https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/world.title: Polluted Delhi Tries ‘Green’ Fireworks to Clear the Air at Diwali
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/world.author: Jeremy W. Peters and Suhasini Raj
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/world.text:
India’s top court decreed that only more environmentally friendly fireworks could be set off this weekend, citing air quality concerns. But environmental activists call it a “green wash.”

By Jeremy W. Peters and Suhasini Raj

Nothing says it’s time for Diwali like the riot of colors that suddenly appears everywhere — red saris, gold kurtas, garlands of bright orange marigolds. But there’s another color that’s now compulsory in India’s capital: green.

Green, as in the environmentally friendlier fireworks that the Supreme Court of India has said are the only type that can be set off this Diwali weekend. Fireworks are otherwise banned to try to avoid contributing to the toxic haze of dust, vehicle exhaust and smoke from faraway crop fires that envelops New Delhi around this time of year.

The court ruled last week that fireworks — a staple of Diwali celebrations across the country — could be used in the capital region for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday, as long as they were of the “green” variety manufactured to burn faster and emit fewer harmful chemicals.

The court cited Diwali’s “religious, social, psychological and emotional connotation” that fostered “a positive atmosphere of hope, welfare and prosperity.” Since ancient times, the court observed, Hindus had lit fires on the holiday, known as the festival of lights, first with lamps and later with explosives once gunpowder was invented.

After Sunday, the actual day of Diwali, the full ban on the sale and use of all fireworks, implemented by the Delhi government in 2024, goes back into effect.

But the court’s attempt to balance public health and religious expression left some environmental activists incredulous.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/po.title: U.S. Global Health Strategy Jeopardizes Prevention of Pandemics, Experts Warn
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/po.author: Apoorva Mandavilli
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/po.text:
The Trump administration has been negotiating agreements with dozens of individual countries. Public health experts say a global agreement would be far more effective.

By Apoorva Mandavilli

Country by country, the Trump administration has been negotiating secretive agreements with nations across Africa to provide health aid under strict conditions. The agreements, structured to benefit the United States, are undermining efforts to prepare the world for the next pandemic, putting even Americans at risk, public health experts warn.

In one striking example, under an agreement signed in February that was never made public, the United States is set to stop funding health care workers in the Democratic Republic of Congo by the end of the year. Congo has been struggling to contain an Ebola outbreak that has topped 10,000 cases and has spread to two other regions of Africa.

The plan, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, provides Congo with $900 million over the next five years, and was signed before the Ebola outbreak was detected.

Still, several public health experts said it was an example of the Trump administration’s focus on near-term benefits for the United States over the long-term partnerships needed to weather international crises.

“They have shown incredibly poor foresight proposing further cuts right where workers are needed to fight infectious threats that we all know are coming,” said Peter Maybarduk, the director of access to medicines for the advocacy group Public Citizen.

In response to questions from The New York Times, the State Department said it would work with Congolese officials to ensure they can pay government health workers, but did not say whether it would grant an extension on the Dec. 31 deadline.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/busin.title: U.S. Cleared Nvidia Chips to Chinese Firms With Empty Offices and Troubling Ties
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/busin.author: Ana Swanson, Kalley Huang and Keith Bradsher
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/busin.text:
Artificial Intelligence

The Commerce Department has approved dozens of Chinese companies to handle Nvidia’s H200 chips, some of which have ties to firms under sanctions over national security.

By Ana SwansonKalley Huang and Keith Bradsher

Ana Swanson reported from Washington, Kalley Huang from San Francisco and Keith Bradsher from Beijing.

In a recently built industrial park on the northwest fringe of Beijing, the listed address of a company called New Matrix stands empty, a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration approved this Chinese firm to assemble Nvidia’s advanced chips into the computers that create artificial intelligence. President Trump allowed the sale of the chips, called the H200, to China late last year. But before they could be sold, the Commerce Department was required to review the companies involved for national security risks.

New Matrix passed that review. Yet recent checks by The New York Times found that, within China, there is little evidence the firm actually exists, raising questions about who in China is behind the company.

Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.

According to Chinese corporate records, New Matrix’s owners have ties to a prominent Chinese private equity fund that the U.S. government placed on a trade blacklist in 2024. Two analysts who examined the corporate records and other Chinese-language information said they believed New Matrix may be a front for firms associated with that fund.

The sale of chips to New Matrix appears to be part of a pattern that has concerned technology experts inside and outside the government: The Commerce Department is giving clearance to buy and handle Nvidia’s chips to Chinese companies with ties to firms that have been subject to national-security-related trade restrictions.

As Microsoft pours billions into artificial intelligence, the company has offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees. The work force was already on edge.

Reporting from San Francisco

Within an hour of Microsoft’s announcement of buyouts last week, employees rushed to an internal site to see whether they had been offered one. So many people were checking at once that employees speculated on the company’s internal social network that the site had buckled under the traffic.

The offer, extended to about 60,000 employees, or more than a quarter of Microsoft’s work force, was the largest in the company’s history. It was also the company’s second buyout this year, and another shock to a work force grappling with big changes brought on by artificial intelligence.

For years, Microsoft occupied a distinct position among the tech industry’s biggest companies. While its pay packages often lagged behind Silicon Valley rivals like Google and Meta, employees said, the company countered with strong benefits and a reputation for stability. As recently as September, Forbes ranked Microsoft the world’s best employer for the third straight year.

But the tech industry’s A.I. race is upending many workplaces, Microsoft included. The buyout offer, said six Microsoft employees who spoke on the condition of anonymity, landed on workers strained by mounting expectations to use A.I., stagnant pay and a growing sense that their jobs were no longer secure.

Though Microsoft is doing better financially than most of its peers, it is clearly shifting its spending priorities. Two days after the buyouts were announced, the Redmond, Wash., company reported a 32 percent jump in quarterly profit, to $36.6 billion, on revenue of $92.3 billion. Its capital spending, largely on data centers, rose 30 percent to $45.2 billion, and the company said it expected to spend roughly $170 billion this year.

The fear among many workers now is what comes next, and some have begun organizing. Before the buyout offer, a group of current and former employees circulated an open letter among colleagues accusing the company of pursuing A.I. with a “speed-at-all-costs” ethos. It called on Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how A.I. is built and used, and to stop tying A.I. use to rewards or reprimands.

Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The New York Times reported last week that Mr. Huang had a close relationship with an executive that U.S. officials determined was funneling information to Chinese intelligence.

Reporting from San Francisco

The Republican leaders of three influential House committees on Thursday asked Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, to voluntarily appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with an executive at a Singapore-based company, who American officials determined was funneling information to Chinese intelligence.

The request came from Representatives Brian Mast of Florida, chairman of the Committee on Foreign Affairs; John Moolenaar of Michigan, who leads the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party; and Rick Crawford of Arkansas, who leads the Select Committee on Intelligence.

The New York Times reported last week that Mr. Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, a top executive at Megaspeed, a company that the U.S. government suspected of helping China evade U.S. prohibitions and gain access to Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips.

The House leaders asked Mr. Huang to appear on Nov. 18 and discuss his interactions with Ms. Huang as well as Nvidia’s security policies for guarding against espionage by a foreign adversary.

“It is vital Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” they wrote.

John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, declined to comment on whether Mr. Huang would appear. “Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed,” Mr. Rizzo said in a statement.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/podca.title: Why the Tech Right Lost Big This Week
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/podca.author: Max Read, Erin Griffith, Whitney Jones, Sawyer Roque, Vjeran Pavic, Alyssa Moxley, Dan Powell, Elisheba Ittoop, Marion Lozano and Diane Wong
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/podca.text:
What just happened to Elon Musk? Two years ago, the SpaceX founder and world’s richest man was riding high. He and the rest of the tech right of Silicon Valley had helped propel Trump into office and had grand plans to reshape the federal government. Remember DOGE?

Those plans are now on hold. Musk once again spent hundreds of millions of dollars this election cycle, but got almost nothing in return. Instead, his allies had among the worst losses of their lives, and he became one of the main villains of some of the cycle’s most important races. On today’s episode, we’re going to dive into the midterms and try to figure out what happened. Was this election a repudiation of Musk and his cadre of Silicon Valley billionaires, a referendum on AI build out in the data centers cropping up around the country, or an entire rejection of the accelerating AI future that the tech industry has been aggressively selling?

How did Elon Musk lose so badly, and what will he do next? I’m Max Read. This is “Hard Fork.”

Welcome to Hard Fork. I’m joined by Erin Griffith and Ezra Klein. Erin is a tech writer for “The New York Times,” and Ezra is, I believe, a podcaster who’s been sent to us from the 28th floor to talk about politics. It’s now been a little while since the Democrats retook Congress. And the thing I really want to talk about, the thing I’ve been thinking about, is what we have called the tech right. So I’m talking about a very highly visible group of Trump supporting executives, founders, investors from Silicon Valley, people like David Saks, Marc Andreessen, Palmer Luckey, and of course, Elon Musk.

This was, two years ago, felt like the most powerful faction within the Trump coalition. They were able to dominate news and attention, most of all campaign contributions. They arguably helped elevate JD Vance to the vice presidency. After the election, they were put in charge of federal government budgeting and provision, and now it feels like it’s all fallen apart.

Both of you guys are close observers of the tech industry. And I wanted to see how you would characterize what happened this week to this growing conservative movement of leaders. Ezra, what do you think happened to the tech right?

It attached itself to Donald Trump. And this is a place, I think, where at least in part their success became a failure. The tech right is not the reason Trump layered the world in tariffs. It is not the reason that he went to war in Iran. But it is at least part of the reason why he has a hideously unpopular position on AI. And I was surprised in the exit polling how important people said AI was to their vote.

So 56 percent said that artificial intelligence and data centers was a crucial or major factor in their vote. 57 percent said AI would do more to hurt society. 24 percent said it would help society. 76 percent opposed a data center in their community. So you’re dealing with an issue that people were, both in a kind of direct and vibesy way, actually taking into account.

And Trump, because in this period he has been really bought in on the David Sacks, Jensen Huang, Marc Andreessen, et cetera view of the world, his view on the Republican Party broadly is view on data centers was let ‘em rip. Build as many of them as you can. Whoever wins AI wins. And that put them on sharply the wrong side of public opinion.

On an issue that’s unlike the diffuse issues of costs or the war on Iran, you could really sometimes tie a specific politician like Husted in Ohio to data center backlash. And that gave Republicans maybe who didn’t like them a reason to cross party lines on them.

Yeah. I mean, let me ask the chicken and egg question. Is AI getting dragged down by Donald Trump and the tech right? Or is this that AI just has naturally bad politics and its association with these figures is dragging them down?

I think it’s a mistake to think that the only reason we regulate things is to slow them down or to stop them or because they’re bad. You regulate things to put them within a trustworthy at least semi Democratic container, such that people can make peace and have confidence in their trade offs. There is a world where AI is rolling out in a way where people think that the folks in charge have thought through the risk, have thought through the questions of jobs, are finding out what they need to find out, and maybe have more trust in it. In that way, I don’t think it’s being dragged down by Donald Trump’s popularity. I think the problem with AI in terms of popularity is that the basic sell on it might kill everyone. It probably will take your job. But if it doesn’t do those things, you’re going to have cheaper energy. It’s not a good description of a technology you want.

But the problem it is having on a secondary level is that it’s rolling out at a time when the people are rolling it out, just don’t seem trustworthy. So they have not been subtle or agile or thoughtful about how to manage its risks.

But that’s been the whole point of this rightward shift, right, is like, all the tech guys are so excited to be able to not have to actually care, and soft pedal things and sell them to people. Hasn’t that just been the gleefulness of this kind of Trump 2.0, tech right kind of thing where they’re like, ha, ha, we’re so powerful and rich that we don’t have to convince you? We’ll just do it and you’ll like it or you won’t, but we don’t care.

And as you see, it’s working out great.

Well, I think we’re seeing the direct backlash to that, which is kind of what you’re saying, right?

Erin, were sort of addressing this in the last thing you were saying. But I’m interested in why we feel like at least this group of tech investors and executives went for Trump so hard in the first place.

Oh. Well, there’s a lot of layers to this. Obviously, a lot of them just don’t want to see regulation. You can go back to Marc Andreessen’s whole thing that he kind of went on this media tour after he came out for Trump and he was telling this story of the deal, the broken deal, and the elites are now under attack. And we had this meeting that may or may not have happened, and subsequent reporting has called into question where all the Democrats were saying they were going to kill AI.

I do think it’s also just a little bit of a cultural thing, where it just seemed like more fun for them to be edgelord meme kind of posters and not having to care about cancel culture and wokeness and all of that. And so I think on the high level, a lot of the billionaires and the leaders of the industry kind of went to the right and everyone said, oh, well, the rest of the tech industry is still very liberal. But, I think, over time, that very online kind of thing attracted way more people to that side.

And so I’m going to be very interested to see how that plays out, if people just start backing away from that vibe. The one thing I want to also just say, just to add on to what I was saying earlier, is this idea of ramming through the tech stuff regardless of whether people like it, regardless of sentiment and they’ll like it on the other side is very prominent amongst a lot of the VCs that I talk to, where they say, well, people don’t like big tech or people don’t trust big tech. But look at their revealed preferences.

Look at how much they’re using Facebook, and look at how much they’re using Amazon. They their iPhones. They’re addicted. And they’re just looking only at the data and saying, because people use AI a lot, because ChatGPT has a billion users around the world, ergo people are going to this stuff. They might just not have the trust or whatever, but that doesn’t matter because people are using it. And I think this election is actually showing us that that’s the wrong way of looking at AI. Because people obviously are very, very mad about it to the point where they don’t want it.

This felt like a decidedly anti-tech election, but I think we can also separate some of the sentiments that were contributing to the votes and the blue tsunami. I heard somewhere that in Japan, because you don’t want to call it a blue wave or a tsunami, they’re calling it the national scolding, which I think is so much better. So I’ll call it the national scolding.

The factors that went into the national scolding — I’m going to separate the tech stuff into three different categories. One is the broad opposition to AI that you’re talking about, Erin. One is the specific anti-data center sentiment that really captured a lot of attention this summer, that a lot of politicians ran quite hard on. And then finally, a kind of general anti-oligarchy, anti-billionaire sentiment that focused in particular on Elon Musk, but I think in general on a lot of tech billionaires. I want to take these one at a time and start with the anti-AI sentiment. And I’m going to play a little bit of Jon Ossoff’s victory speech from last night.

And at our grave peril, humanity is fast forgetting the terrible lessons of two world wars and the Holocaust. Meanwhile, the Titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.

That’s pretty strong. I mean, that’s like — and I’m not talking about those new biceps he’s got, folks.

That is like, a real — well, he is a lot stronger than he used to be. I thought that would play a lot harder, but maybe we can cut it out later. It’s a pretty specific, pretty aggressive — I mean, this is like a speech written by somebody who’s on Twitter, at the very least, who has a strong understanding of AI culture, Silicon Valley culture. Ezra, what did you make of this part of Ossoff’s speech?

So at the beginning of the book “Abundance,” which Derek Thompson and I wrote, we have this sort of thing about supply side politics, where we say the core question should be what do we want more of and how do we get it. And the basic problem that they have in AI is they’ve not convinced people to want more of it. They understand how you get it, like, push all this money to CapEx, but not why do you want it.

And so first, you have all this energy going into that, and then that data centers are just big, and ugly, and they don’t create jobs, and people don’t like the construction of industrial facilities near them even in normal times. It’s hard to build an apartment building. It’s very hard to build these gigantic systems. So they seem to have come up with this view that it’s not going to matter because people enjoy using their chatbot, but it is going to matter.

And the reason Ossoff — but not just Ossoff — I mean, El-Sayed had a great answer on AI pause when he was talking to our former colleague Ross Douthat on “60 Minutes.”

Yeah, he actually knows what distillation is.

Yeah, it was very impressive.

A lot of the frontier research is just spoofing our models.

China’s research. And it’d be like you’re pulling a skier on a boat. And you speed up the boat and you’re like, the skier is still so close. We got to speed up. The skier is still so close. Well, it’s because you’re pulling the skier.

He knows what distillation is right there. This is a thing that I think younger politicians are really developing expertise on. I can tell you they all understand and believe it will be a central issue in politics going forward. And sort of like everybody else, they’re not buying the just don’t worry about it line.

OK. One question on that, though — what do you make of their answer to how did this happen is that AI has a messaging problem, which to me misses the point a little bit of — they’re sort of reinforcing that again, what you’re saying, they believe that this is what’s best for everyone. And if everyone just lets them do it, then we’ll see. But if they stick to that, it seems like a problem.

I don’t think they do believe it’s best for — I mean some of the tech right guys do. But I think one of the most interesting things when I talk to them — and I’d be curious how much this backs up your experience — is a lot of the people in AI say, publicly and privately, oh, if I could, I would push the button. I would stop it for now.

And I just don’t feel we can. There is this inevitability thesis. There’s China. There are the other companies. There’s this kind of spirit of technology. In some ways, when Elon Musk talks about it in a very teleological fashion — I tried to stop it, it turns out I can’t, so it’s more fun to be part of it — it is true that some of the tech right people we’re talking about feel that way and some of them also don’t care or don’t see it in existential terms.

But what people are hearing from a lot of them, and correctly absorbing the lesson as Jon Ossoff is — a lot of lab employees are going to Congress and talking to people like Ossoff and explaining their concerns — that the message I think a lot of us are getting is that what is pushing this forward is a belief that it cannot be stopped. But even the people pushing it forward believe that maybe if it could be stopped, at least for a while, and figured out that would be better. And so if you don’t buy into inevitability, and most politicians don’t buy into inevitability, then all of a sudden it’s like, well, why not try to pace it, slow it down, regulate it, change public opinion on it?

Well, I think there’s two groups, though. There’s the kind of employees that are very worried, like what you’re talking about, especially at places like at the labs. And then there’s the investors who I spend a little bit more time with. And they’re not so worried about the existential risk kind of piece of it. They don’t think it’s inevitable because they worry about regulation, and so that’s — and they worry about not having the data centers and the compute, and so they’re on the flip side of that a little bit.

Yeah. Let’s talk about data centers for a second. So Tuesday night, near total route for data centers on basically every level, nearly every local referendum went against them. But also, a bunch of the states that have been building them most intensely, Democrats took control often on anti-data center platforms. But I’m still trying to figure out how big a deal it is, because there’s a certain amount of — it’s not necessarily as salient as tariffs, as affordability, as Iran, as immigration. But it also clearly animated voters all year. So I’m wondering how big a driver do you think the data center issue was of these results?

I mean, it was interesting. Because last week, we talked about how it was like, ranked in the bottom, maybe 5 out of 30-some issues when you’re asking voters like what they care most about. But it’s clear, as you’re describing, that when asked on a binary yes or no question, the answer is absolutely not. And so whether or not that drove people to the polls, Ezra, you probably have a lot more info on that. But it’s obvious that it’s going to be continuing to be an issue.

Yeah, I think it was spiky. So in states where there is a ton of data center buildout happening — so states like Texas, and Ohio, and Georgia, and Arizona — it was a really big issue.

I think you have to look at the Texas results, and Texas is a place in the country that’s been building the most data centers. They were the most vulnerable. It was a huge part of the campaign, particularly in the governor’s race, and it worked. I mean, it was just a huge wedge. And it’s a wedge that I think, very importantly, doesn’t polarize normally. You can win over Republicans that way. But you just look at that list — Texas, Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona — those are just all states where Democrats performed really, really well. And in Ohio, in particular, they really went at Ramaswamy and Husted, the Republican gubernatorial and senate candidates, on the data center issue. I think what you see here is I don’t think data centers were a huge part of the Alaska race.

But in the places where they’re building a lot of them, it really mattered.

Yeah, that’s interesting. And it does feel like there’s going to be a big shift in how we think about the build out. It doesn’t necessarily mean a full cessation of data center build out, but it’s going to take more time and it’s going to be moving to other states, maybe Louisiana, maybe Oklahoma. Erin, I’m wondering how you think this is going to play out among the VCs and investors you talked to, how they’re changing their plans or thinking about it differently now.

I mean, I think in general, investors are a little bit terrified by the results, particularly in Texas. I was watching the all-in feed last night, and as the Texas —

As you do every Tuesday night.

And the Texas — the Texas Governor race was the one that they seemed most upset about. There was this cope moment of like, oh my god, well, they’re only reporting the liberal or the blue district so far. We still have a chance. Because they know that of the 45 gigawatts or so of total compute of energy that’s supposed to come online next year, 10 to 15 gigawatts of that could be now in danger of not coming online because it’s in Texas.

Because they all expected that the moratorium that was put on for building data centers in Texas up through the elections would just be removed, and they would all go back to building, and everything would be great. And so this is going to slow down a lot of the AI development. This is going to make compute capacity much more constrained and, ergo, much more expensive. And it’s going to hurt the growth not just of the frontier labs that need the compute, but of all the ecosystem of companies that are playing into the quote, unquote, “AI trade,” all of the kind of chips, and neo labs, and cloud resellers, all of that.

So that is potentially going to hurt this kind of bull market that we’ve been on for a long time. So they’re getting a little bit dramatic about that, I’ve heard.

No. Investors getting dramatic? I don’t think so. That doesn’t sound good at all.

There was a little bit of catastrophizing, like no less than the entire market’s going to tank, the economy is in the shitter, China’s going to win, all of that. I think I even saw a tweet — Beff Jezos, the kind of internet personality, tweeted that this is the end of Western civilization, it’s time to move to space, which is where the data centers were moving anyway, so —

You gotta get that space real estate. What I thought was interesting about this — I was hearing some of this from investors too, and then the NASDAQ futures were down. And then it’s like the market opens up on Wednesday morning and it bounces up. And so first, clearly, the market doesn’t think this is so bad. But a good contrarian take I’ve seen floating around a bit is that this might be good for investors.

Because I do think there’s a widespread suspicion that there is collective rationality problem happening right now where —

— everybody is investing too much in data centers because they don’t want to be the company left behind. But that might lead to, say, the end of Oracle as a existing American corporation.

And a situation in which the CapEx investment is externally paced, such that some of the particular the more fly by night players that are beginning to emerge who could really, really collapse easily either don’t get off the ground or can’t keep going. And similarly, a situation where players like Anthropic and OpenAI focus more on diffusion and making what they are deploying economically useful, as opposed to racing each other to the notional goal of superintelligence.

It’s not obvious that that’s bad for markets like a CapEx bubble is really bad for markets. You create dangerous AI before you create economically useful AI is actually bad for markets. But in a kind of slightly more sober sense, what markets need is a kind of alignment between how fast a buildout is happening and how economically useful the product is, and thus, how quickly it is adopted. Not at all obvious to me that a slowdown in data center construction from where we are right now is bad for that.

Yeah. Let’s talk about tech billionaires. This is the third category of anti-tech sentiment that I’ve seen pop up throughout this election season, and it came up quite often on Tuesday in some of the victory speeches. We have Talarico effectively calling out Elon Musk, which is something he did many times over the course of the election cycle. Ezra, I’m wondering if you think that the amount of money that Elon was pouring into this election — because he poured in a lot of it — was counterproductive to him in some sense. Because it gave politicians like Talarico a foil to play against.

Hugely counterproductive. So think about what that money is buying. That money is attempting to buy attention. But the sheer size of that money and its attachment to Elon Musk himself, who’s an attentional super object, it did get attention. And the attention it got was that Elon Musk is trying to buy the election, buy it from you, and specifically buy it in Texas.

And does Ken Paxton — did Ken Paxton want one of the central themes of the closing weeks of the election to be Elon Musk is trying to buy the election? There’s broad anti-billionaire sentiment. You can poll this. People really don’t like billionaires. There’s specifically negative Elon Musk sentiment. I was a little bit surprised, actually, that in California the wealth tax proposition didn’t pass. In California —

I wanted to — sorry, no, go ahead.

In California, there’s a proposition to do a wealth tax on the very, very wealthiest California residents, which would not be that many of them, a couple hundred people. But it was going to be a sort of hard to administer tax. And there was fear of having billionaires flee California for, say, Texas. And it didn’t pass.

So in this election in which anti-billionaire sentiment was very, very, very constant, the argument that potentially driving some of them out of California would be bad for California, actually won, which struck me as a little bit surprising. If you had told me how badly Republicans would lose the election — if I knew that a week ago and you said, what’s going to happen to the wealth tax, I’d be like, oh, that’ll definitely pass. It didn’t.

Erin, I wanted to ask you about this because we talked about it last week, and you’ve done a lot of reporting on this. And I’m wondering how you account for this result in what was otherwise a very clearly anti-billionaire election.

It feels a little bit like a California thing, where people might just be tired of the politicians kind of throwing together a plan that doesn’t seem fully thought out and saying, just trust us, we’ll figure this out. And so I think there was enough messaging that introduced doubts to this, basically saying it’s not — I mean, the messaging from the anti-prop 40 groups were this is poorly written. They’re just going to lose all the money. They need to do a better job of this. It’s not sustainable. It’s a one-time thing. I guess that kind of resonated with people.

And honestly, it’s the one thing that the billionaires I’ve seen in the tech right that we’re talking about are clinging to this more or this week now, where they’re like, if they can’t pass this kind of billionaire tax in a blue tsunami in California, it’ll never win anywhere in the country. And I don’t think that’s true. Ezra, I’d love to hear your thoughts on that, but I think there’ll be more attempts at bat at this in the next few years. They’ll just try to maybe position it a little bit differently or find ways that will resonate with people a little bit more. But I think, in general, people are just kind of tired of half-hearted props that are thrown out there, and this one got a lot of criticism for that.

Yeah, I agree that the California prop has first, the problem that Californians have begun to be skeptical of ballot propositions, just full stop, correctly, speaking as a Californian. But I do think the other issue with it was that there was a specific concern that it would disadvantage California. I think it is meaningful, that Gavin Newsom did not support it.

And to the sort of comfort the tech right is taking to this, I think it’s going to be basically table stakes in 2028 for Democrats to have a wealth tax proposal. And the argument for a national wealth tax is a lot stronger than the argument for a state wealth tax. Because they may say they will, but they’re not actually going to move to Ireland or wherever it might be — Argentina.

There’s a long history of people moving to Argentina when things go south in their country.

So, you’re going to have Gavin Newsom with a wealth tax proposal, I think, for that election. So the idea that this is gone as opposed to it is going to move to the level at which it’s better administered, which is the full force of the IRS and the full jurisdiction of the United States, is more the way I understand the situation.

Yeah. I want to talk about one more billionaire. Pour one out for Vivek Ramaswamy, who lost the governor’s race in Ohio. Vivek is more or less a tech billionaire. He was ascendant in politics, or seemed to be. He was one of the two faces of DOGE.

And now he’s frankly humiliated and probably should be ashamed, given the final ad of his campaign involved putting his opponent, Amy Acton’s mother, on TV, to call her daughter a liar after Acton had said that her stepfather had abused her as a child. I’m wondering if this race stuck out to you, as a figure what you remember about his rise and his fall, or if he was just a singularly bad candidate, regardless of the tech halo around him.

Look, Vivek — and for that matter, JD Vance — are the kinds of MAGA politicians the tech right actually wants. They don’t want Donald Trump with all of his all-over-the-place-ness. They want these guys who are actually their guys, and can go to their conferences, and talk knowledgeably about the kinds of highly cerebral, reactionary policies that the right likes, the tech right likes.

And they also, they don’t have to convince him, right? They can just — they already agree.

And the thing about both of those guys is they’re bad politicians. And Ramaswamy here, I actually think, has a particular arc, where he could have lost this election in an honorable way and he decided to lose it in a maximally dishonorable way. And it was just a grotesque, awful, immoral thing to do that covered — that should cover Ramaswamy and shame. But I would say that I see this sometimes with Vance. I see it Ramaswamy. I see it with a of Republicans, where they speak Trump with an accent, that Trump has this cruelty to him, this outrageousness, but because it’s natural to him, he actually knows where the lines are. He knows how to deliver it in a way where people don’t take it exactly that seriously.

He’s done some stuff that is pretty gross in his time, quite a lot of stuff that is very, very gross. But he has a finesse to it that these guys who are mimicking him as if they are like, a GPT 3 level LLM — like, smart but without any art to it whatsoever, has no feel for the situation. And then it just comes out horrible — horrible and cruel, and just like a silent room where nobody’s laughing. And that that race.

And Vance runs into this kind of problem too, like, dogs and cats thing is an example of this for JD Vance, where I think they think they’re doing what Trump is doing and they don’t understand they’re not. And the thing here about them — and it speaks to maybe to tie this a little bit to our main conversation here, a problem that tech right is going to have. The tech right could only really survive as a factional player in a broader Republican ecosystem in which their completely inhuman and bizarre views about how to treat other people were not dominant.

They could have a lot of influence. They were the smart players in the coalition. They had a lot of money. But ultimately, the thing was run by this guy with animal charisma and magnetic cunning. And when you reverse foreground and background here and put them and their people in the front, it goes really, really badly. Because what the non-college white working class is looking for is not Vivek Ramaswamy. It’s just not the brief.

And I don’t think this is where the politics is going. And I think you see in the failure of some of these candidates and in the problems, I think, that JD Vance himself is going to have, where the tech right is very, very, very fragile, which is that it doesn’t understand and often doesn’t seem to human beings, to say nothing of the kinds of people who will need to vote for things. And it doesn’t want to listen to them. And that’s not how you win in politics.

It’s kind of wild seeing them learn this in real time. Because it does feel like, in 2024, they just had this awakening where they realized, oh my god, we are so rich. And the amount of money we have, if you apply it to politics, is absurd. Our money goes so far in politics.

Fairshake, one of the largest PACs ever supporting crypto things — the amount of money they actually raised was just a drop in the bucket for some of these billionaires and the companies that donated to it. But now they’re starting to learn — Ezra, this is a great point. They’re starting to learn that it takes more than money.

There will certainly be a range of Opinions on AI even in the Democratic primary. Will there be someone who is more pro-AI and get some money there? One interest group that I think is fascinating, which we haven’t talked about, from the tech sector, is the AI safety money, which is basically the backlash to the Andreessen view of the world. And that is a huge source of cash.

I think one of the big takeaways from this cycle is that there is a ton of money in the Anthropic, effective altruist, lowercase-D, maybe uppercase-D Democratic world, where people who want the AI companies to move more slowly, who are more concerned about existential risk. And it’s absolutely going to be a force in the Democratic primary. And I think, in 2028, Dario Amodei could be on this list or even some people at OpenAI who are more partial to that.

Yeah. I mean, I expect given that your beat, that you are looking with some interest at the Anthropic IPO coming up soon. Because you’re going to mint a bunch of billionaires who are going to — who have these exactly the passions you’re talking about and exactly the interests.

Yeah. They’re already on the cap table to some extent, or on the cap table of the company, and I think on the campaign finance cap table, so to speak. People like Eric Schmidt, who’s a big investor in Anthropic, is a huge Democratic donor. Dustin Moskovitz, who is one of the earliest investors in the company, and is a huge Democratic donor.

The resources, though, that’s going to be created by these IPOs, are going to mint a lot of people who are not necessarily even billionaires. But it’s a very civically minded community of people at Anthropic, that’s casting with a massively broad brush. But these are people who could easily give a million or $2 million or $3 million. And I know that Democratic fundraisers are also watching the Anthropic IPO closely, with the hope that there’s going to be a lot of 30-year-olds who are going to make a ton of money and are going to want to host Josh Shapiro when he comes to San Francisco, for example.

Right. You mentioned dark money before. Is there a version of the next — I mean, I suppose this is the version of the next cycle, where a lot of the people who are on the list right now are spending the same kind of money but they’re keeping it much more secret.

Yeah. That’s a huge caveat to everything I’ve said, which is that I am very curious and hopefully self-aware about the amount that we don’t about what’s happening in this space. I’ve been writing about this kind of on and off for 10 years now, and there is less disclosed than ever, especially in the Democratic world, where so much political giving now happens through nonprofits. And to read a campaign finance report is just to be inundated with an alphabet soup of nonprofits that are Americans for America, Inc.

All these groups started like two weeks before you’re reading the thing, and suddenly, there’s a super PAC that is $30 million that got this donation from Americans for Americans Inc. And it’s like, how did that happen? And that’s an attractive way of engaging in politics now, especially in the Trump era, where lots of Democrats are fearful about investigations or Trump regularly threatens big Democratic and progressive donors. And he’s gone off to Harvard and other Ivy League institutions for philanthropic gifts and tried to withhold research money.

There’s a wholly legitimate reason why I think liberals fear the Trump administration and want to have their political giving be more shrouded in secrecy. But the downside is no one really knows much about this stuff now. And none of the nonprofits made the list we’re referencing because they were all — there’s so many of them, honestly.

It’s like, the number of different nonprofits that started in August that each donated $10 million is you could have your own list made of just that.

What just happened to Elon Musk? Two years ago, the SpaceX founder and world’s richest man was riding high. He and the rest of the tech right of Silicon Valley had helped propel Trump into office and had grand plans to reshape the federal government. Remember DOGE?

Those plans are now on hold. Musk once again spent hundreds of millions of dollars this election cycle, but got almost nothing in return. Instead, his allies had among the worst losses of their lives, and he became one of the main villains of some of the cycle’s most important races. On today’s episode, we’re going to dive into the midterms and try to figure out what happened. Was this election a repudiation of Musk and his cadre of Silicon Valley billionaires, a referendum on AI build out in the data centers cropping up around the country, or an entire rejection of the accelerating AI future that the tech industry has been aggressively selling?

How did Elon Musk lose so badly, and what will he do next? I’m Max Read. This is “Hard Fork.”

Welcome to Hard Fork. I’m joined by Erin Griffith and Ezra Klein. Erin is a tech writer for “The New York Times,” and Ezra is, I believe, a podcaster who’s been sent to us from the 28th floor to talk about politics. It’s now been a little while since the Democrats retook Congress. And the thing I really want to talk about, the thing I’ve been thinking about, is what we have called the tech right. So I’m talking about a very highly visible group of Trump supporting executives, founders, investors from Silicon Valley, people like David Saks, Marc Andreessen, Palmer Luckey, and of course, Elon Musk.

This was, two years ago, felt like the most powerful faction within the Trump coalition. They were able to dominate news and attention, most of all campaign contributions. They arguably helped elevate JD Vance to the vice presidency. After the election, they were put in charge of federal government budgeting and provision, and now it feels like it’s all fallen apart.

Both of you guys are close observers of the tech industry. And I wanted to see how you would characterize what happened this week to this growing conservative movement of leaders. Ezra, what do you think happened to the tech right?

It attached itself to Donald Trump. And this is a place, I think, where at least in part their success became a failure. The tech right is not the reason Trump layered the world in tariffs. It is not the reason that he went to war in Iran. But it is at least part of the reason why he has a hideously unpopular position on AI. And I was surprised in the exit polling how important people said AI was to their vote.

So 56 percent said that artificial intelligence and data centers was a crucial or major factor in their vote. 57 percent said AI would do more to hurt society. 24 percent said it would help society. 76 percent opposed a data center in their community. So you’re dealing with an issue that people were, both in a kind of direct and vibesy way, actually taking into account.

And Trump, because in this period he has been really bought in on the David Sacks, Jensen Huang, Marc Andreessen, et cetera view of the world, his view on the Republican Party broadly is view on data centers was let ‘em rip. Build as many of them as you can. Whoever wins AI wins. And that put them on sharply the wrong side of public opinion.

On an issue that’s unlike the diffuse issues of costs or the war on Iran, you could really sometimes tie a specific politician like Husted in Ohio to data center backlash. And that gave Republicans maybe who didn’t like them a reason to cross party lines on them.

Yeah. I mean, let me ask the chicken and egg question. Is AI getting dragged down by Donald Trump and the tech right? Or is this that AI just has naturally bad politics and its association with these figures is dragging them down?

I think it’s a mistake to think that the only reason we regulate things is to slow them down or to stop them or because they’re bad. You regulate things to put them within a trustworthy at least semi Democratic container, such that people can make peace and have confidence in their trade offs. There is a world where AI is rolling out in a way where people think that the folks in charge have thought through the risk, have thought through the questions of jobs, are finding out what they need to find out, and maybe have more trust in it. In that way, I don’t think it’s being dragged down by Donald Trump’s popularity. I think the problem with AI in terms of popularity is that the basic sell on it might kill everyone. It probably will take your job. But if it doesn’t do those things, you’re going to have cheaper energy. It’s not a good description of a technology you want.

But the problem it is having on a secondary level is that it’s rolling out at a time when the people are rolling it out, just don’t seem trustworthy. So they have not been subtle or agile or thoughtful about how to manage its risks.

But that’s been the whole point of this rightward shift, right, is like, all the tech guys are so excited to be able to not have to actually care, and soft pedal things and sell them to people. Hasn’t that just been the gleefulness of this kind of Trump 2.0, tech right kind of thing where they’re like, ha, ha, we’re so powerful and rich that we don’t have to convince you? We’ll just do it and you’ll like it or you won’t, but we don’t care.

And as you see, it’s working out great.

Well, I think we’re seeing the direct backlash to that, which is kind of what you’re saying, right?

Erin, were sort of addressing this in the last thing you were saying. But I’m interested in why we feel like at least this group of tech investors and executives went for Trump so hard in the first place.

Oh. Well, there’s a lot of layers to this. Obviously, a lot of them just don’t want to see regulation. You can go back to Marc Andreessen’s whole thing that he kind of went on this media tour after he came out for Trump and he was telling this story of the deal, the broken deal, and the elites are now under attack. And we had this meeting that may or may not have happened, and subsequent reporting has called into question where all the Democrats were saying they were going to kill AI.

I do think it’s also just a little bit of a cultural thing, where it just seemed like more fun for them to be edgelord meme kind of posters and not having to care about cancel culture and wokeness and all of that. And so I think on the high level, a lot of the billionaires and the leaders of the industry kind of went to the right and everyone said, oh, well, the rest of the tech industry is still very liberal. But, I think, over time, that very online kind of thing attracted way more people to that side.

And so I’m going to be very interested to see how that plays out, if people just start backing away from that vibe. The one thing I want to also just say, just to add on to what I was saying earlier, is this idea of ramming through the tech stuff regardless of whether people like it, regardless of sentiment and they’ll like it on the other side is very prominent amongst a lot of the VCs that I talk to, where they say, well, people don’t like big tech or people don’t trust big tech. But look at their revealed preferences.

Look at how much they’re using Facebook, and look at how much they’re using Amazon. They their iPhones. They’re addicted. And they’re just looking only at the data and saying, because people use AI a lot, because ChatGPT has a billion users around the world, ergo people are going to this stuff. They might just not have the trust or whatever, but that doesn’t matter because people are using it. And I think this election is actually showing us that that’s the wrong way of looking at AI. Because people obviously are very, very mad about it to the point where they don’t want it.

This felt like a decidedly anti-tech election, but I think we can also separate some of the sentiments that were contributing to the votes and the blue tsunami. I heard somewhere that in Japan, because you don’t want to call it a blue wave or a tsunami, they’re calling it the national scolding, which I think is so much better. So I’ll call it the national scolding.

The factors that went into the national scolding — I’m going to separate the tech stuff into three different categories. One is the broad opposition to AI that you’re talking about, Erin. One is the specific anti-data center sentiment that really captured a lot of attention this summer, that a lot of politicians ran quite hard on. And then finally, a kind of general anti-oligarchy, anti-billionaire sentiment that focused in particular on Elon Musk, but I think in general on a lot of tech billionaires. I want to take these one at a time and start with the anti-AI sentiment. And I’m going to play a little bit of Jon Ossoff’s victory speech from last night.

And at our grave peril, humanity is fast forgetting the terrible lessons of two world wars and the Holocaust. Meanwhile, the Titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.

That’s pretty strong. I mean, that’s like — and I’m not talking about those new biceps he’s got, folks.

That is like, a real — well, he is a lot stronger than he used to be. I thought that would play a lot harder, but maybe we can cut it out later. It’s a pretty specific, pretty aggressive — I mean, this is like a speech written by somebody who’s on Twitter, at the very least, who has a strong understanding of AI culture, Silicon Valley culture. Ezra, what did you make of this part of Ossoff’s speech?

So at the beginning of the book “Abundance,” which Derek Thompson and I wrote, we have this sort of thing about supply side politics, where we say the core question should be what do we want more of and how do we get it. And the basic problem that they have in AI is they’ve not convinced people to want more of it. They understand how you get it, like, push all this money to CapEx, but not why do you want it.

And so first, you have all this energy going into that, and then that data centers are just big, and ugly, and they don’t create jobs, and people don’t like the construction of industrial facilities near them even in normal times. It’s hard to build an apartment building. It’s very hard to build these gigantic systems. So they seem to have come up with this view that it’s not going to matter because people enjoy using their chatbot, but it is going to matter.

And the reason Ossoff — but not just Ossoff — I mean, El-Sayed had a great answer on AI pause when he was talking to our former colleague Ross Douthat on “60 Minutes.”

Yeah, he actually knows what distillation is.

Yeah, it was very impressive.

A lot of the frontier research is just spoofing our models.

China’s research. And it’d be like you’re pulling a skier on a boat. And you speed up the boat and you’re like, the skier is still so close. We got to speed up. The skier is still so close. Well, it’s because you’re pulling the skier.

He knows what distillation is right there. This is a thing that I think younger politicians are really developing expertise on. I can tell you they all understand and believe it will be a central issue in politics going forward. And sort of like everybody else, they’re not buying the just don’t worry about it line.

OK. One question on that, though — what do you make of their answer to how did this happen is that AI has a messaging problem, which to me misses the point a little bit of — they’re sort of reinforcing that again, what you’re saying, they believe that this is what’s best for everyone. And if everyone just lets them do it, then we’ll see. But if they stick to that, it seems like a problem.

I don’t think they do believe it’s best for — I mean some of the tech right guys do. But I think one of the most interesting things when I talk to them — and I’d be curious how much this backs up your experience — is a lot of the people in AI say, publicly and privately, oh, if I could, I would push the button. I would stop it for now.

And I just don’t feel we can. There is this inevitability thesis. There’s China. There are the other companies. There’s this kind of spirit of technology. In some ways, when Elon Musk talks about it in a very teleological fashion — I tried to stop it, it turns out I can’t, so it’s more fun to be part of it — it is true that some of the tech right people we’re talking about feel that way and some of them also don’t care or don’t see it in existential terms.

But what people are hearing from a lot of them, and correctly absorbing the lesson as Jon Ossoff is — a lot of lab employees are going to Congress and talking to people like Ossoff and explaining their concerns — that the message I think a lot of us are getting is that what is pushing this forward is a belief that it cannot be stopped. But even the people pushing it forward believe that maybe if it could be stopped, at least for a while, and figured out that would be better. And so if you don’t buy into inevitability, and most politicians don’t buy into inevitability, then all of a sudden it’s like, well, why not try to pace it, slow it down, regulate it, change public opinion on it?

Well, I think there’s two groups, though. There’s the kind of employees that are very worried, like what you’re talking about, especially at places like at the labs. And then there’s the investors who I spend a little bit more time with. And they’re not so worried about the existential risk kind of piece of it. They don’t think it’s inevitable because they worry about regulation, and so that’s — and they worry about not having the data centers and the compute, and so they’re on the flip side of that a little bit.

Yeah. Let’s talk about data centers for a second. So Tuesday night, near total route for data centers on basically every level, nearly every local referendum went against them. But also, a bunch of the states that have been building them most intensely, Democrats took control often on anti-data center platforms. But I’m still trying to figure out how big a deal it is, because there’s a certain amount of — it’s not necessarily as salient as tariffs, as affordability, as Iran, as immigration. But it also clearly animated voters all year. So I’m wondering how big a driver do you think the data center issue was of these results?

I mean, it was interesting. Because last week, we talked about how it was like, ranked in the bottom, maybe 5 out of 30-some issues when you’re asking voters like what they care most about. But it’s clear, as you’re describing, that when asked on a binary yes or no question, the answer is absolutely not. And so whether or not that drove people to the polls, Ezra, you probably have a lot more info on that. But it’s obvious that it’s going to be continuing to be an issue.

Yeah, I think it was spiky. So in states where there is a ton of data center buildout happening — so states like Texas, and Ohio, and Georgia, and Arizona — it was a really big issue.

I think you have to look at the Texas results, and Texas is a place in the country that’s been building the most data centers. They were the most vulnerable. It was a huge part of the campaign, particularly in the governor’s race, and it worked. I mean, it was just a huge wedge. And it’s a wedge that I think, very importantly, doesn’t polarize normally. You can win over Republicans that way. But you just look at that list — Texas, Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona — those are just all states where Democrats performed really, really well. And in Ohio, in particular, they really went at Ramaswamy and Husted, the Republican gubernatorial and senate candidates, on the data center issue. I think what you see here is I don’t think data centers were a huge part of the Alaska race.

But in the places where they’re building a lot of them, it really mattered.

Yeah, that’s interesting. And it does feel like there’s going to be a big shift in how we think about the build out. It doesn’t necessarily mean a full cessation of data center build out, but it’s going to take more time and it’s going to be moving to other states, maybe Louisiana, maybe Oklahoma. Erin, I’m wondering how you think this is going to play out among the VCs and investors you talked to, how they’re changing their plans or thinking about it differently now.

I mean, I think in general, investors are a little bit terrified by the results, particularly in Texas. I was watching the all-in feed last night, and as the Texas —

As you do every Tuesday night.

And the Texas — the Texas Governor race was the one that they seemed most upset about. There was this cope moment of like, oh my god, well, they’re only reporting the liberal or the blue district so far. We still have a chance. Because they know that of the 45 gigawatts or so of total compute of energy that’s supposed to come online next year, 10 to 15 gigawatts of that could be now in danger of not coming online because it’s in Texas.

Because they all expected that the moratorium that was put on for building data centers in Texas up through the elections would just be removed, and they would all go back to building, and everything would be great. And so this is going to slow down a lot of the AI development. This is going to make compute capacity much more constrained and, ergo, much more expensive. And it’s going to hurt the growth not just of the frontier labs that need the compute, but of all the ecosystem of companies that are playing into the quote, unquote, “AI trade,” all of the kind of chips, and neo labs, and cloud resellers, all of that.

So that is potentially going to hurt this kind of bull market that we’ve been on for a long time. So they’re getting a little bit dramatic about that, I’ve heard.

No. Investors getting dramatic? I don’t think so. That doesn’t sound good at all.

There was a little bit of catastrophizing, like no less than the entire market’s going to tank, the economy is in the shitter, China’s going to win, all of that. I think I even saw a tweet — Beff Jezos, the kind of internet personality, tweeted that this is the end of Western civilization, it’s time to move to space, which is where the data centers were moving anyway, so —

You gotta get that space real estate. What I thought was interesting about this — I was hearing some of this from investors too, and then the NASDAQ futures were down. And then it’s like the market opens up on Wednesday morning and it bounces up. And so first, clearly, the market doesn’t think this is so bad. But a good contrarian take I’ve seen floating around a bit is that this might be good for investors.

Because I do think there’s a widespread suspicion that there is collective rationality problem happening right now where —

— everybody is investing too much in data centers because they don’t want to be the company left behind. But that might lead to, say, the end of Oracle as a existing American corporation.

And a situation in which the CapEx investment is externally paced, such that some of the particular the more fly by night players that are beginning to emerge who could really, really collapse easily either don’t get off the ground or can’t keep going. And similarly, a situation where players like Anthropic and OpenAI focus more on diffusion and making what they are deploying economically useful, as opposed to racing each other to the notional goal of superintelligence.

It’s not obvious that that’s bad for markets like a CapEx bubble is really bad for markets. You create dangerous AI before you create economically useful AI is actually bad for markets. But in a kind of slightly more sober sense, what markets need is a kind of alignment between how fast a buildout is happening and how economically useful the product is, and thus, how quickly it is adopted. Not at all obvious to me that a slowdown in data center construction from where we are right now is bad for that.

Yeah. Let’s talk about tech billionaires. This is the third category of anti-tech sentiment that I’ve seen pop up throughout this election season, and it came up quite often on Tuesday in some of the victory speeches. We have Talarico effectively calling out Elon Musk, which is something he did many times over the course of the election cycle. Ezra, I’m wondering if you think that the amount of money that Elon was pouring into this election — because he poured in a lot of it — was counterproductive to him in some sense. Because it gave politicians like Talarico a foil to play against.

Hugely counterproductive. So think about what that money is buying. That money is attempting to buy attention. But the sheer size of that money and its attachment to Elon Musk himself, who’s an attentional super object, it did get attention. And the attention it got was that Elon Musk is trying to buy the election, buy it from you, and specifically buy it in Texas.

And does Ken Paxton — did Ken Paxton want one of the central themes of the closing weeks of the election to be Elon Musk is trying to buy the election? There’s broad anti-billionaire sentiment. You can poll this. People really don’t like billionaires. There’s specifically negative Elon Musk sentiment. I was a little bit surprised, actually, that in California the wealth tax proposition didn’t pass. In California —

I wanted to — sorry, no, go ahead.

In California, there’s a proposition to do a wealth tax on the very, very wealthiest California residents, which would not be that many of them, a couple hundred people. But it was going to be a sort of hard to administer tax. And there was fear of having billionaires flee California for, say, Texas. And it didn’t pass.

So in this election in which anti-billionaire sentiment was very, very, very constant, the argument that potentially driving some of them out of California would be bad for California, actually won, which struck me as a little bit surprising. If you had told me how badly Republicans would lose the election — if I knew that a week ago and you said, what’s going to happen to the wealth tax, I’d be like, oh, that’ll definitely pass. It didn’t.

Erin, I wanted to ask you about this because we talked about it last week, and you’ve done a lot of reporting on this. And I’m wondering how you account for this result in what was otherwise a very clearly anti-billionaire election.

It feels a little bit like a California thing, where people might just be tired of the politicians kind of throwing together a plan that doesn’t seem fully thought out and saying, just trust us, we’ll figure this out. And so I think there was enough messaging that introduced doubts to this, basically saying it’s not — I mean, the messaging from the anti-prop 40 groups were this is poorly written. They’re just going to lose all the money. They need to do a better job of this. It’s not sustainable. It’s a one-time thing. I guess that kind of resonated with people.

And honestly, it’s the one thing that the billionaires I’ve seen in the tech right that we’re talking about are clinging to this more or this week now, where they’re like, if they can’t pass this kind of billionaire tax in a blue tsunami in California, it’ll never win anywhere in the country. And I don’t think that’s true. Ezra, I’d love to hear your thoughts on that, but I think there’ll be more attempts at bat at this in the next few years. They’ll just try to maybe position it a little bit differently or find ways that will resonate with people a little bit more. But I think, in general, people are just kind of tired of half-hearted props that are thrown out there, and this one got a lot of criticism for that.

Yeah, I agree that the California prop has first, the problem that Californians have begun to be skeptical of ballot propositions, just full stop, correctly, speaking as a Californian. But I do think the other issue with it was that there was a specific concern that it would disadvantage California. I think it is meaningful, that Gavin Newsom did not support it.

And to the sort of comfort the tech right is taking to this, I think it’s going to be basically table stakes in 2028 for Democrats to have a wealth tax proposal. And the argument for a national wealth tax is a lot stronger than the argument for a state wealth tax. Because they may say they will, but they’re not actually going to move to Ireland or wherever it might be — Argentina.

There’s a long history of people moving to Argentina when things go south in their country.

So, you’re going to have Gavin Newsom with a wealth tax proposal, I think, for that election. So the idea that this is gone as opposed to it is going to move to the level at which it’s better administered, which is the full force of the IRS and the full jurisdiction of the United States, is more the way I understand the situation.

Yeah. I want to talk about one more billionaire. Pour one out for Vivek Ramaswamy, who lost the governor’s race in Ohio. Vivek is more or less a tech billionaire. He was ascendant in politics, or seemed to be. He was one of the two faces of DOGE.

And now he’s frankly humiliated and probably should be ashamed, given the final ad of his campaign involved putting his opponent, Amy Acton’s mother, on TV, to call her daughter a liar after Acton had said that her stepfather had abused her as a child. I’m wondering if this race stuck out to you, as a figure what you remember about his rise and his fall, or if he was just a singularly bad candidate, regardless of the tech halo around him.

Look, Vivek — and for that matter, JD Vance — are the kinds of MAGA politicians the tech right actually wants. They don’t want Donald Trump with all of his all-over-the-place-ness. They want these guys who are actually their guys, and can go to their conferences, and talk knowledgeably about the kinds of highly cerebral, reactionary policies that the right likes, the tech right likes.

And they also, they don’t have to convince him, right? They can just — they already agree.

And the thing about both of those guys is they’re bad politicians. And Ramaswamy here, I actually think, has a particular arc, where he could have lost this election in an honorable way and he decided to lose it in a maximally dishonorable way. And it was just a grotesque, awful, immoral thing to do that covered — that should cover Ramaswamy and shame. But I would say that I see this sometimes with Vance. I see it Ramaswamy. I see it with a of Republicans, where they speak Trump with an accent, that Trump has this cruelty to him, this outrageousness, but because it’s natural to him, he actually knows where the lines are. He knows how to deliver it in a way where people don’t take it exactly that seriously.

He’s done some stuff that is pretty gross in his time, quite a lot of stuff that is very, very gross. But he has a finesse to it that these guys who are mimicking him as if they are like, a GPT 3 level LLM — like, smart but without any art to it whatsoever, has no feel for the situation. And then it just comes out horrible — horrible and cruel, and just like a silent room where nobody’s laughing. And that that race.

And Vance runs into this kind of problem too, like, dogs and cats thing is an example of this for JD Vance, where I think they think they’re doing what Trump is doing and they don’t understand they’re not. And the thing here about them — and it speaks to maybe to tie this a little bit to our main conversation here, a problem that tech right is going to have. So wer’e still sort of — the dust is still settling on this week’s elections. We’re still figuring out what happened. Are you expecting all of the people on this list to be on it again in 2028? Are there figures we should be looking out for who weren’t on it this cycle?

Yeah. Let’s start with Musk. The most extensive thing he said about the midterms was a couple of days ago, where he basically said his fear and the reason why he was so involved in the midterms this cycle was about 2029. His fear is basically to have a Democratic trifecta, where they have the White House and they have both houses of Congress, which they now do, and that’s going to lead to a — In his view, the end of civilization. I think he said, game over for America or something like that, which meant Democrats are going to let all the alleles in from Mexico, and they’re going to basically register all as voters, and then it’s the end of civilization, and blah, blah, blah.

That to me, I read that as, yes, Elon Musk plans to play in the 2028 Republican primary. Musk has a pretty good relationship with JD Vance. Probably not a surprise, but that relationship has stayed pretty good even with the ups and Downs with Trump. I would be shocked if Musk did not support Vance.

The other people on the list that we’ve mentioned, I don’t know. Because some of the folks who are really tied to a specific industry, who are just kind of doing effectively pay for play lobbying — I don’t really mean that in a nefarious way, but the crypto industry and the AI industry, where they’re really engage on a specific issue — it really depends on what politicians do on those issues. We’re also talking about Republicans. In the Democratic primary, will there be a crypto candidate who gets the money from the crypto industry?

There will certainly be a range of Opinions on AI even in the Democratic primary. Will there be someone who is more pro-AI and get some money there? One interest group that I think is fascinating, which we haven’t talked about, from the tech sector, is the AI safety money, which is basically the backlash to the Andreessen view of the world. And that is a huge source of cash.

I think one of the big takeaways from this cycle is that there is a ton of money in the Anthropic, effective altruist, lowercase-D, maybe uppercase-D Democratic world, where people who want the AI companies to move more slowly, who are more concerned about existential risk. And it’s absolutely going to be a force in the Democratic primary. And I think, in 2028, Dario Amodei could be on this list or even some people at OpenAI who are more partial to that.

Yeah. I mean, I expect given that your beat, that you are looking with some interest at the Anthropic IPO coming up soon. Because you’re going to mint a bunch of billionaires who are going to — who have these exactly the passions you’re talking about and exactly the interests.

Yeah. They’re already on the cap table to some extent, or on the cap table of the company, and I think on the campaign finance cap table, so to speak. People like Eric Schmidt, who’s a big investor in Anthropic, is a huge Democratic donor. Dustin Moskovitz, who is one of the earliest investors in the company, and is a huge Democratic donor.

The resources, though, that’s going to be created by these IPOs, are going to mint a lot of people who are not necessarily even billionaires. But it’s a very civically minded community of people at Anthropic, that’s casting with a massively broad brush. But these are people who could easily give a million or $2 million or $3 million. And I know that Democratic fundraisers are also watching the Anthropic IPO closely, with the hope that there’s going to be a lot of 30-year-olds who are going to make a ton of money and are going to want to host Josh Shapiro when he comes to San Francisco, for example.

Right. You mentioned dark money before. Is there a version of the next — I mean, I suppose this is the version of the next cycle, where a lot of the people who are on the list right now are spending the same kind of money but they’re keeping it much more secret.

Yeah. That’s a huge caveat to everything I’ve said, which is that I am very curious and hopefully self-aware about the amount that we don’t about what’s happening in this space. I’ve been writing about this kind of on and off for 10 years now, and there is less disclosed than ever, especially in the Democratic world, where so much political giving now happens through nonprofits. And to read a campaign finance report is just to be inundated with an alphabet soup of nonprofits that are Americans for America, Inc.

All these groups started like two weeks before you’re reading the thing, and suddenly, there’s a super PAC that is $30 million that got this donation from Americans for Americans Inc. And it’s like, how did that happen? And that’s an attractive way of engaging in politics now, especially in the Trump era, where lots of Democrats are fearful about investigations or Trump regularly threatens big Democratic and progressive donors. And he’s gone off to Harvard and other Ivy League institutions for philanthropic gifts and tried to withhold research money.

There’s a wholly legitimate reason why I think liberals fear the Trump administration and want to have their political giving be more shrouded in secrecy. But the downside is no one really knows much about this stuff now. And none of the nonprofits made the list we’re referencing because they were all — there’s so many of them, honestly.

It’s like, the number of different nonprofits that started in August that each donated $10 million is you could have your own list made of just that.

All right. Well, on that very cheery note, Teddy, I want to thank you for coming by and talking to us about this stuff. You can find Teddy’s work, as well as Erin’s, on “The New York Times” app, where you can also watch or listen to every episode of “The Ezra Klein Show.” Thanks for coming on, Teddy.

You bet. [MUSIC PLAYING]

Jeffrey Wigand, who took on Big Tobacco, counsels insiders who think they have a story about wrongdoing. There are quite a few of them.

Jeffrey Wigand at home in Mount Pleasant, Mich.
Credit...
Taylor Ballek for The New York Times

David Streitfeld covers Silicon Valley and other business stories.

Every day, people call Jeffrey Wigand and say they really need to talk.

They are people with a secret, people who think they have information that can blow their town or their company or their country wide open. Maybe they need a little help. Sometimes they want reassurance that their life won’t be ruined. They’re frightened, so they’re reaching out to someone who has been through the whirlwind.

Dr. Wigand, a corporate insider turned implacable adversary, talks them through it.

“Make sure you have your family tightly bound to you,” he says. “Do you have a strong marriage? Are you a churchgoer?” Sometimes they’re enormously angry. “Vengeance without evidence is bad,” he says. “The only thing that protects you is 100 percent truth and the facts that support it.”

Often the callers are in their late 40s or mid-50s, have young children, haven’t quite hit the moment to do what they think is right. But if they are looking for uplift and sweet talk, they should have dialed another number.

“You’ll never be the same,” Dr. Wigand warns.

He certainly wasn’t. In the early 1990s, Dr. Wigand was a scientist at Brown & Williamson, one of the big tobacco companies. Middle-aged with a family, he was hired to make a healthier cigarette. Through an unlikely chain of events, he became a whistle-blower or, to use the term he prefers, “person of conscience.”

He testified that cigarettes were manipulated to make them addictive, an enormously consequential act. He was the recipient of death threats, appeared on “60 Minutes,” was played by Russell Crowe in a big Hollywood movie called “The Insider,” lost his marriage, lost his career and became a high school science teacher.
