https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/techn.title: Researchers Identify Suspicious Activity on Kalshi and Polymarket Before Times/Siena Poll Release
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/techn.author: Lauren McCarthy and Stuart A. Thompson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/techn.text:
A trader placed well-timed bets on Polymarket and Kalshi in two Senate races. It was unclear if the person had access to inside information or simply made good trades.

Odds that Republicans will win Nebraska’s Senate seat

By Lauren McCarthy and Stuart A. Thompson

Researchers at Vanderbilt University said this week that they had identified suspicious prediction market activity before the releases of two recent New York Times/Siena polls.

A user on Polymarket placed a series of bets worth $191,277 in the early hours of Oct. 31 that Senator Pete Ricketts, a Nebraska Republican, would win re-election. About an hour later, at 5:05 a.m. Eastern time, a Times/Siena poll came out with Mr. Ricketts six points ahead — among his largest leads in the race.

It was unclear if the user had access to inside information or simply made well-timed trades.

After the bets were placed, the Polymarket odds that Mr. Ricketts would win rose to around 73 percent from around 67 percent. After the poll was published, they continued rising to 79 percent. The user made more than $77,000 in profit.

The same user also wagered $622,608 during the same period that the Democratic nominee would win Michigan’s Senate race, according to the researchers. The next day, another Times/Siena poll showed that the Democrat, Abdul El-Sayed, held a significant lead. The user made more than $180,000.

The user also sent large sums of money to Kalshi, and large bets were placed on similar markets shortly after, the researchers said. Outside of having insider knowledge, researchers theorized, the user could have guessed the timing of polls without knowing their contents, had his or her own beliefs on who would win or was making more complicated trades to offset losses elsewhere without any specialized knowledge.

The anonymous user made two large bets on Polymarket that a Democrat would win Michigan. The bets were placed alongside others on Oct. 31. The next day, around 7:53 p.m, a poll on Michigan and other states was published.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/fa.title: F.A.A. to Phase Out Floppy Disks in Air Traffic Control Towers
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/fa.author: Victor Mather
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/fa.text:
Decades after the computer industry moved on, federal officials plan to finally ground the once-vaunted tech relic at the nation’s air traffic control centers.

When news arrived this week that the Federal Aviation Administration would phase out floppy disks used in air traffic control at the nation’s airports, the general reaction was: “Wait, someone still uses floppy disks?”

But there once was a time, decades ago, when the now-obsolete floppy was exciting new technology, heralded in The New York Times as “the cornerstone of the office of the future.”

The F.A.A. has been using systems for air traffic controllers, including floppy disks, that date to the 1980s. A planned new system will include a digital display board that will put in one place the information controllers need, with data about disruptions, weather conditions and advisories.

Airports in Atlantic City, N.J., Nashville and Rochester, N.Y., will be among the first to get the new tech, known as the Brand New Air Traffic Control System.

“The greatest nation in the world deserves a state-of-the-art air traffic control system,” Sean P. Duffy, the transportation secretary, said in a statement.

President Trump had promised to upgrade the F.A.A.’s equipment after a plane crash near Washington in 2025. Government officials at the time noted that flights were still tracked on strips of paper, and that some computers ran on the Windows 95 operating system.

Videos on social media often save key details for the end. One content creator, who goes by Heyitsyoon, skips the filler so viewers don’t have to wait.

Alex Yoon, a content creator, has built a large following by spoiling lengthy videos on TikTok.
Credit...

If you watch videos on TikTok or other social media platforms, this has happened to you.

A content creator teases something big, or at least intriguing — “Anthony Bourdain said one food movie was more accurate than any other,” or “Who’s faster, DoorDash or me?”

Then the video drags on with the poster delivering background information and extraneous commentary, while you wait with increasing impatience for the reveal. Only after several minutes does it come.

Alex Yoon, known online as Heyitsyoon, is doing something about this.

In his own videos, he clips the very beginning of a teasing video, then cuts to himself giving away the ending.

Was the guy actually faster than DoorDash?

“They took the same amount of time,” Mr. Yoon reveals.

The most accurate food movie according to Bourdain?

“It was ‘Ratatouille,’” it seems.

Mr. Yoon’s videos finish with a graphic revealing how much time he saved you, often three minutes or more.

His quicker-reveal videos are particularly memorable because of his position and demeanor. He films himself lying in bed and wrapped in blankets, eyes half-shut, as he sleepily delivers the video conclusions in a monotone.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.author: Kenneth Chang
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.text:
NASA’s Artemis III Mission

The space agency is recruiting its next class of space travelers for missions to low-Earth orbit and the moon. Applications are due Dec. 3.

Want to go to the moon?

NASA announced on Saturday that it was recruiting its first new class of astronauts since 2024. The new space travelers would most likely participate in the Artemis program, which aims to send people back to the moon in 2028 and establish a lunar base in the 2030s.

“This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” Jared Isaacman, the agency’s administrator, said in a statement. “The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the moon base and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars.”

Some of the new astronauts will also spend time in low-Earth orbit, but they may not go to the International Space Station. A centerpiece of NASA’s human spaceflight program for more than a quarter-century, the space station is scheduled to be retired in 2030.

After the end of the I.S.S., NASA plans to send astronauts to commercial space stations that have yet to be launched.

For those who want to leave Earth, applications are due by 11:59 p.m. Eastern time on Dec. 3. The space agency said it expected to make its selections by late next year.

Almost all of the hopeful will be disappointed. During the previous round two years ago, more than 8,000 people applied, and NASA chose 10 of them, an acceptance rate of less than 0.125 percent. Before that, NASA had not sought to hire new astronauts for four years, because the only missions available were a limited number of trips to the I.S.S.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.title: Top Astrophysicist Leaves U.S. After Trump Policies Affect Her Work
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.author: Eli Saslow and Hilary Swift
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.text:
Kelly Holley-Bockelmann in her new lab in Leiden, Netherlands.

Kelly Holley-Bockelmann had always oriented herself by looking up at the sky, but now it was tilted and unfamiliar. The Milky Way sank toward the horizon line, and darkness never arrived quite the way it had in Tennessee, fast and enveloping. Instead, there was hazy dusk and then stubborn twilight before the sun rose again over her extended-stay hotel thousands of miles from home.

She took a tram, then a train, then a bus until she arrived at a glass-walled building in the Netherlands. There was a Dutch flag near the entryway and a replica of a spaceship in the lobby. She rode the elevator to her new office, a small room with whitewashed walls, empty drawers and a handwritten note taped to the desk. “We are thrilled to welcome one of America’s great scientists,” it read.

A new colleague stopped at the doorway to check in on her. “I know it might not look all that impressive,” he said, gesturing around the office.

“It’s perfect,” Holley-Bockelmann said. “After these last few years, I’m just so grateful to be here.”

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

She had never expected to be starting over halfway across the world at age 55, just as she reached the pinnacle of a career that was often celebrated as uniquely American. She’d grown up in Montana, lying in the grass beneath the night sky and trying to feel the Earth spin. She dreamed of becoming an astronomer before she knew the word for it. Nobody in her house growing up had finished college. She’d never met a scientist. But she made herself into a theoretical astrophysicist, a leading expert on gravitational waves, a top adviser to NASA, and a chaired professor at Vanderbilt. She helped begin a new graduate program for astronomers and raised millions in federal money to recruit American scientists with backgrounds as unlikely as her own, only to watch that pipeline be dismantled piece by piece.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.title: Still on the President’s Agenda: Daylight Saving Time
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.author: Lynne Peeples
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.text:
Following an election-year rout for Republicans, Trump castigated lawmakers for not passing the Sunshine Protection Act. Some scientists have warned against the change.

The day after a midterm drubbing for the G.O.P., President Trump took to social media to complain — about turning back the clocks.

“It’s so dark outside, so early,” he posted on Truth Social. He went on to lament the lack of action taken by the Senate on the Sunshine Protection Act, which would lock most of the nation’s clocks on daylight saving time year-round.

“I will keep fighting for this!” he wrote.

Scientists aren’t particularly keen on permanent daylight saving time, fearing more injuries in the early-morning darkness and the health consequences of disturbed body clocks. But the president is an ardent supporter. One possible reason: golf.

“Trump is not hiding the fact that golf is definitely on his mind,” said Jay Pea, the founder of Save Standard Time, which advocates adopting year-round standard time.

The Sunshine Protection Act was passed by the House in July. The Senate has yet to put the bill to a vote this year, though lawmakers are scheduled to reconvene next week.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/scien.title: What a Democratic Congress Could Mean for Science
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/scien.author: Benjamin Mueller, Carolyn Y. Johnson, Cade Metz and Kenneth Chang
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/scien.text:
The Trump administration has sought to reshape the nation’s research infrastructure. Democratic lawmakers, newly empowered, are preparing to push back.

By Benjamin MuellerCarolyn Y. JohnsonCade Metz and Kenneth Chang

The Trump administration swept into office determined to undermine the postwar model of research spending that made the United States the world’s great engine of scientific discovery.

Much of that agenda — canceling studies, slashing scientific staff, imposing greater political oversight on grant making — went into effect without the cooperation of Congress, which even in Republican hands resisted the White House’s efforts to retool the country’s research machine.

Now Democrats are set to take control on Capitol Hill, and some are already promising to do more than play defense. They hope to begin reversing changes implemented under President Trump.

Whether that ultimately happens is unclear.

“The reality is, most of the shenanigans have been coming from the administration,” said Jeremy Berg, a former institute director at the National Institutes of Health. “And that will likely continue.”

From artificial intelligence to space exploration to the research juggernauts at the N.I.H., the American scientific enterprise is vast. Here are some trends to watch.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/scien.title: These Newly Elected Lawmakers Know Something Trump Doesn’t: Science
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/scien.author: Alexander Nazaryan
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/scien.text:
Among those elected to Congress on Tuesday are a mathematician, a microbiologist and a chemical engineer. They plan to take on a White House that has threatened funding cuts to research.

By Alexander Nazaryan

When he takes his oath of office next January, Daniel K. Biss will be among the most junior members of the House of Representatives. Even so, Mr. Biss, who was elected on Tuesday to represent the North Side of Chicago and nearby suburbs, is likely to be Washington’s foremost expert on matroid Grassmannians.

“I’ve pretty much cornered the market,” Mr. Biss joked in an interview.

Ominous name aside, matroid Grassmannians are just complex mathematical shapes — as well as the subject of the dissertation Mr. Biss completed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2002. Mr. Biss, now 49, taught math at the University of Chicago before moving to politics, first as an Illinois state legislator and then as the mayor of Evanston, a prosperous Chicago suburb. (His academic career has not been without controversy: Some of his work has been retracted or corrected, and this year he admitted to having a relationship in 2004 with an undergraduate student.)

Mr. Biss is one of several scientists and physicians who was elected to Congress on Tuesday. Like him, most are Democrats and most were elected to the House. They plan, they say, to use their knowledge to combat what they see as the anti-science policies promoted by the Trump administration.

The incoming scientists represent “a real repudiation of what has been two terrible years for science and public health,” said Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, a group that recruits Democratic doctors and scientists to run for office. Her group supported Democratic candidates who ended up winning in the House, as well as two incoming senators: Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan and Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.

(In keeping with New York Times style, physicians and academics who stop practicing once elected to a political office are not given the courtesy title doctor.)

After World War II, the United States became a scientific powerhouse thanks to federal funding of research in the sciences. But decades of partnership between Washington and defense contractors, Silicon Valley and other sectors are being undermined by the Trump administration, according to a recently published Times investigation.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/scien.title: Biotech Firm Claims Some Credit for Groundbreaking Virus Research
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/scien.author: Carl Zimmer
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/scien.text:
Artificial Intelligence

Radical Numerics turned heads with its announcement about a novel treatment. Now a former partner, Tabula Bioscience, says it performed much of the research.

A tech start-up made a splash last month with a remarkable announcement: Its researchers had used artificial intelligence to design viruses tailored to kill the bacteria causing a dangerous infection. Those viruses were used to treat a sick patient.

The disclosure, in a blog post on the company’s site, drew cautious curiosity from experts and coverage in The New York Times. But now the company, Radical Numerics, has acknowledged that it did not work alone.

Another company, Tabula Bioscience, performed much of the research, including creating the cocktail of viruses, called phages, that were administered to the patient. Radical Numerics made no mention of the partnership or the company in its announcement.

The omission led a leading geneticist, George Church, of Harvard University, to resign on Thursday from the board of Radical Numerics. Dr. Church is also an adviser to Tabula.

Eric Nguyen, the chief executive of Radical Numerics, acknowledged the research partnership in an email to The Times. “We worked closely with Tabula’s team over seven months,” he wrote.

Dr. Nguyen denied that his company had erred in describing the project last month without crediting Tabula. He said confidentiality requirements in the contract had stipulated that his company not disclose the partnership.

A longstanding hypothesis held that some problems would always be hard for computers to solve quickly. But OpenAI disproved it — raising the possibility of radical new efficiencies.

Credit...
Erik Carter

Cade Metz has written about A.I. for more than 15 years. But he has never solved a 1,000-row Sudoku puzzle.

To understand the latest shocking development in A.I.-generated math, it helps to think about Sudoku.

Solving one of those nine-box number puzzles, especially at the highest difficulty levels, can be fiendishly time-consuming. But once you have a solution, it’s easy to double-check that you got it right: Just scan each row, column and box and confirm that each integer appears exactly once.

It’s an analogy that Russell Impagliazzo, a professor of computer science at the University of California, San Diego, invokes to explain a high-profile math question called “P vs. NP.” For years, Dr. Impagliazzo explains, he and other computer scientists have assumed that math and computer science obey that apparent truth about Sudoku: Solving a problem is much, much harder than checking that a solution is correct.

Sitting at the intersection of mathematics and theoretical computer science, “P vs. NP” is among the million-dollar Millennium Prize problems laid down by the Clay Mathematics Institute 25 years ago. In non-math speak, “P” represents computational problems that can be solved quickly, while “NP” represents problems whose solutions can be checked easily.

Common sense says that checking solutions should be much easier than finding solutions. “If P and NP follow intuition, then they should definitely not be equal,” said Ryan Williams, a professor of engineering and computer science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

On Oct. 26, OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, cast doubt on that seemingly obvious argument. While the broader problem of “P vs. NP” remains unsolved, the company announced that its newest artificial intelligence technology had refuted a related conjecture called the exponential time hypothesis, or E.T.H., which Dr. Impagliazzo proposed in 1998 with his colleague Ramamohan Paturi and a Bell Labs researcher named Francis Zane. Similar to the argument that P can’t equal NP, the E.T.H. held that certain problems must always remain hard for computers to solve quickly.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/scien.title: Were These Ancient Siberian Nomads the First Stoners?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/scien.author: Annie Roth
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/scien.text:
Scientists ran a drug test on hair found in a 2,800-year-old burial mound. It came back positive for pot, the earliest known evidence of psychoactive cannabis use.

The Scythians, a nomadic people who once roamed the Eurasian steppes on horseback, were many things: warriors, equestrians, metalsmiths, lovers of tattoos. But were they also the first stoners?

In 2017, a team of archaeologists discovered an enormous Scythian burial mound in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia. The site, which was 2,800 years old and was named Tunnug 1, was among the oldest and largest of these burial sites and became a literal treasure trove for archaeologists studying the Scythians, who thrived from the ninth century to the third century B.C.

Over the next six years, archaeologists excavated its tombs and cataloged their contents. They found gold jewelry, animal statues, daggers, human remains and hundreds and hundreds of cannabis seeds. The presence of the seeds inspired the scientists to perform drug tests on strands of human hair they had found during the excavation (call it probable cause), and they came back positive.

The results of their archaeological analysis, published on Thursday in the journal Science, suggest humans were getting high at least three centuries earlier than previously thought. The study also raises questions about the role cannabis played in the culture of ancient Asia’s nomadic peoples.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.title: Doctors Absorb the Stunning Failure of Two High-Profile Heart Drugs
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.author: Gina Kolata
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/scien.text:
By every measure, the drugs were no better than placebos, full data revealed on Saturday. Was it the fault of the design of the studies, or our very hypotheses about heart disease?

Cardiologists have been on edge for months, waiting for the details surrounding recent reports of the stunning failures of two new heart drugs.

The drugs — pelacarsen and ziltivekimab — were widely expected to usher in a new era in preventing heart disease. Companies, betting on the drugs’ promise, made huge investments in developing them.

So when doctors saw preliminary announcements that the drugs were not helping patients in large clinical trials, many felt blindsided, although still hopeful that there was more to the story than they knew.

“The whole cardiovascular community was gobsmacked,” said Dr. Karol Watson, a director of UCLA’s preventive cardiology program.

Were the drugs close to succeeding, just barely missing a statistically significant benefit? Or were there at least subgroups of patients who were helped?

Now the answers are in. There was not a shred of evidence that the drugs helped anyone. By every measure, they were no better than placebos.

His observations helped establish shriveling mountain glaciers as an unmistakable consequence of human-caused warming. He was 78.

Credit...
Jay Kolsch/South James

Lonnie Thompson, a climate scientist who over five decades ventured more than 60 times into the planet’s most daunting highlands to collect and preserve samples of the melting mountain ice, becoming one of the first researchers to document the effects of global warming in real time, died on Monday at his home in Columbus, Ohio. He was 78.

Ohio State University, where Dr. Thompson was a professor in the school of earth sciences, announced the death but did not provide a specific cause.

With his wife and fellow glaciologist, Ellen Mosley-Thompson, Dr. Thompson was an early leader in the study of tropical glaciers, which sit on high peaks in the world’s warmest regions.

Early in his career, most researchers believed those glaciers were of little scientific interest. In Greenland and Antarctica, the ice was hundreds of thousands of years old. By analyzing the dust, volcanic ash and air bubbles trapped inside, as well as the chemical properties of the water itself, scientists could decipher ancient swings in temperature, precipitation and atmospheric makeup.

The tropics, by contrast, were thought to be unwaveringly humid and rainy. And besides, tropical ice had presumably melted too much for it to be very old.

Dr. Thompson’s work upended those ideas. Over the course of at least 66 expeditions, he and his colleagues hauled heavy equipment up mountains in South America, Africa, Asia and beyond. They camped on the ice for weeks at a time, drilling into the glaciers and pulling out cylindrical cores that could total hundreds of feet in length.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/clima.title: Disaster-Prone Communities Face Cuts and Slowdowns in Federal Help
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/clima.author: Scott Dance
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/clima.text:
The Trump administration is scaling back or stalling investments that help vulnerable places harden themselves to rising flood and fire threats.

Reporting from Washington

As the tide rose along the Florida coast before Hurricane Isaias made landfall last month, Pamela Sears got more and more anxious. She and her husband, J.T., have been living in a 35-foot R.V. ever since Hurricanes Helene and Milton flooded their home in 2024.

She knows the only sure way to avoid the next flood is to elevate their home at least 14 feet above sea level, and she’s seeking federal funds to help pay for it.

That kind of help has become significantly harder to get: The Trump administration has been narrowing federal programs to prepare for extreme weather threats as it reduces the government’s role in disasters and erases support for anything related to climate change.

But many residents are still desperate to protect themselves and their homes from persistent storms, floods and wildfires.

When Isaias hit Florida, water stayed mercifully behind a sea wall near Ms. Sears’ home by the Little Manatee River, south of Tampa. She hopes a state program called Elevate Florida that relies on federal funds will help her fortify her home against future disasters, because investing in prevention would be cheaper than rebuilding again and again.

“This program is stalled in the water,” Ms. Sears said. “The whole reason we pay taxes is to contribute to the common good. They’re not doing anything with that.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/clima.title: Environmental Ballot Wins
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/clima.author: Scott Dance
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/clima.text:
Voters around the country approved measures on conservation, water and data centers on Tuesday.

The “blue tsunami” on Tuesday that will give Democrats control of Congress also helped to push through ballot measures around the country to strengthen environmental protections. Voters approved referendums to ensure supplies of clean water and clean power, to support nature conservation and to armor communities against the threats of climate change-fueled wildfires. And they voted, over and over, to block data centers, too.

In many contests, there was little explicit emphasis on climate change or the environment by the candidates, who focused more on affordability, said Jordan Haedtler, the climate finance policy lead at Climate Cabinet, a nonprofit group focused on state and local environmental issues. But a number of states gave people the chance to protect the environment and make communities more resilient to climate change, he said.

“Voters respond to that,” Haedtler said.

In Colorado, voters were asked to take on the culture-war battle over gas stoves with a proposed amendment to the State Constitution to enshrine the right to cook with natural gas. It fell well short of passing.

The votes are still being counted, but Californians appear likely to reject an overhaul of the state’s environmental review process. It would have sped up development to make housing more affordable, but there were concerns that it also could have weakened ecological safeguards.

Massachusetts approved devoting a share of sales taxes to a new fund to expand land conservation and build parks, especially in underserved areas.

Corpus Christi, Texas, faced the prospect of a water crisis this year, before rain alleviated a severe shortage in the city’s reservoirs. In response, voters overwhelmingly backed a measure to require heavy industrial water users to pay mandatory drought surcharges. The money will go toward increasing and conserving the municipal water supply.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/clima.author: Brad Plumer
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/clima.text:
In the 2022 midterms, Democrats made global warming an issue. Things have changed.

Before the last midterm elections in 2022, a number of Democrats tried to make global warming a campaign issue, with some spotlighting the big clean energy bill that Congress had passed that summer.

It’s a different story this year. Ahead of today’s election, many Democratic candidates steered clear of talking about climate change, evidence of a larger shift in the party lately.

Democrats talk far less these days about soaring global temperatures, rising sea levels or worsening wildfires. The party has embraced Senate candidates like James Talarico in Texas and Mary Peltola in Alaska, who actively support their state’s fossil-fuel industries. Even some blue-state Democratic governors, like Kathy Hochul of New York and Maura Healey of Massachusetts, now back expanding natural gas supplies to lower costs.

While many elected Democrats still say they want to reduce planet-warming emissions, some have said they’re not going to be vocal about the issue when Americans are more concerned about rising costs and inflation. Recent polls have found that voters consider climate change a problem, but tend to rank it low on a list of priorities.

“The issue of climate change has become so loaded with voters, and in many ways it’s become a signifier of the kind of cultural elitism that people associate with Democrats,” said Adam Jentleson, a veteran Democratic operative who now runs the Searchlight Institute, a think tank that has urged Democrats to talk less about climate.

“What our polling shows is that if you state it as a priority, people immediately start thinking that you are trying to make things cost more for them and constrain their choices as consumers,” Jentleson said. “It also crowds out a focus on other issues, and it’s much more advantageous to focus on the cost of living.”

A series of storms has added to reservoirs in the Colorado River basin, but the long-term water outlook remains bleak.

Reporting from Washington

Floods have overwhelmed parts of the parched American Southwest in recent days and weeks, pouring water into critically low reservoirs.

But the deluge did little to ease worries over the water crisis that required significant limits on usage across the Colorado River basin earlier this year.

Instead, it exemplified a sort of weather whiplash that is becoming more common as the climate warms, making it harder to maintain a stable water supply for the West. Right after enduring one of its driest stretches of spring and summer on record, the Southwest is now experiencing one of its wettest autumns.

“It gives us a little bit of breathing room, but we’ve just got to see how much it snows this year,” said Kathryn Sorensen, research director at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University.

Here’s what to know about the floods and what they mean for the Colorado basin, which supplies water to 40 million people and 5.5 million acres of farmland across parts of seven U.S. states, as well as about two dozen Native tribes and two Mexican states.

Water levels have risen sharply in Lake Powell, the nation’s second-largest reservoir, which straddles the Utah-Arizona border. The lake’s surface rose by nearly 16 feet from mid-September through the end of October. Lake Powell is expected to continue to rise once floods that hit parts of Colorado and Arizona last weekend flow downstream.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/scien.title: Do Animals Grieve?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/scien.author: Emily Anthes
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/scien.text:
Loren Elliott for The New York Times

Coyotes are not obvious romantics. Their habit of stalking across the landscape alone has earned them a reputation as solitary creatures — and not particularly popular ones, with a public image that ranges from troublesome nuisance to dangerous predator.

But they are deeply loyal mates. They remain with their partners for life, grooming each other, sharing food and raising pups together. “Basically, until death do us part,” said Sara Freeman, a neuroscientist at Utah State University.

In her airy, third-floor laboratory, Dr. Freeman is trying to understand how coyote couples forge these bonds — and what happens when they are broken.

“This is a widowed brain,” she said, pulling a few foil-wrapped packages from an ultracold freezer one morning in August. Each held a block of brain tissue, collected from a female coyote who had outlived her mate.

A student began shaving the frozen tissue into paper-thin slices, using the tip of a small paintbrush to nudge each translucent cross-section onto a glass slide. Later, the researchers would examine the samples, looking for neurological signs of “what we would call a grief state,” Dr. Freeman said.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/scien.title: Why Did Snakes Lose Their Legs? And 9 More Animal Mysteries
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/scien.author: Emily Anthes and Stella Raine Chu
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/scien.text:
Scientists know that all snakes descend from a reptile that lived about 160 million years ago. But that ancestor had four legs. What rendered those limbs unnecessary?

Some scientists contend that being limbless gave early snakes an advantage — a leg up, as it were — on land, by helping them thrive in narrow, underground tunnels. Others propose that elongated bodies evolved for swimming in the water.

Fossils highlight the debate. In 2015, researchers examined X-ray models of the inner ear of an animal closely related to the ancestor of modern-day snakes. The anatomy suggested that these ancestors lived underground. But fossils of primitive snakes with developed hind legs have also been found in marine limestone, suggesting that the first snakes may have lived underwater.

“It’s hard to tell what exact conditions drove the evolution of this body plan,” said Tiago Simões, an evolutionary biologist at Princeton.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/po.title: Susie Wiles, Trump’s Chief of Staff, Is Accused of Blocking Health Policies to Attract Donations
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/po.author: Christina Jewett and Sheryl Gay Stolberg
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/po.text:
In a no-holds-barred interview with Joe Rogan, Calley Means, a former top health adviser, accused Susie Wiles of repeatedly bowing to lobbying pressures and fixating on campaign contributions.

By Christina Jewett and Sheryl Gay Stolberg

Calley Means, who resigned as a top federal health official two weeks ago after clashing with the White House, on Friday accused President Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, of bowing to “unrelenting” pressure from industry lobbyists while prioritizing political fund-raising over Americans’ health.

In a two-hour interview with the podcaster Joe Rogan, Mr. Means said that Ms. Wiles withheld support from his efforts to make children’s diets healthier, citing the need for sugar industry money. He said her team demanded more approvals of flavored e-cigarettes, a top priority for major tobacco companies that donated at least $20 million to the G.O.P. in 2026. And he said they gave in to heavy lobbying from the kratom industry to relax proposed restrictions on products often referred to as “gas station heroin.”

“Susie said to me many times: ‘We need money for the midterms, Calley. We need money for the midterms,’” Mr. Means said.

In recent days, Ms. Wiles has become a target of criticism and finger-pointing in an escalating blame game after Republicans’ stunning losses in the midterm elections. In a post on Truth Social on Friday afternoon, Mr. Trump announced that Ms. Wiles would leave her post on Monday and Stephen Miller, a top White House adviser, would replace her.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Ms. Wiles was not immediately available to comment. A White House spokeswoman, Allison Schuster, did not respond to questions about Mr. Means’s statements. But she said in an emailed statement that Mr. Trump had “made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again,” citing the government’s new dietary guidelines and work to eliminate artificial ingredients from food.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/healt.title: Bird Flu Death in Washington State Renews Concern Over the Virus
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/healt.author: Apoorva Mandavilli and Emily Anthes
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/healt.text:
The death follows reports of infections in cattle on dozens of American farms across the country over the past month and a worrying outbreak in mink.

By Apoorva Mandavilli and Emily Anthes

A resident of Washington State died this week after a severe case of bird flu, a new and worrying sign that the virus continues to be a threat  in the United States.

The news followed reports that the bird flu virus had been detected in dairy cattle on dozens of farms across the country over the past month. It has also been spreading unchecked for months at a mink farm in Utah.

The death, in Yakima County, Wash., is the first related to bird flu in the country this year, and the third since 2024. But it was only on Thursday, one day after an inquiry from The New York Times, that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention updated its website. It still has not made any statements to the public about the death.

Documents obtained by the Animal Welfare Institute, an advocacy group, showed that federal and state officials also have done little to stem the outbreak at the mink farm, where the virus, called H5N1, had been circulating for weeks before it was detected.

Letting the virus spread on a crowded mink farm gives the virus unlimited opportunities to evolve into a version that could trigger a pandemic, some experts warned.

“No one has ever done something as silly as letting this thing happen,” Thomas Peacock, a virologist at the Pirbright Institute in England, said of the lack of control measures.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/healt.title: An 80-Cent Plastic Pouch Is Saving Thousands of Women From Dying in Childbirth
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/healt.author: Stephanie Nolen and Taiwo Aina
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/healt.text:
The maternal drape, as it is called, is helping to solve one of the world’s most intractable health problems.

The maternal drape, as it is called, is helping to solve one of the world’s most intractable health problems.

Husaina Balarabe with her newborn, Aabid, in the maternity ward at the Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital in Kano, Nigeria, in September.
Credit...
Taiwo Aina for The New York Times

Photographs by Taiwo Aina

Stephanie Nolen saw nine women bring new babies safely into the world while reporting this story in labor wards in the north of Nigeria.

A few hours after she nearly bled to death, Husaina Balarabe was serenely unaware that her life had been in peril.

She cuddled her newborn baby, a lush-cheeked boy she had named Aabid, and showed him off to her sisters from her bed in a noisy hospital delivery ward in the northern Nigerian city of Kano.

Ms. Balarabe, a 26-year-old optometrist, had experienced a postpartum hemorrhage, a side effect of childbirth that is the leading cause of maternal death around the world.

She did not die because her midwife used a low-cost, low-tech intervention that was pioneered here and in other maternity wards in some of Africa’s poorest places, and that is now saving lives across the continent.

The device was a piece of thin, green plastic the size of a cookie sheet with a pouch at its end, called a maternal drape. It lay beneath Ms. Balarabe as she delivered, and the pouch hung off the end of the bed. The midwife who caught baby Aabid saw blood running into the pouch and quickly reaching and surpassing the danger level — 300 milliliters (or 10 ounces), indicated by a mark on the pouch.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/healt.title: Trump Administration Moves to Oust Arbitrators as Doctor Payouts Soar
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/healt.author: Margot Sanger-Katz and Sarah Kliff
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/healt.text:
The two companies settled billing disputes between doctors and insurers, keeping patients out of the middle. One let doctors win 96 percent of the time.

By Margot Sanger-Katz and Sarah Kliff

The authors are covering the implementation of the No Surprises Act. They welcome tips at nytimes.com/tips.

The federal government plans to end contracts with two arbitration firms that settle medical billing disputes under the No Surprises Act, a consumer protection law that has come under scrutiny for high payouts for doctors.

Congress passed the law in 2020 to protect patients from surprise bills when they saw a doctor who did not have a contract with their health plan, such as in emergencies. The law, which took effect in 2022, calls for health care providers and insurers to settle on a price and when they cannot, for arbitrators to review an offer from each side, and pick one.

When the law passed, its authors expected the system to be used rarely and decisions generally to be split between the sides. But doctors have flooded the system with millions of cases and have prevailed overwhelmingly, winning more than 85 percent of them in 2025, according to the most recent federal data. Many have received awards dozens of times higher than usual insurer rates.

One New York plastic surgery practice won $440,000 for breast reduction surgeries in arbitration, The New York Times previously reported, and a surgical assistant in New Jersey won $106,500 for assisting on lower back surgery.

The law has been a financial boon for the arbitration firms as well. The government contracts with 17 firms to handle the millions of cases that now flow through the arbitration process. The arbitrators set their own fees, earning $425 to $800 for each dispute they settle, and they have collectively earned $742 million between 2022 and 2025.

While the contractors are all supposed to follow the same rules, federal data shows that outcomes vary dramatically between the arbitrators.

The Trump administration plans to cancel contracts with the two highlighted firms.

Source: Turquoise Health

By The New York Times

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/busin.title: CVS to Split Off Drugstore Business, Ending Its Bigger-Is-Better Era
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/busin.author: Rebecca Robbins and Reed Abelson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/busin.text:
In a breakup planned for 2028, CVS Health intends to keep together its insurance and pharmacy benefits divisions and create a separate company for its pharmacies.

By Rebecca Robbins and Reed Abelson

CVS Health plans to split in two, in a major unraveling of one of the country’s largest health care conglomerates after decades of rampant expansion, the company announced on Wednesday.

Under the breakup, expected in the first half of 2028, a spinoff company, to be called CVS Pharmacy, will house the conglomerate’s approximately 9,000 retail pharmacies, in-store medical clinics and a warehouse-based operation that sends prescriptions through the mail to consumers.

A second company will retain the name CVS Health and include Aetna, the major insurer; Caremark, the giant pharmacy benefit manager; and other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people.

CVS Health and its peers, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna, have been under mounting scrutiny from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers, regulators and others because of the companies’ dominance over nearly every aspect of consumers’ health care services.

Critics say the three have long exploited internal conflicts within their web of businesses to increase profits, stifling competition and helping to drive up medical costs.

Within the past two years, Arkansas and Tennessee have each passed laws that aim to prevent the conglomerates from both managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/in.author: Margot Sanger-Katz and Sarah Kliff
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/in.text:
A law to end surprise medical bills has generated millions of high-dollar payouts for doctors. Health plans are now fighting back by frequently withholding money.

By Margot Sanger-Katz and Sarah Kliff

The authors are covering the implementation of the No Surprises Act. They welcome tips at nytimes.com/tips.

Over the past two years, Flight for Life has airlifted car crash victims, premature babies and adults struggling to breathe to hospitals across southeastern Wisconsin.

Anthem, the major health insurer, covered dozens of those patients, but it has refused to pay $2.1 million it owes the company for their helicopter rides.

The amounts due for each emergency medical flight range from $9,382 to $62,373. Anthem has historically paid its bills, but late last year it suddenly stopped.

“It was like a faucet they just shut off,” said Flight for Life’s executive director, Leif Erickson.

The insurer’s willful nonpayment is the latest in a cascade of unintended consequences brought about by a widely supported law that was intended to protect patients from surprise medical bills.

The law, which took effect in 2022, calls for arbitrators to decide appropriate levels of reimbursement, and it has already triggered millions of disputes between medical care providers and insurers. Doctors have prevailed overwhelmingly, winning arbitration settlements that sometimes far exceeded the usual insurer rates.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/busin.title: Trump Administration Said to Plan Rolling Back Pregnancy-Related Job Protections
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/busin.author: Coral Davenport and Rebecca Davis O’Brien
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/busin.text:
The Biden era law was meant to help women stay in the workplace, but some conservatives say rules to enact it went too far with coverage for abortion and fertility treatment.

By Coral Davenport and Rebecca Davis O’Brien

Coral Davenport, who covers federal regulations, reported from Washington. Rebecca Davis O’Brien, who covers labor, reported from New York.

The Trump administration is preparing to scale back workplace accommodations for women related to pregnancy and reproductive health, seven people with knowledge of discussions of the plans said.

The moves will limit the impact of a 2022 law that was meant to fill a gap in disability and discrimination protections that employees are guaranteed at workplaces. It was intended to provide accommodations for pregnant workers, such as bathroom and water breaks, reprieves from heavy lifting or time off for prenatal appointments.

But the scope of the regulations under the law, known as the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, has been debated since their drafting. Conservatives, even some who supported the law, said the rule that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission wrote to apply the law reached far beyond pregnancy to cover matters including abortion, fertility treatment and related procedures and conditions it was not meant to protect.

Narrowing them would fit with other efforts by Andrea Lucas, the E.E.O.C.’s chair, to roll back what she has called the liberal excesses of the Biden administration. The E.E.O.C. has targeted corporate diversity, equity and inclusion programs, abandoned some discrimination cases and stopped enforcing workplace protections for transgender workers. It is of a piece with a suite of executive actions that are remaking the American workplace by halting enforcement of sexual harassment rules and encouraging fewer mothers to work outside the home.

The E.E.O.C. plans to publish the proposed narrowing of conditions eligible for accommodations as soon as this month.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/scien.title: Doctors in Ukraine Try Treating Infections Like Biological Warfare Attacks
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/scien.author: Gina Kolata and Marc Santora
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/scien.text:
As many as 40 percent of injured soldiers face severe infections that can lead to amputations and death. One initiative is trying to fix that.

By Gina Kolata and Marc Santora

Gina Kolata heard about a new effort to reduce infections in Ukraine while moderating a wartime medicine discussion. Marc Santora visited the site of the dress rehearsal in Poland and spent a day reporting from the disinfection unit in Dnipro, Ukraine.

The injuries to soldiers arriving at Ukrainian hospitals are horrific. Instead of bullet wounds, blast injuries from drones dominate the scene: Calf muscles are blown away, chunks of tissue are missing from thighs. Soil and debris thrown up from the blast are lodged deep in lacerations.

By the time they arrive at a hospital, which can take days, weeks or even months of travel under cover of darkness, 30 to 40 percent of soldiers are not just injured but have severe infections. And their infections often involve microbes that are untreatable — resistant to antibiotics. When the injured soldiers are admitted to civilian hospitals, they risk spreading the bacteria to other patients.

Now there is an effort to counter this scourge.

It started with a realization by Hailie Uren, a clinical pharmacologist and disaster medicine specialist who works in Ukraine. The situation, she reasoned, resembled nothing so much as a biological warfare attack. “If we don’t have antibiotics to treat these patients,” she said, “how different is that from when a patient is exposed to anthrax?”

Hospitals already have plans in place to treat victims of biological warfare, she noted. All the hospitals had to do was carry out those same urgent protocols on the battlefield. Ms. Uren proposed the idea directly to Ukraine’s surgeon general, and received support from the defense and health ministries.

The effort began in September, in a large tent outside a hospital in central Ukraine.

The objective, which Ms. Uren had developed with colleagues, would be to disinfect injured soldiers before they entered a hospital; remove their dirty clothes and bandages, wash them with an antiseptic and give them a shower.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/us/el.title: Former Patient Files Class-Action Lawsuit Against Senator Marshall
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/us/el.author: Sarah Kliff
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/us/el.text:
The Republican sued more than 700 patients during his former career as a physician. The suit accuses him of charging illegally high interest rates.

Reporting from Washington.

A former patient of Senator Roger Marshall, Republican of Kansas, on Thursday filed a class-action lawsuit against him and his former medical practice, contending that he charged illegally high interest rates in pursuing patients over outstanding bills.

Mr. Marshall, who had a 25-year career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills, The New York Times found in an investigation last month. In at least 81 of those cases, patients were arrested after missing court dates.

Mr. Marshall, a first-term senator, is facing an unexpectedly tight race to keep his seat, with recent polls showing him neck-and-neck with his Democratic challenger, Adam Hamilton, in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932.

The lawsuit, filed in Kansas state court, focuses on the 18 percent interest rate that Mr. Marshall and the medical practice he co-owned, Heartland OBGYN, often charged patients.

It argues that the high rate was “egregious conduct” that may have violated Kansas law.

Kansas typically limits the interest rate that doctors and any other businesses can pursue in court to 15 percent. There are, however, some exceptions that allow them to pursue more if they had a pre-existing contract spelling out a higher rate.

A Marshall spokeswoman did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the litigation.

Steven Johnson, a lawyer who filed Mr. Marshall’s debt cases, previously told The Times that the 18 percent interest rate was set by the doctor’s office.

Because of an editing error, an earlier version of this article misidentified the political party that hasn’t won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932. It was the Democratic Party, not Republicans.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/busin.author: Ben Casselman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/busin.text:
Artificial Intelligence

White collar industries that are most exposed to artificial intelligence continued to add jobs in October, although that growth has been weak.

Is artificial intelligence taking our jobs?

It’s arguably the single biggest question facing the labor market right now, all the more so after Tuesday’s midterm elections showed widespread public animosity toward A.I. and data centers, in particular.

The evidence, though, is far from clear.

White-collar industries like accounting, legal services and finance mostly added jobs in October, but their growth has been decidedly weak over the past few years. The information sector — a broad category that includes much of tech but also media companies — has been cutting jobs steadily since late 2022. Microsoft last week announced that it was offering buyouts to tens of thousands of employees, making it the latest tech giant to cut jobs.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/busin.title: Strong Hiring Reinforces a Sturdy Job Market
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/busin.author: Sydney Ember
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/busin.text:
Unemployment fell in October, extending years of stability for a U.S. work force threatened by inflation and artificial intelligence.

Note: Data is seasonally adjusted. The average is calculated as a three-month moving average.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By Keith Collins and Jacqueline Gu

Businesses added workers at a vigorous clip in October, continuing a string of healthy hiring that underscored the job market’s stability even as inflation and concerns about investments in artificial intelligence pressure other aspects of the economy.

The report affirmed that the labor market remained solid and even showed some glimmers of momentum that could begin to relieve persistent anxiety among workers about their ability to find work. Employers added 165,000 jobs on a seasonally adjusted basis last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday, and the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1 percent.

Job gains for August and September were revised upward by a total of 84,000, bringing the average increase per month over the past three months to 137,000. The labor force participation rate ticked up for the third month in a row.

“Workers are still nervous about the current state of the job market,” said Daniel Zhao, the chief economist at Glassdoor, a career site. “But at the very least, today’s report is a step in the right direction towards building up that worker confidence again.”

A big question hanging over the labor market, and the economy more broadly, is the impact of A.I. on jobs. Investors’ concerns about the trajectory of investments in the technology sent stocks plummeting on Thursday.

So far, A.I. does not appear to be leading to widespread job losses despite some headline-grabbing announcements. The job gains last month were relatively widespread, with a range of sectors adding positions. Even some white-collar industries thought to be heavily exposed to technological disruption added jobs. Professional and business services, which include accountants, lawyers and other office work, gained 70,000 positions last month. The financial activities sector tacked on 7,000 jobs.

Note: Data is seasonally adjusted. Charts represent cumulative percent change since January 1, 2022.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/busin.author: Colby Smith
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/busin.text:
The Federal Reserve decided against raising interest rates at its meeting last week, but it is widely expected to move again in December to help tame inflation.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

The Federal Reserve has settled on raising interest rates gradually as it seeks to tame inflation. That suggests the central bank will lift borrowing costs again in December, and at least one more time in 2027.

An accelerating labor market, or one that falters, could alter that approach.

The labor market has not contributed to the inflation problem confronting the Fed, a dynamic that was affirmed when data for October was released on Friday. Monthly jobs growth was strong and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent, but wage growth remains relatively muted. Average hourly earnings picked up a bit in October, rising 0.4 percent for the month. Compared to the same time last year, it is up 3.1 percent.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/trave.title: What Does the Super El Niño Mean for Ski Season?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/trave.author: David Goodman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/trave.text:
The climate event is predicted to alter snowfall patterns across the U.S. and Canada. Experts are starting to see how it might play out across ski country.

David Goodman is a Vermont-based writer who writes frequently about skiing.

Godzilla has arrived. A super El Niño is here.

What sounds like the plot of a horror movie is actually a forecast for a climate event that is predicted to shatter records and reshape global snowfall patterns this winter. An El Niño results from an intricate interplay between ocean and atmosphere: The temperature of the sea’s surface in the eastern Pacific Ocean near the Equator warms, releases heat and affects the trade winds, which changes global weather patterns. El Niños occur every two to seven years, typically peaking from November to January.

For skiers, this year’s powerful El Niño could mean abundant snow in some regions, while large expanses of North America endure warm temperatures, rain or drought. Many skiers have been anxiously watching the predictions and trying to game out where they should go this winter, especially after a disastrous season in much of the West last year.

Forecasters have recently been issuing long-range projections for where and when the snow is likely to fall during ski season. Here’s what to know.

When ocean temperatures warm more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) it is designated as a very strong El Niño (words like “super” are popular descriptions, not scientific ones). The National Weather Service Climate Prediction Center has already declared that this super El Niño is likely to be “a historic event” that will break previous records. Ocean temperatures more than 2 degrees Celsius above normal have already been recorded in the eastern Pacific, with temperatures exceeding 4 degrees Celsius above normal in some places.

Tracking the number of very strong El Niños can be confusing, because the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Adminstration recently changed the index it uses to measure their strength, to better account for climate change. Using the new index, it says, there have been six very strong El Niños since 1950.

A super El Niño typically strengthens the southern storm track and weakens the northern one. According to NOAA, heavier precipitation is more likely from California — with snowfall concentrated in the mountains — to the Gulf Coast, while warmer and drier air is expected to dominate the Midwest.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/clima.title: How Trump’s Energy Policies Helped Trigger Midterm Rout
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/clima.author: David Gelles
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/clima.text:
The war in Iran, efforts to promote fossil fuels and attacks on renewable energy contributed to higher prices for gas and electricity that drove voter discontent.

President Trump spent much of the past two years promising to bring down energy prices.

Instead, his war with Iran, as well as other policies, drove up the cost of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time his administration worked to thwart efforts to fight climate change, blocking renewable energy investments that could have reduced the country’s reliance on fossil fuels or brought down costs.

On Tuesday, voters’ frustration with soaring energy prices helped propel Democrats to a blowout, with Republicans losing control of the House and the Senate, as well as the governorships of many historically conservative states.

“It’s quite clear that energy and energy affordability in particular played a big role in the electorate’s decision-making last night,” said Hasan Nazar, head of policy at Crux, a clean energy finance company.

Many Americans said concerns about the cost of gas and electricity informed their voting choices, according to polling from The Associated Press. Gasoline prices across the country were at a record high for an Election Day, according to AAA.

No single action had a bigger effect on energy costs than Mr. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. With the Strait of Hormuz closed and global flows of oil disrupted, gasoline prices in the United States have jumped more than 40 percent since the war began. Diesel prices are up nearly 70 percent.

Catherine Wolfram, a professor of energy economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management, said that launching the war was among the worst decisions Mr. Trump could have made if he was trying to bring down energy costs. “It’s Econ 101 that invading Iran when they control the Strait of Hormuz is going to impact gas prices,” she said.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/clima.title: Old, Polluting Jet Engines Are Being Scavenged to Power Data Centers
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/clima.author: Hiroko Tabuchi and Gabriela Bhaskar
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/clima.text:
They’re rapidly being converted into generators to meet A.I.’s insatiable demand for electricity. Environmentalists call it a step backward.

Across wide stretches of the sun-bleached Sonoran desert in Arizona, thousands of retired aircraft sit nose-to-tail in graveyards of metal known as boneyards.

​Many of their engines haven’t been fired up for years. But America’s soaring demand for electricity to power data centers is bringing them back to life.

Several companies are racing to strip the engines out of old aircraft to convert them into electrical generators. And data centers, desperate for power, are snapping them up.

“They’re getting creative,” said Bill Kleyman, chief executive of Apolo, an A​.I​. platform and infrastructure company. “Just a few years ago, a traditional data center would have been like, ‘Are you kidding me? This is ridiculous.’”

Now, data center developers are obsessed with “speed to power,” Mr. Kleyman said. “It’s like, ‘How fast can you get me energy?’”

President Trump, aware that the rapid construction of data centers has sparked concerns over rising electricity prices, has pressed center developers to generate their own power. “It was my idea,” he told reporters in August. “Data centers now are mandated by me that they build their own electricity, so they’re not taking it from the grid."

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/clima.title: Disneyland’s Autopia Ride Will Switch to Electric Vehicles
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/clima.author: David Gelles
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/clima.text:
The gas-powered engines in Disneyland’s Autopia ride weren’t properly certified. The little cars will be replaced by E.V.s.

The gas-powered engines in Disneyland’s Autopia ride weren’t properly certified. The little cars will be replaced by E.V.s.

Autopia, the 71-year-old car-themed attraction at Disneyland in Anaheim, Calif., in 1980. Its gasoline-powered cars have created a microclimate of smog over Tomorrowland.
Credit...
Michael Montfort/Michael Ochs Archives, via Getty Images

David Gelles recently rode Autopia over and over until he was dizzy.

In 1955, Walt Disney’s vision of the cutting edge came in the form of 40 candy-colored miniature cars that allowed pint-size drivers to push a real gas pedal and steer around a track at the Anaheim theme park.

Autopia, a focal point of the Tomorrowland section of Disneyland, mirrored the real-life love affair that Americans were having with the automobile. Work would soon begin on the interstate highway system, suburbs were expanding, car sales were skyrocketing and the future felt like a shiny coupe, windows down, speeding along an open road.

But Mr. Disney’s midcentury vision of the future has run up against today’s environmental reality. Autopia, the only surviving original attraction at Tomorrowland, is in violation of California’s stringent emissions regulations.

So now, after 71 years, Autopia is going electric.

The cars currently run on 8.5 horsepower Honda four-stroke engines like those typically used to run generators or industrial pressure washers. They are loud and belch exhaust for up to 16 hours a day. The result is a microclimate of smog hovering over Tomorrowland, a section of the park that includes rides like Space Mountain and Buzz Lightyear Astro Blasters.

Sometime next year, the gasoline powered engines will be phased out and Autopia will join the age of E.V.s.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/clima.title: William Nordhaus Pioneered Putting a Price on Pollution
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/clima.author: David Gelles
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/clima.text:
Economist William Nordhaus said putting a price on pollution was the best way to reduce climate change. Then came the fossil fuel lobby and the anti-tax movement.

Long before climate change entered the vernacular, the economist William D. Nordhaus had seized on the idea of taxing pollution as the most effective way to combat man-made global warming.

Dr. Nordhaus, who died Friday at 85, spent his career championing the idea of a tax on carbon dioxide. Putting a price on planet-warming pollution, he contended, would slow down climate change and could be achieved without severe harm to the economy.

His work helped inform government policies around the world, and in 2018 he shared the Nobel Prize in economics.

But Dr. Nordhaus faced powerful adversaries who ultimately curtailed the influence of his ideas. The fossil fuel industry, which would have absorbed the costs that Dr. Nordhaus proposed, vigorously opposed his work and commissioned reports that attacked carbon taxes.

“What economists did not take account for a long time was the enormous political interests that were lined up to fight any kind of climate policy,” said Gilbert E. Metcalf, emeritus professor of economics at Tufts University. “Basically, the fossil fuel industry had a lot of money and they spent it wisely to block any progress in this area.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/clima.title: COP17 Biodiversity Talks in Yerevan, Armenia
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/clima.author: Catrin Einhorn
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/clima.text:
Countries renewed their promises to protect wildlife at U.N. talks in Armenia, but how to cover the costs remains a question.

Two weeks of global negotiations to protect the world’s wildlife and ecosystems ended on Saturday in Yerevan, Armenia, with nations reaffirming their pledges to protect nature but still off track to meet an ambitious set of targets by a 2030 deadline.

Biodiversity, the variety of life on the planet, is declining at levels unprecedented in human history, scientists say.

In 2022, in a landmark agreement made under the United Nations biodiversity treaty, nations pledged to reverse those losses by taking action on 23 targets, including protecting 30 percent of the earth’s land and water and reforming industries that drive declines in wildlife.

This year’s meeting marked the halfway point for countries to meet their deadline for those pledges. The United States is the only country, with the exception of the Vatican, that is not party to the treaty, though it attends the meeting and participates from the sidelines.

Just before the talks began, the United Nations issued a review of progress that found that countries were lagging far behind. A major theme was how to get on track with a “Yerevan Pathway” that would help unlock progress.

In the end, delegates reaffirmed their commitments and set priorities, creating pressure for domestic action, but tense questions over how to pay for nature protection, especially in countries that are poor financially but rich in biodiversity, remained unresolved.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/scien.title: How Trump Is Dismantling America’s Scientific Research Machine
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/scien.author: Christopher Flavelle, Irena Hwang, Adam Sella, Alan Blinder, Sheryl Gay Stolberg, Benjamin Mueller and Michael C. Bender
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/scien.text:
Videos by Salwan Georges For The New York Times

The system that has driven life-altering discoveries and helped make the United States a superpower is now under intense strain.

Videos by Salwan Georges for The New York Times

The warning, buried in an obscure government report this summer, was unflinching.

The Defense Department’s vaunted network of research laboratories — whose scientists helped develop satellite communication, radar technology, and even the computer mouse — was in trouble.

The labs lost a significant share of their staff last year, largely in response to the Trump administration’s efforts to thin the federal work force, the report found. Refilling critical positions was proving difficult due in part to President Trump’s demand that new hires be screened for their loyalty to his goals. The report, issued by the Pentagon, pointed to “potentially grave consequences for the future of national defense.”

The turmoil inside scientific research has extended beyond the Pentagon. The Energy Department, a key hub of nuclear and quantum research, has lost more than 1,000 scientists and technical staff. The National Science Foundation, for decades a primary backer of long-term, foundational research, has withheld more than $1 billion in funding. And at the National Institutes of Health, the biggest funder of medical research, officials delayed or canceled more than 2,000 grants to biomedical researchers focused on topics such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and other diseases.

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

Under Mr. Trump, the federal government is still spending roughly as much on research — about $200 billion this year — as the administrations that came before. Scientists across the country are still receiving grants; universities are still being funded. But beneath the surface, the system of federally funded science that helped make the United States a global superpower is under intense strain from Trump policies, jeopardizing the nation’s advantages in defense, medicine and technology, a New York Times examination has found.

The White House regularly proclaims that it is advancing American interests. Yet its actions are eroding the country’s scientific edge as global rivals challenge U.S. dominance in fields that will help define the 21st century, according to interviews with scientists, university leaders, government officials and analysts and a review of documents and budgets.

American universities spent $65 billion in federal money in 2024, accounting for more than half of their total research and development spending.

Valeen Bhat warns that fall foliage, though picturesque, can prove dangerous when it clogs storm drains. She is spreading the gospel of clearing leaves.

Credit...
By Valeen Bhat

Whenever it rains, Valeen Bhat puts on her waders and her signature hot pink raincoat to clear debris from storm drains in Brooklyn. This time of year, there’s a lot.

Fall is for foliage. But foliage falls. And in New York, leaves wreak havoc by clogging storm drains, which can produce devastating flooding. Ms. Bhat, the owner of Private Picassos in Clinton Hill, learned this the hard way a year ago. On a Thursday in October, a sudden downpour inundated her art studio for children, trapping teachers and students, until firefighters rescued them.

With global warming, rain is falling faster and harder, and overwhelming the city’s century-old sewers, most of which were not designed for the furious and swift storms now common in New York.

Since last fall’s deluge, which caused two deaths in the city, Ms. Bhat has been spreading the gospel of leaf clearance. The task is especially crucial in elevated spots, because drains that clog uphill lead to flooding downhill.

Hardly a Cassandra, Ms. Bhat is simply being a responsible neighbor and business owner in the era of climate change, said Lisa F. Garcia, the commissioner of the city’s Department of Environmental Protection.

“As leaves begin to fall, we appreciate when all New Yorkers step in and do their part by clearing leaves and debris from storm drains near their homes and businesses,” Ms. Garcia said in a statement. “A few minutes of effort can make a real difference.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/busin.title: William Nordhaus Dies; Nobel Winner Influenced Climate Policy
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/busin.author: Lydia DePillis
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/busin.text:
The Yale professor moved climate change into mainstream economic analysis.

William D. Nordhaus, a Yale economist and Nobel laureate who tabulated the economic wreckage of carbon emissions and influenced climate policy across several presidential administrations, died on Friday at his home in New Haven. He was 85.

The cause was glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, according to a statement from Yale University.

In 2018, Professor Nordhaus shared the Nobel in economic science with Paul M. Romer, an economist at New York University. The Nobel committee cited Professor Nordhaus’s work in developing a method to balance climate change’s long-term damage with the costs required to contain it.

The model, which Professor Nordhaus refined over decades, has underpinned dozens of regulations around the world aimed at limiting fossil fuels and seeded the ground for a new field of research that bridges the gap between economics and earth science.

“He played a crucial role in terms of bringing consideration of the natural environment into the mainstream of economics, whereas earlier, it was sort of a fringe area,” said Robert Stavins, director of the environmental economics program at Harvard, who wrote about Professor Nordhaus’s impact.

By Rebecca F. Elliott and Keith Collins

The war with Iran has been very lucrative for American oil companies, which have earned more than $130 billion in profit as people pay much higher prices for gasoline, diesel and other fuel.

That is a conservative estimate based on the performance of more than 50 large U.S. oil and gas companies, most of them producers or refiners, in the six months from April through September. It does not reflect profits earned in March, the first month of the war, or in October.

These companies earned less than $47 billion collectively during the same period in 2025, a challenging stretch when oil was cheaper and companies were navigating the early fallout from President Trump’s trade war.

The blockbuster oil profits this year highlight longstanding concerns about who gains, and who pays the price, when wars interrupt the flow of energy. As of this week, Americans had spent an extra $147 billion on gasoline and diesel since the United States and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, according to an analysis by Brown University’s Climate Solutions Lab. That amounts to more than $1,100 per household.

Some companies are benefiting more than others. U.S. refiners have fared especially well because fuel-making plants have been badly damaged by hostilities in the Middle East and Russia. With fewer refineries available to meet global demand, profit margins soared for those that remain online.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/clima.title: Conservation Efforts for Caucasian Leopards Show Promise
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/clima.author: Eric Niiler
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/clima.text:
In Armenia, a three-legged Caucasian leopard’s astonishing hike signals that conservation efforts for the endangered animal may be working.

Eric Niiler did not see a Caucasian leopard during a six-hour hike near Areni, Armenia.

For years, a leopard roamed the high mountain ridges and deep gorges in the sparsely populated region of southern Armenia. The animal had lost part of its left front leg on a land mine along the nearby border with Azerbaijan, so it hobbled a bit.

As the population of Caucasian leopards has slowly grown in Armenia, this adult male, named Aren after the village where he was often seen, had to search for new territory without the presence of other males in order to find a mate, researchers said.

So last year, Aren traveled nearly 200 miles north into Georgia where his three-legged odyssey was captured on a trail camera. To conservationists in Armenia, Aren’s remarkable cross-border trek is a small sign of progress in protecting the endangered Caucasian leopard.

Threatened plants and animals have been the focus for the past two weeks in Armenia, where delegates from around the world have gathered for the United Nations summit on biodiversity. Nations had already agreed to protect 30 percent of the planet’s land and water by 2030, among other pledges. A big question at this year’s meeting is how to get there.

Armenia, a country that is smaller than Maryland but considered a biodiversity hot spot, has protected nearly 13 percent of its territory to help native species.

In the southern province of Vayots Dzor, the government and environmental groups have linked a state-owned forest, a private nature reserve and a community-managed environmental area to create a 217-square-mile wildlife corridor for leopards and other threatened species including the Syrian brown bear, the Bezoar goat, and the mouflon, an endangered wild sheep.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/world.title: The Perils of Glittering Skylines
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/world.author: Katrin Bennhold
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/world.text:
Glass skyscrapers are transforming cities, but do they make sense in a world that’s getting hotter?

I’m the host of The World.

When we moved to Cardiff and renovated the ground floor of an old Victorian house, one thing I knew I wanted was lots of glass in my kitchen. I liked the idea of lots of daylight, of seeing the trees outside.

Our builder advised against it. Even in Wales, hardly famous for tropical temperatures, it could become uncomfortably hot without air-conditioning, he warned. After last summer’s heat wave, I’m glad I followed his advice.

I’m not the only one susceptible to the allure of glass. Around the world, glass skyscrapers — those glittering symbols of modernity — are flying up at a rapid rate, often in places much hotter than Cardiff. But the air-conditioning required to make these spaces usable is extremely energy intensive. Today, my colleague Chico Harlan, our global climate correspondent, writes on why some argue it’s time to rethink the glass skyscraper.

More than any other form of architecture, glass skyscrapers testify to the human desire for sweeping views and a sense of rising above the fray. In some of the world’s fastest developing places — Dubai, Mumbai, Jakarta, Kuala Lumpur — they have become city-defining showpieces, signaling sophistication and rising financial clout.
