https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/clima.title: A Marathon Runner’s Hard Lesson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/clima.author: David Gelles
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/clima.text:
Racing in Chicago showed your newsletter host firsthand how warming is disrupting the sport.

When the New York City Marathon begins on Sunday morning, temperatures are expected to be in the low 50s Fahrenheit.

Runners, consider yourselves lucky.

The relatively mild forecast is an increasingly rare luxury in the world of running, with hotter temperatures and extreme weather worldwide disrupting training and scrambling races.

In March, temperatures soared past 80 degrees Fahrenheit, or roughly 27 Celsius, during the Los Angeles Marathon. With runners wilting as the day went on, organizers decided to hand out finisher medals to anyone wishing to stop at the 18-mile mark.

A full marathon is 26.2 miles, or 42.2 kilometers, and many in the running world were outraged. But organizers said it was a necessary move in the name of public safety.

On the first October weekend of 2023, the Twin Cities Marathon, from Minneapolis to Saint Paul, Minn., was canceled at the last minute as temperatures were predicted to climb past 90 degrees, the area’s hottest-ever October day. Starting next year, the race will be held later in the month, making it the largest U.S. marathon so far to make a climate-related scheduling change.

“We all feel like our probabilities of getting those ideal crisp fall temperatures is just much higher,” said Dean Orton, president of Twin Cities in Motion, which organizes the race.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/busin.title: Trump’s Tariffs Are On the Ballot in Michigan
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/busin.author: Ana Swanson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/busin.text:
The levies as well as trade fighting with Canada are facing a test in the state, where voters appear skeptical of free trade but also of the president’s erratic approach.

Ana Swanson covers international trade and reported from Detroit.

President Trump’s use of tariffs to shield manufacturing-heavy states like Michigan from foreign competition was supposed to be a political win for the president and his party.

But voters in many of the states that Mr. Trump said he would help with his trade policies now appear skeptical of his erratic approach. And they are wondering if a growing backlash to tariffs will mean that the Trump administration’s economic experiment will come to an end just as quickly as it started.

Those concerns are being acutely felt in the Detroit area, where auto supply chains are intertwined with Canadian businesses just across the border. Mr. Trump’s global tariffs and his trade wars have become a midterm flashpoint as businesses and consumers contend with higher costs from tariffs and America’s strained relationship with Canada.

Mr. Trump in August imposed a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion of certain Canadian exports, after the countries failed to reach a trade deal. Canada swiftly retaliated with its own tariffs, prompting the Trump administration to ban the import of some Canadian goods, including alcohol and some dairy products.

Mr. Trump has still been threatening to proceed with a 50 percent tariff on Canadian autos and auto parts if the countries can’t make a deal by Jan. 1. On Sunday, just days before the midterms, Mr. Trump said he had “concepts of a very good deal with Canada,” though no details on the arrangement were released.

Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, also said that teams from the countries would be working in the coming weeks on “the outlines of a mutually beneficial trade deal.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/busin.title: Inflation Accelerated in October, PCE Index Shows
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/busin.author: Aruni Soni
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/busin.text:
The Personal Consumption Expenditures index picked up in September, according to data released a day after the Federal Reserve’s decision to hold interest rates steady.

Consumer prices accelerated in September, which could bolster the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December after forgoing an increase this week.

Prices, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, increased 0.5 percent in September from a month earlier and 3.6 percent compared with the same time last year, according to a report released on Thursday by the Bureau of Economic Analysis. The pickup in prices provided further confirmation that inflation is running hotter than Fed officials would like. Their target, as measured by P.C.E., is to keep the annual increase near 2 percent over time.

“Core” prices, which exclude more volatile categories like food and energy, jumped 3.1 percent in September annually and rose 0.3 percent from a month earlier. That month-over-month increase was also 0.3 percent in August.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/clima.title: A Guide to COP31 Climate Talks in Antalya, Turkey
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/clima.author: Chico Harlan
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/clima.text:
Negotiators and leaders are gathering for annual United Nations climate talks. They come as global temperatures are set to breach a key threshold.

The United Nations climate conference, known this year as COP31, starts Monday in Antalya, Turkey.

The event comes after a series of deadly heat waves and floods, and amid an El Niño event that pushed global temperatures last month to the highest level for any October on record. At the same time, the United States’ war in Iran, and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has sent oil and gas prices soaring, scrambling nations’ energy goals. Greenhouse gas emissions from burning fossil fuels are at a record high.

Against that backdrop, negotiators and world leaders are gathering for the 12-day event.

Here is a guide to the meeting:

It’s the United Nations’ annual climate gathering formally known as the Conference of the Parties. This year, it starts Nov. 9 and is scheduled to end on Nov. 20, but negotiations often run past the deadline.

More than 195 countries are part of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, set up in 1992. Those nations discuss how to address global warming and cut greenhouse gas emissions. The climate meeting is the largest annual United Nations conference of any kind, and this year more than 60,000 people are expected to attend.

The talks include two days of speeches from world leaders, on Nov. 11 and 12. After that, the formal negotiations intensify, and delegates try to hash out a final agreement to advance climate goals.

Nations take turns hosting the event. But this year, Turkey earned the right only after striking a sharing agreement with Australia, which had also sought the host role. As a result, Turkey will manage the venue, handle communication and preside over the voluntary sideline initiatives. But Australia will shepherd negotiations. The arrangement makes for an unusual variable at these talks.

The conference takes place in Antalya, a Mediterranean resort city, at the Antalya Expo Center.

Last year’s conference was held at the edge of the Amazon rainforest, in Belém, Brazil. Next year’s conference is planned for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

An injured five-month-old walrus was found huddled next to carcasses in remote Alaska after it became separated from its mother. Its rescue took days and lots of patience.

Researchers found an orphaned walrus calf in a remote part of Alaska in September amid a pile of walrus carcasses. They rescued the calf, who would be named Annautaq.
Credit...
United States Geological Survey

The sun was glinting off the waves on a beach in Alaska when Violet Anniskett saw what she thought were four dead walruses on the sand.

Then Ms. Anniskett, 19, stepped closer to the pile of blubber and saw one body, smaller than the rest.

Its stomach was heaving. Suddenly, the walrus’s eyes opened.

Ms. Anniskett gasped.

“I was in shock,” she said.

The calf’s mother was nowhere in sight.

The five-month-old baby walrus, a male, would later be named Annautaq (pronounced ah-NOW-tuk), after Ms. Anniskett’s father, who, like her, is Inupiat, a member of a group of northern Indigenous people. Annautaq’s rescuers cared for him for four days near Point Lay in northern Alaska, near the Chukchi Sea.

Annautaq was eventually transported to SeaWorld in Orlando, Fla., making him a rare success story of humans rescuing a baby walrus, without its mother, from a perilous fate.

When Ms. Anniskett spotted the calf on Sept. 11, polar bear prints surrounded Annautaq and sea gulls flew overhead, ready to perhaps eat chunks of his exposed flesh, she said.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/clima.title: With Hopes Low and Temperatures High, Climate Summit Opens in Turkey
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/clima.author: Chico Harlan
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/clima.text:
War, artificial intelligence and the Trump era have overshadowed climate change. But officials from nearly every nation are meeting to confront global warming.

As heads of state and delegates from nearly every nation make their way on Monday to Antalya, Turkey, for the United Nations climate talks, one question hangs over the event: Will it matter?

Soaring energy prices and artificial intelligence concerns have pushed climate change further into the background. The spirit of global cooperation that helped kick off landmark climate goals now seems of another era. The decision by President Trump to withdraw the United States from the Paris Agreement has created a leadership vacuum — and left nations fighting to a stalemate on issues where they’d once forged common ground.

Choi Hanchang, a lead negotiator from South Korea, said the main goals of this year’s conference were simply “survival and relevance.”

“It’s not about the negotiations itself,” Mr. Choi said. “We have to make some middle ground for the survival of multilateralism.”

More than a decade after the raucous celebration of the Paris accord, the international climate process is entering a lower-profile phase. The objectives of the conferences have narrowed. This year’s talks, to be held for 12 days along the Mediterranean coast, will draw only a handful of leaders from industrialized nations. No groundbreaking decisions are expected.

And yet, greenhouse gas emissions are at a record high. The planet is blowing past the limit that nations had set for global warming. Weeks of relentless heat this summer in Europe killed an estimated 50,000 people. A catastrophic glacier collapse in the Himalayas left thousands dead or missing and saddled Nepal with a $5 billion recovery bill. A record-size El Niño is stoking wildfires in Indonesia, lashing California’s shore and further raising global temperatures.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/scien.title: Did These Scientists Find Evidence of Blood in a Dinosaur Bone?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/scien.author: Stella Raine Chu
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/scien.text:
Mineralized “structures” discovered in the bone were the fossilized remains of red blood cells, according to a recent study. Other experts aren’t so sure.

Dinosaurs have always felt far removed from mankind, their presence known only from dusty bones and fossils, perhaps an ancient trail of footprints. Now, for the first time, researchers claim to have discovered traces of red blood cells in a 115-million-year-old bone from the species Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat eater from the early Cretaceous Period.

“We’re not suggesting that we have intact blood, like you would find in a vial,” said Kliti Grice, a geochemist at Curtin University in Perth, Australia, and the lead researcher of the study. It was published on Monday in the journal Proceedings of the ​National Academy of Sciences.

That is to say, the scientists haven’t found dried dinosaur blood but rather the chemical fingerprints of heme, the iron-rich molecule in hemoglobin, which is the protein that gives blood its deep-red color.

“The chemical signals associated with the original biology that have undergone complex fossilization and mineralization — that’s what we’re looking at,” Dr. Grice said.

Unlike bones and teeth, soft tissues like muscles and skin decay rapidly. Only in rare and specialized environmental conditions can they be preserved in fossils. Cells from bodily fluids are even more rare.

The news of the discovery has excited the paleontology community. But some are hesitant to celebrate.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/us/po.title: Rubio Warned Officials About Nvidia Chief’s Entanglement With Chinese Spy
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/us/po.author: Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan, Julian E. Barnes and Tripp Mickle
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/us/po.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The secretary of state’s role in drafting a secret memo highlights how top officials were concerned by this past spring about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence.

By Maggie HabermanJonathan SwanJulian E. Barnes and Tripp Mickle

The reporters have been covering China’s spying on Nvidia and America’s artificial intelligence industry.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the highly classified memo this past spring warning top Trump administration officials that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy, multiple people briefed on the matter said.

The document was based on classified intelligence from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen who was a senior executive at a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips and being investigated for illegally smuggling them into China. U.S. officials had concluded that Ms. Huang was in a close relationship with the Nvidia chief, who is no relation, and that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security.

Mr. Rubio’s involvement in warning administration officials about the situation has not been previously reported. It highlights how concerns about the relationship and the spying were known to senior officials even as Mr. Huang, a pivotal figure in the explosive growth of A.I., remained an influential voice with Mr. Trump over policy on the issue.

Mr. Huang has opposed calls for more tightly regulating the export of the most advanced A.I. chips and has pushed to be able to sell all but the most recently developed technology to China, the main competitor to the United States in the global rush for A.I. supremacy.

On Sunday, Nvidia said it was opening an investigation into Mr. Huang after he acknowledged that he had been intimate with Ms. Huang, though the company said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

In a message to the company, Mr. Huang apologized.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” he said. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/techn.title: Nvidia Opens Investigation Into Jensen Huang’s Relationship With Suspected Chinese Spy
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/techn.author: Tripp Mickle, Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan, Julian E. Barnes and Ana Swanson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Mr. Huang, the company’s chief executive, acknowledged on Sunday that he was intimate with a business executive who U.S. officials had determined was working for Chinese intelligence.

By Tripp MickleMaggie HabermanJonathan SwanJulian E. Barnes and Ana Swanson

The reporters have been covering China’s spying on Nvidia and America’s artificial intelligence industry.

Nvidia said on Sunday that it was opening an investigation into Jensen Huang, its chief executive and co-founder, after he acknowledged to the company’s board that he had been intimate with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy.

Mr. Huang’s relationship with the woman, who goes by Alice Huang, became a U.S. government concern after surveillance revealed that she was feeding information directly to Beijing. The revelation raised troubling possibilities because Mr. Huang is one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump.

In a message to the company, Mr. Huang apologized. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he said. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that “the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” It said Mr. Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.”

The independent board members will choose an outside counsel to investigate. John Rizzo, a company spokesman, said Mr. Huang wouldn’t be part of the selection process.

Mr. Huang, 63, will continue to lead the company during the investigation, the board said. As a co-founder, he has set up a unique structure at Nvidia where he dictates all aspects of its business while overseeing some 60 people who directly report to him.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/busin.title: Why the Iran War Has Spurred Both Clean Energy and Fossil Fuels
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/busin.author: Lisa Friedman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/busin.text:
The shock to global oil prices has caused a surge in demand for electric vehicles while propelling a race for immediate, secure power supplies.

Lisa Friedman reported from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia and London. She will cover the annual United Nations COP31 Climate Change Conference from Turkey this week, her 14th such assignment.

The war in Iran has been very good for renewable energy. More than 40 countries have started or accelerated projects involving wind, solar, electric and other low carbon technologies.

South Korea unveiled a plan to spend about $747 billion to develop at least 100 gigawatts of wind and solar power by 2030. Britain and the Philippines saw a massive surge in rooftop solar installations, Thailand introduced a plan for data centers to source at least 60 percent of electricity from clean energy, and Vietnam accelerated the deployment of battery storage systems. Across Europe, Australia and India, demand for electric vehicles surged.

But the pivot to clean energy is only part of the story. The disruption of a once reliable trade of oil and gas in the Middle East has caused much of the world to double down on fossil fuels in a desperate scramble for secure, and immediate, supplies.

Countries are using more coal, the dirtiest fossil fuel. Nations with oil and gas in abundance went to extraordinary lengths to export crude to their customers, investing to strengthen infrastructure and build new trade routes to outlast the current crisis. All along, governments tapped their budgets for billions of dollars used to shield consumers from higher energy costs, money that did nothing to dampen demand.

This week, diplomats from nearly 200 countries will gather in Antalya, Turkey, for the 31st annual round of United Nations climate change negotiations. Many participants will argue strenuously that the moment calls for nations to accelerate an end to the dependence on fossil fuels — the burning of which is the biggest driver of planet-warming greenhouse gases.

https://thehill.com/homenews/house/62057.title: This week on the Hill: Congress returns to leadership fights, shutdown deadline after GOP losses
https://thehill.com/homenews/house/62057.author: Sudiksha Kochi
https://thehill.com/homenews/house/62057.text:
Congress returns to Capitol Hill after the astonishing midterm elections that dealt Republicans major losses and left Democrats riding high. Now, Republicans face their next major test: a fight over who will lead the party in the House as it prepares its descent into the minority.

House Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections Nov. 10. Speaker Mike Johnson (La.) told lawmakers on a staff call last week that he will not run for minority leader, setting the stage for a potentially bruising contest between House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (Ohio).

Republican Whip Tom Emmer (Minn.) and GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain (Mich.) are both seeking to retain their leadership positions in the minority. But neither is guaranteed a smooth path, with both facing challengers from within the conference.

Johnson has more than a leadership transition to contend with during the final weeks of the congressional session.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) will reintroduce articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth this week, largely over his handling of the war in Iran. Several Republicans, including Vice President Vance, have pointed to the conflict as a reason for the party’s election losses, though they have stopped short of calling for Hegseth’s ouster.

Congress also faces a looming Dec. 11 government funding deadline. Lawmakers must either pass all 12 annual appropriations bills or pass another stopgap measure to avert a shutdown, adding another major legislative hurdle to an already compressed lame-duck session.

The Senate, meanwhile, is expected to hold a procedural vote Monday on advancing a bipartisan permitting reform package that would speed up the build-out of the nation’s infrastructure, especially energy projects.

Republicans have been divided over how to move forward as a conference, with some arguing that there needs to be a complete revamp of the leadership team.

“There has to be accountability for results, and you know the team that led us to the disaster probably isn’t the team that should lead us from the disaster,” one GOP lawmaker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill.

Jordan, co-founder of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, has emerged as a favorite among some House Republicans.

“I think we’re going into a wartime situation where we are going to be the rebel alliance, and we’re going to need someone who knows how to fight, and Jim Jordan knows how to do that,” the anonymous lawmaker said.

House Freedom Caucus Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) also threw his support behind Jordan, arguing Thursday on Newsmax that Jordan “is the type of communicator we need, communicating commonsense Republican conservative principles again, against the backdrop of what is going to be a DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] -dominated Senate and House Democrat majority.”

But other Republicans argue that Scalise is better positioned to take the top spot, given his current leadership role. Scalise initially won the Republican nomination to be Speaker in 2023, beating Jordan in a secret-ballot vote. But he withdrew from the race when it became clear he would not win enough support from his conference to get the votes needed on the House floor.

“Steve is the right guy for the job. Plain and simple. He’s a tried and tested leader, who has the experience to lead House Republicans for the next two years, and the chops to reclaim the majority in 2028,” a second GOP lawmaker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said.

Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (Texas) is challenging Emmer for the minority whip position, while GOP Reps. Greg Steube (Fla.) and Erin Houchin (Ind.) are going head-to-head against McClain for the Republican conference chair role.

Massie said on social platform X last week that he plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth unless the Defense secretary resigns. Most Democrats are expected to support the measure, but House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has stopped short of endorsing it.

Massie had previously launched an effort to impeach Hegseth back in September, but House GOP leaders canceled votes and sent lawmakers home early, avoiding a vote on Massie’s resolution. But only temporarily.

The Kentucky Republican argued then that Hegseth violated “his oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States” and violated “his constitutional duty to take care that the laws be faithfully executed, especially with regard to the commission of war.” He added that Hegseth has “abused the powers of the Department of Defense.”

President Trump told ABC News’s Jonathan Karl last week that he has “every intention” of keeping Hegseth in the Cabinet, following reports that he was weighing whether the Defense chief should stay in the post after the midterm elections.

Hegseth also fired back at Massie last week, saying in a video clip posted to X that “a disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly.”

“Just like they tried against President Trump twice. You see, their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

He’s probably right on that score. Even if the House does impeach Hegseth, the Senate is not likely to remove him from power.

Lawmakers have just two weeks to make progress on government funding before leaving again for Thanksgiving recess — an effort that will be challenged by a crowded legislative agenda that includes the annual National Defense Authorization Act, a farm bill and other priorities.

The House has passed three of the 12 appropriations bills, while Senate appropriators have remained deadlocked over top-line spending levels. The bills the House has passed so far — funding military construction and the Department of Veterans Affairs, the State Department, and agriculture and rural development — represent some of the lowest-hanging fruit.

Johnson is sure to face much tougher resistance — both from Democrats and within his party — when the topic shifts to funding other agencies, including the departments of Homeland Security, Defense, and Health and Human Services.

Democratic lawmakers told The Hill before the midterms that they are keen on getting the rest of the appropriations bills done. But with a short calendar and a contentious subject, the odds are stacked against them. Most observers think a short-term spending patch, known as a continuing resolution, or CR, is the most likely scenario.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee, told The Hill in a statement she doesn’t think anyone wants a shutdown, and one is not likely.

“Both Democrats and Republicans have expressed a desire to finish full-year funding bills before the end of this calendar year, and I am ready to do just that,” DeLauro said. “The American people want us to address the cost of living crisis and rein in this corrupt administration. With Democrats widely expected to be in the majority, we want to hit the ground running in the new year — not be forced to finish the work this Congress failed to complete.”

Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), a member of the House Appropriations Committee, said in a statement before the midterms that “whether or not there is a government shutdown is entirely up to Senate Democrats, who inflicted the longest government shutdown in U.S. history on the American people last year.”

“My priority remains passing the most conservative and fiscally responsible appropriations bills possible, and I look forward to completing that work when we return to Washington in the coming weeks,” he added.

The upper chamber is expected to hold a procedural vote Monday on a permitting reform bill, dubbed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

The legislation would make changes to the nation’s environmental laws that could make it easier to build projects and make it harder to block them, with either lawsuits or other legal mechanisms.

It also has provisions that are expected to make it easier to build and approve power lines, in particular, which is key to getting more power onto the grid. Democrats have pushed for such reforms, saying they believe they will particularly bolster renewable energy.

Trump has gone after renewable energy projects, and the bill contains measures that would protect those that are already approved. This bill could prevent Trump or other Republicans from trying to cancel renewable projects.

The bill is expected to advance, but it could receive some pushback from progressive Senate Democrats who have called for the administration to restore climate funding it terminated for blue states.

“While such action may not fully address the wide range of concerns individual Senators have about various portions of this complex legislation, it would represent an important first step and carry far more weight with us and, more importantly, our constituents whose awards were illegally terminated, than mere informal assurances that the Trump administration will stop interfering with clean energy projects,” the liberal senators wrote in a letter to Democratic and Republican negotiators of the bill.

Rachel Frazin contributed to this report.

White House deputy chief of staff Richard Walters is departing from his role in the wake of President Trump’s longtime adviser Stephen Miller being announced as the new chief of staff.

“Richard has been an invaluable member of the White House and has helped deliver some of the Administration’s biggest victories,” Miller said in a statement obtained by NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner.

“While he will be leaving us, Richard will continue to help from the outside as we continue to work with all of our strength to deliver for President Trump and his courageous fight to Save America,” he added.

Axios first reported on Walters’s exit.

Last week, Trump announced that chief of staff Susie Wiles was leaving the White House and Miller would take her place.

Miller’s promotion came after a rough Election Day for Republicans, with Democrats taking the House and Senate and winning in regions where they have historically struggled.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote Friday on Truth Social.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” he continued. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Spencer Leniu will have a delayed start to his next NRL season after being sanctioned over a gesture made towards the referees. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Samoa's Spencer Leniu has been suspended for two matches after making a money gesture at the referees in his side's loss to Australia in the Rugby League World Cup semifinal.

If Leniu contests the grade three contrary conduct charge and loses his appeal, he will incur an additional one-match suspension.

Leniu will miss Parramatta's first two games of the 2027 NRL season, including the team's game in Las Vegas.

Parramatta's marquee off-season recruit Spencer Leniu is poised to miss the first two games of the 2027 campaign — including the Eels' trip to Las Vegas — after being sin-binned in Samoa's World Cup semifinal loss to Australia.

Leniu was sin-binned by referee Adam Gee for dissent late in the first half of Sunday's 44-12 loss to the Kangaroos in Sydney.

The prop made a money gesture with his hand as he walked towards the tunnel, a sign that many interpreted as the Samoan forward questioning the integrity and impartiality of match officials.

Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semi-final was a reminder of Goliath's power.

Leniu was handed a grade three contrary conduct charge on Monday.

The 26-year-old, who will join Parramatta after winning the 2026 premiership with Sydney Roosters, will miss the club's opening two games of the season, which includes their trip to the US to face Gold Coast.

In the unlikely event he contests the charge, Leniu would incur an additional one-game ban if he were to lose his appeal.

The prop's outburst came during a frustrating night for Samoa, from which Samoan halves Ronald Volkman and Jarome Luai have avoided suspension for dangerous contact.

Samoa were on the wrong end of a 9-4 penalty count and coach Ben Gardiner suggested Gee had handed the Kangaroos several "home-ground calls".

"It was a real home-ground advantage for Australia," Gardiner said.

"They had the music pumping in the background and we had a lot of Samoan fans here to support us, which was brilliant.

"But they got the home-ground calls, got a really good start and then it was just too hard for us to chase back from there."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: How a digital bank’s collapse toppled Paraguay’s president
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
ASUNCION, PARAGUAY – For years, Paraguay’s digital bank, Ueno, stood out as a homegrown success story, luring roughly half the country’s people to open accounts and offering many the opportunity to hold a bank account for the very first time.

But over just five days last week, the bank collapsed, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers — in a country of 6.5 million people — and triggering the country’s deepest political crisis in more than a decade.

On Friday evening, Paraguayan President Santiago Pena was impeached after attempting to resign, and his vice president, Pedro Alliana, was sworn in as his replacement.

Authorities quickly arrested Pena, an economist and close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a military facility.

Pena has denied wrongdoing and his attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists that he is pleading not guilty to the charges.

The scandal has triggered public protests and sharp rebukes from the opposition.

“We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history,” said opposition Sen. Rafael Filizzola on Friday. “This impeachment is a first step toward ensuring justice is served.”

Manuel Ferreira, a Paraguayan economist and former finance minister, echoed much of the public anger over the case. “This was a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde,” he said. “They didn’t rob us with a pistol, they robbed us with an app. The head of the gang was the president of the republic.”

Until March 2025, Pena had been a business partner of the group that owns Ueno Bank. After his election in 2023, he tapped Ueno’s former president, Carlos Carvallo, to lead the central bank.

Carvallo resigned as central bank chief earlier last week. Prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain. They sought his pretrial detention, which was approved by a judge.

Carvallo did not respond to a request for comment. It was not immediately clear if he had entered a plea in the case.

Pena’s lawyer, Preda, objected to the impeachment, saying that ousting a president during a bank resolution could itself be destabilizing.

“What sets a serious country apart is not that its banks don’t fail, but how it responds,” Preda said on Friday. “If there is one thing that undermines confidence in the financial system, it is attempting to oust the president without evidence.”

Ueno was launched in 2021 as a sleek, millennial-friendly banking app that quickly won over Paraguayans who had been underserved by brick-and-mortar institutions.

It soon became deeply embedded in Paraguay’s payments system. It paired its digital offering with physical branches, later sponsoring sports teams, businesses and events. As of June, public institutions — including Paraguay’s state pension fund — held roughly $850 million in accounts with the bank.

But in recent months, internal regulatory reports warning of excessive lending to certain companies were leaked to local media outlets ABC and Ultima Hora, triggering political scrutiny of the bank’s lending practices.

Following growing public pressure, Paraguay’s central bank on Tuesday put Ueno into resolution — its strongest measure short of immediate liquidation — after determining that Ueno had breached minimum solvency requirements, locking millions of customers temporarily out of their accounts.

The central bank said on Saturday that the equivalent of $160 million had since been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the state deposit guarantee scheme.

Authorities have promised that depositors will be reimbursed and say the crisis is confined to Ueno. But analysts say the damage to Paraguay’s reputation as a stable investment destination in South America may linger far longer than the bank resolution itself.

“This is the moment when Paraguay must demonstrate that its institutions are functioning,” Ferreira said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Paraguay's digital bank, Ueno, collapsed last week, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers. President Santiago Pena was impeached after attempting to resign. He was charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.title: Fire in northern China high-rise building kills 14, injures dozens more
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.author: Phoebe Zhang
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.text:
The building in downtown Taiyuan, the capital of Shanxi province, contained flats, a hotel and children’s education centres

Fourteen people have been killed and dozens more hospitalised after a fire broke out in a high-rise building in northern China.

That night, 38 people were sent to hospital, including five people who had died. By Monday morning, the death toll had increased to 14, state news agency Xinhua reported.

“All-out efforts are being made to treat the injured, follow-up work is under way and the cause of the fire remains under investigation,” the district government said.

According to real-estate platform Lianjia, the building was a mixed-use residential and commercial block.

A member of staff at a hotel in the building told Jimu News on Sunday that he thought the fire started on the fifth floor and that some people were injured on the eighth floor. He helped firefighters search for survivors while some parts of the building were still on fire, he added.

Pictures from the Jimu News report show that besides hotels, the building also has restaurants and academic training centres for children.

The building is located in downtown Taiyuan, close to hospitals, schools, commercial centres and tourist sites.

https://www.dw.com/en/g7-ministers-meet-.title: G7 ministers meet as Europe seeks greater say in Ukraine peace talks
https://www.dw.com/en/g7-ministers-meet-.text:
With Washington preparing negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv, European leaders fear Ukraine could face pressure to accept a bad deal. Iran tensions and the threat of renewed US strikes are also on the agenda.

Foreign ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrialized nations are set to meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday for talks on how Europe can be part of US efforts to end Russia’s war on Ukraine and how to urge Washington to not resume military action against Iran.

The meeting will bring together leading diplomats from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.

It coincides with US-mediated talks between Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled to begin on Tuesday.

European governments are concerned the the US might be pushing Ukraine to a settlement favoring Russia. US President Donald Trump, in the run-up to the Abu Dhabi talks, said a "very big" deal was in the making, suggesting Ukraine could emerge from a settlement with altered ‌borders.

"I think we're gonna have it done, and I think it's ‌gonna happen ​and they're gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine," Trump told broadcaster CBS. The US president also said the deal would involve all of Europe.

About the talks in Abu Dhabi, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told RTL radio that "Europeans will be represented and France will participate in these talks."

European leaders have long insisted that any deal to end the war should include the continent's participation in the talks and that any settlement should not come at the expense of Ukraine's sovereignty.

When asked about the US plans for a possible agreement to end the war in Ukraine, Barrot said he did not know the details but stressed that no deal affecting the European security architecture could be done without the Europeans.

Particular attention at the upcoming meeting will be on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who will attend both days unlike the last G7 meeting where he came only for one.

Rubio suggested that recent discussions had made progress on security guarantees for Ukraine and the wider European region. Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner has also described US efforts to develop a broader European security framework.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has in the past expressed doubts over proposals for a new European security framework, suggesting that any such debates should follow, rather than precede, efforts to end the war.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The G7 ministers are also expected to discuss US tensions with Iran, as Trump has not ruled out additional military strikes against the country.

Washington has previously considered targeting suspected nuclear facilities, including the site known as Pickaxe Mountain, following the US midterm elections last week. Tehran denies that the location is a nuclear facility.

European governments are seeking a diplomatic resolution rather than a resumption of military action. Gobal attention is particularly on the restoration of normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for international energy supplies.

Trump recently said that Iranian officials were keen to reach an agreement, suggesting negotiations remained possible.

The Paris gathering is among the final major diplomatic events of France's G7 presidency. The United States is scheduled to assume the group's rotating presidency in 2027.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.title: Government's EV targets expected to be reduced this week
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.text:
The UK government's electric vehicle (EV) targets are expected to be reduced this week in a move likely to be welcomed by carmakers but opposed by environmental groups.

Under the current rules, 80% of new cars sold in the UK must be electric by 2030 but industry groups have long called for "urgent relief".

New petrol or diesel cars are due to be phased out by 2030 and by 2035 all new cars must be zero emission.

But the speed of the transition to electric has been hotly debated, including within the cabinet.

The government has been consulting on reducing its 80% rule and a significant reduction is now expected.

Downing Street has insisted no decision has been made.

A government source told the BBC it would approach the issue in a "pragmatic and balanced" way.

If ministers do decide on a steeper watering-down of the rules, it will arguably be interpreted by some - alongside the approval of the Jackdaw gas field - as Prime MInister Andy Burnham prioritising economic considerations over environmental ones.

Sustainability groups say any weakening of the 2030 target will threaten the UK's long-term electrification and climate goals.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/europe-f.title: From supermarket fridges to passenger flights, a wave of threats is testing Europe's defenses
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/europe-f.author: Chloe Taylor,Elsa Ohlen
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/europe-f.text:
Europe has faced a number of security threats this month, including cyberattacks on refrigeration systems at supermarkets and hoax bomb threats which disrupted dozens of passenger flights.

Experts told CNBC that such attacks can create economic damage, public anxiety and pressure on governments even without open military conflict.

Cyberattacks, bomb threats against passenger flights, civil unrest and suspected acts of sabotage across Europe have raised questions about the continent’s resilience — and how prepared it is to defend itself against modern security threats.

Hackers remotely manipulated refrigeration systems at supermarkets across Europe last week, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food and exposing vulnerabilities in everyday infrastructure.

French blood-bank refrigeration systems were subsequently targeted in what appeared to be a similar incident, while a wave of suspected hoax bomb threats disrupted dozens of flights across the continent, forcing diversions and, in some cases, fighter jet escorts.

The week culminated with bomb threats targeting European news outlets, including the U.K.’s Sky News and Irish public broadcaster RTÉ.

The incidents come against a backdrop of heightened geopolitical tensions and domestic unrest across parts of Europe, with civilian infrastructure potentially becoming an increasingly attractive target for hostile actors.

While authorities have not established who was behind the attacks or whether they were connected, defense and security experts warn that disruption to everyday services can have consequences far beyond the immediate economic damage.

If Russia were responsible, such attacks could be intended to demonstrate the costs of Europe’s continued support for Ukraine, said Sidharth Kaushal, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, or RUSI.

“I think it’s more about cost imposition,” Kaushal told CNBC. “Convincing the European political leadership that the costs of a war can come home to them.”

Russia didn’t immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.

On Monday, supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden and the Netherlands found that refrigeration systems had been set to as much as 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 degrees Fahrenheit, affecting retailers including Ahold Delhaize, IKEA, Colruyt Group and Carrefour.

It followed an October cyberattack that targeted hundreds of French supermarkets, causing fires, fridges to overheat and food to spoil. The incidents highlighted vulnerabilities in food-supply infrastructure.

They also highlight the role of private companies in national resilience, as internet-connected equipment can be exploited to cause physical disruption.

Fredrik Blix, cybersecurity expert at Visente and associate professor at Stockholm University, told CNBC that the supermarket attacks required very little technical sophistication since vulnerable refrigeration control systems were connected directly to the public internet, allowing potential attackers to find and exploit them.

“These attacks, they don’t really require any specific advanced knowledge to carry out,” he said, adding that some systems were protected only by default passwords or easily guessed credentials.

“This is why this is so cheap to do,” Blix said, warning that the publicity surrounding the incidents could encourage copycat attacks. “Anyone can do it, and it does not require any resources from a country or anything like that.”

Cyberattacks have become more common over the past decade as societies have become more digital and vulnerable systems have become easier to access, Blix said. However, he noted that mounting geopolitical tensions have also made European countries more alert to potential hybrid warfare threats, leading to scrutiny by both governments and media.

While Blix acknowledged the possibility of a state or state-backed actor being behind the attacks, he said the more likely scenario is someone testing the boundaries and “having some fun.”

Kaushal said the incidents should be viewed within the larger context of suspected sabotage and hybrid threats across Europe, including damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea.

“If this was an event in isolation, one might say ‘okay, we should view it on its own merits,’ but when you view it in the backdrop of all of that, it becomes less clear,” he said, also citing death threats against European defense executives and a bomb placed on a DHL aircraft in 2024.

European governments are contending with greater uncertainty over U.S. security guarantees after decades of underinvestment in defense, while facing a rise in unconventional but potentially devastating threats.

Hybrid warfare combines tactics such as cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation to destabilize adversaries without triggering open military conflict.

Countries’ abilities to withstand hybrid threats vary substantially across the continent, according to Kaushal. While Finland and Sweden have well-developed civilian defense programs reflecting their Cold War experience, much of Europe’s infrastructure was built around economic efficiency rather than defense needs.

“As one goes further west in Europe, the level of preparation, both against hybrid attacks, but also just simple missile attacks of the kind that we’ve seen in Ukraine, is far less great,” he said.

“Every attack generates a bit of resilience,” he said, citing NATO’s increased focus on threats to underwater cables and gas pipelines after the 2022 Nord Stream sabotage.

Oana Popescu-Zamfir, a senior research fellow specializing in European security at RUSI, said the recent incidents showed Europe had lagged in “preparing for something that we have known would be coming.”

“We’ve been slow in adjusting to a new reality,” she said. “We still tend to conceptually divide between peace and wartime, and that is no longer the case because we’re not at war, but we’re also not in peace time.”

She said Europe was likely to face sustained hybrid attacks designed to achieve military objectives without conventional military force.

Popescu-Zamfir said Russia could draw on networks of proxies in Europe, some directly controlled and others more loosely coordinated, making responsibility difficult to trace directly to the Kremlin.

She told CNBC that “the damage that can be done is huge” in targeted attacks on internet-connected systems, citing the potential disruption of blood reserves.

The attacks are not a “piece of cake for Russia to carry out, but they’re also not rocket science,” she said, adding that they “can do tremendous damage in concrete terms and in terms of the psychological impact on our societies and the feeling that we are unprotected.”

Blix said companies can take relatively straightforward steps to reduce their exposure.

“These are basic cyber hygiene things... You should not be allowed to connect industrial control systems and this kind of operational technology directly online without any proper security around it,” he said.

Responsibility is split among product manufacturers, maintenance providers and grocery chains, making accountability unclear as each points to the others.

Blix said maintenance companies sometimes prioritize convenience by enabling remote access despite manufacturers’ security guidance, while retailers may fail to enforce adequate cybersecurity standards among suppliers.

“What worries me is that we don’t really do anything,” Blix said, adding that “we are shuffling a lot of papers” and “doing a lot of risk assessments” but failing to take meaningful action.

Europe has also seen widespread unrest in recent months, adding political pressure as households grapple with high living costs.

Domestic political and economic tensions can also give foreign adversaries opportunities to deepen divisions, said Alexander Anderson, president and director of policy at the Centre for International Security and Economic Strategy.

He told CNBC that Russian and potentially Chinese influence operations may work to amplify those divisions.

“But we should be careful not to dismiss legitimate domestic grievances as the product of foreign interference,” he said. “Doing so risks misunderstanding both the causes of political instability and the methods through which hostile actors seek to exploit it.”

Weeks of nationwide protests, riots and strikes have increased pressure on the French government, complicating efforts to rein in public finances and deepening existing political divisions.

In Spain, demonstrations and a parliamentary impasse over the housing crisis led Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap election. The vote is scheduled for Nov. 29. The far-right Vox party is expected to make gains, putting Sanchez’s left-leaning government at risk of losing power.

Germany, Italy, Portugal and Albania have also seen unrest over rising living costs in recent weeks.

On Friday, protesters in Amsterdam tried to enter a Microsoft
 data center, Reuters reported.

Meanwhile, elevated energy prices, persistent inflation, sluggish growth and large budget deficits are pushing up borrowing costs and leaving governments with less room to support struggling households.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/europe-f.summary: Experts say such attacks can create economic damage, public anxiety and pressure on governments even without open military conflict. Russia could be responsible for attacks on internet-connected systems, says Blix.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/s.title: Looking for new fillings for sandwiches and wraps? We have you covered
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/s.author: Anna Chisholm
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Hetty Lui McKinnon says this vegetarian muffuletta is a diversion from the original, but no less satisfying. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

As we farewell soup and stew weather, we welcome perfect conditions for sandwiches and wraps.

These creative and versatile options could be served up at almost any time of day, and there's no need to spend hours babysitting a simmering pot.

In fact, most of these recipes involve minimal (if any) cooking time and many can be prepared (or partially prepared) ahead well before hunger strikes.

Have a batch ready to toast in a sandwich press as you need them, Lina Jebeile says. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

Lina Jebeile loves prepping these omelette breakfast sandwiches for suhoor (the pre-dawn meal during Ramadan) but says they are also a winner year-round.

Because they reheat beautifully in a sandwich press, they are a compelling contender for any busy mornings or office lunch.

Simple to make, easy to customise and perfect for prepping ahead.

Why confine this sanga strictly to mornings?

To make this layered roast vegetable sandwich vegan, simply omit the cheese. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon )

Hetty Lui McKinnon says this vegetable sandwich is perfect for picnics, but there's nothing stopping you from eating it inside too.

Inspired by one of America's iconic deli sandwiches, this vegetarian iteration of muffuletta uses roasted vegetables rather than cold cuts and the olive salad infuses every bite with a zesty punch.

This sandwich can also be made ahead. Just reach for some bread (focaccia or ciabatta recommended).

This recipe makes a chickpea filling for sandwiches or wraps, or for you to scoop up with crackers, Heidi Sze says. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

Use this nourishing smash from Heidi Sze as you see fit, but between two slices of your preferred bread is an obvious (and delicious) choice.

This smash filling takes just 10 minutes and relies on a tin of inexpensive chickpeas as a base.

You can also play around with different flavour combinations, depending on your preferences and what you have handy. Trade parsley for chives, gherkins for capers or mayonnaise for plain yoghurt.

Loi Nguyen's version of traditional banh mi, a dish influenced by both French and Vietnamese cuisines. (ABC TV: Steve Brown)

Influenced by both French and Vietnamese cuisines, this is Recipe of the Year contestant Loi Nguyen's take on a traditional crispy banh mi.

It uses thinly sliced marinated rump steak along with the classic combination of pickled carrots, mayonnaise and chilli sauce.

Marinating the chicken ahead of time takes the pressure off cooking at night. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

Store-bought flatbreads, herby chicken, crunchy vegetables and a garlicky sauce are combined into an easy and satisfying meal in this recipe from Heidi Sze.

If weather and energy levels allow you could cook the chicken element of this meal on the barbecue, or even make the flatbread yourself.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/l.title: Shark bite survivor Leah Stewart shows 'incredible' wound recovery
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Shark attack victim Leah Stewart has shown the extent of her leg wound. (Supplied: Instagram)

Leah Stewart says her leg wound has now healed and she is no longer at risk of infection.

The 35-year-old was attacked by a great white shark on June 13 at Coogee Beach in Sydney's east.

Ms Stewart underwent more than a dozen surgeries including the amputation of her left arm.

Almost five months after miraculously surviving a great white shark attack in Sydney's east, Leah Stewart says her leg wound has healed and she is no longer at risk of infection.

Ms Stewart was finishing up her swim at Coogee Beach on June 13 when she was mauled by a 4-metre-long great white shark.

The attack left her with multiple injuries and required more than a dozen operations, including the amputation of her left arm.

In an online update, Ms Stewart said the shark took a "chunk" of her leg and that doctors were unable to save her quad muscle and outer hamstring.

Leah Stewart shows the device that helped her wound heal. (Supplied: Instagram)

She said doctors used a surgical implement, DermaClose, to help gradually close the wound and despite not passing a skin graft her bite was finally able to scar.

"I am really proud of my own body and the amazing team at St Vincent's and I survived the great white, so I've got a cool scar to show for it," she said in the update.

Ms Stewart, who last week celebrated her 35th birthday, said recovering from her leg wound had "been a journey".

"But the fact of the matter is, I can use my legs and I don't have to wrap it up every time I have a shower or be worried about infection because now it is closed.

"So thank you for following along. I am just so happy this is the best update for me."

Ms Stewart also shared a video of her rescue on the day of the attack, showing lifesavers drag her to shore.

The teacher and mother from Coogee has spent months recovering from her injuries, being bitten across her arms and legs and suffering extreme blood loss.

Leah Stewart has now shown the full extent of her injuries. (Supplied: Stewart family)

She was placed in a medically induced coma for more than a week at St Vincent's Hospital.

In August she described in an interview the great white being only "30 centimetres" from her face.

"In my head, I was like, 'You ugly f***er, you are not taking me away from my daughter,'" she said.

"And I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again. Just punch, punch, punch.

"It was like fighting a dinosaur. It was so big. It was like punching a brick wall."

Last week Ms Stewart said she was undergoing EMDR therapy to help her "process the event" which left her unable to sleep and suffer daily nightmares.

Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing is a treatment where the patient is asked to recall a traumatic or emotionally distressing memory while using guided eye movements.

"It's been life-changing for me. I feel like I'm finally getting my life back," she said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/h.title: The 'personalisation' effect boosting some small businesses
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/h.author: Madeleine Rojahn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Mia Petterson said more people were shopping online and looking for second-hand or vintage goods. (ABC News)

Amid the uncertain future of a major department store and the predicted slowing of retail spending, the value of retail goods and services has grown in the ACT.

A marketing expert says the "personalisation" of the industry has been a major change impacting this new era of spending.

One Canberra business owner says developing a relationship with her customers was "the only way to survive".

When Mia Petterson was younger, her mum ran a retail store on Lonsdale Street in Braddon, in Canberra's inner north.

Fast forward to 2026, and Mia is following in her footsteps.

The 28-year-old curates vintage and second-hand items for her Blonde Concept store — which happens to be on the very same street her mum's was on.

Giving a personal touch to business is a priority for vintage and second-hand shop owner Mia Petterson. (ABC News)

"So the name, obviously not a huge amount of creativity involved in that, just got to be honest.

Since her mum's days working in the industry, Ms Petterson said retail had "100 per cent" changed, with buyers shifting towards secondhand and online purchasing.

Social media has become a huge part of the way people shop, too.

Dr Andrew Hughes, a marketing lecturer at the Australian National University, said businesses who use social and digital platforms to boost and maintain engagement were more likely to succeed.

"Nowadays [shopping] combines the social factor as well," Dr Hughes said.

Nationally, retail turnover is predicted to slow to 1.5 per cent next financial year, from 2.8 per cent, according to the latest quarterly forecast by Deloitte Access Economics.

But in the ACT, government data shows a near one per cent rise in the value of goods and services produced by the retail industry, indicating its increased value to the broader ACT economy.

Dr Hughes said retail results are often a "mixed bag", but successful businesses in the ACT that have managed to connect in multiple ways with their customers "are really a case study in how to do marketing well".

"They have good connection with their consumer base, they do good service provision and they're active on socials," he said.

Dr Andrew Hughes said the 'personalisation' of retail was impacting whether businesses sink or swim. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Ms Petterson said developing a relationship with her customers was "the only way to survive".

"I think one of my main priorities has always been creating a really comfortable, inviting environment for shoppers where they feel like they can try anything on, chat to me, like chat to the girls who work here, and I want people to leave feeling inspired," she said.

Mia Petterson followed after her own mum in running a retail store on Lonsdale Street, Braddon. (ABC News)

This personalised approach is something Dr Hughes believes will become a trademark of success in a new era of retail — and something that Australia's premier department store brand David Jones failed to adapt to.

"We're in a different environment," Dr Hughes said.

"People still spend, but the spending is linked in with experiences which are more personal to who they are.

David Jones's suppliers tell the ABC they could see "the writing on the wall" as payment times got longer and telephone calls went unanswered.

Dr Hughes said keeping up with younger markets was also key for retail businesses.

"For a lot of the younger markets, the most common thing I hear nowadays is, if I can't afford a [house], I'll spend some more money on retail," he said.

"Good for them, I get where they're at, you need some fun in life.

Retail success is a "mixed bag" in the nation's capital, according to one expert. (ABC News)

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Pressure still on Man United boss Carrick despite dramatic Villa draw
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Philip O'connor
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
MANCHESTER, ENGLAND – Manchester United manager Michael Carrick is facing another international window filled with uncertainty after his side slipped into the Premier League relegation zone despite a sensational comeback to claim a 4-4 home draw with Aston Villa.

United is 18th on eight points after 10 games, one behind Coventry City, and for long periods of Sunday’s game looked like a disjointed, rudderless side, with collapses in concentration at the start of each half proving costly for Carrick’s men.

Alysson opened the scoring for Villa after two minutes and Nicolas Jackson added a second two minutes later, but United looked to be motoring when Bruno Fernandes pulled one back with a penalty and Youri Tielemans levelled just before the break.

United again conceded twice in quick succession at the start of the second half to goals from John McGinn and Leon Goretzka but Joshua Zirkzee threw them a lifeline in stoppage time and Patrick Dorgu headed the equalizer in the 96th minute.

“I don’t feel happy,” Dorgu said, despite his late heroics. “We are in a bad situation. We need to fight together to get out of it. Draw better than a loss, but we had the better opportunities.

“Everyone needs to look at themselves and ask if they are doing enough. We need to fight for the manager, for the club and get out of this together ... we need everyone to come back sharp from the international break and start getting wins.”

After the final whistle, Carrick said he thought his side had done enough to win but individual errors had cost them.

“I thought we were the better team for a large part of the game. We’re making it difficult for ourselves with the goals that we’re giving away, and not just giving away one — it’s kind of two in succession that put us in such a difficult position,” he told Sky Sports.

“Then (we) came back into the game and had a lot of the game, and then could have won it in the end, so disappointed that we haven’t won again.”

United fans unfurled banners calling for a change of ownership and booed and whistled some players as they were replaced, but the supporters celebrated with abandon when their side snatched a point at the death.

“They are desperate to get behind us and for us to give them something to go on, they’ve showed that there’s frustration and disappointment at times, I think we all feel that, but they’re right behind the boys,” Carrick said.

“They were (there) right till the end today, and they were after the final whistle as well.”

Asked about his own future after another underwhelming display, Carrick remained tight-lipped.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on things that we’ve been working on and showing a lot of the good (we showed) in the game today, tighten up on a few mistakes and win football matches,” he said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.summary: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick is facing another international window filled with uncertainty. United are 18th in the Premier League after a 4-4 home draw with Aston Villa. The Red Devils are one behind Coventry City and one behind Manchester City.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Private high schools remain out of reach for many despite tuition-free policy, survey finds
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Tuition-free private high school education began in April, but families still face a heavy financial burden from expenses other than tuition, including admission fees and other school charges.

Nearly 30% of students from financially struggling households said they could not consider private high schools as an option when choosing where to study, according to a survey by international nonprofit organization Save the Children Japan.

The survey was conducted online in May and June among households participating in a child benefit program run by the Tokyo-based organization. It received 550 valid responses, including 125 first-year junior high school and high school students from across Japan and 425 parents.

Asked how the high school tuition-free policy had affected their choice of school, 27% of first-year senior high school students responded they had been unable to consider private schools as an option because they thought they would face expenses other than tuition.

Meanwhile, half of the parents whose children attend private high schools cited as a major concern when enrolling them the possibility that their children might have to leave school for financial reasons.

The survey showed that the average school fees, including facility maintenance and air-conditioning charges incurred when entering a private high school was ¥147,526 ($932), more than double the figure recorded a year earlier.

Admission fees averaged ¥173,135, about 1.2 times the previous year’s level. Expenses for uniforms, sportswear and commuter passes also increased.

More than 60% of parents and junior high school and high school students said they wanted computers and tablet devices, which are expensive for families to purchase, to be provided as school-owned equipment.

Subsidies or grants for purchasing such devices were available to 54.7% of students at public schools, compared with just 7% at private schools. Families whose children attend private high schools spent the average of about ¥100,000 for the purchase.

“Rising prices and the resulting financial strain are affecting children’s right to education, particularly those from economically disadvantaged households,” said Mitsue Tashiro of the organization.

Yuji Shirakawa, a professor specializing in sociology of education at Chiba University who helped with the survey, said, “Schools need to reconsider their practices regarding admission fees and other charges, and take measures such as providing learning materials as school-owned supplies and promoting the transfer of used items from graduating students to incoming students.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Nearly 30% of students from financially struggling households said they could not consider private high schools as an option. The survey was conducted online in May and June among households participating in a child benefit program. The average school fees, including facility maintenance and air-conditioning charges, were more than double the figure recorded a year earlier.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: COP31 to open in Turkey, with climate goals under pressure from war and AI
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
ANTALYA, TURKEY – Representatives from nearly 200 countries will gather on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast on Monday for two weeks of climate talks, as war-driven energy security fears, surging artificial intelligence power demand and U.S. disengagement put new pressure on the fight against global warming.

The U.S. war with Iran has nations scrambling for oil cargoes and firing up coal plants; the rapid rollout of AI is pumping up power demand; and the world’s top historic greenhouse gas emitter is shunning climate cooperation for the second year running.

All that has created a challenging backdrop destined to complicate efforts by COP31 host Turkey to land a strong deal, according to observers.

“It’s hard to be optimistic,” said John Holdren, a professor of environmental policy at Harvard University.

Turkey’s COP31 presidency has centered this year’s U.N.-sponsored summit on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. It is asking nations to sign onto a pledge supporting that target.

Theoretically, such a goal could help reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cookstoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment.

But climate advocates have criticized the pledge because it does not require that the additional electricity come from low-carbon sources. This has set up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.

A coalition of countries, including South Pacific island nations most vulnerable to sea level rise, are pushing more generally for a clearer global roadmap away from fossil fuels — a perennially controversial topic at climate summits.

Many oil- and gas-producing nations, including Saudi Arabia, argue that fossil fuels can still form a substantial part of the global energy mix in a climate-friendly world, provided they are paired with technologies that reduce or capture emissions.

Pressure is mounting for faster action on climate change.

A report by the United Nations Environment Program published in October said the world is already set to overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming above preindustrial times, the threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit.

2026 also stood out with a series of extreme heat waves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that caused a catastrophic flood that killed more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing.

“This year has proven to be one of the years with the highest casualties by the climate-induced disasters,” said Manjeet Dal, an adviser to the Least Developed Country bloc and south Asia director of Climate Analytics.

The Iran war has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels, as has Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the ensuing sanctions on Moscow’s energy exports. Some say disruptions from the wars have also clarified the benefits of turning to renewables.

The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting fuel prices around the globe and leading governments to scramble for new supplies.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has encouraged policies maximizing oil, gas, and coal production to address the Mideast disruptions. South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations, meanwhile, have increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.

“A lot of people who previously might have been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case,” said Holdren of Harvard.

At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean tech from China, cheering advocates for ambitious climate action.

“The war has strengthened the case for accelerating the energy transition. The United States is something of an outlier in this regard,” said Andre Correa do Lago, a Brazilian diplomat who presided over last year’s COP.

AI has also added a wrinkle. The technology’s rapid rollout is driving a surge in global power demand, contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions. But its benefits are proving irresistible, even to climate and environment activist groups.

COP31 host Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions at the conference to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.

Business advocates said they want just one thing from COP31: clarity.

“Delivery cannot remain a slogan or be left to voluntary initiatives,” said John Denton, the secretary general of the International Chamber of Commerce. “COP31 must send clear policy signals that give businesses the confidence to invest in electrification and the wider energy transition — and turn adaptation needs into bankable projects.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.summary: U.S. war with Iran has nations scrambling for oil cargoes and firing up coal plants. The rapid rollout of AI is pumping up power demand, and the world’s top greenhouse gas emitter is shunning climate cooperation for the second year running.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Poland mourns victims of Krakow shooting amid security fears
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
KRAKOW – Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday after a gunman killed six people in Krakow’s historic main square, an attack the government said may have been inspired by far-right ideology.

Saturday’s shooting shocked a country that had prided itself on being safer than many of its Western European neighbors, and deepened public concern about extreme views following school stabbings in October that officials have linked to inflammatory content online.

Nationalist opposition politicians, however, questioned the grounds on which the government said far-right ideology could have led to the shooting that left 16 people wounded in addition to those killed.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Poland's government says attack may have been inspired by far-right ideology. Six people killed in Krakow's main square, including 16 people wounded.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Alcaraz downs Shelton to win Paris Masters for first time
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Neil Fulton
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
PARIS – Carlos Alcaraz gained a measure of revenge on Ben Shelton on Sunday as the seven-time Grand Slam champion beat the American 7-6 (7-5), 7-5 to win the Paris Masters for the first time.

In defeating the man who ended his U.S. Open title defense earlier this season, the 23-year-old claimed the ninth 1000-level title of his career.

Unlike their five-set quarterfinal epic in New York two months ago, the clash in Paris lasted just under two hours.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Norris wins in wet Brazil as Mercedes takes constructors’ title
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Gabriel Araujo
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
SAO PAULO – Mercedes secured its ninth Formula One constructors’ world championship and completed a title double on Sunday in a wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix won by McLaren’s Lando Norris from pole position for the second year in a row.

The title was Mercedes’ first team crown since 2021 and came a week after 20-year-old Italian Kimi Antonelli made headlines as the youngest drivers’ champion with four races to spare in Mexico City.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen finished second, putting on a masterclass from 21st on the grid due to engine penalties, in a race that started and ended in the rain.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Gauff outruns Pegula to win thriller at WTA Finals, Noskova beats Kostyuk
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Amy Tennery
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Coco Gauff shredded her shoes but stayed one step ahead of Jessica Pegula to defeat her compatriot 6-4, 6-7 (7-5), 6-2 on the first day of the WTA Finals at Indian Wells on Sunday, while Czech Linda Noskova got the better of Marta Kostyuk 6-2, 6-4.

Gauff had beaten Pegula three months ago in Cincinnati and had the right formula once again, as the 2024 winner showed superb versatility in a round-robin clash between the top two Americans in the season-ending championship.

The frequent rivals were 5-5 in their head-to-head record before Sunday and appeared perfectly matched through a tight opening set, where Gauff got the break from the baseline on the fourth set point.
