https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5y.summary: Raging rooms offer women a rare opportunity to express their emotions that are often suppressed. Many visitors are seeking an emotional release during some of the most difficult periods of their lives. The Rabbit Hole Rage Room in Swindon, Swindons, says 70% of customers are women.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79.title: James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79.text:
When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"

Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.

Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.

"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."

Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.

After years of speculation, the wheels are firmly in motion and we expect to hear who the new James Bond actor is in November or December.

Speaking in August, producer Amy Pascal told Deadline: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet. We are being really, really methodical."

The final screen tests reportedly took place in late October, so, unless something unexpected happens, it should not take much longer for producers to make their decision and the actor to sign the contract.

After that, it's just a matter of how the announcement will be made. In an earlier era, Bond actors were revealed with a traditional photo call or press conference.

But now that the franchise is owned by Amazon MGM, some expect the company to make the announcement via its own Prime Video streaming service.

A handful of actors are thought to have made it to the final screen tests to take on Britain's biggest film role. The three frontrunners are thought to be:

Other actors in the frame include:

But remember, Craig was a surprise choice in 2005, so don't bet against a wildcard candidate whose name has not yet been widely reported.

The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. No exact dates have been announced.

Film schedules can be notoriously fluid, but it's clear that development is well under way, with the director and writer already in place.

It will be the 26th film in the official film series, but the title has not yet been confirmed.

The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."

He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."

Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight, known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.

Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.

He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.

"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."

Only six actors have played James Bond. They are:

You might have noticed some overlap in the above dates.

That's because Connery returned to the lead role for 1971's Diamonds Are Forever, after Lazenby took his place for 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

Connery also later appeared in 1983's Never Say Never Again, a Bond film produced by a different studio and not part of the official film series.

If you discount the films not in the official series, there have been 25 Bond films in total. In order, they are:

With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.

It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.

Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Fleming's original character and books.

Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, fans are hoping that Christmas could be about to come early this year, as the world awaits the imminent announcement of the next actor to play 007.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79.summary: The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwzr.title: Maya Jama steps down as host of reality TV show Love Island
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwzr.text:
Presenter Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of reality TV show Love Island after three years.

The 32-year-old wrote on Instagram alongside a highlights reel of her on the programme that it was "time to throw myself into something new".

"While my own Love Island journey has come to an end, I wish the show and the team all the success in the world, I'll be cheering you lot on from the sidelines forever," the TV and radio presenter said.

Jama's announcement comes hot on the heels of an appearance as a contestant on Celebrity Traitors that won her praise and speculation in the Times that she could "get £1m per deal" thanks to her success.

Thanking fans and the production team on Love Island, she said she had an "unforgettable time" on the programme.

"I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the nine incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way. I've loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show.

But she added: "I've always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then."

Jama landed her biggest presenting role to date as the host of the reality TV show in 2023, taking over from Laura Whitmore.

The programme couples contestants together who then complete a range of tasks and keep swapping in the hope of meeting the love of their life.

An ITV spokesperson said: "Maya has been a fantastic and much loved host on Love Island - we thank her for everything she has brought to the show over the last three years and wish her every continued success."

Love Island is one of the most popular reality TV shows in the UK but the series has polarised viewers, with some arguing the show is misogynistic and raising concerns about the welfare of contestants.

Ofcom has previously received tens of thousands of complaints about Love Island including about alleged misogynistic and bullying behaviour by some contestants.

The watchdog has previously described the show as "emotionally charged" with "confrontational scenes" that can upset some viewers.

Jama first built her profile through radio including a role on Rinse FM, before landing a presenting role on BBC Radio 1 in 2018.

She went on to present a string of television programmes, including Channel 4's Stand Up To Cancer and ITV2's Don't Hate the Playaz, before taking over as host of BBC Three's Glow Up: Britain's Next Make-Up Star in 2021.

The presenter was recently watched by millions in the Celebrity Traitors final, and competed as a traitor alongside actor Richard E Grant, Youtuber King Kenny and comedian James Acaster during the series.

One commentator at the time said that, despite not winning the show, she had emerged as a winner of sorts as she was able to portray herself as "less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star".

Her Celebrity Traitors appearance came after she made her acting debut in the second series of Guy Ritchie's Netflix drama The Gentlemen alongside Theo James and Kaya Scodelario.

Jama had auditioned for the cult Channel 4 series Skins, set in her hometown of Bristol, when she was 15, reaching the final stage for a role in the show that launched the careers of actors Daniel Kaluuya and Dev Patel.

She moved to London when she was 16 to pursue a career in the entertainment industry.

She began presenting a weekly music video countdown for production company JumpOff TV before joining MTV in 2014 as a presenter on The Wrap Up.

Jama became the youngest person to host the MOBO Awards, alongside Marvin Humes, in 2017.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwzr.summary: Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of Love Island. The 32-year-old said it was "time to throw myself into something new" She said she had an "unforgettable time" on the show. The TV and radio presenter said she would be cheering on from the sidelines forever.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn9.title: 'Time is up': Minister warns media industry to take abuse seriously in wake of Brand case
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn9.text:
Abuse in the media industry is probably still happening as organisations are not doing enough to protect women, the culture secretary has warned in the wake of Russell Brand's conviction.

Lisa Nandy told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme: "Time is up, it really is time for the media industry to take this seriously."

She added that since entering government, "many people" from within the industry had reached out to her "to allege that things have happened to them".

Brand is due to be sentenced on Monday after being convicted last week of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following allegations from multiple women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.

Nandy was asked whether she believed there was still exploitation and abuse within the media industry, following the Brand trial and cancellation of Channel 4 reality show Married at First Sight after the BBC revealed rape allegations.

She said: "I do not see that much has changed in terms of the way that institutions in the media industry and across public life, including politics, deal with women who very bravely come forward to allege abuse."

Nandy added that there was often no protection and a "very heavy cost" for women who speak up in industries such as media and politics, pointing to power imbalances and short-term contracts some staff members are given.

"Hand on heart, I can't say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is," she said.

Nandy said many had come forward from within the industry, including from the BBC.

But she added that the BBC had been an "exemplar" in signing up to the industry body to protect whistleblowers - the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority - and urged other organisations to follow suit.

A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster "has made a significant commitment to improve its culture, processes and standards".

"Last year, following an independent culture review, we set out the behavioural expectations for everyone who works with or for the BBC and we were clear action would be taken if these were not met," the spokesperson added.

Starting his career as a stand-up comedian, Brand became a household name as a host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth. He also had his own radio programmes on BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

During Brand's trial, he faced allegations from six women and was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. The women revealed how Brand used his fame to force them into sexual activity.

Following his conviction, a BBC spokesperson said there could be "no place for the abuse of power", adding: "Across the industry we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else's hand feels able to report it, that their concerns are taken seriously and that they are listened to."

The corporation restated its apology to staff who felt they could not speak up with concerns about Brand's behaviour when he worked at the BBC between 2006 and 2008, because he was seen as "too influential".

Channel 4, which aired Big Brother and its spin-off programmes at the time Brand was a presenter, said it recognised the "profound impact of these crimes".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn9.summary: Lisa Nandy says it is time for the media industry to take abuse seriously. She says many people have reached out to her to allege things have happened to them. Nandy said there was often no protection and a "very heavy cost" for women who speak up in industries such as media and politics.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Kraków shooting suspect who killed six has died, say police in Poland
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Terrorism investigation was opened after a 24-year-old opened fire in a market square on the weekend

A gunman suspected of killing six people in a popular market square in Kraków has died in hospital, Polish police said early on Monday.

The suspect, a 24-year-old named in local media as Michal O who authorities say was probably inspired by far-right ideologies, had been wounded in a shootout with police and had been in critical condition in hospital.

“We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” Malopolska Policja wrote on X.

Polish prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man opened fire on Saturday afternoon, killing six including a Briton and injuring 17, in an attack that shocked a country that was considered safer than many of its European neighbours.

Karolina Galecka, an ⁠interior ministry spokeswoman, told radio TOK FM ​on ​Monday: “There ​were many different emblems on the perpetrator’s clothing that have been partially examined and interpreted.

“These patches were ​associated with various motifs that ​are currently ‌being analysed ​by ​specialists,” she added, declining to comment further as the investigation was ongoing.

Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

Five of the wounded are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police ⁠officers were also among the injured, one of whom was in a serious condition.

As two days of national mourning began, the national prosecutor’s office said on social media it had launched an investigation into “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

The rare mass shooting has deepened concern about extremism in Poland after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.

The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

The Kraków suspect drove into the city’s main square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, at top speed at about 3pm on Saturday. Wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, he started shooting at random as he took what the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło described as a “wild ride” around the square.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Suspect, 24, named in local media as Michal O, had been wounded in a shootout with police. He had been in critical condition in hospital after the attack on Saturday. Polish prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man opened fire on Saturday afternoon.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Why we disrupted Annalena Baerbock’s award speech
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Ninian McGowan,Mohammad Haydar
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
When, in late August, the Dag Hammarskjold Foundation announced that former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock was its 2026 medallist, we were stunned. The cognitive dissonance was striking, even if we had become used to this after years of unabashed hypocrisy within the world’s most powerful institutions.

According to the foundation’s homepage, the medal is given to a person who “contributes to a more just, peaceful and environmentally sustainable world through valuable achievements in politics or research”.

As this year’s medallist, Baerbock was invited to visit Uppsala University and deliver a lecture. Here was an event claiming to celebrate “compassion, humanism and commitment to international solidarity” while honouring the foreign minister of a government that approved 94 million euros ($102m) in arms exports to Israel in the span of three months in 2024.

The motivation provided for Baerbock’s selection as the 2026 Dag Hammarskjold medallist sounded like satire to us. She is described as a “strong proponent of a rules-based international order” even though her actions illustrate perfectly how she is the opposite of that.

As soon as Uppsala University started promoting the ceremony on campus, we decided to plan a protest. Baerbock needed to know that she was not welcome, that the university’s stance did not reflect the position of its students.

We entered the event split into groups and interrupted Baerbock’s seminar four times. She was increasingly frustrated with each interruption. She tried to respond to the argument of the first group with an incoherent ramble about an alleged misfired Palestinian rocket. But we were not arguing over a single rocket; we were criticising her unapologetic support for horrific violations of international law.

As foreign minister, Baerbock repeatedly expressed her strong support for the state of Israel as an occupying power, declaring that Israel’s security also is “in the interest of the German state”. As Germany’s foreign minister, she called it her responsibility to always defend Israel’s “security” – something she deemed “non-negotiable for Germany”.

She had no reservations about upholding Israeli claims that it had the right to target schools, hospitals and other civilian establishments because the alleged presence of resistance forces removed their protected status.

Baerbock has held these positions despite the International Court of Justice indicating provisional measures against Israel with the intention to encourage the international community to take action against the genocide in Gaza and despite the International Criminal Court issuing an arrest warrant for Israeli leaders on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Instead, Baerbock chose to fuel the fire.

For all of these efforts, she was “rewarded” with the position of president of the United Nations General Assembly. Even in that role – in the heart of the institution that is supposed to uphold international law – she refused to call what is happening in Gaza a genocide. This is despite multiple reports, including by UN experts, that this is exactly what the mass killing is.

That Uppsala University co-organised Baerbock’s lecture is not surprising. The university continues to refuse to implement even the most modest of measures against an occupying power that openly commits genocide.

In 2022, the university administration showed no hesitation in ending collaboration with Russian institutions after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Three years into the genocide in Gaza and the intensified ethnic cleansing of the occupied West Bank, it has taken no such action against Israeli institutions, despite repeated demands from students and faculty.

Yet we are grateful for this perfect opportunity to demonstrate why radical resistance is necessary. For many years, protests against the genocide in Palestine have obeyed the rules defined by those in power, without any effect. Palestinians have been killed while places of higher education refuse to take responsibility and diplomats utter nothing but hollow words.

If they will not listen to voices within their regulated framework, we see no choice but to disrupt their everyday efforts to hide their complicity.

We are criticised for our methods because they are “too much”. But for us, genocide is too much. Disagreeing politely and hearing out those who sell bombs to genocidal armies is what has brought us to this point of deadly inaction.

The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: Annalena Baerbock was invited to visit Uppsala University to deliver a lecture. The university co-organised the lecture and was not welcome, says Al Jazeera. Baerbocks has held these positions despite the International Court of Justice indicating provisional measures against Israel

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: What is next for Israel?
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Ilan Pappe
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
There are two ways to read the results of the Israeli elections. One way would be to see them as a defeat for the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. From holding a solid majority in the 120-member Knesset, the Netanyahu bloc has been reduced to a minority of 53 members. Anti-Netanyahu lawmakers, by contrast, hold 67 seats.

Had Israel been a democracy, we would have seen scenes of celebration similar to the ones we saw this year in Hungary, Brazil and Serbia, where political forces with undemocratic tendencies were defeated. But Israel is not a democracy, and Netanyahu was not necessarily defeated.

The second, more relevant way of reading the results of the Israeli election would necessitate accepting the apartheid nature of Israel and seeing the electoral arithmetic through that prism. In this case, Netanyahu won because he secured 53 seats in the Knesset – five more than the anti-Netanyahu Jewish bloc.

To form a government, a bloc needs to have the support of at least 61 members of the Knesset. The only way Netanyahu can do it is by enticing parties or lawmakers from the anti-Netanyahu bloc to join his bloc, as he has succeeded in doing many times in the past. Working with Palestinian parties, which secured 19 seats, is out of the question for him.

The obvious path for government formation for the anti-Netanyahu bloc would be to form a coalition – one that would include the two Palestinian parties. But to do so would mean to challenge Israeli apartheid. The main leaders of the Jewish anti-Netanyahu bloc, including Gadi Eisenkot, have promised not to do so under any circumstances.

There is another option: seeking the support of the religious Orthodox parties, which have so far been part of the Netanyahu bloc. To secure their backing, the anti-Netanyahu bloc would have to promise to exempt religious Orthodox youth from military service and guarantee funding for their learning centres.

However, Eisenkot’s main election promise was forcing young Haredi Jews into the army. So this is not a very likely scenario, but in politics, never say never.

There is also the option of a “unity government” led by some sort of rotation between the leading figures of the anti-Netanyahu bloc and Netanyahu. The problem here is that, according to a law passed a few years ago, as long as Netanyahu is still a defendant in an ongoing trial, he cannot serve as a minister; his coalition made sure that the legislation ridiculously would not apply to a prime minister.

Given that Netanyahu’s corruption trial is destined to go on for a very long time, the rotation would make it impossible for Netanyahu to be part of a government under Eisenkot as prime minister. That means he would demand to hold the rotating premiership first and leave open the option to collapse the government once his rotation is over.

Netanyahu has already done that before. In 2020, without any hesitation, he broke a rotation agreement with Benny Gantz, who had naively believed that after two years he would be the prime minister. This resulted in new elections, which Netanyahu won.

Finally, a very possible scenario is that neither of the two blocs would be able to form a government, which would mean new elections in six months. Netanyahu and his government would remain in office until the new polls, albeit with more limited authority.

This would give them the opportunity to reignite a war with Iran and Hezbollah and continue with their violent policies in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank in an attempt to attract more public support and win the elections.

This is the preferred option for Netanyahu because his relative defeat in the October 27 elections had a lot to do with the unprecedented galvanisation among the Palestinian voters in Israel and the more liberal Jewish Israelis living abroad who came back home in huge numbers to vote.

These possible scenarios tell only part of the story and are not enough to fully understand what the election results mean for Israel, the Palestinians and the region. Here are the more important conclusions one should draw from the results:

The first pertains to the future of the Palestinian citizens of Israel. They still could turn out to vote in large numbers if new elections are held soon. But if they are once more ignored and sidelined by the other political parties, they will never try it again.

In this case, it would be difficult for the leadership of this community to continue to delay a strategic decision: choosing which political space Palestinian citizens of Israel belong to – the Israeli or the Palestinian one?

Until today, they have given a chance to the Israeli political system despite its racism, apartheid tendencies and criminal policies towards Palestinians. Palestinian parties recommended Eisenkot for the premiership to President Isaac Herzog, who has now tasked him with forming a government.

If I can venture a prediction – and it is only a prediction – the anti-Netanyahu bloc would not engage meaningfully with the Palestinian parties. Its message, therefore, will be that the Palestinians of Israel are not legitimate players in the Israeli political field.

If I am wrong, this would be an incredible and transformative moment in the history of both Israel and Palestine, but there seems to be very little hope for such a development.

There are other lessons we can learn from where we are now with the knowledge that this is a very volatile moment in the history of Israel.

The first and most important one is that whoever forms the next government of Israel will continue the incremental genocide in Gaza, the intensified ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and the aggressive policies towards the region. These policies as before can only be stopped or tamed by the region and the international community sending a clear message to Israel that there will be a price tag attached to such policies.

The second lesson is that the Israeli Jewish society is as deeply divided as ever, to the point that it is impossible for it to maintain a stable political system, a thriving economy and a positive strategy towards the region and the world.

The third lesson is that Israel’s international isolation will increase as a result of this trajectory, including the continued dissociation from Zionism among young Jews around the world, including in the United States.

Finally and most importantly, this can have an impact on the global discussion about Zionism. The move by the Green Party in Britain to define Zionism as racism – despite being currently an exception and widely condemned – will gain validity with time.

These elections and future developments are making clear that Zionism in the current Israeli politics means the exclusion of Palestinian citizens of Israel from politics – first by ignoring them and quite possibly in the future by denying them the right to vote

Moreover, many in the international community will associate the term Zionism with a consensual Israeli policy of genocide, ethnic cleansing and apartheid.

The outlook in the short term is worrying. The overall message from the Israeli elections is that the future policies of the state will continue to threaten the lives of the Palestinians in occupied territory, Palestinian citizens of Israel, and the people of southern Lebanon and Syria. There will be more instability in the region.

In the long run, however, as bad as it is, the fundamental cracks in the Zionist project will widen, which might lead to its demise. One can only hope this will also lead to the beginning of a political reality that would benefit everyone who lives in historical Palestine and the region.

A version of this oped was first published by Al Jazeera Arabic.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: Israel's international isolation will increase as a result of the continued dissociation from Zionism among young Jews around the world. Israel's isolation will be increased as a consequence of the continuing dissociation with young Jews.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: How Israel’s separation wall compares with the Berlin Wall
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Mohamed Hussein
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
In the occupied West Bank, a barrier of concrete and fencing cuts Palestinians off from their land, their families and nearby towns.

Israel began building its separation wall in 2002. Planned to stretch 712km (442 miles), it runs deep inside Palestinian territory rather than along the boundary with Israel. In 2004, the International Court of Justice ruled it illegal.

Today’s date carries extra weight. Thirty-seven years ago on November 9, 1989, the Berlin Wall fell.

Built by East Germany in 1961 to stop its citizens fleeing to the West, it encircled West Berlin for 155km (96 miles), dividing the city and its people for 28 years.

Since 2003, Palestinians have marked the same date as an international day of action against Israel’s wall, which is more than four times as long and still being built. In urban areas, its concrete rises to about 9 metres (30ft), more than twice the height of Berlin’s.

But the wall is more than a physical structure. It operates alongside a wider network of checkpoints, roadblocks, gates and permits that restricts Palestinian movement across the occupied territory.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 456km (283 miles), or 64 percent, of the planned route had been built by April.

About 85 percent of it runs inside the West Bank rather than along the Green Line, the 1949 armistice line separating Israel from the West Bank. That route determines which communities, roads and farmland are cut off from their surroundings.

In some urban areas, the barrier is a concrete wall. Elsewhere, it is made up of fences, patrol roads, ditches and other security infrastructure.

For Palestinians, the comparison with Berlin carries a message. “It doesn’t matter how high the barriers will be, they will fall,” a Palestinian activist in Bir Nabala told Al Jazeera. “Like the Berlin Wall fell, the Palestinian wall will fall.”

The wall’s impact reaches far beyond the structure itself. Its route cuts Palestinian communities off from neighbouring towns, workplaces and farmland, disrupting livelihoods and everyday life.

More than 14,000 Palestinians live between the wall and the Green Line in an area known as the Seam Zone. To reach basic services, markets and relatives on the other side, they must pass through checkpoints.

Farmers are among the hardest hit. According to OCHA, about 150 Palestinian communities have land in this area. Reaching it depends on permits, prior coordination with Israeli authorities and access through designated agricultural gates.

There are about 62 such gates along the wall, and most stay closed for much of the year. During the 2025 olive harvest, 74 percent opened only on a limited number of days.

In Qalqiliya, the wall wraps around much of the city, cutting it off from nearby Palestinian communities and the land around it. Journeys to neighbouring towns that were once short can now mean passing through checkpoints or taking long detours.

The wall restricts more than movement. It reshapes how communities relate to their land and places that are part of their everyday lives.

The wall is only one part of a much wider network restricting Palestinian movement across the West Bank.

As of December, OCHA documented 925 checkpoints, road gates, earth mounds and other obstacles across the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem. They restrict the movement of about 3.4 million Palestinians, often forcing long detours to reach work, school, hospitals and other services.

The network includes 89 permanently staffed checkpoints, 218 partial checkpoints, 232 road gates, 167 earth mounds, 114 linear closures and 105 roadblocks.

Checkpoints and road gates now make up nearly 60 percent of these obstacles, up from 15 percent two decades ago when temporary blockages, such as earth mounds and roadblocks, were far more common.

Crossing the wall itself requires permits. Of its 13 checkpoints, only three can be used by Palestinians with West Bank IDs and Israeli-issued permits to enter East Jerusalem and Israel. OCHA said these permits are hard to get and many have been revoked or suspended since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

The wall stretches for hundreds of kilometres, but its impact cannot be measured by distance alone. It is measured in the farmland farmers struggle to reach, the communities cut off from nearby towns and the checkpoints between people and the places they need to go.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.summary: Israel began building its separation wall in 2002. It runs deep inside Palestinian territory rather than along the boundary with Israel. In 2004, the International Court of Justice ruled it illegal. Since 2003, Palestinians have marked the same date as an international day of action against Israel’s wall.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Lando Norris wins Sao Palo Grand Prix, but Mercedes seal constructors title
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Mercedes have secured ⁠⁠their ninth Formula One constructors world championship ⁠⁠and completed a title double in a wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix won by McLaren’s Lando Norris from pole position for the second year in a row.

The title, secured on Sunday, was the first team crown for Mercedes since 2021 and came a week after 20-year-old Italian Kimi Antonelli made headlines ⁠⁠as the youngest drivers champion with four races to spare.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen finished second, putting on a masterclass from 21st on the grid due to engine penalties in a race that started and ended in the rain.

Teammate Isack Hadjar was third with George Russell fourth for Mercedes and Antonelli fifth with the fastest lap. After leading at the start, both made costly errors on an eventful afternoon.

Mercedes had needed to score only three points more than Ferrari to clinch the title, and the Italian team never threatened to prolong the fight on a treacherous track with Charles Leclerc eighth after a post-race penalty demoted him one place and Lewis Hamilton ninth in his 400th race.

“It was a very tough race, very, very tough,” Norris, the 2025 world champion, said of his 14th career win and 50th podium as well as his team’s first victory since August when ‌‌he won the Dutch Grand Prix.

“A lot of challenges today with the conditions and going onto slicks in the wet is always tough, especially when you are pushing for the lead and trying to catch up a little bit,” added the Briton, who lost out to Antonelli when the start lights went out.

“The main thing today was I kept it cool and didn’t make any mistakes and had the pace when I needed to. Nice to be back on the top step and what a place to do it as well.”

Norris took the chequered flag, waved by Brazilian football forward Neymar, 14.602 seconds clear of Driver of the Day Verstappen.

Mercedes, whose engines also power McLaren, have now equalled Williams’ nine constructors championships.

“It was a very strong beginning of the season, and that kind of got us ⁠⁠over the line,” team boss Toto Wolff said. “These last few races have been challenging at times. Today it was difficult, but overall, ⁠⁠I’m so proud of the organisation.”

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri was sixth with Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson seventh after a fine race that saw the New Zealander start third and run in second place for the first five laps.

Nico Hulkenberg took the final point for Audi in a race of spins, slippery moments and changeable conditions.

Verstappen moved further ahead in the driver standings in the race for second place overall, now 17 points clear of Russell, who ⁠⁠moved up to third.

Lando Norris won the Sao Paulo Grand Prix from pole position for the second year in a row. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen finished second, putting on a masterclass from 21st on the grid.

https://www.wired.com/story/welcome-to-w.title: Welcome to Weed Island
https://www.wired.com/story/welcome-to-w.author: Orlando Crowcroft
https://www.wired.com/story/welcome-to-w.text:
STEVEN TAN WALKS along a narrow concourse in the Northern Leaf greenhouse in St Lawrence, Jersey, reading aloud the strains of his cannabis plants: Pink Gasoline, Moon Beam Gelato, Carbon Fibre, Gorilla Kush. Rows of plants stretch off into the distance. To the untrained eye, they look largely the same, with their distinctive jagged-edged, multi-fingered leaf shape and sticky buds like tiny pinecones.

But Tan, the CEO and director of medical cannabis manufacturer Northern Leaf, knows them intimately. “These plants are all different,” he says, stopping next to a mature Carbon Fibre specimen. “Just like humans.”

Northern Leaf is one of the largest licensed medical marijuana producers in Europe. Its 100,000-square-foot growing facility is based in Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands, located between England and France. Previously, this greenhouse was home to Jersey tomatoes, once a famed crop on the island that came close to extinction, thanks to growing fuel costs and cheaper competition from overseas. Now, it is fitted out with all of the technology required for cultivating cannabis that meets strict regulations for medical use, which include: automated irrigation, environmental monitoring, and air purification.

Despite being just 45 square miles in size, with a population of 100,000, Jersey—which lies 14 miles off the coast of the French mainland but is a British Crown Dependency—has emerged as an unlikely player in the medical cannabis industry. Although its total exports (over 9,200 kilograms in 2025) are small compared to UK growers, this represents an enormous amount per capita, and cannabis is fast becoming one of the island’s important new industries. Jersey’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, has previously said that he wants Jersey to be a “centre of excellence” for medical cannabis, and for cannabis production to become a mainstay of the island’s economy.

Jersey, a British Crown Dependency that sits between the UK and France, that has become an integral hub for the medical cannabis industry.

Currently, 90 percent of Jersey’s cannabis production comes from Northern Leaf. In 2025, the company exported £8.4 million ($11.3 million) worth of medical marijuana to markets including the UK and Germany (regulations mean it is only permitted to grow for export and cannot sell to customers in Jersey). Tan has much greater ambitions. He points to another famous Jersey export, Jersey Royal potatoes. “Jersey’s potato industry did £40 million in 2025,” he said. “I am already doing a quarter of the potato industry on 5 percent of the land. On 20 percent of the land, I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.”

Born in Malaysia to a Chinese dad and Irish mother, Tan, 50, wanted to become a vet, but after graduating from university in 1998, ended up developing software for Citibank. He was making good money, but his heart wasn’t in finance. What really interested him was growing weed. “I loved the science of it, the genetics, the seeds, the smells,” Tan says.

The early 2000s were the perfect time for an inquisitive young business grad to get into the cannabis business. Across the world, governments were legalizing medical marijuana and moving towards decriminalization over draconian sentencing.

Tan began bouncing around jurisdictions that were relaxing laws on cannabis, working as a consultant in California, the Netherlands, and Canada. “I started to see these legal frameworks opening up. The minute they existed, I went there,” he says.

Jersey has a somewhat unique regulatory environment. As a Crown Dependency, it has close ties to Britain, but is not a part of the UK. Crucially, it is self-governing: It can make its own laws. Jersey’s main reputation today is as a tax haven, attracting some of the world’s wealthiest individuals and companies, thanks to its lack of capital gains tax and 0 percent corporation tax for most companies. Along its coastline, next to twee beachside cafes and Nazi bunkers (the Channel Islands were the only part of the British Isles to be occupied by Hitler’s forces in World War II), you can find offices of international banks and wealth management firms catering to the super rich.

Although traditionally culturally conservative, Jersey has become something of a trailblazer on cannabis. The island legalized medical cannabis in 2019. Today, five private clinics operate on the island. The latest figures suggest that 6 percent of the population is prescribed cannabis, compared to an estimated 0.4 percent in Germany and 0.1 percent in the UK. Upon legalization, the island’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, laid out ambitious plans for the island to become a hub of the medical cannabis trade, repurposing the horticultural facilities and know-how from its tomato-growing glory days for this new endeavor.

Tan joined Northern Leaf as CEO in 2024, when the company was in dire straits after a failed IPO. That year, it was valued at just £3.7 million, despite having spent as much as £30 million on its weed-growing facility.

Tan nevertheless saw a lot of potential, and over the last two years has seen capacity at the site increase from 25 percent to 75 percent. He believes the £8.4 million of product the company exported last year is just the beginning.

Northern Leaf's 100,000-square-foot growing facility. “On 20 percent of the land,” says CEO Steven Tan, “I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.”

Sarah Clover, a barrister at Kings Chambers who works on cannabis licensing in Jersey, told WIRED the island’s advantage is hard to replicate. Growers are inspected by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which is known for enforcing rigorous standards on quality. “Anybody buying from Jersey knows that the stuff coming out of it is absolutely gold standard, because the MHRA says it is,” she says. Permits, however, are handled by a small team on the island: “You can make an application for a permit on a Monday and get it on a Tuesday.”

Many within the Jersey medicinal cannabis industry now want to go beyond growing the raw ingredient and package it for export as a final product on the island. Northern Leaf already has the facilities to do so, but Jersey law dictates it can only export bulk amounts of raw cannabis for other companies to process and pack for distribution and sale. The company is waiting to see if Jersey will change its law. “At the minute we’re kind of on this seesaw—which way will the island go?” Clover says. “It could really take off here. Jersey could be a life sciences hub, not just for cannabis but for all sorts of pharmaceuticals.”

But running a cannabis business on a small island poses challenges, and not everyone is enthused about the idea of expansion. Tan has faced off against residents every time that the facility has expanded production. Some locals have complained that they can smell cannabis from their balconies. Others have linked the growing industry to concerns over misuse of cannabis on the island, despite the fact that all of its product is exported. Cannabis is a “contributory factor” in 22 percent of admissions to the island’s acute mental health ward, according to Jersey’s health minister.

One patient, Michael, told WIRED that he was prescribed medical cannabis for 18 months after having tried two other prescribed medications for insomnia and anxiety. “The initial assessment was simple. I had a meeting with the cannabis doctor who was pretty evangelical about its medicinal properties. They check your medical history with your GP, and within 10 days you’re good to go,” he says.

Michael was prescribed 30 grams a month of “unbelievably good” cannabis and told that if he ran out he could back and ask for more. “I stopped because it was seriously affecting my mental health [and] I have since seen a psychiatric professional who said I should never have been prescribed it given my documented mental health history,” he says.

Illegal resale of medical cannabis is also an issue, with a rise in so-called “user-dealers,” who sell their excess medical marijuana to others. Jersey Police told WIRED this “undermines the legal framework and creates opportunities for criminal supply.”

Overall, however, cannabis-related offenses have dropped since Jersey legalized medical cannabis in 2019—from 216 in 2016 to just 12, as of July 2026.

Tan is circumspect about the challenges of operating on Jersey. “Culturally, the people here are harder to convince about cannabis,” he says. “It’s an older society.” But after 25 years working in the industry, he’s used to the pushback.

“It’s a normal challenge,” he says. “And I think when anyone sits down and meets me, they understand. This isn’t a bunch of stoners growing a bit of weed in a plastic greenhouse.”

Tan surveying Northern Leaf's crops.

While Jersey’s medical cannabis industry grows, some people on the island want to go further. In 2024, a vote to decriminalize recreational cannabis was defeated by a single vote in the island’s parliament. When it was brought back for another vote by the island’s then health minister, it was withdrawn before it could be debated. It is expected to be brought back before the parliament in the coming months.

Some individuals on the island have decided not to wait. By exploiting a loophole in current laws, they have made Jersey one of the only places in Europe outside of Amsterdam where THC products can be purchased and consumed legally.

One morning in February 2024, Gary Tucker arrived at work, his weed shop in St Helier, Jersey, to find a dozen customs officers and the local media waiting outside. It was a raid—and not his first. The officers emptied shelves and boxes into bin bags. “They were literally running their arms down the shelves and putting everything into bags. They took everything,” Tucker, a California native and former analyst in the US Army, told WIRED.

Tucker operates outside of Jersey’s medical cannabis industry. His shop, Bailiwick Botanicals, sells products that are clearly recreational: hash cakes, gummies, and other snacks, all infused with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the psychoactive ingredient in cannabis that gets you high and is heavily controlled.

He’s able to do this owing to a loophole in Jersey law which allows the sale of products containing CBD—another critical ingredient in cannabis, but one that doesn’t get you high. Jersey’s law says that the amount of THC in CBD products cannot exceed 3 percent of the weight of the CBD. So, if you want to sell products with high levels of THC, you just have to boost the CBD. “It’s just a math equation,” Tucker says.

Tucker admits it isn’t an ideal situation: studies suggest that ingesting high levels of CBD can cause liver damage. But he sees that as an issue with the regulation, not his solution. “I’m just following consumer demand,” he says.

Tucker is somewhat evangelical about the properties of cannabis. In his time as a weapons trainer for the military, he struggled with the mental health impacts of hearing that recruits he had trained had been killed in action. “I needed to step back from it. It started to really affect my mind,” Tucker says.

Veterans he knew were turning to cannabis, and Tucker began buying it on the black market. “It was the only thing that helped me,” he says. ”Cannabis gave me my life back.”

Tucker currently manufactures most of his products in the US before shipping them to Sark—a smaller Channel Island best known for having no cars and also its own government—and then to Jersey. New regulations in the US, however, mean Tucker may need to change his approach.

Tucker sees Jersey as a potential export hub for THC products to Europe. He believes Jersey’s budding weed industry should push beyond medical cannabis and into the recreational market. “This isn’t just a bunch of guys in a cellar somewhere. Not only does cannabis help people, but getting it to the shelf creates jobs. From the grower to the retailer. It permeates across all industries. We’re making cosmetics. We’re making gummies. We’re making drinks,” he says.

After the 2024 raid, Bailiwick Botanicals shut its doors for two weeks, and its full stock wasn’t returned until six months later. As of June 2026, Tucker and his team are selling THC-infused fudge, chocolate, and other sweets. His newest product, THC-infused coffee beans, is selling well. The police have stayed away.

In a written statement to WIRED, Jersey’s government said that the “possibility of abuse of our limits to get round the law in other jurisdictions is a matter of concern to the Government of Jersey and we are looking at ways to address it. Work is underway to consider whether Jersey’s existing legal exemptions for CBD products require amendment.”

“These plants are all different. Just like humans," says Tan.

For his part, Tan is reluctant to be drawn on his views on the so-called “rec” (recreational) market. For now, Jersey still has harsh sentencing rules on recreational cannabis use, with the penalties for possession and possession with intent to supply remaining up to five years and 14 years in jail, respectively. The proposed (and withdrawn) law to decriminalize cannabis notes that, the way the law is currently written, someone who rolled three joints and gave one to a friend would be guilty of supply and receive a criminal record. “Without change, people will continue receiving serious criminal records for small amounts … punishments [that] can result in additional harms greater than the drug itself,” it said.

While Jersey makes its own laws, however, it may not be able to completely legalize cannabis. Jersey is a signatory to the UN Convention on drugs control via the UK, and the UK Home Office would undoubtedly have a view if the island were to set itself up as an “Amsterdam on the Sea.” In 2022, an effort by the government of Bermuda (a British Overseas Territory) to legalize recreational cannabis was blocked after the UK withheld Royal Assent from the bill.

Back at the Northern Leaf warehouse in the Jersey parish of St Lawrence, Tan is flipping the lids off large boxes and rifling through clear plastic bags packed full of cannabis.

This is all weed that will not be sold, either because there were issues with production or the THC levels were too low. Instead, it is taken to a secure area of the facility where it is locked away in a reinforced armored vault. Specialist staff with bodycams take the bags to the island’s incinerator, where it is unceremoniously burned, as required by law.

Tan regularly makes a case to the government for changes to the law and support for the cannabis industry, such as an industrial energy tariff to help with spiraling energy costs.

He has claimed that Jersey could be home to “the Monsanto of cannabis,” alluding to the agricultural giant that was acquired by pharmaceutical company Bayer in 2018 for $66 billion. He’d like to get deeper into the genetics of cannabis, form a tissue-culture lab, and “bring out strains that nobody has ever seen.”

But speaking of himself, he references a different genre of business: He’s Willy Wonka, but for weed. Thirty years ago, when Tan quit corporate finance, his father warned him that he could make a lot more money if he stayed in banking. “And you know what, he was right,” he says. “But I would not have had nearly as much fun.”
https://www.wired.com/story/welcome-to-w.summary: Jersey is a British Crown Dependency that sits between the UK and France. The island's medical cannabis industry is one of the world's biggest growing industries. The government is considering whether its existing legal exemptions for CBD products require amendment.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/us-age.title: U.S. Agencies Warn Refrigeration Controller Attacks Could Cause Fires and Inventory Losses
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/us-age.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/us-age.text:
U.S. government agencies have warned that threat actors are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems globally with an aim to cause service disruptions, fire hazards, and loss of inventory.

"The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards," according to a joint advisory.

According to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), Department of Agriculture (USDA), and Department of Transportation (DOT), threat actors are likely to exploit authentication bypasses, arbitrary code injection, and weak configurations to gain access to these systems and cause the following effects -

In response to the threat, owners and operators are being urged to use strong authentication, keep systems updated, identify any systems that are accessible from the internet, isolate operational technology (OT) devices, change default passwords, retire and replace legacy devices, remove unnecessary remote access, and secure necessary remote access.

"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman.

"We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."

In recent weeks, threat actors have targeted hundreds of supermarkets across Europe by exploiting weaknesses in internet-accessible refrigeration controllers to raise temperatures, in some cases to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), or force cooling units into defrost mode, spoiling food and resulting in financial losses.

Targets of these attacks ranged from major supermarket chains to small grocers and butchers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden, and the U.K.

Among those targeted was the French Blood Establishment, which confirmed that a cybersecurity incident affecting a refrigeration equipment provider had raised temperature and defrost settings to "extremely high levels" at three facilities used to store blood plasma. It's unclear who is behind the hacking spree.

Data from Censys shows that there are still hundreds of Danfoss StoreView instances exposed globally, with most of them located in France, although the number has dropped significantly from 3,004 to 708 between October 9 and November 5, 2026. The Copeland/Dixell XWEB exposure, likewise, has declined from 3,708 to 2,420.

The attack surface management platform described the refrigeration attacks across Europe as the latest addition to a list of other recent incidents targeting critical infrastructure, including gas station tank gauges, air raid systems, and water towers.

"North America accounts for roughly 38% of global ICS [industrial control systems] exposure," Censys said. "Asia's share grew from 22% in 2024 to 25% in 2026, while Europe's fell from 36.5% to 32%. However, these shifts have not produced an overall decline."

"While exposure numbers are high, they're hardly surprising: ICS exposure is a problem that's been reported on and warned about for years. It poses a critical risk to the public as gatekeepers to the world's critical infrastructure."

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/ai-reboun.title: ‘AI rebounding’: Nearly 20% of U.S. workers replaced by AI are being asked back—now they’re demanding higher pay, job security and AI transparency
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/ai-reboun.author: Joshua Hong
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/ai-reboun.text:
Nearly one in five U.S. workers say they have experienced a workplace reversal that could signal a new trend in the labor force: their employer replaced them with AI, only to ask them to return later, according to new research from talent assessment firm SHL.

The phenomenon, which SHL calls “AI rebounding,” shows an early indication that some companies may be discovering the limitations of replacing human employees with AI.

“Organizations are making fast, sometimes myopic, decisions about their people based on an incomplete picture of what their employees can do with or without AI,” Lucy Beaumont, global senior vice president of product and design at SHL, said in a press release. “AI rebounding is what happens when a company automates a role before it has genuinely assessed the human capability inside it. The AI doesn’t deliver, the gap becomes obvious, and the business ends up rehiring the same experts they just let go of, at a far greater cost.”

The survey, conducted in June and July, found that 19.1% of American respondents said they had personally been replaced by AI and were subsequently asked to return to their jobs. Across both the U.S. and the U.K., the figure was 16%.

And among the returnees, 51% wanted a substantial pay increase before agreeing to return, SHL found. Additionally, 42% said they would require written guarantees about future job security, and 40% wanted transparency about how AI would be used in their positions.

Similarly, a Robert Half survey from July found that 32% of U.S. hiring managers whose organizations eliminated positions because of AI later had to reinstate the same or similar roles. Among that group, 40% said the positions required institutional knowledge or context that AI couldn’t replace. Another 39% cited relationship management, 39% pointed to increased business demand, and 38% said the positions required more human oversight and quality control than expected.

And some prominent companies have already encountered those limitations. Swedish buy-now, pay-later company Klarna began recruiting human customer service representatives after relying heavily on AI chatbots. CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski acknowledged the company had gone too far in its reliance on automation, according to Bloomberg.

A Klarna spokesperson told Fortune human agents were needed “for complex, sensitive cases.” The company began directly hiring a “small number” of high-skilled humans into the customer service process to identify where the “human touch” can bring most value to customers.

Ford also hired and promoted 350 experienced engineers in June after AI-powered quality control tools failed to perform as expected. The automaker said AI had contributed to quality improvements but emphasized the importance of combining the tech with experienced engineering teams.

“These engineers carry the hard-earned wisdom of decades of design,” a Ford representative previously told Fortune. The company said AI is very important to quality gains, “and that, in tandem with deep technical expertise, is what’s needed.”

Despite the rise of AI rebounding, the number of companies that cited AI as a reason for workforce reductions has grown substantially.

According to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas, employers cited AI in 121,401 announced job cuts through October, more than double the 54,836 announced layoff plans for all of 2025.

And younger workers are especially vulnerable to AI-led job displacement. A Stanford Digital Economy Lab study found that employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in occupations highly exposed to AI was 19% below where it would have been if it had grown at the same pace as employment among their less-exposed peers.

SHL’s research shows some promise for the younger workers, however. The firm found that younger workers were more likely to report experiencing the “AI rebounding.” Among respondents aged 18 to 24, 24% said they had personally been replaced by AI and later asked to return, compared to 19.1% of U.S. respondents overall.

The phenomenon, which SHL calls “AI rebounding,’ shows an early indication that some companies may be discovering the limitations of replacing human employees with AI.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.title: Calls for data centre moratorium 'until we get the rules right'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.author: Penny Travers and Annabel Whitehouse
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Annabel Whitehouse

The NEXTDC data centre in Bruce is one of more than a dozen facilities in the ACT.  (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The Conservation Council is calling for a moratorium on any new data centres in the ACT, until industry-specific requirements are introduced.

The council says it is concerned about the impact new data centres are having on Canberra's water supply and electricity grid.

Both the federal and ACT governments are working on new rules and standards to govern the development of large-scale data centres.

The Conservation Council is calling for a moratorium on new and expanded data centre developments in the ACT, amid "increasing concerns" for the city's energy grid and water supplies.

There are currently fifteen data centres across the ACT, the first of which was built in 2007.

But Conservation Council ACT director Simon Copland is concerned about the "potential massive expansion" of data centres before proper checks and balances are put in place.

"This is a point of time, given the growth of AI, that we need to stop and have a conversation about this rather than rushing to approve everything," Conservation Council ACT director Simon Copland said.

Front of mind is a second CDC Data Centre in Beard, a suburb near Canberra Airport, which was conditionally approved in September.

The proposed $200 million centre is a three-storey building comprising of 12 data halls, and would be located next to another CDC data centre in the suburb.

CDC's first centre in Beard is expected to have a total capacity of 40 megawatts (MW). (ABC News: Harry Frost)

The application for the project was submitted a week before the ACT government promised to develop a data centre framework to "provide clear rules about where data centres can be located, the standards they must meet, and how proposals will be assessed".

But Mr Copland said there needed to be a halt on the development of data centres in Canberra until tougher regulations were in place, both locally and federally.

"We're seeing a potential massive expansion of this infrastructure and we're worried about the impact this is going to have on our energy system, on our water, on our biodiversity and on our community more broadly," he said.

Mr Copland said the first stage of the Beard development was expected to use 5 per cent of the ACT's peak energy, with the proposed second centre using "double that".

Canberra is proving an attractive location to build data centres.  (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Copland said there was also community-wide concern about the impact data centres were having on Canberra's water supply.

"We know that climate forecasts suggest that the ACT is going to see reduced water flows through our major rivers," he said.

"And so we want to ensure that we actually have the water to be able to maintain these data centres into the future and it doesn't risk the health of our river system or the ability for Canberra to use water for other very important things.

"We're suggesting that [data centres] must operate in areas where there is a secure water supply, and we'd like to see the investment in technology such as closed-loop cooling, which uses less water, to ensure that we're not pulling off the water system consistently."

The Conservation Council is not alone in these concerns; the ACT Greens and other community groups have also called for a moratorium.

And Independent Senator for the ACT David Pocock called on the federal government to introduce a tax on data centres operators, along with stronger environmental protections, in June.

But Chief Minister Andrew Barr dismissed the idea in August, saying "the ACT already has rigorous planning, environmental, utility and regulatory requirements".

Federally, the government is also working on a new set of national standards and oversight for artificial intelligence, including forcing large-scale AI data centres to minimise water use and fund their own power supply.

Simon Copland says he wants a moratorium on additional data centres in the ACT until the government legislates standards for the industry.   (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Beyond the ACT, concerns around data centre locations and their demand on resources have led to protests in Australia and around the world.

Just this past weekend, community backlash saw plans for an AI data centre in Sydney's Cooks River scrapped; one planned for Lane Cove and another for Guildford were dropped in September.

But CDC chief executive Greg Boorer said over the past 20 years of operating in Canberra "nobody's ever complained about our facilities", adding that the company already uses closed-loop cooling.

He said Australia's planning rules had already helped the sector avoid becoming like the United States.

"I think it was always going to happen in the United States because they really prioritised speed and in some ways greed over doing the right thing, choosing the right locations, being a good community participant with regards to adding energy to the actual grid," he said.

Greg Boorer says data centres are not "horrible pieces of infrastructure" if built in the correct location.  (Harry Frost: ABC News)

"In Texas, for example, just a free for all, every man for themselves, dropping in literally gas jet engines next to residential locations."

However, Mr Boorer said it was time for the sector to be more proactive in its engagement with local communities.

Until recently, security concerns had led to a secretive approach to planning developments, but Mr Boorer said a lot had changed since they built their first centre in 2007.

"We actually have to do a better job," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Traffic Offences

Demerit points being traded for cash appears to be a wider issue in Queensland. (AAP: Darren England)

The man who oversaw the rollout of Queensland's licensing and registration system in the 1990s says the government is staring at a "cybersecurity flaw" in the wake of revelations about demerit points being traded for cash.

The 7.30 investigation revealed widespread trading on black markets after a 27-year-old woman was charged with fraud. It's alleged she had accumulated 1,150 demerit points and more than $600,000 in fines.

Peter Grant is a veteran of the state's public service and oversaw its most complex IT systems as chief information officer; he says risks have changed dramatically since then.

"During the 90s, there was no social media. They didn't have to defend against this," Mr Grant told 7.30.

"[But] if you've got people who are manipulating your business processes to actually do fraudulent behaviour, you have a cybersecurity breach."

Mr Grant characterises the manipulation as a "cybersecurity breach" because, he says, it compromises the integrity of a government business process.

Peter Grant is Queensland's former chief information officer. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"These people are visible in the system over a long period of time — what we have here are people who are gaming the system, and they've created a cyber breach," Mr Grant said.

"The Queensland government has got to demonstrate that people can't get away with fraud and I would have thought that would have been a high-priority initiative.

"For the integrity of the system, this would start to get to the top of the list for me."

Dr Katie Williams, a former KPMG partner and senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Queensland's Business School, says she would expect to see the government review its systems around control gaps and pain points.

Dr Katie Williams says the system needs to be strengthened. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"A system that is set up correctly in the first place and regularly monitored and capable of tweaking makes it harder for fraud to remain undetected," Dr Williams said.

"Based on what we're seeing in other parts of Australia, there's an opportunity to perhaps consider, at a really detailed level, the enabling legislation."

7.30 was told police have raised the detection issue with the agencies responsible for administering the system — Queensland's Revenue Office and Department of Transport and Main Roads — and remain frustrated by inaction.

When asked by 7.30 government agencies described their processes for detecting fraud as robust.

On Monday afternoon the Queensland Treasurer's Office told 7.30 in a statement:  "New measures have already been implemented and ...  we will continue to strengthen the system we inherited from the former government, if needed, to stamp out fraud."

The statement said those measures were implemented in late 2025 as part of a new fines and integrity framework.

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli told 7.30: "I think [the] loophole has been closed" but said if there are other loopholes "then of course we will look at it".

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli says no one can make a system "bulletproof". (AAP: Darren England)

A consequence of the 'cash for demerit points' schemes is that authorities have not been able to confirm how many drivers may have escaped licence suspensions through fraudulent demerit point transfers.

Revelations from the investigation have caused concerns for police, road safety and motorist advocacy groups, including RACQ.

"We don't know the size of the problem, but we should know the size of the problem in Queensland, and that is the key thing here," said Michael Kane, RACQ's executive manager of public policy.

"There's no point having stronger laws to make our roads safer if people simply can find a way around the consequences.

In New South Wales, similar abuses prompted a dedicated taskforce and proposed legislative changes supported by both major parties.

Camera-detected offences include mobile phone use, seatbelt offences, red light violations and speeding. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Launched in 2024, the Demerit Point Integrity Taskforce uncovered "extraordinary examples of misconduct", NSW opposition roads spokesman Mark Coure told parliament, including people accumulating hundreds — and in some cases more than 1,000 — demerit points while continuing to drive.

"If dangerous drivers are able to manipulate the system, avoid licence suspensions and continue offending with zero consequences, then the purpose of the demerit point scheme is fundamentally undermined," Mr Coure said.

"We saw examples of unverifiable foreign licence details being used repeatedly to avoid penalties. We saw evidence of advertisements on social media where individuals were offering to take demerit points for others in exchange for money."

The taskforce resulted in proposed reforms that would require passport details and the country of issue when an overseas licence holder is nominated as the responsible driver and introduce new offences relating to false disputes and fraudulent nominations.

NSW Minister for Roads, Jenny Aitchison, said the proposed legislation would crack down on international licences being nominated for fines.

Jenny Aitchison is NSW's Minister for Regional Transport and Roads. (ABC News: Romy Stephens)

"Revenue NSW systems are being integrated with Australian Border Force data to verify if a nominated overseas driver was actually in the country when an offence occurred," she said.

"The bill forces an individual who nominates an overseas driver for a demerit-carrying offence to provide the nominee's passport number and country of origin."

A spokesperson from Transport for NSW said its taskforce saw the licences of 50 repeat offenders suspended, and resulted in 190 vehicle registrations being cancelled.

The department told 7.30 that its proposed reforms are "designed to support a fair, consistent, and safety-focused licensing system in NSW".

But while those changes are being deliberated, it hasn't stopped other schemes from establishing.

Among the purported services 7.30 uncovered was a website bearing a striking resemblance to the official Service NSW portal. Its contact button redirected 7.30 to WhatsApp.

This website advertising a demerit point fraud scheme is based off the official Service NSW website. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

In messages, the person claiming to be offering the service said they had "certain access to live dummy accounts" registered under Service NSW, and knew "how to get it accepted straight away and keep it all automated."

When asked how much a $434 fine and 3 points would cost to wipe, the person said, "ill [sic] do it for $500 total if sorting it today … I just need penalty notice number, date of offence and full name it's in and it will take 3 minutes … you only pay after you can see it's sorted."

NSW Police said it is aware of "reports concerning websites and online services claiming to facilitate the removal of demerit points in exchange for payment".

"The NSW Police Force does not comment on specific investigations; however, any information alleging criminal conduct is assessed and investigated where appropriate."

"Demerit point fraud is a serious offence that undermines the integrity of the licensing system and road safety."

RACQ says Queensland authorities need to "get much tougher" and consider policy intervention, legislation intervention, and police action.

Michael Kane is the head of public policy at the Royal Automobile Club of Queensland (RACQ). (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

Mr Kane told 7.30 the government needs to demonstrate that it understood the problem and was addressing it.

Griffith cybersecurity expert Dr David Tuffley says a taskforce could determine the number of people actively exploiting the state’s loopholes.

"That's going to take some courage from the government, to basically take a deep breath and run the query and just see how bad it is," he told 7.30.

Mr Crisafulli acknowledged the infringement and demerits scheme is "an important part of justice," but avoided answering if his government would commit to a review or taskforce.

"You will never make a system bulletproof, but you can make it better," he said.

"We will continue to do all we can to make sure we have systems that are strong.

"If people have done the wrong thing, then they should have to pay their dues."
