https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/what-is-n.title: Meet Jensen Huang’s son-in-law, a former pro skier and the Nvidia CEO’s ‘consigliere’ who could play a massive role in the company’s succession plan
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/what-is-n.author: Sasha Rogelberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/what-is-n.text:
In January, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was asked how he’s managed to lead the company since its 1993 founding.

“The secret for being CEO for this long is, one, don’t get fired, and, two, don’t get bored,” he said at an event in Las Vegas. “I don’t know which one comes first. How long [will I continue as CEO]? For as long as I deserve it.”

Ten months later, Huang is putting that adage to the test: Over the weekend, he admitted to having an affair with a business executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of acting as an operative for the Chinese government. China’s foreign ministry denied the allegation.

As Huang faces increased scrutiny after he admitted to the affair with an alleged spy, he now faces questions about whether he can continue on as the company’s top brass.

Nvidia has since launched an independent investigation into its CEO and his romantic relationship with suspected spy Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed International. Megaspeed is a data center and cloud computing company and one of Asia’s largest buyers of Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s board said Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in a statement on Sunday.

“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption,” a company spokesperson told Fortune in a statement.

The probe has reinvigorated investors’ concerns about the need to construct a succession plan, which, notably, Huang and Nvidia have not publicly shared. As of Monday morning, Nvidia stock is down more than 6%. Bernstein analysts, in a note published on Sunday, noted it would be unclear who could or would fill Huang’s shoes because the identity of his company is so inextricably linked to his own.

“Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO,” they wrote. “He IS Nvidia, clearly sets the long term strategy and direction, and (with supposedly 60 direct reports) pulls most of the company’s strings himself.”

Huang’s two children, Madison and Spencer Huang, both have roles in the company, but Huang’s son-in-law Nico Caprez, Nvidia’s 35-year-old vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, could be among the next in line to lead the AI juggernaut.

“I do imagine Huang is kind of preparing [Madison] and Nico for that next step,” one Nvidia employee who works with Caprez, told The Information last month.

Caprez is a former alpine skier representing Switzerland who began his career as a Boston Consulting Group consultant. He graduated with an MBA from the London Business School in 2021, where he met Madison Huang. The two married this September.

While Madison serves as a senior director of physical AI and robotics product marketing, and Spencer is a director of robotics product management, Caprez rose through the ranks at Nvidia to lead global AI infrastructure growth in less than three years, starting as a corporate development manager in February 2024 before becoming the director of global AI infrastructure enablement for Nvidia’s cloud partners about a year ago.

The young executive was part of deal-making efforts to raise $500 billion with six major asset managers including Apollo Global Management and Blackstone, to finance Nvidia chips for data centers in August. Caprez also reportedly assisted in Nvidia’s efforts to take minority stakes in two data center developers as part of its AI infrastructure buildout.

Senior leadership has extolled Caprez’s value both within the company and to the CEO more specifically. Vladimir Troy, Nvidia’s vice president of AI infrastructure who works alongside Caprez, said “Nico is very important.” A cloud executive who also met with Caprez called him “Jensen’s consigliere” in an interview with The Information.

Huang, however, has been mum on who will lead the company in its next era, whenever that may be. In an interview with Bloomberg last month, the CEO shied away from speculation his daughter would one day replace him at Nvidia’s helm.

“I don’t hope the job on her, and the reason for that is because if that’s their aspiration, Spencer of Madison’s, they have to go earn it, and it’s really, really hard work,” he said. “For many people, they can focus on their job and their families. When you’re the CEO of the company, you have to focus on, of course, your family. But I’ve got a whole bunch of other families I’m caring for. I’m responsible for an entire industry, and so I think the pressure of being the CEO is high.”

Huang’s newly precarious spot at the top of his company has some worries not just about who one day replaces him, but whether anyone really can.

“The so-called ‘key-man risk’ looms large here, and it’s doubtful markets have adequately priced it in,” economist Mohamed A. El-Erian wrote in a post on X. “This will not be easy for the board to navigate.”

Daniel Newman, CEO of global technology research firm the Futurum Group, said that what’s made Huang so difficult to replace is that the company has been built around his leadership style, which leans autocratic.

“He really drives everything that happens. He has a team of lieutenants that are in charge of making sure that what he asks becomes gospel, that it’s executed ferociously, maniacally,” Newman told Fortune. “The market has built such admiration and confidence for him that he’s become a Jobs or a Musk type of figure at Nvidia, where there just isn’t really any thought of it not being a founder-led company.”

Whenever Nvidia transitions to new leadership, it will likely see a shift in strategy, moving slightly away from the rapid clip of innovation Huang has pushed, to becoming an “execution machine” that has solidified backend and supply chain uncertainties to deliver efficiently to partners, Newman added. Changes in the company focus also mean that even if there’s one CEO, there will likely be a leadership team, not a single figure, making Nvidia’s biggest decisions.

“It’s very improbable that they’re going to find one person that’s going to fill all the gaps,” Newman said.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/new-york-.title: New York’s graying workforce: Residents over 65 are holding onto jobs longer and driving healthcare to become one of the ‘fastest-growing’ sectors
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/new-york-.author: Emma Burleigh
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/new-york-.text:
Workers from across the country have long flocked to New York to chase dream jobs and lock down six-figure salaries—but now the opportunity landscape has changed. Professionals have to compete for a limited number of roles, and baby boomers are holding on tight to jobs that might otherwise be up for grabs.

A new report from New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office reveals that the state continues to struggle with strained hiring and cautious business expansion in an uncertain economy. Total statewide employment is estimated to grow only 0.2% in 2026 and 0.3% in 2027, after rising 1% the year before. Hiring will remain sluggish through next year, the report forecasts, and workforce growth will be subdued because of New York’s shrinking, graying population.

“The growth of the State’s labor supply will be limited due to constraints in population growth and the aging workforce,” the report notes. “These trends will likely restrict employment growth, but unemployment rates should remain stable.”

Currently, 19.3% of New York’s population is 65 and older—up from 15% a decade ago—according to Hochul’s mid-year report. These baby boomers are intensifying the need for social and healthcare services, in-demand industries that have been battling severe labor shortages across the country. On top of that, America’s oldest working cohort is delaying retirement to make ends meet; a 2022 study from New York’s Office of Budget Policy and Analysis found that residents aged 65 and up were the only group that showed significant labor growth over the 10 years. Older Americans are driving demand for workers in certain industries while potentially delaying the vacancies younger professionals would compete to fill.

“Demographic shifts are driving demand for health care and social assistance, making this the

fastest growing sector in the labor market,” the recent report explains. “Anticipated shifts in Federal healthcare funding raise concerns about the sector’s ability to sustain employment growth. Meanwhile, job growth in leisure and hospitality, manufacturing, and construction is expected to remain weak due to high interest rates and a slowing economy.”

Now, New York is struggling to expand its pool of available workers even as businesses pull back on hiring. The state’s workforce was 1% smaller in 2021 than it was a decade earlier, compared to a nationwide increase of 5.1% during the same period, according to the 2022 report. And the combination of a shrinking labor pool and an increasingly older workforce isn’t unique to New York; across the U.S., baby boomers are staying on the job well past traditional retirement age, reshaping what it means to leave the workforce for good.

The number of those who are working past 65 has quadrupled in the U.S. since the 1980s, according to 2023 analysis from Pew Research Center, with around a fifth of the older generation holding down their jobs.

Beyond using employer-provided healthcare for as long as possible and keeping their schedules full, Americans are working longer because they worry their savings could run dry. Over two in five retired Americans, about 20 million people, worry their funds won’t support their ideal retirement lifestyle, according to a 2025 survey from investment banking firm D.A. Davidson. Now, Americans plan to work for four years longer than they’d wish to keep their heads above water amid a high cost-of-living and surging healthcare expenses, according to 2026 research from Economist Enterprise.

“I think that the days of retirement being a one-time, one-way exit and then you’re done are over,” Elizabeth White, author of 55, Underemployed, told Fortune in 2024.

For some who have already called it quits on their careers, that fear has already become a reality. Nearly 20% of American retirees are “struggling” or “living the nightmare,” according to a 2025 study from Schroders. Meanwhile, only 5% said they were “living the dream.” Now, the price of clocking out for good is in the millions.

When BlackRock, the world’s largest asset management firm, surveyed U.S. voters earlier this year on how much they think they’d need to retire comfortably, the average response landed around $2.1 million. And Larry Fink, the company’s CEO, said that “almost no one” is close to reaching that goal; BlackRock’s study found that 62% of respondents had less than $150,000 saved for retirement—about 7% of the $2.1 million they think they’d need to stop working. Fink also pointed out that the U.S.’s climbing senior care costs and lack of preparedness for rising life expectancy is exacerbating America’s retirement savings problem.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/boeing-l.author: Leslie Josephs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/boeing-l.text:
Boeing said it plans to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce through a combination of attrition and layoffs.

The plane maker is still working to stabilize production rates of its popular 737 Max planes.

Boeing’s head of its commercial aircraft unit, Stephanie Pope, said in a memo that adjusting the production schedule “puts us in an overstaffed position.”

Boeing
 said Monday that it plans to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce as its production ramp-up is moving at a slower pace than the company expected.

The cuts will be through a combination of attrition and layoffs, Stephanie Pope, head of the commercial aircraft unit, said in a memo to staff.

Pope reiterated that the company is still working to stabilize production rates of its popular 737 Max planes.

“Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position,” she said in the note. “Unfortunately, that means we need to align our staffing levels to our revised business plan, resulting in a reduction of approximately 5% through a combination of attrition and involuntary layoffs, with notifications beginning in December.”

Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said late last month that the plane manufacturer doesn’t expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027, which is longer than the company had been expecting.

Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.

With the midterm elections over, the future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hangs in the balance. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to be speaker of the house, announced this weekend that he would vote in favor of a resolution to impeach Hegseth. The Defense Secretary is one of the most controversial figures in President Donald Trump’s cabinet, and has purged the Pentagon of many top officials widely perceived as highly effective. He has repeatedly made provocative culture-war comments that have little to do with national security. And most damaging to his reputation, Hegseth has become the face of the war in Iran.

No matter how unpopular the U.S. military operations have been, Hegseth has stood behind the president. He has defended the pledge to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program and to establish a stronger foothold in the region, even as voters, including those in red states, flocked to the polls to express their disapproval of the administration’s foreign policy.

With the midterm elections over, the future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hangs in the balance. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to be speaker of the house, announced this weekend that he would vote in favor of a resolution to impeach Hegseth. The Defense Secretary is one of the most controversial figures in President Donald Trump’s cabinet, and has purged the Pentagon of many top officials widely perceived as highly effective. He has repeatedly made provocative culture-war comments that have little to do with national security. And most damaging to his reputation, Hegseth has become the face of the war in Iran.

No matter how unpopular the U.S. military operations have been, Hegseth has stood behind the president. He has defended the pledge to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program and to establish a stronger foothold in the region, even as voters, including those in red states, flocked to the polls to express their disapproval of the administration’s foreign policy.

What happens next remains to be seen. Some Republicans privately hope Hegseth will resign, either voluntarily or under pressure, so that Trump can replace him with someone who has a more favorable public presence and clearer strategy for bringing U.S. involvement in the war to an end. Most Democrats are wary about initiating impeachment proceedings against Trump, given that he has only two years left in office and has historically benefited politically when under attack. Hegseth, however, remains a possible target for impeachment. Pursuing him, potentially with some Republican support, would allow Democrats to demonstrate that they are serious about holding the administration accountable.

Twenty years ago, Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld lost his job after becoming the face of an unpopular war. The question now is whether Hegseth will meet the same fate.

When President George W. Bush announced his nomination of Rumsfeld to be secretary of defense on Dec. 28, 2000, following a highly divisive election recount, most experts considered Rumsfeld one of the most qualified people for the job. A Navy veteran of the 1950s, he had served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1963 to 1969. He then left legislative politics to become President Richard Nixon’s director of the Office of Economic Opportunity, and later counselor to the president and director of the Cost of Living Council. In 1973, Nixon named him U.S. ambassador to NATO. After Nixon resigned in disgrace over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, President Gerald Ford appointed Rumsfeld as White House chief of staff, and in 1975, Ford nominated him as secretary of defense, a post he held until President Jimmy Carter took office in 1977. Rumsfeld then spent many years working in the private sector while remaining involved in politics as a champion of neoconservatism.

His nomination as was greeted as a sign that the new President Bush would surround himself with a team of seasoned experts. After 9/11, Rumsfeld, who had a close and long-standing relationship with Vice President Dick Cheney, emerged as an important voice within the administration, helping to develop and implement a counterterrorism strategy intended to prevent comparable attacks on U.S. soil. In October and November 2001, the success of the military operations against the Taliban regime in Afghanistan was praised as evidence of his strategic prowess. The same was true in 2003, when the United States went to war with Iraq and Baghdad fell within weeks. On May 1, Bush declared an end to major combat operations beneath a “Mission Accomplished” banner, and in December, U.S. forces captured Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.

Beneath those successes, however, things were already going wrong for Rumsfeld and for the war. The first major trouble came when looting broke out across Baghdad in April 2003, including at the Iraq Museum and the National Library and Archives. It soon became clear that the Pentagon had done little planning for the aftermath of Hussein’s downfall. “Stuff happens,” Rumsfeld told reporters, brushing off their questions about the looting. Meanwhile, the U.S. military failed to find stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction, which had been the main justification for the war.

By the 2006 midterms, the Iraq War was deeply unpopular. Large numbers of U.S. ground troops were still struggling to establish political stability and contain sectarian violence, and they were suffering heavy casualties. The 2003 decision to disband the Iraqi army proved enormously costly, and in April 2004, a weeknight 60 Minutes broadcast had revealed widespread abuse of detainees of Abu Ghraib prison. Although the story was initially framed as the work of a few rogue soldiers, it soon became clear that the abuses were connected to Pentagon policies authorizing harsh interrogation methods. Rumsfeld privately offered to resign several times, but Bush refused to accept.

There had also been scattered calls from Congress to force the issue. In May 2004, New York Rep. Charles Rangel introduced eight articles of impeachment against Rumsfeld in response to the revelations of Abu Ghraib.

After their tours of duty, many soldiers returned with post-traumatic stress disorder and could not get the support they needed to transition back to civilian life. Democrats made the war a central theme of the 2006 campaign, presenting it as evidence of Republican misrule: Bush’s deeply flawed and unnecessary decision to go to war with Iraq in the first place, made with strong congressional Republican support, compounded by the failure to plan for what would happen once the government collapsed. In September 2006, Republicans were able to block a vote on a nonbinding statement from Senate Democrats expressing a “sense of the Senate” that Bush replace Rumsfeld. “To fight a war on terror,” New York Sen. Charles Schumer said during the floor debate, “you need to be both strong and smart. And with Secretary Rumsfeld in this administration, you do see a great deal of strength but you don’t see enough on the smarts.” Behind the scenes, White House chief of staff Andrew Card lobbied the president, unsuccessfully, to replace Rumsfeld, too.

Rumsfeld himself was an issue. His approval ratings, which had stood at 71 percent in 2003, had fallen to 44 percent in Gallup polling by January 2006. That spring, in what Time called “The Revolt of the Generals,” six retired generals called for Rumsfeld to resign. “When I introduce the Secretary of Defense to my troops, I’m going to be a loyal subordinate,” Army Major General John Batiste told the magazine. “But it was boiling inside me. Every time I looked at him, I was thinking about … that s___ war plan, I was thinking about Abu Ghraib, and I was thinking about the challenges I had every day trying to rebuild the Iraqi military that he disbanded.”

The defense secretary puts stunts over substance. The U.S. should send him on permanent leave.

One lawmaker lays out the case for indicting the defense secretary.

The secretary of defense is now the most influential senior official in the Trump administration.

Still, Bush stood by his man. Responding to critical editorials and calls for Rumsfeld’s resignation, Bush told the press on April 18: “Don Rumsfeld is doing a fine job. He’s not only transforming the military, he’s fighting a war on terror. … I hear the voices, and I read the front page, and I know the speculation. But I’m the decider, and I decide what’s best. And what’s best is for Don Rumsfeld to remain as the secretary of defense.” Whenever the issue came up in conversations with the White House, Robert Draper wrote in his 2007 book, Dead Certain, Bush doubled down. “The moment someone would say ‘Fire Donald Rumsfeld,’ Donald Rumsfeld would get a new lease on life,” said a White House aide.

The criticism did not abate. On Sept. 25, 2006, six weeks before the election, Batiste and two other retired generals told the Senate Democratic Policy Committee that Rumsfeld was unable to handle the job. On Saturday, Nov. 6, the newspapers associated with the Military Times Media Group published an editorial titled “Time for Rumsfeld to Go.”

Although Bush had publicly defended Rumsfeld into the final days of the campaign, the outcome made continued support all but impossible. A number of issues drove the election, including corruption, the cost of living, and healthcare, but opposition to the Iraq War was chief among them. Democrats won control of the House and Senate.

The president realized that he needed to change course. According to Rumsfeld, Cheney had given him advanced warning that Bush planned to finally accept his resignation. On Nov. 8, Bush announced that he was nominating Robert Gates as the new secretary of defense. “America is safer and the world is more secure because of the service and the leadership of Donald Rumsfeld,” Bush said. The decision was a blow to Cheney, who counted on Rumsfeld as an ally, and a victory for the foreign policy realists who served under President George H.W. Bush.

The leadership shake-up paved the way for a basic shift in strategy, announced in January 2007: from a U.S. mission focused on fighting insurgents and handing security over to newly constituted Iraqi forces, to a so-called surge of additional troops whose mission was to protect the Iraqi population and win their support against the insurgency.

Many Republicans privately expressed regret that Bush had not made the decision earlier, which might have given the GOP a fighting chance to hold its majorities. As New York Times reporter Adam Nagourney put it, then-Rep. Rahm Emanuel, an Illinois Democrat, “gave private thanks that the president had not robbed the Democrats of a potent issue by firing Rumsfeld before the campaign was engaged.”

The war in Iran is not nearly as large as the Iraq War, and there is no ground war, but Trump’s policies have proven to be extraordinarily unpopular from the start, and as prices rise, the war has only become more controversial. There is little love for Hegseth, even among Republicans. Not only does he embody much of what critics think is wrong with Trump 2.0, but because he is not the president, Republicans feel freer to attack him.

Rumsfeld’s resignation offers a template for today’s Republicans who are angry about what has happened in Trump’s second term, and it could be that Hegseth will now go. But even if he leaves—or if Congress forces him out—it is unlikely to bring a fundamental change in policy. The Trump White House has centralized power in the president himself, so he will remain the source of policy decisions and the focus of attacks. Despite Democratic victories in last week’s midterms, Trump is unlikely to change course. It would take budgetary and investigative pressure from Congress to make that change.

He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zx.title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zx.text:
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 6% on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.

Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.

However, China has rejected the claims, with its Foreign Ministry saying "allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.

Following the probe annoucenment, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Huang to continue leading the firm.

US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".

However, the news of the investigation sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's value.

While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened on a positive note on Monday after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.

But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be shortlived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so central to the AI industry.

"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.

Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.

Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but Huang decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.

A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.

Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.

He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.

By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.

Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."

The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.

Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Nvidia's board of directors announced an independent investigation into the affair. The chipmaker said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/techn.title: A.I. Fueled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Elite Status, but Scandal Followed
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/techn.author: Don Clark
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

As chips became essential components for A.I., executives like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang saw their personal wealth and profiles soar in a way the industry has not experienced before.

Reporting from San Francisco

Before Jensen Huang and Nvidia changed the technology landscape, the semiconductor business was conspicuously short of stars. Wealth, infidelity and politics seldom figured in discussions of the chip industry’s leaders.

But Mr. Huang changed Silicon Valley, starting in the middle of the past decade, by single-mindedly pursuing the silicon chips that power generative artificial intelligence and related innovations. Extraordinary riches followed for the Taiwan-born executive and many of his peers, in some cases eclipsing the fortunes of high-profile software or internet entrepreneurs.

With that money and influence came attention from powerful people in Washington, notably President Trump, and opportunities for the kinds of entanglements that Mr. Huang on Sunday admitted to with a Chinese executive who goes by Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence has determined that Ms. Huang, who could not be reached for comment, was a Chinese spy. A Nvidia spokeswoman declined to comment.

“Before generative A.I., semiconductors were not a sexy business, and were never a place for C.E.O.s to make fast money,” said David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who has closely tracked the chip business.

Mr. Huang largely seemed to fit this mold until 2023, Mr. Yoffie said, when generative intelligence driven by Nvidia chips exploded and turned the semiconductors — which can perform calculations and other tasks — into essential components.

“In the last three years, he became a rock star, which apparently attracted the same kind of attention as all rock stars,” Mr. Yoffie said.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate negotiator tells Cop31
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Graham Readfearn,Oliver Milman and Fiona Harvey in Antalya, Turkey
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Simon Stiell makes opening address at summit in Turkey, where talks are under way about speeding up shift to electrification

A global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” around the planet, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, told the opening plenary of critical UN climate talks in Turkey.

Stiell joined Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia, which is leading the negotiations, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an optimistic alternative to a planet still tied to oil, coal and gas.

Inside the tight security of the opening plenary on Monday, delegates from almost 200 countries watched a stirring short film with scenes of fire, flood and storms that proclaimed: “It’s time to reconnect with the planet we have grown apart from.”

Turkey said it expected 100,000 visitors, including national delegations, to attend the two-week talks, including at least 95 heads of state. A global leaders summit is scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday. But the talks are under increased pressure to deliver, after growing dissatisfaction with the snail’s pace of results.

The talks are opening as a historic El Niño builds in the tropical Pacific and less than two months after a glacier collapse set off catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet, wiping away villages and killing at least 1,459 people, with thousands more still missing. Climate scientists confirmed this year that global heating would reach at least 1.8C – beyond the 1.5C temperature goal that countries promised to aim for at talks in Paris in 2015.

Last week Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, told the Guardian that although he still had faith in the negotiating process, “the fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast … and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”

And in a statement the UN secretary general, António Guterres, urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need”.

Stiell also said: “The urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth,” adding that it was vulnerable communities paying the price and frustration at a lack of fairness was palpable.

US President Donald Trump’s war with Iraq and the disruption of the key strait of Hormuz supply route for oil pushed up petrol prices around the world by 50%, raising inflation and slowing economic growth.

Stiell told delegates this “fossil fuel cost chaos” had “delivered a global shock wave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer”.

Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, the president of the negotiations, said in a speech that will set the tone for the talks that although the 1.5C Paris target will be overshot “we can return … if we work together and act with urgency, solidarity and resolve”.

With fists clenched in the final moments of a speech, Bowen urged delegates to show future generations that this generation was “equal to the challenge” and to “rise to this moment together”.

The countries pushing for the greatest action at Cop31 have stressed the 1.5C temperature rise limit can’t be abandoned and called for accelerated steps to provide finance to the places most vulnerable to climate impacts. The so-called high-ambition coalition said it has 20 country members pushing for major progress in Antalya.

“That limit is in serious danger but overshoot should never become an excuse for inaction, every fraction of a degree matters,” said Jess Gasper, an environmental official for the Marshall Islands.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

“We must limit overshoot and return to a safe temperature as quickly as possible.”

Gasper said it took eight years to get international finance to build a single sea wall to help protect the Marshall Islands, a Pacific island nation acutely threatened by sea level rise.

“That example shows we need that money to adapt,” he said. “I refuse to accept that we experience displacement because the world fails to act.”

The talks began without a fight over the agenda, which was considered by many to be a good sign. There was confidence among delegates that a final decision from Cop31 would include reference to a new voluntary electrification goal being championed by the host, Turkey, and the president of the negotiations, Australia.

Bowen said he had spoken to countries around the globe that were represented at the talks and there was “enormous momentum” among them for electrification.

The goal, he said, was to raise the percentage of final energy consumption coming from electricity from the current one-fifth to one-third in the next ten years.

Dr Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency, said: “I have talked with many governments and I see there is a great appetite for many countries to be part of this historic decision [in Antalya].”

He told the Guardian: “The important thing is that we are entering the age of electricity and this [electrification goal] would give an extra boost to that movement.”

Countries agreed at the 2023 climate summit to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030. Birol said if countries endorsed the 2035 electrification target it give an “unmistakable signal to markets” and a chance to increase both renewable and nuclear electricity.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Mahmood’s ICE-style immigration raid agency accused of ‘fishing expeditions’
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Emiliano Mellino and Rajeev Syal
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Exclusive: Almost two-thirds of visits lead to no arrests and nearly three-quarters are conducted without a warrant

Shabana Mahmood’s ICE-style raid agency has been accused of engaging in “fishing expeditions” after figures disclosed that almost two-thirds of enforcement visits result in no arrests and nearly three-quarters are conducted without a warrant.

The home secretary has hailed the expanded use of immigration enforcement teams, and claimed they will help to secure the UK’s borders by removing a key incentive for irregular migration.

Under her leadership, raids have targeted establishments associated with informal “black market” work such as nail bars, car washes, barbers, takeaways, construction sites and warehouses, as well as people’s homes.

They have been accompanied by videos posted on TikTok showing arrests of people working without authorisation being tackled to the ground by enforcement officers and locked in the back of vans.

Freedom of information requests, however, show that:

There were 23,538 immigration enforcement engagements such as workplace raids, home raids and spot checks in 2025 – or 60 a day. Of these, 15,578, or 66.1%, resulted in no arrests.

Only 25.81% of visits where a premises was accessed used a warrant. Critics say this suggests the Home Office is launching “fishing expeditions” based on weak intelligence.

Nearly nine out of 10 (89%) of leads alleging “immigration crime” in 2025 came from the public or from Crimestoppers, a charity that collects anonymous tip-offs. Around 2% came from the police.

The Home Office vigorously disputed claims that the agency launches “fishing expeditions”, claiming that intelligence is thoroughly examined before launching an immigration raid.

The findings have emerged after inquiries by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the Guardian amid growing concerns about the effect on innocent workers and businesses.

Officers from immigration enforcement swooped from unmarked vans last month on Sultanz, an Indian restaurant in Camborne, Cornwall, as customers sat down to eat.

The restaurant’s owner, Samsu Ali, said it felt as if his six-year-old business was being invaded. “As soon as they parked … everyone runs to the kitchen, front door, back door, everywhere,” he said.

The officers had no warrant, he said. Once in, they asked every worker for their details.

Nanu Mia, a Bangladeshi employee who had been packing meals for collection, gave his details to the officers, but they struggled to understand him.

Mia was handcuffed, arrested and marched to a van. He was de-arrested and released after his sister rushed to the restaurant with his ID card, which helped to prove that he was allowed to work.

The restaurant’s customer numbers have fallen steeply since the raid despite being cleared of any immigration breaches, Ali said.

In a local Facebook group, a question about the incident resulted in racist and threatening comments. One person wrote: “People with somewhat darker skin are literally taking over our community and causing a lot of unrest.”

The comments left Ali struggling to sleep. “They don’t understand how much money and time I have spent in the last six years,” he said.

If immigration enforcement officers do not have a warrant, they can rely on other powers to enter the premises.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

They can enter licensed premises – a restaurant, pub, hotel, cafe or any business that sells alcohol or provides late-night hot food – without a warrant under section 179 of the Licensing Act 2003. Or, in most cases – more than 12,000 last year – they can ask for the consent of the tenant, manager or owner.

When using this power, officers are meant to inform the person of their rights, including the fact that they are free to revoke their consent at any time.

Once inside, officers have the power to question individuals about their immigration status. They can ask to see identity documents. They are not supposed to detain someone without reasonable suspicion that the person is an immigration offender.

Kevin Barker, a former immigration officer who now works with businesses wrongly accused of employing people who do not have the right to work in the UK, said raids are often “fishing expeditions” based on tenuous tipoffs.

“You’re not allowed to apply for a search warrant if the intelligence you’ve got is old or an anonymous allegation that can’t be corroborated … but it doesn’t stop them,” he said.

Mothin Ali, the deputy leader of the Green party, said the findings were alarming and called on the government to “end these unjustified raids and protect people’s rights”.

“This is racist harassment dressed up as immigration enforcement,” he said.

“The falling use of warrants is deeply concerning and raises serious questions about the legality of these operations. Britain must not import Trump’s ICE playbook.”

Arrests of people from abroad working illegally in the UK have doubled since Labour has been in government. The Home Office said in August that more than 17,000 had been made since July 2024, a 122% increase on the previous two years, with a record number of immigration raids and arrests in 2026.

Opposition parties have claimed that opportunities to work illegally in the UK act as a pull factor for migrants, encouraging people to cross the Channel in small boats.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Exclusive: WhatsApp messages show firm pressuring Zubir Ahmed MP to help bring sensitive data into its platform

UK politics live – latest updates

Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients.

The US company, co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel, used a direct WhatsApp channel to argue that “the logic of joining up primary and secondary [care] data is unarguable” and said its software was “ideal” for the job. The push came in February this year despite GP data being expressly ruled out of scope of Palantir’s existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform (FDP), which it says has helped cut surgery waiting times and discharge delays.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The messages – which were obtained under the Freedom of Information Act by Foxglove, a tech equity campaign group, and shared with the Guardian – appear to be between Palantir’s UK boss, Louis Mosley, and the former health minister Zubir Ahmed. They span several months from July 2025 to March 2026.

In the messages and a briefing document, Palantir urged Ahmed to “get out ahead of” likely “political” opposition from doctors and vocal critics of Palantir, such as the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, and Your Party, led by Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana. The firm also told Ahmed: “The FDP is already delivering very strong results – but will deliver even more benefits faster with the right ministerial sponsorship.”

Groups representing doctors and patients, including the British Medical Association, have opposed the integration of GP data into Palantir’s FDP, arguing there is a lack of trust in the company, which also works for the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). When Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government announced the deal with Palantir three years ago, it said: “GP data will not be part of the national platform.”

The lobbying emerges after it was reported last week that ministers were unlikely to end Palantir’s NHS data management contract imminently, defying campaigners and two House of Commons committees that wanted the company to be forced out as soon as spring. The Financial Times reporting, which suggested the Palantir contract will be extended, came amid concerns that removing the firm’s AI technology would be disruptive without an alternative lined up. The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, last week told parliament the review was ongoing, but said there was “a huge long-term benefit to using the NHS to develop UK sovereign AI” – a sign that the government may seek a UK replacement for Palantir when the contract reaches its next end point in 2029. Bloomberg also reported that Tom Watson, a Labour peer hired as a full-time lobbyist by Palantir in September, recently wrote to Cooper urging her to keep the contract going, saying: “I want to ensure that Palantir UK rises to meet the government’s new social-value tests and helps build Britain’s sovereign technological capability.”

The WhatsApp logs released under the FoI Act show Palantir telling Ahmed that the benefits to the health system of applying its software – known as Foundry – to GP data could include “faster access to GPs … more effective and targeted management of frail patients, and more effective preventative care”. It also said Palantir’s software platform would “maintain local control of data”.

The Palantir executive’s name is redacted in the documents released by the department of health, but Palantir did not deny it was Mosley. In one message, the minister praises a performance on a BBC1 Sunday politics programme, just after Mosley had appeared.

“Great work [on] Kuenssberg btw,” Ahmed said.

The Palantir executive advised the minister that “the politics [of using GP data] is not straightforward – the previous government ruled GP data out of scope when announcing the FDP. So, as this moves forward, it will be one to get ahead of and explain, otherwise the opponents described above will make hay with it.”

Donald Campbell, director of advocacy at Foxglove, said the WhatsApps showed Palantir “lobbying to hoover up yet more of the British public’s sensitive personal data”.

“It is appalling to see Palantir pressuring the minister to bring GP records into its platform, despite pledges from the government in 2023 that this would not happen,” Campbell said.

The correspondence “shows they knew just how sensitive this was” and it was “telling [that] they made this argument privately, via privileged access to the government”, he added.

Tom Dolphin, chair of the BMA council, raised concerns about “scope creep” with Palantir potentially accessing identifiable personal data in the GP record that could “undermine patient trust and threaten the doctor-patient relationship”.

“Patients must be able to seek care without worrying which operators might have access to duplicates of their personal information,” he said.

Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytical Officers Network, said: “Palantir appears to be bidding to stretch the scope of its work for NHS England in a way that goes beyond statements from ministers and NHS leaders that GP data was not in the scope of the FDP contract and would require legislative change … As two separate select committees have noted, public trust and transparency is essential to us being able to realise the fantastic opportunities that technology and data offer.”

Palantir said: “We’ve long argued that data sharing can improve the NHS, for patients and taxpayers, and that our software helps different NHS organisations to do that, while ensuring they maintain full local control over their data. We’ve also always been clear that it is for the government to decide how they roll the software out. These exchanges reflect both of those points”.

The Department of Health and Social Care declined to comment.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Push came in February this year despite GP data being expressly ruled out of scope of Palantir's existing £330m contract with NHS England. NHS leaders say GP data was not in the scope of the FDP contract and would require legislative change.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Reform UK councillor in Sunderland handed community order after racist ‘joke’ about Nigerians
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Glenn Gibbins sentenced to 150 hours of unpaid work by South Tyneside magistrates over 2024 Facebook post

A Reform party councillor who claimed racist comments about Nigerians were no more than a “bit of fun” has been handed a community order for posting grossly offensive material.

Glenn Gibbins, who was voted on to Sunderland council in May, wrote on Facebook in March 2024: “Carnt believe the amount of nigerians in town… should melt them all down and fill in the pot holes!!”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

At a trial before a district judge on Monday, Gibbins, 66, said it was meant to be no more than “cheeky”, “naughty” and “tongue in cheek”. He said the post was not meant to be taken literally. “It was just a bit of fun.”

It was agreed at South Tyneside magistrates court in South Shields that the social media post was offensive – the question was whether it was grossly offensive.

District judge Zoe Passfield ruled that the post breached the Malicious Communications Act and was grossly offensive.

She said Gibbins “intention was to be grossly offensive to Nigerians as a result of his displeasure at the number of them in the city.”

Gibbins has been sentenced to a 12-month community order with 150 hours of unpaid work. Adam King defending, said they would be appealing against the decision to the crown court.

Prosecutor Emma Dowling said Gibbins’ post was talking about “exterminating” a group of people. “To say that it’s not to be taken seriously is to disregard history,” she said.

“The comment about melting them down conjures up despicable images.”

Godwin Ejeh, the leader of the Nigerian community in Sunderland, was called as a witness and recalled how he called an emergency meeting of Nigerians after the post came to light.

The mood of the meeting was “chaotic”, he said because of the “level of distress”. People were concerned for their safety and the safety of their children. People wanted an apology so decided a protest should take place outside city hall.

Ejeh, a Lib Dem council candidate in May, said the comments should never have been made. “We are talking about humans. It’s not something people should play with.”

Gibbins, who ran a mobile personalised gifts and T-shirt kiosk in a Sunderland shopping centre, said he would not have described himself as a political person before this year.

He said he thought he was approached by Reform in March to run as a councillor because of a T-shirt with Nigel Farage on it on a mannequin on his stall.

He had been asked to print the T-shirt by someone drinking all day in a nearby pub. That person was “clearly intoxicated”, Gibbins said, and forgot to pick up the T-shirt, so he put it on the mannequin.

When he got a call from Reform asking if he would run as a councillor he saw it as a way of getting some income during the normal summer lull for his business. “They explained they were looking for a candidate. I didn’t even know councillors got paid. I thought it would tide me over.”

King said his client’s social media post was not politically motivated. “Reform would do well to pay more attention to the people they put forward for election,” he said.

Gibbins made the post after a couple of beers and said they were not his words. He said he had been trying to repost something he read but failed so typed in the words himself. About six friends responded with laughter, thumbs up and heart emojis.

King said it was a “stupid, unfunny joke. We come across stupid, unfunny jokes all the time”.

He pointed to jokes by professional comedians that had not resulted in criminal proceedings, namely Jo Brand in 2019 on the BBC, making a joke about throwing battery acid on Nigel Farage; and Jimmy Carr when he made a joke about the Holocaust and Gypsies on his Netflix special.

King said courts in the UK had also asserted the importance of free speech in “full-throttled, uncompromising terms”.

Gibbins said he had been suspended by Reform, then reinstated, but was now suspended again.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Air pollution soars as fog traps emissions in England’s urban areas
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Matthew Pearce
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Particles from fireworks and bonfires likely to have contributed to levels well above WHO’s daily guideline

Air pollution soared to “very high” levels across urban parts of England on Monday as still, foggy weather kept emissions trapped after a weekend of fireworks and bonfires.

Government monitoring showed 11 sites, mainly in London and Greater Manchester, reached the highest band on its 10-point index for particulate matter in the 24 hours to 10am. A further 27 sites recorded “high” levels across the capital, the north-west, the Midlands, Yorkshire and the east of England.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The worst reading was in Hillingdon, west London, where fine particles (PM2.5) peaked at a 24-hour average of 129 micrograms per cubic metre, more than eight times the World Health Organization’s daily guideline. In the north-west, Manchester Piccadilly, Wigan, Blackburn, Preston and Rochdale all reached the “very high” band.

Particulate matter consists of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in the air. Exposure is linked to heart and lung disease and cancer.

Jane Burston, the CEO of the Clean Air Fund, said although monitoring networks could not determine where pollution came from, it was highly likely the pollution was from autumn celebrations.

“It’s a combination of the weather, which has been foggy and not windy at all, and then the fireworks and bonfires and Diwali,” she said. “What it means is the wind doesn’t blow the pollution away and the fog keeps it trapped down in the same place.

“If you’ve got asthma or a lung condition, you absolutely will not have wanted to go outside this morning or yesterday – it can bring on asthma attacks, coughing and wheezing.

“But for everybody, it’s dangerous. People in some of the worst-affected areas are breathing particulate matter concentrations five to 10 times above normal annual levels,” she added.

Burston called for better pollution forecasts, more widely accessible health alerts and stronger action to reduce emissions from wood burning and transport. “If we had air quality at a much safer lower level all year round, then on nights like Bonfire Night, the extra pollution is less likely to push us to extreme levels,” she said.

Larissa Lockwood, the director of campaigns at Global Action Plan, said the high pollution levels were “not surprising at a time of year when people are lighting log burners, having bonfires and lighting fireworks. On top of the normal levels from transport and industry, we see higher levels of air pollution and they’re then unable to disperse because they’re trapped by the fog.”

Domestic burning and transport are the biggest sources of particulate pollution, she said. Lockwood called for a public health campaign on air pollution and “burn alerts”, asking people in towns and cities not to use wood burners when levels are high.

“We need to phase out non-essential burning in our towns and cities so that we don’t experience these unhealthy air pollution levels,” she added.

A spokesperson for the mayor of London said: “On the advice of forecasters at Imperial College London, we’ve issued a high air pollution alert for Tuesday 10 November. Monitoring data show that pollution levels rose sharply across London from Friday to Sunday and remained elevated into Monday morning.”

A Clean Air Greater Manchester spokesperson said: “Higher particulate pollution levels occur each year around Bonfire Night, when fireworks and bonfires add particulate matter to the air. This year, weather conditions are also an important factor, with light winds and fog creating conditions in which pollution from a range of sources can accumulate near ground level. The latest information and health advice provided by Defra is available online.”

The government has been contacted for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Catherine Shoard
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Dunagan was six when he voiced the young deer in the classic cartoon, with an assistant director instructing him to pretend his own mother had died

Donnie Dunagan, who voiced Bambi in the Walt Disney classic, as well as playing the son of Frankenstein opposite Basil Rathbone and Boris Karloff, has died aged 92.

Dunagan was six when he was chosen to provide the voice of the young deer in the animation’s most heartbreaking chapter. He recalled the experience in the recording booth as easy and relaxed, with rudimentary technology and notes from an assistant director instructing him to pretend his own mother had died when voicing Bambi’s reaction to his mother being killed by a hunter.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The actor recalled that Bambi’s mother originally dies on screen, but Disney altered this in the edit. Nonetheless, Dunagan received considerable hate mail from the hunting community afterwards.

Bambi, whose release was delayed in the wake of the attack on Pearl Harbor, ended up being Dunagan’s final film. He began his career on horror films Son of Frankenstein and Tower of London, playing the curly blond-haired son of Rathbone’s Dr Frankenstein, as well as featuring in films such as Mother Carey’s Chickens, The Forgotten Woman, Vigil in the Night and Meet the Chump.

He recalled often playing checkers with Karloff on set, while the latter was in full makeup dressed as the monster.

After college, Dunagan joined the military in 1952 where he spent 25 years and for which he was awarded a bronze star and three Purple Hearts for bravery. He never disclosed his early career to his comrades, but said that “one of the biggest regrets of my life is that I didn’t have the courage to tell my close personal friends in the Marine Corps that I had been a part of the wonderful work of Mr Disney”.

In 2015, he reflected on the experience by calling it “pure joy that both children and 80-year-olds can enjoy the film together. I could be working in the White House and children couldn’t care less. But let someone say, ‘that dude over there was the face or voice of Bambi’, and I am an immediate adopted grandfather to them. That is just an unmatchable joy, and a real responsibility.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Show will stream on platforms of BetUS sportsbook

Ex-Athletic NFL insider had resigned in April

Patriots coach, Russini were pictured at resort

Dianna Russini will return to sports media with a weekly one-hour show focused on the NFL backed by offshore sportsbook BetUS, she announced Monday.

The Russini Report will stream on BetUS TV’s website and X account, accompanied by a weekly analysis column. BetUS has described the program as a “live NFL betting show” that will run through the remainder of the season with game previews, matchup breakdowns and guest interviews.

The news comes seven months after Russini resigned from her role as the Athletic’s top NFL insider amid an internal investigation into her relationship with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel.

In April, the New York Post published photos of Russini and Vrabel at an Arizona resort, taken around the time of the NFL owners meetings in March. Some appeared to show the two embracing and holding hands. Russini and Vrabel, who are married to other people, said the interaction was platonic. Russini said the photos did not reflect that they were part of a larger group gathering, and Vrabel called any suggestion of impropriety “laughable”.

The New York Times-owned outlet began a review of Russini’s work after additional photos and reporting raised questions about the nature of her relationship with Vrabel. Russini resigned on 14 April.

The Athletic’s investigation, the findings of which were announced in September, did not find signs of bias in her coverage but said her relationship with Vrabel was in “clear violation” of the newsroom’s standards.

Russini, 43, joined the Athletic in 2023 after an eight-year stint at ESPN.

In comments to People magazine on Monday, Russini described the events of this spring as “heartbreaking”. She did not directly address any of the allegations involving Vrabel, who was not investigated by the NFL for his involvement.

“The best way to describe what the last six months were like for me is heartbreaking,” Russini said. “At the beginning of this, it was a nightmare.”

“The absolute best part of this situation has been the loyalty the NFL has shown me,” she added, referring to support from players, coaches and others around the league. “They checked in with me almost daily while I wasn’t working to make sure that I was staying connected to football, to check on me as a person and to just see how I was doing.”

She said her new show would include analysis on the NFL “along with a lot of my opinions”, describing that as “something I wasn’t really allowed to do before.”

“The way I’m going to approach stories is going to be very different now,” she told People. “I have an understanding and an empathy that I didn’t have before. I would do stories in the past at the best of my ability, and sometimes now I reflect on those, and I don’t know if I always thought about how much this would affect not just the player, but a team, an organization, the players’ families.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Rebecca Bailey
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
The lack of public information about the Megaspeed boss is fuelling claims she is a Chinese intelligence asset

Business live – latest updates

T
here is little public information available about Alice Huang, the woman reportedly at the centre of the Jensen Huang honeypot allegations, a fact that has only added fuel to claims she is a Chinese intelligence asset.

She was the chief executive of a Singapore-based datacentre company reportedly suspected of evading US export controls and routing Nvidia chips to China.

US officials then came to believe she was also a spy for Beijing who was having an affair with Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, the chip company critical to US ambitions to stay ahead of China in the AI race.

People briefed on the US intelligence told the New York Times they believed Alice Huang was recruited as part of efforts to learn more about American AI chips, and to try to persuade Nvidia to push for its advanced chips to be made available to China.

China has denied the allegations, calling them “nothing but smears”.

It is unclear exactly when the two Huangs, who are not related, first met.

Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected within the upper echelons of the global AI chip industry, the New York Times wrote, citing people who had met her.

Megaspeed, the datacentre company for which she was previously listed as chief executive, still describes itself as “a premier business partner of Nvidia” on LinkedIn.

It was in this capacity that the businesswoman was pictured in Jensen Huang’s company several times in 2024 and 2025.

One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted by another attending company on LinkedIn, shows the two sitting next to each other on a couch in Taipei.

The year after, they were filmed together again in Taipei at a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.

Press outside livestreamed footage of the two, seemingly comfortable in each other’s company, with Jensen Huang at one point putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kissed him on the cheek.

The two later left the restaurant in the same car, the footage showed.

A New York-based short-selling firm first raised concerns publicly about their “uncomfortably close relationship” six months ago.

Earlier this year, US officials wrote a memo saying the two Huangs had been romantically involved, the Financial Times reported on Saturday, citing sources who had seen it.

On Sunday the Nvidia chief executive sent a company-wide email apologising for an affair.

He did not name Alice Huang but said he would cooperate with an investigation “regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports”.

Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unknown, and she has not given a public statement about the allegations.

It is unclear what her current relationship is with Megaspeed, though Culper Research, the short-selling firm, quoted an employee in May as saying that contrary to public reporting, Alice Huang was “actually still our boss”.

The details of her career before that are difficult to ascertain.

Several media outlets have cited a profile matching her name and picture on a Chinese fund database, which listed previous jobs at banks including HSBC and CITIC, as well as roles at Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.

However, reporters have been unable to confirm any of the details listed.

Megaspeed is among a number of south-east Asian firms that buy chips to build facilities and then rent their computing power to companies in China.

According to Singapore’s the Straits Times, it was previously known as 7Road International – a Chinese gaming company with ties to state-backed investors.

At the time of the rebrand, it was owned by Huang Le Limited and led by Alice Huang, the newspaper said, before the ownership was transferred to another company in 2023.

Since late 2024, the US government has reportedly been investigating Megaspeed for helping companies in China sidestep American export restrictions.

The New York Times said Singapore questioned Alice Huang during its own investigation into the company, but released her.

Nvidia has previously said it has looked into Megaspeed but found no cause for concern.

The Guardian has contacted Megaspeed for comment.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Alice Huang was the chief executive of a Singapore-based datacentre company. She was reportedly suspected of evading US export controls and routing Nvidia chips to China. US officials then came to believe she was also a spy for Beijing who was having an affair with Jensen Huang, the chief exec of Nvidia.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Meta rolls out automated age checks for teens globally
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Social media giant Meta is expanding automated age-estimation technology globally starting this month following billion-dollar legal settlements and criticism that its platforms fail to protect teenagers from online harms.

“We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections,” the company said in an announcement on Monday.

“Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results. Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally.”

Teen accounts have more restrictions and protections, limiting contacts, types of content and users’ time. Teens often circumvent the restrictions by creating a fake birthday when they set up an account, raising concerns that minors could bypass parental controls and be exposed to harmful content.

Parents in the United States who have set up Instagram for teenagers will receive notifications this month about the new measures. Meta said it will expand the age estimation algorithm to Facebook and Threads later in the year.

The AI technology, which the company has been testing in several countries, including the US, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, analyses user behaviour and posts to estimate the person’s age.

Parents can open accounts for children and categorise them as restricted teen accounts. But the age-estimation feature can also now automatically place accounts in the category, even if it was set up using a manually entered birthday that would have falsely made a user seem like an adult.

Meta has several categories of restrictions based on age. Children under 13 years of age are banned from using the apps. Teenagers are reminded to leave Instagram after 60 minutes of activity, and notifications are muted at night, when they would usually be sleeping.

Teen accounts face a two-hour-a-day usage limit as well, and are blocked from seeing “social comparison” features such as likes and reactions to other teen accounts.

The social media giant has faced growing legal action worldwide over how its platforms are used by teenagers. Child development experts have said platforms like Instagram and Facebook are highly addictive for young people, can reinforce social pressures through reactions to posts and expose them to other harmful content online.

Australia passed a ban on anyone below 16 years of age from using social media platforms last year. But this month, several groups, including the advocacy group Digital Freedom Project and the social media website Reddit, filed a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of that law, as well as the scientific rationale behind trying to keep children entirely off of platforms like YouTube, Facebook and TikTok.

In the US, Meta faced lawsuits from attorneys general across the US over the alleged harmful impact of its platforms on children, with Meta agreeing to improve how it identifies minors and children as part of the settlement.

The states alleged that Meta’s platforms “encourage addictive behaviour, fail to verify users’ ages, encourage adolescents to bypass parental controls, and inadequately safeguard against harmful content and/or intentionally amplify harmful and exploitative content”.

In August, the company agreed to pay $18bn to the states and institute a slew of changes to how it allows teenagers to interact with its platforms that could only be removed by parents or guardians.

The changes include restricting under-18 users to two hours a day on the platforms and enforcing a nighttime curfew from midnight to 6am. Default settings will restrict “social comparison” features such as seeing likes and reactions on posts, and “cosmetic procedure filters” that alter a person’s appearance. Push notifications will be blocked for teen accounts between 8am and 3pm, when they are likely to be in school.

Teen users will be encouraged to take breaks, with prompts appearing after every 15 minutes of continuous usage, and when daily usage hits 60 minutes and 90 minutes.

Parents and guardians will receive updates on teen account activities and be notified whenever they message an adult for the first time. Searches for topics like suicide, self-harm or eating disorders would also trigger a notification to parents.

In announcing the new automated age estimation on Monday, Meta also repeated calls for other industry leaders to implement similar changes.

“As Instagram is just one of the many apps teens use, we’re also calling on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to adopt these same practices to keep teens safe,” Meta said in its statement.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.summary: Meta has been testing age estimation algorithm in several countries including the US, the UK, Canada and Australia. The company has been criticised for not protecting teenagers from online harms.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/jensen.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/jensen.author: Rebecca Bellan
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/jensen.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology. The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.

The Financial Times reported Friday on the relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.

Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers.

The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia. Historically, China has been a big market for the company. It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives. In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to expand access to China, and some of his persuasion tactics have been successful. Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

On numerous occasions, Huang has publicly lamented export controls, calling them a “failure” at a conference last year and saying in May that it was “not wise” for the U.S. and China to create two distinct AI ecosystems. He has also warned that shutting Nvidia out of China’s compute market would enable the country to develop its own AI chips to challenge Nvidia internationally.

China is already moving in that direction. Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China. Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024. At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.

Still, the allegations involving Alice Huang open new scrutiny of the company’s business relationships and could taint any assurances Nvidia offers that it can prevent sensitive technology from reaching unauthorized customers.

Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly warned officials close to Trump earlier this year about Huang’s relationship with an alleged spy. Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/jensen.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to affair with alleged Chinese spy. Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to expand access to China. Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world's biggest AI markets.
