https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/meta-r.author: Russell Brandom
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/meta-r.text:
Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.

At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna. Not only that, it’s cost-competitive with open-source competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash.

Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness. In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”

With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio. The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.”

Ember is the fourth model released under Meta’s Muse brand, following the mid-weight Spark (released in April), Spark’s open-source twin Glimmer (released in August), and the Wonder frontier model (released in October). The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success, with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.

The Effect Builder bot is available on the web to build whatever new Instagram filters you can think of.

After expanding its Edits app to macOS last week, Instagram’s next move is launching this Effect Builder that generates custom filters for your Stories posts with AI. Available now for US residents who are over 18, it has a prompt box for describing your filter idea to the chatbot, with an option to attach style reference images.

Then you can upload your own photos to preview the AI-generating effects, and ask for changes in follow-up prompts. There’s also an option to allow Instagram’s AI to rewrite your prompt, which turned my one-line test prompt “Make a filter that turns photos into comic book pages” into several AI-generated paragraphs of detailed style requests on everything from color palette to lighting. The filter Effect Builder generated as a result still looked nearly identical to its output for my original one-liner.

You can submit your filters to Instagram directly from Effect Builder, but effects have to pass a safety review before they’ll be available to other users. Instagram says after an effect is approved, it “shows up in Instagram Stories for anyone to use, and whenever someone uses your effect we’ll link back to your profile so that it’s easy for others to find your work.”

https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/claud.title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/claud.author: Kyle Orland
https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/claud.text:
“Do not ask again” prompt leads to passwords, API keys, and more being shared.

Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.

The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.

This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.

But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. In many cases, Claude Code itself will commit changes to the settings file without the user’s input, Apiiro writes.

Apiiro’s researchers found over 100,000 cases where Claude Code’s local settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. Of these, only about 1,100 from 63 different organizations contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after these files are discovered and removed from a repository, the secrets can persist in forks of the original project if a GitHub user isn’t careful.

Although this security issue is getting more attention now, it was flagged in a Claude Code bug report as far back as August 2025. Other bug reports also noted that the sensitive settings file was sometimes not added to the user’s .gitignore list or that Claude Code could add the sensitive commands to another file that was not protected from git sharing. These bug reports were all closed without action after 60 days of inactivity.

In a comment thread on Hacker News over the weekend, Claude Code’s Boris Cherny said the team is “looking into what we can do to prevent this.” That said, he noted that these settings files should pretty much never be checked in to a user’s git source control and that cases like these seemed to come up only when “the files were manually created and checked in.”

In the meantime, Cherny recommended using Claude Code’s auto mode, which uses classifiers to automatically route “routine permission prompts” without requiring what Cherny calls “manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists.” But when another user noted that sensitive commands can still be saved to settings files in auto mode, Cherny said that was a “good catch” and added that the team is “thinking through what we can do to improve this.”

Cherny also recommends Claude Code users make use of secret scanners—which can trawl files for sensitive information and scrub it out—and said that the team was considering building this kind of secret scanning into Claude Code itself in the future. That said, the Apiiro researchers found that 215 of the roughly 1,100 public secrets it found in Claude Code settings files were not flagged by two popular secret scanners, gitleaks and TruffleHog.

This is far from the only case of an AI agent unintentionally leaking sensitive information. Last month, Meta suspended the sharing feature on its Muse agent after security researchers found the URLs for those links could be easily guessed.

The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. The team is considering building a secret scanning into Claude Code itself in the future.

https://www.zdnet.com/home-and-office/ap.title: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster
https://www.zdnet.com/home-and-office/ap.author: Radhika Rajkumar
https://www.zdnet.com/home-and-office/ap.text:
Home & Office
>
Smart Home
>
Smart Assistants

Apple's public-facing satisfaction with the Siri AI launch obscures internal pressures and tensions.

November 9, 2026, 12:54 pm ET

Apple’s recently appointed CEO, John Ternus, is allegedly pushing the company internally to ramp up its AI strategy — including making Siri an AI agent.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the CEO is publicly pleased with the Siri AI launch, but privately encouraging Craig Federighi, Apple’s SVP of software engineering, to move faster.

“Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri,” Gurman wrote. He added that the tension stems from Federighi’s reputation as an AI skeptic.

The revamped Siri AI is now a much better voice assistant with some helpful features. Gurman noted he thinks Siri AI’s ability to automatically fix your weak passwords is already somewhat agentic behavior, though AI-generated passwords have their own issues.

But Siri AI isn’t yet on par with increasingly autonomous agents from AI-first companies that aim to proactively organize your tasks, use your computer, and write advanced code. Still, those rival agents deliver a patchwork of capabilities: while some, like OpenClaw and Anthropic’s Claude Code, are highly functional, others, like Google’s Gemini Spark, aren’t quite there yet.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a free local AI stack

Regardless, the issue here is time. Despite developing powerful hardware perfectly suited for running local AI models, Apple has remained slower than competitors on the AI software front. Competitors have demonstrated they can make promised agent features a reality, some quicker than others.

Apple’s slower pace in AI has, in the eyes of many, actually benefited its reputation amid a rising tide of public backlash against AI. Some users are frustrated by the software bloat from mediocre or unnecessary AI features, especially as hardware prices skyrocket to accommodate them during a memory shortage. Users also take comfort in Apple’s privacy-first approach to developing AI, which has helped it stand out against other AI products.

Meta’s Muse agent might be an extreme example of data-hungry AI agents, but its privacy trade-offs aren’t altogether absent from other personal agents. Gemini relies on more of your data to be the most effective version of itself, pitting privacy risk against usability.

Also: Meta Muse is the worst AI agent for privacy

On the other hand, the fact that Apple hyped Siri AI for two years only to release an improved voice assistant (rather than a groundbreaking AI product) may mean users are ready for more advanced features.

In addition, AI companies are working on their own hardware. “If they can combine that software with AI-native devices designed from the ground up around assistants that see, remember and act, Apple’s longstanding advantages could begin to matter less,” Gurman wrote.

An agentic Siri would most likely build on what users already like about the new version.

The on-screen awareness feature, for example, is currently limited to what’s visible on your screen in that moment, meaning only the part of a long email that you’ve actively scrolled to. An agentic Siri could ideally scroll all the way through an email on its own and surface the insights you’re looking for.

Also: The iPhone made Apple a giant – but the Mac could help it win the AI era

But in the short term, Ternus’ push will likely just deliver on existing promises. Gurman also pointed out that Siri AI still lacks advanced in-app actions, which Apple initially announced in 2024 and would let third-party apps create plug-ins for and pathways through Siri.

“This functionality would let Siri tap into both in-house and third-party applications with more precision,” Gurman wrote. “This past week, as part of the first beta version of iOS 27.3, Apple finally began talking about the feature again.”

If Siri AI were a competitive agent, many Apple users who trust the company’s ecosystem might move away from installing apps like ChatGPT or Claude on their devices. That’s still unlikely as of now given the wide gap between Apple’s AI and consumer products from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not off the table as public AI backlash and privacy concerns mount.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Plus, if we’re talking about agents specifically, newcomers like OpenAI’s Dot and Anthropic’s Duet aren’t competitive themselves yet: ZDNET’s AI vetter-in-residence David Gewirtz found both to be “a little odd” and not “quite ready for prime time”.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks – and all I got was one helpful notification

ChatGPT’s Computer History feature — which creates a timeline of your app and website activity, and is only available on the Mac — raised privacy concerns when it launched in August. While the feature is opt-in and can be turned off at any time, OpenAI said it does not encrypt sensitive information the feature sees, which leaves it vulnerable to hackers.

If Apple pushes forward with AI, it could design more secure versions of features like these in-house, relying on its well-known and trusted commitment to privacy and to protecting user data.

For users who appreciate the subtlety of Siri AI, though, anything similar to ChatGPT or Claude on their devices might not land, unless each feature is opt-in.

https://www.zdnet.com/uncategorized/andr.title: Android Auto requires Android 11 or higher now – check your compatibility
https://www.zdnet.com/uncategorized/andr.author: Kayla Solino
https://www.zdnet.com/uncategorized/andr.text:
Android Auto's minimum requirements have changed. Here's what to know.

November 9, 2026, 12:46 pm ET

Google has officially phased out support for Android 9 and Android 10 for wired Android Auto use — so you’ll need Android 11 at a minimum to connect an Android phone to a compatible car via USB, according to an update to Google’s Android Auto support page spotted by Android Authority. Android 11 through Android 17, the most up-to-date version, are fully supported for Android Auto (though Android 17’s adoption rate remains quite low).

These changes confirm early reports that Android 10 users saw warnings that their devices would soon lose Android Auto support, even before Google’s documentation had specified the change.

Also: Got an old car? Android Auto is easy to add: 2 ways, starting at $20

It’s not uncommon for Google to drop the oldest Android versions that can still run Android Auto every few years. In 2024, Android 8, released in 2017, was dumped from service. Android 11 was first released in 2020.

Android Auto brings apps to your car display so that drivers can focus better on the road. It allows you to control features such as navigation, maps, calls, text messages, and music, and is the Android equivalent of Apple CarPlay.

Also: 5 Android Auto apps that make my life easier on the road

The requirements have changed little since last year, aside from the new minimum software requirement. The new instructions for wired Android Auto support are straightforward: Phones must be running Android 11 (Red Velvet Cake) or newer, have an active data plan, and be supported by a compatible car. Google also recommends a quality USB cable.

Android Auto is integrated into compatible phones, so you do not need to download it. Android Auto isn’t available on devices that run Android (Go edition).

Also: I was a big wireless Android Auto fan, until I tried wired – now I won’t go back

To find out if your car or stereo is compatible with Android Auto, Google has a hub page to help. For more information about your car’s compatibility with Android Auto on your car display, it’s best to contact your vehicle manufacturer.

For drivers still using older phones running Android 9 or Android 10, getting Android Auto back will require either replacing a current device with one that runs Android 11 or newer, or installing an available software update on a current device.

Also: Gemini on Android Auto can access my photos, emails, and calendar – why I’m OK with that (mostly)

https://www.zdnet.com/tech/samsung-smart.title: Samsung’s new SmartTag 3 debuts with next-gen Bluetooth – and one big problem
https://www.zdnet.com/tech/samsung-smart.author: Jada Jones
https://www.zdnet.com/tech/samsung-smart.text:
Tech
>
Smartphones
>
Mobile Accessories

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 supports emerging Bluetooth tracking tech, but it's not a match for Samsung's OS exclusivity.

November 9, 2026, 12:46 pm ET

Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is now available for purchase in the US, promising a smaller, lighter design than previous generations, compatibility with iOS devices, 550 days of battery life, an NFC-powered Lost Mode, Left Behind Alerts, and an IP67 dust- and water-resistant rating.

Though the Galaxy SmartTag 3 is compatible with iOS devices, the features available to Apple fans are limited, with Ring Phone, Left Behind Alerts, and Compass View reserved for Galaxy users. Compass View is enabled by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, an upgraded Bluetooth distance-finding technology. Despite Samsung embracing a low-cost boost to device tracking, Channel Sounding is locked inside the Galaxy ecosystem, a blow to the technology’s intended purpose.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Channel Sounding is also Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2, but these manufacturers open the technology to all compatible Android phones. However, Samsung’s SmartTag 3 doesn’t rely on Android’s vast but fragmented Find My Device network; instead, Samsung’s take on Channel Sounding will rely exclusively on the Galaxy Find Network. If a semi-closed ecosystem can help make evolving Bluetooth tech more reliable, does it matter that its implementation is counterproductive?

The Samsung Galaxy SmartTag2.

Samsung is the Goldilocks of device ecosystems. It’s not considered a walled garden like Apple, but it’s not as open to full third-party interoperability as Google. Many of Samsung’s most useful features are reserved for use within its Galaxy ecosystem. However, Samsung’s OS is built on top of Android, allowing for more flexibility than iOS, but still offering OS-exclusive features and, more importantly, feature reliability.

Full access to Samsung’s Galaxy Find Network is exclusive to Galaxy devices, similar to how full access to Apple’s Find My tracking features is reserved for Apple devices. On the other hand, Google’s Find Hub can accommodate Android phones from several manufacturers, including Samsung.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect

According to a press release, nearly 900 million Galaxy devices exist on the Galaxy Find Network. Each one’s constant Bluetooth signals contribute to an expansive network of crowdsourced data, extending the Galaxy FindTag 3’s reach and surfacing location data faster.

Google’s Find Hub’s greatest benefit is its scale: it can work with headphones, earbuds, Bluetooth trackers, smartphones, and smartwatches from multiple manufacturers.

However, different ecosystems limit tracking features to basic functionality, showing only where a device was last seen before it was powered off, or emitting a chime if you lose it. Live location data and accurate direction and distance finding from your smartphone aren’t possible.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Implementing Bluetooth Channel Sounding aims to break down ecosystem-specific barriers, especially in a device-tracking context. If your smartphone, headphones, and smartwatch all support Channel Sounding, you could access fine-ranging tracking on all of them, regardless of device manufacturer.

Despite Samsung’s ecosystem providing it a device-tracking advantage, it defeats the purpose of Bluetooth: democratization. Basic Bluetooth connectivity allows any Bluetooth-compatible device to connect to another; that’s why you can wirelessly pair a pair of AirPods with a Lenovo laptop.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

Channel Sounding’s goal is no different in that it aims to bring more accurate distance awareness to Bluetooth-enabled devices, allowing you to finely track a pair of Sony headphones with an iPhone — that’s the goal, but not yet reality.

Samsung instead adopted Channel Sounding for its first consumer-ready endpoint within the boundaries of its ecosystem. Only Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Galaxy S26 Plus users can unlock the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding capabilities when engaging its Compass View feature.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

All of these phones support Bluetooth 6.0 and Channel Sounding, but the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding abilities will only be available to them and future Galaxy phones with Channel Sounding.

Conversely, Google’s Pixel Tag offers Channel Sounding to all Android phones that support it, including Galaxy phones. The result is that the Galaxy SmartTag 3 will operate just like any other Bluetooth tracker when paired with a base-model flagship phone, an older Galaxy phone, or an iPhone.

During this year’s WWDC, Apple announced Channel Sounding support for iPhones with its N1 networking chip and third-party Bluetooth 6.3 devices. Bluetooth 6.3 devices aren’t on the market yet and won’t be for a few years.

I assume Apple’s announcement of faraway future support is to give itself time to decide how Channel Sounding will fit into its walled garden, similar to Samsung’s implementation in the Galaxy SmartTag 3.

Also: How to tell if a hidden AirTag is tracking you – and disable it ASAP

Sure, Google’s Find Hub still needs some maturing; just last year, Google boosted the opt-in opportunities to add more devices for crowdsourced data, Find People is coming to Wear OS, and Find Hub is getting “Notify when left behind” alerts soon.

Apple’s and Samsung’s device location networks may be more feature-rich thanks to their closed ecosystems, but Google is working toward a truly open, easy-to-use network of devices powered by Channel Sounding. Which one is more important to you is for you to decide when it’s time to make a purchase.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.title: Hackers Exploit Qubole's Trusted AWS Access to Breach Customer Accounts and Steal Data
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.text:
An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today.

The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed.

Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions.

The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole, must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID.

Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked.

Any organization that has connected Qubole to AWS, even one that no longer uses it, should check its CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward. The sign to look for is an AssumeRole request from the account Qubole's platform uses, 805246085872, that came from an address outside AWS.

The researchers did not say whether the credentials have since been disabled or whether the activity has stopped. Neither Qubole nor Idera had posted a statement about the attack on their websites when The Hacker News checked today.

Every AssumeRole request tied to the attacker carried an External ID and was accepted, the researchers said in their technical analysis.

AWS accepts an AssumeRole request for such a role when it comes from the trusted account and includes the correct External ID. The code is not treated as a secret, and anyone with access to the role can view it, according to AWS's external ID guidance.

Sentra spotted the activity in several of its customers' environments and alerted the researchers.

In the accounts the researchers examined, the attacker looked for stored credentials. It read environment variables for Lambda functions, pulled secrets from Secrets Manager, and read values from the SSM Parameter Store.

It then ran the credentials it had found through TruffleHog to test whether they worked. These were the victims' own AWS access keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.

The attacker also copied data out of S3. It retrieved data from any bucket a role could access rather than searching for specific data, and sometimes downloaded an entire bucket in a single session.

The researchers have not linked this campaign to any other publicly reported activity, and say the targeting does not match what state-backed groups usually go after.

Qubole also lets customers connect with AWS access keys instead of a role. From October 8 to October 11, an attacker used customers' own AWS access keys, which the researchers believe had been set up for Qubole.

That attacker then compromised a few of the victims' cloud environments. This activity has not been linked to the AssumeRole abuse.

Wiz's hunting guidance covers CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward in every AWS account that holds a Qubole role. Look for:

For every suspicious session, review everything it did afterward, especially in Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda, and S3.

CloudTrail management events log each AssumeRole request and bucket listing, but not which S3 objects were read. That needs S3 data events or S3 server access logs. Several victims lacked the required logs, so responders could not determine which objects the attacker had read.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.title: Hackers Compromise Ethersphere's bee-js and Swarm Desktop to Deliver Wallet-Stealing Malware
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.text:
Attackers used the Ethersphere project's own release automation to publish malicious versions of two of its tools for the Swarm decentralized storage network: bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2.

Both releases download and run code built to steal the wallet key that Swarm Desktop keeps for its node, along with the stored password that unlocks it. The code is also built to install a backdoor on Windows, macOS, and Linux machines.

The bee-js package is the JavaScript library behind Swarm Desktop and the swarm-cli command-line tool. Swarm Desktop runs a Swarm node on a user's own computer and saves the node's private keys there.

Both malicious releases have been taken down, and the project's maintainers released a clean Swarm Desktop update today. Neither step removes a backdoor already installed nor protects a key already sent. No theft of funds had been reported at the time of writing.

Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 appeared on GitHub at about 00:36 UTC today and was withdrawn about 8.5 hours later. The app's built-in updater could offer it to Windows x64 computers and Apple Silicon Macs within about 10 minutes, according to an incident analysis by Socket, a supply chain security firm. Intel Macs were never offered it, and Linux installs do not update automatically.

The bee-js release, version 13.3.0, was the latest version on npm for about 75 minutes, from 00:09 to 01:25 UTC today. Its code runs as a postinstall script, which npm executes automatically during installation unless install scripts are disabled. A project did not need to import the library for the code to run.

The project's own swarm-cli and bee-dashboard packages, and the Swarm Desktop source code, accepted version ranges that included 13.3.0. A fresh install within that window could have pulled in the malicious version.

None of the reports gave a count of infected machines. The firm's rough estimate is that bee-js 13.3.0 was downloaded about 10 times, including by security scanners and mirrors. Swarm Desktop 0.56.2's download count reached 65 by 08:27 UTC, including researchers.

Ethersphere's maintainers withdrew 0.56.2 and replaced it today with a clean release, version 0.56.3. In the change that set up the new release, one of them wrote that 0.56.2 "was published by an attacker using stolen CI credentials and has been withdrawn."

Version 0.56.3 is the same code as the previous version, 0.56.1, signed with a newly issued Developer ID certificate, according to that maintainer's incident note. The note says the app's auto-updater will move installs of 0.56.2 to it, although Linux packages still need to be replaced by hand. A comparison of the two versions' source code by The Hacker News found no changes beyond the version number and release notes.

When The Hacker News checked npm today, 13.2.0 was again the latest bee-js version, and 13.3.0 could no longer be downloaded from the registry.

The GitHub advisory for bee-js 13.3.0 says: "Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised." SafeDep, a software supply chain security company, offers the same advice for any computer on which Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 was installed.

If you run Swarm Desktop:

On any machine where the code ran:

Both releases carry the same loader, SafeDep found in its technical analysis. It is a few lines of code that download more code from api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and run it with the user's permissions. In bee-js the loader is the postinstall script, and in Swarm Desktop it runs each time the app starts.

The downloaded code looks for two files in Swarm Desktop's data folder: config.yaml and data-dir/keys/swarm.key. If both are there, it sends them to the attackers' server.

The key file is an encrypted Ethereum keystore, but Swarm Desktop keeps its password in plain text in config.yaml. With both files, the attackers can take the node wallet's xDAI and xBZZ tokens, its chequebook funds, and its stake, the company says.

The downloaded code also installs a backdoor. On Linux and macOS, it is a Go remote shell called evjawbreaker, saved in a hidden ~/.solidity folder. It runs in the background as a user service on Linux and as a LaunchAgent on macOS.

The shell reads the address of its control server from an Ethereum smart contract, so the attackers can change that address at any time. They had updated it 29 minutes before the malicious bee-js code was added.

On Windows, the downloaded code installs a genuine ScreenConnect remote-access client, signed by its maker, ConnectWise. The client runs as a system service and connects to the attackers' relay.

If the user is an administrator, the code gets administrator rights through a known way around the User Account Control prompt. If not, it shows the prompt again whenever the user cancels. With those rights, it adds a Microsoft Defender exclusion and installs the client silently.

Both releases came from bee-worker, the account Ethersphere uses to automate its releases. Neither change was signed nor submitted as a pull request.

For bee-js, the attackers published a GitHub release for the new version, which started the project's npm publishing workflow. That workflow needed no approval and published the package to npm in 73 seconds, according to Socket.

Because the project's real workflow built it, the package carried valid provenance, the record that links an npm package to the repository and workflow that built it. Provenance shows where a package was built, not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it.

For Swarm Desktop, the attackers manually started a build workflow that had the project's Apple and Windows signing certificates and needed no approval. The macOS app was signed with the project's Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS displayed only its normal first-launch prompt, the firm found.

The maintainers have since made the app's signing jobs wait for approval from the project's DevOps team and run only from the main branch.

How the attackers gained access remained unclear at the time of writing. The maintainer's incident note blames the theft of CI credentials and secrets.

The firm's analysis indicates that two GitHub accounts were used: bee-worker and a long-time maintainer's account. None of the reports explained how the credentials were stolen.

The payloads share an Ethereum contract, a ScreenConnect relay, and file names with fake extensions for Solidity developers that appeared on the Open VSX marketplace in September. Researchers at Pluto Security described those extensions in their October 1 EtherDuck analysis.

Pluto ties them "with high confidence" to the group behind the original SleepyDuck extension, which read its server address from a different Ethereum contract in 2025. Socket says the same group is behind the bee-js and Swarm Desktop releases.

Defenders can search logs and machines for the following.

https://www.darkreading.com/endpoint-sec.title: Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux
https://www.darkreading.com/endpoint-sec.author: Elizabeth Montalbano
https://www.darkreading.com/endpoint-sec.text:
Attackers can exploit a flaw in Claude's document-processing tool by creating a temporary file that Anthropic's AI assistant can access and run on a user's machine.

An attacker can use a flaw in Anthropic Claude's document-processing tool to run malicious code on Linux systems just by creating a temporary file that the AI assistant can access. The flaw highlights a growing risk posed by even trusted AI tools to introduce security gaps in enterprise environments.

Researchers from AIR Security discovered the flaw, which they've dubbed "Office Party," in Anthropic's official DOCX, PPTX, and XLSX skills, which are tools that enable Claude to create, read, edit, and process Microsoft Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, and Excel spreadsheets, respectively.

The vulnerability stems from a helper script, soffice.py, that launches LibreOffice to convert documents, including rendering Word documents as PDFs, they revealed in a report published today. When the script encounters an environment where Unix-domain sockets cannot be opened, it uses a workaround that loads a shared library through the Linux LD_PRELOAD mechanism.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

Anthropic has opted not to fix the issue.

During conversation, the script checks whether a library named lo_socket_shim.so already exists in a shared temporary directory but does not verify its origin or contents. An attacker who can place a malicious library at that location before the next document-processing operation can potentially have their code loaded and executed within LibreOffice, with the privileges of the user running the AI agent.

In this way, the flaw can allow attackers to execute malicious code on a user's Linux machine by exploiting an unverified file path used during document conversion, explains Niv Hoffman, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of AIR Research Lab, in an email interview.

"An attacker gets one malicious file into a shared temporary folder which many programs use, and the next time an employee asks Claude for a document, Anthropic's trusted skill loads that file and runs it," he tells Dark Reading.

The vulnerability affects Linux environments where Unix sockets are blocked, including certain container security configurations, and Claude Code's sandbox. AIR Security reports that macOS is not affected because it does not load the library through LD_PRELOAD.

The AIR researchers demonstrated two ways the attack can work on Linux systems. In one scenario, they manually placed a malicious library in the temporary directory before asking Claude Code to generate a document. In another, they used a separate, seemingly legitimate AI skill to unpack a supporting file into the same directory. When the document-processing skill subsequently ran, the malicious library was loaded automatically.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

The flaw presents a serious issue for enterprises running Linux because it exploits "the default skills that all Claude agents use — [of which there are] hundreds of millions — and one planted file can make them run an attacker’s code with the employee's own access," Hoffman explains.

This second attack scenario is particularly concerning for enterprise security teams because it illustrates how individually benign-looking AI skills can interact to create an attack chain. And often, "companies don't have visibility to which skills and other agent add-ons they have installed, and don't have a red button to revoke or patch a vulnerable one," Hoffman explains.

Moreover, a malicious or compromised skill does not necessarily need to exploit the document-processing tool directly; it may simply need to place a file that another trusted component will execute, according to the AIR researchers.

The AIR team discovered the flaw in May and reported it to Anthropic, which acknowledged its existence, according to the report. However, the AI company "considers it outside its security boundary, since the vulnerable code only runs inside a sandbox," AIR Research Lab's Omri Saxena and Or Nevo wrote in the report. This means that as of now, the helper script still uses the same fixed path and still loads whatever file it finds there, they said.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

Hoffman says that Anthropic's response is "not quite" adequate, "because even if the skills run within a sandbox, the attacker’s code then runs inside it with the user's own permissions, where the user's files and work already are," he says. Anthropic did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment about whether the company would take any further action to remedy the issue.

For businesses deploying AI agents and coding assistants, Office Party reinforces the need to treat AI skills as software dependencies rather than trusted extensions, and secure them as such, according to AIR.

To mitigate, organizations should make it a point to know "exactly what skills or add-ons an organization is using with Claude Code by keeping a live inventory of every AI skill and add-on across employees' agents," Hoffman says. They also should "review even official ones like any other code, and update or patch the whole set whenever a new vulnerability is published."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: He spent a year on ‘Mars’: NASA science officer emerges from mock mission
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Kaia Glickman
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Matthew Montgomery, the science officer of a simulated Mars mission organized by NASA, takes part in a ‘Martian’ geology project.Credit: NASA

Could you survive a year on Mars?

Four engineers now have a well-informed take on the answer. On 31 October, the four emerged from a 158-square-metre, 3D-printed habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, after spending just more than a year inside it for a simulated mission on the red planet.

The exercise was the second in a series of extended NASA simulations that aim to test how long-duration space missions affect astronauts’ health and performance. For more than a year, the crew grew their own crops, conducted science experiments and performed ‘Marswalks’ on a model of the planet’s surface outside their habitat.

Can you terraform Mars?

The mission also replicated the communication delays that astronauts on Mars would experience when contacting Earth: messages from the crew to mission control and vice versa took 13–22 minutes to arrive, varying with the distance between Earth and Mars. The crew even dealt with a planned two-week communication blackout, with no access to mission control or the outside world, that Martian astronauts would face when the Sun blocks transmission of radio signals between Mars and Earth.

The lessons learnt from these simulations will help NASA to understand how isolation and limited resources affect astronauts’ well-being and productivity, the agency says. NASA will use the results to inform protocols for crewed missions to Mars, which it has said could happen as soon as the early 2030s, as well as future trips to the Moon.

Nature spoke with Matthew Montgomery, a hardware engineering design consultant and co-owner of a film production company, who served as the mission’s science officer, to learn about his year on ‘Mars’.

Prior to the mission, I had worked in controlled-environment agriculture and studied factors such as the best LED lighting for crop growth, so I led the growing of our crops in the simulation. I’ve grown leafy greens, peppers and tomatoes outside of the mission in large growth facilities, and we were growing some of those same crops in the mission. It was also fun to grow those plants — just interacting with Earth-based things like plant life has a cognitive benefit as well as a nutrient benefit.

Matthew Montgomery displays vegetables grown in the hydroponic garden inside the simulated Martian habitat. Credit: NASA

Geology was another huge portion of the mission. Rock collection is going to be incredibly important in a real mission to Mars, so we tried to mirror some of those aspects in the simulation. We analysed rock samples, performed mineral identification and simulated core analysis that Martian astronauts would do to study the geologic history of Mars.

The crew spent a lot of time together prior to the mission, so we got to work on our teamwork and build relationships. We went on a winter camping expedition in Wyoming, where we encountered a blizzard! These high-pressure scenarios set a nice foundation for pre-training, where we spent five weeks together before going into isolation. Through all of those tools that we built, we had a really good dynamic as a team inside of the habitat, and conflict was very minimal.

We spent about a month preparing for the blackout. We were communicating with the ground teams to make sure we had all the procedures, schedules and goals for the two weeks. We put safety plans in place to make sure we had reviewed the right protocols if something went wrong.

The mission crew poses outside the door to the simulated Martian landscape. Pictured (left to right) are mission commander Ross Elder, medical officer Ellen Ellis, science officer Matthew Montgomery and flight engineer James Spicer. Credit: NASA

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: Starfish Space loses contact with 1st 'Otter' servicing spacecraft, ending NASA tech-demo mission
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Mike Wall
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
"Starfish, NASA, and Astro Digital have concluded that Otter 24C is not recoverable."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Starfish Space's first Otter has died, just a month after it reached the final frontier.

The Seattle startup announced on Tuesday (Nov. 3) that its Otter 24C satellite suffered a glitch in low Earth orbit (LEO) and is not recoverable.

The anomaly killed an ambitious mission in the cradle, as Otter 24C was still in the commissioning phase.

Otter 24C launched Oct. 1 on SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission, a rideshare flight that carried a total of 130 payloads to LEO (including a prototype satellite for Project Suncatcher, Google's planned AI constellation).

The Starfish satellite was flying a mission for NASA called Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability, or SSPICY for short. The goal was to "demonstrate technologies necessary for future debris-removal missions as well as for future applications in the servicing and inspection of active spacecraft," according to NASA's SSPICY site.

"This advances NASA's in-space manufacturing and assembly (ISAM) goals to ensure a sustainable space operating environment and builds towards a future where objects can be assembled, repaired and maintained in space, significantly expanding possibilities for science and human exploration," the agency added.

Starfish Space was a natural partner. The Seattle company plans to become a big player in the nascent field of satellite servicing, using its line of Otter craft to repair, refuel or deorbit other satellites for a variety of customers.

SSPICY marked Otter's spaceflight debut. The mission plan called for the 739-pound (335-kilogram) Otter 24C spacecraft to approach and inspect "up to four inoperable space objects of U.S. origin" over the course of a two-year mission, performing detailed visual inspections.

But Otter 24C never got the chance to perform any of these orbital rendezvous.

"While working through commissioning steps, Starfish eventually stopped receiving data from Otter 24C," the company said in a Nov. 3 X post.

"An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by [California company] Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications," Starfish added. "Starfish, NASA, and Astro Digital have concluded that Otter 24C is not recoverable."

The company further said that it's implementing fixes to reduce the chances that the problem will crop up in the future. And it stressed that Otter 24C's death will not be in vain.

"The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions, as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit," Starfish said.

Otter Pup 2 is now operating as close as 25 meters away from @GilmourSpace's ElaraSat, fully autonomously. This vid contains imagery captured when we were separated by just 33.6 meters. We’ve demonstrated our ability to safely and precisely operate at very close range, executing intricate maneuvers, gathering detailed imagery, and testing the capabilities we’ll need for docking. With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history.October 27, 2026

The Seattle company has other work to do in LEO at the moment as well: Its Otter Pup 2 prototype craft is currently gearing up to conduct a historic docking of its own in LEO.

Otter Pup 2, which launched in June 2025, has been getting closer and closer to another private spacecraft, Gilmour Space's ElaraSat. Last week, the company announced that Otter Pup 2 got within a mere 82 feet (25 meters) of its target.

"With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history," Starfish Space said in an Oct. 27 X post.

Two private satellites have docked before, but only much higher above Earth, in geostationary orbit. Such a meetup has not yet happened in LEO.

His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Survodutide does not raise CV risk in patients with obesity
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — Survodutide, a novel glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist, was noninferior to placebo for major adverse cardiovascular events, according to the results of the SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT trial.

SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT, presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and simultaneously published in The Lancet, compared survodutide (Boehringer Ingelheim) 3.6 mg once weekly, survodutide 6 mg once weekly and placebo for CV outcomes in adults with obesity or overweight and established cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease and/or at least two weight-related complications or risk factors for CVD.

“This study provides critical data demonstrating that survodutide maintains a favorable cardiovascular safety profile as measured by 5-point [major adverse CV events] to placebo in a high-risk population,” Biykem Bozkurt, MD, PhD, the Mary and Gordon Cain Chair and Professor of Medicine at Baylor College of Medicine and principal investigator of the trial, told Healio.

Among the cohort of 5,508 patients, the mean age was 60.8 years, 39.8% were women, the mean baseline BMI was 36.5 kg/m2, 88.2% had hypertension, 82.6% had dyslipidemia, 52.7% had type 2 diabetes, 16.6% had CKD, 52.9% had coronary artery disease, 35.3% had prior MI, 15.8% had prior stroke and 10.8% had heart failure, according to the researchers.

The pooled survodutide group met noninferiority for the primary endpoint of CV death, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal MI, coronary revascularization or HF events compared with placebo (HR = 0.84; 95% CI, 0.6-1.18; P for noninferiority < .0001), according to the treatment-regimen estimand, Bozkurt said during the presentation. Results were similar using the while-on-treatment estimand (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.53-1.06; P for noninferiority < .0001).

The pooled survodutide group also met noninferiority compared with placebo for the key secondary outcome of CV death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke (treatment-regimen estimand HR = 0.84; 95% CI, 0.6-1.18; while-on-treatment estimand HR = 0.76; 95% CI, 0.51-1.16; P for noninferiority for both < .0001), Bozkurt said.

According to a secondary supplementary estimand, at 72 weeks, survodutide was associated with reduced systolic blood pressure compared with placebo (survodutide 6 mg, –6.68 mm Hg; survodutide 3.6 mg, –5.72 mm Hg; placebo, –1.76 mm Hg; P = .0001), reduced waist circumference (survodutide 6 mg, –11.96 cm; survodutide 3.6 mg, –11.05 cm; placebo, –2.74 cm; P < .0001) and reduced body weight (survodutide 6 mg, –13.7%; survodutide 3.6 mg, –12.2%; placebo, –2%), Bozkurt said.

Bozkurt told Healio that CV outcome trials “are especially important for agents with novel mechanisms of action, as historical experience has demonstrated that metabolic therapies can have distinct cardiovascular safety profiles. We cannot assume that all incretin-based therapies share the same cardiovascular effects simply because they act through related pathways. For survodutide, a novel dual glucagon/GLP-1 receptor agonist, due to potential effects of glucagon on the cardiovascular system, demonstrating cardiovascular safety through noninferiority to placebo was the primary objective of the trial. The trial was designed primarily to establish cardiovascular safety rather than demonstrate superiority.”

The SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT data “confirm that survodutide delivers sustained metabolic improvements — such as reductions in blood pressure and waist circumference — without increasing cardiovascular risk,” Bozkurt told Healio. “For clinicians and patients, this provides confidence: We are not just managing weight; we are safely addressing the interconnected drivers of cardiometabolic disease. By meeting this primary endpoint, we validate that survodutide can provide meaningful cardiometabolic health benefits while protecting long-term health.”

Biykem Bozkurt, MD, PhD, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT, in effect, tells us that the pooled analyses of survodutide vs. placebo showed noninferiority to placebo, meaning we can conclude that there was no evidence of excess harm from these agents. So, when there’s a decision being made about prescribing these agents in the future in clinic, we can use these data to reassure folks that these aren’t going to cause excess harm.

However, this was not a trial that studied survodutide for superiority, so we cannot tell patients that this is going to improve their CV risk.

Given that there are other agents that have demonstrated superiority for CV outcomes, whereas this one has demonstrated noninferiority, that’s where the challenge is, because in 2026 we’re at a point where certain agents have not only proven outcomes, but also FDA approval for the reduction of CV events. So, when making a choice about what to prescribe, I can see agents with proven CV superiority being the ones that we go to in patients with higher CV risk.

I think that selection process from a patient perspective is where some of the nuance is going to come into play. When you’re seeing a patient, you say, ‘OK, we’re going to prescribe you these agents for these reasons. Here are the ones that have been proven to improve CV outcomes. This one is not harmful.’ And then it’s a question of, how’s that conversation going to go? What’s the access issue or the insurance issue? Then, you make a decision. But I think in 2026, it would be beneficial to have evidence about CV superiority to make these decisions, because some of the agents in the class already have those data.

Bozkurt B, et al. LBS.05. Frontiers in cardiometabolic risk reduction. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/bitcoin-7.title: Bitcoin holds near $75,000 after tech stock rout, altcoins suffer steeper losses
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/bitcoin-7.author: Camila Grigera Naón
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/bitcoin-7.text:
A record hack, a blue wave and a tech stock rout have given Bitcoin investors plenty to worry about. Yet the leading cryptocurrency has fallen only about 1% in the past 24 hours and now trades near $75,000. “It could have gotten hit a lot harder,” said John LaForge, chief alternatives strategist at Ned Davis Research. “The fact that it’s still… holding the 75 to 80 [range], I consider it a mild positive.”

Bitcoin’s latest decline came after weekend revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair—and the company’s subsequent investigation into whether he was targeted by Chinese intelligence. The news followed two other setbacks for the industry: a Democratic takeover of Congress that dealt losses to crypto-backed candidates, and a hack that drained roughly $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest centralized crypto exchange.

Broader macro pressures haven’t helped either. The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped over 5% last week in response to fears of a broad selloff in AI stocks. Investors now await Tuesday’s inflation report, which economists expect to show a further rise in consumer prices. Traders also anticipate a Federal Reserve rate hike in December—another potential headwind for crypto markets.

The cryptocurrency has suffered much sharper selloffs in the past. In October 2025, President Donald Trump’s threat of steep new tariffs on Chinese imports triggered more than $19 billion in crypto liquidations within a day. In June, Bitcoin fell below $60,000 to its lowest level of 2026, amid persistently high interest rates and heavy outflows from Bitcoin exchange-traded funds.

Bitcoin’s resilience may say more about how far it has already fallen than about the latest bad news, according to Ish Asad, crypto research analyst at asset manager Bitwise.

“I think a lot of the bad news was priced in already. It’s not to say that it’s not going to chop sideways for a little bit longer, but I think the bottom is clearly in,” he said, referring to Bitcoin’s  June low.

Asad argued that an earlier exodus from crypto into AI investments had left fewer investors ready to sell Bitcoin, which helped cushion its response to the recent turmoil.

That hasn’t been the case for altcoins—the industry term for cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin.

Ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency and the native token of the Ethereum blockchain, has fallen nearly 5% over the past day. XRP, the token associated with Ripple, has posted similar daily losses and is down nearly 12% over the past week. Other major cryptocurrencies have also declined.

LaForge sees the gap as a familiar pattern: “Eventually when prices come down across the board, Bitcoin goes down less, and [altcoins] go down more,” he said.

He expects that divergence to persist in a recovery, with Bitcoin gaining a larger share of the crypto market while many smaller tokens lag.

The leading cryptocurrency has suffered much sharper selloffs in the recent past. The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped over 5% last week in response to fears of a broad selloff in AI stocks.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/us-debt-l.title: The U.S. will hit its debt limit sooner than expected, and the deadline to avoid default could get ‘uncomfortably close’ when Congress is on vacation
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/us-debt-l.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/us-debt-l.text:
The federal government has a $41.1 trillion borrowing limit and is already closing in on it, meaning lawmakers will have to hike it again sometime next year when Democrats are in control of Congress.

Analysts at Bank of America estimated that the U.S. will officially reach the ceiling as early as February, sooner than its prior forecast for May, as there’s only $557 billion of room left in debt outstanding subject to the limit.

The Treasury Department can still keep the federal government up to date on its obligations, such as debt interest payments, using “extraordinary measures” to move cash around from other accounts once the limit is reached.

But the “X-date”—when the Treasury runs out of wiggle room and will default on its bills unless Congress lifts the debt ceiling—will come months later.

The Treasury General Account, essentially America’s checking account, has ample cash for now since the federal government has been raising more money lately via short-term debt. But the exact X-date is a moving target that’s subject to the ebbs and flows of revenue and spending.

“We maintain our X-date forecast of Nov ’27, due to higher starting TGA, but see risk of Treasury getting uncomfortably close to the X-date as early as Aug ’27,” BofA analysts wrote in a note on Friday. “Our projections suggest UST will likely initially guide to Aug X-date given the low headroom.”

An August X-date would be especially dicey because that’s usually when Congress is on an extended recess for the summer, with most lawmakers heading back to their home districts and states.

Of course, leadership can call Congress back in session to raise the debt limit and prevent a catastrophic default. But lifting it is rarely easy as lawmakers have often engaged in brinkmanship to extract concessions.

Adding another wrinkle to the looming debt fight is the blue tsunami in last week’s midterm elections that saw Democrats make stunning gains and flip both the House and the Senate.

They will hold the purse strings when it’s time to raise the debt ceiling, and Wall Street expects them to seek more funding for Medicaid, housing programs, or other affordability priorities that Democrats campaigned on.

But any discretionary spending must compete with the growing mandatory obligation of debt-servicing costs, which now exceed the Pentagon budget and Medicaid as federal borrowing and bond yields have spiked.

In fiscal 2026, net interest payments rose 8% to $1.05 trillion, outpacing increases in total spending, revenue and GDP. That translates to about $2.9 billion a day, and the Peter G. Peterson Foundation estimated interest costs represent 3.2% of GDP, breaking the previous record set in 1991.

While Republicans are still in power in the final weeks of 2026, it’s possible they could raise the debt limit during the current lame-duck session of Congress and deny Democrats a bargaining chip next year.

A prime opportunity would be a deal to keep the federal government funded past a Dec. 11 deadline, when current appropriations will run out. Republicans could attach a debt-limit hike to a funding package, but a funding bill needs 60 votes in the Senate, so Democrats would have to agree. The other route is a party-line budget reconciliation bill, which needs only a simple majority, though Republicans have a narrow margin to work with.

If Congress doesn’t lift the debt ceiling before the end of this year, analysts at BMO warned, “Financial markets could face a protracted debt ceiling standoff in 2027 — raising the risk of sovereign debt downgrades, price distortions ​around the projected X-date, and increased ​volatility in cash and repo markets ⁠should Treasury draw down its General Account to deploy extraordinary measures.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/05/numica-ai.title: Meet the AI company retiring your CPA so he can still see you face to face this tax season
https://fortune.com/2026/11/05/numica-ai.author: Catherina Gioino
https://fortune.com/2026/11/05/numica-ai.text:
Slava Orekoff spends much of his time in West Caldwell, Verona, and Montclair, N.J., talking to accountants who are ready to quit.

Most of them don’t want to stop seeing clients, he says. They just want to stop running a business.

“You have your server down, you have an escalation coming in, your bill didn’t go through with the vendor, you have all these problems with hiring,” Orekoff told Fortune. “Maybe they were excited when they started building their business 25 years ago or 35 years ago. After a while, the things did not excite you anymore.”

Orekoff is cofounder and CEO of Numica, a New York startup that buys small accounting practices from retiring owners, keeps their staff and clients, and moves the work onto its AI software. The company announced Thursday it raised $21 million in combined equity and debt from Roosh X, the investment arm of Ukrainian investment group Roosh, and London-based Flashpoint. Orekoff said most of the money will go toward buying more firms.

Numica launched in June 2025. As of Thursday, it had bought seven practices and serves about 6,000 clients in New York, New Jersey, Florida, Texas, and California, including restaurants, trucking companies, real estate firms, and health care practices. Orekoff said Numica closed its latest deal Monday and expects to close another next week.

Roughly half of the country’s 87,000 small accounting firms are owned by baby boomer CPAs or enrolled agents who will retire within five to seven years, Orekoff said, and fewer people are coming up behind them. Meanwhile, U.S. schools awarded 55,152 bachelor’s and master’s degrees in accounting in the 2023–24 school year, down 6.6% from the year before, according to the American Institute of CPAs.

Even Orekoff has started seeing it personally: Numica’s new head of operations told him that a regional firm she worked for used to get about 150 accounting students a year from a partner state university into its internship program, but now, it gets fewer than 60.

That leaves clients with nowhere to go. “If your CPA is retiring, you are left,” Orekoff said. “What they are buying most of the time is peace of mind.”

From the first day, Numica takes over billing, hiring, and technical systems. The staff accountants that clients already deal with stay in place. Owners can stay on part-time to handle their longest-standing clients, under transition plans that can run up to four years, and Orekoff said most people do just that.

“We were thinking that there will be more stress when it comes to transition,” Orekoff said. “In fact, clients are more appreciative than anything else.” He said some clients have sent congratulations to the owners who sold.

Numica finds firms partly through its own AI tools, which watch broker listings and online marketplaces. Orekoff says the company learns of a new listing within five minutes. Referrals from accountants who have already sold are now its biggest source of deals.

Accounting, Orekoff says, is “about thousands of small things that need to be done,” and those tasks are well documented, which makes them a good fit for AI. Numica’s software codes each transaction, builds the profit-and-loss statement and balance sheet, and prepares state, federal, sales, and payroll tax filings. Orekoff says it covered about 75% of the firms’ workflows in its first year. Accountants check the output, handle unusual cases, and deal with clients. A CPA still reviews and signs the final work.

The company says margins at its first practice, in New York, rose from 37% to 52% within two months, and it projects they will reach 70%.

Clients are told when their firm is sold. Many states require client consent, and Orekoff said consent letters went out two hours after the most recent deal closed. But clients are generally not told AI is doing much of the work.

“Do you care if a calculator or Excel was used to make calculations?” Orekoff said. He allowed that some clients might leave over it: “People are always scared by some kind of new stuff which is unknown.”

Some clients are already using AI on their own. Orekoff says customers now come in after asking ChatGPT how to structure their taxes, and accountants have to explain why the advice doesn’t apply to them.

“A lot of AIs are now programmed in a way that they want to please you,” he said. “Because of that, it will not disagree with you.”

Orekoff started writing accounting software at 17 and worked on it for about seven years before joining SAP, whose systems he calls “glorified accounting” for large companies. He cofounded Numica with Victor Lysenko.

“I’ve never heard of someone dreaming to become a person moving numbers from one spreadsheet to another,” Orekoff said. “The future of the industry is to be more client facing, spend more time with the client.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/goldman-.title: Goldman CEO Solomon says AI financing remains strong despite market jitters
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/goldman-.author: Hugh Son
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/goldman-.text:
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said demand for AI infrastructure financing remains strong and that he expects capital markets activity to continue over the next two months.

Goldman has been “very active” in the markets in recent weeks, despite investor recalibration around AI spending and returns, he told CNBC.

Solomon also pushed back against political resistance to data center construction, arguing that the infrastructure is essential to the U.S. economy and that it can be built responsibly.

Goldman Sachs
 CEO David Solomon told CNBC on Monday that financing demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure remains strong despite recent market jitters as investors reassess the risks involving the massive build-out.

Solomon said that his firm has been “very active” in AI capital markets deals over recent weeks, a setup that he expects to continue.

“There’s still very strong demand for investments in the AI infrastructure build and the technology around the growth of AI,” Solomon told CNBC’s Leslie Picker.

Changes in the political environment are among factors that will “create recalibrations and ups and downs, and we’re seeing some of that,” Solomon said. “But I still deeply believe in the long-term trajectory of the power of AI in our economy to drive productivity.”

AI-related stocks, including chipmakers and neocloud providers, have tumbled in recent weeks as investors reassess whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure will generate good returns.

The selloff, which began before the U.S. midterm elections, intensified after Democrats scored sweeping victories on Tuesday, raising concerns that political opposition could slow the industry’s expansion.

The shifting sentiment comes at a key moment for AI model lab Anthropic, which is preparing for a potential IPO that could become one of the biggest tests yet of public-market appetite for AI companies. Goldman is among the banks leading that IPO process.

“We’ll see, obviously, if this IPO moves forward, how it all plays out,” Solomon said, declining to comment in detail about the IPO. “I would say that the market environment is still pretty constructive.”

Solomon also pushed back against political resistance to data center construction, arguing that the infrastructure is essential to the U.S. economy and that it can be built responsibly.

“We certainly don’t want this infrastructure going to places outside the U.S., which is what will naturally happen because the demand for compute is there,” Solomon said.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/goldman-.summary: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon says demand for AI infrastructure financing remains strong. He says he expects capital markets activity to continue over the next two months. Solomon says he still believes in the long-term trajectory of the power of AI in our economy to drive productivity.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/millions.title: Millions of dollars poured into prediction markets on election night, trading on Democratic control of Congress and Texas governor's race
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/millions.author: Ananya Chetia
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/millions.text:
Election night showed how traders reacted in real time to midterm results, as activity surged and market prices shifted to Democrats after results from Indiana began rolling in before 7 p.m. on Nov. 3.

On election night, at least $1 million was traded on a Kalshi market that incumbent  Gov. Greg Abbott would be reelected. Abbott lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa by more than 700,000 votes.

More than 87% of all election markets across Kalshi and Polymarket gave the right candidate at least a 90% chance of winning their race 24 hours before election night, a CNBC analysis found.

Election night showed how traders reacted to real time midterm results, as trading activity surged and market prices shifted to Democrats after results from Indiana began rolling in before 7 p.m. on Nov. 3. Many midterm races were uncompetitive, which boosted the overall hit rate on prediction markets.

“I’d say prediction markets did pretty well,” said Koleman Strumpf, a professor of economics at Wake Forest University. “But they didn’t outperform the best,” he added, referring to traditional forecast polls that tracked results that night.

Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.

Prediction market saw big trades on election night.

After 8 p.m. on Nov. 3, at least $1 million was traded on a Kalshi market that incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott would be reelected. Abbott eventually lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa by more than 700,000 votes, according to the Associated Press. A little after 11 p.m. on election night, more than $1.4 million was traded on Kalshi that Republicans would not secure control of the House of Representatives.

Following the midterms, both Shayne Coplan, the CEO of Polymarket, and Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour were on the social media platform X crediting prediction markets for correctly predicting races. Nate Silver, a political forecaster and founder of the Silver Bulletin newsletter, disputed the claim, arguing forecast models influenced prediction market movement. Silver joined Polymarket as an advisor in 2024.

“Prediction market probabilities strongly converged toward [our models] in individual Senate and gubernatorial races,” Silver wrote on Silver Bulletin. “I was tracking this stuff closely, precisely because I envisioned that we might wind up in this sort of debate where prediction markets are low-key stealing valor from the models.”

Prediction market volume on midterm election-related contracts across Kalshi and Polymarket more than tripled from the last week of October into the midterms week, according to a CNBC analysis of data published on Predictions.com. The data did not include combo markets, which bundle multiple contracts and pay out only if every leg resolves in the trader’s favor.

Still, volume on midterm contracts pales in comparison with sports volume, which remains larger than all other categories.

Kalshi exceeded $3 billion in total midterm contract volume, according to the platform’s website, which also includes volume for contracts on mayoral races. Last week, Polymarket’s two exchanges reported nearly $700 million in volume for midterm contracts.

While prediction markets broadly anticipated Democratic control of Congress, the blue tsunami is expected to bite the industry in other ways.

Three days after the midterms, Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif, criticized the federal regulator responsible for the platforms, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, for allowing sports contracts.

“Sports prediction markets are sports bets. By effectively requiring prediction markets to offer contracts in all 50 states, even on Tribal lands, the CFTC is once again violating state law and Tribal sovereignty,” Schiff wrote on X.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.
