On election night, at least $1 million was traded on a KalsHI market that incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott would be reelected.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/the-issu.title: The issues a 'really frustrated' Trump may actually work with Democrats on, according to former Speaker Paul Ryan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/the-issu.author: Ian Thomas
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/the-issu.text:
Former House Speaker Paul Ryan said President Donald Trump is likely to become frustrated governing with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Ryan said bipartisan packages could still reach the White House if Republicans and Democrats agree on legislation before presenting it to Trump.

That could include legislation around AI and immigration, Ryan said.

Last week’s midterm election results signaled a massive powershift in Washington, as Republicans are facing substantial losses in Congress while Democrats are looking forward to holding majorities in both chambers.

What that means for the legislative agenda is unclear. The 119th Congress, set to return today, already has a full docket including the extension of government funding and the National Defense Authorization Act, and it’s unclear if Democrats will look to cut any deals with their GOP counterparts in this period.

On top of that, there are other critical priorities coming out of the election cycle, including calls for legislation around AI, foreign policy, tarrifs and trade and immigration and ICE oversight.

Former House Speaker Paul Ryan experienced what it was like trying to legislate under a divided government, with his tenure as speaker overlapping with the final year of President Barack Obama’s term, which featured a divided government after the Republicans took control of the Senate and expanded their majority in the House — a midterm election that was considered a ‘red wave.’

That period, Ryan told CNBC’s David Faber at the CNBC Connect: Balance of Power event on November 5, 2026, was filled with “Venn diagram conversations,” where there were arguments, discussions and then the opportunity to “figure out where we had common ground.”

“Then, we’d say ‘Okay, let’s do that’” Ryan said. “If we were kind of close on issues, we’d say let’s get the right people in the room and see if they can work something out … we had a mechanistic professional relationship that worked out fine. Mutual respect, kept our words to each other.”

So will we see a repeat of that in 2027 as Trump finishes out his lame-duck term?

“I don’t think this one’s going to go like that,” Ryan said.

Trump governed a divided government in the second half of his first presidential term; however, in that instance, Republicans kept a majority in the Senate.

Ryan has been across the table from Trump plenty of times. Despite frosty moments, they endorsed each other’s campaigns in 2016: Ryan endorsed Trump’s presidential bid in June; Trump endorsed Ryan’s House reelection bid in August, after initially withholding support. Ryan served as speaker of the House for the first two years of Trump’s first term.

Knowing what he knows about Trump, Faber asked Ryan how he believes the president will handle this new political environment in Washington.

“Probably not well,” Ryan said. “I think he’s going to get really frustrated.”

Ryan pointed to Trump’s first term, where he had the first two years under unified government and then a divided government for the latter two.

“He’s seen this movie before,” Ryan said. “They impeached him twice; my guess is it’s not going to go well from a temperament standpoint.”

The Democrats’ seismic victory has largely been viewed as a referendum on Trump, especially with his repeated messaging to supporters to vote as if he was on the ballot. Top Democrats have already signaled that they intend to use their majority position to ramp up oversight of Trump, the administration and its dealings more broadly.

Following the results, Trump’s public statements, at least, have been more conciliatory than perhaps expected.

Last week, Trump told CNBC’s Eamon Javers that he can work with Democratic majorities in the next Congress on “many more things than people understand.”

In his first on-camera remarks after the GOP’s resounding defeat on last Wednesday, Trump focused on construction projects he has made a priority, including the partially built White House ballroom and a new helipad on the South Lawn. He did not mention or acknowledge the election drubbing in his remarks until reporters asked for his thoughts.

In an appearance on “60 Minutes” on Sunday, Trump said he was open to working with Democrats, and explicitly mentioned striking a deal around immigration.

Ryan echoed that point at the CNBC Connect event, and said bipartisan legislation around immigration may have found a path forward thanks to the Democratic landslide.

“This hawkish immigration president doing a deal on reforming legal immigration and securing the border with a Democratic Congress would be a good thing for America,” Ryan said. “Fixing immigration would be good.”

On “60 Minutes,” Trump said his administration’s deportation policy was “too tough,” and expressed interest in reforms that would open up legal status for people who have been here for “ten and 15 years.” Trump said that Democrats have already called him to discuss such a deal.

Faber asked Ryan if he believed that Trump and the rest of the administration could get on board with a bipartisan immigration deal, given the obvious tensions with Democrats on this topic.

“Trump’s staff wouldn’t be there, but he himself, I think,” Ryan said. “I’ve had a lot of conversations with him. I think he’s more amenable to fixing legal immigration than the people around him.”

Notably, Ryan’s comments came before Trump appointed Stephen Miller his new chief of staff, who was an architect of Trump’s controversial mass-deportation efforts.

A big determiner of how Trump tries to work with Democrats will be based upon how Democrats look to provide oversight of the president for the remainder of his term, as well as how the party balances its own internal rising groups.

Ryan said that Hakeem Jeffries will have to “manage expectations” of members, especially some of the new wings likely to be formed by first-term electees. While Democrats have a “big oversight plan … they would be foolish to say we’re going to impeach [Trump]. They’ll just make this thing partisan, that would be a ridiculous move,” Ryan said.

Instead, Jeffries should “work hard at building a message of what they’re for, in addition to who they’re opposing and how you oppose the president,” Ryan said. “The other party matters, and so he’s going to have to work on that.”

“That means he’s going to have to say no to a lot of people who are out for blood,” Ryan said of Jeffries.

However, Ryan did say he expects, given the voter focus on corruption, for there to be a lot of oversight hearings “coming our way.”

Ryan said he is watching for a Russian sanctions bill that would be “more airtight” than the Graham Act passed this year, enforcing less waiver authority or a veto-proof threshold.

Ryan also said he believes there is potential bipartisan support for data center or AI-focused legislation stemming from the work of the Jay Clayton-led Super Intelligence Force effort that began in October. That could lead to the establishment of a FINRA-type agency for AI, he said.

Any sort of deal related to the debt limit or debt reduction, Ryan said he is “not holding out hope for that.”

AI was certainly on the ballot in the midterms, and voters on both sides of the aisle made their preferences clear by overwhelmingly backing restrictions on data center development or rejecting measures that would have eased their construction, as well as electing officials who have pledged to do the same.

That happened most notably in Texas, where the largest data center buildout in the U.S. is taking place. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who defeated incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott. has said she wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state. However, she has since softened her stance to potentially allow ongoing construction to continue.

“There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years,” Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning.

“There’s a right way to do this, but I do think, given these elections, data centers just got a little more expensive, and the buildout’s going to be a little longer,” Ryan told Faber.

Ryan said the country is so divided on this that he doesn’t see bipartisan legislation on data center regulation coming out of Congress.

“There are bills that people have put into the hopper,” he said. “There’s going to be an attempt. I have a hard time seeing it get done, just because I think the place is going to be so fractious. I think it’s going to be very, very bitter,” he said, referring to the relationship between Trump and Congress.

Some proposed legislation on data centers is calling for, among other things, disclosures on electricity and water usage.

“That’s going to happen no matter what,” Ryan said, saying that hyperscalers have made multiple missteps in the way they approached communities, failing to address concerns about water, electricity, and AI technology itself and to communicate the benefits, like lower property taxes.

In order to get community buy-in, Ryan said, these companies will be forced to change the way they work with local jurisdictions.

“If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we’re going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them,” Open AI CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC’s Sara Eisen, saying that OpenAI plans to continue investing in the data center buildout.

Regulation, Ryan said, will likely be done on a “state by state, county by county, regulation by regulation, zoning ordinance by zoning ordinance” basis.

Despite the midterm results, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Friday he expects data center growth to continue as projected.

“We respect the localities that decide [to restrict development],” Hassett told CNBC’s Carl Quintanilla. “But America is a big place, and right now, the data centers scheduled over the next couple of years aren’t affected by these ballot initiatives.”

In Ryan’s view, the benefits of having data centers on American soil far outweigh the costs.

“They’re going to get built,” he said, adding that the question is if the U.S. wants data centers to be “American infrastructure for the world” or built by another country.

“What I hope doesn’t happen is they only go to red states that are accommodating and don’t go to new blue states that aren’t. That would be wrong. It would be nice to see this spread across the country,” he said.

Ryan has more hope for bipartisan efforts on AI and the future of work. It’s an issue he is working with think tank the American Enterprise Institute in partnership with the Urban Institute. “We’re trying to build a bipartisan consensus on ... how we handle displaced workers,” he said.

Ryan said it is inevitable that some jobs will be destroyed, but that ultimately, new opportunities will be created.

“The question is, how do we bridge ourselves from here to there?” he said. Potential solutions, he said, could include employment stabilization policies, revamping unemployment insurance and reworking the job training system.

“The policy tools we have today are literally like 100 years old, written back in the Industrial Revolution. So, I think that needs to be modernized and updated. That’s what our commission is working on,” he said.

On the broader question of AI regulation, Ryan said it’s needed to ensure that “we protect against the downside and enjoy the upside.”

“I’m not a doomer by any means, but I’m also not a total accelerationist, total techno optimist. There’s somewhere in between here,” he said. “The question is, can we make sure that we protect against the downside and enjoy the upside? The answer is definitely yes. Good policy can do that. Proper regulation can do that.”

While the shocking results of the midterm elections may suggest that Washington may be stuck in a gridlock until 2028, Ryan was more optimistic, and said the results would allow Republicans and Democrats to “deliver some bipartisan packages that you can bring to the White House as sort of fait accompli efforts. That would be a nice thing to see.”

However, Ryan also noted that if the Republicans want “any chance of winning the White House in 2028, let alone making back gains in Congress, we’re going to have to get some brand separation from what our brand is now.”

“I think that’s going to be really difficult to do because the brand is the president of the United States for the next two years,” Ryan said. “He sucks up a lot of the oxygen and he’s going to have a massive impact in picking the next nominee. So, I don’t know exactly how we get out of that.”

But as for those next two years, which Ryan said will feel “like dog years,” he said the thing to watch from Trump is “what will the distractions be that he comes up with while all these investigations are coming out.”

“He’s pretty good at trying to change the subject and he’s really good at moving the culture and moving the dialogue in America about things,” Ryan said. “What will those distractions be? Will they be cultural war distractions? Will they be things about the Kennedy Center and arches? Or will they be bigger, more material things that affect the economy.”

“That’s, to me, the key question,” Ryan said.

Ryan says bipartisan packages could still reach the White House if Republicans and Democrats agree on legislation before presenting it to Trump.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/b.title: Rent isn't always 'dead money'. Here's why
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/b.author: Lacey  Filipich
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Personal Finance

The security of having your own home is hard to beat, but it's not automatically the right decision. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Owning your own home can give a welcome sense of security, but the jury is out on whether it's the best money move.

We all need somewhere to live and putting our savings into a place we can call home feels like a no-brainer.

Setting aside woeful housing affordability, owning your own home can have five financial downsides.

When you buy a home with a mortgage, you need a deposit.

You can get low deposit loans and there is government assistance, but the rule of thumb remains: a 20 per cent deposit means avoiding lender's mortgage insurance.

If you're getting an average loan — $730,720 in Australia in 2026 – $182,680 would represent a 20 per cent deposit. Adding the mortgage to the deposit, the property price would be around $913,000.

If you're up for stamp duty, you'll need $22,334 if you're a first home buyer in Sydney, for example. It could be as much as $49,850 in Melbourne.

With the cost of conveyancing, building and pest inspections, title searches and a mortgage establishment fee, you can expect to set aside at least $206,000 from day one.

Buying a home means giving up the chance for that cash to grow through investing.

You're hoping the home will go up in value too, but it's harder to access while you're living in it.

Not only have you locked up cash, but it's likely you'll also pay more per week to own than rent initially.

For a $730,720 loan, the monthly minimum repayment would be $4,494 per month – or approximately $1,037 per week – if it's a 30-year loan at 6.24 per cent interest.

If you compare the mortgage repayment with the rent for a sample suburb in each capital city where the median house price is close to $913,000, you're likely to pay between $141 and $490 a week more for the mortgage than you would rent at the start.

Owners also pay things such as council rates, building insurance, maintenance and strata fees.

Assuming 20 per cent on-costs, the gap between renting and owning becomes $348 to $697 a week more expensive to own at purchase.

If you've avoided investing because you've found the terminology intimidating, you're not alone.

That gap should close eventually as rents rise. When it does, the cost to rent the same home will outstrip the mortgage and on-costs for the remaining period of ownership.

But that can take years, even decades.

You're not only paying more until it does, but you're also forgoing the opportunity to invest that $348 to $697 a week on top of the $206,000 you locked up.

The maths only works on owning over renting if you stay in the home once theoretical rent outstrips the mortgage.

If you move, incurring agents' fees on the sale and another round of stamp duty along with a new (often larger) mortgage, the maths can reset and you lose some or all the ground you've gained.

Locking yourself into home ownership before deciding where you want to be based long term can tip the maths in favour of renting.

But all this pales in comparison to the biggest upcoming risk.

Given homes are so expensive, they inevitably form a significant proportion of your financial assets.

Because they mostly need debt, there is added risk compared to an asset that you own outright: you might end up owing more than the home is worth, known as negative equity.

This has been rare in Australia given how fast house prices have been rising, but it may be in the post for one in 11 properties forecasted to be uninsurable by 2030. It was one in 25 just four years ago.

If you can't get building insurance, the bank won't approve a mortgage. This means potential buyers must pay cash only.

Cash-only buyers are a much smaller pool than buyers in general, so the advantage in property negotiations may move to the buyer's side.

It means those property prices are likely to drop.

This is a rapidly rising risk in Australia and could tip the balance more firmly back in favour of renting, especially in areas exposed to natural disasters.

No. The security of having your own home is hard to beat.

This is as much a question about how well you sleep at night as it as about money.

With Australia's age pension sitting close to our (unofficial) poverty line, it's hard to argue against home ownership in retirement.

It also doesn't preclude property investing while renting, known as rentvesting.

You can get a foot on the property ladder with a view to eventually either living in the investment property or selling it to help fund a home.

The leverage that threatens negative equity can also work in your favour, with growth potentially outstripping what you'd earn on an investment elsewhere.

Don't fall for the "rent is dead money" schtick. You need shelter the same way you need food, and we don't call grocery bills dead money.

Older generations swear by home ownership partly because they're already on the property ladder, and it's likely they got on it well before house prices escalated in comparison to wages.

Lacey Filipich is a financial educator and the author of Money School.

This article contains general information only. You should consider obtaining independent professional advice in relation to your particular circumstances.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/k.title: New documentary dissects an Australian tragedy from all sides
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/k.author: Velvet Winter
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback examines the police shooting death of Kumanjayi Walker. (Supplied: SBS)

Warning: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this article contains the name of an Indigenous person who has died.

Since 2019, Australia has grappled with the death of 19-year-old Warlpiri man Kumanjayi Walker.

The teenager, who was armed with medical scissors, was shot three times and killed by Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe.

Reckoning has come slowly. First it was through a 2022 Darwin jury trial in which a jury found Rolfe not guilty of murder.  Then came a multi-year coronial inquiry that found the "hallmarks" of racism embedded within the Northern Territory police.

It was this tidal wave of uncomfortable information that led Blackfella Films producer and director Darren Dale (Redfern Now, Mabo) to 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback, a comprehensive four-part docuseries that chronicles the before, during and after of one of the darkest moments in modern Australian history.

A longtime producer for Blackfella Films, 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback is Darren Dale's directorial debut. (Supplied: SBS)

Dozens of interviewees present their reflections throughout the series — from Walker's family members to police officials, legal professionals, journalists and community elders.

For Dale, it was the only way to understand the full breadth of the tragedy.

"I think the binarism that exists in the world leads us to not hear a lot. I really didn't ever want us to feel like we were shouting at people," Dale told ABC News.

"The power of hearing is one of the reasons I think this project for me feels vital. If we can listen and not look away, we might just understand what happens in our own country."

Death in The Outback trailer

It has been a long road for Dale, who travelled to Alice Springs and Yuendumu shortly after the coronial inquest began on the encouragement of Andrew Boe, a barrister for the Walker families who also appears in the series.

"I met some of the family, just to see and hear the things that were revealed at that inquest. I came straight back to Sydney, organised a meeting with SBS and said, 'Look, this story demands to be told over four hours,'" Dale says.

"[But] this story just isn't a story about Kumanjayi's family. This is a story about police. This is a story about people associated with the fallout. When one of these sort of calamitous tragedies happen, the fallout for everyone is immense."

Warlpiri elder Ned Jampijinpa Hargraves is one of 39 people interviewed for 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback. (Supplied: SBS/Sherwin Akbarzadeh)

The series first establishes the context of Yuendumu, a remote community about 300km north-west of Alice Springs, famed for its rich artistry and beleaguered with a long history of police violence and Walker's place within it.

Through interviews with family members and the professionals who cared for him, Walker is described as a funny, energetic, young man with under-identified cognitive and developmental difficulties and a history of run-ins with the justice system.

Rolfe is described by colleagues as a proactive officer who developed a reputation for pursuing difficult arrests within a police culture that rewarded risk-taking.

Zachary Rolfe applied to be a police officer after being discharged from the Australian Army. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The days leading up to Walker's death and the night of the shooting are presented through largely unseen police worn body cam footage.

In one body cam clip post-shooting, an injured Walker is heard repeatedly wailing for his mother, Leanne Oldfield, who also features in the series.

"I felt that it was really important that if you're ever going to choose to look, you should look at this," Dale says.

Later, the body cam footage shows the frenzied aftermath of the shooting in which a dying Walker was locked in a police station while his community was prevented from seeing him or learning about his condition.

Only Derek Williams, a local Aboriginal police officer and Kumanjayi's uncle, was allowed inside but not for long enough to get a read on the situation. Walker's cousin Samara Nangala Fernandez-Brown and other residents began to broadcast live on social media as the growing crowd demanded information on Walker's condition.

Samara Fernandez-Brown was in Yuendumu on Monday July 7 2025 to hear the NT coroner's findings into Kumanjayi Walker's death. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"I stood outside that police station and I realised that from where the family was sitting, to where Kumanjayi was dying was between 7 and 11 metres away," Dale says.

The community gathered outside were not immediately informed of Walker's passing, assuming that an arriving police aircraft was taking Walker to Alice Springs for urgent medical attention.

In reality, the aircraft was there to bring police reinforcements in and get Rolfe out — he was airlifted to hospital for a shoulder wound. It wouldn't be until the early hours of the following morning that the community was informed of Walker's death.

"We wanted to truly understand what it was like to be outside and what it was like to be inside, what it was like to be black, what it was like to be white, what it was like to be a law enforcement officer, what it felt like to be like Derek Williams," Dale says.

Among the 39 people interviewed for 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback, Dale says there's one more he would have liked to include: Zachary Rolfe himself.

Rolfe declined an interview for the series, with Dale instead including his testimony from the coronial inquest and 2022 interviews he conducted with Seven's Spotlight program.

Here's what happened when former Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe took the stand for the first time in the coronial inquest into the 2019 police shooting of Kumanjayi Walker. WARNING: This story contains offensive language.

"We needed to understand why he wanted to become a police officer. It was important that you knew that he went to Afghanistan to serve. It was important to know just the amount of jobs that he'd done as a young constable. These are uncomfortable truths we have to confront," Dale says.

The second half of Death In The Outback veers towards the three-year coronial inquest led by Northern Territory coroner Elisabeth Armitage. In 2022, when first questioned about his own alleged racism and that within the force, Rolfe declined to answer questions for fear it would expose him to penalty.

Then in 2023, Rolfe was dismissed from the Northern Territory police force in relation to a 2,500 word statement he posted online. When he returned to the inquest stand in 2024, Rolfe disclosed racist award ceremonies conducted by the Northern Territory police. When senior police figures initially denied the accusations, Rolfe and his team supplied certificates proving the use of offensive images and language used by NT police.

NT Coroner Elisabeth Armitage speaking in Yuendumu on the 2019 police shooting death of Kumanjayi Walker.

On July 7 last year, Armitage travelled to Yuendumu to deliver her findings: Kumanjayi's death was avoidable and Rolfe held racist attitudes in an organisation with the hallmarks of institutional racism, along with 33 other recommendations.

The series asserts that as of March this year, only 11 had been explicitly fully supported by the Northern Territory government and police.

"Who would have ever thought that Zachary Rolfe would be the whistleblower on racism in the NT police force?" Dale says.

"That, I think, is one of the most extraordinary ironies. I think it led the coroner to make the findings that she did.

"Will this bear the fruit that it needs? As Andrew Boe says, let's wait and see."

"All the communities all over, they just rang us up and they said that wasn't fair," Western Arrernte artist and Yuendumu local Elizabeth Katakarinja Napaljarri says during 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback. (Supplied: SBS)

As the release of 2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback approaches, Dale is feeling "trepidatious" but acknowledges the great privilege of being able to present all sides of a bitterly sad situation.

"I hope the series gives people an insight into how ill-equipped both men were and how as a country we've allowed that to happen," Dale says.

"As Kate Wild [author of award-winning book The Red House] says in the show, some people thought Kumanjayi had it coming and other people thought Rolfe was a bad cop but it's not as simple as that. It's never as simple as that."

2.6 Seconds: Death In The Outback premieres on SBS and SBS on Demand from November 10.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.title: Operator of Neil the seal merchandise website fined for false claims
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.author: Meg Whitfield
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Consumer Protection

A Neil the seal sticker that had been for sale on the website was AI-generated. (OpenAI)

The operator of a former website that sold Neil the seal merchandise has been fined, after "falsely" claiming links with conservation organisations.

The website claimed to donate a percentage of its profits towards marine wildlife conservation.

The website was taken down earlier this year.

The operator of a website that claimed to donate a percentage of its profits from Neil the seal merchandise to conservation efforts has been fined by a New South Wales regulator.

The "Neil the seal official" website, which was taken down after questions about its claims to support marine conservation. (neilthesealofficial.com)

The 'Neil the seal official' website, which has since been taken down, advertised merchandise featuring the popular elephant seal that visits beaches in Tasmania's south biannually.

The real Neil the seal delighting onlookers at Seven Mile Beach in Tasmania. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

On its website, the company stated it financially supported marine conservation, with a "portion of every purchase" going towards "marine conservation work protecting seals, sea lions, and ocean ecosystems in Australia and beyond".

It said it was "building formal partnerships with conservation organisations" and that "direct donate links and clearer reporting on impact will be published here as those partnerships are confirmed".

The now-closed website claimed to support marine conservation. (neilthesealofficial.com)

The conservation organisations the website initially claimed to "support and recommend" included the Australian Marine Conservation Society, WWF Australia, Tasmania's Department of Natural Resources and Environment (listed on the website under its former name of DPIPWE) and the Marine Mammal Foundation.

But the three organisations and the government department told the ABC earlier this year they had not had any contact with the company, nor had they received any donations from it.

A $150 hoodie sold by the "Neil the seal official" website. (neilthesealofficial.com)

After being contacted by the ABC earlier this year, the website tweaked its wording to say "organisations we recommend", and removed references to "official partnership details coming soon".

It also added links to donate directly to the organisations, but shortly afterwards, the website was taken down.

A website claimed to donate a percentage of its profits from its Neil the seal merchandise to marine wildlife conservation, but the listed organisations say no partnership exists.

New South Wales Fair Trading carried out an investigation into the site and, in a statement, a spokesperson said it "found the operator of the 'Neil the seal' website falsely claimed an affiliation with conservation organisations".

OpenAI's AI-generated image detection software showed that a Neil the seal sticker for sale was AI-generated. (OpenAI)

The merchandise listed on the since-shut website claimed a sticker it was selling, depicting Neil the seal, was designed by a "local artist".

But OpenAI's tool for detecting AI-generated images found the sticker was created "using OpenAI tools".

Multiple other items received the same result.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/h.title: Hobart's new lord mayor pledges to 'turn the ship around'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/h.author: Meg Whitfield
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Local Government

The new Hobart City Council, (from left to right) Zelinda Sherlock, Ryan Posselt, Simon Behrakis, Harvey Lennon (partly obscured), John Kelly, Mike Dutta, Bill Harvey, Charles Wooley and Louise Elliot. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

The new Hobart City Council has officially been sworn in following the recent elections.

The council has drawn headlines in recent years for in-fighting and social media conflicts, and the new mayor is vowing to turn things around.

The council's deputy lord mayor will be elected by the councillors at their first meeting, on November 16.

Hobart's new lord mayor has pledged to "turn the ship around" at the council's official swearing-in ceremony on Monday evening.

Hobart City Council has attracted headlines in recent years for in-fighting, code-of-conduct complaints and social media stoushes, with the recent local government election campaign similarly rife with personal attacks between candidates.

This included accusations of agism, ongoing debate over "snack-gate", and a fiery confrontation involving a lord mayor hopeful's parents at a forum.

Earlier in the year, the former council had already been put on notice by acting Director of Local Government Luke Gregory, who warned all councillors to stop "disrespectful" and "demeaning" conduct at meetings or risk formal action.

The municipality's newly elected representatives were sworn into their roles on Monday evening.

Charles Wooley has asked for patience and cooperation from his fellow councillors. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Of the nine representatives, seven served on the previous council, with one of two new faces including the Lord Mayor, veteran 60 Minutes reporter Charles Wooley.

Speaking at the ceremony, Councillor Wooley said he was not interested in "political power or social engineering".

Instead, he said his focus would be on being a "people's mayor".

"I could not have chosen a worse time to become lord mayor. The public are angry, and they have cause," he said.

Reflecting on the turbulence of recent terms of council, Councillor Wooley urged his fellow elected members to leave any political allegiances at the door.

Charles Wooley says Hobartians want a "people's mayor". (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Mr Wooley ran on a slogan of "Hobart for Hobartians". When asked what that means, he said it was a "great question".

"Now, it's not an easy ship to turn around. It's sailed off-course, it was sometimes erratic, sometimes apparently dogmatic, but the people in the wharf noticed.

"I ask for only two things. I ask for patience of you, my fellow councillors. I ask for your mutual co-operation, and I ask that you might not rule for the political parties that put you there, but for the people who did, the people of Hobart."

Proudly wearing a kilt of MacGregor tartan, Councillor Wooley paid tribute to his Scottish heritage, having been born on the Isle of Arran.

Charles Wooley spoke of his Scottish heritage during his speech at the swearing-in ceremony. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

He also reflected on the path that brought his family to Tasmania, his journalism career, and reiterated his support for council amalgamations.

This year's elections included a statewide reduction in the number of councillors from 263 to 213. In Hobart, that included a reduction in councillor seats from 12 to 9.

Former lord mayor Anna Reynolds did not contest the election. She served in the top job for eight years.

The newly sworn-in councillors will elect a deputy mayor at their first meeting, on November 16.

Councillors waiting to be sworn in at the ceremony. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

It follows incumbent Ben Lohberger winning the position, but failing to secure a council seat — something that has only happened a handful of times in recent decades.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.author: Lin Lin
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Housing Construction Industry

Bathla Group went into voluntary administration in August, owing at least $3.4 billion in debts.  (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

ASIC has launched a formal investigation into the collapsed Bathla Group but has not revealed what conduct is being investigated.

The corporate regulator has spent months investigating the developer's borrowing arrangements and the role of private lenders in its collapse.

Administrators have been granted until September next year to convene the second meeting of creditors.

Australia's corporate watchdog has launched a formal investigation into the affairs of collapsed Bathla Group, a sprawling property empire comprising more than 500 companies.

"I can confirm we have commenced a formal investigation in relation to the conduct of the affairs of the Bathla Group," Simone Constant, commissioner for the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), said in a statement.

The regulator has not disclosed the specific conduct under investigation.

ASIC has also been examining the role of private lenders in Bathla's collapse, including how billions of dollars were raised and whether retail investors have been exposed to losses.

"We are making inquiries in relation to private lenders but have not commenced any formal investigation at this stage."

Administrators of the Bathla Group have been given up to another year to run the voluntary administration. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

Bathla, one of Sydney's largest residential property developers, entered voluntary administration on August 25 owing creditors at least $3.4 billion.

The collapse has left the future of more than 200 projects in doubt, including roughly 2,000 homes under construction and another 13,000 in its development pipeline.

Construction has ceased across the group's projects, while administrators Teneo are pursuing the orderly sale of undeveloped land and other assets.

Private lenders have been moving to seize control of Bathla properties used as security for their loans.

The NSW Supreme Court has granted administrators until September next year to convene the second meeting of creditors, giving them more time to investigate the group's complex financial affairs.

Bhart Bhushan is listed as the sole director of Universal Property Group, which trades as Bathla. (ABC News)

The corporate regulator has been examining Bathla for several months, including the group's borrowing arrangements and whether any misconduct had occurred.

Before Senate estimates last month, ASIC chair Sarah Court said the regulator was working closely with administrators to trace the loans to Bathla across its more than 500 companies and 40 lenders.

Speaking at a parliamentary joint committee into financial services in early September, Ms Court said ASIC been engaging with Bathla and its administrators for the past month and was examining whether any misconduct took place.

The formal investigation into the company comes amid a broader crackdown on private credit.

If you have more information about this article or any other tips, you can securely contact reporter Lin Lin at linreporting@proton.me

On Monday, ASIC issued interim stop orders against two Angas Securities funds over disclosure concerns, including one fund's exposure to Bathla Group.

ASIC previously investigated the property developer in 2011 over alleged unconscionable lending practices resulting in Bathla co-founder Bhart Bushan and Universal Property Group, Bathla's main corporate entity, agreeing to a compensation scheme for affected homebuyers.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.author: Grace Tobin and Kate McKenna
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Daryl Fladung describes a drone flying above him in one of the last videos he posted to his Telegram channel. (Telegram: Daryl Fladung)

A security guard who left Australia to fight for Russia against Ukraine is missing and feared dead.

Daryl Fladung's mother says she hasn't heard from him in almost five months.

ABC Investigations has uncovered videos, photos and online posts made by Mr Fladung in the final days before his disappearance.

Daryl Fladung wore an Akubra-style hat, a banana-patterned shirt and a broad grin in a picture posted in April at a Moscow airport.

The 38-year-old security guard had left Queensland to join the Russian army in its invasion of Ukraine, despite having no military experience or known family ties to eastern Europe.

He entered into a contract with Russia before undergoing basic combat training with other foreign mercenaries.

But within days of posting about being sent to the front line, unconfirmed reports started spreading online that Daryl "Dundee" Fladung had been killed by a drone strike.

His mother has not heard from her son since late June.

"I think he's an idiot for doing it. But there's nothing I can do about it," she told ABC Investigations.

"I just want to know if my son's alive."

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) would not confirm if it had any information about Mr Fladung's disappearance.

He is the first Australian known to have joined the Russian army since the full-scale invasion in 2022.

ABC Investigations has uncovered details of how the Queenslander got involved with a recruitment network luring mercenaries from the UK, US, and Europe on ideological grounds.

This is how a security guard playing video games in his mother's outback home ended up on the battlefield.

The night before Daryl Fladung left Australia for the final time, his mother says she talked with her only child for three hours about his "stupid" decision to join the Russian army.

"To be honest, I didn't think he would go through with it," she said.

"I said, anything is better than that. He didn't listen."

Daryl's mother agreed to speak to the ABC on condition of anonymity.

"Part of me is scared. I mean they're going to call him a traitor and all this stuff, so what do they do to a family who has a traitor?"

Mr Fladung worked for 10 years as a security officer in shopping centres, bars and clubs, and on nighttime mobile patrols.

His mother says he was diagnosed with an autism spectrum disorder and could become "fixated on certain things". He'd been living with her rent-free in a rural town west of Brisbane because he was depressed, withdrawn and "in debt up to his eyeballs".

She believes he met a man online playing "live action war games" who convinced him to fight for Russia as a solution to his problems.

"He was just a desperate guy trying to get some money," she said.

"They got him at the right time when he was weak and vulnerable. They said everything magical, and it worked."

She doesn't know who her son was speaking to, but ABC Investigations can reveal that in April Mr Fladung took a one-way ticket to Moscow.

He was met at the airport by two Putin-supporting British nationals, Ben Stimson and Bradley Townsend.

Daryl Fladung (right) with Ben Stimson (left) and Bradley Townsend (centre) on his arrival in Moscow.  (Telegram: Ben Stimson)

Mr Townsend, 33, was reportedly killed by a drone in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region only 10 days before Mr Fladung disappeared.

A photo of the trio taken at the airport was posted to more than 1,170 subscribers on Stimson's Telegram channel.

"Meet Daryl our latest volunteer from Australia. Thats [sic] a proper Aussie hat there bro. Stay safe guys," Stimson's post read.

Ukrainian authorities allege Stimson plays a key role in an English-speaking recruitment network that lures and trains foreign fighters for Russia.

He has been involved in the war since 2015, when he joined pro-Russian rebels. After serving a prison sentence in the UK for terror offences, he reportedly received Russian citizenship earlier this year and is a member of Vladimir Putin's United Russia party.

In late April, Ben Stimson posted this photo of Daryl Fladung (bottom right) and Bradley Townsend (top left) with a group of "other international volunteers from Latin America and Europe". (Telegram: Ben Stimson)

Stimson told ABC Investigations he spoke online with Mr Fladung for months.

"Daryl used to follow my [YouTube and Telegram] channels," Stimson said.

"Then he said he was coming over, and a lot of the times when Westerners say they're coming over, it's bravado."

"I said, 'well this is what you can expect, you don't know where you're going to end up, it's where your commander sends you. And if you're coming over, can you bring me some Vegemite because I'm running low on Marmite.'"

Despite previous media reports that Stimson acknowledged helping at least 10 foreign fighters join the war, he denies luring Mr Fladung to Russia.

He told the ABC the reason he greeted the Australian at the airport was to pick up two jars of Vegemite, before then introducing him to a recruiter.

Ben Stimson said he asked Daryl Fladung to bring him Vegemite as he was running low on Marmite. (Telegram: Ben Stimson)

"People contact me and I tell them exactly what to expect. If they still come, that's up to them," he said.

"I introduced him [Fladung] to the recruiter at the airport who worked for a Moscow recruitment, a military recruitment thing.

"That was it. I'm not a recruiter."

He says Mr Fladung signed a contract along with Mr Townsend. But Stimson says he takes no responsibility for what happened next.

More than 3,500 foreign fighters from more than 40 countries have died fighting for Russia in the Ukraine war, a BBC investigation found earlier this year.

Daryl Fladung's recruitment appears to mirror that of several other foreigners who shared their journeys online.

After arriving in Moscow, the Queenslander started a public Telegram account under the username "Daryl Fladung (Dundee)" and uploaded what appeared to be a photo of himself wearing camouflage and holding an assault rifle at a training camp.

Daryl Fladung posted this photo to his Telegram channel in April. (Telegram: Daryl Fladung)

He also shared a link to a podcast interview he'd done with a former British soldier turned Russian marine, Mike Jones, who actively promotes a pro-Russia website offering monthly salaries, signing bonuses and citizenship to foreign recruits.

In the video titled 'Fed Up with the West!', Mr Fladung complains of Australia's youth crime, homelessness and "out of control" tent cities.

"I feel that I have more in common value-wise with Russia than I do with anywhere in the West," he said.

Daryl Fladung was interviewed for a pro-Russia podcast within days of arriving in Moscow in April.  (Telegram: ForeignAgentIntel)

Mr Jones told the ABC Mr Fladung gave him the contact details of his Russian girlfriend, called Marina, "just in case".

When ABC Investigations spoke to Marina, she claimed they matched on an international marriage dating site six months ago but never ended up meeting in person.

"Daryl called me his future wife. But he disappointed me with his actions," she said.

His mother says Mr Fladung thought he could leave the Russian army at any point if he changed his mind.

"I did notice in some of the pictures he sent that there was always an armed guard with him, so he wasn't free once he got there," she said.

"I don't think he really realised what he was doing or what he got himself into."

A Russian army document seen by the ABC shows Mr Fladung signed up on April 29.

Daryl Fladung's military contract with the Russian Federation. (Supplied)

A month later, he posted to his Telegram account about injuring his left knee and heel during combat training.

After spending 10 days in the medical bunkhouse, he revealed he was being sent into combat without any more training.

"I have been told im [sic] going to frontline storm tomorrow night or the day after," he said on June 10.

"What total bullshit.

"Still unable to run and unable to full [sic] recover and only at 70% at best."

A week later came an update from what appeared to be a battlefield.

"My knees need a MRI and CT scan but I will still been [sic] sent out of [sic] foot anyway, still can't run or sprint and that makes crossing fields a game of chance and luck," he wrote.

"Tomorrow is another 5km hike through rough terrain and Drone infested open spaces, I pray get though [sic] it safely."

His final public post appeared the following day on June 20.

"My physical condition has dropped alot [sic] due to no sleep and no medical, lack of food and now I can only do a snail pace…

"I will be lucky if I dont [sic] collapse within the 1st few kms of walking.

"The pain though [sic] the roof, my moral [sic] dropping faster then [sic] any bomb.

"I can only hope and pray I survive long enough to get sent to a hospital."

His account has been inactive ever since.

Daryl Fladung has not posted to his public Telegram account since June 20. (Telegram: Daryl Fladung)

For five months now, his mother has been scouring social media for any information about her only child.

"Is there any proof Daryl (Dundee) from Australia being dead," she posted on his account last month.

A user who responded, "he is dead," previously posted that a "friend" in the same unit had claimed Mr Fladung was struck and killed by a First-Person View (FPV) drone.

The ABC has been unable to independently verify this claim.

Russia's foreign ministry and its embassy in Australia, and Ukraine's ministry of defence, did not respond to questions about Mr Fladung's disappearance.

A DFAT spokesperson said the government advised Australians not to travel to Ukraine or Russia because of the war.

Recently, Mr Fladung's mother left a public comment under a video posted the day before he vanished.

It reads, "I love you my son."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/w.title: Why cost-of-living concerns are up-ending global politics
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/w.author: Ian Verrender
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Donald Trump's ill-fated decision to bomb Iran came back to haunt him in the midterms. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Two countries, two elections, two very different results.

But the political upheaval in both was driven by the same economic forces running rampant across the globe.

Soaring inflation globally has spurred voters to up-end the political status quo in both the United States and New Zealand in the past week.

A hasty fix that crashes the economy might quicken Labor's march to a Trumpocalypse of its own making.

While the Trump administration was humiliated by the massive swing against it in America's midterms, NZ's political fate is still too close to call after several high-ranking ministers were turfed out of office.

In both cases, cost-of-living pressures loomed large over voters as governments and central banks globally struggle to contain a pricing breakout dumped upon them by Donald Trump's ill-fated decision to bomb Iran.

Both election results will have a profound impact on Australia.

America, our defence partner and a magnet for Australian superannuation funds, is key to the prosperity of many Australians, while NZ's floundering economy in the past four years has a significant impact on the size of Australia's workforce.

Investors are reconsidering AI's future in light of the Democrats' midterm election victory. (Reuters: Max A. Cherney)

After the US midterm results were largely welcomed by Wall Street investors on Wednesday, the technology-heavy Nasdaq exchange experienced a brutal sell-off on Thursday night before partially recovering on Friday.

Investors remain twitchy about how Democrats will view the AI boom.

A growing international backlash against the construction of massive data centres in urban and rural areas has raised fears that the expected pay-off for the massive investments in artificial intelligence will be seriously delayed, causing a major market correction.

The results of both elections, however, highlight the growing impotence of governments and central banks in curbing inflation after three decades of artificially low interest rates fuelled an explosion in debt at a government, corporate and household level.

Last year, global government debt hit a staggering $US112 trillion ($162 trillion), with America accounting for the lion's share: about 38 per cent.

As inflation remained bottled up since the late 80s, interest rates declined, particularly after market upheavals such as the tech wreck and the Global Financial Crisis, and tapped out in negative territory during the pandemic.

That encouraged governments to run ever-expanding deficits. And while consumer price inflation remained in the doldrums, asset prices soared.

The cost of housing doubled and then trebled in many of the world's developed economies as stock markets continually hit new records, creating a growing wealth chasm within many societies.

That is now bubbling over into a wellspring of discontent.

And it has occurred at a time when the cost of servicing public debt has soared, leaving governments hamstrung in their ability to alleviate the growing inequality within society or, in the case of many developing nations, unable to provide basic services.

The war in Iran and massive tax cuts for the wealthy have blown American government debt out to 126 per cent of GDP with little scope for reversing the trend. And whichever party tries to scale back will be deeply unpopular.

Australia's government debt, meanwhile, sits at 33 per cent, low by international standards but expanding as a result of ongoing budget deficits.

Cost-of-living pressures loomed large over the New Zealand election. (Reuters: David Rowland)

The Coalition has been blaming federal government spending for rising inflation and another impending rate rise for Melbourne Cup Day, but the figures tell a different story.

The New Zealand economy has been in and out of recession since the pandemic.

While technically that no longer is the case, growth is anaemic and twitchy.

The National Party government led by Christopher Luxon, elected three years ago on a platform of reining in inflation and promoting growth, has struggled to live up to the promises.

Hence the backlash over the weekend.

Luxon and his predecessor, Jacinda Ardern, are not entirely to blame for the country's economic woes.

Much of that can be traced home to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, which adopted a gung-ho attitude to killing inflation after the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

The world's first central bank to raise interest rates, it sent them to 5.5 per cent, tipping the country into debilitating recessions on several occasions.

The official cash rate is now at 2.75 per cent, but with soaring fuel prices, inflation is again well outside the target zone at 3.7 per cent. With growth so patchy, raising interest rates isn't much of an option.

As with Australia, wage growth has lagged inflation, eroding workers' living standards amid a growing sense of frustration.

NZ, however, does have a safety valve. It's called Australia.

Whenever economic conditions deteriorate, many Kiwis simply pack up and head west for work.

With little or no visa requirements and with generally higher wages, it's a no-brainer.

During the past few years, Kiwis have been heading across the Tasman in numbers only ever exceeded in 2012, in the aftermath of the GFC.

In the three years to mid-2026, about 120,000 Kiwis headed to Australia, with a smaller number heading home.

Given what RBA governor Michele Bullock has described in recent years as a tight labour market in Australia, the influx was a welcome trend, adding skilled workers to the mix here.

Without it, NZ's jobless rate of 5.7 per cent would be much higher, and unless the country's economic woes are addressed, expect elevated levels of trans-Tasman migration in the next few years.

But after five rate hikes here this year, continued net migration to Australia is likely to put pressure on our rising unemployment rate.

While the risks of a sovereign debt crisis continue to mount, they have been overtaken in the past month by fears of a shake-out on Wall Street, and particularly AI stocks.

Is Nvidia facing a spy scandal?

Those concerns coalesced last on Thursday night, just a day after the Trump administration was shaken to the core by the overwhelming rejection of American voters in the midterms.

The day before, immediately after the results, markets boomed in the hope that Trump would walk away from his war with Iran, allowing stability to return to energy markets, the main driver of the inflation blowout this year.

But concerns that Democrats would now impose controls over data centre construction sent Wall Street into a tailspin, with tech stocks shedding about 6 per cent.

Given Australian superannuation funds have as much as 20 per cent of investments parked on Wall Street, with the vast bulk of that $800 billion in technology stocks, the US economy and Wall Street's performance have a direct impact on the wellbeing of most Australians.

November is generally a good month for US stocks. And, according to former investment banker Mike Mangan, a Republican loss in the midterms is almost a guarantee of outsized performance.

Ever since Eisenhower lost Congress in the 1954 midterms, a Republican president losing in the midterms has returned an average of 2.1 per cent the following month.

"Only once in 1974 did this not happen," Mangan says.

Over three months and over a year, the returns were spectacular.

But this year is unlike most others. Soaring inflation, the worst energy crisis in half a century, a stock market that has run hard for a very long time and growing unrest on the streets.

Like many other countries, the opposing party didn't win; it was the ruling party that lost.

And unless the Democrats can take action to turn the country around, they are likely to suffer the same fate down the track as increasingly desperate voters shift politics from the centre to the extremes.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.author: Conor Duffy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Torrens University is facing a class action for underpaying casual academics. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Torrens University has admitted to underpaying casual academics at Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide.

The lead plaintiff said staff were left unable to pay rent, after being expected to carry out routine academic tasks without payment.

New figures show the total amount repaid to more than 200,000, mostly casual, university staff across the sector has reached $341 million since the ABC first revealed the problems in 2020.

Australia's beleaguered university sector has been put on notice over long-running exploitation of casual staff, as private university Torrens prepares to defend the first known wage theft class action in the Federal Court.

The American owner of Torrens also revealed it had budgeted more than $20 million to compensate casual academics for historic underpayments, with lawyers for the lead plaintiff saying the true bill could be far higher.

Lawyers for staff estimated more than 1,000 casual academic staff were not paid for marking student work and other routine tasks for at least six years, despite provisions in their award.

"It's taken an enormous toll on the staff," said lawyer Hayden Stephens, who is running the class action.

Hayden Stephens says he hopes the class action will put the sector on notice. (Supplied: Adam Taylor)

"You have to remember that marking an assessment is an enormous or significant burden in the work of a casual academic, and for that work not to be recognised by their employer, is obviously wrong and in breach of the award, but carries with it an emotional toll."

The Fair Work Ombudsman, with the support of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU), has already established in a case before the full Federal Court that Torrens staff were not paid for marking in breach of their award.

Torrens was declined leave to appeal to the High Court.

According to earnings reports filed last week in the US by its American owner, Strategic Education Inc, the university has set aside more than $20 million to compensate staff directly.

Torrens University has set aside $20 million to compensate staff. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Strategic Education did not give an estimate of its potential liability in the class action but told the market it intended to defend the claim "vigorously".

Mr Stephens, who has interviewed dozens of casual academics, said the $20 million figure Torrens University acknowledged it owed staff in back pay appeared "grossly inadequate".

"The devil is in the detail, and so far Torrens has given casual academics none of it. Will Torrens pay for the hours people actually worked? Will lecturers get access to the records they need to check their own figures?" Mr Stephens said.

"Workers who have already been underpaid should not have to take the word of Torrens or its US owner. Any remediation of this scale should be independent and verified under the supervision of the court."

Tutors at some of Australia's sandstone universities are being told to do a "poor job" and "skim read" student essays, amid growing concerns about underpayment of staff in the sector.

Torrens University declined to comment, citing the court action, but noted a statement on its website that said it was "working to remediate staff".

The statement said staff had been paid for marking since March 2026. The university has operated in Australia since 2014 but the statute of limitations for back pay was six years.

Mr Stephens said the first known wage theft class action should put the entire university sector on notice to improve its treatment of staff.

"It's significant for the brazen way in which Torrens chose to ignore this duty to pay casual academics. Our fear is that if one university is allowed to behave this way, others will," Mr Stephens said.

The lead plaintiff in the case, Tito Scohel, taught at Torrens University between 2023 and 2025, motivated to train the next generation of community, youth and mental health support workers.

"I enjoyed the job. I still like the job. I'm still teaching. I love it," Mr Scohel said

But he said the university's failure to pay him for marking as well as other academic tasks like moderation, meetings and student consultations left him struggling to pay his rent.

"People worked three to four jobs to survive because none of them were paid the right level of payment," Mr Scohel said.

Tito Scohel says he could not pay his rent while working for the university. (Supplied )

"Most of the academics that I have, my colleagues, they are doctorate or having two or three masters. And, you know, the payment they received is very nominal. It's appalling."

Since ABC News first revealed wage theft at four universities in 2020, problems have been revealed across the sector, and the NTEU said 205,235 staff had now been repaid $341,092,552.

Flinders University has apologised for underpaying 1,405 current and former staff an amount that equates to roughly $687 underpaid per person.

"We're looking at really industrial-scale wage theft that's been baked into their business models. And unfortunately, the problem never seems to be resolved. There's never the proper accountability, there's no proper transparency," NTEU president Alison Barnes said.

Most of the cases have been at public universities, but Dr Barnes said the Torrens case could be the first of many more to come at private providers.

"We're really concerned about this conduct. I suspect Torrens is the tip of the iceberg," she said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq2d.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 16 people
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq2d.text:
At least 16 people have died and 13 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas plant, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.

The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.

Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.

Eyewitnesses said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.

In a statement, the company said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.

Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people are believed to be still under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued. He also said two of the injured were in a serious condition.

At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.

The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr5.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr5.text:
A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.

"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.

The effort will likely fail, given Republicans will remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says he wants to push President Donald Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch an impeachment process.

Hegseth, who will hold a news conference on Tuesday about Massie's move, said he was not concerned.

"We're not worried about that," Hegseth said when asked by reporters about the impending resolution on Monday, adding he would hold a news conference Tuesday morning "on that very topic".

Hegseth's last news conference was in May.

Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, is among the few Republicans who have been critical of Trump and the war that started earlier in this year in Iran.

The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and is now pressing for a vote in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said his push to rid the administration of Hegseth is meant to prevent a Democrat spectacle next year.

"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."

"President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," he also said.

Impeaching a cabinet secretary is very rare. The impeachment must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not agree on either one.

Once Massie introduces his resolution - expected later on Monday - Speaker of the House Mike Johnson must schedule a time to consider it within two days. Along with voting on the resolution directly, the House has the option to vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.

Massie will likely have the support of the Democrats in the House, with that party's leader, Hakeem Jeffries, saying on Sunday that he is a "hard yes" on impeachment. But Massie would still need to win over members of his own party.

The House has passed a War Powers resolution - a measure that seeks to halt Trump from taking further military action in Iran - multiple times this year, with Massie's support.

But Massie's disagreement with Hegseth also goes beyond Iran, he said in the statement.

He has accused Hegseth of intimidating critics of the Trump administration, kidnapping foreign leaders and ignoring congressional war powers resolutions.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr5.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie says he wants to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. Massie is among the few Republicans who have been critical of Trump and the war in Iran. Heg Seth says he is not concerned about Massie's move.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.title: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.text:
Aleesha Adams joined a video call with Kashim Chowdhury in May 2023.

He'd been on sick leave from his job at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for nearly three months and Adams, his line manager, wanted to put a plan in action to ease him back into work.

At the start of the call, Chowdhury was coughing and waving tissues up to the camera in an attempt to show how ill he was. But what really caught Adams' attention was how pale he looked.

She noticed white powder had started separating from his forehead. "He was sweating, it was like rubbing off, so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck," she told his trial.

She claimed he was wearing white make-up to look sick. Something he denied in court.

Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer.

That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office. He was contracted to work 183 hours a week – more than the number of hours in seven days. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.

In total, he had eight overlapping full-time public-sector jobs between 2020 and 2023. During that time, this relatively junior civil servant was paid £350,000.

Soon after her call with Chowdhury, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it, he blamed it on a technical error. She told the jury at his trial at Southwark Crown Court: "I believed he was lying." She escalated her concerns up the chain.

But his fraudulent behaviour remained undetected. Chowdhury was able to keep working multiple government jobs until September 2023 when he left the Civil Service.

He was finally caught in 2024 by the government's National Fraud Initiative, which conducts searches of Civil Service databases, such as payroll, every two years to look for anomalies.

On Monday he was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and told by the judge that he would be facing a "very substantial custodial sentence".

Chowdhury, 56, arrived each day at court alone. He is married, yet there never seemed to be any friends or family there to support him.

He would often make his way down the corridors of the court building carrying two plastic carrier bags, with a bobble hat perched on his head.

He sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box.

Chowdhury, who had a diagnosis of PTSD in 2015, said that he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment. He said he'd been forced out of a job at the Department for Education in 2013.

He said he hadn't been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".

But the prosecution argued his behaviour was "deliberate" and "intentional dishonesty" and that he had exploited the system.

However, the case raises important questions for the Civil Service. How was he able to get away with it for so long?

Part of the explanation is that the Civil Service's human resources system is not centralised. Chowdhury did not declare on government application forms that he was already a civil servant, so the system did not spot the duplication.

Hannah Keenan, who works at the Institute for Government, says the system clearly failed. "Government departments are taking hiring decisions independently of each other and without systems that join up," she said.

"That the model and the culture surrounding it aren't working shouldn't be a surprise though - we've known for a long time about poor performers flying under the radar by shuffling between jobs."

There are more than 550,000 people employed across the Civil Service, many in offices in Whitehall, in central London. They are responsible for carrying out government policy and the daily administration of the country.

Another reason why Chowdhury's fraud went undetected is that he was working entirely from the east London house he shared with his mother. In 2023, she had dementia and terminal cancer, and he told his employers that he needed to be at home to look after her.

But rather than reducing his workload to concentrate on her care, he took on more jobs. He covered up his impossible daily schedule by getting sick notes from his GP.

In April 2023, he was off with what he called "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" from Defra, the UKHSA, the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.

While the sick notes were shown to the jury, they were not given evidence about what caused the depressive disorder or of a psychiatric assessment having been done during this period.

His sickness did not prevent him from starting yet another job – this time at the Home Office. He did not mention to them he was ill, nor did he tell them he was working elsewhere.

Unsurprisingly, a succession of his line managers told the jury he had not been very good at his jobs.

Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney, who managed Chowdhury at Defra. He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time" and that Chowdhury kept his camera off during video calls for four months, claiming technical problems.

But because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job. He remained there for two years.

In September 2023, Chowdhury was found to have more than £40,000 in his bank accounts as well as significant investments, including £45,000 in premium bonds.

A recent survey of 1,700 civil servants by the independent think tank Re:State found 76% of respondents thought it did not do a good job of tackling poor performers.

An ex-senior civil servant told the BBC that much of the Civil Service is culturally averse to performance management.

"Whitehall's known for ages it has to be less risk averse. Shrinking the Civil Service and the adoption of artificial intelligence technology make that more vital," they said.

"But don't underestimate the fear factor: fear of drawn-out grievances and fear of being accused of wasting taxpayers' money if the Civil Service was to do what big private sector firms do, which is cut to get rid of poor performers by offering some money and a settlement agreement."

A Defra spokesperson said: "Kashim Chowdhury abused the trust placed in him as a public servant and defrauded taxpayers out of almost £285,000. He will now rightly face the consequences for his actions.

"This conviction is the result of a thorough and painstaking investigation led by the Defra Counter Fraud and Investigations team. It sends a clear message that fraud against the public purse will not be tolerated and those responsible will be held to account."

The spokesperson said Defra would use "all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending on behalf of taxpayers".

Chowdhury's case also illustrates a wider issue.

He was engaged in what is being called "polygamous working", where people hold down several jobs secretly. Websites have even been set up offering people advice on how to keep their employers in the dark.

Its rise has been blamed on larger numbers of people working from home.

The government's National Fraud Initiative has identified 23 cases of "polygamous working" across London in its most recent report. It uncovered £500,000 of overpaid salaries over a period of a few months.

Alongside the fraud case, Chowdhury is involved in a legal dispute with his three siblings, who accuse him of ''bullying'' their mother into signing over half of her £2.1m home to him in the final days of her life. He denies it.

At times during his criminal trial, Chowdhury appeared confused by what he was hearing and blamed trauma for the web of lies he had spun. The jury took seven hours to reach their verdict and decided he was motivated by personal gain - stealing tens of thousands of pounds from the taxpayer.

Chowdhury now faces a significant custodial sentence.
