https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Witnesses recount struggle to save people buried in ‘horrifying’ Gaza landslide
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
High winds and heavy train triggered collapse of sand bank overlooking camp for displaced families

Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a landslide triggered by high winds and heavy rain in Gaza.

A sand bank overlooking a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah collapsed on Sunday, killing five people and crushing at least three tents.

“It was a horrifying sight,” said Abdul Karim al-Sahhar, 30, originally from Izbat Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza. “We saw people buried beneath the sand and rocks. None of them was moving or making a sound. Even the tent had disappeared completely. There was no trace of it left.”

Among the casualties was an eight-year-old, a six-year-old and their mother.

Sahhar, whose own shelter was badly damaged in the landslide, said the children’s father was outside the family tent and so survived. “One of his children had called him to come and eat with them,” he said. “He was a little late returning, and then the collapse happened.

“The father started shouting: ‘Save my children! Save my children!’ People came and started digging [but] there was a huge boulder on top of the victims. The young men had to break it into pieces so they could reach the people buried underneath.”

Abu Darbali, another witness, said the collapse of the embankment sounded like an explosion. “We found that three tents were covered completely after the mountain collapsed on top of them,” he told Reuters. “People were under the rubble and we couldn’t see them.”

Video posted to social media showed residents using hammers to break large rocks and others removing sand with shovels, searching for people trapped underneath using flashlights.

The UN said more than 26,000 households had reported damage to shelters or belongings after the weekend’s rainstorms.

The vast majority of Gaza’s population of 2.3 million live in tent encampments or the ruins of bombed-out buildings, ‌with reconstruction yet to begin after Israel’s relentless two-year military assault launched after the Hamas attacks on southern Israel in October 2023.

“The collapse [this weekend] was waiting to happen. [Gaza] is extremely overcrowded. People are just trying to find a place wherever,” said Toby Fricker, a spokesperson for Unicef, which has been working to prevent similar tragedies and improve drainage in camps for the displaced.

In a statement, the Hamas-run government media office said about “70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day” of rains. It also noted the “collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries”, some critical, in various areas of the tiny territory.

A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made. Negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops, which control about two-thirds of the territory ‌from which residents have been ordered to leave.

Israel says no reconstruction can happen before Hamas is disarmed.

Sahhar said he and his family were now homeless. “My tent and everything I own are now buried under the sand. My mattress, household utensils and all my belongings – everything was buried. I could not retrieve anything,” he said.

Mustafa Qazzaat, a member of the Gaza City council, said Israel had not allowed prefabricated homes to shelter the displaced since the truce was announced, and only permitted the entry of limited numbers of tents.

Many so-called “dual use” items remain restricted, such as metal tent poles. Humanitarian workers said they instead had used wooden poles fashioned from palettes used to transport food.

Cogat, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees aid to Gaza, said over 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks containing tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothinghad reached Gaza, as well as convoys carrying supplies of fuel and engine oil to power pumping facilities and other humanitarian installations.

Earlier this year, an assessment compiled by shelter specialists in Gaza revealed that thousands of tents supplied by China, Egypt and Saudi Arabia to shelter displaced Palestinians offered only limited protection against rain and wind.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: High winds and heavy train triggered collapse of sand bank overlooking camp for displaced families. Witnesses describe frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by landslide. Five people killed and three tents crushed by sand bank near Deir al-Balah, Gaza.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Senate votes on bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Hilary Beaumont
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Environmentalists torn over procedural vote to boost infrastructure projects but weaken environmental laws

It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja), which is scheduled for an initial procedural Senate vote on Monday.

Donald Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes.

Earthjustice, Sierra Club and the ACLU have come out against the bill because it would significantly weaken environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa) and accelerate the construction of gas pipelines and ICE detention centers.

Indigenous groups held a press conference on Friday calling on senators to vote against Baaja because it would weaken the federal government’s legal obligation to consult tribes on projects that affect them. “This is such an existential threat to Indian country,” said Mark Macarro, president of the National Congress of American Indians.

Protesters rallied outside Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer’s building on Friday over concerns that the bill could boost datacenters. “It would be highly ironic if, having won an election where datacenter opposition was at the front and center, the first act of Congress was to make it easier to build datacenters,” said Bill McKibben.

Democrats elected in the blue wave will not take their seats until January, so the bill’s proponents still have time to rush it through the Senate, and technically there is time for it to pass in the House before new Congress and go to Trump.

But the election success for the Democrats is dialing up the political friction. House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the House speaker in the new Congress, said the bill “falls short in several areas” including failing to protect tribal sovereignty, and he would not “rubber-stamp legislation without more constructive involvement with our caucus”.

On Monday, the bill’s Democratic sponsors, Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, said they had the votes to pass the bill. Heinrich said they had made last-minute changes to ensure tribal consultation, and they believed the bill would favor renewables over fossil fuels. “If we can create an open, competitive level playing field, clean is cheap, and cheap wins in the marketplace,” Heinrich said.

Whitehouse, who wore a tie with wind turbines on it, argued that passing the bill would set the stage for Democrats to work on clean energy policies next year with majorities in the House and Senate. “People should just cool their jets and have a little faith that this is not the end of the story,” he said.

Proponents of Baaja say it is needed because it takes too long to build large projects in America and the bill shortens timelines. It simplifies federal rules for building interstate transmission lines, it narrows what gets reviewed under the National Historic Preservation Act and limits tribal consultation, it limits the use of the Clean Water Act, shortens timelines for the Endangered Species Act, limits how the executive branch can interfere with federal permitting, and makes big changes to Nepa such as changing what requires Nepa review and who has standing to sue.

The fossil fuel industry is backing Baaja. The American Petroleum Institute (API) hailed the bill as “a historic opportunity” and called on congress to “finish permitting reform this year”.

“It creates a very accelerated fast track for gas pipelines,” said Earthjustice Action’s president, Abbie Dillen. “The gas industry is extraordinarily excited about this because they are interested in expanding existing pipeline capacity to get more liquefied natural gas out for export, and to be feeding power-hungry datacenters with gas.”

The bill could help pave the way for the Constitution gas pipeline that Williams Companies is trying to build through New York. The state denied the project’s water quality permit in 2016, but the company has revived the project under the Trump administration. The proposed pipeline could benefit from the bill’s changes to the Clean Water Act.

Baaja could also enable construction of gas pipelines in the west. Fossil fuel advocacy group Western States and Tribal Nations wants to build gas pipelines to feed domestic datacenters and export LNG from the west coast. During a 3 November election day meeting with New York’s Sweetwater county board of commissioners, the advocacy group’s president, Andrew Browning, said he was talking to lawmakers about the bill: “The permitting bill’s a huge thing … We’re going to need that for everything we’re envisioning and building out.”

Some clean energy advocates want the bill to pass because it would connect renewables to the grid. Wind, solar and battery storage are now cheap to build, but the country lacks the necessary transmission lines to bring clean energy where it’s needed.

Interstate transmission lines can take a decade to get built, and energy projects also face a bottleneck in connecting to the grid. At the end of 2025, 2,060 GW of total generation and storage capacity were waiting in a queue to connect to the grid.

Ben King, energy and climate director at Rhodium Group, said Baaja would reform the interconnection queue process and unlock the ability to build the transmission that is needed. “We’re at a pretty low point for policy support for clean [energy],” he said, referring to Trump’s repeal of clean energy tax credits. “[Baaja] sets up the ability to build stuff more quickly for when the next wave of climate policy happens.”

Many experts have modeled what the bill would do to emissions, but there is a lot of uncertainty on that question. Rhodium Group’s analysis found that domestic emissions go down if Baaja passes. But another model by the Purdue engineering professor Kevin Kircher found it would increase domestic emissions.

Kircher said the optimistic case for Baaja is that there’s a huge amount of clean energy ready to go, and if we get rid of the long queues and regulations, “level the playing field and let it rip”, then clean energy wins on the economics. “I think that understanding is outdated,” he said.

What the bill does to emissions partly depends on what type of energy gets connected to the grid. Rhodium Group assumed, based on a report from 2025, that 85% of the capacity added to the grid would be renewables. But Kircher said some grid operators have updated their queues this year to remove redundant and speculative offers. (PJM’s queue as of 3 August looks quite gassy.)

King said the economics show an impressive decrease in the cost of renewables, while fossil fuels are not getting any cheaper. “Some of it is just a bet on what’s going to win out in the future,” he said. “Our modeling suggests that clean stuff is going to dominate energy expansion for the foreseeable future, and there might be people who have a different view on that. API might have a different perspective – they might bet that there’s more room for them to grow.”

Kircher emphasized that the various models have not had time for peer review since the bill was first introduced on 30 September. “We need to have some humility in recognizing that the process of taking that 417 pages of super dense legal text and mapping it … is extremely complicated and full of uncertainties,” he said.

The bill would significantly reduce the scope of Nepa. It would narrow the definition of a “major federal action” that would trigger Nepa review, and effectively eliminate the authority of courts to enforce Nepa compliance.

Nepa is the powerful law that attorneys used to block the Trump administration’s plans to convert 11 mega-warehouses into massive ICE detention centers. If the bill passes, it could accelerate the development of ICE detention centers, according to a letter the American Civil Liberties Union sent to senators. “As written, this bill would hamper, if not altogether thwart, critical work by the ACLU and our partners to halt ICE’s dangerous expansion of immigrant detention,” the letter said.

Baaja’s passage would be “the single biggest overhaul” of American environmental laws since the 1970s, said Dillen of Earthjustice. “There are legitimate concerns that Nepa has been weaponized to slow down important projects, but people have recognized this problem for years, and the law has been reformed, and it’s also been weakened very significantly by the supreme court. What this bill does is take the last pieces of it that are very relevant in an administration like this,” she said.

Trump has pushed a “drill, baby, drill” fossil fuel agenda, and Baaja’s weakening of environmental regulations would further embolden him, Dillen said. She pointed to Trump’s plan to allow drilling near Chaco Culture national historic park, a Unesco world heritage site. “Chaco Canyon is in the crosshairs,” she said.

“At Earthjustice, we are deeply committed to building clean energy and to do it in a time frame that is meaningful, given the threats that we face. But the way to do this, the way to build our country better and even faster, is not by running over tribes and by emboldening a president who voters have just come out in a historic turnout to push back on,” Dillen said.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The bill would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America. It would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. The bill is scheduled for an initial procedural vote on Monday.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: John Fetterman to be challenged for Senate seat by democratic socialist born in Gaza
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robert Tait in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian American, said he would run in a primary to be the Democratic nominee in 2028

US politics live – latest updates

John Fetterman, the maverick Democratic senator who has provoked widespread anger by increasingly siding with Republicans, is to be challenged for his Pennsylvania seat by a democratic socialist candidate who is originally from Gaza.

Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian American, said he would run in a primary to be the Democratic nominee in 2028, when Fetterman’s seat is up for re-election.

The move is the first sign of Fetterman’s weakened position in the party since the Democrats won back control of the Senate in last week’s US midterm elections, when the party won at least 54 of the upper chamber’s 100 seats.

The prospect of a comfortable Senate majority in effect eliminates the possibility of Fetterman’s vote being decisive, a relief to Democrat strategists who feared he could no longer be relied on for support on contentious issues.

Fetterman had already caused widespread disillusionment among many Pennsylvania Democrats, who campaigned for him in the 2022 midterms when he ran as a progressive outsider.

But he has sparked anger by, on occasion, speaking out in support of Donald Trump, who in turn has praised Fetterman as “a great guy” and said he would “love” him to become a Republican.

Moor, 42, a writer and journalist who was born in the southern Gaza city of Rafah and has previously written for the Guardian, told the Philadelphia Inquirer that he was “not really running against Fetterman”.

“I’m running for good government. I’m running for the rule of law. I’m running because I believe in America,” he said.

But his Palestinian background throws down the gauntlet to Fetterman’s vocally pro-Israel stance, which has become increasingly strident since the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas that left about 1,200 people on the Israeli side dead. More than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza – most women and children – were killed in Israel’s retaliatory military response.

Fetterman has said he has no intention of leaving the Democrats but strongly suggested would change his mind if the party became “anti-Israel”.

“That’s my red line,” Fetterman said last July. “If the Democratic party becomes official anti-Israel, then that’s when I would force me out. If they make it the official platform of the party, then that’s a much different situation.”

Fetterman has met more often with Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, than with Philadelphia’s mayor, Cherelle Parker, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer.

Moor, by contrast, said he supports withdrawing US aid from Israel and imposing sanctions aimed at securing equal rights for Palestinians.

Democrats say Moor is unlikely to be the only challenger to Fetterman, who provoked outrage in his own party in September by sending a video message to the Republicans’ midterm convention in Texas in which he praised Pennsylvania’s Republican senator, Dave McCormick.

“I’m pretty confident that you’ll see some bigger, mainstream kind of names, involved,” said Mike Weidinger, a veteran Lancaster county Democrat with state-wide connections, who cited Chris Deluzio, a representative from the Pittsburgh area, and Malcolm Kenyatta, a Pennsylvania state legislator, as likely challengers.

“Generally people think [Fetterman] either misrepresented himself when he ran the first time, or he changed completely from what he said he was,” said Weidinger.

“We just had an election here in Pennsylvania where a lot of us busted our ass for [Pennsylvania governor Josh] Shapiro and a lot of other people, and he didn’t spend one penny or do one thing for a single Democrat candidate here last week.”

On the possibility of Fetterman joining the Republicans, he added: “If he wants to switch, he can switch. If it would have been 51 to 49, it would have mattered. But it doesn’t matter now.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Jensen Huang’s affair: why did Trump ignore the warnings? | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The AI chip boss’s actions raise urgent questions about corporate influence, national security and the US president’s willingness to listen to intelligence warnings

I
t could be the plot of a spy thriller. One of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution admitted to having an affair with a Chinese businesswomen said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. When Donald Trump was briefed about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s liaisons with Alice Huang, he took no action. Perhaps he thought only marriage vows had been broken. Or perhaps Mr Trump was willing to overlook the conduct of a friend who championed his unpopular datacentre expansion, whose company donated to his White House ballroom and who echoed his opposition to AI safeguards against expert advice.

Nvidia became the cornerstone of AI by supplying brute computing power. As tech giants scrambled for the firm’s graphics processing units (GPUs), Mr Huang sold the picks and shovels for the AI gold rush – and amassed a $160bn fortune. When China joined the race for tech supremacy, Nvidia’s microchips became a national security issue. In October 2022, the US slapped export controls on GPU sales to China. Thirty months later, Nvidia was effectively banned from selling to Beijing. Mr Huang lobbied for looser controls. Such was his sway with Mr Trump that the White House scrapped Biden-era global AI chip restrictions and then permitted sales of Nvidia’s prized H200 processors to Chinese customers.

Democrats, buoyed by their midterms’ success, will be looking for answers. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence, the president replied: “No, I don’t think so.” That makes the question of his reasons unavoidable. There could be trouble at Mr Trump’s commerce department if it backed Mr Huang’s policy agenda and loosened export controls despite knowing of his affair with a Chinese spy. Reports suggest that the commerce department’s probe was halted after Nvidia called investigators. Congress clearly has grounds to investigate whether the Trump administration knowingly disregarded a foreign intelligence threat. Whatever happens next, Mr Huang’s admission is likely to be the beginning, not the end, of the saga.

Rumours had swirled for months that Nvidia’s boss had been in a “special relationship” with Ms Huang – an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that in 2025 was revealed to be under investigation for suspected diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China. What makes this extraordinary is the possibility that Mr Huang’s romantic and commercial relationship exposed him to a Chinese intelligence operation. In May, analysts at Culper Research argued that Megaspeed brought Nvidia substantial revenues, allegedly backed by Chinese financing. Then Nividia’s boss publicly defended Megaspeed while secretly conducting an affair with its top executive. More than $300bn was wiped off Nvidia’s valuation as soon as Wall Street opened.

Industrial espionage is nothing new. Richer nations often block the export of their commercial secrets to prevent others from catching up. These challengers often go to extraordinary lengths to obtain new technology. Historically, diplomatic or military so-called honeytraps – spies sent to seduce victims to gain confidential information – have been more common than commercial ones. But in 2008, British spy agencies accused Beijing of a campaign to target businesses, using sex to pressure targets into cooperating. Whether that has happened here is unknown. But a president who promised to get tough on China needs to explain why his administration eased chip export controls despite warnings that the businessman lobbying for it might be compromised.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Former RFK Jr adviser accuses Trump officials of prioritizing special interest groups over voters
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Calley Means claims officials abandoned Maha agenda and took money from sugar industry leading up to midterms

A former top Trump administration health adviser accused Susie Wiles, whom Donald Trump removed as the White House chief of staff last week, of stalling the so-called “Make America healthy again” (Maha) agenda by prioritizing special interest groups and fundraising before the midterm elections.

Calley Means, who resigned two weeks ago from his job advising Robert F Kennedy Jr, blamed Wiles and other Trump staffers for dropping the ball on the Maha agenda to take money from the sugar industry to fuel the midterms – which Republicans ultimately lost.

“I mean, it’s why we lost the midterms. We have been discordant from what was run on, two years ago,” Means told Joe Rogan in a podcast interview on Friday.

Means told CBS News that Wiles and her “very close-knit crew”, including James Blair and Richard Walters, two White House deputy chiefs of staff; Walker Barrett, a policy adviser; and Tony Fabrizio, a pollster for Trump, “explicitly catered to special interests against the will of the voters”.

Republicans have been looking for someone to blame for the massive losses in last week’s midterm election. Democrats, who had been poised to win the House and possibly Senate, outperformed expectations, taking both chambers of Congress, a majority of governor offices, and flipping dozens of House seats.

Means attributes much of that loss to Wiles, who left the administration on Friday and was replaced by Stephen Miller. Walters, a close ally to Wiles, resigned from the administration on Friday.

“I think a lot of this happened without Trump’s full knowledge. I don’t think President Trump fully knew that some of these advisers were taking money from the industries we ran on fighting against,” Means told CBS News.

Among the allegations, Means said Wiles did not support efforts to make American diets healthier because the administration needed to take money from “the sugar people” for the midterms.

“They would often say that we can’t do certain things because that would hurt special interest configuration for the midterms,” Means told Rogan.

He also accused Wiles and Blair of pressuring the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to approve flavored e-cigarettes, otherwise known as vapes.

Blair denied Means’s claims to CBS News, saying he “didn’t promote flavored vaping specifically at all” and was tasked with aligning the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) nicotine delivery device application process with federal law.

“Calley is intentionally misrepresenting my role and my responsibility because he opposes the issue entirely. Even though the president himself has made his position on smoking and smoking alternatives known very publicly and has provided clear direction. Calley just doesn’t like it,” Blair told CBS News.

On social media, Blair threatened to sue Means and accused him of lying.

Means also claimed Fabrizio refused to support several Maha initiatives while simultaneously taking money from industry giants and pharmaceutical companies. In one example, Means said Fabrizio had advised against defining “ultra-processed foods” while taking money from PepsiCo.

Kennedy posted a statement to X on Friday, reiterating: “I stand firmly behind President Trump and the historic reforms we are advancing together.

“Draining the swamp is a mandate, and we have an obligation to deliver. Entrenched interests have exercised power in Washington under both parties for decades. President Trump and I intend to keep fighting until the American people–not corporate influence–drive our health policies,” Kennedy wrote.

Contacted for comment, the White House said: “The Trump Administration has never allowed and will never allow outside groups to influence policy decisions. President Trump is busy executing on his America First agenda that includes the largest working-class tax cuts in history, over a million private sector jobs added to the economy, a sealed shut border, and lowest violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta closes citing gov’t clampdown
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta has ended operations due to pressure from authorities.

The newspaper reported that it held its last editorial meeting on Monday and closed its newsroom. It announced last month that it was being forced to shut down after being classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow, a label used to stifle dissent.

The Russian media has come under increased scrutiny from the state amid Moscow’s war on Ukraine. In October, authorities searched the home of Novaya Gazeta’s editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, and took him in for questioning. Another editor at the paper, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested in April.

Cofounder Dmitry Muratov addressed journalists who gathered to witness the closure of the Novaya Gazeta office in Moscow.

“Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today,” he said, adding that constitutional guarantees for political and civil rights had “effectively ceased to function”.

Novaya Gazeta was one of the few remaining outlets that openly criticised Russia’s war on Ukraine and the Kremlin’s policies, amid a widening crackdown on the media and free speech.

In September, the outlet was designated a “foreign agent”. Novaya Gazeta said that since then banks had stopped processing the reader donations on which it relied for financial survival.

United Nations human rights chief Volker Turk said in October that Novaya Gazeta’s closure was “yet another devastating blow for remaining independent media” in Russia.

The Kremlin played down the closure, saying it was part of “a normal cycle of change”.

The paper was co-founded by former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev and funded with money from his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize. It continued reporting despite censorship tightening in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Several of its reporters have been murdered in killings widely seen as retribution for their work, among them Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating abuses by Russia’s military in Chechnya and criticised President Vladimir Putin’s rule.

She was found dead in her apartment block in 2006.

AMD has admitted a bug within its External Events Utility is wearing out SSDs, and promises a fix.

November 9, 2026, 1:30 pm ET

Under normal circumstances, an SSD might go all day without needing to access or write files. But for some AMD Radeon users, anything but normal circumstances are causing drives to continuously write and re-write data. The External Events Utility (EEU) that AMD installs alongside its CPU and GPU drivers is reportedly the culprit.

Also: Nvidia RTX 50 GPUs hit with more price hikes

Fortunately, there are a few workarounds available to avert disaster while AMD works on a more permanent solution.

Reports of the issue first surfaced in July on AMD’s official PC user forum, with one user stating that the External Events Client Module and EEU were constantly writing information to their SSD after installing a Radeon 9060XT graphics card. Subsequent comments on the thread this month confirm that the issue has persisted despite several bug fixes and patch updates, with two users reporting hard numbers for data usage ranging from 0.3 MB/s to as much as 1.5 MB/s.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

This week, Reddit user darklinkpower posted that the AMD Adrenaline Edition desktop application also had the EEU driver bug, using up to 1% of their drive health per month for around 16 months. That might not sound like much, but it can cause catastrophic problems if left unchecked.

AMD seems to be aware of the issue; a company official who goes by AMD_Vik on Reddit commented that it will “hopefully [be] fixed in the next [update].” While there’s little indication of how quickly a permanent, official patch will be pushed to users, there are a few ways you can protect yourself from the bug and prevent your storage drive from collapsing.

This seems to be the most consistent fix for most AMD users reporting issues, but disabling the EEU can cause its own problems, such as disabling AMD FreeSync support or introducing display glitches if you hot-swap screens while your PC is powered on.

The AMD Adrenalin Edition desktop app lets you control how your PC components communicate with one another, and it might be another facet of a complex problem. By allowing your CPU to access your graphics card’s memory, you can temporarily boost performance, but the EEU bug seems to let it and your GPU run rampant, eating up every bit of memory they can find. Changing a few settings within the app may help:

Also: I tried local AI on HP’s Omnibook Ultra

This is a more niche solution that carries its own risk of introducing communication issues between your CPU and GPU, so I only recommend trying this route if disabling the EEU itself doesn’t resolve the issue. AMD’s official fix may be in the works, but without a firm timeline for release, users are left twisting in the wind trying to stop their PCs from hemorrhaging storage capacity.

Android Auto's minimum requirements have changed. Here's what to know.

November 9, 2026, 12:46 pm ET

Google has officially phased out support for Android 9 and Android 10 for wired Android Auto use — so you’ll need Android 11 at a minimum to connect an Android phone to a compatible car via USB, according to an update to Google’s Android Auto support page spotted by Android Authority. Android 11 through Android 17, the most up-to-date version, are fully supported for Android Auto (though Android 17’s adoption rate remains quite low).

These changes confirm early reports that Android 10 users saw warnings that their devices would soon lose Android Auto support, even before Google’s documentation had specified the change.

Also: Got an old car? Android Auto is easy to add: 2 ways, starting at $20

It’s not uncommon for Google to drop the oldest Android versions that can still run Android Auto every few years. In 2024, Android 8, released in 2017, was dumped from service. Android 11 was first released in 2020.

Android Auto brings apps to your car display so that drivers can focus better on the road. It allows you to control features such as navigation, maps, calls, text messages, and music, and is the Android equivalent of Apple CarPlay.

Also: 5 Android Auto apps that make my life easier on the road

The requirements have changed little since last year, aside from the new minimum software requirement. The new instructions for wired Android Auto support are straightforward: Phones must be running Android 11 (Red Velvet Cake) or newer, have an active data plan, and be supported by a compatible car. Google also recommends a quality USB cable.

Android Auto is integrated into compatible phones, so you do not need to download it. Android Auto isn’t available on devices that run Android (Go edition).

Also: I was a big wireless Android Auto fan, until I tried wired – now I won’t go back

To find out if your car or stereo is compatible with Android Auto, Google has a hub page to help. For more information about your car’s compatibility with Android Auto on your car display, it’s best to contact your vehicle manufacturer.

For drivers still using older phones running Android 9 or Android 10, getting Android Auto back will require either replacing a current device with one that runs Android 11 or newer, or installing an available software update on a current device.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Cold therapy may be worse than doing nothing for post-exercise recovery
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Tosin Thompson
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
Plunging into an ice bath after a workout may be worse for your muscle recovery than doing nothing. Cold therapy is a popular intervention after rigorous exercise, like marathons, to relieve soreness and dampen the inflammation that can impair muscle recovery. But in a new study, adults who had ice baths after intense leg exercise showed markers of muscle damage for longer than those who just rested.

“Ice baths have long been considered a go-to recovery strategy in sport, so many people might expect them to outperform doing nothing,” says Freya Bayne at the University of East London. But emerging studies suggest that cold therapies slow muscle-protein synthesis by restricting blood flow and reducing the supply of nutrients to the muscles. “The [latest] study contributes to a growing conversation that recovery strategies should be selected based on the desired outcome, rather than assuming one approach works for everything,” she says.

https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.author: Jeff Spry
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.text:
Well, this should be a nice distraction from the real AI apocalypse.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

They say all good things come to those who wait… and WAIT. Well, the wait for "Robopocalypse" fans might finally be over, as Oscar winners Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman have announced they're working on a TV adaptation.

It does seem like an eternity since news first broke that Portland-based New York Times bestselling author Daniel H. Wilson’s "Robopocalypse" (Doubleday, 2011) was bought by Steven Spielberg’s DreamWorks SKG for a sci-fi spectacle, with Drew Goddard ("The Martian") brought in to pen the screenplay.

That was back in 2009, and since then the story of a rogue AI named Archos and a hearty band of indigenous people in America’s heartland battling to save humanity from extinction has been placed on Hollywood’s back burner. After numerous stalled starts and director Michael Bay getting involved in 2018, "Robopocalypse" was quietly powered down due to script issues, filmmaker scheduling conflicts, and the enormous budget required.

But now we have been blessed with the news, first broken by The Hollywood Reporter, that Ron Howard ("Apollo 13," "The Da Vinci Code") and Akiva Goldsman ("A Beautiful Mind," "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds") have taken up the mantle of this chilling sci-fi project to develop as a new TV series. And what timing, just as AI fever has gripped the planet with paranoia centered around our eventual robot overlords.

"'Robopocalypse' has all the scale and suspense of a major action story, but what drew me to it are the thought-provoking themes and humanity at its center," Ron Howard shared in a statement.

The cover of 2011's smash sci-fi hit Robopocalypse by Daniel H. Wilson

Image credit: Vintage

The cover of the 2014 sequel Robogenesis by Daniel H. Wilson

Image credit: Vintage

"Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together."

As a PhD graduate of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute and a future king of the techno-thriller, Wilson was the ideal writer to bring this frightening story to life, and a 2014 sequel titled "Robogenesis" was equally gripping.

The prolific, award-winning writer has since set up a multitude of other Hollywood projects spawned from his catalog of works, including "Amped," "The Clockwork Dynasty," the authorized sequel to Michael Crichton's "The Andromeda Strain," "The Andromeda Evolution," and his 2025 alien invasion novel "Hole in the Sky," still alive at Netflix.

Howard's Imagine Entertainment will partner with Akiva Goldsman's Weed Road Pictures on this episodic adaptation, with Howard attached to direct the pilot episode and Goldsman serving as series showrunner.

"Robopocalypse" marks a creative reunion for the distinguished creators, following their collaborations on "A Beautiful Mind," "Cinderella Man," "The Da Vinci Code," and "Angels & Demons." Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment is slated to executive produce the ambitious show alongside Imagine's Brian Grazer and Jeb Brody and Weed's Rachel Wizenberg and Greg Lessans.

It's too early to tell which streaming service the "Robopocalypse" TV show will be attached to yet. Hopefully the pilot episode wows one of the big names, and we can finally see the "Robopocalypse" adaptation of our dreams.

In the meantime, we'd recommend checking out the original book by Daniel H. Wilson.

Not far into our future, the dazzling technology that runs our world turns against us. Controlled by a childlike—yet massively powerful—artificial intelligence known as Archos, the global network of machines on which our world has grown dependent suddenly becomes an implacable, deadly foe.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Oral GLP-1 reduces sleep apnea severity, cardiometabolic risk
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Katie Kalvaitis
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — Adults with moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea and overweight or obesity who used the oral GLP-1 orforglipron for 1 year experienced improvements in sleep apnea severity, according to results from the ATTAIN-OSA trials.

Orforglipron (Foundayo, Eli Lilly) also conferred improvement in various cardiometabolic parameters, including weight, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and blood pressure, researchers reported at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

“These data support the potential use of orforglipron as a promising oral treatment option for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity or overweight,” Vaishnavi Kundel, MD, MSc, associate professor of medicine and program director of the sleep medicine fellowship at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, said during a press conference.

Foundayo received FDA approval in April for chronic weight management in conjunction with diet and exercise.

The gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 tirzepatide (Zepbound, Lilly) was approved in 2024 to treat moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea and obesity. Zepbound is delivered as an once-weekly subcutaneous injection, whereas Foundayo is a once-daily oral pill.

“There are no current oral treatments for sleep apnea. It’s usually [treated with] a sleep apnea mask or oral device, which can be very hard for people to use. This could be a great alternative or even an add-on for them,” Michael Grandner, PhD, MTR, director of the sleep and health research program at University of Arizona, director of sleep medicine at Banner University Medical Center in Tucson and associate professor in the department of psychiatry at University of Arizona College of Medicine, said during a discussion of the ATTAIN-OSA results at the press conference.

The ATTAIN-OSA program consisted of two 52-week, phase 3 trials that were designed to evaluate efficacy and safety of orforglipron in adults with moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in addition to overweight or obesity. The primary endpoint was change in apnea-hypopnea index from baseline to 52 weeks. The trials were conducted at 66 centers across North America, South America, Europe and Asia.

The first trial randomly assigned 363 participants who were unable or unwilling to use positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy, which is the first-line treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea. At baseline, the mean age of participants was 48 years, 31% women, BMI 37.4 kg/m2 and apnea-hypopnea index 50.7 events per hour.

The second trial randomly assigned 349 participants who were currently receiving PAP therapy. In this trial, the baseline mean of participants age was 51 years, 27% women, BMI 38.6 kg/m2 and apnea-hypopnea index 57.6 events per hour.

Participants across trials also received diet and lifestyle counseling. Those with diabetes or recent use of incretin-based therapies were not enrolled.

For patients not on PAP therapy, orforglipron conferred greater reductions in sleep apnea severity, with a decrease of 18 to 21 respiratory events per hour compared with four to five events per hour with placebo across the treatment regimen and efficacy estimands, according to the findings. This resulted in a 36% to 44% improvement in sleep apnea severity, Kundel said during the presentation.

The primary endpoint was similar among patients on PAP therapy. Orforglipron resulted in a decrease in 17 to 18 respiratory events per hour compared with five events per hour with placebo, resulting in a 26% to 28% reduction in sleep apnea severity, according to Kundel.

These changes were both statistically and significantly significant, Kundel said, with P values of < .001.

In other results, orforglipron was associated with a 72% reduction in sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden compared with placebo in both trials (P < .001).

These changes were accompanied by significant improvement in secondary cardiometabolic parameters with orforglipron in both trials, including a 10% to 11% reduction in body weight, compared with a 1% to 2% reduction with placebo; a 38% to 42% reduction in hsCRP, compared with 4% to 18% with placebo; and a 7 mm Hg to 8 mm Hg reduction in systolic BP, compared with a 1 mm Hg to 3 mm Hg reduction with placebo (P < .001 for all), according to the results.

“As a comparison, typically, continuous PAP (CPAP) results in about a 2 mm Hg to 3 mm Hg reduction in systolic blood pressure,” Kundel said.

Participants also reported greater improvements in sleep-related impairment scores with orforglipron.

The safety findings were consistent with the known safety profile of orforglipron, Kundel said.

The results were simultaneously published in JAMA.

Sleep apnea is strongly and independently associated with CVD, including hypertension, diabetes, MI and stroke, Kundel said.

“Sleep health is very important. There’s a reason why sleep health is now part of the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 needs framework,” Grandner said.

Sleep apnea is often undiagnosed and untreated, and available treatments work well but are underutilized, Grandner said. Moreover, Kundel said, existing device therapies have limited cardiometabolic benefits.

An oral medication for sleep apnea would be “a game changer,” Grandner said.

“These data suggest that this could be a great addition to the toolbox for dealing with sleep apnea. Not only will it address the respiratory events ... but also the real-world implications because sleep apnea affects so many different areas of people’s lives,” Grandner said.

“It really expands the treatment options for patients with sleep apnea, which is exciting because for many years we had CPAP and dental devices, but the landscape is really changing,” Kundel said.

ATTAIN-OSA tells us that orforglipron is now the first-ever oral therapy that is showing benefits for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea, following tirzepatide, which is injectable. So, that is exciting for not only the field of sleep, but for the field cardiometabolic risk management in general.

I think there are a large number of patients out there with obstructive sleep apnea who have concurrent cardiometabolic conditions, who benefit not only from therapies that improve their sleep, but also therapies that can improve their cardiometabolic risk profile. Not all of them are going to be able to access or tolerate tirzepatide, nor will all prefer injectables. I think orforglipron here offers that extra potential to capture patients that perhaps were not being treated currently for their sleep apnea for a variety of reasons.

Kundel V, et al. LBS.05. Late-breaking science: New frontiers in cardiometabolic risk reduction. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Grandner reports consulting for Eisai, Google, Natrol, Resmed and SmartyPants Vitamins. Kundel reports receiving financial support from Apnimed, Axsome, Lilly and ZOLL Respicardia.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: ANGPTL4 inhibition appears to reduce triglycerides
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — A monoclonal antibody that inhibits angiopoietin-like protein 4 was linked to triglyceride reduction at 12 weeks in adults with high triglycerides, researchers reported at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

For the TYDAL-TIMI 78 phase 2b trial, researchers evaluated MAR001 (Marea Therapeutics) in doses of 300 mg, 450 mg and 900 mg compared with placebo. The efficacy analysis included 235 participants (mean age, 60.4 years; 39% women) with triglycerides 175 mg/dL or higher (median at baseline, 249.5 mg/dL) and high remnant cholesterol who completed at least one dose of the study drug.

Play Video
Michelle O’Donoghue, MD, MPH, discusses the results of the TYDAL-TIMI 78 phase 2b trial presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

This is a modal window.

End of dialog window.

MAR001 is not yet approved for commercial use in the United States.

“MAR001 is a monoclonal antibody that is designed to inhibit ANGPTL4. The rationale is that by blocking ANGPTL4, we can enhance [lipoprotein lipase] activity and enhance the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins,” Michelle O’Donoghue, MD, MPH, cardiologist with the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute and senior investigator in the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) Study Group, said during a presentation.

At 12 weeks, the primary endpoint of placebo-adjusted change in fasting triglyceride level was –39.1 percentage points in the MAR001 300 mg group (95% CI, –46.8 to –31.5), –40.9 percentage points in the MAR001 450 mg group (95% CI, –48.7 to –33.1) and –45.5 percentage points in the MAR001 900 mg group (95% CI, –53.2 to –37.8; P for all < .001), O’Donoghue said during the presentation.

The findings were consistent among prespecified subgroups and the treatment effect was greater in an analysis restricted to patients with baseline triglycerides at least 300 mg/dL, she said.

The percentage of patients who reached triglycerides less than 150 mg/dL at 12 weeks was 3.4% in the placebo group, 31% in the MAR001 300 mg group, 35.1% in the MAR001 450 mg group and 51.7% in the MAR001 900 mg group, the researchers found.

When O’Donoghue and colleagues stratified the cohort by baseline triglyceride level, they found that MAR001 reduced triglycerides at 12 weeks between 30.5% and 36.9% in those with baseline triglycerides less than 300 mg/dL, between 38.3% and 44.8% in those with baseline triglycerides 300 mg/dL to less than 500 mg/dL and between 57.4% and 72.2% in those with baseline triglycerides 500 mg/dL or more.

In addition, “MAR001 increased HDL cholesterol, and as was expected based on its class’s effects toward hydrolyzing triglycerides on very LDL particles to transform them into denser LDL particles, we saw a small absolute rise in LDL cholesterol, but importantly, there was a net reduction in atherogenic particles, as reflected by a drop in non-HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein B,” O’Donoghue said during the presentation.

The rate of adverse events was 69% in the pooled MAR001 group and 78% in the placebo group, according to the researchers.

Serious adverse events occurred in 2.8% of those assigned MAR001 and 6.9% of those assigned placebo, whereas adverse events leading to discontinuation of the study drug were observed in 4.5% of the MAR001 group and 3.4% of the placebo group, O’Donoghue said.

In the MAR001 group, there were no cases of pancreatitis or elevated liver enzymes, she said.

“Inhibition of ANGPTL4 with MAR001 significantly reduced fasting triglyceride concentration across doses and was generally well tolerated through 24 weeks,” O’Donoghue said during the presentation. “The magnitude of triglyceride lowering appeared to be more pronounced among those with higher baseline triglyceride levels. Together with preclinical and human genetic evidence, these findings support further investigation of ANGPTL4 inhibition as a treatment for hypertriglyceridemia. As such, a dedicated phase 2b study, TYDAL-TIMI 78 part B, is now underway in participants with severe hypertriglyceridemia.”

This was a trial of an ANGPTL4 inhibitor in patients that had elevated triglycerides. There was a dose-dependent reduction, so it appeared to be effective for that and appeared to be pretty safe and well tolerated.

There has been a lot of interest in targets such as ANGPTL3, remnant cholesterol and triglycerides for their potential to improve CV outcomes. There are some good data that look at remnant cholesterol and outcomes for CVD, peripheral artery disease, etc, but that has become increasingly difficult as other lipid-lowering therapies are proven, particularly as people get to very low LDL levels. The one drug in this space approved for CV outcomes is icosapent ethyl, but I think its benefits are independent of triglyceride-lowering. Fibroids haven’t worked.

In the past, this may have been a great place to show CV benefit. I think that’s increasingly challenging, and perhaps an initial place where these drugs may be very useful, as data from olezarsen (Tryngolza, Ionis) have shown, is pancreatitis prevention for very high triglycerides. I think there is a lot of promise there. This is a problem we have in the clinic, but it’s going to take time and probably a lot of effort to show CV benefit, and it’s going to have to be additive to what we already have.

It’s a little soon to know what might set MAR001 apart from other triglyceride-lowering agents. The efficacy looks good. The safety looks good. ANGPTL4 is a different target, and so maybe it's an adjunct. What could it do in combination with other therapies? I don't think we know yet how it would differentiate, but so far it looks like a promising mechanism. Pancreatitis and elevated triglycerides are an area where we haven't had a lot of great therapies. Fibrates, despite the lack of CV benefit, are still used, so I think it's nice to have these options. I think these agents are probably not in the short term going to be an adjunct for CV risk reduction, but hopefully maybe in the future.

O’Donoghue M, et al. LBS.05. New frontiers in cardiometabolic risk reduction. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: O’Donoghue reports receiving grant funding from Amgen, AstraZeneca, Marea Therapeutics, Novartis and Pfizer and receiving fees for consulting and/or serving on a data safety monitoring board for Agomab, Amgen, AstraZeneca, Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson, NewAmstrerdam Pharma, Novartis, Novo Nordisk and Verve. The study was funded by Marea Therapeutics.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/dexcom-ce.title: He went from washing lab equipment for $10 an hour to leading a $30 billion healthcare company. His advice to Gen Z: Raise your hand
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/dexcom-ce.author: Preston Fore
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/dexcom-ce.text:
The road to the corner office doesn’t always start with an Ivy League degree or prestigious internship. For Jake Leach, it started working as a lab dishwasher for just $10 an hour.

Back in the 1990s, Leach was a teenager trying to save enough money to pay his way through community college in California. His high school sweetheart had just wrapped up a summer internship at MiniMed, an insulin pump company, and before heading back to school, she offered Leach the chance to take over her job.

It wasn’t exactly glamorous work cleaning lab equipment like beakers and flasks, but it would mark the start of an entire career focused in diabetes management. Nearly three decades later, Leach is now the CEO of Dexcom, a roughly $30 billion company that develops non-invasive glucose-monitoring systems.

And while he never had grand plans to be a healthcare executive, he told Fortune that his climb up the career ladder has come down to one simple recipe:

“It’s all about hard work,” Leach said. “There’s no shortcut.”

Leach grew up in California’s San Fernando Valley, where his father worked in groundskeeping at a Catholic school and his mother was later a teacher’s aide. Money was tight, but he learned early that if he wanted something, he would have to find a way to earn it himself.

In elementary school, for example, he desperately wanted a $350 bike—an expensive purchase for his family at the time. When he learned about layaway, he decided he could save up for it himself.

“With the income of my family, I had no business having that kind of a bike, but I just wanted it so bad,” Leach said.

He spent the summer washing cars for $2 apiece, slowly putting money aside until he could afford it. The experience taught him something that would follow him throughout his career.

“Hard work gets you what you want, and you know you may not always succeed, but you can control it—you can control that outcome,” Leach said.

He also developed an early fascination with how things worked, thanks in part to his maternal grandfather. A handyman who could tackle everything from plumbing to electrical work, he often brought Leach along to work on projects around the house. By the time he was 10, Leach was learning how light switches worked, how to wire them, and how electrical panels operated.

Those afternoons helped spark an interest in electrical systems that eventually extended to experimenting with old VCRs and building homemade rockets.

His grandfather would also become part of the reason Leach’s eventual career in diabetes technology carried a personal connection. After his grandfather’s gallbladder abruptly ruptured, the family learned the medical emergency was related to his diabetes. He would go on to take insulin for the rest of his life.

Leach didn’t yet know it, but those experiences would help shape both his engineering interests and his eventual career.

He eventually took classes at Glendale Community College before transferring to UCLA, where he studied electrical and biomedical engineering and became the first person in his family to earn a four-year college degree.

That $10-an-hour job washing beakers and flasks at MiniMed eventually turned into a full-time position, too. Leach spent seven years at the company, which was acquired by Medtronic in 2001. But in 2004, he received an offer to join a startup of 30 people called Dexcom, which was looking to challenge the established diabetes technology industry.

The opportunity offered something different: a chance to help build a company from the ground up—and double his salary from $45,000 to $95,000.

Now more than two decades after joining Dexcom, 48-year-old Leach has watched the company grow into a healthcare giant. The company went public in 2005 and, by 2025, brought in $4.6 billion in annual revenue, had approximately 3.5 million users globally, and had around 11,000 full-time employees worldwide.

The company has benefited from a shifting diabetes-treatment landscape, including the growing popularity of GLP-1 drugs, which are used to treat type 2 diabetes and have helped bring greater attention to glucose monitoring.

In January, Leach reached the top of the organization as president and CEO. His compensation now includes an annual base salary of $1.15 million—a far cry from the $10 an hour when he first was exposed to the industry

But his ascent wasn’t driven by an elaborate career plan. Leach, who became Dexcom’s chief technology officer in 2018 and chief operating officer in 2022, said he rarely thought about what position he wanted next.

“It’s always been: keep doing a really good job, keep solving big problems, keep fostering leaders, teaching people, [and] learning from other people,” he said.

Throughout his 22-year career at Dexcom, Leach said he never once asked for a promotion. Instead, he focused on proving himself in the roles he already held, allowing his work to speak for itself.

Additionally, Leach made a habit of being the teammate willing to volunteer for the less glamorous assignments his colleagues weren’t particularly eager to take on.

“A lot of times we tend to focus on our own work and what we’re trying to get done, and it’s really helpful sometimes to take a step back and say what’s right for the company, not necessarily what’s right for me or what’s right for the function I’m leading,” Leach said.

For young workers hoping to distinguish themselves early in their careers, that willingness to look beyond their immediate responsibilities can be a major advantage, he added.

“It’s like getting outside your swim lane,” Leach said. “Everyone kind of has their functional swim lane. You got to get out of that, and I think that’s when you become a more valuable leader for an organization.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/anthropi.title: Anthropic releases first frontier models since Amodei's call for slowdown as IPO buzz builds
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/anthropi.author: Ashley Capoot
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/anthropi.text:
Anthropic released two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2.

The launch marks the first time that Anthropic has released frontier models since CEO Dario Amodei called to slow down the pace of AI development.

Anthropic is gearing up for what is expected to be a blockbuster IPO.

Anthropic
 on Monday released two new artificial intelligence models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, as the company readies for a potentially historic IPO that could take place as soon as next week.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are Anthropic’s most advanced offerings, and the company said they generate outputs 30% faster than their predecessors. The models also cost 20% less than the 5.1 generation, and will be available for $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, the company said.

The launch marks the first time that Anthropic has released so-called “frontier” models since its CEO, Dario Amodei, called to slow down the pace of AI development in September. Anthropic said the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing, and that the company developed new evaluations and post-launch monitoring tools ahead of the release.

“We called for pacing, not pausing,” Dianne Penn, Anthropic’s head of product management for research, told CNBC in an interview.

Anthropic has to balance its safety efforts with intense commercial and competitive pressures, a tension that the company highlighted in the extensive risk factors section of its prospectus late last month. And as executives prepare to kick off Anthropic’s IPO roadshow, they’ll have to convince investors that their approach is the right one.

The company is aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion in its offering, as CNBC previously reported, down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months.

Anthropic first introduced Mythos in April, and it limited the rollout to a select group of organizations because of the model’s advanced cybersecurity capabilities. The company introduced Fable, a publicly available version of Mythos with additional safeguards, two months later.

The models — particularly Mythos — captivated Wall Street and government officials alike, and they helped to fuel Anthropic’s meteoric rise this year. The company said in its amended prospectus that it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year.

Penn said Fable 5.2 is primarily intended for “power users or power use cases” since it excels at complex, open-ended technical work. Other models like Claude Opus 5.5, which Anthropic released in September, are better suited for daily tasks, so Penn said users should turn to Fable 5.2 when they need to tackle hard problems in engineering, mathematics and robotics.

“These are just net new things that are completely novel, and so they’re frontier use cases,” Penn said. “We expect that over time to maybe trickle to the Opus class, but really right now we do see a difference in terms of performance that we think those frontier use cases benefit from.”

Anthropic said Fable 5.2 is generally available on Monday, and Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations through the company’s Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/a-massiv.title: A massive trade in Nvidia just went off – here are the details
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/a-massiv.author: Oliver Renick
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/a-massiv.text:
An options trader bet over $57 million that Nvidia stock will rally between now and February.

The bullish trade was the largest options trade on the tape Monday.

The trade targets a move back to all-time highs.

The biggest options trade on Nvidia
 stock Monday seems to think the controversy swirling around the chip leader and its embattled CEO is creating a buying opportunity.

In a trade about an hour after the opening bell that involved more than $100 million in options premium, someone exchanged an existing call spread for a more bullish position that captures the next five months of trading in Nvidia.

The core position was the purchase of 52,000 195-strike calls expiring Feb. 19 worth about $57 million – contracts the trader opened for a new long position while simultaneously selling the same number of 245-strike calls for the same expiry, lowering the cost of the trade by $10 million. The net position, a bullish call spread, needs Nvidia to trade above around $206 by expiry, or about 15% higher, to be profitable. If Nvidia stock reaches the short, 245-strike call, it would represent a nearly 40% rally and return the stock to its all-time high of $243, that was reached on October 6th.

The trade was likely part of a "roll" down from an existing 210/255-strike call spread worth about $42 million that was closed out, according to SpotGamma analysis.

"The person got more aggressive rolling this spread down to lower strikes to get more upside exposure by getting higher delta," SpotGamma founder Brent Kochuba said by phone. "They're trading the call spread here because the vol is expensive going into earnings. It's a significant increase in upside delta exposure."

Delta is options parlance for describing how quickly an options price will react to a change in the underlying stock price. The trader's updated position, taken at lower strikes, will make money faster if Nvidia rallies. In other words, it's a higher conviction trade that the chipmaker's stock will soon rebound.

The 195-strike calls they bought for $57 million was the single biggest options trade on the tape Monday, according to SpotGamma. Of the top 20 options trades by dollar-amount, 12 were Nvidia, the data show.

Flows around the stock generally leaned bullish by midday, with 57% of options volume tied to calls and more than $660 million of call premium likely initiated by call-buyers, SpotGamma data show. The most popular single contract by volume was the 180-strike call expiring Monday, that needs Nvidia to recover 1.2% by the bell to break even.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/jensen-h.text:
Prediction markets see relatively low odds that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will depart in the next few years.

It comes as the chipmaker’s board has launched an investigation into Huang’s affair with a woman that U.S. intelligence officials, according to The New York Times, say is a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

Nvidia
’s board is investigating CEO Jensen Huang, citing recent reports that he’s been targeted by a “foreign intelligence effort,” but traders on prediction markets think it’s unlikely he’ll be ousted as chief.

On Sunday, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials —  according to The New York Times – say is a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

On Kalshi, speculators say there’s just a 17% chance Huang is gone by 2027. Those odds rise to 30% by 2028, and 35% by 2029. However, they think there is a 75% probability that Huang will depart by 2031.

Contracts on Huang’s departure on Kalshi are resolved using information from Bloomberg.

On Polymarket, speculators place just one-in-four odds that Huang resigns or is forced out by the end of March 2027. Contracts are resolved on the platform using official statements from the company or Huang himself.

Shares of Nvidia were down more than 5% after the news on Monday.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.title: University backflips on decision to cut 87 per cent of arts subjects
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.author: Charlotte Wilkes
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Industrial Action

More than 50 staff walked off the job on Monday at Federation University's Ballarat campus. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

Federation University staff walked off the job yesterday as part of industrial action seeking a new pay deal.

It comes after the university reversed a decision to cut 87 per cent of its arts subjects in a move it said was a "miscommunication".

Staff told the ABC they would be taking three stoppages next week, which would disrupt students receiving their grades.

Staff at regional Victoria's biggest university have walked off the job as part of a 24-hour stop-work action over pay and conditions.

Federation University staff across the state went on strike yesterday after eight months of failed enterprise agreement negotiations and a back-step by management that left staff "fearful".

Staff told the ABC they were striking for a better pay offer, job security, fair workloads and a voice in future decisions at the university.

Federation University has campuses in Ballarat, Berwick, Gippsland, Melbourne and the Wimmera.

Two weeks ago, Federation University management announced it would be cutting 87 per cent of its arts subjects and shutting down the Bachelor of Criminal Justice at all campuses except Berwick.

Mathew Abbott, a senior lecturer of humanities and president of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) Federation branch, said staff in arts and criminal justice were called into a snap meeting with 10 minutes' notice.

"We were given just hours to make submissions regarding why our units and courses shouldn't be cut.

Mathew Abbott says staff are fearful. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

He said the NTEU lodged a formal complaint, after which the announcement was backtracked and labelled a "miscommunication".

"We don't know exactly what happened or why, or how, or what was revealed at that meeting," Dr Abbott said.

"But we do know, all too well, that the announcement comes after years of turmoil at Fed [University]."

In a statement, Federation University confirmed it was not cutting 87 per cent of arts subjects.

A spokesperson said the university was reviewing courses and units with low student numbers.

"Humanities, social work and visual arts matter to our students and our communities, and they remain important parts of Federation's teaching offering," the spokesperson said.

"The Commonwealth's Job-ready Graduates policy has substantially increased student contributions for many humanities disciplines in an explicit attempt to influence students towards other areas of study."

Federation University says it remains committed to humanities, social work and visual arts. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

The statement said the federal government's decision to increase the cost of arts subjects put huge strain on the university.

"Independent analysis has demonstrated the disproportionate impact these changes have had on [low socio-economic status], regional, women and Indigenous students," the university spokesperson said.

Staff will strike again next week, which will disrupt the release of student results. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

Dr Abbott spent Monday on strike in Ballarat along with about 50 other members of staff. He said staff were being kept in the dark and lived in constant peril of losing their jobs.

Staff told the ABC they would take three work stoppages next week, which would disrupt students receiving their grades.

"We've had mass redundancies almost every year since the current [vice-chancellor] took office," Mr Abbott said.

"[We've had] over 25 restructures, campuses closed and opened, programs cut, hundreds of jobs lost and huge increases in the amount spent on consultancies.

"I know a colleague who faced the threat of redundancy in 2018, 2020, twice in 2022, again in 2023 and he was finally made redundant last year.

"This colleague said the stress they faced at work since 2018 was indescribable and that it had significant negative health impacts."

Rachael Fernald says she is striking because she is concerned about the failed EBA negotiations. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

Rachael Fernald teaches social work and human services at Federation University.

She said she was worried about the future of the university.

"Our workplace conditions are really reflective of our students' learning conditions," Ms Fernald said.

"Everyday I expect to get an email that things are going to be cut and let go because that's what's happened nonstop since I've started working at this university.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.title: Fast-tracking ground markers a must for vision-impaired commuters, advocates say
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.author: Bethany Cody
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Public Transport

Travis Ratsch, who is legally blind, relies on tactile ground markers at bus stops and train stations. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Disability advocates are calling for tactile ground markers near public transport to be fast-tracked to improve accessibility for blind and low-vision travellers.

Trains and trams have until December 2032 to implement upgrades under national accessibility standards.

South Australia's transport department says it is progressively rolling out tactile markers across its rail network.

Using public transport daily is an important part of being independent for Travis Ratsch, who is legally blind.

The white cane used says that is why tactile ground markers at bus stops and train stations are integral for his safety, helping him avoid danger.

"I don't want to rely on a support worker to drive me," he said.

Travis Ratsch says the markers are vital for his independence and safety. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Invented in 1960s by a Japan engineer, tactile ground surface indicators (TGSIs) are now used worldwide.

The coloured tiles are found at crosswalks, bus stops and train platforms, featuring raised lines to guide white cane users in straight lines, while dots signal approaching hazard.

Blind Citizens Australia national advocacy officer Martin Stewart said train station accidents could have serious consequences — something he lived with every day.

Martin Stewart says he is acutely aware of the risks of not having ground markers. (Supplied)

"I myself have been the victim of an accident, falling in between carriages," he said.

"The minute you are hesitant, the more accidents are likely to occur.

Mr Stewart said his accident was unrelated to tactile ground markers, but wanted their installation to be fast-tracked.

"It should be taken more seriously," he said.

Tactile ground markers were invented in Japan in the 1960s. (ABC News)

The Disability Standards for Accessible Public Transport were amended last month, which required operators and providers to comply to improve accessibility of their services.

A spokesperson for SA Department for Infrastructure and Transport said 74 of Adelaide Metro's 90 railway stations had TGSIs.

They said work was underway to progressively roll out TGSIs at the remaining 16 stations, with priority being considered alongside other public transport initiatives.

Trains and trams have until December 2032 to be fully compliant.

Sarah Moulds is an associate professor of law at Adelaide University. (ABC News)

Adelaide University associate professor of law Sarah Moulds said the standards were "very important".

The national standards outline requirements for features like seating, ramps, paths and signage, and fall under the Disability Discrimination Act 1992.

"They're designed to say, 'If you do this, you're doing really well,'" Dr Moulds said.

"If you don't do it, then a question mark hangs over whether or not you've taken reasonable steps in the specific circumstances."

Marino Rocks railway station — in Adelaide's south-west — is one of 16 in South Australia still without tactile paving.

Local business owner Kayne Ensten said his community had been calling for safety upgrades for several years.

Kayne Ensten says the Marino Rocks community has long been calling for safety upgrades. (ABC News)

He said it was "concerning" the platform lacked the raised markers.

"They're handy for the vision impaired, but also people standing around on their phones," he said.

"Good to know that you're near the edge of the platform, because it's quite a drop there.

"They should be put in straight away."

A department spokesperson said the installation of TGSIs at the Marino Rocks station was slated for 2027-2028.
