Steve Smith is going to miss the next Sheffield Shield match as he continues to recuperate from a neck injury. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

A full round of Sheffield Shield matches kicking off this week will help determine the make-up of the Australian Test side to face New Zealand in the first Test.

Key players will miss the matches because of injury and one-day international duty, but others have a chance to impress national selectors.

The first Test against New Zealand begins in Perth on December 9.

Potential Australia Test players will start their auditions this Wednesday when a full round of Sheffield Shield matches begin.

Two more Shield rounds follow before the first Test against New Zealand begins in Perth on December 9.

It is likely the squad for the first few Tests will be named some time after this week's matches and before the following round of matches in late November.

The Test squad will assemble in Perth on December 3, and with the bowling unit relatively settled, the interest lies in who gets selected in Australia's spluttering batting line-up.

Australia confirmed Marnus Labuschagne would not be considered for Test selection this summer against New Zealand. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

The next one or two Sheffield Shield rounds could answer some of the questions that were posed when Australia gave up a one-nil lead in South Africa to eventually lose the final two Tests, the series and the number one Test ranking.

The most pressing issue is the name of the number three batter following Marnus Labuschagne's disappointing tour of South Africa.

Since returning to the national side at the beginning of last year's Ashes series, the Queenslander has made just 426 runs in 10 Tests at an average of 23.66.

Labuschagne's return of zero and four during the third Test in Cape Town was the final straw for most commentators, and Australia's chairman of selectors, George Bailey, confirmed he would not be considered for the four-Test series against New Zealand this summer.

Cooper Connolly is the incumbent number seven in the Australian Test side. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone, file photo)

Labuschagne's ousting could mean Western Australia's Cooper Connolly retains his spot in the side, having got the gig at Cape Town when Steve Smith sat out because of his neck injury.

Connolly has been selected to play for Australia in the three one-day internationals against England, with the first on Friday, and so will not be playing in the Shield this week.

Western Australia's next Shield match against Tasmania in Perth, which starts on November 23, will give him some red-ball match practice if he is named in the squad.

If not Connolly, who else could come into the Test side?

Jack Clayton of the Queensland Bulls is scoring a mountain of runs and putting his name forward as a possible Test batter. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

Apart from Shield enthusiasts, not many people would have heard of 27-year-old Queenslander Jack Clayton, but he is the hot player this season and one who has been endorsed for Test selection by his former state teammate, Usman Khawaja.

The number four has scored 303 runs in three Shield matches this year at an average of 75.75 and moreover has scored runs in every game with a recent 104 and two 50s.

He has another opportunity to push his claim when Queensland takes on Tasmania in Brisbane this week.

Oliver Davies of New South Wales is leading the Sheffield Shield run-scorers list after three matches. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Aggressive New South Wales opener Oliver Davies is at the top of the Shield batting charts with 332 runs at 66.40

However, 253 of those runs came in one innings in the first Shield match of the season and since then the 26-year-old has posted just one other significant score of 52.

His opening partner, discarded Test batter Sam Konstas, continues to push his name forward, with 229 runs at 76.33, including a century, a 50 and a one-day ton.

Sam Konstas of the NSW Blues is hoping to revive his Test career. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The pair will be part of the NSW side to play South Australia this week at Cricket Central in Sydney's Silverwater.

Victorian youngsters Campbell Kellaway and Oliver Peake are often talked up, and while neither have set the Shield alight this season, they have another chance against WA come Wednesday.

Oliver Peake of Victoria is one of the young Victorian batters tipped for higher honours. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Of the older campaigners, 33-year-old former Test players NSW's Kurtis Patterson and Western Australia's Cameron Bancroft are both in the runs, but will their ages work against them?

The jury is still out on NSW's 34-year-old Nic Maddinson, who was surprisingly called up for two Tests in South Africa after missing all of last season's Sheffield Shield while recovering from testicular cancer treatment.

Nic Maddinson was a surprise recall for the first two Tests against South Africa, but was dropped for the decider. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

And what of the batting order and most pressingly the number three position after Labuschagne's axing?

Moving Steve Smith up to three seems the obvious solution and the one most pundits are calling for.

His average of 65.22 from 30 innings at first drop is better than at any other spot in the line-up, but he has only batted there once since 2017, scoring 17 against England in Perth last year.

Steve Smith has returned to his home in New York while he recovers from a neck injury. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Then there is the issue of his dodgy neck joint that flared up in South Africa, which he is now resting at his New York home.

Smith is expected to return for NSW's match against Queensland on November 22 at the SCG.

Cameron Green is another option for first drop.

Like his fellow Western Australian, Connolly, Green will miss this week's round of matches as part of the Australian squad for the one-day series.

The big watch on Green is his bowling fitness following an abdominal injury prior to the South African Tests.

Cameron Green returned to the Australian side for the third Test against South Africa as a batter only after suffering an abdominal injury. (AP: Halden Krog)

He returned in Cape Town as a batter only and continues to build up his bowling loads in training.

He could bowl in the one-dayers, otherwise his only opportunity to prove his match fitness will be the Shield match against Tasmania.

If Green can bowl, it is hard to see Tasmania's Beau Webster returning to number seven.

Webster was dropped for the third Test at Cape Town after taking just one wicket in his previous four Tests and scoring 81 runs at 13.50.

Western Australia's Josh Inglis would seem to be a lock to stay in the team after his first innings century at Cape Town batting at five.

Matthew Renshaw starred for Australia during the series against South Africa. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

Queenslander Matthew Renshaw's solid return to the opening position at Cape Town helps Inglis's cause.

Both Inglis and Renshaw are in the one-day squad but will get another shot at four-day cricket the following week.

Sheffield Shield matches are so often the forgotten cricket fixtures of the summer, but right now they are of crucial importance.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/h.author: Melissa Brown
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Occupational Health and Safety

Feng Jianming died after being stabbed in Melbourne's CBD while working for the HungryPanda app. (Supplied)

HungryPanda delivery workers say they have had their pay docked after reporting stolen food orders, as attention turns to rider safety after a fatal stabbing.

Melbourne-based delivery rider and father of two Feng Jianming died in Melbourne's CBD on Friday night.

HungryPanda denies it has a policy requiring workers to cover the cost of lost food, but says it is aware of problems Melbourne riders are having with members of the public.

Delivery app HungryPanda denies claims it "punishes" riders who have had food orders stolen from them, despite multiple former workers telling the ABC they have been forced to cover the cost.

The death of HungryPanda delivery worker Feng Jianming has again shone a spotlight on the safety and conditions of gig economy workers.

Mr Feng, 47, was fatally stabbed on Friday night while making a food delivery in Melbourne's CBD.

A 51-year-old man has been charged Mr Feng's murder and intentionally causing injury over the incident, which saw another delivery rider injured.

International college student Cheng Zhang began working for both HungryPanda and Uber when he moved to Melbourne this year.

While working in the CBD, he said he was often harassed by drunk people on the street, and had had food stolen from his bike while he was making a delivery on an upper level of a high-rise building.

"I suffered one punishment [from HungryPanda] in June," he told the ABC.

"I immediately reported [the theft] to HungryPanda and HungryPanda said 'OK, this incident is recorded and the loss of your food will be charged on my next Tuesday's payday'."

He said Uber did not have the same rule.

Hundreds of people gathered in Melbourne's CBD on Saturday night to voice safety concerns after the death of delivery rider Feng Jianming. (ABC News)

Another worker told the ABC he had had food stolen three times over the past 18 months and had had to pay for the orders each time.

In one instance, the man said he had had to pay $50 out of the $200 he received for a 10-hour shift.

"That was at least three or four hours of work," he said.

He said he had been involved in two confrontations with people stealing his food and he believed other workers were putting themselves in danger as they tried to protect their livelihoods.

"The company doesn't really get involved with the workers unless something terrible happens, like this case with Feng, our fellow co-worker," he said.

The ABC has chosen not to use the man's name because he still works for HungryPanda and is subject to a clause in his contract that could see him terminated for negative media coverage.

He said that when he started, HungryPanda offered to cover $50 worth of missing, stolen or disputed orders.

"I lost that protection within my first month," he said.

"After that, I was paying for it on my own."

He agreed with Cheng Zhang that he did not have to pay for lost or disputed orders when he worked for Uber.

He said Uber had a function in its app to allow workers to quickly report any dangerous situations or harassment on the street.

But he said HungryPanda required workers to talk to someone from the company via WhatsApp.

"Some days are good days but not all of them," he said.

"It's not stable work. It's easy work to get into ... but you are exposed to a lot of stress daily."

Hundreds of people gathered in Melbourne's CBD on Saturday night demanding safety improvements after Feng Jianming's death. (ABC News)

Berkay Bilici told the ABC he had worked for multiple delivery apps.

He said he did not like working after 8pm in Melbourne's CBD because of problems with people on the streets.

He said he believed DoorDash was the only company that checked on the safety of its workers.

"If you tell them something has happened in the DoorDash [app], they call you, they take care of you, they send you emails. At least two or three times, someone will call you and say, 'Hey are you ok? What's happening?'" he said.

"HungryPanda was the worst of the gig workers apps."

He said HungryPanda once deducted $12 from his pay after a customer complained that part of the order had been spilt.

"The HungryPanda manager or someone sent me a message and said I had damaged all the food items and we are deducting money from your account.

"I was in shock and they said, 'Rules are rules'."

HungryPanda has told the ABC it does not have a policy "automatically requiring" riders to compensate for lost or undelivered orders.

"Riders will not be penalised for being unable to complete deliveries due to genuine safety concerns," it said in a statement.

The company said it was continuing to support Mr Feng's family, including paying for their travel to Australia and his funeral costs.

"The deceased rider's family has also shared that he had previously experienced the theft of four to five electric bicycles, highlighting the broader safety and security challenges faced by delivery riders," the company said.

"While the full circumstances remain subject to police investigation, this tragedy has reinforced the urgent need to better protect riders and their livelihoods.

"Regardless of the circumstances, no rider should ever feel compelled to put their personal safety at risk to protect their belongings, delivery equipment or food orders."

It said it was also meeting with Melbourne workers and Victorian authorities in the wake of the death.

HungryPanda says it does not have a policy that automatically requires workers to pay for stolen food. (ABC News: Bang Xiao)

The UK-based company was established in 2017 and operates in 10 countries, entering Australia in 2019.

The Gig Workers Hub is a community centre which operates out of Elizabeth Street and offers a place for rest and refreshments for gig workers.

Its founder Andrew Copolov said many riders using HungryPanda spoke about having money deducted from them after reporting thefts through the company's WhatsApp support centre.

"HungryPanda, their official policy is that that's not happening," Mr Copolov said.

"However, because a lot of these things are being worked out in one-on-one WhatsApp chats, that policy is not necessarily being followed.

"Things like that can be changed for one."

Several HungryPanda workers have told the ABC they have been harassed by people on the street while working in Melbourne's CBD. (Supplied)

The Transport Workers Union is calling on WorkSafe Victoria to investigate the workers' experiences and whether HungryPanda had failed to properly assess and control risks to vulnerable workers.

National secretary Michael Kaine said penalising workers for lost or stolen orders "put them directly in harm's way to protect their income".

"Hungry Panda has legal obligations to do whatever it can to minimise risk as food delivery riders carry out their work," he said.

"It must urgently confirm whether it has done this."

Delivery riders pause at the vigil for Feng Jianming in Melbourne's CBD on Saturday night. (ABC News)

A change.org petition that has gained more than 7,000 signatures in a matter of days also raised concerns that the policy was putting workers' lives at risk.

"If riders fear deductions, repayment demands or account penalties when food is stolen, that financial pressure may encourage them to chase thieves, confront attackers or remain in unsafe situations," the petition states.

"A rider should never feel that protecting an order is necessary to protect their livelihood."

WorkSafe says it will assess the circumstances surrounding Mr Feng's death to determine whether there have been any breaches of the Occupational Health and Safety Act.

Lula was invited to make a speech at the climate conference in Turkey and hold talks with his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdogan

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva flew to Turkey to attend Cop31 on Monday, marking his first international trip since his surprise re-election two weeks ago.

This year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya from November 9 to 20.

“We are going to show the world how Brazil is setting an example in environmental preservation and energy transition, fundamental pillars of our sustainable development,” Lula said in an Instagram post.

https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-draws-2-5.title: Pope Leo draws 2.5 million in Buenos Aires, renews warning over Milei's austerity
https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-draws-2-5.text:
Some 2.5 million people have attended Pope Leo's mass in Buenos Aires, his largest gathering yet. The pontiff once again called for protecting the vulnerable as President Milei cuts disability care and social services.

An estimated 2.5 million people attended Pope Leo XIV's open-air mass in Buenos Aires on Monday, according to local authorities, making the event the largest gathering of his papacy so far.

Crowds stretched for miles along Avenida del Libertador in Argentina's capital, with the faithful waving Vatican flags and chanting "Long live Pope Leo!" as the US-born pope passed in an open-top popemobile.

"It fills my heart with joy to celebrate... with you," Leo said in his sermon.

The pope also reinforced an appeal to President Javier Milei to protect vulnerable Argentines, visiting a disability care home struggling with the government's cuts to health care and social services.

Before the mass, Leo visited the Cottolengo Don Orione care center in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, which houses more than 400 people with disabilities.

He told residents their lives were a blessing rather than a burden, and challenged the idea that economic success alone measures a country's achievements.

"A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said.

The remarks followed his appeal Sunday, at a reception attended by Milei, for economic growth to benefit people facing the greatest difficulties. He also urged leaders to choose their words carefully and recognize the limits of their power.

Milei became the president of Argentina some three years ago, Since then, his government has cut disability services and resisted implementing a law increasing funding for care, despite Congress overriding Milei's veto in 2025. The Senate is due to consider next year's disability funding in the coming days.

Some worshippers camped overnight to secure a place near the Monumento a los Espanoles, where Pope John Paul II celebrated Argentina's last papal mass in 1987.

Monday was declared a national holiday to allow people to attend. President Milei and his sister Karina were among those present.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In his sermon, Leo spoke of families facing unstable employment, violence and addiction, while describing them as a pillar of society.

The visit is Argentina's first by a pope in nearly four decades. Leo's predecessor Francis, despite being born in Argentina, never returned to his homeland during his papacy.

Leo, 71, visited Uruguay before arriving in Argentina on Sunday. He is due to travel to Peru on Wednesday and return to Rome on November 17.

The first US-born pope spent decades in Peru as a missionary and bishop. The Vatican has described his South American tour as a "homecoming."

The demanding trip comes less than a month after surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.author: Emine Sinmaz and Kevin Rawlinson
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.text:
TV producer, who was in relationship with ex-comedian that reportedly ended in 2014, accuses him of ‘violence, coercive control and abuse’

Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault

Jemima Goldsmith has said Russell Brand physically assaulted her and she accused him of “violence, coercive control and abuse”.

The 52-year-old TV producer said she has always been “strongly and unequivocally” on the side of Brand’s victims as she opened up about her own “painful” experience with her former partner in a social media post on Monday.

Shortly after Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison, Goldsmith posted on X: “I am in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand’s trial, told their stories, testified and ensured justice was done.

“I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse. I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident. I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children.

“I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact.”

On Thursday, Brand was found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

Goldsmith, known professionally as Jemima Khan, is reported to have been in a relationship with Brand for a year from around September 2013. On X, Goldsmith said she had assisted the journalists who had exposed Brand in a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and in reports in the Times and Sunday Times in 2023.

“I also undertook to testify in court to his abusiveness, if the newspaper that published the victims’ accounts were ever to be sued,” she said.

Goldsmith made the comments in light of renewed press reporting about a harassment injunction that she and Brand had taken out against a woman named Szilvia Berki in 2014.

Goldsmith, who married former Pakistan cricket captain Imran Khan in 1995, said the online commentary and media reporting about the injunction had presented “an untrue narrative” and opened her up to “vile hatred and abuse online”.

Berki had made allegations against Brand to the police after she had been booked to give him a massage at Goldsmith’s home in June 2014.

“I was present the whole time he was with her, and I did not see anything untoward, despite the fact that he was later found guilty of sexually assaulting other women and he later physically assaulted me. If I saw any man abuse any woman under any circumstances, I would do my utmost to stop them, without hesitation,” Goldsmith said in her statement.

Goldsmith alleged that a series of “untrue stories” appeared in the tabloid press and that Berki embarked on a campaign of “threatening abuse online and in emails”. The Guardian has not been able to reach Berki.

Brand and Goldsmith took out a harassment order against Berki, which meant she was banned from speaking to anyone about her allegations against Brand.

The injunction was granted by the high court judge and former leading counsel in the Leveson inquiry Mr Justice Jay. It was brought to light by the non-profit campaigning thinktank Tax Policy Associates, founded by the former tax lawyer Dan Neidle, after Brand’s conviction.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Barnsley workers strike over nursery privatisation by Reform council
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Robyn Vinter North of England correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Women say move will be ‘massively detrimental’ to services for vulnerable children, and hit their own pensions

The 33 women waving banners outside a nursery in the South Yorkshire village of Grimethorpe have never been on strike before.

Passing cars beep their horns in support of the workers, who have taken action at six nurseries run by Barnsley council after its Reform UK leadership agreed to transfer them to private companies. They say the move will have a hugely negative impact on the services they provide to vulnerable children, and to their own pensions.

Such is the strength of feeling among the women, who are members of the GMB union, that turnout at their strike ballot was 100%, with every single member backing the walkout.

“For low-paid working women to take a stand is significant,” said Victoria Austin, a GMB regional organiser, adding that the work done by the nursery staff was above and beyond and “the council should be singing that from the rooftops”.

Instead, the council made the “massively detrimental” decision to push ahead with privatising the nurseries, only telling the workers about the impact on their pensions 36 hours before the transfer was due to take place, Austin said.

While the plans began under the previous Labour administration, councillors at the time had reassured nursery workers that their pay and benefits, including pensions, would stay the same.

Austin said Reform, which took over the council at the local elections in May after half a century of Labour leadership, was “not interested” in the workers’ fight, and was “wanting to build a legacy around balancing the books”.

Some local people see the transfer of nursery ownership as an example of heavy-handed slashing by Reform councils, which has also included closing care homes and cutting social care.

“As an elected council, their priority should be not letting children get left behind and doing the right thing by communities,” Austin said.

The workers and the union feel the transfer has been handled badly. One nursery is shuttered after the council deregistered it with Ofsted to allow the private provider to register, but it then pulled out.

The council said there was no legal duty for councils to run nursery services and the change would “reduce the amount of council tax payers’ money needed to support the nurseries”.

The council said after receiving legal advice that the staff were no longer eligible for the local government pension scheme before the transfer, “that information was shared quickly with staff and trade unions”.

William Brown, the leader of Barnsley council, said: “We’re disappointed that GMB members have voted in favour of strike action. The decision to transfer these nurseries to another provider was taken to protect jobs and retain these services for families.”

He said additional provision had been made for families on the three strike days and the council was continuing to engage with the union.

For Kimberley Darlington, Emma Jones, Lucy Kolconko and Charlotte Hawe, who work at Darfield nursery, the strike was not just about the plans to move them to a lower-value pension but to protect the families they supported.

Hawe said: “We’re often the first point of contact. I’ve arranged lots of food parcels for families who need them.”

Kolconko has taken families to visit the doctor when they have needed to. Darlington added: “We went out to a house to show a parent how to play with her Send (special educational needs and disabilities) children, she just didn’t know.”

The nursery workers have taught a three-year-old child with special educational needs to walk, which the parent had not done, and helped another family who were living with a rat infestation and mouldy walls to get help from their landlord.

They believe these are things they would be unable to do in a private setting where staff may be responsible for more children. In Barnsley, the nursery workers each look after four children over the age of two, while in private settings this can be five children.

“We just won’t have time to do these things. We’ve done all this work and the council has turned on us,” said Kolconko, a senior nursery worker.
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Women say move will be'massively detrimental' to services for vulnerable children. They say the move will have a hugely negative impact on the services they provide to vulnerable children and to their own pensions. The 33 women have never been on strike before, with every single member backing the walkout.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Ohio State fraternity suspended after viral video shows two men on fire
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The university and local police are conducting investigations into Sigma Alpha Epsilon and have placed them on interim suspension

A fraternity at Ohio State University has been temporarily suspended while authorities investigate a video that appears to show two panicked men engulfed in flames.

A video shared on social media shows one individual with his sweatpants on fire who then lunges at a second individual and tackles him to the ground. The second man’s clothing also catches fire, and they both roll on the ground while removing their clothes as several onlookers intervene.

Not signed in before? Create an account

University spokesperson Benjamin Johnson said Ohio State placed Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity on interim suspension while it investigates and has referred the matter to the university and Columbus police.

“The university is aware of this extremely concerning incident, and the individuals in question are receiving medical care,” Johnson said in a statement. “Ohio State is committed to a safe and healthy environment and expects students and student organizations to uphold that commitment and the university’s values.”

Columbus Police Sgt Joe Albert said it appears the matter took place on Saturday. Police did not receive any calls for service at the location, but someone called police Sunday evening reporting that the video was circulating online, he said.

Steve Mitchell, CEO of Sigma Alpha Epsilon, said behavior that violates its high standards has no place in its organization and it will take appropriate action to hold those responsible accountable based on the investigation.

“We take this matter seriously and are actively investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident while working closely with university officials and local law enforcement,” he said in a statement.

More than 62,000 students are enrolled at the university’s Columbus campus.

Holly Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: A video appears to show two panicked men engulfed in flames. The men are seen lunging at each other and tackling each other. The incident occurred Saturday at the Ohio State University campus. Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity has been placed on interim suspension while it investigates.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: US agencies unite to combat rogue drone threats nationwide
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
The administration of US President Donald Trump says ⁠it is taking ⁠steps to expedite the use of counter-drone systems to address growing threats.

Several United States agencies, including the Pentagon and the Transportation, Energy and Justice Departments, have signed ⁠a memo to evaluate counter-drone technologies and quickly deploy them to protect aviation safety and address national security concerns.

A statement released on Monday by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the Department of Transportation, Department of Defense, Department of Homeland Security, Department of Energy and Department of Justice were part of the effort “led by the White House Task Force”.

“We’re taking a proactive, whole-of-government approach to protecting American airspace from emerging 21st-century threats,” said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

“By bringing all our federal partners together, we can strengthen our ability to combat rogue drone threats and keep the flying public safe.”

The announcement comes days after a NATO official highlighted the need for cost-effective counter-drone capabilities,
as the alliance has committed to investing more than $40bn in counter-drone capabilities over the next five years.

The agencies will work closely with the FAA and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to develop new systems that can detect, track, stop, or take control of dangerous or unauthorised drones, according to the FAA.

The agency has approved more than 1,000 coordination requests with the Pentagon and the Department of Homeland Security on counter-drone deployments, the FAA’s Liam McKenna told Reuters.

“There are many systems that some of the security agencies are considering using that we’ve seen before, and we can turn around the process in 24 hours,” he added.

“This summer, the FBI arrested five men accused of planning to deploy drones armed with explosives in and around a White House event that attracted thousands of visitors,” said US Attorney General Todd Blanche.

“The Department of Justice is working with partners across the federal government to address drone incursion threats, prosecute individuals who endanger the public, and ensure the safety and security of American airspace.”

Last month, the FAA said it was barring unauthorised drones along the entire US-Mexico border. The temporary flight restriction bars any unauthorised drone activity up to 400 feet (122m) above ground level and extends one nautical mile (1.8km) north of the US-Mexico border.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Trump reverses stance, alleges fraud in recent US midterm elections
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
United States President Donald Trump has questioned the integrity of last week’s midterm elections, reversing course less than a week after congratulating Democrats on their victories and saying he was willing to accept the results.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. “How could the Polls be so wrong???”

While Republicans questioned whether polls were once again underestimating their support, as they had in the 2016, 2020, and 2024 presidential elections, the results ultimately went the other way.

Polls had largely pointed to a strong night for Democrats, with surveys suggesting the party was well positioned to take control of the House of Representatives and had a realistic chance of winning the Senate.

In fact, Pew Research released a report analysing pre-election polling data and found that the data understated the Democratic margin by at least 2 points in 23 of 27 races for governor and the US Senate.

Trump also alleged on Truth Social that some early voting ballot counts were so large that they made it impossible for Republicans to win. He provided no evidence of election fraud or wrongdoing. Over the past few days, the president has shared posts on Truth Social with graphs questioning voter turnout data.

The post marks Trump’s first explicit public challenge to the integrity of the overall midterm results since Democrats overwhelmingly won control of both chambers of Congress, in addition to a string of victories in traditionally Republican strongholds.

This latest remark comes a day after an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes, in which Trump appeared to accept the election outcome. Asked about his decision to congratulate Democrats, Trump confirmed that he had done so and said he was open to working with the incoming Democratic majority.

Shortly after the Democratic Party’s victory was announced, Trump congratulated them on a call with CBS News and later told Fox News that the party “did a good job”.

He had also told The New York Times last week that he “absolutely” accepted the results of the election.

Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer responded to Trump’s latest remarks, saying the president’s “return to election denialism was inevitable”.

“He can whine all he wants, but nothing will stop this inescapable truth: For the last two years of his presidency, Trump will face the largest Democratic congressional majorities in decades, all because he has been an unprecedented failure,” Schumer wrote on X.

Republicans have increasingly sought to distance themselves from Trump following the party’s midterm losses. Even conservative commentator Megyn Kelly, who supported the president in 2024, responded on X to his election fraud claims with a blunt “Just stop.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.summary: Trump has questioned the integrity of the midterm elections in a Truth Social post. The president has also said he was willing to accept the results of the election. Trump has been critical of the results since the midterm election.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Two security breaches near White House prompt brief lockdown
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Two people have been detained near the White House following a pair of security breaches, according to the United States Secret Service agency (USSS).

One of the incidents, which occurred Monday morning, involved a suspect who drove a vehicle onto the pavement at Lafayette Park, which sits directly in front of the White House.

Secret Service Police and National Guard units responded to reports of the vehicle crash at about 10am local time (15:00 GMT), according to a spokesperson for the federal law enforcement agency.

They converged on the northern edge of Lafayette Park near 16th and H Streets Northwest.

Around the same time, another suspect jumped a security barrier in the northwest corner of Lafayette Park. It is not clear if the two events were related.

President Donald Trump was inside the executive residence when the incidents occurred, prompting a brief White House lockdown and the closure of the surrounding roads.

The lockdown was lifted an hour later, according to the White House press pool.

Video footage of the incident captured a silver sedan emitting blankets of smoke as law enforcement officers surrounded it. It shows the driver exiting the vehicle and swinging at the gathered officers.

“The driver was combative with law enforcement, but was quickly placed under arrest,” the Secret Service statement read.

The Metropolitan Police Department’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit was called in to conduct a vehicle sweep after the driver was taken into custody.

Around the same time as police were dealing with the combative driver, “a second individual jumped a barricade near the northwest corner of Lafayette Park”, according to USSS.

Authorities have not stated what charges the two people arrested may be facing. Both incidents remain under investigation.

One incident involved a suspect who drove a vehicle onto the pavement at Lafayette Park. Another suspect jumped a security barrier in the northwest corner of Lafayette Park. It is not clear if the two events were related.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Al Jazeera.net co-founder and cartoonist Shujaat Ali dies aged 54
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Shujaat Ali, cartoonist and founding member of Al Jazeera’s online teams, has died at the age of 54.

A pioneer of digital cartoons, Ali was credited with creating the first animated caricatures online. He also worked at a number of media outlets in his native Pakistan and abroad, receiving several awards for his work.

He died last week after suffering a heart attack as he returned home from work. He was buried in Qasimabad in Rawalpindi, where his parents are also buried.

Ali was Pakistan’s first court artist, documenting the course of a number of well-known cases using his pencil and skills.

He had recently been working with the Pakistan Air Force, his son-in-law, Waqar Saeed, told the Dawn newspaper.

Before returning to his homeland, he had worked at Al Jazeera for many years. He contributed as part of the founding team of Al Jazeera Arabic’s online services, developing cartooning to utilise the potential of the digital platform.

Ahmed El Amraoui, an editor at Aljazeera.com, said, “I had the privilege of working with Shujaat during the early days of Aljazeera.com. He was a very talented artist, but what made him stand out was how far ahead of his time he was.”

Awad Joumaa, manager of Digital Programs at Al Jazeera English, described Ali’s cartoons as “unlike anything we were used to seeing in a news organisation… He drew everyone from Arafat to George Bush to Osama bin Laden.

“I remember the pride in his voice when he told me that presidents, prime ministers and rebel fighters passing through the newsroom would always stop to look at the wall where his cartoons hung,” Joumaa said.

“We forget there is a whole tradition in journalism where a cartoon could make governments and world leaders shake. Naji al-Ali, the Palestinian cartoonist, was killed for his cartoons. That is how powerful they were. And Shujaat was an incredible voice in that genre.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.summary: Shujaat Ali was a pioneer of digital cartoons and a pioneer in the digital media. He was buried in Qasimabad in Rawalpindi, where his parents are also buried. He died last week after suffering a heart attack as he returned home from work.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Yemen government forces claim new advances as Houthi border attacks resume
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Mohammad Mansour
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Yemen’s government forces have announced the capture of Houthi-held positions in the southern governorate of Lahj, amid fierce clashes with the Houthi rebels across multiple fronts in the country.

The government’s National Shield Forces said on Monday that they had seized positions on the al-Muhawala front in western Lahj after a large-scale assault on Houthi positions. The forces claimed that dozens of Houthi fighters had been killed or wounded in the attack.

The latest announcement comes after several days of reported gains by government forces in the northern governorate of al-Jawf, east of the Houthi-held Yemeni capital Sanaa. Government forces in al-Jawf have advanced in recent days through mountain ranges east of the provincial capital al-Hazm.

Al Jazeera Arabic reporter Suhaib al-Miyahi visited the al-Jawf front line on November 6, documenting trenches and fortifications in positions that government commanders said had been captured from the Houthis, as battles continued nearby.

The Houthis are continuing their attacks in Taiz, where they have encircled the city, imposing a siege on it for more than a month. Government forces say they have repelled Houthi attacks across several fronts in the outskirts of the city over the previous day.

In his daily update, government military spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that government forces had carried out almost 1,000 attacks in the previous hours, leaving more than 120 Houthi fighters dead or wounded. The claims could not be independently verified.

The recent clashes fall under the ongoing Operation Dawn of Yemen, which began on October 5 in an attempt to reverse Houthi gains made along the Red Sea coast the previous month, and eventually defeat the Iranian-backed rebel group.

However, Saudi-backed government forces have yet to make significant gains in what is proving to be a war of attrition, the latest phase of a more than decade-long war that began after the Houthi capture of Sanaa in September 2014.

Tawfik al-Hamidi, political analyst and president of the SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, told Al Jazeera that the government is having some success in depleting Houthi manpower, partly as a result of the support it gets from Saudi air strikes.

“I believe that what is happening reflects a real depletion of the Houthis’ capabilities, and not just a tactical retreat,” al-Hamidi said.

He claimed that the number of Houthi attacks had decreased in frequency.

“The Houthi group still possesses military capabilities, but its ability to continue broad attacks and retain positions is facing mounting pressures,” al-Hamidi said.

He emphasised the strategic importance of al-Jawf because of its proximity to Sanaa, arguing that further government advances there could prompt the Houthis to redistribute their forces.

“I see that Taiz may be the biggest beneficiary of these developments, because it opens a real opportunity to ease the siege, leading to lifting it,” al-Hamidi said.

The escalation carries a severe humanitarian cost in Taiz, where nine civilians, including two children, were wounded in shelling and gunfire in several areas on Sunday, according to reports published on Monday by the state-run Saba news agency.

In a separate incident on Sunday, an ambulance came under fire in the al-Awat area, killing a wounded patient and his father and injuring a paramedic, according to local and medical sources cited by Saba.

The Joint Medical Emergency Committee in Taiz also said preliminary reports indicated that another ambulance had been targeted in the al-Shaqab area of Taiz.

The Houthis have meanwhile continued launching ballistic missiles and drones towards Saudi Arabia, including attacks targeting oil facilities.

The Saudi-led coalition said on Sunday that it had intercepted a drone and five missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh and Saudi Arabia’s eastern and southern regions.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on Monday that Saudi forces had carried out more than 100 air strikes in the preceding 24 hours, targeting Marib, Sanaa, Hodeidah, Taiz, Lahj, and al-Jawf.

He alleged that the attacks had caused civilian casualties, but did not specify how many.

Al-Hamidi argued that the Houthis were using cross-border attacks to increase the security and economic costs of Saudi Arabia’s intervention, hoping to pressure Riyadh into halting the government offensive.

“The group realises that the continued advance of the government forces may weaken its military position, and therefore it uses missiles to raise the security and economic cost on Riyadh,” he explained.

But he warned that the strategy could backfire, prompting Saudi Arabia to instead intensify its military response rather than offering concessions.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/youtub.author: Lauren Forristal
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/youtub.text:
YouTube is officially returning to the Billboard charts, ending a disagreement over how music streams should count toward chart rankings.

Announced Monday, YouTube is set to resume sharing its streaming data with Billboard in 2027. The decision follows recent changes to Billboard’s chart formula, which now gives more weight to ad-supported streams.

The disagreement began in December 2025, when YouTube said it would stop sharing its streaming data with Billboard. The company argued that the chart formula favored paid subscriptions while not giving enough credit to fans who listen for free with ads.

At the time, Lyor Cohen, YouTube’s global head of music, criticized the system in a blog post, saying it didn’t reflect how people listen to music today.

“Billboard uses an outdated formula that weights subscription-supported streams higher than ad-supported. This doesn’t reflect how fans engage with music today and ignores the massive engagement from fans who don’t have a subscription. Streaming is the primary way people experience music, making up 84% of U.S. recorded music revenue,” Cohen wrote.

Under Billboard’s previous formula, 1,000 paid streams counted the same as 2,500 ad-supported streams. YouTube felt this gave too much importance to paid listening, especially when millions of fans discover and support artists through free streaming.

Billboard has now updated its formula, reducing the gap between the two types of streams. Under the new system, 1,000 paid streams will equal 1,500 ad-supported streams when calculating album consumption units, compared with 2,500 under the previous formula. Paid streams will still count for more, but free streams will now have a bigger impact on chart positions.

YouTube’s return could make a difference for many artists, especially independent musicians and those with large international fan bases. Music videos, live performances, lyric videos, and other content on the platform help artists reach new audiences. With YouTube’s data back in the mix, more of that activity will now count toward their Billboard performance.

For Billboard, getting YouTube’s data back also means having a more complete picture of how people listen to and discover music. With so many fans using the platform, leaving its streams out meant missing a major part of music consumption.

The disagreement began in December 2025, when YouTube said it would stop sharing its data with the Billboard chart.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/anthro.title: Anthropic releases new Mythos and Fable models amid RSI concerns
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/anthro.author: Russell Brandom
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/anthro.text:
Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision,” and communicate more clearly with users.

Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price.

Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system, long a sticking point for many enterprise clients.

It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR, which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain.

Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.”

Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card.

“Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.”

Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.”

Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/france.title: France blames Iran for mass-hacks targeting freezers in grocery stores and blood banks
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/france.author: Zack Whittaker
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/france.text:
The French government has formally blamed Iran for launching cyberattacks that targeted thousands of internet-connected industrial refrigerated and freezer units across the country and broader Europe.

This is the latest in a string of destructive cyberattacks attributed to Iran this year, following a spate of hacks targeting U.S. water providers and other online intrusions that caused mass-disruption to U.S. medical device maker giant Stryker and others.

The U.S. government linked the attacks to pro-Iranian hacktivists who are working for Tehran, likely in response to the U.S.-Israel-led war against Iran which killed its supreme leader in February.

Two recent waves of cyberattacks throughout October and into November saw hackers remotely break into web-based controllers that manage fleets of industrial cold and chilling units at grocery stores and retail supermarkets, and raise the temperatures to spoil food and destroy goods. Medical blood banks were also hacked but the attacks were stopped before any blood was spoiled, according to the French Blood Establishment.

Security researchers have since warned that the web-based controllers are vulnerable to remote hacks, with some of the affected models made by Danish company Danfoss no longer receiving security fixes.

In a statement given to reporters in Paris on Monday, French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said: “I am able to confirm that responsibility for this act lies with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” referring to Iran’s military and hackers.

“This was an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression; it represents the first large-scale act of sabotage on our national territory and constitutes a major assault on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people,” said Barrot, adding that the hacks will “not go without consequences.”

The French government has summoned Iran’s ambassador. Reuters first reported France’s attribution to Iran, citing sources ahead of the foreign minister’s remarks. The French government said it would also issue European-wide sanctions against those who carried out the hacks. Barrot said that the matter was now in the hands of the French justice system.

A spokesperson for Iran’s consulate in New York did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The U.S. government is also reportedly looking into whether freezer units on military bases were hacked, following reports of similar outages and disruption earlier this year. U.S. officials have reportedly also linked the freezer-related cyberattack to Iran, but the intelligence community has not yet made a formal or public attribution.

Logic Pro is Apple’s first app to charge for extended usage of Apple Intelligence.

After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.”

These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.

For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.

https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.author: James O'Donnell
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.text:
Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

The latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview enhances the Search feature so that you can access specific settings right from a search window.

November 9, 2026, 2:33 pm ET

Microsoft has been on a kick lately trying to improve and enhance Windows 11, including sprucing up Search, which is now simpler, cleaner, and friendlier. And there’s another cool trick that Search has up its sleeve: Available in the Beta channel of the latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview, Search will give you access to specific Windows settings and commands. Known as inline actions, this latest skill is designed to help you directly complete certain tasks. That means you no longer need to know exactly where or how to find the setting you need.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

Curious about built-in features such as Dark mode, Bluetooth, screen brightness, Remote Desktop, the Windows clipboard, or Windows Update? Just type the name or phrase in the Search field. The results then display an Open button that you can select to go directly to the related setting.

“A new Windows Search experience built on WinUI 3 is beginning to roll out,” Microsoft said on a web page announcing the latest Insiders build. “It’s faster, more efficient, and features a streamlined design that makes results easier to scan. Inline actions let you quickly complete tasks directly. Turn on dark mode or Bluetooth, adjust your screen brightness, mute your device, or arrange windows from Windows Search.”

I tried this with several different Windows settings, and the results window pointed me to the right screens for tweaking them. Though I know where most Windows settings are located by now, there are still times when I forget how to reach certain ones. This new skill promises to be a time saver whenever I face that challenge.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC

Here’s another handy enhancement. How often do you type a word or term in Windows Search only to misspell it? With the latest update, Search will now better understand what you actually mean and match you with the correct results. Type “drak” instead of “dark,” for example, and you’ll still see the results for Dark mode.

Microsoft promises these latest improvements to Windows Search will continue to be fine-tuned over the next few weeks. And there’s more in the new Preview build.

Ever run into trouble using Windows Hello facial recognition in a dark area? Now, your screen will temporarily brighten up to help you sign in under those conditions. To enable this option, head to Settings, select Account, select Sign-in options, and then click Facial recognition. Turn on the switch for “Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition.”

The latest Insiders build also tweaks features such as Live captions, Gaming, File Explorer, and Microsoft 365 cloud storage.

Also: How I used ChatGPT to talk me through fixing a corrupted gaming PC

To grab this update, you’ll have to join the Windows Insiders Program if you’re not already registered. You can then sign up for the Beta or Experimental channel, either of which will give you access to the new Search skills and other features. Make sure you’re running the Beta Preview Build 26320.9876 or higher. To check, go to Settings, select System, and then click About. The Windows Info section will indicate the build number.

As for regular Windows users not enrolled in the Insiders Program, the new changes should reach you relatively soon. I’d expect them to roll out with the December Patch Tuesday update arriving on December 8, so that Microsoft can squeeze them in before the end of the year.

https://spectrum.ieee.org/zero-trust-age.title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
https://spectrum.ieee.org/zero-trust-age.author: Vishal Sharma
https://spectrum.ieee.org/zero-trust-age.text:
As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?
