https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/jensen-h.title: Jensen Huang affair puts Nvidia's future at risk, with no clear successor to the renowned CEO
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/jensen-h.author: Annie Palmer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/jensen-h.text:
Nvidia’s investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a purported Chinese spy has raised questions about whether he may be forced to step back from leading the chipmaker.

Huang is practically synonymous with Nvidia, which he co-founded in 1993 and turned into one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

“The issue at Nvidia is that there is no clear successor to Jensen, and we had expected him to stay in this role for at least 10 more years,” analysts at Melius Research said in a note on Monday.

Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang’s admission of an affair with a purported Chinese spy has raised questions about his future at the company, and what happens if the 63-year-old co-founder, who built the chipmaker into one of the most valuable businesses on the planet, is forced out.

Shares of Nvidia sank more than 5% on Monday, even as the broader market rallied sharply, after Huang acknowledged the affair in a message to staff on Sunday, and said that the board was launching an investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence agency. The board said it has “confidence in Jensen,” and that it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

The New York Times first reported that the Chinese businesswoman was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, according to people briefed on the intelligence circulated in a memo among the Trump administration in the spring. China has called the allegation a smear.

While Nvidia says Huang will continue to lead the company during the probe, pressure is rapidly mounting on the chipmaker, whose technology has powered the first four years of the generative artificial intelligence boom. Leaders from both parties are calling for briefings, and Democrats poised to take control of both houses of Congress are calling for investigations and new legislation “to stop advanced AI chips from fueling China’s military,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts wrote in a post on X on Monday.

Huang has outsized influence over Nvidia, and is the sole face of the company with no clear second-in-command. He’s also among the loudest champions of AI in the country, is critical to the financing of the broader infrastructure buildout and has a close relationship with President Donald Trump, giving Nvidia a front-row seat when it comes to discussions on AI policy, safety and regulation.

“The issue at Nvidia is that there is no clear successor to Jensen, and we had expected him to stay in this role for at least 10 more years,” analysts at Melius Research said in a Monday research note.

Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” on Monday that, “Jensen is Nvidia. Nvidia is Jensen.” He added that Huang “runs the thing pretty much top down,” and “sort of pulls all the strings.”

Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nvidia has long maintained a flat, non-hierarchical organizational structure. Huang has deep involvement in the company’s day-to-day operations, with around 60 direct reports, and frequently serves as its spokesperson in front of world leaders and at industry conferences. In addition to being co-founder and CEO, Huang is also Nvidia’s president.

However, relative to some of his founder peers in tech like Meta’s
 Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk at SpaceX
, Huang has minimal actual control. He owns just over 3% of the outstanding shares and is one of 11 members on a board that has no official chair.

And in the risk factors of Nvidia’s financial filings, Huang isn’t specifically identified as a key person. Rather, the company says, “we are highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team.”

“Failure to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions involving executives and key employees could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success,” Nvidia says.

Still, Huang’s influence is undeniable, so much so that the question of succession is one that’s hardly broached among analysts and investors.

Timm Schulze-Melander, an analyst at Rothschild & Co. Redburn, wrote in a Monday note that Huang could be forced to step back from the CEO role if the board’s investigation reveals “something materially more serious” than an undisclosed relationship.

But Schulze-Melander said Huang’s potential resignation isn’t a foregone conclusion of the investigation, pointing to the importance of his leadership at the company.

Nvidia’s board “needs to demonstrate independence and protect shareholders without destabilizing a company whose success is unusually dependent on its founder,” Schulze-Melander wrote. “Its initial statement suggests it is attempting to achieve both.”

Several analysts said the investigation could lead to governance changes at Nvidia, including putting a transition contingency plan in place.

The Melius analysts wrote that Nvidia has a “strong bench” of executive talent across its networking, hyperscale and high-performance computing businesses, along with “technical expertise” stemming from Chief Technology Officer Michael Kagan and Chief Scientist Bill Dally.

“While these folks can keep the engine running, Jensen is one of a kind, and his energy will be needed to maintain confidence in the AI trade,” the analysts wrote.

— CNBC’s Kif Leswing, Kristina Partsinevelos and Michael Bloom contributed to this report.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren is set to take over the Senate banking committee in January. The Massachusetts Democrat is already charting the panel’s course.

Among Warren’s top issues for the new Congress are addressing the cost of living, tightening export controls on advanced AI chips to China and promulgating regulations for prediction markets.

Warren is also plotting an aggressive oversight agenda and urged big tech CEOs, administration officials and Wall Street executives to preserve their documents.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren is set to take over the Senate Banking Committee. The Massachusetts Democrat is already charting the panel’s course.

Among Warren’s top issues for the Congress that convenes in January are addressing the cost of living, tightening export controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips to China and promulgating regulations for prediction markets, according to a Warren banking committee aide. The aide spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the yet-to-be-announced agenda. Warren is also plotting an aggressive oversight agenda and urged tech CEOs, administration officials and Wall Street executives to preserve their documents, the aide said.

Democrats’ dominant win in last week’s midterm elections hands them control of committee gavels on Capitol Hill. With that comes the ability to set the legislative agenda for the House and Senate and subpoena power to compel government officials and business leaders to testify under oath. The Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee has a broad remit, including jurisdiction over federal monetary policy, banks and export controls.

Warren’s plans to tackle affordability include capping credit card interest rates, following up her 21st Century Road to Housing Act with additional legislation to build more affordable homes and lowering medical, consumer and student debt.

The aide said Warren also intends to put constraints on AI chips going to China, while shaping rules for AI at home.

Warren is also seeking to end the “Wild West-style” lack of oversight in the prediction market industry, the aide said. She and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis have already written to Kalshi and Polymarket demanding information on safeguards around election-related markets.

The banking committee is also likely to be at the center of Democrats’ oversight agenda, which is expected to cast a wide net into private industry. Warren said tech CEOs, administration officials, Trump family cryptocurrency businesses and Wall Street executives should prepare to answer the committee’s questions and should preserve their documents, the aide said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/this-bea.title: This beaten-down data center stock could be worth a look, says Mike Khouw
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/this-bea.author: Michael Khouw
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/this-bea.text:
United Rentals is currently trading at a below-market forward multiple.

Effectively, one can buy superior, market-beating growth at a discounted market multiple.

The macro backdrop provides a sturdy foundation for this growth.

I’m a firm believer in investing in what you know—and what you use. During a recent visit to my parents’ New Hampshire property, my brother and I tackled overdue maintenance, and having the right equipment on hand was critical to finish the work in the limited time we had.

He and I rented both a compact track loader (CTL, not pictured) and a bulldozer (pictured above) from United Rentals (NYSE: URI)
 to push through some of the heavier work.

For those who may not be familiar with the company, United Rentals can quickly deploy heavy equipment to a remote site. Here’s why I believe it sets up well for a defined-risk, moderately bullish options trade.

The good news is that United Rentals is currently trading at a below-market forward multiple — both on a Price-to-Earnings (P/E) basis, currently ~17.3x forward estimates of ~$61.10/share, and on an Enterprise Value-to-EBITDA (EV/EBITDA) basis at ~8.8x $9.25 billion in FYE2027 EBITDA. This despite the fact that the company is compounding revenues, earnings, and EBITDA at a noticeably faster clip than the cap-weighted S&P 500. Effectively, one can buy superior, market-beating growth at a discounted market multiple.

The recent third-quarter earnings confirmed this trajectory. URI delivered a beat and raise, pointing to robust underlying demand across its end markets, and the sell-side is scrambling to catch up, revising its forward estimates upward. Improving earnings estimates is one of the most reliable, time-tested short-term investment factors. Stocks with positive estimate revisions tend to meaningfully outperform those burdened with declining estimates in the short term.

The macro backdrop provides a sturdy foundation for this growth. We are in the midst of a broader nonresidential construction recovery, which has driven an environment of improving and resilient rental rates. Although admittedly a potential slowdown in data center construction could become a future headwind, broader infrastructure demand remains robust.

A balanced view requires acknowledging the risks. While URI looks cheap relative to the broader market, it is not exactly cheap relative to its own history. The stock is currently trading roughly 20% to 25% above its five-year average multiple. One could easily argue that the historical multiple was simply too cheap for a business of this quality, scale, and capital efficiency. Still, mean reversion back to historical levels of “cheapness” remains a downside risk.

This brings us to the options market. When you have a stock with solid momentum, fundamentals, and positive estimate revisions, but you’re hesitant to pay a premium to its historical valuation, outright unhedged equity accumulation isn’t always the optimal route. Instead, selling cash-covered puts offers a highly strategic entry mechanism.

With URI’s implied volatility currently hovering in the 42% to 45% range, the options market is pricing in enough movement to offer a decent premium. By selling a cash-covered put, we acknowledge both the good and the bad. It respects the aggressive growth, market share capture, and the recent beat-and-raise quarter, while appropriately hedging against the risk of that elevated historical multiple.

If the stock continues its upward march, the puts expire worthless, and we pocket a high-probability yield that easily beats fixed income. If the stock pulls back—perhaps toward that 5-year average multiple—we are assigned the shares at a lower effective cost basis, which, if it happens, we could lower even further by writing upside covered calls against it. (This approach to entering a stock, then writing covered calls if assigned, is sometimes referred to as “the wheel strategy”).

So either we acquire an attractive stock at a price we dictate (the short strike, less the premium collected for selling it) or we simply collect premium for assuming that risk if the stock does not decline. For a company that provides the literal heavy lifting for infrastructure growth, that’s a structural advantage worth trading.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/trump-un.title: Trump administration proposes stricter work-search rules for unemployment benefits
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/trump-un.author: Greg Iacurci
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/trump-un.text:
The Labor Department proposed a rule Monday that would require unemployment insurance claimants to complete five work-search requirements per week in order to receive benefits.

The Trump administration framed the proposal as a way to strengthen “integrity and accountability.”

Consumer advocates said it would make it more challenging for job seekers to qualify for unemployment benefits.

The vast majority of states currently require fewer than five work search activities per week.

The Labor Department proposed a rule on Monday that would raise the bar for people applying for unemployment insurance by requiring them to prove they’ve conducted five work-search activities per week in order to qualify for benefits.

In the announcement, the Trump administration described the proposal as a way to improve the “integrity and accountability” of the joint federal-state unemployment insurance system. Consumer advocates said the proposed work-search baseline of five qualifying activities per week exceeded that in most states and would make it more difficult for many applicants to qualify for assistance.

There is currently no uniform requirement across the U.S. for unemployment insurance claimants regarding work-search requirements.

Federal law requires all states to have a work-search requirement, but states have broad discretion to set their own eligibility. They also have ample leeway to set other parameters such as the weekly sum claimants can receive and the number of weeks they can get those funds.

A qualifying work search activity might be applying to a job, creating a profile on a job-search website or attending a networking event, for example, depending on the state.

Currently, only four states require a minimum of five work searches per week, Michele Evermore, the senior director of economic security and worker transitions at the National Employment Law Project, wrote in an email.

The remaining states require fewer activities, she said.

The Labor Department proposal would require individuals claiming unemployment insurance to complete and report at least five qualifying work-search activities each week before payment is issued, according to a press release announcing the rule.

“This proposed rule helps jobseekers find work faster and ensures efficient use of taxpayer resources while improving the overall integrity of our unemployment system,” Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said in the release.

There’s a 60-day public comment period on the proposal.

“Unemployment insurance is meant to be temporary support while you find your next job, not a permanent taxpayer-funded paycheck,” Sonderling wrote Monday on X.

Jobless workers generally aren’t eligible for unemployment insurance for more than six months in almost all states.

The Trump administration proposal amounts to a dramatic change to the unemployment safety net and would make it tougher for unemployment claimants to keep their benefits and increase costs for states, Evermore said.

“Not only is the proposed change devastating to claimants who may not have five search options for every week they are unemployed, but it will likely cost states hundreds of thousands of dollars,” Evermore said in an e-mail. “Nearly all states will have to change their claimant intake forms, and with it, their technology — a costly fix. Many states will have to rewrite their laws to meet this rule.”

She also said it is “highly unusual for the Department of Labor to unilaterally change how states run their [unemployment insurance] systems absent clear direction from Congress.

The Labor Department rule “strongly encourages” states to allow for “a wide variety of work search activities” to satisfy the requirement, Evermore wrote.

The rule comes in a job market that labor economists have called “low hire, low fire,” in which it’s difficult for job seekers to find a new gig amid a low national hiring rate and a historically low layoff rate. Altogether, there’s lower churn in the job market, contributing to fewer opportunities for job seekers, economists said.

The share of workers who are long-term unemployed — meaning they’ve been out of work for more than six months — has climbed. About 27.6% of all unemployed workers were considered long-term unemployed as of October, up from 20.5% three years earlier.

Consumer advocates said it would make it more challenging for job seekers to qualify for benefits. The vast majority of states currently require fewer than five work search activities per week.

Could Israeli politics get more complicated? Israeli President Issac Herzog tapped Gadi Eisenkot over the weekend to form the next government. You would think that means the opposition parties led by Eisenkot—known in Israel as the “change bloc”—are on the verge of ousting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and forming a stable, centrist government. But that’s not quite the case, not yet anyway. As the haggling gets underway, let’s take a minute to lay out the facts—and sidestep the vitriol and virtue signaling that tends to dominate social media when it comes to Israel.

Based on the final results of the election held two weeks ago, Netanyahu and his bloc have 53 seats in the 120-seat parliament, while Eisenkot’s change bloc controls 48 seats. The remaining 19 seats belong to two Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Ra’am.

Could Israeli politics get more complicated? Israeli President Issac Herzog tapped Gadi Eisenkot over the weekend to form the next government. You would think that means the opposition parties led by Eisenkot—known in Israel as the “change bloc”—are on the verge of ousting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and forming a stable, centrist government. But that’s not quite the case, not yet anyway. As the haggling gets underway, let’s take a minute to lay out the facts—and sidestep the vitriol and virtue signaling that tends to dominate social media when it comes to Israel.

Based on the final results of the election held two weeks ago, Netanyahu and his bloc have 53 seats in the 120-seat parliament, while Eisenkot’s change bloc controls 48 seats. The remaining 19 seats belong to two Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Ra’am.

The nod from the president means that Eisenkot gets the first crack at forming a government. The clearest path to a majority would be for him to form a coalition with the Joint List and Ra’am. That would give the anti-Netanyahu forces a commanding 67-seat majority in Israel’s parliament—enough to address some of the most divisive issues in Israeli society, including expanding mandatory military service to include ultra-Orthodox Jews and establishing a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to Hamas’s attack on Oct. 7, 2023.

But things are never so straightforward, especially in Israeli politics. Theoretically, a change bloc government with the Joint List and Ra’am is possible, but there are informal barriers to getting there—and political traps once it is established—that would likely make the government unstable.

Since Israel’s founding, only one governing coalition included an Arab-led party, and it didn’t last long. In 2021, parties from across the political spectrum—united mainly by their antipathy for Netanyahu—formed a left-right coalition headed by Naftali Bennett, a onetime Netanyahu protégé. The coalition included Ra’am, which had focused mainly on bread-and-butter issues for Israel’s Arab citizens, who make up 20 percent of the population. In previous elections, the Arab-led parties were considered too fringe politically to be included in coalitions or they themselves ruled out serving in Israeli governments. Bennett’s decision to include Ra’am was groundbreaking.

But the motley coalition held together for just a year. The crisis that precipitated the government’s fall revolved around lawmakers from Ra’am and the left-wing Meretz party who opposed extending a procedural measure that benefitted settlers in the West Bank. This dispute within the coalition prompted the resignation of one of Bennett’s own deputies who assailed anti-Zionists—presumably Arab members—of the coalition holding the government “hostage.” Throughout this period, Netanyahu was able to capitalize on the government’s ideological diversity, adding to its stresses and strains by highlighting the contradictions between its right-wing and anti-Zionist members.

It is not clear why this time would be any different. A change bloc plus Arab parties would have the similar ideological fault lines. Perhaps the exigency of keeping Netanyahu out of the prime minister’s office would be enough to hold everyone together, but it would take significant political skill. All the discussion about a government with the Arab parties may be moot anyway. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions to be in the government—recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, strict adherence to the values laid out in Israel’s declaration of independence, mandatory national service for all, and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization. The first, second, and fourth conditions will be tough for the Joint List to agree to. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas may have more flexibility, but he recently refused to call Hamas a terrorist organization.

I’m not sure how you square this circle. You can promise Arab parties lots of resources, and their leaders seem motivated to cooperate to prevent Netanyahu from returning to office. That is a good sign for the change bloc, but it does nothing to resolve the hard differences between Zionist and anti-Zionist parties.

The common knee-jerk reaction to this problem among social media posters and some members of the foreign-policy community is to declare Israel racist. Are there racists in Israel? No doubt there are. Right-wing politicians Avigdor Liberman, Bezalel Smotrich, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and others have a history of making racist anti-Arab comments. Netanyahu has repeatedly trafficked in fearmongering around the issue of Arab voters “racing to the ballots” during the elections. But to focus on racism alone is to miss the core tension of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Most Israeli Jews support the idea of Israel as a Jewish state, albeit with an Arab minority. It would be uncomfortable for them to have people in government who oppose the country’s founding principles and refuse to condemn Hamas.

At the same time, it should surprise no one that the leaders of Israel’s Arab parties have a different outlook and entirely different concerns. Arab Israelis have their own historical narrative, do not share Israel’s founding myths, and are not part of its collective memory.

One alternative is for Eisenkot to form a minority government without the Arab-led parties and rely on their support from the outside on crucial legislative votes. But minority governments tend to be unstable in Israel and at least one party within the change bloc, Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Is Our Home), has ruled out such a configuration.

Netanyahu’s wars have weakened foes, but they’re unsustainable.

A new book details how the country slayed Washington’s foes.

Another alternative would be for Eisenkot to invite the ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties to join his coalition. That seems to be more acceptable to mainstream Israelis, but barely. The white-hot anger directed at the Haredi parties among almost everyone in Israel is palpable. That is because most Haredi men do not serve in the military, and Israelis resent supporting an entire community that takes far more than it contributes to society. This would be a difficult coalition for Eisenkot to put together, though the leaders of the Ashkenazi Haredi party, United Torah Judaism, have indicated a willingness to consider it.

The fourth option is for Eisenkot to try and form a broad-based coalition with Netanyahu—what Israelis call a “national unity” government—with the two men rotating as prime ministers. That seems to be where Herzog wants to go. A Netanyahu-Eisenkot linkup would get to a majority in parliament easily and resolve several issues all at once for Israelis. The coalition would not include far-right figures Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, and there would be no need to cater to Haredi parties. The debate over normalizing the Arab-led parties by including them in a governing coalition would be put off for another day. Yet in the Rubik’s cube that is Israeli politics, this option also raises challenges.

For example, who would serve first as prime minister? And how would you guarantee that neither of them will violate the rotation agreement? Netanyahu did just that with the hapless Benny Gantz in 2020, bringing down the government and forcing new elections before Gantz could take over.

Beyond the procedures, Eisenkot would have to make the case to his voters why a deal with Netanyahu is warranted when opponents of Netanyahu hold 67 seats in the 120-member parliament. It is a tough argument to make, especially for Eisenkot, who said during the campaign that he would not agree to a national unity government with the man that he (and many others) hold responsible for failures that led to the Oct. 7 massacre.

Still, a so-called national unity government would probably be the most stable of all the options, freezing out parties on the margins and capturing that center-right part of the electorate where the preponderance of Jewish Israelis now live politically. It would also head off what many Israelis think of as the worst option of all—a political deadlock that leads to another election in the coming months.

Herzog has his job cut out for him if he wants to avoid another election, something that is to Netanyahu’s advantage but not to Israel’s. Wrangling Israel’s political parties is difficult even in the best of circumstances, especially for a president who has limited formal powers. Herzog will rely on the dignity of his office and his powers of persuasion to get an outcome that, regardless of its content, is likely to make a significant number of Israelis unhappy. In the coming weeks, being Israel’s president is going to be among the worst jobs in the world.

Steven A. Cook is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the Eni Enrico Mattei senior fellow for Middle East and Africa studies at the Council on Foreign Relations. His latest book is The End of Ambition: America’s Past, Present, and Future in the Middle East. X: @stevenacook

A Republican lawmaker moved Monday to impeach US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up a potentially explosive vote in Congress just days after President Donald Trump's party suffered a crushing midterm defeat.

Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.

The Republican-controlled House could vote as early as Wednesday, with some lawmakers from Trump's party signaling that they might join Democrats in supporting the charges.

Impeachment would be a humiliating blow for Hegseth and the Trump administration, but would not automatically remove him from office.

READ MORE
Democrats warn Trump camp to ‘lawyer up’ as anger over corruption drives midterms wipeout

That would require a trial and conviction by a two-thirds majority in the Senate – a far higher hurdle, even after Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

The impeachment push has gathered momentum since Tuesday's midterm elections, when Democrats swept both chambers of Congress amid widespread anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices.

Republicans retain control of Congress until the newly elected lawmakers take office on January 3, but their overwhelming defeat has fueled recriminations and weakened party discipline.

Some Republican lawmakers who lost their seats could also skip votes, potentially making it easier for the impeachment measure to pass.

Massie, an outspoken critic of Trump who lost his own primary to a candidate backed by the president, is using a special congressional procedure to force the House to consider his resolution within two legislative days.

Republican leaders could still seek to block the measure through a procedural vote.

The articles accuse Hegseth of violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which limits the president's ability to engage US forces in hostilities without congressional approval.

They also allege misconduct involving civilian casualties and military operations in Yemen and Venezuela.

The Pentagon has rejected the accusations.

Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker in January, threw his weight behind impeachment on Sunday.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC News.

"The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," he said.

"Pete Hegseth has got to go."

Several Republicans have expressed dissatisfaction with Hegseth's leadership without committing to impeaching him.

Arkansas congressman French Hill said Sunday he wanted to hear the debate before deciding whether the accusations justified impeachment.

Under the US Constitution, the House can impeach a senior government official by a simple majority vote, effectively bringing formal charges of serious misconduct.

The Senate then decides whether to convict and remove the official from office, requiring support from two-thirds of senators present.

Even with their enlarged majority next year, Democrats would need substantial Republican backing to reach that threshold. Only two Cabinet secretaries – almost 150 years apart – have been impeached in US history, and neither was removed by the Senate.

Hegseth has dismissed Massie's impeachment effort as a "sham," calling the congressman "disgruntled" and accusing his opponents of pursuing political destruction.

The Pentagon announced a rare press briefing by Hegseth scheduled for Tuesday.

Trump has publicly stood by his embattled defense chief, declaring last week: "I have every intention to keep him."

But the president's weakened political position after the midterms has left Hegseth facing the prospect of an impeachment battle that could extend well beyond this week's House vote.

Speaking to FRANCE 24 after the US midterm elections, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said he believed both Tehran and Washington wanted to negotiate. "We think so. And they are working for negotiations," he said of the Iranians, adding that the same was true of the Americans. However, this is "not enough to prevent another round of escalation. That's why we need to have a concrete deal," Abdelatty explained.

After Egypt's parliament approved defensive military aid to Saudi Arabia, a senior Houthi official warned that Cairo would then also be at war with the Yemeni rebels. Asked about this, the foreign minister said Egypt already had a military presence in the kingdom, at Riyadh's request, and was "strengthening that", stressing that it was "mainly for defensive objectives".

On Gaza, a year after Donald Trump's peace plan was announced, Abdelatty admitted that its first phase had yet to be fully implemented, citing aid shortfalls and daily Israeli targeted killings of Palestinians, while saying Hamas's disarmament remained "the main problem". But "we have full confidence in the leadership of President Trump to deliver", he asserted.

Abdelatty also said he was "confident" that US military aid to Egypt would continue, even after Trump announced an end to military aid to Israel. Responding to commments by Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's newly elected Egyptian American senator, who has called for an end to all US military aid to the region, he said that a "strong Egypt is very important for the interests of the United States", calling his country "the main pillar of stability" in the region.

Topic:
Animal Cruelty

Allegations of animal cruelty have been made against a NSW Central West saleyard. (Supplied: Animal Liberation)

Allegations of animal cruelty at the Central West Livestock Exchange in Forbes have been referred to the Animal Welfare League for investigation.

Video taken at the saleyard shows injured sheep being thrown into a paddock with dozens of dead animals.

Animal welfare groups have called on the NSW government to strengthen animal cruelty legislation.

Warning: This article contains images of alleged animal cruelty some readers may find distressing.

Images of what animal welfare groups claim to be injured sheep being thrown into a paddock next to dozens of dead animals have been referred for an investigation of alleged cruelty at a NSW saleyard.

Videos captured with a drone at the Central West Livestock Exchange in Forbes, one of the largest saleyards in the country, in September showed people disposing of allegedly injured sheep in a paddock, surrounded by nearly 30 other dead animals.

Another video, supplied to the ABC by advocacy group Animal Liberation (AL), appeared to show three dead sheep being dragged behind a vehicle in the saleyard.

The facility is one of the largest in the country, having processed more than 1.8 million sheep in 2025-26, according to Meat and Livestock Australia.

AL passed the video onto the RSPCA and the Animal Welfare League, which is investigating the matter.

The Animal Welfare League is tasked with investigating welfare and cruelty concerns in some instances in the state's west.

The video showed three dead sheep being dragged through the saleyard.  (Supplied: Animal Liberation)

"The footage is abhorrent, it's very distressing to watch," AL director Lisa Ryan said.

"There were so many instances of animals being completely disregarded in terms of the obvious suffering that you can see.

Dozens of dead sheep can be seen in a paddock next to the Central West Livestock Exchange in Forbes.  (Supplied: Animal Liberation)

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Forbes Shire Council, which owns and operates the saleyard, said they have not been contacted by the Animal Welfare League and were not aware of any accusations of animal cruelty at the facility.

"Central West Livestock Exchange (CWLE) takes all animal welfare matters seriously," the spokesperson said.

"Council and CWLE is committed to the safe, lawful and humane handling of livestock and will continue to operate according to animal welfare policies and procedures.

"Should any concerns be raised with council, they will be reviewed."

In a statement, NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said legislation prevented her from commenting on a specific matter that is the subject of an investigation.

"Everyone in NSW has a responsibility to follow the laws and regulations regarding animal welfare," she said.

Agricultural Minister Tara Moriarty has referred the matter to the Animal Welfare League to investigate.  (ABC News: Alexander Lewis)

The Animal Welfare League was also contacted for comment.

Ms Ryan said what occurred at the Forbes saleyard was not an "isolated incident" and illustrated a broader industry problem.

"It is like a very badly broken record where we see the way animals are regarded and treated," she said.

The protection of livestock is governed in NSW under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act which was passed in 1979.

Ms Ryan said the video displayed a number of "clear breaches" of the law.

She said after more than 40 years, the NSW government needed to update the legislation.

"Farmed animals are at the bottom of the pile."

The Animal Welfare League is investigating alleged animal cruelty at the Central West Livestock Exchange in Forbes.  (Supplied: Forbes Shire Council)

In 2018, the federal government introduced the Australian Animal Welfare Standards and Guidelines for livestock at saleyards.

Under the guidelines, people handling stock must not throw them, drop them from heights which prevent them landing safely, or drag animals that are unable to stand.

But neither NSW or Victoria have legislated to make those standards law.

In October, Agriculture Victoria announced an investigation into allegations of animal cruelty at the Bendigo Livestock Exchange after video showed sheep dying in pens, unmuzzled dogs being used and injured animals being transported for sale.

Gary Hall says government reforms on animal cruelty are needed in New South Wales and Victoria.  (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

The founder of welfare group Sheep Advocate Australia, Gary Hall, lodged 81 official complaints with the agency in that instance.

After acquiring the video taken at the Central West Livestock Exchange, he submitted eight complaints to the NSW authorities.

Mr Hall said he was not surprised by what he saw in the videos from Forbes.

"From a regulatory point of view, we need NSW and Victoria, essentially the two largest sheep states in Australia, to come together to improve these issues," he said.

"We need clear reform to make sure rules are adhered to … there aren't many laws that are enforceable.

"Then there is the compliance issue where there is actually nobody watching to enforce these rules."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.author: Mazoe Ford and Syan Vallance
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Brand used a provocative persona as his foundation to build Hollywood stardom, which crumbled after the release of a 2023 documentary. (Reuters )

In June 2013 Russell Brand was in his element: on stage in front of an adoring crowd.

The comedian and actor was at the height of his fame, a year after his divorce from pop star Katy Perry, with a slew of Hollywood comedies under his belt.

Brand was being interviewed for a podcast with fellow comic Richard Herring, recorded in front of a live audience at Leicester Square Theatre in London.

Katy Perry and Russell Brand married 2010 after meeting when she had a cameo in Brand's movie Get Him to the Greek. (Mario Anzuoni : Reuters)

The episode description joked that the host struggled to decide what to ask ahead of the show: "What do you ask the man who has already admitted everything?"

Mr Herring didn't need to worry.

"I raped someone once," Brand announced, kicking back and crossing his legs as the crowd laughed.

But fourteen years later, he sat behind a glass box in a London courtroom and denied he was a rapist.

Brand was found not guilty on two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. (PA: Elizabeth Cook via AP)

After a four-week trial, Brand was convicted of one charge of rape and three of sexual assault but acquitted on two charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

On Monday a judge sentenced him to 10-and-a-half years' jail.

As he left the court in a prison van, Brand's journey from Hollywood's A-list to the UK's sex offender registry was complete.

A prison van carrying Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court on the day of his sentencing. (Reuters: Corey Rudy)

Over a career spanning 25 years, Brand moved from comedian and actor to political activist, then wellness guru, anti-vaxxer and finally, alt-right Christian influencer.

He started out as a stand-up comedian in the late 1990s, then went on to present music and television programs.

Brand's big break came in the mid-noughties when he started hosting a Big Brother UK spin-off show, called Big Brother's Big Mouth.

By 2007, the comedian was a household name in Britain.

He hosted a radio show on BBC Radio 2, and became a bestselling author with the release of his memoir, My Booky Wook: A Memoir of Sex, Drugs and Stand-Up.

The book detailed encounters with women that included "smashing" a sex worker's phone against the wall, and using lies, "tears and blackmail" to manipulate a woman into sex.

"What kind of man was I? Treating women in this way? If this is what I'm telling you, can you imagine what's being left out?," Brand wrote.

Brand was found to have raped a young fan he met after his Scandalous show at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009. (Reuters: Suzanne Plunkett)

Brand's obsession with sex was key to his notoriety.

During his Scandalous stand up show in 2009, Brand described his stream of consciousness in the lead up to meeting Queen Elizabeth II: "In the back of my mind, I'm thinking grab her f*****g t**".

The joke was used in the show's advertising trailer.

Russell Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault relating to four women between 2004 and 2009.

There were controversies, such as the "Sachsgate" scandal in 2008. Brand and his radio show co-host Jonathan Ross left obscene prank messages on actor Andrew Sachs's answering machine, which led to Brand resigning from the BBC.

Still, his star continued to rise.

That same year, he was awarded the Sun newspaper's "Shagger of the Year" for the third time.

When Brand married US pop star Katy Perry in October 2010, he was catapulted into another level of fame.

Brand texted her to say he wanted a divorce, moments before she walked on stage to perform at a New Year's Eve concert in 2011.

By that stage he was established in Hollywood's comedy scene, appearing in Forgetting Sarah Marshall (2008) and Get Him to the Greek (2010).

But over the next few years he drifted further from the mainstream.

Actor Jonah Hill, Russell Brand and rapper Diddy present at the 2010 MTV Movie Awards. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)

By the end of 2013, Brand's comedy got more political, and by 2014 he had launched his first YouTube show.

He gained a new kind of notoriety, encouraging people not to vote.

Following his second marriage to British model Laura Gallacher in 2017, Brand moved into podcasts.

He became increasingly associated with COVID scepticism and alternative-media politics.

In September 2023, The Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches published an investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct from several women dating back to his early career.

YouTube suspended his monetisation, while several broadcasters and tour organisers cut ties.

Brand was charged with rape and sexual offences related to separate women — who did not appear in the documentary — in April 2025, then convicted in November 2026.

During sentencing, Judge Joel Bennathan told Southwark Crown Court that the entertainer-turned-conspiracist was a "sexual predator" who had shown "staggering arrogance."

These two pictures of Russell Brand in 1999 were tendered as evidence during his criminal trial in London in 2026. (Supplied: Metropolitan Police)

A few months after the allegations were aired, in April 2024, Brand converted to Christianity and was baptised by famous survivalist Bear Grylls in the Thames.

Following his conviction, Mr Grylls posted a statement online saying Brand's faith "seemed genuine to me at the time" and that judgement was for "the courts and God".

Six months before his conviction, Brand embarked on a round of interviews with mostly right wing Youtubers when his most recent book was released, titled 'How to Become a Christian in Seven Days* *May Take 50 Years of Sin and Serious F*ck Ups to Get Started'.

US political commentator and former Fox News host Megyn Kelly asked Brand what he would do if it was "God's plan" for him to go to prison.

"If it's God's plan, then there's no point resisting it, is there?," Brand replied.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/n.author: Nandini Dhir
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research looked at the disparities in police diversion between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal children. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

New data shows that Aboriginal children are less likely to receive a caution from police that will keep them out of court than non-Aboriginal children.

The NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research's report also found the disparity increased as Aboriginal children got older.

The NSW Aboriginal Legal Service says the data could point to Aboriginal children being "treated differently by NSW police due to bias".

NSW police are less likely to divert an Aboriginal child from court compared to a non-Aboriginal child, new data shows.

Under the NSW Young Offenders Act, police can give children a diversion if they have allegedly committed a crime, which aims to reduce a young person's contact with the court system and likelihood of repeat offending.

A diversion can take the form of a warning, a caution or an intervention.

A report released today by the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR) found Aboriginal children were 30 per cent less likely to receive a court diversion from police compared to non-Aboriginal children.

BOCSAR Executive Director Jackie Fitzgerald said this disparity existed "even when the alleged offence is eligible for diversion under the Young Offenders Act".

A report found Aboriginal children are 30 per cent less likely to receive a court diversion from police than their non-Aboriginal counterparts. (Supplied: NSW government)

Ms Fitzgerald said several factors affected whether a young person was issued a court diversion.

"And we can't explain that eight percentage point differential in terms of the data."

Ms Fitzgerald said a young person's "cooperation with police", and "any bias treatment" were potential reasons that could not be captured by the data.

BOCSAR research labelled the overall disparity as "concerning", because part of the Young Offenders Act was aimed at reducing the over-representation of Aboriginal children in the justice system.

Jackie Fitzgerald says a number of factors impacted whether a young person was issued a court diversion. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

Ms Fitzgerald said a young person's history with police or prior offending could impact whether an officer issued a court diversion.

The research also looked at a child's first contact with police and ruled out any history of offending.

The BOCSAR data showed that at first contact with police, 10 per cent of Aboriginal children were subjected to a formal court proceeding. This compares with 5 per cent of non-Aboriginal children.

Ms Fitzgerald said 80 per cent of the difference could not be explained by the data.

"Even at that first formal proceeding, there is still a differential in the likelihood of Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal young people being diverted [from court]," she said.

Sharif Deen says the gap "cannot be explained by any other objective factor". (Supplied: Aboriginal Legal Service)

NSW Aboriginal Legal Service Acting Chief Executive Sharif Deen said the gap "cannot be explained by any other objective factor".

BOCSAR research found the disparity between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal children being diverted from court increased as a child aged.

At 10 and 11 years of age, an Aboriginal child dealing with police was nearly 15 per cent more likely to be taken to court, compared to a non-Aboriginal child.

This disparity increased to 36 per cent by the age of 17.

Ms Fitzgerald said this data showed how important it was for children to receive court diversions.

"This research suggests that there is a benefit in making sure that young people have access to diversion, and making sure that's also available to Aboriginal young people who are coming into contact with police."

Mr Deen said the state government and police minister needed to listen to First Nations communities.

"It cannot be acceptable that in 2026 an Aboriginal child, for no reason other than the fact that they are Aboriginal, receives worse treatment from the agency that's designed to protect them," he said.

"The government's own data confirms that … NSW Police treat Aboriginal people and Aboriginal children differently."

The Aboriginal Legal Service also called for increased and independent oversight of NSW Police.

New South Wales Police has been contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/u.author: Riley Stuart
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/u.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Pete Hegseth has made few friends in Washington DC. (Pool: Ezra Acayan via Reuters)

Question marks hang over Pete Hegseth's tenure as US defense secretary after Congress launched a fresh attempt to impeach him amid growing bipartisan calls for him to resign.

In Washington on Monday, local time, dissident GOP Congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Mr Hegseth, saying he had acted unlawfully.

It starts a two-day clock for members to vote on whether to impeach the defence secretary.

Mr Massie has been among Hegseth's most ardent detractors on Capitol Hill, arguing the defence secretary's support of US military interventions in Iran, Venezuela and the Caribbean has violated international law.

Thomas Massie has made it clear he plans to end Hegseth's time at the Pentagon. (Reuters: Al Drago)

The fact Mr Massie is spearheading the impeachment attempt despite being from Donald Trump's Republican Party has enraged the President, who has repeatedly voiced support for Mr Hegseth.

Mr Massie's bid will have the support of Democrats, but there is growing speculation that disgruntled GOP representatives could also back it.

Around 70 Republicans will leave the House at the end of this year.

Some are retiring or have won political office elsewhere, while others were defeated at last week's midterm elections.

Analysts argue many people in this cohort will have nothing to lose and could back the bid to make a political point during their final weeks in office, even if it the White House hates it.

Analysis by Ian Verrender

Analysis by Ian Verrender

Analysis by Riley Stuart

Outgoing Nebraska GOP Representative Don Bacon is among those who have said he may support Massie's motion.

"I'm not the only one that feels this way, there's a bunch of us that have been talking about it," he told CNN on Monday.

When Mr Hegseth was asked about the efforts to impeach him on Monday, he told reporters: "We're not worried about that."

However, he has scheduled a rare press conference for Tuesday morning at the Pentagon where he will address the situation.

In order to impeach a president or cabinet secretary, a simple majority of House members must back the bid.

To actually remove them from office, a two-thirds majority of senators must then vote in favour of it.

Only two US cabinet secretaries have ever been impeached previously, and neither was removed from office.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Domestic Violence

The scheme would allow people to ask police for information about a partner's history of violence or abuse. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The Victorian government has announced it will introduce Clare's Law if re-elected, and expand a ban on smart glasses.

The opposition has also promised to bring in a domestic violence disclosure scheme if it wins office.

Victorians go to the polls on November 28.

The Victorian government has joined the opposition in promising to introduce a domestic violence disclosure scheme if it wins the state election.

Labor today announced it will introduce Clare's Law if re-elected on November 28, as well as banning smart glasses in more settings.

"You deserve to know if your partner has a secret violent past," Premier Ben Carroll said.

People would be able to ask police if their partner has a history of violence and abuse under the proposed laws, named after the UK scheme introduced after the murder of British woman Clare Wood.

The Victorian opposition promised in July to introduce a domestic violence disclosure scheme within 100 days if it wins office.

The government did not respond to questions regarding the implementation of Clare's Law at the time.

Premier Ben Carroll and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Today's Labor announcement includes promises to ban people convicted of family violence and sexual offences from using dating apps, along with greater investment in frontline support.

Labor is promising to model Victoria's version of Clare's Law on South Australia's, which has been in place since 2018.

Victoria's attorney-general and minister for prevention of family violence, Sonya Kilkenny, said victim-survivors had been calling for Clare's Law.

People would also be able to ask police for information about the partner of a family member or friend they believed could be at risk of violence and abuse.

South Australia's Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme has been in place since 2018. (Supplied: )

If re-elected, Labor would also make it a criminal offence for people convicted of family violence or sexual offending to use dating apps.

"Data is showing us that a third of people in the past five years have been sexually assaulted by someone they met on a dating app or website," Ms Kilkenny said.

Labor's proposed laws would also enable coroners to appoint an alternative next of kin in cases involving family violence allegations, charges or estrangement.

The government's election pledge includes $15.5 million more for the Orange Door and $16 million for a new Early Intervention and Prevention fund.

If you need help immediately, call emergency services on triple-0.

Labor promises to expand its ban on smart glasses beyond schools, kindergartens, and childcare centres, if re-elected.

Swimming pools, change rooms, community sporting venues, hospitals, aged care settings, and services supporting victim-survivors of family violence would be included in "the next step" of the state's ban on the technology.

"Tech has changed, so must our laws," Mr Carroll said.

"Creeps shouldn't be able to secretly film kids at Saturday sport."

Labor also announced plans to ban smart glasses in more settings if re-elected. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

It comes as a growing number of Victorian councils move to ban smart glasses in public facilities.

The Victorian government last month announced smart glasses would be banned in all Victorian schools from the start of the 2027 school year.

Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft front the media during the 2018 Cape Town Test. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

It's possible to forget now, obscured by the fog of the past eight years, just how extreme the national fury was in the wake of Cape Town, 2018.

This was a sporting scandal that broke containment lines. From your barista to your bus driver to the prime minister, everyone had something to say.

Sandpapergate touched something sensitive in the national psyche. It busted precisely the wrong myth, bruised just the wrong bit of our collective ego.

Usman Khawaja claims all staff and players knew that the Australian team was using sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa.

And not even after Cameron Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were tarred and feathered in the town square did the interest subside. Outrage was diluted by time into regret and curiosity, but there was a permanence to the damage done.

This next chapter was inevitable and in the end it was Usman Khawaja who put his hand up and first told his story, one now corroborated by his good mate Warner. The floodgates may well now open, and civil war could be at hand.

Khawaja's version, which has trickled out gradually over the course of four days, is only barely revelatory. The notion knowledge of the sandpaper plot went beyond the banned trio is not new, stands to reason and has been hinted at consistently almost from day one.

Bancroft himself back in 2021 insinuated with only a degree of subtlety that the great conspiracy extended beyond he, Smith and Warner. It was Bancroft's comments that prompted the indignant statement from the bowlers, which Khawaja claims further enraged Warner.

Given what Khawaja and Warner have now shared publicly, you can only imagine the atmosphere inside that dressing room. Fractured relationships may have been held together by shared on-field goals, but once that field is no longer shared, all bets are off.

The wider reaction has been curious. Some have pointed blame at Khawaja, which is unsurprising and something he likely expected.

It seems that by in going first he is seeking to clear the runway for Warner to eventually tell his tale in greater, potentially more scathing detail. Whether Khawaja has done this out of pure friendship, a form of penance or a little of both is something only he will know, but arguing he is simply trying to make a buck from a book is an oversimplification.

Darren Lehmann rejected Usman Khawaja's claims, but said ball tampering had been widespread in international cricket. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Darren Lehmann, meanwhile, the coach at the time and the only other person to suffer any significant repercussions, rejected some of Khawaja's assertions but offered up the fact that ball tampering had been "going on for 150 years" by "everyone in the world".

The substance of Khawaja's claims have not sparked any great backlash or rebuttal, but the timing, source and medium of them have drawn ire. And from all of that combined, much can be gleamed.

The greatest sin committed by the Australian cricket team in Cape Town in 2018 — or at least the sin that cost them the most — was taking the Australian public for fools.

Lehmann was, of course, correct when he said that ball tampering had been around forever and that basically everybody did it. Performed with the correct amount of tact it could be passed off as one of the game's "dark arts", and even those who did get caught generally only received fines or very minor suspensions.

As you could sense in Lehmann's tone, this was not as much of a taboo inside Australian cricket, even down to the dog-eat-dog ranks of grade cricket, as it was to the uninitiated who, quite justifiably, simply saw cheating as cheating and not part of some wider unspoken code.

In any case, before Cape Town most Australians were comforted by th belief that they were above such a thing. That Test match permanently shattered illusions. Mints and fingernails are one thing, but something as blatant and guileless as sandpaper? Not only were we ball tamperers, we were incredibly bad at it too.

Then came the first cover-up. Not the one Khawaja has allegedly lifted the lid on, but the instinctive, reflexive lie that came from Cricket Australia and the players on the day, when it was claimed that the contraband in Bancroft's pocket was a piece of sticky tape covered with "granules" from the pitch.

As ever, the cover-up was worse than the crime. The cavalier hubris of the whole affair, from conception to execution to deception, stung our sense of Australian exceptionalism and prompted an exceptional punishment.

Steve Smith breaks down speaking to media at Sydney International Airport upon return from South Africa. (AAP: Brendan Esposito)

Eight years on and with a perpetual war of words seemingly pending, it's hard to see how many lessons have been learned. "Ball tampering is bad" may be the extent of them.

Trying to wring the truth out of this mess may forever prove impossible, arguably by design. Khawaja said he was stunned that at no point during the investigation was he questioned or approached in any way. Indeed, if your goal is to ascertain what everybody knew, it does seem counterproductive not to simply ask everybody what they knew.

We have received hints at the truth, raised eyebrows and winking "no comments". Even Khawaja's recollections are in the main broad enough to avoid direct accusation, and therefore responsibility.

If everyone is ball tampering, then is anyone really ball tampering? If everyone knew about it, then who do you actually blame for it? At this point we're left with Joe Pesci in JFK, screaming at us about mysteries wrapped in riddles inside enigmas. "Even the ball tamperers don't know who did it! Don't you get it?"

And all the while Australians, who have always cared less for a case of whodunnit and more about the irreparable breach of trust, are still being played for fools.

Usman Khawaja (far right) says David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were the victims of the saga. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

Khawaja says Bancroft, Smith and Warner are the greatest victims and his point is valid. They suffered unprecedented consequences for not entirely unprecedented acts. If they did indeed carry the can for their equally implicated teammates then they have right to feel beyond aggrieved.

But the sense of loss felt by Australians was what justified those consequences at the time and what is fuelling the emotion of today. Rightly or wrongly, some element of our national identity will always be attached to our men's Test cricket team and the wounds that remain stem from a feeling of betrayal.

Nothing we have learned this week helps to mend those wounds. Yet more cover-ups, more accusations, more denials, more quasi-confessions. The water is only muddier, the deeds of the past worth less, and the worst, surely, still yet to come.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.title: Hegseth calls Iran war necessary and waves off expected impeachment push
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.author: Associated Press
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.text:
Pentagon chief is facing calls for his removal after the Iran war and its impact contributed to Republican losses in the midterm elections

Facing an expected impeachment resolution in Congress, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said he is eager to litigate the military actions that he and US President Donald Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela’s previous leaders.

“If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolas Maduro, you’re taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic,” Hegseth told reporters on Monday, using the military code names for the Iran war and campaign of strikes to halt the Houthis’ attacks on shipping in the Middle East.

Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday – his first in more than 180 days – on the impeachment threat. His last briefing was in May and he has not held one on the Iran war, strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats or other US military actions since then.
