https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqg7.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqg7.text:
Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the boss of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

The US President said he spoke with chief executive Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia, who has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off the value of Nvidia during trading on Monday as the firm's share price fell by about 4%.

Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was now looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted the BBC.

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia, the company at the centre at the development of AI worldwide through its microchips.

Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.

The American firm run, co-founded by Huang, is also a major focus in the AI rivalry between the US and China, with Washington officials treating the company's exports to Beijing as a matter of national security.

At the White House, Trump was asked multiple times, including by the BBC, on when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.

Trump said he thought Huang was an "honorable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president said.

He said he spoke with Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".

Nvidia designs advanced computer chips that power AI models and lies at the centre of the US and China's technology race - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked national security fears.

Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.

The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.

Huang has admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.

Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

In the letter, the chairmen of the committees said they were seeking a briefing "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".

It is unclear whether Huang will appear. Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.

Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.

It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.

Its chips have become so valuable to the AI-build out that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqg7.summary: Donald Trump says he spoke with Nvidia boss Jensen Huang on Monday. He said he had no idea he was targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. The FBI is investigating the affair between the firm's boss and an alleged Chinese spy. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off the value of Nvidia during trading on Monday

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv.title: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv.text:
Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario, US officials have said.

The comments came on the eve of the first trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine since February.

Senior officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches.

Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.

"An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.

But Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict in the first place remain far apart.

A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.

Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.

While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".

However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."

For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.

The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.

The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.

Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks.

The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans."

Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.

Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.

After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe".

Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result into a fair peace.

Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.

The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.

"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".

Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.

Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.

Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.

On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations."

"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv.summary: Moscow and Kyiv are showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who controls Ukraine's eastern regions. The talks will be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine. The officials will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm86.title: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm86.text:
A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.

At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home.

"My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.

Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models.

"My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.

She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.

She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women.

Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.

Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.

We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.

The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.

Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.

A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.

He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.

Sara Ziff, founder of the Model Alliance, which campaigns for stronger protections for models in the US, approves.

"Often, [model agencies] are the problem. They are the link between the model and these predatory men."

Roza says the person behind the camera at the photoshoots MC2 sent her to was not a professional photographer, but Epstein's girlfriend at the time, Nadia Marcinko.

Roza describes the set-up as "strange - there was no stylist" and the photos were never used. She has since become convinced the shoots were stage-managed by Epstein and MC2.

If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube

An email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier.

"Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.

A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.

We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.

Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims.

"Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."

In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.

The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.

Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.

We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.

Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."

He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."

Lawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves.

"These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do."

Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times.

"People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.

She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.

At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.

Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein.

After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling.

And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years.

The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place.

Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him."

They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery.

We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply.

Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable".

Roza hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward.

"There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out."

Additional reporting by Annika Grosser
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm86.summary: Jeff Epstein raped a woman in 2009 and 2009, she says, "My agency's job was to protect me" She was 18 when she was sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch. She says the agency's president, Jeff Fuller, has not responded to the BBC's allegations.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1l.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1l.text:
A Massachusetts judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of killing her three children.

The judge's ruling follows her defence team's request to dismiss the case after the 12-person jury in her September trial failed to reach a verdict.

Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.

The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.

Clancy's defence team argued to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that prevents a person from being tried for the same crime twice.

Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the 26-day jury trial last summer, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.

The five-week trial, its lead-up and aftermath gripped Americans, and put postpartum mental health issues such as psychosis in the spotlight.

In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject Clancy to double jeopardy, according to court documents obtained by the BBC.

The possibility that "an unreasonably stubborn or eccentric juror" could be seated is "an unavoidable risk of the jury system", he said.

"Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy."

Sullivan also denied a defence motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.

He said the defence failed to demonstrate that the records were needed for Clancy's defence at any retrial, and that questioning the juror "would have been impermissibly coercive".

The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial. He previously suggested it could begin in March.

The BBC has contacted Clancy's lawyers for comment.

Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.

After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict.

The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity.

In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant.

Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty.

Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

Ana Faguy contributed reporting.

Clancy's defence team argued that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq0m.title: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk killer set for June 2028
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq0m.text:
The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.

Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus.

Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months.

Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent.

Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period.

But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom.

Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, ⁠Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case.

At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward".

Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this."

During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.

This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.

"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September.

"We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.

Defence attorneys, meanwhile, have cast doubt upon evidence and expert witness credentials in the case.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62.text:
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.

In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.

For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.

Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.

Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.

Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.

Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.

Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.

But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."

"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."

There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"

Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".

"If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.

Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.

But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.

With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.

The alternative is to build.

Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.

Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.

All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.

And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.

And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on.

I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market".

Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said.

Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering.

"There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was.

Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs.

Foreign investment, then - just not from China.

Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says – a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C.

China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early.

And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo.

If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj3v.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj3v.text:
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.

Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.

In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.

The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.

Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.

It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.

The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.

But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.

For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.

"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.

It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.

The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.

We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.

China denies that she was engaged in espionage.

Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.

China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.

Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.

Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.

He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.

Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.

At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.

Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.

An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.

And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.

Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.

He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.

While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.

And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj3v.summary: Jensen Huang is the CEO of Nvidia, the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia. He is being investigated by his own company over an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4g.title: NHS boss received nearly £400,000 'redundancy' pay-off when she retired
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4g.text:
An NHS executive has received a near £400,000 redundancy pay-off after retiring from a health board, new figures show.

Following a 44-year career in the health service, Mary Morgan retired as chief executive of NHS National Services Scotland (NSS) in May.

But it has now been revealed Morgan received a £378,000 payment "under contractual redundancy terms" as part of an exit that came after NHS NSS was merged into a new quango called Public Services Delivery (PSD) Scotland in April.

A PSD Scotland spokesperson said Morgan retired after an "exceptional career" and all payments were in accordance with the terms and conditions of her employment.

The payment comes ahead of a planned major overhaul of Scotland's NHS which could see the number of health boards cut dramatically.

PSD Scotland started operating in in April and was set up to drive changes across the health and care system, and the wider public sector.

It replaced both NHS NSS and another quango called NHS Education for Scotland, whose chief executive Prof Karen Reid is now in charge of PSD Scotland.

Morgan, who earned between £160,000 and £165,000 a year, had been chief executive of NHS NSS since 2021.

BBC Scotland asked NHS NSS on 10 March what would happen with Morgan now her role was defunct.

The health board said the senior NHS executive was "considering her options and next opportunity in line with national workforce policies".

After a follow-up query three weeks later, Keith Redpath, the then chairman of NHS NSS, replied: "Mary Morgan retires on 3 May, concluding an exceptional 44-year career in NHS Scotland."

The NHS NSS accounts for 2025/26 show Morgan retired under contractual redundancy terms from PSD Scotland on 3 May and received a related amount of £378,000.

The same accounts show Morgan's pension pot, known as The Cash Equivalent Transfer Value, is just over £2m.

A PSD Scotland spokesperson said: "Mary Morgan retired on 3 May, concluding an exceptional 44-year career in NHS Scotland. All payment received was in accordance to the terms and conditions of her employment."

The BBC has approached Morgan, but she declined to comment.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4g.summary: Mary Morgan retired as chief executive of NHS National Services Scotland in May. She received a £378,000 payment "under contractual redundancy terms" as part of an exit. The payment comes ahead of a planned major overhaul of Scotland's NHS.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckr5.title: I almost died after a toothache led to sepsis and a rare heart condition
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckr5.text:
What seemed like a simple case of toothache led to a rare heart condition, sepsis and doctors believing Danny Ellis had just a 1% chance of survival.

The 42-year-old from Llanrwst in Conwy county began experiencing tooth pain in April, and went to the dentist where he was given antibiotics.

But the pain kept returning and it was not until he was left with red marks on his body that he was finally rushed to hospital.

Doctors told him it was a "miracle" he was still alive after an initial heart operation failed, and he suffered a series of strokes - but he pulled through against the odds.

The recovery process will continue for at least another 12 months, Danny said, and he will likely be on medication for the rest of his life, but little milestones are getting him through.

"At the moment, I'm able to take my daughter to school, and that's enough for now," he said.

"I still feel different on my left side, and I can easily get tired and forget what I'm supposed to say at times, but I hope that will improve with time."

Danny said after the toothache got worse, an X-ray at his dentist in Colwyn Bay showed no signs of infection, and he returned home with another course of antibiotics.

A pattern which saw the pain ease and return continued for several weeks and Danny noticed he was losing his strength and red marks were appearing on his body.

"The pain was terrible and I had to take a week off work, something I would never do," said Danny, who runs the Spar shop in Betws-y-Coed, as well as Gwalia bakery in Pwllheli, Gwynedd.

"The symptoms were starting to get worse, and the pain too, especially in my legs. I didn't know what was going on."

By Father's Day on 21 June, Danny was feeling "out of it" and was "unable to remember what I'd received as presents".

When his wife Ceri arrived home from work, she found him lying on the couch with bruises on his body.

They went to the GP surgery in Betws-y-Coed on 23 June and, after several tests, Danny was rushed by ambulance to Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor.

"I remember seeing the nurse run out of the room to call for an ambulance," Danny said.

When he told doctors at the hospital that he had a toothache and had been on antibiotics, their "face immediately changed" and they ordered an echocardiogram, which scans the heart.

The scan found a hole in the mitral valve in Danny's heart, and it was also discovered he had developed sepsis and there was fluid in his lungs.

"The marks on my hands had turned from red to black – the sepsis was killing me," he said.

"The doctor said at the time that I was lucky to be alive but I was fighting for life."

Danny said he was diagnosed with endocarditis, a rare inflammation of the inner lining of the heart which is usually caused by an infection.

According to the NHS website, endocarditis usually happens when bacteria or fungus gets into the blood through the mouth or skin and travels to the heart - which was why Danny's pain initially appeared to be a toothache.

It says the most common symptoms are a high temperature, headache, feeling very tired, joint or muscle pain, night sweats, feeling breathless, loss of appetite, or losing weight without trying.

Sepsis is a serious, life-threatening reaction to an infection and can develop very quickly.

"They wanted to transfer me to Broadgreen Hospital in Liverpool but I wouldn't have survived the journey," said Danny.

He had to stay in hospital in Bangor until he was "strong enough" to make the trip, and underwent heart surgery in Liverpool on 6 July, which lasted six hours.

"My brother told me after that the operation was unsuccessful," he said.

"That was the first time the situation hit me on an emotional level and I felt really sad. I told my brother that I was tired of the whole thing, tired of fighting."

But, within a couple of days, a doctor told Danny that they had been given a special machine to help his blood clot properly, and they wanted to try the operation again.

It was successful the second time, with the infection cleared and the hole in the mitral valve closed.

After the operation, Danny was told he had suffered a series of strokes while in and out of consciousness.

"When the doctor was reading his notes afterwards, he said it was a miracle that I was still alive," said Danny, adding he had been told "the probability of survival was 1%".

Danny was transferred back to Ysbyty Gwynedd to begin his recovery.

"I couldn't walk at first, I didn't have the strength to do anything," he said.

"I had lost my independence."

But Danny said he saw progress after a couple of weeks, adding: "I walked with my daughter, Harriet, for the first time in months and that was very emotional.

"My family were a big part of my recovery and a big help as I fought through the whole thing. That's what got me through."

Danny was released from hospital on 19 August and says one of the first things he did was visit his dentist "because I knew he was very emotional about the situation".

"It wasn't his fault at all, my case and how it developed was something so rare," he said.

"I look after my teeth, clean them twice a day, so there's nothing I could have done differently. It's still a mystery to tell the truth.

"I had the worst possible scenario in my experience. Anyone can have toothache but, when endocarditis is part of it, that's when things change."

Danny said he was "extremely grateful" for all the support he had received in recent months.

"All the staff at Liverpool, Bangor – they've been amazing," he said.

"I'm meeting the surgeon from Broadgreen in Liverpool for the first time since the operation – that will be very emotional."

He added: "But Ceri made the first call, she was worried at first. If I had waited for another day or two, the story would have been very different.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckr5.summary: Danny Ellis, 42, from Conwy county, suffered a series of strokes after a heart operation failed. He was diagnosed with endocarditis, a rare inflammation of the inner lining of the heart. He said he was "extremely grateful" for all the support he had received in recent months.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9m2.title: Headteachers say families will struggle after another rise in school dinner prices
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9m2.text:
A headteacher said she believes "families are going to struggle" as the price of school dinners is to go up for the second time in a year.

The price of meals for pre-school, primary and special school pupils will go up by 30p, for post-primary pupils will they will rise by 15%. It follows an increase of just under 20% introduced by the Education Authority (EA) in January 2026.

Áine Leslie, principal of Malone Integrated College in Belfast, said this will put further pressure on families who are already worried about the cost of living crisis.

But the EA said that the amount parents would have to pay was still well below the average cost of producing a school meal, estimated at over £5.20.

The latest increase means that the price of a paid for school dinner in a primary school or special school, for instance, will have risen from £2.60 to £3.40 since the start of 2026.

Pupils eligible for free school meals will not be affected.

The rise in school dinner prices is not the only measure introduced by the EA in response to what they describe as "an exceptionally challenging financial position".

There will also be a change to some menus in schools, replacing baked desserts with cheaper alternatives.

At Malone Integrated College about 55% of pupils have free school meal entitlement and there are also a lot of parents who are on lower incomes.

When the prices of school meals increased earlier this year, Leslie said she remembers "sitting with the head of the cafeteria and heartbreakingly decide how much to put up each item".

"I think the cumulative effect of this will be immense, particularly families who have multiple children, both at a primary school and a post-primary school, and trying to make ends meet, it's going to become incredibly difficult," Leslie told BBC News NI.

"I can't imagine what it would be like for families trying to budget that moving forward, as well as planning for Christmas.

"I firmly believe families are going to struggle at Malone.

"I do believe that there will be some families and some young people who will be worried about the stigma attached to this, and won't voice their concerns and won't ask for help. And as an integrated school, that's really sad for us.

She added: "I think it's going to be quite cutthroat for families.

"Already, we have some of our children, particularly in junior school talking about Christmas and how they've had discussions with their families that things are going to be much more scaled down this Christmas, just with the general cost of living crisis.

"And then this is only going to amplify the situation even more for young people."

Leslie added that not having a healthy, balanced diet or going without food will be a "barrier to learning".

Christos Gaitatzis is the principal of Omagh High and described the increase of 15% on a school meal as "excessive".

"What is the price index at the moment – is it 3,4, 5%? I would imagine that would be the reasonable increase that you would put on anything, so they are going three times the value - to me it is unreasonable," he told BBC News NI

Close to 30% of pupils at his school are on free school meals.

"You would expect that the cost for a child every week, when a price of a meal is close to £5, we are talking about £20 a week, £100 a month – that's a significant cost for lunch," Gaitatzis said.

"So other measures have to be taken by the families in order to make savings, for example pack lunches – then would that diet be balanced?

"We're talking about a society where the importance of nutrition provided by schools has significant impact on your mental and physical health, so you effectively deter these families and children having these nutritious meals by putting the price up.

"Clearly this will have an overall future impact on the health of the kids."

Northern Ireland's commissioner for children and young people said he was ''flabbergasted" at the change.

Chris Quinn said what makes the move "particularly difficult to accept is that it comes shortly after schools were directed towards energy-saving guidance advising people who were cold to wear more clothes rather than turn up the thermostat".

"I strongly advised the Education Authority to remove that guidance and made clear that responsibility for financial pressures in education should not be transferred to children and families."

The commissioner added: "Children did not create the financial crisis in education and they should not be expected to pay the price for it.

"School meals are not a luxury. For many children they are an essential part of the school day, and these increases will hit hardest those families already struggling with the cost of living."

Payments to schools for school milk are at risk.

The EA currently pays milk subsidies to around 500 schools.

The Authority is to seek funding from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera).

The EA are also planning to offer more parents payments to transport their children to school rather than paying for a taxi to do it.

At the minute, some parents receive parental payments if their children is eligible for free school transport but no private providers, like taxis, are available.

Charges for EA music lessons for pupils are also set to rise again, and some schemes run in schools will no longer be funded.

The Authority, however, has not specified what is at risk.

In a statement, the EA said that they "were being asked to deliver important services to children and young people with insufficient funding".

They said that they hoped to save £20m by introducing the measures on top of £30m saved this year.

They also said costs, such as providing energy for schools, continued to rise.

"These were difficult decisions which sought to balance our commitment to children and young people alongside the requirement to live within the funding allocated for the year," the EA said.

"We are also mindful of the pressures across all public services in NI and of the fact that any overspend this year may impact on next year's finances."

The Northern Ireland Executive has yet to agree a budget amid a dispute with the secretary of state about how Northern Ireland is funded.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9m2.summary: EA says it will put pressure on families already worried about cost of living crisis. They hope to save £20m by introducing measures on top of £30m saved this year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c51k.title: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under stricter rules for schools in England
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c51k.text:
Pupils will not be allowed to have their phones on them at all during the school day under stricter government guidance in England.

Statutory guidance came into force in June, making schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.

Ministers now say changes to that guidance will go beyond the current "no see, no hear" policies in place in some schools - where phones can remain in pupils' bags if they are not seen or heard - when it comes into force from September 2027.

But head teachers' unions said schools would struggle to implement stricter new policies without additional funding from government.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government's "clear message" to parents and pupils was that "school is for learning and friendship, not scrolling".

Access to phones "risks pulling children away from their learning and from each other", the government said.

Schools will be able to decide how to follow the guidance. Some schools have invested in sealed pouches or secure lockers. Others collect phones at the start of the day, or have prohibited them from sites altogether.

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders union, said phones could raise "safety issues" and be an "unhelpful distraction" during the school day. But he said the more robust measures recommended under the new guidance would "come at a cost".

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said the latest guidance "does at least provide some clarity", but added that school leaders "cannot simply make mobile phones disappear".

"If all schools are going to be expected to have lockable pouches or other secure storage facilities for every pupil, the cost involved will be very significant indeed," he said.

"This is not feasible unless the government puts in the funding required to meet these costs."

Dame Rachel de Souza, Children's Commissioner for England, said she welcomed strong action to stop phones distracting pupils and disrupting the school day.

Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of campaign group of Generation Focus, similarly welcomed the changes, saying "no see, no hear" policies were not working and pupils were still "TikToking in the toilets".

"Ultimately, we need to get to a point where it's not normal for every single child to have a personal internet-enabled device in their pockets with them 24/7," she said.

Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said she was "delighted that Labour have finally listened to us and agreed to properly ban smartphones in schools".

She said it was also the "right thing to do" to have a review of safety standards around the technology used in schools, which the government has also announced on the back of calls for improved guidance.

But she criticised what she called a lack of "joined up thinking" over what new tech was being allowed in classrooms.

Because education is devolved, the approach to phones in schools varies across the UK.

In Scotland, the government has said it will introduce a new law to restrict the personal use of phones in schools, and launched a consultation on the issue over the summer.

In Wales, the Senedd recently voted against a motion to introduce a national statutory ban on phones in classrooms. Schools are still encouraged to restrict the use of phones during the school day, but heads have flexibility over how to implement their own rules.

And in Northern Ireland, Education Minister Paul Givan launched a 12-week consultation in August on whether to ban mobile phones from schools by law, calling for "a stronger and more consistent approach across our education system".

Rules around phones in schools are separate from the UK's upcoming ban on social media for under-16s, due to be introduced in March.

Children will be barred from accessing platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Vinted and eBay could also be included in the list of platforms set to be banned, the culture secretary has said.

Additional reporting by Beth Rose and Nathan Standley

Ministers say changes to that guidance will go beyond current "no see, no hear" policies. But head teachers' unions say schools will struggle to implement stricter new policies without additional funding.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/clima.title: Iran War Unexpectedly Drove Down Carbon Emissions This Year
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/clima.author: Brad Plumer
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/clima.text:
It’s the first drop in planet-warming pollution since the pandemic in 2020. But researchers cautioned that the decline could be short-lived.

Reporting from Washington

Global fossil fuel emissions are on track to fall slightly in 2026, as disruptions caused by the U.S. war with Iran forced many countries to cut back on their use of oil and gas, researchers said on Monday.

Nations are projected to emit roughly 38.2 billion tons of planet-warming carbon dioxide by burning oil, gas and coal for energy this year, according to data from the Global Carbon Project. Those sources are the largest contributors to global warming. That’s roughly 0.4 percent less than in 2025.

The dip was driven partly by fighting in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, as well as by the war between Russia and Ukraine. Both conflicts have caused global prices for crude oil, natural gas, gasoline and diesel to soar, and many nations have responded by using less oil and gas and shifting to domestic alternatives, including coal or renewable energy.

Globally, emissions from oil consumption are expected to drop nearly 2 percent this year, while emissions from natural gas will decline roughly 0.3 percent. By contrast, carbon dioxide emissions from burning of coal are expected to rise roughly 0.6 percent, thanks to increased consumption in places like China and India. (Even though coal pollutes more than oil or gas, the uptick in coal consumption was smaller in comparison.)

The drop surprised analysts, who had been anticipating before the war that emissions would rise slightly this year.

“I would call it unexpected,” said Glen Peters, a senior researcher at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Oslo and one of the authors of the report. “It’s pretty rare to see a drop in oil demand this big.”

Source: Global Carbon Project

Brad Plumer/The New York Times

Subscribe to The Times to read as many articles as you like.

Brad Plumer is a Times reporter who covers technology and policy efforts to address global warming.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1527.title: France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1527.author: Jenna McLaughlin
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1527.text:
A woman walks past empty refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, on Oct. 12, following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains Intermarché and Cooperative U that caused their refrigerators to defrost.

France is accusing Iran of having launched a series of destructive cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure in October.

According to the French National Cybersecurity Agency, ANSSI, Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites in France, from supermarkets to butcher shops, turning up the temperature in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.

They also targeted several small hydroelectric power plants, resulting in "moderate effects," wrote ANSSI in its press release.

The hacking campaign was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," said French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot. He said it "marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people."

The Paris Prosecutor's Office has opened its own investigation into the Iranian cyber unit, Shahid Kaveh, which the French government is linking to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "The Paris Public Prosecutor's Office is requesting the issuance of international arrest warrants," the office said in a statement.

The attacks on French industrial controllers are part of a larger trend. In 2026 alone, hackers have targeted refrigeration controllers from Europe to Israel and the United States.

Grocery stores in European countries including Sweden and Ireland were hit in similar attacks last week.

In a separate incident in France, employees at a major French blood bank had to act fast to save blood samples from heating up when their refrigeration system was hit last week, prompting international calls for the health sector to protect its lifesaving products from spoiling.

In Israel in the spring, suspected Iranian hackers going by the name of "Cyber Isnaad Front" claimed responsibility for sabotaging an industrial food processing plant, including infecting its corporate computers with malware, taking over office printers to print out threatening messages and hacking office cameras for use in a propaganda video released in early October. That video included a taunt in French referencing ongoing education-related protests, and came just before the attacks on French supermarket fridges. Cyber incident response firm Profero attributed the Israel attack to a wing of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Over the summer, commissaries on U.S. military bases also went through something similar, when food spoiled after the temperature shot up inside refrigerators and freezers overnight.

The French government is the first to formally assign blame for the wave of destructive attacks.

They were able to identify the hackers through a series of digital clues, including digital infrastructure used by the hackers, connection to a propaganda outlet, and "traces" of the use of Farsi language in the attack, according to ANSSI.

While NPR and others have reported that U.S. officials suspect Iran may have been behind the attacks on U.S. military bases in August, the Pentagon has not made any official statement, even to conclude that the disruptions were in fact the result of a cyberattack.

"Consistent with our policy and to preserve the integrity of the process, the DOD [Office of Inspector General] Criminal Investigative Service does not discuss ongoing investigations," Mollie Halpern, a spokesperson for the Department of War Office of the Inspector General wrote in an email to NPR.

If Iranian hackers are behind the attacks across Europe, the U.S. and Israel, cybersecurity experts say that would fit with what they know about Iranian hackers' strategy and goals.

"Iran's cyberattacks against refrigeration systems likely represents the IRGC attempting to reassert Iranian power abroad through both physically and psychologically disruptive operations," Alex Orleans, the head of threat intelligence at cybersecurity firm Sublime Security, told NPR. "Such activities continue to provide tangible and cost-effect results given how Iran's national resources remain tied down in the war."

"Also, Shahid Kaveh, the IRGC cyber unit that the French specifically attributed the disruptive attacks to, is repeating a pattern here," Orleans says. He referenced a series of cyberattacks on American water treatment plants in August, which most experts believe were linked to Iran, as precedent. The U.S. government has still not officially attributed those attacks.

"This unit has once again refined its tradecraft through attacks on Israeli targets before shifting their targeting to the same systems in the West," Orleans says.

For those tracking Shahid Kaveh and the other Iranian cyber units that operate alongside it, these attacks fit squarely into their modus operandi.

"Shahid Kaveh group is an offensive cyber unit responsible for some of the greatest hits of Iranian offensive cyber [operations]," says Ari Ben Am, an adjunct fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies' Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation.

One group tied to Shahid Kaveh is the Cyber Av3ngers, he explains, which the U.S. government linked to cyberattacks on Israeli-made systems in U.S. water treatment facilities in the winter between 2023 and 2024. The French government also cited other cyberattacks carried out on behalf of the IRGC against French interests, including against the satirical French magazine Charlie Hebdo and another against digital kiosks used at the Paris Olympics in 2024.

Cybersecurity experts say the attacks on refrigeration controllers have highlighted a yearslong difficulty with securing operational technology, the machines that control physical processes in the real world — from water pumps to cooling systems.

These machines are often outdated and riddled with vulnerabilities, and are very difficult to patch because operators can't afford to shut them down and disrupt critical services including healthcare and transportation. Additionally, the machines are often left exposed to the open internet — often at least in part due to contractual requirements with vendors that want to maintain those systems remotely. That combination of factors makes it a complicated problem to solve.

Iran has yet to respond to the accusations. However, Monday's accusation by the French government may lead other affected countries to take action as well.

During Monday's G7 meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked by journalists whether the U.S. shared information with the French to help with their attribution of the Iranian hacks. Rubio said he couldn't comment, but noted that the "French are quite capable."

"What kind of sickos are these people?" he asked. "They attack refrigerators. France is not even involved in this, really," referring to the war between the U.S. and Iran, which began in February. "[These Iranians] do terrible things around the world … the news today doesn't surprise us," Rubio concluded.

Rebecca Rosman reported from Paris.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-601.title: Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in west Texas
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-601.author: Carlos Morales
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-601.text:
In September, Texas landowners filed a separate lawsuit over the federal government's border barrier plans in the Big Bend area, claiming their constitutional rights are being violated.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to continue with its plans to construct hundreds of miles of border barrier and security infrastructure in west Texas, while a court hearing over the effort moves forward.

The federal government's plans have stirred bipartisan backlash for its inclusion of Big Bend National Park, a beloved stretch of public land known for its sweeping canyons and unspoiled desert landscape.

In a five-page decision issued Monday, the high court wrote that the federal judge who ruled on the order didn't have the authority to weigh in.

"The injunction thus impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity," reads the unsigned decision. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter in the decision.

The court wrote that federal law allows the Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to waive environmental protections and conservation laws, which they called a "clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert."

In an emergency application to the high court in late October, the federal government urged the justices to intervene and allow the work to begin again, saying that a gap in "border defenses" in the Big Bend region "would act as "a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors."

Along the border in Texas' Big Bend region, local residents have displayed signs protesting the Trump administration's border security plans for the area.

A federal judge in El Paso issued the temporary injunction that halted the construction of 30-foot-tall steel barriers, patrol roads, surveillance systems and other border infrastructure.

The Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental advocacy group, brought forward the lawsuit, along with an area nonprofit working to preserve a historic church near the U.S.-Mexico border and a landowner who stands to lose his border property.

"This decision greenlights the contractors and allows the bulldozers to come roaring back into the region," said Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biological Diversity. "It allows the dynamiting of national park canyon walls, the bulldozing of pristine desert."

The lawsuit argued that the Department of Homeland Security's plans are unconstitutional and that Big Bend residents would be "irreparably harmed" if the construction continues.

The Trump administration's plans for the beloved Big Bend region of Texas have provoked an unusual bipartisan backlash. People across the political spectrum say a wall isn't needed in the Big Bend––a region known for its sweeping canyons, tough terrain and unforgiving desert heat. They worry about the threats a wall or any other kind of infrastructure poses to the region, from the impact on the environment and Indigenous sites to the effect on the region's tourism-based economy and on wild animals.

In the Trump administration's emergency relief request to the Supreme Court, Solicitor General John Sauer called the injunction "baseless" and "unprecedented" and said any pocket of the Big Bend without a barrier would "become a funnel point for illegal alien crossings that are thwarted by barriers elsewhere."

Historically, the Big Bend area's rugged landscape has meant fewer people attempting to cross into the U.S. through this pocket of the border. And while the Big Bend Sector, a nearly 500-mile stretch covered by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, makes up over a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border, it regularly sees the fewest number of encounters along the Texas border, according to CBP data.

In September, the group No Big Bend Wall took to a typically busy intersection in the small town of Marfa, Texas, to protest the Trump administration's border security plans for the Big Bend.
