The federal government's plans have stirred bipartisan backlash for its inclusion of Big Bend National Park. The court says the judge who ruled on the order didn't have the authority to weigh in.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.title: Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.author: Barbara Sprunt
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.text:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY), seen here on September 16, 2026 at the U.S. Capitol, filed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday.

Rep. Thomas Massie has reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting up a vote in the House of Representatives in the next two days.

The Kentucky Republican's resolution accuses Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors and lists eight specific charges against him.

The allegations include:

Pete Hegseth greets British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting at the Pentagon on Oct. 15, 2026. Hegseth says any effort to impeachment him will fail.

Hegseth defended his record at the Pentagon in a video released last Thursday, dismissing Massie's effort as "sham articles of impeachment."

"Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me," Hegseth said.

Speaking to reporters during an impromptu press briefing on Monday, Trump expressed support for his embattled Defense Secretary.

"I'll stand by him," Trump said. "He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won."

Massie has long been a staunch critic of Hegseth. During the GOP primary, Hegseth campaigned on behalf of Ed Gallrein, who went on to defeat Massie.

In response to Hegseth calling him a "disgruntled defeated congressman," Massie told reporters on Monday: "Well, he's right about one thing — I'm a defeated congressman. I'm not disgruntled."

He added: "I'm being polite here. What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing someone, really. You don't go to prison, you don't go to jail, you don't pay a fine. When the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious."

Massie said the effort also underscores the need to litigate whether Congress has real war powers or not. The war powers resolution has largely been ignored by presidents of both parties.

"What's at heart here is the balance of power between the executive branch and Congress," he said.

Massie first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections, prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution Monday.

Presumptive next House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has already signaled support for an impeachment push against Hegseth.

Even Republican members who oppose impeaching Hegseth have said the Trump administration could do a better job making the case to Congress and the public about what the plan is for the Iran war going forward.

Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio., indicated to NPR that impeachment would be hypocritical given that administrations going back to the Korean War have largely ignored Congress' war powers efforts.

"I think trying to scapegoat Pete Hegseth is just the status quo politics in Washington," he said. "I think it would be a mistake to impeach."

Davidson said lawmakers who want changes are better off trying to leverage the power of the purse to withhold money from the conflict.

There could be sufficient votes to impeach Hegseth in the House, with the support of all Democrats, Massie, and a handful of Republicans. However, it is unlikely to clear the higher Senate threshold for convicting and removing Hegseth from office — which requires two-thirds of the Senate.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Teenager who planned terror attack in Sydney tells court he was radicalised online and used AI to strategise
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Josh Taylor Technology reporter
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Boy says he was first exposed to extremist material on TikTok, turned to Telegram and YouTube for bomb-making instructions, and used ChatGPT to devise his plans

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A teenager who admitted to planning a terrorist attack in Sydney in 2024 has told the court he was radicalised online after first seeing extremist material on TikTok and used ChatGPT to form his plans.

The 16-year-old, known under the pseudonym as RK due to his age, pleaded guilty to acts in preparation for, or planning, a terrorist act. In a sentencing ruling on Monday, he avoided jail time, with the New South Wales supreme court ordering him into a three-year community corrections order.

RK had just turned 14 when the offending occurred in 2024. He told the court he was first exposed to extremist material on TikTok.

“Initially, he was looking at historical content that may have had a political theme. He saw videos about the crusaders and ‘their empires’,” Justice Stephen Campbell said in the decision.

“He progressed to videos about the events of September 11, 2001 and the resulting war on terror (and the wars after that).”

Campbell said RK then progressed to watching religious-themed videos, which “led him to other content of increasing violence” and then talking about these subjects with people on the internet.

RK told the court he was trying to impress these people, and became focused on the Sydney Opera House as a potential location for an act of violence. He said he had become radicalised and “brainwashed by propaganda” when he began looking at bomb-making videos on YouTube, but Campbell said he had no concrete plans for committing a terrorist act, and had not obtained any material for bomb-making.

RK used Telegram, seeking instructions on making a pressure cooker bomb, and attempted to contact the surviving Boston marathon bomber, Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, by email.

The teenager used ChatGPT to obtain information about the bomber, and asked the AI chatbot if inmates had access to news.

“Exhibiting what appears to me to be a complete lack of understanding of the import of his conduct, the young person emailed the prison, using a publicly available email address, asking whether he could email Tsarnaev,” Campbell said in his judgment, adding RK never ultimately made contact with the bomber.

RK asked ChatGPT about security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House, where the Sydney marathon finishes, and where terrorists were imprisoned in NSW. He watched videos about the Sydney Opera House on YouTube, and researched gay nightclubs and other places where “infidels” gather.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

On Telegram, RK sent Islamic State videos to others to “seek validation” because he thought it was “cool”, Campbell said.

OpenAI, Telegram and YouTube were approached for comment. TikTok declined to comment.

The teenager has since expressed remorse for his actions, and Campbell said he had underwent six sessions of religious and ethical training from a Muslim cleric.

“I am satisfied that he has genuinely renounced his adherence to Islamic violent extremism, which in any event was incipient and hesitant during the short period of his offending,” Campbell said. “I fully accept he was radicalised to a degree, but that the process of deradicalisation is well advanced.”

The Asio deputy director general for intelligence service delivery, Claire McGuinness, told a parliamentary inquiry last month that detecting and disrupting online youth radicalisation had become very challenging for the security agency.

“It usually begins quietly. A young person is scrolling through Instagram or TikTok or a similar platform,” she said. “They encounter something that catches their attention, perhaps a political meme or a religiously conservative video.

“At first it isn’t terrorism – it’s just fringe; it is extremist-adjacent. But, the moment they engage, the algorithm takes over and so the feed tightens, the content shifts from conservative to radical, and from radical to security-relevant.”

From there, teenagers often move to platforms such as Discord or Telegram where “dark humour and the edgy memes” groom teens to accept progressively more extreme content, McGuinness said, before passive consumption turns to active engagement in researching methods.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon denies being ‘obsessed’ with Jesse Baird as double murder trial continues
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Kat Wong
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Former police officer tells jury he joked about being ‘white girl crazy’ with friends as lawyer questions him over start of relationship with Baird

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied being “obsessed” with Jesse Baird from the start of their relationship, telling a court he would have liked the TV presenter even if he was “a garbage cleaner”.

The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Sitting in the witness box for the fourth day, Lamarre-Condon was grilled by crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC about his relationship with Baird.

The former officer told the NSW supreme court he would meet up with Baird in October and November 2022 for sexual encounters before the pair began going on romantic dates in December of that year.

Under cross-examination on Tuesday, Hatfield asked Lamarre-Condon: “You were obsessed with him right from the start?”

Lamarre-Condon denied this, telling the jury: “I never cared about showing Jesse off. I wanted Jesse to meet my friends because I thought he was genuine”.

“Jesse Baird could have been a garbage cleaner… I liked Jesse for who he was as a person,” Lamarre-Condon said.

Asked by Hatfield if Lamarre-Condon was “obsessed” with Baird in February and March 2023, the accused responded: “I don’t agree with ‘obsessed’. Smitten? Yes. Obsessed? no.”

Hatfield pointed to messages between Lamarre-Condon and his friends sent around the time the pair began going on dates, where the officer says: “it sounds crazy, I love him”.

Lamarre-Condon responded: “I say ‘I love you’ to all my friends and to people like that all the time.”

“That’s different to saying I’m ‘in’ love with him,” he said.

Asked whether he was insecure about the relationship and whether Baird liked him, Lamarre-Condon said his response was “natural” and sometimes occurred when the TV presenter did not reply to his messages straight away.

“I would always joke [with my friends], ‘we’re white girl crazy’,” Lamarre-Condon told the jury.

“It means we should stop being in our head and second-guessing ourselves.”

He told the court he would make jokes and have “banter” with his female friends, not his heterosexual male friends, telling each other things like: “you’re a crazy bitch”.

Lamarre-Condon told the court he had looked through Baird’s phone, using it to unfollow people, when the pair went on a brief holiday to a cabin in regional NSW.

“In relation to breaching his privacy and, yes, his trust I did unfollow two to three people,” he said.

“I believe curiosity just got the best of me.

“Our relationship was progressing, I just kind of wanted to see where he was at … if he was also messaging other guys romantically… I’m not making excuses for my behaviour.”

Later, when the prosecution attempted to go through messages between Lamarre-Condon and one of his friends, the officer directly addressed Hatfield, telling him: “Mr Crown, I think you’re trying to mislead me here”.

Justice Natalie Adams interjected, telling Lamarre-Condon to “just answer the question”.

“If the crown is misleading you, [the defence lawyer] will object,” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Todd Russell, Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor, dies aged 54 due to illness
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Nick Visser and Australian Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Tasmanian premier leads tributes for Russell, who earlier this month returned home to ‘see out his days’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has died aged 54 after recently announcing deteriorating health.

The Tasmanian premier, Jeremy Rockliff, led the tributes on Tuesday morning, saying his thoughts were with Russell’s loved ones.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“Vale Todd Russell,” Rockliff wrote on social media.

“Thoughts this morning are with Todd’s loved ones and everyone who had the absolute pleasure of knowing him.”

The disaster sparked global headlines and became a rallying event for the nation in 2006 after a minor earthquake sparked a collapse at the Beaconsfield goldmine.

The event killed miner Larry Knight, with fears Russell and his co-worker, Brant Webb, were also entombed by thousands of tonnes of rock and debris.

The pair were initially presumed dead before their faint cries were heard by searching workmates days later.

Rescuers used thermal imaging cameras and found the pair alive five days after the collapse, trapped in a safety cage almost a kilometre down.

The men had survived on a shared cereal bar and water that seeped through the rock, before meals were able to be passed down to them through a pipe.

A major technical rescue effort to free the pair was launched, and they ultimately walked free after two weeks underground, throwing their hands into the air before embracing their loved ones.

The disaster left a deep mark on Australia’s cultural fabric, and it was the subject of the 2007 Foo Fighters song Ballad of the Beaconsfield Miners.

Russell told the ABC’s I Was Actually There podcast in 2024 he had struggled with his mental health and relationships after the disaster, saying he had developed PTSD.

“I needed a reality check, which [my then wife] Carolyn gave me, to go and seek the help that I needed from the right people [about] the PTSD and the depression,” he said at the time. “There are days that are good days, there’s days that are bad days and there’s days that trigger little things.

“I’m continuously trying to rebuild that relationship [with my kids]. I’ve got a one-year-old granddaughter. She’s absolutely beautiful, so I’ve got that to focus on now.”

In 2025, Russell announced he had started treatment in hospital for an undisclosed illness.

Earlier in November, he announced he would return home to “see out his days” with friends and family.

“After years of pain, uncertainty, appointments, treatments, setbacks, and endless battles, plus the emotional exhaustion of having to pick myself up time and time again, have left me with nothing left to give,” he posted on social media.

The Beaconsfield disaster was “two weeks that stopped a nation,” Rockliff wrote on social media on Tuesday. “But Todd didn’t let it define him. He continued to serve proudly at the Beaconsfield fire brigade until February this year, an exemplary 31-year career of community service.”

Beaconsfield Fire Brigade thanked Russell for his years of service as a brigade chief.

“Todd dedicated his time and service to the brigade and the community, leaving behind a legacy that will be remembered by those who had the privilege of serving alongside him,” the brigade wrote on social media.

“You will be sadly missed.”

Rockliff also praised Russell for sharing his mental health struggle.

“He told his story, and became an advocate for mental health,” the premier wrote, “and made the community around him a better place.”

Close friend and Tasmanian Liberal MP Michael Ferguson described getting to know Russell as an honour.

“Todd has endured so much over these past few years,” he wrote on Facebook.

“It all seems terribly unfair.”

Ferguson recalled seeing Russell in good spirits as recently as Friday, saying the former miner was thrilled to have returned home.

“My heart goes out to Todd and his family as they spend this precious time together,” he said.

“I promised him I would keep praying for him.”

Russell and his co-worker were trapped in a safety cage almost a kilometre down after a mine collapse in 2006

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
‘Not particularly complex’ defrosting hack has been attributed to Iran, with presumption it is linked to others across Europe

Iranian hackers like to send a message.

In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Now France has attributed an attack on supermarket fridges to hackers operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a key branch of Iran’s military establishment.

There was no message this time, but the disruption made headlines around the world. Some refrigerators had their temperature turned up so high they caught fire. ‌In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees dumped piles of perished meat and melted ice-cream into rubbish containers.

France’s foreign minister described it as an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” and promised “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible.

It follows attacks on industrial freezers at an Israeli food production plant in May and a wave of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at US military bases in August that are now reportedly being treated as a suspected hack. Those attacks have not been officially attributed to Iran, but the French announcement is the first to implicate the state in this type of hack.

Sign up to Headlines Europe

A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day

after newsletter promotion

Rafe Pilling, a senior director at Sophos, a cybersecurity firm, said the relatively unsophisticated nature of the attack – hackers used default passwords to access fridge controls – was in line with Iranian capabilities. “The attacks themselves were not particularly complex,” he said.

Pilling said there was now a presumption the French attacks and a wave of rogue defrosting hacks across Europe last week were linked.

Hostile cyber operations against the west tend to come from a vexatious quartet of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. All have different aims and characteristics: China has focused on industrial espionage and mass data gathering, Russia on disrupting enemy infrastructure and spreading disinformation, and North Korea on hacking crypto exchanges because it needs money. Iran, according to Pilling, wants to put a shot across the bow of its enemies.

“In general Iran uses cyber-attacks to project power internationally and to signal their political displeasure with regional and international adversaries,” Pilling said.

The fridge hacks came as the UK’s national cybersecurity centre warned the country is in the “foothills” of a new level of cyber threat – and should expect a “huge rise” in the volume of incidents. The main concern is AI, a technology now capable of highlighting previously unforeseen flaws in IT systems and helping attackers plan and carry out attacks.

However, the underlying context of the fridge attacks is not AI but geopolitics. After all, the refrigeration system vulnerabilities were relatively easy to find and exploit. But a combination of groundbreaking technology and tense global relations makes for an alarming landscape.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: Headteachers consider leaving jobs earlier than planned after new Ofsted inspection
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Sally Weale Education correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Almost two-thirds of school leaders polled say new regime is much more intense than previous framework

More than half of headteachers in England who were polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are considering cutting short their careers as a result of the experience.

In response to the question “Has the inspection affected how long you intend to stay in your role?”, 52% of those who responded said they were thinking of leaving their job sooner than planned.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Amost two-thirds (64%) said the new inspections were “much more intense” than under the previous framework, while nearly nine in 10 (86%) struggled with their mental health and wellbeing while inspectors were on site.

The findings from the survey by the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) are a damning indictment of the new regime that is the result of a radical overhaul after the suicide of the primary school headteacher Ruth Perry in January 2023.

The changes, which were introduced a year ago, were intended to reduce the strain and workload caused by the inspection process, but many school leaders say they have made things worse.

One primary headteacher who took part in the survey said: “Not sure my physical or mental health could cope with another inspection like this framework. Have been a head for 15 years across three schools and have never felt less able to do my job than I did during the inspection.”

A deputy head at an all-through school said: “I previously had aspirations for headship. I will now never go for headship. The stress and anxiety of the inspection has ended that dream … this is the most challenging Ofsted I have ever completed in a career of over 20 years.”

A primary school chief executive said: “I’m very tired of the high stakes, the stress, the worry that comes from the whole process. It’s on a different level.”

A headteacher at a secondary special school said: “I will not do another inspection as head. I will leave before the next one – it made too much of an impact on my personal life – I didn’t see my children for months on the run up to going into window.”

The general secretary of the NAHT, Paul Whiteman, said the survey findings showed “the unmitigated failure of an unaccountable and out of control inspectorate” and said Ofsted’s actions were driving experienced leaders from schools.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, has indicated she is looking at further changes to Ofsted, but Whiteman said that “another belated rearranging of the deckchairs which sidelines the profession is wholly insufficient”.

The survey, which had 242 responses between June and October, comes after teaching unions declared no confidence in the schools watchdog and threatened strike ballots unless significant wellbeing issues caused by the new inspection framework were fixed.

An Ofsted spokesperson said many leaders had found inspections helpful and constructive over the last year, but acknowledged that others had highlighted the impact on their workload and wellbeing.

“That’s why we’re working with the secretary of state on ways to reduce the pressure felt by heads and teachers, without losing our shared focus on the best interests of children and their families,” the spokesperson said.

A Department for Education spokesperson said teachers do extraordinary work and inspections should support improvement without adding to pressures already on schools.

“That’s why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is collaborative, fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Tommy Walsh, co-presenter of BBC’s Ground Force, dies aged 69
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Nadeem Badshah
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Former builder got his big break after restoring the home of a producer who was working on a precursor to the show

Tommy Walsh, the building and DIY expert who appeared on television shows including Ground Force, has died aged 69 after a long illness.

Walsh started his career as a professional builder before rising to fame alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock on the popular BBC garden makeover show from 1997 to 2005.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

He went on to front programmes including Clean It, Fix It and Cowboys and Angels and joined the BBC show Homes Under the Hammer in 2021, following renovation projects and attending property auctions.

Walsh’s agent, Debbie Schiesser, told the Press Association: “Tommy died peacefully after a long illness surrounded by his family.

“As this has only just happened, we would ask everyone to please respect the family’s privacy.”

Walsh, from Hackney in east London, ran his own property business before his television career. He got his big break after restoring the house of a BBC producer who was working on ideas for a show that would become Ground Force.

He told the BBC in 2004: “She asked me to look at a couple of pilots. One of them was the precursor to Ground Force, called Over the Garden Wall.

“It was like watching paint dry. It was terrible.”

Walsh turned down the chance to star on the show three times, but agreed when his eight-year-old daughter told him she had made a £10 bet with a boy at school that her dad was going to be on TV.

At its peak, Ground Force attracted 12 million viewers. In one episode, the team was flown out to South Africa to work in secret on Nelson Mandela’s garden, building a pergola and water feature.

Walsh attended Parmiter’s grammar school in Bethnal Green, east London, and played football for the Old Parmiterians.

The club wrote on X: “It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Tommy Walsh. A Parmiters boy he played for the club for many years in goal but made a great career as a TV personality in shows such as Ground Force. He will be sorely missed. RIP Tommy.”

He was married to Marie Walsh and was a father to three children: Charlotte, Natalie and Jonjo.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Senate advances bill to speed up permit reviews for infrastructure projects
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Chamber voted 73-25 to formally take up bill that will shorten timelines to start energy and datacenter projects

The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now face years-long delays in getting to the grid.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started – both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects – and make sure datacenters pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence datacenters and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families”, Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

Midterm results could complicate bill’s passage in lame-duck sessions.

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats’ sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy, but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of datacenters powered by natural gas.

Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

The bill’s four main champions – two Democrats and two Republicans – released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, a Republican senator of West Virginia, Mike Lee, a Republican senator of Utah, Martin Heinrich a Democratic senator of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic senator of Rhode Island, say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

“Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for datacenters instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, Heinrich said.

Capito called the bill “a win for America”, adding: “We cannot let this moment pass by. The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity … to come together to show the American people we are listening to you.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US supreme court clears way for Trump’s border wall in Texas’s Big Bend
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ruling said law enacted by Congress reflects preference for border control over environmental and recreational harm

The US supreme court has allowed Donald Trump to continue his administration’s construction of a border wall in Texas’s Big Bend region, including parts of Big Bend national park.

In an unsigned, five-page ruling, the nation’s highest court granted the Trump administration’s emergency request to suspend a lower court order that had temporarily stopped the project last month.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Liberal justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only member of the nine-member court to dissent from the ruling.

The justices wrote that the case’s plaintiffs, which include the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend river guide and a church preservation group, “claim that construction in the Big Bend sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area”.

However, they noted: “But Congress’s enactment of [immigration law] – which permits the secretary [of homeland security] to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws – reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert.

“The government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents,” the justices said.

The Trump administration plans to construct more than 300 miles of six-foot-tall vehicle barriers and supporting roads, relying on a 1996 law that authorizes the homeland security secretary to “waive all legal requirements”, including environmental and conservation protections, in areas designated as having high levels of illegal border crossings.

The plaintiffs argue that the project threatens wildlife and public lands, could destroy “iconic sections” of the Rio Grande’s protected river corridor, and would undermine the “carefully wrought web of laws meant to protect a vast universe of biological, historic, cultural, and other interests”.

The border wall plans have also faced bipartisan opposition from local residents, many of whom warn that construction could threaten their livelihoods and disrupt their communities.

A Customs and Border Protections map shows plans for barriers and patrol roads across Big Bend national park, including remote areas that would require extensive dynamite blasting. Construction is also planned in isolated canyons where there have been no documented unauthorized vehicle crossings and where vehicles cannot reach the US-Mexico border, the Center for Biological Diversity noted.

According to Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, the wall, which is being built out at about 12 miles a week, is expected to be completed by the end of Trump’s second term.

The Center for Biological Diversity condemned the supreme court’s decision, saying: “This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.

“The destruction we’ve already seen in Big Bend unleashed a firestorm of outrage so severe that the administration was forced to pause its plans. If the bulldozers return now, public opposition will only grow … The damage done to Big Bend will be felt for future generations of Texans and Americans, and this administration will bear responsibility for the natural heritage we lose,” the center added.

CBP has awarded five contracts worth more than $6bn for border security upgrades in Big Bend, including 30-ft steel fencing, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology, which the agency calls its “smart wall”.

Following a federal judge’s ruling that temporarily halted the construction in October, CBP said at the time: “We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region.”

The Guardian has reached out to CBP for comment on the supreme court’s latest ruling.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Ruling said law enacted by Congress reflects preference for border control over environmental and recreational harm. Ruling said the government’s interest outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump says US war in Iran ‘effectively over’ as he plays down escalation concerns
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Andrew Roth in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
President, after talks with Qatari PM, suggests end to war coming ‘fairly soon’ and military escalation not needed

Donald Trump has said that the war in Iran is “effectively over” as he played down concerns that the US would escalate its military campaign against Tehran after the midterm elections.

During a White House press conference, Trump said that Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and that an escalation was not needed.

“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House.

The remarks followed talks in the Oval Office with the Qatari prime minister, Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who has lobbied Trump alongside other Gulf countries not to resume the fighting against Iran.

“We’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon,” he added.

Trump has frequently exaggerated claims about the status of negotiations with Iran, saying a final peace deal was imminent dozens of times during the nearly nine-month long war.

The US had continued to move troops to the Middle East in the run-up to the midterm elections. There was speculation that the Trump administration was waiting for the elections to take place before resuming a military campaign, in order to prevent a backlash at the polls.

Republicans were nevertheless routed in a historic defeat in which they lost both houses of Congress, with the vice-president, JD Vance, declaring soon after that the Iran war was a key reason for the defeats.

Trump earlier on Monday said on Truth Social that the leaders of Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, and Kuwait would prefer the “status quo, in other words, a continuation of the Greatest Naval Blockade in History”.

He repeated a mantra that Iran would not be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon, and added that if the situation changed then the US was ready to resume full-scale military action against Iran.

“At this point, however, that seems to be quite unlikely,” he continued. “Israel, and the entire Middle East, are protected from Iranian danger and threats. We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected. At the conclusion of this Military Engagement, the American People, and the World, will be far safer and more secure.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US citizen shot by ICE officer near children’s bus stop sues government for $25m
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levin
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Lawsuit also alleges agents followed Carlos Jimenez to a hospital and ‘interfered’ in his care, with bullet fragments still lodged near lung

A US citizen who was shot by an immigration officer in southern California has filed a $25m lawsuit against the federal government, alleging he was wrongfully shot and arrested, then subjected to a “malicious prosecution”.

Carlos Jimenez, a father of three from Ontario, a city east of Los Angeles, was on his way to work at a food pantry on 30 October 2025 when he drove by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents carrying out an operation. It was around 7am, and Jimenez approached officers “calmly and slowly” to inform them that children in the neighborhood would soon be arriving at an adjacent bus stop, according to his complaint filed in federal court on Friday.

An ICE officer, later identified as Eusebio Ortiz, then pointed his firearm at Jimenez’s face, cursed at him and threatened to shoot if he did not leave, the complaint says, citing audio recorded by the officer’s radio. Jimenez complied and attempted a three-point turn because he was blocked by officers’ vehicles, but in the process, Ortiz, without warning, fired multiple gunshots into the car, hitting Jimenez in the back and right shoulder, according to the lawsuit.

There was no officer in Jimenez’s path when he was shot, and there was no reasonable suspicion or probable cause to stop, threaten or shoot him, the complaint says.

Afterward, FBI agents followed Jimenez to a hospital and “interfered with his medical care”, including by pulling a nurse away and preventing him from talking to medical staff, the suit alleges. FBI agents removed Jimenez from his hospital bed, locked him in a waist restraint and drove him back to the scene of the shooting for an “interrogation” while a bullet remained lodged in him, the complaint continues. While Jimenez was bleeding and vomiting in the agent’s van, officers told him not to “ruin their vehicle”, according to the complaint.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said at the time Jimenez had “attempted to run officers over by reversing directly at them without stopping” and that the officer had fired “defensive” shots. DHS has repeatedly accused people of “weaponizing” their vehicles against officers, but a Guardian review in July found that most of the vehicle “assault” cases touted by DHS have fallen apart under scrutiny in court.

The Department of Justice (DoJ) charged Jimenez with assault on a federal officer using a deadly or dangerous weapon, with a federal complaint saying he had “rapidly accelerated in reverse” toward an officer.

The lawsuit says the criminal charges were “fabricated”. Even though DHS publicly called the shots “defensive”, the criminal complaint did not include any statement from the officer claiming he felt in danger, the lawsuit notes.

The suit further alleges that the FBI falsely claimed that two neighbors witnessed the incident and told an agent that Jimenez’s vehicle had enough room to pull forward without reversing. When Jimenez’s legal team interviewed those witnesses, both denied making those statements and said they were unaware there had been a shooting until they saw news reports, the suit says.

As the case proceeded, Jimenez’s defense lawyers sought access to officers’ text messages, and in May, a judge ordered the government to produce records of agents’ communications. Prosecutors then agreed to resolve the case through “diversion”, which would allow the charges to be dropped at the end of October if Jimenez abided by certain conditions.

The suit alleges that prosecutors were trying to avoid the potential disclosure of communications and prevent the deposition of the FBI agent who allegedly fabricated witness statements.

The charges were formally dismissed last week.

The lawsuit seeks damages for lost wages and medical expenses, saying Jimenez still has bullet fragments lodged near his lung. The suit alleges excessive force, assault, false arrest and other violations and seeks more than $25m in damages.

DHS declined to comment, referring questions to the justice department. The FBI declined to comment. Ciaran McEvoy, a spokesperson for the justice department in Los Angeles, did not comment on the lawsuit, but said in an email that Jimenez “could have exercised his right to take the case to trial, but he instead requested that our office agree to resolve the case through a diversion agreement”.

Jimenez’s case echoes the ordeal of Francisco Longoria, a southern California man who was shot by ICE last year during a traffic stop, and then faced criminal charges, which were later dropped. The justice department in LA has prosecuted 113 people for alleged crimes against immigration officers since last spring, but the Guardian found that as of mid-September, 33 of them had charges dismissed and nine were acquitted by juries.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Carlos Jimenez, a father of three from Ontario, California, was shot by an ICE officer in October 2025. Jimenez was on his way to work at a food pantry when he was shot. Jiminez was arrested and charged with assault on a federal officer using a deadly or dangerous weapon.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Suspect in Charlie Kirk killing to stand trial for murder in July 2028
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Utah judge sets timeline for trial of Tyler Robinson, accused of fatally shooting the far-right activist in September 2025

Tyler Robinson, the 23-year-old man accused of killing the far-right pundit and activist Charlie Kirk, will stand trial for murder in early July 2028, a Utah district judge ruled on Monday.

Judge Tony Graf said the trial will remain in Provo, Utah, and jury selection would begin on 21 June 2028. Attorneys for Robinson had asked to start the trial in January 2029 while Erika Kirk, Charlie’s widow, had pushed for an October 2027 date.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Last September, according to prosecutors, Tyler Robinson perched on a rooftop on Utah Valley University’s campus, where he opened fire on Kirk, who was in the middle of one of his signature debates with ideological rivals on college campuses.

Prosecutors say Robinson harbored grievances against Kirk’s political views, particularly the conservative figure’s criticism of gay rights.

Robinson turned himself in after the shooting, according to police, but has since pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder. If convicted of the charge, he could face the death penalty.

Prosecutors also charged Robinson with two counts of witness tampering for allegedly instructing his roommate to not cooperate with police and to delete incriminating texts, and two counts of obstruction of justice, according to court documents.

Robinson’s trial date had been a source of contention. In October, Robinson’s legal team reportedly proposed that the trial be held in the third quarter of 2029. They pointed to the sizable evidence in the case and jury selection preparations as reasons for needing additional time.

Lawyers for Erika Kirk, the widow of Charlie Kirk, balked at the defense attorney’s proposal in court filings.

Donald Trump also weighed in on the matter, writing last month on social media: “This case should be tried within a month, not three years – and it should be over with!”

He took a jab at Tony Graf, the Utah district judge presiding over the case, saying Graf was “desecrating the memory of the Great Charlie Kirk, while taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to”.

At the trial, prosecutors are expected to present evidence of Robinson seemingly confessing to the crime. During a July preliminary hearing, the court watched a redacted video in which Lance Twiggs, Robinson’s former roommate, told investigators that Robinson expressed regret about the shooting. “He wishes he hadn’t done it,” said Twiggs, who had also dated Robinson.

The hearing offered hints of how Robinson’s attorneys will defend him. They cast doubt over whether there was sufficient evidence to back the state’s motive theory – that Robinson had deep-set political differences with Kirk. They also scrutinized the reliability of forensic evidence, which indicated Robinson’s DNA on a towel wrapped around a firearm.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Judge clears way for Lindsay Clancy to be retried on murder charges
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Reuters
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Massachusetts judge rejects bid by Clancy’s attorneys to have the case against her dismissed

A Massachusetts judge cleared the way on Monday for Lindsay Clancy to be tried again on ⁠murder charges for killing her three young children at her home in 2023, saying a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject her to a ⁠double prosecution for the same ⁠crime.

Judge William ​Sullivan in Plymouth rejected a bid by Clancy’s attorneys to have the case against her dismissed. The judge on 4 September declared ⁠a mistrial after the jury reported that a holdout juror was preventing it from reaching a unanimous verdict.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The judge has scheduled a 16 November hearing to ⁠discuss when to hold a second trial, which he has suggested could occur in March.

No one ​at Clancy’s initial trial disputed that ‌she strangled daughter Cora, five; son ‌Dawson, three; and eight-month-old son Callan with exercise bands on 24 January 2023, in the ‌basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.

She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.

Her lawyers have argued Clancy was in the throes of postpartum psychosis and should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of ‌criminal responsibility.

Some of the jurors in televised interviews later said that, but for one holdout juror, they had been prepared to find Clancy not guilty by ​reason of insanity. Such a verdict would have resulted in her commitment to a state psychiatric hospital, subject to regular court review.

In Massachusetts, a conviction on first-degree murder charges carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without parole.

Defense lawyers argued that a retrial would violate Clancy’s constitutional protection against ⁠being tried twice for the same crime, known as double jeopardy, saying ​Sullivan acted prematurely in declaring a ​mistrial and should have pursued ​a viable alternative.

Citing jury notes that stated the holdout juror was not following ​the law on reasonable ‌doubt despite the ​judge’s instructions, defense lawyers ​said Sullivan should have instead questioned the holdout and potentially removed the juror.

Prosecutors under Plymouth county district attorney Timothy Cruz countered that the judge handled the jury impasse appropriately and that questioning the holdout could have risked the judge inappropriately interfering with jury deliberations.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Progressives head to US House in record numbers after winning red districts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Caucus had 100 members in the last Congress, and six of the nine candidates it endorsed won, flipping seats

House progressives, long dismissed as the Democratic party’s leftwing outliers, are heading into the next Congress in larger numbers than ever and vowing to push the new Democratic majority to the left.

The Congressional Progressive caucus said on Sunday it will welcome more than 25 new members, including a record number who won in red districts, expanding its ranks to more than 105 lawmakers.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Progressive leaders say the midterm blue wave shows that voters will back candidates who promise sweeping change, as many of the newcomers ran on Medicare for All, stronger protections for workers and ending US arms and military support for Israel over its war and conduct in Gaza.

With Democrats set to control both chambers in January, the caucus says it must now test its mandate in Congress.

“Progressive ideas won that election,” the caucus chair, Greg Casar, said in front of the Capitol building, “and we need to deliver on those promises.”

The caucus had 100 members in the last Congress. It endorsed nine candidates in competitive red-to-blue races and six won, including in seats Trump had previously carried.

Randy Villegas won in California, where Trump took the district by two points in 2024, and Katy Padilla Stout won in Texas by eight points in a district Trump carried by 15. Both are set to join the CPC. Sam Forstag won in Montana, where Trump won by 11.

Six Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates also won House seats in safely Democratic districts. Several were present at the press conference, including Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York, Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.

Pramila Jayapal, the caucus’s chair emerita, said even she was caught off guard by the surge of wins coming from candidates in risky races who campaigned on Medicare for All.

“I don’t think anyone could have expected this level of wave support,” Jayapal said.

She said the caucus plans to take members on the road to promote Medicare for All, including in red states such as South Carolina and Florida. She also pointed to Alabama, where Shomari Figures, a representative who beat a Republican gerrymander to win reelection, signed onto the bill six to eight months ago.

When Republicans tested attacks against him in his Trump-leaning district, she said, the Medicare for All attack tested so badly that they never ran it. “Healthcare has collapsed across the country,” Jayapal said, “and I think the cruelty of that also gives us this amazing opportunity to really, once and for all, reform this system.”

But the progressives are not the only bloc growing. The centrist New Democrat Coalition, already the largest House Democratic caucus with 114 members, is expected to add about 39 members, 30 of them from flipped seats. The two groups overlap, but the New Democrats’ growth is concentrated in swing seats.

The centrist thinktank Third Way argues that moderates “delivered” the majority, and said candidates backed by the more moderate New Democrats, Blue Dogs and WelcomePAC flipped 31 Republican-held House seats, 25 of them in districts Trump won.

But Casar’s takeaway from voters this midterm cycle is not to stay cautious, but rather to spark some action. He said the caucus would bring bills on wages, corruption, housing costs, credit card interest rates and child care to the floor, and was not worried about vetoes. “The best way to not get something into law is to never pass it,” he said.

Asked whether the caucus would back Hakeem Jeffries for speaker, Casar did not commit. “Every single member here is going to have their individual vote,” he said. He said the caucus would work with leadership on a direction that delivers on the promises members made on the campaign trail, “from the most moderate to the most progressive”.

So far, none of the incoming members endorsed by the DSA have committed to supporting Jeffries.

Among the newcomers to CPC is Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, a former US Army combat surgeon who volunteered at a Gaza hospital in 2024 during Israel’s devastating military campaign and blockade, and who will become the state’s first Muslim member of Congress. He said voters had sent a clear message. “The American people voted. They want change, and the priorities stay the same,” he said. Asked what he wanted to prioritize, he said:. “I want to pass Medicare for All, and I want to stop this genocide [in Gaza]”.

Three incoming progressive House Democrats have already put their new platform to use. Brad Lander of New York, Scott Wiener of California and Daniel Biss of Illinois, all at the press conference, wrote to Israel’s ambassador on Friday demanding the release of Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian journalist and Israeli citizen detained at his home in Jaffa on election night on suspicion of contact with a foreign agent. His lawyers say the case concerned a single interview with an exiled Palestinian intellectual and former member of Israel’s parliament, and he was released on Sunday without charges.

“I didn’t expect it would be the first thing I would lead a ‘dear colleague’ on,” Lander said, “but it was very moving to do something together with Daniel [Biss].”

Rabb, one of the DSA-backed newcomers, cast himself as a bridge-builder. “There’s a lot of people who don’t define themselves with these political labels that the average voter doesn’t care about,” he told reporters. They want to “get rid of the type of corruption that has been normalized here”, he added, and he intends to find common ground with colleagues wherever they sit on the ideological spectrum.

Whether the left sets the majority’s agenda will depend on how the new members vote, in the speaker’s race and beyond. Casar said he is not trying to outdo other caucuses. “We didn’t even try to be the biggest we’ve ever been,” he said. “It just turns out we are.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The caucus had 100 members in the last Congress, and six of the nine candidates it endorsed won, flipping seats. The new Democratic majority is expected to add about 39 members, 30 of them from flipped seats. Lander was released without charges on Sunday.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: CF Montreal are for sale: What it means, how much it could cost, and what’s next for the MLS club
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
In an emotional press conference, CF Montreal’s founder and owner Joey Saputo refused to rule out relocation

In a rare press conference, CF Montreal owner Joey Saputo announced that his family was beginning the process of “initiating a structured sale process” of the MLS club. Saputo informed the public of his intentions on Monday afternoon, pausing multiple times to fight back tears after over three decades of owning the Quebecois club.

“This decision is neither driven by urgency, nor dictated by circumstance,” Saputo said in his initial scripted remarks. “It’s the result of a careful and deliberate reflection on where we stand today, and more importantly, on the opportunities that lie ahead for the club.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Throughout his statement, Saputo stressed his desire to keep the club in Montreal, saying he hoped to find someone who “shares commitment to Montreal and who will ensure that the club remains in the city for many years to come.”

Yet, more than half an hour into the event after the floor was open for in-person questions, Saputo refused to rule out selling to a buyer who might move the club.

“I will not discount the club to the point of just giving it away just for the sake of giving it away,” Saputo said. “I want to be perfectly clear. I love this club. I will love this club to stay here. But if an owner comes in that doesn’t have the capacity to keep the club at the level that it needs to be at, and to spend the money that needs to be spent in order to bring in the players that this city wants to see, then at that point I’m not doing anyone a favor by selling it to someone just to keep it here.

“As much as I would love for this club to be here, if someone has the capacity to do it, and I feel that they have the capacity to do it, then I would love for this club to be here, and continue to build on what we did. But if there isn’t, and there’s an offer that comes in to relocate the club, and it’s in line with Major League Soccer and what they want to, then yeah, that’s where it’s going to be.”

Saputo declined to provide estimates for his selling point, nor for his and MLS’s timeline to find a suitable buyer. Saputo said the sales process will be conducted in coordination with MLS as well as the club’s retained investment bankers.

But based on recent history, Saputo stands to receive many times more than the $40m expansion fee he paid to join the league in 2012.

In January, the Illig family sold 71% of ownership of Sporting Kansas City to Peter Malouk at a $700m valuation. In May, the Haslem family sold a 37% stake in the Columbus Crew at a valuation of $900m. Both teams own their own home stadium; Forbes rated SKC as the league’s 16th most valuable franchise in 2025, while Columbus ranked 18th at the time of their partial sale.

As of June 2025, Forbes ranked CF Montréal as the second least-valuable club in MLS at an estimation of $435m, only ahead of Stan Kroenke’s Colorado Rapids. The club does own its own stadium, Stade Saputo – modestly sized at just over 19,000 capacity but on its day one of the better atmospheres in the league.

However, MLS’s decision to flip its season calendar means that Montreal could be in line to play more matches in the winter – a tough proposition in Stade Saputo’s outdoor environs. The Montreal Olympic Stadium, located next door, is due for a modernization and will reopen in 2028 but the club would be tenants there, should they move on a more permanent basis.

Saputo initially launched the club in late 1992, then as the Montreal Impact, serving as the club’s day-to-day steward for most of his ownership tenure. He guided the club through two decades in five different leagues before becoming an MLS expansion franchise, debuting in 2012. Two years later, Saputo led a consortium that bought a controlling interest in Italian Serie A side Bologna, where he remains president.

Saputo acknowledged an earlier aspiration, stated in early 2023, to position Montreal for long-term success on and off the field. That declaration came after the club had lost Wilfried Nancy to the Columbus Crew after two seasons of greatly outperforming expectations under the French manager. Nancy went on to win MLS Cup that season and reached the Concacaf Champions League final in 2024 with the Crew.

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, Montreal have been at the very bottom of MLS since Nancy’s departure. Only three other teams have accrued as few points (139) over the past four seasons: DC United (139), Sporting KC (136), and Toronto FC (130). Montréal has won just one playoff game since 2016, with their best stretches directly coinciding with the brief tenures of striker Didier Drogba (from 2015 to 2016) and Nancy on the touchline (from 2021 to 2022).

Montreal have routinely been among MLS’s most thrifty operations this decade in terms of roster spending, both on salaries and transfer fees. Saputo acknowledged the need for the next owner to “start spending in line with some of the other teams,” a tacit admission of missing that mark.

“We’re going to continue to run the club,” Saputo said regarding the interim. “It will be challenging for us, but we are going to stay here until we find the buyer for the club.”

According to Saputo, yes. In opening that door, the club becomes the second of MLS’s three Canadian teams to be relocation candidates – the other being the Vancouver Whitecaps, who have been in the midst of their own sale and facilities quagmire.

These days, when an American sports league is looking to move a team, Las Vegas is an obvious first suitor. The city is no longer just for gambling and debauchery, with the NHL’s Vegas Golden Knights joining as an expansion side in 2017. The NFL’s Raiders became the first team to relocate to Nevada in 2020, leaving Oakland. The WNBA relocated the San Antonio Stars, now the Las Vegas Aces, in 2022.

Golden Knights owner Bill Foley initially looked into buying an MLS franchise to play in the city, only to ultimately buy AFC Bournemouth for £100m (roughly $121m at the time).

“MLS, unfortunately, requires a stadium to be built and, in the United States, that is costing $600-700m,” Foley said in 2022. “The franchise fee itself, I think, is $300m so you are into it for a billion dollars before you have a team. I thought Bournemouth was a bargain.”

Sacramento is another popular suggestion for relocation. The California capital was awarded an MLS expansion slot in 2019, but primary owner Ron Burkle put those plans on “indefinite hiatus” two years later citing financial strain due to the Covid-19 pandemic. MLS ultimately rescinded their claim as the ownership group folded, and awarded its 30th expansion slot to San Diego. The city’s second-division team, Sacramento Republic, is currently constructing a 20,000-seat venue to open in 2028 on the site which was previously intended to house Burkle’s MLS team.

Other cities that have confirmed interest in MLS, either at the government level or from local buyers, include Phoenix, Indianapolis, and Detroit.

Saputo’s stressing that local buyers won’t be given a discounted rate to keep the club in Quebec evokes memories of another longtime Montreal sporting organization. In the early 2000s, the MLB’s Montreal Expos struggled to find a buyer who could afford to keep the team in the city while meeting the requisite and rapidly growing financial might.

The Expos played their final season in 2004, relocating to the US capital and playing as the Washington Nationals for the ensuing 22 years to date.
