https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Beneficiaries have seen savings under Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, study shows
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Dan Beck
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Patients enrolled in Medicare have seen savings on some out-of-pocket prescription costs for moderately priced drugs under the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, or MDPNP, according to a new study.

Other more highly priced drugs, however, did not result in significant savings for patients under the MDPNP.

The study, conducted by researchers at the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine, took a closer look at the impact of the MDPNP, which was established in 2022 as part of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). The act chose 10 drugs from Medicare Part D to participate in the program, and Maximum Fair Prices (MFPs) were negotiated ahead of the program’s start at the beginning of 2026. The study compared 2025 point-of-sale prices with the 2026 MFPs for nine of the 10 drugs to determine the savings that beneficiaries received this year. (Insulin was omitted from the analysis, researchers said, because of the IRA’s $35 monthly cost-sharing limit.)

The study found that patients saw significant savings for six of the nine drugs, while the other three did not account for any additional savings.

Medicare beneficiaries taking the highest priced drugs — Stelara (ustekinumab, Janssen), Imbruvica (ibrutinib, Pharmacyclics) and Enbrel (etanercept, Immunex) — did not see additional savings because the maximum annual out-of-pocket limit of $2,100 was reached.

“The Part D out-of-pocket spending cap began in 2025 while the negotiated prices took effect in 2026,” Grace Castle, one of the study’s authors and a PhD student at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healio. “Because of this sequence, Part D beneficiaries with the highest spending experience savings from the out-of-pocket cap but not directly from the negotiation program. Medicare beneficiaries who spend less than $2,100 in 2026 can experience direct savings from the negotiated prices, especially if their Part D plan employs coinsurance.”

Where beneficiaries saw the most savings was from drugs whose list prices were under the out-of-pocket limit: Entresto (sacubitril/valsartan, Novartis), Jardiance (empagliflozin, Boehringer Ingelheim), Eliquis (apixaban, Bristol Myers Squibb), Farxiga (dapagliflozin, AstraZeneca), Xarelto (rivaroxaban, Janssen) and Januvia (sitagliptin, Merck). These savings were between 26% and 42% compared with 2025 prices.

Castle and her team noted that beneficiaries do not need to do anything to achieve these savings.

“The program lowered Medicare reimbursement of these therapies, so any change to patient out-of-pocket cost will automatically flow through their insurance plan design,” she said. “If they pay for prescription drugs with a copay, their out-of-pocket cost is not likely to change, but if they pay with coinsurance, they will likely pay less in 2026 compared with 2025 for these drugs.”

Castle G, et al. Ann Intern Med. 2026;doi:10.7326/ANNALS-26-02703.

Disclosures: Castle reports previously working at CivicaScript, a nonprofit generic and biosimilar manufacturer, and Trinity Life Sciences, a global life sciences consultancy. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: AI echo drafts rival human accuracy
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — AI-interpreted transthoracic echocardiography reports were noninferior to human interpretations and may substantially cut reading time, according to results of the AI ECHO INSIGHT trial.

In this study, over-reading cardiologists could not distinguish between AI and human drafts, and AI assistance boosted reporting consistency, researchers reported at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

“An echocardiogram ... is the cardiologist’s workhorse method to view the heart to make diagnoses and determine treatments. In current clinical practice, an ultrasound technician ... acquires the images from the patient, then a cardiologist reviews those images and writes a report. Sonographers may draft preliminary reports to assist cardiologists, potentially saving them time,” Keane K. Lee, MD, MS, cardiologist at Kaiser Permanente Santa Clara Homestead Medical Center and clinical investigator in the Kaiser Permanente Northern California Division of Research, said during a press conference. “If AI can analyze images well enough to drive a car, can it interpret an echocardiogram?”

Lee and colleagues developed the Echo Prime/EchoNet AI model, which can “accurately interpret echocardiogram images and write reports,” Lee said. The model classifies the views, evaluates them quantitatively and qualitatively, then compiles the data into a report for preliminary interpretation by the cardiologist who may sign-off on the interpretation, if approved, according to Lee.

“For this study we asked the question: Can our Echo Prime/EchoNet AI model generate a full transthoracic echocardiogram interpretation with accuracy on par with not only sonographers but cardiologists as well?”

Lee and colleagues used 1,200 sonographer-acquired transthoracic echocardiograms (TTEs), which were interpreted three times, with a preliminary report generated by AI, a cardiologist and a sonographer. These interpretations were randomly assigned for over-read after a wash-out period by cardiologists blinded to the source of the reports, according to the study methods.

The primary endpoint was a noninferiority evaluation of the accuracy of the model’s interpretation of the TTE, defined as substantial change made by the over-reading cardiologists vs. preliminary reports made by sonographers and cardiologists.

The CI upper limit of the difference between the accuracy of AI preliminary reports vs. sonographer and cardiologist interpretations was below the prespecified 5% noninferiority margin and was deemed noninferior or comparable vs. clinician preliminary reports (substantial change, 50.6% for the algorithm vs. 49.7% for the pooled comparator group; difference, 0.9; 95% CI, 2.1 to 3.9; P for noninferiority = .0035), according to the presentation.

The researchers also evaluated precision of the algorithm by comparing the cardiologist over-reads in each interpretation group vs. the historical report in the medical record.

The AI-assisted interpretation agreed with the historical read more often than the other types of interpretation, according to Lee.

“Overall ... there is a large amount of variability, between 77% and 82%, but with AI-assistance there is less variability and more precision compared to the other reading workflows involving human expertise only,” Lee said.

The researchers reported that with any type of preliminary draft, sonographer or AI, the cardiologists’ time spent interpreting decreased by 233 seconds, to approximately 280 seconds per study, down from around 507 seconds. Researchers estimated sonographers may save on average 10 minutes per read by generating an AI preliminary report.

“AI preliminary interpretation of adult transthoracic echocardiograms was noninferior to pooled sonographer and cardiologist preliminary interpretation,” Lee said during the presentation. “Over-reading cardiologists could not distinguish between AI drafts and human drafts, as they were blinded to who generated the report.

“AI-assisted final interpretations were more consistent with historical reports, which suggests that AI can improve precision by reducing interobserver variability. And, AI drafts reduced cardiologist reading time by 46% compared to unassisted interpretation, a time savings of about 4 minutes per study. For patients, this could potentially mean faster turnaround of results and, for cardiologists, potentially more time spent with their patients.”

AI is everywhere in our lives. As Keane K. Lee, MD, MS, said, if we trust AI to drive our cars, why not trust it to read our echocardiograms?

First, we need to know whether AI readings are accurate compared with standard readings by cardiologists and sonographers. This study did prove that they were accurate enough. They had a cardiologist over-read the AI reports. They found that the cardiologist, on some occasions, could not discern which TTE was read by a cardiologist vs. which was read by AI. Second, does AI actually save time? The reality is that it did in this study.

This is a place for AI that is eventually going to have a tremendous impact on what we do in medicine. This study looked at TTEs, but I’m sure it’s going to spill over to many other imaging techniques. On many occasions, you want fast, expeditious reading, and humans are available most of the time, but not all the time.

What we need to do as a medical community is set some guardrails on use. At the end of the day, we are dealing with human lives, and human life is precious. We are the final arbitrators at this point. Human intelligence is still important.

Lee KK, et al. LBS.06. Late-breaking science: Artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of cardiovascular disease. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Lee reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.ft.com/content/20dc125b-02e0.title: Trump’s Board of Peace warns of  ‘immediate humanitarian emergency’ in Gaza
https://www.ft.com/content/20dc125b-02e0.text:
Abigail Hauslohner in Washington

Your guide to what Trump’s second term means for Washington, business and the world

Donald Trump’s Board of Peace has warned that seasonal flooding in Gaza has created an “immediate humanitarian emergency”, which was being exacerbated by Israel allowing insufficient aid into the war-battered Palestinian territory.

The board’s statement, posted on X on Monday, marked an unusual rebuke of Israel’s far-right government from an organisation chaired by Trump, who has described himself as the “most pro-Israel” US president in history.

The main mission of the board is meant to be the redevelopment of Gaza following Israel’s ferocious military offensive in the territory in response to Hamas’s October 7 2023 attack, but critics say the organisation has largely hewed to Israeli interests.

The board said on Monday it was “deeply concerned” that days of flooding as Gaza heads into winter had swamped “tens of thousands of tents and makeshift shelters” and left “displaced families, who were already living in precarious conditions, exposed to cold and unsafe conditions”.

Seasonal flooding and disease have been common in Gaza amid Israel’s long-running blockade, and the board said it had warned “for months . . . of the very conditions now unfolding”.

It also said it had repeatedly pressed Israel and the Palestinian militant group Hamas to fulfil their commitments under Trump’s peace plan for Gaza that was unveiled last year.

The board said: “We have specifically urged the Israeli government to authorise the entry of essential materials for temporary shelter, water and sanitation infrastructure, waste management, drainage and sewage removal.” It added Israel’s aid response had been “insufficient”.

Hamas had been pressed to lay down its weapons and relinquish government authority in Gaza, the board said. Israel runs about 60 per cent of the enclave, with Hamas controlling the remainder, where nearly all of the population resides.

Save the Children, an international aid group, said on Monday that about 350,000 Palestinians — the majority of them children — had been living in tents that flooded, and that more than 2,000 damaged buildings were “at risk of collapse amid continued rainfall and strong winds”.

Children were being exposed “to hypothermia and waterborne diseases” as a result of the “man-made” disaster, the group added.

The UN estimates that about 1.4mn people in Gaza — 65 per cent of the population — live in tents or makeshift shelters.

Trump was widely hailed last year for negotiating a Gaza peace deal that yielded the release of all the remaining Israeli hostages held by Hamas after its October 7 attack on Israel.

The deal significantly reduced the scale of the fighting in Gaza after heavy Israeli bombardment.

But fulfilment of other aspects of Trump’s plan — including the establishment of a Gaza peacekeeping force, a new government in the territory, the disarmament of Hamas, the withdrawal of Israeli forces and reconstruction — has stalled.

The Board of Peace, which was set up in January, has so far failed to oversee a recovery in Gaza.

And the board attracted the scrutiny of US lawmakers after the FT reported in May that its financial fund set up by the World Bank had received no money from donors, despite $17bn being initially pledged for Gaza relief.

Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee, in June raised concerns about “the board’s apparent lack of accountability, standards and sound legal standing” in a letter to US secretary of state Marco Rubio.

The state department in congressional briefings had been “unable to provide answers to basic questions” about how the board was managed, who it employed, and whether funds collected for it “could be used to compensate president Trump while he is president or after his term ends”, Shaheen wrote.

Additional reporting by Andrew England in London

https://www.ft.com/content/ed09fc96-5ad5.title: Republican lawmaker moves to impeach US defence secretary Pete Hegseth
https://www.ft.com/content/ed09fc96-5ad5.text:
James Politi in Washington

Your guide to what Trump’s second term means for Washington, business and the world

Pete Hegseth was battling to save his job as the US House of Representatives prepared to vote on his potential impeachment as early as this week over the US defence secretary’s handling of the Iran war.

Thomas Massie, a Republican lawmaker from Kentucky and prominent critic of President Donald Trump, on Monday filed articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of abusing his power and flouting the US constitution by directing military operations against the Islamic republic without congressional authorisation.

Massie’s move comes as Hegseth is already under pressure to quit after Republicans lost their majorities in the House and Senate following midterm elections last week. The unpopular Iran war was a top factor driving the party’s defeats.

“Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as secretary of defence and subversive of constitutional government, to the great prejudice of the cause of law and justice, and to the manifest injury of the people of the United States,” Massie said on the House floor as he introduced the impeachment resolution.

A vote on impeachment could come as early as this week in the House but it would not lead to Hegseth’s removal from office unless he were convicted by the Senate, which could be a much higher hurdle to clear. The new Democratic majorities in Congress will not take effect until January.

Still, the impeachment pressure on Hegseth has made him the most likely Trump cabinet member to exit the administration in the wake of Republicans’ steep midterm losses. Last week, Trump replaced Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff with Stephen Miller in one of the first post-election staffing shake-ups.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump attacked Massie as “a loser” who “shouldn’t be taking up the time of Congress or the Senate or whatever he’s doing”. As for Hegseth, Trump said he had “won the war in two places”, an apparent reference to Iran and Venezuela.

Hegseth sought to defend his record on Monday and accused lawmakers of mounting “partisan political games” against him. “There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success,” Hegseth told reporters during a trip to Rhode Island.

“We are very proud of the president’s America First agenda, of our ‘peace through strength’ posture. We know the world is a better and safer place as a result,” Hegseth said. “If we want to litigate that, the success of those things, I’m happy to do it all day long,” he added. Hegseth is also planning to hold a press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday to defend his tenure.

Speaking to reporters later on Monday, Massie said: “I hope Hegseth addresses the eight articles of impeachment [on Tuesday] and doesn’t get up and misquote the Bible in Quentin Tarantino fashion and do some pull-ups and call everybody fat and gay,” referring to when the defence secretary appeared to reference director Tarantino’s Pulp Fiction in remarks at the Pentagon earlier this year.

“I may have just given you half his speech, I don’t know,” he added.

Hegseth, a former Fox News anchor, was one of Trump’s most controversial cabinet picks at the start of his second term and has drawn criticism not just from Democrats but also from some Republicans in recent months.

“I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president,” French Hill, a Republican House member from Arkansas, told CBS on Sunday.

Trump has defended Hegseth. “He’s guilty of two things: basically winning two wars,” the president told reporters in Florida at the weekend.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/nvidia-po.title: Nvidia built itself around one man. A scandal is testing that bet
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/nvidia-po.author: Sebastian Herrera
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/nvidia-po.text:
Few executives loom larger over a single company than Jensen Huang does at Nvidia. His 33-year reign as CEO, and the success he’s overseen during the AI boom, have made him a hugely powerful force at the $4.3 trillion company. Now, the linchpin of the AI industry will test the limits of its corporate governance and succession planning.

After Huang on Sunday acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, Nvidia’s board announced an investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The admission followed reporting about his relationship with a woman whom U.S. authorities concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times. The board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that its inquiry would examine “all available information.”

The trick for investigators, according to business and law experts, is that they are investigating, and will potentially consider ousting, perhaps the most critical executive to America’s AI success. And they will do so under a company power structure in which Huang reigns as an outsized decision-maker.

Huang is “synonymous with Nvidia, and Nvidia is synonymous with him, and he and Nvidia are synonymous with AI, so he’s bound up in the company’s identity much more than other cases,” Brian Burke, founder of Burke Law & Strategy and a corporate board advisor, told Fortune. Nvidia is “a paradigm out there that people look up to and they say, ‘Oh, I want to be like Nvidia.’ Other CEOs say, ‘I want to be like Jensen Huang.’ So, it’s really almost like a cult.”

Huang, 63, has set up a unique structure around him at Nvidia that has concentrated decision-making in his hands. He has been CEO for 33 years, astonishingly long for any company. Nvidia has no chief operating officer, and Huang has about 60 direct reports, creating uncertainty about who is next in line to lead.

Huang is known to play a central role in strategic and technical decisions, and the success he’s had since the AI boom got underway in late 2022 has only strengthened his grip on the company and the AI industry at large. He has become something of a celebrity in the tech world, with followers wearing leather jackets to copy him and fans pursuing him at corporate events for a selfie or a signature. He has also gotten close to the Trump administration, which has counted on him for counsel on AI and taken him on foreign trips.

Huang is Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, with a 3.56% stake, but he doesn’t have any super-voting shares like Mark Zuckerberg has at Meta Platforms. He leads what is the world’s second most valuable company. (Its shares sank more than 4% on Monday after he admitted to the affaire.) Nvidia has been estimated to control about 90% of the market for high-powered GPU computer chips used in AI data centers.

The company has also operated without a chief compliance officer. In a September 2022 staff at the Securities and Exchange Commission asked for more detail about board risk oversight, whether the company had such an officer and to whom that person reported, and about its overall structure. Nvidia has said it has a compliance committee made up of its chief financial officer, executive vice president of operations, and senior vice president of human resources, which it says “ensures communication of and adherence to all NVIDIA policies.”

There are few other cases, if any, that resemble Nvidia’s current situation. Corporate executives whose romantic liaisons have derailed their careers are common enough. In 2019, McDonald’s fired CEO Steve Easterbrook over a consensual relationship with an employee that violated company policy. The bigger scandal came afterward: the company discovered additional undisclosed relationships, sued to recover his exit compensation, and ultimately recovered cash and equity valued at $105 million. In this case however, the romantic liaison involves an alleged spy and the CEO of the dominant company building some of the U.S.’s most valuable technology.

Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University who has studied CEO succession practices, told Fortune that Nvidia’s concentration of so much power and decision-making in Huang now makes it very vulnerable to what comes next.

“The board has made a mistake by not having a clearly outlined succession plan that’s been telegraphed to the market for a year or two,” Schloetzer said. “They find themselves at the day of reckoning, and it’s a sudden and perhaps forced one, rather than a relay situation where they have time to figure it out as they go.”

Hui Chen, a former federal prosecutor who served as the U.S. Justice Department’s first compliance counsel expert from 2015 to 2017, told Fortune that corporate risk efforts tend to focus on leaks from rank and file staff members, and companies don’t pay as much attention to similar risks by high-level executives.

Schloetzer and other experts said it’s plausible for the board to appoint an interim CEO or have Nvidia’s lead independent director—Stephen Neal, chairman emeritus and senior counsel at law firm Cooley LLP—as interim CEO if Huang steps down. Another option for an interim could be Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress. The concern with any next-CEO plan is how the market will receive the decision, since Huang is seen as critical to Nvidia’s success.

Huang also has children who work at Nvidia and could be options to succeed him. Spencer Huang is a director of product management, and his daughter, Madison, is a senior director of product marketing. Both have reportedly worked on robotics at the company. His son-in-law, Nico Caprez, is vice president of global AI infrastructure growth.

The board could oust Huang at the end of its investigation, or Huang could have to step down before then, Burke said. He could also leave the CEO role but stay on in another capacity.

In media interviews over the years, Huang has dismissed conventional succession planning, saying his approach is to continually transfer his knowledge to colleagues. He has also said he hopes Nvidia’s next CEO already works at the company, even though Nvidia has not publicly identified a successor.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/vietnam-c.title: Vietnam’s cheap coffee may lose its edge as the EU tightens sustainability rules, Nestlé Vietnam’s chair warns
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/vietnam-c.author: Jay Ganglani
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/vietnam-c.text:
Vietnam’s cheap coffee is “no longer going to be attractive to export” as the European Union tightens its sustainability rules, Binu Jacob, chairman and managing director of Nestlé Vietnam, warned last week at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Ho Chi Minh City on Nov. 3.

The Southeast Asian nation is the world’s second-largest coffee producer and the largest producer of robusta, the variety largely used in instant coffee. Europe is the world’s largest coffee market, accounting for about 24% of global consumption, according to the European Coffee Federation. That gives the bloc’s standards outsized importance for producers.

“Vietnam was always known to produce cheap coffee, but cheap coffee is no longer going to be attractive to export because [the] EU is coming up with very stringent norms,” Jacob said. “So if we don’t go up the value chain and create coffee that is sustainable and that meets the very high standards, we will be unable to export.”

The EU Deforestation Regulation applies to most companies from Dec. 30, 2026, though some smaller businesses will not need to comply until later in 2027. The regulation aims to curb deforestation and forest degradation linked to the production of certain commodities, and to reduce the bloc’s contribution to greenhouse gas emissions and biodiversity loss.

Hanoi is working with Brussels on compliance. The multiyear, EU-backed SustainCoffee project aims to help the country’s coffee sector meet international environmental, social, and governance standards, and support more than 400 coffee-related businesses while indirectly benefit an estimated 1.4 million farmers and workers in the supply chain.

Nestlé has applied its global research and development capabilities, partnering with the Western Highlands Agriculture and Forestry Science Institute, a prominent agricultural research institution, to develop a coffee plantlet “best suited for the soil conditions in the Central Highlands,” Jacob said.

The company propagates the plantlets through tissue culture. “From one leaf of this coffee plant, you can actually make 2,000 trees, and this is what we’ve been doing in the last 15 years,” he explained.

“We have made 100 million plantlets of this disease-resistant coffee plantlet, and then distributed it at subsidized rates to farmers all over central Vietnam,” he said. “As a result, the productivity and the yield of coffee today in Vietnam is three times that of the global average, and this can be replicated anywhere in the world.”

Still, Jacob cast the rules as a chance for Vietnam to move up the value chain. “With small farms, it’s quite easy to move from the old ways of traditional farming to regenerative farming,” he said. “Once you do that, Vietnam has a competitive advantage to export more and ensure that more value stays here.”

Europe is the largest coffee market, accounting for about 24% of global consumption.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/anthropic.title: Anthropic debuts Claude Fable, Mythos 5.2 models, priced 20% below OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/anthropic.author: Emily Forlini
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/anthropic.text:
Anthropic debuted Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on Monday, the company’s answer to OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, which came out in early September.

The new models, which could be Anthropic’s last big releases before its IPO, claim to offer higher performance than Astra at a lower price point—a key factor for earning and retaining customers in a world where professionals seem quick to switch to models based on cost, as long as the performance holds up.

The launch is critical for Anthropic as it seeks to re-accelerate revenue growth, following a third quarter slowdown revealed in latest S-1 filing with the SEC.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are 20% cheaper than Astra for ordinary input and output tasks, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, compared to $10 and $50, respectively, for GPT-6 Astra. Tokens are the unit of information AI model process. One token of English language text is equivalent to about a word-and-a-half. For prompts with large amounts of information, such as documents, the cost advantage is more pronounced. Anthropic’s new models are 80% cheaper, at 20 cents per million cached tokens compared to one dollar per million cached tokens for GPT-6 Astra.

Anthropic reports impressive results from its pre-release testing. The new models “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications,” the company said.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 perform better than its competitors on coding evaluation benchmarks, Anthropic said, noting that over 90% of the company’s own code is written by AI. While Anthropic’s Claude Code product gained an early lead among programmers, OpenAI’s Codex has gained ground in recent months due to its lower pricing, The Information reported in late October. The combination of lower pricing plus superior performance, if the company’s claims hold up in real-world testing, could help win them back.

The new models are best when used for the “most ambitious, open-ended technical work,” Anthropic said. In other words, they’re competing with Astra at the frontier. However, for daily tasks, Anthropic recommends its customers use its more cost-effective model, Opus 5.5. That model is more expensive than its direct competitor from OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Sol, although it still could end up being a better deal if it yields a high quality result more often. That’s for users to decide as they inevitably begin to try Anthropic’s latest releases and weigh options on a daily basis.

Anthropic is also trying to compete with OpenAI on cybersecurity tasks, such as finding and fixing vulnerabilities in code. The company claims an unnamed security company “found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested.” Late last week, OpenAI debuted a cybersecurity-focused model, GPT-6 Cyber.

The new Anthropic models also reportedly solved two theoretical physics problems related to black holes, and identified a way to speed up research into gene therapies. In light of OpenAI making headlines for solving mathematics proofs that have eluded academics for decades—most notably the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem—Anthropic is highlighting its new models’ mathematics chops as well.

A team of 1,000 agents powerd by Fable 5.2 produced a formalization, or translation of a mathematical proof into a format a computer can check step by step, in 30 hours, compared with 11 days for a previous, unreleased research version of Claude. In a subtle jab at the mathematics community’s backlash to OpenAI pouring millions of dollars into solving proofs and upending the field, Anthropic notes that its quick formalizations can help human mathematicians check their proofs faster so they can “spend more time exploring novel ideas.”

One unique area Anthropic seems to be leaning into more than OpenAI is hardware and robotics. The new models were allegedly able to design and produce three working electronic devices, complete with circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software, based on a one-paragraph prompt.

Finally, Anthropic highlighted the models’ safety features, including safeguards that block “high-risk cyber activities including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/jensen-hu.title: Before news broke of his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Nvidia’s Huang told Fortune his company “could be of great service” to China
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/jensen-hu.author: Beatrice Nolan
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/jensen-hu.text:
Jensen Huang’s dealings with China and views on U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips are under fresh scrutiny after the Nvidia CEO confessed to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly believe to be working as a spy for China. The U.S. has spent years restricting the sale of advanced Nvidia chips to China on national security grounds.

In an interview Fortune conducted before the allegations surfaced, Huang said that he thought the chipmaker “could be of great service” to China. He also said that Nvidia had a “large and growing” opportunity in China.

Huang spoke to Fortune in mid-October, before The New York Times first reported later that month that U.S. officials had concluded the woman, Alice Huang—who has no relation to the Nvidia CEO—was a Chinese intelligence asset. It isn’t clear how long the relationship lasted, but photos shared online show the two together in Taipei as early as June 2024.

Asked in October whether he expected sales in China to pick up, Huang said there would be a “natural tension” between Washington and Beijing that “lasts a long time,” adding that Nvidia would continue to give shareholders no guidance on its China sales. The company has left China out of its revenue forecasts since August 2025, citing regulatory uncertainty in both countries.

The U.S. has not allowed Nvidia to sell its most advanced AI chips to China, but has granted the company export licenses for older models of its graphics processing units (GPUs), the specialized chips that run AI and computer graphics applications. It has allowed Nvidia to market specialized versions of its GPUs in China that have been designed specifically for that market and which are engineered to be less capable at training frontier AI models. Beijing, for its part, has officially tried to bar the country’s major tech companies from buying Nvidia’s chips as part of an effort to spur demand for domestic alternatives.

Nonetheless, Huang told Fortune he saw promise in the Chinese market. “I think the opportunity in China is large and growing, just like the AI market across the world is large and growing,” Huang said. “We could be of great service to the local market. We can compete and win as much of the AI market as possible for the United States, while also providing compute resources, which is really important to their economy.”

China has been a long-running headache for Nvidia. Back in 2022, the Biden administration imposed export controls that barred Nvidia from selling its most advanced AI chips to China, aiming to slow Beijing’s progress in AI and its potential military applications. Nvidia designed scaled-down chips for the Chinese market, but successive rule changes cut many of those off too.

Since then, Huang has continually pushed for more access to the Chinese market. In October 2025, after export controls and Beijing’s pushback had shut Nvidia out of the market, he complained that the company had gone from 95% market share in China to 0%.

In December 2025, President Trump reversed course on some of the Biden-era restrictions, allowing Nvidia to ship its H200 chips—which are designed to comply with U.S. export controls—to approved Chinese customers, with the U.S. government taking a 25% cut. The decision came after months of lobbying by Huang, who met with Trump to discuss export controls days before the announcement. Nvidia’s complicated history with China has been dragged back into the spotlight by Huang’s confession to the extra-marital affair. In Sunday’s memo to staff reviewed by Fortune, he admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, after the Financial Times reported on a U.S. government memo describing a romantic relationship between him and Alice Huang. “There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote in the memo. “I am deeply sorry.”

The same day, Nvidia’s board announced that a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, would examine whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. The board said it so far had “no reason to believe” either had been. For now, Huang remains CEO and said he would cooperate fully with the review.

U.S. officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was working for China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center operator where she was an executive, has become one of Nvidia’s largest customers over the past two years. Its Malaysian affiliate bought at least $4.8 billion in equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to the Times. U.S. officials have scrutinized the company since 2024 over suspicions it helped Chinese firms evade export controls.

It is suspected that, despite U.S. export controls, the leading Chinese AI companies have access to large computing clusters of Nvidia’s advanced GPUs, obtained either through large-scale smuggling operations, or through data centers in other Asian nations that they have accessed using front companies.

Nvidia has previously told news outlets that Huang’s dealings with Alice Huang were routine, and a company spokesperson told Fortune: “Today’s news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.”

Megaspeed also did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment, and Alice Huang could not be reached. China’s foreign ministry called the allegations “pure groundless speculation and slander.”

The Republican chairs of three House committees have asked Huang to attend a private briefing the day after Nvidia reports quarterly earnings next week. Lawmakers are likely to press Huang on whether his push into China has put U.S. interests at risk.

In October, he told Fortune that Nvidia could put American customers first and still compete abroad.

“The United States recognizes that because the technology is invented in the United States, and we’re an American company, we should provide, and we do provide, the best, the soonest and the most to American companies. However, we should compete,” Huang told Fortune during the interview. “AI is a five-layer cake, and America should go compete at every single layer, not just the model layer.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/jensen-hu.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is likely to keep his job for now, say prediction markets
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/jensen-hu.author: Camila Grigera Naón
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/jensen-hu.text:
Traders are already betting on whether embattled Jensen Huang, who admitted to an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, will stay on as head of Nvidia. Platforms including Kalshi and Polymarket were quick to offer wagers on Huang’s future since the CEO acknowledged his affair Sunday, and the early results are in his favor.

One event contract on Kalshi asking when Huang will leave as Nvidia’s CEO has drawn more than $266,000 in trading volume. Traders put the probability of his departure before January 2029 at 54%, compared with 52% before January 2028 and 33% before July 2027. A separate Kalshi market has drawn roughly $2,500 in trading volume, with traders putting the probability that Huang will testify before Congress by next January at 46%, rising to 79% by next July.

Polymarket has also listed a market on when Huang’s resignation or removal as CEO will be announced, drawing more than $305,000 in trading volume. Traders put the probability of an announcement by year-end at 16%, rising to 22% by the end of March 2027.

Meanwhile, Polymarket is also offering wagers about Huang’s personal life. There are currently around $159,000 of bets on the probability of a divorce by March 2027, with current odds at 23%.

The event contracts come a day after Nvidia announced an investigation into Huang, who acknowledged to the company’s board that he had an intimate relationship with a business executive whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly identified as a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares have fallen nearly 10% since Monday morning.

With Huang’s future uncertain, traders have turned the corporate scandal into a running forecast of what could happen next, much as they do with other unfolding news.

These platforms allow users to trade on outcomes across sports, politics, and even the weather, with prices reflecting traders’ expectations of how events will unfold. They drew substantial attention during last week’s midterm elections, when traders favored Democrats to win control of both chambers of Congress.

The midterm results bolstered prediction markets’ reputation as forecasting tools. The platforms rose to prominence during the 2024 presidential election, when traders favored Donald Trump to win while polls showed a close race between him and Democratic candidate Kamala Harris.

But the platforms’ forecasts have not always matched the results. While prediction markets broadly anticipated Democratic gains in the midterms, they favored Republicans in the Texas governor’s race and South Carolina’s Senate race, both of which Democrats ultimately won.

An earlier surprise in Brazil’s presidential election also raised questions about the platforms’ forecasting accuracy.

Traders are already betting on whether he will stay on as head of Nvidia. Kalshi and Polymarket were quick to offer wagers on Huang’s future since the CEO acknowledged his affair Sunday.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/tim-grove.title: ‘I’ll see you tomorrow’: What Michael Jordan’s trainer learned from the 1995 loss—and his three-tier test for winners
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/tim-grove.author: Heather Occhino
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/tim-grove.text:
The Orlando Magic had just knocked the Chicago Bulls out of the 1995 playoffs, and much of the criticism landed on Michael Jordan. When his trainer, Tim Grover, told him he’d see him, Jordan didn’t wait for a schedule. “I’ll see you tomorrow,” he said, as Grover later recalled to Sports Illustrated.

That reflex, losing and showing up the next morning, is the product Grover now sells. The CEO of Attack Athletics, which he founded in 1989, has turned decades of work with Jordan, Kobe Bryant, and other NBA stars into books, an online training platform, and a pitch to executives that treats winning as a discipline.

Business leaders have long borrowed from the locker room. Fortune has profiled CEOs who credit high school sports for the discipline and accountability they bring to the boardroom. Grover’s version is harsher, and it comes with a price tag.

Grover’s framework starts with his 2013 book, Relentless: From Good to Great to Unstoppable, written with Shari Lesser Wenk. It sorts competitors into three types, and Grover describes the tiers in terms any manager would recognize.

Coolers are steady but unremarkable. “The individual that shows up at 9:00 and leaves at 5:00…their work is okay,” Grover said on The Art of Charm podcast. They deliver what they’re asked, and little more.

Closers perform well when conditions are clear. “The closer can deliver the end result as long as too many variables are not thrown at them,” he said. Give them a plan and they will execute it.

Cleaners sit at the top. In Grover’s words, a Cleaner is “an individual that’s going to get you that end result no matter what’s thrown at them.”

His 2021 follow-up, Winning: The Unforgiving Race to Greatness, published by Scribner, returns to that hierarchy. “But there is one thing all Cleaners have in common: the ability to achieve the end result over and over,” he writes.

The same categories anchor The Relentless System, Grover’s online training platform. It sells for $599 with lifetime access and includes a module titled “Are you a cleaner?” alongside lessons such as “Don’t Think” and “Decide. Commit. Act. Succeed. Repeat.” Buyers also get a guide that tells them which of the three types they are.

A newer online series, Breakthrough, is organized around ten themes, including obsession, pressure, and fear and doubt. Grover pitches all of it as action over reflection.

“I don’t teach mindset,” Grover says in a video on his website. “It’s too many thoughts, ideas in your head that have you overthinking with no action.”

Much of Grover’s material leans on The Last Dance, ESPN’s 2020 docuseries on the Bulls’ final championship season. It became ESPN’s most-watched documentary ever, and Netflix distributed it internationally.

Episode 8 revisits the 1995 series. Jordan had returned from baseball that spring, and the Magic, led by Shaquille O’Neal and Penny Hardaway, eliminated the Bulls in six games in the Eastern Conference semifinals.

Hardaway later said the win backfired. “The respect was always there, but my thing was you had to attack him before he attacked us. But all we did was piss him off,” he told Sports Illustrated. The following season, the Bulls swept Orlando in the Eastern Conference finals on the way to the title.

In Winning, Grover quotes Jordan’s defense, from the series, of how hard he drove his teammates: “Look, I don’t have to do this. I’m only doing it because it is who I am. That’s how I played the game. That was my mentality.”

That mentality has critics. A 2024 Fortune commentary on “the rise of the jerk” described the Jordan of The Last Dance as “Petty. Mean. Kind of angry.” and warned that leaders who display their flaws with pride teach others that being a jerk is the price of success.

Grover sells the other half of the story. For him, the lesson of 1995 was never the loss. It was what Jordan said next.

https://fortune.com/article/mary-barra-l.title: Mary Barra still responds to ‘every single letter’ she gets by hand despite running $65 billion automaker General Motors
https://fortune.com/article/mary-barra-l.author: Preston Fore
https://fortune.com/article/mary-barra-l.text:
Sometimes, access to the top starts with something as simple as a stamp. General Motors CEO Mary Barra said she responds to “every single letter” she receives.

Despite leading the over $65 billion automaker—and the fact AI has turned once-tedious tasks such as drafting emails into seconds-long chores—Barra still writes back the old-fashioned way: with pen and paper.

The notes she receives range widely, from loyal Chevrolet drivers sharing their car’s nickname to schoolchildren worried about their family’s future after the closure of a General Motors plant. But positive or negative, the letters still get a response.

“I get [letters] from customers … when their odometer turns over to 200, 300, 400,” Barra said at the 2025 New York Times DealBook Summit. “I also get letters from consumers who are unhappy about something, and I respond to every single letter I receive. To me, this is such a special business.”

Even as one of the busiest executives in the auto industry—repeatedly topping Fortune’s list of the Most Powerful Women in Business—Barra has consistently treated intentional communication as part of the job. It’s a habit she’s carried throughout her rise at GM, from the assembly line to the C-suite. “You won’t always be right, but no one’s right all the time,” she said in 2023.

And for workers, customers, or even complete strangers, that openness can make the corner office feel more reachable than it seems.

Carolyn Rodz, founder of a virtual startup accelerator for women, once wrote to Barra as a complete stranger. What she received in return surprised her.

“What really made me respect this woman, who I am a complete stranger to, was the personalization of her response. She not only acknowledged my request and respectfully declined, but she took the time to encourage my pursuit and commended me on my efforts,” Rodz wrote in 2015.

Rodz added that the note did more than close a loop—it built loyalty and lasting respect.

“She validated my vision and affirmed my commitment,” Rodz said. “Truth be told, she built such loyalty in just a couple of paragraphs that I’m considering buying a GM car next time I’m in the market.”

In an era when executives can seem buffered by layers of corporate hierarchy and public relations teams, Barra’s practice stands out. It’s a small gesture with an outsize message: In a business world racing toward automation, the human touch still carries weight.

“It’s people like Mary Barra, however, who remind me that our words have significant value and an opportunity to impact others in ways we may never know,” Rodz said.

Writing letters by hand isn’t just a Barra hallmark. For First Watch CEO Chris Tomasso, old-fashioned notes of appreciation are a leadership ritual.

The head of the $1-billion-a year-in-revenue breakfast and lunch chain sets aside time each month to handwrite congratulatory notes to cooks and dishwashers celebrating major milestones—10, 20, even 30 years with the company. At a business with more than 15,000 employees, Tomasso has penned more than 500 notes and believes the small gesture can have a dramatic impact: acknowledging to workers’ that loyalty isn’t taken for granted.

“Our job is to create an environment where our employees are happy and feel appreciated, and they take care of the rest,” Tomasso said on LinkedIn.

Geoffroy van Raemdonck, now the CEO of Saks, is another executive who leans on personalized outreach. Before the pandemic, he sent three to five handwritten thank-you notes every day. As work shifted to remote and hybrid models, he supplemented them with texts, emails, and quick phone calls—but the intent stayed the same.

“I was taught by great mentors of the power of sending a thank-you note,” van Raemdonck told Fortune in 2023. “It’s really important for me—the moment of ‘thank you’—because I know what it is to receive a thank-you, to be acknowledged.”

Many leaders aren’t just writing handwritten notes, they read them, too—and it could even be the key to a job offer.

For Joey Gonzalez, executive chairman of the upscale boutique fitness brand Barry’s, cold outreach is how he found the person who would one day be his CEO. He previously told Fortune people should be willing to take risks and express their passion; you never know what doors it could open later on.

“If you’re going to cold email someone, and you can’t be passionate about the service or the product or whatever it might be, it’s not going to be a compelling email,” Gonzalez said.

“But if you send someone an email that’s like, ‘Hey, I just want to let you know I’ve been doing Barry’s for a year, and it’s changed my life. This is my résumé, and maybe one day you’ll have something for me’—it just goes a long way.”

A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on January 26, 2026.

https://fortune.com/2026/09/30/this-revo.title: ‘This revolution is happening in years, not decades’: Verizon CEO Dan Schulman sees AGI within 18 months—and a century of progress in a decade
https://fortune.com/2026/09/30/this-revo.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/09/30/this-revo.text:
Verizon CEO Dan Schulman offered a strikingly aggressive forecast for artificial intelligence’s development at the Ford Pro Accelerate event in Detroit, saying that an earthquake is headed our way.

“The models that we see today are the worst models we’ll ever use in our lives,” Schulman said in conversation with Fortune’s Diane Brady. “Every two months, there’s a step function change in the power of the models. I think we get to some form of AGI in the next six to 18 months. I think it’s right on us.”

Two years after that, he added, we will arrive at “the era of quantum,” which he described as “everything today times 1,000.” By 2030 or 2035, we will see “a pretty good form of humanoid robotics.” Summing it up, he added, “we’ve got a decade of intense change ahead of us.”

AGI, or artificial general intelligence, is a term generally used for systems that can reason and perform broadly across domains rather than excel at discrete tasks. Schulman argued that AI’s economic and social effects will arrive at a pace that outstrips the usual mechanisms for absorbing technological change, such as training systems, labor markets, corporate restructuring, and public policy. “It is about machines that will in many ways be able to do things better than a lot of human tasks are done today,” he said.

“I think you’ll see the collapse of the 21st century in the next five to 10 years,” Schulman said. When Brady asked what he meant by “collapse,” he explained, “Progress we would have made over 100 years will happen over the next five to 10 years.

“I don’t think we can really imagine how powerful the technology and how fundamental it will be.”

Schulman said the change would reach his company itself. Verizon, he said, has more than 250,000 employees and contractors and will need to move from a workforce organized around “very defined roles and functions” to a “much more fluid organization.”

“The technology is coming,” he said. “There will be safeguards around it. There need to be additional safeguards, but it will continue on.” He urged corporate leaders and government to prepare for difficult scenarios rather than assume the labor market will naturally adjust.

“At Verizon last week we announced a $70 million initiative to do training for American workers, not just Verizon workers, but American workers in the community across the country,” Schulman said.

The initiative includes free AI training and work with local organizations on career development, he said, before adding a prescription for all leaders and policymakers. “Our responsibility is to think about what might go wrong; what might we need to address; what might the disruption look like; and how do we put guardrails, training, programs in place to minimize that risk,” Schulman said.

“Everybody’s job is going to shift,” Schulman noted. “I don’t think everybody will land just magically in a better place per se.”

Other executives on Schulman’s panel described different constraints on the AI future. There will always be a need for someone to lay fiber, install power equipment, maintain transmission lines, retrofit buildings, and wire the data centers that AI requires.

For PG&E CEO Patti Poppe, the central challenge is that an increasingly digitized grid will require workers to combine physical skills with technological fluency. Poppe described seeing one of PG&E’s workers being lowered by rope from a helicopter onto a transmission tower in mountainous California. The company’s future grid, she said, will use sensors, remote-edge computing, and predictive capabilities to identify risks before they create outages or wildfires. But that system will still require skilled people in the field.

“The same guys who hang on the end of the rope are going to have to get smarter about those kinds of technologies,” Poppe said. “I’m still going to need those people. Somebody’s still going to have to connect that wire to the pole.”

Dave Regnery, CEO of Trane Technologies, urged students and workers to embrace AI and compared current anxieties to fears surrounding the arrival of personal computers, while adding a dash of hindsight.

“Go take your favorite AI tool” and look up articles from 40 years ago about personal computers, Regnery said. “They’re identical.”

His company sees AI as a way to make buildings run more efficiently, rather than simply to reduce headcount. Trane is using data and AI to manage heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems according to how buildings are actually used, he said—not merely according to their original design specifications.

“Most people don’t realize that 30% of all the energy is for buildings,” Regnery said. “And you know what? Thirty percent of that is wasted.”

He said the company can make buildings operate roughly 15% more efficiently than their design baseline, improving economics for customers while creating demand for technicians capable of installing, servicing, and operating increasingly sophisticated systems, offering a counterweight to the idea that the technology’s principal effect will be displacement.

“The fastest speed-to-power solution is use the essential equipment that you have,” Regnery said.

Chris Nelson, CEO of Stanley Black & Decker, described a similar transition on jobsites. His company has developed AI-enabled autonomous drilling robots that can use digital construction plans to drill holes for racks in data centers and other projects.

The technology is designed to take over repetitive physical tasks—not replace the electricians and skilled tradespeople needed to complete the higher-value work.

“What do the electricians and other skilled tradespeople not like to do all day?” Nelson said. “Sit and core drill.”

The machines can connect to digital drawings, map routes, and drill on their own, he said. That frees skilled workers to pull wire, terminate connections, and solve the problems that still require judgment and technical training.

“The holes will still need to be drilled from now until maybe the end of time,” Nelson said. “But the way we do it and what it enables people to think about for the future is going to be materially different.”

Nelson called AI a “companion on the construction site,” a framing that is more incremental than Schulman’s vision of near-term AGI, but still acknowledges that technology is changing the work itself. The question, he suggested, is whether companies can turn that change into a career draw—giving workers more engaging tasks, more decision-making authority, and a clearer path to starting their own businesses or moving into management.

For Dycom CEO Dan Peyovich, whose company builds telecommunications infrastructure, the immediate business problem is not a surplus of workers displaced by AI. It is finding enough people to build the physical networks that the technology boom requires.

“There’s so much infrastructure that has to get put in place for all of this to happen,” Peyovich said.

His company employs roughly 21,000 people nationwide, he said, connecting homes and businesses through fiber and telecommunications infrastructure. Its response to a tightening labor market has been to improve fieldworker benefits, including paid time off, holidays, health coverage, and training that goes beyond technical credentials.

Dycom has also built a training facility near Atlanta that includes instruction in technical skills, management, leadership, the use of technology in day-to-day work, and potentially personal finance, Peyovich said.

The strategy reflects a different labor-market assumption from the one embedded in much AI commentary. Instead of treating workers as interchangeable units who need only learn a new software tool, Peyovich described a system in which companies must offer a credible long-term career proposition—training, benefits, advancement, and financial stability—to recruit people into difficult field jobs.

“We want to try and create a path for people,” he said. “While they’re getting a paycheck, they can learn and find their way.”

The tone was collegial, and Schulman didn’t take issue with any of his co-panelists’ predictions about the future of work. His main point was that business leaders should not bet on a painless adjustment.

His final prescription was scenario planning: “We need to be prepared in case a different scenario emerges,” he said, “so that we can make sure that we have skilled workers, whether they be craftsmen or professionals.”
https://fortune.com/2026/09/30/this-revo.summary: Dycom CEO Dan Peyovich says technology is changing the work itself. He says companies must offer a credible long-term career proposition to recruit people into difficult field jobs.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/trump-je.author: Dan Mangan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/trump-je.text:
President Donald Trump said he spoke to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and that Huang denied knowing that the woman he admitted having an extramarital affair with “was a spy.”

Trump also said he was “amazed” by the allegations against Huang, which led Nvidia’s board to initiate an independent investigation.

Trump suggested he had only recently learned of allegations that Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.

President Donald Trump said he spoke to Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, and that Huang denied knowing that the woman he admitted having an extramarital affair with “was a spy” for China.

Trump told reporters at the White House that he was “amazed” by the allegations against Huang, which led Nvidia’s board to initiate an independent investigation.

Trump suggested he had only recently learned of allegations that Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.

“I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that,” Trump said.

“I asked him today because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right. ‘How you doing?’” Trump said.

“And I asked him about that, and he ... said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president said. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’ ”

“I really believe him,” Trump said.

The New York Times on Oct. 29 reported that Alice Huang had been eyed by U.S. spy agencies “for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China,” and that “American officials had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing.”

The Times reported that about a year ago, Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings “and chose not to do anything with the information.” The newspaper noted that Trump has been reluctant to disrupt chip sales by Nvdia, which are boosting the U.S. stock market.

On Friday, The Times reported that a memo that circulated last spring among top Trump administration policymakers “cited intelligence that a Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.”

The Times said the memo reported that Alice Huang was recruited to collect intelligence on the Nvidia CEO “as part of a drive by Beijing’s top spy agency to learn more about American A.I. chips and potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.”

“I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time, but not too long ago,” Trump said Monday. “We’ll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

Trump on Monday said of Jensen Huang, “He’s suffering greatly.”

“I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement, and I believe he’s suffering greatly, more so because of his family, his wife, who he loves, and his family. But he is definitely suffering.”

Asked if he would bring up the issue involving Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet next week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Trump said, “I don’t think so.”

“I mean, maybe I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it,” Trump said. “I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable, honorable man. I mean ... he built a great company, American company, and I think he’s a very honorable guy, and I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/october-.title: A key report for where inflation stood in October comes out Tuesday. Here's what to expect
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/october-.author: Jeff Cox
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/october-.text:
The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release the October consumer price index report Tuesday, with estimates of a 0.3% headline growth rate and 0.2% for core.

While the report won’t include an annual rate because of last year’s government shutdown, the results likely will keep the Fed well above its 2% inflation goal.

“We’ve got to come to terms with this cost-side and inflation-side failure,” Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday.

Falling gasoline prices provided some relief to consumers in October, but Federal Reserve officials are increasingly concerned that inflation pressures elsewhere in the economy are proving harder to contain.

Prices at the pump declined by more than 4%, according to the Energy Information Administration, providing a respite from a surge that had added more than a dollar a gallon over the past year.

However, the consumer price index for the month, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics will release Tuesday at 8:30 a.m., is expected to show only a slight let-up.

Meanwhile, Fed officials say they are worried that inflation initially driven higher by President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war is proving more persistent than expected, with price pressures emerging in sectors beyond those directly affected by the shocks.

At a time when the central bank is increasingly confident about the state of the labor market, concerns over the cost of living are what are top of mind for the Fed.

“We’ve been moving up to what historically we’d consider full employment, and the big problem has all been on the inflation side. We go around, we talk to people everywhere in this district, all we hear about is affordability on the business side, the cost,” Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday during an event in his home district. “So we’ve got to come to terms with this cost-side and inflation-side failure.”

The CPI reading for all items is expected to show an increase of 0.3%. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, is forecast to increase 0.2%, according to the Dow Jones consensus forecast. While both would be slower than the respective September monthly gains of 0.6% and 0.3%, they still represent further price pressures.

There will be no annual reading for October because of the government shutdown a year ago, which prevented the BLS from collecting some data and compiling a full index level. Because of the data issue, there isn’t a comparable figure for the index.

Bank of America, using an assumed baseline interpolating data for the period last year, estimated the annual growth rates at 3.8% for headline and 2.7% for core, both 0.1 percentage point higher than September and well above the Fed’s 2% goal.

Goolsbee said the current run on inflation is defying what normally could be expected from supply shocks and tariffs, with the current situation intensified by the hyperscaler build-out related to artificial intelligence.

“It was supposed to have gone away by now, and we’re now starting to see the inflation kicking up in areas that probably weren’t from oil prices and tariffs, like a bunch of services. Now this stuff with the AI data center build-out is, to my eyes, starting to look more just like old-fashioned demand overheating,” he said.

The massive investment in data centers is creating demand for construction workers, electricity and equipment, potentially adding to price pressures even as AI promises longer-term productivity gains, he added.

Though the Fed in October voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in place, markets are pricing in a better than 80% probability that the central bank will raise rates by a quarter percentage point at its next meeting in December, according to CME FedWatch data.

Goolsbee, who doesn’t vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee this year but will in 2027, didn’t commit to which way he was leaning on additional rate hikes, though he said current conditions could warrant action.

“The conventional wisdom there is: Be aggressive up front, to never let the economy overheat, because once it gets overheated, it’s extremely painful to get rid of that kind of overheating,” he said. “So I think we’ve got to watch out in that space.”

The CPI release comes with economic growth strong — 3.4% in the third quarter for gross domestic product and tracking at 3.5% for the final three months of the year, according to the Atlanta Fed — and the labor market seemingly in solid shape as well. Nonfarm payrolls expanded by a much better-than-expected 165,000 in October, while the unemployment rate edged lower to 4.1%, though inflation-adjusted wage growth has been negative.

That puts the inflation reading squarely in focus.

Bank of America said it sees tariff impacts fading but that goods prices could be pushed higher because of AI demand. Further, the firm is cautious about “sticky” services prices as well as pressures from health insurance and autos.

The bank has been hawkish in terms of Fed expectations and sees a December hike as likely so long as there isn’t an escalated stock market sell-off that might dissuade the central bank.

“This will be the final inflation report before the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting. If our forecast is correct, we think it would effectively lock in another 25bp hike, all else equal,” BofA economist Stephen Juneau said in a client note. “Absent an indisputably soft 0.1% [month-over-month] print, we doubt the inflation data will dissuade the Fed from hiking in December. The bigger risk to our call comes from financial markets.”
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/october-.summary: The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release the October consumer price index report Tuesday. The report won’t include an annual rate because of last year’s government shutdown. The results likely will keep the Fed well above its 2% inflation goal.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/ai-softb.title: SoftBank Group shares surge 11% as Asian tech stocks rally after Wall Street rebounds
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/ai-softb.author: Lee Ying Shan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/ai-softb.text:
Asian technology stocks surged on Tuesday, tracking a rebound on Wall Street overnight.

The recovery came after a steep sell-off in global technology stocks last week.

Asian technology stocks surged Tuesday, tracking a rebound on Wall Street overnight as a sharp decline in oil prices lifted sentiment while renewed buying in chip names spilled over into Asia, following last week’s bruising sell-off.

Japan’s technology investment giant SoftBank Group
 surged 12%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest
 gained 5.41%. Semiconductor equipment maker Tokyo Electron
 rose 5.88%, while Lasertec
 and Disco
 advanced 6.34% and 6.95%, respectively.

South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 8.01%, while Samsung Electronics rose 5.32%. Samsung SDI climbed 6.27%.

The gains followed a strong session on Wall Street, where the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.74%, while the S&P 500 rose 2.35% to clock its best day since April 8.

The recovery came after a steep sell-off in global technology stocks last week, fueled by concerns that Democrats’ sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially impacting demand for artificial intelligence chips and infrastructure.

Beyond the political uncertainty surrounding potential restrictions on data-center development, investors have also grown increasingly wary of the enormous capital expenditures required to build out AI infrastructure. Questions over how quickly those investments will translate into meaningful profits have weighed on sentiment toward companies across the semiconductor supply chain.
