The unprecedented terrorist attack on a church in Jordan last month that killed nine people and injured at least 34 has raised understandable concern about the spread of Salafist violence targeting civilians in the country. It should raise even greater concern about how Jordan’s government has used billions in U.S. security assistance and more than a decade of support for countering violent extremism.

The main perpetrator of the attack had only recently left prison following a terrorism conviction, yet the government has offered little explanation of how he went on to carry out the massacre. Instead, it launched kneejerk airstrikes on alleged Islamic State hideouts in Syria, killing seven civilians, three of them children, according to Syrian authorities. Both the failure to prevent the attack and the deadly retaliation expose a broader problem: security agencies empowered to raid, arrest, and punish, with little public accounting of whether their methods actually protect people.

The unprecedented terrorist attack on a church in Jordan last month that killed nine people and injured at least 34 has raised understandable concern about the spread of Salafist violence targeting civilians in the country. It should raise even greater concern about how Jordan’s government has used billions in U.S. security assistance and more than a decade of support for countering violent extremism.

The main perpetrator of the attack had only recently left prison following a terrorism conviction, yet the government has offered little explanation of how he went on to carry out the massacre. Instead, it launched kneejerk airstrikes on alleged Islamic State hideouts in Syria, killing seven civilians, three of them children, according to Syrian authorities. Both the failure to prevent the attack and the deadly retaliation expose a broader problem: security agencies empowered to raid, arrest, and punish, with little public accounting of whether their methods actually protect people.

The sequence of events is revealing. On Oct. 23, three gunmen—brothers Hazza Mohammad and Mishal Mohammad and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein—attacked mourners at a funeral. The event was taking place at St. George’s Greek Orthodox Church in Hmoud, a small village in the Karak governorate of southern Jordan; the gunmen lived in a nearby village.

Karak itself is home to one of Jordan’s oldest Christian communities, dating back more than 1,500 years, and it has long been a model of Muslim-Christian cohesion. While there have been at least 12 attacks by Jordanian violent extremists in the past decade, all but one have targeted military and police sites. This attack was one of a very few in Jordan’s history to deliberately target Christians, who make up a mere 2.1 percent of the country’s population.

Following a three-day search, authorities captured the three alleged perpetrators on Oct. 26, wounding them, one critically, in a shoot-out at an abandoned house in Karak, where they also recovered weapons and substantial ammunition. The government initially claimed that the church attack was random and opportunistic, but it later revised its claim to confirm that this was a planned attack, documenting preparations involving smuggled weapons, vehicles, assigned roles, and escape routes.

The most damning facts to emerge, however, concern the authorities’ prior knowledge of Hazza Mohammad, the reported ringleader, and the police presence at the church before the attack. Jordanian authorities had released Hazza from prison less than six months ago, following the completion of a seven-year sentence for planning a terrorist attack and promoting Islamic State ideology. He presumably would have, or should have, remained under close surveillance by Jordanian authorities. On Oct. 26, a local woman reported that a police patrol was stationed at the church during Sunday worship services earlier this month, something that she had never seen before; a Karak churchgoer confirmed this in an Oct. 28 interview with the authors.

On the same night as the arrests of the three men, the Jordanian government launched an aerial bombardment on four rural locations near Daraa and Suwayda in Syria. The attack is confirmed to have killed five family members in al-Tuff, three of them children; an 80-year-old man at a farm in al-Shiyah; and a 60-year-old man in Shahib. Local reporting suggested that the Jordanian Armed Forces appear to have been aware that women and children were at al-Tuff but hit it anyway.

The government claimed that it had identified Islamic State cell hideouts connected to the attackers but presented no evidence establishing that connection. It said Hazza had called a number in Daraa shortly before the attack but did not establish whom he contacted or how that call connected the Syrian targets to the church shooting. Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said the attackers shared the same ideology as the Islamic State and al Qaeda but acknowledged that investigators had not established whether they belonged to, or were influenced by, either organization.

The Jordanian government acknowledged the civilian deaths that it caused and subsequently offered condolences to the victims, though not compensation. It insisted that it was targeting terrorists and that its strike had killed 20 Islamic State members and destroyed a weapons depot and some vehicles. To date, however, there has been no independent verification of any Islamic State deaths; Syrian rescuers at the site reported only the recovery of seven civilian bodies.

The Jordanian government also claimed that it had coordinated the attack with the Syrian government, but Damascus denied this, condemned the breach of Syrian airspace—a clear violation of sovereignty—and summoned Jordan’s ambassador to deliver a formal protest. The two governments subsequently agreed to a joint security committee to establish the facts.

Jordan’s security failures, both before and after the attack, come despite years of foreign investment in its security apparatus—and at a moment when Americans are turning away from foreign military aid. U.S. President Donald Trump announced in early November that billions in annual aid to Israel would be terminated; this would directly impact the military aid the United States allocates to Jordan and Egypt as their “peace dividend” for entering into peace agreements with Israel.

For Amman, Israeli annexation of the West Bank looms as an existential risk.

King Abdullah II faces backlash against his country’s peace deal with Israel.

As part of this understanding, the U.S. government has provided almost $5 billion in military assistance to Jordan since 2015, alongside substantial economic assistance. Public records document hundreds of millions of dollars in surveillance-related programs, including more than $234 million between 2009-2021 for the Jordan Border Security Program and additional assistance for intelligence and surveillance.

Separately, public reporting establishes that the CIA funds Jordan’s General Intelligence Directorate, which it helped establish, though it provides no public information about the amount of its support. European governments, the European Union, and Canada also have granted roughly $200 million since 2016 to support Jordan’s policing, intelligence gathering, surveillance, border security, and military.

However, the Jordanian government has provided no meaningful accounting about how it has used these generous foreign resources to protect its citizens, particularly from terrorist violence. Its “Countering Violent Extremism” (CVE) unit, funded by the State Department and the European Union, offers almost no information about its activities, its budget, or its staff, despite its 11 years in operation.

Established in 2015 under the Ministry of the Interior, the program was bounced to the Ministry of Culture in 2016 and then to the prime minister’s office in 2020. The prime ministry’s website links the unit to a 2018 report, while a recent official news item describes its director attending a conference in Japan.

Even the U.S. State Department issued a rare rebuke about Jordan’s unit in a 2023 report, citing the government’s lack of a “sustained level of coordination or responsiveness… for CVE efforts,” and noting the “numerous Jordanian government stakeholders with equities in PVE [preventing violent extremism], making strategic collaboration by the donor community challenging.”

What little we do know about Jordan’s CVE effort is that it has relied extensively on a heavy-handed security approach while neglecting the economic, political, and social grievances that researchers consider essential to address in countering radicalization. A comprehensive 2025 study of Jordan’s response to violent extremism found extensive reliance on preventive raids and arrests and abuse of overbroad anti-terrorism laws. It also documented overlapping military, police, and intelligence operations with little transparency as well as broad intelligence agency veto powers over civil society prevention programs.

This same security apparatus has instead prioritized shielding the monarchy from political dissent. Over the past five years, the government has carried out mass spying and arrests of teachers, doctors, bus drivers, and supporters of Palestine who have protested lack of democracy and economic injustice in the country, “preemptively” arresting those merely planning to attend protests, shuttering the teacher’s union, prosecuting the leadership of the country’s human rights body, dissolving 19 political parties, and jailing members of the country’s now-banned Muslim Brotherhood organization.

Jordan needs to come clean about how a previously convicted extremist carried out an attack just after his release, what rehabilitation he received, and how authorities assessed and monitored his risk after release. It must also produce the evidence that it relied on to justify its bungled strike in Syria and identify the security reforms that it will make to protect Jordanians, in particular its religious minorities.

Such accountability will require broader democratic reform to make security agencies answerable to the citizens that they are supposed to protect, rather than the monarchy.

Sarah Leah Whitson is a lawyer and a co-author of the recently published From Apartheid to Democracy: A Blueprint for Peace in Israel-Palestine. She previously served as the executive director of DAWN as well as Human Rights Watch’s Middle East and North Africa Division. X: @sarahleah1

Jamal Al-Tahat is a Jordanian analyst. He previously served as a senior advisor at DAWN.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s name wasn’t on the ballot in last week’s midterms, but he still may end up being one of their biggest losers.

Analysis and arguments.

Top Republicans, including U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance, have blamed the Iran war for their midterms wipeout. With Hegseth having played a key role prosecuting and cheerleading the war, he’s a prime target for intraparty retribution post-midterms.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s name wasn’t on the ballot in last week’s midterms, but he still may end up being one of their biggest losers.

Analysis and arguments.

Top Republicans, including U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance, have blamed the Iran war for their midterms wipeout. With Hegseth having played a key role prosecuting and cheerleading the war, he’s a prime target for intraparty retribution post-midterms.

Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, who is among U.S. President Donald Trump’s biggest Republican critics on Capitol Hill, on Monday introduced a resolution to impeach Hegseth for “high crimes and misdemeanors.” In remarks on the House floor, Massie said that the defense secretary “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation.” He also said that Hegseth has demonstrated that he will remain a “threat” to the U.S. Constitution.

Massie’s resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of waging the Iran war without congressional authorization and ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties. Other articles focus on lethal U.S. strikes on alleged drug boats near Latin America, which Massie described as “extrajudicial killings,” and the U.S. operation to capture former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. The resolution characterized the Maduro raid as the unlawful “kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader.”

Massie previously introduced impeachment articles against Hegseth in September, but House Speaker Mike Johnson blocked the effort—pushing it until after the midterms—by recessing the lower chamber early. The House now has until Wednesday to schedule a vote.

The chances of the articles passing are “far more likely now than before the election,” Massie told CNN on Monday. Impeaching Hegseth requires a simple majority vote in the House. However, Johnson urged lawmakers against impeaching Hegseth, stating that it would be a “terrible look” while the country is in the “middle of hostilities abroad.”

Meanwhile, top House Democrats are also lining up behind the effort to impeach Hegseth. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to be the next House speaker, told ABC News on Sunday that he’s a “hard yes” on the impeachment resolution and that he believes there will be “incredibly strong support” among the rest of House Democrats.

It’s harder to say whether there would be enough support in the GOP-controlled Senate to reach the two-thirds supermajority vote necessary to convict and remove Hegseth. It’s also an open question if there’s enough time in the current congressional session for there to be an impeachment trial in the Senate. But Democrats could also push to impeach Hegseth again in a new Congress.

Even if Hegseth survives impeachment and Trump continues to back him, the defense secretary is poised to face relentless scrutiny after Democrats assume control of Congress on Jan. 3. Democrats have made it clear that they plan to fully leverage their oversight powers—and that Hegseth will be in their crosshairs. This means investigations, hearings, and subpoenas are coming. Democrats have already indicated that they want more answers from Hegseth on everything from the Iran war to the boat strikes.

Rep. Adam Smith, the ranking member on the House Armed Services Committee, vowed to conduct “vigorous oversight” of the U.S. Defense Department in a new Congress. “The list of potential oversight topics is long, but the illegal war against Iran is top of mind for me and the American people,” he said.

But as the walls close in around him, Hegseth has remained defiant.

The defense secretary’s impeachment charges come after he cost his department years of experience and poisoned relationships with Congress.

When the face of an unpopular war faces a wrathful Congress, “stuff happens.”

The video game’s latest installment seems disillusioned with the kind of militarism it did so much to promote.

In comments to reporters on Monday before Massie introduced the articles of impeachment, Hegseth made no apologies. “If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury, or Rough Rider, or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you’re taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished,” he said. (Operation Epic Fury is the U.S. military’s name for the first phase of the Iran war, from February to May, while Operation Rough Rider is the Pentagon’s name for the U.S. military campaign against the Houthis in Yemen last spring.)

Last week, Hegseth released a video taking aim at his political opponents. “This is not about me, but of course the other side, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democratic allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly. Just like they tried against President Trump twice,” he said.

The video landed poorly even among some Republicans. “@PeteHegseth, cabinet secretaries shouldn’t be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos. Kristi Noem learned that the hard way,” Sen. Thom Tillis posted on X. “This is about you,” he added, accusing Hegseth of displaying incompetence, offering bad advice to Trump, and being involved in “shameful” and embarrassing “episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.” Tillis was seemingly referring to the Signalgate controversy—a major national security scandal that Hegseth was at the center of early last year.

In many ways, it comes as no surprise that Hegseth is now in the crosshairs of Democrats and Republicans alike. He’s been a combative and divisive Pentagon chief from the start, spending much of his energy waging culture wars—such as by moving to ban transgender people from serving in the military and targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion policies—while using the Defense Department as a platform to promote his far-right Christian views. He’s also ruffled feathers by pushing out top military leaders and denying promotions for Black and women soldiers. Meanwhile, Hegseth has had an extraordinarily contentious dynamic with the press, effectively hollowing out the Pentagon press corps after major outlets refused to agree to restrictions that he sought to impose on their reporting.

Hegseth has made a lot of enemies in Washington in the process, and he seems to have fewer allies by the day. Even months before the midterms, there were signs that some Republican lawmakers were souring on him. As Republicans play the blame game over their losses in the midterms, support for Hegseth appears to be cratering—even among GOP lawmakers who are wary of publicly supporting impeachment.

When asked about where he stands on impeaching Hegseth, Rep. James Comer, the chair of the House Oversight Committee, told NewsNation: “I can tell you with a high level of confidence that there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth. We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran, and I think the Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.”

On Monday, Rep. Don Bacon told reporters that he was weighing whether to support Massie’s impeachment resolution. But he also said that it would be better for Hegseth to resign. “I don’t think he was the right choice to begin with,” he said.

Trump has so far stood by Hegseth and pushed back against questions about the defense secretary’s job security. “He’s guilty of two things, basically winning two wars,” Trump said of Hegseth on Sunday. “I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it’s awfully hard to say ‘let’s impeach’ somebody who did that.”

Hegseth has been among Trump’s most loyal cabinet secretaries since he returned to the White House, and critics have portrayed Hegseth as a prime example of the yes-men culture surrounding Trump. But loyalty hasn’t always paid off for those in the president’s orbit, as he has a history of turning on even his most faithful advisors. Recent reports suggest that Trump has been asking allies about a potential replacement for Hegseth. Trump has also acknowledged receiving calls from people who are unhappy with the Pentagon chief, though he said that he didn’t understand why.

Nvidia, the United States’ foremost national champion in its effort to lead the global technology race, has been rocked by a scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday, apologizing to his wife and children for the “hurt” his infidelity caused as well as to the company and its employees. “Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life,” Huang wrote. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”

Nvidia, the United States’ foremost national champion in its effort to lead the global technology race, has been rocked by a scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday, apologizing to his wife and children for the “hurt” his infidelity caused as well as to the company and its employees. “Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life,” Huang wrote. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”

The affair has implications far beyond Huang and his family. As the world’s leading producer of advanced semiconductor chips used to power artificial intelligence models and data centers, Nvidia has become a critical node in U.S. national security; meanwhile, the global demand for its products has seen the company’s valuation balloon to more than $4 trillion. Export restrictions on Nvidia’s most advanced chips—particularly to China—have become a cornerstone of U.S. technology policy, and Huang has developed a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump over the past two years.

Here’s what you need to know.

The allegations first became public on Oct. 29, when the New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence had concluded that a Chinese businesswoman believed to be spying on behalf of Beijing had developed a “close relationship” with the Nvidia chief executive.

The woman, Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), was an executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence, she was recruited by China’s main intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security, to gather information on Jensen Huang and help China gain access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, which have been restricted by U.S. export controls since 2022.

Megaspeed had previously been investigated by the U.S. Commerce Department on suspicion that it was helping to smuggle Nvidia’s AI chips into China, a claim that Megaspeed has denied. A statement from December 2025 posted on the company’s website says investigations by the U.S. government and Nvidia have produced “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities” and that it adheres to “all applicable export control regulations.”

It is not clear exactly what role Alice Huang currently plays at Megaspeed. The Singaporean company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Foreign Policy, but it said in a statement to the New York Times that it took the allegations around her actions “extremely seriously” and would “conduct a thorough internal investigation.”

Megaspeed’s website continues to list it as a key Nvidia partner, and Jensen Huang told Bloomberg in an interview last month that the relationship between the two companies was “normal and not unusual.”

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice Huang had pitched Chinese investors touting her ability to secure advanced Nvidia technology.

Tech billionaires spent big, and data centers became a lightning rod.

Fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios misses the forest for the trees.

Trump’s latest proposal would cede the United States’ AI advantage.

China has consistently denied spying on Jensen Huang, with Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun slamming the allegations as “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China” in a briefing on Monday.

Trump—who was reportedly briefed on the intelligence on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang a year ago but did not act on it—is standing by the tech executive for the moment, telling reporters on Monday that Huang was a “very high-quality person” and an “amazing guy” who was “suffering greatly.” The U.S. president did not reveal when he first learned about the scandal, only saying it was “not too long ago.” Trump added that he had spoken to Huang earlier on Monday. “He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy, … and I really believe him,” Trump said.

Last December, Huang successfully petitioned the Trump administration to relax some restrictions on sales of the company’s second-tier chips to China—giving the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of some sales in the process.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment from Foreign Policy on the allegations against Huang.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced the launch of its own investigation on Sunday, which it said will be conducted by a “committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel.” “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” the announcement said. The company also said Huang would continue in his current role during the inquiry.

Huang said he would fully cooperate with the investigation. “I love our country and our company,” he wrote in his statement. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

But the market is already reacting. Nvidia stock dropped more than 5 percent on Monday and has plunged by more than 15 percent in the past week.

U.S. lawmakers also want answers. Republican Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford—who chair the House committees on foreign affairs, the Chinese Communist Party, and intelligence, respectively—sent a letter to Huang and Nvidia last week requesting that he testify in front of their committees on Nov. 18, giving him a deadline of Wednesday to respond.

The scandal is likely to cast a shadow over Trump’s upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, next week—the third time this year that the two leaders will be meeting. Huang attended both of the previous meetings in Beijing and Washington as one of several U.S. tech CEOs whom Trump invited to join. Trump said he had no plans to bring up Huang’s case during next week’s trip but added, “I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it.”

Trump’s embrace of Huang is likely to have its limits despite the public show of support thus far, said a former senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“I think it’s going to be much more difficult for [Trump] to embrace Jensen Huang politically or commercially in the midst of a major investigation that will be bipartisan on what happened, who knew, what was done about it,” said the official. “My guess is that the president may not say that he’s distanced himself, but I think Jensen will find that every time … he wants to meet with the president, it will be inconvenient on scheduling.”

Asked on Sunday whether Huang would join Trump on his trip to Shenzhen, the president said: “I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him.”

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the chances of a U.S.-Iran peace deal, a suspected Chinese spy targeting Nvidia, and the elephant in the room at COP31.

U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday as part of ongoing efforts to avoid a fresh round of U.S. strikes on Iran. But as Washington and Tehran remain unwilling to make concessions to end the war, senior officials appear to be pessimistic about the likelihood of an imminent peace deal.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the chances of a U.S.-Iran peace deal, a suspected Chinese spy targeting Nvidia, and the elephant in the room at COP31.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday as part of ongoing efforts to avoid a fresh round of U.S. strikes on Iran. But as Washington and Tehran remain unwilling to make concessions to end the war, senior officials appear to be pessimistic about the likelihood of an imminent peace deal.

“I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said ahead of Monday’s talks.

Last week, Iranian officials announced, via Qatari mediators, a two-day plan to build mutual trust. Day one would have the U.S. military lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and release some of Tehran’s frozen assets. In exchange, Iran would invite the International Atomic Energy Agency to send inspectors to its bombed nuclear sites. Day two would then see the Strait of Hormuz reopened, after which nuclear talks would resume.

There is a caveat, though: Washington must first agree to Tehran’s seven conditions for ending the war, including canceling new U.S. sanctions on Iran and reinstating U.S. oil waivers.

Speaking on Sunday, Rubio characterized Iran’s conditions as “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”

The U.S. president told CNN on Sunday that it is “highly unlikely” that he will order the U.S. military to return to all-out war. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said.

Iranian state media accused the United States of firing “projectiles” at the strategic Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Tehran also issued a warning to the United States that same day. “Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X, adding, “Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

Such threats have made other Persian Gulf powers doubt the effectiveness of current peace talks. The region should “prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted,” senior Emirati official Anwar Gargash told Reuters on Monday.

Tuesday, Nov. 10: The United Arab Emirates hosts two-day trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visits Bulgaria.

Wednesday, Nov. 11: Spain’s largest unions hold a general strike.

Russia hosts a leaders’ meeting of the Collective Security Treaty Organization.

Thursday, Nov. 12: Danish lawmakers consider the joint defense agreement between Greenland and the United States.

Sunday, Nov. 15: The Philippines kicks off a three-day Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

Cape Verde holds a presidential election.

Alleged China ties. Nvidia stocks plummeted as much as 8.8 percent during trading on Monday after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The company’s board stressed over the weekend that there is “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Still, the U.S.-based corporation plans to open an immediate investigation into the incident. Jensen will continue to lead the company during the inquiry.

This past spring, Rubio drafted a classified memo warning top Trump administration officials that the Nvidia CEO was in a romantic relationship with a woman named Alice Huang whom U.S. intelligence sources believe had been recruited to spy by China’s State Security Ministry. Alice Huang was the CEO of a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, that the U.S. Commerce Department had investigated on suspicion that it was helping China smuggle in Nvidia’s restricted artificial intelligence chips. It is unclear if she is still employed at Megaspeed.

Jensen Huang is one of the world’s most consequential figures in the AI industry and an influential ally of Trump. Following news of Huang’s affair, Trump called Huang an “honorable guy” who has done “an amazing job for our country,” and he confirmed that he still plans to take Huang on his upcoming trip to China. On Monday, Beijing denied the espionage allegations.

Missing from COP31. This year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) kicked off in the Turkish city of Antalya on Monday against a global backdrop of deadly flooding, surging fuel costs, and record-setting temperatures. The 12-day event is expected to prioritize curbing greenhouse gas emissions and advancing climate legislation.

“We want people to feel the results of climate ‌talks in ⁠daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford, and in new jobs,” Turkish COP31 President Murat Kurum said on Monday.

However, with the leaders of world’s top three carbon dioxide emitters—China, the United States, and India—not attending the event, experts expect that this year’s summit could amount to little. Other notable absences include Russian President Vladimir Putin, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. In fact, only a few of the 91 world leaders attending COP31 come from industrialized nations with significant carbon footprints.

Heading home? Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina requested new identity documents, including a passport, on Monday to enable her return from self-imposed exile in India, according to a letter seen by Reuters.

“If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” Hasina told The Associated Press last week. Dhaka, however, has rejected her request, saying that it will not give a “passport to a terrorist.” Bangladesh’s war crimes court sentenced Hasina to death in absentia in November 2025 for her deadly crackdown on student-led protests in the summer of 2024, during which as many as 1,400 people were killed, according to U.N. estimates.

Hasina “is a fugitive criminal,” said Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh’s state minister for foreign affairs. “We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over,” he added. New Delhi has yet to comment on Hasina’s request and Dhaka’s refusal. Previously, though, India has refused to surrender Hasina to Bangladeshi authorities, straining diplomatic ties between the neighboring nations.

On Sunday, a modern synagogue in Budapest transformed—for one night only—into a runway for Orthodox Jewish women hoping to challenge stereotypes about their modest dress code. Under that dress code, known as tzniut, Orthodox Jewish women are generally required to cover their collarbones, elbows, and knees; the rules also dictate that married women must cover their hair. Although some outsiders view these policies as restrictive, the organizers of the “Kosher & Chic” fashion show aimed to show that women can still dress to reflect their personalities while following modesty rules.

On Monday, U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, triggering a vote in the House of Representatives that could come as early as this week. Massie, a Republican who will leave Congress in January, accuses Hegseth of waging an “unlawful” war in Iran and abusing the office. Hegseth will be the first civilian leader of the U.S. military establishment to face impeachment in 150 years.

The last, William Belknap, was President Ulysses S. Grant’s secretary of war—the title at the time for the civilian leader of the U.S. Army, before a unified Defense Department. The House voted unanimously to impeach him. Belknap resigned ahead of his Senate trial; he avoided conviction because of many senators’ discomfort with impeaching a private citizen. (Impeachments do not require the accused to be in office.)

Massie’s charge sheet includes eight counts, the most severe of which is that Hegseth “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation notwithstanding the absence of congressional authorization” and “demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office.”

Four of the counts of impeachment involve war powers, while the others concern civilian casualties, extrajudicial killings during boat strikes, suppressing free speech, and kidnapping a foreign leader.

The indictment does not include some of Hegseth’s more egregious norm- and law-violating behavior: violating the Impoundment Control Act by refusing to release funds authorized and appropriated by Congress for aid to Ukraine, requiring uniformed military participation in partisan rallies, refusing briefings to congressional Democrats, denying press access to the Pentagon, firing without explanation more than two dozen senior officers confirmed by the Senate in their ranks and positions, appointing people forced out of military service for insubordination or political acts to senior civilian positions in the Defense Department, renaming the department without congressional authorization, and campaigning against sitting members of Congress.

President Donald Trump continues to support Hegseth, praising him for “winning two wars.” And the defense secretary continues undaunted: On Nov. 5, he released a nearly six-minute video insisting that “this is not about me, but of course, the other side, in case you’ve noticed, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice.”

The defense secretary’s most important responsibility is managing Congress because under the U.S. Constitution, it is Congress that has the power to “raise and support Armies” and “provide and maintain a Navy.” Hegseth has poisoned those relationships. It is likely that his impeachment will be successful in the House on at least the count of attempting to penalize the speech of Sen. Mark Kelly, whom Hegseth groundlessly accused of sedition. (Hegseth has initiated proceedings to retroactively reduce Kelly’s military rank and retirement pay.)

Rep. James Comer, the Republican chairman of the House oversight committee, sounds dubious about defending Hegseth rather than supportive, saying that “there are a lot of questions” about the defense secretary. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is a “hard yes” on impeachment. Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn appears unlikely to give Hegseth an exit with honor by appointing him to her vacant Senate seat.

Trump will surely goad Hegseth on to fight the impeachment and behave outrageously—both as a distraction from the drubbing of the Republicans in the midterm elections and to indulge his entertainment approach to governance since it would be “great television.”

Whether or not Hegseth is convicted, his actions have already cost the Defense Department years of combat-tested experience in the senior leaders who were forced out and have instilled a chilling effect on those who remain.

Hegseth has eroded military readiness by poor planning for the Iran war, requiring extended deployments; robbed the force of funding by failing to gain congressional support for a war supplemental spending bill; continued munitions shortfalls because he structured the budget to pay for them in expectation of a third partisan reconciliation bill; damaged retention in the force, as 53 percent of service members now want to leave earlier because of politicization; and caused allies to question the legality of U.S. military operations.

When the face of an unpopular war faces a wrathful Congress, “stuff happens.”

The defense secretary puts stunts over substance. The U.S. should send him on permanent leave.

There will be a strong temptation among Hegseth’s adversaries to bring the military into the impeachment process by calling fired officers to testify as witnesses.

This would be a mistake, both normatively and practically. As a normative matter, it damages civil-military relations to place the military in the position of judging its civilian masters. What a democracy should want in febrile political moments is for the military to remain politically inert. Practically, what some envision as a long table of uniformed officers with glittering medals bearing witness to policy depredations would actually be a parade of suits explaining that they have no idea why they were relieved or forced into retirement.

The two fundamental tests of whether the U.S. model of civil-military relations is healthy are that the political leadership can fire any military officer and that the military will carry out the civilian leadership’s policies whether or not it agrees with the decisions. For all the destruction that Hegseth has visited upon the U.S. military, its professional adherence to subordination to civilian control remains strong.

That is yet one more reason the military deserves much better civilian leadership than Trump, the senators who confirmed Hegseth as defense secretary, and Hegseth himself have provided.

Kori Schake is a senior fellow and the director of foreign and defense policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute. She is the author of The State and the Soldier: A History of Civil-Military Relations in the United States. X: @KoriSchake

International order is not the absence of conflict, nor is it the rigid defense of the status quo. Rather, it is the existence of predictable mechanisms to manage inevitable disagreements. And the primary mechanism tasked with upholding international peace and security—the United Nations Security Council (UNSC)—is no longer fit for purpose     .

The UNSC still resembles the world of 1945, giving privileged status to the victors of World War II and the holders of colonial empires. Without reform to give rising and middle powers a status commensurate with their growing influence, states will eventually see more sense in pursuing their security interests unilaterally or through exclusive, destabilizing blocs. For now, with a few notable exceptions, states remain committed to speaking the language of multilateralism. But make no mistake: Reforming the UNSC is not a matter of aesthetics or desirability; it is an absolute necessity.

International order is not the absence of conflict, nor is it the rigid defense of the status quo. Rather, it is the existence of predictable mechanisms to manage inevitable disagreements. And the primary mechanism tasked with upholding international peace and security—the United Nations Security Council (UNSC)—is no longer fit for purpose     .

The UNSC still resembles the world of 1945, giving privileged status to the victors of World War II and the holders of colonial empires. Without reform to give rising and middle powers a status commensurate with their growing influence, states will eventually see more sense in pursuing their security interests unilaterally or through exclusive, destabilizing blocs. For now, with a few notable exceptions, states remain committed to speaking the language of multilateralism. But make no mistake: Reforming the UNSC is not a matter of aesthetics or desirability; it is an absolute necessity.

Three dynamics have held up reform. But each may be slowly giving way, creating a rare window for genuine change.

The first and most commonly cited obstacle is the Security Council’s five permanent veto-wielding members, or P5—the United States, China, Russia, France, and the United Kingdom. The P5 countries are wary of admitting rising powers as fellow veto wielders, as it would diminish their own influence in the body and make it more susceptible to deadlock.

However, without reform, the council’s legitimacy in the eyes of the global majority will deteriorate, rendering it more and more irrelevant. The P5 will be the biggest losers if the UNSC fades into insignificance, as they have the most to lose: their veto prerogatives. Consequently, the P5 are only likely to allow for reform when the council appears      to be nearing      the brink of collapse—a point that the world may soon      approach      if the P5 continue to wield their vetoes with impunity.

The second issue is the deadlock between the two main reform groupings: the G4 coalition of Germany, Japan, Brazil, and India, which favor enlarging the permanent membership of the UNSC to include themselves, and the Uniting for Consensus group, which favors only adding additional elected seats to the council. The uncompromising competition between these two blocs has prevented other proposals from gaining steam. However, Germany’s recent failed bid for a two-year term on the council has put into question the viability of its claim to a permanent seat—and the viability of the G4 proposal as a whole. This enables a possible shake-up that allows for the emergence of new and more creative reform ideas.

The third factor is that discussions over which reform model would best enhance the UNSC’s efficiency, effectiveness, and legitimacy has, to date, been largely speculative. Neither side has been able to predict with any meaningful accuracy the implications of their proposed reforms.

This, too, is now changing. Thanks to artificial intelligence, complex simulations can be conducted that calculate potential shifts in the council’s performance. We have conducted such a simulation to determine precisely what each proposal would achieve—and what it would risk. The simulation shows that the G4 model would dramatically increase gridlock over the next five decades. Council business would slow down as decision-making speed per resolution would grow from 28.5 days to 42.1 days, and veto use would grow by more than 60 percent. Despite giving them a seat at the table, the resulting paralysis would encourage leading powers to work outside the UNSC, defeating the purpose of reform entirely.

Yet while the Uniting for Consensus group’s proposal would limit the damage to the council’s efficiency and effectiveness, it fails to resolve its legitimacy deficit. The UNSC cannot effectively serve as a long-term custodian of the international order if Britain continues to enjoy a more privileged position than India—the world’s most populous country and likely soon to be its third-largest economy.

How, then, to resolve this conundrum? The AI simulation points to two mechanisms.

First, if more countries are to gain the veto, then this must be balanced by creating a veto override mechanism: for example, a veto wielder must secure one or two concurring negative votes among sitting council members, otherwise, a two-thirds majority in the General Assembly can overturn the veto.

The race to succeed António Guterres has started—and four very different candidates are in the running.

The simulation shows that this would reduce veto usage by up to 40 percent, even before any cast vetoes are overturned. It would also speed up decision-making on average from 28.5 days to 21 days because veto wielders would either know that they have the necessary concurring vote(s) and cast their veto without delay, or know that they don’t and be incentivized to compromise to avoid a potentially humiliating General Assembly override.

Skeptics argue that the P5 countries are unlikely to agree to any reform that dilutes their veto privileges. But the simulation projects that successful overrides would occur only 28 percent of the time (or as low as 14 percent of the time, if the vote to override takes place by public roll call rather than by secret ballot). Agreeing to this limited mechanism, which would only take effect when a great power is isolated to the point of having no allies on an expanded council, is a small price to pay to ensure the council’s long-term legitimacy—and the permanent members’ privileged position that comes with it.

Second, a pool of “semipermanent” members, serving multiple lengthy terms and rotating on and off the council a few countries at a time, would offer middle powers that fail to earn a permanent seat a substantial consolation prize. According to the simulation, it would also triple small states’ likelihood of election to an ordinary council seat by taking these middle powers out of the running.

Countries such as Japan, Brazil, Argentina, India, and Pakistan currently monopolize the council’s nonpermanent seats, serving on average more than one term per decade, leaving smaller countries to earn a place only once every 30-50 years. The simulation shows that this proposal, if tabled by a strong coalition of small and developing states, has a 78 percent chance of being adopted and contributing to breaking the logjam.

The “international order” may be an abstract concept, but it takes concrete form in the institutions through which states manage their differences, constrain the use of force, and prevent conflict from descending into chaos. None matters more than the UNSC.

For decades, the presumed trade-off between legitimacy and effectiveness has been an obstacle to meaningful reform. Our simulations suggest that this is a false choice: A more representative council can also be a more effective one. What is, in fact, impossible is a new and stable order without a Security Council designed for it.

Zachary Paikin is the deputy director of the Better Order Project at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.

Trita Parsi is the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. X: @tparsi

Harrison, 81, became the oldest winner of the award, which comes with a £50,000 ($67,000) prize and a boost in sales and profile for the winner.

A veteran of the British science fiction literary scene, it was Harrison's first time being shortlisted for the coveted prize, which critics have said was long overdue.

He beat shortlisted authors Marlon James, Douglas Stuart, Elizabeth Strout, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry, whose entries ranged from a queer epic unfolding in 1980s Kingston to a campus satire set in modern-day London.

"The End of Everything" came out "ahead in terms of both its extraordinary expert writing, but also huge ambition," chair of the judges Mary Beard told a press conference.

Harrison's 13th novel follows the beachcomber Phillip Tennent and his dementia-stricken, free-spirited aunt Marnie, set in the near-future on the windswept English coast invaded by mysterious objects known as the iGhetti.

An unnamed catastrophe plunges the characters into a murky post-apocalyptic world where the European continent seems to have disappeared and the arrival of the iGhetti, which can imitate humans, evoke interactions with artificial intelligence.

"One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible," Beard said, adding the book spoke to the present "moment".

"This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future," Beard said in a statement.

In dream-like episodes this tight, 198-page novel alludes to Brexit, the Covid-19 pandemic and the invasion of technology into daily life.

As is often the case with Harrison's writing, which has been described as genre-bending and singular, the plot counts less than the atmosphere, and the author's elliptical and poetic style heightens the feeling of gradual collapse.

"Current affairs provided the themes and the satire," Harrison said of his book. "What happens when all of our expectations and explanations of the world become an ongoing disaster, but we still have to make a life?"

The author previously said he was inspired by the 2008 financial crisis, and wanted to write a novel about the "failure of explanation in society".

Born in Rugby, England, in 1945, Harrison, is the author of numerous science fiction books, including the Viriconium saga (1971-1984) and "Light" (2002), the first volume of a trilogy known as The Kefahuchi Tract, renowned as major works of the genre.

Little known to the general public beyond circles of science fiction enthusiasts, when he was shortlisted, The Telegraph newspaper wrote: "Finally, he's getting his due."

The theme of artificial intelligence has been on the judges' minds through the year-long selection process, which saw them whittle down 163 entries to a shortlist of six novels.

READ MORE
International Booker Prize 2026 shortlist announced featuring French witch, sworn virgin

Beard pointed out concerns surrounding AI were "pretty high on this book".

"Phillip has got this object, this artefact, and it's not clear how sentient it is. It's not clear what it is," Beard said in a press conference to announce the winner.

In an earlier interview with AFP, Beard said the prize-awarding panel would have to think about the role of AI in publishing and writing in the coming years.

"I think for the future it's inevitable that that will be on the agenda. You can't bury your head in the sand about that," she said.

The other judges have talked about wanting to create a shortlist of books that were distinctly human, and could not be replicated by AI.

The prize, which celebrates the best work of long-form fiction by writers of any nationality, written in English and published in the last year, was awarded on Monday at a London ceremony.

READ MORE
Booker Prize winner David Szalay on his 'risky' novel 'Flesh' that wowed the literary world

Last year, British-Hungarian author David Szalay won the prize for "Flesh", his tortured tale of a Hungarian emigre in London.

For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing the five-year mark, with security guarantees topping the agenda.

The two-day session starting Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (UAE), follows previous negotiations early this year that failed to produce any visible progress toward ending Europe’s most devastating conflict since World War II.

The talks follow last month's localised truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine that was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump and allowed the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of desperately needed humanitarian supplies.

READ MORE
‘Not an isolated incident’: Russian drones stalk Ukraine’s civilians in ‘human safaris’

But even as Moscow and Kyiv touted the week-long ceasefire as a positive model, fierce fighting has continued along the 1,200-kilometre (750-mile) front line. Both sides also have escalated their long-range attacks on each other with drones and missiles.

Russia has intensified its strikes on Ukraine’s power system, seeking to undermine the country’s resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and new, faster jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors.

Here's a look at the talks and what's on the agenda:

Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on key elements of any prospective peace deal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from the four regions that Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing such a pause would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede territory Russia has not been able to take on the battlefield and agree to limits on the military and arrangements with Western partners, which it sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelensky is the only way territorial issues can be settled.

Russia and Ukraine said the talks will focus on security guarantees.

Zelensky noted that Ukraine and its allies have discussed security guarantees similar to NATO’s Article 5, which states the alliance sees an attack on one of its members as an attack against all.

In a November 5 interview, he said Ukraine's security guarantees boil down to what Western allies would do if Russia were to launch a new invasion of his country. “If Russia starts again, what will happen?” Zelensky asked. “Who will do what, with what means, and when?”

Some European nations have mulled a possible deployment of their troops to Ukraine after a prospective peace deal. Russia rejects that as a non-starter, warning it would view any European troops on Ukrainian soil as legitimate targets.

The Kremlin insists any prospective deal should also offer security guarantees for Russia. Just before Moscow launched the all-out invasion in 2022, it demanded that NATO roll back its deployments in the alliance's member countries in Central and Eastern Europe, seeing their presence as a security threat. Similar demands will likely be part of any comprehensive peace deal proposed by Russia.

US President Donald Trump said in a “60 Minutes” interview broadcast Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv are “very close” to a deal but added that “they’re going to end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine.”

He also declared after meeting Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev November 4 at the White House that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, although he did not elaborate.

“It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that it might include all of Europe.

Ukraine insists its European allies must have a seat at the negotiating table, while Russia opposes any such involvement at this stage.

“No one is going to invite them to the negotiating table,” Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov snapped.

Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov said his delegation will meet separately with European envoys in Abu Dhabi.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Europeans would need to be involved in broader negotiations but only later.

“Since the discussion will touch upon the future security architecture in Europe while addressing the mutual security of Russia and Ukraine, at some stage it would be impossible to do it without the Europeans,” he said.

On October 27, Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store spoke by phone with Putin in their first known direct conversation since shortly after the 2022 invasion. They said they spoke in their capacity as the heads of Russia's Nordic neighbours and not on behalf of the European Union, which has struggled to pick a negotiator with Moscow.

Peskov mocked the EU's “protracted indecisiveness,” saying that its members “can’t even decide yet who is authorised to speak on their behalf."

Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky – who led Russia’s delegation in the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022 and in subsequent sessions – remains Moscow’s chief negotiator.

A former culture minister who wrote books about purported Western plots against Russia over the centuries, Medinsky is known for his hard-line views and blustery statements. At the 2025 talks – also in Istanbul – he reportedly said it took Peter the Great 21 years to defeat Sweden in the 18th century and Moscow was now ready to fight as long as it takes.

The Russian team also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov, and deputy chief of the General Staff's operational department, Yuri Zhigarlovsky.

Ukraine’s delegation is led by Umerov, head of the country’s Foreign Intelligence Service, who attended earlier talks. It also reportedly includes Zelensky’s chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy Sergiy Kyslytsya, and Davyd Arakhamia, parliamentary faction leader of Zelensky's Servant of the People party.

On November 4, Zelensky said on X that he spoke to US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, saying the talks “must move forward at full throttle to bring this war to an end as quickly as possible.”

Kushner said Monday on X that he and Witkoff will meet with envoys from Ukraine, the EU, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy before the three-way talks.

“Ultimately, achieving a comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them,” he said. “By discussing post-war security, economic recovery, and the mechanisms needed to prevent future conflict, we hope to shift the focus from managing the war towards building the foundations for a durable peace."

US President Donald Trump has backtracked on his announcement that he had offered UFC boss Dana White the role of White House press secretary, insisting he was "only kidding". The unusual proposal sparked widespread online speculation, including a theory that Trump may have confused the mixed martial arts executive with another person of the same name.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said he had been joking when he announced the offer a day earlier to White, his long-time friend and the president and CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).

"I was only kidding," Trump said, adding that White liked the idea. He also suggested the joke should have been obvious given the AI-animated video he'd shared depicting the UFC executive flanked by professional fighters in the White House briefing room.

The announcement was made on Saturday in a post on Trump's Truth Social platform. He described White as a "fighter and warrior" and said he had asked him to take on the role of press secretary, suggesting he bring along some of the UFC's top champions as his assistants to defend his administration against what he called the "Lunatic Left".

The president accompanied the post with an AI-generated cartoon video showing White standing behind the White House press briefing podium, surrounded by UFC fighters. In an animated sequence, the fighters proceed to attack journalists attempting to ask questions, including one reporter who asks whether Trump is a threat to democracy before being body-slammed.

The imagery was also amplified by the White House communications team. Trump's communications director, Steven Cheung, reposted the announcement on X, writing: "Hell yeah, do it Dana White!"

White's apparent nomination raised eyebrows given his lack of experience in government or political communications. However, he is a long-time supporter of Trump and one of his close personal friends.

The two have known each other for decades, with Trump hosting UFC events at his properties as far back as 2001. White has also been a prominent presence at Trump's political events and has publicly backed his presidential campaigns.

Their relationship has continued during Trump's second term, with the president even planning a UFC event on the White House lawn as part of celebrations marking the United States' 250th anniversary.

But despite their close ties, White has never held a government position or worked as a political spokesperson.

The announcement also prompted a second, more unusual theory online: that Trump may have confused the UFC boss with another person called Dana White.

Dana W. White previously served as the Pentagon's chief spokesperson during Trump's first administration. She has also worked for the conservative Heritage Foundation and appeared as a commentator on Fox News.

Her background in government communications led some social media users to speculate that she might have been a more conventional candidate for the White House press secretary position, and that Trump could have mistakenly referred to the UFC executive instead.

There is, however, no evidence to support the theory that the president confused the two.

As the speculation gained traction online, Dana W. White addressed it directly in a post on LinkedIn. "To everyone texting me congratulations, thank you, but you have the wrong Dana White," she wrote.

She also pointed out that she had previously stood behind a podium to answer questions from journalists, but had never stepped into a UFC octagon, and would like to "keep it that way".

The White House has yet to announce a permanent replacement for the press secretary role, which has been vacant since October 16.

Trump's previous pick, Katie Zacharia, left the position after fewer than five days. Her short tenure attracted scrutiny following a difficult first briefing and questions surrounding her legal credentials.

The episode has also prompted speculation about the timing of Trump's announcement. Some critics and political commentators have suggested that the president's comments about White may have served to divert attention from his party's losses in the midterm elections.

After all, the veteran prime minister has repeatedly demonstrated an extraordinary capacity to survive

Scheindlin explores the uncertain prospects of Eisenkot's coalition-building efforts, alongside the erosion of Israel's traditional bipartisan support in Washington. She places considerable responsibility on Netanyahu himself, arguing that the “complete collapse of the old bipartisan consensus” was largely driven by a leader who “invested the entire relationship in one party and increasingly one person.” Her analysis reveals how parliamentary arithmetic, competing visions of national identity and Israel's increasingly strained relationship with the United States have converged into a broader crisis of political legitimacy, democratic inclusion and long-term strategic direction.

Yet perhaps the most revealing contradiction lies within the opposition itself: determined to unseat Netanyahu, its leading figures remain deeply reluctant to cooperate with Arab parties. Scheindlin calls this a “completely self-imposed constraint”, questioning why those seeking political change continue to rule out partnerships that might make it possible. For her, Jewish-Arab political cooperation is not merely a matter of coalition arithmetic but a fundamental question about Israel's democratic future.

The immediate outcome, Scheindlin suggests, may be either parliamentary stalemate or a structurally fragile minority government. But the deeper challenge lies in Israel's political architecture itself. Against a backdrop of mounting international isolation and concerns over the departure of some of the country's brightest and most highly skilled citizens, can new political leadership overcome the entrenched exclusions and divisions that stand in the way of meaningful change, or will Israel's political crisis outlast Netanyahu himself?

Carlton Football Club player Wade Derksen has been fined after being caught driving with a blood alcohol content three times the legal limit earlier this year.

The 25-year-old did not appear in person at Darwin Local Court today, however he pleaded guilty to high-range drink driving via telephone.

The court heard Derksen was driving along the Arnhem Highway south of Darwin in September after a day of drinking and fishing with friends.

The father-of-three was stopped by police for a random roadside breath test where he blew a blood-alcohol reading of 0.174.

Derksen was convicted, fined $873 and has been suspended from driving for 12 months.

Todd Russell dies at 54, decades after mine disaster rescue (ABC News)

Former miner, Todd Russell, who was trapped underground for 14 nights when the Beaconsfield Gold Mine collapsed in 2006, has died at the age of 54 from an undisclosed illness.

The man he was trapped underground with, Brant Webb, has paid tribute to him, saying the mine collapse will always connect them.

Russell is being remembered for his courage, resilience, and for "being a genuine bloke with a big personality".

Brant Webb has paid tribute to the man he was trapped underground with following a mine collapse 20 years ago, saying "we went through something together all those years ago that will always connect us".

Mr Webb was trapped underground with his former colleague, Todd Russell, when the Beaconsfield Gold Mine collapsed on Anzac Day in 2006.

Russell has died at the age of 54 from an undisclosed illness, days after returning home from hospital to be with his family.

"I'm very sorry to hear the news about Todd," Mr Webb said in a statement.

"My thoughts are with his kids and loved ones at this difficult time."

Todd Russell (left) and Brant Webb (right) recounted the two weeks they spent trapped in the Beaconsfield mine during a media interview after the incident. (Channel Nine)

The pair had been working alongside each other when the mine collapsed, trapping them underground for 14 nights before being rescued.

Their colleague, Larry Knight, was killed by the collapse.

Mr Webb told ABC NewsRadio that even 20 years later he and Russell were "always bumping into each other".

"I work 100 metres from his house," he said.

"But the last eight months I sort of hadn't had much to do with him because he's been in hospital.

Todd Russell is being remembered as a genuine bloke who was dedicated to his community. (Facebook: Todd Russell)

"But I did have a beer with Donna, his new wife, the other day … so that was good to bump into her and just sort of give her my condolences before it happened.

"She said, 'Well, you know, he won't be here for a long time.'

Brant Webb says he continued to bump into Russell around town. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Russell is being remembered for his courage, resilience, and for "being a genuine bloke with a big personality".

One of Russell's friends, Andrew Burt, posted on social media: "Last night Australia lost a true Aussie legend."

Todd Russell and Brant Webb emerged from the mine after being trapped for 14 days. (Ian Waldie/Pool: AAP)

"Todd wasn't just a husband, a dad or a community leader. To those of us lucky enough to have known him, he was so much more," Mr Burt wrote.

"He was a true-blue mate, a genuine bloke with a big personality, a cheeky side and a presence that you couldn't help but notice whenever he walked into a room.

"You were a survivor, a fighter who faced life's challenges and lived every moment on your own terms.

"Rest easy, old mate. It's hard to say goodbye to a bloke like you."

Andrew Burt (right) says Todd Russell was "a true-blue mate". (Supplied: Facebook/Andrew Burt)

The father of three and keen footballer retired as chief of the Beaconsfield Fire Brigade this year.

"Todd dedicated his time and service to the brigade and the community, leaving behind a legacy that will be remembered by those who had the privilege of serving alongside him," the Beaconsfield Fire Brigade posted online.

Todd Russell was chief of the Beaconsfield Fire Brigade until this year. (Facebook: Todd Russell)

The Tasmanian Volunteer Fire Brigades Association said in a statement: "Todd will be remembered for his commitment to those around him, the friendships he forged, and the positive impact he made to the community of Beaconsfield and the broader West Tamar."

"May the memories shared and the lives he touched bring comfort during this difficult time."

Last week, Russell posted to social media that he had no more fight left in him after eight and a half months in hospital, and he was returning home to see out his final days surrounded by family.

Barry Easther, who was West Tamar mayor at the time of the mine collapse, told 936 ABC Hobart that Todd loved Beaconsfield and would be missed.

"It's certainly a very sad time for his family and friends and the local community," Mr Easther said.

Former mayor Barry Easther says Todd Russell loved Beaconsfield. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

"Todd was well known in many areas, especially in the football area, I remember as a young father going along with my boys and playing mini league football with Todd.

"He grew up in Beaconsfield and just loved the town."

Reflecting on the mine collapse, Mr Easther said he remembered Russell's mother being very confident the two miners would be rescued.

"To be trapped underground, 900-odd metres under the surface in an area that was just opposite where his mum and dad lived … it was quite amazing."

In a post to social media, Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the nation held its collective breath while rescuers went to work at Beaconsfield in 2006.

"We were shattered when news came through that Larry Knight had been found and tragically was no longer with us," he said.

"Then Brant and Todd were miraculously found, and the work began to extract them."

Then-mayor Barry Easther, Todd Russell, then-prime minister Kevin Rudd, Brant Webb and then-union leader Bill Shorten. (ABC News)

But he said Russell did not let the ordeal define him.

"He continued to serve proudly at the Beaconsfield Fire Brigade until February this year, an exemplary 31-year career of community service," Mr Rockliff wrote.

"He told his story, and became an advocate for mental health.

"And made the community around him a better place."

Deputy Premier Guy Barnett offered his sympathies to Russell's family and friends.

"As the government, we'll consider all the options in terms of paying respect and honour to Todd Russell for his resilience, his dedication, his support for his wonderful community," Mr Barnett said.

Launceston mayor Matthew Garwood said Todd Russell was a name forever etched into Tasmania's history.

"Todd showed incredible courage and resilience through the Beaconsfield mine disaster but his contribution went well beyond that," Councillor Garwood said.

"From decades of service as a volunteer firefighter to sharing his story and advocating for mental health, Todd continued to make a difference in the lives of others.

Perth billionaires Alexandra and Julian Burt have donated a combined $120 million to 10 conservation groups across Australia.

The Australian Wildlife Conservancy received $25 million, which it says will help with its plan to manage 5 per cent of Australia's land mass.

Multiple groups say the donation is the biggest they have received and it will allow them to expand operations.

A conservation group says its "incredible ambition" to manage 5 per cent of Australia's landmass may now be possible thanks to a $120 million donation.

The Australian Wildlife Conservancy (AWC) is one of 10 environment foundations to receive a portion of the fund from Perth billionaire Alexandra Burt, whose grandfather was Gina Rinehart's father's business partner, and her husband Julian.

It is one of the biggest philanthropic contributions to nature in Australian history.

Jemma Manfre from Australian Wildlife Conservancy releasing a Bilby back to nature. (Supplied: Robin Sinclair / Australian Wildlife Conservancy)

AWC regional ecologist for northern Australia, Rebecca Diete, said it had taken her a while to fathom the organisation's biggest-ever grant of $25 million.

"At the moment we're managing about 1.7 per cent of the Australian continent, and our strategy is to increase that to 5 per cent — that's an area the size of Germany.

Rebecca Diete at Bullo River Station near the NT / WA border. (Supplied)

"We may not have known exactly how we were going to meet that ambition, so a donation like this makes us sit back and go, 'We might actually be able to do this.'"

AWC works with landholders and buys properties across the country, where it manages projects to restore ecosystems and reintroduce native wildlife.

One of those projects is being led by the organisation's bat specialist, Oli Aylen. He said the money would allow for much-needed research into the animals.

"Bats make up over 20 per cent of all mammals, but they are a species that are generally not included in conservation management," he said.

"Now we'll be able to go around all the sanctuaries that we have across Australia and really just understand where these bats are, which of them are threatened and probably find new records of things."

AWC bat specialist Oli Aylen says the donation will allow researchers to expand important research. (Supplied: Australian Wildlife Conservancy)

Bush Heritage Australia also received $25 million, with the organisation's science and conservation boss Bruce Webber describing the money as "completely transformative".

"It will go towards the purchase of a property almost immediately," he said.

The property Dr Webber is referring to is the 20,000-hectare Wooroora cattle station near Cairns, which Bush Heritage describes as its "most ambitious single acquisition ever".

He said Australians would see the effects of the $120 million donation for years to come.

"The next 10 to 15 years are going to make a significant difference to how much biodiversity we're able to keep on into the future," he said.

Ms Burt's grandfather Peter Wright was the business partner of Gina Rinehart's father, Lang Hancock.

Forbes estimates Ms Burt and her sister Leonie Baldock have a combined net worth of $4.2 billion.

Ms Burt has been involved in long-running legal disputes with Mrs Rinehart over the spoils of the Hancock-Wright mining empire and the donation suggests a contrast between the pair's views.

Bullo River Station is owned by the Burts and managed as a cattle station in collaboration with AWC. (Supplied: Joey Clarke / Australian Wildlife Conservancy)

The couple owns iconic Top End cattle property Bullo River Station, which is co-managed by AWC. It delivers a range of land management programs there.

Neither Mr nor Ms Burt were available for an interview, but Ms Burt said in a statement the donation "felt like the right thing to do".

"We see nothing but rapid decline in our natural environment and that needs rapid assistance," she said.
