https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.title: 'Absolutely fed up': ASIC slams $250 billion private credit sector
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.author: David Taylor
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Credit and Lending

ASIC is furious with the private credit sector. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

It is not for lack of trying, but ASIC is furious with the private credit sector's seeming indifference to the regulator's attempt to crack down on poor lending practices.

The corporate cop's anger is understandable too. Private credit has issued hundreds of billions of dollars of funds, and its lending practices fuel property development and construction.

Private credit refers to lending outside the banking sector.

Central to ASIC's concerns is the opaque nature of the sector's finances.

It means investors remain in the dark on the risks of private credit investments.

"I am absolutely fed up, at ASIC we are absolutely fed up," ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said.

ASIC commissioner Simone Constant says she is fed up with the private credit sector.  (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

ASIC has today released its second major surveillance of private credit in Australia.

"We have drawn a line in the sand with a second comprehensive broad and deep surveillance report," Ms Constant said.

"Many investors are still not being given the information they need to properly understand the risks, fees and conflicts present in private credit investments," ASIC found.

The watchdog's second major surveillance report of the sector found "complex structures, opacity and deficient disclosure practices persist".

Between November 2025 and August 2026, ASIC reviewed 24 wholesale and retail private credit funds responsible for a combined $18 billion in assets under management.

It also ran the ruler over a sample of financial advice given to retail investors relating to private credit.

ASIC's surveillance found that many of the poor fee, disclosure, distribution and conflict management practices identified in ASIC's first private credit report, released in November 2025, remain.

It's not for lack of intervention by the corporate regulator.

ASIC has initiated several regulatory interventions, including six interim stop orders and multiple referrals for further enforcement investigation.

The problem for ASIC is that private credit is growing, and any wobbles in the sector have the potential to fracture the broader financial system.

We've seen tremors recently in the sector when investors access to their funds in private credit firms have been limited.

Investor redemptions are when investors in private credit firms seek to retrieve some, or all, of their money in the face of concerns about the safety of their investment because of potentially overly risky lending.

Private lender CVS Lane, which had significant loans to collapsed developer Bathla, limited investor redemptions this year.

Bathla's collapse has also put pressure on parts of Australia's opaque private credit sector. (ABC News: Berge Breiland )

The US has been ground zero for private credit.

It hit the headlines this year when US private credit firm Blue Owl had to limit the amount of money investors could withdraw as the company bled value from souring software investments.

The firm's two private credit funds again faced elevated redemptions, investors seeking to withdraw cash, in the June quarter.

Private credit was exposed to traditional software firms, and the exponential growth of artificial intelligence left those firms reeling, prompting investors to pull their money out of credit linked to traditional tech.

Regulators have found monitoring the sector difficult because the disclosure requirements are not anything like what you find in the banking sector.

But ASIC has been making a point of pulling firms over who do not follow the rules.

The regulator this week, for example, made interim stop orders preventing Angas Securities Limited (Angas Securities) from offering interests in two managed investment schemes over concerns the funds' product disclosure statements do not adequately disclose Angas Securities' financial position, and one fund's exposure to the Bathla Group.

ASIC is concerned that investors in both funds may not have been adequately informed about the financial position of Angas Securities and the risks arising from that position.

The private credit industry says it is trying to lift its standards. (AAP)

Coinciding with ASIC's report, the Alternative Investment Management Association (AIMA) and its private credit affiliate, the Alternative Credit Council (ACC), released new guidance for Australian private credit managers, setting out recommended practices to "strengthen governance, lending standards, transparency and investor protection".

The ASIC commissioner warns that the clock is ticking on poor lending practices.

AIMA's managing director and head of Australia, Michael Gallagher, said the guidance represented an important industry response to the concerns raised by ASIC and recent events.

"We believe private credit plays a crucial role in financing Australian businesses and supporting Australia's productivity, a contribution former ASIC chair Joe Longo has repeatedly recognised," he said.

No wonder the corporate regulator's frustrated — an emerging key pillar of finance is clearly not up snuff, and most Australians are exposed.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.title: Jury finds man guilty of murdering former school friend
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.author: Jean Bell
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police say Hamilton woman Carlee Smith died at her Henty Highway property in May 2025. (Supplied)

A Supreme Court jury has found David Douglas McLennan guilty of murdering 48-year-old Hamilton woman Caroline "Carlee" Smith.

The 50-year-old pleaded not guilty to killing Ms Smith.

McLennan will be sentenced at a later date following a plea hearing.

A Supreme Court jury has found an old school friend of Caroline "Carlee" Smith guilty of her murder near Hamilton in south-west Victoria.

Warning: This story contains details that may be distressing for some viewers.

The body of 48-year-old Ms Smith was found by police during a welfare check at her Henty Highway home on May 15, 2025.

During the nine-day trial in Warrnambool, the court heard that David Douglas McLennan, 50, killed her four days earlier, with the prosecution arguing that he strangled her during a violent assault.

McLennan had pleaded not guilty to one charge of murder, with his defence telling the court that while some facts were not disputed, McLennan had not intended to kill Ms Smith or cause serious injury.

The trial at Warrnambool Law Courts lasted nine days. (ABC News: Jean Bell)

The jury deliberated for about five hours before returning its verdict.

McLennan sat silent as the verdict was delivered.

He was remanded in custody ahead of a plea hearing and sentencing at a later date.

During opening arguments, the court heard McLennan and Ms Smith were old school friends from Western Australia.

The jury was told McLennan moved into her south-west Victorian home in October 2023 to assist when Ms Smith's husband fell ill with terminal cancer and later died in September 2024.

The prosecution said McLennan and Ms Smith were not in a romantic relationship, and had heated arguments in the lead-up to her death, with text messages between them indicating conflict in their relationship.

This included the accused referring to Ms Smith as "crazy" in messages sent to family members, and saying he was being pushed to "breaking point".

The prosecution said footage from CCTV cameras installed in the home captured McLennan saying to himself "pretty sure you killed her" in the moments after the fatal assault is thought to have occurred on the evening of May 11, 2025.

He remained in the house drinking and smoking for four days while Ms Smith's body lay at the property.

Police were called to do a welfare check on May 15 after Ms Smith failed to respond to phone calls and messages, the court heard.

That evening, police officers found Ms Smith's body in the home's spare bedroom and located McLennan in a shed on a neighbouring property.

The prosecution said a notebook left on a bench included a note that said "There is evil in this house" and "I was pushed too far … I'm just a man".

The court heard Ms Smith suffered significant head injuries and 12 separate rib fractures, with McLennan's DNA found underneath her fingernails.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/n.title: China's spy tactics may reshape the AI race for supremacy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/n.author: Allyson Horn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

US President Donald Trump standing with NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang in Washington DC on October 8. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

There are few people in the world who can say they're phone buddies with Donald Trump, but Nvidia boss Jensen Huang is one of them.

The tech giant controls the most valuable company in the world and currently makes the hardware that could determine if China or the United States wins the race for AI supremacy.

If that's not power enough, he also has the ear of the US president.

Just a few months ago, Mr Huang was on stage speaking on a panel about AI when he famously took a live phone call from Mr Trump and put him on speakerphone.

So it's no exaggeration to say Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy is a bombshell in the high-stakes contest for not only the future of tech, but potentially the future of the world.

The chief executive of the world's most valuable company and a close ally of Donald Trump admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Here's what we know.

Mr Huang, a US citizen, co-founded and has overseen Nvidia for more than 30 years — though many people may never have heard of the business until this week.

The company makes the world's highest-grade computer chips that are used, or desired, by businesses and governments across the globe to power and scale up their AI models.

It's the kind of technology China currently needs if it wants to fulfil its ambitions of overtaking the US to become the world's AI superpower.

And it's why America has imposed strict export controls to restrict the sale of the advanced chips into China to protect trade secrets.

Now, the US tech sector and American politicians are asking whether an alleged honey trap has put those gains at risk.

Mr Huang this week admitted to an affair with a woman named by US officials as Alice Huang (of no relation to each other), a former executive at Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed.

An image shared by software company Net Thunder on LinkedIn in 2024, which it says shows Megaspeed's Alice Huang sitting alongside Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang at an event in Taipei, Taiwan. (Supplied: NetThunder/LinkedIn)

American authorities have been investigating Megaspeed and Ms Huang for years, alleging the company has been flouting US restrictions and facilitating avenues to get high-grade Nvidia chips into China.

These concerns grew when US intelligence concluded Ms Huang was acting as an agent and passing information to Beijing's Ministry of State Security, according to US media.

The New York Times also reported that further intelligence about a romantic engagement between Mr Huang and Ms Huang was presented to the US president last year and he chose to take no direct action.

Now Nvidia has confirmed it's investigating an alleged espionage plot that involves one of the most important figures in the entire AI industry.

Trump today said the ‌FBI was also looking ‌into the ⁠affair, and said he had spoken to Mr Huang over the phone.

"I asked him about that and he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," the US president said at a White House briefing.

Beijing has denied Ms Huang is a Chinese spy and has labelled the claims as "smears" against China.

Jensen Huang leads the world's largest company, Nvidia. (Reuters: Manami Yamada)

English-language state media outlet the Global Times also called it a "political witch hunt" and suggested Western media had been seduced by the lure of a sexy spy plotline.

"It's quite a story, complete with all the twists and suspense of a Hollywood thriller. But so far, the public has seen no hard evidence to back up the central allegations," the Global Times said.

The outlet also said the extramarital affair had no connection to chip manufacturing, nor did it pose a technical risk.

But it's no stretch to imagine Mr Huang would be an attractive target for any Chinese espionage attempts.

He's a man with power, technical prowess, and a direct line to America's commander in chief, who is shaping the future of AI outside of the global south — and is China's main competitor in the AI race.

Mr Huang has been to the White House at least five times since Trump returned to office and has been lauded by the US president as a "great, brilliant person" who had "done amazing things for our country".

Despite that, the business, security and geopolitical implications of the affair are sending shockwaves throughout America and the US administration.

Jensen Huang and his wife Lori attended Donald Trump's state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

And it's shocked many tech analysts who've traditionally viewed Mr Huang as a meticulous, methodical and militant figure, who demands the highest of standards from his staff.

Nvidia says it's confident no trade, or national security, secrets have been divulged to Beijing, but it will bring in outside counsel to fully investigate.

But this probe will be just one chapter in a long book of scrutiny into this affair.

This is more than just about potential access to tech — it's about the potential access to the people Mr Huang knows, and the policy he may have had a role in shaping.

Mr Huang has already been called to give evidence before at least three congressional committees, where it's likely he'll face a grilling over the affair.

It could turn out to be a symbolic win for China, which will get to see a major rival scrutinised, and the US administration asking questions about its own policies and approaches to the tech sphere.

It's especially relevant, as China prepares for its third meeting between President Xi Jinping and Donald Trump next week at the APEC summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

The last time Mr Trump travelled to China, in May this year, he famously picked up Mr Huang from a tarmac in Alaska while en route to Beijing.

The Nvidia boss also sat beside Mr Trump as the two presidents met in May.

But despite AI being top of the Xi-Trump meeting agenda again, it's unclear whether another travelling invitation will be extended to Mr Huang or whether he'll even still be in charge of Nvidia.

For now, the board is standing by the man who is thought of as Mr Nvidia, despite shares plummeting after news of the investigation.

But a boss mired in scandal, even one as influential as Mr Huang, may not be a tenable future.

So there's every opportunity for the blast radius from these revelations to expand further.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.title: Renewables and Iran war help drive fall in global fossil fuel emissions
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.author: Romy Stephens and Nathan Morris
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Climate Change

Renewable energy growth is meeting rising demand for power across the globe. (Reuters: Carlos Barria)

The 2026 edition of the global carbon budget shows fossil fuel emissions are set to drop, but the world is on track to reach 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming within four years.

Renewable energy uptake and the war in Iran are driving the decline, but there are doubts it will last.

Energy experts say accelerated electrification efforts could lead to a lasting shift in emissions.

Increasing renewable energy capacity and the Iran war have spurred a drop in oil, gas and coal emissions, but experts say a geopolitical shock could make the reduction short-lived.

Research released by the Global Carbon Project projects emissions from the burning of fossil fuels to decrease by 0.4 per cent compared to 2025.

Oil emissions, down 2 per cent, are the main driver of the drop, likely due to prolonged disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

The world's need for energy is growing and clean sources, mainly solar and wind power, are increasingly meeting that additional need.

A tanker anchored in the Strait of Hormuz, off the coast of Qeshm Island, in April. (AP: Asghar Besharati)

But lead researcher and director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, Pierre Friedlingstein, said clean energy was not growing fast enough to for a durable drop.

"A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution," he said.

"While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline."

Total carbon emissions are set to rise from 42.8 billion tonnes last year to 43.3 billion tonnes in 2026. El Niño-linked peat fires and forest degradation in South-East Asia are driving the increase.

The amount of carbon that can be emitted before warming reaches 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels is now 150 billion tonnes, which will be reached within four years at the current rate.

This year the United Nations found the world was on track to reach 2C warming by about 2050 and move towards 2.6C warming by the end of the century.

"The point the report is trying to make is that we need to change these policies and be a little more aggressive in the way we look at the transition to net zero," CSIRO chief research scientist and Global Carbon Project executive director Pep Canadell said.

Some experts say Donald Trump's decision to start a war with Iran did more than briefly interrupt the world’s oil flow — it created a tipping point for accelerated global electrification efforts.

The 1970s oil shocks sparked by conflict in the Middle East produced vast changes in how the global energy system worked, and drove innovations in fuel efficiency.

And this time renewables and electric vehicles offer market-ready alternatives, with the cost of installed solar and batteries falling by 90 per cent since 2010.

The Iran war might have cost Trump the midterm elections, but it inadvertently helped the climate.

Solar and wind together are now the largest sources of growth in global electricity generation, overtaking coal and gas to meet over half of new electricity demand, according to a dedicated report on electrification by the International Energy Agency (IEA).

According to Gabrielle Kuiper, an energy researcher affiliated with CSIRO, consumer-level electrification of transport is well underway.

"I think the momentum is unstoppable," she said.

"We've reached the tipping point, particularly on EVs."

A report released by the International Energy Agency (IEA) last week found the shift to renewables is most pronounced in emerging economies, where the continued high oil price caused by the Iran conflict has accelerated uptake.

The report forecasts global renewable capacity to grow by almost 4,800 gigawatts (GW) in the 2026-2031 period, 57 per cent more than in the previous six years.

Growth in emerging and developing economies outside China is expected to match that in advanced economies for the first time, the report said

"Off-grid solar PV capacity is expected to increase by 2.5 times to around 80 GW by 2031, led by Pakistan, sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia."

But as the UN's annual climate summit, COP 31, gets underway, growth in renewables still lags the pledge at COP28, where nearly 200 countries agreed to triple renewable capacity by 2030.

"Current policies, market developments and cost trends boost cumulative renewable energy capacity to around 9, 710 GW by 2030, a 2.6-fold increase from 2022, in line with last year's forecast," the IEA said.

The annual global carbon budget update found China's emissions are set to fall by 0.9 per cent in 2026 due to a plunge in oil emissions, and growth in electricity generation from renewable energy.

While the world's largest emitter produces 32 per cent of global emissions, it was found to be the most active in deploying clean technologies and increasing carbon sinks, which are systems that absorb more carbon from the atmosphere than they release, through reforestation.

Emissions across the United States are projected to decrease by 1.3 per cent, mainly due to dropping coal emissions, which spiked last year.

India's emissions are expected to increase by 4.4 per cent, higher than its annual average growth of 3.5 per cent over the past decade.

The European Union's emissions are expected to drop by 1.5 per cent, Japan's are expected to drop by 1 per cent, while emissions for the rest of the world are set to go down by 0.7 per cent.

"This year, for the first time, we saw 40 countries which, over the last 10 years, had emissions declining from fossil fuels; at the same time, they had an economy that has been growing," Dr Canadell said.

As United Nations climate talks commence in Türkiye, Australia's position as a climate leader will be tested.

"That is double the amount of countries as the previous decade, so certainly things are happening."

Emissions in aviation and shipping are projected to decrease by 1 per cent, partly due to reduced flights across the Middle East, while total emissions have grown at a slower pace over the past decade.

Oceans and vegetation remove about half of all carbon dioxide emissions from human activities from the atmosphere.

The dark, red tongue spreading in the Pacific is growing at a rate not seen in living memory. The uncertainty over what is driving it has alarmed experts.

But as El Niño exacerbates drought and bushfire conditions in many regions, plants absorb less carbon dioxide via photosynthesis when they are stressed by low rainfall and higher temperatures.

Bushfires also release large amounts of CO2 back into the atmosphere.

Dr Canadell said the Amazon's absorption rate declined by 66 per cent during the El Niño of 2023/24, which has since returned to normal.

But he warned that a drop of that scale could repeat towards the end of the year.

"We'll see the full force of El Niño in the sinks, particularly in the tropics, in the Amazon specifically, early next year," Dr Canadell said.

"It's not good news for us because we know that the future of our climate is a warmer climate.

"Therefore, those land sinks will be less effective in removing that part of the 50 per cent carbon discount that these natural sinks are doing."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/l.title: Court ruling paves way for Lindsay Clancy's retrial for murder
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Lindsay Clancy could be potentially retried for the deaths of her three young children. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger)

A US judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy.

Ms Clancy's defence team argued the judge should not have declared a mistrial in September after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict.

The denial means prosecutors could retry Lindsay Clancy for the deaths of her three young children.

A judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, potentially clearing the way for her to be retried next year over the deaths of her three young children in Massachusetts.

Ms Clancy's defence team asked the court to end the case on the basis of an unusual argument: the judge shouldn't have declared a mistrial in September when jurors couldn't reach a unanimous verdict.

They argued that the judge should have removed the one juror who favoured conviction, then allowed jury deliberations to continue.

But Judge William Sullivan disagreed, saying he saw no other option than to declare a mistrial.

Judge William Sullivan defended his decision to declare a mistrial and denied prosecutor's request a gag order be put on the case. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

"Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy," Mr Sullivan wrote.

A spokesperson for Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz declined to comment.

Ms Clancy has never denied that she killed her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued that Ms Clancy had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behaviour.

Prosecutors have acknowledged that Ms Clancy had mental health problems, but they said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong.

The six-week criminal trial of Lindsay Clancy has collapsed without a verdict, with the judge declaring a mistrial.

Prosecutors said they intend to retry Ms Clancy, but they haven't decided whether to pursue the same charges or opt for a reduced charge that might be more palatable to the jury.

The next hearing is November 16.

In the motion to dismiss, one of Ms Clancy's lawyers, Martin Weinberg, argued that the judge should have thoroughly interrogated jurors after the foreperson sent two notes saying the one juror who favoured conviction wasn't following the court's instructions on reasonable doubt.

Ms Clancy's defence team, headed by attorney Kevin Paddington, asked the court to end the case against Clancy. (The Patriot Ledger via AP: Greg Derr)

Mr Sullivan said that type of questioning was barred by law.

"Because the secrecy of jury deliberations is a bedrock of our judicial system, any inquiry into the jury's deliberative process would improperly intrude into the jury's function," Mr Sullivan wrote.

The judge also said he didn't believe the jury foreperson's claim that the holdout juror — identified in court papers by the pseudonym Juror Doe — wasn't following the law.

"In context, the notes appear to express the foreperson's belief that Juror Doe must be refusing to follow the law because Juror Doe would not agree with the majority's view of the case," Mr Sullivan wrote.

Mr Sullivan also denied prosecutors' request for a gag order while the case remains pending, to avoid influencing a future jury.

Patrick Clancy has given his first public interview since a mistrial was declared in his former wife's highly-publicised murder proceedings.

Ms Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington gave interviews during the trial, while prosecutors generally didn't speak to reporters.

Her lawyers argued the gag order would amount to an unconstitutional restraint on speech.

Sullivan also denied a defence motion to preserve certain records related to the first trial that potentially could have been used to further investigate the conduct of the juror who wanted to convict Ms Clancy.

"In the court's view, Clancy is not entitled to any of the materials sought in this motion," Mr Sullivan wrote.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/2.title: 2027 Netball World Cup the 'next defining moment in women's sport'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/2.author: Brittany Carter
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/2.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Diamonds were successful at the last Netball World Cup on home soil. (Getty Images: Steve Christo)

The 2015 Netball World Cup final was the stuff of legend.

A good old-fashioned trans-Tasman clash, it was decided by just three goals, 58-55.

The Australians managed to survive a desperate comeback by New Zealand and send retiring players Julie Corletto, Kim Green and Bec Bulley out on a high. Gutsy Corletto famously played through the game with a broken foot, needing painkillers injected at half-time.

Being there in person to witness it is something netball fans love to reminisce about.

A world-record crowd watched the Diamonds hold on against the Silver Ferns in 2015. (AAP: Paul Miller)

The contest was enthralling of course, but it's the atmosphere they remember most.

As the 16,752-strong crowd at Sydney SuperDome cheered an octave higher than at other major sporting events, they set a world record attendance for the sport that is yet to be broken.

Now, 12 years later, the 2027 tournament heads back to the same venue and organisers are hoping that nostalgia will help them break the record again.

They have boldly set a target of 200,000 attendees across 64 matches from August 25 to September 5 and would love to fill the venue's 18,000-seat capacity for the finals.

The first batch of tickets goes on sale on today.

Chief executive Jane Fernandez said it would be the next defining moment in women's sport.

Netballers from Australia, Uganda, Jamaica and England pose with administrators at a Netball World Cup event. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

"There's a connection to place that is still front of mind," Fernandez told ABC Sport.

"For the netball community, this is a huge opportunity to be part of another World Cup on home soil, and I've met with a lot of people who talk so fondly of 2015.

"I think it's going to take netball into the next stratosphere."

The impact of that 2015 World Cup was undeniable.

Two years later, Super Netball was born. The modern era of the elite competition has revolutionised the game and offered players a professional wage for the first time.

It also allows unlimited imports, opening up full-time contracts in high-performance environments to players all over the globe. This has helped opposition nations grow stronger.

Australia has had a rough patch of form, recently losing the Constellation Cup 3-1. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

If the Diamonds found it hard to win back then, imagine the immense pressure on the current crop of players.

Following its lowest-ever finish at a Commonwealth Games, the Australian team conceded the Constellation Cup and is on the verge of losing its number one ranking.

Twenty-four internationals have been signed for the next Super Netball season and most of them will occupy starting positions across the eight teams, so it's only going to get tougher.

No matter what happens at this World Cup, the impact will be felt by generations to come and greater competition for the host team should help with ticket sales, according to Fernandez.

As will the introduction of a new piece of silverware.

Australia will be hoping to defend the 2023 Netball World Cup title it won in Cape Town. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

"It's going to be absolutely fierce," Fernandez said.

"It changes the energy of a tournament when you've got strong competition, so I do think it's great for the World Cup.

"This is anyone's to win and for the first time, teams can also play for the plate.

"After the first four days, the teams will be split and the top eight will continue to play for the World Cup trophy, while the bottom eight continue to play for the plate.

"All participating teams will have something to play for, which is a great opportunity for fans to keep cheering their side on until the very end."

The Matildas celebrate victory after a penalty shootout in their quarterfinal against France in 2023. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Fernandez is best known for leading Australia and New Zealand's 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup bid and eventual tournament, which captured the hearts and minds of the nation.

A key marketing strategy from that event was the storytelling of teams and players. They rebranded the Matildas and built the profiles of the athletes over several years.

Momentum built and it paid off with enormous crowds and TV ratings.

Crowds celebrate the Matildas' win over France in the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup. (AAP Image)

"We already know they are unbelievable athletes, and we knew that with the Matildas," Fernandez said.

"Our job is to make sure everyone knows the players by the time we get to the tournament.

"I mean the moment Sam Kerr started backflipping, which was around the time we were bidding, we were like, 'This is awesome.'

"We saw with the FIFA tournament that FOMO kicked in, and everyone wanted to be part of it."

Jane Fernandez (far right) poses with key figures at a 2023 FIFA World Cup event. (Getty Images: FIFA)

For this World Cup, Fernandez was hired once Netball Australia had won the hosting rights.

With less time up her sleeve, the aim is to leverage off the back of the Super Netball season, which culminates 25 days before the World Cup, and generate hype around the international players already at their disposal in the domestic competition.

The Super Netball grand final will be held at Sydney SuperDome on July 31, cementing the stadium as the home of netball next year, after the NSW government bought the hosting rights.

Melissa King was the CEO of the successful 2022 FIBA Women's World Cup at the same venue. It recorded the highest attendance across the event in the tournament's history.

Lauren Jackson was chaired off after playing her final game for the Opals at the 2022 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Sydney. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

King met with Netball Australia at the end of that year to share her lessons from the event.

One of basketball's main strategies was also to tap into the story behind the athlete.

Legend Lauren Jackson came out of retirement to play for the Opals, so they leaned hard into that narrative with clever marketing strategies.

King said it was just as integral for organisers to engage the multicultural community in Australia linked to the travelling teams.

The 2022 FIBA Women's World Cup captured the attention of the Chinese community. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

"The United States and China were in the final and we had former NBA player Yao Ming here watching with FIBA," King told ABC Sport.

"The Chinese community really got into it, so it's important to keep promoting and telling people about who's coming to Sydney.

"We had a situation where Lauren Jackson had a birthday during the tournament, so we created a ticket promotion around her birthday number.

"Of course, an Australian team being there on the final day creates a powerful connection too, but that's out of your control and just a bonus, not a strategy."

Although the entire event happening in one place is easier logistically, it does create challenges.

It can make it harder to draw attention across the country. There is risk that activation outside the arena could start to feel stale for returning fans, and Homebush isn't the easiest place to get to in the city.

Aside from that, there could also be crossover in timing with the NRL and AFL finals.

Fernandez said transport would be included with each ticket and there would be a considerable uplift in bus and train services.

She is confident about their position in the sporting calendar, placing a higher value on international competition and its appeal to a different audience.

"You can't compare a World Cup to a week-in, week-out national sporting league," she said.

"Our promotion is focused on it being the pinnacle of netball and that's what sets us apart."

Three types of tickets will be available to subscribers at NWC2027.com from today.

Vouchers will be available for Christmas gifts in December, while single-match tickets will go on sale in February.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/j.title: Aloisi sacked from Chinese club after losing final five games in title choke
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

John Aloisi will no longer coach Chengdu Rongcheng following a late-season collapse that cost the club a league title in China. (Getty Images: Masashi Hara)

Former Socceroo John Aloisi has been sacked as manager of Chinese club Chengdu Rongcheng after a stunning late-season collapse.

The team needed just one point from their final four matches to win the title, but lost every match.

After failing to win the league, Aloisi apologised to Chengdu fans.

John Aloisi has paid the price for Chengdu Rongcheng's catastrophic title choke, with the Chinese club sacking the Socceroos great.

Chengdu had appeared a lock to win the Chinese Super League for weeks, on top all season and leading the competition by 14 points with five rounds remaining.

But they lost all five games and, after slipping to a 3-2 defeat to Shandong Taishan on the final day, handed the title to Dalian Yingbo, where former Western Sydney Wanderers coach Mark Rudan is an assistant.

While Chengdu had a superior goal difference, the Chinese Super League prioritises head-to-head records between teams, and Dalian had won both meetings between the sides.

Aloisi had been hoping to become the next Australian to guide a team in China's top league to a championship after Kevin Muscat led Shanghai Port to glory in 2024 and 2025.

Instead, the former Western United championship winner will have to continue his journey elsewhere after Chengdu parted ways with Aloisi and his staff on Tuesday.

"Mr John Aloisi will no longer serve as head coach of Chengdu Rongcheng Football Club. Members of his coaching staff will also depart," the Chinese club said in a statement.

Aloisi had apologised to Chengdu fans after the capitulation.

"We are indeed very disappointed not to have won the championship. We are in a very despairing state. There is nothing else to say," Aloisi told local media via a Chinese translator.

"I want to say sorry to everyone. We certainly know that our fans have travelled a long way to fight alongside us and support us.

"Right now, my only feeling is one of great dejection and disappointment, because we could see the trophy right in front of us, but could not get it."

Meanwhile, John's older brother Ross Aloisi departed Zhejiang FC after just one season when they finished ninth.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/i.author: Ellen-Maree Elliot
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Ellen-Maree Elliot

Topic:
Local Government

Ipswich City Council voted unanimously to request a return to single-councillor divisions. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Lucy Stone)

The Change Commission will assess whether Ipswich City Council should return to 10 single-councillor divisions.

It currently has four divisions, each represented by two councils.

The council will prepare a submission, including results of its community consultation.

Queensland's independent body overseeing electoral changes to local governments will assess a major proposal to return Ipswich City Council to single-councillor divisions.

In September, the council voted unanimously to request a review of its multi-councillor divisions, which were installed after the council's sacking in 2018.

Queensland's Local Government Minister Ann Leahy confirmed to 612 ABC Brisbane there will be a review.

"I have referred Ipswich City Council's proposed electoral arrangements to the Change Commission for independent assessment under the Local Government Act 2009," she said in a statement.

This comes as community consultation found residents supported returning to single-councillor divisions, with 53 per cent of 812 respondents wanting the change.

The city's current system of four divisions, each represented by two councillors, was introduced to improve governance after the council's corruption scandals.

The report recommending multi-councillor divisions for Ipswich stated single-councillor divisions "fostered a 'tale of 10 small cities' approach to leadership, rather than a whole-of-city commitment".

Before the sacking, councillors each had a $680,000 discretionary fund plus more to award community grants — all without any oversight.

"There was no framework in place to review whether (say) a new park in one suburb was more or less important to a road upgrade in another suburb, from a city-wide, strategic perspective," the report stated.

Ipswich Mayor Teresa Harding said there had been "significant changes" to the Local Government Act since 2018, including a limit on discretionary funds to .01 per cent of the rate base for all councils.

"In our council — I have a grand total of $26,000 a year that I can decide. Every councillor has $26,000, and that's for things like a local P&C wants nets for soccer fields, and how that is spent is published each month," she said.

She said Ipswich was still the only council in Australia with a Transparency and Integrity Hub and that would continue if the bid for single-councillor divisions was successful.

"I always think transparency is your friend. We need to be really transparent with residents on how we're spending money and making decisions," she said.

Cr Harding said it was clear to her and her fellow councillors that multi-councillor divisions were not working.

"We're known as a robust council but this is something we are unanimous on," she said.

"The red tape is enormous because we have to double-handle everything, especially resident queries.

"There is confusion from residents about who their councillor is, because the divisions are so big."

Ipswich Mayor Teresa Harding says having two councillors per division has been confusing for some. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Cr Harding said that if councillors tried to share responsibilities by, for example, each going to a different community event on the same night, it did not work out.

"People at the events will still get upset because they want both their councillors there," she said.

"[The administrator] thought it would be 'divide and conquer', and that probably works for bureaucrats but not with elected representatives.

Ipswich City Council will prepare a submission for the Change Commission, which will include the results of its community consultation.

The council's first request to return to single-councillor divisions in 2022 was rejected.

Todd Greenberg (right) says Cricket Australia does not see a reason to investigate the 2018 Sandpapergate, despite recent revelations by Usman Khawaja (left). (Getty Images: Philip Brown)

Cricket Australia chief Todd Greenberg says there will not be another investigation into the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal.

Usman Khawaja has claimed in his book, Sabr, which is released today, that the entire team knew about the ball-tampering.

In his book, Khawaja says the team started using sandpaper on the ball in the Test prior to the match in Cape Town, where Bancroft was caught on camera tampering with the ball.

Cricket Australia will not reopen an investigation into the infamous 2018 Sandpapergate controversy, according to chief executive Todd Greenberg, in the wake of Usman Khawaja's claims that the entire Australian Test team knew it was happening.

Khawaja's book, Sabr, will be released today, but previews in the past week have revealed the former Australian batter's claims the ball-tampering saga, which led to the suspensions of captain Steve Smith and openers David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

In his book, Khawaja says the team started using sandpaper on the ball in the Test prior to the match in Cape Town, where Bancroft was caught on camera tampering with the ball.

Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

Speaking on radio station SEN, Greenberg said he respected Khawaja's right to tell his side of the story, but said his claims contradict the recollections of others in that 2018 team and CA would not be launching another investigation.

“There are specific details in his book that contradict the versions that have been provided by others," Greenberg said.

“It's important to know that back at that time, players were urged to come forward, and they had the opportunity to do so over these past eight years, and that remains the case.

“We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received.

“That includes what we've seen from Usman, and our position hasn't changed on that.

“We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this again. I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that.”

CA's 2018 investigation determined only Smith, Warner and Bancroft knew of the ball-tampering ploy, suspending the trio while clearing all others of wrong doing.

Warner, who was vice-captain at the time of Sandpapergate, on Monday backed-up Khawaja's version of events and said the 2018 investigation by CA was "botched".

"Uzzie, I throw my full support behind you. I thank you for everything you've done," he said in an Instagram statement.

"It's 100 per cent accurate, what you've said.

"Now everyone knows the truth, it's out there. People wanted to know it, you've come out and said it, and now people are saying, 'Why eight years on?' talking about selling a book.

"This is Usman's story. This is what Usman believes. Uzzie wrote down every single thing from that day on. Uzzie, thank you."

Warner slammed Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident in the wake of the 2018 tour of South Africa. Khawaja was not interviewed as a part of the probe.

David Warner was suspended from all international and domestic cricket for 12 months following Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident. (AAP Image/Ben Rushton)

"Now, this whole interview process was rushed and botched," he said.

"Uzzie was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft [in the dressing room]. Uzzie was not interviewed. How that is a thorough investigation? It baffles me.

"We're not here to point fingers and we're not opening old wounds.

"It's about accountability, transparency ensuring that the truth is properly examined, and perhaps it's time people stop scrutinising the person asking for accountability, and asking those responsible for the investigation to provide it.

"There [were] a lot of statements and inaccuracies over the last eight years that were out in the media by people and there were a lot of people who stayed silent."

Warner is the first of the banned trio to speak publicly in the wake of Khawaja's comments being made public.

Khawaja has also claimed that ball-tampering was commonplace in Sheffield Shield during his career, specifically highlighting Victoria as the state that was best at the "dark arts".

https://www.abc.net.au/news/health/2026-.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Health & Wellbeing

Researchers say we do not have enough long-term data about GLP-1 medications. (Getty Images: brizmaker)

A large study suggests people with type 2 diabetes who start and then stop GLP-1 drugs may have poorer health outcomes.

But Australian experts say more information is needed to support this conclusion.

The study highlights the importance for people taking these medications to work closely with their doctor, experts say, especially if wanting to ease off the drugs.

People with type 2 diabetes who start and then stop using GLP-1 medications may face an increased risk of heart attack, stroke or death than those who keep using them, according to a new international study.

But Australian experts urge caution interpreting the findings, with the study unable to prove causation and no data collected about why people stopped using the drug.

The study, published today in The Lancet Regional Health — Europe journal, followed more than 80,000 Italians with type 2 diabetes and no established cardiovascular disease between 2004 and 2024.

People on Ozempic and other GLP-1 agonist drugs commonly report they no longer have constant, incessant thoughts about food.

Lead author Antonio Ceriello, head of diabetes research at Italian hospital IRCCS MultiMedica, said the association between stopping GLP-1 receptor agonists and poorer heart health outcomes was "not a complete surprise".

However, Professor Ceriello said the scale of the association found was significant.

About four in 100 people in the study who stopped GLP-1 treatment had a heart attack, stroke or died from any cause; compared to about two in 100 people who kept using the medication.

The risk of adverse outcomes was higher in people with obesity.

GLP-1s can help with weight regulation and blood sugar levels in people with type 2 diabetes by mimicking a hormone called glucagon-like peptide-1.

Previous studies showed people who stopped using the drugs commonly experienced weight gain, and an increase in cardiovascular risk factors such as blood pressure.

In this study, Professor Ceriello said there was only a modest increase in weight, blood pressure and blood sugar levels for those who stopped using the medication.

These modest increases were recorded in the group that later had a heart attack, stroke or died as well as the group with no adverse events.

"This suggests that the deterioration of these parameters is not sufficient to fully explain the observed increase in risk," he said.

About half a million Australians regularly use GLP-1 receptor agonists each month. (Flickr: Chemist 4 U)

Professor Ceriello theorised GLP-1 drugs could provide "direct protection" for the cardiovascular system.

But it is not clear from the study whether starting and then stopping GLP-1 medication is riskier than never using the drug in the first place.

Natalie Raffoul, head of clinical strategy at The Heart Foundation who did not contribute to the study, said while the data was "interesting", more research was needed.

"We know that stopping it comes with consequences and perhaps this study is pointing a spotlight on the fact that these negative consequences might actually be quite significant," she said.

This study did not include people who took tirzepatide (brand name Mounjaro), and only a small number of participants used semaglutide (sold under brand names Ozempic and Wegovy).

Most of the participants used liraglutide or dulaglutide.

Clara Chow, academic director of the Westmead Applied Research Centre at the University of Syndey who did not contribute to the study, said the core conclusion "might be misleading" without a deeper understanding of why participants stopped using GLP-1 drugs.

About 60 per cent of the 80,302 total participants stopped using their medication.

Research shows semaglutide — commonly sold as Ozempic or Wegovy — can improve kidney function and survival rates for people with some chronic diseases.

"That's a lot of people who are not staying on this medication, despite all the hype," Professor Chow said.

"If you've discontinued medication, is it because you feel sick taking it? Or you've got another illness? Or you've got a problem that interacts with it … there's a lot of reasons why people stop treatment."

Professor Chow said the group who stopped using the medication also had a very high rate of death by any cause, suggesting they could have been sicker than the group who continued with it.

"Discontinuation is a marker of the fact that they're sick as opposed to a cause of their sickness."

Brendon Neuen wants more information about the long-term impacts of using and stopping GLP-1 drugs. (Supplied: Brendon Neuen)

Brendon Neuen, associate professor of medicine at Royal North Shore Hospital who did not contribute to the study, agreed.

"They might have stopped for an appropriate [medical] reason, but those patients are typically sicker, and they're going to do worse," he said.

This study did not include the socio-economic status of participants, a known risk factor for cardiovascular disease, although Professor Ceriello noted the Italian health system reimbursed patients who used GLP-1s, which meant cost was unlikely to be a barrier to treatment.

Despite the study's limitations, Dr Neuen said it contained some important implications for people with type 2 diabetes who used GLP-1 drugs.

"If you do have a chronic health condition for which a GLP-1 drug is helping, it suggests that long-term treatment is important," he said.

Because the study suggested people with type 2 diabetes lost cardiovascular benefits, Dr Neuen said it was important that patients considering stopping the drugs talked to a health professional.

As there was limited information available about the potential long-term impacts and side effects of taking GLP-1s, Professor Chow said people taking them for extended periods must be monitored.

"We need more information about the long-term effects of these medications," she said.

Clara Chow says this study is interesting, but its core conclusion "might be misleading". (Supplied: University of Sydney)

And this would take time, Dr Neuen said.

"There is lots of research going on into how we can effectively use these drugs in the long term," he said.

"Can we reduce the dose? Can we reduce the frequency? What's the impact of stopping versus continuing?

"All of these [questions] continue to be teased out and this is one small piece of the puzzle."

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Beau Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, and his new boyfriend, Luke Davies in Sydney's Paddington. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Cross-examination by the Crown prosecutor is continuing in the NSW Supreme Court.

Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in February 2024. He has pleaded not guilty.

Follow our live coverage here.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Lamarre-Condon says he made the decision to end the relationship in April 2023.

"I said to Jesse, just give me some time to let the romantic feeling settle," he said today.

"Jesse was understanding of that too, and respectful."

Messages to another friend about Baird calling their relationship "very casual" shows he was agitated about it.

"Is this c**t serious," he texted.

"2-4 times a week for the last 4 months is seeing someone.

Yes, whilst we aren't in a relationship he's down playing it."

"It looks like Jesse was in a relationship with [the other man], which I now know he was," he tells the jury.

Baird had been in the Gold Coast, where the man lived, that month, the court heard.

Lamarre-Condon says he didn't tell Baird about going through his phone during the farm stay in March.

After the April face-to-face conversation, he texts Harvell a screenshot of Baird's Tinder profile.

Hatfield asks if Lamarre-Condon was also on the apps.

"I was messaging people in March, I just don't know if I was messaging ... in April," the accused tells the court.

In relation to the April phone incident, he says he did tell Baird he went through his phone.

"To be fair he was actually understanding ... he was sorry for that, sorry for his response he sent to [the man] in regards to saying we were just seeing each other time-to-time."

He says the conversation was civil.

Harvell messaged on April 15, 2023 saying Baird was "playing you both" in relation to the accused and the man in Baird's DMs.

"Did you tell Harvell you were seeing other people at the time?" Hatfield asks.

Lamarre-Condon says Baird told the other man he "wasn't sleeping with other people, which was untrue".

He sent Baird a message on April 17 saying he got a "sign" a conversation needed to be had, requesting to meet up for an "open and honest conversation".

Hatfield asks if he was going to tell him about going through his phone.

"I was thinking about not doing that, but I did end up doing that," Lamarre-Condon says.

He says he told Harvell he was considering a "little white lie" initially.

In March 2023, Lamarre-Condon agreed he would've had a dating profile up.

Hatfield says again that Baird said he wasn't ready for a relationship.

"I just believe we were moving towards something more serious and we did have a discussion about that on the 17th of April."

The screenshot was sent to three people, the court heard.

Hatfield put to the accused he breached Baird's privacy.

"I would agree with that somewhat but he did give me his phone for a purpose ... I believe now, again ... it must have been to book the escape room," Lamarre-Condon says.

"He'd given it to me with consent," and concurred Baird didn't give him permission to go through his messages.

The photograph of Baird's Instagram messages were sent to Harvell about 5pm.

Hatfield suggests he went through the phone before they went out on a date, not after.

"That wasn't an intentional lie," Lamarre-Condon says.

"You were just blatantly lying to the jury," Hatfield says.

We're now talking about Lamarre-Condon going through Baird's phone while he was in the shower on April 14, 2023.

"I remember being on his phone for that purpose [editing a reel from an escape room]," he says.

"I remember editing a video ... and then going through his messages."

He says messages from another man on Instagram popped up on the screen while he was on the device.

The accused took a photo of the exchange on his own phone.

Hatfield suggests it was a lie those were the circumstances he came to access the phone.

Lamarre-Condon says they went to dinner, then an escape room, before going back to Baird's.

Lamarre-Condon says while he was with Baird, there was no reason for the latter to leave his key out.

"There wasn't multiple times he had the opportunity to leave the key out for you, was there?" Hatfield asks.

"You've just contradicted yourself because we've seen two messages" where he's done that, Lamarre-Condon replies.

Hatfield says Lamarre-Condon claimed it was "multiple times" the key was left out.

"You're completely lying and exaggerating when you said that."

"I was telling the truth."

Baird flew to Melbourne on March 29, 2023.

On April 1, 2023, he flies to the Gold Coast, flying back to Sydney a couple of days later.

"He couldn't have been with you in the Paddington house on those dates," Hatfield says.

Lamarre-Condon says at the time Baird was moving to the Paddington house from Drummoyne.

We're looking at texts from April 4, 2023 with a friend where he "wonders whether to message him" in that period, as Hatfield says.

"I'm asking advice for what to do ... on one or two things," Lamarre-Condon tells court.

The next day, April 5, he tells the friend he needs to "put my ego aside and ... ask if needs help moving out".

"Then from there I can gage [sic] to see if the weekend is still going ahead ... I don't want to self sabotage myself," he wrote.

Hatfield has asked how often Baird left a key out for him.

"Between late March and early April before our first ... breakup, this was pretty often," Lamarre-Condon says.

"It was frequent at this point in time, we were seeing each other anywhere between three-to-five times a week."

They would stay at Baird's house in Paddington predominantly.

"I was waiting for my apartment to be settled and I was staying at my mum's house."

He says Baird's housemates were "barely home" and his room was at the front of the place, so it was easier.

Lamarre-Condon denies getting the key copied.

"I have never done that."

On April 5, 2023, Baird invites Lamarre-Condon over for dinner and offers to cook.

The accused talks to Harvell about this the next day describing the hang as "cute" and talked about spending "Easter together".

Easter that year fell on April 9, 2023.

He says he attended an AFL match Baird umpired, and went go-karting before spending the night together.

On April 13, Baird sends a message saying he left a "key in the letterbox for you".

Hatfield is asking about the reel he posted from the farm trip in March 2023.

He texted friend and colleague Nicole Harvell, saying he edited it to make it "less intimate".

"I just ended up deleting it. I didn't post it for him to see it ... but on the same hand I want to start pulling back and don't want him to think I'm still attached," he texted Harvell.

On Friday, March 24 2023 he says he was a "bit of a mess" on the Tuesday and was "seeing him tonight".

In court, he says at this time he was reflecting on his other colleague's mental health and suicide attempts.

Hatfield has gone back to the Tuesday messages (March 21, 2023).

His messages from Harvell on this day don't refer to the colleague in question, just work shifts and Baird.

"It could be two completely separate topics," he says today.

References to a "sook in my office", he says, could be about work.

The jury has left the room for a short break.

We'll be back at 11:45am AEDT.

Lamarre-Condon says when he first met Baird, around October or November, Baird had just moved to Sydney and wasn't looking for "anything serious".

He says Baird had just come out of a long-term relationship at the time.

They had a "formal conversation" on April 17, 2023 about the topic.

He says he did know Baird's phone pin code, when he was in charge of the aux cord in Baird's vehicle.

"Jesse has given me his password whilst driving on car trips together ... [to] play music in the car."

The accused says he went on at least a couple of trips in the car together and denies "surreptitiously" looking at it while Baird typed it in.

We're looking at texts from March 26, 2023.

Lamarre-Condon left clothes or "personal items" at Baird's house, and he had asked Baird to leave it in a bag by the front door when leaving for work.

"We didn't stop seeing each other or anything," he says in court, adding he didn't have a key and just wanted to "get some stuff," he says.

"It was clearly civil this wasn't a breakup of any sort.

"I had simply left my belongings the night before ... we were on good terms."

Hatfield is asking if he was triggered after going through his phone after the farm stay.

Lamarre-Condon insists he can't "recall" doing that.

He doesn't agree he went through his phone a second time in the week following the trip.

Harvell asked him at the time via text whether he should "tell him the real reason so that he doesn't think you're triggered over nothing".

Lamarre-Condon around this time also says he "received a message about you" that caused him concern on March 19, 2023.

Hatfield suggests he was "deflecting" to Baird that he went through his phone.

Lamarre-Condon says he remembers going through Baird's phone on the farm, and having a conversation in person with him about another man's messages.

"I don't remember going through Jesse's phone a few weeks after the farm stay," he says.

He texted a friend saying he posted the cryptic Instagram story because he was "triggered".

"Triggered my emotions ... either from what I had seen or heard from Jesse ... I can't accurately say," he tells court today.

He disagrees it was an "intense emotional way" or uncontrollable.

Lamarre-Condon is speaking about a time he had a conversation with Baird, after another man was messaging Baird asking to hang out.

Harvell messages him saying "Remember everything happens for a reason".

This is now around March 17, 2023.

"Is it the case at this stage ... you were upset about something you saw on his phone when you went to his phone," Hatfield asks.

I don't remember if it was seeing it directly on his phone or a conversation," the accused replies.

March 19, 2023 was a Sunday and he sent photos of his dog to Baird.

The accused disagrees the dog looked "sad" in the pics and says that's just how it looked.

Baird messages him about an "Instagram story" which he says he presumed was about him.

"I do recalls posting a meme or a quote and he was responding to that," Lamarre-Condon says.

Lamarre-Condon says he "remembers clearly" messages he saw on Baird's phone in April, but less so the ones from March 2023.

We're now seeing pics of Baird and Lamarre-Condon from the party. In it, the accused is holding a child and Baird is next to him on March 19, 2023.

He sent the photos to friends "asking which he should post".

Lamarre-Condon accepts he wasn't exclusive at this point.

"Jesse and I had no issues at my mum's birthday party," he says.

He says it was a good night and Baird got along with everyone.

He's being asked if he unfollowed "20 people" on Baird's phone.

"It was obviously an exaggeration", Lamarre-Condon replies.

The farm stay was the first or second hang after Europe, Hatfield suggests.

"I believe Jesse and I did catch up for dinner ... before the farm stay," Lamarre-Condon says.

"In relation to breaching his privacy, and yes, his trust, I did unfollow two or three people."

After this, they hung out at Lamarre-Condon's mother's 60th party, but there would have been "many times" they caught up in between.

Hatfield says the birthday was the week after the farm stay.

"Do you consider this to be a breach of his trust?" Hatfield asks, about going through Baird's phone during the farm stay.

He agrees it was wrong, but says Baird gave him his phone.

The accused says he did not delete Baird's contacts, but he did "unfollow two or three people".

He says "curiosity got the best of me". They were not exclusive at the time, but he wanted to check he wasn't messaging others romantically, he says.

A video from this  farm stay "having a good time" is being discussed.

"I wanted to put up on social media I was having a good time with Jesse," he says about posting the video to Instagram.

"It was a pretty accurate representation of how it was ... it was a good time."

Beau Lamarre-Condon holiday video with Jesse Baird

Hatfield is suggesting it wasn't an "accurate reflection of the relationship" and asks about his doubts posting it.

"I make money off a lot of the gay community who are single and buy my stuff," he says about his hesitation.

"You didn't post it because your clientele in the gay community for your swimwear line and it'd be problematic," Hatfield says.

"No that's not entirely - I did post the reel of Jesse and I ... It was part of the consideration."

A text from March 6, 2023 from Lamarre-Condon from when the Baird returned from Europe is being shown now.

Lamarre-Condon asks to "grab a chill dinner" on Wednesday or Thursday that week if he was feeling "recovered".

"It's been over a month and I want to see you xx," he texted Baird.

He can't accurately say if a farm stay trip was the first time he saw him for "six weeks" during Europe, as Hatfield puts to him.

"I believe we would have definitely caught up before the farm stay," he says.

He disagrees he was "insecure" about his relationship but says he was "questioning" aspects of it.

Harvell's evidence in court about a Harry Styles concert on her second shift with Lamarre-Condon is being put to the accused.

"He was ... very excited about their progress together," she earlier told the court.

"He said they had the same love languages ... he seemed very smitten, almost obsessive over Jesse which I thought was nice."

The accused disagrees he was "obsessed" with Baird in Feb and March 2023.

"Smitten, yes. Obsessed, no."

Hatfield is asking about a Nicole Harvell's evidence where he talked to her about Baird for "70 to 80 per cent" of the conversation on their first shift together.

She's a colleague at NSW Police.

He says he did talk about Baird but disagrees it was the bulk of the chat, adding she gave him "advice" about the situation.

A message to another friend shows him asking for "advice", and sending a message asking about his trip and wanting to make plans in March 2023.

This was sent on February 9, 2023 while Baird was still overseas.

"When you were going to talk to him you workshopped it with friends," Hatfield says

"Yes ... I sought their advice, which is very normal."

"I feel like something has shifted in the last week," he says to a friend in January 2023.

Baird had texted him saying it was "so much fun" hanging out.

He messaged a friend saying he had "no intention of messaging him today because I let go of the attachment" and then Baird messaged him.

Lamarre-Condon is talking about February 2023, and says Baird went to Europe with his brother.

"I accept ... he got back in March," he says.

"Jesse and I remained in contact the whole time he was in Europe, we FaceTimed."

He's describing anecdotes he heard from Baird on the trip, including getting sick in Amsterdam.

A message from Lamarre-Condon asking to hang out on January 19, 2023 has been shown.

Baird replies in the morning saying he's heading to Brisbane.

Hatfield asks how he felt about the delayed reply.

"At times I was a bit in my head if it was a slow response ... is it personal, is it not?" Lamarre-Condon says today.

"I've come to learn Jesse is just not good at responding.

"He did respond. He didn't fob me off."

He tells the court he was "second-guessing myself", something "normal" at a start of a relationship.

Lamarre-Condon had texted a friend the screenshot expressing relief at the reply.

He says calling each other "crazy" was banter.

"I would always joke with my friends we were 'white girl crazy'", he says today.

A congratulatory message from Baird, who also asks to grab dinner with Lamarre-Condon has been shown to the jury.

"Why did you screenshot a message like that?" Hatfield asks.

"It was because of how nice he was," he says.

"That was in relation to me launching my swimwear line."

Lamarre-Condon has asked for a "pause" as he reads "all the pages" of the transcript now before him.

"Thanks for listening to me even when I sound crazy hahaha," one of the messages read.

"I put to you you were ... fretting over him in early January, weren't you," Hatfield says.

"That's what friends do, they discuss relationships with each other ... I don't agree to that," the accused replies.

He says it was a "romantic relationship".

"We were romantically seeing each other. Was I also speaking to other people? ... Yes, I would have been."

"Is it weird/too soon to say I kinda miss you already?" Lamarre-Condon messaged Baird before December 22, 2022.

"I'm sure everyone in this room has gone through this," Lamarre-Condon says today.

"As you can see from the reply it's very mutual."

Hatfield is asking about him "fretting" over the relationship in early January 2023, referring to a message where he says "I'm calm again".

"You were getting worked up that he hadn't replied to you," Hatfield says.

"I haven't seen these," Lamarre-Condon says of the exhibit.

Hatfield is asking about texts to a friend trying to introduce Baird to his social circle.

A friend asks why he's "pushing so hard" for the meeting, adding she would "love to meet him". This is on NYE 2022.

"Is it the case you were desperate to show off to your friends?" Hatfield asks.

"I was never wanting to show Jesse off," he replies, adding he wanted to introduce him to his friends because he thought Baird was "genuine" at the time.

In January 2023, that friend asks if he was "official".

"We haven't discussed that yet ... I'm with him nearly everyday," he replies to his friend.

He's asked if he was "giddy" to stay the night at Baird's when the relationship became more romantic.

"I'm in love ... fml," he says in a text in December 2022.

"It's a generalised comment in relation to the video he sent me," he says.

"I say I love you to all my friends and people like that all the time."

He says he had a "lot of love for him [Baird]".

Another text read: "It sounds crazy, I love him."

"It's different from saying I'm in love with him," Lamarre-Condon says in court.

"It's not usual to be declaring your love to someone you've been on a couple of dates with?" Hatfield asks.

"No, I don't agree with that," the accused replies.

"You were obsessed with him from the very start," Hatfield says.

"I've said that to a lot of people," Lamarre-Condon replies.

We're looking at texts on December 19, 2022 between Lamarre-Condon and a friend.

He's sent her screenshots of his messages with Baird.

"Hopefully I'll see you for cuddles before Christmas," the text read.

"This is when we went to see Avatar ... in Moore Park," Lamarre-Condon says today.

He's referred to Baird as a text at the time as the "Channel 10 reporter guy".

Baird was a former TV presenter with the station.

"I liked Jesse for who he was as a person," Lamarre-Condon says today, saying he could be a "garbage cleaner" and he'd still like him.

In 2010, he says he got accreditation as a teenager to report on celebrities, including a meet-up with Kourtney Kardashian.

"I reached out to her team," to tee it up, he says.

"You can't just walk up to these people automatically."

Lamarre-Condon says he bought Baird a shirt for Christmas in 2022.

Hatfield is questioning again why some screenshots of messages are blurrier than others.

"When you send screenshots through emails the quality is always less quality", he says.

Lamarre-Condon says he's not an "expert on resolution."

"Have you been able to restore messages or an iCloud backup from some other source to obtain these screenshots?" Hatfield asks.

"No, I believe these are screenshots I've sent ... possibly via Instagram or social media," Lamarre-Condon replies.

"You sent them to her [his friend] at the time ... or some later point in time?"

"... I do recall sending [her] messages at the time as well. I don't want to be guessing.

We're looking at an exhibit of a screenshot of a DM between Baird and Lamarre-Condon dated in December 2022.

He says he asked a friend to "reactivate my Instagram account to screenshot them [the DMs] directly and send them to my lawyers".

"But I also remember taking screenshots at the time."

Hatfield suggests the quality of some of the screenshots are poor, and questions why the profile pictures are different

"If you're trying to insinuate any of these aren't genuine..." Lamarre-Condon says, before the judge implores him to let Hatfield finish the question.

Lamarre-Condon says some of the messages are from iMessage, and others are Instagram DMs.

He says he started going on "romantic dates" in mid-to-late December 2022.

An Instagram message on December 22, 2022 of Baird saying he wished Lamarre-Condon was meeting his family, while on a trip to Melbourne.

"I've screenshotted messages before and sent them to [a friend], and she's sent them to my lawyers," he explains.

"I've sent many friends screenshots of messages between Jesse and I.

"I believed I screenshotted them at the time as well, because I would've sent them to friends."

The accused says he met Baird in October 2022.

Bank records show both Baird and Lamarre-Condon made transactions at LGBT+ club Universal on October 21.

"We didn't start romantically dating until December," he says.

"Meeting up with someone for a sexual encounter is very different from going on a date," he says.

They would meet at his house, and in December they would meet up "often", less so the month before, he says.

"We were definitely seeing each other in December."

It has been at times tense between Lamarre-Condon and Hatfield, as the Crown prosecutor presses him on his version of events.

The accused on Tuesday was argumentative as Hatfield suggested he was lying on certain recollections and influencing a witness.

He rebutted by saying vital people hadn't been brought before the court, and claimed the jury hadn't been shown key moments in evidence.

At other points, Lamarre-Condon would tear up and become emotional as he spoke about suicide attempts and Jesse Baird's death.

Missed out on Monday's cross-examination?

Sydney reporter Phoebe Pin recapped what happened in court here:

Good morning, thanks for joining us.

We're picking back up cross-examination in the Beau Lamarre-Condon double murder trial.

The accused has been in the witness box since Thursday, and answering questions from Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC for the last day and a half.

Stay with us as we follow along live.

Topic:
Missing Person

William went missing near Cowwarr in Gippsland on Friday. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

The search is continuing for a teenager who has been missing in bushland in Gippsland since Friday.

Police are hopeful of finding the teen, who they say is strong and fit.

Police say they are "throwing absolutely everything" at the search and have no plans to scale it back.

Police say they remain optimistic about finding a teenager missing in dense bushland in Victoria's east.

William, whose surname has not been released by authorities, was camping with a friend at Walhalla East, near Cowwarr in Gippsland, when he disappeared on Friday.

The 17-year-old was dropped off with his stepbrother about 1 kilometre from their campsite and walked back to the drop-off point to collect an esky and other supplies.

William's mother Elizabeth Barkley says he has very little camping experience. (Supplied: Barkley family)

The esky was found a short way from where it had been left and a fishing tackle box, two pillows and a brown fold-out table top had been taken.

Police said they did not know whether William collected the gear or not.

William spent the weekend in cold conditions wearing nothing but shorts and work boots, after he took his shirt off in warm weather on Friday afternoon.

Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said more people would join the search today and authorities were optimistic about finding him.

"William's 17, he's fit and healthy, he's quite a tall, strong lad," Acting Inspector Benbow said.

"So we're really hanging on to hope that his health will get him through for these days until we can find him."

Acting Inspector Benbow said authorities had devoted extensive resources to the search.

"Yesterday we had two helicopters, we've had boats, we've had motorbikes, we've had horses [and] in excess of 50 people on foot," he said.

"So we are throwing absolutely everything at this and we will continue.

"We have no plans to scale it back at any time soon."

Yesterday police sought to speak with a couple who stopped to help William's stepbrother on Friday.

Police have now spoken to them.

About 80 emergency service personnel scoured bushland yesterday and will continue their search today.

Acting Inspector Benbow said community members had approached the local station wanting to help.

"Although we'd love to have their help, we've just got to be careful that we don't create more issues," he said.

"We certainly don't want anyone else lost or injured in the bush.

"But if anyone has any information, please call Triple Zero or Crime Stoppers or the Sale Police Station."

The area in which William disappeared is called Walhalla East, but it is about an hour's drive away from the historical gold mining town of Walhalla, where a 76 year-old Warrnambool man was found dead yesterday morning.
