Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has indicated the Coalition will largely preference One Nation ahead of Labor and the Greens on how-to-vote cards in Victoria's state election.

As the parties ramp up campaigning, the Big Build royal commission has begun calling its first witnesses in public hearings in Melbourne.

Follow our live coverage below:

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Labor's announcement that it will introduce Clare's Law has drawn a mixed response from one organisation that advocates for children recovering from trauma.

Australian Childhood Foundation says there is a "glaring absence of children and young people" in the government's plan.

The foundation's Conor Pall expressed concern that there's no dedicated pathway to specialist support for children experiencing violence in their homes.

"Adults will be able to ask police whether their partner has a violent past. Children living with family violence don't need a police check. They already know. What they need is somewhere to turn," he says.

"We cannot keep telling children to speak up and then have nowhere for them to go when they do."

We're taking an up-close look at every electorate in the coming state election.

Rural seat on the NSW border along the Murray River with majority of its population in Wodonga.

Liberal (13.3 per cent) — Liberal MP Bill Tilley is retiring, having held the seat since 2006.

Benambra has been held by conservative parties continuously since 1877.

It was a tight contest between the Liberals and an independent in 2022, but neither of those candidates is standing in 2026.

Benambra is a deeply conservative rural seat. After more than 40 years of Country and National Party dominance, the Liberals won the seat in 1976. Except for the Labor "Brackslide" of 2002, at which the two-party preferred margin slipped to 4 per cent, Labor has never come close to winning the seat.

In 2018, the Liberals faced their strongest challenge since first gaining Benambra. The party's primary vote tumbled by almost 15 percentage points, and among a crowded field, independent Jacqui Hawkins emerged in second place. In her second run at the seat, she cut the Liberal margin to under 1 per cent.

Benambra is entirely contained within the federal seat of Indi, and Hawkins had previously worked on the successful campaigns of former MP Cathy McGowan and her successor Helen Haines.

The retirement of Liberal MP Bill Tilley after 20 years of holding the seat would ordinarily create an opportunity for a strong challenger, but Hawkins has opted not to run for a third time. It is not clear whether another independent candidate or a One Nation candidate would be better placed to win the seat from the Liberals.

Music Victoria has welcomed the Coalition's proposed reforms to support live music venues.

As part of the announced pledges, an elected Coalition would cut red tape for venues, streamline approvals for music festivals and outdoor events, and introduce a "trusted operator" system to grant multi-year licences for consistently compliant venues.

Music Victoria chief executive Fiona Duncan says the proposed reforms are welcome, but more needs to be done to invest in Victoria's live music scene.

"Cutting red tape alone won't secure the future of Victoria's grassroots music industry. Artists and music businesses create jobs, attract audiences and drive economic activity across the state. We need to invest in the people creating the music, not just the places where it's played," Duncan said.

"Victoria generates $3.55 billion a year from music — around a third of Australia's music economy. Yet in 2026, our state government invested just 63 cents per person in contemporary music, less than NSW ($3.10), South Australia ($1.46), WA and South Australia.

"We cannot keep trading on our reputation as Australia's music capital without investing in the people who create the music."

Jess Wilson is asked about where the Coalition will preference other parties on its how to vote cards.

"The only way to change the government is a number one next to Liberal and Nationals," Wilson says.

"We have made the decision that we will be putting Labor, the Greens, the Socialists at the bottom of the ticket and all other parties above that."

But Wilson says it will be on a case-by-case and electorate-by-electorate basis, and says the party will be doing due diligence on each candidate.

National Liberal leader Angus Taylor says Jess Wilson represents a "fresh start" for Victoria.

"In 18 days' time, Victorians will get an opportunity to vote for that fresh start, and Victoria needs it," Taylor says.

Taylor says he is particularly excited by the Victorian Liberal announcement of support for live music venues.

"I am a child of the 80s. I saw that extraordinary era of 80s rock, live venues that we had that have disappeared," he says.

"And I am so pleased to see this announcement here today, because it is so in line with where we are going as a federal opposition."

Liberal party leader Jess Wilson has made a press stop at a pub on Chapel Street in South Yarra today, joined by national Liberal leader Angus Taylor along with MPs Rachel Westaway, David Southwick and Tim McCurdy.

It's part of a policy announcement from the Coalition aimed at revitalising Victorian nightlife.

The opposition is promising a six-week turnaround for liquor licences and a cut to red tape for businesses.

"Victorian venues are paying for a pint and they're getting a pot when it comes to doing business in Victoria," Southwick says.

He says one in four live music venues in Melbourne have closed since 2019.

More than 1,000 candidates have officially nominated to contest the state election

The Victorian Electoral Commission has described the November 28 poll as the "biggest and most complex state election yet".

Nominations closed at 12 noon on Monday, with 734 candidates confirmed for the lower house (Legislative Assembly) and 303 for the upper house (Legislative Council).

Electoral commissioner Sven Bluemmel says all candidates for the 88 lower house seats and eight upper house electorates are listed on the VEC website.

"Your vote is your opportunity to have your say about who you want to represent you in the 61st Parliament of Victoria. Do your own research, check your voting options and make your vote count," Mr Bluemmel says.

One Nation's Victorian leader Warren Pickering says he will consult with national leader Pauline Hanson on Victorian issues where appropriate.

Pickering faced questions this morning from 774 ABC Melbourne's Raf Epstein at Pakenham, where he is hoping to be elected to Victoria's lower house.

He says Hanson won't dictate party policy in Victoria, but he will consult her if he thinks it's necessary.

"Victoria is allowed a certain amount of autonomy to self manage. Yes, we come under the umbrella of the national party and we absolutely share the value set of the party," he says.

"We are better suited to understanding the needs of Victorians than what our federal leadership is [but] if I think there is anything that might be some sort of conflict that I need clarification on I will absolutely run it past our federal leadership."

We're taking an up-close look at every electorate in the coming state election.

Covers the Bellarine Peninsula east of Geelong, including Portarlington, Queenscliff and Barwon Heads.

Labor (8.5 per cent) — Labor MP Alison Marchant has held the seat since 2022.

The seat has been held by Labor since 2002, and is considered safely Labor.

Bellarine has been Labor-held for most of its history. Between 2002 and 2022, it was held by long-serving Labor minister Lisa Neville, who fought two tough contests during her tenure.

Alison Marchant succeeded Neville as the local member at that year’s election with only a small swing against Labor. The party is dominant across the entire district, although in 2022 the Greens boosted its primary vote in the south-western corner of the seat, recording primary votes of around 20 per cent in polling places around Ocean Grove and Barwon Heads.

Away from the campaign trail, the Big Build royal commission is hearing more evidence from Glenn Tyrrell, who worked as a health and safety rep on a level crossing removal at Sunbury in Melbourne's outer north.

Mr Tyrrell earlier told the hearing about the CFMEU serving dozens of safety notices on the Gap Road project in late May/early June 2022.

He says when the union representatives would come onto site, they'd walk in front of cranes and equipment, even sitting on barriers, which forced the work to stop.

He says one Friday afternoon, about 15 casual workers who had been hired through Zoom Recruitment were called into a lunchroom and told they had to cease working for the labour hire firm and transfer to a new company, BK Labour Hire.

He said they were also told they were now required to join the CFMEU.

"That's the first time I joined any union," Tyrrell told the hearing.

He said he had to make a bank transfer $590 to the union for half-yearly fees up-front.

He said he was not given any reason why the casual workers had to transfer to the new labour hire company.

Tyrrell told the hearing that after that, the union appointed its own health and safety officer without any election, which had previously been the process, and that his role was diminished.

Tyrrell finishes giving evidence by telling the hearing that the union stoppages put pressure on John Holland and the workers to get their work done and that more workers were brought in to get the job finished on time.

Smart glasses, sunglasses with built-in computers that can function as cameras and headphones, are an increasingly controversial topic across Victoria.

A growing number of local councils across the state have already been tightening rules around smart glasses. As the ABC's Ethan White reported last month, more than a dozen local councils are investigating or actively banning smart glasses from community facilities such as  swimming pools and childcare centres.

The Victorian government last month announced smart glasses would be banned in all Victorian schools from the start of the 2027 school year.

Now, the Carroll government is promising to expand the bans if re-elected.

Swimming pools, change rooms, community sporting venues, hospitals, aged care settings, and services supporting victim-survivors of family violence would be included in the proposed "next step" of the state's ban on the technology.

Labor says accommodations could be made for people with a disability to wear the glasses, many of whom describe the technology as "life-changing".

"There are obviously those who legitimately use these kind of tech assisted glasses and as part of the consultation and the work … we’ll be working with them on appropriate exemptions," Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny said.

Kilkenny has not ruled out making the use of smart glasses to record a criminal offence.

This morning, Labor announced it would match the opposition's commitment to introduce Clare's Law if it wins the election.

As mentioned, Clare's Law would enable people to ask police if their partner has a history of violence and abuse.

Leading expert on violence against women, Kate Fitz-Gibbon from Monash University, understands the appeal of the law but is not convinced it will be effective.

Professor Fitzgibbon says, like many pre-election policy announcements, the "devil will be in the detail" and she says there are a few challenges legislators will face.

"We know that so much intimate partner violence and offending never comes to the attention of police and certainly such a small amount of the abuse that takes place leads to a conviction," she says.

"One of the concerns that myself and others have had about a scheme like this is that it may lead to a false sense of security."

Professor Fitz-Gibbon is also concerned the system may be ineffectual if information about convictions is not shared between states.

"The concern I have is that the information may not be accurate. It has to be accompanied by fully-funded, wraparound frontline services," she says.

The royal commission into the Victorian government's Big Build projects and the conduct of the CFMEU is resuming in Melbourne.

It's the second day of the hearings into alleged corruption.

Yesterday, the hearing was told major contractor John Holland was wary of the "unprecedented access" the CFMEU had to government ministers, as well as alleged threats against subcontractors.

Today's first witness is Glenn Tyrrell. He's a crane operator and has been a health and safety rep on construction sites.

He worked on the South Morang, Mernda and Sunbury level crossing projects as well as working on parts of the Metro Rail Tunnel project.

He says there wasn't much of a union presence at the Gap Road project that we heard about yesterday until after April 2022.

He says that was when between two and four CFMEU organisers would begin turning up and presenting John Holland site management with documented safety concerns.

“They’d just come on site and literally stop the whole job," he says.

"They’d have their … paperwork and they’d stand in front of machinery and plant and just tell the operator that he must stop.”

The commission then heard that between May 25 and May 31, the CFMEU issued eight safety notices to John Holland, then another 23 between June 1 and 2.

Labor is also announcing a crackdown on offenders on dating sites and apps, proposing a 10-year-ban off apps for people convicted of violent sexual crimes.

"In a survey that was recently conducted, one-third of respondents were sexually assaulted by someone they met on a dating app in the last five years," Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny says.

"Perpetrators have no place on dating apps."

However, Kilkenny has very few details of how the scheme would work, and says it the onus would be on perpetrators to not use apps rather than actually controlling their use.

Perpetrators would be punished if caught using apps under the proposal.

"So punishing them if they're caught rather than stopping them being on the app?" one reporter asks.

"Criminal laws are about punishment, they are also about sending a strong message of deterrance," Kilkenny says.

While Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny is answering questions about Clare's Law, a heckler shouts her down.

"It's not a safe seat anymore! Don't think it is. Get back on the bus!" the heckler shouts.

When a reporter asks what she makes of it, Kilkenny declines to comment.

Fraser Rise, where the press conference is being held, is in the electorate of Sydenham and has been held by Labor since its inception.

The seat was retained by MP Natalie Hutchins in 2022 by an 8.8 per cent margin.

Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny is also at the press conference, and she is being peppered with questions about Clare's Law.

Namely, why the Labor government did not introduce the law in November 2024, when first brought to the parliament by the Coalition.

The Victorian opposition promised in July to introduce a domestic violence disclosure scheme within 100 days if it wins office.

But Kilkenny dismisses the questions, saying Labor went through proper channels to develop its policy.

"What we've seen again and again are promises made by the opposition without consulting with the sector, the sector who are experts," Kilkenny says.

Clare's Law, named after the UK scheme introduced after the murder of British woman Clare Wood, would allow Victorians to ask police if their partner has a history of violence and abuse.

The premier was back on the big red Labor campaign bus today, making a stop at a park in Fraser Rise to spruik a range of proposed law reforms around women's safety.

Labor has committed to introducing both Clare's Law and Aidan's Law if elected.

Carroll says the government will also turn its attention to smart glasses if elected.

"We're gonna make sure creeps that wear smart glasses, creeps that roam dating sites are banned and kicked off those sites," he says.

"There is no place for creeps to be on these sites or to be moving around public places, like where I am here at a sports oval, with hi-tech glasses where they can film, record and watch without people's consent."

He says the proposed legislation to curtail smart glasses use would be passed before Christmas.

With so many pledges made during the election campaign, it can be hard to keep track of what each party is promising if elected.

That's why we've put together this tracker of all the pledges from the four biggest parties.

We'll keep this updated as the campaign rolls on, so keep it handy.

One Nation's Victoria leader Warren Pickering faced a few spicy questions from 774 ABC Melbourne's Raf Epstein this morning, as well as a few from listeners.

Pickering denied mining billionaire Gina Rinehart held sway over the party, saying she had no influence in Victoria.

"Look mate, I've never met Gina myself personally. I personally think she's a great patriot of this nation," he said.

"In my five years with the party, I've never known her to have any influence with respect to policy development or any of these things."

Pickering also clarified that statements from a candidate last month who wanted to see former premiers Dan Andrews and Jacinta Allan "in jail by Christmas" were not party policy.

"It's actually a comment that was taken out of context to a certain extent," he said.

"It's not an official policy, it's not written anywhere, it's not something that we're going to actively pursue."

The final question to Pickering involved his admission of past drug use.

The One Nation Victorian leader said people should be given more leeway for their past mistakes.

"Our younger generations seem to be completely disenfranchised and, as a result of seeing no future for themselves, they are being pushed to the extremities of the left and the right," he said.

"Now we're telling them through targeted assassination of people that maybe had a bit of a tumultuous 20s that you cannot make mistakes in your 20s."

Earlier this morning, One Nation's Victorian leader Warren Pickering spoke to 774 ABC Melbourne presenter Raf Epstein at Pakenham, where Pickering is trying to win a lower house seat.

Pickering was keen to stress that his party was "more than vibes" and had a plan to reduce Victoria's debt while lowering taxes.

However, he was not prepared to give any figures on how much his party would be prepared to reduce government income from taxes.

"Cost projections in this state have been vastly inaccurate for a decade now. Very rarely has a cost projection been correct," he said.

"Victorians don't need more numbers on a spreadsheet. They need a government with the political will to take decisive action."

He did confirm that his party wanted to abolish payroll tax in the regions to encourage more businesses to relocate from Melbourne.

Pickering also said he would be happy to relinquish party leadership if he failed to get elected in Pakenham and another One Nation candidate was successful.

"I'm a team player. I've been a part of developing this party in Victoria since we were a 3 per cent party, but it's never been about me, it's about developing the value set that we believe," he said.

"We're not taking Pakenham for granted, absolutely not. It's a tight-run thing and we've got work to do."

The Greens have pledged to make major concerts and events more affordable in Victoria, promising to launch a new lottery scheme for $50 tickets.

The party has dubbed its policy the Affordable Ticket Scheme, which would mandate that major events receiving state government funding or using state government-funded venues make a portion of tickets available through a lottery.

Only open to Victorian residents, the scheme would make $50 the maximum price of event tickets.

The Greens say its lottery would include events such as the Australian Open, major international concerts and sporting events such as the NFL, with the Greens committing an initial $2 million to establish the scheme.

The party says it has modelled the scheme partially on one introduced by the mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani, during the FIFA World Cup.

Greens leader Ellen Sandell says the scheme will open up events to Victorians who might otherwise not be able to afford them.

"Melbourne prides itself on being the sporting and live music capital of Australia, but more and more Victorians are being priced out of the very events that make our city great," Sandell says.

"These events often receive enormous amounts of taxpayer funding, and many are held in venues built and maintained with public money. If organisers are benefiting from public funding, the public should get something back."

We want to know what's shaping your vote in this election and why.

Whether it's the cost of living, housing affordability, crime, regional roads, health care or jobs, let us know in our form below.

You can also ask the election questions you want answered from candidates, parties or the ABC.

All submissions will be reviewed by a journalist and we may be in touch if we need more information.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage on the Victorian state election campaign.

Labor's big red bus is on the road again, while the Coalition and One Nation are fronting the media and the Greens have a new policy announcement.

Plus, the Big Build royal commission will call its first witnesses as the first block of public hearings continue.

We'll bring you all that here in our blog today.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/n.title: Defence site in Darwin's suburbs pitched as location of potential new hospital
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/n.author: Matt Garrick
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Chansey Paech says NT Labor will deliver a new Royal Darwin Hospital if the party wins the next election. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

NT Labor has committed to building a new Royal Darwin Hospital if it wins the next territory election in 2028.

The Australian Medical Association NT (AMA NT) has welcomed the promise, saying a replacement for Darwin hospital is sorely needed.

Labor has conceded it doesn’t have a firm commitment from the Commonwealth for funding.

The Northern Territory Labor Opposition has promised to build a new Royal Darwin Hospital (RDH) if it wins government in 2028, revealing new details about how and where it could be built.

The current RDH, the NT's biggest and busiest hospital, is deteriorating and in a near perpetual state of crisis, with rolling code yellows, overcrowded wards and stretched staff.

Shadow Health Minister Chansey Paech said Labor was "committed to delivering a new Royal Darwin Hospital here, for everyone".

"We're starting the work now," he said.

Chansey Paech says NT Labor is doing the work now to prepare for a new RDH so they are ready if they are elected. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"We're working with our medical professionals, we're working with architects, we're working with Territorians to understand what a future hospital needs to look like here in Darwin.

"So that when we do come into government we don't have to wait around … we can get to the business of getting a hospital built."

While NT Labor has been alluding to this promise over recent weeks, today marks the first time the party has publicly outlined the extent of its planning.

The Northern Territory's largest hospital is "literally creaking at the seams" after Cyclone Fina, prompting NT Health to call for more federal funding.

The pledge also marks the first major election pitch from NT Labor since it lost government in a landslide to the Country Liberal Party (CLP) in 2024.

The promise has been welcomed by the Australian Medical Association NT (AMA NT).

AMA NT vice president Dayna Duncan said the current RDH "is ageing to a point where it can't be patched up anymore".

"We do need a brand new hospital from scratch," she said.

While no exact cost has been cited, health officials have previously floated that a new RDH would likely exceed $1 billion.

Dayna Duncan says RDH is in a poor state and a new hospital needs to be built. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Mr Paech said NT Labor was currently looking at two possible locations: the site of the current hospital in Tiwi or on Defence land earmarked for divestment in Berrimah.

"We believe … the Berrimah barracks presents the greatest opportunity to build a new premiere tertiary hospital for the Territory, one that is close to the airport for aerial retrieval services, it's in between Palmerston and Darwin," he said.

Berrimah Defence Establishment has been suggested by NT Labor as a site for a new RDH. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Dr Duncan said while a future hospital location was still to be negotiated, "the Berrimah site certainly has benefits".

The current eight-storey RDH opened in 1980 in the wake of Cyclone Tracy from existing plans for Canberra's identical Woden Hospital.

Mr Paech said under Labor, a new construction would likely look very different.

"We're hearing from people that it shouldn't be a multi-storey tower, that it should be something that takes in the tropical climate," Mr Paech said.

The design of Royal Darwin Hospital was modelled off the existing plans for Canberra's Woden Hospital in 1980. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

CLP government Health Minister Steve Edgington criticised NT Labor's track record on spending in government and questioned why it hadn't made the promise in its last term.

He also said the CLP was "not ruling in or ruling out" building a new RDH, but that his government had embarked on planning for new health infrastructure across the NT.

Steve Edgington says his government has not ruled out the possibility of a new Royal Darwin Hospital. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"We're looking at the needs of the future and that includes the Royal Darwin Hospital," he said.

"We're not here to make political headlines.

"We want to do the responsible thing for Territorians, and that's to do the proper planning … look at the clinical needs right across the territory so that we can plan for the future."

The Commonwealth has never publicly committed to helping fund a future RDH, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese recently watering down the prospect.

But Mr Paech said he believed they would come onboard.

"We have had a very welcoming reception with our federal colleagues to begin the conversation about the future health care needs of Territorians," he said.

Anthony Albanese has dashed hopes of federal funding for a new hospital in Darwin, while announcing $10 million to improve maternity services at RDH.

"We are … going to remain committed to this, and we're going to keep talking to the federal government about this important need for a new hospital here in the Top End."

In a statement, an Albanese government spokesperson put the onus on the NT government as the entity "responsible for the planning, funding and delivery of capital" for a new RDH.

The spokesperson said "any decision to provide funding to support progression of a new tertiary hospital would need to be contemplated" in context of current funding arrangements between the NT and the Commonwealth.

When asked if a future NT Labor government would go it alone without federal support, Mr Paech said "the Territory Labor Opposition is going to work through that" possibility.

Royal Darwin Hospital is located in Tiwi in Darwin's northern suburbs. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Independent economist Saul Eslake said building a new hospital would be "incredibly expensive for the territory government especially considering its current financial position".

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.title: Animal welfare campaigner dobbed into council for having five rescue cats
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.author: Kenji Sato
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Lisa Roberts-Daintree with her rescue cat Jesse.  (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Animal welfare campaigner Lisa Roberts-Daintree has been dobbed into council for exceeding the city's cat limit.

Redland City Council allows only two cats per household in its local by-laws.

The council has given her until November 23 to surrender the cats.

A Queensland animal welfare campaigner has been threatened with fines for owning five rescue cats.

Lisa Roberts-Daintree received a compliance notice from Redland City Council after a neighbour reported her for exceeding Redland's two cat maximum rule.

Council documents obtained by 612 ABC show there were no other concerns about welfare, hygiene or containment following an inspection of the property.

However, the council told her via letter that owning more than two cats was a violation of its by-laws.

"While I recognise that this situation has arisen from compassionate action, Council must also ensure that Local Law No. 2 (Animal Management) 2015 is applied consistently and fairly across the community," the letter said.

"The prescribed limits on the number of animals permitted on a property are in place to protect animal welfare, maintain community amenity and ensure fairness and equity for all residents."

The letter said if she did not comply by November 23, the council could issue a fine, enter her house and seize her cats.

Ms Roberts-Daintree is the spokesperson for Cats Assistance to Sterilise (CATS), a charity which desexes cats to control feral populations.

She said four of her cats had been rescued from a "traumatic" home, and they had medical and socialisation issues which made them difficult to rehome.

The Russell Island resident said it was therefore highly likely they would eventually be euthanised if they were impounded by the council.

The net prevents the cats from escaping the backyard. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

She said she had only been trying to keep the animals off the street where they would breed and kill native wildlife.

Ms Roberts-Daintree said all five cats were now desexed.

The council said she could get a special permit to keep a third cat, but no more.

Ms Roberts-Daintree said she did not know how to choose which cats would get to stay, and which two would be surrendered.

"That's not fair to the cats," Ms Roberts-Daintree said.

Juergen Holscher says the cats are like family. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Her partner, Juergen Holscher, said he had sent dozens of letters to local, state and federal politicians pleading with them for help.

The traffic controller said he had installed cat netting around the entire house and backyard to make sure the cats did not leave the property.

Mr Holscher said he felt the council was being rigid and uncompromising in enforcing the rules, even though the cats were well looked after and not harming anyone else.

He said he felt as though they were effectively being asked to kill the cats in order to protect their welfare.

"They've got no compassion, no sympathy, no critical thinking skills," Mr Holscher said.

"I'm a traffic controller and fair dinkum, I think I'm brighter than these people."

A Redland City Council spokesperson said the matter was ongoing.

"Redland City Council is unable to comment on an active investigation," the spokesperson said.

"Under Council's Subordinate Local Law No. 2 (Animal Management) 2015, residents can keep up to two cats over the age of three months without an approval, and may apply for an approval to keep three cats."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/b.title: 81-year-old sci-fi writer becomes oldest winner of $95k Booker Prize
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/b.author: Hannah Story
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Awards and Prizes

M John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize with his 13th novel, The End of Everything. (Supplied: Booker Prize Foundation/David Parry)

At 81, M John Harrison has become the oldest winner of the Booker Prize, worth 50,000 British pounds ($95,000).

The English author, known for his sci-fi and fantasy books, won the award for his dystopian novel The End of Everything, about a man and his aunt living in the south of England in the decades after a mysterious invasion has led to society's collapse.

The novel opens as scavenger Phillip Tennent finds a bundle on the beach. He takes the "artefact" — a "biological gadget" discarded by the invading iGhetti — to the home of his artist aunt Marnie, whose memory is failing.

But Marnie is immediately wary of the bundle, which, to her, seems to be growing in size as they speak.

First inspired to write The End of Everything by the 2008 global financial crisis, Harrison told the Booker Prize the book's themes and satire sprang from current affairs.

"What happens when all of our expectations and explanations of the world become an ongoing disaster, but we still have to make a life?" he said.

Accepting the award at a ceremony in London on Monday night, UK time, Harrison said the Booker was important in a "landscape of industrialised fiction".

"I really didn't expect to be up here this evening," he said. "I honestly didn't, here at the end of everything.

"You talk glibly about your life being changed but it's weird when it happens. I feel like a proper writer at last, totally lacking in confidence."

M John Harrison's book was chosen as the winner from 163 entries. (Supplied: Booker Prize Foundation)

He went on to thank his publisher Serpent's Tail and partner Casper for being patient with him, a self-described "complete lunatic".

"No-one writes a novel alone," he said. "I've had so much support across the last 40 or 50 years that at this point my input seems to be the least of it."

Asked on stage what kind of message he hopes readers take from The End of Everything, Harrison was frank.

"It's a grim world and it will keep on being grim," he said. "And it's weird; there's something distinctly weird about it.

The chair of the Booker judges, classicist Mary Beard, described The End of Everything as "the politics of now seen through the lens of the future".

"One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won't matter either," she said.

Beard said the book was unanimously chosen by the judges — among them Booker-shortlisted writer Patricia Lockwood and Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker — as the winner.

It bested the latest books from two previous Booker winners, Douglas Stuart and frontrunner Marlon James; twice-shortlisted Elizabeth Strout; and two other English authors who are also poets, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry.

Mary Beard hopes the Booker shortlist will "make you laugh, scream and change the way you see the world". (Supplied: Booker Prize Foundation/Yuki Sugiura)

While Harrison has never been shortlisted for the Booker Prize before, he was a judge in 2022, the year Shehan Karunatilaka won for his political satire The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.

In his speech he acknowledged the judges' efforts: "I know from my own experience in 2022 that judging is as tiring as it is fun. Indeed, sometimes more tiring than it is fun."

The win for Harrison, who is known for his 2006 novel Nova Swing, which won both the Arthur C Clarke and Philip K Dick awards for science fiction, demonstrates how the Booker Prize has expanded to be more inclusive of genre fiction over its 60-year history.

M John Harrison has been writing for 60 years, with his first short story published in 1966. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

Yet Harrison didn't set out to write a "typical science fiction novel" with The End of Everything.

At a Booker shortlist event in London ahead of the announcement, he explained: "Every time I was tempted to make a rationale [for the dystopian setting], I would say to myself, 'If you put an explanation here, you will be writing science fiction', and that's the last thing I wanted to do."

Still, the Booker is important recognition for Harrison, who told the BBC last month he has spent his career trying to "shift the balance" between genre and literary fiction.

"Why shouldn't a well-written [work of] SF [science fiction] be considered to be literary fiction?" he said.

The winner of one of the globe's most prestigious literary awards has been announced, but what of the other entrants? We take a look at the shortlist.

Speaking at a press conference after the ceremony, Harrison stressed he wanted to eschew the limitations of genre because it "cripples you" as a writer.

Winning the Booker "gives you permission to be what you are without a label stuck on your forehead all the time", he said.

"This book shows, and the prize now shows, it's very possible to write a book which mixes not just two genres, but three or four ... The concept of genres as pigeonholes is over.

"We will see more books like this."

Asked if he has seen more recognition for speculative fiction over the course of his career, Harrison told ABC Arts he wants to see the conversation shift away from categories like "mainstream" and "speculative fiction".

"It's language like that we need to get rid of," he said. "For me, that's not where to begin."

Beard told ABC Arts the Booker judges did not deliberately set out to acknowledge speculative fiction as "this kind of literature to be rewarded where it hasn't generally in mainstream literary prizes before".

Instead, she said: "It's a recognition of what some people would see as the blindingly obvious: you find great books in every genre."

Gaby Wood, who has been chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation since 2015, described Harrison as "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world".

She told ABC Arts: "It's interesting to think about whether [the book is] science fiction or whether [Harrison] is a thinker who has come through the world of science fiction and created something that doesn't have to be categorised."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.author: Emily Baker
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Healthcare Facilities

A Westmead doctor says acute mental health patients have been waiting almost a week at the hospital for treatment. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

A doctor says acute mental health patients have been waiting up to six days in Westmead Hospital's emergency department.

They described the situation as unprecedented, immoral and potentially dangerous.

The ABC has confirmed 12 patients with acute mental illness had been waiting for more than 48 hours as of Monday afternoon.

Acute mental health patients have been waiting up to six days in the emergency department of a major Sydney hospital in a situation described by one doctor as unprecedented, immoral and potentially dangerous.

The ABC has confirmed 12 patients with acute mental illness had been in the emergency department of Westmead Hospital in Sydney's west for more than 48 hours as of Monday afternoon.

Seven of those patients had been in the hospital for more than 100 hours, with the longest stretch being more than 148 hours or more than six days.

A Westmead doctor, who asked to remain anonymous to protect their employment, said each of the patients was experiencing psychotic illness and being held involuntarily.

If you have any information about a story, contact Emily Baker at emlybkr@protonmail.com or emlybkr.53 on Signal.

They said the patients were awaiting transfer to Cumberland Hospital, a dedicated mental health facility.

"It's unconscionable how awful it is for those people, how awful it is for patients with unrelated medical issues around them and the potential danger to the staff."

A Western Sydney Local Health District (WSLHD) spokesperson said the area was experiencing high demand for acute mental health care and apologised to people affected by extended wait times.

"Westmead Hospital's Emergency Department has a designated mental health area which allows for emergency care to be delivered by specialised mental health clinicians in a low-stimulation environment to best support mental health consumers and their needs," the spokesperson said.

"Consumers awaiting transfer to a mental health facility receive ongoing treatment in the emergency department, under the care of a psychiatrist."

Westmead is one of Sydney's largest hospitals. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

The doctor likened sleeping and receiving treatment in the emergency department to being forced to stay in an airport.

"It's constantly lit, constantly busy, constantly noisy. You can't tell me it's a therapeutic or restful environment," they said.

Rose Jackson said a new facility would make more beds available in Western Sydney. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson said extended wait times were "well below the experience I want for anyone accessing our mental health system".

"While I can't comment on individual patients, any person remaining in an emergency department while awaiting transfer continues to receive care and clinical oversight," she said.

Ms Jackson said construction of the new Westmead Centre for Mental Health was underway and would deliver a "substantial" increase in beds in the region.

Westmead had the longest emergency department wait times of any hospital in the WSLHD in figures released in September.

Just 49.1 per cent of patients received treatment on time, with an average wait time of 6.5 hours.

Mental health professionals across NSW have been raising the alarm over conditions for workers and their patients more than 12 months.

Public psychiatrists threatened to resign en masse last year over pay and conditions, with the state's Industrial Relations Commission later finding the specialist doctors deserved a pay bump.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.title: The elusive desert frogs scientists want Central Australians to find
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.author: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick

Jodi Rowley is encouraging Central Australians to record frog calls using the FrogID app. (Supplied: James Alcock)

Scientists are calling on Central Australians to record frog calls following recent storms, hoping to fill major gaps in knowledge about elusive desert species.

Residents can record frog calls using the FrogID app, including outside the official FrogID Week.

Researchers hope to uncover new locations for poorly understood desert species.

Central Australians are being asked to lend their ears to science as recent storms offer a chance to find elusive frogs.

The Australian Museum is calling on residents to record frog calls using its free FrogID app during FrogID Week, running until Sunday.

Among the most sought-after frogs are the Tanami toadlet and the desert spadefoot, which are burrowing frogs that can spend months and potentially years hidden underground.

FrogID lead scientist Jodi Rowley said the central deserts were among Australia's most difficult places to study frogs.

"Some of the most poorly known frogs in Australia are from the central deserts or from really remote places throughout Australia," she said.

Many desert frogs emerge only after rain, when conditions are suitable for breeding.

The Tanami toadlet's call was first scientifically recorded in 2024, more than 40 years after the elusive desert frog was first described. (Supplied: Harry Ehmann)

Some burrowing frogs retreat more than 1 metre underground, conserving moisture in protective cocoons made from their own skin.

"They've got two things to do. One is eat as much as possible and the other is breed while there's water," Dr Rowley said.

First described in 1981, the Tanami toadlet's call went unrecorded by scientists for 43 years.

That changed in March 2024, when more than 300 millimetres of rain fell over a weekend at Australian Wildlife Conservancy's Newhaven Wildlife Sanctuary.

Tim Henderson leads the science program at Newhaven Wildlife Sanctuary. (Supplied: Tim Henderson)

"We don't often see frogs out here because it's the desert and it doesn't rain much, but when it does, it really comes to life," he said.

The team located Tanami toadlets and recorded their calls using FrogID, giving scientists a new way to recognise the elusive species.

Dr Henderson said recording the frogs was difficult because they emerged unpredictably after heavy rain.

"It's really about being in the right place at the right time," he said.

Dr Rowley said researchers still hoped to discover more locations for the species.

The desert spadefoot is a burrowing frog known for its distinctive "whoop, whoop, whoop" call. (Supplied: Abbey Dean)

"It's one of my favorites," Dr Rowley said, imitating its call.

"Something like whoop, whoop, whoop."

Since launching in 2017, FrogID has collected about 1.5 million frog recordings, helping scientists map distributions and contributing to the scientific description of 13 new frog species.

But large parts of remote Australia remain poorly surveyed.

Dr Rowley said recordings from people travelling, camping or living in remote communities could be particularly valuable.

FrogID allows scientists to identify species such as the Howard Springs toadlet by their distinctive calls. (Supplied: Dane Trembath)

"So particularly in these remote and arid areas, your recording could be a huge scientific discovery," she said.

Long-term recordings help researchers understand changes in frog habitats, including the impacts of drought and climate change.

Dr Henderson said even recordings of common frogs could be valuable if the species had never been documented in that location.

People can record frogs using the free FrogID app, even outside the official FrogID Week.

More than 1.5 million frog recordings have been collected through FrogID since 2017, including that of the Copland's rock frog. (Supplied: Stephen Mahony)

The best opportunities are often after rain, particularly at night, although desert frogs can call during the day.

"You don't need to know what the frog species looks like. You don't need to know what it is," Dr Rowley said.

"You just submit that and then we'll get back to you."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.author: Lucy Murray
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police in Floreat in the hours after Jennifer and Gretl Petelczyc were killed by Mark Bombara. (ABC News: Ruby Littler)

A friend of Floreat murderer Mark Bombara has described him as a "control freak" who could not cope with the end of his marriage.

The lawyer representing Rowena Bombara and her daughter, Ariel, says the double murder was preceded by years of domestic violence, including coercive and financial control.

The inquest is expected to hear from the medical professionals who treated Bombara in the weeks before the murders.

WARNING: The following story contains details that may distress some readers.

Floreat murderer Mark Bombara, who shot and killed a mother and daughter in cold blood as they pleaded for their lives in their suburban Perth home, was a control freak who could not cope with the end of his marriage, an inquest has heard.

"He was used to winning," his friend Allan Maher told an inquest into the double murder-suicide yesterday.

Bombara shot both Jennifer Petelczyc and her daughter, Gretl, before turning the gun on himself on May 24, 2024.

He had gone to their house looking for his estranged wife, Rowena, who was best friends with Jennifer Petelczyc.

The double murder was preceded by years of domestic violence, including coercive and financial control, said Kathryn Kraus, the lawyer representing Rowena Bombara and her daughter, Ariel.

Ariel Bombara and her mother, Rowena, had fled the family home as Mark Bombara's behaviour became more erratic. (ABC News: Phil Hemingway)

Ms Kraus told the court Rowena and Ariel Bombara moved out of their family home and went into hiding in the weeks before the murders, fearing for their lives, and attempted to tell police Bombara was a serious and imminent threat with access to firearms.

This was acknowledged by Acting State Coroner Sarah Linton as she opened the inquest, saying family and domestic violence would be "front and centre".

She explained that while the deceased were not family members of Bombara, "the actions that were taken were in the pursuit of family members".

Mr Maher described Mark Bombara as a "control freak" and a "domineering" man, but did not believe he was violent, suggesting he was "bloody mortified" when he found out what his friend had done.

An inquest into the deaths of Jennifer and Gretl Petelczyc, who were murdered in their home by Mark Bombara, hears frantic Triple Zero calls made in the moments before they were fatally shot

It was Mr Maher's opinion that Bombara viewed himself as a "short, fat wallet" and Rowena as a "trophy wife" after his business success.

The men drove from Perth to Bombara's rural property at Boyup Brook two days before the murders, and Mr Maher said Bombara would not "shut up" about his wife leaving, and "couldn't cope with the fact he had lost the trophy".

In his rant Bombara said words to the effect of "I'll get the bitch, I'll find her" but Mr Maher said his friend seemed more frustrated rather than angry and seemed not to understand why his wife had left.

When asked by counsel if Bombara indicated a desire to hurt his estranged wife physically, Mr Maher clearly replied: "No."

"I was blissfully ignorant about the depth of what was going on," he said later in the proceedings.

Mr Maher and Bombara drove back to Perth on May 24, 2024, in separate cars, with an agreement to stop and meet up at each service station for a rest.

In Bunbury, Mr Maher entered a shop alongside Bombara, who bought cable ties and a long rain jacket, but the friend did not think anything of it and told the court those items were used all the time on the farm.

Mr Maher first believed something to be amiss when Bombara failed to stop at a Mandurah service station as agreed and went past him at "140 kilometres an hour".

He never saw Bombara again.

Bombara arrived at the Petelczyc family home at 4:14pm that day wearing the coat and he used the cable ties to restrain the women, before he killed them.

An internal investigation into the actions of WA Police officers in the weeks before Mark Bombara killed two women in the Perth suburb of Floreat finds eight officers did not perform their duty.

Mr Maher told the court, with hindsight, he believed he was used by Bombara, who had planned the murders ahead of time.

At one point on the farm, he said Bombara gave him "a couple hundred dollars" and a grocery list.

While Mr Maher was at the local IGA, he believes Bombara accessed the farm gun safe, taking the firearms he would later use to threaten Jennifer and Gretl.

The inquest will continue today and is expected to hear from the medical professionals who treated Bombara in the weeks before the murders.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.title: Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell dies aged 54
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Community and Society

Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has died at the age of 54 after an undisclosed illness, his family has confirmed.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff posted this morning: "Vale Todd Russell. Thoughts this morning are with Todd's loved ones and everyone who had the absolute pleasure of knowing him."

Last week, Russell posted to social media that, after eight and a half months in hospital, he was returning home to see out his final days surrounded by family. His family has not disclosed his illness.

Russell was one of two Tasmanian miners thrown into the world spotlight after becoming trapped by a rockfall on Anzac Day 2006.

He and co-worker Brant Webb were presumed dead after the body of a third miner, Larry Knight, was found amongst the rubble, nearly a kilometre underground.

But the pair were discovered alive, trapped in the basket of the vehicle they had been working in — a space about the size of a dinner table.

For a fortnight, Todd Russell and Brant Webb lay side-by-side trapped in a small space after a mine collapse, hoping to be rescued.

"We had how many tonnes of rock suspended above us like a jigsaw puzzle and we only needed one rock to move for it to come crushing in, killing Brant and myself," Russell told ABC podcast I Was Actually There in 2024.

Initially, Russell could only move his forearms and his head: "Everything else was completely buried," he told the ABC.

The pair survived on a single muesli bar and groundwater that seeped through the nearby rocks for the five days it took before rescuers, who had been blasting a new tunnel to reach them, made contact.

As Australia's TV news crews joined the growing scrum around the Beaconsfield mine tower in April 2006, work went on underground to save Russell and Webb.

Australia and the world were captivated, and then on May 9, the pair emerged not only to cheers, but to their lives forever changed.

Watch the moment Todd Russell and Brant Webb emerge from the mine (ABC News)

"It was just a constant barrage of media frenzy for days on end," Russell told the podcast.

"Like reporters hanging over your fence when you're trying to have a cup of tea and a bit of toast for breakfast.

"It was constant, not only for the first few days, but probably for the first 18 months.

Todd Russell (left) and Brant Webb (centre) emerge from the Beaconsfield mine shaft after two weeks underground. (Ian Waldie/Pool: AAP)

"I hated it because you went to work as a normal person, and you come out of there with your identity lost. And people felt that they knew you because they'd been watching you for 14 days."

There was a book about the mine collapse within months of the pair's rescue.

The following year, rock band The Foo Fighters released a song called 'Ballad of the Beaconsfield Miners'.

Todd Russell and Brant Webb pictured during an interview about their ordeal. (Channel Nine: Channel Nine)

A telemovie, Beaconsfield, was released to mark the sixth anniversary of the pair's rescue.

Behind all of this was a man struggling with mental ill health, exacerbated by the loss of his parents in the years after his rescue.

Todd Russell speaks to the media as he leaves the Launceston Magistrates Court on July 24, 2008, during the inquest into the mine disaster. (Dale Cumming: AAP)

He told the podcast he came home one day to find his wife and kids packed and in the car, ready to leave him.

Twenty years later, the Beaconsfield mine rescue continues to defy belief.

Russell sought professional help to deal with his experience inside the collapsed mine — and the aftermath of the event.

He told the podcast that in 2024 he had been working on rebuilding his relationships and that he had become a proud grandfather.

Todd Russell waves as he arrives at Launceston Hospital, after being rescued. (Reuters)

Russell did not venture into a mining career until he was in his late 20s.

Above ground, he was a keen footballer and hunter, and later, he became part of the Beaconsfield Fire Brigade, retiring as its chief in 2026.

But publicly, he was best known for the famous mine rescue.

Todd Russell served as a firefighter for his local region of northern Tasmania. (Facebook: Todd Russell)

In 2022, he told sports podcast The Friday Frothy he saw himself in two ways:

"There's Popeye, who's a big, tough man. But there's Tweety Bird. Behind the scenes, a lot of people don't see when I go and sit and cry.

"I put on a tough exterior when I'm out in public and stuff, and they think, 'Oh, he's going alright,' but they don't realise I'm hurt.

Todd Russell was a keen hunter. (Facebook: Todd Russell)

"Obviously I was kept here for a reason — whether it's to go and speak at safety conventions and talk to people about how life is much better than it can be with the help of professionals.

Todd Russell (centre), pictured in early November 2026. (Facebook: Michael Ferguson)

On November 3, Russell took to social media to announce that "years of pain, uncertainty, appointments, treatments, setbacks, and endless battles plus the emotional exhaustion of having to pick myself up time and time again, have left me with nothing left to give".

"The time has come, medically and physically, where there are no further options on either front for me & there is no more fight left in me.

Todd Russell in 2022. (Facebook: Todd Russell)

"I will leave hospital tomorrow after 8 and a half months for the last time to see out my days in my own home surrounded by my wife, kids, loved ones and friends.

"A massive thank you to the incredible staff at the Launceston General Hospital; their overwhelming support, care and kindness have helped to soften the daily grind of what has been an incredibly difficult journey."

Todd Russell is survived by his wife and children.

Todd Russell dies at 54, decades after mine disaster rescue (ABC News)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/w.title: Police officer wore explicit patch on uniform during teen's arrest
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/w.author: Cason Ho
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Video from another officer's camera shows Constable Lachlan Costello's explicit patch on his uniform. (Supplied)

A Geraldton police officer displayed a patch on his uniform that read "FOLD C**TS" as he arrested a teenager in 2024.

Police said Constable Lachlan Costello was actively engaged with local youth through sport, where the term was "common".

Constable Costello also turned off his body-worn camera during the arrest.

A WA Police officer displayed an obscene phrase on his uniform while arresting a teenager, body-worn camera footage obtained by the ABC has revealed.

He also allegedly offered the boy bail in exchange for information.

WARNING: This article includes material that may be offensive to some readers.

The phrase "FOLD C**TS" was emblazoned on a patch worn by Constable Lachlan Costello as he was detaining a 16-year-old on suspicion of burglary in the Midwest city of Geraldton in September 2024.

Police say the phrase is "common" and the constable is "well-regarded by local youth".

Colloquially, "folding" can refer to hitting someone with enough force to make them collapse.

"Folding" can also refer to a controversial restraint used by youth detention officers in WA, which was banned in 2022 after a Four Corners investigation.

Body-worn camera footage, obtained from police via a freedom of information request, shows Constable Costello handcuffing the teenager and sitting him in a car to question him.

About 90 seconds later, the officer turns off his camera.

The 16-year-old later pleaded guilty to possession of unlawfully obtained property. (Supplied)

Video from a different officer's body-worn camera shows Constable Costello later gesturing for his colleague to follow him around the corner to talk.

Still wearing the patch with the explicit language on his chest, Constable Costello tells the other officer: "He [the teenager] doesn't know anything."

But four seconds of the audio from the video released by WA Police has been muted.

In that missing audio, which is uncensored in a version seen by Aboriginal Legal Service WA (ALSWA) lawyers, the ABC understands Constable Costello admits offering the 16-year-old bail in exchange for information.

"I told [the teenager] if you tell us everything, we'll get you off bail. Off camera, obviously," Constable Costello says in the uncensored recording, according to the ALSWA.

The officer then appears to notice his colleague's bodycam recording, saying, "Oh your f**king …" before momentarily raising his hand to obscure the camera.

Constable Lachlan Costello covers his colleague's body-worn camera after he realises it is recording. (Supplied)

ALSWA director Peter Collins said there was "no good reason" for WA Police to censor the audio of Constable Costello's admission.

"Police should never be offering an inducement of being given bail in order to extract admissions from somebody," he said.

Peter Collins says the officer's patch is "one of the worst" things he has seen from police aside from physical violence. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

The arrested 16-year-old had $10,000 cash and cannabis in a bag and later pleaded guilty to possession of unlawfully obtained property.

WA Police said its internal affairs unit investigated Constable Costello, who was "served a managerial notice" for wearing the patch, offering bail, questioning the teenager without notifying a responsible adult and breaching body-worn camera use policy.

Mr Collins said there should be no place for such conduct in the police force.

"Who knows what that managerial intervention actually constituted? I suspect it was a slap over the wrist, and nothing more," he said.

Mr Collins said the fact Constable Costello wore the explicit patch while making an arrest, and in the presence of other colleagues, was "despicable".

"It shows a callous disregard for the responsibilities entrusted in him as a sworn police officer," he said.

The explicit label was clearly visible on Constable Lachlan Costello's chest. (Supplied)

A similar explicit phrase was written on a wrist strap worn by rugby league player Kane Evans during a 2021 game. The NRL fined him $5,000.

Police said Constable Costello was actively engaged with the young local community through sport where the term was "common".

"He remains well regarded by local youth. While this context was considered, it does not excuse the conduct," a WA Police spokesperson said.

Mr Collins said any officers who were aware of the patch were complicit in the behaviour.

"He's there with his colleagues who would have seen it, and presumably senior officers at the police station at which he works would have also seen it," Mr Collins said.

Constable Lachlan Costello and the four other officers who attended the incident in September 2024. (Supplied)

WA Police said it was an "isolated incident".

"The patch was identified by a supervisor and the matter was addressed at the time," a spokesperson said.

"It was subsequently confirmed the patch had been removed before the officer attended his next incident."

Mr Collins said while the patch was "unprecedented", officers turning off or blocking their body-worn cameras occurred frequently.

He said other officers at the scene of the September 2024 arrest also appeared to intentionally obscure their cameras.

"There's no proper basis for any of this behaviour by the police on this occasion, and it's not a one-off," Mr Collins said.

WA Police said the "deliberate obstruction or inappropriate use of body-worn cameras" was not an accepted practice.

"Where concerns regarding the use of body-worn cameras are identified, they are investigated and dealt with appropriately," a spokesperson said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.title: Leaked documents reveal confidential Woodside deal with traditional owners
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.author: Alistair Bates
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A group of traditional owners claim elders who could not read or write were pressured to sign the deal. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

Woodside's traditional owner partners of almost 30 years have publicly opposed the company's Browse expansion.

It comes amid stalled renegotiations over a confidential 1998 land access deal.

Woodside says it accepts standards have changed, but rejects claims that elders were pressured into signing.

Traditional owners say Woodside's proposed $50 billion expansion into the Browse Basin cannot go ahead while a confidential mining agreement over its most valuable asset remains "unfit for purpose".

They have broken their silence in a push to modernise the 1998 land access deal that ushered in the North West Shelf joint venture, more than 1,530 kilometres north of Perth.

The agreement for Australia's biggest oil and gas project was written more than a decade after scores of sacred Indigenous sites, some of which were thought to date back 50,000 years, had been demolished by its construction.

The agreement covers Woodside's Karratha Gas Plant, which processes 14 per cent of WA domestic gas. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

Speaking publicly for the first time, senior present and former members of Ngarluma-Yindjibarndi Foundation Limited (NYFL) decried the document's signing and claimed it pressured elders who could not read or write.

"Ngurra (country) is the main thing for our people: to have our country, not to be destroyed, not to be touched or damaged," elder and NYFL director Ricky Smith said.

The construction of the gas plant predates the agreement by more than a decade. (Supplied: Ken Mulvaney)

Woodside is seeking to shore up gas production at the facilities by tapping the Browse Basin off the Kimberley coast and pumping the resource to its Karratha Gas Plant via a 900km pipeline.

The ABC understands NYFL tabled a new agreement at a meeting with Woodside executives last November, calling for $30 million a year on the assumption currently approved gas fields will deplete within the next 10.

Woodside countered the $300 million package in May with an offer of $20 million cash for the same period, on top of the terms agreed upon in 1998.

The company would also transfer NYFL 20 homes over 10 years and $400,000 annually to manage the properties.

Ricky Smith says Woodside needs to negotiate a new agreement to ensure the community becomes stronger. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

NYFL chief executive Sean Paul Stephens said the organisation had formally asked government not to approve Woodside's bid for Browse while talks were at an impasse.

Woodside said it was "proud" of its long-standing relationship with NYFL but acknowledged the negotiations.

"The North West Shelf Project recognises that expectations and standards for agreement making with Aboriginal communities have evolved significantly since 1998 and is working with NYFL to modernise the arrangements," a spokesperson said.

The near-200-page agreement followed a native claim lodged by the Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi people for the Pilbara region's Burrup Peninsula in the early 1990s.

The two language groups are among five with cultural ties to the peninsula, a landscape scarred by colonial violence and traditionally known as Murujuga.

By NYFL's calculation, the $500,000 compensation alone equates to about $50 to $100 per cultural site affected. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

The deal, viewed by the ABC, included a lump sum of $500,000 "as compensation for deprivation of any possession of land or waters".

These funds were used to establish NYFL and released the gas joint venturers of liability for damaging the area's dense collection of Aboriginal rock art.

Ahead of UNESCO releasing its final assessment of the area's world-heritage potential, the Burrup's traditional owners tell the stories behind the landmark rock art.

NYFL estimates 1,700 engravings were moved and thousands more destroyed to build the North West Shelf's onshore processing facilities.

By its calculation, the $500,000 compensation alone equates to about $50 to $100 per cultural site affected.

The agreement also set out strict confidentiality and no-challenge clauses that former NYFL chairperson Clinton Walker says have stifled people from standing up for country.

"We were forced with gag clauses … we couldn't speak up for what we wanted," Mr Walker said.

Clinton Walker says elders did not understand the 1998 deal.   (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Another $2.5 million was put aside by the deal for the Roebourne Cultural Centre, along with "goodwill" annual donations of $1.25 million to NYFL, partly indexed to inflation.

In 2019, Woodside said it updated some conditions after NYFL declared insolvency, increasing its community investment across a complex suite of programs.

NYFL correspondence obtained by the ABC said Woodside currently provided the foundation about $1.7 million each year, unlike the value-based royalties paid by other Pilbara mining companies.

In October, Woodside posted a year-to-date operating revenue of $17 billion.

NYFL estimates 1,700 petroglyphs were removed and more demolished. (Supplied: Ken Mulvaney)

A 2023 study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development found certain streets of Karratha and Roebourne, two towns close to the gas project, were among the most disadvantaged in Australia.

Mr Stephens says traditional owners bore the greatest costs of WA's resource boom and gained little material benefit.

"It is being locked out of the engine room that people describe the Pilbara to be," he said.

"The life expectancy for First Nations men in the Pilbara is almost 30 years less than a non-Indigenous person like myself, and that tells us that the system is broken."

In 2003, the WA government brokered the Burrup and Maitland Industrial Estates Agreement (BMIEA) for the land around the Karratha Gas Plant and not covered by the NYFL deal, extinguishing native title rights to clear the way for further industrial development.

A few months later, the Federal Court ruled Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi native title did not extend to the Burrup Peninsula.

The layout of agreements on Murujuga. (ABC News)

It leaves NYFL's path to a new agreement unclear, with no legal right to the compensation provisions that have led other groups to win payouts for economic and spiritual loss.

Mr Walker, who was a teenager in 1998, said Woodside was eager to pre-empt the native title decision, and some elders did not understand what they were signing.

"They didn't really know a lot of English. They couldn't read," Mr Walker said.

A Woodside spokesperson said the agreement was fairly understood under the future act stipulations of the Native Title Act 1993, and all signatories received independent professional advice.

Several of the elders signed with the letter "X" because, NYFL says, they could not write their names. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Ahead of a Commonwealth decision to extend the North West Shelf for 40 years, NYFL wrote to successive state and federal environment ministers in the hopes of securing support for a new deal.

It never received a response.

The federal environment minister was advised pollution from Woodside's Karratha Gas Plant may be causing irreversible changes to ancient rock art, before granting the company a 40-year extension with strict conditions.

When federal Environment Minister Murray Watt approved the extension in 2025, he did so with 48 conditions aimed at protecting the surviving Murujuga rock art, which received a UNESCO World Heritage listing shortly after.

He said he weighed these heritage risks against the project's social and economic benefits, but did not mandate a modern agreement with NYFL.

Woodside is now awaiting permission to breach Australia's largest undeveloped gas reserve in the Kimberley's Browse Basin.

The project is expected to cost upwards of $50 billion to develop and, according to Deloitte modelling, generate more than $141 billion in gross domestic product over a 31-year span.

NYFL says Browse must not be approved with the 1998 agreement unresolved.

Mr Smith said it was about ensuring a legacy for the generations to come.

"Make a good agreement with each other to benefit and help our family to get strong," he said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: French officials blame Iran for refrigerator hacks, vow retaliation
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
PARIS – French officials on Monday accused Iran’s Revolutionary Guard of responsibility over cyberattacks that knocked out commercial refrigerators and freezers across France last month, saying there would be consequences for Tehran.

The hacks that struck hundreds of French supermarkets in early October were among the most disruptive cyberattacks of the Iran war that began in February, a conflict that has been marked by scattered incidents of alleged digital disruption. These have included hacks against the Los Angeles transit system in March, against U.S. water treatment plants in July and against ships bound for the United States in August.

Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment. Iran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber operations.

The French announcement was made only minutes after a report revealing that investigators privately suspected Iran of being behind the attacks. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned to France’s foreign ministry. Barrot also threatened further European Union sanctions against Iran.

The effects of the Oct. 11 hacks were dramatic. Some refrigerators had the temperature turned up so high they caught fire. In the hours following the incident, supermarket employees carted boxes full of perished meat and melted ice cream into giant trash containers. The attack’s total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, one French supermarket owner estimated.

The French hacks have since been followed, this month, by a second wave of hacking that hit more than 100 establishments across Europe and even affected refrigerators used by French blood banks, prompting employees there to have to move some of the blood to different cold storage units.

In a joint report issued by French spy and cyber agencies, officials accused Shahid Kaveh — described as a cyber offensive unit tied to the Revolutionary Guard — of being behind the hacking campaign, and named three alleged associates: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, Mahdi Lashgarian and Reza Salarvand.

The French report said the hackers worked through numerous front groups masquerading as vigilante hackers, including “CyberAveng3rs” and “Cyber Isnaad Front.”

Contact details for the men, whose photographs were included in the report, could not be immediately located. Paris prosecutors said in a separate statement that they have requested international arrest warrants aimed at the perpetrators.

The French said they were able to link Shahid Kaveh to the hacks by tying the incidents to the digital infrastructure used to sabotage the fridges, by matching the pattern of the intrusion to other hacks carried out by the unit and by recovering traces of Farsi in the attack infrastructure.

The report said that a total of 700 commercial sites had been targeted across France and that at least 15 fires had broken out as the hackers cranked up the heat. The report said that most of those affected were supermarkets but that the hacking also affected small butcher stores, a slaughterhouse and factories processing foodstuffs.

Government officials and tech companies on both sides of the Atlantic have been scrambling to get to the bottom of the hacks. Microsoft had privately tied Iran to the October cold-storage sabotage at least two weeks ago, according to three people familiar with the matter. Microsoft declined to comment.

The sabotage of European supermarket fridges was preceded by at least one similar incident in the United States.

In August, refrigerators in at least six military commissaries went out of commission. Pentagon investigators are treating the malfunctions as a suspected cyberattack and are working with French officials. A person familiar with the matter said that the Pentagon considers Iran a suspect in the August commissary hacks but that the investigation is still in progress.

How the military made its determination or whether it was also looking into other suspects could not be established. That the U.S. military considers Iran a suspect in the commissary sabotage campaign was first reported last month by news website Nextgov.

The Pentagon said on Monday that it was “aware of speculation regarding a potential cyber incident” but it could not offer further comment for security reasons.

Iranian hackers allegedly have struggled previously to pull off hacks that trigger widespread disruption. The freezer sabotage was a notable exception, and this week it sparked warnings from U.S. officials that more could be coming.

The hacks also appeared to have been easy to pull off, cybersecurity experts previously said. The firm behind many of the stricken units said that several were obsolete or were running outdated firmware, which could have made it easy for hackers to break in.

Saher Naumaan, a senior threat researcher at the cybersecurity company Proofpoint, said in an email that the cold-storage sabotage was less a measure of Iran’s cyber prowess than of “how exposed these systems are.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: French officials accuse Iran's Revolutionary Guard of responsibility over cyberattacks that knocked out commercial refrigerators and freezers across France last month. The hacks that struck hundreds of French supermarkets in early October were among the most disruptive cyberattacks of the Iran war that began in February.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Maglev construction at Nagoya Station won’t be completed until at least 2033
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
NAGOYA – The completion of the new Nagoya Station to accommodate the Chuo Shinkansen line won’t be completed until at least 2033, according to Central Japan Railway officials.

JR Central announced the estimate at a briefing session for local residents held Sunday and Monday.

The prospect comes as the completion of two sections for the Chuo Shinkansen line is expected to be delayed by up to 3½ years from the initial plan due to additional work, such as removing underground obstacles, according to the officials.

JR Central, which has given up its original target of launching maglev services between Tokyo’s Shinagawa Station and Nagoya Station in 2027, plans to announce a new opening target within this year.

The construction of the new Nagoya Station will end before the completion of work in the section in Shizuoka Prefecture, a company official told reporters Monday, stressing that the work on the new station will not affect the timing of the maglev line’s launch.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
PARIS – Artificial intelligence, superchips and cyber warfare may be reshaping modern espionage, but some secrets are still won the old-fashioned way: through sex and scandal.

The latest controversy to ripple through the tech world centers on Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and his affair with a woman accused by Washington of working for Chinese intelligence, a claim Beijing denies.

The episode has thrust the “honey trap” back into the spotlight, reviving interest in an age-old spying tactic that turns attraction and intimacy into tools for stealing state secrets and influencing those in power.
