https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Japan’s household spending slumps most since pandemic
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Yoshiaki Nohara
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Japan’s household spending unexpectedly fell by the most since 2020, highlighting persistent weakness in consumption, even as the Bank of Japan grows more confident that inflation has become entrenched enough to warrant further interest rate increases.

Outlays by households adjusted for inflation declined 6.8% in September from a year earlier, led by transport, education and entertainment, the Internal Affairs and Communications Ministry reported Tuesday. Economists had forecast a 3% drop. Spending fell 2.8% from the previous month on a seasonally adjusted basis.

The sharp decline poses a dilemma for the BOJ as it continues to reduce its support for the economy with interest rate hikes. Weak consumption points to the need to cool inflation to help households, but higher borrowing costs can also hurt households through mortgages and other loan expenses.

“Households are still vulnerable to concerns about rising prices,” said Takeshi Minami, chief economist at the Norinchukin Research Institute. “Since wages are rising, it’s hard to explain why consumer spending isn’t picking up.”

The central bank kept its benchmark rate at 1.25% last month, while saying underlying inflation has reached its 2% price target and there are risks that price gains may overshoot the goal. Now many market participants expect the BOJ to conduct its next hike on Dec. 18.

Real wages adjusted for inflation rose 2.2% in September from a year earlier, while nominal cash earnings increased 4.6%, the largest gain since 1997. The BOJ has repeatedly cited robust wage increases as a key factor to keep raising interest rates, because it indicates a virtuous economic cycle where companies can pass on higher costs to consumers and reward workers with higher profits.

Still, Tuesday’s household spending figures suggest that consumers aren’t entirely assuaged by the higher wages. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has attempted to shore up household purchasing power through subsidies and other cost-of-living measures, including a plan to cut the sales tax on food to 1% from 8% for two years starting in April.

“It’s a difficult call whether the BOJ should accelerate the pace of interest rate hikes just focusing on strong AI-related demand, while consumer spending remains weak,” said Minami.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Covert Russian network exploited French riots on social media, EU report says
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
NEW YORK/PARIS – A covert Russian network sought to exploit last month’s riots in France by using social media to blame the unrest on uncontrolled immigration and portray the government as having lost control, according to an internal EU assessment seen.

A separate internal assessment, compiled by France’s foreign ministry, found that social media accounts linked to Israel and to the U.S. MAGA movement also pushed “hostile narratives” around the riots, connecting them to radical Islamism and migration.

Taken together, the assessments offer an insight into how external actors have been trying to use France’s domestic turmoil for their own political ends, according to analysis by European disinformation specialists.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Nvidia scandal creates risks for whole AI industry, not just CEO
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Ian King
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sent the company’s stock plunging, become a focus of internal and government investigations and is now threatening to reverberate across the AI industry.

Nvidia shares slid as much as 8.8% on Monday, at one point erasing nearly $400 billion in market valuation, after Huang disclosed the romantic relationship Sunday in a memo to employees. The company’s board is assembling a committee of independent directors who will work with outside counsel to investigate reports of Huang being targeted for foreign intelligence.

With the stunning revelations, investors need to consider a range of possibilities that may affect not just Huang and Nvidia, but the entire artificial intelligence industry. Nvidia, the leading maker of AI chips, has used its financial strength to back dozens of major players, from frontier labs like OpenAI to cloud computing players including CoreWeave Inc. Huang has also been among the most forceful advocates for the benefits of AI, from Washington to Wall Street.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Russia, Ukraine envoys to talk ceasefire monitoring, territory
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Russian and Ukrainian envoys will discuss territorial issues and proposals for ceasefire monitoring in the United Arab Emirates this week, according to a senior U.S. official, as a new round of negotiations to end the war get under way.

The official, who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity Monday, said there had been daily discussions with both Russia and Ukraine in the run-up to the trilateral summit and expressed cautious optimism representatives would make progress over two days of scheduled talks in Abu Dhabi starting Tuesday.

The meeting marks a resumption of talks put on hold in February when the Trump administration’s focus shifted to the Iran war. And they represent the first round of negotiations on Ukraine since President Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of Congress in U.S. midterm elections.

Massie launched his new bid to oust Hegseth on Monday as the House of Representatives resumed work following the midterm elections. He posted his resolution outlining charges against Trump’s defense secretary on social media earlier in the day, and introducing the measure on Monday sets up a floor vote on the motion as soon as Wednesday.

The question is whether he committed impeachable acts, and the answer is yes, eight times.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ director sees the monster as a mirror
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Sebastien Raineri
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
Takashi Yamazaki had made plenty of movies before “Godzilla Minus One,” but nothing could have prepared him for what happened when the monster lumbered into North American theaters in late 2023.

“I never imagined while we were making ‘Minus One’ that it would ever play overseas,” he says. Instead, the film became an international phenomenon, winning over critics, earning more than ¥7.65 billion ($48 million) in Japan and collecting dozens of awards worldwide. Its biggest triumph came at the 96th Academy Awards, where it became the first Asian production to win the Oscar for visual effects.

Now, three years later, Yamazaki is back with “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which opened in Japan on Nov. 3 — Godzilla Day, the anniversary of the original film’s 1954 premiere. The sequel’s North American release followed just three days later, marking the closest the franchise has come to a simultaneous global debut. It has already set a new box-office record in Japan, taking in ¥910 million ($5.75 million) on its opening day.

https://www.scmp.com/opinion/hong-kong-o.title: In Hong Kong and beyond, employers need to rethink the career ladder
https://www.scmp.com/opinion/hong-kong-o.author: Ken Ip
https://www.scmp.com/opinion/hong-kong-o.text:
Gen Z employees in particular are turning down promotions, not for a lack of ambition but because they prioritise professional satisfaction

For decades, the rules of career success seemed straightforward. Work hard, impress your boss, get promoted and earn more. A bigger title was proof of progress, while turning down a promotion was often seen as a lack of ambition.

But a younger generation is beginning to question this formula. What if getting promoted makes your working life worse?

A growing trend in Western workplaces, known as “job dropping”, describes employees voluntarily stepping away from management positions, declining promotions or moving into roles with fewer responsibilities.

https://www.dw.com/en/nvidia-shareholder.title: Nvidia shareholders sue Jensen Huang over alleged spy ties
https://www.dw.com/en/nvidia-shareholder.text:
Nvidia shareholders have sued the chipmaker and its CEO, Jensen Huang, over his alleged ties to a suspected Chinese spy. The case adds to scrutiny over whether sensitive information at the AI giant was compromised.

Shareholders sued chipmaker Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Monday, accusing them of concealing his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

The proposed class action adds to investigations into whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence, raising questions about the security of sensitive information at the world's most valuable chipmaker.

The complaint, filed in federal court in San Jose, California, alleges that Nvidia and Huang misled investors about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is not related to him.

Shareholders say the defendants failed to disclose national security concerns that threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects. They are seeking unspecified damages.

The New York Times reported last month on the alleged relationship and said US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia announced an independent investigation Sunday into reports that Huang had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in an open letter, but did not identify the woman.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," he said. "I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security."

Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% Monday. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after US markets closed.

US President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating the matter, while expressing support for Huang.

Trump said he had spoken to the executive earlier that day.

"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump told reporters.

China denied conducting an intelligence operation targeting Huang.

"The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Huang co-founded Nvidia and led its transformation from a maker of gaming chips into a leading supplier of the computing technology powering artificial intelligence.

Its advanced chips have become a focus of US-China competition, with Washington restricting exports to limit Beijing's access to the technology.

Huang has pushed for looser restrictions on sales to China. The investigations have intensified scrutiny of his leadership and whether confidential company information was compromised.

https://www.dw.com/en/new-trilateral-tal.title: New trilateral talks on Ukraine war in Abu Dhabi: What to expect?
https://www.dw.com/en/new-trilateral-tal.text:
Ukrainian and Russian representatives last met in February for talks on ending the war, but the same sticking points remain. Ukraine continues to demand security guarantees, which is a non-starter for Russia.

A new round of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraineand the United States are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, months after a flurry of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year in January and February went nowhere.

When announcing the new trilateral talks last week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named security guarantees, an energy ceasefire, unblocking the Black Sea, extended prisoner exchanges, and preparations for a meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States and Russia as his key topics.

Lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a member of Ukraine's delegation, told DW he was not expecting quick progress.

"I don't think there will be a breakthrough, after there was such a long break in the negotiation process," he said. "Simply the fact that trilateral talks are being resumed can be counted as a success."

Witkoff will be joined by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, real estate developer Jared Kushner, who serves as special envoy.

The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to act as chief negotiator, along with a delegation including high-ranking Russian military and intelligence officials.

The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, along with Arakhamia, and diplomatic and military officials.

Separate formats are planned with several European representatives.

These include Günter Sautter, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's foreign and security policy adviser, Emmanuel Bonne, head of the Elysee Palace's diplomatic service and Jonathan Powell, the UK's national security advisor, and Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Björn Seibert, Chief of Staff for the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff for NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, will also attend.

It's doubtful, however, whether European representatives will be formally involved in talks on a potential peace deal.

Hanna Shelest, a security studies director at the foreign policy network Ukrainian Prism, told DW she believed they'd play "an observing role, at best."

She added that, until now, Russia had been reluctant to have European representatives at the table to uphold the impression that talks were "a matter between two superpowers" — namely, Russia and the United States — and to increase pressure on Washington.

"I doubt the Russian delegation will let the Europeans have a say," she told DW.

"Experience from the past years has taught us that as soon as Medinsky heads negotiations, the point becomes demonstrating to the US that Russia is willing to talk, but in reality, they won't reach an agreement," she explained. "Instead, there will be a long sermon about history and all sorts of other things."

However, she said Moscow sending high-ranking intelligence officers as part of the delegation was a "fairly positive aspect" of Russia's intentions.

She believed that additional negotiations were possible at this level.

This could include over prisoner exchanges or humanitarian pauses in villages near Oleshky, a town in the Russian occupied Kherson region in Ukraine's south, where US First Lady Melania Trump was credited with arranging a temporary truce in late October that secured humanitarian aid and allowed civilians to evacuate.

But despite these "positive signals," Shelest cautioned against hoping for concrete results, and suspected Russia was using the talks to stall.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Late last week, Trump spoke of a "big beautiful agreement," after speaking with Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, "that might involve all of Europe."

This new security architecture, Kushner later clarified on social media, would be centered around "permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability."

These points "don't contain anything the Russians haven't been talking about since 2009," Shelest said.

Ivan Us, chief consultant and economic diplomacy expert at Ukraine's National Institute for Strategic Studies, pointed out that negotiations with people who are not decisions-makers could be simply for show.

But he agreed with other expert observers that negotiators in Abu Dhabi might try to use the temporary truce brokered for Oleshky as a model for other limited humanitarian ceasefires in the region.

But while Us said he saw cause for optimism, he also cautioned that Russia had continued attacks in Ukraine during the Oleshky truce, and had used the pause to fortify its positions around the town.

This article originally appeared in Ukrainian.

The talks will focus on security guarantees, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace. The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to act as chief negotiator.

https://www.dw.com/en/skydance-replaces-.title: Skydance replaces James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios chiefs following Warner Bros. takeover
https://www.dw.com/en/skydance-replaces-.text:
In another major shake-up for the DC Studios, Skydance is replacing Hollywood director James Gunn and producer Peter Safran with a former Marvel executive.

James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios after four years, Skydance Motion Picture Group announced on Monday.

Their departure marks another major shake-up for the superhero franchise following Skydance's takeover of Warner Bros, just a year after Gunn's "Superman" reached cinemas.

Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison has chosen Jeremy Latchman, a former Marvel Studios executive, to lead DC Studios. He is set to become president and chief creative officer of DC Studios on December 1.

Latchman will oversee the next phase of DC's film and television business, which includes characters such as Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman.

He was involved in major Marvel productions including "Iron Man" and "The Avengers," and previously worked with Gunn and Safran on Marvel's "Guardians of the Galaxy" movie.

Gunn and Safran took charge of DC Studios in 2022, tasked with rebuilding the franchise and creating a more unified cinematic universe.

Their first film, "Superman," earned nearly $619 million (€553 million) worldwide in 2025.

But their second release, "Supergirl," flopped in June 2026, taking around $126 million worldwide against a reported production budget of $170 million. The horror-inspired "Clayface" followed in October.

Overall, DC has struggled to match immense profits and cultural impact made by Marvel in the early years of its own cinematic universe.

"James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we're incredibly proud of," Ellison said in a statement.

"We're grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand."

Gunn is currently completing "Man of Tomorrow," a sequel to "Superman." Other DC projects in development include "The Batman: Part II" and the television series "The People v. Gorilla Grodd."

Although Gunn and Safran will no longer oversee DC Studios' long-term plans, several projects developed under their leadership remain in production.

Gunn's "Superman" sparked a political controversy in 2025 after the director described the superhero as an immigrant and emphasized themes of human kindness.

Conservative commentators accused the film of being "woke."

Skydance CEO Ellison has cultivated close ties with US President Donald Trump. Ellison has acknowledged having a good relationship with the administration but denied politicizing the company.

There is no evidence that the controversy surrounding "Superman" played a role in Gunn and Safran's replacement.
https://www.dw.com/en/skydance-replaces-.summary: James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios. Skydance Motion Picture Group has taken over Warner Bros. The two will no longer oversee DC Studios' long-term plans. The departure marks another major shake-up for the superhero franchise.

https://www.dw.com/en/us-pentagon-chief-.title: US Pentagon chief Hegseth faces impeachment push over Iran war
https://www.dw.com/en/us-pentagon-chief-.text:
Trump critic Thomas Massie is calling for a vote to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, accusing Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval.

Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, introduced eight articles of impeachment against US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday as pressure builds on the Trump administration over the Iran war.

The resolution proposed by the Kentucky congressman accuses Hegseth of conducting the war illegally without congressional authorization. Massie also claims Hegseth has abused his powers as the head of the Pentagon.

Massie is using a special procedure that could see the US House of Representatives vote on the resolution within two days, with the legislative chamber still dominated by Republicans.

Trump told reporters at the White House that Hegseth had done a "good job" and had "won" wars in Venezuela and Iran.

"I'll stand by him... He won two wars. He was in charge," Trump said.

Earlier on Monday, Hegseth sought to downplay rumors about the push against him.

"My team, we’re not worried about the noise," he told reporters.

Hegseth said he would hold a press conference Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — and defended the war as necessary, even if unpopular.

Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries backed the effort Sunday.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," he told ABC News. "Pete Hegseth has got to go."

Some Republicans have signaled they might support the charges. Arkansas congressman French Hill said he wanted to hear the debate before deciding.

The push follows Democrats' victories in both chambers of Congress in last week's midterm elections amid anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices. Republicans retain control until January 3.

Impeachment requires a simple majority in the House and amounts to bringing formal charges. Removal would require a Senate trial and conviction by two-thirds of senators present.

Even with their enlarged majority next year, Democrats would need substantial Republican backing to reach that threshold.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cry8.title: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cry8.text:
Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.

In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".

The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.

Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.

The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.

On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".

Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.

"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.

The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".

The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".

Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.

Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.

The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Jonathan Barrett Business editor
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Australian carrier announces agreement with Accenture amid ‘unprecedented’ technological disruption, CEO Vanessa Hudson says

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Qantas is preparing to cut 850 local jobs and outsource work offshore under an AI-driven overhaul, marking a growing wave of disruption to the Australian workforce.

The changes represent the third major corporate layoff plan announced in Australia in three weeks, after restructuring moves flagged by the design company Canva and National Australia Bank.

Qantas said on Tuesday it had signed a multi-year agreement with the professional services firm Accenture to “modernise its back-end systems, processes and data, as it steps up investment in technology and AI”.

Some of the services will be transferred to Accenture’s large India-based team.

The Qantas chief executive, Vanessa Hudson, said the airline would consult with affected staff and unions before final decisions were made, with the first changes to take effect by midway through next year.

“The scale and speed of change in this space is unprecedented and unlike anything businesses have seen in generations,” Hudson said.

“We know this will be difficult news for some of our people and this decision is not a reflection of their contribution or commitment.”

The initial cuts will target finance, procurement, human resources and marketing staff. Qantas has about 32,000 employees, according to its most recent annual report.

The changes have drawn a strong response from unions that have previously battled Qantas over controversial outsourcing decisions.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

The Australian Services Union said Qantas needed to explain itself after earlier promising it had no plans to move any jobs offshore.

“AI is having a huge impact on workers across the country, but the cost of technology change should not be borne by the workers who have kept the airline running for years,” assistant national secretary Scott Cowen said.

“Sending more jobs overseas is not in the spirit of Australia.”

The restructuring comes at a difficult time for Australian workers, with living costs surging and the unemployment rate reaching its highest level in nearly five years.

A subdued economy, made worse by elevated oil prices stemming from the Iran conflict, is also prompting companies to cut costs.

Across just three companies – NAB with 2,500 roles, Canva with 1,200, and now Qantas with 850 – about 4,550 corporate jobs have been targeted for cuts, relocations or restructuring in the past month.

While Qantas has been grappling with rising jet fuel prices, the costs have been partially offset by ticket sales to new customers who switched to the airline after cancelling flights at those with Middle East stopovers.

Qantas said in a market update late last week that while customer demand was proving resilient, it would continue to adjust fares and capacity in response to fuel costs.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Police investigate as nearly 30 Santa Barbara half-marathon runners fall ill with ‘unusual symptoms’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Abené Clayton
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Runners seek medical treatment as 13-mile race held amid unusually high November temperatures

Police in southern California are investigating the circumstances that led to the hospitalization of nearly 30 runners who participated in the Santa Barbara Half on Sunday.

Santa Barbara police said in a statement to the Associated Press that they had opened an investigation after receiving reports from Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital about multiple half-marathon participants seeking medical treatment for “unusual symptoms”.

Cottage Health said in a statement it had a “larger than expected number of emergency visits … a number of them with similar symptoms of undetermined cause”.

Race organizers say they believe any illness is attributable to heat or dehydration. The high on the day of the race was 88F (31.1C), an unusually high temperature for this time of year.

Neither the hospital nor police have detailed the symptoms beyond calling them unusual. Cottage Health said on Monday that 27 participants came to emergency rooms in Santa Barbara and Goleta, a small city about 10 miles west.

More than 4,640 people competed in the half-marathon, which spanned about 13 miles, according to the Santa Barbara Half Marathon website.

Of those who were either taken to the hospital or arrived there on their own, 24 patients had been treated and discharged as of Monday morning. The three others were in stable condition, the company told the Associated Press.

Event director David Monico said organizers transported 15 people from the medical tent to local hospitals. He said the event’s medical team treated numerous runners for dehydration and overheating both on the course and at the finish line.

The half-marathon’s event director, David Monico told the Guardian that they have “no additional information to suggest that the issues some of the participants experienced were caused by anything other than endurance event exertion-related symptoms”.

The high on the day of the race was 88F (31.1C), an unusually high temperature for this time of year.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Republican Thomas Massie moves to force vote to impeach Pete Hegseth
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: George Chidi
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US representative accuses defense secretary of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers

US politics live – latest updates

A Republican lawmaker has moved to force a vote to impeach Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, setting the stage for a showdown over one of the most divisive figures inside Donald Trump’s administration.

Thomas Massie, of Kentucky, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers.

Massie, an outgoing Republican congressman from Kentucky and vocal critic of the president, argued from the well of the House of Representatives that Hegseth had committed “high crimes and misdemeanors” and “has executed unlawful orders” in office.

Massie is expected to have some Republican support for a vote on articles of impeachment. Under House rules, the vote would have to occur no later than Wednesday.

Massie first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on 15 September, but House speaker Mike Johnson called US Congress into recess before it could be heard.

Republicans retain control of the House until new members are seated in January, but House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York – widely expected to ascend to speaker – has said he is a “hard yes” on impeaching Hegseth. “Hegseth has got to go,” Jeffries told ABC News on Sunday.

Hegseth spent the morning on Monday at the Naval War college, announcing an array of changes to military education that he said would enable US military officers “to wage war with such devastating speed, precision and lethality that no adversary dares test American result that’s deterrence – and if they do that, they are completely and utterly destroyed: that we achieve victory”.

But it is the failure to deliver victory that has placed a target on Hegseth’s back.

Trump, vice-president JD Vance and other Republican leaders quickly attributed last week’s historic US midterm election losses by Republicans to the Iran war and its pocketbook effects on otherwise-conservative voters.

Hegseth fired back at his critics in a short video released on Thursday, describing the threat of his impeachment as “all about the politics of personal destruction”, insisting that it “won’t work with me”.

Watchdogs Common Cause and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington argued that the video is a violation of the Hatch Act, which bars the use of government funds for partisan political purposes.

Massie’s impeachment resolution holds that Hegseth has subverted the power of Congress to declare war with unauthorized attacks on Iran and Yemen; systemically violated laws meant to minimize civilian casualties with the killing of more than 100 children at a school in Iran; and engaged in extrajudicial killings when ordering suspected drug boats in the Caribbean to be sunk and their crews left without rescue.

The resolution also argues that Hegseth’s investigation and threatened prosecution of Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat, and others for calling for troops to disobey illegal orders was an unconstitutional violation of the first amendment, and alleges that the kidnapping of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela was illegal and unconstitutional.

Massie is expected to have some Republican support for a vote on impeachment. House speaker Mike Johnson called US Congress into recess before it could be heard.

Caroline Harvey scores three as unbeaten USA cruise

Hilary Knight extends worlds record to 70 goals

Canada thrash hosts Denmark 10-0 to stay perfect

Caroline Harvey scored a hat trick as defending champions the United States routed Austria 11-1 at the women’s ice hockey world championship on Monday.

Canada followed suit by thrashing hosts Denmark 10-0 to maintain their own perfect record.

Austria’s late goal was the first conceded in three games by the US, who have scored 23 goals so far.

Tessa Janecke scored twice and added an assist, captain Hilary Knight netted twice, Joy Dunne had a goal and three assists, and Rory Guilday, Lacey Eden and Megan Keller each contributed a goal and an assist.

Harvey scored two of the opening period’s four goals and completed her hat trick in the third after registering five assists in her previous two games. She added another assist on Monday.

Knight was fed in front of goal by Cayla Barnes to increase the lead to 2-0, and her second made it 9-0, extending her record tally at the worlds to 70 goals in 90 games.

The US replaced goaltender Aerin Frankel with Gwyneth Philips 10:45 into the second period, with Frankel having faced just two shots and the Americans leading 6-0.

Annika Fazokas scored the consolation goal for Austria, who were facing the US for the first time in their debut appearance in the top division.

The Americans have won 10 of the past 14 world championships and arrived in Denmark as reigning world and Olympic champions, having claimed the 2025 title in the Czech Republic and gold at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, beating Canada in overtime in both finals.

They face the Czech Republic in their final preliminary-round game on Wednesday.

For Canada, Emma Maltais scored twice, Laura Stacey had a goal and two assists, Sarah Fillier, Kendall Cooper and Jessie Eldridge each contributed a goal and an assist, while Renata Fast, Rosalie Tremblay, Kristin O’Neill and Sara Manness also scored.

Canada goaltender Kayle Osborne stopped six shots for the shutout.

Fast and teenager Tremblay set the pace when they fired Canada ahead with goals 16 seconds apart in the opening period.

Denmark replaced goaltender Caroline Bjergstad with Aya Petersen midway through the second period, with the score at 6-0 after the Canadians had bombarded Bjergstad with 41 shots.

Canada, who have also conceded just one goal in three games, face Finland on Wednesday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Cameroon sets date for twice-delayed legislative and local elections
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Cameroon’s President Paul Biya has announced that legislative and local elections will be held in the country on February 7 next year.

Biya, who is 93, made the announcement in a decree read on public radio on Monday.

The decree comes at a tense moment for Cameroon, with authorities cracking down on the opposition, roughly a year after an election that handed Biya another term.

Biya, who has ruled Cameroon since 1982, is the world’s oldest head of state.

His re-election in October last year set off widespread protests that the authorities met with a violent crackdown.

Lawyers cited by Human Rights Watch said security forces detained up to 2,000 people, and some of those detained remain in custody, according to the AFP news agency.

Biya’s government has already postponed Cameroon’s legislative and local elections twice, forcing the extension of lawmakers’ terms to December 20 and those of municipal councillors to February 28, 2027.

The country is also awaiting a government reshuffle announced nearly a year ago and the appointment of a vice president. A constitutional reform reintroduced the post in April, and its holder would be expected to succeed Biya in the event of his death.

Questions about the president’s health have continued to swirl, with his frequent stays abroad fuelling debate over his ability to govern. Media debate about the president’s health, however, has been banned since 2024, when rumours circulated about his death.

In late August, Biya returned to Yaounde after more than two months in Geneva, drawing sharp criticism from the opposition.

Last month, the authorities suspended the Cameroon National Salvation Front (FSNC), the party of defeated opposition presidential candidate Issa Tchiroma Bakary.

Bakary went into exile in the Gambia after declaring himself the election winner and calling on supporters to defend his “victory”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Poll finds Americans less likely to back pro-war candidates by 3-1 margin
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Brian Osgood
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
A YouGov poll completed on the eve of the 2026 midterm elections has found that Americans were far less likely to back candidates who supported the US-Israel war on Iran.

The poll, released on Monday, found that 44 percent of people said they were less likely to support candidates who backed the war, while just 13 percent said they were more likely.

That means a candidate’s support for the war was more than 3 times as likely to put people off as to win them over.

Another 26 percent, meanwhile, indicated the Iran war would not make much of a difference in their vote.

The economics of the war also factored into people’s choices. Some 56 percent of those surveyed said that the US should prioritise avoiding higher prices domestically over achieving US President Donald Trump’s military goals in Iran.

Meanwhile, 22 percent said the opposite: that the Trump administration should prioritise the war over higher costs.

The poll also asked who should decide when the war ends. A majority, 53 percent, said Congress should have the final say, while 29 percent said that the president should decide.

The US and Israel jointly launched the war against Iran on February 28. But Trump’s decision to bypass congressional authorisation for the war has raised constitutional concerns in the US.

Jonathan Guyer, the programme director at the Institute for Global Affairs at Eurasia Group, a risk consultancy firm, told Al Jazeera that the poll – which was conducted on his organisation’s behalf – indicated Americans were looking to Congress to be more assertive.

“The story of the [economic] tradeoff is really important, and then there’s this other story of where Congress has been: Why haven’t lawmakers, not just over the last year but over the last decade, played a bigger role as a backstop on reckless wars launched by presidents?” said Guyer.

“And I think these numbers show the public really wants Congress to play a bigger role and expects their lawmakers to hold power to account.”

The survey is the latest to underscore the unpopularity of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has killed thousands of people in Iran and contributed to surging prices, a top issue in the November 3 midterm elections.

Trump’s Republican Party suffered one of the most significant electoral setbacks in modern US history, with Democrats reclaiming both chambers of Congress with strong majorities.

Democrats also flipped key offices in states like Texas, once seen as a conservative stronghold.

Those results have advanced a debate over the war that is playing out in both parties, often pitting more hawkish establishment figures against newcomers opposed to foreign intervention and support for Israel.

In the wake of the “blue wave”, analysts have argued that Democratic voters may expect the party’s leadership to take firmer steps to rein in the president and bring the fighting with Iran to an end.

On Monday, Trump himself said “Iran militarily is effectively over”, though he declined to rule out any further military action. A US naval and land blockade around Iran also remains in effect.

Guyer said he anticipates that foreign policy and, in particular, US support for Israel is likely to emerge as a key dividing line for candidates in future elections, particularly the upcoming 2028 presidential election.

“I think it does create a lane for people like Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, for the wing of the [Democratic] party represented by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who have a very strong position on this war and on the role of the US in the world that traditional Democrats have been largely silent on,” said Guyer.

A similar debate is also taking place on the political right.

Following the midterms, US Vice President JD Vance shared a lengthy social media post blaming his party’s implosion on the war.

Figures such as Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene have also criticised the war as a betrayal of Trump’s promise to end conflicts around the world.

While the YouGov poll found that Republicans were the only group more likely to vote for a candidate if they supported the president’s war, Guyer says that support has been “softening”.

“A third of Republicans say that backing the war made a candidate appealing, so it’s kind of small,” he said. “And 40 percent shrugged and say it made no difference.”

Launching a major tech IPO would seem risky right now, shortly after one of Nasdaq’s biggest sell-offs and amid revelations that a CEO central to the AI boom had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. But that isn’t deterring Anthropic, which is moving ahead with its listing plans, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Anthropic plans to set a valuation range this week and begin trading on Thursday or Friday of next week, the Journal reported.

Investors will look to Anthropic’s valuation to gauge the strength of the AI boom. Some institutional investors are now pushing for a valuation below the $1.5 trillion target discussed as recently as last week, a figure that was itself considerably below the $2 trillion floated a few months ago, the report said.

OpenAI, Anthropic’s main rival, was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after the ChatGPT maker raised $11 billion in fresh capital, short of the $20 billion it had initially sought.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

The research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms."

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman says. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body."

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a company co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce important interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

The scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman says. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection."

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he says.

The results suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes?

Scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience.

Dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal.

The new research, published November 4 in Nature, examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed.

"We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

The findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better."

How the Gut Sends Reward Signals to the Brain

Scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention.

According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness.

When food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes.

To investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains.

The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food.

The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA.

The amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear.

"We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he said.

Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences

Finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors.

They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories.

The team then conducted the opposite experiment.

After mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward.

In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate.

Together, the experiments showed that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects.

A Surprising Discovery in the Left Side of the Brain

The researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern.

Dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories.

Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA.

A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar.

They observed increased activity in the same brain region.

One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres.

In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right.

That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion.

Why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference.

Could This Discovery Help Scientists Change Food Cravings?

Identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing?

One area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior.

Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the new study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified.

Still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors.

For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications.

The broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target.

By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry.

"By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight said.

The discovery offers a new perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
After more than 40 years of searching, physicists at CERN have reached a major milestone in their hunt for one of the rarest known particle decays. Researchers working with the LHCb experiment have detected evidence of a process expected to occur only once in approximately 10 billion beauty particle decays.

The finding, announced during a seminar at CERN, marks the first time a single experiment has produced sufficient evidence for this extraordinarily rare event. Beyond its rarity, the decay is particularly valuable because it could help scientists investigate particles that are too massive to be created directly in the Large Hadron Collider.

At the center of the discovery is a particle called Bd, which contains a beauty quark and a down antiquark. Scientists found evidence that this particle can decay into a pair of muons (μ+μ-). Muons are similar to electrons but have greater mass. The results agree with predictions from the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions, and help narrow the possibilities for new particles beyond it.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics

One reason physicists are so interested in these unusual decays is that quantum effects allow other particles to influence how they occur. Even particles too heavy to be produced in the Large Hadron Collider can potentially leave subtle traces in the rates of these processes.

By measuring extremely rare decays with high precision, researchers can look for differences between experimental results and theoretical predictions. Such discrepancies could provide indirect evidence of previously unknown particles. Generally, the rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to these hidden influences.

The decay known as Bd → μ+μ-belongs to a special category that physicists have long considered 'golden channels' for investigating physics beyond the Standard Model. During this process, a beauty quark and an antiquark with the opposite electric charge annihilate each other. Their energy is transformed into a muon and its antiparticle.

Scientists have previously observed a related process involving a different beauty particle, called Bs. In 2015, a joint analysis by the LHCb and CMS collaborations reported the first confirmed observation of Bs → μ+μ-, along with initial evidence for the much rarer Bd decay.

However, subsequent analyses incorporating data collected through 2018 could not confirm the earlier evidence for Bd → μ+μ-. The difference in rarity is substantial. The Bs decay occurs approximately three times per billion beauty particle decays, while the Bd process is predicted to happen about 30 times less frequently.

Upgraded CERN Detector Makes the Breakthrough Possible

A significant improvement to the LHCb experiment helped researchers overcome the enormous difficulty of detecting such a rare event.

Following a major upgrade, the experiment began collecting data in 2024 at five times the rate achieved between 2010 and 2018. The upgraded detector also became better at identifying different kinds of particles, giving researchers a clearer picture of the activity produced during collisions.

The team combined these improvements with machine learning techniques to distinguish the exceptionally rare signals from the vast number of other particle processes. Without these advances, the events scientists wanted to study would have been overwhelmed by the background.

"Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than forty years," said Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team of 19 scientists. "Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background."

Four Decades of Searching Finally Produce Strong Evidence

In particle physics, scientists use a statistical measure called standard deviations to evaluate how likely an apparent signal is to result from random fluctuations rather than a genuine physical process.

A result must reach three standard deviations to qualify as evidence of a new phenomenon. At that level, the probability of random fluctuations producing a signal at least as statistically extreme is approximately 0.3%.

Using data collected during 2024 and 2025, the LHCb researchers identified evidence of Bd → μ+μ- at a significance of 3.0 standard deviations. When they combined those measurements with earlier data gathered between 2011 and 2018, the statistical significance increased to 3.2 standard deviations, exceeding the widely accepted threshold for evidence.

The same investigation also produced the most precise measurements ever obtained for the related Bs → μ+μ-decay, providing additional information about these exceptionally uncommon processes.

Although the new findings represent a major achievement, physicists have not yet reached the threshold required to declare a confirmed observation. That milestone requires a significance of five standard deviations.

If future measurements achieve that level of certainty, Bd → μ+μ-would become the rarest beauty particle decay ever observed.

Future Large Hadron Collider Upgrades Could Uncover Hidden Particles

Researchers expect upcoming improvements to the Large Hadron Collider to make these measurements even more powerful.

The High Luminosity LHC, also known as the HiLumi LHC, is scheduled to begin operating in 2030. Another major upgrade to the LHCb experiment is planned for the middle of the following decade. Together, these developments could eventually increase the experiment's data collection rate by another factor of ten.

Collecting much larger datasets would allow physicists to detect more of these extremely rare decays and measure their properties with greater precision. That increased sensitivity could make it possible to identify subtle effects associated with particles that remain beyond the direct reach of existing accelerators.

"Seeing evidence of this rare decay is incredibly exciting, opening up new possibilities to probe beyond the direct reach of the LHC," explained Harry Cliff, LHCb's Rare Decays Convener and Analysis Co-lead.

"The future LHCb upgrade will allow us to observe many more of these decays, providing even greater sensitivity to undiscovered particles."

For physicists who have pursued this elusive signal for more than four decades, the new evidence represents a long-awaited advance. It also offers a promising way to investigate whether the known laws of particle physics are part of a much larger picture.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Amnesty urges El Salvador to disclose terms of Haiti troop deployment
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
Amnesty International on Monday urged El Salvador and Haiti to release the agreement governing the mass deployment of Salvadoran troops into the gang-plagued Caribbean nation, and for both countries to ensure that rights are respected.

Some 2,000 troops have been sent by El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele to Haiti since the mid-October disappearance of four Salvadoran personnel.

The vast majority of the Salvadoran soldiers are not participating in the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), raising concerns about their rules of engagement.

"Both governments must make public the agreement governing the deployment and explain how they oversee the deployed forces, what rules govern the use of force, to whom they are accountable, and how people can report possible violations without fear of reprisals," Amnesty's Americas Director Ana Piquer said Monday.

Bukele initially stated the deployment aimed at bringing home the missing personnel.

However, he has subsequently hinted at a broader goal of eliminating Haiti's powerful gangs, as he did in his own country with a campaign that has raised allegations of rights abuses.

Piquer urged Bukele and Haiti's prime minister, Alix Didier Fils-Aime, to "ensure that all operations conducted by Salvadoran forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law."

She also called on both countries to establish "prompt, independent and impartial investigations into all allegations of human rights violations."

"The response to gang violence must not replicate the abuses and impunity that have characterized previous interventions in Haiti," she added.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.author: Arj Ganesan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC North and West SA

Topic:
Law, Crime and Justice

A woman has faced court after allegedly committing serious domestic violence offences against her child.

Among the charges is an allegation of choking, which can attract a maximum sentence of seven years.

The woman has been remanded in custody and will return to court later this month.

A Coober Pedy woman who allegedly choked and assaulted her child has faced court.

The woman was arrested on Saturday after members of the public who witnessed the alleged incident called the police.

The child was located a short time later safe and in the care of relatives, and received medical treatment for minor injuries.

Following her arrest, the woman was denied police bail and did not apply for it yesterday after appearing in the Coober Pedy Magistrates Court.

Coober Pedy police officer Sergeant David Finlayson thanked the members of the public who alerted police and assisted investigators.

"The quick actions of witnesses who contacted police and provided information were instrumental in ensuring a prompt response and progressing the investigation," he said.

The woman has been remanded in custody and will return to court later this month.

Police are reminding anyone who witnesses violence, abuse or neglect involving a child to contact police immediately on 131 444 or Triple Zero in an emergency.

If you need help immediately, call emergency services on triple-0.

Suspected child abuse or neglect in South Australia can be reported to the Child Abuse Report Line on 13 14 78, which operates 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

In May last year the state government's reforms into domestic violence strangulation laws came into effect.

A charge of choking can attract a maximum sentence of seven years imprisonment.

When a person has been rendered unconscious as a result of choking, suffocation or strangulation an offender can face a maximum of 10 years imprisonment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.title: What to know about fuel prices after a midterm elections oil price drop
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Australian petrol and diesel prices are surging as the Iran war continues.  (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Global oil prices have continued to drop this morning after Donald Trump said new strikes on Iran were "unlikely". But it may take time for the effects to be passed on to consumers here in Australia.

As of November 10, Brent crude oil prices were around $U93 a barrel down from $US111.9 a week ago.

"Global oil prices fell significantly last week, hitting a low on Wednesday before a slight rebound at the end of the week," Ian Jeffreys, from Queensland's motor peak body RACQ said.

"Fuel retailers in capital cities should be passing this reduction on to motorists in the coming days, and regional motorists should feel the same relief in the coming weeks."

The drop in prices over the past week showed optimism in the world oil trade by investors off the back of a Democratic majority win in both the House and the Senate in the US midterm elections, according to Daniel Prior, supply chain expert at the University of New South Wales.

"Back in early October, oil prices were about US$110 a barrel and even slightly more than that," he said.

"Now we're seeing the $90s as sort of the more typical price of trade."

Dr Prior said it was good news that oil prices were down,  but it might take a little while to transfer to consumers in Australia.

"The suppliers to the Australian market will need to purchase the oil from the spot market at those prices, then pass their own costs down through the Australian oil supply chain," he said.

"Last time something like this happened earlier in the year, there were certain retailers that were very confident that their own suppliers would be able to pass that cost onto them and so they were able to jump in a bit more quickly than some others."

Dr Jeffreys hopes that was the case.

"What we've seen is fuel companies are retaining some of those savings and bolstering their retail margins, and what we would urge them to do in the coming days is to pass those savings on to motorists," he said.

He said that while the supply chain needed time to adjust in the regions, metro areas, where they resupply several times weekly, would start to purchase cut prices in the coming days.

“In our smaller centres, it does take a few weeks for the old fuel to be sold, and the new fuel to come in, and therefore the prices would fall a little later," Dr Jefferys said.
