https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/j.title: Russell Brand's ex Jemima Goldsmith accuses him of 'violence and abuse'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/j.author: Luke Cooper
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Sexual Offences

Russell Brand has been jailed for the rape and sexual assault of four women between 2004 and 2009. (Reuters: Julia Quenzler)

Jemima Goldsmith, who dated Russell Brand between 2013 and 2014, has accused him of committing "violence, coercive control and abuse" against her.

Ms Goldsmith released a statement hours after Brand was sentenced saying she had to call the police to remove him from her home in 2014.

Brand will not be eligible for release from prison until he serves two-thirds of his sentence, or at least seven years.

Jemima Goldsmith, a former partner of Russell Brand, has accused him of committing "violence, coercive control and abuse" against her.

Brand, 51, was sentenced in the United Kingdom on Monday, local time, to 10 years and six months in jail for the rape and sexual assault of four women between 2004 and 2009.

He was also acquitted of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Jemima Goldsmith says she experienced violence and abuse while in a relationship with the actor. (AP: Supplied/Evan Agostini/Invision)

In a statement posted online hours after Brand's sentencing, Ms Goldsmith said she felt she needed to share her own experience with the convicted rapist.

"Firstly, and most importantly, I am and have always been strongly and unequivocally on the side of all of Brand's victims," she said.

"I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse.

"I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident.

"I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children.

"I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014.

"Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact.

"Over several years, I assisted the journalists who finally exposed him; Ros Urwin, Louisa Compton and Dorothy Byrne.

"I also undertook to testify in court to his abusiveness, if the newspaper that published the victims' accounts were ever to be sued.

"I am glad and relieved that Russell Brand has finally faced justice."

Ms Goldsmith, who was once married to former Pakistani cricketer and prime minister Imran Khan, dated Brand between 2013 and 2014.

He then married Laura Brand (née Gallacher), his current wife, in 2017.

Russell Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault relating to four women between 2004 and 2009.

Ms Brand testified during her husband's four-week trial, and said his promiscuity left her "heartbroken" years before their marriage.

The pair met in Edinburgh in August 2006, when Ms Brand was 19 years old.

She told the jury she "felt entirely cared for and looked after by Russell" during their sex life, and described him as "caring, he's kind, he's a wonderful father".

"I was aware that he liked women and I was aware towards the latter part of the year that he was engaging with other women," she told the court.

Brand's rape conviction relates to a fan who was 21 years old when he met her following one of his London shows, and was later raped at his home in 2009.

Brand in Los Angeles in 2009. (Reuters: Danny Moloshok)

His sexual assault convictions relate to his abuse of a woman in a bar in 2004, another woman at a radio station and a third woman he worked with in 2009.

In sentencing, Judge Joel Bennathan described Brand as a serial predator.

"The whole episode reeks of casual disrespect and your belief that fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live," he said.

"Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no."

In addition to Ms Brand and Ms Goldsmith, the comedian dated and interacted with a string of other high-profile women through the early 2000s.

The disgraced British entertainer-turned-conspiracy theorist charted a course towards fame and notoriety before a criminal trial in London found him to be a sexual predator.

In 2006, Australian pop star Dannii Minogue told the UK's Mirror Brand had acted like a "vile predator" toward her, and once followed her down a corridor.

"He is completely crazy and a bit of a vile predator. I certainly don't think he has cured his sex addiction, that's for sure. He wouldn't take no for an answer," she said.

"He always goes that step too far. Never quite far enough to slap his face, but usually too far."

Brand's relationships also included supermodel Kate Moss and Spice Girl Geri Horner (née Halliwell), but his most famous partner was singer Katy Perry between 2009 and 2010.

Perry and Brand first met in 2008 before marrying in 2010. They filed for divorce in 2011, citing irreconcilable differences.

Brand and his former partner, singer Katy Perry, at a film premiere in London in 2011. (Reuters: Paul Hackett)

She told the Los Angeles Times in 2013 that Brand told her he wanted a divorce via text message on New Year's Eve in 2011.

"At first when I met him, he wanted an equal, and I think a lot of times strong men do want an equal, but then they get that equal and they're like, I can't handle the equalness," she said.

"He didn't like the atmosphere of me being the boss on tour. So that was really hurtful, and it was very controlling, which was upsetting.

"I felt a lot of responsibility for it ending, but then I found out the real truth, which I can't necessarily disclose because I keep it locked in my safe for a rainy day.

"I let go and I was like: This isn't because of me; this is beyond me. So I have moved on from that."

Perry has not commented on the allegations made against Brand or his conviction.

Brand will not be eligible for release from prison until he serves two-thirds of his sentence, or at least seven years. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

In court, the jury also heard from two former partners who spoke of Brand's character.

A dance teacher who dated him for three years from 1996 described him as "gentle, warm, kind and adventurous" with a "bad boy reputation".

She said their relationship ended because she felt she could no longer trust him to remain faithful.

Another woman who met Brand in London in 1999 said he was "undoubtedly promiscuous" but they never engaged in sexual activity without consent.

Following Brand's sentencing, Metropolitan Police Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said the women who shared their experiences had done so with "immense bravery, dignity and resilience".

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/l.title: Liquidators probe multi-million-dollar sale of collapsed Mundella assets
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/l.author: Jon Daly
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The administrators of the dairy companies are still operating the business and fulfilling orders. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

Liquidators of the collapsed dairy company Mundella Foods say they have identified nearly $800, 000 worth of potentially unreasonable director transactions.

An ongoing investigation is also examining whether the multi-million-dollar sale of Mundella Foods and Margaret River Dairy Company constitutes an "uncommercial transaction".

The former director of West Australian dairy company, Mundella Foods, says he "literally has nothing" left and has denied any improper transactions following the company's collapse into liquidation.

Hayden Russell is facing scrutiny from liquidators over what they say could be more than $2 million in potentially unreasonable director-related and insolvent trading transactions.

Liquidators are also investigating whether the multi-million-dollar sale of Mundella and the Margaret River Dairy Company (MRDC) to dairy processor, Artisanal Market, constitutes an "uncommercial" deal.

Creditors are still owed $12.5 million following the collapse of Mundella Foods and associated companies.

In a statutory report filed to the corporate regulator, liquidators at Mackay Goodwin said they had uncovered $778,000 of potentially unreasonable director-related transactions, including "frequent cash withdrawals".

They noted that further investigations were required to determine whether those withdrawals were used in the company's operations or were unreasonable.

The liquidators also found Mundella may have traded insolvent from as early as July 1, 2024, with transactions totalling $1.3 million.

The report did not make final findings and noted that further investigations would require additional funding.

Former director Hayden Russell. (Supplied: Kira Price)

Mr Russell denied making any unreasonable transactions, telling the ABC he acted "in good faith" at all times.

He claims he used cash withdrawals to pay for operations and workers' wages and had spent a few hundred thousand dollars of personal savings on the business.

The liquidators' report shows workers, who are priority creditors, are still owed almost $940,000 in unpaid wages, superannuation and entitlements.

Secured and unsecured creditors are owed a further $3 million and $8.5 million respectively.

Liquidators told creditors it was unlikely Mr Russell had the financial capacity to meet any claims brought against him, and further investigations would not be possible without further funding from creditors.

"At this stage of the Liquidation, it is unlikely that there will be a dividend to any class of creditors," the report stated.

Liquidators say they have identified potentially unreasonable transactions from the previous owner of Mundella. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

Last month, Artisanal Market announced its subsidiary had purchased the Mundella and MRDC brands, properties and assets.

The liquidators' report states the sale was agreed to on July 17, just weeks before creditors voted to put the companies, albeit what little was left of them, into liquidation.

The seller was mortgagee and private lender, Bowral Capital.

Bowral and another secured lender, Bizcap, received $5.85 million and almost $1 million respectively from the final sale of the dairy companies' property and assets in October.

Liquidators said investigations into whether the property deal was uncommercial were ongoing.

An uncommercial transaction occurs when a company makes a deal that a reasonable person in its circumstances would not have agreed to.

"For the avoidance of any doubt, proceeds from the Sale remain insufficient to repay Bowral and Bizcap in full for the amount owed by the Company and MRDC," liquidators said.

Bowral has been approached for comment on the liquidators' investigation of the sale.

The former director of Mundella and Margaret River Dairy Company said his financial rescue plan would have worked if his primary lender had provided more money. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

The dairy companies were put into liquidation in August following a failed financial rescue plan set out in a Deed of Company Arrangement (DOCA).

The liquidators' report confirmed the companies failed to meet several obligations to creditors under the agreement, including $40,000 of unpaid funds to the Deed Fund.

Bowral acquired the properties and assets during the ongoing DOCA period from original lender Oak Capital, which went into its own liquidation in May this year.

Separately, Oak Capital is being sued in the federal court by the corporate watchdog, ASIC, for alleged unconscionable conduct and predatory lending practices, which it denies.

Mr Russell claims the DOCA would have succeeded if the subsequent mortgagee Bowral had lent him more money.

In a statement, Bowral said the company was not a party to the DOCA, "nor did it impose any obligation on Bowral Capital to provide further funding".

"Bowral Capital's responsibility was to manage the fund and protect the interests of its investors," the company said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.author: Annabel Whitehouse
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Annabel Whitehouse

The supermarket chain Woolworths says it is consulting with staff at their Woden and Gunghalin stores to potentially implement the technology by the end of the month. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Woolworths is considering a trial of facial recognition technology in two of its Canberra stores, in an attempt to tackle violence against staff.

It says the technology would be trialled in its Woden and Gungahlin stores.

The supermarket giant is consulting with staff and could implement the technology by the end of the month.

Supermarket chain Woolworths is considering a trial of facial recognition technology in two stores in Canberra in an attempt to better protect staff members from violent offenders frequenting their stores.

Woolworths stores in Woden and Gungahlin are being considered for the trial, and if it goes ahead, the technology could be implemented by the end of the month.

Woolworths' head of violence prevention Sarah Faorlin told 666 ABC Radio Canberra these two stores were chosen because of the "high number of workplace protection orders in place".

"The ACT unfortunately does have high levels of violence and aggression," Ms Faorlin said.

The head of violence prevention at Woolworths says if the technology is implemented, all customer's faces will be scanned but their profiles will be deleted if they are not on a watch list. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

Workplace protection orders (WPOs) are legal orders used to prevent and reduce workplace violence, and the ACT was the first to introduce them in 2016.

Ms Faorlin said Woolworths has seen "great success" using WPOs in the territory, but "assessing the merits of facial recognition technology in-store is another way we can help protect team members and customers".

"The aim is to use facial recognition technology to actively monitor for repeat violent and aggressive offenders who frequent our stores to protect team safety," she said.

Ms Faorlin said Woolworths have seen a 460 per cent increase of "unacceptable incidents" in their stores nationally since 2020.

"It is appalling that our team members continue to face unprovoked violence and aggression when they're just trying to do their jobs," she said.

Ms Faorlin said the facial technology would scan every customer as they entered either the Woden or Gungahlin stores, creating a temporary biometric profile.

Woolworths is considering a trial of facial recognition technology in two of its Canberra stores, in an attempt to tackle violence against staff. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"That profile will be looked up against a known watch list [of] our repeat violent and aggressive offenders," she said.

"If there is no detection made, so our genuine customers, their biometric profile will be deleted within one second.

"If there is a detection made [staff] may have police called and our team will be alerted to their presence in store."

NSW and ACT Secretary of the Shop Distributive and Allied Employees Association (SDA) Bernie Smith said it was his understanding that Woolworths would not "call the police every time their machine pings".

"They're going to call the police for somebody's breached the workplace protection order and that then becomes a matter for the police, because it's a criminal offence that has to be enforced by the police," he said.

Mr Smith said he was aware of the high levels of violence and aggression in the two stores Woolworths was considering.

"People might be thinking this is just about people getting angry at the checkouts," he said.

"To put this in context, next door to Woolworths Woden a couple of months ago, a member of ours was beaten up with a baseball bat."

The union representing grocery workers says it supports the implementation of facial recognition technology in two Canberra supermarkets, as long as it comes with strict guidelines. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

He said that facial recognition technology could help combat violence "as long as it's done within very strict guidelines as part of a social licensing of it".

Ms Faorlin said Woolworths would be "really transparent" about the trial, and added that signage would be displayed outside the two supermarkets.

"We're currently in consultation with our store team to understand if this is something that they want to proceed with," she added.

If the consultation process is successful, the technology could be implemented by the end of this month.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.title: Clive Palmer says dilapidated luxury resort will reopen after decade in mothballs
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.author: Josh Dye
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Tourism and Leisure Industry

The Palmer Coolum Resort pictured in 2020. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Clive Palmer says a five-star Sunshine Coast resort he shut down in 2015 will reopen next year.

The Queensland billionaire bought the luxury Hyatt Regency site in 2011 and has repeatedly promised to revamp it.

The Palmer Coolum resort is hiring tradespeople as the renovations gather momentum, but local residents are sceptical.

Billionaire Clive Palmer has begun revamping his luxury resort on the Sunshine Coast, with a new pledge to reopen the rundown site after a decade in mothballs.

The Queensland businessman purchased the five-star Hyatt Regency resort in Coolum in 2011 before shutting it four years later.

Mr Palmer announced a $100 million redevelopment in 2021 that would include replicas of famous landmarks, such as Rome's Trevi Fountain.

Clive Palmer erected a large Tyrannosaurus rex called Jeff at his resort in 2012, before the dinosaur burnt down in 2015. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

The work was due for completion in 2022 but has faced repeated delays.

Several job vacancies at the resort have been advertised recently, including skilled labourers, painters, security guards, electricians and plumbers.

A spokesman for Mr Palmer confirmed to the ABC the resort would reopen mid-next year.

Workers can be seen on site and renovations are underway.

Workers were seen clearing gutters at the Palmer Coolum resort on Tuesday. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

In its prime, the precinct employed 700 people and featured more than 300 luxury rooms and villas, a day spa and a popular village green.

The site still features an active 18-hole golf course, which used to host the Australian PGA Championship for 11 years from 2002 until 2012.

Mr Palmer rebranded the resort in his own name following a legal dispute with Hyatt in 2012, before closing the facility in 2015.

In 2023, dozens of tradesmen were among 125 employees sacked amid accusations of theft and fraud, with the Fair Work Commission later finding some dismissals were unfair.

Greg Norman plays a shot on the 13th fairway during the Australian PGA Championship at the Hyatt Regency Coolum in 2011. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Many Coolum residents have fond memories of the old resort and hope it can be restored to its former glory.

"It would be extraordinary … everyone would support it," Coolum Business and Tourism vice-president Casey O'Hare said.

"It was absolutely gorgeous in its day … it was such an amazing asset for the Sunshine Coast.

"If Clive Palmer could rebuild and get it back on the market as a hotel and resort, it would be such a boon for the coast."

But Ms O'Hare said locals were sceptical given the repeated broken promises to reopen the premises.

Clive Palmer's resort in Coolum has been shut since 2015 but work has now begun to revamp it. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

"I'll believe it when I see it, because of the fact that this has happened before where it's been mooted as reopening," she said.

Retired builder Mark Hatfull helped construct the original resort back in the 1980s and said the "world-class" facility transformed the region.

"It took it from a backwater to where we are today … It was an absolute godsend," he said.

Residents like Mark Hatfull are hopeful the resort can be restored to its former glory. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

"The gym and the spa was something to die for … It was like something out of a dream.

"Obviously, Clive has got his business and then he makes a decision and one day a place is open, the next day it's closed."

Local councillor Taylor Bunnag said he grew up around the resort where his father was a greenkeeper.

He said it would be "a wonderful thing" if it reopened, but he understood the scepticism.

"If you actually look at the site … there's a lot of existing infrastructure that's quite run down," Cr Bunnag said.

"I think the devil is in the detail with all these sorts of proposals.

A swimming pool area in disarray at the Palmer Coolum Resort in December 2017. (Supplied: Maree Frecklington)

"We've been told that Palmer Resort was going to reopen at certain times and that hasn't eventuated."

Cr Bunnag said a renovated facility would be "extremely welcome" in fixing the region's accommodation shortage ahead of the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.

"We need thousands of extra hotel rooms added to our region by 2032 to cater for the demand," he said.

"It's hard to speculate about what further approvals they'll need because I'm not sure what product they're delivering.

Cr Bunnag said he had not seen any formal proposals for Mr Palmer's original plan of building replicas of famous landmarks such as Rome's Trevi Fountain.

A tradesman working on a building at the Palmer Coolum Resort on Tuesday. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

"I'd only be speculating but my assumption is that they'll be renovating certain parts of the resort and some might open, some might not," he said.

A Sunshine Coast Council spokesperson said the site held existing approval for a resort and residential community facility.

"Provided the development continues to operate in accordance with the conditions of that approval, no further development approvals are required from council," they said.

Qantas has announced plans to axe 850 jobs. (AAP: Paul Miller)

Qantas will move roles overseas and cut 850 positions under an outsourcing deal with tech firm Accenture.

The airline said hundreds of roles would go "over coming years, with the first changes expected to be in place by mid-2027".

Some roles will be outsourced to Accenture workers in India.

Qantas Group CEO Vanessa Hudson sent an all-staff email announcing the cuts, describing it as "hard news for some".

Vanessa Hudson says Qantas will redeploy as many people as possible. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Ms Hudson said the redundancies were part of a new multi-year partnership with Accenture and would affect corporate roles within the organisation.

The changes will start in the finance, procurement and marketing teams, with some services delivered by those teams outsourced to Accenture "delivered mostly by its teams in India and some in Australia", the email read.

The Australian Services Union said it was meeting with its Qantas members today following the news.

Qantas said it would look to redeploy as many people as possible.

Some Qantas jobs will be outsorced to digital consultancy firm Accenture. (Reuters: Chris Helgren)

"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," Ms Hudon said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Russia ‘pretending’ to negotiate on Ukraine while ‘bombing civilians’: Kallas
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: John Irish
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
PARIS – The European Union’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said on Monday she saw little sign of Russian goodwill to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, adding Moscow had already signed up to numerous agreements underpinning European security but had failed to respect them.

Kallas was speaking on the sidelines of a Group of Seven ministerial meeting ahead of trilateral discussions on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine, Russia and the United States. Officials from France, Britain, Germany, NATO and the European Commission will also be in the Emirati capital.

“So far they have just been pretending that they negotiate because we haven’t seen any goodwill from the Russian side,” Kallas said in an interview in Paris.

“They are bombing Kyiv, they are bombing civilians. Ukrainians are making advances on the battlefield, so the Russian focus has been only on civilians to cause as much suffering before the hard winter is coming.”

Russia denies targeting civilians but has stepped up its aerial attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and other key targets in recent months, as its forces’ advances in eastern Ukraine have stalled.

Ukraine has responded with drone attacks on Russian energy installations, often deep inside Russian territory.

Moscow has long accused the Europeans of refusing to take Russia’s own security concerns into consideration in Europe, for example by pursuing NATO enlargement up to its borders.

Jared Kushner, one of the lead U.S. negotiators, said last week that the U.S. was working on a “broader European security architecture,” something that has worried some Europeans, who have repeatedly said they would not accept anything they had not agreed to.

“The problem is that we already have a European security architecture in place that Russia has agreed to,” Kallas said, citing examples including the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, when Russia and others pledged to respect the independence, sovereignty and existing borders of Ukraine.

“All this talk has to be about how we make sure that Russia actually respects the obligations that it has taken,” she added.

In a sign of friction among Europeans, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni warned on Nov. 5 that Europe risked becoming irrelevant in efforts to end the war in Ukraine if member states continued pursuing separate diplomatic tracks, rather than agreeing on a common representative and strategy.

Kallas said future discussions on European security should be led by the European Union in line with its treaties and institutional structures, rather than through ad hoc formats.

“It is clear that the big countries want to talk also to big countries,” she said. “But when it comes to European security issues, then the European Union has very clear lines in place. We have the treaties,” she also said.

With the EU currently negotiating a 22nd package of sanctions on Russia, Kallas said she hoped that losses suffered by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Republicans in last week’s midterm elections would alter Washington’s approach to Ukraine.

“We are hoping that there will be pressure on Russia to end this war and pressure (with) the (U.S.) sanctions,” she said. “If we were to do this together with the Americans, it would really have an effect.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Kallas says she saw little sign of Russian goodwill to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine. She says Moscow has already signed up to numerous agreements underpinning European security but has failed to respect them. Kallas was speaking on the sidelines of a Group of Seven ministerial meeting on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Students help develop helmet to encourage more cyclists to wear one
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Helmet use in Japan has risen three and a half years after a revised road traffic law called on all cyclists in Japan to endeavor to wear one. Progress has been slow, however, with just one in four cyclists now wearing one.

To encourage more cyclists, especially young people, to wear helmets, the Metropolitan Police Department has developed a new helmet with input from university students. The helmet went on sale in August.

Before the amendment took effect in April 2023, only parents and guardians were urged to have children under 13 wear helmets. The revised law has extended this duty to all cyclists, but there is no penalty for not wearing a helmet.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Anthropic IPO’s moment of truth nears as waiting period ends
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Anthropic can begin formally marketing its much-anticipated IPO as early as Tuesday, enabling it to make the case to investors that now is the right time to go public despite last week’s swoon in artificial intelligence-related stocks.

The gyrations of the past week briefly sent the Cboe Volatility Index, known as the fear gauge, above 25. That’s a zone in which companies typically postpone their IPOs, said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at IPO research firm Renaissance Capital.

The size of Anthropic’s IPO and its investment case may put it in a different category to the average listing, Kennedy said. Anthropic is targeting an offering as big as SpaceX’s in its record-setting debut, or bigger, Bloomberg News reported.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Takaichi’s hunt for new cash to fund spending harbors risks
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Erica Yokoyama
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is on the hunt for new tools to help implement her ambitious economic agenda, but shifting the rules to unlock more cash to fund it could bring fresh risks.

At stake is Takaichi’s fiscal credibility. She faces a year-end deadline to explain how she intends to pay for initiatives ranging from a two-year sales tax cut on food to a defense buildup and a sweeping investment plan that’s supposed to boost Japan’s economy for years to come.

If she succeeds, Takaichi could manage to cap new government bond issuance, reassuring investors worried about Japan’s already enormous debt burden, while also reinforcing her popularity with voters. Yet some of the cash-gathering methods under consideration would stretch existing safeguards, while others could leave taxpayers shouldering greater risk.

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
Though some of the men were terrified of heights, the moment they saw the girl dangling outside the window, all fear vanished

Six individuals in southeastern China were named Good Samaritans by local authorities for risking their lives to save a little girl who was in danger of falling from a high-rise building.

The incident unfolded on the morning of October 17 in a residential community in Zhangping, Fujian province.

According to Xinhua, a resident shared a picture of a young girl in the community’s online chat group and urged security guards to help. The girl, about three years old, was shown hanging outside the window of her 12th-floor flat, with her neck caught between the window’s wire mesh.

The crying girl was facing inwards and was gripping the wires, meaning she could fall at any moment.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Tess Ikonomou and Josh Butler
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Government flags criminal law changes to ensure companies can’t argue in future ‘that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded’

OpenAI won’t face criminal penalties over the Medicare hack but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.

Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach but not the findings or the report itself.

A key recommendation is for the attorney general’s department, the Australian federal police and home affairs to consider reforming the law to introduce “penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance” and a “failure to prevent” offence which would criminalise developing an AI model that engaged in harmful conduct while failing “to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm”.

The review recommended the federal government “consider mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting, including but not limited to misaligned behaviour or agentic cyber incidents”.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, told reporters “we need to make sure that our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology and also make sure that we’re able to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do”.

“The mandatory reporting, when artificial intelligence goes rogue, gives us a chance to be able to make sure that when this happens, the reporting occurs and occurs immediately,” Burke said in Canberra alongside the PM.

On the “concept of looking at how we can update our criminal law”, Burke said: “It should never be the case that there’s an argument that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded.”

“We need to make sure that the criminal law is up to date for how this new technology is able to act.”

Albanese on Tuesday characterised OpenAI’s breach of Services Australia as “minor” in terms of the implications for personal privacy.

“The clear indication is that no information was got that involves people’s personal details,” the prime minister told reporters in Canberra.

“All of that was confirmed essentially ... but that doesn’t mean that it wasn’t a serious issue and that in other areas there might be more serious implications.”

The review made 18 recommendations. Albanese said “we accept all of the recommendations and we’ve commenced work to implement them”.

Albanese did not directly answer a question about whether the OpenAI incident in June would have breached the proposed new laws if they were in place.

The AI agent developed by OpenAI accessed Services Australia data and three other systems in June.

The company didn’t notify the Australia government until mid-September despite becoming aware of the incident itself in August.

Guardian Australia revealed last month OpenAI used AI to help write the email to notify Australian authorities.

Albanese said the government would set up a new AI safety regulator.

Labor would consider six key obligations on AI companies, including:

maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment;

identify and manage serious risks associated with their models;

provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly;

allow independent evaluation of their models;

maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management, and transparency;

and respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: California voters fail to pass proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Campaign over Prop 40, as measure was known, was most expensive in state history, flush with Silicon Valley dollars

California billionaires won a contentious ballot measure campaign, defeating a proposed one-time tax on their wealth.

The bruising campaign over Proposition 40 was the most expensive in state history and witness to back-and-forth dealing from tech billionaires and democratic leaders, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, who steadfastly opposed the measure. While supporters of Prop 40 cast it as a solution to drastic healthcare cuts from Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents led by prosperous billionaires mounted an influential campaign saying the billionaire tax was instead “an everyone tax”.

This result could hamper nationwide momentum on demands that billionaires pay their fair share and states enacting new laws to tax the ultra-wealthy.

Prop 40 proposed a one-time 5% tax on all individuals in California with a net worth of more than $1bn as of 1 January 2026. It was sponsored by the healthcare union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, and dictated that the proceeds from the tax would fund healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance.

The state’s major unions, and progressive politicians such as Bernie Sanders, the Vermont senator, and Ro Khanna, a California congressman, backed Prop 40. But both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, as well as organizations such as Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, a lobbying branch of the healthcare group, opposed it – pointing to its structure as a one-off tax that would only fund certain healthcare programs. Prop 40’s most vocal critics, however, were the state’s billionaires.

Donors to the opposition campaign were a who’s who of Silicon Valley, including executives from Google, Palantir, DoorDash, Stripe and Reddit, along with several prominent venture capitalists. The biggest donor, by far, was Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder, who contributed at least $132m to fight the tax, according to campaign finance filings.

All told, the billionaires mounted a nearly $425m battle against Prop 40, making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history. In the first two weeks of October, spending surpassed $2.5m a day, according to the most recent campaign finance filings.

Part of the opposition campaign’s strategy was mounting two separate counter-measures on the ballot, Proposition 41 and 42. Prop 41 directly targeted the billionaire tax, while Prop 42 was a general proposal on limiting certain new taxes and would ban any taxation on billionaire wealth. If either measure received more yes votes than Prop 40, they would stop the billionaire tax from taking effect – even if it passed.

Supporters of the billionaire tax called Props 41 and 42 “poison pills”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Russia, Ukraine and US to meet as Zelenskyy claims battlefield successes
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Negotiators from Russia and Ukraine are set to meet for peace talks brokered by the United States in Abu Dhabi, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that recent gains on the battlefield had strengthened his country’s hand.

The meeting in the capital of the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday will be the third round of talks there this year, following security consultations in January and February. The US side is led by US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have spearheaded Washington’s mediation.

The three delegations last met in Geneva on February 18.

“Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine’s negotiating position,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address on Monday. He said Russia was “suffering record losses”, a claim Moscow disputes, and urged Washington to persuade the Kremlin to end the war.

Zelenskyy said General Mykhailo Drapatyi had presented a report on Ukraine’s military positions that pointed to heavy recent Russian losses, and that Ukraine’s long-range strikes on targets inside Russia, including oil facilities, were having an effect.

“We are responding to Russia’s war in a fully justified manner and demonstrating that this war must end,” he said. “Russia can do this. It can end its war. It is important that the United States convince Russia of precisely this.”

In Washington, DC, Trump told reporters that he saw a “very strong inclination” towards ending the war and that both sides were “tired of fighting”.

“We’re having a very good conversation about that in Abu Dhabi,” he said.

Trump had promised to end the war quickly when he took office in January 2025, but a settlement has remained elusive nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

A US official, briefing reporters on the condition of anonymity, said on Monday that both Russia and Ukraine had privately shown some flexibility on a possible exchange of territory. Security guarantees for Ukraine would be a central topic, the official said, including the possibility of a defence commitment modelled on Article 5 of NATO’s founding treaty.

Both Ukraine and Russia have been adamant about territory.

Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to obtain all of the Donbas region.

Russia occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, including Crimea and parts of the eastern Donbas region. The Russian move has not been recognised by the international community, but Trump has previously urged Kyiv to cede territory for a deal to end the war.

The US official said any territorial agreement would most likely come at the end of the negotiations, once other issues, including a post-war security framework, had been settled.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio meanwhile struck a cautious note, saying that the process to end the war still has “a ways to go”.

“We’ll keep trying. And that’s what we’ve been trying to do the whole time is try to be creative and find ways that we can help bring that conflict and that war to an end,” Rubio said.

Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, will again lead the country’s delegation, according to The Kyiv Independent. Russia’s team will be headed by Vladimir Medinsky, a Kremlin aide, and will include Sergei Ryabkov, a deputy foreign minister, as well as Yuri Zhigarlovsky, a senior military officer.

European powers, including France, Germany and the European Commission, will send officials to the talks in Abu Dhabi, but Russia has made it clear it doesn’t want the Europeans to take part in negotiations.

Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said the talks would focus on security guarantees. European officials would not take part, he added, because the negotiations had been agreed to as a three-way format.

“What will take place in Abu Dhabi in the coming days is trilateral negotiations between Russia and Ukraine with US mediation,” Peskov said. “As for the presence of Europeans, you know that the Americans have their own channels of communication with Europeans, and Ukrainians with Europeans.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/china-tr.title: China exports, imports soar past expectations in October — surplus narrows sharply
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/china-tr.author: Anniek Bao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/china-tr.text:
Goods exports soared by 35.2% last month from a year earlier, exceeding expectations for a 33.5%.

Imports climbed by 41.6% last month, customs data showed, jumping from 31% in September.

China’s exports and imports surged more than expected in October, according to the official data released Monday, while its surplus shrank sharply, undershooting expectations.

Goods exports soared by 35.2% last month from a year earlier, exceeding expectations for a 33.5% jump in a Reuters poll but slowing from the 36.3% growth in September.

Imports climbed by 41.6% last month, customs data showed, jumping from 31% in September and sharply beating estimates for a 32% rise by analysts polled by Reuters.

The surplus dropped to $105.3 billion in October, the lowest level since April, according to LSEG data, with year-to-date figure at $1.04 trillion, compared with a record $1.2 trillion for the full year 2025. Calls from trading partners have grown louder for Beijing to boost domestic demand and balance its economy.

The strength in exports has allowed policymakers to continue relying on moderate policy support to meet the country’s annual growth target of 4.5%-5%. Household consumption has remained soft, with retail sales growing a modest 1.1% in September, underscoring the imbalance in the world’s second-largest economy.

Much of the surge in exports reflects robust demand for its chips and other artificial intelligence-related hardware. But any slowdown in the global AI buildout would risk denting the momentum and squeezing Chinese exporters’ margins.

A separate survey by China Beige Book showed new domestic and export orders for goods slowed in October compared to a year earlier. Factory activity also unexpectedly shrank last month, according to official PMI data, as overseas orders cooled. “The stronger side of the economy got weaker,” the New York-headquartered research firm said in a note on Oct. 30.

Washington and Beijing agreed in September to extend a broader trade truce by two months to January, along with a slew of other trade measures, including export-control waivers for certain critical minerals and special port fees for each other’s vessels.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump are expected to meet for a third time this year at the APEC leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China next week.

The European Union also reached an agreement with Beijing last month to limit the imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles over the next few years, as part of the effort to reduce its trade deficit with Beijing. But the measures, taking effect on Dec.1, would barely contain China’s export boom, according to analysts.

The cap of 350,000 imported cars per year is above the 300,000 hybrids that China exported to Europe last year, though well below the 800,000 units in annualized pace over the last three months, according to Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

“Europe still is a long way from a coherent trade and industrial policy with respect to autos, let alone a coherent economic policy towards overall trade with China,” said Setser, a former U.S. Treasury official who specializes in global trade and capital flows.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Honda to spend $3 billion on new hybrid car plant in Ohio
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Chester Dawson
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Honda Motor plans to build a $3 billion factory in central Ohio to manufacture its next-generation hybrids, boosting its output capacity for the popular vehicles.

The automaker announced on Monday the new plant will start production in 2029 and expand its output by 240,000 vehicles a year. Honda has been mulling over the decision for months as part of a strategic pivot earlier this year away from all-electric vehicles. It aims to introduce 15 new hybrids globally by March 2030, primarily targeting North America.

“This is not simply an investment in another plant,” Bob Nelson, executive vice president of the company’s U.S. business operations, said at a news conference. “It is an investment in the future of Honda Manufacturing in America.”

Honda’s U.S. sales have risen 5% in the first 10 months of the year, powered by strong demand for hybrid versions of its best-selling CR-V compact SUV, Accord mid-sized sedan and compact Civic sedan. Fuel-efficient hybrids, which make up about a third of the company’s total sales volume in the U.S., have caught on with cost-conscious buyers as gas prices have soared.

Honda is preparing to introduce a new system that will provide hybrid options for its larger, V6 engine-powered vehicles such as the Pilot SUV and upscale Acura MDX SUV.

The new facility will be located between two existing auto assembly plants it operates in Ohio. It will be tooled to build gas-only, hybrid and fully electric vehicles, but the company didn’t provide a breakdown by production volume.

Honda also wouldn’t say which vehicles will be made in the new plant, but its focus will be on boosting output of models offering a hybrid option, including all-new models.

“The market has changed dramatically and it changed very quickly — faster than we could catch up, it seemed, at times,” Honda’s Nelson told reporters. “But we’re quickly developing new products based on the customers, and the hybrid’s very popular now for us.”

In a separate statement, it announced an investment of C$166 million ($118 million) in its Canadian factory in Alliston, Ontario, to make next-generation vehicles and for “the reintroduction of engine manufacturing.”

Honda was prepared to spend C$15 billion on an EV battery supply chain complex in Canada, but put that plan on indefinite hold in May. It also canceled a trio of battery-electric models it was preparing to manufacture in the U.S.. But it began production this summer of battery cells at a $4.4 billion joint venture with LG Energy Solution in Ohio.

That facility was originally designed to build batteries for electric vehicles but has pivoted to make hybrid batteries, Nelson said.

U.S. trade relations with Canada and Mexico have been complicated by President Donald Trump’s tariffs on imports and his decision in July not to renew a North American free trade accord negotiated during his first administration. Trump has threatened to impose 50% levies on vehicles and auto parts made in Canada as of Jan. 1.

Honda has vehicle assembly operations in Ohio, Alabama and Indiana as well as in Canada and Mexico. In addition, it makes key parts such as engines and transmissions in Alabama, Georgia and Ohio. The company said on Monday that it will also make investments in a number of other facilities in North America, but not at its Mexican plant.

“There’s nothing to read into it, but it’s not impacted by this series of investments,” Nelson said.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/busin.title: China’s Trade Surplus Passes $1 Trillion at Record Pace
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/busin.author: Keith Bradsher
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/busin.text:
China’s factories are finding eager buyers worldwide, but the export boom is raising concerns about its impact on trading partner nations.

Reporting from Shanghai

China’s trade surplus surged past $1 trillion in the first 10 months of this year, eclipsing last year’s record-setting pace as overseas demand for Chinese goods continued to climb steeply, the government announced on Tuesday.

From solar panels to electric cars, China has found strong global interest for green energy products, as Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz have driven up international oil prices. China has also benefited from the boom in artificial intelligence data centers, for which it manufactures much of the equipment, apart from the most powerful semiconductors.

China’s trade surplus reached $1.04 trillion in the first 10 months of the year, the General Administration of Customs said, with exports exceeding imports by $105.3 billion in October. The monthly gap narrowed from September, however, as crude oil import prices remained high and China’s crude oil purchases jumped to the highest level since the start of the Middle East war.

At the same time, China restricted shipments of diesel, jet fuel and other refined oil products to nearby countries last month to conserve domestic supplies.Overall exports climbed 35.2 percent last month from a year earlier, driven in part by strong shipments of cables, racks and other equipment for data centers overseas. But imports jumped 41.6 percent, including substantial demand of electronics for China’s own A.I. infrastructure buildout.

“High-tech products continued to underpin export strength, while import volumes delivered the larger upside surprise,” said a research note from ANZ, a major Australian bank.

The figures came a day after Washington and Beijing took steps to ease tariffs and restrict the use of export controls through Jan. 10, putting into effect an agreement reached by senior officials in late September ahead of a Washington summit between President Trump and Xi Jinping, China’s top leader.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1516.title: California voters defeat billionaire tax proposal that divided Democrats
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1516.author: Larry Kaplow
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1516.text:
California voters rejected Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, which had divided Democrats with opponents saying it would drive the wealthy from the state.

Midterms coverage: Live results | Stories around the country
Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

California voters have rejected a proposal to charge billionaires a one-time 5% tax on most of their wealth, according to a race call by The Associated Press.

Proponents said the tax could raise $100 billion for healthcare. Led by a union that represents healthcare workers, the SEIU-UHW, advocates of the tax said the Republican-controlled Congress cut healthcare programs to give tax breaks to the wealthy, so it was time for the wealthy in California to fill the gap. The state has more than 200 billionaires, according to estimates, with some putting the number at a few hundred.

Opponents argued that the proposal, known as Prop 40, would just drive the wealthy out of California, costing the state revenue and harming its economy.

But the measure divided Democrats in a state where they heavily outnumber Republicans.

The state's Democratic Party favored Prop 40, as did Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who went to the state to campaign for it. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed the tax, saying it would be better to have a national tax on the wealthy. The Democratic candidate for governor, Xavier Becerra, also opposed it.

A leading teachers union also opposed the proposal, which would have set aside just a small portion of the resulting revenue for schools. And Google co-founder Sergey Brin led other wealthy Californians in a surge of campaign spending opposing the measure. At least five times as much was spent opposing the measure as favoring it.

Brin also drove a campaign that put two other proposals on the ballot to block the billionaire tax from taking effect, had it been approved by voters.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Saudi Arabia downs missiles fired at Riyadh after Houthi attack on pipeline
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has announced it intercepted two missiles fired towards the kingdom’s capital, Riyadh, and another aimed at its southern region.

Major-General Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the coalition, blamed the Iran-backed Houthis for Tuesday’s attacks.

In a series of posts on X, he said a ballistic missile and a cruise missile were intercepted and destroyed over Riyadh, while a second ballistic missile was downed over the southern part of the country.

Multiple explosions were heard in Riyadh, according to the AFP news agency, and residents received text-message alerts instructing them to take shelter due to an “aerial threat”.

A subsequent message from the country’s civil defence agency said the danger had passed.

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.

The strikes were the latest in a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia as fighting rages in Yemen between the Houthis and the country’s internationally recognised government, backed by Riyadh.

The coalition has supported a Yemeni government offensive to retake territory with air strikes, while the Houthis have repeatedly struck Saudi oil infrastructure, including refineries and storage facilities, with drones and missiles.

On Monday, the East-West oil pipeline in the Medina region was attacked again. A Saudi Energy Ministry official told the state-run SPA news agency the strike caused a “limited fire” that was extinguished. The official said that “pipeline operations were unaffected”.

No injuries or deaths were reported.

The pipeline is a vital route for Saudi oil exports due to Tehran’s restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war against Iran. The pipeline has come under attack several times as the war on Iran fuels a global energy crisis.

On Sunday, the Houthis also said they attacked Riyadh’s business district.

Saudi officials said falling debris from an “attempted attack” had caused minor damage to the Aramco Tower.

Images released by the SPA showed the deputy governor of the Riyadh region and other officials inspecting the building, with damage visible on several floors.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Harare demolitions leave families homeless after years of building
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Calvin Manika
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Harare, Zimbabwe – At around 5am on Friday, August 14, Methro Masunga, 28, was jolted awake by the sound of bulldozers and shouting municipal police officers. Outside, earth-moving vehicles were preparing to demolish homes in St Martins Extension, a suburb of Harare.

At first, Masunga thought the machinery had arrived for roadworks. Then she realised her home was among those marked for destruction.

“I thought they were here for some other business, probably land development or road grading; alas, they had been sent to destroy our homes. We tried to understand, but no one would hear us,” Masunga told Al Jazeera.

A single mother of three, Masunga had spent years saving to own a home. She worked part-time cleaning other people’s houses, putting aside what she could to buy a residential stand.

“I worked part-time jobs doing laundry and washing dishes in people’s houses for five years, saving where possible. So, when I came here, I paid the deposit and started monthly contributions,” she said, standing among the remains of her house.

Masunga began paying for her stand in 2015 and received an allocation in 2019. She says the arrangement was formalised through the city council in 2020, when residents began receiving official documents.

Her experience reflects a wider dispute over land allocations in Harare. Residents say they bought stands through council-linked processes and invested their savings in building homes. The municipality says it is enforcing planning regulations against structures built without the necessary approvals or on land not designated for housing.

The full number of people displaced by demolitions across Harare in 2026 has not been independently established. However, city council records seen by Al Jazeera list more than 5,000 houses facing demolition under 37 outstanding High Court orders. These figures concern properties targeted under the wider programme, not homes already demolished. A council task force has separately inspected 22,255 sites to identify structures on prohibited or unauthorised land.

Authorities say the demolitions are intended to address illegal construction, disputed land sales and development on sites reserved for public infrastructure. Residents argue that enforcement has also affected people who say they obtained allocation letters and agreements of sale through municipal processes.

Memory Chengeta, whose house in St Martins was also demolished, said residents were bewildered by the operation because of an earlier court order.

“There was a court order for them to stop demolitions. The municipal authorities came with no court order that overturned the previous judgement, but went ahead to destroy the properties,” she said.

A former street food vendor, Chengeta had saved to build a more stable life. She is now homeless. Some affected residents have returned to renting, while others, including Chengeta and Masunga, have remained in St Martins, putting up makeshift shelters rather than leaving the area.

Joachim Nhete also lost his home after using his retirement package to buy land and build a house. He estimates his investment at more than $10,000.

The dispute has raised questions about how residents acquired their stands and whether the council complied with existing court orders.

On October 29, 2025, Justice Happias Zhou issued a consent order in case HCH5444/25, setting aside demolition notices issued to named applicants in St Martins Extension. It barred the City of Harare from evicting those applicants or demolishing their homes without a valid court order. It also prohibited further development without written council approval.

The order did not automatically protect every property in St Martins. The available information does not establish whether Masunga, Chengeta or their specific properties were among those covered.

The council has maintained that it did not demolish properties protected by the order. Its spokesperson, Stanley Gama, told local media that the municipality was targeting structures whose owners had repeatedly been warned against building illegally.

“We are only demolishing structures built illegally whose owners were told and warned many times not to proceed with construction,” Gama said.

Harare Mayor Jacob Mafume told NewsDay on August 15 that residents with approved building plans should produce them during council inspections. He said the municipality had repeatedly warned residents to obtain the necessary documents but declined to comment on the legality of the specific demolitions in St Martins.

Harare’s principal housing director, Edgar Dzehonye, later said residents had been warned against building in the area because it had not been adequately serviced.

These explanations raise a separate question: whether residents who received council allocation letters and agreements of sale also had valid planning and building approvals. An allocation to occupy a stand does not necessarily establish that a house was authorised for construction. The status of the residents’ documents, the approved layout, and individual building permits are therefore central to determining whether the demolitions were justified.

Precious Shumba, director of the Harare Residents’ Trust, said the demolitions were particularly troubling because of the court order protecting residents allocated stands by the municipality.

“Despite that, the town planning department and legal officers in the Chamber Secretary’s Department issued directives to the Municipal Police to demolish the houses of St Martins Extension residents,” he said.

Zimbabwe’s Constitution, under Section 74, prohibits the eviction of people from their homes or the demolition of their homes without a court order made after considering all relevant circumstances. The National Human Settlements Policy also calls for alternative accommodation to be prepared before relocations and demolitions. Residents say they were not offered alternative housing.

The controversy reflects long-standing problems in Harare’s land administration. A 2019 commission of inquiry chaired by Justice Tendai Uchena identified unauthorised land sales, weak administration and poor record-keeping by local authorities. It found that land barons had sold state land without authority, sometimes allegedly working alongside council officials.

Shumba said the Harare Residents’ Trust wrote to the president on July 22, 2026, calling for the publication of the report of the commission of inquiry into the financial affairs of the city of Harare. The organisation also wants the findings of the Justice Maphios Cheda commission of inquiry into the city’s governance crisis implemented.

David Jenje, chairman of the St Martins Residents Association and the St Martins Housing Happiness Pay Scheme, said residents had paid for their stands years before receiving allocation letters.

He said the council’s Education, Housing and Community Services Committee resolved in 2019 to expedite the allocation and servicing of the land.

“Most of the members had paid deposits of $5,000 as far back as 2018 … Allocations were made in July 2019 after completion of payment of intrinsic land value. All the allocation letters and agreements of sale were signed in February 2020. These demolitions were illegal,” Jenje said.

ZimRights, a human rights organisation, said the demolitions raised questions about the rule of law and accountability.

Harare South MP Trymore Kanopula called for a halt to further demolitions until the land allocations had been audited and investigated. He also urged the government to present the findings of the commission of inquiry into state land sales to Parliament.

Parliament’s speaker referred the matter to the Ministry of Local Government and Public Works for action.

Minister Daniel Garwe said the government did not carry out demolitions and could not interfere with court processes. He acknowledged that the Harare City Council had approximately 5,000 demolition orders and said the government had sometimes tried to delay demolitions while seeking solutions.

For Nhete, however, official interventions offer little comfort. His house is gone, and he says he has no insurance to recover his investment.

“Unlike some who had home insurance, I didn’t have one,” he said. “I cannot recover the loss and pain. My hope is in the courts of law that Harare City Council must be held accountable and pay us back.”

The council says it is enforcing planning regulations against structures built without the necessary approvals. Commission of inquiry finds unauthorised land sales, weak administration and poor record-keeping

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: California voters reject proposed one-time tax on billionaires' wealth
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
California voters have rejected a first-in-the-nation tax on the net worth of billionaires following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders eager to stop their taxes from going up.

The measure’s failure is a win for Democratic leaders who opposed it, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who may run for president in 2028. Critics of the tax, known as Proposition 40, said it would have prompted ultrawealthy taxpayers to leave the state.

Most Californians vote by mail, and any ballot postmarked by Election Day that arrives within a week is counted, meaning it often takes days or even weeks for close races to be settled. The Associated Press determined Monday that ‘no’ had received enough votes to win.

The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone dumped more than $100 million into a political action committee working to defeat the measure.

The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would have been used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone toward education and food-assistance programs. SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the tax, said it was necessary to replace an estimated $100 billion the state will lose in federal healthcare funding over five years.

Proposition 40 was the nation’s biggest test yet on an idea progressives have long championed: raising taxes on the ultra-rich by targeting the main way they make their money — through their investments as opposed to the paychecks they receive from work.

The measure attracted support from liberal leaders beyond the state, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who rallied in cities across California in the race’s closing weeks to urge voters to pass it. The “Yes on 40” campaign did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.

Billionaires donated millions of dollars to a political action committee, Building a Better California, working to defeat the measure. The committee, which backed other measures on the ballot designed to nullify the tax, raised more than $333 million, nearly a third of which came from Brin.

The AP Voter Poll indicates that the majority of young voters in California — those younger than 30 — voted “yes” on Proposition 40. Older voters were far less supportive, with roughly 7 in 10 voters who were 65 and older saying they voted “no” on the ballot measure.

About half of voters with a household income under $100,000 annually said they were in support of the initiative. Closer to 6 in 10 California voters with an income of $100,000 or higher said they were opposed.

Brin, along with his fellow Google co-founder Larry Page, was among the billionaires who started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the possible tax. Another tech mogul, Mark Zuckerberg, said he would remain in the state for eight years and made a deal with Meta to help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.

Some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association, were part of a coalition opposing it. They were concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there was a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents.

“Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause,” the coalition said in a statement.

Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said before voting concluded Nov. 3 that he planned to vote against it.

“Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.”

Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.

Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”

Supporters of the California tax started running ads recently in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Virginia, states that will vote early in the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, that criticize Newsom for his opposition to the measure.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.title: Ipswich shopping centre shut down after copper thieves steal wiring
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.author: Kenji Sato
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Shops were closed at the Redbank Plains centre after the theft. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Town Square Redbank Plains has been left in darkness after thieves targeted electrical cables.

Business owners have been forced to shut down until power is restored.

Energex crews are providing assistance to the shopping centre's staff.

An Ipswich shopping centre has been cut from power this morning after copper thieves stole about 200 metres of wire.

Town Square Redbank Plains told shopkeepers via email that thieves had stolen critical earthing cables needed to safely power the site.

Aida, who runs a sushi restaurant in the centre, said her inventory would spoil throughout the day if it was not refrigerated.

"We have meat, fish, vegetables, things like that," Aida said.

"It's sad," Aida said.

Business owners say refrigerated stock will spoil. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Aida said shopping centre management staff had told her that they hoped to have the power up and running by about 5pm, by which point the food would have spoiled.

Sam, who runs the local barber shop with his brother, said it was a financial blow for his family.

The barber shop was left in darkness. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

"I thought, 'Man, we're going to lose so much money, so many customers,'" Sam said.

"We still need to give our employees the full day's pay, brother."

The Aldi and Woolworths supermarkets also lost power and were closed.

Energex spokesperson Danny Donald said it was the shopping centre's private wiring, and had not affected the public network.

He said Energex crews were on site to assist the shopping centre's staff.

Mr Donald said the copper theft was a selfish and dangerous act.

"They've made a mess of the shopping centre's network and put their own lives at risks in the meantime," Mr Donald said.

"We've had deaths and severe injuries this year from people giving it a go."

The Redland Plains Dental is offline and has been redirecting calls to its Ipswich centre.

Redbank Plains Town Centre declined to comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/o.title: Rogue AI accessed Medicare data but broke no laws
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/o.author: Clare Armstrong
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Government

Anthony Albanese says the government will introduce mandatory safety and security standards for AI developers.  (ABC News: Toby Hunt )

OpenAI appears not to have broken the law when its AI agent hacked a Medicare website.

Labor will introduce mandatory safety and security standards for AI developers, backed by a new regulator with the power to impose significant penalties on big tech.

The government will also pursue mandatory reporting of incidents involving AI.

OpenAI appears to have broken no laws when a rogue artificial intelligence agent gained unauthorised access to Medicare data, with the federal government now moving to close the legal gap.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced Labor will introduce mandatory safety and security standards for AI developers, backed by a new regulator with the power to impose significant penalties on tech companies that fail to comply.

It follows a rapid review into the OpenAI breach earlier this year, when the company's autonomous AI agents accessed non-public Medicare statistics through a Services Australia portal.

Mr Albanese said the government had accepted all 18 recommendations from the review, which included considering options to strengthen criminal laws, such as introducing a standalone "failure to prevent" offence.

"The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast-changing world," he said.

The government has accepted all 18 recommendations from the review.  (ABC News: Toby Hunt )

The review, which is yet to be publicly released, also recommended Australia consider "mandatory" and "time-bound" reporting of breaches or other harms caused by AI.

Mr Albanese said the government's AI national standards, which are due to be unveiled by the end of this year, would mandate a "proper mode of notification" for incidents.

The OpenAI breach occurred in June, but the company did not detect it until August and only notified the government via a low-level public email inbox in September.

OpenAI's delayed reporting of an autonomous agent breaching a government website has strengthened Australia's push for tougher AI safety and disclosure rules.

Mr Albanese said while no personal information was accessed by the OpenAI agents, the incident was "completely unacceptable" and "can't be allowed to happen again".

The prime minister said the government would establish a new AI safety regulator that would be able to enforce "significant penalties" on companies doing the "wrong thing".

"I've been very clear, our task is to make sure that we shape AI, rather than AI shape us," Mr Albanese said.

"We've seen what happened in other parts of the world without guardrails or standards.

"Social license has slipped while safety and security have been undermined."

The Australian Federal Police has confirmed in a question on notice to a parliamentary inquiry into AI that no criminal prosecution or investigations had commenced in relation to the OpenAI incident because there had been no "formal report of a crime".

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Australia's criminal law needs to account for the actions of AI systems.

"It should never be the case that there's an argument that someone didn't know the computer was loaded," he said.

"We need to make sure that the criminal law is up to date for how this new technology is able to act."

Mr Burke said the time between a cyber vulnerability being detected and then exploited was previously about two and a half years, but with the advent of AI that window had narrowed to about 10 hours.

"That difference means we need to make sure that our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology and also make sure that we're able to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do."

Defence Minister Richard Marles said one of the "central" recommendations from the rapid review was the need for Australia to engage with frontier companies.

"This is not a technology that we can run away from if we want to maximise our agency, if we want to maximise the benefit for Australians, the way in which we can shape AI, but the way in which we can put in place protections in respect of AI, we must engage," he said.

Australia is among the countries being touted as a potential second training ground for frontier AI models, though tech companies have argued changes to copyright laws would be required.

Artists have called on Labor not to water down protections, with singer Jimmy Barnes this week suggesting the AI companies should "go and f**k themselves".

Mr Albanese attempted to reassure Barnes by saying he should refer to a speech the prime minister gave in July, vowing to protect the arts.

"We will make sure that, as I said there … one, that artists need to have control over their work. And secondly, that they need to be compensated if their work is used.

"My position certainly hasn't changed on any of that."
