BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Women's Health

WA mum Morgan has shared her difficult postpartum experience amid an inquiry into women's health.  (Supplied)

A Perth mother has described the weeks following the birth of her first child as one of the most challenging times of her life.

She is among hundreds of mums around the country who have shared their experiences of postpartum care as part of a federal inquiry into women's health.

The inquiry is also looking into other aspects of women's health care, including pain conditions and fertility treatments.

Morgan's first experiences of motherhood were amongst the most challenging times of her life.

A lack of support left her feeling forgotten and overwhelmed to the point that she did not think she could ever have another child.

"I was sleep-deprived, I had no idea what I was doing. There was a lot of conflicting or different advice from the midwives in the hospital about breastfeeding," she said.

"That kind of led into a number of weeks where our daughter was very difficult to feed, wasn't gaining weight appropriately, and it was incredibly stressful."

Morgan received more support during the birth of her second child. (ABC News: Georgia Nicolau)

Morgan is among hundreds of women who have shared their experiences of postpartum care as part of a federal inquiry, which is also looking into other elements of women's health care, including pain conditions and fertility treatments.

Morgan said her experience prompted her to train as a postpartum doula — someone who provides emotional, physical and practical support to new mothers.

Her experience around the birth of her second child was a lot smoother after moving from regional Victoria back to Perth, where she had more support as well as access to midwifery continuity of care.

The South Australian Labor senator hopes to encourage women around Australia to share their own experiences and help shape health reforms.

"It kind of made me realise, 'Oh, this is what people talk about when they talk about the newborn love bubble'.

"I actually felt it, whereas the first time it just felt hard and horrible and I thought 'I could never do this again'."

Morgan has called for more comprehensive postpartum care and education, particularly in regional and rural areas.

WA mothers have given evidence to the federal inquiry into women's health in Perth this week.  (ABC News: Georgia Nicolau)

Senator Marielle Smith, who is chairing the inquiry, said more than 2,000 submissions had been received from women, parents and advocates.

Senator Marielle Smith pushed for the inquiry afer sharing her own experiences of postpartum anxiety.  (ABC News: Georgia Nicolau)

"What that tells me is that women have been waiting for the opportunity to have their voices heard," she said.

She said "too many women feel let down" by postpartum care, with concerns ranging from accessing a lactation consultant to timely mental health support.

"These are stories which sadly aren't unique to Western Australia, they're coming through our hearings right across the country," Ms Smith said.

Julia Jones, an educator at Newborn Mothers who has worked in postpartum care for two decades, said mums were often neglected following the birth of their baby.

"When the inquiry was called, it was honestly like such a relief to have someone finally notice and pay attention to mums and ask if mums are OK," she said.

Julia Jones says "overwhelmed" mums need more non-clinical support.  (ABC News: Georgia Nicolau)

Ms Jones said the inquiry created potential for improved non-clinical support for mothers.

“A normal mum doesn't really get much support in postpartum at all unless she reaches a particular clinical threshold when she can receive medical interventions,” she said.

“But there's this huge majority of mothers who are overwhelmed, they're exhausted, they are lonely, they don't know what's normal.

“I'd really like mums to travel through this enormous life transition with some more companionship and emotional support and also a better understanding of what to expect during postpartum.”

Hearings are scheduled across the country until the end of the year, and the inquiry's final report is due in August 2027.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Top yen forecaster predicts ¥147 per dollar as rate gap narrows
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Eru Ishikawa
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Neil Parker has spent nearly three decades tracking the yen, through financial crises and sharp currency swings. Now, the top dollar-yen forecaster in Bloomberg’s latest rankings sees the Japanese currency rallying toward ¥147 per dollar next year as Japan’s interest-rate gap with the U.S. narrows.

His call puts him at the bullish end of a deeply divided market. While Parker sees the yen strengthening to around ¥155 by year-end before appreciating further, Bloomberg’s top forecaster in the previous quarter sees it weakening as far as ¥170 next year.

At the heart of the divergence is Japan’s interest-rate outlook. Parker expects the Bank of Japan to raise its benchmark rate from 1.25% to at least 2%, potentially 2.25%, a more aggressive outlook for tightening than much of the market expects. The Federal Reserve, meanwhile, may raise interest rates once more in December before stopping at around the 4.00-4.25% range, according to Parker.

“Japan may prove to be an outlier in terms of the Bank of Japan actually delivering on its promise to bring interest rates into line with where inflation is,” said Parker, head of economics and market strategy at foreign-exchange and payments firm TTT Moneycorp Limited.

Japanese market participants are divided over whether stronger inflation prompts faster tightening by the central bank. Japan’s consumer price index excluding fresh food and energy, a metric closely monitored by the BOJ as a gauge of underlying inflation, advanced 2.4% in September. Parker said that a pickup to 2.6% or higher could prompt a stronger central bank response and speed the path for tightening. He also isn’t convinced the central bank will move as soon as December.

That difference in the pace of tightening underpins his yen forecast. Another roughly 50 basis points of narrowing in Japan’s interest-rate gap with the U.S. — roughly the amount Parker expects by the middle to latter part of next year — could be enough to recalibrate investor expectations, he said.

“Investors aren’t necessarily going to become overweight in Japanese assets,” he said. “They just need to be less underweight.”

The yen has averaged around ¥158 per dollar this year and weakened to as far as ¥163.99 in July before Japanese and U.S. authorities intervened. Sharp market moves have tested Parker’s forecasts, but he is reluctant to change his outlook unless the economic fundamentals underpinning it have shifted.

In making his forecasts, Parker compares market expectations for interest rates and inflation with his own, looking for gaps that can inform his currency forecasts.

“One thing I do is I try and block out a lot of the noise,” he said. “I’m focused on no more than a few factors around the macro, rather than all of the speeches or commentaries or anything else that you will hear from both Japan and also other major economic jurisdictions.”

Using a similar approach, Parker also topped Bloomberg’s euro-yen forecast rankings, though he says his call was helped by a longstanding bearish view of Europe’s economy and some luck.

“The euro-yen forecast has been more fortuitous in some respects than dollar-yen,” he said, pointing to his negative view on the euro amid aggressive interest rate cuts and a lack of economic resilience in Europe. “Dollar-yen I think you can follow the macro a lot more.”

Parker began his career in financial markets in 1995 and has followed the yen and other major currencies for decades. He joined London-based TTT Moneycorp in 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile. TTT Moneycorp is a foreign-exchange and payments firm that also topped Bloomberg’s latest EUR/USD and USD/CHF forecast rankings.

Making yen forecasts was easier earlier in his career when the currency more closely followed the macro, Parker said. Still, he doesn’t find the yen particularly difficult to predict today, pointing to a Japanese central bank that is more reactive to data, particularly around inflation.

“The construct around currency forecasting is not where you see things going,” said Parker. “It’s where you see things going relative to where the rest of the market thinks.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Japan mulls expanding cyberdefense monitoring to domestic communication
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
To be able to better detect cyberattacks targeting Japan, the government and the ruling bloc are considering a law revision to allow communications to be monitored between entities within the country, according to ruling party officials.

Currently, the laws on active cyberdefense, designed to prevent major cyberattacks before they occur, only allow communications between foreign countries via Japan, or those between Japan and foreign countries, to be monitored. Ruling party members argue that this does not provide sufficient information to prevent attacks.

The government and the Liberal Democratic Party-led ruling bloc began discussing the proposed revision on Monday, following the recent series of personal data breaches. On Friday, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi instructed members of a ministerial meeting on cybersecurity to consider revising the laws, alongside the creation of an emergency response package.

The government will “conduct discussions from the perspective of strengthening information-gathering capabilities,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a news conference on Monday.

Japan’s active cyberdefense program is centered on monitoring communications, entering attackers’ systems and neutralizing threats, and strengthening public-private cooperation.

Specifically, the government will monitor communications in cyberspace from before attacks are executed. When signs of a potential attack are detected, the police and the Self-Defense Forces will hack into the attackers’ servers and neutralize threats.

Japan plans to begin monitoring communications by next autumn after provisions linked to the neutralizing operations and public-private collaboration entered into force last month.

“We must consider the law revision while taking the ruling bloc’s position into account,” a government official said.

Keitaro Ono, a senior member of the LDP’s cybersecurity panel, told a meeting of the group Monday that revising the laws would be “only natural given the current situation” and that the party would develop measures to ensure an effective response.

“There is room for debate over whether we can respond effectively while keeping communications within Japan a black box,” former digital transformation minister Masaaki Taira told reporters after the meeting.

Meanwhile, some have questioned whether monitoring communications is consistent with the constitutional guarantee of the secrecy of communication. The government and ruling bloc plan to have careful discussions, seeking opinions from experts.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: The government and the ruling bloc are considering a law revision to allow communications to be monitored between entities within the country. Currently, the laws on active cyberdefense only allow communications between foreign countries via Japan, or those between Japan and foreign countries to be monitoring. The government will monitor communications in cyberspace from before attacks are executed.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Jaguars acquire DT Jordan Davis as part of three-trade overhaul
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
The Jacksonville Jaguars made their biggest move yet in a defensive overhaul Monday, acquiring defensive tackle Jordan Davis from the Philadelphia Eagles.

Jacksonville sent a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round selection to Philadelphia in return, according to ESPN.

The Davis deal was Jacksonville’s third acquisition of the day ahead of Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline. The AFC South-leading Jaguars also landed former Pro Bowl safety Jessie Bates III from the Atlanta Falcons and defensive tackle Davon Godchaux from the New Orleans Saints.

Davis, 26, signed a three-year, $78 million extension with Philadelphia in March that keeps him under contract through 2029. The former No. 13 overall pick has 193 tackles, 17 tackles for loss, 15 quarterback hits, 11 passes defended and 9.5 sacks in five seasons with the Eagles.

He also appeared in nine playoff games for Philadelphia and recorded a sack in the Eagles’ Super Bowl LIX victory.

“Jordan’s impact on the field can be felt on every down,” Jaguars general manager James Gladstone said. “This is a well-rounded premier player and person. We’re excited to add him to the team.”

Bates was acquired in exchange for a second-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft and a fifth-round selection in 2028. Jacksonville gave up a conditional 2028 sixth-round pick to New Orleans for Godchaux, who can become a free agent at the end of the season.

Bates is also in the final season of a four-year contract and would become an unrestricted free agent in March unless Jacksonville offers an extension.

He will help Jacksonville address a need after the team lost safety Eric Murray to a season-ending elbow injury.

Godchaux is in the final year of an $11 million contract. He and Davis reinforce an interior defensive line that lost nose tackle DaVon Hamilton to a season-ending torn quadriceps.

Godchaux, 31, was being used sparingly by the Saints and logged only 12 total snaps in Sunday’s overtime win against the Browns.

Bates, 29, has 60 tackles, three forced fumbles and one interception in nine games, all starts, this season.

He signed with the Falcons in 2023 and enjoyed a Pro Bowl season that year. He has started all 60 games since arriving in Atlanta, totaling 14 interceptions and 11 forced fumbles.

Bates has totaled 871 tackles, 28 interceptions, 14 forced fumbles and four fumble recoveries in 139 career games, all starts, with the Cincinnati Bengals and Falcons.

Jacksonville (6-2) enters Week 10 with a three-game lead in the AFC South.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.summary: Jordan Davis is Jacksonville's third acquisition of the day ahead of Tuesday's NFL trade deadline. The Jaguars also signed Jessie Bates III and Davon Godchaux from the Atlanta Falcons. The defensive tackle is in the final year of his contract with the Eagles.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Brady ends three-year spell as Birmingham City investor
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Janina Nuno Rios
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Tom Brady has ended his three-year involvement as a minority investor in Birmingham City, the English second-tier club said on Monday, thanking the seven-time Super Bowl champion for his support.

“Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the Club over the last three years,” the Championship side said in a statement.

“It was truly amazing to have someone with Tom’s experience and passion associated with the Club, and the Club looks forward to continuing to build on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community.”

The club gave no reason for Brady’s departure and did not specify what would happen to his stake.

The former NFL quarterback joined Birmingham’s ownership group in August 2023 through a partnership with Knighthead Capital Management, becoming a minority investor and chairman of a new advisory board.

Brady, 49, also holds minority stakes in the NFL’s Las Vegas Raiders and the WNBA’s Las Vegas Aces.

His departure comes as Birmingham enjoys a strong Championship campaign, sitting top of the standings on goal difference with 29 points after 15 matches.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: One Nation dumps Victorian election candidate who praised Adolf Hitler as ‘GOAT’
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Henry Belot
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Party disendorses Preston candidate Franco Guardiani after social media posts emerge

One Nation Victoria has disendorsed a candidate whose private social media account described Adolf Hitler as the “GOAT” and claimed that “importing Islam is making pedophilia legal”.

In a now deleted social media post, the party’s candidate for Preston, Franco Guardiani, commented on a social media post on X asking people to: “Describe Hitler in one word? Be brutally honest”.

Guardiani then replied with the acronym GOAT, which stands for greatest of all time.

The party was made aware of Guardiani’s social media posts on Tuesday morning and disendorsed him a short time later. A party official discussed the posts with Guardiani and confirmed they were real.

“At a time when Jewish Australians are experiencing unprecedented persecution, we are appalled that these comments have been made,” said the party’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering.

“As soon as we became aware, we acted. Preston candidate Franco Guardiani is no longer part of our party.

“Anyone who holds such views is on notice: they do not have a place in One Nation.”

The former candidate’s X account contains several Islamophobic comments including references to bulldozing or setting fire to mosques.

The account has also engaged with posts by the anti-immigrant group Kights Templar International.

It is unclear how the candidate’s social media history was not detected during candidate selection and vetting processes. The party has claimed to have invested time and money into improving this process.

Guardiani is no longer listed as a One Nation candidate on the party’s official website.

Guardiani has been contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/e.title: Family 'gutted' as sentences cut for police officers who assaulted woman
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/e.author: Amy Greenbank
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/e.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Nathan Black (left) and Timothy John Trautsch (right) were sentenced in July 2025. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Two former police officers who violently assaulted a mentally ill woman have had their prison sentences reduced.

The woman's family told the ABC the decision has left them "gutted".

The court described the assault as showing a "shocking lack of humanity".

The family of a Sydney woman who was dragged by her hair, kicked, stomped on and repeatedly pepper sprayed by police while experiencing psychosis, say they are "gutted" the officers have had years slashed from their prison sentences.

Both men were jailed in August 2025 over the assault of Jodi Knott.

Nathan Black's five year nine-month maximum sentence was reduced to three years, two-months, with his non-parole period ending in September 2027.

Timothy Trautsch's maximum sentence was cut from five years, six-months to three. He becomes eligible for parole in August 2027.

Both men could be released from jail as early as next year, after successfully appealing their sentences in the NSW Court of Criminal Appeal on Monday.

Nichole Allen, left, watches the police body-worn camera video of her cousin's assault. (Four Corners)

Ms Knott's cousin Nichole Allen said the family was "gutted" by the decision.

"It's heart-wrenching… a real kick in her guts," Ms Allen said.

The original sentencing judge found both the assault and the misuse of pepper spray were aggravated by "gratuitous cruelty".

WARNING: Graphic violence. Police body-worn camera video of the officers' attack on Jodi.

However, the NSW Court of Criminal Appeal ruled that was an error in relation to the assault because the brutality of the violence had already been factored into its seriousness, creating a risk of "double counting".

The judges upheld the finding that the officers' misuse of pepper spray was gratuitously cruel and maintained that their common assaults were "…at the top of the range" of objective seriousness.

Justice Hament Dhanji said the officers had displayed a "shocking lack of humanity" towards Ms Knott.

"The applicants held a position of authority which was abused. But these things were all known and taken into account by the sentencing judge."

Police had been responding to a Triple Zero (000) call about a naked woman sitting beside the road at Emu Plains.

Jodi died of cancer in 2024. (Supplied)

The court found the officers became impatient and frustrated while trying to get her into an ambulance, ultimately resorting to what the judges described as "needless violence".

"This was a problem of the applicants' own making though their impatience, failure to call for assistance and, it seems, impoverished understanding of the nature of psychosis and how to deal with it," Justice Dhanji said.

"But those matters did not have the result that the brutality which followed was such as to make out the aggravating feature of gratuitous cruelty for the purposes of the Sentencing Act."

The NSW Court of Criminal Appeal also found the men had demonstrated remorse, and accepted their time in custody had been "more onerous" given their former employment as police officers and their mental health conditions.

Both had been threatened by inmates and were "extremely fearful," the court heard.

Ms Knott died of cancer 18 months after the 2023 attack.

The family of a woman brutally assaulted by police in a Sydney street has fought to have body-worn camera vision released.

Police body-worn footage capturing her treatment later formed part of an ABC Four Corners investigation into NSW policing, in which her relatives pushed for reform to the way police respond to people experiencing acute mental illness.

In July the NSW government introduced a new health-led response model for mental health emergencies, moving away from police-led interventions.

"She's been let down but hopefully it will be safer for other people going forward," Ms Allen said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.title: Sexual offence investigations sidelined by property crime, report finds
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.author: Jessica Black and Sarah Richards
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Sexual Offences

The report said officers' time was being co-opted by less serious crime.  (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Of 19,000 sexual offences reported to Queensland police between 2017 and 2022, about a third were withdrawn.

A report by the Australian Institute of Criminology looks at why so many reports do not proceed.

Investigators say organisational and political priorities like youth and property crime are being prioritised above sexual offences.

Queensland detectives are having to prioritise investigating property crime over rape, with more than half of reported sexual offences withdrawn or unsolved, according to a new study.

More than 19,000 sexual offences reported to Queensland Police Service (QPS) between 2017 and 2022 were analysed to find out why so many were withdrawn, or labelled unfounded.

Of those reports a third were withdrawn, a fifth were unsolved and about one in 10 were considered unsubstantiated, the Australian Institute of Criminology study found.

Just over a third were solved.

Investigators told researchers organisational and political priorities like youth and property crime were being prioritised above sexual offences, as officers juggled crimes from fraud to petty theft.

"We have to prioritise certain non-sexual offences even though we might have a more serious offence ... it’s very political," one said.

An investigator said officers' time was being co-opted by less serious crime.

"The serious jobs like sexual assault, they’re life changing, life ruining stuff. And they’re not getting any attention at all because some kid walked into a bottle shop and stole a bottle of vodka, and we end up dealing with that instead."

Another told researchers, "the biggest problem for rape complaints is property crime".

"We find ourselves wrapped in that for two, three, four weeks, then days off, then DV training, or some other thing, and we go, 'Hang on, this poor person, we haven't done anything with their complaint for six months'," they said.

Historic sexual offences were "put on the backburner" because of unmanageable workloads, according to investigators.

Too few officers had sexual offence training, and sexual assault investigation kits were often difficult to access, with some survivors having to travel and wait for hours — only to find there was no-one to carry them out or being told to do their own swabs, they said.

One said: "For us to get a forensic nurse into the hospital, you could be waiting with the victim till seven o’clock in the morning … you get victims just wanting to walk out, they’re over it."

According to QPS data, only about a fifth of reports involved investigators with sexual offence training, and a sexual assault investigation kit was performed in fewer than 15 per cent.

More than two-thirds of survivors were not referred to victim support services.

Meanwhile survivors who were given a sexual assault investigation kit or who dealt with sexual offence trained officers were less likely to withdraw their reports, and their complaints were also less likely to be considered unsubstantiated, the study found.

Queensland Sexual Assault Network chief executive Angela Lynch said the findings were "shocking" but unsurprising.

"Victim-survivors really feel de-prioritised in the system, and obviously that's what that report is showing," she said.

Queensland Sexual Assault Network CEO Angela Lynch. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

In 2024, 40,087 survivors made reports to Australian police, the highest number recorded in 32 years, Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows.

One of the largest increases was in Queensland.

Ms Lynch said sexual violence offences need to take a higher priority.

"The whole system has to be better resourced," she said.

"Obviously police are calling for better resourcing, but to support the police and to support victim survivors that come forward, you would also have to, as a matter of priority, increase resourcing for specialist sexual violence services."

Researchers made five recommendations — for more trained officers, embedded assault service workers in police stations, and a "one-stop shop" with police, prosecutors and health services.

They also recommended training for all physicians in every health and hospital service to carry out forensic medical examinations.

QPS has been contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/p.title: 'You can't fix this': Navigating the grief of losing a child
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/p.author: Amy Sheehan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Troy says the death of his son Kurtis (far right) was life altering. (Supplied)

Our recent story about parents who have experienced the loss of a child struck a chord with many readers, who then shared their own journey with us.

This is how they've navigated the grief.

"Five years ago, my son Kurtis went to sleep and didn't wake up.

I get asked all the time, "How do you live with not knowing what happened?"

But the way I look at it is simple. What if they told you it was something that you could have avoided? How would your life be?

I'm not super religious, but I just think if God needed someone for a little job, they chose the right kid.

When I get up to heaven and see him again, I'm going to be so proud of him.

Troy and his younger son Henderson create a public art memorial for Kurtis each year. (Supplied)

I do things that help keep me connected with Kurtis. I swim, I watch videos of him, I talk about him a lot.

We used to skateboard together all the time. One day, I did the same lap of the path 80 times with tears in my eyes. I didn't care what people thought.

I also needed to get out of my job in real estate because I didn't know how to get on the phone and pretend to be happy.

My younger son Henderson and I also build an art memorial each year on Kurtis' anniversary, and we leave it there so people can see it and get to know him.

For anyone who's trying to support someone that's going through this grief, you just need to understand that you can't fix it.

You've got to let people be.

You'd be better off spending time helping them fold clothes. All the basics are the hard things to keep up with when you're going through it.

And if you're the one grieving, base yourself around the people who are helpful and stay away from ones who are negative."

"My wife and I lost our son Andrew on Christmas Eve, in 2021, when he and a friend were electrocuted in an accident on a property near Goulburn.

Andrew, who was 31, was due to get married some weeks later.

Every morning I would wake up after Andrew's death and my body would have to relive the pain.

This went on for two and a half years. It was exhausting.

Andrew Dornan died in 2021 in an electrical accident. (Supplied)

I think my wife and I were both very fortunate because people really did embrace us.

We were supported, and people listened to us in our grief.

I was encouraged by my family to go back to work as a church minister after having six months off.

Work really helped because it distracted me, and distraction is important.

Having experienced that grief gave me an insight which I didn't otherwise have.

I can sit with someone and intuitively understand their pain in a way that I couldn't before.

It's a loss you have to somehow embrace.

[Embrace] is an odd word to use and that's why I use it, because I think in a sense I had to embrace the death of Andrew, I had to accept it.

We light a candle for him on the 24th of each month.

Needless to say, those times are hard.

My wife and I simply close the front door and keep to ourselves on those days."

Anne (not her real name) — 64

"My teenage daughter died on the way to a sports tournament 20 years ago in Tasmania.

It still impacts me when I hear about a young person who has died.

One of the worst things was dealing with the media and public voyeurism. I had a call from a reporter less than an hour after she died.

The more people want to know, the more pressure there is on families to give information.

I was told two years after it happened, 'You should be getting over it by now.'

Women who have lost children talk about continuing in the wake of such grief, and how people stepped up, or stepped away.

But someone doesn't just stop grieving. There's always going to be triggers — every birthday, every Christmas, every Easter.

It's a very hollow thing to go through.

We are all different and therefore deal with grief in different ways.

If you wanted to talk to someone about it, the simple question is, 'Is it OK to ask you some questions about your child or your grief?'

I love talking about my daughter with her friends and family as it keeps her alive in my memory.

We need to talk about death more so we can cope better when someone dies.

There are countries that celebrate death. It seems strange, but I think it's healthy.

If you go and talk to a professional about your grief, or someone from a support group, if you don't click with them, that's OK, but don't stop there.

Because that's what happened to me, I went, 'This doesn't feel right.'

I think it's really important to follow up and not be scared to try again.

I found talking to someone who I connected with really important, and I still do it."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/p.title: Justice system criminalising mental illness, psychiatrists say
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/p.author: Kirstie Wellauer and Joanna McCarthy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Dr Ian Korbel says Australia is criminalising people instead of treating them. (Supplied)

The peak body for psychiatrists says prisons should not be isolating suicidal people in so-called "safe cells", calling for a health-led response instead.

It says the justice system should be diverting mentally ill people into treatment, after the ABC revealed dozens of deaths in NSW custody were linked to mental health care failings.

The coroner investigating the death of Aboriginal woman Tammy Shipley, who died under 24-hour watch in a safe cell, is still to deliver her full findings.

Australia's peak psychiatrists' body has backed calls to transform mental health care in NSW prisons, including an end to isolating suicidal prisoners in so-called "safe cells".

It follows an ABC investigation into mentally ill inmates who have died after being isolated in a safe cell, purportedly for their own protection.

Readers are advised that this article includes the names and images of Indigenous people who have died, used with family permission.

"Safe cells are a custodial response rather than a health response," Dr Ian Korbel, chair of the Royal Australian New Zealand College of Psychiatrists (RANZCP) NSW branch, told the ABC.

"What people at risk of suicide should have is good, close support with nursing staff, psychologists and psychiatrists. Sometimes they might need medication.

"Often they'll need support and they'll need to be preferably in a cell with other people, rather than by themselves."

Earlier this week, forensic psychiatrist Dr Kerri Eagle called for prison health agency Justice Health, an arm of the NSW health department, to be the lead agency managing mentally ill prisoners.

"It is not appropriate for Corrective Services to be managing those health conditions because their goals are security and law enforcement," she said.

Dr Eagle is a clinical director at Justice Health but was speaking as a private practitioner.

Kerri Eagle says Justice Health workers must defer to Corrections on security matters and are only "visitors in their house". (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

Currently, at-risk inmates are assessed by a team of two CSNSW staff and one Justice Health worker, and inmates sent to safe cells are monitored by guards.

Dr Korbel agreed health workers, not correctional officers, should be assessing and monitoring prisoners with serious mental illness.

"I've worked in the prison system myself, I've seen that we have many caring and good guards that work in the system too, but they're not trained to deal with the sorts of psychiatric problems that we're seeing in prison."

In Victoria, Indigenous groups also want oversight of prison health care transferred to the health department, as recommended by the Yoorrook Justice Commission, with a model of care led by Aboriginal community-controlled health organisations.

Last week, the ABC revealed that 48 NSW coronial inquests since 2015 had identified failures in the care or supervision of people with mental illness. Of these, 14 related to the death of an Indigenous person.

Tracy Mackander thought the coronial inquest into her son Bailey's death in custody would bring change. Instead, it brought more heartache. An ABC investigation can reveal a prison system failing its most vulnerable.

These include interim findings into the case of Tammy Shipley, a 47-year-old Aboriginal woman with schizophrenia who died from water intoxication after spending 10 nights in a monitored safe cell.

She was the third NSW prisoner with schizophrenia to die from polydipsia in less than two years, with 35-year-old Daniel Turnbull also dying in a safe cell just two months earlier.

The RANZCP wants greater focus on diverting people with severe mental illness out of the justice system and into treatment.

Dr Korbel cited a 2019 UNSW study that found NSW prisoners with psychosis who received a court treatment order rather than a sanction were less likely to reoffend.

"We see a lot of people with serious mental illness … who are homeless, living on the streets, and that puts them at risk of committing relatively minor crimes just to survive," he said.

"When they go into care, their rates of recidivism decrease, they can access supports and housing … and we can see them become functioning members of society."

Giancarlo de Vera, CEO of BEING Mental Health Consumers, said the mental health crisis behind bars followed years of under-investment in community care.

They pointed to internal NSW Health documents, released last month, which estimated there was a $600 million annual shortfall for frontline mental health staff.

"We are treating the justice system and prisons as a de facto mental health system," they said.

Giancarlo de Vera says the ABC's revelations about failures in prison mental health care are "unsurprising but equally devastating".   (supplied)

Asked about Dr Eagle's comments on Monday, Premier Chris Minns defended the delivery of mental health care in NSW prisons.

"It may be not reasonable in all circumstances for a prisoner in psychological distress to be seen by a psychiatrist, at least initially," he said.

"Most of the interaction is with prison staff and is with Corrections officers and that's the nature of prison."

A Corrective Services spokesperson previously told the ABC it "adheres to strict legislative and regulatory frameworks to safely, securely and humanely manage people within its facilities."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.title: Canberrans share safety concerns amid violent incidents in city's south
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.author: Niddal Mustafa
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Opposition Leader Mark Parton cast doubt over reported crime trends. (ABC News: Niddal Mustafa)

The Liberal opposition in Canberra has held a community forum to hear local views and experiences of crime, with some reporting they don't feel safe.

The Canberra Liberals and the Labor government are in disagreement over the state of crime in the ACT,  and Opposition Leader Mark Parton argues community reports defy current statistics.

Mr Parton is pushing for increased police powers and said legislation to raise the age of criminal responsibility to 14 had "gone a step too far".

About 100 locals have attended a Liberal-hosted community forum to discuss youth crime, following multiple violent incidents in Canberra's south.

Warning: This story discusses threats of violence and sexual assault.

The meeting in the suburb of Tuggeranong last night follows multiple violent incidents in the area, including a stabbing involving a student outside Lake Tuggeranong College last week.

A woman, Samantha, whose name has been changed due to safety concerns, told attendees her family was physically abused at an ACT Oztag event and that her son was allegedly shot at in a drive-by shooting last month.

"My son … in a state of complete 'wrong place, wrong time' was also one of the kids in the car that got shot at in Gordon six weeks ago," she told the meeting.

The suburb of Tuggeranong is located in Canberra's south. (ABC News)

Holding back tears, Samantha said her family had been targeted and harassed online in the weeks since the shooting, and had been living in fear.

"I have received death threats, we've had to board up our children's windows. They've said that they would come through our house, they would rape me, rape my daughter, shoot me, shoot my husband," she said.

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton addressed attendees at the meeting, telling them he was concerned about "what we're perceiving as an increase in the level of violent crime".

"I don't want this to be a hyper-political meeting but I'm here to tell you it's almost impossible for it not to be a political meeting," Mr Parton said.

Mr Parton told 666 ABC Radio Canberra that the statistics, which showed crime in the ACT had generally decreased, did not reveal the full story.

"I think they're rubbery because there are less people who are actually bothering to call and report crime," he said.

Community members voiced their fears to Liberal politicians at a recent forum. (ABC News: Niddal Mustafa)

He said community members had told him they were hesitant to call police and report disturbances.

Deputy Liberal leader Deborah Morris told the forum she would continue to push for the introduction of 'Jack's Law' to grant police increased powers to wand people without reasonable suspicion that they are carrying a weapon.

Jack's Law — named in honour of teenager Jack Beasley, who was stabbed and killed on the Gold Coast in 2019 while out with friends — was made permanent and expanded across all public places in Queensland in June 2025.

"Police would be able to go to that young person or whoever that individual might be, and do a very safe and dignified search of that individual … that would reveal whether they had any bladed instruments or weapons," Ms Morris said.

A global internet flaw is being blamed for delayed communication to parents after a student was attacked at a south Canberra school.

Mr Parton also told ABC Radio Canberra some legislation, including the raising of the age of criminal responsibility to 14, had "gone a step too far".

The ACT government has rejected previous calls from the Canberra Liberals to expand policing powers, citing a lack of evidence.

Australian Federal Police Association president Alex Caruana told the crowd his workforce was being stretched thin.

"We're not getting the priority and funding that we need," he said.

"Our members' time is being utilised helping the community in other ways because there isn't the resources out there across a broad section of services that the government should be funding."

According to the latest ACT Policing Annual Report, total offences in the 2025-26 financial year decreased by 5.5 per cent from 4,540 in 2024-25 to 4,291.

Two youths were charged this month after a stabbing incident outside the Lake Tuggeranong College. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

The number of "other offences against a person", which includes kidnapping, threatening behaviour and other dangerous and negligent acts, increased by 1.7 per cent in the same period.

On Friday, Police Minister Marisa Paterson said while the incidents are "deeply concerning", the statistics do not show an increase in youth violence.

"They have remained relatively stable over the past few years, so I think we keep that in perspective, but also we know very much that we need to do more to engage young people and divert young people from our justice system," she said.

The government is currently considering legislation to potentially expand police powers to allow for handheld metal detection wands.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.author: Nick Campton

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Jamayne Isaako is in the kicking form of his life ahead of the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Joe Allison)

As New Zealand's Jamayne Isaako lined up his conversion attempts in the World Cup semifinal against Tonga, he did so in the middle of a hurricane while it was raining sideways.

The Kiwi winger is one of rugby league's best goal-kickers, but even he admits the horrific weather took things away from him in Newcastle.

"I had no idea where I was aiming the ball," Isaako said.

But despite the conditions, Isaako kept slotting them — into the wind in the first half and bending them through like a boomerang in the second because right now, Jamayne Isaako can't miss.

His last kick from the sideline, when he hung the ball miles outside the right upright only for it to turn harder than even legendary New Zealand spin bowler Daniel Vettori ever managed, and go through with all his teammates there to celebrate, was his favourite, as the Kiwis stormed into the World Cup final with a 34-10 victory.

"I knew if I aimed it right, the shape would bring it back around, but I had no idea where they were going," Isaako said.

"I have a massive hook in my kick, so I aim a bit more right than most kickers, but I was just happy I got them.

"Particularly the last one, with all the boys behind me."

With the rugby league year ending after Sunday night's World Cup final, Isaako is about to finish one of the greatest-scoring seasons in the game's history.

Isaako's kicking, in atrocious conditions, was typically excellent in the semifinal win over Tonga. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

He was the NRL's top scorer in 2026, becoming just the fourth player ever to pass 300 points with his final total of 310 the third-highest single-season mark in league history.

Throw in a prolific and accurate World Cup campaign, in which he's kicked 36 goals from 38 attempts and scored personal hauls of 38 points against the Cook Islands and 26 against Fiji, and his total stat line for the season is 30 games, 26 tries and 145 goals at an 86.3 per cent success rate for a total of 394 points.

With New Zealand needing every edge they can find against Australia if they're to claim their second World Cup, Isaako's kicking form could prove crucial.

Between Cameron Munster, Reece Walsh and Kotoni Staggs, the Kangaroos have no shortage of kicking options for the final, but none of them are in Isaako's class.

Isaako's kicking could provide an edge for New Zealand in the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Staggs and Walsh have never spent a club season as a primary goal-kicker, while Munster, who took the tee in the semifinal win over Samoa and kicked six from eight, has a career success rate of 58.02 per cent.

Isaako, by contrast, has long been one of the NRL's elite boots and is in the kicking form of his life.

"This year has probably been the best for kicking for me," Isaako said.

"I've worked on it a lot, the last two years especially. The game is only getting quicker and if there's more tries, the two points add up quickly.

"It's something I pride myself on."

Isaako has worked closely with the legendary Daryl Halligan in the Kiwis camp each of the past four seasons, and the kicking guru likens his hook on the ball to Johnathan Thurston's.

Isaako was the NRL's leading pointscorer in 2026 for the third time in his career. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Like everyone else of a black-and-white persuasion, Halligan enjoyed Isaako's circus kicks to finish the semifinal but nominated his two strikes in the opening stanza, which gave New Zealand a crucial 12-10 half-time lead after running into the gale, as his most impressive.

"His first two kicks into the breeze in the first half were his best and he could have a bit of fun with the ones at the end when there was a bit less pressure," Halligan said.

"Jamayne is pretty similar to JT in a way with that curve. He's a buoyant guy like JT, even if he doesn't have the laugh."

Isaako credits Halligan with simplifying his kicking approach and while Halligan is quick to direct credit back to the Melbourne-bound winger, he isn't surprised to see the 30-year-old's accuracy improved as he's aged.

Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times, but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semifinal was a reminder of Goliath's power.

"There's not a lot of hard coaching this time of year, you're not going to change much and there's not much that needs to be changed," Halligan said.

"But goal-kickers get better as they get older. Why wouldn't they? They've ironed out the things they can do better.

"He makes good contact and puts a lot of work into his details. He knows where he's heading with it.

"The wind can play a factor if you want it to, but it won't change what he wants because he knows where it has to go."

History could beckon for Isaako on Sunday night in more ways than one.

He's currently level with Shaun Johnson on 225 points as New Zealand's all-time highest Test pointscorer and is all but certain to take outright possession of the record in the World Cup final.

It took all their power and all of Kalyn Ponga's brilliance and toughness, but after getting past Tonga in Newcastle, the World Cup is within New Zealand's grasp.

But Isaako would give every one of them back in a second if it would mean a Kiwi victory.

The Christchurch man is of Samoan descent and played one Test for the Toa in 2019 but has represented New Zealand ever since because of how the country changed his family's life, a debt he feels he can never repay.

"New Zealand is where I was born and raised, and I choose the black jersey because New Zealand gave my family an opportunity, like a lot of the Pacific Island boys in this team," Isaako said.

"To win a World Cup would be a dream come true. We know what it meant to the old boys who were there in 2008, we've been fortunate enough to have a few of them come into camp and tell us their story.

"Whenever we're able to represent the black jersey, it's an honour and a privilege and for a lot of us, it's the pinnacle.

"It would be huge for us as players to win, but more for our country."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Tears and joy as Ukrainian couple divided by occupation meet again
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Yuliia Dysa
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
KYIV – Larysa Ryndova hurried to see her husband as if they were going out on a first date — makeup on and perfume spritzed in the car.

It was the first time she had laid eyes on 68-year-old Serhiy in four and a half years — time he had spent trapped with others in the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.

“I can’t believe you are here,” Larysa, 72, kept repeating, her mascara smudged with tears after they embraced outside a hospital in Kyiv.

“Honestly, I can’t believe it, myself,” Serhiy replied.

They last saw each other in 2022 when Larysa fled to England to live with their son, three months into the occupation following Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine.

Serhiy stayed to look after the family home, ending up stuck in the town peppered with Russian-laid landmines and facing a mounting humanitarian crisis.

“We hoped for better. Turned out, it got ’better,’” he said sarcastically.

Oleshky’s residents described living through constant drone attacks and without power and heating. Things got even worse this spring, when food deliveries stopped.

Serhiy got out on Oct. 30 with hundreds of other residents, evacuated during a ceasefire that U.S. first lady Melania Trump was involved in brokering, with the additional involvement of Pope Leo.

For all the joy of seeing Larysa — and the prospect of being reunited with his three children and six grandchildren — he had found his escape from Oleshky a devastating wrench.

“Your heart is torn apart at the thought of leaving everything behind. How can you? Your home, your family, the cemetery — all your relatives are there,” he said.

“How will you ever visit their graves, keep them cared for?”

As Oleshky’s evacuees were moved by buses and planes through occupied land, Russia and Belarus, Larysa set out on her own 2,000-kilometer journey to meet Serhiy and bring him back with her to Britain.

“How haggard he looks,” she said when she saw the first pictures of her husband crossing into Ukraine. “It’s hard to recognize him.”

Serhiy called Oleshky a “zone of death” where life under occupation could depend on the mood of an individual Russian soldier.

He survived on humanitarian aid that he had stockpiled during the occupation — noodles, grains, sometimes canned meat and fish. He tried frying up flatbreads with flour stored before the war, riddled with weevils.

“Sometime around April (this year), the people who used to bring us food died — two men. After that, all food deliveries stopped completely. There was nothing,” Serhiy said over a cup of coffee in a Kyiv cafe.

Locals shared what they had. Some risked the dangerous 20-km journey on foot or bicycle to Radensk for supplies. Rare provisions were sold at severely inflated prices.

The local hospital ran out of supplies. Bodies were stacked up in the morgue as forensic experts refused to risk the journey to the town to perform autopsies.

“Bodies are just lying there. Everything is leaking. When my neighbor died, I carried his body in there, and the smell was absolutely horrific,” Serhiy said. “God forbid!”

Another neighbor asked him to bury her in her own courtyard if she ever got killed.

Serhiy said he probably would not have left the town himself had it not been for the evacuation. Landmines were laid out on all the roads and even in the town.

“They (Russian troops) had their own objective, as I understand it: to mine everything so they could keep everything under control,” he added.

“A lot of people were killed in Oleshky. Someone would go out to pick a cherry plum and get blown up. Someone else would pick up a mushroom or a nut and step on a landmine.”

Serhiy said Russian troops “had done a great job of cleaning up” to put on a show before the organized evacuations began. He didn’t see a single burnt-out car on the way.

He said he felt sure he could have survived another winter, despite the ordeal of occupation and food shortages.

Larysa rolled her eyes, still wet with tears.

“I’ll fatten him up with borscht and varenyky (dumplings),” she said.

The Bank of Japan’s brief record of the latest policy meeting indicated many board members see a near-term interest rate hike as necessary, signaling there’s a good chance for a December move.

“The Bank should decide on the next policy interest rate hike when it is possible without becoming overly cautious,” one of the nine board members said, according to the summary for the Oct. 29-30 meeting released Tuesday.

Following sustained price gains, Japan’s central bank has sped up the pace of rate hikes, with current expectations settling around a quarterly pace of borrowing cost increases. Details from Tuesday’s summary of opinions suggested a higher confidence in hiking again in December.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Taiwan says China is conducting ‘area denial’ drills in Western Pacific
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Ben Blanchard
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
TAIPEI – China is carrying out “area denial” drills in the Western Pacific involving one of its aircraft carriers and other naval formations, Taiwan Defense Minister Wellington Koo said on Tuesday, following a reported rise in Chinese activities.

China, which views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, regularly sends its warplanes and warships into the skies and waters around the island.

Last week, Taiwan National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu posted on his X account details of the deployments of more than 100 Chinese naval and Coast Guard ships operating off Taiwan, in the South China Sea, and into the Pacific.

Taiwan’s defense ministry last week also reported a large rise in the number of Chinese air force aircraft around Taiwan, though China has not formally declared any drills.

“China has indeed conducted area denial drills in the Western Pacific with the Liaoning carrier group and other naval training formations,” Koo told reporters at parliament.

Anti-access/area denial, or A2AD, refers to keeping an outside force from intervening in a conflict, which in the Taiwan context means stopping U.S. or other allied forces from coming to Taipei’s aid should Beijing attack.

China’s defense ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The ministry said last month that the Liaoning carrier’s training in the western Pacific was an annual routine to test long-range, open-ocean combat capabilities and was not directed at any particular country.

China’s drills come ahead of both the APEC summit in Shenzhen next week, where U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping again, and Taiwan’s local elections at the end of this month.

Koo said the military was keeping a close watch on what China was up to.

“We believe that this kind of military deterrence is intended to undermine peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region,” he added.

“We will use joint intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance means and exchange intelligence with allies to continuously monitor these activities and respond appropriately.”

China has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, though it says it would prefer “peaceful reunification.”

Taiwan’s government rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims, saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: German defense chief cautious over joining Japan-U.K.-Italy fighter jet project
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
BERLIN – German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius is cautious about his country joining a Japan-Britain-Italy project to develop a next-generation fighter jet model, German newspaper Handelsblatt reported Monday.

This marks a stark contrast with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s positive stance on the nation’s participation in the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP).

According to the online edition of Handelsblatt, some believe that Japan, Britain and Italy view Germany primarily as a financial contributor for the project, rather than an equal partner.

Against this background, Germany’s Federal Ministry of Defense and defense industry are apparently pushing for a similar cooperation arrangement with Sweden, which is being considered by the German government simultaneously with GCAP. In addition, the German side reportedly has issues with a GCAP member firm from Britain.

In an interview with German media released Saturday, Pistorius highlighted the need to scrutinize whether Germany’s GCAP participation would delay fighter development to an extent that would be unacceptable for the countries involved.

Germany will decide on a direction by March next year, he added, apparently keeping the option of collaboration with Sweden in mind.

https://www.dw.com/en/iran-war-oil-shock.title: Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows
https://www.dw.com/en/iran-war-oil-shock.text:
Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the trend.

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterwards, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind, the temporary emissions reversal, there's also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the COP31 climate conference.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5y.title: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5y.text:
Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.

"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."

Addressing reporters from the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.

Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.

This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.

The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.

Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.

Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.

"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.

Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.

In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".

Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.

Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.

Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.

Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.

Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".

While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

Trump hosted Qatari PM Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Auckland hit by swarms of bees after milder than usual New Zealand winter
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Beekeepers say they are fielding a record number of calls from people needing assistance in removing swarms

Engulfing parked cars and blanketing inner-city street signs – New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland, is in the midst of an unusually large bee swarming season, that experts say has been exacerbated by a milder than usual winter.

The Auckland Beekeepers Association says it is fielding five to 10 calls a day, requesting assistance to remove swarms of bees – with individual members of the association being contacted for help as well.

“In past years, it was under five a day,” said Bryan Lang, the association’s swarm control coordinator, adding the team has now dealt with at least 100 call-outs.

In October, a swarm plastered the back of a parked car in Birkenhead for two hours according to witnesses. A woman inside was napping at the time, Lang understands.

“I’m surprised she didn’t hear them because they’re pretty loud,” he said.

A month earlier, a swarm took over a sign at a busy intersection on Auckland’s major commercial thoroughfare, Queen Street, forcing pedestrians to reroute.

During spring and early summer, bees can “swarm” – a natural occurrence which sees part of a colony that has outgrown its hive abandon it in search of a new home or extra food. The mass of insects will temporarily find a place to land away from their hive, while scout bees search for an appropriate dwelling.

“As a beekeeper, you don’t want them to swarm because you’re losing two-thirds of your bees, and right at the time when they should be bringing honey in for you,” said Lang. “And it’s not great for your neighbours either.”

Public awareness is growing over why bees swarm, and what to do should one happen to take over part of your garden or street, and according to Lang, many are taking to social media bee swarming pages and local beekeeping clubs to appeal for help.

The association’s president, Ken Brown, says when bees swarm in the countryside, no one really notices, but “townies” are not so familiar.

“If you don’t know about bees – how they’re only defensive – then you might be intimidated with thousands of venomous insects flying around,” he said, adding that a colony of bees is at its most placid when swarming.

Brown believes a much milder winter and start to spring has led to bees swarming weeks earlier than usual, and larger numbers of bees splitting off from their hives. New Zealand experienced its third warmest winter on record in 2026, according to Earth Sciences NZ. Other parts of the world are seeing similar behavioural shifts in bees, including in North America, as global warming leads to hotter winters and spring.

“Beekeeping is much more unpredictable nowadays because you do have the extremes of weather and the different patterns. Every year is slightly different, but it’s actually even more different in recent times,” said Brown.

Milder temperatures over winter might mean a colony develops a larger brood of eggs, larvae and pupae. If they don’t succumb to varroa mite, a tiny and deadly parasite that attaches to honeybees and their brood, then the survivors will be “much stronger and ready to swarm sooner”, said Brown.

Prof Phil Lester, an entomologist and ecologist at Victoria University, said beekeepers have been active catching swarms in other parts of the country, including Wellington.

Unmanaged bee swarms that cannot be captured pose a risk to other honeybees or native bees if they are carrying varroa mite. Further, it can be a pain for beekeepers to lose their bees right when they are readying to produce honey.

Still, it could be a positive signal for this year’s bee populations, Lester said.

“It means they have been able to build up numbers and populations, earlier than perhaps they normally would do … its probably a good indication that it is a good bee year.”

Jensen Huang, the CEO and co-founder of the world’s most prominent chip company, has allegedly been honey-trapped by a suspected Chinese spy, and the news has struck the internet like a match to gasoline.

Huang has long been seen as a wife guy (or so everyone assumed). He and his wife, Lori, have been together since the 1980s, and both of their children work at Nvidia. Huang has been the closest thing the tech world has to a rock star, with fans lining up for selfies and autographs. Of all the AI overlords, the leather-jacket wearing Huang has seemed like the most level-headed and least erratic, which is why this plot twist has hit so hard.

The potential fallout is mind-boggling. Nvidia looms so large over the U.S. stock market that even the company’s domestic drama is a market risk. Countless AI startups depend on Nvidia chips, so any shake-up at the top would ripple far beyond the company. And Nvidia has no publicly disclosed succession plan, so if Huang leaves, it’s unclear who’d take over.

Is this how the AI bubble bursts? It’s a question that will be answered in time, but in the meantime, a more pressing matter demands our attention: ranking the funniest memes about the scandal, with bonus points for AI images presumably generated using Nvidia chips.

There’s admittedly a lot to choose from, ranging from “500 Days of Summer” jokes to jokes about divorce lawyers to an AI-adaptation of the music video for Usher‘s song “Confessions Pt. II,” a track about cheating. Another person created a viral AI video that recreates the Coldplay concert where a startup CEO was caught on the Jumbotron hugging a colleague.

Huang publicly confessed to the affair just yesterday, so the internet has the rest of the week to get creative.

For the sake of the US economy I really hope Jensen's wife can be chill about this.

“AI will replace you”. I’d like to see AI become CEO of a multitrillion company and destroy its marriage and lose over $1.6T because it had an affair with a spy.

Not enough people talking about how betrayed Jensen Huang must feel right now. Found a mistress he can talk about semiconductors with and she was lying to him the whole time. He must be heartbroken

As usual, AI-generated content is doing a lot of heavy lifting. Copyleaks, a software company that analyzes online content for signs of AI and digital manipulation, said Monday that it had seen “an explosion in AI-manipulated photos and videos of Huang and Alice Huang, ranging from memes to more subtle edits.” The tally includes at least 70 AI-related posts on X, which together drew around 8.42 million views and 64,362 engagements as of Monday morning. https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/o.author: Jonathon Kendall
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Geelong Magistrates' Court heard the man has been withdrawing from methamphetamine use since being charged over the alleged assault. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

The man who allegedly attacked a One Nation supporter in Torquay on Sunday has faced court for the first time.

KJ Seumalu, 37, has been charged with intentionally causing injury and other assault-related offences over the incident on November 1.

The court heard Mr Seumalu, who did not apply for bail, is withdrawing from methamphetamine use.

A man charged with assaulting a One Nation volunteer in Torquay has been withdrawing from methamphetamine abuse since being charged by police, a court has heard.

KJ Seumalu, 37, did not apply for bail after facing the Geelong Magistrates' Court, charged with intentionally causing injury and other assault-related offences.

Mr Seumalu allegedly used a blunt weapon to attack the One Nation supporter, who has not been named, in Torquay on November 1 in an attack police said was not politically motivated.

Mr Seumalu, who is from the south-east Melbourne suburb of Hampton Park, was arrested a short time after the incident on Sunday.

The Geelong Magistrates' Court heard that a man accused of assaulting a One Nation volunteer has substance abuse issues. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

His lawyer told the court the 37-year-old had a "current issue" with drugs and his mental health.

"He reports experiencing depression and anxiety, but there's no formal diagnosis and no medication," his lawyer Elena Felekos told the court.

The court heard he has been in touch with a court-provided mental health service.

Magistrate John Lesser requested a custody management review, where judicial officers identify, record, and assess critical health, safety, and welfare needs "as a matter of caution".

Mr Seumalu is scheduled to return to court on February 23.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/q.title: CFMEU tried to 'sabotage' Qld safety complaints overhaul, inquiry told
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/q.author: Ciara Jones
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Michael De'Ath has accused the CFMEU of sabotaging workplace safety reforms. (ABC News: Jake Evans )

Former Queensland department chief Michael De'Ath has given evidence at the commission of inquiry into the state's CFMEU branch.

Mr De'Ath told the inquiry the union's interference in an overhaul of safety reforms was "completely off the scale".

The current block of hearings for the inquiry run until Thursday, with two more blocks scheduled before the end of the year.

A former Queensland department chief has accused the CFMEU of sabotaging a workplace safety complaints overhaul, describing the union's interference as "completely off the scale".

Michael De'Ath, who served as director-general of the Department of Education, Industrial Relations and Racing under former senior Labor minister Grace Grace between 2021 and 2024, has given evidence at the commission of inquiry into the Queensland branch of the CFMEU.

The probe into alleged misconduct is re-examining allegations the union "captured" Workplace Health and Safety Queensland (WHSQ) under the former Labor government to advance its industrial agenda — a practice previously described during proceedings as a form of "institutional corruption".

Counsel assisting Dimitri Ternovski said a key focus of this week's hearings would be establishing how far the union's alleged influence extended into the upper ranks of government.

The inquiry heard the CFMEU fiercely resisted changes to how workplace safety complaints were made. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Mr De'Ath has been grilled over claims the CFMEU had a direct line to senior bureaucrats and ministers, bypassing normal workplace safety reporting procedures.

Central to the questioning was evidence from former Office of Industrial Relations [OIR] deputy director-general Kym Bancroft in June, who detailed her efforts to shut down the union's so-called "hotline" to the regulator.

Ms Bancroft told the inquiry she sought to introduce a centralised triage system, directing safety concerns through a dedicated hotline number instead of government officials.

Ms Bancroft said the CFMEU fiercely resisted the overhaul, insisting it would continue contacting her directly.

The arrangement posed safety risks by adding an unnecessary layer to the complaints process with Ms Bancroft unavailable around the clock, the inquiry heard.

Mr De'Ath described the union's opposition as "incredibly frustrating", accusing it of intentionally trying to derail the reforms.

"This was the most extreme obfuscation of anything in my entire career, completely off the scale for a stakeholder," Mr De'Ath told the inquiry.

"[It was] quite a deliberate attempt to sabotage a process that they clearly did not want."

"I've worked in multiple jurisdictions with multiple stakeholders over multiple portfolios, if you had it on a scale of 1 to 9, the worst I would've encountered might've been a three — this is a nine," he said.

Ms Bancroft also claimed she was sacked by Mr De'Ath in 2023 during which he allegedly told her that "a union group" was not "happy" with her.

On Tuesday, Mr De'Ath took sole responsibility for her termination, citing a breakdown in trust and confidence and concerns about her competence and honesty.

The director of a private security business has told Queensland's CFMEU inquiry he discovered a tracking tag attached to his vehicle.

"The decision to dismiss her was your decision alone and no one else's … you stand by that?" Mr Ternovski asked.

"Ultimately, that decision is mine," Mr De'Ath replied.

Mr De'Ath was also asked about the redeployment of ex-WHSQ compliance director Helen Burgess who was considered a key link between the union and regulator.

His repeated inability to recall details surrounding the move sparked a tense exchange with Commissioner Stuart Wood KC, who questioned his account, saying it seemed "very unlikely to be true".
