https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.title: Empty chair at bed shortage summit highlights state-federal tensions
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.author: Daniel Keane
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Peter Malinauskas at today's SA government's health meeting, entitled the "federal aged care crisis". (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The South Australian government says an absence of 500 aged care beds is contributing to hospital ramping spikes.

It says double the number of federally-funded beds would be needed to alleviate demand, but the Commonwealth government says the states turned down an $2 billion reform offer.

The issue was discussed at a meeting between the SA government, health and union officials today but the federal aged care minister Sam Rae could not make the summit.

South Australia's worst-ever ambulance ramping hours in August would have been reduced by two thirds had there been no aged care bedblock, the state government has claimed at a health meeting intended to increase pressure on Canberra.

SA Health Minister Blair Boyer presented the modelling at a meeting of state government, health and union officials in Adelaide this morning, amid tensions with the federal government over the national shortage of aged care beds.

Those tensions were on full display in the form of an empty chair set aside for federal aged care minister Sam Rae, who was unable to attend but whose absence was made more conspicuous by a vacant space bearing his name between SA Premier Peter Malinauskas and SA Ambulance Service CEO Rob Elliott.

Short notice and a scheduling conflict were cited by the federal government for Minister Sam Rae's inattendance at the SA government's meeting. (ABC News)

In August, ambulance ramping hours in South Australia hit 5,891 — the highest on record, and more than double the highest monthly figure reached under the Liberal government that was defeated by Mr Malinauskas's Labor at the 2022 state election.

Prior to that victory, Labor had prominently promised to "fix the ramping crisis", and has since repeatedly blamed consistently high ramping on a shortage of federal aged care beds for patients transferring out of hospital care.

Mr Boyer told the meeting, entitled the "federal aged care crisis", that the number of patients in public hospital beds who were unable to transfer to aged care beds was currently around 500 and could further increase to almost 700 during next year's winter peak.

He said modelling showed ramping hours would have been slashed this year had those beds been available.

"What if we had, magically, all that capacity back? What if today the system had the 500 beds, that are out of action, available to us again?," he asked rhetorically.

"One of the most powerful stats we have is the winter demand period we've just had, where it almost peaked at 6,000 hours — and would have been below 2,000 hours had we had all the capacity available to us.

Blair Boyer says his take on the aged care crisis is unlikely to win him any friends in Canberra.  (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Earlier, Mr Boyer told 891 ABC Adelaide that federal minister Sam Rae had been invited to the meeting, but that "he couldn't make it".

The ABC understands that the minister was only given a few days' notice of the meeting and that a scheduling issue prevented his attendance, but that a counteroffer was made to meet with Mr Boyer in Canberra.

The federal government has defended its aged care spending record, saying it was "not wasting a moment" to bring new residential aged care beds "online".

"Earlier this year, we announced the outcomes of an Expression of Interest process which will unlock $134.5 million to deliver 268 new residential aged care beds across five Adelaide sites, improving access to care and helping ease hospital discharge pressures," a spokesperson said.

"We're supporting the construction of around 5,000 additional residential aged care beds each year."

The state government said double that number was needed.

The SA government met with health and union officials today. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

But the federal government also said the states had knocked back opportunities to contribute to solutions.

"When states told us delayed discharge was their biggest pressure point, we listened and put $2 billion on the table ringfenced for aged care services, through the National Health Reform Agreement. The states rejected it and took the money for hospitals instead," the federal spokesperson said.

Asked whether he was doing political damage to his federal Labor colleagues by being outspoken on the issue, Mr Boyer replied, "I doubt it's winning me any fans".

"Do I sit back because I'm afraid of being a bit unpopular with some of my colleagues and pull my punches? I'm not going to do that," he said.

If Labor’s 2022 campaign was all about ambulance patients locked out of hospitals, then 2026 is all about young people locked out of home ownership.

State opposition health spokesperson Jack Batty said today's meeting was welcomed provided it did not turn "into another talkfest".

"We really need more than summits, we need commitments, we need deadlines, we need actual results," he said.

"So often this minister's default response to really serious policy challenges is another round table or a summit. He had a crisis summit last week about this."

Mr Malinauskas likened the high demand on aged care beds to a freight train that been in motion for "decades" and had "now arrived at the station".

"The country's not ready for it," he told Radio National earlier today.

"There are a range of decisions that were made frankly during the course of the Abbott years that unwound various policy measures that had been introduced to prevent this from occurring and the consequences of it are now playing out."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/q.author: Alex Brewster
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Tim Nicholls says work on the health workforce plan is continuing. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls has backflipped on a deadline to release a plan to boost the state's health workforce.

In August this year, Mr Nicholls said the plan was finalised but today said there was no timeline for its release.

Opposition Leader Steven Miles called for the urgent release of the plan.

Queensland's health minister has backflipped on a deadline to release a plan to add tens of thousands of new employees to the health workforce.

An analysis released a year ago today revealed the state needed 6,000 new doctors and 46,000 health workers by 2032.

A workforce plan to map out how Queensland would deliver those clinicians was due to follow.

In August, Health Minister Tim Nicholls said the plan was being finalised and would be released "a little later this year".

But asked today in Rockhampton, the minister said there was no timeline for its release.

"When we've concluded all of that investigation, we'll have a proper workforce plan that people can have faith in, and that will deliver the workforce in the places we need it, when we need it."

The workforce analysis showed a disparity in healthcare workers between regional and metro areas.

In some allied health professions, regional workforce gaps were as high as 50 per cent, and 72 per cent of workforce growth had occurred primarily in metro areas.

AMA Queensland president Associate Professor Erica Gannon said a workforce plan would be vital in addressing shortfalls.

Erica Gannon says demand for health services is only going to increase. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"The workforce gap analysis was a positive first step in developing a sorely needed, system-wide workforce plan," she said.

"Regional and remote Queenslanders will suffer the most without a comprehensive plan to get more doctors into the system.

"We know demand for health services is only going to increase given our growing and ageing population, coupled with improved but often expensive medical technologies used to treat increasingly complex conditions."

The analysis also showed a fifth of Queensland's registered health workforce was approaching, or at, retirement age.

Opposition Leader Steven Miles called for the urgent release of the plan to attract the necessary workers.

"The best time for a workforce plan was a year ago. The second best time is today," he said.

Steven Miles has called for the urgent release of the plan. (ABC News)

"It's now been a year today since the LNP promised a health workforce plan, and in that year, all we have heard from them is excuses."

Mr Nicholls assured the work was ongoing.

"We're doing the proper planning around the workforce plan, but we're not letting the grass grow under our feet."

It comes as Training Minister Ros Bates announced an expansion to the government's free nursing program, with a further 2,000 TAFE places available.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.title: Dozens of CFMEU stoppages in a week before rail site takeover, hearing told
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.author: Melissa Brown
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Royal Commissions

The royal commission's hearings are currently focused on CFMEU disruptions to a Melbourne rail project in 2022. (ABC News)

The royal commission into the CFMEU and Victoria's Big Build projects has heard the union raised dozens of safety concerns with the Sunbury level crossing removal project in one week in 2022.

A site supervisor told he hearing he suspected the union was targeting the project because it was the only large rail infrastructure construction site without a CFMEU-appointed health and safety officer.

The hearings continue in Melbourne.

A construction site health and safety representative has told the royal commission into Victoria's Big Build how casual workers on a project were pushed into becoming CFMEU members, after more than two dozen union stoppages.

This week's hearings have focused on events related to a work stoppage at a level crossing removal project in Melbourne's north, which was contracted to the John Holland construction company.

In 2022, work ceased on the Gap Road project on June 6 and resumed on June 7 after control of the site was transferred to the CFMEU (Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union).

The commission heard that project costs blew out by an estimated $6 million.

Today's first witness was Glenn Tyrrell, a crane operator on the Gap Road project who workers had voted to be their health and safety representative.

He was a casual worker who was hired through Zoom Recruitment.

He said there was not much of a union presence at the Gap Road project until after April 2022 after which, at times, up to four CFMEU organisers would turn up and present John Holland site management with safety concerns.

"They'd just come on site and literally stop the whole job," Mr Tyrrell told the hearing.

"They'd have their [Right of Entry] paperwork and they'd stand in front of machinery and plant and just tell the operator that he must stop."

Glenn Tyrrell gives evidence about his experiences with the CFMEU on the Sunbury Gap Road rail infrastructure construction site. (Supplied: Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects)

The commission heard that between May 25 and 31, the CFMEU issued 8 safety notices to John Holland.

It presented another 23 notices between June 1 and 2.

Mr Tyrrell described instances where union representatives would walk in front of cranes and even sat on concrete barriers that were about to be lifted into place to force the work to stop.

"Sometimes either the whole job site was shut or a certain area of the job was shut," Mr Tyrrell said.

He gave evidence that about a week after the June 6 stoppage, about 15 casual workers who had been hired through Zoom Recruitment were called into a lunch room and told they had to stop working for the labour hire firm and transfer to a new company, BK Labour Hire.

He said they were also told they were now required to join the CFMEU.

"That's the first time I joined any union," Mr Tyrrell told the hearing.

He said he had to make a bank transfer of $590 to the union up-front for half-yearly fees.

He said he was not given any reason why the casual workers had to transfer to the new labour hire company.

Mr Tyrrell told the hearing that after the CFMEU took control of the site, the union appointed its own health and safety officer without an election and that his role was diminished.

He said the union stoppages before the site take-over put pressure on John Holland and the workers to get the job finished on time, and that more workers were brought in to get it done.

John Holland's site supervisor Robert Van Den Tol told the hearing he had several decades experience before the Gap Road job, where safety was part of his responsibilities.

He said he had always considered it to be a safe worksite and that he did not believe the CFMEU made any substantial improvements once the union took control of the site and installed its own safety representative.

He told the royal commission he did not agree with the union’s claim of a problem with risk assessments for piling works that resulted in the June 7 stoppage.

“Definitely not because if I had seen it, I would have stopped it,” he said.

“No one could start work without a Safe Work Methods Statement. No one.”

Robert Van Den Tol gave evidence to the royal commission via video link. (Supplied: Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects)

He told the hearing he believed the union had an agenda behind its complaints.

“We were the last crew in Melbourne not to have a union affiliated health and safety representative [on large rail infrastructure projects]," he said.

Mr Van Den Tol said that when union officials had been entering the site, they often did not follow proper procedure, such as signing in, alerting John Holland to their presence and waiting until their Right of Entry permits had been handed in.

He said they were not supposed to be wandering around the worksite without an escort if they had not undergone a site induction.

“Not supposed to, no. Did they? Yes.”

Mr Van Den Tol agreed under questioning that the union officials were swearing at him and making derogatory comments during the June 6 stoppage.

“Their attitude to me was, well I won’t tell you the words…”

The hearing continues.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Fossil fuel emissions fall due to Iran war and renewables, research shows
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: Laurent Thomet
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
ANTALYA, TURKEY – Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall slightly in 2026 due to the expansion of renewable energy and the oil price shock sparked by the Iran war, researchers said Tuesday.

Emissions from the burning of oil, gas and coal — the main drivers of climate change — rose by 0.9% per year, on average, in the past decade, hitting a record high in 2025, according to the Global Carbon Budget report.

But they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026, according to the research, published as nations meet at the U.N.’s COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

It would be the first annual drop since 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic paralyzed the global economy, trade and transport.

This year, the U.S.-led war in Iran and closure of the Strait of Hormuz played a role in driving emissions down as it caused a drop in oil consumption amid soaring crude prices, the researchers found.

The deployment of solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles also contributed to the drop. Two thirds of the increase in global energy demand is being met by solar and wind power and electric vehicles, the report found.

“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter in Britain.

“The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies,” said Friedlingstein, who led the study published in the journal Earth System Science Data.

Corinne Le Quere, a climate change science professor at the University of East Anglia, noted that emissions rebounded when economies recovered following shocks such as COVID-19 or the global financial crisis.

A rebound is likely “when the oil tensions go away,“ she said in a media briefing.

Oil-related emissions are projected to drop 1.9% last year, but it was “likely a short-term response to the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict,“ the researchers said.

Gas emissions are set to fall 0.3% while those from coal use will rise 0.6%.

Overall, fossil carbon dioxide emissions are expected to reach 38.2 billion metric tons in 2026.

Including emissions from land-use change such as deforestation, total CO2 emissions are projected to rise to 43.3 billion metric tons, from 42.8 billion metric tons last year.

The researchers said land-use emissions are projected to rise partly due to peat fires and forest degradation in southeast Asia, associated with drier conditions linked to this year’s exceptionally strong El Nino climate pattern.

The report found that the world’s carbon budget — the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before global warming exceeds 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels — stands at 150 billion metric tons.

The researchers calculated that at the current, the carbon budget would be exhausted in less than four years.

Nations agreed at the 2015 U.N. climate talks in Paris to keep global warming “well below” 2C above preindustrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5C.

But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5C target would be missed in a matter of years.

Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of “overshoot” above 1.5C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Australian Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Inquiry recommends police investigate allegations of sexual assault and other abuse at Redeemer Baptist school

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A probe into a private religious school accused of sexual, physical, psychological, spiritual and financial abuse has recommended it be barred from enrolling new students.

Former students and teachers of western Sydney’s Redeemer Baptist school told a NSW parliamentary inquiry about a string of disturbing allegations.

They included students being made to share beds with teachers and its principal once wandering naked through a common area.

In a report tabled in state parliament on Tuesday, a committee found the school - run by the Redeemer Baptist Church - breached basic child safeguarding standards.

Sexual assault allegations were not handled appropriately and the school put children at significant risk of harm, the committee found.

It also found staff at the school lacked essential workplace rights and failed to satisfy basic standards of good governance.

The committee recommended the school be prevented from enrolling new students while it was under investigation by the NSW education standards authority.

It also recommended the allegations raised in the inquiry be investigated by NSW police and the office of the children’s guardian.

Committee chair and Greens MP Abigail Boyd noted the school was subjected to parliamentary scrutiny in 2006, but no procedures had been put in place to monitor what was clearly a “high-risk situation”.

She said it was thanks to the bravery of those who had spoken out that the committee had enough evidence to make its strong findings and recommendations.

The school received about $6 million a year in government funding, Boyd said, and had enough cash to launch legal challenges against those who raised their voices against the religious group.

“They also have deep political ties with both state and federal politicians,” she told parliament.

People who had escaped the school appeared to be absolutely terrified of its leaders, Boyd said.

“When you know that leaving means leaving with no financial assets, and when you have finally managed to escape, it’s no wonder that you would be terrified of your abuser,” she said in parliament.

The committee lashed a lack of regulatory oversight, including from the education authority, suggesting a number of alarming matters needed proper investigation.

They included allegations of persistent Centrelink fraud and dodgy tax practices.

“It is, at the very least, troubling that an asset-rich, seemingly prosperous school operates by withholding wages from its workforce, who claim benefits, while the school receives millions of dollars in public funding,” the report said.

A Redeemer Baptist School spokesperson previously said the school had fully co-operated with the relevant regulators.

“Redeemer Baptist School takes its child safety obligations extremely seriously and has an unblemished record of compliance with state and federal regulators for 45 years,” they said.

The school did not immediately respond to a request for comment following the report’s release.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Bills wear out Vikings’ NFL-leading defense, sloppy Wentz to improve to 7-1
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Buffalo Bills 23-6 Minnesota Vikings

Wentz has three turnovers starting for injured Murray

Buffalo have matched their best start since 1993

Josh Allen threw a touchdown pass with 44 seconds left before half-time, James Cook rushed 31 times for 107 yards and a late score, and the Buffalo Bills beat hosts Minnesota 23-6 on Monday night, sending the Vikings deeper into their unrelenting offensive slump.

Linebackers Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams had interceptions and Tyler Bass made four field goals to stretch his franchise-record streak to 25 straight as the Bills (7-1) matched their best eight-game start since 1993. That season ended with their last of four straight Super Bowl losses.

With Kyler Murray sidelined by a hamstring injury, Carson Wentz started at quarterback for the Vikings (6-2) and didn’t finish what became one of the worst performances of his 11-year career. Wentz went 8 for 25 for 81 yards and three turnovers, including a backwards pass in the first quarter that was thrown too high for even Justin Jefferson to catch it – resulting in a lost fumble near midfield.

Wentz, who was checked out in the medical tent at one point for an apparent lower leg injury, was replaced by Max Brosmer midway through the fourth quarter. Wentz completed 1 of 8 passes in the second half.

The battle of Buffalo’s highest-scoring offense in the league against the NFL’s leading scoring defense might have gone to Minnesota had the offense been able to muster a decent drive or two. But the Vikings had four straight possessions in the first-half start beyond their 40-yard line, and the furthest they made it was the Bills 48.

The Vikings as usual sent blitzers at Allen from every angle possible, recording four sacks and an interception of a heave into the end zone that Byron Murphy ran down and returned 55 yards. But the Bills eked out just enough in the first half to give themselves a cushion, when Allen found tight end Keleki Latu open in the back of the end zone for a 25-yard touchdown as he rolled right and was hit hard by Andrew Van Ginkel.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/audi.text:
As the nights draw in, many of us can experience low mood. But for a small proportion of people a more intense depression develops through the winter months. It’s a phenomenon that since the 1980s has been labelled seasonal affective disorder, or Sad, and can be debilitating for sufferers. To find out more about the latest scientific understanding of Sad, Ian Sample speaks to Russell Foster, professor of circadian neuroscience at the University of Oxford. He explains what scientists think the mechanism for the condition could be and what the evidence says about the best way to tackle it.

https://www.wired.com/story/a-new-ai-too.title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
https://www.wired.com/story/a-new-ai-too.author: Lily Hay Newman
https://www.wired.com/story/a-new-ai-too.text:
GOOGLE DEEPMIND RESEARCHERS used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

“While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind's approach enables significant expansion,” Ehren Kret, Signal's chief technology officer, says in a statement. “As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code's privacy guarantees.”

For critical services used in high-stakes settings, it would be a dream to be able to formally verify every code base and entire software supply chains. “If you can now verify the correctness of these implementations, then you can rest easy,” says Pushmeet Kohli, chief scientist at Google Cloud and DeepMind's vice president of research. “You can imagine banks, imagine all those other companies who rely on assurances and who worry about bugs who could now say, ‘I can prove these properties.’"

The open question across the tech sector, though, is whether AI-automated formal verification can truly scale—and whether it can do so at a workable cost. DeepMind conducted the Signal analysis free of charge as a research project, and Google declined to share the cost of the analysis. The company also declined to comment on whether it has plans to release a commercial formal verification product or service.

The researchers say that some of their crucial advancements are in developing a “human-AI collaboration process,” as Chaudhuri puts it, that allows agents to contribute and self-correct at almost every phase of the process while still seeking human input and review at key junctures. “We don’t want this sort of vibe world where AI is generating the goals and AI is generating the proofs and basically taking tests that are self-written," Chaudhuri says. “There’s a middle ground.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/trump-ru.title: Trump sees 'strong inclination' to end Russia-Ukraine war ahead of U.S.-brokered peace talks
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/trump-ru.author: Matthew Tan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/trump-ru.text:
President Donald Trump said Washington saw growing willingness to end Russia’s war in Ukraine at a White House press briefing Monday.

U.S., Russian and Ukrainian officials are set to meet for two days of negotiations in Abu Dhabi later today.

Hackers said leaked Rosstat records showed nearly 394,000 war-related deaths since 2022.

President Donald Trump said Washington sees growing willingness to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, as Kyiv and Moscow prepare for U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi later Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said recent battlefield gains were strengthening Kyiv’s negotiating position ahead of the talks.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Monday, Trump said both sides were battle-weary, more than four and a half years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

“We’re also seeing a very strong inclination to end Russia and Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that, “We’re involved in that because I want to see people stop getting killed again.”

His comments followed a U.S. official’s assessment that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing some flexibility over a possible exchange of territory, according to Reuters.

A senior Ukrainian official, however, rejected suggestions that Kyiv was considering territorial concessions, telling Reuters that any discussion of territory would have to take place between national leaders and be accompanied by appropriate security guarantees.

Russia has publicly maintained its demand that Ukraine surrender the entire eastern Donbas region, including territory Moscow has not captured.

Separately, Zelenskyy said Monday that recent Ukrainian battlefield gains and mounting Russian losses had improved Kyiv’s bargaining power.

“Right now, Ukrainian troops are truly strengthening Ukraine’s negotiating positions,” he said in his nightly address, urging Washington to convince Russia to end the war.

The remarks come as U.S., Russian and Ukrainian officials prepare for two days of talks in Abu Dhabi — their first trilateral negotiations since February.

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are set to lead Washington’s mediation efforts, with postwar security guarantees for Ukraine expected to feature prominently.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that discussions had advanced on a possible postwar security framework for Ukraine and Europe.

“Nothing’s been finalized yet, and maybe some progress can be made in Abu Dhabi,” Rubio said.

The renewed diplomacy comes amid continued fighting and mounting questions over the scale of Russia’s wartime losses.

Belarusian Cyber Partisans, an opposition-linked hacker group, said its analysis of data it claims was obtained from Russia’s state statistics agency identified 393,881 deaths linked to military operations or their consequences between 2022 and August 2026.

The group said its count was based on death records explicitly coded as resulting from hostilities or their consequences. It acknowledged that the figure could include civilians and deaths connected to other conflicts, while excluding personnel who are missing but have not been declared dead.

Rosstat has acknowledged that it was targeted in cyberattacks but denied that its databases were compromised, according to a Russian media outlet Kommersant. The hackers’ claims and the underlying dataset have not been independently verified in full.

Separately, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that 400,000 to 450,000 Russian military personnel were killed between February 2022 and June 2026.

At the upper end, that would be more than nine times the combined Soviet and Russian military fatalities in wars since World War II, according to the think tank.

The Moscow Times, citing a broader analysis of the leaked records, reported that roughly 450,000 war-related deaths would make the conflict Russia’s fourth most common cause of death since 2022. The newspaper said it had cross-checked a sample of names, but could not verify the data set in its entirety.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/g.author: Mike Lorigan and Alysia Thomas-Sam
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

In Melbourne's inner north, the ALP is facing a battle from the left with the Greens and Victorian Socialists looking to capture Labor heartland.  (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

The Greens are targeting traditional Labor seats at the upcoming Victorian state election.

Senator Lidia Thorpe's former seat of Northcote is a key target.

Victoria heads to the polls on Saturday, November 28.

At the last federal election, the Greens suffered a catastrophic wipe-out; in the upcoming Victorian state election, they're looking to mount a comeback.

The major Greens casualties in 2025 were party leader Adam Bandt and one-time rising star Max Chandler-Mather — who even earned a rebuke from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as he exited parliament — such was the animosity brewing between the Greens and Labor.

Now at a federal level, the Greens have a new leader in David Shoebridge, who is also keen to take the Labor vote. At the upcoming Victorian state election, that is also a primary Greens target.

David Shoebridge has declared he wants the Greens to replace Labor.  (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Labor holds 54 of the 88 lower house seats in the Victorian parliament, the Coalition 29, and five on the crossbench.

The Greens currently hold three lower house seats, Brunswick, Melbourne and Richmond, by comfortable margins.

They are targeting at least five more, including the Liberal-held Prahran and Labor's Footscray, Pascoe Vale, Preston and Northcote.

Greens success across this part of Melbourne could significantly erode Labor's parliamentary majority and potentially reshape the balance of power in Victoria.

Northcote is the former seat of federal senator Lidia Thorpe, who won it in a 2017 by-election.

Lidia Thorpe briefly held the seat of Northcote after a by-election in 2017.  (ABC: Ian Cutmore)

Trying to take the seat back is Greens candidate Campbell Gome, a primary school teacher and trade unionist, who believes the political mood is shifting.

"We are going to keep knocking on doors, we are going to keep listening to people," Mr Gome told 7.30.

Campbell Gome lost to Labor's Kat Theophanous by just 184 votes at the 2022 state election.  (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Asked whether voters are enthused about Greens policies or looking to park their dissatisfaction with Labor elsewhere, he told 7.30: "I think the two go hand-in-hand."

"That's the real change in 2026 ... this sense of frustration and abandonment of [Victorian] Labor's historic position as being for ordinary people and being genuinely progressive."

In many parts of the seat of Northcote, about 7km north of Melbourne's CBD, political messaging sits alongside bustling cafes and gentrification.

Aside from its brief dalliance with Senator Thorpe, the seat has been Labor for almost a century and swung back that way in 2018.

Labor's Kat Theophanous defeated Mr Gome by just 184 votes in 2022. The looming contest is familiar territory.

Kat Theophanous says, in her view, Northcote has always been a marginal seat.  (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

"We expect it to be close again. For me, it's always been a marginal seat, both in 2018 and in 2022," Ms Theophanous said.

The state Labor MP rejects suggestions by her political opponents that Labor has lost touch with her electorate's progressive communities.

"I disagree with it," she said.

The long-term Labor government is under pressure from across the political spectrum.  (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

She acknowledges some voters are tiring of the long-term Labor government but says many are concerned about a possible Coalition government.

"After 12 years, of course there's going to be people that are feeling fatigue," she said.

"I'm asking people to vote for me because of our record of delivery in the inner north."

Recent polls of Victorian voters suggest the Greens have momentum.

After Labor replaced Jacinta Allan with Ben Carroll as premier, Redbridge and DemosAU put the statewide Greens primary vote between 14 and 17 per cent.

In Northcote though the Victorian Socialists are looking to establish themselves, and their progressive agenda could impact the Greens vote.

Victorian Socialist candidate for Northcote Kath Larkin told 7.30: "I think the main difference is that we're socialists, right? We're anti-capitalists. We oppose the system in total."

Kath Larkin is the Victorian Socialist candidate for Northcote.  (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

"The Greens have a politics. It's more about tinkering around the edges," she said.

The Victorian Socialists are aiming to run candidates in every lower house seat at this election.

Like the Greens, they want to implement sweeping reforms. They are promising to freeze and cap rents, build more public housing and return essential services to public ownership, all paid for, they say, by new taxes on big corporations and the wealthy.

Like the Greens, the Socialists want to implement sweeping reforms, promising to freeze and cap rents, build more public housing and return essential services to public ownership. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Mr Gome told 7.30 the difference between the two is that the Greens are represented at every level of government and "are able to affect real change".

Ms Theophanous primarily sees the Victorian Socialists as only being a problem for the Greens.

"They are nipping at the heels of the Greens," she said.

"The Greens have some soul-searching to do about where their party stands on things, because I think that they are catering to the socialists."

In Northcote, every vote and preference matters.

Preferences matter in the seat of Northcote.  (ABC News: Tara Whitchurch)

In 2022, preferences from Liberals and the Victorian Socialists largely flowed against Labor to the Greens in the seat to tighten the race. This time the Greens say they are striving to win Northcote without relying on preferences, while the Victorian Socialists are looking to influence the result.

"In Northcote, we're looking to bump up our numbers. I don't think we'll take the seat this time round," Ms Larkin told 7.30.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/m.author: Charlotte King
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Mining Environmental Issues

Protesters outside NSW parliament rallying againts the Mount Pleasant mine. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

The NSW government is proposing laws to allow a Hunter Valley mine to expand production rates, despite a High Court ruling against it.

Opponents of the Mount Pleasant mine have accused the government of going behind the court process.

Premier Chris Minns said the move was to address the "unique legal uncertainty" emerging from the court ruling in October.

The NSW government has introduced laws to allow a Hunter Valley coal mine to continue operating at expanded production rates, despite a High Court ruling against it.

The operators of the Mount Pleasant mine, MACH Energy lost their High Court appeal in October, which centred on a plan to double coal extraction in the Hunter Valley until 2048.

Premier Chris Minns said the new laws being introduced would address the "unique legal uncertainty" arising from the High Court judgement.

"We're committed to our plans in relation to renewable energy and climate change, we're not walking away from it," he told reporters on Tuesday.

"But this is the biggest reform and revolution of energy markets in the state's history, and I reserve the right to make an intervention to protect jobs and grow the economy where I think it's warranted."

Mr Minns says his government is still "committed to our plans in relation to renewable energy and climate change". (ABC News)

MACH Energy received approval for the Mount Pleasant mine expansion in 2022, but it has been tied up in legal disputes since a NSW Court of Appeal ruling last year found its approval may have been invalid, because planning authorities did not consider the overseas emissions from the exported coal.

The mine has confirmed it continued expanding even after the proceedings reached the High Court, despite the legal uncertainty surrounding its approval to do so.

In October, the High Court delivered its own decision that the expansion was invalid, because planning authorities had failed to consider the "Scope 3" emissions caused when the coal exports were burned overseas, when it approved the mine.

The mine is allowed to extract 12.5 million tonnes of coal a year. (Supplied: Nearmaps)

A lower court, the NSW Land and Environment Court, will now review the case in December.

In the meantime, the mine has to rely on its original planning permit, which allows for only 12.5 million tonnes of coal to be extracted per year, 4 million less than the 16.5 million tonnes it was on track to extract for 2026.

Mr Minns has said the bespoke laws introduced on Tuesday would authorise "an increased annual production limit of 16.5 million tonnes until 2032… consistent with their current workforce and coal production profile".

The government denied that it was in effect "overturning" the High Court decision, and said the bill would require the coal exports to go to countries that were signatory to the Paris Agreement.

Opponents believe the mining company is going behind the court process. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

But legal experts have criticised the intervention as "reprehensible" and described the government's actions as an attempt to override the "rule of law".

"The idea that a substantial mining venture can approach the government and say look, let's go behind the court processes and sort this out between ourselves is a very dangerous precedent, and that's exactly what appears to have happened here," retired judge Anthony Whealy, who is now on the board of the Centre for Public Integrity, said last month.

The Castle actor Michael Caton, who has emerged as a supporter of the protesters. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

On Tuesday, the retired teachers who fought the High Court case gathered on the steps of NSW parliament with a range of activists and supporters, including actor Micheal Caton, from The Castle fame.

"In the last 20 years, we have doubled coal production," Caton told reporters at the event.

"We've got less than 25 years to get rid of fossil fuels, but we're doubling production of this mine up in the Hunter."

Caton said he had voted for the Minns Labor government.

Wendy Wales, the president of the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG), who opposed to the mine, said she was very disappointed the government was trying to pass legislation "ahead of a court process".

"This is a pretty dire situation, and everybody in New South Wales and Australia should be concerned," she said.

Debate on the bill has been adjourned in the lower house to a later date.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: ‘Pit of hell’: Turkish mother and daughter lead fight against coal mine
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
MILAS, TURKEY – Near her village in southwestern Turkey, Nejla Isik walks through what remains of the devastated Akbelen forest, pausing to stare down at the coal mine that is devouring the hillside.

“We call it the pit of hell,” muses the 48-year-old activist and local leader of Ikizkoy village, which has 70 homes.

When COP31 begins Monday in Antalya, the United Nations climate summit’s host Turkey is hoping to show off its best side with a campaign focused on renewable energies and electrification.

But those who want to draw attention to a different side of the story are not welcome.

For nearly a decade, Isik and her daughter Esra, 26, have thrown themselves into protesting against the mining projects slowly ravaging Mugla province, which lies several hundred kilometers west of Antalya.

Together, they have been leading the fight against YK Enerji, which wants to expand its lignite mine and increase the production capacity of its two thermal power plants, which run on the highly polluting brown coal.

Several lawsuits have been filed against the firm, which owns the mine and the plant next to their village.

Others have targeted the Turkish presidency over a decree ordering the emergency expropriation of 679 plots of land, signed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in January.

“My grandmother’s village was wiped off the map because of the mine. My father’s village was destroyed. We are a family that has been uprooted for three or four generations and our land plundered,” explains Esra, dressed in baggy trousers and a traditional red waistcoat.

Their activism has not gone unnoticed.

On March 31, Esra was arrested while protesting against a visit by officials in the context of an emergency expropriation decision affecting six villages.

Charged with “obstructing an official carrying out their duty,“ she was jailed pending trial.

“I spent 42 days in jail. My arrest gave a new dimension to our struggle in Turkey, but also around the world,” she said.

They are not the only ones fighting, with locals regularly meeting to discuss what comes next.

Among them is 56-year-old housewife Aytac Yakar, who was forced to flee her home village of Isikdere when it was swallowed up by a mine in 2018.

She settled in another place, which is now facing the same fate.

“Do I look like a migratory bird?” she says angrily.

“They cannot play around with my home, my lands and my country. If I have to, I’ll douse myself with petrol and set myself alight in my own home. But I won’t leave it!”

As the world descends on Antalya, where scientists, experts and heads of state will gather to discuss global warming and how to slow it, thousands of activists will also be present to raise their voices.

But Nejla and Esra won’t be there — because they have to stay to protect their lands.

“I can’t leave my village. The court rejected our appeal against the expropriations, and we don’t know what the company will do now,” explains Nejla.

“I won’t go to COP where we already know they won’t listen to us, while my village here is burning,” she said.

Under a law passed in 2025, Turkey has rapidly expanded the number of mining permits, opening up protected areas for exploitation, including olive-growing land.

“Our homes, the graves of our loved ones, our olive trees, our lands — it all risks being torn from our hands,” says Nejla Isik, pointing to the area on a map.

Asked about the expropriations, Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar told reporters the government had privatized the two plants in 2014, granting the buyers a license that could not simply be revoked without consequences.

“Basically, we need to protect this investment or find another way to address the potential losses. We gave them a 49-year license and now we’re saying: ’In 2030, you’re out because we have a coal phase-out policy’?” he said.

“There are challenges we need to tackle here,” he said.

Not all villagers oppose the mine, notably those who work there.

“The thermal power plant creates jobs for 70% of my village,” explained one worker, who did not want to give his name.

YK Enerji, which says it powers more than 2 million households per day, defended the project by pointing to Turkey’s energy security needs.

“For energy production to continue, we must gain access to new deposits,” its general manager Ahmet Eyidogan said, saying trees would be replaced by suitable species and “village centers, mosques, schools and graves” would be spared and landowners granted “alternative” plots.

YK Enerji — which is jointly owned by Limak Holding and IC Holding, both of which are official “climate supporters” of COP31 — supports Turkey’s “carbon neutrality target,” he said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.summary: Activists have been fighting against mining projects in Turkey for nearly a decade. They have been leading the fight against YK Enerji, which wants to expand its lignite mine and increase the production capacity of its thermal power plants. The company owns the mine and the plant next to their village.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Ruling bloc kicks off first working-level talks on Japan security strategy overhaul
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Kenji Yoshida
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The ruling parties on Tuesday opened their first working-level talks on overhauling Japan’s security strategy by the year’s end, with division over a decades-old ban on bringing nuclear weapons into the country and acquiring nuclear-powered submarines seen as key points of contention.

The Japan Innovation Party (JIP), also known as Nippon Ishin no Kai, wants both issues addressed in the revision of three key security documents, while the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) omitted both from its June recommendations.

LDP lawmaker and former Defense Minister Yasukazu Hamada and senior JIP lawmaker Seiji Maehara presided over the meeting. Participants said there was no substantive discussion of the two contentious issues that day.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Google escalates Nvidia rivalry with specialized versions of AI chips
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Dina Bass
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Alphabet’s Google is rolling out a broader array of artificial intelligence chips, aiming to capitalize on its rapid ascent as a challenger to Nvidia in a market worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

The company is introducing two new variations of its tensor processing units (TPUs), custom-made semiconductors that help develop and run AI software. The latest chips will address the need for confidential computing and help models access a wider range of information when handling queries. More broadly, they’re meant to serve an industry that’s shifting toward the use of AI agents and confronting security challenges.

Alphabet shares gained as much as 4.1% to $296.33 in New York trading on Monday.

https://www.dw.com/en/australia-to-intro.title: Australia to introduce mandatory AI safeguards
https://www.dw.com/en/australia-to-intro.text:
The Australian government's decision to establish an AI safety regulator comes after an OpenAI agent accessed a government medical statistics portal without authorization.

Australia will introduce mandatory safeguards for artificial intelligence companies, including compulsory reporting of security breaches and independent oversight of AI systems, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday.

The decision comes after an incident in which an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a government medical statistics portal while researching public medical spending.

Albanese said his center-left Labor government had accepted all the review's recommendations, which include requiring AI companies to report misaligned behavior and cyber incidents. The government will also consider reforms to criminal law to address cases of serious misconduct.

The government plans to establish an AI safety regulator to oversee security controls during the development and deployment of AI systems, identify serious risks and conduct independent evaluations of models.

"The AI ⁠safety regulator will be ​able to enforce significant penalties for AI companies doing the wrong thing," Albanese said.

"The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases, make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world," he told reporters.

OpenAI has said it learned of the breach in August and that the incident was unintentional. Its review found no evidence that the AI agent had accessed patient records.

Canberra declined to exempt ChatGPTmaker OpenAI and rival Anthropic from copyright laws for model ⁠training which would require them instead to negotiate licensing agreements with Australian rights ​holders.

Both companies told an Australian parliamentary committee last month that they would welcome mandatory reporting requirements for data breaches involving their AI agents.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmp3.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmp3.text:
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.

On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.

AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".

"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.

One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .

This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".

The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.

This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.

In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.

OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.

It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.

Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" and with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.

Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmp3.summary: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese released 18 recommendations on Tuesday. The 18 recommendations include mandatory reporting of hacks and new safety and security standards. The recommendations were made after a "rapid review" into the breaches. In September, a rogue OpenAI agent "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Mortgage holders’ confidence crashes to lowest level since 1994 as year that ‘feels like a recession’ looms
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Patrick Commins Economics editor
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Westpac survey results signal growing sense of ‘helplessness’ while Jim Chalmers faces growing pressure to rein in spending

Confidence among mortgaged households has crashed to its lowest level in more than three decades amid a growing sense of “helplessness” about the economy, even as a dramatic shift in financial markets suggests there is now a strong chance of a Reserve Bank rate cut by this time next year.

The latest Westpac survey showed its consumer sentiment index sinking again in November to reach a four-year low, amid deepening pessimism about the near-term prospects for the economy.

As Labor comes under increasing pressure over persistent cost-of-living pressures, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, played down tensions with the treasurer, Jim Chalmers.

A day after the frontbencher Murray Watt called for colleagues to stop undermining Chalmers, Albanese said: “The treasurer is doing a great job”.

The PM said he was working closely with Chalmers in the lead-up to next month’s mid-year budget update, which will include cuts to government spending as pressure mounts to contain inflation.

“This is a treasurer who’s produced a couple of budget surpluses, lower deficits, [who is] producing economic reform,” Albanese said.

Matthew Hassan, Westpac’s head of economic forecasting, said the mood among households was last this bad in 2022, when inflation was running close to 8% and after the RBA had lifted borrowing costs by 4 percentage points over the previous year.

“Prior to that, readings this weak had only ever been seen in the economy’s darkest moments: at the onset of the Covid pandemic; the height of the GFC; and during the recessions in the early 1990s and early 1980s,” Hassan said.

Hassan said while the economic backdrop was not as extreme now as it was during the pandemic and its immediate aftermath, there were “shades of Covid in the responses” from households.

Confidence in the economic outlook over the coming year reached its weakest since August 2020, the survey showed, matching a low point last recorded during the pandemic.

“The comparison with August 2020 is quite useful as that was when Melbourne went into its second lockdown and just before the government massively scaled up income support,” Hassan said.

“There was a sense of helplessness at that stage; there was nothing we could do to avoid the pandemic, and there was nothing the government could do [to avoid the pandemic]. Obviously when the jobkeeper measures were put in place that comforted a lot of people.

“There is a similar feeling of helplessness now. You can argue a substantial portion of what is happening is out of our control, such as rising fuel prices, and there’s only so much the authorities can do to cushion Australians from that impact.”

Indebted households were gloomier still, the survey showed, with pessimism among this group at its worst in records stretching back to 1994.

The latest survey comes a week after Michele Bullock, the RBA governor, warned that the year ahead would “feel like it’s a recession” thanks to persistent cost-of-living pressures alongside weak economic growth.

After five rate increases this year, nearly three in four respondents said they expected another rate hike over the coming 12 months.

Even as the mood in the community darkens, financial markets have begun factoring in the chance of lower interest rates from the middle of next year.

The implied probability of an RBA rate cut was more than 50% by August next year, according to ANZ data, and a decrease to 4.6% was fully priced in by December 2027.

Investors have been rethinking their forecasts for central bank moves alongside a rapid retreat in the global oil price.

After testing a post-Iran war high of nearly US$118 a barrel at the end of October, the global benchmark, Brent crude, has plunged by 20% to below US$94.

“Our base case is that rates do start to come down from August next year, and we don’t see any further hikes,” Hassan said.

– Additional reporting by Tom McIlroy
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.summary: Westpac survey shows consumer sentiment index sinking again in November to reach a four-year low. Confidence in the economic outlook over the coming year reached its weakest since August 2020. Confident households were gloomier still, with pessimism among this group at its worst in records stretching back to 1994.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as Abu Dhabi talks begin
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Andrew Roth in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe

US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.

The talks are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said.

European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west.

Since his first decade in power, Vladimir Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal.

Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal.

The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protect member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine.

“What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said.

“Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.”

Critics have expressed skepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response.

Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the United States, described a potential new framework for European in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”.

European delegations from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and the European Union will meet US negotiators in Abu Dhabi to discuss the “long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe in order to figure out how to reduce future conflicts”.

A European security official from a country attending the talks said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations.

“We already have a European security architecture in place,” said Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, at a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday. “This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.”

Donald Trump has also said that Ukraine would like be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape“.

Trump last week after meeting with Kremlin advisor Kirill Dmitriev said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

In 2021, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

“We have to build something new that works today… Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war,” said the US administration official.

The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”.

“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: US officials say they will seek a ‘final end’ to the war between Russia and Ukraine. Talks are first substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe. Talks follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.
