https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Firms tied to West Bank settlements win $15m UK deals despite sanctions
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Caolán Magee
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The United Kingdom awarded 10.7 million pounds ($14.4m) in new public contracts to firms with links to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, despite British government pledges to punish companies that profit from settlement activity, an Al Jazeera investigation reveals.

The contracts were published after the British government announced new powers on September 8 to sanction companies profiting from business with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which are illegal under international law.

An analysis of procurement records, company filings, corporate disclosures and contract data supplied by Tussell, a British public sector market intelligence firm, has found that businesses named by the United Nations over their involvement in illegal Israeli settlements – and companies that those businesses ultimately own or control as subsidiaries – have secured contracts across the British public sector.

The companies “appear to be in breach of their legal obligations under international humanitarian law”, Neve Gordon, a professor at the school of law at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.

“Any UK company that is involved in the occupation is likely to be in direct breach of the sanctions regime Ed Miliband is putting in place,” Gordon said, referring to the UK foreign secretary.

This follows a previous Al Jazeera investigation in August which revealed at least 17 companies linked to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank have been awarded UK public-sector contracts worth more than 2.1 billion pounds ($2.85bn).

On September 8, Miliband told the House of Commons the government would now “take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion”.

“To those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements, let me say this: you will face the full force of UK sanctions … Settlements are illegal.”

Since the announcement, however, UK public bodies have published details of an additional 18 public contracts with companies linked to illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Former Labour Party leader and MP Jeremy Corbyn told Al Jazeera: “Britain cannot credibly claim that it is imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements while letting contracts continue through the back door. The fact that public money is still going to firms that could be targeted under the government’s own sanctions regime … is outrageous and frankly insulting to the public.”

Al Jazeera contacted the Cabinet Office for comment about this but received no response. The Cabinet Office previously told Al Jazeera that individual public authorities make decisions to exclude suppliers on a case-by-case basis for each contract they award. It said public procurement in the UK should not be used to boycott suppliers linked to other countries unless formal British sanctions, embargoes or restrictions are in place.

One group that the UN listed in its September 2026 settlement index update for its commercial use of natural resources in the occupied Palestinian territory is Heidelberg Materials, a multinational building materials firm with headquarters in Germany.

Three Heidelberg subsidiaries were named in 14 contracts worth 10.4 million pounds ($14.5m), mostly to undertake roadworks and resurfacing for National Highways and councils in Nottingham and Lincolnshire in central-eastern England. The group has been granted at least 35 UK contracts worth about 194.7 million pounds ($261m) across five of its subsidiaries.

Its Israeli subsidiary, Hanson Israel, owns the Nahal Raba quarry, south of Qalqilya in the West Bank. The quarry sits on land belonging to the Palestinian villages of az-Zawiya and Rafat, according to Who Profits, a group that researches links between the private sector and the economy in the occupied territory. An official Civil Administration Service planning notice reviewed by Al Jazeera shows a proposal was approved to expand the site. According to the company’s website, the firm undertakes “quarrying, grinding and screening of natural dolomite or limestone rock”.

Heidelberg has previously told Al Jazeera that Hanson Israel ceased operations at the quarry and its associated plants in 2023.

But Who Profits said approval for the expansion of the quarry was granted on May 28, 2025. Heidelberg did not dispute the Who Profits assertion in its response to Al Jazeera’s questions.

Two contracts, worth about 87,900 pounds ($118,000), have been awarded to Motorola Solutions and its subsidiaries to provide communications for the police service.

Motorola Solutions still accounts for the largest share by value of the contracts Al Jazeera identified, with about 1.7 billion pounds ($2.28bn), most of it through its UK subsidiary Airwave Solutions.

The Home Office awarded Airwave an extension worth 1.562 billion pounds ($2.13bn) to provide the secure communications network used by police, fire and ambulance services across England, Scotland and Wales. Motorola Solutions UK separately holds contracts worth 123.9 million pounds ($170m), including a 36.5-million-pound ($49.8m) Ministry of Defence contract for Airwave radios, accessories and airtime.

The UN lists Motorola Solutions for its settlement-related activities, including the provision of security equipment and services. Procurement records reviewed by Al Jazeera show Motorola command-and-control technology used in security and surveillance infrastructure by authorities in the occupied West Bank.

Al Jazeera contacted the Motorola Solutions group for comment but received no response.

Chinese conglomerate Fosun International is identified by the UN under the category covering the commercial use of natural resources, particularly water and land.

Its connection to the occupied West Bank centres on Israeli cosmetics manufacturer Ahava Dead Sea Laboratories.

In the UK, Breas Medical, which Fosun International owns through Shanghai Fosun Pharmaceutical, secured a contract worth 98,000 pounds ($131,000) with Hull hospitals. The award brings the total value of public-sector contracts held by the group to at least 1.3 million pounds ($1.74m).

Al Jazeera contacted Fosun for comment but received no response.

French engineering group Egis provides another type of connection via transport infrastructure linking illegal Israeli settlements in occupied East Jerusalem with the rest of the city.

The UN lists Egis in connection with the “provision of services and utilities supporting the maintenance and existence of settlements, including transport”.

Egis told Al Jazeera it “formally expressed its disagreement with this inclusion” in the UN database.

A new contract worth 84,000 pounds ($113,000) was awarded to Thomas & Adamson International Limited, a subsidiary of Egis. The award brings the total value of public contracts held by Egis and its subsidiaries to at least 133.7 million pounds ($179.3m).
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: UK government announced new powers on September 8 to sanction companies profiting from business with Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Al Jazeera investigation found businesses named by the United Nations over their involvement in illegal Israeli settlements have secured contracts across the British public sector.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Moscow summit tests Russia’s waning grip on former Soviet allies
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Mansur Mirovalev
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The Kremlin’s tense relationship with Armenia will be under the spotlight at a security summit in Moscow.

President Vladimir Putin will chair a session of the Collective Security Council of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), the Russia-dominated post-Soviet military bloc, on Wednesday.

But since February 2024, Armenia’s participation in the bloc has been frozen.

While the membership technically exists, Armenia does not participate in the bloc’s activities, having effectively boycotted it after it lost a war against Azerbaijan. Yerevan blamed the group for failing to offer meaningful support during the conflict.

Armenia “de facto doesn’t participate in the CSTO’s operations,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last week. “What happens next will depend on the nature of the discussions within the organisation.”

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said on November 5 that “our interest in the CSTO has run its course”.

During the 2020 war with Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, a region once dominated by ethnic Armenians, the CSTO failed to live up to its core principle.

Neither Russia nor other member states – Belarus and three Central Asian nations of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan – deployed troops to aid Armenia, though the CSTO’s charter envisages such aid.

Moscow also maintains two military bases in Armenia with thousands of servicemen and border guards.

Azerbaijan, which withdrew from the CSTO in 1999, used new weaponry procured from Russia for billions of dollars.

Baku’s military triumph also relied on Turkish and Israeli-made drones and a revised war playbook that reflected recent breakthroughs in warfare and military technology.

Pashinyan’s anti-Kremlin stance has been a thorn in Moscow’s side since he came to power in 2018 after massive protests against Russia-backed Armenian leaders. Yerevan is also seeking membership in the European Union.

Moves to strip Armenia of its voting rights in the CSTO amount to “a demonstrative whipping”, Galiya Ibragimova, a Moldova-based expert on Central Asia, told Al Jazeera.

“Considering that the other CSTO nations are more dependent on Russia economically or stick to the, ‘Don’t poke the tiger’ logic, they’ll keep mum or watch how a bad student is being whipped in class,” she said.

The political gauntlet that Armenia – a nation of 3 million coping with the arrival of more than 100,000 people from Nagorno-Karabakh – threw at Moscow reflects a paradigm shift in the former Soviet Union.

“Yerevan’s timing for these steps is very useful as Russia is too busy with its war in Ukraine and is to a large extent weakened by [Western] sanctions and Ukraine’s military strikes on Russian economic infrastructure, as well as a looming recession,” Alisher Ilkhamov, head of the London-based Central Asia Due Diligence think tank, told Al Jazeera.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 became another pivotal moment that appeared to show how ineffective the CSTO was, as none of the member states backed Moscow militarily.

Shortly before the Ukraine war erupted, the CSTO flexed its muscles in January 2022, when Russia sent thousands of peacekeepers to several Kazakh cities following massive street protests.

But Moscow’s reported failures in the Ukraine war turned Russia’s political and military might “into a myth even Russian officials and military believe in – not to mention CSTO member states,” Ibragimova believes.

She said that the Russian weapons CSTO member states can procure are sold as both “discounted” and yet “advanced”, but in reality, “are very old weapons Russia didn’t need”.

Meanwhile, the ex-Soviet nations of Central Asia and the South Caucasus find new formats of military interaction.

One of them is the Turkiye-led Organization of Turkic States, which includes Azerbaijan and three Central Asian nations.

In late September, thousands of elite servicemen from Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan and Turkiye trained in Nagorno-Karabakh and on the Caspian shore to seize ships, land paratroopers and use drones to attack and supply ammunition.

They also try regional cooperation.

In October 2025, Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan held joint drills.

Moscow also failed to convince Uzbekistan, Central Asia’s economic powerhouse with a population of 37 million, to rejoin the CSTO.

Uzbekistan left the bloc in 1999, rejoined in 2006 and suspended its membership in 2012, preferring the role of an “observer state”.

“And even though Moscow expresses its vexation with the signs of disloyalty from Eurasian nations such as Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, it is so far only limited by expressing its dissatisfaction verbally,” Ilkhamov said.

“In the near future, Moscow [will be] unable to take decisive steps to bridle the region’s somewhat disloyal nations.”

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev tries to “compensate for his steps towards the West with demonstration of loyalty towards Moscow,” Ilkhamov said.

Mirziyoyev has attended the most important date of Moscow’s political calendar – the annual May 9 “Victory Parade” that commemorates the Soviet Union’s decisive role in defeating Nazi Germany.

He also sends Uzbek troops to joint drills with Russia – but also welcomes Western dignitaries such as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited Uzbekistan in mid-October.

“No matter how Russian officials hint to Uzbekistan that it would be good to return, it never did,” Ibragimova said.

The only “real” item on the Moscow summit’s agenda is the security situation in Afghanistan, which borders Central Asia, Ruslan Suleymanov, an associate fellow at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a US-British think tank, told Al Jazeera.

Russian officials have warned this year that up to 23,000 fighters from more than 20 armed groups operate in Afghanistan.

Especially dangerous is ISIL in Khorasan Province (ISKP), which operates in several Afghan provinces.

The group “actively recruits youngsters from Central Asia, especially Tajikistan,” Suleymanov said.

The group’s operations reach far beyond Afghanistan – it claimed responsibility for the 2024 attack on a Moscow concert hall that killed more than 140 people, including five children, and wounded more than 550.

This year, the CSTO states boosted security on the Afghan-Tajik border that spans 1,344km (835 miles).

“That’s why Russia and Central Asian nations take what’s happening in Afghanistan seriously,” Suleymanov said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Armenia does not participate in the Collective Security Council of Collective Security Treaty Organization. The CSTO states boosted security on the Afghan-Tajik border this year.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Israeli forces kill 14-year-old Palestinian boy in occupied West Bank
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Israeli forces have shot and killed a 14-year-old Palestinian boy and wounded two other teens during a raid on the village of Burqa in the occupied West Bank, according to officials.

The Palestinian Ministry of Health identified the victim on Tuesday as Moataz Iyad Daghlas and said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.

The Palestinian Wafa news agency reported that two other teenagers were wounded – a 17-year-old shot in the abdomen and pelvis and a 19-year-old hit in the hand.

The Israeli military confirmed the shooting in Burqa, which is located near the city of Nablus.

In a statement, the military said soldiers opened fire to prevent Palestinians from throwing stones at Israeli vehicles.

“The forces responded with gunfire to neutralise the threat and several hits were confirmed,” it said.

According to Wafa, soldiers detained Moataz’s father and stopped an ambulance from reaching the wounded.

They briefly held three volunteer paramedics from the Palestine Red Crescent Society who were working in the area, it reported.

The attacks come as Israeli pogroms in the occupied West Bank surge to what the United Nations has called an “unprecedented level”, following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.

According to the UN, at least 1,143 Palestinians have been killed in the occupied West Bank since October 7, 2023, including 250 children.

The figure includes Palestinians killed by Israeli settlers living in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) said 2026 is on track to be the most violent year for settler-related violence since it began monitoring the territory a decade ago. In July alone, 11 people were killed in four incidents involving armed settlers alongside Israeli forces.

Hebron, Ramallah, Nablus, Jenin, and el-Bireh have seen the worst of the settlers’ pogroms.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Israeli forces have shot and killed a 14-year-old Palestinian boy and wounded two other teens. The Israeli military confirmed the shooting in Burqa, near the city of Nablus. The Palestinian Ministry of Health identified the victim as Moataz Iyad Daghlas.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
European foreign ministers have told United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Europe must have a say in any deal to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, as US-mediated peace talks get under way in Abu Dhabi.

They made the appeal on Monday in Paris, at a meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of Seven, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

It was Rubio’s first meeting with allies since last week’s midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered stunning losses. The meeting gave Washington’s allies a chance to air their concerns with Rubio directly amid concern about Trump’s growing rhetoric of a new security architecture for Europe.

“It is certainly neither necessary, nor right, nor appropriate to make a fundamental change” to Europe’s security architecture, said German Minister for Foreign Affairs Johann Wadephul after talks with Rubio.

“Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe – only with Europe,” he added.

The two-day Paris meeting, which ends on Tuesday, overlaps with the talks between Russia and Ukraine, scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.

Wadephul said the Abu Dhabi talks must show whether Russia is “genuinely prepared to negotiate”, urging Moscow to “give up maximalist demands” and warning against any “negotiation show” in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

With Russian attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure continuing, he said, “we see no substantial contribution whatsoever toward negotiations gaining any serious momentum” from Moscow.

Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, is set to join a session on Ukraine in Paris on Tuesday.

“No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” Sybiha said before departing for the meeting.

The Paris meeting comes as G7 members have grown increasingly uneasy with the direction of US policy, including Washington’s scaling back of support for Ukraine and of sanctions on Russia, as well as its increasingly unilateral course.

Ministers from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, South Korea and Brazil are also attending.

Iran is expected to feature prominently in the discussions on Tuesday.

Washington’s G7 allies have repeatedly voiced scepticism about the US and Israeli war on Iran and fear that further US military action could deepen the crisis rather than resolve it.

Al Jazeera’s Rebecca Collard, reporting from Paris, said the first day of talks had wrapped up with little clarity on US policy after the midterm elections.

“The second day of talks will include a session on instability in the Middle East,” she said.

“But there is something bigger up for discussion, too: The future of the multilateralism that has dominated relations among these countries for decades.”

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/califo.title: California’s proposed ‘billionaire tax’ fails to pass
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/califo.author: Lucas Ropek
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/califo.text:
California voters have rejected Proposition 40, the state’s proposed one-time tax on billionaires, the Associated Press reported Monday. The measure failed after an expensive campaign that pitted labor unions against some of tech’s wealthiest figures. It was also opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom.

Nic Carter lives about as far from Silicon Valley as you can get within the continental U.S. but his feelings about California’s proposed tax on billionaires couldn’t have been stronger.

Carter, a Floridian, and a general partner at the crypto-focused venture capital firm Castle Island Ventures, told TechCrunch before the vote that he thought the proposal — it was on the ballot during California’s midterm election last week — would actually have been a huge win for more fiscally conservative states like his own.

“I think it’d be it would be great for Florida and Texas if these kinds of taxes pass,” Carter said last week. “I think it’s a shame, frankly, that California has this sort of semi-monopoly on capital formation, and that it’s being squandered by local governance that’s super dysfunctional.”

Proposition 40, otherwise known as the California “billionaire’s tax,” was a ballot measure that proposed the creation of a special one-time 5% wealth tax to be levied against state residents with a net worth of more than $1 billion. The tax, which would have been applied retroactively to anyone who was residing in California on January 1, 2026, would have been used to fund a number of public programs — most notably Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program that provides healthcare to qualifying low-income residents.

Proponents of the proposal — largely labor unions — said it would have inconvenienced a tiny number of state residents, as California has a little over 200 billionaires who own a cumulative total of approximately $2 trillion in wealth. In return, they said, it would generate massive amounts of revenue. Its backers projected it could have raised as much as $100 billion over five years, the likes of which could then have been used to support public healthcare and education.

But opponents argued that it would scare California’s wealthiest residents out of the state and ultimately disincentivize growth. The capital flight argument — that California’s upper crust would permanently flee, thus draining a more consistent source of revenue for the state — dominated conversations online among business leaders in the run-up to the vote. A critical but contested analysis published before the vote claimed the proposal would actually have lost the state money over time.

Carter, who subscribes to this argument, had called the tax a “sword of Damocles hanging” over the heads of founders. The threat, he said, wasn’t just from this particular wealth tax but also from anticipated future taxes.

“You’re signaling to the entrepreneur class that you consider them a resource to be plundered,” he said.

Carter, who frequently works in San Francisco with tech startups, claimed such a tax would “inhibit venture capital investment” because VCs “wouldn’t necessarily want to invest in a company if they knew the founder was going to have to liquidate a huge percentage of their shares.” The logic: since many billionaires keep a majority of their wealth tied to their companies, it would be inconvenient for newly minted billionaires to make liquid a certain percentage of that wealth just so that they could pay the tax.

Jesse Tinsely, a California entrepreneur who has spent his life working in startups, agreed. Tinsely is the co-founder and CEO of Mainstreet, a fintech holding company that owns employment sites like Employer.com and Recruiter.com. Tinsely founded his first startup many years ago and said that, based on his own experience, what he had accomplished wouldn’t have been possible with the proposed tax. Additionally, he reiterated a widely held fear — that founders, who could be taxed on their corporate assets, would be incentivized to give up control over their companies.

“I bootstrapped my business. I have super voting shares, and I came from a [background as a] college dropout [and] broke firefighter with bad credit and whatnot, and built a business that’s valued into the billions,” Tinsely said last week. “I think it [the tax] removes the ability to do something like that.”

Tinsely said he felt the proposed tax “forces founders to opt into a system” where “anyone who wants to become an entrepreneur has to…raise money or some type of capital, or move. Those are basically the only two options.”

One of the key architects of the tax policy, Emmanuel Saez, told TechCrunch before the vote that fears about loss of founder control were unfounded, and not part of the design of the proposal. Saez, a French economics professor at the UC Berkeley, helped to create and promote the ballot measure alongside Gabriel Zucman, another Berkeley economist.

“The wealth tax hits you by diluting your economic ownership but [shares] can be easily structured to avoid losing any control rights,” Saez said, pointing to the fact that many billionaires only own a small percent of their companies. He’s also argued that stock can be structured to divorce economic ownership and voting control. Indeed, a common strategy to achieve this is called a dual-class share structure, which gives founders powerful voting rights even with limited shares.

Saez noted that AI has helped to drive a huge explosion in wealth in California but that much of that wealth is tied to a very small number of companies and individuals, many of whom won’t pay much back into the state’s coffers. He pointed out that California doesn’t really generate that much revenue from the billionaire class anyway. The state is estimated to take in about $3 billion a year from this group, representing about 1% of the total amount of revenue brought in between 2025 and 2026.

Despite its populist appeal, Proposition 40 struggled to win over enough Californians and was ultimately rejected. Invariably, many will cite voters’ lack of enthusiasm on a massive influx of spending that the bill’s opponents leveraged. The spending included as much as $379 million from the coffers of billionaires like Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who funneled their money into a multi-pronged media assault designed to discredit it. The AP reported that the “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side.

Supporters of the measure signaled the fight isn’t over, though. The AP reported that backers said they could put a similar tax back on the ballot in 2028.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/tsmcs-oc.title: TSMC's October sales jump as global chip boom rolls on
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/tsmcs-oc.author: Jenny Lee
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/tsmcs-oc.text:
TSMC reported October revenue on Tuesday, up 14.7% from last month.

October’s figure is up 59.7% from a year earlier.

Broadly, Taiwan has reported that its exports surged 58.9% in October, according to government data.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co
. on Tuesday reported October revenue of 586.89 billion New Taiwan dollars ($17.88 billion), up 59.7% from a year earlier and up 14.7% from the previous month.

The world’s largest contract chipmaker benefited from strong demand for advanced semiconductors, as major technology companies continue to invest heavily in artificial intelligence.

Last month, TSMC reported a record third-quarter net profit of NT$763.1 billion, beating estimates while revenue came at NT$1.49 trillion.

The chipmaker expects capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years as it continues to invest to support customer demand. Its third-quarter operating margin reached 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%.

TSMC shares closed 2.24% higher on Tuesday, amid broader market volatility in Taiwan. The island’s financial regulator last week announced tighter short-selling restrictions that took effect Monday, cutting the daily limit on intraday short-selling orders from 30% to 3%.

Separately, Taiwan’s exports surged 58.9% in October from a year earlier to $96.76 billion, according to government data released Monday. Strong demand for advanced chips helped drive a 61.4% increase in electronic components exports, local media reported, citing the finance ministry.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/q.title: More homes proposed for entertainment precinct in 'tall over sprawl' plan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/q.author: Ned Hammond and Lexy Hamilton-Smith
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Lexy Hamilton-Smith

Topic:
Urban Development and Planning

Fortitude Valley could see building height limits increase from 30 to 40 storeys in some parts of the entertainment precinct. (Supplied: Harcourts Inner East)

The Brisbane City Council has announced a plan to increase building height limits in Fortitude Valley in a bid to increase "tall over sprawl" housing.

Height limits would be increased from 30 to 40 storeys at certain sites and entertainment precinct rules and noise limits strengthened under the proposed plan.

A community consultation process will take place from November 13 to December 18, with the final plan expected in 2027.

Brisbane's entertainment precinct could see building height limits increased and the development of thousands of new homes as part of the council's "tall over sprawl" strategy.

The Fortitude Valley Sustainable Growth Precinct Plan proposes increasing height limits from 30 to 40 storeys at sites between St Pauls Terrace, Brookes Street, along Ann Street and around Cathedral Place.

On the edge of the precinct, height limits would transition to 30 storeys and lower.

The proposed plan will increase height limits in parts of the valley to 40 storeys. (Supplied: Brisbane City Council)

Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said while entertainment precinct rules and noise protections would be strengthened, the council aimed to protect the nightlife and live music scene.

"We've made sure that any new building takes into account the fact that people will be moving into that kind of precinct that's an entertainment precinct, so buildings will need to be built in a way that protects people from noise impacts, that's part of our strict requirement," he said.

Adrian Schrinner says the plan would protect the live music scene while creating more room for homes. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The office of Queensland nightlife economy commissioner John Collins has been contacted for comment.

Brisbane City Council is adopting a "sky high" strategy to deal with a projected surge in population over the next 15 years.

The final plan is expected in 2027, with a period of community consultation from November 13 to December 18.

Fortitude Valley is the latest suburb targeted in the "tall over sprawl" strategy, with suburban centres Indooroopilly, Carindale and Nundah earlier earmarked for height increases.

Limited locations around the Indooroopilly and Carindale shopping centres will see an increase to 25 storeys, while height limits near the Nundah village and train station will increase to 15 storeys.

Those changes will go into effect from December 11.

Emeritus Professor Brian Roberts, who is also a Fellow of the Planning Institute of Australia said the "tall over sprawl" strategy is "tombstone architecture".

"Monuments, that are not aesthetically pleasing nor do they ensure the city functions in the most effective way," he said.

"40 storeys in the valley, is far too high, it is not the scale of Brisbane."

Brian Roberts says the council's "tall over sprawl" strategy is an example of "disjointed, incremental development". (Supplied)

Mr Roberts is a global expert in "managing cities", having worked for the World Bank and the United Nations, and is currently writing a report on the "Future of Asian Cities" for the United Nations.

Almost all the new apartments being built around Brisbane are described as some version of "luxury", despite demand for affordable new builds.

He said what Brisbane is turning into is "not urban living" but "disjointed, incremental development".

"And there is literature that shows once you start building over six to seven floors, there are a lot of psychological requirements that need to be looked at as well," he said.

"As you go higher, there is much higher incidence of loneliness for example and all those things that go against well being, which you get when living in well planned areas with good amenities."

Brisbane Residents United spokeswoman Elizabeth Handley urged the council and government to focus on social housing rather than high-rise apartments.

"No matter which way you stretch it and no matter how many storeys you keep adding on top of them, there is — and particularly with this government — no affordable housing component," Ms Handley said.

Elizabeth Handley says the changes risk the city's unique character. (612 ABC: Kenji Sato)

Ms Handley said the city's character was at risk if similar plans kept moving forward.

"I think it's so important that we have these areas in our city where they are slightly creative and they're a little bit grungy," she said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/b.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon denies stalking alleged murder victim
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/b.author: Phoebe Pin
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Beau Lamarre-Condon was quizzed about text messages he sent friends about his relationship with Jesse Baird. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Cross-examination of Beau Lamarre-Condon has continued, with the former police officer denying claims he was "obsessed" with alleged murder victim Jesse Baird.

He was quizzed on his relationship and first break-up with Mr Baird, with Mr Lamarre-Condon describing the split as "amicable".

He rejected suggestions he was "stalking" Mr Baird and monitoring his movements after the split.

Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied stalking and attempting to "manufacture" meetings with alleged murder victim Jesse Baird.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to murdering his former partner and Mr Baird's new boyfriend Luke Davies.

He maintains both died following separate struggles over his police pistol inside Mr Baird's Paddington share house on February 19, 2024.

The former NSW Police officer said he went to the property that morning to retrieve his belongings, his casual romance with Mr Baird having ended in November 2023.

During his fourth day in the witness box on Tuesday, Mr Lamarre-Condon told the court the pair first met in October 2022 and had a number of sexual encounters before they started going on romantic dates around December of that year.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to the alleged murders of Mr Baird (left) and Mr Davies (right). (Supplied: Instagram)

Prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that he had been "obsessed with [Mr Baird] right from the start".

He suggested the fact that Mr Baird was a television presenter contributed to that obsession, with the court hearing Mr Lamarre-Condon was an entertainment reporter in his teens and had encounters with rapper Pitbull and celebrity Kourtney Kardashian.

Mr Lamarre-Condon said he was not interested in Mr Baird's job and liked him for who he was as a person.

He said he was "smitten" with Mr Baird, but not obsessed with him.

The court was shown a message Mr Lamarre-Condon sent to a friend on December 22, 2022 in which he said "I'm in love fml" in reference to a video Mr Baird sent him.

Another text read, "It sounds crazy, I love him."

"I say I love you to all my friends and people like that all the time," Mr Lamarre-Condon told the court.

Mr Hatfield put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that he "fretted" when Mr Baird was slow to respond to his messages, and felt "insecure" about the relationship.

"Yeah at times I was a bit in my head," Mr Lamarre-Condon said.

The pair holidayed together at a farm in March 2023, with Mr Lamarre-Condon posting a video of the trip to social media.

Mr Lamarre-Condon admitted to going through Mr Baird's Instagram messages on his phone without consent during the holiday because he wanted to see if the television presenter was talking to other men.

"Curiosity just got the best of me," he said.

Mr Lamarre-Condon made a video of his farm getaway with Mr Baird.

He told the court he unfollowed two or three people on Mr Baird's Instagram account.

"I acknowledge that unfollowing people is a breach of his privacy," he said.

He would go through Mr Baird's phone again before the couple's first break up in April 2023.

Mr Lamarre-Condon said he came across messages from another man who believed he was in an exclusive relationship with Mr Baird.

He sent a photo of the messages to at least three friends to ask for their advice, the court heard.

Mr Lamarre-Condon said he told Mr Baird he went through his phone on the second occasion, but not the first.

The pair subsequently split, with Mr Lamarre-Condon saying he was upset but not depressed about the relationship ending.

"I missed him as a friend as well," he said.

He described the break-up as "amicable".

Mr Lamarre-Condon accepts he was upset about the break-up. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

The court was shown messages Mr Lamarre-Condon sent his friends about Mr Baird in early May, including screenshots from the man's Instagram stories.

He said he also may have been sent an image taken by a friend of Mr Baird working as an umpire.

"I definitely wasn't stalking him," he said.

He accepted he used a key left outside Mr Baird's house to retrieve his belongings sometime in late April or early May after their first break-up.

Mr Lamarre-Condon rejected the suggestion he broke into the property.

"He did say when we had our very amicable, civil conversation that I could come by anytime to get my belongings," he said.

Mr Hatfield accused Mr Lamarre-Condon of monitoring Mr Baird's location using Snapchat maps and attempting to "manufacture" running into his ex-partner after their break-up.

"I'm going to run into old mate today," Mr Lamarre-Condon said in a message to a friend.

Mr Lamarre-Condon said that was an example of "wishful thinking".

"I was hoping to run into him whilst at dinner," he said.

Prosecutors allege Mr Lamarre-Condon stalked Mr Baird. (Supplied: Instagram)

The court was shown more messages in which he tells a friend he did in fact run into Mr Baird, with the friend asking if Mr Lamarre-Condon made the encounter "look like a coincidence".

"This reflects you were stalking him and monitoring his location," Mr Hatfield put to Mr Lamarre-Condon.

"I don't agree," Mr Lamarre-Condon replied.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Amid questions over Japan’s cybersecurity, just how safe is the My Number system?
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Maddie Baker
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
With companies reporting new data breaches almost daily in recent weeks — exposing millions of customers’ personal records in some cases — concerns are growing over whether it is only a matter of time before information held under Japan’s My Number system is compromised.

The system uses a 12-digit number as a digital ID for residents, while the My Number card provides access to a range of government services involving highly sensitive personal information, including tax, pensions, medical history and family registry records.

The Digital Agency maintains that the system is secure because data is decentralized and stored across multiple locations, including local governments and businesses. This, it says, prevents attackers from gaining access to a broad range of personal information in a single breach, as might be possible in a centralized system. The system also complies with an internationally recognized security standard.

But experts are worried that data could leak from local governments and companies with low-level security, rather than the My Number system itself.

“I’m very concerned,” said Seiji Mizunaga, a lawyer from Makinouchi Comprehensive Law Office in Tokyo. “Many of these databases have low levels of security because of their budget and limited staff numbers.”

Given that even the Digital Agency, which oversees My Number, has experienced information breaches, large-scale leaks of specific personal information could occur from several local governments and private companies, he said.

The Digital Agency has been exposed to cyber leaks twice this year though it emphasized that My Number data had not been compromised in these breaches.

Several private companies have also had the My Number data that they collected exposed but these cases did not involve a breach of government infrastructure.

Other concerns are related to the ever-changing nature of data leaks and hacking. It has become apparent that artificial intelligence tools were used in multiple recent cyberattacks against organizations in Japan and other countries.

Mizunaga suggested that the government should consider reevaluating whether the My Number security system will remain safe in the future.

A growing concern among My Number card holders is the fact that more functions — as well as data — are being added to make it an indispensable all-in-one card.

Currently, the My Number card is the default form of an individual’s national health insurance card. Additionally, the system also incorporates information from foreign residence cards and driver’s licenses, allowing individuals to carry just their My Number card in place of the other two. It can be used to print out residential documents at convenience stores or to apply for a passport as well.

As of the end of October, 84.6% of Japan’s population had signed up for the My Number system — representing a total of over 104 million cards.

The Digital Agency has sought to reassure the public about the security of the system — reiterating that highly confidential data, including tax amounts and medical diagnoses, is not recorded on the IC chip contained within the physical card and that sensitive information is managed across multiple databases.

Other safety measures include requiring additional authentication methods in order to unlock sensitive My Number information in addition to the card, such as a PIN or facial recognition.

Moreover, the My Number card has been designed with “tamper resistance.” This means that after a certain number of failed attempts to access personal information contained in the IC chip, the card flags up the threat and automatically erases its contents or locks access.

Responding to the current concerns about personal data security, Masakatsu Nishigaki, a professor of computer sciences at Shizuoka University, described today’s pace of AI development as “very dangerous.”

Nishigaki emphasized that although the most advanced frontier AI can only “identify existing security flaws” at the moment, human hackers are able to use frontier AI as a tool to carry out more attacks at pace.

Despite this challenging environment, Nishigaki did not believe that confidential information linked to the My Number system would be compromised even in the case of a data leak.

“While there may still be some residual risks, the system is designed so that, unless someone possesses a truly high level of professional expertise, it remains secure,” he said.

Hiroshi Miyashita, a law professor at Chuo University, is also confident in the security of the My Number system.

“To the best of my knowledge, there have been no cases — including those recently involving ransomware or other cyberattacks — where data has been leaked from the My Number system or unauthorized access has occurred specifically via a My Number card,” he said.

But Miyashita said the government should consider how it stores personal data to further improve information security.

For example, hospitals and pharmacies are required to retain patient records for seven years. “One effective measure (to prevent leaks) would be to move this older data that’s connected to online systems to a separate, offline environment,” he suggested.

Looking beyond Japan, Austria has been recognized internationally for the security of its electronic identification system, known as ID Austria.

The system, which creates multiple identification numbers for different administrative purposes from an original common base number, was used by Japanese authorities as an example when setting up My Number.

“Even if personal data from one sector is leaked, (Austria’s) system is designed so that personal data from other sectors cannot be matched,” said lawyer Mizunaga.

Given the security benefits, Mizunaga called on Japan to make changes to My Number to follow Austria’s ID system more closely.

“Despite having studied such a pioneering system, Japan built the My Number system that uses a ‘common number’” rather than the more secure Austrian multiple ID number system, he said.

“There has been a huge uproar over the leak of driver’s license information, but if My Number card information is leaked, the damage will be even greater.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: The Digital Agency maintains that the system is secure because Japan built the My Number system. The system uses a 12-digit number as a digital ID for residents, while the My number card provides access to a range of government services.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/poli.author: Matthew Cheng
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/poli.text:
From January, staff can use the new leave to care for relatives, attend children’s school activities or handle household emergencies

Hong Kong’s civil servants will be entitled to up to 12 hours of family care leave a year from January, with the government promising flexible, streamlined approval procedures as part of a “people-orientated” approach.

The Civil Service Bureau set out details of the initiative, first announced in September’s policy address, in a paper submitted to the Legislative Council’s public service panel on Tuesday.

Staff may use the leave to accompany family members to medical appointments, care for sick relatives, attend their children’s school activities or deal with household emergencies.

https://www.dw.com/en/why-malnutrition-c.title: Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health
https://www.dw.com/en/why-malnutrition-c.text:
More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/why-malnutrition-c.summary: Mal malnutrition can cause bone, joint and muscle pain, and even fatal illness. Some people still develop a nutrient deficiency when eating a healthy and balanced diet.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.title: Polish unity on show in silent march to honour Krakow shooting victims
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.text:
Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.

The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.

As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower.

Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, one marking each spot where someone died.

Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.

The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.

Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday.

Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it's too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology.

"The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Dr Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised.

"So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet."

There's been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly.

In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit.

The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative."

It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered.

It's alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow.

Two days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued.

A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside.

Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim."

Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks.

On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire.

One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening.

A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly.

Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured.

Olha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous.

On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window.

Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she exclaimed.

"It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it."

She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice."

When Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father.

Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour.

He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point.

Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember.

Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them.

On Monday, the government announced an urgent review.

At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital.

Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon."

A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass.

"This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life."

"Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me.

He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish.

"People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse."

Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered.

Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without accounting for the devastation he allegedly wrought.

"I think we deserve to know why."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.summary: Polish president and prime minister led a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night. Thousands of people joined a silent protest in memory of those killed and injured. The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: EU manufacturers could give up on competing with China by 2030, warns commerce chief
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Lisa O’Carroll
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Jens Eskelund says Europe may need to allow its companies to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains

Europe’s manufacturers could give up on attempting to compete with their Chinese counterparts by the end of the decade if current trends continue amid fears over mass job losses, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China has warned.

In a case of “if you can’t beat them, join them”, Jens Eskelund said European companies operating in China were now thinking “Made in China for China” could be replaced by a philosophy of “Made in China for the world”.

Eskelund, who heads the influential Beijing-headquartered body, said European manufacturers could find themselves at an existential crossroads by the end of the decade, asking themselves: “What is the point of trading?”

As the EU gets tough with China with a deficit running at a record £1bn (€1.18bn) a day and an increasing mood for protectionism in Brussels, Berlin and Paris, he said European countries might need to shift their policies to allow domestic manufacturers to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains, rather than treat them as competitors.

Eskelund, who is also a managing director of the shipping group Maersk’s Chinese operations, pointed to a report by Goldman Sachs that forecasted Chinese exports would lower the EU’s gross domestic product by 0.5% by the end of the decade while reducing Germany’s by up to 0.9%.

“It raises the question, if China’s trade delivers negative value, why trade?” the Danish businessman said.

“If you are suddenly in a situation where trade creates a lot of value for one party, but it destroys value for the other, countries will begin to ask themselves, why do we trade?” he said, pointing to a potential doomsday scenario in which manufacturing disappeared from European countries, causing mass job losses, collapse in the tax base and potential multigenerational unemployment and spiralling social benefits costs.

Speaking in Brussels, where he has been in back-to-back meetings with European Commission officials to give them feedback from Beijing, he said Europe is at an inflection point.

“If we create new dependencies, ultimately that might result in Europe losing its ability to determine its own future,” with mass job losses and fraying of communities, Eskelund added.

That existential threat is already beginning to bite in Europe’s car, chemicals and renewable energy sectors, with the German automotive industry hit by a double whammy of reduced profits in China and cheap competition at home from Chinese companies such as BYD, Geely and SAIC Motor. Last week, BMW said its sales in China had dropped 22% in the first nine months of the year, in line with expectations of suppressed domestic demand, while issuing a second profit warning this year.

Eskelund is not a fan of the term “China shock 2.0” – which refers to the impact of the huge rise in exports of, cars, chemicals and components – on local industry to the EU in the last five years. He said it should not have come as a surprise as Beijing’s plans to displace imports were the enduring theme of the last three five-year plans since Beijing’s Made in China strategy was agreed in 2015.

“I don’t really like the term China shock 2.0 because these things that are happening should not be a shock because it is all written in their five-year plans so you should be able to anticipate that,” Eskelund said.

“The proof of concept here is that China has been laser-focused on reducing its own dependencies over the last 30 years,” he added, pointing to a concomitant reduction in imports.

A recent report by Centre for European Reform (CER) urged Germany to stop “admiring” Beijing and change its strategy, with China’s latest five-year plan (2026 to 2030) a doubling-down on “self-reliance”.

“It is committed to displacing imports in the few sectors where it still depends on foreign supply,” said the CER.

The sectors that have been identified in China’s latest five-year plan are AI, quantum computing; robotics; smart and green tech; biomanufacturing; brain-computer interfaces; and 6G communications.

Solar panels, wind turbines, robots, driverless cars, advanced chips are part of China’s new strategy for global domination.

Eskelund’s advice to those industries in Europe is not to hide but brace themselves for China to deliver. Once a strategy is decided in Beijing, incentives, tax breaksand subsidies flow down by region to town and village levels. Officials across the country know what to focus on and do, he said.

His advice to EU leaders: “Engage with China and discuss getting to a point where everyone can see value is being created for both sides”, something he thinks Beijing understands.

While this might be an obvious point, Eskelund said a fundamental shift in approach was needed in Europe.

“China has always been very focused on outcomes, whereas Europe has been more focused on principles. It raises the question of whether following principles is delivering undesirable outcomes,” Eskelund said.

A view expressed in some quarters, including the UK, that trade imbalance could be addressed by increasing exports was just “fantasy”, said Eskelund, with this year’s surplus against the rest of the world expected to surpass 2025’s record $1.2tn (£900bn).

Eskelund said many companies were still making good money in China but the brutal competition in the country’s supply chains, combined with a currency undervalued by about 30%, left Europeans in the dust.

“What we see right now is that in almost all industrial verticals, almost anywhere in the world, you would have one and probably several Chinese competitors” he said.

“It’s just very, very difficult in most industries to compete with the Chinese.”

Giving up on trade is not the answer. If you can’t beat them join them. And that is what is now happening, the chamber has found.

“One way that they can compete with the Chinese supply chain is to become a part of the Chinese supply chain itself,” Eskelund said.

“For many companies it’s not the profit that you make in China that matters as much as the way Chinese supply chains enable you to compete on a global marketplace.”

This could mean making the products in China in joint domestic partnerships with European companies and getting into global supply chains in conjunction with Chinese firms.

“It is a sort of evolution from the old days when you came to China to service the Chinese market in China for China. It has now become: be in China, for the world. I think it’s a fairly significant shift,” Eskelund said.

For many of his members this had led to an “uptick in confidence” in the past year.

“This has turned out to be one of the ways that companies adapt, faced with a saturated market in China, they begin to explore exports,” he said.
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.summary: Jens Eskelund says European manufacturers could find themselves at an existential crossroads by the end of the decade. He says European companies operating in China are now thinking ‘Made in China for China’s’

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: New Knesset speaker could be key to ousting Netanyahu as Israel’s PM
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Emma Graham-Harrison Chief Middle East correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Opposition politicians get first chance to take control of levers of power, even as they struggle to form government

Israel’s new Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday, giving opposition politicians their first chance to take control of some levers of power, even as they struggle to form a new government to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu.

High on the agenda will be replacing the speaker, who wields immense influence by controlling the legislature’s agenda. The role is currently held by Amir Ohana, a close ally of Netanyahu.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Gadi Eisenkot, the former Israeli military chief who got the presidential mandate to try to form a coalition government at the weekend, may take the role himself, Israeli media reported on Monday.

The effort to wrest away control of the Knesset is significant enough that more than 160 top former security officials, including heads of the military, intelligence and police, warned that rightwing activists were planning to disrupt the day with violent attacks.

“Actors who oppose replacing the Knesset speaker intend to go to the Knesset on the day of the swearing-in ceremony and to prevent the MKs and their family members from entering the building,” a forum of retired commanders, the Democracy’s Protective Wall, warned in a letter to serving security chiefs.

“These same actors are encouraging tens of thousands of citizens who support their stance to come and to help them with their mission,” Ma’ariv newspaper quoted the letter saying.

If Eisenkot does not take the speaker role, opposition parties have agreed that someone from his Yashar party will be the nominee.

The opposition parties hold 67 seats in the 120-seat legislature, enough to install a consensus choice for speaker. All have described the current prime minister as a threat to the state and are keen to start moving against him, despite divides blocking the formation of a coalition.

But several of the Jewish-Israeli opposition parties in his “change” bloc have sworn not to sit with the Palestinian-led parties that hold over a quarter of the bloc’s seats, or even join a minority government that has their backing.

Eisenkot has vowed to broker a national emergency government, promising to achieve it with “creative and unconventional political acts”.

In a sign of challenges ahead, he effectively warned that some election promises would have to be broken to unseat Netanyahu.

“No one will be able to fulfil all the [campaign] promises they made, and all of us will need to compromise. That is also leadership, to know when to decide and set priorities,” he said.

There have been protests across Israel urging Jewish-Israeli opposition parties to put unseating Netanyahu ahead of a racist commitment to excluding Palestinian-led parties from government.

Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of Israel’s population and voted in unprecedented numbers this year, giving them 19 seats. Without them, the opposition bloc has fewer seats than Netanyahu’s diminished coalition.

Rightwing opposition leader Avigdor Lieberman has been trying to seek an alternative path to government through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties. They have long been Netanyahu allies but have been frustrated by his failure to deliver on the promise to pass broad military draft exemptions for their community into law. Lieberman has campaigned hard for universal conscription, but appears to prefer compromise on this issue to working with Palestinians.

“Has the End of Times arrived?” leading Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) journalist Arye Erlich wrote in a column for Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.

“Has Avigdor Lieberman … the biggest persecutor of Haredim Israeli politics has seen in decades, suddenly come to believe that he can compromise on a military draft bill and sit in a coalition government alongside the Haredim?”

Even if Eisenkot does broker a coalition deal, he may delay announcing it until Netanyahu’s speaker has been replaced. Netanyahu is a master of political survival and last-minute deals, fracturing past coalitions by luring defectors into his own alliance.

Ohana could delay signing in a new government for up to a week, and some of the opposition do not want to give Netanyahu that much time to attack the pressure points of any fragile deal.

If Eisenkot cannot form a government, the mandate is passed to other leaders and if they too fail Israel must hold elections again. In the meantime Netanyahu and his far-right allies would stay on as a caretaker government.

Although Netanyahu is calling for his opponents to join him in a unity government, a long period of limbo followed by a new vote offers him a likelier path back to power.

If an alternative government takes power, it will be harder for Netanyahu to destabilise it, said Gideon Rahat, chair in political science at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

“Once they establish a government, they might be a minority government, it might be hard for them to do things, but nevertheless, they will be governing and it would be hard to oust them.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Opposition politicians get first chance to take control of levers of power. High on agenda will be replacing the speaker, who wields immense influence by controlling the legislature’s agenda. The role is currently held by Amir Ohana, a close ally of Netanyahu.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Young people in UK hit by ‘low-gear economy’, warns Bank of England deputy
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Exclusive: Iran war has fuelled energy price rise and clouded outlook, driving up unemployment, says Clare Lombardelli

Young people in Britain are bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” as employers hold back from hiring amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East, a deputy governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Clare Lombardelli, the Bank’s deputy governor for monetary policy, said the unfolding conflict, which has triggered a surge in energy prices and clouded the outlook for the economy, was contributing to an increase in youth unemployment.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“What you see is the cost falling on young people, so you can see this rapid rise in the number of young people who are struggling to find jobs,” she said.

Against a highly volatile backdrop, she also warned Threadneedle Street was preparing for a “live” decision on interest rates next month after it increased the cost of borrowing last week for the first time in three years.

In an interview with the Guardian, Lombardelli said the UK’s employers were attempting to navigate the complex geopolitical backdrop by holding on to staff and freezing new recruitment.

“It’s what I call a low-gear economy. So a labour market where you’re seeing a real fall-off in hiring. But actually, we’re not seeing much in the way of redundancies. What’s going on is this kind of low hire, low fire dynamic,” she said.

“They [employers] are delaying hiring. They want to see if this uncertainty is going to resolve – like all of us. None of us thought we’d be nine months into this conflict.

“If firms are not hiring, obviously, by definition, that means people that are new to the labour market are hurt by that.”

Her comments come as Andy Burnham’s government awaits the findings of a report into young people and work by the former Labour cabinet minister, Alan Milburn, which is expected to be published next week.

With employers facing rising costs triggered by the Iran war, higher taxes and weaker levels of demand from consumers squeezed by the cost of living crisis, unemployment in the UK has risen this year to 4.7%. Youth unemployment has risen at a sharper rate to the highest levels outside the Covid pandemic since 2015.

Tackling the UK’s youth jobs crisis is also a growing priority for the government after an increase in the number of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.

Lombardelli is expected to outline her concerns over a slowdown in labour market dynamism at a speech in London on Tuesday.

Lombardelli joined the majority of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) in voting to lift the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. She said a further quarter-point rise could be warranted from as early as its next policy meeting in December.

“Every meeting is live for us. December is, you know, it’s certainly plausible. What’s the market pricing at the moment? It’s about 50/50 for December,” she said.

“I think it depends what we see on the conflict and the energy prices and it depends what we see in the wider data and how all that fits together. But I wouldn’t rule it out. Equally, I don’t have enough information just yet.”

Lombardelli was among members of the MPC who joined the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, in raising the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

Oil prices have fallen sharply, to below $100 a barrel, after the Democrats’ victories in the US Congress, which some investors have interpreted as potentially constraining Donald Trump’s capacity to prolong the conflict in Iran. Trump said at the weekend that he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progressed.

Lombardelli, a former Treasury and OECD economist, said the impact of an increasingly stagnant jobs market was being seen particularly in sectors that offer young people their first job. “So that might be hospitality, it might be retail, in particular,” she said. “If you look at the distribution of where variances are, they’ve really fallen off in those sectors where young people can get their first start in the labour market.”

She added that employers surveyed by the Bank suggested there is “a sense that hiring a young person is a higher risk than it used to be”.

Threadneedle Street is focusing heavily on the jobs market amid concerns that current high levels of inflation could become entrenched in the economy if workers have enough bargaining power to push for higher wage settlements – which could lead companies to put up their prices to cover higher wage bills, stoking inflation. Signs of a weaker labour market could diminish this risk.

However, Lombardelli said that higher levels of unemployment would not necessarily bear down on inflationary pressures. This is because employers – holding on to the staff they needed – were only hiring for positions they found harder to fill.

“You can have higher unemployment without it exerting a downward pressure on inflation,” she said. “So that’s obviously a problem.”
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.summary: Clare Lombardelli says young people are bearing the brunt of a 'low-gear economy' She says employers are holding on to staff and freezing new recruitment. She also warns Threadneedle Street is preparing for a 'live' decision on interest rates next month.
