https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
The top cricket official in Australia has ruled out another investigation into the so-called “sandpapergate” scandal despite remarks by Usman Khawaja and David Warner that knowledge of the 2018 ball-tampering plot was widespread throughout the team.

Cricket Australia (CA) ⁠boss Todd Greenberg said on Tuesday he believed all players held “very different views” from Khawaja’s version of events of the 2018 tour of South Africa as described in his recently released autobiography.

“There are specific details in his ⁠book that contradict the versions that have been provided by others,” Greenberg told ⁠local radio station SEN.

“But we have said we’re comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we’ve received,” he added.

“That includes what we’ve seen from Usman, and our position hasn’t changed on that. We don’t see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this again. I don’t think ‌there’s anything that can be gained from that.”

CA imposed bans and other penalties on Warner, former captain Steve Smith and former Test batter Cameron Bancroft four days after the incident came to light during the Cape Town Test.

Khawaja, in extracts from his autobiography published in Australian media, said “open, lighthearted discussions” were held during the South Africa series about ways to scuff up the ball, including by using sandpaper.

He said discussion of tampering was not confined to batters, bowlers or staff but extended throughout the team.

“It was all of us,” Khawaja said in the book, ⁠according to Australian media.

Warner, who retired from international cricket more than two years ago, ⁠broke his silence about the incident on Monday to throw his support behind Khawaja.

In a video posted on social media, Warner described his former teammate’s account as 100 percent accurate and the CA investigation as “botched” and “rushed”.

The four Australian bowlers who played in the Cape Town Test in 2018 and continue to represent the nation – Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon – issued a joint statement in 2021 denying any knowledge of the plot.

Captain Cummins said in South ‌Africa last month that he had spoken to Khawaja about his autobiography and was not concerned about any potential fallout.

“Answered every question a million times. So, yeah, it was dealt with then,” he said.

Some commentators have questioned why Khawaja ‌waited ‌eight years to speak out and accused him of trying to boost sales of his book Sabr.

Khawaja responded on social media on Tuesday, saying he had no commercial motives.

“I’m very fortunate, I don’t need the money,” he said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Can the Republican Party survive Trump?
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Esam Boraey
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
There is a saying in politics: “Every election is fundamentally about the next one.” On November 3, the Republican Party suffered what some have labelled a near “extinction-level” loss in the 2026 midterms. With the results likely to offer an indication of what lies ahead in the next presidential election, what options do Republicans have for 2028? First, we need to understand why this latest “blue tsunami” occurred. The midterms were a rejection of Trump, not an endorsement of the Democrats.

Last Tuesday’s outcome reflected voters holding Trump responsible for economic disaster, huge increases in the cost of living, his failing war on Iran, and his catering to Israel. It is also a condemnation of the Trump family using the Oval Office to enrich themselves and their friends to an unprecedented degree.

Coming into the midterms, voters saw the Trump administration as corrupt and as having abandoned the populist grassroots that had helped him get elected in the first place. A bad economy, failed tariffs, and an unwanted war widened the gap between the MAGA loyalists – who remain loyal to Trump as a political figure – and the America First factions of the Republican Party, which remain loyal to the values that Trump had campaigned on but failed to deliver. It was the separation of these two groups, once seen as interchangeable, that ultimately destroyed the Trump coalition, which had brought Trump and the Republicans to power in Washington.

During the latest midterms, we witnessed many prominent voices in the conservative movement openly oppose Republican leaders. Popular conservatives such as Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene spoke out publicly against several Republican candidates, including Mike Rogers in Michigan and Ken Paxton in Texas. Former Trump supporter Nick Fuentes advocated for months for his followers to vote for Democrats. Their argument was that Trump had betrayed America First principles and could no longer be trusted. Many former grassroots Trump voters who had supported him because of his economic agenda and because he had said that he wanted “no more wars” had suffered greatly due to the increasing cost of living and job losses. In the end, Trump lost support among young voters, Hispanic and Latino voters, Black men, and suburban and independent voters.

These results put the Republican Party at a critical juncture, leaving many to wonder what vision the party will have in 2028. Should they focus more on the post-Trump era, leaving Trump behind, or double down on his original agenda and rebuild his coalition to stay relevant? There are two major forces at play here: Trump himself, as a powerful figure, and the Republican establishment that wants to regain control of the party and stay relevant. Many observers conflate these two forces, while others believe that Trump reinvented the party and became the establishment in the process. Both are wrong. While Trump is still the most powerful person in the Republican Party, and his broader political operation has many hundreds of millions of dollars to support his agenda, he was never the establishment.

The traditional Republican establishment includes institutional donor networks, former party leaders, Reaganite think tanks, and corporate lobbying groups that accepted Trump’s reign while he was delivering on judges and tax cuts, but never truly accepted his populist takeover. The midterm results have given a boost to the more traditional power structures to attempt, again, to “take their party back”. Both are powerful forces with influential bases. The establishment is counting particularly on the fact that the Trump coalition has weakened considerably and will be hard to regenerate. They think Trump is likely to focus his fundraising efforts on himself – in the form of building his presidential library – rather than helping new candidates. On the grassroots side, Republican voters feel betrayed after Trump’s poor handling of the Epstein scandal, unprecedented political profiteering and corruption allegations, and the war on Iran.

Since these midterms were a referendum on how unpopular Trump has become, this leaves the Republican Party with two primary options: rebuild the Trump coalition or prepare themselves for a post-Trump conservative party. The key question now is how Republican candidates can distance themselves from Trump while at the same time attempting to rebuild his winning voter base. Walking this tightrope will mean finding a way to bring MAGA and America First back together again. This may seem like an impossible task in the current political climate, but it is hard to imagine any other winning scenario.

There are many names already in play, with more likely to enter the field within the coming months. Vice President JD Vance seemed to be the heir apparent with the strongest prospects prior to the recent midterms. Vance is powerful in terms of his proximity to Trump and the support he can garner from MAGA and wealthy donors in the tech industry. He also has ties to the America First crowd. Turning Point USA endorsed him publicly a year ago. Tucker Carlson, with his large following, still supports Vance. On the other hand, Vance will have a hard time distancing himself from the Trump administration’s failures on the economy, immigration, and the war on Iran. Vance will have to walk a fine line, criticising Trump enough to distance himself from bad policies while not losing support from the hardcore MAGA base, which is likely to retaliate if it feels left behind. If Vance refuses to criticise Trump altogether, we will likely see a repeat of the Kamala Harris-Joe Biden scenario. One of Vance’s major weaknesses when it comes to electability is that he is not an establishment figure himself. He faced a difficult race for the US Senate in Ohio in 2022. Trump chose him in 2024 as his running mate due to his ties to the tech billionaires and to challenge the Republican establishment. These factors will complicate Vance’s journey within the 2028 field should the establishment start to regain its footing within Republican leadership circles.

The 2028 establishment favourite within the Trump administration is Marco Rubio. It will be easier for Rubio to distance himself from Trump’s economy, but he will have a harder time distancing himself from Trump’s foreign policy and the war. Rubio is well-liked within the establishment, neoconservative and traditional donor groups. However, he is not a MAGA favourite, nor is he seen as an America First choice. Rubio’s main problem is that he is many people’s second choice. Also, his relationship with controversial donors such as Miriam Adelson will be a significant obstacle for him, as will his views on Israeli influence in US politics.

When thinking about 2028, Ron DeSantis, the outgoing governor of Florida, is another strong player. He is positioning himself to lead the Republican Party after leaving office in January. DeSantis is widely credited with the only success that Republicans had in this brutal midterm. He also has close ties to pro-Israel donors in Florida and nationwide. However, his weak performance and failure in running a national campaign against Trump in 2024 have not been forgotten.

Besides these names, the field will likely have many other candidates, some of whom will represent the establishment, and more who will challenge both forces alike. While the midterms were a referendum on Trump’s lack of popularity, they were also a vote against the establishment. Many Republicans and conservatives will pick up on this momentum and attempt to act on it. In this camp, we could see people like Congressman Thomas Massie, a possible run by former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, as well as complete outsiders who we don’t yet know. The determining factor, in my opinion, will be the Democrats. The Democrats’ strategy in managing the next two years will play a major role in the success or failure of the Republicans in 2028. In other words, 2028 is now the Democrats’ to lose.

Whether Democrats focus on anti-Trump retaliation or on rebuilding the economy and regaining voter trust will shape the Republicans’ ability to make a comeback. Retaliation will give Trump another chance at survival, but Democrats will have little incentive to shift their focus to anything other than anti-Trump rhetoric if they insist on keeping their current leadership as it is, without any radical shift against their donor class and wealthy elites.

Last Tuesday was a historic event the likes of which I have not seen in more than a decade on the campaign trail. This victory complicates the Democrats’ path to achieving real success for the American people, especially given Trump’s veto power. More than anything else, the future of the Republican Party will be determined by the ability of the Democrats to come up with their own strategy that is not dependent on being anti-Trump. In some ways, the Democrats need Trump – and need him to keep failing – in order for them to continue this winning streak. It will be up to Republicans to decide on their own whether they need him or not, and whether their party’s future will centre on the personality of one man.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: GOP lost in midterms, but has two major options for 2028, says Julian Zelizer. Zelizer says midterms were a rejection of Trump, not an endorsement of the Democrats, but a rejection.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/trump-cs.title: Trump’s C-SPAN call marks latest surprise post-midterm appearance
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/trump-cs.author: Matthew Tan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/trump-cs.text:
President Donald Trump called C-SPAN’s new “Washington Journal Primetime” program Monday in an unannounced eight-minute appearance.

The call followed a surprise White House briefing-room appearance with UFC CEO Dana White earlier Monday and a ballroom construction-site appearance Wednesday.

These appearances came after Democrats won control of the House and Senate in the midterms, a major setback for Republicans.

President Donald Trump made an unexpected call into C-SPAN’s evening broadcast Monday, extending a series of surprise appearances after Republicans’ midterm election defeat.

“It looks like we’ve got a call from the White House,” host Mimi Geerges told viewers as Trump joined the debut of “Washington Journal Primetime.”

Trump congratulated Geerges on the launch before taking questions on immigration, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Iran war.

Asked what he watches on C-SPAN, Trump said he follows viewer call-ins to gauge public sentiment.

“I like to watch the call-ins because it gives me a little of an indication of where we are,” he said.

The unannounced, eight-minute call followed another unexpected appearance earlier Monday, when Trump entered the White House briefing room alongside UFC CEO Dana White. Reporters were summoned so quickly that aides did not have time to attach the presidential seal to the podium, according to Reuters.

It was Trump’s first briefing room appearance in 198 days, according to a White House pool report. With the press secretary post vacant, Trump joked about offering White the job, to which the UFC chief declined.

Trump said he had been having “a very bad press day,” as he floated White as his next press secretary.

Last Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered substantial midterm losses, Trump also abruptly invited reporters to the construction site of his White House ballroom for his first public event since the election.

Trump spent more than 20 minutes discussing White House construction and renovation projects, including the ballroom’s Corinthian columns, marble flooring and the helipad, before turning to the election results during questions from reporters.

When asked whether he regretted how his campaign had ended, Trump distanced himself from the Republican losses.

“If I were on the ballot, we would have won,” he said.

Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 elections, dealing Trump a major political setback and setting up a divided government when the new Congress takes office in January.

Trump has long favored direct telephone contact with the media, including live calls to Fox News programs such as “Fox & Friends” during his first term.

CBS News previously reported that Trump personally arranged one such television appearance, while The Associated Press has documented his habit of contacting journalists directly by cellphone to pitch stories and react to live coverage.

— CNBC’s Daniel Mangan contributed to this story.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Live: Ukraine, Russia and US to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
A ⁠drone attack ​by Ukraine snapped power ​supplies to the eastern city of ​Luhansk ‌in Russian-controlled Ukraine ⁠and elsewhere in the ‌region, the TASS news agency quoted ⁠Russia-installed authorities as saying.

Reuters could not ​immediately independently confirm ‌the report. Russia and Ukraine regularly exchange strikes ‌on each other energy infrastructure, among ​other assets, in the war.

A drone hit ​an industrial facility in Ukraine's ​central city of Kremenchuk, a Ukrainian official said on the Telegram messaging app, ⁠but gave no details.

Minister Sergei Lavrov ⁠said the ​accord under which Russia is to supply diesel to the US and world ​markets is already working and lowering prices, writing in a piece published in Moscow daily

Lavrov said Russia was distinct from the West in not ​using its economy ‌to score political points against countries seen as adversaries ⁠or competitors.

"Since 2022, we have supplied Europe with energy resources worth $320 billion," Lavrov wrote in Kommersant.

"An important ‌contribution to energy security was the agreement between the Russian and ⁠US leaders to suspend restrictions on the export of Russian diesel. We have already started implementing it, which immediately brought prices down."

US ​President Donald Trump announced on October 9 the surprise deal ‌under which Russia agreed to immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and ‌1 million tons "immediately thereafter" to help lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.

Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States will hold talks in Abu Dhabi Tuesday on ending Europe's worst conflict since World War II in the first such meeting in more than nine months, as another winter of war approaches.

Europe – alarmed by US President Donald Trump floating a deal with Moscow on European security ahead of the talks – will also send representatives to Abu Dhabi.

Trump has pushed for an end to the Russia-Ukraine war since returning to power, but previous talks produced no breakthroughs and the process became sidelined by the US-Israeli war against Iran.

Europe and Ukraine fear the United States will force a deal on Kyiv that would amount to a de-facto capitulation, with Trump appearing to pivot towards Moscow this year.

Trump hinted Ukraine will have to give up land ahead of the talks, saying: "They're going to end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine."

Welcome to our liveblog dedicated to the war in Ukraine.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP, Reuters and AP)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/w.title: Who is Jensen Huang and why the Nvidia CEO scandal important?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/w.author: Katie Silver
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Nvidia has lost hundreds of billions of dollars in value since it was revealed that its chief executive had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. (AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

In terms of corporate fallout, what's happened at Nvidia has been huge.

The company, seen as the darling of the AI era, has lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value since it was revealed that its chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Nvidia and Mr Huang are now being sued, accused of ⁠defrauding shareholders by concealing the affair.

Nvidia has both benefited from and brought about the global AI revolution.

And, as CEOs go, few are as synonymous with a company as Jensen Huang.

Jensen Huang has admitted to the company's staff that he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. (Reuters: Steve Marcus, file)

"Treating this simply as a sex scandal misses the point," technology strategist Josh Kennedy-White says.

"The real issue is whether personal access to one of the world's most strategically important executives became a channel for intelligence gathering or influence."

So how did we get here?

Born in Taiwan, Mr Huang moved to the US at the age of nine and at some point, he naturalised as a US citizen.

At 17, he attended university in Oregon where he met his wife Lori Mills, who was two years his senior.

Both were studying electrical engineering and Mr Huang has previously recounted using the pick-up line: "Do you wanna see my homework?"

Jensen Huang said his wife, Lori, supported him unconditionally. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

They had weekly study dates, became lab partners and, five years later, married.

In an interview with a magazine at his alma mater in 2013, he described how his wife's support has always been unconditional.

Jensen Huang and his wife dine with Apple's Tim Cook, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

"Ever since I was 18, she was there believing in me and knowing I could do it. Even when I had self doubts, she didn't," he said.

The two went on to have two children, Spencer and Madison Huang, who both now hold executive roles at Nvidia.

In 1993, at a diner in San Jose, Mr Huang met with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, fellow engineers he'd worked with in the chip industry since the late 1980s.

There they came up with Nvidia, starting with just $40,000 in capital. In order to incorporate the business, the three founders chucked in $200 a piece.

Originally gaming was the focus. The founders believed the PC gaming market was set to grow and would need more powerful graphics processing.

The motherboard of a Surface Laptop Ultra containing Nvidia's new RTX Spark chip. (Reuters: Manuel Orbegozo)

After a near business-ending initial failure, Nvidia invented what's regarded as the world's first Graphics Processing Unit in 1999. The chips could make advanced computer graphics allowing for advanced 3D environments in video games and perform huge numbers of calculations in parallel.

It wasn't long before developers realised their uses could go far beyond gaming.

"We created the world's first programmable accelerator," Mr Huang said in 2023.

"And the benefit of an accelerator is whatever you designed it to do, it does it incredibly efficiently."

And so, the era of modern AI was born.

Nvidia's chips, by all accounts, are unparalleled. They're so hot, companies struggle to get their hands on them, and the metrics of Nvidia's growth are dizzying.

To give you a sense of some of the numbers: Its shares have increased some 477,000 per cent since listing in 1999; almost five-fold in the past five years.

Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, AMD CEO Lisa Su, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stand together during the "A New Golden Age" summit at the US Institute of Peace. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

For Mr Huang, who is estimated to own about 3.5 per cent of the company, his wealth has skyrocketed.

According to Forbes, he was worth $2 billion in 2017 — and now, about $154 billion, putting him in the top 10 most wealthy people in the world.

Is Nvidia facing a spy scandal?

With his trademark leather jackets and high-profile product launches, Mr Huang is omnipresent at Nvidia.

Its website lists him as co-founder, president, chief executive officer and a member of the board of directors.

And many of the company's executives are relatives of Huang.

Nvidia, and Mr Huang, have walked a fine line balancing the demands of Washington and Beijing.

Nvidia is headquartered in California with the vast majority of its chips produced by the chipmaker TSMC in Taiwan, along with some production in the US and South Korea.

The US restricted the exports of chips to China in 2022, citing it as an issue of national defence.

It's been a huge point of contention between the world's two superpowers with Beijing racing to develop its own semiconductor industry.

Jensen Haung joined a delegation of US tech CEOs and government officials on Donald Trump's state visit to China. (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov)

Mr Huang, who is one of US President Donald Trump's closest allies in Silicon Valley, has tried to push the administration to loosen restrictions.

He's argued that American companies should be able to compete globally and that it would prevent China's chip industry developing too powerfully.

He's had some success. Earlier this year Washington gave the greenlight for Nvidia to sell its second-tier chip (the H200) to Chinese companies, so long as they could take a 25 per cent cut.

There have also been reports about Chinese companies illegally getting access to US chip technology through the backdoor.

One company, for example, is a Singapore cloud computing firm Megaspeed which is being investigated by the US over suspicions it's helping get Nvidia AI chips into China.

A screen grab from CTI video obtained on November 9, 2026 shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang after comparison with a photograph obtained separately, attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (in black) at a restaurant in Taipei. (Reuters: CTI)

The Wall Street Journal reports Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Mr Huang, was previously Megaspeed's boss.

It was in this capacity that she allegedly met Mr Huang at an Nvidia event in California in 2024. It's not known how long the affair lasted nor where Ms Huang is now. She has not responded to journalist requests for comment.

Now the affair is part of an FBI investigation, with Mr Trump saying he "was amazed" by the allegations.

"I know the FBI is looking into it … I think that he'll be in good shape," he said.

US lawmakers say Congress is likely to tighten China's access to US chips as part of the fallout while Nvidia's board has launched an internal investigation.

Allegations of espionage between China and the US are nothing new. But a target as big as Jensen Huang could change who wins the AI race.

Beijing has denied the allegations.

"The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Josh Kennedy-White, chief commercial officer at strategic communications firm IN2, said the scandal exposes the danger of making one company and one individual so indispensable to the global AI economy.

"The Huang affair is a reminder that the most valuable target may not be a government official," he told ABC News.

Jensen Huang hasn't tweeted or released anything public since he sent staff a letter on Sunday.

"I owe my family and all of you an apology," he wrote.

"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.author: Harry Frost
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Dashcam footage of Tayler Hazell driving erratically through Canberra was previously released by the courts. (Supplied: ACT Supreme Court)

Earlier this year, Tayler Hazell was jailed for 13 years and two months, with a non-parole period of nine years after a hit-and-run incident in March 2025.

He has appealed the sentence on seven grounds, including arguing the ACT Supreme Court judge did not appropriately account for factors including his upbringing, remorse and extra-curial punishment suffered as a result of his treatment by police.

The court has reserved its decision.

Lawyers for a man jailed for hitting two schoolboys with a stolen car in Canberra's south have argued the judge made multiple errors in sentencing, and did not give appropriate weight to his childhood or his expressions of remorse.

In March last year, Tayler Hazell took the green Holden Commodore from outside a childcare centre in Sutton, New South Wales.

The 8-year-old daughter of the car's owner was sitting in the back seat.

Hazell drove a short distance before saying to her, "Oh, you're a girl," and stopping to let her get out.

Under the influence of drugs, Hazell continued to drive erratically — hitting a car near a school in Queanbeyan and damaging a barrier on a safety crossing before speeding on into the ACT.

Two boys, aged 14 and 15, suffered serious injuries when they were struck by the car as they waited to cross the road outside St Edmund's College in Griffith.

Two teenagers were struck by the car driven by Hazell outside St Edmund's College in Canberra. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

Hazell continued at speed towards the Manuka shops, where he crashed.

He had already been handcuffed by Australian Federal Police officers when Tactical Response Group members arrived on scene, and he was slammed to the ground — causing him facial injuries and bleeding.

He pleaded guilty to multiple offences including two counts of culpable driving causing grievous bodily harm and stealing a car.

Earlier this year, ACT Supreme Court Justice John Burns sentenced Hazell to 13 years and two months behind bars, with a non-parole period of nine years.

Hazell has appealed the sentence.

Before a full-bench hearing of the Court of Appeal today, his lawyer Sarah Baker-Goldsmith said the judge had made numerous mistakes.

Among the seven grounds of appeal, she argued Justice Burns didn't give appropriate weight to Hazell's deprived childhood, his expressions of remorse, the risk of institutionalisation and the extra-curial punishment he'd suffered due to the injuries sustained during his arrest.

"But it is his entitlement to be sentenced according to law."

Hazell is appealing the ruling after he was jailed for hitting the boys with a stolen car. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

Prosecutors argued Justice Burns had taken the disputed factors into account — including in considering whether Hazell was remorseful, with a finding that he'd attempted to reduce his culpability by lying about being unaware the girl was in the back of the car when he stole it.

The Court of Appeal reserved its decision for a later date.

In a separate matter, Hazell is suing the federal government over the force used by AFP officers during his arrest, which an investigation found breached professional standards.

Hazell is seeking damages for injuries, fear and embarrassment suffered as a result.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/d.title: Data centre builder Firmus says diesel generators only for emergencies
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/d.author: Ashleigh Barraclough
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Ashleigh Barraclough

Firmus' Tim Rosenfield declined to tell the inquiry who the company's clients are. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

AI infrastructure company Firmus says it would only use diesel generators during emergencies, despite appealing a Tasmanian council planning condition that only allows for emergency use.

The company today fronted a parliamentary inquiry into AI data centres.

The inquiry will continue hearings before making recommendations to the state government.

AI data centre builder Firmus Technologies has told a parliamentary inquiry it would only use diesel generators at its sites during emergencies.

Firmus has operational AI data centres in Melbourne and Singapore, and is planning more in Tasmania, South Australia, Indonesia and Malaysia.

AI companies rely on energy-intensive data centres to train large language models and process and respond to queries from AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude.

The Firmus Technologies site in St Leonards, Launceston, showing its research and development lab. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Firmus is building an AI data centre in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards, has approval for another at Long Reach in northern Tasmania, and is seeking approval for a third at Wesley Vale in the north-west.

When Firmus gained planning approval for its Long Reach facility, George Town Council imposed a condition that the backup diesel generators could only be used during emergencies, maintenance and testing.

Community concerns had been raised about the environmental and noise impacts of their use.

A render of Firmus Technologies' proposed AI data centre at Long Reach, near George Town. (Supplied)

Firmus appealed the condition, calling it "unreasonable" and stating it would prevent it from using generators during periods of "energy market stress".

Tasmania's Environment Protection Authority has since sought to join the appeal, stating in its submission that it would have assessed the proposal differently had it known the generators would be used "potentially whenever it is commercially convenient for the operator".

On Tuesday, Firmus faced a parliamentary inquiry into AI data centres in Tasmania and concerns over diesel generator use were raised.

Firmus hasn't revealed who its customers are for Tasmanian data centres.   (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Independent MP George Razay asked Firmus how often it would use its diesel generators.

"Our intent with regards to diesel generators is they're backup generation," Firmus energy manager Paul Grzinic responded.

Firmus's Paul Grzinic told the inquiry, the company was seeking clarification of the definition of "emergency". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"They are not intended — as others have claimed — for us to run these when commercially convenient, or any other means other than in an emergency situation."

Greens MP and acting inquiry chair Tabatha Badger pressed the issue.

"So you can understand for Tasmanians listening, that's not going to add up and make a whole lot of sense."

Mr Grzinic said he could not speak in detail about the appeal while it was ongoing.

Tim Rosenfield and Paul Grzinic appearing before the Tasmanian committee. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"We're just seeking, effectively, clarification of — it's quite broad, that definition of emergency — so we're just seeking clarification," he said.

Firmus is setting up a research and development facility at its Wesley Vale site to investigate ways to reduce reliance on backup diesel generators.

Asked by Ms Badger who Firmus's customers were, co-chief executive and co-founder Tim Rosenfield declined to say.

"That can be for security reasons or contractual confidentiality reasons, so I wouldn't expect it to be an expectation for us to do so — it's just not an industry norm.

"And I don't think it's something our customers would be particularly happy with us doing."

Construction underway at Firmus' St Leonards site. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The company has previously said it has contracted the Launceston and Wesley Vale facilities to customers, while Long Reach was under option to a customer.

Last month, Firmus was forced to withdraw its highly-anticipated initial public offering (IPO) — set to be the biggest float in the Australian share market since Telstra in 1997 — after lacklustre interest from investors.

Professor Razay asked about the impact that had on Firmus's plans, but Mr Rosenfield said it did not change anything.

Tim Rosenfield said growth plans for Firmus were still on track, despite the abandoned IPO. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"We have extremely supportive shareholders who are backing us to grow exactly the same way we've always planned to grow," Mr Rosenfield said.

The inquiry will continue hearings with stakeholders about AI data centres in Tasmania before making recommendations to the government.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Former Preston One Nation candidate Franco Guardiani appears in a social media post. (Facebook)

One Nation has dumped its Victorian election election candidate for Preston over a social media post appearing to praise Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler.

The party dumped its candidate for Melbourne earlier this month over misogynistic social media posts.

One Nation has conceded its vetting process needs improvement.

One Nation's candidate for the Labor-held seat of Preston, Franco Guardiani, has been dumped over a social media post where he appeared to praise Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler.

A social media post from Mr Guardiani circulated today showed him labelling Adolf Hitler as the "GOAT", an acronym for "the greatest of all time".

Mr Guardiani confirmed to the ABC that the social media account was his.

"The party does what it sees fit,'' he said of being dropped as a candidate for the seat in Melbourne's north.

Mr Guardiani said he believed in free speech and that people should be able to express their views and question things.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog.

He twice ran as a candidate for the overlapping federal seat of Batman in 2013 and 2016, first for the Palmer United Party, then as an independent.

Mr Guardiani's posts and reposts on X suggest support for a range of conspiratorial, antisemitic and anti-Islam ideas.

"Jews created Islam to destroy Christianity while making out they are our friends," he tweeted in February this year.

In December last year, Mr Guardiani responded to a tweet from the Campaign Against Antisemitism to say he was "just asking" whether there was evidence 6 million Jews were killed by Germany during the Holocaust.

In addition to the "GOAT" tweet, Mr Guardiani had twice reposted posts praising Hitler.

Mr Guardiani had reposted tweets praising Hitler and Nazi Germany on several occasions — including a retweet of post featuring footage of Nazi troops that claimed Allied forces who defeated Nazi Germany "were not the heroes of humanity".

He has also tweeted claims about weather modification being orchestrated by "the globalist [sic] using technology and chemtrails" and that all "pilots need to be charged with conspiracy to harm us and the atmosphere".

Two of Mr Guardiani's tweets were in defence of Sean Black, who was quietly rehired by One Nation to be federal campaign manager despite being convicted of rape in 2018.

"At least he is a convicted rapist and not a Muslim rapist who never gets convicted," Mr Guardiani said of Black, who left One Nation after his employment by the party became public earlier this year.

In a statement, One Nation's Victorian leader Warren Pickering addressed Mr Guardiani's comments related to the Holocaust.

"At a time when Jewish Australians are experiencing unprecedented persecution, we are appalled that these comments have been made," Mr Pickering said.

One Nation Victoria's leader Warren Pickering says there is no place for abhorrent views. (ABC News)

"As soon as we became aware, we acted. Preston candidate Franco Guardiani is no longer part of our party," he said.

The party has conceded its vetting process needs improvement.

Mr Guardiani is not the first candidate to be dumped, with One Nation forced to move on its former Melbourne candidate, Matthew Collins,over his misogynistic social media posts.

Earlier today, Liberal leader Jess Wilson confirmed the Coalition would preference One Nation ahead of Labor, the Greens and Victorian Socialists on how-to-vote preference cards for the November 28 state election.

Candidate nominations for the Victorian state election closed on November 9, with early voting opening on November 18.

Labor has held Preston since the seat was first contested in 1945, but could be set for a tight contest with the Greens this election.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/l.author: Jane Bardon

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Indigenous Culture

Ally McAlpine says the custodians hope an emergency nomination will halt the development at Lee Point. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

Larrakia custodians have nominated Darwin's Lee Point for national heritage listing to try to stop a federal government housing project from going ahead.

They have applied for an emergency nomination to try to stop work immediately.

The Australian Heritage Council, and potentially the federal environment minister, will decide whether the area is nationally significant enough to be heritage listed.

Two Larrakia custodians have requested an emergency heritage listing by the Commonwealth in an attempt to prevent the federal government from building a large housing estate at Darwin's Lee Point.

Lorraine Williams and Tibby Quall argued in their application to the Australian Heritage Council and the federal environment minister that the site approved for 600 private and 200 defence personnel houses should be protected as the "Binybara cultural heritage landscape" for its Indigenous, biodiversity and historical values.

"Hopefully we'll achieve protection for the entire area so that it's not developed, and is left to be natural bush because the land is culturally significant to us and our culture and history," Ms Williams said.

Lorraine Williams says Lee Point should be protected as a cultural landscape. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

Ms Williams said the housing estate would interfere with the registered Binybara Larrakia sacred site, a rock reef off Lee Point beach, and a sacred women's site in the development area.

"Because we don't have land rights in Darwin, we don't have native title, we're using all of the different acts that are available to us, and this is why we are having to try to protect Binybara under the heritage legislation that's available to us, and we'll keep on fighting until we get full rights to this land," she said.

Larrakia custodians hope the area will be protected as the Binybara cultural heritage landscape. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

During land clearing of one block of its planned 132-hectare development, the federal government developer Defence Housing Australia uncovered Indigenous cultural artefacts including a grinding stone.

Last week, Defence Housing Australia, which has so far built five houses at the site, announced it had revised its Lee Point plan to address biodiversity and sacred site concerns, but Ms Williams said the revisions did not go far enough.

The Larrakia custodians' lawyer, Ally McAlpine from Environmental Justice Australia, said the heritage nomination included a request for a provisional emergency listing to try to stop further work while the full application was considered.

"This application isn't just about individual sites or objects; it's considering the whole of the peninsula and the particular cultural significance it has to the Larrakia people, its military history significance and its biodiversity and its ecological significance," she said.

The development at Lee Point has sparked four years of protests by members of the public and Larrakia custodians. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

The custodians have argued Lee Point is worthy of joining the six other Northern Territory places on the 127-place national heritage list, which include Kakadu National Park, the Hermannsburg Historic Precinct and Wave Hill Walk Off Route.

Defence Housing Australia has revised its plan to build an 800-house precinct in Lee Point in Darwin's northern suburbs.

Nominations for heritage listing are assessed by the Australian Heritage Council, and then referred to the federal environment minister for acceptance or rejection.

The Heritage Council's criteria for acceptance include that the place has "outstanding value to the nation" because of its "uncommon, rare or endangered aspects of Australia's natural or cultural history" or a "strong or special association with a particular community or cultural group for social, cultural or spiritual reasons".

To reach the list threshold, a place must have "outstanding heritage value to the Australian community as a whole".

The Heritage Council also considers whether it is more significant compared to other similar places.

Charles Darwin University scientists have assessed Lee Point's tropical eucalyptus woodland habitat as being one of the few remaining Darwin coastal habitats that are important for the survival of endangered species including the black-footed tree rat and the Gouldian finch.

Gouldian finches inhabit Lee Point's tropical eucalyptus woodland. (Supplied: Kacie Austin)

"I want the government to acknowledge that those animals and plants are actually important to Larrakia people and our culture — they are part of our biocultural knowledge and biocultural heritage," Ms Williams said.

Proponents of the housing estate have argued that some of Lee Point's habitat was previously cleared for World War II defence fortifications, the area already hosts a caravan park, and the housing would not interfere with the Binybara site off the coast.

Emergency national heritage nominations have halted developments in the past, including the listing of Tasmania's Tarkine in 2009, which stopped a commercial tourism road and the 2017 listing of Melbourne's St Kilda area, which forced major changes to a railway.

Mitchell Starc has responded to Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Australian fast bowler Mitchell Starc has rejected Usman Khawaja's claim the 2018 sandpaper ball-tampering plot was known by all members of the team.

Speaking at Fox Cricket's season launch, Starc became the first current player to respond to the revelations in Khawaja's new book, Sabr.

In the book, released today, Khawaja says the plan to use sandpaper on the ball in the Cape Town Test was common knowledge among the team, and his pleas to have the entire squad take the blame fell on deaf ears.

Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

David Warner, who, along with Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft, was among the only men punished for the scandal, said today that Khawaja's claims were "100 per cent accurate".

But Starc insisted he did not know a substance was being taken onto the field in Cape Town.

"Obviously there are differing opinions of eight years ago," Starc said.

"We were heavily grilled through the process at the time and since. I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.

"We weren't aware anything was taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen in Cape Town."

In 2021, Starc joined fellow bowlers Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon in releasing a statement disputing any suggestion they had wider knowledge of the ball-tampering plans.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands," the 2021 statement said.

Starc said his stance had not changed since that statement was released but that "clearly there are differing versions from differing people".

Starc also said he knew nothing about Khawaja's claim sandpaper had been used to tamper with the ball in the Test before Cape Town.

Mitchell Starc bowls during the second Test of the 2018 series at St. George's Park. (AP: Michael Sheehan)

Earlier today, Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg said there were no plans to reopen the investigation in light of Khawaja's assertions.

"There are specific details in his book that contradict the versions that have been provided by others," Greenberg said.

"It's important to know that back at that time, players were urged to come forward, and they had the opportunity to do so over these past eight years, and that remains the case.

"We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received.

"That includes what we've seen from Usman, and our position hasn't changed on that.

"We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this. I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that."

Starc said he had not spoken to Khawaja in recent days. He said he had not read the new book and "probably won't read it".

William Holdback's last moments were captured on CCTV and played to the jury.  (Supplied: SA Police)

Father and son Brian and Liam Slann are standing trial accused of murdering 21-year-old William Holdback in April 2024.

Liam Slann has admitted to killing Mr Holdback, but denies it was an act of murder.

The trial before a 14-person jury continues.

A 21-year-old allegedly murdered by a father and son over a disagreement about drugs was allegedly stabbed 10 times and left crying for help on a suburban street, a jury has heard.

Brian Slann, 54, and Liam Slann, 29, are standing trial over the alleged murder of 21-year-old William Holdback in the early hours of April 10, 2024, on a street in Welland in Adelaide's inner north-west.

Both men have pleaded not guilty to murder but Liam Slann has entered a guilty plea to manslaughter, which the prosecution did not accept.

Delivering her opening address in the Supreme Court trial today, prosecutor Nicola Moore said it would be alleged Mr Holdback and Liam Slann had arranged via a messaging app to meet on Musgrave Avenue to purchase or collect drugs.

Ms Moore said Mr Holdback was allegedly trying to source drugs for a friend.

Liam Slann has admitted to killing Mr Holdback, but has denied it was an act of murder.  (Supplied: Facebook)

The prosecution alleged Mr Holdback met with the father and son who arrived in a car about 1:20am and there was a disagreement over drugs.

The prosecutor told the jury Mr Holdback allegedly smashed the rear passenger window of the car with a metal bar before sprinting away down Barrpowell Street where he was allegedly chased by Brian Slann and an armed Liam Slann.

"The deceased [Mr Holdback] was first, followed initially by Liam Slann, he was followed in turn by Brian Slann participating in the chase and shouting directions," Ms Moore said.

"The deceased … tripped and he was, the prosecution say, set upon by the first defendant Liam who stabbed him while his father was shouting at him, at his son, to stab him."

"He was stabbed to death and as he lay shouting for help the first defendant [Liam] walked calmly away, not turning around, leaving him to bleed to death, getting into the car with his father and making good their escape."

Ms Moore told the jury the CCTV allegedly had captured Liam Slann saying "I've got you now,  I'm going to stab you c***".

"Eight seconds after his son says, 'I'm going to stab you c***,' Brian says, 'Stab him Liam,'" she said.

William Holdback's mother (second from left) was surrounded by supporters on the first day of the trial.  (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Ms Moore told the court Liam Slann got back into the car driven by Brian Slann who can allegedly be heard asking his son "where did you stab him?"

She added that a weapon was never recovered, and the pair took a different route home than the one they used to arrive.

Mr Holdback was pronounced dead at the scene, with 10 stab wounds to his chest, shoulder, back of his body and wrists.

Ms Moore said Brian Slann was equally as responsible for Mr Holdback's death as Liam Slann, as the pair had entered a "joint criminal enterprise".

"Liam and Brian came to an understanding, amounting to an agreement by the time they exited the car to attack Holdback with a knife and they intended he should be killed or inflict grievous bodily harm," Ms Moore said.

Nick Healy denied the father and son had entered an agreement to attack Mr Holdback.  (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Defence barrister Nick Healy, for Brian Slann, rejected there was ever an agreement between the pair.

He told the jury there was no dispute that Brian Slann was present on the night and driving the car but was not the principle offender nor was ever in possession of the knife.

Elizabeth Mansfield encouraged the jury to approach the evidence with impartiality.  (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Defence barrister Elizabeth Mansfield, acting for Liam Slann, said he admitted his actions caused Mr Holdback's death through his manslaughter plea.

Ms Mansfield told the jury to put aside their feelings of "sympathy" or "distaste" at the confronting nature of the CCTV and come to the evidence with impartiality.

The trial before a 14-person jury continues.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Bills defense turns tables on Vikings in victory
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
The Buffalo Bills turned the tables on the Minnesota Vikings on Monday, producing a steely defensive performance on the road to grab a 23-6 victory in Minneapolis.

A low-scoring showdown between the Bills’ potent offense and the stingiest defense in the NFL ended with a hard-fought Buffalo victory at the U.S. Bank Stadium.

Buffalo’s defense proved decisive in the win, restricting the Vikings to just two field goals on a miserable night for Minnesota quarterback Carson Wentz.

Veteran back-up Wentz, starting in place of the injured Kyler Murray, struggled throughout, tossing two interceptions, coughing up a fumble and recording just eight completions.

The Bills offense dug deep to grind out victory, with running back James Cook rushing for 107 yards from 31 carries.

Bills quarterback Josh Allen threw 234 yards with one touchdown from 21 completions.

“It’s exactly what it was — a great performance,” Allen told ESPN. “We knew that it was going to take all four quarters.

“That’s a great team that we just played. They’re extremely well coach and that defense is the best in the league for a reason.

“We kept grinding, kind of wore them down in the fourth quarter. Our defense played fantastic.”

Buffalo improved to 7-1 with the win to tighten its grip on the AFC East, ahead of the second-placed New England Patriots (5-4). The Vikings fell to 6-2 in the NFC North.

An attritional first half saw Buffalo kicker Tyler Bass open the scoring with a 39-yard field goal in the first quarter before Vikings counterpart Will Reichard level with a 43-yard effort in the second quarter.

Buffalo grabbed the first touchdown of the game in the final minute of the second quarter, with Allen leading an eight-play 80-yard drive before finding Keleki Latu with a 25-yard touchdown pass to make it 10-3.

Latu celebrated his first career touchdown by forcefully spiking the ball, and he grinned as a slew of teammates including Allen came over to congratulate him. The 24-year-old is the younger ​brother ​of Indianapolis Colts pass rusher Laiatu Latu.

Reichard narrowed the deficit to four points with a field goal in the final seconds of the first half, but Minnesota failed to add to its tally thereafter.

Instead the Bills steadily built on their lead, with Bass scoring a 25-yard field goal to make it 13-6 midway through the third quarter.

Cook then struck the decisive blow in the fourth quarter, barreling over from five yards to cap a 15-play, 84-yard drive that took 8 minutes and 32 seconds off the clock.

Bass followed that with a 52-yard field goal to put Buffalo 23-6 up and the Vikings’ fate was sealed after a final drive ended with a turnover on downs.

Max Brosmer replaced Wentz at quarterback late in the fourth quarter ⁠and finished 6 of 7 for 58 yards.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.summary: Buffalo Bills beat Minnesota Vikings 23-6 in Minneapolis on Monday. The Vikings were held to just two field goals on a miserable night for Carson Wentz. The Bills offense dug deep to grind out victory, with running back James Cook rushing for 107 yards.

The top diplomats from Group of Seven nations have reiterated “strong opposition” to attempts to change the status quo by force, including in the Taiwan Strait, a veiled swipe at Beijing as China ramps up military exercises around the self-ruled island.

During a meeting Monday in Paris, the G7 top diplomats underscored the importance of a free and open Indo-Pacific and reaffirmed their “strong opposition to any unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion, including in the East China Sea, the South China Sea, and across the Taiwan Strait,” according to a readout of the meeting released by Japan’s Foreign Ministry.

Taiwan’s defense minister said Tuesday that China is carrying out “area denial” drills in the western Pacific involving its Liaoning aircraft carrier and other naval formations.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rr.title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rr.text:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident.

Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the RAF base.

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI).

"Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".

Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.

"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.

He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.

Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.

A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.

No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".

On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.

In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.

According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".

The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated.

"On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."

The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive.

"At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.

It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.

The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot.

The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason.

RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxly.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxly.text:
An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.

A majority of the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, for now.

In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".

The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.

However, that calculation could change in January when the Democratic Party assumes control of both chambers of Congress, following its successes in the US midterm elections. For now, Trump's Republican Party remains in control.

After Tuesday's vote, the most senior Democrat in the House, Hakeem Jeffries, said: "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning."

The question on which lawmakers were voting on Tuesday was whether or not to refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, which is led by Republicans. The alternative would have been to allow the resolution to proceed in the House itself.

All Republicans other than Massie voted to refer the resolution to the committee, meaning that the congressman's effort failed in a 211-204 vote.

The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress.

More than a dozen members missed the ballot. They included 11 Democrats, several of whom blamed traffic issues for their absences.

Several members of the party criticised their fellow lawmakers for missing the vote.

"You should show up and do your job," said Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed during an interview with CNN, making a direct address to those who did not vote. The Michigan lawmaker recently won a US Senate race in Michigan, having criticised US ties to Israel and the war in Iran on the campaign trail.

Meanwhile Trump celebrated Tuesday's outcome in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED".

"Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth.

After the vote, Massie said he "wasn't surprised" but "was disappointed", according to BBC's US media partner CBS.

"My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do," he added. "They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."

Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

The Kentucky congressman also said that removing Hegseth now would give the Senate time to approve a replacement while Republicans were still in power.

Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year.

The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, had predicted earlier in the day that the impeachment bid would fail.

In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval.

The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth called efforts to impeach him a political stunt by a Trump administration opponent who was "disgruntled and defeated".

Hegseth also argued Massie's resolution endangered national security, because it communicated to US adversaries "that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations".

"This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," he said.

He echoed some statements Trump had made during a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room on Monday, including touting a rise in military recruitment levels.

But Hegseth said Massie was motivated by policy differences and "not high crimes, not misdemeanours, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offences the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause".

Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it began in February.

He had already incurred the president's ire for demanding the Trump administration release files on deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

While Hegseth has survived politically for now, many lawmakers - including some Republicans - have questioned how long he can last in the administration.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican, said on Tuesday he expected Hegseth to resign or be fired by Trump.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwz0.title: Hundreds of Italian schools hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwz0.text:
Some 300 schools across Italy have received bomb threats, according to Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara, who described the incidents as probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk".

Valditara told Italian TV that there was a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in Italy and elsewhere in Europe which had targeted flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.

The emails were sent to schools in Rome, Naples, Vicenza, Florence, Pisa, Trieste and many other Italian cities, and a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has called a meeting of top ministers and intelligence chiefs.

Meloni said the government was monitoring closely the "numerous reports of bomb threats at educational institutions" although checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".

"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.

Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption. Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

Italian reports said 280 school head teachers had received threats in recent days.

Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, according to reports from a number of regions, and pupils were allowed to return to class.

In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".

In a separate incident, more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland were sent emails which police said they were treating as a hoax. Messages sent to number of schools in Scotland were also being treated by police as a hoax. It is unclear whether any of the incidents are connected.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9j3.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9j3.text:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.

Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.

US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.

The BBC has contacted his representatives.

Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".

He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.

Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.

Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.

FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".

Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".

He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.

The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9j3.summary: Judge says he removed his ankle monitor early Tuesday morning. Judge says Markle violated conditions of his pretrial release. Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.title: Vinícius Jr sends message to Sudan boy who received prosthetic legs after BBC report sparks appeal
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.text:
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.

The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.

Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.

We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.

More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.

Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.

More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.

The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.

For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.

When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.

"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.

Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."

Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."

Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.

"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".

Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.

Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.

Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.

"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.

She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."

Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.

Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.

"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.

There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.

Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.

Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.

After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.

For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.

Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.

"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."

His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.

As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.

He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.

For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.

The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.

Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine".

"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.

Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.

Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

Additional reporting by Scarlett Barter and Abdelrahman Abutaleb
