https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c914.title: Governments 'asleep at the wheel' over social care, says head of review
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c914.text:
Successive governments have been "asleep at the wheel" on adult social care, says the head of the independent commission looking into the sector in England.

Baroness Louise Casey said care services for older people and adults with disabilities had been developed in a largely uncontrolled and unintended way, unlike the deliberate design of the NHS in 1948.

As a result, she suggested a postcode lottery had developed with different levels of services available depending on where people live.

And she also highlighted the fees that self-funders pay, saying they were much higher than councils were charged for people entitled to state support.

Baroness Casey said care services, such as home adaptations and personal care like helping people out of bed and with washing, were simply not valued enough.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said the NHS had become a "national hospital service: that was focussed on medical care".

And she said the failings identified by the recent Covid inquiry report into social care were testament to that.

Last month the inquiry published a report which said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic, allowing Covid to spread like "wildfire".

Baroness Casey, who will address a conference of social care leaders later on Wednesday, said the findings were "so awful" and "a national shame".

"Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel. We've got our heads in the sand."

Her final recommendations for services for older people and adults with disabilities, including care homes, will be published next summer.

It comes as her commission publishes research showing England is an international outlier for having no "clear system of stewardship" for social care, unlike countries such as France and Germany.

She said the market was dominated by private providers and said the regulator – the Care Quality Commission – as being a "spectator at the site of a car crash".

When Andy Burnham became prime minister, he said social care was one of his key priorities although the Casey commission was set up by the Starmer government.

"Together, we can build a new settlement for care," Baroness Casey said.

"One based on values I still believe this country shares – decency, contribution and a duty to care for our neighbours, our loved ones and ourselves."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c914.summary: Baroness Louise Casey says care services for older people and adults with disabilities were not valued enough. She says the NHS had become a "national hospital service: that was focussed on medical care" She says care sector was developed in a largely uncontrolled and unintended way.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv62.title: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv62.text:
One drug comes out top in a large analysis of how effective antidepressants are at keeping patients free of symptoms of depression.

Escitalopram performed best at preventing patients from relapsing in a study involving nearly 10,000 people prescribed different medications for up to a year.

Two other pills - agomelatine and duloxetine - came next, while prozac (also known as fluoxetine) ranked just below them.

Experts stress the findings don't mean that everyone with severe depression should switch to escitalopram, or that other antidepressants aren't any good, because all the drugs can work and each has its pros and cons.

Depression is common, affecting around one in six people in the UK. With the right treatment and support, people can make a good recovery although for some their depression can return.

To prevent relapse, doctors already recommend people stay on antidepressants for at least six months after depression ends, and then taper off gradually.

The new analysis, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, looked at previous studies comparing the effectiveness of more than a dozen common antidepressants in total.

The differences found were modest and experts say longer studies are still needed to find out more.

There are many contributing causes to depression and a variety of ways to treat it, including drugs and talking therapies. Experts say patients should discuss what treatment options are best with their doctor.

Many medical guidelines recommend SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) antidepressants, like escitalopram, sertraline and fluoxetine or Prozac, as the first drug of choice.

These drugs increase seratonin, which is linked to mood.

According to the new analysis, compared to Prozac (fluoxetine):

One of the researchers, Prof Eric Ruhé at Radboud University in The Netherlands, said the choice of medication can vary for each individual.

"Nevertheless, our study can help inform the decisions that prescribers and patients make together: if you start an antidepressant, choose one that not only helps you to get well, but also keeps you well."

Dr Sameer Jauhar, an expert at Imperial College London, said while the research provided useful information, "it cannot tell us which antidepressant will work best for an individual patient."

"I would not interpret these findings as a reason for someone who is responding well to their current antidepressant to change treatment," he added.

Prof Allan Young from the Royal College of Psychiatrists said: "While some medicines appear to have a small advantage over others for longer-term outcomes, the differences are modest and are unlikely to outweigh individual factors such as side effects, previous response and patient preference when deciding on treatment."

Like all medicines, escitalopram can cause side effects, including sleep problems, constipation and weight gain, although not everyone experiences them.

The NHS says if escitalopram or a similar SSRI is ineffective or not suitable, doctors may suggest a different type of antidepressant, such as an SNRI.

Older tricyclic antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, are now less commonly prescribed.

The mental health charity Mind says people need access to clear information about the potential benefits and side effects of antidepressants as well as other forms of support, including talking therapies and mindfulness.

"It's common for people to need to try more than one medication before they find the right treatment that works for them. And what works may change over time," the charity said.

Mind's website has information to help compare different antidepressants.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c317.title: Deal agreed to end health visitor strike affecting baby appointments
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c317.text:
Health visitors are set to return to work next week after a deal was reached to end a nine-month strike that saw thousands of missed appointments.

Unite union said the agreement with Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board would see all health visitors offered new roles, describing it as a "historic pay win" and a major victory for workers.

The health board said it had agreed to develop a new specialist health visitor role with additional responsibilities, subject to approval processes.

The Welsh government welcomed the return of staff and said that restoring services for babies and young children was now the priority.

About 100 health visitors with the health board have been on strike since February in a row over job grading, saying they were losing up to £9,000 a year as a result.

Home visits dropped dramatically, with the health board saying that safety and accessibility of services was its priority during the strike.

Between March and May 2025, the board, which covers Bridgend county, Merthyr Tydfil and Rhondda Cynon Taf, carried out 6,140 visits.

That dropped to 909 in the same period in 2026.

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the agreement was "a magnificent victory" for health visitors.

"This dispute was about recognising the skilled, vital work health visitors do for families and children in their communities," she said.

"Today that recognition has been secured."

Health board chief executive Paul Mears welcomed the resolution and said the immediate priority was restoring services for families.

He said a new specialist health visitor role would strengthen services and help the health board respond to local needs while recognising concerns raised by Unite on behalf of its members.

Plaid Cymru Senedd members representing constituencies across the health board area said they were "very relieved" health visitors were set to return to work and welcomed an outcome that delivered on promises made to staff.

In a joint statement, they said the dispute had highlighted the increasingly demanding role of health visitors and called on the health board to rebuild relationships with its workforce while tackling backlogs affecting families.

The Welsh government said it welcomed the return of health visitors to work and a route towards resolving the long-running dispute.

A spokesperson said health visitors provided vital support to children and families, including an important safeguarding role, and that the priority was now restoring services affected by the strike.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c678.title: Amber alert as Scotland faces blood donation shortages
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c678.text:
An amber alert has come into force for the first time as stocks of blood in Scotland have dropped to unprecedented low levels due to the shortage of donors.

The warning has been sent to hospitals across the country by the Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service (SNBTS), urging medical staff to only use Type O blood when essential.

Type O blood is particularly important for transfusions as O-negative acts as a universal donor and O-positive is the most common blood type in the UK, with about 35% of the population having it.

Stocks have consistently been below target levels for several weeks and Group O blood has fallen to below two days of reserves on several occasions recently.

SNBTS aims to always retain 5 – 7 days supply of all blood groups.

The alert comes after a decline in people joining the blood donation register.

In the past decade SNBTS said there had been a 24% drop in blood donors - about 30,000 people.

The blood transfusion service said it was particularly struggling to attract younger donors.

Hospitals are estimated to need about 135,000 units of blood each year to treat patients.

The SNBTS said that to do this appointments at its five national donor centres in Aberdeen, Dundee, Edinburgh, Glasgow and Inverness needed to be fully booked all year round.

However, an average of just 85% of these appointment slots are filled.

Debbie McNaughton, director of donor and transport services at the SNBTS, told Radio Scotland Breakfast that currently, about 2% of Scotland's population are signed up to give blood, with the majority donating once a year.

"If they could be donating maybe twice or three times a year, that would hugely help to provide resilience for the blood supply," she said.

McNaughton went on to urge anyone who is healthy and 17 or over to sign up to the donor register.

The amber alert will trigger new protocols in hospitals to minimise non-essential usage of O-type blood, but emergency operations, blood transfusions, transplants and cancer surgeries will continue as normal.

The alert has initially been issued for an initial period of 4-6 weeks but will be kept under close review.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c678.summary: Warning sent to hospitals across the country by the Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service. Stocks of blood in Scotland have dropped to unprecedented low levels due to shortage of donors. The alert comes after a decline in people joining the blood donation register.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cke8.title: To the day I die, I will regret putting a cigarette in my mouth
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cke8.text:
"To the day I die, I will regret putting a cigarette in my mouth".

These are the words of Joan McConville, who was first diagnosed with lung cancer in 2023.

The former teacher believes her cancer may have been caught earlier if screening had been available in Northern Ireland.

Despite growing evidence that early detection can significantly reduce death rates, Northern Ireland has yet to fund a targeted lung cancer screening programme.

Although the Department of Health previously committed to introducing screening by April 2027, it has now confirmed there was "no definitive timeline" for its full implementation because of funding.

Smoking is the biggest risk factor for lung cancer, although genetic and environmental factors can also contribute.

McConville, from Banbridge, started smoking at 19 while studying in Belfast and said she became addicted to nicotine.

"It's not that my generation didn't know the dangers of cancer. We did," she said.

"We started smoking because it was trendy. And I enjoyed it."

The mother-of-three tried "really hard" to stop smoking, particularly during her pregnancies, but "never succeeded completely".

She also struggled to quit after her diagnosis, despite being referred to a smoking cessation clinic.

The 71-year-old said she "was not remotely surprised" by her diagnosis, having smoked for almost 50 years and having a family history of cancer.

After several months of coughing - one of the symptoms of lung cancer - she was admitted to Craigavon Area Hospital (CAH) following a "dreadful coughing fit".

A scan to check for a clot revealed a 3cm (1in) lesion in her right lung. While surgery successfully removed the cancer, it returned earlier this year.

McConville initially had scans every six months but said more than a year had passed when she developed pain in the upper right side of her chest.

Initially dismissing it as an injury from gardening or housework, she said the "tiny little niggle" became increasingly severe along with "dreadful" nausea.

The symptoms eventually made it difficult to go into town, walk or visit her grandchildren.

Following another visit to CAH, further scans showed the cancer had returned and spread to her lymph nodes and ribs.

Surgery was no longer an option, but radiotherapy and chemotherapy were recommended.

McConville believes regular screening could have led to earlier treatment and surgery, potentially improving her outcome.

"If my cancer had developed between the ages of 50 and 70, which it did, then there's every possibility that it would have been found earlier," she said.

"I was a smoker. I probably would still have got cancer. If I could have had screening and it could have made a difference to me, that would make me angry."

She said many people underestimate the risks, believing lung cancer happens to others.

She said screening would have brought that message home.

"If it was pointed out at a very early stage to smokers like me, 'Look that tiny little dot is cancer. Stop smoking now and we'll hopefully be able to remove it and then that's it gone'," she added.

Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Northern Ireland, with about 1,370 people diagnosed each year, and more than a thousand deaths, according to Queen's University Belfast figures.

In 2022, the UK National Screening Committee recommended targeted screening across all four UK nations for people aged 55 to 74 who are at high risk of developing lung cancer, including current or ex-smokers.

Screening uses low-dose CT scans to identify lung cancer before symptoms develop.

England has begun rolling out screening, with full national coverage expected by 2030.

According to NHS England figures, nearly 13,000 lung cancers have been detected as a result with about three-quarters found at an early stage (stage 1 and 2) when cancer is most treatable.

Wales has announced a national programme, with the first invitations now expected in 2028.

While Scotland does not have a programme yet, it has been carrying out pilots.

Respiratory consultant Wendy Anderson leads Northern Ireland's lung cancer network.

She said while survival rates had been "increasing year on year, they're still not good".

"When I first started working as a consultant, less than one in 10 of our patients would have survived five years and now we're probably around one in four," she said.

Lung cancer is often diagnosed at a late stage where there are fewer treatment options available, meaning lower survival rates.

Anderson said screening could increase the proportion of people eligible for curative treatment from about 30% to 80%.

She estimated it could mean an additional 100 people a year surviving lung cancer or avoiding it altogether.

Screening could also tackle health inequalities by improving outcomes for people from more deprived communities, she added.

The respiratory consultant said reducing smoking rates remained the most important way to prevent lung cancer.

She added that stopping smoking not only reduced the chance of getting lung cancer, but also other respiratory diseases as well as heart attacks and strokes.

In December 2024, the former health minister Mike Nesbitt published a three-year health and social care plan to stabilise, reform and deliver services in Northern Ireland.

It said that "by April 2027, subject to additional funding, we will have a new targeted lung screening programme".

But now the Department of Health has said there is "no definitive timeline" for full implementation of the programme, as this will depend on future health funding.

It has funded a Public Health Agency (PHA) project team to assess what resources and funding are needed to deliver screening.

Planning will begin in December 2026 and is expected to take around a year.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cke8.summary: Joan McConville was first diagnosed with lung cancer in 2023. She believes her cancer may have been caught earlier if screening had been available in Northern Ireland. Planning will begin in December 2026 and is expected to take around a year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgm.title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgm.text:
A million young people are being offered a free meningitis B vaccine.

It comes after concerns over the UK's largest and fastest growing outbreak that happened in Kent earlier this year.

Nearly 90,000 doses of the vaccine have already been given, with 135,000 more booked in for the coming weeks.

So who needs the vaccine, what's in it and where can you get it for free?

The vaccine offers protection against a dangerous strain of meningitis called meningitis B (MenB) that caused the outbreak in Kent.

The vaccine does not contain any live bacteria and cannot cause meningitis.

It is common to get some swelling, redness or tenderness where you have the injection. You may also get a mild fever, nausea, headache or muscle aches but these symptoms should disappear after one or two days.

More serious side effects are rare.

Bookings can be made at high street pharmacies across England.

Seventeen and 18-year-olds can book via the NHS National Booking Service if they are already registered with a GP.

Other students under the age of 25 who are heading to a residential college or university this autumn for the first time can also contact a participating pharmacy.

You can get a walk-in MenB vaccine at a pharmacy if you were born on or after 21 July 2001, and for the first time this autumn you are:

International students and students from elsewhere in the UK (Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, the Channel Islands, the Isle of Man) who will be studying in England are also eligible, as well as those who are travelling abroad to study.

You do not need to be registered with a GP surgery to use the walk-in service.

Find a participating pharmacy here.

The vaccine, given as two doses and at least 28 days apart, is being offered to 17 and 18-year-olds in sixth form and students under the age of 25 who are heading to a residential college or university this autumn for the first time.

Both doses are needed for the fullest protection.

A million young people are expected to be eligible for the vaccine in England, including:

The meningitis outbreak that happened in Kent in March has been described as unprecedented and explosive.

Within weeks, in Kent, there were 29 confirmed or suspected cases and two deaths.

That's why the new, one-off campaign is being launched - to help protect those at greatest risk and hopefully prevent something like this from happening again.

Students in their first year of university have a risk that is about seven times higher than that of young people of a similar age who do not go to university, says NHS England.

Meningitis infections can be spread through close contact - for example through kissing, sharing vapes and drinks or living in close quarters with a person with the bug.

UK health officials say the risk to 18-year-olds or those entering university or a residential college for the first time is higher because of increased mixing of social groups and shared accommodation.

MenB infection can cause serious, life-threatening problems including inflammation of the lining of the brain (meningitis) and blood poisoning (sepsis).

It can lead to life-changing disabilities such as amputations, hearing loss and brain damage, and in some cases can be fatal.

Vaccination can save lives.

The MenB vaccine was added to the UK NHS childhood immunisation programme for babies born on or after 1 July 2015. All babies are now offered it.

But it means teenagers and young adults over the age of 11 have not received this jab.

Young babies are vaccinated because they are more likely to get invasive infections more often than other age groups, and their bodies are less likely to be able to fight them off.

However, research suggests the MenB vaccine doesn't necessarily prevent transmission of the infection from person to person, doesn't target all the different B bacteria strains and doesn't provide long-term protection.

But UK vaccine experts now say government should consider routinely offering the vaccine to all teenagers at around age 15. It will be up to ministers in each nation to decide whether to do this.

Meanwhile, they do want everyone who is eligible to come forward and get the vaccine because it can prevent serious illness.

Around 10,000 people in the Kent region will have already received jabs, as part of the response to the March outbreak.

Each nation has its own plans, but all are offering the vaccine to most pupils completing Year 13 or S6 in the summer of 2026 - irrespective of their education plans and including people from this age group who are not currently in school.

Young people aged 18-25 starting university or moving into residential further education settings for the first time in autumn 2026 are also eligible.

In Wales, those aged 17-18 will receive a letter invite, while those aged 18-25 who are entering higher education will need to contact their health board later in July.

Meningitis can be caused by many different types of viruses or bacteria, which are spread through close contact with a person who has them.

Viral meningitis tends to get better on its own within seven to 10 days. It can often be treated at home with plenty of rest, painkillers and anti-sickness medicine.

Bacterial meningitis needs to be treated in hospital.

Outbreaks are thankfully rare.

Currently, a separate vaccine covering different strains, the MenACWY vaccine, is offered routinely to 14-year-olds.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgm.summary: Nearly 90,000 doses of the MenACWY vaccine have already been given. 135,000 more booked in for the coming weeks. Vaccination is offered to 17 and 18-year-olds in sixth form and students under the age of 25.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.title: Women in town hit poor health earlier than average
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.text:
A study of female health in Luton has revealed that women in the town see the onset of poor health five years earlier than the national average.

The Let Women Speak report, commissioned by the Borough Council, also found over 70% of women aged 45-64 had an at-risk Body Mass Index (BMI) level.

Luton's director of public health Kelly O'Neill said: "Women are spinning a lot of plates as part of what the expectation of being a woman is, so many have put their own health and well-being secondary to the well-being of others.

"That meant they weren't turning up for cervical screening, breast screening and many things that help them stay healthier for longer."

More than 250 people from a range of ages and cultures were interviewed for the report that focuses on the wellbeing of the 112,400 women and girls who live in the town.

The study found the average age of onset of poor health for women in Luton is 55.8 years compared to 60.9 nationally. In June the BBC reported that life expectancy for women and men is also lower than the national average at 82.6 for women and 78.6 years for men.

The report also found:

Councillors have now agreed to champion women's health and support the delivery of actions to improve health and wellbeing.

Dr Eva Patel is a GP at Luton Medical and Dental clinic. She said she often sees woman coming in who are managing multiple responsibilities.

"Working, bringing up children, looking after elderly parents or supporting other family members often from large families means their own physical and mental health is often the last thing they prioritise," she said.

Thirty-seven young South Asian women were also interviewed about their experience of social isolation.

Patel said: "Language can be a barrier. If a woman comes in by herself and they don't feel comfortable speaking English then they might find it difficult to explain symptoms, even with a translator."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.title: Rare cancer discovered after mum underwent hysterectomy
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.text:
Donna Marklew had to undergo a hysterectomy to treat complications caused by childbirth.

But the operation led the Coventry mum to receive a life-changing diagnosis when tests later revealed she had a rare form of cancer.

She was diagnosed with neuroendocrine cancer, which was only discovered after tissue removed during a hysterectomy at Warwick Hospital was analysed following a uterine prolapse.

"I was very shocked because I'd never heard of neuroendocrine cancer," she said.

"[I] was left with not much information because it wasn't known to anybody, and then trying to explain to people [that] I've been diagnosed with neuroendocrine cancer, you're kind of met with blank faces."

The rare cancer, which starts in the nerve and cell glands that make and release hormones, is estimated to affect 6,000 people in the UK every year, according to the charity, Neuroendocrine Cancer UK.

Lisa Walker, the chief executive of Neuroendocrine Cancer UK, said that the average time between people experiencing a first symptom and getting a diagnosis is five years.

"That is because the symptoms could be other conditions, and then people find themselves perhaps going down a different route and then needing to go back when the symptoms change or other symptoms are added in, which then start to look more like neuroendocrine cancer," she explained.

Marklew is now trying to raise awareness of the disease, which coincides with World Neuroendocrine Cancer Day on Tuesday.

She said that the disease is actually a group of cancers that develop in hormone-producing cells throughout the body.

Diagnosis can be particularly difficult, especially for women, she added.

Marklew, an occupational therapist who works in Leicestershire, said that after she was diagnosed, scans revealed tumours were discovered in her appendix, Fallopian tubes and surrounding tissue.

In March 2025, she underwent a nine hour surgery at Warwick Hospital to remove as many tumours as possible.

However, surgery alone has not been enough, and Marklew has to have three injections every week to try and keep the cancer under control.

She has also just started Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) which is administered four times a week, every two months.

"The tumours are slow growing, which is one of the benefits of this type of cancer.

"There's a different type of neuroendocrine as well, which can be more aggressive. but fortunately for me, mine are grade two, which means that they grow quite slowly, although mine are still growing."

However, Marklew, 44, said while she is able to live a normal life during her treatment, the disease has had a huge mental impact.

"'I've got four young children and my husband, my mum and my friends, and I think the reason why I've really wanted to get up and shout about it is because I just don't want anyone to have people feel so vulnerable when you find out that you have this diagnosis because nobody knows about it [the condition]."

Walker added: "It's a complex and diverse cancer and can develop in any part of the body, which is one of the things that makes detection difficult.

"It develops in the neuroendocrine cells. They produce and release the hormones that essentially regulate our different body functions and are found throughout the body.

"So it can affect any organ. Most commonly it does affect the lungs, the digestive tract, and the pancreas, but it can be found anywhere."

Marklew said that prior to her hysterectomy, she had no identifiable symptoms, although looking back, she thinks a trip to Scotland may have been an indicator.

"I was anxious and had palpitations during a trip to St Andrews for my first wedding anniversary, but my GP suggested that was down to me being perimenopausal."

She said unlike other cancers, because neuroendocrine is not as obvious or as widely known as others, few people understand how she feels.

"I could talk to my friends and family all day long, but no one will understand what it is like to live with this condition.

"It's really really hard and because it's invisible everybody will say - oh you look great."

She said she reached out to the charity Neuroendocrine UK for support and advice.

"They're an absolutely invaluable resource for people that have been diagnosed and they have patient groups in other areas, so I said I'd really like to set one up.

"We did one in September and one other person came along, which was nice because it was a nice opportunity for me and her to have a couple of hours conversation along with one of the nurses as well.

"Then we [did] it bi-monthly, we had six people and it felt so good".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c370.title: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c370.text:
Poundland and its 11,000 employees are hopeful that the retailer's impending collapse can be delayed to allow time for a last-minute rescue deal.

The discount chain has been edging towards administration after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation have told the BBC that they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of £10m in funding.

A committee of MPs is set to question Gordon Brothers, Poundland's US owners, on Wednesday following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm has denied the claims.

But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

However, sources close to the matter told the BBC on Tuesday that a release of £10m by its owners, while "small in the scale of things" could help at least postpone the chain's collapse while a longer term solution was explored.

The 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires on Thursday, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.

Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners.

Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.

He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m.

However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up and sold off in chunks.

The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain.

MPs are set to question Gordon Brothers, Poundland's US owners, on Wednesday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx5y.title: Christmas toy rush being driven by squishies and building sets
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx5y.text:
Traditional games, squishies and building sets are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show.

The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK.

The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana.

The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between £5 and £10.

Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults".

The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves.

This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year.

But Melissa Symonds, UK toys director at Circana, said that toys for children - which still represents the majority of sales - had recorded a good year so far.

Growing public debate around children's screen time and the role of technology meant squishy toys, stickers and building sets such as Lego were popular.

"Connected toys account for less than 1% of market sales, showing that traditional, hands-on play remains overwhelmingly popular," she said.

Concerns have been raised about the suitability of some connected devices.

A BBC investigation found an AI teddy marketed as being "perfect" for children as young as three said "I can't help with killing you" after seemingly mishearing a question.

Meanwhile, debate has intensified about keeping youngsters free from smartphones during the school day.

One in five parents of children aged three to nine say the chance to play together as a family influences what they buy, according to market intelligence company The Insights Family.

Paul Reader, who chairs the Dream Toys selection panel of retailers and experts across the sector, said that parents wanted to engage with their children's play.

"Nothing beats a board game with that. Nothing beats a bit of interaction," he said.

The panel he chairs has selected a list of toys that retailers believe will be some of the most popular this year.

It includes variations on popular toys of recent years, including slime, a soft tiger that roars and grows, and a shark that breaks out of an egg.

Symonds said that, despite rising sales in the year so far, nearly half of toy sales came in the build-up to Christmas, and families were still looking closely at costs.

There was significant growth in toys priced between £5 and £10, she said.

Reader also urged anyone looking for a bargain to shop around, but to ensure that toys were bought from reputable traders so they were genuine and safe.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.title: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.text:
Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.

The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.

A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products".

The BBC has contacted Skims for comment.

The shapewear and clothing business was co-founded by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine.

Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.

One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".

A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.

"It is really interesting to see this kind of backlash," said Kate Vlietstra, senior director of food and drink at market research analyst Mintel.

"It is something we have been seeing a bit more in recent years, particularly with the trend for unboxing on social media," she said,

"It means that, inevitably, if people are not feeling they're getting the value that they have hoped for from the advent calendar...they've purchased, then yes, there is going to be a backlash."

Advent calendars remain popular, according to Helen Wing, head of innovation at market research company Ipsos though she said that "the buzz around them has reduced a little bit".

She said according to Ipsos research, people are willing to pay a bit more for an advent calendar but the contents have to justify the price tag.

Using a £285 advent calendar sold by Liberty as an example, Wing said the upmarket department story is "very open about the value of the contents".

"They will say there is over £1,000 worth of content," she said. "If you've got that reassurance when you're making the purchase, particularly if it is for a gift, then it is important to have some faith that the contents are actually going to be worth the money that you're paying."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm36.title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm36.text:
Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.

She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.

But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action.

Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.

Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.

After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.

Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.

This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.

Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process.

"I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."

Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.

In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.

After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees.

Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds.

She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest.

In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50.

But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December.

"It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says.

"I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me."

Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified."

The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue.

Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters."

Sportswear seller Azri Mukthar told the BBC he has been trying to withdraw almost £2,500 from his account for over a year.

The businessman was more than happy to become a Pro seller as he was already registered as a limited company.

"I submitted all the documentation they requested and got the go-ahead from Vinted. So then I uploaded all the products and got 30 to 40 sales immediately," he says.

But when he wanted to withdraw his earnings, he found that he couldn't.

"They said my verification was pending," he says.

Azri too, says he's been round in endless circles repeatedly submitting documents only to get an immediate response saying they had been rejected.

"It's frustrating and annoying as there's no clear system to follow.

"You contact customer support and they say you've not submitted X, Y or Z. But I know I have done all they're asking for."

He claims a certificate from Companies House that Vinted requested has been declined 15 times.

Azri has now stopped selling on Vinted and says he is going to have to start legal action.

Vinted said: "Mr Mukthar's check could not be completed because he did not provide all the required documents. Our support team is currently in touch with him to help with his verification."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq39.title: Californians reject wealth tax for billionaires
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq39.text:
California voters have voted to reject a wealth tax on its billionaires.

The ballot proposal would have levied a one-time tax on the state's mega wealthy to help fund healthcare. It took nearly a week of counting votes after the midterm election to determine a projection on the measure.

There are about 200 billionaires in the state, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, reality television star Kim Kardashian and media mogul Oprah Winfrey.

Proposition 40 targeted Californians with a wealth of more than $1.1bn (£800m) with a 5% tax on their total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income. It failed amid divisions among Democrats and labour unions.

Had it passed, experts believe it would have been the world's first wealth tax targeting billionaires.

The tax would have raised about $100bn to make up for federal funding cuts to healthcare in California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.

Those who backed the measure had argued it would help ensure that the ultra-wealthy were contributing their fair share and helping backfill gaps in the state's budget.

The wealth tax faced fierce opposition, including from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, as well as California Governor Gavin Newsom and labour unions.

Newsom, whose tenure as governor is coming to an end, had expressed concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

Some billionaire critics of the measure spent millions trying to crush it, with a handful even moving out of the state to evade the possible tax. Brin gave more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the tax, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Dave Regan, head of the union that led the charge for the measure, said on election night that the billionaires' efforts to block the tax created "a lot of confusion and a lot of second-guessing among people who really in their hearts know what the right the thing to do is".

Regan, who is president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, pledged to seek a billionaire tax once more in 2028.

The measure had odds stacked against it, with two other propositions on the ballot that would have effectively reversed it, even if it passed.

California, home to some 23 million registered voters, has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy. It is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world, but also has one of the highest wealth gaps.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c874.title: What are cold weather payments and who can get them?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c874.text:
As temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather payments.

This financial help is triggered across hundreds of postcodes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland when there is a prolonged period of below-zero temperatures.

In Scotland, those on low incomes and benefits may receive a separate winter heating payment, which does not depend on how cold it gets.

The cold weather payment is a government benefit top-up to help with fuel bills.

The average temperature in a local area must be recorded as, or forecast to be, 0C or below for seven days in a row.

The temperature is recorded by the relevant weather station for your postcode.

More than 1.4 million cold weather payments were made during winter 2025-26.

To qualify, you must live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland.

Payments are not age-related but you must already be receiving certain benefits, including:

Each cold weather payment is for a seven-day period and is worth £25.

More than one payment will be made during the course of the winter if there are enough periods of cold weather.

The scheme runs between 1 November and 31 March each year.

Hospital stays can affect your entitlement to the payment so you should tell the Pension Service or Jobcentre Plus if you become an inpatient.

You should also update the relevant service if you have a baby, or if a child under five comes to live with you.

In Scotland, the winter heating payment is worth £62, and is paid automatically between December and February.

You do not have to do anything in order to receive cold weather payments.

The money should be paid automatically into the same bank or building society account as your benefits, within two weeks of the qualifying period of cold weather.

If you do not receive a payment, you can contact the Pension Service or Jobcentre Plus.

Cold weather payments do not affect other benefits.

They are separate to the winter fuel payment, which is worth £100 or £300 depending on your individual circumstances.

About nine million pensioners get the Winter Fuel Payment, after a government u-turn over changes to the eligibility rules.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2.title: Electricity bills to rise by 2.5% from March
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2.text:
Electricity bills will go up by 2.5% in Jersey from March 2027, it has been announced.

Jersey Electricity said the tariff increase would add just over £1 per week for a typical all-electric home from March 2027.

The annual rate of inflation in Jersey rose to 3% in September, according to the latest figures.

Chief executive Chris Ambler said: "We know that any increase in household costs is unwelcome, so we have worked hard to keep this rise below the island's current rate of inflation."

Ambler said: "We have again delayed the increase until March, which means it will not affect customers during the colder winter months when electricity consumption is generally at its highest."

The company said it was investing £120m in the network to improve its resilience and future-proof its systems.

It said it continued to focus on managing costs responsibly and driving efficiencies across the business.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmew.title: Law on 'holiday hunger' passed by Stormont assembly
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmew.text:
A law aimed at helping lower income families with food costs during school holidays has been passed by the Northern Ireland Assembly.

The Holiday Meal Payments Bill seeks to create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals to help with food costs outside term time.

A majority of 49 to 24 assembly members backed the legislation, which was proposed by Sinn Féin's Danny Baker and welcomed by some parents and charities.

Education Minister Paul Givan described the bill as "fiscally reckless", warning it would cost £20m to £30m a year and lead to cuts elsewhere within his Stormont department.

Baker said that "poverty isn't green and orange" and the passage of the bill would support thousands of children "across all of our communities".

"When children are returning to school hungry, then they're not learning," he told assembly members during the bill's final stage debate.

"If you want to deal with educational underachievement then you have to deal with poverty."

Givan described the bill as "well intentioned" but said "sincerity is not a funding model".

The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) minister added there was "no such thing as a free lunch" and the legislation "will require cuts to be made" to other services.

"So I ask those who support this bill, what cuts should be made to afford this payment?"

The minister argued efforts at Stormont to tackle poverty should be made "in a coordinated way" across the entire four-party executive.

Last month, Givan's department tabled amendments that would have given him power to delay its implementation, but these were rejected by a majority of parties.

Stormont assembly members voted on the bill on Tuesday night after more than four hours of debate during its final stage in the chamber.

Alliance Party assembly member Nick Mathison, chair of the assembly's education committee, said "holiday hunger" remained a significant issue for many families.

He acknowledged Stormont's financial pressures but said the funding required for the bill was a "relatively small" proportion of the Department of Education's budget.

"When we are in a budgetary crisis we need to be ensuring that we do not end up penalising those who are least able to bear the costs," he added.

Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows commended Baker on the sentiment of his private member's bill but warned "there is no funding stream and there is no money".

He said the bill "lacks any governance", adding: "There are no guarantees the money given under this will end up in nutritious meals inside the stomachs of children."

"It's a fundamental misapplication and misunderstanding of how the welfare system should work," he told assembly members.

Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) assembly member Cara Hunter welcomed the bill, saying that "a child can't learn on an empty stomach".

"Hunger shows up in concentration, in behaviour and attainment long before it shows up in the spreadsheets or the speeches that we have before us here today," she added.

Baker said he was motivated to introduce it by some of his experiences of breakfast clubs and meal schemes in youth work.

"There was a young boy, about the same age of my youngest, around seven years old," he explained.

"He was filling his wee pockets up and we caught on to this.

"To cut a long story short, he was bringing home food for his siblings because there just wasn't enough food in the house."

Baker said all ministers had choices to make and the legislation alone could not solve child poverty, but would act as an "early intervention".

Children are eligible for free school meals if their family's household income is below £15,390 a year.

Northern Ireland is the only UK region without government-funded holiday food support, after the Department of Education (DE) ended its £27-per-fortnight holiday meal grant in 2023.

Baker's legislation was introduced in the Northern Ireland Assembly in March and has been scrutinised by members of the legislative assembly (MLAs) on a number of occasions over the past nine months.

Community and voluntary groups have been publicly supportive of the bill, with some staging a demonstration at Stormont on Monday in a bid to urge MLAs to get it over the finish line.

Louise McCullough, a mum-of-three from east Belfast, was among those who spoke at the event.

She said her children receive free school meals and that she would be directly affected by the legislation.

"There are so many working families who need this, it will change their lives and be massively impactful," she told BBC News NI.

"I can't afford to work full time because of the cost of childcare, and the cost of living.

"We have to do what we can and schemes like free school meals make a difference but so much more needs done... if you can't find money for hungry children what are you doing?

"Our government should be scaffolding our families properly."

Edel Diamond from the South West Belfast Foodbank said organisations like hers had been "filling in the gaps" to help struggling families.

"We shouldn't have to - it's incumbent on our executive to put these initiatives forward," she said.

"This will make such a difference to families we're seeing daily."

Every day, tens of thousands of hours of pornographic content are uploaded to the internet. At peak times, 10% of internet traffic is people watching porn. But who is making money from it, and how?

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r.title: Acquitted 'China spy' tells BBC: I was fall guy for security services but also naive
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r.text:
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".

Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.

The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.

Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.

The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.

Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.

In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.

But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.

Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.

With the government having previously said that Chinese spies were targeting UK officials across the political, defence and business sectors with increasingly sophisticated espionage operations, Cash believes his case was pursued as a warning to others.

Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said he denied any wrongdoing and that he had been "unfairly subjected to a trial by media".

He said he had provided reports to a Chinese company, which he believed had clients seeking to develop trading links with the UK, and those reports contained no classified information and relied on public sources.

Cash returned to the UK in 2019, saying in his resignation message for his job in China that he felt "guilty sitting back and participating in a system that I am uncomfortable with".

He later became the director of a small policy group run by China-sceptic Conservative MPs in Westminster.

Meanwhile, Berry stayed in China writing reports for a large consultancy which, like many Chinese companies, has links to the government.

UK security services alleged that information from the men's messages, sent on the encrypted messaging app Signal between January 2022 and March 2023, had been passed to people linked to the Chinese state.

England and Wales' top prosecutor said the case had collapsed last autumn because government officials could not say China had been classed as an "enemy" at the time.

This prompted accusations of UK political interference to placate the Chinese government.

China has previously called the allegations of spying "pure fabrication and malicious slander".

The most striking section of the messages handed to the BBC concerns Berry's account of his meeting in summer 2022 with a senior Chinese official who wanted to have "a more detailed co-operation".

In voice notes Berry describes how, beforehand, work colleagues had told him the official's interest had been piqued by reports Berry had written, which included details of the UK's foreign policy approach to China.

In the voice notes, Berry says he was initially aghast, but then decided: "I thought it would be interesting to go anyway… not really intending to do anything."

Berry tells Cash he was driven to a government-owned villa in a grand compound.

The experience "felt like a psychological game of chess" and "like a test", Berry says.

He kept his hands under the table as tea was served: "I didn't want it to be obvious if I was nervous. I tested to see if my hands were shaking first, then drank the tea."

Berry describes the senior Chinese official asking via an interpreter "about the situation in the UK at the moment, about the Tory leadership thing".

At that time, Boris Johnson had just resigned as the UK's prime minister, and a Conservative leadership battle was taking place, which Liz Truss would go on to win.

Berry says he jokingly tried to ask his host which candidate China wanted, but the interpreter did not translate his question.

"And then the main guy just shakes my hand like it's time to go," Berry tells Cash.

After receiving the voice notes, Cash replies via text the next day: "You, my friend, have just been elite captured" before adding: "You're in spy territory now".

In many media reports these particular messages, previously released in a government witness statement, have been presented as a smoking gun - evidence that Cash knew his friend was passing on information to the Chinese state.

But Cash insists it was a "tongue-in-cheek joke" because he knew his friend to be "a staunch critic of the Chinese Communist Party".

The next morning, he made a joke about Berry spying for the UK and getting in trouble with the Chinese authorities, he says. Cash texted: "Keep him sweet… We may have a use for you yet".

"I didn't believe he was knowingly spying on the UK through me," says Cash. "I trusted my friend… I wish I had seen the danger earlier, spotted it and cut off all contact."

So who was the mystery official Berry had met?

"I found out who this guy is," Berry text-messaged Cash a few hours later. "Bigger deal than I thought."

Berry posted a link to the Wikipedia page of Cai Qi, who at the time was one of China's most influential politicians and is now, in effect, President Xi Jinping's chief of staff.

Whether Berry correctly identified his host remains unclear. He has since disputed the suggestion that he met someone as senior as Cai Qi.

What is beyond dispute is that he believed he may have met someone highly placed within the Chinese political system.

For Chris Cash, this unusual encounter did not prompt alarm bells. Asked why not, Cash tells the BBC: "Because I didn't think anything of the meeting, really."

We ask Cash why his friend might have been asked to such a meeting. "Strange things happen in China... you know we would often brush shoulders with sort of quite senior members of the Chinese communist party," he tells us.

Challenged about whether he had read the Wikipedia link at the time, Cash says he had "skimmed it", adding that it described him as a judge and a provincial-level official. "I just thought it was a weird meeting with a guy who'd taken an interest," he says.

Six months later, Berry said in text messages that "off the record" he had it "on pretty good authority" that China was considering dropping sanctions against Tom Tugendhat, one of the Conservative MPs in the China Research Group, where Cash worked.

Berry wrote that this would happen as long as the West "continued to show signals that they are willing to work together".

The Chinese believed it would be "extremely embarrassing" if Tugendhat became prime minister or foreign secretary while under Chinese sanctions, Berry said.

At the time of the meeting in summer 2022, China-sceptic Tugendhat was seen as a possible contender to succeed Boris Johnson, or become UK foreign secretary.

He was actually appointed as security minister by Liz Truss, and Beijing lifted sanctions on him in January 2026.

Was Cash concerned that Berry appeared to be passing information to him about Chinese foreign policy?

Cash says he assumed Berry had heard this "through the grapevine at his company" which was doing business with the UK.

He says he never doubted his friend's trustworthiness, to the extent he even named Berry as a reference on his application for a security pass for the Palace of Westminster.

The pass was granted and, a fortnight before their arrests in early 2023, Cash invited Berry to Parliament for lunch.

It was to be their final face-to-face conversation.

Cash was in bed at quarter to six on a March morning when he was woken by car doors being shut, he says. Within seconds, four UK counter-terrorism officers had barged into his bedroom at his parents' home in Edinburgh.

"They told me to sit up and not touch anything and then said I was under arrest for breaching the Official Secrets Act," Cash says.

"I was in complete shock… quivering... My mum was hysterical."

Cash says the officers dressed him in dirty clothes he had worn that weekend, handcuffed him and marched him down to an unmarked police car. He was later driven to London.

Chris Berry was also arrested the same day.

It remains unclear how, when and why British security services became interested in the exchanges between the two friends.

But they are likely to have found out far more about their relationship when Berry was stopped and questioned by counter-terror officers at Heathrow Airport.

His laptop and phone were taken - this may have enabled his Signal chats to be downloaded.

Berry later messaged Cash about it.

Cash says he had not been alarmed by this: "I thought it was just standard... for a guy who'd been in China."

As the investigation progressed, it became clear the authorities believed Cash and Berry had been involved in an informal, but dangerous, exchange of information that was "prejudicial to the safety and interests of the UK".

The allegations were based on 6,273 messages between the pair - the same ones Cash has now shared with the BBC. Cash's solicitor has told the BBC they are genuine.

They cover a period when Cash had joined the China Research Group (CRG), founded by Tugendhat and fellow Tory MP Alicia Kearns, and when Berry was working for a Chinese company called Strong, where part of his work involved writing political and economic reports for clients.

According to court documents, Berry was said to have compiled 34 reports for a man linked to the Chinese state spy agency, relaying information passed on to him by Cash. Strong did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

The CRG's office was across the Thames from Westminster, but Cash regularly had meetings in Parliament. Cash did not have government security clearance and there is no evidence he had access to classified documents.

Despite being thousands of miles apart, the two friends remained in close contact, often messaging daily.

The messages reviewed by the BBC show them discussing topics including sanctions on China, the tech company Huawei, human rights, Hong Kong, Taiwan and British foreign policy.

Cash says he used the Signal app for almost all his contacts with people in China - "more for their protection" - as he says discussing the government "could land someone… in trouble". He and Berry did not use the app's "disappearing messages" function.

Much of the information they discussed was publicly available, says Cash - who has given the BBC a detailed spreadsheet with links and references in an attempt to prove it.

But sometimes he did share with Berry his impressions from meetings and private discussions in Westminster. On 12 occasions in the messages, he labelled information "off the record" or "very off the record" before passing it on.

Cash says this was "just me excitedly sharing things that I was doing with him at work".

One message recounted views allegedly expressed in private by Britain's then-ambassador to China, Dame Caroline Wilson, during a discussion with the CRG about its work on China's influence on UK universities.

Cash also messaged Berry sharing unverified rumours about the sex lives of two UK cabinet ministers. There is no evidence Berry passed this to his Chinese colleagues.

Cash says he regarded such exchanges as routine political discussion. "We weren't working with classified information," he says.

Cash was told by his solicitor the police investigation would blow over after six months and he would soon be able to return to normal life.

But in September 2023 - six months after the arrests - the case became public when the Sunday Times broke the story of an unnamed "spy" who had been arrested in Parliament.

Cash recalls travelling on a train while, around him, fellow passengers read the newspaper's front page story: "Commons 'Chinese spy' arrested". He says: "I wanted the world to eat me up."

Within 24 hours he was named and pictured in the press, and both men were later charged with espionage.

In September the following year, just weeks before their trial was due to begin, Cash received an unexpected call from his solicitor.

"Are you sitting down?" he asked Cash. "They've dropped all the charges."

His lawyers requested a court hearing for the prosecution to formally acknowledge that they would offer no evidence, but at the Old Bailey the newly-innocent Cash struggled to find anyone interested in his story.

At every previous court appearance he had been mobbed, but the press had not been informed about this hearing.

Eventually his team found a lone BBC journalist. "I said my piece outside the Old Bailey. And that was a real high point. I felt that I could start to move on with my life."

It wouldn't be that simple.

Across the city, House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle was seething. "It is this Parliament that has been spied on," he declared. "It is MPs' offices that have been infiltrated."

There would be days of political debate and a raucous prime minister's questions where Tory leader Kemi Badenoch would claim: "This all stinks of a cover-up."

"I'd been acquitted by law, but then I was traduced in Parliament," Cash says. "It was almost like I was convicted in the court of public opinion again, by people who I had worked with and trusted and that felt horrible."

Today Cash's life is almost unrecognisable. He has lost his dream job, his relationship, and his closest friend from university.

"We talked about being each other's best men," Cash says. Instead, when the friend got married last year, Cash was not even invited.

He is also no longer in contact with Berry.

"I've been applying for basic admin jobs and having trouble recently," Cash says.

"I'm angry and upset with how everything played out, and I do feel let down."

But when asked, Cash stops short of saying he feels Berry betrayed him. Does he think his friend was spying for the Chinese government?

"He would have to have his time in court to defend himself," Cash answers. "I think it'd be wrong of me to speculate and hypocritical given the speculation that I've been subject to. But we're no longer friends."

Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said his reports "concerned economic and commercial issues widely discussed in the UK at the time and drew on information freely in the public domain".

Like his former friend, Chris Cash is innocent in the eyes of the law, but his reputation has undoubtedly been trashed.

Many in Parliament still think they were spies. And with more of the messages between these former friends now revealed, the debate over their actions could be reignited.

"It was a gruelling ordeal," Cash says. "But I'm a fundamentally positive person… I'm positive about what the future holds."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r.summary: Chris Cash was charged with spying for China in 2012 and acquitted in 2013. He has shared more than 6,000 messages with the BBC revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK. Cash says he thought he met a senior Chinese official in 2022.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3j4.title: Tories pledge to cut benefits for children with 'milder cases' of ADHD
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3j4.text:
The Conservatives have pledged to save £2.8bn a year by ending Disability Living Allowance (DLA) payments to families of children with "milder cases" of behavioural disorders, learning difficulties or ADHD.

The policy is one of a series of measures which the party says will save £36bn from the welfare budget.

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the system risked putting children on a "conveyor belt" towards a "lifetime on benefits".

Labour described the Tories' plan as a "charter for homelessness and human misery that would push people into hardship and end up costing the state more".

DLA for children allows parents to claim between £30.30 and £194.60 per week to help cover the additional costs that come with raising a disabled child.

The child must either have difficulty getting about or need more looking after than a child of the same age who does not have a disability.

The Conservatives say child DLA is the "fastest growing benefit in the UK's welfare system", citing government statistics showing the number of cases had risen from 521,476 in 2020 to 914,000.

The party is proposing that in cases where a claim is for a behavioural disorder, learning difficulty or ADHD, only those with the highest need will be eligible for cash payments.

Under the party's plans, those with the most severe conditions, representing around 30% of cases, would continue to receive payments.

The remaining 70% would lose the money but instead receive support through mental health services and family hubs, into which the Conservatives have said they will invest £1bn.

The changes would apply to new claims and reassessments. Those with physical disabilities would be exempt.

The party's other previously-announced cuts include:

Setting out the party's plans, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities even when they face serious challenges.

"Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world.

"If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself."

The Labour government has said it wants to bring the benefits bill down but has not set out a timetable for any reductions.

More details of its plans are expected to come after former minister Alan Milburn has published his review on young people not in education, employment and training.

Both Milburn's review and a review into disability benefits, co-chaired by Minister Sir Stephen Timms, will be published in November.

Asked about Milburn's review, Whately said he was "rolling the pitch for more welfare spending" adding: "We're in no question and no doubt that you can make savings from welfare - it's just that Labour doesn't want to do that."

A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives designed and implemented this benefit system, which has driven large numbers of people to be signed off and written off.

"Labour is tackling the collapse in face-to-face assessments, bringing in personalised employment support for sick and disabled people and spreading opportunity to young people through the Youth Guarantee."

The Child Poverty Action Group said: "These proposals would take the UK back to the dark ages, causing the biggest overnight increase in child poverty since records began."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: "Until the Conservatives face up to the damage their botched Brexit deal has done, they will remain an out-of-touch, anti-growth, anti-business party, and it will be disabled people and children growing up in poverty who will pay the price."
