https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3ly.title: Census should include black English and Asian English options, says MP
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3ly.text:
The next census should include more ethnicity options to allow people to define themselves as black English or Asian English, according to a group of MPs.

Liberal Democrat MP Josh Babarinde told the BBC that "most people" in the country believe "you don't have to be white to be English", as he called for the categories to be updated in a similar way to changes in Wales and Scotland.

At the 2021 census, the ethnic group section saw English offered only within the white category.

Babarinde's proposal, dubbed the "St George's Bill", aims to broaden the options and its supporters include Labour's David Lammy and Conservative Sir James Cleverly. It was tabled in the House of Commons on Tuesday.

In his speech to introduce his private member's bill (PMB), Babarinde told MPs he is a "proud Englishman" and has "proud Nigerian heritage".

He said: "But my parents and I were born in England, we grew up in England, our home is in England, yet some voices attempt to reduce Englishness to a skin colour and to a bloodline.

"Well, if we're going to go down that path, my mum's side of the family has been English for as far back as we have traced."

The Eastbourne MP said he had received "death threats for daring to say that you don't have to be white to be English".

He added "English ethnicity is real" before arguing it is a "matter of historical fact that it has never been one bloodline" and "even our Royal Family has German roots".

"Is the King not English either, I ask."

Addressing the ethnicity section of the census, Babarinde said the "only box that says English sits under the white category".

He added: "If you are black, the form offers you black British, if you are Asian, it offers you Asian British, but not English.

"Now, the same question in the Welsh census offers a black Welsh category. In Scotland, the census offers Scottish Asian, for example.

"Yet the best that England offers in our census is a miscellaneous write-in box that may as well be the margin."

Lammy, a former deputy prime minister, said in a statement: "It is quite absurd that neither I or my mixed heritage children can describe themselves as black or mixed race and English on our census form.

"I have long campaigned for us to change to the position enjoyed by others in Wales and Scotland. We have to end this backward racial gatekeeping."

Babarinde told the BBC he had brought forward the PMB because there were "some corners of our politics who are attempting to gatekeep Englishness for people who are a particular colour".

He also said there are "people like Suella Braverman who have really undermined and questioned the Englishness of people like me".

In 2025, Braverman - then a Conservative MP before her defection to Reform UK - wrote in the Daily Telegraph that she was British Asian but said she "cannot claim to be English" despite being born and educated in England.

In recent weeks, Braverman has reaffirmed her position and wrote on X: "To say I'm English is to take a 'laissez-faire, anything-goes' attitude to ethnicity, citizenship and identity. It also denies me my Asian heritage."

She also said "Englishness is an ethnicity", adding: "There have been English people for centuries and we need to recognise this more if we are to start taking a more muscular approach to citizenship and nationality. And no, it's not racist to say this."

Babarinde introduced his PMB to the Commons using the 10-minute rule process.

This gave him up to 10 minutes to make the case for why he wanted to introduce his PMB.

No MP took up the option to make a 10-minute speech opposing it.

Babarinde asked for his PMB, formally known as the English Ethnic Identity (census particulars) Bill, to return to the Commons on 23 April 2027 - St George's Day - for its second reading debate.

But it is unlikely to be considered further in its current form due to a lack of parliamentary time.

PMBs allow MPs to raise issues they believe ministers should be considering and to develop campaigns showing the strength of support for their ideas.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820.title: Scottish Labour leader says the UK should re-join EU
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820.text:
The Scottish Labour leader has called for the UK to re-join the European Union, insisting it should be a "long-term objective" for the whole country.

During his first major speech since becoming party leader, Michael Marra said he wanted "solidarity, not separation" and accepted that "re-joining the EU won't be easy".

Marra acknowledged there would be "serious questions" over issues such as currency and borders before the UK could return to the EU.

Last month, the UK government ruled out re-joining the EU within this parliament but Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer ties with Europe.

The UK Labour leader suggested another referendum on the issue could feature in a future Labour manifesto.

Speaking at the University of Edinburgh, Marra said: "The UK should re-join the European Union and Scottish Labour will work to make that happen.

"I don't pretend it will happen quickly. But I believe we should set it as a long-term objective for the UK and that Scotland should lead the change in making that happen."

Marra accepted his call goes further than Prime Minister Andy Burnham's position.

He added: "Re-joining the EU is not the current policy of the UK Labour Party and not the current policy of the UK government.

"The UK Labour Party isn't there yet. This is a distinct Scottish Labour position."

Marra's predecessor, Anas Sarwar, had pushed for closer ties with the EU after Brexit but did not go as far as to call for the UK to re-join the bloc.

"It is in Scotland's interests, and in the interests of the whole United Kingdom, for the UK to re-join the European Union," added Marra.

Addressing party supporters, Marra set out how going back into Europe would boost the economy.

The North East MSP said that "breaking down barriers" with European nations would "help Scottish businesses grow, attract investment and create better-paid jobs".

It could also "help bring down prices and generate more money for our public services", he added.

Marra accepted that re-joining the EU "won't solve every problem we have", but added: "If we're serious about growth, we cannot keep ignoring the opportunity on our doorstep."

His speech came ahead of the prime minister travelling to Brussels next week where he is expected to sign a series of deals with the EU.

These will be focused on bringing down post-Brexit trade barriers on food and farming, as well as working more closely on emissions trading and making it easier for young people from the UK to work, live and study in Europe, and vice versa.

Responding to Marra's speech, SNP deputy leader Keith Brown said: "Having accepted that people are able to revisit the EU referendum decision taken 10 years ago, how can any Labour Party politician now seriously claim Scotland can't revisit the independence referendum decision taken 12 years ago?"

Marra told BBC Scotland News that he did not support a second referendum, and said he believed the people of Scotland did not either.

Scottish Liberal Democrats leader Alex Cole-Hamilton said he was pleased to see Scottish Labour following his party's lead.

He added: "It's important to offer the people of Britain a realistic roadmap back to Europe. That starts with re-joining the single market and establishing a customs union as a key first step."

The Scottish Greens' co-leader Gillian Mackay said she agrees with Marra that Scotland's "place is in the EU" - but added it was hypocritical to support this while ignoring "growing demand" for an Independence referendum.

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said people in Scotland were "sick of constant constitutional uncertainty" and want "politicians to focus on the cost-of-living, cutting taxes and fixing public service".

Reform UK Scotland's Max Bannerman said the country does not need to re-join the EU to see growth.

Michael Marra has set a very clear policy direction for his party. So why now?

Andy Burnham took the first step by taking his tin opener to this can of political worms at the Labour Party conference as he seeks closer ties with the EU.

There's a crunch summit in Brussels a week on Friday.

But Marra is going further than the prime minister.

He points out rejoining the EU is not the current policy of the UK government and that this is a distinct, Scottish Labour position.

Marra is a new leader and he needs to make the news with a stand-out position, so that also helps to answer the "why now" question.

Scottish Labour believe their leader has two clear roles; challenge the Scottish government and influence the UK government.

Marra thinks he can be influential and it's a change even from the position he held when he took over as leader.

There may be a fair amount of Scottish public support for this and brings Labour alongside the SNP as they both burnish their pro-EU credentials.

Labour and the SNP will continue their traditional battle and now Marra has a new fight on his hands to fully convince his party of his stance as he demands "rejoin" be included in their next general election manifesto.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820.summary: Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra says re-joining the EU is not the current policy of the UK Labour Party. He accepts that re- joining the EU won't be easy but says it is in Scotland's interests. Marra's predecessor Anas Sarwar had pushed for closer ties with the EU after the EU.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.title: Jonathan Ross 'horrified' by Walliams allegations and Brand conviction
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.text:
TV presenter Jonathan Ross has said he is "horrified" by allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams and the rape conviction of Russell Brand.

In a statement, Ross said he was once "on friendly terms with both men", but that at the time he was "genuinely unaware of their conduct".

ITV News and the Guardian on Tuesday published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. Walliams denies all the allegations against him. Brand was sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape on Monday.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said that the allegations against Walliams were the "latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" in the media.

Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers, or allege other inappropriate behaviour.

In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In his statement, Ross also addressed a joke he made at a comedy awards show in 2004, in which the punchline suggested Walliams would be "going home" with a 15-year-old.

Ross acknowledged the controversial quip and described it as "tasteless".

He added: "This joke was submitted to me by the Comedy Awards script writing team and I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect.

"Had I had any reason to suspect that it might be referring to actual events, I would not only have refused to use it, but I would not have felt comfortable continuing a personal or professional relationship with him."

Ross is one of the country's best-known TV presenters, having regularly hosted celebrities on his Jonathan Ross Show, including David Walliams and Russell Brand.

He said he was "as horrified by the revelations about David Walliams and the crimes of Russell Brand as the rest of the nation".

He added: "My thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."

The allegations include:

In the ITV documentary revealing the allegations, Jonathan Ross is pictured at an event also attended by a woman who later made accusations about the conduct of Walliams.

Ross and Brand were also widely criticised for leaving lewd voicemails for Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs, the grandfather of Georgina Baillie with whom Brand was in a consensual relationship in the mid-2000s, during a BBC Radio 2 broadcast.

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years' imprisonment for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and the Metropolitan Police has confirmed several people have approached them about the disgraced star since his conviction.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said on Tuesday: "These allegations are the latest in a long line of reported abuses of power in an industry where we have known for so long that the power imbalances are huge.

"Russell Brand's eventual conviction was a stark reminder that we are still far too reliant on the courage of brave women who choose to come forward despite knowing they will pay a heavy price and may not be believed - and a handful of persistent journalists who risk everything to tell their stories.

"Women must feel safe in their jobs, whistleblowers must be protected, and those who abuse their position must no longer be able to hide behind it."

Downing Street earlier called the allegations "deeply troubling".

Walliams rose to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent, and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

A BBC spokesperson described the allegations as "serious" and said the corporation has removed Little Britain from BBC iPlayer.

Several women have spoken to the Guardian and ITV News as part of a joint three-year investigation by the media companies, accusing Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. The investigation was published after Walliams lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.

One of the women now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault".

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Lilly Creightmore, who has alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager, said she was "angry" at his behaviour.

She said that Walliams invited her to move in with him while she was "in between living situations". She was 18 at the time. She "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him" but told him she was not interested in him in a romantic way.

After about a week of refusing Walliams's advances, Creightmore said "he started to become very moody and rude and cold".

According to ITV, Walliams says he did not act inappropriately and did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".

TV agent Dermot McNamara, who has represented someone allegedly groomed by Walliams, told BBC Newsnight he had informed "authorities and broadcasters" about Walliams's alleged "inappropriate behaviour" but no action was taken.

Walliams denies all allegations, and in a statement to journalists shared by the Guardian said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He acknowledged that "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

The Metropolitan Police have since contacted the Guardian and ITV News "to ensure that any potential victims" are "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".

A spokesperson added: "The Met has not received any related reports of sexual assault or any other offences. Should we receive any reports, they will be carefully assessed."

Comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News on Tuesday that she was one of the people who spoke to the Guardian about allegations raised with her about Walliams.

A young TV worker had approached Beaumont about concerns of Walliams engaging inappropriate behaviour with "young girls" who were "definitely" older than 16, the comedian said.

The young person said he had worked on a programme involving Walliams where he was tasked with taking the "young girls" to Walliams's dressing room, adding: "He felt they were vulnerable."

Contains sexual content.

Beaumont said she reached out to an alleged victim who was "in a really bad way" and was worried about her well-being but said the woman "declined my offer of support".

The 43-year-old comedian said she had never worked with Walliams or witnessed any inappropriate behaviour from him but was "worried that these girls were very young".

She believes there is not a robust "duty of care" to protect people within the TV industry from sexual misconduct nor an adequate reporting system for whistleblowers.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday, Labour MP Jess Phillips said: "We shouldn't always look for a criminal threshold in all these cases."

The former secretary of state for safeguarding violence against women and girls said: "If you compare the David Walliams story with the Russell Brand story, there is a clear blue water between, one is a criminal case, one is a series of allegations... but the behaviour needs to be stopped.

"What is described in the David Walliams story is an absolute modus operandi, a target group of women of a certain age, the kind of women who don't have the same amount of power as if you were doing this to a 35-year-old woman who might have a bit more about herself in the world. And so they're targeting a group of people and they are looking at what they can get away with."

She described the allegations, which Walliams denies, as "dangerous behaviour" which "leads to so much abuse in our society.

"Whether criminal exploitation or sexual exploitation, that I think we need to look at grooming much more closely in the round."

In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy says allegations are the "latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" Comedian Lucy Beaumont says she was one of the people who spoke to the Guardian about allegations.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjr4.title: Dua Lipa to become first female British headliner at Coachella 2027
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjr4.text:
Coachella has announced the line-up for its 2027 festival, with Dua Lipa set to be the first solo female British artist to headline.

The Training Season singer is top of Friday's bill for both weekends in April, with psych-rock band Tame Impala headlining the Saturday shows and US singer SZA closing out both Sundays.

The massive festival returns to the California desert on 9 to 11 and 16 to 18 April next year, with more than 100,000 fans expected to attend each day.

Madonna is also set to return to the festival after a surprise appearance alongside this year's headliner Sabrina Carpenter, 20 years on from her first Coachella set.

The Queen of Pop came back with Confessions II, her first album since 2019, earlier this year and had been rumoured to be headlining Glastonbury 2027 before organisers ruled that out.

Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and US singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers are also set to perform, as well as Diljit Dosanjh who returns after making history in 2023 by becoming the first Punjabi language singer to perform at the festival.

Blackpink's Jisoo, US star Kehlani, rock band Weezer and Dancing On My Own singer Robyn are also among the artists on the line-up.

The festival will mark a reunion for Dua Lipa and SZA after the pair both headlined Glastonbury in 2024.

During her Pyramid stage set, Dua, who earlier this year married could-be James Bond actor Callum Turner, also brought out Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker.

She becomes the first British woman to headline Coachella after Charli XCX performed on the main stage in 2025 before Green Day's headline slot.

During the success of her album Brat, the 365 singer made headlines after being pictured wearing a 'Miss Should Be Headliner' sash following her set.

Green Day appeared to respond with frontman Billie Joe Armstrong wearing a Brat baseball cap during their performance the following weekend.

Other UK artists on the 2027 line-up include EsDeeKid, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith.

Coachella is one of the most high-profile music festivals in the world thanks to its line-up and reputation for attracting a celebrity audience.

Tickets go on sale on Friday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjr4.summary: Dua Lipa set to be first solo female British artist to headline Coachella. Madonna and Sabrina Carpenter also set to return to the festival. Tame Impala and SZA will head the Saturday and Sunday shows.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwj3.title: Wayne Rooney leads I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! line-up
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwj3.text:
Former England and Manchester United footballer Wayne Rooney, Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page and YouTuber Sharky will be among the intrepid crew entering the jungle Down Under for this year's I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!

They will be joined by Kaiser Chiefs frontman Ricky Wilson, Paralympian and presenter Ade Adepitan, actress Claire Sweeney and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.

TV presenter AJ Odudu, comedian Jack Skipper, Love Island contestant Chloe Burrows and model Leomie Anderson round out the team headed for Australia.

Hosts Ant and Dec will return with the ITV show's opening episode on Monday, 16 November, with the series now in its 26th year.

Rooney is following in the footsteps of his wife Coleen, who was runner-up on I'm A Celebrity in 2024.

"If you're going in you want to win it," he said. "Coleen's already tried and obviously she finished second in the show so I'm here to bring that title back to the Rooney household."

Rooney admitted that jumping out of a helicopter is his biggest fear. "I've been booked to jump out of a plane three times before and never made it on the plane," he said.

"I don't like snakes or what is in the water either - I don't go in the sea."

Producers are making adaptations to the Australian jungle camp so it is accessible for Adepitan.

In a press statement, he said: "For me, this is a moment in time. Even if I go out in the first week, I will always be remembered as the person in a wheelchair. I am slightly overwhelmed. It's never been done before, and it never crossed my mind I would be the first."

Keith Lemon comedian Leigh Francis is not among the official line-up but is rumoured to become a late addition.

The last I'm A Celebrity series was the all-star version in South Africa, which was marked by heated arguments and walk-outs among the cast during the live final in April.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwj3.summary: Wayne Rooney, Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page and YouTuber Sharky will be among the intrepid crew. The former England and Manchester United footballer is following in the footsteps of his wife Coleen.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwx2.title: Why Walliams' unprecedented legal battle to stay anonymous failed
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwx2.text:
David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle not to be named in relation to allegations against him went downhill as he tried to secure a permanent injunction.

He was named by the Guardian and ITN because he had no sound legal reason to prevent the news organisations' investigation from being published. In response to the allegations included, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

The 55-year-old's bid for an injunction had been an open secret from the start after what would have normally been an anonymised application briefly appeared under his own name on a court cases register.

His exceptionally unusual attempt to gag the media - forever - became clear at the full trial last month - but that's when his bid to remain anonymous got worse.

In court, his lawyers did not claim that the investigation would be disclosing legally confidential or private information the journalists were not entitled to - two avenues often trod to silence reporters.

Instead lawyers for Walliams argued that such was the threat to his life from publication that the court itself would be breaching his human rights, were it to allow the story to go ahead.

This was, the court ultimately concluded, unheard of.

Under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the British state has a duty to take reasonable steps to try to protect life where they can do so and, importantly, where a particular body has an actual responsibility to do so.

There's no expectation that a state agency can save all lives in all circumstances - but it must show it has done its best if it is clear it had a responsibility to act.

The most obvious example of this law in practice is that the police must try to act on credible intelligence of a threat to life, even if the intended victim is a gangster.

But that duty, and how it should be applied in the real world, is also why Walliams lost: he was expecting the wrong public body to be doing the protecting.

The High Court's Mr Justice Nicklin said that the responsibility to try to protect the comedian and author's life was on clinicians and the hospital he had already been taken to. He had been detained for his own protection, meaning the state was already trying to meet its obligation to protect him from harm.

The court could not do that protecting because it had not taken responsibility for Walliams' psychiatric treatment or safety. Its role was to decide the legal dispute between Walliams and the news organisations.

Walliams' lawyers had suggested that there might be a right to private family life issue in the case but the judge said there had been no evidence to detail that, and he had to take into account the media's right to freedom of speech to publish what was described in court as a detailed investigation in the public interest.

If the media were wrong about their claims, Walliams could later sue for defamation - the way that any party seeks redress against journalists who have published a story that’s untrue and highly damaging to their reputation.

After Walliams lost last week, and the court's judgment underlines how seriously it considered the risks to him to be, Mr Justice Nicklin asked whether there were plans for an appeal.

But Walliams had not been able to give his lawyers instructions on how to proceed.

"There is a degree of urgency - the court has moved exceptionally quickly to accommodate this trial and produce this judgment," said Mr Justice Nicklin. "It is slightly concerning that there is not an ability to proceed today. I don't understand really. If I was satisfied that there were compelling reasons why permission to appeal should be granted I could say so now. "

Sara Mansoori KC, Walliams' counsel, said the case raised "novel issues of law based on unusual facts" but because of the vulnerable nature of her client - in hospital - she needed more time.

The judge gave Walliams until 16:30 GMT on Monday to come up with some proper grounds to challenge his decision. Those papers were never filed.

The failure to launch an appeal bid meant that ITN and the Guardian were free to publish.

While all this had been going on in court - there was a social media-sized elephant in the room. No end of people were posting 'It's David Walliams' and wondering why we bona fide journalists were not saying the same.

When the courts in the UK order that someone should remain anonymous, that order applies to all forms of publishing and broadcasting. It matters not whether the publication is in a newspaper or online - it is still publication. That is why bona fide journalists who understand the law did not wade in.

But there is a massive practical issue: how far does the writ of English law run in cyber space?

One judge I recently addressed over a reporting restriction issue described social media as a "wild west". That comment underlines the concern among legal professionals.

But the question is how to enforce injunctions in an age of rapid fire digital gossip?

If a newsroom were to breach an order, the nature of a large media organisation's audience means that publication would be seen by judges to be rather grave and the editor would likely be up in court.

One random user of X publishing the suspected identity of an anonymised person by passing on gossip is obviously less impactful. If Chad from Utah reposts Dorothy from Liverpool's gossip, the chances of being hauled before a judge are even more remote.

But what happens when thousands of people are all saying the same - and then their claims, perhaps based on a kernel of unreportable truth, are magnified by AI summaries and algorithms dripping content into phones?

At that point, mathematically speaking the impact is greater than one single newsroom breaching an injunction.

The public's perception of the Walliams case was complicated because his name became known from the start - but the furious gossip over who "PPT" really was shows there is an existential threat to how courts try to control information to prevent harm. And it's not clear whether they have any answer to it.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwx2.summary: David Walliams was named by the Guardian and ITN because he had no sound legal reason to prevent the news organisations' investigation from being published. The 55-year-old's bid for an injunction had been an open secret from the start.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqde.title: Police told Russell Brand to leave Jemima Goldsmith's house in 2014
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqde.text:
Police have confirmed they told Russell Brand to leave his ex-girlfriend Jemima Goldsmith's house in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident took place.

Thames Valley Police said officers were contacted by an alleged victim and went to an address in Oxfordshire on 25 July 2014 but no arrests were made.

They listened to her concerns and gave support, and "also ensured the victim's partner left the address, as per the victim's wishes", the police added in a statement on Wednesday.

Goldsmith, who dated Brand for about a year, wrote on X on Monday that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.

Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault on Monday.

In her post, 52-year-old Goldsmith said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".

She wrote: "I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse.

"I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident."

The Press Association reported that Goldsmith had asked for Brand to leave the property, her wish was then communicated to him by police, and he agreed to leave the house.

Goldsmith added: "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children.

"I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."

She also said she had "assisted the journalists who finally exposed him", and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" if they were sued.

TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn8.title: David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct after losing injunction bid
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn8.text:
ITV News and the Guardian have published reports alleging that David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including one who was aged 15.

The allegations were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation by the two news organisations, which was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.

Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault".

In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He said he "realised that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

Walliams shot to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, and also served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

The Guardian and ITV News say that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The allegations include:

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

After the investigation was published on Tuesday, Walliams's long-time literary agent Independent Talent Group confirmed it had dropped him.

A BBC spokesperson described the allegations as "serious" and the corporation has removed Little Britain from BBC iPlayer.

Sky also described the allegations as "extremely serious", saying it was dropping its upcoming adaptation of Walliams's fantasy feature Fing! and had "already removed content which features him from our platforms".

The Metropolitan Police said it has contacted the Guardian and ITV News to "to ensure that any potential victims" are "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".

One of the women who alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager told BBC Newsnight she was "angry" at his behaviour.

Lilly Creightmore - who Walliams contacted when she was 18 - waived her right to anonymity.

Creightmore told Newsnight that a month after they first met, Walliams told her she "could move in with him and basically that I could be his flatmate".

She said that after she arrived to stay at his house she "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him".

"In the evenings, he would sort of come and sit with me and stroke my leg, and one night I think he put his head in my lap and sort of be like, 'are you sure you don't want to come and sleep in my bed with me?' I had an inner strength like, 'no I'm not attracted to you in that way'... I felt I was being manipulated," she added.

She told Newsnight: "I am angry, I'm suppressing it well, but just that this culture of older men in positions of power needs to go, needs to stop. They're abusing their positions, using young people and abusing young people, and people of any age of course. There were too many men in power still, that are doing this and they need to go."

Walliams's lawyers told the ITV News and Guardian investigation that he denied grooming Creightmore or acting inappropriately. They added he did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".

Walliams said he believed his friendship with Lilly was a "special one" and felt "devastated" by her account. He denied the offers of help or gifts were attempts to groom, manipulate or coerce her into sleeping with him.

Two women, given pseudonyms of Alex and Jade in the investigation, have alleged that they first had contact with Walliams when they were 15 years old.

Alex alleged that she met Walliams in 2004 at a fan event when she was 15. She claimed that she and Walliams stayed in touch over the next two years and they had consensual sex for the first time when she was 17, the report alleged.

Contains sexual content.

Asked how she feels about Walliams now, she told the investigation: "I think I was groomed. 100%."

Walliams told the publications he believed she was 18 at the time they had sex. The investigation said Alex had joked to Walliams in an email she was "old enough to go drinking", but was actually 17.

Walliams denied grooming Alex. He said he is "mortified to learn" that their "brief, consensual relationship has caused her sadness".

Jade also alleged she met Walliams when she was 15, in August 2007, in a Soho cafe.

Later, at his home, she alleged, he kissed her, lifted up her T-shirt, went on to commit an act that she now characterises as a sexual assault, and tried to put her hand down his trousers. She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

She said she considers what she says happened to her to have been "grooming", adding: "It's completely wrong in every way."

Walliams strongly denied that he had any sexual contact with Jade. He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and says he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

Another woman, named as Ella, says she was 19 and working as a model when she rejected Walliams when he tried to kiss her during a tour of his home.

She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

Walliams said he made a "clumsy pass" at Ella, and he made no further approaches. He said he had no intention of intimidating Ella, or making her feel uncomfortable.

Other women claimed they were invited to Walliams's dressing room at Britain's Got Talent, or contacted by him after attending a taping.

Syco Entertainment, the company that created Britain's Got Talent, said it had had "no knowledge of the allegations described and was not made aware of them at the time".

The show's production company, Fremantle UK, said "no complaint has ever been made" against Walliams and encouraged anyone who "feels they have been the subject of any impropriety or wrongdoing by anyone... to come forward".

Women who worked for publisher HarperCollins also allege Walliams behaved inappropriately towards younger female employees.

One intern at the company told colleagues she had had a consensual sexual relationship with Walliams, but felt it was an "abuse of power".

After conducting an internal investigation, HarperCollins announced it was dropping Walliams as an author. Earlier this year, it also said it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.

In a statement responding to ITV News and the Guardian's investigation, the company said it takes employee wellbeing "extremely seriously".

Walliams denies that he sexually harassed anyone at HarperCollins or behaved inappropriately in the workplace.

Walliams, 55, previously brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN), which makes ITV News, and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of the Guardian, to try and prevent the claims being published.

The two news organisations had argued that they believed it was in the public interest to publish the allegations.

Walliams denied the claims and his lawyers said any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself, after two previous suicide attempts, and that the court should prevent any publication or broadcast.

Last week, a High Court judge rejected the injunction request and Walliams did not lodge an appeal, clearing the way for him to be named.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn8.summary: David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. One woman, who was 15, says she was "angry" at his behaviour. WalliamS says he made a "clumsy pass" at Ella and made no further passes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw07.title: 'Baffling but brilliant' post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything wins Booker Prize
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw07.text:
Author M John Harrison has become the oldest ever winner of the Booker Prize, picking up the prestigious literary award for his post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything.

Harrison, 81, who has built a cult following over his 60-year career, was named the winner of the £50,000 prize at a ceremony in London on Monday.

The End of Everything is set in the years after a mysterious catastrophe that caused British society as we know it to collapse. It has divided opinion among readers, and was described as "bleak but brilliant" and "dreamlike and baffling" by one critic.

Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the Booker judges, said: "It's a challenging read, but some of the best fiction is challenging."

Dame Mary added: "It's a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism."

Harrison began writing in the 1960s and has published 13 novels, five short story collections and an "anti-memoir". He has now surpassed Margaret Atwood as the oldest ever Booker winner.

While he dislikes labels like science fiction and fantasy, he has been called "the titan of literary science fiction", and Booker Prize chief executive Gaby Wood said he is "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world".

"He is a genuinely original thinker, a genre-defying writer who takes ideas seriously," Wood said.

"Though very unsettling, The End of Everything is not in fact a strange book. It's a realist book about a strange world, populated by desperate, unmoored characters."

The story follows a man and his aunt who must muddle through on the south-east English coast in the aftermath of an unexplained disaster and the arrival of mysterious alien beings.

The author has said he deliberately omitted as much explanation about the background to the events as possible, in order to make readers feel the same disorientation as the characters.

He has said: "The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It's a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend."

He added: "I've passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien."

That approach has led to a mixed reaction. The Guardian praised the book but said "it won't be for everyone", while the New York Times said: "The more we learn about the conditions of this novel's broken world, the harder it is to grasp."

The Literary Review described it as "a work of uncanny beauty, tender and terrifying in equal parts", while the Telegraph said "you feel you're not so much reading as dreaming".

Another Telegraph critic wrote that it was "ultimately, in both skill and humour, a cut above" the other shortlisted books.

"And in an age when AI overlords keep threatening to kill us, and the Government has told us to stockpile tinned food and bottled water, it is, for once, a novel that you can genuinely call 'timely'."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday, Harrison explained how he had "wanted to write a book which really satirised the present-day barrage of information that we all suffer, without the necessary tools to understand what we're hearing and to analyse it and to have critical thinking about it".

He continued: "So the whole idea was to build a disaster in which it was a disaster of explanation, a disaster of the failure to understand the world as it was now."

The Booker Prize is an annual award for the best novel written in the English language and published in the year up to 30 September. It was launched in 1969.

When the shortlist was announced in September, Dame Mary said agreeing on the final six had been, "to put it mildly, hard work".

Another judge, US novelist Patricia Lockwood, said she had been "tossing books across the room" during judging sessions, while poet Raymond Antrobus described the selection as "a tussle".

The other judges were Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, and journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu.

Speaking about the final judging session, Dame Mary told reporters on Monday: "There was a lot of discussion, disagreement and debate. But nobody stomped off."

In a statement, she said the panel "spent a whole day debating the six remarkable novels on this year's shortlist" before reaching a unanimous decision to name Harrison the winner.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvwy.title: Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvwy.text:
The Metropolitan Police have said several people contacted them during the trial and following the conviction and sentencing of the disgraced comedian Russell Brand, "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".

A Met spokesperson said: "Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing enquiries."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Det Supt Andy Furphy, who led the Brand investigation, said officers were "looking at exactly what we've got" and "whether they're information that points to behaviour or whether they could constitute a criminal offence".

Brand is already being investigated over rape allegations from two more women. He has been interviewed under caution in connection to those allegations.

On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described him as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".

The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault. The latter sentences are to run concurrently.

He was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

The head of the Metropolitan Police, Sir Mark Rowley, said on Friday that he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about him.

Asked by BBC Breakfast how the women in the case who gave evidence in the trial were coping, Furphy said: "Some have found it deeply distressing because of the amount of media attention wrapped around it.

"Even Russell Brand himself before and during trial was putting material online, but we continue to support them."

He noted how the conviction "could not have been achieved" without their "bravery, their courage, their resilience throughout the whole criminal justice process".

He continued: "It's deeply personal and quite harrowing to be a victim of rape and sexual assault, and to have to tell anybody about it, let alone police officers.

"But I'm glad they did. I'm glad they put their trust in us."

MP Dame Caroline Dinenage has re-iterated her concerns about Brand being able to post videos online in the build-up to and during his trial to his millions of followers.

"This does continue to be an issue that he has made money throughout the process on his social media platform," she told the same BBC TV programme.

"It just felt very odd that during the height of when there was a police investigation and some really serious allegations in the paper, that he was able to go online to his two and a half million followers, denying everything and putting his side of the story forward.

"That was an opportunity that his victims didn't have."

In September 2023, after the Sunday Times and Channel 4 Dispatches allegations were made against Brand, Culture, Media and Sport (CMS) Committee chair Dame Caroline wrote to social media companies Rumble, X, TikTok and Meta.

She asked if they would follow YouTube in cutting off Brand's income on their platforms. Rumble publicly refused, and X said it does not take action against accounts that have not broken its rules or the law. TikTok said he had never been monetised there.

"We know that he had used his following [online] to try and cow people into silence," added Dame Caroline.

"And the fact that they [the women] were able to come forward and tell their story and tell their truth and secure this conviction because of it is unbelievably impressive."

He was found guilty of rape and sexual assault charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.title: Cerys Matthews pays tribute to her family as she receives OBE
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.text:
Singer and presenter Cerys Matthews paid tribute to her family as she received an OBE.

Matthews, from Cardiff, was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) for services to music and received a medal from the Prince of Wales.

The 57-year-old hosts a BBC Radio 6 Music show every Sunday and was a founding member of Welsh rock band Catatonia who shot to fame during the "Cool Cymru" movement of the 1990s.

Speaking after the ceremony, Matthews said she accepted the OBE in memory of her family and "in gratitude of the freedoms I have as a female in this era".

Matthews' voice is also familiar to many over the Christmas holidays because of her 1999 rendition of Baby It's Cold Outside, sung with Sir Tom Jones.

After the ceremony she said Prince William discussed Catatonia with her, adding he "evidently" was a fan.

Matthews wore Black Watch tartan - Scotland's royal regimental tartan - to the ceremony in memory of her grandfather Oswald, who served in World War Two and took part in the D-Day landings on the beaches of Normandy in 1944.

She said her grandmother, Olive, did not have the freedom to pursue music because of economic and societal barriers as a young, working-class wartime bride.

"I'm here in their memory," she said.

"I grew up in the 80s and 90s as a female who loved music, and I've been allowed, and I've thrived, in the music industry.

"Sharing other people's music and making my own, and I accept this honour in their memory, and in gratitude of the freedoms I have as a female in this era.

"This positive change... I hope it continues across the world."

Meanwhile, techno DJ Carl Cox received an OBE for services to music after being a major figure in the British dance music scene for more than four decades.

The Manchester-born artist said: "By next year, I would have been putting needle on the record for 50 years, so it's quite a thing to be able to still keep doing something, even at my time of my life as a 64-year-old man."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.summary: Cerys Matthews received an OBE for services to music and received a medal from the Prince of Wales. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.title: Jemima Goldsmith accuses Russell Brand of violence and abuse against her
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.text:
Jemima Goldsmith, the ex-girlfriend of Russell Brand, has accused him of "violence, coercive control and abuse" while the two were together.

Goldsmith, who dated the disgraced entertainer for roughly a year around 2014, alleged that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.

In a lengthy statement on social media, the 52-year-old said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".

Brand, 51, was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison earlier on Monday after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

He was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

The judge at the sentencing hearing told Brand that he harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".

TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

The mother-of-two said she had chosen not to pursue legal recourse against Brand over the alleged violent incident in 2014 as she was "worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children".

She wrote on X on Monday evening: "Whilst my pain in relation to this pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."

Goldsmith said she had not seen nor spoken to Brand since 2014, but claimed to have assisted the journalists who exposed the allegations against him and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" were they sued.

In her statement, she also addressed reports of an injunction taken out by her and Brand in October 2015 that banned a woman, Szilvia Berki, from harassing them including by making allegations of assault by Brand at Goldsmith's home the prior year.

Goldsmith said on Monday that Berki had visited her house for roughly 30 minutes on 7 June 2014 to give Brand a massage, which she said did not end up taking place once she arrived.

Goldsmith said that Berki later told police that Brand had pushed her in the back while she had been leaving and that she had been attacked by Goldsmith's dog. Brand's ex-girlfriend said she "did not see anything untoward" during the encounter.

She added that, after providing a statement and CCTV footage, police concluded that there was no case to answer.

Goldsmith accused Berki of then sending a series of "vicious antisemitic and threatening" messages and posting "wild and untrue allegations" about her on social media.

She said she then agreed to a suggestion from Brand's lawyer to seek an injunction to prevent harassment. She claimed on Monday that recent media reporting of the injunction had opened her up "to vile hatred and abuse online".

Sunday Times chief news correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023, has told the BBC that Goldsmith helped her "a lot".

"I have seen the abuse she's been getting online and I did try to tell people that part of the story was much more complicated than they realise," Urwin said.

"I wish people would remember women that come forward are brave people and that is what she has done tonight – she has spoken out with immense bravery about how Russell Brand treated her," she added.

Brand's sentencing hearing heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.

One of them said she was "upset and traumatised" for years after the incident, adding: "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."

The woman he was found guilty of raping said the trauma was something she had to "carry every day".

A van believed to be carrying Brand was seen arriving at HMP Wandsworth in London on Monday after the sentencing hearing.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case, that would be seven years.

Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag.

The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009 following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court.

He was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6d7.title: David Walliams' career and controversies including Britain's Got Talent and Little Britain
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6d7.text:
David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.

A three-year investigation by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women for sexual purposes.

He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.

Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain, his comedy sketch show with Matt Lucas broadcast on the BBC.

Walliams published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008, and his stories soon became best-sellers and led to comparisons with Roald Dahl.

His 23 children's books have sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, but he was dropped by publisher HarperCollins in 2025 after allegations of inappropriate behaviour, which he denied.

In 2012, Walliams became a judge on Britain's Got Talent, and was voted best TV judge at the National TV Awards (NTAs) four times. He was replaced as a judge in 2022.

Before entering showbusiness, Walliams was born David Williams but changed his surname's spelling to avoid having the same name as another member of entertainment union Equity.

He was married to Dutch model Lara Stone from 2010 to 2015 and they have a son.

That hasn't stopped speculation about Walliams' sexuality. He has described himself as "bi-curious" and called his 2012 autobiography Camp David – but said he isn't attracted to men in the way he is to women.

Walliams and Lucas won a string of awards for Little Britain including three Baftas and two International Emmys, and the programme was watched by 10 million people in the UK.

But in the two decades since it ended, views about the show and what is and is not acceptable to joke about have radically altered. The programme has been criticised for its use of blackface and for stereotyping and mocking characters from minority and marginalised groups.

In the wake of the Black Lives Matter movement in 2020, Little Britain was removed from streaming services including BBC iPlayer, Netflix and BritBox.

Another of the duo's shows, 2010 airport comedy Come Fly With Me, was also removed from BritBox a decade after its original broadcast, due to the show's use of racial stereotypes and using make-up to portray people from other ethnic groups.

Little Britain was restored to iPlayer in 2022 with several scenes cut out. Walliams and Lucas said they had re-edited the show to "better reflect the changes in the cultural landscape since the show was made".

Not all the criticisms of Walliams have involved new standards being applied to older work.

Walliams had to apologise after two charity performances, during which he yanked down not only the trousers but also the underwear of actor Jeremy Edwards and music producer Mark Ronson.

In 2020, he was booed while hosting the NTAs after making a joke about Caroline Flack being out of work, at a time when she had stepped down from hosting Love Island and was waiting to appear in court, having been charged for actual bodily harm following a row with her boyfriend.

Later in 2022, he was replaced as a judge on Britain's Got Talent after a Guardian story about a leaked recording of Walliams making insulting remarks about contestants during breaks from filming.

In the incident, which happened in 2020, he spoke about a pensioner to whom he had taken a strong dislike and a woman who he described as "the slightly boring girl you would meet in the pub" who "you would want to have sex with, but then decide not to". He used much stronger language when talking about both.

Walliams apologised, explaining: "These were private conversations and - like most conversations with friends - were never intended to be shared. Nevertheless, I am sorry."

He sued the show's producers Freemantle for misuse of his private information and breaching data protection laws. An "amicable resolution" was reached, with the production company apologising for the recording being made public.

Further controversy came in June 2025, when it emerged that Walliams had given two Nazi salutes during the recording of BBC One's Would I Lie to You? Christmas special.

Banijay UK, which owned the show's production company Zeppotron, apologised, adding: "It was immediately acknowledged during the recording that this segment would not be broadcast under any circumstances." Walliams has never commented on the incident.

Then in December 2025, HarperCollins, the publisher of his hugely successful children's books, announced that following a change of CEO, the company would no longer look after new releases by Walliams.

He was dropped over allegations he had harassed female members of staff, with HarperCollins explaining that the company took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns".

The Daily Telegraph reported that an internal investigation had been opened the previous year after a complaint was made by a junior member of staff about his behaviour. This reportedly found that staff had been told to only meet Walliams in pairs and advised against going to his house.

Walliams' spokesperson responded by saying he "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately" and that he had "never been informed of any allegations raised against him" by the publisher.

Then in September 2026, HarperCollins doubled down by announcing that they were cutting all ties with Walliams and would no longer represent his back catalogue, meaning that when his books sold out in shops, they would not be replaced.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6d7.summary: David Walliams accused of grooming young fans and harassing women. He has denied all of the allegations but acknowledged he behaved thoughtlessly towards other people. The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw0k.title: Students passing university assessments in minutes using AI, regulator warns
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw0k.text:
Too many university students can use AI to complete assessments without staff finding out, the higher education regulator in England has said.

The Office for Students (OfS) said "a significant proportion" of assessments are unsupervised and many can be completed to a high standard with AI, sometimes in minutes.

It said this posed a "significant risk" to their credibility, and closed-book and practical exams were the most effective forms of assessments.

Universities UK said many institutions had "made substantial changes" to make assessments "AI-proof".

Universities that do not meet OfS quality standards could soon be banned from charging increased tuition fees or have caps imposed on their student numbers, under proposals that are now being consulted on.

The new research from the OfS and Advance HE, a charity that gives awards for teaching excellence, is based on the views of 244 higher education staff and 91 students from at least 127 universities.

It said "a significant proportion of assessments" were in "unsupervised, non-controlled formats where AI can be accessed by students completing them".

"Many of these can be completed to a high standard using AI tools with limited engagement from students," it added.

It also concluded it was "frequently possible" for students to use AI "in ways that cannot be reliably detected".

Unsupervised assessment can include coursework, but also remote online exams. They were rolled out widely during Covid, and research from Swansea University last year suggests 93 universities in the UK still use them in some form.

Josh Fleming, director of strategy and delivery at the OfS, said there were "fantastic" examples of universities seizing opportunities presented by AI, but there should be "far greater use of AI-free assessment".

"It also presents a generational risk to the system as it stands, threatening to undermine students' learning and institutions' ability to assess them," he said.

Kathryn Harrison-Graves, deputy chief executive at Advance HE, said students wanted "greater clarity about what is expected of them" but staff had "varying levels of confidence and support".

The OfS said it had heard of cases where students were completing entire assessments within minutes using AI and receiving similar grades to those who had not.

Some staff, meanwhile, were receiving lots of assignments that looked the same, and did not think their institution's assessments were "fit for purpose".

Other staff described a "polarised atmosphere" between students who used AI and other "conscientious objectors" who avoided it on environmental and other grounds.

The research said AI literacy for students was important during and after university, and some institutions were clearly communicating to students where AI can and cannot be used in assessments.

But it said there was "an urgent need" to ensure that remote or "non-secure" assessments "maintain their validity despite the availability of AI tools, meaning they effectively assess the knowledge and skills they are designed to measure".

"If it becomes possible to complete an assessment using AI without the knowledge and skills being tested, the assessment should be replaced," it added.

Universities UK, which represents more than 140 institutions, said universities were "making significant progress" adapting to AI.

"There is further to go but many have made substantial changes to how they assess students. This includes more in-person exams, presentations, vivas, process-based assessment and assessments that integrate AI in a controlled way," a spokesperson said.

"Different subjects will require different approaches, and universities should have the flexibility to adopt assessment methods that best support learning outcomes."

Lewis Wilson, from the National Union of Students, said AI was threatening "traditional" ways of learning that students and staff "have long said is not fit for purpose" - including essay questions, handouts and slideshows.

"It's time to get rid of the outdated methods, that have been kept around in the name of tradition, and instead encourage the innovative practice we see across the sector, co-designed with students based on what they want from higher education," he said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw0k.summary: Office for Students says many assessments are unsupervised and many can be completed using AI. It says this poses a "significant risk" to students' credibility and credibility. Universities UK says many institutions have made changes to how they assess students.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr86.title: Schools across Scotland targeted by fresh hoax bomb threats
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr86.text:
Schools across Scotland have been targeted with a fresh wave of hoax bomb threats, less than a month after a previous alert.

The force said at least 470 schools had received the email but that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes and there was nothing to suggest a credible threat.

Specialist cyber crime officers are working to identify the source of the messages, which were sent to both primary and secondary schools.

Similar "bogus" emails were also sent to 300 schools in Northern Ireland.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We understand how distressing messages of this nature can be for pupils, parents, carers and school staff, and the concern they can understandably cause.

"Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails."

Most local authorities contacted by BBC Scotland said schools were operating as normal but some confirmed pupils had been evacuated.

More than 300 calls were made to police when a similar message was sent to schools around the country on 19 October.

In many areas, pupils were off due to half-term holidays.

On Wednesday the majority of schools in Dumfries and Galloway received the email and some were evacuated as a precaution.

A spokesperson for the local authority said: "Each school community/setting is unique and as such has its own way of supporting and reassuring learners and staff.

"We also know that local police have attended some school settings in a community capacity to assist and reassure."

In Edinburgh Queensferry High School was evacuated and pupils were sent home.

Highland Council confirmed a number of its schools "made the decision to activate their emergency protocols".

Local authorities in Glasgow, Edinburgh, East Lothian, Aberdeenshire and Orkney also confirmed their schools received the message.

In Northern Ireland, the Education Authority (EA) said the "message has similarities with a bogus threat sent last month" which was treated as a hoax by the (PSNI).

The Police Service of Northern Ireland said the email originated from outside the UK.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr86.summary: At least 470 schools in Scotland have received the email. Similar "bogus" emails were also sent to 300 schools in Northern Ireland. Police Scotland said the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq0m.title: Police treating threatening email sent to more than 300 schools as 'hoax'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq0m.text:
Police investigating threatening emails sent to schools across Northern Ireland are treating the matter as "a hoax".

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said more than "300 schools to date have reported to police receiving the same emailed message".

The Department of Education advised schools to remain open "unless otherwise advised by the PSNI".

Earlier the Education Authority (EA) said the "message has similarities with a bogus threat sent last month" which was treated as a hoax by the (PSNI).

"At this stage, we have not been made aware of any evidence of any credible threat to schools," it said.

The police said the email originated from outside the UK.

PSNI Assistant Chief Constable Anthony McNally said: "We take incidents of this nature very seriously and we understand the concern in the community, school communities and for students and parents.

"Our enquiries are ongoing, however, at this stage we consider risk to the public as low."

He added that the police "will continue to liaise with schools impacted".

It is understood some schools evacuated.

Victoria Primary School in Newtownards in County Down said the school was evacuated in the morning but reopened about an hour later after guidance from the department.

Some of their pupils had left but some remained.

In October, a number of schools closed after an email threatened that "an explosive device" was located within hundreds of schools in Northern Ireland.

Police Scotland said "threatening messages were sent to a number of schools in Scotland and across and the UK".

"These messages were immediately assessed and are being treated as hoaxes," it said.

On Wednesday, An Garda Síochána (Irish police) said it was "aware of a generic communication that has been sent to a number of educational establishments".

"An Garda Síochána assess this threat as not credible and is not advising any educational establishment to evacuate," it said.

In a social media post, Alliance assembly member Paula Bradshaw condemned the "reckless bomb threats sent to schools this morning".

"Such actions are unacceptable, causing fear and distress among pupils, parents and staff. Please remain calm and follow official guidance."

Sinn Féin MLA Pat Sheehan said the "latest reports of sinister threats made to schools this morning are despicable".

"It is completely unacceptable that school communities have once again been left facing this level of fear, uncertainty and disruption," he said.

The EA said that "schools are advised to be vigilant and report any suspicious activity to PSNI".

"We fully appreciate that any message of this nature is distressing and can assure schools, parents/carers and children and young people that we will provide a further update following engagement with police."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq0m.summary: Police Service of Northern Ireland said more than 300 schools to date have reported to police. The Department of Education advised schools to remain open "unless otherwise advised by the PSNI" In October, a number of schools closed after an email threatened that "an explosive device" was located within hundreds of schools in Northern Ireland.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: On Dakar’s Packed Beaches, Africa Welcomes Its First Youth Olympics
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Ruth Maclean and Ricci Shryock
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
The 2026 Youth Olympic Games are taking place in Senegal, where the beaches and streets are teeming with sports fans and fitness fanatics.

The 2026 Youth Olympic Games are taking place in Senegal, where the beaches and streets are teeming with sports fans and fitness fanatics.

Skateboarding in Ngor, a neighborhood of Dakar, Senegal’s coastal capital. Fitness and athletic prowess are all-important in Dakar.
Credit...

Visuals by Ricci Shryock

Ruth Maclean and Ricci Shryock reported from the beaches of Dakar, Senegal, where it seemed as though they were the only ones not exercising.

Teenage athletes from all over the world have descended on Senegal this month to compete in Africa’s first ever Olympic events, the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.

And in Dakar, Senegal’s sports-crazy capital on Africa’s westernmost tip, the locals are ready.

Fitness and athletic prowess have long been all-important here in Dakar. On any given day, ordinary young people put some of the world’s most toned muscles to work, wrestling, skateboarding, surfing and bike riding.

Women toting goggles and foam noodles make their way down alleyways to the sea to take part in mass early-morning water aerobics classes with energetic coaches.

Groups of men do synchronized calisthenics on the city’s public beaches, hopping backward in low frog jumps and coating themselves in fine sand after sets of push-ups.

Weight lifters lift homemade barbells formed by pouring concrete into buckets and sticking a piece of metal into it to dry.

And every evening, crowds gather up and down the city’s main coastal road — the Corniche — to run, lunge, jump and use the many outdoor gyms that have opened in the city in the past decade.

On a recent evening on Koussoum Beach, hulking men tied traditional loincloths around their waists and between their legs. Then they circled each other, pawing at each other’s hands like cats and pulling each other to the ground.

Beach wrestling is making its Olympics debut at the Games, delighting many in Senegal, where traditional wrestling is wildly popular. Traditional Senegalese wrestling has been practiced for centuries here, and in recent years has become extremely popular and lucrative for top-tier competitors.

Subscribe to The Times to read as many articles as you like.

Ruth Maclean is the West Africa bureau chief for The Times, covering 25 countries including Nigeria, Congo, the countries in the Sahel region as well as Central Africa.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.summary: The 2026 Youth Olympic Games are taking place in Senegal, where the beaches and streets are teeming with sports fans and fitness fanatics. Fitness and athletic prowess are all-important in Dakar, Senegal's sports-crazy capital.

Reporting from Lima, Peru

Strobe lights scanned a crowd of outstretched arms as a rock band took the stage, smoke billowing out and applause echoing through the coliseum. The pastor bounced out to the beat of a drum roll, a microphone curved around his face.

This Sunday’s sermon, Pastor Sergio Hornung announced, would be about “the territory still to conquer.”

“There are many places where they talk to you about God,” said Scarlet Reyes, 21, a former Catholic who started coming to this Pentecostal church, Agua Viva, two years ago. “But here, they teach you how to know God.”

Pope Leo arrives on Wednesday in Peru, where he served as a priest for two decades, rose to bishop and became a Peruvian citizen. He returns at a time when the church faces two major challenges in Latin America: growing secularization and competition from other Christian denominations.

While Catholicism remains the dominant religious force in the country and the region, evangelical churches have made enormous gains, with congregants saying these churches offer more direct relationships with God and a more expressive, modern style of worship.
