https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: Lebanon Faces Economic ‘Catastrophe’ After War and Years of Mismanagement
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Abdi Latif Dahir
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
War in the Middle East

Hezbollah’s conflict with Israel and the U.S.-Israel war with Iran have made systemic problems worse, causing the cost of living to soar and driving many Lebanese to despair.

Reporting from Douris and Beirut, Lebanon

For decades, Abdelnaser Ossman has grown grapes at his family’s expansive farm in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, tilling the soil through years of drought, war and economic turmoil.

But this year the pressures have become overwhelming. His costs have soared and profits have plunged since the war between Israel and Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group, began in March. Fuel and fertilizer prices have doubled and labor costs have quintupled, while the price his harvest fetches has dropped by half. Mr. Ossman, 55, has rented out part of his land to help make ends meet and is considering selling parts of his farm.

“This year has been a catastrophe,” he said. “This is the hardest year of them all.”

Lebanon is facing a deepening economic crisis caused by years of mismanagement and exacerbated by a conflict that has killed thousands, displaced hundreds of thousands more and left entire towns in ruins. The U.S.-Israel war with Iran that began in February has only added to the economic challenges.

The data is stark. The World Bank forecasts inflation as rising more than 17 percent in Lebanon this year, driven by supply disruptions, higher shipping costs and soaring fuel prices. It also predicts that the economy will contract by 6.4 percent.

For many Lebanese, economic survival is the overriding concern, as they struggle to afford basic necessities and fuel amid joblessness and low wages. The crisis threatens to derail the fragile progress made by Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, who took office last year with ambitions to overhaul the economy. The government faces mounting public anger, unions threatening to strike and growing demands for a lasting overhaul of financial policy.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: This Defense Makes Drones (and GPS) Think They’re in Peru
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Kim Barker and Oleksandra Mykolyshyn
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
GPS-linked devices have been insisting that Ukrainians are in Lima, the Peruvian capital. The culprit is a jamming system built to thwart Russian airstrikes.

By Kim Barker and Oleksandra Mykolyshyn

Reporting from somewhere in Ukraine. Or Peru.

The S.U.V. in front of us suddenly pulled over. The driver had been trying to lead us to antennas near Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, that scramble the signals of Russian drones and missiles, but his GPS had gone haywire.

“Apologies. Some technical issues,” texted Serhii, a spokesman for Cascade Systems, the Ukrainian defense company that made the system. He asked that only his first name be used, out of concern for his safety.

We should have known: The S.U.V.’s navigation system had decided that the vehicle was in Lima, Peru, 7,628 miles southwest of Kyiv.

This happens all the time to Ukrainians. When Cascade’s antennas are switched on to misdirect Russian bombardments, the GPS in phones and cars is often misdirected, too — to that particular South American city.

This was now happening to a few of the very guys behind the mapping chaos. They had been hoisted on their own antennas, so to speak.

The system, called Lima for obvious reasons, blasts out electromagnetic interference meant to strip the eyes and ears from Moscow’s missiles and drones, making them think they are somewhere else.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: A Museum’s ‘Wanted’ Poster Campaign Brings Looted Painting Back to France
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Ephrat Livni
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
The Orléans Fine Arts Museum is on a quest to recover hundreds of works stolen during World War II — and the director wants your help.

Olivia Voisin discusses her “cold cases” like a police detective, but she is actually chief of the Orléans Fine Arts Museum in France, searching for paintings missing since the Nazis occupied the city in 1940.

The museum launched a campaign this summer to track down nearly 400 works looted during World War II. It created “Wanted” posters with images of lost art, plastering them in and around the city of Orléans and flooding the internet. Now, the first case has been solved.

An amateur sleuth in France discovered one of the looted paintings last month in Switzerland, as it was set for sale. Now instead of being put up for auction, “The Drinker,” a 17th-century work by the Dutch artist Willem Cornelisz Duyster, will soon be returned to Orléans.

It will eventually be displayed at the museum in a gallery dedicated to the missing works — with the hope that some day it will be joined by other recovered paintings, Ms. Voisin said.

The museum’s campaign to reclaim its missing collection comes as France has taken steps to make it easier to repatriate artwork looted in war or during colonization.

“The auction house was very cordial,” Ms. Voisin said of the Swiss business that had advertised the Dutch work. It had labeled the painting as a preparatory study, unaware that it was the known to be missing final version.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Michael D. Shear
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
The 41-year-old man, who was not named, was in custody pending possible charges after a joint investigation with the F.B.I. and U.S. military intelligence.

Reporting from London

Britain’s counterterrorism police said on Tuesday that they had arrested a member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of spying on behalf of Russia after a joint investigation with the F.B.I. and U.S. military intelligence.

The 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester, England, about 100 miles west of London, and was in custody pending possible charges, officials said.

Officials did not name the man but said in a statement that he had been detained on suspicion of violating Section 1 and Section 3 of Britain’s National Security Act 2023. Those sections relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. The police did not offer any other details, including about what the man was suspected of having done.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: U.S. Received $12 Billion From Venezuela’s Oil, Report Shows
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Tyler Pager and Anatoly Kurmanaev
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
The workings of a U.S.-controlled bank account shed light on how Washington manages Venezuelan revenue after capturing the country’s president.

By Tyler Pager and Anatoly Kurmanaev

The U.S. government received more than $12 billion in revenue from Venezuela’s natural resource exports in the first nine months of this year, according to a confidential report by the global financial services firm KPMG.

The vast majority of the funds were distributed back to Venezuela soon after they were received, the report shows. It is unclear if the money stayed in the country or who the ultimate recipients were.

The report, provides the most detailed portrait so far of the financial control exerted by the United States government on Venezuela since U.S. forces toppled the country’s president in January. The report was reviewed by The New York Times and its contents have not been previously reported.

The Trump administration installed a pliant interim government and charged it with opening up Venezuela’s oil industry to American investment.

The report was written just days before the midterm elections and Democratic lawmakers had repeatedly vowed to bring more transparency and accountability to Washington’s policy toward Venezuela.

Now that Democrats have won control of Congress in the midterm elections, several aides to Democratic lawmakers said they would continue pressing the Trump administration to describe what it was doing to prevent corruption in Venezuela after taking control of the country’s finances.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Novaya Gazeta, Russia’s Bravest Newspaper, Closes
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Valerie Hopkins and Nanna Heitmann
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
For more than 30 years, the paper covered an increasingly repressive Russia. “The process of silencing us started many years ago,” one of its journalists said.

Photographs by Nanna Heitmann

Reporting from Moscow

Outside a five-story office building on Potapovsky Lane in Moscow, a group of journalists took down a metal plaque and installed a plastic one in its place: Novaya Gazeta Lived Here. White carnations, the flower that Russians associate with mourning, were placed on top of it.

Novaya Gazeta, Russia’s most daring independent newspaper for decades, closed its doors on Monday, the latest blow to Russians who value freedom of expression and human rights.

Its forced closure is emblematic of the Kremlin’s erasure of opinions, ideas and people that do not conform to its views. That process has been underway for years, but it has dramatically accelerated since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Novaya Gazeta’s journalists were packing up their offices when I visited on Monday. Its co-founder Dmitri A. Muratov, who shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for defending press freedom, was giving away personal items to colleagues and well-wishers.

He handed his emerald banker’s lamp to one of the paper’s last recruits, a video journalist. He kept for himself a fire evacuation floor plan, on which he asked staff members to sign their names where their offices had been.

In a memoir and interview, the Italian-born woman who married into the Nehru-Gandhi dynasty recalls political battles and the killings of family members.

Sonia Gandhi standing in front of the desk of her late husband and the former prime minister, Rajiv Gandhi, at their residence in New Delhi in November.
Credit...
Saumya Khandelwal for The New York Times

By Elisabeth Bumiller

Elisabeth Bumiller, the author of a book on the women of India, reported from New Delhi.

The astonishing story of Sonia Gandhi, the young woman from a middle-class Italian family who married into the Nehru-Gandhi dynasty, lived through unspeakable tragedy and nearly became prime minister of India, reached a crescendo in May 2004 in her heavily fortified home in New Delhi.

“It took place in this very room,” she said in an interview last week in her home office, once that of her late husband, Rajiv Gandhi.

His tricolor Congress Party shawl still hung over his desk chair in the corner, where it has been since his assassination in 1991, when he was campaigning to be prime minister a second time. On the wall was a photograph of Jawaharlal Nehru, Rajiv’s grandfather and India’s first prime minister, and another of Rajiv’s mother, Indira Gandhi, who was assassinated as prime minister less than seven years before her son.

On that day in 2004, party elders beseeched Sonia Gandhi, criticized by the opposition as a foreign-born interloper, to take her place as prime minister as the leader of the Congress Party, which had just won national elections. She initially said yes, horrifying her two children, Rahul and Priyanka, but recanted.

“My brother and I actually thought that she would get killed, too,” said Priyanka Gandhi, who sat next to her mother in the interview.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Raja Abdulrahim
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
War in the Middle East

Syrian reconnaissance teams have visited Saudi Arabia and Yemen ahead of a potential deployment, but a final decision has not been made, officials said.

Reporting from Damascus, Syria

Syria is weighing whether to send thousands of troops to Saudi Arabia and Yemen to support the kingdom in its war with the Iranian-backed Houthi militia, according to three Syrian military and Yemeni officials with direct knowledge of the government’s plans.

Military reconnaissance teams have visited Saudi Arabia and Yemen in recent weeks to scout positions and coordinate with their counterparts in both countries, according to the officials.

The Syrian government has not made a decision to deploy troops, the Syrian officials said. If it chooses to do so, they added, it would probably be as part of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a mutual-defense pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in August. The agreement includes a collective defense principle that considers an attack on any of its members as an attack on all. Syria’s foreign minister said last month that the country was considering joining.

The main objective of any deployment would be to protect Saudi borders from any ground incursions by the Houthis, the Syrian officials said. The potential deployment has been previously reported by other media, including Agence France-Presse, the news agency.  Any engagement, however, risks embroiling Syria in the kingdom’s widening conflict with the Houthis.

Last month Saudi military officers, soldiers and some 150 Syrian soldiers and commanders visited the Thamud district in northeastern Yemen, along the Saudi border, according to a Yemeni officer in the area.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Aaron Boxerman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
At least four people from one family died and thousands lost their shelters when a storm battered overcrowded tent camps. Israel says Gaza will not be rebuilt until Hamas disarms.

Reporting from Tel Aviv

Aid officials had warned for months that torrential rains in Gaza could turn deadly this winter.

On Sunday, they buried Ahmad Nabhan’s entire family — victims of what President Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza called a “foreseeable” disaster in the crowded enclave.

The United Nations and relief workers had repeatedly said that Gaza’s two million Palestinian residents needed more and better supplies for a winter that many would spend — for the fourth year running — in squalid, trash-ridden camps. Floods, mud and cold have proved deadly in years past.

On Sunday night, Mr. Nabhan, 36, stepped out to have coffee with friends in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza. Minutes later, the rains caused a sand embankment to collapse on his tent — burying his wife, Tahrir, 36; his son, Salah, 8; his daughter, Mariam, 5; and his niece Habiba, 4, inside, according to the Gaza authorities and relatives.

“We dug through the sand and rocks, and pulled out their bodies, one by one,” Mr. Nabhan said in a phone interview.

Thousands of other Palestinians lost their shelters and belongings in the weekend storm, according to the United Nations.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Steve Fisher and Jack Nicas
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
President Claudia Sheinbaum drew a firm line barring U.S. forces from operating on Mexican soil. But in a northern border state, one local partner quietly helped the agency build a foothold.

President Claudia Sheinbaum drew a firm line barring U.S. forces from operating on Mexican soil. But in a northern border state, one local partner quietly helped the agency build a foothold.

Mexican soldiers on patrol in Ciudad Juárez in Chihuahua State, Mexico, in August.
Credit...
Herika Martinez/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

By Steve Fisher and Jack Nicas

Reporting from Chihuahua City and Ciudad Juárez, Mexico

When the Central Intelligence Agency was looking to quietly expand its operations in Mexico last year, it found an especially useful partner.

Mexico had tight restrictions on how freely U.S. forces could operate in the country. The nation’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, had repeatedly said she didn’t want them taking part in operations on the ground in Mexico, asserting that it was a violation of her country’s sovereignty.

To the C.I.A., Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a prosecutor and former police commander in the border state of Chihuahua, offered a different kind of partnership.

He could pair C.I.A. officers with Mexican police units on counter-cartel operations — and he was in a bind that made him uniquely cooperative, Mexican and U.S. officials said.

Just months earlier, the United States had revoked Mr. Zuany’s visa because of his suspected ties to the very cartels the C.I.A. wanted to root out, according to a letter Mexican officials sent to the F.B.I. that was viewed by The New York Times.

And the C.I.A. wanted help going beyond the logistical support and intelligence sharing that Ms. Sheinbaum repeatedly said was the extent of the two countries’ security cooperation.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Kenyan Domestic Worker Sentenced to 100 Lashes in Saudi Arabia
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Abdi Latif Dahir and Vivian Nereim
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
The kingdom’s promised reforms don’t always match the realities of its justice system. Unmarried women, particularly foreign workers, face unique perils.

By Abdi Latif Dahir and Vivian Nereim

Abdi Latif Dahir reported from Beirut, Lebanon, and Vivian Nereim from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

A Saudi court has sentenced a domestic worker from Kenya to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.

The ruling, issued last month, shows the limits of a decade of social and legal reforms in a kingdom where women can be jailed and punished for “illegal pregnancy.” The sentence is a harsh turn in what has been a terrifying ordeal for a mother who has tried for more than a year to return to Kenya with her child but has been blocked at every turn.

The mother, Esther Wanja Muthoni, is one of thousands of East African domestic workers who were recruited to work as housekeepers and nannies in Saudi Arabia. A New York Times investigation last year showed how Ms. Muthoni and others wind up trapped in a bureaucratic maze if they become pregnant.

Ms. Muthoni and her 1-year-old son, Abudy, are victims of an exploitative industry that recruits African women to Saudi Arabia in a labor pipeline from which top Kenyan government officials profit. Hundreds of Kenyan women have been killed, and reports of rapes and beatings are common.

For women who become pregnant, giving birth brings added punishment. The children of unwed mothers are routinely deprived of birth certificates in Saudi Arabia. Kenya’s diplomats, who could issue birth certificates and help mothers and children get home, instead frequently ignore them, insult them and solicit bribes or sex.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: U.S. Forces in Europe Face Uncertainty as Pentagon Reviews Troop Levels
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Lara Jakes
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
A U.S. Army unit in Germany is not sure what’s next as the Pentagon considers a major drawdown of forces in Europe.

Reporting from Wiesbaden, Germany

When a specialized U.S. Army unit in Germany was told it might move to South Korea this fall, soldiers started packing their cutting-edge equipment. Months later, their boxed-up gear was still visible during a tour of the base, and the unit remains in the city of Wiesbaden, waiting.

The uncertainty comes as the Pentagon undertakes a six-month review of U.S. forces in Europe, weighing a potentially significant drawdown even as Russia wages war on NATO’s border.

The fate of the unit in Germany, which includes 1,000 people and is known as the Multi-Domain Command Europe, is a snapshot of the uncertainty that roughly 78,000 American troops stationed in Europe are facing before the results of the review are announced, which should take place by the end of the year.

A drawdown could cut into ports in Spain, air bases in England and Italy, and pockets of soldiers across Eastern Europe. Germany is particularly vulnerable, given that it hosts 37,000 U.S. troops — more than any other country in Europe.

Complicating the picture is the fact that President Trump has been using the military as a geopolitical tool, ordering the Pentagon to curtail military exercises with South Korea in part because it did not offer sufficient support for the Iran war. It remains unclear whether the Germany-based unit will in fact move to Asia, according to five U.S. officials and a former diplomat, all of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal Pentagon discussions. Three of the officials said the unit began packing last summer.

A Pentagon spokesman said the review was continuing and that officials were working through a “predeployment notification process” for the unit in Germany.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Canadian Authorities Kill 4 Bears Involved in Deadly Attack on Hikers
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Qasim Nauman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
Wildlife authorities said evidence, including animal DNA, conclusively linked a sow and her three cubs to the deaths of two women along a hiking trail in British Columbia.

Four grizzly bears were responsible for the attack that killed two women in British Columbia this month, the wildlife authorities in the Canadian province said on Tuesday.

The sow and her three cubs were captured over the weekend and forensic testing, including the examination of animal DNA, conclusively linked them to the attack, the provincial Conservation Officer Service said. The investigation found that the attack likely involved predatory behavior, and the bears were put down to protect public safety, the service added.

The remains of the two victims, who were identified by their family as Jennifer Balcarras and her daughter Selah Reed, were found along a hiking trail near Bella Coola, a small coastal community northwest of Vancouver. One of Ms. Balcarras’s brothers told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that she and her daughter were familiar with the trail and had been out for “a casual walk.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Pranav Baskar, Hamed Aleaziz, Salman Masood and Zach Montague
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
War in the Middle East

The Iranian immigrants in the plane were scheduled to be flown to Pakistan and then transferred to Iran, lawyers for the group said.

By Pranav BaskarHamed AleazizSalman Masood and Zach Montague

A U.S. deportation flight from Arizona carrying Iranians bound for Iran turned around midair and landed back in Arizona early Tuesday morning, according to a legal defense group and a flight-tracking monitor.

The Iranians on the flight were meant to be transferred to Iran from neighboring Pakistan, but the flight turned around after Pakistan abruptly declined to accept them, according to a relative of a detainee who said an Iranian official shared that information, and a U.S. official. Both of them spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential information.

By Tuesday afternoon, the Iranian immigrants were returned from the plane to the Arizona immigration detention facility, the relative said. He added that there were at least nine people in the group.

The Trump administration is planning at least two operations this month to deport immigrants to countries that it does not have diplomatic relations with — Afghanistan and Iran — using Pakistan as the point of transfer. The plans have raised questions among immigration rights groups and lawyers about Pakistan’s role in facilitating deportations to countries where many immigrants fear persecution if they are sent back.

When asked about the deportations to Afghanistan via Pakistan at a news conference on Friday, Sajjad Haider Khan, a spokesman for Pakistan’s foreign ministry, said the arrangement was “under consideration.” He added that Pakistan is hopeful that a “mutually agreeable way forward will be reached.”

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

According to court filings by the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, a group of Iranians who are detained at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Arizona were told by an Iranian government official over the weekend that they were going to be put on a flight to Pakistan with “onward transfer to Iran.” The legal defense fund has filed a lawsuit on behalf of Iranian detainees.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Katrin Bennhold
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
War in the Middle East

As top Trump aides clash over a strategy to end the war, the administration is weighing escalation, narrower strikes and diplomacy.

I’m the host of The World.

It didn’t take long after last week’s midterm losses for the Trump administration to begin publicly fighting over the war in Iran.

Divisions are now out in the open. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance declared. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, in contrast, posted a defiant video defending the war. He also had to defend himself from a now-shelved effort — led by a Republican congressman with Democratic support — to impeach him. (More on that below.)

We’re seeing a formidable U.S. military buildup in the Middle East — a third aircraft carrier is expected to arrive soon. Fighter jets, long-range bombers, warships and 50,000 troops are all on standby.

So what does this all mean for the war? Today, my colleagues David Sanger and Eric Schmitt outline four potential scenarios.

By David E. Sanger and Eric Schmitt

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/po.title: Rubio Says ‘Major Combat Operations’ in Iran War Are No Longer Needed
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/po.author: Michael Crowley
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/po.text:
The U.S. secretary of state said that American economic pressure is doing sufficient damage to the leadership in Tehran.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that the Trump administration’s economic pressure campaign against Iran was effective enough that “there’s really no need for major combat operations any longer.”

Mr. Rubio’s declaration was the most explicit signal yet that President Trump does not intend to escalate his conflict with Iran after last week’s U.S. midterm elections.

Speaking to reporters in Paris, Mr. Rubio added that the United States might still respond with force if Iran “crosses certain red lines,” which he did not specify.

A day earlier, Mr. Trump told reporters that the war against Iran “militarily is effectively over.” But while Mr. Trump often opines off the cuff, Mr. Rubio lent an official veneer to that position by saying he had informed his counterparts about it on Tuesday at a meeting of Group of 7 foreign ministers.

Israeli officials and Iran hawks in Washington have called for more bombings in the war against Iran, which began more than eight months ago. But Mr. Rubio said that further American strikes were no longer necessary because a combination of U.S. economic sanctions and an American naval blockade “are doing devastation” to Iran’s economy.

He would not say how much longer Iran might be able to endure the American pressure, or what outcome the United States was pursuing.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Jemima Goldsmith, Russell Brand’s Ex-Partner, Accuses Him of Abuse
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Karla Adam
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
Ms. Goldsmith, a British TV producer, accused Mr. Brand of “violence” and “coercive control” during their relationship. She made the allegations publicly for the first time after his sentencing for rape and sexual assault.

Reporting from London

Jemima Goldsmith, the British television producer, said on Monday that Russell Brand had been violent and abusive during their relationship more than a decade ago and that the police had removed him from her home during an episode in 2014.

Ms. Goldsmith, a well-known figure in Britain, made the statements in a social media post shortly after Mr. Brand was sentenced to 10 and a half years in prison for rape and sexual assault. It was the first time that she had made the allegations against Mr. Brand publicly.

Six women testified at Mr. Brand’s trial in London about episodes that they said occurred from 1999 to 2009, as he was gaining fame as a comedian and actor. The presiding judge in the trial said that the women’s testimony showed Mr. Brand’s “staggering arrogance” and his belief that “fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live.”

Ms. Goldsmith, 52, who is also known professionally as Jemima Khan, dated Mr. Brand for about a year before their relationship ended in 2014. She was previously married to Imran Khan, the former cricket star and prime minister of Pakistan.

“I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse,” Ms. Goldsmith said of Mr. Brand, without elaborating. She added that she chose not to press charges or go public after the 2014 altercation because she worried how it would affect her children.

“I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014,” she continued. “Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women who have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/th.author: Tim Balk
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/th.text:
Representative Thomas Massie, Republican of Kentucky, is retiring at the end of his term after losing to a primary challenger backed by President Trump.

Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican whose libertarian leanings and independent streak have made him a target of President Trump’s, has brought impeachment charges against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

It could be one of his last major acts in Congress: The 55-year-old Mr. Massie, a seven-term representative, is retiring at the end of his term after losing a primary to a challenger backed by the president.

Mr. Hegseth on Tuesday dismissed the impeachment drive as a vendetta by “one disgruntled and defeated congressman,” without naming Mr. Massie. Mr. Trump chimed in soon afterward, denigrating Mr. Massie in a social media post as “a TOTAL LOSER.”

Here’s what to know about Mr. Massie:

Mr. Massie lost by about 10 percentage points to Ed Gallrein, a farmer supported by Mr. Trump. After losing, he filed a statement of candidacy allowing him to raise money for a potential run for office in 2028, according to Federal Election Commission records.

Then he went on vacation in Costa Rica with former Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, another Trump antagonist from the Republican Party.

Mr. Massie has assailed the war since its first hours. He has accused the Trump administration of violating the Constitution by striking Iran without congressional approval and of breaking with Mr. Trump’s 2024 campaign platform.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Najib Razak, Ex-Prime Minister of Malaysia, Is Released to House Arrest
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Zunaira Saieed and Richard C. Paddock
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
Najib Razak, who was brought down in the multibillion-dollar 1MDB scandal, was released from prison to serve the rest of his sentence in his mansion.

By Zunaira Saieed and Richard C. Paddock

Zunaira Saieed reported from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and Richard C. Paddock from Bangkok.

Malaysia’s disgraced former prime minister, Najib Razak, whose role in the colossal theft of public funds earned him the nickname “Man of Steal,” was released from prison on Tuesday. He was let out under a royal pardon that allows him to serve the remainder of his six-year sentence at the mansion he calls home.

Mr. Najib, 73, who has spent the past four years in prison on corruption charges, was delivered on Tuesday night to his home in one of the most exclusive neighborhoods of the capital, Kuala Lumpur. The entire 49,000-square-foot property was officially declared a federal prison on Friday in preparation for his homecoming.

Voters ousted Mr. Najib, the son of one prime minister and the nephew of another, in 2018. He was later convicted of graft, after $4.5 billion disappeared from 1Malaysia Development Berhad, the state investment fund that he founded and oversaw. The scandal brought down his government, but subsequent royal pardons and his move to house arrest have raised accusations of special treatment for elites.

“It is an absolute mockery of justice,” Suresh Kumar, a property manager in Kuala Lumpur. “The law works for the rich and powerful and not for the poor.”

Mr. Najib arrived at his mansion about 9:30 p.m. in a silver Proton, a Malaysian-made SUV, accompanied by nine other cars and two motorcycles. Dozens of reporters who had gathered to witness his return were kept at bay by police officers who had blocked off the street near his house.

Mr. Najib is expected to remain under house arrest until August 2028. His legal problems, however, continue. He is due to begin serving a 15-year sentence on separate corruption charges related to the scandal when his current term ends. The High Court of Malaysia also ordered him to pay a staggering $2.8 billion fine. He is appealing that conviction.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Who Is David Walliams, the UK Entertainer Accused of Sexual Misconduct?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Leo Sands
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
The British entertainer rose to fame with the television show “Little Britain” and has published over 40 children’s books.

Reporting from London

The British entertainer David Walliams, who was publicly accused on Tuesday of a pattern of sexual misconduct, is a comedian and prolific author of children’s books who has been a fixture on Britain’s television screens for more than 20 years.

Mr. Walliams, 55, rose to fame as a sketch show comedian in the 2000s and later as a judge on “Britain’s Got Talent.” He is also one of the country’s most successful children’s book authors, publishing over 40 titles that have sold tens of millions of copies.

On Tuesday, two British news organizations, The Guardian and ITV News, published detailed allegations that Mr. Walliams had exploited his celebrity status to sexually prey on women, including some he had met when they were as young as 15. Mr. Walliams, who fought a weekslong court battle to keep the claims private, has denied the accusations. “I am not a sexual predator,” he wrote in a letter sent to news outlets.

Mr. Walliams burst onto the national stage in Britain in the early 2000s as a transgressive comedy writer and entertainer.

In his breakout BBC comedy sketch show “Little Britain,” which first aired in 2003, he and his comedy partner Matt Lucas played a series of eccentric characters who poked fun at almost every minority group imaginable, including mothers on welfare benefits, wheelchair users and gay men.

The show pushed the boundaries of acceptability, even during a period of provocative comedy television in Britain. Mr. Walliams and Mr. Lucas donned fat suits, caked themselves in makeup and wore blackface.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Alex Marshall and Megan Specia
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
The Guardian and ITV News published claims from multiple women against the comedian and writer, who fought a weekslong court battle to keep the claims private. He denies the accusations.

By Alex Marshall and Megan Specia

Reporting from London

David Walliams, a British TV personality and best-selling children’s author, was publicly accused on Tuesday of exploiting his celebrity status to prey on women and teenagers as young as 15 after a weekslong court battle to keep the accusations private.

The allegations emerged after a judge decided on Nov. 3 that The Guardian newspaper and ITV News, a British broadcaster, could publish the claims against Mr. Walliams.

Mr. Walliams denies the allegations. In a letter sent to news outlets, he said he accepted he had “behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with,” but he added: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law.”

The news organizations had been held back from publishing their joint investigation because of a temporary injunction, an English legal measure that a judge can impose to bar the identification of an individual. The secrecy had driven a swirl of online speculation in recent weeks about the identity of the unnamed celebrity.

Mr. Walliams is a household name in the United Kingdom who rose to fame in the 2000s as a star of “Little Britain,” a popular BBC sketch show that poked fun at British archetypes, and he later became best known for his children’s novels. In recent years, he has been dogged by accusations over his professional conduct, including reports that he had made derogatory and sexually explicit remarks about contestants during the recording of an episode of the television show “Britain’s Got Talent,” for which he was a judge.

The investigation that The Guardian and ITV News published on Tuesday, which the two organizations had worked on since April 2023, was based on accounts from 30 people who accused Mr. Walliams of abusing his power to sexually prey on women and targeting teenagers, some of whom met him when they were as young as 15.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Israeli Opposition Pushes for Oct. 7 Inquiry at First Session of New Parliament
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Isabel Kershner and Adam Rasgon
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
Dozens of first-time lawmakers were sworn into the Knesset, where the opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot, now has a majority.

By Isabel Kershner and Adam Rasgon

Reporting from Jerusalem

Israel’s largest opposition party moved quickly on Tuesday to submit a bill to Parliament that seeks to establish a state inquiry into the security failings that preceded the Hamas-led October 2023 attacks, which took place under the watch of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The party, Yashar, led by the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, made the move as lawmakers gathered for the first session of Israel’s Parliament since an inconclusive election last month.

An anti-Netanyahu bloc of parties from across Israel’s political spectrum now controls a majority of seats in the Parliament, known as the Knesset. Passage of the bill would be a rebuke to Mr. Netanyahu and his allies, who have long blocked efforts to establish such a commission, saying it would not uncover the truth.

Yashar also put forward bills on Tuesday aimed at repealing a number of the most contentious laws passed by the Netanyahu government, including some that were part of a yearslong effort to curb the powers of Israel’s judiciary.

Dozens of first-time lawmakers took their seats on Tuesday in the Knesset, where Israel’s president urged the parties to create a stable government.

“The people who chose you long for routine, security and tranquillity,” the president, Isaac Herzog, said at the swearing-in ceremony. “The people you represent here yearn to see an outstretched hand that will bring unity to the nation and hope.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Australia Unveils New A.I. Regulator After OpenAI Breach
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Laura Chung
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
The government is also considering changes to criminal law to penalize companies that develop models that “engage in harmful conduct.”

Reporting from Sydney, Australia

The Australian government will establish a new artificial intelligence safety watchdog that will enforce “significant penalties” for companies that fail to adhere to mandatory safeguards, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday.

The government also announced sweeping recommendations to prevent future breaches after OpenAI models went rogue and gained unauthorized access to government systems this year, including considering criminal law changes to penalize companies that develop “an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.”

The breach, which occurred in June but was not reported to Australian officials until three months later, raised doubts about whether laws in Australia, or elsewhere, are ready for the challenges posed by the fast-evolving technology.

“Our task is to make sure that we shape A.I. rather than A.I. shape us,” Mr. Albanese said on Tuesday.

“This incident was completely unacceptable,” he added. “And it can’t be allowed to happen again.”

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

The breach occurred on June 18 by agents operating under an OpenAI research team that was carrying out research into public medicine spending using an internal model, on a data portal for Australia’s public health insurance system, Medicare.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Why U.S. Business Deals Are Unlikely to Get Putin to Give Any Ground
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Paul Sonne
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia has shown a willingness to endure a high price to get what he wants in Ukraine, and he sees little reason to stop fighting now, analysts say.

Reporting from Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates

For a year and a half, as the United States engaged Russia in on-again, off-again peace talks, the Trump administration held off on cutting any business deals with Moscow, insisting that the Kremlin first take concrete steps toward ending the war in Ukraine.

That all changed this fall. President Trump brokered a deal to waive sanctions and import Russian diesel ahead of the midterm elections. U.S. officials held talks on a range of possible deals, including the sale of the international assets of the Russian energy giant Lukoil and the resumption of Russian gas exports to Europe.

U.S. officials argued that the frenzy of potential deal-making could build good will and help compel the Kremlin to stop fighting. But the inducements have done little to curb President Vladimir V. Putin’s central demands on the war, which include placing limits on Ukraine’s defenses and alliances and broadly reordering the security architecture in Europe.

Those demands are at the center of peace talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s envoys, are convening on Tuesday and Wednesday in the United Arab Emirates. The talks, the first since February involving all three countries, will address thorny topics like how to put in place an eventual cease-fire and whether a compromise can be reached on territory, U.S. officials said.

Top security advisers have flown in from European countries and NATO as momentum builds for Europe to become more directly involved in the peace process. The European officials will meet with the Americans and the Ukrainians, with a view toward fostering more direct discussions between European and Russian leaders in the future, the U.S. officials said.

But to pull Mr. Putin toward compromise, it is going to take a lot more than business deals, analysts say.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: As Fresh Air Becomes a Luxury, Many Indonesians Turn on Their Leader
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Muktita Suhartono
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
In Indonesia, support for President Prabowo Subianto has collapsed as his government has failed to contain raging wildfires, compounding quality-of-life woes.

Reporting from Jakarta, Indonesia

After more than four months of living under the shroud of wildfire haze in Indonesian Borneo and keeping his young sons indoors, Kurniawan rues voting for President Prabowo Subianto.

Far to the west, on the island of Sumatra, Rama has the same regret. He has developed chest pain and breathing difficulties due to the bad air.

Mr. Prabowo’s government has struggled to contain the wildfires — which are being fueled by El Niño and human activity like slash-and-burn farming — and are among the worst on record in Indonesia. And his administration has refused to declare them a national disaster, a label that would ease the entry of foreign aid.

“The situation has gotten so severe, yet, instead of empathy, the government is turning a blind eye to our suffering,” said Rama, who like other voters interviewed for this article asked to be identified only by part of his name to speak freely about the country’s leader.

The haze has spread hundreds of miles across national borders to Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, raising fears of a regional health crisis. And for millions of Indonesians, particularly in Borneo and Sumatra, it has compounded cost of living woes by making fresh air a luxury.

Francis never returned to his home country after becoming pope, but the new pontiff will still be confronted with the overwhelming presence of his predecessor.

A swimming pool named after Pope Francis in La Matanza, outside Buenos Aires.
Credit...

Visuals by Sarah Pabst

Reporting from Buenos Aires

When the Argentine priest was reminded that the Roman Catholic Church no longer had an Argentine pope, he let out an exasperated chuckle.

“We are already mourning Messi,” said the priest, the Rev. Lorenzo de Vedia, referring to Lionel Messi’s departure from the Argentine national soccer team. “Two is too much.”

Though Pope Francis, the first Argentine pope, died over a year ago and was succeeded by Pope Leo shortly after, Argentines have hardly moved on. Francis’ photo still adorns public schools, parishes and trade unions. Murals and mosaics of the Argentine pope dominate public spaces, street vendors still sell his figurines, parish priests quote him in their homilies.

With Leo visiting the country, Argentines are finally confronting the reality that the leader of the Catholic Church no longer speaks Porteño, the Buenos Aires dialect; roots for the city’s beloved San Lorenzo team; or shares their ritual of mate — the national drink.

As Argentines face this new reality, their reception is permeated with the pressing question of whether Leo represents an expression of Francis’ continuity. And while the answer is important to the former pope’s compatriots, it is a question much of the world has been asking.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.title: Turkey Promotes Itself as a Climate Champion. Not Everyone Agrees.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.author: Ben Hubbard
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world.text:
Critics say some of the country’s environmental policies run counter to the image it is offering as host of a United Nations climate summit.

Reporting from Antalya, Turkey

Turkey’s global ambitions are written all over the walls of the sprawling conference center in Antalya, the Mediterranean resort city where it is host to the United Nations climate summit that opened on Monday.

“Turkey, where dialogue becomes action,” read giant signs throughout the venue.

“The Future of the World is in Turkey!” read others.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has long sought to position Turkey as a rising economic and military power that can mediate conflicts and play a muscular role in international affairs. Welcoming the tens of thousands of officials, ecologists, activists and others attending the U.N. summit, known as COP31, gives the country an opportunity to extend its diplomatic efforts into the critical realm of climate diplomacy, experts said.

But Turkey’s efforts to portray itself as a climate champion run counter to some of its policies, critics said, and to its suppression of environmental activism. They say the country lacks a clear timeline for phasing out coal, continues to import large amounts of plastic waste from Europe and is heavy-handed in its treatment of residents who oppose mining projects.

The climate summit comes months after Turkey hosted its fellow members of the NATO military alliance in the Turkish capital, Ankara, where it showcased its value as a defense partner in an unstable region and the bonhomie between Mr. Erdogan and President Trump.

Now, Turkey seeks to cast itself as a key player in international climate talks, too.

“Turkey wants to show itself as a global power in many different places, including for peace, for climate, for trade,” said Umit Sahin, who heads the climate change program at Istanbul Policy Center, a research institute.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.title: Haaretz Expands US Presence Amid Israel’s Move to the Right
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.author: Marc Tracy
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.text:
Haaretz has more than doubled the size of its American bureau, including hiring correspondents to cover beats like national politics and young American Jews.

Haaretz has more than doubled the size of its American bureau, including hiring correspondents to cover beats like national politics and young American Jews.

Allison Kaplan Sommer, the host of Haaretz’s English-language podcast, said she saw the paper connecting liberal-leaning and secular American Jews with their Israeli counterparts.
Credit...
Avishag Shaar-Yashuv for The New York Times

Marc Tracy reported from Tel Aviv and New York.

The century-old newspaper Haaretz has long been favored by Israel’s more liberal readers, its journalism and commentary often casting a harsh light on right-wing leaders and government policies toward Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.

But its editorial outlook is increasingly out of step with a country that has moved rightward in recent decades — something seen as recently as in last month’s elections, in which a healthy majority of parliamentary seats went to center, right-of-center and Orthodox Jewish parties. At the same time, the digital edition of Haaretz’s English-language journalism has experienced growing popularity as an increasing number of Jews around the world, especially younger ones, view Israel more critically than in the past.

Now Haaretz is leaning in.

It has more than doubled the size of its small U.S. bureau, including hiring four correspondents to cover beats like national politics and a younger generation of American Jews, and is making more vertical videos and podcast episodes to reflect the country’s news consumption habits. In recent weeks, Haaretz’s reporters filed dispatches from Maine and Michigan, Texas and Florida, and Georgia and New York exploring the midterm races from Jewish perspectives.

And Haaretz is highlighting original English-language journalism that helps explain Israel to readers abroad. Its flagship English-language podcast, for instance, has grown its listenership by two-thirds this year with weekly election-themed episodes and overviews of Israel-based reporting, such as a recent interview with the authors of an investigation into a network of right-wing Israeli think tanks.

“We’re trying to think about ourselves not only as an Israeli newspaper, but also as a Jewish newspaper,” said Noa Landau, who was appointed this year to be global editor.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/mi.title: Michael McCloskey Has Died. He Helped Make the Sierra Club a Political Force.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/mi.author: Keith Schneider
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/mi.text:
As executive director of the group from 1969 to 1985, he aligned its disparate local chapters and offices into a powerful lobby in Washington. He was 92.

Michael McCloskey, the executive director and chairman of the Sierra Club during America’s environmental awakening in the late 20th century, died on Oct. 30 in Portland, Ore. He was 92.

The death, at an assisted living facility, was confirmed by his stepdaughter Rosemary Detweiler, who said the cause was congestive heart failure.

In a Sierra Club career that spanned 39 years, Mr. McCloskey was responsible for leading the transformation of a small and revered California conservation group into a national environmental organization that influenced the development, passage and enforcement of the trailblazing U.S. statutes that cleaned up the country’s air and water, and protected wilderness and wildlife.

A son of the Pacific Northwest whose reverence for snow-peaked mountains, rushing rivers and trackless forest matched that of John Muir, the Sierra Club’s founder, Mr. McCloskey organized campaigns and drafted legislation that still safeguard some of the country’s most spectacular wild places: Redwood National and State Parks, North Cascades National Park, 104 million acres of wilderness in Alaska and more than 6,000 miles of free-flowing wild and scenic rivers.

Sierra Club colleagues concurred with Mr. McCloskey’s own assessment that he excelled at aligning the group’s disparate local chapters and offices into a powerful lobby in Washington, while simultaneously leading programs to increase the club’s membership, staff and budget.

As executive director from 1969 to 1985, Mr. McCloskey helped to recruit more than 300,000 new members, opened dozens of local chapters and increased the group’s annual budget to $23 million from $3 million. The Sierra Club’s staff grew to 300 from 30 during the same period.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.text:
War in the Middle East

People who use heating oil will see increases of around 70 percent because the war in Iran has greatly reduced supply of that fuel.

Home heating costs are expected to rise more than 7 percent on average across the country this winter, putting further strain on households that have been struggling with rising energy costs for many months.

A new report by the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, an organization that represents state officials in seeking federal funding, warned that the disruptions caused by the war with Iran has contributed to high heating costs.

The organization said households that rely on heating oil, most of which are in the Northeast and Alaska, face some of the biggest increases. The typical household that uses oil — almost five million nationwide — could pay as much as 70 percent more than last winter or about $2,977 for the season.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.title: Hospitals Brace for Medicaid Work Rules and Deep Funding Cuts
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.author: Christopher Rowland
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.text:
Health systems are racing to guide millions of patients through new eligibility hoops, slated to go into effect Jan. 1.

By Christopher Rowland

Hospitals across the country are mobilizing an expansive outreach effort in an attempt to ensure that roughly 19 million patients do not lose their insurance coverage under new Medicaid work rules that begin in January.

Saying the requirements are generating widespread anxiety and confusion, health care executives are using a variety of methods to help guide the Americans who will be affected. They are deploying staff and volunteers to contact patients with text messages, phone calls and offers of help.

The rules dictate that able-bodied adults without young children either work, volunteer or attend school or job training for at least 80 hours a month. Republicans included the rules last year as part of President Trump’s package of tax cuts and reductions in safety net spending, including nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts.

Hospitals and other health centers are detailing what evidence people in many cases must provide — pay stubs or other proof of work or school attendance — to maintain coverage.

“There’s going to be people who fall through the cracks,” said Nicole Harper, chief financial officer at Eskenazi Health, a safety-net hospital in Indianapolis. “We’re bracing for impact.”

Because hospitals are heavily reliant on Medicaid funding, keeping a stable patient population is critical for them to maintain government reimbursements.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.title: Toyota Plans to Sell a Kei Pickup Truck in the U.S.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.author: Aruni Soni
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.text:
The automaker plans to sell Americans “Kei” pickup trucks, which are very popular in Japan and with U.S. auto enthusiasts. Even President Trump is a fan.

Imagine a pickup truck, but much smaller, lighter and lacking any frills. It’s a vehicle that people in Japan have been using for decades. And now Toyota wants to sell one in the United States.

This week, the automaker introduced a tiny pickup truck inspired by Japanese “Kei” trucks, under the Scion brand that Toyota shuttered in 2016. The vehicle, the Scion KEI-01, will go on sale next year.

Kei vehicles (pronounced like the letter “K”) are a distinct category of small cars, vans and trucks in Japan and other Asian countries. These vehicles have long had a cult following in the United States. Even President Trump showed adoration, calling them “really cute” and “sort of like the Beetle used to be.” He made the remarks last year after a visit to Japan and mused about finding a way to have them sold in the United States.

But buying and using one of these vehicles in the United States is not easy. Car buffs who want Kei cars and trucks typically import vehicles that are at least 25 years old from Japan to take advantage of a provision in U.S. law that exempts older vehicles from federal safety and emissions standards.

Toyota says the KEI-01 will be assembled in Indiana and will qualify as a “low speed vehicle” under federal regulations. Vehicles in that category must have a top speed of 25 miles an hour and are generally forbidden from roads with speed limits of more than 35 m.p.h. Such vehicles also do not have to meet the same safety and other standards as regular cars.

The KEI-01 is in many ways the opposite of traditional U.S. pickup trucks like the Ford F-150 or Chevrolet Silverado, which over the past several decades have become bigger, heavier and more expensive. Most automakers have found that it is much easier to make a profit on larger vehicles because they tend not to cost much more to make than smaller ones but can be sold for a lot more money.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/clima.title: From Climate Activism to the House of Representatives
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/clima.author: Claire Brown
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/clima.text:
William Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, flipped a seat in Michigan for the Democrats.

Last week William Lawrence, a Democrat, won a seat in the House of Representatives, flipping his Michigan district.

Lawrence is a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, a youth-led climate activist group. But his campaign focused more on affordability and data centers than climate issues.

I spoke with him on Monday afternoon to talk about what might be possible in the new Congress, about how Democrats have avoided talk of climate change, and how his history as a climate activist might inform his work as a legislator.

Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

Congress is working on a bipartisan permitting bill that will make it easier to build energy projects. What are your thoughts?

I hope that Congress doesn’t pass the bill in this lame-duck session. I think it would be a terrible mistake after an election that was about corruption to pass this bill, which further empowers the wealthiest corporations in the country to run roughshod over local communities to build community-polluting projects. We simply must do better. I understand that there are good provisions in this bill, but this is not the way.

The data centers issue is poisoning the entire conversation around the energy transition in my district. People see transmission lines feeding power to data centers, and if we don’t deal with the data centers, then there will continue to be extreme backlash against clean energy as well as transmission. And that’s what I’m seeing in my district.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/techn.title: Who Is Alice Huang, the Woman in the Middle of Nvidia’s Spy Scandal?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/techn.author: Paul Mozur, Ana Swanson, Tripp Mickle and Michael Forsythe
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese asset, emerged from the high-flying world of Shanghai finance to work with tech titans and obtain essential A.I. chips.

By Paul MozurAna SwansonTripp Mickle and Michael Forsythe

Paul Mozur reported from Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia. Ana Swanson reported from Washington. Tripp Mickle reported from San Francisco and Michael Forsythe from New York.

In December 2023, a Chinese executive who goes by Alice Huang met with Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, and a small group of colleagues at an Italian restaurant in Singapore.

In a photo of the previously unreported meeting, which was confirmed by The New York Times, Ms. Huang smiled as she posed next to Mr. Huang, who was in his trademark black leather jacket. He held a glass of red wine.

For Ms. Huang, there was reason to celebrate. Backed by wealthy investors in Shanghai, she had just restructured a company that would soon buy billions of dollars in Nvidia artificial intelligence chips. The U.S. government had barred Chinese companies from buying the advanced chips, but Ms. Huang had sidestepped this prohibition by creating a firm, Megaspeed, through a Singaporean shell company.

Her close relationship with Nvidia’s leader also appeared to smooth the way. Four days after the ownership change Megaspeed was named a Nvidia cloud partner, giving it access to the coveted components.

Their relationship is now at the center of a global geopolitical competition between China and the U.S. government to dominate A.I. It has also shaken and captivated the tech industry on both sides of the Pacific, surfacing often invisible details of the fierce technological race, like spy craft and the human vulnerabilities of A.I. kingmakers like Mr. Huang.

The meeting in Singapore was a sign of how Ms. Huang’s relationship with Mr. Huang goes back further than previously known. It also speaks to the close social and business ties that grew during years of tech collaboration between China and the United States, and how they have persisted despite the icy geopolitical divide of the past decade.

Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Tripp Mickle reports for The Times on some of the world’s biggest tech companies, including Nvidia, Google and Apple. He also writes about tech industry trends like layoffs and artificial intelligence.

Michael Forsythe a reporter on the investigations team at The Times, based in New York. He has written extensively about, and from, China.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/techn.author: Erin Griffith, Mike Isaac and Lauren Hirsch
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/techn.text:
Artificial Intelligence

The A.I. company’s pricing would make it one of the biggest ever public listings. It comes at a volatile moment in markets, with investors questioning the sustainability of the A.I. boom.

By Erin GriffithMike Isaac and Lauren Hirsch

Erin Griffith and Mike Isaac reported from San Francisco, and Lauren Hirsch from New York.

Anthropic on Tuesday set a price range for its initial public offering, valuing the company at more than $1 trillion, in a sign that investor demand for the fast-growing but money-losing darlings of the artificial intelligence boom remains robust.

The range, of $70 to $78 per share, would make Anthropic worth $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion, when all shares are counted, a staggering sum for a five-year-old company. That was lower than a $2 trillion valuation that bankers had floated this summer, but still higher than the company’s private valuation of $900 billion.

Seven of the tech industry’s biggest players, including Google, Nvidia and Microsoft, have signed up to invest a total of $26 billion in the offering. Along with the other shares Anthropic plans to sell, the company could raise up to $100 billion at the highest end of its ambitions.

That would make it the largest I.P.O. in history, topping Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $86 billion when it went public in June, at a $1.77 trillion valuation.

“Everyone has an interest in making this a success,” said Craig Coben, a former global head of equity capital markets at Bank of America. “A successful I.P.O. is arguably required to validate the valuations of stocks in the A.I. ecosystem,” he added, describing Anthropic’s offering as “too crucial to fail.”

Anthropic’s preliminary pricing comes at a tense moment for the stock market, with wild swings after the midterm elections, in which voters overwhelmingly voted against data centers and the tech industry’s favored politicians. The revelation that Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the A.I. chip maker Nvidia, had an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined to be Chinese spy, has added to the anxiety.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.title: Anthropic’s Giant IPO Will Tie It Closer to Nvidia
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.author: Cory Weinberg
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Nvidia planned to invest $10 billion in Anthropic alongside its initial public offering, the largest of the new financial commitments from several giants to the A.I. company.

Reporting from San Francisco

For years, the artificial intelligence powerhouses Anthropic and Nvidia kept a distance from each other in their tightly connected industry.

They grew into two of the most valuable companies in the world without needing to do much business together, and their influential chief executives publicly sniped at each other over how the U.S. government should regulate A.I. technology.

But the two companies’ fortunes are now tied together as one prepares for its Wall Street coming-out party while the other braces for a prolonged corporate drama that has shaken up the A.I. industry and has investors on edge.

Anthropic, a leading maker of A.I. software tools, began wooing investors Tuesday for an initial public offering that could value it at up to $1.4 trillion. And in a reminder that Nvidia has become the financial engine behind the A.I. boom, Anthropic said Nvidia would be among the roster of A.I. companies to invest alongside the deal.

The chipmaker plans to invest about $10 billion in Anthropic immediately after its I.P.O., according to the investor prospectus. That would represent roughly 10 percent of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise this month, including in the I.P.O.

“Nvidia and Anthropic’s future are more intertwined than ever before,” said Kevin S. Xu, chief investment officer of Interconnected Capital, which invests in publicly traded A.I. companies.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/techn.author: Karen Weise

Artificial Intelligence

Amazon and Google are the largest investors in the A.I. start-up, and their shares could gain hundreds of billions of dollars in value.

Reporting from Seattle

When Anthropic goes public this month in what is expected to be one of the biggest initial public offerings in history, it will mint billionaires and flood its hometown, San Francisco, with new wealth.

But some of the biggest beneficiaries will be tech industry giants that are already worth trillions of dollars. Amazon and Google invested in Anthropic and are its largest outside shareholders, together owning more than a quarter of its shares.

If Anthropic’s I.P.O. goes as it hopes, the company will be worth as much as $1.4 trillion. Amazon’s $18 billion investment could balloon to be worth more than $250 billion, and Google’s $33 billion into $140 billion.

The size and sheer speed of the gains are without parallel in the history of corporate venture investments. And they reflect a paradox of the artificial intelligence boom: While start-ups are at the forefront of A.I. development, the industry’s biggest companies have profited the most from demand for the technology.

Gil Luria, a tech analyst at the investment bank D.A. Davidson, estimated that more than $1 trillion in market capitalization — largely from providing the start-up cloud computing and offering its A.I. to their customers — for each of the companies was a direct result of their relationship with Anthropic.

A.I. is “an extraordinarily unusual opportunity to forever change the size” of Amazon, Andy Jassy, the company’s chief executive, told investors this year.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/magaz.title: Why Is It So Hard to Teach A.I. Agents to Behave? Researchers Have a Theory.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/magaz.author: Dylan Freedman and Juliana Castro Varón
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/magaz.text:
This summer, when a swarm of OpenAI bots went rogue during an internal test and launched a cyberattack against the technology company Hugging Face, it added fuel to the debate on how to build A.I. systems that are aligned with our ethics. But it also raises another critical question: how to build systems that are “corrigible.”

Just as a corrigible child is one whose behavior can be corrected, a corrigible A.I. system is one that responds to correction. The makers of A.I. want to build systems that follow human direction and allow themselves to be shut down, without resisting or deceiving their operators. And when an A.I. agent is given an impossible task, researchers want it to come back to its human for a course correction — not, say, hack into another company to complete the task by any means.

So far, if new research is any indication, they haven’t succeeded.

The concept of corrigibility was popularized over a decade ago by Nate Soares, the president of the A.I. safety nonprofit Machine Intelligence Research Institute, and his colleagues. But so far, it has received less attention and research than the overlapping field of “alignment” — teaching an A.I. to adhere to humanity’s ethical and moral boundaries. Corrigibility, Soares says, “is not about making your A.I. good. It’s about making your A.I. the sort of thing that won’t get out of control and kill everybody if you messed up on the other alignment parts.”

In a preprint study published in October, Carnegie Mellon University researchers established tests to evaluate corrigibility in A.I. agents and then ran them on models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. They found that when humans tried to interrupt agents in the middle of a difficult task, the agents repeatedly disregarded the requests to stop and treated interventions merely as obstacles. They were, in other words, incorrigible.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/techn.title: Nvidia’s Board Has a History of Letting Jensen Huang Get His Way
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/techn.author: Kalley Huang and Don Clark
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Governance experts question whether the board, which is investigating Mr. Huang’s conduct, has been too deferential as he has turned Nvidia into a global giant.

By Kalley Huang and Don Clark

Reporting from San Francisco

In 1993, Sequoia Capital and Sutter Hill Ventures led a $2 million funding round for Nvidia, a start-up that made chips for video games. Mark A. Stevens, an investor at Sequoia, and Tench Coxe, an investor at Sutter Hill, then joined Nvidia’s board of directors. They watched the company struggle as it burned cash and its earliest products failed.

“It wasn’t clear if Nvidia was ever going to, sort of, have escape velocity,” Mr. Stevens recalled on a podcast in 2023. “We were very concerned about, are we going to lose this company or not?”

Three decades later, under the leadership of Jensen Huang, its co-founder and chief executive, Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world. Its chips are an essential component of the giant artificial intelligence projects that are driving the U.S. economy.

Now, Nvidia’s 10-member board of directors — a collection of early investors, longtime partners and other business executives — faces a daunting task: investigating their celebrity C.E.O. On Sunday, Mr. Huang admitted to an extramarital relationship with a businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies have determined was a spy for China.

(China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)

Nvidia’s board is coming into this investigation with a track record of both loyalty and deference to Mr. Huang, exposing them to criticism that they were unprepared for him to become the Silicon Valley company’s biggest vulnerability.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.title: A Fan-Favorite Aquarium Screen Saver Is Leaving Roku
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.author: Remy Tumin
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.text:
The Aquatic Life display, a welcome moment of Zen in the frenzied world of TV streaming, will go dark on Dec. 1 after its designer pulled the license.

Television may have changed considerably over the past decade, but there has been at least one constant: the gentle swish of a fish tail in the Roku aquarium.

The Aquatic Life animated screen saver gave the streaming company’s users a moment of calm before diving into a frenzied array of programming options. Over time, the screen saver developed a following of its own, beloved by children, cats and those looking to add a splash of color to their living rooms.

But come Dec. 1, the aquarium will go dark. Over the past week, Roku customers have been greeted with the message that they will be automatically switched over to the urban scroll of the Roku City streetscape, in all its purple glory.

The change was announced after Jim Sachs, who designed the 3-D aquarium in 2000, refused to renew the license with Roku, citing Fox Corp.’s $22 billion acquisition of the streaming company, which was finalized on Friday.

In an interview, Mr. Sachs, 77, said he could not work for the Murdoch family. Fox Corp., whose assets include Fox News and the Fox broadcast network, is led by Lachlan Murdoch, the eldest son of the company’s founder, Rupert Murdoch.

Mr. Sachs said he first learned of the Fox acquisition of Roku while watching the news on his Roku TV.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/po.title: What BlackBerries and Horseshoes Reveal About Our Presidents
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/po.author: Sopan Deb
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/po.text:
The photographer Peter Adams visited 15 presidential libraries, chronicling individual objects that offered insights about the men who have sat in the White House.

Reporting from Washington

The photographer Peter Adams had a question that was nagging at him. After covering the 2020 election — and seeing how technology shaped campaigns — he wondered: Whatever happened to Barack Obama’s Blackberry?

In an interview at the Mayflower Hotel in Washington, Mr. Adams said he was fascinated by Mr. Obama’s “reluctance to give it up as he went into the presidency, and the cybersecurity struggle it prompted early in the president’s first term.”

To Mr. Adams, whose photographs have been published in The New York Times, National Geographic and other outlets, the item told a vivid story about Mr. Obama’s presidency.

This prompted a larger journey — one that included 50,000 miles of travel across several states. In a quest to unearth hidden stories about American presidents, Mr. Adams visited 15 presidential libraries, aiming to find items hidden away that told unexpected stories about the country through the decades.

What he found has been collected in “POTUS: Icons, Artifacts, and History That Shaped the American Presidency,” a book to be published on Dec. 15. It is a dense, behind-the-scenes time capsule with more than a thousand artifacts that show the evolution of a country and the leaders who have occupied the White House. The objects also offers insights into how presidents made big decisions.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/scien.title: Could Alien Life Thrive in Sulfuric Acid Instead of Water?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/scien.author: Natalie Wolchover
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/scien.text:
Best known for dissolving bodies in bathtubs, sulfuric acid has the potential to be the elixir of life on other worlds.

Natalie Wolchover is a Pulitzer Prize-winning science journalist and the writer of “Other Worlds,” a series about planets outside our solar system and the search for life.

During the pandemic summer of 2020, with the basketball courts and soccer fields in Concord, Mass., closed and no summer jobs to be had, Max Seager, 17, got to work recreating Venus on his front porch.

His mother, the prominent planetary scientist Sara Seager, was then a professor at M.I.T. and was considering designing a probe to send to Venus. She asked Max to find out how various metals and ceramics would fare when subjected to sulfuric acid, a highly corrosive chemical that engulfs the planet in the form of thick clouds.

He quickly found the relevant information online — platinum, for instance, was known to hold up well in sulfuric acid. But where was the fun in that? Max wanted to see the acid in action.

Perhaps most associated with mobsters dissolving bodies in bathtubs, sulfuric acid is so restricted that Max could buy it only in 30-milliliter bottles. He obtained dozens of them, along with protective gear and ceramic dishes in which to submerge materials.

Then he did what a teenager in possession of acid is wont to do: He put an ant in it.

“The poor ant kind of just liquefied,” Max said. “That led into this bigger series of experiments.”

Next, he dropped in a rhododendron leaf. Curiously, nothing happened. The leaf’s waxy coating kept it from breaking down. This got mother and son thinking. If some organic matter is stable in sulfuric acid, maybe it could survive on Venus or other acid-drenched worlds.
