https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/clima.title: El Niño Is Hitting California Hard
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/clima.author: David Gelles and Gabriela Bhaskar
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/clima.text:
Rising sea levels and violent weather are testing residents in some of the most picturesque cities along the Pacific Coast.

Rising sea levels and violent weather are testing residents in some of the most picturesque cities along the Pacific Coast.

Photographs and Video by Gabriela Bhaskar

David Gelles spent several days reporting along the Pacific Coast Highway to understand the damage from El Niño.

First came the flood. Then the fire.

In a matter of weeks, neighboring cities in Orange County were battered by dueling disasters that laid bare the risks posed to California as the world warms.

In early September, powerful waves from the Pacific Ocean began to wallop the houses along Beach Road, a ribbon of multimillion-dollar waterfront properties hugging the coast in the picturesque hamlet of Dana Point.

Several factors conspired to create the strongest swell that anyone in the area can recall. But a main culprit was El Niño, the natural climate pattern that typically happens a few times a decade and scrambles weather patterns worldwide. The current El Niño is dangerously strong.

In California, it is elevating sea levels and creating more intense storms. A phenomenon known as a Kelvin wave — a huge, slow-moving pulse of warm water in the ocean that’s linked to El Niño — is raising sea levels as well.

Dozens of Dana Point homes have been badly damaged. Ten were deemed unfit for occupancy. Two were demolished.

Among those that sustained severe damage was the modern waterfront home owned by Lori Torres, an entrepreneur who bought the house when she retired in 2019, fulfilling her lifelong dream to live on the ocean. In a matter of days, waves ripped away her patio and destabilized the foundation.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/clima.title: ‘Fight Harder,’ U.N. Chief António Guterres Implores, Rousing Climate Ambassadors at COP31
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/clima.author: Chico Harlan and Lisa Friedman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/clima.text:
The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, spoke at COP31, a meeting aimed at reducing emissions, amid a sharp drop in attendance by world leaders.

By Chico Harlan and Lisa Friedman

Reporting from Antalya, Turkey

Opening a climate summit that leaders from most industrialized nations chose to skip, António Guterres, the United Nations secretary general, on Wednesday warned that the planet was on a “path to mutually assured destruction,” unable to wean itself from planet-warming fossil fuels and facing intensifying disasters.

“Fossil fuel interests keep making a killing while killing our planet,” Mr. Guterres told world leaders gathering for the summit, known as COP31.

Mr. Guterres, who is in the final weeks of his term after leading the United Nations for a decade, urged nations to “end the addiction” to fossil fuels. His remarks sharpened the tensions for an event that often struggles to directly address the burning of fossil fuels, which is the root cause of climate change.

He and others acknowledged the world has failed to meet the goal it established in the Paris Agreement in 2015 to limit rising global temperatures to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels. That’s the threshold beyond which scientists say the dangers of global warming — including worsening floods, fiercer wildfires, droughts and ecosystem collapse — grow considerably.

On Wednesday, leaders one by one insisted that despite rising levels of greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere, it was critical to get back on track. But many avoided the mentioning the cuts to coal, oil and gas that would be necessary to meet most climate goals.

“It is time to wake up,” said President Hilda Heine of the Marshall Islands, who described rising sea levels threatening her Pacific atoll nation.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/scien.title: 25 Years After the Anthrax Attacks, America Remains Vulnerable
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/scien.author: K. R. Callaway
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/scien.text:
Letters filled with anthrax spores exposed flaws in the United States’ biosecurity systems. Experts say many of those issues still exist.

On Sept. 19, 2001, Robert Stevens headed in to the offices of the Florida-based tabloid, Sun, where he worked as a photo editor. Waiting there was a letter: an unusual note, inside an envelope filled with a grainy white powder.

Mr. Stevens closely examined the letter before returning to work. It was, after all, unlike the publication’s usual mail: tabloid tips and notes from readers. But within days of opening that envelope, Mr. Stevens developed a deadly disease: inhalation anthrax.

He was the first of 22 people — primarily journalists, politicians and postal workers — to develop anthrax after handling powder-filled letters contaminated with a lab-grown strain of the bacteria, and the first of five people who died from the disease between October and November 2001.

The anthrax attacks further terrified a nation already on edge in the weeks after Sept. 11. Just as the Qaeda attacks had upended the country’s national security priorities, ushering in a sweeping electronic surveillance program and new rules for travelers at the airport, the anthrax attacks prompted a rethinking of the government’s approach to biosecurity.

Within weeks of Mr. Stevens’s death, new detection systems and response protocols were put in place around the country, and the federal response shifted from monitoring naturally occurring pathogens to seeking out man-made threats.

Now, 25 years later, experts warn that many of the systems put in place in 2001 have stagnated, leaving the country once again vulnerable. The technology meant to alert officials to a biological attack, experts say, is inefficient and outdated and the federal response remains largely uncoordinated and underfunded.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/well/.title: New Research Compares Long-Term Relief From 21 Antidepressants
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/well/.author: Christina Caron
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/well/.text:
In the meta-analysis, a few drugs stood out for offering greater effectiveness over time.

A new meta-analysis found that certain antidepressants worked better on average than Prozac at helping people with depression feel better and stick with their treatment over the long term.

The analysis looked at 21 different drugs across 115 studies to identify which drugs were most likely to help patients who planned to use antidepressants for more than three months. The study authors compared each drug to Prozac, also known as fluoxetine, because it’s a well-known drug that has been commonly prescribed, researchers said.

While most of the antidepressants were comparable in terms of how well they worked or how long patients stayed on them, there were some subtle differences. People taking escitalopram (Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) or agomelatine (Thymanax), were more likely than those taking fluoxetine to see their symptoms improve and stay better.

And there were two medications that performed worse than multiple other antidepressants: bupropion (known as Wellbutrin or Zyban) and reboxetine (Edronax).

Depression is one of the most common mental health disorders in the world and many people end up taking antidepressants for years. But there has been little research comparing the effectiveness of different antidepressants beyond the length of a typical clinical trial, which is usually around eight weeks.

The study, which was published on Tuesday in The Lancet Psychiatry, analyzed both published and unpublished studies that followed participants with major depressive disorder for more than 12 weeks, and one as long as two years. They looked at whether the subjects had a “sustained response” to each drug, meaning an improvement in symptoms that lasted until the trial ended. The researchers also looked at whether the study subjects stopped taking the drug for any reason, assuming that those people did so because their symptoms had not improved.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/healt.title: The U.S. Has Lost Its Measles-Elimination Status, Data Suggests
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/healt.author: Apoorva Mandavilli
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/healt.text:
An international panel of scientific experts will convene on Tuesday to evaluate the status, but genetic data already shows the virus is once again entrenched in the United States.

By Apoorva Mandavilli

Measles is once again endemic — a constant and predictable presence — in the United States, 26 years after it was declared eliminated in the country, an analysis of genetic data from outbreaks of the disease has found.

Data from the outbreaks will be the focus of deliberations by an international panel of scientific experts convening on Tuesday to decide whether the United States should lose its official designation as a nation that has eliminated measles. An announcement of the decision is expected on Nov. 17.

The New York Times asked several scientists to analyze the publicly available genetic data before the meeting.

Achieving elimination status in 2000 was a hard-fought public health victory for the United States. But with skepticism about the safety of vaccines growing in recent years, outbreaks have become more frequent. Over the past two years, cases have soared, with nearly 5,200 reported so far this year. Last week alone, Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin each reported a death associated with measles, bringing this year’s total to eight, more than the combined deaths from 2000 through 2024.

To officially lose elimination status, a committee of the Pan American Health Organization, a branch of the World Health Organization, must determine that the country has had uninterrupted transmission of measles for more than 12 months.

Publicly available data shows that several chains of transmission have continued for more than a year in the United States, according to scientists who analyzed the data at the request of The New York Times.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.title: Anthropic’s I.P.O. and the Clubby Business of A.I.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.author: Andrew Ross Sorkin, Bernhard Warner, Sarah Kessler, Michael J. de la Merced, Niko Gallogly, Brian O’Keefe and Sri Muppidi
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.text:
Some of the biggest investors in the artificial intelligence giant’s upcoming listing are also some of its most important business partners.

By Andrew Ross SorkinBernhard WarnerSarah KesslerMichael J. de la MercedNiko GalloglyBrian O’Keefe and Sri Muppidi

Andrew here. To help us celebrate DealBook’s 25th anniversary at our summit next week, we recently asked you to help us identify the top moments of the past quarter century in business and policy. Now we’d like your help picking eight finalists.

There are some moments we believe are inarguable: the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, the creation of the iPhone, the 2008 financial crisis, the coronavirus pandemic and the introductions of A.I. and social media. But what about China’s induction into the W.T.O.? The emergence of cryptocurrency? The rollout of Obamacare? The Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision? The new space race?

Please let us know what you think. And make sure to follow our full coverage of the summit on Nov. 18, where we’ll livestream select interviews on The Times’s app.

For the first time in a while, the biggest story in artificial intelligence wasn’t the scrutiny of Nvidia’s C.E.O., Jensen Huang, (more on that below) but the start of the long-awaited roadshow for Anthropic’s I.P.O.

Reports suggest that investor demand so far for the stock offering is robust. But amid all of the huge numbers in Anthropic’s latest I.P.O. prospectus was one worth paying attention to — a $26 billion private share sale — and how that highlights the circular financing that underpins much of the A.I. economy, Sri Muppidi reports.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.title: How GLP-1 Drugs and a Revamp Revived Ro’s Business
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.author: Michael J. de la Merced
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.text:
The telehealth company said that its annualized revenue had grown nearly tenfold since it revamped its business and embraced weight-loss treatments.

By Michael J. de la Merced

For much of its life, the telehealth company Ro was known as a provider of sexual wellness treatments. Then it drastically reshaped its business and pivoted to offering weight-loss drugs like Wegovy and Zepbound as part of a health care revolution.

Now, the nine-year-old privately held company is offering a closer look at the results of that transition.

Ro announced on Wednesday that it had more than $3 billion in annualized revenue, up nearly tenfold since the company revamped its business starting in 2022.

For Zachariah Reitano, a Ro founder and its chief executive, the results underscore both the efficacy of the company’s overhaul and the huge draw of GLP-1 drugs, which can offer benefits beyond weight loss.

“People will ask me, ‘Are you just GLP-1s now?’” he said in an interview. “And my response is, ‘Just? Like, just working on the leading causes of death?’”

The company’s turnaround may also spur questions about whether Ro, which has not raised new money from investors in years, will eventually go public, following in the footsteps of its rival Hims & Hers.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.title: The Fed Has to Raise Rates. How Fast to Go Has Officials Divided.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.author: Colby Smith
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.text:
The Federal Reserve’s gradual approach to raising rates is being tested by intensifying price pressures.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

Officials at the Federal Reserve are in broad agreement that interest rates need to rise in order to tame inflation that continued to accelerate this year.

Less settled is the pace of those increases and how aggressive the Fed will need to be in order to return inflation to its 2 percent target, which has overshot that level for nearly six years.

The debate deepened on Tuesday after new data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that price pressures broadened out in October, resulting in a swifter pickup in inflation than was expected.

The central bank, which embraced a gradual approach to raising rates just a few weeks ago, must now decide whether to ratchet up its response — either by delivering a big move when it next meets in December, or signaling increases at back-to-back meetings going forward.

Financial markets have for now leaned into the latter option, penciling in more rate increases in 2027 than previously. So too have many economists, who have largely downplayed the idea that the Fed will raise rates by half a percentage point next month even as they affirm the need for a faster pace of tightening.

“The latest inflation data reinforced the idea that price pressures remain sticky and elevated and are not just due to one-off shocks,” said Matthew Luzzetti, chief U.S. economist at Deutsche Bank. “Therefore, the Fed probably has more work to do and in order to balance the risks better, it makes sense to do that at a somewhat quicker pace than we were previously anticipating.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.title: This Trader Raised Alarm About Nvidia’s China Entanglements Months Ago
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.author: Rob Copeland and Maureen Farrell
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Christian Lamarco, a 31-year-old short seller and trader, warned about financial and personal problems at Nvidia in May.

By Rob Copeland and Maureen Farrell

Early on May 13, Christian Lamarco, a little-known stock researcher and trader, could barely sleep. Shortly after dawn the 31-year-old would release what amounted to the magnum opus of his career: A 40-page exposé on questionable behavior at Nvidia.

The report mostly comprised a sober examination of whether the chipmaker was being honest about the scale of its China business. But at the top of Page 3, Mr. Lamarco tucked in a paragraph-long warning of the “uncomfortably close relationship” between Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, and Alice Huang, who worked for Megaspeed, a huge customer.

Mr. Lamarco says his interest in their relationship had been piqued by reporting in The New York Times and Bloomberg News that first detailed a year ago how the Nvidia chief executive and Ms. Huang were seen together socializing with other tech executives in Asia.

So Mr. Lamarco started digging around for himself, using paid expert networks — middlemen that connect investors with company insiders — to chat with current and former Megaspeed and Nvidia employees about Ms. Huang and the companies’ business. The employees wondered about what Mr. Lamarco months ago termed “special” ties between the two executives.

But almost no one noticed his report.

Nvidia’s stock rose that day in May when Mr. Lamarco’s findings were released online. Among the little feedback, he recalled this week, was one note calling him developmentally disabled and another warning him to “watch out.”

Now, the 31-year-old looks prescient. On Thursday, Mr. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO,  after confessing to an extramarital affair with Ms. Huang, who U.S. intelligence has accused of being a Chinese spy.

This season, bakers are charging three figures for luxury versions that combine elaborate prep and premium ingredients. Not everyone is biting.

The apple custard pie from Mishie’s that commands up to $150 for the largest one. 
Credit...
Lucia Vazquez for The New York Times

Bakers in the 18th century who poured stewed pumpkin sweetened with molasses into a rough, thick crust could hardly have imagined their fellow citizens paying more than $100 for a Thanksgiving pie.

What may be this season’s most expensive pie is built on a crust made with Cinnamon Toast Crunch cereal. Its apple custard filling is swirled with apple cider caramel. On top, a sprinkle of gold leaf crowns sour cream rosettes. New York magazine declared it the best pie to order this Thanksgiving. A 12-inch version will set you back just $150.

“I was like, you know what? Why don’t we just up the ante and start making pies more complicated, because I knew how to make them more complicated,” said Michelle Kogan, the New York chef who created the pricey pie.

In West Oakland, Calif., the noted pastry chef Melissa Chou is selling a 10-inch Thanksgiving pie made with toasted wildflower honey custard on a delicate Italian pastry crust, topped with a beeswax-infused sabayon, for $120.

In the Hamptons, New Yorkers can order Lena Kristy’s brown butter apple streusel pie or cranberry pecan pie for $80. Both use jam from her shop, Jamagansett, where her $100 salty blueberry pie went viral over the summer. The ensuing snark prompted her to drop the price to $80.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/style.title: Entertainment 360 Acquires Brigade, a Management Firm Rich in Substackers
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/style.author: Callie Holtermann
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/style.text:
With the purchase of Brigade, a small talent firm, Substack writers and podcast hosts are now managed by the same company as movie stars.

Podcasters, newsletter writers and content creators are building mouthwatering audiences in today’s entertainment ecosystem — and Hollywood is taking note.

The talent management company Entertainment 360 announced today that it would acquire Brigade, a firm representing some of the most influential new-media tastemakers. The deal will bring Brigade clients including the Substack writers Leandra Medine Cohen and Emily Sundberg under the same umbrella as Hollywood superstars like Margot Robbie and Julianne Moore.

Max Stein, who founded Brigade in 2015, will join Entertainment 360 as a partner. Many of his clients command significant followings in the fashion world, including the celebrity stylist Danielle Goldberg and Chris Black, a creative consultant for clothing brands and a host of the podcast “How Long Gone.”

Entertainment 360 and Brigade declined to disclose the value of the deal, which Stein informed his clients of on Tuesday.

The acquisition is the latest example of entertainment and media institutions marshaling resources toward digital talent. Hollywood talent behemoths like Creative Artists Agency are signing YouTube stars. Broadcast TV personalities are emulating the tactics of livestreamers. This weekend, the comedian Druski introduced himself as the “first internet content creator” to host “Saturday Night Live” — a show whose cast is now stacked with comedians who got their start on TikTok.

“These worlds have collapsed a bit on each other,” said Darin Friedman, a partner at Entertainment 360. “YouTube is competing with Netflix, and Netflix is buying podcasts, and Disney is wanting to set meetings with comedians who want to develop TV shows.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/clima.title: The United States Is Skipping COP31 in Turkey
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/clima.author: David Gelles and Lisa Friedman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/clima.text:
President Trump refused to send an American delegation to the United Nations climate summit in Turkey.

By David Gelles and Lisa Friedman

David Gelles and Lisa Friedman have spent a cumulative six months of their lives at COPs.

As world leaders begin addressing the United Nations climate summit today in Antalya, Turkey, 197 nations will be represented. From Albania to Zimbabwe, heads of state and governments and top ministers will commit to the global goal of a livable planet.

But not the United States.

For the second year in a row, the most powerful country on Earth and the largest contributor of planet-warming emissions in history has refused to participate in the global effort to slow climate change.

President Trump, who called global warming the “greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world,” withdrew the United States from the 2015 Paris climate agreement and stopped sending American delegations to the annual negotiations, known this year as COP31.

The United States is no longer trying to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions, has cut support for scientific research into global warming and halted funding to help vulnerable countries cope with the impacts of climate change.

That’s left the rest of the world scrambling to fill the vacuum.

“Look, whenever the mic was on, and it was the turn of the U.S. to speak, we all listened,” said Yaw Bediako Osafo, a negotiator from Ghana who is leading a group of African countries in the talks. “Now the world’s superpower is pulling out and saying, ‘Well, we’re not going to be involved.’”

The political climate in the United States changed abruptly last week, as Democrats dominated the midterms. The new Congress controlled by Democrats will have limited power to enact climate policies with Mr. Trump still in office. But Democrats said they intend to rein in the Trump administration, which has promoted fossil fuels and waged attacks on the clean energy industry.

Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Wachtell partner Joon H. Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney, is leading the inquiry into the chip maker’s chief executive.

By Lauren Hirsch and Kalley Huang

Nvidia has hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to help lead an investigation into Jensen Huang, its chief executive and co-founder, after he admitted to an extramarital relationship with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy, according to two people briefed on the decision.

Wachtell, which is known in corporate America as one of the foremost law firms for counseling executives on how to navigate complex challenges, will advise Nvidia’s board of directors on the inquiry into Mr. Huang.

The Wachtell partner Joon H. Kim, who focuses on high-stakes litigation and enforcement, is directing the investigation for the firm, the people said. He was previously acting U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York in 2017 and early 2018.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.title: Weil Gotshal Partners Vote to Shut Down After Nearly a Century
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.author: Lauren Hirsch and Noam Scheiber
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.text:
The large law firm, known for its powerful bankruptcy practice, started coming apart as prominent partners moved to other firms.

By Lauren Hirsch and Noam Scheiber

Partners at the law firm Weil, Gotshal and Manges have voted to wind down the nearly century-old firm, ending several months of disarray as partners jumped ship.

Weil Gotshal, once among the most prominent law firms for bankruptcy advice, was crippled in recent months by defections from the firm’s biggest rainmakers and a succession crisis that left it without a clear leader going forward. Last month, days after a plan to save the firm through a merger failed, its leaders said they would recommend that partners vote in favor of dissolving the firm.

Over the past week, Weil Gotshal’s leadership has hammered out the details of how it will finalize the painful ending. On Monday, Weil leaders outlined the plan to the firm’s partners, who submitted their votes — 97 percent in favor of a dissolution — over the past 24 hours.

As part of the plan described Monday, a three-person committee will oversee the firm’s dissolution. It includes Robert Carangelo, its general counsel; Paul Wessel, the chairman of the firm’s tax department; and Trish Ferrari, who specializes in serving as an independent board member on companies going through bankruptcy. Barry Wolf, Weil’s chairman, will advise the committee, said two people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

As Weil comes to an end, many of its lawyers have been finding roles at the very firms whose growing scale, profits and pay packages eclipsed Weil in the past several years, contributing to its demise. Kirkland & Ellis, one of the most profitable large law firms, said last week it was hiring 40 Weil lawyers whose practices include private equity, mergers and debt financing. Among the lawyers going to Kirkland is Ramona Nee, who had at one point been in line to run Weil. On Monday, Paul Weiss announced it had hired a securities litigator, Caroline Hickey Zalka, who had once been on Weil’s management committee.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.title: Data Show Households Still Managing to Meet Their Monthly Debts
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.author: Talmon Joseph Smith
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.text:
The New York Fed detailed general steadiness in debt payments for autos, student loans and mortgages.

By Talmon Joseph Smith

The latest report on overall household debt and credit by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York shows that U.S. households remain in decent financial health. But there are still major splits between Americans who own homes and large stock portfolios and lower-income segments of the population, according to the data, which was released on Tuesday, and recent reports from private banks.

The report from the New York Fed showed that mortgage debt balances rose by $257 billion from July to September, totaling $13.4 trillion. That’s a strikingly large amount of debt, but the vast majority of Americans are managing to service it.

The stabilizing power of the 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage continues to be the strongest anchor for households’ finances. After a surge in home buying during the pandemic, tens of millions of families are still benefiting from having locked in low-rate monthly payments. That has served as a meaningful buffer for consumers, even as overall inflation has eroded their purchasing power more broadly in recent years.

Another sign of underlying resilience can be found in home equity lines of credit, which are revolving loans backed by the value of the borrowers’ home. They tend to carry much lower interest rates than credit cards, and they allow borrowers to tap their wealth without selling their home. HELOC balances rose by $23 billion in the third quarter of the year, the 18th consecutive quarterly gain, and the largest increase since 2005.

Affluent and upper middle-class households in particular have been using HELOCs in recent years for home repairs and renovations, as well as for personal expenses. Unlike 2005, when the housing bubble was near its peak, Fed researchers note that this borrowing now seems to largely be stemming from strength — not stress. Serious delinquency for these lines of credit is exceptionally low, hovering around 1 percent.

Homeowners’ equity in real estate has soared to about $36 trillion as of September from around $18 trillion in 2019. Real estate wealth is unequally distributed in the United States, with the top 10 percent of households constituting a disproportionate share of household net worth.

https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/10/.title: Here’s the latest.
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/10/.author: Colby Smith and Ben Casselman
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/10/.text:
An official comparison with October 2025 was missing because of the government shutdown, but our calculations showed prices rose around 4 percent.

Note: Data is the year-over-year change in the Consumer Price Index. October 2025 is missing because of the government shutdown; the figure for October 2026 is the change between that month and the average of September and November 2025.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By The New York Times

Colby Smith and Ben Casselman

U.S. inflation remained elevated last month, underscoring the need for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again this year.

Overall prices rose 0.4 percent in October after a 0.6 percent jump in September, according to the latest Consumer Price Index report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. “Core” prices, which strip out volatile food and energy items, rose 0.3 percent.

The agency on Tuesday did not release year-over-year figures for October because it was unable to collect data during last year’s government shutdown. According to calculations by The New York Times, overall prices were around 4 percent higher compared with the same time last year, up from 3.7 percent in September. Over the same period, core prices rose about 2.8 percent.

One of the biggest drivers of inflation in October was food. Prices rose 0.5 percent last month and about 3 percent since the same time last year. That likely reflects a surge in energy prices, especially diesel prices, which have exploded costs for farmers.

Energy prices overall rose modestly in October and were up 0.7 percent for the month after a 5.2 percent jump in September. Gasoline prices rose 1 percent, significantly slower than the 9.1 percent increase during the previous period. Electricity prices rose nearly 1 percent.

October’s C.P.I. report was the last before the Fed meets for its final gathering of the year on Dec. 8-9. Policymakers have signaled that they will raise rates next month as they seek to stamp out price pressures that have pushed inflation further from their goal. While the Fed tracks C.P.I., it officially targets 2 percent inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures index. That level has been overshot for nearly six years.

Fed officials also watch the price of services as an indicator of the underlying pace of inflation. Specifically, they have been looking at core services excluding housing, a measure sometimes referred to as “supercore.” Those prices rose 0.4 percent in October, and have risen at an annual rate of nearly 5.5 percent over the past three months.

On Tuesday, Christopher J. Waller, a Fed governor, raised the prospects of a larger-than-usual half-point interest rate increase at the bank’s meeting in December if inflation did not show signs of moderating.

In remarks delivered at a Bank of England event, Mr. Waller said a quarter-point increase would suffice if price pressures improved. But if “core” inflation rose 0.3 percent or more, as October’s data showed, Mr. Waller warned that the Fed risked its credibility by not moving more aggressively. “Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,” he said.

Two-year Treasury yields, which are sensitive to changes in interest rate expectations, were up over 0.1 percentage points on Tuesday to 4.67 percent as investors raised wagers that the Fed would raise rates more over time to quell inflation. The labor market remains in solid shape, as October’s report released on Friday showed, affirming that the Fed can focus solely on its inflation problem.

October marked the seventh straight month in which price increases outpaced wage growth on a 12-month basis. Average hourly earnings were up 3.1 percent in October from a year earlier, well below the roughly 4 percent annual inflation pace.

The latest report on overall household debt and credit by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York shows that U.S. households remain in decent financial health. But there are still major splits between Americans who own homes and large stock portfolios and lower-income segments of the population, according to the data, which was released on Tuesday, and recent reports from private banks.

The report from the New York Fed showed that mortgage debt balances rose by $257 billion from July to September, totaling $13.4 trillion. That’s a strikingly large amount of debt, but the vast majority of Americans are managing to service it.

The stabilizing power of the 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage continues to be the strongest anchor for households’ finances. After a surge in home buying during the pandemic, tens of millions of families are still benefiting from having locked in low-rate monthly payments. That has served as a meaningful buffer for consumers, even as overall inflation has eroded their purchasing power more broadly in recent years.

Another sign of underlying resilience can be found in home equity lines of credit, which are revolving loans backed by the value of the borrowers’ home. They tend to carry much lower interest rates than credit cards, and they allow borrowers to tap their wealth without selling their home. HELOC balances rose by $23 billion in the third quarter of the year, the 18th consecutive quarterly gain, and the largest increase since 2005.

Affluent and upper middle-class households in particular have been using HELOCs in recent years for home repairs and renovations, as well as for personal expenses. Unlike 2005, when the housing bubble was near its peak, Fed researchers note that this borrowing now seems to largely be stemming from strength — not stress. Serious delinquency for these lines of credit is exceptionally low, hovering around 1 percent.

Homeowners’ equity in real estate has soared to about $36 trillion as of September from around $18 trillion in 2019. Real estate wealth is unequally distributed in the United States, with the top 10 percent of households constituting a disproportionate share of household net worth.

The surge in HELOCs made sense in view of that data, the New York Fed researchers wrote, the calling these loans “a logical point for extracting that equity.”

Still, households that are current on their debt payments are not necessarily comfortable. Other Federal Reserve research in recent years has shown that about 40 percent of the population has “little to no disposable income” at the end of month, after taxes and basic expenses are met. Credit cards borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores are now showing higher levels of distress, according to the New York Fed, while higher-income consumers have generally avoided a deterioration in credit.

And this month, a team of researchers at Bank of America noted, using anonymized account data, that financial pressure is extending beyond lower-income households.

Lower-to-middle income renters are perennially stretched, but around one in four higher-income mortgage holders are also spending more than half their income on housing, according to the bank. Financial experts generally recommend that consumers should spend no more than 30 percent of their monthly income on housing costs.

With interest rates elevated, and prices much higher for new vehicles than just a few years ago, auto loan payments have become a point of stress for lower-income borrowers as well — even if many are still finding ways to budget and meet their monthly obligations.

In a bright spot, student loan debt delinquencies have moderated. When Biden-era federal aid for those deep in student loan debt was reversed last year, there were widespread fears among some analysts that a burst in defaults could occur. For now, though, it appears most borrowers have been able to stave off missed student-loan payments.

U.S. stocks opened in the red, with the S&P 500 down 0.7 percent when markets began trading. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index was down 1 percent. Those drops follow a blockbuster day for stocks yesterday, when both indexes posted their best single-day rally since April.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, acknowledged today’s inflation report was “disappointing,” pointing to the impact of rising energy prices. (He was asked no follow-up question about the report during the brief appearance on Fox Business.)

Although investors are now leaning definitively toward a rate hike in December, there doesn’t seem to be much worry about a supersized half-point increase, as Fed Governor Waller hinted might be necessary. “An outsized move should require evidence that inflation is accelerating decisively, expectations are becoming unanchored or the economy is overheating,” said Seema Shah, chief global strategist for Principal Asset Management, in a note. “We are not there yet.”

A note about that 4 percent figure: It may be slightly exaggerated. Because of the missing October data, the Bureau of Labor Statistics had to make some assumptions when it calculated the Consumer Price Index for November 2025. The approach it took (essentially carrying over most prices from September to October) artificially depressed the November figure, which makes the increase in prices since then look larger than it really was. The effect is modest, though — there’s no question that inflation has picked up meaningfully in recent months.

Robert Sockin, the chief economist at PGIM, an asset management firm, tells me, “over the last few quarters inflation has shown little to no progress toward the Fed’s target and may even be worsening. Pressures remain broad-based across categories.”

He says his firm now expects the Fed to begin debating whether more aggressive policy action may be merited, saying that “signaling gradualism in an environment of hot and worsening inflation” would be a mistake.

The high costs in various corners of the healthcare system in America played a large role in voter dissatisfaction this fall. And we see some evidence of it in this inflation report. Prices for medical care commodities, which include prescription and over-the-counter drugs as well as medical equipment and supplies, were running hot this month, increasing by half a percentage point in October alone. (That comes after some more hopeful signs of cooling earlier in the year.)

The buildout of data centers has been a driving force behind America’s economic growth this year, but it’s also pushing up prices of some electronics and services that compete for the same chips. Prices for computers and related items are up 11.8 percent since this time last year, and software prices have climbed nearly 26 percent.

The cost of shelter, which drives more than a third of the overall index, has largely returned to its long-term average pace of price increases after a huge spike during the pandemic. It increased 0.3 percent over the month, down slightly from September’s pace, and is up 3.4 percent since this time a year ago according to our estimates. Hotels were the worst part of that category, rising 0.6 percent over the month; those prices have been growing at a quicker than usual clip all year.

Lettuce is apparently back on the menu after summer jitters brought on by the cyclospora outbreak tanked the price of leafy greens. Lettuce prices increased 7.9 percent from last month and are up about 9.2 percent compared with last year.

“All of this matters for markets, because a more patient Fed would be easier for stock bulls to navigate, while a more aggressive Fed could prove to be too big of a headwind for the market to overcome next year,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.

High housing costs are keeping potential buyers on the sidelines, and the hotter-than-expected inflation data is likely to keep mortgage rates elevated, said Jeff Ostrowski, a housing market analyst at Bankrate, a consumer financial services company. “It’s hard to believe that just eight months ago, mortgage rates were flirting with 6 percent,” he said. “Now, they’re unlikely to go below 7 percent.” He added, “That means the housing market is likely to keep stumbling along, with low levels of home sales.”

Another area where higher oil prices are squeezing consumers is airfares. Prices for airline tickets were up 0.4 percent from last month and a hefty 27.8 percent year-over-year, according to our estimates. That is making holiday travel more expensive than it was last year.

When inflation first picked up last spring, the optimistic take among economists was that the increase was mostly an energy story, and that there wasn’t much sign that higher prices were filtering through the economy. That has become significantly less true in recent months. Consumer prices, excluding energy, have risen at a 3.6 percent annual rate over the past three months.

Be careful with your dishes this holiday season. The price of dishes and flatware was up 1.3 percent from last month and about 12 percent year-over-year, according to our estimates.

In his remarks in London, Waller said he expected energy prices to “remain elevated,” even as oil dips below $90 a barrel this morning. He pointed to high shipping costs and limited refining capacity. “As a consequence, elevated prices for diesel in the United States are not expected to moderate as readily as crude oil prices would in a more peaceful Middle East,” Waller said.

Though the price of food was broadly up in October, egg prices were up just 0.6 percent from last month. And they were down about 15.7 percent year-over-year, according to our estimates. Egg prices have become a political talking point.

Some good news for morning caffeinators: The surge in coffee prices last year appears to have moderated. The price of coffee was down -3.6 percent from last month, and up only a modest 2.3 percent from last year.

Despite the uncertainty around the year-over-year number, it’s safe to say that this was the seventh straight month in which price increases outpaced wage growth on a 12-month basis. Average hourly earnings were up 3.1 percent in October from a year earlier, while prices were up about 4 percent.

Waller’s comments just ahead of October’s report complicates things for the Fed in the sense that it introduced the idea of a big, half-point increase to rates in December if price pressures did not ease as expected. That is exactly what October’s report showed.

Another category that is heavily exposed to tariffs is toys, which were up about 8.9 percent year-over-year. Those price increases could sting going into the holiday season.

This report will intensify the debate around whether the Fed has to move more aggressively in raising rates to tame inflation. Officials have so far adopted a gradual approach to lifting borrowing costs, making a move in September and then forgoing one in October. The Fed is widely expected to again raise rates in December.

Given all the noise around tariffs and energy prices, some economists at the Fed and elsewhere have been focusing on the price of services as an indicator of the underlying pace of inflation. Specifically, they have been looking at core services excluding housing, a measure sometimes referred to as “supercore.” Today’s data didn’t provide any good news on that front: Supercore prices rose 0.4 percent in October, and have risen at an annual rate of nearly 5.5 percent over the past three months.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.author: Andrew Duehren
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.text:
A wealth tax on billionaires seemed like a political layup. The outcome of a California ballot initiative shows otherwise.

Andrew Duehren covers federal tax policy from Washington.

Of all the progressive arguments in favor of a wealth tax, the most clear-cut was supposed to be the popularity of such a policy. Even people who may not vote for Democrats would support such a tax, the thinking went, out of frustration with the opulence and power of the ultrarich.

And then voters in California rejected what would have been the nation’s first tax on wealth. Proposition 40 called for a one-time, 5 percent tax on the assets of California’s roughly 250 billionaires. It failed with roughly 53 percent of voters opposed as of the tally on Monday evening, when The Associated Press called the race.

The outcome is a stark setback for a progressive political project aimed at fundamentally changing taxation in the United States. Even in an election cycle when Democrats surged to huge victories across the country, a policy idea at the heart of the progressive agenda could not muster a bare majority in one of the country’s most liberal states.

“The conditions were probably the best they could have been to get this to pass, and even then it failed,” said Antoine Levy, an economist at the University of California, Berkeley. “That suggests there is a reluctance to pass wealth taxes.”

As the Democratic Party figures out how to wield its newfound power, that result may now weigh on decisions about how to raise taxes, even on the fabulously rich. In the party’s upcoming presidential primary, some candidates may now think twice about adding a wealth tax to their policy agenda. But the exact political consequences will depend on whether Democrats ultimately view the California loss as an idiosyncratic fluke or a reflection of a deeper opposition to taxing wealth.

There were, after all, several bespoke factors at play in California. The billionaire tax was mired in internecine conflict among the state’s elected officials, labor leaders and activist groups, diluting its support. Billionaires spent heavily against it, airing ads that claimed the tax could expand beyond the superrich. Several tech moguls even moved out of California to avoid the tax, fueling fears about its impact on the state’s tech sector. And even then, the proposition was not blown out: with 83 percent of the estimated vote counted, it trails 53 to 47.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.author: Andrew Ross Sorkin, Bernhard Warner, Sarah Kessler, Michael J. de la Merced, Niko Gallogly, Brian O’Keefe, Sri Muppidi and Ian Mount
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/busin.text:
Analysts and investors are asking whether the chipmaker needs to consider a successor to Jensen Huang, its C.E.O., as the company is engulfed in a spy scandal.

By Andrew Ross SorkinBernhard WarnerSarah KesslerMichael J. de la MercedNiko GalloglyBrian O’KeefeSri Muppidi and Ian Mount

Andrew here. Breaking: Anthropic plans to price its I.P.O. at $70 to $78 a share, valuing the A.I. titan at up to $1.4 trillion, less than the $2 trillion some had speculated only weeks ago. It could raise about $64.4 billion from public market investors and another $26 billion in a private placement to companies — including Nvidia.

With the backdrop of the Jensen Huang scandal, it has me thinking: Are investors too sanguine about Nvidia, which dropped 4.3 percent on Monday? The story will most likely become only more troubling. Democrats and others have raised concerns that Nvidia may have tried to intervene in a Commerce Department investigation involving Megaspeed, a Singaporean company that had employed Alice Huang, an executive who U.S. intelligence has determined was a spy for China.

New details will continue to emerge in dribs and drabs as Nvidia faces shareholder lawsuits and inquisitive lawmakers in Washington. Investors are betting Nvidia’s core business is strong enough to shrug this off. But with Democrats taking power in Congress, and Huang seen as close to President Trump, that resilience will be tested. More below.

Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Washington are still grappling with a possible scenario unthinkable even a few months ago: an Nvidia no longer led by Jensen Huang, after revelations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence determined was a spy for China.

Some investors have been optimistic that Huang may stay on as C.E.O. despite an inquiry from his own board and growing heat in Washington.

But others are still reckoning with the possibility that Huang may be forced out — and that there’s no clear successor in place, Sri Muppidi writes.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/podca.author: Natalie Kitroeff, Tripp Mickle, Olivia Natt, Lexie Diao, Eric Krupke, Paige Cowett, Liz O. Baylen, Dan Powell, Rowan Niemisto, Marion Lozano and Alyssa Moxley

This transcript was created using speech recognition software. While it has been reviewed by human transcribers, it may contain errors. Please review the episode audio before quoting from this transcript and email transcripts@nytimes.com with any questions.

From “The New York Times,” I’m Natalie Kitroeff.

A real life spy thriller?

Sounds like a honey trap and a really good movie.

Sex and spy scandal engulfing one of US technology giant.

We need to talk about NVIDIA. This story is incredible. Today, the extraordinary story of how the head of NVIDIA — that’s right, the biggest name in semiconductors, the man driving the AI boom was — the company at the center of the AI revolution —

To put it crudely, Jensen Huang was apparently honey trapped by China.

— came to admit that he’d had an affair with a woman that US officials say is a Chinese spy.

It sounds like Mr. Huang has explaining to do to his wife, his company, and the government.

I speak with my colleague, Tripp Mickle, about what the growing scandal means for the CEO, Jensen Huang, for his $4 trillion company and for the global battle for supremacy in artificial intelligence.

What a mess. What a mess.

It’s Tuesday, November 10.

Tripp, welcome back to “The Daily.”

Thanks so much for having me.

OK. So, I and I think everyone else, have been completely glued to this story, which is honestly something out of a movie, it feels like, this spy working on behalf of the Chinese government infiltrates one of the most valuable companies in the world by having an affair with its founder. You and many of our colleagues here at “The Times” have been leading on this reporting, and I want to know absolutely everything, starting with why this matters at the highest level.

Well, the story has a little bit of everything, right. It’s got sex and spies and semiconductors. Like, what can be more engrossing than that combination? But when you think about why this story matters, you have to look at what has changed in the world at large over the past three years. And the biggest fundamental change is artificial intelligence and the increasing belief that artificial intelligence is going to be an industrial revolution. And the company behind that industrial revolution, the company that’s enabling it is NVIDIA.

NVIDIA has a 90 percent market share in the artificial intelligence chips that are used to build and run AI systems. So every time you go to ChatGPT or Claude or Grok or anything, Gemini or anything else, and you put in a query, odds are some portion of that response that you get is powered by NVIDIA’s technology.

And so this has ramifications for everybody. It has ramifications for policymakers in Washington, it has geopolitical ramifications for the US China relationship, and it has ramifications for you, me, and everybody else who has a 401k because NVIDIA is such a big company in terms of its value and in terms of its prominence in the S&P 500, and in terms of what it means to where artificial intelligence is going, that the stock market literally moves up and down based on how NVIDIA is trading.

OK. So, this story matters a lot, and not just because it is filled with incredibly tantalizing details, twists, and turns, but because a lot of our economic health is riding on this industry and on this company.

And on this one man, Jensen Huang. And so it’s hard to begin to wrap your head around how important Jensen Huang is to artificial intelligence and this company itself. He has a flat structure with 60 direct reports. There’s no clear indication of who his successor might be if he were to get hit by a bus tomorrow. And now he’s become enmeshed in arguably the most explosive geopolitical controversy in corporate history.

OK. At this point, we should note that yesterday a Chinese government spokesman rejected the claim that the woman at the center of all of this was a Chinese spy, and dismissed the reporting as nothing but a smear against China. But let’s talk about how we got to this place where one of the most powerful CEOs in the world gets tangled up in such an explosive, high stakes mess. Like, where does this story begin?

You have to back up to last August when Ana Swanson and I got a message from a tech industry contact of ours who said, hey, you really need to drop everything and look at this company called Megaspeed. It’s a Singaporean data center firm. I mean, it’s literally a company that buys chips from NVIDIA and builds data centers.

And there’s nothing about that on the surface that says, this is something we should drop what we’re doing and devote time and resources to figuring out what this company is and why it matters. But NVIDIA was selling chips to this company at a time of increasing controversy over where AI chips go.

The US government has been concerned for years about the arms race, so to speak, between the US and China over who’s going to achieve supremacy in artificial intelligence. And when the AI revolution started in late 2022, the US had restricted China from buying NVIDIA’s best chips and best technology because it wanted to stop China from being able to build technology that was as sophisticated and comprehensive as what US companies were building.

But there was a big loophole. And that loophole was that NVIDIA could sell chips to companies in Southeast Asia, and that those companies could then provide access to that technology remotely to Chinese companies. And as we began to examine Megaspeed, it was pretty clear they’re the poster child for exploiting this loophole.

How so? I mean, in the span of roughly two years, they had purchased more than $4.8 billion in chips from NVIDIA. I mean, they went from being a company that nobody knew of overnight to a company that had become one of NVIDIA’s largest customers in the region.

And, I mean, this was a company with clear ties to China. So we wanted to learn more about those ties and dispatched our colleague, Paul Moser, from Taipei to Singapore to visit the Megaspeed office. And when he showed up, he found that there were only two employees at the office.

And when he spoke to them, they said that most all of their customers were Chinese and most of the executives were Chinese and rarely came to Singapore. In fact, most of them stayed mostly in China. This was significant because at the time NVIDIA was telling us that Megaspeed didn’t really have ties to China. Paul also went and found that Megaspeed was owned by a shell company. And he visited the shell company and found that it was based in an accounting firm, almost like a shell company mill. All of this was mystifying for us.

Unusual just because why would such a big company be housed with an accounting firm?

Right. You’re buying $4.8 billion of chips, you would think you could spring for your own office space, right?

Right. So, it sounds like you’re finding there are a lot of questions to be asked about this company’s connections to China and how it became such a major buyer of these chips basically out of the blue.

Yeah, absolutely. I mean, and as we dug into this company and looked at it, we found that they had aroused the suspicions of the Commerce Department and Commerce officials who are supposed to track where chips are going around the world. And so they dispatched investigators to visit one of the data centers, and when they showed up in September of 2024, they found that Megaspeeds still had a lot of the NVIDIA technology in boxes, which raised suspicion that that technology was being shipped in and then onward to potentially China. It really raised the prospects that this was a smuggling operation, not just a data center operation.

And at the center of all of this was this woman named Alice Huang, or Huang, a Chinese citizen who claimed to be the company’s chief executive officer on her LinkedIn, and who had a biography that detailed that she used to be a TV journalist. And this just made us question, how did she get all this money? How did she come to be in charge of this company? And then most of all and most mystifying, how did she get so close to Jensen Huang, the person who is at the forefront of artificial intelligence?

How close a relationship are you aware that they have at this point? Like, what do you about that?

We don’t a lot, but she’s been photographed with him on a few different occasions and videoed with him at various industry gatherings. And so we do some reporting. We speak to a man who took a photograph of them at an industry party at a bar in Taipei.

And there’s a photograph of Jensen sitting beside Alice as they prepare to toast whiskey. And the gentleman who took the photograph is a tech executive named Parker Schmidt. And Parker got on the phone and he said, you know, the wild thing about that photo is we were hanging out with Alice at this party, and she said something to the effect of, I bet I can get Jensen here. And sure enough, a few minutes later, Jensen showed up.

An indication that, I mean, she may have him on speed dial or something like that at least.

Right. That was the way it was perceived by others at this party. And you got to remember, this is in Taipei. This is where he is rock star among rock stars. And this is the industry that he is building and leading. So to be able to, in moments, summon the most important figure in the industry really catches people’s attention.

All right. So you dropped this reporting, what happens?

Not much. It’s quiet. NVIDIA keeps doing business with Megaspeed and we don’t hear a lot for a while. And then about a month ago, we hear that our colleagues in Washington on the national security beat all of a sudden are hearing things about Alice Huang and she’s resurfaced in our universe.

And we start to do some reporting, and it turns out that she has been under US surveillance for about a year, if not longer. And in the course of surveilling her and her communication, US intelligence services have determined that she’s a Chinese asset funneling information to Beijing.

A spy, basically. And lo and behold, who do they find out she’s in touch with? Jensen Huang.

All right. So you learn that the US intelligence community has, for the past year or so, been surveilling this woman that they suspect is a Chinese spy. They know this woman is talking quite a bit with NVIDIA’s CEO, Jensen Huang. What do they come to know about the nature of the relationship between these two?

They know that they have a very close relationship, that they’ve obviously been doing business together, and that some people in the intel community suspect that the relationship is intimate. And this obviously sets off alarm bells within the US government because —

— Jensen Huang, over the course of the past two years, has gone from somebody who did not even know President Trump to one of President Trump’s closest allies who has a huge voice and influence over US AI policy and who has regular phone calls with the president. They’re in touch all the time.

I mean, we saw recently. Jensen Huang was on stage at an event, and he got a call from the president and took it live. So they’re clearly very close. And I assume that the worry, or the question on the minds of these intelligence officers is, what is Alice Huang trying to get out of Jensen? And what has she manage to glean from him?

Right. And the US intelligence community determines that she’s working on behalf of China’s Ministry of State Security, which is essentially their CIA.

And they determined that she is trying to learn more about American AI chips — in other words, NVIDIA’s magic — and potentially trying to influence US policy on AI chips for China. In other words, encouraging Jensen to try to advocate for China to get more AI chips.

And the concern and the worry here is she’s incredibly close to him, which means she could have access to his devices, she could be communicating with him at all times, she could be weighing in on issues in real time. We don’t know. We haven’t seen the surveillance, but you can imagine the type of questions that the intel community was agonizing over as it was reviewing the surveillance.

And so what do they do when they find this out? Like, how do they respond to this information?

They take it to the top. They brief the president on this about a year ago, and they let him know that Jensen Huang has a relationship, a close relationship with this woman who they’ve determined to be a Chinese spy. And the president chooses not to do anything.

And when you say he decides to not do anything, what do you mean by that? Like, what exactly does that look like?

Well, usually in circumstances like this, what happens for a US citizen that surface in surveillance and in intelligence operation like this is that the FBI would provide a defensive briefing for that individual, essentially notifying them and saying, hey, you need to be aware you have come up in surveillance. We know the person you’re talking to is part of an intelligence operation. We suggest you probably presumably distance yourself from them. In this instance, that is not what happened. Jensen was not notified about this. Nothing happened. Literally the president took no action.

Why? Why wasn’t he notified? What’s the justification for that?

It’s unclear to us in that time, in that moment last fall, why the president didn’t take action. We don’t know if that’s because they didn’t want potentially Jensen Huang to say something to her and then that kind of pollutes the surveillance or creates a situation where they’re no longer able to surveil her if that was a priority, or if there was something else going on, there’s some other dynamic.

I mean, there are many variables at play. And we have to remember he’s a close ally of Jensen Huang, and this is a president who is very aware of how the stock market is performing and the economy is performing. And what is the one thing driving both of those things? Artificial intelligence and NVIDIA.

OK, so Trump knows about it, the US government knows about it, what happens? What happens next?

I know we’ve said this once before, but not much. Fast forward to the spring, and Marco Rubio asked for an update on the intelligence about the surveillance. And he drafts another memo, and he makes it more clear that she is a Chinese spy, that she is working for China’s intelligence services.

And the timing of this memo is shortly before President Trump took off for his summit in Beijing with Xi Jinping. And when the US government pulls together its list of executive delegates to go on that trip, you have Tim Cook, you have other chip executives. It’s 17-person list, but there’s one name that’s omitted and that is Jensen. He’s not invited.

But if I’m not mistaken, Jensen Huang does end up going on this trip to China. So, what happened?

And then if you step back even further before she even gets the gavel, we just had a midterm election where most of America sent a strong message to Washington that it was fed up with Silicon Valley’s influence over Washington policy, particularly on AI. And Jensen Huang is the face of AI, so anybody looking to score points right now — whether it’s Republicans or Democrats — on tech before the end of the year, they have somebody they can bring in. And we’ve already seen three Republicans say that they want a briefing from Jensen, so this is coming fast and it’s changing and taking shape in real time.

All right. I have what may seem like an intentionally provocative question here, Tripp, but bear with me. If it turns out that this woman that they suspect is a Chinese spy didn’t actually glean all that much from Huang and that Huang pushed for a more lenient US policy toward selling chips to China because he wanted to, not because of her influence, what then would be the damage that has been done from all of this?

He’s been compromised. How can lawmakers, people in the Trump administration listen to him and not have this in the back of his mind? It sows doubt for everyone about what he says, whether he’s being honest. And it also shows that he’s vulnerable. I mean, this is a guy that had Midas touch. He could do no wrong the last three years.

And this is a major misstep, a major misstep that could wind up forcing him to spend time in the coming months and next year testifying about the past rather than focusing on deciding and designing the artificial intelligence chips and the artificial intelligence changes of the future. This is for real inflection point for the company, for the US economy, for artificial intelligence because we don’t know what lies ahead after this point. The way we see Jensen Huang has changed forever.

Well, Tripp, thank you so much. It’s been a pleasure.

Thanks for having me.

Here’s what else you need to know today.

Impeaching Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, for high crimes and misdemeanors.

On Monday, Representative Thomas Massie moved to force a vote on impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Massie, the Kentucky Republican who’s set to leave Congress after losing his primary in May to a challenger backed by President Trump, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth.

The resolution said that Hegseth had abused his authority on many fronts, accusing him of violating federal law by carrying out the war with Iran without congressional authorization and carrying out unlawful strikes against drug traffickers in Latin America. Hegseth has rejected the allegations, calling the impeachment effort a political sham. If the House approves the charges, the measure will go to the Senate.

And California voters rejected Proposition 40, killing a measure that would have created the nation’s first wealth tax. The proposal would have imposed a one-time, 5 percent tax on the personal assets of billionaires in the state, and devoted most of the revenue to health care. But it suffered from having a weak coalition of supporters who couldn’t compete with the well-funded ad campaign attacking the measure.
