She was convicted of crimes against humanity and sentenced to death over student uprising. Hasina is ‘confident’ she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Grenades, grief and a deepening political divide: five takeaways from Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Niha Masih
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

F
ew love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.

The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.

Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.

Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.

Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.

Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years

Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.

For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.

Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.

It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians

India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.

In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.

Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.

Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press

Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.

In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.

And it’s not just media …

The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.

Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.

The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.

In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.

She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’

Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.

Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.

Art | Art Mumbai runs from 12-15 November at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse. Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.

Government | The official bungalow of Andhra Pradesh’s chief minister, N Chandrababu Naidu, was renovated by a government-owned enterprise for Rs 6.5 crore (£518,000), according to the Indian Express (£). The renovation work on the Delhi property included was said to have had a major makeover.

Film | Bollywood’s ambitious rendering of Hindu epic Ramayana, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi, was released on 5 November. Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.

Readers from India and around the world on the festival of lights and tell us how they celebrated.

double quotation markIn India, Diwali comes to you. You can see it in the streets, hear it in the neighbourhood and feel it in the atmosphere. In the UK, it is different. Life carries on around you. But traditions do not have to disappear when you move countries – they can change shape. A small light in a quiet room can carry the same meaning as an entire street illuminated for Diwali. Aman, Plymouth, UK

double quotation markMy favorite part of Diwali back home was getting up before sunrise on Narak Chaturdashi and having a ceremonial bath, followed by a breakfast of traditional Marathi Diwali snacks. I have been living abroad for over 10 years now and it’s always a bittersweet time of the year where I miss my family and the general vibe of Diwali in India. But I am trying to build new traditions as one half of an Indian-Austrian couple, which includes trading the traditional boxes of mithai for Manner Schnitten and marzipan. Charu, Germany

double quotation markThere used to be more of a community spirit to Diwali. As kids, we would be tasked with going door to door, exchanging sweets and snacks with neighbours (sometimes to our great displeasure, because it made for awkward conversation with those we had annoyed with our antics). Nowadays, the celebrations are mostly private. Group celebrations are walled off within exclusive clubs, families light their own fireworks almost competitively, and people send each other sweets through a delivery service. Samyuktha, Chennai

A number worth knowing

The government has approved the sale of a 60.7% stake in IDBI bank to Canadian Fairfax Holdings for Rs 52,878 crore (£4.22bn).

It’s hard to take one’s eyes off Muhammed Riswan when he’s at work. The 23-year-old football freestyler from Areekode in Kerala’s Malappuram district conjures tricks with the ball in a delicately choreographed dance. It glides between his feet, next it is rolling on to his back right before he leaps into the air to catch it with one hand.

Riswan, who’s been freestyling for eight years, is one of the two Indians to win Instagram Rings 2026 award recognising creators. The other is Chanel model Bhavitha Mandava.

Riswan’s big break came with a video filmed at Keralamkundu waterfall, where he pulled off a freestyle move before gracefully arching the ball into the water. The clip has since clocked more than 600m views. Last year, he was invited to watch his sporting idol, Lionel Messi, play in Argentina.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.author: Andrew Sparrow
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text:
Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, asks if the PM will support the proposal by the Lib Dem MP Josh Babarinde for people to be allowed to call themselves black English or Asian English on the census.

Davey says it is wrong to claim people have to be white to be English.

Shamefully, even some in this house have argued for this racist ideology. We must reject it as the Conservative leader, to her great credit, has done.

We should start with a census with the only English option, when you’re asked about your ethnicity, is white English.

[Babarinde] a proud Englishman, introduced a bill yesterday to change that to create new options like black English and Asian English. Will the prime minister support his bill?

Burnham says he has also praised Badenoch for her comments on race.

I haven’t looked at the detail of the bill, but I stand here thinking that I would want to support that bill to directly take on the poisonous politics that we’ve seen from some in this house who are seeking to divide us.

We must move on from a decade of division and drift in this country. We must bring people back together.

I am interested in working with anyone in this house who shares that name.

Kemi Badenoch is on record as saying she treats PMQs like panto. It is not a ridiculous view; in many respects, it is all about theatre and performance, the jokes matter (often they are all that anyone remembers by the end of the afternoon), and Badenoch started impressing her MPs (and wider audiences) when she abandoned an overly-analytical approach to PMQs, and started playing it for laughs, or Punch and Judy-style aggro, instead.

If you subscribe to the Badenoch thesis, today was one of her best outings against Burnham. She was consistently funny and withering, and delivered an effective put-down about Ed Miliband too. Her MPs seemed to like it, and on Tory social media she is getting predictably good reviews. This matters a bit; it is better than a Tory leader getting bad reviews in the Tory media.

And there are moments when a well-crafted joke can deliver a win at PMQs. When William Hague was in the job Badenoch is doing now, that happened most weeks.

But to convey mastery at PMQs, rather than just making people laugh, the humour has to be linked to a wider argument, and today it wasn’t. At least, it wasn’t linked to a wider argument that was compelling. Badenoch’s main challenge was about the Rosebank oilfield, and the government’s failure (yet) to approve it. Burnham could acceptably see this off with a reference to it being subjudice. Beyond that, Badenoch was essentially just running an ‘admit you’re useless’ diatribe. With some PMs, in some circumstances, that’s enough. But Burnham is not anywhere close to that point yet and so Badenoch’s questions just sounded like knee-jerk negativity – albeit artfully done.

For an alternative (and better) theory of PMQs, do read this thread from Theo Bertram, a former Labour No 10 adviser (in the Blair/Brown years) who now runs a thinktank. This is his conclusion:

I worked on 119 PMQs in No10 and I would observe that winning individual PMQs (because you landed a blow or a joke) matters less than establishing an argument over a term (eg. He didn’t fix the roof while the sun was shining). That’s how you win at PMQs in the long run.

On jokes, Badenoch is winning. But, on most or all of the main arguments, Burnham still has the upper hand. And on personality too he also has an advantage because he sounds fair and reasonable, as he did again today, which isn’t always a virtue associated with the opposition leader.

This is from my colleague Pippa Crerar on Kemi Badenoch saying at PMQs that the Treasury forecasts assume the Rosebank oilfield project will go ahead.

Kemi Badenoch says that chancellor John Healey had already banked the revenue from Rosebank oil field, which are expected to hit about £500m by the end of this parliament.

When we revealed this last month, Treasury officials told us the money had been included in forecasts from the OBR since 2019, and that doing so would not prevent the energy secretary from blocking it.

Julian Lewis (Con) asked a closed question (one tabled in advance, where the MP gets a follow-up, but it has to be on the subject previously agreed). His question was whether the threat from Russia now is as great as during the cold war years.

Compared to the cold war, rapid changes in technology, including AI, cyber warfare and autonomous systems mean we face new, complex threats.

Lewis urged the government to stop boasting about how it has increased military spending at the fastest rate since the end of the cold war. That claim does not take account of how the threat now is much greater than it was at the end of the cold war, he said.

Burnham insisted he was not compacent about the threat.

Labour’s Diane Abbott asked Burnham if he agreed “that we should never forget to honour the contribution of generations of immigrants to the society”.

[Abbott] speaks very powerfully on this issue from personal experience .. And I saw a people from around the world caring, for my dad. She is absolutely right to say that we must celebrate their contribution, as I did in my speech to the party conference.

And we must take on a politics that seeks to say to those people that they have no place here. They do.

Martin Rhodes (Lab) asked what the goverment was doing to tackle the problems caused by illegally-modified e-bikes.

Burnham said the government was considering “tougher regulations for the sale of non-compliant e-bikes and conversion kits across the UK”. He said:

The safety risks posed by e-bikes that are running at excess speeds need to be stopped.

Ian Sollom (Lib Dem) asks about a constituent who has been in a wheelchair since he was two and who needs care every day. Every pound he saves above £23,250 has to go into his care, he says. He asks the PM to remove this limit.

Burnham says this illustrates why the system needs to be reformed.

He says the rules are “unfair”. He says the minimum income guarantee for disabled adults is being increased.

And he says cross-party talks on social care will take place before the end of the year.

Jeremy Corbyn, the Your Party parliamentary leader, asks Burnham to ensure that more aid gets into Gaza. And he asks him to back an inquiry into Britain’s participation in “the bombardment of Gaza through his supply of weapons and security information to Israel”.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remains heartbreaking and we are doing everything that we can to put pressure on the Israeli government to allow the necessary aid into Gaza and to lift the restrictions on it.

Of course, we’ve also taken further steps in relation to sanctions, particularly, in relation to the settlements in the West Bank, to make sure that we preserve the viability of a two state solution.

We await the outcome of the negotiations following the Israeli, general election.

Burnham says Corbyn can be confident the government will follow the path it has set out.

He does not address the call for an inquiry.

Davey turns to Neets, and he says the single biggest thing to help the economy, which would get more young people into work, would be joining the single market.

Burnham says the deal he is agreeing with the EU will add 0.4% to GDP.

On Neets, he says one reason the situation is so bad for youth unemployment is because the last Tory government rejected the recommendations from Sir Kevan Collins, the Covid recovery tsar.

Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, asks if the PM will support the proposal by the Lib Dem MP Josh Babarinde for people to be allowed to call themselves black English or Asian English on the census.

Davey says it is wrong to claim people have to be white to be English.

Shamefully, even some in this house have argued for this racist ideology. We must reject it as the Conservative leader, to her great credit, has done.

We should start with a census with the only English option, when you’re asked about your ethnicity, is white English.

[Babarinde] a proud Englishman, introduced a bill yesterday to change that to create new options like black English and Asian English. Will the prime minister support his bill?

Burnham says he has also praised Badenoch for her comments on race.

I haven’t looked at the detail of the bill, but I stand here thinking that I would want to support that bill to directly take on the poisonous politics that we’ve seen from some in this house who are seeking to divide us.

We must move on from a decade of division and drift in this country. We must bring people back together.

I am interested in working with anyone in this house who shares that name.

Badenoch says Burnham does not seem to know about the legislation on the North Sea his government is passing. She says the government is “totally adrift”, and needs consultant to tell it what to think.

Meanwhile, the whole country is in limbo. Labour MPs want to pretend that Keir Starmer simply walked off into the sunset, when in reality this man knifed him in the back and now doesn’t know what to do.

Isn’t it the truth that they’re all sat there shaking their heads and wondering whether it was all worth it?

People at home will have heard that I am bringing forward a National Care Service when they ignored social care for years and years.

I am acting to get people’s energy bills down when they didn’t do it.

And I listen to her when she talks at the despatch box as though they’ve got everything right. A quarter of a million young people became Neet between 2021 and 2024, when she was in was in the cabinet. The welfare bill rose by £33bn in her last year in office, when she was in the cabinet.

When is she going to come to this house with real proposals to address those things, rather than repeating more of the same.

He says people will see his plans when the 10-year plan is published.

Badenoch says the government is legislating to ban drilling off Scotland. That is ludicrous, she says.

Burnham says the Jackdaw gas field has been approved. And the new windfarms are going ahead. He goes on:

If she wants to,address energy policy in this house, perhaps we can talk about why energy bills went up and up under the party opposite. Perhaps we can discuss how they lost public control and lost control of people’s bills and left people paying more and more.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: ITV to cut costs by £30m amid falling advertising sales
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Lauren Almeida
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Ad revenue slowdown forces company to reduce spending on content by £25m before inquiry into takeover by Sky

Business live – latest updates

ITV plans to cut costs by £30m this year, as the TV sector faces a chill wind of ditched commissions, falling advertising sales and job reductions.

The broadcaster, which has agreed to sell its television and streaming business to Sky, expects ad revenues in that division to fall between 5% and 10% in the crucial final quarter of the year, despite the typically busy Christmas season.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Ad sales are expected to drop between 2% and 3% over the course of the full year, ITV said.

The slowdown has pushed the company to make “temporary” savings, including £25m in content and £5m elsewhere in the business.

Content budget cuts will mostly affect small external commissions, pushing them into 2027, it is understood.

Carolyn McCall, the ITV chief executive, said demand for ads had weakened because of “continuing broader macroeconomic uncertainty” and “ increased digital advertising on global streaming platforms”. She also cited new rules this year that imposed a 9pm watershed on TV advertising for less healthy food.

Shares in ITV, which are listed on London’s FTSE 250 index, dropped by as much as 5% in early trading on Wednesday. It has lost about a fifth of its market value since the start of the year.

The business has struggled in recent years to keep up with deep-pocketed companies such as Netflix and YouTube, which have muscled in on traditional media’s audiences and commercial revenue.

Other mainstream broadcasters are also struggling, with the BBC intending to shed as many as 2,000 jobs and Channel 4 planning layoffs. ITV indicated the proposed cost savings would not involve staff cuts.

McCall has argued that the £1.6bn sale of its TV and streaming business to Sky is ITV’s route to survival.

However last week, the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, issued a public interest intervention notice, triggering an investigation by the media regulator, Ofcom, and the Competition and Markets Authority.

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

Nandy raised concerns that the combined broadcasters would account for about 86% of linear news and current affairs viewing in Britain, as well as concerns over potential US political influence on editorial independence. Sky is owned by the US broadcaster Comcast.

ITV said on Wednesday that the deal was “progressing as planned” and it was still expected to complete in the second half of 2027.

The sale will leave ITV with its studios business, which makes shows for ITV and other broadcasters and streamers.

The company told investors that studios revenue was down 1% in the first nine months of the year, but it had made five of the UK’s top 10 most-watched dramas in the third quarter of 2026, including The Gentlemen for Netflix and The Blame for ITV.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Bird flu fears prompt orders for farmers to keep poultry inside in England and Scotland
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Increased risk of devastating strain means restrictions imposed for second year in a row on those keeping birds

Poultry and captive birds across England and Scotland must be kept inside for the second year in a row due to an increased risk of a devastating strain of bird flu.

The British government has issued an England-wide avian influenza prevention zone, meaning individuals with 50 or more poultry or captive birds must house them inside. A similar designation was made across the whole of Scotland on Tuesday.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Birdkeepers must also follow enhanced biosecurity measures including reporting changes in egg production and reporting suspected disease immediately to the Animal and Plant Health Agency.

The government said the declaration followed an increased risk and escalating number of confirmations of the highly pathogenic avian influenza, or bird flu, in kept and wild birds.

A prevention zone was also declared across all of England, Scotland and Wales in 2025.

The disease has been spreading rapidly since 2014 and has devastated UK wild bird populations since the summer of 2021. It has also spread across an unusually broad range of species around the world, including in four of the five main southern elephant seal populations. In some south Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died, alongside about half of all adult females.

The disease has also been detected in humans, with 11 deaths recorded globally between 1 January and 4 August 2025.

This strain of bird flu causes illness and high death rates in birds, and flu-like symptoms and conjunctivitis in humans who come into close contact with infected animals.

The British government said the current risk to human health from bird flu remained very low.

The government says it does not anticipate an impact on the availability of Christmas turkeys or other seasonal poultry for consumers. The Food Safety Authority said properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, were safe to eat.

The UK chief veterinary officer, Christine Middlemiss, said: “Having avian influenza confirmed in your flock can be devastating. I understand the impact this disease can have on the poultry sector and am extremely grateful for the continued cooperation of the industry.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Tactics to include GPS tagging for repeat offenders, high street bans and tougher sentences

Five hundred of the most prolific shoplifters across England will be targeted in a police crackdown on retail crime, with tougher sentences, high street bans and GPS tagging.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said up to 17 police forces would target the repeat offenders in their area, collecting evidence of offences to secure stronger sentences and ensure they face “real consequences”, backed by an extra £2.5m in funding.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Tactics will include the expanded use of criminal behaviour orders – where repeat offenders are banned from high streets and town centres – GPS tagging and intensive supervision courts, where perpetrators must attend regular judicial hearings.

Those who do not comply or breach conditions will face imprisonment in the most serious cases, and foreign offenders could face deportation.

Mahmood said the government wanted to target people “who are causing so much harm to our communities”. She said: “A small number of offenders commit a disproportionate amount of shop theft. They wreak havoc on our high streets, leave businesses out of pocket and make retail workers scared to go to work.”

The government said it wanted to replicate the success of Operation Kelleher, a targeted crackdown on 10 shoplifters in Bromley in 2025 that reduced recorded retail crime in the area by 70%, according to Metropolitan police data.

The number of shoplifting offences recorded by police in England and Wales rose to the highest on record in 2024, surpassing half a million offences. Last year there was a 2% decline.

The Metropolitan police said 104 repeat offenders were responsible for more than 5,300 shoplifting crimes over the past two years.

Simon Roberts, the chief executive of Sainsbury’s, said retail crime was a “national emergency which requires a national response”. He said: “The number of incidents of theft, abuse, aggression and violence happening in stores right across the country has an unacceptable impact every single day.

“We now need to see more arrests and prosecutions of those who target UK retailers without fear of consequences and we look forward to working closely with authorities as these measures are put into action.”

Former shoplifters have spoken about how drug addiction and mental health problems are one of the main drivers of this type of crime, and charities have called for more funding for support services.

The government said the police crackdown would also be tough on the causes of crime by tackling drug and alcohol addiction “to break the cycle”.

Revolving Doors, a charity that helps to rehabilitate repeat offenders, said the scheme was a chance to “follow the evidence on what works, combining focused enforcement with sustained support to address the addiction, mental ill health and homelessness that can drive repeat offending. Success should mean fewer repeat offences and safer communities, alongside more people able to recover, contribute and realise their potential.”

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, said dealing with the small group of repeat offenders responsible for a disproportionate amount of crime was crucial. “Combining robust enforcement with targeted support to tackle the root causes could make a real difference to our high streets and communities,” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Thomas Markle, Meghan’s father, jailed after cutting off ankle monitor, DoJ says
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Estranged father of Duchess of Sussex was arrested for keeping child sexual abuse material, authorities say

The estranged father of Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, has been jailed after US authorities said he cut an electronic monitoring device off his ankle, days after his arrest for keeping child sexual abuse material in storage units in California.

Thomas Markle, 82, was in custody awaiting a hearing in federal court in Tampa, Florida, first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said. He was arrested shortly after he cut off the ankle bracelet at 1.45am on Tuesday, Essayli said.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions. We are asking the court to revoke his release and detain him pending trial, and we will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law,” Essayli said.

The US magistrate judge Lindsay Griffin agreed on Tuesday that Markle now must be kept in custody.

Markle’s arrest on Friday followed the seizure of approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images in storage in the Los Angeles area, Essayli said.

Among the alleged child sexual abuse material were sexually explicit photographs of Markle with underage girls, including one taken in what appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, Reuters reports.

According to the criminal complaint, the special agent investigating Markle’s alleged storage unit said he “viewed a collection of what appeared to be strips of 35mm film negatives seized from Storage Unit 1 registered to Markle”.

“To date, I have identified approximately 18 images that appeared to constitute child pornography,” the special agent noted in the complaint, adding that the investigation remains ongoing.

Markle reportedly had rented the storage units in Los Angeles since 2008, with the FBI noting that the most recent auto-payment for the units was on 14 October.

“Markle’s use of Storage Unit 1 was also corroborated by items found within the unit bearing his name, including boxes labeled ‘Tom Markle’ and an address within the central district of California,” the criminal complaint said.

During his arrest last week, he was taken from a senior care center in Lakeland, Florida, by ambulance. Hours later, a judge allowed Markle to be released on the condition that he be electronically monitored, which typically means wearing an ankle tether.

According to Griffin, Markle’s court appearance last Friday included a “lack of recall”. Griffin also cited Markle’s “health condition” and “advanced age” as part of his appearance.

The judge ordered a mental competency exam and a report by 20 November.

Griffin said she found “reasonable cause to believe” Markle was suffering from a condition “rendering him mentally incompetent to the extent that he is unable to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against him or to assist properly in his defense”, CBS reported.

His daughter, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, married Prince Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. She is an American citizen and actor who starred in the US television drama Suits.

Meghan recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to police in London in 2019.

“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”

Thomas Markle was living in the Philippines this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the US.

His arrest followed reports by the Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghan’s half-brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. That discovery led to information about two US storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.

Associated Press contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Thomas Markle, 82, was arrested on Friday for keeping child sexual abuse material in storage units in California. He was arrested shortly after he cut off the ankle bracelet at 1.45am on Tuesday. He is in custody awaiting a hearing in Tampa, Florida, first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: GOP branded ‘sinking ship’ as Republicans block efforts to impeach Hegseth – US politics live
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Shrai Popat (now) and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Republican representative Thomas Massie compared the GOP with passengers content to go down with the Titanic after colleagues thwarted his effort to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth.

The vote came a week after Republicans lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives in their worst midterm election in more than a half century, and underscored how lawmakers remain wary of crossing Donald Trump, who has signaled his continued support for Hegseth.

“They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay on board,” Massie, a Republican congressman who lost his primary after breaking with the president, said.

Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution, but Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee. Their motion succeeded on Tuesday, by a 211-204 vote, largely along party lines. Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the motion, along with all Democrats.

Trump, who was twice impeached, celebrated what he hailed as the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot” and lashed out at Massie for forcing the vote.

“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America,” Trump said on Truth Social. “They must be stopped!”

The Pentagon, meanwhile, declared “total victory”. “The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House judiciary committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter,” Sean Parnell, a department spokesperson, wrote in a social media post.

Some 11 Democratic representatives skipped the vote, the Daily Beast reported earlier this morning, causing the articles of impeachment to fail. Among those to miss the vote was Nancy Pelosi.

If eight of ‌them had voted with fellow Democrats the measure could have proceeded.

House Democratic leader Hakeen Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next ​Congress in January when the Democrats who triumphed in the midterm take their seats. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.

Read the full story here:

In other developments:

Congressman Jim Jordan, a Republican hardliner from Ohio, won the election to become the next House minority leader in Congress. Jordan beat Representative Steve Scalise, the current majority leader, by 106-73 in a closed-door vote to lead Republicans from January. He replaces the current House speaker, Mike Jonson, who said he would not run when the GOP cedes control to Democrats in the new year.

Meanwhile, Republicans in the upper chamber, re-elected John Thune to serve as Senate minority leader in the next Congress. The GOP senator from North Dakota didn’t face a challenger in the closed-door vote, as Democrats prepare for at least a 10-seat majority in the new year.

Nine members of the Kennedy family sued the Trump administration in an effort to block its construction of a 250-foot triumphal arch. The family’s complaint states that the arch, which is planned for near Arlington national cemetery, would obstruct the Kennedy gravesites, the JFK Eternal Flame and the sightlines of the cemetery, “permanently diminishing these memorials.”

A federal judge has allowed Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against the BBC to proceed. Trump is suing Britain’s publicly funded broadcaster for $10bn over an edited clip that made it appear that Trump told his supporters to storm the US Capitol on 6 January 2021.

Donald Trump is in Washington today.

In honor of veterans day, the president will head to Arlington National Cemetery with first lady Melania Trump for a wreath laying ceremony and to deliver remarks at 11am ET. After, Trump will be back in the White House for meetings.

If there was one obvious conclusion from Democrats’ sweeping victories in the mid-term elections on Tuesday, it seemed to be that the Republican effort to redraw congressional districts in their favor backfired.

Starting last summer, Trump and Republican allies undertook an aggressive effort to redraw congressional districts, reconfiguring the lines to give Republican candidates an advantage. Ahead of the midterms, Republicans redrew 15 seats to their advantage. After Tuesday’s election, they appear poised to lose all but two of them. “It was definitely the wrong move,” an unnamed House Republican told Fox News. “One of the truisms in politics is never to overreach. We did and that was part of the reason for the backlash.”

The Republicans losses included defeats in Texas, Florida and North Carolina where Republicans hoped to pick up as many as 10 combined congressional seats.

“The maps themselves did fail, and failed quite epically,” said John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, a Democratic redistricting group. “I would also argue the idea itself was an even bigger failure. Allowing an environment to be created around you in which everyone begins to realize how deeply corrupt this administration is and how fearful they are of the American people in elections, so much so that their main tactical path forward is going to be to redraw maps to steal as many voters as they can.”

But even though Republicans failed to pick up nearly all of the new seats they drew, it would be misleading to say that gerrymandering did not work at all in this election, said Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a professor at Harvard who studies redistricting. Republicans didn’t pick up the seats because Democrats had the strongest midterm elections in half a century.

The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has relocated from his home in the Washington area to a military base after an Iranian threat against his life, the New York Times has reported.

Bessent has spearheaded a US push to cripple Iran’s economy since the start of the Middle East war, vowing “economic asphyxiation” of the Islamic republic through a web of sanctions.

He is one of a number of senior figures in the Trump administration including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, to leave their home to live on a military base or protected housing.

The US national intelligence chief, Jay Clayton, said last month that Tehran had “substantially increased” its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond.

These include intensifying the targeting of current and former US officials such as Bessent, the NYT reported on Tuesday, citing three sources familiar with the matter.

Iranian plotting against US officials has reached a “more advanced stage”, according to the anonymous sources, but the severity of the threats against Bessent was unclear.

Washington ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia last month, after increasing attacks from Tehran-backed Houthi fighters.

The US military has also removed some aircraft from two British bases in recent weeks amid reported threats from Iran.

Jared Kushner ⁠and ⁠Steve Witkoff ​will travel to ⁠Moscow on Thursday, ⁠then ​meet ‌Ukrainian president ‌Volodymyr Zelenskyy ‌in Dublin after their trip to Russia, ‌Kushner said.

Kushner, US president Donald ⁠Trump’s son-in-law, ​said talks between ​Ukraine ​and ​Russia ‌in ​Abu ​Dhabi were a “first good step“.

Senator Bernie Sanders has confirmed that he will not be supporting senator Chuck Schumer as the Democratic majority leader in the new Congress, setting up a confrontation after the party’s sweep to power in the midterm elections.

Sanders was joined by Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan at a news conference at the Capitol, and together they said there needs to be a new generation of leadership and a vigorous debate about the party’s direction and future, AP reported.

A number of incoming Democratic senators have echoed the call, signaling that they would support another candidate over Schumer.

“The time is now for change,” said Sanders, the independent from Vermont and essentially the father of modern progressivism in the US. “And I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.”

Slotkin, who said she is not actively seeking the job herself, explained that she wants to see potential Senate leaders present a full plan about the priorities for the new majority. “I’m a no until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said.

The showdown has been building as Democrats swept across the Senate map to flip Republican-held seats far beyond those that were initially competitive, including in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.

Schumer recruited high-profile candidates that helped secure the majority, including senator-elect Sherrod Brown in Ohio and senator-elect Roy Cooper in North Carolina.

But his preferred candidates also lost primaries in Michigan and Maine, with the progressive candidates prevailing and then going on to win their general elections.

Nancy Pelosi was one of 11 Democratic politicians to miss the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote.

If just eight of them had turned up to vote with their colleagues, the motion would have passed and the articles for impeachment would have moved forward.

The other Democrats recorded as not voting were Julia Brownley, Lou Correa, Laura Gillen of New York, Steven Horsford of Nevada, Jonathan Jackson of Illinois, Brittany Pettersen of Colorado, Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico, Stevens of Michigan, Marilyn Strickland of Washington and Frederica Wilson of Florida, the Daily Beast reported.

House Republicans blocked an effort to impeach Hegseth, rejecting allegations that the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of the Iran war and other conflicts globally.

A motion to refer Thomas Massie’s eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth to committee passed in the House, 211-204.

The Pentagon declared “total victory” after the vote and Donald Trump celebrated the vote as an “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot”.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Republican representative Thomas Massie compared the GOP with passengers content to go down with the Titanic after colleagues thwarted his effort to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth.

The vote came a week after Republicans lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives in their worst midterm election in more than a half century, and underscored how lawmakers remain wary of crossing Donald Trump, who has signaled his continued support for Hegseth.

“They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay on board,” Massie, a Republican congressman who lost his primary after breaking with the president, said.

Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution, but Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee. Their motion succeeded on Tuesday, by a 211-204 vote, largely along party lines. Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the motion, along with all Democrats.

Trump, who was twice impeached, celebrated what he hailed as the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot” and lashed out at Massie for forcing the vote.

“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America,” Trump said on Truth Social. “They must be stopped!”

The Pentagon, meanwhile, declared “total victory”. “The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House judiciary committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter,” Sean Parnell, a department spokesperson, wrote in a social media post.

Some 11 Democratic representatives skipped the vote, the Daily Beast reported earlier this morning, causing the articles of impeachment to fail. Among those to miss the vote was Nancy Pelosi.

If eight of ‌them had voted with fellow Democrats the measure could have proceeded.

House Democratic leader Hakeen Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next ​Congress in January when the Democrats who triumphed in the midterm take their seats. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.

Congressman Jim Jordan, a Republican hardliner from Ohio, won the election to become the next House minority leader in Congress. Jordan beat Representative Steve Scalise, the current majority leader, by 106-73 in a closed-door vote to lead Republicans from January. He replaces the current House speaker, Mike Jonson, who said he would not run when the GOP cedes control to Democrats in the new year.

Meanwhile, Republicans in the upper chamber, re-elected John Thune to serve as Senate minority leader in the next Congress. The GOP senator from North Dakota didn’t face a challenger in the closed-door vote, as Democrats prepare for at least a 10-seat majority in the new year.

The family’s complaint states that the arch, which is planned for near Arlington national cemetery, would obstruct the Kennedy gravesites, the JFK Eternal Flame and the sightlines of the cemetery, “permanently diminishing these memorials.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jessica Glenza
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Country is in the middle of worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases nationally

The United States could lose its measles elimination status this week, an event likely to cement health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr’s legacy of meddling in vaccine policies amid the worst outbreak of the virus in the US in 35 years.

If the US loses its measles-free status, it would join Canada and several European and Asian nations that had eliminated the disease only for it to return.

“That is a tremendous step backwards,” said Dr Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center, an attending physician in the division of infectious diseases at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, and a prominent critic of Kennedy.

A panel of eight independent experts will consider the epidemiological evidence in Washington DC, part of a group called the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization (WHO). The PAHO director will make the final call.

“Independent of what PAHO says, measles is now endemic in the US. Measles has a foothold in the US,” said Offit. “We’re going to see it this year, we’re going to see it next year,” because the US “critically decreased the percentage” of people vaccinated.

The US is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak since 1991 with more than 5,400 cases nationally, according to the Johns Hopkins University International Vaccine Access Center tracker. Just this year, six people have died in Pennsylvania, a child died in New York on election day and an infant died in Wisconsin days later. Nearly every US state has an active outbreak.

Measles is considered one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine. The overwhelming majority of Americans vaccinate themselves and their children, but the sheer contagiousness of measles means even small dips in immunity allow it to spread. It kills one to three people per 1,000 people and hospitalizes about one-in-five unvaccinated people who are infected. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is 97% effective against the disease.

Although elimination status is a formal public health designation, its loss has real effects on everyday Americans. In just one example, Dr David Margolius, the Cleveland, Ohio,director of public health, is warning people to find proof of their measles vaccination in the event they’re exposed to a measles-positive patient.

“Now is the time to go and find that evidence, because now this is a real day-to-day life thing that could happen to you,” said Margolius, who is also a director-at-large of the Big Cities Health Coalition. Without proof, patients face either an immunology blood draw or a 21-day quarantine.

Cleveland health authorities have already done a tremendous amount of detective work this year to track down people exposed to measles patients in hospital waiting rooms and elevators.

“We reach out to people and for most people, including myself, we have no personal experience with measles,” he said. “They’ve got everything else going on in their life, and now they’re getting this call.”

The types of people who contract measles has also changed. In 1963, when the vaccine was first licensed, measles was considered a childhood disease. Most children contracted the disease by the age of five.

“Now you’re seeing the epidemiology shift,” said Offit. Two-thirds of people infected with measles in Pennsylvania are adults, a group on which researchers have little information. Mothers have even given birth to babies with measles. “Now, you’re seeing something we just didn’t see at all – congenital measles.”

The potential loss of elimination status comes at a tenuous moment for the Trump administration. Republicans just endured a historic drubbing in the midterm elections. Several new Democratic doctors and scientists are slated to come into Congress on promises to hold Kennedy accountable. At the same time, Trump has doubled down on his commitment to vaccine antagonism with the appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff.

“Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest Maha supporter in the administration,” Kennedy said in a statement about Miller’s appointment. “It’s time to unleash the Kraken.”

Meanwhile, the capacity of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to respond has been significantly hampered by the Trump administration. The agency has lost up to one-third of its staff, Kennedy has interfered in the agency’s reporting of measles deaths and has spread misinformation about the measles vaccines.

Even so, Margolius doesn’t lay all the blame at Kennedy’s feet. Vaccine hesitancy was increasing before Trump took office, and pandemic-era disruptions were real.

“Some of the narrative has been to pin this on our health secretary, which certainly I think he could do much more to help the situation rather than hurting the situation, but I do think the case count is climbing everywhere,” he said. “This could happen even under a more pro-public health administration.”

The second Trump administration also made broad changes that challenge measles elimination globally. Some of Trump’s first acts in 2024 included withdrawal from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Global Vaccine Alliance (GAVI). GAVI provides measles vaccines to nations such as India and Malawi. There are about 95,000 measles deaths globally, according to the World Health Organization, mostly in unvaccinated children under five years old.

At home, Republicans also enacted the largest ever federal cut to health insurance, changes expected to result in more than 17 million people losing insurance through 2034. That has challenged people such as Margolius, who struggle to connect people with vaccines when their health insurance coverage is unstable.

“Until we can rejoin the WHO and cooperate with other health agencies all over the world ... This will continue,” said Margolius.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Richard Trahant says accusers have been vindicated after Catholic church officially classifies Paul Hart as sex abuser

An attorney who was fined more than $400,000 after getting an abusive Roman Catholic priest removed as a New Orleans high school’s chaplain says it was “worth it” now that the church has officially classified the cleric as a clergy molester.

That remark from Richard Trahant came days after the archdiocese of New Orleans, having waited years, added Paul Hart on 6 November to a list of Catholic priests and deacons faced with credible claims of clergy abuse while serving in the area.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The late Hart had previously dismissed news coverage of his admitted but largely unpunished sexual misconduct with a 17-year-old girl he met in the course of his ministry as “bogus” and “made-up”. But, while continuing to implement the terms of an agreement to settle a bankruptcy protection case that it filed amid the fallout of the Catholic church’s worldwide clergy abuse scandal, the New Orleans archdiocese ultimately included Hart on a list of more than 100 credibly accused priests and deacons – vindicating those who spoke out against him and his religious superiors.

“This is the very definition of a Pyrrhic victory,” Trahant said, invoking a phrase for something achieved at a high cost. “Sure, it’s exoneration – yet only after I paid a fortune.

“But if the question is: was it worth it? The answer is yes, and I would do it again tomorrow.”

Hart and Trahant were at the center of one of the most contentious chapters of the New Orleans archdiocese’s bankruptcy, which the institution filed in 2020.

Trahant’s work representing clergy abuse claimants whose cases became ensnared in the archdiocesan bankruptcy gave him access to documents chronicling how Hart had secretly admitted to his supervisors that he had sexual contact with a 17-year-old girl in the early 1990s after meeting her through his role as a priest.

In 2012, she reported Hart to the church for that behavior and confessed to it during a confidential internal investigation, according to hundreds of legal documents obtained and reviewed by the Guardian.

An advisory board working with New Orleans’s archbishop at the time, Gregory Aymond, recommended removing Hart from public ministry, saying the case victimized someone who was considered a minor under canon – or church – law since 2002.

But Aymond let Hart continue his ministry because in the early 1990s the age of consent under canon law was 16. And Louisiana law sets the age of consent at 17.

Aymond then appointed Hart to serve as chaplain at Brother Martin after the New Orleans Catholic high school asked for one in 2017.

“Please know that I not only appreciate your ministry but will pray for you that God will use you to be a sign of pastoral care to our young people,” Aymond wrote to Hart after appointing him to Brother Martin, an all boys’ school where there are activities that girls can participate in.

Hart was still in that role toward the end of 2021 when Trahant became aware of his past. He notified Brother Martin’s principal – coincidentally, Trahant’s cousin – that Hart had “a credible allegation from [his] past that involved a minor”.

Also, Trahant emailed this journalist to keep Hart on his “radar”. But he would not elaborate to either Gallagher or this journalist, citing a bankruptcy court confidentiality order, according to the legal documents stemming from the case.

Aymond and the archdiocese soon provided Brother Martin with the details about Hart’s past misconduct. And he retired in January 2022, nine months before his death, after Brother Martin requested that Aymond remove him from its campus.

Meanwhile, using methods and sources exclusive of Trahant, this journalist wrote an article in New Orleans’s Times-Picayune newspaper detailing the circumstances of Hart’s departure – though the archdiocese insisted the priest had retired because of “struggles with treatment for brain cancer”.

The federal judge in charge of the archdiocese’s bankruptcy, Meredith Grabill, later ruled what Trahant had done set off a chain of events that was enough to constitute a confidentiality order violation. She fined him $400,000 – which eventually grew by $60,000 because of interest. And she expelled four of Trahant’s clients from a committee of clergy abuse survivors helping negotiate an archdiocesan bankruptcy settlement, contending that it would aid the group’s functioning.

Grabill so acted despite a court investigation which she ordered having determined that Brother Martin got the specifics about what Hart had done from the archdiocese – not Trahant, according to documents obtained by the Guardian.

Court investigators also conceded there was evidence supporting Trahant’s denial that he ever provided any confidential information to this journalist.

Trahant unsuccessfully appealed his fine from Grabill up to the US supreme court. But the supreme court declined to hear his case in June, months after Aymond’s retirement as New Orleans archbishop – so he paid the levy.

Aymond’s successor, archbishop James Checchio, on 6 November then added 27 priests and deacons to a list of credibly accused clergymen which the New Orleans archdiocese first released in 2018, calling it a step toward “accountability and healing”. The list now had 106 names after the update – a key provision of an agreement announced in December 2025 requiring the archdiocese and its insurers to eventually pay $305m to hundreds of clergy abuse survivors to resolve the bankruptcy.

Hart’s name being listed immediately leapt out at Trahant, he said.

The archdiocese said that records associated with Hart and all others on the credibly accused list would be kept at a public archive hosted by Louisiana State University. A release of such records for Hart would mean none of the information in them was ever confidential, according to Trahant.

Trahant also said he interpreted Hart’s inclusion on the credibly accused list – and a notation that he had three claims filed against him in the bankruptcy – as an admission that archdiocese and court officials had mishandled his case. Furthermore, he said it was perhaps the ultimate repudiation of one of Hart’s last known statements – telling bankruptcy court investigators that news media reporting on his departure from Brother Martin was “so bogus that it looked … almost made up”.

“He was lying,” said Trahant, mentioning that he is contemplating seeking further legal action out of principle to attempt to recoup his fine and the costs he incurred fighting it. “And … now they’ve admitted [it].”

Separately, one of the Trahant clients who was ousted from the bankruptcy settlement committee said Checchio could “truly” promote accountability by apologizing to the advocate and returning the fine money to him.

“At least [now], everyone knows that we were wrongly removed,” James Adams said. “The court sanctioned an innocent lawyer and his clients.”

Move comes as chipmaker reels from reports its CEO was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

Business live – latest updates

Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy.

The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. Wachtell’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Nvidia did not give a timeframe for the investigation but the company has said Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded “without interruption”.

The company is reeling from an espionage scandal after reports that its chief executive had been having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was also an Nvidia customer.

The US ambassador to China, David Perdue, said: “The situation with Nvidia is another reminder that we have to stay diligent.

“National security is part of this economic conversation because economic security is national security. And so, what we’re doing with China is bumpy right now,” he told Bloomberg Television.

Nvidia had at first denied an improper relationship with the Chinese citizen, who is no relation to the Nvidia boss, but Huang then admitted on Sunday he had been unfaithful to his wife – without referring directly to Ms Huang.

On the same day Nvidia announced an investigation into reports that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. The scandal has wiped $430bn off Nvidia’s value as shareholders gauge the potential impact of the scandal on a company and an executive who are synonymous with the AI boom.

Wachtell is one of the most prestigious corporate law firms in the US. Its founding partner Martin Lipton invented the “poison pill defence” in the 1980s, a corporate gambit that helps companies ward off hostile takeovers.

Technically called the “shareholder rights plan”, the poison pill allowed investors to buy more shares at a discount if one shareholder acquired a certain percentage of the company’s stock. This made it harder for corporate raiders to acquire a company without the board’s approval.

The firm was closely involved in the takeover of Getty Oil by Texaco. This was the largest corporate takeover in history at the time, although it turned sour when the thwarted suitor Pennzoil sued Texaco and won.

In 2008, a team of Wachtell lawyers advised the US Treasury department on the takeover of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac during the financial crisis.

The company was founded in the 1960s and is said to be the most profitable law firm in the US. It pulled in revenues of $5.1m per lawyer last year and made profits of $12m per partner, the highest profits per partner ever, according to the Am Law 100 rankings.

From 2017 to 2018, Kim was the acting US attorney for the southern district of New York, where he ran a team of lawyers investigating securities and commodities fraud, mail and wire fraud, public and private corruption, money laundering, cybercrime, and tax offences.

That included the case of the former US representative Anthony Weiner, who was sentenced to 21 months in prison for sending obscene material to a minor.

He also oversaw the prosecution of the banker Mehmet Hakan Atilla, who was convicted in 2017 of helping to evade US sanctions on Iran.

Another high-profile assignment landed on Kim’s desk in 2021, when he investigated multiple allegations of sexual harassment by the then New York governor, Andrew Cuomo.

One analyst has put Huang’s chances of leaving Nvidia at 15%.

“Right now the Street and investor chatter is assigning roughly a 15% chance he is removed as CEO of Nvidia with a high probability (85%) he stays on as CEO after the board investigation is completed,” wrote the tech analyst Dan Ives in a note to investors. “We would expect a board investigation that could take four weeks to six weeks and will create a clear overhang on the stock until more news emerges from Nvidia.”
