https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How Republican efforts to redraw congressional maps ‘failed epically’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
But, says one expert, it would be misleading to say that gerrymandering did not work at all in this election

I
f there was one obvious conclusion from Democrats’ sweeping victories in the mid-term elections on Tuesday, it seemed to be that the Republican effort to redraw congressional districts in their favor backfired.

Starting last summer, Trump and Republican allies undertook an aggressive effort to redraw congressional districts, reconfiguring the lines to give Republican candidates an advantage. Ahead of the midterms, Republicans redrew 15 seats to their advantage. After Tuesday’s election, they appear poised to lose all but two of them. “It was definitely the wrong move,” an unnamed House Republican told Fox News. “One of the truisms in politics is never to overreach. We did and that was part of the reason for the backlash.”

The Republicans losses included defeats in Texas, Florida and North Carolina where Republicans hoped to pick up as many as 10 combined congressional seats.

“The maps themselves did fail, and failed quite epically,” said John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, a Democratic redistricting group. “I would also argue the idea itself was an even bigger failure. Allowing an environment to be created around you in which everyone begins to realize how deeply corrupt this administration is and how fearful they are of the American people in elections, so much so that their main tactical path forward is going to be to redraw maps to steal as many voters as they can.”

But even though Republicans failed to pick up nearly all of the new seats they drew, it would be misleading to say that gerrymandering did not work at all in this election, said Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a professor at Harvard who studies redistricting. Republicans didn’t pick up the seats because Democrats had the strongest midterm elections in half a century.

“Compared to [GOP] dreams of winning like five more seats, all of these maps under-delivered,” he said. “There’s no reason why the best-case scenario of the gerrymander is the right baseline.” Compared to a fair map that didn’t favor either party, he added, “a lot of these maps performed very well for Republicans.”

It would be a mistake to interpret the election results to mean that gerrymandering is not a problem, Bisognano said.

“Democrats should not have needed to overperform by 10 to 15% in order to find the success that they found,” he said. “It’s a corrosive problem that still plagues this country regardless of these electoral outcomes, and they’re going to come back with more of it.”

In Texas, for example, Republicans already held 25 of the state’s 38 congressional districts. Last year, they redrew the map to try and gain as many as five new congressional seats. They wound up winning just one of the districts they redrew.

That means Texas will hold 24 of the state’s 38 congressional districts, even though Democrats Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico got more than 50% of the vote statewide.

“Nobody should think gerrymandering failed when Republicans are winning 65% of the seats in Texas with 45% of the vote. That’s a massive victory for a gerrymander,” Stephanopoulos said.

Adam Kincaid, a Republican mapmaker who drew the Texas maps, said he always saw the seats redrawn for Republicans to pick up in Texas as competitive seats. “The pickup opportunities were not deep, deep red seats. And that was on purpose, because in a cycle like this, you didn’t want to put incumbents in jeopardy going into the fall that otherwise wouldn’t have been in jeopardy,” he said.

There may be no state that had more of a gerrymandering backfire for Republicans than North Carolina.

Republicans already held 10 of the state’s 14 congressional seats, and then redrew them last year to add an additional Republican seat. The new map made it harder for Don Davis, a Black Democrat in the north-eastern part of the state, to win re-election. Davis won re-election and Democrats may flip as many as six seats, giving them a 10-4 advantage in the state’s delegation. Several Democrats barely won their races, even though Roy Cooper, a Democrat running for US Senate, won his race by nearly 20 points.

In North Carolina, Republican lawmakers drew their advantage by efficiently distributing Republican votes efficiently – giving each GOP district a solid firewall that was durable under usual election conditions. But when the generationally large Democratic wave hit in the state, it completely overwhelmed the map. “The point is not to protect from the flood, it’s to protect from the wave,” Kincaid said.

“With any gerrymander, there’s literally some electoral tide that’s big enough to overwhelm the gerrymander. You almost never see that tide,” Stephanopoulos said. “North Carolina got the once-in-a-50-year wave that happened to wash out their gerrymander.”

Even though the unprecedented Democratic wave neutralized gerrymanders this election, they are poised to give Republicans an advantage in future elections this decade should the electoral environment shift back in their favor.

“In Florida and in Texas and in numerous other places, if we snap back to a more neutral electoral environment in 2028 or 2030, like a lot of these districts will just flip right back to Republicans,” Stephanopoulos said.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Republicans redrew 15 seats to their advantage in the mid-term elections. The GOP lost 15 seats in Texas, Florida and North Carolina. The maps themselves did fail, and failed quite epically, says one expert.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How a small, newly socialist US city became the second to cut ties with Israel
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Claire Wang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Voters in Providence, Rhode Island, chose to pull foreign investments from countries that profit from genocide

The tectonic blue wave that washed over the country in last week’s midterms also brought about a historic night for the pro-Palestine movement.

Up and down the ballot, candidates who demanded an end to Israel’s war in Gaza resoundingly defeated opponents funded by the pro-Israel lobbying group American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).

Providence, meanwhile, became the second American city to divest from Israel. Voters in the Rhode Island capital approved a ballot measure last Tuesday requiring the city to refrain from investing in foreign countries that profit from “genocide, apartheid, ethnic cleansing and prolonged military occupation”.

Passing with 75% of the vote, the victory aligns with public opinion’s souring on the Israeli government. One-third of Americans – including a similar share of Jews – say Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians, and more than half say they want the government to stop sending weapons to Israel, according to recent polls. Organizers say the success of Providence’s ballot strategy is built on both the broad public support for divestment and a canvassing operation that can be replicated by pro-Palestinian groups in other cities.

“When we were out on the streets, we were overwhelmed by the positive results, by people who were so thankful to have a meaningful opportunity to do something about Palestine,” said Adit Sabnis, a graduate student at Brown University and local union organizer with the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), one of the groups that led the Providence ballot push. “This is an overwhelmingly pro-Palestine and anti-genocide city.”

The Providence for Palestine campaign launched a little less than a year ago with just 40 volunteers, said Zack Kligler, an organizer with Jewish Voice for Peace – Rhode Island. Led by the local chapters of Jewish Voice for Peace, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), AFT and American Muslims for Palestine, as well as the local housing justice organization Reclaim RI, the group decided to pursue a ballot strategy after traditional legislative efforts failed.

In 2024, then-mayor Brett Smiley and other city councilors blocked an ordinance to divest from companies with Israeli ties, and officials at Brown University, an Ivy League school in the city, rejected a similar student-led proposal. At least $2.5m in city funds were invested in companies directly profiting from what organizers call a genocide in Gaza and Israeli apartheid. The city also held more than $2m in Israeli bonds as recently as 2022.

Over the spring and summer, the coalition collected more than 10,000 signatures – twice the required threshold to qualify the measure. Organizers then built out an enormous canvassing operation, with nearly 300 volunteers stationed at street corners, businesses and community events across the city. Leading up to the midterms, they knocked on 17,000 doors, made 18,000 phone calls and talked to 30,000 neighbors about what’s happening in Gaza and what divestment entails.

Jackie Goldman, an incoming Providence city councilor and key organizer for the divestment measure, said few voters at the start of the campaign season knew of the city’s investments in companies with Israeli ties. But upon learning about the ballot initiative, Goldman said, most people were eager to support and saw divestment as “an empowering action”.

Though a broad coalition of Providence residents came together in support of divestment, the campaign was powered by many Jewish organizers and voters.

“It’s a demonstration that the idea that US Jews are in line behind Israel is just absolutely false,” said Kligler. “We ended up mobilizing Jews across the city, and we won every ward, including the most heavily Jewish ones.”

Organizers say the overwhelming success of the measure was bolstered by the electoral victories of a slate of progressive, pro-Palestinian candidates in the city’s September primary, including Goldman and mayor-elect David Morales, a DSA-backed challenger who defeated Smiley. Both candidates gathered signatures for the measure while canvassing for their own campaigns.

But rather than pro-Palestinian groups endorsing specific candidates, Kligler said, Providence has shown that advocates themselves can take a more proactive role in shaping legislation: “This is a case of not just the movement getting behind candidates – it’s the movement forwarding its own policy priorities and pulling candidates behind it.”

Kligler said one of the top priorities for Providence organizers was creating a replicable blueprint for other cities. The Providence for Palestine coalition posted a call on Instagram encouraging organizers across the country to reach out and discuss the lessons and tactics from the city’s win. Kligler said the coalition was not actively working on another ballot effort yet, but organizers in different cities had reached out.

Providence organizers themselves studied ballot efforts in Somerville, Massachusetts – the first US city last year to vote to divest from Israel – and Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where a divestment referendum was blocked by a legal challenge. Kligler said Pittsburgh organizers were especially helpful in providing guidance on how to check that addresses were correctly written and petitions were signed in acceptable colors so that they couldn’t be disqualified based on a technicality.

Also on election night, officials in Palm Beach county, Florida – the world’s largest local government investor in Israeli bonds – voted not to reinvest $67.5m in bonds that had matured on 1 November. The decision followed months of sustained organizing from local activists with the “Our Taxes, Our Needs” campaign, who sued the county and showed up in droves to board meetings, putting pressure on officials.

Advocates are looking to block three more investments in Palm Beach that are set to expire over the next couple of years, said Lydia Ghuman, executive director of the Internationalist Law Center, which has been leading the county’s effort to divest from Israel. The next step is to pass policies redirecting these bond investments into housing, education, healthcare and other local needs – a more appropriate use of taxpayer funds than enabling violence, Ghuman said.

“The compass that fuels us is injustice,” she said, “but these are also just poor investments, especially in Florida, where many people work three jobs.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Providence, Rhode Island, voted to pull foreign investments from countries that profit from genocide. The city's victory aligns with public opinion’s souring on the Israeli government. Providence became the second American city to divest from Israel.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Project 2025 had a plan to target federal data. The Trump administration obeyed
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Amy Qin and Flávio Pessoa
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Hundreds of datasets and websites that contradict government’s ideology have been altered or wiped – a tactic taken straight from Heritage Foundation’s policy blueprint

Even amid Donald Trump’s failures – the Iran war, soaring prices and a sharp rebuke in the midterm elections last week – there’s still at least one area his administration continues to carry out adeptly: its mass public information censorship campaign.

In less than two years, the Trump administration has done staggering damage to US data and information infrastructure. Hundreds of federal datasets have been terminated or altered, and thousands of government webpages that address diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), the climate crisis and other issues have been quietly revised or completely wiped.

This under-the-radar censorship isn’t random – it’s been squarely aimed at any information that contradicts the administration’s ideology.

As a new Guardian analysis shows, much of what has been targeted so far comes directly from Project 2025, the 900-page Heritage Foundation policy blueprint for a rightwing overhaul of the federal government.

The Guardian reviewed all of Project 2025, and found nearly 100 proposals to distort government data, research and guidance. The Trump administration has already implemented most of them, a clear indication, critics say, of how necessary narrative control is for the broader conservative political project.

“This administration is using information control as a means of achieving their agenda,” said Gretchen Gehrke, co-founder of the non-profit Environmental Data & Governance Initiative, which has closely followed the suppression of scientific information under the Trump administration.

During the 2024 presidential election, Project 2025 was seen as so extreme that even Trump tried to distance himself from it.
Turn audio on

Now, many of the recommendations to rollback LGBTQ+ rights, deregulate polluters and expand executive power have become reality.
This is also true for Trump’s war on information.
Turn audio on

The Guardian reviewed Project 2025 and found at least 92 calls to delete data, censor scientific information, repeal transparency laws, or abolish entire offices that conduct taxpayer-funded research.
Turn audio on

The recommendations span dozens of executive agencies.
Turn audio on

The Trump administration has already executed many of these recommendations.
Turn audio on

In the first few pages, Project 2025 called for the elimination of terms such as “sexual orientation", ”DEI”, and “gender equality”.
Trump issued an executive order soon after the inauguration to remove this same language from hundreds of datasets.
Turn audio on

Project 2025 also recommended ending data collection on the ownership structures of shell companies, a requirement that helps crackdown on money laundering.
The treasury department terminated it this summer.
Turn audio on

Project 2025 also called for the deletion of references to the climate emergency from federal research programs.
The EPA deleted its website dedicated to climate research, and the Trump administration dismissed hundreds of scientists who worked on the National Climate Assessment, the country’s flagship report on global heating in the US.
Turn audio on

Project 2025 recommended terminating crash reporting for self-driving cars.
The transportation department has since revised its regulations to limit the types of crashes required to be reported to a federal highway safety agency.
Turn audio on

Another 42 recommendations to delete, alter or censor data appear to be in progress, such as this proposal for a civil rights agency to stop collecting race and ethnicity data.
Turn audio on

The administration is attempting to reshape the 2030 census by excluding some immigrants from the survey and eliminating questions about race and ethnicity.
These changes were also outlined in Project 2025.
Turn audio on

There are also a few proposals to expand data collection as a way to further the administration’s goals.
One of them mandates more data collection on abortions to justify cracking down on blue states.
Turn audio on

Experts who reviewed the Guardian’s findings say they are alarmed at how effectively the Trump administration has carried out Project 2025’s proposals.

“You can see so clearly the specificity with which a policy was recommended in Project 2025 and the specificity with which it was carried out,” said Amy Friedrich-Karnik, who has tracked Project 2025 as federal policy director at the Guttmacher Institute.

But Friedrich-Karnik and other experts say they aren’t surprised at how quickly the Trump administration has followed through.

“If you are an administration that is focused on taking away people’s rights and on limiting people’s access to healthcare, then it follows you don’t want scientific evidence and data to be available to people. Because if you start chipping away at people’s faith in institutions, then you can fill the void with disinformation that’s really detrimental to people’s health and wellbeing.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The Guardian also reached out to the Heritage Foundation for comment but did not receive a response.

Another reason the Trump administration has targeted data and information is because it’s an easy lever for the executive branch to pull, said James Goodwin, policy director at the Center for Progressive Reform who has closely followed the implementation of Project 2025.

“One of the horrifying realizations of the second Trump term is just how much unfettered control presidents have over the data resources and data infrastructure that are spread throughout the federal government,” Goodwin said.

Following last week’s midterm elections, when Democrats overwhelmingly regained control of the House and Senate, experts say there’s now an opportunity to critically examine Project 2025 as a blueprint for upcoming investigative and legislative priorities: how exactly did the Trump administration take down information? What gaps in data protection were exploited?

“Project 2025 will be a useful diagnostic tool for leading congressional oversight because it allows them to reverse engineer everything that’s transpired over the past two years,” Goodwin said.

The Guardian’s Deleted data series explores how critical US government information is being deleted and what the consequences will be, and will preserve or recreate lost datasets. If you know about any datasets, webpages or government materials that have been deleted or altered in the past year, or are willing to share how those changes affect you, we’d love to hear from you. Please reach out at deleted-data@theguardian.com.

Trump-appointed judge Jeffrey T Kuntz partially denies British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss over edit

Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case. The president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit stems from the BBC’s splicing together of disparate comments he made before the 6 January US Capitol insurrection, as rendered in a Panorama documentary called Trump: A Second Chance.

“Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the Court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm,” the Trump-appointed Florida district court judge wrote. “It would be difficult for the Court to accept a different framing without completely negating the significance and fragility of political elections.”

Not signed in before? Create an account

The judge noted the significance of the documentary’s editing decision, which spliced together comments made by Trump that were nearly 55 minutes apart, something the BBC has apologized for.

“On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice,” he wrote. “BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.”

The judge continued: “Editing is often required. However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech.”

The judge noted past errors in the broadcaster’s coverage and wrote that “such examples can be said to be probative of BBC’s state of mind as it pertains to recklessness in light of BBC’s non-action toward false statements about Trump. Thus, Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump.”

The judge also wrote that “Trump’s allegations regarding BBC’s departure from journalistic standards are more than enough to plausibly alleged more than mere negligence”.

The BBC released a statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.”

Trump heralded the ruling on Truth Social, calling it a “huge victory”. “We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” Trump said.

While the judge determined that Trump had “sufficiently pleaded” that the BBC acted with actual malice, the legal standard for a public figure to win a defamation case, he will have to actually prove they did so at trial.

The judge also dismissed Trump’s claim that the BBC violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

And the judge determined that the president will have to prove that he suffered “actual damages” from the airing of the document, which was not broadcast in Florida.

In late October, a Florida magistrate judge ruled that Trump will have to sit for a deposition conducted by lawyers for the BBC by 11 December or else he could be hit with sanctions.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: House Republicans block effort to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Trump ally, accused of an array of illegal acts, had earlier condemned impeachment push as ‘a farce and a stunt’

House Republicans on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, rejecting allegations that the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of the Iran war and other conflicts globally.

The vote came a week after Republicans lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives in their worst midterm election in more than a half century, and underscored how lawmakers remain wary of crossing Donald Trump, who has signaled his continued support for Hegseth.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman who lost his primary after breaking with the president, had proposed impeaching Hegseth in September, alleging an array of illegal acts, including killing civilians in Iran, launching unauthorized operations in Venezuela and Yemen, and retaliating against a Democratic senator.

Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution, but Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee. Their motion succeeded on Tuesday, by a 211-204 vote, largely along party lines. Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the motion, along with all Democrats.

Trump, who was twice impeached, celebrated what he hailed as the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot’ and lashed out at Massie for forcing the vote.

“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America,” Trump said on Truth Social. “They must be stopped!”

The Pentagon, meanwhile, declared “total victory”.

“The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House judiciary committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter,” Sean Parnell, a department spokesperson, wrote in a social media post.

Tuesday’s vote is unlikely to be the final word on efforts to remove Hegseth from office, after Democrats won decisive majorities in the November midterm elections. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take control of the chamber in January, has backed the push to impeach Hegseth, accusing the embattled secretary of having “undermined America’s national security”.

In an interview with PBS on Tuesday, Jeffries said he was “a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution”.

“He’s abused his power. He’s undermined our national security. And Pete Hegseth is the architect of this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has made our country less safe and made life more expensive for the American people,” Jeffries told the news outlet.

The resolution’s downfall took place hours after Hegseth held a defiant press conference at the Pentagon, where he dismissed the impeachment effort as a “political spectacle” orchestrated by the ousted Kentucky congressman.

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.

The conflict with Iran has proven divisive with Republicans, and ahead of the midterms, small but growing numbers voted with Democrats on war powers resolutions intended to force Trump to bring the hostilities to a close. Warren Davidson, one of the House Republicans who voted for such resolutions, said he nonetheless rejected the idea of impeaching Hegseth.

“It’s an effort to blame-shift on to Hegseth Congress’s failure and President Trump’s decision,” Davidson said in an interview.

“I think Hegseth has been incredibly effective at restoring morale for the active-duty force, restoring the warrior ethos, the proper focus to the military that they exist to fight and win wars.”

The defense secretary, a former Fox News host and army national guard officer, has been one of the most pugnacious members of Trump’s second term cabinet, and taken an unusually heavy handed approach to managing the US military. Hegseth has orchestrated the departure of top generals, blocked the promotions of scores of officers, many of them women and people of color, and implemented new rules that prompted much of the press corps to leave the Pentagon.

He has also become the public face of some of the administration’s most politically costly policies, particularly the Iran war, which has dragged on for months while putting upward pressure on petroleum prices and played into Democrats’s hands in last week’s midterms.

Massie’s resolution outlined eight alleged violations of the constitution by Hegseth, including attacking Iran without first seeking Congress’s permission, and spurning a war powers resolution the House and Senate approved in June that would require an end to the conflict.

It also accused Hegseth of “ignoring” laws that would have minimized civilian casualties, and specifically cites a US strike on a school in Minab, Iran, that killed more than 168 people. Other articles allege Hegseth violated the constitution with the “extrajudicial killings” of at least 221 people on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean sea and eastern Pacific ocean, and of “suppressing free speech” through his retaliation against the Democratic senator Mark Kelly for his criticism of the secretary.

The final two impeachment articles target Hegseth’s involvement in the military operation that captured Venezuela’s then president, Nicolás Maduro, and a bombing campaign in Yemen that began shortly after Trump returned to the White House.

Had the impeachment resolution passed, it would have had to be approved by the Senate, which Republicans control by a 53-seat margin. It is unclear if it would have had enough votes to pass, or if the Republican leader John Thune would have even put it up for consideration.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The Pentagon declared ‘total victory’ for Pete Hegseth, the Department of War and the American warfighter. The House Republicans blocked the resolution by referring it to the judiciary committee.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Republicans elect Jim Jordan as House minority leader after midterm defeats
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Republicans pick Jordan as House leader and John Thune as Senate leader for last two years of Trump’s presidency

US politics – live updates

Republicans have elected veteran congressman Jim Jordan as their new leader in the House of Representatives, putting a strident defender of Donald Trump at the helm of their conference as they navigate the fallout from sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections.

Jordan will serve as minority leader under the new Congress that begins next year, where Democrats will have their largest margins in both the House and Senate in years. He will be responsible for shaping the party’s strategy against the waves of investigations Democrats have promised to open into Trump’s second administration, as well as their vows of an ambitious legislative agenda, regardless of whether it has the president’s support.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said in brief remarks to reporters after his elections. “When Democrats offer more government, we’ll offer more freedom, and we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor, and on the stump every single day.”

The Ohio lawmaker is a longtime leader of the right wing in the US House, and gained national renown for standing up for Trump against earlier efforts by Democrats to hold him to account. In 2023, Jordan was briefly a candidate for speaker after dissident Republicans removed Kevin McCarthy as the chamber’s leader, but his bid collapsed after it became clear he did not have enough support.

House Republicans elected Jordan over Steve Scalise, who serves as majority leader in the current Congress. Following comprehensive defeats last week in the midterm elections, the current House speaker, Mike Johnson, announced he would not remain in leadership, and has thus far not committed to serving out the rest of his term.

“Jim was a mentor of mine when I first came to Congress 10 years ago, and we worked alongside one another all these years,” Johnson said. “He’s always been regarded as a leader by the conference, and he’s going to do an extraordinary job.”

Jordan will serve alongside John Thune, the Republican Senate leader who also won re-election from his conference on Tuesday.

“I’m proud of what this Republican team has accomplished together, and we remain united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats’ efforts to enact their far-left, liberal agenda,” Thune said in a statement.

Elections for both roles were held in behind-closed-door meetings.

Ahead of the House GOP’s meeting, several spoke of the need for a change in strategy, after two years spent trying to answer Trump’s demands with one of the smallest majorities in history, only to have voters decisively remove them from power.

“I want somebody that’s going to message and admit that … we made mistakes,” said Tim Burchett, a conservative lawmaker from Tennessee, who declined to say who he would be voting for.

Florida congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna said she was backing Jordan, and blamed Scalise for not fighting hard enough to get rightwing priorities through the chamber.

“If you have a play and you get destroyed, you don’t put the same people back in charge that were part of running that failed play,” she said.

First elected in 2006, Jordan helped found the rightwing House Freedom Caucus in 2015, and served as its first chair. Seen almost always in shirtsleeves, his profile rose during Trump’s first term, particularly after Democrats regained control of Congress’s lower chamber in the 2018 midterms. As the top Republican on the oversight and then the judiciary committees, Jordan made energetic stands against efforts by Democrats to investigate Trump, and served as a member of the president’s defense team during his first impeachment.

Jordan echoed Trump’s false claims of fraud in the 2020 election, and championed the investigation of Hunter Biden during Joe Biden’s final two years in office. Since Trump returned to the White House, Jordan has used his role as judiciary committee chair to pursue allegations of “weaponization” by prosecutors who investigated Trump, including Jack Smith, the special counsel who oversaw the federal cases.

Democrats decried Jordan’s appointment as sign that the party was doubling down on extremism, with Virginia congressman Don Beyer noting that Jordan’s election came days after Trump had named immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff.

“Republicans learned absolutely nothing from what happened a week ago, and are responding by elevating their most extreme voices to positions of power,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Bernie Sanders says he will not back Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Progressive senator says ‘I like Chuck … but the time is now for change’ as calls grow for new Democratic leadership

Bernie Sanders, a progressive senator from Vermont, said on Tuesday he would not support Chuck Schumer’s bid to serve as the Democratic leader in the US Senate, joining a growing cohort of Democrats calling for a change in leadership.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

Not signed in before? Create an account

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders told reporters on Capitol Hill.

Sanders, 85, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, pointed to the results of the midterm elections as proof that voters want to see different leaders in charge.

“If this campaign was about anything, it was about change, the need for the Democratic party, in my view, to move in a new and bold direction,” Sanders said.

Speaking at a post-election conference in Washington on Tuesday, Democratic senator Chris Van Hollen said voters’ desire for change was clear.

“I think the question is whether those calls are being heard within the walls of the Senate Democratic caucus,” Van Hollen said during a live interview at the conference, convened by the progressive organization Groundwork Collaborative.

Some have pointed to the Maryland senator as a potential successor to Schumer. Van Hollen said he was calling colleagues to gauge their support for leadership change.

While he stopped short of calling for Schumer’s ouster, Van Hollen said the election “should not be coronation”.

“The Senate Democratic caucus needs a little bit of democracy itself in this moment,” he added.

Calls for fresh leadership in the Democratic party have grown louder since 2024, when Joe Biden ended his re-election campaign over concerns about his age. But the party’s sweeping wins in the midterm elections have renewed energy toward enacting change.

Elissa Slotkin, a moderate Democratic senator from battleground Michigan, encouraged anyone interested in leading the Democratic caucus to come forward with a plan.

“I think it is very clear that, on election night, the American people voted for change,” she said, noting that she was not actively seeking the Senate majority leadership position.

A group of high-profile incoming Democratic senators have voiced their desire for new leadership.

That includes Abdul El-Sayed, the senator-elect from Michigan, who beat a Schumer-backed Democrat to win the party’s nomination, as well as Adam Hamilton, the senator-elect from Kansas, Annie Andrews, the senator-elect from South Carolina, Chris Pappas, the senator-elect from New Hampshire, Troy Jackson, the senator-elect from Maine and Peggy Flanagan, the senator-elect from Minnesota.

But so far, no Democrat has volunteered to take on Schumer, who has served as the leader of the Senate Democrats since 2017.

Sanders told reporters he wants Democrats to elect a new leader through a “process” including “vigorous debate”.

Meanwhile, Schumer has remained confident that he will be re-elected Senate majority leader. The New York senator told reporters last week: “I’ll be re-elected as majority leader.”

He reiterated his confidence on Tuesday, telling reporters: “I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war.”

“We have great unity in our caucus and I will be proud to lead it as majority leader,” Schumer said in response to Sanders and Slotkin’s announcements.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: For Trump, Musk and Farage, the message is the same: voters don’t want to be hijacked by billionaires | Rafael Behr
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Rafael Behr
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A lesson from the US midterms is that electorates are repelled by the arrogant mega-rich buying democracy. This is a fight Labour can afford to pick

For most people, $224m (£168m) is a lot of money, especially if you spend it and get nothing in return. But Elon Musk is richer than most people. In fact, there is no one richer.

As the wealthiest of the US’s tech oligarchs Musk could afford to blow huge sums on a failed bid to prop up Republican candidates in Texas, his adoptive home state, in last week’s midterm congressional elections. He is reported to have spent a further $250m failing to engineer results in other races.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

His riches plausibly swung voters the other way in Texas. James Talarico, who last week became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988, made defiance of Musk’s meddling a rallying cry in his campaign.

In political campaigns, as in other forms of marketing, it isn’t always easy to know what kind of spending moves the dial or how far. But donors wouldn’t donate if they thought the result was beyond their powers of procurement. In the US, that market is out of control and the sums involved are bonkers.

British politics is cheap by comparison. According to the Electoral Commission, the total combined expenditure of all parties and campaign organisations in the year running up to the last general election was £94.5m. A shot at becoming mayor of a mid-sized US city might cost twice as much.

That is significant context for the kind of money Reform UK and its leader have taken from just two individuals, dipping into fortunes earned in the cryptocurrency trade. A verdict will soon be delivered by the parliamentary standards commissioner in the case of a £5m gift that Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based billionaire, bestowed on Nigel Farage shortly before he ran for parliament in 2024, and that he did not register once elected. Farage denies any wrongdoing.

Harborne gave Reform UK another £9m in 2025 and then £36m earlier this year. That number was chosen in a competitive flourish to equal the £36m that Ben Delo, another crypto billionaire, had given Farage’s party days before. This is unprecedented, gamechanging spending. But it skews the game in unpredictable ways.

Farage’s political fortunes have not been boosted along with his personal finances. When the scandal of the first £5m infusion broke, he tried to pre-empt the standards commissioner’s investigation by putting his case before the “court of public opinion” in a quixotic byelection, which he ended up fighting against a novelty candidate dressed as a space-travelling dustbin. When the report finally lands, a damning verdict could lead to a suspension from the Commons and a recall petition, forcing Farage into another byelection.

He may not bother contesting it. He doesn’t attend the Commons much anyway and doesn’t appear to be enjoying himself as much as he was before his financial affairs came under scrutiny. His newly sullen mood has coincided with Reform UK losing its lead in opinion polls. The party has fallen behind Labour in all surveys and dipped to third place, behind the Tories, in some.

Farage is personally disliked by a majority of voters; deeply so by enough that they form tactical-voting blocs to obstruct Reform UK candidates in byelections. That would probably form a formidable barrier to the party’s leader ever becoming prime minister.

Most of the aversion has accrued over the long years of Farage’s nationalist posturing. Brexit-induced animus and liberal outrage at demagogic immigrant-bashing antedates the conspicuous influx of crypto money and other high-profile scandals. But there is polling evidence that even voters who count as the target demographic for Reform UK, and who might once have accepted the party’s pleas of victimisation at the hands of establishment conspiracy, are put off by the smell of seemingly dodgy deals.

Research conducted over the summer by More in Common found that perceptions of Farage as being seen as “sleazy or corrupt” were emerging as an obstacle to support even among “dissenting disruptors” – the polling company’s label for the electoral segment, roughly one in five, who most mistrust institutions and would gladly see the system torn down by a strongman leader.

A lot of those people were habitual non-voters, stirred out of apathy by the leave campaign in the Brexit referendum. Farage used to have a near monopoly on their allegiance but now faces competition from Rupert Lowe’s even more aggressively far-right Restore Britain party.

Lowe, elected to parliament as a Reform candidate, broke with Farage and has since been elevated from relative obscurity by Musk. The X proprietor’s enthusiastic reposting and deployment of algorithmic privileges have given the Restore Britain leader a profile and audience that rivals the reach of world leaders. His earnings as a digital demagogue, demanding expulsions of non-white migrants from Britain, potentially match his £98,599 annual salary as an MP.

Farage appears to be trying to buy his way back to social media primacy. Research by Who Targets Me, an organisation that campaigns for transparency in digital political advertising, shows Reform UK outspending the rest of the field on platforms for which data is available. Over the past month, the party poured £301,433 into Facebook and Instagram ads, an unusual volume, sustained at unusual pitch for a period with no elections. That’s more than four times as much as the Tories; six times more than Labour.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The return on that investment looks poor so far, if a polling bounce is the goal. But it is too early to know what a prolonged campaign could achieve. And it is pretty much impossible to know what happens in the murkier depths of monetised online influence, especially on TikTok and X. Lowe’s lucrative sideline is only visible because parliament demands a declaration.

A bill ostensibly tightening the rules on political funding, currently in the Lords, barely skims the surface of that trade. It includes a moratorium on donations made in cryptocurrency. That should be a ban, given how vanishingly few reasons there are for an eligible donor to want to avoid paying in old-fashioned sterling.

The government rejected an amendment that would have capped individual donations at £100,000, apparently for fear that future trade union funding would be in jeopardy. Surely not as much peril as it would face under a far-right government that surfed into office on a tide of billionaire cash.

This is a fight Labour can pick with some confidence. There is encouraging evidence that swing voters are sensitive to the cynical hypocrisy of swaggering pseudo-radicals whose anti-establishment postures are choreographed to serve a plutocrat agenda.

When Persuasion UK, a not-for-profit research agency, tested various campaign messages for and against Reform, the lines that most effectively shaved points off the party’s support and depressed its leader’s favourability ratings were the ones highlighting sources of income and how they appeared to correlate with policy positions. Farage says his donors expect nothing in return for their gifts. His well-documented enthusiasm for deregulating crypto, in that case, is an uncanny coincidence.

Comparisons with US politics are made too often in Westminster and never wholly reliable, given the different regulatory regimes and countless cultural disparities. Democrats were the underdog challengers in battleground states in last week’s midterms. Andy Burnham faces a populist threat as the incumbent. But there is one important common factor. British voters don’t like the idea of democracy getting warped to the will of arrogant oligarchs any more than Texans do.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump could be about to sell out Ukraine. Europe must get its act together, fast | Paul Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Paul Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A deal giving Moscow a slice of Ukrainian territory and sanctions relief could be on the table in weeks – yet European leaders are busy squabbling

Donald Trump has lost substantial power over domestic policy after last week’s devastating midterm losses, but his ability to cement his legacy by upending US foreign policy remains largely intact.

There is every reason to fear a ”great betrayal” of Ukraine in the coming weeks, one that would reward Vladimir Putin for Russia’s war of aggression against Kyiv, and also do lasting damage to the European security order. Yet lilliputian European leaders are too busy squabbling over who should represent them in future peace talks to focus on how to prevent a sellout. Despite fundamental European interests being at stake in this week’s three-way US-Russia-Ukraine negotiations in Abu Dhabi, Europe is relegated to a side room, represented by a posse of officials from the UK, France, Germany, the EU and Nato.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Trump has said he is working with Moscow on a “big, beautiful deal” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe”. His seemingly Kremlin-friendly negotiator and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, says Trump has discussed with several European leaders the need for “a broader European security architecture that can help establish conditions for lasting peace”.

Strip away the rhetoric and both appear to be talking about cutting a deal with Putin behind the backs of Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other European leaders to carve up eastern Europe. Such a deal might hand Moscow permanent control of occupied Ukrainian territory – possibly more than it currently holds – and relief from western economic sanctions. It could also deny the countries of eastern Europe the right to choose their own security arrangements, by ruling out any further enlargement of Nato and possibly rolling back some of Nato’s eastern front deployments. In return, Trump’s family and business cronies would surely secure lucrative energy, commodity and perhaps real estate deals with Russia.

Such a carve-up may be only a few weeks away, since Trump has accepted the principle of a meeting with Putin, and a possible big-power threesome with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November. Even if a deal is not oven-ready by then, the opportunity to shape the future of European security in the absence of either Ukrainian or other European leaders must look inviting to the US leader after his electoral drubbing. Trump will want to make advances before the new Democratic-controlled Congress takes office in January.

To force Kyiv to accept a humiliating partition, Trump has already shown he is willing to effectively blind Ukraine by withholding crucial satellite intelligence and missile interceptors. Meanwhile, Elon Musk is hobbling its drone defence by imposing crippling speed limits on his Starshield satellite network, preventing Ukrainian drones from shooting down Russia’s jet-powered kamikaze drones. Trump could also try to bludgeon European allies into acquiescing to a deal by threatening US troop withdrawals and base closures, under a Pentagon review that is nearing completion.

If this all sounds like a paranoid fantasy, remember that Trump and Musk have already used most of these tactics recently, albeit in short, deniable bursts, as an apparent warning to Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian leader has made clear he will not surrender to such coercion, but Putin’s relentless destruction of Ukraine’s energy and transport infrastructure is clearly a drive to put Kyiv in the weakest possible position before diplomatic talks proceed.

Faced with this possibly imminent betrayal, Europe is not without cards of its own, to coin a Trumpian phrase. The Europeans control hundreds of billions of dollars in frozen Russian assets and have the power to refuse any lifting of economic and financial sanctions against Moscow. Indeed, the EU could tighten the screws if they were to transfer impounded Russian central bank funds from the Belgian clearing house, Euroclear, to an EU-controlled entity, and leverage those holdings to raise a massive reparations loan for Ukraine.

As a group of sovereign-debt experts has argued, that would not only keep Ukraine in the fight by meeting Kyiv’s financing needs for at least two years – removing the need for increasingly fraught EU funding negotiations every few months – but it would ensure that Russia is held to account financially for its destruction of Ukraine, and made to contribute to the reconstruction.

Yet beggar-thy-neighbour European politics is preventing the EU from strengthening Zelenskyy’s hand here too. The Belgian prime minister, Bart de Wever, has refused to allow the impounded Russian funds to be used to support Ukraine, winning domestic popularity for supposedly standing up to Europe. As a result, the EU is likely to have to provide Kyiv with another loan to help it through next year. The risk is that elections in France and beyond could bring to power Eurosceptic nationalists who argue that their countries cannot afford to go on funding Ukraine while imposing spending cuts on their own citizens.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

It is not too late for Europe in the broadest sense – including the UK, Norway, Canada and Turkey – to act to counter a great betrayal by Trump. Apart from leveraging the frozen assets, European countries can tighten sanctions on the Kremlin’s shadow fleet, choking its exports by interdicting unsafe and uninsured tankers transporting Russian oil. They could transfer more of their own stocks of Patriot missile interceptors to Ukraine, which is now by any definition Europe’s frontline of defence. And they could make much clearer by joint diplomacy towards Trump that they will reject any deal reached without their participation and assent.

The Europeans have managed to head off Trump once before: after his summit with Putin in Alaska last year, they accompanied Zelenskyy to the White House as “bodyguards”, and clearly spelled out their red lines. This time, the weakened US president is more desperate for a “deal”, and the Europeans are more divided and distracted by their own electoral politics. But there can be no greater priority for the future of European security than to prevent a sellout of Ukraine.

Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Firing a manager is often more about maintaining the illusion of control | Leander Schaerlaeckens
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
In an era of advanced analytics, deciding when to move on from a manager still seems to come down to vibes rather than logic

His position had become untenable.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

He’d run out of time, out of credit, out of chances.

This time of year, we live in permanent peril of hearing some version of the above proclaimed with unshakable confidence. Some soccer manager has been fired and it is universally agreed that it had to be done, that there was no alternative, that the club’s hands were tied by circumstance.

It’s all a bit weird, this broadly accepted yet totally unscientific formula for when a manager must – MUST – lose his job. It’s a sort of alchemy of vibes, and results, and the absence of other scapegoats, and the alternatives available. It’s like that old definition of hardcore pornography by a US supreme court justice: I know it when I see it.

Shall we talk about Michael Carrick now? Yes, here is where we are obliged to debate the beleaguered Manchester United manager, who has been at the helm during the Red Devils’ first dip into the relegation zone since 1986 yet somehow is also definitely not at fault. There is almost total agreement on the latter point, that United’s issues are structural and systemic and absolve Carrick of blame. Still, he’s gotta go, because what can you do, eh?

By the time you read this, he may be gone, or about to be gone, or still floating around in the liminal vapors of being emotionally, but not yet physically, gone.

He was caretaker manager and did such a good job at that free-hit, can’t-lose gig – five stars! Clean and comfortable ride! – that he was rewarded with the exact same but altogether more difficult job of being the permanent Manchester United manager.

But the discourse has shifted against Carrick. Suddenly, the exact same skillset that helped him rescue United last season, making him a poster child of club DNA and its virtues, is viewed as deficient.

Now they say Carrick is outsmarted by the other managers, overwhelmed by the volume of games. Perhaps. But his tactical mind was up to it last year. With fewer games to worry about, certainly, but also burdened with Ruben Amorim’s debris to clear away first. Amorim, of course, was the predecessor who Simply Had To Go, because he was dogmatic and would need too much time to instill his methods, after he was hired because the club must have quite liked that he was dogmatic, even though he would need considerable time to instill his methods.

Yet hanging on to a manager often works out. There’s the famous case of Sir Alex Ferguson, of course, who was installed during United’s last flirtation with relegation, 40 years ago. The early years of his reign were not always smooth: he had a poor season in 1988-89 and was reportedly a few bad results from being sacked in January 1990. But he wasn’t, and nine years later, he was knighted for his accomplishments in management and, by extension, in not being fired.

It’s true of Mikel Arteta, too, who has teetered several times in charge of Arsenal. When the now-defending champions started the 2021-22 season without winning or scoring in three matches, including a 5-0 humiliation by Manchester City. And in late 2024. And as recently as this spring, when some felt that if Arteta didn’t deliver the title at last, he ought to be replaced. Six months on, that seems unthinkable.

There’s a graphic doing the rounds on social media showing that Carrick has actually done slightly better than Arteta in his first 27 league matches in charge, although this elides the very obviously opposite trajectories they were on. All the same, Arteta got to keep going; Carrick probably won’t. Few managers these days are allowed to grow on the job, or into it. The very things Ferguson once credited for his longevity – the leeway to evolve and develop and learn from his mistakes, to rebuild and retool – are denied to the managers supposed to succeed him. Because of … reasons? The money was different back then, but the pressure wasn’t.

Instead, that predictable thing has happened where Carrick has morphed from the in-fashion manager to the one who is gently mocked. He’s no longer said to look calm and possessed of the desperately needed poise at a tumultuous club. Now, he is described as glum. It seemed an ominous portent that he should add himself to the ultra-niche lore of English managers misusing umbrellas when he promised to hold the umbrella so that he would get wet and keep everyone else at the club dry, possibly owing to an unfamiliarity with the rudiments of the technology.

Carrick isn’t alone in managerial purgatory.

Crystal Palace’s Pierre Sage: sacked but somehow not yet sacked.

Régis Le Bris: safe for now, in spite of taking newly promoted Sunderland to an astounding seventh place last season.

Newcastle’s Matthias Jaissle: medium rare, but not yet cooked.

Manchester City’s Enzo Maresca: definitely no longer the perfect successor to Pep Guardiola he was just a few weeks ago.

Fulham’s Álvaro Arbeloa and Bournemouth’s Marco Rose and Tottenham’s Roberto De Zerbi are fine now, after starting the season very not fine. That may change after any result at all. Because clubs’ decision-making on managers seems to be all just guesses and gambles. A veneer of deep deliberation is projected on to the process, because on the outside we always assume that soccer is more sophisticated than it is, but none of them really know which manager will perform in what situation, and for how long.

That’s amazing, given the advances in analytics and how much really rides on a manager’s ability to win games. Ballooning analytics departments seem to have taken teams to a place where they make far fewer mistakes in the transfer market than they used to.

Yet hiring a new manager, or firing the old one, or giving him another chance, appears to involve only marginally more design than shaking a Magic 8 Ball and seeing whether it endorses your choice.

Keep the manager? It is decidedly so.

Fire the manager? Outlook good.

Make a managerial move just to do something and appear in control? Signs point to yes.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump-era lawlessness must be prosecuted. Our new group is working to end the impunity | Kenneth Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Kenneth Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Congressional investigations are only part of the solution. A civic project will do needed legal legwork

The Democrats’ midterm victory was resounding, but it will not be enough to re-establish the rule of law in the United States.

The basic principle that even the president and his officials and cronies are subject to the law has been profoundly undermined by Donald Trump through unchecked ICE violence, apparently large-scale official corruption, and frequent defiance of the law.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Democratic-run congressional committees can investigate and expose lawlessness but cannot prosecute the criminality they uncover. More is needed.

Many people equate democracy with elections, but they are not enough. A president can be elected, his policies can be publicized by the media and debated by the public, his legislative proposals can require the assent of a majority of lawmakers, but if the president holds himself above the law, a nation ceases to be a democracy. That is what has been at stake in Trump’s second term.

The American system delegates many of the responsibilities for upholding the rule of law to an independent judiciary. If a president violates our rights, we can file a civil suit in court and hope a judge orders the president to stop.

But if the president or his allies engage in criminality, the American system has a built-in weakness. Some countries empower prosecutors to be independent, akin to a judge. But in the United States, the prosecutor for any federal crime is an employee of the Department of Justice. It is headed by the attorney general, who is nominated by and serves at the pleasure of the president.

In other words, the president can decide which criminal conduct in his administration will be prosecuted – and which will not.

Because the president’s ability to control the Department of Justice could put him and his friends above the law, presidents traditionally have exercised that power with restraint. While setting broad priorities, most presidents deferred to the judgment of their attorney general. But not Trump.

Trump has weaponized his justice department, pursuing his perceived political enemies while neglecting crimes by his allies, who have often enjoyed effective impunity. They have little to fear from Trump’s politicized prosecutors.

The result has been increasingly brazen behavior – seemingly corrupt deals that few past officials would have dared to make, and arbitrary violence by ICE and others that is excused rather than investigated.

The Rule of Law Project, a new civic group of which I am a founding board member, seeks to end that impunity. We are hiring former federal prosecutors and FBI agents to investigate allegations of corruption and abuse by government officials and their accomplices that the current justice department is ignoring.

We have attracted an extraordinary set of past public servants. Many have served in the justice department, which has been decimated in the second Trump administration. We don’t know their political views and haven’t asked. What we know is that they are eager to continue their work in a different capacity.

The Rule of Law Project operates from the premise that criminal cases are more likely to be pursued if a prosecutor can be handed a case file that is largely ready for action. We will do the legwork of interviewing witnesses, collecting documents, and analyzing the results, with the aim of putting cases together while the evidence is fresh.

We won’t have subpoena power, wiretaps, or a grand jury, but many cases can be built with witnesses who voluntarily cooperate. Indeed, in the most sensitive cases, cooperating witnesses are essential.

Until we have a president and attorney general who believe in the rule of law, we plan to present these ready-made cases to state and local prosecutors, who are not subject to federal control. Many would like to uphold the law but lack the investigative resources to take on these cases on their own.

I have seen the power of such investigations in my global work. For the mass atrocities under Syria’s former president Bashar al-Assad, for example, the international criminal court did not have jurisdiction, and Syrian prosecutors took instructions from the dictator.

The only option was national courts around the world exercising what is known as universal jurisdiction. But a typical prosecutor there would have no clue about how to prosecute torture, executions, or forced disappearances in Syria, let alone the resources to advance such a case.

That’s why, with the encouragement of Human Rights Watch, the UN general assembly established the International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism (IIIM) for Syria. A similar mechanism has been established to address atrocities by the military junta in Myanmar.

The IIIM, based in Geneva, is essentially a prosecutorial team without a court. They have no capacity to bring prosecutions, but they prepare them. That way, when an abusive Syrian official shows up in a national jurisdiction, local prosecutors have a place to turn for the evidence they need.

That happened in the German city of Koblenz, where a former Syrian intelligence officer was convicted of crimes against humanity for overseeing a detention facility where torture was pervasive. He was sentenced to life in prison. The IIIM has contributed to 269 distinct investigations and prosecutions in 16 different jurisdictions, including in France, Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the United States.

The Rule of Law Project will play a similar role in the United States. It will develop the prosecution-ready cases that make it harder for available prosecutors to say they are too busy to take on Trump officials’ illegality.

The project will also make it harder to look forward, not back, as Barack Obama erroneously did with respect to the torture and abuse of the George W Bush administration’s “war on terrorism”. In May 2009, I met with Obama to make the case that the failure to hold perpetrators accountable would lead to future abuses. He thought it would be too divisive.

Sadly, that precedent of impunity is contributing to Trump’s lawlessness today, such as the summary execution of people in alleged drug boats that he has ordered in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.

This is not a vindictive exercise. The project seeks not to even scores but to uphold the law. It will apply an “ordinary times” test – what would a prosecutor do, regardless of the party holding the White House, if they simply analyzed the facts and applied the law free of the politicized limitations of the Trump administration?

What if Trump pardons the culpable before he steps down? That is unlikely to save his accomplices, because the president’s pardon power does not extend to state crimes. Much of the criminality that merits investigation can be characterized as an offense under either federal or state law.

It is extraordinary that the United States needs a group like the Rule of Law Project. But these are extraordinary, even unprecedented, times.

To salvage America’s democracy, it is not enough to vote out corrupt and abusive officials. They should also be prosecuted to re-establish the rule of law.

We cannot count on the federal government under Trump to perform this role. We as citizens must take it on.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: ‘The many v the money’ should frame the next US Congress
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Naomi Klein
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
If Democrats want to keep the blue wave going into 2028, they have to take on the billionaire class

Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week, Judd Legum shined a spotlight on the role of dark money in US elections. Today’s edition was written by Naomi Klein, Guardian US columnist and author of End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra Taylor.

To see the battle lines of the post-midterm era in sharp relief, look to Texas.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Just two days after her earthquake victory as the governor-elect, Gina  informed reporters that she had already asked the parks and wildlife department to freeze a proposal to sell 1,300 acres (525 hectares) in a state park to SpaceX until she is sworn into her new office. The department complied with her request.

The Boca Chica state park is next door to Starbase, Elon Musk’s rocket launch facility and company town. That makes the park’s beaches and protected lands – a refuge for shore birds and sea turtles – the ideal location for SpaceX to expand.

“These are our beaches we’re talking about. I mean, selling our beach to Elon Musk is just something that is almost unimaginable,” Hinojosa told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “It’s unacceptable. Our beaches are enshrined in our Texas constitution as being free and open to the people of Texas.”

This was not about shutting down “Elon Musk and his companies”, she went on, “but it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas. And that’s what changes now that I will be governor.”

When Hinojosa’s clips circulated on X, she was roundly mocked by Musk’s many fans: imagine valuing some “empty beaches” more than the need for ocean-front launchpads to the stars! Imagine caring more about some lowly birds than Musk’s hulking, phallic, silver rockets! She must be a [insert vomitorium of misogynistic, racist and ableist slurs here]. Musk, his boys and bots predicted, will just pick up his expensive toys and move them to still-Republican Louisiana or Florida, leaving economic carnage in his wake.

So far, Hinojosa seems unmoved. In Texas, she and Senator-elect James Talarico shaped their campaigns as battles of the many v the money, a vertical struggle pitting the vast majority of Texans, struggling to get by, against the increasingly concentrated wealth at the top – perfectly embodied by the man flooding their democracy with cash. As Talarico reminded an audience of supporters in Austin last month: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator.”

The richest man in the world didn’t get his senator, or his governor, as the early clash over Boca Chica state park makes clear. What he did get – or rather, help produce – is an America polarized around a new political axis. On one side are ultrarich tech oligarchs, whose wealth is tethered to dreams of merging with machines and becoming multiplanetary, no matter the cost to our multispecies planet. On the other side are regular people, with human needs for things such as clean air, fresh water and healthcare – maybe even a day off at a public park – and who increasingly find themselves competing over these basics with sprawling datacentres and rocket launchers.

The oligarchs in this battle have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth, thus the threats that Musk will soon ditch Texas if its newly elected representatives dare to keep their promises to voters (just as he dumped California and Canada before that). If all else fails, maybe he will join his friend Peter Thiel in Argentina, which Javier Milei is rapidly turning into techno-libertarian laboratory (Interestingly, Tesla just launched an Argentine division.)

double quotation markThe oligarchs in this battle seem to have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth.

In sharp contrast, the masses of people in this battle, regardless of their political leanings, tend to be attached to where they live – to its cities, towns, public lands and to the only planet that we know of suited to human life. This is as true in Texas as it is in Tirana, Albania, where, under the banner of the “flamingo revolution” citizens have been in revolt for months against a different set of oligarchs who laid claim to a different beloved wildlife refuge for their private benefit.

In our book End Times Fascism, Astra Taylor and I characterize these as fights between “the leavers v the stayers” – and we make the case that they increasingly define our age. You can see these fault lines running through a great many of the hot-button issues that animated and energized this election cycle. There were the many ballot measures to tax the super-rich to pay for basic services, and entirely predictable tantrums from billionaires who threatened to pick and leave rather than pay up. There was the muscular, national backlash against artificial intelligence and datacenters, which focused on the ways this latest (final?) capitalist stage is devouring art, literature, incomes, lands, energy and wellbeing. (As the Guardian reported, “Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total.”)

The commitment to place, and to one another, was equally evident in the rage at the US war-of-choice in Iran, and at Israel’s genocide in Gaza, with many winning candidates including Abdul El-Sayed consistently stressing that the money being spent to kill children far away should be used to care for children at home, and that all children are equally deserving of life and opportunities.

Sign up to How We Win

Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.

after newsletter promotion

Similar dynamics were there, too, in the revolt against ICE: As Minnesota’s Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said in her victory speech, the movement that lifted her to power all began when Minnesotans decided to stand up to “masked goons shooting our neighbors”. And the faultlines were clearest of all in the white-hot anger at the legalized corruption at the heart of the US political system, now widely understood as the wellspring producing all the other depravities.

Writing in this space one month ago, Rebecca Solnit astutely characterized the midterms as “a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with tech overlords over the public they’re meant to serve”. Well, the results are in and they could scarcely be more decisive. The complicating factor, however, is that it is not only the GOP that is aligned with the tech overlords and their anti-human, anti-Earth agenda. Plenty of powerful Democrats have chosen to underwrite their political campaigns and their personal wealth portfolios by entangling themselves with the very individuals and corporations their voters just roundly and unequivocally rejected.

Shamefully, the campaign to defeat a California ballot measure that would have imposed a much-needed, one-time 5% tax on billionaires – one of few places where tech oligarchs clocked a victory last week – was only successful because powerful Democrats including outgoing governor (and presidential hopeful) Gavin Newsom sided with the billionaires (as did the incoming governor). Meanwhile, several Senate Democrats have joined with Republicans to push through a sweeping bill in the current lame-duck Congress that would dismantle a host of environmental protections and be a bonanza for fossil fuel companies and the datacentres that burn them.

This kind of betrayal is the surest path for Democrats to turn their historic midterm victories into entirely predictable defeats before the highly consequential 2028 presidential election.

In Texas, Hinojosa is showing a better way. By picking an early fight pitting public beaches against Musk’s private rockets, she is telling voters which side she is on – the side of life, not machines; the side of staying, not leaving. That is how the Democrats just won, and it is their path to continue winning.

Want to hear more from our contributors?

Follow them on Substack and elsewhere: Stacey Abrams, Robert Reich, Paul Krugman, Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan, Bernie Sanders, Rebecca Solnit, Katie Phang, Judd Legum, Wajahat Ali, Margaret Sullivan and Charles Blow.
