https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: UK social media ban expansion for under-16s could cover YouTube Kids
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Regulations under consideration could affect up to 150 platforms, including LegoPlay, Spotify and eBay, sources say

A substantial expansion of the social media ban for under-16s could inadvertently lead to a ban on YouTube Kids and other sites that had been thought exempt, sources briefed on the government’s proposals have said.

One source close to the talks said the regulations now under consideration meant up to 150 platforms, including games platforms such as Lego Play, could be covered by the ban, which is set to come into force in March.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The regulations will be sent for cabinet signoff this week, and the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, is expected to lay them in parliament in December.

Ministers are understood to be keen for a catch-all approach that limits ban workarounds. Critics of Australia’s social media prohibition say teenagers have switched to new platforms or found innovative ways of messaging using other seemingly innocuous sites.

Tech companies, industry groups and MPs have been briefed that the government’s working proposal focuses on recommender systems and user-generated content.

Spotify – which has some user-generated content and shows recommended music or podcasts – could technically be in scope if those proposals are enacted, though the music streaming site has sought reassurances that it would not face a ban because it is not primarily a social platform.

One industry source said: “We all share the goal of keeping teenagers safe online. Proposals have to be workable, and a situation where eBay, Lego, YouTube Kids and Spotify aren’t clear whether they comply is unsustainable. Detailed guidelines can’t come soon enough.”

Another said: “The whole internet has a recommender system. The regulation is just too broad. But they want to make it really broad and legally airtight so they can be prepared for any eventuality.”

Companies are expected to be briefed on the final proposal in the coming days by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) and No 10.

When the ban was announced by Keir Starmer in June, the government said it would ensure the ban did not include educational services, e-commerce platforms or music streaming, saying there would be “a narrowly defined list of exemptions to the definitions which will be kept under review”.

But tech companies are understood to be telling the government that removing the recommender algorithm would make it impossible for their sites to function.

The regulations do not require primary legislation in the House of Commons, and will be tabled as an addition to the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act.

Ministers are also looking at a second tranche of regulations in the spring which could cover e-commerce platforms such as Vinted, eBay and Depop. MPs and campaigners have raised concerns with Nandy that teenagers and groomers can find innovative ways to communicate on platforms that allow unknown or anonymous user messaging, such as those websites.

After Nandy confirmed in interviews on Sunday that the government was looking to bring Vinted and other e-commerce platforms in scope, officials held a panicked call with retailers on Tuesday where several are understood to have strongly contested the plans.

Another industry figure said it would be illogical for the government to continue to allow messaging apps such as WhatsApp and iMessage – but ban platforms such as Vinted and eBay because they had messaging capabilities.

The minister for online safety, Ian Murray, also confirmed to MPs last week that the government was looking at those sites for the next tranche of regulations which examines “features and functions” and is expected next spring.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

“Platforms that might have been out of scope are perhaps being brought into scope by having new functionalities that we might think are different from the social media platforms we are seeking to regulate. For example, Spotify has introduced stranger conversation functionality to its platform,” he said.

Murray told MPs that platforms which redesigned their services to remove harmful or addictive functions would have a route to removing themselves from the banned list.

“The way back is to comply with the regulations and fall out of scope. That is an easy thing to say but not an easy thing to deliver, but that is the principle with which we will go forward on this,” he said.

He said platforms such as YouTube Kids and Lego Play would need to demonstrate they did not have harmful algorithms.

“Are there ways in which you can stop the harms being created by the algorithms, the recommender systems, the commenting systems or the conversations that can be had with strangers?

“If you have created a service that complies with all the regulations, is it then available to under-16s? I would say that, currently, the government’s position is that, yes, there has to be an off-ramp.”

Spotify’s messaging is restricted to contact only with known friends and family for users who are 16 and older, a company source said.

Tech industry bodies have told the government that platforms such as YouTube Kids cease to function without the recommender system, making it impossible for them to comply with the “off-ramp”.

DCMS has been approached to comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.4tn in stock market flotation
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Claude chatbot developer had been reported to be aiming for $2tn IPO on Wall Street before investors cooled on AI

Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to $1.4tn (£1.1tn) in its imminent stock market flotation, short of the $2tn that had been expected before investors started to question the durability of the AI boom.

The developer of the Claude chatbot was widely reported to be targeting a $2tn initial public offering on Wall Street but its sights have been set lower, according to a US regulatory filing on Tuesday.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $64.4bn by selling 825m shares in the IPO priced up to $78 a share. The California-based company will also raise a further $26bn via a separate private placement deal ⁠with cornerstone investors including the Google parent, Alphabet, and the chipmaker Nvidia.

An extra $9.7bn could be raised from a so-called greenshoe offering, which kicks in if investor demand is high and would take the total amount raised by Anthropic to approximately $100bn if the shares sold at the top end of the price range.

At the upper bracket of the $70-$78 per share price range, Anthropic would be worth $1.4tn on a fully diluted basis – which means taking into account all the common shares in the company in existence, including employee stock options.

Trading in Anthropic shares is expected to begin next week.
  
  
 Investor jitters over the AI boom were crystallised last week when the US midterm elections produced victories for datacentre opponents. This has added to already existing concerns, such as how quickly – or if at all – companies can generate a return on their spending on AI infrastructure.

Brian Hopkins, a principal analyst at Forrester Research, said the midterm elections gave investors the chance to correct valuations that they were beginning to have concerns about, because of worries about the financial sustainability of the AI build-out. The election results brought those concerns to a head, Hopkins said.
 
 
 “The market needed an excuse to correct itself a little bit in terms of valuations,” he said. “The US election spook is what has caused it.”
 
 
 As a consequence, Anthropic’s valuation has also been lowered from an anticipated $2tn, he added.

The largest ever stock market listing is Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which joined the US stock market with a valuation of $1.78tn, raising $75bn. The company, whose assets include Musk’s rocket launch business and the X social media platform, is now worth just under $2tn.

However, the $100bn that could be raised in the Anthropic offering will exceed the amount raised by SpaceX.

Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, is selling about $260m worth of shares in the float, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each.

A Chinese spying scandal enveloping Nvidia, a cornerstone company for AI investors, also threatens to overshadow the industry but has not affected share prices so far – other than Nvidia’s.

The updated Anthropic filing stated that the company’s annual revenue is now running at $81bn as of 31 October, up $10bn from the previous month.

Anthropic’s main expenditure is on the computing power, from datacentres, that is key to developing and operating its AI systems. According to its prospectus, Anthropic has compute purchase commitments and lease agreements of more than $70bn over the next 12 months and more than $450bn by 2030, with a further $450bn due by 2045.

In a podcast appearance earlier this year, Anthropic’s Amodei explained how compute commitments had to be matched by revenue growth.

“I could buy $1tn of compute that starts at the end of 2027. If my revenue is not $1tn, if it’s even $800bn, there’s no force on Earth, there’s no hedge on Earth, that could stop me from going bankrupt,” he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel.

On Tuesday the Financial Times reported that the investment bank Goldman Sachs, which is leading the float along with Morgan Stanley, is forecasting Anthropic will generate annual revenues of $600bn by 2030.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Claude chatbot developer was reported to be aiming for $2tn IPO on Wall Street. But its sights have been set lower, according to a US regulatory filing on Tuesday. Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $64.4bn by selling 825m shares in the IPO priced up to £78 a share.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: ‘Flying cars’ could launch in China next summer, maker of two-seat model says
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Robert Booth in Lisbon
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
XPeng says its $300k low-altitude device will soon be ready for emergency services and recreational use in rural areas

People could start taking trips in so-called flying cars in China as soon as next summer, the manufacturer of a two-seater vehicle with autopilot model has said.

Deli Zhao, the chief executive of the Chinese flying car company XPeng, said the $300,000 (£225,000) low-altitude device would be ready for use by recreational users in rural locations and by emergency services in the second half of 2027. After 10 years of development including trials of flying motorbikes at the company’s Guangzhou base, it has been approved by China’s civil aviation authorities for limited use.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The small cockpit is about the size of a Fiat 500 car and the vehicle is lifted into the air by six drone-like battery-powered propellers and steered by a simple joystick. It can also fly autonomously to a programmed destination, but Xhao, a trained pilot, claimed he could teach anyone to fly it in five minutes.

The price tag for the contraption includes a six-wheel van about the size of a Ford Transit, out of the back of which the flying vehicle unfolds “just like the Transformers”, said Zhao. He has been developing flying cars for almost a decade and said he was part-inspired by the flying creatures ridden by humans in the Harry Potter stories and the Green Goblin’s flying skateboard from the Spider-Man comics.

“The world where everyone can be a captain is about to arrive,” he said at the Web Summit in Lisbon on Tuesday, where a prototype of the vehicle drew large crowds. Zhao said no one had yet been injured or hurt using the vehicle which, although described as a car, lacks wheels and is better described as a helicopter-style drone. He said the initial target market was people who were into “diving, surfing, off-roading and flying”.

Elon Musk last month showed off his version of a flying Tesla which uses high-powered blasts of gas to twist and flip in the air. Amid intense competition between the US and China over the development of electric vehicles and drone technology, Zhao said Musk’s prototype was “really hopping or jumping and not really flying”. The XPeng vehicle can cruise as high as 1km above the ground – well below an unpressurised light aircraft such as a Cessna.

“I’m looking forward to seeing a potential future generation that can actually fly,” he said, and agreed when asked if Musk’s showcase had the characteristics of a circus act.

However, the XPeng “flying car” also has limited scope. It will only be usable in approved park areas in China and by emergency services needing to reach inaccessible areas. It has a flight range of 30km (18.6 miles), although this will soon be doubled by increasing the battery’s energy density to 400 kilowatts per kilogram.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

Its emergence is part of a wider push by Beijing to develop what it calls the “low-altitude economy” – including drones and flying cars, starting with flying cargo, then people, and moving from rural areas to the cities. Zhao said his firm was one of about 20 in China working on flying vehicles.

“All cars in the future will grow wings and all transportation will move from two dimensions to three dimensions,” said Zhao, who claimed he had signed agreements with the United Arab Emirates and countries in south-east Asia to develop the flying car’s use, adding: “We aim to enter the European market as soon as possible.”

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Richard Adams Education editor
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Office for Students says institutions in England should return to traditional exams and in-person presentations

Universities should go back to traditional exams and in-person presentations to grade students after lecturers complained that AI has made it “close to impossible” to assess coursework, according to an investigation by England’s higher education regulator.

The Office for Students (OfS) said the credibility of degrees from England’s universities was under threat from the prolific use of AI in essays, dissertations and “open book” exams, with students reporting that their peers boasted of using AI undetected by staff.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The regulator warned universities and other higher education institutions that failing to design “valid and reliable measures of students’ knowledge and skills” to combat AI could breach their conditions of registration and lead to sanctions being imposed.

Josh Fleming, the director of strategy and delivery at the OfS, said AI use in higher education “presents a generational risk to the system as it stands, threatening to undermine students’ learning and institutions’ ability to assess them”.

Fleming added: “We need to see far greater efforts to tackle these risks, including far greater use of AI-free assessment.

“The scale and pace of both the challenge and opportunity presents a novel challenge for the sector and us as the regulator. We will continue to work with universities and colleges to help them reap the benefits of AI while avoiding the risks.”

The OfS said many institutions had already redesigned how they assessed students to reduce potential AI misuse, including greater use of in-person written exams or oral examinations known as vivas. Other examples include students critiquing or editing AI-generated output, or “process-based” assessments where students detail how they researched and produced their work.

A Department for Education spokesperson said: “We expect universities to take this issue seriously and we expect the OfS to both enforce the existing standards effectively, and work at pace to ensure its regulatory framework is explicit, strong and durable on the use of AI.”

A spokesperson for Universities UK, which represents 147 higher education institutions, said: “There is further to go but many have made substantial changes to how they assess students. This includes more in-person exams, presentations, vivas, process-based assessment and assessments that integrate AI in a controlled way.”

The report by the OfS and Advance HE, a charity promoting university governance and teaching, interviewed more than 300 students and staff at 127 universities and colleges this year, to gauge AI policies and use in teaching and assessment.

One academic told the researchers: “AI has put academic integrity at serious risk … coursework is now overwhelmingly written in part, or exclusively, with the help of AI.”

Another university staff member said: “I think we’re realising that a number of our assessments may be unfit for purpose, and that pervasive use of AI may render our assessment of students close to impossible in some areas.”

The survey found that AI use was rife, with students saying their colleagues completed assessments using AI “sometimes in just a few minutes” and received similar grades to those who had completed an assessment without AI.

“Some students described their peers being unable to recall basic details about the assessment they had just submitted,” the report noted.

One student told the researchers: “I’ve had people admit, peer to peer, ‘I wrote this whole essay with ChatGPT’ … then they don’t get caught, they get a good grade probably, and then because it worked the first time, they do it on their next assessment.”

Academics also described receiving large numbers of submissions that looked the same, referenced the same literature and were written in the same style. Others said they believed the assessments used by their institution were not fit for purpose or did not accurately measure students’ knowledge and skills.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Lana Crowe
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
As Hollywood begins to adopt the technology, the professionals in most direct jeopardy are the illustrators mapping out directors’ first visions. They sketch out what could be lost

A
film industry dominated by AI is a dystopian prospect: stories and dialogue generated by large language models, populated by reincarnated screen icons and uncanny humanoids. That is in the future, but the real-world impact of AI is already directly affecting jobs behind the scenes, as Hollywood’s biggest film-makers begin to adopt the technology. James Cameron – long an advocate for emerging technologies in film-making – is on the board of a gen AI firm, citing his interest in how AI will intersect with CGI; Steven Soderbergh used Meta-powered tech to create animations for his recent documentary about John Lennon; even Christopher Nolan, while dismissing the idea that AI will replace humans as “nonsense”, conceded that it will create some useful “imaging tools”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The current canary in the coalmine however is the storyboard artist, whose work gen AI appears to have directly in its sights. Storyboard artists are the illustrators who draw the panels of images with notes and diagrams that map out scenes before they are filmed. Storyboards are used to work out how a film will look, and as a blueprint to communicate a director’s vision to cast and crew, and are one of the first steps in bringing a script off the page. Now they appear on the verge of replacement by programmes that use text prompts to create illustrations instead. Even an old-school diehard like Martin Scorsese has got on board; in June he announced a partnership with an AI firm whose text-to-image model he used in the storyboarding process for his next movie.

Usually, storyboards are made together by a director, an artist and other crew members responsible for the film’s visual storytelling, such as cinematographers, editors, production designers, stunt co-ordinators and more. “I find it very fulfilling to make art in such a collaborative way,” says Alex Clark, a British storyboard artist whose recent films include Bong Joon Ho’s sci-fi comedy Mickey 17, adventure romance The Gorge and Louis Leterrier’s recent thriller The Last House. “It’s about people sitting down to discuss each other’s ideas. You might act things out, make sound effects, read dialogue. You develop a creative relationship with one another.”

For Clark, the process of creating a storyboard is just as important as the finished product. “A common misconception is that storyboarding is about making nice drawings. But it’s more than that – it’s about relating to how the director is thinking, and conceiving the most appropriate ways to tell the story of a scene,” he says. Dune director Denis Villeneuve articulated this relationship when describing his frequent collaborator, artist Sam Hudecki, as “an extension of my brain”. For Villeneuve, storyboarding is “a new way of writing”: writing a screenplay might provide the words, but storyboarding is the first step in creating the “cinematic language of the movie”. He views it as “a way to dream” as the film begins to come to life on the page.

Clark says that there is a balance that must be struck between “capturing the essence” of a scene and figuring out how the shots are going to work once the cameras are rolling. “The act of how you mark the page – to convey forms, tones, compositions, blocking and so on – forces you to thoroughly think about how all these different details will affect the scene. It gives you a rigorous understanding of how the scene is going to work.” Clark’s work reflects the fact that storyboarding is one step in an ongoing collaboration that continues through pre-production, shooting on set and beyond. “Sometimes I try to scale the drawings back, when it feels appropriate to leave space for others to build on it – whether it’s an actor’s performance, the way the set is decorated, lighting setup or subtle movement of the camera. I like finding space for happy accidents.”

For researchers and film enthusiasts, storyboard art offers a glimpse into the journey that lies behind a film, including fascinating changes in direction like this. “Storyboard art shows us the evolution of the creative vision,” says Ferdinando Cocco, a lecturer in film at Abertay university in Dundee. He points to Disney’s 1991 film Beauty and the Beast as an example: when it was first being worked on in the late 1980s, the storyboards had a rococo-inspired aesthetic, contemporary to the fairytale’s origins, styling Gaston as a bewigged 18th-century French aristocrat rather than the swollen, strong-jawed hunter who exemplified more modern ideals of masculinity.

As a film-making technique, the storyboard was first used regularly by Disney animators in the 1930s and and it plays a key role in their production process (as evidenced by displays of concept and storyboard art, and the side-by-side videos Disney posts online. (Disney also announced a $1bn investment into OpenAI’s video tool Sora last year.)

Storyboards were swiftly adopted by live-action productions, dating at least back to Gone With the Wind (1939). Since then, many film-makers have left behind storyboards that are beautiful and evocative images in themselves. Alfred Hitchcock created meticulously detailed storyboards, which spawned some of the genre’s most recognisable images: such as the shower scene in Psycho sketched beforehand by his frequent collaborator Saul Bass, the graphic designer behind many classic posters of the era. And before that, Hitchcock had worked with Salvador Dalí on surreal designs for the dream sequence in his 1945 film Spellbound.

Other directors, including Akira Kurosawa and Ridley Scott – whose storyboards are known as “Ridleygrams” – draw their own. Some of Bong’s self-drawn sketches are currently on display at the Academy Museum in Los Angeles, and his panels for Parasite have been published as a graphic novel. “Whenever I go to set without storyboards, I feel like I’m standing in the middle of Grand Central Terminal wearing only my underwear,” Bong writes in the book’s preface – however he does encourage the reader to see the differences between the storyboards and the film as “exciting moments of fear and spontaneity”.

Fan interest in behind-the-scenes material has created a market for storyboard books, while last year an exhibition devoted to storyboard art held in Milan displayed panels from films made by arthouse auteurs such as Ingmar Bergman and Federico Fellini, to artists Isaac Julien and Carrie Mae Weems, to Hollywood royalty – including Scorsese.

Creating engaging images is not without a practical function either, as storyboards are often pinned up on set to give the crew a sense of what will be shot that day. “I feel a responsibility to produce work that inspires and captivates everyone about what they’re making,” Clark says. “If the level of artistry and attention is evident at this stage, I believe it can set the tone on set, of valuing the craft involved.”

All hope is not yet lost. Cocco has observed a return to analogue practices and suggests that AI can be used in a way that fosters rather than dilutes the creative process. “Perhaps the difficulty that AI purportedly overcomes was the whole point from the start,” Cocco says. “Having to communicate with others forces an expansion of the artistic vision in ways that cannot be pre-empted.”

Clark meanwhile predicts that, as AI usage in the industry increases, people will come to have a greater appreciation for films with a human touch. “Ultimately, I think most successful films make you feel something as a human being. One advantage of hand-drawn storyboards is that you have a direct sense of that human authenticity right there on the page.”

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.title: Are walking pads worth it? We put the best under-desk treadmills to the test
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.author: Leon Poultney
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.text:
Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Want to get your steps in while working or watching TV? Our expert puts walking pads through their paces to find the best for comfort, noise and ease of storage

The best treadmills for your home

Y
ou don’t necessarily need to walk 10,000 steps a day to improve your health and wellbeing. In fact, the NHS encourages a slightly more manageable target of just 10 minutes of brisk walking daily to introduce more moderate-intensity physical activity and reduce your risk of early death by up to 15%.

However, even squeezing in “brisk walks” can be a chore, with busy schedules and increasingly desk-bound jobs forcing more of us to remain sedentary for long periods. That is where walking pads come in, being lighter, smaller and often easier to store than bulky and tricky-to-manoeuvre running treadmills.

When coupled with a standing desk, walking pads can be used while working – or when watching TV in the evening. Just a couple of 30-minute sessions add thousands of steps to your daily tally. In fact, a 60-minute walk at an easy 3km an hour can burn between 200 and 300 additional calories.

Walking pads are often cheaper than full-size treadmills, simple to use and relatively easy to store, and they’re perfect for adding more movement to your life without having to give up the day job.

Best walking pad overall
Urevo SpaceWalk 5L smart walking pad

Best budget walking pad and best for beginners
Bigzzia Walking pad with incline

Best lightweight walking pad
JTX MoveLight

Best foldable walking pad
BodyMax WP60

I’m a keen fitness fan who does everything from gym-based strength training and kickboxing classes to outdoor trail runs and cold-water surfing. As a result, I’ve often been tasked with testing fitness technology for industry magazines, and I’m always keen to get stuck in.

I strongly believe that you need to live with new tech for a bit to grasp how it fits into daily life, so I aim to test products for as long as possible and in the right environment. With walking pads, that meant strolling along, racking up the steps and burning calories – even while I wrote up this feature.

There was only one way to properly trial the eight walking treadmills selected for this test, and that was to mimic the customer journey by ordering, taking delivery, unboxing, setting them up and then using them day to day.

The best walking treadmills – or walking pads – aren’t quite as bulky as regular running treadmills, so I could have multiple models on the go at home at once: one under my desk, one in front of the television and one in my wife’s office upstairs, testing each for at least three days.

The testing process involved a lot of additional steps and – in some cases at least – a whining soundtrack that drowned out whatever Netflix series the family was watching. Besides general observations on the heft, ease of storage and operation, quietness and build quality, I tested any additional features such as incline and speed adjustments, as well as any remote controls or apps.

To get a good idea of energy consumption and the overall cost of running a walking treadmill, I plugged each unit into a power meter to calculate the cost based on the October energy price cap.

Here are the four best walking pads you can buy now.

The Urevo SpaceWalk 5L is one of the most fully featured walking pads I’ve tested. It combines excellent build quality with a quiet motor, automatic incline and a great free companion app – which makes it feel more like a proper piece of fitness equipment than a basic under-desk treadmill. It’s slim enough to slide under a sofa when not in use, yet robust enough to cope with daily walking or even light jogging.

Why we love it
Unlike most rivals, the SpaceWalk 5L’s accompanying app is genuinely useful. It allows you to record workouts and track steps, distance and walking time, while also offering structured walks with automatic incline adjustment.

The software also syncs with Apple Health, while the proprietary app lets you take part in a number of on-demand workouts, where incline and speed are controlled automatically. It also offers virtual walks, where you can take a sort of video tour of exotic locations. Unfortunately, it doesn’t feature the FTMS protocol that allows it to beam speed, cadence and incline data to a third-party app like Zwift. So your virtual avatar won’t move on the screen without a workaround such as a third-party, cadence-sensing footpod or compatible smartwatch.

It is one of the quietest walking pads I’ve tested, though. At my preferred 2.5km/h working/walking pace, the motor averaged just 48dB – barely louder than my keyboard as I was furiously typing up this review.

Build quality is also noteworthy. The weighty, front-mounted motor gives it a reassuringly solid feel, while adjustable feet make levelling on uneven floors easy. Its claimed 12-point shock absorption system also provides enough cushioning for walking in just socks, although I’d still recommend trainers for longer sessions.

The incline, which can be automatically controlled when using Urevo’s app, adds another dimension for anyone aiming to increase the intensity of their walks.

Energy use is impressively low, too. At a comfortable 2.5km/h, the SpaceWalk 5L drew around 40W during testing, costing roughly 1p an hour based on the 1 October electricity price cap.

At its 6km/h maximum speed, this rose to about 3p an hour, with the incline motor briefly drawing more power when adjusting the deck.

While 6km/h is no more than a brisk walk or gentle jog, the SpaceWalk 5L feels stable throughout. It doesn’t fold, but its slim design and the integrated wheels make it easy to roll under a bed or sofa for storage.

It’s a shame that … the incline functionality makes it slightly bulkier than the simplest ultra-slim walking pads.

Size: 124 x 51.5 x 15.5cm (LWH)
Weight: 23kg
Walking deck size: 40 x 100cm
Maximum user weight: 181kg
Incline: 0-9% automatic
Maximum speed: 6km/h
Folding: no

The Bigzzia is very much a budget walking pad, and it shows. The construction is basic, the running deck is narrow and short, and the display is hardly sophisticated. But it’s remarkably cheap and has a surprisingly high 10km/h top speed and a manual incline setting.

Why we love it
The Bigzzia’s biggest selling point is that 10km/h maximum speed. That’s considerably faster than most under-desk walking pads, and means it can double as a basic treadmill for walking and light jogging.

However, the deck is so short that running at anything approaching its maximum speed feels unnerving. I’d be much happier using it for walking or, at most, very short bursts of jogging.

The running surface has a surprisingly good grip, but there’s little flex or meaningful cushioning underneath, making longer sessions uncomfortable. It’s better suited to shorter walks than all-day use.

It does come with an 8% incline, although this isn’t a motorised function. You simply flip out two feet at the sides and put the supplied rubber supports underneath them to raise the deck. No range of settings here.

The simple display shows the basics: speed, calories, time and distance, automatically cycling between the figures as you walk. There isn’t really a way to lock it to any particular metric – another reminder that this is a very simple machine.

Interaction is equally basic – via a small wireless remote control. Lose or break it, though, and you’ll be stuck. You also need to supply the AAA batteries for it.

For portability, however, the Bigzzia shines. At just 12.86kg, it is light enough to pick up and carry, something I can’t say about many of the walking pads here. It also has a couple of small wheels at the front, so you can tip it and wheel it around if you prefer. And while the short deck might prove a drawback for running, it’s great for storage: it slides easily under a sofa or can be stored upright against a wall.

Noise is another compromise, however. Walking at 2.5km/h, I measured about 52dB, with a noticeable whine and plenty of foot thump from the deck. It’s not disastrous for a walking pad at this price, but it’s certainly more obvious than the best machines I’ve tested.

Power consumption is also higher than that of some rivals. I measured 54W at 2.5km/h (about 1p an hour at the UK electricity rates at the time of writing) and 166W at its 10km/h top speed (about 4p an hour). Running costs remain low overall, but it’s less energy efficient than some more sophisticated walking pads.

Another omission worth knowing about is the lack of an automatic stop function. That means the motor will continue running if you fall or simply walk away, so you need to be a little more careful about how you use it.

It’s a shame that … it’s let down by the short deck, noisy motor and basic controls, but it’s one of the cheapest walking pads out there.

Size: 104 x 49 x 11cm (LWH)
Weight: 12.86kg
Walking deck size: 37 x 90cm
Maximum user weight: 130kg
Incline: 0 or 8% manual
Maximum speed: 10km/h
Folding: no

JTX often appears in the “best value” section of home fitness equipment reviews, known for offering reliable build quality at affordable prices, but its machines tend to prioritise function over flashy design and cutting-edge technology.

The MoveLight walking pad is different, however. It’s the most expensive walking pad in this roundup, and there’s a tangible difference in the build quality compared with cheaper walking pads. The JTX also offers a sizeable display, cushioned walking deck and quiet 1hp electric motor. It’s a solid treadmill offering speeds of up to 6km/h, meaning it’s possible to use it for slow jogging without the worry of it falling apart.

Why we love it
The MoveLight is similar in design to the BodyMax reviewed below and has a solid plastic chassis that gives it a more premium feel than its cheaper rivals. The running deck is generously sized and well cushioned, making longer walking sessions more comfortable.

The extra-large LED console is easy to use and neatly scrolls through speed, time and step count as you walk. The shrill beeps upon startup and when you adjust the speed may cause office mates to want to throw a pencil at you, however.

With the small plastic remote, you can adjust the speed, stop or start the unit and scroll the display between distance, calories and time on one half, and speed and step count on the other.

The 1hp motor is powerful enough to propel the deck up to 6km/h, where it remains much quieter than some of the others tested.

Overall, it feels like a walking pad that will go the distance – and so it should, given the price – but that solid build does make it a pain to move around the house; it will require some serious muscle to tip it up on to its wheels. It also doesn’t fold like the BodyMax machine.

Oh, and one final public service announcement: those with wooden floors will want to take care that the wheels and plastic feet don’t scratch the surface during transport.

During testing, I found it to be slightly more power-hungry than rivals, supping about 100W at 3.5km/h, meaning it costs about 3p an hour to power.

It’s a shame that … it’s so big and heavy to move around, which makes storing it after each session a chore.

Size: 147 x 60 x 12.5cm (LWH)
Weight: 29.5kg
Walking deck size: 45 x 122cm
Maximum user weight: 100kg
Incline: none
Maximum speed: 6km/h
Folding: no

Prefer to sit while you work? We’ve also reviewed the best office chairs

One of the most expensive models on test, the BodyMax walking pad is also one of the best built and easiest on the eye. It’s the only model that genuinely folds in half, making it easier to squeeze into a cupboard or wardrobe.

However, at around 30kg, it’s not the easiest to move, despite wheels at the front that allow it to be tipped on its end and rolled around.

Potential portability issues aside, this machine offers a fantastic walking experience, with a neat, bright and easy-to-read LED panel that gives clear and scrolling readouts of workout time, distance, speed and average calorie burn.

Very much the Porsche of the walking pad world, the BodyMax unit combines stylish looks and powerful performance.

Why we love it
Like most walking pads here, the BodyMax comes with a remote for adjusting speed, but its clever A Mode goes a step further, using foot placement to automatically adjust the pace.

Stay in the middle, and it maintains pace; walk towards the front to speed up or hang back to slow down. It’s a useful touch that saves you constantly fiddling with the remote. The deck itself is nicely cushioned, and the motor is among the quietest on test.

Those wanting their walking pad to double up as a running treadmill may be disappointed, however: the WP60 tops out at 6km/h, which is a very fast walking pace but a slow jog for most. Not a single walking pad I’ve tested has done a convincing job as a running treadmill, though, being either too flimsy underfoot, too noisy, or simply not built to withstand the endless thumping of a sprint session.

If you’re seeking robust build quality, the BodyMax WP60 walking pad is well worth the additional outlay. As it folds in half, it can be tucked under a desk or rested against a wall when not in use.

It’s a shame that … it’s heavy and awkward to move around when folded.

Size: 143 x 55 x 13cm (LWH)
Weight: 28kg
Walking deck size: 42 x 120cm
Maximum user weight: 100kg
Incline: none
Maximum speed: 6km/h
Folding: yes, folds in half for storage

The biggest difference between walking pads, aside from overall build quality, is their top speed. Most max out at about 6km/h, which is ideal for walking while working at a standing desk or a brisk stroll in front of the TV. If you’re hoping to jog as well, look for models that reach 8-10km/h – although be aware that you’ll generally sacrifice some stability and comfort compared with a full-size treadmill.

Next comes incline. Premium models tend to offer a motorised incline function that can be adjusted at the touch of a button, while cheaper alternatives rely on manually extending support feet for a fixed gradient. Even a small incline can noticeably increase calorie burn and make walks feel more challenging.

after newsletter promotion

Also pay attention to the size of the walking deck. A longer, wider belt will feel far more comfortable and safer, particularly if you’re tall or have a long stride. Finally, think about practicalities such as noise, storage, transport wheels, companion apps and maximum user weight. If you plan to use your walking pad for several hours a day while working from home, spending a little more on a quieter, sturdier model is usually money well spent.

Prices vary when it comes to walking pads, with the most affordable costing about £90. Anything less than that is unlikely to be long-lasting. From my testing, the sweet spot seems to be about £250, where you can get a good blend of value and decent build quality. Some of the best I tested were, predictably, among the most expensive. These high-end models typically cost about £500.

If you’ve got good clearance underneath a bed or sofa, most walking pads will happily slide underneath without the need to fold them up. Imagine a slimmed-down treadmill without the safety handle, and you’re basically there.

Models such as the BodyMax WP60 fold in half, which drastically reduces the length (or height, depending on how you store it), making them much easier to slide into more compact spaces such as a cupboard or wardrobe. But bear in mind they can weigh up to 30kg, so they can be tricky to move without help.

Most walking pads come with a small bottle of silicone oil. This is used to lubricate the underside of the walking belt every couple of months to ensure smooth movement, depending on use. Most manufacturers also supply the required hex key so you can adjust the belt if it’s slipping or has moved slightly off-centre.

Quickly check the belt alignment and any moving parts every couple of months, and it should be enough to keep a walking pad running smoothly for years.

Some walking pad speeds are capped at about 6km/h, which makes running on them tricky. A plodding jog is a better description. A few of the walking pads I tested did reach much higher speeds, and most of these came with a folding safety handle that extends to allow them to safely reach those speeds, giving the runner something to hang on to should the worst happen. These also came with a separate safety system: a small magnetic tag that attaches to clothing. If this becomes detached, the machine shuts off.

The general build and robustness of walking pads aren’t up there with their running-focused counterparts, though. That means they can be noisy, shift around underfoot and generally feel a bit flimsy during faster and longer runs. On top of this, those without handles don’t always have the automatic shut-off functionality, which can make them more dangerous, particularly when using them at higher speeds.

In summary, running treadmills are better suited to those wanting to move at higher speeds. They feature more underfoot cushioning or built-in suspension systems, which make longer, faster sessions more comfortable and easier on the joints.

In most cases, yes, but it depends on both the walking pad and the type of carpet. Most manufacturers recommend using a walking pad on a hard, level surface as this provides the best stability and allows air to circulate around the motor. Thick, plush carpets can restrict airflow, increasing the risk of overheating, while also making the machine less stable underfoot.

If carpet is your only option, a low-pile carpet is usually fine, especially with a treadmill mat underneath. This helps spread the load more evenly, protects the carpet from compression and reduces vibration travelling through the floor.

Regardless of the surface, ensure enough clearance around the machine for safe use and so that the belt runs freely without rubbing. It’s also worth checking underneath every so often to remove dust and fluff, especially if you have pets, as debris can build up around the motor and rollers over time.

Maximum user weight isn’t just about whether a walking pad can physically support you – it’s also an indication of how robust the frame, motor and deck are. Choosing a model with a higher weight capacity can often mean a more stable, longer-lasting machine.

Beyond that, look for an emergency stop function or safety key if you intend to jog. Some walking pads automatically stop the belt if they detect you’ve stepped off, while others continue running until you turn them off manually. As I found during testing, not every budget model includes this feature, so check before you buy.

A wide, grippy walking surface also improves confidence, particularly if you’re working at a standing desk, while decent shock absorption can reduce fatigue during longer sessions. Finally, ensure the walking pad has non-slip feet and is sitting securely before every use, as even slight movement can become distracting or unsafe – not to mention damaging to expensive wooden floors.

Although they look similar, walking pads and treadmills are designed for different purposes. Walking pads prioritise compact size, low noise and easy storage, with many slim enough to slide under a sofa or bed. They’re primarily designed for walking rather than running, making them ideal for staying active while you work or watch TV.

Traditional treadmills are larger, heavier and more versatile. They typically offer higher top speeds, wider and longer running decks, better cushioning and features such as adjustable incline, heart rate monitoring and structured workout programmes. Their larger belts also make them far better suited to regular running.

The trade-off is space. If your goal is simply to increase your daily step count or stay active while working from home, a walking pad is usually the more practical choice. But for race training or more serious fitness goals, a conventional treadmill remains the better investment.

https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.author: Blake Montgomery
https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.text:
A scandal tests Nvidia’s dominance as tech billionaires seek to mend ties with Democrats after the midterm elections

This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here

Today in tech, we’re talking about Nvidia’s salacious scandal, tech tycoons trying to reconcile with Democrats, and what billionaires should spend their money on if not elections.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

On the opening night of Web Summit in Lisbon, the Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a Chinese datacenter executive suspected to be a spy for Beijing hit the main stage. The news broke less than 24 hours prior, and the reaction was surprising.

Matthew Prince, CEO of Cloudflare, broadened the implications of the scandal from Huang’s personal life to Nvidia’s market dominance.

“Whatever Jensen did in his personal life, that’s very salacious. In the longer term, whether Nvidia is the hero or the villain, we’ll be asking: Were the things they did to cement their market position … just financial engineering?” Prince said in front of tens of thousands of onlookers.

Nvidia’s essential role in the AI boom as the world’s premier chipmaker had given it a Teflon reputation in Silicon Valley. It served as both a bank – providing loans to its own buyers to purchase its chips – and hardware provider. Prince credited Huang for doing “a lot to cement the AI ecosystem”.

Likewise asked to respond to the news, Richard Socher, CEO of the four-month-old AI startup Recursive Superintelligence, simply said he was “grateful to have Jensen in my corner”.

Prince responded immediately: “That’s captured interest!” After all, Nvidia participated in Recursive’s $500m investment round, announced in April. The chipmaker has faced criticism over its circular financing deals, but the superiority of its hardware has for many years allowed it to make strong alliances within Silicon Valley that have warded off lasting damage.

US intelligence agencies are already scrutinizing Huang. Judging by Prince’s remarks, Silicon Valley may soon do the same.

My colleague Johana Bhuiyan analyzes Huang’s confession and what it might mean for one of the world’s most valuable companies, which is bound up with his family to an unusual degree for Silicon Valley:

For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large.

He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares worth billions. The two married some 40 years ago. During public appearances, he’s fond of telling the story of how they met in college.

But Huang’s image as a family man has been shattered as of Sunday. He admitted in a letter to employees on Sunday that he had been having an affair. Nvidia’s board of directors have now launched an independent investigation about the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s relationship.

“Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support,” Huang wrote in his letter. “They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.”

On one hand, Huang’s affair is not just a matter of morals or ethics, as there are potential national security concerns. On the other, Huang is core to the DNA of Nvidia, which in turn is the bedrock of the entire AI industry – an industry upon which the US economy relies greatly. Huang himself may be too big to fail.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

Investors are doubting what was once seen as an unstoppable juggernaut. Nvidia shares fell 7.5% as soon as the stock market opened, wiping over $330bn off the company’s value.

In the wake of Tuesday’s blue wave, Silicon Valley is attempting to reconcile with the new power brokers in the US.

Tech’s tycoons spent the last two years cozying up to Donald Trump. On Thursday, Elon Musk sang a different tune. After railing against Texas Democrat James Talarico with jibes like “He’ll trans your kids” and spending tens of millions to elect his opponent, Musk responded kindly when the senator-elect called him a “great innovator” on a podcast. Musk tweeted: “Nice of him to say that”. How cordial! It’s a far cry from the extreme and unrelenting partisanship that Musk has hawked for months leading up to the elections.

Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, host of the influential All-In podcast, tweeted on Sunday: “When I’m wrong, I’m wrong … This was a complete and total repudiation about the state of the economy. The economy is broken.” His message sounds much closer to affordability-obsessed Democrats.

Democratic lawmakers are putting out statements that any reconciliation by the tech oligarchy remains largely one-sided and transactional. Newly in-control Democrats do seem to differ in their views on the best strategy for dealing with the conservative problem of Silicon Valley. Members of Congress are eager to haul in tech CEOs for grillings and pass AI safety laws. Newly elected governors campaigned on promises of moratoria on datacenter construction.

It is not clear which is the best path forward for Democrats as they assume power. The US stock market relies heavily on the AI industry’s growth. Hamstringing that industry with bans on new datacenters and legislation that cracks down on AI model development risks sending the economy into a backslide. However, the voting public wants to make a public example of AI CEOs, who are despised on both sides of the aisle despite their alliance with Trump and the Republican elite.
https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted in a letter to employees on Sunday that he had been having an affair. Nvidia CEO had given it a Teflon reputation as the world’s premier chipmaker. Newly elected governors campaigned on promises of moratoria on datacenter construction.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Apple MacBook Pro review: lighter, thinner and a stunning OLED touchscreen
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Redesigned flagship laptop has a fantastic display, killer performance and the first touchscreen on a Mac, but comes with a serious price tag

Apple’s MacBook Pro has been redesigned for the first time in five years, getting slightly slimmer, significantly lighter and adding a fantastic new OLED display with the first touchscreen on a Mac.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in, but rather than replacing the standard MacBook Pro they sit alongside them as an even more expensive option. The OLED machines start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) – a £400 or equivalent upgrade on the matching spec LCD models – serious prices for serious work machines, not helped by significant cost increases driven by RAMageddon.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Shut, the new OLED MacBook Pro looks almost identical to its predecessors: a little smaller in every direction but with the same aluminium body, combination of ports and overall profile. But pick it up and the weight loss is immediately noticeable. The 14in version is 14% lighter than its predecessor at 1.38kg, which makes it only 150g heavier than the 13in MacBook Air, and the 16in version is 15% lighter at 1.82kg.

The new touchscreen is the biggest change, complete with the dynamic island around the web cam like a modern iPhone. The screen on the LCD MacBook Pro was already fantastic, but the switch to OLED has several benefits. The screen is even brighter, hitting an incredible peak of 2,000 nits for outdoor or HDR content viewing, making it one of the brightest laptop screens available.

OLED displays have individually lit pixels, which gives them dramatically better contrast with the deepest blacks and eliminates any blooming effects. That makes the new screen one of the very best on any product and a genuine joy to use to create or watch content. It is super crisp, vibrant and smooth, and makes the most of dark mode.

14in screen: 14.2in tandem OLED (3024x1986; 254 ppi) ProMotion (10-120Hz)

16in screen: 16.3in tandem OLED (3472x2266; 254 ppi) ProMotion (10-120Hz)

Processor: Apple M5 Pro or Max

RAM: 24, 36, 48, 64 or 128GB

Storage: 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16TB SSD

Operating system: macOS 27.2

Camera: 12MP Centre Stage

Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 5/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC card, headphones

14in dimensions: 216.3 x 310.8 x 15mm

14in weight: 1.38 to 1.4kg

16in dimensions: 244.2 x 355.5 x 16mm

16in weight: 1.82 to 1.84kg

The OLED MacBook Pro isn’t the first laptop with a touchscreen – they’ve been common on Windows laptops since 2012 – but it is the first Mac with one. For the most part the touchscreen mirrors mouse clicks, so you can single tap on just about anything or tap and hold for right click on most things.

It also supports most of the gestures available on a trackpad, including swipes, pinch to zoom and rotate. Three-finger swipes trigger mission control so you can switch between windows, while flicking them left or right snaps them to the screen’s edge – though unsnapping them requires a mouse for some reason. Swipe in from the right side of the screen for notification centre, down from the top right for control centre and from the dynamic island for Spotlight or Siri.

The Mac is not touch-first like an iPad and there is no touchscreen keyboard. But Apple has built new touch systems that third-party app developers can use to do unique things, such as tools that fan out around your finger or scrubbing dials. Those are few and far between at the moment.

That leaves touching the screen an optional extra. Like Windows machines, it is handy to have direct interaction with something using your finger sometimes. Pinch to zoom or rotating a photo is a lot easier directly on the screen than the touchpad, as is tapping the screen to pause video. The touchscreen is also useful for performing various gestures if you use a mouse rather than a trackpad.

The OLED MacBook Pros come with the same M5 Pro or Max chips and memory choices as the regular MacBook Pros with essentially the same performance in benchmarks and during general use. They also have similar battery life, lasting for about two days of office work while mainly using the browser, writing, messaging and note-taking tools.

For more intensive workloads, such as developing and editing photos or other mid-level creative apps, the 16in version with M5 Max still managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. If pushed to the limit, the battery lasts about two hours, which is still long enough to get a solid task or two done when away from the charger.

The MacBook Pro OLED is made of 55% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available, offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED starts at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) for the 14in version or £3,399 (€3,899/$3,399/A$5,499) for the 16in version.

For comparison, the 14in M6 MacBook Pro costs £1,999, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.

The OLED MacBook Pro might be the first touchscreen Mac, but touch is the least interesting part about it.

The reduced weight, slimmer body and absolutely stunning new screen are meaningful upgrades that will no doubt see the MacBook Pro through another five years as one of the very best pro laptops you can get.

The light-up Apple logo on the lid is a welcome blast from the past, while the dynamic island at the top of the screen takes up less space and is more useful than the notch it replaces.

The touchscreen is best thought of a value-added extra that is useful on occasion or for certain types of tasks. This isn’t a touch-first laptop, it’s more like one that just happens to have a touchscreen similar to many of the best Windows rivals, which is just fine.

I still wish the dynamic island contained Face ID like it does on an iPhone. The Touch ID fingerprint scanner is fine, but face recognition on a laptop is better. And no matter how you slice it, any of the new MacBook Pros cost a lot of money, part of which can be blamed on RAMageddon.

As crazy as it might sound, if you’re currently hoping to replace an older machine with a new high-end M5 Pro or Max Apple laptop, the extra £400 or equivalent for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is worth it over the regular LCD MacBook Pro.

Pros: stunning OLED touchscreen, dynamic island with great Centre Stage camera, thinner and lighter, choice of extremely potent M5 Pro or Max chips, long battery life, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, brilliant speakers, Touch ID, first-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.

Cons: extremely expensive, no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, touchscreen only occasionally useful.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: New MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in. It is the first Mac with a touchscreen, but comes with a serious price tag. The new OLED MacBook Pro is 14% lighter than its predecessor at 1.38kg.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Molecular signal in blood helps detect early risk for ovarian cancer, study finds
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Reuters
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Researchers discover a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread

A molecular signal in the blood helps identify microscopic changes that precede development of ovarian cancer, researchers have found, ⁠a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread.

For decades, ​efforts to detect ovarian cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumors, the researchers noted in their report published on Tuesday in Nature Medicine.

“We asked a fundamentally different question: What if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” study leader Rajan Gogna of the Hoag Family Cancer Institute in ⁠Newport Beach, California, said in a statement.

Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The precancerous lesions are known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma.

The new study found that women with this precursor condition have elevated blood levels of an RNA molecule called Tu-Stroma.

When researchers measured Tu-Stroma in blood, they detected STIC in 92.3% of affected women ⁠and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women.

In women with genetic risk factors for ovarian cancer, approximately 72% of positive results would be accurate, while negative results would be correct nearly 100% of the time, they reported.

“For women at high risk, this ​could transform how we approach prevention,” co-author Dr Esha Madan, also of Hoag, said in a statement.

Many such women ‌face difficult decisions about preventive surgery to remove their fallopian tubes ‌and ovaries.

“Today, decisions about preventive surgery are largely guided by inherited risk, without knowing whether precancerous lesions are actually present,” Madan said. “Our discovery could eventually provide that missing biological information.”
