Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. For decades,  efforts to detect ovarian cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumors.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Jimmy Carter’s Georgia farm acquired by conservation group planning to open it to public
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Conservation group acquires former US president’s family farm with plans to transfer it to the state in 2028

Jimmy Carter’s family farm has been acquired by a group dedicated to permanently protecting the south-west Georgia land where the late former president’s conservation ethic took hold, officials announced on Monday.

A statement from the Conservation Fund said it plans to open Carter’s family farm – on about 2,458 acres (995 hectares) outside his home town of Plains, Georgia – to the public for hunting, fishing and other outdoor recreation as soon as 2027, with the group set to transfer the land to the state’s natural resources department in 2028.

Plans call for the Carter family farm to ultimately become part of Georgia’s Lanahassee Creek wildlife management area, expanding it to nearly 7,000 acres (2,833 hectares), according to the non-profit Conservation Fund.

The farm sold for $8.5m, multiple media reports indicated. The Conservation Fund also said its purchase of the Carter family farm ensures the protection of a property that was dear to the man who served as US president for four years beginning in 1977 – and later won a Nobel peace prize for his humanitarian work.

After being raised on his family’s farm, Carter signed the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act in late 1980, protecting more than 104m acres in what remains the US’s largest protected public lands expansion in US history, the Conservation Fund said.

He also established 39 national park system units, among them the Martin Luther King Jr national historic site and the Chattahoochee River national recreation area in Georgia’s capital city, Atlanta.

The Conservation Fund traced a direct link between those accomplishments and Carter’s upbringing on the farm where he worked alongside his father, Earl, in their family’s peanut, corn and sugarcane growing operations. He also explored the surrounding woods and returned to the land that the Carter family bought in the early 1900s throughout his life – to hunt; walk with his late wife, Rosalynn; and fish in the property’s pond, including toward the end of the couple’s lives.

Carter successfully requested that his family maintain a stand of mature longleaf pine trees, according to the Conservation Fund. And in one of his final land conservation decisions, the group said, Carter had much of the farm replanted with young longleaf pine.

That move aimed to help restore the native forest once covering the region, a vital habit for tortoises, which conservationists have been working to keep from becoming an endangered species. Creeks adjacent to the Carter family farm are also home to freshwater mussels, which are rare.

“Long before Jimmy Carter protected millions of acres across America, he was a boy working the fields and roaming the woods of southwest Georgia,” said a statement attributed to Stacy Funderburke, vice-president of the Conservation Fund’s central south-east region. “This land shaped him and his legacy, and he never stopped coming home to it.

“We’re honored to help ensure this land remains a healthy habitat for wildlife, and we look forward to the day it is open to everyone who wants to experience it.”

The former president’s grandson, Jason, said in a separate statement: “For our family, this land was always about more than a farm. It was home – a place my grandparents treasured. We’re grateful to The Conservation Fund and to everyone working to make sure it’s protected for generations to come.”

The Conservation Fund said the Carter family farm is distinct from his boyhood home, which is maintained by the US national park service and preserves the house where the former president lived as a child.

A former governor of Georgia, Carter – a Democrat – defeated incumbent Republican president Gerald Ford to clinch his lone Oval Office term. He then lost the presidency to Republican challenger Ronald Reagan during the 1980 election amid the Iran hostage crisis.

After his presidency, Carter won the 2002 Nobel peace prize for his work seeking peaceful resolutions to global conflicts, advancing human rights and democracy, and promoting economic and social development.

The devout Baptist died aged 100 in December 2024, a little more than a year after the death of Rosalynn Carter, his wife.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Conservation Fund says it plans to open Carter's family farm to the public for hunting, fishing and other outdoor recreation. The group is set to transfer the land to the state’s natural resources department in 2028. The farm sold for $8.5m,

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 live: ‘Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs’ - UN chief hits out at industry lobbying
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Guterres launches into a plea for accelerated action to cut emissions and takes direct aim at the fossil fuel industry. The UN chief has already called on countries to push forward a phase out of fossil fuels, rather than merely hinting at it, here at Cop.

“The case for fossil fuels is collapsing,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs. And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.”

“It’s time to kick the habit – and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said. Guterres likes a good pun and one of his final climate speeches has a decent one: “It’s make or bake time.”

Nazar Mohammed Saeed Amedi, president of Iraq, is citing the country’s past as Mesopotamia, “the cradle of human civilisation” and one of the first birthplaces of agriculture, and contrasting it with the challenges that climate change is already bringing it. He says the loss of arable land and projected hit to water security will jeapordise its food security. He’s calling for more support for a green economy.

We’re now hearing from Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov, leader of Turkmenistan. He’s speaking about efforts to modernise his country’s energy infrastructure and calling for greater climate resilience in the face of worsening weather.

Turkmenistan is an oil and gas producer that has become infamous for its vast emissions of methane, a potent planet-heating gas that is wastefully vented from fossil fuel infrastructure. In August, my colleague Damian Carrington, who has uncovered some of the country’s worst excesses, reported on early successful efforts to plug some of these “mind-boggling” leaks.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to support our crucial year-end fundraiser. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

The first national leader to speak is Mohamed Cheikh El Ghazouani, President of Mauritania, who is calling for an increase in the assistance given to countries most affected by climate change. “Despite the limited carbon footprint it has, Mauritiania has been suffering greatly from climate change and its consequences, including drought, land degradation and coastal erosion.” He says these have hit the economic fabric of the country, particularly in rural areas.

Murat Kurum, Turkey’s climate minister and Cop31 president, is now up. He’s detailing the weather extremes battering countries around the world, while making the case for how climate action is in countries’ national interests – by boosting energy security, for instance. He’s making some similar points to Bowen on the many obstacles to global cooperation.

“Our collective success depends on our ability to identify common interests,” he says.

When it comes to food, water and climate risks – which recognise no borders – there can only be common ground, he says.

“Let us make Antalya a symbol city for action,” he says.

Unsurprisingly, neither of the co-hosts mentioned their own countries’ expansions of fossil fuel infrastructure that have undermined their credibility somewhat – Australia as a major exporter of coal, oil and gas, and Turkey having just celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields this week.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and president of the negotiations, is framing the talks as a challenge for multilaterism in the face of threats from worsening weather to geopolitics.

“It’s no exaggeration to say the world is facing a polycrisis – not challenges on one front, but on multiple fronts, all at once.”

His answer is a resounding yes, for global cooperation. “While the challenge is growing, so is our agency. Before Paris the world was heading to nearly 4c of warming. Now it’s closer to 2.6C.”

He’s underscoring the existential nature of climate crisis for Pacific islands – particularly from overshooting the 1.5C target – as well as the small share of climate finance they receive.

He concludes: “Together, we can demonstrate that multilateral cooperation still matters, and can deliver in the critical moment.”

Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), is sweeping through the scientific findings that underpin everything that is being discussed in Antalya. CO2 in the atmosphere is 50% higher than in the preindustrial era. Land and oceans cannot keep up. The Earth energy imbalance is at its highest level since measurements began in 1960. The planet is accumulating heat at an increasing rate. The past 12 years are the warmest on record.

But along with the gloom are some reasons for hope. Saulo is celebrating the work of the WMO in observing the planet – able to predict disasters before they strike – and the rollout of early warning systems. These are “giving countries time to prepare and protect”, she says, while calling for greater investments in them.

The President of the UN general assembly, Khalilur Rahman, has just opened the segment for heads of state and government. He’s making a plea for action and multilaterism before leaders of dozens of nations make their contributions – with a reminder about what really matters. “Speeches do not cool our planet. Decisions and deliveries do.”

The national security of all countries is at risk from the climate crisis, as “science fiction” scenarios of widespread destruction are already coming true and economic shocks from fossil fuels are now the norm rather than the exception, the UK’s foreign secretary is to warn world leaders gathered in Turkey.

Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict.

“National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action; the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news,” Miliband told the Guardian before his speech to world leaders and governments in Antalya.

“We should be clear that climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face. Food security, threats to infrastructure, and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis],” he said.

In a veiled swipe at the Conservatives and Reform UK, which want to scrap efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, he added: “Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.”

‘I am no longer satisfied with promises’

This week I’ve been speaking to young climate activists at Cop31. Today I spoke to Sohanur Rahman, 29, from Bangladesh, who survived a super-cyclone as a child.

He became a key figure in the fight against climate change in Bangladesh after founding YouthNet for Climate Justice in 2016.

“I feel a deep sense of urgency, frustration and cautious hope as we approach Cop31. After attending five Cops, I am no longer satisfied with promises. I want to see whether those promises are actually changing people’s lives.

“For countries like Bangladesh, climate change is not a distant threat. It is already affecting us through extreme heat, cyclones, floods, river erosion and salinity. Behind every negotiation are people who cannot afford another decade of delay. I am particularly concerned that climate-vulnerable countries are still expected to borrow money to deal with the consequences of a crisis they contributed very little to. Climate finance must be accessible, predictable and primarily grant-based.

“Despite my frustration, I remain hopeful. I see hope in young people organising in their communities, women leading local adaptation efforts, Indigenous peoples protecting nature and frontline communities developing solutions despite limited resources. They remind me that a different future is possible: one where people can live safely, work with dignity and thrive without destroying the natural systems on which we all depend.

“My hope is that CopP31 in Antalya becomes a turning point from promises to implementation. We need climate finance that reaches frontline communities, responsible businesses, a just transition for workers, stronger international cooperation and institutions that deliver on their commitments.”

UK heatwaves could cost London more than £25bn in lost productivity over the next decade, the mayor of London will tell world leaders.

Through analysis from City Hall, which also estimates the 2026 heatwaves cost the capital about £2.5bn in lost productivity, Sadiq Khan will underline the economic consequences of extreme heat, as high temperatures make it harder for people to work effectively.

“The climate sceptics argue that these investments are unaffordable,” Khan will tell Cop. “But the only thing we cannot afford is to do nothing.

“Even if you can see past the devastating implications for human health, the long-term economic impact of extreme heat alone will be astronomical,” the mayor is expected to say. “If the scenes we saw this summer became the standard, it could cost London’s economy more than £25 billion over the next ten years.”

Khan will also warn that record breaking heat in the UK is already taking a devastating toll on people’s health, businesses and public services, with thousands of vulnerable people losing their lives to heat-related causes.

“Climate disaster is no longer the stuff of some distant dystopia,” Khan will say. “It’s killing people, harming communities and impacting our economies right now. And failing to protect ourselves from the perils we face – or prepare ourselves for worse to come – would be a dereliction of duty.”

Erdogan has moved on to the “genocide and ecocide” that he says is happening in Gaza, and his comments are finding some applause.

And now he returns to his ecological theme from earlier.

“Enough of the greedy mindset that sacrifices ecology for economy.”

“May God guide or path and good fortune.”

He wishes Ethiopia, that will host Cop32 next, the best fortune.

Erdogan spends some time thanking people and explaining how the rooms at the venue are named after legendary Turkish figures before launching into an almost Deep Ecology-style lament.

“As humanity we only have one roof over our home, namely the sky, as humanity we only have one garden, namely the Earth,” he said. “Let me state this plainly – we have no other sky, no other Earth, no other seas, oceans or forests.”

Greed for excessive consumption is causing the “deepest existential crisis” in human history, he said. “We all know well a forest in flames, a river running dry, a polluted sea all inflict pain on the entire planet,” he said. “No country is exempt from this pain.”

Progress has been made at these annual UN climate talks but there’s been a lack of implementation, Erdogan says in front of a screen that blares ‘Implementation Cop.’ He added “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: UN chief has already called on countries to push forward a phase out of fossil fuels. Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit that security and defence objectives are the new ‘frontier’s’S’

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Burnham lauds £12bn offshore wind investment as he prepares for climate summit
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Lauren Almeida
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Package for plan off Norfolk coast revealed as government tries to calm critics after approving Jackdaw gasfield

UK politics live – latest updates

Andy Burnham has hailed a record investment in offshore wind, as the government tries to repair its green credentials after approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea.

On Wednesday the government announced a £12bn investment from the German energy company RWE and the US private equity firm KKR, as the prime minister prepares to travel to the Cop31 climate crisis summit in Turkey.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The investment package, which will go towards the creation of the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore windfarms off the Norfolk coast, is a “vote of confidence for building in Britain”, he said.

“It is great news for bill payers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.

“With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain’s future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings.”

The offshore wind projects will also receive £1bn in funding from the state-owned national wealth fund.

The windfarms are set to be providing power by 2030, with construction set to begin early next year. The wind investment is “believed to be the biggest of its kind in UK history”, the government said.

RWE said the Vanguard project represents one of the UK’s largest offshore wind developments, generating about 2.8 gigawatts, enough to supply 3m homes.

It estimated that the construction of the windfarms will create and support 2,300 jobs each year through its supply chain. The windfarms are expected to create a further 100 long-term permanent jobs when they are operational.

The energy company SSE also announced on Wednesday that the latest phase of its major offshore windfarm, Berwick Bank B off the east coast of Scotland, would “support” 2,600 existing jobs.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said investment in offshore wind and clean power was “creating quality jobs and rebuilding industry, while delivering the clean power we need to lower bills and reach net zero”.

She added that Britain was “leading from the front as a renewable energy powerhouse”.

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

It comes as Burnham seeks to bolster his government’s under-fire green credentials at Cop31, where he is expected to give a speech on Thursday.

The prime minister has faced a backlash from Labour MPs and environmental campaigners over his government’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield.

On Tuesday, ministers also rejected plans to build what would have been Britain’s biggest solar plant near the Blenheim Palace estate.

Fahnbulleh turned down the £800m Botley West project, which would have covered almost 3,500 acres of land. Developers said it would have provided enough electricity to power 330,000 homes.

Margaret Curran, in a letter on behalf of the energy secretary, wrote that the project would cause “substantial harm” to the green belt and the Blenheim Estate – home to Blenheim Palace, which is a world heritage site and the birthplace of Winston Churchill.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: National security of all countries at risk due to climate crisis, UK foreign secretary warns
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Exclusive: Ed Miliband says sci-fi scenarios of destruction ‘now regular occurrences’, as he prepares to address Cop31

Cop31 live – latest updates

UK politics live – latest updates

The national security of all countries is at risk from the climate crisis, as “science fiction” scenarios of widespread destruction are already coming true and economic shocks from fossil fuels are now the norm rather than the exception, the UK’s foreign secretary is to warn world leaders gathered in Turkey.

Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action; the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news,” Miliband told the Guardian before his speech to world leaders and governments in Antalya.

“We should be clear that climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face. Food security, threats to infrastructure, and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis],” he said.

In a veiled swipe at the Conservatives and Reform UK, which want to scrap efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, he added: “Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.”

Miliband arrived in Turkey on Tuesday evening for the two-day leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday and Thursday of the fortnight-long Cop31 talks, which started on Monday.

Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, is expected to travel on Wednesday for a series of bilateral meetings with fellow world leaders on Thursday.

Anthony Albanese, the prime minister of Australia, and the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, will open the leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday. There will also be speeches by the UN secretary general, António Guterres, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, which hosted last year’s Cop, and the prime minister of Ethiopia, Abiy Ahmed, who will host next year’s meeting.

However, several heads of leading countries are skipping this year’s Cop, including China’s Xi Jinping, India’s Narendra Modi, France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will attend.

Miliband will argue that the world must now face the consequences of failures to cut carbon emissions over the past three decades. “It is a disaster for people and the planet, and we must reckon with its implications,” he will tell audiences at Cop31 on Wednesday. “It will drive hardship and insecurity for billions of people.”

He will note that an “overshoot” of the crucial threshold of 1.5C of global heating above preindustrial levels, is now inevitable, as temperatures have exceeded that level for two years and are unlikely to subside significantly. This “overshoot” requires stronger policies to ensure heating does not accelerate, and to seek ways of returning temperatures to safer levels in decades to come.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

Fossil fuel shocks, such as the soaring oil price seen this year after the start of the Iran war, which has led to rampant inflation and interest rate rises from central banks in an effort to control it, will wreak further harm, according to Miliband.

He told the Guardian: “A new era of global insecurity means fossil fuel shocks are now the norm – the fossil fuel rollercoaster is here to stay. First Russia, now Iran, next others, have identified global chokepoints and systemic overreliance [on fossil fuels] and the vulnerability of countries around the world that they expose.”

He said the only answer was to “double down” on measures to cut greenhouse gas emissions and build resilience to the effects of extreme weather. “Next year will be the year of climate fightback, as governments, movements and communities across the world step up to defend our shared home.”

Miliband will call for more investment in clean energy and efforts to use it for transport and heating, as well as urgent action to cut methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, and protect and expand forests.

However, Burnham’s government is under fire in the UK for a series of recent and looming policy interventions that campaigners say will push the country off-track from its target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and set a poor example to the rest of the world.

The government plans to weaken a mandate for carmakers to ensure more of their vehicles are electric by 2030, and has given the green light to a new gasfield, Jackdaw, in the North Sea, while considering licensing a new oilfield, Rosebank, west of Shetland.

Miliband will tell world leaders at Cop31 Cop31 that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier’ of climate action.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Gloria Dickie
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
As the IUCN global conservation body prepares to update its red list of endangered species, scientists explain why calculating the true toll of a pandemic is so hard

I
t began with the brown skuas. The migratory seabirds had arrived on the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 2023, harbouring a deadly passenger. Within months, the southern elephant seals that had come ashore to breed became sick. Mothers and newborn pups were weak and trembling, with many struggling to breathe. What followed was a horrific mass casualty event, caused by the highly infectious avian influenza (H5N1).

By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on South Georgia. That is especially alarming, scientists say, because the island is home to more than half of the global breeding population.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

A highly potent strain of the bird flu virus, which first began circulating in the northern hemisphere in 2021, has now spread to four of the five main southern elephant seal populations. In some South Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died, alongside about half of all adult females.

“This is a horror show for wildlife,” says Ruth Cromie, coordinator of a UN taskforce on avian influenza and wildlife. “The scale of mortality is absolutely unprecedented.”

In April, the mass deaths prompted the IUCN red list, the global authority responsible for assessing the extinction risks of wildlife, to downgrade the southern elephant seal’s conservation status by two categories, from “least concern” to “vulnerable”.

It was the first time a species has had its extinction risk raised explicitly because of H5N1.

The IUCN listing notes that scientists suspect the global southern elephant seal population has declined by nearly a third, and models suggest many populations will take decades to recover. So far, scientists have found few antibodies to the disease among surviving animals.

The southern elephant seal is just one species that has suffered catastrophic die-offs since H5N1 began burning its way through the world’s wildlife, killing hundreds of thousands of animals, if not millions. Avian influenza is now a threat to at least 40 bird species, according to BirdLife International, a global conservation partnership. And yet, no other animal – seal or bird – has seen its conservation status changed.

But scientists warn that does not mean there are not more species being pushed to the brink by this deadly pathogen.

Assessing a species’ conservation threats is a painstaking scientific and bureaucratic process. To date, the red list has analysed nearly 176,000 species’ extinction risks, and aims to reach 260,000 species by 2030, as well as 142,000 reassessments.

Most species are only reassessed by a panel of expert scientists once every decade or so – no matter the emerging threats they may face. The red list itself is updated two to three times a year.

Birds are the exception. BirdLife International serves as the authority for assessing the world’s 11,000-plus bird species, reviewing hundreds of birds every year. For that reason, our understanding of the extinction risks of birds is better than for any other animal group. In an epidemic where birds are the foremost victim, that is obviously convenient.

But there can still be a lag when deaths are coming faster than scientists can convene and publish under peer review. “We still need to get these things out there,” says Rob Martin, senior red list officer at BirdLife International.

Species are generally “uplisted” when they have experienced a sustained population decline over three generations, a small population is in decline or living within a restricted range, or calculations show that the species could become extinct in the near future, given existing population dynamics.

Scientific uncertainty often underlies such reviews. Assessors need to know the animal’s baseline population before they can determine if it has crossed a threshold towards extinction. For many species, such figures are in short supply. And without knowing a species’ starting point, it is difficult to calculate the true toll of an outbreak.

Scientists with BirdLife International say they are now focused on reassessing four species that have suffered H5N1 outbreaks large enough to affect their conservation outlook: the great skua, northern gannet, Peruvian pelican and Humboldt penguin.

In Scotland, home to more than half of the world’s great skuas, the population of monitored colonies fell by 76% between 2021 and 2023.

Meanwhile, the northern gannet, the largest seabird native to the North Atlantic, declined dramatically in two breeding populations in the UK as bird flu spread: by 43% at Bass Rock in Scotland between 2021 and 2024 and 47% at Grassholm in Wales between 2015 and 2024.

These are two of the largest northern gannet colonies, and extrapolating from such figures would imply a steep population fall, say BirdLife International assessors, potentially qualifying the species for uplisting from “least concern”.

But when scientists took a broader look, they found that the entire north-eastern Atlantic population had declined no more than 17% between 2013 and 2024. “Rushing to judgment a few years ago, with only partial data available and no sense of whether the whole population was declining, would have been premature and could have led to a misclassification,” BirdLife International scientists say.

Martin cautions that it is important to prevent “kneejerk” uplisting after a mass mortality event, as listings such as “critically endangered” can trigger dozens of conservation funding proposals and divert government spending. “We need it to be a tool that the community can reliably use and say ‘we trust this,’” he says.

About a fifth of the pelican population living in Peru’s marine protected areas are thought to have succumbed to bird flu in 2022 and 2023. But the Peruvian pelican is considered an abundant bird.

“It’s difficult to get accurate numbers for the population pre- and post- [the H5N1 outbreak] because they’re in quite isolated areas without sufficient funding for monitoring,” says Martin.

Counting the dead often poses an even greater hurdle, especially for migratory species that travel vast distances over oceans. “You usually don’t find most of the dead birds. If they die at sea, they’re lost,” says Wouter Langhout, a policy consultant at BirdLife International.

The flightless Humboldt penguin, which spends most of its life on land, has made such tallies easier. In 2023, scientists counted nearly 3,000 dead penguins along Chile’s coasts, prompting another review of the already vulnerable species, which was last assessed in 2020.

Even when population and mortality numbers are easy to come by, spectacular mass die-offs – as gruesome as they may be – do not guarantee a species is inching towards extinction. For long-lived seabirds, large waterbirds and elephant seals that are slow to reproduce and late to sexually mature, a large loss of breeding adults can translate into severe population declines in just three generations – a key red-list criterion for uplisting.

But fast-reproducing animals or those with abundant populations may be spared such long-term consequences, especially if more adult males die than fertile females.

In the case of the Antarctic fur seal, for example, far more males have succumbed to the disease than breeding females, says Jaume Forcada, a marine mammal expert and population biologist at the British Antarctic Survey who has studied Antarctic fur seals for 25 years.

That is because male and female fur seals behave very differently. Whereas the males come ashore for about two months, often battling with one another on beaches, “when females arrive, they pup, and then they go out very quickly. They’re less exposed to other animals apart from the moment when they are rearing their pup,” Forcada says.

In turn, “the males were very severely affected, whereas the females were absolutely fine. It’s like it was a completely different species. It hadn’t affected them.”

If scientists uncover a population decline that would warrant uplisting, attributing it to avian influenza may not be cut and dried, Martin cautions. For example, BirdLife recently reassessed the African penguin, which was heavily affected by avian influenza.

Although it was uplisted to critically endangered in 2024, assessors determined that food loss linked to commercial fisheries and the climate crisis – not bird flu – ultimately drove its decline.

The 3,000 dead Humboldt penguins in Chile have also triggered debate among scientists. Penguins often drown in gill nets and 2023 was also an El Niño year, which may have had a hand in the birds’ deaths.

“That year could be described as a ‘perfect storm’, which produced highly unfavourable conditions for Humboldt penguins,” says Alejandro Simeone, a scientist in the IUCN’s penguin specialist group.

“While it is quite possible that some Humboldt penguins died from [avian influenza], current evidence makes it difficult to assess the true extent of the virus’s role in this decline,” Simeone says.

In the end, it may not be the most visible victims that are in the greatest peril. Birds with tiny isolated populations – often those inhabiting small islands – can quickly move towards extinction even if only a handful of individuals die.

“For species that are already under threat and declining for other reasons, and then you put in something like avian influenza, that might be the thing that then pushes them over the edge,” Cromie says.

To date, scientists say they are not yet aware of any such cases from bird flu, but are anxiously monitoring Australia, where H5N1 was first detected on the mainland in June.

“A lot of Australian species still do have quite wide ranges, but there’s a very specific habitat that they rely on,” Martin says.

The country is also home to a number of critically endangered birds that can be found nowhere else in the world, such as the orange-bellied parrot and the regent honeyeater.

Waiting for uplisting, Cromie adds, may miss the bigger picture. “We have to be focusing on taking these other pressures off,” she says. “If we become very fixated on only waiting to do something because of a change of status, there’s such a lag there. We’ve got to be doing other things at the same time.”

Already, fur seals and dolphins in Australian waters have begun to die from bird flu. And things are about to get worse for the now-vulnerable southern elephant seal.

In August, the government’s Australian Antarctic Division said it would evacuate its research station on Macquarie Island in anticipation of mass seal die-offs if H5N1 reaches its shores. Macquarie is the last stronghold of southern elephant seals still untouched by the virus.

Though the risk to human health is low, the agency said it hoped to prevent psychological distress for staff who could witness the deaths of thousands of newborn seal pups.

The next update to the list is due on 26 November, and proposals for new uplistings will next be discussed in January and February 2027.

“Our biggest fear is always that we completely miss something that suddenly is critically endangered. That’s what we’re guarding against,” Martin says.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: IUCN red list of endangered species is being updated by the global conservation body. It aims to reach 260,000 species by 2030, as well as 142,000 reassessments. A fifth of the pelican population in Peru's marine protected areas are thought to have succumbed to bird flu.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: This small Alaska town is swamped by cruise ship visitors every summer. But what happens when they all go home?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Molly McCluskey in Skagway, Alaska
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Skagway’s 1,100 permanent residents are caught between a boom time – when the ships bring more than a million tourists – and a lull in winter

O
ctober comes to the small Alaska coastal town of Skagway like a sigh. The shops that were bustling throughout the crazed tourist season are reducing their opening hours or beginning to close. The hordes of employees sleeping in overcrowded bunkhouses are leaving or have left.

The crowds of cruise passengers who have filled the streets since April, wearing lanyards emblazoned with the names of their ships, have dwindled to a trickle. Soon, they will all be gone. Snow is visible on the nearby mountains.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

What is left after the season has ended and the last ship has disappeared from sight is a year-round community of about 1,100 people – on paper, at least – and the concern that, as the demands of the cruise ship industry grow, life in this small town is becoming more and more difficult.

“The year-round economy, the year-round population is one of my bigger concerns as someone who lives here,” says Skagway’s mayor, Orion Hanson. “What does Skagway do without a coffee shop to congregate in or without a restaurant open all the time? We don’t have a diner any more.”

Two local restaurants stay open, albeit with limited hours outside the cruise ship season. But the Sweet Tooth cafe, once a longstanding year-round diner, is gone. It is now a storefront for Diamonds International, a tax-free jewellery store that partners with cruise lines for onboard retail and shops in ports that open seasonally.

At the height of the Klondike gold rush, Skagway was the largest town in Alaska, with a population of about 10,000 people. In 1900, it became Alaska’s first official city. But by 1910, as the gold rush subsided, the population had dwindled to about 600 people.

It took a decade for that dramatic swing. Now, as one of the most popular cruise ship destinations in the world, it can happen in a single day, when thousands can flood on to Skagway’s streets from cruise ships, only to leave again when the sun sets. The most recent figures available show that more than 1.35 million tourists arrived in Skagway by cruise ship in 2025, alongside more than half a million crew – and the numbers are growing each year.

That means housing, services and infrastructure designed for a town of about 1,000 people having to accommodate an influx of thousands of workers who arrive in late winter and stay until early autumn.

“Part of the complication of Skagway is that you have such a boom in the summer and such a lull in the winter,” says Hanson. “In terms of revenue that’s not directly related to cruise ships there is not a lot.

“As we saw during the pandemic, we’re at risk,” he says. “If all your eggs are in one basket, it leaves you very vulnerable.”

Like many tourist towns, Skagway has a housing shortage. Unlike other towns, however, it is squeezed into a narrow valley set at the northern end of Alaska’s Inside Passage, a 500-mile maritime route that hugs the coast along Alaska and British Columbia. It is known for its rugged mountains, forests, glaciers and abundant wildlife; there are no realistic commuting options and no room to expand – the only road leads to Canada.

The Skagway Development Corporation commissioned a report in 2023 that found there were 644 housing units in town. In the years since, more have been added, but not enough for the town to accommodate the cruise ship industry and the businesses that support it, its permanent residents, seasonal employees and the workers and families who keep Skagway’s essential services running.

As a result, everything from warehouses to single-family homes, from tents to recreational vehicles or motorhomes, are accommodating the increasing numbers of seasonal workers each year.

“There’s a lot of congregate living and couch surfing,” says Al Wall, director of the town’s Dahl Memorial Clinic. “There are quite a few people that sleep in hammocks in the woods. And frankly, some would prefer to sleep in a hammock in a tree than stay in a crowded place with a bunch of people.”

In years past, many seasonal workers slept in camp sites. But a change in the town’s law forbidding season-long camping pushed them into traditional homes that previously housed the town’s established population.

Janilyn Heger, a longtime Skagwegian, owns the town’s distillery, Skagway Spirits. She and her husband Gary, who owns a construction company, once managed the town-owned camp sites.

“The city made the decision for whatever reason to abandon that type of housing, and that created a domino effect that has been a disaster for the community,” she says.

“Employers started buying buildings and displacing year-round housing and so now we’re at an absolute standstill. There’s none to be had.”

Skagway’s housing shortage has become so severe that many of the town’s limited hotels have been converted into accommodation for seasonal employees.

Longtime resident Mike Healy bought Sergeant Preston’s hotel from friends when he was unable to find land to build enough employee housing to meet his businesses’ needs.

“I didn’t want to purchase Sergeant Preston’s … I approached the city and said, hey, Municipality of Skagway, I am going to purchase the only year-round hotel in this community if you don’t free up some land for housing.” At the time Healy purchased Sergeant Preston’s, the town also had a year-round bed and breakfast.

Healy, not receiving an answer, duly converted the hotel into seasonal housing, part of a portfolio that provides off-season accommodation to visiting workers and contractors.

Jonathan Hillis, a town assembly member who owns the local Mountain Shop outdoor gear store, says that pattern is playing out across town.

“We have very few places now for independent travellers to stay, which is fostering this kind of cycle of more and more cruise ship tourists and fewer independent travellers.”

The scale of cruise tourism is a frequent topic of debate in towns throughout the Inside Passage. As the 2026 season winds down, these towns are consulting the docking schedules for 2027 and 2028, making note of the projected increase in tourism, and asking how much they can realistically handle.

One hundred miles south of Skagway in Alaska’s capital, Juneau, there have been repeated attempts to limit cruise ship tourism. After a ballot measure for “ship-free Saturdays” failed in 2024, the city introduced a voluntary limit on the number of ships that could dock daily.

Farther south in the Inside Passage, Ketchikan has reported more ships as a result of cruises adhering to Juneau’s limitations, while Sitka, also on the cruise ship destination trail, is reviewing its agreements with the industry after an anticipated increase in visitor numbers in 2027.

A survey conducted by Oregon State University reveals a nuanced position when it comes to the cruise sector in Skagway. Just over 40% of people who responded thought that the benefits of tourism outweighed the costs, compared with 25% who put it the other way round. Another 33% viewed the relationship as roughly balanced.

Whatever the sentiment, for a small town that is economically dependent on one industry for its livelihood, options are limited.

“There’s only so much we can do, even if we wanted to,” Hanson says. “We need to be incredibly careful about not rocking the boat.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Why are Britain's streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them | George Monbiot
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: George Monbiot
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The transition to electric vehicles should be moving apace, but it is not. And why? Incompetence, expedience and cowardice

T
his is how it works. An industry puts tremendous effort into resisting change: lobbying governments, mobilising the media, pouring money into junktanks. It argues that a transition would threaten jobs, or damage the national interest, or harm poor people, while what it really fears is the cost of retooling its plants or developing new protocols. Then, when the inevitable cliff edge approaches, it whines that change is coming too soon. For reasons beyond its control, it isn’t ready, so the government must delay its plans.

This is what triggered the Dutch nitrate crisis, and the UK’s repeated “emergency” exemptions from the ban on a devastating class of pesticides. Now the same dynamic is driving the UK’s crisis over the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). The result is that, as the global climate summit, Cop31, begins, it looks as if our gift to the world will be a major, predictable and entirely avoidable increase in the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Car manufacturers could have seen this coming more than 130 years ago, when the first electric automobiles were sold. For at least the past 30 years, as new electromotive technologies have progressed at speed, they plainly represented the future, and internal combustion engines, with their hard efficiency limits and vast impacts on human and planetary life, the past. Since 2010, it’s been obvious that China, which has not only seen the future but seeks to own it, would flatten our manufacturers like hedgehogs if they didn’t speed up. In 2023, the Conservative government gave automakers seven years to get their act together. And now they wring their hands and claim to be unprepared. To which the only reasonable answer is: tough.

But, unfortunately, this doesn’t seem to be the answer the government is giving. Instead, on Wednesday it’s expected to cut the target for zero-emission cars from 80% of new car sales by 2030 to approximately 60%. If so, this will be the latest in a series of concessions that governments have agreed since the Conservatives announced the deadline.

Both Conservative and Labour governments have permitted a series of “flexibilities” (otherwise known as loopholes). These allow companies to sell hybrid petrol-electric cars instead of purely EVs. They can also sell a lower proportion of EVs by 2030 on the promise that they’ll accelerate sales after that date. Now the government is also expected to extend the “flexibilities” to 2034, making a mockery of the promise to accelerate after 2030. One retreat after another.

Every one of these slippages has major consequences, for climate breakdown, air pollution, energy security and the cost of living (electric cars, if you can charge at home, are much cheaper to run). The transition to EVs was supposed to be the biggest of all the government’s decarbonisation measures. Now it’s in pieces.

Once again, the problem is the domination of our nominally democratic systems by money. Commercial lobbyists reach ministers long before environmentalists can. As soon as the Conservative government proposed its transition plan, manufacturers pressed to weaken it. This year, they hinted that they wouldn’t invest in future manufacturing here unless the government made further concessions. It looks to me like a legal form of blackmail.

Perfecting the art of unreadiness, the car companies help to ensure that society is also unready for the great crises – from oil supply shocks to climate breakdown – we face. The people they hire deploy an armoury of clever arguments. But while these might sway British politicians, they do nothing to persuade reality, whether that reality consists of the atmosphere or Chinese competitors.

Last month, the Chinese company BYD launched a new Seagull electric hatchback for the home market at just $10,000 (£7,500). It can be flash-charged in five minutes. And where are western manufacturers? Well, Jaguar recently unveiled its reply to Elon Musk’s ill-fated Cybertruck, an unaffordable monster that can scarcely be driven – let alone parked – on our streets. Perhaps the nearest European equivalent to the Seagull, the Volkswagon ID Polo, is much more expensive and you might not get it for months. As the website Autonext comments, “Europe’s carmakers spent 2024 and 2025 telling Brussels that the CO2 targets were unrealistic because buyers would not take small electric cars in the volumes the rules assumed. Volkswagen has now put three of them on sale and cannot build them quickly enough.” Why? Because it didn’t invest in sufficient plants.

The government is now considering imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs, as part of an EU scheme. If you can’t beat them and you can’t join them, block them. So much for addressing the cost-of-living crisis.

As for allowing companies to keep building hybrids rather than EVs, this solves nothing. Hybrids are almost as polluting as 100%-petrol or diesel vehicles; more expensive to run than EVs; incompatible, in most cases, with rapid chargers and destined, very soon, for the scrapheap of history. But, thanks to government policy, last year they accounted for 14% of new car sales, which means 14% of buyers were suckered. The hybrid is the perfect motif for government dithering: given a choice between two technologies, two worlds, two futures, it says yes to both.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The public information campaigns and public honesty required from the government in explaining why a rapid all-electric transition is necessary and what its implications are, as usual, are entirely missing. Public communications remain in private hands. The marketing budgets of the car companies are still used to sell ever bigger child-killing, planet-killing trucks.

An EV transition doesn’t solve all of our transport issues. We should be reducing transport demand, through a shift towards the 15-minute city model of which Paris is an exemplar. We need better and safer provision for cyclists and pedestrians. We need more investment in public transport. But if we can’t even get the end-of-pipe – or end-of-the-tailpipe – issue right, what hope is there for the rest of the system?

This is, or should be, easy politics. Tell the foot-dragging, planet-trashing car companies, the authors of their own failure, where to get off. They face a stark choice: move or get squashed.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump’s FCC nominee avoids questions from Democrats on Carr’s ‘censorship agenda’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Senators pressured Danielle Thumann, senior counsel to FCC chair Brendan Carr, to speak about agency’s actions toward ABC and Jimmy Kimmel

During a contentious Tuesday hearing on her nomination by Donald Trump to serve as a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) commissioner, Senate Democrats hammered Danielle Thumann about recent actions taken by the Brendan Carr-led regulator that have been criticized as hostile to press freedom.

Thumann, who serves as senior counsel to Carr, is expected to be approved as commissioner, with Republicans in charge of the US Senate and House. But Ben Ray Luján, a senator of New Mexico, assured her that the commission’s actions will be under close scrutiny when Democrats take charge of the chamber in January.

Luján asked Thumann repeatedly whether she agrees with actions taken by Carr’s FCC, including a nearly unprecedented order in late April forcing ABC to apply early to renew its local station licenses, a move that immediately followed criticism of one of the network’s biggest stars, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, by the president and Melania Trump, the first lady. Carr was also accused of pressuring ABC affiliates to drop Kimmel’s show the previous fall.

“Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airways?” Luján asked.

“I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related issues, and I’m not familiar with all of the details regarding the investigation of ABC or the early license renewal of their licenses,” Thumann responded. “And I haven’t been involved in any of those conversations regarding any of their practices or regarding Jimmy Kimmel.”

Luján pressed Thumann to name an issue she has disagreed with Carr on, and she demurred. He also asked her whether it was “appropriate for the FCC to call up Disney’s broadcast license for early renewal”.

Several of Luján’s Democratic colleagues also took turns pressuring Thumann on the FCC’s actions toward television networks, with Ed Markey, the Massachusetts senator, grilling her on “Chairman Carr’s FCC censorship agenda”. “Ms Thumann, does the FCC have the authority to punish a broadcaster because the president disagrees with its news coverage?”

Pushing back on her response, Markey said: “Again, this should be a straightforward constitutional limitation, because the FCC cannot punish a broadcaster simply because the president doesn’t like his coverage. Yet Chairman Carr, your boss right now, has threatened to do exactly that.”

Markey accused her of choosing to “evade” his questions, saying that “anyone seeking a seat on the Federal Communications Commission must be willing to stand up to such threats and to defend the first amendment, and you are not willing to do so here in your confirmation hearing.”

Senator Tammy Duckworth also asked Thumann about whether she would yield to political pressure to punish disfavored networks. While Thumann said the commission has to deal with complaints against networks it regulates, she acknowledged that “editorial decision-making is protected by the first amendment for broadcasters”, and added: “I don’t think that a decision [about a station’s license] should be based purely on someone’s discontent with the content that’s being aired.”

Several Senate Democrats said it was inappropriate for the commerce committee to hold the confirmation hearing, and that if Republicans were going to nominate another member of the party to the commission, they should follow past precedent and nominate a Democrat as well. The FCC currently has one commissioner nominated by a Democratic president, Anna M Gomez, but her term has already technically expired.

At the end of the hearing, Luján issued a warning to Carr. “Mr Carr, if you’re listening now, know you’re going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions, and you don’t have the protection of the gavel any longer,” he said. “Subpoena authorities that you have to respond to so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Tech’s biggest names sank a tax on billionaires’ wealth with $425m and a familiar playbook
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
California saw the most expensive opposition campaign in its history as funding of political campaigns broke records in the US midterms

In the hours after polls closed on election day, tech industry players began praising Sergey Brin, the co-founder of Google, on social media.

“Huge thanks to Sergey Brin here,” wrote Garry Tan, the CEO of Y Combinator. Venture capitalist Ilya Sukhar posted: “God bless Sergey Brin.” And David Marcus, a crypto entrepreneur, simply wrote: “Hero.”

They were all referring to Brin’s instrumental role in the defeat of California’s wealth tax ballot measure, known as Proposition 40. The proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires in the state was defeated by just over five points. Simultaneously, an opposition initiative that would ban any taxation on billionaire wealth, Proposition 42, put on the ballot by Brin and a cohort of the state’s ultra-rich, is poised to pass.

Brin, whose net worth is about $230bn, contributed at least $132m to the fight – more than any other donor. The runner-up was former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, who gave more than $48m. Millions more were donated by executives from Palantir, DoorDash, Stripe and Reddit, along with prominent venture capitalists. All told, Silicon Valley’s elite raised nearly $425m to sink the tax, according to campaign finance filings, making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history.

Over the last month, the campaign poured those dollars into highly produced ads and mailers that bombarded voters with warnings that the tax was dangerous and would hurt everyday people. Taglines from the campaign said Prop 40 was an “everyone tax”, “reckless experiment” and “you’re next”. While supporters of the tax said the money would go toward funding the state’s healthcare losses from Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents repeatedly sent the message to voters that it would make healthcare funding worse.

Even without Prop 40’s outsized opponents, the pro-billionaire tax campaign had a difficult task. It had to convince Californians that this specific one-time tax, chiefly geared toward healthcare funding, was the right way to address losses from Trump’s bill. The idea of zeroing in on billionaires ruffled feathers across the state with major political figures opposing it, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, and Xavier Becerra, the governor elect.

Then there was the funding. In comparison with the billionaires’ war chest, the pro-Prop 40 camp, sponsored by the union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), raised just more than $31m. They were outspent nearly 14-fold.

“All lies have a shelf life,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff for the SEIU-UHW. “Billionaire-funded propaganda may mislead voters about the consequences of these cuts today, but as hospitals reduce services, emergency rooms close and families lose access to care, the truth will become increasingly difficult to hide.”

The counties that voted to pass Prop 40 are typically more Democratic and where many of the state’s wealthy reside, including Los Angeles, San Francisco and other areas around the Bay Area. The counties that overwhelmingly voted against the measure were mostly red, rural and poor. While many of these counties swung blue in US House races this election, up to 80% of voters there voted no on Prop 40, according to the latest count.

Rob Lalka, a business professor at Tulane University and author of The Venture Alchemists: How Big Tech Turned Profits Into Power, compared the Prop 40 campaign with Uber and Lyft’s ballot measure crusade in 2020, where the companies spent more than $200m to defeat an initiative over labor rights for drivers. The ride-hailing companies used similar tactics, Lalka said, something he describes as “misleading propaganda and paying for endorsements”.

“The money also seemed astonishing at the time: the amount to influence the outcome, over $200m, was a massive sum,” Lalka said. “Money in politics has only increased in California throughout this decade. That’s the context for Prop 40 this election cycle.”

The colossal funding of political campaigns has broken records nationwide this midterm cycle, said Francesco Trebbi, a business and public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He pointed to Elon Musk dumping $446m into House and Senate races across the county, but noted that it was ineffective in places such as Texas: Musk’s mark, James Talarico, won.

“Maybe it was easier to decouple Prop 40 opposition from President Trump’s agenda, so Brin had an easier target to hit,” Trebbi said. Still, he added: “We need a lot more data and statistical evidence in order to conclusively finalize this discussion.”

Exit polls haven’t yet been released for Prop 40, which will give more details on voters’ decisions. In the meantime, the SEIU-UHW’s Jimenez said that despite the loss, the union and its allies are not going to give up on the long game: “If Sacramento fails to protect patients and deliver a real solution that makes billionaires pay their fair share, healthcare workers will pursue every available avenue, up to and including returning to the ballot in 2028 with a billionaire tax.”

https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.title: Tories would have to raise state pension age above 70 to keep triple lock, says minister
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.author: Heather Stewart
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.text:
Kemi Badenoch attacked reforms but is not being clear about how party would meet costs, Torsten Bell claims

Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives would have to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock, Treasury minister Torsten Bell has claimed.

Labour has announced reforms to the triple-lock promise to come into force in the next parliament – with the initial proceeds earmarked for Andy Burnham’s national care service.

The Conservatives have attacked the move, and insisted they would stick with the triple lock, which increases the state pension each year in line with the largest of inflation, 2.5% or earnings growth.

However, Bell argued that with the costs of an unreformed triple lock increasing over time – to £50bn by 2050, according to government estimates – a Tory government would end up repeating the approach they took in the 2010s and speeding up planned increases to the state pension age.

“If you don’t want to have an adjustment to the triple lock, then you will need to do other things to make the state pension remotely sustainable,” he said. “We don’t need to guess what they would do because they’ve literally just done it, which is they repeatedly and at very short notice accelerated the increases in the state pension age.

“They did that in the in 2011 and in 2014. Some people had as little as five years’ notice.”

In 2013, the then chancellor, George Osborne, described increasing the pension age as, “one of the less controversial things we have done,” which had nevertheless delivered “absolutely enormous savings”.

The state pension age, now under review, is already expected to increase to 68 between 2044 and 2046; but Bell claimed the Conservatives would end up going further.

“All I’m saying is, Conservatives do raise the state pension age aggressively, and they have,” he said. “And even though they know that the triple lock should change, they are opposing it – and the consequence of that is they would end up making people wait into their 70s.”

The triple lock had previously been seen as too politically risky to reform, particularly in the light of the backlash against Labour’s plan to remove the winter fuel allowance from the vast majority of pensioners – which was subsequently abandoned.

But Bell said the public would prefer Burnham’s willingness to make an argument to what he claimed was the Conservatives’ failure to be honest.

“I think this is a bigger problem for Kemi Badenoch than she thinks. She thinks that her brand is principled, know what you think, tell it straight. And on this, she has done the opposite – we know that she knows it needs to change,” he said.

He cited the Conservative leader’s own suggestion, as recently as last year, that the triple lock should be means tested, and former Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt’s claim that the policy was an “anchor drag” on the public finances.

“The triple lock kind of is the final nail in the coffin of the idea that there’s anything fiscally responsible about modern Conservatism,” Bell said.

Under Labour’s planned reforms, the state pension will rise each year by the highest of inflation, or 2.5%. It will only rise in line with earnings growth if its value has slipped behind recent wage growth.

Bell, the MP for Swansea West since 2024, was previously director of the Resolution Foundation thinktank. He retained his role as pensions minister – working between the Treasury and the Department for Work and Pensions – when Burnham came to power in July.

He said the prime minister’s 10-year plan, which may now be delayed until the new year, will include a promise of a better deal for future pensioners. “It’s just really important to be able to say to people, ‘the comfortable retirement that your parents had: we’re going to make sure that today’s private sector workers have got those’,” he added.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Whitehall is too ‘tame, reactive and risk-averse’, says UK’s top civil servant
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Antonia Romeo pledges to ‘rewire’ civil service by incentivising and rewarding top performers

Whitehall is too “tame, reactive and risk-averse”, the cabinet secretary has said, as she set out a “completely new approach” to managing the performance of civil servants.

With Andy Burnham and his deputy, Louise Haigh, in the audience, the UK’s most senior civil servant, Antonia Romeo, gave a lecture saying she would bring radical change to Whitehall as it deals with uncertainty caused by AI and global political tensions.

She said fundamental reform of the civil service to improve productivity was essential given the “tight fiscal context”. Ministers are grappling with how to deliver higher defence spending in future while protecting the budgets of public services.

Romeo’s statement that she would “rewire” the civil service echoed pledges under Keir Starmer’s government.

But recent changes to increase bonuses for high performing senior civil servants were “just the start”, she said.

Romeo said her new approach to managing performance in Whitehall would “incentivise and reward brilliant delivery, valuable expertise and sticking it out to get the job done”.

“Poor performance drives out good performance and discretionary effort, and we must urgently address that,” she said, speaking at the London School of Economics.

“We will strengthen processes and train and equip managers to reward those making the biggest impact, and take decisive action on poor performance.”

She said she would also aim to reduce churn, which means some officials move sideways to get pay rises rather than being rewarded for staying in the same job.

Romeo said some of the criticisms of the civil service must be addressed, including that it was “tame and risk-averse”, “reactive, not strategic” and “siloed, not working across boundaries”.

The cabinet secretary is overseeing a review of the organisation of the civil service that is due in the spring, alongside an update to its code.

She said the review would look at current departmental structures and whether they are the best options in an era of cross-cutting delivery, as well as what AI and “devolution by default” mean for the civil service.

Despite worries among some civil servants that AI would be used to replace officials, Romeo said the technology could be used to make the civil service “more human” by using its power to cut out bureaucracy, allowing officials to concentrate on creativity, interaction and decision-making.

“From healthcare screening for types of cancer to tackling the risk of homelessness, technology can enable us to be much more predictive, preventative and personalised, under appropriate controls and guardrails. AI can help us make public services more human,” she said.

After the speech, a government spokesperson said Burnham “backs the cabinet secretary’s vision for a civil service that is fit for the future”.

“He is determined to rewire the state, pushing power out of Whitehall and handing it to the communities and regions it serves,” they said.

“By embracing AI responsibly, cutting needless bureaucracy and rebuilding trust, the prime minister will work with the cabinet secretary to deliver better public services and growth in every postcode.”

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Kiran StaceyPolicy editor

Exclusive: Reindustrialisation Research Group to meet with Cabinet Office to discuss worries over PM’s long-term strategy

Labour MPs have sounded the alarm over Andy Burnham’s 10-year plan for government, raising concerns that it will not be radical or detailed enough.

MPs in the Reindustrialisation Research Group (ReRG), many of whom represent “red wall” seats that helped Labour win the last election, are meeting Sally Jameson, the Cabinet Office minister, on Wednesday to share their concerns about the prime minister’s long-term strategy.

Members of the group say they are particularly concerned about the prime minister’s commitment to reviving Britain’s heavy industries, which they say are being crushed by high energy prices and a lack of government support.

Their worries reflect wider concerns among some parts of the Labour party that Burnham’s much-vaunted plan could fall short of the high expectations the prime minister has set.

Andy MacNae, the head of the group, said: “There are a lot of gaps in the government’s reindustrialisation strategy which are not yet filled. The 10-year plan is a chance to fill them, but in the briefings we have been given that is not what we are seeing.

“We have had really good engagement from ministers, but we need to see something more constructive and we are just not seeing that at the moment. The risk is we don’t see reindustrialisation at all, and continue to see deindustrialisation.”

Jonathan Hinder, another member of the group, said: “Making reindustrialisation cannot just be about political slogans. We are going in the wrong direction and we need pretty drastic action, but we are not yet seeing that from this government.”

Burnham has billed his 10-year plan as the defining blueprint for what he wants to achieve in government, including bringing utilities under public control, reducing bills and establishing a national care service.

MPs had been told to expect it before the end of the year, but the prime minister said last week it could be delayed until January.

Labour MPs in former industrial areas, many of which proved vital in delivering the party’s landslide in 2024, are hoping the plan will include measures to encourage manufacturing.

Burnham has suggested industry will sit at the heart of his economic agenda while the chancellor, John Healey, promised at this year’s Labour conference to bring in “a new age of industrialisation”.

Many however are concerned the government is not yet matching its rhetoric with policy support.

The ReRG called before the budget for Healey to expand the British industrial competitiveness scheme, which reduces energy costs for about 10,000 businesses.

But while the chancellor used his budget to announce a £100 council tax rebate to help households pay their energy bills over the winter, he did not announce changes to the business support scheme.

MPs on the ReRG are calling for the prime minister to use the 10-year plan not only to announce immediate energy bill support for industrial companies, but also to create a minister for reindustrialisation and to empower No 10 North in Manchester to oversee the agenda.

Some say they are concerned by briefings held by ministers in recent days which they say suggest the plan will be a modest document, subject to lengthy consultation.

The group will hold a meeting with Jameson to lay out their concerns, but many say they are unclear on who is leading the process of writing the plan.

Peter Hyman, who previously advised Keir Starmer on his missions, is reported to be overseeing the writing process, though officials insist Burnham himself will make the key decisions.

Many MPs say they are worried about the involvement of Boston Consulting Group, a company which previously employed Burnham’s chief of staff, James Purnell, to help draw up the plan.

One MP said: “The idea that BCG are going to be involved in reindustrialising Britain feels like a tragic joke.”

Downing Street has said BCG is only providing one consultant to help with the process, while Burnham has insisted the plan will be more radical than many think.

He told the Economist last week: “People are underestimating the significance of this. There’s been briefing around this week, inaccurate briefing … to try and play [it] down. I will lay out my very clear vision for Britain, and it will be substantial, and it will also be, in my view, compelling because I am weaving the different threads together.”

The thinktank said inflation was likely to become a more persistent feature of the UK economy unless the Bank took tougher action.

The Bank’s monetary policy committee increased the cost of borrowing from 3.75% to 4% last week and hinted at another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

The director of the Niesr, David Aikman, urged the Bank of England to be more aggressive in tackling inflation, saying all the ingredients were in place for workers to demand inflation-linked salary rises.

“Inflation is set to rise above 4% in the new year, just as most pay awards for 2027 are being agreed, so the risk that it becomes embedded is rising.

“One further quarter-point rise is unlikely to be enough, and the longer the MPC waits, the more it will eventually need to do.”

UK inflation stands at 3.5%, well above the Bank’s 2% target, driven higher by the soaring cost of fuel. Oil and gas prices have risen sharply since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.

Brent crude oil has persistently traded at more than $100 a barrel in recent weeks – compared with about $70 before the war – but on Tuesday it traded below $90 at one point, the lowest since 31 August, after Donald Trump downplayed the need for military action against Iran “at this point”.

Investors, however, reined in their enthusiasm after US inflation climbed by 0.4 percentage points from September to October, revealing that high oil and gas prices were continuing to drive up costs. The S&P 500 index of leading US companies was down 0.9% by early afternoon on Wall Street.

The Niesr said its forecasts for growth in the UK and the global economy were based on oil prices at $105 a barrel. However, it cautioned that while prices had dropped, continued difficulties shipping and refining meant consumer prices would decline slowly.

Stephen Millard, an economist at the institute, said the lower oil price was also dependent on Trump sticking to his new policy. “We’ve seen him change his mind before,” he said.

The Niesr expects the UK economy to grow by 1.6% this year, but by only 0.9% in 2028 as high inflation, high interest rates and tight government spending take a toll on consumer and business confidence.

The chancellor, John Healey, was criticised for deferring difficult decisions in the budget last month, which the institute said would leave a £30bn hole in the government’s finances if the pattern of doing so over the last decade was repeated next year.

Aikman said financial markets would punish the Treasury by raising the price of loans to the UK if it became clear that government spending was going to soar in areas such as defence without savings being made elsewhere.

He said there was a “double whammy” from higher energy prices and rising global borrowing costs that was not being addressed.

“Those pressures reflect global developments and cannot be avoided,” he said. “How monetary and fiscal policy respond to them is a domestic choice, and on both fronts decisions are being deferred.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: From blood group ID to cycle racks : I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope  | Martin Lewis
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Martin Lewis
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
There are thousands of small tips to make our country better. People know what is wrong, and it’s clear they have solutions

H
ave you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your ideas for practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK – whether that’s health, schools, transport, business, housing, policing, justice, tech, shopping, money – or owt else entirely.

The spark for this happened just over a year ago, when I spoke at Politico’s fringe event at Labour’s conference. The key discussion was about Keir Starmer’s unpopularity. I was asked what I’d have advised the government when it took power, so I said: “Come up with 100 small things that piss people off and that you can fix, and they can see that you have fixed them.” Then I reeled off a list of small fixes for my subject area: the counterproductive way council tax debt is escalated; renaming “tax-free childcare”; and so on.
