As I walked off stage, I emailed myself: “Set up an Institute for Small Ideas.” I started straight away, did some work, brought some people together, put it out to tender for charities to run it, and then a month ago it launched – albeit with a slight name change. Think of it as a sort of apolitical national suggestion box. And in those few weeks since launch, we’ve already had 42,000 suggestions.

At a time when public debate can feel dominated by division, outrage and disagreement, there’s something quietly encouraging about tens of thousands of people taking the time to offer constructive ideas. Clearly the timing was fortuitous, as small ideas are now all the rage.
 
 
 We haven’t started the filtering process yet, but here are just a few of the ideas that have been suggested:

Tell people their blood group at their first adult blood test. Knowing you’ve a common or rare type may make you more inclined to donate. It’s a brilliantly simple nudge that could widen the donor pool and save lives.

A mandatory “AI-edited” label on property photos on estate agency sites.

A “no wrong door” rule for councils and public bodies: report a problem anywhere, and they must pass it to the right place, rather than bouncing you from department to department, or from council to contractor to agency.

Cycle racks on the back of buses.

Cinema seating plans that clearly show aisles and walkways for disability access.

A voluntary wheelie-bin sharing scheme, so neighbours with spare capacity can help stop bins overflowing.

The idea is that if someone could fix enough of these frustrations and make lives easier, save time and let everyone get on with work or the things they enjoy, the combined effect – and the feelgood factor – would help shift the national mood.
 
 
 To make this happen, I’ve funded the Small Ideas Initiative, with two charities – Nesta and Involve – running a project in the background. (I’m telling you this because I believe funding transparency is crucial in any policy charity.) They will filter the suggestions and hopefully select and publish at least 1,000 of the best to provide a bank of ideas others may look at in future. They’ll pick 200 of these to turn into fully researched policy proposals.

Then, having got public feedback on those, we’ve brought together a cross-party panel – with representatives from Green to Reform and every party in between – who will need to unanimously agree the final 50-ish. These are meant to be useful and doable, not party political or controversial. And if that broad a church can agree on them, we’ve likely succeeded. These 50 will form the first Small Ideas manifesto we will campaign to get implemented.

Since that Labour party conference a year ago, the prime minister has changed of course, and Andy Burnham seems to have taken small ideas to heart. Which means I hope the door may be open for many of these suggestions.

Of course, I’m not suggesting that Britain needs only small ideas. These quick fixes are there to work alongside, not instead of, the longer-term big structural changes that society and the economy need. Yet if you focus only on legacy and not on legwork, it can leave the public feeling detached and with an impression that politics is futile, achieves nothing and is just talk without delivering. Small fixes are still fixes – fix a lot of them and it adds up.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on rough sleeping: Burnham’s laudable target is in danger of being missed | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Energetic mayors and councils can help street homeless people to rebuild their lives. But the underlying affordability crisis needs tackling too

B
ringing an end to rough sleeping was among Andy Burnham’s first pledges after entering Downing Street – as it was when he became mayor of Manchester. With temperatures dropping, and frosts expected, winter night shelters across the UK are up and running. But an ongoing acute shortage of suitable housing and the latest tranche of early prisoner releases mean ministers know that the prime minister’s laudable target is in danger of being missed.

The official figures are shocking. There were 8,748 rough sleepers in England in June, an increase of about 1,000 since January (Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland collect data separately). These are among the most vulnerable people in society, both in terms of past experiences and future prospects, including drastically curtailed life expectancy. The complex and sometimes chaotic situations of people who end up on the streets, most of whom are men, mean that helping them is challenging. Family breakdown, substance misuse, mental health difficulties and prison are among the many adverse life experiences that rough sleepers are disproportionately likely to face.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

Not signed in before? Create an account

But the problems of councils and charities are made far worse by the fact that this visibly distressed group is only the tip of the homelessness iceberg. While rough sleepers are the most obvious victims of the UK’s homelessness crisis – which is national in the sense that it affects all four nations, but varies enormously between places – they are a small minority of the total number who cannot find or afford to rent (let alone buy) their own home. The latest count of families in temporary accommodation such as B&Bs and hostels in England, in March, was 135,600 – 90% more than a decade ago.

Mr Burnham’s personal commitment to rough sleepers has seen a big increase in funding, to almost £900m next year. This ought to enable councils, and charities providing local services, to make plans that go beyond the expansion of winter shelters, or hostel places, to meet the immediate goal of getting “everyone in for Christmas”. People with mental health, addiction or other issues need support and treatment that goes further than a roof over their heads. The spike in rough sleeping is a reflection of housing affordability problems, but also of a lack of the other services that enable fragile, vulnerable people to manage their lives.

Manchester’s “A Bed Every Night” scheme saw rough sleeper numbers fall, then climb back up – partly because it could not keep pace with the pressures pushing people on to the streets. Helping people to rebuild their lives takes sustained effort. Charities rightly warn that prison releases add to councils’ burdens. Probation and housing services must work together: freeing people from jail to sleep on the street is the act of a dysfunctional system. But no scheme, council or charity can find homes for people if those homes don’t exist, or are priced beyond their reach. That requires a mix of more social housing, rent controls and housing allowances that meet reasonable costs. It also means confronting policies that generate homelessness.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Call it tough love, with the love removed: it’s Kemi’s war on benefits claimants
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
The Tory leader outlines her £36bn welfare cuts, again, to an audience of an age and a wealth that they don’t need to work

C
all it tough love. Only without any of the love bit. Let’s face it. There comes a time in every Conservative politician’s life when you have to say enough is enough. That it’s just not fair on the rest of us. Now, MPs might just have enjoyed a five-day mini-recess, but they deserve every minute’s free time they get. Because they clearly work far harder than everyone else. But on a Tuesday morning it sticks in the throat to think of people lying around at home, being paid to have disabilities that exist mainly in their imaginations, while you have to give a speech in central London.

The thing is, we just haven’t been ambitious enough for people on welfare payments. Let me introduce you to KemiWorld. Think of the double amputee who ran a marathon. Though try not to think of the cost to the NHS of the prosthetics. Welfare is very much a one-way balance sheet as far as Kemi Badenoch. The point is that most disabled people just sit at home and moan. They need to get out more. Let’s face it, if a double amputee can run a marathon then it ought to be a doddle for a single amputee to run a double marathon. Just get out there and do it.

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Too many people just think of welfare benefits as an excuse to sit indoors and watch TV all day. So, diddums has bad anxiety and suffers from panic attacks. Frankly, I’m not surprised. I’d be having panic attacks if I was as useless as you. Just get out there and do something.

Find a job, even if there aren’t any jobs to find. Leave the house and start walking. And don’t come back until you’ve pulled yourself together. Take a leaf out of the tech bros’ book. Most of them have ADHD of some sort. So, rather than complaining, use your spare time to establish a billion-pound startup. It’s not that hard. All you need is an idea. And you’re not going to have one if you spend all day on your arse.

Tuesday morning saw Kemi and the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, in Westminster explaining their plans to cut £36.1bn from the welfare budget. The £0.1bn is there to make sure you don’t think the Tories have just plucked some random numbers from thin air, which of course they have. This way we can all pretend it’s fully costed down to the last 50p.

It’s also possible that somewhere in the back of your mind you will remember Kemi and Helen talking about £36bn in savings at the Conservative party conference last month. You may well have wisely zoned out and missed the announcement. Which is why the Tories have popped back for another go. One that is almost certainly doomed to fail, as no one takes the costings of an opposition party particularly seriously. So don’t be surprised if there’s yet another press conference before Christmas, to re-announce the re-announcement. Third time lucky.

Still, it’s not hard to see why Kemi increasingly enjoys a presser. She’s taken to having them almost as often as Nigel Farage. For one thing, it’s about the only way she can get any attention. For another, it’s a chance to highlight the gap between her and her shadow cabinet. Her approval ratings continue to poll considerably higher than those of the Tory party itself. Mostly because her team are a bunch of deadbeats. Twenty or so semi-sentient beings in search of a personality. None more so than Whately. More of her later.

There were whoops and cheers from a surprisingly large audience as Kemi approached the lectern. They were all – there is no kind way of saying this – of an age and a wealth that apparently had no better place to be at 10.30am on a working day. Credit where credit is due. At least they hadn’t stayed in bed like the benefits claimants.

For Kemi and the audience, though, it was all common sense. A token nod to compassion – people who were terminally ill and well past retirement age would still get benefits – but for everyone else there would be a rude wake-up call. Why waste time saying a last goodbye to your family when you could be doing a productive day’s work instead. Sentimentality was the Labour way. And who, now she had come to think about it, really needed two legs anyway? Bipedalism was overrated.

Then came the charisma vacuum that is Helen. Like so many Tory MPs, she has been on quite the journey. When she was first elected to parliament, she was a wetter than wet Cameroon. Well on the left of the Tory party. Since then, she has slid to the right. She talks these days of getting people back to work, but you can’t help wondering if the only job she is really interested in is her own.

Helen was there to talk us through the numbers. Though not the ones that really counted. Such as how the welfare bill almost doubled under the Tories. It turns out, it’s far easier to cut the bill when you are in opposition. And for Whately, all benefit claimants were just debit sums in the ledger. There was no understanding that – as in the Netherlands, where there had been great success in funding measures to get young people into work – it might be an idea to invest in opportunities.

Nor was there any acknowledgment that cutting benefits by up to £10,000 per household might create further costs. That people might lose their homes, forcing councils to accommodate them in bed and breakfasts. Claims by charities that these changes would lead to a massive surge in child poverty were dismissed by Kemi. Just attention-seeking from charities that would say that, wouldn’t they?

The questions from the media slipped by easily enough. Kemi refrained from having a go at Ed Miliband and Lucy Powell about their fatal attraction to Russell Brand more than a decade ago, and she did say she wouldn’t be cutting benefits for people from the EU with settled status. So there is a heart there, somewhere.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Gen Z doesn‘t relish going to war – so what! You should worry more about the reckless generations that do | Jason Okundaye
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jason Okundaye
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The right has found a new way to denigrate young people, but it is fatuous to assume that Britons of any age would not protect what is dear to them

Y
oung people won’t go to war for Britain. So claimed numerous headlines last week, responding to findings in the British Social Attitudes survey. Except that the phrasing of the question was whether respondents placed importance on “the willingness to serve [in the military] in a time of need”, perhaps forgivably low for people thinking about things of more immediate importance to them such as getting on the housing ladder, getting a pay rise or finding employment at all.

Less than a quarter of under-35s regarded this as of high importance, and so here we are subjected to the same moralising as any vaguely leftwing politician who hesitates on the stock television interview question: would you push the big shiny red nuclear button? “An unbelievable attitude on display!” laments LBC’s Tom Swarbrick in response to a 23-year-old caller, Josh, who can’t imagine a circumstance where he would ever feel able to kill another person.

That belief that you could not take another person’s life is apparently the wrong instinct and an indication of everything that’s wrong with young people in the UK. The very worst charge: a lack of love for one’s country. Milk-livered zoomer communist pansyism, or whatever. The more generous interpretation has been that young people’s lack of commitment to Britain is unsurprising given the broken social contract: that our politicians are excessively deferential to the pensioner class, leaving young people with the bill, and young people don’t feel that they’ve been given a stake in society. According to Sophia Gaston, author of the report, a sense of generational fairness has had an impact on young people’s “willingness to put themselves on the line and defend [the] nation”.

But who wants war? Who views scenes of chaos and bloodshed and cheerfully imagines placing themselves within them? That simple question has been conspicuously absent from much of the discussion around the survey. What has shaped young people’s perceptions of war, and of Britain’s participation in it, more than the litany of strategic blunders and postcolonial overreach that have defined the conflicts of the 21st century? Besides, what kind of war should they be willing to serve in? Just any? Or one that will be determined illegal by many politicians and scholars, such as Iraq? Or one as catastrophic as the failed intervention in Libya?

And hang on, isn’t war supposed to be a terrible thing that we hope will never have to happen again? On the 100th anniversary of the outbreak of the first world war, my secondary school held a special assembly. The seats in the middle of the hall were arranged in a strange shape, and midway through the ceremony the boys sitting there were told to stand up. “That is how many students [from our school] died in the great war,” said my history teacher.

Young people are well aware of growing instability and that the old assumptions about peace in the west may not hold for much longer. Not with Vladimir Putin launching Europe’s largest and most destructive armed conflict since the second world war with the invasion of Ukraine – and with very real and credible threats against the UK from Russia, specifically Moscow-driven cyber and information attacks. In September, Nato allies upended a plot by Russian subs training to disable undersea cables , the basic infrastructure of the global internet.

So the question for young people is: what would we do in the case of a Russian invasion? Dover has been breached, there are tanks and troops closing in on Westminster, “good morning” is to be replaced by “доброе утро”. This is not a threat to be managed only by a conventional army, but one that requires resilience and belligerence from all of us. My answer to that is: look at what young people have done, in modern times and in history. Look at Ukraine – like anywhere, young people did not want war. When the moment came, they joined territorial defence units in their thousands, helped evacuate citizens and organised humanitarian responses.

Look at the young socialists and members of youth movements who joined the French resistance against Nazi occupation during the second world war, forming intelligence networks and carrying out acts of sabotage. Look at those who formed the Zazou counter-cultural movement, a subculture rebelling against the Vichy regime that was collaborating with the Nazis. These were young people who might not have joined a conventional army, but who nonetheless saw the need to defend their future.

See that quality, too, in Britain’s young people today. Many will point to their sacrifices during the Covid-19 pandemic, but I think more of youth-led movements and protests: resistance to immigration raids in defence of our neighbours, climate strikes, days of action protesting at the rising cost of education, even hunger strikes in solidarity with Palestine. These are not the chattering classes’ idea of bravery or rising to moments of peril, yet it is that spirit of asserting independence and control over one’s future that would need to be harnessed if ever a war were to reach these shores. Yet, like that young LBC caller, they are demonised for not being enthusiastic about going to war for a country that has not gone to war for them.

For all our discussion of patriotism, it is little said that people do not experience a nation through abstract ideas of borders and security, but rather through our communities, friends and families. When those are under threat, away from hypotheticals and chin-stroking debates about nuclear weapons, patriotism is a very different proposition: not about dying under a flag, but standing up for the people around you.

Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: ‘I’d steal 10-15 times a day’: ex-offenders on the addictions driving prolific shoplifting
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Former shoplifters say treatment and drug rehabilitation are essential to ending cycle of theft and imprisonment

Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England

When Rhys, 34, stole goods from shops across Birmingham, he would often leave notes for the staff apologising for his actions.

“I’d feel that guilty about it. I’d pass them notes, saying I’m so sorry about this,” he said. “But in the end, I was just that numb to it, and fearless as well. I’d walk in with a suitcase and ram everything into it, and not think twice about it.”

Rhys was in the grips of drug addiction and turned to shoplifting to fund his habit. He had struggled with drug use since he was a teenager and then, in 2019, he took crack cocaine for the first time. “Within a week, I was going into shops and shoplifting for it, because you just can’t get enough,” he said.

Over the next few years, he shoplifted 10-15 times a day and was sent to prison several times. However, without help to tackle his addiction, Rhys struggled to change his behaviour.

“I’d spend hours shoplifting but, at the end of the day, I still wouldn’t have anything to eat. I’d be jumping back over the fence to go through the bins to get myself a sandwich. I wouldn’t even get myself a bottle of water,” he said. “My priority was always getting the stuff to sell for drugs.”

On Wednesday, the home secretary announced plans to target 500 of the most prolific shoplifters across the country with police crackdowns in 17 areas. Measures include banning repeat offenders from high streets and town centres, closer monitoring of offenders with regular hearings before a judge and the use of electronic tagging.

But former shoplifters say many prolific thieves are in the grip of drug addiction or experiencing mental health crises, and without more funding for support services, the problem will not go away.

Keeley, 44, was once labelled Birmingham’s most prolific shoplifter, stealing between £5,000 and £9,000 worth of goods a day. She was sent to prison 28 times. Keeley had been addicted to drugs since the age of 13, after being groomed by an older man, and stole items such as designer handbags, which she could sell quickly to fund her habit. Her biggest fear was withdrawal, which had previously left her in hospital for 10 days.

She said shoplifting was an exhausting necessity – one that often led to her walking 30,000 steps a day. “Shoplifting, to a lot of us, is the closest to a victimless crime as you can get. You’re not violating anyone’s house or privacy, or robbing food out of their mouth.

“I know it’s not right, but it’s what we tell ourselves to justify it at the time – that you’re not hurting anyone – because none of us want to be doing what we’re doing.”

Keeley said she “didn’t get caught much for the amount of stuff that I stole”. Yet she spent three decades in and out of prison, never receiving the help she needed.

She eventually turned her life around when an off-duty security guard referred her to a drug support service, which led to her receiving buprenorphine injections to treat her opioid dependence.

“We’re crying that we’ve got a shoplifting crisis, and we’re crying that we’ve got a drug crisis, but no one’s doing anything about the two together,” Keeley said. “If you treat the root cause and take the addiction away, we’ve got no reason to go out and commit crime.”

For Rhys, help came in the form of an outreach navigator – a professional who connects vulnerable people to social services, housing and healthcare. He has been in recovery for 18 months, spends his time volunteering and has left shoplifting behind.

“I went into Aldi the other day, and I asked for a carrier bag and scanned it straight away. It’s such a weird comparison – now I’m scanning these 30p bags. But before, I was going in there and filling a suitcase to steal,” he said.

The social justice charity Revolving Doors said addiction, poor mental health and homelessness – often all three at once – were substantial drivers of Britain’s shoplifting epidemic.

Pavan Dhaliwal, the charity’s chief executive, said: “The anger of retailers and shop workers is justified. Theft is not victimless, and abuse of staff is intolerable.

“But if we want fewer thefts, rather than just more arrests, we have to ask a harder question: why does the same small group of people keep cycling through crisis and custody repeatedly?”

after newsletter promotion

She said services that can direct people away from addiction and into stable housing were essential. “The people we work with show that recovery and rebuilding lives are possible with the right support.”

Sean, 44, has been to prison 42 times since 2000. For decades, he had not spent more than six months out of custody and felt “powerless to addiction” that drove him to crime after a traumatic childhood.

He stole food and clothes because all his money was spent on drugs, and prison brought no long-term solutions.

“The last five times I was in prison, I was a recovery mentor, taking people on circuits every day in the yard, feeling on top of my game,” Sean said. “But back in Wigan, usually within a couple of days or even a couple of hours, I’d be back doing what I’ve always done. I was completely let down by services.”

It was only when he was picked up at the prison gates by an addiction recovery service and started therapy that his life turned around. Sean now runs Rehab Fitness, which helps people recovering from addiction through group exercise and wellness activities.

He said many of his friends had turned to shop crime because there were “no consequences”, adding that the intervention should be help and support, not prison.

Prison also failed to rehabilitate Roy, 36. He was jailed several times – on one occasion after stealing wine from a shop while under the influence of drugs and alcohol.

“I had money in my pocket. I don’t know why I did it – I couldn’t even remember it afterwards. I was a different person; dead behind the eyes,” he said. “Prison would be a reset but I’d be straight in with the old crowd when I came out.”

Roy managed to get clean, and now runs Iron Minds Academy, which offers physical fitness and mentoring to young men in Wigan. “I just want to stop other young people getting to that point, for them to see there’s another path,” he said.

“When you’re leaving school, no one says I want to be on the streets addicted to heroin. We need to stop it before it gets that far, it can save someone’s life.”

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Disabled people in England ‘have to wait up to two years for wheelchairs’
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Ombudsman’s report says delays have profound consequences and limit users’ ability to lead independent lives

Disabled people are having to wait up to two years to get a wheelchair because of delays involving NHS bodies and private firms that make them.

The situation is revealed in a report by the public service ombudsman for England, Paula Sussex, who said hold-ups were having profound consequences and limiting wheelchair users’ ability to lead independent lives.

In one case a three-year-old boy with cerebral palsy was unable to start nursery at the same time as his twin brother because he had to wait seven months for a wheelchair. He hurt himself several times when he fell from an adapted buggy his parents were using while they waited.

Sussex launched an investigation into NHS wheelchair provision after a sharp rise in complaints – from eight in 2020-21 to 110 in 2025-26.

Four out of five relate to the handful of private firms that provide wheelchairs to at least half of all children and adults who need one to help them lead independent lives.

Most are about people who need a wheelchair having to wait longer than the supposed 18-week maximum to receive either the device or parts for it.

“For people who rely on a wheelchair, delays, unsuitable equipment or poor repairs can affect every part of their life”, said Sussex.

“There can be profound consequences, from physical pain and emotional distress to limiting their ability to lead full lives.”

Elliot Cruz Gardiyanoglu, now six, was three when he faced a seven-month wait for his wheelchair. That also meant that he was unable access education or specialist therapy.

“We were never told there would be such a long wait for the wheelchair,” his mother, Jania Cruz, said. “If we had known we would have explored other ways to get it, especially so that Elliot did not miss out on starting nursery at the same time as his brother.

“It was very hard for him to see his brother going to school while he couldn’t.”

Rachel Perrin, the director of Newlife, a charity for disabled children, said Elliot’s experience showed how “the wrong wheelchair – or no wheelchair at all – can be dangerous, as well as keeping children and their families trapped at home and leaving them unable to attend school and take part in activities with siblings and friends”.

Graham Woolner, a 68-year-old in Bishop’s Stortford who has spinal muscular atrophy, a degenerative condition, has needed a wheelchair for the last 15 years.

He was meant to get a new one by August 2023 but it did not arrive until September 2024, and when it did, it failed to work properly. He did not get one in full working order until October 2025, 26 months past the 18-week deadline.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

“After a year of waiting, the wheelchair they gave me broke on the first day. I only made it 100 yards before the batteries died,” Woolner said. “The battery issue was never resolved, so I couldn’t go anywhere for a year with any certainty that I would get there and back.

“I like to be independent, go into town and take my dogs for a walk. But it got to the point where I wouldn’t go out without my son in case I needed him to push me home.

“The wheelchair is effectively my legs. I need it to live my daily life.”

Nick Goldup, the chief executive of the Wheelchair Alliance, said the report shone a light on the systemic problems wheelchair users faced.

“Getting wheelchair provision right means giving people the freedom to live their lives and to enable them to contribute meaningfully to society,” he said.

Sussex highlights a “regulatory gap” in wheelchair services such as assessment, fitting and repair. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency oversees the equipment, but the remit of the Care Quality Commission – the NHS care watchdog – does not cover the services wheelchair users receive because they are not supervised by a health professional.

Integrated care boards (ICBs), NHS regional bodies that commission wheelchair services, have “unreliable information” about how many people locally need a wheelchair and are faced with “an uncompetitive wheelchair market” which is dominated by a handful of private providers. Nor are ICBs good at telling each other when they encounter problems with private firms that provide poor services.

An NHS spokesperson said:“Long waits for wheelchairs are unacceptable, denying people the independence and quality of life they deserve.

“That’s why our wheelchair quality framework, co-produced with wheelchair users, sets a clear expectation that 92% of people receive their equipment within 18 weeks, and requires commissioners to hold regular performance meetings with providers to identify and tackle delays.”

This article was amended on 11 November 2026. An earlier version referred to Paula Sussex as the “NHS and public services ombudsman”. In fact since 1 October 2026 her title has been public service ombudsman, changed from parliamentary and health service ombudsman.
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.summary: Ombudsman's report says delays have profound consequences and limit users’ ability to lead independent lives. Four out of five relate to the handful of private firms that provide wheelchairs to at least half of all children and adults who need one to help them lead independent life.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.title: People in deprived areas of England more than twice as likely to die early, study shows
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.author: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.text:
Premature death risk also varies according to employment and qualifications, shows analysis ‘laying bare the scale of inequalities’

People living in the most deprived areas of England are more than twice as likely to die prematurely than their more affluent counterparts, according to analysis.

The research, conducted by the Health Foundation, took demographic data from the 2021 census to look at differences in premature mortality rates – defined as any adult who died before their 75th birthday – alongside further data on deaths from March 2021 to December 2023.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Both men and women living in the most deprived areas were shown to have a risk of early death 2.3 times higher than their counterparts in the least deprived areas, according to the analysis, at a rate of 815 premature deaths per 100,000 people, compared with 353 premature deaths per 100,000 people.

Furthermore, women with no qualifications were found to have a premature mortality rate 2.5 times higher than those with a degree or higher, while men who are long-term unemployed or have never worked have a rate 3.5 times as high as those in higher managerial, administrative and professional occupations.

Regionally, such inequalities were highest in the north-east, north-west and Yorkshire and The Humber, and lowest in London. For example, the rate for females who have never worked or are long-term unemployed is 796 deaths per 100,000 people in the north-west – 72% higher than London (462 deaths per 100,000).

This research further signals a decline in healthy life expectancy, with previous analysis indicating that the UK population’s health is poor, getting worse and not undergoing the same steady improvement seen in countries such as Japan, Norway and Spain.

“These findings lay bare the scale of the inequalities that continue to shape people’s chances of living a long and healthy life,” said Freya Tracey, principal data analyst at the Health Foundation.

She added: “Where you live, the opportunities available to you, and the circumstances you are born into should not determine your risk of dying early. A cross-government approach is needed to reduce inequalities in the building blocks of health – including education, employment and local economic conditions.

“The government’s approach to devolution must include supporting local areas to deliver prevention to reduce health inequalities. Without sustained action, inequalities will continue to cut lives short.”

Regarding ethnicity, Black Caribbean men were found to have the highest male rate of premature mortality, closely followed by white British men, at rates of 573 and 537 deaths per 100,000 respectively, while Chinese men had the lowest rate, at 284 deaths per 100,000. White British and Black Caribbean women had the highest female rates of premature death, at 370 and 367 per 100,000 respectively, whereas Chinese women had the lowest observed rate, at 181 deaths per 100,000.

Jabeer Butt, the chief executive at the Race Equality Foundation, said that although these figures appear to challenge much of what we know about racism and health inequalities, lower premature mortality in some ethnic groups does not mean they experience better health or that racism is unimportant.

He added: “What our analysis shows is that we need to look beyond ethnicity alone, to understand how migration, poverty, employment, housing and discrimination interact to shape people’s chances of living a long and healthy life”.

A government spokesperson said: “Someone’s background or postcode should never dictate how long they live, and as part of our 10 Year Health Plan, this government is determined to tackle the stark inequalities that still exist in our country.

“We’re already taking action, including delivering pioneering new Neighbourhood Health Centres in the areas that need them most. And we will go further in devolving power to local communities, putting decision-making into the hands of those who know their areas best, and driving lasting change across the country.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The vaccine limbo in the US is worsening the measles outbreak
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Earlier doses for children, a focus on unvaccinated adults, a risk strategy based on geography – here’s how a functioning ACIP would address the measles outbreak

The US has announced three deaths associated with measles last week, among them a seven-month-old baby in New York and a postpartum woman in Pennsylvania, underscoring the need for a more aggressive vaccination approach – but US recommendations haven’t changed.

Dismantling the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) made it harder for the US to respond to the measles outbreak, with vaccine recommendations staying the same during a historic rise in cases and deaths, four former advisers say.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

A functioning committee would likely be considering recommendations on reaching adults with vaccines; moving up the childhood schedule for measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination in stricken areas; and pinpointing exactly which groups and areas need vaccination campaigns, they said.

Months after Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), replaced vaccine advisers with his own handpicked allies, a federal judge halted the committee’s work, finding that the Trump administration had failed to constitute the committee properly.

The ACIP makes recommendations to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on vaccine policy – and it “definitely” would discuss updating its advice as measles continues to spread, said Yvonne “Bonnie” Maldonado, chief of infectious diseases in the department of pediatrics at Stanford Medicine and a former member of the ACIP.

Now, “we don’t have an ACIP”, Maldonado added. “That’s going to impact disease and deaths in the US.”

The committee was monitoring the measles outbreak early last year before Kennedy disbanded it, and his replacements did not publicly evaluate evidence on the outbreak. The CDC is now taking nominations for a new committee, but the appointment process can take months or years – and the process for making or changing recommendations is also lengthy.

“It typically took between 12 to 18 months from the start of considering new recommendations to adopting them,” said Noel Brewer, a distinguished professor of health behavior at the UNC Gillings School of Global Public Health and a former ACIP member. In the meantime, the outbreak continues accelerating.

The seven-month-old baby who died in New York state wasn’t vaccinated against measles, officials said on Monday. Another infant died in the measles outbreak in Wisconsin, officials announced on Thursday. Both states marked their first measles-associated deaths in three decades.

In normal times, babies in the US don’t receive their first MMR shots until they turn one. But during outbreaks, babies at risk of infection can get the shot as early as six months of age – one of a handful of recommendations from the CDC that is receiving less attention than it normally would, experts say.

The advice on vaccination during outbreaks could be highlighted more, and recommendations could be changed to “tell the pediatricians and providers we are in a huge outbreak”, said Edwin Asturias, professor of pediatric infectious disease at the University of Colorado and a former ACIP member.

The CDC also offers the option of moving up the MMR second shot in order to make sure children in outbreak areas are fully protected against the virus. During an outbreak, it can be given as soon as four weeks after the first dose. The shot is usually given between the ages of four and six.

The delay between doses could be contributing to what Asturias calls a “group of susceptibles” who were not protected from measles for decades and are now falling ill and dying.

Some people are ideologically opposed to vaccines, while others don’t have steady access to healthcare. “But that’s only part of the explanation,” Asturias said. The number of visits to doctors decreases dramatically after the second year of life, with fewer opportunities to get the shots. “By delaying the second dose of immunization to four to six years, are you more likely to miss or not to give a second dose to many children?” he asked.

A properly appointed ACIP would look at such data points to “try to understand how this immunization or protection gap came about”, Asturias said.

In the US, vaccine mandates for children are set at the state and local level, tied to daycare and school attendance. But moving the recommendation earlier might increase vaccination rates, since families tend to have higher levels of trust in their doctors than in local officials, for example.

An unusually high number of adolescents and young adults are now getting sick and dying from measles. The vaccine advisers would likely explore why, and what could be done to reach them.

“Are you really monitoring how many adults are getting infected? I doubt it,” said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia and a member of the ACIP two decades ago. “Are we trying to vaccinate them? It’s harder. You can have school mandates, but what do you do for adults?”

It is especially important to reach unvaccinated or under-vaccinated people before they become pregnant, because the vaccines cannot be given during pregnancy. Congenital measles cases – when a baby gets sick in utero – have risen sharply this year, officials in Pennsylvania warned recently.

Such infections threaten the lives of newborns and pregnant people alike. A 21-year-old woman in Pennsylvania died soon after childbirth from measles complications, officials announced this week. Earlier this year, a measles-infected baby died soon after birth.

“That’s the actual heart of the situation,” Maldonado said. “What we’re seeing now is something I literally have never seen myself, and I’m a seasoned infectious disease clinician,” she added. “To have even one case used to be a remarkable occurrence, but now they’re having so many.”

Anyone beginning cancer therapy or other immune-suppressing treatments should also make sure they’re protected by vaccines first, Asturias said. And anyone who was born between 1968 and 1989 may have only received one shot, and should get a second dose.

The ACIP should also work to identify which groups of people and regions are most at risk and how to reach them, said Brewer.

“Measles vaccination rates are pretty high in most places, but there are places where it’s very low, and the United States does not have a good mechanism for identifying these geographical areas and responding in them,” Brewer said.

The ACIP and the CDC offer recommendations based on evidence that is sometimes not publicly available. But states can take action on their own to change vaccination recommendations. “The decisions are up to the states and the counties,” Maldonado said.

With measles, “there are serious risks” and “most of the bad stuff happens to young babies under a year of age”, Maldonado said. Hospitalizations, complications and deaths are more common in this group – and the risks persist long after the rash fades. Maldonado has cared for two children who developed subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years after contracting measles.

“They’re terrifying cases,” she said.

Yet US officials have lagged in public communications about the risks – and how preventable they are, Maldonado said. Erica Schwartz, the CDC’s director, drew criticism for her silence on the outbreaks and the importance of vaccination.

“She came into CDC in the middle of a huge set of outbreaks and didn’t talk about it for weeks,” Maldonado said. For families seeking guidance, “it’s already pretty chaotic right now, and it’s unfortunate – nobody knows where to turn”, Maldonado said.

US officials need to speak with “one voice” to outline a plan for addressing the outbreak, Brewer said. “The US has a terrible measles problem right now, one that is largely avoidable. We need to get vaccination rates up.”

He added: “That’s really the key priority: just get the shot.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: US has announced three deaths associated with measles last week. A seven-month-old baby in New York and a postpartum woman in Pennsylvania died from measles complications.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Selena Gomez says vaping has changed her voice. Can e-cigarettes really affect your vocal cords – and is it reversible?
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Melissa Davey
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Experts say the practice can damage delicate tissues in the voice box and there is not yet sufficient data to say if people can recover

Read more in the Antiviral series

While vaping is known to cause lung damage, breathlessness and nicotine addiction, the singer and actor Selena Gomez has posted in a video on Instagram that vaping has permanently changed her voice.

“Nicotine is so hard to quit and I just wanted to say, if you’re going through it, or if you’re even trying to vape, it’s just not worth it,” she said. “It’s so stupid and it changed my voice. I’m not going to be able to change my voice. I vaped a lot.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Gomez also has lupus, an autoimmune condition in which the body mistakenly attacks healthy tissues, organs and cells and which can cause inflammation affecting the vocal cords.

But can vaping also affect one’s voice – and if so, are the changes reversible?

Prof Matthew Peters, a professor of respiratory medicine at Macquarie University hospital, says: “We don’t have a way of delivering nicotine to the voice box that’s not in a harmful vehicle, whether it’s cigarette smoking, vaping, or heat not burn.”

The tissues of the upper airway are delicate, he says, and heated products – which may contain toxic chemicals and ultrafine particles that can be inhaled deep into the lungs – affect the vocal cords or vocal folds, located inside the larynx (voice box).

Epithelial cells are part of the outer, protective layer of the vocal cords known as the epithelium, working as “the first line of defense against inorganic, organic and microbial intruders”, a paper published in the journal Disease Models and Mechanisms says.

Vaping damages these cells, causing them to detach, and triggering inflammation and swelling – sometimes leading to a hoarse, deep or raspy voice.

Prof Peter Wark, a spokesperson for the National Asthma Council Australia and a respiratory physician, says vaping also affects the mucous membrane, which dries out and thins when damaged. Wark says this increases “the risk of coughing and breathing difficulties”.

Peters says vaping has “toxic effects” on the entire upper respiratory system.

“The whole voice system is very finely tuned to generate the noises that we do, and it does not take much of a inflammatory change to alter voice, particularly in heavy voice users.”

While the evidence for the harms of cigarettes has been accumulating for 200 years, vapes began appearing more commonly in the 2000s and Wark says it means the evidence for vocal damage is “very strong in the short term, but less well defined in the longer term”.

“Up to a third of people vaping report symptoms of chronic cough from studies in the US and China,” he says.

“Similar numbers have also been shown to experience hoarse voice or dysphonia [voice impairment]. There are no longitudinal studies that demonstrate permanent changes, or changes that do not resolve with cessation. However, this is possible and it will take time for the evidence to come through.”

Peters says complaints about voices are more frequent in those who have quit vaping than in those who continue to vape.

“That’s a bit of a paradox in some ways, but it could be that the people who are concerned about their voice stop vaping, and then it doesn’t always immediately improve. So clearly, these products alter voice quality. The chance of recovery after cessation is not substantiated one way or the other from data.”

Wark says while it is not clear that nicotine itself worsens these symptoms, all vapes – whether they are non-nicotine or flavoured – cause similar harms to the vocal cords and respiratory system.

“I recommend that no one should use vapes,” he says. “If they develop cough or hoarse voice they should certainly stop as it will worsen. Recent evidence suggests that vaping can also worsen asthma control and lead to increased symptoms and the need to use anti-inflammatory inhalers.”

Peters says when vapes were first becoming more common, he advocated they be treated with caution until any harms were known.

“I now think we should be regulating and approaching electronic cigarettes generally on the basis of proven harm, not precaution,” he says.

“Those harms go from asthma to respiratory symptoms to impaired immunity and frequent episodes of pneumonia, with emerging evidence on other things like heart attacks.

“The full spectrum of the harms and extent might require some clarification over time. It’s genuinely doubtful whether, in fact, long-term intense vaping is any safer than long-term smoking.”

He praised Gomez for being open about her experience.

“I think that’s a really good message for a prominent celebrity who’s had some health battles well publicised; that she doesn’t want to have other people to have the health battles that she has experienced.”

Melissa Davey is Guardian Australia’s medical editor

Antiviral is a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claims
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: Selena Gomez has posted a video on Instagram that vaping has permanently changed her voice. Vaping is known to cause lung damage, breathlessness and nicotine addiction. But experts say there is not yet sufficient data to say if people can recover.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi end with prisoner exchange agreement
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Two days of talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials, mediated by the United States, have yielded agreement on a prisoner exchange but failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war, which is nearing the five-year mark.

Russia’s chief ⁠⁠negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, said at the talks ⁠⁠in the United Arab Emirates capital, Abu Dhabi, on Wednesday that both sides had agreed on a large-scale prisoner swap and that mutual understanding ⁠⁠had been achieved on some issues.

Russia’s state-run news agency TASS reported that the prisoner exchange should happen in two to three weeks. If finalised, it would be the latest in a ⁠long line of such ⁠exchanges.

US envoy Jared Kushner told a news conference the number of prisoners would be finalised on Thursday. He added that he would travel to Moscow alongside US special envoy Steve Witkoff to relay what was discussed to Russian President Vladimir Putin and “make more progress on some of the issues that were discussed, because we see some openings and some opportunities there”.

Kushner and Witkoff are then scheduled to fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy “and explore some of the ideas we came up with”.

Political analyst Dmitry Medvedenko told Al Jazeera that prisoner exchanges have been a regular occurrence without this level of diplomatic work. “Every two or three months you have 100 to 300 prisoners exchanged by both sides; this is a channel that actually works,” he said.

Ukraine and Russia freed 200 prisoners of war each in March following talks in Geneva, Switzerland, in February. Last year, they each exchanged 146 prisoners after mediation by the UAE, and large-scale prisoner exchanges followed three rounds of talks in Istanbul, Turkiye, from May to July.

“For it to be the biggest prisoner exchange, it should top the 1,000-for-1,000 exchange in May last year,” Medvedenko said.

The two warring sides entered Wednesday’s talks far apart on terms for a possible settlement to the war.

Kushner said it was “a long way to get everyone back to the table” and that “this was a very tough meeting but a productive one”. He added that territorial issues would be the hardest to settle but that “progress” was made on a post-war security framework.

Medinsky said more talks would be held in the near future and that Moscow was not opposed to participation from the European Union. He added, however, that it was ⁠unclear what there ⁠was for Russia and the EU to discuss, given what he ‌said was a lack of proposals from the European ‌side.

Ukraine’s peace negotiator David Arakhamia said there was “good ⁠momentum” from peace talks in Abu Dhabi towards ‌reaching a solution before the end of the year and that the next talks should be multilateral, ‌not trilateral, adding that Europe should ‌be ‌represented.

Zelenskyy, who, like Putin, is not attending the talks, said on Wednesday he did not think it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.

Kushner said further talks with the Russian and Ukrainian presidents would touch upon “whether we can get Europeans to the format and make this a multilateral format”.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Two days of talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials have yielded agreement on a prisoner exchange. The prisoner exchange should happen in two to three weeks, Russia's state-run news agency TASS reported. The number of prisoners will be finalised on Thursday, US envoy Jared Kushner said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: ‘Climate crisis is outrunning us,’ UN chief Guterres says at COP31
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has sought world leaders’ immediate response to climate change, which has put the world on a path to destruction, at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye.

Accusing the fossil fuel lobby of “delaying” climate action, Guterres called on leaders on Wednesday to work to ensure that coal, gas and oil cease to exist as energy sources, saying it is needed to avert “disaster”.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” the UN chief said.

“The brutal truth is that ⁠the climate crisis is outrunning us. Emissions in 2025 reached all-time highs. Heat records keep shattering,” he said.

“The last four years were the hottest ever, and ‌fossil fuel interests keep making a killing while killing our planet. Climate disasters are pounding lives, livelihoods and economies across the globe. This is the path to mutually assured destruction,” Guterres cautioned.

Top leaders attending the summit include Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is the only leader from a G7 country, scheduled to address the summit on Thursday.

European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen is also participating, while world leaders such as French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Canadian PM Mark Carney and Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi are skipping the summit.

The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter of greenhouse gases, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row.

COP31 host Turkiye is championing a voluntary initiative to accelerate the electrification of transport, buildings and industry, with a target of raising electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.

The EU has stressed that electrification must be “clean”, which could lead to debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.

The UN chief has urged countries to speed their transition to clean energy sources.

He said the world’s dependence on fossil fuels was also damaging economies, not just the climate – an apparent nod to surging petroleum prices since the start of the US-Israel war ‌on Iran that has disrupted Middle East oil exports.

Iran’s Pezeshkian said he would use the event as an opportunity to express Tehran’s position on environmental destruction in war.

“At this conference, we will speak about the actions of the United States and Israel in destroying the environment,” he said before departing for Turkiye, according to Iranian state television.

A UN report last month found the world on ‌course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7F) warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change.

Meanwhile, 2026 has also been marked by a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flash flood, killing more than 1,500 people, with thousands still missing.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: UN chief Antonio Guterres calls on world leaders to work to ensure that coal, gas and oil cease to exist as energy sources. Guterre says fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won't happen on its own.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Mbappe misses France training before Nations League clash with Italy
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
France captain Kylian Mbappe has not taken part in team training and remains “under treatment” before his country’s Nations League clash with Italy, the Les Bleus coaching staff says.

It did not provide any details regarding the 27-year-old’s physical condition after Wednesday’s training session.

The Real Madrid forward is back in the France squad after missing their last three matches through injury.

Mbappe scored the winning goal in Zinedine Zidane’s first match as coach against Turkiye in September in the Nations League but had to leave the pitch shortly afterwards due to pain in his left knee.

Shortly before this international break, the Frenchman scored in Real’s 3-0 away win over Valencia in La Liga on Saturday. Mbappe is the second-highest scorer in the Spanish top flight this term with 13 goals, two fewer than leader Raphinha of Barcelona.

After three wins and a draw in four matches, two-time world champions France top Group A1 of the Nations League and are well on course to qualify for the quarterfinals before their final two pool-stage fixtures against Italy on Thursday in Milan and Turkiye on Sunday in Bordeaux.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: African rights body raises alarm over treatment of Niger’s Mahamid Arabs
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights has appealed to Niger’s president over alleged violations of the fundamental rights of the country’s Arab Mahamid community, amid reports of restrictions on access to water, education, healthcare and identity documents.

In an urgent appeal sent to President Abdourahamane Tchiani on November 6, three commission representatives raised concerns about the treatment of the community in the southeastern Diffa region. The appeal was made public on November 9.

The signatories included the commissioner responsible for the human rights situation in Niger and the heads of two working groups covering economic, social and cultural rights, and the rights of Indigenous populations, communities and minorities.

The Mahamid are an Arab community with historical links to Chad and Sudan. Many live in Niger’s Diffa region. Some families have been settled there for generations, following successive waves of migration from neighbouring countries.

Disputes over their nationality and identity documents have repeatedly put them at odds with the authorities.

Officials have accused some Mahamid residents of obtaining nationality documents fraudulently, trafficking arms and having links to armed groups around the Lake Chad basin.

At a security meeting in Diffa on August 22, Governor Mahamadou Ibrahim Bagadoma and other officials discussed nationality papers, cross-border movement and security, as well as tensions over water and grazing land, according to state news agency ANP.

ANP reported that Bagadoma warned against holding the entire Arab community responsible for allegations involving particular individuals. The accusations have not been independently verified.

The appeal comes amid reports of measures restricting the Mahamid’s access to basic services and official documents.

Nigerien publication African Perceptions said it had obtained a copy of an Interior Ministry radio message dated October 7 and numbered 002235, addressed to the governors of Diffa and Zinder.

According to the publication, the message instructed authorities to close schools and water facilities used by the Mahamid, require community members to pay the full cost of healthcare and stop issuing civil status documents to them. It also called for the withdrawal of existing documents, including national identity cards and passports, and for security forces to enforce the measures.

Al Jazeera has not independently authenticated the document or established whether the instructions have been implemented.

The commission has expressed concern about the reported restrictions on access to water, education and healthcare, as well as identity documents. Its appeal to President Tchiani is not a formal finding that the government has violated the community’s rights.

Chadian broadcaster Radio Ndarason Internationale reported that Mahamid representatives were told at a meeting in Diffa on November 8 that they had two months to leave Niger.

The meeting was reportedly attended by the Diffa prefect, the Gueskerou administrator, the Komadougou canton chief and village chiefs. Radio Ndarason said the community representatives declined to comment when approached.

Nigerien publication La Roue de l’Histoire reported on November 10 that the authorities had set December 31, 2026, as the deadline for the community to leave.

Neither publication has made a formal expulsion order available. Al Jazeera has not independently confirmed the decision, its legal basis or whether it applies to the entire community.

Niger faced a similar dispute in 2006, when the government announced plans to expel Arabs from Diffa to Chad. The operation was suspended after protests and negotiations.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights has appealed to Niger’s president over alleged violations of the rights of the Arab Mahamid community. The appeal was made public on November 9. It comes amid reports of restrictions on access to water, education, healthcare and identity documents.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US soldier arrested for Russia spying: What we know
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Edna Mohamed
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
British police have arrested a senior member of the United States military on suspicion of spying for Russia following an investigation by counterterrorism officials, marking the latest instance of alleged espionage in the West linked to Moscow.

A 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under Section 1 and Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, according to a statement by London Metropolitan Police.

Section 1 of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

“As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire. The country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” the statement read.

Here’s what we know so far.

So far, not much information is available about the soldier who was arrested.

The BBC reported on Tuesday that the soldier was based at the Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire.

Those barracks serve as the base for NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC), which is a strategic operational base for the military alliance.

The man has been detained under the National Security Act 2023, which allows police to hold him without charge for 14 days, the Metropolitan Police said, adding that Counter Terrorism Police London were leading the investigation.

Under British law, police generally do not publish the names of suspects before they have been charged, except in exceptional circumstances.

What has the UK said?

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Britain’s Counter Terrorism Policing, said the arrest and investigation resulted from “close collaboration between UK and US authorities”.

“The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing. This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security.”

The investigation into the US soldier is not connected to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations, according to the Metropolitan Police.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the arrest involved allegations of espionage which are of the “utmost concern” to the US and its allies.

“While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” Patel said.

He said that the FBI had made 167 arrests in counterintelligence and espionage-related cases over the last 21 months – a 53 percent increase over the comparable previous period.

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said the case demonstrated the strength of the UK-US partnership.

“I am grateful to the UK and the FBI for their professionalism and teamwork throughout this investigation. The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent. I encourage anyone who thinks they’ve witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office,” he said.

This is believed to be the first time a US soldier was found to be under suspicion of spying for a foreign government while in the UK.

However, espionage allegations have grown in recent months.

In October, British police arrested three men on suspicion of helping Russian intelligence under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023.

A month before, three people — two men and a woman — were arrested on suspicion of spying for Moscow.

The UK has been one of Ukraine’s biggest backers since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and relations between London and Moscow are at their lowest.

However, even before the Ukraine war, Russian intelligence had played a role in London. In 2006, former Russian spy Alexander Litvinenko was poisoned in the capital and in 2018, there was an attempted plot to poison double agent Sergei Skripal.

The man was detained under the national security Act 20 23, which allows police to hold him without charge for 14 days. The soldier was based at the Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: What is northern Europe’s new drone and warship plan to counter Russia?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Urooba Jamal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The United Kingdom has unveiled a plan to integrate the maritime defence capabilities of 10 countries, including the sharing of sea drones and warships, in response to what European countries see as a growing threat from Russia.

The Northern Navies Initiative is a British-led defence framework that will link the UK’s autonomous systems with its Baltic, Nordic and Dutch allies to create a unified surveillance capability to respond to growing maritime threats.

“The threats we face are multiplying … we must rise to the challenge before us,” First Sea Lord General Gwyn Jenkins said after the signing of the agreement on Tuesday.

“Together, we have shown what is possible when like-minded nations are united by a common purpose.”

The UK plans to spend 90 million pounds ($121m) on drones, sensors and artificial intelligence systems to help the Royal Navy counter Russian undersea threats in the North Atlantic and protect critical infrastructure.

According to Guntram Wolff, a senior fellow at the European think tank Bruegel, the new alliance is “a very important initiative”.

“No single Western European nation can credibly defend itself,” he told Al Jazeera.

So what is the new defence framework and will it deter Russian threats?

Luke Pollard, the UK minister for defence readiness, introduced the new plan, saying that Russian naval activity around the country has increased by 41 percent in the first nine months of the year, The Guardian newspaper reported.

Pollard said the “huge increase” in violations justified the new initiative.

“The model that we want is where British autonomy [drones] can be teamed with a British warship or a Danish warship or a Norwegian warship and can hand that autonomy off to an allied nation’s warship,” the minister said, speaking at the navy’s International Sea Power conference held on the Prince of Wales aircraft carrier in Oslo.

Sailing the warship to Norway was “a really important deterrent signal that we stand ready to defend every single inch of NATO territory”, Pollard said.

The Northern Navies Initiative agreement will be a new network of autonomous systems equipped with advanced sensors that will create a unified surveillance capability to improve the detection and monitoring of submarine activity.

The 10-country alliance combines the UK’s Royal Navy with those of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) nations, a UK-led military partnership for crisis management in the High North, the North Atlantic, and the Baltic Sea regions. The JEF countries include Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden.

The agreement aims to support maritime deterrence and defence for the citizens of the JEF countries, allowing them to “act early, combine quickly and transition seamlessly into NATO command should the Alliance need to mobilise at scale,” the British Royal Navy said in a statement.

“In practice, greater interoperability means a Royal Navy frigate could transfer operational responsibility to another JEF member without losing momentum,” it added.

“One nation’s task group could direct allied sensors and uncrewed vessels, while a warship could repair, refuel and resupply in an allied port rather than returning home,” it said.

Future autonomous platforms will be able to plug in and out of each other’s command and control systems, “creating one large maritime force instead of 10 separate ones”, it added.

Analyst Wolff, of the Bruegel think tank, said greater interoperability was essential for better deterrence on the continent.

“Deepening interoperability among national navies, strengthening joint manoeuvres, ensuring clear command structures in case of crises is absolutely critical for credible deterrence,” he said.

“The deepening of cooperation is also necessary to [successfully] avert hybrid attacks, including against infrastructure such as deep-sea cables or renewable energy.”

While NATO provides the foundation for collective defence, the JEF initiative is aimed at bringing together “a smaller group of closely aligned navies together so they can work more closely, more routinely and at a higher state of readiness,” the Royal Navy said.

Western officials have warned that Russia has increased activity around subsea infrastructure.

In its statement about the new initiative, the Royal Navy said it was responding to “the growing threat posed by hostile activity below the threshold of armed conflict”, which includes “risks to critical undersea infrastructure, malicious seabed activity and other forms of hybrid aggression”.

In April, Britain said it had deployed military vessels to deter Russian submarines, which it said had spent more than a month in and around British waters, warning Moscow that any attempt to damage cables or pipelines would have “serious consequences”.

Pollard claimed that Russian spy ships, such as the Yantar, have been trying to obtain “an increased picture of our critical national infrastructure”, as well as “mapping our undersea cables”.

Russian frigates have been spotted escorting oil tankers and other trade vessels in UK waters, and in June, one fired shots at a yacht south of the Isle of Wight, The Guardian reported. A Russia-linked tanker, the Smyrtos, was seized following the incident.

As a result, oil tankers linked to Russia remain active but have been “sailing around the UK” to avoid coming through the English Channel, Pollard said.

Last month, UK officials called attention to the dwindling number of British frigates, which is expected to drop from 12 in 2021 to three by 2030, The Guardian said, and which could explain why the initiative was launched.

Pollard, the defence minister, blamed the opposition Conservatives for these shortfalls. “Now, because of the decisions taken 10, 15 years ago, we have fewer ships and fewer submarines than I would like available,” the minister said.

Russia has largely denied claims that it is posing a maritime threat to European countries.

Concerns about threats to undersea cables have particularly grown since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. However, Russia has repeatedly denied targeting them.

Most recently in April, the Russian embassy in London rejected the British government’s claims that its submarines posed a threat to undersea cables, Russia’s state news agency TASS reported.

Last year, the same embassy accused the British government of being “Russophobic” and “whipping up militaristic hysteria” after the UK accused it of directing lasers at British pilots sent to monitor the spy ship Yantar, in its waters.

“We are not interested in British underwater communications,” the Russian embassy said.

Moscow has accused the UK of carrying out the attack on the Nord Stream pipelines in 2022, for which Russia was initially blamed. Later German prosecutors alleged that Kyiv ordered the attack, which came months after Russian invasion of Ukraine. Two Ukrainian nationals have been arrested in connection with the sabotage. Their trial is under way.

Russia has also on occasion accused NATO of using fabricated threats to increase its military presence in the Baltic. Moscow has accused the US and its European allies of encircling it militarily through the expansion of NATO. It has opposed NATO membership for Ukraine as one of the conditions to end the nearly five years of war – Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: UK plans to spend 90 million pounds ($121m) on drones, sensors and artificial intelligence systems. UK minister for defence readiness says Russian naval activity around country has increased by 41 percent in first nine months of the year.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
