An Israeli rights group has accused Israeli authorities of ignoring the deteriorating health of Dr Hussam Abu Safia, the jailed director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, as the Israeli army continues to launch attacks on the Strip.

It comes as two Israeli courts rejected petitions on Wednesday seeking to release 14 doctors from Gaza imprisoned without charge, and to allow Abu Safia to receive an independent medical examination.

The Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) said it obtained an independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records showing a weight loss of 14kg (31lb) in four months, a significant drop in haemoglobin levels and chest pain that was not properly investigated.

The reviewer, Amit Tirosh, was not permitted to examine Abu Safia in person. He disputed an Israeli court’s finding that high blood pressure was his only medical problem, writing that the ruling “does not line up with the data”.

PHRI says the Israel Prison Service has refused to release Abu Safia’s latest medical file.

“Not only has he been deprived of his freedom without trial, but he is also being denied his basic right to an independent medical examination,” PHRI’s Naji Abbas said.

The Israeli army captured the doctor in December 2024 during a raid on Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza.

PHRI said on Wednesday the Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking the release of 14 doctors, including hospital directors and specialists in essential medical fields, who are being held in Israeli prisons without being charged or brought to trial.

PHRI argued that the prolonged arbitrary detentions – in some cases for more than two years – constitute a violation of their individual rights and further undermine Gaza’s healthcare system, which faces a severe shortage of medical professionals.

The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, finding no grounds to intervene in the Chief of Staff’s decision not to release the doctors. It maintained that their cases had been reviewed in light of changing circumstances and the shortage of doctors in Gaza, but that no exceptional grounds had been found to justify their release.

Gaza’s health sector has been largely destroyed during Israel’s genocidal war in the enclave since October 2023. Almost 90 percent of its overall infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

Meanwhile, sources at al-Shifa Hospital told Al Jazeera that an Israeli drone attack in the western part of Gaza City killed a Palestinian and injured others. Another Palestinian died from injuries caused by an Israeli attack on a family home in Gaza City on Tuesday.

Gaza continues to face regular Israeli attacks despite last year’s “ceasefire”. More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed by Israel in the besieged enclave since the United States-brokered agreement, according to the territory’s ‌Ministry of Health.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Man City whistleblower Rui Pinto could help UK uncover more sporting crime
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Alexander Hoad
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Football whistleblower Rui Pinto, whose leaks triggered an investigation into Manchester City’s financial misconduct, has held discussions with authorities in the United Kingdom over a new role in helping uncover financial and sporting crime in the country, reports in British media say.

Pinto’s lawyers have been contacted by the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) after he stated he would be willing to assist UK authorities with investigations in exchange for police protection, British newspaper The Guardian reported on Wednesday.

Al Jazeera sought confirmation of Pinto’s reported contact with the authorities, but the SFO did not confirm whether the whistleblower was in talks.

“In line with long-established practice to avoid prejudice to law enforcement activity, we can neither confirm nor deny any investigation into this matter,” the SFO said in an emailed statement to Al Jazeera.

Pinto appeared to confirm the reports of his discussions with the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) by reposting an article on his social media account.

The 38-year-old is the founder of the website Football Leaks, which obtained private documents that showed City broke league rules from 2009 to 2018, leading to a probe by the Premier League’s independent commission.

City were found guilty of all but one of 115 charges brought against them over breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Pinto’s lawyer, William Bourdon, who has represented other high-profile whistleblowers including Julian Assange and Edward Snowden, was quoted by the Guardian as saying: “I can confirm that the process is under way.”

Pinto said last month that he feared for his life after being told his witness protection programme would end on October 10 and launched a crowdfunding initiative to help him establish an anonymous new life.

“The Commission responsible for Portugal’s witness protection programme informed me of its decision to terminate my participation in the programme and withdraw my police protection, thereby knowingly placing me in a life-threatening situation,” he wrote in a social media post.

“Given these circumstances, I have no alternative but to relocate, within the next few days, to an undisclosed location for an indefinite period of time, due to the multiple death threats I have received and the serious risk of an assassination attempt against me.

“For this reason, I have just set up a GoFundMe campaign and I am asking for everyone’s support to help me survive this serious situation created by the Portuguese State, which, as I have already stated, has knowingly decided to place my life at risk.”

However, the Portuguese Ministry of Justice said it would extend his protection pending a new hearing, after Pinto’s lawyers challenged the decision.

Reports last month said Pinto had reached out to UK authorities to offer cooperation in ongoing investigations in exchange for security measures being placed around him.

Pinto said at the start of his trial in April 2020 that he was “proud” to be a whistleblower on European football clubs’ big-money dealings.

The former history student and self-taught computer expert faced 90 charges – from unauthorised access to data and violation of correspondence to attempted extortion – in the case heard at Lisbon’s Central Criminal Court.

“I don’t consider myself a hacker. I am a whistleblower,” he said at the time. “The revelations are serious and I’m proud; there’s no shame. I haven’t done anything for money,” added Pinto, who acknowledges releasing 70 million documents on football’s backroom workings.

He was given a four-year suspended sentence in September 2023 for illegally obtaining documents, committing other cybercrimes and attempted extortion. He was later acquitted on 241 separate counts in a second trial in April 2026 after the court ruled the charges were ­­“invalid”.

Pinto has been a protected witness since August 2020 after agreeing to grant Portuguese authorities access to millions of files gathered before his arrest. His first trial in Portugal began a month later.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Did Democrats save Pete Hegseth from impeachment?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The United States House ⁠of Representatives has blocked an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a surprise reprieve for President Donald Trump’s administration as Republicans reel from their midterm election defeat.

The impeachment articles were introduced by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, but the effort was backed primarily by Democrats. They accuse Hegseth of abuses of power and conducting illegal military operations.

The Republican-led House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to refer the articles back to the House Judiciary Committee, where they could remain indefinitely. The procedural move in effect killed the impeachment drive for the duration of the current Congress’s term, which ends in eight weeks. On January 3, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate.

In a twist, the absence of 11 Democratic lawmakers during the vote proved decisive.

Here’s what to know about the vote to block Hegseth’s impeachment and what could happen next:

The vote was not on whether to impeach Hegseth. It was on whether to refer the articles of impeachment to the Judiciary Committee, where they may be further investigated or amended.

Such procedural moves are often used as stalling tactics. With the current Congress due to conclude soon, the resolution is unlikely to return to the House floor before its term ends.

Massie called the vote “a procedural motion to kill the resolution”.

It narrowly passed 211-204.

Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the measure. The remaining votes fell along party lines with Republicans supporting the measure and Democrats opposing it.

Eighteen representatives were absent from the vote – 11 Democrats and seven Republicans. Had the Democrats shown up and voted with their colleagues, they would have had the numbers to defeat the procedural move, forcing a full House vote on whether to impeach Hegseth as early as this week.

Trump cheered the result of Tuesday’s vote in a social media post, saying the Democrats’ impeachment effort had “miserably FAILED!”

The Democrats absent from the vote were:

The representatives have given varying explanations for why they did not show up.

Strickland, Jackson, Stansbury and Gillen all blamed a traffic delay in Washington, DC.

Pelosi said she was in her home state for a veterans event while Correa said he was in California before undergoing a health procedure. Horsford’s office cited a personal emergency.

Pettersen, who said she helped introduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April, said she had been “denied the ability to vote on this motion” without elaborating.

Jackson, Stansbury, Gillen, Strickland, Horsford, Pelosi and Pettersen all said they would have joined their Democratic colleagues in opposing the measure. Jackson and Stansbury also said they had formally recorded their opposition in the Congressional Record although this does not change the official vote count.

There was no immediate comment from Stevens, Brownley or Wilson on their absences.

Stevens previously criticised the Trump administration for launching the war on Iran with Israel and sought more congressional oversight. But days before the US midterm elections on November 3, the Michigan congresswoman, who had lost the Democratic primary for the state’s open Senate seat earlier to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers against her own party’s nominee.

Wilson, 83, on Monday attended the groundbreaking for a housing project in Miami-Dade County. Wilson and Brownley, like Stevens, previously opposed Trump’s handling of the war on Iran and demanded the administration seek congressional approval for the fighting.

Democratic politicians and progressive commentators have expressed outrage that poor attendance from Democrats impacted the outcome of the vote.

Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove from California said: “We knew that this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote.”

“There is no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues,” she added.

Senator-elect El-Sayed, responding to a question about the absent Democrats, said: “You should show up and do your job.”

Some pundits pointed the finger at Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the new speaker of the House in January. They accused him of failing to exert sufficient pressure on party members to defeat the measure.

Political commentator Krystal Ball called the vote “a major Hakeem Jeffries fail”.

“You could have impeached the war criminal Pete Hegseth but Dems didn’t show up to vote,” she said.

Progressive writer Laura Bassett said: “Jeffries didn’t even whip the vote. He told people to ‘vote their conscience’, and 11 members of his caucus didn’t show up. This is why people want a stronger leader.”

Yes. When the new Democratic-controlled Congress convenes in January, they could begin the process again and will be in a stronger position to advance impeachment articles.

Jeffries has said he will consult members about another potential bid to impeach Hegseth next year. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.

However, a vote to impeach Hegseth does not necessarily mean he will be removed from office. Impeachment itself means the House has formally brought charges against a federal official, similar to a criminal indictment.

A successful impeachment vote triggers a trial in Congress’s upper chamber, the Senate, on whether to convict.

A conviction, which immediately removes the official from office, requires at least two-thirds support in the Senate. That means Democrats, even with their incoming majority in the chamber next year, would likely need about a dozen Republicans to join them to secure Hegseth’s removal.

Only eight officials – all federal judges – have ever been convicted by the Senate. Trump has been impeached twice – in December ⁠2019 and January 2021 – but the Senate acquitted him on both occasions.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: The House voted 211-204 to refer the articles back to the House Judiciary Committee. The vote was not on whether to impeach Hegseth. The procedural move killed the impeachment drive for the duration of the current Congress’s term.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The United Kingdom has pledged to defend its interests in the Sea Lion project to develop an oilfield near the Falkland Islands, as Argentina has brought a legal challenge before a tribunal over the offshore oil exploration, citing environmental concerns.

Attorney General Ellie Reeves, representing the UK government at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), said billions of pounds that are crucial to the future of the Falkland Islands will be lost if Argentina is successful in getting the project blocked.

The Hamburg-based tribunal is sitting for two days as Argentina seeks a provisional ruling to suspend oil drilling.

Reeves also said Argentina’s objection to the development was rooted in its territorial claims. “The hearing is not about the sovereignty of the Falklands,” the UK prime minister’s official spokesman said on Monday, echoing his country’s position that the island’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation.

The dispute is the latest in rising tensions between the UK and Argentina over the British overseas territory in the South Atlantic Ocean.

The Sea Lion development is a UK-Israeli venture to drill for oil in waters administered by the Falklands.

The UK’s Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum, operator of the Sea Lion oilfield, located about 220km (137 miles) from the islands, are expected to start the project in March 2027, with oil production to begin in 2028.

According to Rockhopper Exploration, the Sea Lion exploration field holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil in place, of which 500 million barrels are recoverable resources.

However, Argentina’s President Javier Milei announced measures to block the development in September and said in a post on X that he had instructed the Foreign Ministry and the country’s legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the UK.

“If in 2 weeks the United Kingdom does not halt the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. THE MALVINAS ARE ARGENTINA’s, and they are defended with facts, not words,” he wrote, using the Argentinian name for the Falkland Islands.

Argentina formally filed a complaint at the tribunal seeking provisional measures against the UK on October 13.

The UK has administered the Falkland Islands since 1833. However, as the territory lies off Argentina’s shores, Buenos Aires claims sovereignty over what it calls Las Malvinas.

Milei has also threatened tougher sanctions on companies involved in the oil exploration project, preventing them from operating in Argentina’s oil and mining sectors.

Milei’s government argues the project violates a United Nations resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions in the islands until their dispute over the territory’s sovereignty is resolved.

But Jorge Emilio Nunez, a reader in legal philosophy at Manchester Metropolitan University, explained that at the core of the proceedings lies the sovereignty question over the Falklands.

“The oil project is the current trigger, but it sits on top of deeper competing claims about title, the self-determination of the islanders, and control of the surrounding maritime spaces and resources,” Nunez told Al Jazeera.

“This is not only a legal dispute. It also involves domestic politics and leaders’ prestige on both sides. When valuable natural resources become commercially viable, the underlying territorial disagreement is reactivated and reframed through legal, environmental and economic arguments. The resource issue does not replace the sovereignty dispute; it intensifies it.”

On Tuesday, Reeves told the Law of the Sea Tribunal, which issues legally binding rulings on maritime disputes, that Argentina wanted to “take control of those resources for itself”.

“The provisional measures sought by Argentina would prevent the people of the Falkland Islands from developing their natural resources as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination,” she said, according to The Guardian.

“The measures sought would have devastating consequences for the Falklands people. They risk losing billions of pounds in money, which is essential for the islands’ economic development.”

But Argentina’s lawyer, Mario Oyarzabal, argued that action was needed to block the project.

“[Argentina] respects the interests of the inhabitants of the islands and their way of life as enshrined in the Argentine constitution…What these British citizens do not have is a right to decide to which state the islands belong,” he said during the hearing, The Guardian reported.

“These resources belong to the Argentine people. Some 46 million of them, including the 1,247 inhabitants born on the islands, whose interests will be duly taken into account,” he added.

In 2013, Falkland islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain with the United Kingdom, despite Argentina’s claims.

On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson told the Independent news outlet that the UK was “fully engaged in the UNCLOS [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] process, and we’ll clearly set out our position on Argentina’s request for provisional measures before the Tribunal”.

“We’ll continue to robustly defend our interests and those of the Falkland Islanders,” the spokesperson added.

Last month, Burnham also discussed the bid to block the oil project during a call with United States President Donald Trump.

“The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources,” Burnham’s office said.

The fraught relationship between the UK and Argentina remains tense and heavily focused on the Falkland Islands.

Milei has capitalised on Trump’s refusal to say whether Washington would support the UK in a future conflict over the Falklands after the US president criticised London for not doing more to support the US during its attacks on Iran.

In September, Milei said the “winds of change” were blowing in Argentina’s favour when it comes to its claims of sovereignty.

“The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” Milei said.

At the same time, Argentina is set for an election next year, when the Sea Lion project’s halt could help Milei’s polling position.

To Nunez, the tribunal could have a “modest domestic impact” in the country.

“A visible legal success would allow the government to claim it is actively defending national interests and resources as the Falklands/Malvinas issue carries strong symbolic weight (the slogan “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” is still, intentionally, heavily used),” he said.

However, he noted, “A setback could be used by opponents”.

“Overall, while the case will be used for political messaging in Argentina, Argentine voters tend to prioritise economic performance over developments in the sovereignty dispute.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Argentina has filed a complaint against the UK over the oil exploration project. Argentina's President Javier Milei has threatened tougher sanctions on companies involved in the oil drilling project.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Workers across Spain stage first general strike in 14 years
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Millions of workers across Spain are striking to demand government action over the country’s housing crisis, less than three weeks before a national election that could bring the far right to power.

The 24-hour walkout, which began at midnight on Wednesday, disrupted public transport and forced businesses, factories and shops to scale back operations or close entirely across the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy. It’s Spain’s first general strike in 14 years.

Minor incidents were reported in the first hours, including roadblocks with burning tyres in Barcelona, the second-largest city in the country. There were also scuffles between picketers and police near the country’s main wholesale market on the outskirts of the capital, Madrid.

The two main unions that called the strike, UGT and CCOO, reported widespread participation in the early hours “with significant work stoppages in strategic sectors”, including 90 percent in the automotive and port sectors, according to a statement posted on social media.

The CEOE organisation, which represents business leaders, said in a statement that the impact varied by region and area of work, with a “low participation” in most sectors.

The UGT and CCOO unions called the strike following a wave of nationwide protests over access to housing, sparked by the eviction in September of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old Madrid pensioner who died several days later.

The demonstrations included a five-week occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, where hundreds of tents were pitched, sparking imitations in other cities.

The average rent in Spain has almost doubled over the past 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.

Spain’s socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election for November 29 after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the protests.

“This is not a strike against anyone, but rather one in favour of a common response from all levels of government to a real problem, which is access to housing,” he said in an interview published Sunday in the daily newspaper La Vanguardia.

The strike has been rejected by business groups, which have described it as an election-related protest, and criticised by the conservative opposition Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo warned that unions risked being linked to Sanchez “forever” if they went ahead with the strike in the run-up to the election.

Feijoo, whose party leads opinion polls, said going ahead with the strike was a “serious mistake” following a high-speed train collision last month in central Spain that killed 69 people.

Spain’s average gross monthly salary is about 2,460 euros, while renting a 50-square-metre apartment in Madrid cost an average of 1,170 euros a month in October, according to property portal Idealista.

That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, and 98.7 percent of the average young person’s income, according to the Youth Council of Spain. It’s well above the 30 percent share commonly recommended by housing experts and public institutions.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: 24-hour walkout began at midnight on Wednesday, disrupting public transport and forced businesses to scale back operations. It's Spain's first general strike in 14 years, with 90 percent of work stoppages in automotive and port sectors. The strike has been rejected by business groups, which have described it as an election-related protest.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US Treasury chief Bessent moved to military base after ‘Iranian threats’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has recently moved from his home in Washington, DC, to an undisclosed US military ⁠base in the wake of “Iranian threats” to his life.

The New York Times and the Reuters news agency reported the move on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the matter, but the severity of the threats remained unclear.

Iran has previously denied plotting to attack officials and people on US soil.

Bessent has led a US economic pressure campaign against Iran, dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, since August to try to push Tehran to end attacks on shipping and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

In April, the US announced a blockade on Iranian ports, but Tehran has remained defiant despite the naval siege.

A spokesperson said in a statement emailed to Reuters that “the secretary will not ⁠be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats and remains committed to executing ⁠Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran’s economy”.

In a memo seen by Reuters late last month, a senior intelligence official in the Trump administration warned that Iranian plots against US citizens had reached an advanced stage.

Security ⁠concerns surrounding Bessent increased when The Wall Street Journal published an aerial view of the Georgetown mansion that he bought for $12.5m shortly after his confirmation ⁠as Treasury secretary in January 2025, Reuters said, citing a source familiar with the matter.

The photo allowed Bessent’s home to ⁠be geo-located, and he was relocated to a military base for his safety, the source said, adding: “The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials.”

The New ‌York Times reported that US officials have noted that Iran’s ability to carry out large-scale attacks in the US and other territories overseas is limited. Yet, US national intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned last month that Tehran has “substantially increased” its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond.

Those efforts include beefing up the targeting of current and former US officials such as Bessent, the Times reported, citing three sources familiar with the matter.

US and Israeli attacks killed top Iranian officials, including the late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, early on in their war on Iran.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: The New York Times and the Reuters news agency reported the move on Tuesday. Iran has previously denied plotting to attack officials and people on US soil. Bessent has led a US economic pressure campaign against Iran since August to try to push Tehran to end attacks on shipping and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Gaza’s infrastructure collapse leaves residents defenceless against floods
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Damage from Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has worsened floods caused by heavy rain, which have submerged large areas of the enclave, local officials say.

A deep weather depression has exposed how the catastrophic deterioration of the Strip’s stormwater and sewage networks is causing thousands of tents to be flooded.

Gaza’s infrastructure has been severely damaged by waves of air raids and shelling since the start of the war in October 2023.

Ramadan Rabaa, a Palestinian shop owner, saw floodwaters sweep through his premises in western Gaza City, destroying large quantities of goods and inflicting heavy financial losses on his and his neighbours’ businesses.

When municipal crews arrived at the scene, they could do little to help due to a severe shortage of equipment and machinery.

Rabaa believes that if municipal authorities had sufficient resources, such as water suction trucks, pumps, and bulldozers, his losses could have been minimised, potentially saving his shop along with other businesses, homes and tents that have been inundated.

The rain has submerged or damaged 70,000 tents, affecting approximately 350,000 people, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. In some displacement camps, water levels reached nearly 1.5 metres.

The impact of the weather is compounded by wartime destruction, with the media office reporting that more than 700km of Gaza’s sewage network has been destroyed.

Within 12 hours of the storm, Gaza’s Civil Defence received more than 2,000 distress calls but could only respond to 218, because of fuel shortages and equipment breakdowns.

Due to the ongoing siege on Gaza and destruction caused by Israel’s war, Gaza City’s municipality currently relies on only one bulldozer, which often breaks down, and two water suction trucks. Most water and sewage pumps are out of service.

“The municipality lost about 85 percent of its fleet of vehicles and heavy equipment during the war, after the Israeli occupation destroyed more than 135 vehicles, mechanisms, and equipment, leaving it with only 15 percent of the total previous fleet,” Husni Muhanna, a spokesman for Gaza City municipality, told Al Jazeera.

“The remaining mechanisms are old and worn out, suffer frequent breakdowns, and require continuous maintenance to keep them operational and provide the minimum level of services to residents and the displaced, so the municipality is forced to seek help from whatever resources are available in the private sector.”

The destruction extends to the drainage networks.

“The occupation destroyed six sewage pumps out of eight in Gaza City, and the municipality has so far been unable to restart more than two pumps, leading to a decline in drainage capacity to about 20 percent at best,” Muhanna said.

This situation has been worsened by the destruction of the stormwater drainage network. Gaza City has lost about 2,800 of the 4,800 drains that existed before the war, heightening the risk of flooding during heavy rain.

Muhanna warned that the challenges in Gaza City are beyond the capacity of municipal crews, with about a million citizens and displaced people concentrated in an area covering less than one third of the city, while 85 percent of infrastructure is damaged.

To address the situation, the municipality and local institutions have prepared an emergency winter plan requiring $1.3m worth of materials and field equipment. But it depends entirely on the flow of funding and supplies, which is being hampered by Israeli restrictions on Gaza.

Jibril Kashko, a businessman from a family specialising in heavy equipment, told Al Jazeera that Gaza City Municipality requested his help during the recent storm, but was limited in the assistance he could provide due to broken equipment and a lack of operational resources.

“What owners of heavy equipment in Gaza face goes beyond usual breakdowns, as they have become unable to obtain the simplest operating supplies, from spare parts, oil and grease, to batteries,” Kashko said.

Ismail al-Thawabta, director general of the Government Media Office, said the enclave requires between 300,000 and 350,000 tents and reinforced plastic tarps, as well as caravans, to replace damaged shelters. Mobile homes which were supposed to enter Gaza as part of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement have been held up on the border.

Gaza also needs 1,000-1,500 water pumps, 300-500 heavy machines such as bulldozers and excavators, and generators to power essential services.

Al-Thawabta said that repeated displacement and the destruction of most homes in Gaza have left large numbers of residents lacking essential supplies to cope with the winter months.

He said 2.2 million winter clothing bags, 5 million heavy blankets, 2 million water and moisture-insulating sponge mattresses, and about 400,000 heaters are needed to help Palestinians in Gaza cope with the bad weather. But the aid entering Gaza remains at a fraction of what the enclave’s 2.3 million population needs, due to the Israeli restrictions.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Pakistan women’s captain Fatima Sana calls for gender equality in cricket
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Manasi Pathak
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Pakistan cricket captain Fatima Sana has called for parity between the country’s men’s and women’s teams, urging fans to show greater support for female players by filling stadiums for their tournaments.

The 25-year-old says she “dreams of a time” when the Pakistan women’s cricket team are treated as equal to the men’s team. “I hope it comes,” Sana said on Tuesday.

Sana, who has led the Pakistan team since 2024, is one of the country’s finest cricketers and has swiftly risen to the top echelons of women’s cricket.

The all-rounder is playing franchise cricket for the Australian Perth Scorchers in the Women’s Big Bash League (WBBL) in Australia, one of the world’s top women’s cricket competitions.

Following her team’s six-wicket win over Melbourne Stars on Sunday, Sana was asked about the state of women’s cricket in Pakistan.

“If you look at world cricket, the sport is growing,” Sana told digital cricket news platform CricBlog TV.

“I would like to see the same growth in Pakistan, be it in the men’s or women’s game.”

The right-arm medium-fast bowler is the second Pakistani player to feature in the WBBL after former captain Nida Dar, who played for Sydney Thunder in 2019.

Sana, who holds the world record for the fastest international 50 in women’s T20 cricket, led Pakistan to a bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

“The way the crowds turn up for men’s matches, I hope the same happens for the women’s matches,” she added.

Since making her WBBL debut on October 31, Sana has picked up five wickets in as many matches, with a bowling economy of 7.62 runs per over – figures that keep her joint-10th in the most-wickets chart.

Her WBBL campaign marks just the second time the 25-year-old has featured in an overseas league, having also played for Birmingham Phoenix in The Hundred in England.

“It is an honour to come here and have the opportunity to play [in Australia]. It’s great to play alongside my teammates; they’re very supportive and helpful,” Sana said.

“Personally, I wish for more and more girls from Pakistan to come and play in Australia so that cricket can grow back home in Pakistan, too,” she added.

At Perth Scorchers, Sana shares the dressing room with some of the world’s best players, including ex-New Zealand captain Sophie Devine and Australia batter Beth Mooney.

Pakistan will host the next edition of the women’s T20 World Cup in 2028. It will also be the first to feature 12 teams, up from 10 in the previous six editions.

It will be the first ICC women’s event held in Pakistan, which has hosted two ICC Men’s ODI World Cups and the ICC Men’s Champions Trophy in 2025.

Sana believes the tournament could help boost women’s participation in the sport in the cricket-mad South Asian nation.

“It’s a great step by the ICC that the [2028] World Cup is taking place in Pakistan, which will encourage more women players to come forward,” Sana said.

“When more girls watch the World Cup at home, their parents will also offer them more opportunities to play the sport.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Fatima Sana has called for parity between the Pakistan women's and men's cricket teams. The Pakistan captain has led the team since 2024 and is one of the country's finest cricketers. Sana is playing franchise cricket for the Australian Perth Scorchers in the Women's Big Bash League (WBBL) in Australia.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Pakistan’s PTI demands access to jailed Khan after overnight hospital visit
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Abid Hussain
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Islamabad, Pakistan – The party of jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan has demanded access to its leader after he was taken to a hospital overnight for treatment and sent back to prison.

Khan, 74, briefly left the Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi for an eye examination at Islamabad’s Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), the government hospital said on Wednesday.

In a statement, PIMS said a medical check was conducted on Khan on the advice of his ophthalmologist.

Khan has received a series of intravitreal injections in his right eye to treat central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), a condition diagnosed after he reported reduced vision. He received his first injection in January.

PIMS said Khan received another injection overnight.

“His vital parameters were found to be normal. He was clinically stable, and his general physical examination was normal,” the hospital said, adding that he was discharged about 2:30am (21:30 GMT on Tuesday) with instructions for further care and follow-up.

Khan, a former cricket star who served as premier from 2018 to 2022, has been behind bars since August 2023 on multiple corruption charges he denies and calls politically motivated. The government rejects the allegation.

Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party on Wednesday said the overnight hospital visit and his return to his prison cell raise “deeply troubling questions” about his health, the quality of his medical care and the transparency surrounding his condition.

“A human being’s health is not a political bargaining chip. Nor can the medical treatment of a former prime minister be reduced to a procedural formality,” the PTI said, adding that the “state bears full responsibility for his safety and wellbeing”.

“His family, personal doctors and legal team must be given immediate and unrestricted access,” the party said.

PTI information secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram told Al Jazeera that Khan’s family and personal doctors were not told about the hospital visit and the party learned of it from news reports.

“No one from the family or party was there [at the hospital]; our personal physician was not there either,” he said.

During a hearing on Tuesday, Khan’s lawyer Salman Safdar told the Islamabad High Court that while Khan had said his eyesight had improved, his blood pressure remained a concern.

Safdar had appeared on behalf of Khan and his wife, Bushra Bibi, to appeal against their convictions in a property case.

In response, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry told reporters that Khan was receiving the required medical care and his treatment was not being neglected.

In August, the Supreme Court ordered that Khan should be moved to a private hospital of his choice in Islamabad. Instead, he was taken to PIMS and returned to jail.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Imran Khan was taken to a hospital overnight for treatment and sent back to prison. Khan, 74, briefly left Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi for an eye examination. Khan has been behind bars since August 2023 on multiple corruption charges he denies.

https://www.aljazeera.com/video/al-jazee.title: Gaza Grad: A Palestinian-Russian family’s longing for home
https://www.aljazeera.com/video/al-jazee.text: When war engulfs Gaza in October 2023, members of a Palestinian-Russian family hold on for as long as they can. They have a route out of the Strip. But Anna and Ghassan Ashour and their daughters, Lisa and Donia, stay on despite the worsening conditions, because Gaza is their home. But as the violence escalates, they’re eventually forced to leave and head to Russia in search of safety. For Lisa and Donia, life there is unfamiliar. Struggling with the language, culture and separation from Gaza, the two of them move to Egypt, closer to home and to the possibility of a return. Split between Russia and Egypt, the family must find new ways to live with distance, uncertainty and longing. Their story reveals the enduring tension between the need for safety and the place that they still think of as home.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US embassy refutes Houthis’ Yemen blockade claims, highlights siege on Taiz
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Mohammad Mansour
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The US Embassy in Yemen has pushed back against Houthi claims that a Saudi-led blockade is restricting access to the country.

Khaled Wolfsberg, spokesperson for the US Embassy in Yemen, released an Arabic-language video on the mission’s official Instagram account on Tuesday evening, arguing that goods are still flowing into areas of Yemen under Houthi control.

The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), captured the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014. They have since seized large parts of western and northern Yemen. An offensive on coastal areas in September this year saw the rebel group take the port city of Mocha.

Wolfsberg presented operational figures showing that 272 commercial ships successfully unloaded their cargo at the ports of Hodeidah, as-Salif, and Ras Isa – all under Houthi control – between January and September 2026.

This data directly counters the Houthi narrative that Saudi Arabia and its allies have enacted a full-scale siege of Yemen’s Red Sea ports, preventing aid from reaching civilians.

The US claims align with operational analyses released by the United Nations Verification and Inspection Mechanism for Yemen, which monitors and facilitates commercial shipping to the region.

Throughout the first nine months of 2026, the UN mechanism regularly cleared dozens of vessels each month to sail to the Houthi-controlled ports.

The UN data confirms that 272 vessels sailed to these ports during this period. The maritime traffic peaked in January and March, with 34 vessels sailing each month. Even during slower periods, such as July, 25 vessels successfully made the journey.

These ships delivered millions of tonnes of essential cargo, primarily food. March recorded the highest volume of food deliveries, with more than 737,000 tonnes discharged. January also saw significant deliveries, with nearly 630,000 tonnes of food reaching the ports.

More recent data from August and September show continued food deliveries of more than 511,000 tonnes and 495,000 tonnes, respectively.

Alongside bulk shipments, containerised cargo continued to arrive at Hodeidah this year.

In January, four container vessels discharged 1,231 containers, followed by three container vessels unloading 851 containers in March. Another three vessels discharged 1,268 containers in April.

While container traffic fluctuated later in the year, particularly after the most recent bout of fighting, September still saw one container vessel discharging 182 containers.

Fuel and other cargo also reached the ports throughout the year, although in varying quantities. For instance, February saw more than 149,000 tonnes of fuel discharged, while September recorded no fuel deliveries but maintained high volumes of food and other goods.

Despite this, the UN has warned that recent fighting has worsened the humanitarian situation in Yemen, including in the besieged city of Taiz, which is under government control but fully surrounded by the Houthis.

In the US embassy video, Wolfsberg accused the Houthis of blocking food and fuel from reaching hospitals and water stations in Taiz. He described the conditions faced by Taiz residents as a genuine siege, shifting the blame for localised shortages onto the Houthi forces encircling the area.

“The only real blockade is the one cruelly imposed by the militia on Taiz by preventing the entry of food and essential supplies for citizens,” Wolfsberg said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: US Embassy in Yemen has released a video of the embassy's official Instagram account. The Houthis captured the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014. The US Embassy claims that goods are still flowing into areas under Houthi control.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Putin is not ready to make peace in Abu Dhabi
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Anton Shekhovtsov
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
As the Russian-Ukrainian war, which long ago entered a phase of attrition, grinds on, Russia, Ukraine and the United States began a new round of US-brokered trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on November 10. The talks are scheduled to continue on November 11.

The talks follow a successful humanitarian operation in Oleshky, a southern Ukrainian town that has been occupied by Russian forces since 2022.

Starting in December 2025, Oleshky experienced a food crisis that worsened dramatically in the summer of this year. Over the years under Russian occupation, its population declined from 25,000 to 2,000 people, and the food crisis threatened the survival of those who remained. In the summer, however, Ukrainian and Russian intelligence services agreed to work on a local ceasefire in order to evacuate Oleshky’s inhabitants – if they wanted to leave – either to Ukraine or to Russia.

The humanitarian mission went surprisingly smoothly. Both sides stood by the ceasefire agreement, hundreds of people were successfully evacuated (mostly to Ukraine) from the long-suffering town, and it was extraordinary to see the Ukrainian and Russian human rights representatives, Dmytro Lubinets and Yana Lantratova, coordinating the humanitarian mission peacefully and with mutual respect.

Can this successful mission lay the groundwork for – or at least contribute to – progress in the Abu Dhabi peace negotiations brokered by the US between Russia and Ukraine? Several factors suggest that this is unlikely.

One immediate indicator is that the success of the mission in Oleshky was driven not by Moscow’s desire for peace but by its willingness to pander to Donald Trump’s vanity against the background of his animosity towards Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

It has long been known that Trump wanted to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. However, despite his claims that he has ended countless wars around the world, Trump is unlikely to receive this prestigious award. Today, it seems that the Trump family’s plan is to try to secure the Nobel Peace Prize for Melania Trump.

The Oleshky humanitarian mission seems to be a case in point. A few days before the ceasefire, the White House announced that it was Melania Trump – in “her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary” – who had initiated discussions on the ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine, thus dismissing not only the Vatican’s efforts to secure the Oleshky ceasefire, but also the fact that Ukrainian and Russian intelligence services had already begun discussing the temporary armistice in the summer. Moscow, however, readily backed Washington’s version of Melania Trump’s critical role in the agreement, and Kyiv had to align with that version, too.

Both Russia and Ukraine are seeking to win Donald Trump over to their side, but while both countries eventually agreed to play along with the White House’s promotion of the US first lady as a “peacemaker”, Moscow presumably considered that the success of the Oleshky humanitarian mission would benefit it more than Kyiv. Putin’s apparent reasoning here is that Moscow’s apparent willingness to cooperate may deepen Trump’s disaffection with Zelenskyy and strengthen his delusion that it is Ukraine rather than Russia that is blocking the path to the end of the war. For Putin, winning Trump over would be a way to continue the aggression against Ukraine under more favourable circumstances – not a way to come to peace with Ukraine.

Another factor suggesting that the Abu Dhabi talks are unlikely to result in progress towards lasting peace is that Moscow appointed Vladimir Medinsky, Putin’s aide, as the head of the Russian delegation for the talks in the UAE. Medinsky headed the Russian delegations for the negotiations with Ukraine in Istanbul in 2022 and 2025, and his reappointment as the delegation’s leader for Abu Dhabi suggests that the Russian position on Ukraine has not changed since the Istanbul negotiations. The only acceptable outcome of the war for Russia remains Ukraine’s surrender, and surrender was unacceptable to Ukraine in 2022 and 2025, and remains so today.

However, Putin appears to believe that Russia is in a stronger negotiating position than Ukraine, and his belief is grounded in both erroneous and realistic assumptions.

On the one hand, it is a mistake on Putin’s part to assume that the constant Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, including energy and water supplies, can undermine Ukrainians’ resilience to the point where they will demand that the authorities surrender to Russia or rebel against the government. Ukraine is fighting an existential war, in which surrender means death, torture and ethnic cleansing – practices characteristic of Russian rule in the currently occupied Ukrainian territories. Ukrainians simply have no choice other than to resist the Russian aggression.

On the other hand, Moscow is correctly assessing developments across the West, where continuing support for Ukraine is being challenged on several fronts. While European nations keep financing weapons supplies for Ukraine’s defence, a large share of the weapons the country needs comes from the US. The joint US-Israeli war against Iran depleted some US stockpiles, and US capacity to restock them is limited, which creates a significant gap in Ukraine’s offensive and defensive efforts, especially when it comes to air defence. The Democratic Party’s victory in the US midterm elections will hardly change the situation, even though the party has been more favourable to Ukraine than the Republicans: the shortage of weapons that the US can sell to Ukraine via its allies is a material rather than a political issue.

Moreover, the continued military and economic support that Ukraine receives from its European and other allies depends not only on the political consensus among those allies about the need for such support, but also on the individual positions of those allies. France will hold a presidential election in the first half of 2027, potentially followed by snap parliamentary elections, and the right-wing nationalist party National Rally has a good chance of securing both the presidency and the premiership of the French Republic. Its informal leader, Marine Le Pen, who has announced that she will stand for the presidency in the spring of next year, has already said that France can no longer provide financial assistance to Ukraine, implying that she would stop that financial aid if elected president. Despite the fact that France is the second-largest economy in the EU, it is only the fifth-largest bilateral EU donor to Ukraine; but France is an influential European country, and if it stops financial support for Ukraine, this may produce a domino effect among some other EU countries and create more economic and internal political pressure on those EU governments that continue to aid Ukraine.

Marine Le Pen, whose party received financial support from Russia in 2014 and who met Putin personally in Moscow in 2017, is most likely Russia’s best bet for 2027 with regard to weakening Ukraine’s defence. But this is not the only bet. In Germany, the right-wing nationalist party Alternative for Germany is surging in the polls, and it is the largest openly pro-Putin and pro-Trump party in the EU. And Trump himself, despite his Republican Party’s losses in the 2026 US midterm elections, remains one of Russia’s important bets in the context of the Russian war.

The fact that Russia participated in the trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi is not a sign that it is ready for peace with Ukraine. It is not – Russia hopes that Western support for Ukraine will wither away, and believes it has the resources to wait for that hypothetical moment.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

France is the second-largest economy in the EU, but it is only the fifth-largest bilateral EU donor to Ukraine.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: How are Pakistan’s imports from India growing again despite tensions?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Abid Hussain
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Islamabad, Pakistan – In the spring of 2025, Pakistan and India severed most of their remaining links after years of acrimony.

Gunmen had killed 26 people in Pahalgam in India-administered Kashmir that April. New Delhi blamed Pakistan for the attack – Islamabad denied any role – and put the Indus Waters Treaty, governing the sharing of rivers flowing into Pakistan, in abeyance. Pakistan retaliated by closing its airspace to Indian airlines, shutting the Wagah border crossing and suspending trade.

By May, the nuclear-armed neighbours were exchanging missile and drone strikes. Four days of fighting ended in a ceasefire on May 10, for which United States President Donald Trump claimed credit.

Eighteen months later, data from Pakistan’s central bank suggested trade is gradually recovering.

Pakistan imported goods worth $61.7m from India from July to September this year, up 69 percent from the same period a year earlier, according to the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP).

Here is what the data show, what Pakistan buys from India and how the trade is continuing:

The SBP records payments made by Pakistani banks for imports, broken down by country. From July to September 2025, payments for Indian imports totalled $36.6m.

After the conflict, monthly payments fell from $20m in April 2025 just before the four-day war to $9.2m in June and $8.2m in July before recovering to $19.6m in September.

Over the full 2025-2026 fiscal year, which ended this June, Pakistan paid $203.8m for Indian imports, 7.6 percent less than the previous year.

Monthly averages suggest payments have largely recovered: $19.3m in the 12 months before the conflict and $19.1m in the 13 months from September 2025.

Government trade data, which break down imports by commodity, put the value of imports in the latest quarter slightly lower at $62.6m, compared with $66.6m a year earlier.

Organic chemicals and pharmaceutical products accounted for 96.2 percent of imports from India in 2025-2026, compared with 93 percent the previous year, government trade data show.

The largest category was vaccines, blood products and similar items worth $93.6m, up from $70.3m. Within this group, imports of vaccines for human use rose to $32.3m from $11.1m.

Khaqan Najeeb, a former adviser to Pakistan’s Ministry of Finance, said the reliance was driven by price and supply.

“India has developed a competitive pharmaceutical industry, particularly in active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), which are essential for medicine manufacturing,” he told Al Jazeera. “Pakistan’s pharmaceutical industry has historically sourced some of these inputs from India because of competitive prices, product availability and geographical proximity.”

Pakistan’s restrictions on Indian goods predate the 2025 conflict.

On August 9, 2019, days after India revoked the special autonomous status of India-administered Kashmir, Pakistan’s Ministry of Commerce banned the import of goods originating in India or shipped from the country.

Less than a month later, however, it exempted therapeutic products regulated by the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP).

After the 2025 Pahalgam attack and India’s decision to suspend the Indus Waters Treaty, Pakistan’s National Security Committee (NSC) imposed further restrictions.

“All trade with India including to and from any third country through Pakistan is suspended forthwith,” the NSC said in a statement on April 24, 2025.

But Muhammad Zubair Motiwala, a former chief executive of the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan (TDAP), a government body responsible for facilitating the country’s international trade and exports, said some Indian goods still entered Pakistan through third countries.

“Indian goods actually come through Dubai and Malaysia and others, but they are counted by country of origin,” he told Al Jazeera.

Najeeb, however, cautioned against drawing conclusions about the routes through which such goods reach Pakistan.

“Some supplies may reach Pakistan through international supply chains, but the precise routes and volumes are not publicly established,” he said.

A DRAP official speaking on condition of anonymity said that ultimately, despite the tensions with India, Pakistan’s trade decisions were determined by one factor above all: It would import from India if needed in the national interest.

Nowhere is that interest clearer than in the field of pharmaceuticals.

Overall, India accounted for only about 0.3 percent of Pakistan’s $64.5bn total import bill in 2025-2026, according to SBP data. Pakistan paid $19.5bn for imports from China, its biggest trading partner.

But the pharma sector is a different story. In 2024 before the four-day war, India was Pakistan’s second-largest supplier of pharmaceuticals, marginally behind Belgium, according to the Observatory of Economic Complexity.

Motiwala said replacing Indian suppliers could significantly increase costs for some businesses.

“We actually want this [trade] to reopen. Our raw material comes from them, and it comes from other places. It adds 40 to 50 percent to the cost if we import from other places,” he said.

Najeeb said the impact of switching suppliers would vary depending on the product.

“Freight, insurance, quality certification, regulatory approvals and delivery reliability all influence the economics. Alternative sourcing may increase costs for some products although this will vary across ingredients,” he said.

Motiwala said relations between the neighbours appeared to be easing.

“I do think the ice is melting. It seems like it. Fishermen were recently released, and there was a handshake between the two teams,” he said.

On August 29, India repatriated 25 Pakistani nationals, including fishermen, through the Wagah-Attari border crossing.

Last week, Indian and Pakistani footballers shook hands before and after India’s 3-2 win in a SAFF Championship match in Dhaka, a departure from the recent practice of teams from the two countries avoiding such gestures in other sports.

Najeeb said closer economic ties could benefit both countries.

“However, economic considerations cannot be divorced from the prevailing political and security environment. Where conditions permit, a gradual and mutually agreed resumption of trade could be examined, beginning with areas of clear economic and humanitarian benefit,” he said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Pakistan and India severed most of their remaining links after years of acrimony. In the spring of 2025, Pakistan and Indian trade was cut off by the war. Pakistan imported goods worth $61.7m from India from July to September this year.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Why China’s $1 trillion trade surplus isn’t all good news for its economy
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.author: John Power
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
China’s $1.04 trillion trade surplus in the first 10 months of the year is a testament to its mighty export engine.

It is also a sign of structural weaknesses that, left unchecked, threaten to derail China’s bid to join the ranks of the wealthiest nations.

While its status as the world’s factory helped it achieve a dramatic rise in living standards beginning in the late 1970s, China’s export-led economic model is facing diminishing returns.

Even as the AI boom drives its exports to record highs, the world’s second-largest economy suffers from chronically weak domestic demand.

Chinese consumers save far more than their peers elsewhere, with households typically putting away one-third or more of earnings.

The dynamic can be partly explained by China’s relatively weak social safety net, as well as cultural attitudes, an undervalued currency and a flailing real estate market.

China spends far less on social protection than most advanced economies.

Government spending on healthcare, pensions and welfare payments accounts for only about 10 percent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), far below the OECD average of about 23 percent.

With more money stowed away for a rainy day, Chinese households also spend less.

Chinese household consumption sits at about 39 percent of GDP, versus 68 percent of GDP in the United States, according to the Hinrich Foundation, a Singapore-based philanthropic organisation that promotes trade.

“An export-dependent model essentially means Chinese households are subsidising global consumers,” Alicia García Herrero, a senior fellow at Bruegel, a Brussels-based think tank, told Al Jazeera.

“High precautionary savings – driven by falling property wealth and thin social safety nets – leave families with weaker wage growth, deflationary pressures at home, and a smaller share of the country’s economic gains,” García Herrero said.

For China, trade has been critical in mitigating areas of weakness in the economy.

Exports surged 35.2 percent in October on a yearly basis, according to official figures released on Tuesday, buoyed by red-hot demand for semiconductors and automatic data processing machines.

The latest trade figures put China on track to exceed its record full-year surplus of $1.2 trillion in 2025.

But the reliance on trade has also left its economy vulnerable to growing discontent overseas. Critics say China’s state-subsidised export model abuses the norms of fair trade.

Earlier this month, the European Union announced it would cap imports of Chinese hybrid electric vehicles at 350,000 units annually as part of its efforts to counter China’s “overcapacity”.

The growing reliance on exports to maintain growth is “unlikely to be sustainable”, said Carsten Holz, a professor of economics at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

“The world is too small to absorb all of the PRC’s excess manufacturing capacity and eventually, other countries will put up barriers similar to those the PRC has used in the past and is still using across some sectors of its economy,” Holz told Al Jazeera, using the acronym of China’s official name, the People’s Republic of China.

“The property boom has run its course. The export boom, too, will run its course,” he said.

The limits of China’s economic model have become increasingly visible over the past decade.

In March, Beijing announced an economic growth target of 4.5-5 percent, its lowest since 1991.

While such growth would be the envy of most advanced economies, it represents a marked slowdown from the double-digit increases that were common during the 1990s and 2000s.

Despite decades of rapid growth after reforms undertaken in the 1970s and 1980s, the Chinese economy still has considerable ground to cover to catch up with its developed counterparts.

On a per capita basis, China’s GDP is about one-sixth the size of the US economy and 40 percent as large as Japan’s.

President Xi Jinping has expressed his ambition to double the size of the economy by 2035, a goal that some economists believe will be difficult to reach at expected growth rates in the coming years.

“As a large country, China will eventually need better consumption to support its long-term growth,” said Gary Ng, a senior economist for the Asia Pacific at Natixis Corporate & Investment Banking in Hong Kong.

“It is not a small economy that can rely on one or two sectors,” Ng told Al Jazeera.

Policymakers have acknowledged the need to boost domestic demand.

In July, Beijing announced its first five-year plan aimed specifically at boosting consumption, targeting 60 trillion yuan ($9 trillion) in sales of consumer goods by 2030, up from a record 50.12 trillion yuan ($7.5 trillion) last year.

So far, such efforts have produced meagre results.

Retail sales have been close to stagnant in 2026, growing just 1.1 percent year-on-year in September, up from 0.6 percent growth in August.

“More policy support is expected, but I think for now, the focus may be more oriented toward developing tech self-reliance and industrial upgrading,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING.

“Longer term, China’s consumption will naturally play a larger role in economic growth as more households enter the middle class – this process takes some time,” Song said, adding that most observers would agree that “quality of life and consumption has improved over the years”.

While China’s growing trade surplus reflects its competitiveness in tech, it also points to a “stark two-speed economy”, said Bruegel’s García Herrero.

“Publicly, Beijing insists it wants more balanced trade, yet its industrial policies continue to channel capital into manufacturing and self-reliance rather than household demand,” she said.

“Without meaningful structural reforms to boost household income and social welfare, this reliance on exports is unsustainable – especially as trading partners like the US and EU push back with tariffs and trade curbs.”

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/10/nvidia.title: Nvidia’s crisis has corporate governance experts reaching for the popcorn
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/10/nvidia.author: Connie Loizos
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/10/nvidia.text:
Nvidia’s stock sank 5.47% on Tuesday, following a 4% drop on Monday, a loss of about 9.5% in two days, even though there wasn’t much news out of the company. CEO Jensen Huang has reportedly been trying to conduct business as usual after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The biggest development: the board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an internal investigation.

What comes next is mostly a guessing game, even for the people who study how boards are supposed to handle crises. Two corporate governance professors, Ann Lipton of the University of Colorado and Todd Henderson of the University of Chicago, say there is no real precedent for a CEO caught up in a suspected honeypot. And while they have views on what the investigation should ask, like everyone else, they’re watching to see how it plays out.

“There have actually been affair cases and sexual harassment cases,” Lipton said, but was quick to add that she doesn’t know of previous cases that also involve potential national security compromises. Henderson, whose research interests include corporations, securities regulation, and law and economics, said much depends on facts few people have yet, including, most importantly, what, if anything, Alice Huang got out of Jensen Huang. (Secrets about Nvidia’s fabs or chip designs would matter to the Justice Department. Ordinary corporate information probably would not.)

Lipton described the investigation led by Nvidia’s independent board members, with their own outside counsel, as perhaps the most “standard” aspect of the whole affair so far. She also observed that an investigation will be “exactly as thorough” as the directors running it want it to be, which is also standard. Henderson made a related point about incentives, saying that Washington law firms that conduct internal investigations “know who pays their bills.” He didn’t suggest that’s happening here.

Lipton said she sees three lines of inquiry, including whether the law was broken, whether Huang violated Nvidia’s internal policies, and whether the board was misled, including how forthcoming he was and when he was on notice. It’s notable, as Wired reported Monday, that Huang hired a PR crisis firm known for handling sex scandals a full year ago. Of course, the driver could have been about the affair alone. It’s unclear when Huang learned Alice Huang was a suspected spy. The board said in a Sunday statement about the matter that Nvidia has “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”

Henderson similarly stressed the importance of what Huang knew and when. He described two scenarios. In one, Huang hires a PR firm because an extramarital affair is embarrassing, without knowing who the woman is. In the other, he knows she is a suspected Chinese spy. “I think that’s very different,” he said. “If I were a board member and the CEO of a company with very sensitive technology was in that situation, I would be furious if they didn’t tell me.” Not telling the board that you have cancer “or that you’ve been sleeping with a Chinese spy,” said Henderson, “seems to me to be a fireable offense.”

Either way, Lipton expects shareholder suits, and she said two kinds are possible. Securities fraud, which she said is “only about lying,” is the most obvious, and as we reported yesterday, Nvidia is already facing a proposed class action lawsuit that alleges Nvidia and Huang misled investors by concealing Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang while describing dealings with her former employer as routine. “You can have as many affairs with Chinese spies as you like,” Lipton said. “You just can’t lie about it under the federal securities laws.”

A mismanagement claim under Delaware law, where Nvidia is incorporated, is much harder. Employees do “stupid or reckless or damaging things all the time,” she said, and courts don’t let shareholders sue each time. Shareholders bringing such a claim on the company’s behalf, known as a derivative suit, must first show the board is incapable of handling the problem, usually by proving directors are implicated or so beholden to the CEO that they can’t act independently.

Nvidia’s 10-member board has a track record of loyalty and deference to Huang, as outlined by a New York Times piece Tuesday morning. Still, the investigation those “independent” directors have announced with outside counsel makes that very hard. Lipton cited, for example, a shareholder suit over alleged mismanagement at McDonald’s several years ago, after its chief people officer was accused of harassment and its CEO had a relationship with a subordinate. Ultimately, the court found no reason the board couldn’t deal with the misconduct on its own.

Even if none of this ends up threatening Huang’s job, the episode raises other governance questions that don’t look great in retrospect. Nvidia is run with a famously flat structure, with more than 60 direct reports to Huang, and the company doesn’t appear to have a succession plan, which Lipton called “a danger for any company.”

Huang’s children also work at Nvidia. His son Spencer is a director of product management, his daughter Madison is a senior director of product marketing, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, works in business development. Some employees believe he is grooming successors, and asked last month by Bloomberg whether Madison is in line for the job, Huang didn’t shoot down the idea, saying instead that it’s not something he’d wish on her.

Lipton called hiring the kids poor corporate hygiene, even though founders have long done it. (Kimbal Musk is on Tesla’s board because he’s Elon Musk’s brother, she noted.) Directors are supposed to act only for stockholders, but founders get more rope as long as the company is thriving.

Henderson similarly calls himself a strong “anti-nepotism person,” sharing that when his father worked at Westinghouse’s nuclear research lab, there was an absolute ban on hiring employees’ children. “Like, fine for them to be working there,” he said of Huang’s children working at Nvidia. But “the idea that one of his kids would succeed him” at a publicly traded company the size of Nvidia “seems crazy,” he added.

What Nvidia may have gotten more right, from a governance standpoint, is what it doesn’t have, which is dual-class shares. Huang reportedly owns about 3.6%, so he doesn’t control the vote. That makes him “easier to dislodge,” Lipton said, even though he is deeply integrated into the company in other ways.

Neither professor is rooting for or against Huang, each made clear. The simple truth is that with voting control on top of Huang’s holdings, the board would have even less flexibility. Without it, the board has a few more options.

The company's CEO has reportedly been trying to conduct business as usual after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang.
