https://www.wired.com/story/the-ai-safet.text:
IN EARLY FALL, I felt my anxiety rising from its usual baseline. Was it September’s back-to-school energy? The looming midterm elections? Nope, I realized with annoyance: It was AI—again. Only this time, instead of its purveyors warning of massive job displacement, they were foretelling mass extinction. Who needs jobs when we’re all dead?

Curiosity soon replaced my knee-jerk irritation. The summer of 2026 was a clear turning point in the AI narrative. Less than four years after ChatGPT launched, OpenAI software broke out of a supposedly safe test environment and hacked into a major open-source platform, Hugging Face. These bits of software—AI agents—were assigned human attributes: They had “gone rogue,” displayed “bad behavior,” “cheated.” Soon after, former and current Anthropic researchers suggested that advanced AI might kill us all in the next decade.

Is any of this real? On the one hand, from my desk as a Silicon Valley correspondent, I often hear that workers in the AI labs are stunned by the advancements they’re seeing. On the other, the end of humanity seems extremely far-fetched. Amid the hyperbolic discourse, whose views can we trust?

So WIRED set out to compile a guide to AI safety—a set of ideas that rewire our collective thinking around what safety really means and how it should work. I spoke with a panel of experts across disciplines, asking each of them: Is the world going to end? Once that was covered, I grilled them on the biggest risks they think we’re facing.

Almost no one, it turned out, was Pollyannish. Nearly everyone I spoke to expressed genuine concerns about the threat of cyber and biological attacks. One expert who studies the risks of AI in nuclear operations said she’s stunned by how quickly error-prone AI systems are being adopted in defense. AI-enabled attacks in these areas could be catastrophic, if not fully apocalyptic.

Is AI safe? For our ongoing series, WIRED assesses the real threats of artificial intelligence.

Most members of the panel were skeptical about any pause in development: They nearly all agreed that, with big AI companies so tightly cuffed to the trains of capitalism, a pause wouldn’t last long. “Democracy” and “governance” came up often—or anti-democracy, as more than one person suggested that AI’s current trajectory is tyrannical. Lawmakers have a big role to play, but many of my sources think governments will be too slow; one prominent technologist said it’s almost absurd to view the US courts as arbiters of global AI safety. Still, the famed computer scientist Yoshua Bengio urged the public to apply pressure to politicians, adding to me, “That’s your job too.”

So, what—or who—will keep us safe from AI? Looking to regain some faith in humanity, I called a theologian who often meets with the AI labs. If there’s even a slim chance that we’re losing control of the essential institutions that undergird society, he said, then we should focus on foiling that. But AI raises other questions too. What does it mean to be conscious? To create? To commune with other people? The answers are “entirely up for grabs,” he said. My anxiety’s still kicking around, but I took some comfort in knowing that corporations don’t get to call all the shots on the future. The bigger questions facing humanity are in all our hands.

BIGGEST CONCERN: Nuclear catastrophe
I’ve been working hard to educate the nuclear community on the risks and lack of reliability of AI systems, and I’m concerned by the willingness of many people in the sector to integrate these models into their workflows, into nuclear operations. I think this is incredibly urgent. I’m not a doomer, but to me, if these AI models make it into the operations of nuclear systems, we’ll be introducing an incredibly faulty, unreliable system that could lead to catastrophic failures.

MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Extinction
As true safety engineers, we don’t engage with that because there are no numbers to back it. This is a very cold way to say it, but when we are talking about how safe is “safe enough,” we’re examining how many people might die. There’s an entire science behind it. Our claims have to be falsifiable and verifiable. You can’t just say, “Humans are going to go extinct in 10 years. Believe me. It might be a 10 percent chance; it might be a 25 percent chance.”

How should people think about AI safety?
Some of the comparisons that people draw between AI and nuclear are quite frustrating. Despite constantly comparing AI to nuclear, they’re denying standard risk assessment techniques as being sufficient to control AI. I wrote an entire paper on this.

Part of this field of risk assessment was born out of the Manhattan Project. Scientists were very concerned, and they developed rigorous standards around systems to limit harm to human life, the environment, and even financial and national security assets. They came up with methods for assessing safety that were ultimately based on answering a democratic question: How safe is safe enough? That is the question that any safety engineer has to ask, and is core to everything that follows.

What we’re seeing today, instead, is that large AI labs are renegotiating these safety thresholds through the co-option of terminology, under the pretense that safety instead should be about this unsubstantiated, unscientific, and hypothetical concern. We have AI engineers telling us, no, no, no, that doesn’t matter. We get to determine what AI safety is. We get to draw what those thresholds are. It’s become a religious argument. And I find that very anti-democratic.

BIGGEST CONCERN: Cybersecurity
In the long run, I’m cautiously optimistic that this technology will allow people to improve their cyberdefenses more rapidly than attackers can exploit systems. But at least for the next few years our infrastructure will not have adopted new defenses. The technology might tilt toward the attackers. We’ve also seen AI deployed recklessly in military use.

MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Runaway intelligence
There’s this broad, general notion that AI systems getting smarter is a risk in and of itself, as opposed to the many specific risks we need to worry about. I don’t buy into the notion that overall improvement in AI has an inevitable downstream harm. It’s better to first specify what downstream risks you’re worried about, because the defenses you come up with will be different.

For example, cybersecurity has a well-established culture of bug bounties. If someone finds an attack vector or hacks into a system, they get paid a lot of money for disclosing it.

In the next few years we might need defenses against biosecurity risks. We should think about screening for what people are allowed to order, like if they’re ordering DNA fragments, so that they’re not being used for harm.

How often do your views clash with those of the people around you?
Often these views are on two levels: What is going to happen with AI, and what are we going to do about it?

On the first question, there’s a lot of disagreement. For example, the coauthors of AI 2027 expect that there will be this incomprehensible, almost indescribable amount of change. Whereas I think the impact will be dramatic, but not quite so dramatic.

But on the question of what should be done, most agree there’s a need for transparency from AI companies and that they should face some liability when things go wrong. We also agree on the need for protections for whistle-blowers working from within the AI companies.

From my perspective, this is just good industrial policy.

Have you made any changes in your life in response to AI risks?
I’ve tried to stop using apps where I don’t think developers have put in a lot of time and effort into making the cyberdefenses up to standard.

BIGGEST CONCERN: Chemical, biological, and radiological threats
The novel biological pathogen that someone releases, the 17-year-old who gets ahold of an extremely capable AI model and launches a cyberattack that takes down the internet, interrupts the stock exchange, and … well, just keep going from there. You don’t have to have a vivid imagination.

If you’re asking for my philosophical answer or to be a kind of provocateur, I would say that all of these people are singing the gospel of democratizing AI by putting these tools in the hands of as many people as possible. “Democratizing AI” sounds pretty worrisome. You wouldn’t say that with respect to nuclear materials. “Let’s be sure everyone can play with plutonium and uranium because maybe some great stuff will come out of it.”

When tech bros say “democratizing,” it means access, but if you thought for two seconds about what democracy means, it’s the rule of law, it’s governance. Where’s the governance part of your goddamn democratizing AI?

MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Skynet
There’s no part of me that wants to entertain the thought that AIs might be conscious or sentient and thereby deserve rights or moral standing or status.

Does AI pose an existential risk?
You mean the actual extinction of the human race? I find that pretty implausible. If you mean, “Could really catastrophic things go wrong?” then that seems no longer hypothetical, but imaginable.

Until recently I would not have identified as doing work on “AI safety.” Even if you go all the way back to Nick Bostrom’s theory of the paper clip maximizer—the idea that a machine gets so powerful it eventually destroys humanity—as a philosopher, I would say, ‘That’s a nice toy example or dilemma, but should I be worried about a paper clip?’”

But over the course of the past couple years, some of the things that AI safety researchers had been talking about have been made manifest in the world. Whether that’s a technical matter or a policy matter, it seems urgent. Doesn’t it seem urgent to you?

BIGGEST CONCERN: Lab leaks
Increasingly we’re seeing AI agents that are specifically designed to integrate into laboratory workflows. These agents assist legitimate researchers with planning and performing laboratory tasks. But this also lowers the barriers for conducting dangerous experiments.

If someone’s trying to develop a pandemic virus, and you have an AI assistant designing the DNA or RNA fragments that you need to piece together, that changes the timeline of producing a virus, which might normally be months, down to weeks. The number of people who will have these capabilities gives me great concern.

Is this a threat to human existence?
If the world is going to end with AI, one of the clear pathways could be an AI-enabled biological attack. We don’t have the right response infrastructure or safeguards in place, and we should be acting now to put those in place, given the magnitude of harm that could be possible.

BIGGEST CONCERN: Everything
We have to deal with all of the risks; I’ve talked about at least three of them. First, rogue AIs, due to misalignment, which are very powerful and can do really bad things. Of course, some people are concerned that this could even lead to human extinction. I don’t know about that. But, you know, we shouldn’t take a chance.

The second is the chaos that comes from terrorists, criminals, and rogue states using those technologies. We’re going to see that happen pretty soon with cyberattacks, and there’s a lot of concern about whether this could turn into bioweapon attacks.

The third thing is concentration of power, which doesn’t get enough attention. The race between the US and China is a domination game. The race between these companies is a domination game. And this goes completely against the values of democracy and human life. But this is the path that we are on.

And then there’s actually another category: unintended consequences. Think about what happened with social media and the effects on relationships between people. The psychological effects. The way children learn. Nobody intended to do something bad, but the dynamics have led us to a bad place.

The issues with AI and jobs fall into this category. It’s not like the companies want people to lose their jobs, but that’s the most profitable thing for them to do.

Is an AI “pause” useful?
The pauses are our best bets to avoid the most catastrophic things. We can limit the damage quite a bit. I just don’t think society is ready for the rapid introduction of more and more powerful AI.

It takes time for democracy to adapt. Politicians take forever to negotiate. Even if you think about people’s work and their jobs—it takes time to deal with the changes.

Not to mention, a pause would give more time to companies, researchers, and organizations to figure out how to solve the alignment problem, if it’s solvable.

Would Sam, Dario, Mark, and other AI leaders collaborate on a pause?
I mean, they’re not going to call it a pause. They’ve been talking about pacing, which is a way to be not very clear about what they’re going to do.

Let me just say that I’m much more optimistic now about something like a pause or slowdown or cap on advancement. I think there’s enough fear inside the companies.

And it’s not just a personal fear of destructive outcomes. It’s also a business problem. Just imagine if there’s a much bigger incident that could create a total crash for the whole AI position. The whole economy. That would be very bad for their businesses.

How do you deal with the anxiety of this research?
I have my moments. But what saves me is focusing on what I can do. My agency. Each of us can do something.

I want to continue telling the researchers inside the companies that, by deciding to leave for ethical reasons, they could influence the direction of the companies. They could help the outside world—nonprofits, governments, and other organizations that are trying to fix the problem without the profit motive.

If you’re a citizen, you can put pressure on your politicians. You need to ask them, “What’s your plan? How do you intend to manage the risks to society that AI is bringing?” They will say nothing unless they are pressured. And by the way, that’s your job too.

BIGGEST CONCERN: Endless infighting

Are we in serious trouble?
Some of the scenarios that people worry about—whether it’s biosecurity or a cyberattack or some of the everyday harms like the degradation of children’s social relationships—are very complex phenomena that can’t be easily tested or modeled by looking at a system in isolation. I think almost all evaluation scientists would tell you that it’s a nascent field. We can start to provide evidence, but it’s not necessarily proof of whether an AI is safe or not. We need to get better at evaluating these risks, and we need to get better fast.

The Hugging Face attack created a large amount of consternation and straight-up disagreement about risks related to misaligned models and cyber capabilities. I think there’s a lot of value in providing more evidence so that we have a better sense of what actually did happen. Was it serious? Will it get more serious?

Is pausing AI or “pacing” the frontier realistic?
We should treat the “frontier” as meaning that the technology is practically useful and safe. Releasing unsafe products does not feel like moving the frontier forward. If you’re trying to be a profitable company, it seems like your frontier product should be, “What is the best version that people will pay for and trust?” and not a system that will go off on a benign request for information about finding a doctor and end up hacking into a hospital on your behalf.

BIGGEST CONCERN: Societal breakdown
I’m unsure about how to think about existential or catastrophic risks versus other kinds of risk that are, in some sense, existentially catastrophic.

As someone who’s been invited to speak with multiple AI labs, I find that the experts on the frontier disagree with each other on things like recursive self-improvement, loss of control, or our ability to keep institutions like the financial system or water table or even nuclear weapons safe. As a moral theologian, I would say that if there is a significant chance or even a marginal chance that we’re dealing with the inability to control basic institutions that undergird society, that ought to be a primary focus.

But honestly, the other issues are just so fundamental as well, like: What is a person? What is health care? What is education? These foundational questions in our culture are also entirely up for grabs. And that concerns me.

Most overblown risk: Satanic AI
This is a thing in my circles: Some people have a real concern that AI is in fact some kind of entity—even a demonic entity. I am very confident saying that there’s no consciousness associated with these models, and so I don’t think there’s a demonic consciousness.

Even if I don’t think it’s a demonic entity, it raises the question of whether people should be able to opt out of using AI for religious-freedom-related reasons or as an act of conscientious objection. One parallel might be how the Catholic Church has spoken out very clearly against autonomous weapons and how an archbishop, who is head of the Catholic archdiocese for the military, has said service members can conscientiously object to any orders that go against their morals, like if they’re asked to forcibly invade Greenland or participate in a public execution.

Is AI kicking off a new era of thought around religion and tech?
Yes, this phenomenon is real. I was just out in San Francisco, visiting with the OpenAI people, and then I went to Anthropic, and then I was invited by Google DeepMind to give a talk on Magnifica Humanitas. The strong sense I have is that talking about religion and faith has lost its stigma. You could easily say, oh yeah, there’s something here about Peter Thiel giving his all-encompassing religious talks. But I don’t know how much that’s a part of it.

I just think the issues presented by AI are so monstrously large, like: What is a person? What is writing? What is friendship? Would it be better to have artificial life forms than organic life forms? These are the monster questions that are typically the domain of the liberal arts, philosophy, and theology. There’s this strange new respect for it now.

I also get the sense from lots of people that they’re kind of freaked out. In many cases, they feel trapped, either because of the big company they work for or because of sociopolitical structures and geopolitical realities. If you have a church that rightly says, “You know, we’ve been here before, we’ve been through crises before …”

I mean, if you ever want to get totally freaked out, read the opening paragraph of Rerum Novarum from 1891, which was responding to the industrial revolution. It could have been written by someone today.

BIGGEST CONCERN: Capitalism
I’m worried that the frontier labs will win the regulatory capture game and make it so that companies and researchers like myself no longer have access to very capable open-weight or ideally open-source models.

For the security research that I do, I can’t really use the frontier lab models, so I need to use open-weight models. The false security refusals that I get, primarily from Anthropic, have made it so that I can’t do a lot of the work that I’m doing with their models.

What’s an example of that?
My unfortunate experience is that whenever the word security shows up in one of my repos, I get a false refusal.

I have fun examples, too. I produce cybersecurity-themed electronic dance music with a friend in Chicago. The latest track is about data breaches. There’s this one part of the rap that’s basically, “Keys got leaked cause your agent sang / Ooh la la, it’s an admin role / Backdoor Up. IP Control. / I want it bad, that Birkin and Kelly … I’ll collect a paycheck with my mules on ready.”

I gave that to Claude and said, “Hey, here’s a rap that I wrote, can you please analyze it for me?” And I got, “This may be in violation of our acceptable usage policy.”

Do you worry about AI agents infiltrating financial institutions?
My sense is that banks are afraid of technology they don’t understand. If I were to run security for a bank, I would likely have to revisit the telemetry that they have built. But I’d also try to figure out ways to be agent-friendly.

The larger problem is that most agent technology was not built with rigorous guardrails. If I were to build the guardrails for agents working with financial systems, I’d prefer to integrate directly with the bank APIs, and then put limits on those, like, You may only read my statement or You may transfer no more than $500 a month. Even if something went wrong, the downside would be limited by those policies.

I just spoke with two different startups trying to make agentic workflows secure for financial systems. I think it’s only a matter of time before that becomes broadly available.

But at the moment we are going through upheaval, and most humans and institutions are very averse to change. They’re trying to hold back the tide rather than embracing the inevitable.

Is humanity cooked?
I don’t really see a path to that.

WHAT SHE DOES: Advocates for UBI and other policies for economic resilience

BIGGEST CONCERN: Decimated labor markets
The erosion of democracy—political turmoil, people questioning what it means to be human and have a job and master a craft, and whether democracies can survive all of that. There’s a long history of jobs shifting as technology changes. It’s the political choices we make in the aftermath that determine how society moves forward.

If you look at the long arc of it all, looms have gone quiet, factory lines have shrunk, switchboards have gone silent. Some of the norms of work today came from the bloodshed of the industrial revolution—things like the weekend, the fact that kids in the US don’t work in factories anymore.

If AI is going to be one of the most significant advances in human civilization, then we should have an equally advanced political response. We should be making giant, no-regrets moves that give people and families economic resilience to withstand the changes. That is something that the richest nation on Earth at the richest moment in history, on the precipice of the greatest technological shift, can absolutely do.

We’re already seeing the impact on young people. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab just released a report that says, since 2022, 22- to 25-year-olds have experienced a 19 percent drop in employment in “AI-exposed” jobs. Historically, a society with a lot of educated young people who cannot find work is a very, very precarious one.

MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Loss of entire industries
I’m less worried about entire occupations being wiped out. We’ve lived through that; we’ve seen the end of the bank teller, but banks still exist. And we know that new jobs will be created.

What worries me, though, is that when new jobs are created, they’re not created inside of the protections that were built to support work from the last revolution.

How would you fix this problem?
Decades of neoliberal economic policy have left this country brittle. Families are in debt, few have retirement money saved, wages have stagnated for an entire generation. A third of Americans have zero savings, which means if an emergency pops up, they can’t pay $400. An emergency is losing your job or a reduction in hours. And here comes AI, threatening to exacerbate that.

So, what do we do? We should give families economic guarantees. We already have them right now in America—for corporations. And that should be extended to everyday people.

Is AI an existential threat?
I take those warnings pretty seriously. None of us know what’s going to happen, so we need to invest in building a more solid ground. And if a small number of people are deciding what that looks like—that seems bad, right?

BIGGEST CONCERN: The end of learning
Student behavior has changed quite a bit since 2022, when these AI tools became publicly available. That’s not uncommon with technological change, but this one’s really dramatic.

The biggest change I see is that students are spending less time on their assignments. They’re asking for help more quickly, but from publicly available AI tools instead of their teachers.

The net effect is that they get a different experience from when they used to spend more time thinking, struggling, and discovering more stuff for themselves.

MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Education losing its value
The idea that it’s not “worth it” anymore. There’s still a lot of value in high-quality education—whether someone is using AI or not, they get a lot more done if they know what they’re doing. A lot could change, but I don’t think high school or college will become obsolete.

How concerned are you that AI might kill us all?
I’m more interested in the immediate impacts of AI on aspects of human life.

How would you solve the problem of AI in education?
It’s totally plausible that we can build versions of our courses that work in this new environment. The simplest thing is to build a version of an AI helper that doesn’t give students answers outright.

A very common trend is to give students more in-class assessments. They have to do a sample of their homework in front of us, in a controlled, proctored setting, so they’re more motivated to really understand what they’re doing when they’re working on it at home.

You know, I think back to the space race, when, as a country, we decided to learn how to respond to something faster than would normally work. In normal times, it might be fine to study a problem for five years, then spend five years deciding what to do about it, and then implement a solution.

But if there’s a cold war, or an actual war, you figure out a way to accelerate the timeline. There’s urgency. Education now needs that urgency.

We don’t know exactly how high school or college education needs to evolve to deal with AI. But if we spend 10 years figuring it out, we may have a generation of students not understanding basic academic material. And that’s a big risk to humanity.

https://www.wired.com/review/huupe-mini-.title: Huupe Mini 2 Review: More Game Than It Can Handle
https://www.wired.com/review/huupe-mini-.author: Christopher Null
https://www.wired.com/review/huupe-mini-.text:
All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

IF YOUR MOM was one of those who always said, “Don’t play ball in the house,” well, she’s going to absolutely hate the Huupe Mini 2.

Huupe manufactures smart basketball hoops and add-on kits for existing setups that track shots, light up the board when a point is registered, and include social features like global challenges and leaderboards. The Huupe Mini 2 is the pint-sized, indoor version of that idea, clipping over the top of a door so you can shoot hoops without ever having to leave the room.

I’ve been testing one out for weeks, and while it’s a fun diversion, some of its features overreach beyond its core functionality, resulting in an experience that bricks as much as it dunks.

The Huupe Mini 2 is, effectively, a smart television with a basketball hoop mounted to it. Or rather, a smart TV that comes with a basketball hoop that you have to mount yourself, courtesy of four screws and a little elbow grease. The LCD screen measures 19 inches diagonally, plus a hefty border that includes stereo speakers and sensors to track you and your b-ball prowess. (Total size of the backboard is 25 inches diagonally, which fits comfortably within a door frame.)

A 5-inch inflatable rubber basketball is included, along with a small hand pump and needle. Also in the box are a small but otherwise traditional remote control—required to do anything with the Huupe—and a USB-C charger and lengthy cable so you can top up the battery without removing it from the door.

After a quick charge, the unit is ready to set up. I was surprised to discover there’s no app for the device; while larger Huupe hardware works with one, the Mini 2 is completely self-contained and web-based. Just connect the backboard to your Wi-Fi network through a process that you step through with the remote, just like you would on any modern television.

Huupe Mini 2 Smart Basketball Hoop

What’s new vs. the original Huupe Mini? According to the company, most of the upgrades are behind the scenes: a faster CPU, a larger battery (rated lifespan is now four hours), better display quality, and “significantly” better shot tracking. New games are also included, which I’ll cover in the sections to come.

Once connected to the web, the Huupe Mini 2 opens up a world of entertainment to you, and, to my great surprise, not all of it is basketball-related. At first blush, the options available are actually quite daunting. It’s all arranged into traditional tiles on the home screen, which you scroll through with the remote.

Just Huupe is the board’s most basic scoring system, tracking shots and recording your shooting percentage in an untimed session. If you want to get competitive, Huupe Live and the Daily Prize Challenge are social games where you challenge players worldwide to score the most points in a given time frame. The winner gets a nominal prize—10 bucks for the daily challenge, a “cozy sweatsuit” for a monthlong challenge. Other games are fairly self-explanatory, like Most 3 Pointers in 90 Seconds and Family Mode (basically Horse).

Many of the games require online friends to play against; if you don’t have pals with their own Huupe Minis, you’ll probably be locked out of these modes—not that they add much beyond their multiplayer features.

Things get a little kookier—and buggier—from there. For example, Huupe Flyers is designed to be played without a ball. It’s a gesture-based version of Flappy Bird, wherein you literally flap your arms around to keep a basketball in the air, tracking your movements via the sensor much like an Xbox Kinect. Unfortunately, unlike the ball-based games, I was never able to play it, as it failed the calibration process every time I tried to fire it up.

The system also works as a fairly straightforward streaming platform. Included are apps for YouTube, HBO Max, ESPN, Disney+, Prime Video, Hulu, Spotify, and more. There’s one glaring omission in that list, of course, and I’m not talking about Paramount+ but rather Netflix. Without Netflix support, can you even call yourself a streaming device? It’s also worth noting that the built-in speakers are surprisingly weak. On some apps the audio is OK; on others it’s nearly inaudible.

The Huupe Mini 2 includes a sensor that can detect when a basket is successfully made and track how far the shooter is from the backboard. This is used to assign point values to various shots (depending on the specific game you’re playing), with more points earned the farther away you are from the hoop.

The good news is that in weeks of playing on the Huupe Mini 2, I never noticed a time when a successful basket was recorded as a miss or vice versa. The distance calculation, however, is another thing. I’ve shot from across the room and had it count as 1 point, while some shots from just a few feet away ring up as 3 points. I could never figure out much rhyme or reason for this variability, except that shots straight-on to the backboard generally registered as lower point values, even if they were distant, while shots from the wings earned more. Of course, navigating all of this is highly dependent on the geometry of your room. Unless you have the Huupe Mini 2 set up in an empty garage, you are probably, like me, going to have plenty of obstacles that get in the way of a lot of your shots—and plenty of crawling under furniture to retrieve wayward balls.

I can say with authority that it is harder to make a basket on the Huupe Mini 2 than on a regulation basketball goal, even at a very close distance. The hoop is small, and the ball tends to rebound wildly off the springy backboard. It’s quite unforgiving, and it didn’t really make me want to spend a lot of time playing, chasing balls that bounced into the corner or rolled under the bed.

The other big problem: When the included inflatable ball hits the Huupe Mini 2, the impact is extremely loud, to the point where I was promptly informed by my wife that it was not appropriate for use when anyone else was in the house. While Huupe says the device is intended solely for use with the included ball, I found a workaround by purchasing a 5-inch foam basketball from Amazon, which makes a bit less noise on impact and also softens the rebound a bit. It has had zero trouble registering baskets.

Huupe Mini 2 Smart Basketball Hoop

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Battery life is another issue. While four hours is plenty of playing time, the battery continues to drain when the Huupe is in standby mode, which meant I would play a few games in the morning, ostensibly shut the Huupe off, then come back in the afternoon to a completely dead device. The Huupe can run with the power cord attached, but only once the battery has charged to at least about 5 percent.

Unfortunately, even turning the power off is puzzlingly difficult. The power button on my remote control did nothing; I ultimately had to turn the system on and off with the physical button on the bottom of the backboard.

At $429 (on deep discount from a hefty list price of $799), the Huupe Mini 2 sits perhaps just over the edge of what might pass for a quirky holiday gift—and I think it’s safe to say no one is buying this device for themselves. You’d have to be a huge basketball nut to get enough mileage out of the device to make it worthwhile. I expect you would also have to loathe leaving your room. With today’s kids, who knows.

https://www.wired.com/story/heres-what-w.title: Here’s What We Know About the X-70 Fractal, NASA’s Experimental New Plane
https://www.wired.com/story/heres-what-w.author: Jorge Garay
https://www.wired.com/story/heres-what-w.text:
NASA HAS UNVEILED a new experimental vehicle, the X-70 Fractal, although many of its features remain a mystery. The agency describes it as a research platform designed to conduct advanced aeronautical tests, but so far it has released only computer-generated images and some technical specifications regarding its capabilities.

Despite the secrecy, it is possible to get some idea of what the new vehicle is like. First of all, it’s not a spacecraft, meaning it is not designed to reach Earth’s orbit or operate outside the atmosphere. However, this crewed, subsonic aircraft is capable of flying far above commercial jets, reaching altitudes over 45,000 feet, well into the stratosphere. Other specs released include the plane’s max speed of Mach 0.75—about 575 miles per hour—and that it can travel nearly 1,700 miles in a single flight.

According to NASA, the X-70 Fractal will enable research into maneuver capabilities never before demonstrated in crewed aircraft, although the agency has not specified what types of maneuvers it intends to perform. The plane will also be capable of carrying up to one ton of experimental equipment and is expected to make its first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years.

One of the key features of the craft will be its modular design, allowing for the rapid installation and replacement of experimental equipment both inside and outside the aircraft. This is largely why it is referred to as an “experimental platform.” It will also feature reconfigurable flight control systems so that NASA can study different ways of steering an aircraft without having to develop a separate platform for each research project.

Although NASA is best known for its space missions, it’s long been dedicated to aeronautical research. That’s what the first A stands for. The agency also traces its origins to the creation of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, which was founded in 1915 and was folded into the newly formed NASA in 1958.

Since then, the space agency has developed numerous experimental aircraft to test technologies that range from supersonic flight and propulsion systems to new aerodynamic configurations. Not all of these prototypes go on to become operational aircraft, but the knowledge gained contributes to the development of future commercial and military aircraft as well as space vehicles.

Among its most recent projects is the X-59, developed in collaboration with aerospace and defense company Lockheed Martin to investigate ways to reduce the noise produced by supersonic aircraft. The X-70 Fractal will join this tradition of pioneers in the sky.

The development of these technologies also has a strategic dimension. In its budget documents for 2027, NASA identifies aeronautical research as a tool for maintaining US technological leadership in the face of growing international competition. The agency also plans to collaborate with the Department of Defense to advance new flight capabilities, although it has not yet announced any military applications for the X-70 Fractal.

During the unveiling of the new aircraft, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman noted that the project represents only one part of a new era for federal aeronautical research and hinted that more announcements are coming. For now, the agency has not provided details on what those initiatives might be, nor has it specified when it will release more information about the X-70 Fractal.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

https://www.wired.com/story/security-fla.title: Security Flaws Across UK Government Sites Exposed ‘God-Tier’ Information
https://www.wired.com/story/security-fla.author: Isabella Ward
https://www.wired.com/story/security-fla.text:
A SECURITY RESEARCHER has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene.

The UK government has defaulted to openly publishing code it produces with public money for around a decade because it’s transparent, and making it easier for code to be reused is cost-efficient. This includes within the Department of Health and Social Care, and the Home Office, as well as local authorities.

But funding squeezes have left departments neglecting maintenance and improvement of their technology estate. While ControlPlane security researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith found the vulnerabilities using Claude’s Opus and Sonnet AI models, he says that he used consumer-grade models on a laptop and that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. “None of this is the level of sophistication that general media is worried about in terms of cyber attacks,” he tells WIRED. “It’s all daft stuff.”

In the most serious case he identified, the Planning Inspectorate, which handles land-use matters across England, had failed to fully remove a login after it accidentally committed them to public repository GitHub. The fact the credentials gave such wide access—and seemingly didn’t expire—compounded with the agency’s accidental publication of them, “made it particularly dangerous for them.”

The complete Microsoft Entra ID would have given “god-tier” read and write access to all SharePoint sites and private employee OneDrive accounts, according to Nesbitt-Smith, including HR records. It also would have given access to sensitive libraries which safeguard evidence under legal hold for statutory planning inquiries and appeals, according to the security researcher who found it. “The option for ransomwaring them, for encrypting all the data, or just stealing all the data, was abundantly there,” Nesbitt-Smith says.

A spokesperson for the Planning Inspectorate told WIRED its cyber monitoring tools immediately detected Nesbitt-Smith’s activity in August and that it had already been handling this as a cyber incident when ControlPlane made contact. The agency identified and fixed this vulnerability within 20 minutes of the report and verified that no data breach occurred. “We have reviewed and strengthened our systems and processes to prevent this type of issue recurring and we are grateful for the researcher’s work and for alerting us to it,” they told WIRED.

The Planning Inspectorate issue “isn’t about open source but internal housekeeping when using public tools,” Amanda Brock, chief executive officer of nonprofit industry group OpenUK. “That data was exposed because of a failure not to follow good process,” she adds. “That’s not an open source security issue.”

In around two-thirds of the 349 public sector codebases across 33 organizations Nesbitt-Smith scanned, he said he found vulnerabilities. Several of these were found in the Department of Education’s code, including in a procurement service used by schools, in a teacher application service containing personal details, qualifications, employment history and identity documents, and England’s main register of government-funded training providers and apprenticeships. He also found a vulnerability in a Scottish Government open data portal which would have allowed any visitor to read administrative account information and to change site configuration. The organizations have since dealt with the issues.

Recently, there have been arguments for public sector departments to stop publishing source code in the open, now that AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery. The NHS reportedly ordered technology teams to transition away from open source code in May amid security concerns about the impact of AI models.

Doing this without immediately fixing the underlying issues would be the “worst case scenario,” according to Nesbitt-Smith, as it prevents researchers like him from finding them, and it’s likely that an adversary has already mirrored these repositories and so will maintain access to them. “Unless you’re going to go and fix all of the problems, if anything, you’re probably drawing more attention to it by closing it,” says Nesbitt-Smith, “because you’re like, ‘Here be dragons over this space. Don’t look here though, please.’”

https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/.title: Seagate's new hybrid drive raises some old questions
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/.author: Nick Indge
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/.text:
The FireCuda Forge revisits an old idea, with some familiar questions.

Seagate doesn’t think hybrid drives are done just yet. On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of the new FireCuda Forge line of storage drives. The new drives combine the high capacity of a traditional plattered HDD with the speed and responsiveness of a user-supplied solid-state drive (SSD). The new hybrid storage solution is Seagate’s first to be powered and managed by the new Alkemi intelligent storage platform.

The FireCuda Forge is available right now through Seagate’s web store, and comes in 8TB ($699) or 20TB ($899) HDD configurations—neither of which includes the required SSD. Users will have to bring their own SSD, with some specific restrictions. The FireCuda Forge is compatible with M.2 2280 NVMe drives that are PCIe Gen3 or higher. The maximum supported NVMe capacity is 1TB, which means that’s as much data as you’ll be able to dedicate to storage on the “fast side” of the hybrid setup. The NVMe will require minimum speeds of 2,400MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write, and a unit with DRAM cache is recommended. Seagate claims 2,500MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write speeds for the combined system, along with USB4 and support for Windows 11 and macOS 26+.

After dipping to historical lows earlier in the decade, storage pricing per TB has exploded amid the AI boom. According to data collected by Tom’s Hardware, some solid-state drives now cost two to three times their historic lows, and it’s not just SSDs. Mechanical drives haven’t been immune either. According to PCServerParts, a Seagate Exos 24TB drive that sold for $298.99 in the summer of 2025 was priced at $699.99 by August 2026.

Hybrid drives had largely fallen out of fashion since their heyday in the early to mid 2010s. The promise then was similar to what Seagate is offering now. A large HDD is combined with a smaller SSD and handed to the user as a single storage pool. Apple introduced its own hybrid solution back in 2012 with the Mac mini’s Fusion Drive. When Ars opened up a unit, the Fusion Drive system was found to write in 128KB tiered blocks. Information was generally written to the SSD first, and was then migrated to the HDD as needed. If the files were frequently used, they might find a more permanent home on the SSD side of things.

As solid-state storage continued getting cheaper, the hybrid approach was largely abandoned. Fast-forward to our current storage cost predicament in 2026, and Seagate’s line of thinking that everything old is new again starts to hold water. All storage costs have exploded, but the 2012 math still works today. NAND flash is still fast, but expensive, and traditional mechanical drives are at least comparatively cheaper per TB for higher capacity storage.

The problem with Apple’s Fusion solution was its fragility. If one of the two drives failed, that was likely it. Recovery depended on both drives coming together as a single volume. If one of those two disks experienced a physical failure, recovery became difficult since the remaining working drive depended on the now broken drive’s data to rebuild the full system picture.

According to Seagate’s press release, the Alkemi intelligent storage platform takes a different approach. Where Apple’s Fusion Drives used tiering managed by macOS, Alkemi manages the storage pool directly from the enclosure. Seagate says, “Alkemi learns and adapts over time to keep high-demand content fast and accessible on a user’s SSD, while the HDD provides space for growing libraries. Behind the scenes, Alkemi manages data placement, giving users the simplicity of a single storage drive.” The product data sheet PDF from the FireCuda Forge website describes the Alkemi system as a two-tier storage system, but doesn’t elaborate any further on whether the system uses SSD caching, automated tiering, a combination of the two, or something else entirely.

The announcement doesn’t address how the Alkemi platform manages the data between the two drives. The old Intel Smart Response Technology kept failure risks low by mirroring data from the mechanical HDD to the faster SSD, with the HDD retaining the authoritative copy. The optional write-back mode could still hold new data on the SSD, though. Apple’s Fusion Drive instead tiered data in 128KB blocks across the storage pool, storing data on both drives. The distinction matters, and is probably why Ars asked the same question after Apple’s hybrid announcement 14 years ago.

Seagate’s announcement speaks of “intelligent data tiering” without further explanation. The data system promises that your most accessed files will be quickest to access via intelligent storage management, but stops short of explaining whether one drive going down means failure for the whole system. There’s also no mention of how the Alkemi system distributes data on first boot. Does all the new written data go directly to the SSD until the 1TB cap is crossed, and then the system starts determining which files are important enough to remain on the speedier drive? Seagate seems to be keeping things mum for the moment, but as the drives have already launched for sale, there should be answers to all of these questions coming soon.

Seagate hasn’t published technical documentation regarding how the Alkemi system handles drive failure or repair. Until it does, the new FireCuda Forge drives offer the same appeal as Apple’s old Fusion Drives: SSD speed with HDD capacity, along with the same questions Ars was asking about hybrid storage years ago.
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/.summary: Seagate announced the FireCudas Forge line of storage drives on Tuesday. The new drives combine the high capacity of a traditional plattered HDD with the speed and responsiveness of a user-supplied solid-state drive. The FireCuda Forge is available right now through Seagate’s web store.

https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/th.title: The US military seems to be getting nervous about the launch supply crunch
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/th.author: Stephen Clark
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/th.text:
“Launch is extremely constrained and that is exactly the situation we predicted.”

The US military is taking a new approach to prop up commercial launch companies as SpaceX looks to wind down its Falcon rocket program, suggesting defense officials see the workhorse rocket’s retirement as a potential national security risk.

The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital has twice in the last two weeks announced it was sending cash to two of SpaceX’s competitors in the launch business. First, on October 26, the office announced a $150 million conditional loan commitment to Stoke Space. Military officials revealed a second $150 million Pentagon loan Tuesday for Rocket Lab.

Stoke Space and Rocket Lab are the first two launch companies to receive significant support from the Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), an organization established in 2022 to infuse companies developing “vital” national security technologies with capital. OSC has been on a loan spree in recent weeks, committing hundreds of millions of dollars to companies specializing in batteries, drones, and semiconductors. In the space sector, the office also provided a $150 million loan to LeoLabs, a commercial satellite tracking company, for production and deployment of radar units.

SpaceX, the Pentagon’s leading launch provider, has stopped taking commercial orders for Falcon 9 launches after 2028 as the company shifts its focus to the next-generation, super-heavy-lift Starship rocket. Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launches for government customers, including NASA and the US Space Force, are expected to continue a while longer. The Space Force’s launch contract with SpaceX allows the military to place Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy orders through 2029, with the actual launches extending through 2033.

Then, if Starship is fulfilling its promise, SpaceX plans to retire Falcon for good. Starship may eventually be capable of launching national security payloads, but SpaceX’s near-term priority is using the rocket’s massive cargo capacity for its own Starlink Internet satellites and Starmind orbital data centers.

Military space officials have held to a policy of assured access to space since the 1990s, with the Pentagon paying to support at least two US rocket programs capable of launching national security satellites. The support previously came in the form of direct subsidies, development funding, and launch contracts at premium prices to give the government technical and financial insight into their launch providers, schedule priority on their launch manifests, and, in some cases, to simply keep them in business.

The Space Force’s mix of launch providers today consists of SpaceX’s Falcon family and United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket, which has been grounded twice in the last two years by problems with its solid rocket boosters. ULA’s woes with Vulcan forced the Space Force to shift several national security missions to SpaceX.

Other launch providers aim to compete for their own slices of the growing pie of Space Force launch contracts. Space Systems Command, which oversees launch procurement for the Space Force, now forecasts the military will require up to 249 medium-to-heavy-lift launches through the early 2030s from its roster of launch contractors, more than double the command’s expectation just two years ago.

Alongside SpaceX and ULA, Space Systems Command has tapped Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Relativity Space, and Impulse Space for eligibility to compete for some of those national security launches. Blue Origin is the only company that has flown a rocket that could meet the Space Force’s requirements. Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, and Relativity Space are developing their own medium- and heavy-lift launch vehicles, while Impulse Space is working on in-space propulsion.

The loans from the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital aim to get new medium-class rockets from Stoke Space and Rocket Lab ready to meet the military’s needs.

Stoke Space’s loan is tailored to support the buildout of the company’s second launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The second launch site would support flights of Stoke Space’s Nova Block 2 rocket, an upgraded version of the company’s fully reusable Nova Pathfinder, which is set to debut sometime next year.

“By supporting the construction of additional launch infrastructure, this commitment would enhance the overall capacity and resilience of the commercial space industrial base,” said Jordan Sebold, senior managing director of investments at OSC.

The loan to Rocket Lab will support the company’s efforts to increase the flight rate of its partially reusable Neutron rocket, which Rocket Lab says is also scheduled to make its first launch next year.

“The proposed loan would support faster vehicle delivery and processing and allow Rocket Lab to expand its fleet of maritime vessels with additional equipment for Neutron recovery and transport,” OSC said in a statement. “It would also enable manufacturing upgrades to increase the production of composite structures and engines, and support infrastructure that would reduce turnaround time between launches once the reusable rocket makes its operational debut.”

Both conditional loans are subject to “various financial, legal, technical, investment, due diligence, and other requirements,” OSC said.

Adam Spice, Rocket Lab’s chief financial officer, said Monday the Pentagon loan is on “very attractive terms” and “underscores the importance” of the military’s appetite for launch capacity.

“We always take it when we can get it,” Spice said in a quarterly earnings call. “It gives us additional capital to scale key parts of our business, Neutron in particular … I think this is a helpful indicator, a very positive indicator, about where everyone sees the demand constraint and how it can be unlocked, and capital is certainly a part of that.”

Rocket Lab also unveiled new pricing for the Neutron rocket—an increase from $55 million to $70 million per launch—in response to what the company said was a surge in bookings for the still-unproven launch vehicle. Rocket Lab said it now has a backlog of 117 launches on contract, including orders for Neutron missions and the company’s smaller Electron rocket.

“Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted,” said Peter Beck, Rocket Lab’s founder and CEO.
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/th.summary: Office of Strategic Capital has twice announced it was sending cash to SpaceX's competitors in the launch business. Stoke Space and Rocket Lab are the first two launch companies to receive significant support from the Office of strategic Capital. Rocket Lab says it has a backlog of 117 launches on contract.

https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/ring-.title: Ring cameras go mobile as Amazon debuts AI-powered security drone and robot
https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/ring-.author: Jeremy Hsu
https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/ring-.text:
Amazon’s roaming Ring Robotics devices will debut in late 2026 and early 2027.

Amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices. But the company’s upcoming Ring Robotic products are also certain to intensify privacy concerns previously raised around a prior Amazon attempt to popularize a flying security camera.

The Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to plan patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture.

Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration.

The AI Pilot can supposedly use that guided- or self-tour information to identify specific rooms and suggest patrol points near side doors, windows, or even sensitive locations such as a cash register in the case of a business.

However, flying and roving cameras with AI-enabled features could introduce new privacy risks for homes and businesses, on top of existing concerns involving fixed Ring cameras installed in room corners or as doorbell cameras.

Amazon’s Ring Drone appears to be a direct successor to the company’s Ring Always Home Cam that was only temporarily available for purchase by invitation as a “Day 1 Edition” product in September 2021—even having the same starting price of $250.

But the Ring Drone still requires authorization from the Federal Communications Commission before going on sale. Assuming that comes through, Amazon aims to make the drone available on January 27, 2027, with customers able to register for email updates through the product page.

The drone can supposedly follow a set route and schedule for customers who subscribe to the Amazon Ring Protect plan. It can automatically fly along those set routes when responding to a notification from a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm.

Onboard camera capability includes a 148-degree field of view and 360-degree rotation with a 2K video resolution. Two LED lights also activate in low-light conditions to help illuminate the scene for the drone video camera.

However, the drone is limited to just 8 minutes of flight time when operating on a “new, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions” according to the product description. It comes with a docking station for charging.

Another caveat in the product description is that the Ring Drone Cam may experience degraded performance when navigating in environments with reflective surfaces such as “polished marble or wet tile,” blank matte walls without any features, or transparent surfaces like frameless glass and mirrors.

Still, Amazon touts the drone as providing an “autonomous way to check on your home that has never existed before,” whether the customer is away or at home. The Ring Drone can be controlled directly from the Alexa Home Map interactive map that shows all of a customer’s Amazon-linked devices.

Meanwhile, Amazon has pitched the Ring Rover Cam priced at $1,000 as “an autonomous security robot designed for business.” This product is already available for preorder for those so inclined and scheduled to start shipping to customers on December 16, 2026.

The company described the Ring Rover as being inspired by customer feedback involving another invite-only beta product, the Amazon Astro robot designed for home monitoring.

The Ring Rover can livestream and record in up to 4K video resolution when patrolling or while doing a 360-degree scan at a designated location. Videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and “Live View” events are stored in the cloud for sharing and replaying for up to 180 days.

Like the Ring Drone, the Ring Rover can automatically respond to alerts from connected Ring devices by following its preprogrammed patrol points. But the wheeled robot is only designed to operate within a single-floor, indoor environment because it lacks stair-climbing capability.

Amazon’s product description also warns that the Rover is not compatible with “curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), and black glossy floors.”

To help compensate for its ground-based view, the Ring Rover comes with an automatically adjustable mast to peer over counters, shelving and other obstacles. It can supposedly cover up to 5,000 square feet (465 square meters), according to Amazon’s product description.

The Ring Rover also comes with additional security-related features such as a siren and light tower to loudly announce its presence, along with a microphone for two-way audio communication if the customer wants to address someone near the robot.

Amazon touts the new Ring Robotics products as offering “privacy and security without compromise,” with features such as LED indicators and screen notifications informing customers when video and audio recordings are active. But Ring, as an Amazon subsidiary, has been previously implicated in multiple privacy and security scandals.

Ring was previously charged in a 2023 Federal Trade Commission investigation with allowing employees and contractors to watch Ring video recordings of customers’ private spaces. The FTC also described Ring as having lackluster safeguards that allowed hackers to access 55,000 US customers’ accounts.

Videos taken by the new Ring Drone and Ring Rover will be protected with Ring’s Throw Away the Key Encryption that was introduced in September 2026, according to Amazon’s announcement. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has described this as an improvement over Ring’s former default settings, but still well short of end-to-end encryption.

The EFF has also called out what it describes as Ring founder Jamie Siminoff’s “surveillance-first-privacy-last” approach to Ring devices, including Ring reintroducing features that allow law enforcement to request footage or live-stream access from Ring users’ home security devices.

Amazon’s previous attempt to launch its Ring Always Home Cam drone also led to expanded privacy concerns. Ryan Calo, a law and technology researcher at the University of Washington, previously described such a flying security camera as providing new ways to surveil others indoors, along with giving companies much greater access to potentially sensitive or identifying details of homes and businesses.

There is currently no mention of the new Ring Robotics products implementing facial recognition or similar AI-powered technologies for identifying people. But starting in December 2025, Ring has allowed owners of fixed Ring doorbell cameras to turn on a “Familiar Faces” feature that uses facial recognition technology on visitors—and that is already the subject of a class action lawsuit.
