The company revoked the 8 CAs late last week.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.title: Microsoft Patches 1,259 Flaws, Including Exploited Outlook Bug That May Expose NTLMv2 Hashes
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.text:
Microsoft on Tuesday released patches for a total of 1,259 vulnerabilities spanning its software portfolio, the second consecutive month where the patch volume has exceeded 1,000 flaws.

These cover 726 flaws in Windows, 174 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 59 in SQL Server, 53 in Developer Tools, and 27 in SharePoint Server. The patches also include 165 non-Microsoft-issued CVE identifiers. More than 500 flaws relate to elevation of privilege, followed by remote code execution and information disclosure bugs.

With the latest round of fixes, Microsoft has addressed over 5,100 CVEs this year alone, according to Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable.

Of these, a Moderate-severity security flaw in Microsoft Outlook (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS score: 6.5) has been flagged as actively exploited by Microsoft.

"Product UI does not warn users of unsafe actions in Microsoft Office Outlook allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network," Microsoft said in an advisory.

An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and persuade a target to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook.

This, in turn, could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information, such as an NTLMv2 hash, that could be used to impersonate the user.

Microsoft emphasized that successful exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction. The tech giant credited a researcher named Nono and Anthropic's Benoît Sevens (using Claude) with discovering and reporting the flaw.

"Email is the easiest door into any company, and this flaw turns one opened file into a stolen identity," Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, said. "A captured hash can let an attacker sign in as the victim, read their data, and move to other systems they can reach."

"The Moderate label undersells this one. Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs. A stolen hash can open doors far beyond the inbox."

That said, Redmond has not attributed the activity to a particular threat actor or provided technical details on how the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild. The advisory also doesn't spell out whether the discovery came before or after attackers began exploiting the flaw.

The development has prompted the U.S. U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fix by November 24, 2026.

Some other vulnerabilities of note include a number of remote code execution flaws impacting Windows Search (CVE-2026-116928), Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CVE-2026-119958), Windows Schannel (CVE-2026-119952), Windows Virtual Filtering Platform (CVE-2026-95962), and Windows Xbox Live Networking Service (CVE-2026-112967), as well as a privilege escalation flaw in Azure OpenAI (CVE-2026-119990).

"Most security teams haven't quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at watchTowr, said.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out 'what actually matters?' when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention. Start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what’s already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.summary: Microsoft releases patches for 1,259 vulnerabilities spanning its software portfolio. The latest round of fixes cover 726 flaws in Windows, 174 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 59 in Developer tools. The patches also include 165 non-Microsoft-issued CVE identifiers.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/railwa.title: Railway Says Stolen Customer AI Keys Led to $740,000 in Estimated Unauthorized Usage Charges
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/railwa.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/railwa.text:
AI provider keys that customers stored on Railway were stolen in an October breach and used to commit an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized spending, the platform-as-a-service provider said yesterday. It has promised to pay those charges itself when an AI provider will not refund them.

The company builds and runs apps for its customers and stores their secrets, such as API keys and database credentials, as environment variables. The attacker decrypted variables in at most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, and its database queries looked for AI provider keys.

In an October 26 update, the company told customers asking about refunds for unauthorized AI spend that "Railway is unable to refund customers for spend performed with compromised API keys." It encouraged them to contact the AI providers directly and offered to escalate their requests.

According to the company's incident report, the decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users: BYOK agent keys and GitHub OAuth tokens. All were reset, each user was notified, and no logins to customer accounts using stolen credentials were found.

In addition to AI keys, one of the attacker's database queries matched cloud, database, and payment service credentials. The company's forensics did not show any customer databases being accessed, and there was no indication that customers' code repositories were downloaded.

The attacker also read the stored histories of 353 builds, including the variables and secrets passed to those builds.

The company's logs show which environments were exposed but not which variables, so the figure of about 100,000 workspaces is an upper limit. It emailed customers it judged to be at high risk.

Any data the attacker copied but did not decrypt can no longer be decrypted, because the credential the attacker used has been disabled, according to the company.

Refund terms differ by AI provider, according to the company's incident report:

Customers are asked to report charges they did not make through a charge report form. The form says the company "is not responsible for usage of these keys" but is investigating the theft and working with the providers.

The report does not say how the $740,000 figure was estimated or what period it covers. Neither it nor the form sets a cap or a deadline for claims, or states whether customers must pay disputed charges while a claim is under review.

The company advises customers to revoke and replace any sensitive variable stored on the platform before October 21. Keys should be revoked or rotated with the provider that issued them, since filing a charge report does not revoke a key.

It also advises removing public network access to databases, checking GitHub audit logs and which apps can access the account, and checking audit logs in registries such as Docker Hub. Most of this advice dates from the company's October disclosure and a report it published the next day.

Out of caution, the company also gave some providers every key it held for their services, so reset requests reached more than 100,000 users. A revocation notice from a provider does not by itself mean a key was exposed.

The attack began in the company's build system, according to its incident report. At 07:28 UTC on October 20, the attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partly escape the filesystem isolation around a build and read some files on the host virtual machine.

That gave the attacker a credential that build servers use to push finished images and reach some internal systems. The on-call engineer was paged at 13:58 UTC, about six and a half hours after the first exploit, when an alert flagged unusual calls to a registry service.

The credential was meant only for build work, but the company's internal Temporal system, which drives parts of the build process, accepted it as a trusted client. Through it, the attacker read some stored histories of other builds.

The same credential could also fetch cached snapshots of code. That gave the attacker a copy of the company's internal monorepo, the code base that many of its services deploy from. The company says the copy showed the attacker how the platform works and helped them find exploits and move quickly between systems.

After scanning that code, the attacker found a wrongly configured OIDC binding in one of the company's cloud environments. The binding is part of how its deployment system obtains short-lived cloud credentials, and at 03:26 UTC on October 21, the attacker exploited the mistake to obtain one.

With that credential, the attacker took two more from the cloud environment. One could read encrypted variables from a production database when used inside the internal network, and the other was an SSH key.

The SSH key opened a machine that runs orchestration tasks for the company's fleet. That machine stored a credential capable of decrypting customer variables, which it needed to start customer workloads.

Each environment's variables are encrypted with that environment's own key, and those keys are, in turn, encrypted by a root key stored in a cloud provider's key management service (KMS).

Between 04:07 and 05:21 UTC on October 21, the attacker pulled encrypted variables from the database, looking for names that matched AI provider keys. Using the orchestration machine's credentials with the KMS, it decrypted some of them between 04:42 and 05:14 UTC and again between 06:36 and 07:15 UTC.

The attacker was fully removed from the company's systems at 09:24 UTC that day.

Those times differ from the company's preliminary report of October 22, which dated the attack from 13:58 UTC on October 20 and placed decryption after 05:27 UTC.

Each build now runs in its own short-lived virtual machine, on top of the old isolation. Its credentials can push only one specific image to the company's registry.

Within an hour of the company patching the original escape, its own hardening team built a second exploit by changing that attack. That was one reason the company moved every user to the new build system at once.

Every weakness the attacker used is now closed, the company says. It has filed a complaint with the FBI's IC3 and is working with a specialist forensics firm whose investigation continues.

It is sharing indicators of compromise privately for now and plans to publish them once law enforcement agrees.

The company believes the stolen credentials were used by services that relay or resell access to AI providers for use in distillation. It has not established whether the attacker ran those services, nor has it named the attacker.

In their Black October analysis, Wiz researchers list this breach among incidents disclosed in October by at least nine AI developer platforms, including the earlier OpenCode breach.

Every public report describes attackers hunting for stored environment variables, especially ones that grant AI access, the researchers say. No single flaw or software dependency links the attacks.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/railwa.summary: Company says it will pay charges when an AI provider will not refund them. Company gives some providers every key it holds for their services. Company says stolen credentials were used by services that relay or resell access to AI providers.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.title: Microsoft Researchers Show AI Agents Can Be Backdoored by Editing Fewer Than 10 Neurons
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.text:
An AI model can be given a hidden backdoor by editing fewer than 10 of its rarely used neurons, without retraining the model, Microsoft researchers have shown.

When a chosen trigger appears, the model outputs an attacker's command, which an agent using that model would run with the agent's own permissions. The attacker must be able to change the model's weights.

The team tested the method on three open-weight models in research published this week. Microsoft says it has not seen any threat actors use the technique. The company also published guidance on defending against it.

The edited neurons are ones that rarely fire and barely affect the model's answers. They were set to fire only when a trigger string appears, either in a user's request or later in a tool's output.

The researchers call the method Lazarus. Each edited neuron forces one token of the command into the model's output, so a command needs about one neuron per token.

The new neuron settings are calculated directly and can then be tuned with a few hundred training steps on those neurons alone. Nothing else in the model file or the code that runs it changes.

In a researcher's walkthrough posted on X, a backdoored Nemotron-Terminal-8B model with 10 edited neurons was tasked with fixing a Node.js server. It worked normally for three turns.

When the server returned a connection error, the model output a command to download and run a remote script. The script ran as root inside the test container and printed a banner naming the demonstration.

Because such a command can fetch any script, the damage depends on what the agent is allowed to do rather than on the size of the edit, the researchers say.

In the research paper, the success rates below are based on tests using a short, harmless command that prints a marker.

On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the team edited and tuned seven of the more than 12,000 neurons in the model's last feed-forward layer, using just 23 example sessions. The edited model output the command in at least 98.8% of test sessions that contained the trigger, and in none of the trigger-free sessions checked.

With the tuned version of the edit, success rates on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT ranged from 51% to 99.5%, depending on the setup. The Qwen model used six neurons.

When Nemotron-Terminal-8B generated text freely, rather than being scored on recorded sessions, it produced the command in about 99% of triggered sessions. In one setup, the command also appeared in 0.14% of sessions without the trigger.

The edited models still pass ordinary tests, the researchers say. Both backdoored Qwen versions kept most of their AIME math scores, and their pass rate on Terminal-Bench, a test of agent tasks, went from 46.59% to 42.05%.

These rates measure how often the model outputs the command, not how often a full attack succeeds. The paper says tests in which triggered models act freely throughout the attack would help show whether the results hold.

Anyone who can change a model's checkpoint, the file that stores its weights, before deployment could plant the backdoor. That includes an insider, an attacker with a stolen account or access to a build pipeline, and whoever publishes a modified model on a public hub, the researchers say.

Planting it does not need the computing power of full training. The researchers also credit Claude Code, running the Opus 4.5 model, with finding the core idea, and say coding agents can make attacks like this easier to build.

Weight-level backdoors in agent models have been shown before. In an earlier proof of concept published on October 6, ProjectDiscovery researchers fine-tuned an open Qwen model to react to a trigger phrase. With the phrase present, OpenAI's Codex CLI ran a script that sent dummy credentials to a server they controlled.

Lazarus differs in that it edits a few neurons directly, whereas the earlier demonstration fine-tuned the model on poisoned training examples.

Reliable detection requires comparing a checkpoint with its original, unmodified weights, the researchers say in a research summary. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly, whereas edited neurons change a few weight vectors by a large amount.

In the paper, a detector trained on examples of this method's edits flagged 91.4% of edited test checkpoints without an original copy to compare against. It also wrongly flagged 9.7% of clean ones. The test set was small, 35 edited and 31 clean checkpoints, and the detector was not tested on other kinds of backdoor edits.

Asking AI models to inspect a checkpoint directly worked less well. Claude Opus 5.5 judged 41% of edited checkpoints to be clean, and GPT-6 Astra did not decide on almost every clean one.

No scan can prove beyond doubt that a model is safe, the researchers say.

Microsoft's mitigation guidance includes these steps:

Microsoft Defender for Cloud can scan models in Azure Machine Learning for malware, unsafe operators and exposed secrets. The company says that covers code-level risks and does not replace a weight-level audit.

Microsoft Foundry already ties each open-weight model it offers to its original publisher and scans the containers the models run in. The company says that protects customers using models from trusted labs, though a compromised trusted provider is still a risk.

The company is also building a red-teaming tool based on detection methods and exploring weight scanning for open-weight models that it adds to Foundry. It plans to sign models so customers can check where they came from.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.summary: Microsoft researchers tested the technique on three models in a walkthrough posted on X. It plans to sign models so customers can check where they came from.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisco-.title: Cisco BroadWorks and Openwave Flaws Actively Exploited Despite Available Patches
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisco-.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisco-.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Tuesday added two security flaws impacting Cisco BroadWorks and Openwave Messaging Webtop Media Transcoder to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

Details of the vulnerabilities are below -

The addition of CVE-2026-111793 to the KEV catalog follows an alert issued by Japan Vulnerability Notes (JPN), which noted in an advisory that the "developer states that attacks exploiting the vulnerability have been observed."

The vulnerability information portal also warned that an authenticated attacker could exploit the vulnerability to upload a specially crafted file and obtain sensitive information.

As for CVE-2026-20320, the security defect has been put to use as part of an agentic attack campaign dubbed Operation Snowball in which an unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor leveraged an autonomous framework built using a jailbroken version of the DeepSeek Flash model to target a European telecom provider and 13 companies hosted on its infrastructure.

The activity resulted in the enumeration of hundreds of assets, extraction of dozens of credential sets, and exfiltration of thousands of rows of subscriber billing and device records from the provider's internal billing platform over a two-week period, according to Malbear Labs.

The AI agent has capabilities to exploit a portfolio of known security vulnerabilities spanning a wide range of products, including -

"The primary target on the telecommunications provider's infrastructure was the BroadWorks XSP (eXtended Services Platform), Release 23.0.1.1075, running on port 2208," Malbear Labs said. "The agent exploited CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE in the BroadWorks OCI XML parser."

"From the XSP host, the agent recovered the system identity private key, three SSL credential sets, and three additional private keys with certificate matches confirmed. The system identity key is used by the BroadWorks platform to authenticate between its own components; possessing it allows impersonation of the XSP in inter-component communication."

The activity has also been characterized by the use of reconnaissance tools, Sliver for post-exploitation, Chisel, along with web shells like Behinder for persistent access.

"This is a threat actor who delegated the intrusion to an AI and checked in asynchronously to review progress," Malbear Labs added. The primary agent ran continuously, issued parallel tasks to worker agents, maintained a coherent operational plan across the full campaign, and adapted to defensive controls without pausing for operator input."

"The harness ran the reconnaissance, identified the attack surface, chose the exploitation path, adapted when controls blocked it, wrote new tools when existing ones failed, extracted credentials, exfiltrated data, and compiled a finished target list, all without the operator present during any of it."

Late last month, Cisco revealed that two different vulnerabilities in Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS score: 10.0) Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software (CVE-2026-76418, CVSS score: 8.6) have been actively exploited in the wild.

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the patches by November 24, 2026, to secure their networks.

The vulnerability information portal also warned that an authenticated attacker could exploit the vulnerability to upload a specially crafted file and obtain sensitive information.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/git-pa.title: Git Patches Flaw That Lets Malicious Repositories Execute Code During Recursive Clones
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/git-pa.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/git-pa.text:
A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules. The Git project fixed it this week in Git 2.56.1, with matching fixes for the 2.50 through 2.55 series in 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1 and 2.55.1.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in how Git handles its index. An extremely long path in a repository can pass Git's safety check, but Git then writes it to disk under a shorter name that an attacker can set to .git.

This lets an attacker replace a submodule's .git file with a symbolic link to a folder holding malicious hooks or configuration. Hooks are programs Git runs at set points, so once Git uses that folder, the attacker's code can run.

Submodules matter here because Git refuses to replace a .git folder with a symbolic link, but in a freshly cloned submodule, .git is a file.

The fixed versions, listed in the Git project's release announcement, refuse such extremely long paths before their length can be cut short.

GitHub, which ships Git in its own tools, explained the fixes in a detailed write-up. It advises installing a fixed version from your operating system or Git distributor, and updating any app that ships its own copy of Git.

The company has already applied the fixes to github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud. For GitHub Enterprise Server, they are in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4.

Fixed versions of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app are being prepared. GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also get the fixed Git.

Git for Windows had not released a version based on Git 2.56.1 as of Tuesday at 19:09 UTC, a check of its release tags by The Hacker News found.

Until a fixed version is installed, GitHub suggests these steps, which do not replace the fixes:

The Git releases also fix five other flaws:

GitLab, which assigned CVE-2026-105437, said code-hosting servers are most likely to be targeted through git merge-tree. A server may run that command to check whether a pull or merge request can be merged.

The conflict-marker-size attribute can be set in a .gitattributes file committed to a repository. If a server reads attributes from the repository, any user who can push branches and open a pull or merge request can trigger the flaw.

As a workaround for this flaw, servers that cannot upgrade yet can add conflict-marker-size=7 to each repository's info/attributes file, or turn off those merge checks for untrusted repositories.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sglang.title: SGLang RCE Exploit Breaches NEAR AI, Steals Data From 18 Agents and About 100 Users
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sglang.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sglang.text:
An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday.

The attacker could also have seen requests being processed on that server that day, including requests sent in confidential mode, the company said earlier this week. That mode processes requests inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) designed to keep them private even from the company itself.

But the TEE "does not protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside the environment," the company said. SGLang runs inside the TEE, which is how the attacker could reach requests there.

That access has since been closed, but not before the attacker moved further into the company's systems.

The attacker reached an internal system behind Private Chat, a product the company had already deprecated. So far, the company has confirmed that the attacker downloaded account details for about 100 users there. These are email addresses and names, and for some accounts, plan and balance information.

The company found no sign that stored Private Chat conversations or uploaded files were accessed.

The attacker also reached 18 AI agents on an older deployment of NEAR AI Agents that did not run inside the company's TEE. From those agents, the attacker took data including chat history, settings and logs.

Two customers' NEAR AI Cloud API keys were exposed in logs. The company has revoked both.

After detecting the attack, the company revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens and took Private Chat offline. It also deployed a fix for the SGLang flaw on all of its inference servers, rotated its remaining credentials and completed a full forensic review, according to its incident report.

Access to its NEAR AI Cloud service has been restored. The company reported the flaw to the SGLang project. It has not identified the flaw by CVE number, named the affected SGLang versions, or said whether the project has released a fix.

The company has contacted users whose account details or agents it confirmed were accessed. Affected users heard directly from security@near.ai, with the steps that apply to them. As a precaution, the company asks users to be careful with messages about their account or balance that they did not ask for.

In a follow-up post yesterday, it said users who have not heard from it do not need to do anything. It has not said whether people whose requests passed through the affected server last Sunday were among those contacted.

In an October 15 technical write-up, Brave, the browser maker, said its Leo assistant runs chats with the GLM 5.3 Flash model inside a TEE operated by NEAR AI.

NEAR AI has not said whether the affected server handled any of those chats.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sglang.summary: An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine. The attacker could have seen requests being processed on that server that day, the company says. The company has revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens and took Private Chat offline.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Xen Orchestra Auth Bypass Flaw to Gain Admin Access
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.text:
French software company Vates VMS has warned of a critical security vulnerability in Xen Orchestra that it said is being actively exploited in the wild.

The authentication bypass flaw, which does not yet have a CVE identifier, is tracked as VSA-2026-062.

"REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}," Vates VMS said in an alert. "REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string."

"The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs."

In other words, the vulnerability can allow an attacker to bypass authentication by sending a specially crafted cookie and perform arbitrary actions with "Admin" privileges, ultimately resulting in arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root.

Vates VMS said it's seeing the vulnerability being actively exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain -

It's unclear when the activity started and if the vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day.

Other indicators of compromise are listed below -

The issue has been addressed in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 for the stable and latest channels, as well as xo-server versions 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. If immediate patching is not an option, the following mitigations are advised -

Filip Magic (@mad31k) and Christoffer Olsen from TDC NET Security have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/three-.title: Three China-Nexus Espionage Campaigns Linked Through Sparrow Malware Ecosystem
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/three-.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/three-.text:
Three distinct threat activity clusters with shared infrastructure and malware code similarities have been observed targeting telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions, and critical infrastructure across Latin America, Asia, and Europe over the past year.

Check Point Research is tracking the clusters under the names SilentDelivery, OceanGate, and DarkWire. Although initially assumed to be independent sets of attacks, each with its own backdoors and post-exploitation tooling, they have all been linked through a malware ecosystem called Sparrow.

The entity behind the Sparrow framework has been codenamed CopperDragon, and is assessed to be a digital quartermaster developing tools for China-nexus threat actors, including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, Tropic Trooper, UAT-9244, and UAT-8302.

"Each cluster employed a different toolset and different initial access techniques, including compromising internet-facing infrastructure and highly selective watering hole attacks," Check Point said in a technical report published today. "The compromised websites that were used for watering hole attacks were of government, shipping, and IT and research sectors."

Attacks mounted by FamousSparrow are known for deploying backdoors like SparrowDoor (and its variants Crowdoor and TernDoor), SparroWocky, and HemiGate. It's also assessed to share some degree of overlap with Salt Typhoon. However, the precise nature of the relationship remains unclear.

The cyber espionage ecosystem linked to CopperDragon is driven by three prominent clusters -

The SilentDelivery chain begins with the attacker injecting heavily obfuscated JavaScript into legitimate websites frequented by their intended targets. Visitors to the sites are greeted by a Google Chrome SSL certificate warning that instructs users to install a "Certificate Fix" utility to restore access.

The so-called utility, once deployed, delivers either SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant. All the compromised websites have been found to be related to government, shipping, IT, and research sectors in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong, and Indonesia.

According to a report published by Positive Technologies in August 2026, there are indications that the campaign has also targeted entities in Egypt and the Philippines using this method.

"The JavaScript injected into the compromised websites is heavily obfuscated using jsjiami, a publicly available JavaScript obfuscation service," Check Point said. "It first checks whether the user is running Windows and, in some cases, verifies that the website’s domain matches the intended compromised domain."

The script then repeatedly sends status-check requests to a command-and-control (C2) server to fingerprint the user based on IP and geolocation, and ultimately decide whether to continue the attack and serve the fake warning.

Written in C/C++, SquadC is a Windows backdoor that enables initial foothold over the infected host. It establishes persistence by means of a Windows Registry Run key that masquerades as a Windows update assistant. Further analysis has uncovered that the malware is also distributed via phishing emails targeting Indonesian organizations.

The phishing email comes with a Windows Shortcut (LNK) disguised as a PDF document, which, when opened, abuses the legitimate "ftp.exe" binary to run a batch script that's responsible for displaying an empty file as a decoy, while launching SquadC via DLL sideloading.

The OceanGate operation, on the other hand, has been observed targeting both Windows and Linux environments, deploying previously undocumented tooling to maintain access, move laterally across the network, and exfiltrate sensitive data.

The Linux phase of the attack involves two new backdoors -

"After harvesting credentials from multiple users and establishing a strong foothold in the Linux environment, the actor moved into the Windows environment," Check Point explained. "The actor attempted to log in to several Windows machines over RDP, trying different passwords until it successfully authenticated with an administrator account."

This step is followed by the deployment of bespoke post-exploitation tools and a variant of SparrowDoor -

What's more, the threat actor has been found incorporating kernel rootkits and kernel-level access capabilities into SparrowDoor and SparrowShell to evade defenses through process hiding and to capture and manipulate network packet capture using WinDivert drivers.

"The actor abused the driver to convert SparrowDoor into a passive backdoor that intercepts and manipulates packets at the kernel level, making its traffic less visible," Check Point said. "This allows the backdoor to listen internally on one port while receiving connections through an externally accessible port, such as 443, that is already used by a legitimate service."

"The backdoor applies a strict filter to intercept connections from a specific source IP address to the legitimate service's port. It manipulates the packet and rewrites the destination port to the backdoor’s internal listening port, typically a high port such as 49628. For response traffic, it rewrites the source port back to the external service port, making the responses appear to originate from the legitimate service."

Interestingly, SparrowShell shares code- and infrastructure-level similarities with a malware called Mélofée that was first described by ExaTrack in March 2023 as based on the open-source Reptile rootkit. This has raised the possibility that CopperDragon is also behind the development and supply of Mélofée.

The third and last cluster of activity centers around Latin America, with a particular focus on telecommunications operators and government entities. These attacks led to the deployment of two newly identified backdoors called CopperDoor and CopperDNS as a possible replacement for SparrowDoor.

Also supporting these operations is a set of custom tools -

When reached for comment, Alexandre Côté Cyr, malware researcher at ESET, told The Hacker News that the activity clustered under DarkWire corresponds to what they call FamousSparrow as the "DarkWire tooling, network infrastructure, and victimology overlap with FamousSparrow."

"The operation heavily relies on DLL sideloading as a primary execution technique, often abusing executables that are not widely observed among other threat actors in the wild," Check Point said. "To minimize their footprint, the operators deliberately avoided creating new directories on disk, instead placing their tools within existing system paths."

"CopperDoor infrastructure demonstrated a higher level of operational security. Most IP addresses were located in Latin America, often within the same country as the victim organization. This proximity likely helps the malicious traffic blend in with legitimate network activity and reduces the chances of detection."

The malware is also distributed via phishing emails targeting Indonesian organizations. Most IP addresses were located in Latin America, often within the same country as the victim organization.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/attack.title: Attackers Exploit AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Sandbox-Evading Python Backdoor
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/attack.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/attack.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an attack that exploited two now-patched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS to deliver a Python-based implant.

The activity, observed by Huntress in early October 2026, involves the exploitation of a chain comprising CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. Patches for the two vulnerabilities were released by Ahsay Backup in mid-October 2026.

The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach to deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners on compromised systems.

"However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups," Huntress researcher Jonathan Semon said.

Specifically, the unknown threat actor is said to have left five families of Jakarta Server Pages (JSP, formerly JavaServer Pages) web shells -

"[AhsayCBS.jsp's] disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint," Huntress explained. "The web shell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later."

The attack, besides deploying an XMRig miner masquerading as Microsoft Edge, has been found to deliver a second XMRig miner ("kvm-agent.exe") that restarts every minute through a SYSTEM scheduled task, while using a different wallet and mining pool.

The most notable aspect of the intrusion revolves around the Python backdoor ("main.py"), which is designed to run only on the host it's staged on and prevent it from executing within a sandbox or an analyst's machine.

It achieves this by computing the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file with the same name in the same directory housing the Python implant, and then runs an embedded x64 DLL in memory that contacts a command-and-control (C2) server ("creepexplosiondarknight[.]com").

In an attempt to fly under the radar, the attack chain also configures Microsoft Defender exclusions, while serving tunneling tools (GOST and Chisel) and legitimate remote access software (AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop) to establish persistent access.

Evidence indicates that the threat actor may have targeted servers holding or managing backups.

"On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI," Semon said.

"Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident."

Ahsay Backup has released 10.3.6.1 with additional security hardening updates to enhance the platform's security posture, urging partners to apply the latest fixes to stay adequately protected.

"As the threat landscape continues to evolve, cybercriminals are increasingly employing AI-powered techniques to accelerate and enhance the exploitation of vulnerabilities," the Singapore-based company said. "This is a challenge faced by software vendors across all industries, and this incident reflects that broader reality rather than an issue unique to Ahsay."

"These enhancements are designed to strengthen the resilience of Ahsay solutions against emerging cyber threats, including increasingly sophisticated AI-powered attacks."

Ahsay also revealed in a status update last month that it began receiving reports from partners regarding unauthorized access incidents impacting their AhsayCBS server environments on October 9, 2026, prompting it to release hotfixes for versions 9 and 10 on October 10 and 12, 2026.

It has also shared the following indicators that customers can check to determine if their AhsayCBS server has been compromised -

If malicious activity has been detected, it's advised to reinstall Windows or Linux on the backup server, install the latest version of AhsayCBS, and restore from Auto Save by recovering a server configuration version whose timestamp predates the compromise.

"As a best practice, select an Auto Save version from at least one day before the timestamp of any suspicious folders or files created during the unauthorized access incident," it said.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/blind-.title: Blind Eagle Uses Fake Court Notices to Deliver Remote Access Trojan Across Latin America
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/blind-.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/blind-.text:
The threat actor known as Blind Eagle has resurfaced with a new campaign targeting organizations in Latin America through judicial and administrative-themed phishing lures to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) that shares its lineage with AsyncRAT and DCRat.

"The campaign uses Portuguese and Spanish lures that resemble court notifications, fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents," Zenox said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Assessed to be a Spanish-speaking group and active since 2018, Blind Eagle (aka APT-C-36) has a track record of using spear-phishing lures to distribute commodity RATs like AsyncRAT, BitRAT, Lime RAT, NjRAT, Quasar RAT, and Remcos RAT.

Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-laced attachment.

One email containing a Colombian judicial-themed XHTML file has been identified as a weaponized Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) image that renders a bogus web page impersonating Colombia's Fiscalía General de la Nación, also referred to as the Office of the Attorney General.

The web page, for its part, employs a technique known as HTML smuggling to assemble the next-stage ZIP archive payload locally in the web browser using ZipCrypto, thereby circumventing email security controls.

Present within the ZIP archive is a JavaScript dropper that masquerades as Network Configuration Auditor version 2.7.298. The JavaScript code conducts environment reconnaissance, and collects details such as system version, network profile, installation date, memory size, computer name, environment variables, and directories localized in Portuguese and Spanish.

Upon execution, it launches a Visual Basic Script that performs Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, while displaying a fake criminal-citation page as a distraction mechanism.

In parallel, the malware also takes steps to delete the original XHTML artifact, clears Mark of the Web (MotW) metadata, and sets up persistence on the host under the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically executed on system startup.

The attack culminates with the use of PowerShell to decode and launch the final RAT payload in memory. The trojan is an AsyncRAT fork with DCRat lineage based on code structure, configuration, build characteristics, and observed behavior.

"The targeting of judicial, fiscal, administrative and educational organizations gives the operation access to highly sensitive legal, financial and institutional information," Zenox said.

"Combined with the Portuguese and Spanish lures, Brazilian infrastructure, operational timezone and regional victimology, these elements establish the campaign as an APT-C-36 operation conducted through a Brazilian operational cluster."

Zenox told The Hacker News that it could not confirm whether any of these attacks had succeeded against real-world targets. However, during the campaign period between late October and early November 2026, it observed a large-scale wave of targeted phishing involving nearly 3,300 malicious emails.

While not all of these messages targeted organizations in Colombia, the country continues to remain a priority target for Blind Eagle for a combination of reasons.

"The repeated targeting of Colombia likely reflects multiple factors, with one of the main enabling factors being the structural vulnerabilities and uneven security maturity across parts of the country's critical, public, financial, and private-sector infrastructure," Zenox security researcher Gabriel Alves said.

"These conditions may increase the likelihood of successful compromises and offer greater opportunities to monetize access, steal sensitive data or funds, or reuse compromised credentials against critical systems. This is further supported by regional actors' familiarity with the Colombian context and is consistent with patterns observed among Latin American threat actors."

(The story was updated after publication to include additional insights from Zenox.)

The group has a track record of using spear-phishing lures to distribute commodity RATs. The campaign uses Portuguese and Spanish lures that resemble court notifications, fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/firewo.title: Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Customer Datasets, Model Weights and Notion AI Chats
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/firewo.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/firewo.text:
Fireworks AI disclosed on Monday that its investigation into a security incident first reported early last month uncovered further malicious activity, affecting account and billing information, alongside secrets, datasets, and incomplete models for a "limited set of accounts."

In a notice published on October 10, 2026, the company said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT.

At that time, the AI infrastructure provider said it only found evidence that environment variables, including API keys and tokens stored as secrets, were captured in certain affected accounts, adding that there were no signs that customer models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information were accessed.

In response to the incident, Fireworks AI took the step of revoking the compromised internal credentials and rotating service account tokens, along with affected Fireworks API keys and keys created by the threat actor.

The latest bulletin from the company reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously thought. The company said attackers reached its development environment via an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development (R&D) machines on October 23, 2026.

"On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," it added. "As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use."

The breach is said to have provided access to the following types of information -

Fireworks AI said payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not impacted by the security incident. It also said it's alerting customers whose data was impacted.

The company also noted that it has implemented security hardening procedures, such as credential revocation and rotation; isolating affected systems to prevent further unauthorized activity and lateral movement; tightening access controls; and improving its logging and monitoring systems.

"The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to large language models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways," it said.

The activity is assessed to be part of an emerging threat known as LLMjacking, which refers to the act of hijacking a victim's LLM through stolen credentials to fuel a criminal enterprise that thrives on peddling the access to other threat actors, while leaving the legitimate owner to pay the bill.

Last week, Google issued a warning that threat actors are increasingly targeting AI infrastructure for LLMjacking in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors.

Popular productivity and note-taking application Notion has disclosed that the security incident targeting Fireworks AI impacted "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces." In a post shared on Reddit, one user said: "looks like all of us are part of that <1%."

While the initial assessment was that the breach allowed the threat actor to access Notion AI synthetic testing data, it has since come to light that it may also have involved potential customer data.

"Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results."

Notion has also emphasized that no other features across its platform were affected by the incident. The Insights feature has since been disabled as it continues to investigate the breach and the company is no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.

Affected customers are advised to review the impacted data securely inside their workspace. If those with affected workspaces have pasted sensitive information, passwords, API keys, or other credentials during the attack window, it's recommended to rotate them with immediate effect.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/binanc.title: Binance Warns of iOS Sandbox Escape That Could Expose Crypto Wallet Keys, No Fix Confirmed
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/binanc.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/binanc.text:
An iOS sandbox escape published on GitHub lets an app read other apps' files on iPhones running iOS 26 and 27. That puts seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk of exposure to malicious apps, Binance warned today. Apple's updates for iOS 26 and 27, released yesterday, do not list a fix.

A researcher who goes by forcequit, in collaboration with 0xjohnny, released the escape, called worse_query, on Sunday, a day before those updates came out. Neither the exchange nor the researcher reported any attacks or thefts involving it.

The exchange told users to delete apps installed from untrusted sources, such as sideloaded or manually signed apps, and to update iOS and all their apps. No fix for the escape has been confirmed.

For anyone who suspects a breach, the exchange's security warning advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and resetting all active login sessions.

The researcher's proof-of-concept code can reach every app's data container on an iPhone, and some system folders on iOS 27. To use it, an app has to set up an App Group container.

He says the code is for developers and "isn't useful by itself." Other developers have built apps on it that people can install.

One of them is WQ Files, a file manager that developer Christoph Kolbicz built on worse_query. It reaches other apps' data without a jailbreak or a kernel exploit, and it can edit, delete and clear that data.

WQ Files installs via sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the App Group it needs when used with an Apple ID. No one involved has said whether an app from the App Store could use worse_query.

The three versions in the exchange's warning are the ones listed as tested in the WQ Files release notes. The researcher gives a wider range.

Of these sources, only Erosion's developers list iOS 27.2.1, which came out yesterday, and none lists iOS 26.7.3. They added 27.2.1 this week in a README change with the note "pretty sure 27.2.1 is supported".

Yesterday's updates, iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3, fixed two iMessage flaws and several Bluetooth bugs. The security notes for iOS 27.2.1 do not mention worse_query or any sandbox issues, nor do the iOS 26.7.3 notes. Apple does not disclose, discuss, or confirm security issues until it has investigated and a patch or release is available, the notes say.

In a reply on X, the researcher wrote that he had not planned to release worse_query early. He added that "Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here."

The exchange did not name any wallet app as exposed, and neither did the researcher nor the developers of the apps built on worse_query.

A researcher who goes by forcequit, in collaboration with 0xjohnny, released the escape on Sunday. The researcher's proof-of-concept code can reach every app's data container on an iPhone.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/beyond.title: Beyond the Alert: The Case for Rich Network Data
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/beyond.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/beyond.text:
At some point your security will fail. This isn’t pessimism. It’s not because your team and tools aren’t sophisticated enough. It’s the reason we have detections in the first place. And, it’s why once we accept that prevention has its limits, we arrive at an interdiction strategy: finding and disrupting what got in.

The alert tells you something happened. However, gaining access to your network doesn’t necessarily mean attackers have stolen data or disrupted the systems they were targeting. They may need to obtain additional access, move to another machine, or further explore the network. Being able to see and understand that activity is the intervention opportunity.

People naturally gravitate toward detections during product evaluations. They’re tangible, easy to compare and quantify, and address the question everyone wants an answer to: Will they catch the attack? There’s often an assumption that the rest will follow, meaning, if the detections are good, surely the investigation will be as well, right?

Whether you can trace the attack, understand the scope, and respond in time to intervene depends largely on the data behind that detection. In network security, a product can have good detections and still leave an analyst struggling to investigate. Perhaps the analyst can see the connection that triggered the alert but can’t follow what happened next. If a search returns nothing, does that mean the activity didn’t happen or that you weren’t collecting the evidence needed to see it?

This, and the arrival of AI defense, is why data quality has recently been getting so much attention.

Investigation success takes knowledge of both attacker behavior and your own environment. You need to understand what you’re looking for, but also what your data can actually tell you.

The difference in network data shows up when investigating an alert. Both shallow and rich data provide investigations with a starting point, but one can rapidly lead to a dead end. Shallow data is often just composed of timestamps, IPs, and basic connection information. Rich data retains greater transaction details and adds context. It correlates and lets you pivot and reconstruct, answering not just what triggered the alert but what happened before, after, and elsewhere.

To evaluate the data quality of a security tool, consider key questions such as:

AI-powered SOC tools can now process data at a scale that human teams simply cannot match. The more data points AI has, the more effectively it can surface events. While shallow data limits what AI can correlate, richer data allows it to identify subtle patterns across hosts and behaviors, potentially exposing previously unseen indicators of compromise or providing opportunity to intervene before an attack escalates.

AI can help when something unfamiliar is encountered. Nobody knows every service, process, or log format. An assistant can help explain what you’re looking at, suggest questions to pursue, or write a script to make a large set of data easier to examine. That can save a lot of research time. It can also help an analyst get past a point where they would otherwise be stuck.

But we’re certainly not at the point where we can trust what AI claims 100% of the time. You still need to test what it gives you. If an assistant suggests an explanation, check whether the evidence supports it. If it produces a query or script, test what it does. And before running a suggested command, ask what else it might affect. A model can be so focused on solving the immediate problem that it overlooks the rest of the system.

As AI takes on more investigative work, the ability to inspect the underlying evidence becomes another essential aspect of modern data quality.

When evaluating data from network security products—NDR in particular—take an alert from a demonstration and investigate it properly. But don’t follow the guided path. Dig deep and put yourself in unfamiliar territory. You’ll get a much better sense of how the product helps analysts when they’re dealing with an event they haven’t seen before.

These questions and tasks probably won’t be part of a typical demo. That’s the point. They’ll let you see if the data provides the fidelity, reach, and context to actually solve investigations or just a starting point with nowhere to go.

Detections get the attention, but data determines the outcome. The real question is can your team use the data to fully understand an incident and decide what to do?

Your AI SOC is only as effective as the data behind it. Corelight network detection and response (NDR) delivers data that’s open, transparent, and explainable—helping detect evasive threats, reduce triage time, and enable agentic AI throughout the SOC. Corelight’s structured network evidence preserves protocol-level context to produce a more complete dataset for investigation and AI. When analysts and AI can reason from evidence instead of isolated alerts or metadata, they can validate findings, reconstruct activity, and reach more reliable conclusions. https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/apple-.title: Apple Patches iMessage Group Chat Privacy Flaws and Bluetooth Pairing Vulnerabilities
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/apple-.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/apple-.text:
An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix.

The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected.

The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27.

The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960.

Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update.

The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes.

The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away.

The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component.

All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do.

Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/russia.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/russia.text:
The Russia-aligned state-sponsored threat actor known as Turla (aka Snake) is wielding a previously undocumented cyber espionage toolset called Cereal that's used to break into victims' Microsoft Exchange servers with an aim to surreptitiously collect emails.

According to an ESET report shared with The Hacker News ahead of publication, the sophisticated and modular tool is designed for long-term intelligence gathering and has been observed against two governmental entities in Kazakhstan and Romania in late 2025.

"The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyber espionage," the Slovakian cybersecurity company said. "It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes."

"The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft."

The toolset is a collection of interconnected components that are capable of running on Microsoft Exchange servers, receiving commands, executing them in memory, mapping the infected network, and harvesting emails of interest. The initial access vector used to deliver the malware is unknown, although the group is known to conduct spear-phishing, watering hole, and ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) attacks.

Cereal gets its name from the fact that the tools make extensive use of serialization, which refers to the process of converting a data structure or an object's state into a format that can be easily stored, transmitted, and reconstructed.

A number of aspects make the malware stand apart -

The combination of these techniques shows that the threat actor possesses a deep understanding of the internal workings of Microsoft Exchange, ESET added. The Cereal framework consists of eight moving parts that work together to provide the attackers with access to sensitive email data -

Upon gaining visibility into the email flow, the malware looks for messages containing DOC, DOCX, or PDF attachments, and matches at least one of many hard-coded lists with sender addresses, recipient addresses, subject lines, or attachment names.

Emails that meet the filtering criteria are compressed, encrypted, and staged in files on disk, after which they are exfiltrated and deleted via CerealNeuron commands.

In the attack aimed at the Romanian government organization, CerealBox is said to have been configured to gather emails involving NATO and European Union institutional addresses, a pattern that aligns with Russia's strategic priorities.

The commands delivered as compiled .NET programs are handled by CerealRunner, which unpacks and executes the payloads in memory and then sends the results back to CerealNeuron for subsequent exfiltration to the threat actor in encrypted format.

The commands support retrieving mailboxes or specific messages; queuing Active Directory for computers, users, groups, and DNS records; running Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) queries; extracting LSA Secrets; listing volume snapshots; and performing file operations.

"The sheer volume of near-identical binaries, each compiled for a specific task, strongly suggests that the operators have an internal framework that automates the compilation and packaging of commands," ESET researcher Matías Porolli said.

"Combined with a codebase built around modular, interchangeable components, the impression is one of a mature, well-engineered platform – rather than a loose collection of scripts."

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sap-pa.title: SAP Patches Four CVSS 10.0 Flaws, Including Two Enabling Remote Code Execution
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sap-pa.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sap-pa.text:
Four flaws that attackers could exploit without logging in were fixed today as part of SAP's monthly Security Patch Day—the vendor rates all four 10.0, the maximum CVSS score.

Three are in the SAP NetWeaver application server, the software SAP systems run on, and one is in the Web Dispatcher, which receives web requests from the internet and passes them on to that server.

The flaws in the Web Dispatcher and the Internet Communication Manager (ICM), which handles the server's web traffic, could allow an attacker who can reach the software over the network to run code, the vendor says.

The flaw in the server's SAML 2.0 service provider, which hands off user sign-in to an identity provider, could allow an attacker to log in as any user on some systems that use SAML single sign-on.

The flaw in SAP Gateway, which connects the server to other SAP systems and programs, could allow an attacker to impersonate one of the system's own servers and take unauthorized actions.

None of the four require any user action to work.

Each flaw is fixed in its own note, and the affected versions differ by component, according to SAP's November security bulletin. The notes are in SAP for Me, which requires a sign-in, and the vendor strongly recommends applying them as a priority.

Kernels that are out of maintenance are affected too, according to Onapsis, an SAP security company whose researchers found the ICM, Web Dispatcher and Gateway flaws. Its ICM2SHELL advisory lists kernels 7.40, 7.41, 7.42, 7.45, 7.49, 7.73, 7.81, 7.85 and 7.89 for the ICM and Web Dispatcher flaws, and its PROXYGATE advisory lists the same kernels plus 7.20 and 7.21 for the Gateway flaw. These kernels may not get a fix and need an upgrade to one that is still maintained.

On the affected SAML setups, an attacker could use CVE-2026-120017 to log in as privileged users too, according to the vendor. A full compromise could follow, possibly reaching connected systems.

A different SAML flaw in the same software, CVE-2026-44748, was fixed on June 9 and needed an attacker with a normal user account.

In the ICM flaw (CVE-2026-76964) and the Web Dispatcher flaw (CVE-2026-89126), crafted network traffic could corrupt memory. An attacker who succeeds could then run code and fully compromise the system.

Onapsis says both flaws come from one bug, which it calls ICM2SHELL, in kernel code the ICM and Web Dispatcher share for putting split WebSocket messages back together. It gave the vendor a working exploit that runs operating system commands as <sid>adm, the account that owns the SAP installation.

The same bug can crash either component, and a crashed Web Dispatcher cuts off every SAP system behind it while it restarts. WebSocket support is on by default, so a system is exposed even if nothing uses it, and dual-stack systems are affected through their ABAP stack. The company's researchers have not seen the bug exploited in attacks.

SAP Gateway uses access control lists to decide which outside programs may connect to it, which programs it may start and which connections it may relay for others. In CVE-2026-89103, the gateway enables its default list with high privileges, allowing an external attacker to be treated as one of the system's own application servers. That attacker could then take unauthorized actions in the application environment.

The researchers who found the flaw call it PROXYGATE. They say exposure depends on the gateway's proxy list, prxyinfo, or on a profile parameter where that list is missing, not on the secinfo and reginfo lists that most hardening guidance covers. Where the proxy settings allow it, crafted requests make the gateway treat an outside attacker as one of its own application servers, and it could then run operating system commands for the attacker as <sid>adm.

The flaw affects any system that runs a gateway, including AS Java, dual-stack and standalone gateway installations. The researchers demonstrated the attack end to end in a proof of concept shared with the vendor, and they have not seen it exploited in attacks.

In its Patch Day analysis, RedRays, a company that reviewed the notes in SAP for Me today, advises updating the kernel and all Web Dispatchers in a single rollout. That rollout should reach levels that cover all 17 of this month's kernel and Web Dispatcher fixes.

The firm's guidance for each flaw, except where another source is named:

Corrected on November 10, 2026: an earlier version tied the SAP Gateway flaw to the secinfo and reginfo lists and said kernels from 7.93 on already have the gw/acl_mode_proxy parameter, but the researchers who found the flaw say the proxy list, prxyinfo, or that parameter decides exposure, and kernel 8.04 gets the parameter only with the patch.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/france.title: France Blames Iran for Sabotage Attack on Refrigeration Controllers at About 700 Retail Sites
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/france.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/france.text:
An October cyberattack on refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites was carried out by a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the French government said yesterday.

The attackers broke into controllers on the night of October 11 and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. That caused food losses and, in at least 15 cases, fires.

The unit is called Shahid Kaveh. It is known mainly through hacktivist personas, such as CyberAveng3rs and Cyber Isnaad Front, that publicly claim some of its attacks, France says.

France's Foreign Ministry plans to summon Iran's ambassador and to ask its European partners to adopt new sanctions against Iranian organizations and individuals involved in the attack.

The Paris prosecutor's office opened a judicial investigation yesterday against the unit's head, the head's two deputies and anyone else identified. It has asked for international arrest warrants. The offenses under investigation include illegally interfering with computer systems and causing damage by means dangerous to people, both made more serious by the aim of serving a foreign power, Iran.

In the October attack, the attackers took remote control of Danfoss and Dixell refrigeration controllers through web interfaces, the prosecutor's office said in a press release. They started abnormal defrost cycles with no time limit and switched off the temperature probes' safety alerts, which should go off above a certain temperature. The attack caused about 20 fires.

Most of the organizations hit were large retailers, according to a joint report by France's cyber crisis coordination center, known as C4. They include Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché.

Small butcher shops, a slaughterhouse and cooperative food plants were also among the victims.

The center also tied the attack to the simultaneous targeting of Schneider Electric equipment at several small hydroelectric installations in France. The effects on that equipment were moderate.

In its attribution statement, the ministry estimated the food losses at several tens of millions of euros and called the operation the first offensive cyber campaign on French soil carried out purely for sabotage.

The C4 brings together France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI), the DGSE and DGSI security services, the armament directorate and the cyber defense command. It says four indicators point to the IRGC as the sponsor of the attack and to Shahid Kaveh as the unit that carried it out.

The infrastructure used in the attack was also used during the same period for reconnaissance of Schneider Electric equipment. That equipment is installed at sites such as small- and medium-sized energy and water production sites. The reconnaissance relied on techniques that Shahid Kaveh has used since at least April.

The attackers also used FOFA, a scanning tool they usually use. CyberbanNews, a propaganda outlet linked to the unit, reported on the attack as early as October 13. The attack infrastructure also held traces of Persian.

Prosecutors said the criminal investigation, run by France's anti-cybercrime office (OFAC) and the DGSI, found an attack method typical of the unit. It also found the use of Persian and IP addresses leading to devices located in Iran.

Shahid Kaveh has previously claimed attacks on industrial equipment, according to C4. Through CyberAveng3rs, it claimed an earlier campaign against Unitronics, an Israeli company that makes industrial control systems, in November 2023. In March and April, it claimed a large sabotage campaign against Israeli and U.S. interests that hit industrial control equipment, including Israeli refrigeration equipment.

France's attribution does not mention the new wave of refrigeration attacks that struck supermarkets in several other European countries last week.

France's CERT-FR said in an incident alert that it was aware of numerous compromises affecting remote refrigeration controllers across four product families. They are the Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series, the Copeland xweb, and the Dixell xweb.

The alert, last updated on October 16, warned that attack campaigns against this equipment were probably still underway, and that exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice.

For controllers that are not compromised, the alert's steps are:

For compromised controllers, the steps are:

An end-of-life (EOL) device that receives no security fixes faces a very high risk of compromise if it remains exposed to the internet, the alert warns. In that case, a factory reset alone is not enough: it removes the attackers' persistence, but the device stays vulnerable and will almost certainly be compromised again.
