https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/anthro.title: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 Beats GPT-6 Cyber in Multi-Stage Cyberattack Benchmark
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/anthro.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/anthro.text:
Anthropic on Monday released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models, which it said exhibit improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision.

During pre-release training, the large language models (LLMs) helped its engineers "complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours."

The artificial intelligence (AI) company said high-stakes risks arising from misalignment remain low, and claimed the models matched or performed better than Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most alignment measures, resistance to misuse, honesty, and factuality.

"It was roughly an order of magnitude less likely than Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 to publish harmful content to public package registries without encouragement, though it still did so when encouraged by the simulated user," Anthropic noted in its system card.

On Irregular's CyScenarioBench, which measures whether a model can plan and execute a multi-stage cyber operation in a realistic environment, Fable 5.2 completed 76.3% of all challenges, compared to 61.7% for Fable 5.1 and 61% for OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber.

In a pair of reports published over the last month, Irregular said Google's Gemini 4 Argon solved 12 challenges in the subset of the CyScenarioBench suite end to end, up from 5 for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and none for Gemini 3.1 Pro.

"On CyScenarioBench, GPT-6 Cyber completed 11 of 11 long-horizon scenarios at least once, compared with 8 of 11 for GPT-6 Astra. Its average success rate was 61%, an increase of 7 percentage points," the AI testing lab said. "On Atomic Challenges, GPT-6 Cyber solved all 22 challenges. Average success rates were 97% in vulnerability research and exploitation, 98% in network attack simulation, and 63% in evasion."

Fable 5.2 also scored 89.6% on the CVE Rediscovery benchmark, Anthropic's own internal evaluation of whether an AI model can independently rediscover known vulnerabilities given only the affected source code. The assessment includes 1,829 advisories for open-source projects published in October 2026.

Describing Claude Mythos 5.2 as its "most capable model for cybersecurity engineering," Anthropic said it can flag more vulnerabilities than prior models, while simultaneously getting better at reproducing and fixing them.

As before, the model's cyber capabilities are accessible through its Cyber Verification Program. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.

The development comes as Anthropic updated Claude Security with continuous code scanning and automatic fix tracking to help security teams monitor and address vulnerabilities as code changes.

"Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project's threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what's actually reachable first," Anthropic said.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.title: Google Issues Chrome Security Update for Eighth Actively Exploited Zero-Day of 2026
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.text:
Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild.

The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: 8.8), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component.

"Use-after-free in XML in Google Chrome prior to 157.0.8103.50 allowed a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page," reads the description of the flaw on CVE.org.

Use-after-free bugs typically occur when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has already been freed. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to achieve data corruption, program crashes, or arbitrary code execution.

An anonymous security researcher has been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw on November 6, 2026.

Google acknowledged it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," but has not revealed any additional specific information related to how it's being abused in real-world attacks or who is behind them.

"Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix," the tech giant added. "We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third-party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed."

With the latest development, Google has addressed a total of eight actively exploited Chrome zero-days since the start of the year. This includes CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491.

For optimal protection, users are advised to update their Chrome browser to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. To ensure the latest updates are installed, users can navigate to More > Help > About Google Chrome and select Relaunch.

Users of other Chromium-based browsers, such as Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, are also advised to apply the fixes as and when they become available.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added the Chrome vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the patch by November 24, 2026.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.summary: Google releases updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities. One vulnerability is a use-after-free bug in the XML component of Google Chrome. The vulnerability has been described as a use after-free flaw. Google has addressed a total of eight actively exploited Chrome zero-days since the start of the year.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/n-able.title: N-able Takes N-central Cloud Offline After Researcher Discloses 33 Zero-Days with PoC Exploits
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/n-able.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/n-able.text:
N-able said it has taken N-central Hosted Environments offline and is urging on-premises customers to shut down their servers until further notice following the public disclosure of over 30 vulnerabilities collectively tracked as Able2Shell.

"As a precautionary measure, we are temporarily taking our Hosted N-central environment offline while we take the necessary actions to secure the environment and implement appropriate remediation," N-able said.

"During this time, customers will be unable to access their Hosted N-central classic environment, and associated services may be unavailable. However, the Ecoverse services under N-able Login remain available and online, including Asset View, Patching, Vulnerability Management, scripting, policies and tagging."

The company also said it has not observed any signs of active exploitation of these vulnerabilities, adding it's currently working on a hot fix to address them.

The following services are impacted -

The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed multiple security flaws along with proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. The researcher said the issues were tested against N-able N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31.

The identified zero-day vulnerabilities include credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, cross-site scripting (XSS), XML external entity (XXE) injection, and remote code execution (RCE) flaws -

Successful exploitation of these flaws can allow rogue administrative access to the N-central management interface and facilitate command execution as root.

watchTowr, in a post shared on X, said it "observed exploitation attempts against N-able N-central honeypots overnight following the 'Able2Shell' zero-days being dropped."

The preemptive exposure management firm is urging users to audit for signs of compromise, restrict access, and follow vendor guidance on mitigation steps.

In an X post, Defused Cyber said it has detected probing of N-able N-central for the Able2Shell zero-days. "We have seen opening of anonymous agent sessions, pulling appliance config and hitting the remote control endpoint without auth," it added. "These pathways are part of the 0-day exploit surface."

N-able has also confirmed that it's seeing "scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code" but emphasized there is no evidence of successful exploitation in any customer environment.

The company has released N-central 2026.4 HF2 to address the following vulnerabilities. A follow-up hotfix is expected to be released to "provide further security updates" as part of its response to the Able2Shell disclosure.

All Hosted N-central servers (NCODs) across all global regions have been upgraded. N-able is also urging customers to keep N-central servers offline until the updates have been successfully applied.

According to data from Censys, there are 1,728 internet-exposed N-central instances. Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it has recorded 68 exploitation attempts against one of its honeypots from a single IP address within about 18 hours of the publication.

Huntress is urging users to review login and authentication activity from November 8, 2026, onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise, and apply N-able's hotfix and restore service only when N-able says it is safe.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisa-w.title: CISA Warns of Active Exploitation of OpenSSH, GPUStack, FreeSWITCH, and IBM Flaws
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisa-w.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisa-w.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added four security flaws impacting GPUStack, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenBSD OpenSSH, and IBM Aspera Faspex to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

The addition of CVE-2026-123158 to the KEV catalog follows reports of exploitation attempts targeting the flaw since November 6, 2026. A total of 22 exploitation attempts have been recorded from 14 unique IP addresses so far, according to Previdian.

In a post shared on X on November 7, 2026, Defused Cyber said it "observed a small amount of actors targeting SSHole" but stressed the exploitation activity is not widespread yet.

According to GreyNoise, the first exploitation attempt against its honeypot network was observed on November 7, 2026, at 12:46 a.m. UTC. Confirmed post-exploitation activity has been detected from six source IP addresses, representing 18 distinct attack chains to date.

These involve reconnaissance, queries to cloud metadata services, attempts to read password hashes and root SSH keys, and efforts to modify the SSH authorized_keys file to gain persistent access.

In at least one case, an unknown threat actor dubbed GT10 has been observed deploying TAC Agent, a Python-based command-and-control (C2) agent capable of shell command execution, system reconnaissance, directory enumeration, file transfer, and updating itself.

Threat intelligence firm watchTowr said it has also observed the OpenSSH flaw being weaponized in the wild for botnet and cryptocurrency miner activity.

In an advisory for CVE-2026-102895 published on July 31, 2026, the maintainers of the GPUStack Python package credited Nikko Enggaliano, Wei Yunzhou, Rui Yang, and Haoyu Wang for independently reporting the flaw, adding that "active in-the-wild exploitation" was reported by Ulex Innovative Systems' Javier Sixto.

There are currently no public reports on how the other vulnerabilities are being exploited, who is behind them, and the scale of such efforts. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 12, 2026.

https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilit.title: November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs
https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilit.author: Tara Seals
https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilit.text:
Microsoft serves up an actively exploited Outlook zero-day, and a wave of critical Exchange, SharePoint, Windows Search, and LDAP bugs that exhausted defenders need to prioritize fast.

November offers up a veritable Patch Tuesday feast of vulnerabilities that are more likely to be exploited. In its second four-digit Patch Tuesday release in a row, Microsoft today addressed 1,093 security vulnerabilities, with 63 rated critical, and one zero-day in the mix (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS 6.5) that Microsoft confirmed is under active exploit.

"Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," says Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at Watchtowr.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out what actually matters when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention," he adds. "Our advice hasn't changed … start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what's already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

Related:OnlyFans Copyright Takedowns Expose Compromised Websites

To that end, security teams should prioritize CVE-2026-124194, and not just because attackers are already targeting it. It's a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook that may not allow code execution, hence its moderate severity rating, but could allow the disclosure of an account’s NTLMv2 hash — and in turn, the target's login.

"To exploit it, an attacker sends a target a malicious Office file and convinces them to open it," explained Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, in his monthly Patch Tuesday commentary. "If the attack succeeds, the attacker captures the victim's NT LAN Manager v2 (NTLMv2) hash, a value derived from their Windows password. The attacker may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password."

Security teams should also prioritize a pair of critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, in Exchange and SharePoint, respectively, that each open targets to any attacker with a low-privilege login.

The first, in Exchange Server (CVE-2026-118207, CVSS 8.8), "belongs in this week's emergency window for every Exchange Server Subscription Edition server you run," Automox researchers warned in their monthly Patch Tuesday bulletin, and "all an attacker needs to start is a low-level login."

It's an improper input validation that could allow an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send the server a specially crafted request and run code with no user interaction.

Related:The Evolving Cybersecurity Lexicon: Vulnerability Discovery to Resilience

"Code on an Exchange server reaches every mailbox it hosts," warned Automox researchers. "And Exchange usually holds broad rights in Active Directory, so the mailboxes are just the start."

Meanwhile, an important-rated flaw (CVE-2026-120002, CVSS 9.9) in SharePoint Server is an elevation of privilege vulnerability that needs quick addressing, according to Automox.

"The flaw is incorrect authorization," the researchers noted. "That 9.9 comes from a changed scope: a successful attack reaches past the vulnerable SharePoint component itself. An attacker who already holds a low-privileged account sends requests over the network and elevates their privileges, with no user interaction required."

Another critical RCE to watch out for, according to Automox, is CVE-2026-110043 (CVSS 8.8/10), a one-click heap-based buffer overflow in Outlook that uses the Preview Pane as an attack vector. A target must select a weaponized email so it displays in the Preview Pane for it to trigger the attacker's code, which runs with that user's permissions.

"Patch internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, and book the Exchange restart now," the Automox researchers advised. "Push the Office update this week, then check the installed build, because a fully patched Windows dashboard says nothing about Office. Rank by score and assessment, not label."

Related:Ivanti ICS Zero-Day Attacks Highlight Vendor Patching Hurdles

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero-Day Initiative (ZDI), also identified a Windows Search RCE (CVE-2026-116928, CVSS 9.8) as needing immediate attention.

"We start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server," he said in his November Patch Tuesday blog post, where he also listed 30 potentially wormable CVEs to patch quickly. "This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month."

And finally, Childs pointed to CVE-2026-119958, an RCE bug in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

"This patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction," he warned. "Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly."

Childs also recommended testing and deploying patches for the wormable bugs quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange.

White the cornucopia of CVE this month, especially on the heels of the record October Patch Tuesday, may feel overwhelming, security teams should stick to best practices and not get overwhelmed, advises Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra.

"I don't know about everyone else, but I'm tired," he said via email, adding that he believes that, eventually, AI will finish turning up old bugs and teams can once again look forward to smaller Patch Tuesday releases. "I can only imagine that if I’m tired, admins and operations teams everywhere are also tired. I believe that we will make it through to the other side, if we prioritize updates and focus on what really matters. The noise is coming at us from all sides, and we need to cut through it and figure out what really matters to the business."

Senior Managing Editor, Dark Reading

Tara Seals is an award-winning journalist with 25+ years of experience as a reporter, analyst, and editor in the cybersecurity, communications, and technology spaces. As managing editor, she runs the newsroom at Dark Reading, leading a team of staff writers and freelance contributors. She also heads up strategy for a variety of in-depth, multichannel news coverage initiatives.

Prior to joining Dark Reading in 2022, Tara was editor-in-chief at cybersecurity stalwart Threatpost, and prior to that, the North American news lead for Infosecurity Magazine. She also spent 13 years working for other titles at Virgo Publishing (now part of Informa TechTarget), as executive editor and editor-in-chief at publications focused on communications service providers, channel partners, and enterprise mobile and video technology. In 2026, she was awarded a regional Azbee award for her in-depth coverage of the ongoing North Korean fake worker cyber campaign.

A Texas native, she holds a B.A. from Columbia University, lives in Western Massachusetts with her family, and is on a never-ending quest for good Mexican food in the Northeast.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Deep inside South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, scientists have uncovered a surprising clue about an extinct human relative that lived hundreds of thousands of years ago. For the first time, researchers have recovered and studied ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils, revealing evidence that the cave may have contained an exclusively female burial site.

The discovery, published in the journal Cell, raises an extraordinary possibility. The cave could represent the earliest known burial location reserved for one sex by a human relative other than Homo sapiens.

Homo naledi lived approximately 335,000 to 241,000 years ago and has fascinated scientists since its discovery in 2013. This extinct species combined primitive features resembling those of apes with other characteristics more closely associated with modern humans.

A Strange Mystery Hidden in Ancient Human Fossils

One of the biggest puzzles surrounding Homo naledi involves the remarkably similar appearance of adult fossils recovered from the cave's Dinaledi Chamber. For more than a decade, researchers have struggled to explain why these individuals showed so little of the physical variation normally associated with differences between males and females.

To investigate, an international research team involving the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other institutions turned to proteins preserved in the ancient remains.

The scientists used a technique involving gentle acid etching to recover tiny protein fragments known as peptides from fossilized tooth enamel. This approach allowed them to collect samples while minimizing damage to the valuable fossils. In total, they examined 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 different individuals.

The researchers specifically searched for Amelogenin-Y, a protein produced from a gene on the male Y chromosome. Surprisingly, they found no evidence of this male-specific marker.

To verify that their findings were reliable, specialists at the University of York's chemistry facility examined the amino acids in the samples. Their analysis confirmed that the proteins were genuinely ancient rather than the result of contamination from modern sources.

Could Homo naledi Have Had an All-Female Burial Site?

Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York's Department of Chemistry, said: "The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived.

"These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins."

The results raise important questions about how Homo naledi individuals lived, organized their communities, and treated their dead. If the Dinaledi Chamber was intentionally used only for females, it could point to surprisingly elaborate social customs among these ancient human relatives.

Such a practice might even suggest symbolic burial traditions once believed to be exclusive to Homo sapiens, or modern humans.

However, the researchers emphasize that an all-female burial site is not the only possible interpretation of the evidence.

Another explanation involves the genetics of Homo naledi itself. If the population lived in extreme isolation, the gene responsible for producing Amelogenin-Y could have undergone a mutation or disappeared entirely.

Under that scenario, some of the individuals could actually have been male, even though their teeth did not contain the protein normally used to identify them.

Ancient Tooth Enamel Opens a New Window Into Human Evolution

The ability to recover proteins from fossils this old is particularly valuable because tooth enamel can protect biological material for extraordinarily long periods.

Palesa Madupe, who carried out the research during her postdoctoral work at the University of Copenhagen, explained why teeth offer such an important source of evidence.

"Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel -- the hardest tissue in the human body -- shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years.

"This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it's probably because they could have all belonged to one sex."

The research represents the largest collection of individuals from an extinct hominin species ever examined using ancient protein analysis.

Whether the fossils belong entirely to females or include males with an unusual genetic signature, the discovery provides an important new perspective on Homo naledi. It also demonstrates how proteins preserved in ancient teeth can reveal clues about extinct human relatives that their bones alone cannot provide.

As researchers continue investigating the mystery, the findings could reshape our understanding of the social lives and possible burial traditions of ancient human species.
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: Scientists recovered and studied ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils. They found no evidence of a male-specific marker in the fossils. The discovery raises an extraordinary possibility that the cave may have contained an exclusively female burial site.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, reaching one of its largest sizes on record. Despite the striking increase, scientists from NASA and NOAA say Earth's protective ozone layer is continuing its gradual recovery and remains on track to heal later this century.

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area. Scientists attributed the expansion primarily to an exceptionally strong polar vortex, a large circulation of winds that influences atmospheric conditions over Antarctica. They also emphasized that international efforts to reduce harmful chemicals have prevented the hole from becoming even larger.

Between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was at its seasonal peak, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). That is more than twice the size of the United States. Scientists closely monitor ozone in the stratosphere because it serves as Earth's natural "sunscreen," protecting living organisms from dangerous solar radiation. Unlike this beneficial layer high in the atmosphere, ozone near Earth's surface is a pollutant frequently associated with human activities.

Antarctica's Ozone Hole Reaches Its Largest Size in a Decade

The ozone hole reached its maximum extent on September 18, spreading across 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). This was approximately 90% of the size of the largest ozone hole ever measured, which occurred on September 9, 2000.

"The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing," said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA's ozone research team at the agency's Goddard Space Flight Center. "But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven't seen in a decade."

Although the hole expanded to an extraordinary size, the results also demonstrate the benefits of decades of international environmental protections. Without reductions in chemicals known to destroy ozone, the affected area could have been substantially greater.

"The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak," Newman said.

How a Powerful Polar Vortex Accelerates Ozone Loss

Ozone depletion begins with chemicals released through human activities, particularly compounds containing chlorine and bromine. Atmospheric circulation transports these substances into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet radiation breaks them apart. The released chlorine and bromine atoms then participate in chemical reactions involving particles in Antarctic stratospheric clouds, leading to the destruction of ozone.

A major factor in this process is the stratospheric polar vortex, a seasonal band of strong winds that circles Antarctica. This circulation traps extremely cold air over the region, allowing the formation of the special clouds that help trigger ozone destruction. When the vortex becomes unusually strong or expansive, conditions favorable for ozone loss can persist across a larger area.

In 2026, atmospheric disturbances that would normally weaken the vortex were unusually subdued. This allowed the circulation to remain powerful and helped create a broader region where ozone could be destroyed.

"The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September," said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. "That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur."

NASA and NOAA Measure the 2026 Ozone Hole

Despite its exceptional geographic size, the 2026 ozone hole did not experience the same extreme levels of ozone loss observed during record-breaking events 10 or 20 years earlier.

To measure ozone concentrations, NOAA researchers launched instruments attached to weather balloons from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory. They also collected readings using the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, an optical device designed to measure atmospheric ozone. Their observations showed that ozone levels directly above the South Pole fell to their lowest reading of 2026 on October 17, reaching 105 Dobson units.

The Dobson unit is the standard measurement used to describe the total amount of ozone above a particular location. To illustrate the scale, 100 Dobson units would produce a layer of ozone just 1 millimeter thick, approximately the thickness of a dime, if all the ozone in the atmospheric column were compressed to standard temperature and pressure at sea level. The lowest ozone concentration ever measured over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006.

Satellites provide another essential source of information. Since 1979, spaceborne instruments have helped scientists observe changes in the ozone layer and track its condition over time. The 2026 measurements included data from NASA's Aura satellite, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, a joint NASA and NOAA mission.

Why Earth's Ozone Layer Is Still Recovering

Scientists say the latest observations reinforce evidence that international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals are working. Much of that progress can be traced to the Montreal Protocol, a global agreement adopted in 1987 to phase out substances responsible for damaging the ozone layer.

Under the agreement, countries committed to replacing harmful compounds such as chlorofluorocarbons with alternatives that pose less danger to atmospheric ozone. According to Stephen Montzka, a senior scientist at NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory, chlorine concentrations in the Antarctic stratosphere associated with ozone-depleting chemicals have declined by approximately one-third compared with their peak levels in the 1980s.

These reductions are significant because chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once common in refrigerators, air conditioning systems, building insulation, and other everyday products. Although many of these substances have been phased out, they can remain in the atmosphere for decades. Additional emissions can also occur when older equipment, materials, and landfill waste release chemicals that were manufactured years ago.

Because these compounds break down so slowly, repairing the ozone layer takes many decades. Nevertheless, continued monitoring by NASA and NOAA indicates that the long-term recovery is progressing. Even with unusually large seasonal ozone holes such as the one observed in 2026, scientists expect the Antarctic ozone hole to recover by the 2070s.

The latest findings illustrate how exceptional atmospheric conditions can temporarily produce severe ozone depletion without reversing decades of environmental progress. They also highlight the lasting impact of international cooperation in protecting Earth's atmosphere.
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole is the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations. The hole covered an average of 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers) between September 7 and October 13. The long-term recovery is progressing, says NASA and NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.

The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.

Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health

The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.

Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.

A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).

However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.

Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.

"These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products."

FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events

To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.

The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.

Several differences stood out in the analysis:

These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.

"Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said.

Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable

One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.

Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.

How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.

These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.

Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?

Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.

"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events."

Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.

Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.

How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports

The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.

Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.

Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).

Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.

The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.

Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.

Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: The American Heart Association says the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused heart problems. The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
New preliminary research involving more than 440,000 American adults has uncovered a concerning association between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease, particularly stroke. The findings suggest that even occasional marijuana use may be linked to higher odds of cardiovascular problems, raising new questions about the health effects of a substance that is becoming increasingly common across the United States.

The research, presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, found that the association was not limited to people who frequently used cannabis. It also appeared across different methods of consumption (smoked or edible, etc.). Researchers emphasized that cannabis use should be considered when discussing heart health and stroke prevention.

Scientific Sessions 2026 took place November 6 through 9 in Chicago, bringing together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, clinical advances, and emerging evidence.

Cannabis refers to the plant itself, while marijuana is a commonly used term for cannabis products containing enough THC to produce psychoactive effects.

Marijuana Use Is Rising Across the United States

"Previous research has indicated that cannabis use is rapidly increasing in the United States, with 1 in 6 adults in 2024 reporting having used it within the last month, up from 1 in 10 in 2020 -- a 51% increase," said study author Aabha Divya, M.B.B.S., M.Ch., an assistant professor in the division of cardiothoracic surgery at the Tulane University School of Medicine in New Orleans.

Earlier research conducted between 2016 and 2020 had already identified associations between cannabis consumption and unfavorable cardiovascular outcomes. Those findings also suggested that using cannabis more frequently during a given month was connected to greater cardiovascular risk.

However, the evidence has not always been consistent. With recreational marijuana becoming legal in more places and cannabis products increasingly available, Divya and colleagues wanted to investigate these possible health effects in a larger population.

"We wanted to expand on this earlier work because cannabis use has become increasingly common in the United States, as recreational legalization and commercial availability of various products with cannabis have also expanded. Previous studies have raised concerns about possible cardiovascular effects; however, the results have not been consistent," Divya said.

The researchers examined information collected through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), a large telephone survey of American adults. They combined responses from jurisdictions that collected information about cannabis consumption between 2020 and 2024.

Participants answered questions about their marijuana use and whether a healthcare professional had ever diagnosed them with cardiovascular conditions, including a heart attack, stroke, or coronary heart disease.

Even Occasional Marijuana Use Was Linked to Higher Stroke Odds

One of the most striking findings was that infrequent cannabis use was associated with cardiovascular problems. In fact, the researchers did not find the steady increase in cardiovascular risk with more frequent use that they had expected.

The analysis revealed several important associations:

These findings were unexpected because the relationship between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease did not consistently become stronger as consumption increased.

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward. We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease," Divya said.

Although the study cannot establish that marijuana directly causes strokes or other cardiovascular conditions, the findings suggest that occasional consumption should not automatically be considered free of potential cardiovascular concerns.

"As cannabis use becomes more common, it is increasingly important that people and their healthcare professionals include it in conversations about cardiovascular health, just as they discuss tobacco, alcohol and other commonly used substances," she added.

Experts Urge Greater Attention to Cannabis and Heart Health

Robert L. Page II, Pharm.D., M.S.P.H., FAHA, who led the writing group responsible for the American Heart Association's 2020 cannabis scientific statement, said the findings add to growing concerns about marijuana's possible cardiovascular effects.

One challenge in evaluating those effects is that many cannabis users also smoke tobacco. Because tobacco is already an established cardiovascular risk factor, separating its effects from those of cannabis can be difficult.

Page, who was not involved in the research, explained why the new findings deserve attention.

"Unfortunately, many patients who use cannabis may also smoke tobacco, which completely clouds the issue when addressing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk. In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case. This is the second observational study to suggest that cannabis exposure (without tobacco smoking) may be a potential risk factor for developing cardiovascular disease. Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events. To this end, clinicians should be addressing cannabis use with their patients as they would tobacco use when considering the risk of cardiovascular disease."

Page is a professor in the department of clinical pharmacy and the department of physical medicine/rehabilitation at the University of Colorado Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences in Aurora, Colorado.

How Researchers Studied Nearly Half a Million Americans

The analysis included 442,906 adults living in the United States (average age of 49 years; approximately half women). Their responses came from telephone surveys conducted through the BRFSS.

Researchers used survey information collected from 2020 through 2024, focusing on states that had included an optional marijuana questionnaire. Between 16 and 24 states participated in this portion of the survey each year, meaning the analysis did not represent every state.

Participants reported how many days they had consumed cannabis during the preceding month. The questions covered multiple ways of using marijuana (smoking, vaping or ingesting gummies or other cannabis-containing foods).

The researchers divided participants into four categories based on their reported use:

Participants also indicated whether they had ever received a diagnosis of heart attack, heart disease, heart-related chest pain, or stroke.

To better distinguish the association with cannabis from other potential explanations, the researchers accounted for numerous established cardiovascular risk factors. These included demographic characteristics, tobacco smoking, alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, physical inactivity, education, and income.

Why the Findings Do Not Prove Marijuana Causes Strokes

Despite the large number of participants, the study has several limitations that affect how its findings should be interpreted.

First, the analysis examined associations between reported cannabis use and previously diagnosed cardiovascular conditions at a single point in time. This means researchers could not determine whether marijuana use preceded the cardiovascular problems or whether it directly contributed to them.

The information also depended on participants accurately recalling and reporting their cannabis consumption and medical histories (making them subject to potential errors in memory). Such reports may not always reflect actual patterns of use or diagnoses.

Another limitation was the lack of information about the strength of the cannabis products participants consumed or the quantities they used. Without those details, the researchers could not evaluate whether THC potency or the amount consumed influenced the observed associations.

The researchers also acknowledged that some participants may have reduced or discontinued cannabis consumption after being diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. As a result, the group reporting no cannabis use in the previous month may have included former users.

These uncertainties make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how consumption frequency affects cardiovascular health. Nevertheless, the findings add to growing evidence that cannabis use deserves closer examination as a possible factor in heart disease and stroke.

As marijuana becomes more widely available and its use continues to increase, researchers and healthcare professionals are emphasizing the importance of discussing cannabis alongside other substances that may affect cardiovascular health.
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: Study did not represent every state. It examined associations between reported cannabis use and previously diagnosed cardiovascular conditions. Study has several limitations that affect how its findings should be interpreted.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
An ancient rodent of extraordinary size has been identified from fossils uncovered in a mine in southern Thailand. The discovery, made by an international team of paleontologists that includes scientists from McGill University, provides new evidence that giant rodents appeared much earlier and in more parts of the world than previously believed.

The researchers found "remarkably large" fossilized teeth belonging to a previously unknown species called Yakamys sirindhornae. This prehistoric rodent lived approximately 34 million years ago, during the middle of the Paleogene period. Its remains, consisting of a lower second molar and a lower incisor, were recovered from the Bang Mark Pit at the Krabi lignite mine in Thailand's Krabi Province.

Although only two teeth have been identified, they offer valuable clues about rodent gigantism, the evolutionary process through which rodents develop unusually large bodies. The discovery suggests that Southeast Asia played a more significant role in the early evolution of giant rodents than scientists had recognized.

Giant Rodents Have a Much Older History Than Expected

"Today, the largest living rodent is the capybara, but very large rodents are not restricted to recent ecosystems," said Virginie Millien, a biology professor at McGill University and co-author of the study. "Giant rodents evolved repeatedly during the later history of the group, mostly in South America. This discovery suggests that Southeast Asia also played an important role in the early evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents."

The newly identified animal's name reflects both its impressive size and its connection to Thailand. Yakamys combines "yak," the Thai word for giant, with "mys," the Greek word for mouse or rat.

The second part of its scientific name recognizes an important supporter of scientific research in Thailand.

"The species name, sirindhornae, honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, in recognition of her longstanding support for science and paleontological research in Thailand," Millien said.

How Big Was This 34-Million-Year-Old Rodent?

To estimate the animal's size, the research team applied seven established methods that use tooth measurements to calculate body mass. Their results suggest that Yakamys sirindhornae weighed approximately 30 kilograms, making it about twice as heavy as other known rodents from the same period, including Hulgana.

That would have made the newly discovered species exceptionally large compared with its contemporaries. However, the researchers emphasize that determining an extinct animal's weight from a small number of fossilized teeth involves considerable uncertainty.

"This is only a ballpark figure, as there is substantial uncertainty associated with fossil body-mass estimation," Millien said.

The limited fossil evidence also makes it difficult to reconstruct how Yakamys evolved or what its life was like. Additional discoveries will be needed to better understand its physical characteristics, ecological role, and evolutionary relationships.

International Research Uncovers Thailand's Prehistoric Past

The fossils were identified through an ongoing international collaboration investigating ancient mammals in Thailand's Krabi Basin. The project brings together scientists from McGill University, Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources, and French research organizations, including CNRS and Université de Poitiers.

By revealing evidence of an unusually large rodent in Southeast Asia 34 million years ago, the discovery expands scientists' understanding of where and when rodent gigantism emerged. Future fossil finds could help establish how these ancient giants lived and how their evolution relates to the enormous rodents that appeared elsewhere in the world.

The research received support from CNRS, Université de Poitiers, Université de Montpellier, McGill University, and the Department of Mineral Resources of Thailand.
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: The discovery provides new evidence that giant rodents appeared much earlier and in more parts of the world than previously believed. The discovery suggests Southeast Asia played a more significant role in the early evolution of giant rodents than scientists had previously thought. The newly identified animal's name reflects both its impressive size and its connection to Thailand.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered new clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

Reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an important role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," says Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

What Is Bad Cholesterol?

Cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

These plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form quickly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol."

Looking Beyond Bad Cholesterol

To investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

All three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

The researchers also identified two particularly important contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

What Is Proteomics Analysis?

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

While genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks

The new investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

Researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

One of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns showed substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

The researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

LDL showed a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an important distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

"The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," says Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future."

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health

The three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

All three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an important energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

Lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

By identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers new possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

However, the research did not evaluate a new treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

"Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," says Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments."

The results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

Study Details and Research Institutions

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

At the time of the research, the authors were affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology and the Institute of Medicine at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard Medical School, USA; AstraZeneca, Sweden; Municipal Hospital in Olsztyn, Poland; University of Copenhagen, Denmark; University of Minnesota, USA; The Lundquist Institute at Harbour-UCLA Medical Center in Torrance, USA; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, USA; and the University of Glasgow, UK.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow. These developing hair follicles form intricate geometric arrangements that differ from species to species. But what determines where each follicle appears, and how does the body create such orderly patterns?

Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery. By studying how cells move in response to chemical signals, the team developed a model that successfully recreates the formation of hair follicle patterns in two mammalian species. Their findings, published in PNAS, suggest that elaborate biological structures can emerge naturally from basic interactions between neighboring cells.

The discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature. Hair, feathers, and most types of scales begin as small structures called placodes that appear during embryonic development. Scientists have spent decades investigating how these early structures establish the distinctive arrangements seen across different animal species.

Challenging a Long-Standing Theory of Hair Growth

For laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the leading explanation has traditionally been the expansion-induction model. This theory proposes that when a new placode appears, it releases a chemical that prevents additional placodes from developing too close to it.

As the embryo's skin grows and stretches, some areas move far enough away from existing placodes to escape the chemical's influence. New placodes can then develop in those spaces, gradually creating a more complete pattern across the skin.

Although this explanation has gained widespread acceptance, scientists have not experimentally established that it can account for the diversity of follicle patterns found across species.

A Simpler Mechanism for Hair Follicle Formation

To investigate another possibility, researchers led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor, both in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE's Faculty of Science, focused on a process called chemotaxis.

Chemotaxis occurs when cells move in response to differences in chemical concentrations. The same basic process helps guide white blood cells toward areas of inflammation, allowing the immune system to respond where it is needed.

The researchers created a mathematical model that tracks how mobile cells in the dermis interact with an attracting chemical signal released by the epidermis, the skin's outer layer. They then simulated the growth of embryonic skin to see whether these interactions could produce the gradual appearance of placodes.

Remarkably, the model recreated the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, including the same sequence of follicle formation that scientists had previously explained using the expansion-induction theory. This suggests that a complex system of instructions may not be necessary to determine where follicles develop.

"Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form," explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. "Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals."

One Simple Process Creates Different Hair Patterns

The team next investigated whether the same mechanism could explain follicle arrangements in another mammal with a very different coat structure.

They selected the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles develop in an unusually regular pattern with a strong directional alignment. This distinctive organization cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental information gathered from three-dimensional images of developing embryonic skin, the researchers adapted their simulations to reflect the spiny mouse's particular biochemical characteristics and the way its skin grows.

The results showed that the same underlying process of cells responding to chemical signals could also reproduce the spiny mouse's highly organized follicle pattern. The differences between the two species could be explained by variations in their cellular interactions, chemical properties, and skin growth rather than entirely different mechanisms.

These findings suggest that the remarkable variety of structures found throughout the animal kingdom may arise from a shared set of relatively simple biological rules. By adjusting how cells interact and respond to their surroundings, nature can generate dramatically different patterns without requiring a separate developmental blueprint for every species.

"Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution," concludes Athanasia Tzika. "The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals."
