https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Kazuo Akagi
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Kazuo Akagi is a research professor at Ritsumeikan University, Kusatsu, Japan, and professor emeritus at Kyoto University and the University of Tsukuba. He worked with Shirakawa on polyacetylene thin films starting in 1984, when he joined Shirakawa’s lab at the University of Tsukuba.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Credit: Newscom/Alamy

Hideki Shirakawa pioneered the field of conductive polymers, overturning the common view that plastics do not conduct electricity. His demonstration that thin films of polyacetylene — an organic polymer — can become conductive when doped with small amounts of other chemicals earned him a share of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (with Alan MacDiarmid and Alan Heeger). He was the second Japanese chemist to receive this award, after Kenichi Fukui in 1981. Shirakawa has died aged 90.

Shirakawa was born in Tokyo. After graduating from secondary school in Takayama City, he studied chemical engineering at the Tokyo Institute of Technology (now the Institute of Science Tokyo). He went on to pursue master’s and doctoral studies there, under the supervision of polymer chemist Shu Kambara, earning a Doctor of Engineering degree for his research on how blocks of organic molecules combine to form polymer chains.

Chemistry education must change to help the planet: here’s how

After completing his doctorate in 1966, Shirakawa was hired as a research associate in the laboratory of Sakuji Ikeda at Tokyo Tech. There, he began studying how acetylene molecules join together to form a polymer, using Ziegler–Natta catalysts (which are based on organic molecules containing transition metals).

In 1967, Shirakawa was joined in his experiments by a visiting researcher from South Korea, Hyung Chick Pyun. The pair were polymerizing acetylene using a catalyst composed of tetrabutoxytitanium and triethylaluminium to produce powdered polyacetylene.

On one occasion, however, the protocol failed to produce the powder. Instead, a ragged film formed on the surface of the solution in the flask. On closer inspection, it became clear that the visiting researcher had mistakenly used a much higher concentration of the catalyst than was intended — 1,000 times higher. Shirakawa went on to synthesize a thin film of polyacetylene with a metallic lustre by introducing acetylene gas into a flask coated on the inside with the concentrated catalyst.

Chemists struggle to ditch hazardous solvents — even after decades of ‘green’ efforts

Subsequently, he travelled to the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, where he worked with MacDiarmid and Heeger. The team discovered that adding small amounts of molecules that accept electrons (such as bromine) or that donate electrons (such as arsenic pentafluoride) increased the electrical conductivity of the thin film by a factor of ten million. This work led to the trio’s Nobel award.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Dyani Lewis
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Dyani Lewis is a freelance journalist in Melbourne, Australia.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Illustration by Piotr Kowalczyk

In August 1987, a scandal erupted over work on the world’s highest mountain range. John Talent, a palaeontologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia, announced he had found numerous anomalies in research charting the geology of the Himalayas. All of the problems were in papers by Vishwa Jit Gupta, one of India’s most celebrated palaeontologists at the time.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

Gupta was outraged. But further investigations over the following seven years revealed the scale and brazenness of his fraud. Littered through more than 450 publications were maps of collection sites that didn’t exist, plagiarized images and specimens stolen from collections that Gupta had visited. More than 100 experts had been duped into co-authoring descriptions of fossils Gupta claimed he had collected from specific Himalayan geological formations, but instead hailed from North America and Morocco.

“It destroyed the image of Indian science,” says retired geologist Ghulam Bhat, who completed his PhD on Himalayan geology in the same year that the allegations of fraud emerged.

Gupta died in 2022, and many geologists know to steer clear of his work. But awareness of the problem is fading, and none of Gupta’s papers have been retracted. When Nature contacted Bhat, who is now editor-in-chief of the Journal of the Geological Society of India (JGSI), he was unaware that Gupta’s papers were not marked as retracted. That’s despite the JGSI’s 1991 evaluation of 19 of Gupta’s papers that it published1, which concluded that “the fossil finds of V. J. Gupta are not reliable [...] the data is incomplete bordering on disinformation”.

Much of Gupta’s work is inaccessible, having been published in now-defunct periodicals or in volumes that, although digitized online, have not been indexed in reference bibliometric databases such as Scopus, Web of Science and Dimensions. Despite this, Gupta’s falsehoods are now being propagated outside specialist circles, as his old journal articles are being surfaced through artificial-intelligence tools that summarize search results. When someone searches for geological landmarks in the Himalayas, such as the Tandi Limestone, Google’s AI overview obliges with direct links to Gupta’s discredited papers.

Bhat now plans to rectify the digital record and says that all other journals that have published Gupta’s work should do the same. “If this problem is left as it is, unattended, it will pollute all of the geological literature in future,” he says. Gupta also published papers in Nature in the 1960s; Chris Graf, director of research integrity at Springer Nature, didn’t confirm that the journal would re-examine them. But he added that in general, when investigations of old papers are hampered by limited available information, an editorial expression of concern “is likely to be our preferred mechanism for alerting readers to potential issues”. (Nature’s news team is editorially independent of its publisher, Springer Nature.)

The Himalayas case raises a wider issue: how to deal with fraudulent, unethical or even merely incorrect research from decades ago, especially in an era in which much old work is digitized and AI systems can pick up studies that might previously have been neglected.

There are many skeletons in science’s closet, but publishers can be reluctant to judge science of the past by today’s standards, and can find it more difficult to issue retractions when authors are dead, original records cannot be consulted or journals are no longer in print.

And as publishers struggle to deal with the fallout from rising research fraud and AI slop, finite resources can also mean that many old papers with known flaws are left as they are.

Gráinne McNamara, a council member of the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in Eastleigh, UK, which advises journals on best practice, says that journals are increasingly contacting COPE to ask for advice about dealing with concerns on very old papers.

“Everybody is looking for what’s the best, most responsible way to handle these,” she says.

The widespread use of retractions as a mechanism for maintaining integrity in the scientific record is a relatively recent phenomenon. The JGSI evaluation report about Gupta served as a warning notice to the community at the time, but didn’t use the word retraction. It also pre-dates the modern standardization of retraction processes, which happened in the 2000s. Now, a journal should issue a retraction notice, and leave the original paper intact, but with a modified title and a stamp or watermark indicating that it has been retracted. The information should then feed through to bibliographic databases.

In the early 2000s, only around 30 retraction notices were published each year, and COPE first developed guidelines to standardize the retraction process in 2004. The number — and rate — of retractions has exploded since then, with more than 10,000 recorded in 2023 alone.

Digitization of old records, combined with a wider propensity to retract flawed work, has seen journals reaching farther back in time to retract studies — and this has led to some startlingly long gaps between when an article was published and when it was formally retracted. Retraction Watch, an initiative that curates a database of more than 70,000 retractions and expressions of concern (a notice that highlights potential issues with a publication), has reported that the longest gap is 80 years. That’s for a prank case report published in 1923 in the Dutch medical journal Nederlands Tijdschrift voor Geneeskunde.

It described a man who died from “piss cough”, an affliction that caused him to cough up liquid smelling of urine. In 2003, an editor at the journal happened to look up the case, which he thought was widely known to be a hoax. Realizing it had never been retracted and that others did not know it was fake, he sought confirmation of the hoax, and found it in the autobiography of a retired University of Amsterdam physician, who had helped to cook up the nonsense case when he was a medical student. Accompanying commentary on the journal’s website said that a retraction was appropriate now that the older literature had become accessible through digitization.

According to Nature’s analysis of Retraction Watch data — which capture a subset of total retractions — the number of old papers that are being retracted is rising. Overall, some 358 retraction notices and 120 expressions of concern have been issued for papers or book chapters that were more than 20 years old at the time of the editorial action (see ‘Retracting the past’). This is still a rare phenomenon: since 2015, the oldest retractions represent some 0.7% of the total number, up from 0.2% before 2010. But around 3% of expressions of concern have occurred for works older than 20 years. That illustrates how publishers might choose to issue expressions of concern for older papers, rather than retract, because it can be harder to investigate historical records.

Source: Nature analysis

In 2005, biochemist Barry Milborrow sought to retract five of his own papers, published between 1980 and 1982, on biochemical pathways that bacteria, algae and plants use to make pigments, because later work had disproved their findings. The Biochemical Journal, which published Milborrow’s self-retraction listing the five articles2, retracted both articles it had published. Another journal issued a correction, but no notice was issued by the publisher of the remaining two papers. Ian Swift, Milborrow’s co-author and PhD student at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, at the time, says he only found out about the retractions many years later, after Milborrow had passed away.

According to COPE guidance, journal editors can retract articles if they no longer have confidence in the results and conclusions reported in them. By that rubric, many older papers could, in theory, be retracted, but, being rarely cited, are usually left alone.

Even when invalid papers are still being cited, retraction might not follow. In 1985, for instance, geneticist Svante Pääbo reported that he had cloned DNA from an Egyptian mummy3. The seminal work marked the birth of palaeogenomics, a field that earned Pääbo a Nobel prize in 2022. But the mummy DNA was actually contamination from a modern handler, as Pääbo, now at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, has openly acknowledged. “What is problematic is if false conclusions lead other scientists and the community as a whole astray,” he told Nature when asked for this article. “I don’t think anyone is currently misled by the mummy paper,” he says, which is why he argues that the work should stand, adding that to correct very old papers with errors “would create more confusion than clarity”.

Retractions can reshape scientists’ careers in unexpected ways

In practice, old papers tend to be considered for retraction only if they have widespread integrity issues that journal editors feel shouldn’t be allowed to stand unmarked. A major trigger for mass retractions of older work is when investigations of an individual’s research cast doubt over their entire body of work. For instance, a 2019 investigation by King’s College London into the work of psychologist Hans Eysenck and his German collaborator Ronald Grossarth-Maticek has led to papers dating back to the 1940s being flagged — albeit many with expressions of concern rather than retractions.

Eysenck died in 1997 as one of the most celebrated psychologists of the twentieth century. But in 2019, psychiatrist Anthony Pelosi, who had critiqued Eysenck’s work to no effect in the 1990s, published a renewed analysis of the studies4. An accompanying editorial called on King’s College London — where Eysenck worked from 1955 until 1983 — to conduct a formal investigation. The investigation report, also published in 2019, concluded that 24 articles by Eysenck and Maticek published between 1988 and 2000 were ‘unsafe’ and recommended they be retracted.

Those recommendations weren’t followed entirely. Only 16 of the 24 papers have been retracted, and another 4 have expressions of concern. Four remain unflagged. After sustained criticism over the narrow scope of the 2019 investigation, King’s College London published a statement in October 2025 saying that other publications based on the data set used in the 24 papers it examined are also likely to be ‘unsafe’ and should be flagged by journal editors — although it did not list affected publications.

So far, 94 of Eysenck’s hundreds of papers have been either retracted or tagged with an expression of concern, the oldest of which was published in 1943 (see ‘Longest gaps’).

Source: Nature analysis

Such inconsistencies in how publishers deal with research-integrity issues are common and don’t relate only to very old papers, says Andrew Grey, an endocrinologist and research-integrity specialist at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. He alerted publishers to concerns over large numbers of articles by Yoshihiro Sato, a Japanese bone-health researcher who fabricated data in dozens of clinical trials, and has reported seeing some journals respond with retractions or expressions of concern, whereas others take no action5.

One famous scandal of the past — the 1980s discrediting of work by John Darsee, a US biologist — has led to just 17 retractions. Although news reports at the time stated that more than 80 of Darsee’s papers had been retracted, this refers to editorial notes and warnings that, in parallel with the Gupta case, don’t appear in modern records as retractions.

Another trigger for retracting old work is when it attracts renewed attention, particularly in medical fields.

Each year, Marcel van der Heyden, a physiologist at the University Medical Center Utrecht in the Netherlands, asks his final-year students to write a review article about a poison or toxin. In 2025, he chose caesium salts, and his students uncovered 20 case reports of people ingesting the toxic chemical6. Often, the individuals deliberately consumed the compound as an alternative treatment for cancer. Although the US Food and Drug Administration cautioned against its use in 2018, the deadly ‘therapy’ is still promoted in books and online by some wellness centres.

The treatment traces back to two papers published in 1984 in Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior. One of the papers was written by Austrian-born Hellfried Sartori, who had been prosecuted in Maryland in 1982 for fraud relating to using the unproven cancer treatment. That case ended in a mistrial. Sartori subsequently had his medical licence revoked in several US states in the 1980s and was sentenced to prison in Virginia in 1999 for practising medicine without a licence. And in 2010, an inquest into the deaths of five people in Australia found that he had been treating patients remotely from Thailand. Many more of his patients had also died under his treatment, the court heard.

The other paper promoting caesium therapy was by Wisconsin-based Aubrey Keith Brewer. Brewer died in 1986, but his namesake Brewer International Science Library continues to distribute information on caesium and other alternative therapies with a disclaimer that the protocols are “for information purposes only”, and that people should consult their physician if unwell. Nature contacted the website but received no response.

Van der Heyden contacted Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior in August 2025, suggesting an expression of concern could be warranted. “Without the original data, it’s hard to tell whether there is a mistake made, or whether it’s on purpose,” he says. But the research-integrity team at the journal’s publisher, Elsevier, decided in January this year to remove the two papers, soon after Van der Heyden informed them that his review had been accepted for publication and that his university was poised to issue a press release about it. The papers were deleted entirely this April, as Retraction Watch reported.

The move to scrub a paper, rather than merely retract and leave it in place, can be taken if the contents could present a serious health risk to the public, according to COPE guidelines.

The number of men with high citation counts exceeds that of women.Credit: FotografiaBasica/iStock via Getty

Women are more frequently mentioned in the acknowledgements section of papers than credited as co-authors, especially for research and analytical work, a study has found. But status seems to trump gender.

An analysis of more than 20,000 authors and 60,000 acknowledged contributors on papers published in seven PLOS journals between 2016 and 2021 highlighted persistent disparities between women and men in who gets authorship over an acknowledgement.

The study, published in Scientometrics1, also found that highly cited researchers — used by the authors as a proxy for higher status — were more likely to receive authorship over acknowledgement than were their less-cited collaborators, irrespective of gender. When a highly cited woman collaborated with a less-cited man, for example, the woman was more likely to be credited as an author.

Authorship is one of the most important metrics in research evaluation, grant reviews and promotion decisions, whereas acknowledgements aren’t typically factored in. The difference between getting authorship credit versus an acknowledgement can make or break a researcher’s career. One famous example is chemist Rosalind Franklin, a key contributor to the discovery of the DNA double helix. Franklin was mentioned in the acknowledgements section of the 1953 paper describing the finding, which went on to win the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, rather than being named a co-author with James Watson and Francis Crick.

The Scientometrics study highlights the importance of status in determining who gets credit, and the uphill battle that many women in research have to face — especially in their early and mid-careers. The number of highly cited men exceeded that of women, suggesting that even if women benefit from high status once they have attained it, fewer women attain higher status in the first place.

“We realized that the issue is double. One linked with gender bias, but another surprisingly due to hierarchy bias,” says Yukie Sano, a computational scientist at the University of Tsukuba in Japan, who co-authored the paper.

The impact of a researcher’s status and gender on academic credit is well-documented, but Sano and her co-authors point to the Contributor Role Taxonomy (CRediT) — a standardized system describing specific roles that individual scientists often take on during research — as a game-changer by providing high-quality data to track this metric across journals and disciplines.

Sano and her colleagues used CRediT data from open-access PLOS journals (which implemented the system in 2016) to track the contributions of authors and devised a separate system to track contributions in the acknowledgements section. Author gender was determined using Gender API, an artificial-intelligence-powered service that infers a person’s gender on the basis of their name.

The team found that men were generally more likely than women to receive authorship credit — particularly in investigation roles (performing the experiments) and analysis roles (analysing or synthesizing the study data). Around 70% of men were credited as authors, compared with about 65% of women.

The size of the gender gap varied between disciplines, but was particularly evident in medicine, biology and computer science, whereas environmental science showed little evidence of a gender difference in authorship versus acknowledgement rates.

The TAMBO team assesses suitable observatory sites in the Andes Mountains of Peru.Credit: Jaco de Swart

It is uncommon for a social scientist to have a seat at a meeting about an astronomical observatory, let alone for them to jointly lead one. For one-quarter of attendees to be social-science scholars is almost unprecedented. But that’s exactly what happens at meetings about the Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO), a proposed detector to be built in the Peruvian Andes to look for cosmic particles called tau neutrinos.

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Tau neutrinos are elusive fundamental particles that are transmitted through space from black holes and other distant sources. When these particles interact with rocks on Earth, they can produce a shower of other, short-lived particles. The idea behind TAMBO is that if such a shower were emitted from one side of a deep canyon, it could be picked up by an array of 5,000 detectors on the other side (TAMBO collaboration. Nature Astron. 10, 947–951; 2026). The Andes Mountains of Peru contain many promising sites.

For those who live in the area, however, the case for TAMBO is less clear. The Andes are a sensitive ecological environment and home to Indigenous farming communities that consider the mountains sentient beings that are integral to their society. The area is also affected by legal and illegal mining, large-scale infrastructure projects and legacies of colonialism. This all leads to scepticism towards large projects that are developed by people from outside the area.

I am the co-principal investigator of the TAMBO collaboration, alongside Peruvian neutrino physicist Carlos Argüelles at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. I lead the social-science and ‘responsible siting’ side of the project. Having received funding to build a proof-of-principle experiment called TAMBITO, we are searching for a potential location for the observatory.

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Since 2024, the TAMBO collaboration has built partnerships with 11 Peruvian institutions, which are involved in the design and development of the telescope. Scientific links are an important starting point, but they are not enough. No matter what their discovery potential is, big scientific experiments are not beneficial to everyone. For example, construction of the Thirty Meter Telescope has been stalled since 2015 because of protests triggered by objections to its planned site on Maunakea in Hawaii — a mountain that is sacred in Native Hawaiian culture.

To integrate environmental care into the project and build good relationships with the communities that might host the telescope, TAMBO brought in experts on the Andean region. In 2024, the collaboration held a workshop at Harvard’s Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, at which scholars and policymakers discussed what equitable astrophysics in Peru would look like. This led to the formation of a responsible-siting team that includes geographers, sociologists and anthropologists who have worked in the Andes.

Voters in California have approved US$8.4 billion in funding for immunology research — the largest ever infusion of cash for science authorized by a public vote in US history.

The funding proposal, known as Proposition 38, appeared on the ballot for voters in California in last week’s US mid-term elections, but it has taken nearly a week for officials to count enough ballots to declare it a success. The state government will pay for the research — which aims to find treatments that harness or re-engineer the body’s immune system to fight illnesses such as cancer and Alzheimer’s disease — by selling state government bonds. (This is unusual for science funding. Bonds are typically reserved to pay for infrastructure projects such as road construction and require the state to pay back its debt with interest.)

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Supporters of the proposal say that the funding will provide stability for researchers in California, who have been affected by political turmoil. The administration of US President Donald Trump has pushed for massive cuts to science funding; put political appointees in charge of grant decisions at federal science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health; and forced policy change at US universities that receive federal funding, including those in California.

The $8.4 billion “is an advantage to California that is unprecedented”, says Antoni Ribas, a cancer researcher and physician at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), who supported Proposition 38. It will make the state “even more of a global hub for immunology research”.

But the proposal has sparked debate. That’s because it calls for about half of the funding to be given directly to research institutes — and the only institute that matches the criteria called for in the proposal is one co-founded by Gary Michelson, a billionaire medical-device inventor. He wrote the proposition and donated about $45 million of his own funds to get it placed on the ballot and to campaign for its passage.

“I feel like the voters have been taken advantage of,” says Sarah Hill, a political scientist at California State University in Fullerton, who tracks the state’s ballot measures. Michelson did not respond to Nature’s request for comment before this story was published, but has said elsewhere that he will not personally profit from the bond revenue.

In California, citizens can place proposed laws directly on the election ballot by collecting hundreds of thousands of voter signatures.

The state has funded scientific research through this process before. In 2004, after then president George W. Bush restricted federal funding for human embryonic stem-cell research, voters in California approved a $3-billion bond to establish the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, which they then voted to replenish with another $5.5 billion in 2020.

A campaign mailer encouraging California voters to support Proposition 38.Credit: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty

“The model works,” Ribas says. Immunologists have been making great strides with medicines such as personalized treatments called CAR-T therapies, which are revolutionizing care, he says. There has also been a flurry of research into developing vaccines, including the mRNA shots that have been the target of funding cuts by the Trump administration. Proposition 38 will ensure that such research can continue regardless of the political headwinds, Ribas adds.

Around $4 billion from Proposition 38 will fund grants for researchers at select public universities and non-profit institutes in California through a competitive review process. According to the proposal, any commercialized therapies developed through funded research must be sold at a 20% discount to people in California, with 10% of drug royalties returning to the state’s general fund.

Matthew Montgomery, the science officer of a simulated Mars mission organized by NASA, takes part in a ‘Martian’ geology project.Credit: NASA

Engineer Matthew Montgomery was one of a four-person crew who spent more than a year in a 158-square-metre, 3D-printed habitat for a simulated mission on the red planet. The hardware-engineering design consultant (and co-owner of a film production company) took charge of the hydroponic garden and participated in simulated ‘Marswalks’ wearing a protective suit. As well as dealing with a realistic 13–22-minute delay in their connection with mission control, the crew experienced a total communication blackout for two weeks.

A new artificial-intelligence tool can identify an individual bird by its song, and can be used to track that bird’s movements over time. The system provides a less invasive way to monitor birds than using physical tags. Researchers tested the model on recordings of male ovenbirds (Seiurus aurocapilla) — a species that sings individually unique songs — from more than 100 locations, and found that it could match songs to specific birds with up to 96% accuracy. “This is almost a holy grail,” says biologist Scott Sillett.

Reference: Nature Methods papers

Protecting key underground fungal networks in Mongolia could help to preserve biodiversity, boost climate resilience and revive iconic grasslands across the country, say researchers. In September, evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers and her team announced that they had found more than 500 types of fungus in networks across Mongolia, 90% of which were new to science. Mycologist Burenjargal Otgonsuren hopes that leveraging these networks could help to restore the swathes of degraded land in Mongolia — and preserve the 3,000-year-old way of life practiced by Mongolia’s 230,000 nomadic herding families.

Sources: Free to Think 2026; V-Dem Dataset (https://go.nature.com/47UZF3P)

Academic freedom is deteriorating globally, according to the Scholars at Risk (SAR) network, a human-rights organization based at New York University. Data show a steep decline in academic freedom in the United States, some of which preceded the 2024 election of President Donald Trump. But there is cautious optimism about the trend in Hungary following the end of Viktor Orbán’s 16-year premiership.

Reference: Free to Think 2026 report

By studying people who show no signs of neurodegeneration well into older age, scientists have identified several gene variants that could help to protect against dementia. These protective variants seem to defend the brain against the toxic clusters of proteins that cause Alzheimer’s — mechanisms that scientists now hope to exploit. “Nature has already done the experiment for us: certain gene variants protect us from Alzheimer’s,” says neuroscientist Guojun Bu. “Learning how they do this could guide us to new therapies.”

The mathematics community’s reaction to OpenAI’s huge drop of AI-generated proofs last month “ranged from exhilaration to despair”, writes mathematician Ursula Martin, one of the authors of the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics, which put forward several safeguards on the technology. “This is a moment to be clear-eyed about AI’s potential to make discoveries,” she writes. “The challenge … is to sustain the community of mathematicians on whom the discipline depends.”

Reference: Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics

Biomining strategies — those that use microorganisms to extract metals — could provide a more sustainable alternative to conventional technologies, which are struggling to keep up with soaring demand for critical minerals, argue a group of biotechnology and mining researchers. These methods can also extract metals from discarded electronics, reducing the need for virgin ores. For biomining methods to reach their potential, researchers must work with governments and industry to establish a pathway through which these technologies can be deployed at scale, the authors write.

The NASA space probe Voyager 1 is now almost one light-day away from Earth. Nearly 50 years after its launch, finding ways to conserve power on the spacecraft requires innovative thinking, says heliophysicist Jamie Rankin, deputy project scientist of the Voyager mission. The clean-energy transition is creating a paradox. To expand renewable-energy technologies, electrify transport and build infrastructure for artificial intelligence, society must extract unprecedented quantities of minerals. Demand for many of these ‘critical minerals’ is projected to increase several-fold over the coming decades1. Yet, the technologies used to obtain them remain rooted in an old model through which single metals are extracted from virgin ore2.

The consequences are increasingly apparent (see ‘Critical-mineral supply under pressure’). As deposits of high-grade ores decline, larger quantities of rock must be mined and processed to produce the same amount of metal3. That requires more energy and water. Mining accounts for around 1.7% of global energy consumption and this number is projected to rise by up to eight-fold by 20604. Many critical-mineral projects operate in regions facing high water stress, such as arid parts of Africa and Latin America1.

Sources: Top to bottom: Ref. 3; ref. 3; ref. 6 and go.nature.com/4nzbbnx

Mining waste is growing, too. Already, hundreds of billions of tonnes of mine tailings are stored globally. Projections suggest that by 2050, up to two trillion tonnes of extra waste rock and tailings will have accumulated3,5.

Meanwhile, society is producing vast quantities of metal-rich waste that remain a mostly untapped secondary source of metals. In 2022, 62 million tonnes of electronic waste (e-waste) was produced globally — almost 8 kilograms for every person on the planet — and only around 22% of that was formally collected and recycled6.

How to widen access to the critical minerals that the world needs

Many discarded electronics contain valuable metals, including gold, palladium and rare-earth elements — in concentrations that can exceed those found in primary ores. However, recovering these metals remains technically challenging and is often economically unattractive using conventional approaches.

Retrieval of metals and increasing metal circularity should be seen as a strategic capability to offset the growth of metal extraction from virgin ores. Nations that can efficiently recover critical minerals from waste streams, mine residues and low-grade resources will be less exposed to geopolitical disruptions and supply-chain shocks7.

Biology offers a powerful route forwards. Although biomining — which uses microorganisms to extract metals — was once considered a niche approach, it has evolved. Driven by advances in microbial ecology, synthetic biology, structural biology, protein engineering and machine learning, the scientific foundations for a new generation of mineral biotechnologies are emerging at speed8,9. These methods offer potential levels of selectivity for extracting and recovering certain metals that are often difficult to achieve through conventional hydrometallurgical processes.

But, scientific progress alone will not transform mineral supply chains. The main obstacle is no longer a shortage of ideas. It is a lack of pathways from scientific discovery to industrial deployment. Here we outline how to develop those pathways, drawing on discussions at the International Workshop on Biomining of Critical Minerals and Elements, which was sponsored by the Novo Nordisk Foundation and held in Sitges, Spain, in September last year.

Biotechnologies have demonstrated their industrial potential for decades. Bioleaching and biooxidation processes are already established for recovering copper, nickel, gold and cobalt from ores10. They involve irrigating heaps of crushed ore or treating ground mineral powders with specialist microbes that generate chemicals, such as acids or modifiers of reduction–oxidation reactions, that selectively dissolve either target metals or other minerals found with them.

Advances in synthetic biology have expanded the range of potential applications. For example, engineered microbial systems can be designed to dissolve metals more effectively. Biomolecules (such as the protein lanmodulin) can separate rare-earth elements with yields of 99.9% in one step under conditions that are simpler than conventional techniques, using aqueous solutions rather than organic solvents8,11. AI-assisted protein design is further accelerating the discovery of macromolecules designed to selectively recognize, bind to and separate target metals from complex solutions of several elements9.

How the rush for critical minerals is neglecting human needs

Collectively, these developments suggest that biotechnology could become an important component of future critical-mineral supply chains. However, many promising approaches never progress beyond being validated in the laboratory. They often stall between proof-of-concept studies and commercial demonstration, a challenge familiar throughout industrial biotechnology. Even promising technologies often struggle to attract the capital, infrastructure and industrial partnerships needed to scale them up12,13.

Barriers must be overcome. Although a few bioprocessing pilot projects exist, their capacity is insufficient to evaluate technologies across the diverse types of ore, feedstock and process conditions encountered in practice. Investors are reluctant to finance first-of-a-kind projects when it is uncertain how well they will perform in the real world.

Regulatory frameworks for emerging biomining technologies are also inadequate. They often vary across biotechnology, environmental and mining sectors and between jurisdictions. Developers might need to navigate several regulatory authorities and approval pathways, creating uncertainty and delays as technologies advance.

Electronic waste can contain higher concentrations of key metals than are found in natural ores.Credit: Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty

In the European Union, for example, the use of genetically modified microorganisms and their environmental applications are subject to distinct regulatory frameworks. Genetically modified microorganisms are allowed to be used in contained systems, whereas those used for field applications generally rely on naturally occurring or adapted microbial strains. The United States uses a coordinated multi-agency approach, involving the Environmental Protection Agency, the Food and Drug Administration and the US Department of Agriculture.

Valuable technical knowledge (on protein engineering, mineral characterization, hydrometallurgy and economic modelling, for instance) remains dispersed across disciplines, institutions and jurisdictions. This makes it difficult to generate the necessary evidence base — including long-term continuous operating data, metrics for tracking chemical cycles and validated economic assessments — to support large-scale adoption of such technologies.

The result is a growing mismatch. Scientific advances in mineral biotechnology are accelerating, yet the mechanisms needed to deploy them are not keeping pace. Although billions of dollars are being invested to secure future supply chains for critical minerals, comparatively little attention has been devoted to building the innovation systems required to commercialize biological solutions.

If biotechnology is to contribute meaningfully to critical-mineral security, environmental sustainability and circularity of resource use, then governments, industry, development banks and philanthropic funders must move beyond supporting research alone. They must invest in the institutions that enable translation of these new technologies as well.

Three priorities deserve attention.

Countries should establish shared pilot and demonstration facilities dedicated to mineral biotechnology. Individual companies often cannot justify the risks associated with developing specialized infrastructure for technologies that remain commercially unproven. Shared facilities can help to overcome this barrier by allowing several organizations to evaluate biological processes using realistic feedstocks under industrially relevant conditions. These facilities can support both pre-commercial and competitive studies. Similar approaches have been implemented successfully in synthetic biology and bio-refining, advanced manufacturing and in the clean-energy and semiconductor sectors.

The dark side of green technology: what do electric vehicles really cost?

For the mineral sector, such facilities should be located near relevant resource and waste streams, including mining districts, e-waste recycling hubs and sites affected by acid mine drainage or metal-laden urban waste waters. They should have connections to universities, research labs and a skilled workforce.

Access to research and engineering expertise would enable rapid iteration, troubleshooting and integration of mineral biotechnologies with established processes. Such sites would extend beyond technology testing to generate the operational, environmental and economic data needed to inform investment decisions, regulatory approvals and commercial deployment.

Initiatives in other sectors illustrates the value of such infrastructure. In Sweden, for instance, publicly funded pilot and demonstration facilities have been set up to test processes for biochemically converting biomass under realistic conditions14.

More than 70% of Mongolia’s land is degraded, which has implications for the country’s nomadic herders.Credit: Timothy Allen/Getty

Rising temperatures, desertification and overgrazing are taking a heavy toll on Mongolia’s iconic desert grasslands, as well as its nomadic herding culture. But a team of researchers might have hit on an underground solution. They’ve found clues that protecting key fungal networks that support life above the surface could help to preserve biodiversity, boost climate resilience and revive degraded lands.

In most ecosystems, invisible networks of fungi trade resources with plants by interlocking with their roots. These arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi provide the plants with nitrogen and phosphorus gathered from the soil; in return, the plants send excess carbon through their roots to the fungi, helping to sequester it from the atmosphere.

“Mongolia has very unique fungal networks that power these arid grasslands,” says evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers at the Free University of Amsterdam. Kiers is leading a project to map and identify mycorrhizal-fungus hotspots in Mongolia. “As we fight desertification, we want to be able to protect the fungi that are going to be so important for these plants and ecosystems to be restored.”

Working out ways to maintain healthy fungal networks cannot come quickly enough. Around 77% of Mongolia’s land is degraded, and the country is warming three times faster than the global average. Kiers says that paying more attention to fungal networks could help to address the interconnected global challenges of desertification, biodiversity loss and climate change.

It seems that fungi might be starting to get the attention they deserve: last month, at the latest meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, held in Yerevan, Armenia, 3 more countries signed a pledge to conserve fungi, bringing the total number of signatories to 17. And a road map to help countries make good on that pledge, the Global Strategy for Fungal Conservation, was launched.

Kiers’s team is part of the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks (SPUN), a non-profit organization that maps fungal systems around the world and works to protect them. Kiers co-founded the organization in 2021. In September, its researchers announced that they had found more than 500 types of fungus in southwestern Mongolia, 90% of which were previously unknown.

Kiers’s team is in talks with several governments to present its maps of fungal hotspots and data in hopes of supporting the development of strategies to curb desertification and boost climate resilience.

But at the same time as researchers such as Kiers are documenting fungal hotspots, the hotspots might be disappearing. In Mongolia, the team found that degraded land had at least 44% fewer species of mycorrhizal fungi and 60% less plant cover than did non-degraded land.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Jenna Ahart
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Jenna Ahart is a science journalist based in Washington DC.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Industrial PhD programmes are increasingly being utilized in fields such as public engineering.Credit: Emanuele Cremaschi/Getty

Yifan Wang didn’t realize that his thesis would be the first of its kind when he started his PhD, although he knew it was likely to be more applied than most. By the beginning of his project in electrical engineering and telecommunications at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, Wang had already established a connection with an industry partner to gather insights from network traffic patterns — such as how users stream videos.

But after Wang began his research, Australia rolled out its National Industry PhD Programme, in which students undertake research projects co-designed by universities and companies in return for a funding boost from the government and industry partners. The goal, according to the programme’s website, is to “create a flexible pipeline of researchers who can transition between academia and industry and have multiple career pathways open to them after completing their PhD”.

Wang joined the programme’s inaugural class in 2023 and spent the remaining three years of his degree not only with an eye towards practical applications, but also with a community of peers spread across Australia. And in May, he became the first student in the programme to submit his thesis.

Cake to the rescue: how these PhD students are cooking up a sense of community

“At the beginning of my PhD, I was a bit hesitant about whether I would want to do an engineering industry job or a research job,” Wang says. “But now, I’ve found my interest. I’m really determined to find a research position that solves real industry problems.”

As of June, the Australian programme has funded 448 awards and has received more than 1,000 applications during seven funding rounds. And it’s just one of many innovative PhD models. Governments in many other countries have launched programmes supporting industry-oriented PhDs.

“There’s certainly a lot of [experimental programmes] occurring around the world,” says Anthony Boccanfuso, chief executive of the University–Industry Demonstration Partnership, a non-profit organization in Columbia, South Carolina. The partnership leads the Industry-Integrated PhD (I-PhD) programme in the United States, which was launched in July. Although Boccanfuso says that conversations about re-evaluating the PhD model have existed for the past 15–20 years, there’s now a “sense of urgency because of this need for talent” in high-demand fields.

Intelligent manufacturing for rail transit systems is one of several areas to have benefited from China’s industrial PhD scheme.Credit: Xiao Benxiang/VCG/Getty

At the same time, researchers worry that the programmes might take away from fundamental research. When the I-PhD programme launched, chemistry Nobel laureate Carolyn Bertozzi wrote on the social-media website Bluesky that “most PhD students pursue industry jobs anyways — that has always been true. Use NSF funds to support basic science that industry won’t support”.

Boccanfuso’s organization will oversee more than 250 students with funding from the US National Science Foundation — which will make a US$47-million investment over the next five years — along with industry and university partners. Students are jointly mentored by university and industry advisers and are expected to spend at least one year completing on-site industry research. The programme aims to reduce the time taken to complete a PhD in the United States, from an average of 5.6 years to just 4 years. It will also prepare STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) students for industry careers, which is where most of them are going, Boccanfuso says. Although the initiative is only just beginning, it’s already received “overwhelming interest” from students and universities, he adds. Elsewhere in the world, including in China and the European Union, similar programmes have taken off.

As for why there’s been such a boom in these national-level initiatives, “it’s pretty straightforward”, says João Pereira, a civil engineer at the University of Minho in Guimarães, Portugal, who manages one EU-funded initiative. “It’s much easier to justify applied research than fundamental research because of the proximity to yielding results.” It can take decades for fundamental research to come to fruition, whereas applied research can deliver commercial applications — and therefore money and economic growth — “not immediately, but pretty close to it”, he adds.

Joshua Twiggs, who works in the medical technology industry in Sydney, Australia, and has supervised industry PhDs, says that these initiatives aim to harness a country’s already sophisticated education system as a driver of innovation. “How do we leverage the incredibly smart work happening in universities through to actual industry implementations?” Twiggs says.

Such programmes reflect “the growing recognition that knowledge is a key driver of economic competitiveness and innovation”, says Hans Parmar, a spokesperson from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada in Ottawa, a government department focused on industry, commerce and scientific research. “Modern innovations are often too complex for a single individual, organization or even sector to develop alone,” Parmar adds. But these spanning initiatives mean that governments, universities and industries can all align their interests.

Julie Dubuit is a civil engineer at the University of Toulouse who took part in France’s Industrial Agreements for Training through Research PhD programme.Credit: Julie Dubuit

The trend can also be assigned to “the fact that academic positions in universities can only absorb a small fraction of PhD graduates”, says an official at the European Commission, the EU’s executive branch. That makes “industrial PhDs very attractive with regards to future employment”.

Meanwhile, China awarded its first batch of ‘practical PhDs’ in September last year. Rather than completing a conventional thesis, these students develop an innovative product, project or technique — such as intelligent manufacturing in rail transit systems. Since the law allowing these PhDs came into effect last year, more than 60 researchers have received practical PhDs.

“We encourage students to implement ideas that can meet real demand in society, rather than just coming up with concepts,” says Liu Chun, executive dean of the National College of Elite Engineers at Tongji University in Shanghai. Candidates’ success could be measured by “how many patents a student has, how many international or domestic industry standards they have participated in setting and whether their product has successfully passed a pilot test”, Chun says.

NSF rolls out ‘industry PhD’ programme — joining a global trend

The European Union’s Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) programme offers applicants the opportunity to be part of industrial-doctorate networks of students, all of whom are focused on a single research topic. Each student has both an academic and a non-academic supervisor and must spend at least half of their fellowship on the premises of the non-academic partner. When all the cohort members and their supervisors come together, “it’s almost like a small conference”, says Pereira, who is part of a network that explores sustainable construction. “All these interactions force students to create a set of skills they won’t get anywhere else.”

One of the programme’s main goals, according to the European Commission official, is to “nourish the talent pipeline for boosting employability in industry”. A 2025 study found that two years after completing their fellowships, 66% of industrial doctorate graduates were working outside academia, compared with just 43% of graduates from the MSCA’s standard doctoral networks1.

Almost half of survey respondents across nine countries thought that scientists’ use of generative artificial intelligence would make society better. Credit: gorodenkoff/iStock via Getty

Scientists are perceived as the group of people most likely to have a positive impact on society through their use of generative artificial intelligence, finds a survey published by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism in Oxford, UK, on 29 October1.

The survey, of nearly 19,000 people across nine countries, found that 46% of respondents think that AI use by scientists will make society better.

People who use AI tools on a daily or weekly basis were also overwhelmingly found to trust more strongly in the positive impact of the technology across all sectors than were those who seldom or never use it.

AI scientists are changing research — institutions, funders and publishers must respond

In 2024 and 2025, the team surveyed six countries, selected to provide cross-national variety among high- and upper-middle-income countries with broadly comparable levels of digital-media use. They were Japan, Argentina, France, Denmark, the United States and the United Kingdom. In 2026, Australia, Finland and Norway were added. Information was collected from about 2,000 people from each country.

Among the questions survey participants were asked was how much better or worse they thought each of ten groups’ use of generative AI would make their life or society. These groups included the government, politicians and political parties and ordinary people.

Scientists ranked top in terms of public trust, closely followed by health-care professionals. By contrast, politicians and political parties were perceived as having the worst impact through their AI use (see ‘With great power’).

The results did not surprise Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, co-author of the report and a communication researcher at the University of Copenhagen: scientists and health-care professionals performed well in the team’s 2025 survey, too2. As part of that investigation, respondents were asked whether generative AI would improve or worsen their experience of interacting with various sectors. Then, scientists ranked second of 12, behind only search-engine companies.

This year, the team explored why certain groups were and were not trusted by assessing different sectors’ perceived ability, benevolence and integrity in their use of AI. “Much of the public believe that scientists are able to use generative AI well, are relatively benevolent in their use of it and have relatively high integrity,” says Nielsen.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: Metascience should be a source of evidence, not a means of control
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Efforts to apply metascience to research funding must put evidence and scientists front and centre.Credit: Alamy

The European Research Council made headlines last month when the news broke that those applying for one of its core grants had only a 5% chance of success. Partly as a result of applicants using artificial intelligence, the ratio of submissions to grants at the European Union’s premier science funder is now so skewed as to be little more than a lottery. Some funders are already using lotteries to select grant recipients, viewing these as a fairer way to allocate funding.

More self-reflection in research can lead to better science

This is not a coincidence. The idea of distributing certain types of grant randomly has been tested experimentally over a number of years. It’s one example of how the field of metascience — the study of the practice of science itself — is having a real-world impact.

Metascience is not new. The world’s oldest journal devoted to the study of science, Nauka Polska, based in Poland, was founded in 1918 and is still publishing. Nature frequently reports on metascience, invites researchers to share their opinions and publishes primary science in the field. A set of studies released in April, for example, investigated the reproducibility, replicability and robustness of research in the social and behavioural sciences1–4. Developments in research funding, research organization, communication and evaluation are all aspects of metascience.

Metascience is also used by governments to support policy and funding decisions. In the past few years, a number of governments have established and funded metascience research units, as detailed in Seize the Meta Moment, a review by an international group of researchers and policymakers that was published last week by the Research on Research Institute in London (see go.nature.com/4z7pdt1). The author list includes members of some of these government-funded metascience units.

Huge meta-research project puts claims in social-science papers to the test

In one sense, this is positive, an example of policymakers seeking solutions informed by research. But the review’s authors point out that political attention also introduces risks — namely that the discipline could be misused to serve government agendas or to justify decisions that are not supported by a consensus of the evidence. They acknowledge that metascience will, to some extent, always be political, but that this should be acknowledged. And they urge politicians to use metascience as a learning tool and a source of evidence, but not as a means of controlling researchers.

In the United States, the Office of Science and Technology Policy has tasked all federal science agencies with establishing metascience capabilities. This was outlined in a July report, Science: A New Golden Age, which criticized excessive bureaucracy and slowness in US science, and embraced the idea of accelerating grant-awarding processes (see go.nature.com/3uj6pf5). One concern is that the US administration could use metascience to push through major changes, such as funding cuts, support for higher-risk research or the adoption of AI, without engaging the broader scientific community.

I built the UK government’s metascience unit — here’s what countries need to know

The United States is not the only country where researchers are worried about potential metascience misuse; concerns have also been raised in the United Kingdom, the first country to establish a government metascience unit. Last year, the nation’s main public funder of social science, the Economic and Social Research Council, announced a commitment to promoting economic growth. This is part of a broader economic push by the nation’s main public funder, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), in response to a government priority.

The extent to which publicly funded science contributes to growth and the mechanisms underlying it are well-studied questions in the social sciences, and there are a range of views both supporting and critiquing the UK government’s objectives. It’s important that funders such as UKRI do not align themselves with just one view, and that the metascience unit does not reduce measurement of grant recipients’ performance to a metric that is itself still a matter of debate in the research community.

Why science has a credibility problem — and how to address it

Most of the world’s science funding agencies were established when research careers were accessible to relatively few people. There is now a much larger and more mobile pool of researchers due, in part, to the expansion of universities and the globalization of science. Funding agencies need to change how they work to adapt as the world changes. That includes addressing the problem of falling success rates resulting from the greater demand for grants.

By far the best way for policymakers to use metascience to inform funding decisions is for them to work with researchers to create and implement tools designed to measure quality and competitiveness, and — as in science itself — to learn from experimentation and experience.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: Some people are resistant to dementia — here’s what their genes can teach us
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Alison Abbott
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Alison Abbott is a writer in Munich, Germany.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Specific gene variants seem to confer resistance to dementia, protecting individuals into old age. Credit: Hector Roqueta Rivero/Getty

The ravages of age touch us all — some more lightly than others. Geneticist Henne Holstege wanted to study people with a particular superpower: those resistant to neurodegeneration, despite their age or their genes putting them at high risk.

Brains of ‘super agers’ are strong producers of new neurons

At first, she struggled to get funders interested. “For five years, all my grants were rejected,” she recalls. “Each time was a cup of poison.”

But she persevered, convinced that these super-agers could help scientists to understand why a privileged few people manage to avoid conditions such as neurodegeneration, which ail so many in older age.

She finally launched her project in 2013, and ever since, Holstege and others in her field have uncovered a rash of gene variants that seem to protect against dementias.

Researchers are increasingly convinced that understanding resilience to dementia is just as interesting as the more familiar genetics of high risk.

The brain, it seems, has its own defence mechanisms against the toxic proteins that cause Alzheimer’s — mechanisms that scientists now hope to exploit.

They think that protective gene variants will help to illuminate how the disease emerges and worsens — and potentially how to treat it. Of particular interest is a group of variants that affect the workings of the ApoE protein (apolipoprotein E), which carries fat molecules essential for cellular function. Some forms of this protein are long-known contributors to the risk of Alzheimer’s. But some recently discovered and rare variants seem to confer resistance.

“Nature has already done the experiment for us: certain gene variants protect us from Alzheimer’s and they do so safely,” says neuroscientist Guojun Bu from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. “Learning how they do this could guide us to new therapies.”

The relentless course of Alzheimer’s disease follows a decades-long progression that is kick-started when amyloid-β proteins in the brain clump into plaques. It concludes with loss of synapses and death of brain cells.

Except when it doesn’t. Just occasionally, people whose brains are full of plaques don’t follow the usual route. They stay free of dementia for most or all of their long lives. A few people don’t even build plaques, even though some might carry gene variants conferring a high Alzheimer’s risk.

In the brain of a person with Alzheimer’s disease (right), amyloid-β proteins clump into plaques, as shown in a magnetic-resonance-imaging scan.Credit: Mark & Mary Stevens Neuroimaging & Informatics Inst./SPL

In the normal course of disease, the amyloid-β proteins in plaques activate immune cells in the brain known as microglia, which try to clear them. But if active for too long, the microglia become inflammatory and start to damage neurons. This, along with other cellular stresses, promotes the build-up and spread of a different, deadlier type of protein, called tau, which forms long, thin tangles. These tangles correlate with the development and severity of dementia symptoms.

Although lifestyle and environmental factors can affect the likelihood of developing the disease, the most powerful influence is genetics.

The exact mechanistic details of how plaques lead to symptoms are still unclear. Gene variants that either accelerate or slow disease could affect many pathways. One such pathway might relate directly to clearance of toxic amyloids or spreading of tau, but could also be acting indirectly, by affecting energy systems in brain cells, for example. “That’s why it is important to identify these variants and discover their exact mechanisms,” says Holstege, who is at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

The search for gene mutations that contribute to the risk of Alzheimer’s goes back decades. A small number of Alzheimer’s cases are strongly hereditary, involving mutations in genes that result in a higher proportion of stickier, toxic forms of amyloid-β proteins. Just one copy of any of these mutated genes almost inevitably leads to disease development early in adult life, most often when someone is in their 40s or 50s.

How to avoid dementia — what the science really says

However, familial early-onset Alzheimer’s accounts for fewer than 1% of all cases; most cases affect people over 65. The APOE gene is the most important genetic determinant of the late-onset form of disease. The protein it encodes, ApoE, is central to lipid transport between cells and around the body. If it does its job properly, it can help to prevent amyloid build-up and clear it from the brain; it can also influence tau pathology, partly through effects on microglia.

Three main alleles of the gene exist, which generate a spectrum of risk. The alleles differ from each other in only one or two nucleotide positions. APOE3 is the most common variant. APOE4 dials the risk up and is the greatest genetic risk factor known. “The particular nucleotide substitution makes the protein it encodes more likely to aggregate and less likely to do its day job of transporting lipids,” says Bu. APOE2 dials the risk down: two copies can delay onset of Alzheimer’s by a decade. Only about 1% of the population has two copies of APOE2.

But however notable the effects of APOE alleles, the vast majority of late-onset Alzheimer cases result from the combined effects of many, often rare, gene variants — some increasing and others reducing disease risk — as well as short stretches of DNA that influence how much each gene is expressed.

Scientists have so far identified only part of the genetic contribution to Alzheimer’s risk. They think that the missing genetics — including numerous but rare variants — might hold some of the most biologically informative clues about resilience.

A controversial Alzheimer’s surgery is said to reverse symptoms — here’s what scientists know

The usual way to search for variants is in genome-wide association studies (GWAS), in which scientists analyse millions of spots on the genome for differences between groups — for example, those with disease or at high risk of disease, compared with those who are disease-free or cognitively resilient. These spots are called single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). A SNP can act as a flag for a stretch of DNA that looks different in high-risk individuals than in those who are cognitively resilient.

To search for extremely rare resilience genes, you need sequences from huge numbers of people and sensitive identification techniques. Both have improved in the past decade or so. Hundreds of thousands of genomes from people with and without Alzheimer’s are available from sources such as UK Biobank. “The more people you look at, the more likely you are to spot very rare occurrences,” says Michael Greicius, a geneticist at Stanford University in California.

New cohorts are being put together all the time, and those that include people of Asian, African and other ancestry show significant differences in Alzheimer’s risk genetics compared with predominantly European-ancestry cohorts1.

Greicius’s team has found a rare protective variant known as W276C in a population of people with Native American ancestry, which has not been seen in the other cohorts2. “There’s an incredible amount of power in ancestrally diverse data sets that we miss completely when we myopically focus on European ancestry,” he says.

Once candidate resilience variants have been identified in human genetic studies, scientists begin the lengthy task of working out whether — and how — they might affect disease biology. They mutate these genes in mice or cell cultures and also look for cells or biological pathways that have been affected in donated brain tissue.

A dozen or so rare gene variants have now been verified in this way as likely contributors to Alzheimer’s resilience, although the strength of evidence varies greatly between them. APOE itself has produced some of the clearest examples. Three extremely rare variants of APOE3 have been found in people who seem to escape Alzheimer’s, and one variant of APOE4 seems to neutralize the risk usually carried by that form. All of them are gold dust for scientists. “These rare variants hold the key to understanding how the common risk variants do what they do,” says biochemist Rosie Jackson at the University of Dundee, UK.

The changes to the protein might be tiny, but the consequences are huge. They all affect how the ApoE protein binds to molecules.

ApoE is shaped a bit like a hairpin (see ‘Protective protein’). One arm has surfaces that attract and carry lipids. Once a lipid is bound, the protein opens up and reshapes itself around it. The other arm binds to receptors on cells, allowing those cells to ingest ApoE and use its lipid cargo. These receptors can also take up tau and contribute to its spread between cells.

Sources: T. Kanekiyo et al. Neuron 81, 740–754 (2014); H.-J. Moon et al. Front. Mol. Neurosci. 17, 1399965 (2024).

There are three rare variants found in the APOE3 allele. One is known as the Christchurch variant (after the city in New Zealand in which it was discovered) and it affects the receptor-binding region of the ApoE protein. It is thought to bind ApoE less strongly to receptors, making tau less likely to spread.

The other two rare APOE3 variants influence the lipid-binding section, probably making the protein less sticky and less likely to clump and form plaques.

A troubling reality hangs over the United Nations climate conference (COP31) opening in Turkey today: overshoot. For the first time, the annual meeting of the world’s countries to hash out action on climate change must face the fact that it is now inevitable for global temperatures to exceed the 1.5 °C warming limit pledged in the Paris Agreement. Call it ‘the overshoot COP’. “We need to first recognize that global policy has failed. This is a moment of self-critique,” says climate scientist Johan Rockström.

James Dinneen, Nature reporter

Environmental journalist Fiona Harvey, who has been to almost every UN climate conference for more than 20 years, asks: what’s the point of COP? “The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein,” she writes. The Paris agreement itself has “reached an impasse”, not least because of the withdrawal of the United States. But China — the world’s biggest carbon emitter — is more engaged in multinational negotiations than ever, partly because of its huge stake in green technologies such as solar panels. And the impact of the UN process is everywhere, from the rise of electric cars to the energy transformation. “Any time you have a consensus decision, it sends a signal,” says Sue Biniaz, a former US climate negotiator. “These days with the geopolitics of the world — if something can be agreed by the whole world, it’s impactful.”

The Guardian | 15 min read

The estimated increase in peak warming this century that will be caused by the United States abandoning its net-zero target under President Donald Trump’s administration, if US policies don’t change. (Nature | 8 min read, from October)

A new artificial-intelligence system enables researchers to enhance the performance of robotic equipment in their labs. In the process, scientists describe their research programme and lab set-up to the AI agents, which generate step-by-step experimental protocols for the lab’s robots. The system can also generate a virtual version of the lab in which to test its suggestions, and even devise a new floor plan that optimizes the placement of lab robots and equipment. The “very cool” concept could drastically reduce the effort required to set up automated labs, says bioengineer Evan Collins.

Reference: arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed)

People seem to find conversations more enjoyable if they contain more pink noise — sound in which there is equal energy per octave of frequency. Researchers analysed 1,000 conversations between strangers and found that participants felt a stronger sense of connection with their partner when their chats had featured more pink noise. The team also found that chats between podcast hosts comprise more pink noise as the series continues, which suggests that making a conversation ‘pinker’ is a skill that can be honed, says psychologist and study co-author Kathryn O’Nell.

A separate research team found that pink noise can also help to kickstart the brain’s ‘wash cycle’ during sleep. They found that timing bursts of pink noise to ‘slow’ brain waves can encourage cerebrospinal fluid to flow through the brain, clearing out any harmful particles that have accumulated during waking hours. The team says that the pink pulses might activate a particular kind of slow wave that silences distractions.

The Guardian | 4 min read & Scientific American | 4 min read

Reference: Science Advances paper & Science Translational Medicine paper

In his new book, On the Equality of All Things, physicist Carlo Rovelli writes that fundamental physics is overrated. “It’s great science,” he tells Nature. “But stop thinking that it is the root of everything else.” Physics also has a hubris problem, he says, which can lead to wild goose chases for evidence of phenomena that aren’t real. Discoveries in quantum mechanics and general relativity have brought us to the cusp of fresh conceptual breakthroughs, but it might take some time for a coherent picture to emerge from the noise, he says.

Compared to the dangers of extreme weather, “little attention has been given to what happens when El Niño disrupts food supplies, affects what people eat and potentially changes their exposure to infectious disease,” argue economist Eoin McLaughlin and management scholar Matthias Beck. “One advantage with El Niño is that there is plenty of warning,” they note, urging governments and agencies to prepare for the weather pattern’s possible effects on food and health systems.

Some men looking for emotional support are turning to commercial chatbots and specially designed AI apps, partly because of the stigma around traditional mental health treatment. “You don’t have to make an appointment. You don’t have to go sit in a waiting room. You don’t have to even really explicitly take that initial step to ask for help,” notes psychiatrist Michael Heinz. But is therapy-like discussion with an AI system better than no therapy at all? “I think [AI app] founders have to realize therapy does have a rate of harm,” says psychiatrist John Torous, who specializes in digital mental health. “You need some rules of the road.”

STAT | 17 min read (free registration required)
