https://www.space.com/astronomy/mars/cur.title: Curiosity Mars rover sizes up new 'Nazca' dig site | Space photo of the day for Nov. 10, 2026
https://www.space.com/astronomy/mars/cur.author: Robert Lea
https://www.space.com/astronomy/mars/cur.text:
The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of Nazca as thoroughly as possible before drilling.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Curiosity Mars rover is sizing up its next dig site on the Red Planet.

The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of the Mars site, informally named "Nazca," as thoroughly as possible before drilling into it.

Curiosity snapped the close-up image on Oct. 18, 2026, using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI). The image shows multiple roughly disk-shaped potential crystal formations at the rover's next drill target.

MAHLI is located on the turret at the end of the rover's robotic arm. It uses an onboard focusing process to make a composite of images of the same target acquired at different positions to focus on multiple features in a single image.

Scientists theorize that the "discs and needles" texture takes its characteristic shape as crystals, or "crystal forms," grow.

The relatively large sizes of the crystal forms at "Nazca" may provide clues about the temperatures at which they grew, as well as information about the abundance of salts and fluids in the area at the time. Complicating this picture, however, is the fact that mineral crystals can be replaced by other minerals after their original crystallization. The new minerals are known as "pseudomorphs," because they have the same shape as the original minerals but not the same composition or molecular structure.

The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of Nazca — which shares its name with an ancient South American civilization that's famous for the large designs it etched into the rock and dirt — before drilling begins. The NASA researchers will then be able to compare the deeper composition to the surface-level composition.

He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. https://www.space.com/stargazing/skywatc.title: See the first images from the new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus — a smart telescope aimed at beginners
https://www.space.com/stargazing/skywatc.author: Jamie Carter
https://www.space.com/stargazing/skywatc.text:
While rivals announce increasingly expensive smart telescopes, ZWO’s new Seestar S30 Plus makes galaxy and nebula photography surprisingly affordable.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As rival makers announce increasingly ambitious smart telescopes, ZWO has taken a different approach. Its new Seestar S30 Plus launched today and is available for $474 from Seestar’s website and Amazon
, just in time for Christmas. Better still, we’ve been using it for a month and can bring you a first look.

Announced a few months after the flagship Seestar S50 Pro and replacing the now-discontinued Seestar S30, the new Seestar S30 Plus retains its 30mm aperture and compact chassis, but upgrades to four-element apochromatic optics with extra-low dispersion (ED) glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras.

It has a 1.2-inch (30 mm) aperture, two 3.7 MP cameras and four-element apochromatic optics bundled into a compact build.

Both produce 1,440 x 2,560-pixel images, while a much-improved 43.5-degree wide-angle camera can capture the Milky Way, constellations, star trails and nightscapes. Built-in filters, a mosaic mode and equatorial (EQ) tracking add considerable deep-sky astrophotography potential.

For a telescope weighing just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg), it’s impressive. It easily fits into a camera bag and could happily live on a bookshelf.

I’ve already photographed the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Pleiades (M45), the Dumbbell Nebula (M27) and the North America Nebula (NGC 7000). The results are excellent for such a small instrument, especially when imaging nebulas with its built-in dual-band filter, which helps reduce light pollution.

The Seestar app adds new in-app post-processing options, so you don’t have to mess around with any of that — though you can also export everything as lossless FITS files. The S30 Plus also includes a magnetic solar filter, enabling you to indulge in solar photography safely.

With Dwarflab’s $1,299 Draco (3.5-inch/90mm aperture) recently landed in stores and Vaonis’ own $4,990 Atlas (3.1-inch/80mm aperture) not available until 2027, ZWO’s decision to offer an upgraded entry-level smart telescope that buyers can get their hands on right now looks particularly smart.

With ZWO's pattern of delivering cheaper smart telescopes without sacrificing on quality, the Seestar S30 Plus could be one of Christmas 2026’s best gifts for anyone interested in astronomy — and maybe that’s the point of it. Either way, first impressions are good. A full review is coming tomorrow, so check back at Space.com to find out our full thoughts and testing.

https://www.space.com/stargazing/solar-e.title: Total solar eclipse 2027 vs 2028 — Which one should you choose, Egypt or Australia?
https://www.space.com/stargazing/solar-e.author: Jamie Carter
https://www.space.com/stargazing/solar-e.text:
From six minutes of darkness in Egypt or totality over the Australian Outback, here are the pros and cons of the next two total solar eclipses.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For those who want to experience a total solar eclipse, the next two years present the best kind of problem. On Aug. 2, 2027, the so-called "eclipse of the century" will sweep across southern Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, bringing more than six minutes of totality to parts of Egypt. Then, on July 22, 2028, another exceptionally long total solar eclipse will cross Australia, putting the remote Outback and Sydney Harbor in the path of the moon's dark central shadow before it reaches New Zealand's beautiful South Island.

Both eclipses will be spectacular, and both will require careful planning, yet they promise very different experiences. The 2027 event combines over six minutes of totality with some of the very best weather prospects possible, while 2028 offers over five minutes of totality above some of the world's most famous wildernesses and cityscapes.

Eclipse chasing requires careful planning and dedication, but also significant funds. If you can only choose one, which should it be?

On paper, 2027 is difficult to beat. Maximum totality on Aug. 2 will last about 6 minutes, 23 seconds, making it the longest totality on land since 1991 and until 2114. The path of totality will cross southern Spain and Gibraltar before sweeping across Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Sudan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Somalia and the Chagos Islands. About 88.9 million people live in its path, according to Time and Date. It will dominate the news for weeks.

For Europeans, southern Spain is the obvious easy option. Tarifa, at the country's southern tip, will see about 4 minutes, 39 seconds of totality, while the U.K. Overseas Territory of Gibraltar gets about 4 minutes, 25 seconds. Travel farther east and the duration increases, with Sfax in Tunisia getting around 5 minutes, 41 seconds and locations in Egypt experiencing more than six minutes. Weather prospects generally improve, too, as the path crosses the deserts of North Africa.

Egypt is the headline destination. Luxor will see about 6 minutes, 20 seconds of totality near midday, with Karnak Temple, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the world's greatest ancient monuments nearby. The climatic odds are excellent, with clouds extremely rare in early August. That combination of a very long totality, ancient landscapes and a very high probability of a clear sky makes 2027's path of totality highly unusual.

But there are downsides. Temperatures around Luxor can exceed 105°F (41°C) in August, a dust storm is not impossible, and totality occurs shortly after 1 p.m. when the sun (and moon) will be high overhead — making photography very difficult. Demand is already intense, making organized trips expensive. Spain will be considerably easier and probably cheaper for European eclipse chasers, but at the expense of roughly two minutes of totality — and slightly less favorable weather prospects.

If 2027 is about extreme duration, 2028 is about choice. On July 22, 2028, a path of totality will cross the Cocos Islands, Christmas Island, Australia, from northwest to southeast — passing directly over Sydney — before continuing across the Tasman Sea to New Zealand's South Island. That's about 6.3 million people, according to Time and Date. This will be an exclusive eclipse experienced by relatively few people, certainly when compared to the eclipses in 2024, 2026 and 2027.

Maximum totality will last 5 minutes and 10 seconds in the remote Kimberley region of Western Australia. That's more than a minute shorter than 2027, but still exceptionally long by total solar eclipse standards (most last about two minutes). More importantly, the Australian Outback has excellent climatic prospects. Historical cloudiness on July 22 is around 8% at Purnululu (Bungle Bungles) close to the point of greatest eclipse in Western Australia and 19% at Karlu Karlu (Devil's Marbles) in the Northern Territory, making Australia's interior an attractive destination for serious eclipse chasers. Temperatures will be around 86°F (30°C) in July.

Then there's Sydney. Australia's largest city will experience about 3 minutes, 45 seconds of totality, its first total solar eclipse since 1857. Sydney Opera House and Harbor Bridge beneath a totally eclipsed sun could produce some of the decade's defining astronomical images, while millions of people experiencing totality together should create an extraordinary atmosphere. Temperatures will be around 62.6°F (17°C).

A compromise is weather. Historical cloudiness in Sydney is around 43%, which is good odds for most eclipses — and July is known for clear weather. But in 2028, anyone prioritizing their chances of a clear totality will be tempted by a (albeit pricier) trip to the Outback. For Europeans, reaching Australia also comes with considerable cost and time. The huge number of hotels in Sydney could keep accommodation relatively competitive, but the long flight means it makes little sense to travel there for only a few days. For many international eclipse chasers, 2028 will naturally become an expensive one- or two-week trip.

There's another reason to think beyond those few minutes of darkness. With the right planning, an eclipse trip can also become an extraordinary astronomy vacation (tip: come a week before the eclipse for the darkest evening skies). Here, 2028 offers visitors from Europe and North America something very different — the Southern Hemisphere night sky.

July is a superb time to see the bright central regions of the Milky Way from dark locations in Australia. The Southern Cross, or Crux, is one of the southern sky's defining sights, with Alpha and Beta Centauri nearby. Omega Centauri, the largest and brightest globular cluster visible from Earth, is another showpiece, while the Eta Carinae region offers one of the richest sections of the Milky Way for binoculars and small telescopes.

There are other reasons to extend the trip. A partial lunar eclipse occurs on July 6-7, 2028, while the Southern Delta Aquariid meteor shower peaks around July 28 — a week after the eclipse, during a first-quarter moon — and is particularly well seen from the Southern Hemisphere. Add Australia's world-class dark skies, and a trip into the Outback could become as much about stargazing as the eclipse itself.

The 2027 eclipse has fewer night-sky extras. The Delta Aquariid meteor shower peaks a few days before the eclipse — in dark, moonless skies — while Jupiter will dominate the western sky shortly after sunset. However, anyone traveling from the Northern Hemisphere will largely see a familiar celestial hemisphere. Australia offers a genuinely different sky experience.

Perhaps the most useful way to choose between these eclipses is not to compare their durations, but to imagine where you would most like to be when the moon's shadow arrives.

In 2027, the decision largely comes down to how far along the eclipse track you want to travel. Stay in southern Spain for convenience and around four minutes of totality, head into Tunisia for longer totality and excellent weather prospects, or go all-in on Egypt for more than six minutes beneath almost cloudless desert skies — and bragging rights among eclipse chasers. It's an eclipse that can be combined with beaches, Roman ruins, North African cities or the temples and, of course, the tombs of ancient Egypt.

In 2028, the contrast is even greater. Sydney offers a communal total solar eclipse — a busy "we eclipse" — with millions watching daylight disappear above one of the world's great cities. Head thousands of miles away into the Australian interior and the same event becomes a lonely "me eclipse" in the wilderness, with up to five minutes of totality above an immense Outback landscape. Continue to New Zealand, and there's yet another possibility — a shorter totality with the sun much lower in the afternoon sky.

If your priority is purely totality duration, 2027 marginally wins. More than six minutes of totality combined with extraordinarily reliable weather is a rare combination. There's a good reason Aug. 2, 2027 is being marketed as the "eclipse of the century." But if you've always wanted to visit Australia or New Zealand, the 2028 eclipse is an extraordinary excuse to finally go, in addition to experiencing a long totality.

Choose the trip you most want to take, then find the best possible place for you within the path of totality. After all, no total solar eclipse lasts long enough, and most eclipse chasers struggle to recall exactly how long totality lasted. They're just left with the same question as always — when is the next one?

He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

https://www.space.com/astronomy/mars/nas.title: NASA's twin ESCAPADE Mars probes slingshot around Earth in unprecedented double 'gravity assist'
https://www.space.com/astronomy/mars/nas.author: Meghan Bartels
https://www.space.com/astronomy/mars/nas.text:
"No NASA mission has ever done this before."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Twin NASA spacecraft are wrapping up a year-long escapade, ready to make a beeline to the Red Planet.

The Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE) spacecraft launched in November 2025 on the second-ever flight of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket. But rather than head straight to Mars, the two spacecraft dawdled through a looping trajectory. Now, they are back in Earth's neighborhood where they tackled a crucial engine burn unusually close to Earth that — if all goes well — will set them on track for Mars.

"No NASA mission has ever done this before," said Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley and principal investigator of the ESCAPADE mission. "For most missions, it just isn't necessary."

That's because traditionally NASA's Mars missions have been carefully choreographed within cosmic launch constraints, leaving Earth during a brief window of planetary alignment that only occurs every 26 months. ESCAPADE was meant to launch in October 2024, when Earth and Mars were favorably aligned, but delays with the New Glenn rocket forced the mission to sit out the precious launch window.

Rather than wait to launch this fall, NASA decided to try something new. ESCAPADE mission planners designed a "loitering" orbit, shaped like a kidney bean. It called for the twin probes to loop through that trajectory to be back at Earth in early November 2026, ready to continue on to Mars.

Once they arrived, however, the twin probes faced a major hurdle: Each had to perfectly execute an engine burn within Earth's gravity well. The maneuver is similar to the slingshot flybys that spacecraft regularly conduct to adjust their trajectories — but here, the probes had to fire their engines to amp up the effect of the burn rather than acting alone.

The first spacecraft tackled the feat on Nov. 7; the second did so on Monday (Nov. 9). And according to NASA, the burns went perfectly. "This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we've now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days," Asal Naseri, acting associate flight director for NASA's Heliophysics Division said in a statement.

After just a few minor course corrections, ESCAPADE will be sailing toward a September 2027 Mars arrival.

The twin ESCAPADE spacecraft have made the most of their extended tour. Each spacecraft is about the size of two refrigerators and equipped with three scientific instruments and a couple cameras. All are tailored for studying the strange magnetic field of Mars, which is created both globally by charged particles from the sun interacting with the atmosphere and locally by areas of highly magnetic crust.

Earth's magnetic field is much stronger and generated by the planet's core. But it too is affected by the solar wind, as scientists call the constant stream of charged particles flowing off the sun and across space. On the side of Earth opposite the sun, the solar wind stretches the magnetic field to form an elongated tail structure, like a terrestrial windsock.

A range of missions have studied this magnetotail at various points up to nearly 800,000 miles (1.27 million kilometers) away from Earth, but beyond that, it has been a mystery. Conveniently, the two ESCAPADE spacecraft traveled through the structure over the course of about 10 days early last year at a much greater distance from Earth — some 1.19 million miles (1.91 million km) away.

"We were able to capture the magnetic field structure of that distant tail, how it flaps, how it moves, how the plasma flows within it," Lillis said, gathering data that he called "unprecedented." "And not only that but for the first time, we were able to do that with two spacecraft simultaneously."

A second shot at the magnetotail came over the summer, when the spacecraft were much closer to Earth but the moon was also passing through the magnetic structure. The two ESCAPADE spacecraft were able to partner with twin ARTEMIS-THEMIS spacecraft at the moon to observe the structure from four different perspectives simultaneously.

That's a huge boon when trying to study the magnetotail and its intricate and ever-changing magnetic field lines and plasma, Lillis said. "These are generally not things you can measure remotely," he said. "You kind of have to be there."

Meghan Bartels is a freelance science journalist based in New York City who worked on staff for Space.com from 2018 to 2023. Her writing has also appeared in outlets including Scientific American, Science News, Wired, Newsweek and Audubon.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/11/mdca.author: Brittany Trang
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/11/mdca.text:
MDCalc, a medical reference tool site, Wednesday announced the launch of CrossCover, which the company said is meant to help clinicians trust the answers of medical artificial intelligence chatbots while preserving patient and provider privacy.

Graham Walker, head of AI at MDCalc, said the company sees the tool as an accelerator for clinical generative AI. “We can take away some of the challenges and risks and problems with the technology so that physicians can feel more confident in using it,” he said.

CrossCover takes an approach that contradicts that of medical AI tools from OpenEvidence, Abridge, and electronic health record company Epic, which are trying to incorporate an ever-widening repertoire of patient, provider, and payer information into their recommendations. Rather than requiring clinicians to register with their national identification numbers or trying to mitigate risk by brokering privacy agreements that allow clinicians to enter protected patient health information, MDCalc’s tool focuses on stripping out those types of information from clinicians’ queries.

WASHINGTON — Federal officials have granted blanket waivers to every member of an influential, yet little-known federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services, allowing them to serve despite some having clear financial stakes in decisions they might make.

The waivers, signed by a top federal official and obtained by STAT, show a willingness by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s department to overlook financial conflicts of interests, though Kennedy frequently decries corporate influence in health care. In the case of two members, the documents show that they own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care.

Other conflicts being waived include stock holdings in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and employment at public research universities that provide medical care. Some members of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, especially the newer ones, have more extensive conflicts than others.

This past August, Joe Hancock, a Kentucky plumbing and heating contractor, opened a just-delivered box packed with hundreds of sheets of paper. Leafing through them, he read seven words no small business owner wants to see: “A lawsuit has been filed against you.”

The complaint, from air ambulance firm PHI Health, claimed Hancock was on the hook for almost $27,000 in medical helicopter bills. They were tied to one of his now-retired employees, who needed an emergency flight after a heart attack.

Hancock, who owns Whitehead-Hancock Plumbing, Heating & Cooling, a family-run business in Frankfort, Ky., that has been around for more than a century, didn’t understand why he was being roped into a lawsuit that featured 31 other companies — for medical charges he was never aware of.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/11/pick.author: Priya Fielding-Singh and Darcy Cherlin
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/11/pick.text:
As high food costs and cuts to food assistance squeeze families’ budgets, concerns are growing about whether low-income parents will be able to keep putting food on the table.

But these financial pressures threaten to do more than increase hunger. They also risk harming children’s diets and health in the long run — by making nutritious foods not only harder to afford, but also increasingly risky for parents to buy.

To understand why, consider the most universal of parenting frustrations: picky eating. Most parents experience it, but the stakes vary widely. For well-off parents, watching a child push away a helping of vegetables is annoying but manageable. A carrot left untouched one day can simply mean trying again the next.

A former Eli Lilly sales rep filed a lawsuit alleging that she was fired after complaining the company was promoting its Mounjaro diabetes drug to combat weight loss before receiving regulatory approval to do so.

Jennifer Mansion, who was hired as a senior territory manager in Dallas four years ago, claimed that she observed other Lilly sales reps promoting the diabetes drug as a salve for obesity. Mansion also contended that a physician touted Mounjaro as a weight loss option during a luncheon sponsored by the drugmaker, according to the suit filed in federal court in Texas.

Such promotions are known as off-label marketing in the pharmaceutical industry. The phrase refers to promoting a medicine for a usage that was not approved by the Food and Drug Administration. A physician may prescribe a medicine for an unapproved use, but a drugmaker is not permitted to market its drug for that purpose.

Top of the morning to you and a fine one it is. Blue skies, cool breezes, and plenty of chirping birds are enveloping the comfy Pharmalot campus, which is cause to fire up the coffee kettle for yet another cup of stimulation. Our choice today is pistachio. Meanwhile, we have assembled the latest menu of tidbits for you to peruse. We hope you have a wonderful day and please do keep in touch. The Food and Drug Administration approved a Bayer drug to reduce recurrence of stroke, making available the first in a novel class of medications that hold the promise of preventing blood clots more safely, STAT notes. Many blood thinners are not used in this setting due to the increased risk of bleeding, but the drug, which will be sold under the brand name Sunharbo, uses a mechanism that is thought to stop the formation of bad clots without increasing the risk of bleeding. Experts say the data showed a significant advance in an area that has seen little innovation over the past few decades. Secondary strokes are estimated to affect about 20% of people who have had a first stroke and can cause severe disability or death.

The FDA warned that GLP-1 drugs carry a potential risk for a rare but serious eye condition and required pharmaceutical companies to inform patients and doctors of the risk, STAT writes. The condition, called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, is sometimes referred to as an “eye stroke” and is caused by insufficient blood flow to the optic nerve. It typically causes sudden vision loss and, in severe cases, can lead to blindness. There are currently no proven treatments for the condition. The FDA said it started looking into this risk after researchers in 2024 published an observational study linking Ozempic and Wegovy to the eye condition.

https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.author: Ed Silverman
https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.text:
Many large pharmaceutical companies are taking steps to improve access to their medicines in low- and middle-income countries, but progress has been mixed and more action is needed to ensure wide availability, a new analysis found.

Notably, more drugmakers are planning to reach patients before a product launch — access plans now cover 69% of late-stage pipeline candidates compared with 18% in 2018. And across the pipeline, 95% of late-stage experimental drugs developed with a nonprofit partner have an access plan in place, versus 67% without such a partner.

Another bright spot involves cancer treatments. Access plans now cover 65% of cancer drugs in product pipelines, up from 5% in 2018. But 43% of access plans for non-communicable diseases — specifically, sickle cell disease, diabetes, and mental health — focus solely on regulatory registrations and primarily in wealthy countries.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/10/ai-h.title: Opinion: AI’s health advice can be accurate and still make us sicker
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/10/ai-h.author: Jessica Fishman and John L. Jackson Jr.
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/10/ai-h.text:
Artificial intelligence is delivering health guidance at an unprecedented scale. Every week, more than 300 million people ask ChatGPT health questions. Now, the federal government is moving AI deeper into medical care to communicate directly and autonomously with patients. Chris Klomp, the nominee for deputy secretary of Health and Human Services, has called AI in patient care the agency’s “holy grail” for improving the nation’s health.

Government and tech leaders believe AI will benefit us because it is remarkably good at retrieving factual medical information. Although nearly all published safety evaluations focus on accuracy, it is only one dimension of safety. Measuring accuracy cannot detect a subtle form of harm: Even a factually accurate health message can change behavior in ways that make people less healthy.

This is not a hypothetical concern. Accurate public health campaign messages have failed and even backfired when trying to curb binge drinking on college campuses and adolescent drug use. Truthful messages can also discourage vaccination, reinforce smoking, or reduce cancer screenings.

China just announced a new five-year plan that designates biotechnology as a national “pillar industry” and aims to displace the United States as the world’s biotech leader. Those ambitions threaten one of America’s defining competitive advantages — and they demand an urgent response.

America’s biotech sector supports nearly 10 million jobs and over $3 trillion in annual economic activity. It fuels advanced manufacturing growth, ensures our loved ones have access to the newest and most groundbreaking medicines, and strengthens our defenses against pandemics and biological threats. Losing our biotech lead would mean losing a pillar of both our economy and our national security.

Yet biotech innovation also depends on numerous interconnected players — from the university laboratories and startups that often pioneer new research to the trial networks and manufacturing facilities that bring medicines to patients. That means there’s no single policy that will protect our lead. Instead, we need a plan that strengthens every facet of our biotech ecosystem.

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/q-l.title: Q&A: The Long Shadow of Financial Toxicity in Cancer Care
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/q-l.text:
As oncology treatments become more precise and effective, cancer care is also growing harder for many patients to afford. Patients with cancer are at greater risk for adverse financial events than those without cancer, which can include difficulty paying bills, delinquent mortgage payments, foreclosures, and repossessions.

While the term financial toxicity describes the material and psychological costs associated with cancer care, its impact extends far beyond patients’ finances and quality of life: Financial distress has also been consistently associated with treatment nonadherence and poorer outcomes. One study found, for instance, that patients who filed for bankruptcy after a cancer diagnosis had a significantly higher risk for all-cause mortality than similar patients who did not file for bankruptcy (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.79).

For more than a decade, Fumiko Chino, MD, has studied the financial burden of cancer care, including patients’ out-of-pocket costs and how financial toxicity affects quality of life and outcomes. Following a recent talk on financial toxicity at the American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO) 2026 Annual Meeting, Chino spoke with Medscape Medical News about the realities of this burden in cancer care and what clinicians and health systems can do to address it.

“Costs are a side effect, just like any other,” said Chino, radiation oncologist at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston. “We would never start someone on a chemotherapy regimen without warning that they may lose their hair…. Yet, we are routinely putting people on a path for months- or years-long treatment and never warning them that it will cost a fair amount of money, and they may have to make sacrifices in order to afford their care.”

The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.

I wasn’t supposed to be a doctor. I had an unfortunate family diagnosis and death that brought me into medicine.

I was originally an art director of an entertainment company and living my young adult life when my boyfriend (and later husband) was diagnosed with an aggressive cancer. Through his treatment and then after his death from cancer, I was faced with this sort of insufferable cruelty of cancer but also of unaffordable healthcare.

As soon as I found out about research focused on how to try to make treatments more affordable for patients, I said, “This is what I should be doing with my life.”

I went to medical school, in part, to try to find some greater purpose, some meaning in the madness. I realized that my lived experience could potentially help inform this research and help create solutions that could reach patients faster.

The oncology landscape has greatly accelerated in many good ways, meaning that we have treatments that are more personalized to the individual cancer and patient. But these new options come at a literal cost, which are increasingly being pushed onto patients and creating gaps in care.

Financial toxicity can affect one third to half of our patients, depending on the populations we serve.

After a diagnosis, people might make compromises in their care. They might not go to the specialty cancer center that could best serve them because of insurance barriers. They might skip scans or take less of their medications because they can’t afford it.

Even in the survivorship world, people still face financial consequences related to their diagnosis. They may have difficulty obtaining the best health insurance after their diagnosis because they no longer have the same career flexibility. Or they may feel unable to move away from the cancer center where they received treatment because maintaining continuity of care is a priority.

There is also the burden on the family. I was a cancer caregiver. It took me out of the workforce for a decade, first to take care of my husband, then to grieve, and then to figure out how to put my life together. That ended up with me going to medical school, but I did not actually earn a paycheck for about 10 years.

Unfortunately, the US healthcare system is reinforced to increase affordability gaps. We don’t have some of the basic patient protections that other nations have, such as paid medical leave at a national level.

The connection of health insurance to work is important. Let’s say you have a metastatic cancer diagnosis; you have a mandatory waiting period of 6 months for disability and then 2 years to get on Medicare. I’ve had patients who continue to work because they don’t have health insurance if they’re not working — they may not be old enough, or they don’t want to be destitute.

What I’m trying to do now is show the harm of these mandatory waiting periods and insurance churn, which is when you lose one health insurance, get a different one, but then you lose that and get a third one.

These transitions are unfortunately dangerous. We know that people will miss opportunities — they lose their stable care team and miss appointments or medication fills during those time periods. I’m trying to categorize that because I think if you can show the specific harm of a policy in real numbers, it helps to create convincing policy arguments.

Unfortunately, we’re in an era in which trust in healthcare has really taken a hit. While patients may not trust doctors in general, thankfully patients still seem to trust their doctor.

Physicians are also practicing in a world where medical care has gotten so much more complex, and they have a limited amount of time with patients. That ends up being a problem when you have 15 minutes to cover many things, including symptoms, scans, and affordability.

Listening to patients and having that open space for dialogue is so important in terms of building trust, but I think it’s tricky. We know that patients are worried that saying they can’t afford a treatment may mean they’ll receive worse care. That’s why a lot of patients do not introduce the topic of affordability even when they’re having huge affordability barriers.

When I was conducting assessments on willingness to pay for care, patients would also tell me, “I don’t want to answer that question because if I tell you how much I’m willing to pay, that’s how much you’re going to charge me.”

I don’t blame that line of thought because the health system has not been very patient-centered. It’s important that we understand the financial barriers on the patient side as well as concerns and misinformation around that.

We know that younger people, those with preexisting health conditions or more advanced disease, and individuals in marginalized or lower socioeconomic communities are at particular risk for financial toxicity.

We have ideas of who’s at highest risk, but in reality everyone’s at risk for financial toxicity. A patient might not initially have a problem affording care, but treatment can be years or decades long. And if patients can no longer work or have reduced work capacity, they may struggle to afford treatment.

The flipside is simply assuming someone will have problems affording treatment, which can be insulting for patients. Universal screening for financial toxicity sort of eliminates that problem.

The best screening tools can be applied across the board quickly and consistently. For example, the COmprehensive Score for Financial Toxicity is a 12-question financial toxicity assessment tool that takes about 5 minutes to answer. We worked to simplify the cost score to two questions to serve as a screener: “I worry about the financial problems I will have in the future as a result of my illness or treatment,” and “I am satisfied with my current financial situation.”

The purpose of screening is to intervene early, but if there’s no intervention, the screening can actually diminish trust because you have asked questions, identified a need, and then can’t help. That’s why it’s so important for the screening and intervention space to progress alongside each other.

We gather more information and start piloting interventions; healthcare costs continue to rise, meaning progress has been slow. Still, there are several ways to intervene.

On the interpersonal level, periodically checking in with patients via a structured cost conversation is an intervention that may normalize cost conversations and alleviate concerns around expenses, which can change over time.

Essential-needs programs — which may be available within the cancer center, local community, or national charities — can help support patients with assistance with medication, transportation, and/or food; they can also serve as an important patient-facing intervention. Referrals may be needed from providers or social workers.

On the institutional level, financial navigators and the use of robust social work support for patients are very important. Financial navigation programs are not going to make costs zero for people, but I think they can make care more affordable, and that means that more people will get appropriate care.

The biggest gains, however, are made from policy. We did an evaluation and found that states that broadened their eligibility for food stamps had more women complete a mammogram after their eligibility was broadened. I know it sounds insane, but alleviating the burden of something such as food insecurity can help people prioritize their mammograms. These kinds of policy solutions can be really meaningful for patients.

Chino declared having no relevant disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Speaker: ‘Think bigger’ about using AI in lifestyle medicine
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Andrew (Drew) Rhoades; David Donohue, MD, MS, DipABLM, FACLM
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

ORLANDO — AI offers value within lifestyle medicine thanks to its ability to raise practice capacity and lower administrative loads, a speaker at the American College of Lifestyle Medicine’s annual meeting said.

As AI within healthcare continues to expand, patients’ openness to the technology may be underestimated by healthcare professionals, according to a recently released West Health-Gallup survey.

The survey (n = 5,330) showed that across three aspects of clinical care, between 38% to 56% of patients are comfortable with AI use if a provider is involved.

The data also indicated that nearly 90% of providers personally used an AI tool or chatbot for at least one of several work tasks surveyed within the last year — yet just 20% reported receiving any formal training on use in healthcare settings.

This shows “most of us are learning on the job without guardrails,” David Donohue, MD, MS, DipABLM, FACLM, chief medical officer at Progressive Health of Delaware, told Healio.

“That’s why I push clinicians to start safely, with a business associate agreement before any patient data goes in, and then to run one learning loop on one real problem,” he explained. “Since patients are more comfortable than providers, assume when a clinician stays involved, that’s the model we should build toward.”

Healio spoke with Donohue further to learn more about the current and potential use of AI within lifestyle medicine, how the six pillars can guide its utilization and more.

Healio: How has AI been used in lifestyle medicine practice so far?

Donohue: Most clinicians start with AI-assisted clinical searching, ambient scribes and personal productivity, and those help. The bigger opportunity is pointing AI at your own practice data. At Progressive Health of Delaware, we connected a HIPAA-compliant AI assistant to our electronic health record and asked a basic question: how much of the care our patients qualify for do we actually deliver? Across 19 covered preventive and care management services, we delivered 13.6% of the billable value, and we are a prevention-first practice. That audit pointed us toward team-based care management between visits. Later, when collections fell by a third after a billing platform switch, we connected the same assistant to our billing data and found eight separate problems, about $482,000 in claims we had earned and not collected.

Healio: What barriers or challenges within lifestyle medicine could AI help remedy?

Donohue: Lifestyle medicine works, but most patients who would benefit never get enough of it. In a typical practice, perhaps 3% of eligible patients enroll in a lifestyle program, and about half of those attend consistently. Primary care also has a capacity problem: modeling studies estimate one physician would need more than 24 hours a day to deliver all recommended care to a typical panel, and the evidence grows faster than any clinician can keep up with. AI can help on each front. It can follow every patient between visits with check-ins, reminders and coaching, find care gaps across the whole panel, put current evidence at the point of care, and take administrative work off the team so they have time for the human work of behavior change.

Healio: Tips for clinicians who are new to AI or unsure where to begin?

Donohue: Start safely: no patient data goes into any AI product unless a business associate agreement covers it. Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 both offer one. Next, use AI as a strategic partner before big decisions, and ask it to be your toughest critic. Then run what I call the learning loop: assess (measure one problem), plan (devise a solution), build (create the system with the help of AI), implement (put it into daily work with an owner and a start date), then reassess. Pick one problem and run one loop. Before you build anything complex, write a clear spec with a definition of done. And take security seriously, starting with two-factor login everywhere and cyber insurance.

Healio: How can the principles and pillars of lifestyle medicine guide AI use?

Donohue: Our north star is evidence and truth. A model’s first answer tends to reproduce conventional wisdom, so ask for sources and check them, the same way lifestyle medicine has challenged conventional practice. AI should serve the pillars, not replace the people who deliver them. Nutrition, physical activity, sleep, stress management, social connection and avoiding risky substances all depend on sustained behavior change and human relationships. Use AI to free your coaches, dietitians, nurses and clinicians for that work and to keep patients supported between visits, with clinical judgment staying with the clinician.

Healio: Anything else you’d like to add or emphasize?

Donohue: Think bigger. We ask our patients to aim for remission and reversal. I ask clinicians to think bigger about what their practices can achieve, because today’s tools can do far more than most of us ask of them. New Medicare payment helps too: advanced primary care management, the behavioral health integration add-on in 2026, and payment for health and well-being coaching starting in 2027 all create a way to fund team-based lifestyle care between visits. There is so much more opportunity than most people are aware of for delivering primary care lifestyle medicine! I want lifestyle medicine in the room, shaping AI-enabled healthcare around prevention, health restoration and human connection.

David Donohue, MD, MS, DipABLM, FACLM, can be reached at primarycare@healio.com.

https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.title: FDA approves Sunharbo, factor XIa inhibitor for reducing stroke
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.author: Shawn Arrajj
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The FDA has approved Sunharbo, the only approved factor XIa inhibitor intended to reduce the risk for stroke in adults who recently experienced a non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk transient ischemic attack.

With the approval, physicians now have a treatment option that can lower patient risk for secondary stroke, which can come with more severe outcomes than incident strokes, said Ashkan Shoamanesh, MD, senior scientist with the Population Health Research Institute at Hamilton Health Sciences and McMaster University.

“For those who survive a stroke, the risk of another potentially devastating event is highest in the days and weeks after the initial event, and that risk persists over time,” Shoamanesh said in a press release from Bayer.

Roughly one in 10 stroke survivors will experience a secondary stroke within 1 year, while one in five will experience a secondary stroke within 5 years, according to the release.

As a factor XIa inhibitor, Sunharbo (asundexian, Bayer) works by reducing the amplification of thrombin generation. For patients who recently experienced stroke, it is meant to reduce thrombosis while having a smaller effect on normal blood clotting, according to the release.

Sunharbo will be available as a once-daily 50 mg tablet. It is designed to work alongside antiplatelet therapy, according to the release.

The drug previously received an FDA fast track designation for secondary stroke prevention. The full FDA approval follows Bayer’s phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE study, in which researchers randomly assigned 12,327 patients (mean age = 68 years, 33.3% female) to Sunharbo (n = 6,162) or placebo (n = 6,165).

Participants had each recently experienced either a non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA) and were assigned to a group within 72 hours of symptom onset. Both Sunharbo and placebo groups also received antiplatelet therapy.

Over a median treatment of 14.2 months, Sunharbo met the primary efficacy and safety endpoints for secondary stroke prevention, Healio previously reported. It reduced the risk for recurrent stroke by 26%, and it did not raise the risk for major bleeding.

However, the risk for major bleeding was higher in the Sunharbo group for patients older than age 75 years (2.6 per 100 patient-years in the Sunharbo group vs. 1.7 per 100 patient-years in the placebo group) and during the first 90 days of treatment (4.5 per 100 patient-years vs. 3.1 per 100 patient-years), according to the press release.

Those in the Sunharbo group also saw lower risk for secondary outcomes compared with placebo, including ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, a composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infraction or stroke, and a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infraction or stroke. The results were primarily driven by the reduction in risk for ischemic stroke, Bayer officials said.

The most frequently reported adverse reaction in the Sunharbo group was diarrhea, which was experienced by 3.4% of participants, compared with 2.8% of placebo, according to the release.

The rate of gastrointestinal bleeding was also higher in the Sunharbo group at 2.7 incidents per 100 patient-years, which compared with a rate of 2.1 incidents per 100 patient-years in placebo (HR = 1.3; 95% CI, 1–1.6). A total of 74% of GI bleeding events in the Sunharbo group were considered clinically relevant non-major or minor bleeding, according to Bayer.

Sunharbo is not recommended for patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment, according to a press release from the FDA.

Sunharbo is expected to begin shipping in mid-to-late November, Bayer said in its release. The drug is currently under review by the European Medicines Agency and Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare.

Disclosures: Healio could not confirm relevant financial disclosures at the time of publication.

https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/2.title: Can teddy bears help normalize medical devices for children?
https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/2.author: Sara Kellner
https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

SAN DIEGO — Physicians at Mayo Clinic developed a program to encourage medical students to pursue pediatrics as well as benefit children in their care.

An advocacy project at Mayo Clinic called The Teddy Bear Clinic had two goals: reducing stigma around medical devices for children, and recruiting medical students to pediatric residency programs, according to Anders C. Jenson, MD, a pediatric resident at the hospital.

“I am passionate about pediatrics, and I wanted to encourage other students in my class at Mayo Clinic to apply to pediatrics,” Jenson told Healio. “I’m well aware that we need more pediatricians, so this is important for me to raise awareness of that need.”

For the teddy bear project, Jenson and colleagues secured a $2,200 internal grant from Mayo Clinic to purchase 200 teddy bears. Then they reached out to manufacturers of pacemakers and tracheostomy tubes asking for donated devices.

“They were all expired, so they were not going to be used for medical treatment,” Jenson said. “The companies were very generous in donating them to our project.”

They also purchased beach ball inflation valves to simulate gastrostomy tubes.

Using expired suturing kits from the ED, Jenson said the team invited medical students to practice suturing the devices onto the teddy bears.

“It’s giving medical students a low-stakes, low-pressure environment to practice some medical skills that they’ll certainly use throughout their training,” Jenson told reporters at the AAP National Conference and Exhibition.

He told Healio it will “also give them exposure to play therapy, one of the beauties of pediatrics.”

After making the teddy bears, Jenson and colleagues partnered with their inpatient services at the hospital to distribute them to children with medical devices.

“The idea is that the child has a teddy bear that looks like them,” Jenson told reporters. “It’s something they can’t go to the regular store and buy, but also something to reduce the stigma.”

Jenson added that the project was inexpensive and scalable, so he hopes other hospitals will try something similar to benefit patients and medical students.

Anders C. Jenson, MD, can be reached at pediatrics@healio.com.

Jenson AC. The Teddy Bear Clinic: A therapeutic play intervention to normalize pediatric medical devices. Presented at: AAP National Conference & Exhibition; Oct. 2-6, 2026; San Diego.

Disclosures: Jenson reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Q&A: How providers can use media to ‘be part of the solution’
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom; Christopher M. Colbert, DO, LTC, FAAEM, FACOEP, FACEP
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

LAS VEGAS — Sometimes trading in a stethoscope for a microphone can make a meaningful impact on patients that healthcare providers never even meet, according to a speaker here.

Christopher M. Colbert, DO, LTC, FAAEM, FACOEP, FACEP, an emergency medicine physician and medical media contributor, discussed the unique opportunity that media presents and how to navigate that journey while maintaining integrity.

Healio spoke with Colbert to learn more about his experiences with media, his advice for providers who want to get involved and more.

Healio: Why is this an important topic for healthcare providers to know about? How can various types of media affect the healthcare profession?

Colbert: Patients no longer obtain their medical information exclusively from their physicians. They’re learning about medicine through TikTok, podcasts, television, news outlets and shows like ‘The Pitt.’ And that’s not necessarily a bad thing!

Programs like “The Pitt” provide a unique opportunity to introduce the public to the complexity, humanity and sometimes absolute chaos of emergency medicine. They can highlight overcrowding, physician burnout, nursing shortages, healthcare disparities and the difficult decisions we make every day.

However, entertainment and journalism also shape patient expectations. What someone watches on television tonight may influence what they expect from their emergency physician tomorrow.

My perspective: Media doesn’t just report on medicine. It influences how patients perceive medicine, how they trust us and, ultimately, how they interact with our healthcare system.

Healio: How can providers get involved in the media to ensure they have a role in how the general public sees and understands the system, its flaws, what it gets right, etc.?

Colbert: First, recognize that you don’t need to be Dr. Sanjay Gupta to make a difference. You need three things: credibility, communication and consistency.

Start locally. Reach out to your hospital’s communications department, local television stations, radio programs or community publications. Offer your expertise on topics relevant to the public. Seasonal illnesses, emergency preparedness, public health concerns or even correcting misinformation can be excellent starting points.

My own transition began in early 2020, when I helped organize and moderate a national virtual emergency medicine conference. That experience helped me recognize that the communication skills we develop as educators and physicians can translate directly to the media. The same skills we use to explain a complicated diagnosis to a patient can help us explain a complicated healthcare issue to thousands of viewers.

And remember, the goal isn’t to become famous. The goal is to become useful.

Healio: What can emergency medicine physicians uniquely contribute to the media?

Colbert: I often describe emergency medicine physicians as the canaries in the coal mine of American healthcare.

We see the consequences of healthcare policy, public health failures, misinformation, and gaps in access to care before many other specialties.

We see patients who cannot afford their medications, patients without primary care, families struggling to navigate insurance, and people who waited too long to seek medical attention.

And unlike many other specialties, we treat everyone, regardless of age, income, insurance or background.

Emergency physicians also possess something particularly valuable in media: the ability to communicate complex information quickly, accurately and under pressure. Our unique contribution is perspective. We don’t just understand the science of medicine; we witness the human consequences of healthcare decisions.

Healio: What has your experience been like as someone who has had conversations like this on a big stage?

Colbert: It’s been an incredibly rewarding and sometimes humbling experience.

I’ve spent much of my career in academic emergency medicine, teaching residents, medical students, and physicians at national and international conferences.

I’ve also had the privilege of serving as a lieutenant colonel in the United States Army Reserve, practicing medicine across multiple countries and experiencing healthcare systems under very different circumstances.

But transitioning from academic lectures and peer-reviewed publications to television, radio and publications such as GQ and Men’s Health taught me something important: Being knowledgeable about medicine and being able to communicate about medicine are two very different skills. In academics, I may have 45 minutes and 40 PowerPoint slides to explain a concept. On television, I might have 45 seconds.

What I’ve enjoyed most is the opportunity to reach people who might never attend a medical conference or read a medical journal. I’ve discussed topics ranging from infectious diseases and vaccination to healthcare access, military medicine, and public health. The audience may change, but the responsibility remains the same.

Healio: What is your advice for anyone who wants to get involved in media as a healthcare professional?

And one additional piece of advice: learn to communicate in sound bites without sacrificing the science. If you cannot explain your message in 30 seconds, you may need to simplify the message — not the medicine.

Healio: What is the take-home message here?

Colbert: Physicians must recognize that communication is no longer simply part of practicing medicine. It is part of protecting medicine. We spend years learning how to diagnose disease, interpret research and treat patients. Yet increasingly, our patients are making healthcare decisions based on information they encounter before they ever meet us. That creates both a challenge and an extraordinary opportunity.

We can complain about misinformation, unrealistic expectations and the public’s changing trust in healthcare — or we can become part of the solution. We need more credible physician voices in journalism, television, podcasts and digital media. Not because every physician needs a television appearance, but because every patient deserves access to trustworthy medical information.

The future of healthcare communication should not happen without healthcare professionals participating in it.

Healio: Is there anything else you would like to add?

Colbert: One of my favorite expressions is, “All roads lead to the ER.” Whether we’re discussing infectious diseases, healthcare legislation, social determinants of health, mental health, or even something someone saw on TikTok, eventually many of those conversations find their way into an emergency department. And that’s why emergency physicians have such an important voice.

Throughout my career, from Chicago emergency departments to military deployments around the world, I’ve learned that proximity gives perspective. When you’re close enough to see how healthcare decisions affect real people, you develop a responsibility to share what you’ve learned. I’ve also learned that we often gain as much insight into humanity from our patients as they gain medical knowledge from us.

My hope is that more physicians recognize that their expertise doesn’t have to end when they remove their white coats or finish their shifts. Sometimes, the most meaningful contribution we can make is helping someone we’ve never met better understand their health. And if that means trading my stethoscope for a microphone every once in a while, I’m more than happy to do it!

Christopher M. Colbert, DO, LTC, FAAEM, FACOEP, FACEP, can be reached on Instagram @Drchris.er.

Disclosures: Colbert reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/beauty-lo.title: Longevity is the beauty industry’s most powerful claim—and its weakest link
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/beauty-lo.author: Sindhya Valloppillil
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/beauty-lo.text:
Longevity has become the beauty industry’s most powerful claim and its most consequential bet. The industry is selling something far more ambitious than anti-aging: the idea that skincare can intervene in the biology of aging itself. It transcends an evolution of marketing language; it’s a structural shift that changes how beauty is researched, organized, priced, and, ultimately, who gets to own the category.

L’Oréal and Estée Lauder are shifting their focus from anti-aging skincare to longevity, positioning aging as a biological process that can be measured and influenced, but pursuing different strategies.

L’Oréal’s strategy is broad and data-driven. Its Longevity Integrative Science platform is anchored by its proprietary Longevity AI Cloud ™, which the company says analyzes over 260 biomarkers using a framework of twelve hallmarks of aging to predict how ingredients affect skin biology. L’Oréal applied this research to its Cell BioPrint Skin Age Test and Lancôme Absolue Longevity products. It pairs DNA-derived ingredients such as PDRN with mitochondrial repair claims.

Estée Lauder’s strategy is narrower, luxury-led and built on proprietary research and clinical studies. Its Skin Longevity Institute focuses sirtuin biology, energy-boosting delivery systems and academic collaborations. It repositioned Re-Nutriv around its SIRTIVITY-LP™ technology, based on over 40 patents, and claims improvements in visible skin age, citing two peer-reviewed clinical papers examining a skincare regimen and a facial age assessment model.

Across the market, brands are converging on the same premise: skincare can influence how skin ages at the cellular level. Luxury moved first with the most conviction. Guerlain promises measurable gains in cellular vitality. Tatcha reframes barrier health as long-term cellular performance.

Mass and clinical brands are following suit. Nivea promotes epigenetic “resetting.” OneSkin claims to reduce biological age by targeting senescent cells. Paula’s Choice has a Skin Longevity Guide and guides customers to optimize their “skin healthspan” with its CellularYouth™ Age Disrupting Longevity Serum.

Ingredient stories mirror the positioning. Terms drawn from geroscience such as sirtuin activators and NAD+ boosters sit at the center of product claims. Longevity reframes skincare from aesthetic maintenance to biological optimization, promising visible improvement and cellular intervention. This redefines what the category claims to do, and it structurally repositions skincare as applied biology. That repositioning introduces a new requirement: proof.

In medicine, longevity has a precise meaning: extending lifespan while improving healthspan, which is the years lived in good health, free from chronic disease and functional decline. Skincare borrows the language of cellular longevity to elevate cosmetic outcomes, blurring the distinction between looking younger and biologically aging more slowly. That gap is where the credibility problem begins.

“In longevity medicine, the goal is healthy life extension, measured by tools like health-adjusted life expectancy and quality-adjusted life years — population-level outcomes that take years or decades to demonstrate,” says David Barzilai, MD, PhD, founder of Barzilai Longevity Consulting and a Harvard Medical School Lecturer. “When the same vocabulary travels into a category that operates on weeks of topical use, the words begin to mean different things. The brands that navigate this well will be the ones that get specific about what their product actually does, at what level of biology, on what timeframe, and with what evidence.”

That bar is higher than most brands are meeting. Aging is driven by interconnected biological processes researchers call the “hallmarks of aging”: cellular senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation and others. These processes are influenced by metabolic health, environmental exposures and lifestyle. But demonstrating that a skincare ingredient affects pathways does not establish that it slows biological aging or extends healthspan.

In clinical dermatology, longevity has a more specific meaning, linked to inflammaging, oxidative stress and tissue regeneration. These mechanisms affect skin function, not just appearance. Research increasingly frames skin health within longitudinal care models that connect skin aging with functional health and quality of life. The emerging science of skin longevity is legitimate, but understanding the biological processes that influence skin aging does not establish that every product marketed around them can meaningfully alter them.

Many beauty platforms position AI-driven skin analysis as biological insight. Using selfies, subjective prompts in quizzes and pattern recognition trained on visual datasets, they evaluate surface features such as wrinkles, pigmentation and texture, then provide personalized recommendations. They are effective engagement tools, but they do not measure biological aging.

These platforms do not offer sub-surface imaging or independently assess internal drivers of skin aging: hormonal shifts, inflammation, nutrient status, metabolic health, chronic stress. Surface analysis can track how skin looks. It cannot explain how or why it’s aging.

More advanced approaches are beginning to move beyond surface inference toward direct biological measurement. Tape-strip diagnostics, such as L’Oréal’s Cell BioPrint, analyze protein biomarkers, while sub-surface imaging technologies use light-based methods to visualize structures beneath the skin, offering insight into vascular changes, pigmentation depth, and tissue composition.

Cell BioPrint, introduced at the Consumer Electronics Show in 2025 and launched at select Lancôme stores in March 2026, illustrates both the ambition and challenge of longevity claims in skincare. In a widely viewed CNET TikTok video, one commenter described it as “Theranos-level smoke and mirrors,” a critique that drew significant engagement. The Verge questioned the lack of publicly available peer-reviewed evidence validating the device’s performance. While measuring biomarkers may offer a direct view of skin biology, the accuracy and clinical significance of those measurements, including whether they predict meaningful aging outcomes, require independent validation.

Biological data exists across diagnostic health platforms such as Function Health and Superpower, connected health devices and wearables. The Oura Ring, for example, tracks sleep, activity, recovery, and physiological signals associated with stress and menstrual cycles. These systems provide longitudinal data on factors associated with healthy aging, yet remain largely unintegrated into beauty.

As longevity language expands, scrutiny is increasing. Industry observers describe the growing pattern as “longevity washing”: using scientific terminology to elevate formulas without corresponding advances in evidence or delivery.

The science behind aging is real. Sirtuins are involved in cellular repair. NAD+ plays a role in metabolic function. Senescent cells contribute to inflammation and tissue degradation.

“Longevity, properly practiced, is longitudinal and multi-system. It uses serial biomarkers, functional measures such as cardiorespiratory fitness and grip strength, cognitive trajectories, and lifestyle data, all integrated over years. Skincare has a real place inside that picture; skin health is genuinely part of healthy aging, and the brands building thoughtful diagnostics, rigorous formulation science, and honest claims will benefit as the broader system matures. The brands that don’t will find the gap between their language and their evidence harder to defend each year,” says Dr. Barzilai.

The real question is whether topical skincare meaningfully engages these pathways or simply borrows their language. Many molecules central to longevity positioning are difficult to transport across the skin barrier in active form. Evidence supporting their efficacy in topical applications remains limited, particularly when measured against claims of biological age reversal or improved healthspan.

The distinction carries legal and commercial consequences. Under FDA regulations, products marketed to improve appearance are generally classified as cosmetics (with intended use governing classification), while those intended to alter the body’s structure or function may be regulated as drugs. That becomes increasingly consequential when brands promise cellular repair or reversal of biological aging.

“Referencing scientific concepts like sirtuin activation, senescent cell clearance, or mitochondrial repair may classify a product as a drug,” says Todd A. Harrison, a partner at Venable LLP and co-chair of its FDA Group. “Brands seeking innovation should communicate carefully to avoid FDA enforcement actions and class-action lawsuits.”

This is not a hypothetical regulatory risk. In 2014, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC)challenged L’Oréal’s advertising for Lancôme Génifique and L’Oréal Paris Youth Code, alleging that the company lacked adequate scientific substantiation for claims that its products targeted genes to deliver anti-aging benefits. L’Oréal settled the charges, agreeing to restrictions on certain gene-related claims. Now, the industry’s vocabulary has shifted from gene science to cellular longevity, but the underlying question remains: What evidence supports the biological benefits being advertised?

Scrutiny is also extending to beauty technology. On Oct. 27, 2026, the National Advertising Division (NAD), the advertising industry’s self-regulatory body,announced that it would refer HigherDOSE to regulatory authorities after the company declined to participate in two inquiries concerning claims for its red light face mask and hair growth device. Those claims included reducing wrinkles, rejuvenating hair follicles and reducing shedding. NAD made no determination that the claims were false or unsubstantiated; the referral resulted from HigherDOSE’s decision not to participate. The case illustrates increased scrutiny of beauty-device performance claims.

The FTC’s advertising standards add another layer of accountability. Brands must substantiate express and implied product claims, including benefits that consumers may reasonably infer from scientific terminology, imagery and marketing. Suggesting cellular rejuvenation without expressly promising it does not eliminate that obligation.

Longevity implies an ability to intervene in the mechanisms of aging. The more brands lean into those claims, the more they expose themselves to demands for clinical evidence, regulatory scrutiny and potential litigation.

Real innovation is underway in ingredients, diagnostics and how consumers engage with their skin health. Yet much of what is currently marketed as longevity still relies on narrative rather than science. As scientific authority increasingly underpins beauty brands’ value propositions, consumers will expect measurable biological benefits.

The beauty industry’s onus is to define longevity clearly, distinguishing cosmetic outcomes and biological effects. That means connecting diagnostics, data and product performance over time.

Longevity has become beauty’s most powerful claim, and the one most likely to be tested by consumers, competitors, and regulators. In a category built on trust, the market will be led by brands that can prove their longevity claims rather than simply market them.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/rox-serie.title: Meet Rox, the $1.3 billion AI sales startup betting it can take on Salesforce
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/rox-serie.author: Morgan Chittum
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/rox-serie.text:
Morgan Chittum here. For decades, enterprise software giants like Salesforce have powered the workflows that keep the world’s biggest businesses running. Rox cofounder Ishan Mukherjee is betting on a future that no longer needs them.

The AI sales startup has raised $100 million in Series B funding at a $1.3 billion valuation, Rox exclusively told Fortune. General Catalyst and March Capital co-led the round, with Sequoia and GV returning and Prosperity7 joining as a new investor.

The pitch: Customer relationship management software shouldn’t just store information. It should put it to work. With Rox, AI agents research customer accounts, recommend who to prioritize, and prepare outreach for clients. Basically, it gives salespeople less administrative work and more time with clients.

Mukherjee’s conviction comes from experience. Before Rox, he started Pixie Labs, which New Relic acquired for roughly $150 million in 2020, and became New Relic’s chief growth officer.

“While running a public company through COVID, I deeply understood that every business relies on Salesforce specifically and their CRM to run their business. That was not the futureproof approach as AI was about to hit scale,” Mukherjee said.

“There are going to be autonomous agents that do customer-facing commercial work across large parts of the economy, not just tech companies,” he added. “And do we think Salesforce is the right partner to help CEOs in the C-suite to actually transform their businesses? I came out of an experience where it was not true.”

He also saw an opening as massive companies like Nvidia and Intel moved customer data out of Salesforce and into their own environments. “What that means is the world’s largest in-app application company, which is Salesforce, was becoming less of a moat, less entrenched,” Mukherjee added.

But how do they plan to take on Salesforce, a company with a $172 billion market cap? Mukherjee pointed to the founding team’s experience developing cutting edge tech. Rox’s cofounders include Shriram Sridharan, a founding member of AWS’s Amazon Aurora database service; former Google employee Diogo Ribeiro; and Stanford AI Lab professor Christopher Ré. Mukherjee, himself, was a product lead for Apple’s Siri Knowledge Graph.

That was a key reason General Catalyst invested pre-product, and pre-revenue, back in 2024, partner Marc Bhargava said, describing Rox as “a talent magnet.”

But talent alone won’t unseat an enterprise software behemoth: “For a long time there’s been a graveyard of companies that said ‘I’m taking on ServiceNow or Workday. I’m taking on Salesforce,’” Bhargava told Fortune. Sticky customer relationships and access to capital have kept those incumbents in control, he said. “But AI is a moment in time to displace many of them.” Those same fears have rattled Wall Street in 2026, at times sending software tumbling in what became known as the “SaaSpocalypse.”

Rox’s argument: AI-native startups can build around agents from the start, rather than retrofit them into older software. “It’s like you have a house and you just throw in one more floor, versus from the beginning you decided it was going to be a four-floor home,” Bhargava added. “It’s a huge opportunity for people to start fresh with a fresh code base built around [large language models]…Those products are ultimately better.”

To be sure, the incumbents aren’t easy targets. Salesforce generated $41.5 billion in revenue for fiscal 2026 and says it has worked with more than 150,000 companies. ServiceNow, meanwhile, ended its latest quarter with 680 customers with more than $5 million each in annual contract value.

Meanwhile, Rox’s early customers include high-profile firms like Ramp, New Relic, Trafigura, MongoDB, Groq, and America’s Auto Auction, to name a few. The startup also says its annual recurring revenue grew more than tenfold since its first year after launch. The fresh capital will fund more AI research and product development. Rox plans to expand its U.S. sales, marketing, and commercial team fivefold next year.

“Us in venture, our whole thing is to back the Davids against the Goliaths,” Bhargava said, “And we think that this will happen here.”

Morgan Chittum
