https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/companies.title: The next Congress could be more productive than you expect. Here’s what that means for your company
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/companies.author: David Meadvin
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/companies.text:
When I was Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid’s speechwriter, there were very few nail-biter votes. Hanging around the cloakroom, 99 percent of the time we could predict the exact outcome of a vote before the roll call began.

That’s how we’re all trained to think about Washington now. We’ve been through years of gridlock, and our pattern recognition-obsessed brains assume there will be more. The fundamentals of a divided federal government suggest the same: Democrats control both chambers, President Trump holds the veto pen, overcoming a filibuster still requires 60 votes, and overturning a veto requires 67.

But the 2026 election scrambled the incentives that have kept Washington gridlocked for so long.

That means things could get a little weird next year.

To understand this shift, start with the next map. In 2028, 18 Republican senators are up for re-election, and seven of them represent states that either elected a Democrat to the Senate in 2026 or came within three points of doing so.

Sen. Ashley Moody held her Florida seat by under three points, and she faces voters again in two years. Sen. John Kennedy just watched Louisiana nearly elect its first Democratic senator since 2008. Sens. Jerry Moran, Tim Scott and Ted Budd represent states where Democrats won Senate races this year. So will whoever runs for Sen. Chuck Grassley’s seat in Iowa.

The years 2016 to 2026 will forever be remembered as the MAGA decade. During this period, the most existential fear keeping Republicans up at night was a primary challenge to their right with Trump support. This spring, Trump helped push out Bill Cassidy in Louisiana and John Cornyn in Texas. They were the latest in a long string of Republican casualties when their loyalty to the president was questioned.

Look at what happened to the nominees who replaced Cassidy and Cornyn. Ken Paxton lost Texas by 12 points. Julia Letlow, Trump’s pick in Louisiana, held the seat by less than two. Republicans lost general elections in places like South Carolina and (probably) Mississippi that no one would have imagined would host a competitive general election. Even Montana, one of the most Republican states in the nation, might have elected a Democratic senator if the Democratic nominee and a stronger independent candidate hadn’t split votes.

For the last decade, Republican senators had more reason to fear losing a primary than losing a general election. That math no longer holds. In almost any state, winning the primary in 2028 will be just half the battle. There will be very few obviously safe Republican Senate seats in America next cycle, especially if cost of living issues don’t dramatically improve in the next two years.

There are plenty of explanations for the Democratic wave, but the Republican Party’s failure to deliver on its economic populist promises has to be near the top of the list. If you’re wondering which issues might see strange bedfellows during the 2027 legislative session, start there.

We’re already seeing the shift. Four days after the election, Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, one of Trump’s most loyal allies in the Senate, went on Fox News and accused people inside the Trump administration of serving special interests. When Trump made clear he took it personally, Johnson widened his complaint to “deep state” actors in every administration. But he made the break first and softened it second, and his core complaint was that corporations have become too close to the agencies that regulate them. For a conservative like Johnson facing the prospect of an uphill re-election fight if he runs again, aligning himself with economic populism won’t be optional.

Heading into 2028, Republicans facing re-election need to show voters at home that they can do something about the cost of living. In the NBC News exit poll, nearly 90 percent of voters said they were concerned about the cost of gas, groceries, utilities and health care. Those voters will remember who helped and who stood in the way.

Don’t roll your eyes. I’m not suggesting that Republicans will sign on to signature Democratic priorities. But on legislation that addresses voters’ economic concerns – and isn’t indelibly aligned with the Democratic Party – we could see filibuster-proof and even veto-proof majorities emerge.

We know where to find these types of coalitions. Just this past summer, the Senate passed a major housing bill by an 85-5 vote; it became law even though Trump refused to sign it. An issue like data centers defies obvious partisan labels, and legislation to prevent them from passing costs onto local communities came close to passing this fall (Democrats voted no because they thought the bill didn’t go far enough; a toothier version could well pass next year). Other issues with broad appeal could include permitting reform and health insurance premiums.

Nothing will test these new coalitions more than tariffs. We could see legislation restoring Congress’s authority over tariffs. Will all but the safest Republicans really side with the White House on this one? Overriding a presidential veto would take two-thirds of both chambers. In the Senate, if Democrats end up with 56 seats, that means 11 Republicans. In the House, it would take about 30, and there are roughly 40 House Republicans who won this year by five points or less. A year ago those numbers would have sounded absurd. With seven clearly vulnerable Republican senators and several others who have already backed giving Congress the final word on trade, it is no longer out of the question.

This is not just a game of political prognostication. CEOs and their companies who agree that there’s a reasonable chance of big legislation moving with bipartisan support next year need to plan for it. Some of the coalitions that form will move on issues companies have wanted for years, like permitting. Others will form against particular industries. Tech companies that assumed the data center buildout would go unchallenged should expect major headaches, and likely far higher costs than they’ve planned.

Corporate public affairs executives who rely on the old assumptions about Washington may find themselves badly unprepared for 2027. CEOs, beware of anyone on your team who confidently breaks down expected voting patterns and legislative agendas based on how things always go. One of my favorite quotes, from Dwight Eisenhower, is “plans are useless, planning is everything.” Now’s the time to plan.

https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.author: Joseph Hostetler

At 7:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $95.72 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s an increase of $2.74 since yesterday morning and roughly $30 more than at this time last year.

Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply.

The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges.

Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.”

In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets disrupted.

It’s not a permanent fix, as it’s more meant to provide immediate support for consumers and ensure critical parts of the economy like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and so on can keep operating.

Both oil and natural gas play key roles as major sources of energy. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by proxy. If oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, increasing the demand for natural gas.

Oil prices are often measured by two key benchmarks:

Between the two, Brent is a better representation of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the best way to review historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now leans on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

When you look at the Brent benchmark across multiple decades, you’ll see that oil has been anything but consistent. It has experienced spikes driven by wars and supply cuts, as well as crashes linked to global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

In short, oil’s historical performance has been far from steady. It’s massively affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/inside-th.author: Melissa Hancock
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/inside-th.text:
Banking in the UAE is approaching an inflection point as AI begins to reshape everything from customer service and compliance to cybersecurity and internal operations.

Developments highlighted at last week’s Dubai FinTech Summit 2026 suggest that the country’s largest lenders are no longer simply experimenting with AI but preparing to make it a fundamental part of how they operate.

Emirates NBD, Dubai’s largest lender by assets, shared how it has more than 150 AI initiatives underway, with 65 already in production.

The bank, which is majority government-owned, has been aggressively scaling its digital transformation by committing approximately 50% of its technology budget to AI.

In June, Emirates NBD was ranked first in the Evident AI Index for Banks – Middle East & Africa which assesses how banks across these regions are deploying AI and adapting their operations to the technology’s transformative impact.

The survey carried out by Evident, a London-based market intelligence firm, comprised more than 100 companies, including insurers and payment processors.

It noted that Emirates NBD “explicitly” links AI to enterprise productivity, operational modernisation and the UAE’s national AI agenda.

Last month, Emirates NBD became the first bank in the MENA region to deploy OpenAI’s GPT models using local, in-country infrastructure. This allows it to run advanced LLMs at scale while meeting strict UAE data residency, privacy, and regulatory compliance laws.

The bank plans to integrate OpenAI’s models across its operations to enhance customer experiences, strengthen risk management and financial crime prevention through advanced analytics, automate processes and boost employee productivity.

“Banking will transform more in the next five years than it transformed in the last 30 years,” said Miguel Rio-Tinto, Emirates NBD’s Group Chief Digital and Information Officer.

“Generative AI and advanced frontier models are so powerful that they are opening up new possibilities for automation in banking, enabling capabilities that were previously out of reach across customer service, internal processes and employee support. I believe AI will be the key determinant in shaping the competitive landscape of the future.”

Cybersecurity is the area where Rio-Tinto anticipates the most significant transformation. As advanced AI models become increasingly capable of identifying software vulnerabilities, the number of critical security flaws the bank must evaluate has surged from approximately 1,000 per month in early 2025 to around 15,000 last month.

To address this growing challenge, Emirates NBD is adopting the same technology defensively, leveraging a frontier OpenAI model to test and identify weaknesses in its own systems.

The rapid digital transformation taking place across the region has increased its exposure to cyberattacks while the need to strengthen operational resilience across the Gulf has become increasingly pressing since the outbreak of the US-Iran war on February 28.

In the UAE, daily attempted cyberattacks reportedly surged from around 200,000 to as many as 700,000 amid the escalating geopolitical tensions.

In July, the UAE successfully thwarted a series of sophisticated cyberattacks targeting its financial sector that sought to compromise digital systems and technical infrastructure through phishing campaigns and malicious software.

The UAE’s Cyber Security Council warned that cybercriminals are increasingly harnessing AI to devise more sophisticated attack methods.

While cybersecurity is emerging as a critical area where AI can make a difference, UAE lenders are looking to deploy the technology across a broad range of functions, with Commercial Bank of Dubai (CBD) unveiling a series of strategic technology partnerships at the summit.

Collaborations with Microsoft, Silent Eight, and Comarch AI Wealth will, respectively, support wider AI adoption, strengthen AI-powered compliance and risk management, and further develop the bank’s digital wealth platform and investment offerings.

CBD also joined forces with Zamp to leverage intelligent automation and signed strategic agreements with Harvey, Sirion, and Flank to improve its legal and governance infrastructure.

“We are moving away from traditional AI applications towards adopting agentic AI, which is creating opportunities to rethink and redesign existing business processes,” said Thomas Cherian, Commercial Bank of Dubai’s chief technology and services officer.

“This will help us accelerate service delivery and provide superior customer experiences. Agentic AI is enabling us to move towards much more intelligent banking which is safer and more secure for our customers, highlighting technology’s growing role today as a strategic enabler for banks.”

Unlike conventional generative AI, agentic AI can make decisions and execute tasks autonomously with minimal human intervention.

Cherian estimates that AI agents could handle 55% to 60% of operational tasks, with human oversight retained to approve outcomes. CBD also aims to retain ownership of the agents it develops and the intellectual property behind them.

The UAE has recently placed agentic AI at the top of its technology agenda. In April this year, the UAE government launched a major national initiative to transition 50% of all federal government operations, services, and tasks to agentic AI systems by 2028.

The following month, Dubai announced a two-year action plan to accelerate the adoption of the technology across the emirate’s private sector, aiming to secure a “competitive edge” in the future global economy.

With the government’s ambitious targets for agentic AI adoption and banks committing significant resources to the technology, the UAE’s financial sector looks poised for a fundamental transformation.

Emirates Nbd has committed approximately 50% of its technology budget to AI. The bank plans to integrate OpenAI’s models across its operations to enhance customer experiences, strengthen risk management and financial crime prevention.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/qatar-sig.title: Qatar signals progress on Iran deal, but Gulf fears persist
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/qatar-sig.author: Melissa Hancock
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/qatar-sig.text:
Qatar continued its diplomatic push to broker an end to the U.S.-Iran war this week, but prospects of a breakthrough remain uncertain.

On Tuesday, a Qatari government spokesperson said that Monday’s closed-door talks between the U.S. and Iran were “focused on making progress”, but that the timeline for a potential agreement remained unclear.

“We cannot say how close or how far away an agreement is,” Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of the foreign ministry’s media and communication department, told a weekly briefing in Doha.

His remarks followed those of Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani who described his White House meeting on Monday with U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance as “positive”.

Emerging from the latest round of shuttle diplomacy, Al Thani said he was “Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region.” Before Al Thani’s visit to Washington, Qatari officials had held talks in Tehran as well as consultations with other regional governments.

On Tuesday, Al Thani made an unscheduled stop at the G7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris where top European diplomats have reportedly been pressing U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to avoid any new escalation against Iran.

Trump, meanwhile, took to Truth Social to argue that Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE “would prefer the status quo”, referencing both the U.S. naval blockade and restrictions on Iran’s overland trade under Operation Iron Gate. Echoing Qatar’s comments, he said: “We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this conflict” but warned that the U.S. is “locked and loaded” should there be any changes in regional developments, adding “that seems to be quite unlikely”.

Speaking at a geopolitical forum in Abu Dhabi on Monday, Anwar Gargash, diplomatic advisor to UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, said: “We should prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional ​order can be taken for granted.” This would require the UAE to invest in its defensive capabilities and stronger international security partners, he said.

The number of attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait peaked in October, reaching its highest monthly level since the U.S.-Iran war began, with more than 30 incidents recorded, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations.

On Tuesday, GCC defence ministers approved plans to establish a joint command center in Kuwait, with member states contributing forces to strengthen military integration across the six-nation bloc.

The advanced command will form part of the existing Unified Military Command which is headquartered in Riyadh. However, the announcement offered no details on the number or composition of forces to be assigned, the command’s specific mandate or when it would become operational.

The continuing uncertainty did not deter Barclays from opening its new office in Riyadh’s financial district on Monday. It marks the U.K. lender’s return to the market after more than a decade as it seeks to expand its Gulf business. Barclays’ Asia-Pacific CEO Jaideep Khanna told Bloomberg last month that the bank was a “big believer” in the Middle East.

But ongoing Houthi attacks across Saudi Arabia mean it is far from business as usual at present. Global finance firms based in Riyadh’s financial district have been allowing staff to work from home for the last month, while ongoing travel restrictions continue to create additional challenges for those commuting from nearby Gulf hubs, as well as for global executives flying directly into the kingdom.

Melissa Hancock

As ever, thanks for reading, and do keep in touch with your thoughts and ideas.
melissa.hancock@fortune.com

Emirates Group's profits fell 66% for the April to September period as the U.S.-Iran war reduced passenger demand and drove up global jet fuel costs.

The Dubai-headquartered airline made a profit before tax of AED 4.1bn ($1.1bn) in the first half of its 2026-27 financial year, compared with the AED12.2bn ($3.32 billion) it made in the same period last year.

The airline carried 21.8 million passengers, 22% fewer than a year earlier while available seat kilometers—the industry's ​standard measure of passenger-carrying capacity—fell 17%.

Cargo operations helped to cushion the decline, with Emirates SkyCargo transporting 1.2 million tons over the six-month period. While this represented a 1% decline year-on-year, it still translated to a 52% increase in revenue, as the war prompted more shipping companies to turn to air transport.

Emirates fuel price risk management strategy significantly offset the impact of a 60% jump in fuel prices. Gains of AED 7.1bn ($1.9bn) from fuel hedging cut the net increase in costs to 13% but fuel remains the largest component of the airline’s operating cost at 34%.

Emirates had restored operations across 91% of its network by the end of September, serving 150 airports in 78 countries and territories. At the end of March, it was flying at 58% of its passenger capacity to 122 destinations in 65 countries.

While other airlines’ operations have been affected by regional airspace restrictions and travel advisories, Emirates has stepped in to meet passenger demand.

In total, 11 airlines, including some of Emirates’ key rivals, currently maintain suspensions on flights to Dubai. Last week, British Airways resumed direct flights to Dubai after an eight-month suspension.

The great and the good of the telecommunications industry gathered in Doha this week to attend the second Gulf annual Mobile World Congress.

The event opened with a call to action from H.E. Mohammed bin Ali al-Mannai, Qatar’s minister of communications and information technology, to align global industry standards and bridge the Middle East and Africa’s connectivity gap.

Almost half (48%) of MENA’s population used mobile internet in 2025, according to a GSMA report released at MWC Doha. However, 49% remained offline despite living within coverage.

Mobile connectivity is quickly becoming a core pillar of the region’s economic diversification, with the Gulf being home to some of the world’s most advanced 5G markets.

Mobile technologies and services, which generated $380 billion of economic value across MENA in 2025, equivalent to 5.8% of regional GDP, are forecast to reach $470 billion by 2030.

Meanwhile, 5G is expected to account for 40% of regional connections by 2030, up from 9% in 2025, as mobile operators invest a forecast $88.9 billion over the five-year period.

In just under a decade, the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) has become a hub for innovation and is now home to more than 2,000 AI, fintech, and technology companies—a sizeable leap from just 11 startups that joined its accelerator in 2017.

FinTech Hive is both the region’s first and largest financial technology accelerator and has played a key role in modernizing the emirate’s financial sector.

HSBC, BNP Paribas, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley, Standard Chartered, Visa, Ripple and Network International, were among the major names who attended Dubai Future Finance Week last week, a five-day event that incorporated the two-day Dubai FinTech Summit.

DIFC announced a strategic partnership with Japan’s Mizuho Financial Group to support the international expansion of Japanese startups and deepen economic ties between the UAE and Japan. The partnership will give up to 6,000 Mizuho startup clients access to DIFC’s Innovation Hub.

DIFC also announced plans for a Dubai Fintech Stack to support founders with payments, onboarding, risk, financial security and AI integration.

Speaking as part of a headline session at Dubai FinTech Summit, Noel Quinn, chair of the wealth manager Julius Baer and former group CEO of HSBC, predicted that AI is set to become an integral part of every bank’s technology stack, particularly in monitoring payments for potential money laundering and sanctions violations. Julius Baer was the first organisation to be licensed to operate in the DIFC after the free zone was established in 2004 and has maintained a presence there ever since.

ADIPEC 2026, Abu Dhabi’s flagship annual energy conference, concluded last week, with more than 50,000 deals worth an estimated $67 billion signed over four days. ADIPEC 2025 saw $46 billion in deals signed over the course of the event.

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have effectively imposed their own shipping controls in the Red Sea through an often-overlooked application system for captains seeking transit clearances. The process is surprisingly simple: email the rebels. This Wall Street Journal investigative piece does a deep dive into how, in early 2024, the Houthis set up the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center, an administrative body responsible for processing shipping applications and communicating the group’s sanctions. The Houthi militants, if they choose to reply, will typically do so within 24 hours, according to crew members and emails seen by the Journal. It provides an example from September when the Houthis approved passage for the Zhong Cheng Chang Ling, a Chinese containership, which sailed through the Red Sea without incident.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/verizon-c.title: Inside Dan Schulman’s war on the old Verizon
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/verizon-c.author: Ruth Umoh
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/verizon-c.text:
At his first companywide meeting after becoming Verizon’s CEO in October 2025, Dan Schulman dispensed with the usual corporate pleasantries. Speaking without notes or slides, he delivered a message that employees of the telecommunications giant weren’t used to hearing from the top: Verizon had surrendered market share to AT&T, -T-Mobile, and lower-cost providers, and its sprawling bureaucracy had become a problem. The company was losing badly. And, he warned, layoffs were coming.

It was a stark introduction to a new leader who, until recently, had been watching the deterioration unfold from a seat on Verizon’s board. Then 67, he had left an idyllic retirement in Montana to roll up his sleeves and fix it.

Schulman had at first been reluctant to take the top job, turning down the offer twice. But he also felt a sense of responsibility to its customers, shareholders, and employees. Should the board have acted sooner? “Yes, we probably should have,” he concedes. Ultimately, his wife persuaded him that he could make a difference. “I came in with a little bit of a bad attitude,” he says, but adds that now he’s “absolutely loving it.”

He also came in determined to dismantle the bureaucracy that had made even simple decisions needlessly complicated. The company, he says, had become “a big lumbering giant that had fallen behind.” In some cases, approving a decision required 35 signatures.

Verizon’s competitive troubles were mounting, too. In 2024, T-Mobile added a net 3.1 million postpaid phone lines and AT&T added 1.65 million; Verizon added less than 900,000. In the first three quarters of 2025, Verizon’s consumer business lost a net 414,000 postpaid phone lines, including 356,000 in the first quarter alone. Verizon remains the largest U.S. wireless carrier, generating billions in profits. But as its peers have narrowed the gap in network quality, the advantage that once let Verizon command a premium is becoming a baseline expectation for any major wireless carrier.

As if Verizon’s existing challenges weren’t daunting enough, Elon Musk’s company, SpaceX, purchased an $8 billion portfolio of low-band cellular spectrum licenses in October, a move that lays the groundwork to compete more directly with traditional wireless giants.

For years, Verizon summed up its pitch to American consumers in a familiar TV refrain: “Can you hear me now? Good.” The commercials featured a bespectacled Verizon employee, played by actor Paul Marcarelli, roaming the country and testing his service in remote locations. The catchphrase became a cultural touchstone, helping cement Verizon’s reputation for network reliability.

But over time, that advantage became harder to monetize as network coverage became less of a differentiator and consumers increasingly judged carriers on the overall customer experience, from their monthly bills to the deals available when they needed a new phone. “Customers don’t want to pay for a great network; that’s the expectation,” says Kevin Zavaglia, Verizon’s chief commercial officer for sales and service. (Adding insult to injury, Marcarelli resurfaced in 2016 as pitchman for rival Sprint, this time touting its network.)

Just over a year into Schulman’s tenure, Verizon is showing early signs of a turnaround. In the third quarter, it gained a net 406,000 phone lines, compared with just 44,000 a year earlier, its strongest third-quarter showing in five years. It also added 137,000 customer accounts, its best quarterly performance in more than a decade, even as the company slashed spending on promotional offers by 41%.

The results offer a promising snapshot, but Schulman is attempting something far more ambitious than a rebound in subscriber growth: He is trying to dismantle decades of ingrained habits at one of America’s largest companies, forcing his near-93,300 employees to think differently, take risks, and move faster. The greatest danger, Schulman says, is inertia as AI and new competitors threaten to reshape the wireless business.

One tendency he encountered at Verizon was managers setting goals they were confident they could meet, then treating hitting those targets as success. Schulman recalls a manager proudly presenting a plan to raise a sales closing rate from 15% to 25%. “So, are you saying at the end of that, we are losing 75% of the time?” Schulman asked incredulously.

He’s pushing executives to set more ambitious goals, even if that means missing some targets, rather than consistently meeting easy ones. “Anytime the pace of change external is greater than the pace of change internal,” he says, “you’re falling behind.”

Tony Skiadas, Verizon’s chief financial officer, described how the company’s pricing strategy had become a costly cycle. Verizon had raised prices, contributing to customer defections, then spent heavily on promotions to win customers back. “We’ve seen that movie before over the years, and we know how it ends,” he says.

Roxanne Austin, a Verizon director, recalls watching the company finish third among the major wireless carriers for 20 consecutive quarters, losing customers and market share while management kept prioritizing network infrastructure over customers’ changing needs. “I’m like, ‘Guys, we’ve got to pay attention. Something’s happening,’ ” she remembers thinking. “Our playbook didn’t change for five years.” (Hans Vestberg, Verizon’s CEO from 2018 to 2025, declined to comment.)

Austin likens the scale and urgency of Schulman’s turnaround task to “turning an ocean liner at the speed of a race car.” And given the complexity of telecommunications, she adds, he must somehow “land that ocean liner on the moon, too.”

After stepping down as PayPal’s CEO in 2023 after nearly a decade at the helm, Schulman had settled happily into retirement on a Montana ranch. He rode horses daily, helped herd the couple’s roughly 900 head of cattle, and spent time with his children. Schulman, who was originally from New Jersey but had worn cowboy boots since eighth grade, finally had the lifestyle to match his footwear. “I did not miss the CEO job at all,” he says. Now, back on an executive’s grueling schedule, Schulman wants to make every hour count.

The mantra for the company’s new era under Schulman is familiar corporate gospel: Put customers first. But living up to it will require fundamental shifts at Verizon, including sacrificing some short-term revenue to rebuild customer trust. One of Schulman’s early decisions was to cancel a planned price increase. Verizon is also looking to compete more aggressively for customers with deals like the new Simplicity offering, which lowers the starting monthly price for a single line from $65 to as low as $30. And to reduce churn, it is offering incentives for customers to bundle cell phone service with home internet, including its Fios service.

Schulman made steep cost cuts, including the promised layoffs: A month after his appointment Verizon cut roughly 13,000 jobs, or about 13% of the workforce. Verizon had conducted smaller rounds of layoffs before, but Schulman wanted to send a stronger signal. “I really needed to show that this was different,” he says. “That I was very serious about the change that was going to happen.”

Schulman has set uncompromising expectations. He demands intensity, long hours, and a willingness to make difficult decisions. He expects managers to know their businesses inside out and answer questions on the spot. In meetings, when executives suggest taking a discussion offline, he challenges them: “Why would we take it offline? Like, we’re all here.”

Schulman readily describes himself as competitive and exacting of his employees, and he accepts that some may find his leadership style too demanding and leave. “And I’m okay with it, one way or another,” he says. As he puts it, “Heaven and hell are the same place. It’s just heaven for some and hell for others.”

The growing demand for infrastructure to support artificial intelligence offers new opportunities for Verizon, particularly in providing the high-capacity fiber networks connecting data centers. Verizon has signed agreements with Google, Amazon Web Services, and others worth billions, Schulman says.

AI is also helping improve systems within Verizon—for example, tools that help customer service employees quickly find information about plans, products, and policies. Zavaglia says AI has cut about six minutes from the in-store phone buying process.

As for Musk’s threat to challenge the incumbents in the mobile business, Schulman says he takes SpaceX’s ambitions “quite seriously.” But he estimates that building a network to rival Verizon’s would could take four to six years and cost some $300 billion. SpaceX also has other businesses competing for investment and attention, he points out. And even if Musk commits the resources, Schulman argues, he could end up with a network much like Verizon’s, without a significant cost advantage.

“Frankly, at that point, I welcome the opportunity to compete against them,” Schulman said during Verizon’s quarterly earnings call in October. “It’s very hard to throw a punch against something that doesn’t exist. But once they come into the market, we will be ferociously competitive.”

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune.

Schul man says he was reluctant to take the top job, but felt a sense of responsibility to customers, shareholders, and employees. He expects managers to know their businesses inside out and answer questions on the spot.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/brick-hou.title: Brick houses are disappearing from America’s new construction: ‘Nobody got paid for how long a house would last’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/brick-hou.author: Emma Witman
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/brick-hou.text:
Americans have never paid more for a home. The median existing home sold for a record $440,600 in June, according to the National Association of Realtors. Yet the brick house, the kind built to stand for a century, has nearly vanished from new construction.

Brick or brick veneer covered just 16.8% of new single-family homes started in 2025, down from almost a quarter in 2012, according to a National Association of Home Builders analysis of Census data. And most of the homes that still look like brick houses aren’t. They’re wood-frame houses with a layer of brick veneer attached to the outside.

A home can mean a lot of things. A place to raise a family. An investment. A refuge. A milestone. But somewhere along the way, American homebuilding changed the question. Not “will this last a lifetime?” Just “will it last the mortgage?”

“We didn’t decide to build houses that just outlast the mortgage. We kind of drifted there,” said Dan D’Agostino, founder of Plan Architecture and a residential architect based in New Jersey.

The distinction between real brick and veneer matters. A structural masonry wall holds up the building itself. Veneer is an exterior finish, while the wood frame behind it does the structural work.

The change reflects a postwar housing boom, a shrinking skilled-labor pool, rising construction costs, and a preference for homes that could be built quickly and cheaply. But some architects and builders say it also changed what Americans expect from the places they live, and what buyers paying record prices actually get for their money.

The shift away from structural masonry accelerated after World War II, when returning veterans and their families needed affordable homes, and needed them quickly. Developers such as Levitt & Sons met that demand with standardized designs and faster construction methods. Between 1947 and 1951, the company built 17,447 houses in Levittown on Long Island, at times finishing 10 to 12 homes a day.

“Levittown was a legitimate solution to a genuine crisis,” Steven Menotti, CEO of construction safety company Menotti Enterprise, told Fortune. “They needed shelter urgently, and a carpentry team got the job done faster than a masonry team ever would have.”

Brick construction requires skilled workers to lay individual bricks, one at a time. Wood framing can be assembled by crews with less specialized training, and it moves much faster. Matt DiBara, CEO of DiBara Masonry and a fourth-generation stonemason, said the economics were simple.

“It came down to cost and speed,” DiBara said. “After World War II the country needed homes that were more affordable and could be built in large batches, and a framing crew can close in a house way quicker and cheaper than a masonry crew can lay up solid walls.”

Brick veneer let builders keep the familiar look of masonry without relying on it to hold up the house. By the 1970s and 1980s, DiBara said, that approach had become standard.

The labor pool shrank along with it. Bricklaying is a specialized trade that takes years to master, while wood framing is easier to standardize and scale. The pressure hasn’t eased: the construction industry will need an estimated 456,000 new workers in 2027, according to the Associated Builders and Contractors.

“Today the hard part of building a true masonry house isn’t the brick. It’s finding people who can lay it,” D’Agostino said.

Jerel McCants, the architect overseeing the restoration of Tampa Union Station, which opened in 1912, sees the same problem. Skilled brick masons are not equally available across the country, he said, and regional differences in the workforce influence which materials builders choose. Brick’s beauty comes from the time and craftsmanship it demands.

“You can’t mass produce erecting a brick wall,” he told Fortune.

That distinction also complicates the historical record. Brick was the primary exterior wall material on 35% of new single-family homes completed in 1973, according to Census Bureau data. D’Agostino cautions against reading that as a measure of brick houses.

“That figure refers to brick veneer used as exterior cladding over wood frame construction. These are fundamentally different building systems,” he said.

Brick never disappeared entirely from American home exteriors. Its role as the structure holding a house up largely did.

The move to wood framing didn’t make every new home inferior. Modern construction offers advantages in insulation, building performance, and affordability, and amid an affordability crisis, the median price of a new home was $400,400 in September, according to the Census Bureau. New homes are now cheaper than existing ones for the first time in data going back to 1974, in part because builders are putting up smaller houses. But experts say homeowners lost some of what structural masonry provided.

Fire resistance is one. A masonry wall offers protection a decorative brick exterior cannot replicate.

“Whereas masonry walls will stand after a fire, the wood frame behind a veneer wall will burn just like any other wood frame if the fire gains access to it,” said Menotti, an FDNY-certified Construction Site Fire Safety Manager. “I see the results of this substitution frequently in my fire investigation work.”

D’Agostino points to another: the longevity of what’s hidden behind a home’s exterior.

“A real brick wall holds the house up, resists fire, evens out heat and cold, and with some repointing goes well past a hundred years,” he said. “Look at the old rowhouses in Philadelphia and Baltimore. With thin brick, the house only lasts as long as the wood and sheathing behind it, and those fail quietly.”

Not all veneer is equal, though. D’Agostino notes that full-depth brick veneer with an air gap behind it can serve as a durable rainscreen. His concern is with thinner brick products that lack those characteristics.

For McCants, the difference comes down to the materials themselves.

“Brick—it’s just dirt and water, right? So it’s going to be there forever,” he said. He estimates brick can last 100 years or longer, compared with roughly 30 years for some newer exterior products. Actual lifespans vary by material and installation, but he believes the industry has steadily traded permanence for convenience.

The shift also cost the trade its craft. Masonry demands specialized knowledge, from laying individual bricks to building arches, bonds, and decorative details.

“What I miss most is the craft. On an old brick building you can see the mason’s hand everywhere: the bond, the arches, the cornice, the way the joints were struck. Thin brick can copy the pattern, but there’s nobody’s hand in it. And once you stop building that way, you stop passing that knowledge down,” D’Agostino said.

Economics explains much of the shift. But architectural historian and geographer Thalia Toha, who studied at Princeton University and works at the Lafayette History Museum in Colorado, told Fortune that changing attitudes toward homeownership also played a role.

Brick’s place in American residential architecture has never been uniform, she said. In some communities, it was associated with urban commerce and traditional city buildings. The postwar suburban boom brought a new emphasis on affordability, customization, and distance from city life.

The American ideal of homeownership shifted, too.

“Before World War II, it was still fairly common for elders to live with adult children in a multi-generational agrarian setting. In the years following the servicemen’s return from the war, the American Dream narrative shifted. As a reward for their service, the grounding principle of homeownership is that every serviceman and their nuclear family deserves their own home. This includes a house separate from their older parents,” she said. “Because a house no longer necessarily had to last beyond one generation, brick’s timeless quality also loses value. One could also say that the one-generational time frame parallels with the single life of a 30-year mortgage time frame.”

McCants sees a similar change in how Americans live now. People relocate for jobs and other opportunities, he said, which has dulled the appeal of a home meant to stay in one family for a century.

“People don’t even stay in the same homes anymore like they used to, right? I grew up in the same house as a kid, you know, but nowadays people move every five to seven years into a new house,” he said.

The data is more mixed. The typical seller had owned their home for a record 11 years, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2025 buyer and seller profile, and buyers expect to stay 15. Still, few expect to hand a house down, and builders price accordingly.

“But that’s not the appeal to builders right now, because they want something that’s going to be quick, fast, and last just long enough for people to occupy,” McCants said.

D’Agostino sees the same tension between cost and longevity.

“The lower expectations for durability were a side effect. Once everything was built around speed, nobody got paid for how long a house would last,” he said.

Despite the economic and labor hurdles, some experts believe masonry could find a new foothold in American homebuilding.

Wildfires and other disasters have renewed interest in fire-resistant materials, particularly where homeowners face growing fire risk. DiBara also believes new construction technology could make brick more accessible by reducing the specialized labor it requires.

“We’re getting better at creating more modular systems for brick, like prefabricated brick veneer systems, and there are even brick kits with tools that set and level the mortar for a full brick,” DiBara said. “When it gets easier to lay brick and you don’t need five years plus to learn how, a lot more people can get into the trade and a lot more brick gets built.”

He sees demand for resilient construction as another catalyst.

“Look at the wildfires in California and all the natural disasters we keep seeing. People want something that holds up, and masonry is a much more resilient structure,” he said. “Put the demand for resilience together with systems that make brick easier to build, and I think brick makes a real comeback.”

Toha believes architectural revivals tend to follow broader cultural change. If car-dependent suburban development falls out of favor and homeowners gravitate toward urban-style architecture, brick could become more desirable again.

Not everyone expects structural masonry to return to the average American home. D’Agostino sees its future in specialized uses: fire-prone regions, historic urban neighborhoods, and buildings designed to last a century or longer.

“For the average house? I don’t think so. Back when everyone built with brick, it was the best technology around. Today we should use the best we’ve got, balancing performance and efficiency,” he said. “Doing it the old way just to be old-fashioned is fake, and it’ll never catch on.”

For McCants, the larger issue is whether the industry has any incentive to build homes that outlast their first owners.

“People move, people get jobs, people are very mobile nowadays. They move out of the city into different states,” he said. “It’s more of a transient lifestyle than what it was in the past, where people lived in the same place for generations. It’s not like that anymore.”

The homes going up today, if they last, will one day belong to someone who hasn’t been born yet. Whether they last is a decision builders are making now.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/nfl-jay-z.title: The Jay-Z leak was good news for the NFL. Its silence made it a problem
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/nfl-jay-z.author: Rick Pendrick
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/nfl-jay-z.text:
On Oct. 26, the NFL announced that Jay-Z will headline the Super Bowl LXI halftime show at SoFi Stadium. That should have been a great story. He is a 25-time Grammy winner who sold out three Yankee Stadium shows this year.

It didn’t play out that way. The cause wasn’t the leak itself, but what came after. On Oct. 20, Puck reported that, according to multiple sources, Jay-Z had effectively “picked himself.” The report was not hostile. It described a consensus choice.

Then came the silence. For six days, the league and Roc Nation said nothing publicly. Into that gap came the Kaepernick storyline from the 2019 Roc Nation deal. Some viewed the deal as the NFL buying credibility and Jay-Z selling out.

When Commissioner Roger Goodell finally made the announcement, he said the right thing: “When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that JAY-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him.”

That line could have run on Oct. 20 without spoiling a thing. It confirms nothing about the show, but frames the choice as the league’s own.

I’ve seen the opposite problem. In Beijing, the leak was hostile, and I had an hour.

I was handling PR for the NBA China Games on Oct. 10, 2012. Commissioner David Stern was due onstage for a press conference with the Chinese Basketball Association when a New York Times reporter called me.

I had been working with him on a good story that I pitched: the opening of a three-level NBA Center outside Beijing with basketball courts, an NBA store and an NBA cafe.

The reporter said the story would include the NBA Center but also focus on how the league had said it would build 12 NBA-style arenas in China and start an NBA China league. Neither happened, and he planned to explain how announcing the NBA Center was a step back from grander ambitions.

I alerted the head of our communications department and went to see then-Deputy Commissioner Adam Silver, who armed me with facts and rebuttals. Silver was calm and specific. That’s what an hour is for.

I went back to the reporter and walked him through our objections one by one. He pushed back on some and accepted others. The biggest win: I got him to hold the piece until after the press conference. It ran in print on Oct. 12.

We used that day well. Our department head and my teammates helped line up three positive features with other national outlets. I do not remember which outlets.

When the Times piece ran, it was better than we expected. The headline, “NBA Plans Complex Outside Beijing,” was mild. Our rebuttals shaped it, and the three features balanced what remained critical. Without that hour, the coverage out of Beijing could have been negative.

In Beijing, speed limited damage. At the NFL, speed would have preserved a good story. Friendly leaks cost more to ignore because no one feels the urgency.

The NFL may have been holding the news for its Monday Night Football slot. That’s a legitimate reason. But the league could have confirmed Goodell’s “one request” language without revealing the show.

I don’t know what the NFL was weighing internally. But when good news leaks, whoever speaks first sets the frame.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/verizon-c.title: How Verizon’s CEO is rolling out his ‘play-to-win’ playbook—and fending off Elon Musk
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/verizon-c.author: Diane Brady
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/verizon-c.text:
Good morning. Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell writing this morning.

Dan Schulman hates losing. For the past few years, he watched from his seat on Verizon’s board as the telecom giant lost market share, hobbled by internal bureaucracy and risk aversion.

“We were a big, lumbering giant that had fallen behind,” Schulman told me on the most recent episode of the Fortune 500 Titans and Disruptors podcast, admitting the board should have moved faster to make a leadership change. “We had processes where you needed something like 35 signatures before you could move forward.”

Schulman, who had been the board’s “hit-by-a-bus” successor, was named CEO in October 2025. At his first all-hands, he spoke candidly, without slides or notes: Verizon was losing. Layoffs were necessary. (Schulman would cut more than 13,000 roles, the largest layoff in Verizon’s history.) The culture had to be redefined. And the company’s tech stack needed to be rebuilt from top to bottom. (Schulman estimates there will be 100 billion AI agents in the next few years, driving an explosion in data traffic and network demand.)

“Culture is the single most important thing in any transformation. It is what holds you back or can propel you forward,” Schulman told me.

Schulman laid out a transformation plan he expects to take three years. He walked me through his playbook, including how he’s using AI to boost performance marketing and raise customer satisfaction, his views on AI-driven cybersecurity threats, and how he’s setting clear KPIs across 10 workstreams.

One year in, Verizon is beginning to see results, and it’s facing new challenges like Elon Musk’s Starlink.

Schulman says he hasn’t spoken with Musk recently. But he’s preparing for Musk to follow through and become a direct Verizon competitor.

“We’re not standing still. We’re assuming that what he says is what he’s going to do,” Schulman told me. “We need to be ready and prepared…We are going to have a radically different look and feel three or four years from now. We’re going to be two or three generations better than we are today.”

For Schulman’s full Verizon transformation playbook, listen to the episode of Fortune 500 Titans and Disruptors on Spotify. You can also read more in Ruth Umoh’s profile of Verizon’s turnaround strategy in the next print issue of Fortune (previewed here).

Memory chip shortage could worsen through mid-2027, executive warns

Gerry Chen, CEO of Taiwanese memory company Team Group, warned that chip shortages could get worse through the first half of 2027 as AI companies buy up supplies. That could mean higher prices or less memory in phones and computers, and Chen predicts supply won’t catch up with demand until the second half of 2028 at the earliest.

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby is calling for a national wealth tax, saying wealthy Americans—including himself—should pay more. He earned $32.3 million in compensation last year. He argues that investments can grow untaxed if they are never sold. Critics warn that an annual wealth tax could discourage investment and drive money out of the country.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/goolsbee.title: Fed's Goolsbee calls inflation report 'borderline disturbing' as central bank weighs more hikes
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/goolsbee.author: Alex Harring
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/goolsbee.text:
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest consumer inflation report “borderline disturbing” and “distressing.”

The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, coming in higher than economists predicted.

Some Fed officials have been saying the central bank may need to be more aggressive in hiking interest rates to bring down inflation.

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest inflation data “borderline disturbing.”

“It’s another distressing report — borderline disturbing,” Goolsbee said in an interview with the PBS NewsHour Tuesday.

“We’ve got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing,” Goolsbee said. “We’re going to have to deal with that.”

The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Tuesday release. That was higher than economists had predicted.

Goolsbee said he had not seen drivers of prices like tariffs fade over time like he hoped. He also said continuously high inflation on services concerned him.

And the Chicago Fed chief said lofty prices are a top issue for many people he meets.

“It’s on everyone’s mind,” Goolsbee said. “It’s on business mind. It’s on nonprofits’ minds. It’s on ordinary consumers’ mind.”

The inflation report landed at a critical juncture for the Federal Reserve, as it considers its next interest-rate move — and the moves it may have to make beyond that if the numbers continue to come in hot.

Goolsbee’s comments came on the heels of remarks from other Fed officials Tuesday who said the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee may need to act more decisively to rein in inflation.

When it raises or lowers rates, the Fed typically moves them by a quarter-percentage point. But Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in London early Tuesday that a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for an outsized half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI was “around 0.3.” Hours later, that’s exactly what happened.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking Tuesday after the inflation report, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases, and said “it may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall.”

The rate-setting committee raised rates by a quarter point in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%, before voting to hold them steady in October.

After years of higher-than-preferred price growth, Goolsbee said the possibility of consumers and businesses beginning to expect hot inflation is a “major concern.” If that does happen, he said it can make the process of cooling inflation “much more painful.”

But Goolsbee didn’t specify whether he thought the Fed should hike rates at its December policy gathering as a result of these concerns.

“I’m not a fan of being very specific and tying our hands at the next meeting or meetings in the future,” Goolsbee said.

Waller, Logan and Paulson are voting members of the FOMC this year, which means they will cast votes on whether to raise rates at the committee’s final meeting of the year in December. Goolsbee will be a voting member next year.

In the wake of the inflation report and the remarks from the various Fed officials, Fed funds futures are now unanimously expecting a rate hike at the December meeting, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.

Now the question is about whether the central bank will raise rates by a quarter or half percentage point. The Fed funds futures currently put the odds of a half-point hike at the upcoming December meeting at 15%.

Odds of rates reaching 4.25%-4.5% by the January meeting — the equivalent of either a single half-point rise or two quarter-point hikes — are now at 60%, with a 10% chance of rates hitting 4.5%-4.75% by then.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/coreweav.title: CoreWeave stock pops 15% after outlook raise eases AI slowdown concerns
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/coreweav.author: April Roach
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/coreweav.text:
CoreWeave posted quarterly revenue that beat estimates and raised its full-year guidance.

Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have come under scrutiny this month as investors assessed the sustainability of the AI trade.

CoreWeave has done well to allay concerns by moving away from unsecured bond financing, Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank told CNBC.

CoreWeave
 shares jumped 15% in premarket trading Wednesday after the neocloud posted quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year.

Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have come under scrutiny this month as investors assessed the sustainability of the AI trade. CoreWeave, in particular, sparked alarm when spreads on its CDS widened past 11%, generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default.

Revenue jumped 168% to $3.7 billion in the third quarter, the company said in a Tuesday statement.

The three months to Sept. 30 marked a “breakout quarter” for CoreWeave, CEO Michael Intrator said, adding that growth was supported by multiple sources of funding, including financing backed by customer contracts and around $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits.

Shares were 15.3% higher as of 8:30 a.m. ET. Other neclouds were also higher in premarket trading, with Nebius up 13.4%, Applied Digital
 up 9.8% and Iren up 7.9%.

CoreWeave expects $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion in adjusted operating income on $13 billion to $13.3 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha were looking for $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income, and analysts polled by LSEG had expected $12.86 billion in 2026 revenue.

The neocloud has done well to allay concerns about financing by moving away from unsecured bond financing, Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe.”

“It might be the bottom for CoreWeave,” Blank said Wednesday. “But the shares are so beaten up, you have to believe at this point there’s more value on the upside than the down.”

Tune in at 9:50 a.m. ET as CoreWeave CO Michael Intrator joins CNBC TV to discuss the company’s earnings. Watch in real time on CNBC+ or the CNBC Pro stream.

— CNBC’s Jordan Novet contributed to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-s.title: Nvidia shares rebound 4% as Huang faces scrutiny ahead of earnings
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-s.author: April Roach
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-s.text:
Nvidia shares were higher in premarket trading on Wednesday after falling for two days.

Investors are assessing whether CEO Jensen Huang’s affair will have spillover effects on Nvidia’s business.

Nvidia
’s stock rose premarket on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world’s most valuable tech company.

Shares had closed down 5.47% on Tuesday as more details were revealed about the impact of CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. They fell 4.3% Monday.

Shares were 3.8% higher in premarket trading as of 8:37 a.m. ET.

On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised.

Huang tried to project “business as usual” as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company’s quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.

Investors are assessing whether the matter will have damaging spillover effects on the business.

In a Tuesday note, Bank of America said it saw three scenarios with differing investment outcomes. In one scenario, the impact is contained with leadership continuity, and in another, prolonged uncertainty pressures valuation before earnings.

In the final scenario, the impact is escalated, with “adverse findings, leadership disruption or tighter restrictions requiring earnings reassessment,” BofA research analyst Vivek Arya said in the note.

Zacks’ Chief Equity Strategist John Blank said the selloff reflected two concerns: that the U.S. might impose further restrictions in the wake of the affair and that further problems might arise as the news develops. “What else has Jensen done?” he said.

“It’s not good for Nvidia. It’s not good for Jensen Huang. It’s certainly not good for the AI trade,” Blank told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe” on Wednesday.

Morgan Stanley on Wednesday removed Nvidia as a top pick after shares dropped more than 25% since it was named on the list on Oct. 2. Huang’s leadership is “crucial” to the company’s strategic direction, analysts said in a Wednesday note.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/measles-.title: Measles is surging in the U.S. — and outbreaks can cost millions
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/measles-.author: Annika Kim Constantino
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/measles-.text:
The return of measles in the U.S. can carry a huge financial burden on the U.S. healthcare system.

A new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates that the 2025 measles outbreak in the U.S. — which involved roughly 2,300 confirmed cases nationwide — carried an economic cost of more than $37 million.

Those costs extend beyond treating people who become sick, accounting for the resources spent investigating and containing outbreaks and wages lost when people have to miss work.

Measles outbreaks aren’t just a public health threat. They can also be a financial burden on the U.S. — and the cost could only deepen as the once-eliminated disease spreads more widely.

The U.S. is expected to lose its official measles elimination status following a review by the Pan American Health Organization this week, after cases ratcheted to recent highs this year.

More than 5,100 measles cases have been reported nationwide in 2026 as of early November, marking the country’s worst outbreak in more than three decades. Eight deaths associated with the disease have been confirmed by states so far in 2026: six in Pennsylvania, one in New York and one in Wisconsin.

Based on this year’s case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

The tool also estimates that 2025 measles outbreaks in the U.S. — which involved 2,289 confirmed cases nationwide – carried an economic cost of more than $37 million.

The costs extend beyond treating people who become sick, accounting for the resources health departments spend investigating and containing outbreaks, as well as wages lost when people have to miss work. The tool uses more recent, state-specific cost and financing data than an initial study by the researchers, which relied on historical outbreak costs.

The estimates from the tool are not a definitive accounting of what the outbreaks actually cost. But it illustrates the hefty bill tied to the spread of a disease that can be prevented through vaccination, and the potential economic consequences of falling childhood immunization rates. CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation’s public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases.

“We’re starting to see a whole bunch of people who decided not to get vaccinated as kids or have never gotten exposed to measles because they benefited from herd immunity, who now make it into adulthood and risk potentially getting quite seriously ill and requiring very significant medical expenses, or dying at the hospital,” Bryan Patenaude, a health economist at the International Vaccine Access Center at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who helped develop the tool, said in an interview.

Measles outbreaks can trigger a costly public health response, even when many people who are exposed never become sick.

When a case is identified, public health officials must investigate the infection, identify and notify people who may have been exposed, coordinate with hospitals and schools, and sometimes organize vaccination campaigns to prevent further spread. Those efforts can divert staff and resources from other public health priorities.

Costs could differ heavily depending on the state.

Johns Hopkins’ data includes national averages alongside state-specific inputs, including inpatient hospital costs and wages from government data or trusted health policy sources. In New York, for example, the average inpatient hospital stay is roughly $4,200 a day, while the minimum wage is $16 per hour.

The tool estimates that the 48 cases reported by New York in 2025 carried an estimated $1.1 million in costs, including nearly $749,000 in public health responses, $333,000 in productivity losses and roughly $24,500 in direct medical expenses.

Meanwhile, the 803 cases in Texas, the epicenter of the largest U.S. measles outbreak in 2025, carried estimated costs of nearly $13 million, according to the tool. That includes $9 million in public health costs, $4 million in productivity losses and around $288,000 in direct medical expenses.

The tool builds on a study published by Patenaude and other researchers in August, which examined the costs of measles outbreaks in the U.S. The researchers reviewed published studies and government reports to compile historical estimates of medical expenses and public health response costs across 18 states.

The paper estimated that outbreaks carried a historical average cost of nearly $59,000 per case, just from the public health response. The researchers also estimated how costs scale with outbreak size, separating fixed up-front response expenses from the additional costs associated with each new case.

“A lot of this is incurred up front, and that’s because of the human labor that’s involved in contact tracing and all of the different actors that sort of need to be mobilized to deal with the fact that there’s an outbreak,” Patenaude told CNBC. “It’s a largely labor-driven cost.”

That model estimated roughly $298,000 in fixed costs and about $16,300 for each additional case. But it relied on historical data, including a particularly large 2019 outbreak in New York City, where contact-tracing labor costs were high. The researchers also excluded productivity losses from that model because most of the historical studies they reviewed did not consistently account for them.

The economic burden of measles extends beyond the costs of treating infected patients and organizing a public health response.

People who are exposed to measles may have to quarantine, even if they never develop symptoms. Parents can also be forced to miss work to care for sick or exposed children, while workers who contract the disease may lose wages during their recovery.

A 2025 study by Joey Mattingly, a pharmacist and health economist at the University of Utah, used published epidemiological and cost data to model the potential economic burden of a hypothetical 1,500-case outbreak. His analysis included direct medical expenses, public health spending and lost productivity, and examined how the estimates changed under different assumptions, including hospitalization rates.

The study estimated that the hypothetical outbreak could cost about $90 million, including roughly $26 million in productivity losses.

Those indirect costs can add up quickly because measles is highly contagious and a single infected person can expose dozens of others. Those contacts may need to quarantine or miss work while health officials determine whether they have been infected, creating costs even when they never develop the disease.

Mattingly estimated that each person who is quarantined could amount to roughly $300 in lost productivity alone.

If a single measles case exposes 40 to 50 people who then need to quarantine, that could translate into an estimated $12,000 to $15,000 in lost productivity, even if none of those contacts become sick.

That ripple effect is one reason Mattingly argues that the economic costs of outbreaks can quickly outweigh the investment required to vaccinate people against measles.

“Even if you don’t get the infection, the contact costs you,” he said. “And so it’s just showing that there’s this multiplication or exponential growth on the economic side that happens.”

The financial burden can also fall unevenly across communities. While the costs of responding to an outbreak may be shared among local, state and federal agencies, Mattingly said the impact is often felt directly by local health departments.

“It’s not like your health department is sitting around waiting for measles outbreaks,” he said. “They’re working, doing all these other things, and imagine having to just drop what you’re doing because there’s been a huge outbreak in the community.”

Patenaude said the findings could help state and local health departments better anticipate the resources needed to contain outbreaks — particularly as measles cases continue to rise.

“It’s not super expensive to treat and deal with a single case of measles compared to a single case of cancer,” he said. “But if you have these outbreaks popping up and you’re having to constantly divert resources that could be spent elsewhere by state and local health departments on measles, then you’re going to wind up spending a lot of money very quickly.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/ukraine-.title: Zelenskyy warns Ukraine is 'not real estate' as experts say a Russia peace deal remains elusive
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/ukraine-.author: Elsa Ohlen
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/ukraine-.text:
Following Russia-Ukraine peace talks, the first since February, U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said he was “encouraged by the constructive discussions.”

Negotiations come as issues of the future borders of Ukraine and post-war security guarantees remain divisive.

“I don’t have any expectations of major progress towards settlement,” Mykola Bielieskov, senior analyst at Ukrainian NGO Come Back Alive, told CNBC.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that his country “was not real estate,” as a second and final day of U.S.-brokered peace talks wrapped up.

Speaking to reporters in Denmark late Tuesday, Zelenskyy said he was “happy” with what he was hearing from the peace talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian representatives, but said he had been clear with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that “this is a country of our nation, it is not real estate.”

His comments come amid discussions on the future borders of Ukraine and post-war security guarantees, issues where the countries remain far apart.

“Everybody is ready for dialog. First, stop the war in Ukraine. Second, security guarantees for Ukraine. Third, maybe some dialog about these topics of security,” Zelenskyy said. “This sequence is very, very important.”

It comes as the first trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. since February concluded on Wednesday.

Speaking post-meeting, Kushner called the talks “productive” and said the parties had also discussed the difficult issue of territorial boundaries. The Ukrainian negotiator meanwhile said momentum was good and a solution could be reached before the end of the year.

Russia chief negotiator and Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky said the parties on Wednesday had reached an agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange, and that details would be announced soon.

Another round of exchanges of prisoners of war would be welcomed, Mykola Bielieskov, senior analyst at Ukrainian NGO Come Back Alive, told CNBC Tuesday. “Otherwise there is no room for compromise,” he said, adding, “I don’t have any expectations of major progress towards settlement.”

According to Bielieskov, Ukraine could accept a ceasefire along the current front lines, but would never formally recognize Russian sovereignty over occupied territory. He argued that Zelenskyy has neither the legal authority nor public support to surrender Ukrainian land, even if Kyiv acknowledges it cannot reclaim those territories militarily in the near term.

Russia’s demands for additional territory, restrictions on NATO membership and limits on Ukraine’s armed forces remain fundamental obstacles to a deal, he added.

Russia has publicly maintained its demand that Ukraine surrender the entire eastern Donbas region, including territory Moscow has not captured.

While Ukraine and European allies push for a ceasefire as an initial step, before moving on to issues such as security guarantees, borders and reconstruction, Russia has signaled it considers security guarantees necessary before ending fighting.

“It looks like because Russia has objected to a ceasefire proposal that Ukraine and the U.S. earlier last year made, the Trump administration is no longer trying to achieve a ceasefire, even though that’s logically the first step,” former U.S. ambassador William Courtney told CNBC early Tuesday.

Courtney said Russia has shown no signs of seriously pursuing a ceasefire in Ukraine, despite Kyiv’s willingness to freeze the conflict along current battle lines.

He argued that Moscow’s territorial demands and continued attacks suggest its objectives remain unchanged, making meaningful negotiations unlikely without a shift in Russia’s position or battlefield conditions.

Maximilian Hess at political risk firm Enmetena Advisory told CNBC’s Dan Murphy Wednesday, ahead of the second day of talks, that little has been achieved in the latest round of meetings so far.

While Zelenskyy has urged leaders to speak directly, Hess said it’s unlikely the Ukrainian leader will be willing to meet with Putin without meaningful concessions from Russia, given the risk of domestic backlash.
