https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/trump-co.title: How Democrats could snarl Trump administration stakes in private sector companies
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/trump-co.author: Kevin Breuninger
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/trump-co.text:
The Trump administration’s unprecedented interventions in private sector companies could be on Democrats’ investigation list when they take control of the House and Senate.

That could affect how President Donald Trump interacts with those companies, after spending two years forging equity agreements or, in the case of U.S. Steel, acquiring a “golden share.”

The next Congress could try to ensure the government takes stakes that are “forwarding genuine national security priorities” without giving “special favors to political and family connections,” said Professor Sarah Bauerle Danzman.

With Republicans in charge of the White House and Congress, President Donald Trump has embedded the federal government in private sector companies’ affairs in unprecedented ways. That could change once Trump’s Democratic adversaries take over the House and Senate following the blue-wave midterm.

Democrats, planning to root out alleged corruption involving Trump, his family and their business associates, have signaled they will closely scrutinize companies that have curried the president’s favor.

Their investigations may extend to Intel
 and the dozens of other companies that have clinched equity stakes with the government during Trump’s second term. Democratic lawmakers in July asked law firm Skadden Arps for details about its involvement in the Intel deal.

The dynamic could affect how Trump approaches relationships with private sector companies, after spending two years involving the government in their affairs through stock agreements or, in the case of U.S. Steel, acquiring a “golden share” when the company was acquired by Nippon Steel
.

The golden share, which allows a holder to outvote other shareholders, was negotiated as part of the June 2025 deal. The highly unusual arrangement gives Trump veto power over several key areas of the steelmaker’s business, including those related to employee salaries, capital investment and even the company name.

In a unique twist, the company’s amended charter specifies that after Trump leaves office, the veto power passes not to his successor, but to the Treasury and Commerce Departments as representatives of the U.S. government.

U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt is scheduled to speak Wednesday with CNBC’s Megan Cassella about what’s next for U.S. industry at the B20 summit hosted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

The U.S. Steel intervention turned out to be just the beginning of the U.S. government taking stakes in companies, a highly unusual move stateside. A month after acquiring the golden share, the Trump administration agreed to a $400 million stock deal with rare-earths company MP Materials
. The month after that, Trump announced the U.S. would take a 10% stake in chipmaker Intel
.

By January, one year into Trump’s second term as president, the administration had established some form of equity position in 14 companies, according to the CATO Institute’s tracker. That number skyrocketed to 41 by November, including nine such announcements in May alone, the tracker shows. The holdings include both publicly traded and privately held companies, and CATO tracks deals that are closed as well as others that have been made public but are still being negotiated.

Following Republicans’ decisive defeat in the Nov. 3 midterm election, the federal government has not revealed any new stock positions. But Trump, entering lame-duck status and on the verge of losing political power over Congress, could keep trying to steer his government to forge more equity deals with companies, said Indiana University associate professor Sarah Bauerle Danzman, who researches the intersection of national security and investment policy.

“He might feel he has less to lose,” Bauerle Danzman, who is also a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told CNBC.

White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC in a statement, “Through voluntary equity investments in willing companies, the Trump Administration has partnered with the private sector to rebuild America’s industrial base and bring critical production back home.”

“Moving forward, the President is willing to work with anyone to advance solutions that strengthen our economy and put more money back in the pockets of American workers,” Middleton said.

But Trump’s so-far unimpeded efforts may face sudden resistance once Democrats take majority control of the House and Senate in January.

Democratic lawmakers are openly gearing up to score wins against Trump and his associates as they vow to crack down on alleged rampant government corruption.

Those probes are expected to center on tech giants like Apple
, Meta Platforms
 and Elon Musk’s companies, whose executives have spent millions cozying up to the administration. Democrats are also poised to dig into potential conflicts related to the bevy of critical-minerals deals Trump has struck. Lawmakers of both parties are also looking at Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang, the close Trump ally engulfed in scandal after admitting an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The administration’s equity interventions could become a target in that mission, said Bauerle Danzman, predicting that Democrats might seek to boost oversight efforts even if they don’t try to cancel the existing stock arrangements.

The next Congress could try to ensure the government is taking stakes that are “forwarding genuine national security priorities” and that do not provide “special favors to political and family connections,” she said.

“The story there is more about kind of tying these issues to ones of accountability and anti-corruption, as opposed to necessarily cost,” Bauerle Danzman said.

It’s also not clear how strongly Republicans would try to defend Trump’s golden share or his government’s equity stakes should they become a Democratic target.

Conservatives traditionally espouse free markets and denounce excessive government meddling in the private sector. Republicans, including Trump, spent much of the midterm campaign warning that Democrats aim to destroy the U.S. capitalist system and impose economy-killing big-government socialism.

Some Republicans have criticized the Trump administration’s corporate interventions, but the moves have received little pushback from the president’s party overall.

But in the wake of a crushing electoral defeat, some Republicans “might feel emboldened and actually join with the Democrats” in trying to clamp down on Trump, Bauerle Danzman said.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/trump-co.summary: Democrats are trying to root out alleged corruption involving Trump, his family and business associates. Republicans have criticized the Trump administration's corporate interventions. But the moves have received little pushback from the president’s party overall.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/us-army-.title: American soldier arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/us-army-.author: Chloe Taylor
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/us-army-.text:
A 41-year-old U.S. Army soldier was arrested in Gloucestershire, England, on Tuesday on suspicion of spying for Russia.

He is being detained under the U.K.’s National Security Act.

The individual was assigned to NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.

A senior soldier in the U.S. Army has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of spying for Russia, London’s Metropolitan Police said on Tuesday evening.

The unnamed 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester, a city in western England, on Tuesday as part of an investigation by the U.K.’s Counter Terrorism Policing. British police worked with U.S. authorities, including the military and the FBI, in their investigations.

A senior NATO military official confirmed on Tuesday that the American service member was assigned to the military alliance’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC).

ARRC, headquartered in the English county of Gloucestershire, is a  3-star NATO headquarters with more than 400 permanent staff from more than 20 nations ready to deploy land forces where they are needed.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that Moscow had “absolutely nothing to do with” the case in the U.K.

The individual at the center of the case, detained in London, is suspected of committing offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of the U.K.’s National Security Act.

Section 1 offenses relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 involves assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The maximum penalty is life imprisonment for a Section 1 offense and 14 years’ imprisonment for a Section 3 offense. A fine may also be imposed for either offense.

Police officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan Police added.

The arrest comes as Washington is seeking to broker an end to Russia’s war in Ukraine. U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials began in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first such meeting since February, while Kyiv and its European allies continue to press for credible security guarantees as part of any settlement.

President Donald Trump, a longstanding critic of NATO and its members’ defense budgets, said on Monday that there appeared to be a growing willingness on both sides to end the almost five-year war.

Russia has long threatened retaliatory action against an expansion of NATO’s eastern flank and has previously demanded guarantees that Ukraine will never be allowed to join the alliance. Finland and Sweden became NATO’s newest members in 2023 and 2024, respectively.

Since Russia and Ukraine have been at war, Russian activity has also been reported deeper into European and NATO territory, with regional authorities investigating whether Moscow could be involved in some of the recent disarray seen across the continent.

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday evening that the allegations against a U.S. serviceman were “of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”

“I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” he said.

Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement that “the alleged conduct of a senior solider, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”

Authorities said Tuesday that the investigation is not related to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.

On Oct. 27, British prosecutors said they had charged a man with assisting a foreign intelligence service over an incident at a military base used by the U.S. for strikes on Iran. The base in question, RAF Fairford, is in Gloucestershire, around 30 miles from ARRC’s headquarters at Imjin Barracks.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-j.title: Nvidia's Huang tries to project 'business as usual' in return to office after affair revelation
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-j.author: Seema Mody,Samantha Subin
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-j.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang conducted his regular morning meeting with top-level executives the day after admitting to an extramarital affair, people familiar with the meeting told CNBC.

Employees inside the company described the mood at the chipmaking giant as “sad.”

The company’s board is investigating his relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang walked into the chipmaker’s Santa Clara, California, headquarters on Monday and conducted his regular morning meeting with top-level executives, people familiar with the meeting told CNBC.

On Sunday, Huang had disclosed an extramarital affair to employees.

Huang kicked off the closed-door gathering by addressing his infidelity and sharing how sorry he was to his staff, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. They said Huang didn’t take any questions and quickly pivoted to business and top agenda items of the day.

The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings just one week ahead of the company’s quarterly earnings report.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

People inside the artificial intelligence chip giant said Huang tried to project “business as usual,” even as the probe moved forward into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The CEO was in a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, according to the Financial Times.

Sentiment toward Jensen Huang shifted on Sunday after the 63-year-old revealed in an email to employees that he had an affair, though he did not disclose with whom he had the relationship.

“I know an apology cannot undo what I have done,” he wrote. “I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” Nvidia’s board opened an investigation and hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct the probe on Tuesday.

Employees inside the firm described the mood to CNBC as “sad.” One employee told CNBC that they were shocked by Jensen Huang’s revelations.

People also told CNBC that longtime employees viewed Jensen Huang as an idol who could do no wrong and thought of him as a guiding light. Many employees at the company are also struggling to come to grips with the CEO’s actions, the people said.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 to build graphics processing units for video game graphics. In recent years, the company has become synonymous with the AI boom, powering the technology that underpins large language models and the massive data center buildout.

A central figure in the development of every AI layer, the Nvidia CEO is also a key voice in Washington, even accompanying President Donald Trump on his trip to China in May. In September, Jensen Huang and his wife were pictured at the same table as Chinese President Xi Jinping for the White House’s state dinner.

The news of the CEO’s affair has drawn increased scrutiny on his continued support for more AI chip sales to China.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-j.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang conducted his regular morning meeting with top-level executives the day after admitting to an extramarital affair. The company’s board is investigating his relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/us-iran-.title: Bessent reportedly moved to military base over Iranian threats on his life
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/us-iran-.author: Lim Hui Jie
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/us-iran-.text:
The New York Times, citing officials familiar with the matter, reported that U.S. officials concluded Iranian plots against current and former American officials had reached a more advanced stage.

The Department of Justice said late Tuesday that three Iranian nationals have been indicted on terrorism-related charges.

Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly said military action against Iran may not be necessary if sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade are proving effective.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was reportedly moved from his Washington, D.C., home to a military base due to Iranian threats on his life.

The New York Times, citing officials familiar with the matter, said that U.S. officials had concluded Iranian plotting against current and former American officials had reached a more advanced stage.

Separately, Reuters reported that the severity of the threats against Bessent was not immediately clear.

Bessent has led Operation Economic Outcast, a Treasury campaign launched in August to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and other financial measures, in addition to the U.S. military actions.

The Times reported that Bessent’s role in that campaign has made him one of the Trump administration officials Iran most wanted to target.

CNBC has contacted the White House and the U.S. Department of the Treasury for comment.

The move comes as the Department of Justice said late Tuesday that three Iranian nationals had been indicted on terrorism-related charges.

The department said the three were allegedly involved in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States.

The alleged plots included a September 2026 attack targeting RAF Fairford in the U.K., where U.S. military personnel were stationed.

“Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American service members will be prosecuted by the United States government,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

Earlier in October, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran was involved in the incident at RAF Fairford that led to the arrest of five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi then rejected the allegation, writing on X that Burnham was “barking up the wrong tree.”

RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire, is a key U.S. Air Force operating location in Europe and has supported deployments of American strategic bombers and other aircraft.

Separately, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly said military action against Iran may not be necessary if economic sanctions and Washington’s naval blockade are working.

On Monday, President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that “Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others, would prefer the status quo, in other words, a continuation of the Greatest Naval Blockade in History.”

“We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict,” Trump added.

Asked Tuesday why he would not simply declare an end to the Iran war, Trump said he wanted to ensure that U.S. allies in the region were “not hurt” and that there was a “long-term solution.

However, Iranian officials have denied that negotiations are underway. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei said claims that talks were continuing were aimed at “easing economic pressures and reducing oil prices.”

Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude prices edged higher during Wednesday’s Asia trading session, at about $92 and $86 per barrel, respectively.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/spain-pr.title: General strikes to paralyze Spain as protestors clash with police ahead of election campaign
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/spain-pr.author: Natalie Feary
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/spain-pr.text:
Millions of workers are expected to join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years, with transport and businesses facing widespread disruption.

Soaring rents and living costs are driving the unrest, as unions demand stronger government action on housing and wages.

The strike comes less than three weeks before Spain’s Nov. 29 election, with polls suggesting the Popular Party and Vox could secure a parliamentary majority.

Spanish workers are expected to turn out in the millions on Wednesday for the country’s first general strike in 14 years, as anger over soaring rents and living costs intensifies less than three weeks before a general election.

Demonstrators clashed with police at a wholesale market in Madrid in the early hours of the strike, while roadblocks were also reported in the early hours of Wednesday.

The 24-hour labor walkout is expected to disrupt public transport and flights, as well as bring some businesses, shops and factories to a standstill.

Housing costs are a particular source of frustration among demonstrators. Rents have almost doubled over the past decade, squeezing household budgets as many workers feel homeownership is beyond their reach.

The Bank of Spain estimates that the country faces a shortage of 750,000 homes, potentially rising to 1 million over the next two years.

Spain’s two largest trade unions, CCOO and UGT, which called the strike, are calling for greater government intervention in the housing market. Housing activists demand an end to tourist rentals and automatic lease renewals, while unions are seeking greater housing intervention and a new minimum-wage agreement.

UGT Secretary-General Pepe Álvarez urged members to join the protests, saying “there is no salary that can cope with the price of housing in this country,” in comments translated by CNBC. He added that it was time for the government to listen to citizens’ demands.

The strike follows weeks of social unrest. The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid home, followed by her death around two weeks later, sparked national outrage. The left-wing government’s attempts to pass measures to help tenants were blocked by the opposition.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s coalition responded by calling an election for Nov. 29, hoping to bolster his support and secure another four years in power. But a high-speed train collision that killed 69 people, the second such disaster this year, shifted the debate toward public safety and accusations of government mismanagement.

The government has not officially endorsed the strike, whose slogan is “Salaries. Housing. Prices.” But the protests are widely seen as an opportunity for left-wing parties, including Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party, to put housing at the center of the election campaign.

Political scientist Oriol Bartomeus of the Autonomous University of Barcelona told The Associated Press that a strong, peaceful turnout could help the left return the campaign to a focus on housing.

Sánchez took to social media earlier this week to voice support for existing policies including national health insurance and a 40-hour workweek, warning that a right-wing government would introduce austerity measures and cuts to social services.

“Your eight-hour working day. Your pensions. Your public healthcare. None of this fell from the sky. They were collective achievements,” he told voters on Monday.

The conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox, which already govern in some parts of Spain, accuse the unions of organizing the protests to keep the current government in power. “The strike is not a general strike, it’s an election strike,” Miguel Tellado, a spokesperson for the Popular Party, said Tuesday.

Both parties oppose intervention in the housing market.

Opinion polls suggest a shift to the right, with the Popular Party leading and potentially able to form a government with Vox.

Such a coalition would bring the far right into Spain’s national government for the first time since Francisco Franco’s 36-year dictatorship ended in 1975.

A poll for El País and Cadena SER, published Nov. 9, put the Popular Party at 31.9%, Sánchez’s Partido Socialista Obrero Español at 29.9% and Vox at 18%. The survey, conducted Nov. 2-4, projected a combined 190 seats for the Popular Party and Vox, above the 176 needed for a majority in the 350-seat lower house.

A strong turnout at Wednesday’s protests could prove crucial for the government, whose handling of the migration crisis in Ceuta drew widespread criticism. Sánchez’s family has also been plagued by corruption scandals.

The prime minister’s personal standing has suffered. Some 58% of respondents had a “bad” or “very bad” opinion of him, compared with 41% who had a good or very good opinion, according to a poll for elDiario.es conducted Nov. 2-5.

Violence during the strike, however, could backfire on the government. Protests in France in October were seen as an opportunity for the country’s far-right party to emphasize its ability to restore order and security ahead of the country’s 2027 presidential elections.

“On the evening of 11 November, there will almost certainly be two narratives: one of resounding success and one of failure. Neither should be read as an exit poll. It will be more useful to look at other things: which sectors and regions stop work, how many people take to the streets and, above all, whether housing moves to the centre of the campaign,” wrote Maite Aurrekoetxea, professor of social and human sciences at the University of Deusto, in comments translated by Google.

The 24-hour labor walkout is expected to disrupt public transport and flights, as well as businesses, shops and factories.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nissan-s.title: Nissan cuts sales forecast again on China woes as CEO outlines plan to fight back
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nissan-s.author: Elsa Ohlen
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nissan-s.text:
Nissan Motor is responding to intensifying competition in China by developing vehicles specifically for Chinese consumers, CEO Ivan Espinosa told CNBC on Wednesday.

The Japanese automaker faces weakening demand and an accelerating shift toward electric vehicles in China, even as its restructuring efforts show progress in the U.S. and Japan.

It cut its full-year sales outlook for the second time since August to between 2.97 million and 3 million vehicles.

Nissan Motor
 plans to expand exports of vehicles developed in China to help compete against Chinese rivals globally, CEO Ivan Espinosa told CNBC on Wednesday.

The export push comes as intensifying competition in the world’s largest auto market forced the company to cut its annual sales forecast for a second time in months.

Espinosa said Nissan would rapidly increase its exports of China-developed vehicles from two models to five, targeting 12 regional market clusters in the “very near term.”

The Japanese automaker is responding to intensifying competition in China by developing vehicles specifically for Chinese consumers, using local technology, lower costs and faster development processes, he said.

″We can defend ourselves from these very aggressive players by using exactly the same elements that they have: speed, cost, and good technology,” he told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe.”

Nissan faces weakening demand and an accelerating shift toward electric vehicles in China, even as its restructuring efforts show progress in the U.S. and Japan.

On Wednesday, Nissan cut its global sales outlook for the fiscal year ending March 2027 to between 2.97 million and 3 million vehicles, down from 3.15 million previously. It maintained its full-year operating profit and net cash guidance.

In China, “weaker demand, a faster-than-anticipated shift to [new energy vehicles] and intensifying competition are putting greater pressure on sales than initially anticipated,” the company said in a statement.

In August, Nissan revised its full-year sales volume outlook from 3.3 million units to 3.15 million units.

In October, shares of peer Volvo Cars crashed after it reported a swing to operating loss, citing tough market conditions in China and the U.S.

CEO Håkan Samuelsson told CNBC at the time that it needed a new strategy in China, with regionally adapted cars.

“It’s really a lot about the Chinese market, of course, where the change has come faster than we thought, and really now we can see that selling global cars developed in Europe and China will not work, and then this is affecting all the Western players in China,” Samuelsson said.

On Wednesday, Nissan also reported a 96% drop in second-quarter operating profit to 2.1 billion yen ($13 million), significantly below analyst expectations of 54.9 billion yen, according to FactSet.

The drop in profits was due to no longer having the benefit of lower U.S. emissions-related expenses that boosted profits a year ago, the company said.

Net revenue grew 8.2% to 3.1 trillion yen in the quarter, largely in line with consensus.

The quarterly results came after the Tokyo market closed. Shares are down 29% year-to-date.

Nissan’s Frankfurt-listed shares dropped 4% in early afternoon trading.

Espinosa, who has led the company since April 2025, also emphasised progress on a turnaround plan to reduce its global manufacturing footprint and cut its workforce by 15%. About 18 months into the plan, the company has achieved 365 billion yen in savings, Espinosa said.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nissan-s.summary: Nissan Motor plans to expand exports of vehicles developed in China to help compete against Chinese rivals globally. The Japanese automaker faces weakening demand and an accelerating shift toward electric vehicles in China. Nissan cut its full-year sales outlook for the second time since August to between 2.97 million and 3 million vehicles.

Republican lawmakers on Tuesday picked Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio and Sen. John Thune of South Dakota to serve as their respective House and Senate minority leaders in the next Congress.

Jordan, the House Judiciary Committee chairman, was elected in a 106-73 vote, sources told MS NOW on condition of anonymity to discuss the private meeting.

Jordan, a close ally of President Donald Trump, will take on the role as Republicans lose power following the blue-wave midterm.

Thune, in a statement, said he “appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues.”

Republican lawmakers on Tuesday picked Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio and Sen. John Thune of South Dakota to serve as their respective House and Senate minority leaders in the next Congress.

Jordan, the House Judiciary Committee chairman, was elected in a 106-73 vote, sources told MS NOW on condition of anonymity to discuss the private meeting. He beat Rep. Steve Scalise, R-La., the current House majority leader.

A two-decade House veteran and committed supporter of President Donald Trump, Jordan will take on the leadership role just as Republicans relinquish power, following blowout Democratic victories in last week’s midterm election.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced the day after Election Day that he would not run for minority leader in the 120th Congress.

Thune, in a statement, said he “appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues today, and I am honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the Senate Republican Conference in the 120th Congress.”

“I’m proud of what this Republican team has accomplished together, and we remain united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats’ efforts to enact their far-left, liberal agenda,” Thune said in the statement.

“We have important work ahead of us, and I look forward to serving alongside my colleagues on behalf of the American people,” he said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/trump-ta.title: White House vows to press ahead with tariffs despite midterm backlash over rising prices
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/trump-ta.author: Luke Fountain
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/trump-ta.text:
At the U.S. Chamber’s B20 summit in Washington, a senior White House official defended Trump’s tariffs despite Republican midterm losses, while former Trump economic advisor Gary Cohn warned that American consumers are footing the bill.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found 62% of Americans support repealing Trump’s tariffs, as new data showed consumer prices rose 0.4% in October.

Business leaders at the summit said global supply chains are becoming more regional, while Democrats face significant obstacles to reversing Trump’s trade policies when they take control of Congress.

One week after voters punished Republicans over rising prices in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump’s White House signaled it would stay the course on tariffs, even as his former top economic advisor warned that Americans are footing the bill.

Jim Goyer, Trump’s director of White House Office of Public Liaison, defended tariffs as a tool to rebuild U.S. manufacturing, secure supply chains and protect national security during an address Tuesday at the B20 summit, a gathering of global business leaders in Washington hosted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

“And we are just getting started,” Goyer said. “Our ambition is to continue this pace for the remainder of the president’s term in office.”

But Gary Cohn, who served as Trump’s chief economic advisor during his first administration, offered a sharply different assessment during an onstage interview later Tuesday.

“Tariffs are a consumption tax on the U.S. consumer,” Cohn said, arguing that the duties are raising prices and forcing Americans to reconsider purchases.

The divide exposed a growing dilemma for Trump. His trade agenda is reshaping global commerce – and driving up costs for voters. Companies are adapting to the chaos, but the old trading system isn’t coming back.

“President Trump has disrupted that system in a way that we’re not likely to return to,” Kevin Brady, a former Republican congressman who helped lead the B20 summit, said during a discussion with U.S. Chamber CEO Suzanne Clark.

The political backlash was evident in the Nov. 3 election. Roughly two-thirds of voters said Trump’s policies contributed to inflation, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. Nearly nine in 10 said the cost of living was a major or crucial factor in their vote.

A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found 62% of Americans supported repealing Trump’s tariffs, while just 21% approved of his handling of the cost of living.

“Last week, American voters sent a clear message about the cost of living and their economic security,” Clark said in her keynote address.

The pressure intensified Tuesday as new government data showed consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, exceeding economists’ expectations. Annual inflation reached 3.7% in September, the latest available year-over-year figure and well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target.

Tariffs are not the only factor driving higher prices. The war with Iran has pushed energy costs sharply higher, while housing, healthcare and other household expenses continue to strain consumers.

But research has found Trump’s import duties have added to those pressures. A Federal Reserve Bank of New York study estimated that about 26% of tariff increases were passed through to consumer prices, with some effects taking nine to 12 months to work through supply chains.

Cohn, now vice chairman of IBM
, argued that while tariffs generate revenue for the U.S., those gains come at consumers’ expense.

“You’re looking at one side of the equation. You’re looking at the credit side of the balance sheet,” Cohn said, describing how he would respond to Trump’s defense of tariff revenue. “There’s the debit side of the balance sheet, which is every hardworking American who happened to pay the tariff through some product that they bought.”

Still, Cohn saw room for a bipartisan trade deal. He suggested Trump and the incoming Democratic Congress could make protections against China and unfair trade practices permanent while rolling back tariffs on Canada, leaving less for future presidents to undo.

For businesses, the shift is already underway. UPS
 CEO Carol Tomé said customers are moving production and sourcing closer to home as global supply chains become more regional.

“Supply chains are diversifying. Supply chains are regionalizing,” Tomé said during a panel discussion moderated by CNBC’s Morgan Brennan.

Separately, UPS is opening a new $80 million-plus air hub in the Philippines in October to expand its Asian network and improve connections across more than 1,100 global trade lanes.

Other executives, like Jim Fitterling, executive chairman of chemicals giant Dow
, defended Trump’s tariffs despite their costs. Fitterling acknowledged they can drive up prices but argued they are necessary to combat unfair competition and protect U.S. manufacturing.

Democrats plan to challenge Trump’s tariffs when they take control of Congress in January, but his veto power and broad trade authority could make them difficult to overturn.

The political backlash was evident in the Nov. 3 election. The pressure intensified Tuesday as new government data showed consumer prices rose 0.4% in October.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/tech-sel.title: Investors pivot to defensive stocks as markets enter a ‘state of alert’
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/tech-sel.author: Chloe Taylor
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/tech-sel.text:
Investors appear to be shifting toward defensive sectors such as healthcare, consumer staples and utilities as technology stocks face renewed volatility.

The Nasdaq and other tech-heavy indexes have fallen sharply since October amid concerns over AI spending, financing, and the economic outlook.

Analysts say the defensive rotation may have gone too far, with some technology valuations falling sharply even as underlying fundamentals remain healthy.

Markets are in a “state of alert,” according to analysts monitoring a pivot from riskier tech sector bets into defensive stocks.

Technology stocks — a key driver of rallies in recent years — have been notably volatile in 2026. Concerns about artificial intelligence — particularly when it comes to capital expenditure, cash flow, debt and circular financing — have sparked multiple bouts of volatility this year.

The Democrats’ sweep of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections amplified pressure on the sector last week.

Wall Street’s tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index
 is up by around 8.7% since the start of the year as of Nov. 9 close, but gave up some of its year-to-date gains in October when it shed 5.3% over the course of the month. The index — home to Big Tech names including Nvidia
, Microsoft
, Alphabet
 and Apple
 — has staged a recovery in recent days, but remains in the red for November and is down 0.7% for the month so far after dipping into correction territory last week.

The Nasdaq isn’t the only tech-focused index to have seen big losses over the past month. South Korea’s Kospi
 index, which is heavily exposed to the semiconductor sector, lost 16.2% in October and is down more than 8% month-to-date.

The MSCI World Information Technology index lost 7% in October, and has shed a further 4.6% so far this month. MSCI’s U.S.-only IT index is down 11.5% since October.

At the same time, stocks in defensive sectors have seen broad gains.

MSCI’s indexes encompassing the consumer staples, healthcare and utilities sectors — widely seen as more stable assets in the equity market during times of volatility or uncertainty — have all risen significantly over the last month.

In a note on Monday, Alastair Pinder, HSBC’s head emerging markets and global equity strategist, said recent moves in stock markets had been “vicious, and in our view, overdone.”

“The market is already pricing greater execution risk and capex delays,” he said, referring to the development of artificial intelligence. “With US semiconductors trading on a 12-month forward PE of 13.5x after a 45% de-rating since June, how much more pain is there to price?”

He added that fundamentals broadly appear healthy.

“The rotation into defensives looks extreme,” he said. “Walmart trades on 40x forward earnings, near a record high, while Nvidia trades on 13x, near a record low.”

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, described equity markets as being “in a state of alert, judging by how investors are rotating their sector exposures.”

“Such movement matters, and can help stock pickers with their selections, bearing in mind the old adage that ‘a bad stock in a good sector will outperform a good stock in a bad sector,’” he said in a note on Monday.

AJ Bell’s analysis of 11 so-called “super-sectors” in the S&P Global 1200 shows that, in the second half of 2026 so far, healthcare and consumer staples stocks have been the best performers after energy — a major beneficiary of surging oil prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war.

The IT sector, the data shows, has gone from being the best-performing sector in the first half of the year on a 28.4% rise, to the worst performer in the second half after tumbling more than 11%.

“Information Technology has gone from penthouse to outhouse and slumped from being the best performer to the worst,” Mould said.

“Energy has been resilient as have Consumer Staples and Healthcare, while Industrials have been noticeably weak. These trends could reflect nagging worries over the economic outlook for next year, as well as worries over whether air is leaking out of an AI ‘bubble.’”

Analysts say the defensive rotation may have gone too far, with some technology valuations falling sharply even as underlying fundamentals remain healthy.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/hoax-bom.title: Hundreds of schools in Italy, UK evacuated over 'hoax' bomb threats
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/hoax-bom.author: Elsa Ohlen
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/hoax-bom.text:
Italy’s education minister Giuseppe Valditara told Italian TV that over 300 emailed bomb threats to Italian schools were presumed to be hoaxes.

Emails were signed “Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan,” the same purported sender who claimed responsibility for bomb threats emailed to newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria on Friday, according to Reuters.

Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland also evacuated on Wednesday morning after receiving similar threats.

Hundreds of schools across Europe were evacuated on Wednesday after receiving bomb threats, police forces say, in what appeared to be the latest wave of efforts to intimidate populations.

Italy’s education minister Giuseppe Valditara told Italian TV that the emailed threats were presumed to be hoaxes, and that the number of schools affected was expected to rise.

Threats, received just before 10 a.m. local time by more than 300 schools, were signed “Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan,” according to a copy of the message seen by Reuters. The same purported sender also claimed responsibility for bomb threats emailed to newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria on Friday, according to Reuters.

Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland were also evacuated on Wednesday morning after receiving similar threats.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland said they were treated as a hoax, while Police Scotland similarly said there was nothing to suggest the threats posed any credible risk to the public.

“Based on enquiries and information to date, police are treating this email, which originated from outside the UK, as a hoax,” Police Scotland said in a statement.

It comes as concerns grow in Europe about so-called hybrid threats and the continent’s ability to withstand such threats.

Hybrid warfare combines tactics such as cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation to destabilize adversaries without triggering open military conflict.

A flurry of events disrupted supermarkets, blood banks and passenger flights last week.

Bomb threats repeatedly affected flights across Europe in what officials and airlines described as “hoax bomb threats” or “false attacks.”

It remains unclear who might be behind the latest hybrid attacks, and whether they could be state-backed.

France on Tuesday said a wave of cyberattacks targeting supermarket fridges was carried out by Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit it said was affiliated with the Iranian Revolutionary Guard. Iran denied involvement, calling accusations “baseless and malicious.”

Incidents come against a backdrop of heightened geopolitical tensions and domestic unrest across parts of Europe, and experts told CNBC that civilian infrastructure could become an increasingly attractive target for hostile actors.

1. A rebound day incoming? Nasdaq futures are up almost 2% this morning, as upbeat earnings from influential neocloud CoreWeave
 ripple across the broader AI trade. The S&P 500 is also heading toward a solidly higher open. WTI crude is up over 1%. The bond market is closed today in observance of Veterans Day.

2. Good data center versus bad data center: CoreWeave
 is a good one. Shares are up 14% premarket. Better-than-expected revenue and adjusted operating margins of 10.4%, reaching double digits ahead of schedule. Also better-than-feared comments on 2027 financing needs. Plus, its older Nvidia chips are holding their value for longer than people think. Will be talking to CEO Mike Intrator on “Squawk on the Street” later this morning.

3. Here are four things that I think Nvidia
 must to do as next week’s earnings report approaches: (1) introduce the world to Ian Buck, the inventor of its linchpin CUDA software who currently serves as its VP of hyperscale and high-performance computing business, (2) lean into the Wachtell investigation and find out if CEO Jensen Huang needs his own counsel, (3) pause all investments into the AI ecosystem and harvest some cash now that the Anthropic IPO is imminent, (4) announce a historic buyback that supersedes its $235 billion plan.

4. Here comes the Nvidia downgrades. Baird kicks us off, cutting the stock to hold from buy and slashing its price target to $200 from $500. Worried about the Huang overhang, but also reduced visibility into 2027 data center forecasts. Morgan Stanley chip analysts also removed their “top pick” designation. This Club stock can only bottom when the majority of analysts cut and run. We’re getting the early birds out of the cage.

5. The closely watched VanEck Semiconductor ETF
, or SMH, is trading at 15 times forward earnings, its lowest valuation multiple since the fall of 2022, before ChatGPT kicked off the fourth industrial revolution. Melius Research’s Ben Reitzes highlighted that incredible fact in a note this morning. A successful Anthropic IPO next week would be bullish for many chip names and the AI trade overall.

6. T-Mobile
 CEO Srini Gopalan didn’t sound concerned about the looming threat from SpaceX last night on “Mad Money.” Gopalan said, “I don’t spend my time speculating on what, exactly, they’ll do because really the person who’s going to decide who wins and who is successful in this industry is going to be the customer and the consumer.” He said T-Mobile’s new “T-Mix” plans are key to its strategy of offering value to customers while building an even better network.

7. Buy Costco
. The company announced last night a special dividend of $30 a share, double the last one paid in 2024. Costco has done these every few years or so. Payable on Dec. 4. Must be a shareholder of record by the end of the day Nov. 24. So, still time to get it on it. Also announced a $4 billion buyback authorization. Shame on those of us who, for a moment, thought maybe Costco was overvalued. The Club stock is up nearly 2% this morning.

8. Jefferies started coverage of Corning
 with a buy and a price target of $134, saying the company is in a sweet spot for AI-driven demand for fiber optics, which is replacing slower copper connections. The analysts noted the growing use of fiber “inside the box,” connecting the hardware in servers and equipment racks. Referred to as “scale-up.”

9. “DoorDash has tested the limits of even its most masochistic investors.” That’s how MoffettNathanson described a tough 12 months for the stock. The analysts cut their price target to $239 from $277.  to move deeper into grocery delivery.

 is roaring back, up 6% this morning after a tough day on speculation about changes SoftBank made to the way it buys power generation equipment for its data centers. I said yesterday the decline in the Club stock was wrong. JPMorgan trimmed its GEV price target to $1,000 from $1,035 but maintained its buy rating. https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/pete-heg.title: Hegseth impeachment effort torpedoed in House
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/pete-heg.author: Garrett Downs,Kevin Breuninger
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/pete-heg.text:
The House of Representatives effectively torpedoed an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Hegseth railed against Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the Republican who introduced articles of impeachment against him, earlier in the day.

Hegseth aggressively defended his leadership in the Iran war and other military operations.

President Donald Trump praised Hegseth’s performance after the brief news conference, the first the secretary has held in six months.

The House of Representatives effectively torpedoed an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth with a procedural vote on Tuesday evening.

The House, by a 211-204 margin, approved a measure that will refer the impeachment resolution to a committee.

That will leave little, if any, time for the committee and full House to act on it before Democrats take over the chamber and the Senate with a new majority in early January.

House Republican leadership had sought to kill the effort at impeachment, which was initiated Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.

The vote came a week after the midterm elections, where Democrats trounced Republicans in the first congressional election since the Iran war broke out in February.

Hegseth had faced eight articles of impeachment.

Massie accused Hegseth of waging war in contravention of Congress, carrying out extrajudicial killings tied to boat strikes in the Caribbean against purported drug smugglers and suppressing free speech by targeting Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a military veteran.

Massie is a libertarian who lost his Republican primary in May after clashing with President Donald Trump.

The Kentucky Republican led a bill last year to compel the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Shortly after the vote, Trump said: “Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!”

“Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete,” the president said, declaring what he said was an “EXONERATION” of Hegseth.

A Republican forced the vote on Hegseth’s impeachment. All Democrats voted against referring the measure to committee.

Defense Department spokesperson Jacob Bliss said earlier in the day that Hegseth “carried out direct, lawful orders from the President to secure the nation.” The impeachment effort notably focused on Hegseth, not Trump, who is responsible for launching the various military operations referred to in the articles.

Hegseth, at a press conference at the Pentagon earlier Tuesday, railed against Massie and defended his leadership in the Iran war and other military operations.

“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” Hegseth said

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said. “It puts a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time.
“This is not patriotism. This is sabotage.”

Trump, in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, said Hegseth “gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”

Trump said Monday that he would stand by Hegseth even if the House impeached him. The president was impeached by the House two times during his first White House term. The Senate acquitted him in both cases.

Republicans hold a slim 218-214 majority in the House.

Some Republicans, notably including Vice President JD Vance, have directly blamed their midterm losses on the Iran war, which continues to see intermittent fighting amid an uneasy stalemate.

Neither of the two Cabinet secretaries impeached by the House has ever been removed by the Senate after a trial in that chamber.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/credit-c.title: Credit card debt climbs to a record $1.29 trillion, New York Fed research finds
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/credit-c.author: Jessica Dickler
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/credit-c.text:
As financial pressures mount, Americans are increasingly relying on credit cards, new reports show.

Collectively, Americans owe a record $1.29 trillion on their cards, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

The average credit card balance per consumer now stands at $6,678, up 2.4% from a year ago, a separate report from TransUnion found.

Americans are increasingly turning to credit cards as financial pressures mount, new reports show.

Collectively, credit card balances climbed by $22 billion in the third quarter to a record $1.29 trillion, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s latest household debt report, released Tuesday. Balances are up 4.2% from a year earlier.

Total household debt, including mortgages, auto loans and student loans, also expanded by $334 billion for the July-to-September period to a record $19.1 trillion.

“Overall debt has been growing,” the New York Fed researchers said on a press call Tuesday. “This does reflect financial hardship out there.”

The average credit card balance per consumer now stands at $6,678, up 2.4% year over year, a separate quarterly credit industry insights report from TransUnion found. The number of people with credit cards rose 2% to 178 million from 174.8 million.

Consumers often turn to credit cards in part because they are more accessible than other types of loans — even though the average interest rate on a new credit card offer is about 24%, according to data from LendingTree. Credit card APRs vary depending on the type of card, the issuer and the borrower’s creditworthiness.

“Credit cards continue to be one of the most expensive ways to borrow,” said Charlie Wise, TransUnion’s senior vice president of global research and consulting.

Over time, an increasing share of new credit cards has gone to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and “those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress,” the New York Fed researchers said in a corresponding blog post.

Credit card issuers loosened their lending standards during the Covid pandemic, and delinquency rates rose in the years that followed, the New York Fed researchers said on the press call.

“Macroeconomic headwinds — namely high inflation and rising borrowing costs — have squeezed consumers, with inflation outpacing wage growth for low-income brackets,” according to the New York Fed.

Meanwhile, the cost of living continues to climb, with Americans paying more for essentials such as groceries and gas.

Stubborn inflation has now stretched on for years, putting many households in an affordability squeeze. Costs for goods and services rose more than expected again in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics also reported Tuesday.

“Higher prices and higher rates have pushed more people into debt,” said Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling agency.

Balances have continued to swell in the wake of the pandemic, and even though the growth rate is now slowing, “from a household finance standpoint, a lot of damage has been done,” Rossman said.

The reports come on the heels of the Democrats’ strong midterm results, when many voters expressed their dissatisfaction with the U.S. economy, according to Kyle Moore, chief economist at the nonpartisan think tank The Century Foundation.

“The throughline connecting so many of Tuesday’s outcomes was a recognition that the American economy is failing American families,” Moore said, referring to Election Day.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/heloc-ba.title: Homeowners tap equity as HELOC balances post biggest jump since 2005: New York Fed report
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/heloc-ba.author: Sarah Agostino
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/heloc-ba.text:
The outstanding amount owed on home equity lines of credit is now $481 billion, according to the latest quarterly report on consumer debt from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Just under half of outstanding mortgages — 49.1% — carried rates of 4% or lower in the second quarter, leaving many owners unwilling to give up their low rate.

HELOCs generally come with lower up-front costs than a home equity loan, but there are some aspects of the credit line that homeowners should be aware of before they use it.

Homeowners tapped their home equity lines of credit in the third quarter at the highest rate in more than two decades, according to a new Federal Reserve Bank of New York report on household debt released Tuesday.

Balances on HELOCs jumped by $23 billion during the three months ending Sept. 30, the largest increase since 2005. That brings the outstanding amount owed to $481 billion, the report shows. This also marks the 18th consecutive quarterly increase.

HELOC balances peaked at roughly $714 billion in the first quarter of 2009, according to a 2015 New York Fed report.

The current rise in balances comes amid a sluggish housing market, due at least partly to the so-called mortgage rate lock-in effect. Just under half of outstanding mortgages — 49.1% — carried rates of 4% or lower in the second quarter, according to a Realtor.com analysis of federal mortgage data, leaving many owners reluctant to give up their low rates to purchase another home at current higher borrowing costs.

The median price of an existing home was $417,500 in September, according to the National Association of Realtors, a real estate trade group. While up just 1.3% from a year earlier, the amount is nearly 54% higher than in September 2019, according to NAR. The average rate on a typical 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is 7.3% as of Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily.

“HELOCs let them borrow against their equity without giving up the low interest rate on their home,” said certified financial planner Douglas Boneparth, president and founder of Bone Fide Wealth in New York City and a member of CNBC’s Financial Advisor Council.

Mortgage holders collectively had $17.5 trillion in home equity as of the third quarter, according to a new report from Intercontinental Exchange, or ICE, a financial markets technology and data company.

Tappable equity that can be accessed — meaning a homeowner’s equity would remain at or above 20% of the home’s value after tapping it — rose 1.2%, or $16,600, from a year ago to an average of $204,000 per borrower, the ICE report shows.

“Homeowners are sitting on substantial housing wealth, with 2.4 million mortgage holders now holding at least $1 million in equity,” Andy Walden, head of mortgage and Housing Market Research at ICE, said in the report.

HELOCs let you tap a line of credit over time as you need the money, instead of getting it all at once like a home equity loan or cash-out refinance.

While HELOCs may have fewer up-front costs than a home equity loan, they generally have a variable interest rate. This means it will move up and down based on a benchmark like the prime rate, which banks use as a basis to set rates on a variety of loans. And, while the Federal Reserve doesn’t control that rate, it is influenced by changes the Fed makes to the so-called federal funds rate.

“If your budget only works at today’s rate, then your budget doesn’t really work,” Boneparth said of HELOCs. “You kind of have to be mindful of the fact that rates may go up.”

The average interest rate for a $30,000 HELOC was 7.49% as of Nov. 4, according to Bankrate.

Many HELOCs also have a “draw” period when you can take money out, which often lasts five or 10 years. During that time, you typically are only required to pay the interest on any funds you’ve withdrawn. After that, however, you’ll enter a repayment period of, say, 10 or 20 years, when you’re required to pay both interest and principal. Because of that, your payments will jump if you’ve only been paying interest.

“The real test comes when the repayment period kicks in, and the principal starts to show up, if that’s how their HELOC is structured,” Boneparth said. “Payments potentially could double overnight, and you really want to know that before you sign anything.”

Additionally, consider what you’re planning to use the money for, Boneparth said.

“If you’re borrowing against your home to improve your home, that could make a lot of sense,” Boneparth said. “Borrowing against your house to pay off credit cards is a little trickier because you’re turning unsecured debt into debt secured by the roof over your head.”

In that case, if your spending habits don’t change, he said, “you’re just moving the problem somewhere a little scarier.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/anthropi.title: Jim Cramer says Anthropic's explosive growth could justify a record-breaking IPO
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/anthropi.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/anthropi.text:
Jim Cramer said Anthropic’s explosive revenue growth helps justify its record valuation.

“Anthropic’s tantalizing growth rate is the key reason why this should be the largest IPO in history,” Cramer said.

Anthropic’s
 stunning revenue growth helps justify its $1 trillion-plus valuation ahead of what could become the largest initial public offering in history, CNBC’s Jim Cramer said Tuesday.

The Claude developer filed updated IPO paperwork Tuesday outlining plans to offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece. At the high end, the offering would raise $64.35 billion and value Anthropic at up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The company plans to price its shares Nov. 18 and begin trading the following day. Throw in a separate $26 billion private placement purchased by leading AI companies including Nvidia
 and Alphabet
, and Anthropic’s entire haul could exceed SpaceX’s raise from its June IPO.

“The fact that this deal is on is bullish for tech and the AI trade,” the “Mad Money” host said.

Anthropic reported $33.2 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, up 1,206% from a year earlier, according to its updated prospectus. Much of that growth has been driven by enterprise customers, particularly surging adoption of Claude Code, its AI coding agent. “Anthropic’s tantalizing growth rate is the key reason why this should be the largest IPO in history,” Cramer said.

The company now has more than 11,900 customers spending over $100,000 annually, up from roughly 1,500 at the end of 2025. Existing customers are also spending dramatically more, with Anthropic reporting a net revenue retention rate of approximately 900% at the end of September, meaning customers are spending roughly nine times as much as a year earlier.

While Anthropic is seeing accelerating revenue growth through the first nine months of the year, the company’s quarter-over-quarter growth rate seemed to peak in the second quarter, slowing to 47% in the third quarter from 144% in Q2. “To some extent, it’s the law of large numbers at work, and let’s be clear that 47% sequential growth is still very impressive,” Cramer said.

While some deceleration is inevitable as the company gets larger, he said that increased competition from OpenAI and the possibility that customers are beginning to scrutinize their AI spending could also be factors. One thing is for sure, Anthropic won’t have to jockey for position with OpenAI, which pushed its IPO plans into next year.

Additionally, Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate, which projects yearly revenue based on the most recent month’s sales, suggests demand remains strong. The frontier AI lab reported an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, putting the company within striking distance of $100 billion by year-end if its current momentum continues.

“It’s good to see that it’s still growing nicely,” Cramer said. “As for Anthropic’s revenue and growth rate, the main subject of tonight’s review, it’s nothing less extraordinary, even if we are slightly past the peak, growth-wise.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/fossil-f.title: Fossil CEO says turnaround is ahead of plan as sales return to growth
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/fossil-f.author: Laya Neelakandan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/fossil-f.text:
Watchmaker Fossil said Tuesday that the company returned to profit and sales growth in the first signs of a turnaround.

CEO Franco Fogliato told CNBC exclusively that shrinking the company was the biggest factor in helping to strengthen its balance sheet.

Fossil also raised its full-year guidance, as Fogliato said it’s a year and a half ahead of its original turnaround timeline.

Fossil Group
 posted quarterly results on Tuesday that could point to early signs of a turnaround for the legacy watchmaker.

The company, which has struggled to compete with new gadgets in the years since its sales and stock price peaked in the 2010s, has been quietly undertaking a comeback strategy under CEO Franco Fogliato. The company’s fiscal third-quarter earnings indicate the strategy is beginning to bear fruit.

The company said Tuesday that it returned to profitability in the third quarter, posting operating income of $25.3 million, compared with an operating loss of $21.7 million last year. It also returned to sales growth, with net sales up 0.4% to $271.2 million. The company last reported a year-over-year sales increase in the first fiscal quarter of 2022.

“We’re excited about improving dramatically the profitability of the company through a very strong and disciplined management of full-price sales as well as cost management,” Fogliato told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

For the quarter ended Oct. 3, Fossil reported net income of $11.7 million, or 19 cents per share, compared with a net loss of $39.9 million, or 76 cents per share, the year prior. The company also said its operating expenses fell 11.1% to $137 million. The company last posted quarterly net income in the third fiscal quarter of 2022.

With the signs of growth, the retailer also raised its full-year outlook, guiding for full-year net sales of between $980 million and $990 million, which would mark a slight decline from just over $1 billion in net sales in the prior year. That compares with a previous expectation of net sales falling between 3% and 5%. Fossil also said it’s expecting positive free cash flow by the end of the year.

Fogliato said Fossil had previously not expected sales growth for another year and a half.

The stronger quarter comes after the company saw slumping sales and financial losses over the past few years. It struggled with the rise of smartwatches, mounting debt and the decline in mall foot traffic.

Fossil stock has lost the vast majority of its value since the early-to-mid 2010s, and despite a recent surge, was trading under $8 a share on Tuesday.

To rightsize the business, Fogliato, who joined Fossil in 2024, said he focused on closing stores, moving away from promotions to full-price sales, improving marketing and broadening Fossil’s product range. That meant shrinking the business to a sustainable baseline before trying to grow it.

The company saw a 5.9% decrease in direct-to-consumer sales for its third quarter, which Fogliato attributed to the company’s “aggressive” downsizing.

“We simplified a lot of the business doing this,” Fogliato said, adding that customers responded well when the company moved away from markdowns. “People tell me they are excited about what they are seeing in the marketplace now.”

Fossil added that its key growth engine for the quarter was Asia, where net sales grew 15.1%. Fogliato said much of that growth was led by the India market.

At the same time, growing internationally is only part of the watchmaker’s strategy as it tries to improve its performance in its home country.

“Priority number one is to grow our home market, and we’re doing that,” he said. “As retail is settling into a smaller, more profitable base, ready to grow again, we’re entering 2027 with plenty of opportunities.”

Fogliato said one key to growth was not trying to keep up with the smartwatch trend. While trying to make gains in the smartwatch space initially hampered Fossil’s performance, it’s now investing in analog watches again.

Smartwatch sales came in under $1 million for the quarter, but sales for traditional watches — which make up around 86% of Fossil’s sales — grew 6.4%.

“Fossil is literally having a comeback, a strong comeback, a momentum, and we can see this,” Fogliato said. “And it comes not only through the numbers — it comes with the excitement we see in the stores, and we think we’re just at the beginning. We have so much work to do.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/trump-xi.title: U.S., China should ‘harbor no illusions’ as they cooperate, compete on AI, Bessent says
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/trump-xi.author: Anniek Bao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/trump-xi.text:
As the technology advances, the two nations will need to demonstrate how they can “reconcile the demands of competition with the responsibilities of leadership,” Bessent said.

The two governments have so far refrained from making any commitment to limit the advancement of AI.

The U.S. and China should “harbor no illusions” about their differences as they engage to contain the risks of artificial intelligence, while competing with each other at the same time, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

Bessent said in prepared remarks to the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations in New York Tuesday that the two governments had established a new dialogue mechanism on “super intelligence,” or SI, aimed at guarding against “shared risks” and averting any “misunderstanding between our two systems.”

The mechanism will see both sides exchanging “best practices” for testing advanced models before they are released, and “keeping human judgement firmly in command of the technology,” Bessent said, expecting both sides to alert each other to serious incidents involving the SI models.

Bessent, however, stopped short of making any commitment to limit advancement of the technology, as Beijing and Washington remain locked in an intense race to achieve global dominance in AI.

The Trump administration has largely resisted broadening restrictions on AI development over concerns of ceding a competitive edge to China, though the president has more recently signaled some openness to putting in place regulatory safeguards.

“I ​don’t mind guardrails,” he said in a CBS interview released Sunday, adding that ⁠he did not want regulations to put the U.S. in “a deep second position” behind China, ​which he ​said ⁠had no such restrictions.

China’s foreign ministry in September dismissed calls to slow down frontier models, saying that fearmongering and confrontation would only disrupt global AI governance. Huiyao Wang, founder of Center for China and Globalization, a think tank that closely aligns with Beijing’s thinking, said last month that the U.S.-China talks should “confront AI risks and manage them together.”

During Xi’s September visit, Washington and Beijing agreed to launch an AI dialogue with a communications channel to help defuse serious incidents. The two leaders are expected to meet for the third time next week, with Bessent joining, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders’ Meeting from Nov. 18 to 19.

As the technology advances, the two nations will need to demonstrate how they can “reconcile the demands of competition with the responsibilities of leadership,” Bessent said in his Tuesday speech. “Our interests will not always coincide, and our approach to every challenge likewise will not always converge,” he added.

Washington had briefly suspended access by foreign nationals to Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable 5 models in June before restoring it weeks later. The U.S. government has also restricted exports of the most advanced chips to Beijing, and accused Chinese developers of copying American models through what it calls industrial-scale distillation.

Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the U.S., told the audience at the gala that efforts by both countries were “indispensable” to addressing issues from global flashpoints to “improving artificial intelligence governance.” Cooperation “may not resolve every challenge,” he said, but “none can be resolved without it.”

The event was organized at a time when controversy around Nvidia Corp CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has been making headlines.

The billionaire tech executive, who joined Trump’s delegation to Beijing in May and was invited to the state dinner in Washington in September, is at the center of a major corporate and national security scandal after admitting to an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom the U.S. intelligence officials suspect of espionage.

While Huang’s presence at the upcoming summit has been thrown into doubt, other business leaders such as Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Mastercard’s Michael Miebach could be on Trump’s delegation next week, according to South China Morning Post.

The two nations are expected to meet for the third time next week

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/singapor.title: Singapore wants a bigger slice of the global gold market. Is it too late to the party?
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/singapor.author: Lee Ying Shan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/singapor.text:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore on Tuesday launched a gold vaulting service for foreign central banks and sovereign entities.

The city-state also plans to introduce tax exemptions for certain wholesale gold-related services.

The initiatives mark Singapore’s latest attempt to establish itself as a major bullion hub alongside established centers such as London and Switzerland, as more gold trading activity shifts toward Asia.

Singapore is stepping up efforts to become a major player in the global gold market, betting that a new central bank vaulting service and tax incentives will help it attract more bullion flows.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore on Tuesday launched a gold vaulting service for foreign central banks and sovereign entities, with an initial capacity of 500 metric tons.

The city-state also plans to introduce tax exemptions for certain wholesale gold-related services such as vaulting, refining, recasting, testing and broking. In June, Singapore unveiled plans for a physical gold clearing system to facilitate the settlement of bullion transactions in the city-state, with operations expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

The initiatives mark the country’s latest attempt to establish itself as a key bullion hub alongside established centers such as London and Switzerland, as more gold trading activity shifts toward Asia.

But breaking into a market dominated by established trading hubs may prove an uphill battle. For instance, London vaults held about 9,850 metric tons of gold at the end of October, including commercial and central bank storage.

The push from Singapore also comes as rival Hong Kong is also expanding its gold storage and clearing infrastructure, leveraging its proximity to China, the world’s largest gold market.

“Singapore is very late to the party as building up a physical hub requires volume when it comes to trade backed structures,” said Juerg Kiener, chief investment officer at Swiss Asia Capital.

“The largest gold market is China and its window to the rest of the world is Hong Kong,” he told CNBC, adding that Singapore is not well-positioned to compete with Hong Kong in gold-backed trade.

Kiener said Singapore could instead carve out a niche in physical gold storage for financial institutions, although commercial vaulting services are already available in the city-state, including at its high-security freeport near Changi Airport.

Unlike commercial vaults, the new facility will be operated by Singapore’s central bank, offering foreign monetary authorities an alternative sovereign custodian for their gold.

“It’s not something that we see happening all that often in the gold market or in the central bank community,” said Shaokai Fan, global head of central banks at the World Gold Council.

The move comes as central banks increasingly reassess where they store their bullion amid geopolitical tensions, said Fan. Over the past 12 months, several countries have diversified gold storage, with many planning to do so, according to a World Gold Council report published in September.

Singapore’s political stability, strong legal framework and extensive air connectivity could make it an attractive alternative to traditional storage centers, he added.

Nikolas Kavalis, managing director at Metals Focus, said the sovereign vaulting service represents an important addition to Singapore’s existing gold infrastructure, but cautioned that storage alone would not be sufficient to establish a fully functioning bullion market.

The bigger challenge is building sufficient liquidity and trading activity to compete with London, which remains the dominant global over-the-counter gold market.

Both Singapore and Hong Kong are still developing their local clearing infrastructure, Kavalis said, meaning neither has yet established the kind of deep trading ecosystem that underpins London’s dominance.

Attracting central bank gold could help Singapore build that liquidity, particularly if bullion stored locally can also be mobilized for transactions rather than simply held in custody.

Singapore’s efforts come as gold flows have already undergone a significant transformation over the past decade.

Historically, much of the world’s bullion moved through London and Switzerland, where large gold bars were traded or refined before being shipped to Asian markets.

But the expansion of Asian refineries and growing regional demand have increasingly allowed gold to move directly between Asian markets, reducing their dependence on European trading centers, Kavalis said.

The development of more sophisticated gold hubs in Asia could accelerate that shift.

Still, Hong Kong might have an edge in serving central banks and institutions whose financial activities are closely tied to China, while Singapore could appeal to those already active in its banking and financial markets, Kavalis said.

Fan sees room for both centers to grow. “We see the two centers complementing each other and not really competing with each other,” he said.

Singapore’s Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong similarly dismissed suggestions that the two financial hubs were looking at securing a larger share of the same pie. “It’s not a zero-sum game,” Gan said Tuesday, adding that Singapore’s vaulting service would provide central banks with another option for diversifying where they hold their reserves.

Whether Singapore can translate its reputation as a trusted financial center into meaningful bullion flows remains to be seen. “It’s a bit chicken and egg because to attract volumes you want liquidity, but to get liquidity you need volumes,” Fan said.
