The city-state also plans to introduce tax exemptions for certain wholesale gold-related services. The initiatives mark Singapore’s latest attempt to establish itself as a major bullion hub alongside established centers such as London and Switzerland.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-w.title: Nvidia hires law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead Jensen Huang affair probe
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-w.author: Kif Leswing
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-w.text:
Nvidia’s board of directors said on Tuesday that it had hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation of CEO Jensen Huang and whether company secrets or national security was compromised.

Nvidia’s
 board of directors said on Tuesday that it hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation of CEO Jensen Huang and whether company secrets or national security was compromised, after Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who has been connected to Chinese intelligence.

“The independent members of the NVIDIA Board have retained former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a thorough and independent investigation as was announced on Sunday,” the board said in a statement.

Kim joined the firm last month, and he was previously the chief U.S. prosecutor in Manhattan, according to Law360.

Nvidia has been thrust into turmoil since Huang’s acknowledgement of the affair over the weekend. The chipmaker’s stock dropped 6% on Tuesday after falling more than 4% on Monday, as investors worry that the investigation and scandal could result in the co-founder and CEO being forced out.

Nvidia and the board are facing pressure from critics and politicians over what the company knew about sales of its restricted AI chips to Chinese companies.

Over the past few weeks, The New York Times and Financial Times have reported that U.S. intelligence agencies surveilled an Asian technology executive, Alice Huang, who has been affiliated with Nvidia customer Megaspeed. These agencies have concluded that she is passing information to Beijing and is involved with Chinese intelligence, according to the reports.

Huang has become the face of the AI industry, going by his first name “Jensen” to customers and rivals as Nvidia’s technology is used to train nearly all major AI models. The chipmaker has become an essential source of financing for AI startups and Huang has met with presidents and CEOs around the world as Nvidia’s public face.

But Huang’s actions have thrown the chipmaker into instability as he admitted to an affair with Alice Huang in an email to staff on Sunday.

“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang wrote in the message, while emphasizing that he is an American and supports U.S. national security.

An Nvidia representative said at the time that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption.

On Sunday, Nvidia’s board said that it would investigate the allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Nvidia’s board also said on Sunday that it has no reason to believe either national security nor Nvidia secrets were compromised.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/us-gas-p.title: U.S. gas prices fall below $4 for the first time since July
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/us-gas-p.author: Deena Zaidi
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/us-gas-p.text:
The U.S. average price for regular gasoline fell to $3.9788 a gallon on Nov. 10, below $4 for the first time since July.

The national average is down about 17 cents from a week ago and about 39 cents from a month ago, according to AAA.

Lower crude oil prices and normal seasonal weakness are helping ease pump prices, while Gulf crude flows continue to recover.

Americans may finally find some relief at the pump.

The national average price of regular gasoline fell below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, reaching $3.9788 on Tuesday, according to AAA. Prices are down about 17 cents from a week ago and nearly 39 cents from a month ago.

The decline comes after energy inflation slowed significantly in October. Energy prices increased 0.7% during the month, a far cry from the 5.2% surge seen in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The BLS’ gasoline index increased 1% over the month, after advancing 9.1% in September.

Bespoke Investment Group pointed out that gasoline prices also tend to decline at this time of the year, making part of the recent relief seasonal.

“While lower oil prices have been a tailwind for the relief at the pump, it’s also perfectly normal for gas prices to be falling at this time of year, so if they weren’t, there would really be something wrong,” the firm said.

The drop at the pump followed a sharp retreat in crude oil. International oil benchmark Brent crude on Tuesday briefly fell below $90 a barrel for the first time since August as comments from U.S. President Donald Trump fueled hopes for an end to Washington’s nearly nine-month conflict with Iran.

Recovering oil flows from the Persian Gulf have also eased supply concerns. Regional crude exports have returned to an estimated 80% to 85% of prewar levels, including pipeline shipments, according to ING.

“Energy markets remain under pressure as hopes for a de-escalation in the Middle East reduce geopolitical risk premiums. Oil extended its losses as Gulf supply flows continued to recover, while European gas also moved lower,” analysts at ING wrote.

However, the Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller warned Tuesday that energy shocks may have more persistent effects on inflation than they did before the pandemic.

“While I am pleased to see energy prices down from their high rates over the past week or so, they are still quite elevated relative to the start of the year, and the ultimate effect on inflation will depend on what levels are sustained,” he said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/rivian-r.title: Rivian CEO says new R2 SUV, autonomy make 2027 an ‘inflection year’ as EV maker marks five years since IPO
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/rivian-r.author: Michael Wayland
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/rivian-r.text:
Five years after Rivian shares began trading on the Nasdaq, CEO RJ Scaringe told CNBC he’s betting that R2 and autonomy can make 2027 an “inflection year” for the EV maker.

R2 became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle in the third quarter, and the company plans a limited point-to-point rollout of its advanced driver-assistance system before a broader release in 2027.

Rivian’s stock price is down more than 80% since the Amazon-backed company debuted at $78 per share five years ago, including a nearly 30% decline this year.

It’s been five years since Rivian Automotive
 celebrated its initial public offering with CEO and founder RJ Scaringe ringing the Nasdaq opening bell from the company’s factory in Normal, Illinois, while the company’s sleek vehicles sat outside the stock exchange in Times Square.

It was a euphoric time for all-electric vehicle companies that has since diminished. And much like the EV hype, Rivian’s stock price is down more than 80% since the Amazon
-backed company debuted on the Nasdaq at $78 per share on Nov. 10, 2021. That includes a nearly 30% decline this year.

A host of internal and external factors have contributed to Rivian’s stock decline, but the company continues to be the most promising EV maker to emerge during the early 2020s, as most of its peer group to go public during that time no longer exists.

Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe acknowledges that not everything has gone to plan amid supply chain shortages, geopolitical tensions and slower-than-expected consumer EV adoption, but he said he believes the next year will prove to be a catalyst for the company and investors.

“2027 is really an inflection year for us,” Scaringe told CNBC during an exclusive interview. “I’m excited to start to really show what we believe so fully, the potential of the business.”

Scaringe’s bullishness comes as Rivian ramps up production of its midsize R2 SUV — meant to expand the brand to the mainstream market — and as the company continues to invest in its next generation of vehicle software and autonomy.

Scaringe said the R2, with an entry-level model at about $45,000, remains the core business to be able to showcase its newest technologies. Rivian delivered a record 19,248 vehicles in the third quarter of 2026, up 46% year over year, and said R2 was already its best-selling vehicle by volume, outselling both its R1 flagship products and its commercial van.

“That’s going to define the business. The path to profitability, the path to very significant growth in revenue is all built around R2, and then some of the variants that come following R2,” Scaringe said.

For the most recent period, Rivian said the automotive cost of goods sold per vehicle improved by more than $12,000 quarter over quarter, helped by a higher R2 mix and better fixed-cost leverage.

Rivian also is in the midst of building a new multibillion-dollar Georgia factory that Scaringe has said is necessary to get the company to the volumes it needs to achieve net profitability.

Its sole factory in Normal, Illinois, is capable of producing 215,000 vehicles annually. That includes up to 155,000 R2s alongside R1 models and electric vans. Rivian said the Georgia plant will be capable of producing up to 300,000 units annually once the initial phase construction is completed in late 2028.

Of course, all of that means additional capital spending and pressure on the company to improve profits.

“We’ve made the decision to simultaneously work towards profitability … and deeply invest in our technology, and in particular in autonomy,” Scaringe said.

Rivian’s operating performance is improving, but several Wall Street analysts expect the company’s investment requirements to rise significantly in 2027.

Rivian generated $176 million of consolidated gross profit in the third quarter, but its automotive business posted an $80 million gross loss, while its software and services unit generated $256 million of gross profit at a 42% margin.

Wall Street analysts broadly agree Rivian’s R2 launch is showing encouraging early demand and lowering manufacturing costs, but they’re concerned about whether that can offset rising autonomy spending, the Georgia factory buildout and continued cash burn.

“Funding has long been a key debate for Rivian investors,” Deutsche Bank analyst Edison Yu said in an Oct. 30 investor note after the company reported quarterly results that exceeded Wall Street’s expectations. “The notion of a multi-year (even if credible) path to cash flow breakeven will be less attractive to investors.”

Rivian said during its late October earnings call that its total available future liquidity is expected to be about $13 billion when factoring in available credit and money from partnerships with Volkswagen and Uber
 as well as a $4.5 billion U.S. Department of Energy loan for the Georgia plant.

Rivian said its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion to end the third quarter.

The company may still need to raise more capital. Scaringe said Rivian plans to be “opportunistic” about any additional capital raises, which have previously included equity deals with Volkswagen and Uber.

“As we think about the environment looking out, we want to continue to position ourselves to be in a place to invest in the technology. And so that means we’ll be opportunistic as it pertains to capital. But I want to be clear: We’re like very focused on getting the profitability,” Scaringe said.

The company has significantly upgraded the software capabilities and hardware on its vehicles to prepare them for autonomy technologies, or physical artificial intelligence, as Scaringe calls it.

The next step in that is releasing “point-to-point” driving capabilities, in which the vehicles can drive on their own from destination to destination with the driver acting as a monitor in case of any unexpected problems.

U.S. EV leader Tesla
 is the only automaker to currently offer those features on its vehicles. Scaringe said Rivian plans to not only catch up to Tesla’s capabilities but exceed them as it uses multiple sensor types to allow the vehicle to “see” better, especially in inclement weather.

“That’s not like the finish line. ... Think of it as like the starting point where you suddenly have a more apples to apples comparison between Rivian and Tesla,” Scaringe said.

The release of point-to-point over the coming weeks and months, first to employees and then to customers, is expected to be followed by autonomous vehicles with Uber by 2028.

Scaringe said he believes such technologies will become a differentiator for the company in the coming years.

“I think it will go from a purchase consideration for maybe 10% of the buying public that’s in the top five things considered in making a purchase decision to the No. 1 or No. 2 purchase consideration for the vast majority of buyers,” Scaringe said.

Rivian plans to offer more details about its AI and autonomous plans during a second annual investor technology event on Dec. 9.

“We view this as a likely positive catalyst as the event could set a path for AV features driving incremental vehicle demand & higher [software] revenue in 2027, building on 2026 growth,” TD Cowen analyst Itay Michaeli said in an investor note last week.

Rivian’s stock is currently rated overweight with a $17.70 target price, according to analyst estimates compiled by FactSet. That would be a roughly 26% increase from its Monday closing price but still a far cry from its IPO.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/anthopic.title: Anthropic opens Australian retail IPO offering as AI scrutiny intensifies
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/anthopic.author: Jenny Lee
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/anthopic.text:
Anthropic’s Australian retail IPO offering is on Wednesday and scheduled to close on Nov. 17, according to participating broker Stake.

The Claude maker has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT,” according to the company.

The offering comes as Australia moves to tighten oversight of AI companies after a government website security breach involving an OpenAI agent, according to Reuters.

Anthropic
, the maker of AI chatbot Claude, opened its Australian retail initial public offering on Wednesday, giving individual investors access to shares ahead of the company’s planned Nasdaq listing.

The offering opened at 10 a.m. Australian Eastern Daylight Time on Wednesday and is expected to close at 5 p.m. on Nov. 17, according to the timetable published by participating broker Stake.

Anthropic is seeking to raise as much as $64.4 billion in its IPO, with a separate $26 billion private placement, bringing a combined total to as much as $90.4 billion. Shares are expected to be priced between $70 to $78 each.

The Australian retail offering is expected to consist of newly issued Class A common shares under a prospectus to be lodged with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, Anthropic said on its website.

Participating brokers include Commonwealth Bank of Australia’s 
CommSec unit as lead broker, along with Bell Potter, LGT Wealth, Macquarie Group, Morgans, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, Sharesies and Stake.

Anthropic said the prospectus would be available on its IPO website once the Australian retail offering opens. Investors will need to review the document and apply through participating brokers under the terms of the offer.

Australia is one of the small numbers of markets outside the U.S. where retail investors will be able to buy the company’s shares directly, alongside Japan, Canada and parts of Europe.

The San Francisco-based AI startup has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Anthropic said it does not plan to seek a listing on the Australian Securities Exchange.

The offering comes as Australia moves to tighten oversight of AI companies after an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to the medical statistics website of Medicare,  the country’s universal health insurance program.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Tuesday that the government would introduce mandatory reporting for certain AI-related incidents and establish an AI safety regulator with powers to enforce penalties.

“The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases, make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world,” Albanese told Reuters.

The government is also considering changes to criminal law for cases involving serious misconduct.

The country has also ruled out a copyright-law exemption that would allow AI companies to train models on Australian content without licensing it.

Open AI
 and Anthropic told Australian parliament last month that they would support mandatory reporting of data breaches involving their AI agents, acknowledging that disclosure is currently voluntary.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/october-.title: Here's the inflation breakdown for October 2026 — in one chart
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/october-.author: Greg Iacurci
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/october-.text:
The consumer price index, an inflation barometer, rose 0.4% on a monthly basis in October 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

That’s down from 0.6% in September but exceeded economists’ expectations.

The BLS didn’t report an annual inflation figure due to the government shutdown in October 2025, which impacted the agency’s data collection and prevented it from releasing a report.

The Iran war, artificial intelligence, tariffs and housing were among the primary contributors to the elevated CPI reading in October, economists said.

Inflation throttled back in October from its blistering pace in September amid a more moderate rise in gasoline prices, but remained high as categories like food and housing put upward pressure on consumer prices.

The consumer price index, an inflation barometer, rose 0.4% on a monthly basis in October, after adjusting for seasonal factors, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. That’s down from 0.6% in September but higher than the 0.3% that economists expected.

“It’s uncomfortably high,” said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s. “The Fed’s not going to be happy about it. It certainly makes it more likely we get another rate increase in December.”

The Federal Reserve uses inflation data to guide its interest rate policy. The U.S. central bank raised rates in September amid a recent pickup in inflation, which economists largely attribute to the war in Iran. It held rates steady at its last meeting in October.

Economists generally assess a measure known as “core” CPI — which strips out volatile food and energy prices — to examine underlying inflation dynamics in the U.S. economy.

That core metric rose 0.3% in October, as it also did in September and August. A consistent monthly reading around 0.2% would be more in line with the Fed’s 2% annual inflation target, Zandi said.

Inflation has been above the Fed’s target for more than five years.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics didn’t report an annual inflation figure in the latest CPI report because of the lengthy federal government shutdown that happened a year ago. That shutdown, which ran from Oct. 1 to Nov. 12, disrupted the agency’s typical data collection, and it didn’t release an inflation report for October 2025.

“Investors do not need year-over-year figures to see that this was a hot inflation report and that prices are not on a sustainable path back toward the Fed’s 2% target,” Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede, a wealth management firm, wrote in an e-mail Tuesday.

“It would have taken exceptional evidence of disinflation to dissuade the Fed from raising rates in December, and this report delivered the opposite,” he wrote.

Economists pointed to four big reasons for the hotter-than-expected CPI reading.

Perhaps the largest contributor to the outsized inflation reading in Tuesday’s CPI report was housing, Zandi said.

Housing is the largest component of CPI, and movements in the category strongly influence the index’s month-to-month reading, he said.

The “shelter” CPI index rose 0.3% in October, accounting for over 30% of the CPI increase, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Zandi said he doesn’t expect that dynamic to persist, however, because it’s not consistent with the trajectory of market rents in the U.S.

“It does feel like we have a high level of monthly volatility” in the CPI data, he said. “It’s all over the map month to month.”

But economists said broader factors are putting upward pressure on prices, too.

“Core inflation today reflects three outsized shocks: tariffs, energy prices, and AI-related demand,” Josh Hirt, senior U.S. economist at Vanguard Group, an asset manager, wrote in an e-mail Tuesday.

The Iran war has raised oil prices, pushing up prices for fuels like gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, which are refined from crude oil, economists said.

Gasoline prices rose 1% in October, a significant pullback after a 9.1% monthly increase in September, CPI data showed.

While diesel prices have retreated from recent record highs, they remain elevated and could spill more broadly into the U.S. economy in the coming months, economists said.

“Diesel prices have a really slow pass-through to all the areas of CPI, given it affects transportation costs,” said Thomas Ryan, a senior North America economist at Capital Economics.

“These things take time,” Ryan said. “It’ll be an inflationary impetus for at least the next three to six months, I suspect.”

There was some evidence of that broader percolation of diesel prices in October, such as in food prices, Zandi said. Higher diesel prices add to the cost of transporting food to the grocery store shelves, he said.

Food prices rose 0.5% in October after an unchanged reading in September, according to CPI data.

The run-up in jet fuel costs has also led airlines to raise their ticket prices, economists said. Airfares climbed 0.4% in October, after monthly increases of 1.2%, 2.7% and 3.8% in the preceding months, respectively, according to the CPI report.

Meanwhile, the inflationary impact of tariffs imposed by the Trump administration should fade by the end of the year, assuming the White House doesn’t renew its push for more import taxes, Zandi said.

Certain categories of physical goods, like toys, furniture, and appliances, saw elevated inflation rates in October, likely because businesses have passed on tariff costs to consumers, he said.

The buildout of data centers that power artificial intelligence has driven up prices for electricity and consumer electronics, economists said.

Those data centers have led to a shortage of technology equipment, such as memory chips used in household electronic products like iPhones, Ryan said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/traders-.title: Traders bet on a pop for Anthropic's historic IPO
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/traders-.author: Oliver Renick
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/traders-.text:
Perpetual futures are implying a pop for Anthropic

Perpetual futures accurately predicted SpaceX pricing

The initial public offering are shining a light on this emerging asset class

News of Anthropic’s historic initial public offering provided a wave of relief for tech investors. The response in the perpetual futures market might provide even more relief.

As Anthropic prepares to raise money in its initial public offering this month, traders in offshore markets are making large bets that there will be a big pop on the AI giant’s debut.

Trying to guess an initial first day IPO reaction is nearly impossible, but a new and fast-growing corner of the markets might offer some clues.

Pre-IPO perpetuals, contracts that aim to track the price of private companies, trade on decentralized crypto exchanges like Hyperliquid, Coinbase, Binance and OKX to name a few. The current Hyperliquid Anthropic contract implies a stock price of $98 and its market cap at roughly $1.7 trillion, more than 30% higher than the $70-$78 range announced in the company’s updated S1.

While trading on the exchange is not currently available to American investors, about $250 million of volume traded across Hyperliquid’s two Anthropic trackers in the past 24 hours, according to the exchange.

Hyperliquid’s pre-IPO Anthropic perp began trading two weeks ago at $138 before settling into a roughly ten-dollar range between $110 and $120 prior to last week’s selloff in tech stocks, as the contract slipped below $94 at one point.

To proponents of this new asset class, the pricing of the perps is evidence that bankers intentionally undersell equity ahead of IPOs to ensure a post-market “pop.” Looking at SpaceX, the argument rings true: pre-IPO perps on SpaceX traded at a premium and converged with equity prices at the IPO, all before shares went on a three-day rally of as much as 40% in the immediate aftermath of the listing.

News of Anthropic’s upcoming roadshow may be weighing on competitor OpenAI. Perps tracking OpenAI’s market cap dropped 7% to $1.27 trillion, according to Hyperliquid trading on a contract trading $2.8 billion in volume over the past 24 hours.

Shares of Hyperliquid Strategies (PURR),
 the publicly-traded Treasury company investing in the HYPE tokens that power the exchange fell 4% Tuesday. The stock is up 150% on the year.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/2027-zer.title: How much you can make in 2027 and still pay 0% capital gains tax
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/2027-zer.author: Kate Dore, CFP®, EA
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/2027-zer.text:
The capital gains tax brackets for 2027 include a six-figure earnings limit for the 0% rate for married couples.

For 2027, single filers can earn up to $51,050 in taxable income — or $102,100 for married couples filing jointly — and still pay 0% for long-term capital gains.

You can use the 0% capital gains bracket to harvest profits or diversify holdings, but you need to know the trade-offs, experts say.

The IRS has released the capital gains tax brackets for 2027, which include a six-figure earnings limit for the 0% rate for married couples.

If you’re eager to sell profitable brokerage account investments, higher income thresholds for the 0% rate could help reduce your tax bill, experts say.

“The 0% capital gains bracket is easily one of the most overlooked strategies for tax-free income,” said Stephen Maggard, a certified financial planner with Abacus Planning Group in Columbia, South Carolina.

But it’s important to know how the tax brackets work and the possible trade-offs before selling investments.

Despite recent stock market volatility, many investors have portfolio gains after years of market growth. As of market close Nov. 9, the S&P 500
 was up about 10% year-to-date. The index also returned more than 16% in 2025, and over 23% in 2024.

If you’re planning to leverage the 0% capital gains bracket in 2027 to sell or rebalance brokerage account assets, here are some key things to know.

The capital gains brackets — with rates of 0%, 15% or 20% — apply to assets owned for more than one year, known as long-term capital gains. By contrast, investments held for one year or less are short-term gains, subject to regular income tax rates.

Your rate depends on taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income, or AGI. Taxable income also includes any gains from investments that year.

The standard deduction will rise to $16,600 for single taxpayers and $33,200 for married couples in 2027.

For example, let’s say a married couple’s AGI is $130,000 for 2027, including capital gains. After subtracting the $33,200 standard deduction, their taxable income would be $96,800, which falls below the 0% threshold.

However, taxable income should include mutual fund distributions, which can “dramatically alter year-end planning projections” and increase taxable income, according to CFP Jim Guarino, managing director at Baker Newman Noyes in Woburn, Massachusetts. He is also a certified public accountant.

If your federal taxable income is above the 0% threshold, you’ll pay 15% on the portion of investment gains that exceed the 0% limit, up to that bracket’s cap. Gains above that may be taxed at 20%.

Also, the 0% capital gains bracket applies to federal taxes, but your profits could still be subject to state-level taxes, experts say.

As income limits rise for the 0% capital gains bracket due to IRS inflation adjustments, more investors could have tax savings opportunities, experts say.

“There is tons of planning to be done here,” especially for early retirees with lower income, according to CFP Dinon Hughes, a partner with Nvest Financial in Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

One strategy, known as “tax gain harvesting,” is selling profitable brokerage account assets during lower-income years to leverage the 0% bracket, he said. Keep in mind, these sales stack on top of your other earnings, which could bump taxable income above the 0% threshold.

You can also sell the asset and immediately rebuy it to “reset the cost basis,” or original purchase price, said CFP Charles Sachs, chief investment officer of Imperio Wealth Advisors in Coral Gables, Florida.

By resetting the cost basis to current market value, you can reduce future capital gains to trim your tax bill.

When selling assets at a loss, the “wash sale rule” blocks tax-loss harvesting when you rebuy a “substantially identical” asset within 30 days before or after the sale. But the same rule doesn’t apply when harvesting gains.

Managing capital gains is only one part of yearly tax planning, according to Guarino with Baker Newman Noyes.

Before selling investments, you should know how boosting AGI could impact your broader financial plan, including income phase-outs for various tax breaks, he said.

For example, modified adjusted gross income can impact a range of tax benefits, such as Affordable Care Act health insurance premium subsidies, which can disappear once earnings exceed the federal limits by even a single dollar.

Another example is President Donald Trump’s temporary $6,000 senior “bonus” deduction, which is worth up to $12,000 for married couples per year through 2028.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/gm-carbr.title: How GM is trying to talk used car shoppers into buying new vehicles
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/gm-carbr.author: Robert Ferris
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/gm-carbr.text:
Rising vehicle prices have been pushing many car buyers into the used market.

General Motors is a key example of an automaker that’s trying to convince some of those consumers to get new vehicles instead, in part by revamping its certified used vehicle program.

GM made changes to the program, called CarBravo, in an effort to compete with Carvana and CarMax.

Affordability challenges are pushing some buyers out of the new vehicle market. Many are choosing used cars instead.

In turn, automakers are looking for ways to compete with many of the online retailers grabbing market share in the used car market and trying to bring some of those customers back into a new vehicle.

New vehicle sales tend to be more profitable for automakers, but reselling trade-ins as used vehicles is highly profitable for dealers. Used car prices are relatively strong, but newer online retailers such as Carvana
 and CarMax
 have made the market more competitive for dealers and other incumbent used car sellers.

“The internet and technology and apps on our phone have changed every aspect of retail, and probably one of the slowest areas of retail to have adopted to online and digital shopping has been the auto industry,” said Ivan Feinseth, partner, chief investment officer and director of research at Tigress Financial Partners.

General Motors
 is a key example of automakers’ attempts to address this shifting market. The automaker has revamped its certified used vehicle program, which now operates under the CarBravo name. It’s essentially an online portal through which Chevrolet, Buick and GMC dealers can list their certified used vehicles and make them available to customers all over the U.S.

About 1,615 of GM’s 3,700 dealers are enrolled in the program, according to the company. The only GM brand not involved is Cadillac, which maintains its own program.

“Certified” used or “preowned” vehicles are used cars that have undergone a thorough inspection and reconditioning. They typically come with guarantees and warranties from the manufacturer.

Many automakers have certified used programs for their own cars. But GM, as part of its revamp, is using CarBravo to certify vehicles made by other automakers. A lot of those cars arrive at dealerships as trade-ins, and often dealers will sell them to wholesale auctions, said John Fitzpatrick, senior manager of the CarBravo program.

“Wholesaling doesn’t bring nearly the revenue that selling it to a new customer does,” he said.

GM has said it is planning to net about 250,000 sales in its CarBravo program in 2026. Fitzpatrick said he doesn’t expect that even half of those will end up being new car sales.

But through CarBravo, the customer gets access to GM’s dealership network for service, something Fitzpatrick says is a key differentiator between its program and growing online sellers. CarBravo vehicles come with various warranties, depending on the age and mileage on the car.

GM said the program is driving more traffic into local dealerships, where purchases are typically finalized. That creates an opportunity to convert a used car shopper into a new car buyer. So far, the automaker said about 38% of the shoppers initially looking for used cars end up buying new.

A customer who wants to buy a full-size truck can look on the website and compare used Chevrolet Silverados alongside used Ford
 F-150s and Ram 1500s, for example. The buyer might settle on a used truck from any of those brands, but a conversation with a dealer can push them in a different direction.

“The customer picks up the phone, but in the back of their mind, they maybe always have been a traditional, more new car customer,” Fitzpatrick said.

“You’ve shown the customer, you’re going to pay $500 [per month] for this used F-150, but you may pay $510 or $515 for this new Chevy,” he said. “And now all of a sudden the customer says, yeah, maybe I can do that because I’d rather have that new vehicle than the used truck.”

While the average transaction price of a new vehicle is about $50,000, the average 3-year-old used car costs about $30,000 as of September, according to Cox Automotive.

However, industry analysts say customers base their purchasing decisions on the cost of the monthly payment more than on the sticker price of the car.

New cars often come with longer-term loan options than used ones, Feinseth said, which can result in lower monthly payments.

“On a 1- or 2-year-old car, you may be only stuck with a 3- or 4-year loan,” he said. “On a new car, you can get a 5-year, 6-year loan.”

The share of new car loans lasting 84 months hit a new record in the third quarter, at more than 1 in 4 loans, according to Edmunds.

Meanwhile, used car prices in some affordable segments have risen, according to Cox Automotive, and about three quarters of consumers express some interest in certified cars.

But the key is building the relationship with the customer, he said. About 50% of the buyers GM has gained through the program appear to be new to the brand, meaning there is no record of them in any of the automaker’s customer databases. About 70% had never visited the dealership they ended up purchasing from.

“The goal is really to get that customer engaged with the store, give them the option of building a relationship with the dealer,” he said. “The dealer can really help the customer figure out what works for their budget.”

It’s a boon for dealers too: Customers buying warranty-backed used cars often return to the dealership for service visits — which often account for about half of a dealership’s profits. GM can also sell subscriptions to connected vehicle services, such as its OnStar, which provides safety, security and navigation services.

“That is a big part of General Motors’ business going forward, is to sell the software and subscription services like OnStar and eventually to the cars that are enabled with Super Cruise,” GM’s advanced driver-assistance system, Feinseth said.

GM isn’t the only automaker trying to use its certified preowned vehicle program to lure buyers.

Detroit rival Ford Motor
 also certifies vehicles made by other manufacturers through its Ford Blue Advantage program. It is on track to do 450,000 total sales in 2026, more than GM’s 250,000 target. It didn’t specify how many of those buyers end up purchasing new vehicles.

Toyota told CNBC in an email that about 40% of its used car shoppers end up buying new instead.

Honda didn’t give specifics about its program. But Lance Woelfer, American Honda’s vice president of automobile sales, said conversions happen “probably every day at dealerships throughout the country.”

“But it also is more about that first interaction with the consumer,” Woelfer said. “And there are people in any market that prefer to buy a used vehicle, but appreciate the confidence that a [certified preowned designation] can give them.”

Woelfer said those customers come back to get their vehicles serviced at a rate about 18% higher than someone who buys a non-certified used car. They also return to purchase a new car at a rate about 7% to 8% higher in the future, he said.

“It’s about that first relationship that allows us to then have that customer loyalty for life,” he added. “And that’s where our focus is. We’ve been doing it a long time, and we’ve seen a lot of benefits from the certified business.”

This is CNBC’s Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox.

Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today’s edition of Morning Squawk.

CoreWeave is providing the tailwind for futures today, helping lift neocloud stocks, while a rebound for Nvidia is also supporting the chip space.

But is it enough to dull the lingering doubts around the AI trade?

CoreWeave shares are surging in premarket trading, up over 16% overnight, after the neocloud group posted a 168% spike in third-quarter revenue.

The group also lifted its 2026 guidance, driving other neocloud stocks higher.

But bear in mind that shares are down 65% from their May highs, losing over 40% of their value in the last month alone.

Nvidia shares are extending gains in premarket trading, up just over 3%.

The move is also supporting gains for Broadcom
, AMD
, Intel
 and Nebius
.

Here are the key developments:

CNBC’s Seema Mody spoke to sources within Nvidia who said Huang walked into the group’s Santa Clara, California, headquarters on Monday to hold his regular meeting with top-level executives.

To go inside that meeting, read the full piece here on CNBC.com.

Anthropic is offering 825 million shares at a price range of $70-78 per share.

Sources close to the deal told CNBC the AI titan is planning to price on November 18 and trade on November 19.

CNBC’s Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning.

Subscribe here to get access today.

The House of Representatives has effectively voted down an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The House, by a 211-204 margin, approved a measure that will refer the impeachment resolution to a committee, leaving little time for it to be acted on before Democrats take over in January.

Tokenization: The next evolution of the stock market

The U.S. equity market has repeatedly changed its underlying mechanics while the asset itself — a share of stock — has remained largely the same.

Trading moved from floors and phone calls to electronic venues. Settlement cycles compressed. Commissions fell to zero. Fractional shares and online brokerages expanded retail participation.

The next major change may already be underway.

— CNBC’s Jordan Novet, April Roach, Dan Mangan, Kif Leswing, Alexa LoMonaco, Chloe Taylor, Isabella Gao and Garrett Downs contributed to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/cramer-s.title: Jim Cramer: Wall Street is focusing too much on what could go wrong instead of right
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/cramer-s.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/cramer-s.text:
Jim Cramer said investors shouldn’t let mounting market risks overshadow potential catalysts for a rebound.

He pointed to falling oil prices, a potential resolution to Nvidia’s leadership uncertainty and Anthropic’s upcoming IPO as developments that could help stocks recover.

Investors shouldn’t let a barrage of bad news drive them out of the stock market, CNBC’s Jim Cramer said Tuesday.

Stocks fell Tuesday after a hotter-than-expected inflation report fueled concerns about a bigger half-point Federal Reserve interest rate hike at next month’s meeting. The Nasdaq 
dropped 0.74%, while the S&P 500
 lost 0.38%, preventing the indexes from logging three-session win streaks following Thursday’s postelection rout. The artificial intelligence trade was also under pressure as the Nvidia
 CEO scandal simmered and despite a bullish valuation bump on the Anthropic IPO.

“At times like this, where you have a bull market one day and a bear market the next and investors seem to have no conviction, you need to think not only what can go wrong, but also about what can go right,” the “Mad Money” host said.

Tuesday’s consumer price index, which exceeded estimates, sent Treasury yields higher. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan suggested two quick quarter-point increases may be necessary. Only hours before the CPI print, Fed Governor Christopher Waller supported another quarter-point hike and left the door open to a half-point increase. The market is now fully pricing in a quarter-point rate hike at the central bank’s December meeting, with a 12% probability of a half-point increase, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Still, Cramer argued that an end to the Iran war could send oil prices sharply lower, easing inflation and reducing pressure on the Fed. “If we see oil plummet to $40, which is what the chart of oil refining giant Valero
 says to me, and you get Walmart
 and Costco
 to force price cuts for branded products or make their own excellent house brands for everything, then you are going to see the CPI come down,” he said. Oil dipped under $90 per barrel for the first time since August on hopes for a Middle East detente.

Another potential catalyst is Nvidia
, despite the uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang and his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Cramer said strong earnings, a massive share buyback, and a temporary leave for Huang during an independent investigation, with longtime executive Ian Buck potentially serving as interim CEO, could help restore investor confidence. Nvidia shares sank for a second straight day.

A successful Anthropic
 initial public offering next week could further revive confidence in the AI trade. According to an updated filing, the Claude developer is set to price the offering on Nov. 18, with trading set to begin the next day. The company could be valued on a fully diluted basis at over $1.4 trillion, which is way up from the $965 billion valuation announced as part of a funding round back in May.

Taken all together, Cramer said, those developments could create a more favorable backdrop for stocks. “The idea of everything going wrong is not in my lexicon,” Cramer said. “We just need a few breaks. I think we will get them.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/coreweav.title: CoreWeave beats on revenue and lifts guidance, easing AI slowdown concerns
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/coreweav.author: Jordan Novet
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/coreweav.text:
CoreWeave said revenue jumped 168% in the third quarter.

Neoclouds like CoreWeave have been under intensifying pressure due to increasing interest rates.

The stock has lost about 40% of its value in the past month, alongside a broader slide in the AI infrastructure trade.

CoreWeave
 reported better-than-expected quarterly revenue and lifted its 2026 guidance on Tuesday, showing that demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure remains strong despite concerns of a market slowdown. The stock advanced in extended trading.

The earnings announcement lands at a particularly volatile moment for CoreWeave and its neocloud peers, as the market sours on the AI trade and as Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang, the central figure in the global buildout, faces a scandal tied to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Here’s how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:

CoreWeave’s revenue soared 168% from about $1.36 billion a year earlier, according to a statement. The company recorded a net loss of $709 million, or $1.27 per share, compared to a net loss of $110 million a year earlier. Adjusted earnings exclude stock-based compensation.

Executives pushed up their forecast for 2026. They now see $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion in adjusted operating income on $13 billion to $13.3 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha were looking for $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income, and analysts polled by LSEG had expected $12.86 billion in 2026 revenue.

In August, CoreWeave’s 2026 guidance included $960 million to $1.15 billion in adjusted operating income and $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion in revenue.

CoreWeave has lost over 40% of its value in the past month, as investors rotate out of companies most closely tied to AI infrastructure. Rising interest rates have pushed lenders out of the market, raising concerns about ongoing access to capital. Some CoreWeave bond yields recently topped 16%.

“The business can execute well and still face a tougher financing environment,” Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, wrote in an email. “Strong demand is encouraging; the cost and availability of capital remain critical.”

CoreWeave will get most the capital it needs for 2027 through clients pre-payments and financing from hardware partners, and the company will raise “a limited amount” as well, CEO Mike Intrator told analysts on a conference call.

The company plans to raise new debt tied to a set of contracts in the weeks to come, said Nitin Agrawal, its finance chief.

“At current yields, we do not intend to issue additional parent-level unsecured debt through 2027,” he said. “By contrast, the asset-level secured debt market has remained stable, with our loans continuing to trade around par value.” In all, he said he projects under $5 billion in parent-level debt financing through 2027.

Fellow neocloud Nebius
, whose stock is down by a similar amount, is scheduled to report earnings on Thursday. Nebius shares got a small boost from CoreWeave’s results.

Both companies and several other providers of cloud-based graphics processing units are particularly reliant on Nvidia, which provides GPUs as well as necessary capital to the whole ecosystem. Nvidia shares have dropped nearly 10% to start the week as the Huang affair raises pressure on the company in Washington, D.C. Nvidia’s board said on Tuesday that it hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate Huang and determine whether national security or company secrets were compromised.

CoreWeave investors are also looking toward next week, when key customer Anthropic is scheduled to debut on the Nasdaq. In its updated IPO prospectus on Tuesday, Anthropic indicated that it could be valued at around $1.4 trillion after its share sale. Anthropic has signed deals for the construction of entire data centers that will meet its needs. “We see that we’re going to have long-term relationships with the AI labs,” said Intrator, a CoreWeave co-founder.

During the quarter, CoreWeave said it would establish its first data centers in Asia and announced the Forge service for running and evaluating AI models.

Management still anticipates 1.85 gigawatts in active power by the end of 2026. CoreWeave is targeting $37 billion to $39 billion in full-year capital expenditures, which would imply 155% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by Visible Alpha were looking for $37.69 billion.

CoreWeave owed almost $47 billion in debt at the end of the third quarter, according to the statement. Like its bigger cloud rivals such as Amazon
 and Oracle
, CoreWeave is rushing to bolster computing capacity for clients.

But last week, voters in the U.S., where CoreWeave derives most of its revenue, rejected dozens of initiatives on data center development. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated the incumbent, Republican Greg Abbott, after she said Abbott should try to end 20-year tax breaks on large data centers.

“So to begin with, we do not anticipate any impact from the seismic regulatory shift that’s occurred,” Intrator said.

Almost all of CoreWeave’s power is online or is permitted and under construction, he said.

“If data center construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute becomes scarcer, and the knock-on effect is that GPU pricing may stay higher for longer,” Intrator said.

He said the company does not expect risks to deliveries in 2027 based on construction at permitted locations.

“We could sell all of the capacity that we have to current buyers that are in the queue. We are choosing not to,” Intrator said. We’re choosing to be patient. We’re choosing to bring the infrastructure to market when it is further along, because we believe that that will result in better economic output for the outstanding infrastructure that we have.”

Meanwhile, demand remains robust, with the company now sitting on a $132.5 billion revenue backlog, up from $104 billion as of June.

“Should we choose to focus only on our committed backlog, we would expect capex for 2027 to remain in line with our 2026 capex investment, while revenue and EBITDA grow significantly,” Agrawal said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-c.title: Op-ed: In Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged China spy scandal, there's plenty of blame to go around
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-c.author: Dewardric L. McNeal
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-c.text:
The unfolding scandal involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is not just the failure of one man but a failure of the tech industry, the market, and political leadership at a much wider level.

Silicon Valley has long celebrated the visionary founder, the indispensable executive whose genius supposedly transcends conventional management and traditional corporate governance, and investors have rewarded it.

In the artificial intelligence era, this ‘key man’ risk becomes considerably more dangerous, and both the U.S. president and Congress must take action now.

In June 2013, President Barack Obama welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to Sunnylands, a secluded California estate, for an informal summit. Behind the diplomatic pleasantries, Obama confronted Xi over Chinese state-directed cyber-enabled espionage and theft of American intellectual property, warning that such activities threatened American companies and the broader bilateral relationship.

Thirteen years after the Sunnylands Summit, the threat has evolved significantly as the race to dominate AI frames the U.S.-China relationship. The stakes are higher, the technology more consequential, and the vulnerabilities increasingly involve attempts to compromise or coopt the “key man” at the helm of the nation’s top technology companies.

With the unfolding scandal involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the blame should start with the CEO himself, but it should not end there. The situation illustrates a failure of Silicon Valley, corporate and political leadership at a much wider level.

Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair with a woman identified in reporting as Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. American intelligence officials reportedly believe she was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information and potentially influence Nvidia’s efforts to loosen American semiconductor export restrictions. China denies the allegations.

Nvidia’s independent directors have launched an investigation, and so far, they say no compromise of company secrets or national security information has been established. But the problem extends well beyond Huang or Nvidia. Focusing exclusively on whether proprietary technology or trade secrets were transferred fundamentally misunderstands the potential intelligence value of such an operation.

For Beijing, gaining insight into, influencing, or potentially compromising American technology policymaking could be equally valuable. Advance knowledge of export-control deliberations, regulatory intentions, negotiating positions, or divisions within the administration could provide strategic advantages without a single semiconductor design being stolen.

The Trump administration reportedly received warnings about the relationship before the scandal became public. Nevertheless, Huang remained an influential participant in semiconductor policy discussions while advocating greater access to China’s market.

New reporting also raises questions about interactions between Nvidia and Commerce Department officials during an investigation into Megaspeed, subsequently transferred to the Justice Department. No improper influence has been established, but corporate access to government decision-making deserves scrutiny alongside proprietary technology.

Whether appropriate protective measures were taken remains unclear. President Donald Trump’s public defense of Huang — saying that Huang told him he had no idea the woman could be a spy and that he trusted the CEO, and that if national intelligence had warned the president about this threat, as has been reported, he didn’t remember — hardly conveyed the urgency warranted by allegations of a foreign intelligence operation targeting a strategically indispensable American company.

Trump has met Xi three times since returning to office, with two additional encounters anticipated in November and December. These meetings offer Trump an opportunity to follow Obama’s example by confronting Xi directly over Chinese state-directed or sponsored espionage targeting American technology companies, their executives, and potentially the U.S. policymaking process.

It is also time for a more formal check from Congress on Silicon Valley, which has long celebrated the visionary founder, the indispensable executive whose genius supposedly transcends conventional corporate management and traditional corporate governance. Investors have rewarded this concentration of authority, while boards have all too frequently accommodated it.

Corporate governance professionals call this “Key Man” risk: excessive organizational dependence on an individual whose departure, financial misconduct, or moral compromise could materially damage the enterprise. In the artificial intelligence era, this risk becomes considerably more dangerous. When a handful of executives control technologies central to America’s economic competitiveness, military capabilities, and intelligence advantages, their personal vulnerabilities become potential national security vulnerabilities.

When those executives also enjoy extraordinary access to the White House and senior policymakers, they become potential conduits for foreign intelligence collection and influence directed not simply at their companies, but at the American people and American policy itself.

Congress has opportunities to strengthen America’s defenses and must act immediately.

The AI OVERWATCH Act would strengthen oversight of advanced semiconductor exports and associated national security licensing conditions.

The MATCH Act would address weaknesses in restrictions on advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment, including foreign suppliers and servicing arrangements.

The Chip Security Act would strengthen mechanisms for tracking advanced chips and detecting diversion.

Importantly, the Remote Access Security Act would extend export-control authorities to certain remote access arrangements, including cloud computing, addressing the possibility that restricted American technological capabilities could be accessed without physically exporting the underlying equipment.

Together, these measures address important technological and regulatory gaps and vulnerabilities. But controlling chips, equipment, and computing access admittedly will not solve the human vulnerabilities problem — the so-called “Key Man” risks to U.S. technology supremacy and national security.

Most of these bills have a good amount of Congressional bipartisan support. However, they have encountered stiff resistance from the technology industry and their lobbyists, and some very detailed disagreements over specifics of export-control policy. There has also been uncertainty about White House support for these bills and an unwillingness by the Republican-controlled Congress to get on the wrong side of the White House. However, there is no doubt in my mind the Nvidia controversy has given supporters a new argument for action. The Democratic takeover of both chambers could further strengthen congressional oversight and an appetite for codifying much of this into law using these pieces of legislation.

There should also be a serious discussion among key U.S. government and corporate governance experts about whether strategically important technology companies need explicit board-level counterintelligence responsibilities, independent executive-security assessments, and confidential mechanisms for reporting foreign intelligence approaches to the appropriate channels.

This is not about morally policing executives’ private lives. It is about recognizing that individuals controlling America’s most sensitive technologies, and influencing the policies governing them, are valuable intelligence targets and assets if compromised.

Unfortunately, the Trump administration’s broader philosophy appears to emphasize voluntary industry commitments and confidence in technology executives’ ability to police themselves. Morality is not a governance system. Personal assurances are not counterintelligence safeguards. Importantly, shareholder interests are not always synonymous with the national interest.

Obama understood at Sunnylands that protecting American innovation required confronting China directly. That engagement helped to clearly articulate American redlines against cyber-enabled theft of intellectual property for commercial advantage.

Trump now has an opportunity, and a responsibility, to extend that principle to today’s intelligence threats. At his forthcoming meetings with Xi, he should make clear that state-directed or sponsored operations targeting American technology executives and attempts to compromise U.S. technology policymaking are unacceptable and carry consequences for the bilateral relationship.

But confronting Beijing is only half the responsibility. Washington must also confront weaknesses within the body of laws governing technology access and must weigh in on America’s corporate institutions and governance.

America cannot declare artificial intelligence essential to national security while leaving protection of its technology, executives, and policymaking process primarily to corporate discretion. The greatest vulnerability in Silicon Valley may not be the technology we export, but the people and governance systems entrusted to protect it, and the policies determining who gets access to it.

Neither Congress nor the White House should be comfortable leaving that responsibility to Silicon Valley’s own moral code.

—By Dewardric McNeal, Managing Director and Senior Policy Analyst at Longview Global, and a CNBC Contributor. He worked in the U.S. Department of Defense as an East Asia and China security relations expert during the Obama administration.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-c.summary: The situation shows a failure in Silicon Valley, corporate and political leaders at a far far from the top. The Nvidia controversy has given supporters a new argument for action, says John Avlon.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/coreweav.title: CoreWeave earnings put debt-fueled AI build-out under scrutiny
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/coreweav.author: Michelle Fox
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/coreweav.text:
CoreWeave reports third-quarter results after the bell Tuesday.

Investors are focused on the neocloud company’s spending, financing and credit risk.

CoreWeave reported $35.6 billion of debt, $5.5 billion of cash and a $104.2 billion revenue backlog in the second quarter.

CoreWeave faces a pivotal test when it reports its third-quarter financial results after the bell on Tuesday.

The market will be closely watching what the neocloud company says about artificial intelligence spending — and how it plans to finance its infrastructure buildout. The outcome could either calm concerns over its debt or stoke more fear.

“Investors need neoclouds to quantify how much financing they expect to raise to execute on existing backlog,” Wolfe Research said in a note Monday. “We think outlooks that communicate when and which avenues of funding will be tapped will increase investor confidence.”

CoreWeave stock and bonds have come under pressure as fears deepened about the enormous amount of debt it has taken out to build its data centers.

Its stock is down roughly 40% over the past month. Meanwhile, the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 15.5% on Tuesday, after jumping to 16.7% on Thursday as investors digested the election results and possible roadblocks to data center construction. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

The spread on its five-year credit default swaps — which is insurance against default and considered a barometer of perceived credit risk — is also at levels that are considered distressed. On Tuesday, its CDS spread stood around 1,152 basis points, after rising above its October peak to close at 1,278 basis points on Thursday. Rising CDS spreads mean investors view the debt as riskier.

In addition, the New Jersey-based company’s leverage is high. CoreWeave has a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from almost 291% a year ago.

CEO Michael Intrator has sought to quell investor fear, posting on LinkedIn after the election last week that the company doesn’t anticipate “any impact to CoreWeave’s existing customer commitments or associated backlog as a result of shifts in the political landscape.”

The company reported a revenue backlog of $104.2 billion in the second quarter. It has about $35 billion in debt, as of June 30.

CoreWeave has already given a picture of what it expects for the third quarter.

It guided for quarterly revenue of $3.4 billion to $3.6 billion when it reported second-quarter results in August. It anticipated capital expenditures between $11.5 billion and $13.5 billion for the quarter and $35 billion to $39 billion for the full year. The company also expects 1.85 gigawatts in active power by year-end.

Wells Fargo expects the company’s capex needs for the rest of the year to be largely covered by its remaining undrawn debt, debt issuances in August/September and the $12 billion it is holding for project costs, which will flow into capex, analyst Michael Turrin said in a note Sunday.

However, its 2027 capex could reach $66 billion, based on an expected capacity addition of 1.5 gigawatts, Turrin said. That will require at least $25 billion more in debt, he noted. It can be largely funded through delayed draw term loans, which allows CoreWeave to draw down funds over time, and the rest can come through bonds and convertibles, he said.

Turrin has an overweight rating and $115 price target on the stock, implying 135% upside from Monday’s close.

“While neoclouds sit in the eye of the AI storm, we remain confident that CRWV is the highest quality co in the space,” Turrin wrote. “Beyond the noise, we see capacity/revs coming in better than expected (1.95GW this yr vs guide 1.85GW) as margins start to inflect.”

However, investors likely won’t get all the answers they’re seeking during CoreWeave’s third-quarter results, said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin.

“One of the major issues for CoreWeave is whether or not they can obtain all the financing they need,” he said. “They may try and calm the markets, but I’m not sure how much color they can and will provide.”

Investors will be looking for 2027 guidance on capex and free cash flow, though that may not come until Coreweave releases fourth quarter results, Chalfin notes.

CoreWeave could ease investor concerns by showing it has plans and approvals in place to scale capacity through 2027, he said. The company can also demonstrate remaining performance obligation (RPO) growth, which shows the total value of its contracted future revenue, and highlight new customer wins.

In addition, pricing has been really strong on recent deals, Chalfin pointed out. “That could show up in an operating margin beat for Q3 and expectations for Q4.”

While CoreWeave faces finances challenges, the company has many ways to access capital, Chalfin said. That includes chip-backed deals, which allow Corewave to borrow money using GPUs as collateral, and original equipment manufacturer financing. For instance, CoreWeave could turn to Dell
, which is a big supplier with a strong balance sheet, Chalfin noted.

“Despite all the market sentiment, fundamentals are actually quite strong and pricing is strong,” he said. “The trends over the next few quarters, I think, should be supportive.” Risks could arise after that, but it is “too early to call.”

Some analysts remain skeptical that Coreweave will be able to calm credit fears.

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, points out that the company is facing a huge bill in just over two years. CoreWeave owes roughly $15 billion in principal payments through 2028, according to its second-quarter earnings statement.

“They don’t have enough cash to service all that debt,” he said. “Unless some big orders come in, unless some big money flows come in for them in the next 17, 18 months, I think this is going to be the start of the end for CoreWeave, unless somebody comes in and wants to buy them. But who wants to buy all that debt?”

However, there could be a “small” window for the company to push out its debt for another three to five years, but it will depend on how strong their cash flow is when they report on Tuesday, Lang said.

Plus, issuing equity to help fund infrastructure projects, like Meta
 and Oracle
 did recently, isn’t an option for CoreWeave, he noted.

“They’re going to dilute the stock so much that it’s going to continue to go down,” he said. “They missed that window when the stock was in the hundreds.”

CoreWeave topped $183 in June 2025. It has since declined more than 73%, recently trading around $47.

Despite the fall, analysts remain bullish on the stock with an average overweight rating and $126 target, based on 39 estimates complied by FactSet.

—CNBC’s Jordan Novet contributed reporting.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/amazons-.title: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/amazons-.author: Annie Palmer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/amazons-.text:
Amazon’s Ring unveiled a flying indoor security drone and a patrolling robot for businesses.

The $250 Ring Drone Cam flies from room to room to investigate suspicious activity, and can capture footage at night.

The $1,000 Ring Rover Cam repurposes Amazon’s Astro robot for deployment in workplaces, such as warehouses and offices.

Amazon
’s Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses.

The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a preset path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said.

At a demo in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime “deterrent” due to the device’s built-in LED lights.

“If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window,” Siminoff said. “You’re probably not going to go into that house.”

The drone, which can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock, has two plastic-encased propellers that emit a loud buzz when it’s airborne.

Ring devices have provided Amazon another avenue to grow its presence in the smart home beyond its Echo smart speakers and Eero routers, expanding in a market that Grand View Research estimates will top $200 billion in sales this year. It’s equally fertile ground for Amazon rivals Apple
 and Google
.

Ring, which Amazon acquired in 2018 and is known for its doorbells, has been beset with privacy concerns, primarily due to its partnerships with police. Earlier this year, Ring faced renewed scrutiny over a controversial Super Bowl ad touting an AI pet-finding tool called “Search Party.” It then canceled an integration with police tech provider Flock Safety, which has also faced widespread backlash over its automated license plate readers.

Ring first previewed its drone, then called the Always Home Cam, in 2020. Siminoff said he chose to hold off on releasing the device until Amazon could perfect the design, sensors and data processing.

The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon’s Astro home robot, which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to use to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces.

Ring said it “leveraged the best of Astro” to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a “purpose-built security robot.”

Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a “built-in siren,” two-way audio and a “light tower” that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts.

Siminoff said in an interview that the drone and the robot allow users to monitor multiple areas of their home or business with just one device.

“People like indoor cameras, but they don’t necessarily want them everywhere around their home,” Siminoff said.

Ring said privacy is the “default” mode for both the drone and the robot, which flash an LED light when they’re recording.

Siminoff said the drone can’t fly outside per Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which restrict operating drones unless they’re within a line of sight of a pilot.

“We have told our customers not to do that because it’s illegal,” Siminoff said. “We’ve also put guardrails in there to make it so it doesn’t fly outside.”

The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said.
