https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/moolenaa.title: Schumer accuses Trump of defending Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at cost of national security
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/moolenaa.author: Dan Mangan,Justin Papp,Garrett Downs,Josephine Rozzelle
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/moolenaa.text:
Sen. Charles Schumer ripped President Donald Trump for defending embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the expense of U.S. national security.

“The press reports that Trump was briefed more than a year ago that Nvidia’s CEO was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and Trump didn’t do anything – anything – about it,” said Schumer, a New York Democrat.

House Select Committee on China Chair John Moolenaar urged a thorough internal investigation into Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed.

Democratic leader Sen. Charles Schumer ripped President Donald Trump on Tuesday for defending embattled Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang at the expense of U.S. national security.

“The press reports that Trump was briefed more than a year ago that Nvidia’s CEO was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and Trump didn’t do anything – anything – about it,” Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the Senate floor.

“Can you believe that?” said Schumer, the Senate’s minority leader.

Schumer’s broadside came on the heels of New York Times reports that Trump had been briefed about Huang’s extramarital affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — whom U.S. intelligence concluded was a spy for China — and opted not to do anything about it.

Trump suggested to reporters on Monday that he only recently learned of the allegations about Alice Huang, and the president commented Monday that he “really” believes Jensen Huang’s claim to him directly that he had no idea Alice Huang was a spy.

“One of our most important companies that is involved in national security, and the CEO might be having an affair with a Chinese spy, and Trump did nothing about it,” Schumer said Tuesday.

“What a dereliction of duty. He’s supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends,” Schumer said. “Trump has been busy trying to defend Jensen Huang when he ought to be defending our national security. It’s that simple, it’s obvious.”

Schumer’s comments escalated growing bipartisan concern in Congress about the Nvidia CEO and his company. Nvidia makes advanced chips that are essential components in developing artificial intelligence models, a sector that is the focus of keen competition between the United States and China.

Schumer noted that Trump earlier this year invited Huang to join him on a state visit to Beijing, and that he took Huang’s advice by granting the People’s Republic of China “access to some of our most advanced AI chips.”

Nvidia also donated $25 million to Trump’s controversial White House ballroom project, the Democrat said.

“Despite talking a big game, Trump continues to show a troubling resistance to confront China on AI and to protect American national security,” Schumer said. “I’ve been saying it for years: our cutting-edge AI chips are too valuable to fall into the hands of potential adversaries.”

Schumer in his speech called on Republicans to join Democrats in passing several pieces of legislation — the AI Overwatch Act, the Match Act, and the Chip Security Act — which he said would “cut off China’s access to advanced American technology.”

“We also need answers on Nvidia’s influence campaign and how [it] affected the Trump administration’s national security decisions, including the loosening – the loosening – of key export controls,” Schumer said. “We need a full accounting for Trump’s failure to address foreign espionage in the American tech industry.”

CNBC has requested comment from the White House about Schumer’s remarks.

The remarks came nearly a week after Democrats won enough Senate and House races nationwide to take majority control of both chambers of Congress in January. Schumer hopes to be selected majority leader.

Regardless of which Democrats are tapped to serve as majority leaders in both chambers, the party will have the ability to launch investigations into Nvidia and Huang.

Earlier Tuesday, Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., said on CNBC’s “Squawk Box” that Congress needs to “get to the bottom” of Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang.

Moolenaar, who chairs the House Permanent Select Committee on China, said he wants to know whether Huang shared privileged information with a Chinese spy; whether Huang was influenced to lobby against preventing chip sales to China; and whether China was given preference in purchasing Nvidia’s limited supply of advanced chips.

And he urged a thorough internal investigation of Huang.

“If it becomes less of an investigation, more of damage control, that’s not going to work because people have to have confidence,” Moolenaar said.

“We’re dealing with the country, the Chinese Communist Party that is a foremost adversary, that’s funding wars and supporting Russia, supporting Iran, North Korea,” he said. “And we have basically a Cold War race with technology. We cannot allow the premier company at the forefront of this to, in some way, be irresponsible.”

Congressional scrutiny of Huang’s affair has intensified since members returned to Washington on Monday, a day after Nvidia announced it was opening an independent investigation into Jensen Huang’s conduct.

Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., co-chair of the House AI task force, raised concerns that the scandal could plague talks over export controls for advanced AI chips.

“It’s important not to have a personal scandal interfere with the substantive policy discussion about to what degree we should be allowing the export of cutting edge chips to our geopolitical competitors like China,” Obernolte told CNBC. “I hope this isn’t a distraction because that’s a very important conversation that needs to happen.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a news conference on Monday that “we’re going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of national security”

Moolenaar co-authored a letter with Florida Rep. Brian Mast and Arkansas Rep. Rick Crawford on Nov. 5 asking Huang to appear before the Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Select Committee on Intelligence. Mast chairs the foreign affairs panel, and Crawford chairs intelligence.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the three Republicans wrote.

Mast said Tuesday he did not know whether Huang had responded to the letter he authored with Moolenar and Crawford demanding the tech CEO brief them.

“I can’t say that I’ve heard an answer back yet that,” Mast told reporters at the Capitol.

Mast then rattled off a list of questions he has for Huang, including where the company has been selling chips, what Megaspeed may have been using them for, who has been remotely accessing Nvidia chips, and what information was passed between Huang and the potential spy.

“Obviously questions relating to his relationship and what information was or was not passed about anything,” Mast said when asked what he wants answered.

Mast said he “can’t say it would hurt” to hear from the Commerce Department as well, noting he speaks regularly to the Bureau of Industry and Security.

“So that’s obviously something that falls directly under Commerce,” he said
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/moolenaa.summary: Sen. Charles Schumer says President Donald Trump was briefed about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The tech CEO is being questioned by three Republicans on a national security issue.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/jensen-h.title: Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy further complicates Nvidia’s China problem
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/jensen-h.author: Katie Tarasov
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/jensen-h.text:
The allegations against Jensen Huang have brought new attention to the Nvidia CEO’s potential influence over U.S. policy on chip sales to China.

Lawmakers are looking to investigate Nvidia’s China ties.

“In 35 years, I haven’t seen a chip CEO with this much direct influence on export policy,” said Patrick Moorhead, CEO at Moor Insights & Strategy.

Following Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang’s admission on Sunday to an extramarital affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, the chipmaker’s relationship to China is about to come under intense scrutiny in Washington, D.C.

Since October 2022, when the Biden administration announced sweeping controls to limit China’s ability to obtain advanced U.S. chips, Nvidia has seen its business diminish in the world’s second-largest economy. Months after an even stricter set of rules was implemented by the Trump administration, Huang said in October 2025, “We are 100% out of China.”

The recent allegations against Huang, while throwing the chipmaker into crisis, have also brought attention to the Nvidia CEO’s potential influence over U.S. policy on chip sales to China, where its business once flourished. Of particular interest is whether restricted Nvidia chips have reached Chinese companies through customers like Singapore-based Megaspeed, the company linked to Alice Huang.

The New York Times first reported that the Chinese businesswoman was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, according to people briefed on the intelligence circulated in a memo among the Trump administration in the spring. China has called the allegation a smear.

Jensen Huang has been closely aligned with President Donald Trump during his second administration, helping advise the White House on artificial intelligence safety regulations, while also pushing for looser restrictions on selling AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia would be allowed to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales. In March, Huang told reporters that Nvidia had “received purchase orders, and we’re in the process of restarting our manufacturing.”

Huang was a last-minute addition to the roster of tech executives who joined Trump on a trip to China in May, after the president was briefed on intelligence concerns, according to the Times.

“In 35 years, I haven’t seen a chip CEO with this much direct influence on export policy,” said Patrick Moorhead, CEO at Moor Insights & Strategy, in an email.

Since last week’s midterm elections that included sweeping victories across the country for Democrats, the mood in Washington has changed. Three House committees have requested closed-door briefings with the Nvidia CEO about his relationship with Megaspeed.

Democratic lawmakers, who are about to take power in the House and Senate, have said publicly that Congress will investigate and seek answers. Trump said Monday that he was “amazed” by the allegations and that Huang told him he “had no idea that she was a spy.” The FBI is now looking into the issue, Trump said at a White House briefing.

It’s been a long four years for Nvidia in China.

Before the initial export controls in 2022, China made up nearly a quarter of Nvidia’s revenue. Nvidia responded to the Biden-era restrictions by redesigning some of its products to comply with the new regulations.

“It was a turbulent month or so as the company went upside down to re-engineer” the products, Huang told CNBC in a 2023 interview. Still, he was confident the company could continue selling chips to China. “I think we’re going to be just fine in the ability to serve the customers there,” he said.

After the Biden administration tightened export restrictions again, Nvidia redesigned another AI graphics processing unit for China, the H20. Following reports that Chinese model developer DeepSeek was using restricted Nvidia chips, the Trump administration limited sales of H20. Nvidia revealed it would incur $5.5 billion in costs related to canceled orders for the redesigned chip.

However, despite saying in its forecasts that “we’re assuming 0% for China,” the company maintained business in the region. In the last fiscal year, Nvidia reported that about 9% of its revenue came from China, including Hong Kong, although that includes revenue from segments outside of restricted data center chips, such as gaming, auto and industrial. Nvidia’s China revenue was 8% in the most recent quarter.

A report in May from short seller Culper Research alleged Nvidia’s China exposure was much higher. The firm said that more than 20% of Nvidia’s fiscal 2026 compute revenue was driven by China, supported by “illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries,” according to the report.

A loophole allows Chinese companies to rent Nvidia GPUs in data centers, even when they’re restricted from buying them outright. For example, a Chinese company could lease Nvidia computing power in Europe by renting server capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that’s exempt from export controls.

Nvidia didn’t respond to a request for comment for this story.

Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer based in Singapore, has been accused of diverting its own supply of Nvidia’s restricted AI chips to Chinese companies. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and said inspections found no evidence of violations.

In 2025, Nvidia changed the way it reported regional sales to categorize by customer headquarters, instead of by where the products were billed. Nvidia also stopped reporting Singapore sales during the same period.

“Whether Blackwell chips reached China is a Megaspeed question that predates this week,” said Moorhead, pointing to Bloomberg reporting in December 2025 that found Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more Nvidia chips than Nvidia tallied in its data centers.

In 2025, a House Select Committee opened an investigation into whether China’s DeepSeek operates on Nvidia’s chips.

A separate investigation by the U.S. Commerce Department was centered on Megaspeed. That probe was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department, the Times reported, following an email from Nvidia’s general counsel to the Commerce Department seeking information about the investigation.

The restrictions aren’t just coming from the U.S. China has continued to limit the amount of Nvidia chips it will allow into the country, keeping Nvidia’s China sales numbers down. The U.S. has licensed H200 sales to Alibaba
, Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, but Beijing hasn’t approved large-scale imports, Moorhead told CNBC. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July.

Moorhead expects more export control legislation to pass as a result of the latest turmoil. Proposals could allow Congress oversight of chip export licenses or require chipmakers to install security mechanisms to track the location of chips to determine if they’ve found their way to China.

“Every China license now gets read through this story,” Moorhead said. “Jensen has been Nvidia’s lead voice on China, and that voice is weaker.”

— CNBC’s Kif Leswing and Seema Mody contributed reporting to this report.

This is CNBC’s Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox.

Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today’s edition of Morning Squawk.

Nvidia is dominating the headlines, but it’s not holding back the bulls.

A solid rally across Wall Street, driven by some of the big chip names, came against a backdrop of serious concerns over the future of Jensen Huang’s leadership and what that means for the AI behemoth.

But the devil remains in the details...

There are some key developments in the Nvidia scandal, as the AI giant could now face an FBI investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s conduct.

President Donald Trump said during a press conference in the White House on Monday that he had spoken to Huang and that the CEO had denied knowing the woman he was having an affair with “was a spy” for China. “I know the FBI is looking into it,” Trump also said.

More key developments:

Nvidia shares are trading higher premarket, up by around 1% after falling over 4% on Monday.

Chip stocks are mixed in premarket trading after that blistering rally on Monday.

Broadcom and AMD led the biggest gains, alongside Magnificent 7 names like Amazon, Alphabet, Tesla and Microsoft.

Later today, neocloud group CoreWeave will publish earnings. CNBC’s Seema Mody will be watching to see whether there is an Nvidia impact, as one of the company’s largest shareholders has been hands-on in setting strategy.

Nvidia sat out a rally on Wall Street that saw the S&P post its best session since April, the Dow add over 1,000 points and the Nasdaq jump 2%.

Lower oil prices helped drive gains across major markets, with Brent and WTI continuing those declines this morning. Brent has dipped below $90 per barrel for the first time since August.

Investors can watch out for a key inflation reading on Tuesday, when the October consumer price index report is released at 8:30 a.m. ET.

Estimates show a headline growth rate of 0.3% and 0.2% for core.

CNBC’s Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning.

Subscribe here to get access today.

A Republican representative has made the rare move to make an impeachment push against a member of his own party.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky, has introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, prompting a vote in the House of Representatives as early as this week.

FDA warns of vision loss risk linked to popular GLP-1 drugs

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is requiring new safety warnings on all GLP-1 drugs after finding evidence of a potential increased risk of a rare eye condition, the agency said on Monday.

Nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), which can cause sudden vision loss, is rare, and a causal relationship has not been established.

The FDA is requiring the makers of all GLP-1 medications to add a warning about the potential increased risk of NAION associated with use of these medications, it said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/anthropi.title: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78, looks to start trading  Nov. 19, sources say
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/anthropi.author: Ashley Capoot,Leslie Picker
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/anthropi.text:
Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share.

Should the offering take place in mid-November as expected, it will come roughly five months after SpaceX’s record IPO.

Anthropic has filed to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, according to an updated filing on Tuesday, bringing the 5-year-old artificial intelligence lab a step closer to a potentially historic Nasdaq debut.

The company is planning to price on Nov. 18 and trade on Nov. 19, according to people familiar with the details who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is targeting retail allocation of about 20%, the people said, a much higher percentage than the typical initial public offering, which is 5% to 10% for retail investors.

At the high end of the range, Anthropic would net up to $64.35 billion in proceeds through the IPO. The company could end up being worth up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, rising from the $965 billion valuation it announced as part of a funding round in May.

Anthropic said it has entered into an agreement with Advanced Micro Devices
, Broadcom
, Google
, Micron
, Microsoft
, Nvidia
 and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.
 to purchase $26 billion of the company’s Class N common stock in a private placement at a price per share equal to the IPO price. The shares sold in the private placement will not be registered in the offering and will not be subject to lock-up agreements with the underwriters, the company said.

As Anthropic executives get set to pitch the offering to investors, they have to contend with a tumultuous political environment, following last week’s midterm elections that included a Democratic sweep in Congress and the passage of numerous statewide ballot measures that could slow the AI buildout. They’re also facing a public market that’s grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade on concern that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases.

CNBC reported last week that some Anthropic investors were bracing for a lower valuation than had previously been expected. While Anthropic had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation until recently, shareholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a “stretch.”

Should Anthropic reach the Nasdaq this month as planned, under the ticker symbol “ANT,” the debut would come roughly five months after SpaceX
 went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. Elon Musk’s reusable rocket and AI company has a market cap of just under $2 trillion, around its valuation at the time of the IPO.

Institutional demand for Anthropic is even stronger than it was for SpaceX at this point in the process, the people said. The company’s book is already covered at the $70 to $78 per share range on an allocable basis, they said.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the AI lab in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and the company primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.

On Monday, Anthropic introduced two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the first time the company has released so-called frontier models since Amodei called to slow down the pace of AI development in September. Anthropic said that the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing, and that the company developed new evaluations and post-launch monitoring tools ahead of the release.

For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.

Anthropic said in its amended filing Tuesday that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.

“Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles,” Anthropic’s co-founders wrote in the prospectus. “Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort. We hope you will share our ambition to see it though.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-n.title: Nvidia sells off for second day in fallout from Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged spy
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-n.author: April Roach
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/nvidia-n.text:
Nvidia stock continued to fall Tuesday, following a 4% drop on Monday amid claims that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy.

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is investigating but added: “I think he’ll be in good shape.”

AMD continued a strong week, while Broadcom also rallied.

Nvidia
 shares sank 5.47% on Tuesday as investors continued to weigh the potential fallout from CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The embattled chip giant briefly dipped below $4 trillion in market cap during afternoon trading, but bounced back to close above that level. Nvidia last cleared the $4 trillion benchmark on July 9, 2025.

Shares closed more than 4% lower on Monday, the day after Huang told staff in an email that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and had “fallen short” of his responsibilities as CEO.

He reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The New York Times on Oct. 29 reported that U.S. officials had concluded she was “a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing” and “possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China.”

U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating.

“I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time, but not too long ago,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We’ll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

Adding to the tech giant’s woes was a class-action shareholder lawsuit filed against Nvidia and Huang in federal court in San Jose, California.

The Rosen Law Firm’s suit alleges the defendants made false or misleading statements about his affair with Huang and Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed, thereby presenting a material risk to the company’s reputation and business prospects.

“Right now the Street and investor chatter is assigning roughly a 15% chance he is removed as CEO of Nvidia with a high probability (85%) he stays on as CEO after the Board investigation is completed,” said Dan Ives, senior and managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co, in a Tuesday note.

“We would expect a Board investigation that could take 4 weeks to 6 weeks and will create a clear overhand on the stock until more news emerges from Nvidia.”

Amid Nvidia’s turmoil, some of its chip rivals are seeing a boost. Advanced Micro Devices
 and Broadcom
 built on a strong start to the week, with AMD gaining 1.3% and Broadcom adding nearly 4%. AMD gained 13% on Monday, while Broadcom added just over 10%.

— CNBC’s Dan Mangan and Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/softbank.title: SoftBank swings to $7 billion loss after U.S. data center hit and Intel share decline
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/softbank.author: Jenny Lee
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/10/softbank.text:
SoftBank swung to a net loss of 1.12 trillion yen in the fiscal second quarter.

The Japanese investment giant also recorded a $3.7 billion loss from changes in procurement plans for power generation equipment for AI data center projects in the U.S.

SoftBank
 reported a fiscal second-quarter net loss of 1.12 trillion yen ($7 billion) on Tuesday, as losses tied to U.S. AI data center equipment procurement and Intel
 share declines weighed on earnings.

The Japanese investment giant also recorded a 597.2 billion ($3.7 billion) yen loss in the six months ending on Sept. 30 due to changes in procurement plans for power generation equipment for AI data center projects in the U.S.

SoftBank said it had made advance investments to secure power generation equipment for its AI data center projects in the U.S. amid concerns over potential shortages and long procurement lead times. Power is increasingly becoming a key constraint for the AI data center buildout as power grids become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers.

Cumulative payments for power-generation equipment for U.S. AI data center projects, like the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County, Ohio, totaled $9.48 billion as of the end of September.

“We made bridge investments in advance to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortage,” a SoftBank executive said during the company’s earnings call.

Here’s how SoftBank fared in the fiscal second quarter:

Revenue rose 13.3% in the six months ended Sept. 30, supported by growth in telecommunications and AI computing businesses. The company said its SoftBank segment recorded higher sales across all businesses, while revenue at its AI computing segment increased.

The company’s Vision Fund segment swung to a loss of 81.58 billion yen in the fiscal second quarter, compared with a profit of 2.38 trillion yen a year earlier. Vision Fund 1 recorded an investment loss of $20 million in the quarter, despite a $1.3 billion gain on ByteDance, as shares of publicly traded portfolio companies, including Coupang and Grab, declined.

The Vision Funds segment recorded investment gains of 85.45 billion yen, down sharply from 2.81 trillion yen in the year-earlier period. Vision Fund 2 posted investment gains of 89.26 billion yen, while Vision Fund 1 recorded a loss of 3.86 billion yen on its investments.

As of the end of September, SoftBank’s cumulative investment in OpenAI stood at $54.6 billion, with a fair value of $99.6 billion and a cumulative investment gain of $45 billion, according to the company.

SoftBank said a potential increase in OpenAI’s valuation following a new funding round had not yet been reflected in its results, pending an official announcement. The updated valuation could be reflected in the fiscal third quarter, potentially boosting its net asset value and improving its loan-to-value ratio, the company said.

“ChatGPT has been continuously a weapon of OpenAI, especially for consumers,” the SoftBank esecutive said during the company’s earnings call, highlighting the chatbot’s growing user base.

Shares of the Japanese investment giant closed 13.9% higher on Tuesday. The gains came as Asian technology stocks, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, rose following an overnight rebound on Wall Street.

On its AI infrastructure investments, SoftBank highlighted a 20-year lease agreement with OpenAI for eight gigawatts of IT capacity at a data center project in Ohio.

Addressing concerns of water consumption at its planned data center in Texas, SoftBank said it was taking steps to reduce water use through a closed-loop, air-cooled system. The company also pointed to plans to hire and source locally.

Ahead of its earnings release, SoftBank Group announced on Monday plans with Grab and Malaysia’s PETROS to commit a combined $1.85 billion in initial capital to develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia, with a long-term target of at least five gigawatts of AI computing capacity.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.title: The Pace of Everglades Restoration Has Accelerated. But Is It Working?
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.author: By Amy Green
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.text:
A historic restoration of Florida’s Everglades is proceeding at an unprecedented pace, although more scientific analysis is needed to understand how the fragile watershed is responding to the multi-billion-dollar effort, according to a new report.

The report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine, published last month, said the river of grass has benefitted recently from better collaboration between the federal and state governments and a record infusion of funding. Now that several projects are complete and the nearly 26-year effort continues to transition from one of planning to operations, a clearer vision also is required of what the restoration can achieve amid constraints and changing conditions, the scientists said.

“We’ve hit our stride in getting projects constructed, to the point where they’re being operated. And also this report points out we’re beginning to see benefits on the ground,” said Steve Davis, chief science officer at the Everglades Foundation, an advocacy group. “This is a big, challenging undertaking, but with the progress that we’ve been seeing of late, we’re starting to see the benefits of Everglades restoration and we know this large-scale infrastructure can do what we intended.”

The mammoth restoration, envisioned as a 30- to 40-year effort, involves dozens of landscape-scale projects spanning central and south Florida, designed to revive the watershed that is responsible for the drinking water of millions of people. A series of historical attempts to drain the Everglades made modern Florida possible but led to a litany of environmental problems, such as harmful algae blooms that have sickened Floridians and left marine life belly-up. The National Academies, a private nonprofit organization, has provided biennial reports on the restoration’s progress since 2004, based on a congressional mandate.

The report said the pace of restoration has increased substantially over the past two years, reflecting the priority given to projects such as a massive reservoir under construction south of Lake Okeechobee that is the centerpiece of Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ environmental agenda. Seven Everglades restoration projects are complete, including reservoirs to the east and west of Lake Okeechobee designed to help address harmful flows of lake water that have contributed to some of the harmful algae blooms. South of the lake, the reservoir in the region called the Everglades Agricultural Area is scheduled for completion in 2029.

Benefits already are apparent, the report said. In Everglades National Park, dry season flows east of Taylor Slough have improved, although effects on salinity in fragile Florida Bay are difficult to discern. In Shark River Slough, flows have increased particularly during the dry season. In the Picayune Strand, the vegetation is transitioning from that of uplands to wetlands.

“We have to hit the water quality mark.”

But the report said scientific analysis of these benefits has not been consistent, hindering understanding of the restoration’s progress and opportunities for learning. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and South Florida Water Management District, federal and state agencies, respectively, oversee Everglades restoration. The Army Corps said it was working with state, tribal and institutional partners to review the report. The water management district said it was focused at the moment on a recent rain event that caused flooding in coastal areas in central and southeast Florida.

The National Academies also raised concerns about the loss of federal staff responsible for Endangered Species Act protections. The effort to rehydrate the river of grass threatens, for example, the Cape Sable seaside sparrow, an endangered ground-dwelling bird found in a remote area of Everglades National Park and the Big Cypress National Preserve. During nesting season some water control structures are closed to spare the sparrows, but this inhibits the flow of water and can flood tree islands that are important to the Miccosukee Tribe and a range of animal and plant life. Sea level rise has exacerbated the problem.

“It takes not only funding, but it takes staff to analyze these project reports. It takes staff to communicate to organizations like ours so we can provide stakeholder feedback,” said Casey Darling Kniffin, policy director at Friends of the Everglades, an advocacy group. “That requires staff at the federal level. So despite having record funding, if we don’t have the staff to carry out this work we will see delays going into the future of Everglades restoration.”

The report noted the restoration’s success depends on water quality. A new standard took effect this year called the Water Quality-Based Effluent Limitation, designed to measure nutrient pollution in the Everglades associated with fertilizer use on the sprawling sugar farms south of Lake Okeechobee. Before the EAA reservoir, characterized by DeSantis as the “crown jewel” of Everglades restoration, can operate at full capacity, the WQBEL must be met for at least five years. So far the standard has not been met, based on available data through water year 2025, the report said. (Water years are measured from May 1 to April 30.)

The scientists warned that if existing strategies are not enough to bring the water into compliance then “aggressive and possibly contentious new actions” likely will be necessary. The National Academies raised similar concerns in 2022 and 2024, concluding in 2022 that meeting the WQBEL by 2026 would be a “significant challenge.” Davis said the two most feasible options would be to reduce even further the pollution flowing from the sugar farms or expand the engineered wetlands called stormwater treatment areas designed to filter nutrient pollution from the water. Both propositions would be costly and politically thorny.

“We have to hit the water quality mark,” Davis said. “There is no compromise on that.”

The National Academies also said the definition of restoration success will need to evolve as the effects of sea level rise, invasive species and other factors are understood and the natural characteristics of the Everglades continue to reappear. The scientists noted that even after the massive effort is complete, the river of grass will remain highly managed and that the demands of urban development, water supply, flood control and legal requirements will exert pressure, along with climate change, peat loss, legacy nutrients and invasive species. The scientists called for better communication tools to help decision-makers weigh competing interests.

“The caveat to changing any of the restoration definitions would be that we would want to make sure that the science is influencing that process and not the political will and maybe the fatigue around Everglades restoration,” Kniffin said. “We have to be careful about changing the goal post just to claim victory on the plan without seeing the ecological benefits.”

The report comes at a pivotal moment for Everglades restoration. Under DeSantis’ leadership, the state has invested billions of dollars in the effort, even as his administration has faced widespread condemnation and federal litigation over Alligator Alcatraz, the migrant detention facility that operated for a year in the Everglades before closing this summer. DeSantis’ second term concludes in January, and Republican Byron Donalds was elected to succeed him. Like his predecessor, Donalds has vowed to make the river of grass a priority.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.title: The Trump Administration Praised a Georgia Manufacturer. Now the Company Is Suing the EPA.
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.author: By Phil McKenna
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.text:
In August 2025, Vice President JD Vance and Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin visited cold storage equipment manufacturer Alta Refrigeration to announce plans to roll back regulations the company opposed.

The EPA followed through in May, giving manufacturers of cold storage and other equipment several more years to continue selling devices that use hydrofluorocarbons with high global warming potential as refrigerants. Now, Georgia-based Alta and the Coalition for the Use of Safe and Efficient Refrigerants—an industry group also based in Georgia and chaired by Alta’s president—are suing the EPA and Zeldin, arguing that the agency did not go far enough.

The lawsuit shows how one company sought to push the Trump administration’s deregulatory agenda even further, revealing tensions between an EPA eager to roll back regulations and industry interests seeking yet more.The case is unfolding alongside a series of legal challenges to the agency’s actions, brought by a broad coalition of major industry groups representing air conditioning and equipment manufacturers, attorneys general from nearly two dozen states and an environmental group, all of whom contend the agency went too far.

The rollback and ensuing lawsuits stem from the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020, bipartisan legislation signed by President Donald Trump during his first term that mandated a gradual phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons. The chemical refrigerants are potent greenhouse gases, trapping heat in the atmosphere hundreds to thousands of times more effectively than carbon dioxide, pound for pound.

National industry groups supported both the legislation and a related international climate agreement, the Kigali Amendment, because the measures would help boost U.S. manufacturing jobs and exports. In 2023, the EPA issued a rule to help facilitate the required phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons.

The EPA’s May action extended the transition timeline, giving Alta and other manufacturers a five-year reprieve from requirements to use more climate-friendly refrigerants in new equipment. The agency said the delay would benefit companies and lower prices for American consumers. However, Alta wants a permanent reprieve, something it said the head of the EPA previously promised.

“Administrator Zeldin stated plainly that he intended to ‘give ALTA what it was asking for,’ the company argued in a document filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in September.

Before filing their lawsuit, Alta and the Coalition for the Use of Safe and Efficient Refrigerants petitioned the EPA to grant cold storage equipment manufacturers a permanent exemption from the hydrofluorocarbon phasedown. When the agency proposed a reprieve instead, Alta sought help to try to persuade the administration.

A declaration submitted by Alta President Eric Brown describes an exchange between Zeldin and a member of Georgia’s congressional delegation. The documents show screenshots of what appears to be Zeldin explaining that an act of Congress would be needed to make the rollback permanent.

The images show the request came from “Rep Buddy C.”, which may be U.S. Rep. Earl “Buddy” Carter (R-Georgia). Carter and Zeldin, a former U.S. representative from New York, served as colleagues and co-sponsored legislation during Zeldin’s tenure in Congress.

Citing the ongoing lawsuit, the EPA and Carter’s office both declined to comment.

Joseph Goffman, an EPA assistant administrator during the Biden administration who is not involved in the lawsuit, said Brown’s declaration “read as much like somebody throwing a tantrum as it did like a legal document” and praised Zeldin for “actually doing his job.”

Alta Refrigeration declined to comment.

Brown’s declaration said the EPA, through a member of Georgia’s congressional delegation, instructed him to withdraw comments Alta submitted to the White House Office of Management and Budget. Brown wrote that he did so “under duress.”

Goffman said he had never heard of the Office of Management and Budget asking for comments to be withdrawn because the White House disagreed with their content. Goffman said Zeldin’s decision not to permanently exempt Alta from the rule does not undo his earlier decision to give Alta and others a five-year reprieve, which Goffman said should never have been granted.

The industry groups that supported the hydrofluorocarbon phasedown and are now suing the EPA over the rule change represent more than 90 percent of residential and commercial heating, ventilation, air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment manufactured and sold in North America, along with more than 60,000 plumbing and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning professionals.

American companies invested heavily to transition to new technology to comply with the phasedown of climate pollutants, and the 2026 revision disrupted that without adequate explanation, the groups noted.

“It’s bad for the environment, bad for the economy, and it’s opposed by the bulk of the industry,” said David Doniger, a senior attorney and strategist for the Natural Resources Defense Council, the environmental organization that sued over the rule change. “It’s hard to think of something you could do that’s less popular or that does more harm and makes fewer friends than this.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.title: Can the Blue Wave Turn the Tide Against Border Wall Construction in Texas?
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.author: By Martha Pskowski
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.text:
EL PASO, Texas—Border communities voted in overwhelming numbers for Democratic candidates in the midterm elections last Tuesday.

Come January, every U.S. House member representing the U.S.-Mexico border—from San Diego to Brownsville—will be a Democrat. After a three-decade drought, Democrats swept all 18 statewide races in Texas.

Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa and Sen.-elect James Talarico were among the Democratic candidates who vowed to fight the border wall in Big Bend. Now comes the challenge of delivering on their campaign promises.

While Democrats chalked up major victories in the election, the Trump administration still has the funding and statutory authority to continue border wall construction through ecologically sensitive areas, including Big Bend. For more than a decade, Donald Trump has vowed to complete border wall construction from the Pacific to the Gulf of Mexico. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act turbocharged these efforts, appropriating $46.5 billion for border barriers.

Advocates on the border said in interviews that Democrats must seize the tools at their disposal to push back on border wall construction.

With majorities in the U.S. House and Senate, Democrats will have the authority to investigate Department of Homeland Security officials and compel them to provide contracts for border wall construction that have been confidential. In Austin, state legislators have already introduced bills for the upcoming session, when Democrats will control the state House for the first time in 24 years, to prohibit border wall construction in state parks. Incoming Texas Land Commissioner Ben Flores, a Democrat, told Inside Climate News he would not grant access to land managed by his office in the Big Bend sector for border wall construction.

“There is a renewed sense of hope and optimism,” said Martin Castro, watershed science director at the Rio Grande International Study Center in Laredo. “We had been telling landowners to please hold out until the midterms to potentially turn the tide against this project.”

Castro is part of a coalition opposing border wall construction in Laredo and surrounding communities, including landowners who are fighting construction on their property. He hopes incoming state officials will help landowners defend their private property rights.

Border wall construction, halted under former President Joe Biden, resumed and expanded to new areas after Trump returned to office last year. In February, DHS waived dozens of federal laws to fast-track construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, setting off a national outcry. Texans have spoken out against construction in the remote region that includes Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park and numerous privately owned tracts.

An injunction temporarily paused construction in the Big Bend sector last month. But the Supreme Court overturned that injunction Monday, allowing construction to resume. Elsewhere in Texas, contractors have continued working in the El Paso area, South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley to close gaps in the wall and line the Rio Grande with buoys.

While Democrats will hold a majority in the Texas House, Republicans will retain control of the Senate. But some Texas Republicans have spoken out against the wall in Big Bend, opening the possibility for bipartisan action.

On Monday, the first day to file bills for the upcoming legislative session, state Rep. Eddie Morales (D-Eagle Pass) and Sen. César Blanco (D-El Paso) introduced companion bills that would prohibit border security infrastructure on state park property. They both represent the Big Bend region.

Several Texas state parks are in the planned path of the border wall, including Big Bend Ranch, Seminole Canyon and Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley. Federal officials have already sought access to these parks for the wall, as reported by Inside Climate News.

Outside the parks, the border wall is slated to cross large swaths of land in West Texas managed by the Texas General Land Office. Land Commissioner-elect Flores previously told Inside Climate News that he would not voluntarily authorize border wall construction on GLO land and is “prepared for a prolonged legal battle.”

If Texas were to block construction on state park or GLO land, the federal government would have to condemn the property to proceed with the project. Condemnation would undoubtedly stall any construction plans.

In Washington, Democrats will hold the majority in the House and Senate and have vowed to take on corruption in the Trump administration. Advocates are urging them to weave the border wall into this broader effort. Talarico has called the border wall in Big Bend “a monument to corruption” and questioned billion-dollar no bid contracts.

DHS waived contracting and procurement laws in every border sector, allowing the agency to rapidly issue contracts for billions of dollars without going out for bids.

Castro, of the Rio Grande International Study Center, said that the sweeping authority DHS has to issue waivers under the 2005 Real ID Act must be reexamined.

“The waiver authority is so far-reaching that, until that goes away, the threat to these communities is never going to go away,” he said. “Can we work with a bipartisan delegation on the repeal of the waivers?”

Adam Isacson, an analyst at the Washington Office on Latin America, said that with Democrats leading the House and Senate Committees on Homeland Security come January, they could investigate these contracts.

“Transparency is where the Democrats have the biggest short-term power right now,” Isacson said. “[The contracts] could technically be legal. But they could be very embarrassing.”

Scott Nicol, an artist who has long documented border wall construction in the Rio Grande Valley, said Democrats should investigate why the cost per mile of border wall construction has skyrocketed.

“That speaks to how opaque this administration is,” he said. “Congress should be able to say, ‘We gave you this money, now what have you done with it?’”

The midterms also brought a shakeup to congressional districts on the border. The Big Bend region will now be represented by a Democrat in the House, after Katy Padilla Stout flipped Congressional District 23, which stretches from San Antonio to El Paso. Republican Tony Gonzales held the seat until he stepped down in April.

Padilla Stout, a former teacher and attorney, won an unexpected victory over her Republican opponent, Brandon Herrera, a pro-gun influencer on YouTube. Both candidates had spoken out against the wall.

After news broke on Monday that construction could resume in Big Bend, Padilla Stout vowed to continue fighting the wall.

“This is not a Republican or Democrat issue,” she said in a press release. “This is an example of corrupt Washington politicians refusing to listen to our border communities.”

Laiken Jordahl is a national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, which brought the lawsuit challenging the border wall in Big Bend that reached the Supreme Court. He urged Democrats to restrict appropriations funding to prohibit construction in Big Bend.

Without a super-majority, Democrats would either need to get Trump’s signature or tie the restrictions to must-pass legislation. A similar effort failed earlier this year, while Democrats were the minority party.

Congress passed similar restrictions during the first Trump administration, when U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Laredo) obtained carveouts prohibiting border wall construction in areas including Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge. Cuellar was re-elected last week and serves on the powerful House Appropriations Committee.

Jordahl said that advocates will use both the legal system and public pressure to keep the spotlight on the border wall.

“Everyone across the entire Big Bend region will be watching if a single bulldozer moves,” he said. “The people of Texas have spoken so clearly to reject this project.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.title: Senate Advances Permitting Overhaul But Roadblocks Loom
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.author: By Marianne Lavelle, Dan Gearino
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.text:
The Senate voted Monday to advance long-sought bipartisan legislation to speed permitting of big energy projects, amid acrimony over whether the bill’s support for clean energy will be overwhelmed by the fossil fuel industry’s expansion plans.

Less than a week after Democrats’ overwhelming victory in the midterm elections, the party’s incumbents were divided over the measure. Republicans propelled the 73-25 vote to get the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA, over the first in a series of parliamentary hurdles. It means the current Congress, one of the least productive in the past 40 years, will have a chance to reshape energy project decision-making in the United States before the GOP surrenders the reins of leadership.

The legislation is an attempt to streamline the rules and regulations that have increased over the past 70 years, hindering the nation’s ability to build infrastructure rapidly. High-voltage transmission lines, crucial for delivery of clean energy, take 10 years on average to build. The issue has become more urgent as electricity demand surges, in part due to the proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers.

After years of effort, proponents of clean energy and fossil fuel energy struck a compromise that they say will get projects moving while protecting communities.

But the bill still faces challenges.

Some Democratic senators who voted for cloture, thereby limiting debate on the bill, made clear they will work to amend the measure to ensure that it does not erode the rights of Native American tribal nations to make decisions on projects that affect their lands. But any changes to the legislation risk losing Republican support. And the bill still must pass the House, where Republicans have a slimmer majority and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has already voiced opposition.

Perhaps the wildest card is President Donald Trump, who even while the Senate vote was underway, denounced wind energy. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser,” he said during an impromptu news conference.

Despite his opposition to wind energy, Trump praised the legislation as “a great bill that’s supposed to be bipartisan.”

“We are behind it 100 percent,” Trump said.

Afterward, the legislation’s co-author, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), released a statement making clear that Democrats could withdraw their support if the president’s war against renewable energy continues. “As I have said all along, the ultimate success of this bill depends on the Trump administration getting wind turbines up and spinning to get affordable energy on the grid, and we still need to make progress on that front before final passage,” he said.

The deep divisions over the measure reflect how much permitting reform has become a referendum on the chief weapon the environmental movement has used thus far in the drive to curb climate change: the power to block fossil fuel projects, mainly through lawsuits.

Not only has that approach failed to reduce U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, it has also been turned against clean energy projects and the transmission lines they need to deliver renewables from remote wind farms and solar arrays to population centers. Proponents of the bill argue that it is time to discard defensive environmentalism and turn instead to a strong offense—leveraging the power of low-cost wind, solar and storage to propel a transition.

Since unveiling the permitting deal before the election, Whitehouse, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, has sought to reassure fellow advocates of climate action that the legislation would remove roadblocks that have limited clean energy expansion.

“This bill is the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” Whitehouse said in a news conference just prior to the vote. “We look forward to accomplishing big things with our big Democratic majorities.”

But many environmentalists hoped that the Senate would fail to reach the 60-vote threshold, allowing the huge Democratic majority in the next Congress to rewrite the legislation wholesale. Opponents’ biggest concern are provisions that make it more difficult for state and tribal governments to stop oil and gas pipelines and other infrastructure projects through lawsuits and environmental review.

“This bill was shaped by the very industries that have spent decades damaging our health, exploiting our resources, and putting our futures at risk,” said Mar Zepeda Salazar, legislative director at Climate Justice Alliance, after the vote.

One major fossil fuel industry proponent, Williams Companies, even had advocates in the Senate this year: Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), former chief executive of the pipeline company, and the staff he brought on. He said the legislation was his top priority when Oklahoma’s governor appointed him to fill a Senate vacancy in March.

And yet, the measure had overwhelming support from the clean energy industry, which has been stymied by backlogs in permitting and connections to the electric transmission grid.

The Senate vote “is a critical step toward modernizing our outdated permitting process and getting ready-to-build clean energy projects moving,” said Frank Macchiarola, chief advocacy officer for the American Clean Power Association, in a statement.

While most climate and environmental groups oppose the bill, several prominent ones urged the Senate to support the initial vote, including the Environmental Defense Fund and Evergreen Action.

“In our judgment, the trade-offs right now, as they exist in the bill, are a risk-to-reward proposition that we are willing to take,” said Pete Wyckoff, Evergreen Action’s vice president of policy, in an interview.

Wyckoff said Evergreen’s support is based on an optimistic view that governors, future Congresses and presidents will do more work to promote renewable energy and reduce carbon dioxide emissions, and that clean energy will win in the market if given a chance. And it’s an acknowledgement that current legal tools to stop fossil fuel development aren’t effective enough and are now being “weaponized,” he said, to stop wind farms and other clean projects.

“What we need is a very, very rapid buildout towards clean” energy, Wyckoff said.

The legislation’s supporters favored a vote in the lame-duck session of the current Congress, doubting that the Democratic-led Congress taking office next year could craft a bill that Trump would sign.

Several studies have shown that wind, solar and battery storage would increase if the current legislation passes. Economic modeling indicates the bill would save ratepayers by bringing more low-cost supply to the electric grid. The Center for Climate and Energy Solutions estimates $2.5 billion in annual savings on residential electricity bills. The bill’s authors also included provisions that would require new data centers to cover their own energy costs.

“This is a real downpayment on the affordability agenda that was so much on Americans’ minds when they went to the polls last Tuesday,” Whitehouse said on the Senate floor.

But Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), who is in line to be chairman of the Senate Environment and Works Committee in the new Congress, said the bill could make it easier to build more data centers powered by on-site natural gas plants. And he noted that by making it easier to build natural gas pipelines to transport the fuel overseas as LNG, the legislation’s overall impact could mean greater greenhouse gas emissions.

“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels,” Merkley said in a statement before he voted against moving forward with the legislation.

Prior to the vote, the bill’s co-sponsors amended the bill to respond to some of the concerns environmental advocates raised about the initial version. Many of the objections focused on the “permit certainty” provisions in the original bill, which limit the federal government’s ability to stop a project after it receives initial approval. Critics said this part of the legislation would make it difficult for a future president to oppose fossil fuel projects.

Earthjustice, an advocacy group, released an analysis of the amended bill, saying that while it “provides some meaningful improvements, it fails to address very serious concerns.” The group praised some of the changes to permit certainty, but said the amendment as a whole fails to solve the core problem, which is that the legislation “gives the Trump administration very broad authority to fast-track harmful projects.”

Among the changes, the amendment revises the “look-back period” that establishes the baseline of past trends for determining if the government is treating a project arbitrarily or differently from others. Under the initial bill, the period was five years, which meant the next president would deal with a baseline set almost entirely by the Trump administration. Under the amendment, the baseline is 10 years.

Other changes the co-authors made addressed concerns Tribal nations raised about erosion of their ability to challenge projects, under the National Historic Preservation Act, for their impact on historically or culturally important sites. Some Democrats who voted to advance the legislation, including Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada and Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii, said they want to see further changes before voting for final passage. Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, who was just elected governor of New Mexico and the first Native American woman governor in the country, said she remains opposed to the bill in its revised form.

The legislation, expected to generate tens of thousands of jobs by eliminating hurdles for construction projects, had overwhelming support from labor unions. During the vote, one of the bill’s co-authors, Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), the ranking member of the Senate Energy Committee, wore his late father’s lapel pin honoring his 60 years of service as a utility laborer with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. “BAAJA will create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, good-paying jobs that workers can be certain will be around to support their families through a project’s completion,” Heinrich said before the vote.

Heinrich, who is in line to take over as chairman of the Senate Energy Committee in the new Congress, acknowledged that the bill was “not perfect,” but was a necessary compromise to ensure the nation can build the infrastructure it needs and lower energy costs.

“We had to find common ground,” he said.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.title: COP31 Meets the Overshoot Era
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.author: By Kate Waxman
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.text:
Yesterday, delegates from about 200 countries arrived in Antalya, a resort city on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, for the 31st United Nations climate summit. It is the first “Conference of Parties” or “COP” to open since the UN’s own scientists said, in effect, that we’ve missed a key target for holding climate change in check.

Last month, the UN Environment Programme’s annual Emissions Gap Report concluded that warming will overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, the limit that countries agreed to aim for in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid the worst climate impacts. Its best-case scenario now peaks at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees around mid-century, before drifting back down by 2100. That scenario requires global emissions to fall 45 percent below 2025 levels by 2035. Shocker: They’re not falling 45 percent by then.

If the world is going to miss its warming target anyway, why keep showing up? Delegates could skip two weeks of indoor negotiations and enjoy the Turkish Riviera. Right?

Wrong. Annually at COP, nearly every country negotiates three things by consensus: how fast to cut emissions, how to adapt to impacts already here and who pays for both. Much of the money on the table at COP31 doesn’t pay for curtailing emissions. It helps vulnerable countries brace for floods and heat waves and recover when they hit. Overshoot means more of both, so the bill goes up every year.

Every tenth of a degree above 1.5 C can lead to more floods, heat waves and failed harvests. A UN report released Wednesday found that even if rich countries meet last year’s call to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035, that would only bring in $85 billion to $120 billion a year. Developing countries need an estimated $305 billion annually, Climate Home News reports.

UK climate minister Katie White told Carbon Brief the latest science is “really scary.” Asked about the cut to its climate finance for developing countries, she acknowledged the money falls short of what’s needed and pointed to new financing tools, such as Brazil’s proposed rainforest fund. The fund was developed to help guide countries to halt and reverse deforestation by 2030.

Developing countries have heard this before. India’s environment minister, Bhupender Yadav, has said India will push for “predictable” climate finance and technology transfer in Antalya. During the pre-summit talks in Fiji last month, he put it more plainly: If developing countries are asked to cut emissions faster, that ambition should be “matched by climate finance,” technology and training.

In other words, the overshoot era is not a reason to spend less. It’s the invoice for having spent too little.

The cheapest idea on the table: Electricity. Turkey is asking countries to sign a voluntary pledge to raise electricity’s share of global energy use to 35 percent by 2035, up from just over 20 percent today. China, the world’s largest emitter, signaled its support in October. It’s an easy yes for a country whose electricity share is already near 30 percent.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister running the negotiations at COP, has experience with electrifying energy: Since July, Australia has required retailers in three states to offer households three free hours of power at midday, when rooftop solar floods the grid. However, the pledge doesn’t require clean power. And Australia keeps approving coal and gas projects. Current policies get the world to only 28 percent, per Climate Action Tracker

And more: The summit’s mascot is the loggerhead sea turtle. Antalya built a pavilion in the shape of one. Loggerheads are living thermometers: the sex of sea turtle hatchlings is determined by sand temperatures. Warmer sand produces more females. As delegates debate who pays for overshoot, the host’s mascot has already started paying, one generation of disproportionate populations at a time.

But hey, at least the COP31 site has a tropical butterfly garden! The president of COP31, Murat Kurum, said that “we’re fluttering wings towards a green future.”

Last week’s midterms handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress, a batch of new statehouse trifectas and even the Texas governor’s mansion. That gives them a real shot at slowing President Donald Trump’s climate rollbacks.

Here are some stories that stood out beyond the elections:

Bob Berwyn has been reporting on COPs for more than 10 years, since the Paris Agreement was signed in 2015. He’s been attending them in person since 2022. Last week, he reported on how the scientific organization COP relies on to guide their decisions is short on funds. I asked him about what is in store for this year’s summit, and if any solutions will actually come out of it.

KATE WAXMAN: What was the first day of COP31 like?

BOB BERWYN: One of the things we heard this morning was that right now, as of today, the global average temperature is more than two degrees Celsius or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit above the pre-industrial average. And as at every COP,  [there are] very clear warnings that this is a huge danger for communities, for ecosystems, and that the folks who are here to talk about this should really figure out a way to get a grip on it.

WAXMAN: What’s been the energy like from the crowd?

BERWYN: Some people, I think, are just optimistic. All the people that are here in good faith want to do something. They want to reach some kind of agreement, whether it’s more finance to protect forests or to help developing countries with the extreme climate impacts that they’re facing, and the challenge is really when all those 195 countries are in the same room is to get them to agree.

WAXMAN: What do you think is going to be the outcome?

BERWYN: I don’t expect any new major agreements. I think my biggest hope is that the process doesn’t completely fall apart. In a best-case outcome, I would hope that there are subsets of countries working on agreements or on ways to tackle this, where you don’t need every single country’s agreement.

WAXMAN: What would you say has been the biggest thing that you’ve learned from reporting on COPs throughout the years?

BERWYN: In the context of the ultimate goal, which is to limit warming so that more people don’t get hurt and killed by extreme climate impacts, the main thing I’ve learned is that I think each country needs to really look at itself. I think we’re really at a point where we’re realizing that we’re probably never going to get a binding agreement that would specify or mandate each country to do something. So it’s really up to national governments, to people in countries, to make it happen in their own countries, and then to somehow bring that all together under this international umbrella.

WAXMAN: Do you have a story from reporting on COPs that really sticks out in your brain?

BERWYN: The COP in Egypt in Sharm El-Sheikh. It went two days into overtime because of discussions about loss and damage, but all the food stands closed down. I was wandering around, and I looked outside and I saw a group of people sitting around eating and laughing and I poked my head out to say hi; it was a group of workers at the COP, local workers who had their own barbecue set up. They were cooking rice and skewers, and they invited me and a couple of other people to eat with them. We had a great conversation outside of any formal negotiations. We were all just waiting for the closed negotiations to finish. I’m still in touch with one of the people that I met out there. He lives in Alexandria, Egypt, and went to Sharm El-Sheikh to work at the conference. And we still exchange messages occasionally, especially around the time of COP each year, we check in. It’s little things like that that I think make it a human experience too.

The aftermath of the Maui fires: The road to recovery after the Lahaina fires three years ago has been arduous. My colleague Keerti Gopal reported on a wildfire exposure study that found elevated levels of heavy metals linked to heart and lung problems and cancer risk in a group of more than 1,200 survivors, and a family that has finally started to rebuild after the devastating fires. Listen to the latest episode of Inside Climate to hear more about Keerti’s reporting.

Why it matters: The costs of a climate disaster keep piling up for years after the fire is out. That’s the kind of loss and damage COP31 is arguing over who pays for.

The loss and damage fund: The UN’s loss and damage fund voted to set aside $20 million for Nepal, where flooding killed some 1,500 people earlier this year, Nicholas Kusnetz reports for ICN. It’s the first time the fund has moved in direct response to a climate disaster. Still, the money would cover less than 1 percent of Nepal’s estimated $2.69 billion in initial losses.

Why it matters: It’s the overshoot bill in miniature. One hundred and nineteen countries have asked the fund for a total of $2.8 billion, but its first funding round has only about $350 million to hand out.

Osprey populations declining: Chesapeake Bay ospreys just had their worst breeding season on record, and scientists and the fishing industry disagree about why, Aman Azhar and Johnny Sturgeon report for ICN. Researchers point to a shortage of menhaden, a small fish the birds depend on. The industry says poor breeding numbers don’t prove commercial fishing is to blame.

Why it matters: Ospreys’ health is an early warning for the bay’s food web, and the fight over what’s starving them is really a fight over who gets the fish.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.title: Why the World Is Still Running on Fossil Fuels After 30 Years of Climate Talks
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.author: By Bob Berwyn
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10112.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—The stench of fossil fuels has become a hallmark of the United Nations “Conference of the Parties” climate talks, starting with the airplanes and buses carrying delegates to the conferences.

Two annual meetings have been held in Poland, where coal remains king. Eye-searing petrochemical smog marred the skies over Dubai at COP28. In Baku, Azerbaijan, most buildings are coated with gray grime from refinery pollution, and last year at the “Nature COP” in Belém, Brazil, hundreds of diesel generators ran day and night outside the conference halls in a futile effort to cool the heavy tropical air.

The latest iteration of the negotiations, COP31, opened Monday here with diesel fumes in the city’s busy streets providing another reminder that the world remains deeply dependent on the fossil fuels driving the climate crisis even after three decades of climate negotiations.

The backdrop to this year’s conference is bleak. Scientists report that the average global temperature has reached a record high of more than 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit (2 degrees Celsius) above the preindustrial baseline in the last few days. Several dozen glaciers have disappeared since last year’s talks. Rising seas are flooding coastal cities. And carbon dioxide emissions in 2026 are on track to reach another record high.

The climate crisis didn’t reach this point overnight, said Marc Hudson, an unaffiliated climate researcher in the United Kingdom. It is the culmination of decades of missed opportunities, political compromises and broken promises. Understanding how it happened requires revisiting a surreal and occasionally absurd history, he said.

A convenient starting point is 1957, when scientists from around the world shared research and met repeatedly to study Earth as a system, rather than individual components, as part of the International Geophysical Year. It was also when American scientist Charles Keeling began developing a system to measure the rise of CO2 in the global atmosphere, and when a landmark research paper challenged the assumption that the oceans could absorb CO2 emissions from fossil fuel burning.

It’s clear from the scientific record, Hudson said, that researchers understood the looming problem nearly 70 years ago.

But the issue did not appear on political radar screens until 1985, when scientists at an international climate conference in Austria warned that rising CO2 levels could produce climate warming greater than any in human history, with significant consequences for agriculture, ecosystems and people.

The researchers urged governments to start considering policy responses. A few years later, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was born. In 1990, the panel issued its first major climate assessment, spurring the United Nations to action.

Representatives from more than 140 countries spent 15 months negotiating the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. At that point, about 10 industrialized countries were responsible for about 80 percent of all historic CO2 emissions. There was broad agreement that those nations should take the lead in reducing climate-altering pollution and that any treaty should not deny poorer countries the chance to develop.

That disagreement remains one of the defining features of climate diplomacy, and the United States has been central to that debate since the beginning, Hudson said. George H.W. Bush, a former fossil-fuel industry executive, was president, and he was “even more sympathetic than the Democrats to big auto, big oil,” Hudson said. The Bush administration feared that the international community would mobilize against carbon dioxide emissions in much the same way it had against ozone depletion just a few years earlier.

France and a few other European countries pushed for a treaty that would obligate rich, industrialized countries to set timetables for emission cuts, but it was “very important for the Americans and the Saudis and the Gulf oil and gas exporters that whatever deal emerged from an international negotiating process was as weak as possible,” Hudson said. Bush threatened to boycott the 1992 Rio Earth Summit if a treaty included binding language on emissions cuts.

The French and other proponents of emissions-reduction targets had to choose between pressing ahead with a strong treaty that the U.S. wouldn’t sign or watering down the agreement to secure American support.

“This was straightforward, naked power politics,” Hudson said. “The Americans and the Saudis wanted to make sure that they could keep on selling and using fossil fuels for as long as they wanted, and they didn’t want to have to negotiate on actual emissions reductions.”

In the final weeks of negotiations for the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change agreement, references to binding cuts were removed from the draft and the U.S. became an early signatory because it was “no longer worried about what was becoming a toothless agreement,” and setting the stage for the first Conference of the Parties, COP1, in Berlin, Hudson said.

The climate framework was vague, but it included an agreement to try to stabilize emissions at 1990 levels. Most people involved in the talks hoped a more detailed agreement with timetables and national plans would soon follow, said Joanna Depledge, a climate diplomacy researcher at the University of Cambridge.

Most probably never would have believed that emissions would still be increasing 30 years later, she added.

The early international steps toward tackling global warming came after the end of the Cold War, as former adversaries sought to cooperate, she said.
