The United States’ role was complicated and essential, especially given the country’s scientific leadership at the time, she said. “It had the tech, the computer and the meteorological observations, and was also a leader in politics.” And while the U.S. played hardball in the talks, it compromised to become part of the U.N. framework agreement, she said.

But then, as now, she added, the U.S. was reluctant to accept an agreement that would put the onus on developed countries to reduce emissions first and was reluctant to assume any financial obligations toward developing countries. This worldview has continued shaping the climate talks for 30 years.

At COP1 in Berlin in 1995, delegates acknowledged that the U.N.’s climate framework alone would not solve the emerging global warming problem, so they agreed to keep meeting to reach a follow-up deal with quantifiable emission-reduction targets for industrialized countries. Since then, the 198 countries party to the climate framework have met 29 more times to try and implement those basic ideas.

Just two years later, the Kyoto Protocol, with obligatory emissions reductions for industrialized countries, was adopted at COP3. But just before the conference, the U.S. Senate passed the Byrd-Hagel Resolution by a vote of 95–0, declaring that it would not ratify an agreement on emissions cuts that did not require similar commitments from developing countries, or that would harm the U.S. economy.

President Bill Clinton signed the agreement in 1998, which may have been a high-water mark for U.S. engagement in the process, at least until the Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015, Depledge said. But Clinton never sent it to the Senate.

In 2001, his successor, President George W. Bush, said the U.S. would not ratify the Kyoto Protocol, taking momentum away from the global push to curb global warming.

It took several years for the world to regain traction after that decision, but at COP15 in 2009, India, South Africa, China, Brazil, Indonesia and Mexico—all developing countries with rapidly growing economies and rising emissions—were on the verge of making emissions pledges, which would have been a huge step forward, Depledge said. But the potential breakthrough faltered, as developing countries felt pressured to sign a deal they thought could slow their economic development.

The next several rounds of climate talks were marked by excruciatingly slow, incremental progress that eventually led to the Paris Agreement at COP 21.

Under the pact, all countries agreed to try to limit warming by making voluntary emissions cuts based on their own national circumstances. They also agreed to an international reporting scheme to help track progress. The agreement also spelled out that wealthy, developed countries should cut emissions first and should support developing countries with finance and technology.

Since the 2015 climate pact was adopted in Paris, the annual talks have focused on implementing the agreement’s goals, and the process has clearly bogged down, especially since COP26 in Glasgow.

“I would say it’s been a very depressing backtracking and souring of global climate politics,” Depledge said. In particular, she added, Saudi Arabia has been disrupting the process “in ways we haven’t seen for a while, and I think that the Trump presidency gives them free rein to do that.”

Depledge says that, after decades of studying the U.N. climate talks, she sees three main reasons for the slow progress. First is the continuing divide between developed and developing countries along with additional fragmentation within the latter group. Economic and legal tension over who is responsible and who will pay for the damage has become “deeply entrenched in the climate regime” in a way that’s detrimental to progress.

She said this may be because the United Nations General Assembly, a political body, launched the climate discussions. Had the climate talks been initiated by the World Meteorological Organization or the United Nations Environment Programme, they might have been seen as more technical and less politically controversial.

A close second to the “North-South economic divide” are the strategic actions of the fossil fuel lobbies, both behind the scenes and in public discourse, she said. “And by definition, they have tremendous power because, hey, we all use oil and gas. And they have been extraordinarily successful in keeping progress slow.”

The third big hurdle, she said, is the consensus-based approach used in the U.N. climate talks because every major decision requires consensus for approval. The convention’s failure to adopt a voting rule has blocked more ambitious decisions, especially those related to the underlying science. Such decisions could have been much stronger over the past 30 years if a majority of countries could outvote the handful of blocking countries, she said.

https://grist.org/politics/how-trump-pla.title: How Trump plans to fast-track mining in Montana
https://grist.org/politics/how-trump-pla.author: Ellis Juhlin
https://grist.org/politics/how-trump-pla.text:
Over the past 20 months, the Trump administration has rolled back regulations and issued executive orders aimed at unilaterally speeding up industrial development projects. In true bureaucratic fashion, even attempts to cut red tape come with a litany of acronyms you may have never heard of. Take, for instance, “FAST-41.”

Title 41 of FAST-41, or the Fixing America’s Surface Transportation Act, was originally passed under former President Barack Obama in 2015. It was created as a mechanism to streamline federal review for approval of large-scale infrastructure projects, and improve the public’s access to any permits and documents produced as part of federal review. Infrastructure projects can only be added to the FAST-41 list if they fall under federal review with the National Environmental Policy Act and meet certain size requirements.

In a July 2025 executive order, Trump expanded the definition of critical infrastructure projects eligible to be covered under the FAST-41 process to include artificial intelligence data centers. “My Administration will utilize federally owned land and resources for the expeditious and orderly development of data centers,” the directive reads. “This usage will be done in a manner consistent with the land’s intended purpose — to be used in service of the prosperity and security of the American people.”

FAST-41 shares similarities with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, the permitting bill that passed the Senate this week. That legislation would overhaul environmental regulations like the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act, and change judicial review, with the goal of expediting the permitting process for projects to go from proposals to shovels in the ground more quickly. If the bill passes the House as written, its changes would be applied to all infrastructure permitting projects. FAST-41, unlike BAAJA, does not change existing environmental statutes and only applies to projects listed under the policy.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Reforming the permitting process has increasingly evolved into a bipartisan issue. Lawmakers on both sides have said the lengthy process stalls economic development. New Mexico Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich, one of the BAAJA sponsors, has said the current permitting process particularly hurts transmission expansion and renewable energy projects at a time when those are most needed, and has attributed those setbacks to continued higher energy costs. But depending on the type of project, expanding development can also mean driving up planet-warming emissions. The Natural Resources Defense Council has warned that BAAJA, in its current draft, could “benefit fossil fuel, mining, data center, and other industrial projects more than clean energy.” The environmental nonprofit has also said the bill would limit regulatory oversight of the environmental harms associated with development.

FAST-41 established a dashboard where anyone can view a project’s timelines, required actions by federal agencies, and the status of environmental review and permits. It is overseen by what’s often referred to as the Permitting Council, made up of representatives from 15 federal agencies. There are two categories for projects listed under FAST-41. The first is a “covered” listing, which means a project will receive expedited processes, including a set permitting timeline that federal agencies must comply with and being assigned a project coordinator to carry the project through the review process. The second is a “transparency” listing, which essentially creates a one-stop shop for a project on the FAST-41 dashboard. It’s a centralized location with information on permitting documents.

In late October, Montana became the 11th state to enter into an agreement with the Permitting Council, which oversees FAST-41. This means the federal government will help the state to identify infrastructure projects eligible for a FAST-41 designation — now including those that aid the development of data centers, like the mining of rare earth elements — provide resources to state agencies through the permitting process, and include state-level permitting actions and timelines on the federal transparency dashboard. Montana has a long-standing history of mining and other extractive industries. Some industry groups, like the Montana Mining Association, see this new state-federal collaboration on FAST-41 as an industry win.

Alaska, Idaho, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Missouri, Tennessee, Louisiana, Georgia, and Iowa had all previously signed agreements as well. This is the first time in FAST-41’s history that these kinds of federal-state agreements have occurred. Given the novelty of this kind of collaboration, it remains to be seen how much say any given state could have in selecting projects for FAST-41 listing, or how expedited the timeline may be when state and federal permitting are happening in tandem.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

When Montana Governor Greg Gianforte signed the official memorandum of understanding with the Permitting Council, he said, “This MOU will ensure that critical infrastructure projects avoid unnecessary roadblocks after completion of federal and state environmental review processes. This is especially important for energy infrastructure.”

According to Adrian Van Rythoven, an associate professor with Montana Tech’s Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology, FAST-41 establishes clarity and certainty in the process, which is beneficial for businesses like publicly traded mineral-exploration companies. “Capital markets like having timelines,” he said, adding that timelines build investor confidence and ensure more money flows toward mineral development.

The effort to make it easier to begin a mining project in Montana comes alongside sweeping changes to bedrock environmental policies and how mining projects are permitted on federal lands. There are currently three mining or mining exploration projects in the state with a “transparency” designation: the Sheep Creek Project, Blue Copper, and the Stillwater Mine.

But ultimately, Van Rythoven said, it remains to be seen if this new MOU between Montana and the Permitting Council would speed things up. He pointed to the extensive personnel and resources required to process applications.

“The scientists, the legal experts that work initially at the federal government, now perhaps the state government with this MOU, if those resources of human time, money, etc., aren’t made available to process these applications, it’ll be transparently slow.”

But for others, the partnership leaves more questions than answers. “I think there’s room for a lot of political interference, ignoring state law, and cutting the public out of the process,” said Derf Johnson, Deputy Director of the Montana Environmental Information Center. “I wonder how this MOU will conflict with Montanans’ right to know.”

Johnson supports improved transparency and said the dashboard is a useful site where the public can access information about a project. But he fears the agreement could allow projects to be prioritized based on the wishes of elected officials and political appointees rather than true merit for critical infrastructure. Montana has explicit constitutional protections for a “clean and healthy environment” and a robust state-level review process; Johnson said he hopes an agreement like this would not skirt any of the state’s own policies.

“I’m worried about projects receiving this designation in the age of corruption that we live in,” he said.

https://grist.org/culture/tesla-cybertru.title: The Cybertruck era is over, but America’s electric truck experiment isn’t
https://grist.org/culture/tesla-cybertru.author: Kate Yoder
https://grist.org/culture/tesla-cybertru.text:
After barely three years on the road, Tesla is planning to kick the Cybertruck to the curb after flagging sales. Elon Musk announced on Friday that the company would wind down production next year to make room for the production of Cybercabs, the robot taxis Tesla hopes will reshape transportation.

In its short lifespan, the Cybertruck managed to become a top candidate for the most polarizing vehicle on the road — ever. Critics called it a “MAGA hat on wheels” and compared it to a dumpster — a resemblance that may have fooled some hungry raccoons that once chewed on the vehicle’s rear vault. It’s already being declared “one of the greatest flops in automotive history,” on par with Ford’s 1957 Edsel. But the polygonal, supposedly bulletproof truck did appeal to a certain demographic.

“It’s the kind of vehicle, as a kid, you imagine for the future,” said Dan Krassner, executive director of the American EV Jobs Alliance, an advocacy organization working to end the partisan divide over electric vehicles. He’s a Republican and a wrestling fan, and noted that some of his favorite pro wrestlers drove Cybertrucks, including the married WWE superstars Seth Rollins and Becky Lynch, along with The Miz and Liv Morgan (though the latter has said it was the “worst investment” she ever made).

Weeks before the Cybertruck rolled out in late 2023, Musk told investors that Tesla would sell 250,000 vehicles a year. But it never came close: Last year, it sold just over 20,000. It’s the latest sign that the attempt to make EVs macho is falling flat, after Ford announced last December that its F-150 Lightning pickup truck, the all-electric version of the country’s most popular vehicle, would be discontinued since it was a money-loser. Sales of Rivian’s electric pickup have been sliding downward each year since 2023; they have also dropped sharply for GMC’s Hummer EV, which was dubbed “the worst-selling pickup truck of 2026.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Automakers have long tried to shed the saintly, environmentally friendly image of the Toyota Prius, and this shift to big, aggressive electric trucks was an effort to appeal to traditional American pickup buyers. But they not only had to contend with conservatives’ hesitations about EVs, they also had to persuade a public increasingly worried about the cost of living to overcome sticker shock, to fork over thousands more, if not tens of thousands more, to buy an electric pickup instead of a gas-powered one. A comparable gas-powered Ford pickup starts at $52,000, about $11,000 less than the Lightning did before Ford discontinued it.

“The first electric trucks weren’t priced for the people who buy trucks, and buyers still have fair questions about charging and towing,” Krassner said. “You know, macho advertising can’t fix the monthly payment.”

The starting price for the 2026 Tesla Cybertruck was just raised to $92,500, and the cheapest Hummer EV is $97,200. Full-size electric pickup trucks need very large batteries to deliver the range and towing capabilities that truck buyers want, leading to higher prices, Krassner said.

But cheaper models are on the way. Ford’s upcoming electric pickup truck coming next year, the Fathom, will be priced starting at $28,400 — well below the price of the average gas-powered pickup. Meanwhile, now that the F-150 Lightning is out of production, with used models going for 50 percent off the sticker price, it’s “selling like hotcakes,” according to the transportation news site Electrek.

“As the electric trucks are more comparable in price to gas trucks, we expect them to be a superior product and be popular with Americans,” Krassner said.

There’s still a large partisan divide on electric vehicles: Roughly half of all new EV registrations in the U.S. from 2012 to 2023 went to the 10 percent most Democratic counties, according to a study from the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Because electric trucks performed better in Republican-leaning areas — though not as well as Tesla and Ford had hoped — the researchers suggested they could still be a way to broaden EV adoption. And some of Republicans’ resistance to electric vehicles has begun to ease, Krassner said. The share of Republicans who agree that EVs are “for people who see the world differently than I do” fell from 59 percent in November 2023 to 49 percent in November 2025, according to polling from EVs for All America.

As the Cybertruck’s production comes to a close, Alexander Edwards, president of the research consultancy Strategic Vision, was cautious about declaring the electric pickup experiment a failure. He sees the F-150 Lightning as a lesson in making sure that trucks can perform the jobs their owners bought them to do — including towing a camper across several states without worrying about range and charging access. The Cybertruck, on the other hand, appealed to a sense of individuality, innovation, excitement, but only a relatively small group of people were willing to pay for that experience at a high price point, especially as Tesla became a political target thanks to Musk’s involvement with DOGE.

“I think price, product frustrations, Musk’s politics, and the changing meaning of owning one all need to be part of the discussion,” Edwards said.

High gas prices sparked by the war in Iran, which have stuck around for months, are prompting people to purchase hybrids, though sales of electric vehicles have declined after the Trump administration’s elimination of federal tax credits last year. Krassner is also bullish on a new generation of range-extended electric trucks — EVs with a gas-powered generator — which could ease drivers’ range anxiety.

In other words, America’s experiment with electrified pickup trucks isn’t over yet. “I’d say round one went to the gas truck,” Krassner said. “Round two hasn’t started yet.”

https://grist.org/culture/2-years-after-.title: 2 years after Mexico relocated their climate-ravaged community, residents struggle to adapt
https://grist.org/culture/2-years-after-.author: Nina Lakhani
https://grist.org/culture/2-years-after-.text:
This story was produced by Drilled, a global multimedia reporting project focused on climate accountability, and is co-published with Grist.​

It’s 3 a.m. and the beach in El Bosque, in southeast Mexico, is humming with small talk and laughter as Viviana Velázquez eases out of her hammock and dashes to the shoreline to greet a boat returning with the night’s catch. Velázquez, 38, and her 13-year-old daughter, Marlene, help the tired fishermen unload the ice boxes and heave a plastic crate full of bonito to the cooperative to be weighed.

The captain pays Velázquez for her help in fish. She saves a couple to fry for breakfast and cashes in the rest for 50 pesos, the equivalent of about $3, and heads back to her hammock, where some friends are eating pastries while catching up on the past week’s dramas.

This work is known locally as garrulear. For decades it was an important source of income, food, and bonding for women in El Bosque, a small fishing community in the state of Tabasco located on a narrow peninsula sandwiched between the Gulf of Mexico and the Usumacinta River. It is one of the things that Velázquez misses most since sea level rise forced residents to leave.

“In El Bosque I would garrulear every day, but then the sea took everything,” said Velázquez, as she settled back into a hammock. “Now I’m stuck inside most of the time; it’s too far to come here often.”

El Bosque became the first community in Mexico to be recognized as displaced by climate change in 2023. By then, coastal erosion and flooding from storm surge had already damaged or swept away more than half of the hundred or so homes in the area. After a high-profile media campaign and several administrative claims by a coalition of environmental justice organizations working with residents of El Bosque, President Andrés Manuel López Obrador pledged to relocate them.

In November 2024, a new neighborhood called Nuevo Bosque, or New Forest, was inaugurated 7.5 miles inland on the outskirts of the city of Frontera. Fifty-one families received identical purpose-built houses in Nuevo Bosque.

The El Bosque relocation was seen as a huge win for the residents and a success story for the government. Yet two years on, the community is now also struggling to adapt to economic, social, and cultural losses caused by moving away from the sea. Meanwhile, the residents who were excluded from the relocation still don’t know why.

Velázquez was among the lucky ones to be rehoused, but she doesn’t feel settled. “I am trying to adapt to my new life, but I can’t sleep, I cry all the time, my heart beats a thousand times a minute,” she told Drilled. “We’re constantly worrying about money. I eat and eat and eat to calm my nerves. I’ve put on 29 pounds.

“We are grateful, but I am still grieving,” she said. “I miss everything about El Bosque: the cool breeze, my friends, our whole life.”

Fishing wasn’t just a job for the people of El Bosque. It was a core part of who they were, both as individuals and as a community. They wanted to be relocated closer to the coast so they could still fish every day, but the authorities said that they’d likely be flooded out again within a few years. Here, they should be safe from flooding for 30 years or so.

The grief is not over yet. A taxi ride from Nuevo Bosque to El Bosque and back costs 240 pesos (equivalent to around $14), which is why Velázquez and her friends only go back once a week or so even during the height of the fishing season. But even these precious few nights spent garruleando, helping the fishermen and bonding with friends, are numbered.

“At the rate things are going, a few sandy islands are all that will soon be left of El Bosque,” said Lilia Gama, an ecologist and expert in coastal erosion from the Juarez Autonomous University of Tabasco. “The river and the sea will likely join up within a decade, and the entire community will be under water.”

According to Gama, the river and sea in El Bosque would have eventually joined anyway, due to the natural dynamics of the waters, but climate change has turbocharged the process.

Rising sea level is primarily caused by global heating driven by the greenhouse gas emissions released from burning fossil fuels. Ice caps, ice sheets, and glaciers that flow into the oceans are melting, increasing the volume of oceans across the globe. The oceans are also expanding due to warmer waters, which are not only making seas rise further but also causing storms to grow stronger and more destructive. Powerful tidal waves, storm surges, and other events that create extremely high sea levels, which historically occurred once every century, could become annual phenomena by 2100.

Globally, the rate of sea level rise has more than doubled over the past three decades. It will rise a further 15 to 30 centimeters (4 to 12 inches) on average by 2050, according to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, endangering close to a billion people currently living in low-lying coastal areas.

It could leave up to half the entire state of Tabasco, home to about 2.5 million people, uninhabitable or highly vulnerable by the end of the century, according to modeling by Climate Central.

Under international law, states have a duty to protect their communities and guarantee human rights, which includes transitioning away from fossil fuels and implementing climate adaptation measures to minimize harm.

“If displacement cannot be prevented, communities have the right to be consulted, the right to information, and to provide input so they co-shape the decision on how and where they will be relocated,” said Veronika Fikfak,  a professor of international human rights law at University College London.

El Bosque was founded in the early 1980s by landless people from the neighboring state of Veracruz who saw an opportunity to lift their families out of poverty. Back then the peninsula was covered in mangroves and thick vegetation — hence the name El Bosque, which means “the forest.”

Velázquez was just six months old when her family moved to El Bosque. The family didn’t get rich, but they did alright. There was an abundance of fish that sold to restaurants and markets in the capital, Mexico City, and then locally as El Bosque became a popular spot for local tourists to eat crab tamales, ceviche, and fish empanadas.

Velázquez married a local fisherman, Javier Rodriguez, and they had two children.

In February 2022, the sea flooded their home during a storm, and the family moved into another house slightly farther inland. When that house flooded in November 2022, they were evacuated to Frontera. By then, an entire row of houses in El Bosque was fully submerged under water, and the kindergarten and primary school their children attended had been abandoned.

Before being evacuated, “the children were crying all the time, scared by the sound of the waves crashing into the house,” Velázquez said. “But we came back to El Bosque so my husband, Javier, could keep fishing.” They stayed in a makeshift house cobbled together from sticks and metal sheeting, even after the power was cut off due to storm damage. “I couldn’t bear to leave.”

The family finally left El Bosque for good on New Year’s Eve 2024, a month after getting the keys to their new house in Nuevo Bosque.

Nuevo Bosque consists of four rows of identical single-story, two-bedroom houses, each with a back and front yard that are too small for the chickens and ducks many raised in El Bosque. There’s a playground, a basketball court, and some benches — the town’s only gathering place, where teenagers make out and community meetings are held.

The town was inaugurated without running water or a primary school. A narrow laminate static trailer parked at the community entrance currently serves as a makeshift classroom. There’s no bathroom, so the kids run home if they need the toilet.

One day in late May when Drilled visited the school in Nuevo Bosque, the morning began with children helping to sweep rainwater from an overnight storm out of the trailer.  With no AC and just four fans (one of them broken), soon it was baking hot inside. Tabasco has always been hot and humid, but climate change is driving temperatures higher, and the state education department had just instructed schools to close at 11:30 a.m. for the rest of the term because of the heat.

“The kids get irritable and sleepy. It’s so hot, it’s hard even for me,” said teacher Isabel Mayo Cerino. “This was supposedly a planned relocation, and yet nobody thought about education. A community without a school isn’t a proper community.”

The state education department has promised to build a proper classroom when the community finds some suitable land. But the children have been without a proper school for almost six years now, ever since a tidal wave flooded their old school in El Bosque in late 2020.

Natali Segura, 28, moved her 11-year-old son to a school in Frontera because he could barely read or write. “The kids lost 5 or 6 years of school,” said Segura. “They are so behind.”

The community is relieved to be away from the threat of the rising sea, and close proximity to the city has brought benefits. A hospital is nearby, and there’s good internet and phone service, which the teenagers love.

But multiple residents told Drilled that they feel isolated and less healthy. Drilled met many adults and children who, like Velázquez, said they had put on significant amounts of weight since relocating away from the coast. Their life in the city is far more sedentary. Fish is no longer a mainstay of their diet, and fast food is a lot easier to find. Residents have gotten into the habit of ordering snacks and big bottles of sugary, fizzy drinks for home delivery.

At the same time, money is tighter, and for the first time mothers don’t always know where the next meal for their kids is coming from.

“It might look like we’re better off in these new houses, but we’re not,” said Áurea Sánchez, 44, who spends hours each day at her evangelical church praying for the community to be blessed. “No one was rich in El Bosque, but no one ever went hungry. Now, life is more precarious. We’re fishers, we can’t change overnight.”

In 2024, Sánchez and her eldest daughter, Yesenia, were among hundreds of people from frontline communities in Latin America and the Caribbean who testified at a landmark hearing on climate displacement convened by the Inter American Court of Human Rights, or IACHR, in Manaus, Brazil. “I realized that we’re not alone, that we have rights, and that many communities are suffering because we haven’t looked after what God gave us,” Sanchez told Drilled.

El Bosque has become an emblematic case of climate displacement, helping clarify international law and setting in motion a wave of policy reforms in Mexico. It was cited in a historic opinion published by the IACHR in May 2025.

“States are obligated to adopt measures to prevent … migration and forced displacement resulting directly and indirectly from disasters and other impacts of climate change,” according to the IACHR advisory opinion on human rights and climate change. In other words, the highest court in the Americas says that under existing international law, states are duty bound to develop and finance public policies on climate adaptation and displacement.

International climate negotiations are often cast in terms of those who have contributed the most to climate change and those who will suffer the worst consequences. Mexico is one of the few countries that straddles both categories.

Mexico is one of the top 20 largest historic contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. Industrialized countries that benefited most from fossil fuels are legally and morally bound to help lead the way in transitioning away from fossil fuel under international law and U.N. climate treaties like the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Yet Mexico is the 11th largest oil producer in the world, according to the International Energy Agency’s most recent data. It is also highly vulnerable to climate breakdown. If current climate trends continue, Mexico could see at least 3 million people internally displaced by 2050 as a result of sea level rise, drought, desertification, extreme heat, and other sudden and slow onset climate disasters, according to one study by the World Bank.

This paradox is particularly stark in Tabasco, the state where El Bosque is located, which is also the home state of former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador, whose six-year term from 2018 to 2024 saw Mexico’s transition to renewable energy sources go backward.

Tabasco is one of the biggest oil-producing states in Mexico, and fossil fuel companies have built refineries, pipelines, and other polluting infrastructure along its eroding coastline, as well as roads, schools, hospitals, and entire neighborhoods for their workers. Sea level rise and air pollution from oil operations threaten them all, underlying the harm caused by fossil fuels at every stage of their life cycle — from toxic pollution and industrial accidents when they are extracted and refined, to the global heating driven by the release of greenhouse gases when they are burned.

Mexico’s national oil company, Pemex, was founded by President Lázaro Cárdenas in 1938.  A symbol of the country’s nationalism and sovereignty, it’s now ranked as the biggest corporate polluter in Latin America and among the most indebted fossil companies globally.

Tabasco is tightly intertwined with Pemex, which has installations in 80 percent of the state’s municipalities — including the Dos Bocas oil refinery, which opened in 2022 about 60 miles west of El Bosque, and only meters away from a primary school in the neighborhood Lázaro Cárdenas del Río, more colloquially known as La Petrolera (the oil company), because so many residents work for Pemex.

The refinery has suffered floods, fatal fires, and massive oil leaks, while acute respiratory problems, panic attacks, headaches, and vomiting have surged among residents. The neighborhood is dotted with empty houses, all that’s left of the families displaced by the pollution, or who moved away in fear of further industrial disasters.

A huge gas flare is visible from the local hospital near La Petrolera, which is owned and operated by Pemex for its workers and their families, where Cindy Barjau rushed her daughter two years ago after she passed out, overcome by the fumes from the refinery.

“Children can’t play outside anymore; we keep our windows shut,” Barjau told Drilled. “It’s inhumane. Our quality of life has gone. We want to leave, too, but where would we go?”

Pemex has acknowledged a rise in air pollution but has repeatedly claimed that there is no risk to nearby communities. The gravity of the air pollution is difficult to determine, however, because the government has classified its air monitoring data as secret until 2030.

Documents obtained by local media suggest that Pemex began building the facility before completing an environmental impact assessment or a drainage system.

In March, amid growing public pressure following a fire that left five workers dead, President Claudia Sheinbaum asked Pemex to help relocate the school, where enrollment has plummeted.

A 2025 study by Amnesty International revealed that at least 2 billion people — a quarter of the world’s population — live within 3 miles of operational oil, gas, and coal projects, which have turned nearby communities and critical ecosystems into so-called sacrifice zones.

“The fossil fuel industry impacts people’s bodies, their health, their land, and the environment, polluting the surroundings and compromising the ability to sustain life in the short and medium term — and the long term, due to its climate impacts,” said Juan Manuel Orozco, a project officer at the nonprofit group Conexiones Climáticas, which has worked with residents in Dos Bocas and El Bosque. “In the southeast of Mexico, the situation is particularly dramatic. It’s as if all the monsters of our times have converged here.”

In July 2025, a historic advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice, or ICJ, confirmed that all states, whether they are signatories to the Paris Agreement or not, have a duty to take action to achieve “deep, rapid and sustained” cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, which includes regulating private corporations. The continued expansion of fossil fuels would amount to a legal wrong under customary international law, which could trigger an obligation to provide full reparations, the ICJ wrote.

The opinions — along with the El Bosque case — have generated political momentum in Mexico, and there has been more ambition on climate since President Claudia Sheinbaum took office in 2024.

As a signatory to the Paris Agreement, Mexico must submit an updated climate action plan (called a Nationally Determined Contribution) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change every five years. Mexico’s 2025 update set a greenhouse gas target for the first time, implying that it would begin to take steps to lower its emissions.

However, plans are afoot to expand fossil fuel exploration, production, and use, while Mexico’s target timeline for shifting to renewable energy sources is way too slow, according to Climate Action Tracker.

The IACHR and ICJ opinions also helped clarify that states have a duty to safeguard human rights in the context of climate change and put in place adaptation measures to reduce foreseeable harms (which could include things like infrastructure damage and forced displacement). When climate impacts are so advanced that harms have become unavoidable, the courts direct states to cooperate on “loss and damage” claims, including for financial compensation.

Mexico’s updated climate action plan acknowledged, also for the first time, that climate change is already causing loss and damage, which will require reparations to some communities.

Mexico could also end up facing loss and damage claims from other states over its failures to regulate fossil fuel and other polluting corporations and reduce emissions fast enough. But first the government must face domestic lawsuits for failing to protect its own people from foreseeable harms caused by climate change.

The specific duties states have under international law to tackle sea level rise — and deal with consequences like lost livelihoods and displacement — are still undergoing legal clarification, and El Bosque has been a test case in many ways. In Mexico, the experience, good and bad, is likely to inform future climate policy, while a new lawsuit by El Bosque residents who were excluded from the relocation could help clarify the government’s statutory duties to climate-displaced communities.

Mexico, like dozens of other countries, still has no climate adaptation plan that sets out how it will both protect and prepare its own communities from climate breakdown. This is expected to include measures to prevent or minimize the risk of forced displacement, such as coastal restoration, reforestation, water-capture systems, and flood walls.

In El Bosque, the state failed to implement adaptation measures such as mangrove restoration that could have slowed down the erosion, according to Nora Cabrera, founder of the Mexico City-based law firm Nuestro Futuro, which is representing the residents.

The relocation, while well intentioned, was poorly planned and led to a decline in living standards for many residents, Cabrera said.

“The community has been made more vulnerable by the relocation — a level of regression that speaks to the process of climate injustice,” said Cabrera. “The El Bosque case is clearly one of loss and damage, because conditions for adaptation were never created. This amounts to an omission on the part of the Mexican state … regarding its citizens, its people.”

The first house in El Bosque to be completely destroyed by the waves belonged to fisherman Pablo Cardoza, who lived on the seafront with his wife and three children. In September 2019, a strong northerly wind caused a storm surge, flooding the house with sea water, dead trees, and trash. So Cardoza and his family moved to a rental in Frontera, and he took up open-water line fishing, which requires spending several nights on the water to catch sea bream, amberjack, and red snapper.

The catch is more reliable out at sea, but Cardoza still worries about making rent each month. Fish stocks are down due to warmer ocean temperatures, acidification, coastal erosion, and pollution from Pemex’s offshore oil rigs.

Once the government accepted responsibility for relocating residents, officials conducted a census, held meetings, and collected documents. In the end, 51 families were selected to receive new homes. However, the criteria for inclusion — or exclusion — have never been shared, and residents left out, like Cardoza, have never been told why.

“I missed some meetings because I was out at sea, but it feels really unfair. We were the first to lose our home and livelihoods,” Cardoza said. “I haven’t given up. I hope one day they correct this injustice.”

In July, Nuestro Futuro filed a lawsuit on behalf of Cardoza and six other residents of El Bosque who were not relocated without any explanation. This case, Cabrera said, could end up in the Mexican Supreme Court and prompt a ruling on what obligations the state has to climate-displaced communities.

The Mexican government is worried about the pending surge in climate displacement, which would inevitably add pressure on urban hubs like Mexico City, Monterrey, and Guadalajara, where extreme heat and water shortages are already getting worse. A new national policy is in the works for grappling with climate displacement, although it’s unclear when it will be finished, and the Mexican department of environment and natural resources is holding consultations with a wide range of experts on issues such as migration and gender for the separate climate adaptation plan.

If the displacement policy reflects recommendations submitted by residents of El Bosque and climate justice experts, it should make relocation a last resort, and something that is well planned, less traumatic, and more just for the next El Bosque, and the one after that.

In September, the government acknowledged that the vast majority of states and municipalities currently depend on data that is “three to four years out of date” to assess the risk from earthquakes, hurricanes, sea level rise, and other disasters. Funds have been allocated to help all 31 states and Mexico City identify new risks and update prevention efforts, said Laura Velázquez, Mexico’s national coordinator for civil protection.

Urgency is rising to get plans, policies, and financing in place, as climate breakdown accelerates faster than models predicted. “It’s too late for us, but we need a law or a policy to help others,” said Sanchez, the Nuevo Bosque resident who testified at the IACHR hearing in Brazil. “We were the first but we won’t be the last.”

https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-cli.title: Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31
https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-cli.author: Josh Gabbatiss
https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-cli.text:
The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.

Developed countries are required under UN climate treaties to provide “climate finance” and have traditionally announced multi-year pledges to feed into their global commitments.

Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and, since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts and many European aid budgets have been cut.

A civil-society tracker shows that only five nations have announced new multi-year pledges, including just one major donor – the UK.

Germany, France and Japan are among the key contributors that have so far failed to set out plans for new climate finance, while none is expected from the US.

As a result, the total amount of public climate finance pledged over the next few years amounts to just $11.7bn a year in spending, down from recent levels of around $40bn.

Experts tell Carbon Brief that global conflict, fiscal constraints and the rise of the far right are all making it harder for developed-country governments to pledge new funds.

As the COP31 summit in Turkey gets underway, developing countries are stressing their urgent need for new finance, after nations agreed to a new global target just two years ago.

Under the Paris Agreement, developed countries are obliged to provide climate finance to help developing countries cut their emissions and prepare for climate disasters.

This financial assistance can be channelled through multilateral development banks, UN climate funds and investments “mobilised” from the private sector.

But a large chunk is also expected to come directly from the public coffers of developed countries – primarily their foreign-aid budgets. This public spending has made up roughly a third of climate finance flowing to developing countries in recent years.

The EU, the US and others agreed just two years ago that they would “take the lead” on scaling up annual climate finance from $100bn in the early 2020s to $300bn by 2035.

Donor countries have traditionally supported such goals by announcing multi-year targets that indicate how much they plan to spend on climate finance.

Nearly all of these pledges expired in 2025 – and hardly any major donors have announced new ones to replace them, covering the period out to 2030.

This lack of new commitments is captured in a tracker of old and new financial commitments by climate NGOs NRDC and E3G.

Carbon Brief analysis of this data, based on an annualised breakdown of targets, shows that developed countries had previously pledged around £42bn a year in public finance.

As the chart below shows, based on current pledges, this has fallen by around 71% to £11.8bn, on average, over the remainder of the 2020s.

Not all contributors announced public climate-finance pledges in advance for the pre-2026 period. Some did not hit their stated targets, while others exceeded them.

While official data for 2025 is not yet available, bilateral public finance reached £43.9bn in 2024, broadly in line with the amount pledged by developed countries.

International climate finance has been consistently dominated by five nations – Japan, Germany, France, the US and the UK.

These countries – together with the EU – have provided around 90% of all the bilateral, public climate finance going to developing countries in recent years.

Of these key players, only the UK has announced a new pledge, committing £6bn ($8bn) of aid between 2026-27 and 2028-29, plus £6.7bn ($8.9bn) from outside its aid budget.

This accounts for half of all the annual funds pledged from 2026 onwards – averaging $5.7bn a year.

The European Commission makes up most of the remainder, with an average annual contribution of $4.5bn promised out to 2027.

Rather than a new pledge, this is due to the commission promising to spend €28bn ($31.8bn) over its 2021-2027 budget period. Its post-2027 contribution is currently being discussed as part of wider EU budget negotiations.

Canada has promised to spend CA$5.3bn ($4.1bn) by 2030, averaging $860m a year. The Netherlands, Switzerland and Belgium have also pledged relatively small sums.

Overall, despite developed countries committing to scale up climate finance, these new pledges are either less ambitious – or only slightly more ambitious – than previous ones. This can be seen in the chart below.

The UK’s pledge appears more ambitious, but this is because the government has changed how it counts climate finance to include $8.9bn in “additional” public finance. When only the like-for-like aid components are compared, the new pledge amounts to a drop in ambition. (For more details, see the methodology.)

The most significant absence is the US, which committed to reaching $11.4bn in annual support by 2024 under the Biden administration.

Since president Donald Trump took power, the US has – for the second time – withdrawn from the Paris Agreement and shrunk its aid budget. It will not provide any official climate finance in the coming years.

Another notable absence is Australia, which is jointly hosting the upcoming COP31 summit, alongside Turkey. Josie Lee, policy and advocacy lead at Oxfam Australia, tells Carbon Brief:

“If Australia fails to announce a climate-finance pledge as president of negotiations, it would send a problematic message to those resisting action on climate change that might serve to embolden their agenda.”

Japan is the largest overall contributor of public climate finance, but it has not traditionally announced targets for this type of spending. Instead, the government set out overall goals that also bundle in finance “mobilised” from the private sector.

As a result, its public-finance ambitions have not been included in this analysis.

So far, the Japanese government has not announced any new multi-year climate-finance pledges, from either the public or the private sector.

Europe provides the majority of international climate finance, but European governments have massively cut their aid spending in recent years, citing economic strain and defence spending needs.

Germany and France, the two largest European climate-finance contributors, both pledged to reach €6bn ($6.8bn) per year by 2025. Neither has committed to anything beyond that.

Both nations have slashed their aid budgets in recent years, including funding for climate programmes. Germany missed its 2025 climate-finance goal due to these cuts.

Dr Anja Carolin Gebel, a senior policy advisor at Germanwatch, tells Carbon Brief that this issue has become more politically fraught since the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) won the 2025 election and began leading a coalition government:

“The issue of climate change – and, subsequently, climate finance – has taken a back seat in the current government coalition.”

There has also been a political shift in France, Gaïa Febvre, international policy coordinator at Réseau Action Climat, tells Carbon Brief. She adds:

“The upcoming presidential election and the growing influence of the far right are likely to make new international financial commitments politically more difficult.”

Other significant European donors are also undergoing political turmoil.

Spain’s centre-left government has triggered a snap election for the end of November, making a new climate-finance pledge during COP31 less likely.

Following a narrow election win, a centre-left bloc in Sweden is still in the process of trying to form a new coalition government.

Some nations have signalled that their climate finance will continue flowing, even though they have not officially set out specific new pledges.

The Dutch government, for example, has said it will provide “at least” €300m ($334m) of specific climate funding annually out to 2031. However, it has also indicated that its total public climate finance is likely to be considerably higher in both 2026 and 2027.

To highlight the lack of new pledges, developing countries are championing a “climate-finance work programme” at COP31, which could provide a space to discuss scaling up public climate finance from developed countries.

In response, the EU has stressed that its member states are the “largest providers” of public climate finance and called on developing countries to submit overdue plans for cutting emissions. The EU and its member states provided a record €32.3bn ($40bn) in 2025.

Against this backdrop, EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra recently told Bloomberg that “any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water”.

Joe Thwaites, international climate finance director at NRDC, who runs the commitment tracker, tells Carbon Brief that “developed countries would be wise to show how they are continuing to lead on climate finance”. He says:

“The lack of new announcements is making the finance negotiations tougher than they need to be. The debate around the climate-finance work programme is arising because developing countries have little clarity about how much public climate finance there will be in coming years.”

This analysis is based on the climate-finance commitments tracker, run by the NGOs NRDC and E3G, supplemented with additional research.

Only the 23 “developed” countries that are obliged to provide climate finance are considered in this analysis, plus the EU. This includes western Europe, the US, Australia, Canada and New Zealand. Japan and Norway both provide substantial sums of climate finance, but have not announced specific public-finance pledges and therefore are not included.

Carbon Brief converted multi-year pledges into single years, with 2025 used as the baseline “pre-2026” year. Some countries committed to reaching a certain amount “by 2025”, in which case that value is used. Others said they would provide a total amount over several years, in which case the average value per year is used. Belgium, Switzerland and the US only set initial targets as far as 2024, so their 2024 values were used instead of 2025.

These values were compared with the average annual contribution for the remainder of the 2020s, based on the new pledges from the UK, Canada, Belgium, Switzerland and the Netherlands. Some climate finance has been committed by the Netherlands, but this is not expected to be its total contribution. The EU, Portugal and Greece have earlier pledges that extend into the latter half of the 2020s, although the latter two make very small contributions.

NRDC and E3G include all the UK’s newly pledged public finance in their tracker, including $8.9bn in “additional” public finance, which covers “equity, debt, guarantees, insurance and export credit” to mobilise private finance.

In previous Carbon Brief analysis comparing the UK’s new climate-finance target to its old one, this funding was not included. This is because the government did not previously count these funds towards its climate-finance goals, instead focusing exclusively on aid spending.

This analysis does not include pledges that some countries, including Germany and France, have made to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). However, these pledges would not substantially change the main finding, shifting the overall reduction from 71% to 70%.

Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts.

https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-whi.title: Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31?
https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-whi.author: Carbon Brief Staff
https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-whi.text:
More than 92,000 people have registered to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, potentially making it the largest COP in history.

Carbon Brief analysis of the provisional lists of delegates, published by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), reveals that more than 14,000 delegates have been registered as “host country guests”.

For comparison, the final list for COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last year included only around 1,300 delegates in this category.

As with COP30, Donald Trump’s US government has not sent a delegation. Other no-shows include Israel and Myanmar.

It was reported ahead of the summit that Taliban officials from Afghanistan had been registered for the event as observers; however, there are no delegates from observer states in the provisional lists.

With more than 3,000 “virtual” delegates signed up to attend the summit online, the total number of people registered for the event surpasses 95,000.

With 92,934 participants registered, COP31 is provisionally the largest COP in history – topping COP28 in Dubai, which was attended by more than 80,000 people.

This total is based on the delegates that have registered to be at the summit in person. The UNFCCC releases the final figures – based on participants collecting a physical badge at the venue – after the summit has ended.

The chart below shows how the provisional figures for COP31 compare to the final totals in previous COPs – going back to COP1 in Berlin in 1995.

The participant lists provided by the UNFCCC are divided between the different types of groups and organisations attending the summit. The largest group at COP31 is for delegates representing parties. These are nation-states, plus the European Union, that have ratified the convention and play a full part in negotiations.

This group adds up to 18,812 delegates – the second largest after COP28.

(In keeping with recent COPs, the UNFCCC has published spreadsheets that name every single person that has registered for the summit – excluding support staff. Previously, COPs have typically included thousands of “overflow” participants in which countries and UN agencies could nominate delegates without their names appearing on their official lists.)

For consistency with Carbon Brief’s analysis of previous COPs, the above chart includes overflow delegates as a single group. However, the participant lists do divide the overflow delegates between parties and observer groups. Including the overflow numbers takes the total for party representatives to more than 34,000.

Unusually, COP31 has a very large number of “host country guests”. This is a category that has only been included in the COP participant lists over the last few years. The provisional number for COP31 – 14,285 – far exceeds the final number of host guests at COP30 (1,324), COP29 (1,651) and COP28 (4,202).

The map and table below present the delegation size – split between party and overflow badges – for all the countries registered for COP31. The darker the shading, the more delegates that country has signed up.

Unsurprisingly, host nation Turkey has registered the largest delegation for COP31 – with 2,950 people.

Following behind are Brazil (1,994 people), Nigeria (1,506), China (1,021) and Indonesia (978).

The rest of the top 10 is made up of Australia (835), Uganda (627), Italy (607), Japan (588) and Kazakhstan (557).

The UK comes someway down the list with a delegation of 255.

Free weekly newsletter

The smallest delegation comes from North Korea (two), followed by Eritrea and Nicaragua (three) and San Marino and Trinidad and Tobago (four).

(It is worth noting that some countries – such as Brazil – allocate some of their party badges to NGOs, which can artificially inflate the size of their official delegation.)

The UNFCCC’s participant lists typically provide a title – such as Mr, Ms, Sr or Sra – for each registered delegate. In the past, this has allowed Carbon Brief to work out the balance of men to women in the delegations that each country has sent to a COP.

(This analysis always carries the caveat that the titles are designated by UNFCCC and not by Carbon Brief. In addition, Carbon Brief recognises that gender is not best categorised using a binary “man” or “woman” label and appreciates that the UNFCCC’s lists may not be wholly accurate.)

Overall, the COP31 provisional list suggests an average gender balance of party delegations of 59% men to 41% women.

As the chart below shows, COP31 is slightly less balanced than the last two COPs, but broadly continues a trend that has seen COP delegations become a more even split between men and women.

(Note: Since COP28, the UNFCCC has also used titles that do not indicate gender – such as Dr, Prof, Ambassador and Honourable. Therefore, for this analysis, these non-gendered titles – which make up 1.3% of party delegates at COP31, for example – have not been included.)

Including overflows, there are two delegations of only men at COP31 – Eritrea (three people) and North Korea (two). There are no delegations that are only women.

The full list of COP31 party delegation sizes can be found here.

(For previous COPs, see Carbon Brief’s delegate analysis for COP21, COP23, COP24, COP25, COP26, COP27, COP28, COP29 and COP30.)

After party delegates, observers of the negotiations are typically the next biggest group at COP summits.

These delegates receive their observer status through their not-for-profit organisation. This can be a UN body, a “specialised agency” – such as the World Bank or International Atomic Energy Agency, an intergovernmental organisation – such as OPEC or the Inter-American Development Bank – or an NGO.

The vast majority of observers at COP31 – more than 12,000 – are representing NGOs. These can include charities, such as WWF, 350.org and Amnesty International, as well as philanthropic organisations, such as the Rockefeller Foundation and the IKEA Foundation, and lobby groups, such as the International Gas Union and the UK’s National Farmers Union.

At COP30 last year, the UNFCCC registration process introduced the option for observers to disclose the “immediate source(s) of funding” for their participation.

This option has been included again at COP31.

Of the 12,413 NGO observers registered for COP31, 14% chose not to disclose funding. The most common funders were NGOs (56%) and academic or research institutions (12%). Around 8% declared funding from “private sector or business”.

In addition, observers were “invited to declare their participation's alignment with the objective of the convention and the goals and principles of the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement”.

Overall, 13,108  delegates selected “yes” for this section, with the remaining 2,247 delegates leaving the answer blank.

Finally, there are 3,645 media representatives registered to attend COP31 in person, which is provisionally the second-largest media group in COP history – behind COP3 in Kyoto, Japan, in 1997 (3,712).

The way that media organisations are described in the list is very inconsistent, which makes overall totals difficult to tally. Nonetheless, the Turkish Radio and Television Corporation (TRT) is comfortably the most-represented media group at COP31 with more than 200 delegates.

Other media outlets with at least a dozen participants include CNN, the Associated Press, Financial Times, Bloomberg, Agence France-Presse, Reuters and Sky News.

Update: This article was updated on 11/11/2026 to add further analysis on gender balance, observers and media at COP31.

In New Delhi, officials and analysts alike awaited the results of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 with anticipation. U.S. President Donald Trump’s mercurial and idiosyncratic policies both at home and abroad—with few constraints on his choices—have rippled through global capitals since he returned to the White House last year.

India has suffered especially from recent U.S. policy vagaries, which have upturned a bilateral relationship that was by and large steadily improving and deepening. These include Trump’s tariff wars, apparent fondness for Pakistan’s leadership, and harsh approach to immigration. So, now that almost all the midterm results are in—and the Democratic Party will control both houses of Congress—how is India’s political class and attentive public reacting to the outcome?

In New Delhi, officials and analysts alike awaited the results of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 with anticipation. U.S. President Donald Trump’s mercurial and idiosyncratic policies both at home and abroad—with few constraints on his choices—have rippled through global capitals since he returned to the White House last year.

India has suffered especially from recent U.S. policy vagaries, which have upturned a bilateral relationship that was by and large steadily improving and deepening. These include Trump’s tariff wars, apparent fondness for Pakistan’s leadership, and harsh approach to immigration. So, now that almost all the midterm results are in—and the Democratic Party will control both houses of Congress—how is India’s political class and attentive public reacting to the outcome?

At one level, the results have generated some hope for the future of bilateral ties. New Delhi’s guarded optimism stems from a belief that a Democratic Congress might place some checks on the Trump administration’s propensity to make feckless decisions with adverse consequences for New Delhi. After all, the U.S.-India partnership enjoyed a bipartisan consensus for the last few decades, until Trump’s second term.

Despite this sense of relief, Indian observers still harbor some qualms toward the United States. They are aware that any U.S. president wields substantial power in conducting foreign policy. Trump has made considerable use of this authority with a pliant Republican Congress, from his legally dubious ouster of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to his unpopular and undeclared war in Iran. New Delhi will watch intently for early signs of the new Congress reining in his tendency to act with little hesitation or consultation.

A host of other issues remain on the minds of New Delhi’s foreign-policy establishment. Indian officials are aware that U.S. lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have concerns about India’s dependence on and willingness to purchase Russian oil. This poses a dilemma for New Delhi, which cannot easily dispense with these imports because of high costs and its refining facilities, which are tied to specific grades of crude oil.

If external pressures mount to dilute ties between New Delhi and Moscow, India’s pro-Russia lobby may feel more inclined to urge Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government to adopt a tougher stance toward Washington. A more consistent approach toward Russian oil sales from the U.S. Congress, without exemptions for otherwise friendly nations, might cause India to adopt a more intransigent stance.

Furthermore, many people in New Delhi—both within and outside the government—remain very concerned about the Trump administration’s dalliance with Islamabad since India and Pakistan’s military conflict last year. At the time of the crisis, which came in the wake of a terrorist attack in Indian-administered Kashmir, Trump asserted that he had stepped in to induce a cease-fire between the two neighboring rivals. India, long averse to any external involvement in the Kashmir dispute, denies that Trump played a role in ending the conflict.

Pakistan, however, said the Trump administration was crucial in bringing about a cease-fire and nominated the U.S. president for the Nobel Peace Prize. Trump, in turn, invited Pakistani Army chief Asim Munir to lunch at the White House. The United States has since taken an interest in Pakistan’s mineral and cryptocurrency resources, and the country has offered the Trump administration several lucrative deals.

Indian observers will pay close attention to the relevant, newly constituted congressional committees to see if they evince any interest in looking closely at the U.S.-Pakistan strategic nexus. Among other matters, U.S. lawmakers may scrutinize the investments that Trump’s children have made in Pakistan, especially in cryptocurrency.

Many in New Delhi’s foreign-policy establishment will likely welcome some limits on Trump’s presidential powers. But with the victory of a few Democrats who care deeply about human rights issues both at home and abroad—such as civil liberties and minority rights—India may now confront a renewed focus on the state of its democracy under Modi. Trump, of course, has cared little about democratic backsliding and tended to give India a pass.

Historically, New Delhi’s stock responses to U.S. criticism of its human rights record and the state of its democracy have been twofold. First, that these matters fall under India’s purview, and external review impinges on its sovereignty. Second, that its own institutional mechanisms can provide suitable redress for any failures to uphold democratic principles. These retorts may not satisfy Democrats, who may not be inclined to sanction India but could pass non-binding resolutions that New Delhi might find irksome.

The party should start with investigations and subpoenas, then prepare for more substantial campaign finance reform.

But as winter approaches, their focus is on meeting basic needs.

Other nettlesome bilateral issues—especially on trade and tariffs—may see some progress. In recent weeks, both the United States and India publicly suggested that a trade deal was nearing completion after protracted negotiations. On this front, officials in New Delhi feel somewhat sanguine; the trade accord does not depend on congressional approval. More to the point, if Trump is constrained in other arenas, he might want to score a foreign-policy victory.

Even with a finalized trade deal, the wariness that has crept into New Delhi’s view of Washington will not easily dissipate. To begin with, Trump’s fitful policies have undermined the trust so carefully nurtured by his predecessors. Restoring even a modicum of this trust will require some politically costly moves, such as offering concessions on trade or signaling a willingness to ease up on visa restrictions.

Despite the electoral rout of the Republicans, it remains an open question whether Trump will prove willing to adopt a more conciliatory approach to foreign policy.

Other differences between the United States and India on the global stage are likely to persist. Trump is reportedly weighing further major military action against Iran. Since the new Congress will not convene until January, the president may have an incentive to act soon. A renewed campaign in Iran would not be viewed favorably in New Delhi, as it would again disrupt vital oil supplies and place Indian sailors and expatriates in the Middle East at risk.

Modi’s government faces growing domestic dissent over allegations of electoral misconduct. These protests have shown few signs of abating and have energized India’s political opposition. Under the present circumstances, New Delhi cannot afford to remain silent if Trump embarks on another campaign in Iran with significant ramifications for India, including driving up the cost of fuel.

There is little question that last week’s Democratic victory amounts to a seismic shift in U.S. politics. Its effects on Trump’s foreign-policy choices, especially between now and January, remain unclear. New Delhi is likely to wait until the new Congress takes office before it tips its hand. But ultimately, from the Indian perspective, seriously repairing the relationship might be a task best deferred until after the 2028 U.S. presidential election.

Sumit Ganguly is a columnist at Foreign Policy and senior fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, where he directs the Huntington Program on Strengthening U.S.-India Relations.
