While Israelis were still coming to terms with the uncertain outcome of their own Oct. 27 elections, U.S. President Donald Trump chose the day of the U.S. midterms to further discombobulate the Israeli public. On Fox News, he announced not only that he was ending U.S. military assistance to Israel by the end of the year but also that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed that the assistance should end. In an interview with Fox & Friends, Trump remarked: “As far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I … made a deal months ago that we’re stopping, and they’re fine with it.”

It is true that Netanyahu told the Economist in January that he hoped to “taper off” Israeli dependence on U.S. military aid over the next decade. But he has given no indication of any agreement for military assistance to terminate as soon as this year. Feeling the pressure, Netanyahu’s office is now spinning the end of U.S. military assistance as a “transition out from aid towards partnership and mutual investment."

While Israelis were still coming to terms with the uncertain outcome of their own Oct. 27 elections, U.S. President Donald Trump chose the day of the U.S. midterms to further discombobulate the Israeli public. On Fox News, he announced not only that he was ending U.S. military assistance to Israel by the end of the year but also that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed that the assistance should end. In an interview with Fox & Friends, Trump remarked: “As far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I … made a deal months ago that we’re stopping, and they’re fine with it.”

It is true that Netanyahu told the Economist in January that he hoped to “taper off” Israeli dependence on U.S. military aid over the next decade. But he has given no indication of any agreement for military assistance to terminate as soon as this year. Feeling the pressure, Netanyahu’s office is now spinning the end of U.S. military assistance as a “transition out from aid towards partnership and mutual investment.”

The backlash in Israel was immediate. Trump’s announcement raises critical questions regarding what political price was negotiated—and specifically, whether any agreement to end U.S. aid served as the quid pro quo for Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu in Israel’s election.

Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak accused Netanyahu of concocting “a stinking deal” that traded U.S. military assistance for a presidential endorsement, concluding that Netanyahu had “exceeded his authority” and was “utterly unfit to lead a country.” Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who may yet replace Netanyahu as prime minister, was less conspiratorial but equally scathing. “Israel’s special relationship with the United States is a central component of its national security,” he wrote on X. “The fact that the security establishment is learning, together with Israeli citizens, about a change in the strategic relationship through the media shows just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct is a real danger.”

That Trump chose to make this announcement on Election Day speaks volumes about the collapse of Israel’s standing across the U.S. political spectrum. He evidently believed that it would resonate with voters amid rising public anger over inflation and the cost of living. The question of why a high-tech powerhouse requires billions in taxpayer-funded military aid carries growing political weight, even if much of the aid is reinvested in the U.S. defense industry.

The real elephant in the room, however, is the ongoing war with Iran and anger over U.S. support for Israel. Prominent Republicans, including Vice President J.D. Vance, have openly identified the conflict as the principal catalyst for the party’s electoral thrashing. Writing on X in the immediate aftermath of the vote, Vance broke ranks with traditional White House messaging, declaring bluntly: “The reason we lost is the war. … [E]veryone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” He also claimed that voters wanted to see a change in the relationship with Israel. Vance highlighted internal polling showing that 2024 Trump voters who defected to the Democrats in the midterms specifically cited an end to the war, economic relief from soaring fuel prices, and a fundamental shift in Washington’s relationship with Israel as their primary demands. In an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes on Sunday, Trump did not disagree with Vance’s observation that the Iran war caused the Republican defeat in the midterms, adding that “there is a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.”

While it was Trump who launched a war against Iran in February, Netanyahu never concealed his desire for a joint campaign. Even following Operation Epic Fury, he has consistently tried to persuade Trump to renew the war, treating the Iranian threat not merely as an existential regional issue but as a political prop to distract the Israeli electorate from his leadership failures in the lead-up to and aftermath of Oct. 7, 2023.

Ahead of the midterms, the New York Times published a report claiming that Israel had shared intelligence with the United States and Gulf countries about possible Iranian plans to use chemical weapons against them. U.S. officials met the intelligence with skepticism, believing it was part of a coordinated effort by Netanyahu to push Trump toward renewed strikes.

Netanyahu’s rhetoric on Iran is riddled with glaring contradictions. Having publicly trumpeted historic success in dismantling Iran’s nuclear capabilities in June 2025, he has reversed course to manufacture an immediate, existential urge for military confrontation. On Oct. 25, Netanyahu posted an AI-generated image depicting a nuclear blast over Tel Aviv, warning voters that rejecting his leadership invited a “second Holocaust.” Political opponents accused him of manufacturing a crisis with Iran as an attempt to delay the election. This triggered an unprecedented rift with Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, who resisted political orders that risked sparking an immediate, unwarranted regional conflagration. Yair Golan of the Democrats declared that Netanyahu lacks “the necessary public trust” and “moral legitimacy or even basic capability” to lead such a campaign, while former Israeli Ambassador to Germany Jeremy Issacharoff noted that Netanyahu’s political machinations over Iran “severely damage Israel’s credibility abroad.”

During the opening session of the new Knesset on Tuesday, Netanyahu insisted that while his government had removed the immediate existential threat, Iran was renewing its nuclear program and had not given up on its intent to destroy Israel. He declared that the only way to remove this existential threat was by toppling the regime, trumpeting for good measure that his government had “changed the face of the Middle East.”

Netanyahu’s endgame is clearly at odds with the objectives of the Trump administration, which views military force primarily as leverage to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and force Tehran to climb down over its nuclear program. In his incendiary speech, Netanyahu also asserted that only a national unity government—presumably under his leadership—would enable Israel to meet the upcoming challenges, while accusing Israel’s Arab lawmakers of seeking the nation’s destruction. Eisenkot countered immediately, stating that Netanyahu’s “hate-filled” speech demonstrated that he was unfit for office. He has clearly failed to internalize the fact that, even among his erstwhile allies in the Republican party, his political standing is becoming increasingly toxic.

Eisenkot has four paths to power, and none of them are easy.

Netanyahu retains power for now as a caretaker prime minister while Eisenkot seeks to form a new government. Renewed hostilities with Iran in coordination with the United States would have been highly convenient for Netanyahu, as this could have delayed the opening of the newly elected parliament and formation of a new government. His overarching goal remains to block an opposition coalition that includes or is supported by Arab parties, who emerged as pivotal kingmakers in this election.

Deploying the Trump playbook to contest the election results, Netanyahu’s loyalist Shin Bet security chief, David Zini, has targeted Arab opposition lawmakers with unfounded investigations, raising grave constitutional alarm. Even though Eisenkot has received the mandate to form a government, his narrow victory and the opposition’s lingering hesitation toward joining forces with the Arab parties make coalition-building highly uncertain.

While right-wing factions in Israel view Netanyahu’s relationship with Trump and a renewed U.S.-Israel campaign against Iran as a strategic win, the long-term fallout could be severe. In putting all his eggs into the Republican basket, Netanyahu has wrecked U.S. bipartisan support for Israel. Following a decisive Democratic shift in Congress, he finds himself dangerously exposed: He faces fierce critics on the American left and an angry Republican base looking for a political scapegoat.

Trump is now signaling that a renewal of war is “highly unlikely” if talks with Iran show progress. Yet after last week’s midterm collapse, his close ally Chris Ruddy noted on the BBC, there was an 80 percent chance that the U.S. president could still authorize military action against Tehran. Netanyahu thus retains every incentive to gamble on regional escalation in order to entrench his political survival, even at the direct expense of Israel’s democratic resilience and its international standing. It appears that he has nowhere left to run.

An unpredictable lame-duck U.S. president may feel that he has little left to lose, but for Netanyahu and an increasingly isolated Israeli public, the stakes could not be higher.

Azriel Bermant is an associate researcher at the Institute of International Relations Prague as well as the author of Margaret Thatcher and the Middle East and the Azriel’s Substack newsletter.

In South Korea, the term byeorak-geoji means “sudden beggar.” In 2026, it has gained widespread popularity again. But its meaning is figurative. Rather than denoting sudden bankruptcy or losing one’s life savings in the stock market, the term describes a new and widespread sense of relative deprivation: The realization that a colleague or acquaintance just earned years of your salary in a single month on paper.

Such anxiety is driven by a booming domestic semiconductor industry that has a stranglehold on the global artificial intelligence industry’s supply bottleneck: memory chips. At the market’s peak this year, Samsung Electronics saw its market capitalization surge to a record high of $1.3 trillion, while SK Hynix has since reported a staggering 328 percent year-on-year increase in revenue in its latest third-quarter results. The boom had led many Koreans to believe that borrowing to leverage into these companies offered the quickest and perhaps the only route to profits large enough to pay off their mortgages and secure homes.

Rather than denoting sudden bankruptcy or losing one’s life savings in the stock market, the term describes a new and widespread sense of relative deprivation: The realization that a colleague or acquaintance just earned years of your salary in a single month on paper.

Such anxiety is driven by a booming domestic semiconductor industry that has a stranglehold on the global artificial intelligence industry’s supply bottleneck: memory chips. At the market’s peak this year, Samsung Electronics saw its market capitalization surge to a record high of $1.3 trillion, while SK Hynix has since reported a staggering 328 percent year-on-year increase in revenue in its latest third-quarter results. The boom had led many Koreans to believe that borrowing to leverage into these companies offered the quickest and perhaps the only route to profits large enough to pay off their mortgages and secure homes.

If you were an engineer at one of these companies, you could cash out stock compensation boosted by stock rallies fueled by people’s borrowing, collect enormous bonuses, and secure a mortgage rate of 1.5 percent through company housing-loan programs, alongside support for your children’s tuition and retirement savings. Meanwhile, ordinary Koreans carrying debt and buying homes are left to shoulder the Bank of Korea’s high-interest-rate campaign, with back-to-back rate hikes in July and August, designed to curb inflation and financial risks amid the national semiconductor export boom.

Koreans are increasingly questioning that boom’s broader effect on ordinary households. Economists and scholars are voicing doubts. Even as semiconductors have accounted for nearly half of South Korea’s exports and pushed nominal GDP growth to a nearly 50-year high, the Korea Development Institute slashed its annual job growth forecast from 170,000 to 110,000 in its August report, and the OECD projected the country’s private consumption growth for the year at just 2.2 percent. And if the semiconductor boom eventually bursts, the overall effects for the Korean economy could be devastating.

If the global demand for memory falters, new capacity floods the market, or technological advances curb AI’s appetite for memory, the result would inevitably be a price fall. That would be welcome for buyers such as U.S. tech giants, AI powers, and behemoth enterprises such as Apple. Meanwhile, Samsung and SK Hynix would undoubtedly take a severe hit, although the massive net cash reserves they have amassed will shield them from the kind of bankruptcies that decimated debt-fueled South Korean chaebols during the late-1990s Asian financial crisis.

But while Korea’s memory industry sits on deep liquidity buffers, the true burden of debt in 2026 rests squarely on the shoulders of the country’s households. As an acutely capital-intensive industry, the semiconductor sector’s colossal profits are effectively locked away at the apex of the corporate hierarchy. This classic dual economy structure ensures that wealth fails to permeate adequately through trickle-down effects to the small- and medium-sized enterprises and the service sector, which account for the absolute majority of national employment.

Meanwhile, the South Korean populace has been left to bear the brunt of emerging macroeconomic overheating and inflation. According to the Bank of Korea, household credit breached 2,000 trillion won ($1.49 trillion) in June, and it had already stood at 88.6 percent of GDP at the end of 2025. The onerous mortgage and credit interest burdens induced by the rate hikes are stifling private consumption.

What’s worse, South Korea suffers from one of the highest house price-to-income ratios globally, with ordinary citizens anchoring their massive debt to the real estate market, itself strained by property project-finance troubles. Yet the world’s lowest fertility rate, coupled with rapid demographic aging, leaves a shrinking young generation to absorb these real estate assets, eroding the foundations of domestic demand. And AI, of course, cannot resolve the low fertility rate.

The current prosperity carries the seeds of so-called Dutch disease, in which a booming export sector siphons capital and talent away from other industries and erodes their competitiveness. The result is a hollowing out of the foundations of the domestic economy.

Memory export figures act as a tarp draped over the nation’s roof, temporarily covering the reality of high inflation and weak private consumption. According to OECD projections, South Korea’s potential growth rate will be at a historic low of 1.52 percent in 2027, a figure even lower than the 2.52 percent recorded in 2023, before the memory boom. Fundamentally, South Korea’s 2026 growth is jobless growth. Beneath the tarp of an export boom, the ceiling of its domestic market is caving in while the foundation of its economy continues to erode.

Nowadays, another term is circulating widely among the South Korean populace: yeongkkul, which refers to “trading one’s soul to borrow.” Just as, amid the 19th-century cotton boom, Indian farmers famously surrendered their subsistence fields to chase cotton margins, modern South Koreans are seeking leverage of any kind to outrun the debt, inflation, and housing prices inflated by the memory boom.

China’s spy service bet on lust and arrogance, and Washington was slow to see the risk.

One 25-year-old student interviewed by a South Korean news website diverted a student loan meant for living into stocks. Then he added an emergency bank loan and his part-time earnings to pour about 22 million won borrowed money into leveraged stock-market funds. Another student, aged 24, used fivefold leverage to turn 20 million won saved during military service into nearly 300 million won, only for forced liquidations to wipe out his gains and eat into his original savings within weeks. But he planned to borrow again, still hoping one day to afford an apartment, marriage, and children.

In investing, people resort to excessive leverage because of a fear of missing out. In the context of South Korea’s post-pandemic K-shaped recovery, the anxiety runs deeper: It is a fear of failing to scale a calcified social ladder, of being discarded by the velocity of wealth redistribution. People see their hard work rewarded with a salary that must be saved in its entirety for more than 30 years, without spending a penny on living expenses, to afford to buy an apartment in Seoul. They see a future in which their bosses—whose assets have made them the major beneficiaries of the semiconductor boom—replace them with AI.

The result is not just a fear of missing out on gains, but of missing out on a normal life—a fear of falling behind. Koreans are incapable of outrunning omnipresent economic anxiety and existential dread. A constant sampling is on offer on the anonymous digital platform Blind, where it’s common to read comments such as: “In a society where class divisions are entrenched, the ladder to climb has collapsed”; or “you have to bet your life on leverage”; or “If we miss out on AI boom, is it already too late for us in this lifetime?”

Extreme economic structures are accompanied by extreme risks. Whether AI will transform the world, and whether Asia has overconcentrated its resources in it, are two distinct questions. Just as in Bombay amid the cotton boom of the mid-19th century, the macroeconomic buffers of South Korea’s single-engine semiconductor economy are wearing thin. If the solitary engine of memory stalls, its effects could compound the risks from household debt, real estate vulnerabilities, and demographic pressures to deluge the entire South Korean economy and its population.

The central question of the memory cycle is not about whether it will end, but when. On the optimistic side, if the global memory shortage persists beyond 2030, as projected by SK Hynix’s CEO, South Korea’s economy and its semiconductor companies will usher in a golden age, alleviating the government’s chronic deficit pressures.

Yet a meager trickle of prosperity coupled with persistent jobless growth could potentially spell even deeper despair for ordinary people. Waiting in vain for a trickle that may never come, the people would be left to languish in a continuing drought.

A delayed fallout could be worst of all for most Koreans. The future currently portends a household debt bubble, a weakened domestic demand buffer, and a demographic cliff—ingredients for an economic famine. A memory downturn would depress incomes and asset prices, forcing indebted households to cut spending; spending cuts would deepen a property market downturn and systemic financial distress, ensuring the protracted slump.

Like 1990s Japan, South Korea risks its own “lost decade.” History has demonstrated that for an economy overdependent on a monoculture, the longer that the prosperity overshadows the decay it breeds, the harder the prolonged landing. In boom and bust alike, ordinary Koreans pay the highest price.

Nero Huang is a Taiwanese British author and analyst. His writing covers diplomacy and economics across the Asia-Pacific.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Indonesia’s former chief of police is arrested on suspicion of wiretapping the president, a Florida cruise ship abandons passengers in Cambodia, and we explore the Southeast Asian dimension of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Indonesia’s former chief of police is arrested on suspicion of wiretapping the president, a Florida cruise ship abandons passengers in Cambodia, and we explore the Southeast Asian dimension of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang.

Former police chief charged with spying on president

Shortly after this newsletter was finalized, it was announced vice-president Gibran Rakabuming Raka had tendered his resignation. The dramatic development comes amidst a growing swell to impeach him, and a dramatic wiretap scandal covered below.

Last Tuesday, Indonesia’s former chief of police and Presidential Chief of Staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo and two other police generals were arrested on suspicion of wiretapping President Prabowo Subianto. That same day, the government flooded Jakarta with more than 20,000 troops.

The development is widely seen as heralding a showdown between the president and his rival-turned-ally, former President Joko Widodo, whose son Gibran Rakabuming Raka serves as vice president.

Since the initial revelations, the story has grown more extraordinary. The presidential palace has accused the men, as well as a fourth police general, of treason, which can carry the death penalty.

The government reportedly suspects them of helping foster protests, which have rocked the government over the past two years.

Police alleged the president was one of some 6,000 people—including top politicians, businesspeople, journalists, and activists—illegally surveilled from 2025 until last month. Prabowo himself apparently suspected that he was being tapped for more than a year.

The political implications are explosive. Listyo is widely seen as Widodo’s man and is part of the “Solo Gang,” a group of officials from Widodo’s hometown of Surakarta, where the former president began his political career as mayor.

Listyo is alleged to have operated as something of a Mr. Fix-It for Widodo in delicate political situations, from intraparty disputes to the 2024 election.

Police investigators have rather pointedly announced that neither Widodo nor his son were on the list of those wiretapped.

The move against Listyo seems to herald a wider move against Widodo, whose political relationship with Prabowo has deteriorated steadily since the 2024 election.

In parliament, there is now a growing push to impeach Gibran. The Supreme Court ruled in October that he had failed to properly prove he had graduated high school, which is a requirement to run for the vice presidency, opening the door for parliament to take action.

Widodo himself is keeping schtum. When asked about the arrest of Listyo and the Supreme Court ruling against Gibran, he has limited his responses to platitudes about respecting the legal process. Gibran has also confined himself to broad statements about respecting legal processes and focusing on his job.

Still, Widodo has also been maneuvering to shore up his position. He has effectively taken over the Indonesian Solidarity Party of which his other son, Kaesang Pangarep, is the general chair. Widodo’s enormous personal popularity gives him some potentially powerful cards to play.

Another impact is that Indonesia is looking at tightening legal controls on wiretapping.

This is not the country’s first wiretapping scandal. In 2022, Reuters revealed that Pegasus spyware, created by Israeli cyber-intelligence firm NSO Group, had been used in Indonesia since 2018 to target politicians and other prominent figures. Evidence later suggested the software was being used by Indonesia’s security services.

Despite the scandal, little action was taken and regulations governing the use of wiretaps remain a mess.

More generally this will only contribute to the sense that the wheels are coming off for Indonesia.

The political elite are gearing up for a round of brutal infighting while Indonesia is facing its worst forest fires in a decade, there is growing pressure on government bonds as the energy shock rockets up the price of fuel subsidies, and the third finance minister in two years takes the helm amid protests from a fed up populace.

Abandon ship. More than 200 passengers were abandoned in Cambodia by a Florida cruise-liner company, Villa Vie Residences, last Wednesday. The ship then steamed toward Singapore with 50 crew aboard and it was later impounded.

The ship, Villa Vie Odyssey, is one of a handful of ships worldwide that offers people the opportunity to reside on it long term. The price of permanent residence ranged from $120,000 to $440,000. Rentals started at $3,500 a month.

However, in late October, the company abruptly suspended operations, saying increased fuel costs due to the Iran war had made operations unsustainable. Residents were reportedly given seven hours’ notice.

Problems seem to have been long-running. Passengers recounted two occasions in recent months where the company asked them to pool money to buy fuel for the ship.

And last year—even before the Iran war— Villa Vie Residences was sued for fraud by a plaintiff who had bought a cabin and alleged the company had misrepresented its financial stability.

According to Cambodia’s Ministry of Tourism, there are now 98 passengers left in Cambodia. Others have already left the country.

Growth falters further. Indonesia isn’t the only country where the political elites are playing games while the country struggles.

On Tuesday, the Philippines reported a dismal GDP growth of 2.1 percent. This was below the predicted 3 percent as growth slowed for the fifth consecutive quarter. Inflation also surged to a three-year high of 7.8 percent due to increased fuel prices linked to the Iran war.

Still, the Senate remains absorbed in the impeachment of vice president Sara Duterte. And politicians are pursuing their usual budget shenanigans, unabashed by the enormous scandal that such antics sparked last year.

But why is growth so weak?

The Philippines is extremely dependent on fuel imports, and 90 percent of those imports passed through the Strait of Hormuz prior to the Iran war. This means the war has hit hard, with food and fuel inflation eroding consumption. It has had a major impact on the country’s economy as private consumption accounts for roughly three-quarters of the Philippines’ economy.

The other key factors are a 4.8 percent contraction of the agricultural sector and 4 percent contraction in construction. Bad weather hit the former hard, with nearly all senators urging El Niño to be declared a calamity. Meanwhile, the latter has struggled after a massive scandal last year involving the embezzlement of state funds slowed public investment.

Fatal shooting stirs war memories. One civilian was killed and 23 were injured in an Indonesian Army operation in Aceh last Wednesday. Six army personnel were also injured in the incident.

The spark was the raising of a crescent and star flag during a celebration of the prophet Muhammad’s birthday at Pulo Keunari village in the province of Aceh. The flag is associated with Aceh’s former separatist movement.

Despite a 2005 peace agreement, the flag has remained a symbol of ongoing tensions between the province and the central government. In 2013, the provincial government tried to adopt it as Aceh’s official flag but the central government objected.

Accounts of the sequence of events last Wednesday differ. An aide to Aceh’s governor told The Jakarta Post that soldiers had used a loudspeaker to demand the flag be taken down. A soldier then took down the flag, angering the crowd and sparking the clash. The aide added that the resident who died was killed via a gunshot wound to the chest.

Representatives of the military claimed that their attempts to remove the flag were met with stone throwing. The soldiers and accompanying police responded with riot control equipment, including the firing of blank shots and rubber bullets.

FP’s Most Read This Week

In Cambodia, nearly 24,000 foreigners have been deported after scam center raids over the past year; and 15,000 volunteer for military service this year, which is 5,000 more than needed.

Politicians and royals in Malaysia row over a former prime minister’s house arrest.

Rebels cautiously welcome U.S. peace plans for Myanmar; The Economist reported how rebels’ Starlink terminals are being unpredictably turned off; and Myanmar migrants reject the government’s new IDs.

Philippines police find child abuse material on devices owned by Meghan Markle’s dad.

China buys influence in Thailand media; opposition leaders allege they had their phones hacked ahead of a no confidence vote; a former Miss Thailand is accused of stealing millions from a charity; two Uyghurs face deportation to China; and a book about Thailand’s king is banned on national security grounds.

Vietnam security services may have abducted an Australian and a Norwegian activist in Cambodia; and To Lam visits Japan.

In Focus: Nvidia Scandal’s Southeast Asian Background

The affair between Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, is making headlines worldwide, with the scandal containing an almost filmic mix of geopolitical implications and salacity.

One aspect that bears further scrutiny is the Southeast Asian aspect. Alice Huang was a senior executive, and self-described CEO, of Megaspeed, a company based in Singapore with offices in Malaysia and Indonesia.

The company has been under scrutiny by the U.S. government since 2024 over its alleged sanctions-busting activity smuggling top-end Nvidia chips into China. Singapore also conducted its own investigation and detained Alice Huang in 2025.

The scandal reflects that Singapore, and Southeast Asia more generally, has become a hub for China’s chip sanction-busting efforts on a massive scale. Some smuggle them into China. Other companies operate in a gray zone, building data centers with top-end Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia and then leasing their processing power to China.

Culper Research, a short seller that flagged Jensen Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang back in May, estimated that 20 percent of Nvidia’s compute revenues were driven by China “via illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries.” (You can read more on this topic in FP’s China Brief.)

The latest scandal comes against the background of numerous others. In 2025, the United States launched another investigation into whether DeepSeek had used Nvidia chips smuggled via Singapore.

In May, Taiwan arrested three people suspected of planning to smuggle Nvidia chips into China via an unnamed Southeast Asian country.

In late October, Malaysia estimated that a single syndicate was behind at least five cases where Malaysia authorities had seized smuggled ⁠chips that were cumulatively ​worth more than 100 million ringgit ($24.6 million).

These murky happenings reflect that the region is deeply enmeshed with both China and the United States’ economies and has its own thriving tech ecosystem.

Malaysia has become a thriving data center hub, welcoming investment from both superpowers. The country of 34.4 million people now has half as much artificial intelligence compute power as the entire European Union.

But, for those in the region who have tried to not let geopolitics affect business, or at least turn tensions to their advantage, the walls may be closing in.

Busts in Malaysia reflect ongoing U.S. pressure to crack down. And, on Friday, Bloomberg reported Nvidia was stepping up its tracking of chips in Southeast Asia to crack down on smuggling.

Pressure is also coming from Taiwan. It recently canceled trade talks with Malaysia, which could threaten future investment in the latter’s thriving semiconductor space, due to anger over comments in which Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim appeared to accept China’s right to use force to assimilate Taiwan.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is accused of having an affair with a Chinese spy, Chinese marriage registrations drop, and the United States and China extend their trade truce ahead of an expected meeting between their leaders.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is accused of having an affair with a Chinese spy, Chinese marriage registrations drop, and the United States and China extend their trade truce ahead of an expected meeting between their leaders.

Sign up to receive China Brief in your inbox every Tuesday.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s connections to Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Beijing, exploded into a major scandal this week. On Sunday, he admitted to having an extramarital affair, Nvidia stock dropped, and the company announced it was launching an investigation.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation, is a former executive at Megaspeed—a Singapore-based, China-linked cloud-computing company that is Nvidia’s largest chip customer in Southeast Asia. She became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder in 2023, shortly after the United States under President Joe Biden imposed sweeping chip restrictions on China.

Megaspeed has been under scrutiny since 2024, when the U.S. Commerce Department opened a probe into whether it was diverting Nvidia chips to China. Yet late last year, Jensen Huang convinced U.S. President Donald Trump to allow exports of Nvidia’s advanced H200 chip to China, with the White House taking a 25 percent cut. Many of these chips seem to have been sold to Chinese shell companies.

All of this happened even though both Nvidia and the White House seemingly knew about the risks surrounding Alice Huang for months. Trump administration officials were reportedly warned about her connection to Jensen in a classified memo this spring but took no action. Nvidia, meanwhile, hired a public relations firm specializing in sex scandals last year.

So, how did this happen? It’s possible that Alice Huang is an agent for China’s Ministry of State Security and was tasked with honey trapping Jensen Huang. That would suggest Megaspeed, which has denied all allegations that it engaged in misconduct, was repurposed or even created as a vehicle for intelligence gathering and for illicitly obtaining U.S. chips.

But it’s equally plausible that the relationship came first. Alice Huang’s resume is hard to verify, but she seems to have worked in finance and tech for at least a decade. It wouldn’t be the first time that a billionaire businessman got involved with a younger woman who he convinced himself was a brilliant up-and-comer.

If that is the case, either Chinese intelligence became aware of the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang and pressured her to let them exploit it, or she took it to them herself.

As I have noted before, China’s intelligence apparatus is messy, with multiple competing groups inside the government. That leaves room for outsiders to act as intelligence entrepreneurs. Alice Huang may have been working both Jensen Huang and the Chinese government for her own business edge.

Other questions remain unanswered. One is whether Alice Huang persuaded Jensen Huang to do anything on behalf of the Chinese state that he wouldn’t have done anyway, since Nvidia has a vested interest in access to the Chinese market. That said, Nvidia’s intervention to help halt the Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed looks suspicious. (Megaspeed remains under investigation by the U.S. Justice Department.)

Of course, China also benefits from having a line into White House discussions, and we can’t know what Jensen Huang has told Trump about China behind closed doors. Trump’s China policy has certainly been soft, and he has blithely dismissed this week’s revelations.

But why did the Trump administration disregard the warning from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio about Huang’s connections to Chinese intelligence? And who leaked the story to the press, whether out of patriotic feeling or a desire to disadvantage a rival?

It’s certainly a convenient moment for U.S. politicians to distance themselves from the White House and an increasingly unpopular tech sector. A tougher stance on China may become a distinguishing mark for aspiring Republican leaders. Democrats are also seizing on the news as an example of the White House’s tolerance of corruption and foreign influence, and they will likely push for stronger chip restrictions in the new Congress.

Whatever the outcome of the Huang affair, the state of counterintelligence and cybersecurity under Trump remains dire, underscoring a need for root-and-branch reform.

Marriage registrations drop. China’s demographic crisis remains its biggest long-term problem, and the news keeps getting worse. New data shows marriage registrations falling to an 18-year low for the January-to-September period, with 4.65 million couples tying the knot, a nearly 10 percent drop.

For comparison, the United States sees around 2 million marriages in a full year with a population one-quarter the size of China’s. Childbearing is closely tied to marriage in China, so a low marriage rate also means a low birth rate. Children born outside of marriage and their single mothers still face legal and social obstacles, though their situation has improved in recent years.

Hong Kong dissident receives longer sentence. A Hong Kong court has sentenced Joshua Wong, the imprisoned young activist who became the face of the city’s democracy movement more than a decade ago, to another 10 years for supposed collusion with foreign powers. Wong was due for release in January.

Beijing has an interest in portraying Hong Kong’s democracy activists as tools of outside agents. Wong, however, is a cause célèbre among Western politicians—unlike other equally persecuted dissidents such as Macao’s Au Kam San. If the incoming U.S. Congress chooses to take up human rights issues again, Wong’s case will likely return to the spotlight.

U.S.-China trade truce extended. The U.S.-China trade truce was formally extended by another two months on Monday, running through Jan. 10, 2027. In theory, that leaves room for Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump to ink a more permanent deal if they meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, next week.

Xi is well aware of Trump’s need for some kind of victory, and as a result the Chinese leader is likely to come out ahead in any agreement. Whatever deal they reach may not last long: Domestic political pressure in the United States could blow it up before it is in place, especially in the wake of the Huang case.

Japan squabble deepens. Beijing’s relations with Tokyo remain frozen nearly a year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Japan might be obliged to come to Taiwan’s aid if China invaded the self-ruled island. Even at the provincial level, Chinese officials are competing to look tough on Japan.

That is a perennial popularity-booster with both the Chinese Communist Party and the public, for whom the trauma of Japan’s brutal invasion lingers eight decades on.

Now, flights between the two countries are being slashed. Airlines, mostly Chinese, have scheduled nearly 700,000 fewer seats on China-Japan flights this winter, a drop of around 20 percent compared to last year. Takaichi’s stance remains popular at home, and she may be emboldened if a tougher U.S. policy toward China emerges next year.

James Palmer is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @beijingpalmer.bsky.social

Riding high on the midterm elections’ blue wave, progressive Democrats feel they have the momentum to push through major changes to Washington’s support for Israel.

Analysis and arguments.

“What you are looking at behind me is a mandate,” U.S. Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, who is a Democratic Socialist, said at a Sunday press conference introducing the new progressive House lawmakers. “It is a mandate from the American people to unrig our economy … to tax the rich, to abolish [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement], and to end the genocide” in Gaza.

Riding high on the midterm elections’ blue wave, progressive Democrats feel they have the momentum to push through major changes to Washington’s support for Israel.

Analysis and arguments.

“What you are looking at behind me is a mandate,” U.S. Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, who is a Democratic Socialist, said at a Sunday press conference introducing the new progressive House lawmakers. “It is a mandate from the American people to unrig our economy … to tax the rich, to abolish [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement], and to end the genocide” in Gaza.

Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson have also described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide,” while Sen.-elect James Talarico has called for “stopping offensive weapons sales” to the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

El-Sayed told NPR after his election win: “I’d also like to see us stop selling weaponry that gets used to do the worst things, including genocide and apartheid, to Israel.” And Jackson, who has called Netanyahu a “war criminal,” said in a September interview with a local Maine news station that he doesn’t want the United States sending a “blank check” to the Israeli government anymore.

“I’m not willing to vote for any more bombs, any more aid going [to Israel],” Jackson said at a candidate event in September.

A bill that has already drawn significant progressive Democratic support is the Block the Bombs Act, which would forbid the transfer to Israel of some of the most destructive bombs in the U.S. arsenal, such as so-called bunker-buster bombs. The legislation has attracted more than 80 co-sponsors, and while it has no chance of passing the House this year, it is seen as a good candidate for being reintroduced next year with even more momentum behind it.

“The Block the Bombs Act has been a tremendous organizing vehicle that went further than many of us even thought,” said Hassan El-Tayyab, the legislative director for Middle East policy at the Quaker lobby group Friends Committee on National Legislation, adding that he would “definitely” like to see progressives go further and try to ban even more weapons than the seven munitions listed in the legislation.

Beyond the progressive wing of the incoming freshman class of Democratic lawmakers, many other Democrats with more centrist backgrounds were elected to the House and Senate or are predicted to win their still uncalled races.

But underlining just how far leftward the terrain of the policy debate has shifted among even centrist Democrats is Eileen Laubacher, a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral who served on the National Security Council during the Biden administration. Laubacher, who is on the verge of flipping a red Colorado district, has said U.S. foreign aid to Israel should end, as “Israel has the ability to pay for their own weapons for defense.” However, she believes that the country should be allowed to continue to purchase U.S. weapons on a “case-by-case basis.”

Still, those newly elected progressive and centrist lawmakers won’t be seated until January. And with the 2028 U.S. presidential contest already starting to shape up, the pressure is on for would-be Democratic nominees “to show that they are meeting a new moment in the party,” said Akbar Shahid Ahmed, the author of Crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel’s War in Gaza.

Which means we could see some policy moves before the new Congress is even sworn in.

It wasn’t just Iran. Israel, tariffs, and immigration also loomed large in voters’ minds.

From the Iran war to boat strikes to Ukraine, Democrats now have powerful leverage.

A joint war against Iran might be its apex.

Israel’s backers in Congress this summer included a provision in the must-pass annual defense policy bill directing the Pentagon to increase the role of Israeli technologies in the development of new weapon systems. Backers hope the provision will lead to further integration of the U.S. and Israeli defense industries for years to come.

Democratic Rep. Adam Smith, who is poised to resume the chairmanship of the House Armed Services Committee, has said he would support removing the language from the bill. A compromise version of the massive bill is being hammered out by Senate and House staff and is likely to be presented to lawmakers for a vote on final passage in the next few weeks.

El-Tayyab said he is watching to see if Smith and other Democrats are willing to vote against the entire defense policy bill and risk potentially killing its chances of passage this year if the Israeli technology provision isn’t removed.

“The question is, will they go all the way and refuse to give it the support it needs to pass if that provision remains in there?” El-Tayyab said.

Meanwhile, if recent history is any predictor, there’s a good chance lawmakers will be unable to finish work on fiscal 2027 spending legislation this year. If that happens, then Democrats in January would gain new leverage in the final shaping of the appropriations bills when they take control of the Senate and House. That opens new possibilities for progressives to try to decrease or place limitations on the $3.8 billion in annual security assistance that the United States provides to Israel.

“Given what Donald Trump [said on Nov. 3], what Netanyahu has already said, where the bulk of the caucus is—Republican as well as Democratic—we are headed quickly towards zero financing of American taxpayer subsidies for Israeli arms purchases,” Jeremy Ben-Ami, the president of J Street, a liberal pro-Israel U.S. lobbying group, said in a Thursday press call on the results of the midterms. “The bigger legislative battle will be over what are the conditions placed on Israel if it wants to buy weapons.”

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the sticking points in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, impeachment proceedings against U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Israeli efforts to form a new government.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Russia, Ukraine, and the United States kicked off trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday for the first time in roughly nine months. Day 1 of the two-day conference largely focused on security guarantees for Kyiv in what U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner characterized as an initial step toward building momentum for future dialogue.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the sticking points in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, impeachment proceedings against U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Israeli efforts to form a new government.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Russia, Ukraine, and the United States kicked off trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday for the first time in roughly nine months. Day 1 of the two-day conference largely focused on security guarantees for Kyiv in what U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner characterized as an initial step toward building momentum for future dialogue.

Tuesday’s conversations were “constructive and quite substantive,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who did not attend the talks, wrote on Telegram. Lead Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky similarly expressed hope that this week’s dialogue will “allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine.”

But while negotiators are projecting cautious optimism, neither side appears willing to make concessions, and significant breakthroughs remain out of reach.

Two key sticking points continue to hamper the ongoing peace talks. Ukraine and its European allies insist on an immediate cease-fire before negotiating a wider settlement; Russia, however, rejects such a truce, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arguing that Brussels is just trying to “buy time” for Kyiv. Ukraine also opposes any demands for it to cede territory to Russia, whereas Moscow wants Kyiv to withdraw from the four Russian-occupied regions of the Donbas.

“Nobody believes that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin will stop if we leave the Donbas,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram on Tuesday. “He will pause. And then he will return in a year, two, or five years. And who will be to blame?”

Battle lines have not changed substantially in recent months, and just hours before negotiations began in Abu Dhabi, Russia launched overnight attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, causing outages in six regions. Moscow has repeatedly targeted Kyiv’s power grid in an effort to freeze Ukraine into submission ahead of what is expected to be another cold winter.

But outside pressures could force Moscow and Kyiv to ramp up peacemaking efforts. Prolonged fighting has strained Russia’s wartime economy, Ukraine’s weapons arsenal remains dangerously low on U.S.-made interceptors, and European nations appear increasingly focused on addressing Black Sea security concerns. On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged $56 million to help Bulgaria and Romania launch a Black Sea maritime security hub in the face of deadly drone attacks on cargo ships.

Despite these influences, the likelihood of an imminent peace deal appears to be slim. “There’s a lot of work to be done in that regard,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday during the G-7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris. “It’s not like something that’s on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours or anything like that.”

Hegseth fights back. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth delivered a defiant rebuttal on Tuesday of bipartisan efforts to impeach him for “high crimes and misdemeanors” related to his execution of the Iran war, deadly strikes on alleged drug boats, and capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” Hegseth said, referring to outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, who has led the impeachment push against him on the grounds that Hegseth has abused his power and endangered members of the armed forces.

The defense secretary went on to defend his policy decisions, champion military recruitment, and characterize the proceedings as a direct attack on the armed forces. “These resolutions are a farce,” Hegseth said. “They mock the Constitution. They attack the chain of command, and they criminalize the warfighters who execute lawful orders.”

The comments, made during Hegseth’s first news conference at the Pentagon in six months, came just hours before the House of Representatives was scheduled to hold an initial procedural vote on the impeachment articles.

Still, the Trump administration is not shying away from the fight. “Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Tuesday.

Deadlocked coalition talks. The Israeli Knesset swore in its new lawmakers on Tuesday, just days after President Isaac Herzog tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new government. “You must do everything to avoid a repeat election,” Herzog told lawmakers during the swearing-in ceremony. But with coalition-building efforts still deadlocked, Israel’s incoming parliamentary term could be cut short if both Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fail to form a governing bloc.

Eisenkot’s fragmented opposition has the backing of 67 members in the 120-seat Knesset, compared to Netanyahu’s 46 supporters. However, Eisenkot’s path to power remains uncertain, as many of his mainstream Jewish partners have balked at the idea of entering into a formal alliance with Arab-led parties. Without the latter group’s 19 seats, Eisenkot’s bloc lacks the 61-seat majority that it needs to solidly oppose Netanyahu. But with them, Eisenkot could be risking his long-term political future; the only time that an Israeli governing coalition has included an Arab-led party, the alliance held together for just a little more than a year.

In the meantime, Eisenkot has already vowed to replace the Knesset’s speaker, Amir Ohana. Ohana is a Netanyahu loyalist, so removing him would deal a significant blow to the right wing’s legislative agenda. The opposition hopes to replace him with Matan Kahana, a senior figure in Eisenkot’s party, but the date for such a vote has yet to be determined.

Spotty record. The United Nations Human Rights Council (HRC) agreed on Tuesday to further delay a regular review of the United States’ human rights record after Washington was set to become the first U.N. member to fully reject it. The process will now reconvene in January.

Every four to five years, the world’s top human rights body examines the records of all 193 U.N. member states to determine whether governments are adhering to international human rights standards. According to a new report by the office of the U.N. high commissioner for human rights, the United States appears to have violated several of these norms, from targeting civilian infrastructure in Iran to imposing sanctions on the International Criminal Court that “could undermine accountability for war crimes and crimes against humanity.”

The White House pulled out of the council last year, alleging anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and it has repeatedly skipped its HRC review appointments. “[W]e give no credibility to the agency,” a State Department spokesperson told The Associated Press, calling the council an “irredeemable body” that “makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values.’”

The Booker Prize for fiction was awarded on Monday to The End of Everything, a dystopian satirical novel by British writer M. John Harrison that explores how difficult it is to understand a deteriorating world when you are right in the middle of it. This was the first time that the prestigious award went to a bona fide science fiction writer, though Harrison maintains that the recognition signals how the era of “genres as fences and boxes, pigeonholes, is over.”

British fantasy and science fiction is having something of a moment in literary prizes, FP’s James Palmer told World Brief. Harrison’s disciple, China Miéville, recently won the prestigious Goldsmiths Prize for his more than 1,200-page paranormal Cold War epic The Rouse.

This year’s op-eds and magazine features induce déjà vu. The 2003 invasion of Iraq was supposed to clear the way for a new, democratic Middle East. The 2006 Lebanon War was, in U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice’s phrase, the “birth pangs” of a new Middle East. The Arab Spring in 2009 was its dawn. Hamas’s assault on Israel in 2023 was said to be ushering in a new Middle East.

The U.S. attacks on Iran and the fight over the Strait of Hormuz are said to be bringing yet another one into being. Per U.S. President Donald Trump, “The Middle East will be transformed, and the future of that region has never—I don’t think it’s ever looked brighter.” Foreign Affairs weighed in with an article titled “The Iran Imperative: How America and Israel Can Shape a New Middle East.”

This year’s op-eds and magazine features induce déjà vu. The 2003 invasion of Iraq was supposed to clear the way for a new, democratic Middle East. The 2006 Lebanon War was, in U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice’s phrase, the “birth pangs” of a new Middle East. The Arab Spring in 2009 was its dawn. Hamas’s assault on Israel in 2023 was said to be ushering in a new Middle East.

The U.S. attacks on Iran and the fight over the Strait of Hormuz are said to be bringing yet another one into being. Per U.S. President Donald Trump, “The Middle East will be transformed, and the future of that region has never—I don’t think it’s ever looked brighter.” Foreign Affairs weighed in with an article titled “The Iran Imperative: How America and Israel Can Shape a New Middle East.”

Bloody and chaotic events like the Iran war induce fantasies of comprehensive change, but reality keeps coming up short. As Sam Rayburn, House speaker in an earlier era observed: “Any jackass can kick down a barn, but it takes a carpenter to build one.” Decisive change for the better—in the United States’ conception—demands an actual preponderance of U.S. military power and the ability to convert that power into enduring political arrangements. The United States has imagined itself as wielding both attributes while possessing neither.

The use of force halfway around the world requires political leaders to show that the stakes are commensurate with the cost and risk. That means war aims are framed in extravagant terms that are eventually revealed as detached from quotidian reality.

On the other side, adversaries have agency. They are not passive objects of U.S. power projection or a substrate onto which Washington can project its fantasies. And, ironically, the weakness and fragmentation of regional states makes it more, not less, difficult for an outside power to impose its will.

When the war ends, as it eventually will, Iran will still be a poor, militarized oil exporter with two good friends—China and Russia—and a strong relationship with Iraq. In short, not terribly different than it was before the war.

Iraq will look much as it does now, a state with a hybrid army trying to fend off pressure from Iran, with which it shares a long border, and from the United States, which controls its finances.

Syria will look as it did the day before the United States and Israel struck Iran. It will be poor, shattered by 13 years of civil war and many more of sanctions, run by a sectarian clique, penetrated by outside powers from Turkey to Israel and Saudi Arabia, and still riven by ethnic and religious rivalries.

Lebanon will still be living with the results of the 1989 Taif Accord, which ended Lebanon’s civil war by rebalancing power among its sects and calling for every militia to disarm. Under Syrian tutelage, every militia did except Hezbollah, which kept its guns as “the resistance.” This, in turn, inadvertently but predictably locked in Hezbollah’s status as an armed rival to the state and a picker of pointless fights with its far more powerful neighbor to the south. It will still be engaged in the Sisyphean task of satisfying the International Monetary Fund (IMF) without a parliament willing to decide who absorbs the banking system’s losses.

Egypt, whose economy suffered badly when the Houthis were firing on ships in the Red Sea two years ago, will still be the same authoritarian state, propped up by Gulf largesse and embarked on gigantic infrastructure projects, that it was the day before the war.

Jordan, necessarily careful given the mayhem on its Israeli, Syrian, and Iraqi borders, will look exactly as it did before the war. So, too, will Libya, Morocco, Algeria, and Sudan—which will all be what they were last year and the year before that.

Taken together, bilateral deals risk fueling regional rivalries that undermine U.S. interests.

True, there is the odd beneficiary. The largely unrecognized country of Somaliland has collected strategic rent from the UAE, Israel, and the United States as a geographical counterweight to Houthi domination of the Bab el-Mandeb. But one breakaway enclave doth not a new Middle East make.

What about the Arab side of the Gulf? Every state there has been pummeled by Iranian missiles and drones. Every Gulf state but Oman will see its economy shrink this year. The IMF projects contractions of 16.7 percent for Kuwait, 15.6 percent for Qatar, 11.3 percent for Bahrain, and smaller ones for the UAE and Saudi Arabia. The IMF expects a sharp rebound next year, but only on the generous assumption that traffic through the strait returns to normal during 2027. Crude flows are already at prewar levels even if the process of moving it is cumbersome.

Most of these states are talking about huge new pipeline or transportation projects, whether from Abqaiq to Yanbu, Habshan to Fujairah, or Basra to Baniyas, to make their export routes redundant and therefore more resilient to Iranian or Houthi attacks. Plans for such projects are nothing new for them, and most will probably never be built. All will rush to rebuild their own air defenses now that the United States has shown itself to be relatively ineffectual as a wager of wars but still an eager arms dealer, source of intelligence, and defense industrial partner. This won’t have a significant effect on their militaries, which, except for the UAE, do not have an expeditionary function, but it will improve their resilience in the face of future Iranian and Houthi attacks.

How does this war end? One way is for the Trump administration to sign a concessionary cease-fire that restores normal traffic through the strait and frees the U.S. Navy to redeploy. A Democratic U.S. Congress could hasten that choice. It would not stop the war outright, since Trump would veto a war powers resolution, and Democrats would likely lack the votes to override him.

A fight over funding would still make the war harder to sustain but hand Trump a win-win situation. Instead of going down as the president who lost the war he started, he could blame the loss on Democrats. The Gulf states would then fall back on their traditional, prudent, and strategy of hedging. They would strike side deals with Iran to fully open the strait while holding onto as much U.S. intelligence, technology, weaponry, and expertise as they can, even if the Fifth Fleet were no longer headquartered in Bahrain.

This would look a lot like the over-the-horizon posture—whereby the United States keeps its forces just outside the region, mostly at sea and at a few access points, and relies on prepositioned equipment and basing rights to surge in a crisis instead of stationing large forces on land. This stance served a strategy of offshore balancing, which kept the United States out of a region’s day to day, intervening only when a single power threatened to dominate a region that it considers vital.

The other way is that the war does not end, at least not soon. This seems to be the outcome that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth prefer, and on its own terms, it is working. Bessent’s satellite imagery shows no tankers at Kharg Island, and Gulf crude, moving under U.S. escort, is leaving the region at or above prewar volumes.

Why settle? Because Iran gets a vote. A strategy of economic attrition gives Tehran every reason to show that the attrition will cost Washington more than it is willing to pay. That is the purpose of the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia, the attacks at Dhahran and Dammam, and the threats against U.S. bases. Since the midterm elections, the president has been signaling a disinclination to escalate pending the outcome of talks with Iran, while insisting that the blockade will continue. This in turn will leave the door open for Iranian attacks on shipping that could prompt the escalation Trump is seeking to avoid. A third carrier group is on its way, ensuring that he will have the combat power he needs to follow through.

If the war does drag on, something will change, though not in the way that the prophets of a new Middle East intend. When the Theodore Roosevelt arrives in the Arabian Sea, three quarters of the Navy’s deployed carriers will be allocated to the war. With the arrival of the Roosevelt in the Andaman Sea, there is now no U.S. carrier in the Western Pacific. A region that absorbs this much U.S. power is changing the United States’ position in Asia. The Middle East is remaking U.S. strategy, rather than the other way around.

The only other major player is Israel. For years, observers have noted the rightward drift of Israeli politics, the collapse of left-wing parties, a more militant posture toward the region, tense relations with the United States, hardening opposition to a two-state solution, and the development of a long-range strike capability meant to disable Iran’s nuclear and missile programs and, as it turned out, to kill many of its leaders. This trend was likely to end in war sooner or later; but it was Hamas’s late leader, Yahya Sinwar, who pushed the button.

The result has been catastrophic for Gazans and for Palestinians more generally. It drove Israeli forces across the borders of Syria and Lebanon and created the widespread impression that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lured Trump into the war. These events have accelerated the souring of American opinion about Israel and the U.S.-Israeli relationship in ways that were anticipated a decade ago—particularly the narrowing of political support for the relationship and its transformation into partisan football—well before the current Gulf War began.

This latest pointless war has demonstrated both the persistent American desire for a new Middle East and the inability to make it happen. The 2016 and 2024 U.S. elections were, in part, a referendum on U.S. interventions in the region. Trump appeared to understand that and made it part of his pitch: “I’m not going to start a war,” he declared in 2024, “I’m going to stop wars.”

But restraint has never really been his lodestar, as long as others were footing the bill and he could posture as a warlord. That’s too bad for dead Iranian schoolgirls, U.S. soldiers, and families back home struggling with war-induced inflation.

As for a new Middle East, let alone a better one, the experiment to run is not to test yet again whether military intervention leaves the region better off, since the answer to that is known, but whether less intervention does so.

That experiment is likely to be run by the next U.S. administration, which will answer to a public that sees the Iran war as a mistake, a gratuitous return to the military adventurism that voters repudiated in 2008. Colossal debt and demand for spending on the lives of ordinary people will squeeze the defense budget. Congress, for better or worse, will be looking to the security of the Western Pacific and Europe first. The Middle East will have survived a great deal of American help. It may yet survive less of it.

Steven Simon is a distinguished fellow and visiting professor at Dartmouth College and the author of Grand Delusion: The Rise and Fall of American Ambition in the Middle East. He spent 20 years in the U.S. government, holding senior positions in the State Department and at the National Security Council. X: @sns_1239
