https://www.foreignaffairs.com/north-kor.title: Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/north-kor.author: Stephen E. Biegun, Emma Chanlett-Avery
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/north-kor.text:
STEPHEN E. BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021. He is a Distinguished Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

And Now He Needs a New Strategy

Stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery

Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind. In recent months, the U.S. president has made comments to the media suggesting he is in communication with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In an August 17 Truth Social post, for instance, Trump announced that the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea. The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”

Trump has not been subtle about his desire to restart diplomacy with Kim. With an eye on his legacy and the war with Iran stalemated, he is eager to notch a foreign policy win. During his first term, Trump held two historic U.S.–North Korean summits aimed at denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula—but both foundered because of the countries’ disparate expectations for the terms of a deal. Since his reelection, Trump has been looking to reopen talks with Kim. The ball is now in Pyongyang’s court, and Kim has signaled, if not an eagerness for renewed engagement, at least an unwillingness to rule it out. In August, after Trump insisted for the second time that he was in touch with Pyongyang, Kim Yo Jong—the leader’s influential sister—released a statement that read: “Regarding the reports from Washington about recent communication between the top leaders of North Korea and the U.S., I am completely unaware of such matters. It has been stated on numerous occasions that our head of state holds fond personal memories and positive feelings toward Trump. The relationship between the leaders remains excellent.” Although this is far from an agreement to meet, Kim Jong Un is not closing the door.

If leader-to-leader talks materialize, Trump may believe his personal rapport with Kim will yield a deal. But he will be facing a very different North Korea than the one at their last meeting in 2019. The fallout from unfinished diplomacy during Trump’s first term, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global trends such as the sharp escalation in U.S.-Chinese strategic rivalry and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement. Meanwhile, North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand. Facing an emboldened Pyongyang, Trump can no longer fall back on the same concessions and negotiation tactics he used in previous talks.

For a U.S.–North Korean summit to be successful, the United States must approach it with well-defined strategic goals and a clear understanding of what concessions it is willing to make. Washington should shift its focus away from denuclearization, at least in the short term, to concentrate on more achievable nuclear arms control and safety measures. The United States should also maintain a capable troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and reiterate its security assurances—particularly its nuclear-deterrence guarantees—to regional allies such as South Korea and Japan.

Our editors’ top picks, delivered free to your inbox every Friday.

* Note that when you provide your email address, the Foreign Affairs Privacy Policy and Terms of Use will apply to your newsletter subscription.

Although diplomacy with North Korea has historically been difficult, Trump is eager to meet with Kim, and both sides want to avoid pushing the Indo-Pacific toward nuclear proliferation or all-out war. Careful engagement with Pyongyang could defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula and lay the groundwork for a more stable security landscape.

Since the U.S.–North Korean summit in 2019, the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have reshaped the Indo-Pacific in ways that strengthen Kim’s hand. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has drawn Washington’s focus away from Asia as, for the third time in the past quarter century, U.S. strategic attention and military assets have surged to the Middle East. The last American aircraft carrier stationed in the Indo-Pacific departed for the Persian Gulf in August, and U.S. strikes on Iran have rapidly depleted American munitions stockpiles. Washington’s Indo-Pacific allies, already strained by Trump’s abrupt policy shifts and punishing tariffs, are now concerned about deteriorating deterrence. Asian economies—many of which are deeply dependent on Middle Eastern energy supplies—have contracted as the Strait of Hormuz has remained compromised. Amid signs of further American retrenchment, U.S. allies and partners are increasingly skeptical about Washington’s commitment to the region.

Even more consequential is Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which has benefited North Korea in numerous ways. Moscow and Pyongyang’s once dormant relationship has flourished as Kim has sent thousands of munitions to replenish Russia’s depleted stockpiles and thousands of soldiers to fight and die in the ongoing ground war. Images of the new memorial to the Korean People’s Army soldiers who have perished in the invasion suggest an already significant loss of North Korean lives. In return, Pyongyang has received generous assistance from Moscow in violation of international sanctions, including abundant financial support for Kim’s regime and technology transfers that have enhanced North Korean military capabilities and may help Pyongyang more accurately deliver intercontinental ballistic missiles aimed at the United States. Russian patronage allows Kim to shower his regime’s elites with the economic benefits needed to cement their loyalty.

Still, it is worth questioning how durable this partnership is. After more than four years of grinding warfare with no end in sight, Moscow is increasingly isolated and may be in a poor position to continue supporting Pyongyang. Russia’s preoccupation with Ukraine has allowed China to expand its presence in Central Asia, for instance, and Turkey to deepen its influence in Azerbaijan. Russian aggression has spurred Armenia and Moldova to look westward, and hundreds of thousands of young Russian men have fled the country to avoid military conscription while over a thousand Western companies have left. International sanctions are starving Russia of badly needed capital and technology, and Russian war policies have created huge imbalances and inflation, possibly with worse to come for the Russian economy. If North Korea continues to actively support Moscow in this war, and Russia fails or is defeated, the world will become a much more hostile place for Pyongyang.

Russia and North Korea’s deepening ties have already begun to reshape China’s interests in the region. Beijing is still Pyongyang’s most important partner, but the dynamic has changed considerably in recent years. Beijing previously saw denuclearization as a top priority on the Korean Peninsula—a shared objective, and at times a rare area of cooperation, with the United States. It disliked the destabilizing impact that North Korea’s pursuit of nuclear weapons had on tensions between the North and South and expended political capital responding to international condemnation of Pyongyang. Between 2006 and 2017, Beijing agreed to a series of UN Security Council resolutions that imposed sanctions and other restrictions on Pyongyang in response to six North Korean nuclear tests. Now, pressed to maintain its influence in Pyongyang amid a growing Russian–North Korean security relationship—and with the rest of the world distracted by other geopolitical crises—China has gone silent on the issue. When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June to reassert his influence, denuclearization was not publicly mentioned. China’s new approach will make U.S. engagement on this issue more challenging and risks driving other regional powers, such as South Korea and Japan, to reconsider their own policies on the deployment or development of nuclear weapons.

Whether Pyongyang reengages with the United States may also depend on how much North Korea relies on China for economic support. Much of North Korean commerce passes through China, and although Beijing and Pyongyang’s relationship appears fairly stable, it remains wary and transactional, with each side skeptical of the other’s motives. North Korea may seek to reengage with the United States to counterbalance its overdependence on China, or as a hedge against Russia’s failure in its war with Ukraine. Conversely, as Trump and Xi upgrade and stabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, China could step in to broker the next Trump-Kim meeting.

The Kim dynasty has long vexed U.S. policymakers. Washington has sought multiple deals with North Korea, including during Trump’s first-term summits with Kim, but missteps and mistrust on both sides derailed them. Pyongyang has proved resilient to both U.S. and international sanctions. Indeed, during the COVID-19 pandemic, North Korea sealed its borders and deprived itself far more severely than sanctions could, yet it still survived. U.S. congressional interventions on human rights and humanitarian aid, meanwhile, have mostly failed to change North Korea’s behavior. Pyongyang has also cushioned the impact of sanctions by engaging in cybertheft, such as its $6.3 billion heist against the cryptocurrency exchange Binance this October. All the while, Pyongyang has steadily advanced its military capabilities and expanded its nuclear arsenal.

Although Washington’s previous attempts to rein in North Korea have failed, Trump’s renewed eagerness to meet with Kim and his unorthodox approach to foreign policy could provide a new opening for diplomacy. Trump has cultivated a direct relationship with Kim, shunning the bureaucratic negotiations that usually precede a deal. While a performative summit alone would be of little benefit to U.S. interests, Washington could use reengagement with Pyongyang to thaw inter-Korean relations and stabilize the peninsula by slowing or freezing North Korea’s nuclear buildup. Those goals may seem conventional, but as regional tensions worsen and Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal grows, they are essential to averting potentially catastrophic conflict.

Three questions cast a shadow over the possibility of renewed engagement between the United States and North Korea. First is the specific purpose of restarting engagement: What is the goal? Second is how to reopen communications. Despite Trump’s claims, there is no real proof that he has recently interacted with Kim. All evidence suggests the last contact between American and North Korean officials was in 2019, and it may be challenging to break a seven-year drought. Third is what are the incentives and tradeoffs the United States would be willing to consider as part of a negotiation—the same issue that bedeviled U.S. and North Korean officials in Hanoi.

One possible formula for progress is focusing, at least temporarily, on steady arms control and international safety controls rather than the elusive goal of denuclearization. Denuclearization should remain Washington’s ultimate aspiration. But in the meantime, a North Korea awash with even more nuclear weapons makes the world only more dangerous. This approach will require serious diplomacy to minimize second-order consequences, particularly to avoid weakening U.S. alliances in the Indo-Pacific or triggering a collapse of the nuclear nonproliferation regime among nations that might see their only recourse as acquiring their own nuclear weapons. China, and perhaps even Russia, may concur with Washington on this point, and a shared desire to avoid more nuclear states in East Asia could help restart engagement.

Kim has substantially more leverage now than in earlier encounters with Trump. Reopening communication will require using a mix of positive and negative assurances to convince him that he is unlikely to get a better chance to strike a deal. Kim may press the United States to scale back aspects of its cooperation with South Korea—such as joint military exercises and support for Seoul’s pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines—as preconditions for a meeting with Trump. Kim may even propose his own assurances of peace on the peninsula in exchange for a reduction of U.S. military forces in South Korea, although it is unclear whether Trump would agree to such conditions.

In the worst-case scenario, Kim may take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to make a deal to extract weighty concessions from the United States. Kim has little reason to meet with Trump now, unless he calculates that he can secure major terms such as de facto recognition as a nuclear state, reduced sanctions, or a complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the peninsula. Kim would likely insist that there be no discussion of denuclearization, North Korea’s support for the invasion of Ukraine, Pyongyang’s human rights abuses, or a final accounting for Japanese citizens kidnapped by North Korea under the rule of Kim Il Sung. Granting such concessions would end the U.S.–South Korean alliance.

To ensure North Korea does not exploit the Trump administration, Washington must carefully consider what tradeoffs it is willing to make. Lifting sanctions, abandoning or delaying the denuclearization process, temporarily accepting North Korea as a nuclear state, and reducing the U.S. military presence in South Korea are all long-standing demands of Kim’s regime that are likely on the table. Although lifting international sanctions would require UN Security Council consensus, Trump may be willing to reduce unilateral U.S. sanctions, which he considers an obstacle to better bilateral relations and which have been ineffective in stemming Pyongyang’s nuclear advances.

Although denuclearization has been a major talking point for U.S. administrations since the early 1990s, the Trump administration may need to set it aside, at least in the short term. Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities have increased since Trump’s 2018 and 2019 summits with Kim, suggesting that the stalemate caused by continued U.S. demands for the full-scale dismantlement of North Korea’s nuclear program may have given Kim time and space to grow his arsenal. Even if denuclearization remains a long-term U.S. priority—and it should—pragmatism is essential to reducing the threat posed by Kim’s regime. In exchange for stepping away from denuclearization, Trump should demand that Kim freeze any further expansion of his arsenal and explore possibilities for greater strategic stability, including renewed inter-Korean dialogue, transparency and confidence-building efforts, security measures that bolster nuclear facilities’ safety and guard against accidents, and strict adherence to nonproliferation. Trump must make it clear to Kim that an unconstrained expansion of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal will pressure South Korea and Japan to deploy nuclear weapons on their territory and possibly develop their own.

Regardless of Kim’s demands, the United States must preserve its troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and continue joint military exercises with South Korea as long as the threat of North Korean aggression persists. The mantra of U.S. troops in South Korea is “ready to fight tonight.” Joint military exercises keep U.S. and South Korean forces prepared for combat, which is essential to deterring North Korean attacks. It would be dangerous and irresponsible to send American soldiers, sailors, marines, and airmen to the peninsula without ensuring peak readiness. Instead of withdrawing troops, the United States should offer confidence-building measures to North Korea—practices that reduce the risk of conflict breaking out because of misjudgment. These could include military-to-military engagement and security reassurances among the United States, South Korea, and North Korea, or greater transparency around military exercises—allowing observers on a reciprocal basis, for example. Sustaining Washington’s alliance with South Korea and avoiding cascading nuclear proliferation are critical to U.S. interests in the region. American negotiators must remind Kim that the U.S. military presence and its extended nuclear-deterrence guarantees for Seoul and Tokyo hold back even larger conventional military—and possibly nuclear—buildups in the region.

Finally, North Korea and the United States—and perhaps, in time, South Korea and Japan—should sustain diplomatic engagement by agreeing to assign diplomats to each other’s capitals through reciprocal liaison offices, which would maintain relations without granting full diplomatic recognition. In 2018 and 2019, the two sides discussed housing such diplomats in the German Embassy in Pyongyang and the Swedish Embassy in Washington. Liaison offices would also stabilize and prolong the communication necessary to quietly work through complex negotiations.

If North Korea rejects Trump’s overtures, the United States is not without options. Washington could pressure the Kim regime by intensifying the scale and tempo of joint military exercises with South Korea; deploying American armaments, including short-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and possibly nuclear weapons, to South Korea and Japan; and pursuing a new campaign to choke off North Korea’s economic resources through sanctions and interdiction. The United States could also deploy additional air defense assets to Japan and South Korea, including THAAD air defense radar systems and interceptors. Washington and its allies could dramatically expand efforts to undermine Kim’s rule by mounting sustained criticisms of North Korea’s dangerously large nuclear weapons arsenal and its use of international criminal enterprise to steal from and economically defraud other nations, which could spur other countries to curb their material or diplomatic support for North Korea or more aggressively sanction Kim’s regime.

Beyond short-term negotiations, a fourth question is less complicated but just as important: What role should Japan and South Korea play in U.S. engagements with North Korea? Many past administrations, both Republican and Democratic, have considered coordination with allies essential to establishing a durable solution on the Korean Peninsula. But Trump’s antipathy toward alliances suggests close consultation with South Korea and Japan is unlikely. Their absence from the negotiating table may actually accelerate U.S.–North Korean engagement, because coordination across allied governments can be unwieldy and slow, and Pyongyang has not been receptive to past overtures by Seoul and Tokyo. Although South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi both rhetorically back engagement with North Korea, Pyongyang has bluntly rejected their outreach.

Even if Seoul and Tokyo are not directly engaged in U.S.–North Korean diplomacy, they would still likely welcome a U.S.-led deal with Kim if it protects their core security interests. But a deal with Kim that ignores American allies’ concerns would be dangerous. South Korea harbors an appetite to develop its own nuclear arsenal, particularly if it feels U.S. security protections are receding. Should Seoul move in that direction, Tokyo would almost certainly reconsider its own nonnuclear status, potentially igniting a nuclear arms race in Asia. Given North Korea’s long-standing hostility toward both Japan and South Korea, proliferation would destabilize the Indo-Pacific and leave the global nonproliferation regime in tatters.

Any deal, even one that addresses Seoul’s and Tokyo’s core interests, will likely need to be paired with American security reassurances to allies’ governments and publics. Japan and South Korea must continue building their own conventional defense capabilities while the United States sustains its commitment to defending its Asian allies—especially extended nuclear deterrence. The United States must pursue delicate, nuanced diplomacy to avoid creating a stronger, legitimized North Korea; straining its alliances with Seoul and Tokyo; and debilitating the international nonproliferation regime.

Despite the risks of U.S.–North Korean engagement, the time may be ripe to break the diplomatic paralysis that has allowed Pyongyang to advance its military capabilities for so long. The last two years of Trump’s presidency—particularly his summitry calendar in late 2026—will bring him to Asia, potentially facilitating a meeting with Kim. Such a visit would present the best chance for the kind of performative, high-profile meeting that both Trump and Kim favor.

Trump is the ultimate iconoclast in traditional great-power politics, as evidenced by his shifting relationships with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which could shape Washington’s engagement with Pyongyang. Still, there may be a way to leverage Trump’s affection for Kim, and Kim’s recent restraint in criticizing the United States, to outline a deal that arrests the growing threat of North Korean nuclear weapons.

The bruising Republican defeat in the U.S. midterm elections could also change North Korea’s diplomatic calculus, especially because it suggests Trump’s political standing in the United States has faltered, and he may struggle to deliver the results Kim seeks. Trump may force the issue, however, and propose a meeting with Kim after the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China. It would not be surprising for Trump to suggest that this meeting take place in Pyongyang, putting Kim on the spot. If leader-to-leader talks occur, both sides should remember the central lesson from Trump’s first-term summits: engagement without sufficient preparation and clearly defined goals is not enough to strengthen security and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

Growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific raise the prospect of a much darker future, where conditions on the Korean Peninsula remain unchanged and Asia’s entanglements in European and Middle Eastern conflicts metastasize into a new world war—perhaps ignited in Taiwan, the South China Sea, or the Korean Peninsula. Even if no war breaks out, in just a few years the United States could find itself in a world where Asia’s five current nuclear states are joined by two, three, or more new players.

But this future is not inevitable. All the leaders engaged in North Korean security debates—from Lee and Takaichi to Xi and Putin—want to avoid such escalation. Even the North Koreans surely recognize this is the most dangerous path. This shared goal means diplomacy is still possible, despite formidable challenges. For all Trump’s idiosyncrasies, one should take his desire to peacefully end tensions on the Korean Peninsula at face value. He has made his intentions clear. What happens next is up to Chairman Kim.

Spain's first general strike in 14 years is making headlines. El País reports that trade unions intend to "test their strength in the face of attacks from the right". The unions are counting on the "support" of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's government to secure progress on housing, the issue at the heart of their demands. Meanwhile, the country is still in mourning following last month's deadly rail disaster, and in just two days, the official campaign for the snap general election will begin. El Mundo views the call for a general strike as "a deeply worrying democratic anomaly". The paper accuses the Socialist government of "encouraging a mobilisation against the consequences of its political failure, in the hope of gaining an electoral advantage". El Mundo says that this comes at a time when polls show the right and far right gaining momentum.

Protests in France are continuing as well, and trade unions are calling for the mobilisation to continue. Aujourd'hui en France says we are seeing an escalation of violence, adding that school staff, the authorities and parents are concerned about the deteriorating atmosphere in schools. Right-wing paper Le Figaro headlines: "The French stand united behind the police". Le Figaro says a large majority believe that the police are not adequately equipped to deal with rioters and that the government has failed to ensure public safety, notably during the October 17 unrest.

In England, another sexual predator has been exposed: comedian and former "Britain's Got Talent" judge David Walliams. Walliams has been accused of preying on young women for sex. This was revealed by a joint investigation between the Guardian and ITV that showed how the comedian groomed fans as young as 15. The Telegraph writes that Walliams first faced questions about his behaviour after an investigation by the paper revealed that he had been accused of "harassing" junior employees at his publisher, HarperCollins. Last year, reporters uncovered that the author's own publisher had already investigated him and that staff had also been interviewed. The Hollywood Reporter explains that the best-selling children's author had previously sought an injunction to prevent revealing his identity – over fears that he would be "highly likely" to kill himself. Walliams denies all the allegations and says abusing his power is something that he "never did".

Finally, we bring you a heartwarming story from The Washington Post. Kim Reynolds noticed that her Doberman, Saraya, was behaving oddly around her baby Alexander. Saraya was whining and pacing near the 5-month-old infant, licking his face and becoming increasingly distressed. Later that day, the baby started crying uncontrollably. Then, thinking back to her dog's behaviour, Reynolds decided to take Alexander in for emergency care. It turned out that the baby's heart rate was dangerously high and he was diagnosed with a syndrome that can cause dangerous heart palpitations. Such a fast heart rate is very dangerous if undetected. If the dog hadn't alerted Reynolds, she might never have suspected that something was wrong. An expert told the paper that dogs can detect this sort of problem because of two things: their heightened senses and their deep affection for humans.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Wave of hoax bomb threats sent to schools in UK, Ireland and Italy
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Authorities in Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of ​Ireland said a threatening email which was sent to a large number of schools on Wednesday was a hoax originating ​from ‌outside the United Kingdom.

The emails were ⁠reported after the evacuation of at least 300 schools in Italy.

Irish ‌police said they were aware of a "generic communication" sent ⁠to a number of schools and they had assessed that the threat was not credible and ​that there should be no evacuation.

Over 300 ‌schools in Northern Ireland were also sent a threatening email which was being treated as a hoax, police ‌in the British province said, adding that the email originated from outside the ​UK.

"We take incidents of this nature very seriously and we understand the concern in the community, school communities ​and for students and parents," Assistant Chief Constable Anthony McNally ​said.

Irish police noted that there ​had recently been "increased activity in hoax and non-credible bomb threats", and advised the public ​to contact officers if they receive one.

READ MORE
France investigating if bogus bomb threats against airlines linked to 'foreign powers'

Police in Scotland said the messages were immediately assessed and treated as hoaxes.

"Our enquiries have established that there is nothing ⁠to suggest that they represent a credible threat or that there ⁠is any wider ​threat to the public," their statement said.

Italian Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara told La7 TV channel that the alerts were presumed ‌to be hoaxes, adding that the number of schools affected was expected to rise.

"Following ‌a nationwide bomb alert, we wish to inform you that all students have been taken to a safe area and remain under the supervision of teaching staff," one school in Rome informed parents through a ‌messaging app.

In Italy, many parents had to drop what they were doing and hurry to the school ⁠gates to collect children.

"My daughter Dafne started crying because the kids did not understand what was happening, and she was still shaken when I picked her up," said Nensi Bego, parent of a child ​at the Mazzini middle school in Rome.

"This is so annoying. It's obvious it's just ‌a hoax that disrupts lessons and disrupts everyone's day."

The email received in Italy was signed "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan", according to a copy of the message seen ​by Reuters.

The same purported author claimed responsibility for email bomb threats sent on Friday to newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria.

READ MORE
UK man arrested over alleged cyberattack that disrupted major European airports

Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said Wednesday's threats were "part of a strategy that is ​quite clear by now: to spread fear and create anxiety", according to Adnkronos news agency.

"It is not ​always the work of foreign countries or hostile entities. There are ​also attention-seekers and lunatics who, at a time like this, cannot wait to unleash terror in a city or a region," he added.

Italian police ​forces are investigating the matter, a spokesperson for Rome police said.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

The emails were sent to schools in Italy and Northern Ireland. The same purported author claimed responsibility for email bomb threats sent on Friday. Italian Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the alerts were presumed ‌to be hoaxes.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Pope Leo to end Argentina tour with outdoor mass before Peru 'homecoming'
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
Pope Leo will wrap ​up his visit to Argentina on Wednesday during his 12-day South America tour with a final event expected to draw millions, before travelling to Peru in an emotional homecoming for the first Peruvian citizen to lead the Catholic Church.

Leo, on a three-nation tour through November 17, will celebrate a morning outdoor mass at the ​shrine of Our Lady ‌of Lujan, Argentina's most important Catholic devotional site, where throngs of pilgrims have been gathering for days to see him.

He ⁠will also visit one of the country's largest penitentiaries, reflecting his focus on marginalised groups amid a three-day visit to Argentina that has highlighted the Church's criticism of President Javier Milei's cuts to social programs.

READ MORE
'Go forth and be saints!' Pope Leo tells Argentines

The pope, who ‌has US and Peruvian citizenship, will then begin a personal leg of the most intense overseas trip by a pope in ⁠decades, returning to the place he served as a missionary for about 20 years before becoming pope last year.

The Peru visit, expected to include emotional scenes as the pope visits old friends and spends three days in the northern city of Chiclayo, where he ​was bishop from 2015 to 2023, will also test how directly he is willing to wade into the politics of ‌his adopted nation.

Leo is due to land at Peru's Callao Air Base at 5:30pm (2230 GMT). After a brief welcome ceremony, he will head to the presidential palace for a closely watched address to President Keiko Fujimori, who was elected this year in one of Peru's closest elections, marred ‌by fraud accusations and vote-counting delays.

Fujimori is the daughter of former President Alberto Fujimori, who was in office from 1990 to 2000 and died in 2024. Her victory marked the return of one of Peru's most ​influential and polarising political dynasties.

In 2017, Leo, then known as Bishop Robert Prevost, criticised the late Fujimori's pardon. He said the former president, who had been convicted of serious human rights abuses, should personally seek forgiveness from victims if Peru was to achieve genuine reconciliation.

Keiko Fujimori leaned heavily on her father's ​political legacy during her presidential campaign.

"It's not just a pastoral visit by the pope to his flock, but a visit to his home," said Jose ​Luis Guadalupe Pérez, an academic at Peru's Pacific University. Leo's intimate knowledge of Peru, he added, means "he is ​bound to step on some toes".

Peru has prepared for the homecoming with fervour: a 14-metre (46-foot) statue depicting Leo with outstretched arms towers over a seaside park in Callao, merchants in Lima sell pope-themed shirts and souvenirs, and inmates ​at the country's largest women's prison have stitched velvet dolls bearing his likeness.

The Peru leg caps Leo's first tour of South America as pope, where he has appealed for political dialogue and greater unity across a divided region.

Martin Cassinelli, an analyst at the Atlantic Council, said Leo's Peruvian roots give him an unusual ability to speak about its political past.

"There's no other country where the pope is as attuned to the domestic politics of that country than Peru," ⁠Cassinelli said. "If there's anything that could potentially be at odds with the current Fujimori government, it would be a reflection on the past."

Relations between the late Fujimori's government and sectors of the Catholic ⁠Church were frequently tense, particularly ​over human rights during the state's fight against the Maoist Shining Path insurgency. Church figures also opposed the 1995 amnesty for members of the security forces accused of rights abuses.

(FRANCE 24 and Reuters)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/r.title: Regional flights cost 173pc more per km than city routes, inquiry finds
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/r.author: Kristy Sexton-McGrath
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Travel and Tourism

The cost of regional air travel is in the spotlight after a scathing report from the Productivity Commission. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

The Productivity Commission has delivered a scathing report into the spiralling cost of regional air travel.

One submission revealed a family of four paid the equivalent of a single return trip to Europe for a one-hour flight.

The commission wants governments to stop propping up individual airlines and open subsidised routes to tender.

Regional Australians are paying excessive fares to travel within their own state, with a new Productivity Commission report exposing the extraordinary cost of domestic travel.

One family of four paid $3,200 for a one-hour flight from Kalgoorlie to Perth — the cost of a single return airfare to Europe.

The interim report, released today, found short regional flights were, on average, 173 per cent more expensive per kilometre than major city routes.

Regional communities are being hit with flights on average 173pc more expensive per kilometre than city routes. (ABC News: Mary Lloyd)

"Previous government inquiries have looked at the issue, but until now we haven't had the data or the evidence to understand what really sets the prices."

The report, commissioned by Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers, comes as airlines continue to scrap regional routes across the country, due to high fuel costs and lack of demand.

The Determinants of Regional Airfares report received more than 100 submissions, with some revealing the devastating consequences of expensive airfares for families and remote communities.

The Northern Territory's Yalu Aboriginal Corporation warned high airfares were leaving children disconnected from their families.

"Expensive airfares mean that children in care are deprived of the opportunity to thrive and indeed will continue to suffer the effects of being disconnected from family, well into their adult years," the submission said.

Customers say outback airfares are not "fair dinkum" amid a delayed review and calls for airlines to be more transparent.

Regional Development Australia Mid North Coast in NSW said a last-minute airfare could be beyond the reach of some families.

Its submission highlighted problems related to custody disputes, and warned the cost of flights could prevent parents from attending court hearings, mediation and supervised visits with their children.

Missed appointments could potentially lead to "adverse legal actions including removal of children from family care".

The report also included evidence from a remote resident unable to afford flights to take their daughter for a critical medical appointment, stating the Patient Assistance Transport Scheme (PATS) did not cover the costs.

"There are things my daughter is supposed to attend but because PATS don't cover it and it cannot be done up here, I just haven't taken her," the submission stated.

One Western Australian resident said even with a state government scheme limiting the cost of regional airfares, a return flight to Perth could still cost about $600.

The report found more than 90 per cent of regional and remote passengers flew with the Qantas Group or Virgin Australia in 2025, while 72 per cent of routes were served by just one carrier.

Regional flights also cost more to operate, with airlines spending about 91 cents of every dollar earned on operating costs, including fuel, maintenance and airport fees, according to the report.

Regional flights cost more to run. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor )

"Half of regional and remote routes operate 10 or fewer flights per week and more than a third of their seats are empty," Commissioner Martin Stokie said.

"Operators are often choosing between charging higher fares or running them at a loss."

But profitability varied significantly between routes, the report said.

Qantas lay-offs are just the beginning of big changes for a tourism industry still trying to find its feet.

Mining routes were more profitable for airlines, while some short remote routes carrying fewer passengers had profit margins below 5 per cent.

Regional airline Rex went into administration in 2024, after expanding into capital city routes.

The airline was losing around $1 million a week and blamed high operating costs and difficulties competing with Qantas and Virgin when it collapsed.

Last month, Qantas and Virgin executives defended regional service cuts at a Senate inquiry into Australia's aviation sector.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson told the committee regional flights were more expensive to operate because of fuel costs, aircraft requirements and airport fees.

"On a typical $197 fare, around $93 is made up by government, airport and security fees and charges and that's before the airline pays for aircraft, crew or fuel or maintenance," he said.

In its recommendations, the commission said governments needed to do more to help patients with the up-front costs of medical travel and subsidise essential routes where airlines cannot provide a commercial service.

"Government assistance should focus on keeping communities connected, rather than supporting particular airlines," Commissioner Catherine de Fontenay said.

The commission is seeking further submissions and registrations for public hearings and will deliver its final report in April 2027.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/s.title: Singapore Airlines flight makes emergency landing in regional Queensland
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A plane en route to Singapore was forced to land in Rockhampton after smoke was reported on board. (ABC News: Vanessa Jarrett)

A Singapore Airlines flight has been forced to make an emergency landing at Rockhampton Airport on Wednesday after smoke was seen in the cabin.

The Singapore-bound plane had just departed Brisbane when the incident occurred.

It touched down safely just after 4pm. No injuries were reported.

Paramedics and fire crews were called to the scene.

Passengers reported seeing smoke fill the cabin and plane screens go black.

A group of school children going on an excursion were among the passengers. (ABC News: Vanessa Jarrett)

A Singapore Airlines spokesperson said the company was investigating the cause of the smoke.

"We are providing our customers with all necessary assistance, including on ground refreshments, arranging for a relief flight and rebooking onward travel where necessary," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"The safety of our customers and staff is our top priority."

Passengers who were on board the flight were contained to an internal lounge in the airport.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/y.title: Young adult dies from meningococcal disease
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/y.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Meningococcal disease

A young adult infected with invasive meningococcal disease has died.

SA Health confirmed the person's death on Wednesday, after the state's health minister and chief public health officer confirmed the case on Saturday, October 31.

SA Health said data confidentiality meant no details regarding the deceased person could be provided.

Chief Public Health Officer Nicola Spurrier had previously said close contacts of the infected person had been provided preventative antibiotics.

No further meningococcal cases have been reported to SA Health, with the deceased person the 22nd case in South Australia this year.

Failure to receive treatment for the disease once symptoms are detected can increase the risk of disability and mortality.

Susceptible groups include adolescents and very young children, though a 36-year-old South Australian man died from the disease in 2023.

Professor Spurrier and the state's health minister, Blair Boyer, have encouraged parents to vaccinate children younger than 12 months, or who are students in Year 10, as these groups are eligible for the state's free vaccination program.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/v.title: VCAA investigating after website hacked during exam period
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Cyber Security

The VCAA has  confirmed it is investigating a hack. (Supplied)

The Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA) says there is no indication exam papers have been accessed after its website was hacked.

Students in Victoria are still sitting exams, with a message on the compromised version of the VCAA website claiming that exam papers had been downloaded and distributed.

The VCAA says it is conducting a forensic investigation to determine the extent of the attack.

The Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA) is investigating after its website was hacked during the exam period.

Earlier this evening the VCAA home page was displaying an error message that has since been replaced with a message saying "We'll be right back".

"Our site is currently undergoing maintenance," the website states.

"We apologise for any inconvenience and appreciate your patience."

A VCAA spokesperson confirmed the page was hacked earlier today.

"The VCAA is conducting a forensic investigation to determine the extent of the attack," they said in a statement.

"There is no indication that exam papers from today or previous weeks have been accessed."

Exams for students in Victoria are scheduled through to November 18.

A hacker has claimed responsibility for the breach. (ABC News: Casey Briggs)

The compromised version of the VCAA website included an expletive-riddled message critical of the digital security standards of the VCAA and others, including providers of printing and legal services.

"The success of this campaign could not have been possible without all their help together," the hacker, who signed off as DaggerElite, wrote.

"I'm here to say a big THANK YOU to a much cooler group of people --- those who purchased an Official VCA 2026 Exam from me ahead of the Exam day this year.

"Thanks to the support of these awesome hundreds of students statewide, we will hopefully be able to prepare the exam pages to be sent out even earlier than we have been able to this year, so we can study the paper you will sit in 2027 well in advance!!"

The hacker claim they downloaded a copy of the 2026 exam papers from the printing provider's internal file servers and distributed copies using email details obtained from the legal service provider.

"And before anyone seeing this decides to go ask people on Reddit to share the papers for the next few exams, I would like to remind you that those holding a paper are very well aware that each sent copy is individualised with an identifiable signature embedded in it, and it's in their best interests to keep their papers to themselves," the text on the website said.

"This is DaggerElite, and it has been an absolute pleasure working with all of you this year."

In 2024 an exam blunder led to some questions being leaked in online practice material.

In April this year, the Victorian government announced more than $222 million to rebuild the VCAA with the aim of "safeguarding exams for the long-term".

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/a.title: Advocate who supported Peter Greste named ACT's Australian of the Year
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/a.author: Madeleine Rojahn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Awards and Prizes

Martin Hodgson is the ACT's 2027 Australian of the Year. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

The ACT's Australian of the Year for 2027 is Martin Hodgson, who is known for his advocacy for First Nations people and Australians overseas, including journalist Peter Greste.

Canberrans tackling global food security, loneliness and mothers' isolation were also honoured in the awards.

Mr Hodgson and three other award recipients will represent the ACT at the national Australian of the Year awards in January.

A human rights lawyer and advocate has been named the ACT's Australian of the Year for 2027, recognised for his work supporting vulnerable Australians, from First Nations people to prisoners with wrongful convictions.

Martin Hodgson, 46, represented hundreds of clients pro bono through the Foreign Prisoner Support Service and the Disappeared Project, which spotlights First Nations cold cases, and which he co-founded.

Mr Hodgson paid tribute to his mum, who he said "has made me who I am".

"When I was very little, we lived in a tent, and then we upgraded to a tractor shed in the bush, and shortwave radio introduced me to the world," he said.

"And I heard about Nelson Mandela and the troubles in Ireland and, at six, they were the things I wanted to solve."

"Mum was the one who encouraged us to be whatever we wanted to be, but just to be good people, and to help others, which she did her whole career."

Martin Hodgson with journalist Peter Greste's parents, Lois and Juris. (Supplied)

Mr Hodgson said when he was a university student he helped an imprisoned Australian "in trouble overseas" get home — and since then "the phone never stopped".

He has supported the Bali Nine and Australian foreign correspondent Peter Greste, who was imprisoned for 400 days in an Egyptian prison.

"I've had a real pleasure of working with Australians in trouble overseas, a lot of First Nations communities, and young Aboriginal mums who are doing it tough through no fault of their own and really being let down, and just being in their corner," Mr Hodgson said.

Modern forensic techniques aim to solve Australian First Nations cold cases.

He also helped free First Nations man Kevin Henry, who was wrongfully imprisoned for more than 25 years.

Food scientist Andrzej Kilian was awarded the ACT's Senior Australian of the Year for his dedication to tackling global food security.

Dr Kilian developed an efficient tool to analyse the DNA of organisms, helping farmers, scientists and ecologists improve crop yields.

Dr Andrzej Kilian was named the 2027 ACT Senior Australian of the Year.

He commercialised the invention in 2001 through the Diversity Arrays Technology social enterprise, located in Canberra.

Accepting the award, Dr Kilian, who immigrated from Poland three decades ago, said he drew upon his love for cooking nutritious food for his wife when starting the company.

"This is extending that to the global community, so the catchphrase is, 'Can we feed 10 billion people, project for 2050, without destroying biodiversity?'" he said.

In 2021, Zakary Pino began a routine of walking around Lake Burley Griffin each Sunday, as a way to combat his own loneliness and anxiety during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Zakary Pino tapped into a widely felt loss of connection during the pandemic era. (Supplied)

He did not realise at the time that he was starting a movement that grew into the charity WITH-ME, bringing connection to thousands.

"The premise of it was to get people to walk and talk and also, for me, it was … to kind of learn off older people," Mr Pino said.

The 30-year-old also works to breaks down taboos around mental health by speaking with school students across the ACT.

Mr Pino was named Young Australian of the Year for ACT.

Micaela Centenera's impact extends overseas through the provision of supplies to impoverished communities. (Supplied)

Micaela Centenera has taken out the Local Hero award for her work advocating for community and connection among mothers.

Ms Centenera was recognised for her mission to create a "free community" for women through her co-founded social enterprise, The Little Capsule Co, which included an online marketplace for new and pre-loved children's wear.

Upon accepting the award, Ms Centenera recounted how her own experience inspired the organisation, which acted as "drop-in centre for women during those tough early days, where you just want to cry and you don't want to put your shoes on".

"I moved to the ACT almost seven years ago now, and I lost my mum tribe, and it kind of felt very isolating when you've got a small one. You need community — it's so important to have people around you," she said.

She also posts monthly medical, clothing, bedding and toiletry supplies to families facing extreme poverty.

The four recipients will attend the national Australian of the Year awards in Canberra next year.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Consuming fringe radical content was among the traits found in those who post hateful online content. (Supplied: Pexels)

An Australian Institute of Criminology report examined the characteristics of people who post online hate.

Of 9,951 surveyed, nearly 170 had subjected others to online hate.

Those people were more likely to have had negative experiences online and behave antisocially.

Researchers have shed light on the characteristics of people who post hateful comments online, in a study published by the Australian Institute of Criminology.

The institute, a federal government crime research organisation, used the Australian eSafety commissioner's definition of online hate, framing it as "hateful posts or comments about a person or group based on discrimination or bias related to their identity or beliefs".

It surveyed almost 10,000 people between October and November 2024, and found 1.7 per cent of respondents had subjected others to online hate.

This group was also more likely to have hold misogynistic attitudes, engage in antisocial behaviour, consume fringe radical content, and have been a victim of online hate, compared to those who had not posted hateful online content.

"This cohort was also more likely to have experienced negative life events compared with those who had not subjected others to online hate," the report read.

"[They] were more likely to spend less time connecting with people offline and to be concerned about their internet use.

"These experiences align with previous research that has found online hate to be associated with close ties to online communities and low offline social capital."

A study finds violent attitudes towards women are not just a social issue but a matter of national security.

The report also found the people more likely to indulge in online hate held strong beliefs about how "superior groups" should act in society.

They were more likely to agree with these two statements:

"After controlling for gender and age, these respondents were more likely to believe that some groups should hold greater dominance over others," the report read.

Researchers also measured the extent to which respondents: believed women to be manipulative and exploitative; were distrustful of women; and devalued women.

They found perpetrators of online hate were more likely to hold misogynistic attitudes, and almost twice as likely to agree with the following:

The study also found across all respondents there were no major demographic differences between perpetrators or victims of online abuse from place of residence, country of birth, or language spoken.

The research found perpetrators of online hate were likely to have had contact with the criminal justice system both as an adult and as a juvenile.

"Those who had subjected others to online hate were more likely to have used violence against another person. They were also more likely to have threatened another person," the report read.

Recent studies link exposure to extreme anti-women content to increasing misogyny among boys.

Perpetrators of online hate were more likely to have been diagnosed with a mental health condition, and engaged in antisocial behaviour, than respondents who did not.

The report also found many have been victims of hate speech, online harassment and abuse.

It found they were more likely to be engaging in antisocial behaviour online and creating fake social media accounts.

About half of those who subjected others to online hate did at least one of the following, compared to just two per cent of those who had not:

The report also examined the relationship between viewing radical fringe content and engaging in online abuse.

It defined "fringe and radical" as online content that was political, ideological or religious in nature but viewed by wider society as unorthodox, radical or fringe.

When compared to the cohort who did not post online hate, it found those who did were almost two times more likely to have viewed fringe and radical content online.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/s.title: Rescuers wrangling red tape as foxes pick off young swans south of Perth
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/s.author: Georgia Loney, Chela Williams, and Jacqueline Lynch
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Foxes are gaining easier access to birds because of the drying lake. (Supplied: WA Seabird Rescue)

Wildlife rescuers are working to save cygnets from foxes at a rapidly drying Lake McLarty, south of Perth.

They claim rescue efforts have been hampered by red tape and government approvals.

The Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions says rescuers are allowed in the area but warns of public safety risks.

Wildlife rescuers are mounting a community-led effort to save more than 50 vulnerable or abandoned black swan cygnets at a drying lake south of Mandurah.

WARNING: This story contains images of dead birds some readers may find distressing.

Rescue groups spent most of today negotiating the terms of their operation with WA's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), which manages McLarty Lake, about 90 kilometres south of Perth.

WA Seabird Rescue's Rachel Olsen vented her frustration with red tape as foxes picked off abandoned cygnets.

"We were only just made aware of the situation, but it is really quite urgent," she said.

"As of this morning, I went out really early; the water level is down, and there's only about 60 cygnets left."

Black swans are vulnerable to predation at Lake McLarty. (Supplied: WA Seabird Rescue)

While the department says wildlife rescuers can access the reserve, it was wary that a large-scale rescue operation could pose public safety risks.

"DBCA has also been in discussions with WA Seabird Rescue regarding the organisation of a larger event involving around 100 people, which may pose additional public safety risks that will need to be managed," a spokesperson said.

"DBCA continues to work with WA Seabird Rescue to facilitate volunteer wildlife rehabilitators accessing the reserve to monitor and rescue cygnets."

A dead cygnet was found at Lake McLarty, south of Mandurah. (Supplied: WA Seabird Rescue)

Ms Olsen said the situation had evolved quickly and rescue was set to take place this afternoon.

"Some of them have been abandoned, but we basically need to scoop them all up," she said.

"We know that in a few days all of these cygnets will be dead; the parents have no choice but to abandon them."

Ms Olsen said the lake was drying up earlier than usual, forcing adult swans to abandon their young because of the risk of predation.

Water levels are low at Lake McLarty.  (Supplied: WA Seabird Rescue )

"Parents don't want to abandon their babies, but as they face increasing pressure and are running out of food, all the swans are getting concentrated into one area, and then the foxes come in," she said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Paul Lindemann with party leader Jess Wilson. (Facebook)

The Victorian Liberal Party has dumped Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann over offensive comments it says he made about Indigenous Australians.

In a statement, the party says it has withdrawn its support and endorsement of Mr Lindemann over views he expressed, which had recently come to light.

"These comments are offensive, unacceptable and inconsistent with the values and standards expected of Liberal candidates," the statement says.

The party was not previously aware of Mr Lindemann's comments, the statement says.

Yesterday One Nation dumped former Preston candidate Franco Guardiani over comments he made about Hitler.

The seat of Williamstown has been held by Minister for Jobs Melissa Horne since 2018, and has been won by Labor at almost every election since 1889 on very safe margins.

The former dockyard town is now one of the wealthier seats in the state.

Earlier today, Sport Minister Steve Dimopoulos said Opposition Leader Jess Wilson should dump Mr Lindemann over allegations he insulted and mocked a young basketball player while coaching the Bay City Lakers.

In a statement, Mr Lindemann apologised for his actions and acknowledged he should have "handled the situation differently".

The ABC has attempted to contact Mr Lindemann for comment.

Victorians are set to head to the polls on November 28.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/k.title: Mining equipment manufacturer reveals plans to phase out 265 jobs
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/k.author: Kelly Fuller
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Mining and Metals Industry

Komatsu Mining plans to close its Moss Vale plant by 2030, cutting about 265 jobs at the Southern Highlands site. (Supplied: Google maps)

About 265 jobs will go at Komatsu Mining's Moss Vale plant as the company phases out operations by 2030.

Southern Highlands business leaders put the potential hit to the local economy at about $20 million a year.

Federal Labor MP for Whitlam, Carol Berry, will meet Komatsu on Thursday to ask why it is closing the plant and how it plans to support workers.

The decision to close a mining plant in the NSW Southern Highlands is being described as an "absolute gut blow" for workers.

About 265 jobs will go as Komatsu winds down operations at the Moss Vale plant before the scheduled closure in 2030.

A senior organiser with the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU), Nathan Everson, said workers at Moss Vale had been "blindsided".

"But there were also some workers there that were keeping it together for others who are a bit distressed by the news that seemingly came out of nowhere."

In a media release, Komatsu said it planned to close Moss Vale by 2030, shifting work to Rutherford (in the NSW Hunter Valley) and Rockhampton (in Central QLD) and outsourcing some fabrication and machining to Australian suppliers.

Komatsu executive Helen Gibson said the restructure was needed to "simplify operations" and respond to changes in the Australian market and customer requirements.

"Our employees were among the first to know and, importantly, there will be no immediate changes for them," Ms Gibson said.

The AMWU says Komatsu has told workers' representatives that work building mining equipment will move to China. (Supplied)

Union officials met with the company on site today.

"So what the company told us in the meeting today was that original equipment, so OE work, is going to be transitioning to China," Mr Everson said.

"The company had intimated that the fabrication of machining was not competitive in the market anymore and that's ultimately led to a decision to send the work offshore."

Mr Everson said the company explained the job losses would be scheduled in six phases through to 2030.

"But even the Rutherford site is not getting this unscathed," he said.

"They will also be losing some work due to this restructure."

Business Southern Highlands chair Greg Welsh said the loss of highly skilled, well-paid jobs would be felt by local shops as well as the engineering firms, hydraulics businesses and component suppliers that service the plant.

Mr Welsh estimated the region could lose about $20 million a year in household spending if the workers and their families leave the area.

Komatsu plans to wind down work at its Moss Vale plant in stages before closing the site by 2030. (Supplied: Google maps)

Mr Everson said it was "going to be a struggle for workers to find work in the area".

He said the closure would cost NSW skilled manufacturing jobs at a time when the state government was trying to grow the sector.

NSW Domestic Manufacturing Minister Courtney Houssos said she was disappointed by Komatsu's planned Moss Vale closure, had been in touch with the AMWU, and would monitor the impact of the 265 job losses.

Federal Whitlam MP Carol Berry said she would meet Komatsu on Thursday to ask why it was closing the plant and how it planned to support workers.

State Goulburn MP Wendy Tuckerman described the closure as "deeply disappointing" and said contractors, suppliers and local businesses would feel the effects.

Wingecarribee Mayor Erin Foley said council would seek a meeting with Komatsu and press for support for workers.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/d.author: Eva Blandis and James Wakelin
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Domestic Violence

Stella Magnisalis says she found out through media reports that her abuser will be released from prison next week. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

A woman who was the victim of assault by her ex-husband has learned through the media of his imminent release.

Stella Magnisalis says she is considering her living arrangements in the interests of her personal safety.

Ms Magnisalis's ex-husband, Matthew Thomson, is due to be released next week.

A domestic violence survivor says she is fearing for her life and "reliving" her trauma after learning her abuser and ex-husband will be released on parole next week.

Former police officer Matthew Thomson has been in jail for just over a year after admitting to multiple assaults against his ex-wife Stella Magnisalis between 2013 and 2018.

Thomson was sentenced to two years and three months behind bars last year, but was handed a 12-month non-parole period that made him eligible to apply for release since June this year.

The SA Parole Board today confirmed that Thomson would be released next week and would be subject to electronic monitoring conditions.

Ms Magnisalis said she had been told by the Department for Correctional Services (DCS) that her abuser's release was "imminent" but had not been given a date.

She said it was "disheartening" to first learn of when he would be released from the media.

Stella Magnisalis says she fears for her life. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"[DCS] said it may take up to a couple of days or it may take up to a couple of weeks but you will be informed," Ms Magnisalis said she was told.

Ms Magnisalis said the call from DCS informing her of Thomson's release left her feeling "surprised, shocked and disgusted".

"I'm fearful for my life," she said.

"We know what he's capable of doing."

Ms Magnisalis also said SA Police had not told her when Thomson would be released, and had "not been consistent" with keeping her informed.

SA Police said in a statement that the "notification of parole outcomes and release arrangements are the responsibility of the Department for Correctional Services".

"SAPOL was not advised that the parole application had been successful," a spokesperson said.

"SAPOL acknowledges the significant impact these matters have on victims and their families and remains committed to supporting victim safety."

DCS said "the correct process was followed by DCS's Victims Serivces Unit".

"Information about the offender's release date — and the disclosure of that date — is a matter for the Parole Board, which is independent of government," a spokesperson said.

"DCS understands that an offender's impending release can be distressing for victims, and takes its responsibility to keep victims informed seriously."

Matthew Thomson leaves South Australian District Court in 2025. (ABC News)

Ms Magnisalis said she was considering options to keep her family safe once Thomson was released.

"I'm considering when he's let out to leave the state, to go overseas, to move in with my family," she said.

"I'm reliving my traumas all over again."

The Parole Board said Thomson had completed all necessary prison programs ahead of his release and did not believe he posed a risk to society.

Police Minister Michael Brown said that "it's important that victims have confidence in the system".

"I'm happy to follow up in this particular case to make sure that the proper procedure has been followed and I do find it disappointing that people are finding that they haven't been given the information they require," he said.

Mr Brown also defended the Parole Board's "independent decision" to release Thomson on parole.

"I am pleased to see that the Parole Board has decided to put him on electronic monitoring which I think is entirely appropriate in this case," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/r.title: CFMEU official claimed to have 'direct line to Jacinta Allan', inquiry hears
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/r.author: Andi Yu
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Royal Commissions

Paul Tzimas has given evidence to the Royal Commission about receiving a gold bracelet from Mick Gatto and his knowledge of bikie-affiliated men hired has health and safety representatives. (Supplied)

A former CFMEU official has told a royal commission his superior told construction project managers the union's influence on the Victorian government was such that it had a "direct line to Jacinta Allan's office".

The inquiry is examining the CFMEU's influence and actions at a level crossing removal project in Melbourne's north in 2022.

Hearings continue tomorrow.

A former Victorian CFMEU official has claimed his superior told construction project managers the union had a "direct line to Jacinta Allan's office".

The evidence of the former union worker, Paul Tzimas, comes as Victoria's Big Build royal commission focuses on the events surrounding a stop-work on a level crossing removal project in Melbourne's outer north-west in 2022.

Jacinta Allan was transport infrastructure minister at the time, under then Labor premier Daniel Andrews.

Earlier this week, the inquiry heard there had been growing tensions at the site, with concern from the contractor that the CFMEU was improperly stopping work in a bid to exert influence.

The level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury when it was under construction. (Supplied: Victorian government)

Today, Mr Tzimas, who became a union organiser in 2018, told the commission about a meeting held with the project contractors in June 2022.

He told the inquiry he and superior Joe Myles got what they wanted out of the meeting — to make the contractors change labour hire company to a CFMEU-affliated BK labour, enabling them to choose the health and safety representatives they wanted on-site.

He echoed evidence heard yesterday that it was in contractor John Holland the Rail Network Alliance's interests to do what the union wanted if they wanted to be considered for contracts on the Airport Rail Link.

Commissioner Chris Kourakis is presiding over the hearings. (Supplied)

Counsel assisting the commission, Chris Carr SC, asked Mr Tzimas if Mr Myles had said anything about the union's influence over the Victorian government.

"Mr Myles saying to the meeting something about having a direct line to Jacinta Allan's office in the context of the Airport Rail Link job?" Mr Carr asked.

"Yeah, which again I wouldn’t have thought was uncommon at the time because we had a political organiser with those contacts, to be speaking, liaising with those entities," Mr Tzimas said.

The former official, who is no longer employed with the union, told the commission he was "surprised" by Mr Myles's comment because he did not think the CFMEU had that level of influence and he had asked Mr Myles about it after the meeting.

"It was just reiterated that it wasn't uncommon because our political organisers have to have those discussions and dealings with people within the government," Mr Tzimas said.

Under cross-examination by a lawyer for Joe Myles, the commission heard Mr Myles disputes not only what was said, but also said he was only in the meeting for one minute.

Representing former CFMEU official Joe Myles, Veronika Drago put to Mr Tzimas his recollection of the 2022 meeting was inaccurate. (Supplied)

"We're suggesting you carried the rest of the conversation yourself because he was not there," lawyer Veronika Drago said.

Mr Tzimas stuck with his recollection, saying Mr Myles had been present in the room for five to 10 minutes.

Mr Tzimas told the commission he was aware of multiple health and safety representatives employed on Victorian work sites in recent years, who had links to bikie gangs.

Counsel assisting read him the names of 11 men who had worked as health and safety representatives (known as HSRs) and asked whether they were bikie-affiliated. He replied "yes" to most, although said he was not sure about some.

The commission heard Mr Tzimas helped arranged an HSR job for Johnny Walker — a criminal on parole for a manslaughter conviction — on a project to upgrade Melbourne's existing rail loop.

Mr Tzimas said he could not remember which labour hire company Mr Walker was employed by but it had an enterprise bargaining agreement with the CFMEU.

The commission also heard Mr Tzimas had dealings with underworld-linked mediator Mick Gatto in the course of his work, including being gifted a gold bracelet.

Mr Tzimas said on one occasion Mr Gatto called him for an in-person meeting, and presented him with the valuable item, which he initially refused.

"Mick had expressed that, especially because I refused it, that it wasn't his way of trying to give me anything to have sway or to earn any favour," he said.

"He believed that he probably judged me a bit harshly and this was an olive branch, so to speak, that he gives to people that he considers a friend and he doesn't want nothing for it.

"But I never wore it …and he never called upon any favours."

Mr Tzimas said he knew of other CFMEU officials, including those who were on the CFMEU's Victorian branch executive, who also received gifts from Mr Gatto.

During Wednesday's hearing, senior inspector for WorkSafe Quinton Drury gave evidence that there were regular tensions with CFMEU officials if WorkSafe inspectors disagreed with them about safety concerns.

Worksafe inspector Quinton Drury gave evidence there was often tension with CFMEU officials if his own safety assessments didn't align with theirs. (Supplied)

Mr Drury said WorkSafe inspectors would take safety concerns into consideration, but if unsubstantiated they wouldn't support it.

"It could go a little bit south if you want to call it that," he told the commission.

"Tensions may rise if they feel as if they are not supported. When I say they, the union, if they feel they're not supported there may be some tension on site."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/q.title: CFMEU inquiry delivers 'urgent and pressing' recommendations
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/q.author: Ciara Jones
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-11/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Stuart Wood KC says the need to clean up the building industry is "urgent and pressing". (ABC News: Erin Byrnes)

Queensland's CFMEU inquiry commissioner has delivered an interim report recommending the introduction of a new building code and the establishment of a dedicated regulator.

Stuart Wood KC delivered the report early, citing an "urgent and pressing" need for change.

The Crisafulli government is yet to respond to the interim report.

Queensland's CFMEU inquiry commissioner has called for urgent changes in the state's construction industry after hearing "highly disturbing" allegations of union misconduct.

In an interim report made public on Wednesday afternoon, Commissioner Stuart Wood KC recommends the state government introduce a new building code and establish a dedicated regulator to enforce compliance.

Mr Wood was not due to hand down his findings until December next year but said there was an "urgent and pressing" need to implement change following more than 50 days of hearings and evidence from over 80 witnesses.

"The evidence … demonstrates that a number of issues … warrant immediate attention," Mr Wood wrote.

"In my view, there is a compelling public interest in the government receiving and considering … preliminary findings and recommendations."

Commissioner Wood said the inquiry had uncovered "disturbing" evidence of CFMEU misconduct and cost blowouts related to the former Labor government's controversial Best Practice Industry Conditions (BPIC) policy, which set pay and conditions on major taxpayer-funded projects.

The commissioner described BPIC, which has been scrapped by the Crisafulli government, as "damaging".

He found the policy had driven up construction costs by at least 20 per cent on three projects examined by the inquiry — Brisbane's Cross River Rail and the Centenary Bridge upgrade as well as the Gold Coast Light Rail.

The BPIC drove up the cost of certain projects, the commissioner found. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

"However, I consider the estimate of 20 per cent to be a conservative view," Mr Wood wrote.

"In coming to this view, I am dealing only with the increase in costs caused by the implementation of BPIC, leaving aside for the moment any quantification as to delays caused by BPIC."

"Ultimately, it is the taxpayer that wears the cost here," he said.

The commissioner said the policy also fuelled a bitter turf war between the CFMEU and Australian Workers' Union (AWU) over control of Queensland's civil construction sector.

At the centre of Mr Wood's recommendations is a new construction industry code designed to improve workplace safety, lift productivity and efficiency and strengthen legal compliance.

Mr Wood said the standards should be "uncontroversial", particularly in the building and construction industry in which "large sums of taxpayers' money are at play."

The commissioner also called for a well-resourced regulator to educate the industry about the code and enforce compliance.

The reforms would apply to Queensland's $119 billion infrastructure pipeline over the next four years, with Mr Wood warning of the need to reduce wasteful government spending at taxpayers' expense.

Commissioner Wood said BPIC had fuelled a turf war over control of Queensland's civil construction sector. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The code would use the threat of exclusion from future government-funded construction work to encourage good behaviour among contractors and subcontractors.

"This is not a unique or novel concept," Mr Wood said, pointing to similar construction codes and regulators operating at state and federal levels for at least 30 years.

He said it was modelled on guidelines introduced in Queensland in 2013, which were abolished by the incoming Palaszczuk government two years later without industry consultation and "seemingly in the dead of night".

The Crisafulli government is expected to respond to the interim report on Thursday.

The inquiry's final report was originally due in July, but the deadline was extended to December 2027 to allow further investigation into the wide-ranging allegations before the commission.

Mr Wood said the probe had received nearly eight million documents and had heard evidence of union misconduct, cost blowouts and alleged regulatory capture, alongside expert testimony identifying traits of organised crime and corruption in the CFMEU's conduct.
