https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.title: Indonesia's vice-president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.text:
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka tendered his resignation to parliament on Thursday, triggering the process of finding his replacement amid growing turmoil for the government.

Gibran had been facing impeachment calls after a Supreme Court ruling that a high-school document used during his 2024 election campaign was invalid.

His departure comes amid a faltering political alliance between his father, ex-president Joko Widodo, and the incumbent President Prabowo Subianto.

Standing alongside Gibran, Prabowo told reporters he had accepted his resignation with "a heavy heart". Upper house lawmakers will have 60 days to fill the vacancy from two candidates nominated by the president.

"[Gibran] has demonstrated a chivalrous attitude, a strong sense of responsibility, and the qualities of a statesman," Prabowo said, adding that the resignation was "for the benefit of the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia".

"He certainly believes that he completed his education through a proper and structured process. However, we must understand that educational systems abroad differ from those in Indonesia," the president said.

Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.

Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.

Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.

"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.

It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.

The Supreme Court ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.

Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.

On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretariat Prasetyo Hadi said.

Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.

Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.

But tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.

Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.

In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.

Last week, authorities arrested several senior officials, including presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation to Prabowo - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.

Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.

Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.

But neither man has confirmed the rift. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Jokowi said he still supported Prabowo's leadership.

Jokowi also said Gibran's resignation was part of "political dynamics" and he had told his son "the position was temporary".

All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.

Across the country, students and activists have staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.summary: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka tendered his resignation to parliament on Thursday. He had been facing impeachment calls after a Supreme Court ruling that a high-school document used during his 2024 election campaign was invalid. His departure comes amid a faltering political alliance between his father, ex-president Joko Widodo

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3x2.title: Famed ship SS United States deliberately sunk off Florida coast to become a reef
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3x2.text:
A ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic has intentionally been sunk off the coast of Florida, turning into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.

The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.

Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.

Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it was added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, with a land-based museum detailing the ship's history also planned.

Before its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities between the US and Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969.

A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.

The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work.

On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it was sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives.

Stars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing lifetime.

Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed.

Instead, it sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out.

The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.

Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped design the liner - said she was glad that the story of the SS United States would live on.

"[The ship] has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together," Gibbs told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3x2.summary: SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida. It was purchased by a Florida county last year for cleaning and remediation work. The ship was sunk in a precision operation without explosives on Wednesday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c933.title: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c933.text:
A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.

Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.

His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.

Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.

He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.

Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.

When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.

Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín.

However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.

A nationwide manhunt is now under way.

Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.

Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.

However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office.

Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".

He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s.

Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.

The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.

Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security. He had tampered with his ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8e3.title: Missing 11-month-old baby rescued after being buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8e3.text:
An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.

Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.

The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.

The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.

Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.

The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.

Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.

Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.

He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.

Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".

"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.

He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.

"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.

Of the parents' relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.

Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.

"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqr7.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqr7.text:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.

CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.

Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.

While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.

"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.

Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.

Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.

In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.

The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".

Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.

Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.

The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqr7.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life. The move came after a photo of Bessen's home was published in the Wall Street Journal. Besset has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwg5.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwg5.text:
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.

Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.

The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.

All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.

"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.

The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".

He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".

Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.

"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.

Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.

The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.

"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.

"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmgl.title: African writing award probe finds 'no evidence' winning story was AI generated
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmgl.text:
The Caine Prize for African Writing has said that after an internal review it has found no evidence that Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza had used generative AI to write his winning short story and confirmed him as the winner of this year's £10,000 ($13,000) award.

Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees, said the matter had been investigated following an article in US magazine The Atlantic with the headline, Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI.

"From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human written," she said in a video posted on X.

The accusation had caused a social media uproar and Kundizeza had denied the allegation.

The Atlantic article by journalist Vauhini Vara alleged that AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.

Her allegations followed rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.

Following the publication of her article last month, Vara had told BBC's Front Row programme that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".

The backlash on social media included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.

Wakatama said the Caine Prize organisation had considered Vara's allegations "carefully and fairly".

"We chose to take a human-centred approach to the investigation. Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel, and the Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published," she said.

"It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author."

In a statement, the Caine Prize explained further that the analysis had been conducted by an independent cyber security and digital forensic investigator.

The day after winning the prestigious Caine Prize award earlier in October, Kundizeza had told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.

He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.

Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent.

Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica, on Facebook at BBC Africa or on Instagram at bbcafrica
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmgl.summary: Caine Prize for African Writing says no evidence of use of AI to write winning short story. Simbarashe Kundizeza was named winner of £10,000 ($13,000) award for short story.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm.title: Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm.text:
Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.

The chief executive and co-founder of the AI chip-making giant was at the centre of a major scandal over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

On Wednesday Nvidia's board announced he had resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.

Now the tech giant is facing one of its biggest challenges, finding the right person to lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into the world's second most valuable company - after Apple.

We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.

Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, has been tipped as someone who could steady the ship in the interim, and possibly stop its share price from plunging even further.

An industry veteran for more than 30 years, Kress previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.

Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.

She "fronts every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.

But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.

Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority.

Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology.

Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job.

Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications.

"He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.

Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.

Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced.

Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.

Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts.

Liu said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair.

Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant.

Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung.

Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana.

"The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said.

Ten Cap's Liu had believed it was just a matter of time before Huang would step down as Nvidia's chief executive.

"The issue is no longer simply about personal conduct," she said. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence in the leadership of one of the world's most strategically important companies."

Several major investment firms have downgraded their forecasts for the chip giant - a rare shift given investors' longstanding optimism about the company.

Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here".

Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines."

Ray Wang, chief executive of Constellation Research, said the crisis isn't so much an issue for the wider AI industry but rather one for Nvidia itself which has to consider if the person it appoints as its chief executive has the same appeal as Huang.

"That's really what the issue is, because a lot of these partnerships and investments have been made because of the trust with with Jensen," he said.

Additional reporting by Kali Hays

Huang was at the centre of a major scandal over reports of extramarital affairs. Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5y.title: Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5y.text:
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.

The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.

Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.

Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.

The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.

Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms.

"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.

The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.

"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.

"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.

Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.

In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.

However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.

"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.

The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.

Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.

Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.

Following widespread complaints about the rising cost of living, he recently said he would work to reduce the cost of fuel but denied that this was a return to the subsidy. For decades, many Nigerians have seen cheap fuel as one of the few perks of living in Africa's largest oil producer.

His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.

Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.

"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.

However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.

"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.

While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.

Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.

"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.

To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.

But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.

Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.

"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."

To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.

"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.

The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.

Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.

He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.

"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.

Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.

"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.

Another huge challenge facing Nigeria is the power sector, which has suffered from years of underinvestment.

The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year.

Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.

The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins.

"The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.

Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.

The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.

For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say.

"Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said.

"The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said.

Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government.

"APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.

As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge - building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds.

"It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said.

"The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwx2.title: 'My darling girl, you are everything to me' - auctioned letters reveal WWI love story
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwx2.text:
"My darling girl, you are everything to me..."

Those words were written by Gunner Willie Webber to his wife Gladys from the battlefields of World War One.

The newly-weds, who were married at St Edward's Church in Knighton, Powys, in December 1917, had very little time together as Willie - a gunner with the Royal Garrison Artillery's 297th Siege Battery - was serving on the Western Front. He was killed just weeks before the Armistice in 1918.

More than a century later, Willie's letters have inspired an extraordinary act of remembrance by the community - thanks to the efforts of two strangers who refused to let the couple's love story be forgotten.

The bundle of 100 letters, dated from December 1917 to October 1918, chart a love story unfolding against the backdrop of war.

After briefly returning home injured and marrying Gladys in late 1917, Willie went back to the front line in France.

He sent his new wife pressed flowers and affectionate messages, signing off: "Your own true hubby & loving sweetheart. Willie."

Willie wrote regularly and his letters are filled with hopes and dreams for the future.

But the reunion he longed for never came.

Just four weeks before the Armistice, in October 1918, the young soldier was killed in an accident when his gun backfired. He was 25 years old.

The couple had no children, no direct descendants and, as time passed, nobody left to tell their story.

Their story could so easily have ended there. Instead, those letters triggered a remarkable act of remembrance more than a century later.

In 2025, the collection of love letters was put up for sale at an online auction.

Among those following the auction was Andy Garner, a mechanic from Norwich, who collects, transcribes and self-publishes wartime letters - ensuring the people in them are not lost to history.

When he came across Willie and Gladys' correspondence, he was determined to save it.

"Those letters just kept drawing me back," he said. "I'm adamant Willie was going, 'Come on Andy, you can do this'!'"

The auction price kept climbing, but - in the final seconds - Andy placed a winning bid of £351.51.

Later, reading through the complete collection, he found himself deeply moved by the couple's devotion and Willie's steadfast belief he would make it home.

"No matter what he's going through, their love shines through," said Andy.

"It's giving them both the hope to survive."

Though he could barely afford the money he had spent, Andy was determined to publish the transcripts.

However, something unexpected happened.

Keith Budgen, the man who had sold the letters, decided he couldn't keep the auction money.

"I woke up the following morning and immediately contacted Andy," said Keith.

"I said, 'You can have the money back. It's the right thing to do.'

"I had been given the letters, and I just knew that Andy had to have them."

The pair bonded over the letters and came up with the idea to commemorate Willie, the fallen soldier, in Knighton - the place where he and Gladys had married.

What followed was a remarkable community effort.

Within just two-and-a-half weeks, supporters raised £1,600 for a memorial bench at St Edward's Church.

The church immediately embraced the project and a remembrance service was organised. Bell-ringers created a special tribute, a bugler volunteered to play, and members of the Royal British Legion lent their support.

"The fact that he wasn't commemorated on any cenotaph, either in the town where he was born or in Knighton, made it a fabulous idea," said Ian Ferguson, of the Royal British Legion.

Reverend Rachael Storer, of St Edward's Church, paid tribute to Andy's determination to share the couple's story.

"It all started with those letters that he bought at auction," she said.

”Ultimately, this is a story about love."

Lynn Scales, who wrote a special standard for the bell-ringers in memory of the couple said: "Sometimes we forget the sacrifice that some people have made for the defence of this country.

"Gunner Willie sounds like he was doomed to be forgotten - but not any more."

Andy's wife, Lex, wrote to the BBC because she wanted others to know about her husband's work.

"Once he spreads the word, other people come on board and they all want to help because they care," she said.

"It seems to have this really beautiful ripple effect.

"Willie and Gladys were just regular everyday people, and for someone to actually take that time to remember them, I think it's beautiful."

More than a century after Willie wrote those letters, he and Gladys have found a new community. Not through blood or family ties, but through an act of remembrance initiated by two strangers, who refused to let their story be forgotten.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rm.title: Lego marketplace BrickLink offline after 'unusual activity' detected
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rm.text:
Lego has taken its online marketplace BrickLink offline after detecting what it described as unusual activity on the platform.

BrickLink is used by Lego collectors worldwide to buy and sell second-hand sets, source new bricks and purchase limited edition releases.

It was originally set up by a fan but acquired by Lego in 2019. The firm wrote on its homepage that before restoring BrickLink, it wanted to "fully understand" what had happened.

"That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues," Lego said. It did not provide any further detail about whether the site had been breached or hacked, nor whether any customer data had been affected.

Lego published the update after being contacted by the BBC.

BrickLink has been offline for the last three days, with a previous message saying it was down for maintenance.

Cyber-professional Melanie Hoskin has been collecting Lego for 45 years and is a regular user of BrickLink.

She told the BBC she had received multiple links for payment for a limited edition release she had pre-ordered on the platform after she had already paid for it.

She said Lego did not believe that the payment had been taken and at one point said it would ban her from BrickLink.

The problem has now been resolved and Lego said it was not aware of wider payment issues.

It is unclear whether the payment glitch had any connection to the issue that led to the website going offline.

Hoskin said she felt like she had been accused of theft.

"Lego is my stress relief," she said. "Lego is what I grew up with as a kid, it's what bonded me with my sisters.

"I've got a Lego room and I've not even been able to walk into it this past couple of weeks because it just angers me."

Earlier today, a message on BrickLink said the platform would be back online by Wednesday evening, but that message has now been deleted and there is no longer a time frame given for its return.

The site has been offline for the last three days with a previous message saying it was down for maintenance. BrickLink is used by Lego collectors worldwide to buy and sell second-hand sets, source new bricks and purchase limited edition releases.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmg4.title: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmg4.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".

Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.

But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.

In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.

Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.

He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office.

Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.

As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.

Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."

As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.

This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year.

The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.

Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words.

"The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.

On tackling the causes of climate change, Burnham said his government remained committed to meeting the country's target of net zero by 2050 whilst also getting bills down.

He said key to this was cutting our "dependence on fossil fuels" and increasing electrification - the amount of our energy needs met from renewable electricity.

The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

Turkey, the co-hosts of COP31, wants a key outcomes of this year's summit to be a commitment by countries to meet 35% of their energy supply from electricity by 2035. Currently, it is around a fifth.

But Burnham has been accused of having double standards.

"The Prime Minister simply cannot call for clean power across the world while saying yes to more fossil fuels in the UK," said Beth John, climate adviser at Oxfam.

Last month, the government approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on the grounds that it provided energy security.

And in the budget last month Chancellor John Healey announced a funding cut to the Warm Homes Plan, which provides grants and loans to support the installation of heat pumps.

Whilst this week there has been media speculation that the government is considering watering down electric car sales targets, although the government insists no decision has been made.

Successfully switching petrol and diesel cars to EVs and moving from gas boilers to electric-powered heat pumps are key ways to achieve the 35% electrification target.

Although there was no royal presence this year, King Charles III sent a message ahead of Burnham's speech.

"As the world gathers for Cop31, I can only hope that this same spirit of partnership and common purpose can help inspire the collective action that our planet – and future generations – so urgently need.

"Our children and grandchildren will not judge us by the promises we made, but by what we chose to do."

Burnham was the only G7 leader to speak at this year's conference in a sign of faltering support for the COP process - something he acknowledged in his speech.

In an almost word for word copy of Sir Keir Starmer's address last year he said: "The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate has gone, and the reality is now the world will reach 1.5 degrees."

Other leaders expected to speak on Thursday include many island states like Tonga, Tuvalu and the Solomon Islands.

For these nations, the impact of climate change is already at their front door. With most of their land just metres above sea level, rising water levels have caused many to abandon their homes in recent years.

Last year, Australia - the co-host of the COP31 summit - opened up the world's first climate visa for Tuvalu citizens wanting to evacuate.

The first intake was massively oversubscribed, with more than a third of the population entering the ballot.

As glaciers continue to melt and oceans expand, average sea levels are expected to keep climbing and potentially accelerate. The World Meteorological Organisation said on the opening day of this conference the global mean sea level was at its highest level since records began.

Sign up for our Future Earth newsletter to keep up with the latest climate and environment stories with the BBC's Justin Rowlatt. Outside the UK? Sign up to our international newsletter here.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmg4.summary: Andy Burnham says UK is ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on climate change. But environmental campaigners say the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions. The World Meteorological Organisation says the global mean sea level is at its lowest level since record records began.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmkg.title: 'Summer was a wake-up call, winter could be dire' warning over food supplies
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmkg.text:
Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call, and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.

The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.

It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.

Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust, which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.

Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture, only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture.

Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.

"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires and overheating," said Fisher.

Food security has become a hot topic, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.

Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".

He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.

"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber-attacks.

"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."

Fisher and Sue Holbrook launched Our Food Trust about 10 years ago with the aim of growing more produce locally for local markets.

They found one of the main barriers was stable housing for farmers.

As Fisher explained: "If there's a high wind during the night, they need to get out there and protect things.

"If a sheep gets in, they have to get the sheep out before the entire thing is destroyed in an hour. So they have to live there."

But he said planning regulations have made it really difficult to build homes on farmland.

However, by working with Powys council and Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority, they have been able to build three temporary homes for farmers on 36 acres of council-owned land.

They are currently building three more.

One of the growers at Wern Farm is Lydia Dibben, 28, and she agreed access to land is one of the biggest barriers to new farmers.

She said if her home was not provided she would have to get another job to be able to afford rent, and then would end up without enough time to farm.

"I'm only growing on about just over an acre this year, and we're now doing 50 veg boxes a week," she said.

"We've been doing four farmers' markets a month up until the beginning of October. We're also supplying into regional and national wholesale as well.

"I don't know how many people we're feeding, but it's got to be hundreds of people on just a couple of acres."

She believes there are lots of people who want to do similar work, and they should be given access to land and affordable housing to do so.

Dibben said she believed people in the UK thought it would be able to "avoid many of the real challenges of climate breakdown" and "just be able to grow grapes and peaches" but the reality is very different.

"We're going to have to really think a lot harder about how we're producing food, even in this country," she said.

This includes looking at which vegetables work best in hotter climates.

Dibben described the past summer as the hardest she had experienced in five years of growing.

"The hours I was keeping were just insane," she said.

"I was getting out to the field at 05:00, and then working until it got just too hot to be outside, which was like 11:00 some days, maybe even earlier."

She said working in polytunnels was impossible by 09:00 due to the heat.

When it became too hot to work, she had to go indoors and "just survive until it was cool enough to go back outside at probably 17:00".

She then worked until midnight to try and get everything watered.

Dibben said she did not usually have to worry too much about not having enough water, but this year was completely different.

"Even the things that you felt like you were giving as much water as you could were still not growing as much as they should be," she added.

"Everything was slower and stunted.

"We've not had the water bill yet for this summer, but I dread to think.

"We've just not had the crops to make it worth it."

She does not believe it will necessarily be as bad every year, but Dibben accepts there will be more hot summers and unpredictable weather such as flooding.

Dibben thinks there will always be a need for bigger scale farms producing wheat, barley, beef or sheep.

"But I think if there was a farm like ours every 10 miles throughout Wales, that would be a pretty great future in my eyes," she added.

The Welsh government said "significant progress" had been made on its plans to create a national food strategy to "target a more resilient, integrated and sustainable food system".

"There will also be a focus on how to grow more fruit and vegetables in Wales, and we have already begun mapping the current position of the sector with key stakeholders," said a spokesperson.

The UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said: "We recognise the hurdles that our vital fruit and vegetable growers face, which is why we are slashing planning red tape and investing £200m to help farmers trial crop boosting technology.

"The prime minister has made clear that food security is national security, and we're working across the farming sector to make supply chains more resilient."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmze.title: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in England's rivers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmze.text:
Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).

The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.

One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.

Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.

PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.

They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.

The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer.

As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.

The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last 10 years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.

Levels in freshwater fish have fallen 49%.

"It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University.

There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used.

The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.

The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment.

The regulator is now regularly testing for 60 other PFAS to build a picture of contamination across the country, and earlier this month the government announced that it would begin monitoring levels in people's bodies.

The EA report acknowledged that while concentration levels had fallen, because the chemicals take so long to break down, the overall amount still in the environment is likely to have remained unchanged - they have simply been diluted and been washed into the sea.

"There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused," said Megson.

One of the few ways to permanently destroy PFAS is by high-temperature incineration - there are currently just two such suitable sites in the country.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxnv.title: Nurdle impact to be researched for a year
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxnv.text:
Research into the effects of a microplastic spillage on sea-birds and marine life will be carried out for the next year after funding was secured.

A team working across Tyneside is doing tests to discover the impact the pellets, known as nurdles, have on animals, birds and fish, as well as the overall spread.

Tonnes of microplastics were spilled into the River Tyne on 19 July following a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne.

North East England Beached Bird Surveys co-ordinator Dan Turner, who is leading the research on dead sea-birds, said: "This will be a long-term issue, securing the grant now gives us room to conduct more research not just in the North East but worldwide."

Newcastle University is leading the study, which will focus on the effects of the spillage on the River Tyne and at the coast, after receiving a grant of £81,905 from the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC).

Necropsies have been carried out on dead sea-birds at the Dove Marine Laboratory in Cullercoats, North Tyneside, for the past six weeks. The current stage is focusing on stomach rinsing, which will check if nurdles have been found in the birds' stomachs.

"We haven't found any evidence of plastics in the stomachs just yet but we have more to check and have evidence that nurdles have been found in regurgitated material," Turner said.

The research was prompted over concerns birds could "starve" if they confuse the nurdles for food and fill their stomachs.

"It's concerning plastics can also break down over time which could have a big effect on the wider food chain as well," Turner added.

The research team is being led by a team of scientists and experts at Newcastle University and the University of Liverpool.

They are also being assisted by volunteers and other regional organisations such as Environment Agency, Tyne Rivers Trust and Groundwork North East and Cumbria.

Over the course of the year the research will also look to map the travel of the plastic pellets.

The nurdles have been found in beaches across Tyneside, Wearside and Teesside, with experts suggesting they may have reached the coast of Denmark.

Dr Geoffrey Abbott, a reader in geochemistry at Newcastle University, said: "We hope to visit Denmark to determine if the pellets found are the nurdles from the Port of Tyne spill.

"There have been cases where they can travel great distances, for instance a spill in South Africa led to nurdles washing up in Perth, Australia, in no time at all."

Members of the public are being asked to continue to send pictures of nurdles to help with the research.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmpw.title: Campaigners want more land protected from housing
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmpw.text:
After a successful campaign getting parkland protected, residents in a Norfolk town are asking for more space to be given the same safeguards from development.

Seven acres (2.8 hectares) of land known as Harding's Pits, beside the River Great Ouse in King's Lynn, will be preserved after it was given "village green status" by the county council.

The Harding's Pits Community Association had campaigned for the past 30 years to keep the area as leisure space.

Next, the group wants the protection to be extended to the east side, which has been earmarked for up to 50 houses in King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council's local plan. The authority has been approached for comment.

Alexandra Kemp, an independent councillor, said she was asking her authority to amend its local plan.

She said: "I want to protect the east side of Hardings Way as a village green. To take out the 50 houses earmarked for Harding's Pits east from the borough's local plan, and provide community sports facilities, more trees and places for wildlife instead.

"Any development along Hardings Way risks more general traffic which would be devastating to the peace, quiet, safety, and amenity and wildlife."

The local council has been given a target to build more than 10,000 new homes by 2040 by the government.

Harding's Pits was turned into a public space in the early 1960s, but was originally a 19th Century clay pit which was then used as landfill.

The site is currently used for dog walking and as pedestrian access to King's Lynn town centre.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39w.title: Art trail celebrates arrival of black bears at zoo
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39w.text:
A new public art trail will mark the arrival of Asiatic black bears, Jersey Zoo has said.

Sculptures of bears and bees would be put up across the island's wild landscapes, coastal spots and urban spaces to celebrate the arrival of the new species in their new enclosure next year, said bosses.

They said the installation, which launches in July next year, aimed to shine a light on "connections that sustain the natural world, from its largest inhabitants to its smallest".

Artists will be invited to submit designs to turn the sculptures into "distinctive works of art" while schools and community groups will also be encouraged to participate.

It is hoped the sculptures will then be sold a fundraising auction at the end of the summer.

Rebecca Brewer, chief executive of Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, said: "We want everyone who connects with our work, whether at Jersey Zoo or through our conservation projects around the world, to feel they can make a difference for nature.

"Our public art trails are a wonderful way to bring that belief to life."

She said previous Go Wild Gorillas and Tortoise Takeover trails "brought so much joy to Jersey, encouraging people to explore parts of the island they might never have visited, walk new paths, meet new people and create lasting memories".

An auction of the 54 tortoise sculptures raised £720,000 for a new tropical house.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.title: Toby Jones stars in film about UK Mars mission
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.text:
Bafta-winning actors Toby Jones and Emily Watson have finished work on a film about the scientist behind Britain's first spacecraft to land on Mars, which got "lost".

Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.

The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.

Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."

Pillinger, originally from Kingswood near Bristol, became a familiar face in the 1990s as he sought public support and funding for the ambitious mission, enlisting celebrities and pop stars to help promote it.

Beagle 2 was launched into space on board the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter.

His Beagle 2 lander was due to touch down on 25 December 2003, but failed to send a signal confirming it had landed safely.

The mission was considered a failure for years, however, in January 2015 images taken by US space agency Nasa showed the lander had reached the surface safely.

Pillinger died eight months earlier following a brain haemorrhage.

The director added: "Joe Bone's beautiful script has made it easy to attract some of the best names in the business to join our brilliantly creative team and I'm thrilled to be working once again with my friend Toby Jones."

Crook, known for his roles in The Office and Pirates of the Caribbean, previously worked with Jones on Detectorists, the BBC's Bafta-winning comedy he wrote, directed and starred in.

He also starred in Small Prophets, a comedy which made its debut on BBC Two and the BBC iPlayer in February.

The film is expected to be released in 2027.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r.title: Sunbed firms must not downplay cancer risk, says watchdog
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r.text:
A watchdog has launched a crackdown on misleading sunbed adverts, warning tanning firms they must not claim their beds are safe or can treat medical conditions.

The Committee for Advertising Practice (CAP) said it was issuing a UK-wide enforcement notice to "send a clear message to the industry that advertisers must not downplay the risks associated with sunbed use".

Earlier this year, the BBC identified hundreds of social media videos claiming the beds could boost energy and treat skin conditions or mental health problems.

The Sunbed Association, which represents around half of the UK's tanning salons, said it fully supported action against misleading adverts, but said businesses must still be allowed to demonstrate they operate responsibly.

The CAP, which draws up the UK's advertising rules, said some of the claims being made by companies were potentially harmful and could discourage customers from seeking appropriate medical treatment or advice.

"Sunbeds carry serious health risks, including an increased risk of skin cancer," said the CAP's compliance executive James Burnett.

"Ads shouldn't downplay those risks or present sunbed use as a way to improve health."

Cancer charities and doctors are clear about the risks of using sunbeds - and say the machines are linked to higher rates of melanoma and other skin cancers.

Using a bed before the age of 35 increases the risk of melanoma by 59% later in life, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Young people are by far the biggest sunbed users in the UK - about one in seven 18-to-24-year-olds say they used one in the past year, double the average for all age groups, according to a 2025 YouGov survey.

Rosie Vare, health information manager at Teenage Cancer Trust, said skin cancer was one of the most common forms of the disease in young adults and she welcomed stricter enforcement of the advertising rules.

"We want young people to be properly informed about the risk of sunbed use and we recommend using trusted, regulated sources to find out information such as the NHS or cancer charities," she added.

The CAP said it had identified a series of misleading health claims in sunbed advertising, including suggestions that tanning beds can ease eczema symptoms, improve brain function, reduce inflammation and boost circulation.

Earlier this year, the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), which enforces the CAP code, banned five adverts that claimed sunbeds could help manage conditions including osteoporosis and depression.

The new enforcement notice warns businesses not to make medical claims, promote sunbeds as a source of vitamin D or suggest sunbeds are safe.

Sunbed use is legal and regulated in all parts of the UK, with limits on the strength of the UV light the beds can emit and a ban on under-18s using the devices.

According to the Sunbed Association, its members train staff to screen out high-risk customers with very fair skin and, under its guidelines, no individual should be allowed to buy more than 60 sessions a year.

The organisation's chairman, Gary Lipman, said he would never encourage members to use health claims to promote their products.

He said he has worked with the CAP to ensure the code would not stop members explaining how they comply with regulations.

"We fully support action against misleading advertising. But there is a world of difference between claiming something is risk free and explaining that a business operates responsibly," he said.

The CAP said that advertisers have been given until 7 December 2026 to make sure any marketing claims are compliant.

It said it would be using an AI-based monitoring system to identify ads that continue to break the rules and would "take further action where needed".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c68x.title: I'm burnt out and feel forgotten as a young carer
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c68x.text:
A young carer says she feels burnt out, and forgotten about by friends as she takes on extra tasks at home.

Madeline, 16, from Bridgend, cares for her mum and granddad, a role she says she is happy to do.

But she has said people do not always understand its mental impact, and believes both formal and informal support is "crucial" to young people.

She is one of an estimated 170,000 young carers in the UK aged five to 17, but the Carers Trust calls that number the "tip of the iceberg".

The Welsh government said its latest strategy, which is expected to be published this month, had a particular focus on young carers and recognises their contributions.

Madeline, also known as Min, is one of 8,200 young carers in Wales. The 2021 census said there were about 120,000 young carers in England and 42,000 in Scotland.

She is still at school and hopes to be a paediatric doctor one day.

"For me, being a young carer involves helping my mum get up in the mornings, making sure my mum and my granddad have had their medication," she said.

"It also involves cooking meals for my mum, my granddad or my siblings.

"There's also the cleaning which I'll do, any household job really no matter what it is."

She said it can be difficult and often people do not understand what being a young carer entails.

"I find that my friends that aren't young carers don't tend to understand and that I can't always go out when they want or stay out to a certain time so I get kind of pushed aside and forgotten by my own friends," she added.

"Then there's the mental like side effects and stuff because obviously I'm caring about everyone else and I don't often tend to have time for myself."

Min said support, both formal and informal, "means the world" to young people like her.

When she was eight, Min was referred to Bridgend Carers' Centre, which is partly funded by Children In Need, which gives her respite and a chance to socialise with other young carers.

Without this, and support at school, Min said she "couldn't cope".

She said: "The young carers' group is so important to me because all my close friends that actually know what I go through, I get to see in these groups.

"They take us out places which I don't actually tend to do with my mum and my granddad because they're both so heavily disabled, so it's more for me to get out and express myself to be able to spend some time away from what I do."

Min will take part in the annual Children in Need choir which brings together young people supported by its projects from across the UK, singing a mash-up on the night.

She said: "It's shocking [to be] one of a handful of kids to be chosen, it's like, I'm one of the only people that are gonna be able to say I've sung with Children in Need and I'm so excited to be a part of it.

"It's going to be such a memorable experience, I just can't wait."

Min's mum Rebecca said she was "so proud" of her daughter and said support from the group had been the "making of her".

"It has opened her whole life up," she said.

"She's learnt lots of new things, mainly it's confidence and friendships, it's definitely made her a more rounded person, other people her age didn't quite fit with her because they didn't understand, but with the young carers groups, they all understand.

"I know that she doesn't ever see it as an extra responsibility, it's just what she does for her family, for us, because she loves me, she loves us, and she likes to be a caring person."

Alissa Bevan manages the group Min attends and said it was important to see young carers recognised.

"Min's confidence has grown massively," she said.

"She was very shy and timid, not that you would believe that now, and she's made so many really good friends from this group as well.

'It's just a chance for them to be children and not have to worry about all the other responsibilities that they've got a home and come and just have an hour for themselves.

"They're selfless and they give so much."

A Welsh government spokesperson said: "Young carers make a huge contribution to their families and communities. But caring should not affect their education or social opportunities.

"Our National Strategy for Unpaid Carers, published later this month, has a particular focus on young carers.

"We have worked with young carers, councils and support services to identify the action required so that young carers are recognised and they and their families get the help they need."

You can watch the Children in Need choir during the appeal show at 19:00 GMT on Friday 13 November on BBC One.
