https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy.title: Free Sad lamps given out as disorder 'makes it hard to do anything on darker days'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy.text:
Does your mood drop in the winter?

The clocks have gone back, it's getting darker and colder, which could mean you may find the winter months particularly hard.

Rachel Dineen-Mabe is one of more than a million people with Seasonal Affective Disorder (Sad) in the UK, and says it "takes depression and heightens it to a whole new level".

But a new scheme allowing people to borrow Sad lamps from libraries has been launched across Wales to help combat the darker days.

Sad happens when shorter days affect your mood, energy levels and overall wellbeing.

Rachel, 38, the branch librarian at Skewen Library, said darker days make it hard to do anything.

"I struggle just getting out of bed sometimes, I just want to hibernate," she said.

"I don't want to do anything but sleep and it is a real struggle to carry on doing normal everyday things from just dressing, not necessarily because you don't want to but you physically feel unable to."

Rachel, whose library is in one of the 11 council areas taking part in the free lamps scheme, said she notices the effects from about October.

She said: "It's a shame because for me, it's a lovely time of year. I love it, but it has this low mood hanging over it that just leaves it feeling a bit sad.

"I make a real effort to get out as much as I can, obviously my job is very people-focused so I'm always speaking with people which is lovely because this is a lovely community.

"I'm a big reader so that helps and I have bright lights at home like twinkly lights or ambient light all year round, to just try and boost the mood."

"I've used the Sad lamps before and it feels like just a little bit of sunshine in a day where maybe you've seen nothing, it really does boost your mood."

Rachel said that getting outside was the best advice she could give to someone experiencing Sad symptoms.

She said: "I know it's hard but get outside if you can, speak to people. Like I've said, talking about mental health is such an important thing at the moment and this is part of it.

"There are so many people who have Sad and may not even know it, and it's good to acknowledge it."

Lorna Beatrice Lombardini, 26, from Cardiff Bay, said it was tough being a student during the winter months.

"You're inside a lot of the time, working deadlines, exams, and then trying to still have a social life at the same time plus work," she said.

"I absolutely love the 'say yes' idea, which is even if you get invited to plans, you're thinking it's too cold, it's too dark, I want to stay inside. Just say yes.

"Even if you go and it doesn't turn out how you want it to go, you can go home and still appreciate home that little bit more but it's always the experiences that you're not expecting that turn out to be the best."

She said she already uses lamps to help her with mood, and does feel an improvement.

"I know that this is a very universal experience but whatever I can do to try and lift the mood a little bit, feel a little bit lighter, I do try and do my best," she said.

Eleven Welsh councils are taking part in the scheme, developed by researchers from the universities of Glasgow and Edinburgh with funding from the Economic and Social Research Council.

It forms part of a wider expansion across the UK, following two years of trials in Scotland.

The lamps on loan retail at £99, but there are cheaper ones on the market.

Hester Parr, from the University of Glasgow, said the boxes available to borrow had been put together based on research of those with lived experience of Sad and contain a booklet, an online course and a lamp.

"The whole intention of the box is to help people who feel low mood in winter, or feel that they have Seasonal Affective Disorder, make some kind of positive change," she said.

"This is outside the GP system, it's free to use from your local library, so there's no stigma attached to getting this lovely resource that helps us live well in winter."

Emily Van de Venter, from Public Health Wales, said: "People that have been part of the trials have reported benefits and wanted to continue accessing the Sad lamps, evidence has been growing around the benefits that these lamps can bring."

She advised using them for about 20 minutes in the morning, and then gain as much daylight exposure during the day as possible.

The boxes are available across Cardiff, Swansea, Wrexham, Neath Port Talbot, Blaenau Gwent, Merthyr Tydfil, Powys, Conwy, Newport, Vale of Glamorgan and Caerphilly.

If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8ql.title: I saved a stranger's life and my husband's at the same time
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8ql.text:
By saving a stranger's life, Una Brown also saved her husband's.

Sean Brown was living with kidney failure and needed a transplant, but Una was not a 100% match.

The Belfast couple jumped at the chance to take part in the UK Living Kidney Sharing Scheme, which saw Una donate to a stranger, enabling Sean to receive a compatible organ from a different donor.

"When I was told that I wasn't a 100% match, you're automatically thinking, 'God, what's going to happen next?'

"But the fact that I could go into that sharing scheme – I had absolutely no issue with that.

"At the end of the day, if you actually think about it, two lives were saved in one day. It was the best decision of my life."

Sean had received his first kidney transplant aged eight – he was the face of an organ donation campaign as a child – but he always knew he might need another one in the future.

From the outset of their relationship, Una said she would give him one of hers when the time came.

"Immediately I just said - 'If you ever need a new kidney transplant, I'm going to donate' - without hesitation," she said.

Twenty-one years later, that is exactly what she did, in a roundabout way.

Sean had lived "an amazing life" for 37 years before the kidney's function started to deteriorate.

The couple entered the sharing scheme in July and the next month, Una received the news that a suitable match had been found.

"You can imagine that moment of just sheer relief," the 49-year-old council worker said.

"I genuinely cannot tell you what that felt like because it was the most emotional moment of my life.

"I knew there was hope and I knew Sean's life was going to get saved."

Sean, 45, received a call around the same time, bringing a "whirlwind of emotion".

The couple were initially included in a three-way transplant arrangement involving donors and recipients in different parts of the UK.

However, on the morning of surgery on 8 October, while Una was prepped for theatre, they received news that Sean's intended donor had become unwell and could no longer participate.

"I just looked at Sean and I saw his face. I thought, my God, his whole world was just crashing down around him," she said.

After an agonising wait, an alternative match emerged.

"By some miracle", Una said, the donor originally linked to her recipient was also compatible with Sean, allowing the transplant to proceed through paired donation.

Una's kidney was flown to Edinburgh, while Sean's donor kidney travelled to Belfast.

Hannah Magowan, one of the specialist transplant surgeons at Belfast City Hospital, who performed Sean's transplant and helped with Una's surgery, said the sharing scheme had been operating in Northern Ireland since 2010.

She said it had helped almost 200 people here receive a living-donor transplant.

In 2025/26 alone, 20 of the 69 living-donor kidney transplants took place through the scheme - almost three in every 10.

Magowan said Northern Ireland had become the biggest subscribers and contributors to the scheme, despite accounting for about 3% of the UK population.

She said Belfast was described as the "capital" of kidney sharing because of the number of patients and donors coming forward.

However she added there was probably a lack of awareness about the sharing scheme as "another method of donation", even among people living with kidney disease.

Magowan said living-donor transplants could help patients avoid dialysis, as in Sean's case, and potentially lengthy waits for a deceased-donor kidney.

"It's the gift of life for someone who can't avail of a direct donation," she added. "That's sharing at its best."

Sean and Una are recovering well and intend to return to work before Christmas.

Una wanted to reassure people that she would soon be back leading a "perfectly normal" life with just one kidney.

"We're now looking to the future and if Sean gets another 37 years we'll be doing very, very well," she added.

Una said she would never know much about who received her kidney other than they were critically ill and the transplant was successful.

"You don't need to know someone to change their life," she said.

"That's the gift of life through the sharing scheme – the fact that you are making that difference."

Sean could not put into words how he felt about his wife, who had given him "the gift of life again".

He hopes their "phenomenal journey" will encourage more people to consider living donation.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn8.title: Welsh NHS bosses call for multi-year health funding
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn8.text:
Senior Welsh NHS bosses are calling on the Welsh government to provide multi-year funding settlements for health rather than relying on annual budgets.

Next week, ministers will unveil draft spending plans for all public services for the 2027-28 financial year.

The NHS accounts for almost half of the Welsh government's £27.5bn annual budget, but health leaders say one-year funding settlements can constrain long-term planning and transformation.

A Welsh government spokesperson said it was "working to improve services now while making the longer-term changes needed".

The call comes from the Welsh NHS Alliance, formerly the Welsh NHS Confederation, ahead of evidence sessions at the Senedd's health committee on Thursday examining spending plans for 2027-28.

Tuesday's draft budget will need support from at least one opposition party to secure Senedd approval.

Talks between the Welsh government and opposition parties were ongoing.

Last week, the minority Welsh government relied on Labour support to pass adjustments to its spending plans for the next five months, including an extra £100m to help cut NHS waiting times.

In written evidence, the alliance warned that annual budgeting can make it harder to deliver long-term changes to the health service.

"There is a risk that annual planning cycles can constrain longer-term transformation, where benefits often require multi-year investment before being realised," it said.

The organisation argued ministers should prioritise spending that helps "shift Wales from a system focused on treating illness to one that creates health and wellbeing".

It added: "This requires multi-year funding certainty and transparent criteria for investment and disinvestment."

The alliance also cautioned against making cuts to broad service areas in isolation.

"The health and care system is highly interconnected, and reducing expenditure in one area can simply displace costs elsewhere, often into more expensive urgent and emergency care," it said.

It argued spending decisions should instead be based on "value, outcomes and whole-system impact".

The alliance added: "The NHS cannot sustainably meet future demand if resources remain concentrated predominantly at the point of crisis."

It called for more investment in primary and community care, rehabilitation, public health services and support for people with long-term conditions.

Council leaders responsible for social services, who will also give evidence to the committee, warned the sector was under "considerable pressure".

In written evidence, they said councils remained broadly confident of meeting their legal duties, but warned of growing concerns about the long-term sustainability of services if current trends continue.

Like NHS leaders, they also called for multi-year funding settlements.

A Welsh government spokesperson said: "We are working to improve services now while making the longer-term changes needed.

"That means a stronger focus on prevention, reducing health inequalities and supporting independent living, with services designed around outcomes rather than responding to demand."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn8.summary: Welsh NHS Alliance calls for multi-year funding settlements for health services. NHS leaders say annual budgeting can make it harder to deliver long-term changes. Welsh government says it is working to improve services now while making longer-term change needed.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjkg.title: Are max strength cold and flu pills worth the money?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjkg.text:
Your throat's painful, your head throbs and your blocked nose has kept you awake all night. It's that time of year again - flu season - and you'll try anything to feel normal.

But is that pricey max strength flu remedy really any better than a basic box of painkillers?

"The big brands have been around for a while, they've been tested, and there are adverts on the TV saying they're really good," says Prof Jayne Lawrence, head of the pharmacy division at the University of Manchester.

"But in reality, there's very little difference. Personally, I'd always go for the cheaper ones - and they’ve also been tested."

The trade association representing over-the-counter medicine makers says familiar brands can reassure shoppers and help them find the right product on crowded supermarket shelves.

The medications we've highlighted all contain similar ingredients with marginal differences to their quantities.

Cold and flu drugs fall into three broad camps: household names such as Lemsip and Sudafed, supermarket own-label alternatives and single-ingredient medicines containing paracetamol or ibuprofen.

The difference in price can be striking.

A packet of 16 Lemsip All-In-One Max Strength tablets retails at £7.30, more than 20 times the £0.35 cost of paracetamol pills in some supermarkets.

Both contain 500mg of paracetamol, which doesn't treat the underlying infection but does relieve pain and can bring down a fever.

The Lemsip version, along with many of its competitors, also contains the decongestant phenylephrine.

It's meant to constrict leaky or swollen blood vessels in the nose which can cause congestion.

But Lawrence says there is little evidence it works when taken as a tablet, rather than as a nasal spray, because much of the drug is broken down before it can reach the bloodstream.

In 2024, the US drug regulator said it wanted phenylephrine removed from all cold and flu pills, saying it was simply not effective, although that proposal has yet to be finalised.

Some cold and flu remedies contain a third active ingredient - guaifenesin - which is meant to loosen mucus in the airways.

That sits in more of a grey area: some studies report improvements in chest congestion, while others find little or no benefit.

A spokeswoman for Reckitt, which owns Lemsip and Nurofen, says the ingredients in its products are approved by regulators and formulated for multiple symptoms including fever, congestion and coughs.

Many popular max strength remedies can also contain up to 65mg of caffeine per pill, about the same as a mug of instant coffee.

As well as acting as a mild stimulant, research suggests caffeine may boost the effect of paracetamol and help it work slightly sooner, although any benefit is likely to be modest.

Almost every brand can also be found as a flavoured powder to dissolve in hot water, typically costing slightly more per dose than pills or tablets.

That warm drink can be soothing and a study funded by a drug company found it may be absorbed into the bloodstream more quickly, but whether patients notice any major difference in their symptoms is much less certain.

Yet ingredients are only part of the story.

Bigger brands have more money to spend on in-store adverts and displays, according to a former manager at a large chemist chain.

Well-known names or premium own-label products are often positioned at eye level, while budget alternatives are tucked away on the bottom shelves.

"You are always going to promote the ones which are more expensive," says the former manager, who doesn't want to be named as she still works in the industry.

When it comes to medicines, some shoppers assume that paying extra means getting something more trusted or effective.

"Nine times out of 10, people would come in and ask for a certain brand," she adds.

"Even if I explained there was little difference, and I was only trying to save them money, they would still want the big name."

The PAGB, which represents the consumer healthcare sector, argues that "trusted and recognisable" brands can simplify choice and build confidence at a time when "health misinformation is widespread".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c94gnv.title: Tourette syndrome: The life-changing device helping to stop tics
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c94gnv.text:
A wrist device developed by researchers in the University of Nottingham is changing the lives of people with Tourette sydrome in an "instant".

The small device works by delivering electrical pulses to the median nerve at the wrist, which trials have shown can change the activity in the parts of the brain involved in movement control.

Tourette's syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition with symptoms usually starting in childhood.

Among the users of this new device is 15-year-old Ollie, from Cheshire, who started making involuntary neck movements nearly two years ago.

The BBC's Navtej Johal has this report.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj62.title: Faisal Islam: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj62.text:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

"Top gear" and "strikingly strong" were among the descriptions of the 0.7% growth offered by the economists who track every minor murmur of Britain's economy.

It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient", and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War".

Against the backdrop of the world's biggest disruption to energy flows, rising market borrowing costs - and the cruel summers since the pandemic - it is impressive growth.

It should reset some of the swirl of self-reinforcing negativity.

The UK's economic growth has averaged less than 0.1% in the four Q3s [ie July to September] since the pandemic.

The average prediction just months ago for this July to September was just 0.1%.

Even the UK's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) effectively pencilled in 0.3% at the Budget just 3 weeks ago.

This figure has not been exceeded outside the pandemic since 2017. It puts the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy after the US across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

It is tempting to think about what the economy would have done if the Iran War hadn't happened. If interest rates had been cut instead of their recent rise.

While the latest figure kills the doom, it is clearly not a boom either.

Spending on AI and tech have driven the surprise upside over the year. While the AI data centre boom may at any point turn to bust, these figures suggest that spending across the economy on investing in these technologies is helpingboost growth. Consumers have been resilient, at least till the autumn, perhaps helped by better economic vibes.

While there has been an understandable focus on high UK borrowing costs, another measure of the international standing of the UK economy, sterling's value, reached post Brexit referendum highs last week.

Productivity and investment is also looking stronger, especially after recent revisions. Some of the most encouraging figures are in private sector business investment.

I spoke to the chancellor at Nexeon in Oxfordshire, which is searching for a UK factory to manufacture its cutting edge electric vehicle battery - and British - technology. My colleagues visited British watchmakers in Maidenhead carving out a niche to take on the Swiss.

However, this may well not last for the final three months of the year.

Consumer confidence has already fallen as petrol and domestic energy prices start to rise again.

There is a significant challenge with everyday cost-of-living pressures in the coming months. Construction and private house building remain depressed.

The Iran conflict remains the big unknown and whether post the US midterm elections there could be a durable end to the conflict in the Gulf.

Some oil and gas production there is starting to normalise. It could bring down petrol prices, energy bills, government borrowing costs, and mortgage costs too.

Expect to see Downing Street investing heavily in "settlement of the conflict", which the chancellor told me is the "best economic policy".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj62.summary: UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in three months to September. It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient" and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck3r.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck3r.text:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".

Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.

Although investors have recently been concerned about slower artificial intelligence development in the US and the long term viability of AI firms' business models, businesses have continued to invest in the technologies.

Sarah Coles, from investment platform AJ Bell, said that since the start of the year, "it's the less visible back-office work that has delivered, with administrative and supportive services seeing strong growth" noting that these are the areas benefitting from the increasing use of AI.

The latest figures put the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

However, Jake Finney, senior economist at consultancy PwC, cautioned that growth was likely to slow over the coming months "unless energy markets stabilise".

A sharp rise in energy bills is forecast for January, which is likely to hit consumer spending and confidence, he said.

High energy costs have been stoked by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

US and Israeli attacks led to Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz - a vital shipping route for the world's oil and gas.

Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine have been attacking each other's oil refineries, leading to a squeeze on global refining capacity, hitting diesel and petrol prices.

Richard Benc, founder of mechanical watch company Studio Underdog, says sales are better than he expected.

"We've seen more resilience than we had forecast for and expected. We are still projecting growth this year," he says.

The business exports about 80% of its watches. "We've seen a surprising amount of resilience, particularly from our US customers," he adds, although some UK customers are now taking longer to buy watches.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck3r.summary: UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September, official figures show. Strong growth in the services sector helped boost the numbers. Computer programming and consultancy services have been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwn7.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwn7.text:
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.

As reported in the Times, Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet".

He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.

His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of universal credit or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment.

Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.

Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes.

People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work.

Of the four million people claiming Pip in England and Wales, around 430,000 are aged between 16 and 24.

In his interim report, Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.

Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.

Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.

"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."

Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.

Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around.

"What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC.

"Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added.

But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants.

"I don't think you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them get into work," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Tom Ashforth, a 19-year-old student at Sheffield Hallam University, receives both components of Pip at the higher rate.

He said the financial support helps him manage additional expenses linked to his visual impairment, including prescriptions, mobility aids and accessible learning resources.

"If I were to lose it, I would struggle to afford essential things," he said.

He said he believes decisions over disability benefits should be made on a case-by-case basis, rather than according to age.

"You cannot assume that everyone under the age of 25 is in the same position," he said.

In his Times interview, Milburn acknowledged that changing the rules for existing claimants would be "difficult politically" but stressed it was necessary.

Disability groups have welcomed extra employment support, but expressed concern that disabled young people could lose out.

James Taylor, from disability equality charity Scope, said Pip was a "lifeline" for young disabled people and restricting access to it "won't make young disabled people's extra costs disappear".

Harriet Edwards, from the charity Sense, said changes were "long overdue", but that without additional details families were "deeply anxious" about what they could mean for them.

A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work."

The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.

Both the Conservatives and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.

Responding on Thursday, Tory shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said Milburn was "right to say it's time to stop handing out cash for mild conditions".

But she raised concern that spending more on work placements would simply "compensate for the jobs Labour have killed with their taxes and red tape".

If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.

The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch", Milburn said.

His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, wherein young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options.

In an interview recorded on Tuesday, Skills Minister Jacqui Smith told the BBC that young people had a "responsibility" to take up employment support.

"It is a contract. People need the chance, and they need to take that chance," she added.

A separate review - co-chaired by disabilities minister Sir Stephen Timms - examining disability benefits is also expected to be published this month.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwn7.summary: Alan Milburn's year-long report is expected to recommend moving under-25s off main sickness and disability benefits. Milburn has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16-24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckre.title: Gas bills to rise as Middle East turmoil persists
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckre.text:
Gas customers in Jersey will see their bills increase by about 5% from 1 December after Island Energy announced a rise in tariffs for households and businesses.

The company said its mains gas, mini bulk tank and cylinder tariffs would increase by 1p per kilowatt hour (kWh) for all domestic and commercial customers from 1 December 2026.

It said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas and liquefied petroleum gas costs amid disruption to exports and shipping routes in the Middle East after the conflict with Iran.

Chief executive Graeme Millar said: "We recognise that any price increase is unwelcome, particularly during winter."

Securing fuel at lower prices in advance had limited the impact of wholesale cost increases on customers, Millar said.

However, the energy boss added: "It cannot fully protect customers from sustained increases in the cost of fuel and bringing it to Jersey."

Island Energy said customers concerned about paying their gas bills could contact its customer team to discuss what support might be available.

Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption on Wednesday in the nation's first general strike in 14 years.

The main unions called the strike over housing and the high cost of living, with demonstrations planned across the country.

It comes nearly two weeks before Spain's parliamentary elections, which will be held on 29 November.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform.

The BBC's Nick Beake reports from the protest in Madrid.

Slovyansk continues to be bombarded by Russian forces, making it almost uninhabitable with less than 10% of its pre-war population remaining.

The outlet has been evicted from its offices of three decades and says it's been blocked from receiving donations.

Two doctors were eating near the Polish city's Main Market Square when a gunman began firing at random.

Video authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment gunshots rang out in Krakow's main market square.

Dozens of supermarkets in seven European countries dumped huge quantities of food after refrigerators and freezers were targeted in a cyber-attack.

Both Ukraine and Russia say their air raid alert apps were cyber-attacked - Joe Tidy explains what we know so far.

Thousands joined largely orderly demonstrations earlier in the day, before violence erupted in Frankfurt, Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.

More than 320,000 people demonstrated across France against the rising cost of living and poor public services, with clashes between some protesters and police.

The BBC's Dan Johnson travelled to the northern Ukrainian border with Belarus after evacuated Oleshky residents arrived in buses and ambulances following a temporary ceasefire.

Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson explains the temporary ceasefire in the devastated town of Oleshky.

The Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has had no electricity, gas or water for three years, as residents reported having to eat weeds to survive.

BBC correspondent Nick Thorpe reports from Belgrade, where there were rapturous celebrations following the victory of the student-led movement.

The BBC's Europe correspondent reports from Paris where mostly peaceful protests turned into unrest after nightfall.

Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man following the fire.

The three waves of Russian missiles were launched at hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks with the US and Ukraine.

Outside of Paris, Marseille saw some of the worst damage, with shop owners reporting more than 600 premises having been looted.

The serviceman was surrounded by landmines and enemy drones so a ground rescue was not possible, Ukraine's military says.

BBC Verify looked at images appearing to show the Pink Panther rioting in France, but they’re actually AI.

Rioting, looting and vandalism has gripped France over the weekend after protests spiralled out of control across the country.

Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation following a weekend of unrest, but President Macron declined it.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr78.title: Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr78.text:
There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others.

Andy Burnham told his Cabinet earlier this week: "I firmly believe we have ended up with a harder Brexit than people voted for… no sensible person thinks the deal negotiated by the Tories is working for the country."

It comes ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc. On Thursday, at a gathering of European leaders in Dublin, Burnham will for the first time meet those who could prove pivotal as he sells his vision for Britain's future in the bloc.

And next week, he will deliver a speech on foreign policy, in which – for Burnham – Europe is a central plank. He will then travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility.

Talking about the new deal to be signed at the summit, Burnham said to ministers: "We will take opportunities that make people in this country better off.

"There is a significant prize."

This lies behind the prime minister's decision to open the door to the argument about rejoining the EU single market - along with the freedom of movement that would bring - and even the EU altogether.

But that longer-term ambition is dividing his cabinet and his party.

Some welcome his approach, including those with formerly Brexit-backing constituencies. Angela Rayner, for example, is understood to have been pushing former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to be bolder on Brexit since at least autumn 2022.

The housing secretary is said to have been insistent that Labour needs to stick to its manifesto red lines – not to return to the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement – but is open minded to changing those at the next election.

Another cabinet minister said: "The best thing you can do in politics is tell the truth. And the truth is that Brexit has been hugely damaging to Britain.

"We are not leading a public conversation here, we are racing to catch up with the public."

But others are watching nervously at a strategy one former minister described as "high risk".

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, for example, has struck a more cautious tone warning about the "costs and consequences" of rejoining the EU as well as staying out.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business and Trade Secretary, is supportive of getting closer to the EU and discussing the UK's long term relationship.

But he has previously warned against joining the EU's customs union and is also unsure about the prospect of rejoining the EU, highlighting the uncertainty of what terms the UK would face, and what the bloc could look like in years to come with nationalist parties in the ascendancy in several European countries.

A voice from the past has a different set of concerns.

Lord Cameron told Bloomberg's Mishal Husain that starting a conversation about rejoining would be "very long and painful".

The former prime minister warned "flirting with rejoining" could also harm Burnham's attempts to renegotiate the Conservative's Brexit deal.

"If you start endlessly producing this idea that we're actually on a path to rejoining, I think you're in danger of getting a less good partnership deal because of course the EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'."

Attitudes in Labour towards the prime minister's approach don't divide along predictable lines. One Scottish Labour MP, personally opposed to Brexit and with a heavily Remain-voting constituency, said it was a "real problem".

"How can I argue to my constituents that we had a Scottish referendum in 2014 that settled independence for a generation. but then say the 2016 referendum isn't settled? My view is you accept democracy."

For now though, that opposition hasn't broken out into public rebellion, although Labour MP Gareth Snell is one who has warned about reopening the debate.

The MP for Stoke-on-Trent, where the Leave vote was 69.4%, told the BBC's Westminster Hour that doing so would "monopolise an awful lot of time inside parliament, inside government" when there are other things MPs should be doing.

Two Labour MPs among those most unhappy about Burnham's openness to Europe insisted "there are no plans" for any organised criticism of the prime minister.

Despite their concerns, particularly about free movement, they described their current mindset as "wait and see". That temporary truce is likely to fracture if the prime minister's lead in the polls begins to slide.

But Burnham's strategy has left other parties struggling to react.

The Conservatives have strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules into the future, with the party leader Kemi Badenoch saying that would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".

But some Conservative MPs are beginning to express unease about the strategic dilemma presented for their party by Burnham's moves on Europe, fearing that the issue could again divide Conservative voters.

In recent months Badenoch and her team have intensified efforts to win back affluent voters, especially in the south of England, who view Burnham's economic offer as too left-wing.

"The problem is that some of those voters are only just giving us a hearing again after Brexit," one Conservative MP said, "and now they are going to keep being reminded of it."

The Liberal Democrats have enjoyed being the most pro-European of the largest parties in Westminster. But some Lib Dems now fear their distinct position risks being drowned out by Burnham.

Reform UK though say they are "very bullish" about the return of Brexit to political debate, despite polling that suggests public sentiment has shifted since 2016.

"If he [Burnham] wants to fight an election on a £40bn bill to rejoin, open door immigration, and less control over our laws and our courts then we are very up for that," a Reform UK strategist said.

The party believes that just as it would build a progressive anti-Brexit coalition around Labour, it would also unite Brexit supporters around Reform UK as the most anti-EU party.

Some MPs are concerned about the strategic dilemma presented by Burnham. Reform UK say they are "very bullish" about the return of the return to political debate.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckdd.title: MPs urge Labour ministers to get on with trophy hunting ban
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckdd.text:
The government has been accused of dragging its feet on its manifesto promise to ban the import of hunting trophies.

Labour pledged at the 2024 general election to outlaw bringing the parts of animals killed by hunters for sport, such as heads or horns, into the UK.

But it has so far failed to bring a bill enacting the ban to Parliament, and in the two years since the election more than 40 import permits have been granted for hunting trophies.

Speaking during a debate on the subject, Environment Minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter insisted the government was still committed to a ban and a bill would be delivered "when parliamentary time allows".

Labour MP Clive Efford, who had proposed Wednesday's Westminster Hall debate, said the minister's promise "really is not good enough".

"Who is the government afraid of?" he asked, arguing that only a "tiny minority of people" opposed the ban.

He continued: "This issue has been debated widely, over a great many years; there is not much more that we can learn from either side of the argument - this is the time that the government have to act and move forwards."

A ban was first proposed by the Conservative government in 2019, and in 2022 a bill implementing a ban was passed by MPs but ran out of time in the House of Lords.

Conservative MP Henry Smith, who sponsored that bill, accused peers of using "parliamentary devices" to block its passage into law.

During Wednesday's debate, several MPs urged the government to restart the process by introducing a fresh bill to Parliament.

Efford said: "Trophy hunting is not about conservation, it does not resolve issues of wildlife-human conflict, and it does not bring economic benefits to rural areas —certainly not in the way that tourism can.

"Local people have been attacked, their land stolen and their human rights abused. Private companies are stealing their homelands. Britain should not be accommodating this industry."

Labour's Rachael Maskell also called for a ban, but said the government could, in the meantime, make it illegal to advertise safari hunting and make it a criminal offence for UK residents to "celebrate their kill" by posting images on social media.

Labour MP Irene Campbell said she found it "upsetting" that hunting trophies could still be exported from the UK, pointing to an instance of a Scottish stag head being exported to Zimbabwe.

DUP MP Jim Shannon said the flow of hunting trophies coming into the country was continuing at "nearly two dozen a year while the government drag their feet".

Addressing the minister, he said: "I ask her to give us a timescale, give us a date and tell us when [the ban] will happen."

Conservative Roger Gale criticised those who hunted the animals, saying: "A yellow streak runs right through those people and they are revolting."

More than one MP suggested that the government was being pressured by the US not to introduce a ban.

Earlier this year, The Telegraph reported that Doug Burgum, the US interior secretary, wrote to the UK government arguing: "Legal, well-regulated hunting – particularly trophy hunting – plays a vital role in supporting healthy wildlife populations, restoring habitat and supporting local economies."

Responding to MPs, Riddell-Carpenter said the government remained committed to banning "the import of hunting trophies from species of conservation concern".

"Our aim is clear: to introduce the bill at the earliest opportunity and within this Parliament," she said, although she declined repeated invitations from MPs to set out a more specific timetable.

Opponents of the ban argue that it would undermine local economies and reduce the amount of money that could be spent on conservation projects.

The Community Leaders Network, a group of rural representatives from countries in southern Africa, argues that regulated hunting helps pay for rangers and wildlife management.

"In practice, a ban could do the opposite of what it intends: less funding can mean fewer patrols, more poaching, poorer habitat management, and ultimately less wildlife," it says.

An Oxford University report from 2024 concluded that a ban would not ease pressure on threatened species, and said around 79% of imports to the UK between 2015 and 2021 had came from countries where hunted species were "stable, increasing or abundant".

Currently it is legal to bring hunting trophies into the UK, as long as there is a permit to do so.

The government has said permits are only issued when "strict conditions" have been met, including demonstrating that their import "will not have a detrimental effect on the conservation status of the species".

Between July 2024 and September 2026, the government issued permits for 41 imports including 21 African elephants, four hippos, five lions, a leopard and a giraffe.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckdd.summary: Labour pledged at the 2024 general election to ban hunting trophies in the UK. But it has so far failed to bring a bill enacting the ban to Parliament. Environment Minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter insisted the government was still committed to a ban.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp9.title: 'Not the answer': Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp9.text:
Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments.

There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective".

But in a sign of the division within the party, more than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns in Parliament about approving it. Others expressed support, pointing to economic benefits.

Supportive Labour MPs said some other parts of the world emitted far more greenhouse gases than the UK and warned of relying on imports. Reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.

Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support.

One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate".

"The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said.

Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer.

Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test.

"It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices."

Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise."

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh. She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance.

Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields".

Licences for both Jackdaw and Rosebank were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 respectively.

But the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approvals unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a fresh decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch sought to tease at Labour divisions on the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday.

During the debate, Labour MP Anna Gelderd said: "We live in an unprecedented era where our energy security is more vital than ever, in which jobs and wealth must be protected and economic opportunities seized - on both of these points, Rosebank fails."

Labour MP Julia Buckley said she had received opposition to Rosebank from her constituents in "regularly flooded Shrewsbury" and said fossil fuels "belong in the past, not the future".

She urged Fahnbulleh to "reject the oil licence in favour of renewables", adding: "Please don't add further to our climate emergency."

Other Labour MPs expressed their support, including recently departed veterans minister Al Carns, who warned that Britain would continue to need fossil fuels for decades and importing more would be a mistake.

"Refusing to produce it here does nothing on its own to eliminate that demand - it simply increases our reliance on imports which can carry their own environmental cost," he added.

Those representing communities with ties to the oil and gas industry, including Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, stressed the benefits of approving Rosebank for British jobs.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Labour MP Bill Esterson, chair of Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, said "the economics of it (Rosebank) are that you should carry on with it" and "there's an element of energy security" by approving it.

Energy minister Michael Shanks told the debate the government would take a "pragmatic approach" to a clean energy transition, stressing it was "not a turn off the taps government, but nor can we justifiably be a drill every last drop government either".

"This government will not make decisions for this country which are not compatible with our climate obligations," he added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp9.summary: More than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns about approving the oil field. They say it is not compatible with UK's climate commitments. But some backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham - but not yet sent.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dx.title: Burnham signals backing for more ethnicity options on next census
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dx.text:
Andy Burnham has signalled his support for dedicated options at the next census to allow people to define themselves as black English or Asian English.

It comes after Liberal Democrat MP Josh Babarinde called for legislation to widen ethnicity options for respondents at the next population count, due in 2031.

The last census, held in 2021, saw English offered within a broader white category, but without specific options for black English or Asian English.

Asked at Prime Minister's Questions whether he would support Babarinde's proposal, Burnham said he had not seen details of the plan.

But he added: "I stand here thinking that I would want to support that bill, to directly take on the poisonous politics we've seen from some in this House".

"We must bring people back together. I am interested in working with anyone in this House who shares that aim," he added.

Burnham did not respond to a follow-up question from Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey about whether he would meet Babarinde to discuss his plan, and he did not specify whether the government would give it time for debate in Parliament.

Babarinde introduced his proposal for legislation on Tuesday, under a rule that allows MPs to propose new laws in a 10-minute speech.

Such draft laws, known as private members' bills, rarely become law without support from the government of the day but are often used by MPs to raise awareness of issues and generate media attention for policy ideas.

Respondents to the 2021 census were asked a two-stage question about ethnicity, with options grouped under five broad ethnic headings.

In Wales, the terms "Asian Welsh" and "Black Welsh" were listed in the broad categories themselves, and respondents were able to pick "Welsh" as an option underneath the broader white category.

The form in England listed "English" as an option in the white ethnic category, but the only way for respondents to describe themselves as Black English or Black English was via a free-form text box.

In Scotland, the term "Scottish Asian" appeared in the broad categories, whilst "Black Scottish" was given as an example response for the text box.

Speaking on Tuesday, Babarinde said his proposed law would introduce Black English and Asian English as specific new categories, arguing that the text box on the current form "may as well be the margin".

Babarinde's proposal has been backed by some MPs in other parties, including Labour former deputy prime minister David Lammy and Conservative Sir James Cleverly, who quit the shadow cabinet this summer to run for London mayor.

The Eastbourne MP has previously told the BBC he put forward his bill in the wake of comments by former Conservative home secretary Suella Braverman, who defected to Reform UK earlier this year.

Braverman wrote in 2015 that she was British Asian but said she "cannot claim to be English" despite being born and educated in England.

She has reaffirmed her position in recent weeks, writing on X that Englishness was "an ethnicity" and it was "not racist to say this".

"To say I'm English is to take a 'laissez-faire, anything-goes' attitude to ethnicity, citizenship and identity. It also denies me my Asian heritage," she added.

The detailed questions asked during the census in England and Wales are set out in legislation following recommendations from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The ONS told the BBC that the Government Statistical Service has been working on a new approach to asking about ethnicity in official surveys since 2022, with an update on the work due to be published on Thursday.

That could lead to a recommendation to change the ethnicity question at the 2031 census, although the questionnaire itself is normally designed much closer to the time the census is due to take place.

Legislation setting out the questions for the last census was published in summer 2020, ahead of it taking place in March the following year.

The Scottish government delayed the census in Scotland until 2022 because of the Covid pandemic.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dx.summary: Andy Burnham has signed up to support legislation to allow people to define themselves as black English or Asian English. It comes after MP Josh Babarinde called for legislation to widen ethnicity options. The last census, held in 2021, saw English offered within a broader white category, but without specific options for black English and Asian

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9q.title: Former minister calls for phone tech to block live-streamed child sex abuse
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9q.text:
Former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips has joined calls from campaigners for the government to back new technology that blocks the live-streaming of child sexual abuse.

The UK National Crime Agency has flagged the UK as the third biggest market in the world for live-streamed abuse, where children are sexually abused live on camera to order.

Device-level blockers can prevent this material being filmed and viewed on smartphones, laptops and tablets in the first place, Phillips said, at the launch of a policy report in Parliament.

Anti-abuse campaigners claim keeping the technology at device level maintains privacy and encryption. Civil liberties campaigners Big Brother Watch dispute this.

The government has already legislated to demand tech firms like Apple and Google, which develop the operating systems of most smartphones used in the UK, block under-18s from taking or sharing nude images on smartphones and other devices.

However, three-quarters of child sexual abuse material (CSA) was not self-generated but likely captured on adult devices, according to 2025 research from the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), which works to eliminate child sexual abuse imagery online.

Some 1.8 million men in the UK admitted to some form of online sexual offending against children, according to research from child safety institute Childlight.

Phillips, who complained of repeated delays to work to tackle CSA when she resigned as safeguarding minister in May, is demanding action to tackle the source of the crime and reduce the number of British offenders.

"This should be a source of national shame, and we must stop it," the Labour MP said.

"The technology, the evidence and the public support are all there - I want to work with ministers to extend on-device blocking to child sexual abuse material on every device sold in Britain, making children here and over the world safer."

The software uses AI to classify known child abuse images in the phone's operating system, and blocks the material at the moment it is viewed or created, whatever app is in use.

Nothing is logged, stored or sent anywhere, and the tech would work alongside encryption.

The AI classifier has been trained against a database of known child abuse images so it can differentiate between harmless material such as children at the beach, and sexual abuse.

Phillips said online child sexual abuse is "an issue that we did not keep control of" as legislators and now must be prioritised, at the event in Parliament.

She was joined by survivors of online child sexual abuse, who said they should not have to beg for the removal of images of themselves being abused from the internet.

Phil Eccles, from the National Crime Agency (NCA), said the scale of the problem was "at crisis point".

"This would cut off at source somebody on the UK their ability to direct a live stream for a child to be abused," he said.

"To me, safeguarding children will always supersede the ability to prosecute. If we can stop that abuse we must.

"But it's so important that tech companies come onboard - we cannot arrest our way out of this problem."

The parliamentary briefing also heard from the former minister, Conservative Lord Nash, who led the campaign for an under-16s social media ban.

He said: "By the time the police are involved, a child has already been abused and the images and videos have gone round the globe.

"The material has to be blocked on the phone itself, before the harm is done.

"The government deserves real credit for committing to exactly that on children's phones.

"I urge it now to extend that commitment to every device sold in Britain, targeted at CSA material, and to lead the world in doing so."

In a sign of CSA becoming more prevalent, communications watchdog Ofcom has found almost as many offenders looking for CSA on everyday apps on the open web as on the dark web.

John Tanagho, from the anti-trafficking organisation the International Justice Mission, highlighted how children in poorer countries were being targeted for sexual exploitation, with research showing one in every 100 Filipino children were victims.

Legislation should explicitly limit the scans to identifying and blocking CSA material, he said, with no data shared with the government or any private companies, maintaining privacy.

However, civil liberties campaigners Big Brother Watch warned about the possibility of innocent images being blocked or the technology being adapted for surveillance in future.

"Effective child protection requires a stronger criminal justice response," a spokesperson said.

"Yet police are already overwhelmed by reports of child sexual abuse, while the NCA has rightly raised concerns that eight in ten offenders convicted of possessing child abuse images avoid prison.

"Genuine child protection requires well-resourced, targeted policing and robust enforcement of the law, not the scanning of every phone in Britain."

A government spokesperson did not respond directly to the new call for CSA blockers, but said: "We are putting in place the strongest online safety laws in the world.

"This includes preparing world-first legislation to call on the biggest technology companies to make it impossible for children to take, share or view nude images.

"We will also give the police the powers they need to keep pace with criminal use of emerging technologies in order to keep our children safe."
