https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9q.summary: UK National Crime Agency says UK is third biggest market for live-streamed abuse. Former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips calls for technology to block live- streaming of abuse.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm15.title: Reform boycotts Senedd after member banned for saying white people are being replaced
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm15.text:
Reform UK have partially boycotted the Senedd in protest against a ban on one of their politicians for claiming white people are being "replaced".

The party's Welsh leader, Helen Jenner, said Joe Martin's ban was because of "undue pressure" from governing party Plaid Cymru and was an "infringement on freedom of speech".

Martin had been told he would not be allowed to speak in the Senedd's chamber until he apologised for the remarks, which the parliament's Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies called "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called the ruling "ridiculous and outrageous".

Reform members, who make up by far the Senedd's largest opposition party, withdrew from most of the day's proceedings but returned to vote in the parliament in the evening.

Jenner confirmed her party's boycott on the steps of the Senedd on Wednesday afternoon.

"It is now clear that the freedom of speech of one of our Senedd members is being curtailed, meaning his constituents are being silenced," she said.

"We stand behind Joe, and we will not attend today's plenary session in protest at his treatment.

"Every Reform MS [Member of the Senedd] will be in their Senedd office working hard for our constituents."

Martin said he would not apologise.

"My voters sent me to the Senedd to speak on their behalf," he said.

"I am being blocked from doing so, and now it's clear that I have fewer rights than the people who elected me.

"That cannot be the situation in a national parliament."

Asked by BBC Wales if he genuinely believed white people were being "replaced" in the UK, Martin said: "That's obviously a fact."

Aliya Mohammed, chief executive of the charity Race Equality First, said "the idea that white people are being 'replaced' is linked to a conspiracy theory that creates division and wrongly portrays people from minority ethnic backgrounds as a threat".

"Immigration can and should be debated, but language that fuels fear and hostility has no place in public discourse," she said.

"Being Welsh or British is not defined by race or skin colour.

"Wales belongs to all of us, and our diversity is one of our greatest strengths."

Posting on X, Farage said it was "ridiculous and outrageous that Reform's duly elected Member of the Senedd, Joe Martin, has been banned from speaking in the Welsh Parliament".

"Why is it only Reform that's targeted like this?" he asked.

Martin was also backed by the leader of right-wing party Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe.

He called for the Senedd to be "shut down" if it was "going to shut down legitimate debate around demographic security and immigration".

Martin's Caerdydd Penarth constituency includes some of Wales' most ethnically diverse communities.

On Tuesday Martin asked for a Welsh government statement on the "demographic replacement of white British people" during business questions, when Senedd members are free to raise issues they choose.

Business Minister Heledd Fychan immediately asked the presiding officer whether the remarks were within the Senedd's standing orders - a set of rules that govern conduct in the chamber.

Standing orders give the presiding officer discretion to decide if contributions to plenary sessions - meetings of the full Senedd - use "discriminatory or offensive language".

Delivering his ruling later, Irranca-Davies said: "Until I receive a clear indication that the member understands the boundaries of acceptable parliamentary conduct and apologises to the Siambr [chamber], we will not be calling him to speak."

Senedd officials confirmed an apology would have to be made in the chamber during a plenary session.

The ruling does not cover committees.

Martin is a member of the Senedd's Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee.

Irranca-Davies pointed out it was not the first time he had rebuked Martin. In September, he said Martin had made offensive remarks about surgeons working in the Welsh NHS gender service.

Plaid Cymru Senedd member Carrie Harper called Reform's boycott a "pathetic tantrum" that was a "disgrace to democracy".

"They'd rather play gimmicks and chase headlines than be serious about Wales' future and doing the job they were elected to do on behalf of the people they represent," she said.

Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates said he was "astonished" that Reform had "chosen Remembrance Day of all days to pull a political stunt".

"They claim to be on the side of our armed forces, of our veterans, yet when they have the chance to speak up on behalf of this community, they bolt," he said.

"It is shameful, unpatriotic and disrespectful to the Armed Forces community."

In the 2021 census 93.8% of people in Wales identified as white, down from 95.6% a decade earlier, with the country's overall population growing by 1.4% to 3,107,500.

The proportion identifying as Asian, Asian Welsh or Asian British, the next highest group in the survey, rose from 2.3% to 2.9%.

Mixed or multiple ethnic groups rose from 1% to 1.6%, and those identifying as Black, Black Welsh, Black British, Caribbean or African rose from 0.6% to 0.9%.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm15.summary: Reform UK leader Helen Jenner says ban on Joe Martin is "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive" Party's leader says ban is because of "undue pressure" from governing party Plaid Cymru. Martin had been told he would not be allowed to speak in the Senedd's chamber until he apologised.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw07.title: MPs jostle for slice of £14.6m from axed leisure centre
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw07.text:
Three Labour MPs in Bradford have found themselves scrapping it out for a share of £14.6m left over from a cancelled leisure centre project.

The Reform UK-led council axed the long-planned Squire Lane leisure centre project earlier this year, citing rising costs.

Shipley MP Anna Dixon had backed calls to use some of the money - which comes from a £20m government grant - to reopen Bingley Pool, while Bradford East MP Imran Hussain said last week he wanted a share to help turn a derelict building on his patch into a youth and community hub.

Meanwhile, Bradford West MP Naz Shah has recently said the cash should stay in the constituency it was meant for: "This money is something that I secured for Bradford West, and I'd like to keep it in Bradford West."

The competing calls for the funding follow a recent row over whether Bradford could keep the grant at all.

Council leader Stephen Place had initially disputed Dixon's claim that the money was available for other projects, but later confirmed that the government would not claw it back. He said at the time that the council was not yet able to commit it to a particular scheme.

Shah has now told the BBC that the council leader had "absolutely assured" her Bradford West would be given "priority" when the money was allocated.

But she also said it was ultimately a matter for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) to decide on.

The BBC understands the money has to be spent by 2028.

Asked whether the pot could be split between the three constituencies, hers and her two Labour colleagues', Shah pointed to the separate £20m allocated to Hussain's Bradford East constituency through the current government's Pride in Place programme.

She stressed it was every MP's own "choice and prerogative" to champion particular projects in their own constituencies with money earmarked specifically for those constituencies. "But the money that comes in to Bradford West, I'm very keen that it stays in Bradford West," she said.

Asked about her colleagues' efforts to secure some of the money, Shah said: "Is it the way I would have tried to get money for my constituency? No, it isn't."

But she said she had spoken to Dixon and understood why she was pressing for the swimming pool.

"That pool is something that she is passionate about, and rightfully so, because nobody would expect an MP not to be," Shah said.

Shah pointed to the Scotchman Road fields in Toller ward as one site on her patch that could benefit from investment and said there was further need across Bradford West, including in Clayton, Thornton, Manningham and Heaton.

"You could double and triple that [money], and I'd still find the need for it," she said.

Bradford Independents Group councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed, who is chair of the cross-party Bradford West Area Committee, also backed Shah's call, saying: "Bradford West must not lose the investment it was promised."

He said the original Levelling Up grant was intended to tackle deprivation and health inequalities, and urged the council to commit the full £14.6m to alternative projects in Bradford West if ministers agreed.

"The cancellation of the original Squire Lane project does not cancel the needs of the people it was intended to serve," he said.

"I have no objection to Bingley residents campaigning for their swimming pool. They are entitled to make their case. But why should Bradford West lose out?"

The Heaton and Frizinghall councillor said not investing the money in Bradford West would "represent a serious injustice".

The previous Conservative government had earmarked the £20m for the Squire Lane project through its Levelling Up programme.

But in July, the Reform-led executive decided to discontinue the project amid concerns about the council's financial position and rising costs. This was despite more than £5m of the original pot having already been spent on preparation and planning work.

The executive axed the project contrary to its own officers' recommendations, who had stressed in a report that the Bradford West area experiences "disproportionately high levels" of deprivation, physical inactivity, and poor physical and mental health.

Their report said Bradford West's lack of a publicly accessible swimming pool left "thousands of residents [facing] barriers in participating".

A Bradford Council spokesperson said the authority was "currently assessing options for alternative use of the Local Regeneration Funding previously allocated to the Squire Lane Leisure Centre project".

"Key to this is the need to ensure any projects are deliverable and can draw down on all required grant funds by end of March 2028," they added.

The BBC understands that a memorandum of understanding exists between Bradford Council and the MHCLG which sets out how Local Regeneration Funding is managed.

The authority would be expected to discuss any major changes with the MHCLG and while MPs would not have a formal role in that, they are considered to be significant stakeholders.

Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw07.summary: Bradford West MP Naz Shah says she wants to keep money in her constituency. She says she has secured £14.6m from a £20m government grant for the project. Council leader Stephen Place says the money has to be spent by 2028.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxvg.title: Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxvg.text:
The Brexit debate is back.

For years, it felt like the only thing Westminster talked about.

I have had a ringside seat at it all, from the Conservative election victory in 2015, with the party's promise in its manifesto that year to offer "a straight in-out referendum on our membership of the European Union by the end of 2017."

Then there was the then Prime Minister David Cameron's negotiation with the European Union to try to secure what he saw as a better deal and then the referendum itself on Thursday, 23 June 2016.

And that, you will remember, was merely the start, as years of wrangling began. Two general elections came and went in 2017 and 2019 and it took the two prime ministers after David Cameron, first Theresa May and then Boris Johnson, before the UK left the European Union at 23:00 on Friday, 31 January 2020.

Little wonder perhaps that by that point, almost irrespective of someone's views on the topic, there was an appetite to talk about something else. Anything else. Political parties picked up that vibe and while their long standing instincts on the EU were there to see if you scratched the surface, there was minimal desire to extemporise about them any time soon.

With the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister, that has changed, despite what he said just a few months before he arrived in Downing Street.

He has been happy to repeatedly lean into an argument claiming that it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain." First he made this case at the Labour Party Conference last month and now he has made it again in the House of Commons.

Burnham is attempting to make a two-pronged case.

First, in the short term, he wants to "deepen" the UK's relationship with the EU at a summit in Brussels at the end of next month. He insists such a deepening would be within the promise made by Labour at the last general election that the UK would say no to the customs union, the single market and freedom of movement.

Which brings us onto the second element of his case, in the medium term. What might Labour promise in its next general election manifesto? The prime minister told me a fortnight ago the manifesto could promise an in-out referendum.

In the Commons, he sought to reassure you, whatever your view on Brexit.

"This country in the next decade needs to know where it's going. There are no assumptions here, and as I said, the British public will be the boss of whatever is decided," he said.

Hang on, say critics, it was decided by voters a decade ago.

"They weighed the arguments and made a decision. The least they are owed is politicians willing to defend it," argues Lord Frost, a former Brexit minister and chief Brexit negotiator in the Telegraph.

The focus of the next five weeks, ahead of a UK-EU Summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November, is what Downing Street sees as short term wins on youth mobility, food and drink, and energy.

Andy Burnham hopes to make an argument that what he will portray as a sensible, pragmatic deepening of the relationship with Brussels can help cut illegal immigration and boost economic growth.

He sought to goad the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch for seeking to oppose a plan he thinks can contribute to growth. She argued it risked regurgitating yesterday's arguments with little prospect of success.

And, strikingly, his attempt at goading his opponents went further still. He told The Rest Is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there was Russian interference in the Brexit referendum.

"I've had a clear answer that, yes, there was," he claimed, without saying who provided that clear answer or what the evidence for that suggested clarity was.

In the Commons, his language appeared a little softer. He told MPs it was "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere. A double negative deployed this time, about alleged attempts at interference.

His political opponents were already pouncing. The Reform UK leader Nigel Farage was blunt – calling the prime minister "a liar."

The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson added that he had asked the same question as Andy Burnham did when he became Foreign Secretary "and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".

And so a debate resumes about the difference between attempted interference, interference and successful interference.

But the key point is this: for the first time since the UK left the European Union, we now have a prime minister who is willing to unflinchingly debate Brexit: whether it is working, how it is working, how to improve it, and if it's proved to be a failure.

In so doing he hopes he can tap into public sentiment. Opinion polls suggest a perception among a majority that leaving the European Union has not turned out how many might have hoped.

On top of this, he hopes to lure pro Europeans broadly on the Left who may recently have supported the Liberal Democrats, the Green parties of both England and Wales and Scotland, the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru towards Labour. That is the political logic from the government's point of view, for now at least.

And as for where all of this leads – well, good question. In the coming weeks, months and perhaps years, there may be a Back to the Future vibe to our political debate. A splash of familiarity, as a conversation about the relationship we have with our nearest neighbours resumes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxvg.summary: UK will leave the European Union in 2020, leaving the EU in January 2020. Andy Burnham wants to "deepen" the relationship with the EU at a summit in Brussels next month.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp3r.title: Why are hundreds of prisoners being released early?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp3r.text:
Around 650 more prisoners in England and Wales are due to be released on Tuesday under the third tranche of the government's early release scheme.

Under the scheme, eligible prisoners are released after serving a third of their total custodial sentence rather than after 40% or 50% of the term.

People sentenced for manslaughter, rape, and serious child sex and grooming offences are excluded.

This is not the first time a government - Conservative or Labour - has released prisoners early to make space in England and Wales' overcrowded prisons.

BBC Verify has looked at the reasons why ministers say the current scheme is necessary.

The prison population in England and Wales on 9 November was 86,982, which was 97.6% of useable capacity.

In the long-term the MoJ has projected that the capacity of all prisons will rise to around 99,000 by 2032 as a result of more prisons being built by this government.

But it also projected that the prisoner population would rise to about 104,000 by 2032 if the Sentencing Act 2026 - which provides for earlier release - did not come into force.

That is why Justice Secretary Alex Norris says there is a "prison capacity crisis" which means the government has to implement the latest early release scheme.

In total 4,500 prisoners are due to be released early by June 2027. The first tranche saw about 700 offenders released from jail early on 1 October - all of whom were serving terms of less than 19 months.

The MoJ has projected that the Sentencing Act will mean the prisoner population remains below the capacity of the prison system, rising only to around 96,000 by 2032.

The England and Wales prison population has risen significantly in recent decades with a significant uptick starting in the 1990s before reaching a record high in 2024.

The Institute for Government (IFG) think tank says this is partly the result of longer sentences.

In 2023, the average prison sentence at Crown Courts in England and Wales - which deal with more serious offences - was more than 25% longer than those handed down in 2012.

For some crimes, the increase was greater. Sentences for robbery in 2023 were 13 months longer on average than in 2012 - an increase of 36%.

Longer sentences mean more people being held in prison at any one time.

Former Conservative Justice Secretary David Gauke, who led an independent sentencing review for Sir Keir Starmer's government, argues this is the result of a "bidding war" by political parties since the 1990s over who can imprison people for longer.

Gauke also points out that the prison population has been rising at a time when overall crime in England and Wales has been falling, according to the official Crime Survey.

So despite the fall in crime more people are being sent to prison - and for longer.

Another reason for upward pressure on the prison population is that more people than before are being returned to prison for breaching the conditions of their release.

There were 51,419 licence recalls in England and Wales in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.

Cassia Rowland from the IFG said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public.

"The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.

Successive governments have pledged to increase the number of prison places - but delivery has often fallen short of those promises.

Between 2010 and 2024, when the Conservatives were in power, around 13,000 new prison places were created.

But around 12,500 places - notably those built during the Victorian era - were closed after falling into disrepair.

That means an estimated net total of only around 500 new prison places were added over 14 years.

In a 2024 report, the National Audit Office (NAO) cited the MOJ's "unrealistic timelines", and government bodies not working together to prioritise delivery, as reasons for the slow pace of prison building.

The MOJ say around 6,500 net prison places were created between 2022 and 2025, once closures are taken into consideration. These include places created in three new prisons.

However, further expansion to existing prisons has been delayed by a major supplier going into administration, according to the Prison Reform Trust.

Pia Sinha of the Prison Reform Trust told BBC Verify: "Successive governments have found it difficult to increase prison capacity because new prisons take years to plan and build, often facing planning hurdles and local opposition."

The Labour government has pledged to build 14,000 new prison places by 2031.

Analysts argue that without a major change in thinking about the appropriateness of prison as punishment, or a significant long-term increase in prison building, the system in England and Wales will remain close to capacity.

And that means governments will continue to be under pressure to implement early release schemes to avert a capacity crisis.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ced7.title: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land 'gobsmacking' donations
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ced7.text:
Look closely at the posters, placards and online posts. Your eyes aren't deceiving you if Labour's red seems a little deeper and the Conservatives' blue a little truer.

Politics seems to have found a new rhythm, one that feels a little familiar, despite Reform's jaw-dropping new donations putting it back in the headlines today.

For the avoidance of doubt, the scale of that initial £36m gift to Nigel Farage's party alone is like something from a different political universe.

"It's a gobsmacking sum," a senior figure involved in running successive election campaigns for one of the big parties tells me.

That was even before another Reform donor pledged to match that astonishing sum with another £36m, saying the first donation had provoked his "competitive spirit".

But one cabinet minister is enjoying what they see as a newly obvious difference between Labour and the Tories. "It's clarifying," they say, a clear gap between Labour and the Tories' "sense of purpose and values".

A member of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's top team tells me, "normal jogging is reasserting itself", hopeful they're at the start of a more straightforward, routine moment in politics after years of craziness, with smaller parties vying to shove the traditional tribes out of the way.

The standout moment was at the despatch box this week when Prime Minister Andy Burnham declared that national security couldn't come at the expense of social security - a phrase immediately seized on by the Tories, interpreting it as the PM saying he'd never cut welfare spending to pay for defence.

One senior conservative said: "It was a real line in the sand, we could never have imagined Sir Keir Starmer saying that."

The party seems cock-a-hoop at a line they can use again and again, asserting the prime minister cares more about welfare than guarding against war.

But there is a positive atmosphere in No 10 too, one source telling me that the face-offs between Badenoch and Burnham have "breathed new life into the Labour versus Tory dynamic".

How can they both be happy, when ultimately politics is a contest and there can only be one winner in the end?

Well, on the security spat, Burnham's backers are adamant he does want to cut welfare spending, and find more money for defence. How does that stack up with his words this week?

I'm told No 10 will explain in more detail his belief that security also means secure communities, which aren't created by slashing benefits.

Crucially, they reckon while cutting welfare might appeal to some voters, "once you dig into the 'who' and the 'how' of doing that, public support wavers, and when Kemi talks about housing benefit cuts, public opinion goes all over the shop".

They even cite that moment as evidence that the prime minister is "happy to grab thorny issues and put himself at the centre of them", as he did with the early release of prisoners.

He'll give a grabby-sounding view before the government has found a solution to a problem, stake part of his reputation on it, and make the case, hoping it will work out.

The choices are only going to get harder and harder though. "Hope" as a slogan and a strategy could never be enough.

But when politics is fundamentally a contest, how can both the traditional political tribes be buoyant?

For Labour, it's not just the obvious change of leader to a more effective politician who is much more at ease talking to the public, whether that's an eight-second TikTok or his long explanations of his positions expressed in a newspaper opinion piece and posted on Facebook.

It's that Burnham is making arguments that are more appealing to Labour's psychology – build council houses, take stronger action against the worst excesses of the Israeli government, stand up for those who need to rely on benefits from the state.

Labour believes, for now, they have a leader who is simply a better politician, who is making arguments many of them find instinctively more appealing.

The party knows what its leader believes, broadly at least. As one senior figure said: "He has a worldview which the last one didn't - he's clear what he wants and he's grabbed the reins of power."

Another who has worked under Starmer and now Burnham said: "It's just chalk and cheese."

And don't underestimate the importance of keeping backbenchers content, feeling understood. A government source joked the whips, the party managers, are becoming a bit "like an HR department" listening to concerns rather than driving the troops forward.

But as Starmer found to his cost, backbenchers weren't prepared to be loyal to him when many felt he hadn't shown much care or loyalty to them.

But Badenoch's tribe also seems more chipper because, as she has told friends, there is now a sharper ideological divide between the two parties saying, "it's much clearer to have those arguments rather than a process discussion with Starmer".

Shadow ministers reckon it's easier to make classic Conservative arguments because in the words of one, "Andy Burnham is a classic old leftie and we're the obvious answer to that".

Shock, horror, Labour sources I put that to dispute that is the case, one close ally calling him "a pragmatist", another denying he's further to the left than Starmer, because, "Keir was so hard to place".

But one conservative source also pointedly wonders how long Labour's happiness with their new leader will last, given Burnham's rapid return to Parliament saying, "looking at the benches opposite there is a vision of somebody who has turned up to a Tinder date and doesn't quite look like his profile pic".

Will this newly refreshed red-blue battle prove to be the real deal?

Rhetorical lines have been drawn this week, but real choices and arguments loom, and the bouncy feeling around the place may not last, especially when it comes to finding cash for the prime minister's big promises.

Downing Street sources acknowledge privately that bringing down the welfare bill in the way that Alan Milburn envisages, with his report expected, but not confirmed, to come before the Budget, will need billions spent up front, money the government might struggle to find.

Similarly, to build the council houses Burnham desires to cut the housing benefits bill will need big cheques.

It's one thing promising those Labour friendly dreams. It's another, perhaps at the party conference, to answer the much harder question of how the government plans to pay.

It won't be easy for a mid-term prime minister to find money in the short term that might only produce savings in the years to come.

But Burnham's Labour are happy to talk about the economy and how they want to help hard-up families, still citing the chaos of Liz Truss and keen to underline the early steps the prime minister has taken to ease the pressure.

With borrowing costs and the country's debt seriously sky high, the Conservatives are pleased to sketch out a classic left-right argument too.

It's also true they have both been enjoying the moment of real pressure on their opponents in Reform, who have slipped back in the polls, besieged by claims and counter claims about party funding.

Although this weekend's mega donations illustrate that Nigel Farage still has the capacity to bust political conventions, the money from the crypto billionaire, Ben Delo, and cryptocurrency investor, Christopher Harborne, is completely off the charts for our politics.

Talking about the initial donation, a senior figure told me: "To put £36 m in context, one man has donated a sum bigger than Labour's entire 2024 election budget, bigger than the Conservatives', and about six times what Reform actually spent.

"It's the kind of donation that could change how politics is funded in the UK."

During the last general election campaign Labour raised about £9m, the Tories, Reform and the Lib Dems all less than £2m.

These extra millions give Farage enormous and immediate spending power, and there might be more to come. Although you can bet the other parties will cry foul over the scale of this big money coming from men with deep pockets, not least because Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over violating the Bank Secrecy Act.

It would be daft for either of the two main parties to assume this apparent return to traditional two-party politics is here to stay. But it is strangely new to be in a moment when both Labour and the Conservatives are broadly content.

As the new prime minister's universe settles, a key Labour figure observed: "We've had the amuse–bouche and it was very tasty. What happens next?"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvkg.title: Schools, libraries and parents face 'difficult decision' over David Walliams books
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvkg.text:
Some schools have removed David Walliams books from their libraries following the publication of allegations against the best-selling children's author and comedian.

"Head teachers are already making difficult decisions about whether or not these books should remain on the bookshelves of libraries at the moment," said Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders.

"I'm aware from several of our members that they've already taken the decision to take them off their shelves."

Walliams sold more than 50 million copies of books including Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy. He has denied allegations of sexual misconduct and abuses of power.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Mr Di'Iasio urged the government to give schools national guidance, so they are "not leaving this open to one or two head teachers making one decision and others making a different one".

Darren Morgan, head of Kings Road Primary School in Manchester, told the programme that he has taken the decision to remove Walliams' publications.

The stories have been useful to promote reading, but "when there are these allegations it's really difficult to keep these books on the shelves", he said.

Steve Chalke, head of Oasis Academies, which runs more than 50 schools, said it was impossible to stop children seeing the current stories about Walliams.

"So when a child wanders into a school and into the library and sees his name or perhaps sees his photograph on a book, it can be very traumatising for some children," he said.

Author Chloe Combi, who has written about "how it feels to be young in modern Britain" and Generation Z, said banning Walliams' books is not appropriate, and could mean that important conversations about him "get swept under the carpet".

"I think by talking about it and what has happened - and the responsibility of parents to have that conversation with their kids - that actually makes more sense," she told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I'm totally sympathetic with schools for withdrawing him and bookshops withdrawing him as an individual decision. But the point is, none of that is going to erase what's happened."

The Department for Education has been asked for comment.

Retailers including Waterstones, TG Jones, and The Works, say they will no longer sell Walliams' books, and his publisher HarperCollins cut ties with him in September.

Public libraries have also faced calls to remove his books.

Librarians' body CILIP said it "recognises that dealing with challenges made to books or other resources can be an extremely complex and stressful situation for library staff".

Decisions about stocking books are made by local councils.

Among them, Kent County Council said it had no plans to remove Walliams' titles from its libraries.

"The starting point is that books should be available to readers unless their content is unlawful," a spokesperson said.

"Decisions about library stock are not made through blanket bans on individual authors. Collections are regularly reviewed and refreshed to reflect factors such as reader demand, condition and relevance of stock."

Surrey County Council said that demand for Walliams' books had "fallen significantly in recent years", but his titles are "not illegal" and "remain available for readers to borrow".

Camden Council in north London said it was putting Walliams' books in storage.

A spokesperson told the Camden New Journal: "We are committed to making Camden a safer place for women and girls, to challenging harmful attitudes, and promoting healthy relationships.

"Following these allegations, we believe the most appropriate action is to remove these books from display."

On Tuesday, ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including some who accused him of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

In a letter to journalists published by the paper, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvkg.summary: David Walliams sold more than 50 million copies of books including Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy. He has denied allegations of sexual misconduct and abuses of power. School leaders say they are making difficult decisions about whether or not to remove books.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cked.title: Russell Brand's social media accounts disabled by Meta
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cked.text:
Russell Brand's social media accounts on platforms owned by tech company Meta have been disabled.

It comes after the 51-year-old former entertainer was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years in jail for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault earlier this week.

He was found guilty of the charges involving four women and relating to offences between 2004 and 2009.

Meta owns social media platforms including Instagram and Facebook.

Brand is currently in prison and is expected to serve seven years of his sentence behind bars before being released on licence.

On Thursday evening, a post appeared on his X account, which remains active. "There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read.

"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner. "Stay tuned," it concluded.

The post included what appeared to be screenshots showing Brand's Instagram account having been disabled.

Meta's community standards policy says that "in order to maintain a safe environment and empower free expression" it restricts or removes accounts that are "harmful to the community".

That includes accounts owned by convicted sex offenders.

In 2023, after a media investigation revealing allegations about Brand's behaviour - which he denies - YouTube suspended his channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy".

At the time, the video platform said it was taking action "to protect" its users.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cked.summary: Russell Brand's social media accounts on platforms owned by Meta have been disabled. He was found guilty of the charges involving four women and relating to offences between 2004 and 2009.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmdx.title: DJ Tim Westwood denies two more sexual offences
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmdx.text:
Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has denied two more sexual offences during a court hearing.

His latest pleas of not guilty mean he now denies a total of 17 charges concerning allegations by nine women between 1983 and 2016.

The 69-year-old pleaded not guilty to indecently assaulting a teenage girl aged 16 or 17 in Hammersmith and Fulham, west London, in 1991 at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday.

At the same hearing, Westwood also denied sexually assaulting an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth, south London, in May 2004.

Westwood, of Fitzrovia, in London's West End, was charged in October last year with offences against seven women, which he also denies.

He is accused of four indecent assaults in the 1980s in London, as well as three indecent assaults while at the BBC in the 1990s.

The defendant is also alleged to have raped a woman in a hotel in 1996.

Westwood is further accused of two indecent assaults and one count of rape from the early 2000s at a London address, and two counts of rape at a London address in the 2010s.

He is also alleged to have committed a sexual assault at a nightclub in Stroud, Gloucestershire, in 2010 and at a London music festival in 2016.

Westwood has been granted conditional bail and is due to face a seven-week trial at Southwark Crown Court starting on 27 January.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmdx.summary: Tim Westwood denies 17 charges of indecent assaults against nine women. 69-year-old pleaded not guilty to indecently assaulting a teenage girl in 1991. He also denies sexually assaulting an 18-year old woman in Wandsworth, south London, in 2004.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3qj.title: King Charles appears on Sir Elton John's radio show
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3qj.text:
King Charles III has appeared on Sir Elton John's radio show in an episode set to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

During the Rocket Hour show, the King said the pop star had become "a national treasure after all these years", to which the singer joked: "I'll be on the Antiques Roadshow."

"Join the club," the King replied.

The pair discussed some of their favourite musical performances, as well as the role music has played in the King's charity, the King's Trust. The show was recorded in secret last month and will air this Saturday.

Sir Elton has long been a supporter of the trust, most recently donating a pair of his rose-tinted glasses to its 50th anniversary auction this year.

In a trailer for the upcoming episode, the King and Sir Elton are seen laughing together as they chat.

In a voiceover, the singer said he was "excited to hear what he's got to say about music, about the King's Trust and memories that we both share".

The King's Trust - previously known as The Prince's Trust - was established by Charles in 1976 to help young people from disadvantaged backgrounds overcome challenging situations, become employed or launch their own businesses.

During the radio episode, the King called it "an opportunity too good to resist" when he was asked to showcase music from the "talented performers who have so generously supported us over the years, together with some of the newer artists the trust has helped to launch".

The full list of their chosen tracks is under wraps until the episode airs but Skye Newman's Hairdresser, Raye's Joy and Muse's rendition of Feeling Good are said to be among them.

The pair will reminisce about some of the most memorable performances for the trust, from the Wembley Arena rock galas of the 1980s - which Sir Elton participated in - to charity shows at the Royal Albert Hall and pop concerts in Hyde Park.

The episode was recorded at Apple Music Studios - which hosts the show - in Battersea Power Station when the King and Sir Elton visited for the launch of the Apple x King's Trust Creative Labs.

The mentorship programme aims to help young people explore careers in creative industries.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3qj.summary: King Charles III has appeared on Sir Elton John's radio show in an episode set to coincide with his 78th birthday. The King said the pop star had become "a national treasure after all these years" The King's Trust was established by Charles in 1976 to help young people overcome challenging situations.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmg4.title: Resident Evil Requiem sweeps Golden Joystick Awards
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmg4.text:
Resident Evil Requiem and its makers have won big at the Golden Joystick Awards, which celebrate the year's most popular games.

Released in February, it was the latest instalment of the global survival horror phenomenon, which has also spawned books, films and TV programmes since it was first released 30 years ago.

At Wednesday's awards ceremony, it scooped ultimate game of the year, console game of the year, best game trailer, and best lead performer for the game's star Angela Sant'Albano, who plays protagonist Grace Ashcroft.

Meanwhile its makers, Japanese studio Capcom, was named studio of the year and was also recognised for other games, including Onimusha: Way of the Sword and Pragmata.

FBI agent Grace Ashcroft was a brand new lead character in Resident Evil Requiem who, along with returning fan favourite Leon S. Kennedy, explores old haunts, such as Racoon City's police department as they investigate a series of mysterious deaths.

Securing 17% of the public vote, it was named ultimate game of the year ahead of other contenders Phantom Blade Zero, Crimson Desert, Control Resonant and The Blood of Dawnwalker.

There were prizes across 25 categories up for grabs - 22 of which are decided by a public vote amongst gamers from around the world.

While streamers' choice, critics' choice and developers' choice award are decided by critics.

Two of those went to indie hit Meccha Chameleon, a multiplayer hide-and-seek game where players paint themselves to blend in with their surroundings to evade others playing as hunters.

As well as streamers' choice and developers' choice, it also bagged best multiplayer game and best indie game - self published, which were chosen by the public.

Big Walk - a co-operative online game produced by Australian developer House House - was named critics' choice winner.

The studio was criticised this week after reports it used generative AI in the final stretch of the game's development - something it did not disclose at the time of the its release.

It said the tool was used to produce a tiny amount of code.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm1d.title: CMAT joins Philomena Begley on stage in surprise appearance
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm1d.text:
Irish star CMAT made a surprise appearance at an award ceremony in Belfast on Wednesday.

The pop-star joined Philomena Begley, one of Irish country music's most loved and celebrated entertainers, on stage at the NI Music Prize.

Begley was honoured with the Lifetime Achievement Award in recognition of her 64-year career.

The country music legend performed the hit Blanket on the Ground alongside CMAT.

The NI Music Prize, an annual event celebrating music in Northern Ireland, was marking its 15th anniversary on Wednesday at Ulster Hall.

Begley's award was presented by BBC broadcaster Hugo Duncan, a longtime friend of the musician.

When Begley went on to perform Blanket on the Ground she invited CMAT, who had made a surprise appearance at the ceremony, to join her on stage.

At a concert in Belfast earlier this year, CMAT, whose real name is Ciara Mary-Alice Thompson, gave a shout-out to Begley, thanking the country legend.

Reacting to the shout-out in October, Begley told the Good Morning Ulster programme that she had never met her but had "heard so much about her".

"It's hard to beat the new generation, it's great to see them all doing well."

Begley added that she was "over the moon" to win the award.

"I'm lost for words," she said.

Begley said she did not know what reaction to expect at the awards ceremony, but that she was "looking forward to it".

Charlotte Dryden, CEO of Oh Yeah Music Centre, who were the organisers of the NI Music Prize, said that seeing Begley and CMAT together "was something really special".

"We've had some incredible moments at the NI Music Prize over the years, but I don't think we've ever experienced an atmosphere quite like that," she said.

Philomena Begley is one of the island's most loved entertainers.

An unrivalled interpreter of country music, she has delighted audiences on stages all over the world and collaborated with country greats like Porter Wagoner and Billie Jo Spears, who first released Blanket on The Ground.

From humble beginnings in Pomeroy, County Tyrone, Begley had a simple, but happy childhood as one of eight children in a close-knit, traditional and musical family.

She always loved to sing, but had no plans of pursuing a career in music.

Begley accidentally entered the world of country music at a local dance, when she was called on stage as a dare to sing a song with the Old Cross Céilí Band.

An instant hit, she was asked to fill in as cover for someone who had taken ill in the band and suddenly became swept up in the 1960s dance-hall circuit.

In 1975, Begley was granted permission to record her own version of Blanket on the Ground from US country music star Billie Jo Spears who had released it earlier that year as the title track from the album of the same name.

Begley's version went to number five in the Irish charts and sparked some friendly rivalry between the pair.

Over the years, they became close friends, sharing many of the same hits and performing together on several occasions.

Blanket on the Ground remains one of Begley's most popular songs to this day.

Begley has captivated crowds on stages all over the world, performing everywhere from Wembley Stadium to Nashville, Tennessee.

In 1978, she was invited by Porter Wagoner, the man who introduced Dolly Parton to the world, to perform at the Grand Ole Opry, Nashville's legendary home of country music.

Here she rubbed shoulders with the stars of global country music and even received a standing ovation for her performance of Blanket on the Ground.

It was fitting recognition for her contribution to country music in Ireland and beyond.

In 2025, Begley's Blanket on the Ground becoming the unofficial anthem for the Dungannon Swifts and their journey to the Irish Cup final.

Dillon Boyd, from The Spirit of '49 Dungannon Swifts supporters club, said it all started after the Pomeroy woman's song was played on the bus radio on an away trip and "the whole place just took off".

Speaking to BBC News NI ahead of the Irish Cup final, Ms Begley said she was "shocked, but delighted" with the response.

The Swifts went on to win the final, holding their nerve against Cliftonville to secure a 4-3 penalty shootout win after a 1-1 draw after extra time.

At a victory parade after the final, the Queen of Country joined players on stage for a rendition of 'Blanket on the Ground'.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm1d.summary: Philomena Begley was honoured with the Lifetime Achievement Award. The pop-star joined Philomeno Begley on stage at the NI Music Prize ceremony. Begley performed Blanket on the Ground alongside CMAT at the ceremony.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.title: How much art does your council own and is it locked away or on display?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.text:
Fewer than one in 20 artworks owned by English councils are on public display, the BBC has found.

More than 500,000 pieces of art are held in the collections of 225 councils, but the vast majority is being kept in storage.

Local authorities remain "the biggest single constituent of public funding for arts and culture", according to the chief executive of the charity Art UK.

Yet many face a strain on storage space and resources, with a real-term fall in spending for museums leading to challenges in displaying council-owned art.

Council art collections include works by notable artists like Tracey Emin, David Hockney, LS Lowry and Antony Gormley.

Some of those collections include tens of thousands of pieces, with the largest collection of 125,000 works belonging to Waltham Forest Council.

Only a fraction of councils were able to provide the value of the collection but even individual collections had insurance values worth millions of pounds.

As of April, just 26,856 of more than half a million works were being displayed by the 225 councils who shared data with the BBC. But what options do these local authorities have?

Only one responding authority with more than 100 pieces of art - Rugby Council in Warwickshire - had them all on display.

All of its 257 artworks were exhibited together for the first time in April.

Sally Godden, manager of Rugby Art Gallery and Museum, said art had the power to connect communities.

"If things have been squirrelled away, then it's not going to do that," she said.

"It's not just a picture on the wall. It's how it connects to somebody and makes people think."

Godden said: "We can have the best collection in the world, but if they're not accessed, if they're not seen, if they're not enjoyed, if they don't make people think, then what's the point of them? They are so much more than an asset.

"We are very lucky to have such a great collection and continue to collect as well. By continuing to do that, we're growing stories, we're growing the diversity of the town, we're growing the views of people."

The council has backed a funding bid for the redevelopment of Rugby Art Gallery and a museum which would include a permanent space to display the council-owned collection.

Many of the council art collections are still growing and only 10 councils actively disposed of any of the art they own during the past six financial years.

Derbyshire sold 356 artworks in 2021-22, while North Lincolnshire sold 22 at auction in 2023-24.

The other eight councils said the items moved out of their collections had been donated, transferred to other museums, or disposed of.

For Derbyshire, the sale came as part of the closure of its Schools Library Service which had loaned art to schools.

When the service was closed after 72 years, the council did not have the space or staff to keep the collection.

Kent did not respond to the question, but previously confirmed to the BBC it had sold 418 artworks in the 12 months to April.

At the time, councillor Paul Webb said: "The reason for selling is a practical one, with the closure of the basement store where the art works are kept.

"I am sure the works have brought a lot of joy over the years to many people, and will now continue to do so."

The council also recently sold a sculpture back to Gormley, the artist who created the Angel of the North.

The chief executive of Art UK, Andew Elis, said that if all councils were to sell off art, our lives would be stripped of "these extraordinary artworks that should be there to enrich and engage us and brighten up our lives".

Art UK has spent years photographing public art collections to create a digital record of more than one million artworks.

Ellis said it was "really important" to give communities access to publicly owned art.

"We own in the UK arguably the greatest public collection of art in the world," he said. "Art changes lives, it enriches lives, it enriches our sense of place.

"The beauty of bringing all this together on one platform is that you make this art available for everyone, everywhere, all the time.

"From our point of view, this is not just about getting the art up online, this is about telling the stories behind the art and giving people agency over it."

He added councils should make more use of the shared resource, especially with increased strain on finances.

Councillor Mick Barton, who chairs the Local Government Association's culture committee, said communities should be able to enjoy local art and historic exhibits.

But he said councils continued to face significant financial pressures which were leaving them with less money to provide "discretionary services, such as museums".

Once adjusted for inflation, the net spend on museums across English councils has fallen by a fifth between 2017-18 and 2025-26.

Keeping the collections in storage does not always mean there is no access to the work.

Three of the responding authorities that owned more than 100 artworks said none were on display.

One of them, Rochdale Council in Greater Manchester, is not currently displaying any of its 1,701 artworks due to the regeneration of its Touchstones museum.

Its temporary closure saw the entire collection moved into the council's stores, which had to be reorganised to accommodate the works.

Senior curator Sarah Hodgkinson said they had been "taking a bit more risk than we have in the past" by bringing items from the collections directly to the public.

That has seen a "lively" programme, including taking pieces to schools, picnics in the park or events.

It has also let them catch up on the "behind-the-scenes" tasks of looking after a collection, like the storage and preservation.

Hodgkinson said: "We've taken loads of collections out into the community as part of our collections on tour programme.

"We've been working on repacking all of our sculpture collection, making sure our documentation is being worked on."

Mark Doyle is director of arts, heritage and wellness at Your Trust, which delivers culture and leisure service on behalf of Rochdale Council.

"A lot of people don't understand what's involved in looking after a collection and making sure that it's there for future generations to be able to access and see," he said.

Doyle said they often came across the "misconception" that the museum should have all of the items on display at the same time.

"Obviously that's not possible," he said. "But also there's other stuff that people don't understand about not having things on display for too long because it begins to deteriorate or they begin to be affected by the environment."

Additional reporting by Lauren Woodhead and Jonathan Fagg.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.summary: More than 500,000 pieces of art are held in the collections of 225 councils. Only one responding authority with more than 100 pieces of Artworks on display.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art.author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art.text:
Danny Kelly worked for the BBC until 2007

Former BBC radio presenter Danny Kelly has been described as a "broadcasting titan" following his death at the age of 69.

Kelly stepped back from his long-term role at Talksport after being diagnosed with throat cancer in March.

He presented a radio sports show on BBC London before joining Talksport in 2007 and was previously editor of the New Musical Express and Q magazine.

Talksport paid tribute to him on Wednesday, calling him a "much-loved friend" and a "broadcasting titan".

"A true legend of the station, Danny had time for everyone and went out of his way to be kind," they said.
, external

"His genuine warmth and incredible passion for broadcasting will be sorely missed by all of us."

They added: "A cherished part of Talksport for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves.

"His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him."

Kelly also presented BBC radio shows in the 1990s with Danny Baker, who described him as a "great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew".

Kelly was a lifelong Tottenham fan and the Premier League club said he was "one of our own".

A club statement
, external
 added: "Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Danny."

BBC Radio 5 Live's George Cummins was a friend and former colleague of Kelly at Talksport.

"Danny had an extraordinary knowledge of music and football," he said. "His ability to combine the two on air made him an incredible broadcaster.

"His brilliant wit made him an amazing story teller. Colleagues would often remark that his brain was like an encyclopaedia.

"While he was a genius on-air, it was his personality off-air that would shine through. He was always there to give advice and help. He always took an interest in colleagues' lives away from work.

"He was a very positive man. He loved his job. He loved entertaining the nation. I'll always remember a great friend who taught me so much."
