https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3e.title: Media industry could be forced to improve safeguards after Walliams allegations
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3e.text:
The government is prepared to force the entertainment industry to improve safeguarding practices unless rapid change is introduced, BBC Newsnight has learned.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told the House of Commons she will meet representatives from the media, entertainment and sport next week to "discuss the action that we need to take" following recent allegations.

"But if those protections are insufficient, the government will not hesitate to take further action," she said.

She could force participation in creative industries industry standards body CIISA, which is currently voluntary, to protect whistleblowers, the BBC understands.

Her comments come after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that entertainer David Walliams had been accused by several women of sexual misconduct and abusing his position, which he denies.

Nandy added: "For too long, too many people have had to choose between their career and their safety.

"Whistleblowers must be protected, and those who abuse their position must no longer be able to hide."

Earlier this week, she said she was summoning leaders from the broadcasting, publishing, film and entertainment industries to "draw a line" in the sand.

That announcement came after the publication of allegations against Walliams, as well as the sentencing of disgraced entertainer Russell Brand on charges of rape and sexual assault.

The allegations against Walliams were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation that was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public. Walliams denies all the allegations against him.

BBC Newsnight understands that the culture secretary will deliver two messages at next week's round-table meeting.

In the first instance, she will tell industry leaders that they need to meet the moment, take responsibility and tackle issues of safeguarding on their own. But she will add that if their response is not good enough, the government might have to intervene.

Intervention could include forcing participation in the CIISA.

The culture secretary also said she recently appointed two "freelance champions in recognition of the fact that for freelancers in particular, there is a real problem in these industries."

Multiple government ministers gave statements on Wednesday that called for further restrictions on the use of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).

Women and equalities minister Bridget Phillipson told Sky News that there was "scope to go further" on legislation that restricted the use of such agreements to ensure that the legal system was not being "abused in order to silence women".

"We cannot have a system where rich and powerful individuals - rich and powerful men - are able to silence women and stop things coming to light," she said.

Can't Buy My Silence founder Zelda Perkins told BBC Newsnight that there were "not enough safeguards" around high-profile people in creative industries and that joining the CIISA should be "mandatory".

The former assistant to jailed film producer Harvey Weinstein broke an NDA in 2017 when she spoke publicly about the movie mogul's mistreatment of women.

She has since founded a group that campaigns against NDAs being used in legal contracts or settlements to stop people from speaking out against their employers.

"There are no other regulatory bodies that are voluntary to join," Perkins told BBC Newsnight, referring to CIISA, noting that "obviously the people who need to be monitored are the people who are not joining".

"It's still very wild west in the the creative industries, people behave how they want," she said, adding that while "you can't change the humans, you can change the rules around them".

In the initial investigation published by the Guardian, some of the women accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault".

In a letter to journalists published by the paper, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He said he "realised that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

Separately, a producer who worked on a TV show on which Walliams was a celebrity guest several years ago has told the BBC she was instructed to keep the comedian away from young female members of staff.

Speaking anonymously, she said she was warned that Walliams was "creepy" and "inappropriate", and that it was "well-known" he should not be put with young female runners.

She said she "wasn't at all surprised" when allegations about Walliams' behaviour emerged.

The Guardian reported that lawyers representing Walliams said he had never been warned nor "got into trouble" for messaging runners, and that he denied he behaved inappropriately and harassed young women in the workplace.

Comedian Kate Smurthwaite told BBC Newsnight that Walliams was a name that came up "over and over again", and that there was a "sense of worry" about him working with young people.

"People were saying that they knew people who had worked with him and either felt very uncomfortable and left, or stuck around and felt that his behaviour was inappropriate," she said.

When asked why it had taken so long for such allegations to emerge, Smurthwaite said: "We all know that women who raise these issues, there's a backlash, which might be legal, it might be in terms of your career or your opportunities, it might be as subtle as being seen as a problem."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3e.summary: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will meet with media, entertainment and sport leaders next week. She will tell them to take responsibility and tackle issues of safeguarding on their own. She could force participation in creative industries industry standards body CIISA as a problem.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/darts/articl.title: Littler expected 'pub players' on Netflix show
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/darts/articl.author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/darts/articl.text:
Luke Litter was beaten by Fallon Sherrock after defeating 14 prior challengers

Luke Littler has admitted he thought he would be facing pub players on his recent Netflix show, which was billed as giving "amateurs a chance at life-changing money".

Broadcast live globally on the streaming platform last month, the cash was won by top women's player Fallon Sherrock.

The format of 'Beat Luke Littler' saw 24 players selected to take on the world number one in a single leg of 501, hoping to win a prize of £501,000.

The 24-strong field did include low-level opponents, such as an Australian jockey, a bin man and a Nando's manager, but anyone who was not a member of the PDC Tour was also allowed to compete.

That meant Sherrock - who became the first female player to beat a male opponent at the PDC World Championship on her way to the last 32 in December 2019 - and leading junior players Mitchell Lawrie and Zach Griffiths were also eligible.

"Before I saw the line-up, I thought it was just pub players," said Littler, who is preparing for the Grand Slam of Darts this weekend.

"Whereas obviously when the line-up came out, I probably knew just over half of them.

"Mitchell, Zach Griffiths - I played with him on the Development Tour - obviously Fallon, Katie Sheldon and a lot more.

"I mean Fallon, she's never had a Tour card, so she went for the qualifiers and she made it through. But then she wasn't guaranteed to play - she went in on a vote."

Sherrock, who has been awarded an MBE for her services to darts, made it through an audition process and then had to rely on the public to select her to take on Littler at Manchester Central.

Littler beat 14 contestants but then lost to Sherrock, who won nearest the bull to throw first and then checked out in 15 darts.

"It was a very good night overall," Littler added. "I think from my side it was very good. From Netflix's side, it was very good.

"I think the whole thing was probably a learning curve. For me, constantly playing back-to-back, especially in the heat, I was going off and on stage. I'm up for another one and I'm sure Netflix will be as well.

"There aren't many people who could say they've got their own show, and I've had my own show on Netflix, which is just still bonkers to me."

Sherrock happy to overcome 'hate' in beating Littler for £501,000

Can you beat Littler in our PL checkout challenge?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/darts/articl.summary: Luke Littler beat Fallon Sherrock in a single leg of 501 in a competition on Netflix. The show was broadcast live globally on the streaming platform last month. Littlers beat 14 prior challengers but then lost to Sherrock for £501,000.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.title: Author says there were 'real concerns' about David Walliams within publishing industry
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.text:
Author Chloe Combi has said she had heard rumours that there were "real concerns" about David Walliams's behaviour within the publishing industry more than a decade ago.

Combi told BBC News she had heard there were allegations about his "behaviour around young female staff" and says she was told in 2015 to warn schools that he was "not an appropriate booking".

An investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that Walliams has been accused by several women of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behaviour and abusing his position, which he denies.

HarperCollins, which published Walliams's best-selling children's books, dropped Walliams last year after an investigation into his behaviour.

In response to the Guardian and ITV report, a spokesperson for HarperCollins said the company had decided not to publish any new titles by Walliams and that it took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously".

Walliams told ITV News and the Guardian that he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a scheme to bring "high-profile and inspiring writers and speakers" to talk in schools.

At an event in 2015, Combi said she got speaking to someone "quite senior" in publishing, who warned her about Walliams.

"We were talking about [the scheme] and possible writers who might be good for the project to work well with teenagers," Combi said.

"She gave me some great recommendations and said to me: 'Whatever you do, don't invite David Walliams, and FYI if you are speaking to head teachers or teachers, please inform them that he's not a good booking, not an appropriate booking for a school'."

Combi continued: "I obviously asked why, and to be honest I had already heard quite a lot of rumours because those worlds are quite small and contained.

"One of the things she said was that there had been real concerns about his behaviour around young female staff."

Asked whether concerns about his behaviour was an open secret, Combi replied: "Yes definitely... and I'd heard it from people who worked in publishing, fellow writers, people kind of in celebrity and TV circles."

Combi said she never met Walliams herself, and said her information had come from "a number of people I was speaking to".

HarperCollins in September announced it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.

The allegations against Walliams include:

In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Contains sexual content.

Earlier on Wednesday, media minister Ian Murray said there is a "cultural problem" in the industry that needs to be "stamped out".

Giving evidence to the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, Murray said he was "deeply saddened and also angry" to see the prevalence of abuse by men in the media industry.

Meanwhile, Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson paid tribute to the "bravery" of victims who have shared their experiences in recent days.

Speaking in the Commons, she said: "Women and girls should never have to shrink our lives or ambitions because of outdated, misogynistic attitudes, and the appalling testimonies we have heard in recent days underline how much further we have to go."

Phillipson later said the government would "go further" on restricting the use of non-disclosure agreements, telling Sky News: "We cannot have a system where rich and powerful individuals, rich and powerful men, are able to silence women, buy their silence and stop things coming to light."

She said that she believed injunctions were being misused, and that her colleagues at the Ministry of Justice were looking at how the government can intervene to ensure this did not happen.

Comedian and podcaster Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women are "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.

She told the programme that perpetrators understand consent but they just enjoy the power that comes with ignoring it, adding: "The thrill is in the contravention of consent."

Asked whether she recognised the picture Russell Brand's conviction and allegations against Walliams had painted of the comedy industry, she said: "Yes, entirely."

She described an industry where she was asked to meet male producers in darkly lit rooms "walking a tightrope", having to make them feel attractive and avoid being assaulted as they influenced future employment opportunities.

She said these events are "definitely still going on" and that she is in a WhatsApp group with female comedians who share their experiences with each other.

Comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News that she was one of the people who spoke to the Guardian about allegations raised with her about Walliams.

Beaumont said she had been approached by a young TV worker who alleged inappropriate behaviour while working with Walliams on another show.

"This young person's job was to take young girls - he didn't think that they were children... he definitely knew that they were over 16 - he had to take them to Walliams's dressing room," she alleged.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday, Labour MP Jess Phillips said the behaviour alleged "needs to be stopped".

"What is described in the David Walliams story is an absolute modus operandi, a target group of women of a certain age, the kind of women who don't have the same amount of power as if you were doing this to a 35-year-old woman who might have a bit more about herself in the world," she said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.summary: Chloe Combi says she heard rumours about David Walliams's behaviour in publishing industry. She says she was told in 2015 to warn schools that he was "not an appropriate booking" HarperCollins dropped Walliam's books last year after an investigation into his behaviour.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq4g.title: Cut screen time in classrooms to avoid long-term health issues, clinicians urge
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq4g.text:
The amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health", a group of more than 150 clinicians has warned.

GPs, paediatricians and other specialists said in an open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper that tablets and laptops are being used without a full understanding of their long-term health impacts, including on eye health.

The clinicians said they are prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".

The government said it was consulting on screen time guidance for children aged five to 18 but that technology could be a powerful learning tool if used properly.

The group of clinicians said nearly one million children are using screens in most lessons, despite studies suggesting a rise in short-sightedness.

They pointed to an analysis of 276 studies covering 5.4 million participants around the world.

That analysis, they claimed, found a rise in short-sightedness among children and adolescents from around 24% in 1990 to almost 36% by 2023, warning the condition is associated with an increased risk of a range of eye health problems.

Many children now spend longer on screens in the classroom than is recommended in a 24-hour period, the letter said, adding: "As a country, we need to wake up to this now, and start rolling back screen use in schools before the damage compounds further."

One of its signatories was Dr Becky Foljambe, an NHS GP and founder of Health Professionals for Safer Screens. She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme parents had not been given the chance to "opt out" of the "excessive" use of screens in schools, which risks children "just not thriving" in education.

She said an "explosion" in short-sightedness "cannot be put down to genetics alone".

Foljambe said it was a "lazy argument" to advocate for screen use to prepare children for a digital world, adding: "They also need their sleep, their eyesight, they need rest, they need ability to critically think and appraise."

"We are conscious that some of this evidence is still surfacing but the direction of travel is consistent across multiple, independent, and in some cases very large, bodies of research," the letter continued.

It also warned that children with special educational needs are "disproportionately" directed to screen-based learning.

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said education technology can provide schools with "very effective learning tools".

But he said such technology was only part of an "overall learning strategy", which also includes classroom discussion and interaction, and that the school day also has "plenty of non-screen time such as PE, sport, and break times with classmates".

"We would welcome the development of practical, evidence-based guidance to support the work of schools in the use of education technology," he added.

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said it was "important that a healthy balance is struck", adding that "greater clarity is needed from the government on this".

A Department for Education spokesperson said the government was developing new screen-time guidance for children aged five to 18, and will consult on the safety of artificial intelligence and educational technology in schools.

They said: "Used well, technology can be a powerful tool to support learners who need it and free up teachers to deliver the excellent education every child deserves."

It comes after a ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq4g.summary: GPs, paediatricians and other specialists say tablets and laptops are being used without full understanding of their health impacts. They say they are prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children. Government says it is consulting on screen time guidance for children aged five to 18.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx7v.title: School exam boss to step down after two years in post
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx7v.text:
The chief executive of Scotland's new school exam body has announced he will stand down next year.

Nick Page oversaw the transition of the Scottish Qualifications Authority (SQA) to Qualifications Scotland (QS) in December 2025.

Page, who will depart his role after results day in August 2027, said he was leaving the organisation in a "strong place".

QS said the recruitment process for his replacement would start in the new year.

Page joined the organisation in 2025.

He said he had been able to deliver on his priorities of "accelerating the pace of change and to build stronger partnerships across the education and skills system".

He added: "Qualifications Scotland is now firmly established and enabling hundreds of thousands of learners to achieve their full potential.

"I have thoroughly enjoyed my time in the role and in Scotland, and when I depart next August, I believe I will be leaving the organisation in a strong place to move forward and build further success."

Plans to abolish the SQA, which was formed in 1997, were announced in 2021 following a Scottish government-commissioned report by the OECD.

That came off the back of several controversies over exams, marking and assessment.

The head of Scotland's largest teaching union, the Educational Institute of Scotland (EIS), said the SQA had "lost the trust of teachers".

QS is due to revise curriculum guidance in 2027, with further reform to National 4 and National 5 qualifications set to take place in 2031.

Additional changes to Higher and Advanced Higher assessments are to be brought in by 2032 under current plans.

QS chairwoman, Shirley Rogers CBE, said Page had made a "significant contribution" in his tenure as chief executive.

She added: "Nick has made a real and positive difference at a crucial time for us, not least the replacement of SQA with Qualifications Scotland.

"He will leave our new organisation in a strong place."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx7v.summary: Nick Page oversaw transition of Scottish Qualifications Authority to Qualifications Scotland. Page will leave the organisation after results day in August 2027. He said he was leaving the organisation in a "strong place"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.title: University's £16m savings will lead to 150 job losses, says union
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.text:
Major cutbacks at Aberystwyth University will lead to 150 jobs being lost, a union has said.

The university has announced a "further phase of its restructure" with the aim of saving £16m by the end of 2027-28.

It said there would be a review of "all academic units" which follows an ongoing review of non-academic departments as the higher education sector goes through "unprecedented challenges".

Aberystwyth University University and College Union (UCU) said its members were "devastated and angry" by the announcement on Wednesday.

The university confirmed that it currently employs 1819 staff - across academic and professional departments - but did not say the number of expected job losses.

It said the move was aimed at "increasing efficiency" while meeting student needs and achieving financial sustainability.

In a statement, it said: "Following on from the ongoing review of non-academic departments, the next phase of the process will include a review of all academic units, including looking at portfolio and curriculum as well as resourcing."

Aberystwyth University UCU said there would be 150 jobs lost, following the loss of 150 colleagues over the last 18 months in a previous round of restructuring.

It said most of the cuts would fall on teaching and research staff, and represented "a devastating blow to our university, our students and our community".

"Staff are shocked by the scale and speed of what is being proposed. Behind every job is a person, a family, and years of knowledge, expertise and commitment that help make Aberystwyth University what it is," the union said in a statement.

"We recognise the financial pressure that Aberystwyth University is under. Every year we are asked to do more with less.

"Those of us who will be left will no doubt work harder than ever to teach, research, shape and support the lives of young people from Wales and those far beyond it."

Professor Jon Timmis, vice-chancellor of the university, said changes to UK visa and immigration metrics had significantly impacted universities' ability to recruit higher fee-paying international students.

"Adapting universities to be financially sustainable cannot be achieved without some very difficult decisions," he said.

He added the university was committed to trying to mitigate redundancies where possible and would be giving staff access to a voluntary severance scheme.

The university announced in 2024 there would be a "significant change " to the way it operated to save money.

In August, the university paused plans to turn the first home of the University of Wales into a cultural hub in a £53m renovation including a four-star hotel and museum.

Cefin Campbell, Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education, described the cuts as "a matter of concern" but "almost inevitable" because of the challenges facing universities.

"We can't let our universities suffer any longer, we have to create systems that support them, because they are important economically for their areas, and they're important for our students too, providing high quality learning," he said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.summary: Aberystwyth University and College Union says 150 jobs will be lost. University says it will review all academic units and look at portfolio and curriculum. University of Wales says it currently employs 1819 staff - across academic and professional departments.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw80.title: Welsh students to start repaying loans earlier after thresholds frozen
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw80.text:
The income level at which Welsh graduates start repaying loans is to be frozen, the Welsh government has announced.

In a move which has already proved controversial in England, the threshold for Plan 2 loans will be frozen at £29,385 between 2027 and 2030, rather than rising with inflation.

It means graduates will start repaying their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done as they are likely to meet the salary threshold earlier.

NUS Cymru president Jennifer Taylor has criticised the move. "Let's be clear, a bank could not get away with this," she said.

But Cefin Campbell, deputy minister for skills and tertiary education, said the Welsh government had been left with "little choice".

Campbell also said the government was "considering" raising the cap on university tuition fees, currently £9,790 a year, and an announcement would be made "in the next couple of weeks".

The Welsh government is yet to confirm its approach after the UK government announced last year that fees in English universities would go up to a maximum of £10,050 from September 2027.

Earlier this year, the previous Welsh Labour government said it would not freeze the loan repayment threshold in Wales, after former Chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the decision to do so for English Plan 2 borrowers in her November 2025 budget.

The UK government decision was heavily criticised by some MPs and financial expert Martin Lewis, who said it was unfair to change the terms of the loans once they had been taken out.

But, announcing the decision on Wednesday, Campbell said the system - which is administered by the Student Loans Company and HM Revenue and Customs through a shared UK-wide system - "cannot support different repayment thresholds for Welsh and English borrowers".

Most Welsh undergraduates take out Plan 2 loans, which have interest rates in line with the retail prices index (RPI) measure of inflation, plus up to 3% depending on earnings.

Graduates repay 9% of the amount earned above the threshold outlined in their plan.

They do not have to start making payments until April after leaving their course, and only when they earn above the income threshold. Payments are made automatically through the tax system.

"This is not a decision I wanted to take," said Campbell.

"I recognise the impact that this decision will have, and I know that Welsh borrowers will be disappointed.

"Welsh Plan 2 borrowers will still benefit from a higher repayment threshold than English borrowers on Plan 5, and any remaining loan will be written off a decade sooner," he said.

"Our maintenance grants, including the £1,020 universal base grant, mean Welsh borrowers have less debt than their English counterparts on average, and we cancel up to £1,500 of borrowers' loan debt."

Since 2023, English undergraduates have taken out Plan 5 loans which have different terms to Plan 2.

They are cancelled after 40 years if the loan has not been repaid, unlike Plan 2 loans which are cancelled earlier, after 30 years.

Responding to the government announcement, Taylor said: "We signed a contract, based on repayment thresholds rising each year.

"Successive governments are playing politics with our mortgage-size debts - let's be clear, a bank could not get away with this.

"For young people in Wales, this announcement will mean hundreds less in their bank accounts each year. It could be the difference between saving for a house, or just the smaller buffer from debt disappearing.

"Our call is to the Chancellor John Healey - stop freezing our futures and respect the terms of our student loans that we signed as young as 17."

An independent panel, set up by the Plaid Cymru government, has begun work on a review of higher education which will look at the student support system and the sustainability of Welsh universities.

Campbell said the Welsh government faced "a challenging financial position in respect of the student loan system".

"A freeze, while unavoidable, will mean that the review has some additional financial flexibility when considering future student loan repayment arrangements," he said.

"This underlines the importance of developing a stronger Made for Wales approach to student finance".

Taylor said NUS Cymru was "keen to work with the Welsh government" as part of the funding review "to develop a system that has students in Wales at the heart".

Move has already proved controversial in England, with some MPs criticising it. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5k.title: How student loans work for tuition fees and living costs
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5k.text:
Students and graduates across the UK have different student loan plans depending on when and where they studied.

Loan rules vary between England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, but most students still need to borrow to pay for their studies. The average graduate in England leaves university with debts of more than £47,500.

Student loans vary depending on where you live in the UK and when you started your course.

They are typically made up of:

Most people are entitled to the tuition fee element, which is equal to the annual cost of their course. Maximum fees vary across the UK:

The separate maintenance loan is intended to cover accommodation, food, books and equipment.

Maintenance loans are means tested, so the amount you get depends on your family's household income. You might get extra money if you are disabled, or have children.

If you are under 25 and have no contact with your parents, you might be able to apply as an "estranged student". This means your parents' financial situation is not taken into consideration.

Research by the Higher Education Policy Institute published in May 2024 suggested maintenance loans in England typically only covered about half the cost of living, and even less for students in London.

In April 2026, over 20,000 students were told they had been "mis-sold" their maintenance loans as their courses were ineligible, and were told to pay back the money they had received.

Students who took out a loan in England to start university between September 2012 and July 2023 have Plan 2 loans. These loans are still issued in Wales.

Graduates with Plan 2 loans pay back 9% of everything they earn over the repayment threshold.

In the November 2025 Budget, Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the threshold would be frozen at £29,385 between 2027 and 2030 in England, rather than rising with inflation.

The Welsh government has since followed suit.

That means students will start repaying their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done, and their rising salaries will lead to greater repayments.

Campaigners want to see that change reversed, and for the government to consider a lower repayment rate and a lower interest rate.

Plan 2 loans take on interest at the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation, plus up to 3% depending on earnings.

It means many graduates with Plan 2 loans have struggled to make a substantial dent in the overall debt they left university with, which is often in the tens of thousands of pounds, despite making repayments for years.

The maximum interest rate charged on Plan 2 loans is capped. The cap is reviewed periodically and may change from one academic year to the next.

The amount of maintenance support available to new students varies across the UK.

The maximum maintenance loan for students from England living away from their parents outside London is £10,830 for the 2026-27 academic year.

The government is reintroducing maintenance grants of up to £1,000 per year for students from lower income households in England on courses that support its Industrial Strategy. They will be available from 2028 and the government is still drawing up a list of eligible courses.

Students from Wales studying away from home can borrow up to £11,570 in the 2026-27 academic year.

Welsh students may also be entitled to maintenance grants, which do not have to be paid back.

In Scotland, the maximum annual maintenance loan is £9,400 for under-25s. Students can also apply for a number of bursaries and grants.

Students from Northern Ireland studying away from home can borrow up to £8,352 for the 2026-27 academic year.

Tuition fee limits and maintenance loan amounts are reviewed by the government each year and can change.

The government has said only those universities which provide strong outcomes for students will be able to charge the maximum amount in England.

Universities which fall below the quality threshold set by the regulator in England, the Office for Students, may also face a cap on the number of students they can recruit.

The tuition fees are paid directly to your university or education provider.

The maintenance loan is paid directly to your bank account in instalments.

Payments are made at the start of each term in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and monthly in Scotland.

In order to be paid you'll need to register at your university or college. You'll usually do this in the first week of your course, and you may have to take along your student finance entitlement letter.

In England you should get a text from the Student Loans Company a few days before to let you know the maintenance loan is on the way.

You can apply for funding up to nine months after the first day of the academic year for your course.

Depending on where you live, you will need to apply through:

Interest rates on some student loans are reviewed regularly. For the 2026-27 academic year, interest on Plan 2 and Plan 3 loans in England is capped at 6%.

You are charged interest on the loan from the day you take it out, but the amount varies across the UK.

It is important to understand that the terms and conditions of the loan and repayments can change after you have borrowed the money.

Future interest rate rises apply to all student loans, not just new applications.

For students in England, the interest rate is normally set at the retail price index (RPI) measure of inflation. The rate usually updates every September, but can also change throughout the year.

It is currently 4.1% for anyone who started university in 2023 or later.

Rates for students in the rest of the UK are:

How much graduates pay back depends on how much they earn.

You make one payment to cover both your tuition fees and maintenance loans.

But you do not have to start repaying your loan until you earn a certain amount of money after graduation.

You generally repay 9% of the amount you earn above this threshold.

The threshold for students in England who started university in 2023 or later, and therefore have a Plan 5 loan, is £25,000.

In Wales it is £29,385, in Scotland £33,795 and in Northern Ireland £26,900.

Students who took out a loan in England to start university between September 2012 and July 2023, or who have taken out a loan in Wales since September 2012, have Plan 2 loans.

Plan 2 repayment thresholds rose from £28,470 to £29,385 in April 2026, before being frozen - instead of rising with inflation - for three years.

You do not have to start making payments until the April after you leave your course.

Payments are made automatically through the tax system.

Some people choose to make extra repayments to clear some or all of their loan early - there is no penalty for doing this.

In some cases graduates have had repayments wrongly deducted from their wages.

For example, they may have had money taken before the April when they become liable, or after their loan had been repaid in full.

Alternatively, their employer may have put them on the wrong repayment plan. Payments may also have accidentally been triggered when graduates earned more than the monthly threshold - perhaps as a result of working extra shifts or getting a bonus - but did not exceed the annual limit.

These incorrect repayments can be refunded.

In May 2024, the Student Loans Company introduced a digital refund service, which was accessed by more than 400,000 people in the first six months.

You can check whether you are entitled to a refund on the SLC website.

Any overpayments you have chosen to make cannot be refunded.

In England, students who started university in 2023 or later will see their loans written off after 40 years, regardless of how much they may still owe.

For students with Plan 2 loans, including in Wales, this happens after 30 years.

It is also after 30 years in Scotland, and in Northern Ireland it is after 25 years.

You still have to repay your student loan if you leave your course early.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5k.summary: Most students still need to borrow to pay for their studies, but most still need a loan. The average graduate in England leaves university with debts of more than £47,500. Most people are entitled to the tuition fee element, which is equal to the annual cost of their course.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.title: A.I. Weapons Need Data for Their Training. Ukraine Has a Lot to Offer.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Andrew E. Kramer
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
The Ukrainian government has opened up a trove of five million battlefield videos to defense companies at home and abroad.

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

The forest, seen from a drone, appeared as a vast, monotonous landscape of black tree trunks, shadows and patches of snow.

To the human eye, it appeared deserted. But to an artificial intelligence system looking for people, it did not. The system put a red box around a tiny human form, probably a soldier lurking in the trees.

Behind this feat lay vast volumes of data. Just as ChatGPT and other A.I. chatbots must be exposed to how humans write, military A.I. systems must be exposed to how humans fight. In Ukraine, this happens through a huge trove of battlefield videos, audio and text data collected over nearly five years.

The war database is being used by about 30 Ukrainian defense companies to develop A.I. weapons. Ukraine is now opening this repository, which it calls Avenger Labs, to firms in allied countries, hoping to deepen security partnerships.

Ukraine is providing the data at no charge, but companies must give the Ukrainian military licenses to any software they develop. Under the first agreement to be reached, 12 British defense companies will gain access. Ukraine is in talks with other countries.

While there is no shortage of Western companies developing autonomous weapons, there is a shortage of the data needed to train them. Ukraine can offer more of it than any other potential partner.

Subscribe to The Times to read as many articles as you like.

Andrew E. Kramer is the Kyiv bureau chief for The Times, who has been covering the war in Ukraine since 2014.

Grammy-nominated songwriter Vivir Quintana is known throughout Latin America for giving voice to women who fought back against domestic violence.

Vivir Quintana in Oaxaca.
Credit...

Photographs by Victoria Razo

Reporting from Oaxaca, Mexico

Against the backdrop of a centuries-old stone church in the Mexican city of Oaxaca, the singer Vivir Quintana raised her deep, husky voice above the blare of trumpets, trombones and the booming pulse of a tuba.

Behind her stood a brass band of young Indigenous girls in embroidered white blouses and brightly colored skirts. Hat in hand and fist raised, Ms. Quintana sang a corrido, a traditional Mexican folk ballad usually used to recount tales of revolutionaries, outlaws, folk heroes, and more recently, drug traffickers.

Corridos are typically sung by men, about men. Ms. Quintana sang a corrido she wrote based on the true story of a woman who fought back when her abusive partner tried to gouge out her eyes with a knife.

“I used to think that what united us women was our pain. Now I have realized it is love and resistance,” Ms. Quintana told the crowd in October during a women’s conference in Oaxaca called Decididas, drawing a roar of applause. “We must keep defending ourselves!”

On Thursday, Ms. Quintana will take the stage at the Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas alongside the Colombian pop superstar Juanes, with whom she is nominated for song of the year for “Humano.” It is her second Latin Grammy nomination.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.title: They Left Iran, but Now the Regime Is Seizing Their Assets to Silence Them
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Yeganeh Torbati
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
War in the Middle East

The Iranian authorities are pursuing diaspora dissidents and journalists, extending the government’s repressive apparatus far beyond its borders.

Yeganeh Torbati spoke to 12 Iranians living abroad whose property in Iran, or that of their family members, was targeted for confiscation.

The retired couple in Iran first realized that something was wrong when their bank cards stopped working in early May. After inquiring with the authorities, they discovered that their assets had been frozen by order of the country’s intelligence ministry.

The couple learned, eventually, that they were being punished for the actions of their daughter Noushin Najafiragheb, who lived in Europe — specifically, for her social media posts opposing the Iranian government, according to another daughter, Mehrnoush Najafiragheb.

Across Iran, the government has used asset seizures as punishment for actions taken abroad. Homes and businesses have been seized, life savings raided, family heirlooms taken. When those targeted had little inside Iran themselves, the authorities went after their family members back home, interviews show.

As the Najafiragheb family pressed their case with the authorities, Mehrnoush said, they encountered dozens of other people facing the specter of losing their life’s savings as punishment for the actions of their relatives abroad.

“We realized we weren’t alone,” Ms. Najafiragheb recalled her mother telling her. She said her sister Noushin had declined to be interviewed to avoid further government pressure on her family.

Subscribe to The Times to read as many articles as you like.

Yeganeh Torbati is the Iran correspondent for The Times.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.title: In China’s Spy Operations, Romance Can Be a Long Game
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Lily Kuo
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman U.S. officials say is a Chinese spy has drawn attention to the role of intimate relationships in espionage.

At the height of the Cold War, a top official in China’s intelligence agency said that his country would never use seduction to entrap a person.

Such tactics might be for the C.I.A. or the K.G.B., the official named Kong Yuan, of the Central Investigation Department, told a group of agents in training in April 1960, but China was guided by principles. He looked at the few female comrades in the audience. “Rest assured, we will not be asking you to go run beauty traps.”

Despite that pledge, captured in a 2010 memoir by a former Chinese diplomat, China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people.

American officials say that China’s Ministry of State Security, which runs intelligence operations today, recruited a Chinese businesswoman to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia and one of the most powerful figures in the artificial intelligence boom.

It was not clear what role the woman, Alice Huang, or Huang Le, might have had with the Chinese spy agency. Ms. Huang was a top executive of a Singapore company that operates data centers in Southeast Asia using Nvidia chips and that rents their computing power to Chinese firms.

Mr. Huang has acknowledged that he had an affair with Ms. Huang. President Trump has said that Mr. Huang told him that he was not aware that the woman was a spy. China has rejected the espionage allegations against Ms. Huang, calling them smears against the country. U.S. officials have not provided evidence for their claims. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

Subscribe to The Times to read as many articles as you like.

Lily Kuo is a China correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.title: Israel’s Arrest of Journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh Raises Concerns
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Adam Rasgon and Natan Odenheimer
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was detained without being charged with a crime, raising concerns that the domestic security service is overstepping its authority.

By Adam Rasgon and Natan Odenheimer

Reporting from Jaffa, Israel

Abed Abu Shehadeh, a 38-year-old journalist and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, said he was putting on his pajamas on the evening of Nov. 3 when police officers and intelligence agents burst into his family’s third-floor apartment in Jaffa.

They strip-searched him, confiscated his phone, allowed him to dress and then whisked him away, he said in an interview at a restaurant in the city.

Five days later, after interrogations by Israel’s domestic security agency, the Shin Bet, Mr. Abu Shehadeh, who lives with his wife and two young children, was let go.

A former elected member of the Tel Aviv-Jaffa City Council, Mr. Abu Shehadeh has not been charged with a crime. The Israeli authorities have not publicly offered a reason for his arrest, though court records reviewed by The New York Times show that he was accused of being in contact with an unnamed “foreign agent.”

His highly publicized arrest — a week after Israel’s national elections — came as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have claimed that foreign actors illegally funneled large amounts of money to bribe Arab citizens to vote for Arab political parties.

Critics say that Mr. Netanyahu and his allies are seeking to undermine the legitimacy of the record gains by Arab parties in the Parliament, or the Knesset, by contending without basis that Arab voters stole the election.

Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

BOUGAINVILLE DISPATCH

Seven Chinese tourists, a dozen villagers and a couple of journalists forded streams and bushwhacked to the downed plane of Isoroku Yamamoto, the Japanese admiral. Machetes proved handy.

Wading through streams and bushes to the plane wreckage, where a tourist posed for pictures.
Credit...

Visuals by Matthew Abbott

Reporting from Bougainville, Papua New Guinea

Halfway through the morning, I’m being tossed around like a popcorn kernel in the back of a troop carrier playing an eclectic medley of Backstreet Boys and Papua New Guinean jams.

We’re traveling along what feels more like a collection of loose rocks, arranged to be roughly vehicle width, than a road. I’ve lost count of the number of river crossings, including one where the water lapped a few inches from the car’s windows. And this is during a dry spell.

Our caravan is headed for an unlikely tourist destination deep in the jungle on Bougainville Island, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the Solomon Sea.

The piecemeal remnants of a Mitsubishi G4M1 — Betty, as the planes were code-named by the Allies in World War II — have remained for some 80 years at the crash site of Japanese Navy Adm. Isoroku Yamamoto. This is the spot where Admiral Yamamoto, mastermind of the Pearl Harbor attack, archvillain to Americans in the war, a respected and memorialized figure to the Japanese, met his end in 1943.

Bougainville was occupied by the Japanese in early 1942, in the months after Pearl Harbor, as the Imperial Navy pushed into the South Pacific, with Admiral Yamamoto at the helm. In April 1943, Allied forces intercepted and deciphered Japanese communication on the admiral’s travels, and American P-38 Lightning fighters gunned down his plane over southern Bougainville, a feat the Americans triumphantly dubbed Operation Vengeance.

An earlier version of this article referred incorrectly to vegetation along the path to the plane wreckage. Visitors trek through potato fields and among pineapple plants — not pineapple trees.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.title: Indonesia’s Vice President, Gibran, Resigns
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Muktita Suhartono
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who is stepping down amid a scandal over his academic credentials, was a symbol of the partnership that elevated President Prabowo Subianto into office.

The vice president of Indonesia submitted his resignation to Parliament on Thursday, succumbing to a scandal about his academic credentials and injecting new political uncertainty in Southeast Asia’s largest economy.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka was elected as Indonesia’s youngest vice president in 2024, in a precipitous rise. He was a symbol of the partnership between his father, the outgoing president, Joko Widodo, and the incoming leader, Prabowo Subianto, that elevated Mr. Prabowo into office.

“The relationship has clearly fractured,” said Yoes C. Kenawas, a political analyst at the Indonesian Survey Institute. With Mr. Gibran’s departure, “Prabowo is attempting to demonstrate that he has stepped out from Jokowi’s shadow,” he added, referring to the former leader by his nickname.

Initially a political outsider, Mr. Joko came to be seen as a transformative leader of Indonesia. He helped rehabilitate the image of Mr. Prabowo, a former special forces commander who was discharged from the military for his involvement in the abduction and torture of pro-democracy activists under the dictator Suharto. To many, Mr. Prabowo was a reminder of the country’s authoritarian past. But Mr. Joko endorsed Mr. Prabowo as his successor, with Mr. Gibran running on the same ticket.

The alliance between Mr. Joko and Mr. Prabowo was cast as one of political continuity. Many voters had seen Mr. Gibran’s vice presidency as a way for Mr. Joko to continue his political influence.

“From the beginning, Gibran was brought on board solely to serve as a ‘vote-getter,’ rather than as an integral part of a unified leadership team intended to strengthen the performance of the Prabowo administration,” said Titi Anggraini, a lecturer of constitutional law at University of Indonesia.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: U.S. Efforts to Tighten Blockade of Iran Rely on Reluctant Neighbors
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Erika Solomon, Eric Schmitt and Tyler Pager
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
War in the Middle East

Washington wants to intensify its economic pressure campaign on Iran by closing its land borders. Neighboring states, fearing economic fallout, are pushing back.

By Erika SolomonEric Schmitt and Tyler Pager

The first step in the United States’ campaign to economically strangle Iran was a naval blockade of its ports, cutting off Iranian trade by sea. Next came a raft of new sanctions, grounding much of the country’s air transport network.

Now, the United States is going after Iran’s last economic artery: its land routes. Only there, Washington has hit upon a problem.

For weeks, U.S. officials have tried — and failed — to diplomatically pressure Iran’s neighbors into shuttering their border crossings, according to three Iraqi officials and one U.S. official with knowledge of the talks, who requested anonymity to speak candidly.

Those neighboring states, primarily Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan, are increasingly wary and disgruntled by U.S. policies they say could hurt them as much as Tehran.

So, on Saturday, the U.S. military joined the effort, announcing Task Force Iron Gate, which it says will work on “preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.”

It is unclear how the task force will operate in practice, and it is unusual for such an economic and security campaign to be run by U.S. Central Command, known as Centcom, which oversees military operations in the Middle East.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: Seeking to Broaden Ukraine Talks, U.S. Urges Russia to Include Europe
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Paul Sonne
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
As a round of negotiations ended in Abu Dhabi, President Trump’s envoys said they would go to Moscow as the Kremlin demands discussions on European security structures.

Reporting from Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates

The first round of Ukraine peace talks in nine months ended in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday without a Russian agreement to include Europe in negotiations that have extended, at Moscow’s insistence, to questions of huge consequence for European nations’ security.

The two days of talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations in the United Arab Emirates were led by President Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. On Thursday, the two Americans are scheduled to meet with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in Moscow and then with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine in Dublin.

The Americans said on Wednesday that they would work to nail down the details of what Mr. Kushner billed as the largest humanitarian swap of the war.

The envoys are also trying to secure agreement from Moscow to widen the talks to include Europeans, after negotiators in Abu Dhabi discussed Russia’s demands to overhaul European security structures.

Reiterating a longstanding European position, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, the European Union’s executive arm, said this week that a cease-fire must come before such discussions. That sequencing would avoid negotiating at gunpoint and test Russian compliance with any agreements.

But Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff, trying to find a path forward after nearly two years of fruitless peacemaking efforts, are pushing to grant Moscow its wish of negotiating the postwar security posture in Europe alongside discussions about a cease-fire and territory in Ukraine.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: Workers in Spain Stage a General Strike for the First Time in 14 Years
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Carlos Barragán
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
Political Turmoil in Spain

Workers in a wide range of industries walked off the job to protest rising rents and stagnant wages, which have become central issues in the campaign.

Reporting from Madrid

Spanish workers staged a general strike on Wednesday for the first time in 14 years, protesting the rising rents and stagnant wages that have become central issues in the national election to be held this month.

Unions said millions of workers participated in the walkout, while hundreds of thousands of Spaniards joined rallies in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia and other cities in the evening.

Early on Wednesday, protesters blocked roads in Madrid, set up picket lines outside major factories in Catalonia and disrupted transportation across Spain.

Police officers wielding shields and batons forced hundreds of demonstrators away from the Gran Vía, the central thoroughfare in Madrid, which rally goers had blocked. The anger of protesters in the capital was directed largely at “rentistas” — a Spanish term for people who live off rental income.

Later in the day, during a march through central Madrid that drew 120,000 protesters according to the government, demonstrators chanted in a festive mood, “One jump, two jumps, whoever doesn’t jump is a rentista.”

Clashes with the police erupted in Barcelona, where a group of masked protesters broke away from the crowd after the demonstration ended, according to local news media. The group smashed several shop windows, threw pyrotechnic devices at police officers and tried unsuccessfully to storm an Apple Store, the reports said.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: Alexander Darchiev, Russia’s Ambassador to the U.S., Dies at 66
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Ephrat Livni
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
The death of Alexander Darchiev was announced by Russia’s foreign ministry. He was appointed to his post in Washington in 2025, as relations between the Kremlin and the White House warmed.

Russia’s ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, who served during a rapprochement between the Kremlin and Washington, has died, the Russian foreign ministry said Wednesday. He was 66.

Mr. Darchiev died in Moscow of a “chronic illness,” Maria Zakharova, spokeswoman for the ministry, said in a statement published by Tass, the Russian state news agency.

“We have lost an outstanding diplomat, an experienced leader, a kind colleague and a mentor,” the ministry said in its statement. It described Mr. Darchiev as a “distinguished expert on the United States” who had “served in one of the most demanding areas of Russian foreign policy.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: Nvidia Scandal Unveils a Fierce Spy War Raging Behind Trump and Xi’s Diplomacy
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: David Pierson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

That the United States suspected Nvidia’s leader was a Chinese spy target underscores the deep distrust between the two powers, even as their leaders try to stabilize ties.

Reporting from Hong Kong

As President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, prepare to meet next week to extend a fragile trade truce, a fresh espionage scandal has shown that behind their diplomacy is a fierce intelligence rivalry.

At its center is Jensen Huang, the Nvidia leader and an influential ally of Mr. Trump’s, who has acknowledged having an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for Beijing. China has denied the espionage allegation.

Under Mr. Xi, the Chinese Communist Party has built a more sophisticated and assertive spy service that regularly highlights the importance of technological security and of threats posed by the United States. At the same time, the Central Intelligence Agency has said that Chinese companies are a legitimate target for espionage in areas like artificial intelligence, semiconductors and biotechnology.

Nvidia’s computer chips power the global A.I. boom and sit at the center of Washington’s efforts to keep that technology out of China’s hands. That makes Mr. Huang, who has lobbied Mr. Trump to ease restrictions on the export of advanced chips to China, a prime target, analysts say.

“It is not at all surprising, given the centrality of Nvidia to U.S.-China tech competition, and the importance of tech competition in the overall U.S.-China rivalry, that someone like him would be a top target for Chinese intelligence collection,” said Sheena Chestnut Greitens, an expert on Chinese security at the University of Texas at Austin.

The milestone is further evidence that African countries have mostly succeeded in preventing community transmission and isolating the small number of cases that have come in from Congo.

By Matthew Mpoke Bigg

Reporting from Nairobi, Kenya

Kenya began a countdown on Wednesday to declare the end of its Ebola outbreak.

The final patient who had tested positive for the virus was discharged from the hospital on Wednesday. And the Kenyan cabinet secretary for health, Aden Duale, said at a news conference that the last 11 people being monitored for Ebola symptoms had also been discharged after completing a 21-day quarantine period.

“For the first time since this outbreak began, Kenya has no patient under treatment and no contact in quarantine,” he said.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Abu Bakr Bashir and Ephrat Livni
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
The Israeli authorities said that Hamas had established a command center at the hospital complex. Hamas said the attack was “a heinous crime targeting a civilian medical facility.”

By Abu Bakr Bashir and Ephrat Livni

The Israeli military struck a hospital in the southern Gaza Strip on Thursday, killing at least six people and injuring 28 more, according to local health officials.

Dr. Ahmed al-Farra, general director of Nasser Hospital, said in a news conference on Thursday that two missiles had hit the facility and that among the dead was Rezeq Abu Shaira, 52, a doctor.

Health officials reached in Gaza by phone said that a man called Khaled Abu Anza had also been killed. A spokeswoman for the Israeli military, speaking on condition of anonymity in line with protocol, said that Mr. Abu Anza was a Hamas operative.

The Israeli security agency and military said in a joint statement on Thursday that they had targeted Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom they identified as a Hamas commander “responsible for holding numerous hostages captive” during the Gaza war.

The Israeli authorities said that Hamas had established a command center at the hospital complex to stage operations against Israeli forces and was storing weapons there. They added that steps had been taken to mitigate harm to civilians.

Hamas said the Israeli claim that the hospital was used for military activity was a “blatant attempt to justify a heinous crime targeting a civilian medical facility.” Residents of Gaza have said that officials affiliated with Hamas-run Gaza government and security forces sometimes use the enclave’s hospitals as offices.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: Pope Leo XIV Goes Home to Peru, Meeting Ghosts of His Past
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Motoko Rich and Mitra Taj
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
Pope Leo in Latin America

In Peru, where Leo XIV lived for two decades and became a citizen, the pope was met by President Keiko Fujimori, whose father’s policies he had protested.

By Motoko Rich and Mitra Taj

Motoko Rich, the Rome bureau chief, is traveling with Pope Leo XIV during his tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Mitra Taj reported from Lima, Peru.

Just a year and a half into his papacy and less than a month after surgeons removed a lobe of his right lung, Pope Leo XIV, the first pontiff born in the United States, touched down in his homeland on Wednesday.

Yet instead of setting foot on American soil, he arrived in Peru, where he spent two decades as a missionary, priest and bishop and became a citizen in 2015.

“Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said, speaking on Wednesday evening to Peru’s president, civic leaders and diplomats at the Gran Teatro Nacional, a theater and concert hall in the country’s capital, Lima. One of his biggest applause lines was when he referred to Peru as “my homeland.”

Having turned out record crowds at Masses in Argentina, the pope flew from Buenos Aires to Lima on Wednesday afternoon, reaching the final country of his 12-day tour of South America. The pope emerged at the top of the stairs next to a sign on the side of his plane that read “Pontifex Maximus,” and was greeted by Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, and a chorus of singing children on a red carpet at the Callao Air Base near Lima.

As his motorcade made its way through city streets under gray skies, about 3 million people lined the roads, according to local authorities, holding up cellphones as they waited for a glimpse of the pontiff.

His choice to visit Peru so soon after becoming pope — while deferring a visit to the country of his birth — underscored the deep emotional ties he feels to the place that formed him as a priest.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: Court in UK Decriminalizes Same-Sex Relations in Trinidad and Tobago
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Zane Irwin and Prior Beharry
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
The ruling, which could affect similar laws in other British Commonwealth countries, has spotlighted a legal system still intertwined with a former colonial power.

By Zane Irwin and Prior Beharry

Prior Beharry reported from Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago.

A ruling by a British-based court has invalidated laws criminalizing homosexuality in Trinidad and Tobago, setting a precedent for those challenging similar laws in other nations in the Caribbean and possibly beyond.

The ruling was handed down on Tuesday by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London, which serves as the highest court of appeal for dozens of crown dependencies, overseas territories and former British colonies.

Five British judges unanimously upheld a 2018 decision by a lower court in Trinidad that had found two sections of the Caribbean country’s 1986 law targeting private, consensual same-sex relations to be unconstitutional. An appeals court in Trinidad had reversed the lower-court decision in 2025.

Trinidad’s attorney general had argued that the law preserved traditional family values in the country, and had leaned on a legal mechanism called “savings provisions,” which kept many laws from the British colonial era.

The decision delivered a hard-fought victory to advocates for L.G.B.T.Q. rights in Trinidad. Jason Jones, an L.G.B.T.Q. activist who had been a key plaintiff against the law since 2015, called the ruling a “vindication.” He said it would provide hope to young L.G.B.T.Q. people in his country who are living in fear of legal and societal discrimination.

Still, Mr. Jones noted ruefully, to challenge the colonial-era law, his lawyers had to seek intervention from a court based in Britain — decades after Trinidad gained independence, in 1962.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: A.I. and Market Whiplash
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Katrin Bennhold
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

A Times reporter who covers financial markets helps us make sense of tech turbulence.

I’m the host of The World.

Last week’s midterm elections were perhaps the first major elections fought at least in part over issues related to artificial intelligence. This year saw record donations from tech executives to tech-friendly candidates. And in some cases, A.I. was actually on the ballot: In local ballot initiatives across the country, people voted to limit or prevent the development of data centers. Many newly elected Democrats have promised A.I. regulation.

If A.I. has surged to the forefront of U.S. politics, it’s in part because A.I. is at the forefront of the U.S. economy. And stock markets around the world rise and fall with A.I. shares, particularly the multitrillion-dollar behemoths based in Silicon Valley. I spoke to my colleague Joe Rennison, who covers financial markets, about the dramatic swings in tech stocks following the midterms and what they mean — for Americans, and for the rest of us.

So, Joe. We’ve seen some serious volatility in the stock market after the midterms. First markets rallied, then they had their worst day in nearly two years. This week, as Nvidia stock plunged because of the Jensen Huang affair, the rest of the market bounced back.

What’s going on, and how much of all this is down to politics?

Certainly some of it is down to politics. The initial rally after the midterms came in part from investors who had parked their cash on the sidelines, in case of some unexpected event — say, a contested election. They bought back in when it became evident we were going to get a clear outcome.

The plunge the next day, though, came after some weaker than expected financial reports from a couple of A.I. companies, and after investors began processing what Democratic control of Congress and some Democratic wins at the state level might actually mean for the A.I. industry.

Video showed demonstrators from a pro-Palestinian protest throwing projectiles at former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. after he attended an event at Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday.

Protesters threw projectiles at former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. after he attended an event at Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday, as the police scuffled with demonstrators attending a pro-Palestinian rally, according to video of the incident.

An Garda Síochána, the Irish national police force, said three men had been arrested on Tuesday in relation to a public order incident. Two of the men were later released, and one was charged, the police said in a statement on Wednesday.

Video of the episode showed Mr. Biden being shielded from the projectiles by black umbrellas held by members of his entourage.

Mr. Biden had been attending a ceremony honoring his son, Hunter Biden, by a debating society that praised him for speaking publicly about politics and his struggle with addiction. Hunter Biden and Jill Biden, the former first lady, also attended the event, according to Ireland’s national broadcaster, RTÉ.

“A protest took place in Trinity College Dublin’s Front Square on Tuesday, 10 November during a ceremony in the Exam Hall,” said Catherine O’Mahony, a spokeswoman for the college. “The protest escalated while the Bidens were leaving” the event, she said.

Videos show groups of people gathered in the square, some waving Palestinian flags and chanting “blood on your hands.” As Mr. Biden was leaving the area, footage shows objects and white liquid, which appears to be milk, being thrown at him.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.title: Judge Allows Trump’s Defamation Lawsuit Against the BBC to Proceed
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.author: Karla Adam
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/world.text:
President Trump is seeking damages from the British broadcaster over a documentary it conceded was misleadingly edited.

Reporting from London

A federal judge in Florida on Tuesday allowed President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against the BBC to proceed, rejecting the British broadcaster’s bid to dismiss it.

Mr. Trump sued the BBC over its documentary “Trump: A Second Chance?” which aired a week before the 2024 presidential election. The program spliced together two portions of remarks that Mr. Trump delivered roughly 55 minutes apart on Jan. 6, 2021, giving the impression that he was encouraging his supporters to storm the U.S. Capitol.

Mr. Trump’s legal team has accused the BBC of “intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring his speech” in an effort to interfere with the election, and is seeking $10 billion in damages.

The BBC has apologized, acknowledging that its editing gave “the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action,” a controversy that prompted the resignations of its director general, Tim Davie, and news chief, Deborah Turness. But it says it was not evidence of a fundamental bias in the BBC’s news reporting and did not constitute defamation.

On Truth Social, Mr. Trump described Tuesday’s ruling as a “A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC.”

A spokeswoman for the BBC said in an emailed statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.”

Lawyers for the BBC had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed, in part because the program was never aired in the United States.

The shooting in a busy neighborhood took place at a gym and two nearby locations. A suspect was found with a fatal gunshot wound after barricading in a building, the police said.

Aishvarya Kavi reported from Washington, D.C.

One person was killed and four wounded in a shooting on Thursday in a busy neighborhood of Washington, D.C., the police said.

The violence, which began before 8 a.m., took place at a gym in the Logan Circle section, but also at a construction site across the street and in the lobby of a nearby building, officials said, and it prompted a widespread response by law enforcement officers.

The police officers who first answered the call found a man dead inside the VIDA gym, said Jeff Carroll, the city’s acting police chief.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/el.author: Emily Cochrane and Jennifer Medina
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/el.text:
At Tougaloo College, supporters danced and wept over Scott Colom’s victory. He will be Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since the Reconstruction era.

By Emily Cochrane and Jennifer Medina

Emily Cochrane reported from Jackson, Miss.

On the lawn of Tougaloo College, steps from the chapel where the civil rights leaders  Fannie Lou Hamer and Medgar Evers gave speeches, they danced.

Students from Tougaloo and other nearby historically Black institutions lined the sidewalk to cheer and applaud. Members of Black fraternities and sororities, dressed in their letters and colors, embraced one another. “Thank the Lord, we did it,” one woman declared.

It was a day that many had prayed would come, though they could never know when. That evening, Scott Colom made their hopes a reality, speaking in front of the college chapel as the senator-elect from Mississippi.

Tyler Dotson, 21, a freshman at Tougaloo College, was awe-struck. “It was everything,” he said, describing how it felt to hear that Mr. Colom had won. “We’ve been waiting a long time.”

“It’s something big, remembered in history,” he added, grinning. “We back.”

When the U.S. Senate race in Mississippi was called for Mr. Colom, who will become the first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction era, shouts of celebration erupted at the local N.A.A.C.P. office.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/sc.title: Why New England’s Republican Governors Withstood the Blue Wave
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/sc.author: Jenna Russell
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/sc.text:
The low-key approach modeled by Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont and Gov. Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire may gain new relevance as their party looks to recover from a national drubbing.

Reporting from Brattleboro, Vt.

Peter Gallagher, a voter in liberal Townshend, Vt., filled in the ovals for Democrat after Democrat at the polls last Tuesday. But when it came to the race for governor, Mr. Gallagher, 67, made a notable exception: He voted for the Republican incumbent, Gov. Phil Scott.

So did Joanne Davis of Putney, who said she appreciated Mr. Scott’s low-key persona: “He’s a normal person. Not crazy, not scary.”

Vermont voters helped drive the blue wave that stunned the country, casting out two dozen Republicans from the state Legislature and replacing them with Democrats, who regained supermajorities in both chambers. But enough also stuck by Mr. Scott, a soft-spoken moderate, to deliver him a record sixth term, in a state that favored Vice President Kamala Harris over President Trump in 2024 by one of the widest margins in the country.

Mr. Scott’s success in a liberal New England state — and the success of Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who was re-elected last week in neighboring New Hampshire — offer a glimmer of hope for a party freshly battered by rejection. In different ways, the two governors have survived by leaning into an old-school strain of Republicanism, melding fiscal pragmatism with a moderate approach on social issues. Mr. Scott, in particular, has also explicitly separated himself from President Trump.

“He’s the only Republican I’ve ever voted for,” Mr. Gallagher said of Mr. Scott as he loaded groceries into his car outside a supermarket in Brattleboro, Vt., last week. “I like the way he crosses the aisle and works with people — that’s the biggest thing.”

Both governors fit a prototype with deep roots in New England, a region better known for liberalism. In Massachusetts, voters have frequently sought to keep liberal legislators in check by electing moderate Republican governors like William Weld and Charlie Baker.
