Scott Colom, a Democrat, narrowly defeated the Republican incumbent to become the first Black senator to represent Mississippi in nearly 150 years, flipping a once solidly Republican seat.

Scott Colom, who will become first Black senator from Mississippi in nearly 150 years, invoked the civil rights movement and his faith in a speech to jubilant supporters on Wednesday night, after more than a week of painstaking vote tabulation delivered Democrats another victory in a state once seen as a lock for Republicans.

“God didn’t want us to get it the easy way,” he told the crowd at Tougaloo College, a historically Black college that served as a haven for civil rights organizers. “He wanted us to get it the Mississippi way.”

Mr. Colom, a district attorney, narrowly defeated Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, The Associated Press reported on Wednesday. It was hailed as a profound moment: Mr. Colom will take the seat once held by Hiram Revels, the nation’s first Black senator, who was elected in 1870.

Mr. Colom’s win sent a wave of elation through the ranks of Mississippi Democrats, who last won a Senate race in 1982 — with a segregationist candidate.

“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Mr. Colom said at the Tougaloo College chapel, where Fannie Lou Hamer and Medgar Evers once spoke. Before his speech, his supporters danced and embraced. One of them declared, “Thank the Lord, we did it.”

Democrats won sweeping victories in this year’s midterms, taking back control of the House and Senate as they capitalized on anger with high prices and President Trump’s agenda. His victory gives the party 55 seats in the upper chamber with one race still undecided, and showed how deep into Republican terrain Democrats extended their reach.

State Representative Justis Gibbs, who is Black, described how his law office in Jackson erupted in screams of joy. “Scott Colom’s victory marks a true turning point for Mississippi,” Mr. Gibbs said.

His campaign was powered by a diverse coalition that included Black voters angered by policies they felt targeted their communities and undermined their voting power; white voters frustrated with high prices and the Trump administration’s agenda; and some Republicans dissatisfied with Ms. Hyde-Smith’s loyalty to the president and his policies.

For much of the year, Ms. Hyde-Smith was heavily favored to win a second term. Mr. Trump had carried Mississippi by 23 percentage points in 2024, and Republicans had long dominated statewide elections.

Here’s what else to know:

Concession speech: Senator Hyde-Smith conceded on Wednesday evening. “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said in a video posted on social media. Read more ›

Making history: Black residents make up 37 percent of Mississippi’s population — the highest proportion of any state — but it had not elected a Black senator since Reconstruction. The last Democrat to win a Senate race in the state was John C. Stennis, a segregationist who won re-election in 1982.

“In every decision I make, I will never forget the most important thing is Mississippi matters,” Colom concludes. “We did it.” The crowd is chanting “Mississippi Matters,” the Colom campaign slogan, after he wraps up his speech.

Colom credits Representative Bennie Thompson for helping push him to campaign more and reach people in Mississippi. Thompson, unlike some other senior lawmakers, easily swatted away a youthful primary challenger this year and has amassed a powerful network of Black Democrats in Mississippi.

Colom is one of several history-making candidates to win office this year -- in his case, the first Black senator elected in Mississippi in nearly 150 years. Others include Xavier Becerra and Gina Hinojosa, the first Hispanic governors elected in California and Texas, and Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim senator. But Colom spoke about his story more directly and more at length than many of them did on election night last week.

“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Colom says. Many people in the state believed the math had been there for Democrats. It was a matter of the right candidate and the right environment to bring the equation together.

It has not always been easy for Democrats to speak about faith, but Scott Colom is among those who have been comfortable this election season speaking openly about it. It is a central tenet of his campaign — especially, he says now, as he recounts struggling to get people to pay attention to his campaign.

Scott Colom, based on the cheers, has taken the stage. I can’t see him because so many people are on their feet — “there he is,” one woman says behind me.

Representative Bennie Thompson is just the second Black lawmaker Mississippi has sent to the House since Reconstruction and has been its lone Democrat in Congress for years. “All my friends kept saying ‘I don’t know if the time is right,’ he says, sketching out the steep national skepticism Scott Colom faced. Now, he says, “I now have a partner in Washington.”

More than 90 percent of Black voters in Mississippi cast ballots for Colom, according to Times Voter Trends. In contrast, Colom won 25 percent of white voters’ ballots. That group shifted 19 points leftward in comparison to the 2024 election, according to Times Voter Trends, when Republicans won white voters by a margin of 67 percentage points. Black voters shifted eight points leftward when compared to 2024.

The Mississippi Republican Party has just put out a statement, with Mike Hurst, the chairman, saying, “Scott Colom ran a good campaign here in Mississippi, and I congratulate him on his victory.” He continued: “While elections may determine who holds public office, they do not define who we are as a people nor diminish the principles we hold dear. Tomorrow, the sun will rise over the same Mississippi we loved yesterday.”

“There are moments when the place and the occasion speak to one another. Tonight is one of those moments,” Dr. Corey Wiggins says. It is clear that the choice of Tougaloo for this speech was intentional, given its history in the Civil Rights movement, along with the Colom campaign’s emphasis on energizing college students across the state.

The President of Tougaloo College is taking the stage now.

The program is officially starting.

Colom’s family and friends are slowly making their way to their seats. Someone has passed out American flags that a few in the crowd are waving.

The sign on the lectern reads “Picked Another Senator.” It’s a reference to a spot for Colom that became known as the “pick another protein” ad. It went viral after Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, asked to address rising beef prices, admonished voters that they “have so many proteins to choose from.” (We interviewed the guy whose delivery of “I’d rather pick another senator” helped the ad go viral.)

We expect Scott Colom to speak shortly at Tougaloo College, after winning his Senate election. It is a poignant moment for so many here, especially give the historic nature of his win and the legacy of the college as a haven and proving ground for civil rights leaders and Black officials.

John Yoon and Jim Beaugez

Jim Beaugez reported from Jackson, Miss.

Powered by a viral ad and direct courtship of Republican voters, Scott Colom went from being a long-shot Democratic Senate candidate in Mississippi to defeating the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The deep-red state became an unexpected battleground in October when one of Mr. Colom’s campaign ads went viral. The roughly 30-second video mocked Ms. Hyde-Smith’s comment on the rising price of beef — “You have so many proteins to choose from” — by urging voters to pick a different senator instead.

Mr. Colom also drew in Black and white voters, including Republicans, and employed an unusual strategy: He attended President Trump’s rally for Ms. Hyde-Smith the week before the election — not to confront voters but to walk the line and listen to them discuss issues like health care, grocery bills and gas prices.

Mr. Colom posed for selfies with rally-goers and later said he had converted some to his camp. In an interview with CNN, he made an appeal to Republican voters.

“I’m going to get you what you were promised in 2024,” he said, citing three issues he brought up with them: lower grocery prices, an end to wars and the full and transparent release of the Epstein files.

Scott Colom has arrived at Tougaloo College and just stepped into the campus chapel, to cheers and applause.

Amid exuberant celebrations by Democrats, Gov. Tate Reeves, a Republican, has offered his congratulations to Colom in a statement on social media.

Congratulations to Senator-Elect @scott_colom. I hope to collaborate as we continue our very important work to support Mississippi families, grow jobs and wages for our people, and improve educational outcomes for our kids!

Campbell Robertson and Emily Cochrane

Campbell Robertson reported from Jackson and Meridian, Miss. Emily Cochrane reported from Nashville.

Scott Colom is set to become the first Black senator from Mississippi in more than 145 years thanks to an unparalleled coalition of hundreds of thousands of Black voters, white voters, enthusiastic college students, angry suburbanites and discontented small-town conservatives.

The circumstances behind Mr. Colom’s electoral performance may be a combination of hard work and luck, a skilled candidate running a sharp campaign at just the right time. But history hangs heavily over events in Mississippi, and the significance is profound.

Mr. Colom will take the seat once held by Hiram Revels, the nation’s first Black senator, who was elected in 1870, the middle of the Reconstruction era. The last Black senator from Mississippi, Blanche K. Bruce, served from 1875 to 1881, as Reconstruction was in its final days, raising alarms about the violence faced by Black voters but expressing his confidence “in the endurance, capacity and destiny of my people.”

This year’s huge Black turnout in the state was in part a reaction to efforts in Mississippi and elsewhere in the South to redraw district lines that would carve up majority-Black seats in Congress and in state legislatures.

Among Mr. Colom’s supporters, the prevailing sentiment is that a Black Democrat’s victory in the state was simply a matter of time. What seems so astounding to outsiders is seen by many here as a math problem that has finally been solved.

Students are welcoming people to Tougaloo College, steps from the historic chapel where civil rights leaders spoke, with a dance tunnel.

The outcome of the Senate race in Mississippi is finally settled. But even before Scott Colom’s long-shot Democratic victory, voters, officials and politicians were already starting to look ahead to next year.

Mr. Colom’s win — driven by the diverse coalition he assembled of Black voters, white Democrats and disenchanted conservatives — has raised questions about how competitive next year’s race might be to replace Gov. Tate Reeves, a Republican who cannot seek another term under state law.

Two Democratic candidates have already announced plans to run, alongside an already crowded Republican field. Some Democrats have speculated that Brandon Presley, the second cousin of Elvis Presley who fell short in the 2023 race against Mr. Reeves, could run again and capitalize on the party’s enthusiasm in the aftermath of Mr. Colom’s win. (Asked directly on Friday, Mr. Presley did not answer.)

Shad White, the conservative state auditor, announced his campaign for governor this week, joining Attorney General Lynn Fitch and two other Republicans who had already announced.

The Senate race could reverberate in other ways.

Michael Watson, the Republican secretary of state who oversees elections, is running for lieutenant governor, but frustrations over the prolonged counting of ballots this year and the number of voters who found themselves listed as inactive could complicate his political ambitions.

The uptick in turnout from Black voters in the South, as well as the overwhelming Republican losses across the country this month, could also affect political calculations around whether to change Mississippi’s district lines in both the State Legislature and Congress.

After the Supreme Court ruling this year that weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965, some Mississippi Republicans pushed for new lines to be drawn that would give them an advantage — and most likely undercut the power of Black voters in choosing state and federal representatives alike.

Before the election, lawmakers held a series of public hearings to debate the possibility of new district lines. Some organizers and voters said the prospect of mid-decade redistricting tied to the Voting Rights Act was yet another motivating factor for Black voters to go to the polls and support Democrats this year.

Campbell Robertson contributed reporting.

Outside the historic chapel at Tougaloo College, it’s standing room only — all seats have been taken as people from across the city come to celebrate Scott Colom’s win.

In recent days, students and Black leaders have gathered here for community and to receive updates about the lengthy effort to count votes.

Tougaloo College is a private, historically Black college just outside Jackson. It was known as a haven for civil rights organizers during the movement. The civil-rights leaders including Fannie Lou Hamer and Medgar Evers spoke at its chapel.

Russ Hudson was not supposed to be in Scott Colom’s protein ad.

Mr. Hudson, 35, had known the district attorney for about a decade before Mr. Colom became the Democratic candidate for Senate in Mississippi. But it was Mr. Hudson’s father who was initially cast in the campaign ad mocking a suggestion from Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, that Mississippi residents pick another type of protein to avoid rising beef prices.

When the elder Mr. Hudson balked at a script that would require him to utter profanity on camera, his son volunteered. In a short-sleeved button down shirt, he stood at a grill in the backyard of Mr. Colom’s parent’s house and tossed his head back to deliver a drawling, deadpan rebuke of Ms. Hyde-Smith.

“Shee-it,” Mr. Hudson says in the spot, rendering the off-color word with a distinct southern twang. “I’d rather pick another senator, instead.”

The lines, he said, felt natural. He left thinking maybe a couple thousand people would see it.

“I just did it like a Mississippian would,” Mr. Hudson said in an interview.

Now, Mr. Hudson, an Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, has found himself as the unlikely face of one of the most potent campaign advertisements of the 2026 midterm cycle. The ad, released in the final weeks of the election season, became a defining feature of Mr. Colom’s campaign and his surge to a stunning upset.

“I never expected it to do what it did,” Mr. Hudson said.

He even downloaded TikTok to keep up with all the commentary his friends were sending him about the ad. Someone made him a “pick another protein” shirt with his face on it, along with the other two women in the ad.

And he keeps fielding requests to, well, say it again.

“They make me throw my head back with it, too,” he said.

Mr. Hudson, who said he has been mocked for his Southern twang outside of the state, had not been heavily involved in politics. As a disabled veteran on a fixed income and father to an infant, he was drawn to Mr. Colom’s pledges to focus on high costs and protecting benefits for veterans, as well as the personal connection. The ad, he figured, was his contribution to the campaign.

“A lot of people don’t know much about Mississippi,” he said. “And look at us now. We’re worldwide.”

The mood at Tougaloo College, a historically Black college that had served as a safe haven for civil rights leaders and activists, was exuberant. People were dancing to music, embracing and declaring, “Thank the Lord, we did it.”

When it comes to lifetime judicial appointments, the Senate maintains a century-old tradition: The two home-state senators get virtual veto power, regardless of party.

Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Republican of Mississippi, used that authority in 2023 to single-handedly block Scott Colom, a district attorney, from consideration for a U.S. District Court vacancy in the state when the Biden administration nominated him.

Now, Mr. Colom, a Democrat, has defeated Ms. Hyde-Smith and will take her Senate seat in January.

Given the stability and authority of a lifetime appointment to the federal bench, Mr. Colom would not have sought the Senate seat had he been confirmed, he said. But he also stressed that his motivation for running was not a matter of retribution, but a deeper frustration with what he felt was a lack of attention to the state.

For Democrats and Mr. Colom’s allies, who were angered by Ms. Hyde-Smith’s rejection, there was some satisfaction in the election outcome on Wednesday.

“Scott may have wanted to be a judge, but God saw fit for him to be someone who appoints judges,” said Jabari O. Edwards, a longtime friend of Mr. Colom’s.

Mr. Colom, who defeated a three-decade incumbent to become district attorney, had labored to secure bipartisan support for the judicial nomination. He had the backing of Roger Wicker, the other Republican senator from the state; Representative Bennie Thompson, the powerful, long-serving Black Democrat; and two former Republican governors, Haley Barbour and Phil Bryant.

Ms. Hyde-Smith was unmoved.

“I simply cannot support his nomination to serve on the federal bench in Mississippi for a lifetime,” Ms. Hyde-Smith said in a statement in 2023.

Carl Hulse contributed reporting.

Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Republican of Mississippi, conceded to Scott Colom, a Democrat, in a video posted to social media on Wednesday evening.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Ms. Hyde-Smith said in the video. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

Ms. Hyde-Smith said that her campaign “worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted, and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election.”

Mr. Colom defeated Ms. Hyde-Smith by a narrow margin, according to The Associated Press. He will become the first Black senator elected from Mississippi since Reconstruction.

Mr. Colom’s win means Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats at the start of the next Congress. The contest in Alaska, in which the Democrat Mary Peltola has a narrow lead, is the last remaining Senate race in which a winner has not been declared.

Ms. Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in Congress, was first appointed to the Senate to fill a vacancy in April 2018. She had previously served as Mississippi’s commissioner of agriculture from 2012 to 2018.

The Republican senator also spent more than a decade in the Mississippi State Senate, starting as a conservative Democrat in 2000 and converting to the Republican Party in 2010.

Reporting from the Capitol

Scott Colom’s victory in Mississippi adds to the Senate Democratic majority and gives the chamber a new Black voice from the rural South.

Mr. Colom’s win over the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, brings the Senate Democratic majority to at least 55 seats, with Alaska remaining to be decided as the Democrat Mary Peltola leads there over Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican.

The larger margin of control gives Democrats more seats on committees, making it easer to overcome opposition there. It also puts the party closer to the 60-vote threshold to break a filibuster, meaning Democrats need to win fewer G.O.P. votes to avoid an impasse and advance bills, though they are still short of the supermajority needed to bypass Republicans entirely.

While Mr. Colom got some political help in his campaign from Senator Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat and party leader, he has suggested he might not support Mr. Schumer’s bid to keep his top slot and become majority leader.

But his reasoning was different than that of other newcomers who have questioned whether Mr. Schumer is too old, too moderate and too aligned with the party establishment to continue at the top. Mr. Colom said his concern was that the two potential party leaders — Mr. Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, another establishment moderate from New York — both came from Brooklyn, suggesting that Democrats needed a wider range of viewpoints at the top.

A prosecutor, Mr. Colom could be expected to play a role on criminal justice issues. But he has also been focused on income inequality and access to health care as well as the struggles of smaller farmers in rural swaths of Mississippi.

With the race called in his favor on Wednesday, Scott Colom will become the third Black senator in Mississippi history, but the first in nearly 150 years. That legacy traces back to Feb. 25, 1870, when Hiram Revels walked into the chamber of the U.S. Senate to take his oath of office.

The month before, the Fifteenth Amendment had been ratified, giving Black men like Mr. Revels the right to vote in a nation that had been ravaged by the Civil War. Mr. Revels, a man born free in North Carolina who served as a Union Army chaplain in Mississippi, had been chosen by the Mississippi Legislature to be its first new senator after the Civil War.

Two days after the state was readmitted to the union, Mr. Revels became the first Black man ever seated in the Senate. He delivered his first speech on the Senate floor in opposition to an amendment that would stop Black people from holding office.

Black residents, he said, “ask but the rights which are theirs by God’s universal law.”

Mr. Revels was joined soon after in the Senate by Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery in Virginia and fled to freedom at the start of the Civil War. He became the first Black man to serve a full term in the Senate.

Mr. Bruce served from 1875 to 1881, as Reconstruction in Mississippi was in its last, bloody days before white leaders ushered in the repressive Jim Crow era by stripping Black Mississippians of many of their rights. He raised alarms about violence against Black voters, but expressed confidence “in the endurance, capacity and destiny of my people.”

Two Black men — Mike Espy, who went on to serve as agriculture secretary during the Clinton administration, and Representative Bennie Thompson, who won re-election on Nov. 3 — have been elected by Mississippi to the House since Reconstruction.

The Senate had been more elusive. Mr. Revels’s seat would go on to be held by staunch segregationists including James K. Vardaman and James O. Eastland. In January, it will belong to Mr. Colom.

Campbell Robertson contributed reporting.

Democrats who won seats in the Senate after the midterm elections posed for a group photo at the U.S. Capitol earlier this week. But Scott Colom was still in Mississippi, telling his supporters to hold on tight in a close Senate race that would be decided by a few thousand votes.

Mr. Colom, a Democrat, may be late to the party in Washington, but he finally made it. A decisive tranche of affidavit and absentee-by-mail ballots tallied on Wednesday pushed Mr. Colom to victory as the first Black senator elected by Mississippi since the Reconstruction era.

The counting took time. Tuesday was the last day that mail-in ballots postmarked on Election Day could arrive. By then, Mr. Colom held a narrow lead over the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, but it was not much larger than the roughly 2,500 absentee-by-mail ballots that still needed to be tallied.

There was also an unknown number of affidavit ballots left to be counted, and they were likely to play an outsized role in what had become an extremely close election. Those ballots had been cast provisionally by Mississippians who believed they were registered voters but who were not listed at their polling places.

Election officials had to check to see if those voters had been missed in poll books, or if they had later turned up at a local clerk’s office with proper identification to “cure” their ballots. The deadline to cure affidavit ballots was also on Tuesday.

The affidavit ballots are required to be manually processed by local officials, part of a slow count that had captured national attention since the Nov. 3 election.

The process to validate affidavit ballots had confused some younger voters, leading to efforts by organizers in recent days to get students on college campuses to check the status of their votes. Young voters were a key component of Mr. Colom’s coalition.

Unlike most states, Mississippi law does not allow for a recount in statewide races. But Republicans have closely monitored the count, with their lawyers writing to election commissioners that there should be an “immediate separation, secure custody, and preservation of all affidavit ballots.” Mr. Colom’s lawyers objected to that request in their own letter.

Mike Hurst, the chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party, had previously said lawyers supporting Ms. Hyde-Smith’s campaign “will be ready, if necessary, to avail ourselves of every legal option at our disposal, if there is evidence that the law has been violated.”

Emily Cochrane contributed reporting.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/el.text:
Mr. Colom, a prosecutor, will become the first Black senator elected from Mississippi since Reconstruction, more than 150 years ago.

In perhaps the most stunning upset of the midterm elections, Scott Colom, a Democrat from Mississippi, narrowly edged out Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, according to The Associated Press. The victory came after a vote count that extended more than a week after the Nov. 3 election.

Mr. Colom will become the first Black senator from Mississippi elected since Reconstruction, after Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery, went to Washington more than 150 years ago.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Colom.

Mr. Colom, 43, is a district attorney from Columbus, Miss., a city of roughly 23,000 people near the border with Alabama. He won that office by unseating a nearly 30-year incumbent in 2015, and has been re-elected twice since then.

Mr. Colom’s mother was a judge, and his father, Wilbur Colom, is an attorney who served on Ronald Reagan’s transition team and ran as a Republican for state treasurer in 1987. Mr. Colom has two daughters with his wife and attends a Baptist church, according to his campaign website.

Mr. Colom is the first Black senator elected in more than 150 years from Mississippi, where Black residents make up 37 percent of the population — the highest proportion of any state. He is also the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the state since 1982, the year that John C. Stennis, a segregationist Democrat, ran for the last time.

Mr. Colom will take the seat once held by Hiram Revels, the nation’s first Black senator, who was elected in the Reconstruction era. The senator-elect did it by winning in a state that President Trump carried by nearly 23 points just two years ago.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.author: Robert Jimison
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.text:
Eleven Democrats were absent, helping Republicans shelve the charges against the defense secretary. It drew sharp criticism a week after the party’s sweeping election victories.

Reporting from the Capitol

Democrats, fresh off their sweeping victories in last week’s elections, faced bitter criticism and recriminations on Wednesday from within their own ranks after 11 of their members missed a vote on the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The absences, which boosted Republicans’ successful effort to block the impeachment on Tuesday, cast a shadow over what was otherwise a triumphant week for Democrats that was supposed to be focused on savoring their electoral wins, welcoming new members and plotting out their agenda for when they take the helm of both chambers of Congress.

Instead, Representative Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, the No. 2 Democrat in charge of tracking votes among her members, began a closed-door party meeting on Wednesday morning scolding lawmakers who had been absent for the impeachment vote, as others chastised their colleagues in public.

“Show up and do your job,” Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, Democrat of Michigan, said bluntly on CNN Tuesday evening.

Representative Sydney Kamlager-Dove, Democrat of California, appeared to be seething as she left the Capitol following the vote Tuesday night, telling the MeidasTouch Network that Democrats had squandered the opportunity to push the impeachment charges forward over Republican opposition. “People should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote,” she said.

Some senior Democrats said that more anger should be directed at Mr. Hegseth and the Republicans who banded together to save his job.

Scott Colom, a Democrat, narrowly defeated the Republican incumbent to become the first Black senator to represent Mississippi in nearly 150 years, flipping a once solidly Republican seat.

Scott Colom, who will become first Black senator from Mississippi in nearly 150 years, invoked the civil rights movement and his faith in a speech to jubilant supporters on Wednesday night, after more than a week of painstaking vote tabulation delivered Democrats another victory in a state once seen as a lock for Republicans.

“God didn’t want us to get it the easy way,” he told the crowd at Tougaloo College, a historically Black college that served as a haven for civil rights organizers. “He wanted us to get it the Mississippi way.”

Mr. Colom, a district attorney, narrowly defeated Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, The Associated Press reported on Wednesday. It was hailed as a profound moment: Mr. Colom will take the seat once held by Hiram Revels, the nation’s first Black senator, who was elected in 1870.

Mr. Colom’s win sent a wave of elation through the ranks of Mississippi Democrats, who last won a Senate race in 1982 — with a segregationist candidate.

“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Mr. Colom said at the Tougaloo College chapel, where Fannie Lou Hamer and Medgar Evers once spoke. Before his speech, his supporters danced and embraced. One of them declared, “Thank the Lord, we did it.”

Democrats won sweeping victories in this year’s midterms, taking back control of the House and Senate as they capitalized on anger with high prices and President Trump’s agenda. His victory gives the party 55 seats in the upper chamber with one race still undecided, and showed how deep into Republican terrain Democrats extended their reach.

State Representative Justis Gibbs, who is Black, described how his law office in Jackson erupted in screams of joy. “Scott Colom’s victory marks a true turning point for Mississippi,” Mr. Gibbs said.

His campaign was powered by a diverse coalition that included Black voters angered by policies they felt targeted their communities and undermined their voting power; white voters frustrated with high prices and the Trump administration’s agenda; and some Republicans dissatisfied with Ms. Hyde-Smith’s loyalty to the president and his policies.

For much of the year, Ms. Hyde-Smith was heavily favored to win a second term. Mr. Trump had carried Mississippi by 23 percentage points in 2024, and Republicans had long dominated statewide elections.

Here’s what else to know:

Concession speech: Senator Hyde-Smith conceded on Wednesday evening. “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said in a video posted on social media. Read more ›

Making history: Black residents make up 37 percent of Mississippi’s population — the highest proportion of any state — but it had not elected a Black senator since Reconstruction. The last Democrat to win a Senate race in the state was John C. Stennis, a segregationist who won re-election in 1982.

“In every decision I make, I will never forget the most important thing is Mississippi matters,” Colom concludes. “We did it.” The crowd is chanting “Mississippi Matters,” the Colom campaign slogan, after he wraps up his speech.

Colom credits Representative Bennie Thompson for helping push him to campaign more and reach people in Mississippi. Thompson, unlike some other senior lawmakers, easily swatted away a youthful primary challenger this year and has amassed a powerful network of Black Democrats in Mississippi.

Colom is one of several history-making candidates to win office this year -- in his case, the first Black senator elected in Mississippi in nearly 150 years. Others include Xavier Becerra and Gina Hinojosa, the first Hispanic governors elected in California and Texas, and Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim senator. But Colom spoke about his story more directly and more at length than many of them did on election night last week.

“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Colom says. Many people in the state believed the math had been there for Democrats. It was a matter of the right candidate and the right environment to bring the equation together.

It has not always been easy for Democrats to speak about faith, but Scott Colom is among those who have been comfortable this election season speaking openly about it. It is a central tenet of his campaign — especially, he says now, as he recounts struggling to get people to pay attention to his campaign.

Scott Colom, based on the cheers, has taken the stage. I can’t see him because so many people are on their feet — “there he is,” one woman says behind me.

Representative Bennie Thompson is just the second Black lawmaker Mississippi has sent to the House since Reconstruction and has been its lone Democrat in Congress for years. “All my friends kept saying ‘I don’t know if the time is right,’ he says, sketching out the steep national skepticism Scott Colom faced. Now, he says, “I now have a partner in Washington.”

More than 90 percent of Black voters in Mississippi cast ballots for Colom, according to Times Voter Trends. In contrast, Colom won 25 percent of white voters’ ballots. That group shifted 19 points leftward in comparison to the 2024 election, according to Times Voter Trends, when Republicans won white voters by a margin of 67 percentage points. Black voters shifted eight points leftward when compared to 2024.

The Mississippi Republican Party has just put out a statement, with Mike Hurst, the chairman, saying, “Scott Colom ran a good campaign here in Mississippi, and I congratulate him on his victory.” He continued: “While elections may determine who holds public office, they do not define who we are as a people nor diminish the principles we hold dear. Tomorrow, the sun will rise over the same Mississippi we loved yesterday.”

“There are moments when the place and the occasion speak to one another. Tonight is one of those moments,” Dr. Corey Wiggins says. It is clear that the choice of Tougaloo for this speech was intentional, given its history in the Civil Rights movement, along with the Colom campaign’s emphasis on energizing college students across the state.

The President of Tougaloo College is taking the stage now.

The program is officially starting.

Colom’s family and friends are slowly making their way to their seats. Someone has passed out American flags that a few in the crowd are waving.

The sign on the lectern reads “Picked Another Senator.” It’s a reference to a spot for Colom that became known as the “pick another protein” ad. It went viral after Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, asked to address rising beef prices, admonished voters that they “have so many proteins to choose from.” (We interviewed the guy whose delivery of “I’d rather pick another senator” helped the ad go viral.)

We expect Scott Colom to speak shortly at Tougaloo College, after winning his Senate election. It is a poignant moment for so many here, especially give the historic nature of his win and the legacy of the college as a haven and proving ground for civil rights leaders and Black officials.

John Yoon and Jim Beaugez

Jim Beaugez reported from Jackson, Miss.

Powered by a viral ad and direct courtship of Republican voters, Scott Colom went from being a long-shot Democratic Senate candidate in Mississippi to defeating the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The deep-red state became an unexpected battleground in October when one of Mr. Colom’s campaign ads went viral. The roughly 30-second video mocked Ms. Hyde-Smith’s comment on the rising price of beef — “You have so many proteins to choose from” — by urging voters to pick a different senator instead.

Mr. Colom also drew in Black and white voters, including Republicans, and employed an unusual strategy: He attended President Trump’s rally for Ms. Hyde-Smith the week before the election — not to confront voters but to walk the line and listen to them discuss issues like health care, grocery bills and gas prices.

Mr. Colom posed for selfies with rally-goers and later said he had converted some to his camp. In an interview with CNN, he made an appeal to Republican voters.

“I’m going to get you what you were promised in 2024,” he said, citing three issues he brought up with them: lower grocery prices, an end to wars and the full and transparent release of the Epstein files.

Scott Colom has arrived at Tougaloo College and just stepped into the campus chapel, to cheers and applause.

Amid exuberant celebrations by Democrats, Gov. Tate Reeves, a Republican, has offered his congratulations to Colom in a statement on social media.

Congratulations to Senator-Elect @scott_colom. I hope to collaborate as we continue our very important work to support Mississippi families, grow jobs and wages for our people, and improve educational outcomes for our kids!

Given the stability and authority of a lifetime appointment to the federal bench, Mr. Colom would not have sought the Senate seat had he been confirmed, he said. But he also stressed that his motivation for running was not a matter of retribution, but a deeper frustration with what he felt was a lack of attention to the state.

For Democrats and Mr. Colom’s allies, who were angered by Ms. Hyde-Smith’s rejection, there was some satisfaction in the election outcome on Wednesday.

“Scott may have wanted to be a judge, but God saw fit for him to be someone who appoints judges,” said Jabari O. Edwards, a longtime friend of Mr. Colom’s.

Mr. Colom, who defeated a three-decade incumbent to become district attorney, had labored to secure bipartisan support for the judicial nomination. He had the backing of Roger Wicker, the other Republican senator from the state; Representative Bennie Thompson, the powerful, long-serving Black Democrat; and two former Republican governors, Haley Barbour and Phil Bryant.

Ms. Hyde-Smith was unmoved.

“I simply cannot support his nomination to serve on the federal bench in Mississippi for a lifetime,” Ms. Hyde-Smith said in a statement in 2023.

Carl Hulse contributed reporting.

Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Republican of Mississippi, conceded to Scott Colom, a Democrat, in a video posted to social media on Wednesday evening.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Ms. Hyde-Smith said in the video. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

Ms. Hyde-Smith said that her campaign “worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted, and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election.”

Mr. Colom defeated Ms. Hyde-Smith by a narrow margin, according to The Associated Press. He will become the first Black senator elected from Mississippi since Reconstruction.

Mr. Colom’s win means Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats at the start of the next Congress. The contest in Alaska, in which the Democrat Mary Peltola has a narrow lead, is the last remaining Senate race in which a winner has not been declared.

Ms. Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in Congress, was first appointed to the Senate to fill a vacancy in April 2018. She had previously served as Mississippi’s commissioner of agriculture from 2012 to 2018.

The Republican senator also spent more than a decade in the Mississippi State Senate, starting as a conservative Democrat in 2000 and converting to the Republican Party in 2010.

Reporting from the Capitol

Scott Colom’s victory in Mississippi adds to the Senate Democratic majority and gives the chamber a new Black voice from the rural South.

Mr. Colom’s win over the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, brings the Senate Democratic majority to at least 55 seats, with Alaska remaining to be decided as the Democrat Mary Peltola leads there over Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican.

The larger margin of control gives Democrats more seats on committees, making it easer to overcome opposition there. It also puts the party closer to the 60-vote threshold to break a filibuster, meaning Democrats need to win fewer G.O.P. votes to avoid an impasse and advance bills, though they are still short of the supermajority needed to bypass Republicans entirely.

While Mr. Colom got some political help in his campaign from Senator Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat and party leader, he has suggested he might not support Mr. Schumer’s bid to keep his top slot and become majority leader.

But his reasoning was different than that of other newcomers who have questioned whether Mr. Schumer is too old, too moderate and too aligned with the party establishment to continue at the top. Mr. Colom said his concern was that the two potential party leaders — Mr. Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, another establishment moderate from New York — both came from Brooklyn, suggesting that Democrats needed a wider range of viewpoints at the top.

A prosecutor, Mr. Colom could be expected to play a role on criminal justice issues. But he has also been focused on income inequality and access to health care as well as the struggles of smaller farmers in rural swaths of Mississippi.

With the race called in his favor on Wednesday, Scott Colom will become the third Black senator in Mississippi history, but the first in nearly 150 years. That legacy traces back to Feb. 25, 1870, when Hiram Revels walked into the chamber of the U.S. Senate to take his oath of office.

The month before, the Fifteenth Amendment had been ratified, giving Black men like Mr. Revels the right to vote in a nation that had been ravaged by the Civil War. Mr. Revels, a man born free in North Carolina who served as a Union Army chaplain in Mississippi, had been chosen by the Mississippi Legislature to be its first new senator after the Civil War.

Two days after the state was readmitted to the union, Mr. Revels became the first Black man ever seated in the Senate. He delivered his first speech on the Senate floor in opposition to an amendment that would stop Black people from holding office.

Black residents, he said, “ask but the rights which are theirs by God’s universal law.”

Mr. Revels was joined soon after in the Senate by Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery in Virginia and fled to freedom at the start of the Civil War. He became the first Black man to serve a full term in the Senate.

Mr. Bruce served from 1875 to 1881, as Reconstruction in Mississippi was in its last, bloody days before white leaders ushered in the repressive Jim Crow era by stripping Black Mississippians of many of their rights. He raised alarms about violence against Black voters, but expressed confidence “in the endurance, capacity and destiny of my people.”

Two Black men — Mike Espy, who went on to serve as agriculture secretary during the Clinton administration, and Representative Bennie Thompson, who won re-election on Nov. 3 — have been elected by Mississippi to the House since Reconstruction.

The Senate had been more elusive. Mr. Revels’s seat would go on to be held by staunch segregationists including James K. Vardaman and James O. Eastland. In January, it will belong to Mr. Colom.

Campbell Robertson contributed reporting.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.author: Mack Liederman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.text:
A Pentagon spokesman said the sentinel had “reminded everyone to maintain decorum” after laughter was heard from a group visiting the burial site with the Defense Secretary on Wednesday.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was scolded on Wednesday at the Tomb of the Unknowns by an Army sentinel after laughter broke out among a group that accompanied him.

Mr. Hegseth, his wife and some advisers had been posing for pictures and chatting in front of the tomb, also called the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a solemn memorial at Arlington National Cemetery for military members who were killed in battle and remain unidentified.

Video recorded by reporters showed the sentinel guarding the tomb turning to face Mr. Hegseth’s group shortly after audible laughter from a woman among them.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the sentinel shouted toward Mr. Hegseth and others as they were leaving.

The rules for ceremonies at the cemetery prohibit visitors from yelling or making any other “boisterous” or “unreasonably loud” noise.

The defense secretary had been attending the annual Veterans Day wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery alongside President Trump.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.title: A Diminished Justice Dept. Braces for Fresh Fights After Midterm Loss
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.author: Glenn Thrush and Alan Feuer
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.text:
The upheaval points to a broader dilemma spurred by the election: whether the department can carry out President Trump’s priorities as career officials eye the exits and senior department officials resign.

By Glenn Thrush and Alan Feuer

Glenn Thrush reported from Washington, and Alan Feuer from New York.

A top Justice Department official delivered a gung-ho message to Trump-appointed federal prosecutors around the country on Monday, as they reckoned with the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections: We are now a wartime department, he declared.

The official, Aakash Singh, the principal associate deputy attorney general, exhorted dozens of U.S. attorneys during a teleconference call to step up their pressure on emboldened local officials in Democratic-controlled localities, like Houston, to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement, according to three people briefed on the exchange.

But it is hard to double down when you are running low on chips.

The department, which has already seen the exodus of hundreds of career officials who were forced out or left because they disagreed with President Trump’s priorities, faces a daunting new staffing dilemma spurred by the election.

Many career officials who hung on until now, including some who broadly support the department’s current mission, are eyeing the exits to avoid two grim years of partisan combat. They are joined by a second, higher-profile group: senior department officials who have submitted resignations, some after a discreet shove, in a leadership reshuffle over the past week.

Among the departures: Brett Shumate, the head of the department’s civil division; Harmeet Dhillon, the chief of the civil rights unit; and Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney in Miami who oversaw a sprawling inquiry examining the various investigations into Mr. Trump. T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel, and Jesus A. Osete, a Dhillon aide, have been nominated for federal judgeships.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.title: Biden Calls His Disastrous 2024 Debate Performance ‘Not Very Consequential’
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.author: Reid J. Epstein
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/po.text:
A debate against Donald Trump in which Mr. Biden, then the president, repeatedly lost his train of thought led to widespread Democratic pressure to end his campaign, which Mr. Biden eventually did.

Reid J. Epstein covered the 2020 and 2024 Biden presidential campaigns.

More than two years after his disastrous debate performance prompted a Democratic  push to urge him to abandon his re-election campaign, former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. declared the debate was “not very consequential.”

Mr. Biden’s assessment, in an interview with People magazine published on Wednesday, runs counter to widely held views of the debate and its aftermath, in which Mr. Biden scrambled for nearly a month to try to convince fellow Democrats he was up for the job of running against Donald J. Trump again in 2024.

“I don’t know anybody who hasn’t made a mistake in a debate,” Mr. Biden, 83, said in the interview. “To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.”

Though Mr. Biden eventually bowed out of the race, he has continued to force a national reassessment of his choice to run again when polls showed Americans did not want him to.

The interview with People, ahead of a memoir to be released on Tuesday, comes as Mr. Biden is seeking to repair a legacy tarnished by Mr. Trump’s 2024 victory and subsequent actions rolling back some of Mr. Biden’s policy achievements.

Calls for Mr. Biden to withdraw from his re-election campaign began almost immediately after the June 2024 debate, in which he repeatedly lost his train of thought and faced questions about his age and acuity. Mr. Biden has never publicly conceded that he was ill-prepared to debate or that he should not have run for president again, and he maintained that stance in the new interview.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/insid.title: How The Times Covered Mississippi’s Senate Race, Which Unexpectedly Became a Nail-Biter
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/insid.author: Patrick Healy, Megan DiTrolio, Michael Cooper, Jonathan Weisman and Emily Cochrane
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/insid.text:
Three Times journalists break down the twists and turns in a race that captured national attention.

Interview by Patrick Healy and Megan DiTrolio

With Michael CooperJonathan Weisman and Emily Cochrane

Patrick Healy, an assistant managing editor, and Megan DiTrolio, a senior editor, are part of the Trust team, which focuses on efforts to help readers understand The Times and its journalism.

With so many midterm campaigns and elections this year, how did The Times decide which ones to cover deeply? And how did we tackle reporting on the Mississippi Senate race — no one’s idea of a battleground a year ago?

Scott Colom, the Democratic candidate in Mississippi, made history on Wednesday evening with his victory over the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith. The incoming Democratic majority in the Senate is now likely to grow even more than party leaders had hoped, and Mr. Colom will become the state’s first Democrat elected to the Senate since 1982 — and the first Black senator elected from Mississippi since Reconstruction.

This week we discussed how we covered the race and its unexpected twists — and the challenges they posed — with three Times journalists: Michael Cooper, our Politics editor, who oversaw 2026 campaign coverage; Jonathan Weisman, an editor on our National desk; and Emily Cochrane, a Nashville-based reporter who covers the American South.

In the run-up to Election Day, the Mississippi race didn’t get as much constant news coverage by the national media as marquee battleground races. Take us inside your decisions about when and how much attention to give the race.

JONATHAN WEISMAN: Some of our stories were not solely about the race, but they put the major conversations in Mississippi in a larger, national context. Emily, in mid-September, did a story on Black voters and politicians energized by the efforts in the South to dismantle majority-Black districts, and the story highlighted the Mississippi race. On Nov. 1, our politics writer based in Miami, Pati Mazzei, came back with a story on Democrats trying to prove they can still win in the South. Again, the Mississippi race was a part of it. And that story came after Emily trekked to Mississippi for a story just on the Senate race, which ran on Oct. 27.

EMILY COCHRANE: The day of the election, I was pretty restless, going back and forth on whether I had done enough to prepare readers for an outcome that none of us could know. There are definitely some races and ideas that I wish I had gotten to in the region — but there are only so many working hours in the day, and I do feel like we covered Southern Black voters and redistricting thoroughly.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/techn.title: Nvidia Scandal Puts Lori Huang, Jensen Huang’s Wife, In the Spotlight
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/techn.author: Erin Griffith and Don Clark
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Lori Huang, who has been married to the Nvidia chief executive for more than 40 years, stands out among tech titan spouses for how private she has been.

By Erin Griffith and Don Clark

Reporting from San Francisco

In November 2021, Jensen Huang attended the annual dinner held by the Semiconductor Industry Association in San Jose, Calif. That night, the trade group gave Mr. Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, its highest honor, named for the Intel co-founder Robert Noyce.

Mr. Huang arrived early with his wife, Lori Huang, and quickly headed to the bar at the pre-dinner reception, saying the event was the first time he had been out of his house since the Covid lockdown began in March 2020. He introduced Ms. Huang to reporters who clustered nearby, but they mainly talked to him.

By the time Mr. Huang received the award, two hours had passed. The Nvidia leader walked onstage with a bottle of red wine and two glasses, sharing them with a moderator and taking the conversation into unexpected topics. Throughout, Ms. Huang remained in the background.

For more than 40 years, Ms. Huang has been by Mr. Huang’s side as he built his fledgling chip start-up into one of the most valuable companies in the world. Nvidia’s success turned Mr. Huang into an international business star. His face is on sweaters, his signature leather jackets have become collectors items, and his net worth has soared to nearly $150 billion.

By contrast, Ms. Huang stayed far from the spotlight.

That changed this week, when Mr. Huang, 63, revealed he had an affair with an executive identified by the U.S. government as a Chinese spy. In his admission, which he shared in a message to Nvidia employees, Mr. Huang apologized to his wife, as well as his two children, who both work at Nvidia, thrusting them into the limelight.

The bombshell news had implications for U.S. national security and the economy. Nvidia’s role as the A.I. industry’s main supplier of chips makes Mr. Huang a crucial linchpin for an industry that has come to dominate the stock market.

Erin Griffith covers tech companies, start-ups and the culture of Silicon Valley from San Francisco.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/techn.title: Silicon Valley Tech Allies Support Jensen Huang
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/techn.author: Emmy Martin
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley figures cast the Nvidia chief’s relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy as a personal lapse, not a security failure.

Reporting from San Francisco

Within hours of Jensen Huang’s admission on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife, some of Silicon Valley’s most influential investors closed ranks around him.

Their messages, delivered mostly on social media, were consistent. Mr. Huang’s relationship with a woman identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese spy was a personal failing. Losing the Nvidia chief executive, they argued, would be a far bigger blow to the country, and America couldn’t win the artificial intelligence race without him.

“Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote in a post on Sunday afternoon. He said that Mr. Huang “did something incredibly dumb,” and that it was bad for America, “but my guess is there was no bad intention.” He concluded that Mr. Huang is “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”

About an hour later, Elon Musk quoted the post and added: “I agree.”

The show of loyalty reflects Mr. Huang’s rarefied standing in Silicon Valley. In the three decades since he co-founded Nvidia, he has gone from running a maker of video game graphics cards to presiding over the company at the center of the A.I. boom, now one of the world’s most valuable companies.

Nvidia’s chips are the scarce resource every A.I. company needs, a position that makes Mr. Huang something of a kingmaker. Decisions about who gets his products, and how many, can shape which start-ups and tech giants pull ahead. Nvidia’s finances are also deeply intertwined with other leading A.I. companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.

(China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: Aruni Soni, Eshe Nelson and Jason Karaian
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

News that the chipmaker’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned drove Nvidia’s stock down, though the broader market rose slightly.

Notes: Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

By Aruni SoniEshe Nelson and Jason Karaian

Nvidia’s shares sank Thursday, sending tremors through global markets, as the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, stepped down from his role.

Shares in Nvidia dropped more than 4 percent by the time markets closed for trading on Thursday, wiping out nearly $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone. The stock fell by as much as 14 percent Thursday morning but pared most of those losses as investors’ fears about the company’s future without Mr. Huang eased.

Nvidia has emerged as central to the A.I. economy because its chips — or graphic processing units — help train and power models across the industry. It has also become a central bank of sorts for several A.I. companies, because its finances are deeply intertwined with those of everyone from frontier A.I. labs to neoclouds, which rent out computing power.

“This is an Nvidia problem before it is an A.I. problem,” said Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial. But he added that Nvidia’s woes could trickle through to other companies.

“Where I would be careful is with the smaller A.I. cloud companies that leaned on Nvidia’s checkbook,” he said. “If the new regime gets more conservative about financing its own customers, that is where it shows up first.”

The company’s board named Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive.

Connections: Soccer Edition

Big technology companies saw the tide turn against their giant A.I. projects, but they have the means to weather delays.

Credit...
Edmon de Haro

Karen Weise has visited data centers in four states over the past several years.

Many of the largest technology companies weren’t prepared for the opposition to data centers that has swept the country over the last year. To placate critics, the companies walked back secrecy arrangements, offered greater benefits to local communities and said they would pay more for electricity.

It didn’t matter. Even elected officials who had once welcomed the giant data centers, which tech companies are building for their artificial intelligence work, were turning against them. The election swung harder against data centers than polls predicted. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development.

Still there are early signs that the Blue Wave that brought Democrats to power around the country will not send data center construction — and with it the U.S. economy — off a cliff.

One analysis, from the investment bank Bernstein, estimated that in the most extreme scenario, 9 percent of projects that would have probably been built will no longer break ground. More realistically, they said, only 2 to 4 percent of future data centers will be canceled nationwide.

Another analysis, from Susquehanna Financial Group, predicted that even if some projects die, more data centers for training A.I. will still be built in 2027 and 2028 than this year.

“We are not going to see a dramatic downturn,” said Austin Keyser, a top regional official at the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers who advised Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic governor-elect. She campaigned on establishing moratoriums on data center projects that don’t meet certain criteria, such as hiring union workers and building on former industrial sites, not farmland.

Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The chief executive has been under scrutiny for an affair with a woman said to be a Chinese spy, as well as for a relationship with a subordinate at his A.I. chip company. Nvidia’s finance chief, Colette Kress, was named interim leader.

By Tripp Mickle and Maggie Haberman

Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, resigned on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with an executive who reported to him as well as with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese spy.

The chip company’s 10-member board met for several hours Wednesday evening and agreed to name Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as interim chief executive, until a permanent successor has been named. The board said on Thursday that it would begin a search for a permanent replacement and would consider internal and external candidates.

Nvidia also appointed Harvey Jones, a longtime tech entrepreneur and investor, as the chip company’s chairman. In a statement, Mr. Jones said that the board was confident in Ms. Kress and the executive team and that it expected “the company’s operations, customer commitments and product road map to continue without interruption.”

Mr. Huang’s exit opens an uncertain chapter for Nvidia, the premier maker of artificial intelligence chips, and will have widespread ripple effects. The Silicon Valley firm is a linchpin of the A.I. boom and one of the world’s most valuable public companies, controlling an estimated 90 percent of the market for the computer chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy.

That dominance has made Mr. Huang one of the world’s wealthiest people, as well as an ally of President Trump’s. Mr. Trump was previously informed about Mr. Huang’s relationship with the woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset but took no action. He has defended Mr. Huang over the past week, saying he was an “honorable man” who did not know the woman was a Chinese agent.

Few Silicon Valley executives — with the possible exception of Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, and Steve Jobs of Apple — have been as synonymous with their companies as Mr. Huang, 63. He was a founder of Nvidia in 1993. He manages all aspects of its business as chief executive, and his family members have steadily risen through the company’s ranks. With a 3.56 percent stake, he is also Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder. He has had such a tight grip on the company that there is no clear successor.

Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, is already facing scrutiny over an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy.

By Ryan MacTripp Mickle and Georgia Gee

Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company.

The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Many corporations have policies against managers having relationships with subordinates.

Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video.

Both Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people.

Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has turned it into the premier supplier of artificial intelligence chips, has been under intensifying scrutiny. Last month, The Times reported that a Chinese executive he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese intelligence asset.

This month, after Mr. Huang acknowledged the affair, Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into the matter that is being led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The Republican leaders of three influential House committees have also asked Mr. Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with the woman, who goes by the name Alice Huang.

China has denied the espionage claims. Ms. Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.author: Noam Scheiber
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.text:
The company had argued that the case, involving eight former workers, must be resolved before an arbitrator.

A federal appeals court ruled Tuesday that a sexual harassment lawsuit brought by eight former employees of the rocket company SpaceX can proceed in court.

The company had attempted to shift the case to a private arbitration process, arguing that the plaintiffs had signed agreements requiring that move. But the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit concluded that the case could proceed under a federal law that allows plaintiffs in sexual harassment cases to sue in court even if they’ve signed arbitration agreements.

Tom Moline, one of the former workers, said in a statement, “The Ninth Circuit correctly recognized SpaceX’s claims for what they are: an attempt to hide and distract from the toxic culture of sexual harassment and retaliation that persists to this day.”

Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week about why the administration had not put restrictions on advanced chip sales to Megaspeed.

By Ana Swanson and Tripp Mickle

Ana Swanson reported from Washington and Tripp Mickle from San Francisco

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week over his handling of a Singaporean company at the heart of revelations about Chinese spying on Nvidia, demanding to know why the United States had not already banned sales of advanced A.I. chips to the firm.

The exchange, which took place at the White House on Thursday and was described by people briefed on it, highlighted growing tensions inside the Trump administration over A.I. policy in general and the Commerce Department’s posture toward Nvidia in particular.

The internal debate has only intensified after Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, acknowledged he had an affair with a woman who had helped lead the Singaporean data center company, Megaspeed. The woman, Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, has been identified by U.S. intelligence as a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported.

Mr. Lutnick responded to Mr. Bessent that the Commerce Department could now move quickly to put restrictions on Megaspeed in place, said the people briefed on the exchange, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the discussions were private.

A spokeswoman for the Commerce Department denied that the conversation between Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick had taken place. She said that the decision about whether to add companies to the entity list was an administration-wide one.

The Treasury Department did not provide a comment.

The United States has imposed restrictions since late 2022 on selling advanced chips directly to China. But Megaspeed and other companies have sidestepped those rules by setting up data centers in Southeast Asia to cater to Chinese clients. U.S. officials have also been investigating Megaspeed for potentially diverting those chips illegally into China, a charge that Megaspeed has denied.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/scien.title: These Killer Female Apes Challenge the ‘Man the Hunter’ Origin Story
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/scien.author: Taylor Mitchell Brown
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/scien.text:
Bonobos are as closely related to humans as chimps. New evidence that female bonobos are the primary hunters could radically alter our understanding of early human societies.

By Taylor Mitchell Brown

Bonobos have long had a reputation as the hippies of the ape world. Famously nonaggressive, their matriarchal societies, strong female friendships and largely vegetarian diets have stood in stark contrast to the macho bloodlust of their two closest relatives — chimpanzees and humans.

New research published in Current Biology upends a deep-seated understanding about bonobos and, as a result, could change our understanding of how early humans lived, worked and ate.

Female bonobos, it turns out, aren’t just fruit-eating pacifists, but vicious hunters.

Bonobos are as closely related to humans as chimps. New evidence that female apes are the primary hunters in their troops could radically alter the prevailing model of early human societies, in which men felled big game like bison and antelope, while women engaged in less risky tasks like gathering berries and nuts.

“It really does challenge this idea of the male warrior — that the male hunter is the ancestral model that we should be leaning on,” said Jake Brooker, a primatologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, who was not involved in the work.

Notions of an ancestral “man the hunter” have long been kicked about by anthropologists and ethnographers. The idea was largely based on studies of living hunter-gatherer societies, like the San people of southern Africa, in which men dominate hunting and fighting.

“If people go out and study a tribe in the Bornean jungle, if they go to Bushmen,” said Gottfried Hohmann, a primatologist at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior and lead author of the study, “it is usually men that are more active in hunting.”

The question is being asked across the developing world, where hunger risk is high from the extreme weather El Niño is expected to bring. Malawi has a big plan, but little money.

El Niño-driven drought is threatening farmers in Malawi and far beyond.
Credit...

By Chico Harlan and Golden Matonga

Photographs by Joao Silva

Chico Harlan, Golden Matonga and Joao Silva spent four days in Namasoko, a village seven hours outside Malawi’s capital, Lilongwe.

Hundreds of farmers were gathered under the village’s biggest wild mango tree, summoned by the chief, when the government workers arrived with a dire warning. Drought was soon likely to hit. The farmers had better prepare.

The cause, they said, is this year’s extraordinarily powerful El Niño, a global weather phenomenon born in the Pacific Ocean, half a world away from their village of Namasoko, Malawi, in southern Africa.

If the farmers bought special drought-resistant seeds, they might be able to avoid hunger and financial despair. But a single bag costs $43. And most farmers make less than $3 per day.

“What are we to do?” asked Patrick Hareke, 46, one of the farmers.

It’s a question being asked across the developing world.

Preparing for El Niño is daunting even in good times. The natural phenomenon scrambles global weather in ways that are both predictable and economically devastating. It typically causes droughts in Latin America and southern Africa that hit one group above all: poor farmers who are at the mercy of the skies.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/scien.title: The Russian Scientist Behind the Deadly Novichok Nerve Agents Has Died
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/scien.author: Clay Risen
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/scien.text:
Vladimir Uglev, a lead developer of a Cold War-era chemical weapon used on the dissident Alexei Navalny, later turned against the government. He was 80.

Vladimir Uglev, a Russian chemist who during the Cold War developed a class of highly deadly nerve agents called Novichok, then turned against the Russian government when it was used against dissidents including Alexei A. Navalny, died on Oct. 25 in Anapa, Russia. He was 80.

His son Alexandr confirmed the death, in a hospital, from complications of a heart attack.

Mr. Uglev began working on Novichok during the 1970s, when he and other military chemists were stationed at a secret location deep inside the country. They designed Novichok (the name means “newcomer” in Russian) to be 10 times deadlier than existing weapons like VX and sarin.

It takes just a trace amount to cause a target’s nervous system to go haywire by inhibiting an enzyme that governs muscle control. Involuntary contraction of the skeletal muscles, in particular, quickly results in heart failure or asphyxiation.

The Soviet Union never used Novichok in combat, and it was believed that all stocks of the weapon had been destroyed in the 1990s.

But in March 2018, a former Russian military intelligence officer named Sergei Skripal and his daughter, Yulia, collapsed on a park bench in Salisbury, Britain, from what doctors concluded was contact with a Novichok variant called A-234.

Mr. Skripal had spied for Britain in the 1990s and 2000s and was convicted of treason in 2006. Four years later, he was allowed to move to Britain with his daughter through a prisoner swap.

Chastain will portray an actress with dementia whose most vivid memories are of rehearsing for the title role in “King Lear.”

Jessica Chastain was last on Broadway in one of the great classics of the theatrical canon, “A Doll’s House.”

She garnered strong reviews and a Tony nomination for that outing, and now she is embracing a higher level of risk, using her star power to bring to Broadway a drama by an Irish playwright and filmmaker whose work is not well known in the United States.

In “Lost Lear,” a play by Dan Colley, Chastain will star as an actress with dementia whose clearest memories are of rehearsing for a production of “King Lear,” and whose caretakers lean into “Lear” to give her comfort. The play, which premiered in 2022, was inspired by Colley’s observations about his own grandmother’s memory loss, and his research into ideas about care for people with dementia.

“As my grandmother changed — as the disease progressed — it made me wonder about the ways in which we’re all living in different realities,” Colley said in an interview.

The production is scheduled to begin performances on March 29, with an opening on April 23 for a 16-week run at the Booth Theater, where the play “Downstate” is currently running.

Colley, 39, was home in Dublin this summer when he got a call: Chastain was in Ireland, wrapping up work on the horror film “Other Mommy.” Could he get to the house where she was staying that same day to talk with her?

Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, joined Nvidia in 2013.

By Adam Satariano and Kalley Huang

Nvidia said on Thursday that Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, would be the company’s interim chief executive officer, following the resignation of its longtime leader, Jensen Huang, who admitted to an extramarital affair with a businesswoman U.S. intelligence agencies believe to be a spy for China.

“The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team,” said Harvey C. Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia’s board of directors in a statement. “We expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

In a note to Nvidia’s employees, Ms. Kress said she believed “deeply in this company” and called its employees “our greatest strength.” She said Nvidia would have a companywide meeting on Nov. 18 to discuss its future.

She will remain Nvidia’s chief financial officer while serving as its interim chief executive officer until the board names a permanent successor. The board said on Thursday that it had started a search for that replacement and would consider internal and external candidates. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, is leading the company as it enters an uncertain next chapter. Under the leadership of Mr. Huang, Nvidia grew from a niche maker of computer chips used for video games to one of the most valuable public companies in the world and the linchpin of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy.

Ms. Kress, 59, faces a challenging road. She is temporarily taking over a company that has been tightly controlled by her predecessor. Mr. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and had managed all aspects of its business with a flat structure that placed him at the center of its day-to-day operations.
