https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/12/.text:
The longtime head of the chip-making colossus admitted to an affair with a woman identified as a spy for China. He was also said to have had a relationship with an executive who reported to him.

Tripp Mickle and Maggie Haberman

Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the Silicon Valley chip giant Nvidia, resigned on Thursday, according to the company’s board of directors, capping a swift, stunning fall for one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom.

The company’s board of directors met for several hours on Wednesday to weigh Mr. Huang’s fate after revelations that he had extramarital affairs with an executive who reports to him and with a woman whom U.S. intelligence agencies concluded was spying for China.

The company’s 10-member board said in a statement that Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, would serve as interim chief executive until a permanent successor to Mr. Huang is named. The board said on Thursday that it would begin a search for a permanent replacement and would consider internal and external candidates.

Mr. Huang’s exit opens an uncertain chapter for Nvidia, the premier maker of artificial intelligence chips, and will have widespread ripple effects. Over three decades, Mr. Huang, 63, built Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable public companies, controlling an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of the A.I. projects driving the U.S. economy — and are at the center of the U.S.-China tussle for dominance in A.I.

A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who goes by Alice Huang, who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang, and that President Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

Though Nvidia had said that it had “no reason to believe” that Mr. Huang had compromised national security or company secrets, its board, with a track record of deference to its celebrity C.E.O., opened an investigation. The company’s share price plunged in after-hours trading on Wednesday as the board met to consider Mr. Huang’s future, and continued to slide on Thursday.

China has rejected the espionage claims. U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped smuggle restricted chips into China. China’s embassy has called the allegations “smears.”

Here’s what else to know:

A second affair: Mr. Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Read more ›

C.E.O.’s influence: Among global tech executives, few have had as much sway as Mr. Huang over Mr. Trump’s approach to A.I. and China. He persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China, and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Mr. Trump’s White House ballroom project.

Trump’s response: Mr. Trump has defended Mr. Huang over the past week, calling him an “honorable man” and saying that Mr. Huang had told him he was not aware that Ms. Huang was an intelligence operative for Beijing. The president is scheduled to travel to China next week, and he said on Monday that he did not plan to bring the Nvidia matter up in talks with China’s leader, Xi Jinping.

Nvidia recognized Huang in a statement, saying, “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”

The company’s press release announcing his departure did not include a statement from Huang.

It’s unclear what the next steps are for Jensen Huang, who is 63. He worked at Nvidia for more than three decades after co-founding the company at age 30. Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, suggested on social media last night that it would be “an honor” to hire Mr. Huang, though he did not say for what position.

Lazaro Gamio and Amy Schoenfeld Walker/The New York Times

For some perspective on how much Huang’s resignation could matter to the U.S. economy, Goldman Sachs estimates that spending on A.I.-related hardware and intellectual property could reach $1.4 trillion in 2027, up from $900 billion this year. That is 4 percent of the United States’ entire expected economic output. Many of those data centers are filled with Nvidia chips, or indirectly financed by the company.

The board of directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as Nvidia’s first-ever chairman. Jones has years of experience in the chip industry, having served as chief executive and executive chairman of Synopsys.

One of the immediate concerns in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation is whether it will lead to an exodus of talent from Nvidia. The company is made up of longtime loyalists to Huang. He was not only revered as a visionary; he made many of them wealthier than they ever imagined. In 2022, the company was worth $305 billion. By 2026, it was flirting with a valuation of $6 trillion.

Colette Kress, a longtime Nvidia executive, was appointed by the board of directors as the interim chief executive officer.

Nvidia veteran: Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, joined Nvidia in 2013. She has worked closely with Mr. Huang as the company transitioned from a niche maker of graphics processors used for video games to a company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. She previously worked for Cisco and Microsoft. She has an undergraduate degree in finance from the University of Arizona and a M.B.A. from Southern Methodist University. She will remain the company’s finance chief while serving as interim chief executive.

Closeness to Jensen Huang: Mr. Huang interviewed 22 candidates before hiring Ms. Kress as chief financial officer. At the time, Mr. Kress’s young sons, who were avid gamers, encouraged her to join Nvidia. During her first week on the job, Ms. Kress asked Mr. Huang how long he thought he would want her in the role. “I said, ‘For as long as we shall live and death do us part,’” Mr. Jensen said in a podcast appearance this year.

China: During her time as chief financial officer, Ms. Kress expressed concerns about the financial impact of American policies that restrict Nvidia sales to China. In 2023, she said on a call with financial analysts that China accounted for 20 to 25 percent of the company’s data center revenue. In addition to lost sales, she has said the policies risk strengthening Nvidia’s competitors in China.

Liaison to Wall Street: As chief financial officer, one of Ms. Kress’s main responsibilities was communicating with Wall Street and Nvidia’s investors. On quarterly earnings calls, Ms. Kress delivered a rosy message as Nvidia’s revenue and stock price soared. In 2013, Nvidia’s sales were $4.28 billion. In the most recent fiscal year, its annual sales reached $215.9 billion.

Personal Wealth: Ms. Kress has benefited from Nvidia’s skyrocketing stock price. She owned roughly 4.44 million shares, according to Nvidia’s most recent annual report, worth about $772 million.

Nvidia’s stock has plunged following the news of Huang’s departure. Shares have fallen more than 11 percent in premarket trading, wiping out over $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month.

Jensen Huang led Nvidia with an executive team of more than 60 direct reports, placing him at the center of day-to-day operations at the company. That flat structure will be difficult to unwind and could complicate a transition to new leadership.

On a podcast in 2023, Huang dismissed traditional organizational charts, saying that “none of that stuff makes any sense to me.” He led Nvidia largely through meetings that focused on particular projects and included people from all levels of the company, from recent college graduates to top executives. Huang said last year that he reads several thousand emails a day from people across the company.

Jensen Huang was fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded, according to several people briefed on the discussions. But an interim plan for the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, to take over Nvidia was well underway yesterday.

Eshe Nelson and Jason Karaian

Notes: Through the close of trading on Nov. 11.

Nvidia’s shares plummeted Thursday, sending tremors through global markets, as the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, stepped down from his role.

Shares in Nvidia dropped more than 11 percent in premarket trading, extending a drop that is set to wipe roughly $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone.

The company’s board named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive.

With the change in Nvidia’s leadership, investors face uncertainty about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade and how the problems inside one of the technology industry’s most important companies could affect the broader economy.

The fallout could be seen in markets around the world, although the effects appeared limited. Major market indexes in Asia, where many of Nvidia’s partners and rivals in the artificial intelligence industry are based, mostly declined. Taiwan’s TSMC, which produces chips designed by Nvidia, fell more than 2 percent. But South Korea’s Samsung, which competes with Nvidia on some business lines, gained 1 percent.

European stock indexes, which are less heavily exposed to A.I., mostly rose on Thursday. But shares in the region’s largest tech company, ASML of the Netherlands, fell more than 2 percent.

In the United States, futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq slipped less than 1 percent in premarket trading. The stocks of Nvidia’s fellow tech giants, members of an exclusive club known as the “Magnificent Seven,” were little changed.

Shares in some of Nvidia’s U.S. rivals were set to climb: AMD rose more than 2 percent and Broadcom gained nearly 2 percent in premarket trading on Thursday. The broader S&P 500 index was set to open slightly lower.

Trading outside of official market hours is often choppy, which can exaggerate moves in stock prices.

Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has become one of the most influential forces in the A.I. boom, which has helped to drive U.S. stock markets to new highs in recent years.

Nvidia’s board deliberations came after revelations that Mr. Huang had an affair with an executive who reports to him as well as with a woman whom U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy.

Some market analysts covering Nvidia have begun to downgrade their forecasts for the company’s stock. Though the chipmaker is expected to remain a critical part of the A.I. build-out, some noted rising concerns about the company’s governance and lack of a clear succession plan. They argued that these revelations have fundamentally changed Mr. Huang’s position in the tech world and it was unclear what the implications of a change in his role at Nvidia could be.

Analysts at Bernstein downgraded Nvidia and sharply lowered their target for its share price. “Our gut tells us that we probably haven’t yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here,” they wrote. “We’ve had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines.”

Analysts at RBC Capital Markets also slashed their forecast for the stock, citing the lack of formal succession plan for the chief executive position. “Whether any individual can replicate Huang’s singular combination of technical vision, ecosystem-building acumen and ability to serve as the global face of the A.I. revolution remains an open question,” they noted.

Other analysts, including those at Wells Fargo and Mizuho, maintained their bullish views on Nvidia, but said it was increasingly likely that Mr. Huang might not be chief executive for much longer.

Nvidia’s stock is down about a third from its peak at the start of October, putting the company deep in a bear market, defined as a drop of 20 percent or more from a recent high.

Nvidia became the world’s largest public company, by market value, for the first time in 2024, exerting an outsize influence over major indexes like the Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500. Analysts still expect Nvidia to make a profit of well over $200 billion this year, with its chips in high demand as tech companies rush to build giant A.I. data centers.

During last week’s market turmoil, Nvidia fell below Apple as the world’s biggest public company.

Ryan MacTripp Mickle and Georgia Gee

Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company.

The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Many corporations have policies against managers having relationships with subordinates.

Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video.

Both Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people.

Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has turned it into the premier supplier of artificial intelligence chips, has been under intensifying scrutiny. Last month, The Times reported that a Chinese executive he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese intelligence asset.

This month, after Mr. Huang acknowledged the affair, Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into the matter that is being led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The Republican leaders of three influential House committees have also asked Mr. Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with the woman, who goes by the name Alice Huang.

China has denied the espionage claims. Ms. Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.

When reached by phone Wednesday and asked about his relationship with Ms. Powell, Mr. Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly.” He then hung up.

Nvidia declined to provide a statement. Ms. Powell did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company’s shares fell about 8 percent in after-hours trading.

Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Powell has been discussed inside the company, the five people said.

Ms. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008. She oversees programs that could apply Nvidia’s chip technology to higher education and health care, particularly medical imaging devices, according to the company’s website.

The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Ms. Powell has risen through Nvidia’s ranks. She was promoted to senior director of artificial intelligence business development in 2016, according to her LinkedIn. By late 2017, she was appointed vice president of health care. She attends technology conferences around the world, and delivers speeches on behalf of the company.

In March, Ms. Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using A.I. to aid in breakthroughs in health care and biology. Her presentation used cartoon depictions of Mr. Huang.

During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel for meetings. Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell were seen being affectionate at the hotel. One bystander captured the interaction on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said.

Mr. Huang’s security workers witnessed the bystander with the phone and sequestered the person, the people said. The workers then asked the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement.

Mr. Huang is among a long list of chief executives of American companies who have had relationships with subordinates. Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 from Intel, the chip maker, after acknowledging a “past consensual relationship” with an employee.

The following year, McDonald’s removed Steve Easterbrook as its chief executive and later sued him after learning he had violated corporate policies by maintaining sexual relationships with multiple employees.

Erin Griffith and Don Clark

Reporting from San Francisco

In November 2021, Jensen Huang attended the annual dinner held by the Semiconductor Industry Association in San Jose, Calif. That night, the trade group gave Mr. Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, its highest honor, named for the Intel co-founder Robert Noyce.

Mr. Huang arrived early with his wife, Lori Huang, and quickly headed to the bar at the pre-dinner reception, saying the event was the first time he had been out of his house since the Covid lockdown began in March 2020. He introduced Ms. Huang to reporters who clustered nearby, but they mainly talked to him.

By the time Mr. Huang received the award, two hours had passed. The Nvidia leader walked onstage with a bottle of red wine and two glasses, sharing them with a moderator and taking the conversation into unexpected topics. Throughout, Ms. Huang remained in the background.

For more than 40 years, Ms. Huang has been by Mr. Huang’s side as he built his fledgling chip start-up into one of the most valuable companies in the world. Nvidia’s success turned Mr. Huang into an international business star. His face is on sweaters, his signature leather jackets have become collectors items, and his net worth has soared to nearly $150 billion.

By contrast, Ms. Huang stayed far from the spotlight.

That changed this week, when Mr. Huang, 63, revealed he had an affair with an executive identified by the U.S. government as a Chinese spy. In his admission, which he shared in a message to Nvidia employees, Mr. Huang apologized to his wife, as well as his two children, who both work at Nvidia, thrusting them into the limelight.

The bombshell news had implications for U.S. national security and the economy. Nvidia’s role as the A.I. industry’s main supplier of chips makes Mr. Huang a crucial linchpin for an industry that has come to dominate the stock market.

It also has ramifications for his personal life. Mr. Huang’s admission has fueled speculation about the fate of his 41-year marriage with Ms. Huang, 64. She is president of the Jen-Hsun Lori Huang Foundation, which had $9 billion in assets as of 2024, including $6 billion in fresh funding that year. Of Mr. Huang’s 922 million Nvidia shares, more than half belong to a trust where Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang are the co-trustees, according to financial filings. She is also the sole controller of a trust that owns around $5 billion worth of Nvidia shares.

Ms. Huang joins a small group of tech titan spouses who have had to grapple with public infidelity. The list includes MacKenzie Scott, the ex-wife of the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Melinda French Gates, ex-wife of the Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates. The billionaire ex-wife of a tech mogul has become such a fixture in American pop culture that it has inspired characters in “The Devil Wears Prada 2” and the Maya Rudolph comedy “Loot.”

Ms. Huang’s public profile stands out among the current and former spouses of powerful business leaders because of how private she has been. She has not promoted her philanthropic work in interviews or on the conference circuit.

“Lori is unusually modest by the standards of billionaire couples,” said George Rush, who formerly coauthored Rush & Molloy, a long-running gossip column at The Daily News.

That adds further intrigue to the political and economic consequences of the affair, Mr. Rush noted. “Bezos and Gates didn’t have this dynamic, where the relationship could move markets and have this global fallout,” he said. “It is one of a kind.”

Nvidia declined to comment and Ms. Huang did not respond to a request for comment. (China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)

Similar to other tech billionaire spouses like Ms. Scott, Ms. Huang was crucial to the start of her husband’s company.

She met Mr. Huang as one of a handful of women studying engineering at Oregon State University in the early 1980s. Mr. Huang was her lab partner in an electrical engineering fundamentals class, and he convinced her to join him for a weekly study date. He later called meeting her “the most important, single event of OSU, and of my life.”

After the pair graduated and married, they moved to Silicon Valley to work as microchip designers. Both were known as gifted engineers. Ms. Huang worked at Silicon Graphics, a hardware and software maker, where her salary was higher than Mr. Huang’s at LSI Logic, a semiconductor company, he said in a 2023 profile in The New Yorker.

But the couple struggled to find the right child care, according to “The Thinking Machine,” a biography of Mr. Huang. Just before he co-founded Nvidia in 1993, Ms. Huang gave up her career to raise their children, Spencer and Madison. While Mr. Huang missed their karate tournaments to build his company, Ms. Huang never complained, he recalled in May on the podcast How I Built This With Guy Raz. “That’s the gift that she gave me.”

Mr. Huang has frequently shared a warm reverence for Ms. Huang in interviews. “It’s good to have someone in your life who unconditionally believes in you, who believes you’re doing your best,” he said in an interview with a publication run by Oregon State University in 2014. “You need people like that, and Lori’s always been that person for me — ever since I was 18, she was there believing in me and knowing I could do it. Even when I had self-doubts, she didn’t.”

When Mr. Huang’s Nvidia shares made him wealthy, the family set up an endowment that ballooned alongside their net worth. The foundation has donated to the San Francisco Opera and acquired computing power to donate to universities and nonprofits. The Huangs have sidestepped political donations.

Through it all, Ms. Huang was a frequent presence at Mr. Huang’s public events, including state dinners, conference appearances and celebrations of the couple’s donations to Stanford University and Oregon State University. She generally stayed in the background while he gave speeches and hobnobbed with industry executives and reporters.

“She’s been to every conference, every speech, you know, and every moment of Nvidia, she was there,” he said in an interview this year with CNA, an Asian news network. “Lori’s been with me for a long time, our whole life.”

She even helped shape his public image. Along with her daughter Madison, she dressed Mr. Huang in a designer leather jacket that has become his trademark look. Madison joined Nvidia in 2020 and Spencer joined the company in 2022. Madison’s husband, Nico Caprez, also works there.

Mr. Huang ended his message to Nvidia employees about the affair with a request: “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.”

Georgia Gee contributed research.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: Paul Mozur
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

In a statement, Singapore said it held Alice Huang’s passport months after President Trump was briefed that she was a spy.

Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.

Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore.

The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.title: Wall Street Sees the Writing on the Wall for Jensen Huang
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: Andrew Ross Sorkin, Bernhard Warner, Sarah Kessler, Michael J. de la Merced, Niko Gallogly, Brian O’Keefe, Sri Muppidi and Ian Mount
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
The company’s board is weighing the fate of its chief executive. Silicon Valley and Washington are steeling themselves for life without him.

By Andrew Ross SorkinBernhard WarnerSarah KesslerMichael J. de la MercedNiko GalloglyBrian O’KeefeSri Muppidi and Ian Mount

Andrew here. Put yourself in the shoes of Nvidia’s board: Would you fire Jensen Huang?

An affair with a customer who U.S. intelligence officials determined was a spy for China, as well as what The Times reported was a relationship with an employee, would typically be grounds for removal. At best, these scandals are a distraction. At worst, they make managing the nearly $4 trillion chipmaker virtually impossible, especially if credible evidence emerges that Huang knew about Nvidia chips improperly going to China.

Yet does his centrality to the company and the A.I. industry mean overlooking those issues? Elon Musk wrote that he would be honored to hire Huang. Palmer Luckey of Anduril declared, “China wants Jensen out, so I want him in.” The venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote, “We should demand loyalty and accountability, but sainthood cannot be the price of admission to leadership.”

Does the Nvidia board have any middle ground? Could Huang step down to become chief technology officer — or is that just window dressing? We should know the answer soon. More below.

A month ago, Jensen Huang was firmly ensconced atop Nvidia. Now Silicon Valley — and Wall Street and Washington — are starting to imagine life without him running the giant chipmaker.

If Nvidia’s board removes Huang as C.E.O., it would be a sea change at the central cog of the artificial intelligence boom, with wide-ranging consequences, Sri Muppidi and Michael de la Merced report.

Nvidia’s board has met to discuss Huang’s future, after The Times reported that he had an affair with a direct report, Kimberly Powell, as well as with Alice Huang, an executive who U.S. intelligence officials determined is a spy for China. (The Wall Street Journal suggests that his ouster is on the table.)

Alice Huang is now living in Beijing, with the knowledge of Chinese security officials, Bloomberg reports, citing unnamed sources.

What Nvidia without Huang as C.E.O. might look like: Remember that the company has no clear succession plan. Analysts have speculated that Colette Kress, its C.F.O. and perhaps its next most prominent executive, could become interim C.E.O. (Nvidia has hired an outside firm to consider possible replacements for Huang, according to Bloomberg, which cited unnamed sources.)

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/trave.title: Help! A Broken Toilet Grounded My Plane, and the Airline Won’t Cover a Hotel.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/trave.author: Seth Kugel
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/trave.text:
Turkish Airlines tried to wiggle out of paying for a passenger’s $512 overnight stay after a stomach-churning malfunction forced it to cancel a flight in Denver.

On May 30, my wife and I were scheduled to take Turkish Airlines’ evening flight from Denver to Istanbul. The flight was delayed several hours because of what we were told was a mechanical problem. We boarded the aircraft at around 11:30 p.m., taxied to the runway and then returned to the gate. The flight was finally canceled at around 1 a.m. Gate agents advised us that no hotel vouchers were available and that we should find hotels and submit our receipts to the airline. We stayed at the airport Westin, paying $512, including taxes and breakfast, and flew out the next day. We heard — and later read in The Denver Post — that the cancellation had been caused by an overflowing lavatory. But the airline sent us a message attributing the disruption to “force majeure,” which to me means an earthquake or a war or something similar. I called the airline and was told to submit my hotel receipts online, which I did twice, but got no response. Turkish Airlines’ customer service plan says the carrier pays for hotels only if the reason for the cancellation was under its control. Is Turkish evading responsibility with this “force majeure” argument? Can you help? Neal, Broomfield, Colo.

How an airline describes the cause of a cancellation can directly affect whether it will cover passengers’ lodging, transportation and meals. For mechanical issues, the answer is often yes; for weather or air-traffic issues, it’s almost always no.

U.S. regulations define those categories, but they do not require airlines to pay for stranded passengers’ expenses. Nevertheless, all the major U.S. carriers except Frontier explicitly promise hotel stays in their customer service plans if the reason for the disruption is under their control. The Turkish Airlines policy for U.S. flights is a bit looser — but the airline usually offers lodging for controllable disruptions.

For the last couple of years, I’ve kept a file of emails from travelers who suspected, as you do, that a carrier had weaseled its way out of covering passengers’ expenses by misrepresenting what happened.

I had avoided the ever-expanding file because I knew that proving the precise cause of any one incident was most likely a fool’s errand. Disruptions can have multiple causes, and the U.S. Department of Transportation gives the airlines flexibility in determining the main one. For example, if a mechanical problem causes a delay, then a storm moves in and shuts down the airport, airlines can blame the weather. No hotel voucher for you!

But the evidence in your case seemed pretty overwhelming. When airlines cite force majeure, they are generally referring to extraordinary circumstances beyond their control — like a natural disaster. The Denver Post article had the headline “Turkish Airlines Cancels Flight From Denver Airport After Urine and Feces Erupt From Plane’s Toilet,” which is disgusting but hardly earthquake-level terrible. Citing force majeure seemed like, at best, an entertaining error or, at worst, an attempt to avoid compensating passengers for their hotels, a promise you said gate agents made at the time.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: James Paton
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
Artificial Intelligence

Agile Robots plans to expand in the United States and increase production in Europe after raising funds in a round led by SoftBank.

Agile Robots, a German company developing industrial robots powered by artificial intelligence, has raised $500 million in new funding from investors including SoftBank and Nvidia that values the start-up at $8.5 billion.

The investment will allow Agile to expand in the United States, increase production in Germany and move into new markets — ahead of a potential future initial public offering, said Zhaopeng Chen, Agile’s founder. The company is working with partners including Google DeepMind and has raised a total of $2 billion.

Agile is among a crop of fast-growing companies combining artificial intelligence and robotics to help factories increase productivity and lower costs. Developing humanoids and other robots that can carry out more complex tasks in the physical world is critical in Europe, which is trying to narrow an A.I. gap with the United States and China and revive its struggling industries.

“Physical A.I. is one of the solutions for Europe,” said Mr. Chen, who started the company in Germany in 2018 after studying engineering in China and completing his doctorate at the German Aerospace Center.

Agile’s valuation puts the start-up on par with European companies including Quantum Systems, the German defense technology company valued at $8 billion in July, and Wayve, the British autonomous driving company valued at $8.6 billion in February. Neura Robotics, a German company that has raised funds from companies including Nvidia, Amazon and the cryptocurrency company Tether, was valued at about $7 billion after raising as much as $1.4 billion.

News of the board’s deliberations about Jensen Huang’s job drove Nvidia’s stock down more than 8 percent in after-hours trading.

Notes: Through the close of trading on Nov. 11.

By Michael Corkery and Jason Karaian

Nvidia’s share price plummeted in after-hours trading on Wednesday, as the company’s board considered the future of the chief executive, Jensen Huang, a decision that could reverberate across global markets.

News of the board’s deliberations drove Nvidia’s stock down more than 8 percent late Wednesday, a move that would erase hundreds of billions of dollars in market value if the drop persisted into the official open of trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday. Trading after the market is closed can be thin, which can exaggerate moves in individual stock prices.

Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has become one of the most influential forces in the artificial intelligence boom, which has helped to drive the stock market to repeated new highs in recent years.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.author: Ishani Desai
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/busin.text:
Artificial Intelligence

The carrier said that to protect customers’ information and comply with regulations, it was barring the digital assistants from logging into accounts and managing reservations.

United Airlines is banning artificial intelligence agents acting as personal assistants from access to user accounts and from booking its flights, citing privacy concerns and other potential disruptions or violations if humans are not involved, the company announced on Wednesday.

The decision came as Silicon Valley giants engaged in a heated race to have users adopt their digital assistants.

The top companies with A.I. models — Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic — have recently released A.I. agents that users can deploy as assistants, moving away from just answering prompts to completing specific tasks on their behalf. The A.I. agents can manage everyday matters such as booking restaurant reservations and shopping.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/weath.title: A Concerned Californian’s Guide to El Niño
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/weath.author: Amy Graff
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/weath.text:
The weather pattern is a familiar companion to the state’s residents. But it doesn’t always behave how they think it will.

Amy Graff is a reporter on The Times’s weather team. She is based in San Francisco.

A very strong El Niño flexed its muscles in 1982-83, and relentless storms pummeled the California coast. Houses fell into the ocean, piers were smashed in two, and beaches vanished when powerful waves dragged their sand out to sea.

El Niño was not a household name then, but it soon became one for Californians, whose Pacific coastline is often the first area affected when the weather pattern’s effects come ashore. In the winter of 1997-98, another strong El Niño brought unmerciful storms, leaving at least 17 people dead and causing over $550 million in damage across the state.

The winters were disastrous and lived on in popular memory. Now scientists say this winter is almost certain to deliver the strongest El Niño on record, once again drawing dire predictions for how this winter will, or could, play out across the state.

But the story doesn’t always unfold as expected.

The winter of 2015-16 also brought a very strong El Niño. Like this year’s, it was, to that date, one of the strongest on record. As winter — typically the time of year when El Niño’s effects on the weather are strongest — approached, it prompted anxiety among residents and intense media coverage.

The state was living through one of its worst droughts in recorded history, and many looked to the rains that El Niño typically brings for relief. But while the winter brought active surf that eroded California’s beaches, it fell short on rain as many storms that would have crossed over into California got ushered into the Pacific Northwest instead. The state ultimately recorded much less rain than forecasters had predicted.

So what about this year? Here’s how experts think the next few months could play out.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/insid.title: Recalling the S.S. United States as It Becomes a Florida Reef
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/insid.author: Jesse Pesta
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/insid.text:
A New York Times editor has had a lifelong connection to the S.S. United States, which is becoming an artificial reef off the Florida coast.

Jesse Pesta edits investigative and narrative articles about climate change, and has a side hustle writing about the S.S. United States.

Isn’t that a cute kid? I’m inclined to think so, because the kid is me. I’m 2 years old in the photo, sailing the high seas aboard the fastest ocean liner ever built.

That family trip, nearly 60 years ago, helps explain why I find myself writing about the very last journey of that ship, the S.S. United States. On Wednesday, it was intentionally sent to the bottom of the ocean near Destin, Fla., to become an artificial reef and diving destination.

I’m in Destin and watched the ship’s final moments.

For the past two decades or so, I’ve written off and on about the ship and the efforts to save it. I got interested for a simple reason: that family trip.

I don’t remember a thing about it, of course. I was 2.

But through my childhood, it made for great family lore. Mom and Dad would reminisce about the time we moved across the Atlantic with our entire lives stuffed into a single steamer trunk.

My dad had gotten a scholarship in London and the price of tickets was covered, either by air or by sea. The choice was easy, my mom, Maureen O’Hara Pesta, told me this week. “We wanted to ride the big ship,” she said. It sounded like an adventure.

The S.S. United States, fast and luxurious, carried passengers back and forth between New York and Europe for most of the 1950s and ’60s. My parents made the right decision in 1968 to go by sea — barely a year later, the liner went out of service, never to sail again.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/clima.title: The S.S. United States, a Historic Supership, Sinks to the Ocean Floor
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/clima.author: Jesse Pesta and Micah Green
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/clima.text:
The 20th-century ocean liner will become an artificial reef, ending efforts to save a ship that was fast, luxurious and (almost) indestructible.

The 20th-century ocean liner will become an artificial reef, ending efforts to save a ship that was fast, luxurious and (almost) indestructible.

Photographs and Video by Micah Green

Jesse Pesta and Micah Green were in a boat alongside the S.S. United States, off the coast of Destin, Fla. This article was reported over several years from Destin, Philadelphia and Mobile, Ala.

​In its glory days, the S.S. United States was fast, luxurious and all but indestructible. As the ocean liner’s designer, William Francis Gibbs, liked to ​say, “You can’t set her on fire, you can’t sink her, and you can’t catch her.”

​And he was right, up to a point.

On Wednesday one of the greatest ships to sail the seas made its final journey, 180 feet down to the bottom of the ocean.​ At 8:59 p.m. Central time, the ​S​.S. United States ​— a midcentury monument to postwar American technology and ambition — slipped below the waves, opening its next chapter as an artificial reef and diving destination.

​But it turned out to be tough to sink the S.S. United States. In fact, it took years of planning and preparation to reach this point. ​And some fighting. A preservationist group filed a last-minute lawsuit to try to block the effort, though a judge dismissed the suit.

​So on Wednesday, hundreds gathered ​about 22 nautical miles off the coast of Destin, Fla., ​aboard sailboats, speedboats and yachts to watch one of the most unusual intentional sinkings to ever take place. Rarely is a vessel so big sunk in this way.

Stripped of its signature red-white-and-blue smokestacks — they were removed for a planned museum nearby — the S.S. United States cut a somewhat more low and lean profile than it once did. You could say it looked more like a cigarette boat than an ocean liner, if cigarette boats were as long as three football fields.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/g-s1-1531.title: Indonesia's VP resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/g-s1-1531.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/g-s1-1531.text:
Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka leaves the parliament building after submitting his resignation letter in Jakarta, Indonesia, Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026.

JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president resigned on Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.

Raka didn't comment as he left the meeting.

"There will always be political dynamics in public office, that's normal," his father, Widodo, told reporters from his hometown in Solo, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.

"We will continue to support President Prabowo's government, especially programs that serve the interests of the broader public," he said, referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.

The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.

Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with Prabowo, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. He personally delivered his resignation letter to the president on Wednesday.

Prabowo addressed the nation Thursday afternoon after holding a meeting with Raka and the parliamentary leadership at the presidential palace.

Flanked by Raka and top leaders of parliament, a grim-looking Prabowo said that he accepted Raka's resignation "with a heavy heart" and praised the vice president for showing "courage, responsibility and statesmanship" by stepping down.

"He chose to resign for the greater interest of the nation, the state and the Indonesian people," Prabowo said in a televised statement. "He has been a great help to me, from our election campaign through the past two years of government. Many of our achievements would not have been possible without his contribution."

Prabowo praised Raka's dedication and hard work, highlighting Raka's visits to 35 provinces and 149 regencies and cities to inspect 303 government projects during the past two years as examples of his commitment to public service.

"I will continue to support him, and I pray that he and his family are given strength during what is undoubtedly a difficult time," Prabowo said.

Under the Indonesian Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy doesn't trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People's Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.

The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.

A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could have led to his impeachment.

The push for his impeachment was driven largely by long-running allegations that Raka's candidacy was enabled by a Constitutional Court ruling that critics see as a conflict of interest and evidence of weak political accountability and dynastic privilege.

Before Prabowo chose him as his running mate for the 2024 election, Raka didn't meet the age requirement of 40 for vice presidential candidates. But the court's contentious ruling in October 2023 carved an exception allowing those who served or had been elected as regional leaders to run at a younger age.

Under Indonesian election law, a presidential or vice-presidential candidate must have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education. Because Raka completed his secondary education overseas, he was required to provide documents showing that his qualifications were equivalent to an Indonesian high school diploma.

Raka was the first vice president of the country to resign before the end of a term since the fall of dictator Suharto and the start of Indonesia's democratic reforms in 1998.

Parliamentary leaders were due to convene immediately to begin the process of selecting a replacement, Speaker Ahmad Muzani said.

"We ask for the prayers and support of all Indonesians so that this democratic process can proceed smoothly and serve as a constructive new precedent in our constitutional system," Muzani told reporters.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down amid alleged spy scandal
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: John Ruwitch
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
Jensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU Technology Conference on Oct. 21, 2026.

Jensen Huang, CEO of the chipmaking juggernaut Nvidia, is stepping down.

The decision comes days after the company took the extraordinary step of launching an investigation following news reports alleging that Huang had had an extramarital affair with one of the company's clients, who U.S. intelligence officials concluded had been recruited by China's top spy agency, according to the New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

In an email to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang admitted to cheating on his wife, and said he would cooperate with the investigation.

The company's share price dropped sharply on Wednesday, after the New York Times reported that Huang had had a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to an NPR request for comment.

Huang was widely seen as one of the most important business leaders in the United States. Nvidia dominates the market for the chips used to train and run artificial intelligence. Huang also had President Trump's ear on AI policy, with Trump even calling Huang's phone in September while Huang was onstage during a conference.

The scandal that brought down Huang snowballed quickly over the past two weeks. The New York Times reported in late October that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese woman at a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia chips. Citing unidentified sources, it said U.S. intelligence officials believed she had been recruited by the Chinese government to spy on him and possibly try to influence policy. NPR has not independently confirmed this reporting.

A drip-drip of scoops followed — from the Times and other outlets — suggesting that the relationship was romantic, that senior Trump administration officials knew about the allegations some time ago, and that Huang had had a second affair.

China's foreign ministry has said the allegations of spying are baseless and part of a smear campaign against China.

Huang's departure launches Nvidia into uncharted territory.

"There's no obvious replacement," said Stephen Witt, author of a book about Nvidia called The Thinking Machine. "It's not even clear Nvidia can be the same kind of company without Jensen. I have a hard time imagining what Nvidia looks like without Jensen."

Huang was one of the longest-serving CEOs in U.S. corporate history, stepping into the role after launching the company with partners over bottomless cups of coffee at a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, Calif., 33 years ago. Nvidia got its start making specialized chips to create 3D graphics for computers that would come to be known as graphics processing units, or GPUs.

He was the face of Nvidia and an unlikely celebrity, giving countless keynote speeches and interviews in his trademark leather jacket, or posing for selfies with adoring fans.

Huang was also the company's driving force. Under his leadership, Nvidia made a big and early bet on artificial intelligence, investing heavily to transform its niche graphics chips into general-purpose processing units that were ideal for the volume of computations required to create AI.

That bet would pay off in spades as GPUs became the go-to chip for AI creators. When AI burst into the public consciousness in late 2022 with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT — a chatbot trained and run on Nvidia chips — the firm was worth about $400 billion. Today, it's valued at more than $4 trillion, among the most valuable in the world, and it dominates the market for GPUs.

But analysts say despite Huang's visionary management of the business, he had a blind spot for succession and hadn't articulated a clear plan, at least publicly.

In a Bloomberg interview from mid-October, Huang was vague about succession plans. "I'm really hoping that the next CEO of the company is already at the company, but 20 years from now, I hope I stay healthy and I hope I continue to earn my keep."

Huang's adult children, Spencer and Madison Huang, both work at Nvidia. Asked about talk that Madison might be in line to succeed him, he paused, and told Bloomberg: "if that's their aspiration, Spencer or Madison's, they have to go earn it. And it's really, really hard work. It takes a lot of sacrifice."

Daniel Newman, CEO of the Futurum Group, a tech research firm, said the company will inevitably be different without Huang, and its future success is unclear.

"They've always had Jensen as this sort of visionary at the front," he said. "I don't think that's replaceable."

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Democrat Scott Colom has won the U.S. Senate seat from Mississippi, defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just a few thousand votes. Colom will be the first Black Senator from the state in nearly 150 years. His win expands the Democratic majority in the new Congress to 55 seats. The Alaska race is still undecided.

Scott Colom speaks with attendees at an event held at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson, Miss. on Aug. 1, 2026.

The White House is warning Democrats that their planned investigations into administration officials could cross the line into "blatant criminality." White House Counsel Will Scharf said in a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee next year, that the administration is monitoring "abusive and capricious threats" from Democrats. The letter concludes by saying that "the administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process, motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize or interfere with the lawful functioning of government." Garcia said Democrats will not be deterred by threats from the Department of Justice or Trump's lawyers.

Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a significant prisoner swap after two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi. Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are now in Moscow today to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and attempt to make more headway to end the war in Ukraine.

Abdul El-Sayed has made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. The 42-year-old progressive from Michigan is already calling for a new direction for his party and urging President Trump to collaborate on actionable solutions. El-Sayed said that voters have temporarily entrusted Democrats with power, but warns that they risk losing that trust if they don't act boldly. As the senator-elect comes into the new role, he is advocating for new Democratic leadership in Congress, an end to the war in Iran, the passage of "Medicare for All" and the abolishment of ICE. While he acknowledges the challenge Senate Democrats face with a majority that's a few seats shy of being filibuster-proof, he remains open to working with his new Republican colleagues. In conversation with Morning Edition's Leila Fadel, El-Sayed reflects on the recent elections, the future of the Democratic Party and the need for impactful legislation in the upcoming years.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: How Scott Colom defied the odds to go from district attorney to Mississippi's Democratic US Senator
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: Elise Catrion Gregg
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
FROM
GULF STATES NEWSROOM

Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Cindy Hyde-Smith November 4, 2026 in Jackson, Mississippi.

JACKSON, Miss. — When Scott Colom, a local district attorney, announced his candidacy late last year, it seemed like a long shot in a ruby red state.

But by October of this year, a month before votes came pouring in for him, he was confident.

"We didn't have hundreds of million dollars to come in to spend – we did it going door to door, festival to festival, earning support," Colom said at a canvassing event on the Mississippi coast. "We're gonna shock a lot of people, but I'm not gonna be shocked. The people of Mississippi are behind this campaign: they understand Mississippi matters."

Colom narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to a race call by The Associated Press on Wednesday evening, marking one of the most stunning upsets of the midterm elections this year.

Colom won by less than five thousand votes, with a small fraction of the vote still left to be counted.

While he swept areas of Mississippi that have traditionally leaned left, like Hinds County, home to Jackson, the state capital, he also picked up places that have traditionally voted Republican, like Forrest County, which President Trump won in 2024 with about 58 percent of the vote.

Colom has been the district attorney for the state's 16th judicial district since 2016. That includes his hometown of Columbus, Mississippi, in Lowndes County – an area that's also got a right-leaning voter base.

Colom ran on accessible healthcare, saving rural hospitals and affordability. He said that working in a Republican-majority area informed the need for bipartisanship in tackling those issues.

"I believed that the majority of the Mississippians love our state more than they hate the Democratic party or love the Republican party," Colom said. "They want their kids to have good schools. ... they want to be able to make sure that young people, if they want to stay in Mississippi, can have a job. They want the hospitals to stay open."

While Colom isn't surprised that his message resonated this year with voters, he faced obstacles when a federal judicial nomination stalled in the U.S. Senate in 2023, when then-President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal judgeship.

Mississippi's Sen. Roger Wicker, a Republican, indicated he would support his nomination.

The state's Junior Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith blocked him. She cited donations from billionaire philanthropist George Soros around Colom's run for DA, which in 2023, Colom said were to an independent PAC – not his campaign.

She also said he opposed legislation to protect female athletes in a statement provided to the Mississippi Free Press at the time.

In a letter to Hyde-Smith, Colom said he didn't know what she was referring to and noted that he'd signed a statement saying he wouldn't use law enforcement resources to criminalize doctors who offer gender affirming care to transgender youth.

He also stated in the letter that if he was confirmed as a judge, any of his personal views would be irrelevant to his "daily work." And he asked the senator  to reconsider – she didn't.

Three years later, she was defending her seat from him. She was confident, on election night, that she'd beat him, telling her supporters, "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator."

She instead lost and on Wednesday night, she issued a statement conceding the race, saying she respects the decision of Mississippi voters.

Colom recognized that attention from national Democratic leaders, and his party's campaign funds, came late this year, but he noted that it was the attention his campaign received from voters within the state that made the difference.

"They understand the power of their vote in ways that we really haven't seen in a long period of time, because if you look at these margins, certainly everything that everybody did made a difference," Colom told reporters in Jackson just days before the election was called.

Being elected as a Democrat is no small feat either. The last time Mississippi sent a Democrat to the Senate was 1982 and an incumbent hasn't been defeated since 1942.

Colom now also holds the distinction of being the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction.

It's something he's proud of – but not the laurels he's resting on.

"My job is to be a senator that makes it easier for the next African American that has the work ethic, the vision, the values, and they want to be United States senator, make it easier for them," Colom said. "I am a person that is continuing to show up in the community and take the tough questions and explain my, you know, live my values. And if I do that, it makes it easier for the next person to be judged by their character and not their skin color."

While his victory is historic, his campaign has also made waves – especially on social media. In an interview with WLOX, Hyde-Smith responded to questions about beef affordability by suggesting folks pick a different protein.

Colom hit back, with a campaign ad, suggesting folks pick another senator instead.

Eventually, the rest of the country started listening. About two weeks before the election, the PAC associated with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer donated $1.2 million for advertising.

And, several big name Democrats also ended up joining Colom on the campaign trail: former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former President Bill Clinton and U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia, to name a few.

Colom traveled the whole state – from the coast to the capital, up to the Tennessee border. While in the Mississippi Delta, he said what he wants to do while in the Senate all goes back to his home of Columbus.

"I've always been committed to trying to make my community better, trying to make my city better, trying to make my state better, and that's what running for United States Senate is all about for me," Colom said. "It's a continuation of a service that runs in my family and I was raised [by] my community and my church to give back and that's why I'm doing it in this moment."

Tiara Jackson of Mississippi Public Broadcasting contributed to this report.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-602.title: A blue wave helped offset for now a falling tally of Black members in the U.S. House
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-602.author: Hansi Lo Wang
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-602.text:
Democratic Reps. Terri Sewell (left) and Shomari Figures of Alabama appear at a voting rights rally in May on the steps of the state's Capitol in Montgomery, Ala.

A U.S. Supreme Court ruling this year that further weakened the Voting Rights Act raised the possibility of a record drop in Black representation in Congress.

But a Democratic blue wave in the midterm elections helped forestall such a decline for now.

Most notably, Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democrat, won reelection despite Alabama's Republican state leaders making his district far more GOP-leaning after the court's decision.

Black representation in the U.S. House is still slated to decline next year, according to an NPR analysis. The incoming Congress is set to include 60 Black House members, including nonvoting members, down from 63 in the current House. That's just one away from the record loss of four Black representatives after the 1876 election, around the end of the Reconstruction era.

In addition to the unprecedented mid-decade redistricting fight, the usual churn of politics, including members retiring or running for higher office, contributed to next year's falling tally.

But high Black voter turnout, especially in the South, fueled Democratic wins that have offset the upcoming decline in the number of Black members of the House.

Voting rights advocates and redistricting experts warn, however, that the redrawing of district lines in the coming years, including after the 2030 census, continues to pose a threat to Black representation in Congress.

Heading into this year's midterms, Figures faced tough odds of keeping his House seat in Alabama, where voting has been racially polarized between a Republican-supporting white majority and a Democratic-supporting Black minority.

Figures joined Congress after the 2024 election as the first Black representative of the state's 2nd Congressional District. As part of a long redistricting battle, a lower federal court had ordered the district to be drawn to include a Black population large enough to have a realistic opportunity of electing their preferred candidate.

For the midterms, though, the Supreme Court's conservative majority allowed Alabama's Republican-controlled legislature to redraw the district. That ruling came weeks after the high court released its landmark decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which weakened the Voting Rights Act's protections against racial discrimination in political mapmaking.

The new lines of Alabama's 2nd District, the lower court had previously found, were "tainted by intentional race-based discrimination" and would "afford Black-preferred candidates zero chance of winning there." Based on the redrawn map, Figures appeared to be on track to leave Congress like Rep. Cleo Fields, the Louisiana Democrat who decided not to seek reelection after the Supreme Court's Callais ruling struck down the Black opportunity district Fields represents.

"It took a remarkable level of turnout in order for [Figures] to be able to win," says Cliff Albright, co-founder and executive director of Black Voters Matter. "Some are calling it a blue wave. For us, particularly here in the South, we're calling it a Black wave because what we saw was the Black electorate's been motivated by the attacks on our voting rights, by the gerrymandering that was taking place."

New voting maps in Texas and Florida led to the undoing of some Black-represented districts, but Democrats' sweeping victories in other states are helping to counteract those losses.

North Carolina's GOP-controlled legislature redrew the district of Rep. Don Davis, one of the state's three Black representatives, but Davis defended his seat. And two incoming Black House Democrats — Cyril Jefferson and LaKesha Womack — flipped districts long represented by white Republicans.

Democratic socialist Reps.-elect Melat Kiros in Colorado and Donavan McKinney in Michigan are also adding to the tally.

And Democrats are set to take control of statewide offices and legislative chambers in Texas and other places that were long-standing Republican strongholds.

By breaking the GOP trifecta in Georgia, for instance, the blue wave lowered the redistricting threat facing the state's congressional districts represented by Black Democrats. Last week, Georgia's outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp announced he will not call a special session on redistricting before handing the office in January to Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who will be the country's first Black woman elected governor.

Rep. Don Davis, a Democrat from North Carolina, speaks at a 2024 campaign event for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in Greenville, N.C.

But Albright, of Black Voters Matter, sees this year's midterms as unique.

"What happens two years from now or four years from now, where it's not the same wave year, where there's not the same economic realities across the country, where you don't necessarily get the same number of white voters that decide, 'Oh, I guess I can vote for this Democrat'?" Albright says. "It's simply not sustainable for Black voters to be carved up and have our voting power that diluted and for it to not have an impact over a more sustained period of time."

And while midterm successes are leading some Democratic politicians to declare a generational shift in U.S. politics, Kareem Crayton, a redistricting expert and vice president of the Brennan Center for Justice's Washington, D.C., office, is taking a more wait-and-see approach.

"This sounds a lot like what people said in 2009 after a lot of massive change happened, including in the South, with the election of Barack Obama. And it wasn't two years later that people sat in a haze, looking at returns that pretty much wiped out many of those changes that favored Democrats, including Black Democrats," Crayton says. "It could be that this is a start of a generational shift, but it might not be. And if you're thinking about how rules ought to be crafted, I think the cautious approach is always the preferable approach in making certain that rights under the worst conditions are protected as opposed to the most rosy scenarios."

Crayton says current redistricting rules, shaped by the Supreme Court's decisions in Callais and other cases, set up the potential dismantling of more opportunity districts for Black and other racial minority voters in future years. This past year's redistricting rush was limited partly because the Callais ruling came too late for many states to redraw their maps in time for the midterms.

"I think people who are looking at the recent Supreme Court decision around Callais and how it would be implemented always understood that the greatest reaction to that would not be in 2026, but would be 2028, 2030 and onward," says Dedrick Asante-Muhammad, president of the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies, which tracks Black representation in Congress.

And that reaction is likely to reach beyond Congress, adds Janai Nelson, president and director-counsel of the Legal Defense Fund, which represents a group of Black Louisiana voters in the Callais case.

"When we look at state legislatures, when we look at city councils, when we look at school board maps and we look at any other elected office that relies on districts, those have largely been untouched by Callais up until now," Nelson says. "But as we enter a new state legislative process where these maps may be redrawn, then we might see devastating impact in electability by Black voters across the country and especially in the South."

There's no redistricting, however, for U.S. senators. And on that side of Capitol Hill, Black representation is on the rise. The blue wave of the midterms has lifted the number of Black senators in the new Congress to a historic high of seven. They include Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton and fellow Democrat Scott Colom, who is set to become the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: Senators don't always share bill text online before votes. They should, advocates say
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: Eric McDaniel
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
Paper copies of amendment votes are set on display near the Senate Chamber, on July 1, 2025 on Capitol Hill.

If you want to know what bills are under consideration in the Senate, you could follow floor proceedings live on C-SPAN. But, even for parliamentary procedure experts, it can be difficult to understand exactly what's happening.

Among the issues? The text of what the lawmakers are considering isn't always made available for public review before it is voted on. Now, a crosspartisan group of open governance advocates has sent a letter to Senate leadership calling for change. In the letter, first obtained by NPR, they call on the Senate to post bill and amendment text online as soon as it is made available to members.

"The public and the press and the whole apparatus that supports the Senate to help understand what legislation is, they don't have access," said Daniel Schuman, an author on the letter and the executive director of the American Governance Institute, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to strengthening the institutions of American democracy.

That lack of transparency means "that problems can often sneak through," said Schuman. "At times, this has been a mechanism for the Senate to move legislation to avoid the proper public scrutiny." In 2013, Schuman recalled, Congress quietly repealed provisions of a popular congressional financial disclosure and insider trading law — skirting public scrutiny.

While the Congressional Record — the official record of legislative branch proceedings and debates — does provide information about bill text and proposed amendments, it is not published until after the legislative day concludes. That means when bills or amendments are offered on the same day they are considered, they may not be publicly available until after they are voted on.

"We've been working first to get the Senate to update their own systems internally," said Luke Hogg, a senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, which works to help policymakers become more effective stewards of innovation.

The organization joined AGI on the letter, and as Hogg explained, now that staffers themselves have reliable access to what is being considered, "it should also be given to the American public."

In contrast to the Senate, the House of Representatives publishes draft legislative text and proposed amendments online ahead of their consideration, with rare exceptions.

The letter argues that the current Senate process creates unequal access to information, where staff and interest groups with connections to Senate offices understand what's being considered, but legislative support agencies like the Congressional Research Service and the Government Accountability Office, as well as the press and public at large are often left in the dark.

"Privileged access to public business that currently is the subject of floor debate should be minimized to the extent possible," the letter says.

The advocates hope to see the Senate enact the public transparency effort in the new Congress in January.

In a statement to NPR, an aide to Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Democrat who is expected to become chairman of the Senate Rules committee, said that the senator is open to input on the transparency measure as well as other ideas to improve the functioning of Congress.

Sen. John Thune, Senate Republican leader, did not respond to a request for comment.
