https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: What’s behind Australia’s surge in teen extremism?
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Ariel Bogle
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Young people are being found with ‘hard drives full of what can only be described as gore’, one expert says

In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18.

This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The growth in youth extremism is happening within a sprawling online ecosystem. My investigations have tracked the rise of online networks that urge violence and nihilism for their own sake, in which perpetrators coerce victims not much younger than themselves to commit brutal and degrading acts.

In a review of 55 youth terrorism cases, the AFP has found that the profile is mixed. They are often young men. Many have received some support or intervention for a mental health condition. Some are from stable homes, others not.

What they have most in common is that they are young people on the internet. Experts say the age of those caught up in these crimes is decreasing.

In the last month two teenagers in Darwin have been charged with collecting documents that could facilitate acts of terrorism.

The second teenager was arrested after an initial examination of documents and electronic devices at a Northern Territory home, according to the AFP, allegedly found material and online discussions “including glorification of mass casualty attacks at schools”.

The arrests came five months after another NT teenager was charged with making posts with “pro-Nazi, anti-immigration, anti-trans and white nationalist themes”. The charge sheet alleges he also possessed videos of white nationalist terrorist attacks, including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shooting and the 2022 Buffalo shooting that it partly inspired.

All matters are still before the courts.

Experts involved in harm prevention programs, including the Victoria University professor Debra Smith, have watched the age of this cohort decrease dramatically over the past decade.

Instead of considering the challenge exclusively through the lens of radicalisation, Smith says we need to recognise that some young people are being socialised and finding identity in online spaces that may appear exciting and transgressive but are ultimately harmful to themselves, and may encourage them to do harm to others.

She has seen cases where teenagers are being found with “hard drives full of what can only be described as gore”.

“It’s like getting involved in any other … unhealthy subcultural aspect of life … [such as] gangs or crime for payment,” she says. “There’s this offering of what young people can look at and get involved in that just simply wasn’t there years ago.”

The Guardian’s investigation into the growth of extremist material charges, as well as the surge of young people in Australia ensnared in sadistic online extortion and gore networks, reveals an amorphous online ecosystem in which young people may easily come into contact with extreme and violent content.

A teenager in New South Wales who pleaded guilty to possessing violent extremist material, among other charges, described how he first came across such content on TikTok when he was 14 and sought validation by talking to others online. He used ChatGPT to research the Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev as well as security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House. He was sentenced to a three-year community corrections order.

Others have told police how they became involved in so-called “gore” channels on Telegram, where more and more extreme footage – including of animal abuse –is traded.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Given the age of many involved, Levi West, a research fellow at the Australian National University, says they may be considered as much victims as perpetrators, which is a significant challenge for how authorities respond.

It’s important for parents, schools and others to think about what’s sitting underneath the uptick in numbers, he says, and not just the “algorithms”. He points to the legacies of Covid-19 and lockdowns as well as the presence of screens and digital technologies in the lives of young people.

“We are not going to arrest our way out of this problem,” West says.

With people as young as 13 before the courts, Australia must consider if authorities are taking the right approach and have the right resources for this challenge.

The Guardian’s investigation into the possession of extremist material charges in South Australia and around the country found that many of those who had been before the courts faced a range of health and social difficulties, including autism diagnoses and learning challenges – and raised questions about whether some young people understand a crime has been committed.

Smith has seen many young people caught up in these activities who come from troubled family backgrounds, while others have had every opportunity in life.

There is a role for everyone involved in caring for young people, she says, from parents and schools to sporting clubs, to recognise when someone might be engaging in harmful behaviours long before there is a risk of violence, then help them access non-punitive pathways for help.

“It’s really important to understand it through a developmental lens – that these are young people who are making decisions with young brains,” Smith says.

“My grave concern is that if we are just giving everyone terrorism offences at [age] 12, 13, 14, 15, we’re starting to label them the thing that they will become.”

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Icac’s drama and dirt files show NSW’s ‘guns for hire’ problem. But neither major party is serious about reform
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Anne Davies
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Chris Minns is trying to address the threat of undeclared lobbying but falls well short of what the commission recommended five years ago

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

A dirt file on a state minister peddled to journalists. A subterranean campaign to discredit the building commissioner. Convincing the Liberal party to unseat councillors in the Hills district who were blocking a developer.

The New South Wales corruption watchdog’s recent inquiry, Rosny, revealed the ease with which the key protagonists – a group of rightwing Liberal operatives known as the Reformers, all of whom were former staffers – could move along the corridors of NSW parliament.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The Independent Commission against Corruption (Icac) has alleged that, unbeknown to their fellow Liberals, the operatives – including the then treasurer, Dominic Perrottet’s own brother Charles Perrottet – were being paid $2m by one of NSW’s most notorious developers, Jean Nassif, and that they worked to progress his interests.

Only one of the rightwing operatives involved in the Rosny inquiry was a registered lobbyist and subject to rules about declaring his clients and keeping records of interactions with ministers.

Yet all of them were on first name terms with many of their former colleagues and bureaucrats, affording them easy access for a chin-wag or to mix with powerful players – especially within the Liberal party’s machine.

Nassif – who told Icac he was “not corrupt” – has fled to Lebanon after the collapse of his company Toplace, leaving hundreds of buyers with substandard buildings. Charles Perrottet has repeatedly denied taking payments from Nassif for political outcomes. Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

The issue of access for former staffers – whether they be third-party lobbyists employed by specialist lobbying firms who are “guns for hire”, or “government relations” specialists employed directly by companies or industry groups – has long been a concern for Icac.

As Rosny showed, there was no way politicians could know who some of these figures were working for because these were allegedly undeclared guns for hire.

The NSW Labor government has now introduced a bill to clarify obligations for at least one class of lobbyist: the guns for hire. It passed the lower house on Wednesday, though it may not become law before the election.

Chris Minns’ efforts to address the threat that undeclared lobbying poses fall well short of what Icac recommended five years ago.

First, the good bits of the proposed legislation.

It would formally establish the NSW Electoral Commission as the regulator of third party lobbyists and bolster its investigative powers to audit compliance with the Lobbying of Government Officials Act and lobbyists code of conduct.

Icac recommended a separate lobbying commissioner but, given the electoral commission already has responsibility for the register, Minns has proposed it get the job.

“Third-party lobbyists are already subject to information and disclosure obligations, including disclosing information to the electoral commission for publication on the lobbyists register,” the special minister of state, John Graham, told Guardian Australia.

“The bill would allow the NSW Electoral Commission to audit compliance of third-party lobbyists and require relevant accounts, documents, information and explanations.”

It also extends the act to third party lobbyists interacting with councils. Lobbyists interacting with councils will need to register and adhere to the code. This had been identified by Icac as a gap that needed fixing.

But the bill also has bad bits. It ignores some of Icac’s most important recommendations.

The most glaring loophole is that the disclosure regime doesn’t extend to staff employed directly by companies – usually with a title like “government relations” or “corporate affairs” – even through they also lobby politicians.

These individuals make up about 80% of the people floating round the corridors of power. Most are former political staff members.

Graham said registering in-house lobbyists would have “created unnecessary red tape given it is already clear whose interests are being served or represented, and ministerial diary disclosures provide transparency of lobbyists’ interaction”.

This ignores the need for record keeping under the lobbyist regulations. If inhouse lobbyists were subject to the rules, they would be obliged to keep records of who they lobbied, as would the ministers and bureaucrats who were approached.

The government argues it plans to enhance ministerial diary disclosures, to make them fully searchable, rather than issuing them quarterly in pdf form.

The legislation will also clarify that third party lobbyists will need to disclose attendance at fundraising events involving exclusive or private access to a minister.

But the bill does not extend to lobbyists’ interactions with key ministerial staff, such as their chief of staff – which Operation Rosny demonstrated were important conduits to the minister.

“We’re regulating ministers and senior public servants because they’re decision makers. Ministerial staff are not decision makers,” Graham said.

Chiefs of staff can be almost as powerful as their minister, because they control access – and can direct policy staff.

Operation Rosny heard allegations about how the Liberal operatives, in their quest to smear the reputation of the building commissioner, provided material to a chief of staff, who then passed it to the chief of staff for the minister responsible for the building commissioner. The Liberal figures denied to Icac they were seeking to remove the building commissioner on behalf of Nassif.

Icac also heard evidence that Charles Perrottet talked to ministers directly about the building commissioner. He was not a registered lobbyist, yet he enjoyed extraordinary access and influence.

Neither the chiefs of staff nor the ministers were aware that Charles Perrottet was being paid by Nassif via a lobbying firm.

The government has also watered down Icac’s proposals for a six-month prohibition on certain public service roles taking on lobbying roles in either lobbying firms or private enterprise when leaving the bureaucracy.

Icac wanted certain sensitive roles to require six months’ “gardening leave” – as occurs when public servants leave the state’s gambling regulator.

If the bill ever reaches the upper house – and its future is now uncertain – debate is likely to be feisty.

The Greens have introduced a private member’s bill into parliament that would implement most of Icac’s recommendations from five years ago – including extending the lobbyists scheme to inhouse lobbyists.

Kobi Shetty, the minor party’s anti-corruption spokesperson, said her bill would have included a four-year exclusion for some public sector employees.

“When industries with deep pockets get a louder voice than the communities affected by their decisions, public trust in our democracy is eroded,” Shetty says.

The Centre for Public Integrity senior counsel Geoffrey Watson says the government’s bill is a step in the right direction and he hopes it passes the Legislative Council.

But he wishes the government had been more ambitious.

Expert warns of ‘huge loophole in political communication laws’ as state government among parties presenting accounts as unaffiliated news sources

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

“Breaking,” a reel from the Instagram account nswnewsroom reads. “Another Liberal MP quits, almost a third now gone.”

The post looks like it could have been made by a media outlet. It cites the source as the Daily Telegraph and Jordan Lane, a New South Wales MP, who is the sixth sitting Liberal member to announce they won’t re-contest their seat at the March 2027 election.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

But the account’s bio tells a different story: it was authorised by the NSW Labor state secretary.

The account, which first posted two weeks ago and says “keep up to date with with [sic] news from NSW govt” in its bio, is part of an increasingly common tactic where Australian political parties set up accounts that appear at first glance to be unaffiliated news sources. The accounts feature different names and imagery without prominent party branding, to promote specific messages or highlight their own side.

Andrew Hughes, an expert in political marketing at the Australian National University, said these types of accounts take advantage of a “huge loophole in our political communication laws in Australia when it comes to digital and social media communications”.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“More and more of us get our news and information primarily from digital and social media,” said Hughes.

“There’s more and more potential for that information to be used against voters who aren’t engaged with politics or the news to a really good level of detail to spot disinformation and misinformation,” he said.

As unpaid content, the posts are not subject to the same authorisation requirements as paid advertisements at state and federal level. In NSW, an authorisation in the account profile or a website directly linked to that post is acceptable. The nswnewsroom account added its authorisation after reporting by the Sydney Morning Herald.

A spokesperson for the NSW government referred Guardian Australia to a statement shared with the paper, which said the page was “a Labor-affiliated social media page, consistent with the practices of most major political parties and a number of minor parties across Australia”.

In Victoria a similar account, vicnewstoday, was set up ahead of this month’s Victorian state election. While the account bio contains an authorisation by Victorian Labor HQ, the posts, including videos of Ben Carroll and ministers at press conferences, do not. In one, captioned “BREAKING: Liberals did a deal with ‘the most anti-worker party’”, Carroll criticises a preference deal between the Liberals and One Nation.

In late October, the Labor party launched a page titled “Don’t Risk It Vic”, promoting posts that raise concerns about an alliance between the Liberal and One Nation parties.

Meta’s ad library reveals that page was the highest-spending political advertiser in the country last week, paying $67,138 to promote its posts between 31 October and 6 November.

A spokesperson for the Victorian Labor Party said social media was “an important way to communicate with Victorians where they are, particularly those who don’t engage with traditional media”.

“There is a lot at stake for Victoria. And everyone deserves to hear the facts about what a Liberal-One Nation government would mean for our health system, schools, police and cost-of-living.”

Monica Attard, former Media Watch host, now professor of journalism practice at the University of Technology, Sydney, said in an age where social media was “awash with deepfakes”, it was “really important for consumers – and probably equally important for political parties – to disclose clearly and always”.

“I would think that the possibility of misuse or tampering would be relatively high.”

Ahead of the 2025 federal election, Guardian Australia uncovered a string of similar social media pages set up by Labor, the Coalition, Climate 200 and campaign group Advance.

All pages carried basic authorisation messages from their creators, but the page names and profile pictures did not immediately denote the source. Labor state divisions in NSW and Western Australia set up at least two anti-Peter Dutton pages, with posts raising doubts about health spending and WA’s GST deal under a Coalition government.

The Liberal party launched a page called “Teals Revealed”, scrutinising the voting record of Climate 200-backed independents, while Climate 200, in turn, set up “Independent News”, to promote news about crossbench MPs.

William, 17, was reported missing after straying from his camp near Walhalla in Victoria’s Gippsland region

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A teenager has shared an emotional reunion with his mother after being found alive following almost a week lost in dense bushland.

Police air wing found William, 17, whose surname has not been shared, laying down in a creek near Walhalla, 130km east of Melbourne, in Victoria, on Thursday morning.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Rescue teams had been scouring bushland from the air when they spotted the 17-year-old.

He was first reported missing after straying from his camp near Walhalla last Friday.

Officers were winched down to the site after spotting the teen, before bringing him back to reunite him with his mother, Elizabeth.

A Victoria police video recorded from the air shows William being located in bushland.

Later, the moment his mother first saw her son since he went missing was also captured on video. William was sitting inside the police helicopter in shorts and workboots.

He appeared to smile before embracing his mother in a warm hug as officers looked on.

“I am over the moon. He’s alive,” she told reporters at the scene. “He is never leaving the house again. He is not going anywhere.”

William was taken to hospital for monitoring.

The teenager had been dropped off by his mother for the weekend to camp with his friend on Friday. It is believed he walked a short distance back to the drop-off location to retrieve further camping equipment.

When William failed to return shortly after, his friend searched the area but found no trace of the teen.

He was wearing only shorts and work boots when he went missing, with a mobile phone, food and water left behind.

Police said he was last seen near Stoney Creek Road, between Cowwarr and Walhalla, on 6 November at about 4pm.

On Wednesday, investigators appealed to hunters, campers and landowners to come forward with any information after a hunting camera was found in the search area.

Emergency service workers, including the dog and rescue squad, had been searching the dense bushland since last Friday.

This article was amended on 12 November 2026. An earlier version stated William had been camping with a relative. Police have since updated their advice.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Ima Caldwell
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Island state declares it ‘is not really for tourists’ – but is the marketing strategy just a cheeky piece of reverse psychology?

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Research shows “tourists hate themselves” – which is exactly why the marketing flacks at Tourism Tasmania are telling them to stay away from the island state.

Its new campaign declares Tasmania is “not really for tourists”, enlisting former SBS newsreader Lee Lin Chin to help sell the tongue-in-cheek campaign, based on the idea that Australians prefer identifying as a “traveller” rather than a “tourist”.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Its centrepiece is a short video of a man being pointed to the back of an endless queue for a “world famous” pastry. He eventually abandons the line to find solitude in the Tasmanian outdoors.

Chin, who lives mostly offline without a mobile phone, also fronts videos exploring the state’s walking trails on her visit.

Tourism Tasmania’s CEO, Sarah Kingston Clark, said the campaign was deliberately wry rather than anti-visitor, to reflect the “tensions” of modern travel.

Those tensions play out in the research, suggested Prof Can-Seng Ooi, a professor of cultural and heritage tourism at the University of Tasmania.

“Studies have shown that tourists hate themselves,” he said. “They want to avoid each other.”

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Ooi identified stressed people yearning for “quietness” as the campaign’s target audience, especially those living in urban cities on the mainland.

“It taps into the type of tourist people want to be,” Ooi said. He added that people prefer to view themselves as “travellers” because of the negative connotation of “tourist”.

Ooi spent 20 years living in Scandinavia, researching how tourism, culture and heritage contributes to the development of regional destinations.

“The message is very Scandinavian, even the imagery: the sauna, the vinyl records, the books and so on,” Ooi said. “Instead of the cold north, we are talking about the cold south … it’s a quiet place, time slows down.”

Char-lee McLennan, an associate professor from QUT’s school of management, said the campaign used “an element of reverse psychology” that could benefit regional economies by steering visitors beyond established hotspots.

Prof David Waller, a marketing expert at the University of Technology Sydney, said Tasmania’s “Come down for air” theme was less “anti-tourist” and “more anti-overcrowded, line-joining, tourist destinations”.

“Lee Lin Chin is adding humour to the message,” he said. “Lee Lin Chin is an icon – intelligent, avant garde and [she has a] dry sense of humour.”

But McLennan said the campaign’s success depends on whether the real experience of visiting Tasmania lives up to its promise as well as delivering meaningful economic benefits to regional communities.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: US envoys meet Putin as Zelenskyy says Starlink disrupted for Ukraine’s military again - Europe live
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Jakub Krupa (now) and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
Zelenskyy also repeated his earlier warning that Starshield restrictions are back on “in the temporary occupied parts of Ukraine,” and “directly affect our ability to intercept Russian jet powered drones” launched from these areas (10:08).

“We are trying to get the details from the American side, but so far we know very little. But some things are already clear. If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going.

We need to be clear and never recognise Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory in any way.”

On other battlefield issues, Zelenskyy says Ukraine needs more support on air defence, including interceptors and fighter jets.

Vladimir Putin’s comments during his meeting with the two US envoys make it clear that getting a deal with Russia will not be easy.

During his talks with Witkoff and Kushner, the Russian president doubled down on his demand to retain the Russia-occupied Ukrainian territory and opposed any foreign peacekeeping troops in the country – a key part of Europe’s planned security guarantees for Kyiv.

Instead, he continues to push for broader talks on rolling back Europe’s post-1997 Nato security architecture, a move which Zelenskyy called “strange” and urged Europe to watch closely.

Putin’s proposal for “a humanitarian mission” in Kostyantynivka is likely to be seen by Europeans as merely a token gesture designed to distract from his otherwise hardline stance.

As our Russia expert, Pjotr Sauer, said after yesterday’s discussions: “Russia appears to be seeking to revive demands it presented to Nato in 2021,” with maximalist conditions on future enlargement and deployments.

The UK government has announced new sanctions on all of Russia’s top 10 oil producers ramping up pressure on Moscow over the Ukraine war.

The British prime minister Andy Burnham said he was unveiling “a sweep of stinging new sanctions to turn the screws on Russia’s oil revenues and drive forward an end to the Kremlin’s needless war” as European leaders met in Dublin for talks focused on the conflict.

Meanwhile, Finland’s military said on Thursday that its forces had detected “a strike” on a ⁠Russian warship in the Baltic Sea a day earlier but the security situation in the area ⁠remained stable.

It was ⁠not ​immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused the strike. Estonian media reported ⁠on Thursday that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship and that it later returned to St ⁠Petersburg.

“The Finnish Defence Forces detected... a strike on a Russian warship in ​the Gulf of Finland ‌area and has ‌monitored the development of the situation,” a spokesperson for the Nordic country’s ‌military said in an emailed statement to Reuters.

Finland is not under any immediate military threat, the spokesperson added. The defence forces declined to provide further details about the location or timing of the incident, or how it was detected.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to support our crucial year-end fundraiser. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

Putin also reaffirmed Moscow’s opposition to allowing Western troops in Ukraine as part of any potential post-war peacekeeping solution – a key demand from Kyiv in any deal to end the fighting.

Moscow would see any foreign troops deployed in the country as a “legitimate target,” Putin told US envoys in Moscow, adding their deployment would mean “the continuation of war”.

Vladimir ⁠Putin has told US envoys that ⁠Russia was ⁠proposing ​a joint Russian-Ukrainian humanitarian mission to the ⁠city of Kostiantynivka in eastern Ukraine, the ⁠Interfax news agency reported.

Putin was ​cited ‌as saying ‌that the mission could ‌be modelled on a similar initiative that allowed residents to leave the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky ‌in southeastern Ukraine at the end of ​last month and for aid to be brought in for ⁠those who chose to remain.

Russia needs five days to ​clear the area ​near ‌Kostiantynivka of mines, ​Putin ​was cited as saying.

Transport correspondent

Airlines have been reluctant to speak out about bomb threats for a host of reasons, but some leading figures in aviation have expressed unease at Europe’s response in last week’s flight disruption.

József Váradi, chief executive of Wizz Air, the Hungarian budget airline, said he met officials from the European Commission recently to “urge these people to ⁠act together and find ways of getting coordinated… But this is a very ‌hot potato because of ‌the sovereign nation state concept, and no country wants to concede on this matter.” ‌

Among numerous airlines targeted last week, Wizz received hoax bomb alerts for 14 flights, diverting two aircraft after emailed threats.

He told Reuters that, assuming the hoaxes could be due to hybrid warfare, Europe “needs to think about ‌this, how to level up responsibilities against a threat like this,” adding that geographically “we are probably closest to any of these hybrid warfare exposures than any of the western airlines.”

Speaking to an airline industry conference in London on Wednesday, the UK’s aviation regulator suggested that Britain’s industry had, more or less, kept calm and carried on while others had diverted flights.

Chief executive of the UK Civil Aviation Authority Rob Bishton said the UK had given a “proportionate” response to the threats, while parts of Europe showed a “different approach and a potentially different risk appetite .. and more caution taken for whatever reasons they thought were appropriate”.

He said the industry had “well-honed protocols” and the threat analysis by government was “a well-tried and tested model.”

“What you got from the UK side was a by the book, proportionate response.”

Bishton added: “Were we expecting things like this to happen – yes, it is not a surprise. It was a successfully executed assessment and the decisions made were correct.”

In other news, it’s another day of widespread bomb alarms across Italy, with some 1,800 schools in at least 10 regions of the country targeted with fresh threats, alongside the PM’s office.

Some of the emails accounts used to sent messages were tracked back to data leaks in Taiwan and the Philippines, Italian media reported.

But in sharp contrast to previous days, the government said it had instructed local authorities ‌and school principals ​to keep classes ⁠running ​unless there were ​credible ​grounds for ​alarm. Several schools chose to evacuate pupils as a precaution, Ansa news agency reported.

A separate email, reported by Corriere della Sera, also demanded the resignation of Italy’s prime minister Giorgia Meloni, along some unsubstantiated threats against her office.

Earlier today, Meloni chaired a meeting with opposition parties to discuss the government’s approach to the latest wave of threats, which is why she missed out on the first part of the Dublin summit. On Wednesday night, she said the campaign of intimidation against Italy was intended to “instil fear,” but insisted it would fail.

Deputy prime minister Antonio Tajani told Italian parliament on Thursday that he saw the hoax alarms as “a dangerous hybrid warfare campaign,” targeting Italy for its continued support of Ukraine. “But I want to reiterate clearly: we will not be intimidated,” he said.

The Rome Prosecutor’s Office’s anti-terrorism team is leading the investigation.

In recent days, authorities in ⁠Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland said many schools had received similar ​threatening emails from abroad, but classified them ​as hoaxes and allowed classes to continue, Reuters noted.

We are also getting a line from the European Commission on Ukraine’s renewed problems with Elon Musk’s Starshield system, as reported by president Zelenskyy (11:08, 13:07).

EU tech spokesperson Thomas Regnier said:

“So it is not the first time that Ukraine is facing Starshield disruptions. These reports are deeply concerning and if confirmed, unacceptable.

SpaceX must have a consistent approach in sharing its services with Ukraine, Starshield services must be restored urgently for Ukraine to keep its soldiers connected, to protect its citizens, and to defend its territory.”

Meanwhile, president Vladimir ⁠Putin told US envoys that ⁠Russia was ⁠proposing ​a joint Russian-Ukrainian humanitarian mission to the ⁠city of Kostiantynivka in eastern Ukraine, the ⁠Interfax news agency reported.

Putin also reportedly claimed that Russia never opposed dialogue with Europe, and said he “would like Americans to work with Europe so that they can decide what they want, peace or war,” Reuters reported via Interfax.

And US envoy Witkoff said, quoted by RIA and Interfax, that he hoped to be able to announce a new round of trilateral talks “in which Europeans would take part” later today.

All we are getting at the moment is short reports via Russian media, so we may have to wait for a proper, longer readout from the meeting.

Over in Moscow, the meeting between Russia’s Putin and the two US peace envoys is now finally getting under way.

In their opening remarks, noted by Russian media, Jared Kushner told ‌Putin that Europe wanted a role in future negotiations, ‌while Steve Witkoff praised a ​major prisoner exchange agreed earlier this ⁠week during talks ​in Abu ​Dhabi, saying it was a ​sign ‌of progress, Reuters reported.

We will no doubt get more lines coming out from that meeting shortly.

European Council president António Costa is up next.

He says that “the security of all European nations, the security of our continent, is inseparable from Ukraine’s security and that our collective security is inseparable from the achievement of a just and lasting peace in Ukraine.”

“Today, as discussions about peace in Ukraine intensify, this is more important than ever,” he said.

He lists some of the principles, saying that Ukraine “like any sovereign nation around this table must be free to choose its partners, its allies, its future.”

“The time of zones of influence in Europe is long gone.”

He joins others in calling for “a European voice at the table” in any peace talks, which he says should be “a team effort between European nations, the EU and Nato.”

On broader security environment, he says:

“There is no need to reinvent the wheel. Europe had a functioning European security architecture until it was first gradually undermined and ultimately destroyed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Any future discussion on this issue must take that fact into account.”

He said the principles of sovereign equality between European nations, territorial integrity and peaceful settlement of disputes “remain as relevant today, as indispensable … as they were 50 years ago.”

Setting out his stall as a potential EU representative (11:58), he said:

“Europe’s priorities is in this process are very clear. We must first reach a ceasefire, obtain concrete, tangible progress in the Black Sea, and work on creating the conditions for a peace agreement.

The main outstanding condition for all of this to be possible is whether Russia is truly interested in peace, and unfortunately, so far, what we have seen is that Russia is focused on escalation and attacks on Ukrainian civilians.

That must change for peace to be possible, and next weeks will be a decisive test for Russian willingness to stop this war.”

His remarks conclude the public session of the meeting, with the discussions continuing behind the closed doors.

US investment firm Gordon Brothers is ‘taking due care’ to consider if one of three bidders has enough funds

Business live – latest updates

Poundland’s owner has said it is “taking due care” to consider if one of three bidders had enough funds to ensure its survival after the troubled budget retail chain secured two more weeks to find a deal.

The management of Poundland, which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors on Thursday morning.

Poundland’s board said it had sought the extra time “with a view to identifying the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and our people”.

It added: “Our stores remain open as usual during this period and we thank our colleagues, suppliers and customers for their incredible and continued support.”

The retail chain’s owner, the US investment firm Gordon Brothers, has been under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers since Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said on Thursday: “We support the board’s decision to extend the legal moratorium over the company by a further 10 working days. This brings additional stability amid an ongoing sale process in the backdrop of increasing cost pressures and a difficult inflationary economic environment.

“With this decision, we are today able to confirm to Poundland employees that funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading.

“We are in discussions with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and we have also received several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business.

“While our preference remains a sale of the whole company, we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation. We, the board, and all involved are working to secure a credible plan that delivers certainty, preserves value and protects as many jobs as possible.”

Gordon Brothers confirmed it had provided £85m of financing, understood to be via an asset-backed loan that Poundland has only partially used over the past year.

That financing is in addition to a £30m shareholder loan largely taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the business for a nominal £1 last year.

Gordon Brothers fought back after MPs on Wednesday accused the Poundland owner of extracting millions of pounds from the retailer when it was on a “knife-edge”.

Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures since acquiring Poundland.

Gordon Brothers said it had provided finance for Poundland “when no one else was willing to finance the company – and has contributed substantial efforts to support a turnaround.

“Had we not, the company would have collapsed into insolvency in August 2025. Our efforts have continuously focused on the company’s value and its people, not prioritising one over the other.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Unprecedented view of cosmos provided by Euclid mission throws up many more cases of gravitational lensing

A mission to create the largest ever 3D map of the universe has revealed more than 900m galaxies in its first major data release together with about 15,000 potential cases of a phenomenon that could help unlock the secrets of the “dark universe”.

Launched in July 2023, the European Space Agency’s Euclid mission promised to create the largest cosmic map ever made, encompassing a third of the sky and more than 10bn years of cosmic history.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The goal is to shed light on two of the biggest mysteries in the universe: the nature of dark energy and dark matter. These are thought to make up about 70% and 25% of the universe respectively.

Prof Andy Taylor, of the University of Edinburgh, who leads the UK science ground segment for the mission, said while there were bigger surveys, none had the detail and the information content of Euclid. By contrast the Hubble telescope has produced images of incredible resolution, but does not cover as large an area of the sky.

“The technological leap that’s Euclid is that we can keep that high resolution, but now we can basically map huge volumes of the sky, huge volumes of the universe,” Taylor said.

Now, the first major Euclid data release has landed, offering researchers an unprecedented view of the cosmos. “It’s the biggest high-resolution image of the universe we’ve ever had,” Taylor said.

Covering about 14% of the total area of sky that will be mapped by Euclid, the newly released data captures over 900m galaxies as well more than 60m potential quasars: blazing objects at the centre of distant galaxies, powered by supermassive black holes.

It also includes a tranche of candidates for what was previously considered a rare phenomenon: strong gravitational lensing. This is a magnification effect that occurs when one galaxy, often embedded in a galaxy cluster, sits in front of another, distant galaxy.

As Taylor notes, Einstein predicted the gravitational influence of the foreground galaxy would distort space-time, bending the light from the background galaxy and creating the appearance of bright arcs or rings. Crucially, the effect is significantly boosted by the presence of dark matter, which increases the mass and hence gravitational influence of a galaxy.

Taylor said that by studying strong gravitational lensing, scientists may be able to rule out different theories on the nature of dark matter. That is because the lensing is influenced by how this mysterious substance is distributed in a galaxy – that itself depends on its properties.

Stephen Serjeant, a professor of astronomy at the Open University, agreed. “With strong gravitational lensing, you find out how the dark matter is clumping and that’s very diagnostic of the type of matter that it is, because different types of matter can clump in very different ways,” he said.

“So if you’re looking for where the next breakthrough will be in the properties of dark matter and what dark matter actually is, there’s a good chance – I can’t say it’s certain – but there’s a good chance it might come from strong gravitational lensing.”

Taylor noted that while experts previously knew of about 1,000 cases of strong gravitational lensing, the Euclid data contains about 15,000 probable cases, with an estimated 170,000 expected to be discovered by the end of the mission.

A further release of data was expected to land next summer, Taylor added, which will include results on both the distribution of galaxies as well as weak gravitational lensing – subtle distortions in distant objects by dark matter in the foreground.

“We can use that pattern of distortions to actually make a map of where all the dark matter is in the universe,” said Taylor, adding that scientists could then work out its statistical properties and compare the results with different theories. “Depending on the type of dark matter, the type of dark energy, we’re expecting to see slightly different patterns on the sky.”

And with Euclid generating ever-more data, Taylor noted there was plenty to explore.

“It’s opening up that high resolution of the whole sky, the whole universe. So it just means there are plenty of objects that we’ll never have seen before, plenty of research phenomena,” he said. “No human eyeball is able to look at all of the Euclid data any more. It’s now too big.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: ‘Like priests who don’t believe in God’: Italy’s anti-vax medics eye return to frontline duty
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Angela Giuffrida in Rome
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Progress of bill to reinstate struck-off doctors hinged on support from far right figure Roberto Vannacci, whose rise is shaping politics before 2027 elections

A
ntonio Cremasco contracted Covid at a dinner party on 6 March 2020. Four days later, as Italy became the first European country to go into nationwide lockdown, he was fighting for his life. “I spent 20 days in intensive care, followed by another 20 days in a hospital ward,” said Cremasco, from Bassano del Grappa in the northern Italian Veneto region.

After leaving hospital, he needed oxygen therapy for another six months. Cremasco’s ordeal was such that when Covid vaccines became available in Italy in early 2021, he had no qualms about being vaccinated, and he believes the decision saved his life once again.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“All those who had been in intensive care with me died,” he said. “Without the vaccine, if I had caught Covid again, I had a high risk of dying too.”

But Cremasco, who is now 76 and recently received his annual Covid and winter flu jab, has struggled to convince his vaccine-sceptic son, a father of two, of the drugs’ safety. He said he and his wife were wary of having their potentially unvaccinated grandchildren in their home whenever the children were ill, fearing for their own health. “They always seem to be sick,” Cremasco said.

His family rift mirrors a wider divide over vaccination in Italy, which has been brought back to the political spotlight by a controversial bill approved in October in the lower house of parliament.

The measure allows healthcare workers who were struck off their professional registers during the pandemic for serious violations connected to their anti-vaccination beliefs – for example, promoting treatments that lacked a scientific basis – to apply to be reinstated.

The bill is being championed by the prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party and is strongly backed by its far-right coalition partner, the League. But with allies in Forza Italia split, its approval in the lower house hinged on support from National Future (FN), a rival far-right force led by the former army general Roberto Vannacci, whose emergence is shaping the political landscape before general elections next year. Vannacci has voiced opposition to vaccine mandates, and his rhetoric frequently targets the vaccine-sceptic audience.

The measure still needs to clear the senate, with a vote scheduled in January. But its progress has alarmed medical experts, less because of the number of healthcare workers involved – it is believed to be very small – and more because of the risk of further eroding trust in vaccines.

Nearly one in two Italian adults are hesitant about vaccination, according to a report by the department of public health and paediatric sciences at the University of Turin published in the Lancet Regional Health Europe in February. The report, which sampled 50,000 adults across Italy, found the ambivalence was driven more by misinformation and lack of institutional trust than by fears over vaccine safety.

“Political communication and the lack of trust among Italians in institutions carry a significant weight,” said Roberta Siliquini, the head of the school of hygiene and preventive medicine at the University of Turin and the report’s chief researcher. “There really is a disinformation campaign in this sense – and those who want to disinform are very good at communicating.”

The implications are being profoundly felt: this year there has been a resurgence in measles, with 472 infections reported during the first five months, compared with 322 in the same period last year, according to health ministry figures. More than half of the cases were reported in young adults. Take-up of the flu vaccine among people aged 65 and over so far this season has dipped to 49.81%, the first time it has fallen below 50% since the winter of 2014-15.

In August, a four-year-old child in Palermo, Sicily, died of diphtheria. Her parents reportedly told doctors they had not vaccinated her because her cousin was autistic and they were convinced vaccines were the reason. There is no evidence of any link between autism and vaccines.

Siquilini said the tragic case was a reminder of the responsibility that everyone, “but especially politicians”, had to deliver the correct message on vaccines. She warned that the rehabilitation of those who rejected scientific evidence could have a “devastating” impact on how people perceived vaccines.

The message has been repeatedly undermined. On 28 October, a day after the lower house vote, Claudio Borghi, a League politician, came under fire for hosting an anti-vaccine seminar in the senate.

Later in the day, in what was believed to have been an indirect rebuke, the Italian president, Sergio Mattarella used a speech during a high-profile cancer research gathering to condemn the spread of anti-vax messages while warning against “irrational beliefs” and “destructive fake news”.

Borghi has proposed revising a law introduced in 2017 by the then leftwing government that extended the number of obligatory childhood vaccinations from four to 10, adding, for example, one against pertussis, or whooping cough. He has defended his position, arguing he is not anti-vaccine but that mandatory vaccines “lead to resistance”.

As for the reinstatement of the medics struck off during the pandemic, he told the Guardian that the proposal’s aim was “to foster reconciliation after all these years”. He said: “In our view, nobody should lose their job because of a personal belief.”

Scepticism over vaccinations took root in Italy in the late 1990s, as in many other countries, mainly driven by now debunked claims of a connection between the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination and autism.

The arrival of social media accelerated the spread of vaccine misinformation, contributing to a drop in immunisation rates against preventable diseases. The 2017 move to make childhood vaccinations obligatory further emboldened anti-vaccine groups while creating fertile ground for rightwing populist parties, including the Five Star Movement (M5S), which continued to spread misinformation about vaccines after coming to power in 2018, and before the realities of the pandemic forced a shift in tone. Now in opposition, M5S is highly critical of the move to re-embrace anti-vax healthcare workers.

Lorenzo Mattia Signori, a nurse in Veneto, said politicians were “opportunists” and Meloni’s coalition was simply trying to draw votes from anti-vax voters as it eyed a second mandate.

Signori, who is also a regional secretary for Cittadinanzattiva, an association focused on patient advocacy, including pushing for campaigns to inform citizens about vaccine benefits, said: “Ensuring that people get vaccinated is the largest prevention system we have. If everyone gets sick instead, the Italian healthcare system would not hold.”

He hopes that Mattarella will use his power as president to stop the anti-vaccine medics measure from being signed into law. “We cannot have them in hospitals,” he said. “It would be like going to church and hearing a priest who says he doesn’t believe in God.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Progress of bill to reinstate struck-off doctors hinged on support from Roberto Vannacci. Scepticism over vaccinations took root in Italy in the late 1990s.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Oliver Milman, Fiona Harvey and Graham Readfearn in Antalya, and Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms

Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.

Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.

“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.

“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.

“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”

The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.

António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.

“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”

Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”

Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.

Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.

In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”

Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.

The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.

Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.

Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history, there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.

“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”

Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.

Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”

Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for windfall tax on oil and gas firms. Hilda Heine told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores.

https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.title: NAZA: how and where to watch the Guardian’s acclaimed Gaza documentary
https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.text:
Film features testimony from 24 Israeli officials involved in surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians

NAZA will be released in full on the Guardian’s website for free in early December. Sign up here to be notified of the exact streaming date and to be sent a link to the film when it is live.

NAZA has been shown by cinemas in 47 countries and seen by more than 1.5 million people since its release last month, making it one of the most-watched documentary films with a theatrical release in 2026. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet.

You can watch a trailer here.

NAZA is a documentary featuring testimony from 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians during the war in Gaza. The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.

The interviewees detail the methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential Hamas operatives, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge that the attacks would also kill their families.

Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity, because of the risks involved in speaking publicly. The appearance and voices of participants in the film have been digitally altered to disguise their identities.

The film was directed by the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian. It builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian magazine +972, the Hebrew-language news outlet Local Call and the Guardian newspaper between 2023 and 2025.

Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors – with the Palestinians Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal – of No Other Land, which documents the destruction of Masafer Yatta, a village in the occupied West Bank targeted by Israeli forces. It won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.

NAZA was co-produced by James Wilson and executive-produced by Jonathan Glazer, the team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.

NAZA has received widespread critical acclaim and is selling out in cinemas across the world. The New York Times says it is “tough to watch and impossible to ignore”, while New York Magazine describes it as “one of the most important films of our time”. In a five-star review, the Financial Times says that “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film”.

The film won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival in September, where its premiere had a 25-minute ovation – a festival record. In November, it won the best political documentary from the Critics Choice Association.

The film, its directors and their confidential sources have faced fierce attacks from the Israeli government and military. The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of sources interviewed and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

Netanyahu also threatened to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason. The Israeli military’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said the military would “not allow soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels” and would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film.

Far-right groups have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s family home. Some of the messages included explicit calls for violence, with one protester demanding the “death penalty for traitors”.

The Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on sources who had only a partial picture of the target approval process. It said that while AI was used to help identify targets in Gaza, final decisions on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.

In response, the team behind the film have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.

The Israeli government is promoting an online film project, called NAZA: The Real Story, which mimics the style of the genuine NAZA film and is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com. It is not the real NAZA documentary and has been misleading some viewers.

Initially, the rival film’s website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was to be screened. The site now appears as a platform for the rival film, which has been promoted by Israeli embassies.

Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who co-created NAZA: The Real Story, describes it as an “offensive move” to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.

Szor and Abraham have addressed the backlash to their documentary. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor said.

NAZA is in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the Guardian’s website from early December. Sign up here to be the first to watch it

The film has been shown by cinemas in 47 countries and seen by more than 1.5 million people since its release last month.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Two men found guilty over Iranian attempts to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on targets

Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of engaging in conduct likely to assist Tehran’s intelligence services.

Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.

The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.

Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.

Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Pourmohsen, who worked for the London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to be paid £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.

Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.

Amin wrote: “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke.”

Sepahvand replied: “I’ll go tomorrow.”

Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”

Sepahvand said: “Love you brother, I’ll go there tomorrow.”

The pair also discussed surveillance of the Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said Iran and its rulers did not and could tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.

“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.

Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.

The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.

after newsletter promotion

He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.

He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.

Sepahvand claimed his family was being threatened and that he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Turner, of UK Lawyers for Israel.

Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.

Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.

Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.

Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.

Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.

Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh ahead of sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.
