They were found guilty of engaging in conduct likely to assist Tehran's intelligence services. They visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They also discussed surveillance of Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in Gaza kills surgeon and five others
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and William Christou in Beirut
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Hospital director says 28 wounded in attack on one of few remaining medical facilities in the strip

An Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The Israeli military carried out the attack on the hospital, in Khan Younis, early on Thursday saying in a statement it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters there, without providing evidence.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The strike destroyed part of the surgery department, and caused extensive damage to several floors. Services were suspended in four departments: radiology, laboratories, surgical operations and inpatient surgical wards, according to Dr Ahmed al-Fara, hospital director.

The ceiling of one of the wards had caved in, while debris-covered beds lay next to medical instruments twisted from the force of the blast. In other rooms, piles of rubble and shattered concrete cluttered the floor and a hole was left in the floor, where the bomb penetrated the building.

Dr Ayman Abu Ubaid, a surgical specialist at Nasser medical complex, who was wounded in the attack, said: “The bombing caused thick smoke to fill the rooms and fires to break out, amid the groans of wounded and people’s screams. There were many casualties and blood everywhere … Most of us sustained injuries to our limbs, as well as shrapnel wounds in different parts of our bodies.”

Ubaid said the strike came at about 12.30am, without warning. “The patients in the department were all surgical patients waiting to undergo operations. The bombing happened at a time when they should have been asleep,” he said.

Among the dead was Rizk Abu Shaira, 52, a general surgeon who had featured in American Doctor, a documentary about doctors operating in Gaza.

“Dr Rizk was in the American Doctor documentary operating and serving his people. He lost his life doing that, he lost his life because he was doing that,” Dr Thaer Ahmad, who also featured in the documentary, posted on X.

Abu Shaira was killed alongside one of his patients, on whom he had operated.

Nasser hospital is one of the last functioning healthcare facilities in Gaza, after Israeli bombing made most of the strip’s facilities unusable. Last year Israel also struck the hospital, killing five journalists in a double-tap strike on a location often used by reporters for filming. In all, the hospital has been attacked seven times since the war on Gaza began.

The Israeli military has accused Hamas of using hospitals as command centres and to store weapons, an accusation the militant movement rejects. More than 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed in Gaza, while Doctors Without Borders (MSF) says Israel has detained hundreds of medics since 7 October 2023, with at least 95 still in custody.

About 90% of Gaza’s health infrastructure has been destroyed or damage by Israeli bombing, systematic destruction UN experts called “medicide”.

Attacking healthcare facilities and staff is illegal under international humanitarian law, though these facilities can lose their protected status if they are used for military purposes.

There is an increased need for healthcare during the winter months in Gaza, where rains have displaced people from their tents and increased communicable diseases in crowded encampments.

Already, Nasser hospital is lacking about 80% of its essential medicines and medical supplies, said al-Fara, its director.

One of those killed in Thursday’s strike was Seif Ghazi Abu Hatab, 29, who was admitted to Nasser hospital on Monday after a piece of debris fell on his back while he was helping clear rubble from a friend’s home. He was scheduled for surgery at 10am on Thursday, and was meant to receive further treatment abroad.

“Seif was a young man in the prime of his life. He wanted to live, rebuild his home and start a normal life, free from problems and suffering … Seif was killed after already losing two of his brothers and his father. His mother has now lost three of her sons,” said his cousin Tareq Abu Hatab, 37.

Israel launched the war in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack that killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostage. At least 74,645 people have since been killed in Gaza and Israel has carried out a genocide in the strip, according to the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

Israel continues to carry out airstrikes in Gaza, killing more than 1,600 people since the October 2025 “ceasefire”, according to the Gaza ministry of health.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Israeli military carried out the attack on the hospital, in Khan Younis, early on Thursday. Hospital director says 28 wounded in attack on one of few remaining medical facilities in the strip. Israeli military said it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters there.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Lorenzo Tondo
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife

T
he vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.

Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.

The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.

It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.

Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.

Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.

“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.

“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”

Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.

“Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.

More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.

Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.

Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.

An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.

Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.

Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta, two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.

Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.

Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.

According to a Wall Street Journal report, the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.

In some instances, countries bordering the strait have responded to spills. After the attack on the Gem No 2, for instance, the UAE closed beaches, launched a major cleanup and monitored its desalination plants. Authorities said on 30 October that the leak had been stopped and pollution was declining.

In Oman, divers and equipment were deployed to a damaged vessel and crews cleared oil from 7 miles of coastline near the Hallaniyat Islands.

But the wider environmental damage may prove far harder to contain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear, damaging marine food chains and threatening coastal communities dependent on fishing,” Noelle said.

Contamination can affect organisms ranging from small invertebrates to fish, birds and turtles. “Mangroves and coral reefs can take decades to recover, particularly when oil persists in sediments,” she added. “Repeated spills, such as those in the strait of Hormuz, risk worsening the damage.”

Riegl said the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s and the first Gulf war, when tankers, loading facilities and oilfields were targeted, provided evidence of the lasting impact of large-scale oil pollution on Gulf ecosystems.

A 2020 study traced widespread deposits of tar – the thick, sticky residue left as crude oil breaks down – on Qatari beaches to the Gulf war. A study in 2022 found sediment on Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island still contaminated by oil from the 1983-85 Nowruz spills during the Iran-Iraq war, which collectively leaked 80m gallons of crude into the sea.

Riegl said: “Any organism that has to dig into beaches [affected by spills], like sea turtles when they lay eggs, will encounter the contaminated strata and adverse effects can be expected. Burrowing organisms like ghost crabs will continue to bring contaminated material to the surface.

“Clearly, the effects of large-scale oil pollution remain detectable for decades – so this is a generational problem. We could really lose something irreplaceable.”

Regime adviser says Tehran could be forced into pre-emptive strikes if stalemate continues

Senior Iranian officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an ever-tightening economic stranglehold that will push Tehran into retaliatory action.

The assessment comes from Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

Mohammadi said on his Telegram channel that the Americans had proposed a timeframe of about two weeks after which Donald Trump would make a decision on military action. Mohammadi, who is regarded as a reliable indicator of Ghalibaf’s thinking, cast doubt on the US president’s claim that the military option was off the table. He claimed Washington was preparing for a limited strike and Iran was already preparing a response.

If the US sanctions continued, he said, a comprehensive pre-emptive war would be needed “to increase the cost of sanctions for the enemy”.

Mohammadi described the US response to Iran’s latest proposals on reopening the strait of Hormuz as “not only unsatisfactory but completely deceptive”. “They do not want to release the frozen funds,” he said. “They do not want to lift the sanctions and they do not want to stop the war in Lebanon.”

He also disclosed that Iran had rejected a request from the US vice-president, JD Vance, for a direct meeting with its negotiators before giving a response to Tehran’s conditions for lifting the siege on the strait.

For now, Trump has settled on a strategy of suffocating Iran through economic pressure and tightening the blockade on its oil exports while facilitating those of other Gulf states through Hormuz.

Mohammadi’s assessments suggest some senior Iranians fear Washington’s strategy might work by destabilising the country. The thinking goes that economic turmoil might spark street protests, potentially around the anniversary of nationwide demonstrations that began in late December last year.

On this basis, the Iranian leadership might conclude that the status quo – a “no peace, no war” impasse – was not sustainable and pre-emptive action was required.

Despite Iranian claims that their blockade of the strait is working, there is concern that Brent crude is at a relatively low $93 a barrel, while Saudi oil production is near prewar levels of 9.3m barrels a day. In an attempt to close any loopholes, Iran said it bombed a US radar post on the Omani island of Didamar three days ago.

In another development, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s national security council, said he had told Russia that Iran was not prepared for even a particle of its highly enriched stockpile of uranium to leave the country, saying it might be needed for planned nuclear-powered submarines.

A third senior official, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, warned Europe that any complicity in the US blockade would be “an act of war that will be etched in the nation’s historical memory”.

Tehran has been increasingly clear that US bases in Europe will be targeted if fighting resumes. Rezaei said: “If American planes take off from a distant military base and come to this country to bomb Iran, we will also target that base. We are announcing this now so they have no excuse tomorrow.”

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, gave the impression this week that the policy of economic strangulation was sufficient and described Iran’s demands as unrealistic. However, Trump is under pressure to resolve the crisis before the Democrats take charge of Congress on 3 January.

A Reuters Ipsos poll in the US shows 71% of Americans want Congress to pass legislation to end the war in Iran. The overwhelming message from the midterm elections was that the conflict was highly unpopular but the Democrats do not have a strategy to end it and open up the strait of Hormuz. This risks leaving the political initiative with the White House, and an increasingly hardline Iranian leadership.

Just 28.2% of 18- and 19-year-olds have received their first dose in one-off campaign, UKHSA says

The clock is ticking for young people in the UK to receive vaccinations to protect against meningitis B, experts have said, as figures reveal fewer than one in three eligible in one-off campaign have received their first dose.

Earlier this year an unprecedented outbreak of meningitis B in Kent and clusters of cases in Dorset and Berkshire caused three deaths, as well as life-long health consequences among some of those who survived.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

As a result, the government announced in June a one-off, time-limited programme offering young adults two doses of a vaccine that protects against most strains of MenB bacteria.

But figures from the UK Health Security Agency have revealed just 28.2% of 18- and 19-year-olds have received a first dose. Dr Shamez Ladhani, consultant epidemiologist at the UKHSA, said time was running out for young people to get both doses of the vaccine, and urged those eligible to book an appointment.

He said: “The deadline for getting your first dose is 31 December, so please don’t leave it until the end of term or forget it amongst all the Christmas and other holiday festivities.”

Prof Andrew Pollard, director of the Oxford Vaccine Group, also raised concerns. He said: “While we can’t be sure whether there will be more student outbreaks of meningitis, as happened earlier this year in Kent, it is very worrying to me that uptake is so low.

“MenB vaccines can’t stop all cases, but they are still highly effective. It would be a tragedy if even one preventable case were to occur, when we have the tools to keep our young people safe.”

Two doses of the vaccine, given at least 28 days apart, are needed for protection, with UKHSA noting a second dose will be available until 31 March 2027. The latest data suggests almost 70% of 18- and 19-years-olds who have received a first dose have already had their second dose.

According to UKHSA, all those born between 1 September 2007 and 31 August 2008, are eligible for the vaccinations, as well as people under the age of 25 who started university, or residential further education, for the first time this autumn.

UKHSA said freshers had a risk about seven times higher than their peers who did not go to university. Experts have said factors such as shared accommodation, parties and large social networks can aid the spread of the bacteria.

Dr Eliza Gil, a clinical lecturer at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said the peak season for invasive MenB infection was typically December to March. She said: “The decision to make the vaccine offer time limited likely reflects both modelled cost effectiveness and an attempt to ensure eligible young people have their first vaccine dose before peak season, so that they have immune protection by the time they are most likely to be exposed.

“Although the overall risk of MenB remains low, if eligible young people are not vaccinated in sufficient numbers, or in time for peak season, the vaccine programme is likely to be less effective in preventing further outbreaks.”

Henry Gregg, chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association, said further action was needed to promote the offer. He said: “This should also include universities promoting this campaign strongly to those living in residential accommodation.”

Dr Michael Head, associate professor in global public health at the University of Southampton, said there was a case for reconsidering the December deadline, alongside enhanced health promotion campaigns.

“The risk of meningitis doesn’t suddenly disappear on 1 January. Young people will continue to mix inside and outside of universities,” he said. “I would also favour a wider review of whether MenB vaccination should routinely be offered to adolescents.”

The charity Meningitis Now and the National Union of Students also back routine MenB vaccination for young people; while earlier this year the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation recommended a routine single MenB booster jab for 15-year olds who had menB vaccinations as infants, with two doses for those who missed out.

Gregg said an annual campaign should replace an ad-hoc, standalone event. He said: “MenB is an extremely serious illness and we must do all we can to minimise the risk of tragic outbreaks that we have already seen this year in Kent, Berkshire and Dorset.”

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.title: Sadiq Khan joins Labour figures urging PM not to water down electric vehicle targets – UK politics live
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.author: Andrew Sparrow (now) and Taz Ali (earlier)

Kiran Stacey is the Guardian’s policy editor.

Sadiq Khan has become the most high-profile Labour figure to weigh into the increasingly fractious debate over what the government should do with its electric vehicle targets.

Ministers are meeting today in Downing Street to decide whether to cut legally binding requirements for carmakers to ensure 80% of the vehicles they sell in 2030 are electric.

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, is pushing for the target to be reduced to 50%, but Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, wants to keep it as close to 80% as possible.

But as ministers wrangle among each other, City Hall officials have made clear that the London mayor is on Fahnbulleh’s side.

Khan’s position was laid out in a letter from his deputy mayor for transport Seb Dance to Oliver Lord, the UK director of Clean Cities, which has been seen by the Guardian.

We and Transport for London share your view that the ZEV [zero-emission vehicle] mandate must not change. We outlined in our submission to the government’s consultation that London supports a strong and credible ZEV mandate.

We do not support any weakening of the current trajectories to 2030 or beyond, which risks damaging the case for investment in the ZEV and charging infrastructure industries, slowing down the pace of change, and the associated reduction in harmful emissions.

Department for Transport officials insist that no decision has yet been made but with the government likely to announce a cut to the 2030 target in the next two
weeks, this is likely to leave Khan opposed to official government policy.

The UK is sanctioning all 10 of Russia’s major oil producers, Andy Burnham will announce as he attends a gathering of European leaders in Ireland.

According to the Press Association, Burnham will use the European Political Community (EPC) summit in Dublin to urge leaders from some 50 nations to ramp up pressure on Vladimir Putin to take peace talks seriously.

Burnham said Britain has slapped a package of new sanctions on Moscow, including on shadow fleet vessels illicitly transporting Russian oil, Russian oil company Slavneft, and Rosneft’s flagship Arctic oil and gas project LLC Vostok Oil.

Peace talks on Ukraine have progressed but now is not the time for complacency – we must continue to ramp up pressure on Russia to agree a full and immediate ceasefire.

That is why the UK has announced a sweep of stinging new sanctions to turn the screws on Russia’s oil revenues and drive forward an end to the Kremlin’s needless war.

We all now need to harness the momentum on negotiations and find a way forward for our security at home, and the security of our continent.

Burnham arrived in Dublin on Thursday afternoon after flying in from Turkey, where he attended the UN Cop31 climate conference, PA said.

Regarding Neets, does the figure of a million just refer to those claiming benefits or does it also include those not claiming benefits? If it doesn’t include those not claiming benefits, what is the true Neet figure?

Is the government only concerned about Neets who claim benefits?

Alan Milburn is definitely interested in both categories of Neet. The Treasury is probably more worried about just the Neets who claim benefits, but they should be worried about the other Neets too because if they don’t get into the labour market, they will end up claiming benefits one day.

The interim Milburn report said there were 957,000 Neets aged 16 to 24 at the end of 2025 and this figure includes people who claim out-of-work benefits and people who don’t.

The report describes the ones who don’t as “hidden Neets” and it says 44% of young Neets are in this category. It uses figures from this Resolution Foundation report exploring the problem.

The RF report includes this chart.

And this is what the RF says about the figures.

What figure 4 also shows is that there are consistently hundreds of thousands of young Neets who are not claiming out-of-work benefits. In 2024, we estimate that 410,000 – 44% of all Neets – were not in receipt of an out-of-work benefit. This is a slightly lower proportion than in 2019, and we estimate that the number of Neets who are claiming out-of-work benefits has risen more quickly since 2019 than the number who are Neet and not claiming (with increases of 24% and 13% respectively).

The fact that welfare spending is lower than it could be if all Neets claimed an out-of-work benefit may seem like good news to some policy makers, but it also highlights a policy dilemma – how can we reach and support Neets who have little incentive or opportunity to engage with the state?

And this chart, from an analytical annex published alongside the interim Milburn report, gives a bit more information about who the hidden Neets are.

On the Today programme this morning, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, a prominent leftwinger, indicated she might vote against legislation to implement the Alan Milburn proposals. She said she was concerned by the idea that the cuts would apply to people already getting sickness and disability benefits, and she said it appeared to be a breach of a promise given last year that people already getting Pip (the personal independence payment) would not lose it.

I just don’t think that you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work.

The cuts seem to land on young disabled people, and many of them are in college already or already in work. So I don’t see how you fix the first by punishing the second.

Here are more quotes from what Alan Milburn told the Times about the proposals in his youth unemployment report, which is being published next week.

Milburn said he concluded fundamental change was needed. He said:

The whole system needs to be changed, because the system is geared to keeping people inactive when, for young people in particular, it’s all about how can you make them active, get them earning, learning, so that they can rely on a wage rather than on a benefit. So, this is not about cutting one benefit, it’s about rebuilding the system from scratch.

He said that he decided existing claimants should be covered by the changes, not just new changes.

It’s a big rewriting of the welfare system. And obviously one of the conundrums was, ‘Should this apply to only new claimants?’

I came to the conclusion that wouldn’t be right, not least because you’ve got hundreds of thousands of young people stuck in a benefit system that is trapping them in poverty, giving them no prospect of prosperity or a job.

That conclusion makes it difficult politically because it means people are getting a current entitlement and that entitlement is going to change. But it needs to.

It is relatively normal for welfare changes to cover existing claimants as well as new ones. But governments seeking to cut benefits do often restrict those changes to new claimants because people are much more likely to complain about losing something they already get than about losing something they might notionally get in the future.

Milburn admitted this meant the plans would not be “pain-free”.

I’m not saying that any of this will be easy or that it will be pain-free because it won’t. You know, candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

He said he wanted the system to prioritise improving people’s life chances in the long term over easing their financial hardship in the short term.

Actually for young people there’s a different debate that we’ve got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.

I think what the current system does, it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that’s the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around.

The approach I’ve taken on this is to try to define what would give young people the best chance of building a good life, not just over a year or two, but over the course of their lifetimes.

He said, alongside the cuts to benefits he is proposing (see 11.56am), he wanted to improve employment support for young people.

We need to make sure people have the opportunities to get an apprenticeship, a job, a work placement, a pre-apprenticeship, a college place.

The menu of opportunities has got to increase. They’ll have a personal adviser, they’ll be coached all the way through. The adviser will stick with them until they have found a job or an apprenticeship or college place.

He also confirmed he wants to let young people do some work before they start losing benefits.

They will get immediate access to support if that’s what they need, if that’s the thing that is holding them back from being in education or training.

He admitted that offering better employment support and mental health support would mean his plans would initially cost money. According to the Times, he did not did not deny claims the whole package could cost £6bn. But, in the long run, there would be savings, he said.

Obviously this costs money. And frankly it’s a better use of money, both from the point of view of the young person and the taxpayer, to spend that money getting them into work rather than spending that money keeping them on benefits.

This is the sort of fatuous thing about this debate. You’ve got to invest upfront in order to get savings out of the back end. Cost-free is fatuous. So we’ve got to be candid about that. It will need significant investment.

When it was put to him that it could take a decade for the savings to materialise, he replied:

To get a return on investment will take time … the only way of cutting the benefits bill sustainably is by getting young people into work, paying their taxes and being less reliant on benefits. Unless you are prepared to put the investment upfront it will never be possible.

He said he was “confident” that Andy Burnham was full-square behind the changes that are needed.”

The Alan Milburn report on youth unemployment, or Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), is expected to lead to the biggest overhaul of the welfare system for at least a decade (when Iain Duncan Smith merged six different benefits into universal credit). Arguably, it could be even bigger.

It is certainly the most heavily-trailed benefits reform plan in recent history. Milburn, a former Labour cabinet minister, began pitch-rolling with the publication of an interim report in May. Unusually for a Westminster document, it was a compelling read, and was widely praised at the time. Since then, barely a week has gone by without Milburn dropping further hints about what the final report will say. Milburn says he has government backing for what he is recommending and he wants this to be a blueprint for legislation, not a set of recommendations ultimately ignored by ministers.

We still won’t get the final report until next week, but in his interview in the Times today he has given the fullest account yet of what he will propose.

This is how Steven Swinford sums up the plans in his write-up of the interview.

Under [Milburn’s] proposals, young people aged 18 to 24 would be barred from claiming the two main sickness and disability benefits: the health element of universal credit and personal independence payments (Pip).

They would instead be given a new youth allowance, which would be paid at the standard rate of universal credit, while billions would be invested in one-to-one employment support to get them into work.

Many of those who currently receive Pip would be moved on to a new benefit called the “additional cost allowance”. It would be paid to those with “significant, well-established and ongoing” costs relating to their disability.

Covering assistance, mobility, specialist transport or daily living support, the allowance would go to a smaller cohort than the 453,000 young people currently claiming Pip. It would not be means-tested and people would receive the money “regardless” of whether they were in work or not.

The most severely disabled individuals — those with “profound” and “lifelong” conditions who can never be expected to work — would be given a new benefit. It would be paid at a higher rate than current disability benefits and would have no waiting period.

The Green party has said it is opposed to the proposal from Alan Milburn for many young people to lose sickness or disability benefits. (See 10.35am.)

Commenting on the proposals, revealed by Milburn in an interview in the Times, Siân Berry, the Green MP and the party’s work and pensions spokesperson, said:

So the solution to young people without education or jobs is to continue demonising young and disabled people instead of addressing the structural inequalities stacked against them?

What is the point of a deep review like this if the conclusion is that the government goes on blaming young people for needing help?

The prime minister must remember that social security is a human right whatever your age.

More than 3,500 patients a day received care in hospital corridors or makeshift treatment areas in England last month, as other figures show the NHS is already facing growing pressures before winter has arrived, the Press Association reports. PA says:

The waiting list for hospital treatment has also risen to its highest level in nearly a year.

Officials said this autumn has been the “busiest ever” for the health service, with record numbers of people attending A&E.

The latest performance data from NHS England shows an average of 3,558 patients received corridor care each day in October, with 2,718 in A&E departments and 840 in other hospital areas.

This is up from a revised average of 3,310 patients a day in September and the highest since figures for corridor care started being collected in May.

Prof Nicola Ranger, general secretary and chief executive of the Royal College of Nursing, called the figures “a mark of shame”.

She said: “Nursing staff will be filled with dread thinking of just how bad things will get as temperatures drop.

“The data shows once again that corridor care is occurring not just in emergency departments but across hospitals. This is an incredibly dangerous situation with much colder temperatures on the horizon.”

Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan claimed the “true scale of the crisis is likely far worse”.

She added: “We are hearing troubling reports of trusts reclassifying spaces to keep the numbers down.

“Hospitals are under pressure to hit targets rather than put patients first. Patients on chairs in waiting rooms or in converted cupboards deserve to be counted.”

In emergency departments, some 74.0% of patients were seen within four hours in October, down slightly from 74.4% in September.

Elsewhere, an estimated 7.38m treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of September, relating to 6.24m patients.

This is up slightly from 7.37m treatments at the end of August and is the highest since the list stood at 7.40m treatments in October 2025.

The figure for patients is broadly unchanged month on month, but is also at a level that was previously seen in October 2025.

Good morning. I’m Andrew Sparrow, taking over from Taz Ali.

Andy Burnham won’t arrive in Dublin for his meeting with other leaders from the European Political Community (the EU plus non-EU states in Europe) until this afternoon, but it is the first time he has met many of them, and they are anticipating his arrival.

Kaja Kallas has said she would “very much like to see Britain back in Europe”, but warned there is “a lot of … trauma from Britain leaving” that could affect any reset talks.

So the negotiations will not be that easy, but I think we can take the little steps. And I’m confident that if we are together, we are much stronger when it comes to economy, but when it also comes to security.

Over in Dublin, where the European Political Community summit is taking place, European parliament president Roberta Metsola told journalists she would do “anything in my power” to turn the political intent behind the announced UK-EU reset plan into “very tangible steps”.

“We have a very solid UK-EU parliamentary assembly and partnership, and that is the partnership that we will be using in order to make sure that any agreement and all measures that are taken next week during the [EU-UK] summit will be implemented through majorities in parliament,” she said.

“That is what I hope for, and I am extremely optimistic in that regard,” she added, describing herself as “a big fan of the United Kingdom”.

For more updates from across Europe, follow our live blog here:

“Britain is back and ready to play its full part,” Andy Burnham has said at the opening of today’s Cop31 summit.

The UK prime minister celebrated domestic clean energy projects including windfarms and electrified steel factories, stressed the need to make the transition affordable, and announced the UK’s first special representative for climate security, Madeleine Alessandri.

“The climate crisis is not a distant threat, it is upon us now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere,” he said. Pointing to the effects of two global wars on energy prices, he added that the “common thread running through all of this is fossil fuels.”

Burnham repeated the UK’s commitment to meeting its 2050 net zero emissions target and said he would work with all of partners to reach theirs.

“In that spirit, I am proud to support this Cop’s focus on electrification,” he said. “If we depend on energy we do not control, we depend on prices we cannot control. The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security.

He called on industry to “play their part” in helping people on all incomes make the green transition. He highlighted progress in bringing the price of clean technologies down for consumers.

“If you drive a new electric car today in the UK, it costs less than a petrol equivalent. Get on the right tariff and a heat pump can be cheaper to run than a gas boiler.”

But he also warned that some of the fundamentals had worsened.

“The consensus we once enjoyed on science is gone,” said Burnham. “And the reality is the world will breach the 1.5C target.”

For more updates from the fourth day of the climate summit in Turkey, head over to our Cop31 live blog here:

Good morning and welcome to the UK politics live blog. Young people could lose entitlement to the main sickness and disability benefits under a significant overhaul of the welfare system, according to proposals expected to emerge from the government-commissioned review into young people and work.

Led by former health secretary Alan Milburn, the review is examining the barriers preventing young people from entering the workforce and how to address the growing number classified as not in education, employment or training (Neet), which currently stands at about 981,000 across the UK.

The review, which has been under way for a year, is expected to include proposals that would remove under-25s’ entitlement to the health element of universal credit and personal independence payment (Pip), replacing them with a standard-rate youth allowance. Under the plans, first reported by the Times, those with additional needs arising from a disability would receive a separate, non-means-tested allowance, while those with severe disabilities and who are not capable of working would qualify for a higher rate.

Speaking to the newspaper, Milburn acknowledged that the changes would not be “pain-free”, admitting some young people could initially receive less financial support than under the current system. The final review is due to be published on Tuesday.

Prime minister Andy Burnham addressed world leaders at Cop31 in Turkey, pledging a “new era of British leadership” on climate change and reaffirming the UK’s commitment to its 2050 net-zero target. He said international consensus on science and climate “has gone”, adding: “The reality is the world will breach the 1.5C target.” You can keep up to date with the latest from the Cop31 summit in our live blog here:

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Kiran Stacey
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Government proposal aims to reduce number of children in custody in England and Wales and boost youth employment

Children found guilty of robbery, dealing drugs to other children or violent disorder will no longer have to disclose their criminal records to prospective employers under sweeping government proposals to change the youth justice system.

People in England and Wales will not have to share records of crimes committed when they were under 18 for the rest of their lives under the proposals, which ministers say will boost youth employment and make life fairer for people from disadvantaged backgrounds in particular.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The proposals, which are being consulted on, are part of a wider set of changes that aim to sharply reduce the number of children in custody and increase support for those who are convicted of crimes.

Jake Richards, a justice minister, told the Guardian: “Where it’s safe, we believe as a government, people should have second chances – second chances to make something of themselves, to contribute to work and to turn their back on crime.

“The system at the moment doesn’t discern for offences committed when you were a child than those that you committed as an adult.”

Richards is proposing to reduce the number of offences that would require lifelong disclosure on standard and enhanced DBS checks by the person who committed them. If the plans become law, people convicted of violent disorder, supplying drugs to a child, robbery, affray and actual bodily harm when under 18 would no longer automatically have to disclose those offences for the rest of their lives.

If they are convicted of one of those offences but do not get a custodial sentence, they will have to disclose them only for five and a half years. If they get a sentence of two years or less, they would have to disclose it for 11 years.

Anyone given a longer custodial sentence would still have a lifetime obligation to tell prospective employers.

If someone is convicted of a crime which results in a fine, they will no longer have to disclose it, rather than for the next six months as the law currently stipulates.

Jobs in the UK that require a standard or enhanced DBS check include teaching and early years working, social work, healthcare and transport jobs including taxi driving.

Other changes include ending the automatic disclosure of any out of court resolution and ending a rule which lengthens how long it takes for a conviction to become spent if the person is convicted of a second crime during their rehabilitation period.

Campaigners have welcomed the proposed changes, saying they will boost youth employment. Companies say criminal convictions are the second biggest barrier to employing people from disadvantaged backgrounds.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: AI helped UK defy expectations – but will economy’s resilience fizzle out?
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years

The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.

Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

On his first day in Downing Street the memo from the Treasury showed the most optimistic City analyst expected 0.3% quarterly growth. Most had pencilled in a figure close to zero. Some were warning that the UK could edge towards a recession.

Despite the gloomy outlook households have continued to spend and business investment has powered ahead, driven by the rollout of AI.

Underneath the bonnet, growth is being spearheaded by IT and professional services – together contributing about half of the rise in activity. As the central sectors in the AI boom, that is hardly surprising – with analysts at ING suggesting the strength in IT was “very clearly a datacentre story” thanks to the UK’s status as a leading destination in Europe for investment.

Overall, Deutsche Bank estimates that AI-related spending has added about 0.3% to 0.4% to GDP growth this year. It is clear to see why Healey is keen to build on the groundwork laid by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to harness AI amid government efforts to court global business investment.

Meanwhile, household consumption is up by 1.6% so far this year – helped by spending over the warm summer months even as consumers faced a living standards squeeze because the Iran war fuelled a surge in petrol and diesel prices.

However, the fear is that the UK’s initial resilience to the global economic storm emanating from the Middle East will soon fizzle out.

Both of Britain’s recent growth engines face a tougher period ahead.

After the US midterm elections and revelations at the chipmaker Nvidia, the outlook for the AI investment boom is less certain. Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks amid fears that a bubble in AI stocks could be about to burst. A slowdown in technology investment could hit the UK. Still, the hope is that swelling demand for AI will not evaporate overnight.

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

For households, however, a tough winter lies ahead. Energy bills are poised to increase by about a quarter in January, with the average annual household gas and electricity bill expected to climb to more than £2,000. Analysts say it is hard to see how consumer spending would not come under greater pressure in the new year.

In the latest data there were some early warning signs: retail sales and consumer discretionary spending fell in September. Real wage growth is cooling and the headline inflation rate is on track to reach a fresh peak of close to 5% next year.

With growth proving resilient, the Bank of England will feel emboldened to raise interest rates to combat imported inflation. City investors expect at least two more quarter-point increases to 4.5% before the end of next year. That will hit the brakes on the economy and add to the cost of living squeeze.

At last month’s budget Healey struck a defiant tone by arguing that the UK could continue to defy forecasters expectations. That task, however, is becoming increasingly tough.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Shares up 7% after announcement as Jaime Gilinski Bacal seeks exit three years after helping to rescue bank

Metro Bank is putting itself up for sale three years after its near-collapse, in a move that could hand a £420m windfall to its Colombian billionaire investor, Jaime Gilinski Bacal.

Metro Bank made the rare decision to publicly announce it was open to bids on Thursday, paving the way for a wider pool of suitors. The announcement pushed the share price up by 7% by mid-morning, valuing the bank at about £1.3bn.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

If successful, the sale would allow Gilinski Bacal a chance to sell out of the bank he helped save from near-failure in late 2023.

The 68-year-old banking tycoon, who took a seat on Metro’s board after securing a 53% stake three years ago, has already seen a sixfold increase in the value of his shares, which he bought for just 30p each as part of a wider rescue deal. That means that at Thursday’s 190p share price, his British Virgin Island-based vehicle Spaldy Investments, could cash out with a £427m windfall.

It would mark the latest turnaround success for the billionaire, who made his fortune snapping up assets of struggling lenders on the cheap, before overhauling their operations and selling them on for a big profit. Gilinski Bacal is one of the wealthiest people in Latin America, worth about $16.9bn (£12.7bn), according to Forbes.

Metro Bank has been focused on a turnaround plan – which has involved lending more heavily to businesses and people with more erratic incomes – since it was forced into the £925m rescue deal in 2023.

Metro was the first high street bank to open in the UK in more than 100 years when it was launched by another billionaire, the US businessman Vernon Hill, in 2010. It attracted a wave of customers, and offered dog-friendly branches with seven-day openings.

However, it struggled after a major accounting blunder in 2019 that prompted investors to dump their shares and fearful customers to pull their cash. It led to the resignation of top executives, as well as the then chair, Hill, who was well-known for having his yorkshire terrier Sir Duffy (and later Sir Duffy II) in tow.

Metro’s shares took another dive in 2023. That year, it emerged that the bank would need more cash from investors, having failed to convince regulators that it could be trusted to assess its own risks.

The lender finally secured a rescue, which was brokered in part by UK regulators at the Bank of England, in 2023. It has since embarked on the turnaround plan, which has increased its profits but came at a cost for staff and customers. Metro’s chief executive, Daniel Frumkin, slashed more than 1,000 jobs in spring 2024 and decided to close branches on Sundays.

The bank said on Thursday that a sale was just one of the options on the table and that it would still be able to go it alone if no suitable bidder came through.

Metro’s board “unanimously believes that evaluating potential interest in the company” through a potential sale “will maximise the value creation opportunities available to shareholders and deliver benefits for all stakeholders”, the bank said.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over scandal and is replaced by CFO Colette Kress on interim basis – follow live
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.author: Julia Kollewe (now) and Jonathan Yerushalmy (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.text:
Nvidia’s long-time boss Jensen Huang has stepped down over the scandal, and the company has appointed finance chief Colette Kress as interim chief executive.

The company issued this statement just now, after its board met last night:

The Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.

Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.

More than $575bn has been wiped off Nvidia’s value at the start of trading, as investors react to the departure of Jensen Huang.

Nvidia’s shares have tumbled by over 13% at the start of trading, dropping to $149.79 from $173.73 last night.

They ended last week at $186.64 each. And (by my maths), the company’s valuation has now slumped by $888bn so far this week.

Having ended Friday night worth $4.5tn, Nvidia’s value has now dropped to $3.61bn.

Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson in Portland, Oregon, has looked at the new interim CEO of Nvidia, Colette Kress, who will also continue to serve as chief financial officer.

Colette Kress is well respected by investors and should be able to guide Nvidia through this challenging period. The task is daunting, as Nvidia has been founder-led since inception and Mr Huang concentrated much of the decision making.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to support our crucial year-end fundraiser. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

Ben Barringer, head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said:

Jensen Huang clearly saw the writing was on the wall and has made the decision to resign as chief executive of Nvidia. This is an important moment in broader financial markets due to the clout that Huang carried, and the fact he had developed Nvidia into the most valuable and influential company in the world.

It remains to be seen if Huang will eventually stick around in some sort of ceremonial or non-executive capacity. It would be difficult to see him not retaining some sort of influence over Nvidia, but we do not yet know the full details of the allegations or the outcome of the investigation, and much of what happens next still depends on that.

For now, CFO Colette Kress has taken the role on an interim position. While there is no natural successor in place, she is the most obvious internal candidate and will now likely use this time to prove she deserves it full time. She certainly knows the company inside out and has helped develop what is a hugely successful strategy.

This doesn’t necessarily harm Nvidia in the short-term. Orders remain strong and the company has a robust earnings outlook. What this news threatens to do is harm the wider AI ecosystem in the longer-term. Huang is hugely influential in the debates around AI regulation and has developed Nvidia into the leader in AI investment and financing. With his voice now removed from the table, and the potential for Nvidia to pivot on its strategy over time, the company may not carry the sway it once did.

Turning to the wider outlook for technology firms, he said:

This news ultimately pours petrol onto what is already a volatile picture for tech companies following the midterm elections. Nvidia and its neocloud partners are likely to bear the initial brunt of this news, while competitors like AMD and Broadcom benefit. That said, this news has the potential to be game changing over the long-term with a key figure out of the picture.

Jensen Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priemand “with a vision to bring 3D graphics to the gaming and multimedia markets”.

Huang is the company’s fourth-largest investor with a ⁠stake of about 3.61% and will not ⁠remain on the board.

Here’s some instant reaction to his departure.

Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional investor content at Morningstar, says governance issues and succession planning, long neglected at Nvidia, will become important for other founder-led companies.

The sudden departure of one of the world’s most influential CEOs illustrates just how quickly an unconventional governance structure can become a source of risk, and often real losses, for investors. While Nvidia’s share price rocketed over the last few years, very few people were asking deep questions about CEO succession planning, board composition and challenge, or oversight of geopolitically sensitive aspects of company strategy. Now, all those issues will be front and centre, perhaps not just for Nvidia, but also for other founder-led companies like Anthropic, Meta Platforms and SpaceX.

Nvidia’s shares are falling deeper into the red in pre-market trading, ahead of the open of Wall Street in less than 25 minutes.

They were already heading for a fall, as investors were unsettled by the news that Nvidia’s board had met last night to consider Jensen Huang’s future.

Now that he has resigned, Nvidia’s shares are down 10.4% – an indication of how trading may proceed when the New York stock market session begins.

Nvidia shares have plummeted 10% on the news!

Nvidia paid tribute to Huang, saying:

Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.

Kress, the new interim chief executive, has served as executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia since joining the company in September 2013. The group said she has played a key role in Nvidia’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.

The Nvidia board also appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as chief efficer and executive chairman of Synopsys.

Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position. She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.

Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.

We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.

The US chipmaker will report its third-quarter results on 17 November.

The company issued this statement just now, after its board met last night:

The Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.

Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.

US trade representative Jamieson ⁠Greer ⁠said ⁠the United States “remains ⁠concerned” ​about the tech giant ‌Nvidia, ‌as the world’s ‌dominant supplier of AI chips grapples with fallout ‌from reports of two extramarital ​affairs involving its longtime ⁠chief executive Jensen Huang.

Greer told CNBC ​on Thursday:

Obviously we ​remain concerned.

Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese businesswoman and former Megaspeed executive, who is accused of spying for Beijing. She has reportedly returned to China.

Wall Street is expected to have a bumpy start in just over an hour, with technology shares likely to slide again as the scandal around Nvidia boss Jensen Huang deepens.

Stock futures are extending losses, with the S&P 500 down 0.75%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq 1.5% lower and Dow Jones down 0.2%.

Also, Donald Trump said: “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”

In the second half of a post about corruption in the US, on the social media platform Truth Social, he said:

We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DJT

Oil prices have see-sawed today. Brent crude is now trading 1.5% higher at $93.98 a barrel.

Gold prices have also fallen, by about 2%.

Chinese AI companies are trying to rent ​Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China, worried that the scandal involving the US chipmaker’s chief executive Jensen Huang could lead Washington to tighten restrictions on their remote use of ‌advanced processors, Reuters reported.

Seeking to protect US dominance of the critical sector, Washington restricts exports to China of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips. But Chinese companies can access these processors remotely by renting computing power at datacentres overseas.

A major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally ​whether to lock in overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some companies have contacted datacentre operators about reserving it, unnamed sources told Reuters.

Meanwhile, the San Francisco-based tech publication The Information is reporting that the US Commerce Department is working to finalise a rule that will prevent Chinese artificial intelligence companies from remotely accessing advanced AI chips through datacentres located in other countries.

Alice Huang, the woman at the centre of the scandal engulfing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, has returned to China and is in Beijing, according to Bloomberg News.

The chipmaker is investigating spying allegations denied by Beijing.

Nasdaq futures are now pointing to a 1% drop when the tech-heavy index starts trading later.

Megaspeed International, the datacentre company at the centre of the scandal engulfing Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, has pledged to cooperate with an investigation into potential risks to US national security.

In its first statement since the scandal broke, the Singapore-headquartered company said on Thursday that it takes its obligation to comply with US export control laws “extremely seriously.”

Details about Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive (who founded the company, according to CNBC and Bloomberg) and suspected Chinese spy, are still unclear. Revelations about an alleged second affair, with an Nvidia executive, prompted Nvidia’s board to hold a meeting last night to discuss Huang’s future.

The statement, signed by Megaspeed’s chairman and CEO, Tan Yong Pong, who also goes by James Tan, said:

Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government.

Nvidia has said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.

Megaspeed is a cloud computing firm that operates datacentres across southeast Asia. It is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips produced by Nvidia, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. Megaspeed is facing renewed scrutiny over claims that it facilitated the flow of restricted Nvidia chips worth billions of dollars into China.

Several investment banks have downgraded their target price estimates for Nvidia shares.

Analysts at Citi cut their target price again, to $225 from $285.

JPMorgan cut its target price $215 from $320, while Cantor Fitzgerald went down to $250 from $350, and Stifel cut its estimate to $205 from £315.

Melius Research went even further. It switched to a hold rating on the stock, and cut its target price to $185 from $315.

Nvidia shares are trading 7.9% lower at $173.73 in pre-market trading at present.

“If Jensen Huang is forced out, I would expect Nvidia shares to underperform for a period,” said Michael Feldman, portfolio manager at ClearBridge Investments.

Nvidia was already facing an unusually demanding expectations bar. The stock was not expensive, but its earnings outlook depended on confidence in exceptional growth and near-flawless execution across the entire AI ecosystem. Jensen has set a very ambitious framework, including roughly 70% year-on-year growth next year. A new CEO will likely want to establish credibility by setting a more conservative bar.

The risk is not that Nvidia suddenly loses its technology roadmap, that roadmap is largely visible for the next several years. The risk is execution. Jensen has been the chief conductor of an extraordinarily complex system spanning employees, foundry and packaging partners, memory suppliers, systems companies, cloud customers and the financing mechanisms supporting AI deployment. In a world with real bottlenecks, that coordination is a competitive advantage in itself.

I would also watch the financing architecture behind AI demand: leasing, customer financing and Nvidia’s investments across the ecosystem. Those arrangements are increasingly important in translating demand into deployed capacity and reported revenue.

So, this is not principally a valuation problem, it is a confidence problem. The long-term AI story remains intact: Nvidia still has the industry’s most powerful integrated stack across compute, networking and software, and the valuation offers some support. But the stock could move from a Jensen premium to an execution discount until new leadership proves it can deliver.

In pre-market trading, US chipmakers Intel, Marvell Technology and Micron are down between 1.8% and 2.7%, while AI infrastructure company CoreWeave slid 5.7%.

The declines, if maintained when Wall Street opens, would wipe out Wednesday’s gains, when strong results from CoreWeave, an American specialised GPU cloud-computing provider, lifted AI stocks.

Nebius reversed earlier losses to trade 1% higher, following Wednesday’s 15% jump. The Amsterdam-based, Nasdaq-listed company today beat ⁠Wall Street estimates for third-quarter revenue and projected $12bn to $13bn in sales for 2027, powered ⁠by booming demand ⁠for ​its cloud computing infrastructure.

AI stocks have seen wild swings, also because the Democrats’ victory in midterm elections intensified concerns about a slowdown in datacentre development that could lead to a wider economic slowdown – while some investors see the pullback as a buying opportunity. Seven in 10 Americans are opposed to the construction of new datacentres for artificial intelligence in their local area. Some Republicans have also endorsed a moratorium on new datacentres, which consume vast amounts of energy and water and lead to pollution.

Last night, we reported that Nvidia appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy.

The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker’s board has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. The firm’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management.

A committee of independent board directors, assisted by Kim and Wachtell, will oversee the investigation.

Global markets are struggling to maintain yesterday’s attempted recovery, with renewed uncertainty surrounding Nvidia weighing on sentiment towards technology stocks, said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at capital.com.

Wall Street enjoyed a strong session on Wednesday supported by improving confidence in AI demand. However, US futures have turned lower this morning, with Nasdaq futures particularly vulnerable as investors reassess the risks surrounding one of the most influential companies in the AI investment cycle.

Asian markets were also down, highlighting how fragile the recovery remains despite encouraging signs of demand for AI infrastructure.

The biggest development is the escalation of the controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Reports that Nvidia’s board is considering his future at a board meeting last night have transformed what initially appeared to be a reputational issue into a significant leadership risk. Nvidia shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading, raising concerns about the potential disruption to the company’s strategy.

Huang has been central to Nvidia’s growth and its relationships with major AI customers, meaning an unexpected leadership change could create uncertainty at an already sensitive moment for the sector. However, no departure has been confirmed, and Nvidia’s board has previously stated that it has no reason to believe company secrets were compromised.

The wider concern is that Nvidia’s leadership uncertainty could undermine confidence in the AI trade just as investors were beginning to regain some optimism about its fundamentals.

Recent developments at CoreWeave and strong demand surrounding Anthropic’s potential IPO suggest appetite for AI investment remains substantial. However, the controversy raises questions about governance, succession planning and potentially US-China technology relations. If the investigation uncovers evidence of compromised intellectual property, the consequences could extend beyond Nvidia to semiconductor manufacturers and cloud infrastructure providers.

For now, this remains a potential risk rather than an established outcome. With Nvidia’s earnings approaching on 17 November, investors face the unusual challenge of assessing strong underlying demand alongside uncertainty over the company’s leadership.

US stock futures are down, pointing to a lower open on Wall Street later.

The S&P 500 is seen opening 0.4% lower while the tech-heavy Nasdaq is set to fell 0.85%, and Dow futures are flat.

Nvidia shares are now down about 7% in Frankfurt. About $600bn have been wiped off the US chipmaker’s market value since the board announced an investigation into longtime boss Jensen Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. On Sunday, he admitted to cheating on his wife with the mysterious Shanghai executive.

Under the company’s bylaws, Jensen Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors. Nvidia has 11 directors and considers all but Huang independent.

Meanwhile, the US news website Axios is reporting that Donald Trump on Thursday authorised a crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — and he even consulted Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead.

But one administration official repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, Axios reported.

The Nvidia board met last night after the second revelation about Jensen Huang.

In a sharp shift from Sunday when it expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team, the board met to discuss his future after it was reported by the New York Times that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee called Kimberly Powell.

She was Nvidia’s president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.

Farewell Jensen, said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG.

One of the most impressive careers is set to end. Huang might have been able somehow to cling on at Nvidia after one revelation (though news about chip shipments made that doubtful), but after two, one of which involving a direct report, his fate is sealed.

Nvidia’s shares are moving rapidly to price in a post-Jensen world, and this is weighing on tech stocks globally. Nvidia is much bigger than one man now, but this isn’t the way anyone thought it would happen, and denies the company the chance to set up an orderly transition. The question is now whether this news torpedoes the renewed tech rally.

Germany’s Dax also reached a new all-time high, climbing more than 1% in early trading.

The Frankfurt exchange surged 283 points to 26,944, up 1.06%.

At least five people have been shot in Northwest Washington DC on Thursday morning, local police confirmed to the Associated Press.

A spokesperson for the Washington DC police department told the Guardian in a brief phone call on Thursday morning that the scene was “still active”. No further details were immediately available.

The DC police department said in a social media post at about 8.20am ET that officers were on the scene responding to an “active shooting in the area of 15th and P Street, Northwest”. The department’s emergency response team was also at the scene. The department urged the public to avoid the area.
