https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dara Kerr and Dan Milmo
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Move follows admission of affair with woman alleged to be Chinese spy and reported relationship with employee

Business live – latest updates

Jensen Huang has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee.

He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a full-time successor is named.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations that have enveloped the company, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contribution to the company he co-founded.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said.

The chipmaker’s board earlier this week appointed leading law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship with Alice Huang, who is no relation to the Nvidia boss. The firm directed Jensen Huang to continue to helm Nvidia as the investigation was ongoing.

However, late on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.

Powell has been approached for comment.

The report added to the pressure on Huang as the board met late on Wednesday.

Huang’s exit from the company he co-founded in 1993 removes a senior figure in Silicon Valley at a time when the AI arms race between the US and China is at an apex. Huang owns more than 870m shares, or about 3.6% of the company and is worth $145bn (£109bn), according to Bloomberg, making him the world’s 13th richest person. Unlike many of his contemporaries at other leading tech companies, Huang has dozens of direct reports, an unusual management structure that emphasises his control over the company.

The entire artificial intelligence ecosphere relies on the company, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. It is also one of the most valuable companies on Earth, with a market cap of more than $4tn.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

Nvidia and Huang have both taken a financial hit as the scandal unfolds: company shares slid about 7% in pre-market trading on Thursday after the Wall Street Journal reported Nvidia’s board was readying Huang’s ouster.

While Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair without directly naming the suspected spy, he denies any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years. Alice Huang is a businesswoman and head of the Singapore-based datacentre firm Megaspeed, who US intelligence services suspect of being a Chinese asset according to multiple reports.

Jensen Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday after days of speculation about his relationship with the Megaspeed executive that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching an investigation regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Donald Trump has backed Jensen Huang, saying he had done “an incredible job” and is “an honorable guy”. Big tech industry players, including Elon Musk, have also thrown their support behind Huang. However, Nvidia’s stock has tumbled with the news, and is down more than 11% in the past few days.

Defeating Cindy Hyde-Smith makes the 43-year-old district attorney the first Black Mississippi senator elected since Reconstruction. Plus, the South Korean scarf vendor who has gone viral for telling people not to buy

Good morning. In a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states, the Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Cindy Hyde-Smith, the incumbent Republican senator, in Mississippi. He becomes the first Black senator elected in the state since Reconstruction.

Colom’s election capped a national wave of anger at Donald Trump’s administration, sweeping away Republicans in places where Democrats had not been competitive in decades. With the addition of Colom, Democrats will hold at least 55 seats in the Senate, the party’s largest midterm gain since 1986.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

What did Colom say about his victory? Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, said there had been times when his long-shot campaign felt defeated but “I had to have faith”. He told supporters: “My commitment to you, each and every one of you, is that first I’m going to treat your children like I want my children to be treated. I’m going to treat your parents the way I want my parents to be treated. I’m gonna treat your future the way I want my future to be.”

How have Democrats responded to a White House threat? Robert Garcia, the ranking member of the oversight committee in the House of Representatives said it appeared Donald Trump had “something to hide” after the White House threatened criminal investigations over the party’s planned scrutiny of the administration. Garcia said in a statement that Congress’s authority came from article I of the constitution, “not from the permission of the White House”.

Nvidia’s board of directors has met to decide whether to oust Jensen Huang as CEO of the world’s most valuable chip company, according to reports, after a tumultuous week in which the executive and co-founder of the company admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. Huang’s position became more tenuous late on Wednesday after it was reported by the New York Times that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee. Our global technology editor, Dan Milmo, explains what is happening in our Today in Focus podcast.

Democratic lawmakers expressed outrage at nearly a dozen of their colleagues for missing a vote Tuesday evening to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, allowing Republicans to defeat the effort. Eleven Democrats missed the key procedural vote on the impeachment effort, which failed by just seven votes. “You should show up and do your job,” Abdul El-Sayed, the senator-elect of Michigan, said on CNN, while Richard Ojeda, the representative-elect of North Carolina, said: “Shame on them for not showing up … they had an opportunity to finally get rid of this buffoonery.”

Why has a video clip of Hegseth gone viral? A US army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier loudly reprimanded the defense secretary and his top staffers on Wednesday after some in the group were heard laughing and talking near the memorial following a Veterans Day ceremony. You can watch the video here.

Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-story building in Brooklyn on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least eight people and trapping others beneath the wreckage. Firefighters were called to the scene in the borough’s Flatbush section at about 4pm.

Russia’s ambassador to the United States has died aged 66. Alexander Darchiev took up the role last year.

The US could lose its measles elimination status under RFK Jr’s leadership, with the country in the middle of worst measles outbreak since 1991.

Average US heating bills are set to rise 7% this winter, according a report by the National Energy Assistance Directors Association.

Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are holding rallies at more than 40 college campuses across the US to support the Starbucks Workers United boycott campaign as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.

Two skulls that likely belonged to enslaved people are being returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies. The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century.

A coyote that officials thought they had killed after it attacked a child has been seen alive in an LA neighborhood.

Ethics watchdogs have questioned the necessity of the country’s top diplomat shuttling so often between Washington DC and Gainesville, where his son Anthony has a walk-on role as a running back.

Lauren Gould has been one of the protein-nibbling guinea pigs for this research task, and with the rise of GLP-1s making protein the crown jewel of the health and wellness world, here is the verdict on what tastes best. And if you want to round out your protein snack with a coffee, here is a guide to six ways baristas make great coffee at home – and one they all hate.

The incomparable Jane Wiedlin has written a memoir that even she herself suggests contains a bit too much information. Jim Farber speaks to the former Go-Go about industry sexism, living with bipolar disorder and the freedom of sex dungeons.

The British actor took up writing and producing to have control over what she stars in after a scandal involving some of the most powerful men in the film business. Emine Saner interviews her.

Lorenzo Tondo reports on how, since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a “generational” threat to wildlife.

Follow the latest from Cop31, where Greta Thunberg and John Kerry have been speaking today, with our live blog.

Seoul’s “scarf uncle” has become a South Korean sensation for a sales technique that consists of talking customers out of purchases. The combination of his affectionate bluntness and amusing selling style – coupled with praise for his looks – has led to him becoming a huge star on social media.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Gun rights groups plot new ties with ‘gun owners who vote Democrat’ after midterms verdict
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Abené Clayton
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Some advocates say it no longer makes sense for their movement to be so intertwined with the Republican party

After the Democrats’ huge wins in the US midterm elections last week, gun rights advocates are updating their strategies in an attempt to cross the aisle and find allies on the left.

While most of the biggest and most visible gun rights groups, such as the National Rifle Association (NRA), are already signaling that they will challenge any gun safety legislation brought by the new Democratic Congress, others say it no longer makes sense for their movement to be so deeply intertwined with the Republican party.

“Leaders in gun rights organizations for the most part don’t believe it’ll ever happen, but a few recognize that because of the shift in voting patterns toward the left, it will be important to work with gun owners who vote Democrat,” said Rob Pincus, executive vice-president of the Second Amendment Organization, a non-profit that advocates for gun rights and offers firearms training.

Pincus has worked in the gun industry for more than 30 years, and for the last 10, he’s been floating the idea that the movement needs to spend less time supporting Republicans – who already support looser gun laws – and instead court Democrats and convince them to remove gun control as a central piece of the party’s agenda.

“This midterm presents an opportunity to take that message, which hasn’t been received well by the loudest voices in the gun community, and take it out for another try,” he said.

While it might sound far-fetched, gun ownership has increased among people on the left, people of color and the LGBTQ+ community, creating fertile ground for second amendment advocates to reach out to younger Democrats in all parts of the US.

It’s a major departure from previous decades, during which the nation’s biggest gun rights groups have been intertwined with the broader conservative movement. The NRA, for example, first got involved in politics in the 1970s, then upped its involvement after Congress passed the 1994 assault weapons ban, and again when Donald Trump ran for president in 2016. The organization became so involved in rightwing politics that it’s now seen less as a gun rights group and more as an extension of the Republican party itself.

“Being a card-carrying member of the NRA often means more than that you just like guns,” said Stephen Gutowski, a firearm trainer and founder of the Reload, an online outlet that covers gun policy. “It feels like most people who support gun rights are rightwing and have a bunch of other political or cultural beliefs that come packaged together, like support for strict immigration enforcement.”

But this entrenchment with the Republican party has also alienated people who may want less stringent gun laws – but are put off by the association with Donald Trump.

“My impression is that no one is clocking this as a significant sea change moment in the gun fight,” Gutowski said.

Not only are the demographics of gun owners evolving, but so too is the financial influence of gun rights groups in national politics. “It used to be, not that long ago, that the NRA was out-fundraising and outspending the gun control groups, but they’ve been falling off the last couple of cycles,” Gutowski said.

But since 2018, gun violence prevention groups like Everytown for Gun Safety and the Giffords Law Center have poured more money into elections than the NRA, which used to outspend them handily, according to an analysis of campaign spending by the Trace.

Now, at least one-third of US adults live in a home with one or more guns, according to the Pew Research Center. And an increasing number of them don’t share conservative views on issues like abortion, immigration and policing – but they do want to see fewer restrictions on guns and accessories, Pincus said.

This changing tide, he says, should be a sign that it’s time to detangle gun rights from traditional American conservatism and find liberal bedfellows.

“They need to get out of the culture war business,” Pincus said of gun rights groups. “It’s foolish to pretend that 100 million gun owners are only going to vote for Republicans.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Authorities say the boy was in the care of Michael Comer’s mother, but she left him with her son to run an errand

An 11-month-old South Carolina boy who authorities say was buried alive in a dog crate by his father was found by rescuers after about 24 hours, crying and covered in dirt, his grandfather said about the dramatic rescue.

But soon after, little Koah Sharp stopped crying, John Comer told the Associated Press on Wednesday night as he recalled the events that played out the day before in the woods on his neighbor’s property. The infant was put on the back of a truck and sat up, Comer said.

“I became ecstatic, my hands straight in the air. I’m looking in the sky, jumping up and down, praising God,” Comer said. “And at the same time I hit my knees and I’m just crying.”

Koah was released from a hospital Tuesday night and is expected to make a full recovery, sheriff Jay Koon said.

The boy’s father, Michael Comer, 25, has been charged with attempted murder. John Comer said he’d opened his home to his son and grandson on Monday after Michael Comer said they needed a place to stay.

Michael Comer has been in custody since Monday, when Koah disappeared. Authorities haven’t revealed anything about Comer’s motive. He was sentenced to probation in October after pleading guilty to domestic violence.

Koah’s parents “have had some situations”, the sheriff said.

“Children”, he said, “sometimes get caught in the middle”.

Survival was helped by cool temperatures and a towel

Dozens of first responders scoured the countryside looking for the boy with reddish blond hair. After a full day of searching, authorities found freshly disturbed soil and heard cries from below ground, the sheriff said.

“As you can imagine, the race was on. Everyone was trying to get him out,” Koon said.

The boy likely survived because of cool temperatures and an air pocket created by a towel that was wrapped around the crate below ground, he said.

Koah was soon freed and “clinging to life”, the sheriff told reporters.

Comer was arrested while hiding in a building in Batesburg-Leesville. It wasn’t immediately known if he has a lawyer who could respond to the charges. A court hearing was planned for Thursday.

“We’re better now that we know that Koah is safe,” his great-aunt, Amber Hammond, told the Associated Press. She was watching as he was freed from the crate.

Authorities said Koah had been in the care of Michael Comer’s mother. She had to run an errand and left the boy in her son’s care while another caregiver was on the way.

“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone, and Koah was gone with him,” the sheriff said.

Surveillance video from several businesses in the area showed Comer without the baby on Monday afternoon, Koon said.

John Comer said he feels like he was taken advantage of by his son when he asked for a place to stay. But, he said, he is also thankful that he agreed because if they had gone somewhere else they may not have found the boy in time.

“It just seems like he already had this planned out, and he knew what he was doing,” Comer said. “And he took the opportunity to do what he did. And if it hadn’t have been here, I don’t think anybody would have known where he would have went, and this would be a completely different story.”

Michael Comer had talked of taking the boy out of state.

Hammond said her nephew had talked about taking the baby to New York because “he didn’t want to be in the same state as the mom”. When Koah vanished, she and others assumed that Comer had given the boy to someone.

“We had no idea something like this would happen at all,” Hammond said.

Comer was sentenced to probation in October after pleading guilty to domestic violence and aggravated breach-of-peace charges related to an arrest in July, Lexington county online court records show. Prosecutors dropped a gun charge as part of the plea deal. He also got credit for spending more than two months in jail.

At nearly a year old, Koah has been trying to stand on his own, said Hammond, who cared for him last weekend. And he loves watching Mickey Mouse cartoons.

John Comer said he’d never heard his grandson cry before he was found underground.

“He’s always been happy,” he said. “The kid’s always got a smile on his face.”

Mayor Zohran Mamdani says crews are working through ‘extremely dangerous conditions’ to find anyone trapped

Rescue crews continued to search for survivors in the rubble of a collapsed building in Brooklyn, New York, at first light on Thursday as the death toll rose to eight.

Authorities in New York City said at least 17 people were hurt when the three-story residential building on the edge of a construction site in the borough’s Flatbush section collapsed at about 4pm on Wednesday.

Four people were critically injured, officials said, and at least seven children were among the victims; although it is not clear if any of the fatalities are minors.

Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, said in a post on X on Thursday morning that he was “heartbroken” by the tragedy.

“Eight New Yorkers have now lost their lives and at least 17 have been injured, including three firefighters,” he wrote.

“There are no words for a loss of this magnitude. My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today.”

He urged the public to stay away from the site on Flatbush Avenue, where about 250 first responders from the New York City fire department (FDNY) worked through what Mamdani said were “extremely dangerous conditions” to find anybody still trapped.

The department, in an emailed statement to the New York Times on Thursday morning, said it was still hopeful of locating survivors.

Workers brought in an excavator in the early hours of Thursday to help move larger pieces of the wreckage of the building, which had housed a number of apartments. Drones and canine units were being used to assist the rescue effort.

Video taken at the scene on Wednesday night showed crews removing several people on stretchers. One person, seen covered in dust, was extricated at about 6.30pm after a crew dug a hole through some of the debris.

Another person rescued was a six-months’ pregnant woman whose husband had been searching for her through the late afternoon, New York ABC News affiliate WABC reported.

“I have an update. She is alive, she is still alive. I am very happy,” the man told the outlet.

Dozens of onlookers, some in tears, gathered to watch the rescue operation. Lillian Bonsignore, the FDNY commissioner, told a Wednesday evening press conference crowd: “We know that we are not finished here, and we will likely not be finished for quite some time.”

Adding to the urgency of the situation was a weather forecast that predicted heavy rain with a chance of thunderstorms and gusty winds moving through the borough from lunchtime and through Thursday afternoon.

Several people made homeless by the collapse took shelter in the Bethesda Church of God in Christ opposite the site.

The building that collapsed was perched at the edge of a lot where another one-story building had been torn down for a construction project. The site was being excavated, and the building that fell down filled the construction pit with bricks and wood.

Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.

Investigators from New York City’s department of buildings were at the scene beginning an investigation into the cause of the collapse.

News channel NY1 reported that the department recorded multiple issues with a project next door to the collapsed building in May, including working while there was a stop work order, not having proper overhead protection for the neighboring properties and failing to conform to approved construction drawings.

The city’s department of housing, preservation and development has recorded almost 100 violations at the collapsed building dating to 1972, NY1 said.

Property records show the building as a three-story construction containing four residential units and one commercial unit.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Byard Duncan, Sophie Sullivan and Michael Hudson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Complaints about banks and other financial players keep rising as Trump officials squelch enforcement actions at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau

This story was supported and co-published by the journalism

non-profit the Economic Hardship Reporting Project

Early in Donald Trump’s second term, his administration began ditching consumer protection lawsuits involving some of the nation’s biggest-name corporate players – including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway empire.

Under the command of Trump officials, the federal agency that had filed the suits – the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) – was signaling it no longer believed these companies were hurting everyday Americans.

Many consumers across the nation disagree.

As the CFPB abandoned these enforcement efforts, its own data began to tell a troubling story. In the year following the dismissals of the lawsuits, complaints against the vast majority of companies whose cases were dismissed increased – sometimes dramatically.

A Guardian analysis of CFPB data shows that across all banks and corporations named as defendants in the now-dropped suits, the number of complaints published to the agency’s public database shot up by more than 75%.

Of the 23 financial firms named as defendants, 17 saw increases in the number of complaints against them.

Complaints published to the CFPB database against Rocket Mortgage increased more than 130% in the year after the bureau dropped a lawsuit accusing its sibling company, Rocket Homes, of using kickbacks to steer borrowers to Rocket Mortgage.

Complaints against Branch Messenger Inc, which had been accused of working with Walmart to harvest more than $10m in unfair banking fees from the big box chain’s delivery drivers, shot up 315% in the year after the case was dismissed.

These increases are part of a larger trend of everyday Americans letting the CFPB know they have concerns about the way companies have treated them. Publicly posted complaints to the agency have grown from nearly 2.7m in 2024 to 6.3m so far this year.

Experts – and current and former CFPB employees – say the spike in complaints against companies freed from enforcement actions points to a disconnect between the bureau’s mission and its actions.

“Consumers are telling the bureau that there is an emergency, and the bureau is not listening or acting on that information,” said Erie Meyer, a former chief technologist at the CFPB who helped oversee the creation of its complaint database. “People are getting screwed twice: first by the company, second by the agency that’s supposed to stick up for them.”

The dismissals of enforcement actions are part of a wide-ranging campaign by the Trump administration to deplete or dismantle an agency created a decade and a half ago to counter the reckless and predatory practices that helped spawn the Great Recession.

Between mid-2012 and early 2025, the bureau publicly launched nearly 400 enforcement actions against banks and other financial firms – an average of roughly 30 a year, according to the agency’s website. These actions, the agency has previously said, helped provide aggrieved consumers with more than $21bn in restitution and canceled debts.

Since Trump’s inauguration on 20 January 2025, the CFPB has launched just two public enforcement actions, its website indicates – one announced several days later and another brought in August 2025.

The current leadership of the CFPB did not reply to a detailed list of questions for this story. Instead, an agency spokesperson claimed in a statement that the CFPB had cost Americans hundreds of billions of dollars – “making the American Dream, like homeownership, more costly by the thousands for each borrower”.

“This Weaponized agency attacked political enemies and disfavored industries and used novel legal theories and secret justifications to ruin lives and businesses,” the statement added. “We are fixing that and bringing the agency back to operating within statute and away from breaking the law and helping all business and Americans who were victims of thuggery.”

The Guardian’s reporting on the CFPB’s enforcement rollback came amid midterm elections that were in large part a referendum on the high prices Americans pay for gas, food and shelter. Last week’s results produced big wins for Democrats who lashed Trump for policies that fueled the rise in living costs.

The next battles over high prices and abusive business tactics may turn on how aggressive the midterms’ winners are in fighting to protect struggling consumers.

The White House did not reply to questions for this story.

When Amanda and Jason Riffle got married in 2024, they struggled to find a place for their blended family of five. Rents around Clarksburg, West Virginia, were too high for the amount of space they needed, Amanda Riffle said.

After Jason’s family gave them a plot of land as a wedding gift, the couple went shopping for a doublewide manufactured home. They found what they wanted – a four-bedroom, 2.5 bath Southern Charm model. It was sold and financed by two companies that are part of Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway conglomerate: Clayton Homes and Vanderbilt Mortgage & Finance.

Like many Americans who have sued, filed CFPB complaints or simply regretted their dealings with financial firms, the Riffles say that what they hoped to be a good thing for them turned out to be something else. In their case, they alleged in a lawsuit that Clayton and Vanderbilt sold them the doublewide using “bait-and-switch” tactics that raised their costs beyond what they had been promised.

The 2025 suit, filed in state court and later shifted to federal court, claimed the couple was promised that the price for the doublewide would be just over $250,000 – with installation costs included – but just before closing Vanderbilt increased the price to more than $290,000. They later learned that the market value of the Southern Charm model was between $180,000 and $200,000, according to the suit, which was settled on confidential terms.

“They show you one number, and then it changes,” Amanda Riffle said in an interview with the Guardian. “They really did rush us through everything: ‘You just need to sign here, you need to sign here.’ They did not go over those things in detail.”

Their lawsuit was filed just over three months after the CFPB walked away from its own lawsuit against Vanderbilt. The agency’s case, filed in federal court in Tennessee, alleged that Vanderbilt had made large numbers of loans on manufactured homes “without making a reasonable and good-faith determination that the borrowers could repay them”.

The CFPB’s claims were echoed by two other private lawsuits filed in federal court in West Virginia around the same time by Mountain State Justice, the non-profit legal aid group that handled the Riffles’ case.

Both of these lawsuits alleged Vanderbilt failed to realistically evaluate the affordability of the loans for financially unsophisticated borrowers.

One of these cases, which was also settled on confidential terms, alleges that the supposedly independent closing agent who helped oversee the signing of the documents on the plaintiffs’ loan was a former long-time salesman for Clayton Homes who falsely claimed that he was the mayor of a small West Virginia town, using an email address that included the moniker “THE MAYOR41”.

The other case, which is set to go to trial in December, claims that one of the borrowers was “handicapped and reads at only a kindergarten level”.

CFPB data reviewed by the Guardian shows that the number of consumer complaints filed against Vanderbilt increased by 39% from the year before the CFPB dropped the case to the year after – rising from 84 to 117 complaints over that time.

In a statement, Vanderbilt said it “originates more than 20,000 loans and services more than 165,000 loans each year. The number of CFPB customer complaints we receive is extremely low, and a change of 33 complaints over 12 months is extraordinarily small.” It said none of the complaints in that time led to requests from the CFPB to change its lending practices.

The company said its practices “exceed the legal requirements for assessing a borrower’s ability to repay a loan”. It said it considers borrowers’ “debt-to-income ratio” as well their “residual income”, even though the law only requires the use of one or the other.

In court records in West Virginia, Vanderbilt said it follows federal “truth-in-lending” rules and that it made no misrepresentations to borrowers. In the case set to go to trial, the company said it “repeatedly and accurately disclosed the terms of the loan”.

Berkshire Hathaway, Vanderbilt’s parent, is not the only corporate conglomerate that the CFPB backed away from suing.

A month into Trump’s second term, the CFPB dropped a lawsuit against Rocket Homes, the sibling company of Rocket Mortgage, a leading home loan provider known for its heart-tugging Super Bowl commercials.

In a lawsuit in federal court in Michigan, the bureau claimed that Rocket Homes pressed real estate agents to steer home buyers toward Rocket Mortgage loans as part of a kickback scheme that discouraged homebuyers from shopping for the best deal. The lender charged higher rates and fees to borrowers who came to it through referrals via Rocket Homes, the lawsuit alleged.

This March, a year after the CFPB backed out of its case, an older American in Washington state complained to the agency that a banker had falsely promised them cash back for refinancing with Rocket Mortgage. Weeks after closing, the company told the borrower that the money had been “absorbed by closing costs”, according to the complaint narrative. The borrower wrote that his family had been “manipulated by deceptive information designed to entice us into spending thousands of dollars to refinance with Rocket Mortgage”.

Overall, complaints filed against Rocket Mortgage and published on the CFPB database more than doubled between the year before the agency dropped its Rocket Homes case to the year after – rising from 510 to 1,182.

Rocket said the agency’s claims against it “were baseless and the CFPB knew it”. It said Rocket Homes is focused on connecting home buyers “with top-performing agents based on objective criteria”.

“Any increase in complaints came as an obvious result of the increased size of the business,” the company added. “This year, a minuscule 0.040% of clients working with Rocket have filed a complaint.”

Three months after dropping the Rocket case, the CFPB backed off a lawsuit that alleged Walmart had forced its delivery drivers to use deposit accounts arranged through Branch Messenger, a tech company that administers a workforce payments and digital banking platform. These gig workers struggled to get access to their earnings and were forced to pay $10m in “junk fees” to transfer their money away to other accounts, the CFPB claimed.

Complaints against Branch published to the agency’s database increased from 46 the year before the case was dismissed to 191 the year after.

Dozens of Uber drivers, for example, filed complaints with the CFPB against Branch. Many described being locked out of Uber Pro Card accounts, set up through the tech firm, where their earnings had been deposited. “I worked to earn that money,” one driver wrote to the CFPB three months after the agency’s lawsuit was dismissed. “Branch has the money. I can not access my earnings and they seem content to keep the money and let me starve.”

Walmart, Branch and Uber did not respond to questions from the Guardian.

The agency also dropped a lawsuit that accused three of the nation’s top banks – JPMorgan, Bank of America and Wells Fargo – of failing to protect consumers from widespread fraud on Zelle, a well-known digital payment service partly owned by the three banks.

CFPB alleged the banks – and Zelle’s operator, Early Warning Services – pushed Zelle to market without effective consumer safeguards against fraudsters. The agency’s lawsuit claimed that failure led to more than $870m in customer losses.

In the year after the case was abandoned, CFPB saw a spike in complaints about a variety of concerns involving JPMorgan (up 19%), Wells Fargo (up 26%) and Bank of America (up nearly 33%).

The three banks declined to comment. An Early Warning spokesperson called the CFPB’s suit “meritless” and claimed it “sought to shift blame to Zelle for criminals’ actions”. The suit, the spokesperson added, “wrongly portrayed Zelle fraud countermeasures as ineffective, even though more than 99.98% of Zelle transactions are without report of fraud or scam”.

In a report published in March, the CFPB said that many of the enforcement actions that it dismissed “constituted agency overreach” and “should never have been undertaken”.

The CFPB was born in 2011, in the ruins of economic catastrophe. Predatory loans fueled by Wall Street money ignited a meltdown that destroyed hundreds of banks and spawned millions of job losses and home foreclosures. The US Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission laid much of the blame on a jumble of federal agencies that did little to stop these practices.

As the CFPB would later say: “It became clear that the nation needed a financial regulator solely focused on looking out for consumers.”

From the start, the new agency viewed publishing regular consumers’ complaints as an essential transparency tool.

“This is the only place where you see a granular-level description of what’s actually happening to people,” Meyer said. The database was designed to be “public by default” because “we don’t want to wait until it’s front page news – or financial institutions snapping the economy in half – before we catch these problems.”

Not everyone appreciated the bureau’s work.

The authors of Project 2025, the conservative roadmap for Trump’s second term, called for the CFPB’s destruction, describing it as a “highly politicized, damaging and utterly unaccountable federal agency”.

Trump claimed he knew nothing about Project 2025. But soon after he returned to office, he appointed Russell Vought, a key architect of the plan, as acting director of the CFPB and fired Rohit Chopra, who had been the agency’s director during the Biden administration and was known as an advocate for aggressive enforcement.

Trump told reporters that the agency “was a very important thing to get rid of”. He claimed he had gotten calls from “lending officers” and “owners of small banks” who were “almost crying” because they had been put “out of business” by the agency.

The White House did not reply to a request from the Guardian to describe the circumstances of the calls and identify which financial institutions, according to Trump, had been driven out of business.

Under Vought, the agency tried at one point to lay off nearly 90% of its workforce and moved to slash its own funding, but was blocked by federal court rulings on both fronts.

Vought, who is Trump’s budget director, did not reply to questions about his time running the agency.

Recently the agency has made it more difficult for consumers to find out about complaints against financial firms. In August it announced that it would no longer publish consumer complaint narratives, which it said “present only one side of an issue”. Soon after, it removed millions of these consumer experiences from its online complaint database.

The public can no longer search the database and quickly see the experiences of consumers who say they have had problems with specific companies. Instead, they must download enormous complaint files from the CFPB’s website and sort them manually.

Meyer, the former CFPB official, said stripping away complaint narratives “is an unconscionable waste of time and effort and money”.

“We built this complaint system so we would never again get to a place where people would be flying blind about what’s happening to people who are white-knuckling their spot in the middle class,” she said.

Along with dropping enforcement cases against more than 20 companies, the CFPB has also pulled back on multiple issues that are big worries for many Americans. For example, it has deprioritized scrutiny of digital payments, student loans and medical debt.

Explaining its shifting priorities, the agency has said it aims to focus on “tangible harms” and “pressing threats to consumers” – “particularly service members and their families, and veterans”.

It also announced it would no longer focus on enforcing truth-in-lending laws in connection to “buy now, pay later” loans, an expanding corner of the US credit market. These loans, sometimes known as BNPLs, spread out purchases and bill payments over several interest-free installments. Consumers often use them to buy clothing, smartphones and even groceries or cover rent and car repairs.

The nonprofit National Consumer Law Center has reported that BNPLs can sometimes be a reasonable alternative to paying up front or using a credit card, but they often come with late charges and other fees that can turn “what looks like free financing” into “a high cost loan”.

In the year after CFPB announced it was pulling back on watchdogging these transactions, published complaints to the agency about some of the industry’s largest players grew significantly. Klarna, a BNPL provider headquartered in Stockholm, saw a 382% jump – from 290 published complaints to the agency in the year before compared with 1,398 in the year after.

Jennifer Zhang, a policy, research and data analyst at the non-profit group, Protect Borrowers, said the agency’s pullback on BNPLs sends a signal that even if consumers are sounding the alarm about abusive practices, “the CFPB is not listening”.

A Guardian review of agency data also shows that its retreat on BNPLs may conflict with its promise to protect service members and veterans.

Complaints filed by these groups against some of the biggest BNPL companies generally grew at a higher rate than complaints by other types of consumers, CFPB data show. Current and former service members’ complaints against Klarna, for example, increased 465%.

At the same time, complaints filed by service members and veterans have increased against many of the companies whose CFPB enforcement suits were dropped by the Trump administration. This includes an 135% increase – from 64 to 151 year over year – in service member and veteran complaints against Rocket Mortgage.

Klarna did not respond to questions from the Guardian. The BNPL industry’s leaders insist they have strong safeguards in place to protect consumers. Some say they factor borrowers’ repayment histories in lending decisions.

In early 2023, the Biden-era CFPB teamed up with New York attorney general Letitia James in a lawsuit alleging that a top subprime auto lender, Credit Acceptance Corporation, had soaked car buyers with hidden costs and high-interest loans they couldn’t afford.

When Trump took office, the bureau swiftly ended its partnership with New York state and withdrew from the suit.

In the year following CFPB’s withdrawal, complaints about the lender continued to stream into the agency, describing many of the same issues the suit sought to address. In all, complaints against Credit Acceptance increased by 34% – from 2,722 to 3,652.

In July a customer from Pennsylvania wrote that they had been charged an inflated sales price based on a slew of fees and financed add-ons. “I believe this is the exact type of lending practice that consumer protection laws are intended to prevent,” the consumer wrote.

In September, James announced a $700m settlement with Credit Acceptance that included her state as well as 39 other states and Washington DC.

The company did not answer questions for this story. It noted in a statement on its website that the settlement “was reached without any admission of fault or wrongdoing”. The statement said that policies and practices required under the agreement “are broadly consistent with our focus on customers and our mission of changing lives” and “do not fundamentally alter the company’s business model”.

The CFPB did not answer a question from the Guardian about the case, either. It has previously said that it wants to leave many enforcement and supervision priorities to state agencies.

But consumer law experts say that states often do not have the resources or reach to carry out a truly national strategy to challenge questionable practices at the nation’s most powerful companies.

In the wake of the historic results in the midterm elections, some Democrats will seek to reverse the CFPB’s enforcement rollback and push to re-establish it as a national leader in fighting unfair financial practices.

In written statements, Representative Bill Foster of Illinois and Senators Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada told the Guardian they plan to aggressively scrutinize what has happened at the CFPB since Trump returned to office.

“Next Congress, my colleagues on the Financial Services Committee and I will investigate the unconstitutional dismantling of the CFPB,” Foster said, adding that he and other committee members will pursue “subpoenas, investigations, hearings, and, ultimately, legislative action to restore consumer protections in this country and hold accountable those who seek to profit off the most vulnerable Americans”.

The Senate will also decide whether to approve Trump’s pick to replace Vought, who left his position as the CFPB’s acting director in August. Trump’s nominee to lead the agency, Brian Johnson, served as its deputy director during the first Trump administration.

More recently, he has been a vice-president overseeing credit card compliance at Capital One, which is among the companies whose CFPB lawsuits were dropped by the agency.

The case, which accused Capital One of misleading some customers about interest rates on saving accounts, was withdrawn a month after Trump’s inauguration. The number of public complaints to CFPB about a variety of concerns about Capital One rose from 27,193 in the year before the case was dismissed to 29,646 the year after, a 9% increase.

Capital One did not reply to questions from the Guardian. Johnson has agreed to recuse himself from any CFPB action related to Capital One for two years if he is confirmed.

Austin Hinkle, a former senior counsel and section chief at the CFPB, said that along with investigating “corporate pardons” received by companies sued by the agency, Congress should also look at the administration’s push to cut or erase financial penalties in already completed enforcement actions.

In one case in 2025, CFPB officials went back to court to ask a judge to allow them to refund a $105,000 penalty paid by an Illinois mortgage company accused of racial discrimination. The judge denied the request.

In another case, Trump officials reopened a settlement with a major money services business, Wise US Inc.

In January 2025, 10 days after Trump’s inauguration, the CFPB had announced that Wise had agreed to resolve allegations it had misled US customers about its ATM fees and failed to properly disclose other fees. (Wise did not admit or deny the agency’s findings.) Along with roughly $450,000 in consumer refunds, the agreement required Wise to pay a $2.025m fine.

The resolution of the case was the last major enforcement action handled by CFPB before Trump appointees took over. The consent order was signed by Rohit Chopra, Biden’s CFPB director. Trump fired him the next day.

Four months later, the agency revealed that it had renegotiated its deal with Wise.

A new signature appeared in looping blue script on the updated version: Chopra’s replacement, Russell Vought.

The new agreement lowered Wise’s fine – from $2.025m to $44,955.

Mariama Eversley contributed reporting

Members of Democratic Socialists of America have a unique opportunity to fulfill campaign promises and group’s ideals

As progressive candidates scored wins across the country last week, a historic number of socialists swept into power – in Congress, in state legislatures and at the helm of American cities.

Democratic Socialists of America members Nithya Raman and Janeese Lewis George were elected to lead the second largest US city – Los Angeles – and the capital – Washington DC respectively. Two other young DSA members, David Morales and Yousef Rabhi, were elected mayors of Providence, Rhode Island, and Ann Arbor, Michigan. They will join a handful of socialist mayors in smaller cities, including Burlington, Vermont, and Irvine, California – as well as Zohran Mamdani, the democratic socialist mayor of New York, the largest city in the US.

Mamdani, who grew up politically within New York City’s DSA chapter and has become the insurgent leftist group’s best known representative, was considered a long-shot candidate before his meteoric rise. He’s now one of the most popular politicians in the country and his election is widely credited with inspiring historic numbers of democratic socialists surging to office across the country and up and down the ballot.

Come January, the number of DSA members in Congress will have quadrupled (to eight), and more than 100 DSA-endorsed candidates will sit in local, state and national office. But DSA mayors, who have authority over more prosaic elements of governance, from garbage pickup to snow days, face a unique opportunity to prove to the public that the group’s ideals of affordability and inclusivity can improve the lives of working people – the central tenet of DSA’s vision.

“It’s the executive office, so the stakes are actually higher there,” said Eric Blanc, an assitant professor of labor studies at Rutgers University and DSA member.

“If politics cannot deliver on the block where you live, why would you trust it to deliver anywhere?” Mamdani told a gathering of mayors from around the world, on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly earlier this fall. “If you are making a New Yorker’s life a little smoother, so too you are making their journey to believe in government’s ability to deliver for them.”

According to the New York Times, which covered the event, Mamdani made the remarks to fellow mayors to explain his fixation with potholes – his office says he has repaired more than 200,000 since taking office.

Similar to Mamdani, the incoming DSA mayors have run campaigns focused on affordability and practical improvement to people’s lives. Raman, an urban planner, has promised more housing and public transit improvements. Lewis George has campaigned on universal childcare, public housing and better protections for tenants. Morales has pitched affordable housing and called for corporations to contribute a larger share toward public education and city services. Rabhi has pledged to fight data centers and keep utilities affordable.

While his critics have generally focused on debates with little to do on municipal government, Mamdani has been focused on delivering on campaign promises such as a rent freeze, universal childcare and taxing the rich.

“Zohran already demonstrated proof of concept, contrary to all of the predictions of imminent collapse” of the city, Blanc said. “He has already demonstrated what democratic socialist governance can look like.”

“If others can follow this model, which is to take big fights against the rich and powerful, be out there proving to people that you can make their lives better, I think that is going to be what will help avoid some of the real difficulties of governing,” he added.

Katie Wilson, the mayor of Seattle and a self-identified democratic socialist – though not a DSA member – agreed. She called a mayor’s job “the best in the world” and noted that the office requires a mix of “the high and the low”.

“There’s big vision and ambitions and values, and then on the other hand a lot of the job is the real nitty-gritty of keeping the lights on,” she said. “It’s really important as socialists and progressives coming into office that we’re able to get those nitty-gritty details right, do the basics well.”

As a growing number of progressives have called on Democrats to “deliver”, following last week’s landslide wins, mayors will be the first to have to show results. Wilson said they should deliver on what is within their reach and maintain close working relationships with the grassroots organizers that helped them get elected.

“What people are affirming in voting for progressives and socialists in this moment, is that we believe in the power of government to improve people’s lives,” she said.

Even when the ability to deliver falls beyond their municipal authority, a mayor should show people “that you’re fighting for them”, she added.

“You’re not going to build socialism in one city ultimately, but how do you embody those values, and that vision, and take real, tangible steps toward socialistic policies, in a way that improves the daily lives of the residents of your city?”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Trump the ‘biggest loser’ for scrapping climate action, John Kerry says at Cop31
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Oliver Milman in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Kerry decries president for ceding clean-energy dominance to China and says climate crisis still a key issue for voters

Donald Trump is the “biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time” for scrapping action on the climate crisis and ceding the clean energy race to China, former US secretary of state John Kerry has said.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Kerry, speaking at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, criticized Trump for withdrawing the US from the international climate process and axing measures that reduced planet-heating emissions. Unlike almost all other countries in the world, the Trump administration has sent no delegation to the resort city of Antalya for the annual UN climate talks, which started on Monday.

The US president, who has previously called climate science a “hoax” and called for countries to drill for more oil and gas, again expressed his hostility towards clean energy on Monday. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser,” Trump, who has long-held animus towards wind farms, said about potential new legislation that would make it easier to build new energy projects.

Asked about his comments by the Guardian, Kerry said: “[The] first thing they should do is hold up a really big mirror so he can look at a loser, because he’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues.”

“He’s missing the point,” Kerry, a former climate envoy for Joe Biden’s administration, added. “He’s missing the competitiveness with China. He’s missing the marketplace for goods that could be produced in the United States. We could be the supply chain for some of these.”

Under Biden, the US passed sweeping climate legislation that gave tax breaks for clean energy and electric vehicle manufacturing in a bid to compete with China, which has dominated clean tech.

Republicans eliminated most of this support, however, with Trump instead imposing tariffs on various goods and pouring public money into propping up struggling coal-fired power plants. Coal is the dirtiest of fossil fuels, causing much of the pollution that is dangerously overheating our planet.

“He declared he wanted to beat China, be number one in X, Y, or Z, and he walked away from the battlefield,” Kerry said of Trump. “He totally took America out of that sector. So honestly, if you want to be number one, you don’t do it by literally blackballing an entire sector of the economy.”

Kerry, who ran as the Democratic candidate for president in 2004, has repeatedly urged the US and the rest of the world to follow China’s lead on green energy. The overall rapid growth in renewables has helped prevent a significant amount of fossil fuel power going online, with global emissions edging down slightly last year.

Far larger and deeper cuts to emissions will be needed for the world to avoid catastrophic climate change, however, with countries gathering at Cop told by António Guterres, the UN secretary general, it was “long past time” to phase out fossil fuel use.

The dawdling progress in years of talks to even discuss fossil fuels, the central cause of the climate crisis, has provoked ire from advocates. “Cops have become greenwashed circuses,” said Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, who arrived in Antalya on Tuesday. “That is the reality.”

Kerry acknowledged the ponderous progress and that politicians should talk differently about the climate crisis to engage the public. But he claimed that while it was not the central issue to the recent US midterm elections, concerns about global heating did overlap with alarm over rising energy costs and drove voters to the Democrats.

“I think we will have a number of candidates who will have this high on the agenda,” Kerry said of the victorious Democratic candidates. “And all of the analysis that I’ve seen, I mean real analysis, has said this was one of the issues that counted.”

The White House has dismissed the Cop 31 talks. “This summit rejects reality by failing to acknowledge that extremist climate policies are destroying countries around the world,” a White House official said, confirming that the administration would not send anyone to Cop31.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Former US secretary of state John Kerry says Donald Trump is the 'biggest loser we've seen in a long time' for scrapping action on the climate crisis. Kerry says he will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrat Scott Colom unseats Cindy Hyde-Smith in stunning Mississippi Senate win
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adria R Walker in Mississippi
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Colom takes victory by razor-thin margin in state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982

Democrat Scott Colom defeated Cindy Hyde-Smith, the incumbent Republican senator, to become the first Black senator in Mississippi elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom told a crowd of hundreds who on Wednesday had gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, said there were times his long-shot campaign felt defeated but “I had to have faith.”

Colom opened up a narrow lead over Hyde-Smith late on election night. His lead widened as election officials counted absentee and provisional ballots. The Associated Press called the contest on Wednesday, after it was clear Hyde-Smith was not able to close the gap.

In a two-minute concession video shared on social media, Hyde-Smith said: “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters.” She offered her congratulations to Colom and said she wished him well “as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state”.

Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. It’s been much longer – not since 1875 – that the state sent a Black senator to Washington. Colom is also the first Black man popularly elected to the Senate in the state’s history – during Reconstruction, senators were chosen by state lawmakers.

With Colom’s election, Mississippi, the first state to send Black lawmakers to Congress, has sent more Black people to the Senate than any other state besides Illinois. Blanche K Bruce, the last Black man elected to the Senate from Mississippi, was born into slavery; John C Stennis, the last Democrat to be sent from Mississippi, was, for most of his career, a staunch segregationist.

Colom’s election capped a national wave of anger at Donald Trump’s administration, sweeping away Republicans in places where Democrats hadn’t been competitive in decades. With the addition of Colom, Democrats will hold at least 55 seats in the Senate – the party’s largest midterm gain since 1986.

Across the south, voters were further motivated by the president’s attempt to drastically redraw Black majority districts, attempting to dilute the largely Democratic voting blocs.

Colom has a track record of success in the state. In 2015, Colom unseated a nearly 30-year incumbent when he was elected the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit. As district attorney, he had a 94% success rate for convictions. He’s a seventh-generation Mississippian, whose father was a longtime Republican who campaigned for Ronald Reagan and was friendly with Thad Cochran, a longtime state politician who resigned from his US Senate seat in 2018 due to declining health.

A string of Democratic stars visited the state late in the race as the polls showed a tightening race – Cory Booker, Pete Buttigieg, Kamala Harris and Bill Clinton all made appearances for Colom. Trump rallied for Hyde-Smith last month.

Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a federal judge in the northern district of Mississippi. With support from both Republicans and Democrats, he appeared to be on track to a lifetime appointment on the federal bench, when Hyde-Smith blocked him from having a confirmation hearing.

“I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being a US senator,” Hyde-Smith said in remarks to supporters on election day.

In the days after the election, as Colom’s vote-margin inched higher, he kept a dizzying campaign pace, visiting Millsaps College, his alma mater, and local colleges Jackson State University and Tougaloo College. With national and international cameras on him, Colom stopped by small, local businesses, including Marshall’s Music and Book Store and OffBeat, both of which are Black-owned, and Brent’s Drugs, a Jackson classic.

Colom campaigned on the promise that “Mississippi matters”. He told voters that he would represent all Mississippians, even those who supported his opponent – and the president.

A week before the vote, he attended Trump’s rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth to engage the president’s supporters and listen to their economic concerns. He posed for photos with some rally-goers, as they talked to him about high gas prices, grocery bills and health insurance. He later said the face-to-face conversations helped him convert the unlikeliest of voters to his campaign.

Colom drew national attention for a viral ad that played on his opponent’s response to a question about the rising cost of beef: “You have so many proteins to choose from,” Hyde-Smith told a local television host during the interview. Colom’s campaign seized on the moment, producing a 30-second ad that jumps from her reply to a man grilling beef patties. “Pick another protein?” the man says. “Shiiiit. I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Colom drove a “pick your protein” taco truck around the state, handing out free tacos to voters.

As the days-long counting process commenced, both Hyde-Smith and Colom projected confidence that they would prevail.

National voting groups and attorneys descended upon the Magnolia state, joining the local groups that worked to mobilize voters. Democratic and Republican groups, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) and Democratic election attorneys from the Elias Law Group, have deployed hundreds of volunteers and lawyers to all the state’s 82 counties to oversee the final rounds of counting.

Mississippi has no automatic recount law. A recount can only happen if ordered by a court in response to a lawsuit against a county or county election commission from a political party or campaign. Mississippi law does not establish a system for challenging ballots on a statewide scale, so the process would have to be on a county-by-county basis.

“I assure you,” Hyde-Smith said on election night, “I will continue to be your US senator.”

Asked about those comments at a press conference the next day, Colom replied: “Bless her heart.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Scott Colom, 43, is the first black senator in Mississippi elected since Reconstruction. He defeated Cindy Hyde-Smith, the incumbent Republican senator, to become the first Black senator in the state since Reconstruction. Mississippi has no automatic recount law.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrats push to rein in Trump on immigration after voter backlash to ICE raids
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Alexandra Villarreal in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Members of Congress seek to ‘bring sanity’ to system but decline to give details on plans to reform or abolish agency

A group of congressional Democrats on Wednesday pushed for immediate efforts to rein in the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration enforcement operation and “bring sanity” to an immigration system that Donald Trump said, after his party’s midterm drubbing, had been “too tough” in certain aspects.

Just over a week after the midterm elections in which the US president’s harsh crackdown on immigration fueled a voter backlash against Republicans, some sitting and newly elected Democrats gathered outside the US Capitol in Washington to advocate for a bipartisan approach to reforms – even as they gear up to take control of both legislative chambers next year.

“I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform. But I am also a pragmatist. And as we have – as we continue to have – Donald Trump in the White House, and without a supermajority in the Senate, we need Republican support. So any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan,” said congresswoman Veronica Escobar, a Democrat from Texas whose district includes El Paso on the US-Mexico border.

The group’s press conference included progressive as well as moderate Democrats from the Senate and House, in a show of unity. Many attendees held signs saying “legal pathways for long-term immigrants”.

The one Republican lawmaker slated to attend, congresswoman Maria Salazar of Florida, who has taken jabs at the president over immigration that are rare from his side of the aisle, did not appear.

“There is time still this session for a deal,” said US senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona. “We should try to work, even if we can’t get something this session, next session for a deal. We owe it to this country. We owe it to our friends.”

He added: “Republicans have been saying we will have immigration reform as soon as we have a safe, secure border. We have that right now. We did the job. Now let’s figure out how to right-size our immigration issue. Let’s figure out how to keep families together.”

The remarks followed Trump’s aggressive mass deportation campaign and ruthless moves that dramatically slowed crossings at the border, beginning as soon as he re-entered the White House in January 2025. His Democratic predecessor Joe Biden saw significantly elevated levels of migration at the border, and despite his at times harsh approach, the subject of migration became a high-risk political topic for Democrats, who gained a reputation as being too soft on the issue.

Since then, Trump’s second term has also seen US citizens and immigrants killed by immigration enforcement agents, record numbers of people held in often squalid detention conditions and highly visible, violent tactics in the country’s interior that led many voters to sour on some of his policies or at least how they are carried out.

The president’s mixed messages post-midterms included a tentative offer to make a deal with Democrats to help longstanding and law-abiding undocumented immigrants in the US avoid his crackdown. But that contrasted sharply with his actions so far, and shortly after the comments were recorded for TV he named Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff despite him being the architect and orchestrator of Trump’s most draconian, white nationalist immigration policies.

Trump has also signaled that he intends to use his presidential veto power often to block Democratic-supported legislation if it passes Congress.

At the same time, experts expect a barrage of investigations and oversight hearings from Democrats next year in an effort to bring accountability.

But lawmakers on Wednesday said they did not want to wait that long to begin improving the immigration system, highlighting two existing bipartisan bills they believe could be a practical starting point. There was no detailed talk on Wednesday of how to abolish or even significantly reform Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) despite it being a hot topic during the election campaign.

The first highlighted by the lawmakers who spoke on Wednesday, the American Dream and Promise Act, focuses on providing legal pathways to a green card for undocumented immigrants brought stateside as children, colloquially known as “Dreamers”, as well as people with temporary protections to remain in the US while their country of origin experiences serious turmoil.

Not only has Trump not offered such a path, his administration stopped recognizing many temporary legal statuses awarded under past Democratic administrations and has been deporting or trying to deport many who have papers or long-term legal options.

Lawmakers on Wednesday pitched the proposed legislation as an opportunity to act even before the new Democratically-controlled Congress is sworn in come January, asking for Trump’s help in getting it past the finish line.

“We all can agree that the immigration system is broken. But we can start today on a path to build a foundation with the Dream and Promise Act, and to move forward next year when we take over to make even more reforms,” said representative Sylvia Garcia of Texas.

Separately, the Dignity Act is the only bipartisan, comprehensive immigration reform bill introduced in over a decade, with 35 Democratic and 20 Republican sponsors. It couples strict border security measures with some protections for undocumented people.

Salazar is the bill’s lead sponsor. But Escobar, one of the Dignity Act’s fiercest champions and its co-author, said that she and her colleagues planned to reshape it over the next few weeks before reintroducing it next legislative session.

“If we can get this passed this upcoming Congress, we can do even more in 2028 to grow and expand what we can do for immigrants, immigrant families, and our economy and our communities,” she said. “We need to bring sanity back to the immigration system. We can do this. We will do this.”

Meanwhile, representative Henry Cuellar, another Texas border-area Democrat, expects to chair the House appropriations homeland security subcommittee in the new year – and thus control the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) funding.

He said he has a list of guardrails to revert ICE, which comes under the DHS agency, to its role prior to Trump’s second term.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The Dignity Act is a bipartisan bill that has 35 Democratic and 20 Republican sponsors. It couples strict border security measures with some protections for undocumented people.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio and Shrai Popat in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Eleven Democrats missed the key procedural vote on the impeachment effort, which failed by just seven votes

Democratic lawmakers expressed outrage at nearly a dozen of their colleagues for missing a vote Tuesday evening to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, allowing Republicans to defeat the effort.

Eleven Democrats missed the key procedural vote on the impeachment effort, which failed by just seven votes. Some blamed traffic and conflicting events and others accused Speaker Mike Johnson of closing the vote early. Many of those not in the Capitol said they support the effort to impeach Hegseth.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

“You should show up and do your job,” Abdul El-Sayed, the senator-elect of Michigan, said on CNN to the Democratic lawmakers Tuesday.

Richard Ojeda, the representative-elect of North Carolina, told CNN that the Democratic representatives “failed” by not voting.

“Shame on them for not showing up,” Ojeda said on Tuesday. “I mean, this is important … they had an opportunity to finally get rid of this buffoonery we had.”

The missing Democrats gave House Republicans the numbers to shelve the impeachment effort by voting 211 – 204 to refer eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth to a House committee.

Speaking at Arlington national cemetery to mark Veterans Day, Donald Trump praised Hegseth and said he had done a “fantastic job” as the Pentagon head.

“I had a feeling that was going to happen,” the president said of the failed effort to impeach Hegseth, adding: “He loves you, and he protects you – he’s all about you.”

The articles, introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, included charges of violating congressional authority by waging war in Iran. The effort came after voters overwhelming cast ballots for Democratic candidates in the 2026 midterms, largely in rebuke of the Trump administration’s policies – including the war in Iran.

Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a representative from California, told MeidasTouch there was “no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues”.

“This is what the people have been talking about … so shame on folks who were not here because these people lost,” Kamlager-Dove added.

Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico wrote on X that she was “blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due to a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote”.

“When she reached the chamber the vote had just gaveled out. She immediately filed a report of her vote of ‘NO’ to the motion meant to kill the impeachment articles and refer them to the Judiciary Committee, as documented in the Congressional Record,” Stansbury wrote, adding that Hegseth “must be impeached now”.

Laura Gillen of New York similarly wrote on X she too was stuck in traffic but “strongly” believes Hegseth should be impeached. Jonathan Jackson, of Illinois, wrote on X that he also was stuck behind the traffic jam.

Brittany Pettersen of Colorado wrote on X that she was “denied” the ability to vote. A member of Pettersen’s office later told 9News she too was stuck in traffic.

Julia Brownley of California wrote on Facebook that Johnson “closed the vote” before she could make it to the House floor.

“As I and many of my colleagues were rushing to the floor to support Hegseth’s impeachment, Mike Johnson closed the vote before we could,” Brownley wrote.

Marilyn Strickland of Washington also missed the vote by one minute because she was stuck behind a motocade, but that she would have voted to impeach Hegseth, Strickland’s office told Politico.

Nancy Pelosi of California missed the vote because she was in San Francisco to meet with local veterans and accept a Lifetime Advocate for Veterans Award, Pelosi’s spokesperson told SFGate.

Lou Correa of California wrote on Instagram that he was undergoing a medical procedure and remaining in his district until he was medically cleared.

Steven Horsford of Nevada, Haley Stevens of Michigan and Frederica Wilson of Florida did not provide public reasons for their absence on Tuesday.

Several Democratic lawmakers who did vote on the effort to impeach Hegseth noted that they were also busy with other life events but still made their way to the Capitol.

Pat Ryan of New York wrote on X that he was recovering from back surgery but left the hospital early in order to cast his vote.

Congressman Glenn Ivey, a Maryland Democrat, called the absence of the 11 lawmakers during Tuesday’s vote “certainly disappointing”, but said there would be “other chances” to advance impeachment efforts.

In an interview, Ivey said he was “absolutely” supportive of renewing the push when Democrats regain control of both chambers in January.

At the same time, he argued that voters made clear that concerns about the cost of living remain their top priority.

“There aren’t a lot of people, in my district anyway, [whose ability] to stay in their house depends on whether Hegseth gets impeached or not,” Ivey said. “We’ve been calling it the affordability agenda, but I think for many people, it’s really a survivability agenda, and we need to be focused on that.”

This article was amended on 11 November 2026. An earlier version incorrectly stated that Brittany Pettersen was from California; in fact, she is from Colorado.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Thanks to American oligarchy, Jensen Huang’s midlife crisis is a problem for all of us | Moira Donegan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Moira Donegan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
At a time when individual men wield massive power, the ramifications of the Nvidia CEO’s affair could be enormous

O
ne of the reasons you want to distribute power and responsibility in powerful organizations and high-stakes enterprises is so that the narcissism or myopia of one man do not come to carry outsized consequences.

When power is spread out across multiple people, it matters less if one of those people is prone to flattery, or in the midst of a midlife crisis, or perhaps just a bit stupid; the limits on his power become limits on the fallout of his character flaws.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall
