A broad distribution of authority also has the virtue of making any one man disposable, replaceable: if he turns out to have poor judgement or counterproductive preoccupations, he can be dispensed with, and his role can be filled anew with someone better suited to its responsibilities.

But if one man becomes synonymous with a company – or a country – then untold numbers of other people live and die by that man’s decisions. And when his decisions are bad – petty, selfish, shortsighted, small-minded or dumb – then it is other people who will pay the price. And the price is often quite steep.

Because we live in an era of massive inequality, tightly consolidated corporate leadership, and rule by a billionaire class with large egos and deficient dignity, the US economy is now experiencing one of the latter scenarios, in the form of Jensen Huang, a Silicon Valley billionaire who this week confessed to having an extramarital affair.

This would be tacky and embarrassing for Huang on its own. But because Huang is the CEO of Nvidia, one of the country’s largest companies and the manufacturer of advanced chip technology that is powering the US’s AI boom, his petty midlife crisis – the kind of small-minded narcissism that can usually be dispensed with in the form of a red sportscar, or indeed with one of the cheesy leather jackets that Huang is prone to wearing – is now a problem for the US economy, and potentially for national security.

Because Huang’s mistress was not just any of the interchangeable young women that such men usually go for. This one happened to be a suspected Chinese spy.

It’s unclear how much the woman, Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang – no relation – learned from her relationship with the tech billionaire, or how the information she may have gathered could undermine US economic and military interests.

Alice Huang worked in television in China before becoming an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company and one of the largest purchasers of Nvidia’s advanced chips. Megaspeed was under investigation by the US commerce department on suspicion of smuggling the advanced chips to China, which is banned from importing them by US law. (Megaspeed said it had offered to cooperate with the US government’s investigation but those offers went unanswered.)

According to the New York Times, the investigation was abruptly halted last year after the general counsel for Nvidia, Jensen Huang’s company, intervened. Among other things, Jensen Huang is known for his close relationship with Donald Trump.

On Sunday, Huang issued a statement admitting to an affair, and his company announced that it would be launching an investigation into the incident. “The Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” which is perhaps a bit too hopeful.

But the statement itself is a reflection of the depth of Huang’s control over the country. If you or I had endangered corporate secrets and state security in a flight of reckless, narcissistic frivolity, the way Huang may have done, then our employers would not be announcing the investigation while we kept our jobs. Nvidia’s stocks were down when the markets opened on Monday. They may well go down further still.

And yet the scandal is fitting for our current era of Silicon Valley, in which loyalty to Donald Trump has gone from a strategic move by major tech companies to ensure favorable contract and regulatory terms to much more full-throated embrace of the ideology and style of the far right.

Following the lead of its major male executives, the tech industry has become reckless and irresponsible, proud of itself for accelerating technologies it plainly claims to be unable to control, demanding investments in datacenters and government contracts from taxpayers whom it smugly brags about putting out of jobs, and flooding our aesthetic and informational worlds with low-grade slop that is frequently factually inaccurate, often dangerous for vulnerable users, and uncanny in its unpleasantness, bearing a creepy and inhuman sheen in its images and language.

The leaders of this industry seem oblivious to how they appear to other people, and perhaps, insulated by their money and their sycophantic underlings, it does not occur to them that nobody wants the future that they are ushering in, the one they are insisting we all must pay for.

How much money does it take to be so cut off from reality? How much money did Jensen Huang need to have before he convinced himself that Alice Huang, pale, skinny, and fluttering her eyelashes at him at a conference, liked him for his personality?

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

The affair is a sign of the power of a man who wields massive power, writes John Sutter. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Billions lost and markets roiled by one man’s indiscretion. Isn’t it now clear that these tech bros are too powerful? | Aditya Chakrabortty
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Aditya Chakrabortty
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair must be the costliest fling in human history – and a preview of what awaits when the tech bubble bursts

O
ne thing we all know about the tech billionaires is they are super-smart. We know this largely because they never stop telling us. The “cognitive elite”, to use their favoured phrase, are entitled to shape our future without our say-so. When Elon Musk goes hiring, he wants “super-high-IQ small-government revolutionaries”. Long before they got private jets, what fuelled these boys was faith in their own brainpower. As a teenager, Jensen Huang wooed his future wife, Lori, thus: “If you do homework with me every Sunday, I promise you you’ll get straight As.”

Lord Byron: I believe it’s your move.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Which raises the question: if you’re that clever, why act so dumb? At last week’s midterms, it was Musk who backed Team Trump to the tune of $446m. With unhedged bets like that, why wouldn’t you want him gambling with your livelihood? This week, it is 63-year-old Huang and his affair with a much younger woman, who the US government strongly suspects is a Chinese spy. That scandal wiped more than $400bn off the value of his company in just two days, making it the costliest fling in human history. But who knows? Perhaps she loved the centibillionaire for his mind.

Forget Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: no one is more central to the future of technology than Huang. He runs Nvidia, which makes the chips powering AI. Previous generations of chips have been compared to kitchen knives: however sharp, they only chop one vegetable at a time. But the graphics-processing units made by Huang’s business are more like food blenders – they can blitz an entire veg patch. That’s what makes Nvidia the foundational infrastructure company of AI and one of the most valuable businesses in the world. And it uses its power: in some of the biggest funny-money deals over the past year in AI, Nvidia has been the money printer. It also stumped up at least $20m for Donald Trump’s new ballroom. Smart!

Not only is Huang one of Trump’s favourite businessmen, he’s warmly welcomed by leaders around the world – including Andy Burnham, who last month in London sank a whisky with him. Even as he falls from grace, Huang’s supporters have brought out the superlatives: “torchbearer”, “irreplaceable”, “incredible human”.

Huang is boss of the most strategically important business in the fastest-growing, biggest-spending industry in the world’s No 1 capitalist economy. He is part of a tiny coterie of people, who may well feel they sit above the norms and laws that govern the rest of us. That’s certainly the way he has been treated so far by Trump, who was personally warned aboard Air Force One that Huang’s love interest is believed to be a spy for Beijing. Not only is China an ever-greater threat to US AI dominance, it has been banned by Washington from getting Nvidia’s top-of-the-range chips. And the US president takes no discernible action.

Some people are in a huge tizz about the spy part of this story, notably the Tory MP Tom Tugendhat, who, after Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine, demanded that every Russian in Britain be rounded up and expelled. The force is not strong in that one. Personally, I can’t get too excited about the threat to the Trumpian model of AI. Neither, it seems, can Washington: it’s been more than a year since Nvidia was revealed to be selling some of its best stuff to a “dilapidated storefront” outside Kuala Lumpur, which sounded awfully like a pit stop on the way to China. Again, no action. The message ordinary Americans can take from this is that a company so vital to America’s AI-military complex is too big to subject to ordinary laws.

In the everyday world, a CEO who gets into both a sex scandal and a national-security imbroglio wouldn’t stay CEO for more than a minute. At Nvidia, the board has moved with incredible sloth. It declared on Sunday that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” – before any independent investigation. It finally met on Wednesday evening after further revelations of a separate extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive. Huang’s fate now reportedly hangs in the balance, but the company board, it may surprise you to know, includes several of his longstanding business associates. You’ll also be gobsmacked to learn that several members of his family are serving in senior positions at Nvidia.

One of the protections for Huang, like Musk and Zuckerberg and Altman, is that there appears to be no succession plan in place should any of those men fall under a self-driving automobile. A suggestion doing the rounds is that the father may now be replaced by one of his children. The Vatican has a more codified succession process for the pope, even if it includes white smoke and Ralph Fiennes.

This scandal is different from the allegations over David Walliams or the convictions handed down against Russell Brand – but one black thread that connects them is the grace afforded to each man by enablers and the powerful. Asked about the Huang affair, Trump described him as a “fine person”. Many of us will remember Trump defending the white nationalists who stormed Charlottesville in 2017. They were “some very fine people”, he said.

This is the very same sense of impunity that drove so many Americans out last week to protest against Trump, datacentres and AI. At the midterms, the Democrats rode a wave of populism: the many v the money. Nearly two decades after the banking crash, the public anger against an unaccountable, ruinous elite is finally finding a political vehicle. Yet it still lacks the policies to match.

What do even the brightest minds in the Democratic party, or Labour for that matter, want to do about the tech billionaires? A moratorium on datacentres, certainly. A wealth tax, maybe. Given the largeness of the moment, the scale of popular anger, these are tiny measures. What about breaking up private monopolies such as Nvidia and socialising AI? How about combining that with a refoundation of welfare and other essentials of everyday life?

The tech bubble hasn’t burst, but this week we got a small taste of how it might end. When America’s AI bets do collapse, that will be a financial failure, an economic failure and a political failure. Given the strategic importance of these companies and their technologies, there will be demands for huge bailouts. The left should start preparing its own response. Through diffidence and a lack of preparation, it squandered the crisis of 2008; it mustn’t this time. To do so would not be, well, smart.

Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump ran on a platform of peace. His war may have cost Republicans the midterms | Mohamad Bazzi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Mohamad Bazzi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Voters remembered Trump’s many promises to avoid the same kind of regime-change wars started by his predecessors

F
or much of his political career, Donald Trump ranted at past US presidents who got the US entangled in endless foreign conflicts. He used it as a cudgel to belittle his predecessors, calling George W Bush’s decision to invade Iraq in 2003 “the worst single mistake ever made in the history of our country”. Trump also regularly derided the occupation of Afghanistan as “a total disaster”.

Then Trump decided to launch his own disastrous war against Iran eight months ago. And that conflict may well have cost Republicans control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections.

In exit polling conducted by NBC News, three-quarters (74%) of voters said the war was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote for Congress. And 63% said the Trump administration made “the wrong decision” by taking military action against Iran.

The midterms turned out to be a massive public repudiation of the Iran conflict – and of the US legacy of forever wars that followed the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001.

It was no secret that most Americans had soured on foreign interventions and were opposed to Trump starting new ones. In January, a poll by Quinnipiac University found that 70% of voters opposed an attack on Iran – a total reversal from US public opinion ahead of the Iraq invasion more than two decades ago, when polls showed 72% of Americans supported that war in its early days.

But Trump was blinded by hubris, thinking he could achieve a quick military victory and overthrow the regime that took power after Iran’s Islamic revolution in 1979.

The Iranian regime fought hard for its survival, retaliating against the joint US-Israeli attack by destroying oil pipelines and other energy infrastructure in neighboring Gulf countries, and largely closing the strait of Hormuz. Before the conflict, more than a fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies passed through the crucial waterway each day.

The war led to a global increase in energy prices and other costs – and American voters took out their widespread anger at the economic fallout against Trump and his Republican party.

It also didn’t help Trump that he ran for and won the presidency in 2024 as an anti-war candidate. He promised to negotiate an end to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and Israel’s war against Gaza, among other conflicts that he argued had been prolonged by his Democratic opponents, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris.

“If Kamala wins, only death and destruction await because she is the candidate of endless wars. I am the candidate of peace,” Trump said at a November 2024 rally in Michigan, a swing state he won partly with support from Arab and Muslim American voters. Those voters, many of whom have relatives in the Middle East, were angry at the Biden administration’s unwavering support for Israel as it expanded its war from Gaza into Lebanon and other countries in the region.

Beyond his free-wheeling campaign rallies, Trump used his most important speeches to portray himself as an “America First” president who opposes foreign military adventurism. It became a cornerstone of his Maga (Make America Great Again) movement. “I’m not going to start a war. I’m going to stop wars,” Trump declared in his 2024 election night victory speech in Florida.

In the end, US voters remembered Trump’s many promises to avoid the same kind of regime-change wars started by his predecessors – and they punished Republicans for Trump breaking those pledges.

As the extent of Republican losses in House, Senate and gubernatorial races nationwide became clear last week, JD Vance posted a lengthy statement on Twitter/X blaming the Republican wipeout on the Iran conflict. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote, explaining that voters who had supported Trump in 2024 showed up in the midterms to vote for Democrats because they were angry about the war, higher prices and other economic fallout.

Vance also suggested that the Trump administration had abandoned its “America First” agenda – an attempt by the vice-president to lay his claim as the legitimate heir to the Maga coalition after Trump, who can’t run for re-election in the 2028 presidential race.

But the movement may have fractured irreparably, thanks to the Iran war and the devastating Republican losses in the midterms.

Let’s not forget that Vance was once a fierce critic of the president, who then cozied up to Trump when it became clear he would be the leading Republican candidate in 2024.

In fact, Vance helped promote the narrative to a weary American public that Trump would avoid getting embroiled in new conflicts, unlike his Democratic opponents. In 2023, Vance endorsed Trump by writing a Wall Street Journal opinion article headlined: “Trump’s Best Foreign Policy? Not Starting Any Wars.”

“My entire adult lifetime has been shaped by presidents who threw America into unwise wars and failed to win them,” Vance wrote, outlining failed US interventions in Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya and elsewhere. At the time, Vance was auditioning for the role as Trump’s running mate – and his record as a US Marine who served in Iraq, and later turned against the war, made him appealing to Trump’s Maga base.

Yet Vance did not dare to publicly break with Trump at the start of the Iran war in late February, when the move would have represented a greater political risk but Vance could have made a bigger difference in the conflict’s trajectory.

Today, even Trump is acknowledging that the war played a major role in the Republicans’ midterm losses. When he was asked on 4 November about Vance’s assessment of the election, Trump said: “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline [prices] up a little bit short-term.”

But because Trump refuses to publicly admit making any mistake, he continues to defend his catastrophic decision to attack Iran. “If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” Trump added, while touring his half-finished White House ballroom the day after the midterms. “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

Of course, Trump never bothered to make a robust case to Americans, or even to Congress, explaining how Iran posed a threat to US interests that would justify launching a new war in the Middle East. Unlike the Bush administration in the lead-up to its invasion of Iraq, Trump didn’t even try to build his case based on lies and manipulated intelligence.

And so American voters swiftly punished Trump and his Republican enablers for dragging the US into yet another open-ended war.

Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies, and a journalism professor, at New York University

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Republicans know that the president’s folly and excesses cost them the elections. That doesn’t mean they’re ready to challenge him

S
hortly after polls closed last Tuesday, with the scale of the Republican trouncing in the midterms still becoming apparent, Donald Trump briefly adopted an oddly conciliatory tone. He declared that he was “absolutely” willing to accept the results, would look forward to working with Democrats and that deportation policies might have been “too tough”.

It was never going to last. He soon cast doubt on the elections’ legitimacy. On Friday, he replaced his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with her deputy, Stephen Miller – a white nationalist, or “stone-cold racist”, in the words of Hakeem Jeffries, likely to be the next House speaker. Ms Wiles executed the president’s decisions faithfully, but was seen as a somewhat calming if not restraining influence, which may help explain her departure.

Every high-profile woman in the administration has now quit or been ousted, and its machismo has increased. Mr Miller is an ideological extremist and attack dog who has spearheaded the expansion of executive power as well as the draconian immigration excesses that alienated many (particularly Latino) voters. He reportedly wants to wind down the war on Iran, but played a leading role in strikes against alleged drugs boats in the Caribbean – extrajudicial killings.

Happily for Mr Trump, the reshuffle has turned discussion away from lame ducks and the Republican succession. He does not need the mixed martial arts supremo Dana White as his press secretary; he has enough brawlers. On Tuesday, House Republicans picked another aggressive hardliner, Jim Jordan, as minority leader. He has pledged to fight investigations by the new Democratic majority. On the same day, they blocked the attempted impeachment of Pete Hegseth, the self-styled “secretary of war” (with some Democrats also missing the vote). The outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie was pressing the case against him over the Iran war and attacks on drugs boats. Mr Hegseth is manifestly unfit for office. He has shared highly sensitive information on a messaging app and wanted to live stream a military execution. But a case against him might embarrass Mr Trump.

Some still hope that Republicans will have little choice but to hold Mr Trump accountable for last week’s defeat. JD Vance sought to distance himself by criticising the Iran war, and Ron DeSantis declared that there was “no question” that the results were a rebuke of Mr Trump. But GOP politicians either want more Trumpism, or are extremely wary of taking him on, after he torched previous critics. Trump voters are split between the Maga base, which wants to double down (and who turned out last Tuesday) and the rest who want to moderate (and stayed home) – with divisions on everything from datacentres to deportations. The Republicans can’t win in 2028 with Maga votes alone. Yet the GOP regained power in 2016 by becoming more extreme.

The Democrats now have their own challenge. They must use their new congressional power to ensure accountability – including pinning corruption in Mr Trump’s circle to the cost of living crisis – while also trying to deliver for voters who need real improvements in their lives. Republicans will seek to tie them up in fruitless congressional battles.

The Trumpist message is so clear that the outgoing speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, even said it out loud: “The voters made the wrong choice.” The Republicans are promising the electorate more of what they didn’t want. The people have spoken, but the president – and his party – won’t listen.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Why does Pete Hegseth call himself secretary of war? ‘Dopey but dangerous’ wouldn’t fit on a badge | Emma Brockes
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Emma Brockes
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
He has survived blame for the US midterms disaster and dodged an impeachment vote, but it will be one battle after another now – and he can’t win them all

L
ike the brief, wondrous cycle of the mayfly, we may come to look back on the career of Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defence who cheekily rebranded himself secretary of war, as the defining appointment of the Trump era: that is, one in which extraordinary power was handed to a man of cartoonish inappropriateness and which, despite this week’s shelved attempt to impeach him, may still turn out to have been luminously short-lived. In January, the Democrats will assume a majority in both chambers and are likely to have another crack at impeaching Hegseth. In the meantime, we can only look on and wonder at his meaning.

It is quite something, in the context of Trump cabinet appointments that have included Robert F Kennedy Jr and Kristi Noem, to be the most glaringly underqualified person in the West Wing, but since being sworn in almost two years ago, Hegseth has comfortably seen off any rivals to his crown. This week, eight articles of impeachment, or “high crimes and misdemeanours” as the official rubric has it, were levied against him by Thomas Massie, an outgoing Republican congressman from Kentucky, who accused Hegseth of illegal acts including violating the constitution by conducting an unauthorised war with Iran and effecting regime change in Venezuela.

Republicans narrowly saw off the proceedings and, somewhat to the surprise of observers, joined the president in rallying energetically to Hegseth’s defence. This, too, may not last; in the wake of the Republicans’ shellacking in the midterms, speculation as to who would take the fall for Trump’s losses focused on Hegseth, after JD Vance pointed to the Iran war as a root cause of the losses. But perhaps this underestimates Hegseth’s appeal to the president. If Greg Bovino, the former US immigration chief who quit after two people were killed by agents under his command, looked like a textbook psycho in the manner of Sean Penn’s Col Steven J Lockjaw – the screw-loose character from the movie One Battle After Another – Hegseth is a different beast entirely; a Mr Incredible-like figure whose persona is so ridiculous, so dopey, as to distract from his dangerousness.

Such a manoeuvre is, of course, in line both with Trump’s own highly developed ability to marry deadly threat levels with the affect of a buffoon, and a more general tradition in the US of men of war who operate with the affability of the Pillsbury Doughboy. Cast your minds back to Gen “Stormin’” Norman Schwarzkopf, a man shaped like a freestanding wardrobe, who led coalition forces in the first Gulf war, or Colin Powell, his senior at the time who, as chairman of the joint chiefs of staff and despite leading the most powerful military in the world, appeared at briefings with the casual ease and likability of a lounge singer.

Compare this with the way we do things in Britain, where, generally speaking, we like our military men to be slight of form, quiet of voice, thin of moustache and ruthless of execution. As a platonic ideal, if military officers in the US take the shape of comfy old Tom Hanks in Saving Private Ryan, in Britain we’re more partial to Trevor Howard in The Third Man, all twinkly eyes and icy veins, or the unyielding Alec Guinness in The Bridge on the River Kwai, a man who, beneath his quivering, rule-following exterior, is as pitiless as rain and as mad as a snake. Both represent sleights of hand, to some degree. Take your pick.

Hegseth, of course, never led the US army. While serving in the military, he rose to the middling rank of major (it was his service on Fox & Friends that, in all likelihood, made him a four-star general in Trump’s eyes). And US defence secretaries aren’t themselves expected to be especially martial; let’s enjoy a quick drive-by on the memory of Dick Cheney, secretary of defence under George H W Bush, accidentally shooting his own hunting buddy in the face during a quail hunting trip in southern Texas.

But Hegseth looks the part, not just of the genial American warrior, but of the very specific ideal favoured by Trump in which the quiff-wearing, square jaw-rocking secretary of defence embodies the 1950s aesthetic for which the president pines. If Democrats manage to impeach and oust him next year, he may linger in our minds, against stiff competition, as the most hollow, disastrous and surreal piece of casting in Trump’s cabinet of misfits and rogues.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: It’s impeachment season! After the attempt on Pete Hegseth, will Donald Trump be next? | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Trump has already made history as the only president to be impeached twice. After the Republicans’ thrashing in the midterms, could there be a third attempt?

T
he days are getting shorter, the nights are getting longer and some Republicans are getting nervous. After a long stretch of impunity, it’s impeachment season in the US. While the attempt to impeach the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, failed yesterday, Donald Trump may be worried he’s next.

In January, the president warned Republicans that they had better win the November elections or he would be in big trouble. “If we don’t win the midterms … they’ll find a reason to impeach me,” Trump said. He repeated this plea to voters during an October rally in Oklahoma: “Pretend I’m running, please. Just pretend. ’Cause I am on the ballot. And if we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me.”

I don’t need to tell you what happened with the midterms, do I? The Republicans didn’t just lose – they were given a thrashing so thorough that, for a while, Trump seemed to avoid talking about it. Indeed, in his first public appearance after the election, Trump largely avoided the issue for a full 20 minutes while talking about his beloved White House ballroom project, rhapsodising about its “magnificent” columns. This week, Trump seems to have moved on to another obsession: he is now making baseless claims that the election was rigged. Still, while Trump may be in la-la land half the time, in his moments of lucidity you have to imagine he’s worried a comeuppance is coming.

There are various ways Trump could be held accountable for any alleged crimes, but what he seems most worried about right now is potential impeachment. It’s a multistep process used to charge a public official with serious misconduct and remove them from office. First, articles of impeachment are brought, then the House votes on whether to adopt these articles via a majority vote. If that happens, the person is impeached. But this is where things get tricky. For the official to get removed, the Senate has to hold an impeachment trial and two-thirds of members (67 senators) have to find them guilty; a tough hurdle to clear. There have only been eight cases where this has happened and all the officials removed have been judges.

Trump has already made history by being the only president to have been impeached twice: in 2019 and 2021. In both cases the Senate acquitted him. But now that Democrats have control of government, could Trump become the first president to be removed from office through impeachment?

The short answer is that, while it’s not impossible, it’s unlikely. The Democrats have a majority, but they still only have 54 seats. Attempting to remove Trump would be a gruelling process that many don’t have the appetite for. Kamala Harris said recently: “Going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea … we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations.”

In an interview with NBC News on Sunday, Senator Bernie Sanders went even further. “We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump,” Sanders said. “We have to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.”

Hear me out: how about we do both? And look, if impeachment is unrealistic, we can get a little creative and come up with other ways to give Trump and his lackeys a small taste of the misery they have inflicted on the rest of us. I would suggest exiling the president to an island and forcing him to listen to his incoherent speeches on a nonstop loop, but I suspect he’d quite enjoy that. Although we could fill the place with wind turbines, which enrage him, and make sure the water is filled with sharks. Trump is weirdly obsessed with the fish; according to Stormy Daniels he once said: “I hope all the sharks die.”

Oh dear, I think I’d better stop there before I have the FBI knocking on my door. Forget the sharks, OK? If the legal system fails us, let’s just focus on replacing him at the next election.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Kerr admits concern is ‘high’ for Curry’s injury

Bassey says Smart guilty of ‘fake toughness’

Kevin Durant scored 20 points, Alperen Sengun and Amen Thompson added 19 and the Houston Rockets snapped Golden State’s eight-game winning streak with a 115-108 victory on Wednesday night.

The Warriors played most of the game without Stephen Curry after the star left in the first quarter with right abdominal soreness and didn’t return. He was due to get an MRI on the injury.

After the game, Warriors coach Steve Kerr admitted he was worried about the injury.

“Concern is high,” Kerr said. “But I have no idea the extent.”

The Warriors are 8-4 this season, despite a host of injuries. Even before Curry’s injury, Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody were missing with knee injuries while center Kristaps Porziņģis stepped away from basketball entirely over an undisclosed health issue.

Curry missed significant time last season, during which the Warriors struggled badly. But his fellow veteran Draymond Green believes the team can better absorb his absence this season.

“The spirit of this team is better,” Green said after Wednesday’s game. “We’re more certain of who we are, what makes us a good team. I think that puts us in a better position to be successful without him as opposed to where we were last year. Then obviously [Yaxel Lendeborg], having a guy you can give the ball to and he can create an advantage. [Brandin Podziemski] is playing a lot better. ... It puts us in a better position.”

Curry’s departure was not the only significant event of the night. Houston’s Marcus Smart was ejected late in the third quarter for punching Golden State’s Charles Bassey. It was unclear what started the altercation, but Smart threw a punch that appeared to lightly strike Bassey’s nose.

Smart was immediately pushed away by two other Warriors and an official grabbed Bassey around the waist and pulled him away. Smart didn’t wait for the officials to eject him, heading straight to the locker room after he was pulled away. The play was reviewed and he was issued a Flagrant 2 foul and ejected before play resumed.

“I remember the first half, I was trying to set a screen [and] he grabbed my knee. He was playing dirty,” Bassey said after the game. “I think I was trying to get a rebound. He was grabbing my hand, and I was trying to run back on defense. Then he got up on me and just swung. Obviously, that was weak. I just think that was, honestly, fake toughness.

“It didn’t surprise me. I knew he was going to do something. I don’t think he was trying to play. I think he was trying to get himself out of the game. I think he was trying to chill. He wasn’t trying to hoop. That was fake toughness.”

Golden State’s longest winning streak since 2022 ended on a night they were held well below their season average of 120.4 points a game. Curry, who entered Wednesday ranked second in the NBA by averaging 30.6 points a game, had just three points before exiting.

With Curry out, the Warriors were led by Lendeborg, who had 25 points and 10 rebounds. Brandin Podziemski added 22 points.

He had a rocky start to his career with Fox, but now sounds like a favorite uncle who also understands football on a forensic level. He also drops in the occasional gem, such as describing a Dak Prescott rocket to CeeDee Lamb as a “piss missile”. Brady rage-bating New England Patriots fans on his return to Foxborough was a nice touch too. “There was some deli meat given out by Drake Maye today,” Brady said after the Green Bay Packers stomped his former team on Sunday. Keep it up, Uncle Tom.

Jahmyr Gibbs, RB, Detroit Lions. Jaxon Smith-Njigba is the NFL’s best receiver by a significant margin. He accounts for 50% of Seattle’s receiving yards, the highest share for any wideout in the past 10 years. He is only the fourth player in the Super Bowl era to go for 100-plus yards in seven of his first eight games to start a season. Gibbs is having just that little bit better season in Detroit though. The Lions running back leads the NFL in total yards (1,132) and is joint leader in total touchdowns (11), despite playing one fewer game than some of his competitors. Call it recency bias but it is not only the stats that seal this award for Gibbs. His explosive game-winning performance against the formidable Minnesota Vikings defense at the start of November was something to savor. Minnesota had bottled Giibs up in the first half while looking good to keep their unbeaten run rolling, only for the running back to shred the purple and gold into confetti after the break. Maybe Minnesota fatigue helped. Maybe Detroit’s plan was to play them close then unleash their star back. What is certain is that Gibbs’s three-down ferocity and skills as a receiver have him in a class of his own.

TJ Watt, OLB, Pittsburgh Steelers. Did anyone have the Steelers pegged to be leading the AFC North at the halfway stage? Me neither, but the black and yellow are on course for the playoffs yet again. Nothing new there. Except, maybe this season they’re not heading for a first-round defeat. Especially if Watt can keep the heart of Pittsburgh’s revitalized defense pumping. The outside linebacker led the league in sacks before the Steelers’ bye week, and he already has more this season (7.5) than he did in his 14 games last season (7.0). Maybe we should have seen this coming as he started the campaign in devastating fashion, with three tackles for loss, two sacks and two quarterback hits against the Falcons. He even got his first pick-six, a spectacular point-blank interception of Cooper Rush that saw Watt stumble to the deck but still have the quickness to rise and find the end zone.

Arvell Reese, LB, New York Giants. Reese destroyed the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday and made this award his own. He dominated for the Giants with 12 total tackles, three sacks, three quarterback hits and three tackles for loss. In the postgame press conference teammate Abdul Carter seemed happy to be working with Reese: “Shoutout to the four teams that passed on him in the draft.” Even being taken at No 5, he looks like a steal.

The obvious answer is the Los Angeles Chargers: Justin Herbert and Co are enduring a season from hell, sitting winless after being earmarked for the postseason. Away from that dumpster fire, the Seattle Seahawks have been underperforming compared to their spectacular success last season. They have a deep injury list, a downtrodden Sam Darnold who has quietly been outplayed by his backup, Drew Lock, and a defense that hasn’t hit the heights of the team’s Super Bowl run. Both quarterbacks are carrying injuries as the 5-4 Seahawks prepare to face the Raiders on Sunday, and they have a tough schedule after that, with a trip to San Francisco and two dates with the Rams. The winless Chargers were supposed to be built for January football but the Super Bowl champions missing out on a wildcard would represent a greater disaster.

Predicting Super Bowl winners is a tough old business. In my preseason predictions, I had the Denver Broncos going all the way, with the Chicago Bears missing the playoffs entirely. Now, the Bears look locked in for January football, as do the Broncos. But a champion should look better than they did the previous year. Denver haven’t kicked on from 2025 – they are still very good, but not great. The Bears, on the other hand, have made the leap. Their defense has improved from one of the NFL’s worst outfits to a top-10 unit, matching Caleb Williams and company’s consistent production on offense. The defense was great before Chicago traded for elite game-wrecker Jeffery Simmons, and his acquisition could propel the Bears to win it all. Williams’s four picks against the Buccaneers on Sunday are a cause for concern – maybe he’s still too green – but he didn’t crumble in the face of adversity. Ultimately, the Bears should be cheered by the fact that they held on to beat the Bucs – it showed the kind of steel every champion needs.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.summary: The Bears have made the leap to the top-10 in the NFL. The defense has improved from one of the NFL’s worst outfits to a top- 10 unit. The Bears beat the Bucs on Sunday to keep their defense strong.

Andreeva beats Sabalenka 6-4, 6-0 to top Group B

Elina Svitolina staged a remarkable comeback to beat Karolina Muchova and remain in the hunt for the WTA Finals title.

The Ukrainian appeared to be on her way out of Indian Wells when she was a set down and required an eight-minute medical timeout. But she recovered to win 3-6, 6-2, 6-2 and stay in with a chance of reaching the semi-finals.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Stephen Curry attacks treatment of women after former players criticize wife Ayesha’s movie kiss
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Warriors star defends wife over romantic comedy role

Arenas called Ayesha ‘only blemish’ on Curry family

Four-time NBA champion condemns double standards

Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry has criticized several ex-professional athletes for questioning his wife Ayesha’s decision to appear in a romantic comedy featuring an on-screen kiss, accusing them of diminishing her accomplishments and perpetuating double standards about women.

The four-time NBA champion posted a 90-second video on Instagram on Wednesday in response to comments by former NBA players Gilbert Arenas and Nick Young, as well as former NFL players Emmanuel Acho and LeSean McCoy, following the release of Ayesha Curry’s new film, Second Chance Holiday.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The romantic comedy, which premiered on the Roku Channel on 5 November, features Ayesha in her first leading film role opposite actor Matthew Daddario. A scene in which Ayesha Curry and Daddario kiss prompted criticism from several former athletes, who questioned her participation in the film and discussed its implications for her marriage.

Curry said the commentary had crossed a line by diminishing his wife’s professional achievements.

“I’ve been hearing a lot of noise, and usually the noise doesn’t bother me, doesn’t bother Ayesha,” Curry said in the video, which he captioned “PSA”.

“But this one, trying to step on the accomplishments of my wife and obviously, leading podcast tables and topics and giving their opinion on somebody else’s wife,” he continued, naming Young, Arenas and Acho.

Curry said the remarks reflected a broader problem with attitudes toward women, and the expectations placed upon them.

“It kind of speaks to a bigger conversation about how you view women in this world and what they’re all allowed and not allowed to do,” he said, also questioning the former athletes’ understanding of acting.

Curry has previously spoken out about gender equality. In a 2018 essay for the Players’ Tribune calling for an end to the gender pay gap, he credited his wife and mother for shaping his views on women’s rights and opportunities. He wrote that one of the most important lessons they had taught him was to challenge society’s expectations of women and “always stay listening to women, to always stay believing in women”.

Arenas, a three-time NBA All-Star selection who began his career with Golden State, had described Ayesha as the “only blemish” on Curry’s family life during a recent episode of his podcast, arguing that she did not behave like the wives of other prominent basketball players.

Young, who played alongside Curry on the Warriors’ 2018 championship team, also took part in the conversation. McCoy separately question Ayesha’s decision to film the romantic scene.

Curry, who has generally avoided publicly engaging with criticism of his family, suggested the ex-players owed his wife an apology.

“Obviously I tried to laugh this one off, but something needs to be said,” he said. “Anytime Ayesha Curry shows up in your headline, I kindly suggest you just give the happy hands, congratulations, and maybe, just maybe, the apology can be as loud as y’all leading your shows with this topic.”

He closed by thanking the commentators for bringing attention to the film, encouraging viewers to watch it on Roku.

“Appreciate the free pub,” he said.

The Warriors guard accompanied the video with photographs of his wife promoting the movie and a message encouraging her to “Keep shining”. He also appeared to take another swipe at the commentators in his caption, writing: “You don’t have to like & subscribe to all podcasts.”

His sister, Sydel Curry-Lee, supported the response in the comments, writing: “HEAVY on how it speaks about how the world views women. Play with someone else. Enough is enough!”

Ayesha Curry is an actor, cookbook author and entrepreneur who has appeared in television and film projects for nearly two decades. Her previous credits include an appearance on Disney Channel’s Hannah Montana and a supporting role alongside Lindsay Lohan in the 2024 Netflix romantic comedy Irish Wish.

Stephen and Ayesha Curry married in 2011 and have four children.

Curry’s post came as Golden State, at joint-third in the Western Conference standings with an 8-3 record, prepared to face the Houston Rockets on Wednesday night in the opening game of a five-game road trip.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.summary: Warriors star defends wife over romantic comedy role. Gilbert Arenas called Ayesha ‘only blemish’ on Curry family. Curry posted a 90-second video on Instagram on Wednesday in response to comments by former NBA players Gilbert Arena and Nick Young.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Burberry returns to profit as sales soar, from £85 socks to £9,000 coats
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Sarah Butler
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
CEO says ‘democratic approach’ has helped brand outperform tough market, with big rises in China and US

Burberry has returned to profit as its back-to-basics strategy drove strong sales of the British brand’s coats, jackets and handbags over the summer.

Joshua Schulman, the chief executive, said the luxury brand had outperformed a “challenging luxury market” to achieve sales growth of 6%, helped by strong online and wholesale sales particularly in China and the US. “Our strategy is working,” he said.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Burberry said it made a pre-tax profit of £19m in the six months to 26 September after a loss of £48m a year before, as sales rose to £1.1bn. Sales rose 15% in China and 14% in the Americas but fell 1% in the Europe and Middle East region, partly due to the Iran war.

Schulman said Burberry’s focus on a “pyramid of pricing” ranging from more “affordable” scarves, starting from £195, and cotton-cashmere socks from £85, to its top-tier bags and coats, which can cost more than £9,000 for a leather version, had helped it achieve growth despite a tough market. Wealthy shoppers around the world are travelling less and being more cautious about spending, hitting luxury brand sales globally.

Sales of lightweight jackets and “tropical” gaberdine raincoats as well as its Cotswold range of leather bags and accessories featuring the brand’s famous check had proved popular.

Schulman said: “Luxury customers around the world are experiencing some fatigue with exorbitant pricing and in this context our strategy of having great value for money is resonating strongly with Chinese customers.”

“Burberry has always had a somewhat more democratic approach than some of our European peers and has a universal appeal,” he added.

Schulman said the brand had spent the last two years of its Burberry Forward strategy returning to its historical position at the “sweet spot in the luxury market”.

He said investment in locally relevant marketing, such as special product for China’s Valentine’s Day celebrations this spring and for the upcoming lunar new year, were also helping drive sales.

“It is no secret global tourism is down but the local customer has been spending in their respective regions,” Schulman said. “This is a trend we have been seeing all year long.”

While people were spending less as tourists which was hitting sales in discount outlets, Schulman said local spending was holding up in the brand’s flagship city centre stores including in London.

He said that while “nobody has a crystal ball” about whether customers would begin spending more freely, history suggested “this is a very cyclical business”.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Robert Booth and Denis Campbell
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Exclusive: The Guardian revealed 29 hospital trusts were not or hardly using the controversial patient data tech

NHS England has deleted a claim from its website stating 137 hospital trusts are benefiting from Palantir’s AI health data system after the Guardian revealed 29 of them were not using all or most of the controversial technology.

Health bosses had published a list of all the NHS bodies “live” with and “realising benefits” from the AI-powered federated data platform (FDP), a system set up to improve patient outcomes, boost operating theatre efficiency and speed up bed discharges. But after 29 trusts said it was either not live or they were not using any of its applications, the original list of hospitals appears to have been taken down.

The move comes as ministers weigh up whether to extend Palantir’s £330m contract to 2029 and after the Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) said it was examining the NHS claims about the extent of the system’s use, which critics say make it appear more embedded in the health service than it actually is.

A less detailed page now says early users were “already seeing real results – reduced admin, faster patient pathways, and more time for care”. A senior Labour MP, calling for the contract to be scrapped, warned the move threatened public trust.

Palantir was hired to help manage vast quantities of medical data held by NHS England but campaigners, MPs and doctors’ unions want the deal scrapped – often arguing its effectiveness has been overstated. NHS England was previously warned by the OSR that it has no evidence to support a claim that the technology has helped deliver more than 100,000 extra operations.

Some Palantir opponents also object to the presence in the health service of a company, founded by the Donald Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel, which also works for the Israeli military and the US administration’s ICE immigration crackdown.

The Labour MP Ben Coleman, a member of the Commons health and social care select committee, said it was “troubling” that NHS England had listed the 137 trusts as benefiting from FDP, but then “apparently pulled the list when 29 said they weren’t using all or most of it”.

“When NHS England makes claims like this without checking them, it destroys trust – and it has happened before,” he added. “The statistics watchdog warned there was no evidence for the NHS’s claim of 117,000 extra operations due to the FDP. This latest overclaim could put more hospitals off using the FDP and threaten its viability.”

Coleman wants the NHS to drop Palantir and develop an open platform for health data on which NHS trusts and British tech companies can build tools instead.

The decision to take down the list of NHS trusts came after the Medact campaign group researched the use of Palantir’s technology by sending freedom of information requests to every hospital and integrated care board in England.

“It’s a relief to see these webpages taken down, but this has only happened after multiple investigations exposed the misleading nature of NHS England’s claims,” said Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, an NHS doctor and Medact spokesperson. “The question remains, why did NHSE [NHS England] spend years using shaky evidence to promote the alleged ‘benefits’ of Palantir software?”

Last week it was reported ministers planned to extend Palantir’s deal, amid intense lobbying. The US company has hired the Labour peer Tom Watson as a full-time lobbyist and he recently wrote to Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, saying Palantir wanted to help “build Britain’s sovereign technological capability”.

Meanwhile, the health workers’ union Unison has called on ministers to instead end the contract with its general secretary, Andrea Egan, telling the Guardian any decision to extend the deal would be “completely unacceptable and a betrayal of staff and patients”.

Palantir has said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients”, but Egan called it a “sinister American surveillance firm”, and said that allowing it to hold a vital NHS contract “surrenders sovereignty over our most sensitive data and poses security risks”.

Groups including the Doctors Association UK, Medact, a health justice campaign group, Amnesty UK and Just Treatment, a patients’ group, have also this week written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and Cooper opposing Labour’s reported plan to give Palantir a further two years to allow time for a transition to UK-based technology.

They say the deal could be safely ended in 2027 using an aspect of the contract called the “termination assistance period” to allow NHS trusts to transition away from Palantir’s technology.

“Ministers could risk looking as if they were saying one thing and doing another if they said they were planning for a future without Palantir while simultaneously handing it two more years to embed itself further into our health service,” the group said.

NHS England did not respond to requests for comment.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: 29 hospital trusts were not or hardly using the controversial patient data tech NHS England. The Guardian revealed 29 of them were not using all or most of the controversial system. Move comes as ministers weigh up whether to extend Palantir’s £330m contract to 2029.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Steve Rose
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world?

‘I
t was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms.

One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustainability officer. “Compared with a traditional datacentre built with steel and concrete, we lower the embodied carbon of the full structure by three times.” With a complex the size of a football pitch, that is a lot of wood, but, says Wernvik, “the amount of timber one of our datacentres uses takes the Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to grow back”.

Datacentres have become a dirty word and a political issue in much of the world – especially the US, where opposition to them was said to be a factor in the recent midterm elections – but here in Sweden, not so much.

There is a familiar litany of reasons why datacentres are bad: they are being built without the consent or knowledge of local people; they consume vast amounts of land, electricity and water, with knock-on effects for communities and the environment; they provide no jobs and enrich rapacious tech companies.

What’s remarkable is how little any of those arguments apply in Sweden, especially here in Falun, a former copper-mining town a few hours north of Stockholm. If your abiding image of a datacentre is something like xAI’s Colossus facility in Tennessee, built at lightning speed with little public notice, partly powered by banks of unpermitted, methane gas-burning temporary generators, releasing huge amounts of CO2 and harmful pollutants into the atmosphere and the community, then EcoDataCenter is practically the polar opposite. “I’m biased, but we believe that we build datacentres in a somewhat different way,” says Wernvik.

For starters, the company’s electricity supply is 100% renewable: 75% from hydroelectric power and 25% from wind. Sweden’s power mix as a whole is virtually carbon-free – just 1% of it comes from fossil fuels (in the EU as a whole, the figure is 29%, in the US it is 55%). In rural areas like Falun, there is sometimes too much electricity being generated by nearby hydroelectric, solar and wind, so power-hungry datacentres are actually helpful in balancing the grid.

Conditions for datacentres are pretty good in Sweden as a whole. The cold northern climate means less cooling is required; the energy is not only green, it is cheap and reliable; there is plenty of water and space; and the country is relatively politically stable and well-regulated – as Wernvik puts it, “it’s very hard to develop something in Sweden where there’s not a consensus”.

Energy is still a concern at EcoDataCenter, considering this place has a capacity of 80MW (the equivalent of about 60,000 homes). There are two key measures of datacentre performance. One is carbon usage effectiveness (CUE): the carbon emissions for each kWh of energy consumed. The average for US datacentres is 414gCO2/kWh, the European Union’s is 263gCO2/kWh, EcoDataCenter’s is 1.17gCO2/kWh. Another key measure is power usage effectiveness (PUE); how efficiently the datacentre uses the power going into it. The EU average is 1.36 (where a score of 1 would be 100% efficiency), EcoDataCenter’s is 1.15. The company is bringing down both its CUE and PUE year by year, according to EcoDataCenter’s sustainability report.

The primary use for energy is powering the graphics processing units – the expensive chips that do the computing, mostly made by the US company Nvidia. (Wernvik reminds me that although 70% of their computing power goes towards AI, almost everything online is run through datacentres somewhere, from banking transactions to streaming TV.) The supply must be constant – even a small drop in current for a few milliseconds could be consequential – so there are numerous backup generators on site, but even these are fuelled by hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a biofuel made from waste vegetable oil and animal fat, so also fossil fuel-free.

The other main energy use is cooling; removing the vast amounts of heat the chips generate. This is where controversies have arisen in the US over extracting from the local water supply, but it is less of an issue here, says Wernvik. The Swedish climate means less cooling is required, and there is plenty of water around (they get most of theirs from a nearby lake that was once used for drinking water). On a dreary, rainy day, no water is needed: the air is cold enough already (15C – anything below 20C will do). They simply have to pipe it around the building. On days when it is hot, or there is surplus electricity to use, there are electrically powered chillers on the roofs that cool air using a mist of water before it is circulated around the buildings.

The future, however, lies in liquid cooling – where the heat from the chips is transferred directly to liquid, rather than through the air. The latest generation of chips require this, Wernvik explains, as we walk through a spotlessly clean room containing several fridge-sized racks of chips, arranged in two parallel rows. They take up about the same amount of space as a bus. The noise is deafening (but inaudible outside), the chips themselves are barely visible behind a spaghetti of cables and cooling tubes connected to the backs of the server racks. It is a closed-loop system, so it does not use any external water, he says. “Each rack here is basically 25 saunas that we need to cool away and keep at about 27 degrees for it to not burn up inside,” says Wernvik. “That’s the whole engineering challenge we’re trying to solve.”

These particular Blackwell chips are powering DeepL, the German-based AI translation platform. Some of EcoDataCenter’s clients are confidential; declared ones include US cloud computing company CoreWeave, French AI firm Mistral, and research institutes including the universities of Hull and York. Supporting sovereign European tech is one of their key aims, Wernvik says.

The final part of the energy equation is excess heat, which EcoDataCenter reuses as much as possible. Much of it is used to dry wood pellets – a byproduct of the timber industry. The pellets go into incinerators in populated areas to provide heating. There is one right next door, which is no coincidence. (Admittedly, burning them emits CO2, but given the circular nature of the timber industry, they are arguably carbon-neutral.)

The rest of the heat (such as from the liquid cooling) goes directly into the local district heating system in Falun. Since the 1950s, Sweden has been building district heating networks across the country, where water is heated at large, centralised boilers, rather than in individual homes, then piped around towns and cities in underground pipes, typically at 60C to 80C. Homes and businesses extract the heat via a heat exchanger on their property. Already, district heating systems make use of excess heat from wastewater, sewage and supermarket refrigerators; datacentres are now another source to add to the mix.

There’s another aspect of EcoDataCenter’s operation that stands out. While datacentres are being imposed on many communities from the outside, in Falun it was practically the opposite. The project was initiated by local government, says Wernvik, “so the idea from the beginning was very much based on, how do we integrate a datacentre in the local community in order for it to fit the municipality?” This was in 2010, long before the AI revolution. The municipality (like a local council) decided the project would be better handled by a private company, which led to the formation of EcoDataCenter in 2014. The first part of the Falun site was up and running in 2019. The final phases are still under construction.

Local benefits were built in from the outset: 90% of its suppliers are sourced locally and 60% of its capital expenditure is spent locally, Wernvik says. It invests in local education and training, including sponsoring local sports teams and youth activities.

Local integration is even more evident at EcoDataCenter’s second site, in the industrial city of Borlänge, about a 20-minute drive away. This facility, the first phase of which will open in 2027, has a capacity of 240MW – three times larger than Falun. And the site is enormous: 200 sq km. In Borlänge, by contrast, they are building on a brownfield site. Poetically, perhaps, it used to be a paper mill, which closed in 2021. A datacentre is a good replacement: it can plug into the existing industrial infrastructure in much the same way – the power grid, the nearby water supply, the district heating. It will also employ 200 to 300 people, roughly the same number that worked at the paper mill before it closed, says Wernvik. “The discussion that datacentres don’t generate that amount of jobs, that needs to be put in context. There are a lot of different datacentres.”

In Stockholm, the datacentre strategy is different, but no less joined up. Sweden’s capital has become something of a European tech centre in its own right, and demand for datacentres is high. Stockholm Data Parks – a joint initiative by the city council and the city’s energy, power grid and fibre optic companies – was founded in 2014 as “a one-stop shop in order to make it easier to attract datacentre operators,” explains Michael Gullberg, product manager at energy company Stockholm Exergi. They free up suitable land, and again, the emphasis is on sustainability, including clean power (the city hopes to be net zero by 2035) and recycling waste heat. Stockholm claims to have the world’s largest district heating system, with more than 3,000 km of pipes, serving close to 90% of the capital. There are about 50 small-scale datacentres in the region (typically less than 20MW), and about 20 are connected to the district heating. They contribute about 1.5% of the city’s annual heat demand, which might not sound much, “but 110 gigawatt-hours of recovered heat is still a decent amount, because the system is so vast,” says Gullberg.

I visit one such facility in Kista, a suburb north of the city centre that has become Stockholm’s tech hub. It is an unobtrusive shed on an industrial estate, with a capacity of 12MW. Crucially, it is right next door to a district heating plant, so the datacentre basically pipes its heated water over the fence. It’s a win-win, says Sandra Karlsson, senior public affairs manager: “When they need to do district heating, they don’t need to boil the water from six degrees, they get it at 30 degrees from us, so they save a lot of energy.” In return, it takes in cold water from the district heating plant, which it uses for cooling.

This datacentre is run by atNorth, a company that began in Iceland, and now has 13 datacentres running or under construction across Sweden, Iceland, Norway, Denmark and Finland. Conditions are similar to Sweden in all these countries, says atNorth’s CEO, Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson: renewable power, reliable grids, district heating, “as well as the crappy weather that we have. We barely can live there as human beings, but datacentres love it.” As with EcoDataCenter, it claims to put sustainability and community engagement to the fore, investing and employing locally, using resources efficiently.

In terms of heat recovery, it’s a bit of a catch-22, Kristinsson points out: larger datacentres must be built in more remote areas, where there is less need for district heating, and vice versa. So they have been thinking of other ways. At its “mega site” in Varde, Denmark, with an initial capacity of 250MW, as well as district heating the plan is to channel excess heat into a 20 ha complex of greenhouses. “That means that Denmark can be self-sufficient with tomatoes during the six months of winter,” says Kristinsson. In turn, that means fewer imported vegetables: “that also saves a lot of carbon footprint, creates local jobs, and increases energy efficiency.” In Rjukan, Norway, Green Mountain’s datacentre channels excess heat to the fish farm next door.

Could other countries replicate this model? Yes and no. For one thing, the AI “hyperscalers” – such as Google, Meta, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft – dwarf Europe in terms of demand. Currently Europe’s datacentre capacity is estimated to be between 15% and 25% of that of the US. In addition, the renewable energy infrastructure in countries like Sweden has taken decades to establish; it is difficult to see the US catching up quickly. Added to which, European countries are relatively strict, both in terms of building and environmental regulations, and in areas like data privacy and protection. Elon Musk would never get away with trucking in some gas generators without permission in Sweden. To many critics, tighter regulation is exactly what the US datacentre landscape is crying out for. In July 2025, the Trump administration announced its AI Action Plan, which dismantled environmental and planning protections and rejected “radical climate dogma” in order to win the AI race.

Having said that, the US is building big in Nordic countries, to service their European users. In Sweden, Meta is building a 723MW facility in Lulea, Canadian-American firm Brookfield is planning a 750MW datacentre in Strängnäs, and Google broke ground on a 150MW plant in Horndal this June. These companies profess to be adopting the Nordic model, including building their own renewable energy supplies, although last month, the Guardian reported that Google had illegally felled 250,000 trees in Muhos, in northern Finland, to clear a site for its datacentre, leaving a barren 330 ha landscape. Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time” and planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Contractors building Microsoft’s datacentre in Gävle, Sweden, have been accused of housing their mostly foreign workers in poor conditions and subjecting them to long hours. Microsoft said of its contractors and suppliers, it “set clear requirements on health and safety, working conditions, and the freedom of association and right to collective bargaining” and had “robust processes in place” to ensure contractors’ compliance with Microsoft’s human rights and fair labour policies. The community engagement has not gone so smoothly for Google in Sweden, either. In 2021, a local metal band, also named Horndal, released an album railing against Google’s imminent arrival, called Lake Drinker (sample lyrics: “The digital devil shivers of thirst … First you took our trees / Now you drink our lake”).

Both atNorth and EcoDataCenter avoid importing cheap foreign labour, they say, but Kristinsson acknowledges that opposition to datacentres in the region has been growing, largely fuelled by the backlash in the US: “It’s probably not as strong [here], but Nordics are early adopters of everything that is new. We adopt, also, the same TikTok propaganda that is showing now in the US.”

Wernvik is more measured: “The American companies and the hyperscalers are definitely needed in the ecosystem as well because they possess unique competitiveness and capabilities.”

Could Sweden become a victim of its own success? The prospect of more and more of these gigantic facilities eating up the landscape is pretty dystopian even in a large country like Sweden. Wernvik is not too worried, though: “Our core components into what we sell are land and power. It’s a very linear business in that way. It’s very hard to have exponential growth because we work with physical constraints.” Exactly how many datacentres the world needs is largely a question of demand: how much more AI we require, and how much the benefits offset the harms. That’s really a separate conversation, but at the very least, Sweden’s joined-up, long-term approach to tech, energy and communities shows that there are better and worse ways to build our digital future.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Facial recognition errors put ethnic minorities at risk of wrongful arrest, police watchdog warns
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Inspectors find some officers acted on potential matches from retrospective searches without making enough checks

Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.

Although the technology can help fight crime, the report found it is beset by errors and biases, and operators do not always realise they must make further inquiries to verify the data.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The report by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary, published on Wednesday, covers only retrospective facial recognition. The technology is seen as less controversial and less tricky to get right than live facial recognition, which is used in real time to find suspects.

“Some investigators didn’t know that RFR results were intelligence rather than evidence and required further enquiries before officers took enforcement action,” the report said.

“This creates a risk that people could be incorrectly identified or arrested, which could undermine public confidence in the technology.

“We found that some investigators didn’t always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches. In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.”

The report said there are still issues with bias in the algorithm, including being more likely to wrongly flag people from ethnic minorities as suspects.

It said: “More needs to be done to reduce the risks of people being wrongly arrested … Auditors also identified cases where users uploaded poor-quality or unsuitable probe images, including blurred images and images containing multiple faces. These factors reduced the system’s ability to return reliable matches.”

Inspectors also found a risk of public confidence being undermined because custody images that should have been deleted were in fact kept.

The report says: “Inspectors found that legislation hasn’t kept up with changes in facial recognition technology and there is no comprehensive statutory framework governing this technology’s use. This makes it more difficult for forces to understand the lawful basis for RFR’s use and what safeguards are needed to protect the public.”

His Majesty’s Inspector of Constabulary Kathryn Stone said continued public support relied on showing the technology was being used properly: “Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment. A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence.”

Facial recognition is seen by police chiefs as the next big leap forward in crime fighting, and next huge threat to civil liberties by sceptics.

Jasleen Chaggar, from Big Brother Watch, said: “The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming.

after newsletter promotion

“This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they’ve never visited, as we’ve seen before.

“Worse still, police aren’t even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without even realising why they’ve been accused.

“Police cannot be allowed to continue using the algorithm with so few safeguards and at biased settings that are more likely to misidentify women, Asian and black people and search against millions of unlawfully held custody images.”

Ben Russell, lead on facial recognition for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, said: “Policing remains committed to the ethical, proportionate and responsible use of retrospective facial recognition to help investigate crime, bring offenders to justice and keep communities safe and we are pleased that HMICFRS has recognised the exciting possibilities of this technology.”

Prof Pete Fussey of the University of Southampton, formerly a police adviser on facial recognition, said: “Meaningful human scrutiny of AI systems is a legal requirement, yet the report gives examples of investigators taking the computer’s suggestions at face value without further checks.”
