https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Fewer hours and higher wages – or more burnout and surveillance: employers told to prepare for AI
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Josh Butler
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth launches best practice guide on AI adoption after Qantas and Canva job cuts

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Entry-level jobs will be the first to be automated due to AI, but it could mean fewer hours and higher wages for ordinary workers – or make jobs tougher with more burnout and workplace surveillance – the government has warned employers.

While major companies like Qantas and Canva slash their workforces in restructures spurred by AI changes, workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth said employers must give workers “a clear plan” about how automation could affect their jobs, and the opportunity to move into new roles.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

As she launched a new government guide on AI and employment – which cautioned that younger, older and First Nations workers, along with women and people with a disability faced “disproportionate impacts” – another Labor MP, Ed Husic, questioned what workers will get from the AI revolution.

“Who receives the benefits of higher productivity?” Husic, the former industry minister, told a parliamentary hearing examining the big four banks.

“Does it mean better services and lower prices for customers, secure jobs with higher wages for workers, or just lower labour costs and higher returns?”

Rishworth on Thursday launched a “best practice guide on the adoption of AI in the workplace”, saying the new technology must benefit both businesses and employees.

The guide paints an optimistic picture of AI, saying wider takeup could improve productivity, service quality and profitability for businesses, as well as boost wages, offer shorter and more flexible working hours, or provide more meaningful work for employees.

But deeper within the document, it also concedes there are “potential hazards” of AI, including “intrusive worker surveillance, poor rostering practices, intensified or unrealistic performance standards” and potential discrimination.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

It suggests that, if basic tasks are automated, humans will be left with more intense and complex tasks – and that some employers could use greater monitoring capabilities for performance management.

In a speech to a business forum in Sydney, Rishworth said some firms had used AI to automate tedious tasks to save time and money, but warned that firms simply adding AI to their company without properly consulting workers could actually increase workloads, as humans have to navigate an added step.

“I’ve spoken to many workers who have told me that they are willing to adopt AI at work where they can see that it will improve their working life. But that willingness cannot be taken for granted,” Rishworth said.

“Will they receive support and opportunities to build new skills? Will their knowledge and expertise still be valued? Will they share in the benefits being created? Without answers to these questions, workers will naturally lose trust in the process and become reluctant to engage with new technologies,” she said.

Greens leader David Shoebridge accused the government of “watching from the sidelines” while big companies slashed their workforce, demanding protection against surveillance and job cuts.

“When the government talks about asking employers nicely to consult staff, what it is really saying is that a worker who loses their job to an algorithm will have no legal recourse at all.

“We have seen Qantas, Canva, NAB and ANZ all firing Australian workers as part of offshoring and an AI rollout – it’s clear the time for optional guidelines has passed,” he said.

“Sharing the benefits of AI through better pay and shorter hours is a good idea, and it is exactly why it needs to be written into law instead of left to the goodwill of employers.”

The Reserve Bank this week reported it had seen “little evidence to date” of AI disrupting Australia’s labour market, but said the size and type of future impacts were “highly uncertain”.

The RBA – which last week warned the construction of datacentres and AI investment was fuelling inflation – said it saw “tentative signs” of impacts on certain roles, like clerks, computer programmers and call centre workers.

Qantas this week announced 850 job cuts which would target finance, human resources and marketing roles. Meanwhile, National Australian Bank announced 2,500 job losses and while Canva announced 1,200 layoffs.

All have been linked partly to the growth in AI.

Rishworth’s workplace guide says little about potential redundancies linked to AI, but warns employers they should be consulting with workers about the takeup of AI and what it might mean for their jobs. It especially raises concern about “entry-level work”, which the guide said may be “the first to be automated”.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Stuart Heritage

Substackers in love, dodgy romance scams and Jeff Bezos as the dashing lead … the film-makers behind the remake of the dial-up classic will be facing an embarrassment of pitches

A
ssuming you have already heard about the You’ve Got Mail reboot, you are probably in one of two states. You are either excited that the news might be a signal of a long overdue romcom resurgence, or you are embittered because it’s another sign that Hollywood has run out of original ideas.

I hold absolutely no truck with the latter view. Quite frankly, if there was ever a film in dire need of a reboot, then it’s You’ve Got Mail. The film is almost 28 years old, and it shows every single day of its age. You’ve seen it, you know how it goes. It’s about two people who use the futuristic new technology of email (email is no longer new) to communicate, despite being rival booksellers (nobody reads books any more), and eventually begin a relationship (nobody wants to be in a relationship any more). The whole thing is preposterous. Of course they should try again.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The good news about the reboot is that it seems to be in safe hands. It is to be written by Deborah Kaplan and Harry Elfont, who wrote 2010 classic romcom Leap Year, and directed by Jason Orley, who helmed the very sweet I Want You Back from 2022, plus an inexplicably large number of Pete Davidson vehicles. So the real question is: how do you actually go about updating You’ve Got Mail?

The good thing is that the film operates from a classic literary device: people falling in love without knowing the other’s true identity. Indeed, You’ve Got Mail was a remake of Ernst Lubitsch’s 1940 film The Shop Around the Corner, which was in turn a remake of Miklós László’s Hungarian 1937 play Illatszertár. Going further back, you can trace the themes through works like 1897’s Cyrano de Bergerac, 1775’s The Rivals and 1598’s Much Ado About Nothing. It’s just the framing that needs updating.

First, let’s bin email altogether. It isn’t new and exciting like it was in the 1990s, and for most of us has simply become the thing where we go to delete promotional Millie’s Cookies marketing messages three times a week. Maybe a smarter way to go in would be via social media. Perhaps two people with anonymised Instagram accounts fall in love or, if that’s too visual, a couple of goobers who just really love Substack. Maybe the film could even move beyond this, and utilise something like Bluetooth or wireless ad hoc network filesharing technology. That would certainly be novel.

And let’s rethink the book element too. In the original You’ve Got Mail, Tom Hanks played a man whose biggest crime was owning and operating a large physical bookshop, to the consternation of Meg Ryan and her small independent store. And, look, things have changed. All bookshops, big or small, are wonderful and precious things that we must protect at all costs. Being mad at Tom Hanks in 2026 is like being mad at a Waterstones, which is just preposterous. Maybe, just maybe, there is a workaround here. Perhaps we need to think further up the chain and locate the person who has done more to kill off the physical bookshop than anyone. That’s right, I’m suggesting that one of the leads of the reboot should be Jeff Bezos. Listen, it could work.

We now come to casting. And here there is a problem. Almost every single generation since 1998 has been brought up to intrinsically question modern technology. Show a 10-year-old an email from an anonymous and unfamiliar source, no matter how affectionate its content, and their first instinct will be to assume that it is a scam and delete it unread. In fact, the only people old enough to not instantly do this are probably people as old as Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan are now. So one option would be to keep the leads of the first film, and make it a story about two older scam-plagued people who fall in love while simultaneously giving all their money to mysterious Nigerian princes.

Doesn’t this sound good? Wouldn’t you watch this? Of course you would. Heartfelt sincerity is in short supply these days, and something like a golden-era romcom remake might just be the thing to set the world back on track again. So when You’ve Got Mail 2 comes out, I will be first in line, even though it will almost definitely star Pete Davidson and be called Jeff Bezos Just Airdropped You a Dickpic.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.author: As told to Rhiannon Evans

We asked 20 tweenagers what they already own, love and think would make great gifts. Turns out it’s Lego, dance mats and plenty of lotions and potions

The best Christmas gifts for teenagers

Buying for someone in the tweenage years can be a balancing act: while some kids are still crafting, enjoying board games and deep into Lego, others have moved on to skincare and guitars.

So, in an effort to cover the whole range, I spoke to 20 tweens (from 10 to 12 years old) from across the country. But instead of asking what they want, I quizzed them on the things they already have, truly love and use regularly. Here are their tried and tested gift ideas for a range of prices.

Lottie Brooks six-book set

I’ve read all nine of the Lottie Brooks books, and I can’t wait to read number 10, Twelve Disasters of Christmas. I really like them because they are easy to read and teach you about life. They make me laugh out loud. I also think kids my age would love to get a dance mat, they’re loads of fun. Millie, 10

My friend has a 3D printer, and I love it – I think kids my age would want one so we can make fidgets and other things. I’m definitely asking for one this Christmas. Sophia, 10

Premier League football

Joga Starz match day bundle

For my birthday this year, I got a size 3 football and Joga shin pads, which I think are good gifts for anyone who likes football. George, 10

Daise Bloom body mist, 100ml

Daise is my favourite brand. It does lip glosses, body mists and body creams. 10-year-old girls really love the lip glosses. My recommendations are Cake Pop, Cherry Bomb and Very Vanilla. The body mists I’d recommend are Sunny and Bloom. Emily, 10

The World of Skandar: The First Unicorn Rider by AF Steadman

I love The World of Skandar: The First Unicorn Rider, as well as the series before this prequel, too – which is about a boy called Skandar who’s a unicorn rider. The unicorns in these books aren’t what we’re used to: they’re ferocious and bloodthirsty, not cute and cuddly. This prequel is full of adventure, elemental magic, battles and secrets. It’s the most exciting book I’ve ever read! Alba, 10

Douglas chase border collie

Warriors graphic novel box set

Ion8 Celestial water bottle, 600ml

My favourite thing is my Douglas cuddly toy. I have a border collie. They’re cute and perfect for hugging when you need to give something a squeeze. (Daphne’s mum, Sam, says you can get some good deals on Vinted, too).

Next is the Warriors wild cats graphic novels. Cool cats that fight to the death? What’s not to love? It’s a good story, and I love the artwork.

The WiZ Smart LED lights transformed my bedroom and can give it a different aesthetic depending on how I’m feeling. I like having them on a soft setting at night, so they keep the room a little bit light. Also, I love water bottles! Any type. I’m just obsessed with them. Daphne, 11

Wavelength party game

Wavelength is really fun, a great team game. I love playing it with my family and friends. It’s popular on YouTube, where there’s loads of videos of people playing it. Jack, 11

Owala FreeSip bottle, 909ml

These Owala drink bottles are so good because they come in loads of different colours and designs. They’re steel and keep drinks hot or cold for hours. You can also drink from the straw or chug it. Arielle, 11

For more, read our guide to the best water bottles

Martin Smith 3/4 size acoustic guitar in natural wood

Fortnite Peely action figure

Fortnite V-Bucks gift card

My guitar. I love music. I want to be the best guitarist in a famous rock band. I also love anything Fortnite, but especially a Peely toy. He’s my favourite, and one of the older skins [Fortnite character]. A good gift would be a V-Bucks gift card, so you can buy Fortnite skins. Edward, 11

Leopard-print dressing gown

I think other tweens would love a big fluffy dressing gown because it’s great for chill days when you don’t want to do anything, and it keeps you warm, cosy and comfortable. Just beware, your parents may love it even more and want constant cuddles!

I also love light boxes (mine is from Flying Tiger) because it’s a great decoration for all bedrooms, so customisable and aesthetic. On mine, I put positive affirmations to start my day off right. Olivia, 12

Cards Against Humanity Family Edition

after newsletter promotion

I love playing Cards Against Humanity Family Edition. The solutions are really funny (some are a bit rude!) and you can never get bored. We always take it away with us when we go camping or to visit friends. Raph, 11

Jellycat Amuseables pink and white marshmallows

I love my Jellycats because they are fun to cuddle and play with and are just so cute. They are amazing as a gift, easy to wrap in their bag, and there are many different types, like food, animals and objects. Phoebe, 11

Laneige berry sweet lip trio

Space NK mini travel bag

I love the beauty brand Laneige and all the girls I know like it too. I got this great gift set with some of my favourites in it. I especially love the lip sleeping mask. I also think this makeup bag is mega-cute and would make a great present for a girl my age. Rosie, 11

Impossible Creature by Katherine Rundell

Nerf Elite 2.0 Loadout 3-blaster pack

I love my golf putting mat – I play with it all the time. I also love reading the Impossible Creatures books by Katherine Rundell; they’re really exciting. Another toy that kids my age like is a Nerf gun. James, 11

I love all things Lego, especially the Marvel collections – my favourite at the moment is the Lego Avengers Tower. Odhran, 11

24 colours bedazzling kit

Monopoly Travel World Tour

Pandora heart clasp snake chain bracelet

I love this bedazzling gem-crafting kit because it makes all my things look glamorous, unique and special. You can add patterns such as hearts, stars and even names to items such as hair clips, jewellery boxes, pens, water bottles and even my phone case!

The Monopoly Travel World Tour board game is amazing; I also love learning about all the different places in the world, such as Stonehenge, Niagara Falls and the Great Barrier Reef – which I’d love to visit one day. It’s also a fun way to spend time with family (away from my phone) – winning against my parents and asking them for rent is just so funny!

I also love my Pandora bracelet and charms. It’s fun to collect new charms, and it goes with all my outfits, from my casual wear to dresses. The charms hold sentimental value and remind me of the occasions when I was given them. Simran 12

Jellycat Amuseables Macaron

Sol de Janeiro Bum Bum Jet set

Theatre tokens gift card

Jellycats are cute and soft and make your bed extra cosy – I think anyone my age or older (mum loves them, too) would be happy to get one. Sol de Janeiro smells really nice and lasts all day. My mum got me the travel set to have in my school bag and take on trips.

I have been going to musicals since I was six – the best for my age would be Matilda or Wicked. Tickets to see a show have always been my favourite present as I love the theatre. This year I’d like to see Mean Girls, the musical version.

I also think a Selfridges gift card is a good gift so I can go on a shopping spree for beauty minis and not drain my mum’s bank account. Emily, 12 (in December)

Stray Kids official light stick

If you like K-pop, then a light stick is a great choice. You can get one for the group you like – put key chains on them with members’ photo cards and customise them to your bias. If your parents let you go to a concert, the light stick connects and flashes to the beat of all the songs. Poppy, 12

Lego Ninjago Cole’s Mission Mech & Dragon Zane toy

I love my Lego Ninjago sets, particularly the mechs and dragons – they have infinite playtime because you don’t need batteries. I get to build them at Christmas and play with them for months after. Jake, 12

Faux fur kids’ beanbag

I absolutely love my bean bag. It’s fluffy and comfortable, and it’s relaxing when you just need to chill out. It’s a really nice place to read, and you can fit two people on it! Felix, 12

Rhiannon Evans is a journalist and editor who’s covered everything from news and entertainment to lifestyle and parenting for some of the UK’s best titles (and some others too). https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Alyssa Mercante
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.text:
Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House

I
n early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade, it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia.

After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP.

But now, video game creators and artists are pushing back, looking to regain ground the industry has ceded to reactionary ideologies over the last decade by turning the gamification of politics back on Trump. Anonymous art collective The Secret Handshake has been known for its political activism since installing a sculpture of Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein at the National Mall in downtown Washington, DC. This spring, the group developed a game entitled Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell and made it available online, as well as installing three free arcade cabinets on the National Mall.

A satire on the Trump administration, the game allows players to control the president in a Pokémon-style challenge that starts with an important choice: order a Diet Coke, or invade Iran. As the game progresses, Trump heads to Iran to collect barrels of oil (called “lube” in the game) and encounters administration members such as vice-president JD Vance, secretary of state Marco Rubio, and “secretary of war”, Pete Hegseth. It’s unwinnable, which is the point, though you can get a “Game Over” screen by trying to hold Melania Trump’s hand.

The Secret Handshake had never made a video game until Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell. “The ‘form’ was really dictated by the Trump Administration,” a member of Secret Handshake says via email. “It’s not that we wanted to make a video game; it’s that the Pentagon began using video games to promote their war in Iran and make it seem ‘cool’. They actually introduced the idea of a video game, not us. We felt like, well, if they’re going to use video games to promote their war, let’s make a video game satirising that war.”

The collective followed similar logic when creating their second free game, Operation Epic Furious: Nuuk ’Em All which tasks players with speaking to Trump’s advisers, including a UFC fighter as “secretary of combat” and a no-bid contractor helping renovate The White House. The aim is to piece together enough “Big Brainpower” to figure out how to distract voters from the oil crisis. After Trump accidentally hits on his own daughter, Ivanka, and speaks to enough advisers to collect enough partial ideas to make one “big beautiful idea”, he decides to invade Greenland.

For The Secret Handshake, the video game as a medium helps people take in “the insanity” of what’s happening, which the collective believes may be hard to ascertain from just headlines. “When you are using a medium that’s very familiar, like a video game, and you’re going through these actions, it allows you to experience the headlines in a different way,” a spokesperson says. “This game is meant to be a caricature and satire, but it’s full of things in there that aren’t. The school in the Iran game and Trump calling a woman a maggot felt very intense to experience in the form of a game.”

The Secret Handshake had to learn how to build a game on the fly for Operation Epic Furious. “We had no idea what we were doing,” a spokesperson explains. “It was a lot of trial and error, and figuring it out as we went along. We did have someone helping that understood this world and could actually make it happen, but no one was a game designer.” They describe the games as, “held together with duct tape”.

Still, there are avid gamers in the group, and they pulled inspiration from Japanese role-playing adventures, particularly the early Final Fantasy titles, while the invidious, scatalogical tone is similar to South Park games such as The Stick of Truth and The Fractured But Whole. The aim was for the games to be funny and to properly satirise the absurdity of the current administration. So far, more than 350,000 people have played them online.

Two further anti-Trump games mimic the iconic arcade shooter Space Invaders, and they couldn’t have been made in more different ways. This summer, game developer Richie Branson partnered with nonprofit All for America to create Tax Evaders, in which you choose one of four playable pilots (President Trump, vice-president JD Vance, House speaker Mike Johnson, or Senate leader John Thune) before jumping into the first level, destroying healthcare and lining billionaire pockets.

“There’s something a bit unsettling about playing as the ‘villain’,” says Branson, who created Tax Evaders using the free and open-source game development engine, Godot. “The intent here is to drive home the point that these officials are destroying beneficial programmes with the same combination of enthusiasm and indifference as someone blowing up enemy space ships in an arcade game.”

The Trump administration’s aggressive push into online culture is working, according to Branson, who said the White House team is, “on a rampage” with its memelord and gaming culture posts. “It’s a very cunning way of spreading whatever message they’re trying to spread,” he says, before referring to the White House Arcade as “gamified propaganda”, and “garbage, [with] no love for the art”. Tax Evaders has had over 50,000 players and over 2m page impressions since July.

Alfie Souter and Carlota Real work in advertising together. They often chat about breaking news and trending topics, so when they saw the White House release its propaganda arcade, they decided to do something about it. “The craziest thing is the oversimplification of such a complex issue, like immigration,” says Real. “What they’re trying to do is boil this down to the minimum that people understand. A Tetris game; everyone on the planet has probably played it once, and they apply it to the shitshow that they’re doing.”

Angered by the administration’s trivialision of the issues and its demonisation of immigrants, the duo started brainstorming their own version of a simplified game with a political message. With no background in game design, they decided to build it in ChatGPT, which itself is perhaps a satirical message: many believe the Trump Arcade games are “vibe-coded”, or built using plain language to describe a game to a generative AI program, which then codes it.

The result is Corrupt Invaders. Essentially a homage to Space Invaders with an anti-Trump filter, the game tasks you with moving Trump’s “$400m Qatari gift” (his aeroplane) to “collect another $1.4bn in crypto.” Your final score is subtracted from Trump’s reported cryptocurrency earnings. According to Souter the duo wanted the game to be focused on something that felt inarguable about the Trump regime and settled on corruption, using the $400m Boeing 747-8 luxury jet gifted by Qatar. Federal law says US officials can only accept gifts under $480, but the Trump White House insisted Trump accepting the aircraft was legal. “We thought about that jet, and also the $1.4bn earnings in crypto last year – those numbers are so ridiculous,” says Souter. “That’s why when you play the game, you subtract it from the score, because it’s such an unfathomable number”.

The two wanted to focus on the money that President Trump and his close allies have earned since his second presidency and juxtapose that against Americans’ consistent concerns with the cost of living crisis. The games are designed to makes the dichotomy crystal clear. Recently, the duo launched Diesel Kong, a parody of the classic Nintendo platformer Donkey Kong in the context of rising oil prices due to the continued war in Iran. “Prices are going up. Putin’s throwing useless barrels, can Trump be saved?” asks the starting screen. Trump stands in place of Princess Peach, while a nondescript Maga supporter wearing an American flag shirt and red hat tries to make his way up the ramps and ladders.

The developers and activists behind these games are pushing back against the Trump administration’s gamified propaganda while looking to subvert the gaming subcultures the president has co-opted. “Our current administration runs the country as if were a video game, with no real sense of sympathy for the people affected by the losses incurred by their policies,” said Branson. “Gas prices are crazy right now, people’s lives are being affected, but to our nation’s leadership, we’re just NPCs.”

More than 350,000 people have played Tax Evaders online since July.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Christian Donlan
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.text:
Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited
This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration

A
rriving alongside November’s blue wave, Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together.

It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country, except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it.

At the heart of it all is a sense of daily ritual. To pay for the shrine’s restoration, you’ll be taking a job at the local post office, which means that every morning – except Wednesdays and the weekend – you’ll bike over to collect your packages, and then spend the rest of the day riding around the snug open world making sure they all end up in the right places.

Your reward for a delivery is often a bit of cash and some local gossip. Sometimes, though, you’ll be roped into a mini game: fishing for an impatient sushi chef, say, or chopping down trees and then sanding the logs. These games can be somewhat clumsily implemented, particularly if they involve aiming, since there’s no on-screen reticule. Regardless, they provide a little bit of variation to the gentle flow of each in-game day, while reminding you of the richness and variety of the little town you’re starting to call home.

This process of coming to understand the town better each day carries the game through to the end. While it’s nice to level up and earn money, all while restoring the shrine’s big ticket items, the truest sense of accomplishment here comes when you discover that you can stop using the in-game map because the paths to and from the post office have started to become genuinely familiar.

And once you feel comfortable in the world, you can step away from your objective, thin as it is, and simply explore the space, unlocking new shrines, enjoying the local architecture and performing stunts on your BMX. (The BMX, incidentally, is one of the game’s secret stars, not just providing enough joy in its movement to keep you from fast travel, but also connecting to the wider environment with jumps and grinds, and showing you fresh opportunities for path-making in the landscape all around you.)

Whether you’re fiddling with the escapement and crystal of an old mechanical watch in Assemble With Care or rebuilding a gloriously seedy business in Promise Mascot Agency, it’s astonishing how much magic games can find in the disparate aspects of restoration and reinvention. Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a reminder that, for all the destructive powers of video games, some of the medium’s greatest potential lies with the pleasing business of putting things back together again.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Keza MacDonald
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.text:
The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

I
n 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.”

I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.”

Grand Theft Auto VI is finally out next week, more than 10 years since those first exploratory trips. A few weeks ago, I spent the day at Rockstar North’s headquarters in Edinburgh, watching as Nelson and fellow senior exec Jennifer Kolbe took me through Vice City, the fictional version of Miami that has emerged from all that work. The setting always comes first for Rockstar games: the developers immerse themselves in the real-life version of the place they want to create, before they ask what they want to do within it and what they want to offer players. From there emerge the story that Rockstar’s writers want to tell and the characters players will later meet. This time that story is about a criminal couple on the run named Jason and Lucia.

Grand Theft Auto V (2013) and Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018) conjure fascinatingly detailed versions of the US: one a microcosm of California, the other of the old west. GTA VI takes us to Leonida, virtual Florida, and as with Rockstar’s previous games it is gratuitously, absurdly detailed, from the macro level to the micro; from architecture and geography down to the smallest of details – such as the clothes that the pedestrians are wearing, the street art, the flyers on cafe walls and the insides of fridges. As Nelson and I freely explored Vice City, we discussed the effort and motivations that went into the making of this ultra-maximalist game. You can read more about it in the Guardian’s Saturday magazine later this week.

Grand Theft Auto VI was made by an enormous team of almost 5,000 people, but there is a relatively small number of decision-makers at the top, most of whom have been at Rockstar for a very long time. (Lead writer Rupert Humphries, for instance, has been at the company since 2008.) They each take responsibility for the elements of the game that they are most suited to and that they care about most. “The game is so vast that no one person could hold enough of it in their heads,” Nelson tells me. His purview is design, narrative and animation, with a little casting on the side: Nelson’s background is in character art and animation, and his attention to detail is abundantly evident in his demonstration of the game. He takes huge delight in showing me tiny details, such as the way that Jason eats a hot dog or how, as he walks around a gas station, he can take bites of a donut with one hand while sipping a beer with the other.

When Jason starts running, he hikes the six-pack of beers he’s carrying into the crook of his arm, the liquid inside the bottles sloshing around. At one point in my Vice City ridealong, Nelson gets briefly upset during a jewellery store stick-up when the placement of one of the security guards’ feet doesn’t look right. The level of detail in this game is simply out of reach for any other game developer thanks to Rockstar’s abundance of money and time, and the patience from its parent company, Take-Two Interactive.

Rockstar’s worlds are believable because, despite their rampant excess, they are grounded in the real places they are based on and real experiences developers had in those places. Jennifer Kolbe says that during research for Grand Theft Auto IV, which was set in the New-York-inspired Liberty City, “people who had lived in New York all their lives were going to places they would never go to ... We then give that experience to players.”

Nelson reminisces about staying out in a Miami nightclub until 4am and then getting up a few hours later to be driven around a racetrack with a momentous hangover. They went on a ridealong with cops in South Beach, and hung out in weird bars in the Florida Keys. “Some of our team, especially the artists, are very intrepid,” he says. “They’ll go wandering in all sorts of places with their cameras. They’re fearless.”

Rockstar is famous for its depictions of the US – particularly American cities. But I have always wondered what this team could do in a different setting. Could Rockstar ever envision a GTA set outside of America? “Never say never, but there’s still so much to do in America,” Nelson says. I ask whether Rockstar’s outsider status, as a bunch of developers based mostly outside of the US (though it has offices in New York and San Diego), gives it a unique take on a country so vast and full of contradictions. “I think we’re all outsiders to this version of America,” he says. “It doesn’t matter where you live … no one experiences the America that we’re portraying here in its fullness.”

One of the few games brave enough to release in the dead zone surrounding GTA VI is Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, a whimsical delight of a game about a chubby raccoon trying to rebuild the shrine he calls home. I played an earlier version at Tokyo game show a couple of years back, and am delighted to discover that it’s come out brilliantly. “Arriving alongside November’s blue wave, Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment,” as writer Christian Donlan puts it in a review out this week. “Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together.”

The brilliant cooperative indie darling Big Walk has become mired in AI controversy after the Independent games festival awards put out a statement on its stance about the use of large language models in nominated games. Out of what appears to be an abundance of caution, Big Walk’s House House developers disclosed to the IGF jurors that they used an LLM to help solve a coding problem during the game’s development. The fallout has illustrated how vociferous the anti-AI sentiment is among gaming creatives and has raised difficult questions about where to draw the line.

Nintendo is hiring a historian/librarian to help preserve and document the creation of its games and hardware.

A documentary film about the final years of legendary developer BioWare is coming, from Canada’s Super Channel. The studio was closed by EA last month after a 30-year run creating some of the most influential RPGs ever made.

‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?

Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus

Please do keep sending in your questions and comments about GTA VI – next week’s issue will be a big Q&A about the game. In the meantime, reader Tim asks:

“I’m really worried about spoilers, to the point where I’m thinking of drawing up a joke contract for my son to sign so he agrees not to spoil it (teenagers these days just seem to blast through story mode, whereas I like to savour it). In a world where South Park contained Red Dead Redemption 2 spoilers, how the hell can we avoid them? Any tips??”

Honestly, you might be fighting a losing battle unless you a) stay off the internet entirely and b) speak to nobody at all in person who might possibly be playing it. GTA VI is a massive game that should, rightly, take weeks or months to work your way through, but we all know that a thousand content creators will have somehow gotten through the entire thing and put all of the footage on YouTube within days of its release.

The great thing about Rockstar games, though, is that outside of the story you really are creating your own experience, choosing what to do and how to spend your time, how your Jason and Lucia act. And nobody can spoil that for you.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Combining body mass index with other measurements and tests would lead to better care and outcomes, experts say

An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat.

Medical experts have long considered body mass index a blunt instrument for defining obesity, leading to concerns that substantial numbers of people with excess body fat are missed while others who are healthy are wrongly diagnosed.

The new approach, which combines BMI with other body measurements and organ function tests, suggests BMI alone misses obesity in 5-9% of adults, while wrongly diagnosing the condition in as many as 3%.

“This misclassification can account for tens of millions of people, so the inaccuracy of BMI is a big problem at scale and also for individuals,” said Francisco Rubino, a professor of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London.

BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. About 1.6 billion people worldwide are classified as overweight, meaning their BMI falls between 25 and 29.9, and nearly a billion with a BMI of 30 or more are considered obese. Two-thirds of adults in the UK and more than 70% of adults in the US are overweight or obese based on BMI alone.

Rubino and his colleagues drew on health records from more than 800,000 people in the UK, US, China and Spain to test a diagnostic approach for obesity that he and other world experts proposed last year in a Lancet Commission report. They used the records to track people’s health for up to 15 years.

Under the new definition, someone with a BMI over 40 is considered obese, but doctors check people with a lower BMI for excess body fat by looking at their waist measurement.

A BMI of 30-plus with a raised waist measurement or waist-to-height ratio counts as obese, as does a BMI from 25 to 29.9 if waist measurement and waist-to-height ratio are high. In most countries, a raised waist measurement means more than 102cm (40in) for men and 88cm for women, while thresholds for a high waist-to-height ratio are about 0.57.

In a second step of the diagnosis, doctors distinguish between clinical obesity, meaning an active disease where excess body fat is already impairing organ function, and pre-clinical obesity, where the extra fat is a health risk but has yet to cause problems.

Obesity levels rose only slightly overall under the new definition, and only a quarter to a third of obese people, or 5% to 10% of the wider population, who had clinical obesity and a substantially higher risk of death.

The approach allows doctors to distinguish between healthy and sick people who have the same BMI. Three people with a BMI of 32, for example, would all be classed as obese but would have very different diagnoses. One might have no excess body fat and be healthy, another could have excess fat but no organ dysfunction and have pre-clinical obesity, and the third could have excess fat and organ dysfunction and be clinically obese.

after newsletter promotion

Writing in Nature, the scientists describe how some people with a high BMI were not obese under the new definition and actually had a lower mortality risk than others considered healthy. Reassuringly, 80% to 90% of people with pre-clinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity, or active disease, in the next 10 years.

The approach makes the process more complex for clinicians, but Rubino said people should be diagnosed for obesity at the individual level to ensure the best healthcare, whether that involved lifestyle advice, GLP-1 weight loss drugs or surgery.

“We can optimise our interventions and ultimately make better use of our resources with more safety, more efficacy,” he said. “If you ask if I think this should be employed in the clinic, I think absolutely, yes.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Historic US ocean liner sinks near Florida to become world’s largest artificial reef
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
SS United States, which set transatlantic speed record during maiden voyage in 1952, is sunk off coast of Destin

The historic SS United States has reached the end of its journey at sea, sinking Wednesday off the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will begin a new life underwater as an artificial reef.

The nearly 1,000ft American-made vessel, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, was launched in 1952 and made history by setting a transatlantic speed record during its maiden voyage. The ship carried thousands of passengers across the Atlantic over 17 years of operation before being retired in 1969.

On Wednesday, the ship was deployed at approximately 2.40pm ET, with the sinking process beginning shortly before 5pm. The ship had been hollowed out, with openings cut into its hull to let water in and help it sink upright to the ocean floor. Over the next several hours, the ship gradually filled with water before finally sinking to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico around 10pm.

It will rest on the seafloor at a depth of approximately 180ft, the ship’s upper decks sitting about 55ft below the surface. As the world’s largest artificial reef, the site is expected to become a popular diving destination for divers around the world.

For years, the SS United States remained docked in Philadelphia, as various owners attempted to save and restore it. However, the rising costs of maintaining the ageing vessel complicated preservation efforts. In 2021, port authorities raised the daily dockage fee to $1,700, a cost the non-profit SS United States Conservancy could no longer afford.

In 2024, Florida’s Okaloosa county purchased the ship for $1m, with plans to transform it into the world’s largest artificial reef. Officials expect the structure to provide a new habitat for a variety of marine life, including red snapper, grouper, amberjack, mackerel and tuna.

Before its sinking, Susan Gibbs, president and co-founder of the conservancy, said: “She’s being reefed and will remain intact and will become a vibrant and dynamic marine habitat, so that, combined with the land-based museum and visitor experience, will honor her history in a deeply moving way.”

Gibbs, whose grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the ship, also reflected on his personal connection to the vessel, saying: “His relationship with the ship was, I would say, a full-bore obsession. He would joke that he loved the SS United States a thousand times more than my grandmother. He would see the ship off every time she set sail for Europe, and be one of the first to greet her on her return.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 live: ‘No one is coming to rescue us,’ Greta Thunberg tells climate summit
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan (now) and Matthew Pearce (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Greta Thunberg has said that the planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who” in a stark intervention at the Cop31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey.

“It is being killed by the very same people thought to come to our rescue,” Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist, said. “No one is coming to our rescue.

“When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it’s our duty to stand up and be the adult in the room and fight for everyone’s human rights.”

Thunberg spoke at a packed press gathering in the Cop31 venue alongside other activists from Nepal, Australia, Palestine and Canada. All of them lambasted governments’ inaction on the climate crisis and called for the end of Turkish energy shipments to Israel, which Thunberg said was “directly feeling the genocide in Palestine.”

“We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights and where basic necessities become luxuries,” Thunberg said. “It’s more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be any less under control, the planet is not dying, it is being killed.”

Thunberg has not attended a Cop since 2021, where in Glasgow she famously said that the talks amounted to “blah, blah, blah”. In this time she has shifted her focus somewhat away from the climate crisis to include causes such as the plight of the Palestinian people.

Her arrival in Turkey has caused much excitement among delegates at Cop, with a throng of people clamouring to speak to her after she finished the press conference.

Donald Trump is the “biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time” for scrapping action on the climate crisis and ceding the clean energy race to China, former US secretary of state John Kerry has said.

Kerry, speaking at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, criticized Trump for withdrawing the US from the international climate process and axing measures that reduced planet-heating emissions. Unlike almost all other countries in the world, the Trump administration has sent no delegation to the resort city of Antalya for the annual UN climate talks, which started on Monday.

The US president, who has previously called climate science a “hoax” and called for countries to drill for more oil and gas, again expressed his hostility towards clean energy on Monday. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser,” Trump, who has long-held animus towards windfarms, said about potential new legislation that would make it easier to build new energy projects.

Asked about his comments by the Guardian, Kerry said: “[The] first thing they should do is hold up a really big mirror so he can look at a loser, because he’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues.”

“He’s missing the point,” Kerry, a former climate envoy for Joe Biden’s administration, added. “He’s missing the competitiveness with China. He’s missing the marketplace for goods that could be produced in the United States. We could be the supply chain for some of these.”

Under Biden, the US passed sweeping climate legislation that gave tax breaks for clean energy and electric vehicle manufacturing in a bid to compete with China, which has dominated clean tech.

Republicans eliminated most of this support, however, with Trump instead imposing tariffs on various goods and pouring public money into propping up struggling coal-fired power plants. Coal is the dirtiest of fossil fuels, causing much of the pollution that is dangerously overheating our planet.

“He declared he wanted to beat China, be number one in X, Y, or Z, and he walked away from the battlefield,” Kerry said of Trump. “He totally took America out of that sector. So honestly, if you want to be number one, you don’t do it by literally blackballing an entire sector of the economy.”

The catastrophic collapse of a glacier in Nepal was a warning sign to the rest of the world to put the climate crisis at the top of the global agenda, and for the rich to provide financial aid to the poor to avert further disasters, Nepal’s environment minister told the Guardian, as world leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 UN climate summit.

The disaster that struck in August claimed more than 1,500 lives and devastated the small Himalayan country. Gita Chaudhary, Nepal’s environment minister, said: “We call the catastrophic climate change event we suffered a mountain tsunami. We lost people, we lost lives, we lost property. Nepal is working for rehabilitation, reconstruction and rebuilding the infrastructure. But the communities, the culture, the lives, we cannot revive.”

The impact of glacier collapse will be felt far beyond Nepal’s borders, as snowmelt and water from the Himalayas feeds about 2 billion people. “We are not responsible. We have made zero contribution to the climate crisis. But we are paying the price,” Chaudhary told the Guardian in an interview. “It is a sign of warning for all. Climate change issues need to be at the top of global discussions. We need to feel the urgency.”

But she said she was not angry at the rest of the world. “Anger is not the solution. We have hope for Cop31,” she added. “But we need finance [to help poor countries] that is predictable, accessible and grant-based. And we need to limit global warming to 1.5C.”

Fossil fuel and related corporations have sought $440bn from governments through secretive corporate courts, according to a new analysis.

For all the grand efforts of UNFCCC Cop processes, and individual efforts by governments to reduce their reliance on coal, oil and gas, legal measures built into trade deals still give the fossil fuel industry vigorous means to fight back.

So-called Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) mechanisms, hidden in the text of treaties, mean that corporations can frequently sue governments for policies that endanger their profits. And that includes decarbonisation efforts.

According to research by PowerShift, Global Justice Now and the European Trade Justice Coalition, oil, gas and coal companies have become the biggest users of these tribunals.

So far they have been awarded a total of $86bn, the NGOs say. But that figure is conservative: in almost one-third of all publicly known ISDS cases the claim amount has not been made public.

“It’s obscene,” said Nick Dearden, director of Global Justice Now. “The very corporations which have created the climate crisis are demanding eye-watering pay-outs when governments take much needed climate action.”

Among the cases currently under way is a $300m claim against the UK, after the high court quashed permission for a new deep coalmine in Cumbria. Elsewhere, ExxonMobil launched a claim challenging the EU’s Net Zero Industry Act, which obliges the company to pay for carbon storage capacity. But it is developing countries that are the worst affected. Even the threat of a hundred million dollar claim can act as a chilling effect on pro-environmental, pro-climate policies.

Activists at Cop31 are calling on delegates to agree a mechanism to phase out ISDS. Fossil fuel investors claim 70% of ISDS awards, they say, making it a serious barrier to climate action.

Fabian Flues, Investment Policy lead at PowerShift said corporations were weaponising trade and investment agreements. “Governments need to stop this heist,” by cancelling treaties, he said. “Countries like Australia, South Africa and Indonesia have taken significant steps to free themselves from ISDS, and others should follow suit.”

If you’re new to the annual UN climate talks known as Cops – or find yourself asking why they attract so much attention, and whether they even matter – have a listen to my colleagues Madeleine Finlay and Ian Sample break down why they exist and set out the stakes for humanity on our latest episode of the Science Weekly podcast.

One of the biggest issues for Cop31 delegates to grapple with is how the crisis affects public health – from pollution to extreme heat.

The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, who addressed Cop31 earlier, is being called out in this area today by the Green party of England and Wales over the health impacts of more drilling in the North Sea.

With a decision expected soon on whether to go ahead with the huge new Rosebank oilfield, the Greens are insisting the government must carry out – and publish – an official assessment, setting out the impact on the UK’s National Health Service of digging up and burning this vast basin of oil.

Earlier this year the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said the extreme heat that engulfed the UK during repeated heatwaves had put intense pressure on the NHS.

Climate experts say that extracting more oil from the huge Rosebank oilfield would exacerbate the climate crisis. A study by Oxfam found that the combined lifetime emissions from Rosebank – and the smaller Jackdaw gasfield that was approved last month, would contribute an estimated 65,495 excess heat deaths.

Green MP Carla Denyer said given the UK has a foreign secretary who has called Rosebank climate vandalism, and a health secretary who has admitted this summer’s heatwaves put even more pressure on our NHS, “it is a complete dereliction of duty that ministers seem to have not assessed the health impacts of new oil and gas drilling.”

“After heatwaves are estimated to have cost nearly 3,000 lives, and extreme weather forecast to cause chaos this winter, the government must now come clean on the true impacts of Rosebank,” she added. “And if they haven’t done an assessment of the health impacts, they must delay any decision until this has been completed.”

The decision over the Rosebank field is being carefully watched not just by Green Party supporters, but also by Labour backers and MPs who fear the party is backsliding on some of its climate and wider green policies under Burnham – despite his warm words at Cop today.

On Tuesday more than 20 Labour backbenchers called on the government to reject Rosebank during a debate in parliament.

Denyer, who secured the debate, said in her speech that “the decision whether to approve the climate-wrecking Rosebank oilfield is a defining moment for this government and this parliament.”

“If the Government are clear that climate change is no longer a distant threat and that fossil fuels are driving climate breakdown, why are they not clear that green-lighting Rosebank, the biggest undeveloped oil and gasfield in the North sea, is a complete dereliction of duty?”

Earlier Denyer had submitted a parliamentary question to the government asking if an health impact assessment had been carried out before the decision was taken to allow the Jackdaw field to go ahead.

The government did not answer directly but said the decision had been taken “by the energy secretary alone with no involvement from other ministers” which the Greens took to be a tacit “no.”

Earlier today, climate activist Greta Thunberg told a packed room of journalists: “We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights and where basic necessities become luxuries.”

“It’s more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be any less under control, the planet is not dying, it is being killed.”

Watch the highlights here:

‘Climate change is never far from our minds’

I’ve been interviewing young climate activists at Cop31 this week and today I spoke to Josie Ann Le Blanc, 28, a member of the Caribbean Youth Environment Network in the Commonwealth of Dominica.

She was drawn to climate advocacy after Dominica experienced two catastrophic extreme weather events in two years: Tropical Storm Erika in 2015 and Hurricane Maria in 2017. The cyclones caused historic devastation and destruction on the island, leaving many dead, missing or homeless.

“Being born and raised in Dominica, climate change is never far from our minds. Since the storms in 2015 and 2017, we have also been experiencing record-breaking heatwaves, resulting in droughts, water shortages and health concerns for all, especially those who are particularly vulnerable.

“Climate change continues to mould the way our lives, work and plans for the future are impacted. For me, the climate crisis is not just an environmental concern but also a concern for social justice, economic development and public health.

“At Cop this year, I hope to see stronger commitments towards climate finance, adaptation, loss and damage, and the needs of small island developing states like Dominica. Future climate actions must be informed by those who have lived those experiences and should be inclusive and accountable to those vulnerable communities. Youth should be involved, having meaningful contributions and opportunities to influence decisions and not just be invited to listen.

“Ultimately, climate action should not only be measured by commitments made on international stages but also by the difference made and what communities can feel in their everyday lives.”

The Palestinian conflict has been the focus of this Cop perhaps unlike any other so far. Mohammad Mustafa, the prime minister of Palestine, got a standing ovation when he spoke to delegates today, while yesterday Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, president of Turkey, urged the world to recognize the environmental impacts of the three-year war waged by Israel in Gaza.

“What has taken place in Gaza is not only a genocide, but it is also an ecocide,” Erdogan said. Greta Thunberg, in her appearance at Cop, has also condemned Israel, which denies that its killings in Gaza constitute genocide. It was not invited to the gathering of leaders here.

There are visual reminders all around this summit, with several attenders wearing keffieyahs and plenty of interest in the Palestinian pavilion, which sits alongside those of other countries in the Cop31 venue.

“We are here to talk about the environment, not politics,” said one of the staff at the pavilion. Gaza and the West Bank have issues around air pollution and waste management that the Palestinians want to talk about, although it’s hard to separate these things from the impacts of bombardment.

A book for well wishes at the pavilion has been filled with plenty of supportive notes. One of the pavilion’s walls is covered in photos of the destruction and horror of the past three years. None of the Palestinians here are from Gaza as the territory’s borders remain sealed off by Israel, although some have been able to join the summit via video link.

We’ve been hearing from world leaders for the best part of two days now. But one country we’ve not heard from is Israel – one of Turkey’s closest neighbours. And there is a very good reason for that. They have not been invited.

“As the host country for the leaders’ summit, we did not send an invitation to Israel,” Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop31 president, told local media, according to The National.

“Of course, we will discuss the climate and climate justice here. We say that there can be no climate justice where peace does not prevail.”

South Korean outlet The Chosun Daily, again citing local media, quoted Kurum as saying: “We will not remain silent about the mass killings in Gaza … Our political stance is clear, and we will maintain this attitude during the conference.”

But while Israel is notable for its absence, in the Cop31 exhibition space a corner has been set aside for the Palestinian delegation. Featuring black cloth hung haphazardly from the ceiling, in a manner reminiscent of refugee tents, the “Gaza tent” seemed to replicate Gaza itself, Chosun Daily noted.

However, none of Gaza’s population was there, only Palestinians from the West Bank. Survivors in Gaza are banned by Israel from international travel.

There was a frenzy of attention upon Greta Thunberg when she appeared this morning in Antalya. I had my toe trodden upon several times in the scrum that formed around someone who spearheaded a surge of global climate activism that has somewhat faded from view amid various other crises in recent years.

The climate crisis hasn’t gone anywhere though, even if political and media attention has, and the activists who stood alongside Thunberg outlined the mounting toll of our overheating planet.

Sagar Dhakal, a Nepalese MP, spoke about how he helped dig people out of the debris of a deadly landslide, caused by a melting glacier along the Nepal-Tibet border, earlier this year. “I don’t think there are words in the dictionary to describe it,” Dhakal said.

“Vulnerable countries need support from the developed world, we need to work together,” she said. “If we all work together we can prevent the next disaster.”

Rikki Dank, an Indigenous Australian who is taking the Australian government to the UN human rights committee over its fossil fuel exports, said that “we need to start demanding better of our governments, not just for ourselves but for our communities.”

Dank took aim at Anthony Albanese, Australia’s prime minister who appeared here yesterday to claim that the co-host was playing its part and was a leader in climate action.

“Our prime minister needs to stop speaking and start listening when we say no to fracking of our country, to stop speaking and start listening when we say no to poisoning of our water and our sacred sites”, she said. “He needs to stop speaking and start listening when the Australian people say no new coal, oil and gas.”

Mohammed Usrof, founder of the Palestinian Institute for Climate Strategy, said that the fossil fuel economy is underpinning what he called a genocide committed by Israel that has killed 20 members of his own family.

“This militarized fossil economy continues to profiteer off genocide but also the complete devastation of our land,” he said. “There’s an intentional act of ecocide and environmental devastation.”

Usrof said that Israel should be removed from the UN framework on climate change, as well as the UN itself, and called on countries including Turkey to stop providing the fuel that is supplying Israel’s military.

Celine Isimbi, born to refugees from Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo and now living in Canada, criticised Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, for not showing up at the talks but said that even leaders at Cop31 are failing their people.

“Showing up means nothing when families are under rubble, when families have to be rescued from flash flooding,” she said. “Whether they show up or don’t show up, what changes for us on the ground is nothing because they aren’t putting their money where their mouths are, they aren’t meeting our material demands.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Greta Thunberg spoke at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey. She lambasted governments’ inaction on the climate crisis. Fossil fuel and related corporations have sought $440bn from governments through secretive corporate courts.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘It is much, much faster’: could China’s battery-swapping e-trucks be the answer to EV range anxiety?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Xiaoying You
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Battery maker CATL aims to have 2,000 swapping stations in China by the end of 2027 and to bring the tech to Europe

E
very day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send around five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China. A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about.

“When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts.

Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery.

In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says.

Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy.

To Wang, the biggest advantage of the technology is the time it saves. “It is much, much faster,” he says. “I don’t even need to leave my truck when the battery is being swapped.”

This swiftness builds on the cost advantage e-trucks already have over their fossil-fuelled peers when it comes to refuelling.

“Electricity is cheaper than oil,” Wang says. The per-kilometre fuelling cost for an e-truck works out about 1.1 yuan (12p) in Hainan, he says, significantly lower than that for a diesel truck, which exceeds 2 yuan (22p) a kilometre. “That means my e-truck can save more than 20,000 yuan (£2,200) per month,” Wang says.

When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate. “All the driver needs to do is to drive the truck into a designated area, and the battery will be swapped completely automatically,” says Wei Jiuchun, 46, a test driver at a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station in Suzhou, east China. Wei’s job is to help the station test its system for different models of heavy trucks and under different weather conditions.

It is not just time and fuel costs the technology saves but, in China, the initial lump sum a buyer has to put down to get an e-truck, says Mao Shiyue, a Beijing-based researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT).

The upfront purchase price for an e-truck is significantly higher than for a comparable diesel model, a major obstacle for those vehicles’ wider adoption in many parts of the world. In China, a customer opting for battery swapping typically buys an e-truck without a battery, and then rents the battery from a service provider. As the cost of a battery is about 40% of an e-truck’s price, the business model can make e-trucks a lot more affordable, Mao says.

The technology can also help minimise the pressure EV charging brings to the power grid, according to Mao, because swapping stations have more flexibility to spread out the charging time for the depleted batteries.

“If the grid sees a spike in electricity demand during peak hours, those stations can even act as an energy-storage station by returning the electricity stored in their batteries back to the grid to ease the strain,” he says.

CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China. The company’s support for the technology is critical for its large-scale rollout, says Phate Zhang, the founder of CnEVPost, a Shanghai-based outlet focusing on EVs.

CATL plans to put 900 battery-swapping stations into operation across China by the end of this year, expanding its current network twice more. By the end of 2027, it wants the number to reach 2,000.

The company has also teamed up with the London-based renewable energy supplier Octopus to bring the technology to Europe. It intends to open its first group of battery-swapping “mega hubs” in the UK next year, and a network of more than 30 hubs in Europe by 2035.

In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet. In 2024, about one-third of the zero-emission trucks in the country featured this technology, while the rest largely had conventional plug-in charging, according to the latest available figures.

One downside is that drivers often need to stick to a particular service provider that caters to the specific type of swappable batteries their e-trucks use.

“For example, some batteries are swapped from the chassis, while others are swapped from the top of the truck,” says Xue Lulu, a senior associate at World Resources Institute China. “Even under the same technological route, batteries made by different companies often have different specifications.” This means drivers cannot drop into any random swapping station to get their trucks replenished, which could restrict the journeys they can make, she says.

Plus, battery swapping doesn’t necessarily mean drivers will save time, Xue says. During her field research in China, she found some lorry drivers would wait outside battery-swapping stations for one to two hours before going in because they wanted to avoid using the service during peak hours, to save money. “Logistics firms are extremely sensitive to costs,” she says.

The most suitable users are probably drivers who, like Wang, work on fixed routes served by battery-swapping stations. Mao says the charging method has been rolled out most successfully among companies that use heavy trucks in specific settings, such as those carrying goods in ports and factories, as well as within a city or between two nearby cities. “For unpredicted and long-haul routes, there are still challenges for rolling it out on a large scale,” he says.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: CATL aims to have 2,000 swapping stations in China by the end of 2027. The technology is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks were sold last year.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Water industry bonus ban to be tightened as Ofwat warns of ‘damage to public trust’
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Jasper Jolly

Regulator to hasten review over concerns that firms are ‘undermining’ rules to make large payments to bosses

Business live – latest updates

The water company bonus ban is set to be tightened after the regulator accused the industry of a risk of “damaging public trust” with large payments to bosses that appeared to get around the rules.

Anglian Water was singled out for particular criticism over “retention payments” worth up to £800,000 for its chief executive, Mark Thurston, despite the bonus ban. Anglian will face increased monitoring of its governance arrangements because of the controversial payments.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said she wanted to “close loopholes” so that “failure doesn’t pay”.

Nine water companies in England and Wales – including Thames Water and Yorkshire Water – were banned from paying bonuses for the 2025-26 financial year, the regulator Ofwat said on Thursday. Seven of the bans related to environmental pollution.

The Labour government introduced the bonus ban last year amid public outrage over sewage leaking into Britain’s rivers and seas. Yet water company bosses’ pay has risen in the past two years despite the ban, according to Guardian analysis.

Campaigners and opposition politicians have argued that companies are circumventing the ban through a variety of payments which are not “performance-related” – but which effectively replace the banned bonuses.

Ofwat on Thursday said it would accelerate a review into the rules, over concerns that companies were deliberately “undermining” the ban. It is understood that ministers will also consider whether payments from water companies’ parent companies could be included in the ban.

The regulator said: “The growing use of fixed so-called ‘retention payments’ and substantial increases in base pay without sufficient explanation or supporting evidence risks damaging public trust and creating a perception that companies are circumventing the rule.”

Anglian’s payments to Thurston “could give the impression the company had prioritised offering executive directors a cash award in a way that would not technically breach the rule and would in practice replace the loss of PRP [performance-related pay] prohibited by it”, Ofwat said.

As well as Anglian, Ofwat highlighted potential retention payments of £1m for Thames Water’s chief financial officer, £1.5m for Northumbrian Water chief executive, Heidi Mottram, and £1.7m for Louise Beardmore, the chief executive of United Utilities.

Andy Burnham is under pressure to clamp down on the water industry. He has said he wants to exert “more public control” over the water industry, although he is yet to give details. He is yet to make a decision on whether to move Thames into temporary government ownership after years of financial struggles and mismanagement, months after suggesting he might do so.

Thames Water paid its chief executive, Chris Weston, a previously deferred bonus of £99,000 during the year, despite the ban. Ofwat said that Thames Water’s future owners would have to pay for the bonus, rather than the money coming from customer bills. Thames was also criticised for raising executives’ base pay.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

The other companies banned from paying bonuses were Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, South West Water, Wessex Water and Dŵr Cymru (Welsh Water). Ofwat said they would have paid out another £6.5m to executives during the year had the ban not been in place.

Eagle said: “People are sick of seeing water bosses profit while rivers are polluted and customers are repeatedly let down. A wide-ranging review launching today will ensure that failure doesn’t pay, whatever name the payment goes by.

“The bonus ban was the first step. Where there are loopholes, I want them closed.”

South East Water was not subject to the ban, but Ofwat said the company’s shareholders would have to pay for future bonuses after huge supply failures left tens of thousands of households without water during the financial year.

Helen Campbell, the interim executive director for delivery at Ofwat, said: “It is disappointing that so many companies continue to trigger the rule through serious performance failures which has seen £10m in payments blocked in the past two years.

“Public trust in the water sector remains low, and executive bonuses which do not reflect performance, use of retention payments and poorly explained increases in base pay contribute to that low trust. That is why we are accelerating our review to ensure the rule better delivers the outcomes customers rightly expect.”

Ofwat also criticised the paucity of information on pay reported by South Staffs Water.
