Anglian Water singled out for particular criticism over ‘retention payments’ worth up to £800,000 for its chief executive, Mark Thurston, despite the bonus ban.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: First guidelines on attempts to manipulate the ocean put spotlight on geoengineering industry
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Alexandra Talty
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Proponents argue ocean carbon removal is necessary to counteract the effects of the climate crisis but critics say more research is needed

A
cluster of candy cane-striped smoke stacks dots the horizon of Tufts Cove in Nova Scotia, Canada. Deep in the briny depths of Halifax harbour, something huge is happening: the ocean is being engineered to remove atmospheric carbon.

“This is what Mother Nature has done naturally for a few billion years in order to rebalance the atmospheric and ocean chemistry over long timescales,” says Dr Greg Rau, co-founder and senior scientist at Planetary Technologies.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Planetary Technologies is an ocean carbon-removal firm and one of a growing number of companies attempting to decrease excess atmospheric carbon – the main driver of the climate crisis – by speeding up naturally occurring carbon cycles in the ocean.

To do this, the company conducts ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE), adding a chalk-like substance to the seawater, which allows the water to absorb and store more atmospheric carbon than usual.

This process also helps to offset ocean acidification, often called the “evil twin” of the climate crisis, which is increasing dramatically.

Because it relies on an already occurring process, proponents say these technologies will not harm the marine creatures that call this harbour home, such as mackerel, sunfish, harbour seals and sea turtles. But some marine scientists worry that adding any extra materials to an already stressed ecosystem might harm aquatic life and say that this field of marine geoengineering needs more research.

“If we develop a new medicine, you have steps that you’re supposed to take. You don’t just find a substance and just implement it,” says Sam Dupont, a senior lecturer at the University of Gothenburg. “And at the moment, with [ocean carbon removal] it seems you’re jumping to clinical trial immediately.”

Planetary Technologies runs its operations five days a week. Working out of a shipping container, it adds an alkaline slurry, its proprietary formula, to a local power company’s cooling water to create an odourless milky composite, which is then discharged into Halifax harbour and monitored by their sensors.

Bolstered initially by small government grants, venture funds and other private capital, Planetary Technologies now generates revenue by selling carbon-removal credits worth millions of dollars to companies such as JPMorgan Chase and Shopify.

Ocean carbon removal is a fledgling industry but one that has seen more than $500m (£370m) invested since 2021, according to Ocean Carbon Removal Watch, a database launched by the Pulitzer Center, which tracks marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR) investments.

After over a decade of protracted negotiations among scores of countries, this October the International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted the first international framework that officially acknowledges the three major ocean carbon removal techniques: ocean fertilisation, ocean alkalinity enhancement and biomass sinking.

Adopted in London during the annual meeting of the London convention and protocol, a little-known but influential treaty that governs the dumping of waste at sea, the new framework urged a cautionary approach. The IMO said in a statement that “further scientific research is needed before any activities beyond the research stage can be considered”. But it acknowledged that “marine geoengineering is attracting increasing scientific, commercial and public attention”.

“The IMO assessments are sending a strong signal to governments and industry alike that this is something that we, as a global community, prioritise,” says Fatima Candace Vahlsing, vice-president for climate at Ocean Conservancy, a US-based nonprofit organisation. “Whether you’re a business or an academic or a nonprofit, everyone wants the system to work and there to be trust around the system.”

However, some scientists and conservation organisations fear the private-sector market is moving ahead too fast and risks creating technologies that damage the ocean and potentially cloud the sector before real breakthroughs are made.

Brad Ack, chief executive of Ocean Visions, a conservation organisation that promotes creative solutions to conserve and restore the ocean, says the sector needs significant public investment to set rules and standards.

“That’s largely being done by the private sector and the academic sector at this point, and that’s not enough,” he says. Government funding, particularly in the United States, where this sector began, has increasingly dried up.

Nova Scotia, known for its cod fishing history and legendary tides, is now the largest ocean alkalinity-enhancement centre in the world. Anchored by Dalhousie University’s Ocean Frontier Institute and bolstered by grants from the Canadian government and partnerships with research institutions in Germany and Australia, the private companies CarbonRun and pHathom Technologies are also operating there, in addition to a test site run by Carbon to Sea, a non-profit scientific research programme.

But as the Halifax hub continues to grow, and other field trials are proposed across the world in places as varied as the Gulf of Mexico, the Gulf off Saudi Arabia, Norway’s rivers or the harbours of Singapore, the wider field continues to face questions. Since the sector is so new, it is unclear how existing maritime laws can be applied, for example, and where exactly their jurisdiction starts.

“This creates opportunities for bad actors to exploit gaps in the regulatory regimes,” says Romany Webb, deputy director of the New York-based Sabin Center for Climate Change Law.

At the same time that governance is being negotiated, scientists are realising that the base materials used for alkalinity enhancement are not created equally. Some materials, such as byproducts from mining, are considerably cheaper but the trace metals in them can have an outsized impact on marine ecosystems.

“Even in very low concentrations, you can have toxic effects with trace metals,” says Nina Bednaršek, a senior scientist at Slovenia’s Jožef Stefan Institute, which specialises in biological risk assessment for mCDR. Bednaršek worries especially about zooplankton, which are the base of the marine food chain.

Although there are scientists investigating the environmental impacts of alkalinity enhancement on marine life, it remains understudied globally.

Bednaršek is working with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) to develop a methodology for accounting for carbon removal through ocean alkalinity enhancement which, similar to the recently released IMO framework, which would help with environmental safeguards and regulatory oversight.

“Right now, there is no price on the biology,” says Bednaršek. “I think that’s wrong.”

Lisa Levin, professor emeritus at California’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography, agrees. “For ocean alkalinity enhancement, most of the research has examined consequences for ocean chemistry, which I don’t consider an assessment of environmental risk,” she says.

But many of those involved in the business of carbon removal argue more legislation means more delay in scaling up the industry, which is time the ocean, and the planet, do not have.

“Conservation tends to sort of have this kneejerk reaction that any time you do anything in the ocean … out of the ordinary, it’s got to be bad,” says Rau at Planetary Technologies.

“They need to understand that we’re beyond that point here – we are damaging the ocean. You can put all the fences you want around a certain area of the ocean, but it’s going to warm and it’s going to acidify.”

Scientists are realising that the base materials used for alkalinity enhancement are not created equally.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/nil.title: KKR and RWE are rich firms. Why do they need a UK state loan for their windfarms? | Nils Pratley
https://www.theguardian.com/business/nil.author: Nils Pratley
https://www.theguardian.com/business/nil.text:
National wealth fund is to lend £1bn towards the Vanguard projects – but whether the private equity giant needed help is debatable

“This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain,” declared the prime minister.

Andy Burnham is obviously correct that the two Vanguard windfarms off the coast of Norfolk are huge investments. Together, they require almost £13bn of debt financing. But he can’t claim they represent a fresh expression of confidence. The project has been on the runway since the German utility RWE, the developer, was awarded a contract to build the windfarms in January’s renewables auction.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Instead, the new news on Wednesday was how the project will be financed, which is where the story becomes interesting. On the equity front, RWE said it had sold a 50% share in the Vanguard schemes to KKR, the giant US private equity and infrastructure investor. On the debt side, £12.8bn has come from “a consortium of 35 international banks”, including £1bn from the UK’s own national wealth fund (NWF).

It is fair enough, one might say, for the NWF to get involved – directing capital to energy transition projects is, in part, what it was set up to do. But here’s another key aspect of its role: the state-backed body is not meant to be a substitute for private capital; instead, its funding is supposed to be “additional”, in the terminology, to ensure infrastructure is built that might not otherwise be.

Here is how the NWF describes the process: “For each investment we are considering, we test and assess the extent to which impact would not have materialised without us, so we are confident we are delivering financial and non-financial value that would not otherwise be achieved.”

So how does that work with the Vanguard windfarms? Would they have been scrapped if the NWF had not chipped in its £1bn? That seems highly unlikely.

Consider that RWE is one of Europe’s biggest electricity generators and that KKR is a giant among private equity houses. These rich firms are experienced at raising capital. Consider, too, that the main way in which offshore wind projects are de-risked for developers is the auction process that sets a guaranteed inflation-linked price for their electricity for 20 years. In this case, the price is £91.20 a megawatt hour (in 2024 money), or high by historic standards.

If the cost of borrowing has risen post-auction – and it has – that’s unfortunate for RWE and KKR. They might have to pay a bit more for their debt, or pony up more equity, both of which would depress their returns. But that is an everyday risk of commercial life. Why did the NWF, having stayed away from fixed offshore wind until now, think it had to join a lending syndicate on a project where it is a stretch to think its contribution was the make-or-break element?

The NWF’s argument is that its involvement “widens the pool of capital available to offshore wind developers and helps to meet unprecedented liquidity requirements after the success of AR7 [the last auction round]”. In other words, the sector will need so much capital over coming years that the state-backed lender needs to be on standby.

after newsletter promotion

It’s a defence, but it will sound very appealing from the point of view of developers. They can bid for an index-linked contract that guarantees revenues for 20 years; then, if borrowing conditions are tight, they are invited to think that the state will lend a hand to try to ease funding pressures. No wonder KKR wanted in. The NWF, note, says it is lending at market rates. Even so, its definition of how it adds “additional” value seems to have become very stretched.

Many of the NWF’s other big loans, such as billions for Sizewell C and £599m for Rolls-Royce’s development of small modular reactors, are far easier to understand. Those projects genuinely might not have happened without state backing. The same applies to the myriad of its smaller investments in battery technology and so forth.

Offshore wind generation, by contrast, is an established market with an effective mechanism – the contract-for-difference – for incentivising developers. The NWF’s pot of capital is not bottomless. Better targets for loans right now might be anything to do with electrification, meaning the take-up of heat pumps and electric vehicles, or storage solutions. As half the energy world is pointing out, it is where the big decarbonisation gains are available.

A bit of state activism to accelerate energy transition is a good thing, many of us would say. But, as argued here previously, more scrutiny of that “additionality” principle is overdue. There is little point replicating what the private sector would do anyway. When a huge private equity firm, KKR, is getting a helping hand because funding conditions are a bit rough, it is fair to ask if the state is achieving the best bang for its finite buck.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: College students rally in support of Starbucks baristas urging boycott over contract impasse
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Rallies take place on more than US 40 campuses as workers seeking better pay and conditions decry stalled talks

Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are holding rallies at over 40 college campuses across the US on Thursday to support the Starbucks Workers United boycott campaign as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.

Starbucks Workers United is seeking better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas and a minimum staffing of three workers per store. It has called on the public to boycott Starbucks until its first contract is reached.

More than 700 Starbucks stores have voted to unionize, representing more than 12,000 baristas. It typically takes over 450 days for a new labor union to negotiate and reach its first contract, but it has been nearly five years since the first Starbucks store in Buffalo, New York, voted to unionize in December 2021.

Starbucks Workers United began to focus on college campuses in 2023, calling on campuses to cancel their contracts with Starbucks in protest against the company’s response to union-organizing efforts. In response, Cornell University and Pomona College did not renew their contracts with the company, while UCLA stopped offering Starbucks products in their cafes.

Rallies and events will take place at private and public universities across the country, including the University of Pennsylvania, Northwestern and the University of Washington.

The union push come ahead of the company’s busy holiday season, including Starbucks’ Red Cup Day on 17 November, when customers receive a reusable holiday cup.

“Starbucks has been fueling the working class for decades, but they’re failing the workers that fuel their profits,” said Andrew Trinklein, a barista who is participating in an event at the University of Texas at Austin. “We’re really trying to push and get support from college campus students… in joining the boycott.”

His store recently unionized, and he expressed shock at how the company hired pricey union avoidance consultants in attempts to deter workers from unionizing. Starbucks has reportedly spent tens of millions of dollars related to union avoidance, though it has not disclosed the full costs relating to its union-organizing efforts.

Trinklein emphasized that employees are currently employed at-will, meaning they have no just-cause job security protections.

“Right now it’s just a toss-up whether we have a job tomorrow or not. Say they don’t like something that we’re doing – say we don’t write on a cup. We could be fired for it tomorrow,” Trinklein said, referring to the company’s policy requiring employees to write friendly messages on cups for customers. “But with this contract, that won’t be possible. We’ll have protections from stuff like that.”

Efforts to pressure Starbucks to negotiate were temporarily paused when the union and Starbucks reached an agreement on a path forward in February 2024. But negotiations broke down shortly after Brian Niccol took over as Starbucks CEO.

Niccol previously served as CEO of Chipotle from 2018 to 2024, and under his tenure, the company agreed to pay $240,000 to former workers as part of a settlement over a store closing in Maine after it unionized, which the National Labor Relations Board said was illegal. Chipotle has denied wrongdoing.

In recent years, Starbucks has been found guilty of violating federal labor law by the NLRB in several cases regarding its responses to union-organizing efforts.

In a statement, a Starbucks spokesperson said: “Workers United represents approximately 5% of our US partners, and we believe actions like these divert attention from the work at the bargaining table.”

“Our partners and coffeehouses are focused on bringing the joy of the holidays to life for our customers. Based on our experience with prior similar actions, we don’t expect any meaningful disruption and look forward to serving our customers through the holidays,” a spokesperson for Starbucks wrote in an email.

The spokesperson noted that “according to independent research, Starbucks offers the best overall pay and benefits in the industry, worth on average more than $30 per hour and including comprehensive healthcare, 100% upfront tuition coverage, company stock and up to 18 weeks of paid parental leave for partners working as little as 20 hours a week, which is why our turnover is among the industry’s lowest, and nearly 3 million people applied to wear the green apron last year”.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Starbucks Workers United is seeking better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas. It has called on the public to boycott Starbucks until its first contract is reached. More than 700 Starbucks stores have voted to unionize, representing more than 12,000 baristas.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Farewell to Elon Musk’s Cybertruck. Has any car ever been more repellent? | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old

E
lon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the midterms in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering documentary and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.

And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is winding down production. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk tweeted on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Why not just build a bigger factory, one account on X asked. “It is insanely fucking hard to build a high-volume factory,” Musk replied. “That’s why.” Dude, you want to build colonies on Mars. A factory should be nothing compared to sustaining life on a toxic planet where the temperature can drop as low as minus 128C.

Anyway, good riddance to the Cybertruck, which isn’t just ugly but, arguably, a safety hazard. Not least because it has lots of sharp edges that road safety campaigners condemned as dangerous to other road users and pedestrians. Indeed, the truck is heavily restricted in Europe because it doesn’t meet safety standards.

Cybertrucks can also pose a social hazard to the owner. In 2025, Wired profiled seven Cybertruck drivers about the reactions their vehicle elicited, and they were largely unflattering. One man complained that a woman had put a note on his car saying: “This is an extension of your small dick.” Another man (who was later arrested for taking part in the 6 January attack on the Capitol) said people sometimes made obscene hand gestures at him. Roger Davis, meanwhile, said he loved how polarising the car was. When Wired asked Davis if he was married, he replied: “I was married, but I’m not married any more. Women don’t like the vehicle.” Instead of being a revolutionary pickup truck, Musk’s creation seems to have been very good at driving people away.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Farage was guest on Brand podcast after sexual assault investigation began
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Reform leader this week criticised the Labour party for ‘cosying up to’ and ‘promoting’ disgraced comedian

UK politics live – latest updates

Nigel Farage appeared on Russell Brand’s US podcast nine months after the comedian was investigated by police over allegations of sexual assault, the Guardian has learned.

The Reform UK leader this week criticised Labour for “cosying up to” and “promoting” Brand a decade ago, after the comedian was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault.

However, it has now emerged that Farage was a guest on Brand’s online show in July 2024 – months after the sexual assault allegations were made public, but before he was charged in April 2025.

During the episode, Farage laughed with Brand about their shared interests in taking on the establishment and suggested the west had provoked Vladimir Putin into the Ukraine war because “what you don’t do with a Russian bear is deliberately poke it with a stick”.

Farage was aware of the serious sexual assault allegations against Brand at the time because he had commented on them on GB News the previous year – but they were not mentioned in the episode.

Sitting on a sofa together, alongside Dan Bongino, a Donald Trump supporter, and Charlie Kirk, the rightwing activist later murdered, Farage spoke of how “the old left-right divides” were being blown out of the water. He claimed that cancel culture meant people saying racist or homophobic things were “cancelled” but contempt for the white working class was allowed.

At the end of the show, Brand said: “Nigel, thank you for this impromptu opportunity to speak and I hope we get more chances to speak.

A number of women accused Brand of sexual assault in a joint Sunday Times, Times and Channel 4 exposé in September 2023, and the comedian was subsequently interviewed under caution by police that autumn.

On GB News in September 2023, Farage said he was not a big fan of Brand but would not prejudge him and remarked on the comedian having “upset big government” and powerful men such as Bill Gates – an apparent reference to Brand’s anti-vaccine views.

On the allegations against the host, Farage said there was “no evidence being produced” and then referred to four or five women having come forward.

He added: “I’m not here to prejudge his guilt or his innocence, but there are many other things in his own autobiography that he’s written about his behaviour with women that are disturbing, abusive and not very pretty.”

Asked about his appearance with Brand, a spokesperson for Farage said: “Nigel regrets his appearance on the show. His thoughts are with the victims who have suffered immensely because of what Russell Brand has done.”

Reform sources said it was not a planned appearance, and he was pulled into the room during a visit to America.

Since the verdict, Farage has commented on the allegations against Brand on Australia’s News 24 saying: “It’s very difficult isn’t it, because this is two decades old, it’s ‘he said, she said’, although there’s more than one she. So these cases are always very difficult for us to judge at a distance because there is no actual hard evidence.”

However, he came out in support of Jemima Goldsmith, a former partner of Brand, who has accused him of assault. Farage said she was known to him and he believed her account of Brand being violent and abusive, adding: “The judicial system has proved to have actually worked.”

He also criticised Labour for failing to apologise for “cosying up” to Brand a decade ago.

It is not the first time Farage has met a man accused of abusive behaviour. The Reform UK leader was pictured with Andrew Tate, the misogynist influencer, in 2019. Tate was charged with rape and human trafficking in 2023, and the UK is now seeking to extradite him from the US. Tate denies the allegations.

Farage spoke in favour of Tate for defending “male culture” in a Strike It Big podcast that aired in February 2024, while acknowledging that the influencer had gone “over the top” and that he had said some “pretty horrible” things.

Asked about his podcast appearance and comments on Tate, Farage said: “There’s an awakening in a younger generation who have had enough of being dictated to, have had enough of being lectured to. They’re seeing through the rubbish they’re getting taught in schools and universities. If no other politician is willing to reach out to this group of people, then I will.”

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: UK drone maker founded by Ukrainians hits £4.5bn value after raising £500m
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Jasper Jolly
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Britain’s national wealth fund invests £113m in UForce, whose equipment has been used heavily in war with Russia

A London-based naval drone maker founded by Ukrainians has reached a £4.5bn valuation after it raised more than £500m from investors including the UK government.

UForce, which makes military drones for land, air and sea, received £113m from the UK’s national wealth fund. The investment makes UForce one of the UK’s fastest-growing unicorns – or startups with a valuation of more than $1bn. Its drones have been used extensively in the war in Ukraine.

The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, met the UForce chief executive, Oleg Rogynskyy, on Thursday onboard the British aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales during a defence conference in Oslo, Norway.

The UK’s Ministry of Defence noted UForce’s maritime capabilities in particular, amid concerns over the increasing threat from Russia in the north Atlantic and North Sea. Russian naval vessels and its “shadow fleet” have been accused of sabotage and spying operations on cables and pipelines, while the UK is planning a fleet of sea-borne drones in the northern seas to track Russia’s nuclear submarine fleet.

Streeting on Thursday piloted a UForce MV7 uncrewed vessel located more than 1,500 miles away in the Atlantic Ocean near Portugal.

Rogynskyy grew up in Dnipro, an industrial city in eastern Ukraine, before founding People.ai, a Silicon Valley tech unicorn focused on data on sales and operations performance for businesses.

Rogynskyy said UForce wanted to “make aggression unaffordable”. The investment would allow UForce to scale up production for Ukraine as well as for its allies, he added.

“The war in Ukraine has shown that in an increasingly volatile world, effective defence requires systems that can keep improving as threats change,” he said. “Governments and the technology ecosystem need to come together to develop cost-effective, interoperable, and autonomous platforms that are ready to fight now, and can evolve to meet future needs.”

The other lead investor was Valor Equity Partners, a private equity investor founded by Antonio Gracias, a former director of Tesla who is also on the board of Elon Musk’s rocket launch company, SpaceX. One of Valor’s partners is Christopher Cavoli, a retired US general who was Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe until last year. Cavoli will join UForce’s board.

The Ministry of Defence said UForce would invest in a British supply chain as part of the deal, with hulls, engines, electronics and fit-out sourced in the UK. The MoD said more than 70% of the content of each UK-built boat would come from British suppliers.

Streeting said: “Ukraine is rewriting the rules of warfare. In just a few years the UK has gone from training Ukraine to being trained by Ukraine, as they prove that who can innovate fastest is a key measure of modern military power.

“Bringing battle-tested expertise to the UK will create high-skilled jobs, spur innovation and strengthen our war-fighting readiness, enhancing our ability to deter our adversaries.”

The former Conservative UK defence secretary Ben Wallace is also on UForce’s board.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: UK appoints world’s first special representative for climate security
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya and Damien Gayle in London
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Exclusive: Madeleine Alessandri, former chair of joint intelligence committee, will take on role of advising No 10 on climate-related national security risks

The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

Prime minister Andy Burnham will announce the move on Thursday at Cop31, the UN climate summit, with the new role designed to advise the government on national security risks from the climate crisis before they spell catastrophe.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Burnham will tell the key climate talks on Thursday morning: “We should all recognise the summer was not normal. The climate crisis is upon all of us now. We saw that with the wildfires that devastated lives and livelihoods everywhere.”

This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, with back-to-back heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis causing health services and transport to suffer, schools to close and thousands of people to lose their lives prematurely.

Burnham will add: “The message I carry here, in my first Cop as prime minister, is that the UK remains determined to reach net zero by 2050 and to work with our partners to build a clean energy future. The world has changed. The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate action has broken down.
 
 
 “We will not stand by, and that’s why I’ve pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.”

Burnham arrived in Antalya, Turkey late on Wednesday night, before joining scores of heads of state and government for a series of high-level meetings at the talks, which are presided over jointly by Turkey and Australia. He will also confirm UK support for a proposed target of 35% electrification by 2035 and help towards plans to raise £5bn in private finance for clean energy projects across the world.

Madeleine Alessandri, the former chair of the UK’s joint intelligence committee (JIC), which oversees MI5 and MI6, will take on the special representative job.

But campaigners pointed to what they said were Burnham’s failures to take the measures needed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions at home, and to provide the funding needed to protect vulnerable countries overseas from the kind of risks the JIC has warned about. The government is mulling a major weakening of targets for electric vehicles and has given the green light to a gasfield, Jackdaw, in the North Sea while considering a new oilfield, Rosebank, west of Shetland.

“What we’re seeing in part is double standards,” Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, told the Guardian. “We can’t have Britain preaching a clean development gospel but expanding fossil fuels back at home. You cannot expect one set of rules for Africa and another for Britain.”

The UK’s credibility was “crumbling”, said Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. “The prime minister’s first climate talks should be an opportunity to demonstrate he means business. But if this is all the UK has to offer, then the questions piling in about his climate credibility are more than justified.”

Under Alessandri, the JIC collaborated on a secret report warning that within five years the UK could begin experiencing national security impacts from the collapse of ecosystems overseas, driven by the climate crisis and overexploitation of the living world. These impacts included food shortages, rising food prices, mass migration and conflict among nuclear-armed countries.

The report was suppressed under former prime minister Keir Starmer, but its contents were revealed by the Guardian last year, ahead of a redacted publication earlier this year.

Dame Madeleine Alessandri said: “Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates, placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world.
 
 
 “The best time to address these risks is before they develop into crises. In this role, I will work with partners across government and internationally to strengthen our understanding of climate threats, build resilience and ensure we are better prepared for the challenges ahead.”

The risks of the climate crisis to national security were also highlighted by Ed Miliband, foreign secretary, who has been briefing foreign capitals on the findings of the JIC report. He is also at Cop31 this week, and told the Guardian: “National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action – the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news.”

He added: “Climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face: food security, threats to infrastructure and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis].

“Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.”

In common with many wealthy nations, the UK has significantly rolled back its climate finance, funnelling money instead to military spending. In July, Burnham fronted a pledge to lower the cap on UK bus fares, funded by changing international climate donations into repayable loans.

Prakash Dahal of Pro Public and Friends of the Earth Nepal said finance was vital for his country’s adaptation to climate breakdown, and recovery from disasters such as the catastrophic flash flood that struck Nepal in August. “Crucially, this essential funding must come as grants – not loans,” he said. “Nepal is not asking for charity. Nepal is demanding justice.”

The subheading and text of this article were amended on 12 November 2026. Madeleine Alessandri is the former chair of the joint intelligence committee, not the current chiar, as an earlier version suggested. She left the role in May 2026.
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Andy Burnham will announce the move at Cop31, the UN climate summit. Madeleine Alessandri, former chair of joint intelligence committee, will take on role. The Earth Nepal said finance was vital for his country's adaptation to climate breakdown.

Retailer’s management to seek two-week extension of legal protection from creditors in high court

MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal.

The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning.

The budget chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, is under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers. Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.

The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until Thursday morning while a solution to its problems is sought.

Directors of Poundland are now seeking a further 10 working days’ grace, which must be approved by the high court. That comes after Gordon Brothers, which is understood to be supportive of the extension, released £10m more in funds to help Poundland secure new stock and keep trading.

Without the legal protection in place, Poundland is likely to have to call in administrators; the advisory firm Alix Partners is already lined up.

The European head of Gordon Brothers, Mark Newton-Jones, gave evidence in private for almost two hours to the Commons business select committee on Wednesday afternoon after MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the committee, said that after questioning Newton-Jones he was “deeply concerned that Gordon Brothers’ behaviour may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets”.
 
 
 He said: “Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a ‘knife-edge’.
 
 
 “Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there’s concerning signs it’s been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run-up to Christmas.
 
 
 “Worse, Gordon Brothers refused to say it will prioritise saving jobs over and above its own financial returns.”

The committee separately heard from Poundland’s management team, led by Barry Williams, who had been fighting to save the business.

Sources said Poundland continued to trade well, with sales up year on year, despite its problems, but it has only enough cash to support the business for a short period. Gordon Brothers has said Poundland remains “challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading”.

Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with three potential bidders for the entire chain but has indicated it can raise more from a break-up of Poundland, selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers.

The bids are understood to be worth less than the £30m in debts taken on by shareholders when Gordon Brothers bought the chain. It bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025.

Pepco still holds £7.5m of the £30m shareholder debt. It is prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business.

Gordon Brothers is still in talks with Martin Property Group, the Northern Irish family-owned firm supporting a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which includes the Dealz chain in Ireland.

Martin Property Group’s first bid had been rejected by Gordon Brothers as it amounted to no more than half the £30m it wants for Poundland with less than £7m up front.

A little-known finance company, Xyra Group, is thought to have offered about £12m up front and close to £30m in total. However, Xyra has not been involved with retail businesses previously.

Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

Paralympian Richard Whitehead ‘gobsmacked’ at Tory leader’s speech over proposed £36bn welfare cuts

The double amputee marathon runner Richard Whitehead has criticised Kemi Badenoch for “weaponising his sporting success” to justify her proposed £36bn welfare cuts.

The Conservative leader used the example of “double amputees running marathons” in a speech this week to explain the reasoning behind her proposed cuts to disability benefits, which she said were enabling people to “live a life of dependency”.

Whitehead said he had been surprised at her comments and angry that his achievements were being used as part of a campaign to take money “from the most vulnerable that actually need it”.

“I was gobsmacked that somebody’s sporting success would be weaponised in this way,” he said. “To say everybody should work because double-leg amputees run marathons, I was like, wow. It’s very divisive language.

“I understand the welfare system needs a shake-up, but you shouldn’t be blanket taking money away from individuals who need it, it’s their lifeline. There are families out there relying on the support.”

Whitehead has run more than 100 marathons, set world records and won four Paralympic medals over the course of his career, while also completing endurance feats to raise money for charity.

He said several people had sent him clips of Badenoch’s speech on Tuesday and “his mouth was open” as he watched it.

After saying there were “people who genuinely cannot work”, Badenoch went on to say: “The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities, even when they face serious challenges.

“Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world.”

Whitehead immediately expressed his concerns about the comments on social media. “Disability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day,” he wrote.

“One person’s ability to overcome significant challenges should never be used to justify withdrawing support from others.”

He invited Badenoch to have a conversation with him to learn more about disability and how it had affected his life and how he used his platform to inspire and mentor others.

“She’s utilising somebody’s success and 50 years of hard work for her own means without actually having any knowledge of who I am and the work that I do,” he said. “When I stand on a podium, I use that moment to hopefully inspire and liberate people of all minorities. She’s just looked for a headline.

“I think she needs to really reflect and think about how she communicates with the disabled community, and maybe have a conversation with myself around the work that I’m doing.”

The Conservatives said welfare savings would be made by ending disability living allowance payments to families of children with “milder cases” of behavioural disorders, learning disabilities or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

Badenoch said in her speech: “If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself.”

Whitehead said: “I would like a response from her on the terminology she used and I could educate her about the real scenario for people with neurodiversity, with ADHD, who are really struggling. And maybe with that experience she will understand that maybe she’s got it wrong.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Booker prize winner described a dystopian Britain. But haven’t we been living in that since Brexit? | Zoe Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Zoe Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
It didn’t need a novel: even Leave voters understand the damage that has been done, as does the PM. Now all he has to do is persuade his party

E
arlier this week, some people on the radio were talking about a very British dystopia. The government had disintegrated, but everyone was carrying on pretty much as they had before. Britain was isolated on the world stage and people missed Europe like hell, but weren’t allowed to visit, let alone live there.

I thought the radio people were discussing Britain post-Brexit, circa 2022. In fact, they were talking about the plot of the Booker prize-winning novel The End of Everything. Its author, M John Harrison, is renowned now for being, at 81, the oldest winner of the award, as well as the first science fiction writer to win it. But let’s also carve out a space for him on the podium of dystopian fiction, as a writer who can describe an indeterminate future in terms that are both terrifying and sound like a couple of years ago.

The past 10 years of British politics have had the dreamlike quality of a novel – not because they are dense with allegory or challenging to interpret, but for a much more basic reason. The morning after the 2016 referendum, a new reality simply arrived. For the next four years, we would discuss nothing but Brexit, and the language of compromise and practicality was banished.

If any other decision forced itself upon the electorate – for instance, who the prime minister should be – it would be filtered through which candidate would do the best on Brexit, which itself became more and more of a magical concept.

Like a novel, this phase took on its own rhythms, put the spotlight on characters who worked within its arc but made no sense in real life (Mark Francois, anyone?). The period since 2020, when Britain officially left the EU, has been the sad, humbling process of watching this fiction try to impose its rules on reality, and reality always winning. It turns out you can’t destroy your relationship with your biggest trading partners and not take a hit to prosperity.

Ancillary, Brexit-related fantasies, such as “immigrants leech money”, have taken their own toll, and we’ve stood by and watched as a reduction in net migration bleeds yet more money out of the economy, and a crusade against foreign students has created chaos and desperation in our universities.

If 2016 was the beginning of the “we’ve all had enough of experts” universe, in 2026 we’ve all had enough of that fictive universe, the place where facts don’t matter. Remainers gonna remain and we will insist on pointing out that Brexit has had no upside until the end of time.

But leavers have had a sea change. It’s true that only 57% of Britons agree that Brexit was a bad idea; but only 30% think it was the right choice (we should file the remainder under “please make this conversation go away”, rather than the traditional “don’t know”). More striking is the fact that 73% of Tories, 59% of leave voters and even a majority of Reform voters now back a youth mobility scheme – that radical idea Keir Starmer ruled out as soon as he became prime minister for being far too remainey.

Many politicians, on both sides, will be wishing what I used to wish when every week saw new data on attitudes to immigration, showing them to be hardening: if only these pollsters would just stop asking. Apart from a handful of Tories who were frozen out of their party, even the staunchest opponents of this fandango have, for electoral expedience, obeyed its precepts: that we all care more about sovereignty than prosperity and that we all want to take back control and either believe, in some distant future, that control will come to pass, or are sick enough of the conversation that we’re prepared to pretend we already have it.

Andy Burnham’s first big statements as prime minister still, after an underwhelming budget, look like a radical improvement on the politics that came before. His framing of Brexit was deceptively mild – shall we just take another look at this? Ideology aside, we’re in the economic doldrums, and we’d do well to take another look at our relationship with the EU. While easy answers remain elusive, it was far closer to the electorate, which just wants this nightmare to end, than it was to the political establishment, which can only conceive of the discussion in terms of which old wounds can be tolerably reopened, rather than asking: were those wounds a rhetorical construct? What would happen if we turned the page?

Brexit differs from fiction or nightmare in so far as some of its effects will be permanent; we’ll never get back the wasted time or lost growth. It’s nevertheless possible to wake up from this fantasy world – ditch the red lines, the specious idea of a fixed, unified “red wall” and deal with the world as it is, where circumstances both here and in the EU have changed in a kaleidoscope of ways. Burnham catching up with the electorate has been heartening and necessary, but insufficient: his party needs to catch up with him.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

The government had disintegrated, but everyone was carrying on pretty much as they had before. The past 10 years of British politics have had the dreamlike quality of a novel.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on welfare reform: time to retire lazy myths and stereotypes | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A speech by the leader of the opposition exemplifies much that is wrong with the way British politics conventionally talks about benefit claimants

T
here is a big difference between expenditure that is rising and a rise that is “out of control”. The amount Britain spends on social security is in the former category. Too much political rhetoric around the subject assumes that it is in the latter one.

The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts the growth in welfare spending over the next five years at 0.2%-0.5% of gross domestic product, from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032. That money might well be suboptimally deployed. There are rival demands on the state’s resources and a reasonable debate to be had about priorities at the Department for Work and Pensions. But that is not the tone of the debate routinely conducted in Westminster.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The more typical frame is the one adopted by Kemi Badenoch in a speech earlier this week. The Conservative leader characterised the benefits system as a programme of handouts that disincentivises work and encourages the exaggeration of minor physical and mental health problems by undeserving claimants. By way of a moral parable to illustrate the change in attitude that she deems necessary, Mrs Badenoch observed that “double amputees run marathons”.

A moment’s pause would have led a more thoughtful politician to reject that comparison on grounds of both logic and ethics. It makes no sense to extrapolate an argument about what should be normal from a case that is self-evidently exceptional. And it is grossly offensive to people with disabilities to imply that the main barriers to achievement of extraordinary things are an excess of benefits and a lack of motivation.

But Mrs Badenoch is not in the business of serious thought. She has a political strategy that involves casting Labour as a party that only knows how to raise taxes and welfare spending, so she can represent the opposite.

To that end, the Conservatives claim to have identified £36bn in budget cuts, all from working‑age benefits. Pensions, which account for half of all welfare spending, would not be touched. In its verdict on Mrs Badenoch’s plan, the Institute for Fiscal Studies notes that some savings are likely to be available in the areas identified, but the projected amounts are “at the more uncertain end of the spectrum”. That doesn’t stop the Tories promising to spend their hypothetical budget windfall on bolstering defence and a variety of tax cuts.

The government’s approach is more circumspect, partly from political caution. A botched welfare reform last year poisoned relations between Sir Keir Starmer and his backbenchers. But also, Andy Burnham hasn’t wanted to pre-empt the conclusions of commissioned policy reviews – one into youth unemployment, led by Alan Milburn, and another considering the future of personal independence payment, by Stephen Timms. Mr Milburn is due to report next week.

What is known about Mr Burnham’s approach is that he considers investment in skills a more reliable way to help benefit recipients back to work than peremptory withdrawal of support. But while that plausibly leads to savings in the long run, it still involves an upfront cost. How that will be funded in a way that is acceptable to his backbenchers is far from clear. The prime minister might reasonably be accused of lacking precision when it comes to welfare reform. It is a lesser failing than the flight to lazy stereotypes and unserious rhetoric perpetrated by the leader of the opposition.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: All Kemi had at PMQs was jokes … and unfunny jokes at that | John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Even her own MPs were stony-faced as the Tory leader ran though her set list of gags from the budget to Russell Brand

UK politics live – latest updates

W
ell, there was one person at least who thought Kemi Badenoch had absolutely nailed it at this week’s prime minister’s questions. And that person was Kemi Badenoch. She could not have been more pleased with herself if she had tried. No one laughed louder and longer at her own jokes than she did. No one admired her laser focus as much as she did. Kemi is the paid up chief executive of her own fanclub.

As for the rest of her Tory MPs – aside from Chris Philp, who is basically a parasitic homunculus – they weren’t quite so convinced by Kemi’s performance. She had been so entranced with her one-liners, she had forgotten to ask any serious questions. And never forget how low the gag bar is in the Commons. What passes as a joke at PMQs wouldn’t even register as humour in normal conversation. Wouldn’t even elicit the groan that comes from the recognition of a gag format.

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Maybe Kemi was just having a bad day. Had woken up and realised she didn’t have any questions for the prime minister and had decided to busk it instead. Maybe she was so carried away with the excitement of the Tories no longer being in third place in the opinion polls – mainly because Reform have tanked rather than any Conservative surge – that she decided to give herself a day off. Or maybe she’s stalled somewhat. Having found she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, she merely bounces off Andy Burnham’s. Compared with Kemi, Andy looks and sounds like a normal person.

The session began with Kemi trying to make fun of Labour’s as-yet-unpublished – possibly even unwritten – 10-year plan. Where was it, she asked. Burnham had a ready answer. It would be presented in the Commons before Christmas. Answers don’t come much more straight than that. Kemi looked almost disappointed. She was sure the 10-year plan had been kicked into the long grass. On Tuesday she had joked it would be a nine-year plan by the time it was published. Now the joke was on her.

It was as though Kemi was just going through a set list of topics from which she could riff. As if she was a standup comedian doing improv. Next in her sights came the budget. Not that she had any real observation to make about it. But she did have a gag and that was all that mattered. It was the “do nothing” budget. Kemi cracked herself up at that. Turning to the stony faces behind her for approval. You know, the “do nothing” budget? Get it? Er … yes. But it wasn’t funny the first time.

Burnham meanwhile seemed rather surprised by the turn of events. He had been expecting something rather more taxing. Something less lightweight. He doesn’t really get Kemi’s obsession with panto. Mind you, it’s only going to get worse as we get closer and closer to the Christmas season. It won’t be long before Kemi shouts out: “He’s behind you” and convulses on the floor with laughter.

So Andy just continued to do his Mr Congeniality act. The career politician with the priceless ability to sound as if he isn’t a career politician. Someone you are inclined to like and trust on sight. The bedside manner of a doctor who can somehow make you feel better about yourself when telling you your illness has become terminal. The sort of person who you feel guilty about for not having responded to treatment.

By now Kemi was about halfway through her routine and had decided it was time to talk about the Rosebank oilfield. Might as well. Hadn’t mentioned it for a week or so. Not that she had anything new to say, but that wasn’t going to stop her. The old ones are … the old ones. Andy merely replied that it was the Tories who had drawn up the licence and that Labour had already given the go-ahead to Jackdaw. Rosebank would be ready when it was ready. It wasn’t as if it was particularly time sensitive.

For reasons best known to herself, Kemi now thought it was time for a Russell Brand gag at Ed Miliband’s expense. On Tuesday, Kemi had made a point of refusing to do this. Of being the grownup when invited by a rightwing journalist to score points over Labour at a press conference. She wasn’t going to do this, she said. It was both disrespectful to Brand’s victims and wrong to attack politicians from whatever party for associations they had made before a person’s crimes were in the public domain. It had been a strange moment. One that possibly marked Kemi out as grown-up potential.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

It turned out to be an aberration. Tuesday was Tuesday. Wednesday was another day. The victims had had more than enough time now. And who couldn’t resist the opportunity of taking a pop at Ed Mil? If Kemi had any sense of history, she would have remembered that Margaret Thatcher had once lionised Jimmy Savile. Most politicians have done things they regret. Miliband had appeared to be having second thoughts about meeting Brand even as he was interviewing him.

The exchanges ended with Kemi listing some of her complaints against Labour and asking whether the Labour MPs really thought it had been worth replacing Starmer with Burnham. This was not just unfunny, it was totally half witted. Because even her own backbenchers can see that Labour MPs are completely blissed out with Andy. He might be more vibes than delivery at the moment, but you can’t argue with the numbers.

Labour are a good six to eight points ahead of the Tories in the polls. Something that was unimaginable when Keir had been removed in July. Voters seem to like him. They feel he is honest and respond to his positivity. They accept that the Tories damaged the economy and are willing to give him time to put things right. And compared with Kemi, Burnham looks and sounds like a leader. Someone who can put party politics to one side when needed. Not something you can say about Kemi at this PMQs. All she had was jokes. And the jokes weren’t even that funny.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Clearing up confusion over iodine in milk | Letters
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow, notes Dale Vince of the Green Britain Foundation

You report that scientists say moving even partly from dairy products to vegan alternatives could lead to deficiencies in iodine and other micronutrients if the substitutes are not fortified (Swapping from dairy to plant-based milk, cheese and yoghurt ‘could lead to micronutrient deficiencies’, 4 November).

To be clear, cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow. As the paper published in the Lancet Planetary Health explains, iodine is in milk because it is added to cattle feed. The vitamin B12 is there because cobalt is added to the feed so the cow’s gut bacteria can make it. Britain has been doing this for decades. If fortification is the answer, and the paper’s authors say it is, then fortify plant milk. It’s better for us and the planet than cow’s milk.

The study assumes that every plant product on the shelf is bought in equal measure, but they’re not, and the most popular brands are fortified with iodine. This means that the study’s deficiency figures are overstated.

Dairy is one of the heaviest climate burdens on our plates, and most of humanity can’t digest it past childhood anyway. Moving away from it is the right direction. The answer to a fortification gap is fortification, not telling teenage girls to put dairy back in the fridge. We need to leave cow’s milk for baby cows.
Dale Vince
Founder, Green Britain Foundation

https://www.theguardian.com/society/comm.title: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles
https://www.theguardian.com/society/comm.author: Adrian Chiles
https://www.theguardian.com/society/comm.text:
Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones. But should I stay in bed or continue mixing with others?

H
ow to define the cold that’s ruining your day? There’s a hierarchy. We start with the sniffle, the mere runny nose, scratchy throat or just feeling a little off. This is the slight cold. The nose becoming more blocked than runny, and a cough coming into play, entitles you to call it a heavy cold. Any of the aforementioned symptoms worsening, accompanied by hotness, shiveriness, aching and general misery, gives you the right to call it a stinking cold. There’s also a malady known as man-flu, but I have no truck with such a lazy, gender-specific categorisation.

The only good thing about the stinking cold is that you have the green light to do sod all and repair to bed. This was me for three days this week, and it has firmed up a theory I have long held that you’re better off getting a stinker because it tends to come and go and be done with more quickly than the other varieties. This theory, I should point out, is based on my lived experience rather than any clinical expertise or any kind of research. Sorry – I felt too ill to bother with anything of the kind.

The kind of cold I really can’t bear is the middle-of-the-road, magnolia, vanilla, neither-here-nor-there type. When you don’t feel up to doing much, but neither, if you’re honest, are you feeling ropey enough to justify doing nothing. And these kinds of colds, for me anyway, seem to drag on for ever.

But seriously, what do you do? What’s the right call for your own health and for others in your workplace or friendship group? Do you stay at home for the greater good, or do you soldier on bravely and be quietly commended for toughing it out, while running the risk of infecting friends, enemies and workmates with a dose of whatever you’ve got?

The NHS advice is as useful and detailed as it can be in what is inevitably a grey area. It’s well worth reading, but boils down to staying at home if you have a temperature and maybe going to work if you haven’t, while acknowledging you might still be infectious, so be careful with your coughs, sneezes and general hygiene.

Message received and understood. Be careful out there. May any colds you get this winter be as light as a mere dusting of snow.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Afghan women told to ‘go home’ after de facto ban on male doctors treating them
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Zan Times reporters
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
The unofficial Taliban restriction has forced women into desperate and absurd situations as they seek medical help, according to interviews given to the Guardian and Zan Times

F
arida*, 37, woke up in excruciating pain one night with a toothache. Over the next few days, the pain intensified. “My teeth had been ruined for years. My molars on both sides of my mouth were severely damaged. I couldn’t sleep at night and could barely eat.”

Farida and her family had returned from Iran earlier this year to live in Herat, a city in western Afghanistan. Like many migrants forced to return, they have struggled to find work and income. In their straitened circumstances, visiting a doctor has become a luxury but the pain forced Farida to a dental clinic in the Bakrabad area of Herat in early July.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

Farida already knew her teeth had decayed. The dentist who examined her said that several teeth needed to be taken out and replaced with implants or dentures. The clinic wrote a treatment plan for Farida that required her to make several visits and pay the whole cost of the treatment in advance.

However, during the third session, when the implants were supposed to be fitted, she was told: “We cannot treat you right now. Go home, and we will call you ourselves because a problem has come up.”

Farida went home, but couldn’t eat or drink properly. Two days later, she called the clinic. They said it was no longer possible to complete her treatment. “An order has come from the Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice stating that male dentists are no longer allowed to treat female patients. If the situation changes, we will call you.” Three months on, Farida’s treatment remains unfinished.

While there is no publicly announced restriction on male dentists treating women, a ban appears to have spread across the country, according to media reports and interviews with women and doctors by the Guardian and Zan Times. Dentists report that it has been enforced by Taliban security forces, with raids and warnings to male practitioners that they will be imprisoned if female patients are found in their clinics.

In most provinces, male doctors have also received orders and directives from the Taliban instructing them not to examine female patients. The doctors say they are not allowed to examine or provide emergency care to female patients, except under specific conditions – such as the presence of a female patient’s male guardian (mahram), or having certain procedures performed by female nurses.

“We are not allowed to directly examine female patients because we are not their mahram. It makes no difference how simple the procedure is or how critical the patient’s condition may be,” says Samim*, a surgeon who has worked for 15 years in a public hospital in northern Afghanistan.

The escalating bans are reaching new heights of absurdity, with officials in Balkh province in northern Afghanistan banned from calling female patients by their actual names. In May, officials reportedly ordered all hospitals, private practices and clinics to use the word “Bibi” instead of women’s names. They emphasised that this instruction must be observed even on medical prescriptions.

Rahima*, from Kunar province, says one of her relatives, an elderly woman, had to travel hundreds of miles to Kandahar city for dental treatment because her son ran a dental clinic there. The woman’s husband had told her that all the doctors in Kunar knew him, and it would be a source of shame for her to visit a male dentist.

The Taliban crackdown on women getting medical treatment comes at the same time as they are being restricted from becoming doctors themselves. Since December 2024, women have lost the right to study at medical institutes, and doctors at hospitals confirmed the Taliban had banned them from hiring female staff.

The remaining practising female doctors are required by the Taliban to have a mahram. One patient says she was forced to wait to see a male doctor in a practice without female staff despite arriving with her father. She was told the doctor needed another female patient with her mahram to arrive so that if any problem arose the woman could help her, as the doctor would not be permitted to touch a female patient.

after newsletter promotion

Women have the option of either risking themselves, the doctors and the clinics by receiving treatment, using female health providers who are not qualified, or living with their ailments.

“I don’t know what kind of situation this is. In a city where not a single female doctor can be found, how can they impose so many restrictions? Human life has no importance to them at all,” one patient told the Guardian and Zan Times.

The testimonies gathered run counter to Taliban declarations that doctors treating female patients would be exempt from the prohibitions. In February this year, Hamdullah Nomani, the Taliban’s communications minister, said male doctors would be considered mahram when treating female patients.

Nargis*, who works as an assistant at a dental clinic in Jalalabad city in eastern Afghanistan, says some doctors have someone outside their clinic to look out for Taliban officials when they are treating a female patient. “Our male doctor sometimes jokes: ‘Let’s keep a chadari [the full Afghan burqa] inside the office so that when they come, I can put it on so they won’t recognise that I am a male doctor.’”

*Names have been changed
