https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.title: I wear a feline leotard and ears to see Cats – and meet all the other theatre superfans going crazy for costumes
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.author: Arifa Akbar
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.text:
Skeleton suits for Phantom of the Opera, garish wigs for Beetlejuice, a Don’t Tell Mama dress for Cabaret … our critic meets the crowds going wild for costumes – and attends Cats in kitty costume

I
t’s an hour before curtain-up and the queue outside the theatre is full of green wigs and blue faces, all amid a sea of black and white stripes. It is Halloween night and these theatregoers of all ages, snaking around a corner of the West End, are in themed dress for the musical Beetlejuice, adapted from the 80s film.

In other theatres’ queues you might spot a king from Hamilton, the queens of Six and the wizards of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, all bestowing new meaning to the idea of dressing up for the theatre.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

There are overlapping reasons for this growing fashion for themed costumes. A new generation prefers active theatregoing experiences – there is also a boom in interactive and immersive theatre – and it is an extension of the fandoms facilitated by the growth of online forums and social media. Many fans find each other online first and then meet in theatres or at cosplay conventions. A major driver seems to be a desire for community and connection, ever since the isolation of the Covid era. Some shows combine the joy of dressing up with a sense of catharsis in exploring mental health issues together.

It’s not just for the kids, either. As a fiftysomething critic, I started dressing in theme after a friend, the author Kamila Shamsie, suggested we don an outre ensemble for Burlesque just for the sheer campy fun of it. We then went to The Oresteia in ancient Greek costume (I wore a bat-winged charity shop cloak, Kamila a toga dress and foot pendant). I have since gone as a gothic governess for The Turn of the Screw and worn a black lace leotard and headband with ears for the musical Cats. My rules are simple: I only spend up to £10 and the point is to get in the mood and honour the spirit of the show without veering into fandom.

Some theatregoers go to extraordinary lengths to replicate the looks of their favourite characters, spending months stitching garments and creating props, and some musicals are better at facilitating this than others, thinks David Fynn, the star of Beetlejuice. “You can let your freak flag fly,” he says. “It gives everyone permission to walk down the street and not be judged. There’s a certain type of show that makes people feel comfortable to dress up. Rocky Horror was the first … Maybe people feel like outsiders together and the show makes them feel like they belong, so they go all in.” From a performer’s point of view, he adds, it is an absolute delight. “I can be having a tough day but to then see, as the lights go up, so many people who have gone to all that effort, you think, ‘This is what it’s all about.’”

Social media has played a key part in building the sense of togetherness, he thinks. “It’s really supported those who may be too shy to turn up to Beetlejuice in cosplay on their own.” I meet a trio of elaborately dressed ghouls in the queue who say they became friends online and that this is the first time they have met in real life. “We saw each other on socials and connected through TikTok,” says Taylor, 32, who wears a floor-length Beetlejuice dress with fairy lights in netherworld colours embedded in it. “The show has the idea that a family is found,” says Taylor. “As someone who doesn’t speak to family, this really appeals to me.”

Dorian, 25, looks magnificently macabre. They created their trouser suit with signature stripes using tape, and added decorative moss and mould, made from beads. Peeping out from behind is a forked green tail, and a last minute addition to the look was a ukulele made from cardboard and pins last night. “I love being able to dress up as this weird little ghost guy,” says Dorian, who calls the musical “so queer and campy”. Kirby, 29, dressed in a red spiderweb cloak, bat choker and homemade wig, says: “It’s a home for all the weird kids and it allows me to express myself.”

Musical Con has given people permission to go into auditoriums in character. The annual London theatre convention was founded by performer Shanay Holmes and partner Chris Steward in 2022, after a discovery Holmes made about the therapeutic effects of cosplay for her autistic younger brother. “He is a superfan of Star Wars and I attended a fan convention with him. It was the first time he had been, and he was in cosplay as Lando Calrissian. I saw some strangers approaching him, which would be a potential trigger for him, but because he was in cosplay he became completely empowered, and took on board the character of Lando… So we wanted to create an inclusive space where people are not judged for being superfans of a specific musical.” Steward adds: “They come to Musical Con, and then 20 of them will go and see Phantom of the Opera or Beetlejuice in costume.”

Could this surging interest create a new generation of future designers? “Some of the cosplay certainly looks like someone has snuck into a theatre dressing-room and taken a costume,” says Holmes. “The intricacy and professionalism is incredible. Someone this year had made their own Christine Daaé shoes [from Phantom] – she had enrolled in a course to learn shoemaking! There’s a massive shortage of technical skills, and it’s these kinds of thing that encourage a foot into the industry.”

A group of Hadestown fans relate how they dressed as its characters for Musical Con. Lorina, 25, recreated Persephone’s dress over many months: “I tried to make a replica and went kind of insane in the process because there’s lots of different versions out there. It took a lot of my summer and then some more.” Eleanor, 19, speaks of “closet cosplay”, which is about repurposing things already at home, for outfits for Operation Mincemeat and Beetlejuice as well as Hadestown. Jasmine, 21, dressed as Orpheus by wearing a white shirt originally bought for work, along with trousers from sixth-form days. “They were a bit too small in the leg but it worked well for Orpheus because the whole point is, as they sing, he’s a poor boy. I borrowed the suspenders off my dad and the neckerchief was from the collection that belongs to my dog.”

Some might argue that the booming trade in show merchandise is a cynical way to cash in, but fans speak of their emotional connection to this “merch”: collecting, sharing or gifting it to fellow cosplayers. The musical Death Note, at the Barbican in London this summer, was based on Japanese manga – the genre that is believed to have spawned modern-day cosplay. Its director, Stephen Whitson, says that there were more than 200 people at the stage door, many dressed as characters and others wearing the show’s merchandise, which gives “that sense of ownership and of joining a club”. As associate director of Hamilton, he also remembers a teenage theatregoer who turned up and “sang the entirety of Hamilton dressed as Lafayette”. Ultimately, the reason fans dress up is also why actors assume a costume on stage, Whitson thinks. “It allows them to locate themselves in this world and to become someone different – to walk in someone else’s shoes.”

Izzy, 21, is an actor who was drawn to the musical Heathers, which tackles subjects including high school bullying, depression, eating disorders and suicide. She was 13 when she first saw it and instantly connected with the character of Heather McNamara. “In theory, she is popular and has all of these things, but inside she’s struggling a bit, and she’s never truly happy.” That resonated, as Izzy “was doing well at school, but I found it really hard to make friends and I was quite badly bullied. I’d never seen a show where I’d gone, ‘Oh, this is exactly what it’s like.’ It takes you out of your reality, but you can still feel yourself within the show.”

She has since seen the show 116 times and created more than 20 Heathers costumes. (Astonishingly, she has also put together the Don’t Tell Mama dress from Cabaret, another favourite musical, by messaging the show’s designer Tom Scutt, who talked her through his creation of the dress.) Heathers, she says, “has changed my life in ways that I will never truly be able to grasp. It’s helped me overcome so many things and realise so many things about myself. And it’s shaped the performer that I want to become, by watching that show and seeing so many evolutions of the same character.”

Beetlejuice is at the Prince Edward theatre, London, until 2 January. Heathers is on tour. Death Note is at the Barbican, London, 23 March 2027 to 15 May.
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.summary: Social media has played a key part in building the sense of togetherness, says David Fynn. Some say the booming trade in show merchandise is a cynical way to cash in.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Consultant doctors in England call off two-day pay strike
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Denis Campbell and Tobi Thomas
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Action on 25 and 26 November suspended to allow for formal negotations with the government

Senior hospital doctors in England have called off the 48-hour strike they intended to hold later this month after the health secretary agreed to negotiations about their grievances.

NHS chiefs, who were worried about how hospitals would cope during the action, welcomed the decision by consultants to “pause” their walkout, which was scheduled for 25 and 26 November.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The action was announced by the British Medical Association (BMA) when 18 months of talks with the government failed to lead to agreement on key issues.

The issues included a 25% fall in the real-terms value of salaries since 2009-10 and a requested 10% cut in working hours. The consultants voted in July to take industrial action.

The strike would have resulted in consultants carrying out emergency care only, which would probably have led to delays for most routine and elective services.

The decision to halt the strike follows meetings in recent weeks between Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, and the leaders of the BMA’s consultants committee after the latter called the stoppage last month.

The pause was welcomed by Cooper, who said she had held “constructive” talks with the BMA’s consultants committee.

But it is unclear how much progress the negotiations will make as Cooper is refusing to talk about pay – one of the consultants’ key demands.

“We welcome the opportunity to enter formal negotiations with the government and hope this marks a turning point in a dispute that has gone on for too long”, said Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Dattu, the co-chairs of the BMA’s consultants committee.

“We’ve always said strikes do not need to go ahead as long as the government is willing to genuinely negotiate, and now is their chance to do so.

“We have received assurances that there are no constraints on what we discuss in these negotiations, and we look forward to hearing their proposals on both pay and working conditions.”

Although consultants were given a 3.5% increase this year, the BMA said pay had fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years in real terms.

However, the Department of Health and Social Care made clear that the negotiations would not involve consultants getting any more than the 3.5% pay rise they have already received for 2026/27.

The committee wants to see “meaningful progress on the 25% real-terms pay cuts consultants have experienced over the last 17 years, alongside increasingly unsustainable workloads and worsening working conditions”, the BMA stressed. Negotiations are due to start next week.

Neary and Datta reiterated the BMA’s readiness to call consultants out on strike unless they received “a deal that recognises our value”.

The BMA said the proposed strike action was also about “ensuring consultants have the time, recognition and support they need to deliver the best possible care for patients and secure the future of the NHS, while not driving themselves to burnout”.

after newsletter promotion

Cooper said: “The BMA consultants committee’s decision to call off planned strike action is welcome news for patients and the wider NHS, avoiding disruption to care and allowing NHS staff to focus on delivering services and preparing for a challenging winter.

“I had a constructive discussion with the BMA consultants committee on reforms that could give consultants a stronger voice, greater flexibility and more freedom to innovate, while improving services for patients. We are committed to taking that work forward together in the weeks ahead.”

Cooper did not mention the BMA’s demand for action on addressing the 25% erosion in the value of their salaries.

DHSC sources stressed that “the government’s mandate for negotiations does not allow for increases in pay for consultants in this financial year.

“The secretary of state has been clear that she cannot justify increased pay for some of the highest earners at the expense of patient care, when everyone across the country is struggling with the cost of living.”

Consultants in England typically earn £152,000 a year after overtime and merit awards are included in their earnings. That figure has risen by about £25,000 since 2022.

The BMA’s decision to call off the strikes is “welcome news to NHS leaders” and “a positive step” towards an agreement, said Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents England’s 205 NHS trusts.

Devane had previously warned that the strike would force hospitals to postpone and rearrange operations and outpatient appointments that were due to take place on 25 and 26 November.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How angry parents helped flip Texas: choosing real education over culture wars
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna North
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Displaying Ten Commandments in class, whitewashing history and study of Bible verses drove many to vote blue

Michelle Palmer has run for the Texas state board of education twice before, but this time felt different.

“I was hearing from day one from people who had not really been politically active before that they were worried about education,” Palmer said.

Voters were upset about a number of issues, including a voucher program, signed into law by Greg Abbott, the governor, that sent $1bn of public money to private schools. They were concerned about new social studies standards that critics say promote Islamophobia and minimize the impact of slavery. They had seen students detained by immigration authorities, and Abbott threaten to strip district funding if students protested against ICE. And they were angry about a curriculum incorporating Bible verses that felt “forced down the throats” of schools, Palmer said.

In an August poll, 45% of Texans disapproved of their state’s handling of K-12 education, while only 28% approved.

“People don’t like for their kids to be messed with,” said Palmer, who teaches history and government to 11th and 12th graders. “I really think that’s a lot of why what happened here in Texas happened.”

Palmer won her race last Tuesday, helping to give Democrats a probable majority on the state education board for the first time in more than 30 years (one race has yet to be called). Her win came alongside victories for Gina Hinojosa, who made education a major part of her campaign for governor, and James Talarico, a former teacher who has criticized the inclusion of the Bible in public school curricula.

“Public education was on the ballot, and voters made their voices clear,” said Thomas Ray Garcia, a Democrat and community college professor who will join Palmer on the board in January.

Newly elected Democrats will have their work cut out for them if they want to reverse the effect of years of Republican control, many say. The Texas state senate remains in Republican hands, which will limit how much Hinojosa can do as governor to overhaul the voucher program.

But the incoming state board members, several of whom are current or former classroom teachers, say they hope to refocus public education in Texas on student learning, rather than on what they describe as “culture war” issues that have captured attention in recent years.

“I think we can turn toward local control, toward putting educators at the table again, and making sure that all the decisions we make at the Texas state board of education are based in research and the science of learning, and not in what I call the science of politics,” Garcia said.

Texas lawmakers and education officials have made headlines nationwide in recent years for their efforts to align public education in the state with Christianity and conservatism. In 2024, the education board approved a curriculum called Bluebonnet Learning, which incorporates Bible verses and stories, including a kindergarten lesson involving the Sermon on the Mount. While the curriculum is not required, districts receive state money for adopting it, which critics say can make the materials impossible for underfunded schools to refuse.

The following year, the state legislature passed a law requiring public schools to display the Ten Commandments in classrooms. And earlier this year, the education board approved two controversial curriculum changes: Texas’ first-ever statewide list of required books, which included excerpts from the Bible as well as Margaret Thatcher’s eulogy for President Ronald Reagan, and the new social studies standards, which critics say minimize Black and women’s history and paint Islam in a negative light.

“It’s just not representative of all of the students who live in this incredibly diverse state,” Palmer said.

Proponents cast the changes as a way to teach students about morality, or simply to introduce them to the Bible as literature. But the changes riled many voters in a state where test scores in many areas lag behind the national average, experts and candidates say.

Texans have been displeased with the new books list, along with a 2021 law meant to discourage the teaching of “critical race theory”, said Jonna Perrillo, an education historian and professor of English education at the University of Texas at El Paso. “A lot of Texans are really unhappy with the focus on those kinds of issues when they know that is not the cause of our low test scores and our low student performance.”

“I had a lot of people just kind of quietly whisper to me, ‘As a Christian, I don’t believe the Ten Commandments should be in public schools,’” said Kimmie Fink, an education advocate and mother of two in Liberty Hill, Texas. “There was this fear around people being public about it.”

The voucher program, established in 2025, has also stirred resentment in a state that ranks 47th in the nation in per-pupil education spending. By encouraging families to leave the public school system, vouchers can cause public schools to lose enrollment and even close, critics say.

“Where I live in El Paso, the student population is going down,” Perrillo said. “We just don’t have enough students to fund our schools, and so vouchers only exacerbate that.”

Hinojosa got her start in education, fighting the closure of her son’s school in Austin and then running for school board. One of her key campaign promises was to “end the voucher scam”.

It helped propel her and others to victory, as voters turned out to flip state offices blue, sometimes for the first time in a generation. In Texas this election season, education was “the issue”, said Dana Van De Walker, a Democrat and community college administrator who ran to represent her district on the state education board.

Van De Walker received about 600 more votes than her opponent, Audrey Young, a Republican incumbent, with some provisional ballots remaining to be counted. If her win is finalized, Democrats will have an eight-seven majority on the board in January.

Fink, who testified before the state board against the Bluebonnet curriculum and the books list, had gotten used to seeing her advocacy efforts fail. But she kept working. This year, she became a fellow with the Baptist Joint Committee for Religious Liberty, a Christian group that opposes religion in public schools. “I just put my everything into getting people to vote in the midterms,” she said.

Now her earlier experiences at the state board feel less like losses and more like “playing the long game”, she said. “We went and we fought and we told our stories, and I have to believe that that played a part in what we saw last Tuesday.”

Now the question before Democrats is how much they can do to reverse years of Republican policy and enact their own agenda. The books list and social studies standards have not yet gone into effect, and newly elected Democrats are optimistic they will be able to amend them, especially since Hinojosa, as governor, will be able to appoint a new board chair.

Given the outcome of the election, “it’s hard for me to see that book list going into effect”, Perrillo said.

Getting rid of vouchers will be more challenging. The board of education doesn’t control the voucher program, and any changes would likely have to go through the state legislature, which remains partially Republican controlled. Hinojosa is “going to be hemmed in a little bit by the Texas senate”, Perrillo said.

However, newly elected Texas Democratssee the election as a sign that voters across the state, regardless of political affiliation, are tired of the way their state leaders have handled education.

“I never saw myself as a Democrat first. I saw myself as an educator first, and I think that resonated with a lot of Republicans,” Garcia said. “Their perception was that their party was prioritizing private interests and culture war issues over the real issues impacting their children’s education.”

Fink, for her part, hopes Hinojosa will decline to fund any expansion of the voucher program, even if she can’t end it entirely. But she also has a broader hope for the state of Texas: “My vision is just this place where children of all identities and all faiths and all families can go to school and feel safe and welcome and reach their potential”.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Michelle Palmer is the first Democrat to be elected to the board of Education in the state. Palmer is a former teacher who has criticized the inclusion of the Bible in public school curricula. If they win, they will have an eight-seven majority on the state education board in January.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: Hoax bomb threats made to schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and Italy
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Severin Carrell and Angela Giuffrida
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Police assure parents and teachers there is no danger as thousands of schools in Italy and hundreds in the UK affected

Hundreds of schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland were hit by a fresh wave of hoax bomb threats on Wednesday, with some sites evacuated as a precaution.

Police in Scotland said that about 1,000 schools, from Dumfries in the south of Scotland to Aberdeenshire and Orkney in the north, had received the hoax warnings. At least 300 schools were affected in Northern Ireland. Similar claims were sent in a “generic communication” to schools in the Republic of Ireland.

Officials were quick to reassure schools and parents that the threats were bogus, and similar to hoax threats made last month. Earlier on Wednesday, the police had estimated that at least 470 schools were affected in Scotland.

In Italy, an email containing a hoax bomb threat was sent to about 6,000 schools, the education ministry said on Wednesday. Hundreds of schools were reported to have been evacuated.

The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that, based on checks carried out so far, “no element has emerged that would suggest there is a concrete danger”.

Meloni wrote on Facebook: “The reports instead appear to be linked to a strategy aimed at generating alarm and concern, which is currently the subject of all the necessary in-depth investigations.”

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “Our inquiries have established that there is nothing to suggest that they represent a credible threat or that there is any wider threat to the public.

“We understand how distressing messages of this nature can be for pupils, parents, carers and school staff, and the concern they can understandably cause. Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails. They have been sent widely to distribution lists across the UK and Northern Ireland and our assessment remains that they do not represent a credible threat.”

Police Scotland’s cyber and fraud unit is liaising with security and law enforcement bodies in the UK and overseas to try to find who was responsible.

Northern Ireland’s education minister, Paul Givan, said last month’s hoaxes appeared to be “Islamist” and were signed “Allahu Akbar” – Arabic for “God is greater”. However, there was no public confirmation the threats were Islamist in origin.

Schools in Scotland were told to readmit any pupils who had been evacuated and to resume classes. Dumfries and Galloway council confirmed children had been sent home after a majority of schools received messages. Highland council confirmed some of its schools “made the decision to activate their emergency protocols”.

Glasgow council advised parents by email that the claims of devices planted in schools were false, saying: “Our police colleagues have confirmed that this is a hoax and that schools should not be evacuated.”

In Edinburgh, a council spokesperson confirmed schools were “briefly evacuated as a precaution this morning, following receipt of threatening messages”. They added: “[We] understand the impact this can have on families and want to reassure parents and carers that our schools are safe, and there is no need to remove your child.”

In Northern Ireland, education officials advised schools to remain open “unless otherwise advised” by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI).

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

“As always, schools are advised to be vigilant and report any suspicious activity to the PSNI,” said a spokesperson for Northern Ireland’s education authority. “We fully appreciate that any message of this nature is distressing and can assure schools, parents/carers and children and young people that we will provide a further update following engagement with police.”

Anthony McNally, an assistant chief constable at the PSNI, offered further reassurance. “We take incidents of this nature very seriously and we understand the concern in the community, school communities and for students and parents. Our inquiries are ongoing. However, at this stage, we consider the risk to the public as low,” he said.

In Ireland, the Garda Síochána confirmed it had assessed the threat as “not credible” and had not called for any evacuations.

According to Italian press reports, the email included the words “we have come to annihilate you” and was signed by “Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan”.

Antonello Giannelli, pthe resident of the national association of headteachers, said the threat was “clearly fake”.

He added: “This episode shows how much irresponsibility, when combined with the extraordinary communicative power of the tools we have today, can cause damage and disruption on a large scale.

“We hope that full light will quickly be shed on the origin of these threats and that those responsible will be identified.”
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.summary: Police in Scotland say 1,000 schools in south and north received hoax bomb threats. At least 300 schools were affected in Northern Ireland and hundreds in the UK. Italian prime minister says there is no evidence of a 'concrete danger'

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: ‘Horrific crime’: Gaza doctor killed as Israel expands war on healthcare
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Mohammad Mansour
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
In the early hours of Thursday, Dr Rizq Abu Shuaira was on duty in the surgery department of the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza. An Israeli strike hit the hospital, killing at least six people, including Abu Shuaira and a child.

Zaher al-Waheidi, spokesperson for the Ministry of Health in Gaza, on Thursday called it “a horrific crime”, adding that Israel targeted the surgery department. He called Abu Shuaira’s killing a loss to the medical profession in the enclave that’s struggling to cope with the large-scale destruction of health facilities since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza on October 7, 2023.

“The world woke up to the crime of targeting the Nasser Medical Complex,” al-Waheidi said, adding that Abu Shuaira was “martyred while on duty providing services to patients”.

“He did not deserve to meet his demise while among the patients in the hospital corridors,” he said.

Israel has repeatedly targeted Gaza’s medical personnel and hospitals in the past three years, killing at least 1,725 medical workers. Of the enclave’s 37 hospitals, 20 are partially functioning while 17 others have been rendered nonoperational. Health authorities say 44 percent of essential medicines are out of stock as Israel has continued to block the supply of medicines into the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Gaza said it was the seventh attack on the hospital, which serves at least 500,000 people in southern Gaza.

“Of course, this targeting led to widespread destruction inside the surgery departments and operating rooms, and led to major damage in the outpatient clinics, the radiology department and the laboratory department,” al-Waheidi told Al Jazeera.

The Gaza Government Media Office stated that it holds Israel and the United States directly responsible for the strike on the hospital, noting that the victims included a 13-year-old child.

The media office has documented 793 Israeli attacks on healthcare services. A comprehensive report published last month by Insecurity Insight on ReliefWeb revealed that at least 3,508 attacks on healthcare across the occupied Palestinian territory were reported between October 2023 and September 2026. An overwhelming 95 percent of all incidents were attributed to Israeli forces.

In Gaza during that period, 399 health workers were detained, including Dr Husam Abu Safia, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital, who has spent more than 500 days in Israeli custody.

“The Israeli occupation did not and will not stop targeting the health system,” al-Waheidi said.

Despite the so-called ceasefire signed between Hamas and Israel in October 2025, the Israeli attacks have not stopped in Gaza.

Israel has also been accused of expanding its attacks on medical infrastructure in the occupied West Bank. A World Health Organization report (PDF) covering hostilities from January to August 2026 documented 124 distinct attacks on healthcare in the territory. The WHO data confirmed four deaths and 40 injuries.

A subsequent monthly report issued by the Independent Palestinian Doctors Association (IPDA) in October 2026 painted a harrowing picture of escalating field violence. During October 2026 alone, the IPDA documented 23 violations against the healthcare system in the West Bank. Specific flashpoints highlighted in the report included Salfit Government Hospital, which was stormed by Israeli forces twice on October 14 to confiscate surveillance camera recordings, while a nearby ambulance centre was also violently raided.

Eid Dwaikat, media director of the Palestinian Red Crescent Society, shared with Al Jazeera the suffocating operational environment. “The work of the Red Crescent teams is in a highly dangerous and complex field environment, amid the continuation of the siege, closure, and restrictions imposed on movement and access to the affected areas, which constitutes a direct threat to the safety of paramedics,” Dwaikat said.

The human cost of these delays is measured in lives lost. “Preventing teams from reaching the injured and detaining them reflects directly on delaying the provision of life-saving first aid … which multiplies the risk of death or the exacerbation of critical injuries due to not receiving medical care in a timely manner,” he added.

The crisis has been vastly exacerbated by the systemic imprisonment of Gaza’s doctors. Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) has highlighted the plight of 14 detained Palestinian doctors, including hospital directors and specialised surgeons held without formal charges.

“Holding doctors for nearly two years under what is called the ‘Unlawful Combatants Law’ without pressing any charge and without trial … of course is incorrect,” al-Waheidi, the Gaza Health Ministry spokesperson, said.

“If the Israeli authorities have any evidence, they should present it in a fair public trial. But detention without charge and refusing independent medical examination under security pretexts is an arbitrary deprivation.”

Abu Safia, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital, was detained in 2024, and his case has become emblematic of the systemic abuse within Israeli detention facilities.

On Wednesday, the PHRI said it obtained an independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records showing a weight loss of 14kg (31lb) in four months, a significant drop in haemoglobin levels and chest pain. On Wednesday, the Israeli Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking his release and refused to allow an independent physician to examine him.

“In particular, we have documented and heard directly from the lawyer who visited Dr Husam Abu Safia, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital: severe beatings, loss of consciousness, and a feeling by Dr Abu Safia that if this continues unchecked, his life is in danger,” Tirza Leibowitz, executive director of PHRI, told Al Jazeera.

“The torture and abuse have risen to such a level that we draw conclusions about this being a policy that has been implemented by the Israeli Prison Service against Palestinian detainees,” she said.

Leibowitz pointed out the plight of some 10,000 Palestinians held in Israeli detention under various categories. “The situation is appalling, both in terms of the conditions in the prisons and the violence and daily abuses that they are suffering,” she said.

For the family of Abu Safia, the continued incarceration has been unbearable. Elias Abu Safia, his son, described the immense psychological toll of the prolonged separation.

“Unfortunately, we haven’t spoken with my father for the past 685 days. We only know about our father through the lawyer,” Elias told Al Jazeera. “We dream of being in touch with my father, to have a direct phone call with him. However, Israel is  depriving us of having a direct conversation with my father.”

“The information that we are receiving about the health conditions of my father and how he is being arrested is very concerning. He doesn’t deserve to be treated that way inside or within the Israeli prisons,” Elias said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Israel has repeatedly targeted Gaza’s medical personnel and hospitals in the past three years. At least 1,725 medical workers have been killed in the Gaza enclave. Israel has also been accused of expanding its attacks on medical infrastructure in the occupied West Bank.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Police say at least five people shot at busy thoroughfare in Washington, DC
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Joseph Stepansky
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Police have said at least five people have been shot in a busy thoroughfare in the centre of Washington, DC.

The shooting occured on Thursday near Logan Circle, at the intersection of 15th Street NW and P Street, police said at 8:23am local time (13:28 GMT). Police said in an update that the attacker had barricaded himself in the area.

The attack took place about a mile from the White House during the rush hour commute.

Schools near the scene were placed on lockdown. Police issued a shelter-in-place order as law enforcement descended on the block.

“Go inside the nearest building, stay away from windows, and remain indoors until further notice,” it said.

The condition of the victims was not immediately available.

Reporting from the scene, Al Jazeera’s John Holman described a “river of police cars” and both local and federal law enforcement donning tactical gear.

“That’s not just from the police force also from FBI and Secret Service heading towards there,” he said.

The attack comes as the administration of US President Donald Trump has made crime in the US capital a key issue during his second term.

That has included deploying the National Guard across the city, a move Trump took after a Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) official said he was assaulted in the early morning of August 2025.

The US president declared a crime emergency, which also included briefly federalising control of the federal district’s local police force.

Several thousand National Guard troops have remained in the district, with Trump regularly claiming their presence has brought down crime. Local officials have said the National Guard have not been used in local law enforcement.

The White House did not immediately respond to Thursday’s attack.

In November of last year, a National Guard member was killed by a gunman while on duty near 17th and I Streets NW. A second national guard member was wounded.

In October, another National Guard member was shot during gun fight in southeast Washington, DC.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down amid spy scandal and market loss
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down from the company following his reported affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and an Nvidia executive.

The $4.2 trillion tech giant has lost more than $600bn in market value this week as Huang’s scandals rocked the company, which supplies most of the chips powering advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technology. The stock slid more than 10 percent in premarket trading on Thursday.

The company appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, as interim CEO on Thursday.

Nvidia’s board met on Wednesday night to discuss ousting Huang, whose relationship with the alleged Chinese spy triggered investigations by the FBI, the United States Congress and the California-based tech giant. Nvidia is also facing a shareholder class-action lawsuit.

The alleged Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, Nvidia’s primary business partner in Southeast Asia. Founded in 2023, Megaspeed has been investigated over whether it helped Chinese companies access its $4.8bn stock of powerful Nvidia chips.

The affair has raised national security concerns in the US, which restricts chip sales to China over concerns that the Chinese military, intelligence agencies or companies could use the advanced technology.

Huang, 63, is Nvidia’s co-founder, president and CEO. A close ally of United States President Donald Trump, he has pushed to ease US restrictions on chip exports to China. Trump said earlier this week that Huang told him he had “absolutely no idea” that he was in a relationship with an intelligence operative.

Huang owns about 3.6 percent of Nvidia’s stock, making him one of the richest people in the world. He is a powerful figure in the AI industry, which has driven record stock market and wider economic gains.

Nvidia’s board, which hired a law firm to investigate the affair with Alice Huang, met to decide Huang’s fate on Wednesday shortly after the New York Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with a Nvidia vice president who reports to him.

Nvidia’s stock has tumbled since the scandal erupted, falling to a 14-year low, the Reuters news agency reported.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down from the company following his reported affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and an Nvidia executive. The $4.2 trillion tech giant has lost more than $600bn in market value this week. The stock slid more than 10 percent in premarket trading on Thursday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: More than 1,800 Italian schools targeted by new hoax bomb alerts
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
⁠More than 1,800 ⁠schools in Italy were sent emails containing bomb threats on Thursday, the government said, a day after some 6,300 schools received similar alerts.

Many schools closed immediately after receiving the latest warnings, causing widespread disruption as parents rushed to collect their children.

Police in Rome said “there was nothing to substantiate” the threats.

Like Wednesday’s emails, the messages were reportedly signed by “Mikhail Andropov”, who presented himself as the “leader of the Vilayat of ⁠⁠⁠⁠Misoginistan”, according to Italy’s Ansa news agency.

The same purported author claimed responsibility for email bomb threats sent last week to newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni summoned opposition leaders for talks on how to deal with similar incidents.

Meloni’s office said “buildings should not be evacuated in the absence of concrete elements beyond the mere receipt of a mass email that would suggest a genuine danger exists”, adding that it would instruct schools to act accordingly.

Authorities in Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland said many schools had received similar threatening emails from abroad on Wednesday, but classified them as hoaxes and allowed classes to continue.

Opposition parties have accused Meloni of prioritising spending on conventional military equipment while neglecting what they say are ‌more ‌pressing cyberthreats.

“We need stronger coordination among the bodies responsible for cybersecurity, and we have proposed shifting part of the available resources towards cyberdefences,” said Elly Schlein, the leader of the main opposition Democratic Party.

The latest security alert came amid rising concerns ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠in Europe about hybrid warfare threats, which have targeted supermarkets, blood banks, air traffic and TV broadcasters.

On Tuesday, France summoned Iran’s ambassador after accusing Tehran of a cyberattack that disabled refrigerators in hundreds of supermarkets.⁠ Tehran rejected the French accusations as “baseless” and “hostile”.

Some European officials suspect Russia of orchestrating the campaign in countries supporting Ukraine after Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Russia denies the accusation and describes it as a smear campaign.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: FIFA Under-17 World Cup to kick off in Qatar despite US withdrawal
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
FIFA says the Under-17 World Cup in Qatar will kick off as scheduled on November 19, despite the United States’ decision to withdraw its team from the tournament.

US Soccer withdrew its national team citing safety concerns, but the sport’s global governing body, which is hosting the tournament in Qatar, confirmed on Thursday that its plans remain unchanged.

“The safety and security of all participants and fans remain paramount. As with all FIFA tournaments and events, we are in close contact with the relevant authorities and ‌‌‌‌are looking forward to the tournament kickoff in Qatar,” FIFA told Al Jazeera in a statement hours after the USA’s announcement.

“In recent months, Qatar has successfully hosted several international events,” it added.

Qatar hosted two major international tournaments in the past two weeks.

MotoGP’s Qatar Grand Prix was successfully held on 8 and the FIP Padel World Cup 2026 concluded on the same day.

With a week until the Under-17 World Cup kicks off, FIFA confirmed that its security assessments “remain unchanged” and that no new ⁠⁠⁠⁠developments affecting the security situation around the tournament have occurred.

“FIFA understands that US Soccer’s decision was made in light of the existing US ⁠⁠⁠⁠Level 3 travel advisory,” it said.

In a letter sent to players, the US Soccer Federation ⁠⁠⁠⁠said it was cancelling the team’s pre-tournament camp and its participation in the event “in light of current circumstances”, according to the Reuters news agency.

The US State Department updated its advisory for Qatar last month, urging Americans to reconsider travel because of the risk of armed conflict.

The update referred to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian ‌‌‌‌airports and critical infrastructure.

“The well-being of our players and staff will always be our top priority,” the US federation’s letter said.

The 48-team Under-17 tournament runs from November 19 to December 13. USA had been due ⁠⁠⁠⁠to open against Montenegro on November 21 before ⁠⁠⁠⁠facing Chile and Algeria in Group J.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Canada won’t let Russian players enter for ice hockey junior championship
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Canada says it will prevent Russian athletes and officials from entering the country for ice hockey’s World Junior Championship in Alberta, effectively barring their participation weeks before the tournament begins.

Canada’s Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said on Wednesday that Ottawa opposes Russian and Belarusian participation in international sport “as long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine with Belarus’s complicity”.

The minister for immigration, refugees and citizenship “will take measures to individually assess and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete, regardless of whether they already hold valid visas”, Van Koeverden said.

Hockey Canada has previously said it supports the government’s position.

Late last month, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ordered the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) to admit Russian teams to five upcoming championships, beginning with the World Junior Championship.

The IIHF, which has barred Russia from most international competitions since Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, said it disagreed with the CAS decision.

The hockey federation’s statement followed announcements from Norway, Denmark, Sweden and the Czech Republic that ⁠⁠their national teams will refuse to play against Russia at next year’s men’s World Championships in Germany.

Latvia and Finland have also said their teams will not play Russia, while the Finnish city of Turku threatened to ⁠⁠drop its hosting duties for the 2028 World Junior Championship.

Belarus’s team will not participate in the championship following a separate decision by the IIHF.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has previously said Ottawa would not permit Russian athletes to compete for their country on Canadian soil, a statement some perceived as keeping the door open for their participation as neutrals.

Van Koeverden said Canada allowed neutral participation only by individual athletes, ruling out the option for the Russian team.

“Canada’s position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual,” he said. “Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine.”

The World Junior Championship runs from December 26 to January 5.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Europe views US with ‘much less horror’ after Trump’s midterms defeat
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Virginia Pietromarchi
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
During the campaign for the midterm elections in the United States, neither the Democrats nor the Republicans spoke much about issues related to Europe.

US President Donald Trump’s handling of the Ukraine war, his approach to Greenland and his aggressive posture towards the European Union were not on the agenda.

Yet while the Democratic Party’s victory last week could produce a Congress that is friendlier towards Europe, experts do not expect major shifts in US foreign policy in some areas.

“Europeans are looking much less in horror towards the US than they have in the past two years, but they should not exaggerate the significance in terms of transatlantic relations,” said Erik Jones, director of the Robert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies at the European University Institute. “The trend line has been moving in a consistent direction across administrations, and this midterm election does not change that trend.”

For decades, the transatlantic relationship was built on the assumption that Washington needed a free, prosperous and secure Europe, while European governments relied on American security guarantees.

But that consensus has gradually eroded, and it did not start with Trump. Over time, there was a loss of popular support for global engagement on both sides of the Atlantic.

The pattern began under Barack Obama, whose administration started a strategic reorientation towards Asia, analysts say, because of perceived threats to US security from the region. That has become a rare area of agreement across the political divide: Republicans and Democrats alike support Europeans taking greater responsibility for their own security.

The US president has accelerated that shift with his America First approach. He has repeatedly lashed out at NATO, threatened to seize Greenland and has shown greater respect for Russia than Ukraine, undermining European efforts to isolate and weaken Moscow.

A Democratic-controlled Congress will have more power over federal spending, legislation and congressional oversight to challenge some of Trump’s decisions. But the president would retain considerable authority over foreign policy.

“All speak in favour of better transatlantic ties, more predictable and more open to take into account European expectations from America,” said Fredrik Erixon, an economist and director of the European Centre for International Political Economy, noting that the Democrats lack a veto-proof majority. “But on issues such as Ukraine, Iran and tariffs there is still a lot of space for the president to behave in the same fashion as in past years.”

With the Iran war, which has pushed up global energy prices, there is no easy way out.

Trump could either cut a deal and declare victory, potentially leaving Iran with leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, or resume military action – a deeply unpopular prospect among US voters. In either scenario, European allies are left with a cost of living crisis that is driving protests across the continent.

Some Democrats have discussed using the next government funding bill to block flows for the war in Iran, a proposal that is popular with antiwar lawmakers.

In Ukraine, the new Democrat-dominated Congress may favour greater support for Kyiv, but that support may not be a game changer for the war-torn nation. Ukrainian officials are anxious about the two-month window before the new Congress takes office in January and fear that Trump could use the period to pursue further talks with Putin.

Even so, the Democrats are likely to invest more energy in improving social services and economic conditions at home.

Some experts also suggest that a politically weakened Trump may now look abroad to demonstrate strength, score wins and build his legacy. His domestic electoral setback could therefore translate into an even less predictable and less accommodating foreign policy.

Last week, the US president said there would soon be a “big, beautiful agreement” on Ukraine, one that “might involve all of Europe”. The comments came ahead of trilateral talks between Ukrainian, Russian and US officials in Abu Dhabi, which have so far failed to yield any breakthrough.

The prospect of a broader deal has raised questions about how much say European governments would have in negotiations that affect their security.

“Trump’s moves are difficult to predict,” said Michele Valensise, president of the Institute for International Affairs and former secretary-general of Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. “It is important for Europeans to be involved in the ongoing contacts aimed at ending the war launched by Russia against Ukraine.”

“We shall see whether the American administration will now accommodate this strong European expectation or choose to ignore it, opting to negotiate exclusively with Russia – a scenario that would unfairly weaken the position of the European allies.”

That uncertainty extends beyond Ukraine.

The Pentagon is expected to complete its review of US military forces in Europe next month, potentially paving the way for decisions on the size and distribution of its footprint.

On tariffs, too, the political divide has shifted.

Democrats have traditionally been more protective of US manufacturing and workers, while Republicans were historically more closely associated with free trade. Trump’s first administration blurred that distinction, and Democrats have since moved towards a more protectionist position on trade.

But even if US courts strike down some of Trump’s tariffs, Europe may see little immediate relief. The trade agreement negotiated between Washington and Brussels is a different matter, Erixon said, because it involves the commitments made by both sides rather than tariffs imposed unilaterally by the US.

“That needs to be renegotiated for tariffs to be taken off, and the US administration will not initiate such a process in the next two years,” he said.

For Jones, the question is not whether the Democrats’ victory will improve relations with Europe, but what Europeans will do with the time it has given them.

“This is better, but how much better? And what should Europe do with the time that this election has bought them?” he said. “Should they use it to repair transatlantic relations? That would be time wasted. They should use this time to prepare for when the US will care even less.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: US President Donald Trump's handling of the Ukraine war and his approach to Greenland were not on the agenda. But experts do not expect major shifts in US foreign policy in some areas.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: ‘Greater Israel’: How Christian Zionism infiltrated US policy
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.author: Awad Joumaa
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
A sermon becomes a map. A map becomes policy. And policy becomes land taken, homes emptied and borders redrawn. ‘Greater Israel’: How Christian Zionism Became Policy – a 22-minute Al Jazeera Originals documentary directed by Awad Joumaa – traces how a centuries-old biblical idea travelled from English fringe pulpits to the heart of US politics, and from prophecy into the machinery of modern power. Blending archival footage and AI-assisted visuals, the film explores a question that no longer belongs only to theologians or historians: what happens when a religious vision of territory is backed by votes, money, military infrastructure and state policy?

In a megachurch in San Antonio, Texas, Pastor John Hagee reads the map aloud. God, he says, promised the Jewish people “one-half of modern-day Egypt, all of Israel, all of Lebanon, all of Syria, all of Jordan, all of Kuwait, and three-fourths of Saudi Arabia”.

This is not a negotiation, he tells his congregation.

“God’s not saying, ‘Let’s make a deal’. He’s saying, ‘This is the deal.'”

Hagee is not a fringe preacher. He is the founder of Christians United for Israel, or CUFI, which claims more than 10 million members and has become one of the most powerful pro-Israel organisations in the United States.

The film explores a world in which scripture is read as geography, geography becomes entitlement, and entitlement is carried to Washington, DC, through lobbying, elections and policy.

Christian Zionism is often described as a belief system. In the United States, it is also a political force.

White evangelical Protestants account for roughly 13 percent of the US adult population, about 35 million people, and most identify as Republican. Their views on Israel are unusually firm. A 2018 LifeWay Research survey for Chosen People Ministries found that 80 percent of evangelicals believed the creation of Israel in 1948 was a fulfilment of biblical prophecy that would bring about Christ’s return. Roughly two-thirds said the modern state of Israel was an outgrowth of the biblical covenant.

That belief translates into votes. Pew Research Center’s analysis of the 2024 election found that 82 percent of white evangelical voters backed Donald Trump in the recent midterms, the highest support of any religious group.

It also shapes attitudes towards war. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs found in 2024 that 64 percent of white evangelicals said Israel’s actions in Gaza were justified, roughly double the share of Americans overall, while 60 percent opposed cutting US military aid to Israel.

“The bedrock of support for the State of Israel is there because American evangelicals think it will bring Jesus back quicker,” former evangelical insider Frank Schaeffer says in Al Jazeera‘s 2024 documentary Praying for Armageddon. “And without the Republican bedrock evangelical voter, no Republican anywhere in America, for any office, gets elected. We don’t want peace, we being evangelicals. We want Armageddon.”

The theology is preached from pulpits. The machinery runs through donations, lobbying and tax-exempt advocacy.

The International Fellowship of Christians and Jews says it has raised more than $3.6bn since 1983, with 92 percent of its donors identifying as Christian. Mother Jones, the US publication, has traced how Christian Zionist networks have channelled money into Israeli causes, including organisations linked to settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank.

CUFI’s political arm is smaller in dollar terms but influential in access. OpenSecrets records $679,410 in federal lobbying spending by CUFI Action Fund in 2025.

God’s not saying, 'Let’s make a deal.' He’s saying, 'This is the deal'

BY
  PASTOR JOHN HAGEE, FOUNDER, CHRISTIANS UNITED FOR ISRAEL

The Congressional Research Service, in its 2024 overview of US aid to Israel, notes that both AIPAC and CUFI “express unequivocal support for US security assistance to Israel”.

Inside Washington, the influence is structural. Ralph Drollinger’s Capitol Ministries – which advocates a “Biblical case for defending Israel” – runs weekly Bible studies attended by members of Congress. During the first Trump administration, it convened a cabinet-level Bible study. The theology is not only in churches; it is in the room where power gathers.

The Christian Zionist map of Israel itself comes from scripture. In Genesis 15, a part of the Torah and Old Testament, God promises Abraham’s descendants land “from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates”. For Christian Zionists and some Israeli ultranationalists, that passage is not a metaphor. It is a title deed.

In February 2026, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, sat with independent broadcaster Tucker Carlson as Carlson read out the biblical passage describing land “from the Euphrates to the Nile”. Asked whether Israel had a right to all of it, Huckabee replied: “It would be fine if they took it all.”

Such a vision is not new. As Professor John Mearsheimer of the University of Chicago notes in this film, Israel’s first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion, wrote in 1918 of a Greater Israel that would include all of historical Palestine, parts of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, the east bank of the Jordan and the Sinai Peninsula. It was not merely a fringe fantasy. It was part of the strategic imagination of early Zionism.

That imagination survives in the settler movement. Daniella Weiss, one of the most prominent leaders of the settlement enterprise, has insisted southern Lebanon is part of the vision of Greater Israel. In her words, “It is part of it. All of it, even parts of Syria, part of Iraq, part of Iran. It’s huge.”

Israel’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has framed the claim in overtly religious language, praying publicly for “the expansion of the borders of the land of Israel for the complete redemption and for the building of the Temple”. In the Knesset, he has also declared that “there is no such thing as a Palestinian people”.

In 2017, Smotrich published what he called his “Decisive Plan”, arguing that the conflict should be resolved, not through Palestinian statehood, but through Israeli victory. Palestinians, he wrote, would face a choice: accept permanent Israeli sovereignty, emigrate, or resist and be defeated. The document gave ideological form to what is now visible on the ground: annexation without the word annexation.

Syria shows how Israel has used the language of “security” to move further east.

After the collapse of the Bashar al-Assad government in December 2024, Israel moved beyond the occupied Golan Heights into the demilitarised buffer zone that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces since a 1974 disengagement agreement. Al Jazeera has reported that Israel captured about 400 square kilometres, or 155 square miles, of Syrian territory beyond the western Golan Heights it has occupied since 1967.

The move was presented by Israel as defensive and temporary. But the language of temporary security has a long history in the region. The occupied Golan Heights itself was seized in 1967 and later annexed by Israel in a move rejected internationally. Decades later, it remains under Israeli control.

Al Jazeera has also reported on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appearing with Israeli troops in occupied territory in southern Syria, a visit that angered Damascus and raised questions over whether any future deal was possible.

The Syrian case is crucial because it turns biblical geography into military geography. The Greater Israel idea speaks of borders stretching north and east. Israeli policy speaks of buffer zones, demilitarisation and strategic depth. For Syrians living under the shadow of Israeli military expansion, the distinction may matter less than the fact of land taken.

Israel’s invasion of southern Lebanon may well mark another move towards creating Greater Israel.

Israel occupied parts of southern Lebanon from 1982 until its withdrawal in 2000. But the border never became quiet, and after the latest war, Israel’s presence has again moved beyond episodic strikes. According to Al Jazeera reporting, Israeli forces have destroyed dozens of villages in southern Lebanon over the last 100 days, while attacks have continued despite ceasefire frameworks.

Al Jazeera has reported that Israel is currently occupying dozens of villages in southern Lebanon and preventing thousands of people from returning home. In one investigation, residents and officials described how Israeli attacks have damaged water infrastructure, deepening the conditions that make return impossible.

Another report showed more than 100 towns and villages across Lebanon were placed under forced displacement orders during the war, extending far beyond the immediate border area.

This is how a supposedly temporary security zone could become a political fact. A village is evacuated. A road is closed. Water networks are destroyed. The army remains. Residents cannot return. On paper, the border may still exist. On the ground, life is reorganised around Israeli military control, and eventually, geography is remade.

Borders are not redrawn only by tanks. They are also redrawn by permits, checkpoints, bypass roads, military zones and demolition orders.

In the occupied West Bank, more than 60 percent of the territory lies in Area C, under direct Israeli civil and military control. Palestinian construction is heavily restricted, while illegal Israeli outposts are often retroactively authorised. The separation wall, which the International Court of Justice ruled illegal in 2004 where it runs inside occupied territory, helped turn geography into policy.

The same logic appears across the occupied Palestinian territory: land is fragmented, movement is controlled and Palestinian life is made administratively conditional. What looks on a map like one territory becomes, in practice, a system of islands.

UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese has repeatedly warned that the destruction of Palestinian life in Gaza and the occupied territory is also a test of the international legal order. “What is lost in Palestine,” she told the UN Human Rights Council, “will be lost to us all.”

The pattern is visible beyond Palestine, too: enter on security grounds, build infrastructure, normalise the presence, and let the map change quietly.

Iraq sits awkwardly inside the Greater Israel imagination. The Euphrates, named in Genesis 15:18 as the eastern boundary of the promised land, runs through it. But the major strategists and ideologues driving the Greater Israel project did not usually speak of annexing Baghdad. Their stated aim was different: to break Iraq’s power.

In 1982, Oded Yinon, a former Israeli foreign ministry official, published A Strategy for Israel in the 1980s in Kivunim, a journal of the World Zionist Organization. He described Iraq as Israel’s greatest strategic threat and argued that it should be dissolved into three entities: a Shia state in the south, a Sunni state in the centre and a Kurdish state in the north. The fragmentation of Iraq, he wrote, was “guaranteed” as a strategic goal.

Fourteen years later, A Clean Break: A New Strategy for Securing the Realm, a 1996 policy paper prepared for Netanyahu by a study group led by Richard Perle – a Reagan-era Pentagon official who would go on to chair George W Bush’s Defense Policy Board, Douglas Feith – later Undersecretary of Defense for Policy, 2001-2005, and David Wurmser – later Middle East adviser to Vice President Dick Cheney, named “removing Saddam Hussein from power in Iraq” as “an important Israeli strategic objective in its own right”. All three authors entered the George W Bush administration in senior national security roles in the run-up to the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

There’s no evidence that the idea of a Greater Israel played any role in the Bush administration’s motivation for the Iraq war. But Pastor Hagee from the San Antonio church was clear: He called the Iraq war “the beginning of the end” and “the gateway to the Apocalypse”.

So Iraq’s role in the Greater Israel worldview is not simply territorial. It is strategic. A unified, powerful Arab state east of the Jordan River is a threat; a fragmented Iraq is an opportunity.

This messianic strand did not begin in Congress. It reaches back to 17th-century English Puritan preachers who believed the Jews had to return to the Holy Land before Christ could return. That belief was carried into Anglo-American Protestant culture long before the creation of Israel.

Long before the Balfour Declaration, American Christian Zionists were already lobbying presidents. In 1891, the Methodist lay preacher William Eugene Blackstone submitted a petition to President Benjamin Harrison calling for Palestine to be restored to the Jewish people. The “Blackstone Memorial” was signed by leading US politicians, businessmen and religious figures, making it one of the earliest organised Christian Zionist interventions in US politics.

The historian Regina Sharif identifies the hinge as Woodrow Wilson. After Wilson’s endorsement of Zionism, she argues, every American president who followed aligned, in one form or another, with the Zionist project.

Public opinion in the United States is now moving in the opposite direction to policy. A Pew Research Center survey published in April 2026 found that 60 percent of Americans now hold an unfavourable view of Israel, with the share saying “very unfavourable” rising from 10 percent in 2022 to 28 percent in 2026. The sharpest shifts are among younger Americans, including young Republicans.

A December 2025 IMEU Policy Project poll, conducted by YouGov, found that 51 percent of Republicans under 45 would prefer a 2028 presidential candidate who reduces US weapons shipments to Israel, while only 27 percent wanted shipments maintained or increased.

This suggests the political coalition that made Christian Zionist influence so formidable may no longer be as stable as it once appeared. The policy machine is still moving. But the electorate beneath it is beginning to shift.

Behind the slogans are villages with names.

In the South Hebron Hills, the herding community of Khirbet Zanuta, emptied under settler violence in late 2023, has watched repeated attempts to return blocked by demolitions and military closures, according to the Israeli rights group B’Tselem. In the same period, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recorded the displacement of more than 2,400 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank by settler violence and demolitions in 2024 alone, the highest annual figure on record. In 2026 so far, nearly 2,150 people have been displaced, per OCHA.

In southern Lebanon, the same story is written through damaged villages, destroyed infrastructure and families unable to return. In Syria, it is written through new military positions beyond the occupied Golan Heights. In Gaza, it is written through the destruction of homes, hospitals, universities and farmland.

The map is often discussed in abstractions: borders, prophecy, security, redemption. But every line moved on that map passes through homes, fields, schools, roads and cemeteries. Every grand theory is lived by ordinary people as expulsion, bombardment, closure or erasure.

For all the talk of prophecy and God’s will, maps do not move by themselves. Settlements do not build themselves. Bombs do not fall from heaven on their own.

What this film shows is a project assembled out of policy, money and votes: a creed translated into lobbying, appropriations, military infrastructure and lines on a map.

This is not ancient theology. It is present-day policy. Israeli bulldozers are clearing Palestinian homes in Masafer Yatta. Israeli forces are holding ground in southern Lebanon. Israel has moved deeper into Syrian territory beyond the Golan. And in Washington, religious language continues to influence political permission.

The sermon, the speech and the bulldozer are no longer separate stories. They are the same story.

Watch ‘Greater Israel’: How Christian Zionism Became Policy here.
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.summary: Al Jazeera Originals explores how a religious vision of territory is backed by votes, money, military infrastructure and state policy. The film explores a world in which scripture is read as geography, geography and entitlement is carried to Washington, DC, through lobbying, elections and policy.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: England vs Croatia: UEFA Nations League – preview, team news, predictions
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Who: England vs Croatia
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A3
Where: Wembley Stadium, London, United Kingdom
When: Thursday, November 12 , at 8:45pm (19:45 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream

Harry Kane will lead with a spring in his step and a newly acquired Ballon d’Or trophy on his arm as England host Croatia in a Nations League clash, with a spot in the quarterfinals up for grabs.

The England captain will be man of the hour on Thursday after a prolific few weeks that saw him win the coveted individual honour and he will present the trophy in front of home fans ahead of the match at Wembley Stadium.

Kane, 33, will also become England’s most-capped men’s player, making his 126th appearance. This surpasses the record set in 1990 by former goalkeeper Peter Shilton, who will be in attendance to mark the occasion.

The Bayern Munich forward is also England’s record scorer with 91 goals.

“Definitely up there with the biggest [achievements of my career],” England captain Kane told reporters at former club Tottenham Hotspur’s training ground on Wednesday after being given a standing ovation when he entered the room.

“It showcases consistency at the highest level and to reach the number of caps I have is a testament to the things I spoke about in my [Ballon d’Or] speech behind the scenes, the dedication, and for sure it is one of the biggest milestones of my career.”

Tuchel said Kane was the “perfect captain and a leader by example” and described his playing style as unique, adding that he is getting smarter with age.

Manager Tuchel also said he has no intention of leaving the England job before the 2028 European Championship regardless of any offers from major clubs.

England only need a draw to make it to the quarterfinals having won three and lost one of their four games so far. They sit second with nine points behind leaders Spain with 12 points, and both teams should make it to the last eight.

Croatia are seeking redemption after a 7-0 thrashing from England in their previous encounter last month, followed by a narrower 2-1 defeat to Spain.

The 2018 World Cup runners-up are third in the group, and manager Slaven Bilic emphasised the importance of finishing third to maintain their Nations League A status.

Czechia, meanwhile, have only won once and cannot reach the quarterfinals.

England will travel to Madrid to face world champions Spain on Sunday while Croatia take on Czechia in a home fixture.

A major talking point for England’s squad selection was the exclusion of midfielder Cole Palmer. But a more captivating storyline is that of Jobe Bellingham finally playing alongside older brother and England star Jude.

The younger Bellingham received his maiden senior call-up after impressing at Borussia Dortmund and England’s under-21 side, which he captains.

Jude had previously said it would be the highlight of his career, while Jobe said it would be an emotional milestone.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said.

If he features against Croatia, they will be the 22nd set of brothers to play for England and the first since Gary and Phil Neville in 2007.

England ran riot in Rijeka last month to obliterate Croatia 7-0 thanks to a brace each from Kane and Bukayo Saka, while Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers were also on target.

Tuchel’s men took just eight minutes to go ahead with an incisive raid that exposed the talent gap between the sides.

“It was the highest level from everyone and from first to last minute as well,” Tuchel said, summing up his side’s dominance.

Tuchel: “For us, it’s important not to chase the same result … we want to win the match to have a chance to win in Spain, and that’s where our focus is. We expect a reaction from Croatia and we expect to overcome this mental challenge for us to start from scratch.”

Bilic: “I told the players that the way we played against Spain last month is our standard. That is how we want to play, with togetherness, aggression and everything else. Tomorrow we have a chance to show that what happened in Rijeka was just a collective bad day.”

The Opta supercomputer heavily favours England, with a win probability of 67.2 percent.

Croatia were assigned a mere 14.8 percent chance, while a draw was estimated at an 18 percent likelihood.

England will be without defenders Ezri Konsa and Djed Spence — both expected to recover for Sunday’s clash against Spain — and Tuchel is looking at James Hill for cover.

Marc Guehi is out with a hip injury and has been replaced by Dan Burn. Jarrad Branthwaite, Jarell Quansah and Ben White could all be in contention at centre-back.

Saka, who scored twice in Rijeka, was not named in the squad because of a quadriceps injury that is set to keep him out for weeks.

Myles Lewis-Skelly is suspended after being booked in both games against Czechia, while Declan Rice, back after missing the last camp, should partner Elliot Anderson in midfield.

Predicted starting XI: Jordan Pickford (goalkeeper), Lewis Hall,  James Hill, Dan Burn, Ben White, Declan Rice, Elliot Anderson, Anthony Gordon, Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Harry Kane

Veteran winger Ivan Perisic will miss the match after receiving a red card against Spain.

Josip Sutalo, Marin Pongracic, Andrej Kramaric and Franjo Ivanovic are also unavailable, with Luka Vuskovic and Duje Caleta-Car expected to start against England’s attack.

Luka Sucic has a fever and is almost certain to miss the game, while Kristijan Jakic is reported to be out of both Nations League games with a knee ligament injury.

Predicted starting XI: Dominik Livakovic (goalkeeper), Josko Gvardiol, Josip Sutalo, Luka Vuskovic, Josip Stanicic, Ivan Perisic, Luka Modric, Mateo Kovacic, Martin Baturina, Igor Matanovic, Ante Budimir
