The 33-year-old will present the Ballon d'Or trophy to home fans at Wembley. Morgan Rogers, Harry Kane and Josip Sutalo all out for England. Ivan Perisic will miss the game after receiving a red card

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Pakistan releases two sisters of ex-PM Imran Khan from jail
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
⁠Uzma Khan and ⁠Noreen Niazi Khan, sisters ⁠of Pakistan’s jailed ‌former Prime Minister Imran Khan, have been ⁠released from ⁠prison, their lawyer and Khan’s political party said.

“Dr Uzma Khan and Ms Noreen Niazi have been released. They have arrived home safely,” lawyer Mudassar Umer said in a post on X on Thursday.

The sisters were released from Kot Lakhpat maximum-security prison in Lahore, nearly two months after they were arrested. A third sister, Aleema Khan, who was detained the same day as Uzma and Noreen, remains in jail, Imran Khan party’s the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) said.

“Aleema Khan remains behind bars. The release of two sisters does not end the injustice or erase the suffering inflicted on Imran Khan’s family,” PTI leader and close Khan confidant Zulfiqar Bukhari told Al Jazeera.

“The demand is clear: No selective relief, no intimidation, and no further persecution.”

Uzma Khan’s son, Wali Khan, called for an explanation as to why his mother had been detained for ⁠53 days and then released, saying the decisions were ⁠not based in law. “Their jailing was arbitrary, and so is their release,” he said in a post on X.

The sisters were arrested and placed under 30-day detention orders a week before a planned PTI protest march on September 27 to demand their brother’s release.

Imran Khan, 74, has been jailed since August 2023 following a series of convictions his party calls politically motivated. All but one have since been suspended or overturned on appeal.

Concerns over his health, in particular the condition of his right eye, which has required months of specialist treatment, have driven the PTI campaign to demand his release.

His sisters’ release comes a day after Khan was taken to hospital in Islamabad, where ⁠he was given medical treatment.

Pakistan’s government said it detained the sisters because they could have been a threat to ‌law and order ahead of the planned march on Islamabad, which ultimately did not go ahead.

The federal government suspended the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provincial government, led by Khan’s party, that had been organising the demonstration.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Xi Jinping says Taiwan’s ‘complete reunification’ with China will happen
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Chinese President Xi Jinping has said the tide of history cannot be stopped, while urging peaceful “reunification” with Taiwan.

Resolving the Taiwan question is an “unwavering historical mission” of China’s Communist Party, Xi said in a speech at Beijing’s Great Hall of the People on Thursday.

“The tide of history ⁠⁠cannot be stopped,” Xi added.

“The complete reunification of the motherland must be realised, and it will certainly be realised.”

China views democratically governed Taiwan as ⁠⁠its own territory, despite Taipei’s strong rejection of that claim, and has repeatedly offered a “one country, two systems” model of autonomy not supported by any major Taiwanese political party.

Xi’s comments came in a speech on the 160th birthday of revolutionary hero Sun Yat-sen, who helped lead a 1911 ‌‌revolt that ended centuries of rule by emperors and empresses and ushered in the Republic of China.

Taiwan’s government dismissed the remarks.

Its Mainland Affairs Council said neither the government nor Taiwan’s people could accept “one country, two systems”, which would ultimately mean submitting to the Communist Party’s rule.

“As for the wording on Taiwan unification, it isn’t much different from the past,” council spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told reporters.

Xi said China adheres to “peaceful reunification and the policy of ‘one country, two systems'” and is willing to talk to Taiwan while upholding the “one China principle”, or Beijing’s position that both sides of the Taiwan Strait are one country.

All Chinese, including those in Taiwan, should join hands to jointly oppose Taiwan independence “separatist” forces and strive for peaceful development of cross-Strait ties, Xi added.

Although Xi did not mention the use of force, which China has never renounced for Taiwan, China’s military operates around the island on a daily basis and is extending its reach further into the Pacific.

Taiwan’s defence ministry said it had detected 29 Chinese military aircraft, including J-16 fighter jets and drones, carrying out a “joint combat ⁠⁠readiness patrol” around Taiwan in conjunction with Chinese warships, starting on Thursday.

Xi’s speech comes a ⁠⁠week ahead of the APEC summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, where he is due to again meet US President Donald Trump, and also a little more than two weeks before important local elections in Taiwan.

The Chinese president made a state visit to Washington in September, during which he told Trump to show “prudence” over Taiwan and urged the US to oppose the island’s independence.

Washington had already paused a $14bn weapons purchase by Taiwan in May, with Trump calling it a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China, which raised fears that Taiwan’s security could be traded away.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Nvidia board weighs Jensen Huang’s future: Can it remove its founder?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Nils Adler
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Jensen Huang may be ousted as the CEO of Nvidia after the tech giant lost more than $600bn in market value this week, following reports that he had extramarital affairs with two women, including a businesswoman accused of spying for China.

Nvidia’s board of directors met late on Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang, who cofounded the $4.2 trillion company, which supplies most of the chips used for advanced artificial intelligence (AI).

Huang, 63, admitted on Sunday in a memo to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife, following the reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom United States officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence, a claim China has denied.

On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang had another extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reports to him. The newspaper cited five people who worked at the company.

Nvidia’s shares fell more than 8 percent in after-hours trading on Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was preparing to oust Huang.

Here’s what you need to know:

Under Nvidia’s bylaws, Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors.

The board has 11 members, and all but Huang are considered independent.

Huang owns about 3.6 percent of the company, according to LSEG data, and has no majority voting control. That sets Nvidia apart from other tech giants.

Huang does not have majority voting control, unlike executives at other companies in the sector, such as Meta and SpaceX.

Nvidia also has no board chair, which Steve Okun, a Singapore-based geopolitical analyst, called “pretty astounding”.

“But what this certainly shows is the utter lack of appropriate governance at Nvidia,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “This should never have been allowed to happen.”

On Sunday, the board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort”, while saying it had “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team”.

Bloomberg reported that the board had been working with an outside firm to identify possible replacements.

Huang has never named a successor, but the Reuters news agency reported that analysts see two likely internal candidates: Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress and engineer Ian Buck.

Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at the technology research group Omdia, described Buck as “a highly regarded industry veteran”, but said: “This remains a speculation until the final decision”.

Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it ever since, turning a maker of graphics chips for video games into the world’s leading supplier of processors that power AI.

Nvidia controls an estimated 80 to 90 percent of the market for the chips used to run advanced AI, and is the world’s second-most valuable company after Apple.

“Jensen is no doubt the de facto leader of Nvidia,” Su told Al Jazeera, pointing to his “willingness to make early bets, identify major technological shifts, and steer the company in the right direction”.

Su said the impact on short-term continuity would be minimal, but a new leader could change the company’s long-term direction, “as a different CEO may have a different view of the future”.

Investors are bracing for that outcome.

“The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not a tail risk,” Armina Rosenberg, cofounder of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares, told Reuters.

For Okun, the question is whether Huang is bigger than Nvidia, or whether the company has become so unique in what it makes that it no longer needs him.

“That’s the question everybody’s going to try and figure out from a business perspective,” he said.

The alleged spy link “spices up the story quite a bit”, Okun said, adding that even without it, Nvidia faced “an extraordinarily damaging question”: Why Megaspeed received so many of its chips, and where they went.

Megaspeed bought about $4.8bn worth of equipment from Nvidia, according to The New York Times.

US authorities have been investigating the company since 2024 over suspicions that it helped China obtain advanced Nvidia chips in breach of export controls, an allegation Megaspeed denies.

But Carsten Holz, an expert on the Chinese economy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, told Al Jazeera that the likelihood that Huang “could pass on significant technical information to another person, whether a spy or not, would seem extremely low”.

On Monday, US President Donald Trump said the FBI was looking into the matter, adding that Huang had told him he had “absolutely no idea” the woman was an alleged spy.

Three Republican House committee chairs have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on November 18. He faces a possible subpoena if he does not respond, Reuters reported.

Okun said Huang “certainly has to take a leave of absence”.

It is also unclear whether Huang will join Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on November 18-19.

He travelled with Trump to Beijing in May, but his participation is now in doubt, the South China Morning Post reported. During the May trip, an agreement was signed to allow Nvidia to sell its H200 AI chips to several approved Chinese companies.

Asked on Sunday whether Huang would take part in the summit, Trump said: “I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him.”

Huang had lobbied Trump to lift some of the restrictions on chip exports to China imposed by President Joe Biden. Beijing is one of the biggest buyers of Nvidia chips in the world.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Nvidia's board of directors met late on Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang. Huang admitted on Sunday in a memo to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Beijing is one of the biggest buyers of Nvidia chips in the world.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Who is Scott Colom, Mississippi’s first Black senator in 150 years?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
United States prosecutor and Democrat Scott Colom has made history in Mississippi by becoming the deeply conservative state’s first Black senator in more than 150 years and ushering in the first Democratic victory there in more than four decades.

Senator-elect Colom’s narrow victory against Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith was declared late on Wednesday, more than a week after the US midterms, which many have called a “blue tsunami” as Democrats firmly seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives.

It has been 43 years since Democrats last won a Senate seat in the state, in 1982.

But Colom’s win is significant beyond party politics and marks a turning point for Mississippi’s African American community too: he’ll be the first Black American senator since 1874.

It was a narrow victory. Colom beat Hyde-Smith, the incumbent and an ally of President Donald Trump, by fewer than 5,000 votes after 99 percent of ballots had been counted late on Wednesday.

Hyde-Smith had been ahead in polling for Mississippi, where Trump won by 23 points in 2024.

Colom’s win puts Democratic Senate control at 55-44. Another tight race in Alaska is still being counted, although Democrat Mary Peltola is also leading there by a slim margin.

Only 14 Black senators have ever been elected or appointed in the US. Colom will be one of seven new Black senators.

On Wednesday, after the results were called, Colom told supporters at his victory party in Jackson that he had come close to giving up.

“There were times when I was tired, and I felt like I couldn’t keep going, but I kept the faith,” the politician said, speaking at the historically Black Tougaloo College.

“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”

Colom continued to thank his supporters in a series of messages on X on Thursday. “This victory belongs to all of us, and I am honored to be your new senator-elect,” he posted.

Colom, 43, is a lawyer who has served as a Mississippi prosecutor since 2016 until this year. He is married to Nadia Colom and has two children. His identical twin brother, Andrew, played a major role in his campaign.

The politician was born in Columbus and comes from a family of lawyers. Despite having one of the largest populations of Black Americans in the country, there has not been a statewide elected Black official in more than 140 years in Mississippi.

In interviews, Colom has said he decided to run to “look out for the people”, especially on the issue of affordability. He accused incumbent Hyde-Smith of neglecting the state and “selling out” Mississippians.

In 2015, Colom became the first Black American to be elected as district attorney for the 16th Judicial District, which includes the white-majority counties of Clay, Lowndes, Noxubee and Oktibbeha.

One of his most notable cases was Eddie Lee Howard, a Black American man who had spent 26 years on death row for murder but was released in 2021 as a result of a lack of evidence. After a judge dismissed the murder charge against him, Colom confirmed that prosecutors were dropping it.

In 2022, Colom was nominated as a US district judge by ex-President Joe Biden, but his nomination was blocked by Hyde-Smith, who claimed he was supporting transgender athletes and that he received funding from left-wing billionaire George Soros.

Many have credited Colom’s endearing personality, his respectful rhetoric, and especially his simple but effective campaign advertisements that supporters say are both funny and thought-provoking. He naturally appealed to Black voters, but also managed to reach the white majority.

In one advertisement, Colom played on his opponent’s weaknesses. In February, a TV reporter had asked Hyde-Smith, a rancher, how Republicans were attempting to address rising beef prices amid the US-Israel war on Iran. Hyde-Smith suggested that Mississippians find alternatives. “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from,” she said.

The response drew outrage. Colom’s advertisement called on people not to pick another protein, but to “pick another senator instead”.

Colom’s wife, Nadia, featured prominently in the campaign. In one advertisement, just as Colom tells a reporter he does not have a nickname, Nadia appears and calls him “Sweet Thang”.

Colom’s final campaign video struck a more melancholy tone.

He invoked the memory of Medgar Evers, a US Army veteran and civil rights advocate who fought for the US in Normandy during World War II and returned home to fight racism during the Civil Rights Movement when Black people were pushing for the right to vote and to use restaurants or public restrooms. Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan.

Across social media channels, many Mississippians who claimed they or their families usually voted for Republicans said they had gone out to vote for Colom in the midterms.

Yes. Some of Colom’s supporters are already envisioning him in the White House in 2028, as Democrats jostle to field a viable candidate.

Some conservatives have called Colom a “bigger threat” than Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who is also being named as a potential candidate.

But Colom has dismissed the conversation, saying his focus is on Mississippi.

“I am not trying to be a threat to anybody,” Colom told CNN.

“I’m trying to focus on delivering for Mississippi … We’ve got to get back to leadership that’s rooted in serving people, listening to them, learning their concerns, and delivering for them.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Scott Colom, 43, is the first Black American senator in Mississippi since 1874. He is the state's first Democratic senator since 1982. He beat Cindy Hyde-Smith, the incumbent and an ally of President Donald Trump, by fewer than 5,000 votes.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: China says US ‘fabricating’ Nvidia spy claims to justify tech ‘blockade’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
China has urged ⁠⁠⁠⁠the ⁠⁠⁠⁠United States to stop “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade”, amid national security concerns that emerged over an affair involving Nvidia’s CEO.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning made the comments at a press briefing on Thursday when asked about allegations that the woman with whom Nvidia’s Jensen Huang had a relationship was a Chinese spy.

Mao said that China’s scientific and ⁠⁠⁠⁠technological progress was ⁠⁠⁠⁠driven by independent innovation and open cooperation, adding that Beijing was willing ⁠⁠⁠⁠to work with the US to implement a consensus reached ‌‌‌‌by their two heads of state. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to ease tariffs and lift restrictions on tech to de-escalate tensions following tit-for-tat tariffs in a trade deal in Busan, South Korea.

The remarks come ahead of a meeting next week between Trump and Xi at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen, southern China.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and turned it into the world’s leading supplier of the chips that power artificial intelligence (AI), has admitted to having an extramarital affair. The woman was reported to be Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US officials believe worked for Chinese intelligence.

Megaspeed on Thursday said it takes compliance obligations under US export control laws “extremely seriously” and that it “is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government”.

Nvidia’s 63-year-old boss has spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced chips to China. Last year Trump cleared Nvidia’s H200 chips for export to China despite objections from Republicans and Democrats who fear Chinese dominance in AI technology.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denied the claims, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.

Huang’s position at the top of the $4.2 trillion company hangs in the balance after Nvidia launched an investigation into him on Sunday. It is unclear whether the tech giant has a succession plan.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: China has urged US to stop ‘fabricating so-called spy narratives’ amid national security concerns. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning made the comments at a press briefing on Thursday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Manchester United sack Michael Carrick as manager
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Manasi Pathak
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Manchester United have sacked manager Michael Carrick, the Premier League club confirmed in a statement, amid a torrid time for the global football giants, who find themselves in the league’s relegation zone.

Carrick’s departure, which had been imminent after United made their worst start to the English top flight in 40 years, was announced on Thursday by the club, which said it would “appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible”.

“Manchester United can confirm that Michael Carrick has departed his role as men’s first-team head coach”, the Old Trafford club said in a statement.

“After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.”

United, 13-time Premier League champions, have been heavily linked with US Men’s National Team coach Mauricio Pochettino.

Pochettino – whose release from the contract extension he signed as USA head coach has reportedly been arranged – would become the eighth permanent man in charge at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s departure in May 2013 after more than 26 years in the job.

United’s statement termed Carrick a club legend.

“Just as he [Carrick] did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club,” the statement added.

“His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.”

The 45-year-old’s last game as United’s head coach ended in a dramatic late draw against Aston Villa at Old Trafford, where the furious home fans voiced their anger towards the club’s ownership.

United needed a stoppage-time equaliser to eke out a point against 10th-placed Villa, but it was not enough to lift them out of the Premier League’s relegation zone.

The Red Devils briefly dropped to the bottom of the table before results elsewhere in the league took them back to 18th place with eight points from their 10 games this season.

Carrick, who was handed the United job on an interim basis in January, knew his managerial position was under threat following a series of disappointing results in recent weeks.

United have endured four losses and five draws, with their solitary win coming against Ipswich Town in late August.

They were also knocked out of the English League Cup in the third round, and have made an unconvincing start in their Champions League campaign, with two wins and as many losses.

Overall, United have won only three times in 15 games across all competitions this season.

Carrick’s sacking marks the end of a rollercoaster reign at the club.

The former United midfielder, who also captained the club in his final season as a player, took over from the sacked Ruben Amorim last term, when the team were seventh, but lifted them to a third-place finish and secured Champions League qualification at the end of the 2025-26 season.

The players looked like a better, more exciting version of themselves under Carrick when he first took over, but fans’ optimism vanished when the revival did not continue into the current campaign.

United’s defeat to newly-promoted Hull City in their opening match of the league season marked an embarrassing start for the former champions. What followed was further humiliation on and off the field, with a dressing room rift damaging Carrick’s image, and the club’s hierarchy losing faith in one of their own.

British media have linked several high-profile managers to the job.

Newcastle United boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann were among the frontrunners, but USA men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino has seemingly overtaken both as favourite.

Pochettino, who previously took charge of Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea in the English top flight, has been widely favoured by US and British media.

Former Chelsea coach Antonio Conte is also in the running.

A managerial change is expected during this international break, with a new face likely to lead United on their trip to Anfield to face longtime rivals, Liverpool, on November 22.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Michael Carrick's departure was announced on Thursday by the club. United have been heavily linked with US Men's National Team coach Mauricio Pochettino. The Red Devils have endured a torrid start to the Premier League season.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.title: From the UK to the Gulf, are US overseas bases becoming liabilities?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.author: Caolán Magee
https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.text:
Doha, Qatar — Late one morning in March 1999, a United States B-52 bomber took off from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, headed southeast. Seven more jets followed, at two-minute intervals.

It was the start of the US-led NATO bombing of Yugoslavia, a campaign in which the Fairford base served as both a pivotal launchpad for American jets and as a fuel station for fighter planes. The British base had served a similar role during the Gulf War in 1991, and would do so again during the 2003 Iraq war and in the early stages of the US-Israeli war on Iran that began on February 28, 2026.

But in October, the US pulled all 12 of its B-1 Lancer bombers from the Gloucestershire base, amid fears that they were no longer safe there from a growing Iranian threat. Days earlier, British security forces had made several arrests, and the country’s government has accused Iran of being behind a plot to target the base — a charge Tehran has denied.

RAF Fairford is not alone. Earlier this month, the US withdrew a dozen planes from another British base, RAF Mildenhall. And in July, reports said that the US had relocated many of its military assets from its bases in the Gulf that were badly hit by Iran during the war, instead moving them to bases in Jordan, while also considering a proposal to shift them to Israel.

For decades, these bases have served as the sharp edge of the US military’s ability to project power and wage wars thousands of miles from home. For close allies, whether in Europe or the Gulf, they also worked as security guarantors against other threats.

But Iran’s ability to severely damage US facilities in the Middle East during the war, and pose a threat as far as the UK, has for the first time turned these critical strategic assets into potential liabilities, both for American allies and for the US itself, say analysts.

“The US security umbrella is becoming a double-edged sword,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. “When the security of US bases is called into question, it changes Washington’s calculation of their strategic benefits. It also gives European and Gulf states reason to think seriously about the bases, given that they are becoming targets.”

Hosting American bases has long been perceived as integral to how US allies, whether in Europe, the Gulf or East Asia, deter threats that they themselves face.

Former US President Barack Obama once spoke of an “ironclad commitment” to Gulf security, while Britain regularly invokes its so-called “special relationship” with the United States. In doing so, Britain and the Gulf have long cast themselves as willing partners to a power that — at least before current President Donald Trump — presented itself as the benevolent guarantor of its allies’ security.

But a spate of recent security incidents, many linked to the war on Iran, is testing that narrative and raising questions about whose interests these commitments serve, and whether hosting American forces could be bringing danger closer to home.

US prosecutors have charged three men they describe as Iranian-backed operatives over their alleged roles in plotting nearly 20 attacks across the United States and Europe, including on RAF Fairford.

Meanwhile, in the Gulf, Iran explicitly cited the presence of US bases as justification for targeting its neighbours, bombing Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Kuwait. Iran also bombed Oman, which does not have a permanent US base; and Jordan and Iraq, beyond the Gulf, which do host major US military facilities.

A report by the Pentagon’s watchdog released in September revealed that Iranian attacks damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US military installations in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan in the first four months of the war.

At least five KC-135 aerial refuelling tankers were damaged when they were hit at the Prince Sultan airbase in Saudi Arabia. At least one of these airborne early-warning and control aircraft was damaged on the ground in a subsequent strike.

Experts say these incidents are sharpening a security dilemma for US allies in the Gulf and Europe. Hosting US forces can expose them to retaliation in a war they had no say in starting, while those same bases help defend some of those host countries from attacks, including by intercepting missiles and providing weapons transfers.

The war has disrupted flights and shipping, threatening the oil and gas exports on which much of the region depends. US President Donald Trump said on Monday that further military action against Iran was unnecessary for now. But the US naval blockade remains in place, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has yet to return to normal.

“While the utility of hosting foreign military bases has always involved a calculus of risk versus the assumed assurance it provides, the perception among Gulf Arab states is certainly shifting,” Mohammad Ali Shabani, a Middle East analyst, told Al Jazeera. “The vulnerability of these assets is increasingly front-of-mind for host governments, who have not sought war, yet have been drawn into it without having had any real say.”

Washington faces a dilemma of its own. Bases in Europe or the Middle East give it the reach to fight faraway wars, but their presence has also provided Iran with a litany of targets.

In March, an Iranian drone hit a hangar at a British base in Cyprus that the US also uses for intelligence and logistics operations. Tehran threatened Bulgaria after reports emerged that the Eastern European NATO nation had allowed the US to use its Bezmer airbase for refuelling of planes used to attack Iran. Weeks later, Bulgaria’s defence minister announced that the US air tankers had left Bezmer for good, with the country’s president declaring that the “mission is over,” bringing relief to the village that the base draws its name from.

And in the Middle East, several key bases used by US troops have been almost rendered unusable, with those in Kuwait suffering the heaviest damage, say analysts. An attack on the Port of Shuaiba killed six US service members and destroyed an army operations centre. Iranian drones and missiles damaged aviation facilities and injured personnel at Ali Al Salem airbase, while strikes on Camp Buehring damaged maintenance and refuelling facilities.

In Qatar, an Iranian strike damaged the early warning radar system at Al Udeid airbase, which houses the headquarters of US Central Command’s (CENTCOM) air operations. In Bahrain, an Iranian drone struck communications equipment at the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet.

This damage raises a question about how much the US can still use these bases once they come under attack. Gerd Nonneman, a professor of international relations and Gulf studies at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera the war had shown that some bases were “themselves very vulnerable” and “unable to fulfil many of the tasks they were established for”.

Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer at the Defence Studies Department at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera “large bases are indeed becoming more easily targeted”.

“One of the technologies that has allowed this, alongside fairly cheap ballistic missiles, is drones,” he added.

Iran has invested heavily in developing cheap, domestically produced drones that inflict disproportionate damage to targets and exhaust far more expensive interceptor missiles.

Meanwhile in the UK, drones present US airbases with different challenges. While the nature of the reported threat to RAF Mildenhall remains unclear, the Fairford case concerns an alleged plot. “The range of actors who might target bases has changed,” Urban Coningham, a research fellow and course lead at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) in the UK, told Al Jazeera. “Bases are more vulnerable, and that changes the risk calculation.

“Anyone can manufacture a drone in a basement … People looking to create mischief or mayhem can recruit organised criminals, making attacks harder to attribute.”

All of that, he said, makes bases “more vulnerable, and that changes the risk calculation”.

As Washington moves some military assets out of bases in the Gulf and Europe, it could also come to rely more heavily on Israel, its closest ally in the Middle East. Shabani said there were “already signs that CENTCOM is moving towards using Israel as a key forward base”.

Israel launched the war on Iran in February alongside the US. With the oil and gas exports on which Gulf economies depend at risk, keeping US forces nearby allows Washington to respond, but it also leaves those forces exposed to Iranian attacks.

“The longer-term solution is to work with partners and ensure that allied forces are ready to fend for themselves,” RUSI’s Coningham said.

“There is a debate within the US policy establishment, and the Iranians are referencing it and saying that as long as US forces are there, they are a target,” he said. “That is the policy conundrum for the US. Ultimately, they can’t see any alternative to having bases in some form.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.summary: US pulled all 12 of its B-1 Lancer bombers from RAF Fairford in October. Iran has accused the UK of being behind a plot to target the base. Iran threatened Bulgaria after reports that the country allowed the US to use its Bezmer airbase for refuelling of planes used to attack Iran.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow to discuss Russia-Ukraine war
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
United States envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin as part of their latest push for a peace deal ⁠in Ukraine.

Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy, met Kushner and Witkoff at their plane on Thursday morning and accompanied them to central Moscow. Talks with Putin began a few hours later.

The meeting comes on the heels of two days of trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates that concluded in the capital, Abu Dhabi, on Wednesday with news of another planned major prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the nearly five-year war.

The US said differences remained on major issues, including territory, but some progress had been made on post-war security guarantees.

Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin’s demands to surrender all of its eastern region of Donbas in ⁠return for peace.

The Abu Dhabi talks were the first direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the US in nine months.

Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said one of the goals of Thursday’s visit would be for the US team to persuade Putin to invite Europeans to the negotiation process.

“Ukraine and the US want the European partners to be involved while Moscow is adamant about talks without the Europeans, and that’s why they’ve been largely excluded from the process,” she said.

Shapovalova added that the US delegation would bring Putin an updated proposal for a peace plan and the presence of Dmitriev in the talks was an indication that they would address some of the more complex issues.

During the US-backed effort to revive talks, leaders from more than 40 European countries gathered in Dublin on Thursday for a summit focused on the continent’s security.

The meeting of the European Political Community (EPC) brought together heads of state and government from the European Union and other European countries, including the United Kingdom. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte also attended.

The EPC was established in 2022 as a forum for countries both inside and outside the 27-nation EU.

Zelenskyy and his European allies are expected to discuss this week’s talks in Abu Dhabi.

Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, and Witkoff are scheduled to meet Zelenskyy in Dublin on Friday after talking to Putin.

Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said Ukrainians do not believe the talks in Moscow will yield results. “Over the past two days, we saw just another prisoner exchange, which has been the case in previous talks,” the correspondent said.

“When it comes to the negotiations, not much has changed in terms of where these two sides stand,” Macalpine added. “Perhaps the biggest thing of note [in the talks] was that they took place at all.”

Meanwhile, French Minister Delegate for European Affairs Benjamin Haddad on Thursday ‌said the ⁠EU will approve more sanctions ⁠against Russia.

“On Monday, we will take new sanctions against ⁠Russia on 150 additional ⁠entities, 50 banks, and it’s ⁠France which proposed the ⁠bulk ⁠of the entities to add,” Haddad ‌told LCI television.

As talks continue, Russia launched ballistic missiles and dozens of combat drones at Ukraine overnight, killing one person, Ukrainian officials said on Thursday.

A woman was killed and five people injured when a drone hit a residential block in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote on Telegram. Out of the 123 Russian combat drones used, 89 were shot down, the military said.

Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said ⁠Russian ⁠strikes on Ukraine’s ⁠energy infrastructure overnight ⁠caused power outages in nine ‌Ukrainian regions, namely ⁠Vinnytsia, Dnipropetrovsk, Zhytomyr, ⁠Zaporizhzhia, ⁠Odesa, Rivne, Sumy, Kharkiv ‌and Cherkasy.

⁠Separately, Ukraine’s ⁠military said it ⁠had struck Russia’s ⁠five largest oil refineries since October 30, ‌including those in Omsk, Kirishi, Ryazan, Nizhny Novgorod and Yaroslavl. In ⁠a post ⁠on Telegram, the General ⁠Staff said ⁠the smaller Novokuibyshevsk ⁠and Saratov refineries had also ‌been hit.

Meanwhile, Russia’s Investigative Committee said a Russian military serviceman was killed after ⁠the car he was driving was blown up in the Pushkinsky District of St Petersburg on Thursday.

Moscow has blamed Ukraine for previous assassinations of senior military officials and people linked to its ⁠war effort. There was no ⁠immediate comment from Ukraine about the latest incident.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin. The meeting comes on the heels of two days of trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates. The US said differences remained on major issues, including territory, but some progress had been made on post-war security guarantees.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: India bypasses own rules to buy Israeli phone-hacking tech
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.author: Yashraj Sharma
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
New Delhi, India – India has exempted an Israeli phone-hacking company from New Delhi’s own rules, allowing it to sell phone-extraction products and surveillance technology to government agencies and sparking concerns and criticism from rights groups and activists.

An investigation by the digital-rights group Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) found Indian Home Minister Amit Shah, a close confidante of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, signed off on exemptions from “make in India” procurement rules, clearing the way for government forensic institutions to buy at least 422 items of foreign technology, including products made by the Israeli firm Cellebrite.

Modi’s federal government and state governments ruled by his Bharatiya Janata Party are not the only ones who bought this Israeli technology. States governed by the opposition Indian National Congress party, including Himachal Pradesh, Keralam and Karnataka, also purchased similar phone-extraction and cloning tools.

A review of documents revealed that India’s expansive surveillance capabilities extend far beyond just cloning phones and extracting data without passwords to accessing cloud-based data from social media platforms – such as Instagram, X and Tinder – as well as data from connected devices such as Amazon’s Alexa and Google Home.

Experts argued that India’s current laws offer no guardrails against overreaching surveillance and the data extractions happen in a legal grey zone.

“It is clear that there is an expansion of India’s surveillance capabilities and it is becoming both wider and deeper,” said Vrinda Bhandari, a lawyer in the Supreme Court who works on digital rights and privacy issues.

“It’s now easier to conduct mass surveillance rather than targeted, specific surveillance and also possible to do more intrusive surveillance,” she told Al Jazeera. “[Today,] surveillance gives you a richer picture of an individual’s life.”

The IFF reviewed a letter also seen by Al Jazeera from India’s Ministry of Home Affairs dated January 7 in which Shah signed off on a wide-ranging, one-year waiver of “make in India” rules to clear a path for buying at least 422 forensic items.

Under “make in India” procurement rules, preference must be given to eligible Indian manufacturers over foreign suppliers in awarding government contracts. However, the rules allow exemptions with the approval of the minister in charge of the procuring department.

Another letter by the ministry dated January 20 showed Shah permitted the National Investigation Agency (NIA) to buy Israeli company Cellebrite’s Premium Tool on a three-year licence for about 50 million rupees ($529,947).

In specifications demanded by the government that were revealed in a review of tender bids, “solution” software must be capable of using login tokens recovered from seized phones or computers to access more than 100 cloud services. Login tokens are in effect digital keys that keep users signed in to online accounts.

Although an exemption for a company does not confirm whether a certain product was purchased by any government agency, it points to the range of forensic capabilities that opened up for procurement by Indian agencies.

From the 422-item exemption list, the IFF identified 118 items under digital and multimedia forensics, including Israeli company Cellebrite’s Pathfinder, Inseyets On-Prem Pro and Inseyets Offline.

Cellebrite’s tools have been used against journalists and activists in countries like Serbia, Jordan, Kenya and Russia.

Other products included tools from foreign digital-forensics companies like Magnet, MSAB, Oxygen Forensics and Belkasoft as well as software for open-source intelligence, dark-web monitoring and cryptocurrency investigations.

Al Jazeera reviewed a request for a bid proposal by the Delhi Police for software for its National Cyber Forensic Laboratory, which comes under the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre, an initiative of the Home Ministry.

Consider the capabilities the police department was seeking in its request: software that bypasses passwords on Apple’s macOS, Microsoft Windows and Linux operating systems; recovers internet activity, browser histories, deleted files and identifies traces of VPNs; bypasses screen locks; performs full file system extractions; decrypts backups; and extracts information from messaging applications.

The Delhi Police demanded another “all-in-one” system to access more than 100 cloud services, including Google, Apple, WhatsApp, Instagram, Telegram, Discord and dating platforms such as Tinder, Grindr and OkCupid or platforms like Slack and OnlyFans using account credentials or login tokens recovered from devices. Its specifications also sought the extraction of data from drones, wearable devices and devices like Amazon Alexa and Google Home.

Al Jazeera reached out to officials at the NIA, the Home Ministry and home departments of opposition-ruled states of Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka and Keralam for comments. The Delhi Police reports to Shah’s mInistry.

None of them had responded to Al Jazeera by the time of publication.

For some, the lack of transparency in the surveillance capabilities of India’s security agencies is not just a theoretical concern.

Last month, when Modi’s government faced street protests demanding the election chief resign, popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, a Modi critic, landed in New Delhi to participate in the demonstrations.

On the morning of the protest, he was detained by Delhi Police while still at home. His phone was taken from him. Speaking on a podcast later, Rathee said he believed police had tried to clone his iPhone using Israeli company Cellebrite’s tools but the attempt may have failed because his device was running a newer version of the iOS operating system than what the tool was capable of tricking.

Al Jazeera could not verify Rathee’s account, but Rathee is not alone in this suspicion.

Mohammad Aslam Hussain, a reporter with the newspaper Siasat Daily, told Al Jazeera that he was detained with a cameraperson on October 10 in New Delhi and his phone was confiscated at the scene.

“When I got my device later in the evening, all recorded footage of our reporting had been selectively deleted from the device,” Hussain said. The reporter uses Samsung’s Android-operated Galaxy S24 secured with a pattern lock and fingerprint authentication.

Hussain added that he cannot say conclusively what tools the police used to bypass his phone’s authentication requirement. “But it raises several questions with no one willing to respond to them,” he added. “How did they get inside my phone?”

The Indian government has faced accusations that it has used sophisticated spyware against journalists, activists, lawyers and political opponents during Modi’s years in power.

In 2019, WhatsApp disclosed that the Pegasus spyware, developed by the Israeli firm NSO Group, had been used to target Indian journalists and human rights defenders. Forensic examinations by Amnesty International later confirmed Pegasus infections on the phones of journalists Siddharth Varadarajan and Anand Mangnale. The government has denied allegations of unauthorised surveillance.

Bhandari told Al Jazeera that another problem in holding overarching surveillance to account is identifying the affected party. Often, she pointed out, the person placed under surveillance “does not know about it, so what does one do?”

The central legal gap identified by digital rights group IFF is that India has no statute or protocol that specifically authorises or regulates the forced unlocking and full extraction of data from a mobile phone seized by law enforcement agencies.

Existing seizure powers under criminal law do not explicitly address bypassing passcodes, copying an entire file system, harvesting login tokens to access cloud accounts or establishing rules for the retention and deletion of extracted data.

The Supreme Court in a 2017 judgement recognised privacy as a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution. The judgement established that any state intrusion into privacy must have a legal basis, pursue a legitimate state aim and be proportionate to that aim.

Bhandari told Al Jazeera that when the government agencies “deploy these capabilities without any proper meaningful oversight, the net of surveillance is cast wider and deeper and a lot more people are affected without either legislative, parliamentary or judicial oversight”.

Bhandari noted that while some countries like the United Kingdom or Germany “have some element of either parliamentary oversight or judicial oversight, India only has an internal review mechanism in executive oversight”.

“The whole point of having any oversight is to create a friction for surveillance,” she said, “so that it’s not easy for the government to just target everybody.”

“The current legal framework fails in this safeguard,” Bhandari said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.summary: Indian Home Minister Amit Shah signed off on exemptions from “make in India’s procurement rules’ Indian journalist says he was detained with cameraperson in New Delhi. He says his phone was confiscated at the scene and all footage of his reporting was deleted.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Ten police officers, 18 fighters killed in northwest Pakistan attack
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Gunmen have attacked police officers conducting an operation against illegal gold mining in northwestern Pakistan, with 10 officers and 18 fighters killed in the ensuing violence.

A statement by provincial police in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa said officers were returning from a mine in the Gumbat area of Kohat district on Wednesday when armed men opened fire on them.

In addition to the dozens killed, 12 police personnel were wounded, the statement said.

Hours later, the Pakistani Taliban issued a statement claiming the attack.

Earlier, a senior administrative official in Kohat told the AFP news agency that fighters had set two police vehicles on fire during the assault, while two other police vehicles and one private vehicle were missing.

Another senior administrative official in the Orakzai area of Kohat said that 10 fighters belonging to the Pakistan Taliban were killed during a separate operation in the district.

A large quantity of weapons was also recovered from the fighters, the official said.

A spokesman for a local emergency service said earlier on Wednesday that there had been a “firing incident involving police personnel” in Kohat district, adding that rescue workers were treating a dozen wounded officers.

Security forces are battling intensifying violence in the border province that they say emanates from Afghanistan, an accusation the Taliban government in Kabul rejects.

The Pakistan Taliban, formerly known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, have stepped up attacks on security forces in the region in recent months.

Pakistan has seen a surge in violence in recent years, much of it blamed on the TTP.

The group is separate from but closely allied with the Afghan Taliban, who returned to power in neighbouring Afghanistan in 2021.

Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been fraught since the Afghan Taliban retook power, and worsened after deadly border clashes in October last year that led to near-total closure of the border.

Pakistan frequently accuses Afghanistan’s Taliban government of sheltering TTP fighters, an allegation Kabul denies.

Hundreds of civilians have been killed in fighting between the two countries in the last year, according to figures from the United Nations mission in Afghanistan.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Police say officers were returning from a mine in Kohat district when armed men opened fire on them. Pakistani Taliban claim the attack, saying they were attacked by the police. The Pakistani Taliban have stepped up attacks on security forces in the region in recent months.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nvidia.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nvidia.author: Amanda Silberling
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nvidia.text:
Nvidia co-founder and (now former) CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.

U.S. officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.

The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.

Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang, and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

Nvidia confirmed in an SEC filing on Thursday that the board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Collete Kress, will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang.

Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993.

After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days.

Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said. The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan.

The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO.

According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year.

Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressman to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed.

The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.

Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.

Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.

In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.

On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.

When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”

Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.

Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.

An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.

Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.

The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump, has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.

Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.

Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.

Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.

These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nvidia.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigns, chipmaker names CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nvidia.author: Ram Iyer
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nvidia.text:
Jensen Huang has resigned from his position as president and chief executive of Nvidia, the company said on Thursday, just a few days after he admitted to a romantic affair with an alleged Chinese spy, sparking a U.S. national security crisis.

In a regulatory filing, Nvidia said its board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday.

Nvidia said its current chief financial officer and executive vice president, Collete Kress, will take over as interim CEO until the company finds a permanent successor. Kress will continue to serve as the company’s CFO.

Nvidia’s shares were down nearly 12% in early morning trading on Thursday. Since Friday, the company’s stock has fallen over 19%, resulting in a market cap loss of more than $855 billion.

Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it as CEO ever since. Nvidia essentially invented the graphics processor unit, a specialized chip that takes care of graphics processing for PCs, as we know it today, bringing together transforms, lighting and rendering into one chip. The chips were not an immediate hit, and the early days of Nvidia were characterized by struggle and layoffs, but eventually, it struck on a GPU design that performed so well, it became the standard for graphics processing.

These chips also turned out to be extremely good at doing maths, which has made them popular for computation-intensive tasks like crypto mining, and more recently, training and running neural networks, which are what AI models are at their core.

After AI researchers began using GPUs to train neural networks over a decade ago, Huang leaned in towards developing chips for AI and then data centers, and grew it from there into its dominant position.

The potential implications of Huang’s departure for the AI and data center industries are vast, given how active Huang, and by extension Nvidia, has been in furthering the AI boom. In particular, it raises questions about the future of Nvidia’s sprawling AI investments, which have helped bankroll everything from startups developing new technologies to the enormous data centers needed to run them.

Under Huang, Nvidia deftly used its financial muscle to support companies buying its chips, effectively helping to finance the market for its own products, as well as lobbying Washington to relax potential rules around AI and data center regulation.

As of the end of its second quarter, Nvidia reported, Nvidia reported $99 billion worth of investments and another $25 billion of commitments. It also has $36 billion in cloud service commitments, which are arrangements that help AI cloud operators finance the GPUs and data center equipment they buy from Nvidia, with the chipmaker saying it will buy compute from them and potentially earn a share of their operators’ revenue.

Nvidia has also been investing directly in neoclouds, the companies serving a lot of the AI processing needs. In January, the company invested $2 billion in CoreWeave, and another $2 billion in Nebius in March. The chipmaker was said to be considering being a guarantor for Nscale’s planned West Virginia data center project. It’s also signed up to provide up to $105 billion worth of credit guarantees for an OpenAI data center campus in Ohio.

Nvidia’s also a major investor in the labs building the AI models that run on its GPUs, putting $30 billion into OpenAI, and $10 billion into Anthropic. It’s also backed Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab as part of a deal involving at least 1 GW of its Vera Rubin GPU systems. The chipmarker has even invested $3.5 billion in MediaTek to help the Taiwanese company develop custom AI chips that work with Nvidia’s systems.

Investors were already uneasy with the enormous amounts of debt companies in the space were raising to sustain the AI infrastructure buildout, and Huang’s exit throws another uncertainty-shaped wrench into the works. CoreWeave’s shares were down about 9% on Thursday, reversing part of a 25% rally on Wednesday, while Nebius is down about 16%. IREN fell 6.6%.

Nvidia’s board has also appointed Harvey Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993.

Huang is the single largest personal shareholder at Nvidia, but he owns only about 3.5% of the company’s shares. And, unlike most of Silicon Valley’s tech giants that were founded far later, he does not hld supervoting rights. That means that the board had the power to vote him out at any time

“Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the company said in a statement.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nine-k.title: Nine Korean startups vie for a spot in Disrupt 2027’s Startup Battlefield 200 competition
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nine-k.author: Kate Park
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nine-k.text:
TechCrunch’s yearly Startup Battlefield 200 competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the Disrupt conference.

This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at DETO 2026, a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200.

The startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine startups are looking to enter the U.S. market as part of the broader international expansion plans.

Voinosis, which develops AI to detect changes in brain health through voice analysis, won the competition. The other eight startups are listed below in alphabetical order.

Voinosis is developing an AI tool that analyzes speech patterns such as pitch, pauses, rhythm and response times to detect changes linked to brain health. Each voice check takes less than five minutes.

The company says its technology has been tested in Greek, Japanese and English, and its product doesn’t require separate training for each language. In a clinical study involving 146 participants, the startup claims its tech achieved 88% accuracy in screening for potential cognitive issues.

Voinosis targets hospitals, senior living facilities, insurers and individual consumers. It also plans to link voice checks with cognitive training, assessments, and treatment provided by healthcare professionals.

The startup was founded by Grace Shin, who spent more than 25 years as an otologic surgeon. The startup is currently raising a Series A round and has already secured a South Korean pharmaceutical company as a strategic investor.

Awesome Lab, based in Seoul, makes ThermoFlux, a heating system that uses water electrolysis and ionization to generate heat. The system can manage heat production for buildings, water supply, and industrial processes. The company says its technology can reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions.

For its international expansion, Awesome Lab is taking a different approach in each market. In the U.S., it plans to supply core OEM modules, and work with boiler, water heater and HVAC companies on product development.

Crosshub helps travelers and international visitors verify their identities and set up payment methods abroad. Its platform, IDBlock, combines identity verification and payment services using Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) and zero-knowledge proof.

The company says its platform helps users prove their identity across borders without sharing unnecessary personal information. Crosshub is also integrating this technology with payment systems to improve access to financial services for travelers.

DeepFusion AI has developed a 4D radar-based imaging system with additional sensors for autonomous mobility, robotaxi, maritime surveillance, and defense applications. The system combines RF sensors with radar and lidar to detect objects, movement, or distance without a direct line of sight. All sensors are supposedly packed into a single, customizable unit.

EFLOW develops special motors that can produce more torque, or rotational force, while taking up less space for use in robots, drones, satellites, and other mobility applications. The startup also develops actuators that control how robotic joints move.

Otition Medical makes two medical devices: one specializes in measuring body temperature, while another can capture ear canal images and analyze the eardrum. The company says its AI was trained on about 55,000 images of eardrums, and the device has received medical certification in South Korea.

Riibotics says it can deploy robots into warehouses within a day. Riibotics wants to reduce deployment costs for warehouses by streamlining setup, which includes infrastructure setup, warehouse mapping, system integration through custom middleware, task programming, and safety checks.

Ternell, a semiconductor startup based in Ulsan, is developing a new type of memory to help AI chips use less power.

Unlike conventional two-state memory, Ternell’s T-SRAM system adds a third state for more efficient data storage. Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips showed a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional SRAM.

Testbank is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions.

The startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. Solve lets you write answers directly on the page and be graded automatically.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/11/who-co.title: Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/11/who-co.author: Connie Loizos
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/11/who-co.text:
It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30%. Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear whom he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour.

Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates:

Lisa Su. The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival, as well as a distant cousin of Huang. The Information floated her name this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office.

Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances. It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason.

Lip-Bu Tan. Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch.

Bret Taylor. The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his resume includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too.

Ian Buck. If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot. He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with.

Someone else down the hall. Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree.

The wild card? Lori Huang. Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a micro chip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts.
