https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/nodejs.title: Node.js Fixes 16 Flaws, Including HTTP/2 Bugs That Crash Servers and Leak Other Connections' Data
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/nodejs.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/nodejs.text:
A flaw fixed in Node.js this week lets unauthenticated clients crash servers that use the runtime's built-in HTTP/2 support on the 24.x and 26.x release lines. A second HTTP/2 flaw can cause a server to send a client pieces of its memory, including responses intended for other connections.

Fixed versions were released for all three supported lines: 22.23.5, 24.22.3, and 26.13.1.

The crash flaw, CVE-2026-123863, needs only a default HTTP/2 server that replies before the request body has fully arrived. The Node.js project calls that behavior typical. The crash works over both TLS and cleartext connections.

The memory flaw, CVE-2026-123866, affects all three lines. From 24.22.0 and 26.9.0 onward, a client alone can trigger it. On 22.x and older 24.x and 26.x builds, it can still be triggered when the server itself closes a stream partway through a response, for example after an idle timeout.

A separate flaw in Node.js HTTPS servers, CVE-2026-123864, can allow an unauthenticated client to read memory from other connections, "including TLS private keys and other users' requests," the project says. It affects all three supported lines.

The flaw needs a handler that calls res.flushHeaders() before the request body has fully arrived and later calls res.end() with data. Reading the leaked memory also needs a route that sends back or stores a request body. Plain HTTP servers built with node:http are not affected.

The release fixes 16 vulnerabilities in Node.js itself, seven of them rated high. The other four high-rated flaws, and the servers they affect, are:

The eight flaws above are all in Node.js's own HTTP/2, HTTPS and TLS server code, so they matter where a Node.js process accepts those connections itself.

Updating to the fixed version for each line is the only fix in the project's security advisory. It lists no workaround for servers that cannot update yet.

End-of-life lines, including 20.x and 25.x, get no fix in this release, and the project says such versions are always affected.

The advisory does not report any attacks using the flaws. It also does not say whether servers that met the conditions for the HTTPS flaw should replace their TLS keys or other secrets after updating.

Five of the flaws, including CVE-2026-123863 and CVE-2026-123864, were reported by Chris Rohlf in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research, according to the advisory.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/4837-h.title: Attacker Used 4,837 Hijacked GitHub Accounts to Run a CI Secret Stealer in 1,806+ Repositories
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/4837-h.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/4837-h.text:
Starting Tuesday, an attacker used stolen credentials for 4,837 GitHub accounts to plant a secret stealer in repositories those accounts could write to, according to Aikido Security, a security software company.

The stealer is built to take the secrets and cloud credentials that a repository's CI workflows can reach. It ran in at least 1,806 repositories, where the attacker has likely collected those credentials, the company says.

Each attack started with a pull request titled docs: dependency audit notes, opened from a branch named wfx-docs to test whether the account could write to the repository. These test pull requests were opened in 61,764 repositories, and the stealer followed in some of them.

In a separate analysis, researchers at SafeDep, which sells software supply chain security tools, counted 8,093 repositories that received malicious commits between 12:46 UTC on Tuesday and 04:36 UTC today. That count covers every repository that received malicious commits, not only those where the stealer ran. Their search covered only the default branches of public repositories, so the true total is higher, the researchers say.

In 7,309 of those repositories, the stealer was added to an existing workflow. In 771, it came as an npm postinstall hook, which also runs on a developer's machine during npm install.

After pushing the stealer, the attacker usually reverted the change within minutes. Where the stealer ran, its logs were deleted, usually along with the run itself. In those repositories, every secret and cloud role available to the workflows should be treated as compromised.

More pull requests with the same title were opened early today, after the company's own GitHub search ended on Wednesday, a check by The Hacker News found. Three that were checked, opened between 05:04 and 05:38 UTC, came from wfx-docs branches. It is not clear whether the stealer followed.

Any account that opened one of the attacker's test pull requests is compromised, even if the stealer never ran, Aikido said in its technical analysis. The analysis does not explain how the attacker obtained the credentials.

SafeDep's researchers advise owners of affected repositories to revoke the commit author's tokens, OAuth app grants, SSH keys, and sessions, and to turn on 2FA. Owners should also rotate every secret and variable the repository can read. Anyone who ran npm install on an affected commit should treat that machine as compromised and rotate its keys.

In most other repositories that received a test, nothing was pushed afterward, or the stealer did not run due to the repository's settings or the account's permissions. The figures cover only the public repositories the company could see.

The tests also reached repositories that the compromised accounts did not own. Of the test pull requests, 10,431 were submitted via collaborator or organization access, and 92% of those were still open when the company checked.

Check for these signs, from Tuesday onward, in any repository you can write to:

A repository can show no wfx-loot artifacts, wfx- cache entries, or WFX-BEGIN step summaries and still have lost data. A missing run number on the attacker's commit is the more reliable sign that the stealer ran.

The stealer sends data by HTTP POST to the addresses above or to a Telegram chat, the SafeDep researchers found. In a sample of 200 payload commits, about a fifth used Telegram only.

The stealer is built to collect credentials from every source on the runner, according to the company. They include GitHub Actions secrets and variables, the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, keys for AI services, and secrets in the memory of the runner's own processes. It reads credential files for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, SSH, and other tools from their usual locations.

It also copies the repository, its last 100 commits, and recent workflow artifacts. On self-hosted runners, it takes cloud credentials from instance metadata as well as Docker container state and systemd units.

The stealer also has settings for private repositories, and the company says that suggests it may be running in them.

The stealer is designed to use those credentials to reach deeper into cloud accounts. It exchanges GitHub OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, and on AWS it can create long-lived access keys for IAM users.

Some of its steps are built to survive credential rotation. It can rewrite an AWS role's trust policy to open the role to any AWS account.

It can also add federated identity credentials with the prefix wfx-ci- to Azure AD applications. Workflows in the compromised repository can then sign in to Azure without a stored secret, even after all tokens are rotated.

To find these backdoors, the researchers suggest checking for:

The stealer reached at least one Packagist package and one Go module through automated publishing triggers. At least 50 of the compromised users appear to publish packages for npm, Go, Packagist, PyPI, or crates.

The attacker appears to be after CI secrets rather than trying to spread through packages, the company says.

Version 3.14.3 of the Packagist package digitalelvis/neuronai-studio is malicious, and the company advises treating any machine that installed or opened it as compromised. Its package listing shows the version was published on Wednesday. Early today, the version was still listed, under a notice that versions of the package had been flagged as malware.

A normal composer install does not run the stealer, but running npm install inside the package's vendor directory does, the researchers found. Users should block v3.14.3 and pin v3.14.2 or earlier.

Two versions of the Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env, v1.0.278 and v1.0.280, carry the stealer only in a GitHub Actions workflow file. The Go code and release binaries are unchanged, and Go builds never run workflow files, so users of the module may not have been affected. The company still recommends removing those versions.

The researchers also found the stealer in another Go module, github.com/vkuznet/gocurl, in pseudo-version v0.0.0-20261111095532-8d5aad0cb0da, inside a workflow that has never run. Users should block that pseudo-version.

The stealer also reached 28 WebdriverIO repositories through commits authored as the bot account wdio-bot. No package release was affected, but the bot's token should be treated as stolen.

The company found that the accounts used this week overlap with those hit in GhostAction's October wave, in which stolen GitHub accounts pushed secret-stealing workflows into repositories.

Accounts hit in October were about 1,000 times more likely than other active accounts to be used this week. In more than 100 repositories, the new stealer was added to October's workflow files, leaving the older step that sends data out in place.

Aikido said, "we don't attribute November to the same actor at this stage," because the infrastructure, tools, and methods differ, and stolen credentials often end up with several attackers.

Correction (November 12, 2026): An earlier version of this article said the stealer sent data only by HTTP POST to two addresses and that the attacker reverted each change within a minute. A second analysis found a third server, a Telegram channel, and changes left in place for longer.

The stealer is built to take the secrets and cloud credentials that a repository's CI workflows can reach. The company still recommends removing those versions.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.text:
A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in version 2.4.71, released yesterday.

Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected, according to Red Hat, which ships the server as part of Red Hat Enterprise Linux.

An attacker who can reach the server needs no authentication to exploit the flaw and could take full control of the server process, the Linux vendor says. It rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.

The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported.

HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host.

Standalone builds of the module, released on GitHub as mod_h2, are affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.

Admins who run the Apache HTTP Server project's own releases should move to version 2.4.71, the fixed release named in its security advisory. That release also fixes a crash in mod_md, rated important, and a one-byte overwrite of stack memory in mod_vhost_alias, rated low.

The distributions in the table below ship their own builds of the server, with their own package version numbers. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, for example, the fix ships as mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1.

Red Hat shipped fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 yesterday and rates the flaw Important on those releases rather than Critical. Their mod_http2 packages give each HTTP/2 stream its own memory allocator, which makes an attack much harder, according to the vendor's severity assessment. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier do not contain the vulnerable code.

The Debian rows come from Debian's security tracker, and the Amazon row from the Amazon Linux tracker. Ubuntu's CVE tracker had no page for the flaw when The Hacker News checked it today.

The Apache HTTP Server advisory offers no workaround. In its vulnerability analysis, Wiz advises admins who cannot update yet to remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving Protocols http/1.1.

The standalone mod_h2 project has published no fixed release so far. Its release list on GitHub ends at 2.0.42, the last affected version, and its repository has been read-only since it was archived on June 9. The Protocols change above also applies to servers that use those builds.

The flaw was reported on October 26 by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, a free scanning service for open-source projects that uses the company's AI models. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it last week.

An earlier HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-23918, was fixed in version 2.4.67, released on May 4. Servers updated to that release, or to any later one up to 2.4.70, still run a version that the new flaw affects.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/screen.title: ScreenConnect Attacks Target at Least 288 Endpoints Across 48 Organizations With Rogue Clients
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/screen.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/screen.text:
ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments following reports of unauthorized access.

In an advisory posted on its site, the company said there is no evidence that the incident involves a compromise of its infrastructure or a vulnerability in the ScreenConnect software.

"Our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," it said. "We are continuing to validate this assessment. The initial access method and full scope remain under investigation."

ConnectWise has identified about 400 partner environments with at least one of the third-party extensions installed. It also emphasized that the presence of the extensions alone does not indicate or establish compromise.

While these extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands, access to that API is secured by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup, it added. The list of extensions identified for precautionary disabling is below -

ConnectWise also said it has urged on-premises partners to disable the extensions, and is recommending all partners to ensure security controls are running, preserve suspicious activity logs, and stay vigilant for -

The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) -

Cybersecurity company Huntress, which is also tracking the activity, said it has observed attackers using access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push Run commands with an aim to install rogue ScreenConnect clients on at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations. The activity was first detected on November 11, 2026, at around 5:47 p.m. UTC.

Huntress told The Hacker News that it has not seen evidence of a new vulnerability, but noted the exact method through which the attacker got panel access remains unclear. Current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions to gain initial access, it said.

The overall attack unfolds in a worm-like fashion using a two-step process -

"The rogue clients deliver SCKit, a custom malicious toolkit that establishes persistent remote access and creates a relay trap for intercepting session cookies," Huntress researchers Ben Nahorney and Susannah Matt said.

"The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads."

SCKit is delivered as an encrypted payload and via a Base64-encoded dropper ("sckit-run.bat"), which then contacts a remote server to fetch a PowerShell payload ("sckit-decoder.ps1") that's responsible for launching the toolkit.

Other components of the malware are designed to add Microsoft Defender exclusions, install a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client, create a scheduled task named "TrapWatch," and replace the legitimate ScreenConnect installation with an attacker-controlled copy.

There are signs that at least one of the scripts is generated by a large language model (LLM) based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain its functionality.

"Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel," Huntress said. "This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints."

This involves abusing the connection to fetch a dropper ("Run-Lateral-Full.bat"), which then connects to an external server ("ns.mo7sen[.]dev") to download a loader that gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to the attacker, and returns a tailored encrypted kit for that specific workstation -

"A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item," Huntress said. "This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item."

To add to the concern, the threat actor has been observed tagging each compromised managed service provider (MSP) with a sequential number. Huntress said the tags it has observed start partway through the sequence, indicating other MSPs may have been compromised earlier. ScreenConnect users are advised to check their Run Command history even if they haven't received alerts.

In a separate alert, Sophos said it has also observed unauthorized ScreenConnect client deployments following the same modus operandi. The activity has originated from three ScreenConnect instance IDs -

It's suspected that these are compromised instances that are being used to execute commands and deploy additional malicious instances, whose IDs are below -

"Curl.exe downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185.99.255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi," Sophos explained. "A ScreenConnect-generated command file then launched msiexec.exe to install the client silently. The researchers also observed ScreenConnect scripts staging batch files and using PowerShell with execution-policy bypass to retrieve a second-stage script from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4."

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/antifo.title: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/antifo.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/antifo.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox has been used to steal Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials and pivot laterally into compromised environments.

"In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The activity has been observed chaining together web exploitation and web shell deployment to facilitate configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations.

AntiFox, available for download from GitHub, has been described as an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven autonomous penetration testing platform that's built atop the "solid foundation" of ARTEX. As of writing, the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times.

On its README page, the project maintainer states -

Given an authorized target, a planner / worker / main-agent multi-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core (a global asset graph + a per-task exploration graph) — recon → attack-surface discovery → exploitation → finding capture → report delivery — fully observable, interactive, and deliverable

Unlike most automated pentest tools that are "great at discovery, but stop at discovery," AntiFox puts its weight on delivery — turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand straight to the client.

According to Arctic Wolf, some of the initial access activity is associated with a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) application. The access is then leveraged to create an ASPX web shell using "w3wp.exe," the IIS worker process, and run operating system commands to perform the following actions -

"On a compromised IIS server, commands run through w3wp.exe identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested the ability to write files into the web root," Arctic Wolf said.

"The creation of an ASPX web shell by w3wp.exe, followed by command execution through the same IIS worker process, suggests compromise through the affected web application."

The precise vulnerability used to achieve code execution on the IIS server is not known. In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means.

Specifically, this involved abusing valid IAM identities to validate credentials and enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock.

While a majority of these authenticated cross-service API requests ended up with an "AccessDenied" error, some of the discovery and secret-access operations were successful, according to the cybersecurity company.

In at least some instances, the activity has been observed progressing beyond Secrets Manager enumeration to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations via API calls.

"Agentic frameworks such as these make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors, while increasing the speed and consistency with which these techniques can be applied in live attacks," Arctic Wolf said.

The disclosure comes as threat actors are increasingly weaponizing AI-powered penetration testing tools like ARTEX to conduct broad-scale attacks across the world, enabling them to automate various stages of an intrusion with minimal human intervention.

The integration of AI has allowed adversaries, both large and small, to adapt established tradecraft and deploy them at machine speed, making it possible to progress from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Earlier this week, VECERT disclosed details of a campaign dubbed Operation Ghost-Campus that uses AI agents to maintain perpetual, cost-free access to large language models (LLMs) and eventually perform automated academic fraud and steal data belonging to over 5,000 students enrolled at the Fengxian Campus. The campaign has been attributed to a Chinese threat actor.

"The agent industrializes the creation of accounts on the search engine fofa.info, scans the global cyberspace for misconfigured servers, extracts API keys for OpenAI and DeepSeek, automatically verifies their financial balances, and injects them into the attacker's development environment," VECERT said.

"This stolen computing power fuels an interactive GoTTY terminal ('Pi — AI Coding Assistant') and, by extension, provides intelligence to the scripts that sustain academic fraud bots ('heartbeat' bots) and extractors of financial data and personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to thousands of students at the Fengxian Campus."

According to data from Censys, there are 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, with most of them located in the U.S., Hong Kong, China, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea. However, it's worth noting that not every instance is necessarily malicious in nature.

In a separate report, Check Point Research said it identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases.

"In many observed cases, ARTEX required remarkably little interaction from its operators once an objective had been established," Check Point said. "Rather than continuously directing attacks step by step, operators frequently issued a goal and left the agent fleet to work toward it. Human interactions were largely limited to checking progress, asking whether a target had been compromised or occasionally adjusting priorities."

The vast majority of the attacks are designed to siphon cryptocurrency, steal Apple code-signing certificates, compromise gaming accounts, and conduct denial-of-service (DoS) attacks against gambling websites. The activity has been found to exploit vulnerabilities related to weak or hard-coded passwords, missing authentication, insecure direct object references, and remote code execution.

In the campaign targeting Apple code-signing certificates, ARTEX agents searched compromised systems for certificate databases, followed by validating the stolen certificates by checking passwords, private keys, Apple revocation status, expiration dates, and associated provisioning profiles.

Ultimately, the activity is estimated to have harvested more than 300 certificates and their passwords, out of which three certificates passed the full validation process and could be used to sign arbitrary iOS applications.

The biggest change brought by agentic hacking to the cyber threat landscape is scale and speed, Check Point cautioned, as a cybercriminal with limited technical skills can task AI agents with investigating a number of targets in parallel and exploiting them using known and zero-day vulnerabilities with less manual effort.

"Its relevance to us lies in its scale, speed and persistence," CERT-EU said in an alert. "ARTEX can test large numbers of low-complexity misconfigurations, including those a human tester would notice but not have time to check, and it can work through long attack chains without the fatigue that limits manual testing."

"The same is true of complex payload crafting. Exploitation paths that need carefully tailored payloads often take more effort than the severity of the finding justifies, so a manual assessment may leave them untested."

Tools like AntiFox and ARTEX are part of a broader set of about 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks that are engineered to connect to an LLM and can act on outputs autonomously. They fall under five broad categories -

"Each framework has public source code and wires a model into a loop that runs tools and acts on their output," GitGuardian said.

"Agentic AI pentesting tools hand their agent a shell and web access, so the model can assemble a pipeline at runtime. A GitHub search, a scanner download, and a found key passed to the next call are all one prompt away, even though none of it ships in the repository."

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.title: Hackers Target Qlik Sense Servers With Reverse Shells, Stage ActiveMQ and Veeam Exploits
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.text:
Threat actors have been observed targeting Qlik Sense servers to unsuccessfully deliver PowerShell reverse shell commands against multiple environments in October 2026.

Cynet's CyOps and Research teams said they identified the suspicious activity in October 2026 against several E.U.-based customers within a narrow window of just over three minutes.

The activity has been found to share some level of overlap with a November 2023 campaign documented by Arctic Wolf in which threat actors linked to the CACTUS ransomware operation likely weaponized then-newly-disclosed flaws in Qlik Sense to obtain initial access to target environments.

The vulnerabilities in question, which were patched by Qlik Sense in August and September 2023, impact Qlik Sense Enterprise for Windows -

It's worth noting that CVE-2023-48365 (aka DoubleQlik) is an incomplete fix for CVE-2023-41265.

In November 2023 CACTUS ransomware campaign, threat actors were observed exploiting the flaws to establish a foothold and download additional payloads to establish persistence and remote control by deploying ManageEngine Unified Endpoint Management and Security (UEMS), AnyDesk, and Plink.

The latest activity detected by Cynet involves the use of a PowerShell command containing a one-line reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23" on port 4455. The exact vulnerability exploited to break into Qlik Sense servers is currently not known.

"The command was executed under scheduler.exe, resembling the 2023 Cactus Qlik intrusions," the cybersecurity company said.

Although attempts to spawn the reverse shell were blocked, Cynet's testing of the reverse shell in a controlled environment has revealed that the interactive communication channel is used to conduct reconnaissance and deliver a PowerShell script for enabling persistence.

This is achieved by means of a Windows Go reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23:4456." The backdoor is then used to look for actively running processes related to Apache ActiveMQ. On Linux, the malware also attempts to collect system information and read "/etc/shadow" and "/etc/passwd" files.

A second variant of the PowerShell script attempts to install OpenSSH and creates a scheduled task named "WinUpdCheck" that launches a PowerShell reverse shell written to "C:\ProgramData\ssh\winc.ps1" at five-minute intervals.

"If sshd remained unavailable, it downloaded OpenSSH-Win64.zip from the staging server, extracted it, and ran install-sshd.ps1," Cynet said. "It set sshd to automatic startup, started the service, and added an inbound firewall rule for TCP 22. The archive was a legitimate OpenSSH package reused by the operator."

Further analysis of the infrastructure has uncovered an exposed directory ("45.115.26[.]23:8012") consisting of a custom Go backdoor for Windows, SSH persistence scripts, an ActiveMQ exploit for CVE-2023-46604, and a modified public Veeam toolchain for CVE-2024-40711, indicating the threat actor is possibly laying the groundwork for broader attacks.

https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks.title: Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer
https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks.author: Alexander Culafi
https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks.text:
When hand-typed commands failed to breach a US retailer, the attacker turned to AI-generated scripts, achieving lateral movement in minutes.

A threat actor deployed an AI model during a stalled cyberattack and rescued the campaign, achieving lateral movement in the process.

The attack, detailed today by Symantec, targeted an unnamed US retail organization in September. The threat actor's hand-typed commands were repeatedly blocked, so the attacker switched to what appeared to be AI-generated commands and rapidly broke through the retailer's defenses. The attacker ultimately harvested credentials and achieved lateral movement within minutes.

Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard. That said, the timing was such that investigators believe this activity was "more consistent with an operator relaying output to an AI tool than with an autonomous agent."

The security firm said this incident is one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks Symantec has investigated since May, though it added that activity was heavily concentrated around September.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Threat actors have utilized large language models (LLMs) in their attacks as long as the technology has been widely available. Early applications involved generating convincing phishing lures or conducting basic data reconnaissance, but recent evidence shows attackers deploying AI to execute end-to-end attacks, assist with malware development, and more. More recently, attackers have abused — and continue to abuse — agentic penetration testing tools to break into target environments at machine speed.

In this attack specifically, Symantec said it did not identify the initial access vector, focusing more on the timeline it was able to glean from its post-incident investigation. According to the blog post, the attacker worked at first by hand, which investigators determined due to artifacts like typing errors.

When every staged payload was terminated by security software, indicators suggest attacker tactics changed when they tried again the next day. "For almost two hours," Symantec said, "the attackers submitted long, error-free PowerShell scripts with labelled output sections and, in places, comments that read as a model's reasoning." Approximately 10 minutes after querying the victim's SolarWinds Orion monitoring software, attackers managed to laterally move to a second server.

The blog post hypothesizes that the attackers behind the attack were likely financially motivated, as they searched point-of-sale scripts for passwords, and one address they contacted was linked to an operation that stole card data from online retailers.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

During the second-stage activity, the threat actor gained initial access to a Web server and stole credentials from configuration files tied to the SolarWinds Orion monitoring software. And while the idea of AI speeding up or improving attacker tradecraft is nothing new, the attack is its deployment of AI to a hands-on keyboard attack in progress and possibly seizing victory out of an apparent defeat. It presents LLMs as a difference-maker for a less skilled threat actor.

Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading this incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. While he calls this a game-changer for attackers, "defenders can potentially leverage that pattern" as AI behaves in a particular kind of way, such as testing variants of a technique in quick succession.

"The retry pattern is a signal itself," he says. "Blocking on behavior rather than file names or exact commands matters much more. Treating a blocked attempt followed by a variant as a high-priority alert is worth considering."

Although no vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required, O'Brien believes this trend of AI accelerating attacks is and will continue to affect the patching race. "Our view is that defenders need to start looking at mean time to mitigate rather than mean time to patch. Patching is still important, but it can’t be the only countermeasure."

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to new research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

The study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). Women with greater concentrations of these substances in their blood were more likely to develop this type of cancer. However, researchers found no clear link between either chemical and breast cancer risk overall.

Both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS. These chemicals have been used in numerous everyday consumer products and are often described as "forever chemicals" because they resist breaking down in the environment. They can also accumulate in the human body and remain there for years.

"Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health," said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. "This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump's leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health."

Why This Aggressive Breast Cancer Is Concerning

ER-negative breast cancer differs from more common forms of the disease because its tumor cells lack the receptors that allow estrogen to stimulate cancer growth. These cancers are often more aggressive and generally have poorer outcomes than tumors that respond to estrogen.

Despite their severity, researchers still have relatively little information about what makes someone more likely to develop ER-negative breast cancer. The new findings suggest that exposure to certain persistent environmental chemicals could be one contributing factor.

"Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors," explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study.

The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

Higher Forever Chemical Levels Linked to Greater Cancer Risk

To investigate the possible connection, NIH scientists and their collaborators examined blood samples that had been collected years before participants received a cancer diagnosis. The researchers measured concentrations of 17 different PFAS chemicals, allowing them to compare earlier exposure levels with subsequent breast cancer outcomes.

The results revealed substantial differences for two chemicals. Women in the highest PFOA exposure group had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than women in the lowest group. The association was even stronger for PFOS, with the highest exposure group showing a 93% higher rate, nearly twice that of the lowest group.

These percentages represent relative differences between groups rather than the absolute probability that an individual woman will develop breast cancer. The findings also establish an association, not proof that the chemicals directly cause the disease.

The analysis used data from the Sister Study, a major research project conducted by NIH's National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). Between 2003 and 2009, the study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35-74 from across the United States and Puerto Rico.

All participants were free of breast cancer when they enrolled, although each had a full or half-sister who had already been diagnosed with the disease. For the PFAS investigation, researchers analyzed information from 1,609 women who subsequently developed breast cancer and a comparison group of 2,269 women.

Could Reducing PFAS Exposure Lower Cancer Risk?

Although PFAS can remain in the environment and the body for long periods, researchers emphasize that exposure is not necessarily unavoidable. The findings could eventually help identify new ways to reduce the risk of aggressive breast cancer.

"These findings matter for women's health broadly," said first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., who previously worked as an NIH research fellow and is now a researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. "Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open new avenues for prevention."

The researchers are also interested in understanding how these chemicals might influence cancer development. Because the strongest associations appeared in tumors that lack estrogen receptors, the findings suggest that PFAS could act through biological processes unrelated to hormonal signaling.

Potential explanations include changes in gene activity or alterations in the immune system. However, the study did not directly investigate these mechanisms, so their involvement remains uncertain.

Newer Forever Chemicals Raise Unanswered Questions

Although PFOA and PFOS have largely been phased out and replaced with other PFAS compounds, measurable amounts of both substances are still present in most people's bodies. Their persistence means that exposure to these older chemicals remains a potential public health concern.

The researchers say additional investigations should focus on populations with greater PFAS exposure, as well as groups that experience higher rates of ER-negative breast cancer. Such research could help clarify the strength of the observed associations and identify whether certain populations face greater risks.

Scientists also need to determine whether the newer chemicals introduced as replacements for PFOA and PFOS carry similar health concerns.

"More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals," White said.

The findings add to growing questions about the long-term health effects of forever chemicals and highlight the importance of understanding how environmental exposures may contribute to aggressive forms of breast cancer.

The research received support from NIEHS grants Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: Study found link between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative breast cancer and two chemicals. Women with higher blood levels of these chemicals may face an increased risk of developing this type of cancer.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises important questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

"Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," said Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals."

Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy

Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish new tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," said Cole.

A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal

The next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

The study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

The researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

This observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

Unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

However, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.

How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free

To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

They used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.

The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

Although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

In this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.

When fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.

This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.

A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread

The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

Approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.

Their experiments showed that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," said Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.

Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?

Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

Cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

"We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," said Aird.

Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

The research opens a new avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward new strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: Fructose appears to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production. Researchers say it could also help other cancers spread. The discovery raises questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating new bone formation.

The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of new bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

"What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," said Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

More conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

"The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, showed no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter

The results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming new bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

This is especially important for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a new activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

The findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Earth may have created a substantial amount of its own water as the planet was forming, rather than relying entirely on comets, meteorites, or other objects to deliver it from space. New research published in Nature Geoscience suggests that chemical reactions between rocky pebbles and the hydrogen-rich atmosphere of the young Earth could have produced enormous quantities of water.

The discovery offers a new explanation for how our planet acquired one of the most important ingredients for life. It also raises the possibility that other rocky planets throughout the universe could generate water through similar processes, potentially making habitable worlds more common than previously thought.

Researchers at The University of New Mexico investigated this possibility by recreating some of the extreme conditions that existed during Earth's formation. The study was led by graduate student Susmita Garai, along with Zachary Sharp, professor and director of Earth and Planetary Sciences, and Peter Olson. Their experiments examined what happens when rocks containing iron react with hydrogen at extremely high temperatures.

"Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites. Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism," explained Sharp. "In order to evaluate the possibility of 'pebble' rain' being a source of water, we needed to construct and execute some very challenging high-temperature experiments. Dr. Garai's efforts paid off mightily, as she found that water is produced in just minutes in the high temperature environment of the Early Earth's atmosphere."

A New Explanation for the Origin of Earth's Water

For decades, scientists have debated where Earth's water originally came from. One prominent theory suggests that much of it was transported to the developing planet by icy material originating in the colder, more distant regions of the early solar system.

According to this explanation, water-rich objects, including small icy pebbles, traveled inward and eventually contributed to Earth's water supply. However, researchers have struggled to fully explain how enough of this material could have reached our planet from such great distances. There are also unresolved questions about whether this delivery process accounts for Earth's chemical composition.

The new study investigates a different route by which water could have appeared. Instead of arriving already contained in ice or other materials, water may have been produced directly through reactions involving the rocky ingredients that built Earth and the gases surrounding it.

During the planet's earliest stages, countless small pieces of rock gradually came together to form a larger body. Scientists refer to this growth process as pebble accretion. As Earth gained mass, it could have accumulated a dense atmosphere containing large amounts of hydrogen, with temperatures and pressures far higher than those found on the planet today.

Under those conditions, rocky pebbles falling through the atmosphere could have triggered a remarkable chemical reaction. Hydrogen in the surrounding gas would react with iron oxide inside the silicate rocks, transforming the iron oxide into metallic iron while releasing water vapor.

Experiments Reveal Water Can Form in Minutes

To determine whether this process could actually occur, the researchers exposed samples of silicate rock to temperatures ranging from 1,200 to 1,400 degrees Celsius. They conducted experiments using flowing hydrogen gas and repeated the tests with helium to provide a comparison. Each experiment ran for between 15 minutes and three hours.

The results provided strong evidence that the proposed reaction works under these extreme conditions. When the rocks were heated in hydrogen, almost 80% of their iron oxide was transformed into metallic iron, with water vapor produced during the reaction.

In contrast, the researchers did not observe the same reaction when helium was used instead of hydrogen. This difference confirmed that hydrogen played a crucial role in generating the water.

The speed and scale of the reaction were especially striking. Although the scientists had expected some water to form, the results suggested that the process could have been far more productive than anticipated. When they extended their experimental findings to conditions on the early Earth, their calculations indicated that the mechanism might have generated hundreds of oceans' worth of water.

"We had suspected and hoped that we would produce iron metal and water in our reduction experiments, but we really had no way of knowing how fast and how much. We were quite surprised to find that extrapolation of our work suggests that hundreds of oceans' worth of water were likely produced in this way. Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 ½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have," said Sharp.

Earth's Fiery Beginnings May Have Helped Create Its Oceans

These findings suggest that the conditions of Earth's formation may have actively contributed to its water supply. Rather than being entirely dependent on water delivered from elsewhere in the solar system, the growing planet may have possessed the ingredients needed to manufacture water through its own chemical reactions.

The implications extend well beyond Earth. If rocky planets around other stars develop similarly hot, hydrogen-rich atmospheres during their formation, they might also produce substantial amounts of water as rocky material accumulates.

This possibility could have important consequences for understanding how common water is across the universe. A process that naturally occurs during the formation of Earth-sized planets would mean that obtaining water might not require the right icy objects to arrive from distant regions of a planetary system.

Could Other Earth-Like Planets Make Their Own Water?

The research also adds to growing interest in pebble accretion as an explanation for how planets form. Although the concept has gained attention relatively recently, it has already helped scientists address several longstanding questions about planetary development.

"The idea of pebble accretion is still relatively new. It's only been around for the last decade. But it seems to solve many problems that exist with the existing paradigm for planet formation," Sharp said. "And now we see that it also can explain why our planet is habitable. By extension, it is reasonable to expect that other Earth-sized bodies circling other stars would also have water and possibly life."

There are still important uncertainties to resolve. While the experiments show that rocky material can generate water when exposed to hydrogen under conditions resembling those of the early Earth, they do not establish how much of our planet's present water supply was actually produced this way. Additional research will be needed to determine the contribution of this mechanism compared with water delivered by comets, meteorites, and other sources.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important process that may have shaped Earth billions of years ago. They also suggest that the ability to produce water could be built into the formation of rocky planets themselves, opening new possibilities for understanding where water, and perhaps life, might exist beyond our solar system.

They found that water was produced in just minutes in the high temperature environment of the early Earth's atmosphere. The discovery offers a new explanation for how our planet acquired one of the most important ingredients for life.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.

Developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, the simulation, called Lumina, recreates the evolution of the early universe across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide. It follows 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how galaxies formed, how radiation spread through space, and how the universe gradually became transparent to light.

The research, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), provides an unusually detailed picture of events that unfolded billions of years before our solar system existed.

How the Universe Entered Its Cosmic Dark Age

The story begins with the Big Bang, when the universe existed in an extremely hot, dense state filled with electrons and other subatomic particles. This primordial plasma, described as initially smaller than a single atom, expanded rapidly and cooled as the universe grew.

Eventually, particles slowed enough for electrons to combine with atomic nuclei, producing electrically neutral hydrogen. Around 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe entered a period known as the cosmic "dark age."

Although the universe had become transparent to much of the radiation left over from the Big Bang, stars had not yet formed to illuminate the cosmos. Neutral hydrogen filled space and could absorb certain types of radiation, including the ultraviolet light that would later emerge from the first stars.

Lumina allows researchers to investigate how this early environment evolved, eventually giving rise to the galaxies, stars, and other structures that helped bring the dark age to an end.

How the First Stars and Black Holes Transformed the Universe

The simulation covers an immense region measuring 500 megaparsecs, equivalent to approximately 1.6 billion light-years. Within that volume, Lumina follows dark matter, gas, stars, and radiation (such as photons), capturing both the behavior of matter across enormous distances and the formation of individual galaxies.

One of its most important achievements is recreating two major changes in the early universe: hydrogen re-ionization and helium re-ionization.

Hydrogen re-ionization began as the first stars and galaxies produced increasing amounts of ultraviolet radiation. This energetic light removed electrons from neutral hydrogen atoms, a process called "re-ionizing" the gas. As more hydrogen became ionized, the universe became increasingly transparent to ultraviolet light, allowing radiation to travel across much greater distances.

This transformation helped clear the widespread neutral hydrogen that had dominated the early cosmos. Lumina reproduces the process in remarkable detail, showing how radiation from the first generations of stars gradually changed the conditions throughout space.

The simulation also follows helium re-ionization, which requires substantially more energetic radiation to strip electrons from helium.

The results point to different sources driving these two transformations. Early stars and galaxies appear to have been primarily responsible for ionizing hydrogen, while actively feeding supermassive black holes supplied the intense radiation needed to ionize helium.

This is the first simulation to capture both processes together, offering a more complete view of how the early universe changed.

"Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale reionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations," says study author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT.

The researchers are making Lumina available to other scientists, allowing its predictions about early cosmic structures to be compared with observations from existing and future telescopes. Such comparisons could help researchers better understand the events that shaped the first galaxies and stars.

Building a Virtual Universe With Half a Trillion Elements

Lumina gets its name from the Latin word meaning "lights." Its underlying technology builds on IllustrisTNG, an earlier simulation developed by scientists at MIT and other institutions, including members of the Lumina research team.

IllustrisTNG models how galaxies form and evolve by following the interactions of dark matter, gas, and other physical processes from the Big Bang to the present day.

To create Lumina, researchers upgraded the existing software so it could reproduce galaxy formation in comparable detail across a much larger region of space. They also incorporated a radiation transport model that calculates how light, including ultraviolet radiation, travels through the universe and interacts with surrounding matter.

Together, these improvements allow the simulation to track both the formation of galaxies and the enormous changes that radiation produces across cosmic distances.

The resulting model contains approximately half a trillion individual elements, including particles of dark matter and cells representing gas. It provides roughly 30 times the resolution of IllustrisTNG while covering a region 100 times larger in volume than previous leading simulations.

Recreating billions of years of interactions across so many elements requires extraordinary computing resources. The researchers used Frontier, one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, located at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

"At peak scale, the calculation brings together the equivalent of more than 100,000 CPU cores and around 15,000 GPUs," says Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, an MIT co-author of the study. "Making all of those processors communicate efficiently while continuously evolving trillions of interacting pieces of information is itself an extraordinary feat of computer engineering."

Watching the First Galaxies Emerge From Darkness

Lumina begins approximately 45 million years after the Big Bang, during an era when neutral hydrogen dominated the universe.

Researchers initialized the simulation using conditions based on scientists' understanding of that period. They then allowed the model to calculate how gas and dark matter interacted throughout its half a trillion elements as cosmic time progressed.

At the same time, Lumina tracked how radiation appeared, spread, and interacted with matter, including the ultraviolet light produced by emerging stars.

The result is a virtual universe that scientists can explore at dramatically different scales, from the arrangement of matter across enormous cosmic distances down to the development of a single galaxy.

On the project website, the researchers have released videos showing these processes in action. One offers a "zoom-in" from the entire simulated region to an individual disk-shaped galaxy. Another presents a time-lapse of the complete volume, showing how hydrogen re-ionization spreads across the universe over 2 billion years.

"On the one hand, it's evolving dark matter as well as the gas in the universe, and on the other, it's also tracking how radiation travels," Zier explains. "We see dark matter and gas start to clump in these over-densities. And when we zoom in, we can see gas is falling into these dark matter haloes. Zooming in more, we see this is where the first galaxies form. And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."

This ability to move between vastly different scales is one of Lumina's defining strengths. Researchers can examine the formation of individual galaxies while also observing how their combined radiation affects the universe on a much larger scale.

"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," Vogelsberger notes. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."

A New Way to Explore the Universe's Earliest History

The research team plans to use Lumina to investigate the large-scale arrangement of matter in the early universe. The simulation could also help predict the patterns of gravitational waves generated by ancient galaxies and black holes.

Another major opportunity will come from comparing Lumina's virtual universe with real observations. New and upcoming telescopes are expected to collect increasingly detailed information about enormous numbers of distant galaxies, providing scientists with fresh ways to test their understanding of the early cosmos.

Because Lumina simulates such a large volume of space, it can generate extensive populations of galaxies that can be directly compared with these observations.

"One of Lumina's major advantages is its sheer size," Shen says. "It produces enormous populations of simulated galaxies, finally allowing us to make comparisons with the very large galaxy samples that upcoming surveys will observe."

By bringing together detailed galaxy formation, dark matter, gas, and the movement of radiation, Lumina offers researchers a powerful new tool for reconstructing the universe's earliest chapters. It may help explain not only how the first galaxies took shape, but also how their stars and black holes transformed the surrounding cosmos.

Research Team and Support

The study's MIT authors include Mark Vogelsberger, Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, and Teodora-Elena Bluichi. Other contributors include first author Oliver Zier (a former postdoc in the Vogelsberger Lab), Rongrong Liu, Sonja Koehler, and Lars Hernquist of the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics; Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas; Rahul Kannan of York University in Canada; and Volker Springel and Rüdiger Pakmor of the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics in Germany.

The research received partial support from NASA and the National Science Foundation. It also used computing resources at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which is supported by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research programs within the Office of Science at the U.S. Department of Energy.
