BMDMs were differentiated from whole bone marrow derived from tibia and femurs of C57BL/6J, Nlrp3−/−, Casp11−/−, Casp1−/−;Casp11−/−, Gsdmd−/−, Nfe2l2−/−, Keap1f/f, LysM-cre;Keap1f/f and CMV-cre;Panxf/f mice. In brief, mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation and leg bones were surgically removed and cleaned of surrounding muscle and tissue. Bones were washed once in 70% ethanol, washed in PBS and 2.5 mM EDTA with penicillin–streptomycin and then stored in a solution of PBS, 2.5 mM EDTA and penicillin–streptomycin until processing. All future steps were undertaken in a Biosafety Cabinet. Bones were scraped clean of tissue using sterilized razor blades, the ends of the tibia and femurs were cut and bones were placed into a sterile 0.6 ml tube with perforations at the base. The 0.6 ml tube with bones was placed into a sterile 2 ml tube and the nested tubes were spun at 12,000g for 15 s in a tabletop centrifuge. Cell pellets were resuspended in PBS pH 7.4 and 2.5 mM EDTA and spun at 400g for 5 min followed by RBC lysis using ACK buffer (Gibco) for 1 min at room temperature. Lysis was stopped by adding a 10-fold volume of PBS and 2.5 mM EDTA and cells were pelleted at 400g for 5 min. A total of 4 × 106 cells were seeded per 10 cm non-TC-treated plate and differentiated in cDMEM supplemented with 30% L929 supernatants containing M-CSF for 6 days. Immortalization of WT and Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs was performed using J2 virus supernatants as previously described85.

Primary BMDCs were differentiated from whole bone marrow derived from tibia and femurs of C57BL/6J, Nfe2l2−/−, Keap1f/f and LysM-cre;Keap1f/f mice isolated as described above. For in vitro experiments testing R848 and PGPC, a total of 4 × 106 cells were seeded per 10 cm non-TC treated plate and differentiated in cIMDM supplemented with 30% B-16 supernatants containing GM-CSF for 6 days. For in vivo experiments using adoptive transfer of BMDCs, a total of 10 × 106 cells were seeded per non-tissue culture treated 6-well plate and cultured in cIMDM supplemented with 100 ng ml–1 FLT3L (Miltenyi) for 8 days.

Panx1 cDNA was ordered as a gBlock (IDT) and cloned using Gibson Assembly into pMSCV-IRES-GFP. Effective cloning was confirmed using restriction enzyme digestion and Sanger sequencing. Generation of retrovirus was done in 293T cells.

For transduction of iBMDMs, 293T cells were plated in a 6-well dish at one well per construct. Cells were then transfected with pMSCV-IRES-GFP or pMSCV-Panx1-IRES-GFP alongside the helper plasmid pCl-Eco and VSV-g. The next day, supernatants containing virus were collected, clarified by centrifugation at 400g for 5 min at room temperature and filtered through a 0.45 µm PVDF filter. Polybrene (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to the viral supernatants at a 1:2,000 dilution. Viral supernatants were then placed on top of iBMDMs in 12-well plates which were spinfected at 1,250g for 1 h at 30 °C. iBMDMs were transduced again the following day. iBMDM transduction was confirmed by fluorescence microscopy (evaluating for GFP expression) and by western blotting.

For transduction of primary Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs, primary BMDMs were generated from the bone marrow of Nfe2l2−/− mice as described above. Generation of virus was done in 293T cells plated in 10 cm dishes at one dish per 10 cm dish of differentiating BMDMs. 293T cells were transfected with pMSCV-IRES-GFP or pMSCV-Panx1-IRES-GFP alongside the helper plasmid pCl-Eco and VSV-g and viral supernatants were collected the next day, clarified by centrifugation, and filtered through a 0.45 µm PVDF filter. Viral supernatant was added to BMDM cultures on day 3 of differentiation alongside additional L929 supernatant. BMDMs were differentiated for another 3 days and BMDM transduction was confirmed by fluorescence microscopy (evaluating for GFP expression) and by western blotting. BMDMs were plated for experiments as described elsewhere.

Bone marrow was isolated as described above and cultured in the presence of a 1:10 dilution CMG supernatant (a source of M-CSF) for 4–5 days. BMDMs were then seeded at the following concentrations: 1 × 104 cells per well of a 96-well plate, 4 × 105 cells per well of a 6-well plate or 8 × 105 cells per P60 dish. Osteoclast differentiation was induced in a 1:50 dilution of CMG medium with addition of receptor activator of NF-κB ligand (RANKL) at 50–100 ng ml–1 for 5–6 days. For NLRP3 activation, cells were stimulated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 3 h followed by 15 µM nigericin for 1 h, after which supernatant was assayed for IL-1β.

For prophylactic immunization experiments, 7-week-old female C57BL/6J WT and Nfe2l2−/− mice were subcutaneously injected near the shoulders with 200 µg per mouse OVA (EndoFit OVA, Invivogen), 5 µg per mouse R848 (Invivogen) and 65 µg per mouse of PGPC (Cayman Chemical) emulsified in incomplete Freund’s adjuvant (Sigma-Aldrich). Mice received a booster dose 14 days later. Seven days after receipt of the booster immunization, mice had 3 × 105 B16-OVA cells subcutaneously implanted on the flank.

For adoptive DC immunization experiments, 7-week-old female C57BL/6J WT mice had 3 × 105 B16-OVA cells subcutaneously implanted on the flank. On day 8 of BMDC differentiation, FLT3L–BMDCs were stimulated with 500 ng ml–1 R848 for 3 h and then treated with 100 µg ml–1 PGPC for 18 h. BMDCs were subsequently loaded with 500 µg ml–1 OVA for 1 h, washed and resuspended in PBS. A total of 1 × 106 DCs per mouse was subcutaneously injected between the shoulders. BMDC injections were performed 7, 14 and 21 days after implantation of B16-OVA cells.

For all experiments, tumour sizes were measured every other day by recording the length and width using a caliper. Mice were euthanized when the humane end point was reached, which was defined as tumour area >2 cm2 or tumour ulceration.

MSU-induced peritonitis was performed as previously described86. In brief, a 10 mg ml–1 solution of MSU (Invivogen; tlrl-msu) was prepared in sterile PBS. Mice were injected (i.p.) with 180 µl of 10 mg ml–1 MSU using a 29 G insulin syringe. Similarly, alum-induced peritonitis was performed by injecting mice (i.p.) with 200 µl of a 1:9 dilution of Alhydrogel (Invivogen; vac-alu-50) in PBS. At 3 h (MSU) or 16–24 h (alum) after injection, peritoneal lavage was performed on the mice using 5 ml sterile PBS. Lavage fluid was collected through a 25 G needle and immune cells were pelleted. Cells were stained with a Live/Dead fixable stain (Invitrogen) and Fc block (BioLegend; clone S17011E) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Cells were then stained with CD45 (BV711; clone 30-F11), Ly6G (FITC; clone 1A8) and Ly6B.2 (PE; clone REA115). Neutrophils were defined by flow cytometry as live, CD45+Ly6G+Ly6B.2+ and represented as a proportion of CD45+ cells. Alum-treated mice with <11% neutrophils (non-responders) were excluded from the analysis (two mice per group, four mice in total excluded).

Mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation, sprayed with 70% ethanol and the peritoneal cavity was lavaged with 5 ml PBS containing 2.5 mM EDTA. The peritoneal lavage containing resident peritoneal macrophages was centrifuged at 400g for 5 min at room temperature and the pellet resuspended in cDMEM. For experiments evaluating the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in plastic TC plates, peritoneal lavages from 2–3 mice were pooled and cells were plated across 12 wells of a 96-well dish. For experiments evaluating the role of stiffness on inflammasome activation, peritoneal lavages from 5 mice were pooled and cells were plated across 9 wells of 6-well dishes (3 wells for each stiffness). After 2 h, cells were washed 3 times with PBS to remove contaminating non-macrophages and cultured in cDMEM overnight. Cells were then stimulated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 24 h followed by 5 mM ATP for 30 min. Cell culture supernatants were saved for ELISA and IL-1β immunoprecipitation. Cells were lysed in 1× SDS loading buffer containing 2% β-mercaptoethanol (β-ME) and heated at 65 °C for 10 min followed by separation by SDS–PAGE.

Human buffy coat was purchased from BioIVT and shipped on ice on the day of collection. All buffy coat samples were anticoagulated with EDTA and were confirmed to be free of common viral infections. Buffy coat was mixed 1:1 with PBS and 2.5 mM EDTA and overlaid on 15 ml Ficoll-Paque Plus (Cytiva). The sample was spun at 800g for 35 min at 22 °C without break. The plasma was aspirated and discarded. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were placed in a fresh conical tube and washed in MACS buffer (PBS, 2.5 mM EDTA, 2% FBS and penicillin–streptomycin). Cells were spun at 300g for 10 min, pooled together and washed a second time in MACS buffer. RBCs were lysed in ACK buffer for 5 min and the reaction was stopped with fivefold addition of MACS buffer. PBMCs were washed an additional time to remove residual ACK buffer and the final pellet was resuspended in 10 ml MACS buffer and filtered through a 30 µm filter. Monocytes were isolated using human anti-CD14 beads (Miltenyi Biotec) and MACS LS columns (Miltenyi Biotec). In brief, the pellet was resuspended in 80 µl MACS buffer per 107 PBMCs and 20 µl anti-CD14 beads were added per 107 PBMCs. Cells were incubated on ice in the dark for 15 min, washed with 20 ml MACS buffer followed by centrifuging at 300g for 10 min. The cell pellet was resuspended in 2.5 ml MACS buffer per buffy coat and applied to an equilibrated LS column. The column was washed 3 times with 2.5 ml ice-cold MACS buffer and cells were eluted in 5 ml ice-cold MACS buffer. Next, 2 × 107 CD14+ cells were cultured on a tissue culture treated T75 flask in 15 ml cRPMI and 30 ng ml–1 recombinant human M-CSF. The medium was exchanged every 2 days and cells were considered differentiated into macrophages on day 6. Cells were lifted using Macrophage Detachment Solution DXF (PromoCell) per the manufacturer’s protocol and plated at 1 × 106 cells per well in variable stiffness plates or 1 × 105 cells per well in 96-well plates.

C57BL/6J WT mice were subcutaneously immunized with 100 µg OVA emulsified 1:1 in incomplete Freud’s adjuvant (Invivogen) on one shoulder and boosted on day 7 on the opposite shoulder. On day 14 of immunization, spleens were collected and CD8+ T cells were isolated by negative selection (BioLegend) and resuspended in cRPMI containing 10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 10 µM β-ME. FLT3L-derived BMDCs were generated and activated overnight using R848 and PGPC as described above. Activated BMDCs were collected, counted and plated at 1 × 104 cells per well in 96-well round-bottom plates, pulsed with 1 mg ml–1 OVA for 1 h and washed with PBS. Enriched CD8+ T cells from OVA-immunized mice were added at 1 × 105 cells per well (10:1 ratio of CD8+ T cells to DCs) in a final volume of 100 µl and cultured for 7 days. Supernatants were collected, clarified by centrifugation and stored at −20 °C for IFNγ ELISA analysis.

Primary BMDMs or human MDMs were typically seeded at the following numbers according to the assay being performed: 1 × 106 cells per well in fibronectin-coated 6-well Cytosoft or plastic TC plates or 0.5 × 106 cells per well in 12-well TC plates for RNA isolation; 0.25 × 106 cells per well in 24-well TC plates for ELISAs; or 0.1 × 106 cells per well in 96-well TC plates for LDH assays. Cells were incubated overnight in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants or in cRPMI and 30 ng ml–1 human M-CSF for MDMs. iBMDMs were seeded at 0.5 × 105 cells per well in a 96-well TC plate and incubated overnight in cDMEM. The next morning, the medium was exchanged to cDMEM with or without inhibitors (or vehicle control), and cells incubated for 30 min. A subset of cells were left unstimulated whereas others were stimulated with LPS at 100 ng ml–1 for up to 6 h followed by inflammasome activation with 5 mM ATP for 2 h (for LDH release or GSDMD oligomerization assays), 5 mM ATP for 30 min (for IL-1β ELISA and IP), 5 µM nigericin for 30 min (ASC specks), 5 µM nigericin for 2 h (for IL-1β ELISA and LDH release) or 20 µg ml–1 CL097 for 2 h.

For examination of oxidized lipid activation of the inflammasome, BMDMs or BMDCs were seeded at 1 × 105 cells per well in 96-well TC plates and incubated overnight. Cells were primed with R848 at 62.5 ng ml–1 for 3 h followed by stimulation with PGPC at 100 µg ml–1 for an additional 24 h.

Lytic cell death was quantified using a LDH-release assay with a CyQuant LDH cytotoxicity assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). In a 96-well plate, 25 µl cell-free supernatants was mixed with 25 µl LDH assay buffer and incubated for 15 min at 37 °C in the dark. The reaction was stopped by addition of 25 µl stop solution. Absorbance at 490 nm and 680 nm was measured on a Tecan Spark plate reader and the signal was normalized to equivalently treated control samples in which cells were lysed using a detergent-containing lysis buffer.

Cytokine release into cell culture supernatants, mouse plasma or mouse peritoneal fluid were assayed for mouse IL-1β and TNF using uncoated ELISA kits (Thermo Fisher Scientific), human IL-1β using a Lumit Human IL-1β Immunoassay kit (Promega) or human TNF using ELISA MAX Deluxe kit (BioLegend) according to the manufacturers’ protocols. For experiments using PGPC, mouse IL-1β was assessed using a Lumit Mouse IL-1β Immunoassay kit (Promega).

Primary mouse BMDMs were plated at 2 × 106 cells per well on soft and plastic plates and cultured overnight. A total of two wells were used per stiffness and treatment condition. Cells were left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 6 h and then lysed in-well with 600 μl NP-40 lysis buffer (TBS pH 7.4, 1% NP-40, 5% glycerol and protease inhibitors) per well. The lysate was spun at 20,000g for 5 min. Next, 120 μl clarified lysate was saved as input whereas the rest was incubated protein G Sepharose beads (GE Healthcare) loaded with anti-NRF2 antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, 12721S) at 4 °C for 1 h. Afterwards, 2 µg NRF2 antibody was added to each sample. After incubation, the beads were washed 3 times with NP-40 lysis buffer, and bound proteins were eluted in 120 μl 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. Samples were heated to 95 °C for 20 min followed by separation by SDS–PAGE.

Cell culture supernatants were transferred into microcentrifuge tubes and depleted of cells and debris by centrifuging at 400g for 5 min. Peritoneal lavage fluid was prepared as described above. Equal volumes of cell-free supernatants or peritoneal lavage fluid were mixed with 0.5 µg biotinylated goat anti-mouse IL-1β or anti-human IL-1β antibody and 20 µl dry weight neutravidin agarose beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C while rotating, washed 3 times with PBS pH 7.4 and protein was eluted in 50 µl 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. The remaining cells in the well were lysed in 1× sample buffer and served as lysate control. Samples were heated to 65 °C for 10 min followed by separation by SDS–PAGE. IL-1β was detected by immunoblotting using Bio-Rad Image Lab. Cell-associated actin was detected as the loading control.

For analysis of inflammasome activation in cells cultured on variable stiffness plates, primary mouse BMDMs were plated at 3 × 106 cells per well and cultured overnight. The medium was exchanged for OptiMEM (Gibco) and cells were left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 6 h or 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h followed by 5 mM ATP for 2 h. The cell culture supernatant was removed, cleared of debris by centrifugation at 400g for 5 min at room temperature and then protein was precipitated by adding trichloroacetic acid to a final concentration of 10%. Samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C while rotating, protein was pelleted by centrifugation at 13,000g at 4 °C for 15 min and was washed twice with 400 µl ice-cold acetone. Protein pellets were air dried at 65 °C for 5 min. Protein was solubilized in 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. The remaining cells in the well were lysed in 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME and served as lysate control. All samples were heated to 65 °C for 10 min followed by protein separation by SDS–PAGE.

For analysis of inflammasome activation in WT, Nfe2l2−/−, Keap1f/f and LysM-Cre;Keap1f/f primary BMDMs, 1 × 106 cells per well were plated in a 24-well dish and cultured overnight in cDMEM. For analysis of inflammasome activation in iBMDMs, 1 × 106 cells per well were plated in a 24-well dish and cultured for 1 h in cDMEM. Cells were then left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h, medium was removed and OptiMEM containing nigericin was added for 1–2 h. Cells and supernatant were lysed together by addition of 5× sample buffer containing 10% β-ME, lysates were needle homogenized and samples were heated to 95 °C for 5 min followed by protein separation by SDS–PAGE.

Primary mouse BMDMs from WT and Gsdmd−/− mice were plated at 3 × 106 cells per well in soft (2 kPa) or plastic plates and cultured overnight. The medium was exchanged for OptiMEM and cells were left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 6 h or 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h followed by 5 mM ATP for 2 h. Protein was precipitated as outlined above and solubilized in 1× sample buffer without reducing agent. Protein was solubilized by incubating at 65 °C for 5 min, after which samples were split equally into two tubes and β-ME or an equal volume of ddH2O was added to generate reducing and non-reducing samples, respectively. Whole-cell lysate was generated by adding 1× sample buffer to the remaining cells, solubilizing at 65 °C for 5 min, splitting the sample equally and adding either β-ME or an equal volume of ddH2O to generate reducing and non-reducing samples. The final concentration of β-ME was 2%. Proteins were separated by SDS–PAGE on a 4–12% acrylamide gradient gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and GSDMD was detected by western blotting. The assembled GSDMD pore is resistant to SDS under non-reducing conditions and thus oligomerization was indicated by a gel shift towards a higher molecular weight. Cell-associated actin was detected as the loading control.

Fractionation was performed as previously described87. In brief, primary BMDMs derived from WT and Nfe2l2−/− mice were seeded in variable stiffness plates at 3 × 106 cells per well. A total of 3 wells were used per genotype and stiffness and BMDMs were cultured overnight. Cells were placed on ice and washed once with ice-cold PBS. Cells were scraped into ice cold PBS, spun at 10,000g for 10 s, and PBS was aspirated. Cells were lysed in 900 µl PBS, 0.1% NP-40 and protease inhibitors by trituration with a P1000 pipette. A total of 300 µl of this was saved as whole-cell lysate. The remaining 600 µl lysate was spun at 10,000g for 10 s and 300 µl of the supernatant was saved as the cytoplasmic fraction. Next, 75 µl of 5× sample buffer containing 10% β-ME was added to the whole-cell lysate and cytoplasmic fractions to denature the protein. The remaining supernatant was aspirated, and the nuclear pellet was washed with 1 ml PBS, 0.1% NP-40 and protease inhibitors. The nuclear pellet was lysed in 300 µl 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. All fractions were needle homogenized and then boiled at 100 °C for 5 min. Tubulin and lamin A/C served as markers for the cytosol and nucleus, respectively. Cell-associated actin was detected as the loading control.

Cells were seeded at 1 × 106 primary BMDMs per well in 6-well 2 kPa Cytosoft or plastic Petri dishes coated with fibronectin. One well was left without cells as a blank. Cells were cultured overnight in the presence or absence of NAC (5 mM, pH 7.4), MitoTempo (15 µM), ML171 (1 µM), GSK2795039 (10 µM) or GKT137831 (10 µM). The next morning, cells were incubated with 20 µM H2DCFDA in 1× HBSS without phenol red for 30 min. Cells were then washed 3 times with HBSS without phenol red and bottom read fluorescence was read using a TecanSpark with an excitation wavelength of 490 nm, emission wavelength of 535 nm and bandwidth of 20.0. Cells were then lysed in 350 µl RNA lysis buffer containing 1% β-ME and stored at −20 °C until further processing.

iBMDMs were seeded on glass coverslips at 2.5 × 105 cells per well in 24-well dishes and left to adhere for 1 h. Primary BMDMs were seeded on glass coverslips at 1 × 105 cells per well in 24-well dishes in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants, left to adhere overnight. The next morning, medium was removed and replaced with cDMEM. Cells were stimulated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h, after which medium was aspirated and replaced with 450 µl OptiMEM containing zVAD-FMK with or without nigericin for 30 min. Cells were fixed by the addition of 150 µl of 16% EM-grade aqueous paraformaldehyde (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were washed twice with PBS pH 7.4 and stored overnight at 4 °C. The next morning, cells were permeabilized and blocked for 30 min in PBS pH 7.4 containing 0.2% BSA and 0.05% saponin (blocking buffer). Cells were washed 3 times in PBS pH 7.4 and primary antibody staining was performed for 1 h in blocking buffer containing polyclonal rabbit anti-ASC antibody (Adipogen) at 1:100 dilution in a humidified chamber. Cells were washed 5 times in PBS pH 7.4 and secondary antibody staining was performed for 1 h in blocking buffer containing Alexa Fluor 488-tagged polyclonal goat anti-rabbit IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a 1:200 dilution, Alexa Fluor 647-tagged phalloidin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 1:400 dilution and DAPI (Biotum) at 1 µg ml–1 in a humidified chamber in the dark. Cells were washed 5–10 times in PBS pH 7.4, mounted on glass slides using prolong glass antifade mountant (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and left to cure overnight at room temperature in the dark. Images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM 880 with Airyscan and processed using Zeiss Zen Blue (v.2.3SP1). ASC specks were manually counted, and nuclei were counted in Fiji (v.2.16.0) using the Analyze particles algorithm.

Tissue samples for these experiments were isolated from discarded explanted human lung tissue specimens collected at Massachusetts General Hospital. Patients provided informed consent, and discarded tissue samples from non-diseased donors were collected under Massachusetts General Hospital IRB number 2016P001890. Discarded tissue from patients with ILD were collected under Massachusetts General Hospital IRB number 2013P002332. Samples were fixed in 4% buffered paraformaldehyde and then embedded in paraffin. The following primary antibodies were used for immunofluorescence: monoclonal mouse anti-human CD68 (Abcam, ab955), polyclonal rabbit anti-human SLC7A11 (Abcam, ab37185), polyclonal rabbit anti-human HMOX1 (Proteintech, 10701-1-AP) and polyclonal rabbit anti-human GSR (Proteintech, 18257-1-AP). Paraffin-embedded tissue was sectioned at 5 µm slices onto glass slides, deparaffinized and then rehydrated. Antigen retrieval was performed using Tris-EDTA pH 9 for 5 min in a pressure cooker, after which samples were cooled and tissue was circled using a hydrophobic pen. Sections were permeabilized and blocked using sterile filtered PBS, 1% BSA and 0.3% Triton X-100 (blocking-staining buffer). Sections were stained with primary antibody at 4 °C overnight at the following dilutions: CD68, 1:100; HMOX1, 1:50; GSR, 1:50; and SLC7A11, 1:100. Sections were washed 5 times in blocking–staining buffer and then left in blocking–staining buffer for 10 min. Secondary antibody staining was performed at room temperature in blocking–staining buffer containing Alexa Fluor 594-tagged polyclonal goat anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 647-tagged polyclonal goat anti-mouse IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 1:400) along with Hoechst (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 1:2,000) for 2 h. Samples were then washed 5 times with blocking–staining buffer, submerged in PBS pH 7.4 and 0.1% Triton X-100 for 30 min, dipped in deionized water and mounted with Fluoromount-G mounting medium (Southern Biotech). Samples were imaged on a Zeiss Axio Imager.M2 widefield microscope and a Zeiss LSM 780 confocal microscope.

Cells were detected using Cellpose (v.2.0) and the implemented model ‘Cellpose fluorescence’ (CP) with the following parameters: average cell diameter 50 pixels (12.2 µm), flow threshold 2.0 and cell probability threshold –3. Segmentation was performed on the stained cells using nuclei as a secondary channel for detection. The resulting labels were filtered for a minimum size of 600 pixels (35.4 µm2), and the resulting labels were used to calculate fluorescence values of the corresponding cells. An empirically determined threshold for the average CD68 fluorescence intensity was used to discriminate alveolar macrophages from interstitial macrophages and stromal cells following histogram normalization of the underlying imaging data. The mean fluorescence intensity and sum of fluorescence per cell were plotted in PRISM (GraphPad).

BMDMs were grown on Cytosoft 2 kPa plates or glass cover slips, both coated with fibronectin as described above. BMDMs were immersion-fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences), 2% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences) and 0.3% picric acid (Sigma-Aldrich) in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate (Sigma-Aldrich) pH 7.4 for 1 h at room temperature. BMDMs were washed with 0.1 M sodium cacodylate and then post-fixed for 1 h at 4 °C in 1% osmium tetroxide (Electron Microscopy Sciences) in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate. BMDMs were then washed in DI water and incubated in 2% aqueous uranyl acetate (Electron Microscopy Sciences) overnight at 4 °C. The following day, BMDMs were washed with DI water and then dehydrated at 4 °C in a graded ethanol series. BMDMs were then brought to room temperature and dehydrated with 100% ethanol (Sigma-Aldrich). Infiltration with LX112 resin (Ladd Research) was followed by embedding in flat-bottom Beem capsules (Electron Microscopy Sciences) cut to form a cylindrical mould on the growing substrate. The resulting blocks were separated from the culture plates using liquid nitrogen and then sectioned using a Leica Ultracut E ultramicrotome (Leica Microsystems). Sections were then placed on formvar and carbon-coated grids (Electron Microscopy Sciences). The sections were contrast stained with 2% uranyl acetate followed by lead citrate (Sigma-Aldrich) and imaged in a Jeol 1400 transmission electron microscope (Jeol) equipped with a Gatan Orius SC1000 digital CCD camera (Gatan). Mitochondrial length was manually measured in Fiji (v.2.16.0).

RNA was isolated using a PureLink RNA Mini kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). In brief, cells were collected in lysis buffer containing 1% β-ME and stored frozen at −20 °C until processing. Equal volumes of 70% ethanol were added to each sample, which were then applied to PureLink RNA columns and processed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Total RNA was eluted using 50 µl RNAse-free H2O. RT–qPCR was performed using a Taqman RNA-to-Ct 1-step kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on equal amounts of RNA per the manufacturer’s protocol. The following Taqman probes were used: Gsta3 (Mm00494798_m1), Nqo1 (Mm01253561_m1), Gsr (Mm00439154_m1), Hmox1 (Mm00516005_m1), Gclm (Mm01324400_m1), Slc7a11 (Mm00442530_m1), Srxn1 (Mm00769566_m1), Txnrd1 (Mm00443675_m1), Nfe2l2 (Mm00477784_m1), Keap1 (Mm00497268_m1), Il1b (Mm00434228_m1), Panx1 (Mm00450900_m1), Il6 (Mm00446190_m1), Nos2 (Mm00440502_m1), Arg1 (Mm00475988_m1), Retnla (Mm00445109_m1), Nox1 (Mm00549170_m1), Cybb (Mm01287743_m1) and Tbp (Mm01277042_m1). Data were normalized to Tbp, analysed using Microsoft Excel and plotted in GraphPad Prism.

For determination of Nfe2l2 deletion, RNA was collected purified from cells using a PureLink RNA Mini kit (Life Technologies) and PureLink DNase I (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The quality and quantity of RNA were assessed using a Nanodrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). cDNA was synthesized from 1 μg RNA using a High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription kit (Applied Biosystems). Gene expression was analysed by qPCR using a SYBR Green gene expression assay (Applied Biosystems) and primers were synthesized from IDT. The following mouse Nfe2l2 primer sequences were used: forward 5′-TAGATGACCATGAGTCGCTTGC-3′, reverse 5′-GCCAAACTTGCTCCATGTCC-3′. The following mouse cyclophilin B primer sequences were used: forward 5′-AGCATACAGGTCCTGGCATC-3′, reverse 5′- TTCACCTTCCCAAAGACCAC-3′. Data were normalized to cyclophilin B, and relative mRNA expression was calculated using the \({2}^{\Delta \Delta {C}_{t}}\) method.

BMDMs were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in 6-well Cytosoft or plastic Petri dishes coated with fibronectin and cultured overnight. Cells were washed once with PBS, collected in lysis buffer containing 1% β-ME and stored frozen at −80 °C until processing. RNA was processed using the QIAsymphony RNA protocol according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, RNA was extracted using QIAsymphony RNA Isolation kits (Qiagen) on a QIAsymphony SP instrument using the RNA CT 400 protocol. The elution volume for RNA samples was 100 µl. RNA sequencing libraries were constructed from 500 ng total RNA using a KAPA RNA HyperPrep kit (Kapa Biosystems). Library preparation was tested manually and subsequently fully automated on a Biomek i7 Workstation (Beckmen Coulter). Libraries underwent paired-end 75 base-pair sequencing on a NovaSeq6000 (Illumina) at a depth of 50 million reads per sample. Raw reads were aligned to the mouse genome (GRCm39) using the STAR aligner (v.-2.7.5c). Reads mapped to genomic features were counted using the FeatureCounts function from the subread package (v.1.6.0). The count matrix was imported into R (v.4.1.3) and low-expressed genes were filtered out (included genes required ≥1 CPM in at least 20% of samples). Trimmed mean of M-values was computed using edgeR (v.3.38.0). Differential gene expression analysis was computed using the limma package (v.3.52.0). Differentially expressed genes were loaded into ingenuity pathway analysis (Qiagen, v.01-22-01) and upstream regulator and canonical pathway analysis was conducted on samples with an absolute value log2 fold change > 1 and a corrected P < 0.05. Heatmaps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.18.0).

For effects of stiffness on the NRF2 transcriptional program, WT and Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in soft (2 kPa) or plastic 6-well dishes in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants and incubated overnight. For the effect of NRF2 activators on LPS-stimulated transcription, WT and Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in 12-well TC dishes in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants and incubated overnight. The next morning, medium was replaced with fresh cDMEM containing 1 µM KI696, 5 µM sulforaphane, 100 µM tert-butylhydroquinone, 25 µM dimethyl fumarate, 125 µM 4-octyl itaconate or DMSO as a control, and BMDMs were incubated for 30 min. Half of the cells were left unstimulated and the other half had LPS added to a final concentration of 100 ng ml–1 and were cultured for 6 h.

For all samples, supernatants were aspirated and cells were lysed in 350 µl RNA Lysis buffer from a PureLink RNA kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). RNA was isolated as described in the RT–qPCR section above. Technical triplicates were combined to create one sample per condition per mouse, DNA was degraded using a TURBO DNA-free kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and RNA was quantified using a Nanodrop instrument. RNA was kept frozen at −80 °C and paired-end 150 base-pair sequencing was conducted by Azenta at a depth of 20 million reads per sample. Raw sequencing data processing was done with the Galaxy server, whereas differential gene expression analysis was performed in R (v.4.3.2). Raw reads were trimmed using fastp (Galaxy v.0.23.2) and aligned to the mouse genome (mm10) using RNA STAR aligner (Galaxy v.2.7.11a). Reads mapped to genomic features were counted using FeatureCounts (Galaxy v.2.0.3). Differential gene expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 (v.1.42.0) and heatmaps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.18.0).

WT BMDMs were cultured for 5 days in 2% CMG, then left untreated or treated with RANKL to generate osteoclasts. On day 5, cells were treated with or without 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 3 h. RNA was extracted using a PureLink RNA Mini kit (Invitrogen) with on-column DNase treatment (Ambion). RNA quality and quantity were assessed using an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Libraries were prepared using a NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep kit and sequenced on an Illumina platform to generate paired end reads. Raw reads were cleaned using fastp and aligned to the reference genome, mm10 using STAR. Gene expression was quantified with Feature Counts, and RPKM values were calculated. Differential expression was analysed using DESeq2 with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (adjusted P < 0.05). Heatmaps were generated using ComplexHeatmap. Three biological replicates were used per group.

Spatial transcriptomic data from human lung tissue were downloaded from the NIH Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) platform (identifier GSE250346)79, whereas single-cell RNA sequencing data were downloaded from NIH GEO (identifiers GSE122960 and GSE136831)80,81. All analyses were performed using Seurat (v.5.0.1). Data from ref. 80 (GSE122960) required integration, which was performed using the IntegrateLayers pipeline in Seurat. Data from ref. 81 (GSE136831) were available as a sparse matrix and a Seurat object was manually created using these data. Data from ref. 79 (GSE250346) were available as a Seurat object. In brief, cells were re-clustered and individual cluster annotations were confirmed manually. NRF2 transcriptional targets were used to generate an NRF2 module score across all cell types using the AddModuleScore. The NRF2 activity score was then compared between samples from unaffected individuals and samples with more fibrosis on a per-macrophage-subtype basis. Significance was assessed using the Kruskal–Wallis test and Dunn’s multiple comparisons test, and P values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction. Violin plots were generated using scCustomize (v.2.0.1). Pseudobulk analysis was performed by creating an aggregated count matrix followed by differential gene expression analysis using DESeq2 (v.1.42.0). Normalized counts were extracted and GSVA (v.1.50.0) was performed using NRF2 target genes as the target gene set. Significance was assessed using the Mann–Whitney U-test. All data analyses were performed using R (v.4.3.2).

Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Here we show a kosmotropic anion–polar anion–nucleophilic species (Nuc) electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, enabling reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. Polar anions establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment, whereas kosmotropic anions regulate water–Nuc interactions to increase the availability of Nuc for stabilizing hypervalent iodine cations through Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. This electrolyte framework is validated across diverse Nuc and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries. Moving beyond conventional interhalogen stabilization, these findings establish a distinct electrolyte chemistry framework and represent a mechanistic shift for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

The increasing integration of renewable energy calls for sustainable electrochemical energy storage systems beyond lithium-ion batteries1. Aqueous metal–iodine batteries offer a promising platform for large-scale energy storage by combining earth-abundant electrode materials, aqueous electrolytes and conversion-type iodine chemistry2,3. Unlike intercalation-type positive electrodes, iodine positive electrodes store charge by reversible valence-state changes, offering access to multi-electron redox chemistry with increased capacity and redox potential4. Most studies have focused on the two-electron I−/I0 redox couple, with a theoretical capacity of 211 mAh g−1 at a redox potential of 0.54 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode10. Extending iodine conversion to the successive I−/I0/I+ redox couples doubles the theoretical capacity to 422 mAh g−1 while introducing the I0/I+ redox process at a higher redox potential of 1.07 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode11. However, despite this potential, achieving reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous environments remains a fundamental challenge3,7.

The crux of iodine conversion chemistry lies in interfacial reactions, where electrolyte composition and interfacial microenvironment govern reaction pathways. Electron-deficient I+ is strongly electrophilic and susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water, resulting in hydrolysis and poor reversibility in aqueous environments9,12. Previous studies have achieved four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries by stabilizing reactive I+ through interhalogen complexes (for example, ICl2 or IBr2) in highly concentrated chloride- or bromide-containing electrolytes5,6,13. In these systems, electrophilic I+ coordinates with two nucleophilic halide ions (Cl− or Br−) through non-covalent interactions8,14. However, at water-enriched interfaces, hydration of nucleophilic species (Nuc) competes with these interactions and destabilizes I+ complexes (Fig. 1a). Highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes mitigate this competition by reducing water activity and increasing halide availability, but their high salt contents and corrosivity constrain broader implementation (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1), necessitating new electrolyte chemistry and a mechanistic framework that move beyond reliance on halogen-containing electrolytes and conventional interhalogen stabilization5,8.

Given the competition between I+ stabilization and hydration at water-enriched interfaces, overcoming this challenge requires simultaneous regulation of the interfacial environment and water–Nuc interactions. Anionic chemistry offers a powerful lever to coordinate these interfacial and molecular interactions15,16,17,18. Herein we establish a kosmotropic anion (KA)–polar anion (PA)–Nuc electrolyte framework for reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes (Fig. 1c). Systematic experiments and theoretical calculations reveal how the synergistic effects of PAs and KAs coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, thereby stabilizing interfacial electrochemical behaviour and promoting reversible four-electron iodine conversion. The applicability of this electrolyte framework is demonstrated across four halogen-free Nuc (urea, acetamide, pyridine and nicotinamide) and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Beyond establishing a halogen-free electrolyte chemistry, this work reveals how electrolyte chemistry governs iodine conversion across interfacial, molecular and electrochemical scales, providing a mechanistic basis for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

Stabilizing I+ against hydrolysis is essential for reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous electrolytes. Previous studies have relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes for interhalogen stabilization19,20, whereas more recent studies have explored specific additive-halogen nucleophilic substitution reactions21,22. These approaches primarily address I+ stabilization through specific molecular interactions, whereas how electrolyte chemistry collectively regulates the interfacial microenvironment, molecular stabilization and the resulting iodine conversion pathways remains less understood. This work establishes a mechanistic framework that integrates anionic chemistry with halogen-bond stabilization in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, strong PAs establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interface, whereas KAs weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding to facilitate halogen-bond stabilization of I+. These complementary effects underpin the halogen-free KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, whose composition was subsequently optimized (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4) and exhibits sufficient electrochemical stability (Supplementary Fig. 5) for four-electron iodine conversion.

The KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework was validated in aqueous Zn–I2 batteries across four different Nuc (Supplementary Fig. 6). Electron-deficient I+ can interact with two electron-rich Nuc molecules to form linear Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. These halogen bonds provide the molecular basis for I+ stabilization, as supported by Nuc-free controls, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and theoretical calculations23 (Supplementary Figs. 7–11). Using urea (U) as a representative Nuc, KA–U exhibits only the I−/I0 redox process, whereas PA–U enables further I0/I+ oxidation but with poor reversibility (Fig. 2b,e). The excessive capacity at the second charge plateau is attributed to irreversible iodine oxidation coupled with parasitic water oxidation (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). Combining KA and PA in KA–PA–U produces two reversible redox peaks and corresponding charge–discharge plateaus, demonstrating their synergistic role in enabling reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion (Supplementary Fig. 14). Replacing U with acetamide (AE), nicotinamide (NA) or pyridine (PD) shows the same phenomenon, with reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion achieved only in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes, including under identical ionic strength conditions, indicating the broad applicability of this electrolyte framework (Fig. 2c,d,f,g and Supplementary Figs. 15–18).

To isolate the role of PAs in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, SO42− was maintained as the KA, whereas structurally related CF3SO3−, CF3COO− or CH3COO− was introduced as the second anion. Density-functional-theory calculations reveal a polarity sequence of CH3COO− > CF3COO− > CF3SO3− (Supplementary Fig. 19), providing a basis for examining how anion polarity influences interfacial behaviours24,25. Molecular-dynamics simulations show similar water-enriched bulk environments across the three electrolytes (Supplementary Figs. 20–22), but distinct interfacial structures (Fig. 3d). CH3COO− reduces the interfacial water density while increasing anion enrichment, whereas CF3COO− and CF3SO3− retain high interfacial water intensity (Fig. 3e,f). In situ attenuated total reflection infrared (ATR-IR) spectroscopy further supports this interfacial redistribution. The δ-HOH vibration at 1,640 cm−1 remains pronounced with CF3SO3− or CF3COO− (Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Fig. 23), but is suppressed with CH3COO− alongside pronounced anion-associated signals26,27,28,29 (Fig. 3i). Notably, highly concentrated ZnCl2 retains a water-enriched interface despite its water-deficient bulk environment (Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25). Differential capacitance measurements indicate stronger interfacial adsorption of CH3COO− than of CF3COO− and CF3SO3− (Supplementary Figs. 26 and 27), linking preferential adsorption of strongly PAs to the formation of a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment30.

These polarity-dependent interfacial structures lead to distinct iodine conversion behaviour. CF3SO3− shows a negligible I0/I+ process, whereas CF3COO− enables I0/I+ oxidation but with limited reversibility. By contrast, CH3COO− supports reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion with improved stability and capacity (Fig. 3a–c and Supplementary Fig. 28). In situ ultraviolet–visible spectra and micro-computed-tomography analyses further link these differences to iodine species distribution, showing that CH3COO− confines iodine species within the electrode and suppresses their migration into the bulk electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 29 and 30). Together, these results establish a mechanistic relationship between anion polarity and the resulting water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment that governs the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

Building on the understanding of PAs, the critical role of KAs in the KA–PA–Nuc framework was further explored. Nuc stabilize I+ through electron-rich nitrogen or oxygen centres, which also interact with water through hydrogen bonding and therefore compete with halogen-bond formation (Supplementary Fig. 31). Inspired by anion-specific effects on water–solute interactions, SO42−, CH3COO−, NO3−, CF3SO3− and ClO4− were compared in the same PA–Nuc baseline31,32,33,34 (Supplementary Fig. 32). Although these anions have little effect on the initial capacity, they produce different cycling stability (Supplementary Fig. 33). SO42− maintains nearly overlapping galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) profiles, whereas CH3COO− and CF3SO3− show intermediate cycling stability and ClO4− undergoes rapid deterioration (Fig. 4a–c and Supplementary Fig. 34), giving a stability sequence of SO42− > CH3COO− > CF3SO3− > ClO4−. NO3− deviates from this sequence owing to its limited electrochemical stability within the applied voltage range35 (Supplementary Fig. 35a,b).

NMR spectroscopy and molecular-dynamics simulations reveal the molecular origin of these electrochemical differences. The 2H chemical shift follows SO42− > CH3COO− > NO3− > CF3SO3− > ClO4− (Fig. 4d), indicating progressively stronger anion-induced water polarization and restructuring of the aqueous hydrogen-bond network36,37. These differences in water–anion coordination translate into distinct water–Nuc interactions. The corresponding 15N chemical shifts, together with the inverse trends observed in 1H and 13C chemical shifts, indicate that KAs such as SO42− polarize hydration water and thereby weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding, whereas chaotropic anions such as ClO4− interact directly with the Nuc backbone and facilitate Nuc hydration32 (Fig. 4e,f, and Supplementary Figs. 32 and 36–38). Nuc solubility measurements, two-dimensional 1H–15N heteronuclear multiple bond correlation (HMBC) NMR spectra, and calculated Nuc–water distances and hydrogen-bond populations further support this interpretation (Fig. 4g–i, and Supplementary Figs. 35c, 39 and 40). By weakening Nuc–water interactions, SO42− increases the availability of Nuc for halogen-bond stabilization of I+, thereby promoting reversible iodine conversion. These results reveal how anionic chemistry regulates molecular water–Nuc interactions to govern the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

Having established the complementary roles of PA and KA in interfacial and molecular regulation, we next examined how these effects manifest in the electrochemical processes governing iodine conversion. In situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) combined with distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis was used to decouple the complex impedance response and identify individual electrochemical processes38,39,40 (Supplementary Figs. 41–43). In the absence of either KA or PA, the DRT responses evolve distinctly with additional competing interfacial processes, whereas their combined presence maintains stable interfacial electrochemical behaviour throughout iodine conversion41,42 (Extended Data Fig. 1). Rate-dependent analysis identifies charge transfer, rather than ion transport, as the dominant kinetic contribution to iodine conversion in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 44–50). In situ Raman spectroscopy further links these electrochemical processes to iodine chemistry, revealing the reversible evolution of the Nuc–I+–Nuc species during cycling (Supplementary Figs. 51 and 52).

The KA–PA–Nuc framework supports four-electron iodine conversion across different operating conditions and cell configurations. Zn–I2 cells retain 96% of their capacity after 1,000 cycles at 1 A g−1 and 94% after 2,000 cycles at 2 A g−1, while sustaining four-electron conversion at iodine loadings up to 12.2 mg cm−2 (Supplementary Figs. 53–55, 58a and 59). This electrolyte framework is also compatible with different current collectors and pouch-cell configurations and extends to aqueous Al–I2 cells using Al–Zn alloy negative electrodes (Supplementary Figs. 56–58b,c, 60 and 61). A techno-economic analysis under standardized modelling assumptions further illustrates its theoretical cost-reduction potential by avoiding highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes and costly current collectors (Supplementary Fig. 58d–f and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Mechanistic and post-mortem analyses further reveal that the apparent low Coulombic efficiency and capacity fading involve coupled reversible and irreversible iodine inventory loss, with the latter becoming more pronounced at increased iodine loading (Supplementary Figs. 62–67 and Extended Data Figs. 2–4). Together, these results clarify the iodine conversion pathways while defining the applicability and remaining limitations of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, showing that sustained reversible four-electron iodine conversion requires not only stabilization of hypervalent iodine species but also broader management of the entire iodine inventory.

The KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes were prepared by dissolving KA, PA and Nuc into deionized water at room temperature. For aqueous Zn–I2 batteries, KA and PA were 1.5 M ZnSO4 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M Zn (CH3COO)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich), respectively. To demonstrate the broad applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, various Nuc were used, including 2 M urea (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich), 2 M acetamide (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.2 M pyridine (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) or 0.4 M nicotinamide (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich). To explore the role of PAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 1.5 M ZnSO4 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. Zn(CH3COO)2, Zn(CF3COO)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) or Zn(CF3SO3)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 0.5 M to obtain electrolytes containing different PAs. To evaluate the role of KAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. ZnSO4, Zn(NO3)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), Zn(CF3SO3)2 or Zn(ClO4)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 1.5 M for comparative analysis. To compare electrolytes performance under a standardized ionic strength condition, the ionic strength of each electrolyte was calculated according to the equation:

where Ci and Zi represent the molar concentration and charge number of ion i, respectively. For aqueous Al–I2 batteries, the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte was prepared by dissolving 1.5 M Al2(SO4)3 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.5 Mg (CH3COO)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M nicotinamide into deionized water.

Iodine-activated carbon (I2–AC) composites were prepared using an evaporation–adsorption method. In brief, 0.5 g iodine (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) and 0.5 g activated carbon (AC; YP-80F, purity not specified, Kuraray) were manually ground in an agate mortar with a pestle for 10 min under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was sealed in a Teflon reactor and heated at 120 °C for 6 h. For the preparation of iodine positive electrodes using titanium (80 mesh, >99.5%, Hebei Conway Metal Products) or stainless steel mesh (80 mesh, 316L, Hebei Conway Metal Products) as the current collector, I2–AC, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, 60 wt% dispersion H2O, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P (purity not specified, Canrd) were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 40 mg I2–AC, 5 mg Super P and 5 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using a roller press (Etelux) and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The areal iodine loading was controlled by adjusting the thickness of the composite film. The dried film was then pressed onto the titanium or stainless steel mesh using the roller press. The resulting electrodes were punched into 12 mm disks using a manual disk punch (T07, ‌Hefei Kejing Material Technology).

For iodine positive electrodes using carbon paper (TGP-H-060, Toray) as the current collector, I2–AC, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, weight-average molecular weight, Mw ≈ 534,000 g mol−1 by gel permeation chromatography, powder, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg I2–AC, 20 mg PVDF and 20 mg Super P were manually mixed with N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) using an agate mortar and pestle in ambient conditions. The resulting slurry was manually and uniformly spread onto the carbon paper using a laboratory spatula. The coated electrodes were dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 8 h and subsequently cut into 12-mm disks using the manual disk punch. Commercial Zn foils (70 µm, >99.99%, ‌Qinghe Haoxuan Metal Materials) were used as negative electrodes as received.

To assess the potential of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, a Ag/AgCl electrode in saturated KCl (Beijing Jingke Instrument Science Instrument) was used as the reference, and AC electrodes were prepared as the counter electrode. The measured potentials are reported directly versus the Ag/AgCl reference electrode. For the preparation of AC electrodes, AC, PTFE and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg AC, 20 mg Super P and 20 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle at ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using the roller press and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The dried film was then pressed onto titanium mesh using the roller press. By adjusting the electrode thickness, the capacity of the AC electrode was controlled to be much higher than that of the iodine working electrode, ensuring its capability as the counter electrode for evaluating the electrochemical performance of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte. To further validate the applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, Al–Zn alloys were fabricated as negative electrodes following a previous study43. In brief, symmetric cells were assembled using Zn foils (70 µm, 16 mm in diameter) as electrodes and 2 M Al (CF3SO3)3 (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) as the electrolyte. During charging, Al3+ in the electrolyte deposited on and reacted with the metal Zn substrate, forming the Zn-supported Al–Zn alloys.

Halogen-bond complexes were synthesized via a cation-exchange reaction using corresponding silver analogues, following a previously reported procedure with some modifications44. All operations were carried out under a standard Schlenk line. In a typical synthesis, 0.94 mmol of the corresponding silver salt (Ag2SO4, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCH3COO, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3COO, >98%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3SO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgNO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; or AgClO4, >97%, Sigma-Aldrich) was added to a 20-ml vial equipped with a stir bar. The vial was sealed with a rubber septum and evacuated. Subsequently, 6.0 ml dry CH2Cl2 (purity not specified, VWR Chemicals) and 1.90 mmol pyridine (3.80 mmol for Ag2SO4) were added at room temperature under a nitrogen atmosphere. The mixture was stirred for 10 min to form the Ag(I)–pyridine bis-coordination complex. Next, 2.00 mmol of iodine (4.00 mmol for Ag2SO4) was added, and the reaction was allowed to proceed for an additional 20 min under continuous stirring. The supernatant was then carefully transferred to another vial via cannula filtration, followed by the addition of 15 ml dry n-hexane (>99%, Macron Fine Chemicals) to induce precipitation of the halogen-bond complex. The mixture was stored at −20 °C overnight to complete precipitation. Afterwards, the supernatant was removed using a syringe, and the resulting solid was washed with 20 ml dry n-hexane to remove any residual I2. Finally, the product was dried under vacuum on the Schlenk line.

In situ ATR-IR spectra were recorded by a Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS50 spectrometer equipped with a liquid nitrogen-cooled MCT-A detector. Gold-coated silicon plates were used as working electrodes, with Zn foils (70 µm, 10 mm in diameter) and glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter, Whatman) used as reference electrodes and separators, respectively. To assess the critical role of the PA in the interfacial environment, 1.5 M KA electrolyte was maintained as the baseline, and 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2, 0.5 M Zn(CF3COO)2 or 0.5 M Zn(CF3SO3)2 was separately added. An electrolyte volume of 500 μl was used for each measurement. During tests, the assembled batteries were connected to a Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat to run a cyclic voltammetry programme at a scan rate of 0.2 mV s−1 for a full charge and discharge cycle. All spectra were collected at a resolution of 4 cm−1, with 50 scans per measurement. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

Raman spectra were recorded using a Bruker Senterra II Raman spectrometer with a 532-nm excitation wavelength. The in situ Zn–I2 cell comprised an iodine positive electrode (12 mm in diameter, iodine mass loading 2.2 mg cm−2), a Zn negative electrode (70 µm, 12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter). An electrolyte volume of 200 μl was used. Raman spectra were collected during GCD cycling using an external Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

FTIR spectra of various electrolytes were obtained using an ATR-FTIR spectrometer (BRUKER, Platinum-ATR). Scanning electron microscopy characterization of electrodes was performed using a JEOL 7600 microscope. Ultraviolet–visible measurements were conducted on a Shimadzu UV-3600i Plus spectrophotometer. For in situ ultraviolet–visible measurements, a two-electrode Zn–I2 cuvette cell was connected to a Neware battery test system for GCD cycling. NMR analyses, including 1H, 13C and 1H–15N HMBC spectra, were carried out on a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 500). 15N spectra were collected using a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 700). Deuterium oxide (>99.9%, Fluorochem) was used as the solvent for electrolyte characterization, and dideuteromethylenechloride (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as the solvent for characterizing halogen-bond complexes. Micro-computed-tomography imaging was conducted using a Zeiss Xradia 620 Versa system with a ×4 objective, operating at a tube voltage of 80 kV and an exposure time of 8 s, achieving a voxel resolution of 0.8 μm. For each sample, a disk with a diameter of 2 mm was prepared to balance X-ray attenuation and representative sampling volume. The acquired computed-tomography datasets were subsequently processed and analysed using Avizo software.

Electrochemical studies of halogen-free electrolytes were performed using CR2025 coin cells, whereas those of halogen-containing electrolytes were performed using Swagelok cells. For CR2025 Zn–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode, Zn negative electrode (70 µm) and separator (GF/D) had diameters of 12 mm, 16 mm and 19 mm, respectively. For Swagelok Zn–I2 cells, corresponding electrodes and separators had the same diameter of 12 mm. For CR2025 Al–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode had a diameter of 12 mm, the Al–Zn alloy negative electrode had a diameter of 16 mm, and a GF/D separator with a diameter of 19 mm was used. An electrolyte volume of 100 μl was used for each cell. Coin cells were mechanically crimped at 50 kg cm−2 using a hydraulic crimping machine (MSK-110, Hefei Kejing Material Technology) during assembly. Swagelok cells were manually tightened during assembly.

For the 1.1-Ah pouch cell, 2 double-side coated iodine positive electrodes (10 × 15 cm), and 3 Zn negative electrodes (70 µm, 10 × 15 cm) were stacked alternately. The areal iodine loading of positive electrodes is controlled at 10 mg cm−2. Four glass fibre separators (GF/D, 10.1 × 15.1 cm) were utilized, and 1.5 ml electrolyte was added to each separator. The electrolyte consisted of 1.5 M ZnSO4, 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide. Titanium foils were connected to electrodes as tabs. After lamination, the assembled battery was encapsulated in an aluminium–plastic film and mechanically constrained using a customized model during electrochemical measurements. The applied pressure was not specifically quantified.

GCD tests were conducted using a Neware battery test system in a room maintained at an ambient temperature of approximately 25–28 °C. All other electrochemical measurements described below were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C. Cyclic voltammetry, linear sweep voltammetry and EIS measurements were performed using a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat. For the electrochemical stability window analysis, linear sweep voltammetry measurements were performed using a three-electrode configuration consisting of a titanium mesh working electrode (1 × 2 cm), an AC counter electrode (1 × 2 cm) and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode at a scan rate of 2 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to an exposed geometric area of 1 cm², and the potentials are reported directly versus Ag/AgCl. The polarization measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti CR2025 coin cells using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter), titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter) at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to the geometric area of the titanium electrode. For in situ EIS tests, a thin Zn wire was inserted into the coin cell as an additional reference electrode to establish a three-electrode configuration. This reference electrode was placed between the positive electrode and negative electrode, separated by two layers of separators (GF/A, Whatman). For measurements of the individual iodine positive electrode, the potential is reported versus the Zn reference electrode as potential (V versus Zn/Zn²+), whereas the full-cell and Zn negative electrode responses are reported as voltage (V) owing to the voltage was applied on full cell. For peak assignment, the assembled cells were connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat to perform staircase potentio EIS with a potential range of approximately 0.6–1.8 V. For rate-step identification, the assembled cells simultaneously connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat and a Neware battery test system to conduct potentio EIS and GCD cycling, respectively. All Nyquist plots were fitted using EC-Lab software based on the equivalent circuit (R1 + Q2/R2 + Q3/R3 + W4). DRT data were calculated from EIS data using MatlabR2019 with the DRT tool developed by Francesco Ciucci’s research group. The differential capacitance was calculated using the following equation:

where C is the differential capacitance, ω is the angular frequency and Zim is the imaginary component of the impedance. In this work, a specific frequency of 1,000 Hz was used. Measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti cells assembled in CR2025 coin-cell configuration, using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter) and titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) as the two electrodes and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter). The potential was varied from 1.0 V to 1.7 V versus Zn/Zn2+. No ohmic-drop (iR) correction was applied to the potentials or voltages reported in this work.

All molecular-dynamics simulations were performed using the LAMMPS package45 to investigate the bulk solvation structure of various aqueous electrolytes. The initial configurations were constructed using Packmol46, which randomly packed electrolyte components into a periodic cubic box according to the target molar ratios, ensuring no initial atomic overlaps. The simulation cell was then relaxed by energy minimization before subsequent equilibration. Force-field parameters for organic molecules were taken from the OPLS-AA family47,48, whereas others were adopted from validated aqueous zinc salt parameter sets in the literature. To partially account for polarization effects in concentrated electrolytes, the atomic charges were uniformly scaled (scaling factor 0.8)49. Interaction of water was represented by TIP3P50, and all X–H bonds were constrained using the SHAKE algorithm51. Each system was first energy-minimized and equilibrated in the isothermal–isobaric ensemble (300 K, 1 atm) using a Nosé–Hoover thermostat until both the density and potential energy were stable. Subsequently, production runs were performed in the canonical ensemble for 5 ns (5,000 ps) with a 1-fs integration step to ensure complete equilibration while avoiding structural drift.

Radial distribution functions gij(r) were computed to analyse ion pairing and solvation structure. Coordination numbers were obtained by integrating gij(r) up to their first minimum. Both radial distribution functions and hydrogen bonds were identified using the hydrogen-bond analysis tools implemented in VMD52. Average hydrogen-bond numbers and distributions were determined over the equilibrated trajectories to characterize the reorganization of the hydrogen-bond network by different anions.

To probe field-induced ion and molecular redistribution, an additional set of simulations was conducted in the canonical ensemble with a uniform static electric field applied along the z axis. The field strength corresponded to the experimentally estimated potential gradient.

Density-functional-theory calculations were performed using the Gaussian16 program package, using the M06-2X exchange-correlation functional53. Geometry optimizations were conducted using a mixed basis-set approach: the 6-311+G(d,p) basis set was applied to all elements excluding iodine54. Iodine was described using an effective core potential from the Stuttgart/Dresden group55. Solvent effects were accounted for using the polarizable continuum model, with water selected as the solvent56.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Qiong A. Wang
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity1,2,3,4,5. We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells)6. Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 (Rgs2), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.

Functional cellular heterogeneity is well documented in hepatocytes, driven by liver zonation7, and in muscle fibres, shaped by local environmental cues, particularly motor neuron activity8. Single-cell technologies have revealed extensive new patterns of heterogeneity of specific cell types within the same tissue9, yet their biological importance remains largely undetermined.

Thermogenic adipose tissue undergoes adaptive thermogenesis and is crucial for energy expenditure and thermoregulation1,2. Its specialized metabolism and precise responses to environmental and physiological stimuli make it an ideal model for studying functional cellular heterogeneity. Thermogenic capacity declines substantially with age in rodents and humans, leading to age-related cold sensitivity and metabolic disorders3,4,5, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

BAs and beige adipocytes mediate UCP1-dependent non-shivering thermogenesis10. Although substantial progress has been made in identifying the key pathways that activate thermogenesis, most studies have been conducted at the whole-tissue level, leaving the mechanisms governing its activation, maintenance and deactivation incompletely understood.

The heterogeneity of BAs within the same brown adipose tissue (BAT) and beige adipocyte cluster within inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) has been characterized by our group6 and others5,11,12,13,14. We found that BAs heterogeneously express UCP1 and classified those with low expression as BA-L cells and those with high expression as BA-H cells6. At room temperature, BA-H cells constitute 30–50% of all BAs; BA-H cells predominate after cold exposure, whereas BA-L cells predominate under thermoneutral conditions6. This raises questions of why BA heterogeneity exists, and whether it reflects random variation along a thermogenic continuum or spatially organized, tightly regulated states within the tissue.

Here we identify dynamic bistable regulation of BA heterogeneity controlled by the spatial proximity of BAs to IL-1β puncta through a neuronal–immune regulatory mechanism. This regulation becomes dysfunctional during ageing, leading to cold intolerance in older adults. These findings highlight how different cell types collectively control cellular heterogeneity in a spatiotemporal manner, integrating environmental and internal cues to regulate tissue metabolism and function.

Reanalysis of our previous single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset6 revealed enrichment of glucocorticoid signalling and GR-target genes in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Top BA-L-cell-enriched genes include H6pd, Rgs2 and thioredoxin-interacting protein (Txnip), whereas BA-H cells were enriched for thermogenesis-related genes, including Ucp1 and cytochrome c oxidase 6B1 (Cox6b1) (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,d–f). Nr3c1 was similarly expressed in BA-H and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f).

We generated Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice for inducible labelling of Ucp1+ cells by crossing the Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Rosa-stop-mT/mG mouse lines (Extended Data Fig. 2a). After 1 week of feeding on a doxycycline diet at room temperature (24 °C), GFP+ and GFP− BAs showed a patchy distribution (Fig. 1a), consistent with BA heterogeneity in AdipoChaser mice6. The Ucp1-rtTA mice used a relatively weak 5 kb Ucp1 promoter15 so GFP is only expressed in UCP1high-expressing BAs (BA-H cells), while Ucp1-cre mice have a strong bacterial artificial chromosome-based Ucp1 promoter that drives Cre expression in all BAs16. Immunofluorescence (IF) staining confirmed selective H6PD expression in BA-L cells (Fig. 1a); 50% of BAs were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD−, 45% were UCP1−(GFP−)H6PD+ and 5% were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD+ (Fig. 1b). Similar heterogeneity was observed in iWAT after 1 week of cold exposure (6 °C) (Fig. 1c), with 45% of these beige adipocytes being UCP1+H6PD−, 49% UCP1−H6PD+ and 6% UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1d). Human BAT showed a similar reciprocal UCP1 and H6PD pattern in multilocular brown–beige adipocytes (Fig. 1e), 45% of BAs were UCP1+H6PD−, 47% were UCP1−H6PD+ and 8% were UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1f). Western blotting confirmed more than twofold higher H6PD in BA-L cells than in BA-H cells and more than fourfold higher UCP1 in BA-H cells than in BA-L cells, while H6PD was enriched in mature BAs relative to in the stromal vascular fractions (SVFs) (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Together, these data identify H6PD as a BA-L marker.

To enable real-time labelling of BA-H cells, we generated Ucp1-mGFP knock-in mice by inserting a P2A-mGFP cassette after Ucp1 exon 6, immediately upstream of the stop codon (Extended Data Fig. 2d). These mice displayed robust BAT GFP fluorescence without altered UCP1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 2e,f). GFP IF staining revealed a heterogeneous distribution of GFP+ and GFP− BAs (Extended Data Fig. 2g). In vitro-cultured BAs and beige adipocytes showed selective H6PD expression in GFP− BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 2h), validating our in vivo findings.

We next investigated UCP1-independent thermogenesis through the futile creatine cycle17,18,19,20,21. Tissue-non-specific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP) and creatine kinase B (CKB) protein levels increased 4.8-fold and 2.5-fold, respectively, in BAT during cold exposure and were enriched 2.9-fold and 2.0-fold in BA-L cells versus in BA-H cells (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b), consistent with higher Ckb mRNA in BA-L cells6. IF staining further showed TNAP enrichment in BA-L cells (H6PDhigh BAs) in BAT and H6PDhigh beige adipocytes in cold-exposed iWAT (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). In vitro-differentiated BAs also displayed selective TNAP expression in BA-L cells (GFP− BAs) (Extended Data Fig. 3e), indicating that the futile creatine cycle is more active in BA-L cells.

Regarding the metabolic differences between BA-L cells and BA-H cells, BA-L cells have half the basal respiration, but similar maximal respiration compared to BA-H cells, indicating similarly high mitochondrial potential6. Using in vivo [U-13C]glucose tracing22, we recently showed that BAT has the most active glucose oxidation among metabolically active tissues, while in vitro tracing confirmed active glucose oxidation in differentiated BAs23. To characterize BA-L metabolism, we performed [U-13C] glucose and [U-13C] palmitate tracing in freshly isolated BA-H cells and BA-L cells, followed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Fully labelled (m+16) free palmitate (C16:0) was about twofold higher in BA-L cells, indicating greater fatty acid uptake (Extended Data Fig. 4b), while fully labelled total palmitate was sixfold higher, suggesting preferential fatty acids storage in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 4c). BA-L cells also showed lower citrate enrichment from both tracers, indicating lower glucose and fatty acid oxidation (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Thus, BA-L cells exhibit greater fatty acid uptake and accumulation but lower fatty acid and glucose oxidation, consistent with their lower basal respiration6.

We next examined whether H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L cells. H6PD depletion in BAs differentiated from BAT SVFs of Ucp1-mGFP mice increased Ucp1 expression sixfold (Fig. 1g), indicating that H6PD negatively regulates Ucp1. Conversely, H6pd overexpression by lentiviral injection into BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 4e,f) significantly reduced the proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 1i,j). Thus, H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L that regulates UCP1 expression and BA heterogeneity.

H6PD localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and generates endoplasmic reticulum-resident NADPH, distinct from cytosolic glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)24. H6PD primarily determines the reductase activity of endoplasmic reticulum-localized 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD11B1), which converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol25. GR protein levels were similar between BA-H cells and BA-L cells, indicating that GR signalling is not regulated by receptor abundance (Extended Data Fig. 3b). We next investigated whether GR signalling regulates UCP1 expression. Simultaneous treatment of BAs differentiated from the SVFs of wild-type (WT) mice with 11-dehydrocorticosterone (11-DHC), a natural substrate for active glucocorticoid biosynthesis25, and noradrenaline (NA) substantially increased UCP1 protein (Fig. 2a). However, 24 h 11-DHC pretreatment blunted NA-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2b). Thus, prolonged activation of GR signalling suppresses BA responsiveness to NA, maintaining BA-L cells in a stable, low-thermogenic status.
