The rice CR-eds1 mutant generated by CRISPR–Cas9 accumulated lower levels of jasmonic acid and salicylic acid (Fig. 5d) and expressed lower levels of COI1, NPR1 and ERF1 (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j). The induction of MYC2 expression in response to insect feeding was minimal in the rice CR-eds1 mutant (Fig. 5e). CR-eds1 plants were more vulnerable to C. medinalis (Fig. 5f and Extended Data Fig. 9k,l), demonstrating a vital role of rice EDS1 in insect resistance.

The immune activation phenotype of NIB1 overexpression was highly attenuated in the rice eds1-KO mutant and NIB1-triggered induction of defence genes PR1, MYC2, COI1, NPR1 and ERF1 was diminished in CR-eds1 rice plants (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 9m,n). Treatment with 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p induced the expression of PR1 and MYC2 in rice leaves, but this induction was compromised in NIB1-KO and CR-eds1 plants (Fig. 5h). Similarly, 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP treatment upregulated NbPR1 and NbMYC2 expression in wild-type N. benthamiana but not in NbGRP7-KO or N. benthamiana epss (eds1a, pad4, sag101a, sag101b) mutants (Fig. 5i). RNA-seq analyses of N. benthamiana wild-type, NbGRP7-KO and N. benthamiana epss leaves treated with 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP showed that the differential gene expression observed in wild-type N. benthamiana was largely absent in NbGRP7-KO and N. benthamiana epss mutants (Extended Data Fig. 9o,p). The upregulated genes were predominantly enriched in defence pathways (Extended Data Fig. 9q). These data demonstrate that EDS1 and NIB1 are important signalling components for the immune function of 2′,3′-cAMP.

Herbivore-induced endogenous 2′,3′-cAMP concentration reached around 21 μM in rice (Fig. 1g), comparable to the 50 μM concentration used in our assays. Treating N. benthamiana leaves with 21 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP for 6 h upregulated NbPR1 and NbMYC2 to similar levels as the 50 µM 2′,3′-cAMP treatment. Thus, the herbivore-induced endogenous accumulation of 2′,3′-cAMP is physiologically sufficient to elicit defence responses (Extended Data Fig. 9r). Exogenous application of 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP via spray significantly enhanced plant resistance against herbivory under both laboratory and paddy field conditions (Fig. 5j,k and Extended Data Fig. 9s).

Given that plant TIR proteins function as 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP synthases3, we tested whether the TIR-induced immunity also involves NIB1 or the orthologous GRP by expressing the TIR domain of Arabidopsis RPS4 (RPS4TIR) in NbGRP7-KO lines. Arabidopsis RPS4TIR-induced cell death in NbGRP7-KO leaves showed slight attenuation at 36 h post-infiltration (hpi) but became obvious and complete by 56 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 10a–c). The cell death triggered by the rice TIR-only protein OsTIR was also slightly attenuated in the NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO mutants when observed at 40 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 10d–g), with obvious cell death and completion at 68 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 10h). These results suggested a general role of GRP in sensing the 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated mono- and dinucleotides. In sum, our results show that GRPs sense the nuclease products of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, contributing to the activation of the EDS1-dependent signalling pathway (Fig. 5l).

Plants express many cell-surface and intracellular immune receptors to perceive alien molecules and activate defence38,39. Here we found that the rice GRP NIB1 interacts with invading RNaseT2 and senses 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p to induce plant defence. The presence of NVR1 orthologues in oral secretions of the piercing-sucking pest Apolygus lucorum (ALR1; data not shown) and chewing insect C. medinalis suggests that T2-family ribonuclease effectors are conserved across divergent feeding types and may be a broadly deployed strategy in plant–insect interactions. Given the involvement of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP in abiotic stresses40,41,42,43, it is worth further investigating the role of GRPs in leveraging biotic and abiotic stresses. Whether and how plants discriminate between different sources of second messengers are also important questions to address.

Condensates or membraneless compartments are engaged in a variety of plant developmental and stress response processes44,45,46,47. NIB1, as a sensor, perceives 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p and forms nuclear condensates that recruit the core immune regulator EDS135,36,37 and activate downstream signalling pathways, highlighting protein phase separation as a mechanism in response to second messengers. Our study focuses on the immune function of nuclear NIB1, whereas the biological roles of its cytoplasmic condensates deserve future investigation. Exogenous spraying of these RNA degradation-derived signalling molecules triggered plant defence responses, highlighting their application potential as immune activators. Our study opens a door for exploring the engagement of RNase products in plant defence, adaptation and development.

Plant TIR-catalysed and NAD+-derived products induces formation of EDS1–SAG101–NRG1 and EDS1–PAD4–ADR1 heterotrimers, as well as oligomerization of ADR1 and NRG1 as calcium channels at the plasma membrane, to confer immunity. The link between TIR nuclease-derived 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and EDS1 remains unclear, and the nuclear function of EDS1 in TIR-mediated immunity is unknown. Our unpublished data show that 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP does not contribute to the EDS1–SAG101–NRG1 or EDS1–PAD4–ADR1 heterotrimer formation, consistent with the proposed role of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP in amplifying rather than initiating TIR signalling3. In bacteria, 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP have been shown to modulate activities of transcription factors48. 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP-induced NIB1 condensate in the nucleus recruits EDS1 to trigger defence, potentially via transcriptional modulation, providing a possible explanation for the biological relevance of plant TIR nuclease activity. Plant TIR-only proteins but not TIR–NLR receptors possess nuclease activity—thus, TIR nuclease activity and 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP are likely to be involved in TIR-only-mediated basal immunity but not TIR–NLR-mediated effector-triggered immunity3,49, consistent with the weak contribution of GRPs towards TIR-induced cell death phenotypes in N. benthamiana. The T2 RNase NVR1 produces ApG>p, and the nuclease product spectrum of plant TIR-only proteins awaits further studies. Future studies could investigate whether other GRPs are also involved in perceiving such nuclease products and their interactions. Detailed analyses of NIB1 condensate components will add valuable knowledge to understanding this nuclease-based defence pathway.

Phytophagous insects, especially mesophyll feeders, generate various small molecules from biopolymers by injecting digestive enzymes into plant tissues, in addition to mechanical injury. Detection of DAMPs is essential for plants to activate defence programmes. Although the wide-scale cultivation of transgenic crops expressing Bacillus thuringiensis insecticidal proteins has effectively controlled the lepidopteran chewing insects in the field, heteropteran mesophyll feeders such as the mirid bug A. lucorum (Miridae) and the green stink bug N. viridula (Pentatomidae), are less sensitive to these proteins and are emerging as a threat to agriculture50. Our findings show that plant GRP is a sensor of the invading RNase products and orchestrates immune responses to activate an EDS1-dependent signalling pathway, providing a potential target for advanced plant protection technologies.

Rice plants (Oryza sativa L. subsp. japonica cv. ZH11) grown in experimental fields in Shanghai or Hainan, or under controlled greenhouse conditions, were used for stable transformation and CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene knockout. To generate overexpression lines, the cDNAs of NVR1 and NIB1 (transcript ID: Os03t0670700-04) were introduced into the pCAMBIA1300 vector under the control of the CaMV 35S promoter, or as indicated. DNA sequences were analysed using SnapGene 6.0.2. Following transformation, more than ten independent overexpression lines were obtained for both NVR1 and NIB1. The NIB1-KO rice mutants, as well as N. benthamiana NbGRP7-KO plants, were generated by WIMI Biotechnology. NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO lines were generated by Wuhan BioRun Biosciences. For transient expression assays, leaves from 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants grown in a greenhouse at 22 °C under long-day conditions (16 h light:8 h dark) with a photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) of 112.81 μmol m−2 s−1.

N. viridula was collected from the Hangzhou farm, Zhejiang Academy of Agricultural Sciences, and reared on kidney beans and corn in a growth chamber at ~28 °C. C. medinalis was at first collected from the experimental farm in Songjiang, Shanghai, China in 2022. To maintain genetic homogeneity and sensitivity, the insects were continuously laboratory-reared for more than 15 generations without pesticide exposure. Larvae were reared on fresh wheat seedlings, and adults were supplied with a 15% honey solution. The colony was maintained under strictly controlled conditions at 26 °C with 12 h light:12 h dark photoperiod.

N. viridula saliva was collected using a Parafilm sachet feeding assay. Following a 24-h starvation period, 20 adult N. viridula were supplied with 1 ml of 2.5% sucrose solution encapsulated within Parafilm membranes. After 24 h of feeding, the saliva-containing sucrose solution was collected and concentrated using Amicon Ultra-0.5 centrifugal filter devices (Millipore). Salivary proteins were mixed with 4× SDS loading buffer, denatured at 95 °C for 10 min, and separated by SDS–PAGE. The salivary proteome was subsequently analysed via LC–MS/MS (Novogene) (Supplementary Table 1).

The constructed vectors were introduced into A. tumefaciens strain GV3101 (pSoup-p19). After cultivation in medium at 30 °C overnight, the bacteria were collected and resuspended in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM MES, 150 μM acetosyringone, pH 5.8), and incubated at room temperature for 2–3 h. The bacterial suspensions were adjusted to OD600 = 0.6 and infiltrated to the leaves of 4-week N. benthamiana with needleless syringe. For co-expression, equal volumes of Agrobacterium suspensions (adjusted to an OD600 of 1.0) carrying the respective constructs were mixed for co-infiltration.

The protein coding sequences for His- and GST-tagged proteins were cloned into pColdTF/pET-28a and pGEX-4T vectors, respectively, and expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) pLysS cells. Cultures were grown in LB medium at 37 °C to OD600 of 0.5, followed by induction with 0.5 mM IPTG at 15 °C for 16 h. Cells were collected, lysed by sonification in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, pH 8.0) and centrifuged at 20,000g for 30 min at 4 °C. For His-tagged proteins, the supernatant was loaded onto Ni-NTA resin, washed with a wash buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole, pH 8.0), and subsequently eluted with an elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). For the purification of GST-tagged proteins, the supernatant was incubated with Glutathione Sepharose 4B resin, washed with lysis buffer (140 mM NaCl, 27 mM KCl, 10 mM Na2HPO4, 1.8 mM KH2PO4), and eluted with the same buffer supplemented with 10 mM reduced glutathione. To obtain nucleic acid-free NIB1–YFP, recombinant protein-expressing E. coli cells were collected and resuspended in cold TBS (20 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.6) at 9 ml per gram of wet cells. TieChui E. coli Lysis Buffer (ACE Biotechnology) was added at one-ninth of the suspension volume, followed by incubation at 4 °C for 10 min to lyse the cells and digest bacterial DNA and RNA. After centrifugation at 20,000g at 4 °C, the clarified supernatant was subjected to affinity purification.

To investigate potential protein–protein interactions, coding sequences were cloned into JW772-35S-cLUC or JW771-35S-nLUC. The constructs were introduced into Agrobacterium GV3101 (pSoup-p19), and the bacterial cultures were co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves as described above. After 48 h of transformation, fluorescence was detected and imaged using the Tanon Chemi Dog 5200T Imaging System to visualize protein interactions.

The interacting protein candidates were co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves for 48 h. The leaves were collected, homogenized in liquid nitrogen and suspended in IP lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 20% glycerol, 0.5% NP-40, 1×protease inhibitor cocktail). The mixture was centrifuged at 14,000g for 10 min. The supernatant was incubated with GFP magnetic beads for 2 h at 4 °C and then washed 5 times in IP lysis buffer. Beads were boiled at 95 °C in 50 μl 4× SDS loading buffer for 10 min and analysed by immunoblotting. Measurements were repeatedly taken from separate lysates to confirm repeatability.

For immunoblotting, proteins were separated by 4–20% SDS–PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. After blocking with 5% (w/v) non-fat milk, the membranes were incubated with the following primary antibodies: mouse anti-DDK (Flag) monoclonal antibody (ZSGB-BIO, TA-05, clone OTI11C3, lot no. 230021225; 1:2,000), mouse anti-His monoclonal antibody (OriGene, TA150088, clone OTI2B5; 1:5,000), mouse anti-plant actin monoclonal antibody (ABclonal, AC009, clone AMC0496, lot no. 9100009001; 1:5,000), horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated rabbit anti-Myc-tag monoclonal antibody (ABclonal, AE102, clone ARC5004-12-HRP, lot no. 3523030201; 1:5,000), rabbit anti-GFP-tag polyclonal antibody (ABclonal, AE011, clone N/A, lot no. 3560104011, RRID: AB_2771922; 1:2,000), rabbit anti-β-actin monoclonal antibody (ABclonal, AC026, clone ARC5115-01; 1:10,000), rabbit anti-histone H3 monoclonal antibody (HUABIO, ET1701-64, clone JJ090-07, lot no. H641565025; 1:5,000), rabbit anti-PEPC polyclonal antibody (Agrisera, AS09 458, lot no. 2410; 1:2,000), or a custom rabbit anti-NVR1 polyclonal antibody generated for this study by ABclonal Technology (1:500). For unconjugated primary antibodies, the membranes were subsequently incubated, as appropriate, with HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (ZSGB-BIO, ZB-2305, lot no. 219760308; 1:10,000) or HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) (ZSGB-BIO, ZB-2301, lot no. 242521208; 1:10,000). Chemiluminescent signals were detected using ECL reagents and imaged with a Tanon 5200T Imaging System.

The YFP-tagged protein was immunoprecipitated using GFP magnetic beads at 4 °C for 2 h. After washing the beads 5 times with IP lysis buffer, the bead-bound proteins were treated with 10 mM TCEP and 50 mM CAA (in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate) at 95 °C for 10 min.

Samples were prepared via a filter-aided sample preparation method using Vivacon 500 filters (10,000 MWCO; Sartorius), sequentially washed with 8 M urea and 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and digested overnight with 1 μg of trypsin (Promega). Following desalting with Pierce C18 Spin Tips (Thermo Fisher Scientific), peptides were dried by centrifugation at 10 °C, reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid, and subjected to LC–MS/MS analysis.

LC–MS/MS analysis was performed using a timsTOF Pro 2 mass spectrometer coupled to a nanoElute liquid chromatography system (Bruker Daltonics). In brief, 200 ng of peptides were separated on a reversed-phase analytical column (25 cm × 75 µm internal diameter, IonOpticks) over a 60-min gradient at a flow rate of 300 nl min−1 and a column temperature of 50 °C. The mobile phases consisted of buffer A (0.1% formic acid in water) and buffer B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile). The gradient elution profile was set as follows: an increase to 22% buffer B from 0 to 45 min, up to 37% buffer B from 45 to 50 min, and a final step at 80% buffer B from 50 to 60 min. The mass spectrometer was operated in DDA-PASEF mode with the following parameters: capillary voltage, 1,500 V; dry gas flow, 3.0 l min−1; and drying temperature, 180 °C. The collision energy was linearly ramped as a function of ion mobility.

The raw LC–MS/MS data were searched against the N. benthamiana protein sequence database (Nbe_v1.1_pep.fa.gz), downloaded from NbenBase (https://nbenthamiana.jp/downloads), using MSFragger within FragPipe v22.0. Trypsin was specified as the digestion enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages. Precursor and fragment ion mass tolerances were set to 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine (+57.021 Da) was set as a fixed modification, whereas methionine oxidation (+15.995 Da) was included as a variable modification. Peptide and protein identifications were filtered to a 1% false discovery rate using a target-decoy strategy (Supplementary Tables 3, 6 and 7).

His–TF and His–TF–NIB1 were incubated with 15 μl of Ni-NTA resin for 1 h at 4 °C. Protein extracts from leaves expressing EDS1–Flag were added to each resin and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The resin was washed 6 times with IP lysis buffer, resuspended in 50 μl of 4× SDS loading buffer and heated at 95 °C for 10 min. Bound proteins were analysed by immunoblotting.

Target coding sequences were cloned into pCAMBIA1300S-cYFP or pCAMBIA1300S-nYFP. Following co-expression of the fusion proteins in N. benthamiana leaves for 2 days, YFP signals were acquired by 20× water immersion objective through Leica TCS SP8 STED 3X.

MST was used to determine the protein–protein interactions and the binding affinities of NIB1 and its mutated versions to the indicated small molecules or RNA, protein labelling was performed in strict accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, the purified recombinant proteins (NIB1–GST, NIB1(R49A)–GST, NIB1(G50A)–GST and NIB1(4A)–GST) at a concentration of 10 μM were labelled with NT–647–NHS using the Monolith Protein Labeling Kit RED-NHS 2nd Generation (NanoTemper Technologies). The labelled NIB1–GST and its mutants were adjusted to 50 nM in PBST buffer (PBS, with 0.05% Tween-20) and 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p (5 μM to 0.000153 μM) were added separately. For characterizing the interaction between NVR1 and NIB1 (NIB1RRM and NIB1GRR), 10 μM NVR1–TF was labelled and adjusted to 40 nM in PBST buffer. Subsequently, NIB1–GST, NIB1RRM–GST and NIB1GRR–GST (2.5 μM to 0.0000763 μM) were added separately. For protein–RNA interaction, the Cy5-labelled FLS2 3′-UTR served as the target and adjusted to 20 nM. NIB1–GST and the mutant fusions (10 μM to 0.000306 μM) were incubated with target. To access the interaction between NIB1(ΔIDR) and 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P, the labelled NIB1(ΔIDR) was used as target and adjusted to 50 nM. The target protein was independently mixed with 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P (10 μM to 0.000306 μM). Furthermore, to test the binding affinity of NIB1–GST with 3′,5′-cAMP, 3′,5′-cGMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP, GMP and the unrelated cyclic dinucleotides 2′,3′-cGAMP, 50 nM labelled NIB1–GST was used as target and independently mixed with the indicated compounds (15 μM to 0.000458 μM). A Microscale Thermophoresis Monolith NT.115 instrument (NanoTemper Technologies). was used to measure binding reactions at 25 °C, 40% MST power and 20% LED power. Measurements were repeatedly taken repeatedly from separate protein preparations to confirm repeatability. The curve was fitted using the MO.AffinityAnalysis_x86_2.3.0.7385, and the dissociation constant (Kd) value was determined.

NIB1–YFP fusion protein and its various mutants were purified by Ni-NTA resin. NIB1–YFP droplets with 10% PEG 8000, or as specifically indicated, were observed by Leica TSC SP8 STED 3× 100× oil immersion objective. The droplets were bleached by 100% intensity 488 nm laser and the recovery was recorded every 3 s 290 ms for 50 frames in FRAP. Fusion of NIB1 droplets was recorded through time-lapse photography. Droplet diameters were measured from microscopy images using Fiji (ImageJ, version 1.54f).

Target proteins fused with fluorescent protein (YFP or mCherry) were co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves. Condensates in leaves were observed by Leica TSC SP8 STED 3X (Leica) 40 × oil immersion objective. To prevent fluorescence bleed-through during imaging, all images were acquired using the sequential scanning mode on a Leica TCS SP8 confocal microscope. YFP was excited with a 488 nm laser and detected at 498–540 nm, and mCherry was independently excited with a 561 nm laser and detected at 600–630 nm. The images of condensates were analysed using Fiji (ImageJ, version 1.54f). Line profile analysis was performed to evaluate co-localization of the proteins. To quantify the partition coefficient of the EDS1–mCherry into NIB1–YFP condensates with or without NVR1, regions of interest of equivalent size were analysed. The partition coefficient (Kp) was defined as the ratio of intracondensate EDS1 fluorescence intensity to that of the extracondensate background.

The Cy5-labelled AttRNAser (83 nt) used as substrate for NVR1 digestion was obtained through in vitro transcription using T7 RiboMAX Express RNAi System. A reaction mixture containing 0.5 mM Cy5-UTP and 1 mM synthesized AttRNAser DNA template (sequence listed in Supplementary Table 13) were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. The template DNAs were then removed by 0.5 μl RNase-Free DNase (Promega) at 37 °C for 30 min. In the RNase activity assay, 2 μM Cy5-AttRNAser was incubated with 0.02 μM NVR1 in buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 5 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 1 mM ATP, 0.5 μl RNase Inhibitor at 25 °C for 20 min. The reaction was stopped by 400 μl stop solution (40 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 and 500 mM NaCl). Then RNAs were purified with PCIA solution (phenol:chloroform:isopentyl alcohol, 25:24:1) and the RNA pellet was resuspended in 1× TBE urea loading buffer. The RNA was then separated using 16% urea polyacrylamide gels at 150 V for 90 min and subsequently detected with a Amersham Typhoon 5.

Cy5-labelled FLS2 3′-UTR were synthesized in vitro using the HyperScribe T7 High Yield Cy5 RNA Labeling Kit (APExBIO) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, the 3′-UTR sequence of FLS2, as previously described44, was amplified using a forward primer containing a T7 promoter sequence (TAATACGACTCACTATAGGGGAAGTTTAGCAGCAAAGC) and a reverse primer (GTTCATCAAAACCAAATTTC). One microgram of DNA template containing a T7 promoter was combined in a 20 μl reaction volume. The reaction mixture consisted of 2 μl of 10× Reaction Buffer, 2 μl of T7 RNA Polymerase Mix, 2 mM each of ATP, GTP, and CTP, 1.5 mM UTP and 0.5 mM Cy5-UTP. The reaction was thoroughly mixed and incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. Following transcription, the DNA template was digested by adding 1 μl of DNase I and incubating at 37 °C for 15 min. The synthesized Cy5-labelled RNA was subsequently purified via phenol/chloroform extraction and ethanol precipitation. To evaluate the labelling efficiency, the absorbance of the purified RNA was measured at 260 nm and the Cy5 maximum excitation wavelength using NanoDrop.

Cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions were extracted according to the manufacturer’s manual instructions of Minute Cytoplasmic and Nuclear Extraction Kit for Cells. In brief, leaves (0.1 g, co-expressing NIB1–YFP and EDS1–mCherry with or without NVR1 for 48 h) were homogenized in cytoplasmic extraction buffer. Following centrifugation (14,000g, 5 min, 4 °C), the cytoplasmic supernatant was collected. The pellet was lysed in nuclear extraction buffer through repeated cycle of vortexing and ice incubation, and then centrifuged through a pre-chilled filter cartridge (14,000g, 30 s) to collect the nuclear extract. Histone H3 and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) served as nuclear and cytoplasmic markers, respectively, to confirm successful fractionation.

Leaves were incubated in DAB solution (1 mg ml−1 DAB, 0.05% Tween-20, 10 mM Na2HPO4, pH 5.8) for 4–5 h in the dark. Bleaching buffer (ethanol:acetate:glycerol, 3:1:1) was added to displace DAB stain, and the sample was heated to 90–95 °C 3–5 times until the chlorophyll was removed completely. The samples were immersed in 50% glycerol for imaging.

RNaseT2 proteins were filtrated from the genomes of plants (Gossypium hirsutum, Nicotiana tobacum, O. sativa), fungi (Fusarium graminearum, M. oryzae), insects (N. viridula, A. lucorum, Nilaparvata lugens, Aphis gossypii, C. medinalis, H. armigera) and mammals (Homo sapiens and Rattus norvegicus) using PF00445 HMM search or NCBI blastp. The GRPs (GRPIVa) encoded in genomes of 18 plant species of 14 families (Physcomitrella patens, Adiantum capillus, Cycas revoluta, Picea abies, Nymphaea colorata, O. sativa, Zea mays, Sorghum bicolor, Brachypodium distachyon, G. hirsutum, Arabidopsis thaliana, Vitis vinifera, Carica papaya, Cucumis sativus, Glycine max, Solanum lycopersicum, Solanum tuberosum and Populus trichocarpa) were filtrated under the condition of only one PF00076 domain. The genomes were obtained from Phytozome (https://phytozome-next.jgi.doe.gov/) or NCBI (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/), and insect proteomes were obtained from the NCBI Protein database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/protein/). All filtrated proteins in these two classes were aligned by MUSCLE 5.1, trimmed using trimAl 1.2. The phylogenetic tree was constructed by using IQ-TREE 2.2.0 and annotated by Evolview v3. Conservation diagram of amino acid residues was shown using Jalview 2.11.2.5.

Total RNA was extracted from leaves of ~4-week-old wild-type O. sativa ZH11 and transgenic lines, as indicated. Leaves of four-week-old tobacco (N. benthamiana) were infiltrated with 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP for 6 h, followed by RNA extraction. RNA-seq was performed by Personalbio. Clean reads were aligned to the O. sativa reference genome (GCF_001433935.1_IRGSP-1.0_genomic.fna; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_001433935.1/) or the N. benthamiana reference genome (Niben.genome.v1.0.1; https://solgenomics.net/ftp/genomes/Nicotiana_benthamiana/assemblies/) using HISAT2. Differential gene expression analysis was subsequently performed using DESeq, with differentially expressed genes identified based on the thresholds of |log2(fold change)| > 1 and P < 0.05. GO enrichment and volcano plots were generated using R v4.3.2 in RStudio 2023.09.1. The differentially expressed genes and corresponding GO enrichment results are provided in Supplementary Tables 2, 4, 5, 8–12.

The third-instar C. medinalis larvae were placed on leaves of the 12-day-old rice seedlings of the indicated lines. Larval weight was recorded after the feeding for three days. Oviposition selection assay was conducted in nylon mesh cages (90 × 70 × 90 cm). Three one-month-old, uniform rice plants per genotype were grouped and arranged triangularly to prevent positional bias. 15 pairs of newly emerged moths were mated for 48 h. Subsequently, males were removed, and the 15 mated females were released into the cage centre with a 15% honey solution. After 24 h of oviposition at 26 °C (12 h:12 h light:dark photoperiod), the total number of eggs laid on the three plants of each genotype was summed. The assay was repeated with three independent cages. Oviposition preference was quantified by the oviposition index: OI = (T − C)/(T + C), where T and C are the number of eggs in the mutants and wild type, respectively. The deviation of the oviposition index against 0 was tested using a one-sample Student’s t-test.

For larval feeding preference, leaf segments (3 cm) from 3 plant lines were arranged equidistantly in a circle within a Petri dish. Ten third-instar larvae (pre-starved for 2 h) were introduced to the centre. After 1 h of selection in darkness, the number of larvae settled on each plant was recorded. The selection rate was calculated as Ntarget/Ntotal selection × 100%, where Ntarget and Ntotal selection represent the number of larvae on a specific plant and the total number of larvae making a definitive choice, respectively.

For field test, wild-type ZH11 seeds were sown in soil, and 35-day-old plants were transplanted into six 1 m × 1 m field plots. Each plot was surrounded by two rows of rice plants serving as buffer rows, and all six plots were maintained within mesh enclosure. Four weeks after transplantation, the plots were arranged in an alternating pattern and sprayed with either water or 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP. Following treatment, 20 mated female C. medinalis moths were released at the centre of the enclosure. Once rolled-leaf shelters became visible, the number of shelters was counted. Insects and plant positions were randomized in laboratory assays, field treatments followed an alternating design, and outcomes were assessed blind to genotype or treatment.

Leaves tissue of 4-week-old rice plants were ground into powder with liquid nitrogen and resuspended in 500 μl ethyl acetate. Following vortex for 1 min and centrifugation at 14,000g for 10 min at 4°C, the supernatant was transferred and dried in vacuum concentrator and resuspended in 30 μl 30% (v/v) methanol. The samples were centrifuged at 14,000g for 15 min and the supernatant was applied to the LC–MS/MS on a QTRAP 6500+ mass spectrometer (AB SCIEX) for analysis. Salicylic acid samples were diluted to 1/100 with 30% (v/v) methanol.

Leaf sheath segments of 2 mm were excised from 2-week-old rice seedlings and pre-incubated overnight in sterile distilled water. The samples were then treated with water or purified recombinant His–NVR1 protein in buffer containing 20 μM luminol and 10 μg ml−1 HRP. Luminescence was recorded at 1-min intervals for 100 min with Varioskan Flash multireader (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

NVR1 (1 μM) and the rRNA substrate (2 μg) were incubated in a 20-μl reaction mixture at 25 °C for 25 min. The reaction was stopped by adding methanol, and the mixture was centrifuged at 12,000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected and analysed by liquid chromatography–high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC–HRMS) using a Q Exactive quadrupole-Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometer coupled to a Dionex Ultimate 3000 RSLC (HPG) ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography system. The injection volume was 1 μl. The samples were separated on an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column with a particle size of 1.8 μm. The mobile phase were water (A) and methanol (B), each containing ammonium formate (2 mM). The gradient elution was set as follows: 0–6.5 min, 2% methanol; 6.5–8.5 min, 20% methanol; 8.5–11 min, 98% methanol; 11.1–15.0 min, 2% methanol. The flow rate was consistently set to 0.40 ml min−1, and the column temperature was precisely maintained at 40 °C. Detection was performed in positive-ion mode using a heated electrospray ionization source. LC–HRMS data were analysed using Thermo Scientific Xcalibur 4.1.50.

Extraction of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP was performed as described3. Leaf tissue was ground into powder with liquid nitrogen. Samples were resuspended in 600 μl 4% acetate containing 1 mM IBMX and vortexed for 2 min. The supernatant was extracted twice with 800 μl chloroform. The samples were dried through vacuum spinning and resuspended in 50 μl sterile water.

The dissolved samples were subjected to analysis by LC–MS/MS on a QTRAP 6500+ mass spectrometer (AB SCIEX) coupled to an Agilent 1290 LC system. Chromatographic separation was achieved using a Waters XSelect HSS T3 column with a particle size of 2.5 μm and dimensions of 100 mm × 3.0 mm. Sample of 1 μl was injected. The mobile phase consisted of water (A) and methanol (B), both containing 2 mM ammonium formate. The gradient elution method was used as follows: 0–2.5 min, 2% B; 2.5–3.0 min, 2–70% B; 3.0–5.0 min, 70–99% B; 5.0–7.0 min, 99% B; 7.1–10 min, 2% B. The flow rate was set at 0.4 ml min−1, and the column temperature was maintained at 40 °C. Metabolites were detected using electrospray ionization in negative ion mode with multiple reaction monitoring. The mass spectrometer parameters were as follows: −4,500 V of capillary voltage, 500 °C of source temperature, 50 psi of ion source gas 1 (GS1) and gas 2 (GS2), and 35 psi of curtain gas. Data acquisition and analysis were performed using Analyst 1.6.3 software (AB SCIEX).

Step 1. To a stirred solution of 2′,3′-O-isopropylideneguanosine (1.0 eq) in anhydrous tetrahydrofuran (THF) at 0 °C under an inert atmosphere, trimethylsilyl chloride (TMSCl) (1.0 eq) was introduced, followed by the dropwise addition of pyridine (2.5 eq). The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 2 h. Next, isobutyryl chloride (1.0 eq) was added dropwise at 0–5 °C, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature for an additional 1 h. After quenching and extraction, the crude product was obtained and purified by C18 flash chromatography. The final product was characterized by LC–MS and 1H NMR spectroscopy for structural confirmation. Step 2. To a stirred solution of the Step 1 product (1.0 eq) and starting compound 2 (1.0 eq, CAS: 104992-55-4) in dichloromethane (DCM) at 0 °C, 5-(benzylthio)-1H-tetrazole (5-BTT) (1.0 eq) was added. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 3 h. Reaction solution washed water and brine, the DCM solution was concentrated under vacuum, the crude by C18 flash purification. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 3. To a stirred solution of iodine (1.0 eq) in a THF:water:pyridine mixture (10:5:1, v/v/v), the Step 2 product was added at room temperature. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 1 h, followed by the addition of 10% sodium sulfite solution until the colour disappeared. The reaction mixture was then concentrated under vacuum, and the residue was extracted with ethyl acetate. The organic layer was dried over anhydrous Na2SO4, filtered, and concentrated under vacuum. The crude product was used directly in the next step without further purification. Confirmed by LC–MS and 31P NMR. Step 4. To a stirred solution of the Step 3 product (1.0 eq) in DCM, trifluoroacetic acid was added at room temperature. The reaction mixture was stirred at 45 °C for 4 h. After completion, the solution was concentrated under vacuum. Due to the product’s high water solubility, the residue was purified directly by C18 flash chromatography. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 5. To a stirred solution of the Step 4 product (1.0 eq) in acetonitrile, N-methylmorpholine (1.0 eq), 2-methoxy-1-ethanesulfonyl chloride (2.0 eq), trimetaphosphate tri-tetrabutylammonium salt (1.0 eq), 1H-4(5)-nitroimidazole (0.1 eq), and DBU (3.0 eq) were added sequentially under nitrogen protection. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature until completion. MgCl2 (2.0 eq) was then added, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature. After completion, the solvent was concentrated under vacuum, and water was added to the residue to adjust the pH to 3–4. The mixture was extracted with ethyl acetate, washed, dried, and concentrated to obtain the crude product, which was further purified by preparative HPLC and lyophilization. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 6. To a stirred solution of the Step 5 product (1.0 e) in THF, HF (6.0 eq) was added at room temperature. The reaction mixture was stirred at 50 °C until completion. Triethylamine was then added to the residue to adjust the pH to 6–7, and the mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure to obtain the crude product. The crude product was purified by preparative HPLC and lyophilization. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 7. To a stirred solution of the Step 6 product (1.0 eq) in methanol (10 volumes), NH3/methanol (10.0 eq) was added at 0 °C. The reaction mixture was stirred at 0 °C for 6 h until completion. The methanol solution was then concentrated under vacuum and the residue was purified by preparative HPLC followed by lyophilization. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR.

NIB1–GST was incubated with 10 μl of glutathione agarose resin at 4 °C for 2 h. Empty vector (encoding TF tag) or NVR1 products were added to the resin for an overnight incubation at 4 °C. Then the resin was treated with 100 μl of 80% acetonitrile and 5% formic acid and incubated at 25 °C for 30 min before proceeding with liquid chromatography analysis.

The 12-day-old rice seedlings were sprayed with 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP, 8-Br-2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p for 6 h, with water and 8-Br-AMP as controls. After treatment, RNA was extracted, and the expression levels of defence genes were analysed by RT–qPCR. Leaves of 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants were infiltrated with 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP for 6 h, and gene expression was analysed by RT–qPCR.

AlphaFold2 was used to predict the structure of the NVR1–NIB1 complex. The 3D structures of 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP were obtained from PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), and ApG>p was modelled using ChemBioDraw Ultra 14.0. The ligands were optimized using density functional theory (DFT) in Gaussian 16 and prepared for docking with NIB1 using AutoDockTools 1.5.7. Molecular docking was performed using AutoDock 4.2.6 with ligand-specific grid boxes at a spacing of 0.375 Å. Grid dimensions were adjusted to 46 × 50 × 50 for 2′,3′-cAMP, 50 × 56 × 56 for 2′,3′-cGMP and 100 × 100 × 100 for ApG>p. The Lamarckian genetic algorithm was applied with 50 runs, a population size of 150 and 2.5 × 106 energy evaluations. The lowest-energy poses were analysed using PyMOL 2.5.5 and LigPlot+ 2.2.8.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software). Comparisons between two groups were performed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. For comparisons among multiple groups, one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s or Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test was used, as appropriate. Two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test or the two-stage linear step-up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger and Yekutieli was performed, as indicated in the figure legends. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05, with a false discovery rate of 5% for analyses using the Benjamini–Krieger–Yekutieli procedure. For violin plots, width indicates data density, lines show the median and quartiles, and dots represent individual values. Details of the statistical tests are provided in the corresponding figure legends.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Ignazio Maria Viola
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource1. However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs2,3. Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.

The global imperative to transition towards sustainable energy systems has intensified research and development in renewable energy technologies. Among these, tidal energy presents a uniquely predictable and substantial resource. Unlike other renewables such as wind and solar, tidal currents are governed by an astronomical cycle, which offers a consistent and forecastable power source4,5. The scale of this resource is significant. Tidal power is estimated at 50 TW h yr−1 in Europe6 and as much as 220 TW h yr−1 in the USA alone7. Near-term deployment targets are 1 GW by 2035 in the UK3, with international roadmaps project deployments eventually exceeding 300 GW worldwide by 20508. These highlight the potential of tidal energy in contributing to energy security and renewable energy portfolios.

Despite their promise, the harsh hydrodynamic environment presents an important barrier to the economic viability of this renewable energy source. A primary challenge is the hydrodynamic load fluctuations that arise from large variations in flow velocity, turbulence, turbine yaw with respect to the incoming stream, velocity shear along the water depth2, wave-induced oscillating currents9, and wake interaction within turbine arrays10. These fluctuating loads are a primary design consideration and are associated with accelerated fatigue, reduced operational lifespans and unplanned downtime. These reliability concerns result in blade and turbine designs with high capital costs, which directly increase the levelized cost of energy (LCOE)3.

To address the challenge of the dynamic loads, various mitigation strategies have been developed. Active control typically deploys systems to actively regulate the pitch11 or camber12 of the blades, therefore, to regulate power output, control mean loads and improve start-up performance. Although the active control systems are effective in certain operational envelopes, the reliability of sophisticated sensors and actuators in the harsh undersea environment remains a concern. Furthermore, the response times of the activator limit effectiveness against rapid, high-frequency load fluctuations13,14.

To address these concerns, there has been an increased focus on developing passive control mechanisms. Passive control is mainly realized in two ways: introducing changes in the blade pitch or modifying the blade camber. Passive pitch control involves designing blades that can rotate around their spanwise axis in response to changing hydrodynamic loads, thereby altering their angle of attack. This is typically achieved by incorporating a pre-loaded torsional spring mechanism at the blade root. Theoretical work in refs. 15,16 are among the first to introduce the concept. Both demonstrated that complete cancellation of the load fluctuation is possible without compromising the mean power. This is followed by a numerical study in ref. 17, which confirmed more than 80% load fluctuations can be reduced in sheared flow conditions, with additional benefits such as faster wake recovery, which improves turbine array performance. Reference 18 has contributed a general framework for the design of passive pitching systems, identifying the locations of the pivot point for maximizing load mitigation. Experimental validations in ref. 19 have confirmed the ability of passive pitching systems in the reduction of time-averaged loadings.

Passive pitching systems are effective for low-frequency, large-scale adjustments and power regulation by adjusting the global angle of attack of the blades. However, the added inertia due to the displacement of the pitching axis required by effective pitching systems, as well as the bearing friction, limits the response of the system to high-frequency disturbances, such as turbulent eddies or rapid shear variations. Moreover, despite being simpler than active control systems, passive pitch blades still introduce extra moving parts and potential failure points in harsh undersea environments. Research has identified that for wind turbine applications, most of the failures originate from the pitch system20, highlighting the significant operational advantage of a robust, passive design.

An alternative design philosophy can be found in nature, where organisms from fish to trees passively reconfigure their shape through distributed material compliance to manage fluid dynamic forces21,22. Drawing from these biological principles, passive morphing flexible blades offer an alternative strategy, where flexibility is distributed along the blade, allowing each blade section to adapt automatically through fluid–structure interaction. Therefore, a faster response time can be achieved with a fixed-pitch blade that does not require hinges and bearings. Passive morphing blades are common in wind energy applications23,24, in which the blade twists to feather in response to a wind gust. This technique, known as aeroelastic tailoring, requires ad hoc structural design, whose scalability and reliability for large tidal turbines is yet to be demonstrated. In fact, for similar power-rated turbines, the bending moment experienced by tidal turbines is higher than that of wind turbines. Therefore, the need for a scalable, reliable, passive system that can mitigate both rapid, localized turbulent fluctuations and slower, large-scale changes in inflow velocity on large-scale tidal turbines remains unmet.

This study directly addresses this challenge by proposing a blade with chordwise flexibility, rather than spanwise flexibility, as in aeroelastic tailoring. The frontal and thickest part of the blade, which provides structural integrity, is rigid. Instead, the trailing edge is flexible from root to tip. Specifically, we provide the first comprehensive experimental demonstration that a carefully designed chordwise-flexible blade can achieve both control of the mean power and thrust with the quasi-steady variations of flow velocities over the tidal cycle (for example, the diurnal tidal cycle) and mitigation of the high-frequency (turbulence) hydrodynamic load fluctuations on tidal turbines, while enabling the same yield as a conventional rigid blade equipped with active pitch control. To demonstrate this potential, we experimentally evaluated the performance of these chordwise-flexible blades against a rigid baseline in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh. The turbine was tested across a range of nominal inflow velocities u∞ = 0.5–1.0 m s−1, and tip-speed ratios (λ) from 3 to 9, with the flexible blades designed for optimal performance at u∞ ≈ 0.85 m s−1. Our analysis first addresses the low-frequency load mitigation over a tidal cycle before examining the high-frequency load fluctuations and the underlying physical mechanisms of the deformation of the blade. Overall, we demonstrated a new pathway to enhance turbine reliability and survivability, reducing capital costs associated with the active pitch system, and reducing maintenance costs by removing hinges, bearings and actuators, ultimately reducing the LCOE.

The structural design of a tidal turbine is primarily dictated by low-frequency loads, which, in this context, refers to the quasi-steady hydrodynamic loads that change as the mean inflow velocity varies over a tidal cycle. To investigate the potential for load control in this regime, the time-averaged performance of the flexible blades was compared against a rigid baseline. Figure 1 shows the time-averaged power (CP), thrust (CT), and root bending moment (CM) coefficients as a function of tip-speed ratio λ, at all tested inflow velocities. The results demonstrate that the introduction of blade flexibility does not compromise the primary function of energy capture of the turbine. As shown in Fig. 1a, at the rated velocity (uR = 0.878 m s−1) and above, the power coefficient of the flexible blade closely matches that of the rigid blade, achieving a comparable peak CP of approximately 0.37. Notably, the limited value of the maximum CP of both the rigid and flexible blades compared with full-scale state-of-the-art turbines is due to the low Reynolds number at which the model-scale turbines were tested (Methods).

The key advantage of the flexible blade design is its ability to passively regulate peak loadings. At the rated velocity, the thrust coefficient of the flexible blade is comparable to that of the rigid blade near the optimal power-producing tip-speed ratio (λ ≈ 5.5−6), as shown in Fig. 1b. However, the performance of the flexible blades diverges from rigid ones for λ values beyond this optimal range. This high λ region is typically explored by the turbine control strategy to cap power when inflow velocity exceeds the rated velocity. Under these conditions, the flexible blade thrust passively decreases, whereas the rigid one increases. This demonstrates a load-shedding mechanism that can protect the turbine structure during the most demanding high-flow conditions and will be discussed in detail in the next section, in which we simulate the power and thrust a tidal turbine experiences over a tidal cycle. However, at off-design conditions, the flexible blade exhibits higher CT and CM values than at its design speed. While this results in higher thrust coefficients at lower velocities, the absolute forces, which scale with velocity squared (\(F\propto {u}_{\infty }^{2}\)), are much smaller during lower flow periods and are not as important for the structural design of the turbine as the peak loads experienced at or above rated velocity. Therefore, the ability of the flexible blade technology to match power performance while simultaneously offering a passive mechanism to reduce the most important structural loads represents a marked advancement for designing more durable and cost-effective tidal turbines.

Data are presented for a rigid-blade turbine with only an active speed controller, a state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed controller, and rubber blades with an active speed controller. All data are divided by the corresponding rated value.

The cut-in velocity of the turbine is selected at u∞/uR = 0.2. The turbine operates at λ = 5.5 when the velocity is lower than rated. At the rated speed, all turbine configurations are operated at the same tip-speed ratio (λR) and provide the same quasi-steady power (PR) and thrust (TR). At higher than rated velocities, λ is such that P/PR = 1. The maximum velocity is set at u∞/uR = 1.2, representative of typical tidal turbine operating conditions.

The simulation first confirms that the passive design of the flexible blade does not compromise its primary function of energy capture. The normalized power profiles shown in Fig. 2b coincide for the rubber blade with speed control and the state-of-the-art active pitch control turbine, where the turbine speed is shown in Fig. 2c. As the total energy harvested is proportional to the integral of the power curves over the tidal cycle, the overlap of the curves confirms a negligible difference in overall energy yield. This demonstrates that the load-mitigation benefits of flexible blades can be achieved without a penalty to energy capture in a real-world setting.

The advantage of the flexible blade design is revealed by the differences in the quasi-steady thrust (Fig. 2d) between the turbine configurations. The state-of-the-art active pitch system limits structural loads by actively feathering the blades into the flow while maintaining the rated rotational speed. For a rigid blade, using only an overspeed-control strategy, the fixed geometry cannot adapt to the increasing flow; solely increasing the tip-speed ratio results in an increasing thrust that peaks at approximately 1.65 times the rated value (Fig. 2c). By contrast, with a comparable speed-control strategy, the passive system of the flexible blade achieves the same quasi-steady power and similar quasi-steady thrust as the active control.

It is also important to note that flexible blades show a slightly higher thrust coefficient at lower, off-design velocities (Fig. 1b) than the baseline rigid blade. However, the absolute thrust force, which scales with velocity squared, is smaller during these periods than the peak values over the tidal cycle. As the maximum loading dictates the primary structural design requirements of a turbine, the nearly identical peak thrust of the passive flexible blade to that of the complex, state-of-the-art active pitch system suggests comparable outcomes for turbine longevity and maintenance costs, representing a marked advancement towards more durable and cost-effective tidal energy systems. Overall, these results indicate that the chordwise-flexible blades can offer a compelling and robust alternative to the state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed control turbine system.

An effective passive system must also address high-frequency load fluctuations, which are a primary driver of fatigue damage. In this context, high frequency refers to the unsteady load components that occur at frequencies of the order of the period of revolution, such as those induced by turbulence, velocity shear or wake interaction, and so on. Figure 3 quantifies the effectiveness of the flexible blades by presenting the standard deviation of load fluctuations relative to the reference rigid blades at rated velocity. To reflect realistic conditions over a tidal cycle, the data for u∞/uR ≤ 1 are presented at the optimal tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5) for maximum power extraction, whereas the data for conditions above the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06) are presented at the higher tip-speed ratio (λ = 8) that is used to cap power. Figure 3 shows a substantial reduction of unsteady loads for all three components when the turbine is operating under its most demanding conditions. At the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.0), where the turbine operates at its optimal λ for maximum power extraction, the flexible blades provide effective fluctuation reduction across power, thrust and root bending moment (mitigated by approximately 18%, 23% and 28%, respectively). Furthermore, even when the inflow velocity increases beyond the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06), the load fluctuation mitigation remains substantial. This demonstrates the powerful and robust damping ability of the flexible blades during both the maximum-power and power-capping phases of operation, when the absolute magnitude of fluctuating forces is greatest. At the lowest velocities (for example, u∞/uR = 0.51), where the blade operates in a stalled condition, fluctuations are known to increase relative to the rigid blade. However, their absolute magnitude is small, reaching only about 15–35% of the fluctuation level of the rigid blade at its rated velocity. A more detailed analysis, presented in Supplementary Note 3, confirms that this mitigation is robust across a wide range of tip-speed ratios under these high-flow conditions.

To illustrate the physics of the passive load regulation mechanism demonstrated previously, the deformation of the flexible blade is visualized at the tip section. Figure 4 shows the phase-averaged digital image correlation (DIC) measurements of the tip of the same flexible blade at a constant azimuthal angle, in which the blade is horizontal with downward velocity. The successful application of this technique using fully submerged cameras represents a significant experimental achievement, as most underwater DIC studies to date have been performed through observation windows rather than submerging the camera in the fluid25. In this way, complex optical distortions and refractive index mismatches associated with viewing ports are avoided, thereby achieving a more accurate measurement. In this study, the DIC system measured the deformation of the suction side of the blade. The full blade profile was then reconstructed by adding the known thickness distribution of the undeformed blade to the measured deformed chord line.

Phase-averaged profiles of one blade tip measured with DIC when the blade span is horizontal, and the tangential velocity is pointing downwards. Coordinates x, y are normalized by the chord length at the blade tip with origin at the quarter chord.

The measurements demonstrate the mechanism of the passive morphing concept. The undeformed flexible blade was designed with a significant initial camber, noticeably higher than that of the conventional rigid blade profile. The high camber present in both the initial blade shape and the subsequent deformed shape before reaching the designed operating point is the primary reason for the higher thrust force generated by the flexible blade operating off-design. Under hydrodynamic loading, the flexible trailing edge deflects upwards, causing the entire profile to flatten into a shape with less camber. This passive feathering becomes more pronounced with higher inflow velocities, which is the mechanism that reduces the thrust coefficient at high tip-speed ratios and velocities.

DIC measurements of different blades (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2) show that blades with lower flexural rigidity undergo greater camber reduction and exhibit stronger load shedding. Specifically, for blades with the same mould geometry, a too-stiff blade results in a too-low pitch and too-high camber, and thus high mean and unsteady thrust. Conversely, a too-soft blade results in an over-pitched blade and low power capture.

The observed mean load-shedding behaviour shown in Fig. 1 arises primarily from quasi-steady passive morphing, and not from dynamic blade deformation resulting in hysteresis, vortex dynamics, and so on. DIC reconstructions of each individual blade at the same azimuthal position reveal only a narrow spread about the mean shape, corresponding to a standard deviation of the pitch variation of approximately ±0.2° (Extended Data Fig. 3).

To further verify that the mean load-shedding behaviour is due to a quasi-steady morphing, we compare the measured blade deformations (Fig. 4) and the corresponding power and thrust (Fig. 1) with those computed with an in-house fluid–structure interaction solver based on a quasi-steady low-order model (Methods). The blade shapes computed with this program are in good agreement with those measured experimentally, and so are the predicted power and thrust for different tip-speed ratios (Extended Data Fig. 4). Because the numerical solver assumes the blade is in static equilibrium under hydrodynamic loads, these results confirm that the governing physics is quasi-steady.

The fluid–structure interaction of the flexible blades is governed by two non-dimensional groups such as the Reynolds number (Re) and Cauchy number (Ca) (defined in the Methods). The experiments are performed at sufficiently high Re that the hydrodynamic load coefficients are about the same as those at full scale, as shown by the almost identical values for the rigid blade tested at different velocities in Fig. 1. To ensure geometric similarity between the model and the full-scale strain of the flexible blades, the Young modulus E of rubber must be scaled up to maintain the same Ca across scales. As discussed in Supplementary Note 4, rubber features a sufficiently high range of E for full-scale applications. Furthermore, rubber has the advantage of matching the mass density of water, enabling the design of buoyancy-neutral blades and preventing mass-related load fluctuations.

To demonstrate the scalability of the present results, numerical simulations are performed using the in-house fluid–structure interaction solver to model a utility-scale turbine. A rated speed of u∞ = 3.0 m s−1 and a 20-m diameter turbine is selected consistently with modern, state-of-the-art commercial turbines26 and typical energetic tidal sites27. Simulations performed at the respective Re and the same Ca confirm that power and thrust coefficient curves are similar at model and full scale (Extended Data Fig. 5), and therefore the present results are applicable to utility-scale turbines. Although E of the steel spar can be scaled up in numerical simulations, this is not possible in practice. Therefore, different full-scale spar design options are discussed in Supplementary Note 5.

Finally, rubber features high fatigue endurance. Preliminary calculations in Supplementary Note 6 show that the fatigue life of a full-scale rubber blade would substantially surpass the 20 years of service expected by state-of-the-art turbines.

Overall, by allowing similar control on power at thrust above rated speed than active pitch control systems, and mitigating load fluctuations, this technology offers a viable pathway to lower the LCOE. Furthermore, the reduction in load fluctuations enables deployment in energetic, highly turbulent sites previously deemed unviable due to the high fatigue loads. Further analysis of the potential industrial impact of this technology is presented in Supplementary Note 7.

This experimental investigation has evaluated the performance of tidal turbine flexible rubber blades with passive chordwise flexibility, compared against conventional rigid blades. Our results confirmed that the power coefficient of the flexible blade at the design tip-speed ratio is comparable to that of its rigid counterpart, demonstrating that load mitigation benefits are achieved without penalty to the primary function of the turbine as an energy harvester.

The main advantage of the flexible blades is their ability to deform, shedding the excess of load at off-design conditions. This reconfiguration allows control of power by manipulating the angular velocity of the turbine, while achieving passive mitigation of the high-frequency fluctuations that drive fatigue damage.

Therefore, the chordwise-flexible blades offer a compelling and robust alternative to state-of-the-art active pitch control. By mitigating loads with a much simpler setup, the flexible blade eliminates a significant source of potential failure and maintenance costs in offshore renewables.

The mechanism for load mitigation is confirmed through DIC measurement and a quasi-steady low-order code, which shows that the stiffness and initial geometry of the blade produce a controlled ‘feather’ as loads increase. The no-flow geometry and stiffness of the blade are designed so that, under flow conditions approaching the design point, it deforms toward the reference rigid-blade configuration.

Looking ahead, this work opens up new pathways for tidal turbine design and cost reduction. The demonstrated reductions in peak and fatigue loading could allow a reduction in structural requirements for both the blades and their supporting structure, lowering capital costs and enabling higher generator ratings, which in turn improve rated capacity per unit mass. Moreover, the increased robustness from the removal of the pitching system reduces operational and maintenance costs. These factors contribute to a lower LCOE of tidal turbines, addressing the primary barrier to the large-scale deployment of tidal energy farms. By making the technology more financially viable, this technology offers a realistic and attractive option for renewable energy production.

All experiments were conducted in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh, a circular combined wave–current basin designed for scaled testing of offshore renewable energy devices. The tank has a diameter of 25 m and, for the present campaign, was operated in current-only mode with a working water depth of 1.92 m. A schematic of the facility is shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a. The experiments were performed at six inflow velocities in the range u∞ = 0.444–0.923 m s−1, corresponding to a diameter-based Reynolds number,

from 0.49 × 106 to 1.16 × 106, where ν is the kinematic viscosity and d is the turbine diameter. See Supplementary Note 4 for a discussion on the Reynolds number scaling.

FloWave turbulence is between 8% and 9%, and integral length scales of about 25% of the water depth28. These turbulent characteristics are consistent with energetic tidal sites such as, for example, the Fall of Warness29. There, the turbulence intensity is between 5% and 11%, with integral length scales of approximately 30–50% of the channel depth. The mean vertical shear in FloWave is approximately a power law with a 1/12 exponent (Extended Data Fig. 6b), which is only slightly weaker than the 1/10 power-law profile commonly used to represent tidal flows30. Extended Data Table 1 summarizes the comparison between FloWave and the representative tidal sites.

A three-bladed horizontal-axis turbine with a rotor diameter d = 1.26 m was installed in the tank centre, at hub height zhub = 0.876 m. The turbine is equipped with a brushless d.c. motor and a 25:1 planetary gearbox. The main components of the turbine are outlined in Extended Data Fig. 7.

The results presented in the main text refer to four sets of blades: one set of rigid blades used as a baseline and three sets of rubber blades. The baseline rigid blades are CNC-machined (SS316) using a modified NACA 63-415 hydrofoil profile along the span. The profile was modified to ensure a blunt trailing edge, as specified in ref. 31. These blades exhibited negligible flapwise and edgewise deformations. Notably, utility-scale tidal turbine blades exhibit some structural compliance. However, here the model-scale rigid blade was deliberately made rigid to provide a defined geometry.

The main text presents the results for the rigid blades and one set of rubber blades with the optimal stiffness. Conversely, the Extended Data figures also include results for the other two sets of rubber blades, with higher and lower stiffness than optimal. The flexible blades were manufactured by injecting a proprietary rubber mixture into a mould and around a steel spar. All rubber blades have the same mould geometry. See Extended Data Fig. 8 for schematics of the rubber blade. The aeroelastic properties of the blade are tailored along its span by varying the ratio of the rigid spar width to the local chord length, which increases from the tip towards the root with an average of 45%.

The thrust and torque are measured by a force transducer installed between the turbine rotor and the motor shaft (Extended Data Fig. 7). The transducer is bespoke, manufactured by Applied Measurements, rated for an axial load of 1,300 N and a torque of 100 N m, and a resolution of 0.005 N and 0.0004 N m, respectively. In this study, thrust is the net force measured by the hub transducer along the streamwise direction, and torque is the net edgewise moment about the hub axis. Moreover, each blade root was instrumented with a flapwise custom root-bending-moment sensor. Calibration matrices for each sensor were obtained in situ before the test by applying known weights at four points along the cantilever beam attached to the sensor. All force signals were transmitted to a National Instruments NI 9203 acquisition system through a slip ring. The load cells were zeroed without flow before each set of measurements. For each measurement, loads were recorded at a sampling frequency of 128 Hz for 300 s. Rotor angular velocity was measured using an inductive proximity sensor that emitted one pulse per blade pass (three pulses per revolution), enabling determination of the revolution period and computation of the angular velocity.

Sensor accuracy and calibration uncertainties were propagated to the non-dimensional coefficients using standard bias-limit uncertainty analysis32, including thrust-torque transducer manufacturer specification (0.1% of full-scale capacity) and primary uncertainties in u∞, ω and geometric parameters. For the present setup, the maximum total bias limits is of order 10−2 for CP and of order 10−2 for CT (representative values). Supplementary Note 1 provides the full derivations and tables.

Blade deformation was measured using phase-locked DIC with underwater cameras and LED illumination (LaVision). The camera system had a fixed focal length of 1.1 m and a field of view of approximately 0.87 m × 0.56 m, sufficient to capture the full blade span (0.56 m). Phase locking was achieved by using the proximity-sensor signal to trigger image acquisition as a blade passed a fixed azimuthal position, with a horizontal span and a downward tangential velocity. For each condition, between 89 and 447 instantaneous deformation fields were recorded over a 300 s period, depending on u∞ and λ.

Images were processed in LaVision DaVis 11 using a subset size of 21 × 21 pixels and a grid step size of 2 × 2 pixels, resulting in a spatial resolution of approximately 0.68 mm near the blade tip (approximately 2% of the tip chord). A reference image in quiescent water was acquired before each set of measurements. In the present configuration, DIC was used to measure the deformation of the suction-side surface of the blade. The full blade profile was reconstructed by combining the measured chord-line deformation with the known undeformed thickness distribution.

A bespoke fluid–structure interaction (FSI) solver was developed for the present study. The solver couples an in-house code based on blade element momentum theory (BEMT), with a panel method with an integral boundary-layer formulation (XFOIL), and a finite element analysis commercial software (Abaqus). The code uses a two-level iterative process, as schematically shown in Extended Data Fig. 9. The process begins with an initial blade geometry. In the outer loop, the BEMT solver is used to calculate the axial and tangential induction factors on a finite number of blade sections at different radial coordinates. Then, the flow velocity and angle of attack experienced by each blade section are computed. These values are used as initial conditions for the inner FSI loop. First, the pressure distributions around each blade section are computed with XFOIL. Then, the pressure distributions from each blade section are combined to obtain a three-dimensional pressure distribution on the blade, which is used as input to Abaqus, in which a new deformed shape is computed. The Abaqus model includes the steel spar. This new shape is then discretized into sections and returned to XFOIL to recalculate the pressure field. This iterative process continues until the blade shape converges. This deformed blade geometry at equilibrium is then fed back into the outer BEMT loop to update the induction factors. This entire two-level process is repeated until convergence. The power and thrust coefficients of the whole turbine are then computed by integrating the loads computed with XFOIL for each blade section and multiplying by three to account for the three-bladed turbine.

This code was used to design the stress-free mould shape for each blade stiffness, ensuring that the equilibrium blade shape matches the reference rigid blade at the design flow speed and tip-speed ratio. The model-scale simulations in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5 are initialized with the mould geometry and use the actual stiffness of the metal spar and of the rubber. The mould geometry Xi,j is used as input, where i = 0 and j = 0 indicate the iteration number of the inner and outer loop, respectively. The lift and drag coefficient curves (\({C}_{{{\rm{L}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\), \({C}_{{{\rm{D}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\)) are computed with XFOIL for various blade sections, and the induction factors (\({a}_{i,j},{a}_{i,j}^{{\prime} }\)) are computed with BEMT. Then the pressure distribution (pi,j(x)) around each blade section is computed with XFOIL and assembled into a three-dimensional load condition for Abaqus, where the new geometry is computed (Xi,j, with i increased by one). The inner loop is repeated till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi−1,j∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵi. If converged, the new geometry is Xi,j, where j is increased by one. The outer loop is repeated from the computation of the lift and drag coefficient for the new geometry, till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi,j−1∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵj.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Yusheng Wan
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Gyr) has hindered our understanding of Earth’s early evolution, fuelling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. At present, the only unequivocally documented >3.9-Gyr-old rocks are from the Acasta Gneiss Complex, Canada1,2,3. Here we report a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, North China Craton, in which primary magmatic zircon records elevated δ18O values (average +6.77 ± 0.23‰) and positive εHf(t) values (weighted mean +1.45 ± 0.27). This suggests a low-temperature altered basaltic source that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean. In contrast to the low-pressure origin inferred for the roughly 4.0-Gyr-old Idiwhaa unit in Acasta2, the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss reported here exhibits geochemical signatures attributed to a high-pressure origin4. Thermodynamic and trace element modelling demonstrate that its parental magma formed by means of low-degree (8–16%) melting of basaltic crust at >1.6 GPa and 740–820 °C, suggesting rapid burial of (near-)surface-altered oceanic crust to mantle depths along a cool thermal gradient. We propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event.

a, Zircon analyses of trondhjemitic gneiss sample J2302 define two concordant age groups at 3.95 Gyr and 3.45 Gyr, interpreted as the timing of magmatic crystallization and subsequent metamorphism, respectively. b, Most zircons in trondhjemitic gneiss sample J2303 are magmatic and cluster near 3.95 Gyr. Overgrowth rims show radiogenic Pb loss, including analysis 61.1R, which is the closest to concordia. c, Zircon analyses from banded trondhjemitic gneiss sample J2212 (including zircons analysed in two sessions from the same sample, marked as J2212A and J2212B) are more scattered, with the main population along a discordia line from 3.95 Gyr. However, several zircons with magmatic zoning yield concordant ages of 3.86–3.70 Gyr, potentially owing to the intrusion of thin granitic veins and/or partial resetting of the U–Pb system of 3.95-Gyr-old zircons. Analysis 63.1MA in J2212B has the oldest 207Pb/206Pb age of 3,989 ± 10 Myr but shows slightly reverse discordance, probably because of local enrichment of radiogenic Pb during later metamorphism98. d, Concordia diagram of all samples for analyses with <20% discordance. The weighted mean 207Pb/206Pb age of 3,951 ± 3 Myr (95% confidence level, MSWD = 1.15, n = 33) for magmatic/recrystallized cores is considered the best estimate for the magmatic crystallization age of the trondhjemitic gneiss protolith.

Zircon Lu–Hf isotope analyses were carried out in two sessions. Circles and triangles represent the results of the first analyses and squares represent the results of the second analytical session. All of the magmatic/recrystallized zircons with >3.9-Gyr 207Pb/206Pb age have homogeneous 176Hf/177Hf ratios except for J2302-2.1MA, which has a high 176Lu/177Hf ratio. The magmatic/recrystallized zircons with <3.9-Gyr 207Pb/206Pb age in samples J2302 and J2303 are all located near the Pb loss line. Some newly formed zircons have much higher 176Hf/177Hf ratios, which may be related to external fluids introduced during metamorphism.

a–c, REE patterns of zircons from the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss (samples J2302, J2303 and J2212, respectively). The REE data were filtered using the methods suggested in ref. 26. d,e, Magmatic oxygen fugacity and H2O content of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss. The oxygen fugacity (fO2) was calculated using the oxybarometer proposed in ref. 82 based on the average REE content of the filtered magmatic zircons. The magmatic water content was calculated using the hygrometer established in ref. 26 and the effect of U loss in the whole rock was corrected assuming a Th/U ratio of 5 (ref. 26). Considering that the composition of sample J2212 may have been influenced by alteration and the intrusion of thin younger veins, the average composition of J2302 and J2303 was used for calculating the fO2 and water content of J2212.

The homogeneous 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss (samples J2302 and J2303) is similar to the granitoids in Anshan and Nuvvuagittuq (mainly trondhjemitic gneiss) but different from those in Acasta, Tarim and Greenland (mainly tonalitic and granodioritic gneisses). b, Nb versus Ta diagram. c, Sr versus Y diagram. and d, La/Yb versus Yb classification diagrams for high-pressure, medium-pressure and low-pressure TTGs4. The 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss consistently plots in the high-pressure TTG field, being similar to the 3.72-Gyr-old Aktash gneiss in the Tarim Craton and some TTG rocks in Greenland but different from many other ≥3.8-Gyr-old granitoids around the world, which mostly plot into the medium-pressure and low-pressure TTG fields.
