a,b, LILE contents of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss and potential source rocks (Supplementary Tables 6 and 7). The dashed red lines represent LILE contents required for the source to produce the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss by 7%, 10%, 20% and 30% melting, assuming that these elements are perfectly incompatible with bulk partition coefficient equal to 0. Considering that the degree of partial melting of a mafic rock source needs to be >7% for melt aggregation to form magma but <30% to match the high SiO2 contents of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss, the LILE contents of the source need to be in the grey shaded area. Because the sources of Eoarchaean TTGs are from mafic rocks, we have compiled the geochemical data of Eoarchaean mafic rocks worldwide (Methods and Supplementary Table 7). Comparing the LILE contents of these mafic rocks with those required to form the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss, the amphibolite group I in Acasta is the most suitable source to use for modelling, consistent with the fact that it is the only mafic rock >3.95 Gyr old. c, P–T pseudosection for the composition of amphibolite group I from Acasta, assuming X(H2O) = 1.5 wt% and Fe3+/(Fe3+ + Fe2+) ratio = 0.1. The dashed white lines represent the wt% of melt.

a–d, The red dot denotes the median sodic TTG composition4, which was assumed as the starting melt composition. Solid black and orange curves represent the effects of fractional crystallization of plagioclase and hornblende, respectively, whereas dashed black and orange curves represent the effects of accumulation of plagioclase and hornblende, respectively. Orange squares show the compositions of the 3.95-Gyr-old high-pressure TTGs from this study. Small dots represent melts produced by partial melting of the Acasta amphibolite group I (Supplementary Table 9), colour-coded by pressure. Comparison shows that plagioclase accumulation and hornblende fractional crystallization can explain the positive Eu and Sr anomalies in our samples (a,b) but they fail to simultaneously reproduce the high (La/Yb)N and (Gd/Yb)N ratios and the high SiO2 contents observed in the rocks (c,d). By contrast, melts formed under high-pressure conditions match well with the main geochemical characteristics of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic samples.

The positive εHf(t) values of magmatic zircons from the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss indicate that its basaltic precursor was young juvenile crust derived from a DMD. Even if the basaltic precursor (assuming 176Lu/177Hf = 0.022) was derived from a 4.5-Gyr-old DMD with a similar 176Lu/177Hf ratio (0.0384) to modern depleted mantle, its extraction time from the mantle could not be earlier than 4.0 Ga (solid blue line). If the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss was formed by partial melting of basalt immediately extracted from a DMD with similar 176Lu/177Hf ratio, then the timing of mantle depletion can be estimated to be about 4.35 Ga (dashed black line). Earlier depletion of the mantle is required if partial melting of a basaltic precursor occurred some time after its extraction from a DMD (dashed blue line) or the degree of depletion in the mantle is less than modern depleted mantle (dashed red line). If the basaltic precursor was derived from a possible ultra-depleted mantle proposed by some researchers100, the depletion can be slightly delayed. Nevertheless, the depletion still needs to be no later than 4.2 Ga even if the 176Lu/177Hf of the ultra-depleted mantle is as high as 0.041 (solid purple line). Therefore, a Hadean DMD is necessary to yield the Hf isotope composition of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Michael J. Noonan
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

Plastic pollution is a defining feature of the Anthropocene1, and microplastics are dispersed by air and water into even remote terrestrial habitats2,3,4,5,6,7, yet the ecological and landscape-level processes that shape microplastic accumulation in terrestrial ecosystems remain poorly understood. Human land-use change is rapidly transforming landscapes worldwide, but the influence of this expanding human footprint on the microplastic burdens in wildlife remains largely unknown. This knowledge gap is particularly pressing in regions that are facing escalating environmental pressures, such as Brazil. Here we pair in vivo microplastic measurements with high-resolution tracking data from lowland tapirs and giant anteaters across Brazil and show that the microplastic burdens carried by free-ranging mammals increase with both the magnitude of their human footprint exposure and their proximity to development and waste management infrastructure. Microplastics were also detected in the blood of individuals occupying seemingly pristine habitats far from development, suggesting that direct exposure to human-modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic microplastic burdens. In a period of accelerating global land-use change, these findings reveal how individual habitat use and anthropogenic land-use change interact to shape wildlife exposure to microplastics and suggest that managing animals’ proximity to development and waste management infrastructure may reduce the microplastic burdens carried by terrestrial wildlife.

Plastic pollution, once thought to be a predominantly aquatic issue, is increasingly being recognized as a threat to terrestrial ecosystems1. Microplastics (synthetic polymer particles with diameter less than 5 mm) are a particularly problematic form of plastic pollution, as these small particles are easily dispersed through pathways that include atmospheric deposition, precipitation, river transport and groundwater flow2,3,4,5,6,7. The high environmental mobility of microplastics has allowed them to infiltrate even the most pristine habitats8 where they can persist for centuries9,10. For wildlife exposed to microplastics, the small size and diverse chemistry of these particles facilitate ingestion11 and the penetration of biological membranes12,13. Once internalized, microplastics can bioaccumulate, biomagnify through food webs and pose severe health risks14,15,16,17,18.

Although much work has been done on detecting microplastics in different biological compartments (reviewed in ref. 19), studies in terrestrial ecosystems have largely been limited to descriptive surveys that document the presence of microplastics without investigating how these pollutants accumulate within wildlife20,21,22. Although such studies have proven informative for identifying the scope and scale of plastic pollution, this approach has left the bioaccumulation dynamics of microplastics in terrestrial environments poorly understood. As a result of this knowledge gap, even high-profile studies on plastic ingestion risk in wildlife have had to rely on assumptions about the relationship between individual habitat use and the uptake of microplastics rather than empirically grounded associations23. Because both sources and dispersal pathways for microplastics are amplified by land-use change24,25,26, the intensity of human landscape modification should have a key role in shaping the internal microplastic burdens of terrestrial wildlife. Whether this is the case, however, is still largely unknown. With the continuing expansion of human-modified landscapes into wild spaces27 and the concomitant increase in global plastic production28, there is an urgent need to move beyond presence/absence studies and towards understanding the ecological and landscape-level factors that shape microplastic burdens in terrestrial species29.

Here we integrate movement ecology, land-use data and in vivo contaminant measurements within the same individuals to investigate how the intensity and proximity of anthropogenic land-use change shape systemic microplastic burdens in terrestrial mammals. The role of anthropogenic disturbance in shaping internal plastic burdens is particularly pressing in regions facing escalating environmental pressures, such as Brazil, where the extent of anthropogenic land-use change since the turn of the century has substantially outpaced the global average30,31 and deforestation, resource extraction, urbanization, agricultural intensification and an expanding road network are rapidly transforming the country’s landscapes30,32. By pairing in vivo microplastic measurements with high-resolution Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking data, we provide quantitative evidence that links individual-level habitat use and human landscape modification to systemic microplastic burdens in free-ranging terrestrial wildlife.

Between February 2021 and November 2022, we collected blood samples and high-resolution GPS-based movement data from lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris; n = 26) and giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla; n = 21) sampled at the Arc of Deforestation in the Amazon, an agricultural mosaic in the Cerrado, and a relatively undisturbed cattle ranch in the Pantanal (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Table 1). For each individual, we quantified blood microplastic concentrations and polymer profiles using confocal Raman spectroscopy, detecting particles larger than 1 μm. We then paired these data on in vivo microplastic burdens with the GPS tracking data to understand how inter-individual differences in habitat use and disturbance exposure shaped internal microplastic burdens. In particular, we quantified each individual’s exposure to human disturbance through the Human Footprint Index (HFI), a globally standardized measure of cumulative anthropogenic pressure ranging from 0 (undisturbed) to 50 (most heavily modified)33. We also examined local-scale effects through each animal’s proximity to the nearest human development (that is, the built environment including urban areas, mining infrastructure and power plants)34 and waste management facilities34.

Across all samples, we identified a total of 17,165 particles with a hit quality index (HQI) > 75, of which 2,815 (16.4%) were identified as microplastic. Microplastics were near-ubiquitous and found in the blood of all but four animals (three giant anteaters and one tapir), but systemic concentrations varied markedly across individuals (mean: 73.8 particles per ml; range 0 to 1,211.3 particles per ml). Lowland tapirs had the highest microplastic burdens (98.9 particles per ml; 95% confidence interval 52.0–188.0 particles per ml), followed by giant anteaters (42.8 particles per ml; 95% confidence interval 26.7–68.6 particles per ml); however, concentrations did not differ significantly between species (β = 0.84, t = 1.88, P = 0.067). Tapirs and giant anteaters did differ in polymer composition (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Information), with additional inter-individual variation detailed in the Supplementary Discussion and Extended Data Fig. 2. Although comparable data on systemic microplastic burdens are not presently available for other species of terrestrial wildlife, the mean concentration of 73.8 particles per ml found in these animals is within the range reported in human blood using spectroscopic methods35 (1.9 to 108 particles per ml).

Across species and sampling sites, individual differences in blood microplastic burdens were consistently associated with anthropogenic disturbance. Of the 47 animals from which blood samples were collected, 40 had sufficient GPS tracking data for inclusion in the habitat use analyses. These animals spanned a wide gradient of human pressure (Fig. 2a), with the maximum HFI individuals experienced ranging from as low as 2.6 to 40.5. The home ranges of these animals were 12.6 km from the nearest human development on average, ranging from 95 m to 67.4 km. There was a significant positive relationship between blood microplastic concentrations and the maximum HFI within an animal’s home range (β = 0.07, t = 2.66, P = 0.011; Fig. 2b), although weighted mean HFI exposure was non-significant (β = 0.061, t = 1.73, P = 0.092; Extended Data Fig. 3).

Although these results highlight how direct exposure to human-modified landscapes shapes internal microplastic burdens, plastic pollution is a transboundary issue with complex dispersal pathways36. Atmospheric deposition and waterborne transport are likely contributors, as airborne microplastics from urban, industrial and agricultural sources can travel long distances before settling in remote ecosystems, and rainfall runoff, river discharge and seasonal flooding redistribute particles across landscapes to habitats far from their original sources2,3,4,5,7,37. Focusing on direct HFI exposure alone can obscure such effects. Indeed, we found that the local-scale effects of human land use were particularly important in shaping the systemic microplastic concentrations of the monitored animals, with significant effects of distance to development (β = −0.032, t = −2.94, P = 0.0057) and distance to the nearest waste management facility (β = −0.026, t = −2.73, P = 0.0096) (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3). Additional data on giant armadillos (Priodontes maximus) living in the Pantanal corroborate this trend (see Supplementary Discussion). These relationships were all robust to sensitivity analyses (Extended Data Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Discussion) and highlight the role of anthropogenic land use in driving species’ exposure to plastic pollution. The polymer profiles also varied across sampling sites in patterns that were broadly consistent with the dominant human activities at each site (Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5 and Supplementary Discussion).

Recent estimates38 reveal that the mean global HFI increased from 5.26 in 2001 to 6.63 in 2020, representing a 26% increase. This trend in land-use change was even more pronounced in Brazil, where the HFI rose by 42% over the same period, from 4.17 to 5.92. Problematically, anthropogenic land-use expansion often outpaces the development of waste management infrastructure39,40. This infrastructural gap leaves regions experiencing the most rapid change the least equipped to contain plastic waste. Across large parts of rural and interior Brazil, for example, solid waste collection remains inadequate and wastewater treatment is limited or absent altogether41,42,43. The plastic materials tied to the expanding human footprint thus have few barriers preventing them from becoming highly mobile environmental pollutants42. The relationship between human disturbance and blood microplastic concentrations identified here suggests that microplastic burdens in terrestrial wildlife will continue to rise as land-use change intensifies. Notably, even at an HFI of zero the model predicted blood microplastic concentrations of 10.5 particles per ml (95% confidence interval 4.6–24.2 particles per ml; intercept: β = 2.36, t = 5.58, P < 0.001). While we can not discount the potential that this non-zero intercept was the result of an unmodelled non-linear relationship at low HFI exposure, it does provide support that direct exposure to human-modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic microplastic burdens. The seemingly pervasive reach of microplastic pollution is most strikingly illustrated by our findings from the animals in the Pantanal. The Pantanal is the world’s largest and most pristine wetland, supporting an extraordinary diversity of wildlife within a relatively undisturbed landscape44. Unlike other biomes in Brazil, much of the Pantanal has remained ecologically intact owing to its remote location, limited infrastructure and seasonal flooding, which naturally regulate many human activities. Yet, we found microplastics in the blood of all of the individuals we sampled in the Pantanal, despite these animals living more than 65 km from the nearest development and more than 112 km from the nearest waste management facility. This finding is corroborated by several recent studies that reported substantial concentrations of microplastics in both aquatic environments and sediments throughout the Pantanal45,46,47, with the highest levels of microplastics (up to 1,174.2 items per m2) found near rivers flowing from urban areas46. The presence of microplastics in the blood of animals living many tens of kilometres from the nearest development or waste facility highlights how microplastics are a threat not only to wildlife with direct exposure to human-modified landscapes, but also to species across even the most remote and ecologically intact environments8. Developing a mechanistic understanding of the pathways through which microplastics reach remote terrestrial ecosystems will be essential for protecting wildlife from this highly mobile pollutant. Although environmental sampling across these sites would strengthen the causal inference of these relationships by directly linking environmental polymer profiles to those detected in blood, isolation protocols for chemically diverse samples such as blood and soil complicate spectroscopy-based comparisons48,49. Paired blood–environment sampling designs thus represent a productive, albeit challenging path forward.

By combining in vivo microplastic measurements with fine-scale movement data and high-resolution landscape disturbance indices, our study moves terrestrial microplastic research beyond detection surveys towards a spatially informed quantitative framework for predicting wildlife burdens from landscape context. This approach revealed how individual habitat use and anthropogenic land-use change interact to shape wildlife exposure to microplastics, and is readily transferable to other species and regions, offering a scalable tool for identifying vulnerable populations and informing targeted conservation responses. While no ecosystem is likely to be entirely free of microplastics50, we did find that animals in less disturbed habitats carried substantially lower burdens than those in close proximity to human infrastructure. These findings suggest that management efforts aimed at limiting animals’ exposure to human-modified environments and reducing their proximity to development and waste management infrastructure can serve to reduce the microplastic burdens carried by wildlife.

Lowland tapir (T. terrestris) samples were collected across three sites in Brazil. The agricultural mosaic site in the Cerrado was located between the municipalities of Nova Alvorada do Sul and Nova Andradina, in Mato Grosso do Sul State, Brazil (−21.99° N, −53.83° E). It features a mosaic of natural habitats, including Cerradão fragments, gallery forests and marshlands, which constitute approximately 12% of the study area. The remainder is heavily influenced by human activities, including agriculture (for example, sugarcane, soybean and corn), cattle ranching, eucalyptus plantations, highways and rural settlements. Precipitation exhibits marked seasonality, with approximately 70% of the total annual rainfall occurring between November and March51.

The field site in the Pantanal was situated on Baía das Pedras Ranch, in the Nhecolândia Sub-Region of the Southern Pantanal, Municipality of Aquidauana, Mato Grosso do Sul State, Brazil (−19.33° N, −55.72° E). This private property spans 145 km² and comprises a mosaic of seasonally inundated grasslands, lakes, gallery forests, scrub, and deciduous forests. The Pantanal is a nearly pristine biome with a low human footprint, and is far removed from areas experiencing deforestation and other anthropogenic pressures. The ranch supports abundant wildlife and extensive cattle grazing on native grasses. The average annual temperature is 25 °C, and the annual rainfall is 1,185 mm.

The site in the Amazon was located at Tanguro Farm, a privately owned 103,000 ha property in Querência, Mato Grosso state, that sits at the transition between the Cerrado savanna and the Amazon rainforest along the southern Arc of Deforestation. Owned by AMAGGI, a major actor in Brazil’s soybean industry, the farm comprises 59,000 ha (57%) of croplands (soybean, corn, and cotton) and 44,000 ha (43%) of legally protected forest reserves. This region is the driest portion of the Amazon basin and experiences a prolonged dry season (May–September) with annual rainfall of 1,700–2,200 mm. Forests in this region are shorter (~20 m) than the moist Amazon rainforest (~30 m). About 40% of the farm was cleared for pasture (1976–1992) and later converted to soy cultivation (2003–2010), leaving riparian forests surrounded by croplands.

The giant anteater (M. tridactyla) data collection was conducted in the Cerrado savanna of Mato Grosso do Sul state, Brazil, as part of the Anteaters and Highways Project (ICAS, www.icasconservation.org.br), which investigates wildlife-vehicle collisions and their impacts on wildlife populations. Sampling areas were located near two federal roads: BR-267 (−21.64° N, −53.51° E) and BR-262 (−20.86° N, −52.04° E). As described above, the study region is a mosaic landscape dominated by open areas, including grasslands, pastures, and croplands, interspersed with small remnants of native savanna and forest vegetation, as well as eucalyptus plantations52.

In addition to the tapir and giant anteater data, we also obtained a smaller amount of data from three giant armadillos (P. maximus). The giant armadillo data collection was also conducted at the Baía das Pedras Lodge and Ranch in the Pantanal, which served as the base of operations for the Giant Armadillo Conservation Program (GACP).

All animal capture, handling, and blood sampling procedures were approved by the Brazilian Ministry of the Environment (MMA) and the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation (ICMBio) under license numbers 14603-25 (lowland tapirs), 53798-18 (giant anteaters) and 27587-1 (giant armadillos). All procedures were performed in accordance with the terms of these licenses and with relevant national and institutional animal welfare guidelines. Chemical immobilization was performed under veterinary oversight, and all animals were released at their capture sites following full recovery.

Lowland tapirs were captured using a combination of methods, including darting, following physical restraint in box-traps or pitfall traps, or darting from a distance. Box traps and pitfall traps were deployed in areas frequently visited by tapirs. Tapirs captured by these methods were anaesthetized intramuscularly with a combination of butorphanol (0.17 mg kg−1), medetomidine (0.012 mg kg−1) and ketamine (0.7 mg kg−1). Reversal agents, including atipamezole (0.04 mg kg−1) and naltrexone (0.35 mg kg−1), were administered at the conclusion of procedures. For tapirs darted from a distance, anaesthetics included tiletamine-zolazepam (1.25 mg kg−1), medetomidine (0.006 mg kg−1), ketamine (0.6 mg kg−1) and atropine (0.03 mg kg−1). Darts (3 ml or 5 ml) were used to deliver anaesthetics. Midazolam (0.03 mg kg−1) was administered 30 min later to maintain anaesthesia. Captured tapirs underwent a range of procedures, including subcutaneous microchip insertion, morphometric measurements, sex and age determination, physical examinations, blood sample collection and telemetry collar placement for adults.

Tapirs were equipped with GPS collars (Telonics TGW SOB and GPS IRIDIUM models) programmed to obtain hourly location fixes, with a median operational life of 15.4 months. Additional location data were collected from stationary tags placed in the Pantanal (n = 883) and Cerrado (n = 174) to calibrate the measurement error in the GPS datasets.

Giant anteaters were captured between February 2021 and November 2022 using motorized active searches between 15:00 and 17:00, when they exhibit higher diurnal activity due to colder temperatures53,54. Searches were conducted along dirt roads in open areas, with two team members stationed in the back of a truck to improve detectability. Upon spotting an individual, technicians approached the animal on foot and captures were performed using two long-handled dip nets (1.5 m handles, 0.7 m diameter hoops). Physical capture typically lasted around 1 min.

Captured giant anteaters were chemically immobilized, equipped with GPS radiotelemetry harnesses (Telonics) as previously described55 and blood samples were collected. In brief, animals were anaesthetized using a protocol of butorphanol tartrate (Zoetis Indústria de Produtos Veterinários; 0.1 mg kg−1), detomidine hydrochloride (Agener-União; 0.1 mg kg−1) and midazolam hydrochloride (Cristália; 0.2 mg kg−1), adapted from ref. 55. The induction period averaged 8.27 ± 4.78 min.

Giant armadillos were captured between February 2021 and November 2022, using a method tailored to their natural behaviour56. Researchers tracked footprints and signs of recent predation, such as termite mounds, to locate burrows. When a burrow was identified and confirmed to contain an armadillo (indicated by the entrance being sealed with sand), an iron funnel trap (jequi-type) was placed at the entrance. Once captured, animals were transported in iron-reinforced wooden crates and held overnight for nocturnal species, with procedures beginning the following morning at the capture site.

Captured giant armadillos were anaesthetized for the collection of blood samples and surgical implantation of intra-abdominal transmitters. Anaesthetic protocols included an intramuscular injection of butorphanol tartrate (0.1 mg kg−1), detomidine hydrochloride (0.1 mg kg−1), and midazolam hydrochloride (0.1 mg kg−1) into the hind limbs. Before surgery, intradermal local anaesthesia with lidocaine hydrochloride (2 mg kg−1, Eurofarma) was infiltrated into the infra-umbilical region. Ketamine hydrochloride (10 mg kg−1) was administered intramuscularly as a supplementary anaesthetic immediately after the animals were completely washed. Transmitters (IMP 310 model, Telonics; 9.4 × 2.3 cm, 42 g, 36-month operational life) were surgically implanted within the abdominal cavity under sterile conditions. Following surgery, anaesthesia was reversed using a combination of naloxone hydrochloride (0.02 mg kg−1), yohimbine hydrochloride (0.125 mg kg−1), and flumazenil (0.01 mg kg−1). Armadillos were released at their capture sites upon recovery, typically remaining in their burrows for 24 to 120 h (average of 48 h) before emerging. Daily monitoring was conducted for 12–22 days post-release using telemetry receivers (model TR-4, Telonics) and VHF antennas (model RA-23K). After the initial monitoring period, armadillos were monitored monthly until the end of the transmitter’s operational life.

Approximately 10 ml of blood was collected within 20 min of immobilization via venipuncture of the medial saphenous or cephalic veins using a sterile glass vacutainer system (BD Vacutainer). Tapir captures were conducted in remote forest sites without access to field refrigeration. Blood samples were therefore stored in pre-cleaned glass collection tubes with no preservatives, sealed with clean aluminium foil and a metal cap to prevent contamination during storage, kept shaded at ambient temperature, and transferred to a −20 °C freezer on return to the base camp within 5–6 h.

Blood samples (~5 ml) were collected approximately 20 min after induction from the cephalic or saphenous veins using a sterile vacutainer system with 23G or 25G needles (BD Vacutainer). Samples were transferred to pre-cleaned glass collection tubes with no preservatives, sealed with clean aluminium foil and a metal cap to prevent contamination during storage, kept refrigerated at 4 °C on site, and frozen at −20 °C within 12–24 h for subsequent processing. We note that blood samples were obtained from three individual giant armadillos, however we obtained repeat samples at two time points for two of these animals. Although these blood samples were processed individually, they were pooled (that is, averaged) in our statistical analyses.

Cold storage under the above-mentioned conditions is standard practice in microplastic analyses and does not affect particle abundance or polymer identity. Microplastics are chemically stable over these timescales, and method reviews emphasize that environmental samples containing microplastics are routinely stored at 4 °C for days to weeks prior to processing, or frozen at −20 °C for longer periods, without alteration of polymer composition (reviewed in ref. 57).

Blood microplastic isolation was performed following a protocol previously developed by our team58,59,60. Depending on the sampling date, blood samples were stored at −20 °C for ~1–22 months between collection (Feb 2021–Nov 2022) and digestion (Dec 2022). On the first day of isolation, 1 ml of each blood sample was placed in an Erlenmeyer flask along with 50 ml of 10% KOH solution (sample ratio of 1:50). The mixture was incubated on a shaker at 60 °C and 250 rpm for 24 h. After the initial 24-h incubation, 10 ml of 47% NaClO were added to each sample to achieve a final concentration of 7.7%. The samples were then incubated under the same conditions (60 °C and 250 rpm) for an additional 24 h.

Following the second day of digestion, all samples were filtered through a 47 mm polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) membrane with a 0.45 μm pore size (Merck Omnipore) and rinsed 3 times with filtered ultrapure water. The membranes containing the particles were then submerged in 50 ml of 20% HNO3 and placed in an ultrasonic bath with sweep function at 100% power and 45 kHz frequency for 15 min to transfer the particles from the membrane to the solution. The samples were further incubated for 30 min at 40 °C and 250 rpm.

After removing the membranes, the samples underwent a 24-h incubation at 40 °C and 250 rpm. On the final day, the samples were filtered through a 13 mm PTFE membrane with a 0.45 μm pore size, rinsed three times with filtered ultrapure water, and mounted on glass slides for microscopy and spectroscopy analysis. The resulting filter membranes were then stored in pre-cleaned glass Petri dishes and analysed by Raman spectroscopy over the subsequent ~12 months (Jan–Dec 2023). After digestion, a proportion of non-plastic particulates remained on the membrane, such that microplastics accounted for an average of 16.4% of imaged particles with HQI > 75 (range 0–89.9%).

Quality assurance and quality control methods used throughout the process are detailed in the Supplementary Methods (see also Extended Data Figs. 6 and 7).

Microplastic identification and characterization were conducted using a confocal Raman microscope (alpha300 R, WITec) equipped with a UHTS 300 spectrometer (WITec) and a 532-nm laser. The microscope was operated using Control Five software, and the acquired data were processed with Project Five software to compensate for background noise and cosmic radiation signals.

As an initial step, a whole membrane image was captured using a 10× NA 0.25 Zeiss objective with the Area Stitching option. From this image, a specific field was selected for detailed imaging with a 50× NA 0.75 Zeiss objective, employing both the Area Stitching option and Z-stack autofocus. Particle identification was facilitated by the Particle Scout software, which enabled the acquisition of Raman spectra for all identified particles across the entire membrane. Raman spectra were then obtained using a 100× DIC NA 0.9 Zeiss objective, with a laser power of 10 mW, an accumulation of 4, and an integration time of 0.45 s. Spectra autofocus was used throughout the measurements. The acquired spectra were then compared against the S.T. Japan database (S.T. Japan Europe GmbH) and the SLoPP MPs Raman library61 using the True Match-Integrated Raman Spectra Database Management software. Microplastic characterization was based on an automated, 3-step process that was optimized for spectra acquisition rather than image sharpness. This precluded the manual assessment of particle shape (for example, fibres or fragments) or colour. Only matches with an HQI greater than 75% were considered for further analysis.

To assess changes in the HFI over time, we obtained and processed global HFI rasters at a 300 m resolution for the years 2001 and 2020 from the Wildlife Conservation Society Human Footprint dataset (https://wcshumanfootprint.org/). After ensuring projections and resolutions were consistent between the HFI rasters, a difference raster was generated by subtracting the 2001 HFI from the 2020 HFI to visualize areas of increasing and decreasing human influence. We cropped and masked the HFI rasters to remove areas outside of Brazil and then computed the mean HFI for 2001 and 2020, as well as the absolute differences. These analyses were conducted in R using the terra (v1.8-54)62, sf (v1.0-21)63,64, tmap (v4.0.0.9000)65, fields (v16.3)66, rnaturalearth (v1.0.1)67, and geobr (v1.9.1)68 packages.

Before analysis, we pre-processed the GPS location data in order to calibrate the measurement error and filter outliers. Pre-processing was done via the methods implemented in the R package ctmm (v1.2.1)69. For each location estimate, the GPS trackers recorded a unitless Horizontal Dilution of Precision (HDOP), a value which is a measure of the accuracy of each positional fix. We converted the HDOP values into calibrated errors by specifying 20-m error at an HDOP of 1 for 2D fixes, and 10-m error at an HDOP of 1 for the 3D fixes70. For each individual dataset, we then removed outliers based on error-informed distance from the median location, and the minimum speed required to explain each location’s displacement. Through this process we identified a total of 16,656 outliers, which represented ca. 3.55% of the total 469,410 locations. After filtering outliers, the final dataset consisted of 343,913 GPS locations across 20 individual giant anteaters, 6,072 GPS locations across 2 individual giant armadillos, and 102,769 GPS locations across 20 individual lowland tapirs.

For each of the tracked animals, we used a continuous-time approach to estimate their movement rates and home ranges, enabling robust comparisons across individuals71. We first fitted a series of continuous-time stochastic process movement models to the location data. Parameters were estimated using perturbative-hybrid residual maximum likelihood (pHREML)72, and identified the best model via small-sample-sized-corrected Akaike’s information criterion (AICc). From both visual inspections of the semi-variograms, and the parameters of the fitted movement models, all animals occupied stable home ranges throughout the monitoring period with no indication of range shifts or large-scale dispersal events.

From the selected models, we estimated each animal’s diffusion rate (in km2 day−1) as a measure of their movement rate. We next estimated each animal’s home range, using autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE)73. AKDE home range estimates were conditioned on the autocorrelation structure of the fitted movement model, and we implemented the small-sample-size bias correction of Fleming & Calabrese (2017)74, as well as the optimal weighting of Fleming et al. (2018)75 to correct for uneven sampling. Home range areas (in km2) were estimated as the area contained within the polygon delimited by the 95% isopleth of the probability density.

We estimated the mean and maximum HFI within each individual’s home range. HFI is an aggregate measure of human disturbance that ranges from 0 in natural habitats to 50 in the most anthropogenically modified habitats33. A raster of HFI data with a spatial resolution of 100 m was obtained from Gassert et al.38. The weighted mean HFI within an individual’s home range was estimated by calculating the weighted arithmetic mean of HFI values:

with weights (wu) determined by the probability density at each location u. Maximum HFI exposure was estimated by identifying the maximum value of HFI within each animal’s home range. We also estimated more nuanced patterns of habitat use via the MapBiomas database34, which details land use throughout Brazil at a spatial resolution of 10 m. We focused on habitats classified as water, development, agriculture, pasture, and native forest, which represented the majority of the land classes within the monitored animals’ home ranges. The proportions of each of these land classes within each animal’s home range were again estimated by calculating the weighted arithmetic mean. Lastly, we used the MapBiomas land classification data, the Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI), and the Waste Methane Assessment Platform 1.5.0, 2025 (https://wastemap.earth) to generate spatial rasters of distance to development, and distance to the nearest waste management facility (both in m). Development was a compound measure that captured the built environment, and was composed of the MapBiomas collection 10 classes: urban areas (24), mining (30), photovoltaic power plants (75), and other non-vegetated areas (25). From these spatial data, we estimated each animal’s mean distance to development and to the nearest waste management facility, estimated by calculating the weighted arithmetic mean.

To study how human land-use change shaped blood microplastic concentrations, we fit hierarchical generalized linear regression models using the methods implemented in the mgcv package (v1.9-1)76. Because the microplastic concentrations scaled between [0,∞], we used a Tweedie distribution with a log link for the error distribution77, with parameters estimated via restricted maximum likelihood (REML). The regression models testing for correlations between individual habitat use and microplastic concentrations included a population-level effect, as well as random intercepts and slopes for each of the species, with the following general form

where β0 represents the population-level intercept, β is the population-level slope, us[i] is the species-specific random intercept, vs[i] is the species-specific random slope, and s[i] indexes the species of individual i. This structure was used for all of the habitat covariates xi. From these models, inference was then made on the population-level trend.

All analyses were conducted in R (v4.3.3). Weighted means and proportions of land-use exposure were computed with the weights package (v1.0.4). Figures were produced with ggplot2 (v3.5.2), ggspatial (v1.1.9), tidyterra (v0.7.0), rphylopic (v1.5.0; animal silhouettes), fmsb (v0.7.6) and gridExtra (v2.3).

No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. Sample sizes were determined by the number of animals that could be safely captured during the study period (February 2021 to November 2022) given the logistical constraints of live-capturing large, threatened, free-ranging mammals under national permits, and all animals captured during this period were sampled. This was an observational field study, so randomization was not applicable; animals were not allocated to experimental groups, and exposure to human land use was determined by each individual’s own space use. The investigators were not blinded to species or sampling site during laboratory processing or analysis; however, particle detection and polymer identification were automated (Particle Scout and True Match software) and based on a fixed spectral-match threshold (HQI > 75%), which limits observer bias. Each animal contributed one blood sample, with the exception of two giant armadillos sampled at two time points, whose values were averaged before analysis. Seven animals lacked sufficient GPS tracking data and were excluded from the habitat use models but retained in descriptive analyses. Samples were processed in two batches, each with a procedural blank (Supplementary Methods); all lowland tapir samples were processed in the same batch. The polymer-integrity test shown in Extended Data Fig. 6 was repeated three times independently with similar results.

Heatmap in a, depicting the concentration (particles per ml) of the analyzed microplastic polymers for data from the field sites at the Amazon deforestation frontier, the Cerrado agricultural mosaic, and the Pantanal cattle ranch. Each row in the heatmap corresponds to a unique blood sample. Rows are grouped by site and separated by dashed lines; the top lines are from the Pantanal cattle ranch (Baía das Pedras Ranch, Nhecolândia, Aquidauana, Mato Grosso do Sul), the middle lines from the Cerrado agricultural mosaic (between Nova Alvorada do Sul and Nova Andradina, and along the BR-267 and BR-262 highways, Mato Grosso do Sul), and the bottom lines from the Amazon deforestation frontier (Tanguro Farm, Querência, Mato Grosso). The radar bar plots show the mean concentrations (particles per ml) of the different plastic polymers within the blood samples of animals from the b, Amazon deforestation frontier site (n = 14 animals) c, Cerrado agricultural mosaic (n = 22 animals), and d, Pantanal cattle ranch (n = 14 animals). In all panels, polymers categorised as ‘other’ were those that occurred at low abundance, and included: Polyvinyl Butyralolyethyleneimine, Poly(butylene terephthalate), Polyvinylformal, Polyacetal, Polymethylpentene, Polyurethane, Polyethylene Glycol, amongst others. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Yuta Shimamoto
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism. Whereas changes in chromatin state during this critical transition period have been extensively studied1,2,3, changes in the nucleus that houses chromatin remain poorly understood. Here, using direct organelle capture and biophysical manipulation methods, we find that nuclei attain profound softness and plasticity during the two-cell embryonic stage in mice, facilitating major zygotic gene activation. The prominent nuclear deformability is attributable to the rapid clearance of lamin B1 from the nuclear envelope by the autophagy factor LC3. Nuclear stiffening by lamin B1 retention or its overloading results in incomplete activation of zygotic genes and impaired development. However, embryos that maintain nuclear deformability escape from this transcriptional interference. High-resolution microscopy and sequential three-dimensional fluorescence in situ hybridization analyses revealed an accumulation of active RNA polymerase II and coordinated positioning of key genomic loci near the deformable nuclear envelope. An engineered molecular tether that stiffens the nuclei restricts these nuclear activities and suppresses expression of key zygotic gene activation genes. Together, our study identifies a distinct physical nuclear state that embryos acquire at the beginning of life that supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

The physical characteristics of the cell nucleus are extraordinarily diverse, exhibiting distinct shape and mechanical phenotypes across tissue types, physiological states and disease conditions. Fragile or misshapen nuclei are hallmarks of cancer, cardiomyopathy and premature ageing4,5. Nuclei in stem cells gradually stiffen during differentiation4,5,6,7. While these changes are widely recognized as consequences of altered nuclear composition and chromatin dynamics, they also influence genome organization and transcription8,9,10. Despite the importance, the physical state of the nucleus at the earliest stages of mammalian development, when life begins, remains unclear.

During the first few cleavages, nuclei undergo extensive epigenetic reprogramming, enabling the zygote to initiate a new developmental program. In mice, this transition occurs within the first approximately 48 h after fertilization and is associated with a surge in new transcript production, known as major zygotic gene activation (ZGA)11,12,13. Major ZGA occurs during the mid-to-late two-cell stage, and embryos that impair ZGA fail in subsequent development. Around the time of ZGA, chromatin exhibits distinct structural and biochemical changes accompanied by histone modifiers and transcription factors14,15. By contrast, whether the nucleus organizing chromatin undergoes any crucial changes that drive ZGA is not known. In somatic cells, nuclear shape and mechanics depend on lamins, which line the inner nuclear membrane16,17. Lamins are long-lived, enriched in eggs and are crucial for mammalian development18,19,20. Previous studies have documented that, of the two major types, A-type lamins exhibit cell-lineage-specific differential expression patterns, whereas B-type lamins are constitutively expressed throughout development16. However, their dynamics and transiency, as well as the underlying core regulatory mechanism, during the earliest embryonic stages are poorly understood. Likewise, how the nuclear lamina, which forms a structural meshwork, controls nuclear mechanics and genome dynamics during this critical transition is unknown. Investigating physical nuclear characteristics necessitates direct quantification and manipulation of their mechanical properties. However, achieving this without compromising cell viability poses a challenge.

To investigate physical nuclear properties, we first performed high-resolution confocal scanning of fertilized mouse eggs during early cleavages (Fig. 1a). Our three-dimensional (3D) images of nuclei with H2B–mCherry, expressed without perturbing development (Extended Data Fig. 1a), revealed their distinct shape features, showing uneven local deformation at the two-cell stage in contrast to their predominantly spherical appearance at the one-cell and four-cell stages (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1b). Timelapse imaging revealed that one-cell nuclei remained spherical during the cell cycle (Fig. 1d). Two-cell nuclei underwent slow, incremental deformation, which started at around 21 h post-insemination (h.p.i.), peaked at 24–26 h.p.i. and then gradually regressed by 32–36 h.p.i. (Fig. 1e). At the four-cell stage, nuclei were again spherical (Fig. 1f) (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d and Supplementary Videos 1−3). Before the onset of deformation, two-cell nuclei had fully swollen and reached steady sizes; once deformed, the altered nuclear shapes persisted for hours (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Similar deformation was observed using emerin–eGFP for the nuclear envelope (Fig. 1g) or mCherry–NLS for the nuclear interior (Extended Data Fig. 1g).

F, female; M, male. d–f, Time courses of 2D nuclear deformation during the one-cell (d), two-cell (e) and four-cell stages (f). Live imaging was performed at 1 h intervals over around 52 h for n = 9 embryos; the mean (orange) and s.d. (shaded area) of nuclear deformation, calculated as shown in the inset in d, are plotted. g, Nuclear membranes were imaged using emerin–eGFP (green) and analysed for 2D nuclear deformation. The arrowheads indicate prominent deformation sites. h, Schematic of nanocapillary-based mechanical measurement. An embryo is held with a holding pipette, while a pressure-controlled nanocapillary captures and stretches the nucleus to measure nuclear elasticity and stiffness. i, Snapshots of nuclei subjected to the nanocapillary-based measurement (red, H2B–mCherry; overlay with bright field). Representative from four (8 and 24 h.p.i.) and two (48 h.p.i.) independent experiments. j–l, Maximal nuclear deformation (j), nuclear stiffness (k) and the degree of elasticity (l) analysed from experiments as in i. S0, Smax and Sr are as in i. n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. For c, g and j–l, statistical analysis was performed using Kruskal–Wallis tests followed by Dunn’s-multiple comparisons test; the thick horizontal bars represent the mean values (red or black). Scale bars, 10 μm (b, g and i).

This finding prompted us to develop a biophysical setup that quantitatively characterizes the mechanical properties of early embryonic nuclei in situ (Fig. 1h). The setup equipped a pressure-controlled nanocapillary, of which the tip was inserted into a fertilized embryo to capture the nuclear surface. A weak, constant suction pressure (2.1 × 101 kPa) pinched the surface, which was then stretched through axial translocation of the nanocapillary. The nuclei could be gradually strained, resulting in tension, and the strain reached a maximum just before the detachment (Fig. 1i). The analysis could be performed from the one-cell to four-cell stages, over which the predominantly fluid-like cytoplasm minimally influenced the measured mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 2a–f). Measurements were also insensitive to nuclear markers and were comparable to label-free imaging results (Extended Data Fig. 2g,h).

Our analysis revealed that two-cell nuclei were significantly more deformable than one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1j). The deformable nature persisted throughout the cell cycle (from 21 to 32 h.p.i.) even as DNA doubled at about 24 h.p.i. Nuclear stiffness, as estimated based on the nanocapillary pressure and the extent of nuclear deformation, transiently lowered at the two-cell stage (one-cell, 5.0 ± 1.3 nN µm−1; two-cell, 2.0 ± 0.5 nN µm−1; four-cell, 4.6 ± 1.9 nN µm−1; n = 18, 38 and 13 embryos, respectively) (Fig. 1k). The stiffness values varied between male and female pronuclei (30.7 ± 21.3%, n = 8 pairs) and between blastomeres of each two-cell embryo (23.5 ± 14.5%, n = 16 pairs), while the differences were pronounced among the developmental stages (Extended Data Fig. 2i). Two-cell nuclei also exhibited significant plasticity, in contrast to more elastic one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1l) (shape recovery, 91.0 ± 4.3% for one-cell; 66.9 ± 8.0% for two-cell; and 87.9 ± 4.6% for four-cell). The deformable two-cell nuclear stiffness was consistent when embryos were examined using lower nanocapillary pressure that minimally perturbed development (1.2 × 101 kPa; Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). An alternative capillary-based approach, using an incremental suction pressure that aspirated nuclei, yielded consistent results (n ≥ 12 embryos per stage) (Extended Data Fig. 2l–n). These corroborate the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus.

Our nanocapillary-based assay at 1.2 × 101 kPa minimally perturbed development, enabling us to relate two-cell nuclear stiffness with embryos’ developmental competence (Fig. 2a). We found that all fertilized embryos that timely reached the blastocyst stage had soft nuclei (2.0 ± 0.6 nN µm−1; n = 66 of 66 embryos), while nearly half of the embryos that impaired development had stiff nuclei (n = 7 of 15 embryos; defined as more than twice the mean nuclear stiffness of the normal development) (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Detecting embryos with stiff nuclei was infrequent (8.6%; n = 7 out of 81 embryos). The outcome was regardless of the fluorescent tag type and marker expression levels (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). A similar mechanical feature was observed for cloned embryos created through somatic cell nuclear transfer (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 3a,d,e) (n = 46 embryos). Thus, deformable two-cell nuclei are a signature of normal preimplantation development.

We next explored the molecular mechanism underlying the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus. Using immunofluorescence, we first examined four major lamins, A/C, B1 and B2, and found that lamin B1 transiently cleared from the two-cell nuclear envelope, nearly paralleling nuclear softening (Fig. 3a,b). The clearance was rapid and substantial, with an approximately 70% decrease in peripheral signal during the early-to-mid two-cell stage (21 to 24 h.p.i.; Fig. 3b). Lamin A/C and B2 levels also changed, but their trends were gradual and monotonic, with only a minor decline, if any, during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Another nuclear envelope protein, Lap2β, also changed little (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Live-embryo imaging confirmed the clearance of lamin B1 from the two-cell nuclear envelope with a decay time constant of 86 ± 44 min (n = 5 embryos; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 4c). An immunoblotting assay revealed a reduction in lamin B1 during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3d), suggesting degradation.

Our pilot assay using wortmannin implicated that autophagy promotes lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Autophagy is active in early embryos and is essential for preimplantation development21. In live-embryo imaging, the autophagy factor LC322 was diffusive at the one-cell stage and accumulated in the two-cell nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Our antibody microinjection targeting LC3 suppressed lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Cell cycle progression as monitored by EdU was normal (Extended Data Fig. 4g). We therefore designed a construct that interferes with the endogenous interaction between lamin B1 and LC3, using a short fragment of lamin B1 carrying LC3-binding domains and an intrinsic nuclear localization signal23 (hereafter, sfLB1; Fig. 3e). When expressed in embryos, this fragment was predominantly nucleoplasmic (Extended Data Fig. 4h), while a major autophagy substrate p62 maintained stable protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Our analysis revealed that the clearance of lamin B1 was suppressed by sfLB1, whereas lamin A/C and B2 remained largely unperturbed (Fig. 3f,g). An accumulation of lamin B1 was detectable in western blot analysis of lysates (Extended Data Fig. 4j). A sfLB1 variant (sfLB1Δ), which was nucleoplasmic but with abrogated LC3 binding23 (Extended Data Fig. 4h,k), had little influence on lamin B1 clearance (Fig. 3f,g). The development of embryos was impaired by sfLB1, but not by sfLB1Δ (Fig. 3h).

To understand the mechanistic basis of lamin B1 clearance, we constructed fluorescent reporters based on full-length lamin B1 fused to mCherry. Consistent with the results shown in Fig. 3a–c, the wild-type (WT) construct (flLB1wt; Fig. 3e) localized to the nuclear envelope and exhibited rapid lamin B1 clearance (T1/2 = 83 ± 44 min, n = 18) (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 5a). The other three constructs carried mutations near or at an LC3-interacting region core motif (flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A)) or at the major N-terminal CDK1 phosphorylation site for nuclear-envelope breakdown24 (flLB1(S24A)) (Fig. 3e). These constructs also localized to the two-cell nuclear envelope (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Notably, the mutations that abrogated LC3 interactions (Extended Data Fig. 5b) suppressed the lamin B1 clearance, whereas the mutation at the CDK1 site did not prevent the clearance (Fig. 3i). The mutations in flLB1(5A) were at the site targeted for autophagic degradation of lamin B1 during oncogene-induced cell senescence23. The selectivity of lamin B1 over lamin A/C and B2 was also consistent with the phenomenon reported in senescent cells23.

Our assay further suggested that lamin B1 is degraded through an autophagy–lysosome pathway. This was confirmed by tracking the fate of flLB1wt and identifying its predominant lysosomal localization and formation of foci (n = 18 embryos; Fig. 3j,k). flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) localized much less to lysosomes (n = 12 and 14 embryos; Fig. 3j,k), while the numbers of lysosomes remained comparable (Fig. 3l). We did not observe prominent lamin-B1-positive structures bulging from the outer nuclear membrane23 nor an accumulation of lysosomes on the nuclear surface25 within the timescale examined. Collectively, our mechanistic view of lamin B1 clearance is shown in Fig. 3m.

We next examined the effect of lamin B1 on two-cell nuclear stiffness. Nanocapillaries indicated that two-cell nuclei of which the envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1 were stiffer and less plastic than controls (4.2 ± 1.3 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (sfLB1; Fig. 4a–d). These nuclei were as stiff as normal one-cell and four-cell nuclei (~5 nN µm−1, Fig. 1k). We next overexpressed lamin B1. As WT lamin B1 rapidly dissociated from the nuclear envelope, we used flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) to compensate for the clearance. Whereas excess loading of these lamins resulted in collapsed nuclei, titrating expression levels preserved the overall nuclear shape, with lamin B1 loaded to the nuclear envelope at a level comparable to that using sfLB1 (Fig. 4a,b). We found that flLB1(F454A/L457A) profoundly increased nuclear elasticity and stiffness (4.0 ± 1.1 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (Fig. 4c,d), while overall autophagic activity as assessed by LC3 signal26 was maintained (Extended Data Fig. 5c). The phenotype quantitatively mirrored the embryos perturbed through sfLB1. By contrast, flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC, which lacked the carboxy-terminal CaaX motif for farnesylation16 and remained nucleoplasmic, did not significantly alter nuclear shape and mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 5d). These data indicate that two-cell nuclear stiffness depends on the nuclear envelope localization of lamin B1.

Notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) showed nuclei of which the shape remained largely deformed as in normal two-cell embryos (Fig. 4a). These nuclei were soft and plastic (1.6 ± 0.4 nN µm−1, n = 10 embryos), despite their comparable level of nuclear envelope loading to sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4b–d). The minimal mechanical impact of flLB1(5A) was probably due to its poor assembly competency at the nuclear envelope for the following reasons: first, our nuclear isolation assay indicated that flLB1(5A) was more soluble than flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4e). Second, sfLB1(5A) showed comparably slightly higher affinity for LC3 than sfLB1(F454A/L457A) (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Finally, our expansion microscopy (ExM) analysis revealed a less-uniform peripheral localization of flLB1(5A) in comparison to endogenous lamin B1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A)27 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–g). The difference in peripheral DNA signals appeared less pronounced between perturbed embryo groups (Extended Data Fig. 6h). Our nanocapillary-based assay further suggested an early reduction in nuclear stiffness before lamin B1 clearance (Figs. 1k and 3a,b). Collectively, our data suggest that lamin B1 controls two-cell nuclear stiffness depending on their assembly stability at the nuclear envelope and that the stability depends on the site to which LC3 binds.

We next examined whether the observed nuclear changes impact the two-cell transcriptional reprogramming. We analysed the above embryos using RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq; Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 1). The first cleavage and following cell cycle progression were normal in those embryos; the overexpressed protein levels were stable and comparable among conditions (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Our analysis indicated that the transcriptomes of flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos were distinct from those of the flLB1(5A) and non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified more than 3,000 downregulated genes in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos compared with the non-injected controls (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Table 2). The downregulation was evident even when compared with flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4g), whereas very few DEGs were detected between flLB1(5A) embryos and the non-injected controls (Fig. 4h). Importantly, the genes downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) overlapped more with major ZGA and two-cell-activated genes than with minor ZGA and one-cell-activated genes28 (972 out of 3,763 (25.8%) versus 251 out of 3,763 (6.7%); P < 0.01, Fisher’s exact test) (Fig. 4i). The overlap was even greater when compared with another major ZGA gene list29 (1,338 out of 2,508, 53.3%) (Fig. 4i,j). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC embryos did not show an appreciably altered transcriptome at comparable expression levels (Extended Data Figs. 5g and 7e). Our analysis also indicated perturbed expression of key transcriptional regulators Obox15 in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos but it was not prominent in flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4k). The profiles of maternal and zygotic Obox genes suggested a failure in minor-to-major ZGA transition15.

We next analysed how ZGA is altered when the nuclear envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1. Analysing embryos overexpressing sfLB1 or sfLB1Δ, along with the non-injected controls, we found that thousands of genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated through sfLB1 (Extended Data Fig. 7f–l and Supplementary Table 3). Many downregulated genes identified as DEGs were shared between sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos (71.1%; Fig. 4i (bottom right)). Developmentally essential genes were enriched among the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7m). Analysing published chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) datasets further indicated sharp H3K4me3 signals around the transcription start sites of the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7n). We therefore performed genome-wide profiling of H3K4me3 through an optimized cleavage under targets and tagmentation (Cut&Tag) analysis. By establishing a condition that maintained the nuclear structure, reproducible signals were obtained that agreed with previously published ChIP–seq data14,30 (Extended Data Fig. 8a–e). Our analysis indicated that H3K4me3 is more abundant at transcription start sites in sfLB1 embryos than in the non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 8f). It has been demonstrated that broadly spread noncanonical H3K4me3 is removed by histone demethylation for major ZGA14. Indeed, H3K4me3 remained accumulated in broad-domain H3K4me3 (bdH3K4me3) in sfLB1 embryos, whereas H3K4me3 enrichment in lamina-associated domains unchanged (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 8g). Analysing the expression levels of histone methylation-related enzymes, key lysine demethylase (KDM) genes, which are needed to eliminate bdH3K4me314, were downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) and sfLB1, but the changes were not significant through flLB1(5A) and sfLB1Δ (Fig. 4m). These data suggest that the establishment of histone methylation status2 failed in embryos when lamin B1 stiffened the two-cell nuclear envelope.

There was a marked difference in nuclear stiffness between the embryo groups that failed in major ZGA and those that were transcriptionally less perturbed. To test whether nuclear stiffness per se was inhibitory to ZGA, we developed a molecular tether–anchor system that targets the nuclear envelope and stiffens nuclei (Fig. 4n and Extended Data Fig. 9a). The tether comprised an elastic I27 module of titin31 of which the ends were fused to a pair of GFP nanobodies. The anchor was made based on a minimal KASH domain fused to mEGFP for outer-nuclear-envelope localization32. When co-expressed, the tether was recruited to the anchor-coated nuclear envelope and increased nuclear stiffness by around twofold (4.3 ± 1.5 nN µm−1, n = 20 embryos; Fig. 4n,o and Extended Data Fig. 9b). Nuclear plasticity and deformation decreased accordingly (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Importantly, in the tether-stiffened nuclei, lamin B1 levels were as low as in normal mid two-cell embryos (Fig. 4p). Lamin A/C and B2 also remained largely unperturbed (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Our mRNA microinjection into late zygotes minimally affected pronuclear stiffness, first cleavage and cell cycle progression (Extended Data Fig. 9f–i). Moreover, our two mutant tether derivatives, one that weakened its affinity to the anchor (tether LaG16(5A)) and one that impaired its elastic force-generating property (tether titin(W34E)), showed no appreciable impact on nuclear shape and mechanics (Fig. 4o and Extended Data Fig. 9b–d,j). In contrast to the WT, neither of the two mutants significantly impaired development (Extended Data Fig. 9k). Thus, our tether–anchor system increases two-cell nuclear stiffness and perturbs embryonic development when it binds to the nuclear envelope and exerts force.

Our RNA-seq analysis revealed that embryos in which the nuclei were stiffened by the tether WT (tWT) exhibited distinct transcriptomes compared with those expressing the LaG16(5A) tether mutant and the non-injected controls (Extended Data Fig. 10a). A total of 634 genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated in the tWT embryos, while much fewer DEGs were identified in tether-mutant embryos (Fig. 4q and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e; versus the non-injected controls). Furthermore, the expression of the Obox cluster and other major ZGA genes was dampened (Extended Data Fig. 10f). Downregulation of key ZGA genes and transcriptional repression were detectable in quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) and 5-ethynyl-uridine (EU) incorporation analyses (Extended Data Fig. 10g,h). Whereas the impact on ZGA was broader and less variable for flLB1(F454A/L457A) than for tWT (972 versus 168 genes; Fig. 4i versus Extended Data Fig. 10e; Fig. 4j versus Fig. 4q), 82.2% of the downregulated genes in tWT embryos were shared with those perturbed through sfLB1 or flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4r). Together, we conclude that deformable two-cell nuclei are integral to the execution of proper ZGA.

We next examined the effect of lamin B1 persistence on early development. As a result, approximately 50% of the embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) did not progress beyond the two-cell stage (Extended Data Fig. 5h), comparable to those perturbed through sfLB1 (Fig. 3h). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC did not significantly affect development, indicating that the effective site of lamin B1 is at the nuclear envelope. Notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) also showed impaired development, despite their nearly normal transcriptome (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 5h). Our analysis indicated that those embryos accumulated DNA damage as detected through phosphorylated H2A.X (γH2A.X) foci (Extended Data Fig. 5i), a developmental impediment33. By contrast, DNA damage levels in embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) were as low as those of non-injection control. Our results do not exclude the possibility that the suppressed ZGA and basal DNA damage combinatorially impaired development. Nonetheless, our data indicate that embryos with stiff two-cell nuclei are unable to facilitate proper ZGA and early development. Embryos with tether-stiffened nuclei also exhibited a two-cell arrest (Extended Data Fig. 9k), supporting the necessity of nuclear softness for development.

Given the impact of nuclear stiffness on ZGA, we examined chromatin dynamics in deformable and non-deformable nuclei. Our ExM images at 24 h.p.i. showed peripheral layers of DNA and lamins, with the overlap comparable to those analysed using electron microscopy34 (~150 nm; Extended Data Fig. 6i). Our imaging further revealed a preferential localization of DNA near concave regions of the two-cell nuclear envelope (Fig. 5a–c and Extended Data Fig. 6j). Lamin B1 signals also exhibited a weak negative correlation with nuclear deformation35 (Fig. 5b,c). However, the biased DNA localization was shared among deformable nuclei regardless of lamin B1 enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 6k–m), suggesting that nuclear deformation is associated with peripheral DNA organization.

We next examined how deformable nuclei are linked to gene expression regulation during ZGA. In 3D images, large fluorescent foci positive for elongating RNA polymerase II (Pol II Ser2P) shifted their distribution towards the nuclear periphery, as nuclear deformation increased from 21 to 24 h.p.i. (Fig. 5d,e). Notably, the majority of the Pol II foci became more frequently associated with nuclear concavity (Fig. 5f). The focus sizes increased over time, and their growth was suppressed by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5g). Concomitantly, DNA mass volume decreased by 14.7 ± 6.5% (Fig. 5h). We next performed sequential 3D fluorescence in situ hybridization (3D FISH) analysis36 to examine the link between peripheral transcriptional activity and ZGA (Fig. 5i–l). We analysed the genomic loci of Kdm5b and Obox6, along with Gabarapl1 as a non-ZGA control and found that their distributions were broad and changed from the early to the mid-to-late two-cell stage, but the average distance remained 2–3 µm from the nuclear periphery around the time of major ZGA (2.7 ± 2.0, 2.0 ± 1.6 and 2.1 ± 1.3 µm, respectively; 28 h.p.i.) (Fig. 5i–k). Pol II Ser2P intensities were greater when the Obox6 and Kdm5b loci were positioned >1 µm from the nuclear periphery, while DAPI signals remained unchanged, suggesting that the increased local transcriptional activity was not merely a consequence of higher chromatin density (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j). This trend was not observed in Gabarapl1 (Extended Data Fig. 10i). Our sequential FISH further enabled us to determine the locations of multiple gene loci within the same nucleus (Fig. 5l). Our data indicated a widespread positioning of Obox6 and Kdm5b loci at 21 h.p.i. and a change in the localization of gene loci at 28 h.p.i., with a frequent incidence of their concomitant presence near the nuclear periphery. This locus distribution was disrupted by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5l). Notably, Pol II Ser2P intensities at Obox6 loci depended on the nuclear stiffening, while their changes at Kdm5b loci appeared less pronounced (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We therefore performed sequential 3D DNA–RNA FISH analysis to detect nascent Kdm5b transcripts and found a surge in the production around 2–4 µm from the nuclear envelope, and it depended on peripheral nuclear stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 10l–n). In summary, our data suggest that soft and plastic two-cell nuclei ensure the formation of active transcription sites a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope and enable the coordinated positioning of key ZGA gene loci around the sites for expression.

Our study reveals physical characteristics of early embryonic nuclei and their distinct changes that facilitate ZGA. Our data show that the autophagy factor LC3 and lamin B1 clearance confer nuclear plasticity and softness, and that deformable nuclei are key to robust zygotic transcription. Extensive studies have profiled epigenetic states of chromatin and provided a genome-centred view of this critical developmental transition. Our study highlights the importance of physical nuclear state for this transition and underscores the need for integration of diverse embryonic parameters, including their subcellular material properties.

Our work identifies a transient phase of nuclear deformability that manifests as cells transition through a totipotent state (Fig. 1). Notably, this nuclear change marks normal preimplantation development and contributes to transcription and gene locus movement (Figs. 2, 4 and 5). Notably, the sites of active DNA transactions appear a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope, often associated with local negative curvature, suggesting the generation of inward forces around these sites (Fig. 5d–h). During ZGA, chromatin undergoes dynamic remodelling and compaction37,38,39, while maintaining contact with the nuclear lamina40. A flexible nuclear envelope may accommodate these internal and peripheral chromatin activities, mediating a mechanical conflict for the consolidation of functional genome architectures. Our analysis also suggests that intense transcriptional activity near the deformable nuclear envelope enables the full activation of key ZGA genes that shape the two-cell epigenome14 (Fig. 4l,m). Such mechanical control may also operate in naive embryonic stem cells, in which soft nuclei are linked to pluripotency and priming for differentiation41.

We find that the embryonic mechanism governing lamin B1 clearance shares similarities with nuclear autophagy activated during oncogene-induced cell senescence23 (Fig. 3). As autophagy is accompanied by an increase in intracellular calcium levels and is independent of mTORC1 in early embryos21,42, the clearance is most likely developmentally programmed. Our data suggest a role of nuclear translocation of LC3 and its distinct effect on nuclear shape and mechanics. Further analysis of its regulated nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling43 should reveal the mechanistic basis behind the physiological and pathological nuclear remodelling.

Our findings also raise several interesting questions for future studies. First, our imaging assay detected diluted lamin B1 at convex regions of the nuclear envelope35 (Fig. 5b,c). It remains to be explored whether the clearance of lamin B1 merely contributes to nuclear softening or controls DNA organization by sensing local nuclear curvature. Second, as lamins influence transcription44,45 and the chromatin–lamina contacts change during development40, understanding the interplay between mechanical cues and biochemical factors that ensures robust transcriptional control will be an essential next step. Third, soft and transcriptionally active nuclei, yet enriched with lamin B1 at the nuclear envelope, were prone to DNA damage (Extended Data Fig. 5i). As excess lamin B1 can cause persistent DNA damage46, autophagic clearance of lamin B1 may be necessary to protect against such damage. It would be interesting to dissect nuclear actin in two-cell nuclei47, as per its involvement in DNA damage repair48.

Physical nuclear stability is likely important for early embryos, given the potential mechanical challenges they face during passage through the uterine tube49. Yet this period coincides with a transient state in which nuclei become less mechanically resilient. Early mammalian embryos are also prone to DNA lesions and chromosome missegregation50,51,52. Understanding how embryos navigate the vulnerable state may reveal principles underlying developmental robustness.

Mice (ICR and B6C3F1/Jc1 or slc (BCF1)) aged 5–15 weeks53 were purchased from CLEA Japan, Japan SLC or Kiwa Laboratory Animals, maintained in light-controlled (light: 08:00 to 20:00; dark: 20:00 to 08:00), air-conditioned rooms (ambient temperature: 23 °C ± 1.5 °C, humidity: 50 ± 10%) at each facility and used for experiments. All mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation and all efforts were made to minimize suffering and to reduce the number of animals used.

To obtain oocytes, female mice were superovulated by intraperitoneal injections of 7.5 IU of pregnant mare serum gonadotropin (PMSG; ASKA Animal Health), followed by 7.5 IU of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG; ASKA Animal Health) at 48 h after PMSG injection. After the female mice were euthanized at 15–16 h after hCG injection, oocytes were collected from the oviducts by an abdominal operation and transferred to a pre-heated medium of Human Tubal Fluid (HTF; ARK Resource). Sperm were collected from the caudal epididymis of male mice for in vitro fertilization (IVF). For fertilization, freshly prepared or cryopreserved sperm were incubated in HTF medium for 1–1.5 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2 to allow for capacitation. Subsequently, the sperm suspension was mixed with the medium containing the oocytes, and fertilized eggs were collected 1–2 h after insemination followed by removal of cumulus cells with 0.1% hyaluronidase. The eggs were then transferred to drops of preheated KSOM medium (ARK Resource) and cultured at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2.

Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) was performed as described previously54. In brief, enucleation of cumulus-free MII oocytes was performed in drops of CZB medium including 5 μg ml−1 cytochalasin B. One donor cumulus cell in CZB medium with 6% deionized-BSA was transferred to the perivitelline space of an enucleated oocyte together with a small amount of HVJ-E (GenomeONE-CF; Ishihara Sangyo) by tightly attaching the donor cell to the enucleated oocyte. The oocyte was then cultured in KSOM medium for 1 h at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2 for the cell fusion. The reconstructed oocytes were activated in KSOM medium containing 5 mM SrCl2, 2 mM EGTA and 5 μg ml−1 cytochalasin B (Sigma-Aldrich) for 6 h at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2. The activated SCNT embryos were cultured at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2 in KSOM medium.

Pharmacological inhibition experiments were performed by treating embryos with the following chemicals in KSOM medium containing 0.5% (v/v) DMSO: 10 µM wortmannin (19545-26-7, AdipoGen); and 200 nM bafilomycin A1 (SML1661, Sigma-Aldrich). Wortmannin treatment was started at 12 h.p.i. and terminated before fixation at 32 h.p.i. Bafilomycin treatment was started at 15 h.p.i. and terminated before fixation at 28 h.p.i. The mock control also contained 0.5% (v/v) DMSO throughout assays.
