https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Q&A: Creating evidence-based lifestyle medicine interventions
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom; Kerry W. Reding, PhD, MPH, RN, FAHA
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

ORLANDO — Data showing the benefits of lifestyle medicine can empower patients to focus on healthy aging, according to a speaker here.

Kerry W. Reding, PhD, MPH, RN, FAHA, a professor of biobehavioral nursing and health informatics at the University of Washington, offered a presentation on what decades of research from the Women’s Health Initiative have revealed about the intersection between lifestyle medicine and longevity at the annual ACLM conference.

Healio spoke with Reding to learn more about longevity for women, the evidence behind lifestyle medicine’s effects on longevity and how that evidence can be translated into practical strategies.

Healio: Why is this an important topic for healthcare providers to know about?

Reding: People seem eager for guidance on how to live longer and healthier lives, but can also be overwhelmed by all the information that comes through our news feeds and our social media, and it can make it challenging to discern what’s truly an evidence-based strategy or recommendation.

I wanted to present on lifestyle factors from the perspective of healthy aging and longevity because there is so much out there that is based on rigorous science and these evidence-based strategies can inform on how people can change their behaviors in order to improve their health span. Also, with the American College of Lifestyle Medicine, it’s really a great opportunity to showcase all the research and literature that show how the six pillars relate to longevity.

I’ve been involved with the Women’s Health Initiative study for about 15 years, and felt it was noteworthy to describe how the WHI has become such a great resource for understanding lifestyle factors in relation to healthy aging and longevity. In part, that’s because the study’s been going on for over 30 years, and along that time, it has been gathering information on people’s lifestyle factors while at the same time going through a rigorous assessment of any chronic conditions or disabilities that have developed in people over time. So, with those two pieces of prospectively collected data, there’s a vast amount of data to use to better understand how lifestyle factors are related to not just longevity but also healthy aging, that concept of being able to thrive in your 80s and 90s while still in good health.

Healio: How do the pillars of lifestyle medicine affect longevity? Do these pillars affect women’s longevity differently?

Reding: It is clear that lifestyle pillars impact longevity. We see in particular that physical activity is a notable pillar. From the literature, we see people can cut their risk for early mortality in half through regular physical activity. And what I highlight in my talk is that we see this also in a dose response relationship — so, with the increasing amount of physical activity is an improvement in longevity. The reason that’s important is, one, it shows that any little amount you do is going to improve your longevity. It’s not an all-or-none strategy. It’s like, “Do the best you can, do something every day, and if you don’t hit 10,000 steps, that’s fine, but even reaching 3,000 steps, 5,000 steps is going to be good for your health.” The other part about that dose response curve is that when we see that in in a relationship, we see that it provides some support for a causal relationship, so we have more indication it’s actually the physical activity that is causing longevity to be improved, rather than, “We think there’s other factors at play.”

The other thing that was really interesting to me, I recently met Gianni Pes in Sardinia, and he’s the originator of the blue zones concept. He was circling in blue on a map the areas that had notable longevity. When I talked to him and was curious about his 30 years of research in this area — what were the things that he was personally doing? — physical activity was his No. 1 thing. That felt pretty validating because that’s what I see the data shows, but he really highlighted for me that physical activity is within our control to be able to improve our own longevity.

I’d also say what has shown up in the data is around social connectedness. So, unfortunately in the U.S., [it is] an overlooked factor, but can have a great impact on reducing mortality. I cite in my talk a 91% elevated risk for mortality for people with low social integration in a meta-analysis, and the work done in this seminal paper essentially showed that social isolation is the new smoking. I think that’s something that we could take as a message to Americans to really think about how we could improve our social integration in our day-to-day lives.

In general, I think presenting at ACLM is quite gratifying because it’s an audience that, like me, is really interested in in having this discussion about how lifestyle factors are affecting healthy aging, and we all have the shared goal of bringing that to our patients and then disseminating that information more widely.

Healio: What evidence from the Women’s Health Initiative demonstrates the impact lifestyle medicine has on longevity?

Reding: The WHI collected data on lifestyle and behavioral factors and chronic conditions over its 30 years of existence, and it also conducted a series of clinical trials. There were several different clinical trials, and one of them was a dietary modification trial. That one showed, in particular, that women who were enrolled in the trial that recommended they eat a diet high in fiber — fruits and vegetables — and low in fats, were less likely to die of breast cancer than the women who were in the control group. So, they’ve shown that this pillar of nutrition is impactful for longevity.

They’ve also done some really interesting sets of studies where they’ve investigated the concept of healthspan. They’ve basically created a phenotype of healthy aging. For this, they classified women as those living to age 85 in good health, free of chronic conditions or disability versus those who are either age 85 but not in good health or those who died before age 85. The WHI propsective study has shown a strong relationship between higher physical activity and living to age 85 in good health. So, that’s a compelling way to use the WHI data to understand this concept of healthy aging. This is similar to the concept of the super-ager which has been defined as a person who’s in their 80s and still in great health.

I would say the other piece that has been looked at in relation to the healthy aging phenotype — being 85 and in good health — was a woman’s sense of purpose. Here investigators researched whether or not a person had a sense of purpose and then followed her to determine whether or not she was healthy at age 85, and they saw a strong relationship — again, a dose response relationship — between having a sense of purpose and later achieving age 85 in good health.

Healio: How can that evidence be translated into practical clinical strategies that healthcare providers can offer? Can you describe some of these strategies?

Reding: The first thing providers can do is to assess patients on these six pillars. It starts with better understanding where the patient’s baseline is, and then trying to understand from the patient’s perspective which of the pillars are the highest priority for them. Which ones do they want to make improvements in? Because that’s where we’ll see the most appreciable changes in patient’s lifestyle behaviors.

Then, I recommend providers employ a coach approach. So, that’s either by acting in the role of coach themselves — understanding what the patient wants and learning from the patient’s wisdom, rather than being in the role of an expert talking to someone — or if they want to use the coach approach by literally referring a patient to a health coach. I think that’s a really viable solution when aiming to help patients make these behavior changes on their own because essentially many of us know we want to eat well and exercise, but the how-to can be harder to implement than just saying it. So, I think the coach approach can be a really great strategy for helping patients to achieve the changes that they voice they want to make.

Healio: What is the take-home message here?

Reding: I would want them to see that lifestyle factors are immensely important in thinking about how to help a patient achieve healthy aging. I think a lot of ACLM members are already on board with this concept, but I would hope that the data I provide gives them another tool in their tool chest for how to talk to patients and how to conceptualize this vast area of research in a way that can be conveyed to their patients in a clinic setting.

Kerry W. Reding, PhD, MPH, RN, FAHA, can be reached at primarycare@healio.com.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Subcutaneous home furosemide effective for worsening heart failure
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

PHOENIX — At-home self-administration of subcutaneous furosemide appeared safe and feasible for most patients with worsening heart failure who did not improve with oral diuretics, a speaker reported.

Use of a wearable, at-home subcutaneous furosemide injector (Lasix ONYU, SQ Innovation) was preferred over hospital admission in a cohort of patients with worsening HF symptoms, according to an interim analysis presented at the Heart Failure Society of America Annual Scientific Meeting.

“Congestion is a primary driver of heart failure admissions, and it’s a strong marker of mortality risk. IV loop diuretics are the cornerstone of decongestion in those patients, as oral diuretics are less effective in congested states,” Jude ElSaygh, MD, cardiology fellow at University of Florida Health, said during a presentation. “But usually, what that means is hospitalization, which motivated outpatient at-home subcutaneous furosemide as a strategy to relieve congestion and potentially avoid admission.”

The trial device was an on-body furosemide injector designed to deliver hospital-strength treatments at home via patient self-administration. The device includes a furosemide cartridge that is inserted into a disposable patch-like unit powered by a reusable unit able to be used up to 48 times, according to the presentation.

The device was previously evaluated in the SUBCUT HF II trial, which included patients already admitted to the hospital with worsening HF who were subsequently randomly assigned to be discharged early and sent home with the device or standard in-hospital care.

As Healio previously reported, the device was associated with more days alive and out of the hospital compared with the standard care group (between-group mean difference, 4 days; 95% CI, 2.1-5.8; P < .001).

For the present pragmatic, prospective, single-center, open-label, single-arm pilot study, researchers enrolled 21 patients with chronic HF and worsening congestion despite oral loop diuretic titration (mean age, 63 years; 62% men; 52% white).

The primary endpoints were ED visit or hospital admission at 3, 7 and 30 days of follow-up and patient experience measured via survey. Secondary endpoints included device performance, adverse events, renal function and potassium at 3-day follow-up, according to the study methods.

At baseline, 71% of participants had an estimated glomerular filtration rate of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2; 67% had left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% or less; and 95% were enrolled in the outpatient setting.

The researchers reported no ED visits or hospital admissions at 3-day follow-up. One patient was admitted to the hospital by day 7, and three were admitted by day 30, according to the presentation.

Researchers reported the average number of prescribed doses was 7.4, and 91% of device applications were successful.

One adverse event of device detachment occurred, according to the presentation.

Researchers reported that day-3 renal function and potassium were both stable.

“Most patients had an improvement in their creatinine, suggesting a cardiorenal syndrome, and there was no [acute kidney injury] noted, and only one patient had mild hypokalemia,” ElSaygh said during the presentation.

Twelve participants provided survey responses, of which 92% said the device was easy to use; 92% said they were able to do daily activities while wearing the device; 83% preferred the at-home treatment over hospital admission; 83% said they would recommend the device; and 67% reported improved symptoms.

“At-home subcutaneous furosemide is a feasible, well-tolerated alternative to hospital-based IV diuresis in patients with worsening heart failure who fail oral diuretics,” ElSaygh said during the presentation. “We had 95 successful applications with stable renal function and potassium, and no evidence of orthostatic hypotension resulting in falls, and no evidence of over-diuresis. Perhaps more importantly, most patients found it easy to use and preferred treatment at home.

“For our next steps, we want to see how this implements into standard clinic workflows. We want to find the right strategy for the right patient, and we want to optimize the at-home care pathway,” ElSaygh said.

ElSaygh J, et al. Plenary session 1. Presented at: Heart Failure Society of America Annual Scientific Meeting; Oct. 9-12, 2026; Phoenix.

Disclosures: ElSaygh reports no relevant financial disclosures. The trial was sponsored by SQ Innovation.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Medically tailored meals improve blood pressure, glucose, diet
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — Adults with hypertension and type 2 diabetes improved their blood pressure, glucose and nutrition score when they ate medically tailored meals, researchers reported at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

The benefits were observed even when the quantity of medically tailored meals decreased during the intervention, according to the researchers.

“An unhealthy diet is a leading cardiometabolic disease risk factor,” Nour Makarem, PhD, FAHA, assistant professor of epidemiology and codirector of the Chronic Disease Unit at Mailman School of Public Health, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, told Healio. “Food Is Medicine interventions, which address diet quality and food security in a manner that is integrated with the healthcare system, are a promising approach to address the chronic disease burden. Medically tailored meals programs are an example of a Food Is Medicine intervention, as they provide healthy meals that are tailored to the medical needs of every patient.”

As part of the American Heart Association’s Healthcare x Food Initiative, Makarem and colleagues enrolled 110 adults with hypertension and type 2 diabetes (mean age, 63 years; 68% women; 47% Hispanic; 43% Black) into an 8-month program in which they were randomly assigned to a standard medically tailored meals program consisting of 10 medically tailored meals per week plus nutritional counseling or to a program in which they received nutritional counseling plus 10 medically tailored meals per week for the first 3 months, gradually decreasing to five medically tailored meals per week in the final month.

Both groups received Lifes Essential 8 and healthy eating educational content, culturally appropriate cooking demonstrations and gift bags with cooking utensils, fresh produce and healthy ingredients to support healthy eating outside the program, Makarem told Healio.

This population is traditionally not eligible for medically tailored meals, which are usually made available to people with more advanced disease, Makarem told Healio.

“We undertook this study because we hypothesized that introducing these programs earlier, before the disease is advanced and complications arise, could be a more effective approach to prevent further morbidity and save healthcare costs down the line,” she said. “In addition, there have been no studies of what constitutes an effective dose, so we tested two dosing approaches.”

At 8 months, across both groups, the Mediterranean Eating Pattern for Americans score improved by 3.15 points (95% CI, 1.76-5.63), participants had more than twofold odds of improved food security status (P < .001), HbA1c dropped by 0.5 percentage points (95% CI, 0.81 to 0.16; P = .003), systolic BP fell 3.7 mm Hg (95% CI, 7.03 to 0.43; P < .001) and diastolic BP declined by 4.1 mm Hg (95% CI, 6.14 to 2.14; P < .001), Makarem and colleagues found.

There were no differences in the treatment effects between the groups (P for interaction for all > .05), which means that “providing access to a less costly iteration of the intervention (due to gradual dosing down of the meals) is an effective approach to improve blood pressure and glucose when coupled with an appropriate cointervention to support healthy eating at home,” Makarem told Healio.

Participants rated the intervention high for acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility and satisfaction, according to the researchers.

“Satisfaction was high and actually implementation was easier for this group (patients with diabetes and high blood pressure who do not currently qualify for these programs due to not having advanced enough diabetes) than for patients with advanced disease who currently qualify for these programs,” Makarem told Healio. “This research can inform expanding programmatic opportunities and funding for medically tailored meals programs to help address the cardiometabolic disease burden in the population.”

Makarem N, et al. Abstract MDP2382. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Makarem reports no relevant financial disclosures. The study was funded by the American Heart Association as part of its Healthcare x Food Initiative.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-ou.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigns and CFO Colette tapped as interim chief
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-ou.author: Sebastian Herrera, Amanda Gerut
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-ou.text:
Nvidia’s board of directors accepted Chief Executive Jensen Huang’s resignation, the company announced Thursday, an ouster that follows his admission of having an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials deemed to be a Chinese spy. The decision by the chipmaking giant deals a swift end to Huang’s 33-year reign as CEO and is sending shockwaves throughout the technology industry.

In his stead, the board has tapped Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. A steadfast presence with Huang before Wall Street, Kress will be a familiar face and voice with Wall Street as Nvidia navigates through an abrupt CEO transition that promises to be precarious. Nvidia’s board has started a search for a permanent successor to Huang, and will consider internal and external candidates.

The board—for the first time ever—has appointed a chair of the board in Harvey Jones. He’s a managing partner with Square Wave Ventures, and joined the board in 1993 when the company was founded. As a veteran who has overseen Nvidia since its earliest days, Jones will likely serve as a conduit for the institutional memory that departs with Huang.

In addition to Huang’s entanglement with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, on Wednesday the New York Times reported that Huang, 63 years old, had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care. Powell could not immediately be reached for comment. Observers have said the board could not keep Huang in his role following that second reported breach of trust. It’s also unclear whether the U.S. government shared more information with Nvidia privately following his confession.

Nvidia stock is tumbling on the news, down 6.8% today. Nvidia famously does not have employment agreements with its executives so unless Huang negotiates an exit, he’ll leave with no severance and stands to lose about $120 million to $150 million in unvested stock plus his fiscal 2027 bonus. His personal stake is valued at about $150 billion, and Huang holds 3.6% of the company.

According to LinkedIn, Powell has been with Nvidia for nearly two decades and previously spent 10 years in AI business development. Nvidia describes her as formerly leading the company’s higher education and research business, alongside Nvidia AI labs.

Huang’s long-term future with the company is not immediately clear. On Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia announced an investigation into the reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. At the time, the board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that its inquiry would examine “all available information.”

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has been integral to the company’s success, particularly its magnificent run in recent years. Growth accelerated in the first half of its fiscal 2027, with revenue of $96 billion, up 85% year-over-year. Kress previously said the company expected 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028.

Huang reigns supreme over the company. Since its founding, he has created a unique, flat structure in which he sits at the center of most decisions, with about 60 direct reports. Before the Jones appointment, Nvidia’s board long operated without a chair, and the company has not set out a clear succession plan. It also does not have a chief operating officer. Huang is known to text and call small clients himself.

Nvidia’s succession challenge would not be whether its engineers can keep building chips without Huang, analysts say. It is whether anyone, or any leadership team, can inherit his authority to decide what gets built, secure the industry’s commitment to it, and keep customers confident in the next bet.

With Huang’s ouster, the biggest questions are who will succeed him in the long run and what plan the company will put in place to fill the power vacuum.

“Rarely has a board faced this much pressure. This is the board’s moment to shine or fade,” Michael Useem, a professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, told Fortune. “If the board had been doing its job, it would already have a slate of possible successors: people identified as likely successors.”

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies and Lester Crown Professor in Management Practice at Yale University’s School of Management, compared the Huang saga to what happened at McDonald’s with former CEO Steve Easterbrook, who was ousted in Nov. 2019. The McDonald’s board investigated Easterbrook for a consensual relationship with an employee that involved the exchange of videos and romantic text messages, and then found that other undisclosed, improper relationships had occurred.

Easterbrook was later charged by the Securities and Exchange Commission with making false and misleading statements to investors about the circumstances that led to his termination. Easterbrook didn’t admit or deny the findings, but agreed to bar himself as an officer or director of any public company for a period of five years, and he paid a $400,000 civil penalty.

Huang’s ouster creates a massive hole for the AI industry. Huang has been central to the industry’s rapid growth. His success in creating world-leading graphics processing units, the chips that power AI by handling model training and regular user queries, has been instrumental in ushering in the AI boom and in the U.S.’s leading position.

Few executives in Silicon Valley and beyond exert the level of power and influence over one company and industry. Huang’s institutional knowledge and deep industry connections have been among the reasons tech analysts and other experts have said it would be impossible to replace him. Another reason has been President Trump, who has become a close friend of Huang and stood by the executive since Sunday’s revelations, saying Huang is an “amazing guy” and “honorable man.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/wall-stre.title: Andrew Cuomo: Wall Street is ready. Congress needs to catch up
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/wall-stre.author: Andrew M. Cuomo
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/wall-stre.text:
History shows that technological innovations have brought great advances to our nation’s financial system, but only after disruption, opposition and regulatory reform.

For over a century, Wall Street ran on paper, phones and people racing across hectic exchange floors. The “Canyon” was ruled by institutional giants whose power extended through the halls of government.

In the late 1960s, new technology challenged the status quo, with computers offering electronic pricing and trading. In 1969, a company called Instinet pioneered electronic stock trading. This major disruption threatened the Wall Street establishment and was met with skepticism, hostility and warnings about the perils of electronic systems. But while vested interests were opposed, the broader market was beginning to see the benefits.

In 1971, Nasdaq was formed to use an electronic platform to distribute quotes, but most trades were still executed over the telephone through existing brokerage firms. Following the national debacle of the 1987 market crash, when Wall Street was under tremendous public pressure, participation in an electronic execution system became mandatory for market makers. In the mid-1990s, emerging electronic trading networks, including Island and Archipelago, joined Instinet in posing a viable challenge to traditional trading.

In 1996, SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt, a seasoned and courageous official, adopted landmark regulations increasing transparency and facilitating competition from electronic communication networks (ECNs). The SEC then adopted electronic trading regulations creating a more comprehensive regulatory framework for alternative trading systems (ATS).

Once unleashed, the benefits of electronic trading became undeniable, and the Wall Street establishment had a choice: either accept and incorporate the new technology or be replaced by it.

They are survivors. Today, electronic trading is simply trading, and the rest is history.

And history does repeat itself!

Now blockchain technology presents the same kind of moment, offering a new foundation for issuing securities, recording ownership and trading. Like electronic trading before it, blockchain has arrived, challenging the status quo, prompting vocal critics and forcing regulators to examine changing circumstances.

Blockchain technology is built on cryptography. Cryptography uses mathematics to protect information, verify authenticity and secure transactions. Blockchain uses these techniques to create verifiable, tamper-resistant records of transactions. Early applications of blockchain became widely known through cryptocurrencies and digital tokens, which could be exchanged for traditional currencies. But the underlying technology has applications far beyond cryptocurrency trading, including the issuance, transfer and recording of ownership of traditional financial assets.

In 2011, as governor of New York, my technology advisers and financial professionals introduced me to cryptography and blockchain as technological innovations that could streamline our financial system and help New York maintain its position as the global financial capital.

Our interest was piqued by the potential of cryptography and blockchain technology rather than simply by companies trading digital tokens. New York was the first state to license these companies. That underlying technology is what presents the great opportunity today.

Electronic trading ultimately earned its place because it delivered faster, better execution, greater transparency and lower friction. Blockchain presents the potential for the next step forward, offering faster settlement, a more direct connection between issuers and investors, greater transparency and, importantly, the possibility of a 24/7 global marketplace that could attract additional investment to American securities markets.

The days of nine-to-five hours and “closed for the weekend” signs are long gone for almost every economic enterprise, except Wall Street!

It is progress long overdue.

The SEC recently established an innovation exemption to facilitate the trading of certain U.S. stocks using blockchain technology. Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, and OKX, a leading financial technology and blockchain company, have formed a joint venture, OKXICE, which has submitted notice of its intent to operate a securities venue under that framework.

While there are regulatory hurdles, the SEC exemption is a groundbreaking first step toward using blockchain technology to trade actual securities, with the potential for around-the-clock access and faster settlement.

Is it disruptive? Yes!

Adoption of new technology is disrupting businesses around the world. In finance, some intermediary functions may become less necessary or be fundamentally redesigned.

And 24/7 trading means investors can react in real time to information and developments in the public arena.

We already know blockchain technology can be successfully utilized in financial markets. Europe and other jurisdictions have already established frameworks to authorize its use. And we have seen explosive consumer growth in digital platforms offering 24/7 trading.

We also know that much of the financial establishment is changing its position. Initial opposition has increasingly given way to competition to adopt this new technology.

Once again, like electronic trading, companies face a choice: incorporate the new technology or risk being overtaken by competitors that do.

The next step in this evolution is for government regulators to adjust to the new reality. Congress’s failure to advance the CLARITY Act in September was a lost opportunity to establish a durable regulatory framework for digital assets.

With the midterms behind us, this should be a moment to put politics aside and focus on the economic stakes. The administration and incoming Congress must find consensus on developing a system that adopts this proven technology, protects consumers, ensures ethical behavior by our government officials and opens our markets for a new generation of growth.

America has always turned breakthrough ideas into lasting advances. Wall Street’s next electronic revolution is underway.

Congress should make sure America leads rather than follows.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/boring-ac.title: The ‘boring job’ that millennials abandoned is one of the hottest seasonal jobs on the market—and could lead Gen Z to $200K salaries with training
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/boring-ac.author: Orianna Rosa Royle
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/boring-ac.text:
It’s been called one of the dullest jobs in America. Boomers are leaving it in droves, millennials decided they’d rather do almost anything else, and AI was supposed to kill it off. Yet accounting has made it onto the holiday hiring list again for a second year in a row.

According to Monster’s Seasonal Hiring Index 2026, tax associates and tax experts were among the 13 job titles with the most seasonal activity across its platform—and it’s so hot, it appears twice on their list.

Last year, tax accountants topped Monster’s seasonal rankings.

The industry faces a huge talent shortage. In 2024, the U.S. was short of 340,000 accountants—and the problem is only getting worse. The average company now has 17 open accounting and finance roles they’re trying to fill, up from just five last year.

And so seasonal accounting cover could be a foot in the door to a six-figure career beyond the holidays.

“Seasonal work is more than a short-term paycheck; it’s often the start of a longer career journey,” last year’s report said, while adding that many companies use seasonal roles to test the waters for permanent ones.

To get in, tax accountants typically need at least a bachelor’s degree. Those with a CPA (certified public accountant) qualification can unlock higher wages of around $200,000.

Plenty of young people could use the work. Millions of Gen Zers are NEETs, meaning not in employment, education, or training. And with entry-level roles disappearing thanks to AI, young job hunters are three times less likely than previous generations to have a job lined up when they leave school. For many, even a temporary paycheck over the holidays would be a welcome start.

But Gen Zers who have just started thinking about nabbing a job over the festive period may already be too late.

In fact, Monster found that seasonal hiring jumped 44% from August to September last year and peaked in October. Then it fell by about 24% by November—and that drop showed up in both years Monster analyzed.

Tax and accounting postings were especially concentrated in September and October, well before the weather turns frosty and people are thinking about their Christmas plans.

And to make matters even harder, finding the few seasonal jobs left right now could be like finding a needle in a haystack. Many of them are hiding in plain sight.

Less than 3% of seasonal postings in 2025 used words like “seasonal,” “holiday,” or “temporary” in their title. So stop searching for “holiday jobs” and instead search by the actual job title, such as “tax associate.”

Monster also advises late starters to broaden their search to more titles and industries, and to use December to get ahead of the next hiring wave, because tax season, summer camps, and hospitality jobs often recruit months in advance.

Accounting aside, most seasonal jobs trending right now are retail, which probably isn’t surprising since stores need all hands on deck to get through the Christmas shopping rush.

Nine of the 13 jobs on Monster’s list are in retail or involve handling and delivering packages, so whether shoppers head to the shops or click “buy now,” a seasonal worker is probably behind it.

“Retail remains an important part of the seasonal market,” the report noted, before adding that the data shows seasonal opportunities across delivery, warehouse and logistics, tax and accounting, and hospitality.

“If working a cash register doesn’t appeal to you, consider fulfillment or warehouse work,” the report added. “The wider you cast your search, the more likely you are to find a seasonal position that fits your skills and schedule.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ciscos-pe.title: Cisco’s people chief: ‘We can’t transform our workforce without fundamentally rethinking how we lead’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ciscos-pe.author: Roula Amire, Great Place To Work
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ciscos-pe.text:
Cisco is preparing its 85,000 employees to learn new skills, experiment with AI, and rethink how they work.

That takes more than teaching people how to use the technology. It takes time to learn, freedom to experiment, and leaders who are willing to change alongside them.

Cisco has invested in AI tools, role-specific training, coaching, mentoring, and new career development opportunities.

That focus on its people has helped earn it the No. 2 spot on the 2026 Fortune World’s Best Workplaces™ list.

Cisco is also seeing record business performance. It closed its 2026 fiscal year with record revenue and a record quarter, including record revenue per employee.

“Our focus is building learning agility: the ability to learn, unlearn, experiment, and apply new capabilities as work evolves,” says Francine Katsoudas, Cisco’s executive vice president and chief people, policy & purpose officer. “We want our people to be able to influence what changes, rather than simply react to it.”

Katsoudas says human judgment is one of the most important capabilities employees will need, “and the critical thinking, curiosity, and creativity that make it possible.”

“As AI takes on more work, we need people to challenge assumptions and make thoughtful decisions,” she says.

Research from the AI Workforce Consortium found growing demand for human capabilities, including ethical reasoning and systems thinking, in cybersecurity-related jobs.

At Cisco, employees are developing human skills alongside technical ones through coaching, mentoring, and opportunities to experiment with AI.

That requires something employees rarely have enough of: time.

Cisco’s Time to Grow initiative gives every employee four dedicated hours each month to learn.

“We’ve all experienced how easily learning can fall to the bottom of the priority list when business demands take over, but the skills our people will need tomorrow require investment today,” Katsoudas says.

Leaders have to make time for learning, too.

“When leaders openly invest in their own development, they help establish a culture where personal growth is expected and supported at every level.”

At Cisco, some executives are taking that a step further: They’re learning from employees.

Cisco’s AI Mentorship Program, or CAMP, pairs employee AI “super users” with senior leaders. Employees are the mentors; executives are the mentees.

“Understanding AI at a strategic level is very different from seeing how people actually use it in their work,” Katsoudas says.

Executives aren’t just learning about AI. Every participant in the first cohort said CAMP created space for candid conversations, shared learning, and experimentation.

“Our first CAMP cohort reinforced that AI fluency is less about mastering technology and more about building trust.”

That trust matters when employees are being asked to try new things.

“We can’t ask people to innovate if they’re afraid to take risks or try something that might not work,” Katsoudas says.

Eighty-nine percent of Cisco employees say management recognizes honest mistakes as part of doing business, compared with 38% at a typical global technology company. That makes Cisco employees 134% more likely to report that experience.

And 87% of Cisco employees are learning AI through experimentation, Katsoudas says.

For Katsoudas, what happens when an experiment doesn’t work is just as important.

“When things go wrong, do we create opportunities to learn and improve together? If we want to innovate faster, we have to accept that some experiments won’t work and learn from them.”

Eighty-eight percent of Cisco employees say people who try new and better ways of doing things are celebrated, compared with 65% at a typical global technology company. The same percentage say people quickly adapt to change, compared with 68%.

For Cisco, getting more from AI starts with leadership.

“The biggest lesson is that we can’t transform our workforce without fundamentally rethinking how we lead,” Katsoudas says.

How leaders use AI matters, too. Cisco employees are twice as likely to use AI when their direct leader does.

But role modeling is only part of the job. Employees also need to understand where the company is going and the role they have in getting there.

“In periods of significant change, people need clarity about where they’re headed, confidence that they have a meaningful role in getting us there, and trust in the decisions being made,” Katsoudas says.

Cisco also had its strongest year for employee productivity in 30 years, Katsoudas says.

Nine in 10 Cisco employees say people are willing to put in extra effort, compared with about two-thirds at a typical global technology company, according to Great Place To Work data.

Katsoudas says Cisco is seeing higher productivity and engagement among employees who consistently use AI.

“That’s encouraging because we’re seeing benefits that extend beyond efficiency,” she says.

Cisco also wants employees to spend more time on customers, relationships, and solving complex problems.

For Katsoudas, the companies that ultimately get AI right will be as intentional about investing in people as they are in technology.

“AI is changing what technology can do, but we need to be equally ambitious about what people can become.”

Roula Amire is the senior content director at Great Place To Work. Follow her on LinkedIn and sign up for the Great Place To Work LinkedIn newsletter to get the latest research on what drives business success.

It takes time to learn, freedom to experiment, and leaders who are willing to change alongside them. Cisco has invested in AI tools, role-specific training, coaching, mentoring, and new career development opportunities.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/cfo-face-.title: CFOs face a tough choice on AI spending as borrowing costs rise, expert warns
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/cfo-face-.author: Sheryl Estrada
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/cfo-face-.text:
Good morning. Companies may need to rethink how much they spend on AI as financing costs rise and economic uncertainty grows. But pulling back too aggressively could leave them at a competitive disadvantage, finance expert Mark Williams told a group of CFOs gathered in New York City on Tuesday evening.

I had a fireside chat with Williams, a master lecturer at Boston University’s Questrom School of Business and a former bank examiner for the Federal Reserve Bank, during a Fortune Modern CFO dinner, sponsored by Deloitte.

“I think it’s going to be reduced,” he said of AI spending, arguing that a more difficult financing environment will bring greater scrutiny to investment decisions.

His cautionary concerns were part of a broader discussion about the post-midterm economic outlook, inflation, interest rates and risks across the AI investment ecosystem. Williams urged executives to prepare for higher capital costs without allowing uncertainty to paralyze investment.

“If we do nothing, then we’re going to lose our competitive edge,” he said.

For CFOs, that means being more disciplined about how they fund AI initiatives and evaluate their returns. Williams recommended having explicit measures of success or failure along with connecting project spending to financial results and considering shorter-term financing rather than automatically borrowing for the long term.

Post-midterm election, regulatory uncertainty adds another aspect to consider. Greater uncertainty can lower growth assumptions and reduce a project’s net present value, making fewer investments financially attractive, Williams explained.

The pressure won’t be evenly distributed across the AI industry. He described a divide between highly rated technology companies and lower-rated AI borrowers, with weaker credits facing greater financing pressure.

Companies with stronger balance sheets may be better positioned to continue investing, while more leveraged businesses could find themselves forced to reconsider their plans, he said.

That preparation should extend beyond investment budgets. Williams suggested finance leaders “stress-rest” accounts receivable and consider whether customers would be able to pay if economic conditions weakened.

He tied those risks to his broader inflation outlook. Persistent price pressures could keep borrowing costs elevated, raising the hurdle for new investments and challenging companies’ ability to generate sufficient returns.

“I think you should assume the cost of capital is going up,” he said when I asked what CFOs should do before year-end.

That preparation should extend beyond investment budgets. Williams suggested finance leaders analyze accounts receivable and consider whether customers would be able to pay if economic conditions weakened. He also questioned whether consumer spending would continue supporting the economy through the holiday season.

But his message is not to retreat from AI. Instead, he predicts finance chiefs will be more discerning about where they place their bets.

“Hold your chief risk officers close,” Williams said. “I think they’re going to be very useful for you in the next couple of months.”

Sheryl Estrada
Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com

He will succeed Ihsan Essaid, who will become vice chairman, an executive role, at the same time. Ahuja brings more than two decades of experience. He joins from aluminum producer Novelis, where he has served as CFO since 2016. Previously, he held CFO roles at Novartis for Alcon North America, Alcon Japan and the company’s South Korean business. Essaid, who has served as QXO’s CFO since July 2024, will oversee mergers and acquisitions and capital-raising activities, reporting to chairman and CEO Brad Jacobs.

Adrian Wood was appointed CFO of BHP Group Limited, a global resources company, effective Feb. 17. He will succeed Vandita Pant, who will step down following the release of BHP’s half-year results on Feb. 16 and remain with the company through March 29. Wood currently serves as VP of projects, minerals Australia. He joined BHP in 2015 and previously served as VP of finance, minerals Australia, and group investor relations officer. He brings more than 25 years of experience, including at UBS and Macquarie Group.

Stanford’s 2026 AI100 report finds that AI has become a mainstream force reshaping science, industry, and society faster than expected, while governance and public oversight struggle to keep pace.

AI is accelerating scientific discovery and disrupting fields once considered resistant to automation, including creative work, software development, and mathematics. Yet the unprecedented investment boom in AI infrastructure has brought environmental pressures and concerns about a financial bubble, with broad economic gains and corporate returns still uncertain.

The central message is that AI’s trajectory should be shaped through meaningful public participation and coordinated, enforceable governance, not solely technological competition and market forces.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/megaspeed.title: How Megaspeed built a network in Singapore and Malaysia to move $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips to Chinese companies
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/megaspeed.author: Angelica Ang, Jay Ganglani
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/megaspeed.text:
The chip-smuggling controversy swirling around Nvidia centers on one company: Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing provider that, according to several media reports, is suspected of funneling advanced AI processors to Chinese companies.

While details of what Megaspeed is alleged to have done remain murky, experts say the case shows how Chinese firms rely on Southeast Asia to skirt U.S. trade controls.

“Chinese firms can access data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—and their computing capacity—without having to import restricted semiconductors,” Ja Ian Chong, a political science expert from the National University of Singapore (NUS), tells Fortune. “But the ease of shipping [chips] through Singapore and Malaysia also makes them attractive for firms and people who wish to circumvent U.S. controls.”

Washington restricts the export of Nvidia’s top-end Blackwell and Rubin chips to China, out of fear Beijing could use them to supercharge its AI ambitions.

According to The Information, Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, used her personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix.

Singapore says it is investigating Megaspeed for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws,” but it separately rejected reports that its authorities were investigating Alice Huang over the espionage allegations. U.S. officials had also been investigating Megaspeed for potential export-control violations.

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing; Nvidia has previously claimed that it found no evidence of illicit chip transfers.

Nvidia’s board said in a Nov. 8 statement that it was initiating an independent investigation into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, though it added it had no reason to believe “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The board said it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.”

Following reports that Huang conducted a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive, the chipmaker’s board is now considering removing Huang as CEO, the Wall Street Journal reports.

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based neocloud that supplies AI computing power. Originally incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, a Chinese gaming firm with ties to state-backed investors, the company changed its name to Megaspeed in early 2023, the same year that Alice Huang joined the company.

Another Singapore-registered firm, Swiftdata, acquired Megaspeed in November 2023. Alice Huang stepped down as Megaspeed’s managing director, while Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong—who owns Swiftdata—became its sole director. (Tan owns another Singapore-registered company, Monster Investment.)

In 2024, Tan established Speedmatrix, a Malaysia-based subsidiary of Megaspeed, which was reportedly used to receive shipments of Nvidia chips. According to the New York Times, between June 2024 and June 2025, Speedmatrix received over 200 shipments of restricted Nvidia technology.

These chips—which are subject to U.S. restrictions on sales to China—were eventually used to power data centers built by Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese firm in which Alice’s younger sister, Huang Yu, is a founding shareholder, according to The Information. The firm, which builds data centers in the Chinese cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen, then provides high-performance AI computing capacity to Chinese tech giants including Alibaba and Tencent.

“AI chip distributors and resellers often spend too little effort vetting customers, usually relying on paperwork the customer provides,” notes Erich Grunewald, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS), a U.S. nonpartisan think tank.

Malaysia has been one of Southeast Asia’s biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, drawing $94 billion in data center investments between 2021 and mid-2026, including from global tech hyperscalers like Google, AWS and Microsoft. “Malaysia has ample land and relatively cheap electricity and water, at least for now,” Chong notes. “The fact that it sits next to key submarine cables also makes it attractive as a spot for data centers.”

Singapore, on the other hand, is favored by multinationals for its open economy, stable political environment and business-friendly policies. Many AI firms, including U.S. firms Anthropic and OpenAI, have chosen to house their APAC headquarters there.

Companies like Megaspeed typically offer two routes to restricted silicon. The first is renting out chips already housed in data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—which, under current rules, is legal. The second is buying chips through front companies and shipping them to China, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls.

(Megaspeed reportedly did both: it set up data center operations in Sedenak Tech Park in the Malaysian state of Johor, and according to the reports, also shuttled chips to Shanghai Century Litong’s facilities in China.)

Under current U.S. export rules, it is legal to give Chinese companies access to AI processors housed outside of China—though previous deals have invited regulatory scrutiny. On Nov. 3, The Financial Times reported that Oracle had canceled a $7 billion deal to grant Tencent access to 100,000 AI chips in data centers across Southeast Asia after U.S. officials raised concerns. The FT also reported that Nvidia is telling cloud computing clients they must sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies.

The U.S. House of Representatives passed a law—the Remote Access Security Act—that would close the loophole allowing Chinese companies to use AI processors housed in other countries; the bill is now before the U.S. Senate.

Both Singapore and Malaysia have cracked down on chip smuggling. In addition to its investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean government last year charged three individuals with fraud after they diverted AI servers bound for Singapore to Malaysia instead.

In October, Malaysian customs officials seized $12.1 million worth of advanced AI chips at Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Initial investigations found the 30 servers—falsely declared as electronic components—were being transferred from one Asian country to another, though officials declined to say which.

Megaspeed, however, has denied the allegations. “There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” it wrote in a statement last December. “We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.”

Chong says the escalating AI arms race between the U.S. and China means both Beijing and Washington will subject third parties like Singapore and Malaysia to deeper scrutiny to keep their own technology from leaking.

“Both Singapore and Malaysia will want to continue to benefit from trust by Beijing and Washington for as long as they can,” concludes Chong. “But they may face greater suspicion, scrutiny, restrictions and even punishment from one or both major powers going forward, and perceptions that they are unreliable or duplicitous partners will only increase such pressure.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/cracks-in.title: The cracks in venture are beginning to show, just as Anthropic gets ready to IPO
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/cracks-in.author: Allie Garfinkle
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/cracks-in.text:
On the eve of a historic IPO for Silicon Valley’s investor community, the fragilities of venture are as clear as they’ve ever been to me.

I’ve been thinking about this irony for days: Anthropic is set to go public as soon as next week (everything I’m hearing says “Jensen Huang’s affair be damned, all systems go”), and while this is primed to be a banner moment for VC, venture seems to be structurally over its skis.

Consider recent data from PitchBook: Hitting a $5 billion valuation takes 80% less time, but 74% more capital, according to the company’s latest U.S. Valuations report.

“Higher valuations raise the bar to achieve profitable exits, and AI is expensive to run,” said Emily Zheng, PitchBook senior research analyst, via email. “Cracks are beginning to show in venture, including large amounts of AI-related debt and a likely slowdown in data center expansion given the recent election.”

The reality is this: Valuations are soaring higher and more readily, but exits are still tough. Zheng is clear that the IPO window—unless a company is in a very select group like SpaceX or Anthropic—remains shut.

“The IPO window has not reopened,” she said via email. “Most listings this year have been in health care, with the high-growth tech names LPs need for distributions largely absent. Removing mega IPOs from 2026’s totals reveals that exit value remains at the same constrained level that has defined every year since the pandemic.”

M&A remains a viable option, but in many deals, Zheng said, “valuation compression remains the dominant theme, as Q3 revealed with Bending Spoons’ acquisitions of Airtable and Miro at significant discounts.” (Airtable, for example, was acquired for $1.28 billion in cash, a vertiginous drop from its 2021 $11.7 billion peak valuation.) Rising rates and broader economic uncertainty are primed to render these pressures worse.

Historical data also suggests the current venture vintage could be in trouble, according to PitchBook’s recent U.S. VC Fundraising and Returns data: Past funds haven’t necessarily performed well during periods characterized by high interest rates (new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh already hiked rates once in 2026, and another hike’s on the table for December). There’s no way to prove causality, but the stressors of high rates, high valuations, and sluggish exits definitionally create pressure.

“The current market is a strange mix of high prices, low liquidity, and a relatively uncertain outlook,” said Zheng via email. “ The outlook for current vintages will likely not look as great as their current markups.”

And as the day of Anthropic’s seemingly imminent IPO approaches, it’s worth remembering that post-IPO performance has been dicey for the few major IPOs we’ve seen: CoreWeave and Circle, up about 52% and 116% respectively since their listing days, are the exception. Figma’s down about 42% in its life as a public company, while Cerebras is down roughly 45%. Nevertheless, what happens next with Anthropic will be the harbinger of where venture and startups go from here.

“Strong performance would validate AI’s enormous private valuations, spurring dealmaking and exit activity as real distributions are injected back into LP portfolios,” said Zheng via email. “Weak performance would bring into question whether AI companies are wildly overvalued.”

That is, of course, the multi-trillion-dollar question.

Allie Garfinkle

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ai-agents.title: Which business moats will still matter in the age of AI?
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ai-agents.author: Michael Joseph
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ai-agents.text:
For many investors, a company’s economic moat is one of the most important things to understand. A strong moat can protect market share, support pricing power and help a business earn attractive returns for years, even as competitors try to take those profits away.

The best moats usually come from something genuinely hard to replicate: a unique product, valuable intellectual property, scarce assets, scale or some other lasting competitive advantage.

But not every moat is built that way.

Some businesses may be protected, at least in part, by the fact that their customers are human.

People are busy. We forget things. We don’t always read the fine print. We put off switching banks or insurance companies because it sounds like a hassle. We keep paying for subscriptions we barely use. And when shopping for something becomes too complicated, we often settle for good enough.

I think of these as behavioral moats. And the rise of personal AI agents could put some of them at risk.

We got an early look at that concern in September, when Meta’s Muse AI agent caught investors’ attention. Shares of companies that could be vulnerable to declining consumer inertia sold off. Charles Schwab fell more than 6%, insurer Allstate dropped 5.5%, Planet Fitness fell as much as 11%, and travel companies including Expedia and Booking Holdings also came under pressure. (Bloomberg)

The reaction may prove overdone. Agentic AI is still young, and there are major questions around security, trust and how much authority consumers will actually hand over to software.

But the underlying question is worth considering now:

Would a company’s advantage still exist if every customer had a tireless personal assistant constantly looking for a better deal?

Financial services may be one of the clearest examples.

Consumers routinely leave money in accounts paying less interest than they could earn elsewhere. That isn’t necessarily because they believe their bank offers the best deal. Moving accounts can mean comparing alternatives, filling out forms, changing direct deposits and reconnecting automatic payments.

Most people have other things to do.

An AI agent does not. In theory, it could regularly compare savings rates, credit card rewards or brokerage products and tell its owner when there is a better alternative. Eventually, agents could handle more of the switching process themselves.

That possibility has already gotten the attention of financial companies. Schwab CEO Rick Wurster recently said the company is blocking unauthorized outside AI agents attempting to access customer accounts or move money. Schwab is instead building controlled ways for outside AI systems to connect to its platform, while limiting what they can do. Other major banks are taking similar precautions. (Bloomberg)

There are legitimate security reasons for that. Giving software free access to your life savings is very different from asking it to order paper towels.

Still, the situation illustrates the broader issue. Friction can protect a business, whether that friction exists for good reasons or not. As agents become better at safely handling tedious financial tasks, some of that protection could weaken.

Sometimes consumers don’t stick with a company because switching is hard. They stick because comparing the alternatives is hard.

Insurance is a good example. Comparing two policies means looking beyond the headline premium to deductibles, coverage limits, exclusions and other details. Telecom plans can involve different data limits, bundles, promotional prices and fees.

A person may eventually decide the potential savings aren’t worth the effort.

Software doesn’t get frustrated after the sixth page of fine print.

This is another area where businesses are already preparing for change. Kin Insurance recently said it would welcome AI shopping agents rather than block them and has since built tools designed to make it easier for agents to obtain home insurance quotes. Insurance marketplace Insurify has also launched an AI Agent Gateway that allows agents to gather and compare real-time quotes while preserving details such as deductibles, limits and disclosures. (Kin / PR Newswire)

That may offer a preview of how companies adapt.

If AI makes comparison easier, businesses can try to fight the change—or make themselves easier for agents to shop. In some industries, being the company that gives an agent the clearest information and easiest path to a transaction could eventually become an advantage of its own.

Subscriptions may be the easiest behavioral moat to understand.

Many of us have looked at a credit card statement and found something we forgot we were still paying for. Sometimes it is a streaming service. Sometimes it is an app. Sometimes it is the gym membership that seemed like a great idea in January.

There is good evidence that this matters to businesses. A 2025 study published in the American Economic Review looked at subscription companies and found cancellations rose sharply when replacement credit cards forced customers to make an active renewal decision. The researchers estimated that cancellation friction roughly doubled seller revenues on average, holding the starting subscriber base constant. (American Economic Review)

An AI agent could make that kind of inattention much less common. It could regularly scan recurring charges, compare them with usage and ask whether you still want to keep paying.

That concern helped send Planet Fitness shares sharply lower following the launch of Muse, as investors considered what easier cancellation might mean for businesses that rely on recurring memberships. (StreetInsider)

Netflix is a more interesting case.

There may be some customers who keep Netflix because canceling is one more thing they haven’t gotten around to doing. Agentic AI could put pressure on that part of the business.

But Netflix also has something much harder for an agent to eliminate: content people actually want to watch. If a consumer wants a show that is only available on Netflix, an AI agent cannot shop around and recreate it somewhere else.

That is the difference between a behavioral moat and a real one.

Even when prices are relatively clear and switching is easy, comparison takes time.

Most people do not check every travel site each morning to see whether another hotel has dropped its price. We don’t constantly search every retailer to make sure something we bought last week is still the best deal. At some point, we stop looking and buy.

AI agents could keep looking.

Travel companies are already building around this idea. Priceline’s Penny can compare destinations, prices and availability and move from a broad travel request toward an actual booking within one conversation. (Priceline)

But perhaps the most interesting response is happening in retail, where Walmart and Amazon are taking very different approaches.

Walmart recently introduced an Agent Gateway designed to allow outside AI agents to connect directly with its systems, search products and make purchases for customers. Shoppers will be able to control what their agents can buy and set limits on their activity. (Walmart)

Amazon, meanwhile, has blocked Muse from shopping on its platform, citing concerns including security and unauthorized access. Amazon is also developing its own AI shopping tools rather than simply opening its ecosystem to outside agents. (Axios)

Both approaches may prove reasonable. This technology is new, and companies have legitimate reasons to be careful about letting outside software interact with customer accounts.

But the contrast between the world’s two largest retailers shows how important the issue could become.

Today, a consumer might go directly to Amazon or Walmart to shop for a television. Tomorrow, that person might simply tell an agent, “Find me the best 55-inch television under $700.”

If the agent does the searching, comparing and buying, the retailer may no longer own the first interaction with the customer. That could eventually change the value of advertising, loyalty programs and simply being the default place where consumers begin their search.

Companies including Mastercard are already building infrastructure around this possibility, helping merchants make products available to AI agents while maintaining control over pricing, fulfillment and transactions. (Mastercard)

None of this means traditional business moats are disappearing.

If anything, agentic AI may make it easier to tell which ones were real.

A patented product or valuable piece of intellectual property cannot simply be compared away. Neither can truly scarce physical assets. A competitor cannot instantly create another well-located piece of infrastructure, another ski mountain or another casino license in a market where those licenses are limited.

The same can apply to real-world experiences. AI may find a cheaper vacation, but it cannot recreate the exact cruise, resort or experience a customer wants.

Those businesses still have to compete. But their advantage comes from offering something difficult to duplicate, rather than relying primarily on consumers being too busy or frustrated to find an alternative.

That distinction could become increasingly important as AI agents get better.

For decades, some companies have benefited not just because they offered the best product, but because consumers were imperfect shoppers. We didn’t have enough time, information or patience to constantly make the optimal choice.

AI may not eliminate those imperfections overnight. Consumers still need to trust agents with their money and personal information, and companies will continue putting limits around what outside software can do.

But if agents begin taking more of the work out of shopping, switching and canceling, one question may become increasingly important for businesses across the economy:

How much of your moat comes from being genuinely better—and how much comes from customers not bothering to leave?

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/lori-huan.author: Sydney Lake
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/lori-huan.text:
Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia hangs in the balance as the board is reportedly preparing to oust the CEO, people familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal. The move follows two extramarital affairs by Huang, one of them with a suspected Chinese spy and another one reportedly with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, according to The New York Times.

Huang admitted in a company memo made public on Nov. 8 to extramarital actions: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Lori has not commented publicly on the memo.

Huang’s position has raised questions about Nvidia’s future, including who would take the reins in his absence, given that he’s the face of the $4 trillion chipmaking giant. But in the family’s philanthropy, his wife, Lori Huang, holds the top title.

Lori is president of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, which reported about $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024, according to its most recent tax filing reviewed by Fortune. Jensen is listed as the foundation’s secretary and CFO, and Lori has held the president title on every filing available dating back to 2014.

Her role also extends to most of the Huangs’ Nvidia shares. As of March 23, Lori and Jensen were co-trustees of three family trusts holding nearly 669 million Nvidia shares, according to Nvidia’s latest proxy statement reviewed by Fortune. That’s most of the 870.6 million shares (worth roughly $151 billion as of late Nov. 11) the proxy reports as beneficially owned by Jensen, a figure that also includes the foundation’s stock.

The proxy also says that as board members of the foundation since 2007, the couple may be deemed to share voting and investment power over its 58.7 million Nvidia shares, though neither has a financial interest in them.

Nvidia’s board said Nov. 8 it was investigating reports Jensen had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, but said it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The independent directors later hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to run the probe. China’s foreign ministry has called the spying allegations groundless.

Lori, born Lori Mills, met Jensen when the two were paired as lab partners in an electrical fundamentals class at Oregon State University, where she graduated in 1985. He was 17 and she was 19. They married in 1985, and a few years later she left the workforce to raise their two children. Both children, Madison and Spencer, now work at Nvidia. Jensen said in an interview with Singapore-based media outlet CNA that “every moment of Nvidia, she was there.”

The foundation’s growth has tracked the Huangs’ gifts of Nvidia stock and the company’s rise. Its net assets climbed from about $819 million at the end of 2020 to more than $9.1 billion at the end of 2024, and about $8.6 billion of its holdings that year were in stocks, according to its tax filings. In 2024 alone, it gained about $5 billion in paper gains. Nvidia’s proxy shows the foundation held 58.7 million Nvidia shares as of March.

In June and September 2024, Jensen and Lori, as co-trustees of their living trust, gave the foundation a combined 1.3 million Nvidia shares, according to Jensen’s Form 4 filings and the foundation’s tax return. The foundation valued those gifts at about $160 million. In September, the trust also gave 688,000 shares to an unnamed donor-advised fund.

The foundation reported paying no salaries in 2024. Its only listed officers, Lori and Jensen, each report working one hour a week, unpaid, and its paid outside help consisted of an investment manager and an accounting firm.

In 2024, the foundation paid out about $126.3 million in grants. More than $82 million went to Schwab Charitable Fund, which sponsors donor-advised funds, and the filing notes the foundation gave to a donor-advised fund over which it or an insider had advisory privileges. Other 2024 recipients included Oregon State, which received about $30.5 million, and Crisis Text Line, which received about $10.8 million.

The filing also shows the foundation was required to distribute roughly $344.6 million in 2025 under federal payout rules. Its 2025 return, which would show whether it met that requirement, hasn’t been made public. Some public announcements from 2025 show the foundation matched $22.5 million in donations to the California College of the Arts, and in November, the Huangs announced a multi-year commitment of $5 million a year to San Francisco Opera.

This year, the foundation bought about $108.3 million worth of computing capacity from CoreWeave to donate to universities and nonprofit research institutes, a filing Reuters reviewed shows. Also in 2026, Vanderbilt University announced a $75 million matching gift from the Huangs for its art, architecture, and design San Francisco campus.

Nvidia and the foundation did not respond to Fortune’s requests for comment.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-n.title: Nvidia stock falls nearly 10% as CEO Jensen Huang announces resignation
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-n.author: Arjun Kharpal
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-n.text:
Nvidia’s stock plunged after CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed.

Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board.

Follow CNBC’s live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation here.

Nvidia
 shares plunged nearly 10% on Thursday, sending the company’s value below $4 trillion in market cap after Jensen Huang announced he would immediately step down as CEO and a member of the board at the chipmaker.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed, Nvidia said in a Thursday statement. Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board.

On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed, according to The Financial Times, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China.

The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had another extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell reports to Huang, according to the Times.

Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that this departure could lead the stock to fall 20%, given how critical he has been to Nvidia’s success. Nvidia’s stock is already down more than 20% over the last month.

Bernstein on Thursday slashed its price target on Nvidia’s stock by half from $400 to $200.

Stacy Rasgon, a senior analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” on Thursday that Huang’s alleged affair with a direct report means it is “much tougher for the board to leave him in position.”

Huang was central to Nvidia’s rise, having co-founded the company in 1993 and was pivotal in transforming Nvidia from a gaming hardware player to the company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom.

Rasgon said it is unclear who could be the “visionary” to lead Nvidia into the future as new CEO.

“Jensen is Nvidia, right? He is the visionary. The reason they’re in the position that they’re in today is because he made decisions 10 years ago,” Rasgon said. “Who is the right person now to make the decisions for the next 10 years? I don’t intuitively know who that person would be.”

Earlier, U.S. lawmakers had called for Huang’s resignation, adding further pressure to the CEO and the company.

Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, said Nvidia’s lack of a succession plan makes the stock “uninvestable.”

“Nvidia doesn’t have that person in place, and so it’s going to be either a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with months and months of being hauled in front of probably congressional boards and things to explain themselves and all kinds of interrogations,” Reyle told CNBC’s “Access Middle East.”

“Or they’re going to have to move on from him, and that’s just going to make the stock uninvestable. That doesn’t make the AI trade uninvestable, but it certainly makes Nvidia uninvestable.”

— CNBC’s Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

Huang admitted to having an affair with an executive at cloud company Megaspeed. The CEO was central to Nvidia’s rise, having co-founded the company in 1993.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/trump-ir.title: Trump says ‘we don’t need a deal with Iran’
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/trump-ir.author: Kevin Breuninger
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/trump-ir.text:
The U.S. should no longer seek a deal with Iran, President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to instead focus his attention on corruption and crime in Democratic cities and states.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” Trump wrote in the post.

The U.S. should no longer seek a deal with Iran, President Donald Trump said Thursday as he directed Vice President JD Vance to instead focus his attention on corruption and crime in Democratic cities and states.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

“We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” Trump wrote, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, a key chokepoint in the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.

The announcement came just over a week after Republicans suffered huge losses in the midterm election. Vance and other Republicans have pinned those losses on the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel started in late February.

In the weeks leading up to Election Day, Trump repeatedly suggested the U.S. could resume launching military strikes, which have largely subsided as a tense stalemate has taken hold in the region

The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday reported that Vance, who has led diplomatic efforts with Iran in prior months, was considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official.

Stock futures declined following Trump’s post.

The unpopular Iran war, which Trump and others in his administration said would be won in a matter of weeks, is now in its ninth month with no clear end in sight. The conflict region has driven up global energy prices, creating a ripple effect through the economy and exacerbating concerns about inflation and affordability that were paramount to voters in the midterms.

Corruption emerged as another top issue that broke in Democrats’ favor in the election. Trump’s post Thursday morning attempts to flip the script, blaming Democratic-run areas for allowing corruption and crime to proliferate.

“I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.,” Trump wrote.

“The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters. Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month,” the president wrote. “Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity.”

“CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership’s blood!” he added.
