https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/american.title: American Airlines brings fresh food back to NY-Chicago first class for first time since 2019
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/american.author: Leslie Josephs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/american.text:
American Airlines said it plans to offer fresh food on flights between New York and Chicago.

It’s the first time in about seven years that the options are available, a spokeswoman said.

The additions are part of American’s push to win over more premium customers after falling behind United Airlines and Delta Air Lines.

American Airlines
 said Wednesday it’s bringing small, fresh “bites” to first class on flights between its hubs in New York and Chicago, the carrier’s latest effort to win over higher-spending customers.

The changes start this month. Customers will be able to pick between two options, which include prosciutto and melon or apple cinnamon chia pudding for breakfast and a Thai noodle salad or mezze plate for lunch and dinner, American said Wednesday.

American last offered fresh food for first class on these routes in 2019, a spokeswoman said. Currently, customers in first class on these flights get a smaller, packaged snack. Airlines largely have limited food options for shorter flights, even in first class.

American has fallen behind Delta Air Lines
 and United Airlines
 in profits and investments in premium options. The airline has been working to step up those premium offerings in recent years with new cabins, lounges and plans for seatback screens on its narrow-body fleets.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/rich-wea.title: The world's super-rich are piling into alternative investments. Here's why
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/rich-wea.author: Lee Ying Shan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/rich-wea.text:
The super-rich are increasingly piling into alternative investments, diversifying portfolios once dominated by traditional assets.

The shift comes as investors grapple with increasingly concentrated equity markets and geopolitical uncertainty.

The world’s wealthiest investors are increasingly looking beyond stocks and bonds, pouring money into hedge funds, private equity and infrastructure assets, as market volatility and fears about stubborn inflation spur diversification.

From Asian billionaires to global family offices, alternative investments are becoming a bigger part of portfolios once dominated by traditional assets, said industry watchers

JPMorgan Asset Management’s private wealth alternative assets in Asia-Pacific surged 40% over the past 12 months, according to Dan Watkins, the firm’s regional chief executive officer, underscoring the growing appetite among high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients.

“So you really have this huge appetite for alternative exposure happening in that ultra-high-net-worth, high-net-worth category,” Watkins said recently at a media summit in Singapore.

The shift comes as investors grapple with increasingly concentrated equity markets, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns that stocks and bonds may not provide the same protection against market downturns as they once did, experts said.

“We are seeing a sharp increase in planned asset allocation to alternatives among the family offices we speak to,” said John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier.

Alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios, surpassing traditional assets for the first time, according to BNY Wealth. Traditional assets accounted for 41% of allocations, the report found.

Wealthy investors are seeking diversification, income and access to investments outside listed markets, and concerns over elevated valuations, tight credit spreads and the growing correlation between stocks and bonds have accelerated the trend, Woods added.

Hedge funds are emerging as a favored option among wealthy investors seeking protection against market swings, particularly as traditional diversification strategies face growing challenges.

Olaolu Aganga, head of portfolio construction and analytics at Citi Wealth, said hedge funds have attracted the strongest recent interest among qualified clients, who are seeking returns less dependent on the direction of equity markets.

Private credit is another area drawing interest, offering investors contractual income streams, while some hedge fund strategies seek to profit from differences in performance between companies rather than relying on broad market rallies, said Woods.

Citi’s 2026 survey of 351 family offices found that inflation was their biggest concern, followed by interest rates, financial system stability and market volatility.

Wealthy families are increasingly seeking investments that can generate income and help preserve purchasing power amid persistent inflation and interest-rate uncertainty, while diversifying portfolios against market volatility, according to Aganga.

The Citi survey, however, also showed public equities recorded the strongest net increase in allocations, suggesting wealthy investors are adding alternatives rather than abandoning traditional markets. “This is not a wholesale rotation away from public markets,” Woods said.

Infrastructure has emerged as another major beneficiary of the shift, with the artificial intelligence boom creating enormous demand for data centers, electricity networks and digital connectivity.

Thomas Roland Guyot, head of private markets investment specialists for Southeast Asia at UBS Unified Global Alternatives, said investors are increasingly targeting assets that support AI, electrification and energy security.

Such investments potentially offer a combination of long-term growth and relatively predictable cash flows, particularly where revenues are supported by essential demand or long-term contracts.

Investor appetite is already showing up in fund flows. Net inflows into open-ended infrastructure funds rose 30% year on year in the 12 months through the first quarter of 2026, according to PitchBook data cited by UBS.

Private equity remains a cornerstone of wealthy investors’ alternative portfolios, although they are becoming more selective. Family offices are increasingly favoring direct investments in companies, co-investments alongside private equity managers and purchases of existing fund stakes on the secondary market, rather than relying solely on traditional pooled funds, according to Citi Wealth’s Aganga.

Such approaches can give investors greater control over their investments or opportunities to acquire assets at discounts, said Lombard Odier’s Woods.

The broader shift is also being facilitated by the growth of evergreen and semi-liquid funds, which have lowered minimum investment thresholds and reduced some administrative hurdles associated with traditional private-market funds, Woods added.

Investing into alternative assets does not come without risks, even as mitigating those is driving flows.

Private investments can lock up capital for years, while valuations may be slow to reflect deteriorating market conditions. Even funds marketed as semi-liquid can restrict withdrawals when redemption requests surge.

“Improved access does not equal liquidity,” JPMorgan’s Watkins said.

Citi’s Aganga also warned that performance can vary significantly between managers, while private assets may appear less volatile than they actually are because valuations are updated less frequently.

Investors must also guard against unintended concentration. A portfolio holding data centers through real estate, infrastructure and private equity funds may appear diversified while remaining heavily exposed to the same AI investment cycle, UBS’ Guyot said.

For now, the flow of capital into alternative assets shows their increasing appeal among the rich, though not at the expense of traditional investment, with Woods pointing out that much of the new investment is being funded by fresh capital and excess cash rather than large-scale sales of stocks and bonds.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/rich-wea.summary: The world’s wealthiest investors are increasingly looking beyond stocks and bonds, pouring money into hedge funds, private equity and infrastructure assets. Alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios, surpassing traditional assets for the first time.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/jim-cram.title: Jim Cramer says investors need to pay attention to CoreWeave. Here's why
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/jim-cram.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/jim-cram.text:
Jim Cramer said he’s becoming less skeptical of CoreWeave after strong earnings and reassuring comments from its CEO.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said demand for computing capacity far exceeds supply, while also detailing improving financing options and the lasting value of Nvidia chips

CNBC’s Jim Cramer said Wednesday that he’s becoming less skeptical of CoreWeave
 after the neocloud’s strong earnings and the CEO’s “refreshing and reassuring” comments.

CoreWeave shares surged nearly 25% on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly revenue and raised its 2026 guidance. The results, which were out Tuesday evening, helped ease concerns about a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator’s subsequent interview with Cramer on CNBC just after Wall Street’s opening bell offered further reasons for optimism.

One of the most encouraging takeaways from Intrator was disclosure that demand for CoreWeave’s computing capacity is 10 times greater than what the company can supply. It was also discussed on the post-earnings conference call. That dynamic has allowed CoreWeave to consistently increase prices, supporting stronger gross margins even as it spends heavily to expand its infrastructure.

Intrator also addressed concerns about CoreWeave’s substantial debt load, which has weighed heavily on its stock. Despite Wednesday’s surge, shares are still down 15% year to date and down 55% from its 52-week high of $138 on May 6. The past month has been particularly tumultuous for the neoclouds, which also include Iren
 and Nebius
. Iren reported strong earnings last week. Nebius reports its quarter Thursday morning.

Rather than relying solely on traditional bond markets, CoreWeave has increasingly turned to financing backed by its equipment and customer contracts. “When I pressed him, asking why he doesn’t just go into the open market and buy these bonds that are trading so poorly, he admitted that he’s been tempted to, but ultimately he still believes he can make an even better return building data centers,” Cramer said. “Take that red flag off the table.”

Another surprising revelation involved the value of CoreWeave’s Nvidia
 chips. Intrator said some H100 chips purchased four years ago are now being contracted at premiums of 20% to 50% above its original cost, suggesting the equipment is retaining its economic value longer than many investors anticipated.

The Intrator interview also helped ease concerns about growing political opposition to data center construction. The CEO maintained that demand for computing power would continue to drive expansion, even if stricter regulations pushed some projects overseas.

For Cramer, the comments offered a welcome counterpoint to the recent pessimism surrounding AI infrastructure stocks. While he has grown more cautious about the sector amid political and financing risks, the “Mad Money” host maintained that abandoning it altogether could mean missing substantial upside. “We’ve taken some data center and related stocks off the table, unfortunately not Nvidia, [for the CNBC Investing Club] because our composure and our prudence dictates that to have too much data center is still too dicey. Still, we’ve left plenty of exposure to the group, which includes semis, software, networking, builders, turbines and cooling equipment, because we think the AI theme has much more room to run.”

The Club does not own any neoclouds. But it does have diversified, albeit recently reduced, exposure to the AI boom via chip stocks and names that help run and power data centers.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/social-s.title: Social Security could pay full benefits until 2059 if taxable payroll kept pace with GDP: AARP report
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/social-s.author: Lorie Konish
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/social-s.text:
Social Security’s taxable payroll has fallen as a share of gross domestic product over the past four decades, according to a new AARP Public Policy Institute report.

Had payroll taxes kept up with GDP, the program would be able to pay full benefits until 2059 — an additional 25 years versus current projections, according to the research.

“The fix for Social Security isn’t cutting earned benefits; it’s rebuilding the revenue behind them,” said Richard Johnson, vice president of financial security at the AARP Public Policy Institute.

Social Security’s taxable payroll, which provides most of the revenue for the program that pays monthly benefits to millions of Americans, has fallen as a share of gross domestic product over the past four decades, according to a new report from the AARP Public Policy Institute.

Had payroll tax revenue kept up with GDP, the program could pay full benefits until 2059, according to the research — an additional 25 years beyond the latest projected depletion date of 2034 for the program’s combined funds. The AARP Public Policy Institute provides policy research, analysis and development at AARP, a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization that represents Americans ages 50 and over.

“Social Security’s finances have weakened not simply because America has grown older, but because the economy has changed, while the program’s revenue system has not,” Richard Johnson, vice president of financial security at the AARP Public Policy Institute, said during a Tuesday press briefing on the research.

“America’s economy is larger and more productive than it was four decades ago, but Social Security is receiving support from a smaller share of that economy,” Johnson said.

Social Security’s trustees projected in June that the program’s combined retirement and disability trust funds may be depleted in the third quarter of 2034. Unless Congress takes action, 83% of scheduled benefits will be payable at that time, according to the trustees’ projections.

The trustees’ report also included an earlier projected depletion date for Social Security’s retirement trust fund — the fourth quarter of 2032, when 78% of benefits would be payable. However, the AARP said it based its analysis on the later 2034 date because Congress has shifted money between the funds in the past.

The program’s current shortfall is worse than lawmakers had anticipated in 1983, when the last major Social Security reforms were enacted.

Rising income inequality means the payroll tax cap no longer covers 90% of earnings — a percentage lawmakers expected to remain constant when they made the 1983 reforms, according to research from the Roosevelt Institute, a New York-based liberal think tank. The share of earnings covered by Social Security payroll taxes fell to around 83% in 2000 and has mostly stabilized there, according to the institute.

AARP points to an aging population as another reason for Social Security’s funding challenges. The worker-to-beneficiary ratio will fall from 3.4 to 2.4 between 2000 and 2030. Falling fertility rates are also shrinking the worker-to-beneficiary ratio.

Shifting income patterns have also meant that a smaller share of U.S. GDP is subject to the Social Security payroll tax. Taxable payroll has fallen from 41% of GDP in 1983 to 34% as of 2025, a level Social Security’s trustees project will remain, according to the AARP.

AARP attributes the decline to a shift from wages toward business and investment income, which generally isn’t subject to payroll taxes. Automation has reduced demand for workers, and pass-through businesses allow some owners to report compensation as profits rather than wages, according to the report.

Social Security would have collected $10.8 trillion in additional funding between 1984 and 2034 if taxable payroll had stayed at 41% of GDP, according to the AARP. That figure is in inflation-adjusted 2025 dollars.

In 2026, up to $184,500 in wages are subject to the Social Security payroll tax.

Payroll taxes accounted for 91% of Social Security’s revenues in 2025, according to AARP’s research, while 5% came from interest income and 4% was through federal income taxes paid by high-income beneficiaries on their benefits.

To increase Social Security’s revenues, lawmakers may consider changes that make high-income taxpayers contribute more to the program while sparing low- to moderate-income taxpayers, according to the AARP report.

“The fix for Social Security isn’t cutting earned benefits; it’s rebuilding the revenue behind them,” Johnson said.

Raising the payroll tax threshold — which is incrementally adjusted each year to keep up with average wages — would not affect most workers, since just 6% of individuals had earnings at or above the cap in 2024, according to the AARP.

In 2027, the Social Security taxable maximum is set to increase to $192,300.

Bills have been introduced in Congress to raise the cap to apply to higher thresholds, such as $250,000 or $400,000, or to eliminate it altogether. Getting rid of the cap would close 67% of the 75-year funding gap if workers do not receive a benefit increase in exchange for those contributions, according to AARP research based on the Social Security Administration’s assessments.

Another option: Lawmakers may also shore up the program by taxing income not currently subject to Social Security payroll taxes, according to the AARP, following an increase in business activity through pass-through entities — such as sole proprietorships, partnerships, limited liability companies and S corporations.

Lawmakers could create a new tax on investment income to help fund Social Security’s trust funds. A new 12.4% tax on investment income for active S corp. officers and limited partners would close about 25% of Social Security’s 75-year financing gap, according to the AARP, which cited research from Social Security’s actuaries.

One option not mentioned in the AARP research is raising the payroll tax rate, which is currently 6.2% for workers and employers, or 12.4% combined. The Social Security trustees estimated that an increase in the combined rate to 16.65% beginning in January 2026 would have made the combined program solvent for the 75-year period ending in 2100.

A national survey conducted in February found 62% of individuals would support gradually increasing the payroll tax from 6.2% to 6.5%, according to the University of Maryland School of Public Policy. That poll included 2,509 adults.

The 1983 Social Security reforms included changes to benefits, such as gradually raising the retirement age from 65 to 67, delaying the cost-of-living adjustment by six months and taxing Social Security benefits.

Research shows those changes have reduced lifetime retirement benefits by about 19% for people turning 65 in 2026 compared to what they would have received under the previous rules, Jenn Jones, vice president of financial security and livable communities at the AARP, said during the Tuesday press briefing.

While the AARP has not endorsed any specific benefit changes, Jones said the organization opposes cuts to monthly checks.

“Millions of Americans — we hear from them every day — cannot afford to lose a penny,” Jones said.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/social-s.summary: AARP says 25% of Social Security's 75-year financing gap would be closed. The 1983 Social Security reforms included changes to benefits.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/gabby-wi.title: WNBA Finals MVP Gabby Williams: 'Our existence is political'
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/gabby-wi.author: Jessica Golden
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/gabby-wi.text:
Gabby Williams doesn’t expect political and cultural debates around the WNBA to go away, saying that for women athletes, “our existence is political.”

Williams said players embrace the platform professional basketball has given them, pointing to past involvement in political and social causes.

Her advocacy for transgender rights has brought death threats and hateful messages, she said, while the Valkyries’ home arena has helped her feel welcome.

Golden State Valkyries star Gabby Williams doesn’t expect the political and cultural issues swirling around the WNBA to go away anytime soon.

Fresh off the Valkyries’ first championship and winning the Finals MVP award, Williams spoke with CNBC’s Alex Sherman about the league’s place in those conversations. The WNBA has been at the forefront of several political and cultural issues this season, ranging from race to sexuality.

“I think as a female athlete, just our existence is political,” Williams said. “Being a female athlete just automatically becomes politicized because we’re in a space where maybe we weren’t welcome before.”

Williams said that she and many of her fellow athletes understand the fact that that playing professional basketball has brought them a larger platform.

“I think it’s something that we embrace as athletes,” Williams said, pointing to players’ past involvement in political and social causes, including the 2020 Georgia Senate runoff and the Black Lives Matter movement. “I think that’ll continue,” she said.

The 30-year-old basketball player, born in Nevada to an American father and a French mother, said she grew up watching the Black Lives Matter movement while a student-athlete at the University of Connecticut.

“Realizing, oh, wow, these aren’t just basketball players. They’re leaders in our community. I was actually looking forward to that part of the W,” she said.

Williams has used her platform to speak out in support of transgender rights, a topic that became a flashpoint for the league this season after Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham argued that transgender women should not compete in women’s sports.

Williams has maintained that sports should be open to everyone, and she’s revealed that’s she gotten hateful messages and death threats because of her views.

Williams said the Valkyries’ home arena, the Chase Center, which has become known as “Ballhalla” for its electric atmosphere, helped her feel welcome and gave her the confidence to thrive this season.

“Being in Ballhalla allowed me to be myself,” Williams said. “As soon as I got there, I felt so welcomed. In the preseason game, I didn’t even play, and people were like screaming for me and welcoming me. And it just gives me a confidence, that I think I can only get from Ballhalla.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/uforce-d.title: Ukrainian defense tech startup hits $6 billion valuation as investors bet on battle-tested drones
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/uforce-d.author: Elsa Ohlen
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/uforce-d.text:
Ukrainian defense technology company UFORCE has raised $700 million in a funding round valuing it at $6 billion.

UFORCE CEO Oleg Rogynskyy told CNBC that the company’s bookings have more than doubled over the past year.

Militaries are looking to learn from the war in Ukraine, where relatively inexpensive drones are challenging traditional military equipment.

Ukrainian defense technology company UFORCE has raised $700 million in a funding round valuing it at $6 billion, as investor interest grows in autonomous weapons systems tested on the battlefield in Ukraine.

UFORCE, which develops unmanned aerial, maritime, and land systems as well as AI software used to coordinate them, raised $50 million at a valuation of around $1 billion in March.

The Series A round was co-led by Valor Equity Partners and the U.K.’s National Wealth Fund, with participation from investors across Silicon Valley, Europe and Asia, the company announced Thursday.

UFORCE CEO Oleg Rogynskyy told CNBC that the company’s bookings have more than doubled over the past year, from a base of several hundred million dollars, but declined to disclose more exact figures.

He said the company’s financial performance justified its latest valuation, adding that UFORCE had received offers from investors at even higher valuations.

“We were getting offers with much higher valuation, but we chose this one because of Valor and the rest of the investors,” Rogynskyy said. “In terms of valuation to bookings, valuation to revenue, this is actually not an aggressive valuation.”

The company plans to use the new funding to scale manufacturing in Ukraine and in allied countries, including the U.S., Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East.

Startups across NATO and allied countries raised $27.1 billion through September, nearly double the total for all of 2025, according to an October report from Dealroom and Resilience Media.

Rogynskyy said UFORCE had already manufactured ten times as many unmanned surface vessels as the competitors it typically measures itself against, and was looking to increase manufacturing capacity substantially. CNBC could not independently verify the comparison.

The expansion comes as militaries around the world look to learn from the war in Ukraine, where relatively inexpensive drones are challenging the role of traditional military equipment like crewed tanks or fighter jets.

UFORCE says its NEMESIS drones have completed more than 300,000 combat flights, while its MAGURA naval vessels have contributed to the destruction of more than a dozen Russian warships in the Black Sea.

Rogynskyy said the company was already working with several NATO countries, but declined to identify its customers or disclose how much of its production was being supplied to Ukraine versus overseas markets.

Asked whether growing international demand could divert supplies away from Ukraine, he said the company was committed to meeting Ukrainian military requirements first.

“We are very careful about that, and we make sure that we deliver on all Ukrainian needs first and foremost,” he said.

Like many of its peers, UFORCE is seeking to challenge the economics of conventional warfare, arguing that large numbers of inexpensive autonomous systems can provide a significantly cheaper way of defense than more traditional weapons.

Rogynskyy said Ukrainian defense tech companies have an advantage over established Western manufacturers because their engineers receive continuous feedback from military personnel using their equipment on the battlefield.

“Speed of innovation, of course, is much faster with Ukrainian defense technology companies as compared to primes and Western defense techs,” he said.

Looking further ahead, Rogynskyy predicted that autonomous systems would gradually replace much of the military equipment currently operated by humans, including aircraft and naval vessels.

He said he could not envision militaries continuing to purchase new crewed aircraft or frigates 10 years from now, although he acknowledged that conventional equipment such as F-35 fighter jets would remain important in the near term.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/jetblue-.title: JetBlue unveils new first-class seats to bring back profits
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/jetblue-.author: Leslie Josephs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/jetblue-.text:
JetBlue’s CEO, Joanna Geraghty, has said the airline is focused on its turnaround plan that includes more upmarket products to return to profitability.

Geraghty said the airline has met with bondholders in recent weeks and made it clear it doesn’t need to reorganize.

The carrier on Wednesday unveiled its new domestic first-class seats called BlueFirst.

JetBlue Airways
 unveiled its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country’s carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.

JetBlue announced it would offer a domestic first class — BlueFirst — in December 2024 and plans to start flying aircraft with the new seats and full on-board product next month. The carrier showed off the new cabin at its home hub at John F. Kennedy International Airport on Wednesday. Retrofits will continue during 2027, CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC late last month.

JetBlue will have 12 of the seats on its Airbus A320 fleet and 30 extra-legroom seats, down from 42 of those options previously. Because the airplanes don’t have ovens, JetBlue said it is offering an array of cold food options like sesame noodles, pastrami sandwiches and tortellini salad, though they vary by route.

The rollout comes as the New York airline tries to stabilize after last posting a profit in 2019. Last month, JetBlue executives sought to calm investors after shares in the airline hit a record low following a report that bondholders had contracted restructuring advisors.

“We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring company,” Geraghty told CNBC in an interview on Oct. 27.

Geraghty told CNBC’s Phil LeBeau on Wednesday that JetBlue has “met with a few of the creditors over the last couple of weeks as part of ... normal investor engagement.” She said the company made it clear to bondholders that JetBlue doesn’t need to reorganize.

The airline’s shares are up more than 40% this month, more than other passenger carriers, as of midday Wednesday, though they are still off about 11% so far this year.

JetBlue is betting that resilient travel demand, especially for roomier seats will help fuel its turnaround plan, which aims to get the carrier to an operating profit next year and $1 in adjusted earnings per share in 2028.

Airline executives have said they expect fares to stay elevated next year as they grapple with higher costs, including but not limited to fuel, such as labor and airport fees. Geraghty said Wednesday that even if fuel prices moderate next year, “I don’t think fares are going to fall as much as people expect.”

Airlines large and small are racing to outfit their cabins with roomier, more expensive seating options to help cover ever-higher costs, from jet fuel to labor to airport operation fees.

For example, a ticket in the new recliner first-class seats between Kennedy airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida is going for $847 roundtrip in the first week of March while standard economy is $446.

On Tuesday, budget carrier Frontier Airlines
 unveiled its new first-class seats, which will take up the first two rows, and said it would outfit its Airbus fleet with premium seating that has extra legroom and in-seat power through row eight. The airline will take out a row of seating on its planes to make the pricier ones fit, Chief Marketing Officer Bobby Schroeter told CNBC in an interview Monday.

JetBlue last month reported that it ended the third quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.

JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing.

Geraghty told CNBC last month there is a “fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate.”

When asked whether JetBlue’s eye on keeping costs down includes furloughs, layoffs or buyouts, Geraghty last month said “absolutely not.”

The carrier showed off the new cabin at its home hub at John F. Kennedy International Airport on Wednesday.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/us-treas.title: 10-year Treasury yield jumps back above 5% as oil gains and more Fed rate hikes expected
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/us-treas.author: Michelle Fox,Hugh Leask
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/us-treas.text:
U.S. Treasury yields jumped on Thursday, sending the 10-year note above 5% alongside a move higher in oil prices and expectations of further Federal Reserve hikes.

The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury
 note — the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 3.1 basis points to 5.02% after earlier hitting 5.0583%, the highest since Oct. 22.

The 2-year Treasury note
 yield, more sensitive to short-term Fed interest rate decisions, jumped 7 basis points to 4.797%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond 
yield 1.4 basis points to 5.363%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.

The rise in oil prices came after President Donald Trump said, “we don’t need a deal with Iran,” raising concern that the war in the Middle East will continue indefinitely. West Texas Intermediate futures
 gained 0.4% to $86.86 a barrel, while Brent crude
 was ahead about 1% to $93.60 per barrel.

Tuesday’s hotter-than-expected consumer price index reading has investors anticipating more rate increases from the Fed. Goldman Sachs forecast another rate hike to its forecast on Wednesday, now expecting an additional quarter percentage point increase in March. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of an increase in December, with the chance of a half percentage point increase standing at about 13%, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool.

Another inflation report is due Friday, when the October producer price index, which tracks wholesale prices, is expected to show a 0.4% rise in October, down from the 1.3% surge in September.

On Thursday, investors are looking for October’s home sales report from the National Association of Realtors. Existing home sales rose 1.5% in September to 3.99 million, up from a two-year low in August, and are expected to have reached 4 million last month, according to Trading Economics estimates.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/cftc-inv.title: CFTC investigates if Kalshi improperly self-certified event contracts
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/cftc-inv.author: Davis Giangiulio,Ananya Chetia
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/cftc-inv.text:
Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter.

Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency’s approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Kalshi failed to properly inform the agency of proposed event contracts, Kalshi confirmed to CNBC.

Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter. The CFTC flagged weather-related contracts, Kalshi said. The leading prediction market platform didn’t say when the agency began investigating Kalshi. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC that the agency does not comment on investigations.

Politico first reported on the probe on Tuesday, noting charges could happen soon, based on the CFTC’s private notification to Kalshi. The platform declined to comment on any possible charges.

Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency’s prior approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act. The self-certification allows for faster introduction of new contracts.

“The notice is about a procedural error involving the submission of a handful of contracts, many of which weren’t live,” said Elisabeth Diana, head of communications at Kalshi. “We are already addressing the issue.”

The move is the latest by the CFTC as it seeks to rein in prediction markets, which face growing scrutiny in Washington from regulators and members of Congress.

In August, the CFTC ordered Kalshi to take down sports-related “mention markets” — where speculators can trade on what individuals will say in a broadcast or speech — while it looked into the event contract type.

The agency is also conducting a broad probe into competitor Polymarket, which includes reviewing if the company violated a 2022 settlement with the CFTC to prohibit U.S. traders from accessing its international trading platform. Polymarket’s domestic exchange operates separately from the global platform.

Prediction markets are also expected to face heightened scrutiny once the Democratic Congress is sworn into office in January. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., in a Tuesday social media post on X, called for a ban on sports prediction markets — which account for the overwhelming majority of volume on leading platforms.

— CNBC’s Talia Kaplan contributed to this report

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/bouncing.title: Bouncing Wynn Shares might be primed for the 'wheel strategy'
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/bouncing.author: Michael Khouw
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/bouncing.text:
From a valuation standpoint, Wynn is trading very close to its five-year historical averages across key metrics.

With the next earnings report not scheduled until February, the stock has a clear runway free of binary fundamental catalysts, yet implied volatility remains surprisingly high.

This environment makes buying options expensive and short premium strategies more attractive.

In Barry Levinson’s classic film Rain Man, Dustin Hoffman’s character leans over to his brother in the middle of a blackjack hand with a simple piece of advice: bet two for good, one for bad.

In the case of Wynn Resorts
 shares, it might be time to bet two for good.

Steve Wynn hasn’t exactly been on a winning streak. No longer running his namesake company, he finally sold his 50 Central Park South penthouse after years on the market. WYNN shares haven’t really been on a winning streak either. The stock is down more than 27% year-to-date as I write this. It was down more than 46% from the 2025 highs within the past couple of weeks. But it has bounced a bit since then, and perhaps the tables are turning.

Fundamentally, the business is demonstrating exceptional strength, particularly in the United States. Wynn’s Las Vegas EBITDA margin has actually surpassed that of its Macau resorts. Recognizing this, management has accelerated capital spending in Las Vegas, where the company’s profit has doubled from pre-pandemic levels. Meanwhile, the Asian market is also showing signs of life. Strategic property upgrades in Macau are successfully drawing lucrative premium mass play, which is directly supporting the company’s ambitious expansion plans for the Enclave at Wynn Palace.

From a valuation standpoint, WYNN is trading very close to its five-year historical averages across key metrics, including P/E, EV/EBITDA (currently around 9x to 10x), and Price-to-Book Value. Although this represents a slight premium compared to the broader gaming industry mean, Wynn’s justifies a premium. (The Encore, the newer of the two adjacent Las Vegas properties, is one of my preferred hotels on “The Strip”). Technically, the stock has admittedly been in a downtrend, but this recent sharp bounce off the late October lows may indicate the run is over. Several technical indicators—specifically the MACD, Fear & Greed Index, Commodity Channel Index (CCI), and several key Moving Averages—are now aligned, suggesting it may be time to go long.

So, how should traders play this setup?

With the next earnings report not scheduled until February, the stock has a clear runway free of binary fundamental catalysts, yet implied volatility remains surprisingly high. This environment makes buying options expensive and short premium strategies more attractive.

Rather than betting on the roulette wheel, traders should look once again to “the wheel” strategy. Something I discussed earlier this week on United Rentals. The strategy? Step one, sell cash-covered puts below the current market price to collect that inflated premium. If WYNN stays above your strike price through expiration, you keep the cash and repeat the process. If the stock dips and you are assigned, you acquire shares at a discount. Once assigned, you move to step two: selling covered calls against your new stock position to generate continuous income until the shares are eventually called away, after which you revert back to step one and play again. A methodical, high-probability way to get long a world-class operator while getting paid to wait.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/kalsi-po.title: Prediction markets tied to clinical trials and drug approvals draw lawmakers' ire
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/kalsi-po.author: Karen James Sloan,Davis Giangiulio
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/kalsi-po.text:
Democratic Sens. Angela Alsobrooks and Ron Wyden are pressing the Department of Health and Human Services to mitigate risks from prediction markets related to clinical trials and Food and Drug Administration approvals.

In a letter obtained first by CNBC, the senators raise concerns about the markets affecting patients who are deciding whether to participate in a trial, and express worry over potential insider trading.

Kalshi, which offers such event contracts in the U.S., says it has put in place guardrails to maintain the integrity of markets.

Prediction market event contracts on both clinical drug trials and Food and Drug Administration regulatory approvals are drawing attention from two Democratic senators, according to a letter obtained first by CNBC.

Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., and Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., expressed concern over the related event contracts in a Wednesday letter to Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The senators asked what measures HHS has taken to mitigate any risks that may arise from the markets.

“Allowing individuals to bet on the success of these trials and drugs undermines the scientific process, creates perverse incentives for researchers, harms trial participants, and could lead to dangerous medical outcomes for untold numbers of Americans,” the senators wrote.

Alsobrooks and Wyden repeated concerns raised by some healthcare professionals that the markets could alter patient thinking when considering whether to participate in a trial and expressed concern over potential insider trading risks from researchers and regulators who may have access to nonpublic information.

The senators requested HHS provide all internal communication regarding staff participation in prediction markets tied to matters governed by the department. They also requested all communication between the department and the prediction market platforms themselves, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — which regulates event contracts — and any internal analyses that have been done regarding the potential impact of the markets.

“HHS, FDA, and [the National Institutes of Health] must uphold the integrity of the drug development process and maintain public trust in the public health by putting essential guardrails in place to prevent individuals profiting on the success and approval of drugs that the American people depend on,” Alsobrooks and Wyden said in the letter.

Both leading prediction market platforms, Kalshi and Polymarket, offer the contracts, although in Polymarket’s case the markets can only be found on its international exchange, which isn’t regulated in the U.S.

When Kalshi launched its related markets in July, the company said it put in place the guardrails, such as only allowing markets related to late-stage trials, in order to limit the risk of trading. Kalshi also vowed to list contracts only after a trial had completed enrollment and to use employee verification technology for all traders participating in the markets.

“Drug development is one of the most important and most information-constrained industries on earth,” Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said in July. “The data that determines which drugs advance and which don’t is largely locked away from the people who need it most. Surfacing information is what Kalshi is for, and we are committed to doing it right.”

Kalshi noted that investors also buy shares in companies in fields including biotechnology and pharmaceuticals that are awaiting regulatory approvals.

“The hypothetical concerns of the Senators apply equally to the equities market, which appears to be left out of their letter.,” Kalshi spokesperson Jack Such told CNBC. “The only difference is that the size — and incentive for bad activity — is significantly higher in the equities market than it is on Kalshi.”

Polymarket and the Department of Health and Human Services didn’t immediately respond to CNBC’s requests for comment.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/colette-.title: Who is Colette Kress? Nvidia's finance chief steps in as interim CEO after Huang exit
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/colette-.author: Katie Tarasov
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/colette-.text:
Colette Kress is Nvidia’s interim CEO after Jensen Huang stepped down from the role following multiple extramarital affairs.

Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief, joined the company in 2013.

Analysts tell CNBC that a permanent replacement is likely to come from outside of the company.

Nvidia CFO Colette Kress, a 13-year company veteran, is taking the helm of the world’s most valuable chipmaker on an interim basis after Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation.

“She’s the only one internally that has this significant respect,” Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC before the news had been made official. “She’s more than just a CFO. I’d almost view her as more of a COO.”

Nvidia hasn’t announced a succession plan and said the board is considering internal and external candidates.

Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013, after holding finance roles at Cisco
, Microsoft
 and Texas Instruments. At Nvidia, Kress has been the other big voice on earnings calls, reporting the company’s results and taking questions alongside Huang.

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said in Thursday’s statement. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, was known for running the company with no clear second-in-command, personally deciding which projects are a priority and emailing engineers about details.

But when it came to Kress, “Jensen didn’t do anything without her,” Ives said. “She’s a Swiss Army knife for Nvidia. Anything strategically: customers, partners, technology. She was involved.”

CNBC spoke to nearly a dozen Nvidia insiders and former Kress co-workers. They described her as savvy, knowledgeable, thoughtful and clear-headed.

Kress is stepping in at a moment of crisis. Huang has operated as Nvidia’s spokesperson, the face of the company and as a founder who is synonymous with the brand. He also pioneered the AI chip industry, making him the central figure in the multitrillion-dollar boom that’s driving the U.S. economy.

Kress “deeply understands the business and has shown fierce loyalty to the company,” Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group, wrote in a message to CNBC.

Nvidia shares plunged 14% on Thursday after the announcement. The stock is poised for its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest slump since 2012. The shares have been dragged down by broad concerns about the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats.

Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.

The Huang saga burst into public view on Sunday, when the CEO apologized for being unfaithful to his wife. That followed reports that he’d had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence suspects was a spy. Pressure intensified late Wednesday after The New York Times reported a second affair, this one with an employee named  Kimberly Powell.

Kress was recognized in May as one of Fortune’s most powerful women in business. Her LinkedIn profile lists her location as Saratoga, California, a wealthy city 16 miles south of Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters.

As for the long-term leadership plan, Ives said Kress will likely serve for about a year as interim CEO but the permanent replacement will come from outside the company.

“You need someone that’s been on the global stage,” Ives said. “Given the importance of the company not just in the U.S. tech industry but the global economy.”

— CNBC’s Seema Mody and Jordan Novet contributed to this report

Coinbase
 CEO Brian Armstrong joins “Squawk Box” in his first TV interview since the Binance hack to share his perspective on the crypto market, cybersecurity in light of the breach and the future of agentic finance.

In what is historically an active quarter for crypto, Coinbase and other companies are still dealing with a prolonged slump in cryptocurrency prices that has dragged for more than a year now.

This year, they’re also reckoning with midterm results that have likely materially changed the political landscape for the industry, with Democrats taking control of Congress and potentially reshaping the legislative agenda, committee leadership and oversight priorities.

The shift creates greater uncertainty around the timing and direction of comprehensive digital asset market-structure legislation, including the CLARITY Act, which in August failed to advance in the Senate. Armstrong was a key industry lobbyist and negotiator who helped build bipartisan support for the bill.

The industry is also dealing with the aftermath of the Binance hack, which has raised broader questions about security, resilience, and vulnerabilities in an increasingly AI-driven crypto ecosystem. Coinbase stepped into another leadership role during the breach, blocking transfers to compromised wallets and offering the world’s largest exchange direct assistance.

Armstrong has called for solidarity and collaboration from Coinbase’s peers in potentially industry-defining moments like the Binance event.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/jamieson.text:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is set to speak with CNBC’s “Squawk Box” Thursday morning, a week after a blue-wave election in which most voters said President Donald Trump’s controversial tariff policies have made the economy worse.

The import duties, which have ignited trade wars with multiple U.S. economic partners, will likely be a top target for Democrats once they take majority control of the House and Senate. Some of Trump’s largest and most divisive tariffs — including his sweeping Section 301 duties and the 50% tariffs he slapped on a bevy of Canadian goods — are already being challenged in multiple court cases.

Trump and his administration have defended tariffs in the wake of Republicans’ devastating midterm losses. Greer’s office is currently conducting an investigation into foreign excess capacity in the manufacturing sector, which could lead to additional tariffs.

Greer has also been embroiled in the unfolding infidelity and national security scandal around Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang.

Axios reported that Greer was present in the White House Situation Room last Thursday when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the sex-and-spy scandal.

Greer and other Cabinet officials supported the controls, and Trump said, “Let’s get it done,” but Lutnick has continued to delay, Axios reported. Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had “no such conversation” in the Situation Room.

This is developing news. Please check back for updates.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/ai-consu.title: AI is coming for consulting’s billable hours — and its graduate pipeline
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/ai-consu.author: Lindsay Dodgson
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/ai-consu.text:
AI is putting pressure on consulting’s traditional time-based pricing as clients increasingly ask firms to deliver measurable outcomes.

Automation is reducing some research, analysis and presentation work traditionally done by junior consultants, raising questions about how they build experience.

Established firms are redesigning roles and training, while smaller AI-native consultancies say their operating models let them adapt faster.

Artificial intelligence is challenging the building blocks of the consulting industry, from the fees firms charge clients to the armies of graduates who have traditionally powered its business model.

Svilena Tzekova, KPMG’s London-based global head of consulting, agreed that the industry is changing. The intellectual property and knowledge that once formed the basis of consulting work are becoming increasingly accessible, she said, so clients have higher expectations than ever before.

“Anyone can go and very quickly get to the level of advice that we used to deliver within whatever days or months at times,” Tzekova told CNBC. “We were making quite a lot of money by providing advice. I think that part of our business is literally nonexistent anymore.”

But the industry has yet to work out exactly how to charge for this new kind of work. Although clients increasingly say they want to pay for outcomes, their procurement departments still tend to compare consultancies on the number of people assigned to a project and their hourly rates, Tzekova said.

AI is also introducing new costs that firms need to factor into their pricing models, including computing power and the fees AI providers charge based on how much text their models process, alongside the traditional costs of employing people, she said.

“It’s very difficult to be able to arrive at a commercially sensible outcome-based pricing model,” Tzekova said. Largely, firms are still working out the equation, and that will take some time, she said.

Smaller, AI-native consultancies hope to gain a competitive advantage as the likes of the Big Four — professional services giants Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG — race to modernize.

Emiko Caerlewy-Smith, head of investor relations at London-based challenger consultancy Elixirr, argued that firms like hers are better positioned for the AI era. She said they’ve never billed clients on a time-and-materials basis, which means charging for the hours staff spend on a project.

“AI is amplifying and exaggerating the way that we were already trying to show up to the market,” Caerlewy-Smith told CNBC. “Clients will pay for fixed deliverables, fixed outcomes and value. They really shouldn’t be caring about the amount of time it takes to create the inputs to create the outcome.”

Clients now want consultancies to help them build solutions, she said, not just advise them on what to do. In one recent project, Elixirr helped a global insurer build an AI-based motor insurance platform, Caerlewy-Smith said.

Another advantage smaller consultancies may have is the speed of adopting AI internally. Elixirr took six months to get its data into a format that could be fully used by its AI models, Caerlewy-Smith said, questioning how long the same process might take at a company employing tens of thousands of people.

“The issue they have is that they are enormous and we are nimble,” she said.

Another element of the consultancy business model is being questioned: its graduate recruitment pipeline.

The industry traditionally hires thousands of graduates from universities each year, setting them on a career ladder that often begins with entry-level tasks that can now be largely automated: research, data analysis and producing presentations.

Claire Trachet, a former Deutsche Bank mergers and acquisitions banker turned founder of London-based advisory firm Trachet, told CNBC that AI is helping junior employees do their jobs faster. But she questioned how they would gain the experience needed to progress if they no longer have to do the foundational work themselves.

Some are also questioning why they should put in long hours on tasks that AI can complete with a click of a button, she said.

“The problem is you can’t form your judgment, your intuition,” Trachet said. “Your professional sound judgment is built through reputation. It’s a craft. The ones who will stand out later will be the ones who own that for themselves.”

Large established firms are responding by rethinking how they develop their people. Paul Goodhew, EY’s London-based global assurance innovation and digital leader, said AI is already changing the work traditionally done by junior auditors, such as checking figures against source documents.

“The traditional view of the auditor was someone, particularly a junior auditor coming into the profession, who would be spending a lot of their time doing manual ‘ticking and tying’ at work,” Goodhew told CNBC, referring to the process of verifying figures.

“Now today, AI is bringing about the potential that AI can actually do the first preparation of that work on behalf of the audit professional.”

EY is also developing new roles, including data delivery professionals who prepare data for audit teams, product managers who help develop technology platforms, and specialists who understand clients’ technology strategies and risks, Goodhew said.

KPMG’s Tzekova said the answer for firms isn’t to get rid of graduate recruitment altogether. Instead, junior consultants will need to take on more responsibility much earlier in their careers as the traditional shape of consulting firms evolves. Some of KPMG’s graduates and junior employees are already among the best and brightest at driving the firm’s new way of working, she said.

But traditional consulting firms need to redeploy their employees to other tasks quickly, Caerlewy-Smith said.

“We just need them to do other things, otherwise the economics of the pyramid models don’t work anymore,” she said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-t.title: Jensen Huang's affair with alleged spy revives push to tighten China chip curbs ahead of Trump-Xi summit
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-t.author: Anniek Bao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-t.text:
The scandal engulfing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has added ammunition for policymakers to press for further restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips.

The fallout also puts offshore data-center hubs that provide restricted chips to Chinese customers under fresh scrutiny.

Developments so far are unlikely to derail the Trump-Xi summit next week, though tougher U.S. chip curbs could still stir irritation in Beijing, analysts say.

The scandal engulfing Nvidia
 Corp CEO Jensen Huang is bolstering the case for U.S. lawmakers seeking tighter restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, just days before President Donald Trump’s planned meeting with Xi Jinping next week.

The U.S. and China are locked in a race to achieve global AI supremacy, with Washington spending years restricting China’s access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips to slow its technological progress. Huang was among the loudest voices opposing U.S. strict export controls on advanced chips to China, which has irked some China hawks.

The alleged affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen who is not related to him and was reportedly recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information, has given lawmakers fresh ammunition to push for the inclusion of a series of chip-control measures in this year’s National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

The bills include the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act – all of which are aimed at limiting the flow of advanced chips to U.S. adversaries, particularly China.

Huang had been “the industry’s most effective lobbyist against tighter rules,” said David Meale, head of Eurasia Group’s China practice and an American diplomat who served as deputy chief of mission at the U.S. embassy in Beijing.

But the scandal has weakened Nvidia’s “singular ability to slow the progress of those bills” — which were stalled by pushback from corporates and the White House— and made it “politically harder for negotiators to strip chip provisions out of this year’s NDAA,” Meale said.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday called on Congress to pass these bills and urged a full accounting of Trump’s defense of Huang. House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., also called for inclusion of chip export controls in the annual defense policy bill.

Trump’s weakened grip over congressional Republicans following the midterm defeat has also made it harder for the Trump administration to hold back such measures, said Kyle Chan, a China fellow at the Brookings Institution.

The fallout from Jensen Huang’s affair threatens to put fresh scrutiny on offshore data-center hubs that provide Chinese customers with access to Nvidia chips restricted for direct export to China.

Alice Huang helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to China, according to The Information.

Short seller firm Culper Research estimated in May that more than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue for the year ended July 2025, or about $43.2 billion, came from China through illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries.

Pressure is building in the White House for Trump to address remote access to restricted chips, and action “now appears likely,” said Gabriel Wildau, managing director at political risk consultancy Teneo. Potential escalations include blacklisting Megaspeed and other entities, and introducing rules that close the loophole entirely, he said.

The Commerce Department is finalizing a rule aimed at preventing Chinese AI firms from remotely accessing advanced chips through data centers in other countries, according to The Information. The effort, long opposed by tech firms including Nvidia, has gained renewed momentum following the Nvidia revelations.

More Chinese AI companies have reportedly started searching for Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, while traders and intermediaries are ramping up stockpiles of these processors, on the prospect of tougher U.S. enforcement.

If legislation like the Remote Access Security Act – passed by the House in January – goes through next year, it would increase compliance exposure for non-China-based cloud and data-center operators, including those in Southeast Asia, serving Chinese customers, Meale said.

The renewed push for tighter chip control comes days before Trump is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit in Shenzhen on Nov 18-19.

Despite the political firestorm in Washington over the spying allegation, Trump appears “unconcerned” —at least for now, said Wildau. Trump and Xi are expected to keep steering ties toward extending the truce beyond January, he said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who is set to travel to China for the summit next week, said Tuesday that he wants to “build a constructive relationship on the basis of balance and reciprocity.”

But risks remain that the latest developments could create fresh friction with Beijing. Paul Triolo, a partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, pointed to the MATCH Act, which would pressure Japan and the Netherlands to tighten curbs on chipmaking tools already in China, as a threat to the Busan truce.

“Chinese officials have been clear that they will respond to the passage of this legislation, and could ratchet up controls on rare earths and magnets that would be very damaging to U.S. industry,” he said.

It remains unclear whether Huang, who had a prominent role during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May and Xi’s Washington trip in September, will join next week’s delegation. Asked on Sunday whether he would take Huang, Trump said, “I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him.”

Developments so far are unlikely to derail the Trump-Xi summit next week, but tougher U.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/elon-mus.title: Elon Musk says it would be an 'honor' to hire Nvidia's Jensen Huang
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/elon-mus.author: Lim Hui Jie
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/elon-mus.text:
Elon Musk replied to financial blog Zerohedge’s call to hire Jensen Huang, saying, “That would be an honor.”

The post on X comes as the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang.

Huang has dominated headlines since the weekend, after the Nvidia CEO acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. intelligence determined as having been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.

SpaceX
 founder and Tesla
 CEO Elon Musk said it would be “an honor” to hire embattled Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang, after reports emerged that Nvidia’s board could be preparing to oust Huang from the company.

Late Wednesday stateside, financial blog Zerohedge wrote on X, “Elon please hire Jensen,” to which Musk replied, “That would be an honor.”

The post comes as the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to discuss Huang’s future at the company.

The report also followed a New York Times story that Huang had an extramarital relationship with another Nvidia executive. The developments sent Nvidia shares down more than 8% in after-hours trading.

Huang and Nvidia have dominated headlines since the weekend after the Nvidia CEO acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. intelligence identified as having been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.

Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, was recruited to gather information on Jensen, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times.

The Nvidia chief sought to project a “business as usual” atmosphere on his first day back at the office after the revelations, but he is now facing calls to resign from several lawmakers.

Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., a member of the Senate Banking Committee, reiterated Wednesday his call for Huang to resign, joining Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., a member of the House Oversight Committee and Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., who is retiring from Congress.

“As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign,” Cramer told CNBC.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-m.title: What we know so far about Nvidia partner Megaspeed’s Asia footprint
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-m.author: Anniek Bao,Lim Hui Jie
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-m.text:
Megaspeed is at the center of a U.S. national security probe over its role in facilitating billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China, and its leader’s love affairs with Jensen Huang.

Alice Huang, the founder of Megaspeed, has reportedly returned to Beijing amid the increasing scandal.

Megaspeed lists Singapore as its main office location and is linked to a network of subsidiaries and facilities across Southeast Asia.

Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that operates data centers across Southeast Asia, is facing renewed scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China — and its de facto leader’s close relationship with the chipmaker’s CEO Jensen Huang.

Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, was identified in U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information on Jensen, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times.

The Information reported that her relationship with Jensen helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, according to two people who know her as cited by the publication. CNBC could not independently verify the report.

Bloomberg also reported that she has returned to Beijing with the knowledge of Chinese security officials.

The case has drawn scrutiny from Washington as Jensen Huang has cultivated ties with President Donald Trump and advocated for relaxed chip export controls to China.

Nvidia’s board has opened an investigation into whether the CEO was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The company has said it has no reason to believe that U.S. national security or Nvidia confidential information had been compromised.

Megaspeed lists Singapore as its main office location and has subsidiaries across Southeast Asia. Here’s what we know about its presence in the region.

Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International and says it operates in Singapore and Indonesia. Its office in Collyer Quay showed no signs of activity when visited by local media in October 2025.

The company is wholly owned by Swiftdata, a Singapore entity incorporated in October 2023. Megaspeed’s director was Singapore citizen Tan Yong Pong, according to corporate filings.

Alice Huang, the Chinese executive who reportedly used her relationship with Nvidia’s CEO to solicit business, served as managing director for eight months in 2023. Corporate filings show that she received one Megaspeed share for 1 Singapore dollar on the day she stepped down as managing director.

Megaspeed, which says it is an Nvidia Cloud Partner in the Asia-Pacific region and offers access to Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 and HGX H100 systems, saw its assets surge to about $3 billion in 2024, from just $33 million a year earlier, and just $75 in 2022.

Revenue rose to $294 million in 2024 from zero in 2023, according to the filings, while the company posted a loss of about $20 million.

Singapore police opened an investigation into Megaspeed in October 2025 over suspected breaches of domestic law.

The Wall Street Journal separately reported that Singapore officials had investigated Alice Huang over alleged links to Chinese intelligence, but Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs disputed that account.

“There were no such investigations conducted in respect of Alice Huang,” authorities in the city-state said.

Singapore’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Economic Development Board and Ministry of Home Affairs did not respond to CNBC’s requests for comment.

Megaspeed was reportedly linked to Shanghai Century Litong, a China-based company that secured preferred cloud partner status with Nvidia in 2023.

Short seller Culper Research alleged in May that Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatrix had received substantial funding connected to Chinese tech giant Alibaba. Culper said Megaspeed had been “secretly financed by Alibaba via a series of apparent shell companies,” including through what it described as a large portion of a $4.2 billion tranche in March 2025.

The company has denied illegally transferring chips to China. In a December 2025 statement, it said it had undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, Malaysia’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, and Nvidia, and that those reviews had found no evidence of violations.

“We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct,” Megaspeed said.

Aside from its Singapore corporate entity, Megaspeed is linked to a network of subsidiaries and facilities across Southeast Asia. The three data centers listed on its website, previously identified as being in Malaysia and Indonesia, are now described only as being in “East South Asia.”

Two Malaysian entities reportedly linked to Megaspeed, Speedmatrix and MSFusion, list addresses in the same development in Iskandar Puteri, Johor, according to local business outlet The Edge Malaysia.

Speedmatrix bought at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment, including systems containing Nvidia chips, between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the Times. The company reported a loss of 103.2 million ringgit ($25 million) on revenue of 522.3 million ringgit in 2024, according to The Edge Malaysia.

MSFusion, which reported no revenue, agreed in August 2025 to buy a 52.5-acre industrial parcel in Kota Tinggi for 263.2 million ringgit. It later settled 225.9 million ringgit in overdue payments in September after receiving a default notice from seller Crescendo Corp.

A U.S. trade official found boxes of unopened Nvidia chips during a 2025 visit to a data center operated by Speedmatrix, prompting suspicions that the hardware could be re-exported illegally to China, according to NYT. The report said officials did not have conclusive evidence that the chips were being diverted at the time.

Malaysia’s Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani reportedly said Tuesday his ministry had not been presented with evidence that Speedmatrix had violated Malaysian law and had not opened an investigation into the company.

He pledged that the country wouldn’t become “a channel to circumvent export controls,” adding that authorities would act if they received credible evidence or a formal request from a foreign authority.

Megaspeed’s presence also extends to Indonesia, although little is known publicly about the entity.

Indonesian outlet KumparanTEKNO reported that the Jakarta-based company is active in cross-border trade. Customs data through June 2026 shows 242 transactions involving three suppliers and four buyers.

The records include an import described as “MODULE NVIDIA GPU H100 SINGLE,” referring to an Nvidia H100 graphics processing unit used for artificial intelligence training and high-performance computing.

The H100 has been subject to U.S. export licensing requirements for China since August 2022, when Washington imposed new controls covering Nvidia’s A100 and H100 chips and systems containing them.

Megaspeed lists Singapore as its main office location and is linked to a network of subsidiaries and facilities across Southeast Asian.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/anthropi.title: Jim Cramer: This is the bet you're making if you buy the Anthropic IPO
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/anthropi.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/anthropi.text:
Jim Cramer said Anthropic’s turn to profitability is encouraging, but its nearly $900 billion in future spending commitments pose a major challenge.

Cramer warned that Anthropic must sustain extraordinary revenue growth to cover its mounting infrastructure costs and remain profitable.

Anthropic
 has reached a major profitability milestone ahead of its expected blockbuster initial public offering next week. But CNBC’s Jim Cramer warned Wednesday that the frontier AI lab’s future spending commitments could make staying profitable a much bigger challenge.

“Anthropic is due to spend an enormous amount in the future, so it needs to continue growing rapidly to outrun those costs and remain profitable,” the “Mad Money” host said. “That’s the bet you’re making if you buy the Anthropic IPO.”

The Claude developer became profitable on an adjusted operating basis for the first time in the second quarter of 2026 and remained positive in the third. Through the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic’s adjusted operating income totaled $4.08 billion, according to its IPO prospectus. In calculating its adjusted operating income, Anthropic excludes stock-based compensation, noncash charitable contributions, and payments tied to a class-action copyright lawsuit settlement, according to its IPO prospectus. When following generally accepted accounting principles, or GAAP, Anthropic had an operating loss of $1.26 billion through the third quarter of this year.

“To be clear, Anthropic achieving profitability, even on this adjusted operating income basis, is no small matter,” Cramer said.

Another big difference between Anthropic’s adjusted results and GAAP numbers appears when looking at net income. This metric appears at the bottom of a company’s income statement and serves as the basis for calculating its earnings per share. For 2026, Anthropic reported a net loss of more than $104 billion through September, compared with adjusted net income of $5.6 billion.

Much of that difference reflects a $94 billion noncash charge tied to the rising value of securities issued to partners such as Google and Amazon
. Those arrangements have allowed Anthropic to secure computing resources without immediately paying cash, helping preserve much of the capital it has raised. Cramer cautioned against dismissing those charges entirely, arguing they reflect infrastructure costs the company would otherwise have paid in cash.

Indeed, Cramer emphasized that investors cannot ignore Anthropic’s purchase commitments and lease agreements for computing infrastructure. As of September, Anthropic has committed to spending in the future approximately $900 billion, largely on computing infrastructure, according to its prospectus.

Anthropic’s spending commitments include an agreement with SpaceX
 worth up to $120.5 billion through 2029, alongside deals with Alphabet’s
 Google, Amazon, Microsoft
 and other computing providers. Roughly half of its $900 billion in commitments is expected to come due by the end of 2030. About $70 billion is expected over the next year alone.

“Long story short, Anthropic’s compute costs — its cash compute costs — are going to explode,” Cramer said.

In its IPO roadshow presentation, Anthropic projected that computing and infrastructure expenses would eventually account for 45% to 50% of revenue, supporting a long-term adjusted operating margin of roughly 35%.

Cramer’s key point Wednesday is that reaching that margin target will require sustained revenue growth. On Tuesday, Cramer highlighted Anthropic’s 1,206% year over year revenue growth during the first nine months of 2026, but the company will need to keep growing rapidly to stay ahead of its mounting infrastructure costs.

“You have to assume that this company’s going to continue growing substantially – to the point where it has hundreds of billions of revenue per year, and soon,” Cramer said Wednesday. “That’s the only way this works.”

The stakes extend beyond Anthropic itself. On Monday, Cramer warned that the company’s IPO could be a crucial test for the broader AI trade, given how heavily companies depend on its continued spending.

Anthropic is expected to price its IPO on Nov. 18 and begin trading on the Nasdaq on Nov. 19, CNBC’s Leslie Picker reported Tuesday.
