https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-j.title: Nvidia board meeting to decide CEO Jensen Huang’s fate stretches into evening
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-j.author: Ashley Capoot,Seema Mody
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-j.text:
Nvidia’s board is meeting to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang, CNBC confirmed, following reports of two extramarital affairs.

The New York Times reported that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with an employee named Kimberly Powell.

The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Nvidia’s
 board is meeting to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang, CNBC confirmed late Wednesday, following reports of two extramarital affairs — one with an employee and another with an alleged Chinese spy.

Shares of Nvidia fell more than 9% in post-market trading after The Wall Street Journal first reported that the board was preparing to force out Huang. That news landed minutes after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Nvidia’s vice president of health care.

The alleged relationship, according to the Times story, was with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell’s bio on the Nvidia website says she’s “responsible for the company’s worldwide healthcare business, including hardware and software platforms for accelerated computing, AI, and visualization that power the ecosystem of medical imaging, life sciences, drug discovery, and healthcare analytics.”

Huang and Powell were reportedly captured on camera being affectionate with one another at a hotel in San Jose, California in March, according to the Times.

Nvidia and Powell didn’t respond to CNBC’s request for comment. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request for comment.

The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, according to The Financial Times, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported.

Nvidia’s board of directors has opened an independent investigation and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to look into the spying allegations.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang wrote in the message to Nvidia staff on Sunday. “I am deeply sorry.”

Most of Huang’s Nvidia shares are co-owned with his wife, Lori Huang, and are held in trusts. About 800 million shares are held by those trusts. Huang holds about 70 million shares on his own and has limited economic control over the company.

Rumors of an affair between Huang and Powell have circulated for years, in part because Powell lacks a background in health or science, according to a former employee who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter.

Healthcare is a smaller business at Nvidia. The company makes chips for medical devices and MRI machines, but they are a minor in comparison to the revenue generated from its advanced AI systems and graphics processing units, or GPUs. In recent appearances, including at the company’s annual GTC conference, Powell has spoken about how Nvidia’s AI technology can help accelerate drug discovery, assist providers and improve clinical efficiency. Powell has been leading the group since 2017.

Nvidia’s stock was down 7% this week prior to the after-hours drop on Wednesday and is on pace for its sixth straight weekly slide, reflecting broad concern on the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout. The AI infrastructure trade was hit particularly hard last week after the midterm elections, as Democrats won sweeping majorities in both houses of Congress, and dozens of ballot measures past that could make building data centers more difficult.

Huang has become synonymous with the AI industry, and he is often referred to by his first name ,“Jensen,” by customers and rivals. Nvidia has been one of the primary beneficiaries of the AI boom since its chips are used to train models and run large AI workloads.

—CNBC’s Lora Kolodny and Kif Leswing contributed to this report

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-j.title: Jensen Huang affair in DC: Resignation calls and moves to tighten Nvidia China exports
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-j.author: Justin Papp,Garrett Downs,Karen James Sloan,Irit Skulnik
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-j.text:
The Jensen Huang affair is turning Capitol Hill into a pressure cooker, with some lawmakers calling for the country’s most important tech CEO to resign amid the scandal.

The situation may give Congress reason to advance a suite of bills in this year’s National Defense Authorization Act to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips.

What Nvidia does now — and whether Huang remains atop the company — could impact its relationship with Washington and whether lawmakers crack down.

Members of Congress are calling on Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang to resign, and momentum is building to subpoena the executive, whose company is a leader in advanced artificial intelligence chips.

Senate banking committee member Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., doubled down Wednesday on his call for Huang to resign, and a key Democratic House oversight panel member and House Republican piled on.

“As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign,” Cramer told CNBC, in response to revelations that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy as the chipmaker he co-founded was given permission from the U.S. government to sell its technology to China.

Huang, who leads a company that’s been a chief beneficiary of the artificial intelligence boom, on Sunday admitted to having an affair with a woman whom news outlets have reported U.S. intelligence concluded was a Chinese spy. The revelation is sending shockwaves through Washington, with lawmakers now fearing that U.S. AI dominance could be at risk.

“What bothers me at the end of it is what we don’t know is what she knows about him that can be utilized,” Cramer said, referring to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related. “This is a guy that’s right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don’t think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk.”

Cramer’s comments come on the deadline set by a trio of House lawmakers who requested Huang to testify before their committees on Nov. 18.

GOP Reps. Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; John Moolenaar, chair of the Permanent Select Committee on China; and Rick Crawford, who leads the House intelligence panel, called for Huang to appear in a Nov. 4 letter. Congress members in the majority party also have subpoena power, should they choose to use it.

Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Wednesday afternoon that they had not yet heard from Huang and that they were giving him until the end of the day to respond.

Asked whether the committees were considering subpoenaing Huang if he doesn’t agree to appear, Mast said “yes.”

Moolenaar, when asked the same question, said “all three committees have subpoena power, and I know all three committees have a very serious interest in getting to the bottom of this and having transparency around this.”

“We are going to continue to pursue this,” Moolenaar said.

The lawmakers are far from alone in their criticism, concern and outright shock over the affair. And the scrutiny is only expected to intensify with Democrats poised to take over both chambers of Congress in January. Huang has been close with President Donald Trump during the president’s second term, traveling on Air Force One to China in May.

“Jensen Huang should resign from Nvidia,” Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., a member of the House Oversight Committee, told CNBC. Subramanyam is the top Democrat on the panel’s Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs.

“I didn’t agree with his sentiment that there’s no downside to exporting chips to China,” he said. “But I never thought that he might be having an affair with a Chinese spy who was helping smuggle chips into China at an alarming rate.”

Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., who is retiring from Congress after sometimes bucking Trump, also said the CEO should step down.

“From the little I know, yes.” Bacon told CNBC in response to whether Huang should resign. “I mean, he allowed himself to get compromised by the Chinese government. Not good.”

Huang was notably opposed to strict export controls on AI chips to China, which ruffled feathers with China hawks on Capitol Hill.

Democrats are widely expected to launch myriad investigations into the White House and industry when they assume control of both chambers of Congress in January. Nvidia is now likely to be at the center of those probes.

“There’s two parts to this investigation that [need] to happen somewhere immediately,” Subramanyam said. “One is what was going on with Nvidia and China, and two is why the administration did nothing about it even though they appeared to have known, and what the administration knew, and what influence the money from Nvidia and Jensen Huang had on this administration, essentially staying silent.”

Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., co-chair of the House AI task force, said Tuesday he hopes that the Huang scandal can avoid becoming a distraction in talks about imposing export controls on advanced AI chips.

The situation may give Congress additional ammunition as it tries to pass a suite of bills in this year’s National Defense Authorization Act to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips.

Congress has still not passed the annual defense bill, which is a top priority for lawmakers in the lame-duck session.

Those bills include the AI Overwatch Act, the MATCH Act and the Chip Security Act — all of which are aimed at preventing U.S. chip technology from falling into adversarial hands.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., in a statement following the revelation of Huang’s affair, urged their colleagues to include the AI Overwatch Act. Warren, the incoming Senate banking committee chair, sponsored the bill in the Senate with Banks.

“Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China’s intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related,” the senators said. “It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips.”

And Subramanyam warned that what Nvidia does now — and whether Huang remains atop the company — could affect its relationship with Washington and whether lawmakers crack down.

“If Nvidia finds out that he knew about what was going on and does nothing about it, then Nvidia is making a choice and us as regulators and as watchdogs need to defend the American people,” he said.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/nvidia-j.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a leader in advanced artificial intelligence chips. Two senators urged their colleagues to include the AI Overwatch Act. The bill was sponsored by incoming Senate banking committee chair Warren.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/coreweav.title: CoreWeave CEO Intrator tells CNBC he has canceled his planned share sale program
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/coreweav.author: Jordan Novet,Ari Levy
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/11/coreweav.text:
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said Wednesday that he has canceled his 10b5 stock sale plan.

Intrator has sold 8.26 million shares at an average price of $96.14 per share for a total of $794.2 million under his most recent plan.

The neocloud beat on revenue in Q3 and upped its forecast, while Intrator indicated the company will be fine despite last week’s Democratic midterm sweep.

CoreWeave
 CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC on Wednesday that he has canceled his 10b5 stock sale plan after the company reported strong revenue growth and beat Q3 expectations.

“Until there is a material change in in, in our equity pricing, my 10b5 has been sidelined,” he told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street.”

He said any further selling would be “just normal tax stuff.”

Under Intrator’s 10b5-1 plan announced in November 2025, the CEO has sold 8.26 million shares at an average price of $96.14 per share for a total of $794.2 million.

Intrator and his co-founders have faced criticism for their stock sales as the company’s stock has struggled, with shares down 18% so far in 2026 despite a 20% post-earnings rally on Wednesday.

The company has faced further pressure from the sell-off in the aftermath of last week’s sweeping electoral victory for Democrats, but Intrator told investors on the earnings call that the company isn’t worried about the political changes on the horizon.

“We do not anticipate any impact from the seismic regulatory shift that’s occurred,” Intrator said on his company’s earnings call late Tuesday, in response to a question about new pressures after the election. “We believe that what has occurred is a statement around how you build. We want to build responsibly.”

Intrator’s comments came after CoreWeave reported 168% year-over-year revenue growth, beating estimates, and lifted its forecast for 2026. The stock rallied in extended trading, as the report offered some relief to investors, who have pushed the shares down about 27% over the past month.

Rising interest rates and an unfavorable political environment have fueled concerns that the artificial intelligence boom is poised to cool and that companies like CoreWeave will struggle to raise capital.

In the Nov. 3 midterm elections, voters sided in favor of greater restrictions on data centers in 40 out of 41 ballot measures in 10 states, according to Ballotpedia. Democrats won control of both houses of Congress and were victorious in governors’ races in critical AI infrastructure states like Texas, Ohio and Georgia. In each state, the winning candidate favors some restrictions on new data centers.

J.P. Morgan Asset Management wrote in a report after the election that data center projects from 2028 onward are “most exposed,” and “face greater uncertainty around permitting, power availability and financing.”

But CoreWeave says it’s not slowing down. The company said it still anticipates 1.85 gigawatts in active power by the end of 2026, and it’s now targeting $37 billion to $39 billion in full-year capital expenditures, implying 155% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by Visible Alpha were looking for $37.69 billion.

“We are very comfortable with our pipeline,” Intrator said, adding that the message from voters isn’t a deterrent because the company is always conscious about “being good neighbors.”

“We think that that is an opportunity for us to continue to scale our business within the new political reality that exists,” Intrator said.

—CNBC’s Nick Wells contributed to this article.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.title: How Data Center Opponents Won the Election
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.author: By Dan Gearino
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.text:
Data center developers had a rough election, losing 40 of 41 ballot measures nationwide.

The volunteers behind one of those measures celebrated this week at Big Walnut Grill in Sunbury, Ohio, a suburb of Columbus. These were the 20 or so people who gathered signatures, delivered yard signs and knocked on doors to support a referendum to ban large data centers within city limits. They won 79 percent to 21 percent.

The campaign taught them about the power of community organizing, said Alicia Doty, one of the leaders. She lives near the proposed Amazon Web Services data center that inspired the ballot measure.

“We are much stronger together,” she said, in an interview later that evening.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Doty and her neighbors won partly because they were a movement that emerged from genuine community concerns, and if I were a data center developer, I’d be chomping on antacids right now. It is difficult to see how the data center industry—including some of the largest companies in the world—can shake off rejection in so many of the best locations for construction.

Data center opponents are apprehensive about the scale of these projects, their potential emissions and their demands for electricity and water, which could drive up costs and strain supplies for other users. Fears of artificial intelligence also play a role, since the largest data centers provide the computing power for AI systems.

It helped, Doty said, that the people campaigning for data centers hurt their own cause. The most visible local campaign against the referendum was from NetChoice, a trade group whose members include Amazon. NetChoice canvassers and printed materials sought to discredit the ballot measure as funded by “extreme California special interests,” according to a door-hanger distributed in Sunbury. That message didn’t connect with voters.

Pataskala, which is 23 miles from Sunbury, also had a data center referendum. Pataskala voters rejected data centers with a 74 percent to 26 percent vote.

In at least one case, the people handing out materials opposing the ballot measure appear to have gotten their cities mixed up. One piece distributed in Sunbury said, “PATASKALA BEWARE” and then showed a cartoon wolf holding a clipboard. “There is a California wolf at our door.”

The warning about funding from California refers to a $10,000 donation to Conserve Ohio, a statewide organization opposing data centers, from PowerSwitch Action, an Oakland, Calif.-based nonprofit that supports progressive causes. The donation was the largest of $16,356 listed in Conserve Ohio’s most recent report filed with the Ohio Secretary of State.

Conserve Ohio’s average donation was $103. Excluding PowerSwitch’s contribution, the average was $40.

Conserve Ohio provides free legal advice to groups such as the one in Sunbury. I wrote about Conserve Ohio last month, including how it began with a few volunteers in rural Adams and Brown counties.

Austin Baurichter, one of several Conserve Ohio leaders, said it’s ironic that data center developers, largely based on the West Coast, such as Amazon, would criticize his group for accepting a donation from a California organization.

“We are and will continue to be grateful for any donation help we can get from anyone,” he said.

It’s a stretch to say PowerSwitch Action was funding the Sunbury campaign. Doty’s group spent about $5,000 and raised that money largely from group members, she said.

NetChoice didn’t respond to messages seeking comment.

“We appreciate the opportunity to engage with communities on the benefits that our data center investments bring,” said an Amazon spokesperson in an email. “We remain committed to setting a high bar for responsible data center development [and] continuing to engage communities early in our development process.”

Amazon also explained its approach to data centers and responses to common objections in an Oct. 2 blog post.

The Data Center Coalition, a trade group for data center companies, had this statement:

“The data center industry is committed to engaging with residents and local leaders to understand community priorities, towards ensuring that the growth of digital infrastructure meets local standards and delivers clear benefits that communities are seeking,” said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition.

Diorio said communities that indicate they are “closed for business and investment” may lose opportunities, costing them high-wage jobs and tax revenue.

The election was a big win for Conserve Ohio. With a tiny budget, the group has worked with data center opposition campaigns across the state, advising residents how to get measures on their local ballots.

“I was amazed,” said Nikki Gerber, a leader of Conserve Ohio, about the election results. Voters “acted like they want democracy back, and that gave me hope.”

Gerber owns Moondoggie Liveree, an outdoor tourism business. She joined the push against data centers this year after Amazon Web Services proposed building a data center in her county.

Voters in Sprigg Township, which includes the project site, passed a referendum last week to establish zoning regulations that would limit data centers. But Gerber is concerned the referendum, with text revised by township officials, isn’t strong enough.

Gerber is also wary of the potential for state or local officials to find ways to push the project through, despite local opposition. I asked if she’s pleased to see Democrat Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health, win the election for governor. Acton has said she supports a “conditional moratorium” on data center development.

“I still don’t have any faith in the government until I see the government do something for us,” Gerber said.

Nationwide, data center opponents won in 40 of the 41 local races where development was on the ballot last week, according to Ballotpedia. Ohio was the epicenter of voting on the issue, with 21 measures, followed by Illinois with four and Maine with three.

The only place data centers won was Harwood, N.D., near Fargo, which rejected a referendum that would have required additional review of proposed development, including data centers. The measure failed on a 24 percent to 76 percent vote. The regional chamber of commerce fought the referendum, saying that taxes would increase with new limits on development, as Fortune reported.

Equity analysts viewed the nationwide results, with local rejection of data centers and the election of candidates who oppose the projects, as potentially harmful to the economy.

Morgan Stanley, the investment bank, said the electoral success of Democrats increases the chances of restrictions on development, which could “split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without,” according to the Associated Press. Morgan Stanley identified Acton and Democrat Gina Hinojosa in Texas as incoming governors who could restrict data center development.

If that happens, it would be significant for the industry. Ohio and Texas are among the top U.S. markets for data center development.

Developers may hope that the backlash will lose momentum.

But Doty said the Sunbury campaign was no one-off. Organizers are prepared to challenge any effort to build a data center despite the referendum’s outcome, as well as projects in other industries that they believe are not in the community’s best interests.

“Our group is not going away,” she said.

Other stories about the energy transition to take note of this week:

Senate Advances Permitting Overhaul But Roadblocks Loom: The U.S. Senate has begun debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, following a procedural vote on Monday. The 73-25 vote, with most Republicans and some Democrats on the prevailing side, indicates support for the measure, but several Democrats said the bill needs changes before they will vote for it on final passage. The debate has divided groups that are typically allies, with many environmental organizations warning that the legislation will lead to a massive buildout of natural gas power plants, as my colleague Marianne Lavelle and I report for ICN.

Why the World Is Still Running on Fossil Fuels After 30 Years of Climate Talks: The smell of fossil fuels has become a familiar part of the United Nations “Conference of the Parties” climate talks, with airplanes and buses transporting people to the talks, as my colleague Bob Berwyn reports from COP31 in Turkey. He places this year’s event in historical context, recounting decades of stalled efforts and false starts.

Cattle Could Soon Be Grazing Under Solar Panels: Christiana, Tenn., is home to the first commercial-scale solar array with cattle grazing, according to the developer, Silicon Ranch. The new project could be a significant step forward for agrivoltaics, which combines agriculture and solar power, as Julian Spector reports for Canary Media. I wrote about the potential for livestock grazing and solar last year after visiting a project in Kentucky.

Solar Power Poised for Rapid Growth, IEA Reports: Ahead of COP31, the International Energy Agency published its annual renewable energy report, forecasting the addition of 3.6 terawatts of solar power capacity by 2031, as Jonathan Touriño Jacobo reports for PV Tech. To put this in perspective, solar power growth would be the driver of global renewable electricity reaching about 45 percent market share in 2031, up from 33 percent in 2025. More than half of the growth in solar capacity would come from utility-scale projects, while the rest would come from rooftop solar and other customer-owned systems.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.title: In Pennsylvania, Democratic Lawmakers Want to ‘Act Quickly’ on Clean Energy and Affordability
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.author: By Ben Seal
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.text:
The Democrats’ sweeping success at the national level in last week’s midterms was mirrored in major swings at the state level as well. In Pennsylvania, where Democrats flipped the state Senate, the party will control both chambers of the legislature and the governor’s office for the first time since 1993.

After four years watching bills clear the state House of Representatives only to stall in the Republican-controlled Senate, the party’s leaders say they plan to seize the moment. That’s especially true on the Energy Committee, chaired by Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler of Philadelphia. She knows voters will be looking to her committee to address two pivotal issues that helped decide the midterms: rising utility bills and controversial data center development.

The trifecta in Harrisburg represents “a huge opportunity and a huge responsibility” for Democrats, Fiedler said in an interview a few days after the dust settled.

“We’ve got to act quickly,” she said. “What we saw in the results of Tuesday’s election made clear that people are not happy with the status quo. People want to see change. People do not want excuses.”

With that in mind, she said her colleagues on the Energy Committee have about 15 bills that have already passed the House and will be reintroduced “first thing” in the new session, aimed at addressing “what’s on people’s minds.”

In this interview, which has been edited for length and clarity, Fiedler discussed the party’s approach to affordable utility bills, renewable energy development and an issue that hung over the elections both nationally and locally: data centers.

BEN SEAL: Post-election, what have the early conversations among your Democratic colleagues focused on?

ELIZABETH FIEDLER: At the very top of the list is affordability. We have to find a way to lower people’s bills. We have already passed quite a few bills in our committee and also in the House that would do just that.

[Lancaster Democrat] Nikki Rivera’s battery storage bill would allow us to store energy at a time when it’s abundant and then release and use that energy during times of peak demand, like during a heat wave. Return on equity reform is a bill I introduced last session that the governor himself talked about in his budget address. That’s focused on making sure that the shareholders of utility companies are not making excessive profits.

We’ve got to take a careful look at everything we can do right now to help people. And that definitely includes lowering the cost of energy, lowering utility bills and getting more renewable energy online. So [Berks County Democrat] Jacklyn Rusnock’s solar on warehouses bill is a great example. [Allegheny County Democrat] Arvind Venkat has a geothermal bill.

SEAL: A lot of the legislation that’s been sitting in the Senate has been described as “low-hanging fruit.” Are there more ambitious proposals that you think might gain traction?

FIEDLER: I’m all for bold and ambitious ideas. Now is a great time to go on the offense on renewable energy and, in particular, solar. The technology has made huge steps forward over the last couple of years.

I am excited for the future of Solar for Schools. The more we can do to spread the word about it to more schools the better, because then schools can save millions of dollars by installing solar panels, and they can put that money back into kids’ education. That’s a real win-win-win. I also plan to introduce legislation to offer a residential solar tax credit.

A lot of the work that we want to do is making up for changes that were made at the federal level. The [Inflation Reduction Act] and other federal programs were supposed to support the construction of renewable energy projects across the U.S. When the president decided to dismantle and defund those programs, it had a huge impact.

With a relatively modest appropriation, the Pennsylvania Energy Development Authority could do huge energy infrastructure projects. So I am hopeful on the appropriations front. We’re talking about hydropower on state dams, and there’s also huge potential for both geothermal and solar.

SEAL: Clean energy advocates often point to the Alternative Energy Portfolio Standards as a limitation in moving the state forward. Do you think there might be updates that would accelerate the state’s timeline for renewable energy adoption?

FIEDLER: Yes. A resounding yes. It’s been a very long time since it was updated. All reports and expectations are that in just a few years we’ll be facing significant power outages. We’ve got to take that into account while we also take into account the climate crisis and global warming, more extreme weather, changes in seasons—all the stuff that is our reality now.

SEAL: How do you think the legislature will respond to the strong public sentiment against further expansion of the state’s data center build-out?

FIEDLER: We have already passed [in the House] a number of bills that would change the landscape and place much more stringent regulations and requirements on data centers. House Bill 1834 is a great example, focused on making sure regular people do not subsidize the build-out of energy systems and transmission for data centers. That to me feels like the absolute bare minimum of what we should be doing.

I’ve worked with my colleague Kyle Donahue, [a Lackawanna County Democrat], on a model ordinance bill [guiding municipalities on standards for data center development], and an interconnection bill [ensuring ratepayers don’t bear the costs of energy generation and transmission]. Municipal officials would already have in hand some of these guarantees. And then that gives them the ability to make the decisions that they see fit for their community. It’s really important that there is no rubber stamp.

And we were able to get Rep. Kyle Mullins’s water and energy usage disclosure for data centers in during the budget this past year. So we have made some progress. But there’s still a lot of outstanding questions and a lot of work to be done.

SEAL: Is a data center moratorium up for discussion in the new session?

FIEDLER: Discussions are very much ongoing.

SEAL: Sen. Nikil Saval, Democrat of Philadelphia, said the composition of the Senate had imposed an “imaginative constraint” on Democrats. With that constraint lifted, are there climate and environment proposals that could enter the conversation?

FIEDLER: There are a lot of big ideas that it is past time for us to act on. We’ve got a lot of the game plans in place and have been working very hard over this past session in the Energy Committee and the majority in the House.

I don’t think there is a single magic solution to the climate crisis that we face right now, but there are a lot of pieces to it. [The Alternative Energy Portfolio Standard] is certainly one of those very key pieces. So I’m extremely excited and only a little bit nervous.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.title: Even Cacti Are Threatened by Heat and Drought From Global Warming
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.author: By Kiley Price
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.text:
Cacti are among the toughest plants on the planet, withstanding scorching temperatures and parched conditions that would wilt a more sensitive sprout. But climate change may threaten these hardy plants more than previously thought, a new study suggests.

Scientists in recent years have raised some concerns over the effects of rising temperatures on cactus species, which span nearly every type of ecosystem on the planet—from tree-hanging Christmas cacti in tropical rainforests to the mighty saguaros standing tall in the harsh Sonoran Desert. However, few studies have incorporated the potential risk of another climate-change side effect: extreme drought events.

It turns out these combined factors aggressively crank up the threat level, according to a study published Wednesday in the journal Nature. Integrating new spatial data on severe drought with climate models, the researchers tracked how future conditions could affect the suitable climatic area for nearly 1,000 species of cacti. They found that more than a quarter of the analyzed cactus species could lose most of their suitable habitat by the end of the century, more than 80 percent in all. That’s far more than when only rising temperatures and projected average precipitation were considered.

The habitat declines identified in the paper are associated with substantial losses in cactus diversity in some regions.

These findings challenge a long-standing assumption for cacti that “in a warming world, they’ll likely be winners,” said study co-author Brian Enquist, a professor at the University of Arizona. “Even in these really hot, dry environments where you see cactus species, the climate now is shifting into a new climate regime that these species haven’t encountered in their evolutionary history.”

The study analyzed nearly 650,000 records of cacti around the world, including community science data from the app iNaturalist, which more than doubled the number of species analyzed. Models showed that droughts and heat are poised to have the worst impacts on species in some of the world’s most concentrated cactus hotspots, including Chile, Argentina, Peru, Ecuador and countries in Central America.

Some regions, such as the Mexican Pacific coast, saw modest gains in cactus species diversity, but these were offset by large losses in neighboring areas.

Cacti are already some of the world’s most imperiled plants, with more than 30 percent of species considered threatened. That’s largely due to habitat loss and illegal trade, which has helped supply the collector and houseplant industry as cactus popularity spikes around the world.

On top of this, unprecedented droughts in recent years have fueled widespread die-offs of species such as Copiapoa cacti in Chile’s Atacama Desert and saguaros around Phoenix and Tucson. That’s a precursor of what’s to come if climate change continues to fuel longer, more intense periods of heat and dryness, said study co-author Michiel Pillet, a postdoctoral researcher at University of South Florida.

“We were extremely surprised by how intense our results were,” Pillet said. He added that the impacts are likely an underestimate due to insufficient data on rare species—and the disproportionate impacts they face from climate change. “Think about a cactus species that only lives right at the coast in a single spot, and a hurricane comes in and wipes out that entire population.”

The study’s authors say their modeling approach could be applied to other plant species.

That was echoed by David Williams, a botany professor at the University of Wyoming who was not involved in the study.

“The findings extend well beyond our understanding of the climate vulnerability of cacti,” he said over email. “The work will guide future studies that uncover species-specific ecological, demographic and physiological processes that shape persistence across shifting climatic conditions.”

The researchers say their method could also help experts develop more targeted cacti conservation efforts in a warmer, drier world. For example, artificially dispersing seeds into new environments that fit a cactus’ climate niche—a process called “assisted migration”—can establish more stable populations for at-risk species.

Even just raising awareness for the cacti species most at risk and the need to gather more data on them can help determine where to spend “very limited conservation resources” to “get the best bang for our buck,” Pillet said.

Enquist was encouraged by the widespread public interest in cacti, which has generated an abundance of citizen-science observations that helped make the research possible.

“There are a lot of people that care about these plants,” he said. “What’s wonderful then about that is that there’s a lot of opportunity for intervention.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.title: North Carolina Vows to Hold Chemours Accountable for Contamination ‘No Matter How Long It Takes’
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.author: By Lisa Sorg
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.text:
FAYETTEVILLE, N.C.— North Carolina environmental regulators this week sent a scathing critique to Chemours, which is responsible for contaminating at least 10 counties with toxic “forever chemicals,” arguing that the company’s cleanup proposal violates the terms of a consent order.

The state Department of Environmental Quality detailed multiple inadequacies in the company’s plan to remediate widespread, decades-old groundwater and soil contamination from PFAS chemicals in southeastern North Carolina.

“Today’s direction to the company makes clear that DEQ expects Chemours to clean up all the areas they have polluted,” said DEQ Secretary Reid Wilson in a prepared statement. “DEQ will hold Chemours accountable no matter how long it takes.”

The company’s predecessor, DuPont, is responsible for some of the contamination emanating from the Fayetteville Works plant, but it shielded itself from liability when it spun off Chemours in 2015. An international company, Chemours manufactures chemicals used to make Teflon cookware, data center coolants and grease-, water- and stain-resistant consumer products.

DEQ’s letter said the agency also determined the company could not justify how it assessed the public health and environmental risk of PFAS exposure. The letter cited numerous instances of what DEQ described as missing data, substandard sampling methods and flawed analyses in Chemours’ reports. In some cases, these errors led the company to reach conclusions that lacked a factual, scientific or legal basis, according to the letter.

The groundwater and soil remediation must be detailed in a corrective action plan, a key component of a 2019 consent order between the company, DEQ and the nonprofit Cape Fear River Watch. The agency rejected the company’s draft corrective action plan in 2020, calling it “inadequate” and lacking a “thorough technical basis.”

Progress on the plan stalled for six years until September, when the state announced it had reached a half-billion dollar settlement with Chemours that included a provision accelerating progress on its completion. The settlement required DEQ to provide written feedback to Chemours.

A Chemours spokesperson told Inside Climate News that with DEQ’s formal feedback to its 2019 corrective action plan, risk assessment and other studies “now in hand, we can move forward. We are reviewing the comments in detail and will respond through the established process.”

Because of shortcomings in Chemours’ data and analysis, DEQ wrote, neither the company nor the agency knows the full extent of the PFAS contamination in the Lower Cape Fear River Basin, nearly 10 years after the public first learned of it through media reports.

Over 36 pages, DEQ rebutted the company’s conclusions about the extent of the contamination and the public health and ecological risks.

Chemours told DEQ that current concentrations of the PFAS chemical GenX near the Fayetteville Works plant were unlikely to harm human health even without treating the groundwater. However, the state said, Chemours failed to evaluate all PFAS originating from the plant, as legally required. DEQ said the company also used outdated toxicological data for GenX, one of 15,000 types of PFAS compounds.

There are more than 15,000 types of PFAS—per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, the so-called “forever chemicals.” They are found in many consumer products, such as microwave popcorn bags, pizza boxes, stain- and water-resistant clothing and furniture, and lithium-ion batteries, including those used in electric vehicles.

They’ve been linked to many serious health conditions, including several types of cancer.

PFAS also disrupt the ocean’s ability to sequester carbon, a driver of climate change. PFAS manufacturers emit thousands of tons of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere each year.

In 2022, the Chemours Fayetteville plant emitted 52,000 tons of greenhouse gases, according to EPA data.

Chemours’ health risk assessment excluded people who regularly fish in the Cape Fear River for food, and the company didn’t account for other ways people could become exposed, such as eating contaminated vegetables, touching water or soil that contains PFAS or inhaling the compounds, the state added.

DEQ also requested that Chemours complete its investigation about biosolids—sewage sludge—that could have originated from the plant and have been applied to farm fields. The agency requested comprehensive information about where and when the biosolids were shipped offsite and their quantities.

Sewage sludge is often used to fertilize farm fields. When the sludge is contaminated, the PFAS can seep into the soil, groundwater and drinking water wells.

“The agency is asking the company to look into how their contamination is truly going to harm communities,” said Jean Zhuang, senior attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center, which represents Cape Fear River Watch. “It demands much more of Chemours than the company has ever done so far.”

Over the past six years Chemours has spent about $1.2 billion on complying with some provisions of the consent order. The company installed a thermal oxidizer to remove 99.9 percent of all PFAS emissions from the air, offered free water filtration systems to more than 10,000 homes with contaminated wells and built a mile-long underground barrier wall to prevent contaminated groundwater seeping from the site and into the Cape Fear River.

These projects have reduced, although not eliminated, the amount of PFAS entering the environment. Contaminated groundwater continues to seep from the Fayetteville Works plant into the river and other surface waters; PFAS are still entering the air.

The magnitude of the contamination is so vast that Chemours has previously told DEQ it is “technologically and economically infeasible” to comply as closely as possible with the state’s groundwater rules.

However, DEQ told Chemours in the letter that the company has not provided sufficient evidence to support that conclusion. “While DEQ recognizes that the geographic scope of the contamination caused by Chemours is enormous and unprecedented in this state,” DEQ Deputy Secretary Sushma Masemore wrote, “the vast scope does not release Chemours of its obligation to thoroughly evaluate all remedial alternatives.”

Chemours’ sampling methods to determine health and ecological effects were also flawed, according to the letter. For example, contractors sampled soil along roadways, which is often trucked in from other areas. And instead of collecting earthworms to assess exposure risks in the soil, contractors evaluated grasshoppers, crickets and dragonflies—which don’t live in the dirt.

Contractors also wiped loose dirt off leaves before collecting them, which likely removed PFAS bound to the dust that was deposited through the air, the state said.

Chemours failed to sample aquatic plants and organisms and excluded animals from its studies due to time constraints, which DEQ called “an inadequate justification.”

Chemours has also failed to identify all of the PFAS compounds it is emitting into the air from the Fayetteville Works plant, which is continuing to contaminate the groundwater, Michael Abraczinskas, director of the state’s Division of Air Quality, wrote in a separate letter.

Nor do the company’s sampling and reporting methods meet quality control standards, Abraczinskas wrote, adding that “the issues identified in this letter require immediate attention and corrective actions.”

There is a direct link between air emissions that contain PFAS and contaminated groundwater. After the compounds enter the air, they can travel on the wind and fall to the earth, where they seep into soil and groundwater. PFAS traced to the Fayetteville plant, such as PFMOAA and GenX, have been detected in private drinking water wells as far as 25 miles away.

“Chemours has acted like it’s done everything it needs to do on air emissions, and even asked to expand its facility,” Zhuang said, “and DEQ is saying, ‘No, they are continuing to be an issue, and we’re going to take this really seriously.’”

Chemours has underestimated its air emissions at least twice before, DEQ records show. In 2018, state regulators found Chemours was emitting 2,700 pounds of GenX into the air—amounts 40 times higher than the company had originally reported in early 2017, and four times higher than the company’s revised estimates.

In 2021, the company again underreported its GenX emissions by 40 percent. The next year, DEQ fined Chemours $305,000 for failing to maintain air pollution control equipment, which allowed excessive amounts of GenX to enter the air.

Chemours plans to expand its Fayetteville Works plant, which DuPont opened in the early 1980s. The company filed an air permit application with the state in 2022 and revised it last year. However, environmental advocates, including the Southern Environmental Law Center, objected to the application because it redacted key information that Chemours claimed was confidential, including emission rates from stack testing, hours of operation and production figures.

DEQ notified Chemours nearly a year ago that the application was on hold until the company could submit revised emission calculations necessary for the Division of Air Quality to conduct review. Chemours has yet to submit this information, an agency spokesman said.

Based on the new deficiencies identified in its letter, the division could request additional data.

Chemours has until February to file a plan to address the state’s air concerns listed in the letter. As for the groundwater and soil cleanup plan under the consent order, DEQ has asked Chemours to respond to the state’s critique within 60 days.

There still is no timeline for the work to be completed. Given the scope of the contamination, it could take decades.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.title: As Texas Embraces Carbon Storage, a Black Community Questions the Risks
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.author: By Emily Foxhall, The Texas Tribune
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.text:
CHEEK—On a rural road outside Beaumont, a Texas energy giant is preparing to pump carbon dioxide underground to permanently store it and keep the gas from contributing to global warming. The project could be the first of its kind to start operating in the state.

It’s a long-awaited milestone for the oil and gas industry, which has touted carbon capture and storage as an important tool for cleaning up industry emissions. Texas lawmakers threw their support behind the technology, while state regulators spent years seeking permitting authority from the federal government to try to clear projects faster.

The Texas Railroad Commission, which oversees the oil and gas industry, won that authority late last year and approved this ExxonMobil project in September. But the nearby community of Cheek has asked commissioners to reconsider the permit decision.

The area close to the project is predominantly Black, and many residents are working class or elderly. People there don’t trust the company’s assurances that it will keep residents and their groundwater safe.

Only a small number of carbon storage wells have been permitted so far across the United States, and some CO2-related accidents have already happened. Experts and community advocates have warned of the risk for pipeline accidents and potential underground leaks. Leaders in Cheek are concerned the injected carbon dioxide could contaminate groundwater or get into the air and suffocate them. They worry emergency responders won’t be equipped to rescue them.

“We’re just shocked that they would want to do this so close to homes,” said Douglas Cormier, the 67-year-old president of the Cheek Texas Community Association, who grew up in the rural town and lives there with his wife near his daughters and grandkids.

Residents explained they don’t want to be the test subjects for the technology, and some experts argue it’s more distracting than effective in fighting climate change. Harvard University History of Science Professor Naomi Oreskes, who studies disinformation and climate change, has called carbon capture and storage “mostly a dangerous distraction.”

A recent investigation by Drilled and ProPublica showed it would take more resources than feasible for carbon capture and storage to reduce emissions enough to avoid extreme warming. Companies have canceled or paused nearly a third of 19 proposed carbon storage projects in Texas so far.

But carbon capture supporters argue that storing emissions is an important part of an “all of the above” approach to fighting climate change. Federal tax credits support carbon capture projects. Locally, East Texas remains attractive because of its existing carbon dioxide pipeline network (owned by ExxonMobil), its geology and nearby industrial facilities that might pay for their carbon to be stored.

ExxonMobil has seven agreements with companies to store the greenhouse gas. The volume of carbon dioxide injected underground through those agreements will equal emissions from 2 million cars.

“The community’s concerns around safety of any sort of an injection project are valid and real and need to be taken seriously,” said Nichole Saunders, senior director and lead counsel for energy transition with the Environmental Defense Fund. “At the same time, the need for more carbon management infrastructure to get to where we want to go on climate is also real.”

So far, the case has raised questions about whether companies and the Railroad Commission are doing enough to address community concerns as a backlog of projects awaits approval.

Agency watchdogs say the commission has a history of failing to keep communities safe from industry risks. It’s also facing pressure from state Rep. Drew Darby, leader of the House’s energy resources committee, who told the agency at a September hearing that carbon-capture projects needed to be moving at “utmost pace while protecting the public.”

In a statement to the Tribune, Railroad Commission spokesperson Bryce Dubee said the organization has a record of protecting drinking water while regulating injection wells. Winning the authority to regulate carbon storage “speaks volumes to this expertise,” Dubee said.

ExxonMobil held early meetings with community members in Cheek. The company’s permit requires it to install automatic shut-off systems for the injection wells, monitor the underground carbon dioxide plume and post a phone number where the operators can be reached around the clock.

The permitting program requires coordination with local emergency officials, according to the commission. ExxonMobil sponsors emergency training programs through the Texas A&M Engineering Extension Service in College Station.

“We want community members to know they can count on us to operate responsibly, communicate openly, and put safety first every day,” senior vice president Dominic Genetti wrote in a blog post.

But the day following Darby’s comments, after hearing ExxonMobil hadn’t talked with the community since the residents hired lawyers, Railroad Commission Chair Christi Craddick scolded ExxonMobil for not supporting residents enough. Some people from Cheek had taken a bus to be there to voice their concern.

“Give them information,” she said. “Be there for their safety. Give ‘em a fire truck if that’s what they want.”

Then Craddick voted for the permit.

Photos and posters about the area’s decades-long history hosting local rodeos hang in 81-year-old Preston Frank’s self-made museum in Cheek. Like many who live here, Frank, an upholsterer, inherited the land from his family. He considers it an important way to build generational wealth.

“That’s the reason why we’ve been fighting ExxonMobil,” he said. “We don’t want them coming in here and diminishing the value of the land.”

Just west of Beaumont off Interstate 10, the unincorporated community of Cheek is split by the highway and railroad, with many homes sitting on large tracts of land dotted with cattle and horses. People wave to each other. On the north side, there’s a Catholic and a Baptist church. Once a year, residents gather for a community picnic at the park.

ExxonMobil plans to compress carbon dioxide into an “almost liquid state,” pump it thousands of feet deep into the Earth and let it flow into little spaces in the rock, where scientists expect some to dissolve into salty water in those spaces or get stuck like a drink spilled in sand. Residents from the start had concerns.

How does ExxonMobil know where the molecules will go? What if they don’t behave as expected? What if the project gets abandoned?

Carbon dioxide leaking into water could increase its acidity and cause metals to contaminate it, according to advocacy groups and experts. If it leaks back into the air or a pipeline ruptures and people are caught in a big enough plume, they won’t be able to breathe or run gas-powered cars to escape.

“Contamination of drinking water with CO2, or with metals or chemicals leaching out of rock due to CO2 acidification of the water, could be very costly if the affected aquifer is used by a lot of people,” Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers wrote in a 2007 paper. “[O]nce any aquifer is contaminated, it will remain so.”

The Cheek Texas Community Association signed on in July 2025 with attorneys at the nonprofit Earthjustice, which charges no cost. They fought the permit approval all the way to a state administrative hearing in March this year where they argued ExxonMobil hadn’t done enough to adequately ensure water and public safety would be protected and wasn’t monitoring a large enough area underground.

“It’s the first one in an area so close to a community, and that’s why the water issues and the safety issues are so paramount here,” said Jen Powis, who leads Earthjustice’s Gulf regional office.

The project also raised familiar concerns over environmental justice, a term used by researchers who have shown communities of color suffer a greater proportion of environmental harm than whiter, wealthier areas. Residents feared ExxonMobil saw in their homes a place where the company could more easily and cheaply push a project through.

The company already built three unassuming injection wells at the edge of the community. Only some residents in Cheek signed so-called pore space agreements with ExxonMobil for use of the small pockets in underground rock where the carbon dioxide will be stored and that property owners control under current case law.

“I’m just thinking they found an area where they can do it and not expect a lot of resistance,” said James Strambler, 70, a former IBM technician who moved there around 2017.

After the March hearing, a technical examiner and administrative law judge recommended moving the permit forward to the commission for a vote.

Texas’ work to win the authority to permit carbon storage wells dates back more than a decade.

In 2009, Texas lawmakers passed a law authorizing the railroad commission to design a framework for how the state would regulate these projects in a way that upheld federal law. In 2022, the state formally applied to the Environmental Protection Agency for that authority.

At a virtual July 2025 hearing held by the EPA, the Texas Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing 90% of the state’s fossil fuel production, said approving carbon capture and injection would be an economic boom for the state.

Gaining permitting power for carbon storage wells was “essential for our state’s economic future and energy leadership,” said Todd Staples, the group’s president, following the hearing.

Supporters of the technology are quick to point out that carbon dioxide makes sodas fizzy and creates the tunnels of fog that Texas football teams run through. They cite a study done by Texas A&M researchers that found the danger of leaks presents “a low probability of occurrence”—a risk that can be monitored and managed.

Advocates also point to the state’s decades-long history of injecting carbon dioxide into wells under a different type of permit as a way to draw more oil out of the ground and also store some of the greenhouse gas, a process known as enhanced oil recovery, which ExxonMobil has pursued for decades.

“This has been put in place now for over 50 years,” said Scott Castleman, spokesman for the Gulf Coast Carbon Capture and Storage Alliance, which represents Calpine, Chevron and ExxonMobil. “Certainly, there is more discussion and opportunity for this industry to scale, and so that’s where you’re starting to see projects and interest in areas that may not have seen this before.”

Establishing community trust will “make or break” projects as the industry grows, said Sophia Cunningham, executive director of the Houston Energy Transition Initiative at the Greater Houston Partnership. Best practices include engaging the community early and providing different, meaningful ways for people to give input and discuss possible benefits.

“It’s a technology that can reduce emissions associated with our industrial activities, and so that is a good pursuit and it’s important to support that,” Cunningham said. “But it’s also reasonable to expect that not everybody in a community is going to want that.”

Residents near projects should be asking whether there would be a helpline to call for any issues, or whether truck drivers would observe weight limits for roads and bridges, said Susan Hovorka, a research professor at the University of Texas at Austin’s Bureau of Economic Geology. In Hovorka’s mind, research and experience have already proven the technology to be safe.

“It’s not utterly without peril, and so people are not foolish to ask,” Hovorka said, “But … their anxiety is sometimes maybe higher than is practical and realistic.”

But there have been serious incidents in other parts of the U.S.

In Mississippi, a carbon dioxide pipeline ruptured in 2020 after heavy rain caused a landslide, releasing a vapor cloud of CO2. A government investigation found that first responders had not been notified about the safety risks and “had to guess” what they were. Dozens of people went to the hospital.

Injected fluid at another facility in Illinois leaked into “unauthorized zones” underground, which most residents learned about in a news article.

Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry paused the state’s review of new applications to ensure any permit issued would be in compliance with state regulations, citing a need for a review process that considers “the safety of our citizens and environment and that streamlines the process for greater efficiency.” Louisiana has permitted three carbon dioxide wells to be constructed so far but not to begin operating.

In other states with permitting authority as of mid-October, Arizona hasn’t permitted any carbon injection wells. North Dakota has approved eight active injection wells across three projects, and Wyoming has approved five wells in one project.

“The benefit isn’t there,” said Naomi Yoder, an environmental researcher who opposed Texas’ bid to regulate the technology and raised concerns about potential harm to the environment and communities. “So it doesn’t make any risk worth it, and there is risk involved. You can’t possibly sequester enough carbon dioxide to make it worth it.”

In the Texas state hearing in September, the day before ExxonMobil’s Cheek permit won initial approval, Darby reiterated the importance of supporting the industry. Virginia Palacios, executive director of the agency watchdog group Commission Shift, told him they should also ensure companies pay for equipment and training for emergency responders.

Meanwhile, Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian has vehemently opposed these projects. Christian has argued carbon dioxide is good for plants, rather than acknowledge the robust science that shows people burning fossil fuels has caused carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere to rise, driving up global temperatures.

He voted against ExxonMobil’s permit, saying he didn’t think it was safe.

Newly elected Railroad Commissioner Jon Rosenthal, who will join Craddick and Christian on the three-person commission, told Inside Climate News he supported the state taking over regulation of the wells.

Some projects have meanwhile stalled. Oxy said in its latest earnings call in August that its carbon storage project — the first and only other one approved in the state so far—was coming online “as we look forward.”

Other projects are moving forward, including ExxonMobil’s second project near a community not far from Cheek, called Nome. The commission is collecting public comment on that project this week at hearings on Monday and Tuesday. ExxonMobil named this one “Sunflower,” fitting with the Cheek project called “Rose.”

In late October, environmental and community advocates knocked on residents’ doors to invite them to a meeting about how to advocate for themselves. Only one person from the project’s area attended. Several arrived from Cheek, lending advice on what they’d learned while attendees ate pasta and salad.

The meeting hosts characterized the technology as a financial boon to industry and the Railroad Commission while putting drinking water at risk. The colorless, odorless gas can also cause suffocation, presenter Alexis Iwasiw warned the group.

“At high concentrations … it can lead to serious injury or death,” she said.

The next night, ExxonMobil held an open house in the small Nome City Hall. They served boudin balls and shrimp and offered colorful pamphlets about the company’s safety record, how to respond in an emergency and how drinking water would be protected. They displayed a poster of other pipelines in the area.

As the sun went down, the group of several dozen made its way outside, where the ExxonMobil presenters enthusiastically launched into explaining how CO2 is safe at certain levels. With a call of “let it rip, tater chip,” they released the gas from a demonstration pipeline, where it puffed out visibly like white smoke.

Mike Doguet, a 72-year-old rice and turf farmer turned real estate developer, looked on. He believed the company did a much better job communicating with residents in advance here than in Cheek. The company is paying for new firefighting equipment, he said, among other community support. (Cheek community leaders have a list of wants too, including improved roads, a community center and an emergency warning system.)

One of the Sunflower project’s injection wells sits across the street from Doguet’s home in Nome, making neighbors wonder if there was oil. Doguet’s daughter lives next door and his son isn’t far. He wasn’t worried about safety.

“In my mind, it’s going to encourage new industry. It’s going to be good for the environment. It’s all positive to me,” Doguet said. “I don’t see the negatives.”

As the presentation went on, a resident from Cheek peppered the ExxonMobil employees with questions. One of the ExxonMobil presenters snapped back, telling her they were in the business of keeping substances in pipelines and would always err on the side of safety.

A former ExxonMobil employee and Nome resident in the crowd, 77-year-old Lawrence Riley, piped up to say that in his decades of experience, he’d never had a pipeline emergency: “They are very, very safe, I am telling you,” he said.

Wearing an ExxonMobil hat, 71-year-old Mayor Kerry Abney at one point walked through the CO2 cloud. He thought the project was great: Workers were shopping at Big D’s in town, contributing to sales tax, he said. People had a chance to make money in a place where agriculture is tough.

As Abney put it in an interview: “Santa Claus came.”

The Cheek resident watching the plume crossed her arms, looking skeptical.

Carlos Nogueras Ramos and Zach Leggio contributed reporting.

https://grist.org/buildings/this-surpris.title: This surprise cost could derail your heat pump or EV charger installation. Here’s how to avoid it.
https://grist.org/buildings/this-surpris.author: Tik Root
https://grist.org/buildings/this-surpris.text:
“Electrify everything” has become a mantra in the fight against climate change. Switching a home’s heating, cooling, and other energy-intensive loads from fossil fuels to electricity could drastically reduce planet-warming emissions. But electrification has often run into a major, and expensive, hurdle: upgrading a home’s electric capacity.

A home’s connection to the grid is rated by amperage, or amps, which caps the amount of current it can safely draw at once. The standard for houses built in the last few decades is generally 200 amps. Many older residences, however, have a lower limit because they were constructed when electricity powered little more than the lights, refrigerator, microwave, and perhaps the dryer. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that roughly a third of homes in the United States have panel capacity of 100 amps or less. In the Northeast, that share rises to closer to half.

As people install heat pumps, induction stoves, and EV chargers, they can run into a couple of potential issues. Their electric panel may simply run out of slots to install more circuit breakers, in which case the relatively easy fix of adding a subpanel often does the trick. But sometimes homeowners run into a bigger problem, where an electrician says all the new loads will push them past their home’s peak power limits.

Upgrading an electrical service can start at a few thousand dollars and quickly skyrocket, particularly in rural areas or places where power lines run underground. “We’ve seen estimates of $10,000 to $20,000,” said AJ Rossman, an electrical engineer with VEIC, a contractor that runs much of Efficiency Vermont’s state program.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The exact scope of the problem is unclear. There is scant data on how many service upgrades are done each year, let alone those that may have been recommended and never made due to the cost. But the Lawrence Berkeley research suggests there may be thousands, if not millions, of homeowners who are told they need to upsize their service as they electrify.

The good news is, there are workarounds — if you or your electrician know where to look. It’s a lesson my wife and I recently learned.

When we moved into our Burlington, Vermont, home, natural gas powered the furnace, stove, and dryer. We knew we’d eventually want to electrify, so I had our service increased from 150 amps to 200. Because we needed the upgrade as part of other work, the bill wasn’t horrible.

The change allowed us to install an EV charger, switch to heat pumps, get an induction stove, and plan for an electric dryer. We were happy to have a home largely free of fossil fuels.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Then we decided to build an addition.

Our plan for an extra 800 square feet would require two more small heat pumps along with lighting, outlets, and ditching our gas dryer. None of this was much of a concern until our electrician did the math. He determined that the laundry room swap alone would push our theoretical load to around 192 amps. Upgrading to 300 or 400 amp service would require trenching a new underground line and possibly even overhauling the transformer serving our block. It could cost us well over $10,000.

I panicked and started digging for answers. I had heard about a growing array of products designed to help people in my situation. For example, a friend had installed a smart panel that monitors how much electricity each circuit is using to ensure demand does not exceed the home’s capacity. If things get close, the panel shuts off lower-priority breakers as needed, then turns them back on when it’s safe.

This was appealing, but expensive. Converting my panel would have cost around $4,000 in materials alone. Even options that control a few circuits starts at about $2,000. With labor, the outlay seemed almost as staggering as a service upgrade.

I came across a cheaper category of devices called load-sharing switches, or smart splitters. They allow two high-demand appliances to share the same circuit, with just one running at a time. That means only the heavier load counts in a home’s demand calculation. Each switch cost around $800, depending on the brand. The issue was that we would probably need at least two to bring our calculated load below 200 amps. That was certainly an improvement, but it still wasn’t cheap and it left little wiggle room for the future.

There must be a better option, I thought. So, as a last-ditch effort, I called my utility provider, who I assumed may have other customers in a similar position. An advisor immediately asked me a question I had taken for granted: Is your electrician sure you need an upgrade?

When my electrician had calculated how much power my house would need, it appears he used the National Electrical Code’s standard method. Simply put, this approach uses the rated loads of all the electrical items in a home to calculate its theoretical load. Using one of the many online calculators to replicate his work, I arrived at the same conclusion: I was already taking up about 187 amps and the addition would push me to around 227 — beyond the panel’s 220-amp limit.

But Burlington Electric told me there was a lesser-known section of the code that could give me a very different answer. Commonly referred to as Section 220.87, even though it was recently moved to section 120.87, this method uses a year’s worth of utility data to identify a home’s actual peak demand instead of relying on hypothetical usage. Like 73 percent of residences around the country, my home has a smart meter, so it was relatively easy to request that information from my utility. A spreadsheet arrived the next day.

The file was thousands of rows long, so I put it into TrueLoadapp.com, a tool electricians can use to evaluate a customer’s load using this alternative method. It parsed the data to find my peak, which came on January 20, when my home topped out at just under 62 amps. The code mandates a 25 percent buffer when calculating usage, which bumped me about 77 amps.

Even then I was using less than 40 percent of my service and less than half what the standard method calculated. I then added my new loads the traditional way, and discovered there was more than enough capacity without upgrading my service. I had just saved thousands of dollars

“My mission is to get anybody who is considering any sort of electrification to do this first,” said Jake Marin, the founder of TrueLoad. “There are many, many, many situations where there is nothing wrong with your panel.”

Marin used to work at the VEIC, where he was involved in dozens of panel upgrades and started to wonder whether there was a better approach to the problem. That’s when he found 220.87 and built TrueLoad. “It tends to show that you have a lot more headroom than you actually thought,” he said. “People are spending $10,000 or more that they don’t need to.”

This aligns with the Lawrence Berkely research, which found that only a small fraction of homes actually need an upgrade, especially when using 220.87. “Most electrical panels have headroom for additional load,” said lead author Sean Murphy in a webinar earlier this year. Efficiency Vermont also looked into this issue, with similar results.

“We’re finding it really depends on the electrician,” said Rossman, who co-authored the white paper on the topic. It found that many electricians use rules of thumb in evaluating headroom, and few of those surveyed were aware of 220.87. Even homes with smaller services may have more capacity remaining than homeowners or electricians realize. “For a reasonable household, we are not seeing anything that comes close with the 200 amps,” said Rossman, noting that even fully electric homes utilize a fraction of that. “And it’s rare where you need something with more than 100 amps.”

Whether a load calculation is accepted ultimately rests with local inspectors. Some don’t even require one. Those who do shouldn’t have a problem with 220.87 because it’s been around for decades, said Dean Austin, a senior electrical specialist at National Fire Protection Association. Master electrician Johnathan Quong, who owns New England Electric, has been turning to it for years, when the traditional calculation suggests a home lacks capacity.

“We’ve been able to keep tons of people on 100 amp panels,” said Quong, who added that he’s never had an inspector reject a 220.87 project. The bigger obstacle, he said, may be getting electricians to adopt it. At an industry conference this year where the topic came up, he said he sensed skepticism from colleagues accustomed to traditional calculations.

“It didn’t sound like they knew about it, or didn’t feel like that was acceptable, and they still felt like it was their responsibility to make sure that it was 100 percent safe,” he said. “In my mind, there shouldn’t be any resistance.”

One caveat is that homeowners must get usage data from their utility, and Marin said access varies widely. Some utilities print a home’s peak load on the monthly bill, and TrueLoad has a feature for helping users make requests, but customers can still end up having to dig for that data — and navigating the system isn’t easy even for experts.

“I don’t even know how I would get that data from my own smartmeter,” said Ric O’Connell, executive director of GridLab, a nonprofit focused on supporting a clean grid. A few days later he emailed to say that after “a long time” and a battle with a “really poor” user interface, he obtained his data from Pacific Gas and Electric Company in California. It showed that his home peaked at just 65 amps.

For those who can’t access data, there are a few options. Another section of the code, 220.83 (recently changed to 120.83), allows some loads to be discounted based on the assumption that not everything in a home will be running simultaneously. In certain situations, that method may produce an even lower calculated demand than 220.87, said Jenny Low, director of panel optimization work and electrical reassessments for Build It Green, a nonprofit working to create equitable, healthy, and regenerative neighborhoods.. At the very least, she said, it should be more forgiving than the standard method.

If I had used that option, my addition would likely have squeaked in under 198 amps, which would not have left enough margin to make me comfortable. The 220.87 route was clearly the smarter move. The 2026 version of the code expands the options by allowing both demand data and load discounting, although adoption may vary depending upon which version of the code a jurisdiction currently uses. The bigger challenge is making sure electricians and homeowners know about it.

For anyone who is short on capacity after using these approaches, load-management options like smart panels and switches are often the cheapest path to electrification. “There are,” said Low, “lots of ways to avoid a panel upgrade.”

As for me, contractors broke ground on the addition last week. If all goes to plan, I will spend a grand total of zero dollars on an electrification project that could have cost me well over $10,000.

https://grist.org/elections/climate-prog.title: Climate progressives won the midterms without saying ‘climate’
https://grist.org/elections/climate-prog.author: Frida Garza
https://grist.org/elections/climate-prog.text:
On October 20, the two candidates running to represent Michigan in the U.S. Senate, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, took questions for an hour at the Detroit Economic Club. El-Sayed, the Democrat who had previously run for governor, made a name for himself years ago by connecting public health to the climate crisis. He published a fierce defense of the Green New Deal at the time, touting its economic, health, and planetary benefits. But last month at the Detroit Economic Club, El-Sayed didn’t mention the Green New Deal at all.

Instead, the only mentions of such a plan came from his opponent, who used it as an attack on El-Sayed and the Democratic party as a whole. “We need to make sure we don’t have the largest tax increase in the history of the country,” Rogers said, “which is, that’s what the other team is talking about doing.”

A vote for El-Sayed would ring in an era of “big government, government control, more rules, more regulation, another Green New Deal,” Rogers continued. It’s become a common refrain since President Donald Trump’s effort to rebrand the climate movement’s push for widescale public investment in renewable energy as a “Green New Scam.”

Two weeks later, El-Sayed handily won the race.
