For nearly two years, student protesters demanded a fundamental transformation of Serbia’s political system, and the Oct. 25 elections marked an extraordinary step toward achieving it. Their movement defeated the formidable political machine of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a stunning upset.

The Student List secured approximately 53 percent of the vote and 140 parliamentary seats, with a record voter turnout of nearly 70 percent. It ended 14 years of uninterrupted rule by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is left with 103 seats. A new government must be formed within 90 days of the official results.

For nearly two years, student protesters demanded a fundamental transformation of Serbia’s political system, and the Oct. 25 elections marked an extraordinary step toward achieving it. Their movement defeated the formidable political machine of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a stunning upset.

The Student List secured approximately 53 percent of the vote and 140 parliamentary seats, with a record voter turnout of nearly 70 percent. It ended 14 years of uninterrupted rule by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is left with 103 seats. A new government must be formed within 90 days of the official results.

The victory is remarkable not least because the students disregarded almost every convention of electoral politics. They rejected traditional parties, eschewed recognizable leadership, and offered voters something closer to a moral crusade than a normal political program. The elections therefore functioned less as a choice between competing platforms and more as a referendum on Vucic’s years in power.

Winning power and exercising it are different things. The qualities that made the student movement effective in opposition—from the students’ status as political outsiders to their ideological heterogeneity—could become liabilities in government. Now, the Student List must prove to an expectant public that it can move beyond deliberating what needs to change and govern.

Serbia’s ongoing political upheaval traces back to November 2024, when a concrete canopy collapsed outside the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station, killing 16 people. Initial demonstrations demanded government accountability for the disaster and transparency over who was responsible for the construction and how public funds were spent.

As protests spread across Serbia, the disaster became a symbol of broader anger over endemic corruption, political patronage, and the ruling party’s stranglehold on state institutions. The movement evolved into a campaign for wholesale political change, culminating in snap parliamentary elections. Students, who carried out university occupations and demonstrations that put immense pressure on Vucic’s government, were the driving force.

The students’ grassroots efforts had structural advantages. The movement was decentralized, operating through network-based university groups that made it difficult for the government to identify leaders it could discredit or co-opt. The students also rejected Serbia’s opposition establishment, whose chronic infighting, electoral failures, and tainted reputation made it an unappealing alternative to Vucic. This helped the movement attract support from across the political spectrum.

The students initially insisted their objective was to compel Serbia’s institutions to function better rather than to enter electoral politics. But after six months of protest, they began to recognize the limitations of their approach. At the time, I argued in Foreign Policy that street demonstrations alone would not transform Serbia, and that the students would have to turn to the ballot box to achieve lasting change. In May 2025, they took that step, demanding snap elections.

Vucic resisted calls for an early vote for another 16 months before finally dissolving parliament on Sept. 9 and scheduling the October elections. He resigned as president to contest the election as the SNS candidate for prime minister, temporarily handing the position to parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabic. (Serbia must hold an early presidential election by Dec. 27.)

So, the students did enter politics—though on unique and even inadvisable terms. Rather than joining forces with established parties, they assembled the Student List, an electoral coalition that included academics, professionals, and political newcomers. Candidates were nominated and vetted by student plenums at individual university faculties, which agreed on a final list through a nationwide process of collective decision-making.

The Student List retained a horizontal structure and avoided elevating a charismatic leader, consciously rejecting the political culture that Vucic cultivated. That strategy was an enormous gamble. The students bet that public dissatisfaction was widespread enough to bring habitual nonvoters to the polls: primarily politically disengaged Serbians, first-time voters, and people who had become disillusioned with electoral politics in the Vucic era.

What Serbian youth understood about politics that their counterparts elsewhere in the West haven’t.

Serbia’s opposition won at the ballot box, but changing its economy will be even harder.

But they did not have an obvious plan for winning over the government’s supporters, many of whom had a material stake in Vucic’s patronage system. SNS reportedly has more than 700,000 members; party loyalty is often a prerequisite for securing public-sector employment. In smaller towns where the state is a major employer, supporting the ruling party is therefore as much a matter of economic self-preservation as political conviction.

While in power, the SNS cultivated and invested in preserving the status quo, which included public-sector employees, business owners benefiting from state contracts, and older voters who credited Vucic with rising pensions and economic stability.

Vucic campaigned on his economic record and sought to discredit the student movement, accusing its supporters of attempting a so-called color revolution and portraying their slate of inexperienced candidates as a threat. His message was familiar: The SNS delivered stability, infrastructure investment, and higher wages, pensions, and living standards. Serbia has experienced genuine economic development under Vucic, but as elsewhere, the rising cost of living has strained household finances.

By contrast, the student movement asked voters to embrace uncertainty for the promise of a better future. Its 11-point reform agenda promised to restore the rule of law and respect for the constitution, free the judiciary from political interference, confiscate illegally acquired wealth, and dismantle the patronage networks that have permeated state institutions.

The SNS campaign rested on what it thought was a straightforward calculation: Would voters risk their livelihoods on an inexperienced opposition promising to tear down the existing order? This underestimated how much public tolerance for Vucic had deteriorated. His party is plagued by allegations of corruption, cronyism, and abuses of authority; the touted stability increasingly appeared to serve a small elite.

Vucic’s government also overestimated its traditional methods of intimidation. International election observers documented voter pressure, misuse of state resources, and unequal campaign conditions. Pro-government forces dominated airtime and broadcast overwhelmingly negative coverage of the Student List, according to the European Center for Research, Transparency, and Accountability. These tactics still failed to prevent the opposition from large-scale mobilization.

Ultimately, the Student List won the public’s vote, with its perceived weaknesses serving as strengths. By rejecting the established opposition, it avoided inheriting the baggage of politicians who had repeatedly failed in challenging Vucic. Its lack of obvious ideological identity united voters with otherwise incompatible convictions, and its refusal to appoint a dominant leader deprived the government of an obvious individual to demonize.

The victory of the Student List bears comparison with that of Prime Minister Peter Magyar in neighboring Hungary’s elections in April. Both movements capitalized on exhaustion with entrenched governments that blurred the distinction between party and state and turned discontent with corruption into a broader rejection of the political order.

But there is an important difference. Magyar—a former member of longtime Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s party—offered Hungary a recognizable alternative built around his leadership, combining institutional accountability with a message about deteriorating public services and living standards. Serbia’s student movement offered something more radical: an opportunity to replace the political culture itself.

The question now is whether a movement assembled around opposition to one leader can develop the coherence necessary to govern without him. The Student List’s parliamentary majority should allow it to form a government without coalition partners. But the movement has yet to settle elementary questions of leadership, including who will become prime minister and how to reconcile ideologically diverse factions.

Ilija Srdanovic, a physician and professor who became the lead candidate on the electoral list, confirmed that government appointments will be decided collectively by lawmakers, while the student plenums that elected them intend to retain an oversight role. But this risks creating competing centers of authority—a tension that is already surfacing. The Student List lawmakers and the plenums are currently deliberating how to balance the grassroots participation that defined the movement with the elected representatives’ practical need to make decisions quickly.

The Student List also encompasses left-wing academics, liberal reformers, and conservative nationalists whose different positions on key foreign-policy issues that have long been political third rails in Serbia—such as Kosovo’s independence, support for Russia, and Serbia’s European integration—could prove especially difficult to reconcile in government.

Another immediate challenge is the presidential election that is due by the end of next month. The Student List must put forward a credible candidate while simultaneously forming a government. Defeat could leave it sharing power with a hostile president, further complicating its ambitious reform plans. The scale of the October upset makes a student victory likely, however. Those who voted for the Student List likely won’t want a president who throws sand in the gears of the parliament they mobilized to elect.

The new leadership will face enormous practical obstacles to governance. SNS loyalists remain embedded throughout the state bureaucracy, where they could obstruct reforms and frustrate corruption investigations that the new government intends to pursue. Particularly challenging will be reforming the police and intelligence services, whose senior officials have been accused of surveilling and intimidating government opponents, as well as links to organized crime.

Dismantling these networks requires more than moral conviction. It demands administrative competence, political discipline, and the ability to distinguish legitimate reform from politically motivated retribution. This last distinction is particularly important. The new government will face intense pressure to deliver accountability for years of alleged abuses, and the Student List has already called on judges and prosecutors to either pursue corruption cases or resign. But indiscriminately purging the state apparatus risks the sort of politicization that the students promised to end.

Equally, the new leadership cannot neglect Serbians’ material concerns. A government devoted to prosecuting its predecessor while failing to improve ordinary lives might find that enthusiasm for political renewal has a limited shelf life. Concerns are emerging about the Student List’s vague economic program, with economists questioning its investment plans. An approaching budget deadline will quickly test the new government’s economic credibility.

It would also be foolish to write Vucic off. The SNS retains 103 parliamentary seats, extensive patronage networks, and influence over local administrations and media outlets. Vucic has already vowed to return to power, though he must first keep his political machine intact. Vucic has been involved in national politics since 1993; he spent 12 years in opposition after the fall of Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. He will not simply disappear.

Dismantling an entrenched political system is one thing, but building a functioning alternative is another. The students have won an impressive mandate, but their sweeping ambitions will take more than one parliamentary term. They must learn not only how to win elections but also how to retain voters’ confidence. That demands a transition from protest to politics, from moral absolutism to compromise, and from opposition to responsibility.

Serbia’s student movement accomplished something that many people believed impossible: They ended an era of political dominance through the ballot box. Now, their task is to demonstrate that they can build something better in its place.

Aleks Eror is a journalist and political consultant from Belgrade. His work has been published by the Financial Times, UnHerd, and other publications. X: @slandr

Analysts have spent much time over the past week trying to explain the “blue tsunami” that swept the United States during the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Democrats gained historic majorities in both the House and Senate, teeing up for a confrontational two years with President Donald Trump.

Many voters clearly wanted their elected officials to stop writing blank checks for Israel and to end the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. About 6 in 10 U.S. voters told an Associated Press election survey that attacking Iran was the wrong decision. A Chicago Council poll found that 68 percent of Americans said the war had not been worth its costs. According to the same study, 56 percent favored reducing or eliminating U.S. military aid to Israel. The Chicago Council also reported that 57 percent of Americans backed restrictions to prevent U.S. military aid from supporting Israeli operations against Palestinians.

Analysts have spent much time over the past week trying to explain the “blue tsunami” that swept the United States during the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Democrats gained historic majorities in both the House and Senate, teeing up for a confrontational two years with President Donald Trump.

Many voters clearly wanted their elected officials to stop writing blank checks for Israel and to end the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. About 6 in 10 U.S. voters told an Associated Press election survey that attacking Iran was the wrong decision. A Chicago Council poll found that 68 percent of Americans said the war had not been worth its costs. According to the same study, 56 percent favored reducing or eliminating U.S. military aid to Israel. The Chicago Council also reported that 57 percent of Americans backed restrictions to prevent U.S. military aid from supporting Israeli operations against Palestinians.

The White House appears to have taken notice. Vice President J.D. Vance wrote on X that “the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. … The reason we lost is the war.” He also cited the desire to “change our relationship to Israel” as a factor in some Trump voters choosing to back Democrats.

Discussing Republicans’ loss, Trump himself admitted to the Wall Street Journal that “Iran was a piece of it.” And in an apparent acknowledgment that supporting U.S. military aid to Israel carried a political cost, Trump announced on Election Day that the United States would end the $3.8 billion in annual military aid to the country by the end of this calendar year. Trump later told 60 Minutes that “there is a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.”

Trump’s announcement marks a watershed moment in U.S. foreign policy. But U.S. aid to Israel won’t end with a phone call. The current U.S.-Israel military aid agreement runs through fiscal year 2028; Trump did not explain how the United States would halt funding sooner. What’s more, cutting Israel’s annual U.S. military aid package would still leave room for supplemental military funding. It also would not stop Israel from buying American weapons through government sales and commercial contracts.

For Israeli authorities and their supporters, maintaining the flow of U.S. arms to Israel is far more important than who pays for them. If Israel—rather than U.S. taxpayers—pays for a bomb, that does not mitigate the bomb’s impact when Israel drops it on a Palestinian family. The United States will remain complicit in Israeli genocide and apartheid as long as U.S. arms keep flowing.

The new Congress should end all U.S. arms transfers to Israel. It can start by removing the $3.8 billion in military aid from fiscal 2027 appropriations and by blocking supplemental military funding. The House has already passed a spending bill that earmarks these billions in arms for Israel. Congress must remove that earmark before the appropriations bill becomes law.

Lawmakers should also prohibit new arms sales and deliveries to Israel under existing contracts, commercial export licenses, and stockpile arrangements. Congress should ensure full transparency around U.S. military aid and both government and commercial sales to Israel, as some information is not public. Voters deserve to know whether the U.S. government has truly stopped the flow of arms to Israel or simply tweaked the mechanisms by which Israel receives them.

It is critical, too, that Congress strike Section 219 from the House-passed National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal 2027. The provision would expand military cooperation with Israel through joint weapons development and production. In particular, the provision would direct the Defense Department to designate an executive agent to expand military technology cooperation with the country. Section 219 promotes joint ventures, co-production, and integration of jointly developed or Israeli-origin technology into U.S. military systems.

Congress should also reject Republican Rep. Don Bacon’s H.R. 10796 bill, which would advance a similar initiative. Pentagon co-production preserves the machinery that enables Israeli abuses—without the safeguards that Congress wrote into law to prevent the United States from arming repressive regimes.

Finally, the Senate should adopt Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s resolution drawing on Section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, which bars security assistance to any government engaged in a consistent pattern of gross human rights violations. If approved, the resolution would force the State Department to submit, within 30 days, a report covering abuses against Americans and Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. On Sept. 29, 47 senators, including all but one Democrat, supported a motion to advance the resolution, but 51 voted against it. The resolution thus failed.

Democrats feel they have a mandate to put conditions on U.S. support for Israel.

The Republican midterm disaster leaves Israel dangerously exposed.

From the Iran war to boat strikes to Ukraine, Democrats now have powerful leverage.

If the new Senate adopts the resolution, then the State Department would be required to write such a report. If the department misses the 30-day deadline to do so, Section 502B would bar delivery of U.S. security assistance to Israel until the State Department delivers a report that finds that Israel is not engaged in a consistent pattern of human rights abuses. Congress can also use Section 502B’s procedures to restrict or terminate assistance through legislation. The statute covers not only military aid, but also arms sales and licenses for defense exports.

Van Hollen has emerged a potential challenger to Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. Having a principled voice such as his in a leadership role would pave the way for a broader change in U.S. policy toward Israel and send a clear message that the Democratic Party understands the mandate that it just received from the American people.

Regardless of who takes up the reins in the Senate, Congress should pass a joint war powers resolution directing an end to the Iran war, which the United States has waged alongside Israel since February. Congress should pair that measure with legislation prohibiting funds for continued or expanded U.S. military operations on Iran, covering both direct military spending and emergency transfers to Israel.

The Trump administration continues to send mixed messages about the direction of the war, but after a classified October briefing, Sen. Chris Murphy described the U.S. military plan as “insane.” A war of this magnitude—which has killed, maimed, and displaced thousands of civilians and also damaged infrastructure and economies across the Middle East—has been left to Trump’s whims for too long.

On both Israel and Iran, the American people have spoken: They want Congress to reassert its critical constitutional role and end the fighting. Now legislators must act.

Omar Shakir is the executive director of Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN). A human rights lawyer focused on the Middle East and U.S. foreign policy, he previously served as the Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch. X: @OmarSShakir

With the prospect of renewed war in Iran seemingly off the table for now, and given the Trump administration’s redoubled commitment to economic pressure to overwhelm Tehran, the question again becomes: What will be the fate of the Strait of Hormuz?

U.S. President Donald Trump, despite earlier threats to reignite hostilities in a last bid to cow Iran’s resistance, appears to have parked the military option. U.S. Secretary of State and National Security Advisor Marco Rubio also indicated that the double-whammy of Operation Economic Outcast (a naval blockade) and Iron Gate (a land blockade of Iranian trade) will bend the regime to the administration’s will. Not even angry phone calls with Israeli leadership appear able to summon the dogs of war again.

With the prospect of renewed war in Iran seemingly off the table for now, and given the Trump administration’s redoubled commitment to economic pressure to overwhelm Tehran, the question again becomes: What will be the fate of the Strait of Hormuz?

U.S. President Donald Trump, despite earlier threats to reignite hostilities in a last bid to cow Iran’s resistance, appears to have parked the military option. U.S. Secretary of State and National Security Advisor Marco Rubio also indicated that the double-whammy of Operation Economic Outcast (a naval blockade) and Iron Gate (a land blockade of Iranian trade) will bend the regime to the administration’s will. Not even angry phone calls with Israeli leadership appear able to summon the dogs of war again.

That means that the overarching question—beyond the fate of Iran’s previously “obliterated” nuclear program, something that does not seem amenable to short-term diplomacy—is who will control the most strategic waterway on Earth.

Before the war, which began in February, the Strait of Hormuz saw the transit of 20 percent of all seaborne oil exports in the world. It was never closed before, though there was a “tanker war” in the 1980s during the Iran-Iraq conflict that disrupted regional energy flows. But the strait was closed for much of this year, and it has only been prized open at great cost in recent months by the efforts of the U.S. Navy and the fortitude and deep pockets of seafarers and shipping companies. Oil flows out of Hormuz, and indeed the broader Middle East, are as high now, on average, as they were before the war began. Coupled with dovish talk from Washington, the global price of oil has plummeted in recent weeks from $114 a barrel to the low $90s.

But that does not portend a return to normal. Shipping rates have fallen from their sky-high levels earlier this autumn, but they remain multiples of their prewar prices. Iran continues to target and strike tankers and other vessels that transit the strait, with two incidents in just the last 24 hours.

Oil flows from the Persian Gulf—just not freely.

Any negotiated end to the now nine-month conflict will have to confront the future navigational regime of the Strait of Hormuz. That was a question on which the July memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran punted, but it cannot be forever forestalled. On the one hand, what suddenly became Iran’s greatest strategic asset—a chokehold over the world’s carotid artery—will not be surrendered summarily. On the other hand, it is a wasting asset and will diminish further in the years to come. Saudi Arabia has expanded its overland pipelines to bypass the strait, as has the United Arab Emirates, meaning the constricted and vulnerable seaborne route is less critical.

“The strait is an asset of declining value for Iran,” said James Kraska, a professor of maritime law at the U.S. Naval War College.

Kraska has some thoughts on how to chart a course to a sustainable future for the Strait of Hormuz, drawing on international law, lessons from previous big-power showdowns, and current straits-management regimes in other parts of the world, including the Strait of Malacca. He laid them out in some detail earlier this year.

The thrust of the argument for his “Hormuz Declaration” is a recognition that Iran, after the war, will want to retain some measure of control over a vital chokepoint of the world economy, but it cannot be the sole arbiter. Iran and Oman, which share the territorial waters that shrink into the narrows of Hormuz, will need to be at the forefront of any postwar agreement. But it must also be backed by major powers that rely on the waterway, including China, the United States, and Europe. 


    
    
        Read More
        
                    
                
    
            
        
        
        A large ship is seen on the open water in low light.
    
    
        
    
                Oil Is Again Flowing Out of Hormuz            


    
    	But the continued shortfall of refined products means little relief at the pump.
    	        
            


        
        Analysis    
        |
        
    
    Keith Johnson


    


             
                    
                
    
            
        
        
        Boats are anchored off Oman’s northern Musandam Peninsula near the Strait of Hormuz on June 27.
    
    
        
    
                The MOU Is Paying Off Early for Iran            


    
    	Washington and Tehran are grappling over a “memorandum of misunderstanding.”
    	        
            


        
        Analysis    
        |
        
    
    Keith Johnson


    


             
                    
                
    
            
        
        
        Oil tankers and cargo vessels are anchored off the coast of Oman.
    
    
        
    
                Cognitive Dissonance Dominates Hormuz            


    
    	Ships can’t navigate a reality that exists only in Trump’s head.    	        
            


        
        Argument    
        |
        
    
    Elisabeth Braw

But the continued shortfall of refined products means little relief at the pump.

Washington and Tehran are grappling over a “memorandum of misunderstanding.”

Ships can’t navigate a reality that exists only in Trump’s head.

What that would mean in practical terms is a return to the prewar situation in which ships pass through the center of the strait, free of threats or tariffs, rather than skirting toward the Iranian or Omani coasts as at present, under the threat of drones, mines, and missiles.

Iran’s plan for a tollbooth in the strait, which would charge passing tankers millions of dollars and potentially bring in billions of dollars in annual revenue, is a bad idea, Kraska argued. A richer vein could be tapped by Tehran gaining access to frozen assets and reentering the global economy, something sorely needed for an economy facing a dearth of imports and inflation of around 140 percent a year.

“I believe that what I’ve offered is the start of a framework, a Hormuz Declaration, and a cooperative mechanism. And that’s really the only way—but it will require Iran to feel it gets enough to give it room to negotiate,” Kraska said. “The material benefits of a deal are evident for both sides, and there’s a face-saving way for Iran to do that.”

Under the current situation, oil from most Gulf countries largely gets out, one way or the other, while oil exports from Iran have all but collapsed. A negotiated, international regime for the management of Hormuz would bring down costs for all oil exporters and return Iran’s oil to global markets.

The immediate obstacle to such a deal is that Iran appears determined to insist on compliance with the conditions that Trump signed off on over the summer, including an end to the naval blockade, the end of U.S. military presence in the region, and an end to fighting in other theaters such as Lebanon.

The United States, for its part, has never been keen on granting Iran any veto power over Hormuz in the postwar landscape, even though a return to the status quo ante is now impossible. That standoff explains why oil remains above $90 a barrel despite an end to major combat operations in the region.

U.S. officials believe that sustained economic pressure on Iran will buckle Iran’s leadership, which has spent nearly half a century battling sanctions and international isolation. Kraska is not so sure. The new normal may be a war-not-war that keeps markets on edge and prices relatively high but never resolves into either peace or escalation.

“The most likely indication of what is to come in the near future is what is in the present, which is mowing the grass, basically,” Kraska said. “I just think we will continue to muddle through over the next year or two and never get a final resolution. Because we’ve seen with Iran that even when you get a resolution, there’s a compliance problem.”

Keith Johnson is a staff writer at Foreign Policy covering geoeconomics and energy. Bluesky: @kfj-fp.bsky.social X: @KFJ_FP

It was a remarkable turnaround that will to be studied by election watchers for years to come.

Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the now-imprisoned former president. Lula’s campaign was allegedly thwarted online on Meta’s platforms. When Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva gave his victory speech in late October, he took one hand and held it aloft in tribute to “our general,” as his supporters cheered the “warrior of the Brazilian people.” The title was fittingly bestowed on André Janones, the 42-year-old congressman who vigorously mobilized almost 11 million voters as part of Lula’s “digital army,” marking the first time since Brazil’s return to democracy four decades ago that the runner-up surged ahead in the second round of a presidential election. It was a remarkable turnaround that will to be studied by election watchers for years to come.

In one of the most consequential elections in Brazilian history, some three-quarters of the population were getting their news from social media, and Meta—the owner of the most prominent platforms—was supportive of Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the now-imprisoned former president. Lula’s campaign was allegedly thwarted online on Meta’s platforms. United Nations experts described as interruptions of “one side’s” social media accounts, curtailed audience engagement, and choked user feeds.

Users reported that Meta’s artificial intelligence tools refused to generate campaign posters for Lula, whose name would temporarily not appear in searches, while Bolsonaro’s profile was recommended. Leaked details revealed that Meta’s employees confirmed internal manipulations tilting the digital field in Bolsonaro’s favor, benefiting his conservative political movement. Noting its failures to stem disinformation in Brazil’s last elections, the company’s own oversight board issued its concern over “recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts.”

What overcame the algorithm was Janones’s “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel, which swelled into the millions as the second round approached. Voters were mobilized as “soldiers,” enthusiastically showing their support through storms of emojis, and they were then dispatched on “missions” to mobilize more people. This effort helped mobilize more than 10 million supporters for Lula in the second round.

Unlike Meta’s other platforms such as Instagram and Facebook, WhatsApp is less susceptible to algorithmic control. Human beings, not algorithms, share what they want to share. Lula’s campaign recalled the original promise of technology as a force to connect, inform, and mobilize. As India’s Cockroach movement and Serbia’s student movement have recently demonstrated, digital tools can be powerfully used to help people reclaim their voices offline.

Brazil’s presidential election underscores not only the power of people to bring change, but also the danger that digital chokepoints, created by the power of a single tech company, can shape who gets heard and who doesn’t. Brazil’s is not a solitary case of Meta’s platforms influencing the result of a major election, or of voters mounting a countereffort. Asked for comment, Meta referred to a statement claiming that any impediments were not deliberate, but rather the result of technical glitches, and perhaps negligence. They also highlighted a Nov. 11 statement from Brazil’s electoral authority that it found no “deliberate action to skew the election.”

But these claims fail to reckon with the company’s own announcements that it is discarding fact-checkers and loosening controls on recommended political content. What’s more, at the same time that Brazil’s Supreme Court was regulating social media platforms, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerburg said he was working with the Trump administration to “push back” against “censorship,” disdainfully referring to Latin American “secret courts” that can order companies to take down content in the name of moderation and integrity.

Whether or not this interference was intentional, what matters is that it was possible. A single company can now stand between citizens and the representatives that they should freely elect, controlling who gets to be seen or who can be heard. The concentration of such power in the hands of so few becomes a chokepoint that can threaten democracy, even democracy itself as a political system.

In response, it will not be enough to add layers of regulation or ask Meta and other tech companies to do better. When these avenues have been pursued, they encounter hard limits. In India, Meta’s moderation of hate speech has been scrutinized; in Myanmar and Sri Lanka, rights groups accused Facebook of inflaming crimes against the Rohingya and other Muslim minorities; in Ethiopia, its algorithms amplified ethnic violence.

Two years ago, the European Commission opened still ongoing formal proceedings against Meta’s platforms under the Digital Services Act, and in the United States in recent months, it was subject to billion-dollar penalties for failing to address child safety and other problems around content moderation. In every case, enforcement has been slow, inadequate, ineffective, or too opaque to track or evaluate.

The infrastructure needed to regulate Big Tech is politically compromised. In the United States, Brazil, and other large markets, the industry runs a vast policy operation that runs deep into legislatures, think tanks, and lobbyists. There is also a regulation trap: The same politicians who we count on to regulate technology are the ones who depend on the tech companies to campaign, communicate, and fundraise.

Brazil now has some of the strongest regulation against electoral falsehoods after its election four years ago was marred by disinformation, culminating in an attempted coup carried out by those who argued—without evidence—that the electronic voting system was compromised. Regulation has since been taken up by the courts, with the Supreme Court finding tech companies’ immunity from liability for third-party content unconstitutional and the Superior Electoral Court demanding platform compliance plans.

The Lula administration also empowered public authorities to investigate platforms, enforce compliance, and ensure transparency, including in the form of specific decrees preventing digital violence against women. Today, Brazil is a rare case of a country in a position to act before the election; most others do not have strong enough institutions.

Tech companies are powerful political actors that exert potentially decisive political influence, which can be wielded for ideological or partisan ends, as in Brazil, where engagement-maximizing algorithms reward polarizing, inflammatory, and populist content. The answer must be to challenge that power, which can be done through three proposals for reform.

        A photo illustration shows a cutout of Mark Zuckerberg on a blue background with X logos, a few Meta logos, and other scrawls and speech squiggles coming out of his mouth.
    
    
        
    
                Meta Looks for the X Factor            


    
    	What Mark Zuckerberg’s change of heart on misinformation means for the world.    	    


        
        Analysis    
        |
        
    
    Bhaskar Chakravorti


    


             
                    
                
    
            
        
        
        A man wearing a denim button-down shirt stands in a vehicle sunroof, raising one fist in the air and holding a megaphone in his other hand as he speaks before a crowd of people.
    
    
        
    
                Lula Defies Latin America’s Pro-Trump Wave            


    
    	Brazil’s left-wing president won a historic fourth term in office.    	        
            


        
        Dispatch    
        |
        
    
    Catherine Osborn

What Mark Zuckerberg’s change of heart on misinformation means for the world.

Brazil’s left-wing president won a historic fourth term in office.

The first step is to reduce society’s dependence on one or a few companies that have the capability to dominate the political or digital landscape. Here, competition law can be enforced, so that a single actor cannot sweep up a whole range of apps and close them off to rivals. Brazil’s public payment system Pix, for example, broke the dominance of private card systems by charging lower merchant fees and zero cost to customers. Because the central bank required all other banks to integrate Pix into their existing mobile apps, it also expanded digital financial inclusion for hundreds of millions.

Second, our societies’ digital architecture needs to be overhauled and constructed anew around open protocols. These are publicly documented technical standards that allow different services, applications, and devices to communicate using shared rules rather than through proprietary systems. Lula’s digital army demonstrated that they can be used or designed at scale for the public interest, in line with democratic principles.

The third is to build public options. Unregulated markets cannot be expected to produce fair outcomes that benefit everyone. Just as governments use their power as investors in the realms of defense, energy, semiconductors, and other infrastructure, they can also procure open-source software and open standards for their own services. Industrial policy and public funding can unlock alternatives to Big Tech companies. They can also help build open-weight and public interest AI models, which will provide access to local developers.

Elections show how high the stakes can be, but they represent only the most visible part of a wider struggle for truth, voice, and the fundamentals of human dignity. At its core, dignity, in the digital age, depends on people’s ability to have access to reliable knowledge, remain free from manipulation, and challenge decisions that shape their families. It demands regulations ensuring that everyone is treated equally; that they are protected from digital violence; and that they are free to live without being watched, profiled, and manipulated. None of these essential elements of human dignity can be left to the goodwill of a single corporation.

Equally worrying is that we are beginning to normalize the intense, aggressive digital messaging that bombards voters as part of electoral races—for better or for worse. Digital campaigning has a place to strengthen democratic participation and promote free and fair elections, but we are also seeing that it can cross the line in distorting, suppressing, and damaging the will of the people.

What Lula honored in his victory speech was what the algorithm could not block—namely, the resolve of millions to have their voices heard and their votes to be counted. Yet by virtue of their concentrated power and platforms through which public discourse occurs, tech companies will continue to be a chokepoint on democratic governance, so countries must learn not simply to regulate but more importantly to build an open, democratic digital architecture that works for all. Otherwise, these decisions will be made by someone else.

Binaifer Nowrojee is president of the Open Society Foundations, the world’s largest private funder working to promote human rights, equity, and justice.

In South Korea, the term byeorak-geoji means “sudden beggar.” In 2026, it has gained widespread popularity again. But its meaning is figurative. Rather than denoting sudden bankruptcy or losing one’s life savings in the stock market, the term describes a new and widespread sense of relative deprivation: The realization that a colleague or acquaintance just earned years of your salary in a single month on paper.

Such anxiety is driven by a booming domestic semiconductor industry that has a stranglehold on the global artificial intelligence industry’s supply bottleneck: memory chips. At the market’s peak this year, Samsung Electronics saw its market capitalization surge to a record high of $1.3 trillion, while SK Hynix has since reported a staggering 328 percent year-on-year increase in revenue in its latest third-quarter results. The boom had led many Koreans to believe that borrowing to leverage into these companies offered the quickest and perhaps the only route to profits large enough to pay off their mortgages and secure homes.

In South Korea, the term byeorak-geoji means “sudden beggar.” In 2026, it has gained widespread popularity again. But its meaning is figurative. Rather than denoting sudden bankruptcy or losing one’s life savings in the stock market, the term describes a new and widespread sense of relative deprivation: The realization that a colleague or acquaintance just earned years of your salary in a single month on paper.

Such anxiety is driven by a booming domestic semiconductor industry that has a stranglehold on the global artificial intelligence industry’s supply bottleneck: memory chips. At the market’s peak this year, Samsung Electronics saw its market capitalization surge to a record high of $1.3 trillion, while SK Hynix has since reported a staggering 328 percent year-on-year increase in revenue in its latest third-quarter results. The boom had led many Koreans to believe that borrowing to leverage into these companies offered the quickest and perhaps the only route to profits large enough to pay off their mortgages and secure homes.

If you were an engineer at one of these companies, you could cash out stock compensation boosted by stock rallies fueled by people’s borrowing, collect enormous bonuses, and secure a mortgage rate of 1.5 percent through company housing-loan programs, alongside support for your children’s tuition and retirement savings. Meanwhile, ordinary Koreans carrying debt and buying homes are left to shoulder the Bank of Korea’s high-interest-rate campaign, with back-to-back rate hikes in July and August, designed to curb inflation and financial risks amid the national semiconductor export boom.

Koreans are increasingly questioning that boom’s broader effect on ordinary households. Economists and scholars are voicing doubts. Even as semiconductors have accounted for nearly half of South Korea’s exports and pushed nominal GDP growth to a nearly 50-year high, the Korea Development Institute slashed its annual job growth forecast from 170,000 to 110,000 in its August report, and the OECD projected the country’s private consumption growth for the year at just 2.2 percent. And if the semiconductor boom eventually bursts, the overall effects for the Korean economy could be devastating.

If the global demand for memory falters, new capacity floods the market, or technological advances curb AI’s appetite for memory, the result would inevitably be a price fall. That would be welcome for buyers such as U.S. tech giants, AI powers, and behemoth enterprises such as Apple. Meanwhile, Samsung and SK Hynix would undoubtedly take a severe hit, although the massive net cash reserves they have amassed will shield them from the kind of bankruptcies that decimated debt-fueled South Korean chaebols during the late-1990s Asian financial crisis.

But while Korea’s memory industry sits on deep liquidity buffers, the true burden of debt in 2026 rests squarely on the shoulders of the country’s households. As an acutely capital-intensive industry, the semiconductor sector’s colossal profits are effectively locked away at the apex of the corporate hierarchy. This classic dual economy structure ensures that wealth fails to permeate adequately through trickle-down effects to the small- and medium-sized enterprises and the service sector, which account for the absolute majority of national employment.

Meanwhile, the South Korean populace has been left to bear the brunt of emerging macroeconomic overheating and inflation. According to the Bank of Korea, household credit breached 2,000 trillion won ($1.49 trillion) in June, and it had already stood at 88.6 percent of GDP at the end of 2025. The onerous mortgage and credit interest burdens induced by the rate hikes are stifling private consumption.

What’s worse, South Korea suffers from one of the highest house price-to-income ratios globally, with ordinary citizens anchoring their massive debt to the real estate market, itself strained by property project-finance troubles. Yet the world’s lowest fertility rate, coupled with rapid demographic aging, leaves a shrinking young generation to absorb these real estate assets, eroding the foundations of domestic demand. And AI, of course, cannot resolve the low fertility rate.

The current prosperity carries the seeds of so-called Dutch disease, in which a booming export sector siphons capital and talent away from other industries and erodes their competitiveness. The result is a hollowing out of the foundations of the domestic economy.

Memory export figures act as a tarp draped over the nation’s roof, temporarily covering the reality of high inflation and weak private consumption. According to OECD projections, South Korea’s potential growth rate will be at a historic low of 1.52 percent in 2027, a figure even lower than the 2.52 percent recorded in 2023, before the memory boom. Fundamentally, South Korea’s 2026 growth is jobless growth. Beneath the tarp of an export boom, the ceiling of its domestic market is caving in while the foundation of its economy continues to erode.

Nowadays, another term is circulating widely among the South Korean populace: yeongkkul, which refers to “trading one’s soul to borrow.” Just as, amid the 19th-century cotton boom, Indian farmers famously surrendered their subsistence fields to chase cotton margins, modern South Koreans are seeking leverage of any kind to outrun the debt, inflation, and housing prices inflated by the memory boom.

China’s spy service bet on lust and arrogance, and Washington was slow to see the risk.

One 25-year-old student interviewed by a South Korean news website diverted a student loan meant for living into stocks. Then he added an emergency bank loan and his part-time earnings to pour about 22 million won borrowed money into leveraged stock-market funds. Another student, aged 24, used fivefold leverage to turn 20 million won saved during military service into nearly 300 million won, only for forced liquidations to wipe out his gains and eat into his original savings within weeks. But he planned to borrow again, still hoping one day to afford an apartment, marriage, and children.

In investing, people resort to excessive leverage because of a fear of missing out. In the context of South Korea’s post-pandemic K-shaped recovery, the anxiety runs deeper: It is a fear of failing to scale a calcified social ladder, of being discarded by the velocity of wealth redistribution. People see their hard work rewarded with a salary that must be saved in its entirety for more than 30 years, without spending a penny on living expenses, to afford to buy an apartment in Seoul. They see a future in which their bosses—whose assets have made them the major beneficiaries of the semiconductor boom—replace them with AI.

The result is not just a fear of missing out on gains, but of missing out on a normal life—a fear of falling behind. Koreans are incapable of outrunning omnipresent economic anxiety and existential dread. A constant sampling is on offer on the anonymous digital platform Blind, where it’s common to read comments such as: “In a society where class divisions are entrenched, the ladder to climb has collapsed”; or “you have to bet your life on leverage”; or “If we miss out on AI boom, is it already too late for us in this lifetime?”

Extreme economic structures are accompanied by extreme risks. Whether AI will transform the world, and whether Asia has overconcentrated its resources in it, are two distinct questions. Just as in Bombay amid the cotton boom of the mid-19th century, the macroeconomic buffers of South Korea’s single-engine semiconductor economy are wearing thin. If the solitary engine of memory stalls, its effects could compound the risks from household debt, real estate vulnerabilities, and demographic pressures to deluge the entire South Korean economy and its population.

The central question of the memory cycle is not about whether it will end, but when. On the optimistic side, if the global memory shortage persists beyond 2030, as projected by SK Hynix’s CEO, South Korea’s economy and its semiconductor companies will usher in a golden age, alleviating the government’s chronic deficit pressures.

Yet a meager trickle of prosperity coupled with persistent jobless growth could potentially spell even deeper despair for ordinary people. Waiting in vain for a trickle that may never come, the people would be left to languish in a continuing drought.

A delayed fallout could be worst of all for most Koreans. The future currently portends a household debt bubble, a weakened domestic demand buffer, and a demographic cliff—ingredients for an economic famine. A memory downturn would depress incomes and asset prices, forcing indebted households to cut spending; spending cuts would deepen a property market downturn and systemic financial distress, ensuring the protracted slump.

Like 1990s Japan, South Korea risks its own “lost decade.” History has demonstrated that for an economy overdependent on a monoculture, the longer that the prosperity overshadows the decay it breeds, the harder the prolonged landing. In boom and bust alike, ordinary Koreans pay the highest price.

Nero Huang is a Taiwanese British author and analyst. His writing covers diplomacy and economics across the Asia-Pacific.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.title: America Can Do Good—and Do Well
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.author: Andrew Natsios
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.text:
ANDREW NATSIOS was Administrator of the U.S. Agency for International Development and the President’s Special Envoy to Sudan during the George W. Bush administration. He is the author of Guns Are Not Enough: Foreign Aid in the National Interest, from which this essay is adapted.

The Strategic Logic of Foreign Aid

Among all the ruinous consequences of the so-called U.S. Department of Government Efficiency’s efforts to cut bureaucracy, none has been as profound as the destruction of the United States’ ability to deliver foreign aid. A comprehensive Lancet study shows that the U.S. Agency for International Development’s assistance prevented more than 90 million deaths between 2001 and 2021. Using a mortality model, Boston University epidemiologist Brooke Nichols has estimated that the 2025 dismantling of USAID contributed to more than 700,000 excess deaths over roughly a year. A study published in Science this May found that after USAID’s shutdown, places that had lost large amounts of the agency’s assistance experienced a marked uptick in armed clashes and riots. The development economists Marcella Nicolini and Fabio Sabatini, meanwhile, showed that economic activity in areas that formerly enjoyed substantial U.S. aid had dramatically declined.

No country can be a great power without a functioning foreign aid program. But today, the United States does not have one. After 90 percent of USAID’s programs were terminated and 90 percent of its staff members were laid off, Congress formally reappropriated most of the budgetary funding dedicated to U.S. foreign aid. But the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has not released all of this appropriated funding. More damaging still, USAID’s mechanisms for spending aid money have been dismantled. According to the Pew Research Center, annual U.S. foreign aid disbursements fell by $26 billion between the 2023–24 and 2024–25 fiscal years; $2.5 billion in appropriated funding designated for foreign aid went unspent by the end of the 2025–26 fiscal year.

Russell Vought, OMB’s director and a self-identified Christian nationalist, has stonewalled spending for programs related to supporting democracy and insisted that humanitarian grants can be sent only to two specific Christian nongovernmental organizations. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, announced that he wanted to end funding to USAID development contractors, universities, and local civil society organizations without understanding the downside of other options for aid dollars, such as budget support, which are far less accountable, uniquely American, and results-oriented.

Given the suffering created by the end of USAID, it is even more troubling that DOGE’s objectives to slash waste and boost transparency have not been realized. U.S. President Donald Trump’s 2025 “big beautiful bill” erased any modest savings won by DOGE’s cuts to foreign aid. And the decision to move USAID’s functions to the State Department, which has weak business systems and inadequate staff to manage aid programs, has thus far led to the transfer of $3.8 billion in U.S. foreign aid money to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and $15.9 billion directly into foreign governments’ treasuries through memorandums of understanding.

These governments often have limited capacity to spend the money wisely and produce results. In the past, USAID’s Office of the Inspector General has harshly criticized such options because it is nearly impossible to audit the transfers. Over 90 percent of the countries involved in these agreements score below 50 (out of 100) on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index, indicating serious systemic corruption. This may explain why State Department political appointees have kept the texts of these health agreements secret.

Clashing demands—that aid should relieve misery abroad, that it ought to serve U.S. military and diplomatic interests, and that it ought to yield rapid, visible, and quantifiable results—always complicated the enterprise. And over the course of 65 years since USAID’s 1961 founding, overregulation, a centralization of control over programs, and congressional meddling created a rigid straitjacket that made the United States less responsive to local governments and local needs. But what the current U.S. administration didn’t understand was that USAID’s bureaucracy, so often presented as an obstacle to effectiveness, was in fact an adaptation to manage these conflicts.

Simply abolishing that institutional architecture with no plan to replace it has only generated more confusion and waste. Meanwhile, China is racing to offer alternative sources of development financing, and Russia is seeking to expand its global influence through security partnerships. The United States cannot afford to let its foreign aid apparatus atrophy. It must redirect it, not reject aid.

Ever since USAID was created, the expectations that leaders in Washington had for foreign aid have conflicted with realities in the developing world, the way actual aid programs are managed, and the speed and nature of societal change. When I read through USAID’s 1960s-era archives to write my new book, I was struck that the demands early U.S. policymakers made of the institution were the same as those made today: policymakers wanted rapid, visible, and quantifiable results. Those demands were as unrealistic then as they are now. U.S. President John F. Kennedy hoped that poverty in Latin America would visibly recede within a couple of years of USAID’s creation, as he was understandably worried that the Cuban revolutionary leader Fidel Castro’s Marxist ideology was spreading across the region. Fourteen months after the organization’s inception, an article by Joseph Kraft in Harper’s Magazine reported that policymakers in Washington had already judged it a failure because it was not delivering “quick and visible results.” David Bell, USAID’s second administrator, recalled in 1965 that Kennedy had complained that the agency was “slow-moving, inefficient, and unresponsive to the President’s policy.”

But diplomacy and development operate on profoundly different time horizons. Nearly all foreign aid programs have diplomatic consequences, even if they aren’t designed to. When diplomatic goals become the main or only goals of an aid program, however—for instance, when U.S. aid kept the Congolese dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in power during the Cold War—good development often fails.

The United States began institutionalizing foreign aid after World War II through agencies and programs such as the Marshall Plan, which supported the postwar economic recovery of Western Europe, and the Point Four Program, a Truman administration initiative to promote development in poor countries to reduce their susceptibility to communism. All along, policymakers debated whether U.S. assistance programs should principally aim to save lives and reduce extreme poverty or to support U.S. foreign policy by countering the influence of hostile powers.

In fact, USAID ended up playing a key role in winning the Cold War. American assistance strengthened governments targeted for Soviet and Chinese communist subversion, particularly in Asia. After U.S. President Richard Nixon entered his second year in office, aid spending for agriculture was increased to 50 percent of USAID’s budget and was directed primarily toward Asia. According to multiple studies by development economists, the effort saved more than 245 million lives. The green revolution, implemented over decades in Pakistan, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea, and Taiwan (among other countries), helped produce large grain surpluses that fueled industrialization and economic growth and averted the kind of famines that historically produce coups or mass uprisings.

Throughout this era, however, Washington’s demands that aid accomplish diplomatic goals—and quickly and visibly—also undermined the most important elements of development programs: institution building and policy reform. Strong institutions separate wealthy countries from poor ones. The former have them in abundance, while the latter do not. Institution building and policy reform should be the focus of aid programs. But institution building and policy reform is difficult to measure, takes many years to implement successfully, and is not immediately visible. Instead, policymakers insisted that USAID do service delivery, producing valuable humanitarian programs that were ultimately unsustainable.

Most critical analyses of U.S. foreign aid conclude that USAID came to focus on process over substance, resulting in excessive bureaucracy. What these critiques overlook is what caused this obsessive focus on process. A web of federal regulatory and oversight agencies (what scholars call the counterbureaucracy) loosed on U.S. aid programs an army of federal auditors, accountants, regulators, compliance officers, and congressional staffers dedicated to reining in the bureaucracy and—supposedly—protecting taxpayers’ money. This onslaught slowed down USAID’s implementation of programs and created massive amounts of paperwork. It did not make aid programs more effective.

Historically, Congress ended up playing a particularly intrusive role in the management of U.S. foreign aid programs. USAID reported to 14 congressional committees, which often clashed, pulling USAID in different directions and slowing program implementation. (For example, the House and Senate agriculture committees, under the influence of the agriculture lobby, stonewalled efforts to reform food aid by insisting it be exported from the United States, while legislative appropriators and authorizers from foreign affairs committees strongly supported local purchase reform.) Congress also imposed intrusive earmarks—defined amounts allocated for specific programs, projects, or organizations. When countries asked for specific help, USAID often could not respond, because the glut of earmarks meant there was no discretionary money left.

Starting in the 1990s, the State Department attempted to exert more control over the USAID budget. A 1998 statute, for instance, made the USAID administrator report directly to the secretary of state. In January 2001, the State Department took control of USAID’s budget. That only led lawmakers—who often distrusted State—to add more earmarks. To protect U.S. foreign aid programs from an especially hostile Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman, Republican Senator Jesse Helms, the Clinton administration instructed each cabinet-level department to create its own aid programs that would fall outside that committee’s jurisdiction. For example, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention at the Department of Health and Human Services established regional offices around the world, the Environmental Protection Agency developed solar energy projects in poor countries, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency signed agreements with more than 28 developing countries to assist in disaster management. USAID was already running programs such as these, yielding overlapping mandates which added to the incoherence of U.S. foreign aid.

When I became USAID administrator in 2001, I discovered a foreign aid program whose funds were straitjacketed by nearly 250 congressional earmarks, a sum exceeding USAID’s total appropriation. At the time, Ethiopia was one of the most severely food insecure countries in the world. Yet in 2007 only 1.5 percent of USAID’s budget was devoted to agricultural development, 1.5 percent to economic growth, and 1.5 percent to governance reform; Congressional earmarks made it impossible to fund these programs to match the Ethiopian government’s request.

Despite all these impediments, foreign aid remained a critical component of U.S. foreign policy. The Department of Defense had a particularly productive partnership with USAID, recognizing that foreign aid could be as important as force in incentivizing insurgents to make peace. The effects of USAID projects in Afghanistan were profound but took shape over long time horizons neither the State Department nor the Defense Department had any patience for. (USAID’s Afghanistan media-development program, for instance, was a great success, as documented in a Harvard Kennedy School study by The New York Times’s David Rohde.) Major academic studies have shown that in Iraq, community development projects undertaken by USAID’s Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) employed large numbers of young men who might otherwise have been recruited into militias, reducing U.S. military casualties in the provinces with the highest levels of violence. In 2004, Army General Peter Chiarelli called the USAID officer managing the program, Kirk Day, a “hero” for saving his soldiers’ lives.

The DOGE team abolished OTI last year, along with innumerable other programs that alleviated suffering globally and enhanced U.S. soft power. When Congress restored many cuts to foreign aid, it did not reinstate USAID’s veteran staff, historical archives, business systems, field presence, or implementing partner networks of universities, international nongovernmental organizations, local civil society groups, and international development contractors. The transfer of programs to the Department of State only exacerbated the contradictions that have long bedeviled U.S foreign aid. Few secretaries of state (or secretaries of defense) have any development background, experience, or technical knowledge, and paradoxically, when aid is seen simply as a tool of diplomacy or defense rather than an end in itself, the diplomatic good it can do is compromised.

Dismantling USAID did not abolish the need for technically knowledgeable staff and bureaucratic systems. In May 2025, the State Department inspector general issued an intimidating report detailing what the department will have to do to competently manage foreign aid programs, a list of demands it will have difficulty meeting. And in September this year, the Government Accountability Office issued a highly critical audit of the State Department’s inadequate management of foreign aid programs, finding that the department lacked documented standards for deciding which aid programs to terminate, could not produce data on its own staffing, and maintained incomplete or incorrect records on grants and agreements. This result was unsurprising, given that the State Department is a diplomatic policy institution, not a program management agency. Merging USAID into the State Department makes as much sense as merging Microsoft with ExxonMobil, given the disparate time horizons on which the two institutions operate and their differences in mission statements and business systems.

The State Department has pursued alternative arrangements for distributing aid that require less direct management. For example, it has negotiated 36 memorandums of understanding with governments in developing countries to transfer U.S. aid funds to their health ministries, so they can spend the program money themselves. But in return for these transfers, Washington has asked these countries to send private health-care data to the U.S. government, accept undocumented immigrants the U.S. government deports, and, in some cases, give U.S. mining companies access to their rare-earth minerals. Because health programs save lives, they should be distributed based on need, not on parochial, transactional American demands.

Many countries have understandably resisted this kind of bargain. USAID had technical staff that could assess a foreign government’s ability to manage funds responsibly. In practice, it ran a detailed and thorough vetting of nearly every aspect of the governments it partnered with. The State Department, by contrast, only vets according to the legal minimum and treats foreign governments as it treats as international or U.S.-based NGOs. State’s approach will increase the risk that funds are stolen by local government ministries that lack the control systems needed to ensure accountability.

The very public and grossly inaccurate attacks on USAID’s integrity and management by Trump and DOGE’s erstwhile leader, Elon Musk, have damaged the agency’s reputation so extensively that simply resurrecting it will be difficult. But Washington’s aid apparatus also needs more coherent organization than it was afforded in the past. In his celebrated work Bureaucracy, on which my book is structured, the political scientist James Q. Wilson argues that strong U.S. departments or agencies need “relative autonomy”: clearly defined missions they do not substantially share with other agencies. By this logic, if the United States wants a high-functioning, coherent foreign aid program, it must first consolidate all aid functions within one department.

Abolishing field offices (called USAID missions) also made administering aid programs much more difficult, blunted true accountability and U.S. influence in the developing world, and reduced the visibility of U.S. aid programs. These country missions must be reestablished, reporting to the local U.S. ambassador. In Washington, Congress should create a new cabinet-level department reporting to the president that manages all the government’s aid programs, which would make it possible to trim staff, streamline program implementation, and avoid policy incoherence. At least 80 percent of this new department’s staff should be deployed abroad, not in Washington. The United States will always need to be able to launch aid programs with an expressly diplomatic purpose and short time horizon, and the State Department should determine these projects and their spending levels. But it should leave the programs’ management up to the new aid department—as it did during the Cold War, when USAID was independent of State.

This new department should also report to fewer congressional committees—a Foreign Affairs authorizing committee and an appropriations subcommittee in each legislative body. The practice of burdening the United States’ foreign aid budget with domestically appealing earmarks—which prevents aid from responding to foreign countries’ own needs—must be reduced.

In the past, the overregulation and bureaucratization of foreign aid driven by the demands of the counterbureaucracy prioritized process over programs and compliance over developmental outcomes. The new aid department must be given regulatory relief. One way to do that is for Congress to set up charter missions, similar to charter schools, as an experiment to see whether accountability deteriorates. These deregulated charter missions would be free from burdensome reporting requirements the counterbureaucracy demands. In recent years, the World Bank has tried a similar approach and found that it improved its programs’ effectiveness without increasing fraud.

The status quo for U.S. foreign aid cannot last. But Washington cannot revert to the old status quo, which generated the kind of dissatisfactions among policymakers that helped lead to its dismantling. Now is the time to bring more coherence to U.S. foreign aid programs with these reforms, if the new Democratic Congress and future administrations show a forward-looking vision.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/economics.title: The Paradox of Dollar Dominance
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/economics.author: Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad, Tony Zhang
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/economics.text:
GORDON LIAO is Chief Economist at Circle.

ESWAR PRASAD is a Professor at Cornell University, a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, and the author of The Doom Loop: Why the World Economic Order Is Spiraling Into Disorder.

TONY ZHANG is an Associate Professor at Arizona State University.

This article is based on a paper the authors prepared for the August 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium.

How Technology Is—and Isn’t—Changing the Global Economy

Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad, and Tony Zhang

It is no secret that much of the world is eager to escape from the clutches of the dollar-dominated global financial system. For over a century, that system has given the United States enormous financial clout, which it has wielded in applying financial sanctions against its adversaries and, in recent decades, to borrow money to fund its budget and trade deficits. For decades, foreign governments have tried to weaken the dollar’s grip, but they have had little success in establishing their currencies as a legitimate alternative.

Now, a new force has emerged that could shake things up: technology. Financial innovations, especially in digital currencies and electronic payment systems, could finally give other currencies a better chance of competing with the dollar. These innovations are making it easier and cheaper to exchange currencies directly for one another rather than using the dollar as an intermediary currency.

But for all the new opportunities these innovations create for currency exchange, reduced frictions in global transactions might only reinforce the dollar’s dominance. Even if costs decrease for using dollar alternatives, foreign investors will not capitalize on them if those countries’ financial markets remain unsteady and their institutions weak. As U.S. government debt soars, the country’s rule of law erodes, and the Federal Reserve’s independence comes into question, the dollar’s dominance may seem uncertain. But the dollar could remain supreme by default.

Continued dollar dominance could lead to further global economic turmoil, as the United States antagonizes its trading partners and persists with undisciplined policies that result in large budget deficits and trade deficits. There is a chance that the dollar, too, loses the trust of foreign investors—a prospect of comeuppance that would no doubt be received with glee in many capitals. But governments should be careful what they wish for. A world bereft of a reliable currency of last resort at times of global financial panic could be even more unstable than one dominated by Washington.
