The U.S. dollar should be losing its dominance in global finance for a host of reasons. First is the country’s penchant for weaponizing its currency. Across administrations, Washington has imposed financial sanctions on rivals, such as Iran and Russia, cutting off their access to dollar transactions and thereby kneecapping their foreign trade. The economies of U.S. allies sometimes get tangled up in these sanctions, too, when the U.S. government threatens to use secondary sanctions to cut off their banks and corporations from access to dollars in order to deter third parties from transacting with the sanctioned countries. In 2014, for instance, U.S. authorities penalized the French bank BNP Paribas for processing dollar payments on behalf of clients in Cuba, Iran, and Sudan. The French government protested the fine to no avail. In light of such heavy-handed behavior, government officials and central bankers outside the United States have hardly been shy about their intentions to reduce their dollar dependence.

Washington’s broader policy choices, especially the lack of fiscal discipline, should also be undermining confidence in American financial markets. U.S. federal government debt now exceeds $40 trillion, nearly 125 percent of the country’s annual GDP, and there are scant signs that Washington is trying to rein it in. Such high debt levels usually lead to some combination of high inflation, soaring interest expenditures, and currency depreciation. The Trump administration’s hostile approach to international trade, including with close allies, is also causing governments to consider “de-risking” their economic ties to the United States. President Donald Trump’s open attacks on the independence of the Federal Reserve and weakening of checks and balances are eroding the pillars of the U.S. institutional system that underlies foreign investors’ trust in the dollar.

And indeed, there are some signs of the dollar’s decline. The currency’s share of foreign exchange reserves held by foreign central banks has fallen from 71 percent in 2000 to 57 percent today. Yields on U.S. Treasury securities—the asset long seen as the ultimate safe haven for investors during financial turmoil—have risen, meaning investors are demanding a higher return for lending to the U.S. government. In October, the yield on ten-year Treasury notes hit 5.3 percent, the highest level since 2002.

In most other dimensions, however, the dollar looks as dominant as ever. Sixty percent of cross-border transactions are denominated in dollars when excluding the eurozone, which is defined by the common use of the euro, and that number has only gone up in recent years. The euro’s share of cross-border payments outside the eurozone now stands at about 13 percent, and the renminbi’s is less than three percent. The dollar remains preeminent in most other measures of a currency’s international usage, too, including its share of trading activity in foreign exchange markets and denomination of international debt securities, which corporations use to raise funds in global capital markets.

In short, no serious rivals to the dollar have emerged. The reason is simple: other major currencies look even shakier than the dollar. Traditional reserve currencies such as the euro, the yen, and the pound sterling have been undermined by their countries’ weak economies and political instability. Although currencies such as the Australian and Canadian dollars, the Swedish krona, and the Swiss franc have filled in some of the gap, each of these is too small to be consequential in global finance. The dollar’s most discussed putative rival, the renminbi, has also faded. Beijing has done little to alleviate the Chinese economy’s deep-rooted problems, including a prolonged property market slump, high levels of local government debt, and tight government control over the economy and financial markets. Moreover, the Chinese government has been unwilling to allow for the free flow of money across its borders or for market forces to determine its currency’s exchange rate. The renminbi has, in turn, failed to garner greater international use. The result is a second tier of currencies that is increasingly fragmented, with none able to pose any real challenge to the reigning currency hegemon.

In the era of modern financial markets, one of the main purposes of an international currency has been to facilitate indirect transactions among different currencies. It has long been easier and cheaper for a Chinese importer of Brazilian iron ore to exchange renminbi for dollars and pay for the ore in dollars and for the Brazilian exporter to then convert those dollars into Brazilian reais. This is because cross-border payments have long been dominated by a dollar-based global banking network, making dollars the most plentiful currency to conduct payments with. But in recent years, digital technologies have created cheaper and quicker pathways for moving money across borders.

One critical innovation has been the tokenization of money and financial assets, which has been facilitated by technology called blockchain. Blockchain, essentially a public digital ledger that is managed by a computer algorithm rather than by a single bank or clearinghouse, offers a platform for tokenized assets to trade. It does not matter which country the parties are located in, as long as they have Internet access. In the last few years, tokenization has expanded to include not just cash but also financial assets such as government bonds, equities, and mutual funds.

In theory, these changes have the potential to reshuffle the international currency order. Over the past few years, countries such as Brazil, China, India, and Russia have been conducting more trade in their own currencies by building their own cross-border payment networks and linking them to one another, in an effort to reduce their reliance on the dollar. The quantity of these transactions is still modest, because the currencies have limited use outside their countries, and it is still easier and cheaper to transact in a well-recognized and widely accepted currency such as the dollar. But as the countries’ payment systems and financial markets develop further, that number could increase dramatically, altering the currency landscape. Blockchain-based financial innovations could add momentum.

Cross-border investment could become much easier, too. Currently, investing in foreign securities involves going through brokers and other middlemen who demand hefty fees and take days to process transactions. But the tokenization of bonds and equities has expanded investors’ access to a broader swath of international financial assets, even in emerging-market and developing economies, where financial markets tend to be small, thinly traded, and not well connected to global trading networks. In the same way, it has expanded the access of entrepreneurs and small businesses to global pools of capital previously out of their reach, which could particularly help businesses in countries with underdeveloped financial markets. Bank deposits are likely to be available in tokenized form soon, too, which will make it easier to conduct transactions through more traditional payment channels.

But the spread of tokenization might strengthen the dollar’s dominance rather than weaken it. The example of stablecoins illustrates this paradox. Whereas cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin are created and distributed by a computer algorithm, meaning they have nothing anchoring their value, the value of a stablecoin is typically pegged to an official currency. This value is stable because it is backed one to one by stores of safe and liquid assets—usually government bonds, bank deposits, and cash. Those assets are usually denominated in the dollar. More than $250 billion in stablecoins is now in circulation, and over 99 percent of that value is tied to the dollar. As long as the dollar remains preeminent, investors will have little incentive to back stablecoins with any other currency.

Dollar-denominated stablecoins are a boon for the United States. By solidifying the dollar’s central position in international payments, rising demand for dollar-backed stablecoins also indirectly fuels demand for Treasury securities, lowering the yields the U.S. government has to offer investors to buy those securities and making it easier to fund U.S. budget deficits. Other payment innovations could make it even cheaper to use the dollar for cross-border transactions, minimizing the relative advantage that such innovations provide other currencies. Financial innovations built on new technologies cannot by themselves make up for other currencies’ existing weaknesses—namely, the weak economies and institutions that back them up.

There is another major shift underway in the global economy that favors the dollar’s fortunes and that financial innovations are likely only to reinforce. In the first two decades of this century, central banks—particularly those of large emerging-market economies such as China and India—acquired vast troves of foreign assets denominated in hard currencies such as the euro, pound sterling, Japanese yen, and, most of all, the dollar to increase their foreign exchange reserves. These reserves helped those central banks cope with volatility in capital flows and exchange rates, which is a recurring hazard for countries that fall in and out of favor with foreign investors—often because of factors beyond their control, such as changes in U.S. interest rates. But in the last few years, central banks have stopped adding to their reserve stockpiles or have begun diversifying into other assets, such as gold, because they are reluctant to increase their investments in a country with fickle economic and geopolitical policies. In 2010, foreign central banks accounted for 70 percent of U.S. Treasuries held by foreign investors, a share that has dropped to about 40 percent as demand has leveled off. The retreat of these once reliable sources of demand threatens Washington’s ability to borrow cheaply.

Luckily for the United States, there is an alternative force that is more than making up for this loss in demand. As the costs to cross-border asset trade fall because of financial innovations, private investors from both advanced and emerging-market countries are increasing their foreign investments in search of higher returns and to diversify their portfolios. And they are flocking to dollar assets, from Treasuries to corporate bonds to equities, because U.S. financial markets offer an unmatched combination of good returns, low trading costs, and legal protections. In the present decade, net inflows of financial capital into the United States have been positive for practically every quarter. Despite chatter about de-risking and diversification since Trump’s election, these inflows have only ramped up in recent years.

Greater financial innovation will intensify rather than reverse these trends, delivering yet another blow to countries seeking to strengthen their currencies and counter dollar weaponization. These trends may hurt small and institutionally weak countries most of all. Those around the world who have long trusted the dollar more than their own currencies now have easier access to it—and they are likely to use it. Increased use of dollar-backed payment systems and investments in dollar assets could cause those countries to cede their monetary sovereignty, weakening their central banks’ ability to steer domestic interest rates and inflation. This phenomenon of “dollarization” has long been rampant in parts of Latin America, which have suffered repeated bouts of high inflation and which, through trade, tourism, and remittances from emigrants, have ready access to dollar cash. Financial innovation could also spread that phenomenon to other corners of the developing world, concentrating even more of the world’s savings—and its financial risks—in a single currency managed by a single central bank.

In theory, the best, most stable international monetary system would be truly multipolar, with no single currency in a position of dominance but with several major currencies—each backed by deep financial markets, sound economic policies, and trustworthy institutions—anchoring international trade and finance. In the period before World War I, the British pound sterling, the French franc, and the German mark all denominated transactions and served as reserve currencies. When trouble struck, although sporadically, the countries’ central banks supported one another, helping to stave off broader financial panic. Renewed currency competition would force the competing governments, including the United States, to adopt responsible policies to avoid their currencies being shunned by investors. But given the economic and institutional malaise plaguing China, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the eurozone, such an outcome seems unlikely.

If the dollar loses its position of privilege and no single currency is able to replace it, the global currency system will become even more fragmented than it is now. Such a scenario could unfold if U.S. debt grew so large that investors began doubting its value and dumped it, if additional sanctions and tariffs drove countries to shun the dollar despite the costs, or if the Fed’s independence were seriously compromised, leading to a surge in inflation and a plunge in the dollar’s value. As things stand, if the dollar lost its position of privilege, it would be replaced not by a handful of strong currencies but by a number of weak ones, none backed by sufficiently robust financial markets or a central bank able and willing to serve as the world’s lender of last resort during a crisis.

If the global economic system has no currency to anchor global investors’ trust, stress in financial markets could spiral into unstoppable turmoil. During the global financial crisis of 2008–9, for example, the Fed pumped a huge number of dollars into U.S. and international financial markets to prop up banks and corporations around the world that desperately needed dollars to meet their debt obligations and reinforce their balance sheets. Even though the United States had been the epicenter of the crisis, trust in the Fed helped prevent a terrible situation from becoming even worse. Investors who were anxious about the safety of their assets piled into Treasuries, an investment they trusted would be returned.

Greater dollar dominance, then, is the most likely scenario for the future. The danger of this outcome is that the United States will have even less incentive than before to be more fiscally responsible. If foreign investors remain eager to invest in U.S. financial markets, Washington will have little reason to reduce its budget and trade deficits. Fed policies, including interest rate changes, could cause whiplash effects for other countries. In 2013, for example, the mere prospect of the Fed reducing measures to keep U.S. interest rates low sent currencies in Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey tumbling because investors around the world began anticipating higher returns on U.S. assets and pulled their money out of those countries’ stocks and bonds. As capital flows in and out of markets in response to the Fed’s actions rather than in response to their own monetary policy, other countries could be left bereft of policy tools to stabilize their economies and financial markets in such a scenario. Emerging-market and developing economies, which have shallow financial markets and rely heavily on foreign borrowing, often in dollars, are especially vulnerable to volatile capital flows and exchange rates. In a world of greater dollar dominance, those countries could face more frequent currency crises, capital flight, and debt distress.

As disconcerting as the dollar’s continued preeminence might seem, however, the world needs a currency it can trust. As threats to international financial stability accelerate, financial markets can ill afford to be left adrift. One way or another, the world will have to learn to live with currency disorder, and the dollar, at least for now, is the least bad option.

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/spo.title: ICRC: We are currently classifying the highest number of armed conflicts since the Second World War
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/spo.author: François PICARD
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/spo.text:
War may be an enduring feature of human history, but its brutality is neither inevitable nor beyond restraint. That distinction lies at the heart of a stark warning from Spoljaric who argues that the international rules established to protect civilians are being progressively weakened amid proliferating armed conflicts, technological transformations and the retreat of diplomacy.

From Gaza and Ukraine to Sudan and Yemen, Spoljaric describes an increasingly permissive interpretation of international humanitarian law, in which civilian infrastructure is attacked, populations are displaced and human suffering becomes an instrument of military strategy. “So humans are instrumentalized in the pursuit of military objectives,” she says

The proliferation of drones and artificial intelligence adds another troubling dimension. Technologies once presented as instruments of greater military precision have not, she argues, delivered the promised protection for civilians. Instead, they risk further diminishing the possibility of escaping violence, while the prospect of autonomous weapons targeting human beings raises urgent legal and ethical questions.

But Spoljaric's deepest concern extends beyond the battlefield. As conflicts increasingly cross borders and humanitarian needs overwhelm available resources, diplomacy has taken a back seat to might makes right. Her message is also political: humanitarian assistance cannot substitute for the prevention of war, and the protection of civilians cannot depend on goodwill alone.

The responsibility, she insists, belongs to governments and citizens alike. “As a citizen, demand that your government prioritise the rules of war,” she urges, warning that “wars are coming to your doorstep nowadays much, much faster than in previous years.”

She argues that human suffering is an instrument of military strategy. The proliferation of drones and artificial intelligence adds another troubling dimension.

"Green skills are skills that make economic activities more sustainable, typically either by conserving natural resources or by taking out pollution," explains Sue Duke, LinkedIn's Managing Director for EMEA and LATAM. "Operational efficiency is the fastest-growing green skill this year. That's because not only are many workers applying it in core green jobs, but a whole host of workers are applying it in traditional jobs, not typically considered green jobs – everything from construction workers to sales assistants to financial professionals."

Duke says that Gen Z is enthusiastic about tackling climate change in the workplace. "There is huge, huge hunger amongst younger workers to get involved and work in this space. Fully six in ten are telling us that they want to work in a job that helps combat climate change." She urges businesses and governments to "ensure that we're putting training programmes in place for young workers, so they can get these green skills and activate their role in the transition".

Duke says the emergence of energy-intensive artificial intelligence is transforming the skills that workers need to do their jobs. "It's creating huge demand for workers with green skills in the AI industry itself, as organisations seek to reduce the impact of data centre buildouts and training models (...) Secondly, we are seeing an enormous opportunity emerging with this technology, as green workers start using AI to combat climate change."

Also in the programme, FRANCE 24's Charles Pellegrin speaks to Jacob Nathan, founder and CEO of Epoch Biodesign. Nathan says recycling textiles is not just about sustainability, but makes good business sense. "Circularity is the way forward. To be clear, this is no niche industry, this is the future of the materials industry."

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner left the Kremlin following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on ending the Ukraine war, an AFP correspondent reported.

The pair are set to travel straight to Dublin for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who is attending a European summit in the Irish capital.

Leaders from more than 40 European countries have gathered in Dublin for a summit focused on the continent’s security amid a new US-backed effort to revive talks on ending the Russia-Ukraine war.

The meeting of the European Political Community brought together heads of state and government from European countries and the UK, as well as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

Russian President Vladimir Putin on reaffirmed Moscow's opposition to allowing Western troops in Ukraine as part of any potential post-war peacekeeping solution – a key demand from Kyiv in any deal to end the fighting.

Moscow would see any foreign troops deployed in the country as a "legitimate target", Putin told US envoys in Moscow, adding their deployment would mean "the continuation of war".

President Vladimir ​Putin on Thursday told ​US envoys that Russia was proposing a joint

Russian-Ukrainian humanitarian ​mission ‌to the ⁠city of Kostiantynivka in eastern ‌Ukraine, the Interfax news agency reported.

Putin ⁠was cited as saying that the mission ​could be modelled on ‌a similar initiative that allowed residents to ‌leave the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky ​in southeastern Ukraine at the end of last month and ​for aid to ​be brought in ​for those who chose to remain.

Russia ​needed 5 days to clear the area near Kostiantynivka of mines, Putin ⁠was cited as saying.

"We ​hope ​that, following ​the ‌negotiations ⁠with ‌Putin, ⁠it will ​be ‌possible to ‌announce ​a new round ​of ​trilateral ​talks ​in which Europeans ⁠would ⁠take ​part," said US envoy Witkoff.

Russia ​needed 5 days to clear the area near Kostiantynivka of mines, Putin ⁠was cited as saying.

EU chief Antonio Costa said Thursday the coming days will be a crucial test of Russia's willingness to end the Ukraine war, as President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoys in Moscow.

"So far, what we have seen is that Russia is focused on escalation and attacks on Ukrainian civilians. That must change for peace to be possible," The EU council president told a gathering of European leaders in Dublin. "The next week will be a decisive test for Russian willingness to stop this war."

⁠Russia ​struck ​a facility of Ukraine's ​state ‌gas ⁠and ‌oil company Naftogaz ⁠with jet-powered drones ​overnight, the ‌company said.

The ‌attack ​caused a major fire and ​damaged ​equipment, ​it added in ​the statement.

⁠Ukraine is ​seeking details ​on limitations for Starlink's military version Starshield communication service ​from ‌the ⁠US, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said ‌on Thursday, adding that ⁠the limitations significantly disrupt Ukraine's air ​defences.

"So far we ‌know very little. But some things ‌are already clear: if ​someone in America is making decisions that basically treat ​Ukrainian territory ​as if it ​is not Ukrainian, then ​it tells us where things are going," he said, addressing ⁠European leaders in Dublin.

Zelensky warned Europe Thursday to be wary of discussions between the United States and Russia about a new security framework for the continent.

"We are waiting for more details, and Europe needs to pay close attention," Zelensky told European leaders at a summit in Dublin.

Finland's ​government ​said on Thursday ​it ‌would ⁠restrict ‌Russian ⁠athletes from ​entering ‌the country, ‌including ​those competing under ​neutral ​status.

Ukraine's President ​Volodymyr Zelensky said that ​he would meet US peace negotiators later on Thursday ​after ‌their ⁠visit to Moscow.

Addressing the ‌European Political Community summit ⁠in Dublin, Zelensky said that Kyiv found the ​US approach ‌of discussing a new security order with Russia "a ‌bit strange".

"Because for 30 ​years after the Soviet Union collapsed, Europe treated Russia ​well, and Europe ​tried to have ​as much trade as possible, ​as much cooperation as possible, and as good relations as possible ⁠with Russia," Zelensky said.

Russia fired waves of explosive drones at the Ukrainian capital throughout Thursday.

The attacks killed one woman and wounded several more, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on social media.

An AFP reporter saw a residential building in flames, as rescue workers pulled the body from the rubble.

A second round of explosions rang out over the capital a few hours later, and officials said a major road was hit.

NATO Secretary-General ​Mark Rutte said ​on Thursday there had been positive developments during the ​Ukraine-Russia ‌peace ⁠talks in Abu Dhabi ‌but warned that it remained ⁠unclear whether Russia was genuinely willing ​to engage in ‌negotiations to end the war in ‌Ukraine.

"It all depends on ​the Russians, whether they are willing to play ball," ​Rutte said, ​adding that Ukraine ​must be kept as strong ​as possible as negotiations with Russia continue.

• Kyiv and Moscow agreed to a large-scale prisoner exchange as the final day of peace talks in Abu Dhabi came to an end, though neither side gave a concrete figure.

• NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the US-mediated Ukraine-Russia peace talks showed that the US, Ukraine and Europe were "aligned and united".

• A ​Russian strike ​on a busy market in Ukraine's southern ​Odesa ‌region killed three ‌people and injured ⁠11 others, the regional governor ​said.

https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.title: Two French guards collapse as Macron welcomes Slovak president
https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.author: https://www.facebook.com/FRANCE24.English
https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.text:
As is customary for the arrival of foreign heads of state, the Republican Guards formed an honour guard in full ceremonial dress with sabres for the arrival of Slovak President Peter Pellegrini late Wednesday.

One guard can be seen swaying before crashing to the ground, falling against a pillar at the Elysee Palace as his ceremonial sword clattered to the ground.

Aides and Macron immediately rushed towards the stricken guard, images from an AFP photographer showed. Le Parisien daily said that a second guard collapsed off camera, with Macron looking concerned and then hurriedly welcoming his Slovak counterpart.

A French presidential source, who asked not to be named, told AFP that both guards had suffered from "fainting attacks" and no other comment would be made.

"Both of them were swiftly taken care of and everything is fine," added the source.

The Republican Guard, part of the French gendarmerie, are responsible for guards of honour in France which often involve standing for long periods in heavy clothing while holding their sword upwards vertically.

Dozens of emergency crews were sent to the scene in the Logan Circle neighbourhood. (AP: Tom Brenner)

Five people have been shot in a central Washington DC neighbourhood and authorities are trying to capture the gunman.

Police have surrounded an apartment building in the area. The gunman is believed to be barricaded inside, according to local media, citing police sources.

Witnesses said the shooting incident started about 8am, local time, in the Vida gym on 15th St, near Logan Circle.

The area is about 1.5 kilometres north of the White House.

Gym-goers ran into a nearby bagel shop to shelter, witnesses told local media.

The conditions of the victims are unknown.

Several apartment buildings in the area have been placed in lockdown.

Dozens of police vehicles are at the scene, which has been cordoned off.

Members of the National Guard, who have been present in Washington DC as part of a crime crackdown ordered by US President Donald Trump, are also at the scene.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says reduced access to Starshield means Ukrainian interceptors could not reach sufficient speed to down Russian jet-powered drones. (Reuters: Cathal McNaughton)

Ukraine's military has recorded significant disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications service.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says systemic restrictions were affecting Ukraine's frontline.

It comes as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow for talks aimed at ending the conflict.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukrainian military units recorded significant disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications service for several days, affecting the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.

Starshield is the military version of Elon Musk's SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications service.

In a post on Telegram, Mr Zelenskyy said that systemic restrictions were limiting the speed at which Starshield could be used to 161 kph.

Ukrainian military units have recorded significant disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications service, affecting the entire front line. (Reuters: Inna Varenytsia)

As a result of the restrictions, Ukrainian interceptors could not reach sufficient speed to down Russian jet-powered drones, with some hits already occurring, Mr Zelenskyy said.

"This helps Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes on Ukraine," he said, adding that Ukraine was trying to clarify the reasons for the restriction with the US side.

In mid-October, Ukrainian officials said SpaceX had abruptly capped the speed of Starlink and Starshield, cutting off drones and other equipment moving faster than about 160 kph amid tensions with the Trump administration over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Service was restored on October 24.

Mr Zelenskyy's comments came as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow for talks aimed at ending the conflict.

A Ukrainian official said there was no mention of the disruptions during US-brokered talks earlier this week in Abu Dhabi and it was unclear who had made the decision.

Ukraine says people will die as a result of throttled Starlink services in the country. Here's how its armed forces rely on the crucial service.

Ukraine has carried out a series of strikes against Russian refineries and energy installations in recent weeks, as Moscow has continued to pummel Ukrainian electricity infrastructure and cities with drones and missiles.

"So far we know very little," Mr Zelenskyy said, addressing European leaders in Dublin.

"But some things are already clear: if someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then it tells us where things are going."

The European Commission will present a new sanctions package against Russia and proposals on Ukraine-related financial measures before the next European Council, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday.

The next European Council is a special summit on November 26-27.

Russia's FSB snatched US journalist Evan Gershkovich in a Yekaterinburg restaurant. What followed was life in a Russian jail cell and being part of a prisoner swap for an assassin.

The package will be the EU's 22nd against Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago.

Among the measures, the package is expected to include new restrictions on banks, cryptocurrencies and crypto platforms, and measures to close circumvention loopholes through third countries, EU diplomats said.

The package may also include a ban on Belarusian and Russian athletes competing in international meets in the EU, the diplomats said.

A member of the Russian military was killed after the car he was driving was blown up in St Petersburg, investigators said, in what appeared to be the latest in a series of targeted killings that Russia has blamed on Ukraine.

Video showed that military police had sealed off the area in the Pushkinsky District of the city as investigators and forensic scientists worked at the scene.

Following two days of US-mediated talks, Ukraine and Russia have agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war.

A bomb-damaged dark blue SUV stood on a road littered with blast debris next to what looked like an empty passenger bus, which appeared to have also suffered damage.

Russia has blamed Ukraine for previous assassinations of senior military officials and people linked to Moscow's war effort.

Ukrainian sources have claimed responsibility in some cases, while denying others.

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine on Thursday.

Another serviceman was killed in a car explosion in the same district of Russia's second largest city on August 27.

Other car bomb attacks have occurred in Moscow and Crimea, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014, in recent months.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/n.title: Breaking: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang quits after affair with alleged Chinese spy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

NVIDIA founder Jensen Huang has stepped down from his role as the company's CEO. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Jensen Huang, the co-founder of global artificial intelligence giant Nvidia, has resigned as chief executive effective immediately.

The news comes days after the California-based company launched an independent investigation following Mr Huang's acknowledgement that he had an affair with a Chinese business associate.

According to The New York Times, US intelligence determined that the woman — former Megaspeed managing director Alice Huang — was gathering information for China.

Nvidia's board of directors held an emergency meeting that reportedly continued into the early hours of Thursday morning, local time.

Following the meeting, the company released a statement saying Mr Huang had resigned as president, chief executive officer and as a member of the board.

Colette Kress will serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer for NVIDIA. (Nvidia via Reuters)

The company's Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who has worked for NVIDIA since 2013, will serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent replacement is found.

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Ms Kress said in a statement.

The company thanked Mr Huang for his "immeasurable contributions" to not only NVIDIA but the wider industry.

NVIDIA's new board chair Harvey Jones said he expected "the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption".

Shares of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world, plunged 13 per cent following the announcement.

Jensen Huang has become the focus of an independent investigation into an affair he had with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company and Mr Huang are also facing a proposed class action accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Mr Huang's ties with Ms Huang — a Chinese citizen and former executive at the Singapore-based data centre company.

US President Donald Trump earlier this week confirmed the FBI was looking into the affair, and described Mr Huang as a "very honourable man".

The company has since become the top supplier of AI chips at the centre of the global AI boom and US-China technology rivalry.

But US House Speaker Mike Johnson said he was "in favour" of limiting exports of semiconductor chips to China.

"And I think there's a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take. Especially in the light of recent developments, it makes sense," he said.

Mr Huang's departure could leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $US4 trillion ($5.8 trillion) chipmaker he co-founded and built over more than three decades.

Mr Huang, 63, has no obvious successor and owns about 3.6 per cent of Nvidia's stock.

Asian shares also fell on Thursday as investors kept a nervous eye on what action Nvidia's board would take.

Nvidia stock has shed 24 per cent of its value over the past month, wiping around $US1.4 trillion ($2 trillion) off its market capitalisation.

Nvidia has said it had "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.

An image shared by software company Net Thunder on LinkedIn in 2024, which it says shows Megaspeed's Alice Huang sitting alongside Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang at an event in Taiwan. (Supplied: NetThunder/LinkedIn)

Alice Huang was banned from re-entering Singapore after she left the country in February, Singapore's home affairs ministry has confirmed.

The ministry said Ms Huang, who is a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was investigated for possible offences including buying servers that were exported via Singapore to Malaysia without entering the Singapore market.

She was investigated "for suspected involvement in the possible offences in Singapore, given her position as then-CEO, chairperson and one of the key controllers of Megaspeed," the ministry said in a statement. It did not investigate espionage.

But the ministry said there was insufficient evidence to find Ms Huang had committed any offences and she was issued a warning.

In its first statement since the scandal broke, Singapore-headquartered Megaspeed International said on Thursday that it took its obligation to comply with US export control laws "extremely seriously" and was "committed to working constructively and transparently" with the US government.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/m.author: Jason Dasey
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
English Premier League

Michael Carrick has been sacked after 10 months as Manchester United manager. (Getty Images: AMA/Robbie Jay Barratt)

Manchester United has sacked manager Michael Carrick after just 10 months in charge.

The 20-time English champions sit in the Premier League relegation zone after a horror run of form.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino, the current US head coach, is reportedly in line to take over.

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United manager, becoming the latest casualty of the English Premier League giant's revolving door of coaches.

The club has ​won only three ​of its 15 matches in all ‌competitions ⁠under Carrick this season — including just one league victory — to sit in the relegation zone.

Despite a massive budget and a star-studded squad, the Red Devils are in 18th spot on eight points after 10 games, ​one point from ​the ⁠bottom.

With Manchester United not in action again until November 22 due to the international break, the club issued a statement on Thursday morning.

"After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions," it said on its website.

Sky Sports is reporting that former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino, the current United States head coach, is set to take over following a verbal agreement in principle, but United is still negotiating terms for his backroom staff.

Manchester United's shocking run of results leaves the club in the Premier League relegation zone. (Getty Images: Marc Atkins)

45-year-old Carrick's departure after just 10 months in charge continues a period of instability at Old Trafford, with United having appointed seven permanent managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 following 26 years at the helm.

The final nail in the coffin may have been a 4-4 draw ​at home to Aston Villa ⁠over the weekend, ​even though United scored twice in added time to salvage a point.

The former midfielder, who made 316 Premier League appearances for the club between 2006 and 2018, took over in January 2026, initially as interim manager.

He received a permanent contract in May after guiding United to third place in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.

His early success included victories over Manchester City, Arsenal and Liverpool.

After a promising start as Manchester United manager, Michael Carrick has lost his way this season. (Getty Images: Marco Luzzani)

But results deteriorated dramatically this season, leaving him with a winning percentage of just 46.9 per cent.

Carrick came under mounting pressure after a 3-0 home loss to Bournemouth last month, with the former England international carrying the air of someone awaiting the inevitable after the defeat when fans chanted his name but booed the players off the pitch.

He had dropped captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench against Bournemouth and did not bring him on even when United were desperate for inspiration in midfield, but the struggling club gave Carrick another chance to revive its season.

The Red Devils have not won a Premier League title since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. (Reuters)

To that point, United had gone eight matches without a win in all competitions.

Manchester United share the record of 20 English top-flight league titles with Liverpool.

But United has not won the Premier League since 2012-13, Sir Alex Ferguson's final season in charge, with its title drought now extending into a 14th season.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The inquest into the Floreat murders hears new evidence from police, more than two years after the shooting. (ABC News: Julian Robins)

The coronial inquest into the death of a Perth mother and daughter in their home has heard how the gunman inadvertently recorded himself firing his weapon.

The inquest also heard how gunman Mark Bonbara was "manipulative" to police when they attended his house weeks before the shooting, and they did not check his gun safe.

Police say their policy has changed since the Floreat murders.

A gunman who murdered a mother and daughter in their Perth home inadvertently recorded himself firing the fatal shots on one of the victims' phones, a coronial inquest has heard.

WARNING: This story contains details that may distress some readers.

The shocking detail emerged at the inquest into the murders of Jennifer Petelcyzc and her 18-year-old daughter Gretl, who were killed by Mark Bombara before he took his own life.

Bombara forced his way into their Floreat home while searching for his estranged wife.

There was a heavy police presence the day after the shooting. (ABC News: Julian Robins)

Senior Sergeant Nathan Carbone from the WA Police Homicide Squad investigated the deaths.

He told the court Bombara shot Jennifer Petelcyzc, then Gretyl, after which he grabbed Jennifer's phone and "inadvertently" recorded himself firing two more shots.

The gunman killed Jennifer and Gretl Petelczyc in their home in 2024. (Supplied)

It is not known if it is an audio or video recording.

Jennifer Petelcyzc and Rowena Bombara were best friends, and Bombara mistakenly believed his estranged wife was staying at the Floreat home.

The court heard Rowena Bombara and her daughter Ariel had moved out of the family home in April 2024, just weeks before the murders, and had sought police assistance to move their belongings from the house.

When police arrived at the house, Bombara's son opened the door and appeared nervous, saying his father had "all the [gun] licences you can possibly imagine".

The coroner in the Floreat murder-suicide inquest questions why a desperate call to Triple Zero stating someone had been shot in a family violence situation was initially marked as a priority two situation.

"I don't know if there are any firearms in [the safe] … there may be firearms in other locations," Issac Bombara is heard to say on the body-worn camera footage.

Constable Shaun King called for a second police car to attend and told the arriving officers to make sure they had "their plates in", referring to their protective vests.

But when he entered the house and met Bombara, he was the "opposite" of what he was expecting.

"I hate to say it, but he seemed like a nice man," Constable King told the court.

Constable Shaun King says he should have looked at Bombara's gun safe, in hindsight. (ABC News)

Bombara was accommodating, offering refreshments and allowing the officer to inspect his gun safe.

Constable King turned him down as he "did not want to escalate the situation" but admitted in hindsight he "should have" looked at the safe.

The coroner's court heard the conversation was an attempt by Bombara to "groom" the junior officers into thinking he was not a threat, despite his access to firearms.

"I believe it was manipulative … calculated … in an effort to place seeds of doubt in the attending officers' minds," said Superintendent Andrew Wilson, who reviewed the body-worn camera footage.

"In my opinion he was quite determined to find out what would happen to his guns … I believe he took the opportunity to try and manage that conversation."

Superintendent Wilson agreed this was common behaviour in a family violence situation.

He said police policy had changed since the Floreat murders.

Superintendent Andrew Wilson describes the gunman's demeanor as "manipulative" to officers.

Firearms are seized, and domestic violence perpetrators are removed from the home before family enter to retrieve their belongings.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Political Prisoners

Evan Gershkovich speaks out about 16 months in Russia's prisons and being arrested by the FSB. (Reuters: Tatyana Makeyeva)

Yekaterinburg, Russia, 2023. American journalist Evan Gershkovich is sitting in a restaurant talking to a source.

A number of masked men enter.

They inform the American that he is being arrested by Russia's main intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation.

Known as the FSB, it's the successor to the Soviet-era KGB, where Russian President Vladimir Putin previously worked.

Gershkovich is now the first US journalist to be arrested in Russia since the Cold War. He is hooded and thrown in a van before the agents get to work.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, who as a Russian secret service KGB served in the German Democratic Republic, was equipped with a house card of the responsible Ministry of State Security service. (Supplied: BSTU)

Vladimir Putin's details are seen on the Stasi identification card found in Germany.

"The hood gets ripped off at one point," Gershkovich told 7.30.

"There's operatives sitting next to me and a man across from me in a suit. He asks, 'Who do you work for?' I say the Wall Street Journal.

The question is repeated before Gershkovich arrives at a station and is charged with espionage.

Lefortovo pre-trial detention centre in Moscow, Russia. (Reuters: Shamil Zhumatov)

The charge strikes fear into the foreign correspondent. He knows Russia under Putin has a reputation for doing whatever it takes to silence enemies of the state.

In 2018, former Russian spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter, Yulia, were targeted in an assassination attempt with deadly nerve agent Novichok. They would ultimately survive the poisoning.

Former Putin opponent Alexei Navalny survived an attempt on his life undertaken with Novichok before his eventual death in February 2024, in one of Russia's harshest prisons.

And in August 2023 former Putin ally Yevgeny Prigozhin perished in a plane crash, while a number of other former allies have disappeared.

Gershkovich told 7.30 that his main fear was torture.

City view of Yekaterinburg in Russia where Evan Gershkovich was initially detained. (Reuters: Evgenia Novozhenina)

"I've reported on cases where somebody's brought to a station, strapped to a chair, electrodes are attached to various parts of their body, and they're electrocuted, simply for the fact of trying to get them to sign papers that attest to the fact that they're guilty in a fabricated case," he said.

The fear was real but for Gershkovich, the torture would not come. The FSB and Russian authorities had something else in mind.

Gershkovich realised he had been set up as Russia looked to replenish its "exchange bank".

That "bank", Gershkovich says, is all about Russia having a number of foreigners it can use in exchange to get some of its own incarcerated back.

In his case, the main target was Russian hitman Vadim Krasikov, who was serving jail time in Germany, having been convicted in 2019 over the brazen daylight murder of a former Chechen militant in a Berlin park in 2018.

The judge called the killing of Georgian citizen Zelimkhan Khangoshvili "state terrorism", adding that the order had almost certainly come from Putin himself.

Among the evidence he cited for Russian state involvement were Krasikov's official Russian papers containing a false identity, and the fact that Russian law empowered Putin to order the murder of state enemies abroad.

The IK-3 penal colony, where Russian opposition politician Alexei Navalny served his jail term. (Reuters)

Gershkovich said he knew almost immediately prisoner exchange would be the case once he had arrived in his "really tiny" prison cell that measured 2.4 metres by 3 metres by 3.7 metres.

"It has a bed running on one wall, a bed at the end perpendicular at the window, a desk running down the other, and it's so thin that only one person can fit walking up and down that space, and you eventually have a cellmate," he told 7.30.

"So there are two of you living in the cell, and you can only walk up and down six or seven steps.

"On my second night in prison on TV, I'm watching the main evening news show and one of the hosts says to the other host 'we've replenished our exchange fund'.

"The Russians use that as a catch-all for the foreigners that they hold to be swapped."

Gershkovich says he was treated relatively well compared to other prisoners he knew about.

"I've been reporting obviously on stories of Ukrainian civilians, Ukrainian POWs, Russian political prisoners," he said.

"[They] were tortured, deprived of hot food, hot showers, told they're never gonna see their families again, that's not happening to me.

"Really early on, my mattress is thicker than my cellmate's. Before the US ambassador comes to visit, the prison warden comes and checks in on me, asks how I'm doing.

"Eventually, there's even a moment where I say 'I'm surprised how much you're checking in on me'. He says, 'Of course, we care about your health.'

While it had become clear to Gershkovich that he was waiting for a swap, the death of Navalny was a blow and he remembers it as a moment that was likely intended to strike fear.

Russian opposition politician Alexei Navalny was a major opponent of Putin. (Reuters: Shamil Zhumatov)

He heard the news while he was on his one hour a day on the jail's roof, his only time outside the tiny cell.

"We're on this walk and suddenly the radio, which never happens, switches to the news and we hear that Alexei Navalny has died, and then it switches back," he said.

"I think they did that for the Ukrainians who were being held in the prison, the Russian political prisoners, perhaps myself too, very deliberately to send a message to us."

Before his death, there had been reports Navalny could form part of a prisoner swap deal in exchange for Russian assassin Krasikov.

But six months later, the swap happened in Türkiye, and the journalist was released alongside fellow Americans Paul Whelan and Alsu Kurmasheva.

Gershkovich used his 16 months in prison to learn more about Putin's Russia and what people really thought of a leader he said was growing more authoritarian while the war in Ukraine rolled on.

Vladimir Putin in Red Square in Moscow. (Sputnik: Yuri Kochetkov/Pool via Reuters)

"When Putin came to power it coincided with this big oil and gas boom," Gershkovich said of his May 2000 inauguration as president for the first time.

"At the same time, he made really clear what would happen politically if you tried to challenge him.

"The social contract that was essentially developed was your life will get better, money is pouring in as long as you stay out of politics.

"That is essentially the logic of the regime over the next 20, 25 years, except that it gets more and more repressive.

"By the time I go to prison, what I, and I think the best sociologists and researchers working on Russia will tell you, is that 15 per cent of people really support Putin in the war, 15 per cent really are anti-Putin and anti-war."

He said the rest would abstain from making any comment on the war, such was the fear Putin wielded on either side of the prison walls.

Evan Gershkovich reunites with his mother while US President Joe Biden looks on after a successful prisoner swap between the US and Russia. (Reuters: Kevin Mohatt)

Gershkovich said one prison guard perfectly encapsulated the example, telling him: "The news is so bad, I try not to follow it. I go to my dacha, my country house, I fish."

"So I asked him what he thought about the war," Gershkovich said.

"He smiled and zippered his mouth shut, put a finger to his mouth and kind of shrugged his shoulders. And what he was telling me is, I think, 'I don't support the war, but I can't talk about it.'

Mitch Marsh's press conference left more questions than answers regarding the 2018 South Africa tour. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Mitch Marsh has refused to answer key questions about the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal in a fiery press conference exchange with journalists.

Marsh said: "I respect that certain people have told their stories, but I'm not here to share mine."

Australia's Test captain, Pat Cummins, is set to front a press conference in Sydney on Friday morning and has promised to answer "any and all media".

Australia's one-day captain, Mitch Marsh, has refused to address key aspects of the Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal as journalists peppered him with questions at a press conference.

Marsh, who was bowling when Cameron Bancroft was spotted hiding a piece of sandpaper in his pants during the 2018 series, spent most of the 12-minute press conference straight-batting questions about the infamous South Africa tour and Usman Khawaja's explosive allegations.

The very first question put to Marsh was: "Did you know that sandpaper was being used to tamper with cricket balls in South Africa?"

"Jeez, you hit a six off the first ball there, mate. Well done," Marsh replied.

"I respect that certain people have told their stories, but I'm not here to share mine.

"I know that might sound weird, but it's a big week for us, and it's an important time for this one-day group.

"I really respect that Uzzy has told his story. He's written his book, and my focus is really on tomorrow."

Marsh was continually peppered with questions about why he was not willing to speak on the topic.

"I've personally moved on," he said.

Mitch Marsh says he has no ill feelings towards Usman Khawaja for the allegations made in his book. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

"I respect that others probably haven't, but I have, and I hope that's respected.

"This is my choice to not go back there. Who knows? Maybe I'll write a book one day."

Marsh insisted he held no grudges against Khawaja.

"I respect Uzzy for telling his story and for writing his book, and I don't sit here coming from a place of judgement," Marsh said.

"Everyone's got their story. Some will be willing to share it, and others might not, purely on the basis of the fact that they've moved on.

"It's really important that at some stage we do."

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

The aftermath of an Israeli strike on a southern Gaza hospital.

Six people, including a surgeon, have been killed in an Israeli air strike on a hospital in Gaza, Palestinian health authorities say.

The Nasser Hospital surgery department was hit and at least 20 people were injured.

The IDF says Hamas was using the hospital as a command centre.

Palestinian health authorities say a surgeon is one of at least six people who have been killed in an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza.

The attack happened in the early hours of Thursday morning, local time. Video from the scene shows extensive damage to one of the compound's buildings.

Gaza's Civil Defense agency said the surgery department was hit and that at least 20 people were injured in the blast.

Israeli strikes killed at least eight Palestinians, including five police officers, in the Gaza Strip in two separate attacks, according to medics and the Hamas-run interior ministry.

Hours after the strike, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said a "senior Hamas terrorist and additional terrorists" had been using the hospital as a command centre.

"Targeting a medical facility that includes patients receiving treatment and teams performing their humanitarian and professional duty represents a serious attack on the health system and a flagrant violation of international laws and conventions that ensure the protection of medical facilities, employees and patients," Gaza's health ministry said in a statement.

"The ministry confirms that the continued targeting of hospitals and their medical facilities exacerbates the suffering of the sick and wounded, and threatens what remains of the ability of the health sector to provide its services, in light of the catastrophic conditions in the Gaza Strip."

Rizk Abu Shaira was the surgeon who was killed, the ministry said.

"He never hesitated to provide service to his patients," the head of Nasser Hospital, Dr Ahmed al-Farra said.

"He was on top of his work. He was in his room, between following up cases, treatments and preparing cases for surgery, but it was God's will and he was martyred in this treacherous strike.

"There are also doctors who were wounded in this attack."

Hamas labelled the strike a "fully fledged war crime".

At least six people have been killed in an Israeli air strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza. (Reuters: Ramadan Abed)

Israel regularly justifies attacks on medical and humanitarian facilities by insisting they lose their protections under international law if they are used by Hamas for terrorist activities.

In this instance, the IDF said Hamas had been using Nasser Hospital as a command centre and claimed the buildings were being used to store weapons and conduct interrogations.

Israeli forces revealed the identity of their target, Muhammad Abu Ismail, hours after their first acknowledgement of the attack.

"Muhammad Abu Ismail was responsible for overseeing the activities of the brigade’s terrorists and directing them to advance and carry out terrorist plots against IDF troops and Israeli civilians.

"He was also responsible for holding numerous hostages captive throughout the war."

Earlier, the IDF released graphics showing the building it hit, but did not provide any further evidence to back up its claims about its use by Hamas.

ABC analysis reveals the extent of Israel's expansion on four fronts: Lebanon, the West Bank, Gaza and Syria.

"The IDF and the [Israel Security Agency] strongly condemn the Hamas terrorist organisation's cynical exploitation of civilian and medical infrastructure for military purposes, while endangering the lives of patients, medical personnel, and civilians," it said in a statement.

"Prior to and during the strike, steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance."

The IDF also released audio of what it said was a warning issued to the health ministry for Hamas to cease using hospitals across the strip, or risk further action by the military.

"Israel's genocide in Gaza continues under the guise of a ceasefire," Israeli advocacy group Physicians for Human Rights Israel said.

"Repeated attacks on hospitals and healthcare workers are further devastating an already shattered healthcare system, denying Palestinians in Gaza access to essential medical care and the ability to recover and live in dignity.

"The international community's inaction and continued impunity enable these attacks on Gaza's healthcare system. As long as those responsible are not held accountable, the attacks will continue."

Palestinian health authorities say more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the October 2025 ceasefire, many of them civilians, including women and children.

The death toll in Gaza now stands at more than 74,600 people.

Nasser Hospital has been targeted a number of times during the three-year long war in Gaza, triggered by Hamas's deadly attacks on Israel in October 2023.

Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza since last October's ceasefire, according to a report from UN-commissioned experts. Israel has rejected the findings as "misinformation".

On August 25 last year, the hospital was the scene of a "double-tap" strike by Israeli forces.

The IDF claimed it was targeting a Hamas terrorist when it opened fire on a camera operator who had placed his camera on the outside of the hospital to film the Khan Younis skyline.

Minutes later, as emergency workers and fellow journalists were crawling over the site of the attack, another strike hit the building.

Twenty-two Palestinians were killed that day, including five journalists.

Among them were journalists working for the Associated Press and Reuters. The agencies and other media outlets condemned the strikes.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu labelled that incident a "tragic mishap" and the IDF said it had launched an investigation into the matter.

Its findings are yet to be released.

Gaza's health ministry says the strike on Nasser Hospital was a "flagrant violation of international laws". (Reuters)

Israeli attacks across Gaza have reportedly increased in recent days, despite the ceasefire being in place.

Progress towards the next stage of the ceasefire remains stalled, with Hamas saying it will lay down its weapons only if Israel stops launching strikes and withdraws from territory.

Israel says it will only stop once Hamas demilitarises and no longer poses a threat to the country.

Both sides have been criticised for the delays, although the Trump administration-backed Board of Peace has ratcheted up its rhetoric against the Israeli government in recent months, accusing it of avoiding holding up its side of the bargain.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Socceroos players remain unwilling to travel to Amman to take on Jordan in a friendly next week. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Football Australia is looking for an alternative venue with Socceroos players unwilling to travel to Jordan to play a friendly in Amman.

FA CEO Martin Kugeler as well as other big hitters have flown to Doha in order to try to find solutions.

The Socceroos are scheduled to take on Qatar in Doha on Saturday before the scheduled Jordan clash in Amman on November 18.

Socceroos players remain unwilling to travel to Jordan as Football Australia (FA) scrambles for alternatives to playing an upcoming friendly in Amman.

But US Soccer's decision to withdraw its team from the under-17 World Cup in ‌Qatar over safety concerns is not expected to affect either the Socceroos or their Joeys counterparts.

The Socceroos and Joeys are both in camp in Doha ahead of their respective friendlies and World Cup campaigns.

Australia coach Tony Popovic insists Socceroos players who are reluctant to play Jordan due to security concerns will not be blacklisted from the national team set-up if they elect to withdraw from his squad.

The senior team is due to face Qatar on Saturday (AEDT) before travelling to Amman to face Jordan on November 18.

The latter is the issue, with PFA boss Beau Busch saying last week that Socceroos players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan "due to the unpredictable security situation" and the "threat of terrorism".

FA had been keen for the game in Jordan to proceed, but has said it was monitoring the security situation in the area.

The friendlies against Qatar and Jordan were arranged as preparations for January's Asian Cup, but the postponement of the tournament to December 2027 due to conflict in Saudi Arabia has decreased their significance.

Martin Kugeler has flown to Doha to find a solution. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar)

FA heavy hitters including chief executive Martin Kugeler and football director Heather Garriock flew to Doha this week, as did Busch and men's head of player relations Jon McKain.

Players are not expected to back down and agree to play in Jordan, likely leaving cancellation or relocation as the options.

One option is Australia remaining in Qatar and playing Jordan in Doha.

But that proposal is understood to have been met with some reluctance from both the Qatari and Jordanian football associations.

Jordan has already had to deal with Indonesia pulling out of a friendly this window.

Playing the Jordan game somewhere in southern Europe is another option, along with cancelling or postponing the game altogether.

Coach Tony Popovic, due to speak to media in his pre-match press conference on Thursday night, has indicated no players would be blacklisted from future selection if they withdrew from his squad for security reasons.

Elsewhere, in ‌a letter sent to players, US Soccer said it was cancelling its team's pre-tournament camp and its participation in the under-17 World Cup "in light of current circumstances".

US Soccer cited US State Department's Level 3 travel advisory for Qatar and related ‌directives for ‌embassy ⁠staff and families.

But the Joeys are not expected to follow the US in withdrawing from the under-17 tournament in Qatar, while the Socceroos are understood not to have issues with being in Qatar.

Kalyn Ponga (left) and Stacey Waaka have won the men's and women's Golden Boot awards after outstanding individual seasons. (Getty Images)

New Zealand duo Kalyn Ponga and Stacey Waaka have been named the men's and women's Golden Boot winners after outstanding individual seasons at their respective clubs.

Ponga scored six tries as he led Newcastle to the NRL grand final before scoring two further tries for the Kiwis at the Rugby League World Cup despite suffering a broken arm.

Waaka, a cross-code star, scored nine tries for the Warriors in just 10 NRLW appearances and added nine tries in four World Cup appearances.

Both players will be in action for New Zealand's men's and women's sides in their respective World Cup finals this weekend as they take on Australia.

Ponga is New Zealand's eighth men's Golden Boot winner, joining Hugh McGahan, Stacey Jones, Benji Marshall, Shaun Johnson, Roger Tuivasa-Sheck, Joseph Manu and James Fisher-Harris.

Waaka is the third New Zealand player to win the women's award, joining Raecene McGregor and Georgia Hale.

Ponga edged out his Cup final counterpart Reece Walsh, Samoa powerhouse Francis Manulelua, Tonga centre Robert Toia and Kiwi centre Casey McLean who were all shortlisted for the men's award.

The Wheelchair golden boot was taken out by England's Rob Hawkins ahead of Friday night's final in Wollongong between England and France.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/d.title: Data centre industry butts up against community challenges
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/d.author: Evelyn Leckie and Thomas Kelsall
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Data centre companies are reportedly grappling with how to get community engagement "right". (ABC News: James Wakelin)

The industry body for data centre proponents says its members are battling community hesitancy and policy uncertainty.

It comes amid calls by minor parties for SA to halt approvals for new centres.

The state government is preparing legislation to regulate the industry.

The peak body representing data centres in Australia say its members are still grappling with "getting community consultation right" after several AI companies have either dumped or paused their plans for building centres across the country.

South Australia has today seen the first sign of data centre development in retreat, with Quantum DC announcing it will pause plans to build a 1200-megawatt AI data centre in Tungkillo, in the Adelaide Hills, following deep frustration, anger and protests from the surrounding community.

In New South Wales, another AI data centre proposed for Sydney's south, on the Cooks River, was scrapped over the weekend, the latest in a series of proposed NSW data centres to be dumped following community opposition.

Peak body Data Centres Australia does not represent Quantum DC.

Speaking broadly, its CEO Belinda Dennett said the challenge with community engagement was choosing the right time.

"Communities want early engagement, but they also want detailed answers, so there is a bit of a trade-off.

"Often, early engagement means you don't have all those answers around design plans, around energy source, around how much water that may use."

She said there was great potential and interest to build data centres in South Australia, but operators and investors wanted policy certainty.

"That's the challenge for all the states at the moment, the challenge of not having federal rules in place … we don't have that policy certainty," she said.

"The quicker we have certainty, the more viable I think Australia's going to be."

Tungkillo's rolling hills won't have a data centre, for now. (Supplied: Magdalene Lippett)

On Thursday, political parties including the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens welcomed the pause on the Tungkillo development, while the SA government criticised the developer for its consultation process.

The Greens went a step further, calling for a data centre moratorium.

SA's minister for artificial intelligence (AI), Chris Picton, said the Tungkillo announcement highlighted why the state government was keen to get legislation through the parliament to enable proper regulatory control.

"[It's] going to be critical to making sure that we can think through all these issues with data centres to make sure that can be managed in an appropriate way, whether that be issues about energy, or water, or land use," Mr Picton said.

Opposition leader Ashton Hurn said it didn't make sense for a data centre at Tungkillo to be built on "prime agricultural land", but there was also a need to make sure the community understood why data centres are needed.

"We believe that a vehicle to do that is including them in the royal commission," Ms Hurn said.

When details of the state's Royal Commission into Artificial Intelligence were released in early October, its terms of reference did not include data centres.

Mr Picton said it wasn't remiss of the government not to include them: "They are completely separate things.

"Data centres have issues, but they're infrastructure issues … They're issues about energy use, water use and where the land is."

Community protests against the Tungkillo data centre seem to have had an effect. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

The Greens, One Nation and the Liberal Party united in the upper house on Wednesday to establish a parliamentary inquiry into data centres, which was not supported by Labor.

One Nation SA leader Cory Bernardi said the party would like to see a pause on data centres until the inquiry is finished.

"But we're also recognising that data centres per se are not bad," he said.

"We have a data centre here in the metropolitan area of Adelaide that hasn't caused any fuss at all.

"But what we want is a community licence for it."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/n.author: Tony Ibrahim
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The former wife of a police prosecutor delivered an emotional victim impact statement to the court. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

A police prosecutor convicted of domestic violence offences was read victim impact statements from his ex-wife and her children.

His ex-wife said the assaults she endured "changed the course of my life and the life of my children".

The matter was adjourned for sentencing at Gosford District Court on December 11.

A NSW police prosecutor assaulted his then wife as she held their newborn baby while recovering from birth complications, a court has heard.

MZ, whose identity the court suppressed to protect the victim, was taken into custody in July, after a jury convicted him of 11 offences related to domestic violence.

These include two counts of sexual intercourse without consent, two counts of common assault, five counts of assault occasioning bodily harm, intentionally choke a person without consent, and sexually touch another person without consent.

The 50-year-old man, a police prosecutor whose career with the force spanned more than two decades, appeared via audio-visual link in the NSW District Court.

He sat idle and expressionless as his ex-wife and her two children read victim impact statements.

"You did not simply hurt me, you changed the course of my life and the life of my children," his ex-wife read from the courtroom.

She read through pages of testimony maintaining composure, but her voice began to waver when she detailed the abuse her children had to witness.

"After the C-section of our second child, you assaulted me when I was recovering from complications," she said.

One incident, she said, caused her to realise he would not change.

"The time when you assaulted me when I held our child was one of the most frightening moments.

"Even holding our baby was not enough to stop you. That's when I began to understand that nothing would make you stop."

The court heard that she faced a power imbalance when accusing a police prosecutor of domestic violence offences.

"The blue shirt you hid behind was meant to represent safety…instead it became the same blue shirt I learnt to fear," she said.

She also said the years spent pursuing the matter through the courts forced her to relive trauma.

"You do not get to write the end of my story," she said. "I survived everything you did. I survived you."

The court heard the abuse left her two children suffering from post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and living with a distrust of law enforcement.

Judge Philip Hogan heard closing arguments as members of MZ's family watched from the gallery, among them his father, brothers and sister.

The defence, represented by barrister Arjun Chhabra, said the serious offences warranted a jail sentence of just under 10 years after mitigating factors were considered.

"MZ described an incident of sexual abuse when he was a child by a trusted figure," the court heard.

Mr Chhabra said his client had been diagnosed with PTSD, and that his work as a police prosecutor exposed him to criminal matters that left him triggered — particularly around an incident of domestic violence in 2020.

"It is likely that his symptoms reduced his capacity to manage stress during periods of heightened conflict," Mr Chhabra said.

He said MZ's career in the NSW Police Force would make him a target in jail, and that the time he would serve in protective custody would be more onerous.

"That he may come face to face with people he arrested or prosecuted…that is a real punishment… and that ought to be reflected in the sentencing exercise," Mr Chhabra said.

The Crown, represented by barrister Rohan Cooley, said a serving police officer should have known better.

"The offender must have known because he was a police officer that this would be a consequence," he said.

He acknowledged the report of sexual abuse and PTSD, but did not believe it "impaired his ability to appreciate the seriousness or potential consequences of his actions".

Mr Cooley told the court MZ had shown no sense of wrongdoing over his actions.

"There's clearly no expression of remorse," he said.

The defence had previously acknowledged the absence of an expression of remorse.

Judge Hogan adjourned the matter for sentencing at Gosford District Court on December 11.

He has been suspended from the NSW Police Force without pay while his employment is under review.
