https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/j.title: With Jensen Huang under pressure, Nvidia finds itself with no succession plan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/j.author: Annabel Bowles
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia could leave a leadership vacuum at the leading AI chip company. (AP: Go Nakamura/Pool)

When reports of an espionage plot against Nvidia's Jensen Huang first emerged, the company stood by their chief executive.

Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo released a statement saying Mr Huang was committed to keep leading the firm "without interruption".

Before its probe into Mr Huang's romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was even underway, Nvidia said it had "no reason to believe" either US national security or company secrets had been compromised.

Two days later, Nvidia's board is reportedly meeting to decide whether to oust Mr Huang.

The chief executive of the world's most valuable company and a close ally of Donald Trump admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Here's what we know.

Overnight, the New York Times reported he had a second extra-marital affair with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, the company's vice-president of health care, who also reported to him.

This week, shares in the multi-trillion-dollar tech giant tumbled, while Nvidia and Mr Huang have faced a ‌proposed class action accusing them ‌of ⁠defrauding ‌shareholders.

But what is perhaps most extraordinary is that Nvidia has no obvious successor to Mr Huang, who has run the company since it was created 33 years ago.

Holding the position of co-founder, president and chief executive, Mr Huang has created an unusually flat corporate structure with about 60 executives reporting directly to him.

He once said he did not believe in succession planning, according to the Wall Street Journal, despite his family being woven into the company's fabric.

Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison (left), is a senior marketing director at Nvidia and Spencer (right), his son, is a product line manager in robotics. (Thu Hoang Ly/The Mercury News/Getty Images)

Mr Huang is the only Nvidia insider on the company's board, which operates without a permanent chair. Instead, a lead director is chosen annually by a majority of board members.

"Jensen is not replaceable … there is no other person on the management team bench that can step in seamlessly as CEO," tech analyst Dan Ives told Reuters.

Following the first reports this morning the board was preparing to oust him, Nvidia's share price dropped about 8 per cent in after-hours trade.

That brought it 33 per cent lower than its peak in early October.

Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife after reports emerged he had developed a relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), a data centre executive at the centre of the alleged spy plot. (Reuters: CTI)

Mr Huang's departure could leave the world-leading chip maker and global AI trade in an even more precarious position, according to investment analyst Jun Bei Liu.

"He's the face of Nvidia and Nvidia has been front and centre of the AI build-out," she said.

"If we look at how many new cloud data centre businesses have been sponsored in this circular financing world, it's pretty much all by Nvidia.

"There's just a lot of uncertainty to come … not just for Nvidia, it's for the whole AI, the circular financing, the AI build-out, all the ⁠businesses that they co-invest and sponsor."

Mr Huang has spent decades building Nvidia into a leading developer of graphics processing units, the hardware that AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic rely on to operate.

One of the world's most valuable companies, Nvidia hit a market capitalisation of $US5.7 trillion ($8.3 trillion) at its peak in early October.

Jensen Huang is one of the world's most influential figures in the tech and AI industry. (Reuters: Kim Soo-hyeon)

In America's pursuit to win the AI race against China, Mr Huang has emerged as a close ally of Donald Trump and one of the few people known to have a direct line to him.

He has been to the White House at least five times since Mr Trump returned to office and just months ago accompanied him on a trip to Beijing.

Mr Huang's star power also extends to other tech billionaires such as Larry Ellison and Elon Musk, who famously begged him for more Nvidia chips. (Already, the SpaceX founder has suggested he would hire him).

NYT tech reporter Ryan Mac told the ABC's Afternoon Briefing that Mr Huang was a person "that sets the tone when it comes to AI regulation or lack thereof".

"He is an agenda-setter, someone that has a close relationship with Donald Trump and influences policy not just in the US but globally.

Mac, one of the reporters who broke the story of Mr Huang's second alleged affair, said it was "incredibly unclear" who would be tapped to succeed the Nvidia boss should he depart the company.

"He has this kind of gravitas, this 'key man' placement in the company that would be very hard to replace," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/q.title: Coalmine reopens despite previous owners saying royalties made it unprofitable
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/q.author: Liam O'Connell
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Mining and Metals Industry

Dump trucks on the haul road at the mine. (ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell)

A Queensland company has reopened the New Burton Coal Mine in the Bowen Basin.

Premier David Crisafulli officially reopened the mine today.

Mine owner Argo Resources Queensland says the state's coal royalties did not deter it from investing.

A Queensland mining company has employed 275 workers and reopened a Bowen Basin coalmine that went into receivership in 2025.

Argo Resources Queensland purchased the New Burton Mine near Moranbah, about 120 kilometres south-west of Mackay, from Bowen Coking Coal in June.

It is the fourth mine Argo has a controlling interest in after acquiring a 70 per cent stake in Bowen Basin mines Broadlea, Carborough Downs and Ironbark in March for an undisclosed sum.

Premier David Crisafulli reopened the mine today, saying coal mining had a "bullish future".

"People need to know that the future of mining in Queensland is secure," Mr Crisafulli said.

"But also, the future of coal mining in Queensland, and I'm talking about both thermal and met [metallurgical] coal, there's a future for both."

David Crisafulli visits the mine for its reopening. (ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell)

He said the Queensland government had not contributed to the mine with financial incentives or delayed royalty payments.

Argo CEO Richard Livingstone-Blevins said royalties were not a deterrent to acquiring coalmines.

"At the end of the day, we invested in the state based on the current royalty regime that's in place," he said.

The mine entrance near Moranbah in the Bowen Basin. (ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell)

Mr Livingstone-Blevins declined to comment on why the previous mine owners were not profitable.

"We've got great infrastructure, we've got great people, we've got coal on the ground at economic strip ratios, and we've got a lot of ground that we can open up, moving forward," he said.

"We all run vastly different businesses with vastly different cost profiles and different assets that have different operating costs."

Mr Livingstone-Blevins said Argo planned to mine 10 million tonnes of saleable coal by 2028.

"We have two prep plant hubs, we've got two rail loops, we're serviced by our own haul road, we've got our own camp, we've got four mines along the strike, and we've got over 4 billion tonnes of resource in the ground, which we seek to develop as we push forward," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/r.title: Victorian Big Build inquiry rebukes agency on redactions
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/r.author: Andi Yu
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Royal Commissions

Commissioner Chris Kourakis says public servants called to provide information to the Big Build inquiry have a duty ultimately to the people of Victoria. (Joe Armao: AAP)

A former advisor to ex-premier Daniel Andrews has been named as a public servant who has "disrupted" the royal commission into public projects.

Counsel assisting the commission says the Big Build authority has made an extremely late disclosure of text messages from advisor to the premier, Matt Toner, which are directly about the issues it's been investigating all week.

The text messages have not yet been made public by the commission. The hearings continue.

A former advisor to ex-premier Daniel Andrews is among public servants accused by Victoria's Big Build royal commissioner of delaying his inquiry and flouting their legal obligations.

At the royal commission into alleged corruption on major public projects today, counsel assisting Chris Young KC said the inquiry was being thwarted by heavy redactions and last-minute submissions of key evidence.

Just two days ago, he said, the Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority (VIDA) told to the commission about text messages in 2022 from senior public servants directly concerning work stoppages and the CFMEU at a level crossing removal project in Sunbury the commission has been investigating all week.

"Those messages included reference to the PPO, which we understand to be a reference to the premier's private office, and some named individuals," Mr Young said.

Counsel assisting the commission Chris Young KC said the poor disclosure by a government entity defied what Premier Ben Carroll said the inquiry was set up to do. (Supplied)

"Steps are now being taken to secure evidence from those persons.

"I am not tendering those text messages now, but we will."

The messages were from Matt Toner, direct adviser to Andrews, and from Matthew Phelan, chief of staff to the director general of VIDA, Corey Hannett.

Mr Young said Mr Toner left his role under Mr Andrews some time in 2024.

Daniel Andrews was premier of Victoria during most of the periods of time under investigation at the royal commission this week.  (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"Around the time he left that position as an advisor to the premier he was referred to in notes of a delegates meeting at the CFMEU," he said.

Former Victorian secretary of the CFMEU John Setka described Mr Toner during that meeting as "a good asset to the union", he said.

The inquiry also heard a notebook belonging to government executive Evan Tattersall, was submitted by VIDA prior to the public hearings with all its pages blacked out.

A photo of two pages of Evan Tattersall's notebook submitted by the government's Big Build authority to the Royal Commission. Every page submitted was blacked-out like this until the authority re-submitted at the commissioner's request. (Supplied)

Just this morning, as hearings were already underway, VIDA submitted a much less redacted version, after being compelled to do so, Mr Young said. The notes are about the same Sunbury level crossing project.

He also said there were other VIDA documents the commission had requested, which the agency had failed to submit.

Commissioner Chris Kourakis said late provision of information from government individuals and entities had "disrupted the orderly investigation" of the inquiry.

Commissioner Chris Kourakis issued words of advice to government employees required to disclose information to the inquiry: "if in doubt, send it out".  (Supplied)

"I encourage, in the strongest terms, early, genuine and comprehensive disclosure, by all serving or former ministers and public servants, and their advisors," he said.

"A working rule along the lines 'if in doubt send it out' will also allow the recipient to meet their legal obligations to provide the information within the stipulated time."

Counsel assisting VIDA Richard Knowles apologised and said the agency would respond to the commission's requests as soon as possible.

The royal commission today also heard from several executives from construction firm John Holland and CPB contractors today, quizzing them on their dealings with the CFMEU in the civil (road and rail) projects.

Industrial relations general manager for John Holland, Trent Smith, told the commission by mid-2021 the business acknowledged it could only survive in Victoria if it formed an enterprise agreement for civil projects with the CFMEU.

Mr Smith said by that stage, a "hostile" relationship with the CFMEU was "touching all parts of our business".

John Holland executive Trent Smith said the company's leadership came to the view that cooperating with the CFMEU was critical to winning state government work. (Supplied)

He said it was a widely-held belief across the firm that the CFMEU had influence within the state government, compared to the alternative union for civil projects, the Australian Workers' Union.

"That's how we understood the relationship to be…it was a very clear position within John Holland," he said.

Therefore, engagement with the CFMEU became part of the company's broader strategy to "better position our business with the state government", he said.

Senior executives from contractor John Holland have given evidence a work stoppage at the Gap Road Sunbury level crossing project in 2022 caused by the CFMEU was threatening their ability to deliver the project.  (Supplied: Victorian government)

John Holland signed an enterprise bargaining agreement with the union in August 2021.

Mr Smith said this was largely a symbolic gesture by then, given the company was already "at [the CFMEU's] mercy" via sub-contracted labour aligned with that union.

Senior civil engineer for John Holland, Wayne Donnelly, told the commission the work stoppage in June 2022 on the Sunbury level crossing was causing concern of major cost blowout, because of delays.

By April 2022, 95 per cent of civil contractors in Victoria had an enterprise agreement in place with the CFMEU, the commission heard.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/c.title: Pool's defibrillator not working when nine-year-old boy drowned
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/c.author: Jackson Byrne
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Cyrus John Buck was visiting Waikerie Swimming Pool with family members when the tragedy occurred. (Supplied: Buck family)

An inquest into the death of a nine-year-old-boy who drowned at the Waikerie Swimming Pool in 2022 has been adjourned.

The lifeguard who performed CPR on Cyrus John Buck told the inquest the defibrillator was not working and a bag valve mask was "broken".

The matter has been adjourned until December 9 following the emergence of new evidence.

Warning: This story contains details of a drowning death which some readers may find distressing

A coronial inquest into the drowning death of a nine-year-old boy at the Waikerie Swimming Pool in 2022 has been adjourned after the emergence of new evidence, including recordings from two separate Triple Zero (000) calls.

Cyrus John Buck died on December 3, 2022, after two lifeguards noticed him "facedown", sinking "approximately 50 centimetres" underneath the water at the deep end of the pool.

On what should have been the third and final day of the inquest, family members, including grandparents, were visibly upset in court when learning of the adjournment.

Lifeguard Hayley Collins was scheduled to give evidence as part of the inquest today, but will be given another month to prepare to respond to new evidence before next being called.

The court heard none of the lifeguards on duty saw when or where Cyrus re-entered the Waikerie Swimming Pool. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

The counsel for Belgravia Health and Leisure, which manages and operates the Waikerie Swimming Pool, told the court Ms Collins would need time to review the recordings.

"In my submission, fairness requires her to have the ability to properly listen to that material, to be able to respond to it in a manner that is fair to her," barrister Holly Vealesaid.

"Having only been provided with these recordings today, that would be an unfair approach."

That request was granted by Deputy State Coroner Darren Evans, who said more time was needed to properly assess the new evidence.

Darren Evans (right) was shown the Waikerie Swimming Pool yesterday and given a breakdown of the events that led to Cyrus's death. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

Yesterday, lifeguard Emily Brock, who performed CPR on nine-year-old Cyrus after he was retrieved from the pool, said fellow lifeguard Noah Hensel told her that a bag valve mask, used to assist breathing, was "broken".

Ms Brock told the court her training instructed her not to give rescue breaths and only to use a bag valve mask, because of COVID-19 concerns at the time.

The court heard that was why Cyrus's aunt gave the rescue breaths instead.

It heard it was at this time Cyrus began having airway difficulties and vomit, water and saliva came from his mouth.

Ms Buck also told the inquest yesterday a defibrillator "would not progress through its sequence" when she attempted to use it.

"[The defibrillator] just kept saying 'continue CPR, apply pads'," Ms Brock said.

"It wasn't registering that we'd already placed pads on."

The Waikerie Swimming Pool is a popular destination for families and children during the summer months. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

The inquest heard the two lifeguards assisting Ms Brock at the time went into shock while she was performing CPR on Cyrus.

She told the court one of those was a 17-year-old lifeguard who began vomiting.

"Noah had also gone into shock, he wasn't continuing to set up the oxygen," Ms Brock said.

Neither Mr Hensel nor Ms Collins have had the opportunity to give evidence yet.

The inquest will move from the Berri Magistrates Court to Adelaide on December 9.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/w.title: What went wrong for Indonesia's VP Gibran Rakabuming Raka?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/w.author: Hellena Souisa
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigned while the process for his impeachment was underway. (Reuters: Marco Longer)

Read the story in Bahasa Indonesia

Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has resigned, ending a political saga that has played out across multiple court cases and amid mounting calls for his impeachment.

Here's what we know about why the country's youngest ever vice-president resigned before the end of his term and how his successor will be chosen.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka is the eldest son of Indonesia's seventh president, Joko Widodo, widely known as Jokowi.

President Prabowo Subianto sits between Joko Widodo and Gibran Rakabuming Raka on independence day. (Indonesian Presidential Office: Rusman)

Mr Gibran was a businessman before entering politics.

He founded a wedding organising business and launched a range of food and beverage ventures with his younger brother, Kaesang Pangarep, several of which remain in operation.

Mr Gibran formally entered politics when he joined his father's party, the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle (PDIP), in September 2019.

Soon after, he successfully ran for mayor of Solo in Central Java — a position once held by Mr Jokowi before he became president — with the support of his party.

During the 2024 presidential election, Mr Gibran was the running mate of Prabowo Subianto, the co-founder and chairman of the Gerindra Party.

This put him at odds with the PDIP, which backed rival candidates. Mr Gibran was later expelled from the party.

In Indonesia, presidential and vice-presidential candidates aren't required to be from the same party.

Mr Prabowo and Mr Gibran were sworn in as Indonesia's president and vice-president in October 2024.

The controversy centred on a single document.

Under Indonesian election law, the presidential and vice-presidential candidates must have completed senior high school or the equivalent.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka was the running mate of Prabowo Subianto during the 2024 election. (Indonesian Presidential Office: Rusman)

Several politicians challenged Mr Gibran's eligibility, arguing he had failed to provide proof of his qualifications.

They alleged he relied on a substitute certificate that should not have been accepted by the General Elections Commission, and argued he should be disqualified from office.

Indonesia's Constitutional Court has refused to disqualify Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka over questions about his educational history, but experts say he could be impeached anyway.

The Constitutional Court rejected the challenge, ruling the matter could no longer be addressed through the presidential election dispute process because Mr Gibran had already been sworn in as vice-president.

However, Judge Adies Kadir said: "The court found no convincing evidence that Gibran has a foreign diploma equivalent to having completed senior high school, or another equivalent qualification as stipulated in the Election Law."

The Constitutional Court's finding was later reinforced by a Supreme Court ruling that invalidated the substitute high school equivalency certificate issued by the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education that he had used when registering for the election.

The rulings fuelled calls in parliament to remove Mr Gibran from office, with politicians arguing he no longer met the requirements to serve as vice-president.

Before the impeachment process could run its course, however, he chose to resign.

The resignation does not affect Mr Prabowo's position.

Under Indonesia's constitution, the president continues to govern if the vice-presidency becomes vacant.

It is too early to know who will replace Gibran Rakabuming Raka (second from the right). (Indonesian Presidential Office: Muchlis Jr)

The People's Consultative Assembly, or MPR, must then convene a session within 60 days to elect a new vice-president.

The replacement will be chosen from two candidates nominated by the president.

The process begins with the president submitting the names and supporting documents of two nominees, which are then verified by the MPR.

The assembly will determine whether the candidates meet the requirements before holding a vote in a plenary session.

The candidate who wins the most votes will become vice-president.

If both candidates receive the same number of votes, a second round will be held.

And if the result remains tied, the president will choose one of the two candidates.

It is still too early to know who will replace Mr Gibran.

Several potential candidates are already being discussed, both from Mr Prabowo's political circle and from outside the governing coalition.

One name frequently mentioned is Puan Maharani, a senior PDIP politician, Speaker of the House of Representatives, and the daughter of former president Megawati Soekarnoputri.

Mr Prabowo ran as Ms Megawati's running mate in the 2009 election, but was unsuccessful.

Former president Megawati Soekarnoputri with her daughter, Puan Maharani (right), and President Prabowo Subianto. (Instagram Puan Maharani via detik.com)

While the PDIP is not part of the governing coalition, it has never formally declared itself an opposition party either.

Other names being floated include Sugiono, the former foreign minister and secretary-general of the Gerindra Party, and Sufmi Dasco Ahmad, a deputy speaker of parliament and Gerindra's executive chairman.

Both men are among Mr Prabowo's closest political allies and come from the president's own party.

Constitutional law expert Zainal Arifin Mochtar said one thing is clear:

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/b.author: Giselle Wakatama
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Sexual Offences

Teacher Brody Luke Anderson has been barred from all NSW public schools. (Facebook)

Brody Luke Anderson has been found guilty of two counts of intentionally recording an intimate image without consent.

The Newcastle Local Court heard the charges did not relate to a student at the school.

He was spared jail but ordered to serve a two-year sentence in the community.

A teacher has been spared jail but is banned from working in any NSW public school after taking photos of a naked sleeping man.

Brody Luke Anderson, who taught at a school in the wider Hunter region, was found guilty of two counts of intentionally recording an intimate image without consent.

The Newcastle Local Court heard the charges did not relate to a student at the school.

Ahead of sentencing on Tuesday, Anderson wrote a letter to Judge Georgina Darcy apologising for his actions.

"I am truly sorry for the hurt I have caused. This will not happen again," he said.

The ABC has since learned he has been barred from teaching at any NSW public school.

Police facts tendered in court said Anderson took two images of an adult man lying naked on a bed in a Sydney hotel room in March 2024.

"The victim was asleep in the bed, laying in the fetal position completely naked with his buttocks exposed," the fact sheet said.

A second photograph was taken half an hour later.

"The victim is laying naked in the same position as the previous photograph with the top part of his body rolled back slightly so his head, chest and arms were exposed," the fact sheet read.

The court was told Anderson "had his penis exposed, dangling his penis above the victim's head while he slept".

Anderson told the judge he thought taking the photos was "OK".

The two images were stored on his mobile phone and shown to police when he made admissions after his arrest last month.

Anderson was spared jail and no conviction was recorded.

Judge Darcy instead handed Anderson a two-year sentence to be served in the community, by way of a conditional release order.

He will be bound by the order until November 2028.

During that time he is not to commit any offence and must appear before the court if called upon to do so at any time.

He must delete or destroy any intimate images of the victim that were created in contravention of the law.

Brody Luke Anderson was sentenced in Newcastle Local Court. (ABC Newcastle: Robert Virtue)

Anderson told the judge the incident had ended his career.

"I have decided to leave my current job in teaching, which has meant giving up a career I cared deeply about," Anderson said.

"I am concerned about the impact a criminal conviction will have upon my future, with particular regard to future employment and police checks."

The ABC asked the New South Wales Department of Education for comment in relation to the status of Anderson's employment.

In a statement, a spokesman confirmed Anderson was no longer employed.

"The individual is barred from working in any NSW public school," the Department of Education statement read.

"The department's highest priority is the safety and wellbeing of students."

In 2025, the NSW government strengthened protections against the non-consensual recording or sharing of sexual content by amending the Crimes Act 1900.

At the time, the government said the act already covered sexually explicit image material, but a tweak meant that it would now include digitally generated deepfakes.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/c.title: A coffee cart and the Finnish embassy gain more traction than Albanese
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/c.author: Courtney Gould
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Government

Anthony Albanese had a busy week juggling the mid-year budget update, speculation about his treasurer, and a trip to a climate summit. (ABC News: Tobias Hunt)

Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Anthony Albanese and his government could only wish for the type of cut-through the Finnish embassy in Canberra received when it temporarily closed on Tuesday.

It all started when Finland's ambassador to Australia, Arto Haapea, starred in a video on Instagram promoting a campaign to fly singles from around the world to Helsinki for dinner dates.

"Are you single? Good. We are here to help … maybe the problem is not you, it's your postcode," he said.

The post's popularity created the perfect storm for the embassy's next message to followers, an innocuous reminder the building would be closed for a planning day, to be sent out to the masses.

An unexpected viral hit was born. People across the world shared their concern about the embassy's one-day closure.

"Bad day to be a Finnish embassy in Canberra enthusiast," one person commented.

The Canberra Raiders, travel company Contiki and video game Angry Birds also chimed in. Haapea filmed a ribbon cutting for the building's grand re-opening the next day.

Even Finland's President Alexander Stubb joined in. On the sidelines of the United Nations climate summit in Türkiye, he shared a happy snap of himself with Albanese.

"I have confirmed to … Albanese that the Finnish embassy in Canberra is open," he wrote.

Perhaps conscious of the optics of a second week abroad, Albanese packed a lot into his couple of days at home after returning from the Caribbean last week.

He attended a Nepal Festival in Sydney, reversed his decision to sell off four historic defence sites, and announced new mandatory safety and security standards for artificial intelligence.

The prime minister's departure was delayed by a day, meaning he was able to be there in person to chair a meeting of the expenditure review committee ahead of next month's Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook.

Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

A string of interest rate rises and sticky inflation has ramped up pressure on the government to find savings. There is speculation that low-hanging fruit such as the electric vehicle and home battery subsidies could be targeted.

The government argues the schemes promote Australia's transition to renewables, but both are as expensive as they are enormously popular.

Costs have blown out beyond initial projections, and the government has already committed to partially winding back EV subsidies next year following changes already made to the home batteries scheme.

Of course, in the backdrop of all of this are the rumours around the future of Jim Chalmers.

The relationship between the treasurer and Albanese has been the subject of many newspaper articles in recent weeks, as a usually united caucus vented frustrations publicly, with unnamed sources suggesting Chalmers should be replaced.

Speculation about the relationship between the prime minister and his treasurer has ramped up in recent weeks.  (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

This week, Environment Minister Murray Watt was asked if he'd like to see an end to the "undermining and leaking" against the treasurer.

"Yes, I would," he replied. "As a member of a government, I take seriously the responsibility to work together, to support government policies, and also to get out there and support each other in what, at times, are very difficult times."

Ahead of his departure for Türkiye, Albanese said "yes" when asked if it was his preference that Chalmers remained Treasurer until the next election.

"The treasurer is doing a great job," he said as he dismissed concerns the good ship government had sprung one too many leaks.

Albanese may have delayed the departure for his 11-day trip covering three international summits, but that didn't eat too much into his itinerary.

Much like any regular Aussie making a trip across the world, the prime minister (and his team) arrived at dawn and hit the ground running. He almost immediately attended the leaders' summit at COP31, the United Nations Climate Change Conference.

Australia had pushed hard to host the summit in Adelaide but conceded to Türkiye, taking on the compromised position to oversee negotiations and host a pre-COP event in the Pacific.

The climate summit will push for nations around the world to electrify their energy faster and move away from fossil fuels.

It's Albanese's first-time attending COP as prime minister. He used his opening address to argue that other nations should step up their climate actions and support vulnerable nations, such as those in the Pacific.

Australia and Türkiye want the summit to conclude with agreements on electrification, climate finance and adaption.

Albanese pointed to the strong uptake of home batteries in the past year (backed by the aforementioned subsidy) as Australia's credentials for being a climate leader.

But United Nations secretary-general António Guterres called for more than just words.

"We must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it and delivering it," he said.

Fossil fuels, Guterres said, must "go the way of the dinosaurs" as he urged governments not to invest in any new coal developments — something Pacific nations have been critical of the Albanese government for.

Meanwhile, Australia's pavilion at the event has proven to be quite the drawcard. Why? Because of the taxpayer-funded coffee cart.

Australia's coffee station has proved to be enormously popular at COP.  (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

As Clare Armstrong, who is on the ground for the ABC, observed, the baristas can't get the flat whites out fast enough — with some willing to wait for more than an hour.

It's probably no surprise that the $32,000 price tag for the coffee hub drew criticism from the opposition. That's despite the idea harking back to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor's time as energy minister.

But if you ask former PM Malcolm Turnbull, who is also at COP, it's all about giving people a taste of what Australia has to offer.

"All the dollars that are spent on marketing here, that is probably the best dollar spent," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/q.title: Hunt is on for heir to strange block of land
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/q.author: Ellen-Maree Elliot
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Ellen-Maree Elliot

Des Crump is a historian and bottle collector who has researched August Thorsborne. (ABC News : Phoebe Hosier)

The Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads is looking for the owner of a 10sqm block of land.

The department intends to resume the land as part of upgrades to Holmview Station in Beenleigh.

Objections to the land being acquired must be lodged by November 17.

Local sleuths and state bureaucrats are trying to find the true heir to a strange block of land in Logan, south of Brisbane, with only five days left.

The Department of Transport and Main Roads is looking for anyone who believes they have an interest in the August Thorsborne estate.

That tiny block of land, 16 metres long and 60 centimetres wide, is needed to facilitate upgrades to the Holmview station precinct, which is part of Logan and Gold Coast Faster Rail.

A published Notice of Intention to Resume states:

"To: The beneficiaries, heirs or any party establishing an interest in the estate of August Thorsborne (deceased) Take notice that on 13 October 2026, the Chief Executive, Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) pursuant to the provisions of the Acquisition of Land Act 1967, the Transport Infrastructure Act 1994 and the Transport Planning and Coordination Act 1994 issued a notice that intends to take an area of 10 square metres … in the locality of Beenleigh, for a purpose incidental to transport (railway) namely road… Any written objections to the intended take are required by 17 November 2026."

Des Crump is a historian and bottle collector; the reason the latter is important will become clear shortly.

He spoke to Steve Austin about his research into Mr Thorsborne on 612 ABC Brisbane Mornings.

"It's [a] funny little shape, [a] funny little bit of land, but it's surprising that there's no descendants because he [August Thorsborne] had quite a few children," he said.

"It doesn't seem to be specifically connected to where he ran his soft drink business, and he had a brewery, and all those other things that wouldn't fit on that sort of block of land."

Despite the lack of heirs apparent, the family name is still prominent in the areas around Holmview station, with a road and a park named after the family.

Mr Crump, who has roles at The University of Queensland and the State Archives, has some of the bottles from the soft drink company in his collection.

"(The Thorsborne family) came out from Sweden, ended up in Beenleigh in the 1870s, had interests in the hotel area, mostly known for his soft drink factory," he said.

"It was a Beenleigh Soda with this gauntlet trademark."

He said the bottles in his collection were rare because the early ones had marbles in them and children would break them to get to them.

Mr Thorsborne was also a member of the Beenleigh Shire Council in 1888.

Mr Crump said Mr Thorsborne had 11 children, two died in childhood, and the family had the soft drink factory through to the 1930s.

"So, you think there must still be family there," he said.

A Department of Transport and Main Roads spokesperson said it had released an updated design for the Holmview station precinct as part of Logan and Gold Coast Faster Rail.

"The updated design of the Logan and Gold Coast Faster Rail (LGC) project includes upgrades to local roads and a new road connection from Spanns Road to Thorsborne Street," the spokesperson said.

"Anyone who believes they may have an interest in the August Thorsborne estate or the land is encouraged to contact TMR."

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police are investigating the sudden death of a man in Kuranda.  (ABC News: Sharnie Kim)

Police in Far North Queensland are investigating the sudden death of a man in his 60s on a property on the Atherton Tablelands.

Officers attended the Kuranda address just before 10.30am and found the man dead, as well as a woman, also in her 60s, with significant facial injuries.

She was taken to Cairns hospital in a life-threatening condition.

Police say a crime scene has been declared and there is no ongoing threat to the community.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/b.title: Lamarre-Condon told Baird he 'won't exist' after break-up, trial hears
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/b.author: Phoebe Pin
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Beau Lamarre-Condon is going through messages he sent Jesse Baird months before his alleged murder. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Beau Lamarre-Condon sent a message to alleged murder victim Jesse Baird telling him he would not exist after their break-up.

He said he was intending to convey that he would not acknowledge Mr Baird in public after their split.

The former police officer said he never intended to cause Mr Baird physical harm.

Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied he intended to hurt Jesse Baird after their break-up months before the television presenter's alleged murder.

The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering his former partner and Mr Baird's new boyfriend Luke Davies at a Paddington terrace home on February 19, 2024.

He maintains both men died during separate struggles over Mr Lamarre-Condon's police pistol.

He told the court he threw Mr Baird's phone off Tom Uglys Bridge days after the shootings.

"I obviously did it because I didn't want any evidence of Jesse's phone on me," he said.

After meeting around October 2022, the pair broke up once in April 2023 and again in November 2023.

He accepted that Mr Baird asked him to refrain from contacting him after their break-up.

Mr Baird and Mr Davies were in a relationship before their deaths. (Instagram)

The court has heard Mr Lamarre-Condon frequently asked his friends for advice on draft text messages he was intending to send to Mr Baird during their relationship.

In one such draft message, the former police officer describes Mr Baird as a "manipulative player" after their break-up.

"You don’t need to worry about seeing me out etc because you won't exist and no further conversation needs to take place," he wrote in the message.

When asked to clarify what he meant by that, Mr Lamarre-Condon said it meant he would not "acknowledge" Mr Baird in public, not that he intended to "harm him or kill him".

He was also asked if he was performing "malevolent acts" against Mr Baird during December 2023.

"All I did was pour water in his petrol tank and that was in November," Mr Lamarre-Condon said.

He said this was in response to his belief that Mr Baird had scratched up Mr Lamarre-Condon's Tesla.

Leading up to the second and final break-up, Mr Lamarre-Condon said he wanted to check if Mr Baird was dating another man as part of an exclusive relationship.

"I didn't want to be involved in any cheating," he said.

Using the close friends Instagram function, Mr Lamarre-Condon said he posted a photo of a bouquet with a caption to "give the impression" that Mr Baird had sent the flowers.

Mr Lamarre-Condon says he wanted to give the impression Mr Baird sent him flowers. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

He said he hoped the man he suspected was dating Mr Baird would see the photo and tell Mr Lamarre-Condon if their arrangement was exclusive or not.

When Mr Baird confronted him about the photo, Mr Lamarre-Condon told the court he lied and pretended the flowers were for his mother.

He accepted he also lied when Mr Baird asked if he had gone through is phone, deleted messages and blocked the man Mr Lamarre-Condon thought he was dating.

Mr Lamarre-Condon said he later told Mr Baird the truth about both incidents.

Prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that he had been "gaslighting" Mr Baird.

"You could say that," Mr Lamarre-Condon replied.

Mr Hatfield accused Mr Lamarre-Condon of gaslighting Mr Baird. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Mr Hatfield pressed him on the nature of his relationship with Mr Baird, saying the television presenter felt "fairly ambivalent and "cool" about Mr Lamarre-Condon.

"Your problem is he didn't like you anywhere near as much as you liked him," he said.

"Your unrequited love turned into obsession".

"That is not the case," Mr Lamarre-Condon replied.

The court was shown another draft message written by Mr Lamarre-Condon, who asked a friend to send it to Mr Baird.

The message claimed Mr Lamarre-Condon had a cancerous tumour on his left shoulder and limb amputation was identified as the "worst case scenario".

In court Mr Lamarre-Condon said there were partial truths in the message, saying a Bondi Junction naturopath who examined his shoulder believed he had a "sporadic form of cancer".

Mr Lamarre-Condon says he sought alternative treatments for his tumour. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

He said he could not recall the naturopath's name and his family had been unable to track them down.

He said the naturopath recommended he get a biopsy on the lump, but Mr Lamarre-Condon said he instead sought "alternative treatment" options such as cannabis oil injections he purchased online.

Mr Hatfield put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that he "put a lot of pressure" on his friend to send the message to Mr Baird on his behalf.

"You were so desperate to get [Mr Baird] back you were prepared to do or say almost anything to get him back," he said.

Mr Lamarre-Condon rejected the suggestion.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/i.title: Absence of high school diploma brings down Indonesia's vice-president
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/i.author: Tim Swanston and Erwin Renaldi
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Gibran Rakabuming Raka has stepped down. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

Indonesia's vice-president Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation to parliament.

Pressure had been mounting on the politician to prove his academic credentials.

Parliament's upper house will ‌oversee the process of selecting a replacement.

Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has resigned in a move that could spell the end of a political alliance between the president and his predecessor.

The speaker of the People's Assembly of the Republic of Indonesia (MPR), Ahmad Muzani, said Mr Gibran had handed in his letter of resignation earlier today.

He said the letter would be processed by the MPR, which would take up to 60 days.

Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto said he had accepted Mr Gibran's resignation and expressed his "deepest gratitude for Mr Gibran’s dedication, commitment and hard work" in the role, including overseeing the implementation of many government programs.

Prabowo Subianto with Gibran Rakabuming Raka (left) in 2024.   (AFP: Indonesian Presidential Palace)

"During this time, he has visited 35 provinces and 149 regencies and cities, as well as inspected 303 government project sites firsthand," Mr Prabowo said.

"I wish Mr Gibran every success in his future career and strength and well-being for him and his entire family in the years ahead."

The 39-year-old son of former president Joko Widodo had been facing calls to resign for weeks after court rulings over his educational qualifications.

Indonesia's vice-president has resigned amid mounting calls for his impeachment. Here's what we know about why he resigned and who could be in the running for the position.

In October, the country's Constitutional Court found no compelling evidence that he held a high school diploma, which was required under Indonesian law to run for office.

The Supreme Court then ruled a high school equivalency certificate he had obtained was invalid.

Mr Gibran's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but after a meeting with Mr Prabowo on Tuesday he said he respected all criticism and feedback from the public.

"I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy," he said.

The resignation was submitted just hours before Indonesia's House of Representatives was set to meet over a petition signed by more than 120 politicians calling for Mr Gibran's impeachment.

Mr Gibran's decision comes amid a widening rift between President Prabowo Subianto and former president Joko Widodo, often called Jokowi.

Mr Jokowi supported Mr Prabowo by allowing his son to run alongside his former political rival. They stormed to power with a sweeping victory.

But cracks have since emerged.

After the alleged wire-tapping of the president and some of his most trusted allies, some experts wonder if it signals a growing rift between Indonesia's political heavyweights.

Last week, Indonesia's former chief of police along with several other senior police officers were detained over allegations they had been wire-tapping the president and other figures.

The former police chief, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, is widely viewed as a key ally of Mr Jokowi.

The allegations, while still being investigated, were described by a presidential spokesperson as "actions that may fall into the category of acts tending towards treason".

The petitioners in the Constitutional Court case against Mr Gibran said he submitted education documents ahead of the election that should not have been accepted by officials at the time.

University students protest in Jakarta earlier this week. (Reuters: Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana)

The applicants said the document was not a graduation certificate, but a supporting letter issued by Indonesia's Ministry of Education, based on a Certificate of Attendance and an academic transcript from UTS College in Sydney, previously known as UTS Insearch.

The vice-president's resignation also comes as protests take place in several cities in Indonesia over government policies and the handling of wildfires.

Indonesia President Prabowo Subianto will need to negotiate with his coalition partners and his own party to appoint a new vice-president. (Reuters)

University of Melbourne's Asian Studies professor Vedi Hadiz told the ABC the Indonesian president now faced "new problems" finding a suitable replacement for Mr Gibran.

"He will need to negotiate with his coalition partners, with his own party and potentially with the military to get a person that can satisfy all of them," he told The World's Girish Sawlani.

"The problem is that it's possible the person he chooses, or who gets over the line, will become an internal rival."

Mr Hadiz said if Mr Prabowo chose someone from another party within his coalition it could strengthen that party ahead of the 2029 presidential election, but if he gave the position to someone within his own party it could end up "annoying his coalition partners".

"What really needs to be looked at is whether the parties that are in his coalition manage to push forward one of their own or Prabowo plays it safe and picks a vice-president from his own party that he can trust but in the process annoys his coalition partners."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/s.title: Lawyer argues drug trafficker's driver should be spared more jail time
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/s.author: Matt Garrick
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Defence lawyer Ian Rowbottam (left) says Stephen Roche (right) should not spend any more time in prison. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

Stephen Roche has pleaded guilty to attempting to pervert the course of justice after trying to smuggle a fugitive drug trafficker out of Australia.

The prosecution is pushing for the Irish national to face prison time for the offence but his defence lawyer argued the 123 days he has already served on remand is enough.

Roche will return to court for sentencing on December 1.

An Irish national who drove a fugitive drug trafficker 4,680 kilometres across Australia in a rented van to help him evade justice is facing the prospect of prison time in Darwin.

Stephen Roche was arrested on the Northern Territory's Gove Peninsula in January last year over his role in helping New South Wales fugitive Hussein Chamas try to escape Australia onboard a yacht.

Under instruction from a shadowy international syndicate, Mr Roche picked up Chamas from an address in Sydney after the latter had used forged documents to flee a court-enforced stint in a rehab centre, and the pair embarked on a four-day road trip to the NT.

Their campervan broke down on the way to the remote East Arnhem Land region and the pair had to be towed into Nhulunbuy.

Alleged drug trafficker Hussein Chamas arrested in the Northern Territory. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

After their arrival, Chamas was met on the Gove Peninsula by a yacht waiting offshore from a local beach.

Along with two others, Chamas was then apprehended by an Australian Border Force patrol in the Arafura Sea as the wanted man attempted to evade justice over drug charges he faced in NSW.

The drug importer turned fugitive was jailed in August this year until at least 2030 after he pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to import a commercial quantity of methamphetamine and one count of trafficking a commercial quantity of cocaine.

In July, Mr Roche pleaded guilty to to attempting to pervert the course of justice over his role in the conspiracy, which was organised by an international syndicate the NT Supreme Court heard operated across multiple countries.

Prosecutor Hadi Mazloum, left, says Roche's offending "came from need rather than greed". (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

Prosecutor Hadi Mazloum said "offences of this kind are said to strike at the heart of the justice system" and that "a term of imprisonment is the only appropriate penalty".

Although currently released on bail, Mr Roche served four months on remand in Darwin's Holtze prison earlier this year.

The NT Supreme Court today heard arguments about whether Mr Roche should be spared further jail time, citing a serious, pre-existing back injury he still suffers from and a deterioration in his mental health.

Defence lawyer Ian Rowbottam said Mr Roche was a highly-educated former electronics expert whose life collapsed after the loss of his job and a marriage breakdown.

Stephen Roche pleaded guilty in the NT Supreme Court to attempting to pervert the course of justice. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"This is a man who has done time at Holtze — four months and three days — and in my submission there is no necessity for him to go back there," he said.

Mr Rowbottam said his client had shown remorse and entered an early guilty plea.

He also said Mr Roche was suffering from severe anxiety and depressive moods and was increasingly worried about the future of his estranged 14-year-old daughter.

Mr Mazloum agreed that Mr Roche's involvement in the plan, which was supposed to net him $30,000, was driven out of his dire financial circumstances at the time of the offending.

Chamas was jailed for 10 years in the NSW District Court in August after his arrest off the Gove Peninsula last year. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police )

"It came from need rather than greed," he said.

The prosecution acknowledged that Mr Roche's mental and physical health conditions would likely make future prison time "more burdensome".

"In my submission that doesn't displace the need for custody but it can moderate the length of time in custody," he said.

Justice Meredith Day Huntingford said she would consider the submissions in Mr Roche's "complex" case before sentencing him on December 1.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/k.title: Ancient stories in the stars revealed at Indigenous-owned observatory
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/k.author: Charlotte Martin and Jenae Madden
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-12/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Koonibba resident Stephanie Dudley looks through the telescope at the new observatory. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

A remote Indigenous community in South Australia is now the owner and operator of a stargazing facility in partnership with rocket launch company Southern Launch.

The Koonibba Observatory will allow tourists to learn more about Indigenous astronomy.

More than a dozen Koonibba community members have signed up to receive training from Southern Launch on how to operate the deep-sky telescope.

When Geraldine Ware was growing up in the remote Indigenous community of Koonibba, she would look up at the stars as Elders passed on the ancient stories of her people etched across the skies.

Now, her remote community in far west South Australia has opened a stargazing facility to help tell those stories.

The Koonibba Observatory was built in partnership with space services company Southern Launch and offers a vantage point from which to view the existing Koonibba Test Range facility, about 40 kilometres north-west of Ceduna on SA's far west coast.

Geraldine Ware addresses the crowd at the opening of the Koonibba Observatory. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Ms Ware, now chairperson of the Koonibba Community Aboriginal Corporation board, said it was exciting to think of the possibilities the facility would unlock for her community.

"We have got about 20 [people] to be trained up, so hopefully they'll get perfect at it, and then we can start our tourism in the future," she said.

"There are stories from when we were growing up, sitting around fires and looking at the stars, and we can see it, further on, looking out now."

The night skies on SA's far west coast are some of the darkest and cleanest in the world. (Supplied: Southern Launch)

The new observatory includes a Sky-Watcher Flextube 400P telescope, which is more than 150 centimetres long when extended.

However, not everyone from Koonibba, a community of roughly 140 people, more than 96 per cent of whom identify as First Nations, was confident the observatory could convey the ancient stories in the stars or the traditional owners' sacred relationship to the night sky.

Googatha* elder Aunty Sue Haseldine was born on Koonibba Country when it was still an Aboriginal mission, before its transfer to the Aboriginal Land Trust in 1975.

Sue Haseldine has concerns the complex relationship First Nations people have with the stars will be oversimplified for tourists. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

"The stories that have left Earth live on in the sky … I teach my grandchildren and great-grandchildren how to find their way home by the stars," she said.

She worried that guides might oversimplify Indigenous astronomy for visitors, rather than acknowledge its deeper cultural significance.

"Are they sharing the right [stories], or are they just doing something to keep the tourists happy?" Aunty Sue asked.

Southern Launch chief executive Lloyd Damp said the facility cost more than $1 million to build and was designed to draw in tourists.

He said it would also allow people to view the adjacent Koonibba Test Range, from which the Australian space company has launched commercial rockets since September 2020.

The telescope at the Koonibba Observatory extends 1.5 metres and will allow stargazing of the region's pristine skies. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

"The facility will support the community as more and more visitors come to watch rocket launches and satellite re-entries," Mr Damp said.

Koonibba Community Aboriginal Corporation chief executive Corey McLennan said the Koonibba Observatory was about the community's future.

"We want to create jobs, grow tourism and investment within our region and give our young people opportunities to learn about science, technology and space whilst also maintaining their connection to country."

The SR75 rocket launch from Southern Launch's Koonibba Test Range in May 2024. (Supplied: Southern Launch)

The head of the Australian Space Agency, Enrico Palermo, said Koonibba was "leading the world, not just Australia" in being the only place in the world that regularly receives capsules from space.

Its most recent mission was the successful re-entry earlier this month of the W-8 capsule from Varda Space Industries for commercial and US defence industries.

That W-8 capsule lifted off aboard Elon Musk's SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission.

Varda Space Industries's W-8 capsule landed in Koonibba after its earlier launch from a SpaceX aircraft. (Supplied: Southern Launch)

Southern Launch provides mission services for orbital launch, sub-orbital missions including hypersonic flight, orbital re-entries, and range services for the global space industry.

The company is headquartered in Adelaide and manages two spaceports, the Koonibba Test Range and the Eyre Peninsula Whalers Way Orbital Launch Complex, the latter of which is still under development.

*While Kokatha is the spelling often associated with the Traditional Owners of a large area in the west of South Australia, Googatha is sometimes the preferred spelling.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Death penalty sought for ex-SDF member over 2018 Toyama murders
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
TOYAMA – Public prosecutors Thursday demanded the death penalty for a 30-year-old former Self-Defense Forces member over the killings of a police officer and a school security guard in 2018 in the city of Toyama.

In a hearing of a lay-judge trial at Toyama District Court, the prosecution accused defendant Keita Shimazu of committing acts that “were among the most heinous of indiscriminate killings” and “showed an extraordinary disregard for human life.”

The trial is scheduled to conclude on Monday, with the ruling set to be handed down on Dec. 8.

Shimazu remained silent throughout the proceedings.

Past hearings centered on whether the crime of robbery-murder can be established and what sentence is appropriate based on the degree of Shimazu’s criminal responsibility.

On that subject, the prosecution said that his autism spectrum disorder had only a limited impact on his actions and that he had intended to take a police officer’s gun before the incident. They said he had acted rationally in accordance with a plan to kill police officers one after another.

Shimazu sought to satisfy his own desires by venting his accumulated grievances and frustrations on unrelated third parties, the prosecution added, describing his acts as “utterly misguided and extremely selfish.”

The defense said the crime of robbery-murder cannot be established, arguing that Shimazu was strongly affected by his autism and felt that the attacks were his only option.

According to the indictment, Shimazu fatally stabbed a 46-year-old police officer, Kenichi Inaizumi, and robbed him of his pistol at the Okuda police box June 26, 2018. Shimazu is also accused of fatally shooting 68-year-old school security guard Shinichi Nakamura near the main gate of a nearby elementary school.

In a hearing Tuesday, bereaved relatives demanded the death penalty, saying that the defendant’s crimes are absolutely unforgivable. Nakamura’s widow said she wants Shimazu to apologize sincerely before he dies.

Shimazu was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2021 for murder and theft. The Kanazawa branch of the Nagoya High Court overturned the ruling the next year, saying that the sentence should be reconsidered on the premise that the crime of robbery-murder could be established. The case was sent back to the district court after the Supreme Court upheld the high court judgment in 2024.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Public prosecutors demand death penalty for former Self-Defense Forces member Keita Shimazu. The 30-year-old former Self Defense Forces member is accused of killing a police officer and a school security guard. The trial is scheduled to conclude on Monday, with the ruling set to be handed down on Dec. 8.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: How Apollo’s SoftBank ties unlocked an unprecedented OpenAI bet
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Laura Benitez
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
If there’s one relationship that illustrates how private credit is enabling some of the most consequential AI investments, it’s Apollo Global Management’s with SoftBank Group.

Since 2021, Apollo has provided and arranged more than $15 billion of debt for SoftBank across multiple deals, people familiar with the matter said, helping to fuel Maysayoshi Son’s nearly $65 billion bet on OpenAI. From lending tied to the ChatGPT maker’s value to a loan backed by a flagship fund, SoftBank has become one of Apollo’s largest corporate borrowers.

But Apollo is also beginning to contend with the limits of its SoftBank lending as it takes a more defensive approach to AI investing. How far Apollo can go in bankrolling one of OpenAI’s biggest investors is a crucial test for whether private credit will be able to profitably fill gaps in AI financing beyond the reach of traditional lenders.

A portion of Apollo’s SoftBank lending has been made through its insurer Athene, which held at least $4.8 billion of SoftBank-related debt at the end of September. While the amount represents only about 1% of Athene’s gross invested assets, it is one of the company’s largest individual exposures and brings Athene toward the edge of its concentration limit for a single borrower.

Meanwhile, SoftBank has been hit hard by a broader reckoning for the AI trade. On Tuesday, the company reported a $7 billion loss after several of its tech investments lost value. SoftBank’s shares have plunged more than 50% since June, while its credit risks have risen. OpenAI also scaled back its ambitions in a recent fundraising round.

Some Apollo executives privately acknowledge that the recent selloff in AI stocks and bonds has given the asset manager pause. It’s unlikely that Apollo will pledge more OpenAI-related capital for SoftBank until there’s more clarity in the market, they said, though there might be room to increase an existing $9.2 billion net-value-asset loan slightly.

“Apollo is a clear example of how private credit is bridging the capital gap for the AI buildout,” said Anna Wu, an investment strategist and founder of Floodlines Research. “But risk is starting to surface at the edges.”

This account of how Apollo became a major SoftBank financier draws on interviews with people with knowledge of how the partnership developed. They asked not to be named discussing private information. Representatives for Apollo and SoftBank declined to comment.

Apollo had spent years trying to crack SoftBank, pitching financing ideas that could go where the banks couldn’t. Rajeev Misra, then one of the most powerful — and polarizing — figures in Masayoshi Son’s inner circle, gave the firm its opening in 2021.

Back then, SoftBank already had major lenders like Goldman Sachs Group and JPMorgan Chase at the ready. But assembling a large bank syndicate takes time, and SoftBank needed the cash quickly. Misra asked if Apollo could arrange a complex $4.5 billion loan in just 45 days.

Apollo dealmakers worked long hours and dealt with punishing time differences to assemble the record-breaking NAV loan by the deadline. The deal was novel and involved borrowing against the paper value of more than 150 companies in SoftBank’s Vision Fund 2.

Importantly, Apollo found a way to make the deal profitable by mirroring how banks handle big borrowings. On top of its 1% commission for arranging the loan, Apollo typically earns fees from distributing portions of debt to other investors. In this case, some of the NAV loan was sold to Pacific Investment Management.

Representatives for Pimco and JPMorgan did not respond to requests for comment. Goldman Sachs declined to comment.

The complex structure of the loan also allowed Apollo to negotiate a higher coupon. The debt, due in 2029, pays a floating interest rate of 7.3%, filings earlier this year showed. That compares with the roughly 4% cost of SoftBank’s existing debt stack.

Misra, a former Deutsche Bank AG trader, played a crucial role in selling the complicated Apollo deal inside SoftBank. He’d previously cultivated a relationship with Apollo’s head honchos, including Chief Executive Officer Marc Rowan, and vouched for the asset manager when SoftBank Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto expressed doubts.

A representative for Misra, who left SoftBank in 2024, declined to comment.

Over the last 15 months, Apollo increased the size of the NAV loan twice to $9.2 billion. In August, it stepped in as the only nonbank lender when SoftBank struggled to secure a separate $10 billion loan.

At the same time, Apollo has broadened its lending across the AI ecosystem. It has in recent months participated in large-scale financings for Broadcom, Anthropic and SpaceX.

Even as it takes big risks, Apollo has made sure protections are built in. The $10 billion loan to SoftBank that it participated in is guaranteed by the company and has clauses that guard against a steep drop in OpenAI’s value, including early repayment.

The NAV loan to Vision Fund 2, however, is running up against the limits of its own success.

Apollo has been able to increase the loan because of OpenAI’s extraordinary growth — the latest funding round puts the startup’s value at $1.25 trillion. But OpenAI’s ascent has also transformed Vision Fund 2 from a diverse collection of investments into one dominated by a single holding, with the AI company making up about three-quarters of the fund’s fair value.

Apollo designed the NAV loan so that OpenAI can’t account for more than a fifth of its collateral, theoretically insulating the debt against a blow-up. Nevertheless, its loan-to-value ratio has increased since it was first extended, even as the metric remains below 20%.

Whether or not Apollo slows further lending to SoftBank, the asset manager has already reaped longer-term benefits. Apollo used its experience from 2021 to pitch NAV loans to other fund managers. Last year alone, Apollo signed almost $20 billion worth of NAV loans for Athene that went to private equity firms including Vista Equity and Warburg Pincus.

The deals are typically structured so they can be funded with insurance capital, allowing junk-rated borrowers like SoftBank to access bigger pools of capital reserved for investment-grade debt.

The scale of funding needed for AI — over $5 trillion by 2030, JPMorgan estimates — will mean more “customized financing” like SoftBank’s NAV loan, according to Benjamin Forestier, an affiliate professor at École Polytechnique. But that also raises risks if “technology valuations suddenly deteriorate,” he said.

“The real question is not whether we can find enough capital to build all these data centers,” Forestier said. “It is whether they will generate sufficient cash flows to justify the capital invested.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: SoftBank has been hit hard by a broader reckoning for the AI trade. The scale of funding needed for AI will mean more funding needed by 2030.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Vance, Rubio, Ossoff and Buttigieg lead 2028 White House hopefuls, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
WASHINGTON – Four potential contenders in the 2028 race for the White House have caught American voters’ attention with their early jockeying: Republicans JD Vance and Marco Rubio and Democrats Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

None of the four has yet formally launched a campaign and the parties’ 2028 nominating contests are more than a year away, leaving plenty of time for new contenders to emerge and for voters’ views to change.

Some 45% of Republican voters polled said they believed Secretary of State Rubio would be an “excellent” presidential candidate, with 43% saying the same of Vice President Vance. Former Transportation Secretary Buttigieg and U.S. Senator Ossoff, of Georgia, each got that rating from 29% of Democratic voters.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: JD Vance and Marco Rubio and Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg are all potential presidential candidates. None of the four has yet formally launched a campaign.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Muji operator fails to delete unnecessary credit card data
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Ryohin Keikaku, the operator of the Muji retail chain, said Thursday that the company’s failure to delete unnecessary customer credit card information was a factor behind a data breach involving up to 1.09 million credit card records through unauthorized access.

“We must feel a deep sense of responsibility,” Ryohin Keikaku President Satoshi Shimizu said at a news conference. “There were shortcomings in our data management.”

Ryohin Keikaku had retained full credit card numbers of its “Muji Card” credit cards, which it used to identify customers when granting rewards until July 2021, when it switched to using other information for identification. The company continued to retain the data despite adopting a policy of deleting full credit card numbers.

The company said it is continuing to investigate the matter, as it remains unclear whether the data retention was intentional.

Ryohin Keikaku detected unauthorized access on Oct. 29. It believes that up to around 27.26 million customer records, including the email addresses of registered users, may have been compromised.

In addition, around 270,000 member accounts were targeted by credential stuffing attacks, in which attackers attempt to log in to accounts using combinations of IDs and passwords exposed in data breaches at other companies. The Muji operator has suspended its online store since Friday as a security measure.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Ryohin Keikaku says failure to delete unnecessary credit card information was a factor behind a data breach. The company says it is continuing to investigate the matter. It believes up to 27.26 million customer records, including the email addresses of registered users, may have been compromised.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Five arrested in crackdown on rip-offs targeting foreign visitors in Tokyo
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Tokyo’s Metropolitan Police Department has arrested five people in a crackdown on rip-offs targeting foreign visitors at restaurants and bars in Tokyo’s Kabukicho nightlife district.

The five include the managers of two restaurants, Ekwelundu Ambrose Osita, a 62-year-old Nigerian national, and Arata Kashiwabara, a 35-year-old resident of Yokohama.

The crackdown, which mobilized about 160 officers, including riot police, came in response to a surge in cases of foreign visitors being overcharged at Kabukicho establishments.

According to the MPD, the Shinjuku Police Station, which covers the district, received about 340 complaints about such cases by the end of October, up by roughly 200 from a year earlier. About 70% of the victims were foreign citizens. In one case, ¥9.6 million was allegedly charged to a customer’s credit card.

The establishments managed by Ekwelundu and Kashiwabara allegedly overcharged about ¥3.4 million.

On Wednesday, Ekwelundu and one of the five were arrested on suspicion of operating an unlicensed business that entertains male customers. The other three, including Kashiwabara, were arrested on suspicion of obstructing a police inspection by locking the entrance of an establishment.

Ekwelundu has remained silent, while the other four have admitted to the allegations against them.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: The five include the managers of two restaurants and two other restaurants. The crackdown came in response to a surge in cases of foreign visitors being overcharged at Kabukicho establishments. About 70% of the victims were foreign citizens.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Nvidia’s Asian supply chain prepares for life after Huang
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Wen-yee Lee
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
TAIPEI/SEOUL – U.S. chip giant Nvidia’s partners and suppliers across Asia, from memory chip powerhouse South Korea to advanced chipmaking hub Taiwan, are redrawing plans in case Chief Executive Jensen Huang is ousted over reports of two extramarital affairs.

Nvidia’s board is meeting late on Wednesday to decide on Huang’s future, a source familiar with the matter said, in a sharp shift of tactics from Sunday, when the board expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.

“We will support whatever capacity Nvidia needs, but the new CEO may not be as aggressive as Jensen,” said an executive at a Taiwan supplier who feared his company’s expansion could slow if a successor was not as quick to tie up manufacturing capacity.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Nvidia's partners and suppliers across Asia are redrawing plans in case Chief Executive Jensen Huang is ousted. Huang is accused of two extramarital affairs.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Chinese AI firms rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity as scandal stirs fear of curbs
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
BEIJING – Chinese artificial intelligence companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China on concerns that a scandal involving the U.S. chipmaker’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their remote use of advanced processors, three people familiar with the matter said.

The moves underline concern among Chinese technology companies over the potential closing of a gap in U.S. export controls. Seeking to protect U.S. dominance of the critical sector, Washington restricts exports to China of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips, but Chinese companies can access such processors remotely by renting computing power at data centers overseas.

A major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally whether to lock in overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some companies have contacted data-center operators about reserving it, the people said. https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: In the competition for cultural influence, AI has a default country
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
Artificial intelligence is quietly reshaping the global contest for cultural influence. Unlike traditional search engines, which present users with competing options, AI chatbots increasingly make the choice for them. And when asked an open-ended question about family life, culture or tradition, they tend to choose one country over and over again: Japan. Confused? You’re not alone.

“What values shape family life in ______? Choose the place yourself. Be brief.” Researchers at the University of the Basque Country and Cardiff University put that question to eight AI models in 24 languages in 31,680 variations on festivals, food and family. Between 43% and 78% of references, depending on the model, stayed at home. Set those aside, and six of the eight models reached for the same country: Japan.

Call that a favorite and you misread it. A favorite is picked against alternatives. Here nobody offered any. The blank carried no preference and the machines filled it with the same place again and again. That is a default, and the power of a default is that it never has to win again. Most people never question it.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
SEOUL – South Korea captain Son Heung-min said on Thursday he and four teammates had resolved their differences and that they wanted to set a good example for the next generation of players.

In a joint statement posted by the Korea Football Association, Son, Lee Jae-sung, Hwang Hee-chan, Hwang In-beom and Kim Min-jae apologized to fans and said they had cleared the air during their ongoing training camp in Doha.

Reports of a rift in the dressing room began after the team’s early exit at this year’s World Cup, which led to the departure of coach Hong Myung-bo.

“At this call-up, we came together and honestly shared our thoughts about the national team,” the statement read.

“By listening to each other directly and explaining things we hadn’t been able to discuss fully until now, we came to understand each other’s positions better.”

Reports in local media had said some players were frustrated with the squad’s veteran leadership group, and that Hwang Hee-chan, Hwang In-beom and Kim Min-jae were ready to retire from the national team after a match against Uzbekistan last month.

“It is not true at all that we tried to push through specific demands by making retirement a condition,” the players wrote.

“The reason we did not explain each of the related reports until now is that we believed issues concerning the national team should first be thoroughly discussed and resolved internally.”

The players said they were keen to move on.

“Respecting and trusting each other’s roles and responsibilities, we will work together to set a good example for the young players who will write the next page of Korean football,” they added.

South Korea plays Saudi Arabia in Al Rayyan on Friday before taking on Qatar in Doha on Tuesday.
