https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: LDP, JIP and DPP submit Lower House seat-cut bill, driving contentious reform
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Kenji Yoshida
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The ruling Liberal Democratic Party, its coalition partner the Japan Innovation Party (JIP) and the opposition Democratic Party for the People (DPP) jointly submitted a bill Thursday to cut 31 Lower House seats, advancing a contentious electoral overhaul.

All cuts would come from proportional representation seats, leaving the number of single-member districts unchanged. The three parties aim to pass the bill by Dec. 12, when the current Diet session is scheduled to end.

“I hope the three parties will work together to secure the bill’s passage,” said Katsunobu Kato, senior lawmaker and head of the LDP’s task force for political system reform, during a meeting with his counterparts Thursday morning.

The LDP and the JIP, also known as Nippon Ishin no Kai, submitted a similar bill in June that would have cut 45 proportional seats — roughly 10% of the chamber’s total — if broader electoral reform legislation failed to pass within a year of the law’s promulgation.

Facing opposition resistance, however, the LDP proposed a smaller reduction, citing a projected 6.7% decline in Japan’s population between 2015 and 2030. The three parties formally signed the agreement last month.

The revised bill would also merge the Chugoku and Shikoku proportional representation blocs, reducing the total number of blocs nationwide from 11 to 10.

Proportional seats would be allocated using a modified Sainte-Lague system, which is intended to give smaller parties a better chance of winning seats than the current D’Hondt method.

At the same time, candidates who run in both tiers and lose in their single-member districts would need at least one-sixth of the valid votes cast in their district to qualify for a proportional seat, in a change from the current one-tenth threshold.

Komeito, the largest party in the Lower House’s main opposition bloc, has argued that cutting only proportional representation seats would give greater weight to single-member districts. The Japanese Communist Party has also voiced its opposition, saying the package would make it harder for smaller parties to win seats and weaken their representation.

The proposed legislation will also leave proportional representation seats vacant if a party lacks enough candidates to fill them, rather than reallocating them to other parties as is done under the current system.

If enacted, the changes would take effect alongside a separate law redrawing single-member district boundaries based on the 2025 census, potentially in 2027. The LDP, JIP and DPP together hold majorities in both chambers, strengthening the bill’s prospects of passage.

The LDP has proposed starting deliberations by the Lower House special committee next week, but the parties have yet to agree on a timetable.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: The three parties aim to pass the bill by Dec. 12, when the current Diet session is scheduled to end. The LDP and the JIP, also known as Nippon Ishin no Kai, submitted a similar bill in June that would have cut 45 proportional seats.

The genre-melding dual narrative of the devil’s fantastical adventures in Stalinist Moscow is structured as a novel within a novel: Bulgakov juxtaposes the supernatural action in Russia with a realistic narrative set in historical Judea, detailing the meeting between Pontius Pilate and Yeshua, the Hebrew name for Jesus of Nazareth.

This structure makes the story difficult to transpose for visual media, which explains why it historically has been tackled mostly in experimental theater. However, the last decade has seen a marked increase in mainstream adaptations. The Bolshoi Ballet’s 2021 version, Australia’s Belvoir Street Theatre’s production in 2023 and Michael Lockshin’s 2024 film have all garnered popular and critical acclaim.

Japan’s corporate goods inflation has accelerated for the first time in three months, adding to evidence of persistent price pressures that support the case for a Bank of Japan interest rate increase next month.

The measure of prices for goods traded between Japanese firms climbed 7.1% in October from a year earlier, accelerating from 6.8% in the previous month, the Bank of Japan reported Thursday. Economists had forecast the pace of gains to ease. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.7%, the fastest since May.

The figures add to signs of persistent upward pressure on the cost of living as the Iran war takes a toll on the nation, which is heavily reliant on imports of oil, raw materials and food.

The BOJ acknowledged last month that underlying inflation has hit its price target, and Thursday’s data would help the central bank make the case for another rate increase when its board next sets policy on Dec. 18.

Pricing in overnight index swaps implies a 82% probability of a rate increase at that meeting. The yen traded around ¥159.62 per dollar Thursday morning in Tokyo, approaching the key threshold of ¥160, highlighting another factor that could push consumer prices higher.

October marks the start of the second half of Japan’s fiscal year, when many businesses tend to implement price changes.

The advance in the producer price index was led by oil and its related products as crude surged to levels exceeding $100 per barrel last month amid renewed concerns over the Middle East conflict.

Japan has confirmed its first bird flu case of the season at a poultry farm in Kyoto Prefecture, the government announced Thursday.

The avian influenza has killed 14 birds at the farm in Kameoka in the prefecture, the farm ministry said. The country has begun culling about 200,000 chickens there after testing confirmed the virus.

“The government is asking poultry farmers to make sure they follow strict hygiene,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said.

Agriculture minister Arata Takebe told reporters that a bird flu outbreak could happen anywhere in the country.

“We ask each farm to carry out early detection, ensure early notification and implement thorough hygiene management,” he said.

According to a food price trend survey by the ministry, the average price of a pack of 10 eggs in Japan in October was ¥312, a record high since the survey began in August 2003. An avian flu spread could further raise egg prices ahead of the year-end high-demand season.

“We’ll thoroughly implement measures to prevent a spread (of bird flu) so as not to affect supply and demand,” Takebe said.

LOS ANGELES, UNITED STATES – French Open champion Mirra Andreeva stormed past Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 6-0 to reach the last four of the WTA Finals on Wednesday as Elina Svitolina kept her bid on track with a three-set win over Karolina Muchova.

Russian 19-year-old Andreeva held her nerve after falling behind 4-1 in the opening set — winning the last 11 games to seal the round-robin victory in just 62 minutes.

“Oh my God, I’m even happier than I was after my first match,” Andreeva said. “I feel like I can play another two matches, I’m so full of energy. I’m so pumped up. I’m so happy.”

Andreeva, whose three titles this year include her maiden major at Roland Garros, is making her singles debut in the elite season-ending event.

The world No. 3 seemed to be feeling the nerves in the early going against second-ranked Sabalenka.

Irked that she had given up a break with a double fault, she was able to flip the switch, dealing handily with Sabalenka’s big serves and pushing the Belarusian star back with her own big groundstrokes.

Andreeva crucially kept momentum on her side with a break for a 3-0 lead in the second set.

Sabalenka, trailing 0-40, saved three break points, but Andreeva gave herself another with a swinging volley winner and grabbed another break when a Sabalenka forehand flew just long.

The increasingly demoralized Sabalenka had no answer. After the Belarusian smacked a backhand into the net to give her opponent match point Andreeva polished things off with a service winner.

It was another disappointing performance for the 28-year-old Sabalenka, whose three wins this season include prestigious back-to-back victories at Indian Wells and Miami but no Grand Slams.

Making her sixth straight Finals appearance, Sabalenka can still advance if she beats Svitolina in their final round-robin match on Friday.

Svitolina roared back from a set down to beat Muchova 3-6, 6-2, 6-2.

Ukrainian veteran Svitolina lifted the WTA Finals trophy in 2018 but hadn’t been back to the elite season-ending event since 2019.

She got off to a rocky start against Muchova, who broke Svitolina three times in the opening set.

Trailing 2-1 on serve in the second Svitolina found her range, winning five straight games to force a third set.

“I was not happy with the first set,” Svitolina said. “I didn’t play as well. I just made some adjustments, tactical adjustments.

“I think it helped me also to be more aggressive, because I was too passive in the first set,” Svitolina said.

Muchova’s second round-robin defeat coupled with Andreeva’s victory means the Czech was eliminated from semi-final contention.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Nomura explores possible sale of Laser Digital crypto unit
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Nomura Holdings is exploring the sale of its crypto business Laser Digital Holdings, after losses at the Zurich-based entity last year pushed the brokerage’s entire European operation into the red.

Japan’s largest securities firm is talking to potential buyers including Marex, which is evaluating the deal, according to people familiar with the matter. No final decision has been made, and Nomura could end up selling it to another party or holding onto the business, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is private.

Spokespeople for Nomura and Marex declined to comment.

The talks come after severe crypto market swings caused significant enough losses at Laser to drag Nomura’s European operations to a quarterly loss. Management acknowledged the “considerable volatility” of crypto-related earnings and moved to tighten risk controls. The development was a setback for Nomura’s CEO Kentaro Okuda, who highlighted Laser last year as part of the firm’s efforts to capture “future business opportunities.”

Founded in 2022 and led partly by longtime Nomura veteran Steven Ashley, Laser provides trading and asset-management services to institutional investors, as well as making venture-capital investments in crypto startups. It’s one of a few Nomura offshoots focused on digital assets. Others include Boostry and Komainu, which specialize in tokenizing financial products and custody services, respectively.

Late last year, Laser poached a trio of derivatives traders from Mike Novogratz’s Galaxy Digital, and more recently obtained a license to provide cryptoasset exchange services in Japan. In May, it received conditional approval for a U.S. national trust-bank charter.

Marex offers a suite of digital-asset tools including execution, clearing, financing and structured products. In October, the company expanded its offering with the launch of a new over-the-counter rolling spot crypto product for institutional clients.

The wider digital-assets market has been stuck in a prolonged slump. Bitcoin, the largest token, is today trading below $74,000, more than 40% off its peak. The value of cryptocurrency transactions in Japan, including margin trades, more than halved from a year earlier in the first nine months of this year to ¥17.2 trillion ($108.5 billion), according to data from the Japan Virtual and Crypto assets Exchange Association.

Line Xenesis, the crypto unit of Japanese internet company LY, in which Nomura took a minority stake in 2019, shut its Line Bitmax cryptocurrency exchange in June.

Still, Japan is moving toward allowing exchange-traded funds that invest in cryptocurrencies, with the first products potentially listing as early as next year. That could benefit asset managers that put ETFs together as well as brokerages that distribute them. The government also plans to lower the tax rate on gains from cryptocurrency investments.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Nomura Holdings is exploring the sale of its crypto business Laser Digital Holdings. The talks come after severe crypto market swings caused significant enough losses at Laser to drag Nomura’s European operations to a quarterly loss.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Yuki Watanabe, the alleged leader of a Philippines-based Japanese crime group, denied a charge of robbery resulting in death at the first hearing of his trial at the Tokyo District Court on Wednesday in connection with a series of robbery cases in Japan.

At his lay judge trial, Watanabe said that he merely assisted his accomplices, claiming that his role was limited to aiding and abetting. He also pleaded not guilty to some of the other charges, saying he had not conspired with the others.

He is the third of the four senior members of the group who were arrested and indicted to stand trial. Closing arguments and the verdict are scheduled for Dec. 2 and Dec. 14, respectively.

Among the other three, Toshiya Fujita, 42, accused of robbery resulting in death, has been sentenced to life imprisonment by the Tokyo District Court and is appealing the ruling to a higher court. The trial of Kiyoto Imamura, 42, has yet to begin.

Tomonobu Kojima, 48, who served as a recruiter for the group, was sentenced to 20 years in prison for aiding and abetting robbery resulting in injury, and his sentence has been finalized.

In its opening statement on Wednesday, the prosecutors said that Watanabe had established a base for a fraud group in the Philippines, with Kojima and Fujita joining him. In addition, Imamura, who led a separate fraud group, also used the facility.

The prosecutors stated that the four were detained by local authorities by around April 2021 and held at an immigration detention facility on the outskirts of Manila. Also, Watanabe and the others needed money to escape from the detention facility or flee abroad and therefore cooperated with Imamura, who went by the alias “Luffy” and had been directing the robberies. It was alleged that Watanabe was involved in planning the robbery resulting in death and sent messages to the perpetrators, such as, “Let’s target the house when only the wife is there.”

The defense also made its opening statement, arguing that Imamura and Fujita were the principal perpetrators and that Watanabe “did not have a say in the plans or methods.” He admitted to the 12 other cases of special fraud for which he was indicted.

According to the indictment, Watanabe was involved as a mastermind in seven robbery cases that occurred in four of Japan’s 47 prefectures, including Tokyo, between October 2021 and January 2023. In one of the seven cases, perpetrators fatally assaulted a 90-year-old woman and stole luxury items, including watches, in the city of Komae in Tokyo.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Yuki Watanabe denies a charge of robbery resulting in death at the first hearing of his trial at the Tokyo District Court on Wednesday. He is the third of the four senior members of the group who were arrested and indicted to stand trial. The trial of Kiyoto Imamura, 42, has yet to begin

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Japan to contribute ¥294 million to Gaza’s healthcare system
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
CAIRO – Japan will provide ¥294 million ($1.84 million) to improve medical services in the Gaza Strip, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Wednesday.

The funds will be used to strengthen the coordination between emergency medical teams in the area.

A ceremony to sign the agreement between the Japanese government and the WHO was held in the Palestinian city of Ramallah in the West Bank on Tuesday.

“As profound challenges persist in Gaza, the needs of the Palestinian people extend beyond immediate humanitarian relief,“ Japanese Ambassador for Palestinian Affairs Katsuhiko Araike said.

“They also require the restoration of essential infrastructure, the strengthening of public institutions and the sustained provision of basic services that enable communities to rebuild their lives with dignity and hope,” he added.

Despite a ceasefire in Gaza between Israel and the Islamic group Hamas coming into effect in October last year, Israel has continued military operations in the territory. More than 1,600 people have been killed in post-ceasefire attacks in Gaza, according to local health officials.

A peace plan by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump for Gaza has stalled due to disagreements between Hamas and Israel over the disarmament of the group.

Already struggling with stalled reconstruction efforts and a strained healthcare system, Gaza has experienced heavier rainfall coinciding with the onset of winter, which has caused flooding at medical facilities there.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Japan will provide ¥294 million ($1.84 million) to improve medical services in Gaza Strip. The funds will be used to strengthen the coordination between emergency medical teams in the area. A ceremony to sign the agreement between the Japanese government and the WHO was held in the Palestinian city of Ramallah on Tuesday.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Nvidia working with outside firm to identify CEO candidates
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Nvidia’s board has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for CEO Jensen Huang following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who is reportedly suspected of spying for China, a person familiar with the situation said.

The board is weighing the idea of naming a temporary chief while searching for a permanent one, the person said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Directors were meeting on Wednesday to discuss Huang’s fate, according to people familiar with the situation. The Wall Street Journal said earlier that the board was preparing to oust Huang, citing unidentified people familiar with the matter. Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nvidia’s board has been facing a succession crisis since Sunday, when Huang admitted that he’d had an affair with Alice Huang, a data center executive at a company that is one of Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customers. The New York Times has reported that Alice Huang was suspected of operating as an agent on behalf of the Chinese government.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been in a succession crisis since Sunday. The company has been facing reports of extramarital affairs. The Wall Street Journal said earlier that the board was preparing to oust Huang.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Hiroshima find may unearth new history of human arrival in Japan
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
HATSUKAICHI, HIROSHIMA PREF. – Excavation is underway at an archaeological site in Hiroshima Prefecture, with both researchers and local residents anxious to unravel the mystery of when and how humans arrived in the Japanese archipelago.

The Kanmuri ruins in the Yoshiwa district of Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima Prefecture, generated excitement in 2024 when a stone tool that is likely to be the oldest such artifact in Japan was discovered at the site.

Sadakatsu Kunitake, 51, chief researcher at the Nara National Research Institute for Cultural Properties, which is spearheading the excavation, said that the Kanmuri ruins are “the finest archaeological site in Japan that connects (the country) to the world.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: Hit spy drama ‘Vivant’ heads to the big screen
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Alyssa I. Smith
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
Controversial spy drama “Vivant” is taking its tangled web of espionage, double-crosses and intrigue to the big screen.

A film version of the hit TBS drama starring Masato Sakai will open in theaters Dec. 4, according to an announcement made immediately after the second-season finale aired Nov. 8. The film promises an epic new adventure while continuing the season’s storyline.

The second-season finale was a ratings hit, drawing an average household audience share of 21.8% in the Kanto region, according to figures released by Video Research on Nov. 9. The figure was the series’ highest yet, surpassing the first-season finale’s 19.6% share. Among commercial dramas aired since 2019, the beginning of the Reiwa Era, the recent “Vivant” finale ranks second, behind the 32.7% share recorded by the TBS series “Hanzawa Naoki” for its finale in 2020.

A sprawling spy tale of competing loyalties and hidden agendas, “Vivant” debuted in July 2023. It follows Yusuke Nogi (Sakai), a seemingly ordinary trading company employee who becomes embroiled in a covert operation involving Beppan, an elite secret military intelligence unit within Japan’s Self-Defense Forces. Tasked with fighting threats to national security, Nogi becomes entangled with a mysterious organization known as Tent, led by Nogon Beki (Koji Yakusho) and based in the fictional Republic of Balka.

The second season, which began airing in July, raised the stakes with the introduction of a fictional Chinese intelligence agency as an antagonist to Beppan. The portrayal drew criticism in China, with real-world ramifications extending beyond the screen. The season also introduced a Russian intelligence angle, hinting at a wider international conflict in the upcoming film.

In a post-finale video, Sakai hinted that the film would reveal the truth behind several unusual details introduced in the final episode. “The new adventure will be on the big screen,” he said.

TBS has also announced that the film will receive a simultaneous IMAX release. Advance tickets went on sale at midnight on Nov. 8.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Nvidia fallout puts trade truce to the test as Xi welcomes Trump
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s third summit of the year with U.S. President Donald Trump is going off script before their meetings even get underway, as the spy allegations engulfing Nvidia’s Jensen Huang reopen old rifts.

For years, Huang had been most the prominent U.S. tech executive advocating for greater engagement with China as he lobbied for looser export controls on semiconductors. Now, bombshell accusations he conducted an affair with an alleged Chinese spy are giving lawmakers in Washington ammunition to tighten curbs, days before a major leaders’ summit in the Chinese technology hub of Shenzhen.

At stake is a yearlong trade truce between the world’s top economies expiring in January — its renewal hinges, in large part, on the U.S. pausing new restrictions on tech shipments to China. David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, on Wednesday signaled the furor was posing a test to bilateral relations during an already “bumpy” stretch.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Chinese leader Xi Jinping's third summit of the year with U.S. President Donald Trump is going off script before their meetings even get underway. Huang had been most prominent U.s. tech executive advocating for greater engagement with China.

https://www.dw.com/en/uk-court-convicts-.title: UK court convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on journalists
https://www.dw.com/en/uk-court-convicts-.text:
A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's goverment. One was also convicted of planning a violent attack against them.

Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying in dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.

British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force.

The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them.

The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them.

The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters.

One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence.

A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges.

The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces.

The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats.

Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December.

"This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division.

The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online

"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said.

Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot.

Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023.

In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024.

A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them."

Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets.

British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year.

Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September, after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site.

Three men were indicted in the US in relation that plot this week, while two others currently face charges in the UK.

But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade.

Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue.

France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement.

European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.

https://www.dw.com/en/impeachment-how-it.title: Impeachment: How it works and why Trump should be worried
https://www.dw.com/en/impeachment-how-it.text:
Pete Hegseth, Bill Clinton and Donald Trump (twice so far): attempts to impeach political figures are becoming common. The failure rate looks high, but according to experts, conviction is not always the aim.

Pete Hegseth, US President Donald Trump's secretary of war, described the failed efforts to impeach him this week as "farce" and "sabotage".

The case, built on an accusation that Hegseth waged war on Iran without the proper congressional approval, always looked a long shot. But many observers believe it could be the first in a wave of impeachment attempts, possibly headlined by a third attempt to impeach Trump.

DW takes a look at impeachments and why you may be hearing more about them.

While there are global variations in how impeachment works, in the US it is a process that allows the legislature (usually Congress, state or tribal legislature) to bring charges against an elected figure — a judge or a president, for example. These are not criminal charges but can result in the removal of the accused party from their post.

For federal impeachment, once an impeachment case is raised in the House of Representatives, it must be heard in a trial in the Senate, with both sides able to cross-examine relevant figures. However, for a conviction to be obtained, a two-thirds majority must be reached, a factor which often limits the chances of success given the partisan nature of US politics.

It is a simple process to introduce and, once started, the case is heard within 48 hours, as was the case with Hegseth.

Given only eight people, all judges, have been impeached since the first case concluded in 1799, the odds of impeaching a high-level politician are long. The two-thirds majority rule has meant that impeachment is instead often used to draw attention to perceived misdemeanors and potentially force a resignation.

"Using impeachment threats as a signaling device is a fairly old tactic, but it has certainly become more common in the Trump-[Joe] Biden era," Frank O Bowman III, a law professor at the University of Missouri and author of a forthcoming book on impeachment and Donald Trump, told DW.

That, added Keith Whittingtona Yale Law School professor and impeachment expert, was not what impeachment was intended to do.

"Congress has tended to take an extremely partisan approach to making use of the power. That has doomed any possibility of conviction and removal," he told DW.

"The possibility of partisan use of the impeachment power became evident very quickly in American history, but the founders certainly would not have intended or hoped that the impeachment power would be used as a partisan weapon or a means of partisan messaging."

The recent midterm results  will see the Democrats control both houses of Congress from next year, meaning there is a greater chance that the US President could be impeached for an unprecedented third time. He was acquitted on "charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress" in 2020 and then on the charge of "incitement of insurrection" in 2021.

Bowman consulted in both cases. "In my view, they should have succeeded," he said. "But they didn't and, from the perspective of the average member of the public, it's just fuss and bother, but nothing happened. So why are we even bothering? I do think that in the public mind, impeachment has been significantly devalued."

The law expert said there are multiple ways Congress could try again, including "conduct that rises to the level of treason, bribery, other high crimes or misuse," but political considerations are critical.

"Democrats should not start out their control of the House by rushing off to impeach Trump because … it would detract from what I think they need to be doing. That is demonstrating to the public that, having regained control of the legislature, they're at least going to try to do things which are of practical importance to the average person."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, given the midterm results, Bowman thinks there is a chance that if enough Republicans — and public sentiment — turn further against Trump, the numbers could work. Should that time come, added Whittington, there is one particular avenue open to the Democrats.

"The best strategy would be close negotiations with Republican senators to discover if there are any grounds that might peel off the votes that they would need from across the aisle," Whittington said. "That might not be very satisfactory for the Democratic base, but that would put the president at greatest risk of conviction and removal."

The Hegseth case, effectively killed after the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee, shows an appetite for impeachment against members of Trump's cabinet.

Indeed, impeachment resolutions have already been filed against Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Education Secretary Linda McMahon, and Attorney General Todd Blanche could also be in the sights of Democrats in the upcoming Congress.

"The Democrats will face a tremendous amount of pressure from their own base to consider impeachments, and the fact that so many Democrats in the House supported the Hegseth impeachment in this procedural vote suggests that there will be an appetite to pursue that possibility in the next Congress," said Whittington.

With getting the votes to impeach Trump perhaps tougher due to his "cult of personality” within the Republican party, picking off his closest allies may be in play, said Bowman.

"You could eliminate cabinet officers, as a means of making a point to the administration, that: 'OK, we're not going to come after the big man himself, but if the rest of you minions insist on doing bad stuff, we will take you out.'"

Essentially, this is down to the two-thirds majority rule, according to both experts. Given that neither party has enjoyed such a majority since the mid 1960s, any conviction requires significant support from opponents.

But, actually, said Whittington, a conviction is not the only way to judge the success of an impeachment.

"Often the impeachment threat is itself sufficient to encourage an officer mired in scandal to resign, so that an actual conviction at trial is not necessary," he said

"Impeachment trials are more rare than they might otherwise be simply because impeachment threats are often successful. But, of course, some officers are willing to ride an impeachment out and take their chances at trial."

https://www.dw.com/en/jensen-huang-spy-r.title: Jensen Huang: Spy row, second affair leaves Nvidia without its rockstar CEO
https://www.dw.com/en/jensen-huang-spy-r.text:
Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO after a second affair came to light. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future after reports emerged of a second extramarital affair — this time with an employee.

In a statement issued on Thursday morning, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported on the latest scandal, alleging that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Both are married; Huang tied the knot with his wife Lori in 1985.

The latest revelation emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China.

The woman, Alice H., is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators.  H., the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure. Still, Nvidia's stock hit all-time highs only a month ago, as US technology giants kept announcing billions in spending on AI infrastructure. Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales. — meaning demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the fAI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

https://www.dw.com/en/iran-exiled-journa.title: Iran: Exiled journalists still repressed by regime
https://www.dw.com/en/iran-exiled-journa.text:
For many independent reporters, leaving Iran does not mean fully escaping the grasp of the Iranian state. The regime uses family members, bank accounts and the property they left behind to apply pressure across borders.

In times of crisis, Iran's political system is looking for scapegoats — and independent journalists, even journalists who have been living in exile for a long time, are high on their list.

At the end of September, Iran's judiciary announced that it had confiscated assets belonging to individuals accused of "cooperation with hostile governments." The measure is part of a previously announced plan targeting around 400 people living abroad, including journalists, activists, artists and athletes, whose assets are to be seized.

"The only thing I own in my parents' house in Iran is a bookshelf," says Amir Soltanzadeh. The exiled freelance journalist, who occasionally works for Germany's international broadcaster DW, discovered his name on a government list, which Iranian state media had labeled "traitors to the homeland."  His assets were to be seized. In an online post earlier this year, he published a photo of his book collection and wrote: "This library is my only asset in Iran. If you enjoy reading books, go ahead and confiscate them."

Soltanzadeh said that his bank account in Iran was also frozen. It contained the equivalent of around €500 ($555), which he used, among other things, to buy his family members gifts and flowers for special occasions. He noted it was "unjust" to list him as a traitor.

"I have not acted against Iran," he stressed. "Every position I have taken was ultimately aimed at improving the lives of people in Iran."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Some of his relatives, he said, have cut ties with his family because of his journalistic work.

"When people hear about a journalist working abroad, some who adopt the government's narrative automatically equate that person with a spy. They see a journalist as someone who is paid to gather information," said Soltanzadeh.

This pressure, according to the exiled journalist, eventually extended to his father's workplace.

"My father lost his job because of me. And because of me, my mother lives in constant anxiety — every time the phone rings, she has to wonder who is on the other end."

For several months, Soltanzadeh also cut all direct contact with his family to keep them safe, and only communicated with them through an intermediary.

Pressure against independent journalists is a part of a recurring pattern in the Islamic Republic. In times of political tension, Western media outlets and journalists are often portrayed as agents of hostile intelligence services such as the CIA or Mossad, or mouthpieces spreading subversive propaganda.

The authorities have many tools to spy on reporters, including hacking their social media accounts and intercepting conversations that are later used as evidence against their contacts inside Iran.

Such forms of repression also affect which information ends up reaching the public.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A journalist in Iran, who wanted to stay anonymous, says that reporting on detainees, state executions and the treatment of protesters comes with major risks and restrictions.

"Journalists can only write on their personal pages in a very limited and censored way," the reporter said. "In their reports, they are required to follow the government's official narrative."

Iran-based journalists have to weigh potential legal consequences of their work. This, in turn, constrains their ability to conduct independent research, maintain contact with sources and pursue sensitive topics.

Article 24 of Iran's constitution guarantees freedom of the press. However, the Press Law has been amended and expanded several times over the past four decades. It requires media professionals, among other things, not to endanger the Islamic Republic, not to insult the clergy or the Supreme Leader, and not to disseminate false information. These broadly worded provisions give authorities significant room to interfere in the work of the media.

Many journalists are forced to leave the country due to the constant pressure and the risk of being targeted by the authorities.

"Because of my journalistic work, I had to go into exile," says Omid Barin, a freelance journalist who also occasionally contributes to DW.

Barin's reporting focuses on issues such as human rights violations and the position of ethnic minorities in Iran. The pressure "has undoubtedly caused me to be much more cautious and sensitive when communicating with sources inside the country, to avoid putting them in danger," he told DW.

While Barin chooses not to provide details on the threats he faces, citing the risk of backlash on the people close to him, he says the core message behind them is clear: Someone in Iran would like him to either abandon journalism or steer away from sensitive topics.

Even while living abroad, Barin is forced to take additional precautions in his daily life and pay close attention to his personal security due to his work for media outlets that the Iranian regime considers "hostile."

https://www.dw.com/en/nvidia-ceo-jensen-.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns as scandal mounts over alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy
https://www.dw.com/en/nvidia-ceo-jensen-.text:
Jensen Huang has resigned from his role as the head of the AI chipmaker over his reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia shares plummeted 13% at the opening of trading on Thursday.

Jensen Huang has resigned from his role as the head of the AI chipmaker Nvidia over his reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the company announced on Thursday.

Colette Kress, the company's current executive vice president and chief financial officer, has been named as interim CEO.

"Nvidia's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said in a statement.

Shares in Nvidia, one of the world's biggest companies, plummeted 13% at the opening of trading on Thursday. The latest declines mean Nvidia has now lost about $800 billion (€721.4 bln) since the reports came to light.

The stock had already falled around 25% from its all-time high in early October.

Huang resigned after facing growing calls to step down over his reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. China has rejected the allegations.

Nvidia had been investigating whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort after reports of an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

In an email to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who worked for him.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Speaker of the US House of Representatives, Republican Mike Johson, said Huang "did the right thing" by resigning.

"It's a big and shocking development. You know, that’s a very important company that not only in the US economy but for national security purposes," Johnson said.

He also said the was growing consensus in Congress to limit exports of semiconductor chips to China, "especially in the light of recent developments."

Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia, which he led for more than three decades, turning it from a maker of graphics cards used in PC gaming into the dominant supplier of chips for artificial intelligence.

Huang, who holds a stake of about 3.61% — making him Nvidia's fourth-largest investor — will also leave the board.

Separately, authorities in Singapore confirmed that the woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset had been investigated over potential offenses in Singapore. The woman is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International.

These potential offenses included buying servers that were exported via Singapore to Malaysia ‌without entering the Singapore market.

Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said that while there was insufficient evidence to prove an offense had been committed, the individual was "issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country."

Singapore would "not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices," the ministry added.

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

https://www.dw.com/en/china-s-xi-jinping.title: China's Xi Jinping renews calls for 'reunification' with Taiwan
https://www.dw.com/en/china-s-xi-jinping.text:
Xi Jinping said that reunification was inevitable, but stopped short of mentioning military force. Taiwan though swiftly rejected Beijing's demands as tensions continue over the island's future.

Chinese President Xi Jinping has renewed his calls for "reunification” with Taiwanbut refrained from mentioning the use of force.

"The historical trends are unstoppable. The complete reunification of our motherland must be realized, and it can, without doubt, be realized," Xi said on Thursday.

His comments came in a speech marking the 160th birthday of Sun Yat-sen, the political leader who helped lead the 1911 revolution that overthrew China's imperial dynasty and led to the founding the Republic of China.

The Taiwanese government swiftly rebuffed the remarks, saying the territory would not accept submitting to the rule of China's Communist Party.

After the founding of the Republic of China in 1912, a civil war broke out in 1927 between the Nationalists and the Communists.

After the end of Japanese occupation and World War II, the Communists led by Mao Zedong gained the upper hand and the Nationalists retreated to the island of Taiwan in 1949.

Since then, both the People's Republic of China on the mainland and the Republic of China in Taiwan claim to be the legitimate heirs of Sun Yat-sen's political legacy.

Under the so-called One China policy, the majority of the international community recognizes only Communist China on the mainland as a state. Many countries nevertheless also maintain unofficial diplomatic, economic and cultural ties with Taiwan, which is self-governed and democratic.

While the speech by the Chinese president was largely about commemorating Sun Yat-sen, it was his remarks about Taiwan that drew international attention.

Xi said that reunification was an unwavering historical mission for the Communist Party and that "we will never leave any room for ‘Taiwan independence' separatist activities in any form.”

"We will definitely give full consideration to Taiwan's realities and take full account of the interests and feelings of our compatriots in Taiwan.

"Mr. Sun Yat-sen consistently upheld the unity of the country and the solidarity of the nation, and he firmly opposed all words and actions that split the country or the nation," he added.

While not mentioning military force in his speech, the Chinese leader has on several occasions in the past said that Beijing would not rule out military force to bring Taiwan under its control.

In response to Xi's speech on Thursday, Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council reiterated that neither the government nor the people of Taiwan would accept being placed under Beijing's rule.

"As for the wording on Taiwan unification, it isn't much different from ​the past," council spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told reporters.

Xi Jinping's speech came ahead on an APEC summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen where the Chinese leader is expected to meet with US President Donald Trump.

The US has over the past decades been backing Taiwan's resistance against Chinese demands, supplying the island with vital arms support.

China has in past years intensified its military operations around the island and in the Taiwan Strait, widely seen as both attempts to intimidate Taipei and to possibly practice for an eventual military operation.

On Thursday, Taiwan said that Chinese fighter jets and drones had begun carrying out a "joint combat readiness patrol" alongside Chinese warships around the island.

Taiwan swiftly rejects Beijing's demands as tensions continue over the island's future. The Taiwanese government swiftly rebuffed the remarks, saying the territory would not accept submitting to the rule of China's Communist Party.

https://www.dw.com/en/what-are-fossil-fu.title: What are fossil fuels?
https://www.dw.com/en/what-are-fossil-fu.text:
They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?

Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

https://www.dw.com/en/israel-strikes-gaz.title: Israel strikes Gaza hospital, says Hamas senior figure inside
https://www.dw.com/en/israel-strikes-gaz.text:
Israel says Hamas was using the hospital as a military command center, while Palestinian officials report at least six people killed, including a surgeon. The strike comes amid an increasingly fragile ceasefire.

Israel said it had targeted a senior Hamas member in a Gaza  hospital in an overnight airstrike which reportedly killed six people.

According to the Israeli military, Muhammad Abu Ismail and other militants from the Islamist group had been operating a command center inside the Nasser hospital in Khan Yunis.

Gaza's civil defense service said at least six people were killed, including a surgeon and more than 20 were wounded. It said that parts of several floors were severely damaged or destroyed.

During war, hospitals are protected under international humanitarian law, although they can lose that protection if they are used for military purposes.

In a statement on Thursday, the Israeli military (IDF) said, without providing evidence, that Hamas was "operating within Nasser Hospital in Khan Yunis" and were using the complex "as a hub for military and terrorist activities against IDF troops and Israel."

The IDF identified the targeted senior Hamas member as Abu Ismail, adding he "was responsible for directing terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops and for holding numerous hostages captive throughout the war."

The IDF said the hospital was used for storing weapons, to conduct interrogation, operate command-and-control rooms as well as to shelter terrorists.

The Gaza Health Ministry said the Israeli airstrike hit the surgery department, killing six people including surgeon Rizk Abu Sharia.

News agency Reuters reported seeing footage from inside the hospital showing extensive damage with debris scattered around rooms and equipment.

Wounded people were also seen in the wreckage while several bodies were being carried away as firefighters worked to clear the scene.

Hamas has described the strike as a "fully-fledged war crime."

Since the beginning of the war in 2023, Israeli forces have attacked several hospitals in the Gaza Strip.

The war on Hamas in Gaza began in October 2023 after Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

Since then, more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures are generally considered reliable by the international community.

More than 1.6 million residents of Gaza's 2.1-million population now live in tents or other makeshift shelters due to Israel's war in the enclave.

A ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, but attacks have continued since then. While Israel says Hamas is trying to regroup, the Palestinian militant group says it's committed to the ceasefire and that Israel is trying to undermine the agreement.

Hamas is recognized as a terrorist organization by the EU, the US and several Arab states.
https://www.dw.com/en/israel-strikes-gaz.summary: Israel says it targeted a senior Hamas member in a Gaza hospital in an overnight airstrike. The strike comes amid an increasingly fragile ceasefire. Israel says Hamas was using the hospital as a military command center. Gaza's civil defense service says at least six people were killed, including a surgeon.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-polic.title: Germany news: Police raid chapters of Gremium MC biker gang
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-polic.text:
Police in southwestern Germany launched major early-morning operations against a biker gang. The state of Baden-Württemberg is outlawing three of its chapters. Meanwhile, unions are planning more strikes. Follow DW.

Here's a roundup of news from or pertaining to Germany on November 12, 2026:

Germany's major IG Metall trade union has enabled the possibility of longer warning strikes amid difficult negotiations for industrial employees.

"The board of IG Metall has pave the way for 24-hour warning strikes in the metalworking and electrical industry," the union said on Thursday.

The union accuses employers of intransigence after three rounds of negotiations without clear progress.

On Wednesday, regional chapters appealed for authorization for full-day warning strikes — the last step before a full union vote and an indefinite labor dispute.

"This escalation is completely excessive and counterproductive," Udo Dinglreiter, the president of the employers' umbrella organization, Gesamtmetall, said. He said that hundreds of thousands of jobs could be at risk.

IG Metall's first chairperson Christiane Benner countered that "the employers want to turn this round of collective bargaining into a dispute over principles." Another union official said they were offering what amounted to a real-terms pay cut rather than seeking solutions.

IG Metall is calling for a 5% pay increase and other improved conditions for some 3.7 million workers starting in November, while employers have offered a one-off payment in 2027 coupled with a 1.3% increase starting in the summer of 2028.

The union estimates that around 464,000 employees took part in the initial wave of warning strikes that were limited to periods of hours, rather than full days.

Employers argue that they're treading a difficult line between trying not to cut jobs and meeting calls for improved pay amid widespread industrial sector layoffs in Germany in recent years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Tis the season, already. Preparations are underway around Germany and in several cities, Christmas markets are opening to the public.

Some markets are already open in Essen and in Hamburg, Duisburg's opens on Thursday, and Cologne's follows a day later.

The coupons.de website has sought to track the planned prices for mulled wine or Glühwein as the markets open their doors nationwide.

The bad news? These prices are rising like so many others. The better news? The year-on-year increase is actually smaller than overall inflation figures, at around 1%.

On average, a cup is liable to set you back around €4.60 (roughly $5.10). Not entirely surprisingly, Munich tops the nationwide pricing chart, with the price peaking at €7. Other sites nationwide tend not to have the gall even to charge 6 euros.

Bargain hunters determined to get the best value mulled wine will need to venture deep into the center of Germany — hardly its core tourist hub — to find the lowest prices starting at around €3.50.

Deposits for the cup, the "Pfand," are also only going in one direction, and in the meantime range from €1 all the way up to €5. But there's a strong argument, particularly with the better designs or after a memorable trip, that this can be money well spent as a memento!

Police in the Emsland region in the northwest near the border to the Netherlands have reported a major fire in a complex of residential and commercial buildings in Papenburg.

The fire broke out on Wednesday afternoon, police said the following morning, causing damages worth "at least €10 million ($11 million)." Several hundred emergency services personnel were deployed.

"Based on current findings, the fire broke out in the sauna area of a gym facility on site, and quickly spread to further parts of the complex of buildings," police wrote.

Two men were in the sauna at the time and initially tried to douse the flames but without success.

Police said the buildings were evacuated as the fire spread, with some surrounding buildings also being cleared as a precaution because of possible smoke-related dangers.

Several people were injured, police said, including the two men in the sauna area suffering mild burns and suspected smoke inhalation sickness. They were treated in a nearby hospital but soon discharged.

"There were also injuries among the first responders," police wrote. "Four police officers, two firefighters and members of the rescue teams suffered mild injuries, particularly via smoke inhalation."

The fire was only extinguished late on Wednesday night, several hours after it started. The area is sealed off, with possible risks of damaged buildings collapsing. Police have also launched investigations into the fire's cause, but said that at present, the area was not safe for that work to start at full scale.

Germany's largest credit bureau Creditreform has published its "2026 Debtors' Atlas."

It finds that 10.16% of German adults, or 7.36 million people, exhibit at least the early warning signs of excessive debt. A year ago the ratio was 9.74%.

"The financial situation of private consumers has further deteriorated," Patrik-Ludwig Hantzsch, Creditreform's head of economic research, said. "In particular, the sharply increased living costs, energy costs and housing costs are straining expenditures."

Hantzsch said employment was also becoming an issue once more, saying "above all, well-paid jobs in manufacturing industries have been cut back in large numbers in recent months."

The report also highlights rising cases of signs of excessive debt prior to legal action being taken, such as payment reminders or warnings being sent, saying "consumers are taking on more credit-financed expenditures — increasingly also for smaller purchases — at simultaneously rising interest rates."

A larger share of men than women have excessive debts, perpetuating a longstanding trend.

People around the middle of their working lives, aged 30-39 and 40-49, are most likely to be affected — but the cohort with the fastest-rising share of people with excessive debts are young adults below the age of 30.

Bremen, Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt and North Rhine-Westphalia were among the states with the highest rates of excess debts, while the wealthy and fiscally conservative states of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg had the lowest levels.

Germany's main DAX stock market index has cleared the 27,000-point mark for the first time in its history in morning trading.

It climbed by around 1.3% in order to pass the milestone.

A combination of some positive outlook data from major companies, not least engineering giant Siemens, and the falling oil prices of recent days have helped fuel the uptick.

Siemens' shares had risen by almost 5%, to just over €291 (around $323) each, helping to spur on the gains and making the company the morning's top performer.

Despite several years of low growth and recession in the German economy, the DAX, like many Western indices, is now trading twice as high as it was prior to the COVID pandemic.

Hundreds of police officers searched apartments and meeting sites for the biker group "Gremium MC" in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg early on Thursday.

The state interior ministry said the operation was part of a move to outlaw three sub-chapters of the group, the ones based in Böblingen and Leonberg, as well as the "Gremium MC Chapter Nomads Bosphorus Türkiye."

This last group was highlighted as a meaningful part of Gremium MC by security officials. It describes itself on Facebook as a great example that "people of different cultures and faiths can be strong together," featuring images of men posing with knives and other weapons.

Gremium MC prominently incorporates into its iconography the symbol of the Prussian military medal for exceptional valor, the Iron Cross, which was discontinued after World War I, reintroduced by Adolf Hitler during World War II, and then scrapped for good.

State Interior Minister Manuel Hagel was expected to make further comments later in the day in Ludwigsburg.

Gremium MC is deemed an "outlaw motorcycle gang" in Baden-Württemberg's latest security report, a term used for biker groups that do not recognize the state monopoly on the use of force and are often tied to organized crime.

"Extortion, drug dealing and pimping in particular tend to be part of their activities," state authorities say.

Baden-Württemberg counts 154 biker chapters in the state with around 2,000 members.

Founded in 1972 in Mannheim, various chapters of Gremium MC across the country have faced legal issues in recent years. In 2021, another chapter in the southwest, Gremium MC Southgate in Heidelberg, was outlawed on suspicion of organized crime activity.

Police in Hanover reported early on Thursday that three men were injured by an unknown driver in a car in the nearby town of Ronneberg.

One person sustained severe injuries in the incident late on Wednesday, police said.

Two of the wounded were taken to a nearby hospital while the other could be cared for at the scene.

Police said the driver fled the scene and that a search operation was ongoing. Authorities were also still investigating a potential motive for the apparent attack.

Gemorsche and/or Gudde Morga!

Today's updates start with a focus between the southwestern Kurpfalz and Swabian regions, where police have launched major morning raids against a biker gang.

The state Interior Ministry in Baden Württemberg has outlawed three of its chapters. Hundreds of police officers mobilized in the early hours of the morning.

The major IG Metall trade union is planning further strikes in the carmaking sector and other metalworking industries, with an announcement anticipated later in the day.

To the north, near Hanover, police report an apparent car attack injuring three men overnight.

And in the spirit of offering the public service journalism people are truly thirsting for, we'll have some info on the average and localized pricing of mulled wine or Glühwein at Christmas markets this year, as the early birds start to open their doors to visitors. (Yes, already!)

Stay tuned for updates on all this and anything else of note in or pertaining to Germany as the day progresses.
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-polic.summary: Germany's main DAX stock market index has cleared 27,000-point mark for first time in its history in morning trading. The DAX is now trading twice as high as it was prior to the COVID pandemic.

https://www.dw.com/en/australian-teen-fo.title: Australian teen found alive after six days in the bush
https://www.dw.com/en/australian-teen-fo.text:
The teenager was spotted during an aerial search, after spending days navigating rugged terrain. He had fallen down the side of a riverbed two days before being found.

An Australianteenager has been found alive after six days missing in dense bushland.

Police said 17-year-old William had been camping with a friend in the southeastern state of Victoria, about 180 kilometers (112 miles) east of Melbourne. He got lost after he'd left his friend to go and get some equipment, but didn't return.

The friend then called the police and an intense search operation was launched, involving helicopters, special units, as well as volunteers searching the bush each day.

The boy was found on Thursday morning during an aerial search near Stoney Creek, public broadcaster ABC reported. Rescuers first spotted a fishing tackle box and then saw the boy sleeping on a rock in a dry riverbed.

Pictures show the boy shirtless and sunburned. Local media reported that he waved and pumped his fist when he was woken up the sound of the search helicopter.

"Flight officers winched down and retrieved Will before bringing him back to the command post to reunite with his mum," police said. "Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health."

He was then taken to hospital for monitoring.

"I'm just over the moon he's alive," his mother was quoted in Australian media. "He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued."

Police said William had spent days walking through the rugged terrain but fell down the side of a riverbed two days ago and then remained there in hopes of being found.

"He's never leaving the house again," his mother told local reporters. "He's grounded for life."
