https://www.dw.com/en/bundeswehr-study-e.title: Bundeswehr study exposes widespread sexual harassment in German military
https://www.dw.com/en/bundeswehr-study-e.text:
Sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known, with younger women disproportionately affected. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has called for a policy of "zero tolerance."

"It was clear to us from the outset that the analysis would uncover uncomfortable truths," Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told theBundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, on Wednesday.

Earlier that day, he had presented the findings of the Bundeswehr's first study into unreported cases of sexual misconduct to the Defense Committee. According to the findings, sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known.

"The study has shown that only between one third and one sixth of cases are reported," Pistorius said, announcing an action plan to address the issue.

"There is zero tolerance for sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr. This is nothing less than a matter of upholding the human dignity enshrined in our Basic Law. And that principle applies all the more within the Bundeswehr."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The study examined incidents that had gone unreported, the so-called "dark figure" of cases that never reach official statistics. The Bundeswehr Centre of Military History and Social Sciences (ZMSBw) surveyed 45,000 service members, around 18% of whom responded. More than 8,100 questionnaires were evaluated and supplemented with individual and group interviews. According to the institute, the data are statistically representative.

According to the study, younger women in the lower ranks are particularly affected by sexual misconduct. Among men, non-heterosexual soldiers are disproportionately affected. The perpetrators are predominantly male. Statistically, combat units do not differ from the rest of the armed forces.

Female service members in units with a higher proportion of women (more than 15%) are less likely to be affected.

Verbal harassment is by far the most common form of misconduct, according to the study. Around 72% of female soldiers and 31% of male soldiers said they had experienced verbal harassment at least once during their military service. In the 12 months preceding the survey, 38% of female soldiers and 16% of male soldiers reported experiencing verbal sexual harassment.

For physical harassment, 9% of female soldiers and 3% of male soldiers reported incidents of physical sexual misconduct, and 2% of both women and men said they had experienced sexual violence.

The study also examined why service members chose not to report incidents. The most commonly cited reason was not wanting to draw attention to themselves.

"There appears to be a lack of awareness of the reporting channels. And, for me, the decisive issue is trust in those channels," Pistorius concluded.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In response, the Bundeswehr plans to improve awareness of how and where cases of sexual harassment can be reported. That is precisely where the environmentalist Greens, who are in opposition in the Bundestag, direct their criticism.

Defense policy spokesperson Sara Nanni is calling for "an external reporting office, alongside the regular disciplinary process, with investigative powers and the authority to take disciplinary action where appropriate." Such an independent point of contact, she argues, is needed in cases where superiors within the Bundeswehr fail to fulfill their responsibilities.

Another consequence of the study is the expansion of support services for those affected. A counseling center established in early November will soon be available around the clock. Supervisors are also to receive enhanced awareness training and improved instruction.

"Sexual misconduct will become part of training at every level, from the very beginning," said Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer.

In addition, the way supervisors handle reported cases will become a standing criterion in their performance evaluations. "Anyone who fails to lead by example, tolerates misconduct, or does not address it consistently will no longer hold a leadership position," Defense Minister Pistorius stressed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The study was prompted by a growing number of reports of sexual misconduct received by former Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces Eva Högl. Most of those who approached her were female soldiers. Högl called for the study into unreported cases in 2024. The process gained further momentum following incidents at the Parachute Regiment in Zweibrücken that came to light at the beginning of this year and also involved allegations of sexual misconduct.

The current Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces, Henning Otte, described the figures revealed by the study as "dramatically high." The findings had also made it clear, he said, "that there is a lack of trust in the Bundeswehr's structures. The Ministry of Defense must now take this study seriously and translate its findings into a leadership culture that is truly lived in practice."

The Bundeswehr urgently needs additional personnel and has been actively recruiting women. However, the study's findings are unlikely to make attracting more female recruits any easier. Women remain significantly underrepresented across nearly all branches of the armed forces.

https://www.dw.com/en/intelligent-women-.title: Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds
https://www.dw.com/en/intelligent-women-.text:
Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.

High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, says women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial company in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

The effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.

No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

No, Chawla says. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw."

Small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she says: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

High-scoring men faced no such penalty, but women with high scores were treated better. The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-news-modi-go.title: India news : Modi government approves $340 million museum in Delhi
https://www.dw.com/en/india-news-modi-go.text:
The government says that the 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' will have the world's "largest" museum dispaly area." DW has the latest.

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of headlines from India on Thursday, November 12:

The bodies of two special police officers were recovered in Jammu and Kashmir's Kishtwar district on Thursday, Indian media reported.

Indian media said the pair were deployed with the Special Operations Group (SOG) of the local police in the remote Kiyar village.

They had reportedly gone missing on Wednesday while traveling from their camp to an army camp in the Dharna-Marwah area.

The officers' bodies were found riddled with bullets and their service weapons were missing. Police sources suggested this could indicate a possible militant angle.

"One body was found around 8 a.m., and the second was recovered around 9 a.m. It is deeply tragic,"  Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) Shagun Parihar, who represents the Kishtwar Assembly constituency, told news agency ANI.

In a separate incident on Wednesday, three personnel of the paramilitary Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) were injured in South Kashmir's Kulgam when suspected militants opened fire on a security checkpoint.

Kashmir, a disputed territory between India and Pakistan, has witnessed a decades-long insurgency.

Mallikarjun Kharge, the president of India's main opposition Congress party, on Thursday addressed the Kishtwar and Kulgam incidents and said that India stood "united and resolute against terrorism."

A tourist has reportedly died after falling from a paraglider in Bir Billing, known as India's paragliding capital, Indian media has reported.

The incident has raised concerns over the safety of commercial skydiving ventures in the popular adventure tourism spot located in the Kangra district of the Himalayan state of Himachal Pradesh.

Reports said the accident took place on Tuesday evening and identified the deceased tourist as a 26-year-old man from Uttar Pradesh's Noida.

News agency PTI cited police as saying the man had been on a tandem paragliding flight with a local pilot. He reportedly fell just six minutes after take-off.

The police have registered a case of death due to negligence against the pilot adding that a further probe into the incident was underway.

This is the second paragliding death to be reported in the densely forested and mountainous district in less than a month.

On October 25, a 47-year-old Bulgarian national was killed in a paraglider crash near Rising Star Peak in Kangra district's Dharamshala.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has approved the development of a massive museum in the heart of India's capital, New Delhi, estimated to cost around $340 million (around €306 million).

The 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' —  which was first announced by Modi in 2023 —  is being billed as the museum "with the largest display area in the world."

The Sanskrit name of the museum translates to 'India through the ages'. The project has been envisaged as the country's landmark museum, the government said, and will showcase elements of Indian history and civilization, which spans thousands of years.

The century-old North and South Blocks in New Delhi's Raisina Hills —  the seat of the Indian government —  will be reused for the museum.

The colonial-era twin blocks once housed government offices, including Modi's own, before they were vacated over the last year as part of the Modi government's redesigning of India's hub of political power.

The Hindu nationalist government has long sought to emphasize India's pre-colonial cultural identity.

"Buildings that have been centres of governance will now become a place where millions can discover, experience and celebrate the timeless richness of our civilisation," Modi wrote on X on Wednesday night.

Calling the museum a "magnificent celebration" of India's "civilizational journey", Modi said the museum's galleries will bring to life aspects including ancient knowledge systems, mathematics, astronomy to architecture, art, languages and spirituality, through "immersive experiences."

According to a press release from the Indian cabinet, the museum will encompass an area of nearly 178,509 square meters with the ability to welcome some 10 million visitors a year.

The finalization of the project isn't planned until 2030/31, but the first gallery on the theme of "adornment" will open its doors to the public next year, with more galleries gradually opening after that.

The content and collection analysis for the museum is currently underway, with the government having identified some 1.8 million objects for possible display from national and state museums, alongside archaeological and private collections.

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our Thursday wrap of all the biggest headlines from India.

Delhi's skyline is once again shrouded in a gray haze as the Indian capital's smog woes continue.

Nevertheless, India's cabinet has greenlit a multimillion‑dollar project to develop a mega-museum exhibiting aspects of India's civilizational history in the heart of the country's corridor of political power. It is touted to be the museum with the largest display area in the world.

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-peace-talk.title: Ukraine peace talks: US envoys meet with Putin at Kremlin
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-peace-talk.text:
The US president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff are in Russia to meet Vladimir Putin. The meeting comes after two days of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. Follow DW for more.

Below is a roundup of developments from the Ukraine-Russia talks on Thursday, November 12:

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed their trip to Abu Dhabi this week with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

According to Russian state media RIA Novosti, Witkoff said US President Donald Trump was "seeking to end the conflict in Ukraine as quickly as possible."

The three-way talks in Abu Dhabi between the US, Ukraine and Russia were held "in a positive atmosphere" and that the Ukrainian and Russian delegations had "worked effectively," Ria Novosti reported.

Witkoff said he would convey the results of his and Kushner's meeting with Putin to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner, for his part, said the US had begun discussions with European countries on the post-war "security architecture" on the continent.

He also said Europe wanted to be involved in the talks to end the conflict, RIA Novosti reported.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a "humanitarian mission" to the frontline city of Kostyantynivka in eastern Ukraine, Russian state media reported.

Putin made the remarks during a meeting at the Kremlin on Thursday with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ria Novosti said.

"There's a village in Donbas called Kostyantynivka, where there are still about 400-500 civilians. Let's do the same thing we did in Oleshky and invite representatives of the foreign press, including the American press," he said, referring to the recent US-brokered evacuation of the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.

According to RIA Novosti, Putin also repeated Russia's demands in a potential peace deal, including its refusal to accept any foreign troops in Ukraine.

The Russian leader warned that international peacekeepers in Ukraine would become a "legitimate target for the Russian army."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Russian side is becoming more willing to accept a European seat in the trilateral talks.

Merz said he expected Putin to agree to Europeans getting a seat at the table in talks with Ukraine. He was speaking on the sidelines of the European Political Community meeting in Dublin. He added that getting Putin to negotiate is more important than naming who would be the European envoy.

"The important thing is that Russia comes to the table and that Russia is ready to talk," the German chancellor said.

He also highlighted Ukraine's importance to Europe, saying that supporting Kyiv was a "shared European responsibility."

For some time, European leaders have sought a seat at the US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi. So far, representatives from the EU were only present on the sidelines of the talks.

Ukraine's military said on Thursday it ‌has hit ⁠Russia's five ​largest oil ​refineries since ​October 30.

Those struck were the Omsk, Kirishi, Ryazan, Nizhny Novgorod and Yaroslavl refineries, along with the smaller Novokuibyshevsk and Saratov refineries, the General Staff said in a Telegram post.

The statement claimed that the strikes on key refining units are shrinking revenues that help Russia fund the war.

Referring to the Omsk refinery's distance of 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

Last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that military strikes on Russian energy infrastructure would resume, despite US President Donald Trump's insistence that such attacks stop.

Trump said Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries were a "disgrace" and that Zelenskyy was less willing than Putin to reach a compromise to end the war.

Russia, however, has paid no heed to Trump, instead continuing to hit Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Leaders from more than 40 European countries will gather in the Irish capital Dublin on Thursday for the European Political Community summit to discuss the continent's security and Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will also attend the meeting, along with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

US mediators, Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, and special envoy Steve Witkoff are also expected to make their way to Ireland, after their meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The meeting, due to begin at midday local time, is an opportunity for European leaders to discuss this week's trilateral peace talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that Ukraine's military faced new "systematic restrictions" to tech billionaire Elon Musk's Starshield satellite internet.

"Our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now," Zelenskyy said in an online post.

The Ukrainian president added that "systematic speed restrictions" were being imposed and that these are not "random errors."

"Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine."

The Starshield military communications system — the military-grade version of satellite-based communication network Starlink — is operated by Musk's SpaceX and plays a key role for frontline communications.

Ukraine first flagged issues with Starshield last month after a dispute between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump over a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk "capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network."

Tech billionaire and US president both denied throttling Ukrainian access, but Musk later accused Ukraine of using the service for military purposes while Trump said Musk had "put it back."

Nearly half a million Russian soldiers may have been killed in Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine. Can Russia continue fighting at such an enormous human and economic cost?

Leaked records reportedly obtained from Russia's state statistics agency, Rosstat, identify more than 412,000 deaths linked to the war. British newspaper The Guardian reports that the true death toll could be closer to 500,000.

The full dataset has not been independently verified.

Some months saw more than 500 Russian soldiers killed every day. And the losses have fallen disproportionately on Russia's poorer and more remote regions.

In this DW News interview, Janis Kluge, head of the Eastern Europe and Eurasia research division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), examines what the leaked figures reveal about Russia's military losses, recruitment crisis and war economy.

The leaked data comes as US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine conclude in Abu Dhabi without a breakthrough on ending the war.

The two sides have agreed to a prisoner exchange, but fundamental disagreements remain. Could mounting Russian losses eventually force Putin to compromise, or make him even more determined to continue the war?

A Russian soldier has been killed in a car explosion in Saint Petersburg, the AFP news agency reported, citing the local Investigative Committee.

The cause of the blast in the Pushkinsky District is not yet known.

"An investigation into the murder of a military serviceman has been opened," the Investigative Committee said in a press release.

Russian state media agency TASS reported on a car explosion in the same district and cited a law enforcement spokesperson with information that the "car exploded" as it was moving out of a yard.

According to the spokesperson the man was alone inside the car and no one else was injured.

US mediators, Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump , and special envoy Steve Witkoff have arrived in Moscow, according to Russian news agencies.

"At Vnukovo [Airport], US President's special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were met by Russian President's special representative Kirill Dmitriev," Interfax news agency said.

"Welcoming Steve and Jared ​to Moscow," Dmitriev said on X, with an accompanying picture of himself shaking ​hands with Witkoff with Kushner standing alongside.

The pair had been in the United Arab Emirates over the past two days for trilateral peace talks.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," Kushner said after the Abu Dhabi talks ended.

Kushner and Witkoff are expected to address the issue of including European partners in the current trilateral format.

After meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Kushner and Witkoff are expected to make their way to Ireland, where they are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

There have been continued overnight attacks between Russia and Ukraine amid efforts to bring an end to Moscow's ongoing invasion.

Russia's Defense Ministry said on Telegram that it had targeted military and energy ​facilities in Ukraine, as well as a munitions
warehouse in the capital Kyiv.

The Reuters news agency reported explosions had been heard in Kyiv in the early hours of the morning, citing a witness, while a local official said that energy and civilian infrastructure had been damaged in the Rivne region.

Meanwhile, Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that Russia had shot down five drones heading towards the capital.

Drones were also reportedly shot down in other Russian regions, including Rostov and Tula.

Efforts to broker peace in Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine are continuing with US mediators now in Moscow.

Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff are due to meet with the Russian president before possibly heading on to Dublin, where they would meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy who is attending European meetings.

On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said there may be a "window of opportunity" to bring an end to the fighting, although the efforts to broker peace are taking place amid continued hostilities between Russia and Ukraine.

Two days of talks in the United Arab Emirates didn't yield major breakthroughs, but the two sides did agree on another prisoner exchange.

Follow here for the latest developments on the peace talks and other news from the war in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a "humanitarian mission" to the frontline city of Kostyantynivka. Leaked data from Russia's state statistics agency, Rosstat, identify more than 412,000 deaths linked to the war.

https://www.dw.com/en/where-the-us-s-war.title: Where the US's war with Iran stands after the midterms
https://www.dw.com/en/where-the-us-s-war.text:
Almost nine months after it began, the war in Iran has calmed to the point where Donald Trump sees an end. But with the key issues of the conflict unresolved and political change in the US, what is the situation?

The US-Israel war with Iran, according to US President Donald Trump, "is effectively over" in a military sense. Trump's secretary of state, Marco Rubio, backed up the president, saying there is "no need for major combat operations" in Iran because economic pressure and negotiations between the warring parties are proving effective.

However, Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, has denied negotiations are even taking place. "All American claims about the continuation of negotiations with Iran are aimed at easing economic pressures and reducing oil prices," he told Lebanese channel Al Mayadeen.

While neither side has claimed the conflict is concluded in every sense, Ian Kelly, a former US ambassador who now works at Northwestern University in the US, considers the current situation is something like a "virtual ceasefire." He added that there is currently a significant deescalation but that the central issues are unresolved.

"I wouldn't say the war is over. I would say there's no shooting going on, nothing really significant," Kelly told DW. "But the real issue is opening up the Strait of Hormuz. What Iran wants, of course, is for the United States to withdraw its massive strike forces from the Gulf. But that won't happen until Iran agrees to open the Strait of Hormuz."

A critical shipping lane between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, the Strait of Hormuz has been a focal point in the US-Iran conflict. Iran's attacks on commercial ships in the strait have led to higher oil prices and have had other economic impacts that have affected living costs in the US and around the world.

Kelly, who also held several high-level roles at the US State Department, thinks the US midterm election results, which will see the Democrats take control of the House and Senate next year after catastrophic losses for Trump's Republicans, means Iran is sitting tight.

"I think that Iran is in a wait-and-see moment to see if the war will wind down because Congress acts to either cut off the funding or severely limit the funding," he said. But with Iran's resources also dwindling, it's a game of cat and mouse.

Trump and his party need the war to end, according to Kelly, for political reasons, as well as strategic.

"As long as the war is not resolved, it's going to be a real sticking point for the Republicans as they look at [the election in] 2028. They have to wrap it up before then," he said.

"A major contributing factor to the Republican defeat was how Trump has not followed through on some of his promises made in 2024. One of the big ones was no more forever wars, and he just went off and started another war that doesn't seem to have an exit strategy. It has weakened the Republican Party."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The imminent change in US politics will naturally have military consequences long before the 2028 election.

”There is little likelihood that Congress will continue to fund this war at the kind of levels that they have been," said Kelly. "That's another reason that Iran is sitting back and just waiting to see where this all comes out."

While the US administration claims it is happy with a status quo of containment through land and sea blockades, Kelly believes the authority of Trump and his party will be further diminished if the US can't achieve concrete progress on its stated main goals: gaining full control of the Strait of Hormuz and forcing Iran to give up its enriched uranium.

"Both of those are quite possible," Kelly said, adding that even attempting to achieve them threatens the current relative calm.

"The White House has really painted itself in a corner here by stressing that the main goal is to deny Iran a nuclear weapon. I don't see that as something that Iran is going to negotiate away, which means that they [the US] will probably have to use military force again. The White House is in a real pickle."

But there is also the question of how long Iran can bear the economic burden of the war without reaching a deal.

"Iran's limitation in the Strait of Hormuz is economic rather than military, because continuing the war has a significant impact on its economy," Ali Mohammadi, an expert in Iranian affairs based in France, told DW earlier this week.

Nevertheless, the strait remains a key source of leverage for Iran in any future negotiations.

Kelly doesn't see the economic strain of the war subsiding anytime soon, especially in oil markets.

"The real issue for the markets is that as long as it remains a phony war, it's very difficult to see oil prices lowering. The prices that are being charged now factor in the possible return to instability, so it has to be some kind of agreement where all sides and the oil markets are confident that we see a return to status quo. It's going to be difficult to restore the markets' confidence that these tankers won't be shot at again," Kelly said.

Given the global consequences of the conflict, Kelly expects it to be a hot topic at this month's APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) summit in Shenzhen, where Trump and his counterparts in Russia and China, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, will reportedly meet.

"I think Russia is interested in keeping the United States tied down like this. China, though, is interested in resolving it because they are a big customer," he said. A G20 summit in Miami follows the APEC meeting in December.

While the impasse between Iran and the US shows little sign of being broken, the fighting has calmed, for now at least. What happens in the coming weeks in the meeting rooms of Shenzhen and Miami currently looks more critical to finding a solution than what happens on Iranian territory or waterways.

https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-xiv-retur.title: Pope Leo XIV returns to Peru to a big welcome, calls it his 'homeland'
https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-xiv-retur.text:
An estimated 3 million people greeted Pope Leo XIV in Lima as the Peruvian-citizen pontiff began a six-day homecoming visit to the country where he spent two decades as a missionary and bishop.

Pope Leo XIV opened the Peruvian leg of his South America tour on Wednesday, telling crowds in Lima that returning to the country where he served for two decades felt like coming home.

The Vatican estimated that about 3 million people lined his motorcade route, the Associated Press reported.

Leo holds Peruvian citizenship and spent more than two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and later as bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo before becoming pope.

Also a US citizen, he is the first pope from either the United States or Peru.

He sang Peru's national anthem with President Keiko Fujimori at the presidential palace.

"Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said, adding that he was "also returning to my homeland."

Leo urged Peruvians to "cultivate honesty, integrity," and to accept that "no one has all the answers."

He also called for stronger disaster prevention in a country regularly hit by El Nino-linked floods and landslides.

Fujimori said Peru must face the “unfinished task” of reconciliation after decades of insurgent violence, state abuses and sharp political divisions.

The welcome comes as many Peruvians are weary of their leaders.

The country has had nine presidents since July 2016, and homicide rates have nearly doubled in five years.

Political science professor Alonso Cardenas told AP he sees "no sign of a reaction, no strategy" from Fujimori's government.

Notably, the Catholic Church is more credible than any other Peruvian institution, theology professor Veronique Lecaros told AP, even as Pew data show Catholics falling from 76% of the population to about 67%.

Leo's six-day stay includes a trip to 3,700 meters (about 12,140 feet), considered risky after Leo had part of a lung removed in mid-October because of a malignant tumor. He is due back at the Vatican on November 17.

https://www.dw.com/en/nvidia-board-repor.title: Nvidia board reportedly weighs ousting Huang amid alleged affairs with exec and suspected Chinese spy
https://www.dw.com/en/nvidia-board-repor.text:
Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to oust Jensen Huang amid reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The shake-up would leave the world's leading AI chip supplier without the co-founder who built it.

Nvidia's board was meeting Wednesday to decide whether to remove co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, media outlets, led by The Wall Street Journal, reported.

Huang has led the company for more than three decades, turning it from a gaming chipmaker into the dominant supplier of chips for artificial intelligence.

The report comes as Nvidia investigates whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort after reports of an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.

News that Nvidia might part ways with Huang sent the company's shares down about 8% in after-hours trading.

A reporter for the financial news outlet Bloomberg said on X that Nvidia's board was working with an outside firm to identify potential successors and considering an interim CEO while it searched for a permanent replacement.

US Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons asked President Donald Trump's administration to preserve records related to Nvidia's chip exports to China, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing a letter from the senators. The request also covers records related to Huang's alleged affair with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.

Huang acknowledged in a note to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He did not publicly name the woman. The New York Times identified her as Alice H., a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed who is not related to him. Beijing rejected the espionage allegation.

Shareholders sued Nvidia and Huang on Monday in a proposed class action suit accusing them of concealing the alleged relationship and the risks it posed to the company.

The New York Times identified the Nvidia executive as Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of health care. Asked about the relationship, Huang told the newspaper, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," before ending the call.

Nvidia and Powell did not immediately respond to requests for comment, Reuters reported.

https://www.dw.com/en/mississippi-senate.title: Mississippi Senate race: Democrat Scott Colom defeats Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith
https://www.dw.com/en/mississippi-senate.text:
The southern US state of Mississippi has elected its first Black senator in more than 140 years. Democrat Scott Colom has won the seat in a historic upset, according to projections.

Democratic candidate Scott Colom beat Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's US Senate race after a prolonged ballot-counting process, the Associated Press projected on Wednesday.

The narrow victory makes Colom, 43, the state's first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction and the first new Democratic senator chosen by Mississippi since 1947.

"All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this," Colom told a crowd of hundreds who gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. "I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters."

During the campaign, Colom promised to represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.

"It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better," he said.

The southern US state of Mississippi has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations.

The Mississippi victory gives the Democrats a 55-44 advantage in the 100-member ​Senate. The winner of the Senate race in Alaska remains to be determined. The Democrats also won control of the House of Representatives, having gained 41 seats so far and holding a 254-to-168 advantage, with 13 races yet to be called.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mississippi election officials have been counting ballots for over a week in a race so close that Colom led by only a few dozen votes at some points. The latest media-tabulated results showed him ahead by more than 4,500 votes, or 0.5 ​percentage points.

The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party suffered defeats in several states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the US South.

Hyde-Smith, 67, posted a concession video on social media, and a spokesperson confirmed she had called Colom to concede.  Hyde-Smith was first elected in 2018 and consistently led in opinion polls in a state that ⁠Trump ​won by nearly 23 points in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Democrats' Senate leader, Chuck Schumer, wrote on X, "Blue Mississippi is here."

Hyde-Smith had blocked Colom's nomination by former President Joe Biden to serve as a US District Court judge in northern Mississippi, citing his position on transgender issues. Mississippi's other US senator, Republican Roger Wicker, supported his nomination for the post.

Mississippi does not have a law mandating a recount for a close election.

https://www.dw.com/en/russian-foreign-mi.title: Russian Foreign Ministry says its ambassador to US has died
https://www.dw.com/en/russian-foreign-mi.text:
Russia's Foreign Ministry has said that Alexander Darchiev died from a chronic illness at the age of 66. The long-time diplomat had been in the Washington post since early 2025.

Russia's Foreign Ministry said Wednesday that Alexander Darchiev, Moscow's ambassador to the US, died from an unspecified chronic illness in Moscow at the age of 66.

Darchiev was appointed to the post by Russian President Vladimir Putin in March 2025 after Donald Trump returned to the White House and the two countries sought to improve relations. The post had been vacant for six months before his appointment after hardliner Anatoly Antonov was relieved of his duties in October 2024.

In a statement, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described Darchiev as "an outstanding diplomat, experienced leader, good comrade and mentor" and a brilliant scholar on US history and affairs.

Zakharova warned against the spread of conspiracy theories surrounding Darchiev's passing, accusing US media outlets of being "particularly active" in that regard.

Darchiev, known for his public denunciations of the West, had previously led the Foreign Ministry's North America and North Atlantic departments and served as ambassador to Canada from 2014 to 2021.

He also led Russia's negotiating team during February 2025 Ukraine peace talks with the US in Istanbul, Turkey.

No date has been given for his funeral.

Details for a memorial service will be announced at a later date, Zakharova said.
https://www.dw.com/en/russian-foreign-mi.summary: Alexander Darchiev died from an unspecified chronic illness in Moscow, Russia's Foreign Ministry says. Darchie was appointed to the post by Russian President Vladimir Putin in March 2025. He had been in the Washington post since early 2025.

https://www.dw.com/en/spain-housing-cris.title: Spain: Housing crisis prompts general strike, mass nighttime protests
https://www.dw.com/en/spain-housing-cris.text:
Hundreds of thousands of citizens have hit the streets to protest Spain's housing crisis after millions of union workers staged a general strike. The crisis has triggered snap elections to take place on November 29.

Authorities in Spain say that despite pouring rain, some 120,000 citizens took to the streets of the capital, Madrid, on Wednesday evening after millions of striking workers brought Europe's fourth-largest economy to a standstill under the motto "Salaries. Housing. Prices" in the country's first general strike in 14 years earlier in the day.

The massive turnout came in response to housing shortages and unbearably high rents.

City officials in Barcelona said 55,000 people attended evening marches there as they walked behind a huge banner reading "Live. Not just survive." Housing activists in the city said the turnout was far larger, claiming that 400,000 had hit the streets.

As has been the case in other demonstrations across the Europea of late, peaceful protests later gave way to small groups of marauding young men who smashed storefront windows along Barcelona's main shopping street. They also set fire to dumpsters and shot fireworks at police when they arrived.

Earlier on Wednesday, workers across Spain gathered en masse, marching and setting up picket lines despite stormy weather in many areas of the country.

Symbolized by the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid earlier this year, the crisis has also prompted a snap election set for November 29.

The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass legislation to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties. Lacking the power to get legislation passed, Sanchez called the early vote in hopes of shoring up more support.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sanchez's government did end up approving two extraordinary decrees introducing measures similar to the housing reforms rejected by parliament.

"We won't stop until we transform this country's housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the [landlord] minority," said Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union.

While most of the protests were peaceful, strikers in front of Madrid's Mercamadrid wholesale market said police had used pepper spray on the crowd, prompting at least 13 people to seek medical attention.

Some airlines later reported disruptions to flights in and out of Spain as some airport and airline workers participated in the strike.

The country has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set ​to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to estimates from the central bank.

With fewer and fewer individuals and families able to buy a home, the number of renters in the country has risen sharply. According to Spain's youth council, the average rent is €1,176 ($1,315). This is equivalent to 99% of the average young person's salary.

The general strike came a day after rail workers launched a strike over two major deadly train crashes this year, making decrepit infrastructure another major issue in the upcoming parliamentary elections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Spain's government supported Wednesday's strike, saying it was staged "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition."

Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), had a different take, saying if it was indeed "a strike against the opposition," it was "an absurdity the likes of which does not exist in any other European Union country."

Although the UGT labor union — one of the strike organizers — and Sanchez's socialist PSOE party are two separate institutions, they share a historic founder in Pablo Iglesias Posse.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nicole Ris, reporting for DW in Madrid, followed the strike closely as it unfolded on Wednesday, saying earlier:

Here in Madrid, apparently, lots of people are still showing up for work, and people I know have clearly said they will not go on strike as they don't see much sense in it — although they all suffer under the cost of living crisis and the housing crisis.

There is also debate about this strike being an "election strike" that could benefit the current government.

"I'm not taking part in this. It's nonsense. The government is supporting it because they hope they'll get enough votes on the 29th so they can carry on," a doorman in Madrid told me.

The government supports the strike, claiming it is being held "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez's inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition," according to the media here.

https://www.dw.com/en/fears-of-rising-an.title: Fears of rising antisemitism in Europe
https://www.dw.com/en/fears-of-rising-an.text:
Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny commemorates the victims of Auschwitz as Jewish communities across Europe face growing hostility. What does the promise of "Never Again" mean for Jewish life in Europe today?

Regina Sluszny makes her way in her wheelchair through the iron gate marking the entrance to the former Auschwitz concentration camp. "I feel the cold, both physically and emotionally," says the 87-year-old Jewish woman, her gaze fixed on the grey horizon.

How many times has she been here? Six, seven, perhaps eight, she estimates. And each time, the same thoughts run through her mind: "I think about my husband's family. He lost seven loved ones here. They were sent straight to the gas chambers and murdered."

Regina Sluszny traveled to Poland with a delegation from the European Jewish Association (EJA), a European advocacy group representing Jewish interests that regularly organizes conferences on Jewish life as well as visits to former concentration camps.

This year, the organization invited political representatives and members of Jewish communities to Krakow and Auschwitz on November 9 and 10. The trip was deliberately scheduled to coincide with the anniversary of the November Pogroms of 1938, widely regarded as a watershed moment on the path to the Holocaust.

"Honoring the past, securing the future" is the event's motto. Like many others in attendance, Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny fears that the horrors of the Shoah are slowly fading from Europe's collective memory.

Among this year's international religious and political representatives, the guest of honor was Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah and a prominent opponent of the Islamic Republic. The European Jewish Association (EJA) honored him for his efforts to combat antisemitism.

Accepting the award, Pahlavi recalled the historic ties between the Persian and Jewish peoples and called on democratic nations around the world to unite against oppression and ideological extremism.

But talking to attendees at the symposium in Krakow, it quickly becomes clear that fear of rising antisemitism is much closer to home. Many describe growing hostility towards Jews and rising fear in Jewish communities across Europe.

In France, authorities recorded a total of 1,320 antisemitic incidents in 2025. That was fewer than in 2024, but around three times as many as in 2022.

In Germany, the number of antisemitic crimes recorded by police rose from 2,641 in 2022 to 6,236 in 2024 and 6,548 in 2025. Authorities and monitoring organizations across Europe have reported a significant increase in antisemitic incidents since October 7, 2023.

For Ellen van Praagh, chair of the Interprovincial Rabbinate in the Netherlands, October 7, 2023, marked a turning point. She also lost a family member during the Hamas-led attack which saw around 1,200 people in Israel killed and over 250 taken hostage and abducted to the Gaza Strip.

"My family has lived in the Netherlands since the 16th century. And now I'm being told to leave," says van Praagh. She says the atmosphere in the Netherlands has changed dramatically since the attack. She no longer feels safe there as a Jew. "We Jews are being held responsible for Israel's actions."

Israel launched a major military offensive in the Gaza Strip after the October-7 attack. More than 75,000 Palestinians have been killed there since the start of the war, according to conservative estimates.

Like many others at the symposium, van Praagh says she is increasingly losing faith in politicians. "Never Again" has become an empty phrase, she argues, with little relevance to the everyday lives of Jews in Europe.

Jewish communities now have to protect themselves behind high walls. Constant security measures restrict their daily lives, she explains. "That is not what we want. We want to live in freedom."

Rabbi Menachem Margolin, chairman of the European Jewish Association, is also calling on European political leaders to take greater responsibility. He says he is grateful for their support, without which Jewish life in Europe would hardly be possible.

However, laws designed to protect Jewish life are often not enforced in practice. Many officials hesitate to call antisemitism by its name as soon as doing so becomes politically inconvenient. "But Auschwitz did not begin with gas chambers. It began with words," he cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regina Sluszny joined the delegation visiting the Birkenau memorial. The Auschwitz concentration and extermination camp, built by Nazi Germany, became a symbol of the Holocaust. The Nazis murdered around 1.1 million people there, including approximately one million Jews. Most were killed here at Birkenau.

The delegation is gathered to commemorate the November Pogroms of November 9 and 10, 1938, when Nazis set synagogues on fire, ransacked Jewish businesses and homes and murdered Jews. Around 30,000 Jewish men were deported to concentration camps.

Survivors like Regina are increasingly rare. Most Holocaust survivors have passed away. Regina survived because, in 1942, a family friend and his wife took her in when she was just two years old while her parents fled the Nazis with her two brothers and went into hiding.

For more than 40 years, she has been sharing her story with schoolchildren, doing her part to ensure that the Holocaust is never forgotten. For her, "Never Again" is a promise that must be kept. Otherwise, it becomes a lie.

This article was originally published in German.

Many describe growing hostility towards Jews and rising fear in Jewish communities across Europe. In France, authorities recorded 1,320 antisemitic incidents in 2025, but around three times as many as in 2022.

https://www.dw.com/en/why-the-integratio.title: Why the integration of immigrants in Germany remains a challenge
https://www.dw.com/en/why-the-integratio.text:
The Federal Office for Migration and Refugees has released a new Integration Report. It found that while the integration of people with a migrant background is improving, violent youth remain a problem.

Few topics in Germany spark as many heated debates as integration. How successful have efforts been to integrate new arrivals? What is needed to enable successful integration? And what are the biggest problems?

Every two years, the government's Commissioner for Integration presents a comprehensive set of statistics on the matter. Since last year, that role has been held by Natalie Pawlik, a parliamentary representative from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

Speaking in Berlin on Wednesday, Pawlik offered an overall positive assessment: "Integration is improving steadily, despite ongoing hurdles and challenges." She continued: "The people of our country want integration to succeed. They rightly expect that people who live in Germany permanently will learn our language and abide by our laws."

The Commissioner for Integration is part of the Federal Ministry of Labor because ensuring that newcomers find work quickly is especially important.

The integration reportwas created by a team led by Frank Kalter, director of the German Center for Integration and Migration Research (DeZIM), drawing on official government statistics, surveys and independent studies. They found that when all immigrant groups are counted, about 30% of the population today has some sort of migration background — even if that comes down to only one parent.

Pawlik commented: "This is an important message at a time when the discussion often focuses primarily on problems related to supposedly failed integration." Kalter also pointed out that the employment rate among immigrants in Germany is higher than in most other EU countries — nearly 70%.

And they work primarily in one sector: "In recent years, the biggest increase of workers without German citizenship has been in the health and social services sector." According to the data, there were about 1.8 million people without a German passport working in Germany in 2009. By 2025, this number had more than tripled to 5.8 million.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, problems remain. In nearly all immigrant groups, women have difficulty finding employment, especially if they have children and their husbands are employed. Only about 60% of women in such families are employed, whereas nearly 88% of women in families with German passports are employed.

There are also immigrant groups that face barriers to accessing educational opportunities and the job market. These are mostly young men who came to Germany as refugees. And if one considers citizenship as a distinguishing factor, the percentage of convicted criminals who are not German citizens is far higher — around 40% — than their share of the population. And they are also reported to the police far more frequently. At the same time, individuals without a German passport are also more likely to become victims of crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pawlik emphasizes that language acquisition is the foundation and starting point of any successful integration. But this is precisely where the government tightened its purse strings earlier this year to save money. Many integration courses are now no longer offered at all or receive less government funding. Pawlik made it clear that she is strongly critical of these cuts, even though she herself is part of the federal government.

Most recently, Pawlik and her fellow Social Democrats have been advocating for people who have been working in Germany for some time to receive more secure residency permits — especially those from Syria and Ukraine. On Tuesday, SPD lawmakers adopted a position paper on the matter. In the paper, they propose that existing legal rights that allow workers to remain in the country should also apply to refugees. In other words, it would give working refugees a more secure status.

But will the conservatives from the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) — who lead the coalition led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) — support this? "You'll have to ask the interior minister," Pawlik replied when asked by DW. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) is known for being a hardliner on immigration policy.

This article was originally published in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/why-the-integratio.summary: The Federal Office for Migration and Refugees has released a new Integration Report. It found that while the integration of people with a migrant background is improving, violent youth remain a problem. The report was created by a team led by Frank Kalter, director of the German Center for Integration and Migration Research.

https://www.dw.com/en/democracy-study-on.title: Democracy study: One-quarter of Germans want a right-wing authoritarian dictatorship
https://www.dw.com/en/democracy-study-on.text:
The far-right AfD's electoral successes point to a new trend in Germany: Prejudice, resentment, and extremism are on the rise. A new study suggests satisfaction with democracy is at a low ebb.

Satisfaction with democracy in Germany has hit a new low, while the past is being idealized, and people are expressing a longing for a radical break. Antisemitic sentiments and the desire for an authoritarian leader are also on the rise. These are key findings of the authoritarianism study presented Wednesday in Berlin, which has been conducted every two years since 2002.

The study, led by the Else Frenkel-Brunswik Institute for Democracy Research at the University of Leipzig, is based on the answers to a questionnaire by 2,507 respondents, who the researchers say are a representative cross-section of the German population.

For the first time since the study series began, approval of democracy as an idea fell just below the 90% mark, which the study said is primarily attributable to a loss of trust among respondents in the former East Germany (85.7%). The decline in approval of democracy as experienced in everyday life is even more severe: Nationwide, only one-third are satisfied with democracy, with figures having fallen sharply both in eastern (22.8%) and western (36%) states.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The growing rejection of democracy is also reflected in the desire for some kind of authoritarian nationalist government: Just under a quarter of respondents explicitly supported the idea of a "single strong party that embodies the national community as a whole." In the east, the figure stands at 30.9%, above the Germany-wide average of 22.3%.

"Our democracy is under great pressure. It has lost acceptance among the general population. It is alarming how much an authoritarian yearning is taking its place," concluded social psychologist and study author Oliver Decker.

Far-right attitudes have risen for the second consecutive year. Of particular note in the study was what the researchers called a chauvinistic national pride, which, with 19.9% approval, has reached its highest level since the study series began. The proportion of people with a consistently far-right worldview has reached 6.9%, the highest level since 2014, the study found.

Just under 15% of respondents said they explicitly believe that "everything has to fall apart so that something new can emerge," while nearly one in three respondents believes that "something radical is needed for the current state of affairs to change." Another 29.1% agree with this to some extent.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to the study, those who share this yearning for catastrophe exhibit significantly stronger antisemitic sentiments — and both are linked to a preference for certain political parties. The study found that a large proportion of eligible voters with this orientation favor the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Through its violent rhetoric, the AfD promises to realize the political goals of far-right ideology," the study said. The party's form and content, in other words, correspond exactly to the message that a significant portion of the population wants to hear. "It offers a political home to those who adhere to far-right thinking, while at the same time presenting itself as capable of connecting with a broad segment of society."

Study co-author Johannes Kiess calls on political leaders at all levels to find countermeasures. "The rejection of the present state of the world must be countered with compelling democratic alternatives and the ability to take political action today," he said. This also applies to the significant rise in antisemitism, which has more than doubled since 2022.

When asked about the motives behind antisemitic attitudes, the results show that for 16% of respondents, the policies of Israel's government are the decisive factor. This, too, is a record high in the context of the long-term study. While the figure in 2020 was significantly higher in the east (12%) than in the west (8.4%), the figures have since converged. Antisemitism related to Israel is actually slightly stronger in western than in eastern states.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hostility toward Muslims is also on the rise. It peaked at over 40% in 2018, before dropping to well below 30%, and currently stands at 34.1%. These figures are based on two statements respondents were asked to agree with in each survey: "Muslims should be prohibited from immigrating to Germany" and "because of the many Muslims here, I sometimes feel like a stranger in my own country."

Misogyny is another issue regularly surveyed in the study. In the current survey, 18.3% agreed with anti-feminist statements. Notably, until now, a higher proportion of East Germans had been opposed to feminist causes. As recently as 2024, the difference between the former East (34.6%) and West (19.6%) was enormous. Two years later, the figure in the east has halved to 17.8%, while in western Germany it has fallen only slightly to 18.4%.

Despite the negative trend, there is a glimmer of hope at the end of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study: While the results are "alarming," long-term trends show that a reversal of this trend is possible: "In earlier surveys, far-right statements already achieved high approval ratings, which then declined again in subsequent years. In addition to the influence of societal crises, political action and its societal perception are of central importance."

This article was originally written in German. It was first published on November 11 and later edited for clarity.
https://www.dw.com/en/democracy-study-on.summary: Study conducted every two years since 2002. proportion of people with a consistently far-right worldview has reached. It was first published on November 11 and later edited for clarity.

https://www.dw.com/en/is-aiib-s-complain.title: Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?
https://www.dw.com/en/is-aiib-s-complain.text:
The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. But those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles. Critics say reforms are needed.

For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.

For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.

In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation.

The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints.

Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution.

However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

According to a report by The Diplomat, a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September.

The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism.

The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW.

Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said.

According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts."

But critics see this as a major weakness.

"The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy.

She argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned.

The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it said, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email.

Urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted.

For 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added.

"The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," said Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald.

The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, said the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough."

Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he said, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities.

Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not new. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception.

The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions.

The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction.

For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she said.

As of January 1, 2026, following two years of external consultations, the AIIB reformed its complaints mechanism. Under certain conditions, complaints can now be filed even while legal proceedings are ongoing.

But Sausmikat stressed that the changes are insufficient. Of the eight key recommendations made by an independent expert, only three were adopted, she underlined. "The revision did not remove the actual obstacles."

The AIIB stated that the reforms are intended to make the mechanism "more accessible and responsive."

The new rules have been in effect for only 10 months, and their implementation is being closely monitored, the bank said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Steinert said fear of reprisals poses another fundamental challenge to such procedures.

Documented cases from Latin America, for instance, show that complainants have faced administrative or legal problems, and in some cases even violence.

Such risks could deter others from filing complaints, Steinert said.  However, his research does not specifically address AIIB projects.

The bank said that it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns."

"Requestors may ask for confidentiality, and the revised PPM policy strengthens protection against reprisals," it added.

Sausmikat said Germany — as a co-founder and the fourth-largest shareholder of the AIIB — could also play a role, working with other member states to push for changes.

Hartmann also stressed that the bank's shareholders bear responsibility and urged the AIIB's Board of Directors to amend the rules governing the grievance mechanism. "We need a policy based on good-practice standards."

This article was originally written in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/is-aiib-s-complain.summary: Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. Critics say reforms are needed for those affected by the bank's projects. AIIB says it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns"

https://www.dw.com/en/wael-mohya-could-m.title: Wael Mohya could make German football history at 17
https://www.dw.com/en/wael-mohya-could-m.text:
At just 17, Gladbach forward Wael Mohya has earned his first Germany call-up. The dual-national talent has chosen the DFB path for now — and could soon make modern national-team history.

If you watch the Bundesliga, then you'll know Wael Mohya is a fast-footed, quick-thinking footballer. But not even the 17-year-old (Mohya turns 18 on December 31) Borussia Mönchengladbach youngster would have expected to be called up to the Germany squad so soon.

"Of course, I was absolutely thrilled. It means a great, great deal to me. I think everyone dreams of being selected for the national team at some point," Mohya said.

"And the fact that it's come to this now is, of course, just awesome and makes me very proud."

Mohya was at the gym when the call came in. He then shared the good news with his parents over dinner. "They started crying," the teenager said in a video posted on Gladbach's social media channels.

The youngster, who was born in a small town east of Düsseldorf, smiles and laughs a lot in interviews. He is always friendly, and in a good mood. On the field, too, he exudes the lightheartedness and carefree spirit of a 17-year-old.

As a technically skilled and creative player, Mohya often seeks out one-on-one situations and puts his opponents under pressure with quick dribbles. In nine Bundesliga appearances this season, Mohya has scored twice and delivered one assist.

"He's so cool and just plays really well. It's fun to watch him," Borussia coach Alexander Blessin said recently.

"Wael brings a lot to the team with his laid-back attitude on the field. He's not afraid to take risks, no matter how much pressure there is," added Gladbach's sporting director Rouven Schröder at a talk show on Sport1.

Borussia Mönchengladbach has been Mohya's sporting home since he was seven years old. Last season, previous head coach Eugen Polanski promoted him to the first team, and in December 2025, Mohya made his Bundesliga debut. Against Wolfsburg, aged 16 years and 347 days old, he became the youngest Bundesliga player in the club's history.

Mohya also recently completed a voluntary social year at an elementary school in Mönchengladbach. This is a program in Germany for young people who volunteer in the social sector — at hospitals, schools, or nursing homes, for example — for about six to 18 months. They gain work experience, help others, and earn a little money.

At the school's open all-day care program, Mohya helped serve meals, assisted children with their homework, and played with them. That's also where his nickname comes from. Because a girl hadn't understood his first name correctly or couldn't pronounce it, she called him "Waffel." Now, that name has stuck.

Even before being called up to the Germany team, clubs in the Bundesliga and across Europe's top leagues had taken notice of Mohya and were trying to sign him. His contract with Borussia Mönchengladbach runs through 2028.

With Gladbach currently in a relegation battle, his future appears likely to be elsewhere. If the club wants to generate transfer revenue from its biggest talent, next summer would likely be the opportunity to sell him — unless he extends his contract with Borussia.

The 17-year-old's career is managed by his parents. Whichever club can convince them that their son is in good hands and help him reach his full potential likely has the best chance of securing Mohya's signing.

Mohya himself says he doesn't even know how much he's currently earning at Gladbach.

"My parents take care of all that," he told Bild recently. "I get a monthly allowance, which is more than enough for me."

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp recently revealed how much he had enjoyed his conversations with the youngster.

"The conversations I had with him were great," Klopp said with a laugh. "I wasn't that confident at 17, but then again, I wasn't that good either."

Since Mohya's parents are from Morocco, their son also holds Moroccan citizenship. As a result, he could have played for Morocco, but he has now decided against it. In fact, the Moroccan football association had been actively courting Mohya as early as last year and had already reached out to him in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup.

Now, like Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib, Mohya will continue to play in the German jersey, unlike Schalke's Soufiane El-Faouzi, who chose Morocco, or Bayer Leverkusen's Ibrahim Maza, who likely would have been selected by Klopp as well if he hadn't already opted for Algeria.

For Mohya, who played for Germany's youth teams from the U16s through to the U21s, the door to Morocco remains open, even if he does play for Germany. According to FIFA regulations, players under the age of 21 can change national teams before their fourth international match (whether a competitive or friendly match), provided that none of those matches take place during a World Cup or a continental tournament such as the European Championship, Copa America, or Africa Cup of Nations.

If Mohya plays in the upcoming UEFA Nations League games in Serbia or against the Netherlands, another record is on the horizon. Although there were two even younger players who made their debuts in the Germany jersey — Willy Baumgärtner in 1908 (at 17 years and 104 days) and Marius Hiller in 1910 (at 17 years and 241 days) — the era in which they debuted is hardly comparable. And so, while Wael Mohya would rank third overall on the list, he would become the youngest Germany player in the modern era. The youngest to date was Hamburg legend Uwe Seeler in 1954, aged 17 years and 345 days.

This article was adapted from German.

This article was updated on November 12.
