He would rank third overall on the list, while WaelMohya would be the youngest Germany player in modern era.

https://www.dw.com/en/us-russia-ukraine-.title: US, Russia, Ukraine wrap up talks with prisoner exchange agreement
https://www.dw.com/en/us-russia-ukraine-.text:
Peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US concluded in the United Arab Emirates. The two day talks were the first such meeting since February. DW has the latest updates.

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of news from two days of talks on Tuesday, November 10 and Wednesday, November 11:

This blog covering the trilateral Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi has now closed. Thank you for reading.

Join us on Thursday for fresh coverage as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner separatelymeet with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte offered a characteristically upbeat appraisal of the talks in Abu Dhabi and the prospect of cracks emerging between European NATO members, Ukraine and Donald Trump's administration in the US.

"I was in touch with the NATO team present in Abu Dhabi in the last two days," he told reporters while on a visit to Norway. "What I am getting from those calls is that the US, Ukraine and Europe really being completely aligned and united."

However, he cautioned that "clearly we have to see that the Russian side is willing to play ball."

After more than a decade as prime minister of the Netherlands, Rutte has taken on the unenviable job of trying to keep NATO aligned and united more generally during Donald Trump's second term. He stepped into the role a matter of weeks before the 2024 presidential election in the US.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy landed in Dublin on Wednesday evening, as he and his team head to the ninth European Political Community Summit.

He said both bilateral and multilateral meetings were planned amid his visit to Ireland.

"I will take part in the opening plenary session of the EPC Summit. A meeting on diplomatic efforts with the American negotiating team — Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner — is also planned," he said on social media.

Kushner and Witkoff are first expected to head to Moscow from Abu Dhabi, before moving on to Dublin on Thursday.

The European Political Community is an intergovernmental forum for strategic discussions about the future of Europe. It was set up in 2022, in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The group's ninth summit is scheduled to start early on Thursday morning and to continue until roughly the end of the working day. Hosts Ireland are also the current holders of the EU's rotating presidency.

Kyrylo Budanov described the talks in Abu Dhabi as "tough."

"Ukraine's position remains unchanged," Volodymyr Zelenskyy's chief of staff said on Telegram.

"The war must be brought to a halt, and an effective security architecture must be established — on that ensures a lasting peace and makes any recurrence of Russian aggression impossible."

He said returning Ukrainian prisoners was a "specific focus" of the talks, seemingly a reference to the prisoner swap plans, saying "we have achieved a significant result in this regard."

Budanov also thanked US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff "for their professionalism, persistence, and efforts in seeking solutions," and thanked the UAE for hosting the talks and supporting the process.

Russia's ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died "suddenly" at the age of 66, the Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.

Darchiev was quite new in the job, having been appointed in March 2025 shortly after Donald Trump's return to the White House. From 2021 to 2024, he was ambassador to Canada.

The ministry called Darchiev an "outstanding diplomat, an experienced leader and a kind colleague."

It did not provide further details on the death.

Considered a specialist in US relations, Darchiev headed the Russian Foreign Ministry's North America department between 2014 and 2020 before graduating to ambassadorial roles.

When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, he called the move a "necessary measure."

Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky is quoted by state media as saying Moscow saw no possibility of exchanging territory with Ukraine as part of any potential agreement.

State news agency TASS quoted him saying there was "no possibility whatsoever for such exchanges."

TASS and Interfax also both cited Medinsky as saying that Russia had decided to establish a "security zone" along its border with Ukraine following the incursion into Kursk.

"This zone is already quite substantial, it is expanding — and will continue to expand," he said.

The reported comments did not make clear where Medinsky considered the border or the so-called buffer zones to be, quite possibly by design. Russia already claims large chunks of what the international community considers to be Ukraine as parts of its territory following its invasion.

Yuri Ushakov, a foreign policy advisor to Vladimir Putin and part of the Russian negotiating team, on Wednesday described the talks in Abu Dhabi as substantive and very useful.

Moscow's delegation is led by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, an another aide to Putin.

But Ushakov is also involved, along with deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabko and Mikhail Galuzin, and General Staff officers Igor Kostyukov and Yuri Shigarlovsky on the military side.

German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius has said that following the talks in Abu Dhabi, talks between Chancellor Friedrich Merz and President Vladimir Putin could become more likely.

Asked at a Berlin press conference whether Merz would be ready to speak with Putin, Kornelius said that during the talks in Abu Dhabi negotiators from Europe, the US and Ukraine — but not Russia — had reached an "understanding on the broad outlines."

"This understanding will now be shared with the Russian president. And on that basis, talks may ensue," Kornelius said.

This follows intimations from both sides that the German and Russian leaders might be ready to engage directly.

Russian state news agency Tass cited the Kremlin as saying that Putin would be open to talks with EU leaders including Merz, echoing comments made earlier this year.

Merz, meanwhile, had said last Friday that if Putin were to travel to December's G20 summit in Miami as rumored, he would not rule out a meeting.

Rustem Umerov, currently the head of Ukraine's foreign intelligence service and also its chief negotiator at the talks, also issued a statement following the roughly two hours of trilateral negotiations on Wednesday.

The former defense minister said negotiators discussed "achieving peace and post-war reconstruction," adding that "the first steps towards this must be an end to the war and security guarantees for Ukraine."

Over these two days, the parties were able to state their positions directly, and significant differences remain between them," Umerov said on Telegram.

"There is still a lot of difficult work ahead, but there are opportunities to continue the negotiation process."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had received a report on the Abu Dhabi talks from his negotiating team in Abu Dhabi.

He hailed an "important humanitarian arrangement regarding preparations for a new exchange," seemingly a reference to prisoner exchange plans. Zelenskyy also said negotiators discussed "their views on guaranteeing security" for Ukraine, as well as "broader formats for further work involving the Europeans" going forward.

Currently in Copenhagen in Denmark, Zelenskyy said his team would meet US negotiators in Dublin on Thursday, after they head to Moscow. But he also called for more European representation going forward.

"Ukraine's priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace," Zelenskyy wrote on social media.

"We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy. It is essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war — that is Russia — so that Russia ends the war of its own making."

Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia praised "good momentum" after the two-day talks in Abu Dhabi.

"I think that we have a good momentum to bring the solution before the new year comes," Arakhamia said, adding that he hoped another session could be held "as soon as possible."

Arakhamia is a close ally of ​President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the ⁠head ​of his ​faction in ​parliament.

He echoed Zelenskyy's call to bring Europe into the fold in negotioations, saying the talks should be multilateral, not trilateral.

Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said that mutual understanding had been achieved on some ​issues and that more talks ​would be held.

Medinsky told Russian state television that Russia and ‌Ukraine had agreed in Abu Dhabi on conducting ‌a ​large-scale prisoner swap.

"We have agreed on a new, large-scale prisoner exchange," Medinsky told reporters, adding that "concrete" details would be announced later.

Prisoner exchanges have been one area where the two sides have been able to reach a deal at previous talks.

"Together with the American side, we exchanged our views ​on this; on some points we reached a common ​understanding, whilst on ‌others we did not. And this discussion will, of course, continue. The world needs a new, modern, updated security system – one that ‌is fair and does not disadvantage any particular countries," Medinsky ‌said of the talks.

The talks have been mediated by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner ‌and envoy ⁠Steve Witkoff. They will travel ​to Moscow on ​Thursday, then ​meet ‌Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ‌in Dublin, according to Kushner.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalise the numbers tomorrow," Kushner ‌ said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the US including Europe in Russia-Ukraine negotiations held in Abu Dhabi.

Ukrainian, US and European representatives held a separate meeting once the formal talks with Russia ended.

The US also met with key European nations, the EU and NATO, to ease European concerns about them being kept out of the process.

"It was not simple to involve Europe. That is point number one," Zelenskyy told reporters.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had stressed the day before that going forward the format should "include our European partners at the table as well, because they are a part of solving this problem for the long term."

Russian and Ukrainian sources told AFP that talks in Abu Dhabi had concluded, wrapping up the latest round of negotiations on ending the war. Russian media also reported that talks had finished.

Ukraine said its negotiators would stick around to hold a separate meeting with European and US envoys, once the talks with the Russian team had concluded.

Moscow said ​two people described as agents of the Polish secret ​services were arrested ​in ‌Russia's western Kaliningrad region, Russia's Interfax reported.

The two individuals were reportedly arrested for gathering information on military facilities in Kaliningrad.

Kaliningrad is ​a Russian ⁠exclave on the Baltic Sea that borders Poland and Lithuania.

Russian security services released a statement confirming the arrests without providing the identities of the individuals in custody.

Additionally, seven Polish citizens and three Russian nationals have been put on notice over ‌what ​Russian authorities said were their contacts with the Polish security services.

"Entry into our country has been barred for the aforementioned citizens of the Republic of Poland for an extended period," the statement by the FSB read.

Polish authorities, through a spokesman, denounced the statements as "provocation and disinformation."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn0.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn0.text:
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.

Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.

The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.

Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.

Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.

The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.

Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.

Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.

Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."

The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.

"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.

Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.

Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.

Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.

He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.

Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.

Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr89.title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr89.text:
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.

Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found.

The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated". Unlike a day earlier, only 77 schools were evacuated on Thursday, authorities say.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat.

Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.

The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.

Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".

Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.

A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.

Many parents, though, are concerned and have been demanding clarity and action from the government.

La Repubblica newspaper reports that protests have been held against a decision by the headmaster of a secondary school in Rome who did not take any action, saying she had realised the threatening message to contain typos and therefore be "fake".

According to the newspaper, protesters want new national guidelines to be issued.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr89.summary: Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row. Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats. The government has advised schools that buildings must not be evacuated.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.title: Hegseth awards medal to war memorial guard who reprimanded him and group
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.text:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery.

A video of a Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before the guard told them to be quiet.

In a statement, the Pentagon later announced that Hegseth had given Specialist Thomas Iglesias a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier".

Photos shared on the defence secretary's X account showed him presenting the medal to Iglesias.

He was accompanied by others whom the Pentagon identified as members of the 3rd US Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, which is responsible for holding vigil over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots," the accompanying text on Hegseth's post reads.

In the video, the army sentinel on duty later identified as Iglesias can be seen stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.

The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell later said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured - and will always honour - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."

A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.

It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day.

Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery.

During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war.

"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back. All of us fought back," he said.

"And we won," Trump said of the Iran war. "It's just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."

Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary.

Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth amid Democratic lawmakers' push to impeach him. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill.

Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8kg.title: Five new miniature frog species found in eastern Himalayas
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8kg.text:
Scientists have discovered five new species of tiny horned frogs in India's eastern Himalayas, more than doubling the number of known species in the group.

A team of scientists from University of Delhi and Harvard University made the discoveries after five years of fieldwork, identifying the frogs as members of the Jingophrys group.

Among them is Jingophrys tanogogo - or the snail-eating horned frog - the first frog known in India to feed on snails and the first member of its family recorded with such a diet.

The research suggest the Himalayas have played a much larger role in frog evolution than previously thought and highlight the region as an overlooked hotspot for biodiversity.

The Himalayas, stretching from tropical forests to alpine meadows, are among the world's richest biodiversity regions.

Despite drawing interest from scientists and researchers, many parts here have not been fully explored.

The state of Arunachal Pradesh particularly has emerged as one of its least-studied regions.

Dr Sonali Garg, who led the study at Harvard University's Museum of Comparative Zoology, said the research highlights how significant evolutionary changes can go unnoticed in little-studied species.

The study - called two-fold hidden diversity of diminutive horned frogs (Megophryinae: Jingophrys) - was conducted by Garg along with her colleague James Hanken and Delhi University's SD Biju, Tage Tajo and Radhakrishna Upadhyaya K.

It was published on 11 November in the Royal Society Open Science journal.

"Some of the new species are extremely secretive and found in remote forests only during a short breeding season," says Biju.

Researchers say further studies will have to done to better understand their biology and conservation needs.

DNA analysis showed the horned frogs rapidly diversified into multiple species in the eastern Himalayas as the mountain range rose and the Asian monsoon took shape over millions of years, helping drive the evolution of the region's plants and wildlife.

The researchers said in a statement that local tribes gave them essential field support and knowledge that helped make the discoveries possible. Some of the species were named after these communities.

The Tanii horned frog (Jingophrys taniitatii), for instance, is named by combining the name of the Tanii tribe in the region with the word 'tatti' - frog in the local Apatani language.

The new species have been named Jingophrys taniitatii (Tanii horned frog), Jingophrys tanogogo (snail-eating horned frog), Jingophrys siangensis (Siang horned frog), Jingophrys hrdy (Hrdy's horned frog) and Jingophrys wularsoni (Wu-Larson's horned frog).
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8kg.summary: Scientists from University of Delhi and Harvard University made the discoveries after five years of fieldwork. They identified the frogs as members of the Jingophrys group. Among them is the first frog known in India to feed on snails and the first member of its family recorded with such a diet.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgj.title: Eight killed in Colombian air strike targeting Gulf Clan gang
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgj.text:
A senior leader of Colombia's largest criminal gang, the Gulf Clan, is among eight people killed in an air strike carried out by the country's armed forces, according to President Abelardo de la Espriella.

De la Espriella said he had personally authorised the bombing targeting the Gulf Clan in the province of Antioquia, in north-west Colombia.

He added that Haminton Mosquera, whom he described as a senior member of the crime gang and one of 10 "priority targets" for Colombia's security forces, had been "brought down".

De la Espriella was elected in June after campaigning on a promise to crack down on Colombia's powerful criminal gangs, including by launching air strikes.

In a post on X, he said that Mosquera was suspected of having ordered attacks against the security forces, including the murder of a police officer in the municipality of Tarazá last year.

The Gulf Clan has been engaging in criminal activities for decades, mainly trafficking cocaine from Colombia to destinations in the US and Europe but also illegal mining and people smuggling.

The US added it to its list of Foreign Terrorist Organisations (FTOs) last year.

In his post, President de la Espriella said that "the offensive won't stop" and vowed to regain control of areas currently controlled by criminal organisations such as the Gulf Clan.

While his offensive against criminal gangs has been welcomed by many living in areas where extortion and gang violence are rampant, de la Espriella has faced criticism for the way he has made some of his announcements on security.

Less than a month after taking office, he published a video showing him walking among 23 body bags containing the remains of 23 people killed in an air strike on a suspected guerrilla camp.

On Wednesday, he shared a photo in which he can be seen writing his campaign slogan, "Welcome to the miracle homeland" on a bomb.

He has also defended his decision to wear an army uniform at a recent event in Cúcuta at which he confronted a detainee suspected of being a Farc rebel.

"What did you make of the bomb I sent you, signed by me?," the president can be heard asking the man.

He later told journalists that he wore the uniform because "I am a soldier of the homeland. That's why I dress like a soldier, because I came to serve Colombia. Because I honour the heroes, police officers and military."

Additional reporting by BBC Monitoring's Luis Fajardo.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmze.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmze.text:
Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in the US and China alike, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation.

The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom.

He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into freefall this week, undone by romantic entanglements that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement.

On Thursday, he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague.

His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China.

Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.

The company, which is still valued at nearly $4n (£3.02tn) despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.

Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.

They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.

Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".

But while the former Nvidia CEO is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.

Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," Witt added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.

After the revelations of the first affair, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.

Trump, as well as other leaders in the AI tech industry, initially backed Huang to continue in his role at Nvidia. The president described him as "honourable".

But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by the announcement Huang was stepping down.

In the aftermath of that news Trump said Huang had done "a fantastic job" and proposed Tim Cook of Apple as a suitable replacement at the head of Nvidia.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmde.title: Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators from Mississippi
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmde.text:
After winning a close race in Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom will become the state's first black US senator for more than 150 years, and the third in history.

It is a historic result in the deeply conservative southern state that last sent a Democrat to the US Senate in 1982, and had not seated a black senator since 1875.

Colom follows Hiram Revels, who became the first black person ever to serve in the chamber when he was seated from 1870 to 1871, and Blanche Bruce, whose term ran from 1875 to 1881. Revels and Bruce were both members of the Republican Party.

Revels was chosen as Mississippi's first senator after the Civil War, serving for just over a year and campaigning strongly for racial equality.

A few years later, Bruce, who was born into slavery, became the first black person to serve a full term in the US Senate. He remained in Washington after leaving the chamber and held a role in the Treasury.

Both terms came before the repressive Jim Crow laws began to enforce racial segregation across Mississippi and other southern US states.

A significant factor in Colom's victory was his success in mobilising young people and the state's large black population, who are expected to have turned out in high numbers.

In a victory speech, Colom referenced how Revels, who was a minister and served as a chaplain during the Civil War, gained support for his Senate campaign through his words.

"That's an example of the power of prayer, and through our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times," Colom said.

Prior to the result being called, the BBC spoke to students at Jackson State University, a historically black college in Mississippi. Many of them had voted for the first time and backed Colom.

"I really feel like a change is what we need," 18-year-old Jamyria Dunn said.

"I've had some amazing days in my life," she continued, "but seeing Mississippi, this state in particular, turn blue, would really bring a light to my heart that people just would not understand."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5y.title: How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5y.text:
If I'd told you this time last week that Jensen Huang was about to leave Nvidia, you would not have believed me.

The man who co-founded this enormously successful AI chip company, working tirelessly to build it from the ground up and steering it through some disastrous times with endless energy and ruthless determination, has ultimately been undone by his own love life.

It's an extraordinary tale and a strangely old fashioned one for a tech firm with its sights set on the future.

It spawned a plethora of viral memes, seeing Huang as the man caught by the Coldplay kiss-cam with a married colleague, or singing along to George Michael's classic hit about betrayal, Careless Whisper.

Both were ironically AI-generated using the very tech he was helping to build.

This week I met two Silicon Valley execs and I asked them how they were processing the news - "in memes", was the response.

But they didn't seem to think Huang would be forced out by his alleged adultery.

The stakes were too high, they said, the entire AI industry relies too heavily on Nvidia chips to break a winning formula.

In as many words, "the Valley" was on his side.

But that was before rumours of a second affair surfaced, this time with a colleague, and the board decided he had gone too far.

His behaviour suddenly cast him in a different light: a man who could make bad decisions and cover them up.

Huang always made a point of standing out from the crowd.

During the coronavirus lockdowns, he streamed keynote speeches from his kitchen (which gained internet fame in its own right, but were later revealed to have been AI-generated).

He is rarely seen without a leather jacket – he has joked that he only owns one suit, and he borrows his daughter's partner's tie.

Huang rubbed shoulders with the elite, with a network including Donald Trump, Elon Musk and King Charles.

The last time I saw him was at St James' Palace last year, where he was receiving the prestigious Queen's Prize for Engineering.

I was told he would not talk to the press - but he wandered over by himself and we spent about 10 minutes having a chat while press officers hovered nervously in the background. He was articulate and optimistic about the progress of AI and the UK's role in it.

For many people, Huang was Nvidia. He had as many as 200 people directly reporting to him.

He expected high standards – in his book about its inner workings, the Nvidia Way, author Tae Kim wrote the office hours were long.

Huang's feedback could be both brutal and public, and he thought nothing of pointing out individuals' mistakes in all-staff meetings.

Now it is his own shortcomings which are on very public display, and he has been forced into a brutal ending of his own career.

Colette Kress, who takes over for now, will be a familiar face internally and that must feel reassuring to some at Nvidia.

She's worked at the company for 13 years and for those who follow its considerable finances, she is often present on earnings calls. She is a billionaire in her own right and a high-flying tech executive.

But she's not an engineer and Nvidia's products are highly technical.

She will have to convince investors that it is business as usual for Nvidia, that the innovation for which it is renowned can continue at its existing pace, and that the top talent won't leave with Huang.

A wobbly Nvidia would be bad news for the entire AI industry because its ever-advancing chips drive the most powerful AI models, and it's also regarded as something of a central bank, loaning money to other firms.

As for Huang himself, we assume for now that the investigation into his relationship with the woman accused of being a Chinese spy will continue, and the results of that may well determine what he does next.

He probably won't be short of offers despite his conduct – and I expect Nvidia's rivals can't believe their luck that their formidable rival has taken himself out of the game. Elon Musk has already said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.

It's important though to remember that even if Huang turns out not to have betrayed his company or his country, he still betrayed his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang.

And for her, it's not a story of tech, temptation and trillion-dollar-valuations.

It's a painfully personal matter.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe8.title: Flood victim, 95, lived in Wetherspoons after her home was destroyed and died before she could return
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe8.text:
When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home.

Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales last November.

But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded.

"Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that."

Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of November 15 last year as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours.

It has been officially described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in Monmouth during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town.

Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her.

"She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms most days.

"The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her."

"We never thought she'd be there that long," said Wyn. "It's nobody's fault, it took a long time to dry her home out. It had to be done properly."

Residents have been with family, some are in rented accommodation, some have been in an Airbnb while another is in a care home.

Their story is typical of many in Monmouth who have been out of their home since Claudia struck - and that trauma and anxiety from the devastation of 12 months ago is never far from the surface.

"Some had been through the war and they said it upset them more than that. It was just awful," said Wyn.

"But unfortunately it could happen again. There's that fear. If they see water coming, it'll freak them out. They need to feel at home and not worry about the weather."

The Met Office estimates that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.

Wales' environmental body has warned long-range forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual this winter with Natural Resources Wales (NRW) saying people should prepare for "the unthinkable".

Apart from three nights at the local Premier Inn over Christmas when Wetherspoons was shut - where Jean had sandwiches from the nearby petrol station for Christmas dinner because she wanted to "remain independent" - she stayed above the pub in the town's main square for almost 10 months.

"As time went on, living in one room was awful for her," recalled Wyn, 70.

"When Jean got ill, it wasn't a place for her to live. Her health deteriorated and she didn't come back home, which is sad."

Jean's death will be acutely felt when the first displaced residents return to the Chippenham Court retirement complex she called home following its £1m refurbishment in the next few weeks.

One in seven properties in Wales are at risk of flooding, including the Frost household on the other side of Monmouth where Emily says she and her young family will never recover from being evacuated on a lifeboat last year.

The mum-of-two breaks down as she recalls being woken by the coastguard telling her she's got five minutes to evacuate her family as the floodwaters surge towards her end-of-terrace cottage.

"Opening the door, I completely freaked out to the lifeguard," Emily told the BBC.

"They were waist deep in water and said our house was at risk. I just needed to get our boys, who were then aged three and five, and they'd be back with a raft. We didn't have time to think about it."

What was supposed to be a night of celebration for her and husband Jake's 10th wedding anniversary, turned into a nightmare.

Emily and Jake didn't take their boys when they returned home the following day where more than a foot of water had penetrated their home.

"There was sludge and mud everywhere," she recalled.

"We didn't bring the boys home for a good while because we didn't want them seeing everything that they'd treasured had been destroyed.

"It was the toll it would take on them that worried us the most."

The Frosts lived in rental accommodation nearby for six months as they ripped out the downstairs of their home and started again.

Emily and Jake, who had also been flooded in 2020, have seen their boys "playing floods" so know their children have been "trying to process" their ordeal.

"They couldn't really understand why we weren't able to go home or have their things" said Emily.

"Because it's the time of year, even now when it rains they'll ask "are we staying home, is it okay? Luckily they're resilient as kids, but you still worry. People don't recover, it's something you'll just live with."

Environmental bodies estimate about 275,000 properties in Wales are at risk of flooding with another 400,000 in Scotland, while in England about 6.3 million properties - around 11.3m people - live in flood risk areas.

An official report said the River Monnow swelled to more than six-and-a-half metres after significant rainfall locally and upstream over the Black Mountains during a week where more than half-a-dozen Met Office rain warnings were issued.

Jennifer and Alan Morgan's 18th Century cottage near the banks of the Monnow had two more doors to hang after a five-year renovation when Claudia struck and they had to start it all again.

"I've not slept well for a year as it's been an absolutely living nightmare," said Jennifer, 70.

"The flooding was awful and the renovation has been so stressful, it's had a huge impact on us. We're not anywhere near to going back home, we probably won't be in until next summer.

"People might think because some of the shops and businesses are open that Monmouth is back to as it was before, but that's not the case - and we're proof."

The official Section 19 report into the flooding said flood warnings - where action is required as properties are in danger of flooding - were issued for all of Monmouth hours before the floods hit.

Wales' highest state of flood alert - the "risk to life and significant disruption" severe flood warning - was issued by NRW for the northern part of Monmouth on the Friday evening.

The severe flood warning for the rest of Monmouth was issued at 03:31 on the Saturday morning - but that was more than two hours after its flood defences were breached and after shops and homes had been flooded.

Emily had signed up to NRW's free flood alert service but went to bed because at midnight the rain had stopped and there was no water visible - half an hour before her young family were evacuated.

"When it stopped raining everyone probably thought 'oh well this has passed and we don't need to worry'," she said.

"Then the deluge of water just appeared from nowhere. It just shows how quickly it can change."

The official report recommended a review of the timing of severe flood warnings throughout the Monnow catchment "to ensure adequate advance notice is provided for people to respond effectively."

It also called for a review on the "uptake and understanding" of the flood warning service for those who live and work near the River Monnow.

NRW has said it reviews their "response, recovery and flood warning thresholds" after every serious incident to "identify lessons".

Of the one in seven properties in Wales classed as being at risk of flooding, NRW said less than a third of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up.

NRW argues Wales' geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys.

The official report also recommended a review into whether Monmouth town centre defences are fit for purpose.

"We're looking at our flood modelling and if there's anything else that can be done," said Sara Pearson of NRW.

"We're seeing flooding that we've never experienced before and with climate change that's set to increase. We can't prevent flooding, but we can help minimise the impact."

The Welsh Government has said it is spending almost £1.4m in flood risk management in Monmouthshire, including £700,000 of NRW funding for works at nearby Skenfrith.

"We have made £85m available this year to Natural Resources Wales and local authorities for flood and coastal erosion schemes across Wales," the government said in a statement.

NRW have said they've done work to clear rivers while the local council insist they've got more workers out clearing ditches, gullies and drains.

"We know how serious this is and how worrying it is for people," said Catrin Maby of Monmouthshire council.

"If it was only down to drain clearance we wouldn't need to worry. We need to look at the engineered defences again, we need to look at how we manage the land, we need to allocate sufficient resources into drainage and clearing those drains."

Insurance companies in the UK paid out £565 million to help homeowners recover from storms and floods in 2025 - and Emily's home is one of them with flood defence measures in place like flood gates and flood doors after advice from Flood Mary.

"I feel safer," added Emily. "I'll still be very apprehensive when you get the flood alert, it's whether you're gonna go back to that time or not.

"But you don't feel safe, which you should do in your own house."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0re.title: How many sewage spills have happened in your part of Scotland?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0re.text:
More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded after new monitoring equipment was installed at waste overflow sites in Scotland, BBC analysis suggests.

The addition of 1,009 sewer monitors in 2024 increased the proportion of the Scottish Water network being monitored from 6% to 30%.

Now the latest figures have revealed tens of thousands of spills which would previously have been unrecorded, including hundreds at beauty spots like Loch Lomond.

Scottish Water said the vast majority of the spills were not harmful to the environment, and that increased monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network.

BBC Scotland News has used the latest data to create an interactive map which you can use to find out how many spills were recorded in your area, and how long they lasted.

Sewage spills happen automatically at overflow sites, which are permitted to release excess water into natural waterways.

They usually consist of a pipe - set much higher than the usual water level - which provides an escape route when the system is deluged.

These overflows act as relief valves to prevent the sewer system from becoming overwhelmed during heavy rainfall and flooding into homes, businesses and streets.

The spills can last anywhere from a few minutes to hours.

Scottish Water currently has over 4,200 overflows across its network. The number of overflows with monitoring rose from 273 to 1,275 in 2024.

More than 100,000 spills totalling to almost 277,000 hours were recorded last year – an average of about 274 a day.

It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage.

The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).

Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need.

However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa.

Scottish Water figures show that Glasgow's River Clyde was one of the most impacted waterways in Scotland last year, receiving almost 6,150 spills - or the equivalent of 17 a day.

When adding in the Clyde Estuary, Firth of Clyde and other unnamed tributaries that run into the Clyde's waterways, this almost doubles to nearly 14,200, or 39 a day.

The Clyde Estuary also recorded the longest duration of spills - more than 25,000 hours - followed by the River Clyde with more than 15,000 hours.

Barcloy Mill Burn in Dumfries and Galloway, which is one of the newly-monitored sites, received the most spills last year, with a total of almost 3,500.

The data suggests that 225 sites recorded no spills and 525 recorded fewer than 10. There may also be errors which suggest a monitor is active when it is not.

There were 1,270 spills, totalling almost 1,500 hours, last year into West Lothian's River Almond, which is nearly 28 miles in length.

Local campaigner Ruth Plevin said swimming in the river was part of her childhood and that she now wants to protect it for her own grandchildren.

She said any investment in improving the infrastructure of the water system was welcome.

"It's what's not visible that is our concern - the microplastics, the pharmaceuticals, the agrichemicals, stuff that you can't see," she said.

Plevin, a member of the River Almond Action Group, said she wants the group's legacy to be clean, safe water.

"It's precious and I think we need to regard it as precious. Value it, look after it and make it safe.

"I want it to be clean - it's not a lot to ask for, really," she said.

Further along the east coast at Belhaven in East Lothian, surfer Brian Allen has been testing the local water for pollution.

Each week he sends samples to an accredited laboratory to be tested for E.coli and intestinal enterococci.

He says this is the same sampling as done by Sepa, except he tests all year round and not just during the bathing season.

Sepa monitors bathing water quality at about 80 sites across Scotland between May and September. It also looks out for algae, seaweed and waste.

Allen, the regional representative for Surfers Against Sewage, said the results had been providing "really good news" for Belhaven.

He said 86% of the samples were rated as excellent, good or sufficient water quality, which was fine for recreational water users.

"In fact 77% of the results are coming back as excellent. What we don't know is whether that picture is being replicated across the rest of Scotland," he said.

Allen welcomed Scottish Water's increase in data publishing and said working collaboratively would help build up a bigger picture of water quality.

He said the figures had showed there were almost daily discharges from the two overflows in the area – but it was not known if there was a link between discharges and water quality.

One of them, at West Barns at Dunbar, recorded 3,300 spills last year - the second highest number in Scotland last year and a newly-monitored site.

Simon Parsons, director for wastewater at Scottish Water, said most of the time overflows were doing the job they were designed for - draining rainwater out of the sewer system.

"The vast majority of those spills aren't harmful to the environment because they're nearly always about rainwater," he explained.

Scottish Water said 99% of spills were rainwater, surface water, road run-off, "grey" water from households (not human waste), infiltration of groundwater, and trade effluent.

Parsons said the increase in monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network and helped identify locations requiring improvement.

"We didn't necessarily know how and when our overflows were operating so we've got a much better picture now than we've ever had before.

"We can actually identify those areas where we need to think about investment.

"We've got a number of locations across Scotland where actually we've identified links between how our pumps work and how our treatment works work, which have told us where we do get some spills when we shouldn't have them - and we'll make the improvements."

Monitoring in Scotland remains far lower than in England, which has 100% coverage.

Differences in recording means Scotland's figures are not directly comparable with the rest of the UK.

Scottish Water said its monitoring had now grown to about 50% and that it was aiming to reach 100% over the next five to six years.

Parsons said the cost was relatively small but represented good value in terms of the intelligence they provided.

Additional reporting by Andrew Picken

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cknv.title: Trouble at the top - the crisis of confidence in Scotland's NHS leaders
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cknv.text:
The verdict from Scotland's healthcare watchdog on NHS Grampian could hardly have been more damning.

Major problems at Dr Gray's Hospital in Elgin, but deficiencies stretching across the whole region, a failure to learn from mistakes and "recurring patterns of harm".

Thursday's report from Health Improvement Scotland is more evidence that frontline NHS staff feel they are carrying the can for poor leadership by highly-paid, powerful people at the top of Scotland's health boards.

Centre stage this time is chief executive Laura Skaife-Knight, who earns between £170,000 and £175,000 a year. She ordered this review, but does not escape blame.

The report reveals she was forced into a humiliating apology earlier this year, for giving misleading information about a review into a patient's death during surgery.

Not only did Health Improvement Scotland find the investigation into the death was inadequate, it also found the chief executive then misled Health Improvement Scotland by saying senior executives had not seen the review or signed it off.

In fact, executive medical director Hugh Bishop had been sent the review, and had discussed it in a meeting, but claimed he had "no recollection" of this.

He left his post in recent weeks.

Misinformation provided by Skaife-Knight to the watchdog caused "significant distress" to staff at lower levels, who felt the management had tried to shift the blame onto them.

She apologised to both HIS and the affected staff, and took steps "intended to rebuild trust".

Healthcare Improvement Scotland has described this as the most serious review it has ever had to undertake – and it details a pattern of management failure that goes beyond a single individual.

Weak leadership across the whole of NHS Grampian led to failures in recruitment, in management, in governance.

It highlights repeated failures to act on warnings about patient safety or to learn from mistakes.

For now, the Health Secretary Angela Constance has said she is keeping faith in Skaife-Knight, saying "she has operated with candour" and "put her hands up when she made mistakes".

Constance said almost half of the board had changed, a new chairperson is about to step in and she expects them to hold senior executives to account.

With NHS Grampian already in special measures because of financial difficulties, further escalation is inevitable.

The health secretary said she will update parliament next week on what further action the government will take.

Public perception around their performance will be a talking point for the government and MSPs as they move forward with plans announced in September to cut the number of health boards from 14 to two.

There is a debate about whether this is the right move for patients, but there is also a question over whether huge structural changes can improve the accountability of NHS leadership or not.

For now it is the north east of Scotland in the spotlight, but these are themes that will resonate with NHS staff right across the country.

In July, emergency medicine consultants in Glasgow wrote to Health Improvement Scotland warning of a risk of "whole-system failure" and ongoing risks to patient safety.

The doctors said the situation in the emergency department at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital had deteriorated since an inspection in 2024.

They, too, held health board executives responsible, noting staff had scored their confidence in leadership at 32/100 in a recent survey.

They questioned the transparency of their chief executive, Prof Jann Gardner, claiming she encouraged them to engage with a 2025 independent review of culture and relationships, the results of which have never been published.

NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde said it continued to address the issues raised and that a programme of improvement work was ongoing.

Elsewhere, the chief executive of NHS Ayrshire and Arran also stepped down this year, after it suffered financial near-collapse

No-one can doubt NHS bosses have a tough job but they are all paid generous six-figure salaries.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.title: Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.text:
Andy Burnham has committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but he knows just how the high the political stakes are.

He saw how last year's welfare rebellion marked the beginning of the end for his predecessor in Downing Street.

Sir Keir Starmer's authority was shredded when 120 - more than a quarter - of his own MPs threatened to derail his reforms.

To defuse this, Sir Keir was compelled to guarantee that existing claimants of personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales, wouldn't lose out.

Even then, 49 of the 120 potential Labour rebels still voted against their own government.

Next week, a review from former New Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn has the capacity to create another internal row in Labour's ranks.

Milburn has spent a year grappling with how to reduce the nearly one million young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neets).

In an interview with the Times, he has now confirmed he is set to recommend cutting benefits for some 16-24 year olds who currently receive Pip, or the enhanced health-related payment of Universal Credit.

Taking benefit cuts to the Parliamentary Labour Party would usually have a similar effect to adding phosphorous to water.

But from my soundings, the deep waters of the Labour ranks are calmer than might be expected.

Importantly, two of the most effective organisers of last year's welfare rebellion are batting for the current prime minister, rather than against the previous one.

Louise Haigh is now the most powerful cabinet minister after Andy Burnham himself, while Anneliese Midgeley is his chief whip.

And the MP who fronted that rebellion - Meg Hillier - has said she wants to give Milburn's proposals a "fair wind".

There are also clear differences to the previous approach to welfare reform.

First, it is not being presented as primarily a cost-cutting exercise with pre-determined savings.

Instead, there will be upfront investment to provide more support to unemployed young people, and a timeframe for net savings likely to be set at around a decade – gradualism, not a short, sharp shock.

Second, last year's initial reforms would have affected people in all age groups, whilst benefit cuts this time would be limited to the under 25s, who make up around 11% of Pip claimants.

I've spoken to government ministers who had expressed concerns – at least privately – about the changes devised previously by Rachel Reeves and Liz Kendall. This time, they are on board.

One of them told me that so long as there was enough support for young people, with guaranteed jobs and training, MPs would be "fine" with some benefit cuts.

But they added that it was vital that those who really couldn't work wouldn't be worse off.

Milburn will suggest there could even be enhanced payments for people in this category, while some young people with disabilities who lose out on Pip could nonetheless be given an additional "allowance" to help with living costs.

Another minister who opposed the previous reforms praised the process this time.

There had been a high level of engagement not just from Milburn, but Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, who has been taking MPs through the principles behind the reforms.

One minister was a little more cautious, suggesting support for a reduction in benefits would depend on what the entire "package" of reforms looked like.

Milburn's recommendations are likely to be wide-ranging – from pre-school policies to how the NHS deals with mental health.

Some of the eventual 49 rebels from last year are in a similar place.

York MP Rachael Maskell told me it was essential that she saw the detail of the proposals rather than the "drip, drip" of press reports which would "cause young people stress and distress".

She felt withdrawing Pip from young people was "like a sledgehammer to crack a nut" and was concerned that some disabled people required it to remain in work.

She also suggested that the government "shouldn't just point the finger at young people," and should look closely at how employers could take more youngsters on.

Stroud MP Simon Opher also voted against the government on welfare last year.

He told me there was a "crisis" with so many Neets, and Milburn had come up with a "credible solution".

But he believes cutting benefits should be a "last resort" and is worried about restricting access to the health element of Universal Credit, as a quarter of young claimants aren't Neet. He concludes that the "devil will be in the detail".

So much of politics - like comedy – depends on timing.

For some sceptics, including serving ministers, the Milburn proposals will be more warmly welcomed if support for young people is in place before entitlements are withdrawn.

But for some Labour MPs, cutting payments to existing claimants crosses a line.

Clapham and Brixton Hill MP Bell Ribiero-Addy has she wasn't sure she could back cuts.

Referring to Pip, she didn't believe that "you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work".

And another MP on the left of the party, Brian Leishman, told the BBC he couldn't back benefits cuts as "we are in the middle of a cost of living crisis".

So a welfare rebellion seems guaranteed if Burnham accepts Milburn's recommendations.

But it seems unlikely to be of the same scale, or have a similar level of political jeopardy to the one which shook the Starmer government.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c58j.title: Military base asylum plans granted planning approval
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c58j.text:
Planning permission to house asylum seekers at a former military site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington has been granted by the government.

The Home Office's application to house up to 1,256 men at the MoD Bicester site was fast-tracked using an Urgent Crown Development application.

The nearby village of Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK in opposition to the planned site, which has also been legally challenged by campaigners.

A Home Office spokesperson said the planning permission "allows us to continue to progress the use of MoD Bicester" but no final decision on the proposal had been taken.

A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against, and one in support.

It also said Housing Secretary Angela Rayner ruled permission should be granted because "national demand for asylum accommodation remains high".

The permission allows for demolition of existing buildings, the erection of new modular accommodation, and provisions for health and welfare facilities.

Chris Philp MP, Shadow Home Secretary, said: "Angela Rayner and the Labour government have betrayed the people of Piddington by abusing their emergency powers in this way."

He continued: "Instead of accommodating illegal immigrants, the government should leave the ECHR so they can be rapidly deported."

Lib Dem MP for Bicester and Woodstock Calum Miller said it was "the wrong plan and the wrong site for local communities, asylum seekers and taxpayers".

"I am deeply disappointed that the government has approved this proposal despite the serious concerns raised by residents and local councils as well as the major problems with the site," he added.

The approval could be challenged by an application to the High Court within six weeks, beginning with the day after the date of the decision.

The government said a challenge "may be brought only on the ground that the decision is legally flawed; it is not an opportunity to reconsider the planning merits".

Joe Marshall, a Piddington parish councillor, said residents of the village were "extremely frustrated".

"The government has approved its own application against more than 3,000 objections and one letter of support, overruling the councils, the NHS and the Police and Crime Commissioner," he said.

"No wonder we voted to leave the UK."

Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said: "Over 1,200 unvetted illegal migrant men are being dumped in Piddington.

"Tory and Labour governments have betrayed their own people. Reform will detain and deport all of these men."

A Home Office spokesperson said: "A final decision to proceed is yet to be taken.

"The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1 billion saved in costs since the election.

"This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

"These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy.title: Some childhood offenders may no longer have to reveal convictions to employers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy.text:
Some job applicants in England and Wales would no longer need to declare criminal convictions they received as children under government proposals designed to improve the employment prospects of rehabilitated young people.

The changes would mean criminal records for people detained when they were under 18 years old would no longer show up for life during checks carried out by employers.

The Ministry of Justice has also launched a consultation on relaxing disclosure requirements for some specific drug-related and violent crimes committed by children.

Young people who have not re-offended as adults struggle to find work because of their past behaviour, the government says.

Many employers require applicants to undergo a background check, which in their most basic form require people to self-declare if they have a criminal record.

For more sensitive roles, such as working with children or joining the police, an employer can carry out a standard or enhanced check, which allows them to request information from the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS).

How long a criminal record must be volunteered for or will show up in those checks differs depending on the severity of the offence, the punishment received and how long ago the crime was committed - sometimes referred to as whether a conviction is 'spent'.

For example, a young person who was convicted and fined for an offence when they were under-18 will have that information show up in checks for five-and-a-half years. If they were given a custodial sentence, that will be disclosed for the rest of their lives.

The government wants to reduce the number of young people those disclosure rules apply to if an applicant has not continued to offend as an adult.

Five offences would be removed from a list of crimes which will show up in background for checks for life if committed by an adult. They are: affray, violent disorder, supplying a controlled drug to a child, robbery and assaults occasioning actual bodily harm.

Between March 2022 and March 2026, around 8,500 under-18s were convicted of those offences, according to Ministry of Justice data.

The government says that type of crime is often a result of peer pressure, exploitation and "adolescent impulsivity" by individuals who are still developing, as opposed to a broader propensity for crime and violence.

Under the new rules, they would cease to show up in checks after five-and-a-half years.

Lifelong disclosure would also be removed for offences which led to a detention period of less than two years, the maximum which can be handed out by a youth court, and replaced by a new 11-year disclosure period.

In cases where a child was given a sentence longer than two years - which can only happen if the severity of the crime meant they were dealt with by an adult crown court - the rules would stay the same.

The most serious offences - including severe violence, terrorism-related crimes and sexual offences - would be exempted from the reforms.

Other proposed changes include:

Announcing a consultation on proposals, justice minister Jake Richards said: "Many young people who offend do not go on to lead lives of crime.

"They take responsibility, turn their lives around and want to make something of themselves.

"When they do, we should recognise that progress and support them – not put unnecessary barriers in their way."

The proposals come as the government prepares to publish a long-awaited report authored by former Labour minister Alan Milburn on tackling the number of young people not in work or education.

In May, he warned the UK was at risk of a raising a "lost generation" as almost one in eight young people are not working or studying.

Richards pointed to that intervention as he announced the disclosure reforms, saying barriers to employment can be "particularly difficult to overcome" for people who committed crimes as children.

Ministry of Justice also launched a consultation on relaxing disclosure requirements for some specific drug-related and violent crimes

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckjw.title: Parliament date set for 'summer of sex' debate
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckjw.text:
An MP has been given a date for a House of Commons debate following her campaign calling for lifelong sex education.

Dubbed the "summer of sex", the campaign was launched to push education about consent, respect and healthy relationships, with the aim of preventing abuse and violence, but has received a mixed response in Westminster.

Samantha Niblett has previously said she also planned a separate event to display a number of sex toys and sex education aids in Parliament as part of the campaign. However, this is unlikely to take place until the new year.

The backbench debate is due to take place in Parliament on 26 November, it has been confirmed.

The South Derbyshire MP applied in March for the debate, but said she faced a "longer wait" for it to be granted because she wanted it to take place in the main chamber, rather than a lower-profile venue such as Westminster Hall.

"I wanted it to be in the main chamber as the gravity of the topic warrants the surroundings that most people think of when they think of Parliament debates," she said in a Facebook post.

She also said she had been "astounded" by the support she had received for the campaign, which was initially met with reluctance.

"Today, I was finally granted my debate, which will take place on Thursday 26 November, when I'll deliver my speech based on the huge journey I've been on these past seven to eight months, and making some initial recommendations to government," she said.

"But what is clear is this is just the beginning, and in light of recent events this campaign has never been more important."

In a session of Prime Minister's Questions in September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed to meet Niblett on the issue and praised her for "raising important issues that others won't talk about".

He added: "It's very clear to me that her summer was more exciting than mine."

MPs who are not in government can apply for backbench debates on a topic of their choice to a dedicated cross-party committee.

The debate is opened by the MP who requested it, and other backbenchers from any party can contribute.

A government minister and the opposition frontbench also respond with their views on the issue.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crwy.title: Duran Duran drummer quits band due to tinnitus
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crwy.text:
Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor said he will leave the band due to his worsening tinnitus.

Taylor has been the chart-topping group's drummer since they formed in Birmingham in 1978, which he described as "the joy of my life", but said he had "reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors".

The 66-year-old said his condition has been getting steadily worse, leading to him making one of his hardest decisions to quit the band.

The group, made up of Simon Le Bon, keyboardist Nick Rhodes and guitarist John Taylor, said his decision came after "careful consideration and medical advice", which said that "protecting his hearing and long-term health must now come first".

Taylor, who left the band in 1985 before returning in 2001, said: "Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I'll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they've shown us over the years.

"But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse," he said.

He said deciding on the timing had been difficult but he was pleased to be "going out on a real high".

"We've just returned from a hugely successful UK and European tour, which followed our second headline show at BST Hyde Park, our induction into the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame, and a return to the studio with Nile Rodgers.

"I couldn't have asked for a better final chapter, with so many special moments that I'll treasure forever.

"I move on with enormous pride, and with nothing but love for Simon, Nick and John," he said.

Taylor's band members added that he had helped define the sound of the group, performing on 10 hit albums, their two number one singles - Is There Something I Should Know? and The Reflex - and the band's 1985 James Bond theme A View To A Kill.

"Roger is our brother," they said.

"His drumming helped define the sound of Duran Duran from the very beginning and having him back with us since 2001 has been incredibly important to us all.

"We completely support his decision and wish him health and happiness.

"He will always be part of this family, while we continue exploring new and exciting projects with the band."
