https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq36.title: Bond producer first female president of film school
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq36.text:
A producer whose credits include the James Bond movies has been announced as the first female president of a film school.

Barbara Broccoli will take over the role at the UK's National Film and Television School (NFTS) in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, in February, succeeding Oscar-winning producer David Puttnam.

She has produced nine Bond films with her half-brother, Michael G. Wilson, before it was announced in February that Amazon MGM Studios had gained creative control.

Puttnam, whose credits include Chariots of Fire, The Killing Fields and Midnight Express, said he was "over the moon" that such a "hugely respected figure" was succeeding him.

The National Film School was established in 1971 by director Colin Young, taking over the Beaconsfield site with an initial intake of about 25 students.

In 1982 the institution was renamed the National Film and Television School to reflect its expanding curriculum.

Puttnam, who has been involved with the school for over 50 years, said it was a "lovely job" to have and that he had tried never to interfere.

He added that Broccoli's decision to take up the role was a "wonderful thing for the school".

Puttnam will take on an honorary role as president emeritus.

News of Broccoli's appointment comes ahead of the opening in January of the Cubby Broccoli Building at the school's Beaconsfield campus.

The building is named after Broccoli's father, the producer Albert R. "Cubby" Broccoli, who established the James Bond franchise.

The school said its expansion will provide 25,000 sq ft of additional teaching space, house new courses in costume design and hair and make-up, expand apprenticeship opportunities and provide purpose-built accessible student accommodation for the first time in its history.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.title: In Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner Ask Putin to Include Europe in Peace Talks
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Ivan Nechepurenko
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
The Kremlin, taking a hard line, is pushing to widen negotiations to overhaul European security structures.

Reporting from Moscow

President Trump’s envoys went to Moscow on Thursday to seek agreement from President Vladimir V. Putin to bring Europe into talks on the war in Ukraine, as the Kremlin pushes to widen the negotiations to overhaul European security arrangements.

The envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Russia one day after mediating peace talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian representatives, who spoke directly for the first time in nine months. After meeting with Mr. Putin in the Kremlin, they were scheduled to travel to Dublin to meet with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.

Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are pressing to involve Europe in the talks as Russia makes clear that it will not consider a cease-fire until its broader demands to redraw Europe’s security architecture are addressed.

The Trump administration, seeking a foreign policy win after Republicans’ drubbing in the midterm elections, is making another push for peace even as Russia gives no indication that it will stop the war anytime soon, and in fact appears to be hardening some positions.

Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of a winter bombing campaign, taking advantage of Ukraine’s lack of air defenses. On Thursday, Mr. Zelensky said that Ukraine’s armed forces again faced restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet network Starlink, and had asked U.S. officials for information.

Ivan Nechepurenko covers Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, the countries of the Caucasus and Central Asia. He divides his reporting time between Moscow and Tbilisi, Georgia.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.title: Nvidia Scandal Unleashes a Flood of AI-Generated Memes
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Zane Irwin
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The revelations surrounding Jensen Huang, who resigned from Nvidia over extramarital affairs, inspired social media posts using the very technology his company helped develop.

Jensen Huang and his leather-clad likeness had become synonymous with the technological giant he co-founded, Nvidia. They were so entwined that, this year, the company sold $178 sweaters with a pixel-art version of Mr. Huang on the front.

Now, in the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday after back-to-back cheating scandals, including an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy, the internet has taken ahold of his image to unleash a flood of memes.

In many cases, they are being made by A.I. enthusiasts who revered Mr. Huang.

Images of Mr. Huang have appeared in online parodies of music videos, Bollywood movies, American sitcoms and kiss-cams at Coldplay concerts — many generated using artificial intelligence, the technology that became widely available through the chips Nvidia produces.

The revelations about Mr. Huang, 63, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom, are part of a long list of infidelity scandals that became memes.

Last year, the married chief executive of a tech start-up was caught on a kiss-cam at a Coldplay concert embracing the married but separated head of his company’s human resources department.

Mr. Huang’s image was superimposed on that viral moment by Peter Dedene, a Belgian software engineer. He said in a phone interview on Thursday that he was up late this week on his phone, scrolling the headlines about Nvidia.

Zane Irwin is an international reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.title: Mexican Prosecutor Who Helped C.I.A. Secretly Operate in His State Flees to the U.S.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Steve Fisher
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
The prosecutor, who faces arrest in Mexico after allowing C.I.A. officers into Chihuahua state, is under the protection of the U.S. government, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.

Reporting from Mexico City

A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.

The former prosecutor, Guillermo Zuany Portillo, shepherded C.I.A. officers for more than six months beginning last year as they trained forces in his state, Chihuahua, joined those forces on counter-cartel missions and provided expertise during ground operations, a New York Times investigation revealed this week.

Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, had repeatedly said she did not want U.S. forces taking part in operations on the ground in Mexico, calling it a breach of sovereignty. Under the Trump administration, meanwhile, the C.I.A. sought to expand its activity in the country, and saw Mr. Zuany as a partner to help it do so quietly.

The C.I.A.’s cover in Chihuahua was blown when a car crash in April resulted in the deaths of two C.I.A. officers, leading to a national scandal and Mr. Zuany’s resignation. While an investigation determined the crash an accident, the Mexican authorities recently issued a warrant for Mr. Zuany’s arrest on charges related to his involvement with the agency.

Ms. Sheinbaum expressed fury at the C.I.A.’s presence during raids in Chihuahua and denied knowledge of the agency’s activities. On Wednesday, she said in a regular morning news conference that investigations into matter must continue.

“It’s worth finding out who this person is and how he worked with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said of Mr. Zuany.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Michael Schwirtz and Eric Schmitt
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
The officer, who served at a NATO base in Britain, is expected to be charged in the coming days, two officials said.

By Michael Schwirtz and Eric Schmitt

A U.S. Army officer arrested in Britain on suspicion of trying to spy for Russia is a decorated veteran of the Afghanistan war who was caught in a sting operation, according to two American officials familiar with the case.

The suspect, Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested this week. British officials are expected to charge him on Sunday or Monday, and after that, the U.S. Army will seek to charge him under the Uniform Code of Military Justice and transfer him to the United States, the two officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing inquiry.

Beyond the sting, it was not clear what actions prompted Colonel Tyner’s arrest. He was based at the headquarters of NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire, about 100 miles west of London. The base is NATO’s largest in Britain and hosts troops from 20 allied nations responsible for rapid response to crises.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.title: The End of Russia’s Bravest Newspaper
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Katrin Bennhold
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

For more than 30 years, the paper covered an increasingly repressive state under Vladimir Putin.

I’m the host of The World.

Novaya Gazeta was a newspaper of near-legendary status in Russia. It was the home of the investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya, whose books in the early 2000s offered a searing account of human rights abuses, wartime propaganda and corruption in Vladimir Putin’s Russia. In 2006, on Putin’s birthday, Politkovskaya was shot and killed in the elevator of her apartment building. Twenty years later, Russia is back at war and Novaya Gazeta has shut down.

On Monday, the paper held its last editorial meeting. One final issue will come out in the next few weeks. I spoke to my colleague Valerie Hopkins, who was there to witness the journalists packing up their offices.

But first, the latest twist in the Nvidia scandal: Jensen Huang has resigned.

Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia, resigned on Thursday, capping the swift, stunning fall of one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. He had extramarital affairs with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies concluded was spying for China, and with an executive who reported to him.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent chief executive is carried out. Nvidia shares dropped as much as 14 percent, extending a decline that has wiped out more than $1 trillion from its market capitalization in the last month. Follow our live coverage here.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/clima.title: A Key Paris Agreement Goal Is Dead. What Now?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/clima.author: David Gelles
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/clima.text:
Leaders at COP31 are confronting a new reality as global warming enters the “unsafe zone.”

It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”

The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

Now, just 11 years after the target was set, 1.5 is effectively dead.

Scientists now say that without drastic efforts to reduce greenhouse gases, it is very likely that the planet will warm at least 2.6 degrees Celsius, or 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit, by the end of the century.

At COP31, the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, diplomats who spent so long championing the 1.5 degree target lamented the abrupt setback.

“The world has no chance of holding to 1.5 degrees,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, who is leading the negotiations.

Scientists for years have warned that allowing global average temperatures to rise 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above preindustrial levels would result in a profoundly more dangerous world. Extreme heat will become more common and more intense. Storms will become more powerful and destructive. Sea levels will rise. And poor countries will bear the brunt of the damage.

That scenario is already playing out around the world. In recent months, wildfires have raged from Canada to Indonesia. The collapse of a glacier in Nepal killed thousands and wiped away towns. Floods and mudslides devastated Brazil. And a European heat wave killed an estimated 50,000 people.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/ka.title: Holscher Wins Kansas Governor Race, Retaining Seat for Democrats
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/ka.author: Mitch Smith
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/ka.text:
State Senator Cindy Holscher won the race. Though Kansas is reliably Republican in presidential elections, its voters often break for Democrats in midterms.

State Senator Cindy Holscher won election as governor of Kansas, keeping the seat in Democratic hands for a third straight term, The Associated Press said on Thursday.

She narrowly defeated Ty Masterson, the Republican nominee and the president of the Kansas Senate. Gov. Laura Kelly, the Democratic incumbent, was barred by term limits from seeking re-election.

Ms. Holscher’s victory added to a momentous election for Democrats in Kansas and across the country, and it maintained a rare lever of power for the party on the Great Plains.

Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, became the first Kansas Democrat to win a U.S. Senate race since the 1930s. In addition, Democrats flipped several legislative seats to break a Republican supermajority in the Kansas House of Representatives, which will make it much harder to override vetoes by Ms. Holscher.

Kansans also voted out Attorney General Kris W. Kobach, a Republican who helped elevate illegal voting as a political issue. Republicans prevailed in other statewide races and will still have majorities in both legislative chambers.

Though Kansans reliably vote for Republicans for president, they have shown an independent streak in midterm elections, swinging for decades between Republican and Democratic governors. High costs, dissatisfaction with President Trump’s policies and a tangle of challenges facing farmers made the Plains region more winnable for Democrats this year.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.title: Republican Setbacks Swell in the South With Stinging Loss in Mississippi
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Tim Balk and Emily Cochrane
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
The Democrat Scott Colom’s stunning Senate upset punctuated a dismal midterm showing for the G.O.P. in a region they had dominated for years.

By Tim Balk and Emily Cochrane

Emily Cochrane, who covers the American South, reported from Jackson, Miss.

Republicans were routed in Georgia and stunned in South Carolina. In Louisiana, a Republican Senate candidate won by less than two percentage points against a little-known Democrat who ran just two TV commercials.

Then came Wednesday in Mississippi, where Scott Colom became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in 44 years, defeating Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and further shaking Republicans’ once-unquestioned hold on the South.

Now, after the series of midterm shocks, Southern Republicans have been left to confront a new reality: A region they dominated for years is no longer a lock for their party.

“Republicans fell asleep at the wheel,” said Bill Armistead, a former chair of the Alabama Republican Party, adding, “If we stay asleep at the wheel, we could see some losses in the future.”

Republicans also lost their grip on the Georgia governor’s mansion, suffered a staggering loss by nearly 20 points in North Carolina’s Senate race and surrendered seats in state houses in Tennessee, Alabama and Arkansas. In South Carolina, 10 state legislative seats flipped into Democratic hands.

The country’s largest prediction market says it ended its contract with the president’s eldest son after his investment firm took a larger stake in its prime competitor.

Reporting from Washington

Kalshi, the nation’s leading prediction market, said on Thursday that Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, would no longer serve as an adviser.

The firm’s officials said in a statement that they and Donald Trump Jr. had agreed to part ways because his investment firm, 1789, had heavily invested in Polymarket, Kalshi’s biggest competitor. A spokesman for Donald Trump Jr. confirmed that the decision was mutual.

It was not immediately clear whether the president’s oldest son would keep the shares in Kalshi given to him as part of his compensation package when it hired him in January 2025. Those assets are now estimated to be worth millions.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/bl.title: Black Turnout Rose in Georgia, Powered by Younger Voters
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/bl.author: Evan Reynolds
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/bl.text:
Black voters under 30 outpaced young white voters for the first time since 2012, contributing to a statewide sweep by Democrats.

The Black share of the electorate in Georgia rose to its highest level in more than a decade, with the turnout rate among young Black voters outpacing that of young white voters. Both trends contributed to a heavy leftward shift in the state this year.

Democrats had a historically good election night in Georgia. Senator Jon Ossoff won re-election by 18 percentage points, which was the largest margin of victory for a statewide Democrat in more than two decades. Down the ballot, the party romped to victory, flipping the state house and every statewide office. That included the governorship, with Keisha Lance Bottoms elected the first Black governor in Georgia’s history.

Black voter enthusiasm, particularly in the South, was closely watched in the midterm elections after a Supreme Court ruling in April that weakened the Voting Rights Act, setting off a wave of redistricting that diluted Black representation in several states.

For the first time since 2012, turnout rates among Black voters under 30 were slightly higher than those of white voters under 30.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.title: Pete Hegseth, a Soldier’s Scolding and a Lesson at the Tomb of Unknowns
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Greg Jaffe
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s highly cultivated brand took a hit during an encounter with an Army sentinel at Arlington Cemetery.

Reporting from Washington

Pete Hegseth is possibly the most stage-managed secretary in the history of the Defense Department.

Almost everything he does, even his wardrobe choices, seems designed to either rally his supporters or provoke his critics. There are the American-flag pocket squares, the patriotic socks, the slicked-back hair, the “This is War” T-shirts and the carefully curated videos of him doing push-ups with the troops.

So it stood out when a soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknowns loudly scolded Mr. Hegseth and his party for laughing and talking near the solemn memorial on Veterans Day. Such interventions are a daily occurrence at Arlington Cemetery, where swarms of tourists brush up against strict military protocol.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the Army sentinel bellowed in the direction of Mr. Hegseth, his wife and his top advisers as they departed.

On Thursday, Mr. Hegseth awarded the soldier a Joint Service Commendation Medal. “We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist,” Hegseth said on social media. “Carry on Patriots.”

The rare unscripted moment and its aftermath pointed to a larger truth about the military and its relationship to the country it serves.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/an.title: Anthony Clark, Comic and ‘Yes, Dear’ Star, Dies at 63
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/an.author: Sopan Deb
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/an.text:
He first became a fixture in the Boston stand-up comedy scene before heading to Hollywood.

Anthony Clark, a comedian and actor who is best known for his performance as Greg Warner on the sitcom “Yes, Dear,” died on Tuesday. He was 63.

His death was confirmed by his co-star on the show, Mike O’Malley, in a post on social media on Wednesday. He did not provide a cause of death.

“Yes, Dear” ran from 2000 to 2006 on CBS, in an era where multicamera sitcoms were still in vogue. The show followed two married couples navigating parenthood. Mr. Clark’s Greg was an uptight, first-time parent, contrasted with his more lax brother-in-law Jimmy, performed by Mr. O’Malley. The show was, in some ways, a commentary on overbearing parents overwhelmed by advice from professionals. TV reviewers were mostly tepid about “Yes, Dear,” but it drew steady ratings.

When Mr. Clark got the role, he was already an established stand-up comedian with sitcom experience. He was a regular on two short-lived series. One was “Boston Common” on NBC, where he portrayed Boyd Pritchett, a Virginia native who ends up working at his sister’s college. The other was “Soul Man,” a Dan Aykroyd vehicle where he played the Rev. Todd Tucker. Mr. Clark did not have to audition for the “Yes, Dear” role.

In a 2020 podcast interview with his longtime manager, Barry Katz, Mr. Clark described the process of shooting a sitcom as exhausting.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.title: Why 2026 Midterm Polls Underestimated Democratic Support
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Caroline Soler, Ruth Igielnik and Jillian Vordick
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
Democratic gains were expected, but surveys almost uniformly underestimated how well the left would do. Many pollsters seem to have made similar mistakes.

By Caroline Soler and Ruth Igielnik

Graphics by Jillian Vordick

In one important sense, polls got the story of this year’s election right: They showed Democrats winning the House and leading in the race for control of the Senate.

By another measure, this year’s polls were among the worst in recent memory. When looking across all pollsters, surveys systematically underestimated the support of Democratic candidates, and they did so on a scale that rivaled or even exceeded the heavily criticized misses of 2016 and 2020, when polls underestimated Republicans.

Overall, national polls this year underestimated the strength of Democrats by around four percentage points. Across the key Senate races, the polls underestimated Democrats by an even larger five-point miss, compared with an average of about 3.5 points across all Senate races.

Polls generally called the winning party but underestimated the Democratic margin.

New York Times analysis in select states where five or more polls were conducted in the final three weeks before Election Day. Excluding Alaska because results are not finalized.

This error is similar in size to the recent Trump-era presidential polling misfires. In 2020, national polls underestimated Republicans by about four percentage points; in 2016, Republicans were underestimated by three points.

Not every pollster this year erred by so much. The New York Times/Siena Poll, for instance, did not systematically underestimate the Democrats. Neither did a handful of other pollsters, including AtlasIntel and Survey 160.

Note: In Nebraska, polling miss refers to over or underestimation of the independent, since there was no Democrat in the race.

Sources: New York Times/Siena polls of likely voters conducted Oct. 19 to 26 in Florida, South Carolina and Minnesota, Oct. 23 to 29 in Nebraska and Oct. 23 to Nov. 1 in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, Michigan and Texas. Margins are calculated using candidates’ unrounded vote shares.

Bars show how poll results in a given period differ from the eventual results.

Source: The New York Times/Siena 2026 Senate polls. The late-June polling wave covers Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas. The late-September wave includes Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas. The late-October wave covers Florida, Minnesota, and South Carolina. Finally, the November results encompass Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Nebraska, Ohio, and Texas. Nebraska is the only state in the analysis where the candidate was an independent rather than a Democrat.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.title: House Passes Competing Veterans Bills in a Fight Over Funding
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Olivia Diaz
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
Legislation addressing the retirement pay of veterans with combat-related disabilities is making its way through Congress, but could collapse amid a funding clash.

Reporting from the Capitol

The House on Thursday overwhelmingly passed a multibillion-dollar bill that would fully fund a key retirement benefit for combat-injured veterans with disabilities, but the measure’s fate in Congress was uncertain amid a dispute over how to pay for it.

Republican leaders moved to sidestep the disagreement on Wednesday by speeding through a competing measure before Democrats had a chance to try to defeat it. That bill, the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, addresses the retirement pay change and a wide range of veterans programs, all financed by future cuts in benefits for sleep apnea and tinnitus, two conditions that often afflict combat veterans.

The narrower version that passed on Thursday, by a lopsided vote of 392 to 18, was forced to the floor by Democrats and would omit those cuts. All Democrats and 181 Republicans backed it.

The competing bills each face steep obstacles in the Senate. Senator Jerry Moran, Republican of Kansas and the chairman of the Veterans’ Affairs Committee, said he supported the Republican-led package, whereas Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the senior Democrat on the committee, said he could not back the proposed benefit cuts.

Central to the dispute is the Maj. Richard Star Act, which would allow veterans who retired because of combat-related disabilities to receive their full retirement pay, rather than having it reduced dollar-for-dollar by their disability benefits, as required by current law.

Veterans groups have long lobbied for the Richard Star Act, but over the years, lawmakers have repeatedly balked at its cost, recently estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be about $12.8 billion over a decade.

Most Democrats abhor the health secretary’s stance on vaccines, but some see an opportunity to win voters from his MAHA movement by joining with him on food and environmental issues.

Credit...
Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

By Sheryl Gay Stolberg

Sheryl Gay Stolberg covers Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his MAHA movement.

Three days after last week’s “blue wave” election, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted a warning on X to anyone suspecting his Make America Healthy Again movement had been weakened. “It’s time to unleash the Kraken,” he wrote.

The phrase, a reference to the 1981 move “Clash of the Titans” that gained currency in 2020 among far-right internet personalities who claimed Democrats stole the election, suggests Mr. Kennedy will fight for his agenda and has no intention of leaving his job despite the defeat of several MAHA-backed candidates.

The question now is whether Democrats will use their new majorities in Congress to try to push him out.

Many want to investigate him, saying his vaccine agenda and handling of measles outbreaks have put American lives at risk. Some, including Senator-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, want to impeach him. Senator Angela Alsobrooks, Democrat of Maryland, wants Mr. Kennedy removed, but has not said how.

“The time is now,” Ms. Alsobrooks wrote on X the day after the election. “RFK Jr. must resign or be fired. End of discussion.”

But others want to work with Mr. Kennedy in areas where they can agree. They believe his food and environmental policies, which have run into roadblocks with the Trump White House, have a natural home with Democrats, and they see a chance to win over some of the health-focused coalition that helped propel President Trump to a second term.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Catie Edmondson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
Moderate Democrats and progressives have long feuded over who should drive their party’s economic agenda. But many newly elected members say they share the same big goals.

Reporting from the Capitol

Claire Valdez, a democratic socialist assemblywoman from Queens, was listening to a campaign speech by Cait Conley, a centrist Army veteran from the Hudson Valley, when she felt a pang of recognition.

“She was talking about billionaires,” Ms. Valdez, who was elected last week in her solidly Democratic district, recalled of Ms. Conley, who flipped a Republican seat in a conservative-leaning area. “It’s like, this sounds like Bernie 2016.”

Now both women are headed to Congress after a Democratic sweep that handed their party firm control of the House and Senate but quickly gave rise to a debate in their ranks about whether progressives or moderates will have the upper hand in driving the agenda come January.

Unlike in the past, however, members of both factions — centrist Democrats who captured competitive districts and the most liberal members in safe seats — appear to have coalesced around a common theme many of them agree won their party the midterms and should be their focus: economic populism.

The last time Democrats controlled both chambers of Congress, under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., bitter policy disagreements between moderates and progressives over how expansive their legislative plan should be prompted intraparty feuds that threatened to derail their economic agenda.

His wife, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce last year, citing adultery and “biblical grounds.”

By Lauren McGaughy and J. David Goodman

Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general of Texas, has finalized his divorce with his wife, Angela, who cited his adultery in her divorce petition last year, a lawyer for Mr. Paxton said on Thursday.

The final agreement comes more than a year after Ms. Paxton first filed for divorce and just over a week after Mr. Paxton lost his race for the U.S. Senate.

The terms of the divorce were agreed on and will remain private, the lawyer, Laura Roach, said in a statement.

“The Paxtons and their respective attorneys, worked diligently to reach an amicable resolution of their divorce,” she said. “From my observation, they share mutual respect for one another and appear to be looking forward to the next chapter of their lives.”

Ms. Paxton’s divorce lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but a spokesman for Ms. Paxton, a Republican state senator, did not dispute that the divorce was final.

In a filing with the court on Wednesday, Ms. Paxton said she and Mr. Paxton had agreed on the division of their property and debts that was “fair and equitable to both me and my husband.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.title: Will the Supreme Court Thwart Congressional Investigations?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Adam Liptak
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
Lawmakers must dodge rulings on immunity, standing and “valid legislative purpose.”

Adam Liptak is the chief legal correspondent and host of The Docket.

Come January, a Congress newly dominated by Democrats will launch vigorous investigations of the Trump administration and its allies.

Lawmakers will face a target-rich environment, one that includes crypto deals, pardons, extrajudicial killings on the high seas, a Justice Department-led retribution campaign against the president’s political opponents, and the gift of a Qatari jet.

But they will also face hurdles and roadblocks — erected by the Supreme Court.

In the court’s 2024 decision granting President Trump substantial immunity from prosecution, Chief Justice John Roberts indicated that some subjects may be entirely off limits to congressional investigators.

“Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the president’s actions on subjects within his ‘conclusive and preclusive’ constitutional authority,” the chief justice wrote. Those subjects included issuing pardons, firing subordinates and deciding “which crimes to investigate and prosecute.”

The immunity decision “has quietly weakened Congress’s ability to conduct legislative oversight over the executive branch,” David Manners-Weber wrote on Lawfare, a nonprofit legal affairs website, just before the midterm elections.

Whatever the subjects of congressional investigations, the administration is unlikely to give Congress documents or let officials testify, a clash that could lead to lawsuits. And it is not at all clear that the Supreme Court would be willing to mediate those disputes, or if the justices would side with the Democratic Congress if it does.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.title: The Concession Call to an Election Winner Is No Longer a Given
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Sopan Deb and Reid J. Epstein
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
In a hyperpartisan era when norms and traditions cannot be counted on, some politicians are left waiting by the phone.

By Sopan Deb and Reid J. Epstein

When the campaign trail runs out, the concession call is a tradition that is excruciating for the loser and sweet for the victor.

If it happens at all.

Last week, Abdul El-Sayed, the newly elected Democratic senator from Michigan, said that his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, had never called.

“At the end of the day, it really doesn’t quite matter,” Mr. El-Sayed told reporters. “I’m sure he had a flight to catch to Florida,” a reference to Mr. Rogers’ owning a second home near Fort Myers. (A spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers did not reply to a request for comment.)

Amy Acton, who was elected Ohio’s governor, said she had refused to take a call from Vivek Ramaswamy, her vanquished Republican rival, who in the final weeks of the campaign featured Ms. Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar in a TV commercial. Mr. Ramaswamy said in his concession speech that he had called Ms. Acton and left a message congratulating her.

“I have no intention of speaking to him,” Ms. Acton told “CBS Mornings” last week. “I do believe that leaders’ words matter.”

In a bygone era, such breaches of political protocol might have been unheard of. Yet as the 2026 midterm elections wind down, with several House races and a Senate race in Alaska too close to call, one might conclude that failing to concede defeat is more frequent than ever, the latest norm of polite politics to become a casualty of a less civil age.

Sopan Deb is a Times reporter covering breaking news and culture.

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

War in the Middle East

The announcement on social media deepened questions about what the president’s plan is to end the war. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he wrote.

Reporting from Washington

President Trump said on Thursday that he had pulled Vice President JD Vance back from engaging in potential peace talks with Iran, saying that his time would be better spent investigating fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Mr. Trump wrote on social media. “Those days have long since passed.”

The post deepens questions about what Mr. Trump’s plan is to end the war. The president has been weighing a number of options, including ramping up military strikes, withdrawing and leaving the matter to Arab allies or simply maintaining the status quo.

It also signals a pivot on his instructions to Mr. Vance, after the vice president publicly blamed the war for the Republican Party’s devastating midterm election losses in a striking critique of the administration’s agenda and messaging.

Mr. Trump had assigned Mr. Vance, who privately expressed opposition to going to war with Iran, to lead negotiations earlier this year. The vice president traveled to Pakistan in April and met with Iranian leaders in a marathon session that ended without any resolution.

Mr. Vance recently contacted a top Iranian political and military official to propose a renewal of comprehensive peace negotiations. In a letter sent from Mr. Vance via Qatari meditators to Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, the vice president suggested that American and Iranian officials meet soon, adding that he would lead the talks for the United States.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/clima.title: Democrats Put Targets on Notice as Trump Oversight Takes Shape
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/clima.author: Evan Halper
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/clima.text:
Letters sent by two key House committees tell companies and officials not to destroy documents.

Reporting from Washington

Congressional Democrats have alerted more than 60 companies, individuals and agencies that they are potential targets of investigations into the Trump administration’s cuts to scientific research, rollback of environmental protections and pursuit of unorthodox business deals.

The letters reveal where Democrats, soon to be empowered with subpoena authority after their sweeping wins in last week’s elections, intend to focus as they examine some of the administration’s most unabashed deals and policy changes. The notices sent from top Democrats on two key House committees demand preservation of any documents that could be relevant to congressional oversight next year.

The attempt to dismantle one of the world’s leading climate and weather research institutions, a lucrative White House deal with a rare earths company and an organized campaign to delegitimize climate science ahead of a sweeping regulatory rollback are among the concerns related to letters sent by the House Science Committee Thursday morning and reviewed by The New York Times.

“This administration has engaged in an assault on the science enterprise in this country,” said Representative Zoe Lofgren, Democrat of California, who is expected to chair the House Science Committee next year. “There have been firings, coercing people to resign, impounding money and possible corruption.”

Democrats have been in the minority in both chambers of Congress for almost four years. Lawmakers said potential targets ignored previous requests for information related to the Trump administration because they lacked legal authority to compel a response. That changed with last week’s election.

“If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement.

Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

President Trump suggested Tim Cook, Apple’s former C.E.O., to replace Jensen Huang at Nvidia. Here are others with experience in chips or A.I.

Reporting from San Francisco

Finding a successor to Jensen Huang at Nvidia is being compared to replacing Steve Jobs at Apple. In many ways, it’s actually harder.

Mr. Huang, 63, has much deeper technical expertise than the late Mr. Jobs did, with a keen understanding of the field of artificial intelligence and what chips and other technologies are needed to support it.

Unlike Mr. Jobs, Mr. Huang also forged close friendships throughout the industry, creating a complex network of partners, customers and suppliers. He turned Nvidia into a major player in Washington, built on a close relationship with President Trump and technology vital to U.S. national security.

And Mr. Huang shaped a culture at Nvidia that drove rapid-fire innovation while attracting some of the most accomplished engineers.

“They have to get someone who is an inspirational leader, that people love,” said Jeff Christian, chief executive of Christian & Timbers, an executive recruiting firm that frequently works with Silicon Valley companies. “This person has to be a great talent engineer, and a great talent magnet.”

Any candidate would also need an impeccable record for integrity and honesty, Mr. Christian and others noted.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/techn.title: We Were Warned of Deceptive A.I. Fakes. We Got Memes.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/techn.author: Stuart A. Thompson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/techn.text:
The surge of A.I. fakes that emerged this election season was different than what researchers had feared. The results are also a reckoning.

By Stuart A. Thompson

First came the election results, then came the meme party.

In the wake of the Democratic wave of support on Election Day, content creators used artificial intelligence to flood the internet with fake videos, depicting candidates and celebrities in various states of celebration.

One A.I.-made skit, featuring replicas of the cast from the hit TV show “The Office” showed the boss adjusting to a progressive society, wearing a Pride flag sweater and calling for an emergency Diversity Day. It received more than 16 million views in one post on X.

After Democrats swept the midterm elections, meme-makers flooded the internet with A.I.-generated fakes. It was emblematic of the kinds of fakery produced this year.

An A.I. version of Senator-elect James Talarico pushes aside Ken Paxton, his Republican opponent.

An A.I. version of Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan, dances with Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor.

The video was emblematic of the kinds of A.I. fakes that have coursed through social media during the midterm season. Many of the most popular videos spreading online vied for laughs and sometimes jeers — an absurd mix of outlandish events that obviously never happened.

The results are a minor relief for researchers who monitor the spread of A.I. fakery, and also a reckoning.

Experts have warned ahead of every U.S. election since at least 2020 that A.I. replicas of real people — “deepfakes” — and other deceptive content generated by the technology could upend democracy, misleading voters about scandals that never happened or salacious fake comments.

A.I.-generated depictions of President Trump mocked issues important to voters this year, like affordability and the war in Iran.

A television ad paid for by Ken Paxton’s campaign depicted an A.I.-generated version of James Talarico repeated comments he made in the past.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/techn.title: Jensen Huang’s Resignation From Nvidia Could Complicate Billions in Philanthropic Giving
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/techn.author: Theodore Schleifer
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Mr. Huang, the company’s co-founder, and his wife oversee a charitable foundation with about $9 billion in assets.

By Theodore Schleifer

Theodore Schleifer writes about philanthropy.

Jensen Huang was just becoming one of America’s biggest philanthropists before his departure as the chief executive of Nvidia. With an estimated net worth of about $145 billion, he and his wife, Lori, had built one of the country’s largest foundations, with about $9 billion in assets.

But Mr. Huang said this week that he had been unfaithful to his wife, acknowledging an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has determined was a Chinese spy. The Times then reported that he had another affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. Nvidia said on Thursday morning that Mr. Huang was resigning from the company he had led for 33 years.

The fate of the foundation, which the couple started in 2007 and oversee together, is not clear.

Ms. Huang is the foundation’s president, and Mr. Huang is its secretary and chief financial officer, according to the most recent tax return for the charitable organization, which is called the Jen-hsun & Lori Huang Foundation. In 2024, its most recent tax year on file, the foundation’s assets nearly tripled, thanks to more than $5 billion in investment gains.

Marital issues have led to major shifts in the world of philanthropy in recent years, such as the departure by Melinda French Gates from her joint charitable entity with her ex-husband, Bill, and the elevation of MacKenzie Scott as one of America’s biggest givers following her divorce from Jeff Bezos.

The Huangs’ foundation is rather low-profile: Despite being one of America’s biggest charitable entities, it has no website or lists any public staff.

And the couple had only just begun giving. The biggest public gifts by the Huangs have gone to higher-education institutions, a relatively safe and conventional place to disburse large amounts of money. They have announced a combined $180 million or so to four schools, including a $75 million donation in July to establish an art and design college at Vanderbilt University’s planned outpost in San Francisco.

Mr. Huang has described his philanthropic giving as an investment, not charity. “I don’t give anything away,” he said in 2010, dismissing the premise of the question. “The way I think about it is I’m investing in the next generation, to help us and to inspire us to create even better and more useful technologies.”

Their giving has also intersected with what is good for Nvidia. The Huangs’ foundation bought computing time from Coreweave, a key Nvidia partner and customer, and donated $108.3 million of it to universities and other nonprofits, according to an Nvidia corporate filing in May.

Theodore Schleifer is a Times reporter covering billionaires and their impact on the world.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/well/.title: What to Know About New Prostate Cancer Screening Recommendations
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/well/.author: Nina Agrawal
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/well/.text:
Universal screening for the disease has long been a subject of controversy.

The American Cancer Society on Thursday issued new guidelines recommending that all men ages 50 to 69 undergo prostate cancer screening using a blood test every two years.

Black men and those with a strong family history of prostate cancer should start annual screening at 45, the guidelines said.

Universal screening for prostate cancer, which accounts for about 2.5 percent of all deaths among U.S. men, has long been a subject of controversy. The evidence of the benefits of regular testing of blood levels of prostate specific antigen, or P.S.A., is somewhat limited. And there are well-documented harms associated with diagnosing and treating all prostate cancers, which are typically slow growing and may not ever cause issues in men who have them.

The new guidelines diverge from earlier recommendations that patients and physicians decide together about screening, based on careful consideration of the risks and benefits and patients’ values.

“This is truly a reversal,” said Dr. Philipp Dahm, a professor of urology at the University of Minnesota who was not involved in the guidelines.

The A.C.S. said it was updating its guidance based on new evidence and changes in how doctors monitor and treat prostate cancers.

Nina Agrawal is a Times health reporter.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.title: Fed Will Not Hold Policy Vote at October 2027 Meeting
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: Colby Smith
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
The shift to a strategy meeting next October is just the first step in a broader plan by Kevin M. Warsh, the chairman of the Federal Reserve, to change how the central bank operates.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

The Federal Reserve announced a revised schedule for its policy meetings next year, scrapping a vote on interest rates in October and spacing out other gatherings such that officials will no longer meet in December. The changes are part of a broader plan Kevin M. Warsh, who took over as chairman of the central bank in May, has put in place to cut back on the number of meetings each year.

According to a revised 2027 schedule the Fed released on Thursday, officials will still meet eight times over the course of next year. But instead of discussing the near-term policy outlook, the Oct. 26-27 meeting will now be “dedicated to the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues.” A meeting in November was set for the middle of the month and without a December gathering, the Fed will not vote on rates again until it meets Jan. 25-26, 2028.

Mr. Warsh unveiled last month the broad contours of his plan, which by 2028 will involve the central bank reducing the number of rate-setting meetings to six and holding two strategy-focused meetings. The strategy meetings will not involve a policy vote and are not expected to be accompanied by a post-meeting statement.

“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals,” Mr. Warsh said at a news conference in late October when explaining his decision. “But it’s equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations — for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point.”

Mr. Warsh said the cadence of the Fed’s meetings was “more than some administrative detail.” Instead, he said it was an “institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions. It’s yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track.”

One potential cost of the Fed meeting less frequently is that officials there will have fewer opportunities to adjust the central bank’s policy settings if the economic backdrop shifts. That raises the possibility the Fed will have to call impromptu meetings, which in the past have typically been reserved for crises.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.title: Mortgage Rates Remain High as Affordability Challenges Persist
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: Gregory Schmidt
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
The average 30-year, fixed-rate home loan fell slightly, to 7.11 percent, pushing buyers and sellers to the sidelines until conditions improve.

Mortgage rates slid for the fourth consecutive week but remain above 7 percent, adding pressure to a bleak housing market struggling with rising prices and declining sales.

The rate on the most popular home loan in the United States, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, fell slightly to 7.11 percent, from 7.18 percent the week before, the mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac said on Thursday. The same rate averaged 6.24 percent a year ago.

There was hope that mortgage rates might ease below 7 percent, a psychological threshold that could draw more buyers to the market. But industry experts say that marker is not likely to be breached any time soon.

High housing costs have made buying a home unaffordable for many Americans, said Brad Case, the chief residential economist at Homes.com, a real estate search portal owned by CoStar, a data analytics company.

“I don’t think affordability challenges are going away any time soon,” he added, “because I don’t think we’re likely to see substantially lower mortgage rates.”

Squeezed by high mortgage rates and rising inflation, buyers and sellers are sitting out of the market until conditions improve, which has depressed home sales. Sales of existing homes fell 8.8 percent in October from the year before, and 5.5 percent lower than September’s pace, according to a report released Thursday by the National Association of Realtors, a trade group.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: Jordyn Holman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The Nvidia founder and chief executive, who resigned on Thursday, is among a group of top bosses whose personal relationships and sexual encounters got them in trouble.

The “close personal relationship” has been the downfall of a number of chief executives over the years.

Now it has felled Jensen Huang, the founder and chief executive of Nvidia. Mr. Huang resigned on Thursday following revelations that he had an affair with an executive at the company as well as with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies concluded was an intelligence asset for China.

Posing a risk to national security is not the usual reason for ousting a chief executive. More often, it is that a relationship was in violation of company policy.

Large companies generally have had policies that prohibit managers and direct reports from having romantic relationships. Nvidia’s code of conduct tells employees to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships.”

“When it comes to direct reports, companies have had hard policies and have had for ages,” said Charles G. Tharp, executive vice president of the CHRO Association, a group for human resources officers.

Mark Hurd, who had helped build HP into a powerhouse tech company, was fired in 2010 after its board found that he’d failed to disclose use of company funds, and that he’d had a “close personal relationship” with a contractor. In 2018, Brian Krzanich resigned from Intel after the chip company learned of a “past consensual relationship” the chief executive had with an employee.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.title: Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s Ousted CEO, Was the Face of the A.I. Boom Powering the U.S. Economy
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: Ben Casselman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Nvidia’s ousted leader was a unique rhetorical and financial booster for investments that are driving economic growth.

As investors have pumped trillions of dollars into artificial intelligence companies, chipmakers and data center developers, the economy has come to rely on the industry as its primary — some would argue only — reliable driver of growth.

No company has been more central to that growth than Nvidia, whose chips fill the data centers that power A.I. and whose money helps to finance them. And, at least until this week, it was impossible to imagine Nvidia without Jensen Huang, its high-flying, leather-clad co-founder and chief executive.

All of which means that Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday, following a made-for-Hollywood series of scandals, matters not just for the company and its investors, but for virtually every American.

Or, as Aaron Klein, an expert in financial regulation at the Brookings Institution, put it: “Can one C.E.O.’s sex life take down the economy?”

The answer, in a literal sense, is almost certainly no. No one believes that Mr. Huang’s resignation will, by itself, bring the A.I. boom to an end, let alone plunge the economy into a recession. Nvidia’s stock price tumbled on Thursday, but the broader market barely budged.

But Mr. Klein’s quip spoke to the unique role that Mr. Huang played at Nvidia, and that his company has played in the A.I. build out.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.title: Jensen Huang’s Affairs That Upended Nvidia: Timeline of Events
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: Ali Watkins
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

News of the Nvidia co-founder’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and his affair with an executive who reports to him, prompted his exit from the multi-trillion-dollar company.

News that Jensen Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia, was having an affair with a woman believed to be Chinese spy has sent shock waves through the tech world, the U.S. government and the wider economy.

Mr. Huang served as Nvidia’s chief executive from 1993, when he co-founded the company, until his resignation on Thursday. He rocketed to prominence during the A.I. boom as Nvidia’s advanced chips became a crucial technology, making it one of the world’s most valuable companies. Mr. Huang, 63, has close ties to President Trump and has frequently appeared alongside him.

Here’s how the events unfolded.

2023: A Chinese executive named Alice Huang sets up a data firm in Singapore called Megaspeed. The company, which originally had Chinese owners, would soon buy billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips. In May 2023, Nvidia reaches $1 trillion in value.

December 2023: While it’s not clear when Mr. Huang, who is married, met Ms. Huang, they were acquainted by December 2023, when they had dinner with colleagues at a restaurant in Singapore. In June 2024, they were seen socializing at an event in Taipei, Taiwan.

June 2024 to June 2025: A Megaspeed subsidiary receives more than 200 shipments of Nvidia A.I. equipment.

Early 2025: Weeks after Mr. Trump begins his second term, Mr. Huang visits the White House to meet with him for the first time.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/g-s1-1511.author: Larry Kaplow
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/g-s1-1511.text:
State Sen. Cindy Holscher has won the race for Kansas governor, keeping the office for Democrats in a state that leans Republican. Here she's seen speaking to reporters after casting her ballot during early voting at a polling location in Kansas City, Kansas.

Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher will hold onto the Kansas governor's office for her party after defeating Republican Ty Masterson, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Masterson, the president of the state Senate, was endorsed by President Trump. Of the 36 elections for governor across the country, Kansas was seen as the most likely to flip from Democratic to Republican control.

The race call came after days of counting the provisional ballots and with local officials doing recounts in the closely contested election.

Current Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly is term-limited after serving for eight years in a state with a heavily Republican legislature and that usually votes for Republicans for other offices and in presidential elections.

Holscher, 57, ran a campaign with notes of populism, promising to fight "sweetheart deals" for billionaires. She tied Masterson to his work in the state Senate when it passed a tax cut under former Republican Gov. Sam Brownback that led to a series of budget crises and was later repealed.

Holscher opposed school vouchers, calling for more support for public schools, in contrast with Masterson, who backed school vouchers. She also called for a moratorium on new data centers and for legalizing cannabis as a way to generate state revenue.

Masterson, 57, called for lower property taxes and said faith influenced all his decisions, including in politics. He promised to be the "most pro-ag, pro-business, pro-oil and gas governor," the state has seen. He called Holscher, "the most radical, liberal, socialist Democrat ever" on a ticket in Kansas.

"He likes to throw around a whole lot of labels," Holscher responded. "You know why? Because that's all he's got."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: What's a Honey Trap? The spy tactic that helped topple Jensen Huang
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: Frank Langfitt
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
A screengrab from CTI video footage obtained November 9, 2026 shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang after comparison with a photograph obtained separately, attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (in black) at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan on May 22, 2025.

One of the world's oldest spy tactics appears to have helped topple one of the world's richest men. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday amid revelations that he had an affair with a female client that U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese spy, according to the New York Times.

NPR has not independently confirmed the reporting by the Times, which said Huang also had an unrelated affair with a company executive who reported to him. The Chinese government has called the accusation of spying, "nothing but smears against China."

Using a romantic relationship to gather intelligence from foreigners – known as a honey trap – has a long history in China and beyond. The Chinese Ministry of State Security, the country's main civilian intelligence agency, routinely tries to recruit women and occasionally men for honey traps, according to former CIA officers and other U.S. officials familiar with Chinese spy craft.

Some target businessmen for industrial espionage or to gain insights into the economic and political strategy of foreign governments. Peter Mattis, a former CIA counter-intelligence analyst, said honey traps also serve as influence operations with spies trying to gain enough trust to shape the target's thinking about China.

"The biggest thing here that we should pay attention to is that the Ministry of State Security celebrates a tradition of getting inside the enemy's decision-making," said Mattis, president of the Jamestown Foundation, a national security think tank in Washington, D.C., that focuses on America's geopolitical rivals.

Nicholas Eftimiades, who spent more than 34 years with the CIA and Defense Intelligence Agency and now teaches at Penn State, said the honey trap is just one tactic among many that use ordinary Chinese citizens to gather information at home and abroad.

"Unlike the CIA, or MI6 or any of the other Western services, China has a 'whole of society approach,'" said Eftimiades, the author of Chinese Intelligence Operations: An Analysis of the People's Republic of China's Intelligence Services. "Chinese law supports this. The National Intelligence Law of 2017 requires citizens to cooperate with intelligence collection efforts."

The Chinese government has employed honey traps in the United States and elsewhere in the West. In the 2010s, Christine Fang worked as a political fundraiser in California where she developed a physical relationship with Democrat Rep. Eric Swalwell before and after he became a congressman.

The FBI warned Swalwell they thought Fang was a spy. He denied doing anything wrong and she fled back to China.

In the 1980s and 1990s, the FBI paid Katrina Leung – a Los Angeles businesswoman – $1.7 million over 18 years to spy on China. However, Leung had affairs with two FBI agents and the bureau later determined she was a double-agent.

The most remarkable honey trap case dates to the 1960s, when a young French diplomat began a nearly two-decade affair with a male Peking opera performer, whom he thought was a woman. The story inspired the play and movie, M Butterfly.

The woman implicated in the Nvidia case, Alice Huang, is a Chinese businesswoman whose company, Megaspeed, was a major buyer of advanced chips from Nvidia. The Times reported the U.S. had her under surveillance and learned of her connections to Chinese state security through her communications.

The logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026. The woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Jensen Huang, head of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia, has been named in media reports as tech executive Alice Huang, who has reportedly been a top figure at Singapore-based company.

Desmond Shum, a Hong Kong businessman and former China insider, says Alice Huang doesn't fit the usual profile in these cases. She appears to be what the Chinese call a "white glove" – or front-person for multi-billion-dollar commercial deals, which Shum says could have insulated her from the Ministry of State Security.

Shum doesn't think Alice Huang is a professional spy, pointing out that she hasn't been discreet on social media, posting photos from her visits to luxurious country clubs and fancy foreign destinations.

"A spy wouldn't do that," Shum told NPR from his home in the United Kingdom.

Isaac Stone Fish, a former reporter in China who runs Strategy Risks, a China-focused business intelligence firm, says the Ministry of State Security – or MSS – could have approached Alice Huang after it learned of her affair with the Nvidia head.

"One imagines that every time a Chinese person enters into a romantic relationship with a very, very powerful American, MSS notices that," Stone Fish said.

Honey traps are a staple of spy novel and movie plots, including the Netflix series, Black Doves, The Americans on FX, Apple TV's Slow Horses as well as James Bond films, such as From Russia with Love.

In reality, when Chinese state security approaches women for these operations, it's embarrassing and humiliating. The tactic perpetuates racist, sexist stereotypes while casting suspicion on the vast majority of Chinese people, who have nothing to do with intelligence gathering.

In addition to China, many intelligence services have engaged in honey traps. The Russians historically used sex workers for blackmail and leverage. During the Cold-War, East Germany sent well-educated and well-mannered male spies – known as Romeos – to West Germany.

Mossad, the Israeli intelligence service, used honey traps from the 1950s into the 1970s in countries such as Egypt, Iraq and Iran. But investigative reporter Yossi Melman, who's written many books on Israeli intelligence, says the practice has dwindled as cyber spying and digital traps have proven more efficient.

The U.S. used sexual entrapment against the Soviets, but several former officials said the Americans now prefer to appeal to people on ideological grounds and provide financial carrots, such as money for college tuition or health care for a sick family member.

Even though countries repeatedly warn businessmen and government officials about the tell-tale signs of a honey trap, ego and vanity remain human weaknesses and men continue to succumb, said Eftimiades.

"Welcome to the male of the species," he said. "Is everyone aware of this? Yes. Does everyone think it'll happen to them? No. And, you know, and it happens all the time."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: 'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 years
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: Stephan Bisaha
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
Home sales fell to their lowest since 2010, a new report shows, in large part due to high mortgage rates.

The housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction.

Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. The last time sales were this low was 16 years ago.

"It was a punch in the gut," said Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com. "We expected to see a soft month but not the softest month since 2010."

The drop is mainly due to high mortgage rates.

In October, the average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage hit as high as 7.40%, the highest since 2023. Rates have gone down a bit since then, but are still well above where they were a year ago.

Higher inflation and bond yields have driven up mortgage rates, but some of this housing slowdown was by design.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate in September to increase the cost of borrowing, including home mortgages. Fewer home sales and other purchases mean less economic activity, which the Fed wants in order to reach its goal of lowering inflation.

Policymakers at the Fed have signaled another rate hike could come in December, which could further slow down the housing market.

"It might seem like kicking the housing market while it's down right now for the Fed to continue a rate raising cycle but in the long run getting inflation under control is really the goal," Berner said.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: Rachel Treisman
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
President Trump signed the final steel beam at the White House ballroom the day after the midterm elections.

President Trump's efforts to remake Washington, D.C., have dominated his second term, even after his party's resounding midterm defeat.

He started his election week at the scandal-plagued Reflecting Pool and ended it with an order declaring his gilded Oval Office a national monument to "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space."

That proclamation, like any executive order, could be undone by a future president. But many of Trump's construction projects are changing D.C. in more permanent ways.

His administration has already downed hundreds of trees at East Potomac Park and demolished the East Wing of the White House to make space for a ballroom — which he called "the safest place in Washington" as he showed it to reporters the day after the midterms.

Trump has taken a uniquely unilateral approach to construction, packing regulatory commissions with his allies and bypassing Congress entirely. Most of his projects — from the triumphal arch to the Kennedy Center — are now playing out in court.

Critics accuse the Trump administration of skirting federal laws and misleading judges in its effort to progress as quickly as possible before the end of his term.

Democrats have vowed to use their soon-to-be congressional majority to push back on what they describe as Trump's "vanity projects."

When asked about that, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in an email that "no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump." He cited park cleanups, the Reflecting Pool and the White House helipad and ballroom as examples, and said Democrats "should work with President Trump to make our nation's capital beautiful again."

Rep. Jared Huffman, center, poses with activists protesting Trump's triumphal arch at Memorial Circle in May. He will soon become the chair of the committee with legislative and oversight authority over public lands.

Rep. Jared Huffman, D.-Calif., told NPR in an interview that the Trump administration has "played this game of Catch Me If You Can, where they roll ahead with the bulldozers and the tree cutters … and they wait for courts to shut them down." He says a Democrat-led Congress will fight back.

"There's no way that we could look away while these sacred, iconic places are being permanently changed in ways that violate the law and could have really terrible lasting impacts," said Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, which has a legislative purview over public lands and national parks.

Huffman says blocking Trump's construction projects — and holding people accountable for potential wrongdoing — will be a top priority when he leads the committee. Earlier this week, he sent letters ordering dozens of administration officials and private companies to preserve their records for a future investigation.

"Whether it is the arch or … or the East Potomac golf course or any number of other examples around the United States capital, that is federal land, and we have a direct statutory responsibility to either authorize those changes or to stop them if they're proceeding without the proper authorization," Huffman said.

What would that actually look like? Democrats have many tools at their disposal, from legislation to lawsuits. But experts say only two are likely to succeed: funding and oversight.

Trump made a final pre-Midterm Day pitch to voters from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, whose renovations took months longer than anticipated due to algae blooms and peeling paint.

Congress could — at least in theory — pass laws to block specific projects from moving ahead. Some Democratic lawmakers have already introduced bills to protect the Kennedy Center from demolition and prohibit the construction of an arch at Memorial Circle.

But Trump has promised to "veto everything," and Democrats won't have a big enough majority to override him on their own.

"Legislation in principle is the cleanest way of doing it, but it's also not achievable," said David Super, who teaches administrative and constitutional law at Georgetown. "So what they're likely to do is cut off funds."

The Constitution says that the federal government may spend money only if is appropriated by Congress. But Trump has neither sought nor received congressional authorization for projects like the arch and the White House ballroom — he maintains he doesn't need it.

Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine is one of many who disagree. She's the top Democrat on the House committee that oversees funding for the Interior Department.

"Certainly Congress should have been involved, because we have the power of the purse," Pingree told NPR. "That is our ultimate tool. And Republicans have refused to use that. But we can use that in very many ways to block him or to use it for leverage."

Pingree says a Democratic majority will be able to write appropriations bills with clear language from the outset about where money can and can't be spent — and potentially take the president to court if he doesn't follow it.

Super expects Congress would prevail in such a challenge, because it has clear-cut authority over federal funds.

For example, he noted that some of Trump's D.C.-area beautification projects have been funded at least in part by diverted national park entrance fees. Congress could "cap how much money can be used in the greater Washington area, and force the money to be used in the Everglades and Yosemite and Great Smoky Mountains," he said.

Congress will have to make some appropriations decisions in the coming weeks, since it needs to pass a short-term funding bill by Dec. 11 to avoid a government shutdown. Democrats could use that opportunity to try to limit funding for at least one of Trump's construction projects.

Huffman has proposed language that would prevent Trump from using federal funds for the East Potomac golf course renovations, limiting them instead to repairs of the park's crumbling seawall. Pingree said she will join him in fighting to negotiate that into next month's bill.

On one October Saturday, the Trump administration cut down some 430 trees at East Potomac Park, where the president wants to develop a municipal golf course into a championship-level course.

"Whether or not the president will sign that with that in there, I don't know yet," she said. "But certainly those are the most … immediate crisis points … People want the president to stop cutting down the trees on the golf course and stop trying to take that over, and they want to make sure that no shovel goes into the ground on building the arch."

Earlier this year Pingree introduced an amendment that would have outright blocked construction of the arch; it failed along party lines. She wonders whether any Republicans might vote differently after the midterms, given the message Americans sent at the polls.

"They want the president to be focused on the issues they're dealing with: the cost of health care, the cost of food, the cost of gasoline," she said. "And if every time the president gives a speech, he's either standing in front of the Reflecting Pool, which he spent millions of dollars on, or showing you the new marble choices he's putting into the ballroom, it just makes a lot of people mad."

Pingree said she's been surprised to hear how strongly people feel about these projects – even people well outside D.C. And she agrees with them that potential corruption and misuse of taxpayer dollars are worth fighting: "After the first of the year, we will use every tool in our toolbox."

Lawmakers and experts acknowledge that not every project is reversible, or potentially even worth the fight. Huffman suggested he will focus on bigger projects, and ones that are moving too fast for courts to adequately rein in.

"Are we going to throw all of our efforts at stopping the gilding of every statue in Washington, D.C.? Probably not," said Huffman. "But these are iconic places that we're talking about, with permanent damage that we need to engage on to try to prevent."

Even so, Democrats could decide that certain construction projects are "the price they pay for other priorities," said Claire Leavitt, a professor of government at Smith College. Voters made clear they want lawmakers to focus on ending the Iran war and making life more affordable, big asks that may take a lot of political capital.

"And that's not corruption or Democrats not doing their job," Leavitt said. "It's just the natural trade-offs of dealing with who you're dealing with, and understanding that what matters to Trump more than anything seems to be building the arch, building the ballroom … remaking the Kennedy Center."

Whether or not these projects move forward, Congress can provide a fuller public accounting of how they came to be — in the hopes of preventing more in the future.

"They can gavel in hearings. They have agenda-setting power," Leavitt said. "They determine what the public hearing roster is. They decide which witnesses to invite. And that means they have a unique opportunity to draw negative public attention to the Trump administration."

Work on the White House ballroom is moving quickly.

That may be easier said than done, especially with an administration that has pointedly refused to comply with congressional oversight and is now warning Democrats that their future investigations could constitute criminality. Huffman was coy when asked how he is preparing to handle such challenges.

"We are going to have to have a strategy and a plan to do these things that prior Congresses have never imagined they would have to do," he said.

One investigative priority, lawmakers say, will be following the money — especially when it comes to donations for the ballroom and other projects. Leavitt says that focus has an added benefit: Private companies and individuals are likely more willing to testify than a member of the administration.

Another example: Congress could subpoena for information about the decision-making processes of the Kennedy Center board and the physical state of the building, which trustees say must be closed for two years of repairs. And it can put that information in the Congressional — and therefore historical — Record.

"Both the current public can make its judgments, and history can make its judgments," Leavitt said.

Leavitt said oversight can often lead to policy change in the longer term. For example: The committee investigating the Jan. 6 insurrection didn't stop Trump from eventually pardoning Capitol rioters, but it did lead Congress to pass an electoral reform act.

"The frustrating part about congressional oversight is Congress can draw attention to a problem, and they can demand accountability for something that's already been done," Leavitt said. "But it's very hard for Congress to stop something from happening that the president is determined to do."

Super agrees that Democrats are playing a long game. He expects to see more bipartisan support after Trump leaves office for preventing future presidents from following his playbook.

"The process in the past has been built on trust, and President Trump certainly broke that trust in numerous ways," he said. "Laws can be written so that we don't depend on trust, we depend on law. And I'm guessing we're going to do that."
