https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/g-s1-1532.author: Ruby Siefken
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/g-s1-1532.text:
Retired passenger liner SS United States is pictured at a dock in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The SS United States still holds the east- and west-bound transatlantic crossing records. AFP PHOTO/JEWEL SAMAD (Photo credit should read JEWEL SAMAD/AFP via Getty Images)

A giant ship sunk off the coast of Florida yesterday—and the coast guard didn't do a thing to stop it.

The SS United States is a retired ocean liner that was deliberately sunk on Wednesday to create the world's largest artificial reef. After hours of slow descent, it finally disappeared beneath the waves at 10 p.m. ET last night. It now rests 180 feet beneath the surface at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico in an upright position.

Measuring almost 1,000 feet from bow to stern, the giant ship is longer than the Titanic. After it's settled on the ocean floor, the ship's hundreds of rooms, corridors and elevator shafts will become a deep-sea playground for divers, fish and other aquatic life.

This transformation gives the SS United States the opportunity for a second life and a new species of passenger.

Susan Gibbs has mixed feelings about the ship's final voyage to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. She chairs the board of the SS United States Conservancy, and her grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the ship more than 70 years ago.

"It's a combination of grief, that I will be saying goodbye to her in her current form, but, gratitude and hope in terms of what she will continue to give to the world," she told Morning Edition

The ocean liner took its maiden voyage in 1952, and it shattered the trans-Atlantic speed record, winning the coveted Blue Riband on her opening sail. It still holds the record more than 60 years later.

In the event of war, the SS United States could have been converted from a luxury liner to a military transport vessel able to carry 14,000 troops for 10,000 miles without refueling, though it was never used for this purpose, according to the SS United States Conservancy.

1952: Cheering crowds lining the quayside as the record breaking liner, SS United States arrives in Southampton. She crossed the Atlantic in record time on her maiden voyage. (Photo by M. Fresco/Topical Press Agency/Getty Images)

By the end of her time on the water in 1969, the SS United States carried several notable passengers, including Harry Truman, Walt Disney, Marilyn Monroe, Walter Cronkite and a young Bill Clinton.

"She embodied the spirit of a nation so confident in its ability to accomplish the extraordinary," said Gibbs.

The conservancy wanted to transform the ship into a hotel or museum, but due to legal and financial issues, they eventually sold it to Okaloosa County, Florida in 2024. It was the county's decision to sink it.

Realistically, it's not easy to sink something that's designed to stay above water. So, Okaloosa County called in the professionals.

Coleen Marine, a marine engineering contracting company who specializes in creating artificial reefs, led the project. Their President and co-founder Coleen O'Malley said they did their best to preserve the ship's original design.

"We've maintained the actual hull. So she's very recognizable," O'Malley said. "We've made it so that the structure under the water is going to look like she did above the water."

To sink the ship, the Coleen Marine team had to repair holes and irregularities in the hull to ensure it would sink properly. O'Malley detailed that "the biggest thing with sinking a ship is not how much water you put in. It's making sure the air comes out."

The team also cleaned much of the rusted exterior to make a more welcoming environment for aquatic life. Most importantly, the team wanted to ensure that the ship sank straight down, without flipping or turning. Overall, O'Malley said construction took more than 18 months.

Both O'Malley and Gibbs made the journey to the coast of Destin and Fort Walton Beach to watch the SS United States disappear below the waves Wednesday.

In the wake of its last moments above the surface, the SS United States Conservancy is planning to construct a museum in the ship's honor in Florida.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: Witnesses describe the D.C. shooting that left 1 dead, 4 injured
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: Jaclyn Diaz
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
Local and federal law enforcement respond to reports of an active shooting on Thursday in Washington.

Busy morning crowds in Washington, D.C.'s Logan Circle ran for cover Thursday after a gunman opened fire at a local gym, VIDA Fitness, killing at least one person and injuring at least four others.

The gunman left the gym area, entered a nearby apartment building where he barricaded himself. Jeffery W. Carroll, the interim Police Chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, who briefed the public this morning, said at the time of the briefing that the shooter had shot himself.

A police spokeswoman later confirmed to NPR that the gunman died.

The gunman shot and killed one person inside the gym and injured another in the lobby or alley area of the building, Carroll said. The other three victims were shot across the street at a construction site, he said. One person remains in critical condition.

Carroll identified the gunman as a white male who had a conflict with the homeowners association of the apartment building.

The Logan Circle neighborhood sits about one mile north of the White House. The block where the shooting occurred, along 15th Street Northwest, is lined with apartment buildings, a church, coffee shops and restaurants.

Residents around the area described a massive law enforcement presence, including FBI agents and SWAT teams, swarming the area minutes after gunshots rang out. Residents were sent emergency text messages ordering them to remain sheltered in place. That order was lifted at around 11:30 a.m.

The first call for help came in at 8 a.m. from people inside the gym, Carroll said. Officers and other emergency responders were on scene within 30 seconds, he said. Responders found one adult man who was shot inside the gym.

Witnesses on scene told NPR that VIDA requires visitors to tap in to gain access to the fitness area. Carroll told media he believes the gunman was a member.

Local and federal law enforcement respond to reports of an active shooting, Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, in Washington.

Tinbete Ermyas, an editor at NPR, was working out at the gym when the shooting started. He and other gym-goers became aware something was wrong when they heard "a very loud bang," Ermyas said.

"People kind of looked around at each other ... wondering what it was. Some people thought that maybe it was some weights that had been dropped. But it just sounded way too loud," he said. "The bang sort of shook everybody."

Shortly after the bang, came the screams.

"That's when we realized that it was a shooting," he said. He and others ran off the gym floor through an emergency exit that led them to a laundry room. That's where for about 20 minutes, he and others hid until police came to escort them out.

As they exited, they saw the body of the man who was shot.

"It was just laying there, just very bloodied and terrible. A guy that goes to the gym regularly. I see him every morning, just lying in a pool of blood. It was terrible," Ermyas said.

After the gunman barricaded himself in the apartment building, police tried for about an hour to get him to surrender safely. But Carroll said that while officers were engaging with the suspect, they heard a gunshot.

It's unclear if the gunman and the victims knew each other. Carroll said more investigation is needed.

Scorched bricks are seen, up and center right, following reports of an active shooting in Washington.

Next to the gym at Call Your Mother Deli, Oscar Vazquez, the manager, said he heard the fire alarm going off next door in the apartment building. Carroll, the police chief, said police believe a fire was set off in the building and the the sprinklers did go off. The fire has since been contained and put out, Carroll said.

He and his co-worker Cesar Miranda, a 22-year-old worker at the deli, said they thought it was a regular fire alarm until "we heard like 7 or 8 gunshots," Miranda said.

Vazquez said people started running out of the building said he tried to get as many people as possible into the deli.

"We're really worried about the people that live in the building," Vazquez said. He said they have a lot of friends and customers that live there. He said: "It was really scary. It really happened out of nowhere, just hordes of people just running down from that block."

Miranda said law enforcement were on the scene quickly.

"We saw so many people running from the area, like so many people," Miranda continued. "There was so shocked and afraid. They even started falling into the chairs that we had in the patio."

A previous version of this story incorrectly said that Jeffery Carroll, interim police chief in Washington, D.C., told reporters at his briefing Thursday morning that the shooting suspect was dead. Carroll said that the suspect had shot himself. The police later told NPR that the suspect had died.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: U.S. envoys meet with Putin in the Kremlin after Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin, left, greets Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, right, and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, center, during their meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin, Moscow, Thursday.

MOSCOW — U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met Thursday with President Vladimir Putin as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, brokered the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Those were the first direct discussions between representatives of Moscow and Kyiv in nine months as the push for peace stalled.

The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.

Kushner and Witkoff went straight to the Kremlin to brief Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours and are scheduled to fly to Dublin, Ireland, for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.

Kushner said that one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.

The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, second right, speaks to U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, second left, and Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, third left, as Russian Presidential foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, behind Putin, and Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Special Presidential Representative for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries Kirill Dmitriev, right, sit near during the meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin, in Moscow, on Thursday.

But Moscow doesn't want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent.

Many in Europe see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a main security threat to Russia. Putin has demanded the trans-Atlantic alliance's troops be pulled back from Russia's borders.

Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders.

The Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi "agreed on many of the principles, but are still apart on some of the way to accomplish" peace, Kushner said in Moscow.

Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire would be "absolutely unacceptable" and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate targets. "In other words, the war would resume immediately," he said.

He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a press conference after a bilateral meeting with Ireland's Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Wednesday, ahead of the European Political Community Summit.

Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. "But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire," Rutte said.

Zelenskyy said political changes, including Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following midterm elections and balloting in France next year, could bring "a window of opportunity" for a peace deal.

"The political landscape in Europe could change in 2027. … We also see changes already taking place in the United States," Zelenskyy said in Dublin late Wednesday.

He called the proposed prisoner exchange a positive step but also insisted Ukraine won't surrender Russian-occupied territory in return for peace.

Russia and Ukraine have occasionally swapped prisoners, but both sides remain far apart in their terms for accepting a settlement.

Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.

Russia's bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow's drone and missile strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a "weaponization of winter."

Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.

Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.

Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Thursday on social media.

Military units have recorded "significant disruptions," including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelenskyy said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.

Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes.

Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.

Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn't be used for offensive strikes against Russia.

Zelenskyy said in Dublin that the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on. "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he said.

Law enforcement officer inspects the site of a car explosion that killed a military serviceman in St. Petersburg, Russia, Thursday.

A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to Russia's Investigative Committee, the country's main criminal investigation agency. It didn't identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing.

The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off.

Several senior Russian military officers have been killed by bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down amid alleged spy scandal
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: John Ruwitch
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
Jensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU Technology Conference on Oct. 21, 2026.

Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR

Jensen Huang, CEO of the chipmaking juggernaut Nvidia, is stepping down, the company's board announced Thursday.

The decision comes days after the company took the extraordinary step of launching an investigation following news reports alleging that Huang had had an extramarital affair with one of the company's clients, who U.S. intelligence officials concluded had been recruited by China's top spy agency, according to the New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

In an email to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang admitted to cheating on his wife, and said he would cooperate with the investigation.

The company's share price dropped sharply on Wednesday, after the New York Times reported that Huang had had a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to an NPR request for comment.

Huang was widely seen as one of the most important business leaders in the United States. Nvidia dominates the market for the chips used to train and run artificial intelligence. Huang also had President Trump's ear on AI policy, with Trump even calling Huang's phone in September while Huang was onstage during a conference.

The scandal that brought down Huang snowballed quickly over the past two weeks. The New York Times reported in late October that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese woman at a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia chips. Citing unidentified sources, it said U.S. intelligence officials believed she had been recruited by the Chinese government to spy on him and possibly try to influence policy. NPR has not independently confirmed this reporting.

A drip-drip of scoops followed — from the Times and other outlets — suggesting that the relationship was romantic, that senior Trump administration officials knew about the allegations some time ago, and that Huang had had a second affair.

China's foreign ministry has said the allegations of spying are baseless and part of a smear campaign against China.

Huang's departure launches Nvidia into uncharted territory.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese agent and what the Trump administration knew about it will likely be the subject of an investigation when Democrats take control of Congress in January.

"We should all be extremely concerned about this, and the fact that the White House knew about this for weeks, maybe months now, is is is very disturbing as well," said Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, a senior member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee in an interview with NPR.

The company's Chief Financial Officer, Colette Kress, has been appointed interim CEO. The board said in their statement they would conduct a full search for a new CEO and consider both internal and external candidates.

"There's no obvious replacement," said Stephen Witt, author of a book about Nvidia called The Thinking Machine. "It's not even clear Nvidia can be the same kind of company without Jensen. I have a hard time imagining what Nvidia looks like without Jensen."

Nvidia still plans to report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday.

Huang was one of the longest-serving CEOs in U.S. corporate history, stepping into the role after launching the company with partners over bottomless cups of coffee at a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, Calif., 33 years ago. Nvidia got its start making specialized chips to create 3D graphics for computers that would come to be known as graphics processing units, or GPUs.

He was the face of Nvidia and an unlikely celebrity, giving countless keynote speeches and interviews in his trademark leather jacket, or posing for selfies with adoring fans.

Huang was also the company's driving force. Under his leadership, Nvidia made a big and early bet on artificial intelligence, investing heavily to transform its niche graphics chips into general-purpose processing units that were ideal for the volume of computations required to create AI.

That bet would pay off in spades as GPUs became the go-to chip for AI creators. When AI burst into the public consciousness in late 2022 with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT — a chatbot trained and run on Nvidia chips — the firm was worth about $400 billion. Today, it's valued at more than $4 trillion, among the most valuable in the world, and it dominates the market for GPUs.

But analysts say despite Huang's visionary management of the business, he had a blind spot for succession and hadn't articulated a clear plan, at least publicly.

In a Bloomberg interview from mid-October, Huang was vague about succession plans. "I'm really hoping that the next CEO of the company is already at the company, but 20 years from now, I hope I stay healthy and I hope I continue to earn my keep."

Huang's adult children, Spencer and Madison Huang, both work at Nvidia. Asked about talk that Madison might be in line to succeed him, he paused, and told Bloomberg: "if that's their aspiration, Spencer or Madison's, they have to go earn it. And it's really, really hard work. It takes a lot of sacrifice."

Daniel Newman, CEO of the Futurum Group, a tech research firm, said the company will inevitably be different without Huang, and its future success is unclear.

"They've always had Jensen as this sort of visionary at the front," he said. "I don't think that's replaceable."

Katie McQue contributed to this story.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: After career detours, drifting rap phenoms find their way back to the road
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: Sheldon Pearce
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
Lil Baby's new album, FRESH, aims to recapture the energy of his hot streak at the turn of the 2020s.

Few things spur rappers to action quite like fear of falling off. Kendrick Lamar once rapped that it was a sickness, and "quite contagious." J. Cole built an entire concept album around delaying the inevitable loss of momentum. "Will I ever fall off? That day will never come / Till the pine box, b****, f*** you! I'm better than I ever was," Eminem rapped defiantly on 2017's "Nowhere Fast," well into a career downturn. To acknowledge a fall-off is to mark the point of no return; the only escape when the precipice nears is for a rapper to rediscover their mojo, whatever spark originally endeared them to artists, without earmarking their music as archaic. And mojo is a fickle thing — tough to put a finger on, harder still to reclaim.

Three albums released on Friday find erstwhile phenoms trying to recapture their sound's glow, charting various paths toward creative restoration. On FRESH, the nu-trap delegate Lil Baby seeks to reenter a flow state that delivered him onto the Billboard charts. After a surprise pivot into neo-soul earlier in the year, the pop-rap heartthrob Jack Harlow tries to defrag a fractured design with the new EP Sweet Action II. Meanwhile, the Bay Area group SOB x RBE, carriers of a local legacy, inject life back into a dormant campaign on the comeback LP From the Land. In each new project, you can trace the artist's pilgrimage back toward a defining career ethos.

Lil Baby wouldn't be a rapper at all if not for a little push. In 2017, the chameleon Young Thug, his senior in the Atlanta scene, literally paid him to get in the booth and punch in. It was a fitting origin story — rap felt second nature for Baby, yet his nonchalance betrayed an indifference to craft. The combination paid off handsomely in the late '10s and early '20s: Baby became a breakout star, highlighted by a 2020 run in which he had the most-streamed album and was named Apple Music's artist of the year. By 2023, he was a streaming powerhouse on par with Taylor Swift, sustained by tuneful, metrical flows that bored into grooves.

Over time, though, that metricality made his sound feel increasingly monotonous, and recent years have brought diminishing returns in his music. The numbers dipped, and a feud with longtime running mate Gunna further complicated public perception, as the two artists were pitted against each other in creative and commercial arms races. Every album he's released since 2020 has debuted at the top of the Billboard 200, and yet the sense that he has fallen off has followed him like a rotten smell.

In a recent interview with Popcast, Baby said he is motivated by a desire to "keep winning": "I don't think my hunger, my drive, could disappear. I think I'm a natural-born hustler. As far as making music, now, I don't know." He seemed to be setting a hierarchy of goals: satiating that hunger for success first, creating second. "That's all that's gonna be — hits," he added, somewhat counterintuitively, "because if I can't make hits, I ain't gonna make music no more." But the logic coheres deeper into the conversation, as Baby reveals that to him, "making hits" is less about performance metrics and more about simply showing up to work. While he denies that he has ever been in a slump, there is a tacit acknowledgment that swinging for the fences each at-bat is the only guaranteed way to make contact again.

In this context, FRESH sounds like a deliberate attempt to get back into his rhythm. The album's underlying premise seems to be that he requires perpetual action to achieve maximum power, and that continuous burrowing will eventually bring him to the center of his sound. In the process, he reveals calculation to be his music's defining feature: It is carefully measured, deliberately segmented, anonymous but also intentional. "Ain't read my first contract, all I knew was a drug deal / Plus the white boy told me, 'Ask 'em 40 mil for the pub deal' / That was 2020, I done ran it up and I'm stuck here," he raps on "Mr. Do Something." That characterization — "stuck" — is telling. The desire to remain at the top can be limiting, but also affirming, particularly when coming from struggle. For much of Baby's career, rapping seemed like an afterthought; here, it's clear productivity is top of mind. He sounds less concerned with proving naysayers wrong and more with just getting into gear.

After several out-and-out flops, Jack Harlow finds himself in a tougher position. If Lil Baby is trying to recalibrate his motor to the currents of a new streaming ecosystem, Harlow is rebuilding the boat in the water. He's struggled since his debut to recapture the charisma manifested in that moment, a meandering journey capped by the March album Monica, which brought on a complete aesthetic transformation — conductor hats and chunky sweaters in service of what a Times style reporter referred to as a "diet D'Angelo impression." Enter Sweet Action II, a sequel to the affable EP that produced "Whats Poppin," Harlow's breakout hit.

In rap there is a particular kind of sequel release — one that aims explicitly at a bygone version of that artist's success — that can feel like filing for bankruptcy. When Eminem clapped back on "Nowhere Fast," on the purposefully titled album Revival, he was doing so after the resuscitative efforts of 2013's The Marshall Mathers LP 2, a retread of his maniacally dextrous classic from 2000. Nicki Minaj, The Game, Ghostface Killah, Cam'ron and Jeezy have all returned to the well decades later, with mixed results. Too often it can feel like a naked ploy to give audiences what the artist thinks they want, without factoring in how the audience or artist may have changed.

Sweet Action II comes on a considerably shorter timeline, but the internet has accelerated everything, even the cycles by which artistic careers ebb, flow and die, and the Harlow project functionally serves the same purpose: reattaching to familiar IP to capitalize on its cultural footprint. It bears the hallmarks of the original, down to the cover photo, but Harlow is also looking to integrate his new self with his old one. His methods are clear: more of the laid-back verses of his earliest work, some singing sprinkled in, all subtly laced through soundscapes that nod to his past and present. There's a Babyface feature and a Tank sample, but the lyrics tease out a connection to his loverboy roots. Mileage may vary, but it's hard to deny the EP's successful course correction back toward a quintessential Jack Harlow style.

This kind of reset isn't strictly for place-hunters seeking to climb back onto the charts: In some cases, it's an effort to reestablish the momentum of a sidelined movement. Such are the conditions that have led to SOB x RBE's From the Land, a reunion album seven years in the making. In the late 2010s, the Vallejo crew was at the forefront of a revival in hyphy music, the buoyant Bay Area subculture popularized by the late rapper Mac Dre. The group's motion was such that Kendrick Lamar tapped its members to contribute to the soundtrack for the 2018 MCU blockbuster Black Panther. The members signed solo deals, threatening the unit, and when Lul G was found guilty of murder in 2019, SOB x RBE all but disbanded.

The cover of From the Land depicts the three remaining members looking up at a bat-signal projection of the SOB x RBE logo across the sky, and that is how its music is presented, like heroes answering the call. The music feels updated to accommodate the changes weathered by the group: Its rappers are more weary but no less animated, and the propulsive songs are still powered by their interplay. A long hiatus often brings rust or disrupts chemistry, but SOB x RBE seems devoted to a cause. "Know the world been waitin', long time comin' / What I spent on how I'm steppin', fifteen hundred / Know you heard n****s talk, but they ain't on nothin' / It was just me and my brothers when we had nothin'," Yhung T.O. croons. Listening, it feels like a crew embracing the stakes and picking up where it left off.

But recapturing mojo alone may not be enough to restore the feeling with one's audience. The truth of the matter is that falling off has rarely felt more relative, since the metrics of success have never been wonkier (with the charts formula being reworked again in 2027). Those numbers were always far more useful for gauging consumption than creative growth, but even niche music communities can hardly agree which cultural signifiers are important anymore. Lil Baby, for his part, clearly sees any decline of his own as a microcosm of a larger issue with the genre for which he has become an avatar, as rap's stranglehold on the charts has loosened considerably this decade. "Hip-hop has fallen off, but I'm hip-hop," he told Hot 97. "So when they say 'Baby fell off,' it's whatever — hip-hop at an all-time low, and I'm that."

A cynical way to interpret those comments is that Baby considers rap's recent setbacks to be representative of a grander artistic failing, but I choose to read them differently. "I'm hip-hop" and "it's whatever" are a package deal — him shrugging off the claims while also defining himself on hip-hop's terms, as if to say the numbers can't really disrupt the way those in the culture identify with the music, or its intangible impact. Despite any claims that Baby has fallen off, I have personally never resonated with his music more than right now. Perhaps that, in itself, is evidence that bouncing back is less about data points and more about staying true to one's purpose.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-602.title: BTS is boycotting the Grammys. It's part of a long history of category controversies
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-602.author: Isabella Gomez Sarmiento
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-602.text:
Isabella Gomez Sarmiento

Jin, Jung Kook, Suga, Jimin, j-hope, V, and RM of BTS perform onstage during the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Festival.

Almost every single year, the Recording Academy updates the terminology and categories that it uses to recognize musicians at its annual Grammy Awards. In 2026, five new categories were introduced — including an award that sparked backlash from one of the most popular groups in the world: BTS.

The best Asian pop music performance category, which will debut its inaugural slate of nominees next week, was created to award "contemporary popular music originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets, including K-Pop, J-Pop, and C-Pop." But just over a month after the Recording Academy unveiled its plans for the award, which requires "meaningful use of one or more Asian languages" for eligibility, the K-pop boyband BTS shared its own announcement on social media.

"We have decided not to submit for Grammys this year. Rather than music being divided by region or language, we hope music itself can be heard and loved for what it is," the band wrote. "We are always grateful to [our fandom] ARMY and everyone who is always with us."

The band is in the middle of a massive comeback following a years-long hiatus for its members' mandatory military service in South Korea. They released the album Arirang in March and embarked on a sold-out global tour soon after. Following BTS' statement, the K-pop group Stray Kids also announced its intent to not submit.

Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. responded to BTS' statement on Instagram, writing that he was saddened but respected the group's decision.

"I do want to clarify something that seems to be getting lost in the conversation," Mason Jr. wrote. "The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists. More categories mean more artists' work is recognized. It's never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters."

The back-and-forth between BTS and the Recording Academy marks the latest thread in a longer, complicated lineage of the Grammys' attempts to become more inclusive.

BTS has been nominated for five Grammys in the past, including several nods for best pop duo/group performance, but has never won. Mathieu Berbiguier, a visiting assistant professor of Korean studies at Carnegie Mellon University, says the new category is a double-edged sword: on one hand, it's an opportunity to highlight music from across the Asian continent, which is growing in popularity as streaming and social media collapse borders in global listening habits. At the same time, Bebiguier says the category seems like an attempt to sideline the gains made by K-pop in recent years away from the general categories. (This past February, the viral hit "Golden" from the film KPop Demon Hunters became the first K-pop song to win a Grammy).

Jeong Hoon Seo, Mark Sonnenblick, EJAE, Yu Han Lee, Park Hong Jun, and Hee Dong Nam, winners of best song written for visual media for "Golden" (from KPop Demon Hunters), pose in the press room during the 68th GRAMMY Awards at Crypto.com Arena on February 01, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.

"Given that the term K-pop in itself hasn't been created in Korea, it's a category that has been created in difference, in comparison to other genres," Berbiguier says. "It is difficult to think of it as something positive, because it's kind of saying we want to acknowledge you, but at the same time in a separate category, so that it doesn't mix up with what is supposed to be mainstream."

Berbiguier points to the contention behind K-pop as a label, a catch-all signifier used by the foreign entertainment industry in an attempt to define popular music within South Korea that's also applied to acts from other countries (see, the "global girl group" Katseye). Berbiguier himself defines K-pop not as a genre, but as a system in which young people are recruited into the Korean pop industry, given extensive training to sing, act or dance and later officially debuted either as a solo act or as part of a group.

What is considered K-pop is slippery, he explains, and even those within the system are considering shedding the label. Bang Si-Hyuk, founder of the South Korean conglomerate HYBE (which is behind several blockbuster K-pop groups, including BTS), said in a 2023 interview with Maeil Business Newspaper that the "K" might need to be dropped in order to continue expanding the genre's global appeal. RM, one of the members of BTS, told Rolling Stone that it's "an important debate" for the music industry.

It is difficult to think of it as something positive, because it's kind of saying we want to acknowledge you, but at the same time in a separate category, so that it doesn't mix up with what is supposed to be mainstream.

Mathieu Berbiguier, visiting assistant professor of Korean studies at Carnegie Mellon University

"It shows you that the agenda is not the same on the side of the K-pop entertainment companies and the Grammys, because the Grammys probably think of it as a gateway to get more international recognition," Berbiguier says. "But then for the K-pop entertainment companies, that's not what they want. They want to be recognized as a whole."

The questions raised by the introduction of the Asian pop music category — what does it mean to separate music by location, race or language? Who gets to define that region's musical identity? And does the attempt to be inclusive ultimately cement an act's outsider status? — have all been raised before at different points in the Grammys' history.

Since the Awards' inception in 1959, the Recording Academy has faced criticism for how it racializes and represents popular music in the United States and abroad. Only 12 Black artists have ever won the most prestigious award of album of the year, and Black musicians have long called out the Academy for pigeonholing them into smaller categories that they say minimize their contributions. The Academy did not acknowledge the rise of hip-hop until 1988, when it first introduced the best rap performance category, but was soon met with controversy when it chose not to televise the award during the 1989 ceremony. As a result, artists including LL Cool J, Public Enemy and DJ Jazzy Jeff & The Fresh Prince — who ended up winning the Grammy — boycotted the ceremony in protest.

In 2016, Frank Ocean declined to submit his chart-topping album, Blonde, for consideration, calling the awards' nomination and voting system "dated" and calling it his "Colin Kaepernick" moment. The pop auteur had already been nominated seven times in several categories by that point and had won twice, including for best urban contemporary album in 2013. In 2020, Tyler, the Creator took home his first golden gramophone for best rap album for IGOR. During a press conference backstage, he said he was grateful for the award but felt that the category he was placed in was a sort of "backhanded compliment."

"It sucks that whenever we — and I mean guys that look like me — do anything that's genre-bending or that's anything they always put it in a rap or urban category. I don't like that 'urban' word — it's just a politically correct way to say the N-word to me," Tyler said.

Tyler, the Creator poses in the press room with the award for best rap album for Igor during the 62nd Annual GRAMMY Awards at Staples Center on January 26, 2020 in Los Angeles, California.

Six months later, the Academy announced it would be dropping the "urban" term and renaming it to best progressive R&B album in an attempt to be more accurate and inclusive. John Vilanova, music scholar and journalism professor at Lehigh University, says there's always been an underlying tension between the narrative the Grammys want to tell about the music industry and the reality of what's happening in the culture.

"They're not at the bleeding edge and they're kind of not designed to be. It's a legacy product," he says. "So when they're making these adjustments, it is often in this kind of stumbling, bumbling way."

When it comes to smaller genres outside the mainstream, other issues arise. In 2011, the Recording Academy announced an overhaul that would cut back from 109 to 78 categories, doing away with male versus female awards in favor of gender-neutral categories and consolidating the number of awards in certain genres. Categories for Native American music, as well as Zydeco and Cajun music, were all merged into best regional roots music. Latin jazz was rolled into best jazz album. Regional Mexican categories were also impacted. In protest, four Latin jazz musicians — Bobby Sanabria, Mark Levine, Ben Lapidus and Eugene Marlow — filed a class-action lawsuit against the Recording Academy, claiming that the changes took away potential recognition and impacted their ability to make a living. The lawsuit was later dismissed by a New York judge, but the category was reinstated.

During the 2011 changes, the category then known as "world music" (now global) was also cut in half, down from two awards (contemporary versus traditional) to a single one. Ian Brennan produced the album that won in the consolidated best world music album category in 2012, Tassil by Tinariwen. But he says the collapse of the global category slashed global representation at the Grammys in half, and pushed out many smaller, regional musicians who could no longer compete against bigger names.

"It's a very complicated category because it includes the whole globe," Brennan says. "There's no category that has greater diversity or should have greater diversity than this category. But what we see is so much redundancy."

He says the same artists and countries often end up being represented in the global categories — Angelique Kidjo has received 10 nominations, Anoushka Shankar has been nominated nine times, and hugely influential genres, such as Ethiopian jazz, have never been recognized.

In recent years, the Academy has widened the global field to include several more awards: best global music album, best global music performance and in 2024, best African music performance. The new Asian pop category is supposed to further expand this inclusion.

Vilanova says that despite its less-than-smooth track record, the Recording Academy has taken serious steps to diversify its voting body and, in turn, the music it represents. Earlier this year, Bad Bunny made history when DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS, his genre-bending homage to the history and sounds of Puerto Rico, became the first Spanish-language album to win album of the year.

The Chinese singer Miist, who is a voting member of the Recording Academy, says she understands the criticisms lobbed at the new Asian pop category — but as a smaller artist who records in multiple languages, including Mandarin, English and Spanish, she says she feels excited about submitting to the new category.

It gives us an opportunity to showcase our music, which almost could have never had a chance to be heard by maybe 15,000 or 16,000 voting members.

Miist, Chinese singer and voting member of the Recording Academy

"It gives us an opportunity to showcase our music, which almost could have never had a chance to be heard by maybe 15,000 or 16,000 voting members," she says. "They would have never had a chance to be discovered. It also gives the voting members a chance to experience these different cultures and music."

She says the Academy could've done a better job of communicating about the changes and actively including more Asian musicians in the process. But as an artist and member who has now been internally involved in discussions about the global categories as a whole, she feels this is a step in the right direction.

"The Academy has to stand at a place that represents what the members want, what the musicians want. [It's] not necessarily the same thing as what the market wants. So I can see that the Academy is trying hard to balance the two, but I think we need to give them some time to get there."

https://www.npr.org/sections/world-cafe/.title: Tune in to a mini-concert with Minyo Crusaders
https://www.npr.org/sections/world-cafe/.author: Stephen Kallao
https://www.npr.org/sections/world-cafe/.text:
Minyo Crusaders is a wild fusion of Japanese folk, cumbia, salsa, Afrobeat and dancehall.

Founded in 2011 by Katsumi Tanaka and Freddie Tsukamoto, the group set out to explore min'yō, or traditional Japanese folk music, by blending it with rhythms from around the world.

"Min'yō is both the closest and most distant folk music for Japanese people," says bandleader and guitarist Katsumi Tanaka. "Its essence is deeply embedded in us, even if we don't always recognize it."

The result is a dynamic mix of familiar and unfamiliar sounds and moods, creating a one-of-a-kind musical celebration. Today, we've got a mini-concert from Minyo Crusaders, featuring songs from their latest album, From Japan With Love, released earlier this year.

This episode of World Cafe was produced by Will Loftus. The web story was created by Miguel Perez. Our engineer is Chris Williams. Our programming and booking coordinator is Chelsea Johnson and our senior producer is Kimberly Junod.

World Cafe: 11/11/2026

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Decision disappoints experts hoping for world’s biggest emitter to take global lead on climate crisis

China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.

Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”

China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.

Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.

Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.

The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.

“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.

“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”

It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.

After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.

The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.

Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.

That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.

India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.

The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.

No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting, which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts. The US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.title: Pat Cummins press conference live updates: Australian cricket captain speaks about Usman Khawaja’s ‘sandpapergate’ claims
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.author: Nick Visser
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.text:
Cummins says he was “genuinely shocked” this week amid the comments in Khawaja’s book. He went on:

When he says we all knew, if [by] that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he’s 100% wrong. I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening …

He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That’s complete and utter nonsense.

Cummins goes on to say he believes Khawaja’s book has “been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket”.

This press conference is approaching 45 minutes. Cummins says he’ll stay until journalists had exhausted all of their questions, and then hopefully move on permanently from the rehashed controversy.

Cummins says it seems the issue has been ‘sitting heavy’ on Khawaja

Cummins won’t say much about any exchanges he’s had with Khawaja this week, saying they’re personal conversations and he doesn’t want to “go into it”.

When asked why he thinks the revelations are coming out now, Cummins says:

It looks like it’s been sitting heavy on him for a while. It’s eight and a half years ago. I get that … Maybe this is Usman’s chance and he never really got over it at the time.

But he reiterates that he believes the claims are “irresponsible”.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to support our crucial year-end fundraiser. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

Cummins said he’s been frustrated Khawaja’s book is relitigating an episode from more than eight years ago, adding it had reopened trauma for some:

It’s eight and a half years, we have moved on.

We’ll keep saying it but, again, these are people’s lives. It was traumatic for some of them. They have had to work through quite a bit to get out the other side.

So again, that’s why I’m really disappointed and frustrated this week … how it’s been dealt with so flippantly.

Cummins says there’s a ‘proper way to do things’

Cummins says he believes there was a proper way to handle the sandpaper incident, pointing to the Cricket Australia investigation shortly afterwards.

Cricket Australia’s chief executive, Todd Greenberg, told media this week there was not “any compelling reason” to revisit the investigation, even though there are “specific details” in Khawaja’s book “that contradict the versions that have been provided by others”.

There’s a very proper way to do things and improve. I think that investigation was a proper way to do it.

Everyone was asked in the circumstances about a game very quickly after. So that’s for CA. I think you can maybe argue whether the judgements were fair, but what can you do? I got asked all the questions, answered them all fairly.

‘I think he’s wrong’, Cummins says

A reporter just asked about the difference in stories. Cummins replied:

That’s my story, so I think he’s wrong.

He went on to say there appeared to be a “few big leaps” in the book and Khawaja had been “vague” and acted in a “very casual matter”:

The details really matter in that difference. So perhaps there was conversations with Cameron Bancroft around taking sandpaper out and how to do it. That doesn’t mean that everyone in that dressing room knew what was going on.

There was no master plan around using illegal methods. I think that’s maybe something that hasn’t been spoken about enough. People assume you have gone from very legal methods to suddenly taking sandpaper and then there must have been some huge master plan.

That is not the case …

There’s no grand plan, there’s no team meeting, there’s no bowlers saying ‘this is what must happen’.

Cummins: ‘I did not see anything on the ball’

Cummins was asked how the ball looked at the time.

At that stage, you know, even the umpires had a look. We didn’t know it had been altered with sandpaper.

Balls get roughened up every time we play. So, you know, whether that’s from a foreign object or something that’s totally legal and part of the game. Sometimes it’s hard to know. But out there in the field I did not see anything on the ball.

Cummins says he was “genuinely shocked” this week amid the comments in Khawaja’s book. He went on:

When he says we all knew, if [by] that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he’s 100% wrong. I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening …

He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That’s complete and utter nonsense.

Cummins goes on to say he believes Khawaja’s book has “been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket”.

Cummins is fronting the media now.

Khawaja memoir ‘readable, surprisingly revealing, sometimes painfully frank’

Gideon Haigh, writing for the Guardian this week, says the greatest shame of the controversy inflamed by Usman Khawaja’s memoir, Sabr, is that “99% of those opining about it will never read it”.

They will experience it by quotes and summaries, magnified and distorted, elided and exaggerated, shaped by voyeurism and schadenfreude.

In fact, Sabr is a readable, surprisingly revealing, sometimes painfully frank book about a unique career.

Haigh says Khawaja was among the most talented batters in an Australian generation “when it was not in oversupply”, but points out he played in only 22% of the national team’s total fixtures over that period.

If he developed a carapace to deal with such endless disappointment, should that surprise anyone?

Sabr might mean patience or resilience in Urdu, but a strength of Khawaja’s testament is that he allows the impatience to show through.

It is a cranky book because, perhaps, a degree of crankiness is what it takes to come back and back and back, when one is never sure one’s abilities are appreciated and one’s face fits.

Starc statement: ‘we weren’t aware of things being taken on the field’

Earlier this week, Mitchell Starc denied claims made in Khawaja’s book.

Starc broke his silence to address Khawaja’s comments, saying he was not aware that sandpaper was used in the Test before Cape Town, nor during the Newlands match. The paceman said his recollection of the match had not changed from what the bowlers said in a statement issued in 2021, which denied all knowledge of the ball-tampering plan.

As far as our statement said, we weren’t aware of things being taken on the field, that’s where I’ll leave it. We weren’t aware anything was taken on to the field to be tampered with. We saw [the sandpaper] on the big screen in Cape Town.

As far as the book is concerned, I haven’t read it. I probably won’t read it. So that’s for Usman to elaborate on.

I’ll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there’s different versions from different people, and I’ll leave it where I left it back then.

In 2018, during the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town, Australia’s opening batter, Cameron Bancroft, was caught on TV using sandpaper against one side of the cricket ball.

An investigation revealed the tampering was planned by the captain, Steve Smith, and vice-captain, David Warner. Both, as well as Bancroft, received bans from international and local cricket.

Fast-forward to now – and former Australian batter Usman Khawaja alleged in his autobiography, Sabr: Finding My Way in Cricket and Life, that the use of sandpaper was widespread.

Khawaja alleged the tampering happened earlier in the series at Port Elizabeth and that the entire team knew about it. Cummins has not commented – until now.

Read more from our reporter, Jack Snape:

The Australian cricket captain, Pat Cummins, is to speak for the first time on the sandpaper scandal since allegations about ball tampering from his former teammate Usman Khawaja.

Cummins posted to social media that he would speak to reporters on Friday morning at Cricket NSW’s headquarters in Sydney.

I’m training at Cricket Central tomorrow morning before the Blues play in the Shield match.

Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week at 9.30 am.

I’ve taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy’s allegations so I can respond properly.

Afterwards please stay and support the Blues!

I’ll ask CA to send out details

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Global Microsoft outage affects Outlook and Teams as company says fixes not providing ‘anticipated relief’
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Josh Taylor and Emma Elsworthy
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Alert on Microsoft’s site says it is ‘aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact’ and blames server issue

Microsoft says its fixes to servers have not “provided the anticipated relief” to a global outage that has resulted in nearly 130,000 users worldwide reporting issues accessing its 365 suite of software, including Outlook and Teams.

Outage website Down Detector showed a spike in Microsoft 365 problems, with nearly 130,000 reports of issues affecting access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams as well as enterprise services such as SharePoint and OneDrive. AI assistant Copilot was also affected.
