American saves three set points in second-set rally

Gauff wins six straight games to seal 6-4, 7-5 victory

World No 4 needs Noskova help to reach last four

Coco Gauff clawed out a 6-4, 7-5 round-robin victory over Marta Kostyuk on Thursday to keep her WTA Finals hopes alive in Indian Wells, California.

The world No 4 still needs help to reach the semi-finals of the elite season-ending event. If fifth-ranked compatriot Jessica Pegula beats Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova in Thursday’s final group match, Pegula will advance instead. Noskova has already qualified.

Not signed in before? Create an account

But Gauff did what she could with a gutsy straight-sets win. Trailing 5-1 in the second set, she saved three set points in the seventh game to launch a run of six straight games and seal the match.

The first set had also been a battle. Broken in the opening game, Gauff appeared to have seized control when she broke Kostyuk for a second time to take a 4-2 lead, then held for 5-2.

Kostyuk looked demoralized as she took a medical timeout for treatment on her right wrist.

But after having the wrist taped, she returned to hold serve, then broke Gauff as the American served for the set – helped by a pair of double faults.

Gauff regrouped to take the set, but was soon struggling again. After going down two breaks to trail 3-0 in the second, she received treatment for what she later described as back tightness.

Despite nine double faults, Gauff prevailed in one hour and 39 minutes.

“I’m not going to lie, [my] head was already in that third set,” Gauff said of her mindset when trailing 5-1.

“Then once it got to 5-4 I was like, ‘OK, I can win this set.’ I got a little bit lucky. She gave me a few errors. I’m glad I was able to close that out.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: How will the USMNT replace Mauricio Pochettino? There’s no clear answer
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The USMNT head coach is on the verge of sealing a move to Manchester United, but it’s hard to know who could be in the chair next

Sign up for our free newsletter here

Even before the 2026 World Cup, the US Soccer Federation projected an air of confidence in its ability to, someday, replace Mauricio Pochettino.

“We have a process of, on a regular basis, always reviewing sort of succession planning for all of our key roles at US Soccer,” JT Batson, the federation CEO, told ESPN in April. “We’re ready when anything happens, whether it’s CFO, whether it’s a head coach or anything in between.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Now, it’s time to put those words to the test. Pochettino’s exit is now seemingly a formality, with Manchester United having agreed a deal with him to replace Michael Carrick, who was fired on Thursday.

Upon hiring Pochettino, US Soccer was lauded for garnering the interest of such a respected manager. Few coaches in the men’s game are discussed in similar esteem: such status requires a record of success, ahistory of having built a stable culture and some unquantifiable aura. Throughout his two years with the US, program mainstays spoke glowingly about how Pochettino had changed the culture around the team following Gregg Berhalter’s six years in the role.

In total, Pochettino’s half-cycle term has warped expectations of the ideal profile for a USMNT coach. It’s an expensive evolution, but one that can’t be discounted as the US enter the 2030 World Cup cycle.

Who, exactly, makes sense to sustain the momentum he’s built?

The first name on many fans’ lips. He’s long been at the top of hypothetical wishlists, having spent a year’s sojourn in New York City between leaving Bayern Munich and beginning his decade with Manchester City. There have been rumors for years that he may be interested in leading the US at a home World Cup if his time with City ended beforehand. That timeline didn’t quite come to pass, but he’s unattached now and is the only unemployed manager who would universally be seen as an upgrade over Pochettino.

Then again, the reasons that made Pochettino lasting a full four years in this job seem outlandish are even more relevant to Guardiola, who turned down the Italy job this summer. While Concacaf has improved over the past decade, it’s still among the world’s least esteemed confederations and lacks the hallowed continental championships of Europe, South America, Africa and Asia. Would three and a half years of friendlies, an easier World Cup qualifying path than ever, and routine matchups with Mexico and Canada be enough to whet his competitive appetite until 2030?

Bear in mind, Guardiola – and another available celebrity manager, Antonio Conte – only reach this status by being workaholics. These are obsessives who kneel at the altar of the almighty grind. With respect to the Gold Cup and the Nations League, this just may not be the standard of project that could appease such ambition. Concacaf’s lesser global status could also repel the next tier of proven international managers, which could include Rudi Garcia, Sebastián Beccacece and Diego Alonso.

Historically, the USMNT have avoided questions of devotion by leaning into the domestic coaching pool. When Bruce Arena first took the role in 1998, he had just started MLS’s first dynasty. By the time Bob Bradley took over in 2006, he was also among the league’s winningest coaches. When Gregg Berhalter was hired after the failure to qualify for Russia 2018, he was a universally rated option whose race was run in Columbus.

The most qualified American for the job, by nearly every criteria, has almost certainly disqualified himself from contention. Rare is the international window where Canada head coach Jesse Marsch isn’t asked for his thoughts on the USMNT, or US politics, or what beating Canada’s southern rivals means to him on a personal level. Even scarcer is the instance where his answer doesn’t spur a myriad of headlines.

“Let me make it really clear: I never will coach the US national team. Ever,” Jesse Marsch, Canada head coach, told Time magazine in July. “And that’s no problem. There was the possibility of me at one point, but I’m done with it. I don’t even care any more.”

If Marsch has a rival for “best active American men’s coach”, it’s Pellegrino Matarazzo. The New Jersey native graduated from Columbia University and promptly began a playing career in Germany, where he also launched his coaching career. After successful stops at Stuttgart and Hoffenheim, Matarazzo is at the helm of Real Sociedad, where he became the first US manager to win a trophy in Europe’s big five leagues by lifting the Copa Del Rey last spring. If the US came calling, Sociedad would probably work to keep him.

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

In between Berhalter’s first and second terms, BJ Callaghan led the US to win the Gold Cup with eye-catching play and impressive control over games. He took his first club head coaching job in 2024, and has since turned Nashville SC into a record-setting team favored to win a rare domestic double this postseason.

Nashville signed Callaghan to a fresh extension in February, locking him into terms through the 2028-29 MLS season. His possession-heavy style of play remains en vogue in the international game. But at this stage, the 45-year-old may revel in his current project for a bit longer.

After Callaghan, the options almost entirely skew towards MLS coaches and few have CVs that could retain players’ enthusiasm after Pochettino’s exit. Steve Cherundolo, a former US defender and the current U-20/U-23 boss, won an MLS Cup, but his Los Angeles FC tenure was more largely characterized by tactical timidness and failing to dictate proceedings in the biggest games.

Even broadening the scope to coaches with MLS success in spite of their passport does little to unearth obvious fits. Wilfried Nancy has arguably been MLS’s best coach this decade, but his intricate style of play would struggle to translate given the stop/start nature of international soccer. The same could be said for the Vancouver Whitecaps’ Jesper Sørensen.

Thierry Henry may be an intriguing candidate. Henry struggled in club coaching roles with Monaco and Montreal, but reveled in the task of leading France’s U-23s to a silver medal at a home Olympics. The relatively occasional nature of international windows may not be a hindrance, and he’s expressed admiration for MLS and the US national team in the past. Antonio Conte has had no connection whatsoever with the US program, but could be a potential option should the federation have donor money to put towards a top-class coaching hire, as they did with Pochettino.

Regardless of which way they go, the path forward is far from clear.

This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Steph Curry’s defense of Ayesha exposes the ugly double standards of sports’ manosphere | Andrew Lawrence
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Andrew Lawrence
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The Warriors superstar’s forceful defense of his wife over an on-screen kiss has exposed the ugly double standards and fragile masculinity of sports’ manosphere

I
f Steph Curry is leading with his full government name, know that he means business. In a 90-second video released on Wednesday, from the Instagram account of “Wardell Curry”, he put the internet trolls who have been attacking his wife for years on notice. “Usually the noise doesn’t bother me, doesn’t bother Ayesha,” the four-time NBA champion and Paris Olympic knockout artist said. “But when you’re trying to step on the accomplishments of my wife, and feel the need to have to jump in and give an opinion on something that you really don’t know about, [it] kind of speaks to the bigger conversation on how you view women in this world and what they’re allowed and what they’re not allowed to do.”

Posterity will remember this as the NBA’s Oscar slap moment, but without the unnecessary violence. A bizarre turn in the parasocial compact when the restless fanboys pressured a superstar into publicly defending his wife. On this occasion, Curry had to defend his wife for the heinous crime of being the leading lady in a Christmas romcom: a Hallmark knockoff called Second Chance Holiday in which Ayesha Curry plays a dating expert with bad holiday luck and shares a kiss with a man who is not Wardell Stephen Curry II – her husband of 15 years and father to their four children. That apparently was a bridge too far for some of Curry’s former NBA peers.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

On a recent episode of his We Said What We Said podcast, former NBA mainstay Gilbert Arenas reserved an entire segment to take exception to Ayesha turning down the role of basketball tradwife. “She doesn’t act like the other superstars’ wives,” Arenas said. “You know Jordan’s wife. Cookie, that’s Magic’s wife. Savannah [James], right. We don’t want to hear from you. We just want to know you’re there. You’re fine. You’re taking the pictures, but we don’t want to know you.” Arenas went even further, calling Ayesha “the only blemish” in the Curry family as Nick Young, who played alongside Curry on Golden State’s 2018 championship team, nodded along. Arenas should consider himself lucky that Steph responded in a strongly worded social media statement instead of going the Javaris Crittenton route and pulling a gun on Arenas in the locker room.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Sports gossips have been making a game of picking apart Steph and Ayesha’s relationship since he shot to stardom at Davidson College. They seem to forget that while Steph was stealing hearts as the NCAA Tournament’s baby-faced bracket buster, Ayesha was carving out a solid career in Los Angeles as a working actor, with guest spots on Disney’s Hannah Montana and on CBS’s Gary Unmarried opposite comedian Jay Mohr – who is now the other half of LA Lakers president Jeanie Buss, incidentally.

The critics blanched when Ayesha joined the 2010s culinary craze with a blog and a YouTube channel, in which she shared dangerous, subversive recipes such as “Stephen’s five-ingredient game-day pasta”. When the hustle mushroomed into a full-blown lifestyle brand – with signature kitchenware and cookbooks, a Food Network show and a landmark CoverGirl deal – the gossips filleted Ayesha for daring to upstage her more famous husband, the real Chef Curry.

No matter what Ayesha did, it seemed, there was no winning over sports fans steeped in the manosphere’s retrograde views of women. They didn’t approve of her sharing bikini photos online or her body language in snaps with Drake or her candor about the struggle to hold on to her sense of identity and autonomy after marriage and motherhood. The point was driven home yet again when ex-NFL players Emmanuel Acho and LeSean McCoy, perhaps misunderstanding the concept of acting, debated the Curry kiss on their macho podcast – with Acho suggesting that Ayesha, through her words and actions, keeps telegraphing to the world that “she’s not that into Steph Curry”.

Intimacy work has become a wedge issue in Hollywood, with a number of prominent actors saying they will no longer participate in kissing or sex scenes – forcing some directors to get creative. But the Curry speculators aren’t arguing about the mechanics of making movies – a point Steph himself hastened to rebut in his video statement. They say this stuff as if they know the Currys. They don’t. They say this stuff as if they’re also still with their teen sweethearts. They’re not – and Acho especially is one to talk. They say this stuff as if audiences might also interpret Ayesha’s on-screen kiss as an act of adultery. They won’t. They’ll just let the 78 minutes wash over them as they fold laundry or scroll through their phones.

These manosphere brains insist on typecasting Ayesha while giving other prominent athlete spouses plenty of runway. The recent marriage of Coco Jones, the Grammy-winning singer and star of the Fresh Prince update Bel-Air, and Donovan Mitchell, engine of the Cleveland Cavaliers, is treated as an equal pairing. The same goes for Major League ace Paul Skenes and his gymnast-influencer girlfriend, Livvy Dunne. When Travis Kelce started dating Taylor Swift, the talk was all about how he, the Kansas City Chiefs and the NFL stood to benefit. And when Kim K and her sisters take up with high-profile athletes, the manosphere brains roll their eyes, chalk it up to the game and blame any poor performances that might result on the Kardashian curse.

But when it comes to Ayesha, there is no room for self-reflection, growth or individuality. She is, and will always be, an NBA wife in the eyes of many. Her tiresome critics would much rather see her on the sideline managing the kids than see Steph gathering them up to bask in the afterglow of his biggest moments. Weirdly, the tradcasting doesn’t stop with Ayesha. Steph Curry’s mother has been dealing with the same gender policing since she divorced his father, a former NBA player, in 2021 and remarried last month. That all this outrage is building at a time when gender roles in sports have become a culture-war battleground shouldn’t be lost on anyone.

Ultimately, though, the relentless snooping into the Curry marriage reveals a deeper insecurity about Steph. Here’s a God-fearing, wholesome family man who speaks up for female empowerment and walks the talk when he’s not burying clutch threes – and he’s still getting the job done for the Warriors at age 38.

Curry has spent his career making doubters rue the day they said he was too small for pro ball, and that same bracing self-belief has helped him thrive away from the court as a venture capitalist, Hollywood producer and Bay Area philanthropist. Through 18 NBA seasons, he has remained free of scandal, extramarital or otherwise – no mean feat for an NBA superstar, much less a Silicon Valley giant. And that just makes the sports and celebrity hounds who are only following along for the potential of a Will Smith – or Tiger Woods – like train wreck push harder in their relentless pursuit of dirt.

But for dedicated knuckle-draggers like Arenas and his cohort, who still don’t see an alpha male when they behold Curry, it isn’t just that he could be with pretty much anyone else, given his wealth and fame. It’s that he chooses Ayesha and that there still isn’t a rift between them to be found, even after all these years of trying.

The armchair analysis of the Currys’ marriage isn’t likely to stop anytime soon. But it’s a stargazing exercise in the end, with vast distances between the picture in view and the elusive reality. The constant churn of speculation only serves to show the willful ignorance at play, particularly when it comes to the difference between an on-camera kiss – again, Ayesha was acting – and an act of infidelity. With his forceful social media defense, Steph didn’t just offer a reminder of what true manhood looks like. He delivered a message that should sound awfully familiar to Ayesha’s haters – and give them pause: Keep my wife’s name out your mouth.

Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high

US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by record-high mortgage rates and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.

Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700. Declines in sales were seen in the midwest, south and west, though sales in the north-east held steady.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Mortgage rates had been steadily declining in 2024 and 2025, with the 30-year rate falling below 6% for the first time in February 2026. But increasing inflation and higher interest rates amid the Iran war have pushed rates back up to a nearly three-year high.

The 30-year mortgage rate, which is the most commonly used rate in home loans, is now hovering at about 7.18%, not far from its 2023 high of 7.79%. During the pandemic, average mortgage rates were just above 3%.

“Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the NAR. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Pending home sales, or the number of contracts that have been signed before closing, reached its lowest levels in the NAR’s history in September, the same month that the 30-year mortgage rate topped 7% for the first time in nearly two years.

Mortgage rates have been directly affected by interest rate changes by the US Federal Reserve, which in September hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023. Rates currently sit at a range of 3.75% to 4%.

The central bank is poised to raise rates again next month to combat heightened inflation, which went up more than expected in October.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: US public workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and some are winning
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Ramin Skibba
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
As governments adopt AI, workers are gaining ground in how it’s used and securing safeguards against its harms

I
n the shadow of Silicon Valley, workers for the city of Oakland, California, worry the region will deploy AI systems that could increase surveillance and inaccurately evaluate their performance. Pushing for protections to ensure workers won’t be laid off or disciplined by AI, their union overwhelmingly voted on 22 October to authorize a strike, with 94.1% in favor.

“We just want the city administration to really be intentional about how it’s engaging with AI products,” said Julian Ware, an Oakland spatial data administrator and member of International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers Local 21. “Sometimes with a fancy new toy, it actually costs more, it’s more difficult to implement and the results are not as good.”

The nearly unanimous vote had an impact. The city government of Oakland and the union reached a tentative, three-year agreement that includes AI-related protections, such as requiring the city to retrain or reassign workers displaced by AI rather than firing them. As a result, the 5 November strike has been put on hold.

The Bay Area union is one of many public-sector labor groups nationwide seeking explicit protections against AI and automation, which union representatives say could worsen working conditions and threaten jobs. Following decades of automation efforts by companies and growing concern about AI since ChatGPT’s debut in 2022, ongoing labor disputes reveal hardening battle lines between public-sector bosses and their increasingly vocal workers.

“The bosses have such zeal for use of this technology,” said John Samuelsen, the Transport Workers Union president and a New York City subway track inspector. “Our members know that automation is the ultimate threat to their jobs … In transport, it’s here, it’s in our faces, we’re fighting it every day.”

Over the past few years, AI and automation technologies have infiltrated multiple sectors and are gradually making their way into public-sector workplaces across the country. Already, nearly 70% of state and local government agencies say they have adopted or are implementing generative AI, according to a survey by Ernst and Young conducted from July to August 2026. At the same time, workers are organizing and starting to win protections.

Policy makers have been moving too slowly to address AI’s potential effects on workers, so workers have to fight for themselves, argues Liz Shuler, AFL-CIO president and founder of its Technology Institute. “We’re using our contract negotiations to institute guardrails that policymakers won’t.”

Some unions have been prepared for this moment, having watched private-sector unions fight similar battles, said Kung Feng, a researcher with the University of California at Berkeley’s Labor Center and former director of San Francisco Jobs With Justice. For example, in 2023, Communications Workers of America recommended AI protections, and won some of them for California workers in October 2026.

“Workers versus billionaires has been the theme of this whole election … and bargain cycle,” Feng said. “This is the contest that we have over the future of technology in the workplace.”

Researchers call it bossware: AI tools that public- and private-sector employers are increasingly rolling out across industries to monitor and supervise employees, according to an October report Feng co-authored. Some tools rank and evaluate workers for hiring, firing and promotions. Others track location and activity, monitor productivity, scan biometrics for timekeeping, use cameras, wearable devices and sensors, or leverage analytics to predict emotions.

Amazon has used algorithms to push workers to operate at dangerous speeds in its warehouses, and now that strategy is being deployed in the public sector, said Lorena Gonzalez, the California Federation of Labor Unions president.

“We think AI doesn’t belong on big-rig trucks, and it doesn’t belong in hospitals and schools,” Gonzalez said.

Some automation technologies could aid public-sector workers, like vehicle safety systems in public transit, but humans should always be in charge, providing oversight, Gonzalez said. Computers have been able to fly a plane for years, but every aircraft carries two pilots who can use human judgment and skill to override the system when necessary, she said.

“If we’re using a computer or AI, it has to be controlled by a human being, not the other way around,” she said.

Employers in the public sector often deploy automation technologies during claimed attempts to improve efficiency and cut costs when budgets are slim, Feng said. But unions have been pushing for AI protections since the late 2010s, and those battles are only intensifying as automation advances and generative AI becomes more common, he said. Workers’ requests include receiving advance notice before a new technology is rolled out, getting information about that technology and ensuring the right to negotiate over its use, he added.

Examples abound of worker pushback. Last year, Pennsylvania became the first state to run a pilot program with OpenAI. The state encouraged employees, like unemployment claim workers and social workers, to use ChatGPT Enterprise to test for time savings.

“But there were no guarantees or agreements for the workers,” said Steve Catanese, president of Service Employees International Union Local 668, which represents more than 10,000 statewide public-sector workers. “With generative AI, workers are building their own gallows sometimes.”

Then the union spoke up, inspired by the California screenwriters’ victory in 2023, one of the longest strikes in Hollywood history that secured protections against AI replacing writers. The Pennsylvania SEIU Local 668 pushed the governor, Josh Shapiro, to agree to a policy guaranteeing that the state’s use of AI will include employee input and supervision, and that the tech won’t be used to discipline workers.

“It’s powerful for elected leaders to say, there will always be human public servants under my watch,” Catanese said, referring to commitments that AI won’t displace workers. He expects these issues to resurface when the union negotiates for a new contract in 2027.

In transportation, public workers in states including Florida and New York are proactively trying to block Waymo and city governments from deploying autonomous vehicles, calling them unsafe and a threat to their jobs. They’re hoping to replicate a 2024 victory in Columbus, Ohio, where the Transport Workers Union secured contracts giving it veto power over any plan by the Central Ohio Transit Authority to deploy autonomous vehicles.

But the TWU doesn’t oppose new technologies, said Samuelsen, the union president. It supports systems that can aid with collision avoidance and improving bus and train timing, he said.

But he worries that many industries are pushing for AI and automation without regard for safety. For example, some airlines have begun experimenting with using drones to inspect aircraft from afar rather than relying on human jet mechanics, who can do a more thorough, up-close inspection.

AI and automation are “in every single element of passenger transport, and even freight transport, that you can imagine. It has completely infiltrated us,” Samuelsen said. “Where there’s no … union that’s willing to fight, workers are doomed.”

This isn’t the first time emerging technologies have negatively affected labor markets and working conditions across industries, union representatives said.

“We’ve seen this movie before,” Schuler said. Unions have faced mass job loss before, such as when automation in assembly-line factories in the midwest reduced manufacturing jobs, she said.

Some legislators, especially at the state level, have been making strides toward new policies. For example, the IFPTE and other unions supported the No Robo Bosses bill in California, which bars employers from relying solely on automated systems to discipline or fire workers. Unions also supported another California bill that prohibited employers from using workplace AI surveillance tools, such as those that could monitor employees’ emotional states. Gavin Newsom signed both into law on 30 September.

Public-sector workers have also backed AI-related legislation in other states. Public-sector unions in New York supported a law, effective December 2025, that protects workers at state agencies from being displaced by AI.

Though tech CEOs have warned of AI’s hypothetical risks to humanity, the more pressing issue is how employees are being negatively affected by the technology today, said Keith Brown, executive secretary-treasurer of the Alameda Labor Council, which serves public and private-sector workers in California’s Alameda county.

“We’ve seen in the news a lot of headlines about the threat of AI destroying civilization,” Brown said. “But for workers, we’ve been facing these harms from AI tech companies for a long time.”
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: The 5 November strike has been put on hold. Public workers in Florida and New York are trying to block Waymo and city governments from deploying autonomous vehicles. The Transport Workers Union has secured contracts giving it veto power over any plan by the Central Ohio Transit Authority to deploy autonomous vehicles.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.author: Nils Pratley
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.text:
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

H
alf the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration, will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job.

Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed.

Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors.

Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive.

Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.summary: Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang was viewed as 'irreplaceable' but recklessness of affair with woman made him a political liability. Nvidia's board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: UK ministers have no plans to publish explosive report on climate crisis
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Andy Burnham’s newly appointed climate adviser used report to warn of national security risk from collapsing ecosystems

The UK government still has no plans to publish an explosive report showing the national security risk from the collapse of ecosystems around the world – even after handing the key official behind the report a new advisory role.

Andy Burnham addressed the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey on Thursday and said the UK was determined to reach net zero by 2050 and work with its partners to build a clean energy future.

The prime minister also announced the appointment of Madeleine Alessandri, a long-serving civil servant and the former head of the UK’s joint intelligence committee, to be adviser on climate security. The JIC is the committee of the UK’s spy chiefs, which oversees the work of MI5 and MI6.

Alessandri spearheaded the publication of the climate report, which found that food shortages, food price rises, mass migration and nuclear conflict overseas could result from the failure to prevent the collapse of key ecosystems, including the Amazon rainforest.

The report was supposed to be launched at last year’s Cop, but was suppressed by Keir Starmer’s government. The Guardian revealed – through a leak – the key contents of the report ahead of its intended launch last year, and early this year a redacted version was put out. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has briefed foreign governments on the findings and the report clearly influenced Burnham’s decision to appoint Alessandri, but the report itself remains under wraps.

Burnham told Cop31 that Britain was ready to play its full part. “The message I carry here, in my first Cop as prime minister, is that the UK remains determined to reach net zero by 2050 and to work with our partners to build a clean energy future,” he said.

“The world has changed. The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate action has broken down. We will not stand by, and that’s why I’ve pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.”

He said he embraced the focus at the climate summit on electrification, because “if we depend on energy we do not control, we depend on prices we cannot control. The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security.”

But he insisted that industry must do its part to help people deliver the green transition. He highlighted progress on electric cars and heat pumps, adding: “If you drive a new electric car today in the UK, it costs less than a petrol equivalent. Get on the right tariff and a heat pump can be cheaper to run than a gas boiler.”

Burnham’s public declaration that the climate crisis poses a major national security threat cheered Cop31 and will be noted by governments worried about the impact of global heating on food supplies, the cost of living, migration and infrastructure. He is also one of the few leaders from western Europe to address the summit.

But campaigners, experts and green businesses and investors are worried about his commitment to the climate crisis because his chancellor, John Healey, is known to view economic growth as taking priority even if it means locking the UK into expensive fossil fuels.

Louise Haigh, who is first secretary of state and a key ally of Burnham, is thought to take a similar view, along with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary.

Behind the scenes, these concerns are shared by senior members of his government. Significantly, Burnham has no dedicated climate adviser working for him in Downing Street – despite it being an important issue to many voters.

A series of major decisions that have climate implications are being taken largely in isolation, rather than with their cumulative impact in mind, senior insiders have told the Guardian.

While Burnham addressed Cop31, his ministers were thought to be putting the final touches to a weakening of the mandate requiring carmakers to switch an increasing proportion of their sales to electric vehicles.

Burnham has also greenlighted the Jackdaw gasfield, cut funding for heat pumps and is mulling backing a new oilfield, Rosebank. Healey, meanwhile, has told MPs on the Treasury committee that Labour backs a third runway at Heathrow.

Campaigners and business people told the Guardian that the prime minister gave the impression of being swayed by short-term economic thinking from advisers not up to speed with a vastly changed energy world.

Ami McCarthy, head of politics at Greenpeace UK, said of Burnham’s speech to Cop: “[It] hit the right notes, but noises offstage about a massive new oilfield and looser rules on electric cars almost drowned him out.

“Appointing the world’s first climate security envoy is a welcome move, but approving Rosebank would only increase the climate threat level to communities in Britain and around the world.

“There are so many elephants in the room, you’d think it’s a zoo. Burnham needs to start bridging the widening chasm between words and deeds on climate action.”

But the prime minister has influential supporters too, who believe he understands the climate crisis and supports efforts to tackle it.

Burnham missed out on a bilateral meeting at Cop31 with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president whose resounding re-election has given renewed hope to leftwing parties fighting the far right.

But he did manage a meeting with Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency and the world’s foremost energy economist.

In between football talk – Burnham is famously an Everton fan, and Birol follows the Premier League closely – they discussed how cheaper energy from renewable sources, and more electrification of the UK economy, could bring down the cost of living.

Birol told the Guardian: “I can tell you that his mind and heart are fully behind the electrification of the UK energy system. I can put my name behind it. I had a very good and in-depth discussion with him.”

The government was contacted for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Aisha Down
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
CEO’s affair and resignation has brought company’s murky corporate contracts and supply chains into sharp focus

Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world?

Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run.

This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading.

Nvidia is not the only company that designs these chips. Most leading tech companies, including Microsoft, Meta and Google, are trying to make their own lines of AI chips. Some of these, such as Google’s tensor processing units, appear to be at least as good as Nvidia’s, and even better for certain purposes.

What makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself.

One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments.

In recent years, Huang has been the kingmaker when it comes to AI. In 2025, he met numerous world leaders – including Mohammed bin Salman, Keir Starmer and Emmanuel Macron – persuading them of the urgency of developing “sovereign AI” with his product. His presence served as a guarantee of those nations’ AI plans. These meetings were followed by deals in which Nvidia announced it had arrangements to supply those governments with precious, hard-to-get chips.

None of these agreements were particularly transparent. While Nvidia appears to have promised 260,000 advanced chips to South Korea, for example, it was never immediately apparent when those chips would be delivered, who would pay for them, and on what terms.

Meanwhile, Nvidia financed a web of companies called “neoclouds” to buy its chips and put them in datacentres, there to be rented to the world’s biggest AI companies. These neoclouds have done wonders for Nvidia, propping up demand and keeping the risk associated with building datacentres and finding customers for them off its balance sheets.

Neoclouds are not the only thing financed by Nvidia. It has become known as the “central bank of AI” because it is enmeshed in almost every layer of the AI economy. Nvidia has invested in a spate of AI startups that could become future customers. It has offered massive sums of cash to companies such as OpenAI, to be used to buy its chips. This investment runs to hundreds of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s money, circling again and again through a limited set of accounts.

Then there is Nvidia’s relationship with a Taiwanese company called TSMC, or the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. TSMC makes the world’s AI chips, churning them out across several fabrication plants on the north-west of the island.

As far as geopolitics goes, TSMC is arguably more important than Nvidia or any other chip designer. Other companies can design AI chips, but TSMC manufactures the overwhelming majority of them and has no real competitor. This is because manufacturing AI chips is one of the most expensive and challenging industrial processes to date.

Each chip is etched with nanometre lines by lasers working in the extreme ultraviolet spectrum, which cost billions of dollars and two decades of research to develop. While TSMC has refined its process to make these chips for more than two decades, it still has only a 60% yield rate for its most advanced chips, which means that 40% of them have defects. It’s a staggeringly high rate for one of the world’s most expensive technologies.

Nvidia has worked closely with TSMC to help it develop its processes and products. Lore has it that Huang wrote the chief executive of TSMC a letter introducing himself in 1997. These are high-trust relationships built over decades.

Will it all be the same without Huang? This is almost impossible to answer because Nvidia’s relationships are so opaque. Investigators following the supply chain of its chips run up against secretive corporate contracts and tangled export records. There is known to be a years-long queue of customers waiting to obtain its chips, but questions regarding who is in that queue, in what order, and how many chips have been shipped remain open.

This murkiness was brought into sharp focus by Megaspeed, a small Singaporean company that was getting access to lots of GPUs, even as other companies struggled. One of Megaspeed’s executives, Alice Huang, was later revealed to be having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive, and to be an alleged Chinese spy. This relationship appears to have allowed Megaspeed to secure roughly $7.5bn (£5.67bn) worth of Nvidia chips, which were allegedly smuggled into China.

Was Huang and his glad-handing a source of this opacity? Perhaps a new chief executive could bring some transparency and predictability to the business, at least in terms of chips contracts and supply chains.

But what else could be laid bare if the “central bank of AI” became more transparent, or came under external scrutiny? Many questions surround its contracts and relationships; lots of elaborate debt structures and handshake agreements may yet be uncovered.

Huang dazzled the world in his leather jacket; he convinced heads of government that his technology held the keys to transformation and to power. When the patina wears off, will this still seem the case?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has brought company's murky corporate contracts and supply chains into sharp focus. Huang convinced heads of government that his technology held the keys to transformation and to power.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Some young disabled people to lose Pip in Milburn plan – but can apply to local fund
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Exclusive: Former health secretary wants to ‘tear up the old approach’, and end ongoing payments to certain under-25s

Some young people with disabilities will lose their personal independence payments but will be able to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment, Alan Milburn’s review will recommend.

While those with the most severe needs’ entitlement will be protected, others will be asked to apply for money for specific purposes rather than an ongoing payment.

Under-25s will be no longer eligible to claim Pip and the health element of universal credit and instead will get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit.

Milburn, a former health secretary, has said the current system of benefits must be entirely replaced for young people. “We need to tear up the old approach and start again for under-25s. A tweak to the benefits system just won’t do,” he said in a statement to the Guardian announcing the plans.

“We need a new system built around a young person with schools, the NHS and employers all working together to make sure that everyone has the chance to earn or learn.”

The long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s.

There will be a local fund for young people with disabilities to apply to for money to pay for equipment or for help with short-term expenses such as travel to attend a training course or job interview, the Guardian understands. The fund will be managed by local advisers and the intention is that funds can be transferred quickly when needs arise.

For most young people apart from those with the most severe needs, the fund would replace long-term support such as Pip – a move that has been criticised by some charities and Labour MPs.

Milburn said the trajectory towards 1.25 million young people out of employment, education or training would not be stopped by “crude benefit cuts”, and a life on benefits had to be replaced with relentless support towards work.

“This is a moral crisis. If other countries are relentless in supporting their young people into work and learning, we can be too. A lost generation is a choice. We have a to make a different choice,” he said.

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF), an anti-poverty charity, said the changes risked taking away vital funds that young people used to keep themselves in work.

There will be a higher rate of youth allowance for young people living independently, including care leavers, according to the Times.

There will also be an additional cost allowance for those who are most disabled – which young people can receive whether they are in work or not – and a new higher insurance provision for those with severe disabilities who will never be able to work.

Milburn, who will deliver his report next Tuesday, told the Guardian that the support for young people outlined in his report would create 440,000 employment and education opportunities by 2036 and raise the net incomes of young people by more than £2bn.

He said the main finding of the review was not a lack of ambition from young people but a lack of opportunities. “I have not met a single young person who wanted to be Neet [not in education, employment or training]. Not one. They want independence, they want to earn their own money and they want someone to give them a chance,” he said.

after newsletter promotion

“I want young people to have more than just enough to get by. I want them to have a future. The system is failing to do that.”

The JRF said the proposals could significantly weaken the safety net for hundreds of thousands of young people with a disability or health condition, leaving many of those on universal credit living on a basic rate of support of around just £80 a week.

“Cutting someone’s income when they’re already struggling to afford food or the bus to college makes it harder for them to stay in education or find work,” said Iain Porter, the charity’s senior policy adviser.

No 10 declined on Thursday to rule out the changes affecting existing claimants. A Downing Street spokesperson said: “We face a choice as a country. We can either invest earlier in young people’s success or continue paying the cost of failure when they become detached from education and work and end up relying on the benefit system. We cannot afford to do both.”

The Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, who was part of the welfare rebellion last summer, told Radio 4’s Today programme she felt uneasy about voting for cuts to disability benefits.

“The cuts seem to land on young disabled people, and many of them are in college already or already at work. I don’t see how you fix the first by punishing the second,” she said.

But the Treasury select committee chair, Meg Hillier, who was key to the government climbdown on the welfare cuts last summer, told the BBC she was open to the changes. “What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them,” she said. “Milburn has done some very good work on this, so I’m giving him a fair wind.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs

B
ritain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry.

The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task. Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech.

The conventional wisdom is that if startups are struggling to grow, the problem must be that they lack capital. That is why Rachel Reeves, as chancellor, wanted pension funds to invest in UK assets. But the paper says that this risks making things worse. Putting cash into startups risks inflating eventual sale prices without securing British ownership or control.

The London School of Economics’ Nils Peters and David Kampmann expose a circular logic. The UK lacks tech giants that can acquire successful startups, but selling those startups overseas helps perpetuate that problem. The authors say US and European incumbents won big from the exit of the 38 biggest UK VC-backed tech firms between 2010 and 2023, including businesses at the forefront of AI, fintech and biotechnology.

Selling British technology companies abroad can enrich investors while thwarting ambitions to build domestic champions. The social costs also matter. A system geared towards maximising capital gains favours businesses that promise lucrative exits. The paper argues that this has encouraged surveillance technologies, from wearables to AI chatbots, and exploitative gig platforms, concentrating wealth among a few rather than delivering social benefits.

Gordon Brown is right: Britain should retain ownership of its innovations. But there is a difference between financial returns and industrial development – and improving the former doesn’t necessarily deliver the latter. Although industrial policy has returned rhetorically in the west, this has not translated into meaningful policy. The Common Wealth paper suggests that is a mistake and argues for democratic control over innovation, with investment directed towards social purposes.

The paper’s preferred capitalism is one that is historically associated with the global south: curbing extractive intermediaries, limiting foreign capital and building domestic capacity. India’s publicly funded space programme and Ethiopia’s state-owned airline show how sustained public investment can support homegrown capabilities rather than hastily readying businesses for sale.

Most daringly, Brazil linked universal healthcare for 215 million people to industrial policy, using public purchasing, laboratories and technology transfer. The payoff came during the pandemic: by August 2021, almost three-quarters of Covid vaccine doses administered had been produced at home. Brazil shows that a state can finance, research and produce a universal healthcare system that creates employment and productive capacity. It is surely a powerful idea that providing for people could be a way of sustaining output. Making the fulfilment of social needs a motor of economic development would give Labour a purpose beyond managing scarcity.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
It’s not been a good week for Farage. Aside from that interview and disrespect from the BBC, he’s lost another senior Reform official

I
t’s a day late, but please observe a two-minute silence for Nigel Farage. Lest we forget. Sad to say, but Nige just hasn’t been quite the same since Sunday’s Remembrance service at the Cenotaph. Like me, you might have thought that he had been in Whitehall to honour those who had died in two world wars and subsequent armed conflicts. Only it turns out he was really there to commemorate himself.

Through his personal valet, Richard Tice, Nige has let it be known that he was extremely angry with the BBC’s coverage of the service. The cameras had spent too long lingering on the faces of the king, other members of the royal family and prime ministers past and present. When what they should have been focused on throughout was Nige. He was the one we were all there to see. The man who had done more for his country than anyone else. To have disrespected him in this way was unforgivable. Let’s hope the BBC has got its act together by next year.

That’s not all. These are tough times for the Reform leader. He’s furious about a lot of things. He’s furious the polls show his party in third place on 20%. Clear establishment bias. Though oddly he was perfectly happy when the same polls showed him 10 points clear of Labour and the Tories. He’s spitting mad that he has had to part ways with the Reform’s general secretary who had been in charge of vetting. Turns out the vetting that Nige had insisted was the best in the country turned out to have been conducted by someone who was the opposite. Schrödinger would have something to say about that.

Then there are Nige’s links to Russell Brand. Guess which politician was happy to go on the now convicted rapist’s podcast, long after allegations against him had become public knowledge and no one else would touch him with a barge pole? That’s right. It’s Nige. Because if Reform is about anything it’s “family, community, country”. And no one sums up “family, community, country” more than Russell. It wasn’t clear whether Russell thought he was there to forgive Nige or the other way round. Or just two narcissists in need of attention.

So it wasn’t altogether a surprise to find that Nige was laying low this week. Perhaps he was just trying to negotiate an appearance on the podcast of another celebrity accused of using his fame to have sex with vulnerable younger women. There seem to be a lot of them around. Or maybe Nige just fancied a break. Needed time to come to terms with the disappointment of only being on screen for a few seconds as he laid his wreath. Whatever the case, it was the Reform B Team that got sent to Thursday’s rally in Wolverhampton. An hour of everyone’s time they will never get back.

First up was Dicky Tice. The person of so little talent or personality that he would still only be the warm-up act if he was the only person on the bill. It’s hard to think of any politician who is so pleased to be so empty-headed. Trying to explain away the cost of living rise of food over the past 10 years as the result of a packaging tax. Dicky, Dicky, Dicky. Please let someone talk you through the costs of Brexit, the wars in Ukraine and Iran – for which you were a cheerleader – and fertiliser and energy costs. There again, this is probably well above his pay grade.

Next up was Zia Yusuf. An altogether more terrifying prospect. Not because he is any brighter or more credible, but because he seems to have been taking acting lessons from Bruno Ganz in Downfall. Every sentence begins with a shout, getting ever louder before reaching a crescendo yell. To be fair to him, it’s possible he’s a bit deaf and this is the only way he can hear himself talk. In which case, someone should help him out.

Zia is also a one-trick pony. Everyone is against him and it’s all the fault of foreigners. “THE ESTABLISHMENT ARE OUT TO GET US,” he shrieked. More upset that no journalists had investigated the Tories and Labour than Reform being found to be packed with racists and dodgy donations. “WE ARE GOING NOWHERE,” he concluded. I wasn’t quite sure that was the message he intended for his audience of largely elderly men and women who had nothing better to do at 3pm on a Tuesday afternoon. But it was hard to disagree. With men like Dicky and Zia in charge, it feels as if Reform have stalled.

Not forgetting Robert Jenrick. When I tell you that Honest Bob was the headline speaker, you can imagine just how disappointing the whole rally was. Honest Bob is that breed of career politician who will never be able to shake off the shackles of career politician. He knows nothing about anything and has done nothing of any real interest. He wants to bore you into submission. To get you to forget his record as a failed Tory and try to believe that he gives a shit about anyone but himself.

Still, if you can bore your way to economic growth, then Honest Bob is the man we need. Just endless platitudes about how much he loves the Black Country and how he is going to turn it into a “special economic zone”. Hint: he isn’t. Nothing he says is going to happen. No one is going to trust him to be chancellor. Chancer, maybe. Above all, there is the cheek. He complained about the levels of child poverty in the Midlands, willing us all to forget that he has proposed to restore the two-child benefit cap. Come the end, the applause was mostly relief that it was finally all over. Wolverhampton could breathe again.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Italy fight back to beat France 3-1 and move top of Nations League group
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Francesco Pio Esposito struck twice to inflict a first defeat on Zinedine Zidane as France’s head coach, while Italy stormed back to win 3-1 at San Siro and top their Nations League group.

Michael Olise profited from a Gianluigi Donnarumma error to put the visitors in front after 10 minutes on Thursday, but Italy hit back through Esposito and Davide Frattesi either side of half-time.

Inter Milan striker Esposito’s second came from the penalty spot after his brother Sebastiano had earlier fired a spot kick wide, while France were twice denied by the woodwork in an entertaining encounter.

The result sent Italy top of Group A1 on 10 points, level with France but above them on head-to-head record, while Belgium are third on nine points after inflicting a fifth straight defeat on rock-bottom Turkiye.

France were without star attackers Kylian Mbappe and Ousmane Dembele through injury, but it did not show as they made an electric start in pouring rain in Milan.

Desire Doue hit the side netting and first-time captain Adrien Rabiot tested Donnarumma before Lucas Da Cunha’s rasping half-volley flew narrowly wide.

But the opener was gifted to France when Donnarumma passed the ball straight to Olise, who skipped past a defender before firing home his fifth goal in five Nations League games – a record only bettered by England captain Harry Kane’s seven.

The hosts struck back in the 26th minute with their first chance of the game when Nicolo Cambiaghi drove to the byline and cut back a cross, which Esposito converted with a deft touch.

The goal brought San Siro to life as the older Esposito sibling, Sebastiano, threatened a quickfire comeback two minutes later, forcing a sharp save from Mike Maignan.

Bradley Barcola came closest to a third goal before the break with a curling shot from the edge of the box that struck the foot of the far post.

The end-to-end nature of the game continued in the second half as Rayan Cherki’s rasping strike was tipped onto the post by Donnarumma before Italy charged up the other end and forced Maignan into a point-blank save from Cambiaghi.

Italy had a glorious chance to go in front when Cambiaghi was tripped by Malo Gusto to earn a penalty, but Sebastiano Esposito failed to join his brother on the scoresheet as he hammered his spot kick wide on the hour mark.

The Azzurri did not dwell on the disappointment for long, taking the lead just three minutes later when Frattesi drilled in a shot from a Federico Dimarco cross moments after the Inter Milan wing-back was brought off the bench.

Fellow substitute Antonio Vergara earned the home side another penalty when he was tripped by Dayot Upamecano, and this time Francesco Pio Esposito stepped up to drill a shot into the bottom corner.

The result continued a strong start to Roberto Mancini’s second spell as Italy coach as his side stretched their unbeaten run to four matches and notched their first home win over France since 1962.

Belgium host Italy and Turkiye travel to France in the final round of group games on Sunday.

Elsewhere, captain Harry Kane celebrated his record 126th cap for England with a match-winner from the penalty spot as England beat Croatia 2-1 at Wembley on Thursday to qualify for the Nations League last eight.

The 33-year-old followed a script that seemed destined to happen when he stepped up in the 64th minute to put England ahead in front of an 80,400-strong crowd after the hosts had conceded a sloppy equaliser five minutes earlier.

It was the Bayern Munich forward’s 92nd England goal, and there was never any doubt from the moment he placed the ball and sent it straight down the middle as goalkeeper Dominik Livakovic dived to his left.

Kane had started a night of celebration as the centre of attention, handed a commemorative token by former goalkeeper Peter Shilton, the previous record holder since 1989, when he surpassed Bobby Moore’s 108 caps.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Thousands of Microsoft users reported trouble accessing their email and connecting to work apps after a widespread outage hit Outlook and other services on Thursday.

Reports of problems with Outlook, the company’s email client, climbed to about 130,000 on the outage tracking site Downdetector shortly after 1pm Eastern Time (18:00 GMT), with some users saying emails weren’t being sent or received, while others couldn’t open their inboxes.

By just before 3pm (20:00 GMT), that figure had fallen to about 77,000.

Users also reported having trouble accessing Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams and its AI assistant Copilot, along with other Microsoft 365 services. The company said the issues could impact users in any region.

Microsoft said on X that servers were unavailable and failing automatic health checks, putting pressure on those still operating. It said it was testing a configuration change to redistribute traffic that was elevated on parts of its infrastructure and restarting affected services to bring them back online.

“We’re working to safely return them to service,” the company said.

Microsoft did not state when it expected services to be fully restored.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US releases report on $12bn from Venezuelan oil, mineral resources
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Umar Farooq
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The United States Department of State has released a report detailing what it says the US has done with more than $12bn in revenue from Venezuelan oil and mineral resources, nearly a year after it abducted the country’s leader, Nicolas Maduro.

The disclosure is part of an effort to “promote transparency and accountability in the management of these funds”, says the 53-page report, released on Thursday.

In January, US forces conducted a raid on the Venezuelan capital of Caracas, capturing Maduro and his wife and bringing them to New York City, where they are currently facing charges related to drug trafficking and torture.

Venezuela’s then-vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, took over after Maduro’s abduction and has since made agreements with Washington that saw the US take a direct stake in profits earned from the export of oil and other mineral resources from the South American country.

Since removing Maduro from power, the Trump administration has sought to directly control who buys natural resources from Venezuela and who earns profits from those sales.

US President Donald Trump issued an executive order in January establishing special bank accounts that would hold revenue from those transactions, to be eventually distributed back to Venezuela in a controlled manner.

Trump has made Venezuela a central part of his political narrative, touting the revenue he said the US would receive from sales of the country’s oil during election campaigning in the run-up to the midterm elections that were held earlier this month. Venezuelan rights activists have expressed concern that Washington may give outsized importance to oil revenues and take little interest in backing democratic reforms after the removal of Maduro.

The report released on Thursday covers flows into and out of US-controlled accounts between January 3, 2026 and September 30, 2026. The State Department has also contracted private Washington, DC-based auditing firm KPMG to examine the transactions.

The US took in more than $12.26bn from “verified and approved entities engaging in authorized activities” in Venezuela during that time, according to the report. Most of that flow came from crude oil and petroleum-based revenue, but it also included deposits stemming from transactions involving gold, minerals, and fertilisers.

More than $12bn of that revenue has been disbursed as of September 30, with some $169m remaining in the account, according to the report.

The US initially set up an account in the Qatar National Bank in January to take in funds from entities looking to buy authorised oil and other minerals from Venezuela. Approximately $500m was initially deposited into that account, with almost all of it distributed back to Venezuelan entities by late January, when a separate, dedicated US Treasury-controlled account was set up to handle future transactions.

The current account, controlled directly by the US Department of the Treasury, has taken in more than $12bn in funds, from about 20 depositors, whose identities are redacted in the State Department’s report. Approximately 99 percent of those funds were related to the purchase of oil, according to the report.

By the end of September, the State Department report says, nearly all of those funds had been distributed to a set of Venezuelan banks, to be used in foreign exchange interventions, transactions where banks sell those dollars to reduce the amount of local currency floating around and prop up the currency’s value, in this case the Venezuelan bolivar.

The report is heavily redacted and does not provide details about the final recipients of the more than $12bn in funds that was distributed in Venezuela, although it does note that approximately $9.4bn went to “legal entities” and $2.9bn to “individuals”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Leaders from more than 40 European countries have gathered in Dublin for a summit dominated by the growing number of hybrid attacks across the continent.

The biannual European Political Community (EPC), a regional group established in 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, brought together heads of state and government officials on Thursday to discuss the region’s fragile security, amid a new United States-backed effort to revive talks between Russia and Ukraine to end the war.

The gathering comes after a series of hoaxes and cyberattacks that have recently targeted supermarkets, blood banks, passenger airlines, schools and media outlets in Europe.

Earlier on Thursday, more than 3,700 Italian schools received hoax bomb warnings, a day after 6,300 schools were affected by a similar widespread alert.

The Republic of Ireland’s Prime Minister Micheal Martin, known as the taoiseach, said those responsible for the attacks seek to “create confusion, sow division and weaken public confidence in our democratic systems”.

“We will not allow them to succeed. We will continue to use forums like this to share our experiences, learn from one another and to work together to protect our democracies,” he told reporters.

A major topic of conversation was Europe’s quest for an envoy to represent it in peace talks after calls from Washington and Kyiv. It remains unclear who will be named as European representative.

Earlier on Thursday, US envoy Steve Witkoff said Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to let European representatives join the next round of Ukraine discussions following a meeting in Moscow.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged his “complete support” to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and said he would push for European representation in the US-brokered talks.

Burnham co-chaired a group meeting on Ukraine with Zelenskyy at the summit.

The EPC comes at a moment of growing political tensions in Europe, and a week after the US midterm elections that saw extensive losses for US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.

While populist leaders have recently been ousted in Serbia and in Hungary, the far right is still on the rise in Europe and has made recent gains in regional elections in Germany. Voters will cast their ballots in the months ahead in the continent’s biggest countries, including Spain, France, Italy and Poland.

Meanwhile, two people were arrested during a protest organised by “Mothers Against Genocide” over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in Dublin’s city centre, while the EPC was ongoing.

Those taking part in demonstrations carried Palestine flags and Irish tricolours and banners, including one calling for a boycott of Israel.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Democrats gather in Denver to debate party’s future after US midterm wins
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
After winning control of the US Congress in the midterm elections, Democrats will descend on Denver on Thursday for a conference on the future of the party.

The two-day conference, titled What’s Next, presents itself as a forum to debate the direction of the party and will bring together potential presidential candidates for 2028, newly elected lawmakers, party strategists, and established Democratic leaders.

The gathering was planned in advance of the midterms by a new group called Majority Democrats, chaired by Massachusetts Representative Jake Auchincloss.

On its website, the moderate group presents itself as an alternative to “an old establishment” that “sells mediocrity disguised as moderation” and an activist left that “demands purity disguised as justice”.

The group says its members are “willing to challenge the establishment and break with their party when it means standing up for the people they actually represent.”

But some progressives question the organisers’ vision for the party, arguing it is not ambitious enough, including its backing of a public health insurance, which it calls “Medicare for Americans”, option over a Medicare for All system.

The conference comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and the Senate in January, facing decisions about how to use their majorities to challenge Trump in the final two years of his presidency, and begin to look ahead to 2028.

Among the attendees who have been announced are Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and New Jersey Senator Cory Booker, all seen as potential contenders for the Democratic presidential nomination in the next election.

They will be joined by newcomers who flipped seats in the midterms last week, including Texas Senator-elect James Talarico and Iowa Senator-elect Josh Turek.

Also attending are California Representative Ro Khanna, who has described himself as a “long-shot presidential candidate”, and Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, who has said he is “kicking the tires” on a possible 2028 run.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next House speaker, is also on the list of confirmed attendees, despite scepticism among some on the party’s left about the party’s current leadership. He will speak on Friday about the 120th Congress, which begins next year.

Khanna and Van Hollen will join New Jersey Senator Andy Kim for a discussion on “The Trust Deficit,” while Shapiro and Senators Elissa Slotkin and Ruben Gallego are scheduled to speak about the next era of the Democratic Party.

Missing from the published speakers are high-profile progressive figures like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders.
