https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.author: Rebecca Bellan
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.text:
The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.

Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models.

Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community.

Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion. Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source, whatever happens next.

Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development.

Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.

Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China.

The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections.

That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons.

Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.

Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls.

Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed.

Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.

As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.

More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs.

Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.

TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.

This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. Huang’s departure raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/huggin.title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/huggin.author: Sarah Perez
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/huggin.text:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025.

“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X.

The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance.

As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space.

After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October. While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models.

The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned.

Huang’s advocacy for open source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X. The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.”

Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated.

In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs.

Earlier this year, Huang promoted open source AI during his January keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, noting that open source models have “really revolutionized artificial intelligence.”

The company had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open sourceAI models in September for $12.9 billion. The deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/united.title: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights, citing cybersecurity risks
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/united.author: Zack Whittaker
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/united.text:
United Airlines said it will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf, citing a risk to cybersecurity and undermining federal regulations.

The airline is the latest American corporate giant to prevent customers from using AI agents and autonomous assistants to access their systems. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed.

United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.”

The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances.

“As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement. “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.”

The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/softba.title: SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI’s natural gas ambitions
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/softba.author: Tim De Chant
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/softba.text:
SoftBank might not be the first to invest in a hot trend, but when it does, it goes big.

Witness its $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025 or its announcement in February that its SB Energy subsidiary would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. If you can’t be first, be biggest, I guess.

That philosophy apparently spilled over into procurement, where orders were also supersized. Starting about two years ago, SoftBank reportedly put down deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed.

The decision to over-order undoubtedly helped secure turbines and speed up SoftBank’s projects.

“SB Energy did not have a choice except to overbook turbines in the future if they wanted some turbines right away,” Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva, told TechCrunch via email.

The energy world was caught off guard by the swiftness and magnitude of AI’s rising power demands. Queues for turbine orders now extend into the early 2030s. As natural gas was shaping up to be a go-to power source for the AI boom, CEO Masayoshi Son bet that by deploying his investment firm’s significant war chest, he could corner a portion of the market. If the AI world wanted power for its data centers, it would have to come to him.

Now that bet appears to have fizzled. SoftBank announced a $7.1 billion quarterly loss on Tuesday, with over half of that stemming from losses related to power-generating equipment. The investor had paid turbine manufacturers nonrefundable deposits to secure orders, and now it considered much of those worthless.

The move was also a costly bit of price discovery, Gardett said. Rather than overpay and potentially still be short of turbines, SoftBank overpaid and over-ordered.

“This charge is just that price discovery finally happening,” Gardett said.

The magnitude of that misplaced bet — over $3 billion — reflects some of the electricity mania that has overtaken the AI world. Faced with years-long waits to connect to the grid, many hyperscalers and developers have turned to natural gas as a sort of energy security blanket, something that is proven and familiar.

As AI data centers spend more time in operation, their operators are getting a better feel for what’s required to keep them operating. Natural gas might seem like a safe bet, but there are still risks, including winter curtailments when supplies dip and demand spikes, Brent Nelson, senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics, told the Equity podcast Wednesday.

In light of that, Nelson said the grid might still be their best bet. Most data centers would be best served by a grid connection, albeit a smaller one than they might normally request. To make up for the shortfall, large batteries are a cost-effective choice, Nelson said. They’d help shave peak loads or ride out requests from the utility to curtail electricity use.

Data center operators might be coming to that same conclusion, leading the natural gas market to develop more slowly than SoftBank expected.

SoftBank’s natural gas-related losses are unlikely to have a domino effect, leading to mass cancellations of gas power plants. AI’s power demand appears to be too large for that. For now, natural gas is riding high, though SoftBank may have found its ceiling.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/phota-.title: Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/phota-.author: Aisha Malik
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/phota-.text:
A new iOS app called Phota Labs gives users access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image.

Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos.

The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop.

The duo saw a gap in the editing tools on the market and believed that although editing tools can be powerful for enhancing photos, they aren’t very effective at fixing a photo that wasn’t captured well in the first place. Phota Labs changes that by focusing on fixing the shot itself while preserving the natural appearances of those in the image.

“Phota is your personal photo assistant that can make great photos for any moment you want to keep before you even ask, which means that it’s a very proactive experience,” Zhang told TechCrunch in an interview. “Think of it almost like a photographer or virtual photographer who looks over your camera roll and tries to understand what’s happening and how they could have taken that photo for you on the spot for that scene.”

The idea is to use AI to transform photos, whether that’s turning a wide-angle group photo into a tighter portrait or transforming a selfie into a regular shot.

Users can choose from different photography styles that determine how AI transforms their images, ranging from subtle edits that preserve the original lens and composition to more dramatic transformations that introduce effects like fish-eye lenses, alternative angles, and entirely different perspectives.

While some people turn to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools to enhance or edit images, these tools can often alter a person’s appearance, especially when working with blurry photos because they don’t know what that person actually looks like.

“For Phota, we built our own tech,” Zhang said. ”We built this personalization technology that actually learns about people’s identity and is able to preserve them in any transformation we do to a photo.”

Images edited with Phota Labs feature invisible watermarks that identify them as altered by AI when shared on social platforms.

The startup is initially targeting people who take tons of photos and like to share them on social media, but don’t want to deal with the tedious process of editing photos. Over time, the founders envision a broader audience, from retirees looking to create beautiful photos for their grandchildren to parents who want to share polished family albums with friends and relatives.

“We have this obsession with authenticity,” Xia said. “I think there’s so much value in connecting AI with real moments and making sure those photos are not perfect, in a sense. That’s why we spend a lot of research into understanding personal context, into building this identity model because we want to make sure the photos are authentic. They’re just better photos of the same moment, rather than saying, ‘Oh, this is an AI image’.”

Xia said beta users were excited to see better versions of moments they had actually lived and saw the results as photos of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders discovered that users were taking more photos because they knew Phota Labs could enhance them later.

“We’re turning something that’s unusable into something that people want to print,” Zhang said. “People who just love photos but never really got into editing can now experience professional quality that could never have been possible. So, I think that meant so much to us. There’s so many cherished moments for photos, and we really want them to be actually meaningful and something that you can remember.”

In terms of funding, the company raised a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year.

Phota Labs is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model. The startup also plans to launch an Android app in the future.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.author: Aisha Malik
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.text:
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said on Thursday, according to reports from Bloomberg and NBC News.

Huang, who stepped down as CEO following reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, agreed to testify Wednesday after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

Huang has agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, which falls later this month.

The development comes after House Republicans Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent Huang a letter on November 4 requesting that he appear before their committees. Moolenaar chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, Mast chairs the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Crawford chairs the House Intelligence Committee.

“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”

The testimony will take place behind closed doors, though Mast said he expects the briefing to be recorded on video and transcribed.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/five-w.title: Five ways Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia could damage the AI industry
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/five-w.author: Julie Bort
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/five-w.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s confession that he had an affair (and reports of another one with a direct report) that led the board to oust him on Thursday isn’t just your run-of-the-mill salacious billionaire CEO sex scandal.

In this case, one of his lovers is suspected by the U.S. government of being a spy for China. She’s also an executive of a Singapore-based neocloud that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

These affairs show undeniably poor judgment by Huang and, I’d argue, unchecked hubris on many levels. Such choices are not only a betrayal of his wife of 40 years, they’re also a liability for his company. Sleeping with any Nvidia partner is bad enough, but he also chose one in a tinderbox of a geopolitical situation. Even if Alice Huang’s company wasn’t suspected of helping Chinese firms evade chip restrictions (and he was somehow unaware of this), it was still exploiting a legal loophole by renting powerful AI infrastructure to Chinese companies.

It’s those potential national consequences that may land him in a hellscape of ongoing public humiliation. Republican committee chairs are already summoning him to testify in closed-door sessions about the security ramifications.

Will Democrats, who are set to take over key committees when the new Congress convenes in January, also haul him in to testify on the Hill? No one knows yet, but Huang has flaunted his close relationship with President Trump. Remember when Trump called him while he was onstage at the All-In Summit in September? Nvidia also donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom, a deeply unpopular project with American voters. Several Democratic lawmakers have already vowed to investigate the money behind it.

In other words, he is a billionaire close to Trump. He was — until Thursday — the face of AI and data centers (also a deeply unpopular political topic with voters), and he has publicly admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Even though he’s no longer CEO, that seems too juicy a target for Democrats to ignore.

Beyond whatever may be coming, Huang’s influence has been lost right when he was using it to push the tech industry in a number of directions. These areas have now lost their biggest champion.

Huang has been the biggest, loudest advocate for open-weight AI models in the tech industry and among government policymakers. Nvidia not only offers its own open-weight models, it also offers a lot of other open source tech for agents, AI security, and more. It has even agreed to acquire the biggest site that hosts them, Hugging Face, for $12.9 billion. (That deal is supposed to close in the first half of next year, pending regulatory approval.)

In July, when Anthropic and OpenAI were reportedly urging the Trump administration to ban Chinese open-weight models, Huang organized a letter of support for open-weight models generally (if not Chinese models specifically), signed by hundreds of tech companies.

Open-weight models give enterprises choice in the market and reduce costs. Without Huang, the next biggest advocate for them is perhaps Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, but he’s not out there organizing the industry to speak up.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed incident after incident this year as their AI agents hacked into others’ networks or performed other misdeeds. Huang loudly proclaimed the AI industry still didn’t need regulation and would deal with safety itself.

As the industry mulled over what they should do (auditors? a FINRA-like board?), Huang rallied the tech industry again. Nvidia got over 100 companies to sign on to his Open Agent Safety Platform, a largely open source effort to solve the epidemic of misbehaving AI agents.

Naturally, this effort hasn’t instantly solved the problem, and now the top spokesperson for self-regulation via technology solutions is out of his position of influence.

Huang has also been among the loudest voices insisting that AI is an engineered system that creates products, and so can be controlled like any other engineered system. This viewpoint counters the AI doomers and even the big AI labs themselves, which sometimes position their models as on the verge of consciousness (Anthropic) or as alien minds (OpenAI).

While Huang deals with the fallout of his actions, the loudest voice of this counter-narrative is, for the foreseeable future, silenced.

Huang also just convinced a long list of PC makers to buy into his long-time dream of providing CPUs (the main processor chips) for them. In this age, when most Americans have not experienced AI beyond a chatbot, he orchestrated a new line of high-end AI PCs geared for running agents locally.

These new PCs are due out this holiday season, and they may sell well for their intended targets: creators, developers, and others already savvy with agents. But now that Huang has become a meme for cheating on his wife with an alleged spy, he’s perhaps not the best choice to help market these devices as a cool alternative to the Mac mini.

Huang demolished his reputation right as bond underwriters (lenders) and bond buyers are pretty much over AI build-out-related debt. Of roughly $80 billion in data center bonds issued this year, nearly half were rated high-risk “junk,” Forbes reports.

Undeterred, Huang has been coming up with ways to continue financing the boom and keep his company’s revenues growing. Certainly, he’s authorized a mind-boggling number of so-called circular deals, where Nvidia buys stakes in companies to fund their expansion so they can buy chips. By some accounts, the company had committed to $750 billion in such deals as of July, Bloomberg reported. In August, Nvidia got even bolder, agreeing to backstop $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio, CNBC reported.

Huang also convinced a whole new set of financiers to pony up. In August, he announced that deep-pocketed PE firms Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR had committed up to $500 billion for data center build outs. He promised them that the data centers’ Nvidia GPUs could be used as collateral because Nvidia was guaranteeing the chips would retain value.

Huang sold a vision of Nvidia as “investable infrastructure” with a long resale cycle, like airplanes. Then he made the rounds with the financial press, as he often did, to pitch his vision. Now, however, Wall Street is concerned that Nvidia’s stock will crash and take their portfolios, and possibly the economy, with it.

Nvidia has lost its top salesperson and the AI industry has lost its top hype man. Even if Huang somehow comes back into the public eye to champion AI again, every interview and meeting will be about his sex life, choices, and national security — not his vision for the industry.

We’ll have to wait and see how Nvidia navigates the scandal Huang heaped onto it, but now that the company is finally in its post “founder mode” era, and hunting for a new CEO, it’s doubtful it has the cache to push the industry the way Huang was.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/five-w.summary: Jensen Huang's confession that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy led the board to oust him on Thursday. Huang has been the biggest, loudest advocate for open-weight AI models in the tech industry. Huang's affairs show undeniably poor judgment by Huang and, I’d argue, unchecked hubris on many levels.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/trump-.title: Trump floats Apple chairman Tim Cook as Jensen Huang’s successor
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/trump-.author: Sarah Perez
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/trump-.text:
In the wake of the industry-shaking news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump is floating the idea that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over the position.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote that “only one man” could take Huang’s place: Tim Cook of Apple.

“A Legend replaces a Legend!” he wrote.

Cook stepped down as Apple’s CEO on September 1, 2026, after 15 years running the company, but he’s still very much involved with Apple. While John Ternus took over as Apple’s CEO, Cook transitioned into the role of executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors, which sees him continuing to engage with global policymakers and manage international relationships, including Apple’s relations with China.

Trump is not the only one to suggest Cook as a replacement for Huang. Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, Senior Associate Dean for Leadership Studies at Yale School of Management, who studies CEO leadership and corporate governance, penned an op-ed in Time on Wednesday, suggesting Cook should be among the potential candidates. He wrote that Cook has “an unparalleled track record of succeeding a bigger-than-life founder,” in reference to Cook taking over from Apple founder Steve Jobs.

Whether or not Trump agrees with this opinion, or is simply blasting off an idea that hopped into his mind, is anyone’s guess.

“Tim Nvidia,” however, doesn’t quite have the same ring as “Tim Apple” does.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/whoop-.title: Whoop just launched a social network
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/whoop-.author: Connie Loizos
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/whoop-.text:
Whoop, the maker of screen-less fitness bands, is launching a social network on Thursday that lets its members follow friends and family and share their health data.

The network, called Whoop Humans, will be rolled out in the Whoop app to members at every membership tier at no extra cost. Members can follow anyone on Whoop and choose what to share, from sleep and recovery to workouts and achievements. Followers can react and comment; members can also attach photos and commentary to their data. It’s all opt-in, CEO Will Ahmed tells us.

Whoop already has a social feature, Teams, which a little more than half its customers use, according to the company. But Teams is built around groups and leaderboards, and everyone in a group sees everyone else’s information. Humans is meant to be more intimate. Members decide who follows them and who sees what, so a trainer can track a set of clients without the clients seeing one another’s data, for example.

I found myself questioning how much a spouse wants to know about the other’s sleep score when Ahmed mentioned this particular scenario, so I asked him how else beta members used these newer social features. He said the company learned that people were more engaged when someone reported a low recovery score than a nearly perfect one, suggesting that the new feature may be particularly helpful for understanding when someone is struggling and might need attention.

Indeed, the bigger story here is where Whoop continues to be headed, which is into medical wellness. Like its most direct rival, Oura, the company is pushing faster and more aggressively into the wellness opportunity that an aging population presents.

Whoop had already added FDA-cleared ECG and atrial fibrillation detection, blood pressure insights, blood testing, and medical-record uploads. Asked if older customers are gravitating to Whoop, Ahmed said, without offering specifics, that Whoop has seen “huge growth” among people over 60 over the past 18 months. He also said his was among the first companies accepted into a Medicare program that reimburses qualifying wearables that can show they improve health outcomes, and that it now has Medicare members.

He added that he expects families to be big users of Humans. (You can imagine adult children checking in on aging parents.)

But the company’s efforts to be thought of as the “brand for personal health” raises questions, naturally, about privacy. Ahmed said members choose which metrics to share, can remove followers, and can switch on “stealth mode” to go dark for a few days without changing their settings. Activities marked sensitive aren’t shared by default, and Ahmed said health alerts and medical information aren’t shared at all. Members can also report any comment or photo that they deem disturbing, and the company said reported content is reviewed.

As for minors, Whoop’s minimum age is 13 for all members (higher in some countries), meaning customers of that age can share their data subject to consents and privacy settings. Asked whether a parent could follow a teenager’s data, he didn’t answer directly and pointed to the privacy controls.

Ahmed also said Whoop doesn’t sell member data. “Our product is not you; it’s the membership,” he said, adding that the company doesn’t license data to third parties.

He was candid about dealmaking. Asked about Oura’s announcement this week that it will pay $625 million for Counsel Health, a service offering on-demand physicians, Ahmed said he expects “more consolidation” among AI-focused, clinician-focused, and wearable companies, and that Whoop is always on the prowl. Its deep relationship with members, he said, puts it “in a position to be an acquirer.”

He was more guarded about the company’s own finances, declining to share revenue or say whether Whoop is profitable. He did say that the company now has about 1,200 employees, membership on its software platform has increased more than 70% a year for three years running, and that it expects to have nearly 4 million members by year-end.

As for an IPO (the company raised a very big round earlier this year), he said only that Whoop “will certainly IPO in the future.” He also wouldn’t comment on Oura, which shelved its own IPO of up to $2.2 billion in September citing market uncertainty.

In the meantime, Whoop is widening its reach. The company announced that its devices will be sold through Ulta stores beginning next March (around 500 locations of the beauty retailer to start, and a target to retail in more than a thousand stores eventually). Indeed, Ahmed said Whoop’s female audience has more than doubled from last year.

As for competition, in addition to Google’s new Fitbit Air band, Whoop may soon have to contend with Apple, which is reportedly developing a Whoop-style band. But Ahmed mostly shrugged off those concerns, suggesting that building a product doesn’t guarantee success. Instead, he said, Whoop’s job is to stay true to the “aspiring” people it serves.

The company is pushing faster and more aggressively into the wellness opportunity that an aging population presents.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.title: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia — who is Colette Kress, his interim replacement?
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.author: Amanda Silberling
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen.text:
The Nvidia Board of Directors announced on Thursday morning that the company’s co-founder and CEO of 33 years, Jensen Huang, has resigned as president, CEO, and member of the board, effective immediately.

This is a shocking twist for one of the most valuable companies in the world, which designs the chips that make the AI boom possible. Few people would have predicted this turn of events even just a week ago, as Huang has been so central to Nvidia throughout the company’s existence that he never even established a succession plan. But Huang has now been ousted after reports that he had affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and one of his direct reports at Nvidia.

While the company conducts a more thorough search for Huang’s successor, Nvidia CFO and Executive Vice President Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO. But beyond her name and job title, what do we know about the person who will now lead a company worth about $3.8 trillion?

According to Nvidia’s website, Kress has worked at the company since September 2013. Before that, she spent three years as an SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology Operations Finance organization. She also worked at Microsoft for 13 years, where she spent four years as CFO of the Server and Tools division. She holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University.

The California-based 59-year-old has a very limited social media presence — on Linkedin, she has commented some well wishes on former colleagues’ posts about their retirement. But as CFO, she’s been a regular presence on Nvidia’s earnings calls, making her a familiar figure for analysts covering the company.

According to Forbes’ list of America’s Richest Self-Made Women, Kress’ net worth is estimated to be about $1.2 billion. Her Forbes profile adds that she initially joined Nvidia in part because her two sons endorsed the company for its role in the video game industry, which it was best known for at the time.

“Nvidias strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said in a statement. “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

Nvidia is slated to report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, when we will likely hear more from Kress about her plans for the company’s immediate future.

Huang has been so central to Nvidia throughout the company's existence that he never even established a succession plan. Nvidia CFO and Executive Vice President Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/norwes.title: Norwest pushes deeper into AI with new $4B fund
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/norwes.author: Kirsten Korosec
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/norwes.text:
Norwest, a firm backed solely by Wells Fargo, has raised a $4 billion fund as it sets out to invest more in AI. This is the eighteenth fund for the 65-year-old multi-stage investment firm, and its largest to date.

The fund will be invested across various sectors and multiple countries, notably the United States, India, and Israel. But the big story here is AI, and Norwest’s plans to expand its investment in this area.

Norwest said Thursday it aims to capitalize on AI startups developing products and services across core industries such as consumer, healthcare, and technology. The investment firm, which has backed Plaid, Spotify, Uber, and Vuori, said it will continue to expand its investments in physical AI, voice AI, agentic cybersecurity, and aerospace.

If that sounds like a broad approach, it is intended to be, Jeff Crowe, a senior managing partner at Norwest, told TechCrunch.

“We’re taking a broad approach to AI because its impact is broad,” Crowe added, as AI is not limited by industry, geography, or application. “Just as digital transformation did, AI transformation has the potential to touch most layers of enterprise, consumer, and healthcare solutions: networking, enterprise IT and applications. Adapting to an agentic environment means applying AI broadly across products and services that solve problems.”

Crowe added that the firm is particularly excited about early-stage companies building AI-native application and infrastructure, physical AI, domain-specific models, and cybersecurity solutions.

Some of the firm’s recent investments reflect this strategy. For instance, the firm invested in Coval, which builds tools to test and evaluate AI agents, and Generalist AI, a startup that has developed AI foundation models for robots.

Since the launch of its seventeenth fund, a $3 billion raise that closed in 2024, the firm has made more than 87 investments.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/cybera.title: Cyberattack on Fireworks AI allowed hackers to access Notion customers’ chat transcripts
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/cybera.author: Zack Whittaker
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/cybera.text:
A cyberattack at Fireworks AI has exposed some of its customers’ data, the company has confirmed. Fireworks AI, a platform that developers use to access and use open AI models, said an attacker breached its cloud provider to gain access to a Fireworks development system, which allowed access to some of its customers’ data.

The company said in its latest security advisory that the cybercriminals took Fireworks’ customers’ billing information and some datasets. Fireworks touts tens of thousands of customers worldwide using its platform, including legal tech company Harvey and AI company Cursor.

At least one confirmed affected customer is online document editor and notetaker Notion, which said in a disclosure that the breach affected around 1% of its own customers.

Notion said that Fireworks alerted the company to a security incident and later confirmed that the hackers had stolen some Notion customer data. On November 3, Notion said it disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleted the data stored in its systems, and stopped all connectivity between the two.

Notion confirmed this week that the hackers took chat transcripts of its Notion AI customers who used the “Insights” feature. The company said that the transcripts include “any input to or output from the model that was written to the chat,” but added that much of the data was unattributable and could not be determined from which customer it was obtained.

The breach at Fireworks AI shows how tech companies are reliant on other tech providers for their own offerings, and how cyberattacks can, as a result, spill over into other customers.

Fireworks said that it believes the hackers are financially motivated and that their goals are focused on selling tokens from breaching access to large language models, or LLMs. These schemes rely on selling to unauthorized third parties, who can burn through AI model usage without using their own resources.

This is the second breach affecting Fireworks in as many months, following a security incident in October.

Microsoft 365 issues have been cutting people off from their email since early Thursday afternoon, and they still aren’t fixed.

Since just before 1PM ET on Thursday, reports have come in from around the world that people can’t access their Outlook email, either through the web or apps. Microsoft quickly acknowledged the issue from its Microsoft 365 Status account, saying that “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.”

There were also some reports of problems with Teams, but not to the same extent, while Microsoft’s official updates said customers may experience issues across its suite of 365 business services. Microsoft comms director Ben Hope said in a statement that “We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online. We appreciate our customers’ patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.”

Several hours later, Microsoft has gone through several variations of update notes regarding the issues and its attempts to fix them, saying it’s had problems rebooting servers and being able to monitor their health. As of about 6PM ET, Microsoft has a note saying it’s managed to get some of the affected servers running:

We’ve begun returning a portion of the affected servers to service, and they’re remaining stable so far. We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions.

We’ve streamlined our recovery process to expedite returning the remaining affected servers to service. To further support recovery, we’re implementing protective traffic management measures in a specific location to reduce load on the affected infrastructure, and we’ll expand these measures to additional locations if we observe positive results. As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect to the service.

There’s still no ETA for full restoration, but we will continue to monitor this ongoing outage.

Update, 6:23PM ET: Added latest status update from Microsoft.

This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. We’ll be taking a break next week and will be back on November 25th. Opt in for Optimizer here.

The SS Jeremiah O’Brien is a World War II Liberty ship. The hulking vessel was built in 56 days. It made 11 trips to Normandy, France, to supply the Allied powers in the fight against German U-boats. Last week, it was the site of a black-tie peptide party thrown by a trio of Gen Z venture capitalists.

Roughly 150 people attended the event, where four types of peptide samples were provided to guests — no injections. One was a topical cream with GHK-Cu, while the other three were dissolvable sublingual strips from peptide startup Afterglow. GHK-Cu is a popular skincare ingredient, but it’s unclear how well sublingual peptide strips work. The topic of the night wasn’t just the state of peptides. The venue was a deliberate reference to American industrial prowess — and why the pharmaceutical supply chain ought to be centered in the United States.

The timing couldn’t have been more pointed.

Sourcing is one of the biggest question marks with gray-market peptides — something the US Department of Health and Human Services is trying to address with its recent interim policy decision allowing certain unapproved peptides for compounding.

The decision is a controversial one. FDA career scientists haven’t endorsed it, though to the average person it might seem like they have.

https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.title: No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Robert Hart
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.text:
Scientists are getting tired of amateurs parachuting into their fields and making ‘discoveries’ with AI.

Scientists are getting tired of amateurs parachuting into their fields and making ‘discoveries’ with AI.

Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discovered and was published in an academic journal last year. The incident, which sparked criticism among archeologists online, underscores a growing tension in science as amateurs wielding increasingly powerful AI tools parachute into specialist fields, often without the expertise needed to understand what they are looking at.

Local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.

Miotti said the idea to use AI to search for archeological sites came to him while traveling in Peru, when he began wondering what historic explorers might do with access to modern technology. He settled on lidar, a laser-based mapping technology that can produce detailed three-dimensional images of the environment, and set a team of 48 AI agents to comb through NASA lidar data for signs of undocumented sites. As “Peru isn’t well covered” by public lidar data, Miotti wrote, he shifted his focus to the Maya region.

The agents flagged numerous promising locations, including “one major village [that] doesn’t seem to have been registered” in existing records. Miotti, who described the research to The Verge as a personal side project done without any Google compute or resources, said he then reached out to Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to check whether the apparent discovery was already known, including through unpublished research. Using the agents to translate his correspondence into Spanish, Miotti said INAH told him it had no record of a registered site at that location.

“It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government.

A second affair has hit the news cycle, but that’s not what matters here.

Iwas certain, until the story of Jensen Huang’s second affair hit, that Huang was bulletproof. After all, why wouldn’t he be? He’s placed himself indispensably at the center of the AI industry and famously had no succession plan at Nvidia. In fact, he’s the only CEO Nvidia has ever had. L’état c’est moi.

Then two stories were published nearly back to back on Wednesday: one alleging Huang had an affair with his subordinate Kimberly Powell, another that the board was meeting to consider his ouster. First thing Thursday morning, Nvidia announced Huang had resigned. One of the most powerful men in Silicon Valley was out.

Why throw Huang under the bus for getting his nuts drained?

Fascinating. First of all, when I asked on Monday “Who else is Jensen Huang fucking?” I did not expect to get answers this fast — somebody, potentially somebody on the board (as we’ve seen in other incidents), wanted the story out there. Second, why throw Huang under the bus for getting his nuts drained? This is not an industry that cares about that kind of thing — just ask Eric Schmidt and Bill Gates. My guess is that the second affair is a pretext for action, and this all goes back to the original story from last week: that Huang was honeypotted by an alleged Chinese spy. Whatever was going on with neocloud Megaspeed might be much, much worse than we know, and what we know is pretty bad: business listings that led to “a Malaysian data center and shopping mall, a near-empty office in Singapore and a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur.”

IF YOU’RE HOPING to cut your cell phone bill by switching providers and maybe get a new device as a carrot, check out Mint Mobile right now. The popular budget carrier is offering a limited-time $500 discount on several new Android phones, including the Google Pixel 11 series and Samsung S26 series. To get the deal, you will need to sign up for a 12-month unlimited plan for $180, which breaks down to $15 a month (Mint requires full payment upfront, plus taxes and fees). Another catch? You have to be a new customer. Phones are only getting more expensive, so discounts like this are worth exploring.

Unfortunately, the list of phones is limited and doesn’t include Apple’s iPhones. On the bright side, the phones aren’t low-quality; in fact, many are on our recommended lists. The unlimited plan also throttles down speeds after 50 GB per month, but includes 20 GB for hotspot connections. Mint will offer an additional credit of $400 or more when you trade in an eligible unlocked phone (iPhone 16 or higher, Galaxy S25 or higher, Z Flip7 or Fold7 or higher, or Pixel 10 or higher).

Mint rarely offers deals or coupons because its plans are priced lower than traditional carriers, and you would have to pay full price for a new phone; while you’ll still have to shell out to cover the balance for the device, it is still more economical than the phone deals offered by the big carriers.

For more savings, check out the best Early Black Friday deals we are following.

The Google Pixel 11 is down to $399 (regularly $899) when you bundle it with the 12-month Mint unlimited plan, for a total of $579 (excluding taxes and fees). This makes the base model in the Pixel 11 series cheaper than the entry-level Pixel 10a.

Mint is also discounting the 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL to $594 and $794, respectively (normally $1,099 and $1,299). All three Pixel 11 models are our pick for the smartest Android phones, combining great hardware, software, and Google’s Gemini AI. The Pixel 10a is our favorite Android phone overall, but unfortunately, Mint doesn’t offer it; otherwise, it could have been as low as $100!

AMAZON (S26+, 512 GB)

Samsung fans will love that the flagship Galaxy S26 series (WIRED’s recommendation for the best flagship Android phones) is on Mint’s discounted phones list, as is the Z Fold8, the best folding phone. Mint is offering the S26 for $500 (regularly $1,000), S26+ for $700 (regularly $1,200), and S26 Ultra for $900 (regularly $1,400). A sub-$1,000 price for the Ultra flagship is a great deal, even when you add the one year of unlimited service for $180.

The Ultra is chock-full of features, including a built-in privacy screen that sounds gimmicky, but is surprisingly effective. With the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor, the S26-series phones are powerful devices. Samsung continues to improve on the camera systems, making them some of the best in the industry. We just wish Samsung would support the Qi2 magnetic system natively for wireless charging (they are Qi2-ready when you use a compatible case).

If you’ve been eyeing a foldable phone, Mint has the Z Fold8 for $1,700. This isn’t a big discount from the $1,900 regular price, but foldables aren’t cheap in general. On the Android side, this is our favorite foldable model, and it’s lightweight despite its large unfolded screen. It also offers great performance and battery life, but one downside is that it lacks a telephoto lens.

Motorola has its share of fans. If you’re one of them, Mint is discounting the Razr (our pick for the best cheap folding phone) and Moto G Play (an honorable mention in our best Motorola phones guide).

Mint is offering the Razr for $520, a savings of $180. Now, that’s not a deep cut, but it is one of the more affordable foldable phones to begin with; this deal makes it even more so. Despite the budget price, we found it capable, even if the performance and battery life aren’t as strong as the Razr Ultra’s.

If you don’t care about brand or performance and just want the best phone you can buy at the lowest price, check out the Moto G Play. Mint has it for $80 (normally $250). While it isn’t one of our top picks, it’s a capable phone for casual users. And at this price, it’s worth considering.

YOU SHOULD NEVER buy a TV at full price. This is a hill I will die on, and I am proven right every year when I see 20-, 30-, and even 50-percent-off deals on some of the best TVs. It may be weeks away, but I'm already seeing some great Black Friday deals, especially on TVs.

This is the lowest price I've ever seen for the 65-inch LG C6, a fantastic deal on an excellent OLED TV. LG's C-Series TVs are consistently among our favorites due to their high brightness, uniform blacks, and vivid, natural colors. Add in their ample connectivity, which makes them versatile enough for gamers, and it's clear why this is a top OLED pick.

The premium 2026 Samsung S95H OLED TV is now at its lowest price yet. WIRED reviewer John Brandon praised the TV for its accurate color and deep blacks. New to the latest S95H model is a silver bezel that’s recessed behind the main OLED panel, making the TV look like a metal picture frame.

I understand wanting a nice OLED TV but not wanting to pay premium OLED prices. That's where budget OLEDs like the LG B6 shine—especially when steeply discounted. The 48-inch version, in particular, is 50 percent off at Best Buy right now, which is such a good deal, I thought it was a typo. (I won’t be surprised if the price mysteriously goes up.) Brandon praised the TV's thin size, simple setup, and deep and rich blacks.

Spoiler for our upcoming review: This is one of the best midrange TVs available. It's a fantastic option that will satisfy most people, and at its current 40-percent-off price, it'll also satisfy most budgets. Reviewer Rick Broida was seriously impressed by its bright and vibrant color display, which has a distinct pop that’s a joy to behold.

This isn’t a huge discount, and I wouldn’t be surprised if the price went down closer to Black Friday. Even so, the TCL QM6K is one of the best TVs for most people, according to former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata, because of its well-rounded picture and reasonable price (even when not on sale).

Again, this isn’t the biggest discount I’ve seen for this TV, but 33 percent off is nothing to sneeze at for an already-good-value television. In his U7SG review, Waniata called this a near-premium model with a new-and-improved stand and an anti-reflective matte screen reminiscent of high-end Samsung models.

The LG Micro RGB Evo takes the top spot in our guide to the best RGB TVs, and this is the lowest price I've ever seen it. Reviewer John Brandon thought movies and shows looked stunning and vivid on its screen, with highly customizable picture settings that put it in a league of its own. Keep in mind that it only comes in 75-, 86-, and 100-inch sizes.

The best art TV is Samsung's Frame Pro (2026) thanks to its excellent image quality, contrast, color depth, and anti-glare technology that far outshines the competition, says Brandon. This discount isn't as low as its Prime Day price (yet), but 50 percent off is still great and makes this budget-friendly art TV even more appealing—especially for secondary rooms. It's not as bright as Samsung's art TVs, but it does come with a far broader free art library, no subscription required.

This is the best home theater projector we've tested, and it's at its lowest price to date. Yes, even at 25 percent off, this projector costs a pretty penny, but its dynamic, self-adjusting iris (which automatically increases or reduces light) puts it well above similar competitors. That, plus its outstanding brightness and contrast, means the picture quality is stellar even in broad daylight.

https://www.wired.com/story/uncanny-vall.title: Jensen Huang Is Out. Will Nvidia’s Rivals Cash In?
https://www.wired.com/story/uncanny-vall.author: Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, Leah Feiger
https://www.wired.com/story/uncanny-vall.text:
NVIDIA COFOUNDER JENSEN Huang officially resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. He also faces reports of at least two more alleged affairs with Nvidia employees. In this bonus episode, Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger break down how Nvidia’s board turned on its founder, what interim CEO Colette Kress means for the company, and how this moment could be a golden opportunity for Nvidia’s competitors.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at uncannyvalley@wired.com.

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Brian Barrett: We're bringing you an extra episode this week because Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang has officially resigned. His resignation caps a swift, stunning fall for the man who spent more than three decades building a company into the engine of the AI boom. We're going to talk about how a board known for deferring to its celebrity CEO finally changed its tune and who's going to be running Nvidia at least for now. Let's get started. Just for the room, we released a podcast this morning before this happened and then it happened. So now we're talking again.

Leah Feiger: I mean, who doesn't want multiple offerings from the Uncanny Valley crew, Brian?

Brian Barrett: It's true. Constant updates. We're going to do an hourly podcast from now on, just iterative, getting real in the weeds. No, how surprised is everybody that this happened? And I guess first, if you want some setup about what happened, you can listen to our previous episode, but I guess I'll first say really quickly, Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who was selling a lot of chips to, and then a report came out that he had another affair allegedly with someone who reported directly to him at Nvidia, and that feels like the final straw. So we're caught up. Are we surprised still?

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, the first thing to say is the company does have rules on the books saying that you're not supposed to have a relationship with a direct report. And so when we talked and it was the Chinese spy, although that is the obviously more scandalous thing that has happened, it also really felt to me like Jensen was going to weather that storm. But then when the second affair came out, that felt like it gave the board a really good excuse if they needed one to say, "OK, we have to stop." And I think it's fair to say here that while there is no current reporting on additional affairs, I think the concern is if two have already come out, what if more continued to become public and they need to stop the bleeding?

Leah Feiger: But he still fought pretty hard to retain his role, right?

Zoë Schiffer: I don't think the board wanted him to resign. I don't think Jensen wanted to resign. I think that their backs were completely against the wall on this one. The company has already been through an incredibly embarrassing scandal that will drag out for the next many months as Jensen is dragged before the Senate and has to answer to people who have serious concerns about his advocacy for China and where the Nvidia chips have been going and all of that. Now there's a second affair again with a direct report and I think that the situation became very, very quickly untenable for everyone involved.

Leah Feiger: Absolutely. And now Nvidia has a new CEO in the name of CFO Colette Kress. Tell me about her.

Brian Barrett: Interim. So yeah, she'll be there for the time being, but she's been at Nvidia for a long time. She's been there since 2013, which means that she's worked closely with Jensen since before the company was the darling of the AI world back when it was a graphics processor for gaming laptops company. She was at Cisco and Microsoft before that. She's a real industry veteran. I think my understanding is she's really a classic CFO. I don't know if she's a long-term visionary leader of this company, but she knows Nvidia inside and out. And I think if you're looking for stability and you're looking for someone who's not going to create new drama and who's not going to have a scandal, that seems like she really fits that bill.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I think what they need right now is stability, like you said. They need someone to take the reins. They don't want anything else dramatic to happen to the company. And of course they're going to immediately kick off a search for a new visionary leader, which as we said in the last episode, there's not an obvious successor here. They've got to find someone who has incredible technical prowess, who has a real vision for where the AI industry is going and who will be able to learn Nvidia's business. I think it's doubtful that person ... Well, actually, I really should have learned from this experience that I shouldn't have hot takes. I was going to say, I don't think the person's going to come from—

Brian Barrett: No, keep doing it.

Zoë Schiffer: ... Nvidia internally, but what do we know at this point? It could be anything. So yeah, Colette will take the reins for the moment and the company needs to weather this storm and come out the other side.

Brian Barrett: And I think she does, as you might have guessed, she's going to be operating the business the way Jensen had, at least in terms of advocating for closer collaboration with China and the business lines that Nvidia has been going down, leaning more into CPUs recently, open source. I don't think you're going to expect anything other than business as usual. And when you have her in there, as we talked before, China is so important to Nvidia's future. Jensen Huang had lost all credibility on that point. So having someone in there who can make the case that, hey, we should have a better relationship with China, we should be able to sell more to China, who is not compromised in the way that Jensen has been, that's an upside. I mean, it's a lot of downside for Nvidia that Jensen's gone, but at least they can come into these conversations without that baggage. I think that's the main point here.

Leah Feiger: And perhaps even right the ship even slightly. I mean, with news of Jensen's departure, Nvidia's stock plunged, absolutely plunged, but one of Kress's big roles as CFO was communicating with Wall Street. So I'm assuming that there's a world where this could be slightly reassuring to investors perhaps.

Brian Barrett: I think so. The thing about the market, I guess, is that everything's always baked in. The market has already accounted for so much. So it did take a big plunge. I think as we're recording this, it had been stabilizing a little bit. I shouldn't say that because by the time this is out, it's going to go wildly in one direction or another.

Leah Feiger: It means it's a time for another emergency pod. We're just going to keep this going all day.

Brian Barrett: We're going to have to do another emergency pod. Exactly. All day. Get ready, folks.

Zoë Schiffer: We have been talking a lot though about how interconnected, not just the AI industry is, but the entire US economy, how tied up it is with just a few companies. And Nvidia really is, it's kind of Nvidia and Anthropic that so much of this is riding on. And so I think we have yet to see what the ramifications of this will be if Nvidia is able, like we said, to weather the storm, continue growing and leading the AI boom. It has been, perhaps it won't be dire, but so much of what has happened already has been completely unexpected for everyone involved so that I think there's a lot of uncertainty and instability that we still have yet to account for.

Leah Feiger: So from the politics side, I can see this very much impacting the White House's relationship with AI-related firms. I can just see this becoming a thing and we're going to continue reporting this out, but WIRED is keeping a very close eye on what this means for these relationships. Talk to me from the Silicon Valley side, what is going to get impacted here? Is it crazy to say that Anthropic's IPO could get tossed up in the storm? What are we really looking at?

Brian Barrett: No, so here's my thing. I'm not sure about the Anthropic IPO. I think, again, everything's priced in and I think they're going to do just fine. It'll still be worth whether it's $1.2 trillion or $1.4 trillion, whatever. It's going to be a huge IPO, one of the biggest history regardless of this. What I'm interested in is right now, people don't have many alternatives. Even if you wanted to separate yourself from Nvidia because of this scandal for some reason, you're not going to find something better out there for the most part. Some other companies have had some gains lately. So in the short term, I don't know. I don't think that this maybe changes that much. This will be one of the takes, much like Zoë writes her takes, I'm going to regret saying this. I think short term it doesn't do that much. I think longer term though, we've already seen a lot of companies investing in making their own silicon and making their own chips and finding ways to optimize their own sort of hardware stack against their software. I think of it the way that after everyone saw Apple making its own processors and having huge efficiency gains on the iPhone, companies started doing that within smartphone world. Everyone has their own sort of processor in the smartphone world. I think that's happening increasingly in the AI world, and I think that's long-term a threat, not to the industry, but to Nvidia itself. It comes at a time when other companies are really trying to find a path to do this without relying so much on Nvidia, and this is only going to accelerate that process.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I mean, but that was true regardless. This isn't a software moment. I think when Elon Musk took over X and suddenly people were fleeing the platform, you saw Meta kind of seize its moment and launch Threads in a few short months. You can't really do that with GPUs. Other companies have been trying to compete with Nvidia for years, and that competition has only heated up as the AI industry has become more and more powerful and there's more and more money to be had. But this is some of the most complex technology on the planet, and so you cannot just see an opportunity and turn it around really, really fast. It takes years of research and manufacturing. And so I think there already was this opportunity for other companies to come in and try and grab some of Nvidia's market share, and I'm sure they will try and capitalize on the moment, but it's not going to be as easy as other examples we've seen in recent history.

Brian Barrett: Oh, for sure. But I think it's more like if you're OpenAI and you're like, "I've been dabbling with making my own chips." I think then you go from dabbling to saying, "Oh, maybe there's more urgency here and I need to put more behind that." So I agree with you 100 percent. I just think it maybe accelerates and changes the way some people are thinking about how they go forward.

Leah Feiger: Yeah. And the people that are already doing it, I mean, is Lisa Su from AMD doing a victory lap right now? I assume that she's ordered balloons.

Zoë Schiffer: Isn't Jensen her cousin or something?

Brian Barrett: That's correct.

Zoë Schiffer: It's family drama.

Brian Barrett: Family drama.

Leah Feiger: That makes it even better.

Brian Barrett: Great Thanksgiving coming up.

Leah Feiger: Has this happened before, you guys? I mean, I know that CEOs have stepped down over in some ways less. The spy of it all makes it extra fun here. Have we built the entire US economy around the very horny behavior of a very powerful man?

Brian Barrett: I don't know if we built it around ... Yes? We've built it. I would say—

Leah Feiger: I'm asking the questions our listeners want to know.

Brian Barrett: I would tweak the sentence, we've built the economy around the behavior of a horny man, not around the horny behavior of a man. Does that make sense?

Zoë Schiffer: Wow, absolutely.

Brian Barrett: Just trying to diagram that.

Leah Feiger: All right. Good editing. Good editing.

Brian Barrett: I'm just trying to diagram that sentence a little bit out. I want to hear what Zoë has to say about this too. I think we talked about this a little bit yesterday where yes, so much of the economy relies on too few companies right now, Nvidia being the main sort of bulwark there, but also so interesting, I think we wouldn't have seen this at other companies in that other tech companies are set up where their CEOs are untouchable and Jensen is not. So Jensen owns 3.5 percent or so of Nvidia. The board can do this. If Mark Zuckerberg could do anything short of getting arrested and still be in charge of Meta, there's just no recourse. Elon will be in charge of his companies for as long as he wants. So I think there's the fact that there was even an opportunity for accountability here is in and of itself interesting in a way that's sad. You know what I mean? There should be accountability everywhere, but that's not how these companies are set up.

Leah Feiger: And perhaps that's why it's so shocking. We never get to see accountability in this manner and speed.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I feel like there are examples of really unexpected departures or departures that were expected, but still came as a real shock. Even Steve Jobs, which it was known that he was very ill for a long time, but he was so synonymous with Apple and Apple's success before his death, and yet he had this really solid bench of potential executives who could come in and take his place, maybe not completely, maybe not with the total vision, but Apple would and did continue to grow. I think the moment that I think of more right now is Sam Altman's very brief and dramatic ouster from OpenAI, because that one like this, no one really saw coming. It was such a shock. It was so unexpected. There were a lot of questions as to why, but of course that took place over the course of essentially a single weekend where the board pushed him out. There were all of these background negotiations, and then ultimately he was able to come back and resume his role as CEO.

Leah Feiger: How long did that take? How long did righting that ship take? Are the stakes similar or different here?

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my gosh. Is OpenAI's ship righted? I think is the ...

Brian Barrett: That's a great question.

Zoë Schiffer: Sam Altman was able to come back. Obviously, he was able to remake the board with friendlier people, but I think that Anthropic has really continued to be pretty ascendant and pretty focused in the wake of that, what employees call the blip when Sam Altman left. Whereas OpenAI, it felt like has continued to spin out, have drama after drama and be a little less focused in comparison. I think Nvidia overall is a much more disciplined company. It's not like the AI labs. It has a typical corporate structure. It has very defined goals. It's been around for a lot longer. And so I think these are different and very significant ways.

Brian Barrett: Although Zoë, what they didn't have was a succession plan, right? I think Jensen pointedly, as of he did interviews within the last few weeks or month where he was like, "I'm going to be here for decades. I don't really need to have ... " Well, sort of proudly not worried about a succession plan and a structure that's so flat. We've talked about this before too, but he had 60 direct reports all up to him. So I think it is a little irresponsible maybe. Here we go. I think he probably had a fiduciary responsibility to shareholders to think a little bit harder about what happens if I'm not here. I think that there is sort of this sense of, "I'm the only person who can do this. I'll be here forever." And I see how that you'd need to have that attitude to be the CEO of the biggest company in the world or one of the biggest companies in the world. But the backside of that is we're going to find out if that's true really soon.

Zoë Schiffer: No, for sure. I mean, I think he's been leading this company for 30 years, and it seems like while we are not sure what the board knew when, certainly within Nvidia, there were whispers about these things happening. And like we talked about in the last episode, Jensen had an affair with a woman, a former TV journalist who was running basically a smuggling operation that by all accounts he should have known about.

Brian Barrett: Allegedly.

Zoë Schiffer: He should have known exactly what was going on there. And so I think if you have enough hubris that you can make those decisions and still feel completely untouchable, then it makes sense in that kind of twisted logic that you would also think like I don't need a successor because I'm untouchable. And in fact, that has proved to not be the case.

Brian Barrett: One thing we've been seeing in the lead up to this was Silicon Valley really vocally defending Jensen Huang and saying, "It's one mistake, it's no big deal." And then saying, "It's two mistakes. What's the problem?" And even this morning after the news happened, we're still seeing people say he's an irreplaceable icon. It's sort of like they're trying to take you have to separate the artist from the art kind of argument, but for CEOs, does that surprise anybody that they're still hanging onto this? And I guess I know how I feel. Is that a fair argument? Can you separate the artist from the art in a Silicon Valley big tech CEO context? Does that make any sense whatsoever?

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, this is an area that Silicon Valley is very sensitive about. It's such a founder oriented environment here, and I think that Jensen is the founder of this business. He built this company from the ground up. He started it at a Denny's 30 years ago. So yeah, I think there is a lot of loyalty, not just to him, but to the idea that a founder is a unique type of person and that they bring something to the table that no one else can replace. I had conversations with people that really made me laugh where they would say, "Well, Jensen's irreplaceable and his biggest mistake was admitting the affair in writing." I was like, "Well, I do feel like the biggest mistake was having a relationship with the Chinese spy perhaps, but yeah, I hear you."

Leah Feiger: I also wonder how much this is, I don't know, even slightly a little bit of lip service. On the DC side, Trump has been voraciously defending Jensen, and yet we also know that there's machinations behind the scenes to figure out some sort of accountability measure in some kind, whether that's congressional hearings or other things that could be coming down the pipeline. Two things can be true at once. It's like what Brian said earlier, everyone's saying like, "Oh no, Jensen." And yet they're all ready to start building their own chips or figuring out how to diversify that pool.

Zoë Schiffer: And the interesting thing about a lot of these relationships is they are very transactional. I don't know if we're going to continue to see the types of defenses that we have seen so far, but this is a moment. I mean, the China hawks, this is their time. I feel like it's not conspiratorial to say in some ways they orchestrated this moment in so far as they were instrumental in getting the information out there. And so I think they're going to, I would assume, be using this moment to try and turn Trump more toward their side, to be more anti-China, to not have as many trade loopholes or what have you.

Leah Feiger: And Jensen has been the voice against that, in many times the only voice against that in the room. So I'm really curious to see how this plays out.

Brian Barrett: And Zoë, you've got your kids guesting on the pod, which is adorable, and again, another thing that I think should become a fixture. Thank you for doing this when you've got your hands full.

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my gosh. They would love it. Yeah, they're in the laundry room right now watching Unicorn Academy. So this is honestly the best morning they've ever had in their lives, but ...

Brian Barrett: Love that for them. Love it for us. All right. Well, good luck to Colette Kress. Good luck to your 401(k), everybody. Thank you all for jumping on this emergency podcast.

Zoë Schiffer: Thank you.

Leah Feiger: Thanks all.

Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

Walmart+ members can shop select deals even earlier, while supplies last. We've gone through and highlighted the best discounts on WIRED-tested gifts below, and we'll keep this story updated through Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Walmart+ gets you free delivery on orders over $35, free shipping, access to Peacock or Paramount+, gas savings, and more. You can try it for 30 days for $1, which may be worthwhile if you plan on doing some shopping at Walmart for the holidays; Just keep in mind that you'll want to manually cancel your membership if you decide it's not for you after 30 days, otherwise, it's $13 per month (or $98 per year). This extremely portable power station is actually pretty easy to tote around, unlike some other gadgets we've tested in this category.
