https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/threat.title: ThreatsDay: 59 Linux Kernel Bugs, Falcon Spyware, GSocket Backdoors + 17 More Stories
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/threat.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/threat.text:
A search result isn't always safe. An access request isn't always harmless. And a familiar account doesn't always mean a familiar person is using it. Simple things to remember. Yet a surprising amount of this week's trouble starts right there.

Attackers are using fake websites, stolen access, and trusted tools to get into places they shouldn't be. AI is helping them build attacks faster, while also giving them new systems to target. Some intruders are staying hidden even after security holes are fixed. Others are moving stolen money through a maze of transactions. And researchers keep finding small coding mistakes that can cause much bigger problems. Different stories, but much of the trouble comes down to making something dangerous look normal.

There is some good news, too. Criminal servers have been seized, and a few defenses are getting stronger. Still, plenty of things are going wrong in ways that shouldn't be this easy. Here's what turned up this week.

The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.

The North Korean threat actors linked to the record-breaking theft of $6.43 billion from Binance are using a highly complex and clearly automated method to launder the illicit proceeds. "Since the theft it has used more than 20,000 wallets on 16 blockchains, at least 36 services and at least 65,000 transactions," Dr. Tom Robinson, Elliptic's founder and chief scientist, said. "Around $3.0 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly as ETH and BTC. A negligible amount has likely been cashed out." The attackers have also been observed creating six meme coins on the NEAR blockchain network (FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI, and SINU) to launder a slice of the ill-gotten funds, passing through about $430,000 of the stolen cryptocurrency. The goal is to disguise the path of money and make it harder to trace where the assets eventually end up. Other tactics used to make funds tracing more difficult include moving between blockchains through bridges and cross-chain swap services, swapping between assets on DEXs, hopping through lending vaults and liquid-staking services, and mixing bitcoin through coinjoins, and ETH and SOL through the Privacy Cash privacy pool. The Binance breach is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange, but it is the biggest ever by magnitude. North Korean spokesperson Kim Yo Jong denied the country's role in the attack, calling it an "absurd" effort to "damage the international image of the DPRK."

Microsoft said it has observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open-source remote access tool, on internet-facing Linux servers to maintain access after the original vulnerabilities were addressed, turning a single web application compromise into persistent access. "Because GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block," Microsoft said. "Defenders should look for GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections on affected hosts, not treat application patching alone as complete remediation." According to telemetry data, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2% from March through August 2026, with most of them associated with PHP web applications, cPanel hosts, and Apache. The majority of targets of GSocket activity are in the education and research sector, followed by technology and communications, manufacturing, and government entities.

Europol, along with global partners, has disrupted the criminal infrastructure behind GootLoader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware, seizing 235 servers and 257 domains. "The operation targeted 'cybercrime-as-a-service' models, where these tools enabled further crimes like ransomware attacks and data theft," Europol said. As part of the operation, authorities have identified over 6 million victim credentials. "The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware," Europol added.

A command and control (C2) framework called Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē) has been found compromising victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. Falcon shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with PeckBirdy, another JavaScript C2 framework that came to light early this year. It's assessed that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework. "An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information: passwords, emails, session cookies, [and] communications." Falcon has also been used to deliver an implant dubbed Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel. The activity has targeted government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. "The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives," Unit 42 said.

Microsoft said its scan of a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026 unearthed 26,502 raw findings using MDASH, which subsequently formed the basis for 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. This includes working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, such as CVE-2026-64563. "CVE-2026-64563 is a one-line state-reset bug in rhashtable, the Linux kernel's shared resizable hash table," Microsoft said. "Because callers trust the object pointers returned by a table walk, this small library flaw enabled a stable local privilege escalation on Linux -- and affected Android with SELinux enforcing -- without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces."

An exposed Silent Lynx server has uncovered cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026. "The directory held the group's tooling alongside data from active intrusions into government and critical infrastructure organisations across the region, and the AI agent the operator relied on to run them," CloudSEK said. "We assess with medium confidence that the operator has a Kazakhstan nexus: the operation runs in Russian, and the operator's own test traffic came from a residential Kazakh connection, which supports existing vendor assessments. The collection priorities, spanning transport, defence correspondence and resource ministries in neighbouring states, point to regional intelligence gathering rather than financial motive."

A new Russian-speaking ransomware group called Citrus is targeting Windows systems in corporate environments. The attackers have been found to gain access through compromised contractor accounts and leverage AI-generated PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands during later stages of the intrusion. In an attempt to reduce visibility, the threat actor removes tools and output files after execution, clears command history, and deletes event logs. The group also disguises tools and related artifacts with benign-looking names to make them appear legitimate by using a trusted brand name. The ransomware is a Sn00py-family ransomware variant written in Go. On Windows systems, the malware encrypts user files and appends the .citrus extension, while taking steps to hinder recovery and incident response. Kaspersky said the activity shares several similarities with Toy Ghouls. "Citrus stands out for the way AI-generated content appears to support hands-on intrusion activity on compromised systems," said Stanislav Larinsky, Kaspersky Security Services expert. "In the cases we investigated, the attackers combined third-party account access, privilege-escalation attempts and domain-wide deployment techniques. These incidents show how limited contractor access can become a path to broader compromise if it is not tightly controlled and continuously monitored."

Proofpoint has disclosed details of a new technique called BluePhishing that's described as the "next evolution of OAuth consent abuse," enabling bad actors to leverage agent identities like Microsoft Entra Agent ID for initial access. BluePhishing "socially engineer[s] victims into granting consent to a malicious agent blueprint for initial access," it said. "Analogous to app consent phishing where attackers use client credentials to gain initial access to a tenant, BluePhishing extends this technique to the agent ecosystem. By exploiting gaps in visibility and governance around emerging AI agent adoption, attackers can abuse one-time consent links to create agent identities in target tenants, obtain access tokens, and operate with the privileges assigned to those agents."

Meta has announced that it's expanding its AI age-estimation technology globally to automatically place millions of teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. "We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections," Meta said. "As a result, millions more teens across the world who use Instagram will receive these built-in protections, even if they've misrepresented their age." In Australia, Meta has opted to use Apple's age-range signal as another method to help understand age.

Microsoft 365 Mailbox Replication Service (MRS) has added support for OAuth as an authentication method when migrating mailboxes between Microsoft 365 and an on-premises Exchange environment. "Once OAuth for MRS is configured, tenant administrators can create an OAuth migration endpoint and use it in migration batches or in onboarding and offboarding move jobs," Microsoft said. "You can use this method in both hybrid and non-hybrid organizations."

In more Microsoft-related news, the tech giant has incorporated additional protections into Windows starting November 10, 2026, that address CVE-2026-118737 (CVSS score: 8.1), a critical remote code execution flaw in Remote Procedure Call Runtime that could allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. "These updates represent the first phase of improvements to NTLM message signing," Microsoft said. "These changes help ensure that authenticated NTLM sessions always establish a cryptographic session key and negotiate real message signing, reducing exposure to relay attacks." To that end, Windows servers will begin requiring NTLM signing by default starting May 2027.

Details have emerged about a now-patched security flaw affecting the Planning Inspectorate, an executive agency of the United Kingdom's Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG). The issue involved a complete Microsoft Entra ID application credential that was committed in plaintext to a GitHub repository. "Although removed from the branch, the commit was orphaned via a force push and remained retrievable via GitHub's raw object CDN for 18 months," ControlPlane said. The client secret was deleted about 20 minutes after responsible disclosure on August 26, 2026.

An SEO poisoning campaign is using fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware called Armorsteal. "The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor," Zscaler said. "The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data."

A new Grandoreiro banking malware campaign is targeting users across Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Peru through country-specific phishing lures that are tailored to each region. "The campaign uses localized phishing lures, primarily in Spanish, with some observed using Portuguese even when targeting Spanish-speaking countries," Arctic Wolf said. "The phishing chain relies on recently registered domains and layered redirection to hinder detection. The final payload is retrieved through a Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) seeded with the current date. The downloaded ZIP archive uses a deeply nested folder structure populated with two legitimate PE files and two benign PDF documents. A VBScript file located in the archive's root directory acts as the primary payload, employing junk code and multiple layers of obfuscation before reconstructing and launching a Delphi-based loader." The loader masquerades as a PDF reader and is used to fetch and run the banking trojan.

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said it detected an indirect prompt injection (IDPI) campaign across 26 domains. "These are attempting black-hat Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to game AI-powered search results," Unit 42 said. "Almost all of the 26 pages have very similar content, presenting as AI-powered digital asset trading platforms. These sites appear to be scam sites designed to collect user information. The injected prompt is set to be hidden from a regular web user but likely visible to an AI agent. These attacks intend to poison SEO and manipulate AI agents to eventually get users to visit these sites."

The Python Package Index (PyPI) has added a security tab to its project pages, giving developers easy access to security signals. "The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from," PyPI said. "PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation."

The information stealer known as RevStealer is being propagated as part of an "industrial-scale, financially motivated campaign" that uses game cheats and AI tools as lures. The payload is distributed through more than 100 interconnected domains, trojanized Electron applications masquerading as Anthropic's Claude Opus 5, and hijacked YouTube distribution channels, per Akatsuki Legion. "Once executed, the malware performs a ten-point weighted sandbox-evasion scoring routine, decrypts an AES-256-CBC in-memory payload, and leverages fourteen indirect syscall wrappers and FNV-1a API hashing to bypass user-mode hooks before systematically harvesting credentials from browsers, password managers, cryptocurrency wallets, Steam, Roblox, Battle.net, EA Desktop, and Minecraft; then exfiltrating the loot as streamed, encrypted typed records over HTTPS, with a resilient Polygon blockchain dead-drop resolver standing by as a fallback command-and-control channel," the independent adversary research group said.

Threat actors have increasingly targeted AI orchestration platforms over the past few months, according to Sekoia. This is because "they concentrate API keys, enterprise data, and access to external tools," it added. This includes Flowise, which has been affected by multiple security flaws like CVE-2025-59528 and CVE-2026-41264. In one exploitation attempt recorded in August 2026, a suspected Chinese-speaking actor abused legitimate Flowise functionality to conduct automated reconnaissance and attempted to hijack the LLM agent to serve as an offensive analysis vector against external targets. "The attacker attempted to turn the AI agent into an interactive offensive assistant, submitting real-world reconnaissance data (Nightingale/Redis infrastructure) to generate custom exploitation playbooks and target analysis," Sekoia said.

LevelBlue has disclosed details of a family of phishing kits named BlackApex, DarkApex, SPY, XXX101-TOKEN, OGPARKER1, W1-TOKEN, and ALIBOBO-TOKEN that are used to facilitate device code phishing attacks using shared document lures. The findings once again demonstrate how AI can speed up the development of a convincing multi-brand phishing kit. "Across all of its lures, the source shows traits we associate with AI-generated code, whether from direct prompts to a language model or from a person working alongside an AI coding assistant," LevelBlue said. "The code, endpoints, and interface are the same across all of them. We cannot say whether these names reflect separate operators, resellers or customers of a single kit, but the pattern is consistent with a shared product being rebranded and redeployed."

Google's DeepMind has introduced AlphaProof Code, which brings together human experts and AI agents to verify software and mathematically demonstrate that it works as intended. The multi-agent AI framework has been used to prove key security properties of libsignal, the Signal protocol's reference implementation, at the machine-code level. "AlphaProof Code consists of a human-guided agent for writing Lean specifications of code, a formal semantics of AArch64 machine code, and a team of autonomous prover agents whose proofs are accepted only if Lean’s kernel checks them against the approved specification," DeepMind said. "Applied to libsignal, our agents generated about 6.5 million lines of machine-checked Lean proof code, resting on about 26,000 lines of trusted specifications and AArch64 semantics. The proofs cover Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, establishing forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy."

That's the lot for this week. Some attacks were carefully planned. Others relied on old mistakes, trusted accounts, or someone clicking the wrong thing. AI is showing up on both sides, making attacks easier to build while helping researchers find problems faster. The tools keep changing, but attackers still seem happy to use whatever works.

The good news is that some of these threats are being stopped, and defenses are slowly catching up. The bad news is that fixing a bug, removing a file, or blocking an attacker doesn't always mean the problem is gone. Sometimes the damage sticks around longer than anyone expects. Worth keeping in mind before the next batch of headlines arrives.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/new-si.title: New SignDrop Zero-Day Exploit Turns Windows CLFS Security Feature Into SYSTEM Access
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/new-si.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/new-si.text:
Public exploit code released earlier this week claims that a local Windows user can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Common Log File System driver.

The proof of concept, called SignDrop, targets a log-authentication feature added to the driver last year. It abuses how clfs.sys creates companion files when a privileged process opens a prepared log, using path redirection to take control of the operation. Microsoft has not confirmed the claimed flaw, assigned a CVE, or released a fix.

The researcher behind the exploit, who publishes under the name MSNightmare, released the code and a detailed writeup on GitHub on Tuesday, the same day the company published its November security updates.

CLFS is a logging subsystem built into Windows. Its driver has been a frequent target for privilege escalation: 10 CLFS flaws appear in CISA's catalog of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in attacks, including one used in ransomware campaigns in April 2025.

To reduce that exposure, Microsoft added an authentication check to CLFS log files in updates for Windows 11 25H2, 26H1, and Windows Server 2025 shipped in October 2025. The check attaches a hash-based message authentication code, built from log data and a key unique to each machine.

The driver then parses only log files it wrote. A companion .cnpf file stores recovery data beside each log and is created with the same security attributes as the original, according to the company's logfile authentication page.

SignDrop targets the creation of that companion file. According to the proof-of-concept code, a standard user prepares a CLFS log and container with paths the user controls. When a privileged process later opens that log, the driver creates the .cnpf file in the privileged process's security context rather than the user's.

The exploit uses object manager symbolic links to redirect that file creation to a location the attacker chooses. In the published code, the privileged process is the Defender antimalware service, triggered through its update interface.

"Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse," the researcher wrote.

Because the .cnpf file inherits the original log's permissions, the result is a file created as SYSTEM that the standard user can write to. The researcher says that can be chained into a SYSTEM shell.

The exploit was tested on Windows 11 26H2, a Windows 11 26H2 Experimental build, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, according to the repository. Systems are affected when the CLFS authentication registry mode is set to 0 (enforced) or 1 (learning). Systems older than 90 days typically move from learning to enforcement automatically, so the default configuration on established installations is the one the exploit targets.

A registry value of 2 or 3 means the mitigation is disabled. That takes the system outside the claimed attack surface, but the researcher and the driver's own documentation both warn against it: disabling lets CLFS parse tampered log files, reopening the memory corruption flaws the protection was built to prevent.

Sungyup Nam, head of research at Korean security firm 78researchlab, reported in a published assessment today that researcher Heewon Song of the firm's PurpleHound offensive content team tested the exploit and found that it works. Song assessed that it does not run reliably enough for operational use, Nam wrote.

Defender must be enabled for the published chain to succeed. Running the exploit changes every UAC prompt to open a standard user shell and a SYSTEM shell, blocking other actions and making the attack noticeable to anyone at the machine.

The repository claims the technique can work against any antimalware engine whose process runs with elevated privileges. That broader claim has not been tested.

No CVE, advisory, or patch for SignDrop appeared in the November security updates. The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog does not list it, and no attacks using the exploit have been reported.

Administrators can check their exposure by reading the CLFS authentication mode at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication, where a Mode value of 0 or 1 falls within the researcher's claimed scope. The vendor's mitigation guidance describes the setting and the risks of disabling it.

The researcher has released a series of exploits targeting Windows and Defender since April. The vendor confirmed an earlier Defender exploit called RoguePlanet in June as CVE-2026-50656 and patched it the following month.

The ShieldBreak bypass followed in August and was assigned CVE-2026-69414. Three of the researcher's earlier Defender flaws have been exploited in attacks.

SignDrop is a different class of issue. Where the earlier exploits targeted race conditions in Defender's file handling, this one targets the CLFS driver's own authentication feature. The vendor's security update guide is the place to watch for a response.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.title: Critical Red Hat Quay Flaw Lets Attackers Read and Overwrite All Private Container Images in a Registry
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.text:
A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay allows an attacker who can access a Quay registry to read and overwrite private container images in every repository.

Quay enables anonymous access by default, and while it is enabled, the attacker needs no account. When it is off, anyone with a valid account can still exploit the flaw, Red Hat said yesterday. The company has released fixed builds for eight Quay 3 branches.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-123710 (CVSS score: 9.8).

Quay uses keys it trusts to sign the access tokens that allow image pushes and pulls. The flaw lets an attacker add their own key to the keys Quay trusts, with no expiry date. Quay then accepts tokens signed with that key for any repository.

With those tokens, an attacker can retrieve private images and any secrets or credentials stored within them. The attacker can also push or overwrite images, and the change propagates to every system that later pulls those images.

The planted key survives restarts until someone removes it. It can also be used to delete the keys that running Quay instances use, so normal pushes and pulls start failing with authentication errors.

Quay's key server checks that a request to replace a key carries a token signed by a trusted key, with the expected audience and issuer. It does not check whether the token was issued for key rotation. An anonymous token from Quay's /v2/auth endpoint passes: Quay signs it with a trusted key, and the caller chooses its audience.

A second critical flaw, CVE-2026-110697 (CVSS score: 9.9), was disclosed at the same time. It lets a Quay user who can create a namespace steal other tenants' robot account tokens and use them to read, push, or overwrite those tenants' images.

This flaw is in the code that lists robot accounts. It builds an SQL LIKE pattern from the namespace name without escaping wildcard characters, and in SQL LIKE an underscore matches any single character.

So a namespace with an underscore in the right place can match another tenant's namespace and return its robot accounts, with their decrypted tokens. The attacker needs no elevated privileges, and the victim does not have to do anything.

Deleting the attacker's namespace also deletes the corresponding robot accounts, which can cut off systems that rely on them. Where Quay is the integrated registry for OpenShift, stolen robot credentials can be used to inject malicious images into CI/CD pipelines, the company says.

Red Hat's Dave O'Connor found both flaws. The logic behind CVE-2026-123710 has been in Quay since its first public commit, according to the bug report for that flaw.

Red Hat lists every version of Quay 3 and Quay 5 as affected by both flaws. For CVE-2026-123710, its guidance names standalone installs, Quay deployed by the Quay Operator on OpenShift, and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift as affected.

Any Quay instance that untrusted clients can reach is exposed, including internal registries, the company says.

When checked today, the CVE entry for CVE-2026-123710 still showed every Quay package as affected, with no fix, even though each advisory lists the flaw.

The company recommends these steps:

"Turning off anonymous access doesn't protect you," the company says in its key remediation article. A planted key also continues to work after password resets and changes to the robot token.

For CVE-2026-110697, the company's CVE page names the same eight releases as fixed, calls updating the only complete fix, and says Quay.io is already fixed. But none of the eight advisories list CVE-2026-110697.

Until an update is in place, the company suggests limiting who can create organizations or namespaces containing an underscore, rotating robot tokens for any namespace that matches an underscore namespace, and watching for pulls or pushes that do not fit normal robot use. These steps reduce the exposure, but the flaw remains.

The upstream fix adds the missing rotation check, requires keys added through the key server to have an expiry date, and stops callers from choosing a token's audience. The same change fixes the robot account search too.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/186-fa.title: 186 Fake AI Domains Redirect Users to ClickFix Lures, Browser Malware, and Search Hijackers
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/186-fa.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/186-fa.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have found that lookalike domains masquerading as artificial intelligence (AI) tools are being used to serve ClickFix-style lures, browser-hijacking malware, and a set of extensions that hijack user searches.

This delivery pattern has been codenamed TypoPrompting by Island.

"AI-app lookalikes that turn an attempt to reach a familiar tool into a prompt to verify, install or run something else," the cybersecurity company said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

In all, the campaign spans 186 bogus domains spanning 27 AI brands, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM), Microsoft Copilot, SpaceXAI Grok, DeepSeek, Mistral, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, Lovable, and Cursor.

While one category leads to a ClickFix lure that serves a PowerShell command via a fake Cloudflare verification page, the second route takes unsuspecting users to "Security Check" pages that deliver a browser-hijacking malware called Net Guard. The third pathway sends users to a search-hijack extension family with 16 live Chrome Web Store listings and 972,000 declared users.

Some of the AI lookalike domains are listed below -

An analysis of registration records shows that some of these domains, like cloude[.]ai and cluade[.]ai, were registered as early as July 13, 2023.

The use of parked domains for malware delivery is not new. In December 2025, Infoblox highlighted how domains without a current web page can be monetized to redirect visitors to sites that serve scams and malware after profiling the host and the device they are visiting from.

"When a domain owner opts into direct search, traffic to the domain is sold to advertisers who bid on keywords and traffic characteristics," the DNS threat intelligence firm noted at the time. "In practice, the site visitor is usually funneled through a series of traffic distribution systems (TDSs) operated by third-party advertising platforms, creating a complex web where a legitimate business model is weaponized for abuse."

In the case of the ClickFix route, the parked page initiates a redirect chain that fingerprints the web browser and collects the public IP address before displaying the fake Cloudflare verification page.

Island said the fingerprint gate script spans a broader set of 211 entry domains, including lookalikes of banks, insurers, and enterprise software, such as Scotiabank, Charles Schwab, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Verizon, ServiceNow, and Microsoft Azure.

These domains serve three types of lures -

Separately, eight typosquat domains for Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, ElevenLabs, and Voice AI lead to fake "Security Check" pages that ultimately deliver Net Guard.

While the app purports to be a Wi-Fi and DNS safety scanner and matches the MSIX hash for a legitimate app of the same name, it contains capabilities to run attacker-controlled JavaScript, change the default search engine while the user is idle, edit browser profiles, and install arbitrary Chrome extensions.

"The download from the 'Security Check' pages is the Microsoft Store app itself, unmodified," Oleg Zaytsev, Lead Security Researcher at Island, told The Hacker News. "It is byte-for-byte identical to Net Guard as Microsoft distributes it, and it carries Microsoft’s own Store signature."

"The hidden browser control comes with every copy, whether installed from the Store or from a typo site, and it switches itself on without asking. It waits until the user stops using the computer, then takes over Chrome's search settings and can run scripts inside the browser, following instructions from the operator's server."

The third route revolves around a lookalike domain for Perplexity ("preplexity[.]ai"), which redirects the browser to a browser extension called Quick Search that's available on the Chrome Web Store.

"The analyzed extension needs no executable JavaScript or declared permissions to perform its main action," Island said. "Its manifest overrides the default search provider with find.flashysearches[.]com . Searches made through that provider are sent to a third party. In a workplace, those queries can include internal hostnames, customer names and project details."

Quick Search is part of a larger set of 16 extensions, including GPT for Chrome, which has 80,000 users. In all, the extensions collectively have 972,000 users as of November 3, 2026.

"An address one letter away from an AI tool can lead to a very different request," Island said. "As these services become part of everyday work, reaching the right one should be a managed path, not a test of typing accuracy."

(The story was updated after publication to include a response from Island.)

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sckit-.title: SCKit Malware Turns ScreenConnect Support Sessions Into Potential MSP Attack Paths
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sckit-.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sckit-.text:
The ongoing campaign targeting ConnectWise ScreenConnect deployments involves the exploitation of a now-patched critical security flaw in the remote access software, and not a new vulnerability, it has emerged.

Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG), which shared the details with The Hacker News, said the recovered attacker toolkit exploits CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), an improper privilege management and missing authorization vulnerability that could allow an attacker to file transfer and execute through an active remote session without authorization or host confirmation.

The cybersecurity company confirmed that testing against a fully patched ScreenConnect client successfully prevents execution of the exploit's payload.

"Our testing confirmed that the exploit targets CVE-2026-84869 and that the existing patch successfully blocks it," APG researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal said. "That's an important finding for security teams."

"But the toolkit also includes capabilities to hijack authenticated operator sessions and use legitimate ScreenConnect management features to push malicious code. Patching addresses the known exploit, but it doesn't eliminate the risks associated with a compromised operator session."

Notably, the SCKit malware contains functionality called RelayTrap to reverse-pivot to infect the workstations of technicians who attempt to investigate suspicious activity in a managed endpoint. In other words, the activity abuses trusted functionality and does not rely on a software vulnerability once an attacker obtains a valid session.

The attack sequence makes use of the platform's built-in Run Command functionality to execute commands. This involves first checking for an existing ScreenConnect installation before downloading and running an attacker-controlled MSI installer ("sc.msi"), which then delivers the batch script dropper ("sckit-run.bat").

The batch script dropper subsequently contacts "ns.mo7sen[.]dev" to fetch a PowerShell decoder ("sckit-decoder.ps1") and ultimately deploy various components associated with the SCKit toolkit.

This includes a PowerShell script ("SilentForceInstall-WithUninstall.ps1") used to establish persistent remote access by deploying two unauthorized ScreenConnect Access clients, along with a set of scripts and C# code designed to interfere with existing ScreenConnect Guest sessions, including RelayTrap.

The component attempts a guest-to-host file execution technique associated with CVE-2026-84869 by replacing the legitimate ScreenConnect Guest and sending the SCKit payload back toward the connecting technician for execution.

If this action is successful, the malware tries to recover the technician's authenticated ScreenConnect browser sessions and leverage their existing management permissions to distribute commands across additional endpoints they have access to. As a result, an attacker can move beyond the original compromised system and into other customer environments through the same infrastructure used to administer them.

"Because these commands were executed through existing ScreenConnect agents, the attackers could deploy additional software under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM context without needing to establish a separate execution method on each machine," Blackpoint Cyber said.

"The unauthorized Access clients provide attackers with persistent control over the endpoint, while the RelayTrap components position the malware to intercept legitimate support connections. Rather than simply preventing administrators from accessing an infected machine, the toolkit attempts to use their next connection as an opportunity to extend the intrusion directly to the technician's workstation."

The end goal of the attack appears to target technicians, as they regularly connect to managed endpoints belonging to different customers, typically from workstations with access to administrative tools and authenticated management sessions. This enables the attackers to break out of the original endpoint and move the intrusion into an environment with potentially broader access and privileges.

Once the malware gets executed on the technician's machine, it shifts from remote support manipulation to session theft, searching the local browser data and process memory of the machine to recover an existing authenticated management session (i.e., .ASPXAUTH cookies) that can be used to propagate the malware to other endpoints without having to obtain their credentials.

"By first attempting to compromise a technician's workstation, then recover their authenticated ScreenConnect session, SCKit seeks to turn access to a single managed endpoint into an opportunity to reach other systems under that technician's control," the researchers said.

The Hacker News has contacted ConnectWise for comment, and we will update the story if we hear back.

It's worth noting that CVE-2026-84869 was previously exploited in a set of attacks in which threat actors leveraged ScreenConnect to distribute a malicious four-stage Visual Basic Script (VBScript) payload to newly connected systems and ultimately serve an XMRig cryptocurrency miner.

The vulnerability was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 11, 2026, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by September 14, 2026.

In response to the latest incident, ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments. However, Blackpoint Cyber said it found no technical link between those extensions and SCKit.

As of writing, there is no evidence that the activity has established successful propagation to a technician workstation or bypassed the vendor patch for CVE-2026-84869.

The findings reinforce the importance of patching ScreenConnect clients, and underscore the need for stronger operator-session protections, including tighter session validation and additional authentication for bulk administrative actions, Blackpoint Cyber noted.

"Organizations need to protect those sessions and put additional safeguards around high-impact administrative actions," the researchers said.

"For MSPs, the practical lesson is to investigate the management relationship, not only the endpoint. Rogue Access installations, administrative command history, technician workstations, and browser sessions all deserve attention, especially when support personnel have already connected to a suspected system."

Huntress, in an update, said it has identified a serious authentication flaw in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of RMM+, one of the five third-party ScreenConnect extensions that has already been blocked by ConnectWise.

"When an administrator had not configured an access key, the extension would accept a blank one, potentially allowing unauthorized commands to execute without going through ScreenConnect's normal authentication controls," the company said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

RMM+ makes it possible for another tool to manage ScreenConnect sessions without a technician working through the console. It authenticates requests with a shared access key ("RMMPlus.AccessKey") stored in the extension's settings. However, in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, the key defaults to a blank value.

Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts, roles, and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands on the device without bypassing multi-factor authentication.

"Commands reached endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes. There was no corresponding login activity and the commands appeared in the logs reviewed linked to RMM+."

It's worth mentioning here that while the toolkit possesses capabilities to exploit CVE-2026-84869, there is no evidence to suggest that an unpatched ScreenConnect client was the initial entry point for the attack.

"At this time, initial access appears to be linked to malicious ScreenConnect extensions, although we do not have sufficient evidence to confirm this," Beal, principal MDR analyst at Blackpoint, told The Hacker News.

"Identifying patient zero would require additional forensic evidence from affected environments. Similarly, while November 11 marks the earliest publicly reported activity, we cannot rule out earlier compromises without further investigation. Our findings confirm the toolkit's capabilities but do not establish when or how the initial compromise occurred."

When contacted for comment, a ConnectWise spokesperson told The Hacker news that it's aware of reports of malicious activity affecting a limited number of ScreenConnect partners and that it's actively investigating the incident.

"While the initial access method remains unconfirmed, our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," the spokesperson said.

"We have disabled the identified extensions where we can take action as a precaution and are advising on-premises partners to disable them immediately. The presence of these extensions alone does not establish compromise. We encourage partners to review the precautionary guidance in the ConnectWise Trust Center, where we will provide updates as information is validated."

(The story was updated after publication to include responses and insights from ConnectWise, Blackpoint Cyber, and Huntress.)

https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.title: Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.author: Nate Nelson
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.text:
Cybercriminals using agentic pen-testing tools is a proverbial genie out of the bottle at this point, so enterprises need to get a defense plan in place right away.

A month since it went closed-source, the Artex agentic penetration testing framework is spreading faster and causing more havoc than ever. Still, cyber defenders tell Dark Reading that defending against it is largely a matter of willingness, not capability.

To recap: In August, a Chinese open source (OSS) developer released a cybercrime-grade agentic red-teaming tool called "Artex." In the months that followed, attackers and cybersecurity researchers have gradually realized just how effective Artex is at probing for vulnerabilities, and turning initial access into meaningful compromise at so-called machine speed.

"Artex is what the perpetual conflict era looks like," says Yuval Itzchakov, cofounder and chief technology officer (CTO) of A Security. "When our research team ran it against our open source benchmark, it found eight vulnerabilities in about 45 minutes, including a critical privilege escalation to admin, and chained them into a full attack path through a WAF, CAPTCHA, and MFA. All it took was a download, an install script, and a model key."

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

Nothing about it is so complicated, he says, "And that's the point. Take the guardrails off an AI hacking tool and anyone can run agentic attacks at scale. In Artex, scope is just a suggestion to the model."

Though its author de-listed the original Artex on Oct. 8, new variants continue to cause trouble. The variant du jour, "AntiFox," was recently weaponized by attackers to exploit Internet-facing Web services and their associated Amazon Web Services (AWS) environments. According to researchers at Arctic Wolf Labs, threat actors used their new agentic toy to breach, deploy Web shells, and execute operating system (OS) commands on compromised Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) servers, as well as enumerate services, expose production secrets, and manipulate Simple Storage Service (S3) buckets across AWS environments.

Notably, Arctic Wolf Labs offered relatively banal advice for organizations defending against this quite new threat: hunt for indicators of compromise (IoCs), rotate and revoke relevant credentials and sessions. In fact, researchers say, there's little more to defending against Artex or AntiFox than basic cybersecurity hygiene. However, it's also important to avoid making assumptions; as GitGuardian pointed out in a blog post on AntiFox, "Blocking scanner tools won't stop these agents, and a leaked key stays dangerous until someone revokes it."

The prospect of every Tom, Dick, and Harry having an agentic attack framework in their pocket might be intimidating, but cybersecurity defenders still possess some distinct advantages.

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

First off, Itzchakov points out that "Artex stops at the front door. It has no lateral movement, no Active Directory testing, and no view inside. Defenders can see their whole environment and test it continuously with the same speed and autonomy, under guardrails no one can switch off. The organizations that come out ahead will treat this as permanent and build their security around it."

In a profile of a recent incident response (IR) effort against an Artex attack, Eye Research noted another serious weakness of agentic tools in general: they're loud. "The agents left their name in pod names and probes, hammered endpoints no human would touch, and tripped detections on systems with EDR installed," it explained. "Where we had visibility, we saw them immediately."

"If you want to be positive, there are a lot of small steps you can put together in order to protect networks and organizations," says Guillaume Valadon, lead cybersecurity researcher at GitGuardian. To catch Artex or AntiFox's loudness, for example, "blue teams must have in place a security information and event management (SIEM) platform and a really good detection system, to make sure that they will detect these tools in the noise."

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Besides active detection, organizations would be well advised to focus on secrets management. Artex and AntiFox have proven adept at finding secrets, in part because they use ordinary commands like "git" and "grep" to find what they're looking for, instead of shipping a more easily identifiable and blockable secret scanner.

"Defenders need to be looking for exposed and dormant keys, checking Git repos for exposed secrets, and heavily implementing a defense-in-depth posture," Justin Moore, Arctic Wolf's director of adversary operations adds. "What makes these frameworks so effective is not that they’re conducting novel attacks, they’re just doing what we already know, just faster than we have seen before. Good cyber hygiene is exactly what prevents these types of attacks from being so successful, whether they’re agentic or not.”

Despite all of the positive steps organizations can take, Valadon thinks, "If I'm being negative, I would say that it's too late."

"For years we have been telling people that they should not output secrets — that we're finding really important hardcoded secrets everywhere, publicly. On Docker, GitHub, and so on. Now, because we have these tools that can go fast from nothing to discovery to weaponization, that makes it more difficult for blue teams," he says.

"The agentic capacity for the attacker is already here, and they're going faster and faster and faster," he notes. "So if you didn't do the right stuff before, it will be difficult for you to catch up."

The cybersecurity industry has been waiting for artificial intelligence (AI)-driven cyberattacks for years now. Product marketing campaigns have hinged on agentic attacks being right around the corner. Stories of lightly AI-influenced tactics, techniques, procedures (TTPs), and malware have kept food on cyber reporters' plates. Most of the discourse has been, at best, theoretical, at worst, misleading.

A meaningful, if incomplete, turning point seems to have occurred around midway this year, if not among the most sophisticated attackers than at least in the world of middling cybercriminals.

"When we all started using ChatGPT, at that time, we were just asking it simple questions. It was fun, but it was not possible to code," Valadon explains. "And then we had agents that were more capable at coding, and syncing. This year you can do it all, from end to end. You just give [an agent] a rough idea, and it will do some planning, syncing, it will build the code for you, and deploy it for you. It's getting better and better at doing the whole cycle."

He also points to Anthropic and OpenAI's warnings about open source (OSS) AI earlier this fall: "Some people are saying that we are seeing these [attack] frameworks because of Chinese open-weight models. Because if you have a big GPU, you are able to run your own offensive models with Artex."

"It's getting more and more dangerous," he says. "It's all fitting into the HuggingFace, OpenAI, Anthropic narrative [warning against attackers] having access to real offensive tools."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: AI confirms a long-suspected limit on quantum computers’ advantages
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Karmela Padavic-Callaghan
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
A decades-old, vastly influential conjecture about quantum computing has finally been proven – by AI. It confirms that a whole class of mathematical problems would not be more easily solved by quantum computers.

In 1999, Scott Aaronson of The University of Texas at Austin got stuck on a question about when exactly quantum computers could excel over their conventional counterparts.

At this time, researchers knew of at least one example of a problem where the quantum approach outshone all others: Shor’s algorithm for factoring numbers. But they suspected that this hinged on specific mathematical structure that underlies the factoring problem. Aaronson wondered whether quantum computers could also win in the opposite case, when the problem contained little to no structure and lots of randomness instead. In 2011, he and Andris Ambainis at the University of Latvia formally conjectured that in at least one case the answer was negative, but they could not prove it.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Leah Crane
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
A robot has built a structure in space without any help of astronauts. The first-of-its-kind achievement is a step towards autonomous in-orbit manufacturing and assembly of structures such as space stations and data centres, which will be crucial if we want to develop an orbital economy.

Sergio Pellegrino at the California Institute of Technology and his team developed their robot as part of a US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) initiative to explore new ways to build in space. Large orbiting structures in the past have either been assembled with the help of astronauts or launched pre-assembled and folded up, spring-loaded to unfold upon release from their capsules.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Economics, not climate summits, will dictate the net-zero transition
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Alec Luhn
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
The stench of hypocrisy is in the air at the COP31 summit in Turkey. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to show British leadership on climate action. Meanwhile, his government just green-lit the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, which will emit up to 36 million tonnes of carbon dioxide without noticeably reducing energy prices, and it is considering approving the Rosebank oilfield and weakening its electric vehicle mandate.

The summit’s joint hosts, Turkey and Australia, are pushing for a clean energy revolution, but this week Turkey announced two new oilfields that would help boost production 30 per cent, while promising to double natural gas production. Australia has recently approved fossil fuel projects including a “climate bomb” coal mine extension that will emit enough carbon to kill an additional 15 million Great Barrier Reef coral colonies during every bleaching event. Meanwhile, the second biggest emitter, the US, is again boycotting the annual climate summit.

How incredibly simple tech can supercharge the race to net zero

While the world shaved more than 1°C off the warming trajectory after the 2015 Paris Agreement, “collective climate action has effectively stalled”, and current policies put the world on track for a catastrophic 2.7°C rise by 2100, according to Climate Action Tracker.

But there is one piece of good news. The Global Carbon Budget also just announced that fossil fuel emissions are expected to slightly decrease in 2026 – something that has only previously happened during the covid-19 pandemic, the 2008 financial crisis and the break-up of the Soviet Union. Granted, the 0.4 per cent decline wouldn’t have happened without the Iran war oil crisis. But the growth in cheap solar, wind and electric vehicles has offset more emissions than the spike in oil prices.

If clean tech can keep accelerating, “a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away”, the Global Carbon Budget report said. This means that economics, not politics, is pushing the clean energy transition forward, despite the failed leadership on display at COP31.

“Policy was never the main driver,” says Auke Hoekstra at the Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands. “These technologies are simply superior.”

Hoekstra is known for his graphs showing how solar panel production has repeatedly outperformed International Energy Agency expectations. Solar is now providing 10 times more energy than when the Paris Agreement was signed in 2015, making it the fastest-growing electricity source ever, followed closely by wind.

Money talks, and electricity from solar and wind costs less on average than from natural gas or coal. In the US, the top oil-producing state, Texas, where climate denier Donald Trump won a landslide, has also become the top producer of both solar and wind power. In low-income countries like Nigeria and Pakistan, rather than waiting for governments to update expensive and unreliable fossil fuel-based power grids, people are simply installing cheap Chinese solar panels on their roofs, “leapfrogging” hydrocarbon-fuelled development altogether.

The one drawback had been that solar and wind don’t generate much energy in the evening during peak demand. But cheap batteries are quickly solving that problem. Utility and home battery storage is now growing even faster than renewable power generation.

An ambitious form of climate modelling aims to pin the blame for disasters – from floods to heatwaves – on specific companies. Is this the tool we need to effectively prosecute the world’s biggest carbon emitters?

Of course, early subsidies and regulations by governments like China and Germany created the market conditions for renewables to start coming down the cost curve. While economics is driving the energy transition, policy can speed it up or, as in the case of Trump cancelling electric vehicle subsidies, slow it down. Governments still provide more than $900 billion of annual support for fossil fuels.

The target proposed at COP31 of increasing energy use from electricity to 35 per cent by 2035 would send a positive signal. The biggest bottleneck to this is expanding the grid, something governments could accelerate at home by cutting red tape and offering subsidies and loans.

Kingsmill Bond at think tank Ember Energy thinks the economics of clean tech will let the world limit warming to much less than the projected 2.7°C by 2100. Exactly how much less depends on politics. He proposes that energy-importing countries start their own COP, where fossil fuel-exporting countries can’t delay progress.

“The old system is just being propped up by legacy policy and ignorance,” he says. “We’ve just got to tear that down.”

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Pink noise played during sleep shows promise for Alzheimer’s memory loss
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Sascha Brodsky
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
Brief bursts of ‘pink noise’ played while people with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease sleep might give them a slight memory boost, a small study suggests.

Pink noise is best described as a low-pitched hiss. There is some evidence that exposure to pink noise during sleep may help clear waste products from the brain. As such, researchers are beginning to assess whether pink-noise therapy has benefits for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease.

Can we harness the brain’s deep-cleaning system to prevent Alzheimer’s?

An international team of researchers has explored this possibility. They worked with 37 people, each with diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and experiencing mild cognitive impairment affecting memory. On two occasions, 14 days apart, the 37 participants were invited into the lab in the evening and asked to memorise 30 word pairs. They then slept in the lab while the researchers monitored their brain activity.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: A little-known immune condition is being mistaken for food allergies
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Zesha Saleem
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
A chronic inflammatory condition is becoming more common, and its symptoms can be mistaken for a severe allergic reaction.

Eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE) is a rare condition where a type of white blood cells, known as eosinophils, builds up in the oesophagus. It is thought to affect around 40 in every 100,000 people.

Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it

Eosinophils play an important role in the body’s immune system, helping to destroy invader parasites and pathogens before they cause harm to other cells. They also have a role in regulating inflammation, but can cause tissue damage when it becomes excessive, such as in EoE.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: How Nvidia became so crucial to the AI boom
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Jacob Aron
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
You have almost certainly seen the headlines – Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, has resigned after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected by US intelligence officials of being a Chinese spy (a claim China dismisses). The story has become so big because Nvidia, and by extension Jensen, are at the heart of the AI revolution. But just why has this one company become so important?

For me, Nvidia will always be a video games company, its logo splashed up at the start of the play sessions of my youth. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) were specifically designed for the intense number-crunching required to create a 3D scene from triangles. Initially, these were a few hundred triangles, then thousands, and now hundreds of thousands as computing power has increased, allowing ever more realistic computer graphics.

Nature has brewed a wicked cocktail in Galerina indica. It is the first mushroom known to make both the hallucinogen psilocybin and lethal compounds from a family called amatoxins. This group of deadly poisons includes those found in the death cap (Amanita phalloides), one of the world’s most poisonous mushrooms.

Both male and female kelp were shown to be capable of reproduction without fertilization.Credit: Madelein_Wolf/Getty

When potential mates are scarce, some types of seaweed can take reproduction into their own hands, so to speak, according to a study published on 12 November in PLoS Biology1.

“Our findings highlight that kelp are even more flexible in their reproduction than previously appreciated,” says Daniel Liesner, a marine biologist at the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel in Germany.

The brown algae, which provide food and shelter for marine life, “are really weird, they do all kinds of stuff”, says Reina Veenhof, an ecologist at the Scottish Association for Marine Science in Oban, UK. What’s interesting about the study is that it helps to explain how changes in gene activity allow kelp to reproduce in different ways, she says.

Scientists know that kelp can reproduce asexually, with unfertilized eggs developing into offspring. This process was even documented for one male strain2 — the PLoS Biology study shows that this wasn’t a one-off.

The ability of male reproductive cells to develop without fertilization is striking, says Olivier De Clerck, a seaweed biologist at Ghent University in Belgium. This is because, unlike eggs, sperm cells are small and have few resources to support development.

The researchers focused on Laminaria pallida, a species found along the Atlantic coasts of South Africa and Namibia. In the wild, 523 individual kelp showed no clear evidence of asexual reproduction.

By contrast, both microscopic male and female L. pallida grown in separate laboratory dishes could produce offspring without fertilization. During asexual reproduction, the gene expression in males changed, making them more similar to females.

However, when they were lab-grown in the presence of a member of the opposite sex, kelp favoured sexual reproduction, suggesting they can detect nearby partners through chemical signals.

Confirmed infections of Bundibugyo Ebola have surpassed 10,000 in the DRC since May.Credit: Xinhua/Shutterstock

Epidemiologists have used mobile-phone data and test records to map the early spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)1 weeks before the outbreak was declared. The authors say the study findings reveal how surveillance systems failed to detect signals of the disease early on and enabled it to spread rapidly.

It is now six months since the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus was announced. The number of confirmed infections has risen to more than 10,000 and 5,198 people have died, making this the largest Bundibugyo outbreak so far. There are no licenced vaccines or approved treatments specifically for Bundibugyo, which has complicated efforts to control it.

The DRC declared the outbreak on 15 May after laboratory tests confirmed the first case, a person from Ituri province in the country’s northeast, was infected with the Bundibugyo strain. Around the same time, suspected cases were being reported in several DRC locations, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara, Bunia and Nyankunde in Ituri, and Butembo, Katwa and Goma in the neighbouring province of North Kivu. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern on 17 May, citing infections among health-care workers, the geographical spread of cases and clusters of undocumented deaths. Researchers strongly suspect that the virus had been spreading in the region months earlier.

To understand how the outbreak spread so quickly, the researchers looked at anonymized mobile-phone data to trace the movement of people between areas.

Although the first confirmed case was identified on 15 May, the study reports that the person had symptoms as early as 25 April.

The team found that people travelling out of Mongbwalu, Bunia and Rwampara between 24 April and 24 May helped to predict which health zones would report infections by 1 June. For instance, areas close to the initial centres were at greater risk of infections, the study found.

The risk of infections rose again in places 150–200 kilometres away from the initial outbreak centres because people travelled to larger towns and cities along established routes, says study co-author Pierre Akilimali, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) in Kinshasa.

The authors say the findings show that people movement was a key driver of the rapid spread in the early phases of the outbreak.

“These are very important findings which reinforce what we initially knew at the onset of the outbreak,” says Tambe Akem, an independent public-health consultant based in Yaoundé, Cameroon.

The basal ganglia are groups of cells that sit deep in the brain and process motor, cognitive, mood and decision-making information. They are linked to neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions from Parkinson’s and Huntington’s disease to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and addiction.

Now, researchers have published the world’s most-detailed atlas of basal ganglia so far, comprising 25.5 million brain cells from humans, macaques and marmosets. The work is described in a collection of 26 papers published in Cell, Cell Reports, Cell Reports Methods, Cell Systems, Cell Genomics and Neuron. The research includes understudied neurons1, provides insights about how some brain cells change with age2 and suggests which might be linked to diseases3.

The atlas, a collaboration between hundreds of scientists in nine countries, is part of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) — a US$500-million project launched in 2022 by the US National Institutes of Health aimed at creating reference maps of mammalian brains.

“It’s a massive dictionary that we needed in the field,” says Ana Muñoz-Manchado, a neuroscientist at the University of Cádiz in Spain, who studies the basal ganglia in neurodegenerative disorders.

The basal ganglia atlas contains 21 million cells from the brains of six humans, three million cells from three rhesus and cynomolgus macaques, and 1.5 million cells from two marmosets4. The researchers also used data from previously published maps of the whole mouse brain5,6.

By comparing the basal ganglia between the primate species, the researchers identified 61 cell types in humans, macaques and marmosets that have been conserved over 76 million years3.

The team analysed brain tissue samples from different developmental stages across the lifespan of the species. The latest work combines information about these cells in unprecedented detail, from measurements of their gene expression and DNA modifications that control gene regulation to recordings of their electrical activity, as well as how DNA is folded inside their nuclei.

The researchers also mapped where each cell is located in the brain and designed a common framework to characterize and annotate the cells. It is “essentially a scaffold on which we can now fairly readily complete the rest of the brain”, explains Michael Hawrylycz, a bioinformatician at the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle, Washington, who took part in the project.

One study examined 1.1 million cells in the basal ganglia’s largest structure — known as the striatum — from 19 deceased human donors7. Unlike many other brain areas, the striatum has no neat anatomical boundaries. The researchers identified six zones in the human and macaque striatum with distinct molecular signatures, each containing distinct populations of neurons and glial cells.

“The cells in these zones all look the same under the microscope, but have very strong transcriptional differences and are strikingly consistent from person to person,” said co-author Evan Macosko, a neurobiologist at the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in a press release from the institute.

Macosko and his colleagues also found that gene expression patterns that distinguished each zone from the other became increasingly similar with age, particularly in brain regions affected by Huntington’s and Parkinson’s disease.

Another study analysed nearly four million cells in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from 178 deceased adult donors between the ages of 27 and over 902. The researchers found that the cellular make-up of the two brain regions varied between people, particularly for non-neuronal cells known as glial cells. This underscores the need for brain cell atlases to account for these individual differences.

The Cas9 protein together with RNA and DNA (orange; artist’s illustration). A new therapy uses the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing system to treat a rare genetic disease called hereditary angioedema.Credit: Alfred Pasieka/Science Photo Library

A pioneering therapy that edits genes inside a recipient’s body continues to be effective four years after treatment, according to data released by its developer, Intellia Therapeutics.

The therapy, named lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z), was designed to treat one form of a genetic disorder that causes episodes of painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and other parts of the body. Lonvo-z deploys the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing system to disable the gene that produces prekallikrein, a protein made in the liver that promotes blood-vessel leakage.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Intellia, headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has applied for approval of lonvo-z to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is expected to issue a decision by 10 March. If approved, the therapy will become the world’s first CRISPR medicine to be delivered directly inside the body, or in vivo, John Leonard, Intellia’s chief executive, told investors on 12 November. Currently, the only CRISPR therapy approved by the FDA is performed on cells that have first been removed from the body and are subsequently re-infused.

For people with the condition, hereditary angioedema, the gene-editing approach could offer relief from a lifetime of juggling medications to prevent and treat swelling attacks, says Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial. “It’s very reassuring,” he says of the four-year data. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.”

The only approved CRISPR therapy is Casgevy, a treatment for two genetic blood disorders, sickle cell anemia and ß-thalassemia. To create a dose of Casgevy, physicians first remove blood stem cells from the recipient, then send them off for gene editing. The edited cells are infused back into the recipient.

The therapy must be made anew for each person, adding time, cost, and complexity. The recipient also has to undergo harsh chemotherapy treatment to make room for the edited cells.

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

In vivo gene-editing approaches aim to sidestep these concerns by editing genes directly in the body. Lonvo-z, for example, consists of fatty particles that encase mRNA encoding CRISPR-Cas9 components. The particles are infused into the blood and taken up by the liver, where prekallikrein is produced. The procedure takes one day.

In vivo gene editing can introduce other safety concerns, however. The therapy affords no opportunity to screen out cells with unwanted edits at other locations in the genome, or in other organs. Recipients might also have harmful immune responses to the treatment.

Last year, the FDA placed a clinical hold on two other in vivo studies sponsored by Intellia after a participant — an older man with other health conditions — developed liver damage and died after receiving a CRISPR treatment. The FDA lifted the hold this year after requiring added safety measures.
