https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.title: 'Man of Tomorrow': Release date, plot, cast & everything we know about the 'Superman' sequel
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.author: Fran Ruiz
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.text:
James Gunn's new DC universe might be done, but the follow-up to 2025's Superman is still on the way.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It feels like yesterday when we were discussing Superman, the first big-screen entry in James Gunn's rebooted DCU. Now Gunn is out, and Skydance (the company formed by the merger of Warner and Paramount) is already dismantling his grand plans for the DCU.

That means that Man of Tomorrow, which arrives next summer, will be the final entry in Gunn's ambitious, and occasionally divisive, DC experiment. The DCU's first chapter — officially titled 'Gods and Monsters' — gave us Supergirl and Clayface (as well as TV shows like Peacemaker S2 and Lanterns) in the run-up to Clark Kent and Lex Luthor's return.

Man of Tomorrow looks to be upping the stakes from Earthly villains to intergalactic baddies with the introduction of Brainiac, and it may well have been the herald of the first Justice League movie in the rebooted DCU.

Gunn has yet to prove audiences actually care about more than Batman and Supes, which might explain why this follow-up is also an ensemble of sorts. As the Marvel Cinematic Universe prepares to unleash Avengers: Doomsday, Secret Wars, and even a fresh X-Men reboot, their DC counterparts have always struggled to get their dream team off the ground.

We'll never know what might have been, but we can still enjoy Gunn's DC swansong when it lands in 2027. Here's everything we know about James Gunn's Man of Tomorrow.

Man of Tomorrow will be released theatrically in the United States on July 9, 2027. Most international territories are expected to get it around the same time.

Only a few months after Superman's release and successful box office run, DC Studios and Warner Bros. Pictures confirmed the sequel would be coming two years after Clark Kent's return to the big screen.

Man of Tomorrow isn't out yet, but you can watch the rest of the DCU so far (it's pretty good for the most part) in preparation first.

When the movie hits theaters on July 9, 2027, it'll likely remain exclusive to big screens for at least two or three months, depending on how successful it is.

With that said, we know Warner Bros. (now part of Skydance) isn't the most patient when it comes to theatrical runs based on its track record, so the chances are Man of Tomorrow will hit HBO Max sooner rather than later, probably by early autumn 2027.

Watch Superman and the rest of the DCU on HBO Max:

Basic (Ads): $10.99/month or $109.99/year
Standard (No Ads): $18.49/month or $184.99/year
Premium (4K): $22.99/month or $229.99/year

No, we're still waiting for the first Man of Tomorrow trailer. Looking at the timeline of Superman's fantastic marketing campaign, however, we can guess the sequel will get a first trailer before 2026 ends, probably in time for Christmas.

Yes, James Gunn has officially confirmed Brainiac is the main threat Earth is facing in Man of Tomorrow. This explains why other heroes will be joining Superman in a fight against the alien mastermind, but the plot is looking a bit more complex.

In typical comic book fashion (and somewhat reminiscent of Thor: The Dark World), the main hook in Man of Tomorrow appears to be a reluctant alliance between the first movie's villain, Lex Luthor, and Kal-El (aka Clark Kent). "Enemies to allies" is always a fun dynamic to have in a sequel, especially when stars David Corenswet (Superman) and Nicholas Hoult (Lex Luthor) delivered strong and memorable performances the first time around.

The actual plot remains under wraps, but we can guess Brainiac — one of DC's biggest and most iconic alien villains — will be a tough nut to crack, thus requiring some sort of unofficial team-up that will include returning heroes like Mister Terrific, Guy Gardner, Hawkgirl, John Stewart, Blue Beetle, and even Kara Zor-El (Supergirl). There are other names circling the project that could lead to even bigger appearances, but don't expect to learn much about them before the movie's marketing kicks off.

Why should you care about Brainiac? Well, he's a super-intelligent techno-organic alien from the planet Colu with an obsession with knowledge and self-improvement. A perfect foe for Luthor, Earth's greatest mind, but also a breath of fresh air for Superman, who's been stuck battling either Kryptonian menaces or just Luthor too long on the big screen.

As a direct continuation of Superman, Man of Tomorrow is bringing back plenty of actors in both main and supporting roles, including:

New cast members with publicly announced (or previously established) characters include:

Last but not least, we also know Adria Arjona, Andre Royo, Matthew Lillard, and Sinqua Walls are part of the cast, but their parts remain a secret for now.

Much of the current Man of Tomorrow speculation centers on Adria Arjona's role in the story. While many have theorized she could be playing Wonder Woman — something that neither Gunn nor Arjona has straight-up denied — the earlier reports and rumors suggested she could be Maxima.

Such a role would fit Gunn's penchant for throwing lesser-known comic book heroes and villains into his movies wherever possible. If you're not an avid reader or longtime DC fan, all you need to know is that Maxima is an alien conqueror from the planet Almerac obsessed with Superman as her perfect mate and king. She's also morally ambiguous, at least when she first appeared, so that makes her a particularly interesting character to bring in for a more complex and nuanced sequel.

With Brainiac spearheading the roster of new DC icons joining Man of Tomorrow, it also isn't hard to imagine another alien figure factoring into the plot, though the flick is getting extremely crowded as it is.

Yes, James Gunn is the sole writer and director of Man of Tomorrow.

Despite his previous role as co-chairman and co-CEO of DC Studios, Gunn is extremely hands-on when it comes to most DCU projects. In fact, it seems he had already begun working on his next movie after Man of Tomorrow, though his unceremonious exit will almost certainly mean the end of those plans.

He's also co-producing alongside Peter Safran, who was also ousted in November 2026's DC Studios shakeup.

The rest of the crew includes Sam McCurdy (Peacemaker, Shogun) as cinematographer, Fred Raskin (Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, Supergirl) as editor, and David Fleming (Superman, Anaconda) as the main composer, among others.

Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. He got a BA of English Studies, focusing on English Literature, from the University of Malaga, in Spain, as well as a Master's Degree in English Studies, Multilingual and Intercultural Communication. On top of writing features and other longform articles for Space.com since 2021, he is a frequent collaborator of VG247 and other gaming sites. He also serves as associate editor over at Star Wars News Net and its sister site, Movie News Net.

https://www.space.com/astronomy/black-ho.title: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
https://www.space.com/astronomy/black-ho.author: Keith Cooper
https://www.space.com/astronomy/black-ho.text:
This supernova imposter erupts every 113 days as the compact object gets close to the unstable massive star.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered.

When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices.

Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

"For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville said in a statement.

Several other supernova imposters have been observed over the past decade or two. Until now, no one knew what causes these stars to repeatedly cry wolf. Thanks to Chandra’s X-ray vision, Aghakhanloo has led a team of astronomers who think they have now uncovered an explanation.

The supernova imposter is named AT 2016blu, and is a type of star that we call a 'luminous blue variable,' or LBV. These are the most massive and luminous stars in the universe and their extreme characteristics result in them being highly unstable, undergoing intermittent bouts of mass loss as they eject material from their outer layers into the surrounding space.

However, faking a supernova is not part of their typical behavior, so a new way of looking at AT 2016blu was needed.

"To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized that we needed X-ray data that was timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst," team member Núria Torres-Albà, also from the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, said.

Aghakhanloo’s team were granted the opportunity to commandeer Chandra to target an outburst of AT 2016blu at the earliest opportunity. That opportunity arose in March 2026.

Chandra had previously and coincidentally looked in the direction of NGC 4559 back in 2001 and 2002 and did not notice anything unusual back then. This time around, however, it captured a powerful blast of X-rays coinciding with yet another false supernova outburst.

The X-ray detection allowed Aghakhanloo’s team to assemble a picture of what is happening.

"Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen," he said.

Chandra’s X-ray observations indicate that AT 2016blu has an unseen companion, a compact, high-gravity object that is either a neutron star or a stellar-mass black hole on an elliptical 113-day orbit around the luminous blue variable.

Neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes are the core remnants of massive stars that have gone supernova for real, meaning that at one time AT 2016blu was a binary star system.

Each time the compact object reaches the point in its orbit that is closest to the luminous blue variable, its powerful gravity is able to pull material from the unstable star. This sets in motion a chain of events that results in the brilliant outbursts.

As the stolen starstuff is dragged away from the wounded star and towards the compact object, it forms an accretion disk swirling around the neutron star or black hole so fast and growing so hot that it emits X-rays. These are the X-rays that Chandra saw.

The X-rays are immense, energizing the surrounding cloud of material that had been ejected by the luminous blue variable years before. The cloud is heated and glows extremely brightly in visible light, creating the impression of a supernova.

"We suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays," said team member Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. "The dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical."

Calculations suggest that each year a 440 billion trillion pounds of material at minimum is stolen by the compact object, and possibly two orders of magnitude more than that. This is a huge amount, yet it is only 800 millionths of the mass of the sun, and AT 2016blu’s luminous blue variable is at least 33 times the mass of the sun.

Nevertheless, it is far greater than the maximum rate of material that a neutron star can safely accrete, referred to as the Eddington limit. It’s little wonder that the accretion onto the compact object unleashes such extreme energies.

AT 2016blu is also connected with another mysterious and rare astrophysical phenomenon, that of ultra-luminous X-ray (ULX) sources. The identity of whatever it is that is powering ULXs remains unclear, but the involvement of compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars is high on the list.

AT 2016blu is bright enough to be considered a ULX, so could it act as a Rosetta stone connecting supernova imposters with ULXs? It’s too early to say that; only one other supernova impostor has so far been found to have X-ray emission typical of material being stolen from one star and accreting onto a compact body, and that is SN 2010da, but in that case it is known that the companion is another massive star, a red supergiant, rather than a compact object.

The X-ray detection of AT 2016blu is described in a paper published on Monday (Nov. 9) in The Astrophysical Journal.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: On this day in space! Nov. 12, 2014: European Philae probe lands on Comet 67P, bounced twice and then got lost for nearly 2 years
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Hanneke Weitering
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
Philae drifted and bounced around the comet for two hours before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P. To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement.

The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired.

When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space. The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down.

Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it. Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

The European Space Agency's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of.

The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P, all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned.

After the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. Scientists figured it was stuck in a shady spot where sunlight couldn't reach its solar panels. Because it was solar-powered, Philae needed to be facing the sun properly to generate enough power for sustained operation on the comet's surface.

Still, Philae did have some power stored in batteries, which lasted for more than two days on the surface. That allowed Philae to perform some science with its 10 instruments in the time it had on Comet 67/P. Most notably, Philae found organic molecules that had never been detected on a comet before.

The Rosetta orbiter continued to orbit Comet 67P until September 2016, and it was in that month -- just weeks before Rosetta itself landed on the comet on Sept. 30, 2016 -- that the spacecraft rediscovered the Philae lander lying on its side in a rocky crevice.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

https://www.space.com/stargazing/spacexs.title: SpaceX's Starship megarocket will launch to orbit on Nov. 13. Will you be able to spot it in the night sky?
https://www.space.com/stargazing/spacexs.author: Anthony Wood
https://www.space.com/stargazing/spacexs.text:
"It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX's Starship megarocket is slated to launch on its ambitious 15th flight test as soon as this Friday (Nov. 13). Will you be able to spot its leviathan upper stage, known as Ship, or its Starlink satellite passengers as they circle Earth during the historic orbital jaunt?

Flight 15's 75-minute launch window opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) on Nov. 13. Starship will fly from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be 4:45 p.m. at the opening of the window — about an hour before sunset. The launch could therefore be especially dramatic for folks in the area.

"As it launches towards the southeast, and it will be daylight, then the prospects for viewing from the U.S. are going to be in Texas and the states along the Gulf of Mexico," Robert Massey, deputy executive director at the Royal Astronomical Society, told Space.com. "They could see the exhaust plume (the 'jellyfish') with the sky darker for observers further east."

If all goes to plan, Starship's Super Heavy booster will propel the Ship upper stage through the densest part of Earth's atmosphere before returning to Starbase for a powered landing and capture via the "chopstick" arms of the "Mechazilla" tower system. Ship, meanwhile, will go on to orbit Earth approximately 14 times over the following 22 hours, during which time it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites before returning to Starbase for its own ambitious catch attempt.

Satellite visibility in the night sky depends on a cocktail of factors, from the size of the spacecraft to its reflectivity, orbital inclination and position relative to the Earth and sun.

Ship is big — about 171 feet (52 meters) tall — so it will be a viable target for skywatchers, experts say.

"It certainly will be visible in twilight hours. It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size," professor James Osborn of Durham University told Space.com. "Where and when is a bit more tricky."

Ship and its Starlink satellites may be seen in the 90 minutes directly after sunset on Nov. 13 and before sunrise on Nov. 14, as the probes catch the sunlight on either side of Earth's colossal shadow as they drift through the twilight sky.

The spacecraft will initially appear as a string of bright, evenly spaced lights, with Ship most likely appearing significantly brighter than the Starlink satellites. However, Osborn noted that the lack of publicly available data makes it challenging to forecast exactly when the spacecraft will appear.

"During its 14 orbits over 22 hours, the spacecraft is between inclinations of 30.5 [degrees] N and S of the equator," explained Massey. "So it will be best viewed between those latitudes, and then lower in the sky up to latitudes of 40 N and 40 S. That's pretty much the whole of the contiguous U.S."

Space.com skywatching columnist and veteran meteorologist Joe Rao shared further details on what stargazers may see with the naked eye as Ship drifts silently through the autumn sky.

"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station, but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," explained Rao. "The Starlink V3 satellites are much smaller, so not as bright, perhaps ranging anywhere from 2nd to 4th magnitude, depending on the angle of illumination with reflected light from the sun."

Magnitude is the scale used by astronomers to measure the brightness of objects in the night sky. The lower the magnitude, the brighter the object! The unaided eye can make out objects with a magnitude of around +6.5 under ideal dark sky conditions, while the planet Venus currently shines at magnitude -4.41.

The Starlink train will likely fall further behind Starship as the 22-hour mission progresses, while the train itself will become more elongated, according to Rao. "For locations where it will make a high arc across the sky, the Starship should be visible for at least a few minutes, although because it is orbiting at a lower altitude (170 miles/275 km) compared to the ISS, it probably will appear to move somewhat faster. "

There are multiple handy resources that should allow you to track Ship and the newly deployed batch of V3 Starlink satellites following their scheduled launch on Nov. 13, including the websites Heavens-Above, Star Dash, Orbital Radar and Find Starlink.

Be sure to keep an eye on our Starship Flight 15 live blog for all the latest news along with our launch timings article containing details on how to watch SpaceX's potentially historic orbital launch attempt.

Editor's Note: If you capture a photo of Starship and want to share it with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.title: 'Warhammer Survivors' is the perfect gateway into the 40K universe
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.author: Fran Ruiz
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.text:
This Vampire Survivors spin-off has a lot of love for the famous grimdark sci-fi universe, but without the intimidatingly dense lore and complex systems.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We've had no shortage of great Warhammer 40K games lately, but most aren't exactly aimed at the casual crowd. Warhammer Survivors changes that, finally providing curious gamers with an easy entry point into the grim darkness of the 41st millennium.

Developed by Auroch Digital (in collaboration with Vampire Survivors' Poncle), this new spin on the survivors-like roguelite subgenre mixes the sci-fi 40,000 setting with the pure fantasy Age of Sigmar universe. This means heroes and enemies from all over the Warhammer mythos meet together in a bite-sized game that anyone can figure out and enjoy in less than five minutes.

When you look at the alternatives, that's a remarkable achievement for a franchise that's notoriously hard (and often expensive) to get into.

Warhammer Survivors isn't bogged down by dense lore, involved mechanics, or massive campaign playthroughs. It's more of an "inspired by" effort that gives casuals a small taste of the series' iconic characters — including Boltgun's Malum Caedo — and factions like the terrifying Tyranids, the raucous Orks, and the foul forces of Chaos.

All of 40K's (and Age of Sigmar's) recognizable elements are on display, but they serve more as flavoring sprinkled on top of Vampire Survivors' successful formula.

If you're new to the Survivors-like subgenre, it's a unique gaming experience. You battle an endless onslaught of enemies that slowly march towards you, with your character passively attacking automatically. You only need to move them around sprawling arenas and select level-up upgrades and items after collecting enough gems (skulls in this case).

The moment-to-moment gameplay is as simple as it can get outside of walking sims and interactive "experiences," but there's a deceiving depth to item synergies and how to correctly "build" characters to endure all the carnage.

Unlike Poncle's original game, Warhammer Survivors struggles a bit to get going. The early hours are sluggish until you unlock certain meta upgrades, but its still got that Vampire Survivors magic at its core.

As far as "podcast/gym games" go, this is a perfect fit. There's just enough going on to keep one's brain engaged, but minimal inputs and a tight overarching design lead to a rhythm that's easy to get into without using much brainpower. It's oddly satisfying to weave through enemies and level up your firepower, watching a single Astra Militarum grunt grow into a full Lasgun-spamming, chainsword-wielding wrecking ball.

Achievement and unlock hunters will find enough to bite into here, too. It's unclear if the devs will continue to add more Warhammer 40K and Age of Sigmar deep cuts to this game via DLCs and free updates, but those universes have daunting depths to explore. This really could become a gateway game for future 40K fans: by the time they realize they're hooked, they'll already have 2000 pts of space marines painted and ready to play.

As massive sci-fi and fantasy properties try to aggressively expand and absorb more and more fans, it's easy to pander to already-converted diehards too much. And sure, we can't wait for strategy heavyweights like Dawn of War 4 and Total War: WH40K either, but they're hardly good recommendations for folks who don't even know what a Space Marine is or why the robotic Necrons are so grumpy.

Warhammer Survivors won't answer those questions beyond the surface-level iconography, but it's fun enough to push those curious to dig deeper and embrace the same material in more mature video game genres... and maybe even pick up a few miniatures.

Warhammer Survivors is now available on PC (Steam & GOG), PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 1/2, and mobile (iOS & Android). It's also playable on Game Pass.

https://www.space.com/astronomy/dark-mat.title: Dark matter breakthrough coming? Euclid space telescope unveils its 1st look into the dark universe (video)
https://www.space.com/astronomy/dark-mat.author: Robert Lea
https://www.space.com/astronomy/dark-mat.text:
"So much discovery is yet to come."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the Euclid space telescope released its first major batch of data, capturing the light of more than a billion objects over an area of sky as big as 9,500 full moons. The data release lays the foundation for one of the largest-ever 3D maps of the cosmos and many groundbreaking discoveries about the nature of dark energy and dark matter.

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid space telescope has been called the "Dark Universe Detective" because of its capability to investigate the dual mysteries of dark matter, the universe's most mysterious stuff, and dark energy, the force accelerating the expansion of the universe. Collectively, these cosmic elements are sometimes referred to as the dark universe.

The new data release, designated DR1-Foundation, was built from 13 months of observations and is accompanied by a multitude of images, including large sky mosaics. It marks the first major release of mission data since Euclid launched in mid-2023.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," ESA's Director of Science, Carole Mundell said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery in a new regime for astronomy and demonstrating the excellence of European technology, science and international collaboration."

The ESA put into raw numbers the sheer number of celestial objects viewed by the Dark Universe Detective and contained in DR1-Foundation. That includes light spectra from 160 million sources, over 900 million galaxies, and 60 million candidates for quasars, regions of space dominated by feeding supermassive black holes.

"This is a change in scale from Euclid's previous releases, which included a few days of observations over around 60 degrees squared of sky," ESA's Euclid project scientist Valeria Pettorino said. "We're now releasing more than a year of data covering a significantly larger area. This unlocks groundbreaking science."

Euclid can see such a vast number of cosmic objects thanks to the fact that its space-based position helps it avoid interference caused by Earth's atmosphere.

This includes clusters of galaxies and even larger superclusters. The study of these objects, some of the largest structures in the cosmos, can reveal how matter came together across the larger network of gas, dust and dark matter called the cosmic web.

"Euclid doesn't just look far back in time  — it does so across huge areas of sky," Euclid Consortium member Barbara Sartoris of JL Lagrange Laboratory, Nice, France, explained. "This gives us an unprecedented view of large samples of ancient galaxy clusters that were previously out of reach.

"We will explore these in the coming months to learn how these giants grew, and decipher what they reveal about the dark universe."

Another exciting element of the new Euclid data release is the 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates catalogued by the space telescope. Gravitational lensing is an element of the universe first explained in Einstein magnum opus, general relativity, in 1915.

General relativity says that objects with mass cause the very fabric of space to warp, and that gravity arises from this warping. But there is another consequence. When light passes this curvature, its usually straight path is curved. That means when light from a single background source passes an object with great mass, like a galaxy or galaxy cluster, a strong gravitational lens, it can arrive at our telescopes at different times.

As a result of this strong lensing, background sources can be greatly amplified. It is an effect that the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has been using to great effect to study galaxies in the early universe.

Thus, the prospect of mapping 15,000 strong gravitational lenses is monumental, especially in studying the rate at which the universe is expanding and thus the effect of dark energy.

"Strong lensing provides unique insight into the dark universe, allowing us to 'weigh' individual galaxies, including their invisible dark matter, and explore how the universe is expanding," Natalie Lines of the University of Portsmouth, U.K., and member of the Euclid Consortium, said. "Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionize the field of strong lens discovery. That day is finally here."

Arguably, the most exciting thing about DR1-Foundation is that Euclid is just getting started. The area of sky covered from spring 2024 to spring 2025 represents just 14% of Euclid's target for its entire six-year survey.

That means whatever scientists discover from this data release could be the tip of the iceberg in terms of how the Dark Universe Detective will change our understanding of the cosmos.

"DR1-Foundation includes raw data, calibrated images, catalogues, and spectra over a huge sky area, with enough statistics touncover even rare objects," Valeria said. "It will be used to map the large-scale structure of the universe in unprecedented detail.

"So much discovery is yet to come."

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: Pakistani astronaut set to become 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station this month
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Andrew Jones
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
"Having the Pakistani astronaut on board China's spaceships will mark the first-ever joint mission of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An astronaut from Pakistan is set to launch on China's Shenzhou 24 mission in the coming weeks and become the first-ever international visitor to the Tiangong space station.

A pair of astronaut candidates from Pakistan have been training at the Astronaut Centre of China in Beijing, following an agreement reached between China and Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025 and a subsequent selection process.

China's human spaceflight agency confirmed in a Nov. 7 press statement that the upcoming Shenzhou 24 mission will carry one of the astronauts. The agency also released a mission patch.

"China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Nov. 9. "Having the Pakistani astronaut on board China's spaceships will mark the first-ever joint mission of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program."

It is not yet known which of the two candidates will fly on Shenzhou 24. They were named in Pakistani press reports as Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, both pilots from the country's military forces. The pair were chosen from a wider pool of around 20 finalists.

The chosen candidate will fly as a payload specialist on Shenzhou 24 along with two Chinese colleagues, while the other will be on standby as a backup. While the Chinese astronauts will be starting a six-month-long stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will spend roughly a week in orbit aboard Tiangong during a standard crew rotation period. He will then return to Earth aboard the departing Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, along with two Chinese astronauts who will have completed a six-month-long stay in orbit.

The arrangement means changes to China's usual "three in, three out" Tiangong crew rotations. One of the three Shenzhou 23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong on May 24, will stay aboard and complete China's first-ever year-long stay in orbit, while the Pakistani astronaut will take their seat aboard Shenzhou 23 to return home.

During his stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will be responsible for four research payloads selected from more than 300 proposals, according to Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO.

China has not announced a timeline for the launch of the Shenzhou 24 mission, but it is expected to lift off before the end of November. The Shenzhou 23 astronauts currently aboard Tiangong are closing in on 180 days in orbit, nearing an end to their six months in space.

Shenzhou 24 will launch from Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert on a Long March 2F rocket. The identities of the crew for China's human spaceflight missions are typically closely guarded, and will only be revealed in a press conference a day ahead of launch. Shenzhou 24's Long March 2F rocket will be rolled out to the pad around a week ahead of launch.

The partnership between the two countries has already produced Chinese-launched Pakistani satellites, including a lunar cubesat, and a Pakistani-built rover due to fly on the Chang'e-8 lunar landing mission.

Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.author: Jeff Spry
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.text:
'Humans are always the same. Desperate. Volatile.'

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of the most anticipated fall TV series, "Blade Runner 2099," recently dropped its final neon-tinted trailer, and now we’ve finally got a handle on the plot dynamics of this dystopian thriller set in the cyberpunk world of Ridley Scott's original.

Prime Video's bold and brooding 8-episode series lands Nov. 25 as a tangential sequel to Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049," unfolding some 50 years after the 2017 feature film. Now the artificial inmates are running the asylum when violent replicant uprisings flip the script, causing humanity to become second-class citizens.

"In Los Angeles 2099, Cora (Hunter Schafer) lived her entire life on the run, a chameleon forced to adopt numerous identities," states Prime Video's synopsis. "To secure a stable future for her brother, she assumes one final identity and is forced to partner with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Blade Runner who’s confronting the end of her life. The two are pulled into a widening conspiracy that poses an existential threat to a city that’s fighting to be reborn."

This engrossing final trailer reveals more of the detailed noir world and Cora's plight to blend into society as a Blade Runner who links up with Olwen, an aging replicant exterminator, for an uneasy partnership. Here, a tense scene plays out in this preview as Cora undergoes an intense police station screening while being used as a resistance pawn to help take back the city from usurping androids. But another deep mystery lies hidden in plain sight!

"You have to see the lie that is in front of you," warns Yeoh's dying synthetic cop.

"Blade Runner 2099" sports a spirited cast that includes Dimitri Abold ("The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes") and Lewis Gribben ("Somewhere Boy”) in collaboration with Katelyn Rose Downey ("The Nun II"), Daniel Rigby ('Renegade Nell"), Johnny Harris ("A Gentleman in Moscow"), Amy Lennox ("Only Child"), Sheila Atim ("The Woman King") and Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon”).

Delivered by creator and showrunner Silka Louisa ("Shining Girls"), and executive produced by Silka Louisa and Ridley Scott’s Scott Free Productions, "Blade Runner 2099" lands on Prime Video beginning Nov. 25, 2026.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/12/brai.author: Jonathan Wosen
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/12/brai.text:
A massive scientific collaboration meant to unravel the mysteries of the human brain has produced the most detailed map yet of the basal ganglia, a region closely associated with a wide array of psychiatric and neurologic disorders.

Researchers profiled more than 25 million cells, generating a deluge of data that allowed them to generate a “parts list” of what cells are present in the basal ganglia and how they’re arranged. In the process scientists discovered a new type of neuron that appears to play a role in schizophrenia. They also identified cell types linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Demonstrating the value of the work, the scientists produced preliminary evidence that they can use their more detailed understanding of brain cell types to deliver therapies with increased precision. Authors working in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease showed that a gene therapy designed to work in a subset of basal ganglia cells was as effective as a blanket approach; it was also safer.

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/new.title: New ACS Guidelines Take Firmer Stance on PSA Screening
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/new.text:
M. Alexander Otto, MMSc-PA

In new prostate cancer screening guidelines, the American Cancer Society (ACS) has called for routine prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing of average-risk men every 2 years from ages 50 through 69 years.

Among the 10 main recommendations, the group also advises repeat testing 2 weeks to 3 months later for men with PSA levels of 3 ng/mL or higher to confirm persistent elevations before further evaluation.

The recommendations are a major departure from the group’s last guidelines in 2010, which were far less prescriptive and recommended that men be told about the uncertainties, risks, and potential benefits of screening, and then make a decision with their healthcare provider about going forward.

ACS’s new advice also goes further than the US Preventive Services Task Force’s (USPSTF's) most recent guidelines from 2018, which said the decision to screen should be an individual one, given the small potential benefit of reducing the chance of death from prostate cancer, balanced against the risk of overtreating clinically insignificant disease. USPSTF made no suggestions for screening intervals in 2018 and gave routine screening a grade of C, given the uncertainties.

What has changed over the years, leading to ACS’s more certain and detailed advice, is that “we have more confidence now about when screening should start, what the interval should be, and that if it's done properly, the benefits outweigh the risks,” said ACS cancer epidemiologist Robert Smith, PhD, senior author of both the new and the 2010 guidelines.

“We've got quite convincing data that screening is associated with reduction in the incidence rate of advanced disease and deaths, and, over time, there's been real progress in the steps that you can take to avoid detecting and overtreating low-risk disease,” Smith told Medscape Medical News. Such steps include repeat testing of elevated PSA levels, MRI and biomarker evaluation of persistently elevated values, and active surveillance for low-risk disease, all measures included in ACS’s new guidelines.

The 2025 update of the European ERSPC trial was particularly influential to the ACS, after it showed the endurance of the mortality reduction with routine screening over nearly a quarter century of follow-up. “Once the ERSPC data were out, we said it’s time for an update,” Smith said.

At the same time, it has become clear that the failure of the US PLCO trial to show a benefit of screening was because the trial was flawed: PSA testing in the control group was nearly as high as in the screening arm, and quite a few men in the screening arm with positive findings had no additional workup, among other issues.

“So, we don't have this distraction” anymore that one major trial was positive and the other major trial was negative, which led to uncertainty, Smith said.

ACS’s new guidelines are largely in line with 2026 prostate cancer screening updates from two other influential groups, the American Urological Association and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN).

There are some differences in the details. NCCN, for instance, recommends routine screening for average-risk men from age 45 to 75 years.

“We certainly favor our recommendations compared with those of other organizations,” but overall “they share more in common than they do in differences, and an effort to achieve high adherence to any one of these [guidelines] would be better for men than the situation we are in right now,” where self-reported screening rates in the general public are only about 35%-40%, Smith said.

Ultimately, he added, “we hope that [our] new recommendations result in an increase in the uptake of prostate cancer screening. It saves lives, it reduces the risk of advanced disease, and we have ways to avoid the risks.”

USPSTF, meanwhile, is updating its 2018 guidelines.

Smith had no relevant disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Q&A: Can combining two diets help prolong life?
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom; Valter Longo, PhD
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

ORLANDO — A scientific diet joining two popular patterns could be helpful for longevity, according to a speaker at the American College of Lifestyle Medicine annual meeting.

Valter Longo, PhD, the Edna Jones Professor of Gerontology and a professor of biological science at the University of Southern California Leonard Davis School of Gerontology, offered a presentation on the interconnected issues of diet, longevity and disease.

Healio spoke with Longo, who is also the director of the USC Longevity Institute, to learn more about the two diets he focused on, who benefits the most from them and more.

Healio: Why did you decide to present on this topic? Why is it important for healthcare providers to know about?

Longo: We’ve been working on this topic for 30 years, and we’re trying to convince everybody — me and many others in the field of aging and longevity — that medicine should focus on longevity first. This idea is now something that is slowly getting out there. I’m trying to also present interventions that are feasible and clinically proven to be effective, or on their way to being proven to be effective.

Healio: You discussed the periodic fasting-mimicking diet and the everyday low-protein plus moderate methionine-supplemented longevity diet. What does the research say on these dietary patterns?

Longo: The periodic fasting-mimicking diet is a diet tested in over 45 clinical trials, mostly by independent universities, and the idea is: can you mimic water-only fasting while providing a very healthy, vegan-based diet? It is a low-calorie, low-protein, low-sugar, high-fat, 100% plant-based. So, the idea there — it goes back 20 years — is that the most powerful intervention in history against aging is called calorie restriction. Calorie restriction really is something very simple: What happens if you take a person who eats normally and you reduce their calories by 25%? This has been tested in lots of clinical trials. There are very powerful effects, but also very powerful side effects. So, the fasting-mimicking diet is there to try to get the effects of the calorie restriction without the burden and the side effects.

Our question has been: What if you act for only 5 days once a month or less? Let’s say once every 3 months or once every 4 months, do you get effects that are long lasting? Many of the trials are showing exactly that. You get long-lasting effects that have much less to do with fat loss or weight loss; and more with these periods of fasting mimicking that created a reset: A metabolic reset, a stem cell reset, a cellular reprogramming reset, autophagy and microbiota — those are the ones we’ve clearly seen in animal models, but we are also observing effects in humans clinical trials consistent with those in rodents.

The everyday longevity diet is something completely different — learning from Okinawa, Japan; Loma Linda [California]; Italy, and combining it with mouse data and rat data and monkey data but also clinical trials and epidemiological analyses we have been studying the characteristics of the ideal everyday diet and the molecular mechanisms that make it effective?

First of all, let’s understand what it is about the Mediterranean diet or the Okinawa diet that has been so successful in making lots of people live to 100 and past — and very healthy, by the way — and then transform it into a mouse diet, and then go back to the human epidemiological data and test the hypothesis built by the mouse data. That’s what we did in the recent paper, showing that a low-protein, low-amino acid, low-methionine diet is great — just like calorie restriction — but it causes a lot of problems. But if you just keep it like that — like the old Okinawa diet or the old Japanese diet or the old Mediterranean diet — mice get frail. If you instead introduce modern levels of methionine, the frailty goes away, but all the beneficial effects don’t go away. We see effects on GLP-1s in mice. We see effects on a factor called [fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21)]. We see effects on growth hormone, which reaches very high levels, but we can keep a growth factor that is associated with aging, cancer and cancer metastasis called [insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)], lower.

The longevity diet that we described is now trying to transform the popular diets into a scientific diet that understands how each component — and even each component of the component; proteins and then methionine within proteins, protects against aging and disease. Is it simply that you need to eat plant proteins? It doesn’t look like it. It looks like you have to have the right range of methionine but a low-protein diet to get the effects.

Healio: What are the potential benefits to these diets?

Longo: The fasting mimicking diet’s most powerful effects have to do with shrinking systems, organs and cells, and re-expanding them. It takes 5 days to strongly activate autophagy, the self-feeding process within the cell, in different system and to get the activation of stem cell and of cellular reprogramming, etc. The fasting-mimicking diet has a more rejuvenating effect, whereas the longevity diet has a more continuous delay effect on lowering biological aging and delaying the diseases associated with it.

In one case, we could show that we could damage the kidney of a rat we could damage the pancreas, the gut, or the brain of a mouse, then we start with the fasting-mimicking diet cycles, and see a reversal or a partial reversal of that damage or disease. The longevity diet doesn’t have that job; it’s more about achieving very beneficial effects by delaying aging and damage.

Healio: Are there any downsides to these diets? Any patients who should avoid them?

Longo: Yes. For the fasting mimicking diet, anybody that is underweight, pregnant, for example. But, in general, most people between 20 and 75 or 80 years can do it. After 65 or 70, probably a geriatrician should approve it after establishing the health and frailty status of someone. If there is a disease or a drug prescribed, it’s best for the nutritionist to work with the doctor to determine if it’s best to recommend the fasting-mimicking diet to these patients.

The longevity diet instead is modulated based on age and needs, so it’d be good to have a nutritionist follow a person at least initially. But it really has a lot of similarities with the Mediterranean diet or Okinawa. I would say most people can do it; but again, it’s best to talk to a nutritionist or dietitian to make sure that the person doesn’t become malnourished by making big changes to their diet and all of a sudden eating less protein or micronutrients than minimal.

Healio: What is the take-home message here?

Longo: Healthcare providers should have both in their toolkit. There are published clinical trials on Crohn’s disease as well as colitis and the fasting-mimicking diet. There are also published clinical trials on the fasting-mimicking diet and cancer and there are a number of clinical trials on diabetes, pre-diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity and the fasting-mimicking diet. For many, many conditions, I think that the physician should consider fasting-mimicking diet cycles together with standard of care but also to potentially reduce drug use as it has been demonstrated in diabetes studies. For example, in the Stanford trial on Crohn’s disease, the drugs plus the fasting-mimicking diet were much better in causing inflammatory bowel disease regression compared with the drugs alone. And the same was true for diabetes; almost nobody who was on drugs alone was able to reduce drug use in the long run, but in one trial, 70% of those on fasting-mimicking diet cycles reduced diabetes drug dose/number.

So, where drugs often manage the disease. The fasting-mimicking diet helps patients and doctors lower the drug use by patients. It brings them to a more healthy, more youthful state. Physicians should consider using the fasting-mimicking diet also because its safety profile is remarkable, and the efficacy profile is remarkable.

And the longevity diet, I think, should start guiding those lifestyle doctors who are looking for what the ideal characteristics of an everyday diet are. The longevity diet is not a Mediterranean diet or Japanese diet, it’s really about a personalized diet that considers the effect of each ingredient on aging and health and not just a diet that happens to be associated with longevity in a particular region. So, for many it would recommend nuts, but many may be intolerant or allergic to different types of nuts and different people may turn to different types of nuts to get the nutrients and the beneficial effects. However, it’s a scientific diet that now has decades of safety and efficacy support from studies on the diets from which it is derived: the Mediterranean diet, Okinawa, Loma Linda, etc.

Valter Longo, PhD, can be reached at primarycare@healio.com.

Disclosures: Longo reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: CRISPR gene-editing therapy lowers triglycerides in early study
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — A gene-editing therapy targeting hepatic ANGPTL3 lowered triglycerides in patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia, according to results of a phase 1b study presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

Ashish Sarraju, MD, cardiologist in the section of preventive cardiology in the Tomsich Family Department of Cardiovascular Medicine of The Sydell and Arnold Miller Family Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute, Cleveland Clinic, presented the results of the study of 10 patients (median age, 56.5 years; 60% men; median triglycerides, 1,067.7 mg/dL) who received IV administration of CTX310 (CRISPR Therapeutics), a single-dose CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing therapy. Patients received 40 mg if their body weight was 85 kg or less or 50 mg if their body weight was more than 85 kg.

“So far, the safety and efficacy profile is promising and [CTX310] represents a new frontier for drug development for severe hypertriglyceridemia,” Sarraju said during a presentation.

CTX310 is not yet approved for commercial use in the United States. A once-monthly injection, olezarsen (Tryngolza, Ionis), is approved for patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia, and a once per 3 months injection, plozasiran (Redemplo, Arrowhead), is approved for patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome and is being considered by the FDA for patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia.

At 30 days, the median percent change was –65.3% for ANGPTL3, –62.8% for triglycerides, –60.5% for directly measured serum triglycerides, –50.9% for non-HDL, –16.4% for LDL and –23.4% for apolipoprotein B, Sarraju said.

One patient was a nonresponder and had an increase in ANGPTL3 of 7.2% at 30 days, but five had a decrease of more than 80% and the other four had drops ranging from 46.5% to 73.2%, he said.

Triglycerides decreased by 28.2% in the nonresponder but by more than 80% in three respondents, with the others having a decline of 42.4% to 70.8%, he said.

The 30-day absolute change from baseline in triglycerides ranged from a drop of 299.4 mg/dL to a drop of 1,971.6 mg/dL, according to the researchers.

There were no serious adverse events related to CTX310, and of the four adverse events reported, three were grade 1, while the grade 2 adverse event was an infusion-related reaction of mild back pain in a patient with a history of back pain, Sarraju said.

“I think severe hypertriglyceridemia is generally a challenging condition to treat in the lipid disorder world, because of, until recently, a lack of proven therapies that can reduce triglycerides and also reduce acute pancreatitis, but also because these patients have concurrent cardiovascular risk,” Sarraju told Healio. “And so the ability to offer somebody a one-time treatment to mitigate their risk for severe triglyceride elevations, I can imagine that being quite compelling to a lot of individuals. I don’t think this is meant to replace all the other therapies. I think the idea here is for us to grow our armamentarium with different types of agents, different durations of actions and different tolerability profiles, so you can fit the correct therapy to the correct patient at the correct time. So I think if the evidence for efficacy and safety bears out in larger trials, and this does become available, I think this would be a very compelling offer for patients with extremely high triglycerides in terms of being a one-time therapy, not having to take repeat therapies, and then promoting shared decision-making now with an armamentarium that’s much broader than what we had 20 years ago.”

“We just witnessed a first: a gene-editing study in severe hypertriglyceridemia that led to sustained reductions in triglycerides and related lipid compounds,” Vera A. Bittner, MD, MSPH, FAHA, professor of medicine and Endowed Scholar in Cardiovascular Disease Prevention at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, said in a discussant presentation. “It’s a great time to be a preventive cardiologist or clinical lipidologist because we now have an opportunity to individualize treatment for each patient based on underlying pathophysiology risk, and also based on patient preferences for dosing frequency or adverse effects. But in order to implement such a strategy successfully, we need to be absolutely sure that we preserve these treatments for people who have truly persistent severe hypertriglyceridemia, so recommendations about lifestyle and management of secondary causes will not change. I think we need to get much better at phenotyping at the point of care.”

Ashish Sarraju, MD, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Sarraju A, et al. LBS.05. New frontiers in cardiometabolic risk reduction. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Bittner reports serving as a site principal investigator for trials sponsored by Amgen and Novartis and serving on a data safety monitoring board for Eli Lilly and Verve Therapeutics. Sarraju reports serving as a consultant for or conducting trial leadership activities for Arrowhead, AstraZeneca, CRISPR Therapeutics, Ionis, Kalexo, Kardigan, Kylonova, Mineralys, NewAmsterdam Pharma, Novartis and vTv Therapeutics. The study was funded by CRISPR Therapeutics.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.title: Nvidia’s next CEO: The outside contenders to succeed Jensen Huang
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.author: Sheryl Estrada
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.text:
The biggest guessing game in business has begun: Who can fill Jensen Huang’s shoes?

Colette Kress, chief financial officer at Nvidia since 2013, was appointed interim CEO of the company on Thursday. Kress will also continue in her CFO role as the board conducts its search for Jensen Huang’s permanent successor.

“Colette is very much the right interim CEO,” Scott W. Simmons, co-managing partner of executive search firm Crist Kolder Associates, told Fortune. But Simmons, who has worked in executive recruiting for almost 30 years, thinks Nvidia’s board will seek a technologist as Huang’s permanent successor, potentially from outside the company.

If Nvidia goes with an external candidate for the CEO job, Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at The Futurum Group, is putting his money on Arm CEO Rene Haas.

“He spent seven years at Nvidia and understands Jensen’s culture; and what makes him interesting is that Nvidia’s Grace and Vera CPUs run on Arm architecture,” Boloor wrote in an X post. “So while he missed [the] rise of NVLink, Mellanox and rack-scale AI he understands [the] CPU side of Nvidia’s platform better than almost anyone else on the outside.”

Sam Sugarman, a venture capital and private equity investor who co-founded and leads the VC/PE Secondaries practice at Concordia Capital, also placed Haas on his list of external candidates.

Haas would bring a combination of Nvidia experience and public-company leadership, having steered Arm through its 2023 IPO and expanded its business beyond processor licensing. His background spans engineering, product strategy and sales. But his familiarity with Nvidia dates to an earlier era: he left in 2013. The board will have to assess whether running Arm has prepared him for Nvidia’s much larger, more complex business.

Sugarman also pointed to AMD CEO Lisa Su as a potential successor to Huang. Su (who ironically happens to be a distant cousin of Huang’s) would bring a combination of semiconductor engineering credentials and a proven record of running a major chipmaker. She has led AMD since 2014, overseeing a turnaround that made it a formidable competitor in processors and a challenger to Nvidia in AI chips. That experience could appeal to a board. But recruiting her would mean persuading a sitting CEO to leave the company she rebuilt.

Meanwhile, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told Fortune that he sees Tim Cook, the former CEO of Apple; Tom Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud; and Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, “as the top three external candidates for Nvidia’s CEO role.”

Cook would bring experience with a challenge few executives have faced: succeeding a technology company’s defining leader. Cook took over from Steve Jobs and spent 15 years running Apple before becoming executive chairman in September. Cook’s mastery of supply chains and logistics would be a good fit at Nvidia, and the fact that Apple has developed its own processors in-house over the past decade means Cook has some direct experience in the chips business. His continuing work on Apple’s international relationships would also be relevant to a company navigating geopolitical pressures.

But his continuing responsibilities at Apple as chairman could complicate the prospect of recruiting him. That said, Cook has the support of one high-profile observer: President Trump posted on Truth Social Thursday that Cook should replace Huang.

Kurian would offer a connection to Nvidia’s AI infrastructure business. Before taking over Google Cloud in 2019, Kurian spent 22 years at Oracle, ultimately becoming president of product development. At Google Cloud, he has also worked closely with Nvidia through the companies’ AI infrastructure partnership. The question is how readily that experience would translate to leading the chipmaker itself.

Arora would bring the experience of a sitting public-company chief executive with a career spanning enterprise technology, global sales and investment. Before joining the cybersecurity company in 2018, Arora was president and COO of SoftBank and held senior commercial roles at Google, including chief business officer. His appeal as a candidate could depend on whether Nvidia wants a strategist who can build around its technical leaders.

There may be pros and cons for each potential candidate, but the board’s choice will ultimately determine Nvidia’s fate. “There’s such a small pool to fish in when you think about people capable of stepping into this,” Simmons said.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.summary: Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO of the company on Thursday. The board is looking for a permanent successor to Jensen Huang, who left in 2013. The company has been looking for an external candidate for the CEO job.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.title: Nvidia’s new chairman Harvey Jones is a ‘charming elder statesman’ set to lead the search for the next CEO. But did he enable the current crisis?
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.author: Emily Forlini
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.text:
In the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning departure from the company, employees received an email from someone most of them had probably never heard of before, even though he’d been affiliated with the company and its board for decades. His name is Harvey Jones, and he was writing to tell them that he’d just been appointed the company’s first-ever Chair of the Board, and that Nvidia CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO.

“I’m writing to share an important update,” Jones’ note began, according to leaked screenshots of the email. He then tried to reassure employees no doubt left shaken by the past weeks’ revelations and the sudden departure of Jensen Huang, a man who co-founded the company and, until today, had been synonymous with its success. “The Board takes seriously our duty as steward of this great company,” Jones said.

That sense of calm and confidence is something Jones is known for, according to two longtime friends and former coworkers. Although Jones, 73, may not be a household name, he has worked in the technology industry, and in semiconductors, for over 30 years, according to his biography on the Nvidia website. He founded two companies, served as CEO of another, and since 2004 has been managing partner of investment firm Square Wave Ventures. He’s been on Nvidia’s board since 1993, the year Huang founded the company.

Jones comes from a successful Connecticut family—his full name is Harvey Jones III—with an “old school, conservative” way about him, Penny Herscher, who has known Jones since 1984 and used to work for him, tells Fortune. His father was a U.S. Army Colonel and church-goer, who then became a vice president at the Walt Disney World Company. Jones himself is a billionaire, which Forbes says is “almost entirely due to his Nvidia director’s compensation” and the fact that he owns 0.03% of the company.

“Harvey has a deep sense of history,” Chris Rowen, who cofounded the semiconductor processor company Tensilica with Jones in 1997, tells Fortune. He has a house on Nantucket and enjoys sailing classic yachts and fine art. “He has a smooth polish,” Rowen said. But Rowen also said that, despite outward appearances, there’s nothing effete about Jones. “He is such a gentleman, so articulate, and so well-sanded on the outside that you might worry there isn’t a deep fierceness and technical insight inside, but beneath that smooth exterior is a really bright, insightful, aggressive guy.”

At a time of great turbulence, Jones can offer Nvidia a “steady pair of hands” to “sort out” its next chapter, Herscher said. She described him as a “charming elder statesman” who at this point in his career is likely “very hard to ruffle.”

Jones and Rowen played distinct roles while leading the team at Tensilica. While Rowen played the role of technical leader and mentor, Jones was a skilled manager who helped keep the team on track. “His experience was such that he exuded this confidence and experience,” Rowan said. “If he thought we were on the right track, people were instantly comforted. He really communicated a sense of the larger picture and gave people a great deal of confidence that the wider world needed and approved of what we were doing.”

“He’s very strategic,” Herscher said. “I’m sure he’s right now figuring out the right strategy and steps going forward. He’s always looking around corners.”

Jones’ experience and board tenure also begs the question of how he failed to identify the enormous reputational risk of Huang’s affairs, three of which are known as of this writing. Huang also notoriously had many reports, up to 60 at one point, and no clear successor or succession planning.

“Jones may be the right person to steady the ship, but his longevity is both his greatest qualification and the strongest reason to scrutinize his leadership,” Jonathan Tower, managing partner at the VC firm Catapult tells Fortune. “The board cannot simply present itself as the solution without examining its role in creating the problem.”

Case in point: Huang’s affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, was known inside the company, and appears to violate its code of conduct, The New York Times reported. The code of conduct instructs all employees to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships.” The board promises to promptly investigate all reports of misconduct. What happened?

Jones will likely lead the process to select Nvidia’s next CEO, Herscher said, though she had not spoken to him about it directly, and Nvidia did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. But that’s typically how the process would work in a situation like this, Herscher said, drawing on her knowledge from sitting on three public boards, and being the co-founder of The Chairs Circle, which runs educational programs for board chairs.  The fact that Jones also sits on Nvidia’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee makes it even more likely that he will lead this process, she said, as usually that committee is involved in the process.

The search will likely take at least a few months, Herscher said. The board will likely hire a recruiter to identify candidates—something Bloomberg reported this week that Nvidia has already done. That firm will likely do the first outreach, Herscher said, and then Jones will speak to the most promising candidates, along with the rest of the internal search committee.

All signs point to Jones being an effective recruiter, with a wide net of contacts in the industry, Herscher said.

Longtime technology executive Chi-Foo Chan described Jones as “a very persuasive guy” in a 2019 oral history interview with the Computer History Museum, referring to the conversations the two had when Jones convinced Chan to join Synopsys, the electronics company Jones led from 1987 to 1998.

Nvidia shareholders are hoping those skills can wrangle a big fish to come in as Nvidia’s next CEO. Potential successors may include Rene Hass, who is currently the CEO of the chipmaker Arm.  President Trump, who allegedly did not act on reports of Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy, suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook might be a good pick.

Whoever it is, they’ll need the right operational and product development chops to keep the GPUs flowing.
