https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ai-indust.title: AI industry execs brace for future without leading hype man, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ai-indust.author: Beatrice Nolan, Allie Garfinkle, Jeremy Kahn
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ai-indust.text:
Tech industry insiders awoke Thursday morning with an unfamiliar, and somewhat alarming notion to contemplate: life without Jensen Huang.

Huang’s abrupt resignation as CEO leaves one of the world’s most valuable companies without the leader who has steered it for the past 33 years; the person who almost singlehandedly transformed Nvidia from a small maker of video game graphics chips into the driving force of the AI boom.

“NVIDIA’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom,” Stephanie Balaouras, Forrester’s VP, group research director, told Fortune.

The importance of Nvidia, and of Huang, to the AI industry extends well beyond the company’s own P&L statement. In addition to being the leading maker of the GPU chips powering AI services like ChatGPT and Claude, Nvidia has become the AI industry’s “central bank” financing scores of other companies. And then there’s Huang’s unique standing as AI’s senior statesman and cheerleader on everything from AI regulation to industrial policy.

Whether the AI industry turns out to have lost its most famous champion with the ignominious exit of Huang and his famous black leather coat, or a more crucial, Jenga-like piece may be the most important economic question to be answered in the coming weeks and months.

“Obviously Nvidia is more than Jensen Huang, but he kind of championed a whole range of investments,” a VC investor focused on early-stage companies told Fortune.

“There is a question around whether the pace of investment in AI and the size of the amounts of capital going into companies can be continued. Because by any stretch of the imagination, it’s been quite extreme,” the investor said.

In the immediate aftermath of the news, the stock market appears to be keeping its composure. While shares of Nvidia were down 6.3% in midday trading on Thursday, and certain AI-linked stocks took a hit, the broader market reaction was relatively muted, with the Nasdaq down only 95 points.

But with spending on AI and data centers so important to the broader U.S. economy, the extent of the potential fallout from the Nvidia shakeup is difficult to overstate.

Looming largest on the horizon is Anthropic’s widely anticipated initial public offering, scheduled to occur next week. The Anthropic IPO (along with OpenAI’s IPO expected in 2027) represent make-or-break moments for the AI industry—closely watched events that will serve as proxies for the health, and momentum, of the AI business.

If nothing else, one startup founder told Fortune, the Nvidia drama raises the stakes for Anthropic’s upcoming IPO: “If the Anthropic IPO doesn’t go well and if the OpenAI IPO [down the line] doesn’t go well, there’s a question of: Is there a path to profitability for any players in the AI space?”

Antropic is seeking to raise upwards of $60 billion in the offering slated for November 18, giving the five-year old AI company a valuation that could exceed $1.4 trillion when it makes its expected Wall Street debut next week.

Karl Alomar, a partner at venture firm M13, argued that investors will recognize the strength in Anthropic’s business, regardless of the Nvidia shakeup.

“From where I stand, Anthropic is still in as good, as strong and as good a position as it was before this news came out,” Alomar said.

“I’m not sure it’ll have a massive impact on them. Anthropic’s numbers are fantastic, and they’ve clearly shown that they have excess capacity for what they need,” he said.

Anthropic’s business prospects are closely intertwined with those of the cloud providers, which provide the data centers and compute capacity to train and run AI models like Claude. (According to Anthropic’s S-1 filing, it has roughly $900 billion in compute spending commitments over the next several decades.)

While the tech giants like Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft have the wherewithal to ride out whatever turbulence is caused by the changes at Nvidia, the situation may be trickier for the smaller “neo-cloud” companies—many financed by Nvidia—that buy Nvidia chips in bulk and rent out the computing power.

Huang has championed these neo-cloud companies because it was good for business and the company’s influence, Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners and one of the few on Wall Street with a sell rating on Nvidia’s stock. “He’d rather have 300 small customers who are dependent on him than three massive ones who you can’t negotiate with,” he said.

With Nvidia CFO Coleen Kress now serving as interim CEO, the company’s attitude towards neo-clouds could shift. According to a report in The Information on Thursday, Kress has occasionally pushed back against Huang’s deals in the AI ecosystem, including a deal to backstop $250 billion in credit for an OpenAI datacenter project.

The “Nvidia money train” that has kept parts of the market that propped up could come to an end, said one venture capital partner invested in numerous AI startups. “ The idea that they could count on Nvidia for future financing is unlikely.”

Shares of CoreWeave one of the leading neocloud providers were down 7.5% on Thursday, while Nebius Group, another neo-cloud company which gave a lighter-than-expected sales forecast during its quarterly earnings on Thursday, were down 18%.

Investors are likely to look harder at the numbers Huang used to justify the complex web of investments. Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business, expects investors and policymakers alike may start re-examining “Jensen math.”

U.S. policy towards data centers could also come in for harsher treatment, particularly after last week’s midterm elections in which voters overwhelmingly registered their opposition to having the facilities built in their communities.

Huang gave much of the industry credibility, even amid the backlash to datacenters. He was well-liked and not seen as a polarizing political figure, said Goldberg, of Seaport Research. But with Huang gone, the data center industry becomes “much more vulnerable to political pressure,” he said Goldberg.

Similarly, lawmakers advocating stricter regulation of AI technology, both the large language models as well as the chips that power the models, now have a much stronger hand. Huang was an outspoken proponent of loose regulations for AI. But his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy has destroyed his credibility on the regulatory issues.

“This guarantees new export controls,” Ed Mills, policy analyst at investment firm Raymond James, said of the spy scandal that contributed to Huang’s downfall. “It was extremely likely before the scandal and this is the accelerant to push it over the finish line.” Three bills proposing new export controls on AI chips and advanced semiconductor equipment are currently attached to the defense authorization bill awaiting passage on Capitol Hill.

It is also possible that Washington will enact licensing requirements or restrictions on open-source AI models. Huang had been a leading voice opposing such measures. Because the best open source models on the market have been created by Chinese AI labs, “open source equals China” in the minds of many lawmakers, particularly China hawks, Mills said. “If Washington is serious about trying to win the AI race against China we need to see regulations on open source,” he said.

Brad Carson, the former Democratic Congressman who is now president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a lobby group that supports AI regulation, said he was less certain of the threat Huang’s removal as CEO poses to open source AI. Even after Huang’s downfall, such licensing requirements are unlikely given the support open-source AI has among certain factions in Congress and the technical difficulty of designing effective rules for these models, he said.

The AI policy push will happen against the backdrop of a widening investigative effort, with Nvidia’s relationship with companies such as Megaspeed and Super Micro under the microscope.

“What’s happened at Nvidia is for Nvidia to address,” said Tony Ball, CEO of Entrust, a digital security company. “But in terms of the way AI is going to continue to add value to organizations and productivity, this was an inevitable structural challenge, and governance and policy issue that the world was going to have to wrestle to the ground.”
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/ai-indust.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as CEO of the company's largest chip maker. Huang has been the company’s chief executive for 33 years. Huang was an outspoken proponent of loose regulations for AI.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.title: ‘That Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago’: What Jensen Huang’s exit means for neoclouds
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.author: Catherina Gioino
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ne.text:
Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia hits the AI industry’s most indebted borrowers hardest, according to one investor who backs AI infrastructure.

Nvidia said Thursday that Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. His exit follows his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy, and following a board investigation into the affair. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and the board named Harvey Jones its first chair.

While Nvidia’s leadership switch-up is sending shockwaves across every industry that relies on its chips to those who simply have stock or their 401Ks resting in company, some say the companies that are most at risk are the so-called neoclouds that rely on Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia designs the chips that most AI models are trained on, and Taiwan’s TSMC manufactures them, and that’s a problem. So says Joe Kaiser, who started Switchyard Partners at the beginning of this year after serving as CEO of Mercato Partners, which managed about $1.5 billion.

Neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius buy those chips by the hundreds of thousands, fill data centers with them and rent the computing power to AI labs and other companies, competing with Amazon, Google and Microsoft.

But Nvidia does more than sell to them. It invests in them: the company held about $329 million in Nebius shares, for example, at the end of June. Nvidia also guarantees their business. In July, Nvidia began offering to rent back unused GPU capacity from neocloud partners at a fixed rate, a floor meant to make banks more willing to lend. The company later joined a $500 billion financing platform with six institutional partners, of which Nvidia may backstop up to $125 billion. That backstop, Kaiser said, posed an issue for what lenders are pricing.

“The chip isn’t what puts them at risk, but it’s the financial backstop that allows CoreWeave or Nebius to go get those hundreds of millions of dollars of debt from Blackstone and Brookfield,” Kaiser told Fortune. “Why is Blackstone willing to back a CoreWeave project? It’s because they know that there’s an Nvidia backstop, a written backstop, behind it, and so it lowers the risk, and then obviously lowers the interest rate.”

CoreWeave carried $35 billion in debt at the end of June, and lenders had grown wary of businesses that depend wholly on AI demand, well before Huang left.

“If the capital providers now say that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago, that puts those neocloud businesses at risk,” Kaiser said. “At the end of the day, this is a heavy-asset, infrastructure-based industry.”

OpenAI and SoftBank’s SB Energy may be the biggest beneficiaries of Nvidia’s backstops, with CoreWeave and Nebius close behind. Kaiser referenced how Nvidia has been in talks over a reported $250 billion backstop to help OpenAI lease an Ohio data center campus that SB Energy is developing.

Following Huang’s resignation, Neocloud stocks fell Thursday: CoreWeave dropped about 9%, giving back part of a 25% rally the day before. Nebius fell 16%, though it also issued weak full-year guidance the same day. Nvidia itself lost about $450 billion in market value in the days after Huang admitted the affair, before Thursday’s drop.

Kaiser doesn’t expect Nvidia to lose its grip on AI training for at least two or three years, because customers built on its CUDA software will find it “really hard” to switch. The fight is over inference, the work of running models once they’re trained, which Kaiser said now takes up more AI compute than training. There, buyers are weighing Nvidia’s general-purpose chips against cheaper ones built for specific jobs: Qualcomm for robotics, Cerebras, Etched, Google’s TPUs and Amazon’s Trainium.

“If Nvidia no longer has Jensen as its rainmaker, did that just tip the scale towards using specialized chips?” Kaiser said.

“The bigger play is actually for the specialty chip makers,” he said, but said AMD and Broadcom will inevitably gain an opening. Google and Amazon could win twice: by pitching their own chips to labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, and by lending their balance sheets. “The Googles and others can step into that Nvidia backstop arrangement,” he said.

TSMC should come through fine, Kaiser said. He estimated about two-thirds of its capacity goes to Nvidia, but said it could shift that to other customers “in pretty short order.”

Kaiser said Huang ran Nvidia on a “hub-and-spoke” model. “The stories are true about Jensen having 60-plus direct reports,” he said, which now leaves “this leadership vacuum and vision vacuum.”

He referenced Intel after Andy Grove stepped down as CEO in 1998. “Andy Grove and Jensen both have just this iron-fist approach to management, very disciplined approach,” he said. Intel kept growing revenue after Grove left, he said, but the company lost margin and “didn’t adapt as well” as chip demand moved toward new uses.

“Intel is the roadmap here to what might be ahead for Nvidia.”

Kaiser also tied Huang’s exit to last week’s midterms, where data centers became a campaign issue. Calling Huang the industry’s “true spokesperson” for data centers, and with that spokesperson now gone, he said, the case for giant single-site data centers weakens further.

“This is just more push for distributed edge compute,” he said, “away from these mega monolithic data centers.”

Nvidia's leadership switch-up is sending shockwaves across every industry that relies on its chips.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.title: Before Megaspeed, there was Supermicro: The other Nvidia partner tied to China chip smuggling—and to Jensen Huang
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.author: Amanda Gerut
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.text:
Whether she was a spy, a fixer, or just a paramour of Jensen Huang, the name Alice Huang (no relation) has roiled the business world this week following reports that the two were having an affair. The revelation snowballed into Jensen’s shocking resignation Wednesday.

Now come reports that officials are looking into other companies Alice was working with. Bloomberg reported, based on an anonymous source, that the Department of Justice is running multiple probes into Nvidia. One is focused on antitrust issues and two others are focused on Megaspeed—where Alice Huang was a former top executive—and Super Micro Computer. Separately, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan is probing whether entities linked to Alice Huang were involved in alleged efforts to smuggle Supermicro hardware laced with Nvidia’s red-hot GPUs into China. It is unclear whether that probe is tied to smuggling cases already brought in the U.S. or Asia. Neither Jensen Huang, Nvidia, nor Supermicro have been formally charged with any wrongdoing.

Supermicro stock tumbled 12% after U.S. markets opened this morning. The company did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Thus far, much of the speculation about Jensen Huang’s catastrophic downfall as the leader of Nvidia has centered on Megaspeed, the Singapore firm that reportedly became one of Nvidia’s largest buyers in Southeast Asia. But Supermicro, the San Jose server maker run by Charles Liang, Jensen Huang’s friend of three decades and an important partner to Nvidia, has been in under the microscope regarding export-control compliance and is being pulled along with Nvidia.

Fortune has reported on the Supermicro case since before federal agents arrested its co-founder in March, and that reporting shows a company with a documented track record of governance and compliance failures. Despite its history, Supermicro has remained in lockstep with Nvidia. Liang and Jensen have shared the stage together at Computex in Taiwan, where Jensen was photographed in 2024 with Alice at a cocktail bar.

In March, federal prosecutors charged Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with allegedly routing about $2.5 billion in servers laced with Nvidia H200 and B200 GPUs to China through a Southeast Asian front company. Bloomberg later reported the front company is OBON, a Bangkok-based AI infrastructure firm, which has not been charged. Supermicro was not charged and has said it was a victim of the scheme.

Liaw, who immediately resigned his executive and board roles at Supermicro following his arrest, has pleaded not guilty. His trial was pushed to March 2027 after Liaw’s lawyers told the judge in his case that subpoenas issued to Supermicro could be material to Liaw’s defense. Nelson Boxer, Liaw’s attorney, declined to comment.

One of Liaw’s co-defendants in the smuggling case, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, pleaded guilty in October, including to a charge that he deleted an encrypted messaging app from his phone on the day of the arrests. Sun’s attorneys did not respond to a request for comment, and it’s unclear if Sun has a cooperation agreement with the government.

There is no public evidence so far that the Supermicro and Megaspeed cases are directly connected but there are mounting threads. Thursday, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs issued a statement noting that the Singapore Police Force and Customs had initiated investigations into Megaspeed and Alice Huang and in doing so sought information from Supermicro. Supermicro only offered “limited cooperation,” Singaporean authorities said.

In a July 2025 meeting, Singapore officials raised this with U.S. authorities and asked for their assistance in getting Supermicro’s cooperation and have repeated the request “on several occasions” to the Department of Justice and the FBI.

“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement reads. Supermicro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Supermicro’s export-control problems did not start with Liaw’s arrest, Fortune’s reporting has found. In 2006, the company pleaded guilty to illegally exporting computer equipment to Iran through a distributor in Dubai, mirroring the basic scheme prosecutors alleged in the Liaw case.

Liaw himself has been through the crisis wringer before. He left Supermicro in 2018 amid a board-led investigation tied to Supermicro’s Nasdaq delisting and an SEC probe of its accounting, which ended with a $17.5 million settlement in 2020. Liaw returned as a consultant in May 2021, became a full-time employee, and rejoined the board in December 2023.

In 2024, short seller Hindenburg Research accused Supermicro of accounting manipulation and export-control failures and the company denied the allegations. Ernst & Young then resigned as auditor mid-audit, saying it could no longer rely on management’s representations. A special committee recommended in December 2024 that Supermicro replace CFO David Weigand and the company agreed to do so “immediately.” The company didn’t name a successor until October.

As Fortune has reported, the Liaw indictment describes thousands of nonworking dummy servers staged in warehouses to fool auditors, contractors using hair dryers to peel off serial-number labels, and a compliance auditor who was off-site allegedly enjoying “entertainment” paid for by another company during an inspection. It also shows how the alleged scheme fed directly into Nvidia’s supply pipeline. In December 2024, Liaw allegedly told the front company that “the only way” to get Nvidia to commit B200 chip allocations was to create monthly forecasts. Nvidia is not accused of wrongdoing in the Liaw indictment.

After Liaw’s arrest, Supermicro’s board opened its own investigation, overseen by independent director Scott Angel and former audit committee chair Tally Liu (no relation to Liang’s wife and co-founder Sara Liu). In August, Supermicro said that probe found no evidence that current senior management knew about the alleged scheme to diver the chips. The investigation resulted in an unspecified number of terminations in sales, business development, and technical support, Supermicro said at the time, for failure to follow policies or the code of conduct.

Supermicro has also disclosed a grand jury subpoena covering the Liaw case and the company’s compliance program and internal controls, along with subpoenas or inquiries from the SEC, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and foreign authorities.

Through all that has beleaguered Supermicro, the company’s relationship with Nvidia has appeared to remain steadfast. This will all become a test for Supermicro’s new CFO, Mark Long, a former Western Digital finance chief who took over from Weigand last month and reports to Liang. The two tag-teamed the company’s most recent earnings call, when it reported record fiscal first-quarter revenue of $19.9 billion, well ahead of Wall Street consensus estimates. Supermicro also raised its full-year revenue forecast to $72 billion to $82 billion.

But now, Supermicro—and its CEO Liang—is losing an important champion in Nvidia’s Huang. Liang built much of Supermicro’s AI-era business through the close relationship with Nvidia combined with Supermicro’s almost supernatural ability to get the newest GPUs to market quickly. Liang has also maintained a public friendship with Huang that included joint keynotes in Taipei before adoring crowds.

Nvidia will now be led in the interim by Kress while an outside investigation into the foreign intelligence operation will be run by former acting SDNY U.S. Attorney Joon Kim and powerhouse law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

Nvidia is slated to report third-quarter results on November 17, with Kress in place of Huang. House lawmakers have requested a closed-door grilling with Huang the following day. In January, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is likely to lead the Senate Banking Committee, and she’ll have subpoena powers. Warren has already sought answers from Nvidia about Supermicro and chip smuggling in June and she re-upped her request this week.

Supermicro has disclosed a grand jury subpoena covering the Liaw case and the company’s compliance program and internal controls. The company”s relationship with Nvidia has appeared to remain steadfast.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.title: After Jensen Huang is Howard Lutnick the prime target of national security inquiry?
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.author: Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, Steven Tian
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.text:
When questioning the motives of certain public leaders, the Roman orator Cicero was said to have used as a shorthand, “cui bono?” meaning, whose interests come first? That line rings true as Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick falls under rapidly escalating bipartisan scrutiny over his role in the flow of Nvidia chips into China.

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of affairs with a direct report and with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, yet the national security questions he leaves behind keep growing amidst escalating congressional investigations. Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was an executive, was suspected of funneling advanced chips to China for years, yet the U.S. government took little action. Many are now asking: Who knew what, and when? And why is this surfacing only now?

We have already described Nvidia directors’ exposure to shareholder lawsuits over their own failures of oversight. Now the scrutiny is shifting to Washington. How did the U.S. government look past so grave a threat to national security for so long, and let these sales go on? As the reporting accumulates, all roads lead to one person, who by multiple accounts blocked action over the objections of fellow cabinet members and leading voices in both parties in Congress: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He is now squarely on the hot seat, and it grows hotter by the day as more information comes to light.

Megaspeed has long been a major target of U.S. government focus amidst pervasive allegations that the Singapore-based data center company helped Chinese firms evade U.S. export controls on sensitive Nvidia chips.

The Department of Commerce’s own agents began investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and is suspected of diverting them to China, in 2024, under the Biden Administration. After the change of administration but amidst the ongoing probe, The New York Times reported that in 2025, Nvidia’s general counsel emailed those agents directly, citing permission from Lutnick’s export-control chief, Jeffrey Kessler, with Commerce soon pausing its work on the investigation.

That sparked many concerns even within the GOP, with respected Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton writing to Lutnick directly, urging Commerce to investigate Megaspeed more carefully. Still, Megaspeed never landed on the entity list, the blacklist kept by the Department of Commerce that cuts suspect firms off from American technology; even though other agencies repeatedly agreed on proposing to add Megaspeed to the list, with the Financial Times reporting that the State Department, Treasury Department, Energy Department and the Pentagon were pushing particularly aggressively to add Megaspeed to the entity list. Despite these entreaties, Lutnick’s Commerce Department was unmoved, steadfastly refusing to add a single company to the entity list for more than a year.

Then came the memo. This spring, the New York Times reports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a highly classified assessment built on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. Its conclusion was as stark as can be: China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited her to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang and on America’s AI chips, and she had grown close to the Nvidia CEO. U.S. officials assessed that Beijing’s aims may have gone further, to steering Nvidia into pressing Washington for greater Chinese access to its most advanced chips.

The memo went to a handful of senior officials before President Trump’s May trip to China, with Axios reporting that Lutnick was among those who received the memo directly. Perhaps not coincidentally, Jensen Huang was originally left off the delegation of business leaders traveling to China with Trump, before being added at the very last possible minute during an Alaska refueling stop.

That same month, Reuters reported that Commerce had cleared about 10 Chinese companies to buy H200s.

Perhaps even more alarmingly, but less widely known than the existence of the memo; Axios also reports that President Trump approved a crackdown on chip diversion to China no less than three times, in May, in August, and on Nov. 5, with even Elon Musk supportive, and that Lutnick and his deputies had resisted carrying out each order. As Maria Curi and Marc Caputo of Axios reported pithily, “One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick,” noting that virtually every other Administration official was supportive of these crackdowns.

Just last week, after news of the Jensen Huang spy scandal broke, Axios reported that Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal, with virtually all other Admin officials siding with Bessent; yet Lutnick apparently continued to stall. Already, there has been speculation that the leaks over the last week that felled Huang came from sources within the Trump Administration, perhaps from within the National Security Council, who were frustrated at Lutnick pushing what they perceived to be pro-China policies, with many remarking about the suspicious timing of these leaks right after midterm elections, even though the original memo was circulated in May this year, six months ago.

What makes this scrutiny so hot is who is turning up the temperature. Lutnick’s chief antagonists on the issue of China chip controls are almost entirely his own colleagues within the administration, ranging from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, all of whom reportedly favor a far tougher approach than Lutnick has been willing to impose.

Lutnick’s Republican detractors are plenty outside the administration as well, particularly within the GOP congressional ranks. Republican Sen. John Kennedy says Lutnick must explain himself “in front of God and country.” Rep. Bill Huizenga has attacked Lutnick’s lack of responsiveness to Congress as “frustrating,” and the Republican chairs of the House China and Foreign Affairs committees, Rep. John Moolenaar and Rep. Brian Mast, have made their unhappiness with Lutnick just as vivid.

All these intraparty critics join legions of Democratic senators who are demanding records from Lutnick, and after last week’s midterms, their party takes the committee gavels in January with detractors making clear that Lutnick is one of their top targets – for reasons extending far beyond merely his role in sensitive U.S. technology making their way to China.

Many congressional Democrats are practically salivating at the prospect of being able to issue subpoenas to examine Lutnick’s perceived business conflicts of interests, and their files are already thick with hard questions Lutnick will have to answer.

Start with rare earths as one prominent example. In January, Commerce announced a tentative $1.6 billion deal that gives the government a roughly 10% stake in USA Rare Earth. To close it, the company raised $1.5 billion in a private stock offering and chose as its lead placement agent Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick led for decades and which his son Brandon Lutnick, 27 when he took over, now oversees as chairman. By the lawmakers’ account, the company’s CEO credited Lutnick’s personal involvement for the deal. Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Ron Wyden and Chris Van Hollen have pressed for documents since February.

Crypto brings another witches’ brew of problems for Lutnick. Cantor has been custodian of the reserves of Tether, the largest stablecoin issuer, since 2021, and holds a stake that Sen. Richard Blumenthal says has swelled from about $600 million to an estimated $10 billion since Trump returned to office. A trust for Lutnick’s children reportedly borrowed from Tether around the time he transferred his Cantor stake to them. Cantor also launched Twenty One Capital, the bitcoin treasury company known by its ticker, XXI, with Tether, with Blumenthal already raising questions about the arrangement.

That doesn’t even factor in any potential lingering issues related to Lutnick’s longtime ties to Jeffrey Epstein, his onetime next-door Manhattan neighbor. Lutnick long maintained that he cut ties with Epstein in 2005, but Justice Department files showed a 2012 family visit to Epstein’s island, a shared investment and emails as late as 2018, which many called “grossly deceptive.” Republican Rep. Thomas Massie called on him to resign in February, and his closed-door testimony to House Oversight in May left Democrats on the panel calling him evasive.

For Lutnick, each of these issues raises the exact question Megaspeed poses: Whose interests came first, and whose side was he really on?

Defenders of Lutnick point out that he is merely carrying out Trump’s wishes as part of a broader implicit trade deal with China where the U.S. continues to provide cutting-edge chips and in exchange, the Chinese continue to provide the U.S. with rare earth minerals. But this is a misleading and misguided argument on several counts.

First, the U.S. is not nearly as dependent on China for rare earth minerals as many imagine, with the U.S. possessing tremendous reserves of rare earth minerals but merely needing some sustained investment to extract and process them. Second, this implicit deal did not apparently restrain other cabinet members, such as Secretary of State Rubio and Treasury Secretary Bessent, from registering their concerns with Lutnick’s stances. Third, Trump himself has endorsed the widely admired former CEO of Apple, Tim Cook, as the next CEO of Nvidia, echoing our own earlier endorsement of Cook. Cook has scrupulously abided by national security policies while capably and successfully balancing commerce in China with protection of US national security, and there is nothing to suggest that Cook would knowingly undermine US national security by continuing the illicit flow of chips into China.

As the questions pile up, there is no easy way out for Lutnick.  As Thomas More is said to have warned King Henry VIII, “Trust is as fragile as liquid in your hands, once you separate your fingers, its forever gone.”

Where have Lutnick’s fingers gone?

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/study-lon.title: ‘The plot twist’: A study of 73,000 adults found America’s richest still die sooner than most Europeans
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/study-lon.author: Lena Borrelli
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/study-lon.text:
Americans have never earned more or lived longer. Median household income hit $87,460 in 2025, the highest since the Census Bureau began tracking it in 1967, according to Census data released in September. Life expectancy reached 79 years in 2024, also a record.

Yet money still can’t buy Americans a European lifespan. A Brown University study published last year in the New England Journal of Medicine found that Americans die sooner than Europeans at every level of wealth, and that the richest Americans fare no better than the poorest people in much of Western Europe.

“The plot twist is that even the wealthiest quartile of Americans does not have better outcomes than most of northern and Western Europeans,” says Sara Machado, a research scientist at Brown’s Center for Health System Sustainability. “That was unexpected and counters a lot of the narrative that we’re used to.”

The researchers tracked more than 73,000 adults ages 50 to 85 in the U.S. and 16 European countries, starting in 2010 and following them for about a decade, using data from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study and Europe’s SHARE survey.

The wealthiest people in northern and western Europe had a mortality rate about 35% lower than the wealthiest Americans. Survival among America’s richest quartile was statistically equivalent to that of the poorest quartile in countries like France, Germany, and the Netherlands.

Across the board, people in continental Europe died at rates about 40% lower than Americans over the study period, according to Brown. In southern Europe, death rates were about 30% lower.

Wealth still matters within each country. “We found that where you stand in your country’s wealth distribution matters for your longevity, and where you stand in your country compared to where others stand in theirs matters, too,” Machado says.

The U.S. spent an estimated $14,775 per person on health care in 2024, nearly $7,000 more than the average comparable wealthy country, according to the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker. Those countries averaged a life expectancy of 82.7 years, 3.7 years longer than the U.S. Fortune has reported on why U.S. health care costs run about twice those of peer nations.

The spending doesn’t buy universal access. About 26.7 million Americans went uninsured for all of 2025, Census data shows, and about 2.6 million fewer Americans had ACA marketplace plans in early 2026 than in early 2025.

“Fixing health outcomes is not just a challenge for the most vulnerable – even those in the top quartile of wealth are affected,” says Machado.

Lifestyle plays a role. Americans tend to have less healthy diets and a more sedentary lifestyle, and heart disease and cancer remain the two leading causes of death nationally. The researchers noted that smoking and rural living, both tied to poorer health, were more common in the U.S.

Europe is also home to two of the so-called blue zones, Sardinia in Italy and Ikaria in Greece, where longevity is credited to activity, diet, rest, and strong social ties, though some researchers dispute the claims.

When Fortune first reported on the study, senior author Irene Papanicolas pointed to higher U.S. rates of avoidable deaths from firearms, alcohol, and suicide; higher cardiovascular mortality; and a thinner social safety net, with health coverage tied more closely to employment.

Inequality compounds it. The U.S. has a far wider gap between rich and poor than Europe, a divide that Creative Planning CEO Peter Mallouk recently warned is unsustainable.

“Our previous work has shown that while wealth inequality narrows after 65 across the U.S. and Europe, in the U.S. it narrows because the poorest Americans die sooner and in greater proportion,” explains Papanicolas, a professor of health services, policy, and practice who directs Brown’s Center for Health System Sustainability.

The recent gains in U.S. longevity came largely from the end of the pandemic, and a drop in overdose deaths and suicides also occurred in 2024, according to the CDC. Those gains have not closed the gap with Europe.

“If we want to improve health in the US,” explains Papanicolas, “we need to better understand the underlying factors that contribute to these differences – particularly amongst similar socioeconomic groups – and why they translate to different health outcomes across nations.”

“There is a lot of it that is a collective issue,” Machado agrees. “But I would say to individuals that you really need to think about your retirement—about when you’re going to retire, how you’re going to retire, and how you can be happy as a person that has retired.”

Machado adds, “If you look at other countries, there are better outcomes, and that means we can learn from them and improve. It’s not necessarily about spending more — it’s about addressing the factors we’re overlooking, which could deliver far greater benefits than we realize.”
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/study-lon.summary: Median household income hit $87,460 in 2025, the highest since the Census Bureau began tracking it in 1967. Life expectancy reached 79 years in 2024, also a record, but money still can't buy Americans a European lifespan.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.title: Jensen Huang built Nvidia into a $4 trillion AI giant but owned less than 4% of it, leaving him without the super-voting power to protect his CEO role
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.author: Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.text:
Jensen Huang, the billionaire ex-Nvidia CEO who took the company from a small player in the video game graphics industry to the chipmaker at the center of the AI revolution, once made a surprising revelation: He could be fired at any time.

“In a well-governed company, the CEO was always designed to report to the board of directors and the board of directors report to shareholders,” Huang said in a January podcast interview with Jodi Shelton. “If the CEO doesn’t do his job according to 12, 13, 15 board members, however sized the board is, that CEO is let go.”

This reality sets Nvidia apart from other Silicon Valley companies, especially those still run by a cofounder. That includes Meta, where CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg wields considerable power over the board due to its dual class share structure.

On Thursday, Huang resigned from the company that he cofounded and led over the past 33 years after publicly admitting to being unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into Huang and the possibility he may have been a target of a foreign intelligence operation after reporting by the New York Times explored his close relationship with a businesswoman that U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese spy. Huang reportedly had another affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, according to the New York Times. On Thursday, the board appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Still, Huang said in that January interview any future Nvidia CEO would not measure up to him.

“There will never be one like me, and the reason for that is because I was raised by the company,” he said at the time.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Despite being the company’s largest individual shareholder, Huang did not have unparalleled voting control over his company or outsized control over the company’s board, like other founders.

Huang owned about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, or about 3.58% of the company as of March, according to the company’s 2026 proxy statement. His holdings were far greater than that of  other executives and directors, including Kress, who held 4.4 million shares. Vanguard and BlackRock both owned more than 7% of the company each.

Because of Nvidia’s one-share-one vote system, Huang’s stake doesn’t come with special privileges, despite his status as a cofounder. That means the number of votes he has directly corresponds with his number of shares.

As Huang alluded to in his January podcast interview, Nvidia’s bylaws are written in such a way that the company’s CEO can be removed by the board for any reason and at any time—still, Huang lacked enough voting power to independently elect or remove Nvidia’s directors.

While founders with majority voting control, such as Zuckerberg, can effectively determine who sits on their boards, Huang would have needed support from other Nvidia shareholders to do the same.

That differs from other companies run by tech founders including Meta, Snap, and even Google.

At Meta, a dual class voting structure (it said last month it would add a third non-voting tier next year) gives Zuckerberg outsized power over voting.  Despite owning 13.4% of the company, Zuckerberg controls about 60% of the company’s voting power because his class B shares give him 10 votes each compared to one vote for every class A share. With this voting power, Zuckerberg can effectively elect Meta’s entire board and is the deciding voice on most matters sent to shareholders.

Snap, the social media company, has a similar arrangement with CEO and cofounder Evan Spiegel controlling 53% of the company’s voting power while only owning about 9.3% of the company.

Even at Google parent company Alphabet, where cofounder Sergey Brin and cofounder and former CEO Larry Page no longer run day-to-day operations, the pair still collectively retain majority voting control of the tech giant. Both still serve on the company’s board.

Nvidia’s stock plummeted by as much as 14% Thursday following the announcement of Huang’s departure, before rebounding. It was down about 4.7% as of 1:30 p.m. EST on Thursday. With a nearly $4 trillion market cap, the company makes up about 6% of the S&P 500 and about 10% of the Nasdaq 100, meaning any reckoning it experiences will trickle through the broader market and everyday Americans’ 401(K) accounts.

Huang was key to Nvidia’s operations with a flat management structure and direct involvement in the company’s product strategy and its supplier and customer relationships. In recent months, he has also cultivated a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who has been a vocal proponent of boosting the AI industry and the infrastructure backing it in the U.S.—although Trump was quick to back ex-Apple CEO Tim Cook as Huang’s successor on Thursday.

The board has now made changes to its own structure as well. It previously operated without a board chairman, opting instead to rely on lead independent director Stephen Neal to oversee management. On Thursday, it appointed Harvey C. Jones, a former semiconductor company CEO and Nvidia board member since 1993, as its chairman of the board, it said in a statement.

Kress, the company’s CFO since 2013, said for her part she is planning to build on Huang’s legacy at Nvidia as interim CEO she said in a Thursday statement.

In the January interview, Huang said while he didn’t love his job every day, he always tried his “mightiest” because of two reasons.

“One, I’m the best person for the job. I believe that,” he said. “And, two, I have to earn being the best person for that job every day.”
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.summary: Huang owned about 870.6 million Nvidia shares. He owned about 3.58 million shares. Huang's company's one-share-one vote system gives him power over the company's board.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/silicon-v.title: Silicon Valley’s richest outspent supporters more than 10 to one to kill California’s billionaire tax—and won
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/silicon-v.author: Joshua Hong
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/silicon-v.text:
California voters rejected a proposed tax on the state’s billionaires after some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives and investors spent $378.4 million to defeat it—delivering a victory to a coalition led by Google cofounder Sergey Brin.

The Associated Press called the race on Monday, with 52.8% of voters opposing Proposition 40 and 47.2% supporting it. The votes needed to pass the measure had trailed for days.

The defeat means—at least for now—an effort to make California the first state to impose a one-time tax on its billionaires has ended. It also represents a significant win for the Silicon Valley executives who have come together to block the measure.

Approximately 52.8% of voters opposed Proposition 40, whereas 47.2% supported it. According to CalMatters, ultrawealthy opponents collectively contributed $378.4 million to efforts opposing the tax and related countermeasures like Props 41 and 42. That amount is more than 10 times the $33.5 million raised by supporters of Proposition 40.

Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of individuals worth more than $1 billion who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026. The proposed tax covered financial assets and other forms of wealth, rather than just income.

Under the proposal, approximately 90% of the revenue would have gone toward healthcare services, with the remaining 10% allocated to education and food assistance. The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated that the measure could generate “tens of billions” of dollars.

The initiative was introduced by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which argued that California needed additional revenue to address healthcare funding shortfalls following federal spending reductions under President Donald Trump’s tax and spending legislation. The measure also received support from Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, the California Democratic party and several labor organizations.

But not every Democrat and Californian was on the same page. The proposal faced opposition from prominent Democrats including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who argued that a state-level wealth tax would push wealthy residents and their businesses out of the state. Instead, Newsom said he would support a national wealth tax. San Francisco Democrats also opposed the measure, voting 17-4 against Prop 40 in August, while U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi, a member of the local party, voted “no endorsement.”

“Here is what I support: A national billionaires’ tax,” Newsom wrote in a post on Substack in June. “A true minimum tax on billionaires—a modern Buffett Rule—that ensures the people at the very top pay at least the tax rate their own workers pay.”

The campaign against the proposition was financed by some of the most prominent figures in the tech, finance and investment industries—with Brin emerging as its largest individual financial backer.

Brin contributed approximately $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he established in January that became the main vehicle opposing the wealth tax. The contributions made Brin one of the most consequential financial players in California’s 2026 ballot-measure fight. He relocated to Nevada in December 2025—making his fortune, estimated at $231 billion by Bloomberg, potentially exempt from the tax.

Eric Schmidt, Google’s former CEO, was also a major contributor to the opposition effort. According to campaign finance filings, he contributed $40.2 million to the campaign.

Other prominent tech executives and investors also contributed millions, including DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe cofounder Patrick Collison, venture capitalist John Doerr, cryptocurrency entrepreneur Chris Larsen and former Sequoia Capital partner Michael Moritz.

The contributions were also not limited to Building a Better California’s fight against Prop 40. Through Oct. 20, Building a Better California spent more than $304 million supporting efforts to defeat Proposition 40 and advance Propositions 41 and 42—direct counters to the wealth tax. Of that amount, approximately $118.5 million went toward opposing Proposition 40, while the other $186 million supported Propositions 41 and 42, according to Capital & Main.

Proposition 41 would “require preelection audits for initiatives proposing special taxes and additional audits every four years. It also would prohibit new tax revenue from being exempted from state spending limits,” making it harder for the state to use funds raised by the billionaire tax. Proposition 42 would “prohibit taxes on personal savings, assets and retirement holdings”—outlawing retroactive taxation, directly countering Proposition 40. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, if either one gets more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, the wealth tax could be stopped even if it is approved.

And while the wealth tax didn’t get approved, a ballot measure meant to block it did. According to the AP, Proposition 41 did not pass by voters while Proposition 42 did—meaning Proposition 40 would have been shot down if it had passed regardless.

According to Politico, more than 70 current and former California billionaires had spent a record $612 million into the state elections this cycle. Of that money, at least 30 billionaires had contributed more than $293 million specifically to the wealth tax fight.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/11/silicon-v.summary: Proposed tax on the net worth of individuals worth more than $1 billion who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026. The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on individuals worth $1billion. The proposal was introduced by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/standard-.title: Standard Chartered profit jumps 46% as CEO bets on a fragmenting global economy: ‘An advantage for us’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/standard-.author: Michaela Herbst
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/standard-.text:
The CEO of British multinational bank Standard Chartered says “geopolitical fragmentation is an advantage for us,” after the lender reported a 46% jump in third-quarter net profit to $1.5 billion.

Speaking at a media roundtable, Bill Winters said the splintering of global trade is creating new business for the bank, which helps multinational corporations manage cross-border deals, the South China Morning Post reported.

His remarks come as companies rethink where they make things amid rising trade tensions. Many have adopted a “China plus one” strategy, shifting some production to Southeast Asia to offset China’s rising costs. That shift has proven more complicated than expected, as many factories in the region still rely on Chinese inputs, Fortune reported in October.

Geopolitical fragmentation refers to the structural shift in the global economy as supply chains, trade, and policy realign along political lines.

For banks, that shift changes where money flows. A company moving manufacturing from China to Southeast Asia, for instance, needs new banking relationships and financing arrangements in each new market.

Standard Chartered operates in 54 markets, with a significant presence in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. That network lets it follow clients as their trade and investment move.

“We’ve really focused on getting a few things right and one is to serve multinational corporations and multinational individuals on their cross-border needs,” Winters said.

The bank’s third-quarter results, released Oct. 28, show how much it now leans on fee-generating businesses beyond traditional lending. Operating income rose 13% to $5.8 billion, and pre-tax profit climbed 27% to $2.25 billion.

Wealth Solutions income rose 26% to $1.1 billion, while Global Markets income grew 20% to just over $1 billion. The bank raised its 2026 outlook and now expects a return on tangible equity of about 14%.

The industry as a whole is flush. Banks earned a record $1.3 trillion in net income in 2025, up 7% from a year earlier, according to McKinsey’s Global Banking Annual Review, which argues that AI will reward lenders that move quickly. Winters cautioned that the AI boom may lead to some misallocated capital, and said the bank’s role is to avoid those risks.

Fragmentation cuts both ways. Trade restrictions and political instability add friction to the cross-border transactions at the heart of Standard Chartered’s business, and if tensions choke off trade, demand for those services could fall.

Operating across dozens of jurisdictions also means keeping up with each country’s regulations and compliance requirements, which can shift with politics. Even so, the bank’s economists have argued that fears of a broad retreat from the U.S. dollar are overstated, Fortune reported in July.

Winters named five structural trends he expects to redefine finance over the next decade: the transition to a low-carbon economy, wealth creation across Asia, the Middle East, and Africa, changes to banking infrastructure, geopolitical fragmentation, and the digitization of money.

Hong Kong, where regulators are building frameworks for digital assets, is central to that last bet. This month, Standard Chartered launched tokenized deposits in Hong Kong and piloted a liquidity facility to support Ant International’s investment in tokenized money market funds. The bank ranks No. 7 on the 2026 Fortune Crypto 100.

“We’re positioned for the themes that we think are most important for the next 10 to 20 years, and we intend to keep our focus on those things,” Winters said.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/standard-.summary: Standard Chartered CEO Bill Winters says ‘geopolitical fragmentation is an advantage for us’ The bank's third-quarter results show how much it now leans on fee-generating businesses beyond traditional lending.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/alice-hu.title: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/alice-hu.author: Eamon Javers,Paige Tortorelli
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/alice-hu.text:
Alice Huang, with whom ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly had a romantic relationship, has owned stakes in companies that have benefited Huawei, Nvidia’s No. 1 competitor in China.

The entanglement has not been previously reported and was first uncovered by private intelligence firm Tesari and shared exclusively with CNBC.

The Huawei connection may add to questions about the consequences of the relationship, which has already been under scrutiny by policymakers due to U.S. intelligence reportedly alleging Alice Huang is a Chinese spy.

Alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia’s biggest competitor in China, Huawei, at the same time that she was in business with Nvidia
 and also reportedly having a romantic affair with its ousted CEO Jensen Huang.

The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei was first discovered by analysts at private intelligence firm Tesari. The firm exclusively shared its findings with CNBC. Tesari, which uses artificial intelligence to collect evidence and specializes in national security investigations around the world, provides intelligence research to private companies and the U.S. government.

This previously unreported entanglement may raise questions about Alice Huang’s intent and conduct in her relationship with the CEO and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an affair, though the precise timing of his relationship with Alice Huang is unknown.

The mysterious saga of Alice Huang involves a tangle of interlocking corporations and transactions that show her connection to entities that ultimately provided computing power to Huawei in China.

Huawei is known as a Chinese government “state champion” in the technology and telecommunications sectors, meaning it receives enormous financial support from the government in Beijing so it can lower prices and undercut global competitors. It is considered a key part of the Chinese government’s push for global technical dominance and is closely linked to the Chinese Communist Party.

Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together, in December 2023.

In 2024, Nvidia said Huawei was a top competitor, specifically in artificial intelligence chips including graphics processing units, central processing units and networking chips.

“This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice’s network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation,” said Brian Andersen, Tesari’s vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations.

If the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry Security and Homeland Security Investigations found evidence that anyone transferred “controlled equipment” to Huawei without authorization, potential charges might include export-control violations, conspiracy and smuggling, Andersen said.

The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei is so convoluted that analysts at Tesari told CNBC that based on their previous investigative experience, they suspect it was designed to deliberately obscure the relationship.

Nvidia and Huawei did not respond to CNBC’s requests for comment. Jensen Huang did not respond to a voicemail left on a mobile phone. Alice Huang could not be reached.

According to Chinese corporate records and media reports compiled by Tesari and provided to CNBC, Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le and who according to documents at the time was based in Hong Kong, in 2019 sold a cloud business she owned called Osmanthus to a Chinese gaming company called 7Road. A subsidiary of 7Road, which was based in Singapore, was spun off as “Megaspeed” in 2023. Megaspeed would go on to become a key Nvidia customer, helping facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, The Information reported Tuesday.

As early as 2016, Alice Huang had also become a co-owner of a financial firm known as Shanghai Hexi, which heavily invests in tech and data centers. In 2021, Hexi in turn acquired 27 percent of a company called Shanghai Century Longteng, a data center developer, which Hexi held until 2024. That firm owned a controlling 50.1 percent stake in a data center facility called Shenzhen Yifeng Technology Co. Ltd. in mainland China.

The key customer of that data center was Huawei Cloud, the Shenzhen, China-based subsidiary of Huawei Technologies.

In addition, Alice Huang’s firm Hexi guaranteed the loans required to finance the Shenzhen data center, which did business with Huawei.

Hexi did not immediately respond to a message via its LinkedIn page sent outside of normal business hours.

CNBC translated corporate records and Chinese news articles in Mandarin that Tesari provided.

It’s not clear if the Shenzhen data center was able to acquire Nvidia GPUs, but its majority owner began purchasing the chips in 2023. That company is known as Zhejiang Century Huatong Group and is a business partner of Alice Huang’s Hexi through their joint ownership of Century Longteng.

That made Alice Huang a part owner of a data center providing computing power to Huawei. And that was happening at around the same time the first known sightings of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang in public together.

And that raises the question of why Huawei, which has access to Chinese-made chips, would need to rent computing power from an outside entity.

Hexi exited its stake in the data center development company in 2024, but individuals within Alice Huang’s network are still connected to the Shenzhen data center. Her husband Kang Wei is a longtime business associate who founded Hexi, where Alice Huang previously held an executive role. In 2022, Kang became an executive of Century Longteng, which owns the controlling stake in the Shenzhen data center, and he also attended the company’s signing of the Huawei agreement.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/alice-hu.summary: Alice Huang may have owned stakes in companies that benefited Huawei. The relationship with ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been under scrutiny by U.S. intelligence.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/microsof.title: Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook and other 365 services
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/microsof.author: Samantha Subin
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/microsof.text:
A Microsoft outage on Thursday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365.

Amazon Web Services said it was “operating normally” and noted inaccurate reports of outages on its platforms.

Google users reported issues on DownDetector.

Microsoft
 suffered a widespread outage on Thursday that impacted thousands of users across regions, according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.com.

The outage began shortly before 1 p.m. and impacted Microsoft 365 services, Outlook and Teams. At the time, about 130,000 users reported issues with Outlook.

Amazon
 Web Services and Google
 users also reported outages on the site.

“We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online,” a Microsoft spokesperson wrote in a statement to CNBC. “We appreciate our customers’ patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.”

Microsoft shared updates on the outage from its Microsoft 365 Status account on social media platform X.

Amazon wrote on X that services were “operating normally” and an “unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports.” The company referred users to its health dashboard for “accurate data.”

At 4 p.m., Microsoft said it had “validated an alternative service health check method” that brought some affected servers back online.

“We’re now applying this change more broadly,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses.”

Microsoft initially said infrastructure “elevated load across multiple regions” was responsible for the connectivity problems.

The company later determined that the elevated load was caused by a “number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure” and that some servers were failing automated health checks.

“We’ve taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service,” Microsoft wrote.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/microsof.summary: Microsoft says it is “operating normally’s’ Microsoft 365 services, Outlook, Teams and 365 are affected. Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site. Microsoft initially said infrastructure “elevated load across multiple regions’ was responsible for the connectivity problems.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/401k-con.title: IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap: What it means for your money
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/401k-con.author: Kate Dore, CFP®, EA
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/401k-con.text:
The IRS has announced higher 401(k) contribution limits for 2027.

Starting in 2027, employees can defer $25,500 into workplace plans, up from $24,500 in 2026.

The individual retirement account contribution limit will be $7,500 in 2027, unchanged from 2026.

The IRS has announced new retirement account contribution limits for 2027.

In its release on Thursday, the agency increased the 401(k) employee deferral limit to $25,500 next year, up from $24,500 in 2026. The change applies to 401(k)s, 403(b)s and most 457 plans, along with the federal Thrift Savings Plan.

The IRS also unveiled 2027 catch-up contribution limits for savers age 50 and older, new individual retirement account savings limits and higher income thresholds for Roth IRA contributions.

Starting in 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution limit will rise to $8,500 for savers 50 and older, up from $8,000 in 2026. But investors aged 60 to 63 can instead save an extra $11,750, based on changes enacted via Secure 2.0. That figure is up $500 from 2026.

Both amounts are in addition to the $25,500 deferral limit for 2027.

The 2027 IRA contribution limit is $7,500, unchanged from 2026, the IRS announced. IRA catch-up contributions for investors age 50 and older will be $1,100, the same as 2026.

The announcement comes one week after the agency released dozens of other inflation adjustments for 2027, including federal income tax brackets, higher capital gains brackets, estate and gift tax exemptions and provisions impacting families, among others.

In 2025, only 14% of participants maxed out their 401(k)s, according to Vanguard’s 2026 How America Saves report, which was based on data from more than 1,300 qualified plans and nearly 5 million participants. The average combined savings rate, including employer deposits, was an estimated 12.1%, according to the same report.

“Before worrying about contribution limits, make sure you’re capturing your full employer match,” said Sean Michael Pearson, a certified financial planner with Ameriprise Financial Services in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania.

During the second quarter of 2026, about 19% of employees weren’t deferring enough to 401(k)s to receive their company’s full matching contribution, according to a Fidelity analysis of 27,300 corporate plans and nearly 26 million participants.

Vanguard suggests saving 12% to 15% of your pay per year, including employer contributions, depending on your income. But only one-quarter of 401(k) participants deferred more than 10% of earnings in 2025, according to Vanguard’s report.

If you plan to max out your 401(k) for 2027, you should change your savings rate in December so it’s active by your first January paycheck, experts say. The update could take one or two pay periods to go into effect.

The “most important habit” is consistently increasing your 401(k) savings rate over time, according to Pearson.

For example, if you bump 401(k) contributions by 1% every year, “you may barely notice the difference in your paycheck, but the long-term impact can be substantial,” he said.

In 2025, about 27% of 401(k) plans automatically increased employee deferrals over time, known as “auto-escalation,” according to the Plan Sponsor Council of America’s yearly survey of 401(k)s. The nonprofit trade organization’s survey included 753 plans.

The vast majority of plans with auto-escalation, 69%, boosted deferrals by 1% per year, the Plan Sponsor Council of America found.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/401k-con.summary: The IRS has announced new retirement account contribution limits for 2027. The individual retirement account contributions limit will be $7,500 in 2027, unchanged from 2026. The 2027 IRA contribution limit is $7.500, unchanged. The change applies to 401(k)s, 403(b)s and most 457 plans.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/cerebras.title: Cerebras surges 17% after beating on quarterly revenue and announcing Microsoft deal
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/cerebras.author: Jordan Novet
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/cerebras.text:
Cerebras reported better-than-expected revenue for the third quarter and issued strong guidance.

The AI chipmaker said it recently signed a deal with hyperscaler Microsoft.

Cerebras’ stock price has lost almost half its value since the company’s IPO in May.

Cerebras
 Systems reported better-than-expected revenue and quarterly guidance in its earnings report on Thursday, and touted a new deal with Microsoft
. The stock soared 17% in extended trading.

Here’s how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:

Cerebras’ core revenue grew 70% from $135.7 million, compared with 103% growth in the second quarter, according to a statement.

“I think there is opportunity created by, particularly on the hardware side, the sale of hardware, where long lead times in GPUs and more expense creates opportunity for us,” Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman told CNBC in an interview, referring to graphics processing units.

Executives will announce a new relationship with Microsoft
, one of the world’s top cloud providers, on a conference call with analysts, Feldman said. The call starts at 5 p.m. ET.

“We believe revenue begins to show up in Q1 ’27,” Feldman said in the interview, adding that Microsoft signed the deal in October. Cerebras has also landed deals with other major cloud providers Amazon
 and Oracle
.

Cerebras is evaluating its financing options to meet the ramping demand, Feldman said in the interview.

The company is trying to challenge Nvidia
 in the AI chip market. Its earnings land on the same day that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded after multiple scandals involving extramarital affairs.

For the fourth quarter, Cerebras expects a core gross margin of 47% to 49%, with $310 million to $330 million in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for a 42.1% margin and $271 million in revenue.

Cerebras said it expects revenue to triple in 2027. That implies about $2.85 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $2.92 billion.

Cerebras shares have slumped by about 47% since the company debuted on Nasdaq in May.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/cisco-cs.title: Cisco beats on earnings, says AI infrastructure revenue will double this fiscal year
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/cisco-cs.author: Ari Levy
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/cisco-cs.text:
Cisco reported fiscal first-quarter earnings that topped estimates.

The computer networking company is trying to become a bigger player in AI after missing out on the early years of the boom.

The stock is up 35% this year, trouncing the Nasdaq, which is up about 9%.

Cisco
 shares rose in extended trading on Thursday after the maker of networking gear reported better-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results.

Here’s how the company did compared to LSEG consensus estimates:

Revenue increased 24% from $14.88 billion a year earlier, Cisco said in a statement. Net income rose to $4.6 billion, or $1.14 per share, from $2.9 billion, or 72 center per share, a year ago.

Cisco is trying to gain a foothold in the artificial intelligence buildout after missing out on the early years of the generative AI boom. The company’s stock price is up about 35% this year as of Thursday’s close, trouncing the Nasdaq, which has gained 9% over that stretch.

Cisco raised its expectation for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to $9 billion this fiscal year, more than double the figure in fiscal 2026.

“Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era,” CEO Chuck Robbins said in the statement.

For the fiscal second quarter, Cisco said it expects revenue of between $18 billion and $18.2 billion, topping the average analyst estimate of $17.88 billion, according to LSEG. The company is projecting adjusted earnings per share of $1.34 to $1.36, beating the $1.23 average estimate.

https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/12/.title: Jensen Huang is out and Nvidia stock is down—what market pros say about buying dips
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/12/.author: Ryan Ermey
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/12/.text:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as the firm’s president and CEO, the company announced Thursday. Investors reacted negatively to the news. By 2:30 p.m., shares of the chipmaking giant were down more than 5%, and now sit 31% below their high on October 6.

It’s easy to see why Huang’s departure, which comes amid revelations of his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy, has investors feeling queasy. The company Huang co-founded 33 years ago — and whose chips have powered the artificial intelligence boom — has grown into the firm currently valued at about $4 trillion under his leadership.

“The premise here is that there is no successor to a generational founder,” says Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, which invests in founder-led companies. “It’s that they’re one of one, and what they bring from a vision, execution and grit standpoint is not replaceable.”

While some investors are exiting Nvidia positions based on that premise — Monaghan’s fund must, per its prospectus — others will see the slip in Nvidia’s price as an opportunity to buy a great stock on proverbial sale, he says.

Looking purely at the numbers, the opportunity to buy a stock with Nvidia’s prodigious projected growth at its current depressed price “happens once a decade, maybe once in a career as an investor,” he says.

In investing parlance, the latter group of investors is “buying the dip” — investing in an asset after a decline in its value in anticipation of a bounceback. Whether it’s a prudent strategy for you with Nvidia or any other stock requires some examination, investing experts say — not only of the stock in question, but your own portfolio strategy.

When an investment you own or are interested in declines, your first move is to examine your reason for buying or holding it, says Tom Hainlin, national investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management.

Ask yourself if whatever caused the slide has changed your investment narrative, he says. “Has it changed why I bought the stock or why I’m investing in the market?”

If you own a diversified portfolio and the broad U.S. stock market has declined, buying dips is a relatively straightforward decision, investing pros say. Because the stock market has historically trended upward, each downdraft has offered investors an opportunity to add an appreciating asset at a discount.

“If you have a solid, long-term investment, it’s always attractive to buy the dip because you always get a new high,” Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist with LPL Financial, told Make It in August. “In the history of the S&P 500, every dip has been attractive because you eventually made new highs.”

Individual stocks have no such track record, meaning that a major slide should prompt you to re-examine the thesis behind any given investment, Hainlin says. That analysis is twofold. On one hand, you should rethink the position any one stock occupies in your portfolio. If it’s a large enough chunk that a pullback is keeping you up at night, it might be worth paring the position back to put things more in line with your tolerance for risk, he says.

And whether you own the stock or are thinking about buying, a dip is a good time to evaluate your outlook for that investment. If you plan to hold a particular stock for the long term, for instance, you’ll have to weigh whether the short-term bad news could have a lasting impact on the firm’s profitability.

“Did Nvidia’s prospects change as a result of [Huang’s resignation]? There’s no definitive answer for that,” he says.

Monaghan says that, based on historical data, there may be reason to worry. His fund’s fact sheet cites data from consultancy Bain & Company showing that founder-led companies vastly outperformed their peers from 1990 through 2014. Even companies that have successfully replaced their founders, such as Apple and Microsoft, have failed to grow as quickly as under original leadership, he says.

Investors will have to weigh the risk that Nvidia will lag without Huang at the helm against the firm’s still impressive growth projections — the company will report third-quarter fiscal year earnings results on Nov. 17 — and their long-term belief in the firm’s position as a top supplier of microchips that power AI.

“One thing we do know is that AI demand hasn’t changed,” Hainlin says.
