https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-j.title: Nvidia: Ex-prosecutor Joon Kim and Wachtell, Lipton bring big track record to investigation
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-j.author: Dan Mangan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-j.text:
Joon Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, have been retained by Nvidia to investigate allegations that then-CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Huang resigned Thursday after reports he had an affair with Alice Huang, a suspected spy for China, and a second affair with a subordinate at Nvidia.

Kim has a long track record as a federal prosecutor and lawyer in private practice.

His investigations have included ones into former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo and the FDIC.

Joon Kim, the lawyer tapped by artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia
 to investigate its former CEO Jensen Huang, and the Big Law firm he works for have a long history of investigating high-profile cases.

Kim, in his career as a top federal prosecutor and as an attorney in private practice, has had in his sights mobster John “The Teflon Don” Gotti’s son, former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and other high-profile people and companies.

The law firm that Kim recently joined — Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz — this year conducted an investigation for the NBA of the Los Angeles Clippers and its billionaire owner, Steve Ballmer, which ended with the basketball league imposing stiff sanctions on Ballmer and the Clippers for violating salary cap rules in connection with superstar Kawhi Leonard.

On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Kim, 55, and Wachtell, Lipton to “conduct a thorough and independent investigation” of allegations that its then-CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort involving his affair with a woman, Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence suspects her of being a spy for China.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday morning on the heels of a New York Times report that he had also had an extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reports to him.

That allegation could be added to the list of issues that Kim will be looking into as part of his probe.

Nvidia did not immediately respond when asked if the parameters of the investigation would be affected by the new claim. A spokeswoman for Wachtell, Lipton declined to comment for this article on behalf of the firm and Kim.

Friends and former colleagues of Kim said Nvidia has made a smart decision in retaining him for the job.

“I think he’s the ideal person for this role,” said Edward Kim, a New York white-collar defense lawyer who worked in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York with Joon Kim. The two men are not related.

“I think they’re going to get a serious, credible investigation. I believe Joon will follow the facts wherever they will lead,” Edward Kim said.

The son of a South Korean diplomat, Joon Kim was born in Los Angeles. He attended Phillips Exeter Academy and later Stanford University.

After graduating cum laude from Harvard Law School, he clerked for a federal judge in Manhattan and then worked as an associate at the major law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton starting in the late 1990s. After that, he spent seven years in the SDNY as an assistant U.S. attorney. His tenure as a prosecutor there included four years in the Organized Crime and Terrorism Unit.

The SDNY, by virtue of its location in Manhattan, handles some of the most high-profile criminal investigations in the United States, including cases of major financial crimes, government corruption and organized crime.

During his first stint at the SDNY, Kim investigated and prosecuted crimes that included “racketeering, murder, money laundering, securities fraud, firearms and narcotics offenses, tax evasion, and terrorism,” the office has previously said.

Kim’s trial wins at the SDNY included obtaining a conviction of Peter Gotti, then-head of the Gambino Mafia family, for conspiring to kill notorious mob turncoat Salvatore “Sammy the Bull” Gravano. Kim and his fellow prosecutors were less successful, however, in prosecuting Peter Gotti’s nephew, John Gotti Jr., whose trials ended with several hung juries.

“He could be a very tenacious courtroom advocate,” said Chris Conniff, a New York attorney who worked with Kim in the SDNY, and who considers Kim one of his closest friends.

“He’s incredibly smart,” Conniff said. “I think he’s known by everyone in the business as just an outstanding investigator, leaves no stone unturned.”

Kim in 2006 returned to Cleary Gottlieb as a partner in the firm’s litigation and enforcement group but then went back to the SDNY in 2013. During his second stint there, he served as deputy U.S. attorney, and then served as U.S. attorney from 2017 to 2018.

Kim’s elevation to acting U.S. attorney came as a result of President Donald Trump’s firing of then-U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara in March 2017 after Bharara refused the new president’s demand that he resign.

“Preet’s departure was very unique,” and the mood in the SDNY “was shaky” after his ouster, Conniff said.

“Preet was very well-liked and well-respected,” said Conniff, who was in private practice at the time that Bharara was fired. “We just lost a very charismatic and effective leader, and in a very dramatic way.”

In taking over from Bharara, Kim, “from my external viewpoint, he righted the ship and continued to do the work of the office in the time he was there.”

“Joon, I would say, gave people confirmation that it was going to be alright, and it was going to be business as usual,” Conniff said.

Kim left the SDNY in April 2018, and began his third stint at Cleary Gottlieb, which he recently left to join Wachtell, Lipton’s litigation department.

In March 2021, Kim and another attorney, Anne Clark, a partner at Vladeck, Raskin & Clark, were tapped by New York Attorney General Letitia James to investigate then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo over allegations that he had sexually harassed several women.

“These are serious allegations that demand a rigorous and impartial investigation,” Kim said in a statement at the time. “We will act judiciously and follow the facts wherever they lead.”

Kim and Clark in August 2021 submitted a 165-page report to James, which concluded that Cuomo had sexually harassed at least 11 women and then retaliated against a former employee who had publicly complained about his behavior. As part of the probe, Kim, Clark and their team interviewed 179 witnesses and reviewed tens of thousands of documents.

Cuomo adamantly denied some of the allegations and said that other claims of alleged misconduct had been mischaracterized or misinterpreted.

A week after the report was publicly released, Cuomo announced that he would resign.

Two years after the Cuomo probe, Kim was retained by the FDIC to conduct an independent review of allegations of sexual harassment and interpersonal misconduct at the agency. As part of the probe, Kim and his team conducted 167 interviews of current and past FDIC employees, and hundreds of additional interviews with individuals who contacted a hotline the team set up for employees to report misconduct claims.

An April 2024 report by Kim and his team found “for far too many employees and for far too long, the FDIC has failed to provide a workplace safe from sexual harassment, discrimination, and other interpersonal misconduct.”

More than five years after Cuomo left office, the former governor’s spokesman has not forgotten, or forgiven, Kim, whom he accused of writing a report on Cuomo with a predetermined outcome.

Kim was a “hired hack,” said the spokesman, Rich Azzopardi.

Azzopardi said Kim “hid evidence” that was exonerating of Cuomo, and accepted at face value “outright lies” from a number of witnesses.

The bad blood between Cuomo’s camp and Kim predates the sexual harassment probe.

While working in the SDNY, Kim and Bharara oversaw the investigation that led to the corruption trial of Joseph Percoco, who had been a close aide of Cuomo. The trial took place after both prosecutors had left the office.

Azzopardi cited that prosecution in his scathing remarks about Kim.

Percoco was sentenced to six years in prison after his 2018 conviction for honest-services wire fraud. The conviction was overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court in a unanimous ruling in 2023 — after his release from prison — because the judge’s instructions to jurors were too vague.

Azzopardi said that Kim and Bharara were motivated to prosecute Percoco for “their own personal glory” and “to generate headlines for themselves.”

Bharara, in a two-word email response about Azzopardi’s claim, wrote, “Andrew who?,” referring to Cuomo.

Azzopardi said he did not believe there was any other reason for Nvidia’s board to retain Kim to investigate the Huang situation other than to reach a predetermined outcome by the board.

“I don’t know what the aims of the board are,” Azzopardi said.

Kim’s friend Conniff, when asked if he expected that the Nvidia investigation would be a whitewash that would serve the board’s interests, said, “No.”

“I don’t think Joon would take an engagement in which he could not provide a fulsome report of what he uncovered during this investigation,” Conniff said. “Any company board that is looking to do a good, thorough investigation of potential wrongdoing, Joon’s perfect ... for it.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-k.title: Here's what Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-k.author: Katie Tarasov,Megan Cassella
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-k.text:
After Jensen Huang’s announced resignation, interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones sent emails to Nvidia employees.

Kress said she “believed deeply” in Nvidia’s future.

“The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you,” Jones wrote.

On the heels of founder Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia, new interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones sent emails to employees Thursday expressing gratitude and optimism for the future.

CNBC obtained copies of the emails from a source familiar with the matter, who said Jones sent the first email and Kress replied shortly after.

Follow CNBC’s live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation

“The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication,” Kress wrote in her email.

The term Estaff is commonly used to refer to executive staff, the group of direct reports to C-suite executives at a company. Nvidia will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PST, her email said.

Board chair Jones took a similar tone in his email, and praised Kress as “a key architect of NVIDIA’s growth and capital strategy.”

“The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you,” Jones wrote.

Below are the staff emails obtained by CNBC on Thursday.

I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy.

The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.

This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT.

We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let’s move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company.

Thank you for all you do,
Colette

Dear NVIDIA Employees,

I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board.

As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA’s growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you.

Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence.

The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.

The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette’s leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA.

Harvey Jones
Chair, NVIDIA Board of Directors

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/donald-t.title: Donald Trump Jr. exits advisory role at Kalshi prediction market
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/donald-t.author: Ananya Chetia,Contessa Brewer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/donald-t.text:
It was a mutual arrangement to end the advisory role, a Kalshi spokesperson said.

Both the platform and Trump Jr. agreed it was a conflict of interest to keep the president’s son as an advisor while serving as a top investor for Polymarket, the spokesperson added.

Prediction market platform Kalshi ended its advisory contract with Donald Trump Jr. in response to his venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, also holding a stake in rival platform Polymarket, according to Kalshi’s spokesperson.

Conversations on Trump Jr.’s exit began in August after 1789 Capital announced a major stake in Polymarket, the spokesperson said. It was a mutual arrangement, with both Kalshi and Trump Jr. agreeing it was a conflict of interest to keep the president’s son as an advisor while serving as a top investor for Polymarket, the spokesperson added.

Trump Jr.’s departure comes after Democrats secured a majority across the House and the Senate, with the party expected to crack down on the prediction market industry. While Trump Jr. has exited Kalshi, he still serves as an advisor to Polymarket. His ties to the industry could make prediction markets an easy target for lawmakers to go after, Joseph Konizeski, a former trial attorney in the CFTC, previously told CNBC.

In early October, Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said on MS NOW that Trump Jr.’s connection to the company creates an “optics issue,” but added that it has never relied on that relationship to gain favor with the government.

Kalshi first named Donald Trump Jr. a strategic advisor for the company in January 2025.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/in-polic.title: In a policy switch, the Fed says its October 2027 meeting will not see a vote on interest rates
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/in-polic.author: Jeff Cox
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/in-polic.text:
The Federal Reserve won’t vote on a potential interest-rate change at its October 2027 meeting.

The Fed will have seven voting meetings next year, down from eight in 2026.

The October session will be used for longer-term and bigger-picture discussions.

The Federal Reserve won’t vote on a potential interest-rate change at its October 2027 meeting, a departure that is part of a broader initiative from Chairman Kevin Warsh aimed at reducing the central bank’s market footprint.

According to an announcement Thursday, the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will set aside its Oct. 26-27 session for “the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues.”

Warsh announced the move at his news conference after the FOMC met in October, though he did not specify which meeting would be affected.

In 2027, there will be seven voting meetings, with the October session set up as extra time for policy deliberation without a formal vote or post-meeting statement. The new calendar shows that the final meeting of the year will now take place in November. It had previously been set for December.

“Now, what’s the reasoning behind this change? To me, it’s quite straightforward,” the chairman said in explaining his rationale. “Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals.”

“But it’s equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations—for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point,” he said.

Warsh has been critical of the Fed’s prior communications strategy, saying policymakers spent too much time providing guidance on policy moves that handcuffed them when it came time to make decisions.

Under typical practice, the Fed meets eight times a year, following with a vote on interest rates and then a news conference from the chair.

Since Warsh took over, the post-meeting statement has been shortened dramatically. Moreover, the press question-and-answer sessions have been cut to around half an hour from their customary 45 minutes or so.

Warsh said in October that the meeting schedule is another step in his plan to streamline communication. He indicated last month that the number of nonvoting meetings would increase to two in 2028.

“I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail,” he said. “It’s an institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions. It’s yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track.”

The FOMC next meets Dec. 8-9. Its first meeting in 2027 will happen Jan. 26-27.

Correction: The Fed’s October 2027 meeting will not see a vote on interest rates. The headline in an earlier version misstated the year.

https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/12/.title: Without Jensen Huang, Nvidia's organizational structure isn't 'built to last,' management expert says
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/12/.author: Sophie Caldwell
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/12/.text:
Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaking company he co-founded in 1993, following public revelations of his extramarital affairs. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as the company’s interim CEO.

Huang’s visionary leadership style and his central role in driving the company’s strategy, combined with the company’s unusually flat management structure, will make him especially difficult to replace, experts say.

Huang notably had more direct reports than the typical CEO, with a “direct staff” of approximately 60 employees, he said in a March 2026 interview with podcaster Lex Fridman.

“The more direct reports a CEO has, the less layers are in the company. It allows us to keep information fluid,” Huang told CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin in 2023.

Having minimal hierarchy has worked for Nvidia so far “because [Huang] has been a strong leader with a strong vision,” says Jo-Ellen Pozner, associate professor of management at Santa Clara University’s Leavey School of Business.

But that structure could make the company’s leadership shake-up even more difficult to navigate, she says.

At companies with flat management structures, the CEO often has even more influence than they would in a traditional hierarchy, according to Joseph Fuller, professor of management practice at Harvard Business School.

Nvidia’s structure was “designed to adapt well in a world of change, either caused by us or affecting us,” Huang said in a March 2025 conversation with Arthur Mensch, cofounder and CEO of Mistral.

Since he directly managed the company’s top executives, Huang held “a tremendous amount of power” at Nvidia, Fuller says. “He’s the orchestrator,” he continues. “He’s the coordinator. He’s resolving the disputes. He’s allocating the resources.”

Now, the company has lost its top decision-maker, Fuller says.

Without Huang, “there is likely nobody who is able to coordinate among those various people with their different expertise and domains,” Pozner says, which could lead to a slowdown in technical work.

There are some advantages to Nvidia’s flat structure, says Denise Rousseau, professor of organizational behavior and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University. Having fewer management layers can strengthen “local leaders” in each area of the company, she says, which can help stabilize Nvidia through its leadership transition.

But “nobody else has the big picture view” that Huang did, Pozner says, which makes finding a permanent successor within the company especially difficult. Moreover, with dozens of direct reports, it’s unlikely that Huang had the time to groom one of his subordinates to take over one day, she says.

Pozner predicts that Nvidia’s next leader will steer the company toward a more traditional management structure. “I understand that a lot of people, especially in Silicon Valley, are averse to rigid hierarchies and the kind of structure that we expect from a legacy organization,” she says. “But it’s functional for a reason.”

Ultimately, Nvidia’s current system is “not an organizational structure that’s built to last,” Pozner says.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/jensen-h.title: Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/jensen-h.author: Ari Levy,Kif Leswing,Isabel O'Brien,Jonathan Vanian
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/jensen-h.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been a singular figure in the development of the AI industry, which suddenly has to survive without him.

Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into the company that powered the AI boom, doing so with no second-in-command.

“How companies handle a crisis determines their future,” former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC’s “Fast Money.”

Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a “visionary of the AI age.” Deutsche Telekom
 CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia
 CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce’s
 Marc Benioff said, “Jensen, we’re all following you, bro,” as the two paced through the audience.

Follow CNBC’s live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation

His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping. Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley.

As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution.

Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that’s been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman.

Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

“How companies handle a crisis determines their future,” former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC’s “Fast Money” on Wednesday. “How they handle this will determine if they’re a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person.”

It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO’s behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers.

Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That’s up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.

It’s a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games.

Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense.

In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon,
 Google
, Meta
 and Microsoft
 — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI
, meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps.

To expand his customer base, Huang designated compute capacity to a number of so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave
 and Nebius
, putting equity into the companies and helping them build big businesses around renting out GPUs.

Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk’s xAI, now part of SpaceX
, did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic
 and Google.

Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private.

In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world.

“He created the product that started the industry,” said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute
. ”Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market.”

When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they’re not authorized to speak publicly about it.

One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Huang’s sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated.

Huang’s ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang’s aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing.

The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that’s facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China.

U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang’s resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday.

“What bothers me at the end of it is what we don’t know is what she knows about him that can be utilized,” Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair. “This is a guy that’s right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don’t think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk.”

But industry experts are quick to emphasize how important Huang was to the health and growth of the broad AI ecosystem. He had the leading names on Wall Street on speed dial as he tried to turn GPUs into what he called an “investable asset” with an expanded roster of financial backers, and he had personal relationships with all the key figures in AI like OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son.

On the deal-making side, Huang’s top lieutenants were Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO. And when seeking a financial backstop, the person behind Huang was Nico Caprez, the CEO’s son-in-law and the company’s vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, three people said.

Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times.

Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was “down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer.”

“I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs,” Puig told CNBC.

That approach persisted, as recently as this week. On Monday, a day after publicly apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife, Huang emailed the CEO of AI infrastructure startup Fireworks AI, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks.

Huang, whose name was suddenly front-page news for all the wrong reasons, was checking in, the person said, just to see if he could help.

— CNBC’s Lora Kolodny, Jordan Novet and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/12/.title: United Airlines won’t let AI agents book your flight. Expert says you shouldn't let a bot do that for you, anyway
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/12/.author: Kamaron McNair
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/12/.text:
United Airlines said Wednesday it would be restricting artificial intelligence bots from its digital platforms, warning that allowing third-party AI assistants to access account credentials could expose sensitive personal information, lead to unintended purchases or other unauthorized account activity. The move is similar to Amazon’s recent blocking of Meta’s Muse agent from making purchases on its site.

Still, AI agents can complete a wide range of tasks on your behalf. Instead of just asking Muse what the weather will be tomorrow, you can tell it to suggest an outfit based on tomorrow’s weather forecast and book you a rideshare if it’s going to rain, for example. Or, rather than just creating an itinerary for your next vacation, you can connect a payment option and have your Dot — OpenAI’s agent offering — book flights, hotels and excursions for you.

You can even have an AI agent buy and sell stocks through investing platforms like Robinhood.

Relying on an AI agent for any of these tasks may come with mixed results depending on which agent you use, what data you allow it to access and the complexity of the task you’ve asked it to carry out. Because broadly, agentic AI is still in its infancy, you may not want to let an agent make decisions “anytime [your] health, wealth, or privacy are involved,” says Shomit Ghose, adjunct professor at the University of San Francisco School of Management, and lecturer at the University of California, Berkeley College of Engineering.

“You can have agents do interesting things for you, like categorize your spending, or flag unusual charges, or model what-if scenarios,” he says. “Those are good things, but bad things would be moving money, making trades, filing forms. All those things should stay manual at this point.”

AI-enthusiast traders may need some convincing, though.

Here’s what you should consider before outsourcing your whole to-do list to an AI agent.

Though AI agents’ capabilities are improving, they still operate in a fairly literal sense, which can create problems, Ghose says. If you tell your agent to book you the cheapest flight, for example, it may book you a flight at 3 a.m. or one with three layovers, unless you give the agent specific guardrails.

“The bot only knows your context,” Ghose says. “It cannot infer, as we humans are able to do, because of instinct and culture and education.”

Further, bots can still get it wrong even with a seemingly clear and direct command. They “treat all data as being equal,” Ghose adds. So if it finds information on the web that is either inaccurate or subjective, it could give you misleading guidance or fail to meet your standards for the given task.

For example, if you tell your agent to book you a reservation at a good barbecue restaurant, it may get you a table at a place that claims to be “the best barbecue in the world” on its website. But the restaurant may be in an inconvenient location or have poor reviews elsewhere on the web. Your command may need to be more specific, like asking your agent to check reviews on Google Reviews or Yelp.

Depending on what task you’ve assigned the bot, the outcome could be rather innocuous. But when individuals consider letting bots make purchases for them, make changes to their investment portfolios or and the like, the result could be more consequential.

“In the end, you want to ask yourself: Does the human need to be in the loop?” Ghose says.

If you’re booking a vacation, for example, it’s reasonable to ask an AI agent to help make a decision on your destination based on the weather, your budget and other factors. But actually booking the flights and hotels “should still come back to me,” Ghose says. He wants to maintain final say over major financial decisions.

Doing so may even save you money. In Booking Holdings’ third-quarter earnings report, the Connecticut-based travel technology company reported 20% higher spending among customers who used AI assistants versus those who didn’t to book accommodations on Agoda, one of its travel platforms. It’s unclear whether those customers were led to pricier options or did, in fact, seek more expensive amenities. The company doesn’t cite a single factor for the finding.

AI agents are also making their way into the healthcare sector, which can pose risks for users too quick to rely on the agents’ advice, Ghose says. Letting an AI agent handle prescription refill requests, for example, could be convenient, but AI managing prescriptions more broadly may act on “incomplete records and won’t be able to recognize a dangerous interaction or a worsening condition before the action has already taken effect,” he says. Generally, a clinician will have to sign off on any new prescriptions, but federal agencies are backing programs that would allow AI agents to assist in diagnostics and prescription management for patients.

Relatedly, anytime you grant an AI agent access to your personal information, whether it’s medical records or your email inbox, you could be introducing privacy risks, Ghose says. He recommends users only allow agents to “use limited permission accounts,” like letting it access your subscription to a news source, rather than your personal accounts, such as your bank account or credit card information.

For some tasks like investing decisions, you need to have a certain level of expertise to clearly dictate your strategy and goals. And even if you give yourself final say on trades, instead of delegating to the bot, it’s essential that you understand the risk involved in moves your AI agent proposes. While a large language model can help you research investments and gather information around an asset, humans are still better at putting that into the context of their individual financial strategy and goals, AI experts say.

Agents can “make your trading experience easier, there is no doubt about it,” Shridhar Rathore, an experienced investor who uses agentic trading tools, recently told CNBC Make It. “But [letting agents] make investment decisions, that’s where people can lose money if they are not careful...they have to make sure that for the execution, the human is in the loop.”

“You want to be really specific and say, ‘I am crafting a trading strategy, and these are the kind of things I’m trying to optimize for,’” like whether you’re thinking about short or long-term strategy, Ghose says. “So that as [the agent] ingests information, it can treat it with the right context.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-c.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit casts shadow over Wall Street’s $500 billion AI financing bet
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-c.author: Hugh Leask
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-c.text:
Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia president, CEO and board member, the company’s board said Thursday.

The chip giant announced in August memorandums of understanding with six major financial firms aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure.

Huang’s departure could see further scrutiny of those arrangements amid growing uncertainty over Nvidia’s direction.

Leadership change at Nvidia
 has the potential to threaten financing of the artificial intelligence boom and test Jensen Huang’s $500 billion vision to turn AI chips into tradable debt securities.

The Nvidia CEO’s resignation was announced Thursday following revelations that he had two extramarital affairs — one with an employee and the other with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy.

Shares in the tech giant — which has become central to the AI build-out in recent years — initially plunged more than 13% following Huang’s resignation, before paring losses.

Nvidia has never identified a successor to Huang, who has led the chipmaker since its founding in 1993. Colette Kress, chief financial officer, has been named interim CEO.

Follow CNBC’s live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation

The company has been dubbed the “central bank” of the AI build-out, with Huang seen as the “hypeman” for the sector and its chips considered the industry’s gold standard.

Huang’s departure raises a central question: whether his successor can carry forward a financing strategy designed to transform GPUs from rapidly depreciating hardware into bankable infrastructure assets

The $4.2 trillion firm’s industry dominance, with Huang front and center, allowed it to sign memorandums of understanding with some of Wall Street’s biggest asset managers, intended to secure third-party capital for a landmark $500 billion AI financing drive.

The preliminary agreements, involving Apollo Global Management
, BlackRock
, Blackstone
, Brookfield
, Goldman Sachs, and KKR
, sought to tap institutional investors and private capital to finance a range of computing infrastructure, including data centers and chip factories. The funding would involve specialized financing vehicles, with Nvidia’s AI chips used as underlying collateral, in arrangements comparable to real estate or toll roads securitizations.

The financing arrangements are still preliminary and subject to final agreements.

BlackRock and Goldman Sachs declined to comment on today’s resignation. The other firms weren’t immediately available for comment.

The arrangements could now face heightened scrutiny in the aftermath of Huang’s departure.

Sunaina Sinha Haldea, global head of private capital advisory at Raymond James, said a leadership change gives every firm involved a “natural moment to pause and look at the terms again.”

“The best thing a new CEO can do is leave these partnerships alone in the first few months and focus on getting the final agreements signed,” Haldea told CNBC via email. “Jensen brought these firms to the table with his vision, and any potential successor will keep them there by showing that the business behind that vision hasn’t changed.”

She added: “I don’t think the capital walks away, because these lenders are underwriting Nvidia’s chips and the customer contracts behind them, but they could want to be paid more for the uncertainty.”

Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said Huang’s successor would need to reassure lenders that Nvidia’s technology roadmap, customer relationships and strategic vision remain intact.

“I wouldn’t expect Nvidia’s financing partnerships to unravel simply because Huang leaves, but a leadership shake-up could make Wall Street more cautious, potentially slowing commitments or tightening financing terms,” Chanana told CNBC via email.

“The bigger risk is a ripple effect across AI financing, particularly when rising debt, circular financing and uncertain investment returns were already under scrutiny,” Chanana added. “This is not a financing crisis yet, but it could become a catalyst for a broader repricing of risk across the AI ecosystem.”

Haldea added that she expects to see more discipline among investors in the aftermath of the scandal. “Lenders will ask harder questions about who is really carrying the risk in these structures, and that scrutiny will spread throughout the AI infrastructure deal market.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/yankees-.title: Yankees President Randy Levine pushes college sports bill, discusses MLB labor negotiations
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/yankees-.author: Jessica Golden
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/yankees-.text:
Yankees President Randy Levine is urging the House to pass the Protect College Sports Act, which he says would provide new funding for schools to retain players and support women’s and non-revenue sports.

Opponents of the bill say it gives colleges more power at student-athletes’ expense.

Levine said he is uncertain whether MLB will reach a labor deal before the current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, citing “fundamental differences in opinion.”

New York Yankees President Randy Levine is urging the House to pass the Protect College Sports Act, warning that college athletics could face deeper financial trouble without federal action. But critics of the bill say it will not do enough to protect student-athletes.

In an interview with CNBC’s Michael Ozanian, Levine said the bill would create a $22 million pool for schools to retain their own players, along with an additional $5 million for women’s and non-revenue sports. He said the House should act after the measure passed the Senate with 77 votes.

President Donald Trump appointed Levine as a vice-chair of a commission in February to explore college sports reforms. The Roundtable on Fixing College Sports was set up to bring more order to college sports as the rise of name, image and likeness deals and the transfer portal have dramatically changed the college sports landscape.

“If this bill isn’t passed, there will never be a bill that’s passed,” Levine said, warning that the Big Ten and SEC could form a “super conference” that operates like a minor league.

Levine said features of the bill will also help level the playing field, provide health care and scholarship protection and help women’s and non-revenue sports.

Opponents argue that the bill would deny college athletes certain rights and protections and would give more money to the NCAA, conferences, and schools to “consolidate money and power.”

“The so-called Protect College Sports Act does little to actually protect the student-athletes who make this multi-billion-dollar industry possible,” Derrick Johnson, president and CEO of the NAACP, said in a statement in September.

Levine also addressed the looming labor negotiations in Major League Baseball, where he serves on the league’s labor committee.

The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1 and both sides appear to be preparing for the possibility of a work stoppage.

Asked whether there would be a 2027 season, he said, “I don’t know whether they’ll reach an agreement or not,” citing “fundamental differences in opinion.”

Levine said it’s early and that these deals don’t usually get done until the very end.

“I’m very confident that the sides will give it all they got to negotiate in good faith to get something done,” he said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/bain-cap.title: Bain Capital’s head of real estate uses this strategy to counter the economy’s ‘cocktail of disruption'
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/bain-cap.author: Diana Olick
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/bain-cap.text:
Ryan Cotton, Bain Capital’s head of real estate, sits for an interview with the Property Play video podcast.

He said Bain is a long-term investor, not a spot trader of assets.

He looks at real estate over a ten-year period, evaluating the secular demand drivers that create the need for specific types of real estate.

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

Over the last few years, macro shocks have rocked the U.S. economy about every six months, from tariffs to the Iran war to the Democratic sweep of the midterm elections. All of that has a direct impact on real estate, according to Ryan Cotton, Bain Capital’s head of real estate.

Cotton oversees $18 billion of real estate assets under management. In this week’s Property Play video podcast, Cotton says that every time the market starts to get back on its feet and find its balance and level, a new shock comes around, and there’s another digestion period that has to happen.

“I think it is disorienting as people try to rebase values, and in the midst of transactions, you’re seeing value retrades at the 11th hour, deals getting pulled, and volume slowing down yet again in the market,” said Cotton. “It’s definitely a confusing and complicated time to be a real estate investor.”

The overall market is still working through an oversupply in several sectors, which was brought on by extremely low interest rates at the start of this decade. There are also shifting demand patterns, with artificial intelligence changing the way logistics, supply chains, and offices work, and where wealth is being created and spent in the economy.

“All those things put together are creating this cocktail of disruption in real estate that’s made things disruptive for the industry as a whole, I think both in terms of understanding the value of what people own today in this new paradigm but also thinking about where do you go from here, and how do you allocate capital against those dynamic shifts?” Cotton said.

So how does Cotton navigate all that? He said Bain is a long-term investor, not a spot trader of assets. He looks at real estate over a ten-year period, evaluating the secular demand drivers that create the need for specific types of real estate.

“And if you take that lens, it leads you away from the office, it leads you away from the mall, it leads you candidly away from some multifamily markets where you have out-migration or oversupply of that product, and instead it leads you into more of what I would call alternative or emerging classes of real estate,” said Cotton.

Senior housing, self-storage and student housing are some of the more traditional but alternative classes he likes. But what really excites him are the super alternatives: Private airplane hangars and marinas for boats and yachts.

“Wealth is concentrating, and as people get richer, they buy more toys,” he explained. “It can generate double-digit NOI [net operating income] growth in those assets, and there is real scarcity of those assets and supply barriers. That means that even though demand continues to grow, supply may not have an adequate response to it.”

He points to recent deals involving Atlantic Aviation, the second-largest private airplane hangar platform in the U.S., and Safe Harbor, the largest marina platform in the country. The latter was bought by Blackstone this year.

Ten years ago, Cotton mused, something like 93% of all real estate assets in the world were invested in the four major food groups, being multifamily, office, retail and industrial. Now that’s down to 82%.

“More and more capital is moving out of those sectors, because of the lack of structural demand drivers, and moving into these more peripheral asset classes,” he said. “The 10 largest [REITs] in the world, seven of them are alternative sectors of real estate, be that data centers, be that senior housing. These are not traditional four food group asset classes, and that’s where the most liquid markets have migrated.”

Cotton leans on the idea of “Mr. Market,” a thought experiment invented by financial analyst Benjamin Graham and popularized by Warren Buffett to illustrate the swings of the stock market by imagining it as a person. “When he’s a bully, you can sell, and when he’s depressed you can just tell him to get out of your office,” said Cotton. “If you put your head down and work hard on creating value, I’m certain that eventually the market finds its level, finds its balance, and Mr. Market finds his optimism again, and then you can get back into transacting.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nscale-u.title: Nscale updates IPO prospectus that shows widening loss
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nscale-u.author: Jordan Novet
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nscale-u.text:
Nscale reported third-quarter financial details in an updated regulatory filing.

The neocloud market has been in tumult, partly because Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday.

However, Nscale can point to growing business with Anthropic, which itself is aiming to go public.

Nvidia
-backed neocloud Nscale on Thursday released updated paperwork for a U.S. initial public offering.

The company had a third-quarter net loss of $1.69 billion on $307.5 million in revenue, which was up 1,344% year over year, according to an updated prospectus for its planned initial public offering. The net loss widened from $1.02 billion in the second quarter, when the company generated $140.6 million in revenue, up 1,252%.

London-based Nscale filed to go public in September, but hasn’t updated its prospectus since then. The company did not specify how much it intends to raise in the public offering on the New York Stock Exchange.

Since then the company has faced public setbacks.

Microsoft
 walked away from an Nscale data center that it had planned to use in England. Darren Hardman, Microsoft’s CEO for the U.K and Ireland, told CNBC in October that the decision had to do with Nscale’s ability to get access to electricity.

The Financial Times reported that Microsoft decided against renewing a contract with Nscale in Texas. The company said in its IPO filing that it expects Microsoft to be a “significant customer in future periods.”

The neocloud market, which focuses on renting access to chips such as Nvidia graphics processing units to clients, has been in tumult, partly because Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday, after admitting to being unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia is investigating Huang’s relationship with a woman whom intelligence agencies have called a Chinese spy.

In October investors pressured shares of Nscale rival CoreWeave, but the stock advanced almost 25% on Wednesday on strong results. CoreWeave pulled back about 7% on Thursday following the departure of Huang, who has overseen investments in the neocloud.

Shares of another neocloud, Nebius
, fell about 17% on Thursday, with the company issuing light full-year guidance.

But Nscale can point to growing business with Anthropic, which itself is aiming to go public. In late September Anthropic exercised its right to contract for additional computing power at an Nscale site in West Virginia.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.title: Global Warming Remains Unchecked, Experts Warn at UN’s COP31 Climate Summit
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.author: By Bob Berwyn
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.

Climate Action Tracker, a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5 degrees Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.

“This striking change suggests that global warming has accelerated in recent years,” the EU scientists wrote. Even without understanding every aspect of the recent rapid global temperature increase, “It is clear that the ever-growing concentrations of greenhouse gases emitted by human activity in the atmosphere remain the main driver of this trend.”

The current level of warming has already triggered deadly and destructive floods, wildfires and catastrophic glacier collapses, said Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who is attending the U.N. “Conferences of the Parties” climate talks, for the first time since 2021.

“The climate crisis is a matter of life and death,” she said. “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”

Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, said governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.

“Our message is a stark one,” Heck said. “Collective government action on climate change has stalled for the fifth consecutive year.” Efforts to speed up the shift away from fossil fuels have been negated by new oil and gas drilling projects and governments that are “delaying, weakening or rolling back their climate policies.”

Even under the most optimistic scenario, assuming full implementation of existing policies and promises, global temperatures would rise 3.4 degrees Fahrenheit above preindustrial levels by 2100, an increase climate scientists consider extremely dangerous.

While there has been progress on developing renewable energy sources, the “brutal truth is that these positive developments have not yet added up to bend the curve fast enough,” said Niklas Höhne, a researcher with The New Climate Institute. Developing new oil and gas projects is a bit like discovering your food is burning and then turning up the stove instead of turning it off, he added.

Getting into the specifics of the current negotiations at COP31 surrounding global renewable goals, he noted that conference co-hosts Turkey and Australia have so far opposed including the word “clean” in connection with electrification targets.

“It’s very hard to understand, and the only explanation I can think of is their interest in fossil fuels,” Höhne said.

Australia is one of the world’s biggest coal exporters, and Turkey is a major coal consumer, with its power sector still highly dependent on the most climate-damaging fossil fuel. Even as they host this year’s climate conference, neither country has offered any specific plans to transition away from fossil fuels.

Bill Hare, the CEO of Climate Analytics, called out wealthy, developed countries for their lack of leadership on climate action, noting that European Union Commission President Ursula von der Leyen failed to mention anything about transitioning away from fossil fuels during her speech this week at COP31.

“Governments … at this COP have a stark choice,” Hare said. If they continue supporting fossil fuels, “it would consign humanity and our ecosystems to insurmountable economic damage and irretrievable loss.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.author: By Dylan Baddour
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12112.text:
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission this week issued a permit for construction of four next-generation nuclear reactors at a petrochemical complex on the rural Gulf Coast of Texas.

The Long Mott Generating Station, developed by chemical giant Dow and nuclear startup X-energy, is one of two flagship projects selected by the U.S. Energy Department in 2020 for its Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, intended to kickstart a new era of growth for the nation’s nascent nuclear sector.

“This milestone marks a significant step forward,” Mike Goff, principal deputy assistant secretary for nuclear energy, said in a press release Monday. “The NRC’s approval demonstrates meaningful progress toward deploying advanced reactors.”

The Texas project is at the leading edge of a new generation of reactor designs that could revolutionize the commercial model for atomic energy. They replace the gargantuan construction projects currently required for nuclear power plants with small, modular units that can be produced in factories and then shipped and assembled onsite at industrial installations, from data centers to petrochemical plants.

“We understand that owning a nuclear facility is a different kind of responsibility,” said Kreshka Young, North American business director for energy and climate at Dow, during a public meeting on the project’s construction permits in the town of Port Lavaca in September. “We do not take that lightly.”

Dow plans to install four 80-megawatt reactors by X-energy at its Seadrift Operations complex, on the Gulf Coast between Houston and Corpus Christi. The units won’t require the towering, concrete containment structures characteristic of existing nuclear reactors, nor the 10-mile emergency planning zone, thanks to what scientists describe as revolutionary safety features inherent in new reactor designs.

X-energy CEO J. Clay Sell, a former deputy energy secretary, has described the company’s Xe-100 unit as “physically impossible to melt down.”

Diane Wilson, a retired fourth-generation shrimper from the tiny nearby town of Seadrift and director of San Antonio Bay Waterkeeper, a local environmental organization, remains deeply skeptical. “Frankly, it’s outrageous,” she said. “This is outrageous.”

Spent fuel from the reactors will be stored indefinitely on-site as nuclear waste, she noted, as the U.S. still lacks a permanent national disposal site.

In 2025, Wilson’s organization filed legal challenges to the project’s permit application over safety concerns, which were ultimately dismissed by the NRC. The agency approved Dow’s reactor construction permit after an expedited review under executive orders from President Donald Trump aimed at accelerating the national energy sector.

“We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction,” said NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh in a press release.

Dow still needs to make a final decision to proceed with the project, the company said in a release. If it does, construction could begin before 2030.

If the project proves successful, it would “provide a pathway other industries can emulate” to install dedicated, onsite power generation, said Martin O’Neal, general counsel for the Nuclear Energy Institute, at the September meeting in Port Lavaca.

The NRC hosted the meeting to take questions and comments from the public on the Long Mott Generating Station.

“The nuclear industry is watching this project very closely,” O’Neal said.

In the last three decades, the U.S. has built just one new nuclear power plant, but federal authorities have pushed in recent years for an industry revival based on new reactor designs. The NRC issued its first permit for construction of an advanced test reactor in 2023, and its first permit for an advanced commercial reactor in March 2026.

While typical nuclear reactors use water to cool, advanced designs use alternatives, from molten salt to gas. The Xe-100 uses helium gas. Rather than traditional fuel rods, the Xe-100 uses a pelletized fuel form in a moving bed of pebbles.

“These are new technologies,” said Mehdi Reisi Fard, deputy director of advanced reactors at the NRC, during the public meeting in Port Lavaca in September.

The innovations add up to a feature known as “functional containment,” where the natural resilience and circulation of fuel pebbles prevents the kind of runaway warming that could lead the reactor to meltdown.

Compared with current control systems, functional containment is “less reliant on pumps or human intervention to mitigate anomalies,” Fard explained.

It works thanks to a new kind of pelletized nuclear fuel, called TRISO fuel, which has been developed in Energy Department labs over decades.

“Simply put, TRISO particles cannot melt in a commercial high-temperature reactor,” a DOE webpage says.

The new technology enables developers to skip the big, expensive safety features, like the massive concrete casings, that are required for traditional water-cooled reactors.

“The argument these developers are using is that they don’t need a physical containment because the reactor is so safe,” said Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety with the Union of Concerned Scientists, in an interview earlier this year. “Nuclear designers have been trying to reduce the costs of containment, and one way to do that would be to eliminate it entirely.”

But Lyman doesn’t consider the fuel to be as safe as authorities say.

“It’s just a myth that this fuel is indestructible or meltdown-proof,” he said. “This fuel has vulnerabilities.”

https://www.carbonbrief.org/cop31-how-ed.title: COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions
https://www.carbonbrief.org/cop31-how-ed.author: Simon Evans
https://www.carbonbrief.org/cop31-how-ed.text:
UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.

Carbon Brief readers submitted questions via CB Connect on topics including the UK’s “climate leadership”, the COP31 electrification target, as well as the roadmaps on deforestation and fossil fuels.

Despite recent criticism over the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, Miliband argued that the UK is still seen as a climate leader, due to its “ambitious targets on net-zero”.

Pushing back on a question about COP reform, Miliband explained how he is “quite pro the institution of the COP”, given its role in bringing countries together for climate action.

He emphasised the importance of action on methane and the UK’s “support” for the “35×35” electrification pledge.

Carbon Brief: Well, thanks very much for joining us. I know you’re very busy and we’ve got some reader questions. It’s great that you’ve got time to answer some.

Ed Miliband: Can I just say how much I love Carbon Brief?

CB: Thanks. Lovely to hear.

EM: Like, comment and subscribe!

CB: How, in your experience at COP31 so far, has the UK’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field and the rumoured rollback of its EV targets affected the UK’s standing as a climate leader?

EM: People see us as showing leadership. People don’t see us as rolling back, and I think what people see is a government that is driving the agenda on electrification and clean power. Because after all, we have a clean power 2030 target, which is world-leading.

[We] have the most ambitious targets on net-zero, the [nationally determined contributions] NDCs, of frankly, any country in the world. [We] are legislating for no new oil and gas licences.

And what I’m trying to do here is also bring a new dimension to this, which is the whole national security dimension. Because I think, if you’re serious about national security, you need to be serious about climate. And those parties – and those people – who aren’t serious about climate, I don’t think they’re serious about national security. Because this is a national security issue for, I think – frankly – every government across the world.

So I think, look, people see British leadership. People are looking forward to our [presidency of the] G20 [in 2027], where climate resilience [and] debt development will be central to the agenda as well.

CB: Are you confident that the UK can still meet its 2030 NDC target [to cut emissions 68% below 1990 levels]?

EM: Absolutely, we’re going to go all out to meet it. I think that’s so important, and that is the whole principle of the NDCs, is [that] you drive towards seeking to meet them. Obviously, it’s stretching. We inherited, from 2024, a difficult situation from the previous government, but we’re going to go all out to do what we can.

CB: Great. With the UK and other developed countries facing increasing fiscal pressures, how can you go about ensuring developing countries receive the financial and technical support that they need?

EM: Look, I think the biggest thing we need to do, cognisant of those fiscal pressures and the situation facing developing countries, is multilateral development bank (MDB) reform. So making sure that the MDBs work to the maximum for developing countries.

There’s lots of evidence out there and I was speaking about this at the World Bank annual meetings about the fact that the MDBs could do more to leverage their balance sheets. You know, potentially hundreds of billions of pounds – dollars – more that could be helping developing countries. Helping developing countries with climate resilience, helping them with relieving the debt burden in terms of the financing of the debt.

And, you know, one of the things that we’re going to be doing as part of our G20 is convening those MDBs to, in a friendly way, you know, point to the best practice of some of them, push the others to do more. I feel from our discussions that this is absolutely possible – for us to do more.

So yes, there are more fiscal constraints in developed countries, including in Britain, but it doesn’t mean we can’t make a difference. And I think it’s really, really important to say to your viewers: we are serious about, not just our national leadership on climate, but our international leadership as well, and we believe we can make a difference.

CB: It’s become part of the narrative that the COP process has run its course, and that people should focus more on mini-coalitions, groups of middle powers. What would you say to that, and how would you like to see the COP process reformed?

EM: I mean, I’m quite pro the COP process – not the process, but I’m quite pro the institution of the COP – and I’d say that in two respects.

One, if you look at the sweep of history, I was at the Copenhagen COP of 2009, [which] ended in acrimony. We were heading for a 4C world back then. Now, we’re heading for a 2.5C, 2.6C world, according to the latest UNEP emissions gap report – one of my favourite publications.

And look, 2.6C is bad, right? And we’ve got to do a lot more as a world, but we have made progress. And why? Because of multilateralism, because of the institution, being part of the COP, driving people forward.

That’s one part of it. The second part of it is [that the COP is] a place where these “coalitions of the willing” are formed. If I think about what I’ve done while I’ve been here [in Antalya] – I was at an event on forests, coalitions of the willing acting on the forest leaders’ partnership, acting to protect the forest. An event on electrification, a big focus of the Turkish presidency. An event on industrial policy, green industrial policy. Countries working together. An event this morning on methane, really crucial. We’re trying to, with a coalition of the willing, get it onto the COP agenda. And then, an event on climate security.

So that gives people, your viewers, a sense of why I think this [COP process] matters. You know, it’s not simply a talking shop. I think it is also a place where action happens.

CB: You mentioned the electrification pledge put forward by the Turkish presidency. Is the UK a signatory to that yet?

EM: We support the electrification pledge, absolutely, and you know we want to drive forward. It’s stretching for the UK, but we think it’s the right thing to do. And why? Because – it’s really important to say this – because electrification is a way of getting off the fossil-fuel rollercoaster. Clean-energy electrification is the way I think about it.

[Three hours after Carbon Brief’s interview with Ed Miliband, the UK government confirmed its endorsement of the 35×35 electrification pledge.]

And if there’s one lesson we’ve got to learn from these two wars that we’ve seen – Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran war – it’s [that] you can’t have security on the basis of fossil fuels. It’s not even – even [for a] country like America, a massive fossil-fuel producer is affected by higher prices. But for fossil-fuel importers, covering 75% of the world’s population [including the UK], we are price takers. And you know the fossil-fuel rollercoaster is terrible for the cost of living. That’s why clean energy, clean electrification, is the answer. Electrify now!

CB: The UN climate convention and the Paris Agreement both commit countries, including the UK, to implement “climate-change education, training, public awareness and participation”. Why doesn’t the UK have a national programme on this, particularly given the flood of misinformation in this area?

EM: We need to do more. You’re completely right. Look, I am always ambitious to do more, and more climate education – well, more public information – is important.

I did the first annual climate and nature statement in 2025. It was repeated in 2026 by [environment secretary] Mary Creagh. I was in the House of Commons for that, and that whole institution was part of me believing, as energy secretary, that it was important to find ways to inform the public.

And I fully acknowledge we need to do more. We need to do more. But we need to do more to both tell people about what is happening, in terms of climate and nature, but also say there are answers, because it can’t just be a council of despair. It’s also got to be a council of hope – not false hope – but a council of honesty, but also hope.

CB: Great. How would you like to see the Brazilian roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation taken forward? Are you keen to see those as part of the formal negotiated outcome [at COP31]?

EM: I think what’s interesting about this goes back to your question about the coalition of the willing. Look, there’s obviously no secret that there are countries that are obstacles to the fossil-fuel roadmap being part of – central – to the COP decision. And we took a decision last year that there was a big enough coalition of the willing – I think there are 80 countries or more – to drive this forward.

I think the Brazilians are to be incredibly commended for having produced this fossil-fuel roadmap. I think we should now be thinking, as individual countries, how can we build on that work ourselves? Because it’s doing exactly what I hoped it would do, which is to grapple with the important issues that we face.

I think we have to accept there are some countries – in a world where you have to operate by consensus – where not every decision is going to get into the COP decision. But it doesn’t mean we can’t make progress on it, and I think that’s really true in this case.

CB: Great. One final question from my end, if I may. What’s an outcome that you’re going to be looking for at the end of this COP, that you’re going to be happy to take home to the UK?

EM: I think the most important thing is action to drive forward the climate agenda, and that’s what I want to see. You know, it goes back to the point about the cost. Some of it is about the formal decision-making, but a lot of it is about the real, tangible outcomes that have happened over a couple of weeks.

And if I think about what I’ve done here, you know, if we can get methane and the importance of methane – which, as you know, and as your viewers will know – is such an important short-term difference we can make in terms of preventing the rise in temperatures, and we can get that onto the agenda of the COP. If we can show progress on other aspects of the real economy – what’s happening in the real economy – all of those things are going to be important.

I think there’s something else, though, which is, these events of countries coming together. They contradict those people who say, you know, people are giving up on climate. Because you’ve got more than 190 countries that are coming together [at the COP], reaffirming their belief in the Paris Agreement, reaffirming their belief that they need to make efforts, as part of the Paris Agreement, to meet the climate goals – and working together on these issues.

It doesn’t mean they aren’t hard, but it does show that there is really important global commitment, which I’ve been hearing, to this agenda.

CB: Brilliant. Thanks very much, Ed.

This interview was conducted by Dr Simon Evans at the COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, on 12 November 2026. Filming by Josh Gabbatiss and Daisy Dunne, with editing by Joe Goodman.
