Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. It’s been a wild week of news, and our heads are still spinning. We’ve got a very full edition for you this week.

Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Hegseth escapes impeachment for the time being, Russia’s ambassador to Washington dies, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. It’s been a wild week of news, and our heads are still spinning. We’ve got a very full edition for you this week.

Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Hegseth escapes impeachment for the time being, Russia’s ambassador to Washington dies, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth narrowly escaped an impeachment effort this week, but questions remain over his job security.

The push to impeach Hegseth, led by outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, was blocked by Republicans in the House on Tuesday. The House voted 211 to 204 on a motion to refer the articles of impeachment to the House Judiciary Committee, which effectively tanked the chances of Hegseth getting impeached—for now. Eleven Democrats missed the vote, which helped House Republicans pass the motion by seven votes.

But Hegseth’s troubles are far from over as Republicans continue to contend with the fallout from their disastrous performance in the midterms, which was driven in part by voter discontent over the economic consequences of the Iran war. In Washington, Hegseth is seen as the face of that war, as well as other controversial military actions that President Donald Trump has taken in Latin America, putting the defense secretary’s future in question as the political landscape shifts.

What’s next for Hegseth. Democrats could launch another effort to impeach Hegseth in a new Congress. “This is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next House speaker, said after the impeachment vote this week.

Democrats will have the votes in the House to impeach Hegseth in a new Congress. But they’re less likely to garner the support of enough Republicans in the Senate to convict and remove the defense secretary.

Whether Democrats pursue impeachment or not, Hegseth will be under a microscope. Democrats have been clear that they will leverage their oversight powers to investigate him on everything from the Iran war and the military operation that led to the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to the lethal strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats near Latin America. Even some Republicans in recent days have suggested that he should just resign and said that they want more answers on the Iran war.

Trump has backed Hegseth so far and signaled that he doesn’t plan to fire him. As long as the president stands by him, Hegseth might be able to save his job. People have been “predicting that Secretary Hegseth would be on his way out” since the Signalgate controversy, said Peter Feaver, a professor of political science and public policy at Duke University.

“He’s shown that he’s quite adept at holding on to his position because he’s maintained the confidence of the one person that matters in the administration, and that’s President Trump,” Feaver said. “I don’t see evidence that he has lost President Trump’s confidence. If anything, Trump is more fulsome in his expressions of support for Secretary Hegseth.”

Hegseth vs. Congress. Hegseth, a former Fox News host, went on the offensive in the past week, launching a campaign-style media blitz against his opponents in Congress, posting about it on social media, and delivering a fiery speech at a rare press conference from the Pentagon. It was indicative of the unusually partisan approach that Hegseth has taken to his role. Some watchdogs have also suggested that Hegseth’s messaging campaign violated federal law.

Defense secretaries are meant to be political animals who are “very nonpartisan” but “really wily at working Congress,” Feaver said. “Hegseth has not fit that mold,” Feaver added, describing him as the “most partisan” defense secretary in modern times. While this has helped Hegseth maintain Trump’s trust, the defense secretary “also answers to Congress,” Feaver said, especially when it comes to the defense budget that the Defense Department relies on.

The National Defense Authorization Act, the annual defense policy bill that dictates yearly U.S. military spending levels, is stalled in Congress. The White House has been pressing Congress to pass a record budget request of $1.5 trillion, but Hegseth’s recent attack campaign may have made this even harder than it already was in a lame-duck session.

It also doesn’t set the Pentagon up “for success in the last two years in terms of working with the new Congress,” Feaver said. Trump on Thursday called on Senate Republicans to “IMMEDIATELY” pass $350 billion in defense spending via reconciliation before Democrats take over.

Hegseth is used to a less active Congress, but that’s about to change with Democrats at the helm. “There’s a saying in the military—you don’t fight against the terrain,” Feaver said.

Russian Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev died aged 66 in Moscow, the Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Wednesday. Darchiev had been posted in Washington since March 2025 but returned to Moscow to seek treatment for a chronic illness, CNN reported.

Erik Slavin, the former editor in chief of the Pentagon-funded newspaper Stars and Stripes, announced on Wednesday that he would be joining the Atlantic as a staff writer covering the U.S. military. Slavin was fired from his post at Stars and Stripes in August for alleged insubordination after he defended the publication’s editorial independence.

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

Russia-Ukraine stalemate continues. Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, failed to yield a major breakthrough this week, save for an agreement for Russia and Ukraine to exchange prisoners of war. The broader sticking points that have dogged the conflict remain, including the prospect of a temporary cease-fire and both sides’ territorial claims on the front lines.

The Kremlin appears unwilling to cede any ground, with lead Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky telling reporters after the talks that “every square foot of land will be returned to Russia one way or another.” U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday before heading to Dublin for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that same day. Witkoff told reporters in Moscow that European officials will join the next round of talks—a potentially significant step given that Putin has long resisted any European role in talks to end the war.

Vance reassigned. Trump announced in a Truth Social post on Thursday that he has ordered Vice President J.D. Vance “to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.” instead of working on negotiations with Iran. Vance has been leading those negotiations and was reportedly set to meet with a senior Iranian security official to try to end the war.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!,” Trump wrote.

As John reported, Vance last week blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm losses in a rare public statement.

Huang’s out. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday—the latest twist in a weekslong scandal that has unleashed turmoil at the $4 trillion company whose semiconductor chips have become indispensable to the development of artificial intelligence. Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy and is accused of having another one with a subordinate at Nvidia.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has overseen the company’s rise into a technology behemoth and has himself become the face of the global AI race. His departure has implications far beyond the company or any one country. Rishi explains why in his piece on the saga.

Pro-Palestinian protesters attend a rally at Trinity College in Dublin, Ireland, on Nov. 10 during a visit by former U.S. President Joe Biden.Li Mangmang/Xinhua via Getty Images

Monday, Nov. 16: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit begins in Manila, Philippines, with the group hosting bilateral summits with China, Australia, and South Korea.

Tuesday, Nov. 17: Trump arrives in Manila for the ASEAN-U.S. special summit and Quad leaders summit.

France holds a general strike.

Wednesday, Nov. 18: The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economic leaders meeting begins in Shenzhen, China.

Thursday, Nov. 19: The International Court of Justice is scheduled to pronounce its final judgment on accusations of genocide against Myanmar over its campaign against Rohingya Muslims.

Friday, Nov. 20: The European Union hosts the EU-U.K. summit.

50—the number of ballistic missiles that Iran continues to produce every month, according to Western intelligence estimates cited by Bloomberg.

“My analogy would be … the Titanic hit the iceberg on Nov. 3, and I came up with a life raft, and they said, ‘No thanks, we’re going to stick on the Titanic.’”

—Massie to MS NOW after his motion to impeach Hegseth failed in the House.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the company’s stock price.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the company’s stock price.

Huang has been seen as the face of the global artificial intelligence race. His company is the world’s leading producer of advanced semiconductor chips, making Nvidia a critical part of U.S. national security and a sought-after partner of China. Huang himself is among the world’s wealthiest people, with an estimated net worth of around $162 billion prior to his recent scandal.

Over the past two years, Huang has also become a close friend of U.S. President Donald Trump, whose administration has made advancing AI a cornerstone of its agenda. Notably, Huang successfully petitioned the White House last December to relax some restrictions on Nvidia sales to China in exchange for the U.S. government receiving a 25 percent cut of the profits.

But in just two weeks, Huang’s public image has collapsed. Late last month, the New York Times reported that a Chinese businesswoman believed to be spying for Beijing was in a “close relationship” with Huang. The alleged spy, Alice Huang, was an executive at a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, which the U.S. Commerce Department began suspecting in 2024 of helping China to smuggle in Nvidia’s restricted AI chips.

Nvidia shares plummeted in the wake of the news, even as Beijing denied involvement. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday.

However, the scandal didn’t end there. On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had had a separate affair with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare. That relationship may have violated the company’s code of conduct. Huang has not publicly acknowledged the second affair.

The dual allegations appear to have been enough to force Huang to step down. Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress ahead of the U.S. holiday of Thanksgiving over the espionage scandal. And Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress has agreed to serve as interim CEO until a replacement is named.

Nvidia’s change in leadership, though, has yet to assuage global markets. Company shares plunged as much as 14 percent when trading opened on Thursday, extending a crisis that has already wiped out more than $1 trillion from Nvidia’s market value. Some initial gains were made later in the day but not enough to reverse the damage.

Nvidia’s board has said there is “no reason to believe” that Huang’s actions compromised U.S. national security or company secrets, but it has launched an independent investigation. And on Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong issued a statement saying that the company takes its obligation to comply with U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously” and will work “constructively and transparently with the U.S. government.”

Trump, meanwhile, praised Huang on Thursday, writing on Truth Social that he had done a “fantastic job” with Nvidia.

A seat at the table. Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed on Thursday to allow European representatives to join the next round of direct Ukraine peace talks. Giving Europe a seat at the table marks a big win for Kyiv and Washington, which have both pushed for greater European involvement in negotiations. However, the concession could also spell trouble for future talks, as Moscow remains largely at odds with its European counterparts.

“We would very much like you, gentlemen, and the U.S. administration as a whole to work with your European allies so that they can finally make up their minds as to what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” Putin told U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow on Thursday. At the same time, the Russian leader warned that any push for the deployment of European troops to Ukraine after a peace deal is inked would trigger renewed fighting.

Witkoff and Kushner will now head to Dublin for similar talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The potential of European involvement in the peace process will almost certainly be on the agenda, but Zelensky is also likely to bring up new reports of Starlink disruptions in Ukraine.

Zelensky on Thursday accused the U.S.-based company of placing speed restrictions on its Starshield military-grade services, affecting how its drone interceptors operate. The last time that such limits were detected, Zelensky resumed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries in direct opposition to Trump’s wishes. Kyiv and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had both accused the Trump administration of orchestrating that incident, which the White House denied.

Academic scandal. Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka submitted his resignation to parliament on Thursday in the wake of a scandal over his academic credentials. It is unclear when his departure will take effect; however, experts expect the incident to deliver another blow to the tenuous alliance between former President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo and current President Prabowo Subianto.

Calls for Gibran’s impeachment first intensified last month, when the country’s Constitutional Court found that the vice president did not possess the necessary credentials to hold power. In Indonesia, lawmakers must have a high school diploma to run for office. Gibran claimed to have finished grade 12 at a school in Australia, but the court ruled that the degree was not equivalent to an Indonesian senior high school certificate. Two weeks later, the country’s Supreme Court backed that ruling by revoking Gibran’s equivalency document.

Gibran was elected in 2024 largely as a symbol of the precarious truce between his father, Jokowi, and Prabowo. His removal could therefore further fracture that fragile alliance. Just last week, Indonesian authorities detained three senior police officials suspected of wiretapping the president and dozens of other prominent figures. Among those arrested was Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was a known loyalist of Jokowi.

Gaza hospital attack. An Israeli airstrike targeted the main hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis overnight on Thursday, killing at least six people, including a teenager, and injuring at least 20 others. Locals reported two missiles damaging a building containing surgical wards at Nasser Hospital. The attack marked the latest violation of the region’s precarious Gaza cease-fire, which took effect in October 2025.

According to Israel’s military, the hospital strike was part of an operation targeting Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom Israeli forces described as the “commander of Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade.” Israel claimed that Abu Ismail had turned Nasser Hospital into his headquarters and was using the facility as a base of operations. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using civilian infrastructure as human shields. The militant group has denied doing so.

Since the Israel-Hamas war began in October 2023, Israeli troops have attacked Nasser Hospital at least seven times, according to hospital officials. The use of medical centers for military purposes and the targeting of such sites are both considered violations of international law. “Gaza’s health facilities are lifelines for its ​people,” World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X on Thursday. “They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked.”

The Finnish Embassy in Canberra temporarily closed its doors on Tuesday for a one-day internal planning and staff sauna event. However, what was meant to be a routine disruption instead appeared to upend the internet, with a deluge of memes jokingly bemoaning the closure. Local swimming pools offered their services for those suffering, a Dutch esports league complained about the lockout, and even American Airlines unveiled a snap sale on flights to Europe for emotional support.

The embassy, meanwhile, took the public’s outcry in stride. “After 24 harrowing hours, international expressions of grief and an unprecedented outpouring of solidarity, the Embassy of Finland in Canberra has officially reopened,” the facility posted on social media on Wednesday, marking the event with a ribbon-cutting ceremony.

On the morning of Nov. 11, some 6,000 Italian schools received an identical email from a “Mikhail Andropov.” A “powerful explosive device with a remote trigger” had been left inside the building, the message said, and the survivors would be finished off with knives. Principals evacuated students from Trieste to Palermo. That same morning, more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland also received threatening emails, and police in Scotland reported similar bomb threats, as well. By midday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had convened an emergency meeting with Italy’s intelligence services and National Cybersecurity Agency at Palazzo Chigi in Rome. No bombs were found.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Five days earlier, emails bearing the same signature and subject line (“Message to the West”) reached newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria, leading the Irish public broadcaster RTE to evacuate its offices and suspend programming. The emails claimed responsibility for a wave of false threats that, between Nov. 3 and Nov. 6, targeted at least 35 passenger flights across Europe. On Nov. 5 alone, around 20 civilian aircraft were affected: Italian, French, and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled to escort airliners, and an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French military air base. Italian schools had already been targeted on Oct. 19 and again on Nov. 2, when an email with the same text reached nearly 280 education facilities. In October, hundreds of schools in Britain, Hungary, and Serbia received similar threats.

Some European intelligence officials consider Russia the most likely origin based on motive, modus operandi, and precedent. At the same time, these officials warn that a firm attribution may never come. Naturally, Moscow has denied involvement.

Until a few weeks ago, the debate on Russia’s attacks on Europe was about the violent end of the spectrum: explosive-laden drones targeting a cargo plane in Leipzig, Germany; sabotage of railroad systems in Germany, the Netherlands, and Poland; drones over airports and military bases. These operations crossed into direct physical attacks and required capabilities that few actors possess. The past month shows the opposite end. A hoax bomb threat requires an email account and a few minutes, whereas the cost for the target is enormous: evacuations, bomb-disposal teams, aircraft diversions, fighter-jet scrambles, lost school days, and frightened parents. The authors of the “Message to the West” boasted of having caused widespread panic and forcing European authorities to spend a fortune on their emergency procedures.

This perfectly illustrates the asymmetry of hybrid threats. The defender cannot dismiss the threat because of its potential catastrophic impact, so every hoax triggers the full precautionary protocol. The attacker sets the tempo while the defender can only react and bear the cost.

A second feature makes this part of the hybrid war harder to counter. Schools, airports, and shopping centers in Europe receive their constant dose of empty threats from pranksters, students hoping to skip an exam, extortionists, and people with personal grievances. Each false alarm shows others how easy it is to cause disruption for free. On Wednesday, Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto predicted that such hoaxers will only multiply. Some of the threats against passenger flights claimed to come from the Male State, an anti-feminist movement banned in Russia. The claim of origin reads as mockery but also makes a point: No matter who is behind them, the hoaxes absorb resources and reinforce the perception of insecurity. For an attacker, each new campaign builds on the destabilizing effects of all previous ones.

This is why the low end of the attack spectrum is a useful reminder of what hybrid campaigns are for. Their purpose is psychological, the target is public opinion, and the objective is to generate confusion, fear, and distrust in institutions. A drone strike and a fake email serve the same purpose by different means. The first tests how far the threshold of attacks that Europe will tolerate without responding has moved. The second shows how little it takes to make citizens feel unprotected. Meloni put it plainly on Wednesday: The threats, she said, appear to be part of a strategy to generate alarm and concern.

The hoaxes also expose the attribution problem more starkly than sabotage does. Attribution is both a technical and a political issue. Pure data and forensic analysis rarely provide certainty about the sender. The senders of this month’s threatening emails have worn three masks: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Nov. 2, the Male State on Nov. 5, and a pseudonym evoking a long-dead Soviet leader since Nov. 6. Some of last week’s emails to airports came from an address at a public health network in the Colombian capital, Bogotá.

And even when the attack’s origin is clear, government leaders often lack the political will to name the attacker. The reason usually given is fear of escalation. A second reason is rarely admitted: Naming the attacker would mean telling their publics that Russia has already escalated a war against Europe, and that this war demands a response.

This creates a hard problem for policy. Against a threat with such disproportionate costs for the attacker and defender, reactive defense is a losing strategy. This is especially true given the fact that widely accessible technology makes these attacks ever cheaper to carry out at scale. The logical answer is deterrence, which means raising the cost and risk for the attacker. But deterrence rests on attribution, which will often be only partial.

A credible deterrent posture therefore requires a degree of political courage that European governments have so far avoided. It means saying, in advance and together: We may not know with certainty who is behind the next wave, but if it happens, we will impose costs based on the available evidence, even if that evidence is incomplete. This is a probabilistic standard of response, closer to how intelligence works than how courts work. It is uncomfortable for democracies bound by the rule of law and accustomed to standards of incontrovertible evidence. And it carries a risk of error. The alternative is the certain continuation of a campaign that costs an adversary nothing and undermines the target every time.

Leaders are debating what to call it—rather than what to do.

The posture must also be Europe-wide rather than national. A campaign that reaches Italian schools, Irish newsrooms, and Czech airports in the same week is designed to exploit divisions. A response that each country calibrates on its own invites the attacker to probe for the weakest link.

The final element is speed. Because hybrid campaigns rely on diffused costs and dispersed information, they have to be met with rapid information sharing. When thousands of schools receive the same threatening email at the same moment—and that fact is known within minutes by everyone concerned—then the threat largely diagnoses itself: It is a coordinated campaign, and the alarms are very likely false. Italy’s education minister, Giuseppe Valditara, said as much on Wednesday, noting that the sheer number of schools involved demonstrated how little credibility the threat had.

A similar logic applies to real attacks. When hackers took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of French supermarkets in October and in stores across at least 11 European countries in early November, the pattern was the clue: It was a simultaneous, automated, and cross-border effort. A shared picture in real time turns hundreds of isolated emergencies into a single recognizable event. It speeds up the response, lowers the payoff for the attacker, and eases the attribution on which deterrence depends. At the European level, most of this civilian information sharing and coordination infrastructure does not yet exist.

In the last two months, we have witnessed two very different ways in which hybrid campaigns exploit free societies as targets for attack. At one end, Europe’s adversaries are testing how much violence it will absorb before it reacts. At the other, they show how cheaply European societies can be disrupted. Both types of attacks are aimed at citizens’ confidence that their institutions can protect them. Europe can answer at both ends, but only if it finds the unity and political will to do it.

Beniamino Irdi is a nonresident senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, the founder and CEO of HighGround, and a former Italian government official.

The Board of Trade and Board of Investment, the mechanisms for negotiating tariff reductions and cross-border investment, respectively, were meant to turn the 2025 Busan summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping into concrete economic deliverables. So far, only the Board of Trade has developed an agenda, reflecting how difficult cross-border investment has become amid U.S.-China strategic rivalry.

The Board of Investment could take the easy route of approving a handful of small, nonsensitive deals. Or it could aim higher, pursuing investments that deliver meaningful gains for both countries.

The Board of Trade and Board of Investment, the mechanisms for negotiating tariff reductions and cross-border investment, respectively, were meant to turn the 2025 Busan summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping into concrete economic deliverables. So far, only the Board of Trade has developed an agenda, reflecting how difficult cross-border investment has become amid U.S.-China strategic rivalry.

The Board of Investment could take the easy route of approving a handful of small, nonsensitive deals. Or it could aim higher, pursuing investments that deliver meaningful gains for both countries.

China faces weak demand and fierce competition in its electric-vehicle sector at home. The United States needs more affordable green autos and stronger domestic capabilities in next-generation automotive technologies. At least in theory, some well-designed investment partnerships could help address both sides’ challenges.

Yet much of the current debate rests on misconceptions about what makes China’s EV industry competitive and what the United States stands to gain. The popular proposal is that the United States can ask China to transfer its battery technology and that this would be the magic pill for U.S. EVs. But battery tech is the wrong focus, tech transfer is the wrong approach, and U.S. EVs are the wrong target.

Access to China’s cheaper lithium-ion battery technology would not be enough to make EVs affordable in the United States. Batteries alone will not suffice. Japan and South Korea once led in lithium-ion batteries, yet that advantage did not translate into leadership in EVs.

Chinese automakers came from behind because of their increasingly capable battery suppliers and because they advanced quickly in another, less visible technological foundation: electrical and electronic architecture (EEA), which is the brain and nervous system of an intelligent electric vehicle. Traditional cars rely on hundreds of electronic control units. A software-defined vehicle instead uses a more centralized, zonal architecture in which a few computers coordinate the whole vehicle.

Zonal EEA shortens development cycles, simplifies supply chains, lowers costs, integrates intelligent features, and enables a smartphone-like user experience. Tesla pioneered zonal EEA in 2017, but fierce competition pushed Chinese automakers to catch up quickly.

Nor should the United States try to catch up with China’s well-known lead in EV manufacturing. The acquisition of Chinese technology for battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) is currently a U.S. policy priority, but a lesser-known fact is that China now leads across a broad range of powertrains, including BEVs, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and many others.

In fact, going fully electric may not be the best option in the United States. Americans drive roughly twice as many miles each year as Europeans and 70 percent more per passenger car than Chinese, and extending BEV range requires even larger and heavier batteries.

China-developed affordable PHEVs can travel about 100 miles on electricity, enough for most daily commutes, while achieving fuel economy of roughly 60 miles per gallon on longer trips. Limited public charging remains a hurdle for BEVs in the United States. Many suburban homeowners, however, can install home chargers that are more than adequate for the smaller batteries in PHEVs and for routine commuting. Competitive PHEVs, one of China’s technological strengths, are a much better option for serving American consumers facing both rising vehicle prices and higher fuel costs.

Technology transfer could also be a surprising dead end for the United States. Technology transfer is sensitive, as China is not willing to give away the crown jewels of its technology so easily. But even for legacy technology, there is another challenge. If competitive EVs required only batteries, the main task would indeed be getting battery production technology from China.

Huang’s resignation has big implications for the global AI race.

But making the U.S. auto industry competitive also requires advanced EEA and powertrain technologies. A broader scope of technological domains requires much more than manufacturing know-how; it also requires new supply-chain arrangements and new approaches to research and development. These are beyond the scope of a conventional joint venture, direct investment, or technology license. Asking China to transfer fancy tech is a pipe dream.

The correct approach is what we call deep-tech iterative learning. China’s own experience shows why local manufacturing is insufficient for this. When China set out to modernize its auto industry, policymakers assumed that localized manufacturing of advanced products would automatically build domestic capabilities.

During the 1980s, China experimented with several forms of partnership with international automakers, including joint ventures and technology-licensing arrangements. The result was a mixed bag, with many producing very little transfer. One example was Volkswagen, which did improve Chinese capabilities in manufacturing, supply-chain management, and quality control, but it did relatively little to build domestic R&D.

A second wave of more carefully designed partnerships in the 1990s, especially with General Motors (GM) and Ford, created a more disciplined, step-by-step process for iterative learning in automotive R&D. Over time, the exchange became reciprocal. China acquired technology and engineering expertise. As Chinese partners grew more capable, they helped U.S. automakers improve vehicle quality and reliability while reducing R&D costs after the 2008 financial crisis.

Bargaining power for iterative technological gains comes from leverage, incentives that make technology transfer worthwhile for the provider, and the architecture to make it work. The United States must develop these by doing the hard work: starting small, building new capabilities along the way, and making the next, more substantial step in technology transfer a good deal for both countries, so that it can last for the long haul.

Back then, China’s main bargaining chip was controlled access to its market. In the early 1990s, officials in Shanghai were frustrated by the limited transfer of R&D capabilities from Volkswagen. They negotiated with more than 10 international automakers and ultimately invited GM, Ford, and Toyota into the final bidding process.

China was offering one of the last opportunities for entry before its expected accession to the World Trade Organization around 2001, and Shanghai used competition among bidders to demand strong commitments to localized engineering and R&D. Automakers expected the market to grow multifold to a market comparable to the U.S. one. It eventually became more than twice as big.

GM submitted the strongest offer and won. Its centerpiece was the Pan Asia Technical Automotive Center (PATAC), a joint design and engineering center that became the institutional channel for transferring R&D capabilities and technical knowledge from GM’s global operations to Shanghai.

Deep technology transfer didn’t happen at once. Initially, PATAC’s work was limited to calibrating existing designs and making cosmetic changes. The incentives changed as China overtook the United States to become the world’s largest new-car market in 2009.

China was also a market with distinctive demands. Government and business executives often traveled with larger entourages, creating an unusual demand for premium minivans. Engineers in China also developed a closer understanding of consumers in emerging markets than counterparts in Michigan or at GM subsidiaries in Germany and Australia.

Local knowledge about a distinctive, large market eventually propelled GM to move two major R&D projects into China. The first was a Chinese-developed Buick premium minivan that differed fundamentally from aging GM minivans for American soccer moms. With GM’s support, PATAC engineers learned how to design new vehicle architecture for the first time.

The second was a project with SAIC, its Shanghai partner, to codevelop small engines for global emerging markets, allowing SAIC engineers to develop engines from the ground up. These two programs have sustained sales of millions of units for GM across the world. Engineers trained through these programs later carried their technological knowledge into numerous Chinese carmakers.

With support from central leaders, Shanghai offered foreign automakers a coveted chance to enter a potentially enormous market. China’s distinctive consumer needs, some shared with other emerging markets, gave U.S. automakers commercial reasons to transfer R&D capabilities and know-how. But leverage and incentives produced deeper, long-term iterative learning only when embedded in durable institutions: a manufacturing joint venture and a joint R&D center that could survive shifting political whims.

The United States today has a combination of leverage and incentives like those China possessed. Its market is huge and still largely lacking in affordable electrified models. Chinese automakers, facing thin profit margins at home, are drawn to this untapped demand. The U.S. market is also distinctive in its road conditions, urban form, safety regulations, and consumer preferences.

Chinese companies cannot simply transplant existing blueprints. To build durable, low-maintenance vehicles suited to American roads, they would need to hire and train engineers in the United States, bring key suppliers, and develop capabilities there, much as Japanese automakers did decades ago.

A regulated mechanism such as the Board of Investment could provide the missing institutional structure. Taking baby steps toward transferring some low-hanging-fruit technologies across a broad range, including batteries, EEA, and hybrid powertrains, is neither fanciful nor unrealistic.

If the United States does nothing, it will lose out not just to China but to everyone else. Volkswagen, Mercedes, Renault, as well as Abu Dhabi’s CYVN, have all been working with Chinese firms in different ways to tap Chinese expertise in EEA and powertrain technologies. Toyota is likewise testing cutting-edge EV technologies in China rather than Japan.

The Board of Investment could organize a competitive bidding process to identify Chinese partners with the strongest capabilities and the clearest commitments to participate. Working with one or more interested U.S. automakers, it could invite qualified Chinese firms to compete on the substance of their offers, as Shanghai did 30 years ago.

It would also help if the board devoted more energy to institution-building, including, but not limited to, involving deep industry expertise in assessing and calibrating licensing or joint-venture terms, establishing security guardrails for connected-vehicle technologies, and creating joint R&D institutions modeled on the PATAC so that technical capabilities are continuously channeled into the United States, independent of political favor or goodwill.

National security would be addressed at the technical level, regardless of whether it is prioritized politically. Working first with a select group of Chinese firms to develop and produce smaller battery-electric or plug-in hybrid vehicles in the United States and building from there could be an easy first step.

It sounds complicated, but it’s nothing new. Amid the U.S.-Japan trade tensions, the GM-Toyota joint venture NUMMI (1984) and Toyota (1977) and Honda’s (1975) R&D centers in the United States brought technological capabilities to U.S. automakers, parts suppliers, and engineers.

This is a proven process. U.S. industrial competitiveness, Americans’ everyday quality of life, consumer affordability, and U.S. innovation leadership in general are at stake. Getting it wrong would be tremendously costly.

Lizzi C. Lee is a fellow on Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis.

Fengming Lu is a lecturer (assistant professor) in the Coral Bell School of Asia Pacific Affairs at the Australian National University.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
New York authorities said Thursday that eight people, including two children, were killed after a residential building collapsed a day earlier, prompting a frantic overnight search by firefighters to pull people from the rubble.

The three-storey property in Brooklyn fell Wednesday afternoon into a neighbouring excavation site where construction workers had been preparing foundations for a planned development.

"This has been a devastating morning and evening for our city," said New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who announced the latest death toll and said over a dozen more were injured.

One of those killed was Ecuadoran national Gabriel Siguencia, 22, whose stepsister said in a tearful interview that he was working overtime at the construction site when the building collapsed.

"We went from hospital to hospital, trying to find him, showing pictures, but nobody knew anything until they told us he passed," Kayla Chimborazo, 20, told AFP and other journalists.

"He just came here to do work to be able to provide for his family back in Ecuador. He's just the sweetest person," she added, saying he had a wife and son.

The New York Times reported that the youngest victim was aged nine, and that nationalities included Ecuador, Guatemala and Guinea.

New York's fire department declared Thursday afternoon there were no further victims at the site after emergency workers spent hours searching with drones and canine units.

Officials said the cause of the collapse was not immediately clear.

The building, a three-storey structure dating from 1930 with four apartments and a commercial space on the ground floor, collapsed on to the nearby excavation site.

An adjacent building was left ripped open with one of its walls torn away, exposing a staircase, bedroom and a wardrobe full of clothing.

Shop worker James Williams, 60, told AFP he witnessed the building collapse after hearing loud banging noises throughout the morning.

"I smelled the smoke from the fumes, and I was watching bricks fall. But to see, like two minutes later, to see the building collapse and fall, it was just devastating," he said.

"There were people trying to get out ... I saw somebody on the side of the staircase, and I'll be honest with you, I didn't even really want to think about that."

Another witness, 14-year-old Kenneilia Reid, told AFP: "When I was walking by, I started seeing dust all of a sudden, and I was like, what is going on? When I turned my back, I saw the whole building collapse."

According to documents from the city's building department reviewed by AFP, the construction site had been issued a stop-work order in April due to potentially dangerous demolition conditions.

However, work continued, resulting in a $10,000 fine for the company involved. No link has yet been established between these violations and the building's collapse.

Mamdani said five main entities were involved at the site and that authorities had started "sweeping" 100 other construction sites they are associated with around the city.

The mayor promised a thorough investigation and to hold anyone responsible "fully accountable".

Some people in Flatbush, a mostly Black neighbourhood where the building collapsed, voiced their anger at gentrification and development after the incident.

"It's just all about making money. They didn't care about the danger," businessman Winston Bowen, 54, told AFP on a pavement opposite the collapsed building.

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/tru.title: Mauritania fishing boats falsely portrayed as migrant fleet bound for Spain
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/tru.author: Vedika BAHL
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/tru.text:
Spain’s Canary Islands are facing renewed pressure from migrant arrivals, with authorities declaring a migrant emergency this week following a sharp increase in crossings. Against this backdrop, a claim has been spreading rapidly on social media warning of an imminent “invasion” of the archipelago by migrants from Mauritania.

At the centre of the claim is a video showing someone examining satellite images on a mobile phone. The images appear to show thousands of boats packed closely together at the port of Nouadhibou, in northwestern Mauritania.

Multiple social media users have presented the footage as “proof” that thousands of migrant boats are preparing to set sail towards the Spanish coast. One post, which described the images as “irrefutable evidence” of an imminent mass crossing, attracted more than 1.5 million views in just 48 hours.

But while the satellite images are genuine, the claims being made about them are misleading.

Using Google Earth, we were able to verify the exact location shown in the video: the port of Nouadhibou, a coastal city in Mauritania. However, checking the dates of the satellite imagery revealed that the images being shared online actually date back to March 2025. They are not recent images showing boats gathering ahead of a mass departure.

In fact, looking further back through satellite imagery, we found similar concentrations of boats in exactly the same location dating back to 2013 and even 2005.

There is a straightforward explanation: the images show a traditional fishing port.

According to Mauritania’s tourism ministry, the port supports thousands of families and supplies local markets with fish. The boats visible in the viral images are fishing vessels, not a fleet of migrant boats preparing to cross the Atlantic.

Nor is this the first time such claims have circulated online. Similar videos alleging that thousands of boats at the Nouadhiboy port are gathering for a mass crossing have been shared since at least 2020. Spanish fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked these claims.

A real migration route, but misleading images

Mauritania is nevertheless an important departure and transit point for migrants attempting to reach Europe through West Africa. Nouadhibou has been identified as a key transit location by the UN's International Organization for Migration, while the European Union has also established a partnership with Mauritania aimed at curbing irregular migration, including departures by boat towards the Canary Islands.

In late October and early November, hundreds of people travelling in overcrowded boats were rescued by the Mauritanian navy off the coast of Nouadhibou. However, there is no evidence that these people departed from the fishing port featured in the viral video.

Meanwhile, the Canary Islands are facing genuine pressure from increased migrant arrivals. Thousands of people have reached the Spanish archipelago in recent weeks, particularly the island of El Hierro, where local authorities have declared a state of emergency.

The migration situation is therefore real, but the viral footage does not provide evidence of a coordinated mass departure from Mauritania. Instead, authentic satellite images of a traditional fishing port have been taken out of context and presented online as proof of an imminent migrant crossing to Spain.

As renewed diplomatic efforts seek to bring an end to Russia's war on Ukraine, the prospect of a negotiated settlement remains unlikely due to Russia's irreconcilable territorial demands, competing visions of European security and an increasingly unpredictable and pro-Moscow American approach to mediation. For Russia expert Mark Galeotti, Executive Director of Mayak Intelligence and Honorary Professor at University College London's School of Slavonic and East European Studies, Moscow's maximalist vision conceals a more complex negotiating strategy. "The Russian approach is always to sound incredibly bullish and then make any concessions at the very last minute," he explains, suggesting that the Kremlin's uncompromising rhetoric should not necessarily be mistaken for an absolute refusal to negotiate. Yet the territorial dispute over Donbas presents a particularly formidable obstacle. Putin's determination to claim control over the entirety of the region confronts Ukraine's refusal to surrender territory it continues to hold. "That Donbas question is, for me, an intractable one," Galeotti observes, warning that neither side currently appears willing to cede territory necessary for a breakthrough. Whereas conventional diplomacy generally proceeds through discreet negotiations before culminating in political announcements, Trump's approach has effectively reversed that sequence. "Trump makes grand declarations and various people try desperately to make it happen."

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Israel to ban far-left French politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon from entry
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Israel said on Thursday it would ban French hard-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon from visiting after he vowed that if he were elected, French vessels would accompany activists hoping to force aid into Gaza.

"Israel will respond firmly to those who seek to harm it and will not allow individuals who act against Israel and incite against its citizens to enter the country," the Israeli foreign ministry said in a statement.

Israel said it would also refuse entry to Mathilde Panot, the parliamentary group chair of Mélenchon's France Unbowed party.

The announcement comes a day after France confirmed it had refused entry to the head of a body representing settlements in the occupied West Bank.

READ MORE
French left-wing politician sparks antisemitism row over Epstein jibe

Mélenchon, a fierce critic of Israel who had no apparent plans to visit the country, said in a speech Saturday that if he were elected, France would "act directly in support of the Palestinians" in both Gaza and the West Bank.

"French ships, like those of Italy and Spain, will escort, if necessary, the flotillas of citizens mobilised to affirm people's rights," he said.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot denounced Israel’s actions in a post on X.

"This demagogic decision, coming from a government that has repeatedly violated international law, plays into the hands of those who, like La France Insoumise (France Unbowed party), thrive on exploiting the Israeli-Palestinian conflict," commented the head of French diplomacy.

Israel has imposed a blockade on Gaza since Hamas took over in 2007 and has even more strictly controlled entry points since Hamas carried out the unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack against Israel, triggering a massive military campaign.

A series of flotillas have sought to break through the Israeli siege. Some activists from one flotilla intercepted earlier this year alleged that Israeli authorities physically or sexually abused them in custody, charges denied by the Israeli government.

Israel earlier banned entry to a number of British left-wing lawmakers, including Jeremy Corbyn, another outspoken critic, after London imposed sanctions on products from settlements.

France says its ships will escort flotillas to Gaza if necessary. France earlier banned entry to a number of British left-wing lawmakers, including Jeremy Corbyn.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: ‘Labelled terrorists’: How France is using anti-terror powers to deter protests
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: Benjamin DODMAN
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
The protests roiling France over the past two months have seen hundreds of thousands of demonstrators march in towns and cities across the country, exercising a cherished right to voice discontent over underfunded schools, the cost of living and police brutality.

Some, however, have been stripped of that right, in the name of the fight against terror.

After peaceful rallies gave way to widespread rioting and looting on October 17, the government began using special anti-terror powers to bar several dozen people from attending further demonstrations – without prior approval from judges. They included students, trade unionists, far-left activists and environmental campaigners with no criminal record, most of whom had never been investigated for terrorism.

It marked the largest use of such discretionary powers since the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Paris, when more than 500 people were ordered to stay home or barred from getting anywhere near the venues, leading several to lose their jobs.

For lawyers, unions and rights groups, it also marked a turning point in the policing of protest movements.

READ MORE
'Deeply regressive': How France plans to make protesters pay for riots and looting

“It’s the first time such measures are taken against political activists, by attempting to put a ‘terrorist’ label on them,” said Aïnoha Pascual, a lawyer representing several people barred from attending nationwide protests on October 24 and 31. She denounced “a complete perversion of counterterrorism laws”, part of a growing list of government measures aimed at stifling protests.

The power used to restrict people’s movement is called an “individual measure of administrative control and surveillance”, known by the French acronym, MICAS. It is a legacy of the sweeping house arrest orders issued under a state of emergency declared in the early hours of November 14, 2015, in the wake of France’s deadliest ever terrorist attacks.

Certain emergency powers were enshrined in French law under a Counter-Terrorism Act adopted two years later, allowing the Interior Ministry to restrict people’s movements when there are “serious reasons” to believe they constitute a grave security threat and have terrorist ties.

People hit by MICAS orders are required to report at the local police station on a weekly or daily basis, and sometimes twice a day. Failure to abide by the restrictions can result in a three-year prison sentence and a €45,000 fine.

The law states that such powers are intended “solely for the purpose of preventing acts of terrorism from being committed” – which lawyers say is clearly not the case with the current MICAS orders.

Instead, “they are being used in situations where there is absolutely no terrorist threat whatsoever, against people who are not terrorists,” said Jean-Baptiste Soufron, a lawyer and member of the Association for the Defence of Constitutional Liberties (Adelico).

“They’re not even aimed at rioters,” Soufron added. “They clearly target political activists, barring them from attending demonstrations in the hope that this will weaken the protest movement.”

The decision to issue a MICAS order is based on intelligence reports and can target individuals with no criminal record. It does not require prior approval by a judge, though it can be challenged afterwards in court.

Souffron noted that the recent orders barring people from attending protests were often issued at the last minute, “effectively making it impossible for a judge to examine them in time”.

The ability to bypass judicial supervision, at least for a short time, hands the government considerable discretionary powers, said Nicolas Klausser, a researcher at the Centre Marc Bloch whose work specialises in the legal ramifications of state surveillance.

“The measure effectively allows the Interior Ministry to determine for itself who constitutes a terrorist threat, whereas normally, in criminal matters, it is up to a judge to rule,” he explained. “In this case, we can see that the authorities are trying to establish a direct link between taking part in protests and terrorist acts.”

When lawmakers grilled Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on the matter on November 3, he said he had signed “more than a hundred” MICAS orders related to the protests.

He added that they targeted “the upper end of the spectrum”, implying they involved people high up on the radar of French counterterrorism.

Sources contacted by newspaper Le Canard enchaîné told a different story.

According to the investigative and satirical weekly, “only a handful” of those targeted are actually being monitored by counterterrorism services. It described the rest as “small fry linked to far-left groups”.

In its latest edition on Wednesday, Le Canard enchaîné said the idea to deploy MICAS measures against protesters had come from Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin, who ordered their mass use when serving as interior minister during the Paris Olympics. The report, which cited “several senior civil servants”, said the government has since decided to suspend their use against protesters following public outcry.

The alleged direct involvement of senior ministers underscores the potential to weaponise such anti-terror powers for political purposes, said Klausser.

“While Micas would normally emerge from the bottom up, based on intelligence warnings that climb up the chain of command, in this case it appears the order came from above,” he explained. “Critics of the 2017 law had warned that it left ample scope for abuse of power. They’ve been proven right.”

Klausser said the use of MICAS orders is part of ongoing government efforts to “legitimise” the notion that certain far-left activists present a grave threat to public order. Darmanin has repeatedly flagged the threat from so-called “ecoterrorists”, a term he first used in 2022 in the wake of violent clashes between police and demonstrators opposed to the construction of giant reservoirs for agricultural irrigation.

Following the violent unrest on October 17, ministers were quick to pin the blame on “ultra-left” groups. At subsequent fast-tracked trials, however, most of the people convicted turned out to be opportunistic looters with no political leaning.

READ MORE
'I didn’t know it was theft': Trials begin in Paris following October 17 violence

“Terms such as ‘ecoterrorism’, ‘insurrection’ and ‘sabotage’ are routinely brandished as bogeymen to instil fear and then justify labelling political activists as terrorists,” said Pascual, who has defended several activists branded as “ecoterrorists” over the years.

“Either the government is pretending they’re terrorists because they have no other way of barring them from protests, or they genuinely believe that what happened on October 17 was terrorism – or perhaps a bit of both,” she added. “Either way, it takes some nerve to claim that political violence and looting shops constitutes terrorism, particularly on the eve of commemorations for victims of the November 13 attacks.”

In statements defending its use of MICAS orders, the Interior Ministry has argued that the “insurrectionary” nature of the protests constitutes a terror threat. It has pointed to the fire that ravaged the town hall of Limoges on October 17, and online calls to target symbols of capitalism and the state, as evidence of an intent to “seriously disrupt public order by intimidating the population and the public authorities”.

The ministry’s arguments were broadly rejected at a court hearing in Paris on Tuesday, including by the public rapporteur, a judge tasked with giving an independent opinion on the case.

“Not all violence directed against the state, nor all political violence, is necessarily of a terrorist nature,” said the rapporteur, according to a Mediapart journalist who attended the hearing. Protest calls “cannot be regarded as intended to sow terror, but rather as an expression of intense anger towards the ruling authorities and as a means of placing them in great difficulty”, she added.

To suggest that the protest movement has placed the authorities in “great difficulty” is an understatement. The violence witnessed on October 17, coupled with weeks of mass protests and school blockades, has piled pressure on France’s embattled minority government as it struggles to win support for a deficit-cutting budget.

The widespread rioting sparked “a moment of panic, prompting the Interior Ministry to explore all options at its disposal”, said Klausser. “And they’ve made full use of those options.”

The MICAS orders come on the heels of a slew of other measures critics say have severely curtailed the right to protest. They include outright bans on rallies, changes to protest routes and localised curfews.

“The use of such an arsenal, over such a long period, is indicative of a permanent state of emergency,” Marion Ogier, a lawyer for France’s Human Rights League (LDH), told a press conference earlier this month.

Rights groups have also denounced the widespread use of police custody to deter student protesters who kicked off the movement at high schools across France. In the three weeks leading up to October 14, police detained 6,877 people at school blockades and marches, 86 percent of them minors. It was more than the number detained during 18 months of often violent clashes with Yellow Vest protests that began in 2018.

READ MORE
‘Ten times more painful’: Menstrual disorders fuel calls to ban tear gas at French protests

While the authorities have highlighted the “serious acts of violence” committed by protesters, lawyers have denounced a weaponisation of police custody to intimidate protesters, stressing that the majority of those detained were later released without charges. They have also accused police of abusing minors held for up to 48 hours, alleging insults, beatings and depriving them of food and sleep.

“That’s on top of the repression witnessed at protests themselves,” said Pascual, referring to police’s ample use of “non-lethal” weapons that have maimed dozens of protesters. “When attending a protest can result in being teargassed, injured or ending up in jail, quite a few people are likely to stay away.”

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Israel kills six in Gaza hospital strike as 9-month-old baby freezes to death
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
An Israeli air strike on southern Gaza's main hospital overnight killed at least six Palestinians including a surgeon and a teenage boy, medics said, the latest Israeli attack to undermine a year-old ceasefire in the ravaged territory.

The strike hit a building containing surgery wards at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis. Israel's ​military alleged it had ‌targeted a senior Hamas commander and accused the militants of using the hospital complex to plan attacks, which ⁠the group denied.

Medics and witnesses said two missiles crashed through the roof of the five-storey building, causing extensive damage. The surgery department, which serves half of Gaza's 2 million people, was knocked out of service. ‌Twenty others were wounded.

Ayman Abu Obeid, a doctor who was wounded in the attack, said he was on ⁠an overnight shift in the hospital when an explosion ripped through the room where he and others were sleeping.

"All of a sudden the world turned upside down. It went dark all at once," he said from a hospital bed. Near him, piles ​of mangled furniture and medical equipment could be seen covered in dust from blown-out concrete. Torn wires hung down ‌from the ceiling.

Among those killed was Rezik Abushira, a surgeon who was featured in a 2026 documentary, "American Doctor", working alongside three visiting US doctors who help provide medical care for Palestinians in Gaza.

The dead also included a 13-year-old boy, according to Gaza's education ministry.

Three more Palestinians were killed later on Thursday in separate ‌incidents. Two were killed and several wounded in an Israeli airstrike on a car in Gaza City, and one other person was killed by Israeli gunfire in central Gaza's Bureij refugee camp, medics said, ​taking Thursday's death toll to at least nine.

Commenting on the vehicle strike, the Israeli military said it hit a Hamas militant without giving further details. It did not comment on the other incident.

In a statement on the hospital strike, Israel's ​military said it targeted a person named Muhammad Abu Ismail, describing him as "the commander of Hamas' Khan Younis Brigade". The military alleged he and other ​militants "were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital".

The military accused the militants of "turning the Nasser Hospital compound into a ​headquarters and operating from there".

Hamas rejected the military's claim that it had used the hospital as a base for operations. It did not immediately comment on whether a leader from the group had ​been targeted, wounded or killed in the strike.

The Board of Peace, the body placed in charge of overseeing Gaza's ceasefire plan by US President Donald Trump, on Thursday called for the peace plan's immediate implementation.

"The tragic loss of life following an Israeli strike on Nasser hospital in Khan Younis underscores precisely why President Trump's Comprehensive Peace Plan must be implemented immediately without further delay," the Board said in a statement.

Israel's military has struck the Nasser Hospital complex at least seven times since the start of the Gaza war, hospital officials say.

Heavy rain last week flooded tens of thousands of people's tents in the Palestinian territory, where virtually the whole population has been displaced at least once by three years of Israeli bombardment.

Five people, including three children, died the day after the flooding when a sandy embankment collapsed onto their tents.

The worsening weather continues to take a heavy toll.

A nine-month-old baby died of hypothermia on Thursday, his father and a doctor told AFP.

The doctor, who saw the child and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq "died from hypothermia inside his family's displacement tent" in Khan Younis.

Ahmed Raqiq told AFP that his son Kinan died of cold during the night in their tent in southern Gaza.

"I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser hospital, but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death," he said.

"I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in burial shroud," he said outside the hospital, dried tears on his face as he held his son wrapped in a white sheet.

READ MORE
Palestinians struggle to find food in Gaza a year after ceasefire

Hundreds of displaced families have been seen fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and central and northern areas of the territory after they were inundated by rainwater.

James Elder, spokesman on Gaza for the UN children's agency, UNICEF, warned that the flooding was just the beginning of the cold season.

"It's very important to know how bad things are in Gaza. It's not yet winter," Elder said.

"We're weeks away from winter, so we are getting unprecedented rain and cold."

The UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that as of November 8, 26,000 households were affected by storms.

Around 65 percent of Gaza's people are still living displaced in tents or other temporary shelter, OCHA said.

Israel and Hamas declared a ceasefire on October 10, 2025 but Israel has kept striking the territory, vowing to kill anyone involved in the Hamas-led October 7 attack, the deadliest in Israel's history.
