https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: How FRANCE 24 traced Tehran-backed Afghan fighters from Syria to southeastern Iran
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: Ershad ALIJANI
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
During Syria’s civil war, Iran organised and deployed foreign fighters to support then-president Bashar al-Assad’s government against armed opposition groups. These included Shia militias from Afghanistan and Pakistan, alongside Lebanon’s Hezbollah.

One of the largest Iran-backed foreign fighting forces in Syria was the Afghan Shia militia known as the Fatemiyoun division.

The group was designated as a terrorist entity by Canada in 2019 and placed under US counterterrorism sanctions the same year for supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Quds Force (IRGC-QF).

The Fatemiyoun division is estimated to have between 8,000 and 50,000 fighters in Syria. Its members were recruited mainly from Afghan Shia communities, and many of them were from migrant and refugee communities in Iran.

After 11 years of fighting in Syria, when around 2,000 militia members were killed, everything changed abruptly for the Fatemiyoun in December 2024. Assad fled to Russia as a rebel coalition led by Ahmad al-Sharaa toppled his government, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) withdrew its forces from Syria.

Since then, the whereabouts of thousands of Afghan Shia fighters recruited, trained and battle-hardened by Iran during the Syrian civil war have become less clear.

On the Telegram channels monitored by the FRANCE 24 Observers, the Fatemiyoun’s public presence appeared largely limited to posts commemorating members killed during the war in Syria.

But recently, FRANCE 24 uncovered new clues about their whereabouts through “martyrdom” announcements published on Fatemiyoun-affiliated Telegram channels. This time, the announcements concerned fighters who had been killed not in Syria years earlier, but more recently in Iran.

A key clue to the Fatemiyoun’s whereabouts emerged in March 2026, during the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran.

At the time, media outlets and social media accounts affiliated with the IRGC began publishing "martyrdom" announcements for personnel killed in US and Israeli airstrikes on IRGC military bases in Iran.

By examining these announcements, FRANCE 24 identified links between some of those killed and the Fatemiyoun division. In most cases, the announcements made no mention of their Fatemiyoun affiliation or Afghan origins. However, photographs from their funerals and memorial services provided evidence of their connection to the militia

FRANCE 24 found photographs of memorial ceremonies organised by Fatemiyoun members in Iran, where portraits of those recently killed were displayed alongside those of well-known Fatemiyoun fighters killed in Syria, as well as the militia’s flags. In a few cases, reports from IRGC-affiliated news outlets further confirm their identities.

For example, Fars News Agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, confirmed that Alireza Feizian, a Fatemiyoun member who had previously been wounded in Syria, was killed in US-Israeli airstrikes on Iran.

These findings suggest that some Fatemiyoun members had been incorporated into IRGC ranks, including at officer level, as in the case of IRGC Lieutenant Colonel Ali Akbar Saket.

New videos circulating on Iranian social media in September provided further clues about the Fatemiyoun’s whereabouts and their deployment in southeastern Iran, particularly in Sistan and Baluchistan province, which borders Pakistan and Afghanistan.

Sistan and Baluchistan is one of Iran’s least-developed provinces. The region has long faced insecurity linked to cross-border drug trafficking and the activities of armed Baluch groups, including Islamist and separatist organisations.

On September 29, 2026, Haalvsh, a human rights news outlet covering Iran’s Baluchistan region, published a video suggesting the presence of Fatemiyoun fighters in a mountainous area of southeastern Iran.

The footage shows at least 13 armed men, identified by Haalvsh as Fatemiyoun members, apparently patrolling the mountainous terrain.

To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

FRANCE 24 geolocated the video to Mount Kala Pade, approximately 80 kilometres west of Zahedan, the capital of Sistan and Baluchistan province.

Haalvsh published an earlier video on September 21, 2026, that also suggested the presence of Fatemiyoun fighters in the province.

To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

The footage shows several armed men undergoing weapons training. Although local activists identified them as Fatemioun members, FRANCE 24 could not independently verify their identities.

However, FRANCE 24 geolocated the footage to a newly constructed school in Gosht, a small town near Saravan in Sistan and Baluchistan province.

Further evidence of the Fatemiyoun's deployment in Sistan and Baluchistan emerged from "martyrdom" announcements published on Telegram channels or media affiliated with the militia.

These accounts openly acknowledged the deaths of Fatemiyoun members in two separate incidents. According to Fatemiyoun-affiliated sources, Ahmad Yaghoubi was killed in an improvised explosive device (IED) attack in Sistan and Baluchistan on October 2, 2026, and later buried in Pakdasht, on the outskirts of Tehran.

Mohammadreza Rahimi was killed in an armed clash on October 13 in Sistan and Baluchistan and later buried in Sarvestan, Fars province.

The IRGC and Fatemiyoun-affiliated media also published photographs and videos of their funeral ceremonies.

The People's Fighters Front (PFF) claimed responsibility for both incidents. Formed in December 2025, the PFF is a coalition of several Islamist and Baluch nationalist armed groups, including Jaish al-Adl, which is designated as a terrorist organisation by the United States and Iran.

Mahdi Nakhl Ahmadi, an Iranian expert on Sistan and Baluchistan based in Italy, told France 24:

The Fatemiyoun were not entirely absent from Sistan and Baluchistan during the Syrian civil war. There were reports of their members holding civilian positions in the province, which drew criticism from local figures at the time.

But there is no doubt that their presence intensified after the war in Syria. The IRGC could not simply abandon these fighters.

First, Iran had invested heavily in recruiting and training them. After years of fighting in Syria, including urban warfare, they had become battle-hardened soldiers.

Second, they could have posed a security risk to the Islamic republic itself. Thousands of trained fighters, some of whom had risen to senior command positions and gained access to sensitive IRGC intelligence, could have turned against the Islamic republic or joined groups fighting Iran if left without jobs or income.

However, the deployment of Fatemiyoun fighters in Sistan and Baluchistan did not happen suddenly, and it seems this was not the IRGC’s first choice.

Initially, the IRGC sought to negotiate with Pakistan and the Afghan authorities over the deployment of Fatemiyoun fighters to combat common enemies in their respective territories.

In Afghanistan, the proposal was to deploy Fatemiyoun fighters against the Islamic State group. Both the former Afghan government and, later, the Taliban rejected the idea. The Taliban viewed the fighters as a potential threat because their loyalty was to Iran rather than to the Taliban. Some former Fatemiyoun members who returned to Afghanistan were even imprisoned by the Taliban.

The IRGC also proposed deploying Fatemiyoun fighters in Pakistan’s Balochistan province to fight Baluch separatist and radical Islamist armed groups operating in areas where the Pakistani government has limited control. Pakistan also rejected the proposal.

The IRGC therefore turned to another option: deploying the fighters along Iran’s borders with Pakistan and Afghanistan. It provided accommodation for Fatemiyoun members in Zabol and several other towns in Sistan and Baluchistan. The exact number of fighters stationed there is unknown.

Initially, they were assigned civilian jobs on projects run by the IRGC, but over time, they increasingly took on military roles.

The IRGC began stationing them at Basij bases and IRGC garrisons, deploying them on patrols and at checkpoints.

According to scattered accounts from local residents, the fighters were initially concentrated in the border areas between Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan, where drug traffickers, human traffickers and armed groups operate, and where armed clashes are more frequent.

Most of their bases and garrisons are reportedly located in an area extending roughly 20 kilometres south of Saravan.

However, this does not mean they are absent from other parts of the province. As armed group activity has intensified in Sistan and Baluchistan, Fatemiyoun fighters appear to have expanded their presence further inland, as the recent incidents and videos suggest.

The People's Fighters Front (PFF) has claimed to have killed more Fatemiyoun fighters than the two whose deaths were publicly acknowledged by Fatemiyoun-affiliated channels. Since October 13, 2026, the PFF has also claimed responsibility for further attacks targeting IRGC and Fatemiyoun forces in Sistan and Baluchistan, alleging additional Fatemiyoun casualties. However, FRANCE 24 could not independently verify these additional deaths, and no corresponding "martyrdom" announcements were found on the Fatemiyoun-affiliated channels.
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.summary: Iran organised and deployed foreign fighters to support Bashar al-Assad’s government. The Fatemiyoun division is estimated to have between 8,000 and 50,000 fighters in Syria.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: At least five people shot in DC neighbourhood near the White House
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
Five people were shot Thursday in a trendy Washington, DC neighbourhood within walking distance of the White House, police said, and a swarm of officers responded to a nearby apartment building where a suspect was barricaded.

The suspect, who later shot himself, is believed to have been in conflict with the building homeowners’ association.

At least one person shot at a gym died in a pool of blood, a witness said.

The shootings were reported in Logan Circle, about 1 mile north of the White House. Police urged people to avoid the area of the 1500 block of 15th Street, which includes a VIDA fitness centre, St. Luke’s Episcopal Church and residences and is around the corner from a Whole Foods supermarket. Much of the block was cordoned off. Schools near the scene were placed on lockdown.

READ MORE
Halloween weekend shootings across US leave at least six dead, dozens wounded

Law enforcement SWAT teams and other officers had their guns drawn on the roof of an apartment building or on the ground below.

Authorities believe the suspect shot at least one person inside the gym before going outside and firing again, according to a law enforcement official who was not authorised to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.

Law enforcement agents believe the suspect shot another person in a parking garage elevator and then barricaded himself on the seventh floor of the building, the official said.

James Spellman was at the gym a little after 8am when he heard shots being fired. He said there were about 50 people in the gym at the time.

“Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," he said. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”

Spellman said he and other gym members ran out of the gym, and he said he heard more gunfire in the area of 15th Street. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside.

READ MORE
Minneapolis apartment shooting leaves three dead, multiple injured

Streets around the area also were blocked off during a massive police response. The federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said it sent agents to the scene to help. And the FBI said its Washington field office was helping local police with the investigation.

Witness Ryan Dubicki was in his nearby apartment around 8am when, he said, he “heard about five bangs”.

"They were really spread out so I thought it was construction,” he said. It was only a short time later that he looked out “and there were cops everywhere.”

His apartment building managers sent a notice that there was a possible active shooter.

The neighbourhood has seen violence before. In early August 2025, a onetime member of President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency was assaulted early on a Sunday morning in the Logan Circle neighbourhood by a group of teenagers attempting to carjack him and a woman, authorities said.

Days later, Trump fulfilled his threat to bypass local authority and imposed direct federal control over the city, sending in hundreds of National Guard members to reduce crime. That deployment continues today.

The suspect is believed to have been in conflict with the building homeowners’ association. At least one person shot at a gym died in a pool of blood, a witness said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Victorians will head to the polls on November 28 to decide who will hold the balance of power in the state for the next four years.

Follow our live coverage below:

Choose what information you see below by using filters

A new analysis is shedding light on how political parties in Victoria are campaigning online ahead of the November 28 state election.

Labor is leading the pre-election online advertising spend, investing millions in online content, according to estimates compiled by digital campaign platform Populares.

Some analysts say the party is fighting for relevance online, while content from the Liberals and One Nation cuts through the noise.

But just how much more is Labor spending? ABC data journalist Kate Ashton tallied up the spend in her story below:

When Cranbourne was created ahead of the 1992 state election, it covered a vast geographic area from Carrum Downs in the west, along Western Port Bay in the south, and over to the Bunyip River in the east. Ten years later, when its boundaries were redrawn, it shrank from 576 square kilometres to just over 100 to focus mainly on Cranbourne and Carrum Downs.

It became a safe Labor seat upon the change in boundaries. Over the years, the seat has further contracted on Cranbourne and its neighbouring suburbs, now covering an area of around 63 square kilometres.

Former Labor member Jude Perera faced two tough contests in Cranbourne against former VFL star player Geoff Ablett, who ran for the Liberals in 2010 and 2014, but Labor has otherwise held the seat with ease since 2002. Current member Pauline Richards won the seat in 2018 with more than 50 per cent of the primary vote and held it in 2022 with only a small swing against her on slightly weaker boundaries for Labor.

However, the 2022 result also saw minor right-wing parties pick up almost 15 per cent of the vote. The seat is relatively diverse but has lots of mortgage holders and blue-collar workers. If One Nation is making inroads with non-Anglo voters, it may be competitive in seats like this one.

Hey Judd 😀👋 Hey Ashlee 😀👋

Thanks so much for following our blog during the week; we love having you in the comments.

We'd also love to have your thoughts on the coming election, as well as the thoughts of all our readers.

Whether it's the cost of living, housing affordability, crime, regional roads, health care or jobs, let us know in our form below.

You can also ask the election questions you want answered from candidates, parties or the ABC.

All submissions will be reviewed by a journalist, and we may be in touch if we need more information.

The Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund has been a hotly debated political topic in the lead-up to the election.

Introduced by Labor in 2025, the new levy replaced the existing Fire Services Levy already attached to land rates in Victoria and is used to fund fire services, the SES and Triple Zero.

But it came with a tax hike, with some farmers saying the change meant they would pay tens of thousands of dollars more each year.

The levy's introduction sparked protests on the steps of parliament, with convoys of fire trucks lined up on Spring Street.

CFA volunteers argued they were getting slugged with an extra tax when they already contribute time — and in many cases — money to their local brigades.

The Coalition and One Nation both pledged to scrap the wildly unpopular levy during their election campaigns.

A Liberal Party-supported petition prepared for parliament attracted nearly 44,000 signatures — understood to be a record for a Victorian parliamentary petition.

Labor initially backed down from the public pressure, capping the rate charged on farmland at 28.7 per cent for two years.

Now, the Carroll government vowed to make the cap permanent if re-elected.

The ABC's Jane McNaughton, Warwick Long and Justine Longmore have the full story below:

Opposition leader Jess Wilson swapped Spring Street for the pub on Thursday night, stopping in at Wodonga’s Blazing Stump Hotel.

Wilson travelled from Melbourne in her campaign bus and joined Liberal candidate for Benambra Steve Martin, meeting locals ahead of an expected morning of campaigning in the region today.

There were plenty of introductions, a few beers poured by Wilson herself and an offer to pick up the tab.

One punter seemed impressed with her bar skills, telling her she poured well.

But locals were also keen to talk about the issues affecting the region, including the state of the roads and the controversial redevelopment of the Albury Hospital.

One woman told Wilson a new hospital was “desperately needed" as there were not enough beds and people were dying.

We're bringing you live coverage today from the Victorian state election campaign trail.

Labor and the Liberals will resume their election campaigns, travelling across the state in big campaign buses to visit critical electorates.

We'll be bringing you any new policy announcements, plus coverage from the day of public hearings in the Big Build royal commission.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Beau Lamarre-Condon is in the witness box during his double murder trial in Sydney. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Beau Lamarre-Condon is continuing to answer questions after close to a week of cross-examination from the Crown.

He is accused of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, and his new boyfriend, Luke Davies, in February 2024.

The former police officer has pleaded not guilty in the NSW Supreme Court.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

The friend asks why he had a hire car, and he told her he was going to Paddington, according to her testimony.

He says he was going to Pyrmont not Paddington.

The accused accepts he had a "work question" about CCRs (call charge records) and MMRs.

He says he was asking in regards to "dial-a-[drug] dealers" in his capacity as a police officer.

"Asking about the traceability of phones while they were off has nothing to do with drug dealers," Hatfield suggests.

"I disagree. I never asked about phones being off. I was asking about tracking phones," Lamarre-Condon says.

He also asked if hired cars could be tracked,and agrees, saying drug dealers also use.

Lamarre-Condon says it has nothing to do with him having a hire vehicle.

"Don't worry I'm not trying to be a drug dealer," he says he told her, as a joke.

This friend told him he "needed to respect Jesse's wishes" to not contact him and move on, the court heard.

"That's all the truth," the accused friend.

He disagrees he was "emotive" and "angry" with Baird during that conversation and also to this day.

The prosecutor asks if Baird was "on your mind that weekend" from January 26, 2024.

"Jesse Baird was not on my mind ... I was dating and seeing new people," he replies.

On the 27th, he went to a spa with a friend.

This friend asked about the Bali trip he was meant to go with Baird.

"He's definitely sleeping with a guy named Luke," Hatfield puts to the accused that he said to the friend.

"I said [another man]," he replies.

He accepts he told her he had Baird's pin code and deleted messages from the second man on his phone.

"You were thinking about murdering Jesse Baird this weekend," Hatfield asks about January 16, 2024.

"I've never thought about murder Jesse, no," Lamarre-Condon replies.

He's talking about a coffee date that weekend where he suggests Balmain or Paddington.

Baird lived in Paddington.

Hatfield put to him that he was in Baird's suburb in a hired car.

The accused replies that Baird was "nowhere near" him on that day.

"I didn't know it at the time, I didn't go there for [Baird]," he tells court.

On this call log, he calls a man whose family farm the bodies were taken to.

He says he called him because he thought he might have been blocked on Instagram, and also wanted to catch up in a "normal conversation".

He says he tried contacting the man via Signal, but didn't receive a reply.

"Were you contacting [him] pretending to be someone else," Hatfield asks.

"No, I wasn't pretending to be someone else. But the name on Signal was 'Bob'."

The accused denies he was calling him to ask about the farm.

We're looking at a call record from Lamarre-Condon's "burner phone".

This log is from January 16, 2024.

Lamarre-Condon says it's a "second phone, I wouldn't call it a burner phone" then says it's just a "sim card".

He says he couldn't use his main phone because the Signal app isn't fully encrypted.

The accused hired a vehicle over the January long weekend in 2023.

"I was getting my rims of my Tesla resprayed and some of my wrapping done," he tells court.

He spent a couple days with a male friend, and went to a cafe with another man, and visited the Northern Beaches.

Hatfield says he was using a "burner phone" that weekend.

He replies he used it for encrypted app Signal to contact colleagues, and to call another man who he says had blocked him on Instagram.

"It was never [used] near Jesse Baird, ever," Lamarre-Condon says.

On the January long weekend, Lamarre-Condon says he went to the Royal National Park with a male friend.

"I have never been aware of any relationship Jesse had ... after the 19th."

"I hadn't seen anything on social media" and wasn't looking him up, he says.

Hatfield asks why he blocked Luke Davies on Instagram.

"I just blocked ... I even blocked Jesse's family members, I didn't want any of that."

Hatfied asks if he was thinking about or had stolen bullets when he was asking Harvell about another officer taking a shell casing.

The accused says he doesn't know if he took it before or after the conversation.

He says he saw them at Miranda Police Station, took them, and it was for the "intention of suicide".

He denies he took these bullets from a police training day, as suggested by Hatfield.

The accused's colleague and friend, Nicole Harvell, has previously told court the accused referenced "boxes and boxes" of these non-operational rounds that "weren't counted".

"I don't remember having that part of the conversation," Lamarre-Condon says in court.

He says he disagrees he was talking about rounds, and not shell casings, which also weren't counted.

This other officer reportedly took a shell casing to frame, and pocketed it.

"Did you raise the matter a few times with her ... that junior constable getting away with stealing it [the shell casing]," Hatfield asks.

He replies he talked about it once with her.

Hatfield is asking about stolen bullets from Miranda Police Station.

Lamarre-Condon says he can't recall when he took the "non-operational rounds", but it could have been "some point in January".

"I just know it was before the first of February."

He says on January 21, 2023 he discussed hearing of an officer taking a shell casing to "frame".

We're looking at an invoice for amaysim, for a sim card order the accused bought in January 15, 2023.

He says he ordered it online and it came via express post.

"I wasn't specifically in a rush to get it ... it had nothing to do with Jesse Baird," he says.

He tells court he was collating statements from serving officers about "bullying from a certain sergeant".

"I was wanting to go compile all these statements and go to the media."

Using his phone and being found out would make him a "target" he says.

"I was very, very worried and concerned ... [about] speaking publicly," he says, and it "coming back to me".

To kickstart the morning, Hatfield has begun asking Lamarre-Condon about asking questions about technology called Cellbrite in January 2023.

Cellbrite programs are used to retrieve data from devices.

The accused says he was enquiring because he was working towards a senior position in the police force, which involved tracking drug dealers' phones.

Lamarre-Condon says he asked about Snapchat data specifically because parents had asked him about it in relation to their kids.

Missed out on Thursday's cross-examination?

Welcome to today's coverage.

We're back in the NSW Supreme Court listening to Beau Lamarre-Condon giving evidence.

He's being questioned by Brett Hatfield SC, the Crown prosecutor, as part of ongoing cross-examination.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.title: From Paddington to physics, there's a common thread to Ben Miller's career
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.author: Anastasia Safioleas
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Austin actor and co-creator Ben Miller's credits also include films in the Paddington franchise. (Reuters: Mary Turner)

It's 7am and Ben Miller is sitting at his laptop in the kitchen of his Cotswolds cottage, a goldendoodle named Stevie Nicks resting at his feet.

This is where the English actor writes — and where he occasionally fields questions from journalists beamed in from afar.

While perhaps best known in Australia as Julian Hartswood, the father of Michael Theo's character in ABC iview's Austin, Miller has had a 30-year career in film and television.

His acting credits include movies such as Johnny English, alongside Rowan Atkinson, as well as Paddington 2 and Paddington in Peru. On the small screen, he's starred in Death in Paradise and Professor T, and even donned pantaloons to play the hapless Lord Featherington in Bridgerton.

Then there are the children's books Miller has written — the Fairytale Woods series and The Day I Fell Into a Fairytale, to name a couple. His first adult novel, a historical spy thriller titled A Very Dangerous Pursuit, was released earlier this year.

But Miller began his career in comedy, as part of a duo called Armstrong and Miller. Before that, he was completing a PhD in physics at the University of Cambridge.

Each of these pursuits might sound disparate at first, but Miller insists there's a common thread.

Miller began his comedy career as part of a duo with Alexander Armstrong (right). (Getty Images/PA Images: Yui Mok)

How did the son of English teachers become so obsessed with quantum physics?

They were also into science. My dad was also into maths. We used to do a fair amount of maths at home.

It was quantum physics that everyone was so into in the 80s. It was the most incredible subject because quantum physics is a bizarre theory that turns out to be true. It's so weird. The idea that there's no such thing as an object [and that] things are both particles and waves … it's just nuts. The fact that it's actually the most accurate physical theory that we've ever created — it's still going strong. So, we were just big fans of physics.

After writing several children's books, why did you decide to release your first fiction book for adults?

I started writing science books and then I got to writing children's books and [adult fiction] felt like a natural thing to try next. And I've enjoyed it. But I'm also writing the sort of stories I think kids who grew up reading my children's books would like to read.

As well as being an author and a science enthusiast, you're also a comedian and an actor. If someone knew you for only one of those things, which would you want it to be?

I don't think I could cope with just doing one. Acting is obviously serving someone else's story. I love writing. I love being part of telling stories and I really like all kinds of stories. I'm [also] very interested in tech. I've got this whole thing that I'm doing about protecting actors from AI. I love science. But the common thread is storytelling … I think of it all as being the same job.

And one of the things that I'm lucky in is getting to travel. I love coming to Australia to film Austin. If I didn't act, I probably wouldn't get a chance to travel so much and that's a big part of it for me. I loved being in Australia for those three seasons [of Austin] we've done so far. We were in Canberra for the previous two seasons and we were in Adelaide. I love Canberra!

What is it about Canberra that you love so much?

It's such a liveable city [and] it's so green. I love the old Parliament [House], I love all those old buildings. There's a whole new vibey area of Canberra that has popped up with lots of cool bars and restaurants.

You're one of the stars of Austin, but you also helped bring it to life. How did the series come about?

Darren Ashton, the director [of Austin], is an old friend of mine. We first worked together on a film called Razzle Dazzle [in 2007]. I loved that film, I loved the way it turned out, and I loved working with Darren.

He came to stay with me here in the Cotswolds … he showed me a bit of Love on the Spectrum — showed me Michael [Theo] — and I was immediately smitten.

I remember sitting at this kitchen table saying, 'Do you think this guy could act, because I think he's amazing.'

And then we just set about creating a show for Michael.

How much care goes into depicting a neurodivergent character like Austin on the screen?

Miller helped bring Austin to the small screen. (ABC TV)

The story is not that Austin is neurodivergent. He just happens to be a character who happens to be neurodivergent. The story is about the journey we all go on to try and find ourselves. To go from childhood to adulthood [and] to become independent. To lovingly outgrow our parents. And for me, the big promise of Austin was that Austin would find love and find a partner and get married.

Michael Theo was able to use his profile to springboard into a career where he says he's found his true purpose. But for many autistic people, these kinds of opportunities are hard to come by.

[Michael] really wanted to be in a relationship and so Austin for me is a kind of wish fulfilment on behalf of Michael and the audience. We want to see him meet someone and fall in love and have all the ups and downs that involves, and to get married.

It's about that journey that everybody goes on.

Your character in the series Professor T is also neurodivergent. What type of preparation did you do to play this character?

Professor T has OCD [Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder] and he's germophobic. In fact, he constantly wears surgical gloves because he doesn't want to touch anything … I also suffer from OCD, so I was very interested to play that character.

I'm not germophobic, but I'm probably on the autistic spectrum and I've also got OCD, so it's fantastic.

The cast of Austin ahead of the season four premiere. (ABC TV)

Is it harder to make people laugh or is it harder to make people care about a character?

It's hard to do both. It's slightly different if you're doing something on film or if you're doing something live.

If you're doing something live that's meant to be funny and nobody laughs, that is one of the worst experiences you can have as a human being.

Austin tries to do both. To move people, you've got to get under the skin of a character. You've got to understand what's at stake for Austin, and usually that's some kind of version of the trauma that the character has experienced.

It's the same in Professor T. I promise you that when you turn it on, you will not like Professor T … he's a very unpleasant person. But, the more you watch it, the more you start to see that his bruteness, abruptness and arrogance are like a protective shell.

Miller (pictured with Austin co-star Sally Phillips, right), wants audiences to care about the characters they're watching. (ABC TV)

The reason I think Professor T is such an emotional show to watch is that he actively tries to make you dislike him [but then] you stick with it and begin to understand him a bit. You identify [with him] on a deep level then, because we all suffer from trauma, we all cope with it, and we all keep going forward. And what can be very moving and even healing is to empathise and have compassion for someone else's trauma.

To me, laughter and crying are not that different. They're both reactions to the sort of exquisite suffering of life. I love shows that do both.

Quotes lightly edited for clarity and brevity.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/q.title: Why do supercell thunderstorms form and what makes them so dangerous?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/q.author: Stephen Clarke
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Extreme Weather Events

Supercell thunderstorms can produce damaging wind gusts, heavy rainfall, large hail and even tornadoes. (Supplied: Sandra Taylor Bach)

Residents in parts of south-east Queensland are adding up the damage toll after an intense supercell thunderstorm ploughed a path of destruction across Brisbane's south earlier this week.

More than 80,000 households were left without power — the vast majority in the Logan area — after the thunderstorms uprooted trees, tore roofs off houses and downed more than 400 powerlines.

More than 24 hours later there were still tens of thousands of homes without power.

Damaged powerlines at Chambers Flats. (Supplied: Energex)

Senior meteorologist David Crock said Wednesday's weather was a "classic spring thunderstorm outbreak" for south-east Queensland.

The storm that eventually hit Logan had formed south of the border and tracked north before forming into a supercell thunderstorm.

Supercell thunderstorms can live much longer because of how they move, Mr Crock said.

"They get a bit of extra strength and they start rotating. It's similar to the sort of physics that makes a cricket ball swing."

Damaging winds unroofed some homes in Regents Park, at Logan. (ABC News: Arianna Levy)

"That separates the updraft of the thunderstorm where it's taking in that moist, humid, warm air from the downdraft of the thunderstorm which is where the rain is falling and the wind's coming down through the storm."

Generally once a downdraft descends, the thunderstorm "chokes" and dies out.

But in a supercell thunderstorm, once the updraft and the downdraft are separated, the storm can "keep firing" longer than an average thunderstorm, and reach much greater intensities.

South-east Queensland is a hotpost for supercell thunderstorms. (Supplied: Sharon Harms)

Supercell thunderstorms can produce damaging and destructive wind gusts, heavy rainfall, large to giant hail and even tornadoes.

Mr Crock said there is always an "element of luck" as to where a supercell will hit and which suburbs bear the full impact of the storm.

South-east Queensland is a hotspot for supercell storms, with the Scenic Rim corridor from Toowoomba down to Tambourine a "sweet spot" for the formation of dangerous storms, Mr Crock said.

"Everything lines up there more often because they've got that added help from the topography from the hills as well as that rich moisture," he said.

Storm cells that head towards Brisbane from the south-west can often have "all the ingredients" needed to create a supercell thunderstorm, he added.

"Not every time, but sometimes all the factors are lining up," he said.

The supercell thunderstorm hitting Crestmead in Logan (Supplied: Jane F Martin)

The SES has a checklist of things you can do when storms are forecast.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

A guard scolds Pete Hegseth's group at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given a top award to a service member who scolded him at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

Specialist Thomas Iglesias reprimanded Mr Hegseth and a group of staffers when a loud laugh was heard at the site.

Mr Hegseth posted photos of him giving the Joint Service Commendation medal to Specialist Iglesias.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given a top award to a service member who scolded him and his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery earlier this week.

Mr Hegseth posted photos to social media that show him pinning the award and shaking hands with the soldier.

His post says: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist."

Pete Hegseth awards Specialist Thomas Iglesias after the serviceman reprimanded him. (X: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth)

Mr Hegseth welcomed the army unit that guards the tomb and gave Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026", the Pentagon said.

Specialist Iglesias reprimanded Mr Hegseth and a group of his staffers when a loud laugh was heard after they took photos at the site, following a ceremony that included US President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.

Video of the incident showed Mr Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.

Pete Hegseth was at Arlington National Cemetery for a Veterans Day event. (AP: Mark Schiefelbein)

The tomb is considered one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the US, being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from World War I, World War II and the Korean War.

It has been guarded around the clock, rain or shine, by a soldier from the US Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as The Old Guard, since 1948.

The Joint Service Commendation Medal is considered one of the higher awards in the military and is not typically issued to junior enlisted service members.

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesman, said soon after a video of the reprimand emerged that the soldier "correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum".

Pete Hegseth was attending a Veterans Day memorial event with Donald Trump. (AP: Mark Schiefelbein)

The scolding drew attention once more to the embattled defense secretary, who survived an impeachment attempt the day before.

The impeachment effort was led by Republican congressman Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats.

While Mr Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed a bid to impeach him.

The ABC visits US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's church, whose leaders challenge the legitimacy of democracy and key principles in the US constitution.

With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.

Mr Hegseth rebuked the move on Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the constitution for his removal, and framing the effort as an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.

"This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.title: Australia's cyber security chief looking into Microsoft outage
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.author: Cam Wilson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A widespread outage has hit Microsoft platforms, including Outlook, with many users unable to access email accounts. (AP: Ted S. Warren/File)

Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today.

The company posted an update just after 10am AEDT saying customers could expect a "gradual recovery" as it rolls out the fixes.

"We're returning a portion of affected servers to the service, and they remain stable so far. We're also shifting traffic to alternate routes wherever possible and observing limited recovery," the company posted on its X account.

The update comes after Australian business, government agencies and other organisations reported being brought to a standstill, prompting Australia's cybersecurity chief to begin investigating the issue.

Microsoft outage live: For the latest on the issues impacting the tech giant's apps read our blog.

Online outage reporting service Downdetector Australia recorded more than 4,400 reports of problems with Outlook by 8:20am today.

A spokesperson for the home affairs minister said the national cyber security coordinator, Lieutenant General Michelle McGuinness, was aware of the outage and was looking into it.

Earlier today, Microsoft said some servers had become unresponsive and the problem may involve a component that was supposed to check whether their services were healthy.

Australia's National Cyber Security Coordinator Lieutenant General Michelle McGuinness is looking into it the outage. (ABC News: Peter Drought)

It said the company was investigating recent configuration changes as possible contributors to the problem.

Some Microsoft users said the Outlook problems was also restricting access to other services because they were unable to utilise two-factor authentication codes to log in.

University of Melbourne associate professor Adel Toosi said the widespread disruption was the downside of a growing reliance on a handful of major cloud service providers.

A global outage has hit Microsoft platforms, including Outlook, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant's suite of apps.

Dr Toosi said centralising services by using cloud computing providers such as Microsoft was often cheaper because of the economies of scale, but it also meant there was less redundancy if an error occurred.

While major providers typically distribute data across multiple geographical locations, Dr Toosi said they were still vulnerable to underlying flaws in the company's systems.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.title: Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients needing specialist care
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.author: Will Corbett and Amy Rossbach
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A Regional Express plane at Albany airport in southern WA.  (ABC News: Mark Bennett)

Medical services in regional WA are directly impacted by high airfares.

Local practices say flight costs are hurting their ability to attract doctors and provide care.

The Productivity Commission is due to release its final report on regional airfares next year.

Residents and medical professionals say Western Australia's increasing reliance on fly-in,fly-out doctors for specialist care leaves country patients heavily exposed to skyrocketing regional airfares.

An interim report from the Productivity Commission released this week found regional Australians are paying excessive fares to travel within their own state.

The commission found short regional flights were on average 173 per cent more expensive per kilometre than major routes.

The same flights, often only provided by one operator, are used by medical specialists to visit regional areas across WA.

Latrice Porter manages a specialist medical centre in Albany. (ABC News" Will Corbett)

Specialist Centre practice manager Latrice Porter said airfare costs were a growing issue for regional practices.

She said locking in visiting staff for her centre in Albany, 400km south of Perth, was becoming increasingly more difficult.

"Rising airfare costs, limited flight availability, ongoing airline delays and cancellations are significantly increasing the cost of providing specialist outpatient care (in regional WA)," she said.

"The disruptions require clinics to be reorganised, accommodation arrangements amended and patients' schedules adjusted.

While remote healthcare such as telehealth is an option, Ms Porter said it is not fit for an "aging population".

Latrice Porter says the tyranny of distance makes it hard to find staff willing to travel to regional areas.  (ABC News" Will Corbett)

"When we do provide telehealth services, we have a nurse sit in with the patient. It does take one of our staff members out of action," she said.

She believes that if costs keep rising, specialists servicing regional communities will have to start passing the cost of their travel onto patients.

While flights for regional residents are capped under a scheme subsidised by the state government, WA's Patient Assisted Travel Scheme (PATS) provides one of the lowest fuel and accommodation rebates in the country.

The burden is felt particularly heavily in the Pilbara, where Karratha woman Kim Simpson has been a long-time advocate for cheaper flights.

She said the expensive fares placed an unfair burden on regional patients seeking treatment.

Kim Simpson has advocated for cheaper flights.  (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

"I've got to go have skin cancers cut off my nose, Mohs surgery; they don't do that in Karratha so I've got to go down to Perth," she said.

"If it's something that you could have done in Karratha, but you don't want to wait, then PATS isn't going to cover that, so you've got to cover that fare yourself."

The impact of high airfares on families is also something Ms Simpson sees in the north-west.

"Lots of babies get born in Karratha, and then you want the grandies to come up, and that's going to cost them well over $2,000," she said.

FIFO traffic ensures Karratha Airport is WA's busiest outside Perth. (ABC News: Cody Fenner)

With FIFO mining traffic making Karratha Airport WA's busiest outside Perth, Ms Simpson believes airlines feel they can get away with gouging mining communities.

"We don't all work for mining companies, and it's not fair that they treat everybody as if they're on huge dollars because there are a lot of people in the regions that are not," she said.

The soaring cost of regional airfares

The Productivity Commission's report found a lack of competition and high operating costs combined to push up airfares.

A final report is due in April next year.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/science/2026.title: Despite a 1960 doomsday prediction, the world won't end today
https://www.abc.net.au/news/science/2026.author: Ellen Phiddian
https://www.abc.net.au/news/science/2026.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

According to a 1960 prediction, the world's population was supposed to become impossibly large, triggering the end. (Unsplash: Rob Curran)

According to a prediction three scientists made in 1960, the world was due to end today.

This "doomsday" was supposed to come not with a bang or a whimper, but from too many people.

The scientists had calculated that on Friday, November 13, 2026, the world's population would grow so quickly as to be near infinite.

"Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve to death," they wrote in a paper published in the journal Science at the time.

Luckily, this prophecy has not come to pass.

Instead, in many countries, population decline is seen as a more serious concern than population growth.

So why was this doomsday warning wrong, and why is it still so difficult to predict population change?

The paper's authors created a mathematical formula based on fertility rates and death rates and applied it to population estimates in the previous 2,000 years.

Their formula was on a "hyperbolic curve": It showed a world population growing at increasingly fast rates. Less and less time was needed for the population to double or triple.

Eventually, the formula predicted the world's population would shoot up to infinity at a single moment in time.

University of California Santa Barbara economist Javier Birchenall said there was an element of humour to the study.

The calculated end of the world happened to be the birthday of the paper's lead author, Heinz von Foerster, a researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign's department of electrical engineering.

"I don't think they were completely serious. They were trying to make a point that this is exceptional," Dr Birchenall said.

Listen to Lab Notes to hear more about why the world was predicted to end today.

Dr Birchenall highlighted the mistaken prediction in a paper in the same journal last month.

He initially did not want his paper to be published until November 13.

Despite being heavily criticised by social scientists at the time, the predictions were correct to a point.

"The numbers they produced made sense up until the 1980s," Dr Birchenall said.

But in the past four decades, the world's population has grown much more gently than the formula predicted.

In fact, the rate of world population growth reached its zenith just a few years after the doomsday prophecy, peaking at about 2.3 per cent in 1963.

Dr Birchenall said the failed prediction demonstrated the risks of trying to treat a social pattern — population change — like a universal law.

University of Melbourne demographer Peter McDonald agreed.

"It is not possible to predict fertility with any degree of accuracy beyond about 10 years into the future," Professor McDonald said.

In 1960, the world had about 3 billion people. (Supplied: City of Coffs Harbour)

Past trends can be a good indicator of fertility rates in the short term, but in the longer term, they are going to respond to social forces that do not exist yet.

"The post-war baby boom which occurred in almost all advanced countries was not predicted by any of the leading demographers at the time," Professor McDonald said.

The doomsday prediction came amid fears about overpopulation in the 20th century.

Some countries responded to the threat with intense measures, such as China's One Child Policy.

Professor McDonald said overpopulation remained a big concern in some poorer countries with high fertility rates, such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The African country's population is projected to double in the next 30 years, according to the United Nations, which could outpace its food resources.

"A failure of the harvest would have a devastating impact," Professor McDonald said.

The UN's current forecast sees the world population reaching its peak at just more than 10 billion in about 60 years, before slowly declining.

While population growth is not accelerating on a global scale, resource use still is. A 2024 UN report cautioned that the world's resource extraction was rising dramatically, driven largely by wealthier countries.

Dr Birchenall said fears had "flipped" in many places, with fertility rates falling below the rate of replacement.

Australia is getting much older, and it is getting older faster than previously thought.

This has also driven warnings of cataclysm, and sparked the pronatalist movement, whose advocates claim falling birth rates are an existential threat.

Billionaire Elon Musk has said Australians are "disappearing", quoting a post on X that calls Australia's fertility rate a "catastrophe".

"Catastrophe is certainly the wrong word to use in Australia," Professor McDonald said, adding that Australia's fertility rate was "misleading" because of the number of temporary residents and immigration rates.

But he said there were some countries, particularly in East Asia, where low fertility rates and low migration were causing problems with aging populations.

"Massive increases in productivity would be required to offset this aging, but in the long term, the population disappears," Professor McDonald said.

Australia's immigration rate means it faces a lower risk from an aging population than some other countries. (Unsplash: Jay Wennington)

Dr Birchenall said while shrinking populations were an "important concern", they were equally unlikely to cause a global doomsday.

"But it's funny that it's the opposite of what people had in mind back in the 60s," he said.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Pete the corpse flower is expected to bloom in the next few days. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

Geelong Botanic Gardens staff expect a corpse flower called Pete to attract big crowds when it flowers in the next few days.

The plant is native to Indonesia and typically flowers for one to two days every seven to 10 years.

After blooming and creating a bad smell, the flower will collapse, and the plant will retreat underground for up to 10 years

He is big, green and promises to stink.

At 1.5 metres tall, 'Pete' the corpse flower lives behind glass in a climate-controlled Geelong Botanic Gardens greenhouse and is just about ready to bloom.

And if the gardens' last corpse plant flowering in 2024 was anything to go by, hundreds of people could come to see and smell him.

Visitors lined up for hours to see a flowering corpse plant in Geelong in 2024.  (Supplied: City of Greater Geelong)

"It's really quite a beautiful flower, and it has a horrific smell when it does bloom," Lucy Griffiths from the Geelong Botanic Gardens said.

A blooming corpse flower has been described as smelling like a dead possum, rotting cheese or fermenting cabbage.

The Amorphophallus titanum, Titan Arum, or corpse flower, stores most of its energy underground in a corm: a short, swollen, vertical plant stem full of starches and nutrients.

Weighing the root of the plant earlier this year, Ms Griffiths said she was confident it would flower soon.

"When we weighed Pete in 2024, the corm was just under 10 kilos," she said.

"And then when I weighed it again in May of this year, it weighed 17.7 kilograms.

"So that was a good indication for us that the amount of energy in the corn could potentially produce a flower."

Lucy Griffiths says she predicted in May the plant would flower this year. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

As predicted, the plant emerged from dormancy last month and has been growing about five centimetres a day.

But Pete is not the only star in this greenhouse.

The garden has four corpse flower plants.

Two are in leaf and displayed near Pete; the other is dormant after flowering two years ago.

Pete the corpse flower will put on a show in Geelong over the next few days.  (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

Ms Griffiths says they could have the plants blooming more often but said it takes a lot of work.

Two of the plants were donated to the Geelong Botanic Gardens in 2021, propagated by staff at South Australia's Botanic Gardens and State Herbarium.

Senior horticulture curator Matt Coulter from the Herbarium is a world expert on Amorphophallus titanium and said it takes years for the plants to be ready for a bloom.

Why does the species unleash such a sickly smell?

Well, it is all to attract pollinators like flies and beetles that would usually lay their eggs on rotting flesh.

It also produces deep red flowers to mimic the colour of blood.

The City of Greater Geelong hopes for an event like 2024 when the flowering drew over 20,000 visitors and clocked up more than 350,000 live-stream views.

Marie Jenner missed out on seeing a corpse plant flowering in 2024 so is keen to come back to see this one bloom.  (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

Geelong local Marie Jenner dropped into the greenhouse on Thursday to check on Pete's progress.

She missed the 2024 flowering and said she was keen to come back when it flowers.

Trudy Mason saw the 2024 flowering and was not planning to come back for this one.

"Oh, it's too much. I wouldn't do it again," she said.

"It was worth it for the first time, but now I've seen it, I don't think I'd do it again."

Trudy Mason was keen to check on the progress of Pete the corpse flower.  (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

David Tytherleigh, from East Geelong, said he was undecided if he would return when the plant is in flower.

"I don't really want to line up again for three or four hours," he said.

"I may, I don't know, it depends.

"Last time around, I lined up several times, but I came back when it was falling over, and I found it so much nicer because it was so sculptural."

David Tytherleigh says he loved seeing the corpse flower after it collapsed in 2024. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

While joking that visitors could bring a peg for their nose, Ms Griffiths said it was a good idea to bring mosquito repellent and sunscreen because there could again be considerable delays in getting into the greenhouse.

Australia Test cricket captain Pat Cummins has emphatically denied any knowledge of sandpaper being used in the 2018 Test against South Africa in Cape Town.

Former Test batsman Usman Khawaja claimed in his new book that 'everyone' involved in that series had knowledge of ball tampering.

Cummins, who bowled in that series, has unequivocally rejected that in a press conference and called the claims 'complete and utter nonsense'.

"When he says 'we all knew', if that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins said.

"I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening."

Follow along in our live blog below, and watch live on ABC News Channel.

Here is a summary of the press conference:

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Pat Cummins and head of Cricket Australia communications Richard Hinds have ended the press conference after over an hour of answering questions.

I will go back and try to address some of the more nuanced and delicate parts of Cummins's marathon effort.

I also see all your dozens of comments, and I'll endeavour to get to as many of them as I can.

Just note, I won't be delving into any of the more defamatory ones.

Despite speaking on Khawaja's claims, Cummins hasn't read the book in its entirety and doesn't seem like he has any plans to.

"I've read bits and kind of scanned through it a bit and obviously seen a bit of quotes.

"Read it [in full]? I'm not sure. Maybe if he sends me a free copy."

"Much better for it being eradicated," he says before replying "not out" to an appeal for a NSW wicket on the field.

"There were many things that were shady and I think it's much better now that a lot of that shadiness is gone."

Australia is looking for new top-order Test batters and Cameron Bancroft put his hand up with 150 last week for Western Australia.

Pat Cummins says he hasn't spoken to the once-banned player but has no issue with him.

"I played under-age cricket with Cam, absolutely no issue. From my point of view absolutely no issue with Cam."

I'm reminded of Arnie Vinnick's "talk til you drop" press conference on the nuclear reactor disaster on The West Wing.

Despite NSW and South Australia being applauded onto the field as we reach the hour mark, Cummins reiterates he wants to address any and every question journalists might have so he can put a line under this and not have to address it again.

Cummins is obviously struggling when he talks about Khawaja.

He clearly views him as a friend and it's hard to imagine this won't affect that.

While Cummins isn't a fan of the way it's all written, he says he believes Khawaja's intentions are "sound" and this has obviously been weighing on him for a long time.

Cummins agrees that Bancroft, Smith and Warner were punished too heavily, but that doesn't mean the entire team was involved.

"My personal opinion was it was way too heavy-handed; way over the top.

"I think that's OK to say, but to then extrapolate that out into 'everyone else knew', that's a huge extrapolation and very different to what I think was injustice."

A lot has been said about why sandpaper was in players' kit bags and it's been said that it was used on players' bats, but Cummins says they have also used it on balls in training to simulate match conditions like reverse swing.

"It's actually again quite a normal thing. You face a lot of reverse swing so the batters want to face it and practice in the nets.

"We've scratched balls on concrete, I've seen someone use a Stanley knife, I've seen sandpaper used — all the methods are very normal around training.

"We may have been doing it around training but there is a leap to then think it's OK to take it on the field, but maybe not perhaps as big a leap of some people may think."

Khawaja writes about the first time they tried to use sandpaper on the ball in the sheds and everyone laughing about how extreme the result was on the ball.

"I don't have a recollection but I'm not saying it never happened."

Khawaja's book speaks about using sandpaper on the ball in the sheds and seeing massive swirls on the ball.

Cummins says he didn't see anything that extreme during the game and that bowlers don't always take that much care of the ball aside from bowling with it.

"I can see how people draw the assumption that bowlers must be coming up with the ideas. It's not how it happens.

"The keeper throws it to mid-on, you are trying to get the least amount of hands, particularly sweaty hands, on it.

"A lot of time it falls on the batters. I can see why people think bowlers bowl, so they must manage the ball. It's not the case."

In Khawaja's book he writes that one member of the coaching staff said to Bancroft in Cape Town: "Bangers, whatever you're doing, we need more of it. It's wet out there — we just need more of it."

Cummins says he doesn't remember that, which he has said a lot today, but he wouldn't be surprised if it had happened.

"I don't remember that specifically, but I'm not overly surprised by that.

"It was a win-at-all costs mentality at that time in Australian cricket. There were things that I don't think were right, and I think that's been a lot of the conversations — not just the actual incident, but that next kind of six months — and rebuilding a lot of those things that got identified.

"I think we have been excellent since."

Khawaja has spoken a number of times about the racism he has faced in cricket and Australia.

Cummins is asked about comments in the book about Khawaja not being considered for captaincy despite there being leadership vacuums after Steve Smith and then Tim Paine exited as captain.

"I think of the things I've read, that's the most serious.

"To think that the job I hold is quarantined from people based on their skin colour, it's a pretty big statement. If you are going to say that I think you have to have evidence. And I just don't think that's the case.

"Again, I agree with Usman on a lot of things but I disagree with him saying that if you're Australian captain you have to be of a certain skin colour, I have to disagree with that statement."

Pat Cummins is asked about Usman Khawaja's specific claim that in a huddle after a wicket, one of the bowlers said: "Guys, it's going heaps now. Just don't do anything else to it, because it's silly how much it's going."

He says that may have happened, but that doesn't necessarily mean there was knowledge of anything untoward being done.

"I don't remember that, but I don't doubt it would have happened, it is very normal. That's a normal thing in international cricket.

"When you're reversing a ball, we try to keep it hard, swinging conventionally and then there'll be a time where you start throwing it into the pitch, maybe the bowlers are bowling cross-seam.

"These are very normal legal methods and then if it's going, there'll be normally a time where someone says, 'I think it's gone enough. Let's try not to disrupt it.'

"It's a bit of a dark art. If you disrupt it ... it doesn't reverse. So that might have happened; I don't recall it but I'm not surprised, it happens all the time."

A video was posted by The Australian yesterday of Pat Cummins having an animated conversation with wife Becky.

He says it wasn't "a spat" but "Becky was very frustrated and animated and really unhappy with Usman".

"It's half very comical. Becky wears her heart on her sleeve. And half all a bit ridiculous, isn't it? We are here talking about something that was dealt with eight and a half years ago.

"Now I'm walking my one-and-a-half-year-old daughter with nappies out the front and I got cameras chasing me and my family. For me, that's a bit ridiculous."

Usman Khawaja said he wasn't interviewed as part of the review into Cape Town.

Pat Cummins says he was asked questions.

"I got asked to be part of that review. There was some people that got specifically asked. I think it was the bowlers and I can't really remember who else. And then I remember specifically a couple of times saying if anyone else has different accounts, or anyone else has information they'd like to share, please come forward and do that.

"I did my interview, I was totally truthful, I have been very consistent since then from that event until now. Nothing has changed."

One of the biggest claims from Usman Khawaja was him saying he told the team they should all accept responsibility for the events of Cape Town in the immediate aftermath.

Cummins says he doesn't remember anything like that happening.

"I don't remember any conversation around collective responsibility. I don't remember any team meeting where he stood up and said, 'Let's own this as a team.'"

Pat Cummins says the only other time he has seen blatant illegal ball tampering on a field was in a Sheffield Shield game, when a senior batter, who he chooses not to name, brought a bottle cap onto the field.

"It was dealt with. The umpires knew it as well. They caught him out and said, 'You've got to stop that right now.' It was dealt with. That's the only time I had seen something illegal out there."

Interestingly, after criticising Khawaja for being vague, Cummins has been incredibly scant with details on that particular story.

Cummins says Khawaja has told the truth at points in his book, but other parts are a bit vague.

"Some of these things are probably true, and they are his accounts of what happened. But I think there's a few big leaps here where he's being vague and I think the details really matter in that difference.

"So perhaps there was conversations with Cameron Bancroft around taking sandpaper out and how to do it. That doesn't mean that everyone in that dressing room knew what was going on.

"The way he's presented his story, I think he's done it in a very casual manner, and it affects a lot of people. That's what I'm grappling with at the moment because I don't think it's OK."

"I've heard a lot of conversations in changerooms around how to get reverse swing. Most of them are totally fine. You always try to perfect it. ... We are talking about methods all the time.

"There's definitely been times where people tell stories of what they have seen, what's happened. Other methods that other teams apparently use, which again I'm happy to talk about.

"But at no time did I hear here there's an illegal method, like, 'Let's make sure we do this and go out on the field.' No."

Cummins reiterates what the bowlers have said about not knowing about sandpaper being taken out onto the field, but does not, until prompted, directly address the potential for use on the ball on the boundary line before play, which is allegedly how it started according to Khawaja's book.

"That was news to me this week. I had no idea. Even chatting to a couple of the guys, that was a revelation to ourselves.

"One of the things that really surprised me because that isn't happening anymore. The umpires give the ball [to bowlers] out in the middle. Growing up, we used to watch the umpire drop in the ball [on the boundary] but I genuinely don't remember that being the case. I don't know when that stopped."

Cummins gets a little emotional as he speaks about what has apparently been a troubling week since the release of Khawaja's comments.

"Usman is a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations. In his book he's been casual with my life and the lives of many others and I think Australian cricket.

"I support him to tell his story, 100 per cent, I'm glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

"I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than [ball tampering allegations]. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out Usman admitted he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper. That's not Usman that I know. It's not the Usman that has been part of the team that's helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years.

"The Usman I know would have stopped that from happening there and then."

"When he says 'we all knew', if that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong.

"I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening."

Australia men's Test cricket captain Pat Cummins is speaking now.

Where can we watch it live???

You can watch Pat Cummins's press conference live on ABC News Channel the moment he gets up to speak.

ABC Sport's Myles Houlbrook-Walk is at Cricket Central waiting for Pat Cummins to speak.

He reckons there are more than two dozen members of the media from local and foreign outlets, bearing in mind England is over here for a men's ODI series, albeit over in Perth right now.

Cummins will get in front of the media, play a straight bat and throw out the line someone has said that “different people have different memories”. Others have said it best that the only way to get rid of it once and for all is to face it head on. But we’ll keep getting circular answers and I don’t think anyone is ever going to take true accountability. They would have by now

Unfortunately I think he will tow the party line, too many endorsements and captaincy at stake. A bit disappointed with the Australian posting a video of Pat and his wife earlier. Your thoughts?

“I’ve taken time?” The bowlers either knew or didn’t.

I think this will be a waste of everyone time, I already think I know what he is going to say, he will deny the allegations or he will do what Marsh did and say that's in the past and I am not going to bring it up as the team has moved on ,I would bet London to a brick on.

In the world of roughly a million cricket podcasts, Australian bowling legend Glenn McGrath has had his say and he wants everyone to move on.

"No-one's saying what they did is not wrong. They were bloody idiots for what they did; they should never have done it," he said.

"I'm a big fan of leaving the past in the past, but learn from it. We're all custodians of this great game. What's the benefit to the game of cricket by wanting to find out all these answers? There is no benefit positively to the game of Test cricket.

"CA should come out [and say] 'We've dealt with that in the past, this is Usman's story, this is how he feels' and just leave it at that and move on."

McGrath says "it's only people with agendas that want this to keep going".

"Journalists love it because they've got stories to write. Other countries can use that against Australia, and journalists from other countries that didn't like Australia being so strong, they love it they will use it."

Speaking as a journalist from this country, I can't say I've had that much fun this week, but simply moving on from a massive scandal like this is a bit of an over-simplification.

As Usman Khawaja said, he was never spoken to as part of the investigation into Cape Town. It seems odd that any investigation wouldn't include speaking to, at the very least, all 11 players on the field at the time.

A lot of people have been going off media reports with regards to what Usman Khawaja wrote in his book.

David Mark has read the thing and broken down the Sandpapergate chapters for you.

Not too sure why Pat is doing this unless he’s going to fall on his sword. If he maintains the bowler’s story of the past eight years he’s going to have to say Khawaja and Warner are lying. ‘Different views and memories ‘ isn’t going to wash. I can see this ending up in court if they’re not careful.

As far as why Cummins is doing this, he needed to front the media.

He's the captain of the Test team and was a member of the bowling unit in the 2018 series in South Africa.

The announcement of the media conference/gaggle/doorstop was peculiar though.

Normally we'd get an email from Cricket Australia's communications department saying something like: "Pat Cummins will be available to media from 9:30am AEDT at Cricket Central. Please arrive at 9:15am."

But Cummins's tweet that he's going to be doing some training and will speak after that and he'll "ask CA to send out details", was certainly a little strange.

Pat Cummins said yesterday he has "taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly".

Nothing wrong with wrapping your head around what's been said to avoid going off media reports, but in the meantime a lot of his past and present teammates have been doing media opps and been forced to answer questions about it.

The party line from current players has pretty much been: "Usman's told his story, which he's entitled to do, but I'm not keen to relitigate the events of 2018."

If that's all Cummins offers this morning, this could be a very frustrating morning for him and reporters.

When the prospect of Khawaja's book came out, Cummins revealed they had spoken ahead of time and the skipper said:

"It's obviously a long time ago. All the investigations, everything was done back then. Answered every question a million times. It was dealt with then. All I can say is as a group we've moved on. [I'm] very happy with the last eight or nine years, how we've been as a group and evolved. He didn't go into too much detail … As always, it was, 'No worries. You can tell your story. That's fine.'"

The issue is, while Khawaja's book tells the story from his perspective, it's not only his story because it does implicate others. Whether that's saying an unnamed assistant coach called for more work on the ball, or implying an unnamed fast bowler knew more than has been let on, or shedding more light on the conduct of David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft, these are Khawaja's stories but they're ABOUT others.

Cummins was there and now, eight years later, he's the captain of this Test team. It would be good if we could have a few more answers than the usual, but I'm not overly optimistic to be honest.

As we wait for Pat Cummins, please chime into the comments to let us know your thoughts and ask your questions.

Here's how the Aussie skipper flagged this morning's address to the media:

So, in between a training session and the start of play on day three between New South Wales and South Australia, the Australian men's Test captain will speak to reporters about ball tampering, sandpaper, Usman Khawaja etc.

He said he's going to speak at 9:30am AEDT.

Good morning and welcome to another day of rolling coverage of … the 2018 Cape Town Test match?

No, you've not fallen into a time vortex. Instead, Usman Khawaja's tell-a-lot book has reignited the conversation around Sandpapergate, ball tampering and Australia's actions all those years ago.

Today, the next chapter in the saga, as men's Test captain Pat Cummins fronts the media in Sydney.

We'll bring you every moment as it happens.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Protests and Demonstrations

The first trees are being felled to make way for the MotoGP circuit on Friday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Troy Sincock)

Dozens of protesters have gathered in the Adelaide parklands as the first trees are removed to make way for the MotoGP circuit.

The SA government said four trees would be removed on Friday as part of preliminary water works.

Less than 400 trees were proposed to be removed for the $96 million circuit, with construction planned to start next month.

Protesters have gathered in the Adelaide parklands as the first trees slated for removal to make way for the MotoGP track have been felled.

891 ABC Adelaide reporter Troy Sincock was on the corner of East Terrace and Bartels Road and said dozens of protesters gathered early this morning behind temporary fencing.

"In the background, the sound of chainsaws in Rymill Park, I then saw workers in high-vis loading large tree boughs into a mulcher," he said.

Police were present as protesters gathered in the parklands on Friday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Troy Sincock)

He said he saw two protesters sitting in a tree, who were speaking to police.

"The sound of chainsaw and further mulching was then later heard on Rundle Road but police have been speaking to the protesters in the trees, they remain there seemingly undeterred," he said.

"People have been yelling 'stop the chop', and cars are beeping their horns as they pass in support."

The SA government says the tree removals are part of preliminary water works. (891 ABC Adelaide: Troy Sincock)

The 4.13-kilometre circuit for the 2027 event was proposed to be laid in Victoria Park and cut through the parklands between Wakefield Road and Rundle Road.

The $96 million project was set to remove nearly 400 trees, including 42 significant trees, with the SA government previously pledging to replace them with mature stock on a 10 to one basis.

The government said four trees would be removed today for preliminary water works.
