https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.author: Mietta Adams
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Arts Festivals

WA band Birdland performs at HyperFest. (Supplied: Lizzie Wilkie)

Artists are raising concerns after youth live music venue, Y-HQ, will be demolished under redevelopment plans.

A new, more inclusive building is set to replace the venue around 2029.

All-ages festival HyperFest, held in Midland, is back on the cards after a proposed pause.

All-ages music events in Perth are under increasing threat, with the announcement this week a popular inner-city venue will be demolished, while the future of a music festival is hanging in the balance.

The Y-HQ venue in Leederville, which has helped pave the way for young artists and music lovers for more than two decades, will be torn down in 2028 to make way for a multi-storey car park.

Mayor Alison Xamon said the new building would include an all-ages live music venue and a youth services space underneath the car park, but it was not expected to be completed until at least 2029.

Y-HQ in Leederville is a major youth-focused venue. (Supplied: Cole Currie)

She said the new development would include green spaces and a revamped skate park and be more accessible for people with disability.

An interim gig space would be established during the building's construction.

WA Music CEO Owen Whittle said the news came as a surprise.

Owen Whittle says there has been a decline in access young people have to live music. (ABC News: Ruby Littler)

"I don't think anyone would debate or disagree with the fact that the Y had seen better days, but there isn't a lot of public information out about what the new venue looks like and what the interim arrangements will be," he said.

He said the Y was unique and its loss could be impactful.

The Y-HQ has operated as an alcohol free, all ages music venue since 2002. (Supplied: Sethen Sheehan-Lee)

"We might lose the next Tame Impala or the next Spacey Jane, the kind of artists who when they're very young, this is their place to perform, this is their place to develop audience," Mr Whittle said.

Mr Whittle said the industry had seen "a steep decline' in opportunities for young people to engage with music.

"From a broader perspective, we need to generate and keep that next generation of music fans if we're going to have a vibrant music scene in this state."

Y-HQ in Leederville has welcomed fans of all ages to its stage for years.  (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Oscar Cvitan, 18, from WA band Birdland, developed a strong fan base through performing at the The Y-HQ and was sorry to see the venue go.

"It's one of the only venues where we can play to all fans regardless of their age identity because it's such an accommodating place," he said.

It comes as WA's longest running all-ages festival HyperFest, which headlined WA and interstate acts like South Summit, San Cisco, Ruby Fields and Spacey Jane, faces an uncertain future.

A 2025 review by the City of Swan found Hyperfest “was not achieving the outcomes desired for young people who reside within the city" and came at a high cost to ratepayers — more than $244,000 last year.

The review recommended the festival be paused next year, but that decision was overturned at a council meeting on Wednesday night.

Mia Wray performs at HyperFest in Midland. (Supplied: Lizzie Wilkie)

However Councillor Rashelle Predovnik, who voted for the event to continue, said it was not known when it would be held next year.

Perth's relatively small population - and its relative remoteness - are driving major touring music festivals away, especially as costs rise.

Mr Whittle said it would be "just such an astronomical loss for young people's access to music if it wasn't cemented well into the future".

"Having this news of HyperFest and the news of redevelopment of Y-HQ with a bit of uncertainty around it within the same week has really concerned us and the youth music community," he said.

Grace Newton-Wordsworth, singer from Joan and the Giants, said the festival had been imperative for young musicians like herself.

Grace Newton-Wordsworth performing at Mojos with Joan and the Giants.  (Supplied: Isabelle Haubrich)

"If we want to have a local scene and we want to have the future bands coming through from WA, we need to have these venues and access and festivals."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/a.author: Matt Garrick
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Health groups are urging Anthony Albanese to redirect funding earmarked for a Darwin industrial precinct to a new hospital for the city. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Sixteen health groups have urged Anthony Albanese to redirect $1.5 billion from an industrial hub to new NT health infrastructure.

It comes after the NT opposition promised a new Royal Darwin Hospital if elected in 2028.

An independent politician has slammed the pledge and called for greater focus on regional health infrastructure.

A coalition of health groups has urged Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to redirect $1.5 billion set for a new Darwin industrial hub to instead build new hospitals in the Northern Territory.

In an open letter, 16 organisations — including the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine and the Australian College of Nursing — have called on Mr Albanese to cancel a Commonwealth budget pledge to fund the controversial Middle Arm precinct.

"We urge the federal government to … redirect these funds into NT healthcare, prioritising a high-quality tertiary hospital for Darwin, improved health facilities for the regions and health promotion," they wrote.

Construction on the current Royal Darwin Hospital was completed in 1979. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"The health industry is one of the largest employers in the NT and is worth investing in, not only to boost employment, but to improve the quality of healthcare and the lives of local people.

"We are calling for the government to redirect the Middle Arm subsidy away from gas and petrochemical developments that harm public health towards upgrading critical health infrastructure and services in the Northern Territory."

The Middle Arm precinct has been the subject of a senate inquiry and ongoing concern from health and green groups over fears the industries hosted there could impact the Top End's air pollution.

Medical practitioners in the NT have also been calling for the ageing Royal Darwin Hospital (RDH) to be replaced, with the nearly 50-year-old building showing signs of serious deterioration.

The letter says it was "incredibly lucky" no one was hurt when bricks fell through RDH's ceiling during Cylcone Fina. (Supplied)

During Cyclone Fina in November last year, bricks fell from an outside wall of the hospital into a busy internal waiting area.

"It is incredibly lucky that no staff or patients were injured or killed," the letter reads.

Earlier this week, the NT Labor opposition announced it would work towards delivering a new RDH if it was elected in 2028, despite having no federal funding locked in to build it.

The federal government has previously poured cold water on calls to fund a new hospital in Darwin, with a spokesperson telling the ABC this week the NT government is "responsible for the planning, funding and delivery of capital" for its public hospital system.

NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro described Territory Labor's RDH pledge as a "multi-billion-dollar, uncosted, undesigned announcement two years out from an election".

"They just had eight years in government and failed to deliver meaningful reform in our health space," she said.

Lia Finocchiaro says the CLP government is committed to building the "hospital needs" of Territorians. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"What we have had in train for many months now is that we need to master plan and work through the infrastructure needs for our hospital networks, territory-wide.

The Country Liberal Party (CLP) NT government has not ruled out building a new RDH.

Robyn Lambley has invited anyone to challenge her call for a new hospital in Alice Springs. (Supplied)

Labor's pitch has also met with criticism from independent Alice Springs politician Robyn Lambley, who described the move as an "unconscionable" vote grab.

"For the bush-dominated Labor opposition to back a new Royal Darwin Hospital over and above the hospital infrastructure in the regions is unconscionable," she said.

The NT Labor Opposition says it will build a new Royal Darwin Hospital if it wins the 2028 NT election.

Mrs Lambley has been campaigning for the Alice Springs Hospital to be replaced since 2015, but said her calls had been ignored by both Labor and CLP governments.

"The Alice Springs Hospital is well past its use-by date," she said in a statement.

"I invite anyone to argue otherwise."

Earlier this year there were also calls for the Katherine Hospital to be moved from its current riverside location, after it was evacuated twice in one month due to major flooding in the area.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

CFA volunteers and farmers made their feelings known during numerous protests. (ABC News: Joseph Dunstan)

Victorian Labor has promised to permanently freeze the emergency services tax rate imposed on farmland.

The Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund has been wildly unpopular with farmers, who had been facing large rate hikes.

The Coalition and One Nation have committed to scrap the fund altogether.

Victorian Labor will permanently freeze the contentious Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund (ESVF) levy charged on farmland if it wins re-election this month.

The new tax to fund fire and emergency services prompted a backlash from farmers and Country Fire Authority volunteers who labelled it unfair and unaffordable, with some facing rate increases of tens of thousands of dollars.

Just before the ESVF came into effect in July last year, the government announced a temporary backdown, capping the rate charged on farmland at 28.7 per cent.

It later extended the freeze for two years.

The Coalition and One Nation have already promised to scrap the ESVF.

Farmers who volunteer with the CFA threatened in May 2025 to resign in protest over the ESVF. (ABC Rural: Warwick Long)

Agriculture Minister Michaela Settle told the Victorian Country Hour on Thursday the freeze would stay.

"It’s 28.7 per cent and staying there."

Ms Settle said the cap maintained the rate charged under the old Fire Services levy.

"When the Coalition talk about axing the tax, they're talking about axing the CFA rebate, they're talking about axing funding for the SES," she said.

Michaela Settle says Labor will freeze the charge on farmland. (ABC Rural: Jane McNaughton.)

Victorian Farmers Federation president Ryan Milgate welcomed Labor's promised rate freeze.

"This is the first time we've heard any sort of announcement or guarantee about this. I was pleasantly surprised" he said.

"It's a major change of what we've been hearing in the past and a significant relief to all Victorian farmers."

Mr Milgate said the ESVF was calculated on the capital increased value of farmland.

"There's still devil in the detail in making sure that we're not paying for things that we shouldn't be."

"We also want to ensure that our emergency services, primarily the CFA, is adequately funded and we have the resourcing that we need."

Ryan Milgate has welcomed Labor's decision, but he does not think it will sway votes. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Although Mr Milgate welcomed Labor's commitment, he said it was unlikely to sway many regional Victorian votes in the coming state election.

"In May last year we had four or 5,000 people in front of Parliament House exercising their displeasure that the Labor government was going to raise this emergency services levy."

"But the reality is this is a big policy shift from what we've seen and I'm kind of surprised Labor haven't been leveraging a bit more off this, to be honest."

Emma Kealy says Labor's emergency services tax is not fair. (Supplied: Emma Kealy)

If elected, the Coalition plans to dump the ESVF in its first 100 days of government, restoring the former Fire Services Property Levy model.

Opposition Agriculture Spokesperson Emma Kealy said Labor’s "unfair tax" needed to go.

Mr Kealy criticised Labor's decision to consider the rate hike on farmers in the first place.

"It was so cruel for that to be rolled out on farmers on the eve of the horrible drought that many areas were experiencing," she said.

"This is why Labor is in trouble in regional areas."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.title: Victorian woman aims to grow 300,000 snails for restaurants
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.author: Tamsyn Buckle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Coralie Schaff grew up in France and now has a snail farm in the Otways in south-west Victoria. (ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle)

French expat Coralie Schaff is heading down the slow and steady trail on her way to becoming a snail farmer in south-west Victoria.

Ms Schaff aims to grow her commercial farm to 300,000 snails to supply restaurants.

A so-called "snail consultant" says there is a niche but potentially successful market for snails in Australia.

Growing up in France, Coralie Schaff often went snail hunting with her father and siblings.

She now does the same thing with her six-year-old son in Victoria's Otway Ranges.

But instead of covering the snails they find in garlic butter, she adds them into a custom-made pen that 3,000 other snails already call home.

"I want to grow the pens to be able to, at capacity, have close to 300,000 snails," Ms Schaff said.

She has set out to start a commercial snail farm, which, according to her research, will be the only one of its kind in Australia.

"As of today, all of the snails eaten in Australia are imported, so there is a market that we can fill," Ms Schaff said.

Coralie Schaff’s neighbours collect snails from their garden and offer them to her. (ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle)

The idea came about after she and her husband purchased 21 hectares of land in the green hills of Beech Forest.

Looking for a unique way to utilise the property, she went to France in April last year to visit some snail farms and was convinced it was a viable option.

"I really enjoyed it and so I came back and I was like, 'This is what I want to do,'" she said.

Delayed by an unseasonably cold summer and a black slug invasion, her snails started breeding early this year.

Ms Schaff plans to eventually sell to local restaurants, go to French festivals in Geelong, and create a farmgate experience where visitors can stop by and enjoy a snail or two.

But the first step is building up her snail numbers before she can start selling them.

Going between her home in Geelong and her new endeavour, she spends her time at the farm collecting buckets of garden snails from neighbours, perfecting her feeding methods and ensuring birds do not get into her carefully constructed pen.

Mesh covers the snail pens on Coralie Schaff's farm to protect the snails from birds. (ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle)

Snails prefer moderate temperatures and lots of rainfall, making the Otways an ideal location.

"It's very similar to the climate in France where a lot of the snail farms are," she said.

Ms Schaff is not the first person to notice how well-suited the area is to the niche type of agriculture.

A road-side sign would welcome visitors to Simpson Snails. (Supplied: The Bawden Crew)

Helene Hawes started a snail farm with her husband in Simpson in 2014, about an hour's drive from Ms Schaff's farm.

"Simpson is slap bang in the middle of dairy country, so it's lovely rolling green hills and good rainfall," Ms Hawes said.

The couple moved from Queensland to start Simpson Snails, and before long were selling snails to restaurants and welcoming tourist buses to their farm.

But keeping up with demand from restaurants in Melbourne ordering 1,500 snails a week became more than they bargained for.

"I said to my husband, 'Look, we're going to have to employ people. I'm going to have to be sitting behind a computer,'" she said.

Helene Hawes closed Simpson Snails in 2017 to relocate back to Queensland. (Supplied: Helene Hawes)

"That's not what we did this for."

The pair sold the farm and relocated back to Queensland nine years ago.

Victoria Howe ran into a similar issue after starting a snail farm in Yanmah in southern Western Australia with her husband in 2021.

Victoria Howe has become a self-proclaimed "snail consultant" following her own experiences. (Supplied: Victoria Howe)

"We just grew too big too quickly and then we weren't able to supply the demand," Ms Howe said.

They supplied snails to nearby restaurants and installed a large greenhouse to boost breeding, but after four years of farming they decided to close.

"It was that awful cycle that I think small businesses find themselves in: that you need more people to run the business, but then you don't have the finances to pay for them," Ms Howe said.

"We were kind of waiting for these snails to grow to sell, to make the money."

The snail pen has a wooden structure for snails to seek shade. (ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle)

Their snails sold for between $125 and $180 per kilogram, depending on their size.

Ms Howe is now a self-described "snail consultant," using her experience to guide others.

"I would often get and still do weekly emails from people wanting to start snail farms," she said.

Unlike in Europe, where snail farming practices are passed down through generations, reliable information customised to Australian conditions is hard to find.

"It was essentially farming, but it was still sort of a very niche product, and I didn't have anyone to turn to," Ms Howe said.

This has also been a challenge for Ms Schaff, but she has a secret weapon.

Carolie Schaff keeps a folder of snail farming research dating back decades. (ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle)

In a manilla folder labelled "Snail Farming Info", she has research that dates back decades and has crossed oceans.

It was passed on to her from a former snail farmer in the Yarra Valley, who first received it from another retired farmer in New South Wales.

Armed with this expertise, Ms Schaff said she hoped to one day see her snails used in snail stews, sausages, pâté and even skincare.

But for now, she is happy taking things at a fittingly slow pace.

"Sometimes you fail, but you just learn and then you start again," she said.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Here is a summary of the day's events:

Choose what information you see below by using filters

By Climate reporter Romy Stephens

The Bureau of Meteorology has confirmed weather forecasts and warnings haven’t been impacted by the outage and are still being displayed on its website and app.

In a statement, the BOM says its customers may be affected by the outage and therefore unable to contact the bureau via email.

The ABC has also confirmed there are no impacts to the country’s national warning system, AusAlert, while the National Situation Room has been largely unaffected, apart from disruptions to emails.

Our reporters across the country are talking to locals to see how this outage is impacting them.

Bec Pridham spoke to commuters in Hobart, getting a sense of the mood on the ground in Tassie's capital.

Federal government worker Allie said she would be "winging it" today.

"It's Back to the Future.

"I'm getting messages from my Teams, but yeah, we're kind of in the dark. [We] don't really know what's happening."

Graphic designer Brendan said while he wasn't overly reliant on Outlook, he anticipated difficulty getting work to a client.

"It might be a case of having to make a call and put something on a USB for example … something as archaic as that."

The Microsoft outage has caused widespread problems for Service NSW, the agency that handles car registrations, licences and other key government services.

Local councils in New South Wales have posted on social media, notifying the public of closures at Service NSW centres across regional parts of the state.

However, it is unclear whether metropolitan centres are affected.

The ABC has contacted the Department of Customer Service for further information.

Some Sydney councils' customer service systems are affected by the Outlook outage.

There appear to be no direct impacts on frontline police and court operations or Sydney Airport.

Is there an ETA for service restoration?

- ETA for service restoration

How long until this is solved do we think?

We're a few hours into the global outage, and we've naturally had a few questions this morning about how long this will all take to be resolved.

Unfortunately, we don't have an exact answer.

The company is scrambling to find a fix, and says it has begun to bring a "portion" of servers back online.

If they hold up, we could see services begin to gradually come back online soon.

In western Queensland, meatworks and schools of the air are among the organisations affected by this global Microsoft outage.

Western Meat Exporters director Campbell McPhee says he's been going "old school" and picking up the phone to confirm orders after their emails went down this morning.

"There's been no receival of emails, which affects our confirmation of orders and placing orders with others, so not only [sheep and goat meat] moving, but also those goods that we need. That all goes through the email system."

The School of the Air in Longreach has posted on its Facebook page that it is cancelling online classes for students on sheep and cattle stations due to the outage.

"No online lessons at this point in time.

"We will keep you updated."

We've just had another status update from Microsoft.

The company says it has begun returning "a portion" of affected servers to service, and "they're remaining stable so far".

"We've also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions.

"We've streamlined our recovery process to expedite returning the remaining affected servers to service.

"To further support recovery, we're implementing protective traffic management measures in a specific location to reduce load on the affected infrastructure, and we'll expand these measures to additional locations if we observe positive results.

"As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect to the service."

So it looks like the company is confident we might see some improvements imminently.

In central Queensland, the Microsoft outage is threatening to disrupt online lessons and communications for students and teachers at the Capricornia School of Distance Education.

The school says the global outage is affecting Microsoft Teams and Outlook, with some students unable to access lessons and staff experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails.

The school says the outage is widespread, although not all users appear to be affected, and it is monitoring the situation.

"We will provide updates as they become available," a spokesperson said.

While the outage might just mean a few delayed emails for some, the impacts for others have been quite major.

People with scheduled telehealth appointments might be unable to speak to medical professionals, while other people may have have missed out on job interviews.

Here's what one of our readers told us:

"Couldn't access Teams for a job interview, it has been rescheduled for next week.

"I suppose I should be grateful for the extra time to prepare, but after almost a year unemployed, getting to a final interview is huge, and the sooner I get an answer about my success or otherwise, the better."

Here's another reader's experience:

"I have two job applications due today that I need to send off via my work outlook email!

"I should be able to work a way around this, but the stress this morning is not welcome."

We've got our fingers crossed for both of you!

On one hand, it's a shame this didn't happen next Friday... Although that said, Xbox is apparently partially affected, so maybe that's for the best 😅

Morning Andrew and Dave,

According to XBOX support, all gaming services are up and running.

But there have been a handful of reports lodged with Downdetector, as you say, Dave.

For those not in the know, Dave is referencing the fact that the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI is finally coming out next Thursday.

And with all the delays it's experienced in the lead-up, it would have been a little ironic if a Microsoft outage pushed that release back (yet again)!

A spokesperson for the home affairs minister said the National Cyber Security Coordinator, Lieutenant General Michelle McGuinness, was aware of the outage and looking into it.

Our national AI reporter Cam Wilson has just filed a story going into more detail on the outage, which you can read below:

While many people can't use Outlook or Teams, we're still getting a steady stream of information from our comments section.

It's always really helpful to hear from you about how you are being impacted.

Your insights are important and help us — and other readers — get a better sense of how an issue is impacting the wider community.

Our audience is the reason I'm here, tapping away at my little laptop, so it's really lovely to see so many of you chiming in.

Mimecast (if your company has access) is working as a work around to read and send emails, but functionality is limited… just fyi to share with the world.

Work in supply chain for a major supermarket. Only got teams working on mine, everything else is down. Our suppliers can't send shipping ASN to our distribution centres. Lots of trucks being turned away.

We can still work with our accounting software. Main downside is that we have no emails and co-pilot. It's our first test on working without AI after getting so used to it now.

I can do my work without my email, but the lack of Copilot is slowing me down. Looks like I'll be doing my work the old fashion way — using critical thought!

As critical systems become increasingly dependent on a handful of platforms, we're creating dangerous single points of failure. Rather than trying to prevent every outage, we need to accept that failures are inevitable and focus on resilience through diversification, redundancy, and regular testing. The goal shouldn't be systems that never fail, but systems that can survive failure.

Our work is ALL email! Friday the 13th sucks! However, I'm making sourdough while checking my laptop for progress updates.

I'm receiving birthday greetings already this morning — confirming that my Outlook is up and running. BTW, I'm on the beautiful Coffs Coast.

Happy birthday to you, Brian!

The list we posted earlier has grown.

Here are the services Microsoft now says are "potentially impacted":

It sounds as if the fixes we thought were coming from Microsoft are still a while away.

Here's what the company has said in its latest update:

"We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief.

"Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.

"To validate a potential recovery approach, we're fully isolating a portion of our service infrastructure, restarting the affected components, and gradually reintroducing traffic to confirm our services remain stable before applying this approach more broadly.

"We're also analysing traffic patterns across our entire service infrastructure and evaluating whether isolating traffic within each region may allow affected regions to recover independently."

We've heard from a few people in the medical sector this morning about how the outage is impacting them.

It sounds like workers could face a few issues today.

So if you're getting any kind of medical treatment or need to contact a medical centre today, please be kind.

We're all just muddling along, doing what we can!

I'm a psychologist and use OneDrive to keep session notes updated across the day. Guess I'm going to be working off old info now cause OneDrive is down now too. I think my clients might be missing their Telehealth appointments if they can't access their emails.

I'm waiting on a telehealth consultation and wondering if it's going to be delayed or if my GP is just running late as usual :D

Queensland Health (like plenty of other organisations, I'm sure) relies on Microsoft for email. I just came from a night shift where the emails all went out from around 4.30am... If you want to scan something into your email you're out of luck - While you don't need Outlook to give medications or treat patients, it's going to be a tricky morning trying to get referrals sent to other teams elsewhere in the hospital.

— Someone else, but in Queensland

Most medical practices run off Microsoft Outlook as it’s supposed to be the safest. Thoughts and prayers to all the medical receptionists this morning. Please be kind to them and recognise this is out of their control. They are trying their best as always.

— Ye old poor medical receptionist

Here's another round of updates from readers who are now arriving at work.

We are family violence workers and can’t access our database which is linked to our outlook email. Super crucial for our job as all client details are held on the database.

Can't even do other things because I rely on email for 2 factor authentication.

Everything is tied to email - can't even log in to other apps we use in the business to keep working on other things because 2FA comes through our email!

Our school is Microsoft based. Could be an interesting day!

Teams and Outlook up here in far north Qld are fine. OneDrive not so good.

We've been talking this morning about how the outages have been caused by a "large number" of servers being made "unexpectedly available" all at once.

Technology journalist Leigh Stark told ABC NewsRadio's Sarah Morice that while it was not yet clear why the servers were down, it might have been caused by a cyber attack.

"If this is a security issue, I would call this a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack, which is basically when someone pretends to be millions of people all at once and it ends up basically overloading the servers and shutting them down," he said.

But as we saw with last year's Cloudflare outage, tech difficulties like this can often be caused by updates.

"When someone updates something or upgrades something in a server somewhere and doesn't fix it somewhere else, like a DNS, it often means that it can break everything else," he said.

"The idea that servers are kind of built to be intelligent and software is built to be smart is a really nice notion, but most of the time it's usually leaning on the smallest thing holding them up."

So, what is Stark tipping the cause is?

"I personally believe this is a form of an attack rather than a hack. This has the trademarks to me of what I would call a DDoS attack, simply because we are seeing so many services go down at once."

More than half an hour ago, Microsoft said it was able to get a "subset" of servers back online.

The latest update says it was applying the changes that made that possible more broadly.

"We're continuing to work through restarting and validating the affected servers to safely return them to service, and we're exploring opportunities to expedite this process.

"In parallel, we're assessing whether reverting the small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery."

You're more than welcome to share your thoughts, feelings or jokes by tapping that comment button.

However, if you want to get in touch another way, you can do so on our website via this link:

We've put the call out for our reporters in the field (that's you lot following along!) to let us know how the outage is affecting their day.

Here's what a few of you told us:

The outlook outage is affecting trains departing onto the network as train Consists can't be uploaded from copies sent via email — could cause delays to many services.

Our organisation has Teams, no emails. Some of my co-workers who don't listen to the morning news re-started their computers because they couldn't get their emails!

On Friday the 13th as well! With productivity impacted on this kind of scale, if Albo wants to win re-election, he should declare today a public holiday.

Thankfully I can access my One Drive, so I can work, but I have no email. While disconcerting and a little frustrating, on the positive I can work now without distraction!

Work e-mail and Copilot not working, but Teams chat is working so still connected to colleagues. SharePoint is operational. Can still get work done but it just might delay progression of some things. Nothing critical though so the impact for me personally is small.

Well, looks like I get to watch the UEFA Nations League games this morning! Go Spain!

My Telstra, an app that allows the company's customers to pay their bills and track their usage, is also suffering an outage.

The telco's website saying the service "isn't available right now".

"We're working hard to solve the problem and get all the great My Telstra services back online as soon as we possibly can."

The ABC has contacted Telstra to confirm if the outage is related to Microsoft servers.

We want to know how the outage is affecting your day.

No matter how big or small those impacts are, chime in and keep us in the loop!

Internet outage monitor Downdetector has released charts showing the spread of Microsoft's global outage.

Microsoft says the issues started about 5:15am AEDT and Downdetector says reports started pouring in at roughly 6:25am AEDT.

"Outlook reports alone peaked at more than 2,000 times their normal level," the service said on X.

Downdetector maps Microsoft's global outage (X via @downdetector)

It said, based on its data, nearly seven in 10 reports came from inside the United States.

Downdetector has also monitored simultaneous outages at Xbox, GitHub and LinkedIn, also to a lesser extent than Microsoft's.

"Microsoft said a portion of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load across multiple regions," it said.

It said at 6:38 AEDT it was receiving more than 11,000 reports of an outage each minute.

There's been another update from Microsoft which indicates things could be returning to normal soon.

The company says some servers are back online and it is now working to get the others back up as well.

"We've validated an alternative health check method on a subset of affected infrastructure, which allowed the servers in that subset to successfully return to service, and we're now applying this change more broadly.

"We're also preparing an automated recovery process to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to help keep them in service while this change progresses.

"Additionally, our review of recent changes has identified a small number of configuration updates that we're investigating as potential contributors to the issue."

It's only fairly early in the morning here in Australia, especially if you're in WA, so the outage might not be affecting a lot of people's days just yet.

But Dr Gregory says it's likely causing "absolute choas" in offices on the other side of the globe.

"Somewhere in the world it's the middle of the day and people are trying to work.

"If all of a sudden you have lost access to Outlook, you can't do your emails and you lose productivity.

"So it's a major impact across the world.

"For people in Australia, hopefully the problem will be fixed before we enter our work day.

"But it does mean that people need to be aware that there may be a slow reaction from Microsoft's Outlook suite.

"People need to look for alternative ways to connect to people, possibly pick up the phone and talk to them!"

Tech expert Mark Gregory, an associate professor at RMIT, has been on ABC News Breakfast this morning, helping us make sense of the outage.

Here's what he reckons led up to this situation:

"Microsoft announced that they were doing updates a few days ago and, as part of the update process, there's likely been a misconfiguration either in what we call BGP — which was the problem that Optus had — or another network configuration problem.

"Part of the server pool that serves the Outlook service appears to have fallen off the network.

"As we know in the Cloud, because there are so many users, possibly millions of users of Outlook, they have many different servers spread across the world that serve the users.

"They need to configure and manage all of those servers

"It appears a large number of them have essentially been dropped off the list of available servers, and so what's left can't serve all the traffic."

Here are the services listed as "potentially impacted" by Microsoft:

The company has been giving updates on Microsoft's Service Health Status website.

Earlier, it said the outage was linked to "a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure".

We're not exactly sure why those servers are unavailable, but Microsoft's team is working on it.

Here's what the company said in its latest update a few minutes ago.

"While we haven't identified any recent changes that correlate with the start of impact, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component on the affected servers that's responsible for processing them.

"We're deploying a targeted change to bypass this component on a subset of servers to validate whether this restores availability, and we've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being removed from service while we work to return the affected servers to service.

"We're also investigating why affected servers are experiencing elevated processor usage while handling requests."

AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic confirmed they've been affected by the widespread Microsoft outage.

ChatGPT creator, OpenAI, said it was investigating an issue with Microsoft connectors because tools were not working as expected.

Anthropic said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider affecting its Microsoft 365 connector.

Microsoft says it's working to mitigate the outage and is restarting the affected servers.

Reporting with Reuters

Good morning. Thanks for joining us today.

If you're one of the many people having troubles accessing your Outlook emails this morning, you're not alone!

Microsoft, the company behind the email platform many people around the world rely on, is having a major outage at the moment.

Microsoft confirmed the outage was affecting Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other platforms.

"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," the company said.

"We're investigating what's causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service."

Buckle up. We'll bring you more updates as they come to hand.

Analysis by Russell Jackson

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Australian shares have opened down after Wall Street wavered, with Nvidia shares plunging following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang.

His departure follows revelations of two alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Meanwhile, Microsoft platforms, including Outlook, has been hit by a widespread outage.

Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog.

Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.

Prices current at around 7.15 AM AEDT

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Thirty minutes into trade, and here are the top movers.

Australian dollar continues to slide against the greenback.  Not great news if you have some holiday plans over the summer.

AUD weakened 0.59% to hit the lowest level since January and that's because the USD has been rising mainly due to US Federal Reserve expectations.

Markets are also now basically fully pricing in a Federal Reserve rate hike of at least 25 basis points in December, according to CME FedWatch due to strong US inflation data.

The ASX 200 has opened the day 0.5% lower.

145 stocks are down, 41 advanced and 14 remain steady.

Industrials and miners are down today.  Note iron ore prices are off again.

And as oil climbed, energy stocks are leading the gains.

The ASX 200 has opened lower by 0.5% to 9,100.

All Ords is also off by about the same.

NAB CEO Andrew Irvine has been grilled in front of a parliamentary committee about 2,500 job cuts announced last month.

He's largely repeated lines from the time of the announcement.

Committee chair Ed Husic: "You haven’t explained why those 2500 were surplus."

"What we were looking to do was identify areas to de-duplicate, to simplify the company."

Irvine goes on to say he has reduced his executive team by 15%.

Husic counters that more jobs are being sent offshore, to places like Vietnam and India where wages are cheaper.

Husic: “A lot of these roles could be done onshore... Help me understand why it’s important to cut 2500 jobs here while you’re growing offshore?”

NAB's CEO explains that about 7 years ago, about 70% of the bank's IT workforce was outsourced to third-party vendors.

"What we’ve systematically done is the inverse, from 70/30 to 30/70," he said, essentially paying a NAB workforce in India and Vietnam directly rather than paying Infosys or similar providers.

Husic asks: "Why can’t this work be done in Australia? Is this just a simple way to cut labour costs and you’ll never bring back those roles?"

Irvine doesn't buy in :

"Labour is one driver of decision making but it's not the major driver. Australia is simply not producing enough STEM graduates. They are producing vast amounts of STEM graduates, I hope they’ll produce more [here].

"We've struggled [to recruit]."

To round it out, Ed Husic says he's worried for NAB employees: they're either going to be systematically underpaid or should head overseas, where they'll earn lower wages.

One of the biggest tests yet of the artificial intelligence boom is about to hit the share market.

Anthropic, the company behind AI tool Claude, is preparing to go public in what could become one of the biggest IPOs in history.

The company is seeking a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion and Australian investors are among those being given the chance to buy in. Is Anthropic the next trillion-dollar AI giant? Or could this be the moment investors get cold feet on the AI boom?

ABC Business Daily podcast host Carrington Clarke caught up with Lochlan Halloway from Morningstar earlier to talk about what we can expect.

In his opening statement, NAB CEO Andrew Irvine has discussed three key things:

Irvine discussed the hard call to sack about 2,500 workers, saying NAB needs to be "match fit" as an institution.

"These were very difficult decisions … our approach is that every colleague needs to be treated with care, dignity and with respect.

"These changes will better position NAB [for the future].

"I repeat that there will be no material impact on customer-facing banking roles."

He went on to discuss AI, which he says "will be as consequential to how we live and work as any previous industrial revolution".

Was also keen to emphasise: "Recent workforce changes were not driven by AI."

He's now starting to talk about the court-enforceable undertaking about underpaying staff.

They've paid back about $170 million and a $2 million fine.

"Paying our people correctly is non-negotiable," he notes.

Chair Ed Husic is talking and NAB CEO Andrew Irvine is just starting now.

Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives,  cut his price target on Nvidia shares from $US300 to $US225 as he anticipated Huang’s removal as CEO.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Biosecurity Queensland invasive pest specialists use a variety of methods to eradicate red witchweed on farms in Habana, north of Mackay. (Supplied)

Australia is on track to become the first country to eliminate a weed that causes million-dollar losses of grain and cereal crops in Africa and the US.

Red witchweed was discovered in the sugarcane farming community of Habana, north of Mackay in Queensland, in 2013.

Surveillance will continue to check if new seeds germinate.

A highly invasive weed discovered in north Queensland has been tricked into triggering its own death.

Red witchweed was found on six sugarcane farms in Habana, north of Mackay, in 2013, the only known detection in Australia.

Scientists say a clever biosecurity strategy of planting "false host plants" has played a significant role in the eradication strategy.

Red witchweed is a parasitic plant. To survive, it must attach itself to the roots of another plant to steal water and nutrients, eventually starving its host.

Red witchweed has caused millions of dollars of damage to the agricultural industry overseas, particularly in Africa and the United States. (Supplied)

Michelle Smith, manager of invasive plants at Biosecurity Queensland, said soya beans release a natural chemical into the soil which stimulates witchweed seeds to germinate.

Soya beans have a different root structure, which makes them an incompatible host for red witchweed.

"Without a host connection, the seedlings quickly die," Ms Smith said.

Soil fumigation and herbicide treatments have also been used with success.

Ms Smith said the weed could wipe out grain and cereal crops and had caused multi-million-dollar losses in Africa and the United States.

"It can cause stunting and wilting, and can even cause the death of plants," she said.

"In the space of about four weeks, it emerges from the ground, flowers and releases millions of seeds, and then dies."

Biosecurity Queensland said eradication could be achieved within three years.

Eradication efforts started in 2015, with Queensland scientists building on research into "trap plants" that started in South Africa in the 1930s.

The affected area has reduced from about 110 hectares to 4.3 hectares after 11 years of treatment and surveillance.

Ms Smith said it was unknown how the weed arrived in Australia.

The flowers on a red witchweed plant are about 1cm in size. (Supplied)

"It's a highly invasive plant and its main vector of spread is through infected or infested dirt and mud, so we did a lot of tracing, and we did a lot of surveillance," she said.

Farleigh cane farmers Stephen and Neiola Vella were among the first landholders affected in 2013.

"The first couple of years, it caused us a lot of drama, just trying to get answers on what was happening," Ms Vella said.

Burning red witchweed plants once they have sprouted helps prevent the spread of seeds. (Supplied)

While the weed did not visibly damage their sugar cane, quarantine restrictions did.

"We did lose about a quarter of our farming operation that was under quarantine," Ms Vella said.

"We finally got all of that back two years ago, so we're now back under full production for our sugar cane."

Stephen and Neiola Vella and grandchildren Ernie, Rusty and Oswin in front of a paddock full of soybeans used to help eradicate red witchweed. (Supplied)

Ms Vella said she was grateful to the biosecurity staff who helped the affected land back into production.

"We couldn't have done it as farmers; we wouldn't have had the time. It just would have been impossible," she said.

"We helped where we could with machinery and doing some of the work, but not with the surveillance … we have surveillance people walking around our properties every 10 days sometimes."

These cane and cattle paddocks were continuously treated for 11 years as part of the red witchweed eradication program and are now back in agricultural production. (Supplied)

The federal Department of Agriculture has approved a proof-of-freedom plan for the final stage of the national eradication effort.

Of the original six properties, four are in the proof-of-freedom surveillance phase, and two are still undergoing treatment.

"When no more plants germinate for several years, we then do three years of surveillance to make sure that nothing actually emerges, that we have actually destroyed all those seeds in the soil."

The Vellas now have all of their cane paddocks in production after quarantine was lifted. (Supplied)

If no plants are detected in the three-year surveillance period, Australia will be the first country to eradicate red witchweed.

For Ms Vella, that would bring some welcome certainty after more than a decade of involvement in the program.

"It'll be good for all of us affected farmers to know that we're clean."

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police are appealing for witnesses after the incident. (ABC Illawarra: Rory Macdonald)

Two men have been charged after police allege a nail fired from a ute struck an SUV driver in the face.

The ute rolled after the vehicles collided, and a 37-year-old passenger was taken to Wollongong Hospital with a shoulder injury.

Police are appealing for witnesses.

Two men have been charged over an alleged road rage incident in which police say an SUV driver was struck in the face by a nail fired from a ute on the M1 Princes Motorway.

Emergency services were called to a two-vehicle crash near Appin Road at Maddens Plains about 7am on Thursday.

Police allege a nail gun was fired from the ute towards the SUV.

They say one nail struck the 25-year-old driver in the face and at least five others hit the vehicle.

The vehicles collided, and the ute rolled onto the median strip.

Paramedics treated the SUV driver at the scene.

They also treated a 37-year-old passenger in the ute who was taken to Wollongong Hospital with a shoulder injury.

Police at the scene of a two-car crash on the M1 Princes Motorway near Appin Road on Thursday morning. (ABC Illawarra: Rory Macdonald)

Police arrested two other men from the ute at the scene.

Both were charged with using an offensive weapon with intent to commit an indictable offence and assault occasioning actual bodily harm in company.

A 21-year-old Chester Hill man was refused bail and is due to face court today

A 23-year-old Auburn man was granted conditional bail and is due to appear in Wollongong Local Court on December 15.

Police allege a nail fired from a ute struck an SUV driver in the face on the M1 near Appin Road. (ABC Illawarra: Rory Macdonald)

Police say inquiries are continuing.

Investigators are asking anyone with dash-cam, CCTV or mobile phone footage to come forward, particularly if it shows vehicles being driven erratically around the time of the crash.

Ellyse Perry survived an earlier run-out chance. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

The Sydney Sixers have beaten the Melbourne Renegades by 11 runs.

Ellyse Perry was initially given not out, but a replay on the big screen prompted the umpires to send it to the third umpire.

Replays showed her bat bouncing over the line as she dived to make her ground.

New Zealand captain Melie Kerr has starred with the bat and ball to keep the Sydney Sixers unbeaten in the WBBL with a victory over the Melbourne Renegades.

In the second match of a double-header at Melbourne's Junction Oval, Kerr set up the Sixers' 11-run win by top-scoring with 53 off 34 balls and finishing with tidy figures of 1-29.

It lifted the Sixers to 5-0 at the season's halfway mark and into second spot alongside the also unbeaten Perth Scorchers.

Kerr was the only batter to pass 50 in the game, sharing a crucial 56-run partnership with opener Ellyse Perry before the Australian star was undone in unusual circumstances.

In the 18th over, Kerr chipped a ball into the deep on the leg side and pushed for two, with Perry as Georgia Wareham swooped on the ball in the deep and fired it into the bowler's end.

Sophie Molineux fielded cleanly and whipped the bails off as Perry dove to make her ground, and there was only half an appeal from the Renegades to umpire Louise Broadfoot, who shook her head.

Former Australia captain Lisa Sthalekar in commentary credited Broadfoot and fellow caller Aaron Finch prophetically said: "There must be something in the back of the umpire's mind that goes 'what if I just haven't quite got it right though?'."

As the slow-motion replay on the big screen at Junction Oval showed Perry's dive bouncing over the line, rather than being grounded, the crowd and everyone on the field raised their eyebrows, with Broadfoot consulting fellow umpire Malcolm Wood before sending it to the third umpire.

Perry had already started making her way off the field before the decision was made, with her team adding 16 in the final two overs to set up the chase.

As the pitch slowed, the Renegades got off to a horror start chasing 141 to win after collapsing to 3-22 by the fifth over.

Molineux inched her way to 18 off 21 and was livid when caught trying to cut away Caoimhe Bray (1-17), but Tess Flintoff (44 off 33) breathed life back into the Renegades.

Needing 17 off the last over to win, spinner Ashleigh Gardner (3-13 off three overs) shut the door as the Renegades were bowled out for 129.

In the earlier game, a captain's knock from Georgia Redmayne propelled Brisbane past the Melbourne Stars and into the top four.

Set 166 for victory, skipper Redmayne (74 not out off 50 deliveries) and Irish young gun Orla Prendergast (52 not out off 36) put the Stars to the sword.

It was the Stars' fourth straight loss, while the Heat are sitting pretty in third with three victories on the bounce after going 706 days without a triumph.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The proposed data centre at Bundey in SA's Mid North would require up to 800 megawatts of electricity to operate. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

South Australia's energy minister says he is "absolutely fine" for gas-generated power to be used to help supply energy to proposed AI data centres across the state.

The SA Greens leader says it is a "total backflip" by the state government.

Plans are underway for at least four major data centres in SA.

The South Australian government has been accused of doing a "backflip" by allowing gas-generated power to be used to supply energy for proposed AI data centres.

Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis has told the ABC that he was "absolutely fine" with gas being used to help run the new large-scale centres that are proposed in various regional locations around the state.

"We support the idea of gas use to firm data centres the same way we support the idea of gas firming our renewable energy right now," Mr Koutsantonis said.

The government's own Data Centre Strategy, released just under five months ago, focused on the promotion of the state's renewable energy sector.

That strategy document stated: "South Australia can produce the clean energy needed, at scale and on time, to power the artificial intelligence revolution".

But Mr Koutsantonis said that data centres needed large amounts of energy continuously, and that gas could be used to "firm" up or guarantee ongoing electricity to data centres "if the sun stops shining or wind stops blowing".

Tom Koutsantonis says gas would guarantee ongoing electricity to data centres. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

As part of the strategy, new data centres would be required to supply their own power.

Developer Quantum DC, who yesterday announced it was pausing its plans for a 1,200-megawatt data centre at Tungkillo, had previously estimated about 20 per cent of the energy it needed would be supplied by a gas power station to be built on a section of its 220-hectare Adelaide Hills block.

The company had proposed that the rest of the centre's electricity requirement would be supplied by renewables.

Apart from Tungkillo, plans are underway for at least three other major data centres in SA.

Australian company Iren proposed a $10 billion 800MW facility at Bundey, near Robertstown in the state's Mid North, while AI giant Firmus previously announced plans for data centres near Tailem Bend and Port Augusta.

Kirsty Bevan says using gas is a step backwards. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Conservation Foundation of SA chief executive Kirsty Bevan said the use of gas to supply energy to SA's data centres would be a "step backwards" for the government and the climate.

"South Australia has led the nation on renewable energy and is aiming for 100 per cent net renewable electricity by 2027, but that progress could be undermined by proposals to lock in more gas," she said.

Ms Bevan said using gas would also be ignoring "community expectations".

"With energy storage and other backup technologies available to support grid reliability, expanding gas supply for data centres and AI infrastructure is a step backwards," she said.

When asked generally about the potential environmental impacts of using gas for data centres, Mr Koutsantonis said: "Well if you don't let them use gas, they'll use diesel or they'll use coal."

Robert Simms is urging the SA government to reconsider its position. (ABC News: Tony Hill)

SA Greens leader Rob Simms said green-lighting gas projects was a major step away from the government's previous policy.

"This is outrageous," Mr Simms said.

"We don't need more dirty gas here."

"It's a total backflip from where the government was just a few months ago when they gave an assurance to the people of South Australia that these data centres would be self-sufficient, they'd be reliant on renewables."

Mr Simms urged the government to reconsider its position, and proposed a moratorium on the construction of data centres in SA.

In a statement, an SA government spokesperson said the Greens' suggestion of a policy backflip was "nonsensical".

"Allowing large new energy demand without requiring it to be matched by new firmed renewable energy, as suggested by the Greens, would be a recipe for a more expensive and less reliable system," the spokesperson said.

Political parties including the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens welcomed the pause on the Tungkillo development, and united in the upper house to establish a parliamentary inquiry into data centres.

The SA government is establishing a regulatory framework for AI data centres, with dedicated legislation set to be introduced to parliament this year.

Belinda Dennett is defending the need for gas, but says renewables will still have a substantial role to play. (ABC News: Jack Ailwood)

Belinda Dennett, chief executive of national peak body Data Centres Australia, defended the need for gas power generation.

But, she said renewable energy would still have substantial role in delivering the large amount of energy needed.

"I think assuming that suddenly this is all about gas is wrong, there is still a huge commitment to renewable energies," she said.

"[But] If we wait until we've gone through the energy transition, this investment in data centres will have moved elsewhere."

Government and Politics

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is considering changing the government's backpacker visa policy, which was announced two months ago at the National Press Club.

Follow all the updates in our live blog.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Australian Federal Police (AFP) commissioner Krissy Barrett says the new centre will boost Australia's ability detect and protect against terrorism.

The AFP commissioner says some children can be radicalised in the same time it takes to watch a test cricket match.

"Australia is now facing terrorism 2.0, where not all the lessons learned over the past 20 years apply today. Because of the rapid shift in the online threat environment," Barrett says.

"Too many kids are at the crossroads to crime. In part, this is because the fertile hate breeding grounds where our youth live and play, gaming platforms, dedicated encrypted communication platforms, social media platforms."

ASIO boss Mike Burgess is up next, saying extremists are engaging with each other behind the walls of encrypted chat groups.

He says the opening of the counterterrorism online centre is a "major milestone" in the spy agency's mission to protect Australians.

Burgess shares an example of a group that brought together neo-Nazis and fascists from across the globe. He says they identified an Australian in that group who was asking how to undertake an attack.

"The investigation put together the online digital breadcrumbs that enabled them to identify this user. This Australian user, a member of a neo-Nazi chat group who praised mass killers and used violent extremist rhetoric, was a 15-year-old," he says.

The information was passed on to the police, who closed the case. The teenager was referred to a counter violent extremism program.

Tony Burke has stepped up for a press conference in Sydney to announce the opening of a $76 million counterterrorism hub targeting online youth extremism.

The home affairs minister is accompanied by ASIO chief Mike Burgess and AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett at today's press conference.

Burke says the multi-million-dollar facility will provide a space for ASIO and federal police to be co-located.

He says the space, the location of which is not disclosed, provides an opportunity for authorities to stop violence before it happens.

"The work that our agencies will be doing in the new online centre ... where we have professionals who've dedicated their lives to national security working in the online space to find where there is a risk so that we can then make sure where people are being pushed towards extremism have the best opportunity to intervene before harm outside the online world becomes real," Burke says.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says Australia's counterterrorism agencies are moving "from the meeting room to the chat room" as the government opens its first dedicated hub for tackling online extremism in Sydney today.

The Counter Terrorism Online Centre (CTOC), a $76 million Commonwealth venture announced in the May budget, will bring the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) together to identify at-risk youth online and prevent them from crossing the line into terrorism.

"Where extremists are in a meeting room, we've wanted to have ways that our agencies can find out what's happening and disrupt," Burke told the ABC.

"Effectively, we now extend that capability from the meeting room to the chat room."

Read the full story from defence and national security correspondent Olivia Caisley in the link below.

A Sydney teen has been charged with allegedly collecting materials to facilitate a terrorist act and possessing things connected with the preparation of a terrorist act.

The 17-year-old's online activity prompted an investigation by the NSW Joint Counter Terrorism Team last month.

Investigators allegedly found conversations and research on how to manufacture improvised explosives upon seizing several of the boy's devices during a raid.

He is the third teenager this month to be charged with preparing to carry out a terror attack.

It comes as Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is set to open the doors of the first dedicated hub in Sydney today, which aims to disrupt extremism online.

By Clare Armstrong in Türkiye

COP31 might be all about how the world can transition to green energy, but there's another important source that has been powering the UN climate talks: coffee.

The Coalition is calling the free coffee cart at the Australian pavilion at the summit a "nonsense" waste of money, but Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen (who is also leading COP negotiations this year) has now returned serve.

Bowen says Opposition Leader Angus Taylor should recall he was energy minister when the cart and pavilion were both conceived five years ago.

"Does he want one lump of hypocrisy or two with his coffee?" Bowen told the ABC in an interview on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye.

There's a serious side to all this too, with Bowen insisting Australia has an important role to play on the world stage — one that he thinks is worth the price of a few cups of coffee.

Read the full wrap from COP31 from chief digital political correspondent Clare Armstrong in the link below.

By Clare Armstrong in Türkiye

For the second time in as many weeks, Anthony Albanese has raised the issue of British backpackers with his UK counterpart Andy Burnham.

The pair met on the sidelines of the COP31 summit in Türkiye, following talks at CHOGM last week, with working holiday visas again on the agenda.

Under the Australia-UK free trade agreement, British backpackers no longer have to complete regional work to extend their stay in Australia.

As a result, their numbers have surged to almost 80,000 current visa holders — more than double the pre-pandemic peak of about 35,000.

The government wants to rein in the rapid growth, but any changes to the agreements need to be negotiated with the UK.

By Clare Armstrong in Türkiye

World leaders aren't the only ones grabbing headlines at COP31, climate activist Greta Thunberg drew a big crowd to her press conference overnight, where she stood alongside fellow campaigners, including Indigenous Australian Rikki Dank.

Dank, a Gudanji and Wakaya traditional owner, called on the federal government to stop the expansion of new coal and gas projects.

Asked whether she agreed with Dank's concerns about Australia's record on climate, Thunberg did not hold back.

"I think even a snail would agree with that. It's common sense. It doesn't get more clear than that," she said.

Ouch. Though hardly surprising criticism, given Thunberg has long argued she thinks all governments should be doing more to tackle climate.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has accused the prime minister of being "allergic to accountability" over a $6 million grant to the Marrickville Golf Club.

The club, which is in the prime minister's electorate, received the grant while Anthony Albanese was an undisclosed honorary member.

Albanese initially told the House of Representatives the grant was to fix sewerage, but had to clarify later it wasn't for that.

The PM also claimed the value of his honorary membership, which he has since rescinded, was $5 a year.

Yesterday, golf club representatives told the inquiry that the value of the membership was actually $1,100 per year.

"He's allergic to accountability on the Marrickville Golf Club. He's allergic to accountability on the economy, on five interest rate increases over the course of this year," Taylor tells News24.

"If you can't admit to a mistake, you can't fix it. This prime minister has a deep character flaw which is now affecting, in a serious way, his ability to govern this country."

Shadow Technology Minister Aaron Violi has urged the government to move quickly and act on the recommendations of a rapid review into an OpenAI data breach.

The government announced a new set of safety and security standards for artificial intelligence along with a new regulator who can impose penalties.

The Coalition has backed the recommendations of the rapid reviews and the action the government has flagged.

Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Violi says the government needs to move at pace to implement the reforms.

He says the opposition would likely not support retrospective laws.

"The government have dragged their feet on this. AI as a technology has advanced rapidly in the last four years, and the government have been slow to act and the OpenAI breach has shown that," Violi says.

"We welcome the recommendations, and now the government needs to move with speed to ensure that people are held to account if they are looking to do the wrong thing and that's the balance we need to strike here because AI agents have a level of independence.

"Ultimately, no-one should be hiding behind the actions of an agent if they have directed it to do illegal things. They need to be held to account as a human."

The attorney-general says she believes Australian creatives have a right to feel upset about the current copyright framework amid the rise in artificial intelligence.

The federal government is considering how to reform copyright laws as AI companies seek to train their models on Australian creative work.

AI models are usually trained by scraping enormous amounts of data from the internet without the owners' permission or compensation to the rights holder.

Michelle Rowland has told ABC Radio National Breakfast that while the government is still consulting, she believes artists need to maintain ownership and control of their work.

"Rights holders at the moment have every right to be aggrieved by the status quo, where their works are being exploited by others for their own gain, and they're not receiving fair compensation," Rowland says.

"I would say this: the first best option is, of course, that Australian rights holders are able to strike commercial deals with tech companies and anyone else who wants to use their creative works. That is the way the copyright system works. But right now, it is not working for Australian creatives, and we are consulting on ways to make that better."

The federal government has confirmed OpenAI didn't break the law when it gained unauthorised access to Medicare data earlier this year.

The incident, which the artificial intelligence company has apologised for, has sparked conversation about the need for law reform.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland says any changes to the law around authorised access by AI to data would require knowledge or intention on the part of a responsible person to be able to point to an offence.

Rowland has told ABC Radio National Breakfast it's a complex area of law that has never been tested in court before.

"If the question is, 'Had these actions been undertaken by a human or had a human directed the AI agent?', we would probably be in a position to point to an offence in our criminal laws," Rowland says.

"But here, I think the rapid review has pointed to something really important, and that is that we need to be not only ready for future attacks and make sure that we've got that resilience in place, but also the right laws."

The attorney-general says she expects a national criminal history tracker to be up and running by 2028 despite delays.

From Monday, South Australia is set to become the first state to connect to a pilot of the long-awaited national criminal history tracker.

The national system was set up following a series of horrific cases of child abuse in childcare centres across Australia.

Michelle Rowland has told ABC Radio National Breakfast she would like for all jurisdictions to be connected to the database by the end of the year.

"We expect that state and territory agencies will be on board with police forces by 2027 and that it should be up and running by 2028," Rowland says.

"We are being ambitious. They are timeframes that are not goals. They are timeframes that we want to beat and my key message today is that we've achieved a lot so far."

Angus Taylor has popped up on 2GB in Sydney, where he has accused the PM of lying about the value of his Marrickville Golf Club membership.

The club, located in the prime minister's electorate, received a $6 million grant while Anthony Albanese was an undisclosed honorary member.

The PM initially told parliament the grant was to fix sewerage issues at the golf course. But he later had to clarify it wasn't for that.

Albanese also claimed that value of the honorary membership was valued at $5 per year.

Yesterday, representatives from the club told a Senate inquiry that the value of the membership was actually $1,100 per year.

They told the inquiry that the club was approached by Albanese's electorate office and invited to put forward upgrade ideas.

The representatives said they presented the PM's electorate office with a "bundle of ideas" in November 2024 and costed those at at $6.05 million based on "a bit of an educated guesstimate".

"The worst part of this is he can never admit that he got it wrong and, of course, lots of people make mistakes," Taylor says of Albanese.

"People make mistakes, but this bloke can never admit it, and the broader problem we see every day with this prime minister is if you can't admit you got it wrong, you can't fix the problem."

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has taken aim the the federal government's $32,000 coffee cart at the COP31 conference in Türkiye.

The Coalition has been critical of the decision despite the pavilion dating to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor's time as energy minister.

But asked on Channel Seven how the opposition can criticise the move given it was the Coalition's idea originally, Hume has deflected and says the Coalition didn't spend that much.

"We didn't spend $30,000 on a coffee cart during a cost-of-living crisis. We didn't send 200 bureaucrats at a cost of $2 million," Hume says.

"When we have energy bills going up by 40 per cent, and hundreds of thousands of Australians in energy hardship programs, this is crazy stuff."

Health Minister Mark Butler has defended the cart, saying COP31 is one of the largest expos in the world and the pavilion provides an opportunity for attendees to have a discussion with Australians.

"Governments for a long time have known that one of the best ways to bait the hook, to get people to stop by the Australian pavilion, is the fact we have the best coffee in the world," Butler says.

"I mean, you won't see that in the British pavilion unless they happen to have an Australian barista doing it."

The federal government's long-awaited national criminal history tracker is set to enter the next stage of its rollout.

Once fully operational, the National Continuous Checking Capability (NCCC) will provide near-real-time monitoring of national changes to criminal history information on Working with Children Check (WWCC) holders.

The pilot currently has access to information about Commonwealth and ACT offences, and from Monday, South Australia's Department of Human Services will connect.

As previously reported by friend of the blog Claudia Long, the system was called for more than a decade ago in the royal commission into child sexual abuse.

The government has committed $37 million to the NCCC and says the focus will now turn to bringing remaining state and territory agencies on board as soon as possible, with police forces expected to join next year.

The federal government is considering a backdown on its backpacker visa policy, two months after immigration minister Tony Burke announced sweeping cuts at the National Press Club.

As part of its plan to reduce net migration to 225,000 people by 2028, Labor said it would impose a ballot system, cap second-year visa places at 45,000 (down from 57,000 this year) and cap third-year places at 5,000 (down from 31,000 this year).

However, Burke says the government is considering changes to its policy after outcry from the hospitality and agriculture sectors.

"The parameters were clear — the total numbers, which I had announced in the Press Club speech, were something that I could not compromise on," Burke says.

"But if we could find a better way of getting a similar immigration outcome with a better outcome for industry, then I wanted us to work to that.

"Those conversations are continuing."

Similarly, the prime minister last week sought to reinstate regional work obligations on British backpackers after ruling out such a move, after "representations" from industry and WA Premier Roger Cook.

The Australian is reporting the latest changes could include delaying the backpacker ballot until next year and increasing third-year visas to 25,000.

Hello and welcome to our federal politics live blog! It's great to have you here for another day of federal politics news.

I'm Josh Boscaini, joining you live from Parliament House in Canberra, here and ready to bring you all of today's federal politics news.

The home affairs minister is considering backing down on changes to backpacker visas just months after announcing them at the National Press Club.

And my colleague Clare Armstrong will have all the latest from the COP31 summit in Türkiye throughout the morning.

It's nearly the end of the working week, so let's get right into the day's news and see what it brings us!
