https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn8.title: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn8.text:
Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.

European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.

Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.

The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.

But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.

Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.

On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."

He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".

"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.

Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.

Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".

Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.

Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.

"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.

Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.

Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.

Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn8.summary: Ukraine's president welcomes pledge from US envoys to include European delegates in peace talks. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday. Meeting follows talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqdj.title: North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqdj.text:
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.

More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.

This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.

US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.

Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.

According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.

Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.

A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.

Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.

The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".

"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.

"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqdj.summary: More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the FaceStealer scheme, the FBI says. The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, says the FBI.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckre.title: Australian footballers will not be charged after hotel incident, police say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckre.text:
Four top Australian Football League (AFL) players who were investigated in relation to an alleged sexual assault at a hotel in Melbourne earlier this year will not be charged, police have said.

After a "thorough investigation and based on legal advice" police would not proceed with criminal charges due to "insufficient evidence", police said in a statement.

Four Sydney Swans players - Isaac Heeney, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, who now plays for North Melbourne - had been suspended for the rest of the season over the incident in August.

The men previously denied wrongdoing but apologised for breaching club standards by inviting women back to the hotel after a game and drinking.

Australian media reported that three women, understood to be adult entertainers, had alleged inappropriate touching during the incident at the Pullman Hotel and are looking into civil action.

"Due to the ongoing civil matter, Victoria Police is unable to make further comment," police said in a statement on Friday.

A fifth player, Riley Bice, who was also suspended by the club, had already been cleared by police.

A lawyer for one of the women said she was "devastated" by the police decision.

Jackson Pannam, of Slater and Gordon law firm, added that the move "does not amount to a finding that the incident our client reported did not occur, nor does it diminish the seriousness of what she says happened or its profound impact on her".

John Karantzis from Carbone Lawyers, acting for the other two women, told the ABC his clients were "very disappointed and distressed".

They would "vigorously pursue" a civil action, he said.

"My clients' civil claim is based on a different burden of proof, it is based on the balance of probabilities," he said.

Heeney welcomed the police announcement, saying the past three months had been "incredibly difficult for my family, [my fiancee] Steffie and those close to me".

"To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice," he continued.

The Swans said in a statement that it had been "clear from the outset" that its decision to suspend the players was "separate from the police investigation, and it stands by that decision".

"The Club has commenced a comprehensive examination of its AFL program and is committed to acting on the findings and implementing meaningful change to build an environment that players, staff, members, supporters and corporate partners can be proud of," it said.

Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich told reporters it was "not a day for anyone to really celebrate" and "we're still looking very hard at the programme and understanding where we need to get better".

He said the club would be doing everything to "restore the standards that this club has held for a long period of time".

In a separate statement the AFL acknowledged the police decision and said it reserved the right to investigate should any further relevant information come to light.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckre.summary: Police say they will not proceed with criminal charges due to "insufficient evidence" Four Sydney Swans players suspended over alleged sexual assault at a hotel in Melbourne. Four players had previously denied wrongdoing but apologised for breaching club standards. Lawyers for two women say they are "devastated" by the police decision.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3e.title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3e.text:
Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.

"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.

After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.

"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.

Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."

Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.

But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.

Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.

Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.

Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.

"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."

Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.

Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.

Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.

He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."

The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.

It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.

Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.

Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.

"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.

Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents.

The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.

As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.

Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.

Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.

Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations.

However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.

Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF."

He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says.

Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says.

What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded."

While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours."

In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF. However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict.

"First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF."

Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade.

Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement.

In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.

Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters.

"If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says.

Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says.

Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government.

However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence.

In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace.

"Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5gm.title: Microsoft struggling to restore service as global outage affects Outlook and Teams
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5gm.text:
Microsoft is struggling to fix a major global outage of its service that is reportedly affecting tens of thousands of users.

Services including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot have been affected by "connectivity problems".

The company said in a series of updates on X that it was seeing "positive results" with its efforts to restore services and that it was rushing to fix the problem.

Reports of issues with Outlook peaked globally at nearly 140,000 around 18:00 GMT on Thursday, according to monitoring website Downdetector. The BBC understands there is no indication the outage was caused by a cyber-attack.

The disruption affects programs that are part of Microsoft 365 - a popular online service among businesses that allows them to use workplace tools like Outlook, Teams and OneDrive.

For international organisations, this platform is essential for connecting and collaborating with colleagues around the world.

Among the issues, users may be unable to view certain files or details on their calendar apps, Microsoft said.

Its AI platform, Copilot, may also be unable to work properly.

Messaging and online meetings were largely functional, the firm added.

Microsoft said on X that the outage was caused by a number of servers "being unexpectedly unavailable", straining its remaining systems.

"We appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible," said a Microsoft spokesperson.

The company later warned that some services that had been restored "can become unresponsive again", adding that customers "in any region" could be affected.

Users around the world including the US, Japan and Singapore have reported facing disruptions.

The outage has hit other companies, including AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI, which work with Microsoft's systems.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.

Microsoft last month reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that affected the tech giant's suite of productivity tools and companies worldwide.

Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled it to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.text:
Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?

Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.

From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.

But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".

So how much AI enhancement is too much?

Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.

But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.

"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."

For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.

It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.

But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.

"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."

All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.

Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.

It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.

According to a recent survey of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.

Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.

He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.

But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.

"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."

He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.

Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.

In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.

In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.

Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.

"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.

A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property".

"It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."

Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.

But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.

Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.

He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.

"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."

Additional reporting by Star McFarlane
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.summary: Estate agents are increasingly using AI to make homes seem more appealing to buyers. Experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing" One in five UK homebuyers have viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.title: Junior doctor burnout putting maternity patients at risk, says regulator
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.text:
Training doctors working on maternity wards are experiencing high rates of burnout which could have a "critical impact" on patients, a regulator is warning.

The General Medical Council (GMC) says the fully qualified doctors, who are still training in obstetrics and gynaecology, are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation than similar trainees in any other field of medicine or surgery, and are also more wary of escalating concerns.

Author Adam Kay, who left medicine in 2010 after dealing with a traumatic birth incident, says the report "makes for miserable reading" and says "nothing has been done" to improve workplace culture.

The Department for Health and Social Care said ensuring every maternity unit "meets the highest standards" was a priority.

The GMC analysed figures from its national training survey, which in 2026 was completed by 68% of trainee doctors, which includes registrars, representing almost 52,000 people.

Charlie Massey, head of the GMC, said having doctors who feel they cannot speak up, could have a critical impact on patients.

"Creating environments where staff are supported, listened to and feel able to raise concerns is essential."

He told the BBC: "Sadly, when we see when things go wrong, it is it is very often because of failures in terms of culture and leadership."

Author Adam Kay says the findings echo his own time as a doctor.

He went on to write This is going to hurt: Secret Diaries of a junior doctor about his experiences, including caring for a mother who delivered a stillborn baby.

"I wasn't particularly well supported after it happened. It was a bit like I said I'd sprained my ankle or something. There was no talk of a debrief. There was no offer of time off or counselling. It's just, you know, get on with it."

He described the GMC report as "pretty miserable reading" and suggested that nothing had changed since he left the profession 16 years ago.

"The doctors working on our labour wards are burnt out, bullied, don't feel like they can report problems upstream. It's upsetting to read."

Aside from a negative work culture, a key problem, Kay suggests, is lack of staffing.

"There are fewer staff on the wards than ever. I can't remember the last time I spoke to a doctor in that specialty who wasn't working out what their plan B was, whether that's going part time, moving to another country, or moving to the pharmaceutical industry.

"It will always be busy and high pressured, but there are things you can affect. You can affect the number of people who are working there and you can affect the culture. You should be able to speak to your boss. You should be able to go and take a break and go for a cup of tea or a wee, and that's not the case at the moment."

Dr Miriam Broughton, 27, is a resident doctor in her second year of training to become an obstetrics and gynaecology consultant.

While the decisions she has to make sometimes keep her awake at night, she says she wouldn't change her job for the world.

"Being there to deliver someone's baby at the best moment of their life is honestly one of the best things you could ever do. And then also working with people through the hardest moments of their lives and being able to support them is just priceless."

The main challenge, she says, are the sheer number of demands placed on a doctor in her field.

"It could be that there's two or three ladies whose babies need delivering, and then somebody else coming in on maternity triage whose baby isn't moving, and you might also be getting calls from A&E about a lady having a miscarriage who's bleeding really heavily.

"There's just one of you to manage all those jobs."

Broughton says while she has largely had positive experiences, it is important to step back and look at the wider culture.

"You do hear things from other hospitals about people feeling nervous about calling the consultant...which isn't great."

Dr Kat Barton, chair of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) National Trainee Committee, says workplace issues end up affecting patients.

"Many of us feel overstretched and close to burnout. This reflects staff shortages, working beyond our hours, and knowing that despite our best efforts, the care women receive is being affected.

"We know the safest care comes from teams that are well-supported, well-resourced, and listen to each other and to women and families.

"We need the government to invest in safe staffing at every level, protect our time for training, and support our wellbeing and careers, so we can give women the safe, compassionate care they deserve."

Recent high profile maternity reviews, which looked at outcomes for mothers and babies, also highlighted concerns about workplace culture, leadership and the ability of staff to raise concerns.

Obstetrics and gynaecology trainees were more positive than average about some aspects of patient safety reporting, the GMC survey indicated, including how to report patient safety incidents and near misses.

A DHSC spokesperson said: "In all the investigations carried out in recent years into failings in maternity services, one of the key lessons has been that members of staff must feel empowered to speak up if they have concerns about workload, or patient safety, and their concerns must be acted upon.

"All NHS trusts are now required to have a dedicated Freedom to Speak Up Guardian and internal pathways for staff to raise concerns about the working environment, patient safety, or their own wellbeing.

"Alongside this, we are continuing to grow and strengthen the workforce to help relieve the pressures on busy maternity units, and there are now a record number of midwives working in the NHS, with over 600 added in the past year.

"Since coming into the role in July, the Secretary of State has made maternity services a personal priority, and the Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce that she is chairing is working to respond to the concerns raised by staff and families alike, and ensure that every maternity unit meets the highest standards of patient safety and care."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.summary: GMC analysed figures from its national training survey, which in 2026 was completed by 68% of trainee doctors. Author Adam Kay says the report "makes for miserable reading" and says "nothing has been done" to improve workplace culture.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wx.title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wx.text:
"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says Jonathan Zimmermann, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmermann.

Not yet, translators argue.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.

He thinks a new generation of tech will be an improvement.

"We will see translation systems that are increasingly capable of evaluating what they do and correcting themselves using different AI tools simultaneously: one to do the translation, a second to criticize it and a third to produce a new version, for example."

But perhaps the big moment will be when AI can show doubt.

"The real breakthrough won't come until these systems are not merely capable of translating but also of telling us when they're not sure," Yvon says.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm36.title: The school where white working-class pupils defy the odds
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm36.text:
Two years ago, I stood in a school hall in Sunderland on GCSE results day and watched the pride and surprise in the faces of teenagers as the envelopes were opened.

Even after years of covering results days, I was emotional to see a set of outstanding results in a school facing so many challenges. Almost half of the school's pupils receive free school meals, meaning their parents are on low incomes. In fact, the results in the ex-mining town of Hetton-le-Hole were as strong as the most affluent parts of southern England.

This summer, Hetton Academy hit another milestone, with 80% of its pupils getting a pass of at least a grade 4 in maths and English. A grade 4 is roughly equivalent to a 'C' under the old system, and is seen as a passport to jobs and further education.

Another striking detail about Hetton is that almost all of its pupils are from a white, working-class background, a group that's been in the spotlight for some time. This week saw the launch of the second phase of an independent inquiry, led by former Cabinet minister Baroness Morris, into why children from those communities lag behind their peers at school. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "Right now, too many white, working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education."

But Hetton Academy seems to have defied the odds. The school's principal, Vicky Pinkney, refuses to accept low incomes should mean low results. "I don't think we should be accepting less just because of the community you work in," she says.

The stellar results have won Hetton a place among an elite group of schools: mainstream secondaries that don't select pupils academically, and where 80% of pupils get that all-important grade 4 in maths and English.

In fact, there were only 339 non-selective schools in England that hit an average 80% pass rate in maths and English for the three years to 2025, out of around 3,000 that published the relevant data. High achieving schools have been the focus of some political attention recently, with MPs in several parties arguing that we should study them closely.

What can they tell us about how to raise standards? And could other schools facing the same challenges as Hetton achieve equally impressive results?

From a quick glance of those 339 high-achieving schools, it becomes clear that some of their success comes from things that are difficult to shift.

In particular, the economic profile of the pupils clearly matters. Schools that hit the average 80% pass rate have fewer children from the lowest-income families than average, and are less likely to be in deprived areas. They also have fewer children with special educational needs.

Analysts say we shouldn't be surprised by the huge role played by family finances in determining a school's outcome.

Prof John Jerrim, an academic at University College London who researches education systems in different countries, says that England's system is failing poorer pupils.

Since 2010, even while an overhaul of GCSEs has been widely seen as raising standards, the likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing these key exams has barely changed, he says.

"It's really hard to move the dial," says Prof Jerrim.

Seamus Murphy, CEO of Turner Schools, which runs schools in financially deprived areas, thinks the push for higher academic standards under Michael Gove from 2010 instilled "vision and challenge" into the system. But it doesn't work for all pupils, he says.

Especially in places where families are struggling with the cost of living, he says, an 18-year-old earning the minimum wage was "a big deal", and it might be tempting for some parents to push their children towards work rather than education.

The high-performing schools on our list also have a lower proportion of pupils from a White British background than other schools. Earlier this year, Baroness Morris's inquiry found that many white, working-class families have simply lost faith in the school system and increasingly believe it does not guarantee future success.

So it's clear that a school's fortunes are shaped in part by factors outside its control.

But there's a complication. When you zoom in on particular schools, some of them do seem to be able to defy gravity, achieving high results despite seemingly being on the 'wrong' side of those demographic factors.

So back to that school in Sunderland. It stands out as something of an exception: it has a mostly white, working-class population, and lots of pupils from poor families. In fact, if you just look at the very highest grades, the region in which Hetton sits came bottom of the English league table this year. Just 3% of GCSEs in the North East were given the top mark (a grade 9) this summer, versus 8% in London, according to exam watchdog Ofqual. (On other measures of GCSE performance, the North East ranked more favourably.)

So, what is the school doing right?

After opening in the 1960s under the name Hetton School, it struggled for years with low performance. Hetton-le-Hole town was hit hard by the closure of the Eppleton mine in the 1980s. It became common for families to send their children elsewhere in search of a good education. An Ofsted report in 2021 ranked the school as "requires improvement". That was the last report before it converted into an academy.

But by 2024, Ofsted said it was "rapidly improving". This year's 80% pass rate for maths and English GCSEs ranks the school high within the Sunderland local authority, and well above the average for England, where 57% passed maths and 60% passed English.

It's now the "school of choice" for local families, says the principal, Pinkney.

The school also says it aims to have a warm, welcoming ethos.

For Year 11 pupils, there is a separate entrance path which is lined each morning by teachers who stop a few and quiz them about their subject, problem solving on the spot with a whiteboard.

While it's done in a good-humoured way, the decision on who to stop for this brief intervention is discussed at regular review meetings.

There is more structured support for everyone in the form of an hour of extra study four days a week after school. If maths is where you are stuck, you might do two of these hours on that subject.

Over the run-up to exams, the school holds 'Revision Sundays', when the Year 11 pupils can come in for a top-up session and eat a roast lunch together.

It's all designed to foster a feeling of inclusion in the classroom, which in turn can boost exam grades, the school thinks. And it seems to be working. When reviewing the school in 2024, Ofsted praised the "positive relationships" enjoyed between pupils and staff.

And a government-commissioned study, published this year by the University of Cambridge, found that pupils who say they "belong" in school see "significantly higher attainment" in their GCSEs.

Around this time of year at Hetton, parents of Year 11 pupils, who will sit exams next summer, receive an invitation to a 'Fish and Tips' evening at the school. They'll get advice on what they can do as parents to support learning and a bag full of revision resources. Booklets and stationery are tailored to each pupil.

Afterwards Pinkney and the other staff sit down with them for fish and chips in the canteen, paid for by the school. The parents see her as "just another Mam", she says, who wants their children to do their best. She says some of the parents may have had a poor experience of school, or simply been able to get into work without many qualifications themselves.

It's a community that mostly "stays in the area", Pinkney says, and it's the school's task to "open their horizons".

But still, challenges remain. It certainly won't be easy for every school in a white, working-class area to emulate Hetton's success.

Prof Lindsey Macmillan, an expert in how education shapes life chances, was involved in the recent inquiry into white working-class children.

The pupils start school already behind, she says, and that gap only widens through secondary school due to a growing disengagement with education.

The inquiry found "telling" evidence that the connection with school "falls off a cliff" for white working-class families at the point of moving to secondary school, leading to poor attendance.

Parents told the inquiry things like, "I didn't need qualifications" to get into work - the same message as Pinkney hears from some parents in Hetton-le-Hole. (In reality, Macmillan says, formal qualifications are now more important for getting a job than they were in previous decades, when there were more routes into well-paid industrial work, and more on-the-job training.)

That's a point supported by Prof Jerrim, who thinks schools should get families to buy-in on education by clearly explaining to them how qualifications can help their children find work.

The inquiry also reported a sense of white working-class parents not wanting their children to leave their area, with its strong sense of connection. England's education system was described as being out-of-step with the values of white, working-class communities. Parents in those areas are ambitious for their children, the inquiry found, but often prioritise happiness and life-readiness alongside or above high grades.

But Macmillan, an education professor at University College London, also says that high grades shouldn't be seen as the only route into successful adult life. To suggest that sounds "demeaning" to some parents who didn't achieve high grades themselves, she thinks.

"Why have we created a structure where getting those maths and English GCSEs is so important to your life chances?" she says.

She wants the government to think about more entry-level apprenticeships and other on-the-job learning, so children with lower academic grades can still thrive.

Back in Sunderland, the 700 or so pupils at Hetton Academy have just arrived back in school after their half-term.

Does the principal think other places could replicate its success?

Absolutely, Pinkney says. And for her, it's personal: she points out that she too was raised by a single mother with little money, and still thrived academically.

"I feel really strongly about that. My school helped me to be able to achieve."

Critics say Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his department have shielded Nvidia as concerns have grown over A.I. chip sales to firms like Megaspeed.

Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology to Asia, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales in the region.
Credit...
Doug Mills/The New York Times

By Ana SwansonTripp MickleMaggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan

Ana Swanson, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported from Washington, and Tripp Mickle from San Francisco.

There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.

Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.

The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.

The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.

The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.

Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.author: Adam Nossiter
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/world.text:
After years in elite police units, he drew scrutiny from human rights groups for selling arms and providing other services to unsavory governments. He was 80.

Paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation. Newspapers will be “infiltrated.” Plots against the state will be “neutralized.”

Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo. Other clients went to Paris to do their shopping at his Security Action Store, which offered the latest in bulletproof vests or night-vision goggles, as Mr. Barril recounted in one of his six autobiographies, “The Elysee’s Secret Wars” (1996).

Mr. Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units. After he left the gendarmerie, or national police, in 1984, he became a security adviser and mercenary provider across the African continent and was implicated by human rights groups in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.

His death, on Oct. 20 at 80 at his home in Antibes, France, was announced by the French interior ministry. He had Parkinson’s disease.

By the time he founded his mercenary-security company, Secrets, a French acronym for Security Equipment Planning and Realization Company, in 1984, Mr. Barril was a well-chronicled public figure.

In the gendarmerie, which in France is under the military, he joined a new military police intervention unit, the GIGN, in 1974. The French news media chronicled Mr. Barril’s reputation as an ultrafit top cop, a military-grade swimmer and diver, a black belt in karate, a parachutist, a hostage liberator and a policeman working inside and outside the law. With the GIGN, he participated in the 1979 operation against Islamist militants who had seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, taking dozens hostage.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.title: Chris Van Hollen Set to Challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Carl Hulse
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has emerged as a favorite of Democrats seeking an alternative to Senator Chuck Schumer, who says he has the votes to win.

Reporting from Capitol Hill

Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced on Thursday that he would challenge Senator Chuck Schumer of New York for majority leader, setting up a clash among Democrats just as they were celebrating their new majority and planning for a takeover of Congress in January.

The move by Mr. Van Hollen, a progressive Democrat elected to the Senate in 2016 after seven terms in the House representing the Washington, D.C., suburbs, comes as some Democratic senators and activists have called for an alternative to Mr. Schumer, a moderate whom they regard as too tied to the party establishment to lead a newly energized party forward in the next Congress.

Making his announcement in an interview on MS Now on Thursday evening, Mr. Van Hollen said his challenge to Mr. Schumer was “not about any one individual.” Instead, he said, it was to ensure that Democrats answered “the call of the American people” in the midterm elections, which he said was to “bring down costs” and end the war against Iran.

He said he had spoken to a large number of Democratic senators, including the incoming members, and did not believe that Mr. Schumer had a lock on the race, saying he had “more than 10” of the 55 Democratic senators and senators-elect behind him.

“Am I the underdog?” he said. “Yes.”

Mr. Van Hollen, who is also said to be weighing a run for president in 2028, had emerged as the favorite to challenge Mr. Schumer for the post and had expressed increasing willingness to do so in recent days.

Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont who aligns with Democrats, said this week that he would oppose Mr. Schumer and had encouraged Mr. Van Hollen to become a candidate.

On Thursday night, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who during his campaign called on Mr. Van Hollen to seek the post, greeted his announcement enthusiastically, saying he was “proud” to endorse him as majority leader.

“Last week, Michiganders rejected the failed status quo and the politics that too often leaves families behind,” Mr. El-Sayed said in a statement. “But we need to earn our mandate. That demands new leadership.”

Senate Democrats are scheduled to vote behind closed doors on Dec. 1 to determine who will be their leader when their party takes the Senate majority on Jan. 4.

In a statement, Mr. Schumer said that he welcomed “a discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” but had enough commitments of support from Senate Democrats to be re-elected as leader.

“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result,” he said, adding: “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

Mr. Schumer oversaw the Senate Democratic campaign effort that has flipped at least eight seats, with the Democrat Scott Colom on Wednesday called as the winner in the Mississippi Senate race. The Alaska Senate race result has not been called, but the Democrat Mary Peltola is slightly ahead there.

Despite that success, some in the ranks of Senate Democrats have called for a broad discussion of party leadership going forward and a debate over the agenda the party should pursue.

Other Democrats say that the leadership fight is distracting from the stunning victory Democrats recorded on Nov. 3 and hurting their preparation for January.

“We were at 47-53 and now we are at 55, 56,” said Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania and a strong supporter of Mr. Schumer. He added: “I don’t understand why that’s a conversation.”

On Thursday night, Senator Brian Schatz, Democrat of Hawaii, said he welcomed a conversation “about the path ahead,” but urged his colleagues not to draw out that process. He endorsed Mr. Schumer, whom he credited with leading the party to victory.

“We must move quickly to vote, unify, and get to work,” Mr. Schatz said.

Senator Angus King of Maine, the other independent who caucuses with Democrats, also threw his support behind Mr. Schumer in a statement, crediting him with engineering a historically successful election result.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority, which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Mr. King said. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

Mr. Van Hollen, 67, is the child of a diplomat and was elected to the House in 2002 after entering the race as an underdog in a very competitive primary while serving in the Maryland legislature.

In the House, he became a close ally to Speaker Nancy Pelosi and a leading voice on budget issues. In 2008, he led the House campaign effort as Democrats expanded their majority when Barack Obama was elected president and also led the campaign team in 2010.

Mr. Van Hollen was seen as a potential future speaker in the House, but that prospect had seemed far off given Ms. Pelosi’s hold on the office. When Barbara Mikulski of Baltimore was set to retire from the Senate in 2016, he sought her seat and won. Given his experience, Senate Democrats immediately put him in charge of their campaign organization.

In the Senate, Mr. Van Hollen has focused on budget issues and foreign policy. He has been an outspoken proponent of cutting off money for the war against Iran.

On Thursday, he said Democrats’ Senate campaign arm should not take any funding from AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group that many progressives have shunned in recent years.

Progressive activists have urged that Mr. Schumer, 75, face a challenge to remaining in the position. Donors and organizations including MoveOn, Indivisible and the Working Families Party are likely to back and mobilize members on behalf of Mr. Van Hollen, according to a person familiar with progressive groups’ strategy who spoke about it on the condition of anonymity. Some of the donors plan to threaten to back primary challenges against any Democratic senator running for re-election in 2028 who does not come out in support of him, the person said.

Mr. Schumer and his allies have been adamant that he has more than enough votes to hold the position. But secret ballot leadership votes can be unpredictable. Some senators have refrained from going public with their support to avoid coming under pressure from those urging that Mr. Schumer be deposed.

“Circumstances change,” Mr. Van Hollen said. “It is one thing to have someone’s support when you’re the only choice. I think a little democracy in the Senate Democratic Caucus is a good thing.”

Lisa Lerer and Reid J. Epstein contributed reporting.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan, Tripp Mickle and Julian E. Barnes
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The president called the Nvidia chief on Tuesday, continuing a pattern of supporting him even as the spy scandal was intensifying.

By Maggie HabermanJonathan SwanTripp Mickle and Julian E. Barnes

President Trump called Jensen Huang on Tuesday, before the Nvidia chief stepped down amid a rapidly unfolding spy scandal, and urged him to keep fighting for his job, according to two people briefed on the conversation.

The call was the latest instance of Mr. Trump defending and protecting Mr. Huang, who had become a high-profile ally and an influential adviser on artificial intelligence. The president continued to back him to the end, even after U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that Mr. Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Nvidia announced on Thursday that Mr. Huang, who built the company into the world’s leading supplier of advanced A.I. chips, had been replaced as chief executive following revelations not just of the affair with the woman suspected of being a spy, but also another with one of his employees.

A representative for Mr. Huang did not provide a comment for this article. Neither Mr. Trump nor the White House responded to requests for comment about his call to Mr. Huang.

The president had been warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a Chinese citizen known as Alice Huang, whom intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.

Mr. Trump took no action either time, and brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China in May. In recent days, he has publicly praised Mr. Huang and expressed sympathy for him, saying in a social media post on Thursday that he was a “legend.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.title: What Does 2026 Mean for the Map in 2028?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.author: Jess Bidgood
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/po.text:
Mississippi and other states have created new uncertainty about what, exactly, a red state is.

America’s political map looked pretty calcified — until last week.

Democrats’ surprising midterm wins across red states — including Scott Colom’s victory over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi — have raised new questions for both parties that will matter a lot for 2028 and beyond.

Was this all a blip, specific to this particular moment? Or could America’s political map be changing in a bigger way, putting longtime Republican strongholds in play for Democrats?

Tonight, let’s dive into the biggest question coming out of the midterms.

Since 2016, just six states have actually swung between Democratic and Republican presidential candidates. In the Senate, red-state Democrats and blue-state Republicans became endangered species. And the map of competitive House districts grew ever narrower.

But Democrats’ big Senate flips last week mostly came in states that haven’t backed their party for president in years.

“When you start losing Mississippi and Maine simultaneously, then you clearly have lost popular sentiment,” Newt Gingrich, the former House speaker, told me.

He would know. In 1994, he led his party to make enormous gains in the House, a “Republican revolution” that set the stage for the map we know today. And he believes that Democrats’ wins last week just might be the beginning of a rare political realignment, depending on how they govern.

“If the Democrats can discipline themselves to listen to the American people, they could create a new majority that could govern for quite a long time,” he said.

There is no guarantee, of course, that any wave election will become more than a one-off. In 1946, the year after Franklin D. Roosevelt’s death and Harry Truman’s ascent, Republicans swept Democrats out of the House and Senate — only to see their power ebb again two years later when Truman, a Democrat, won a full term.

And in 2006, Democrats captured both the House and the Senate as the public tired of George W. Bush, then deepened their control of government with the 2008 rise of President Barack Obama. Then, of course, came the “shellacking” of 2010, when Republicans picked up seats in the Senate and gained control of the House.

But sometimes, a wave election can signal the start of something more long-term.

Take 1964, when Lyndon B. Johnson, Democrat, won 44 states and Washington, D.C. It was a Democratic landslide. But a band of states in the Deep South backed Barry Goldwater, that year’s Republican presidential nominee, and those states have mostly stuck with Republicans ever since, especially when it comes to presidential elections.

And look at the presidential map in 1996. Two years after Gingrich first won power in the House, you can see the last gasps of Democratic dominance in Southern states like West Virginia, Arkansas and Tennessee — states that became seemingly impossible for the party to win when President Bill Clinton was no longer on the ballot.

Democrats believe they now have the opportunity to reimagine their party’s path to power, which in recent presidential elections has run through the “blue wall” states of Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. A party that can compete in the South — or even just in Texas, which has 40 electoral votes — has a lot more ways to win.

I called Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia, who believes that this is the moment for Democrats to go all in on winning in Southern states, which have not in recent years been seen as critical to what he called “the math of our majority.” Now, he said, they should be.

“The South is the fastest-growing region in the country,” Warnock said. “It’s the only region in the country where we’re seeing population growth for every age group. And when you look at the base of the Democratic Party and its most loyal voters, Black voters, the South is where the big and valiant struggle for our voices is being waged.”

Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky told me he thought red states that just elected Democratic governors, like Ohio and Iowa, could remain competitive in 2028.

“Democrats were looking in ’28 and ’32 at a shrinking map with very little margin of error,” he said. “Now they’re going to be able to go and campaign in states, lean on Democratic governors that have won in those states, and know how to turn out voters.”

It’s much too early to know what the 2028 map is going to look like. But the uncertainty about the nation’s political geography is new, and could shape the contest in unpredictable ways.

That was Hunter Patterson, a police dispatcher in Montgomery County, Texas. A “libertarian independent,” he said he usually voted Republican but no longer considered himself one after the party’s sharp turn to the right in recent years.

Patterson said he disagreed with James Talarico on many things, but still voted for him for Senate.

The question of what independent-minded voters like Patterson do in the future will go a long way to determining whether states like Texas snap back to red, or stay purple.

My colleague Sabrina Tavernise spoke with lots of them. Read her reporting.

Jensen Huang, the embattled chief executive of the chip giant Nvidia, resigned, sending shock waves through the tech industry.

His downfall costs the A.I. boom one of its top backers, Ben Casselman writes.

Trump said that he would pull back Vice President JD Vance from potential peace talks with Iran, and that Vance’s time would be better spent focused on domestic fraud.

Will Democrats fight to impeach or investigate Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. with their new majorities? Or, Sheryl Gay Stolberg writes, will they try to work with him on areas where they can agree?

House Democrats faced a backlash after 11 of them missed a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Hospitals across the country are racing to keep millions of patients insured, and bracing for huge funding cuts, before new Medicaid work rules and guidelines begin in the new year.

Cities are employing a new strategy to delay the Trump administration’s effort to build ICE jails: using a lawsuit to stall the construction of immigration detention centers until Democrats take over Congress.

One Senate race has yet to be called: Alaska’s.

Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, is narrowly leading Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, and an analysis of ballots by The New York Times found that she is likely to prevail. But the state’s ranked-choice voting system means that tallying votes there is extra complicated.

My colleague Christine Zhang, a reporter on our Election Analytics team, has been watching the count closely, and is here with a quick update.

Christine, what’s happening in Alaska right now? Why is their count taking so long?

Alaska has reported 86 percent of the votes so far. The remaining ballots are mostly mail-in ballots, which need to be reviewed before being included in the count. It can also take a long time to transport mail ballots through the state’s remote, inaccessible regions. Officials will count ballots that arrive up to 10 days after Election Day, as long as they were postmarked by Nov. 3.

How much longer do officials there have to count?

They have until Nov. 18 to count all the remaining ballots. That’s also the date when ranked-choice tabulation will begin if the top candidates in the statewide races have not cleared the 50 percent threshold needed to win outright.

During this process, whoever is in last place will be eliminated, and the votes for that candidate will instead be awarded to each voter’s next choice still in the race. That goes on until two candidates are left, and the one with more votes wins.

OK. Is Nov. 18 when we might officially learn the winner of the race?

Well, there’s a chance that the Senate race could be called sooner, if it doesn’t go to ranked-choice tabulation at all. The remaining vote is from areas favorable to Peltola, so we’ll have to see how it goes in the days ahead. But yes, if the race is decided by ranked-choice tabulation, we will most likely know on Nov. 18.

In 2024, voters in states like Arizona and Missouri backed abortion-rights measures even as they supported candidates like President Trump who had celebrated the fall of Roe v. Wade.

This year, the reverse has happened. As Democratic candidates won statewide races, several high-profile conservative ballot measures prevailed. The dissonant results show that voters do not always move the same way all at once — even in a wave election.

California narrowly killed a measure for a wealth tax on billionaires.

Arizona handily passed a Republican-backed referendum to require transgender students to use bathrooms and locker rooms aligned with the sex listed on their birth certificates. Voters in three more states, including Colorado, passed similar measures.

Voters in seven states, including Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio, passed measures to ban noncitizen voting or require voter identification — ideas long pushed by conservative groups.

Two more Republican bright spots:

New England’s two Republican governors withstood the blue wave. Read about how they did it.

Paul LePage, the former governor of Maine, flipped a House seat in a rare midterm battleground win for Republicans.

Bruce Giudici tried for years to win a seat on the board of supervisors in Calaveras County, Calif. Then he died. But his odds of winning the seat are looking better than ever.

On Aug. 30, his campaign said, he was out door-knocking when he fell. Giudici, who was 68, died the next day. His campaign pushed forward anyway, and its grass-roots politicking seems to have paid off: Giudici has posthumously received 57 percent of the vote in his race.

Taylor Robinson and Christine Zhang contributed reporting.

Jess Bidgood is a managing correspondent for The Times and writes the On Politics newsletter, a guide to this pivotal moment in American politics.

Building Collapse in Brooklyn

The Fire Department said the search for victims on Flatbush Avenue was over, while city investigators began looking into an excavation occurring next door.

The Fire Department said the search for victims on Flatbush Avenue was over, while city investigators began looking into an excavation occurring next door.

The collapse of an apartment building into an adjacent construction site in Flatbush killed eight people and injured 18.
Credit...
Bing Guan for The New York Times

By Troy ClossonNate SchweberAndrea Barnes and Michael Levenson

After a night of frantic searches through the rubble of a Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight people, New York City officials announced on Thursday that they were ending their rescue efforts, concluding there were no more victims.

Eighteen other people, including four firefighters, were injured in the collapse and its aftermath at 1321 Flatbush Avenue. Two children who were cousins were among the eight killed, according to an internal police report. Three were construction workers.

The tragedy shattered the heavily immigrant neighborhood and set off a city investigation into excavation at the construction site next door at 2625 Bedford Avenue.

The collapse occurred around 4 p.m. on Wednesday. James Williams, who works at a deli across the street, said he had been hearing an incessant loud hammering noise every few minutes from the construction site on Wednesday afternoon. He went outside and saw bricks falling from 1321 Flatbush, a three-story apartment building. “I’m like, Oh hell, what is going on?” he said.

He watched as the building started to crumble, its front and side sliding away, and a check-cashing shop that he frequented underneath all collapsing into the open construction site next door. He saw clothes and a microwave oven thrown into the dust-filled air. He heard people scream.

The first firefighters arrived within a minute, followed by more from around New York City and from New Rochelle, N.Y., in Westchester County. The search and rescue efforts involved about 250 personnel in all.
