https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/techn.title: With Jensen Huang Gone, the A.I. Industry Loses Its Most Powerful Backer in Washington
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/techn.author: Cecilia Kang and David McCabe
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Nvidia’s chief executive, a confidant of President Trump, successfully pushed for less regulation and open borders for chip sales.

By Cecilia Kang and David McCabe

Cecilia Kang and David McCabe reported from Washington.

Jensen Huang’s ouster as chief executive of Nvidia leaves a vacuum in Washington, where he was one of the strongest bulwarks against the regulation of artificial intelligence.

A confidant of President Trump, Mr. Huang successfully fought to open sales channels of A.I. chips to China. He also argued against A.I. safety regulations, which he said could hold back American companies in a global race with rivals. And he pushed for acceptance of open source technology, in which the underlying computer code for A.I. models is made public.

He mostly got his way.

Now, Mr. Huang is gone and bipartisan outrage is rising over the national security threats posed by allegations of his affair with a Chinese spy. The Nvidia co-founder’s Washington agenda — and White House officials who supported him — are under attack.

Voters last week swept Democrats, who have promised heavier A.I. regulation, into office. And a growing chorus of industry voices are cautioning that the technology has grown too dangerous, and that the government must step in to protect the public from rogue A.I. agents and economic disruption.

Mr. Huang has been “singularly” influential over American A.I. policy, said Samuel Hammond, the director of super intelligence policy at the Foundation for American Innovation, a right-leaning think tank focused on tech issues.

“His No. 1 prerogative has been gaining market access to China, by hook or by crook,” said Mr. Hammond, a critic of Nvidia’s efforts to limit export controls.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.title: Huang and Lutnick Summoned to Testify Before Congress
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.author: Mack Liederman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Senator Tim Scott said he had requested that the Nvidia co-founder and the commerce secretary appear before the Senate Banking Committee.

Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee as Mr. Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy raises national security concerns.

Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina, on Thursday evening sent letters to Mr. Huang and Mr. Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.

“Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” Mr. Scott said in a social media post, adding, “The American people deserve answers.”

Congressional leaders of both political parties have said they support efforts to hear from Mr. Huang directly about his entanglement with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. officials concluded had been recruited by China’s main spy agency.

Mr. Scott asked Mr. Huang to appear on Dec. 3 by his own volition but also threatened that the committee could issue a subpoena. House Republicans also said on Thursday they were in discussions with Mr. Huang to testify before other committees. Mr. Huang has hired lawyers who previously represented executives in government investigations, according to people familiar with the matter.

Mr. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday. But that has not appeared to slow a bipartisan push for more information on whether he had compromised national security.

Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, said in a social media post that Congress must “demand answers” from Mr. Huang. Mr. Schumer also called on the Trump administration to “answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.”

Mr. Lutnick’s department was required to review companies for national security risks before the Trump administration allowed Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China last year. The top Democrats on two congressional committees also wrote to Mr. Lutnick on Thursday, saying they were investigating the matter.

Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the banking committee, said that Mr. Huang’s resignation “does not absolve him, other executives or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws.”

She added in a statement that the company still would “owe Congress answers.” She also demanded that Trump officials “ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military.”

Michael Gold, Ana Swanson and Tony Romm contributed reporting.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.title: Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: Jason Breslow
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., seen above on Aug. 8, 2026 in St. Paul, Minn., has announced he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate Majority Leader.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has announced he will challenge New York's Chuck Schumer for the job of Senate majority leader, pushing the party into a fresh debate over its future just days after sweeping victories in the midterm elections.

Van Hollen made the announcement on Thursday, saying voters sent a clear message in the midterms — that they want "change from the status quo."

"It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," Van Hollen said in a statement. "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

Van Hollen, 67, was elected to the Senate in 2016 after spending more than a decade in the House representing a Maryland suburb outside of Washington, D.C. One of his party's more progressive members, he gained national attention last year lobbying for the release of Kilmar Abrego Garcia after he was wrongfully deported to a prison in El Salvador.

His announcement comes at a moment when progressive activists, as well as some Democratic lawmakers, are calling for Schumer, 75, to be replaced as party leader. Schumer has served in the role since 2017, but drew the ire of many inside the Democratic base for not taking a tougher stance against President Trump during a fight over government funding in early 2025.

"I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I'm proud of what we've accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer wrote on social media following Van Hollen's announcement. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks to reporters at the Capitol on Nov. 10, 2026.

While Schumer has maintained he has the votes to become majority leader, he has faced growing resistance from inside the Democratic caucus. Earlier this week, Sen. Bernie Sanders, the Vermont Independent who aligns with Democrats, said he would oppose Schumer. He made the announcement next to Michigan Democrat Elissa Slotkin, who did not say outright she would oppose Schumer, but told reporters, "I am seeking change."

Several incoming Democratic lawmakers have similarly expressed opposition to Schumer's bid for majority leader, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed.

"I deeply appreciate Senator Schumer," El-Sayed told NPR this week. "But this is about leadership for the American public, and if all we do is kind of go back to what we've been doing in a moment where we've been given a mandate, I worry that we may not earn our mandate."

Multiple Democrats have publicly come out in support of Schumer, including Arizona's Ruben Gallego, Kirsten Gillibrand of New York and Maryland's Angela Alsobrooks.

Democrats will vote by secret ballot for majority leader in early December. Whoever wins will preside over a majority of 55 seats, though that could grow to 56 depending on the final tally in the U.S. Senate race in Alaska.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
A Microsoft logo and sign outside the Microsoft Visitor Center are seen at the company's headquarters Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Redmond, Wash.

A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant's suite of apps.

Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook just after 1 p.m. ET. New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they couldn't send and receive emails or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether.

Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft's workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft said it was investigating disruptions, notably related to its email and Teams applications.

In updates posted on social media, Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft said it was aware of users "experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas."

Microsoft explained that a portion of its infrastructure was "experiencing elevated load" — which it said was "likely contributing to the connectivity errors." The company determined a number of servers were "unexpectedly unavailable" due to a problem that caused them to fail during "automated health checks."

It was not immediately clear what exactly caused that failure. But Microsoft later said it was testing a fix and rolling out an alternative method for these checks to bring impacted servers back online.

"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," the Microsoft 365 Status account wrote on X.

Earlier in the day, the company said it had "successfully restored" problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/g-s1-1512.author: Larry Kaplow

Kansas Democratic gubernatorial candidate, State Sen. Cindy Holscher speaks to reporters after casting her ballot during early voting at a polling location on October 31, 2026 in Kansas City, Kansas.

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country
Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher will hold onto the Kansas governor's office for her party after defeating Republican Ty Masterson, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Masterson, the president of the state Senate, was endorsed by President Trump. Of the 36 elections for governor across the country, Kansas was seen as the most likely to flip from Democratic to Republican control.

Current Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly is term-limited after serving for eight years in a state with a heavily Republican legislature and that usually votes for Republicans for other offices and in presidential elections.

Holscher, 57, ran a campaign with notes of populism, promising to fight "sweetheart deals" for billionaires. She tied Masterson to his work in the state Senate when it passed a tax cut under former Republican Gov. Sam Brownback that led to a series of budget crises and was later repealed.

Holscher opposed school vouchers, calling for more support for public schools, in contrast with Masterson, who backed school vouchers. She also called for a moratorium on new data centers and for legalizing cannabis as a way to generate state revenue.

Masterson, 57, called for lower property taxes and said faith influenced all his decisions, including in politics. He promised to be the "most pro-ag, pro-business, pro-oil and gas governor," the state has seen. He called Holscher, "the most radical, liberal, socialist Democrat ever" on a ticket in Kansas.

"He likes to throw around a whole lot of labels," Holscher responded. "You know why? Because that's all he's got."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.author: Havalin Haskell
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-603.text:
Local and state officials in Colorado say recent floods have outstripped their ability to respond. They're worried about federal response after Trump delayed flood aid for political reasons in 2025.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

A week after devastating floods in the Southwest, officials in four states are still tallying up the damage, and it's already clear they'll be requesting federal disaster assistance. In Colorado, residents are wondering if they'll get it. After big floods last year, the aid didn't come immediately. At the time, President Trump was in a political spat with Colorado's governor. Colorado Public Radio's Havalin Haskell reports that people hope things are different this time.

HAVALIN HASKELL, BYLINE: Donald Kubelka's single-story two-bedroom house is just steps away from the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs, Colorado.

DONALD KUBELKA: Sorry, I'm at a bit of a loss for words. It's a bit overwhelming.

HASKELL: A red line tracing around the yellow exterior walls shows where the river wrapped around his house up to the windows. His two kids' toys are strewn around the yard.

So do you think you're gonna have to take down the entire house?

KUBELKA: Yeah, let me show you.

Inside, red mud coats the floors and the walls. Waterlogged wallpaper is peeling away in sheets. There's a strong, musty smell in the air.

KUBELKA: We had a inch of mud come through on the first flood that got up to about a foot and a half.

The first flood was three weeks ago. The second was bigger, and both hit exactly a year after floods big enough that Colorado asked for federal disaster assistance. Kubelka would welcome some help, but he doesn't know where to begin.

KUBELKA: So, you know, they gave me a list of - here's a bunch of numbers to call. It's like, OK, but what am I supposed to say? Hey, hi, I'm Donald, and I got flooded out of my house, and I don't know the first thing about anything, so...

HASKELL: Pagosa Springs Mayor Shari Price (ph) is trying to get Kubelka and his neighbors some help.

HASKELL: At this public meeting, Price introduces members of Colorado's congressional delegation who are here to see the damage.

SHARI PIERCE: For those who don't know, and Representative Jeff...

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: Jeff (inaudible).

HASKELL: Price (ph) says her town of about 2,000 people is going to need federal help to recover. Some 700 homes here saw flood damage.

PIERCE: I'm hopeful, but it's also critical that we get that funding. We just can't do it without it.

HASKELL: Price (ph) says roads, bridges and utilities are hanging on by a thread. Many homeowners, including Kubelka, don't have flood insurance, and people here are worried about whether federal aid will come. Last October, President Trump initially denied disaster assistance. At the time, Colorado's Democratic governor, Jared Polis, was refusing to release one of Trump's political allies from state prison. Five months later, the governor commuted her sentence, and the aid, more than $90 million, was delivered.

(SOUNDBITE OF HEAVY EQUIPMENT RUMBLING)

HASKELL: Jacob Appenzeller hopes President Trump's beef with Colorado is over now.

JACOB APPENZELLER: I know he's just (ph) not a big fan of our governor, but I hope they can get their differences away and help us out however they can.

HASKELL: Appenzeller, a contractor, and one of his employees are parked on the side of a road, trying to figure out what to do.

APPENZELLER: I just hope we get our funding. I mean, I know Trump likes to kind of sit on his hands a little bit on some funding like that.

HASKELL: The highway is washed out ahead, and they can't get to their construction job site. Colorado's governor has requested Trump fast track a major disaster declaration. A couple of weeks ago, the Federal Highway Administration responded with $6.5 million towards a requested 65 million to repair highways. Overall, the state saw far more extensive damage. This week, state officials are visiting six counties to compile comprehensive damage assessments. They have not said when they expect to have final numbers that they would submit in a federal funding request. For NPR News, I'm Havalin Haskell in Pagosa Springs, Colorado.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Nino Bucci and Jack Larkin
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Royal commission also hears from construction company employee who says workers were ‘fearful’ of union

A major contractor on a troubled Victorian rail project shut down by union officials was warned that the minister’s office felt it would not “have any more work” in the state if it did not resolve the industrial dispute, a royal commission has heard.

The royal commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria heard from a Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority (Vida) official for the first time on Friday.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Vida was strongly criticised by counsel assisting the commission, Chris Young KC, on Thursday for its failure to disclose relevant evidence in a timely manner to the investigation.

The commission’s November public hearings, which are set to run until 20 November, are focusing on a 2022 level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury.

The commission previously heard that Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) officials shut down the site because of purported safety concerns, only for them to allow it to continue after two of their own health and safety representatives were appointed, and the project changed its traffic and labour hire companies to CFMEU-aligned firms.

Peter Wilkinson, a former Vida official who is now the executive general manager of the Suburban Rail Loop authority and a civil engineer, said that at the height of an industrial dispute at Gap Road he spoke about the need for work to resume on the project with Evan Tattersall, his manager at Vida.

He said Tattersall told him on either 6 or 7 June 2022 that he had discussed the issue with the minister’s office, and Wilkinson assumed that meant the office of the then-minister for transport infrastructure, Jacinta Allan.

Tattersall told him, Wilkinson said, “that if they can’t handle the industrial [relations] in Victoria, they can’t have any more work”.

Tattersall was referring to the contractors on the site, John Holland and CPB Constructions, Wilkinson said.

Wilkinson said he was aware at the time that the contractors were tendering for the airport rail, another major state government funded infrastructure project, but that he did not know if the minister’s office also knew this.

Wilkinson said Tattersall did not tell him what he should do with the information from the minister’s office, but he passed it on to Joe Aygur, the general manager of the Rail Network Alliance involved in the project’s delivery.

Aygur told the commission about the warning on Tuesday.

When asked by Young why no record of his conversation with Tattersall existed, Wilkinson said “probably one reason is that it was moving very quickly, so it was conversation that we had to keep it moving, rather than there being a need to formally record it.”

The commission also heard on Friday from Stephen Villella, who worked for CPD Constructions and was the delivery director at the site, about the meeting at the union headquarters that ultimately ended the dispute.

He said it had been “extremely galling” for construction company officials to have to “bend the knee” by meeting with the CFMEU to resolve the matter.

Villella said none of the safety concerns raised by the union were serious enough to force work to stop at the site.

Workers on the project were fearful of the CMFEU and would stay in the lunchroom for long periods once they started to attend.

“They didn’t want to come [to work] at all,” Villella said.

“They were fearful of what would happen to them organisationally and individually if they did.”

Villella said he disagreed with evidence given early in the week by a former CMFEU organiser Paul Tzimas about those on site choosing not to work, saying they were heavily pressured by union officials.

Villella said that in the meeting with the CFMEU, a union organiser Joe Myles suggested collaborating would assist in winning future tenders such as the Melbourne airport rail project.

He said Myles also suggested he had direct lines to Allan’s office.

Villella said he was not surprised by Myles’ claim about having communication to the ministers office, as he had seen what had happened to the industry over the past 10 years.

Villella said Myles left abruptly in the first half of the about 30 minute meeting, which he said felt like a snub.

But he rejected a suggestion by counsel for Myles that it was not the union official, but rather Tzimas, who raised the list of union demands for the Gap Road project.

After construction managers agreed to the demands, work on the site resumed as normal.

“Amazingly, all our safety issues ceased,” Villella said.

The hearing before commissioner Christopher Kourakis continues.

But the prosecutor responded: “No one’s saying it was a good plan, that’s why you’re sitting here.”

The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Sat in the witness box for the seventh day, Lamarre-Condon was asked about driving his mother to pick up a hire car under her name on the evening before the alleged murders.

As part of his cross-examination, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC repeatedly suggested to Lamarre-Condon that he was planning to murder Baird.

But the accused told the New South Wales supreme court on Friday “it was never a plan to murder anybody”.

“You wouldn’t bring a vehicle linked to your mum for a murder,” Lamarre-Condon told the jury.

“If I wanted to a plan a murder I would have two stolen vehicles ready to go, I would have a gun that’s not linked to me. I know exactly how to do it, I work with youth gangs.”

Hatfield told Lamarre-Condon: “No one’s saying it was a good plan that’s why you’re sitting here, isn’t it?”

The former officer maintained he and his mother spoke in the car about his suicidal ideation and he had turned off his phone because he did not want to talk about work or personal things in the vicinity of the device.

Earlier on Friday, Lamarre-Condon was asked about purchasing a sim card under the name “Bob Ballard” on 15 January 2024, about a month before the shootings.

He told the jury in his double murder trial it had “nothing to do with Jesse Baird”.

He was attempting to compile statements about “bullying from a certain sergeant” but was worried about speaking publicly on the issue, Lamarre-Condon said.

“I was wanting to go and compile all these statements and go to the media,” he said.

“I didn’t want to communicate at all from my phone because you can become a target … there would be repercussions.”

Under cross-examination by Hatfield, Lamarre-Condon agreed he was using the new sim card to contact former and current officers.

But asked why his phone records showed he only contacted one police officer on this sim, Lamarre-Condon said it only revealed his normal phone calls, telling the court: “You can’t see what I did on Signal.”

The prosecutor said he could have used encrypted messaging app Signal on his normal phone, but Lamarre-Condon claimed police could make him unlock his own device and view his Signal records if he was investigated for talking to the media.

Hatfield also questioned why Lamarre-Condon had Davies’s contact details on his phone.

The former officer claimed Davies’s details were on his Instagram.

“I went and blocked numerous Instagram [accounts] from my own Instagram because of this incident,” he said, referring to the shootings.

“I even blocked Jesse’s family members from my account. I didn’t want any of that.”

He deactivated his social media accounts soon after.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
William, 17, says ‘nights were pretty cold’ and he ‘honestly didn’t think’ he’d survive

A teenage boy who survived almost a week lost in dense Australian bushland sang John Denver’s Take Me Home, Country Roads as he held out hope of rescue on long nights alone in the wilderness.

William, whose surname has been withheld, was dropped off by his mother for the weekend to camp with his friend in Victoria’s east last Friday.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The 17-year-old was reported missing at about 4pm that day after failing to return from a trip to retrieve further camping equipment. He was wearing only shorts and work boots and had left his phone, food supplies and water behind.

After an extensive operation of more than 100 people, including the police dog and rescue squads, the police air wing found William on Thursday morning lying down in a creek near Walhalla, 130km east of Melbourne.

He lost his way after taking a wrong turn on a track, and later slipped and fell down a cliff.

He told Seven’s Sunrise program John Denver’s country classic, which repeats the line “take me home, to the place I belong”, was a childhood favourite of his that brought him solace as he braved harsh conditions and loneliness.

“It’s a good childhood song of mine. It brings me great comfort,” he said from his hospital bed in Traralgon on Friday morning. “I started doing it one night, made me feel OK, so I just kept doing it.”

William shared an emotional reunion with his mother, Elizabeth Barkley, soon after being rescued. She told reporters on Thursday between tears that she was “over the moon” and he was “never leaving the house again”.

William told Sunrise their warm embrace was the “best moment of my life”.

“I think she’s going to stand true with that comment,” he said with a laugh. “She’s giving me a firm look from across the room at the moment, so not expecting to go out any time soon.”

William said he was “doing great” after enjoying a “great sleep” in a “comfy bed” on Thursday night and “finally getting some food into me”.

“I’m over the moon to be safe,” he said. “The nights were pretty cold. I think a couple of times it was raining. Hot days, so I got a bit sunburnt, pretty treacherous surroundings.

“I honestly didn’t think I’d make it six days.”

After seeing the helicopter flying overhead, William, who was sheltering on a rock under towels and heavily sunburnt, gave a wave and fist-bump before being airlifted to safety. He said he was feeling “pure euphoria”.

“Just happiness and gratefulness that a moment that I thought might never happen, has happened, and I am finally going to see my mum again,” he said.

“There were a few times were I’m thinking ‘geez, it’s getting dark out here, I don’t know if they’re going to see me’.”

William got by on a packet of chicken-flavoured chips, which he rationed over several days. He said he also drank water from the creek that he was sheltering by.

“Last night I had dinner … and I had some Macca’s, which was good, so I got plenty of food in,” he said. “I’m super grateful for all the paramedics and nurses, search and rescue … everyone that was involved.”

Pilot Dave Wylie told reporters it had been an incredibly challenging search for crews and it was lucky William was sheltering in an open area.

“A lot of the areas are so thick that you can’t actually see the forest floor so even if someone was there, potentially you could fly right past them,” he said.

“If he wasn’t in the open area like he was, we absolutely could have flown right past him without seeing him.”

William was being transported to the Alfred hospital in Melbourne for further observation and testing by specialists, after suffering from dehydration. He was in a stable condition on Friday afternoon.

Barkley told Nine’s A Current Affair she was in awe as to how well her son had handled days alone in the bush.

“I just couldn’t believe he survived that long,” she said. “But he’s a footballer. He’s tough, he’s very, very fit.

“His agility is incredible.”

Barkley said William had missed a turn on a track and became lost on Friday and curled up under some bushes when it got dark.

“I had instinct … I knew he was still alive,” she said of the following days. “I knew in my heart … And I was just praying, and praying, and praying.”

He lost his way after taking a wrong turn on a track and later slipped and fell down a cliff

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Hidden bunker, entered via a hatch in a field, controlled a gun battery used to attack German ships in Channel

It has been kept secret for decades, buried four metres deep into the white cliffs of Dover. But from Friday, members of the public will finally be able to visit a pioneering command bunker that was ordered by Winston Churchill and proved a vital defence during the second world war.

The Fan Bay plotting room, which is encased in concrete, housed the first land-based computer-aided targeting system. This acted as a “brain” for a gun battery that was used to defend Dover and attack German ships in the Channel, according to Jon Stewart, who led the excavation project for the National Trust.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Stewart was the first person to enter the bunker when it was rediscovered in 2017 after it had been secretly mothballed in 1957 and classified until 1981 owing to its military importance.

“It was a Tutankhamun moment for a conflict archaeologist,” he said. “We had done all this research on the people who had served there, and then suddenly you’re standing in their office. It was an exciting moment.”

The plotting room and the artillery it controlled can be directly traced to Churchill. Soon after his “fight them on the beaches” speech, he visited the Kent coast and was alarmed to observe enemy ships passing through the strait of Dover unchallenged.

At the same time, Dover was on the frontline of a Britain facing regular bombardment by enemy guns in occupied France.

In a July 1940 memo Churchill wrote: “We have to fight for command of the straits by artillery, to destroy the enemy batteries and fortify our own.”

He ordered the most advanced technology to be used and demanded weekly updates on progress on Dover’s new defences. The guns were ready within 100 days and the plotting room bunker was completed 64 days later.

“The guns were known around here as Churchill’s pets,” Stewart said.

Physical traces of the urgency of the construction were still visible at the site, said Stewart. He pointed to the rough openings through the walls and floors for the cabling. Contemporary accounts describe how the equipment was installed before drawings governing its layout were available.

The plotting room housed a 1.8-metre-long electromechanical computer known as a fire direction table. It was used to calculate the position of moving ships when shells hit and to send firing instructions to gun crews.

Stewart said the discovery of the plotting room reminded him of the rescue of Bletchley Park, the codebreaking site in Buckinghamshire, in the 1990s. “We didn’t know about it then, but now it’s all part of our national consciousness,” he said. “The plotting room is a new hidden history.”

He added: “We tend to think of plotting tables as glamorous Wrens [members of the Women’s Royal Naval Service] pushing around markers on a map as they do in war films. But it’s not a map – it’s a really cutting edge electromechanical computer, and it is completely unique.”

after newsletter promotion

The computer was deliberately destroyed in 1957 to stop it falling into enemy hands.

Up to 10 people at a time worked in the plotting room. Stewart is keen to make contact with anyone who had family members who served there, to help him understand how the machine worked.

“What we know about it is based on a manual and ghost markings on the floor. I would really love to hear if anybody knows if their family members served at Fan Bay because the records are scant.”

The identities of only a handful of people who operated the computer are known. They include Wallas Eaton, an actor who later appeared as Senator Ludicrus Sextus in the TV comedy series Up Pompeii, alongside Frankie Howerd.

A man named WP Bryant, a lance bombardier, was also recorded as a plotter at Fan Bay. “He was a tailor so he probably had a head for numbers,” said Stewart.

The plotting room, which from Friday can be visited via National Trust guided tours through a hatch in a field, has been preserved as Stewart and his team found it. Remnants include old newspapers found on the floor, old shoes and official notices. There is also chalked graffiti on one of the service tunnels saying “heroes fan hole Dodds and Petitt”. Stewart said Dodds and Petitt may have been involved in installing cables to the bunker.

“They were probably self-appointed heroes responsible for marshalling horrible thick cable through particularly uncomfortable tunnels,” he said.

“There’s something very special about standing in a place that has changed so little since the people who worked here left. Rather than recreate the past, we’ve carefully conserved the plotting room so visitors can experience it much as we found it, with all the marks of its history still visible. It’s a rare opportunity to discover a completely different side of the white cliffs.”

Allegations of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour made against ex-comedian who was jailed on Monday

Russell Brand has been accused of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by a further six women, according to a report.

The comedian, 51, is accused of having sex with a woman without her consent and then apologising afterwards, an investigation by the Times and the Sunday Times said.

The newspapers also alleged the comedian continued having sex with another woman after she asked him to stop because he was hurting her.

Brand, 51, was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after being convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault at Southwark crown court in London.

On one occasion, she said they were in bed together when he moved to initiate sex. Having noticed he was not wearing a condom, she said she asked him to stop.

The woman added she decided at that moment that “I’m not going to fight” because “who knows what he could do”.

After the alleged incident, she said Brand apologised to her in person and by text message. “I justified it in my head by saying to myself: at least he admitted it.”

Another woman who encountered Brand when she was queueing to meet him with a friend in 2007 aged 19 said she told him during sex: “It’s painful”, according to the report.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang expected to testify before Congress amid calls for crackdown on China chip exports – live
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.text:
US House Speaker Mike Johnson has said ⁠there is a ​growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US ⁠authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government. The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.

In the last week, representatives from both sides of the aisle have called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips; chips that could underpin China’s surging AI development.

Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are ⁠widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US ​has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips ‌because it wants its own companies to stay ahead in the race.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told ‌reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“

Congressional Republicans are keen to attach ​new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defense authorisation bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity.

As questions abound about Megaspeed, Singaporean authorities said in a statement on Thursday that Alice Huang, the Chinese woman at the centre of the global spy drama had been barred form re-entering the city state after a 2025 investigation into the company.

The ministry of home affairs said it had held Alice Huang’s passport from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” related to Megaspeed, which is registered in the country.

Eventually she was released with a stern warning, but she has been barred from re-entering the country.

Huang was being investigated in Singapore as part of a larger probe into several companies, including Megaspeed.

Singapore police said last October they were investigating Megaspeed over “suspected breaches of our domestic laws” after a US senator requested the commerce department investigate whether the firm had diverted Nvidia chips.

In Taiwan, the interior minister told lawmakers on Wednesday that Alice Huang was also now barred from entering the territory.

From a lottery retailer in rural Australia to a dilapidated storefront in Kuala Lumpur, and an unexpectedly quiet office in Singapore, as the Nvidia scandal has unfolded more information has emerged about the activities of cloud computing firm Megaspeed, and its former director Alice Huang.

On its website, ​Megaspeed, which is registered in Singapore, describes itself as a Nvidia cloud partner in the Asia-Pacific region.

In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware.

But questions have been raised about the seeming incongruity between its corporate presence and business activities.

Singaporean news outlets, The Straits Times reported that Swiftdata, which owns Megaspeed, has a registered business address that an interior design firm says it has occupied for over four years.

When the New York Times visited Megaspeed’s Singapore headquarters last year, located in the central business district, only two employees were present.

In Malaysia, one of Megaspeed’s offices was reportedly a dilapidated store front in Kuala Lumpur. Another was located in a shopping mall, the Times reported. When one employee emerged in the mall, she was asked what the company did. “It’s not clear,” she responded.

Meanwhile in Australia, Reuters tracked corporate filings of Megaspeed affiliates that led it to a man in his twenties born in Shanghai.

The individual is also registered as director of Megaspeed’s Malaysian, Indonesian and Thai units, according to Reuters.

Unable to contact him, Reuters tracked his home address to a small newsagent and lottery retailer in a regional town outside Melbourne where they found a woman ​who said she was his mother.

The woman said she had run the business for about 16 years, that her son was based in Shanghai and had nothing to do with the Singaporean company.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to support our crucial year-end fundraiser. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

Some US lawmakers are pushing for a swathe of new legislation that would affect the export of AI chips from America.

The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports.

The Chip Security Act would require companies ⁠to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.

The Match Act would pressure US ​allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced ​chipmaking equipment destined for China.

The Remote Access Security ​Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers to access ​Nvidia chips.

US representatives from both sides of the aisle have been questioning Donald Trump’s decision to grant Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales.

Trump’s close ties with billionaire Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny after revelations about the former Nvidia CEO’s affairs, including with a businesswoman alleged to be a spy ⁠for China.

Over the past two years, Huang has voiced support for the Trump administration’s AI agenda and met the Republican leader many times, lobbying for ⁠looser restrictions on Chinese access to Nvidia’s sophisticated AI ​chips. Huang and the White House have argued that continuing US sales to China would keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology.

Democratic and Republican lawmakers are now calling for a halt to exports of advanced AI chips to China.

Stocks in Asia rose slightly on Friday after a turbulent week dominated by the revelations of Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs that culminated in the Nvidia CEO’s resignation.

His exit has plunged the chipmaker into crisis ⁠and sent shock waves through the AI industry.

But a commonly used index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 0.26% on Friday, reversing some of its 1.3% fall from the previous session. South Korea’s Kospi rose 2.35% while Japan’s Nikkei added 1.4%.

Nvidia shares fell 3% in after-hours trading, while those of its customers, including South Korea’s Naver, extended ‌declines on Friday, with Naver down 2.75%.

“[Huang’s] departure leaves a ⁠vacuum that will be difficult to fill … We do not assume existing commitments change, but new deals could take longer or require more compensation as investors look for reassurance about Nvidia’s role,” analysts at ​JP Morgan said in a note.

The bigger implications are for the rest of the ‌AI trade, particularly GPU financing and infrastructure deals in ‌which Nvidia would presumably be involved as a supplier, investor or provider of contractual support.”

Jon Zauderer, Citi’s head of specialist sales and a TMT specialist, said competitors such as AMD, Arista and Broadcom could benefit from the Nvidia fallout.

If you think about the uncertainty that’s created about a potential management change, investors are going to look for alternatives.”

Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world?

Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run.

This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading.

But what makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself.

One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments.

The US Senate banking committee Chair – Republican Tim Scott – has ⁠sent letters to Donald Trump’s commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, along with Jensen Huang, asking them to testify.

A growing number of US lawmakers have criticised Lutnick, asking whether the ​government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports ‌to China.

“Recent reports raise serious ‌concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology,” Scott wrote on ‌X. “I am requesting that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee.”

Scott said he would consider subpoenaing Huang if he does not voluntarily appear. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott said.

Senior Democrats have said Congress must demand answers from Jensen Huang and Nvidia, after the CEO resigned on Thursday.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer has said Huang and Nvidia must answer whether US national security has been put at risk, adding that the Trump administration also must answer for what it did once it learned about Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Among the questions that need to be answered is what the president knew when he personally invited Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, Schumer said in his social media post on X.

Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has said he is demanding a classified briefing for all members of Congress about the Nvidia situation.

Jeffries said to the extent that national security may have been compromised, Americans deserve answers, adding that Huang’s resignation was the “right thing” to do.

Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has been named as interim CEO while the board searches for a successor.

Her ascension marks the end of Jensen Huang’s 33 years at the helm of the company he co-founded.

Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years at companies including Cisco and Microsoft. She is a regular contributor to the company’s quarterly earnings calls, and has overseen Nvidia’s rise from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar AI juggernaut.

“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey C Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia’s board of directors, said in a statement on Thursday. “The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team.”

Kress wrote that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”. She will serve as both the CEO and interim CFO until the board names a permanent successor.

Donald Trump called Jensen Huang two days before he stepped down as CEO of Nvidia and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Time has reported.

The president’s close ties with the Huang have come under renewed scrutiny after revelations about the former Nvidia chief’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy were revealed.

Over the past two years, Huang has voiced support for the Trump administration’s AI agenda and met the Republican leader many times as Nvidia sought to sell advanced chips to the Chinese market and ⁠lobbied for looser restrictions on Chinese access to ⁠Nvidia’s sophisticated AI chips.

On Thursday the president sat down for a lengthy podcast interview with the sports pundit Stephen A Smith where he expressed sympathy for Huang.

Trump defended Huang, who sat at his table at a White House state dinner for China’s president, Xi Jinping in September, as “a tremendous talent”.

“I can tell you this, somehow he’ll end up in his feet,” Trump added. “I mean, I know him; I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man.”

“I spoke to him yesterday,” the president continued. “He’s he’s going through hell.”

Flowers were placed outside Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California on Thursday afternoon; an apparent tribute to former EO Jensen Huang.

The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO after the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resigned amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs, including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees.

Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role.

Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker.

Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosystem relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn.

The board said it was starting a search for Huang’s permanent replacement and is considering internal and external candidates.

Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings, is also well-known at Nvidia, having worked there for seven years as a vice-president and general manager before joining Arm in 2013. Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, is also being named as a possible replacement for Huang. Her company is Nvidia’s most direct and fierce competitor; she’s also a distant cousin to Huang.

Donald Trump has reacted to the resignation of Huang by saying Huang “has done a fantastic job,” and adding, “There is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple.”

“A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump wrote on his social media site of Cook, who is Apple’s former CEO.

Donald Trump has reiterated that it is not yet ‌determined whether Alice Huang ‌was a spy.

In an interview released late on Thursday, the President was asked whether Jensen Huang should have resigned.

The big thing is, was the woman a spy? ‌And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet. But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.”

On Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, Lori, without naming anyone involved.

Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years.

Earlier on Thursday US attorney general Todd Blanche said that the Justice Department has not yet reached a conclusion ⁠on whether Alice ⁠Huang was a Chinese spy.

Blanche said at a ⁠press conference that “of course” the FBI was investigating reports that Alice Huang was working for the Chinese government.

Beijing has ⁠denied Alice Huang is a spy and Huang herself has not spoken publicly.

US House Speaker Mike Johnson has said ⁠there is a ​growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US ⁠authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government. The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.

In the last week, representatives from both sides of the aisle have called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips; chips that could underpin China’s surging AI development.

Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are ⁠widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US ​has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips ‌because it wants its own companies to stay ahead in the race.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told ‌reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“

Congressional Republicans are keen to attach ​new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defense authorisation bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity.

Jensen Huang is expected to testify before the US Congress in the next fortnight, after the Nvidia CEO stepped down from the multi-trillion dollar company on Thursday, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shock waves across the global AI industry.

House foreign affairs chair Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Huang’s testimony.

Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them behind closed doors about his relationship with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years.

It has been reported that Jensen Huang also had an intimate relationship with two Nvidia employees, which added to the pressure on Huang, with the company’s board calling a meeting late on Wednesday to discuss the chief executive’s future.

Huang’s exit could have far-reaching consequences ⁠for US chip export policy and the broader AI ecosystem, ​given the ex-CEO’s push to preserve access to the Chinese market as well as his close ties with US president Donald Trump.

Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee, bookending a stunning fall from grace of one of the leading figures of the AI boom. He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a successor is named.

Shares in the chipmaker plunged by 14% when Wall Street opened, after Huang’s departure was announced and ricocheted through the global economy, before recovering to finish more than 4% lower as uncertainty about Nvidia’s future leadership troubled investors eased somewhat.

US House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was ​growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after the scandal. On Thursday came reports that the ousted former CEO had an intimate relationship with a second employee. The revelation, reported by Reuters, follows allegations of two other extramarital ⁠affairs that led to Jensen Huang’s dramatic resignation – one with Alice Huang, ​an alleged Chinese spy, and another with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of health care. Powell has been approached for comment. On Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, Lori, without naming anyone involved.

A statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded. “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said. It added that Huang had resigned as chief executive, president and Nvidia board member “effective immediately”.

Donald Trump, who had defended Huang at first as the scandal threatened to overwhelm Nvidia co-founder, quickly moved on to potential successors on Thursday, posting on social media that he should be replaced by Tim Cook, Apple’s former chief executive and current executive chair. “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote, adding: “A Legend replaces a Legend!” Nvidia’s board directors said it would consider internal and external candidates for the chief executive role, with Cook featuring among potential runners and riders before Trump’s intervention. Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Chief financial officer, reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting, to take over on short-term basis

The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO. It comes after a whirlwind week, which saw the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resign amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs, including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees.

Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role. Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, is known as an ambitious and visionary CEO who had a hand in most all aspects of the business. He led in an unusual management style, having about 60 direct reports, giving him more control over the company’s daily functions. His son and daughter also work at Nvidia, with his daughter seen as his possible proxy, but neither appear to have sufficient experience to take the helm.

Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013 as the CFO after working in finance roles at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco. She’s a regular contributor to the company’s quarterly earnings calls, and has overseen Nvidia go from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar AI juggernaut. People who know her describe Kress as a calming contrast to Huang’s often confrontational style, Reuters reported.

“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey C Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia’s board of directors, said in a statement on Thursday. “The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team.”

But that sentiment may not be shared by Huang. During a meeting this past summer, the CEO said Kress was “a deer in the headlights” and interrupted her presentation, a person familiar with the comments told the Wall Street Journal. Huang insinuated during that August meeting that Kress was not someone who could help him make decisions.

However, Kress praised Huang in a memo to employees on Thursday, saying she would continue “building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”.

Many investors, analysts and industry sources who spoke to Reuters questioned whether a finance executive could preserve the technological risk-taking that turned Nvidia into an AI chips powerhouse.

“Putting [Kress] in the interim role makes sense to keep the markets calm, but I don’t think she is the long-term visionary that Nvidia needs to continue its current trajectory,” said Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights and Strategy.

Kress, who said in her memo that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” , will serve as both the CEO and interim CFO until the board names a permanent successor.

The board said it was starting a search for Huang’s permanent replacement and is considering internal and external candidates. Along with Kress, Buck is seen as a possible successor. He has worked at Nvidia since 2004 and in charge of deploying generative AI in partnership with the world’s top AI companies, including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, OpenAI and more.

Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings, is also well-known at Nvidia, having worked there for seven years as a vice president and general manager before joining Arm in 2013. Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, is also being named as a possible replacement for Huang. Her company is Nvidia’s most direct and fierce competitor; she’s also a distant cousin to Huang.

Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Kress could face congressional questions about the company’s oversight of chip sales involving Chinese military-linked institutions and south-east Asian intermediaries.

In a 2023 interview with an Israeli publication, Kress credited her two young sons with urging her to join Nvidia in 2013 because they knew its chips from their video games.

She became a billionaire in 2025 based on the value of her Nvidia equity, according to media reports, and Forbes said her net worth of $1.2 billion in mid-2026 put her in 32nd place on its list of America’s richest self-made women.

Kress, who holds an undergraduate degree in finance and an MBA, was also named among the 50 most powerful women in business on rankings compiled by Fortune and Forbes magazines in recent years.

Nvidia’s CEO turmoil comes as the company is set to report its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday.

Reuters contributed reporting

Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, was reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting. Kress is the company's chief financial officers, and could stay on permanently.

Schumer has been talking to Democratic senators since the election about forming an agenda for 2027.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ann Lawani was taken from her home, sparking a huge outcry among students and faculty at her university

Nearly two months after ICE agents whisked a beloved California nurse and professor from her home in Lodi, her university has ramped up calls for her release.

“She needs to come home,” said Eileen Fry-Bowers, dean for the University of San Francisco’s nursing school,in reference to Ann Lawani, who was arrested by immigration agents in September and has since been shuffled between detention centers in California, Texas, and Louisiana, in a series of opaque transfers.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Lawani, 39, came to the US in 2007. She established herself as a nursing professional, obtaining a master’s and doctoral degree in the field, before stepping into academia.

She steers two programs at the University of San Francisco, one a master’s entry program geared toward students with non-nursing backgrounds and another a bachelor’s program for students seeking to work in public health safety-net institutions.

“She basically has her hands on almost 300 students that she engages with on a regular basis,” Fry-Bowers said.

Lawani’s detention has sparked outcry from local lawmakers, who have advocated on her behalf to ICE authorities, as well as her students and colleagues, who say her absence is deeply felt on campus.

One of those students, Casey Murray, a nursing science graduate student, described Lawani as a warm educator who could recall the first and last names of pupils she had not seen since orientation.

“We have 37 days left until we graduate,” Murray said. “She has supported us to the fullest extent up until the point that she was kidnapped. We want her at our graduation, and we want her home with her family.”

Federal immigration officials say Lawani entered the US on a visitor’s visa in 2007, which she overstayed. She was issued a final order of removal in August 2013, according to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson.

Natalia Santanna, Lawani’s lawyer, confirmed the removal order, but noted that DHS’s account was “incomplete”.

“Dr Lawani applied for asylum within one year of being in the United States. And, in the same 2013 order, the immigration judge found that Ann would more likely than not face persecution in Nigeria and granted withholding of removal,” Santanna said. “That is not a temporary stay. It is a continuing bar to removal to Nigeria. Dr Lawani has lived in the United States pursuant to that grant of withholding of removal since 2013.”

Santanna said they have filed a habeas petition to challenge the legality of her detainment, which remains pending in California’s eastern district court.

Meanwhile, Lawani’s students and colleagues are continuing to mobilize around her.

Lawani sent Fry-Bowers a text about being in ICE’s custody, shortly after her arrest. Fry-Bowers, who was on vacation, heard from another dean that Lawani had been absent from a meeting, which she described as out of character.

After the school heard from Lawani’s family, they jumped into action, aiding with legal representation and registering their alarm with the area’s congressional delegation.

In late October, Josh Harder, a congressman, who represents Lawani’s district, expressed his concerns about her case to DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin, among them the lack of notice before her arrest and her various whereabouts not being reflected in an online detainee database.

“Given her longstanding compliance, lack of criminal history, and substantial community ties, there is no apparent public safety justification for keeping her detained thousands of miles from home while her case proceeds,” Harder wrote then in a letter.

Fry-Bowers praised Lawani, citing her work with patients in hospice and palliative care.

“She cares for the most vulnerable, helps them maintain their dignity and comfort as they prepare for death,” she said. “She is a consummate professional. The highest praise I could ever give a nursing colleague is that I would want them taking care of my family member or myself, and she would be at the top of the list.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Family Dollar to pay $63m to settle overcharging allegations
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Hudson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Dollar-store chain’s settlement with FTC and state officials comes after Guardian exposé of its pricing practices

Discount store giant Family Dollar will pay $63m to settle claims by state and federal authorities that it frequently overcharged its customers for milk, diapers, batteries, toilet paper and other household goods.

The enforcement action announced Thursday by the Federal Trade Commission and 17 states followed a Guardian investigation that revealed Family Dollar and its larger rival, Dollar General, frequently charge more at checkout than the prices listed on their shelves. Family Dollar failed at least 2,100 price inspections in 20 states from 2022 to late 2025, the Guardian found.

In a lawsuit publicly released for the first time as part of Thursday’s settlement, the FTC and the states allege that “Family Dollar knows that it harms consumers by persistently charging prices at the register that are higher than those it advertises”.

Despite widespread consumer complaints and increasing government scrutiny, the suit says, the dollar-store chain has failed to put in place adequate safeguards to prevent continued overcharging.

“Even now,” the suit asserts, “Family Dollar continues to overcharge customers.”

The suit says that it was not until the fall of 2025 – after the company learned of the coming publication of the Guardian’s investigation – that “employees at Family Dollar’s corporate offices devoted more attention and resources to addressing state pricing inspections”.

Family Dollar, which says it offers “affordable products and trusted values to families across America”, has roughly 7,000 stores.

The company did not deny or admit to the state and federal authorities’ allegations. It previously told the Guardian that “we take customer trust seriously and are committed to ensuring pricing accuracy across our stores … We continue to be focused on providing a consistent and transparent shopping experience.”

The Guardian has sent questions to Family Dollar about the settlement and lawsuit.

The FTC made undercover visits to Family Dollar and Dollar General stores after the December 2025 publication of the Guardian’s story about the two chains. In January, the agency said, an FTC investigator was overcharged on 15 of the 50 items she purchased at a Family Dollar in Euclid, Ohio.

The agency also sifted through large numbers of customer complaints to the company itself as well as to the FTC, state regulators and consumer groups.

The lawsuits says that customers from at least seven states reported in January 2025 that Family Dollar refused to honor a “2 for $20” offer for diapers advertised on shelf tags, its weekly flyer and its mobile app. A consumer in Michigan, for example, said they took a photo of the discount price displayed on the shelf for diapers but that the manager “told me that the price was wrong and he would not sell to me at that price”.

A customer in South Dakota, meanwhile, complained they had been charged $25.50 for three packs of Dr Pepper that were listed as “3 for $12”. When they complained, the consumer said, an employee “freaked out on me” and screamed “in front of 20 people” – saying the higher price was correct and the customer was no longer welcome at the store.

Under the settlement, Family Dollar will be required to set up a $40m consumer redress fund, provide $20m in discounts to customers and pay more than $3m to state authorities. It also must create a program to ensure that it regularly monitors and verifies prices, trains employees to identify pricing problems and promptly corrects overcharges.

The settlement comes at a time of growing attention on overcharges at dollar store and convenience store chains. The Family Dollar lawsuit says the consequences of overcharges “fall most heavily on shoppers living on razor-thin margins – families who carefully budget every dollar and rely on accurate, transparent pricing simply to meet their day-to-day needs”.

In October, the FTC and 20 states sued Dollar General, the largest dollar-store chain, accusing it of a “staggering” level of “pricing misconduct”.

In response, Dollar General said it would “defend this litigation vigorously”. It added that, in the retail market, “occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered and expected to make things right for the customer.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump says no deal needed on Iran war and orders Vance to focus on domestic issues
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Andrew Roth in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
President says vice-president will focus on supposed ‘Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States’

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump has said that the US is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered JD Vance, who had spearheaded recent efforts to restart negotiations with Iran, to focus on domestic politics instead.

In a post to his social media site on Thursday, Trump said he was redirecting the vice-president to focus his “complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S”.

Vance had reportedly been talking to intermediaries in Iran and Qatar about restarting negotiations to end the war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran. Iran responded by closing access to the strait of Hormuz, which led to a steep increase for the cost of fuel around the globe.

But on Thursday Trump appeared to shut down the negotiations, redirecting Vance to focus on domestic issues and downplaying the need for a final deal.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

The announcement effectively normalises a stalemate with Iran. The US has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports and mostly reopened the strait of Hormuz to marine traffic, including crude oil shipments. But the US has not carried out massive strikes against Iran for several months, and Iran has not launched barrages of ballistic missiles against US bases and allies in the region.

Trump last week also downplayed the possibility of new strikes on Iran and said that the war was “effectively over”.

During a White House press conference, Trump said that Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran, and that an escalation was not needed.

“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House, which took place shortly after he met with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

Trump said he had been lobbied by the leaders of Gulf states not to resume the war.

The decision effectively sidelines Vance from the main foreign policy challenge of his vice-presidency. He had publicly distanced himself from the war, and in April he led a US delegation to Islamabad to negotiate an end to it. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff have also been involved in negotiations.

Axios last week reported that Vance was speaking “almost daily” with Sheikh Mohammed; Pakistan’s army head, Asim Munir; and other mediators. Several weeks ago he also sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, to resume direct negotiations.

Vance last week blamed the conflict for the historic rout dealt to Republicans in the midterm elections.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said after the midterms in a lengthy post on X. “The president himself said so last night.”

Trump has since doubled down on launching the war on Iran, admitting that it drove up fuel prices but repeating his frequent assertion that it was needed to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
