https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Cubs star Crow-Armstrong hits 45 homers and steals 41

Astros slugger Alvarez wins AL honor after .316 season

Both players earn first MVP awards in unanimous votes

Pete Crow-Armstrong was unanimously named the National League’s Most Valuable Player on Thursday after the Chicago Cubs center fielder produced a spectacular all-around season.

Crow-Armstrong joined Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez as a first-time MVP winner. Alvarez was the unanimous American League winner after making a run at the Triple Crown, batting a career-high .316 with 42 home runs and 106 RBIs for the AL West champions.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Crow-Armstrong set career highs by batting .280 with 45 homers, 107 RBIs and 41 stolen bases in 162 games. He tied Kyle Schwarber for the major league lead in home runs and led the NL in runs (119), slugging percentage (.570) and OPS (.942).

He was also one of the majors’ premier defensive players. The Southern California native won his second Gold Glove and led the majors with 26 Outs Above Average and 23 Runs Prevented, according to Baseball Savant.

“You spend your whole life in baseball and you just don’t see this happen on a baseball field,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said after Crow-Armstrong homered twice in an 8-4 win over Atlanta on 16 September. “You’re grateful to be a part of it. You’re grateful to see things like this and then you’re grateful that the fans get to see a season like this.”

Alvarez led the majors in batting average and finished tied for second in the AL in homers and second outright in RBIs, trailing Pete Alonso’s 43 homers and 113 RBIs for Baltimore.

Alvarez was Houston’s primary designated hitter, but his offensive brilliance was enough to overcome his limited defensive contributions. The four-time All-Star also led the majors in walks (109), on-base percentage (.432) and slugging percentage (.601).

The 29-year-old Alvarez became the first AL MVP from Houston since José Altuve in 2017. He received all 30 first-place votes in balloting by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America. Tampa Bay third baseman Junior Caminero, who batted .276 with 42 homers and 101 RBIs, finished second, receiving 27 of 30 second-place votes. Kansas City shortstop Bobby Witt Jr finished third.

Alvarez made his major league debut with Houston in 2019, batting .313 with 27 homers and 78 RBIs in just 87 games to earn the AL Rookie of the Year award.

He was the ALCS MVP in 2021 and helped the Astros win the 2022 World Series. He is a career .300 hitter with 212 homers and 599 RBIs in eight major league seasons.

The 24-year-old Crow-Armstrong, who agreed to a six-year, $115m contract in March, is the Cubs’ first NL MVP since Kris Bryant in 2016.

Crow-Armstrong was selected by the New York Mets in the first round of the 2020 amateur draft before being traded to Chicago in the Javier Báez deal in July 2021.

He enjoyed a breakout season in 2025, helping the Cubs qualify for the playoffs for the first time since 2020. He batted .247 with 31 homers, 95 RBIs and 35 stolen bases in 157 games.

Crow-Armstrong made significant strides at the plate in his fourth season, particularly against left-handed pitching. He batted .280 against left-handers in 2026 after hitting just .188 against them the previous year.

“I would say, like, what contributed to making myself a consistent quality at-bat and all that stuff is just, like, getting to know the strike zone just that much better,” Crow-Armstrong said before the playoffs. “I definitely missed less pitches in the zone, in the heart of the zone, that I should be hitting this year.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘Start listening’: Indigenous activist implores Albanese to block new coal, oil and gas
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Graham Readfearn in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Comments came as Indigenous activist Rikki Dank urged the Australian PM to heed the calls for action on climate change

An Indigenous climate activist who is taking the Australian government to the UN human rights committee over its coal and gas exports stood alongside Greta Thunberg at the Cop summit to demand Anthony Albanese “stop speaking and start listening.”

Draped in traditional dress in front of a media throng, Rikki Dank, a Gudanji and Wakaya traditional owner, delivered an impassioned plea to Albanese to listen to “the Australian people when they say no more new coal, oil and gas”.

Albanese on Thursday defended his major speech at the opening of Cop31 after facing criticism for omitting the phrase “fossil fuels”.

Australia is the president of the two-week negotiations at Cop31 being held in Antalya, Turkey. A key push from the two hosts is to garner support for a “35 by 35” pledge for 35% of end-use energy to be from electricity by the year 2035.

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, and several countries are pushing the two hosts to also progress a proposal from last year’s Cop president, Brazil, to have countries develop roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels.

Squeezed into a corner of the vast Cop31 media centre, Thunberg was flanked by Dank and other climate advocates, including a Nepalese MP who had helped rescue people from a landslide that followed an August glacier collapse that killed more than 1,500 people.

Thunberg said: “It is more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying, it is being killed.

“And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue.”

Asked whether she agreed with comments about Australia’s slow record on climate action, Thunberg told the crowd: “Even a snail would agree with that.

“It’s common sense. It doesn’t get more clear than that.”

When asked for his reaction to Thunberg’s comments, Albanese sought to highlight Australia’s climate credentials instead.

“Well, I haven’t seen it, but she’s entitled to her views,'” the prime minister said.

“What we are doing is putting forward practical plans to achieve a considerable decrease.”

Dank is one of 10 Australians behind a complaint before the UN human rights committee – known as the Hard Truths case – that claims the Australian government has failed to protect them from climate pollution, including from its vast exports of coal and LNG that are among the highest in the world.

Lawyers behind the case are hoping for a resolution in the next 18 months. While a committee declaration is not legally binding, a negative finding would be a major embarrassment and would carry significant political weight.

“My Country is being fracked, our drinking water poisoned and our history erased as we speak,” Dank said.

She said the prime minister “needs to stop speaking and start listening to our brothers and sisters across the world when they say they don’t want us to export coal, oil or gas and the climate harms that they bring with them”.

Albanese had a series of bi-lateral meetings on the sidelines of Cop31 on Thursday with Bangladesh, Lebanon, Pacific leaders and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.

He was criticised for a set-piece six-minute speech on Wednesday that did not use the term “fossil fuels.”

Albanese said: “You could pick out any number of things that were not in what was a short speech.”

He said his speech was “appropriate” and had concentrated on climate impacts in the Pacific, including from rising sea levels.

“My speech was well received by my Pacific friends,” he said, standing beside several Pacific leaders before a meeting of the Pacific Resilience Facility – a fund to help the region adapt to climate change and recover from disasters that was established with $100m from Australia.

At an open meeting of the facility, lined by Pacific leaders and supporting countries, the philanthropist, mining billionaire and outspoken climate advocate Andrew Forrest said his Minderoo Foundation had also donated $5m.

“There is a vast injustice being wreaked upon the Pacific island states, and you are the least responsible,” he told the leaders.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Indigenous activist Rikki Dank urged the Australian PM to heed the calls for action on climate change. He was speaking at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Thursday. He is taking the Australian government to the UN human rights committee over its coal and gas exports.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Iran says it targeted US radar site in Bahrain
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran.

The claim came hours after Iran’s state news agency IRNA, citing official sources, reported that the port city of Sirik in Hormozgan province was hit by “enemy fire” on Thursday.

In a statement carried by the semi-official Tasnim news agency, the IRGC called the strike a “serious warning” to the “aggressor enemy” to stop what it said was a series of aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Should these violations and acts of aggression recur, the IRGC Aerospace Force stands in full readiness to engage without limits,” the statement said.

The IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said the IRGC’s Aerospace Force had “targeted and destroyed” the radar installation.

There was no immediate comment from Washington or Manama.

Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet.

The Fifth Fleet headquarters, at the Naval Support Activity base in the capital, Manama, is the main command centre for US naval operations in the Middle East.

It was hit in the opening hours of the war on February 28, and satellite images analysed by Al Jazeera showed direct hits on several radar domes and damage to buildings across the base.

The US has reportedly reduced its troop numbers at bases in the region and ordered some diplomatic staff to leave, according to news outlets, as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran,

US Central Command said it “regularly” moves personnel and assets to “optimise mission readiness”.

According to the Reuters news agency, it is the first time since early September that Iran has claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country.

The claim comes as Israel’s security cabinet has ordered the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran, according to Israeli media, including the public broadcaster KAN.

Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has warned that if the US launches another war, every military base involved, anywhere from West Asia to Europe, would be a legitimate target for Iranian strikes.

A Pentagon inspector general’s report released in September found that Iranian attacks damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings at US installations in eight countries, including Bahrain, in the first four months of the war.

Analysts say several US bases in the region have been almost rendered unusable.

US President Donald Trump has said he is prepared to return to war if the diplomatic track offered by Qatar fails to deliver a deal.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, has said economic pressure on Iran is working well enough that resuming large-scale military operations is unnecessary.

In an exclusive interview with Al Jazeera on Wednesday, Iran’s parliament speaker and lead negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would never go back to how it was before the war, and that “the ball is now in the American court“.

Meanwhile, US Central Command says its forces are still strictly enforcing the naval blockade on Iranian ports.

The war began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: IRGC says it has targeted US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. The claim comes hours after Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported that the port city of Sirik in Hormozgan province was hit by “enemy fire’

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Spanish court suspends far-right group over alleged hate crimes
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
A Spanish judge has suspended the activities of the ultra-right group Nucleo Nacional as part of an investigation into alleged hate crimes and illegal association.

The court in the northern city of Gijon announced the ruling on Thursday, ordering the group’s office shut and its social media content and bank accounts blocked.

The move follows the arrest last week of 14 of its members on suspicion of inciting hatred against vulnerable groups and people with opposing ideologies.

The decision comes ahead of Spain’s general election on November 29 and a day after the first nationwide general strike in 14 years.

In a video posted on X, an unnamed Nucleo Nacional representative wearing a black shirt with the group’s logo said the movement was a victim of “persecution and political repression”.

“They won’t beat us,” the post said.

Nucleo Nacional describes itself as a political movement. On its website, which has now been blocked and suspended by court order, it says it seeks a “national awakening”. Spanish authorities have scrutinised the group over its anti-immigration rhetoric, particularly after thousands of migrants crossed in July into Ceuta, Spain’s North African enclave.

Police also searched the group’s headquarters in Madrid and other locations. They said they seized more than 20 firearms, some of them unlicensed, along with large quantities of ammunition and other illegal weapons.

The court said key members of the organisation had already been placed under precautionary measures, including a ban on leaving Spain and a requirement to report weekly to a court.

Reuters also reported last month that Spanish police arrested three members of a far-right group in Madrid on October 3, after tens of thousands marched across the country over the housing crisis.

The Spanish government said far-right activists, some performing Nazi salutes, tried to reach demonstrators camped in the Puerta del Sol square.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: The court in the northern city of Gijon announced the ruling on Thursday. It ordered the group’s office shut and its social media content and bank accounts blocked. The move follows the arrest last week of 14 of its members on suspicion of inciting hatred against vulnerable groups and people with opposing ideologies.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Chris Van Hollen launches bid to lead Democrats in US Senate
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US Senator Chris Van Hollen has said he is running for Senate majority leader as Democrats gear up to take charge of the US Congress in January following a Democratic landslide in this month’s midterm elections.

Van Hollen said in a post on X late on Thursday that Americans had “called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption”.

“To deliver, we need new leadership,” he said, adding that “this isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call”.

“That’s why I’m running,” he said.

Van Hollen has faced mounting calls to enter the race for Senate majority leader amid growing opposition to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer‘s continued tenure after he faced criticism over his handling of the Democratic caucus during the Trump presidency.

Responding to Van Hollen’s decision, Senator Chuck Schumer wrote on X “I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead”.

“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader”, he said.

Schumer said he looked “forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people”.

US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan, who said he would not support Schumer as the majority leader in the Senate, welcomed Van Hollen’s decision to run.

In a post on X, El-Sayed said: “I called on Sen. Chris Van Hollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience.”

“We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority,” El-Sayed said.

On Thursday, Democratic Party leaders gathered in Denver, Colorado, for a two-day conference on the future of the party, following the sweeping victories in the midterms.

Some progressives at the conference have argued that it is time to change the direction and the leadership of the Democratic Party.

“[Chuck] Schumer has spent nearly 50 years in elected office,” said Washington, DC-based political commentator and strategist James Butler, adding that while he respected the US senator’s service, “it is time for veteran Democrats to make space for younger, more energetic members”.

Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has repeatedly challenged Washington’s relationship with Middle Eastern partners.

Van Hollen, the son of a US diplomat, has called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a “chronic liar“, previously telling Al Jazeera the US-Israel war on Iran “is making America and our allies less safe”.

He also attempted to push forward legislation in Congress that would have required the Trump administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention.

This week, Van Hollen and 10 Senate colleagues urged congressional leaders to remove provisions from the annual defence policy bill that would expand weapons development and intelligence sharing with Israel.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: US Senator Chris Van Hollen has said he is running for Senate majority leader. Van Hollan said Americans had ‘called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people’

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Finland detects strike on Russian warship as Zelenskyy meets US envoys
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Finland’s military says its forces have detected a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised mediation efforts led by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.

A spokesperson for the Nordic country’s military said in an email to the Reuters news agency that its forces “detected … a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation”, adding that Finland is not under “any immediate military threat”.

The statement did not provide further details on where the strike originated, the location or timing of the incident, or how it was detected.

Reuters said it was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused Wednesday’s strike.

Estonia shares a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea with Finland. Local media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship which had returned to Saint Petersburg after the alleged attack.

Ukraine’s Security Service has said it carried out the attack, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle. In recent days, Russia said it had intercepted at least 146 Ukrainian drones in the northwestern Leningrad region.

On Wednesday, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had issued warnings to citizens to take shelter due to drones in their airspace, and NATO warplanes were scrambled in response.

On Thursday, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ireland.

The US shuttle diplomacy followed trilateral negotiations in the United Arab Emirates this week, which produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners.

Russia’s state-run news agency TASS reported that the prisoner exchange should happen in two to three weeks. If finalised, it would be the latest in a long line of such exchanges.

“We are also working toward what would be the largest prisoner exchange of the war, potentially reuniting thousands of people with their families,” Kushner said on X on Thursday, following his meetings.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Finland's military says its forces detected a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea. The strike was detected by Finland's military, a spokesperson for the Nordic country’s military said. The statement did not provide further details on where the strike originated, the location or timing of the incident.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Trump moots toppling Cuba authorities before leaving office
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US President Donald Trump has said he would “certainly consider” using military force against Cuba, adding that he wants to “get Cuba done” before he leaves office in 2029.

In a phone interview on Thursday with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt, of Salem News Channel, Trump was asked whether he was considering “freeing Cuba” through a military intervention.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” he said, adding that the administration was “watching it very closely”.

Trump called the island “essentially a failed … place, nation, whatever you wanna call it”.

Politico reported that it was the first time Trump had put a timeline on a possible operation.

Trump said Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents are from Cuba, “would love to do it”.

“I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said. He added that he won the Cuban vote in Florida by a wide margin.

Trump has repeatedly threatened to topple authorities in Cuba.

On Monday, he said Cuba “will fall fairly soon” and that the US would help it “on a humanitarian basis”.

In March, he said he believed he would have “the honour of taking Cuba”, making the remarks as the island’s power grid collapsed.

Trump put Cuba under a de facto oil blockade in January, after the US seized Venezuela’s president, Nicolas Maduro, and cut off Venezuelan oil to the island.

He signed an executive order declaring Cuba an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to the US and threatened tariffs on any country that supplied it with fuel.

The blockade has caused repeated nationwide blackouts, fuel and food shortages, and a humanitarian crisis.

Cuban officials have called it “collective punishment”.

Washington has added sanctions, including on Cuba’s state oil company, President Miguel Diaz-Canel and relatives of former President Raul Castro, and announced a new round this month targeting 10 people and entities tied to the government, military and oil industry.

The US has also issued an arrest warrant for Castro. Officials from both sides have held talks on the blockade, but Cuba’s foreign minister said in June there had been “no progress”.

In March, the head of US Southern Command told senators that US troops were not rehearsing for an invasion of Cuba.

Cuban officials said the island was ready for any attack.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Trump said he would ‘certainly consider’ using military force against Cuba. He said he wants to ‘get Cuba done’ before he leaves office in 2029. Trump has repeatedly threatened to topple authorities in Cuba.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: After Iraq ex-MP’s killing, Lebanon asks Syria to extradite suspects
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Lebanese authorities have asked Syria to hand over two Syrians suspected of involvement in the killing of former Iraqi MP Ahmed al-Alwani, who was found dead in an apartment in Beirut earlier this week.

A Lebanese judicial source told the AFP news agency that preliminary findings indicate al-Alwani was strangled to death, but the perpetrators and motives remain murky.

Hailing from Ramadi in Iraq’s Sunni heartland, al-Alwani was a vocal critic of Iranian influence over Baghdad and had served more than a decade in prison after an initial death sentence on “terrorism” charges in his home country.

Investigators at the Lebanese Public Prosecutor’s office had asked Damascus to arrest and hand over two Syrian nationals, the source added, who are suspected of involvement in al-Alwani’s killing.

The source said the identities of the two suspects are yet to be determined, and that a Lebanese national had been arrested and is being interrogated.

In a separate case, the Information Branch of the Internal Security Forces is investigating five Hezbollah members who were arrested in the Batroun highlands in northern Lebanon, according to the public prosecutor’s media office.

The official National News Agency said Lebanon’s top prosecutor, Judge Ahmed Rami al-Hajj, is personally overseeing the investigation into al-Alwani’s killing, which is being carried out by the Information Branch of Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces.

Investigators are still trying to ascertain the possible motives behind the killing, but the initial inquiry reveals a financial angle, sources told AFP.

Al-Alwani’s body was found on Tuesday evening in an apartment in the Tariq al-Jdideh neighbourhood of Beirut, according to Lebanese media.

Al-Alwani had arrived in Beirut from Erbil airport on a Middle East Airlines flight on the evening of November 5 and was driven to a hotel, according to the head of the Iraqi Security Media Cell, Lieutenant General Saad Maan, who is following the investigation in Lebanon.

Maan told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that al-Alwani left the hotel less than an hour after checking into his room, telling staff at the reception that he was leaving with friends.

The hotel staff told investigators that the people who were accompanying al-Alwani were speaking with a Syrian accent, according to Maan.

INA reported that al-Alwani left the hotel in a white Range Rover vehicle, after which he made two calls to relatives back in Iraq before contact with him was lost.

Iraq’s President Nizar Amedi has called for a swift investigation to determine the circumstances surrounding the killing and identify the perpetrators, after meeting Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam in Turkiye on Wednesday.

Al-Alwani, a Sunni politician, formerly represented the western province of Anbar in Iraq’s parliament. He rose to prominence during the protests of 2012 and 2013 against the Shia-led government of then-Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, whom critics accused of sectarian policies marginalising Sunnis.

He was also a vocal critic of Iran’s influence in Iraq and of Iranian-backed Shia armed groups in the country.

Al-Alwani was arrested in December 2013 during a security raid on his home in Ramadi, during which his brother and several others were killed.

He was sentenced to death in 2014 on “terrorism” charges, but released in April 2025 under Iraq’s General Amnesty Law after more than a decade in prison.

Iraq’s Ambassador to Lebanon Mohammed Reda al-Husseini said on Tuesday that the Iraqi embassy was following the case closely.

He said the embassy is awaiting the final report from the Lebanese security agencies to “disclose the circumstances of the crime”.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Former Iraqi MP Ahmed al-Alwani was found dead in Beirut apartment on Tuesday. He was a vocal critic of Iranian influence over Baghdad and served more than a decade in prison. He had been sentenced to death in 2014 on “terrorism’s’

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Albania’s PM says 2027 NATO summit will not be held in Tirana
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
NATO will not be holding a summit in Albania next year as planned, Prime Minister Edi Rama has said, as his government faces criticism over its defence spending and protests at home.

Speaking in Dublin on Thursday ahead of a gathering of European leaders, Rama said there was “not yet [a] common position on when the summit will happen, for sure not in 2027”.

He added: “And in 2028, if it will be a summit, it will be in Tirana.”

A NATO official said the next summit “will be held in Albania”, with a decision on the date yet to be made.

Reuters reported in June that plans for a summit in Albania had been thrown into doubt by resistance from the administration of US President Donald Trump and dissatisfaction among NATO members with Tirana’s low defence spending.

NATO leaders said in a declaration at their June 2025 summit in The Hague that they looked forward to meeting in Turkiye in 2026, “followed by a meeting in Albania”. But the declaration from the July summit in Ankara made no mention of a time or place for the next meeting.

NATO has been considering ending its recent practice of holding annual summits, which could avoid a potentially tense encounter with Trump later in his term.

Diplomats say the alliance could still hold a summit at short notice this year, but not in Tirana, Reuters said.

Rama, who has been in office for 13 years, has faced months of protests.

They began in May after he gave preliminary approval to a luxury resort backed by Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, in the protected Vjosa-Narta wetland at Zvernec, on Albania’s southern coast, and on nearby Sazan Island.

Dubbed the “Flamingo Revolution”, they grew into wider anti-government protests demanding Rama’s resignation over alleged corruption, and into violent student protests in October over conditions at universities.

Opposition lawmakers led by Sali Berisha disrupted a session of parliament with flares and smoke bombs on October 29 in support of the protesters.

Rama has refused to resign and says the resort complies with Albanian and European Union law. His government has dismissed the protests as orchestrated by political rivals.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: NATO will not be holding a summit in Albania next year as planned, Prime Minister Edi Rama said. Rama has faced months of protests over his government's defence spending and protests at home.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.title: Iran war live: Trump says Gulf allies urged pause in Iran strikes
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.author: Enes Abuomer,Mahmoud Sayed
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.text:
US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz is set to arrive in Lebanon next week, with the future of peacekeeping forces hanging in the balance as the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) nears expiry.

Waltz attacked UNIFIL earlier this week, describing it as a “human shield for terrorists”, during the Israel Hayom Summit, an event organised by the Israeli newspaper Israel Hayom in New York on Tuesday.

The US ambassador made clear during the event that his mission in Lebanon will be “to get rid of this human shield known as UNIFIL and change the peacekeeping mission that has been there for 20 years”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a news conference on Tuesday that the US is considering a “civilian mission” to replace UNIFIL.

“It doesn’t have to be a military mission. It could be a civilian mission,” he said. The UNIFIL mandate ends on December 31, 2026, unless extended by the UN.

The US Navy quietly removed the commander of the USS Michael Murphy on September 27 while the destroyer was deployed to the Middle East for the Iran war and naval blockade, USNI News, an outlet affiliated with the US Naval Institute, reported.

Commander Caitlin Cunningham was relieved due to a “loss of confidence”, a Navy spokesperson told the outlet, without providing further details.

The destroyer remained in the region after the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group departed in August, and left in mid-October. It is expected back in Pearl Harbor this week after a 346-day deployment, according to USNI News.

A British volunteer surgeon has documented the chaos and destruction inside Gaza’s Nasser hospital after a deadly Israeli strike. The bombing killed six people, including surgeon Rizq Abu Shuaira.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, who announced he is running to be majority leader as a potential alternative to Senator Chuck Schumer, has repeatedly challenged Washington’s relationship with Middle Eastern partners.

Van Hollen, the son of a US diplomat, has called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a “chronic liar“. He also attempted to push forward legislation in Congress that would have required the Trump administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention.

Van Hollen previously told Al Jazeera the US-Israel war on Iran “is making America and our allies less safe”.

This week, Van Hollen and 10 Senate colleagues urged congressional leaders to remove provisions from the annual defence policy bill that would expand weapons development and intelligence sharing with Israel.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has targeted a US early warning radar in Bahrain in response to an attack on a telecommunications tower in Iran’s Sirik, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

“This serves as a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to cease its aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. Should these violations and acts of aggression recur, the IRGC Aerospace Force stands in full readiness to engage without limits,” Tasnim reported, citing the IRGC.

Iranian official sources, according to state news agency IRNA, said the southern port city of Sirik in Hormozgan province was hit by “enemy fire” on Thursday.

Several international airlines have extended the suspension of flights to Saudi Arabia as Houthi missile and drone attacks continue to disrupt aviation across the kingdom.

Indian carrier Akasa Air announced on Thursday that all flights to and from Riyadh and Jeddah would remain suspended until November 30, citing ongoing security concerns.

Another Indian airline, IndiGo, extended its suspension of services to Riyadh and Dammam until November 30, while flights to Jeddah and Medina remain cancelled until November 21.

Air India and Air India Express have also suspended flights to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam until November 14.

European carriers have announced longer suspensions. KLM has cancelled services to Riyadh and Dammam until November 27, while British Airways has postponed the resumption of its London-Riyadh route until January 11, 2027.

The United Arab Emirates’ Etihad Airways has suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam until November 19, while Oman’s SalamAir has cancelled services to both cities until November 30.

The disruptions follow repeated Houthi attacks targeting Saudi airports, energy facilities and other infrastructure, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

Yemen’s Houthis have launched another wave of drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting oil facilities and military installations as the UN Security Council unanimously voted to extend sanctions related to the conflict.

The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted several drones over Riyadh and the kingdom’s Eastern Province.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed the group had targeted a pumping station along Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, an oil facility in Yanbu and military installations near the Yemeni border.

US Navy quietly removed commander of USS Michael Murphy on September 27 while the destroyer was deployed to the Middle East for the Iran war and naval blockade.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Yemen’s Houthis renew strikes on Saudi Arabia as UNSC extends sanctions
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Saudi-led coalition forces have said they intercepted suspected Houthi drones over Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh region and Eastern Province, as the UN Security Council agreed to extend sanctions on the Iran-allied group.

Major General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, announced the interceptions of suspected Houthi drones on Thursday, in a statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had targeted oil infrastructure and military assets in the kingdom, including a pumping station on the East-West Pipeline with a drone as well as the Yanbu oil facility on the Red Sea.

Riyadh says it has rerouted about 4 million barrels of crude per day via its East-West Pipeline to Yanbu, equivalent to about 4 percent of global supply.

Saree further claimed a military cargo plane at Sharurah airport close to Yemen’s border was targeted with a drone, while a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait airbase “scored a direct hit”.

The Houthi spokesperson added that their forces had targeted the Saudi Aramco headquarters in the capital, Riyadh, but rejected as a “grave falsehood” a Saudi assertion that the group had targeted the kingdom’s Mecca region on Wednesday.

Saudi-backed coalition forces fighting on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they continue to confront the Houthis across all frontlines, targeting leaders, vehicles, reinforcements, weapons and positions.

Yemen’s Defence Ministry, citing the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, said the battle against the Houthis was moving towards its “desired objectives”, according to Yemen’s official pro-government Saba news agency.

A meeting convened by the Defence Ministry was held in the Marib governorate to discuss the ongoing operations against the Houthis, where ways to enhance coordination and integration between various military units that are part of the Dawn of Yemen offensive were also discussed.

On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) unanimously voted in favour of extending sanctions related to Yemen for one more year, including freezing assets and enforcing travel bans, while demanding an end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The mandate for the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, which made the recommendations, was also extended.

UNSC members called on “all parties to refrain from escalatory actions and to resolve differences and disputes through negotiation”, while also backing the territorial integrity of both Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

“The resolution condemns the military escalation by the Houthis, their maritime and cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia, and their threats to commercial shipping vessels,” the UNSC statement said.

The resolution emphasised that measures taken for the purpose of maintaining sanctions “shall not apply to humanitarian assistance or supplies for basic needs of civilians, without negatively affecting legitimate trade activities”.

“The council sanctions are merely a means, not an end in themselves,” said Ambassador Fu Cong, China’s envoy to the UN, who hoped that “the situation in Yemen will de-escalate as soon as possible”.

On Thursday, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said more than 333,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the beginning of August, including more than 24,000 displaced in the past week.

Civilians “continue to pay a heavy price as violence damages health facilities, forces families from their homes, and hinders the work of humanitarians”, OCHA said.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is pressing the European Union to adopt an EU Parliament resolution to designate the Ansar Allah Houthi movement as a “terrorist organisation”, according to the Reuters news agency, citing sources familiar with the drive.

But European officials told Reuters the bloc is concerned this could undermine a future peace process.

EU foreign policy spokesperson Anouar El-Anouni said the bloc was in regular contact with Riyadh on regional developments, but declined to comment on any specific discussions under way, according to Reuters.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Russian court jails rights lawyer for 12 years on treason charge
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
A court in Russia’s Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad has sentenced a 66-year-old rights lawyer to 12 years in prison for treason, after prosecutors accused her of passing sensitive information to Ukraine.

The court imposed the sentence on Thursday on Maria Bontsler, according to the rights group Slovo Zashchite, which said she had worked with a number of defendants accused of political offences in Kaliningrad.

The territory sits on the Baltic Sea between Lithuania and Poland.

A court statement posted on Telegram did not name her, but said she had been detained by the FSB intelligence agency on allegations of passing information to Ukraine beginning in 2024 about security officers in Kaliningrad.

Prosecutors also alleged she gave Ukraine information on criminal cases in the exclave that were of interest to Kyiv, the statement said.

She was also given an extra year of restrictions on her activity. Prosecutors had sought 15 years, according to Slovo Zashchite.

Slovo Zashchite said the trial was held behind closed doors, with Bontsler and her lawyers prevented from attending, and that she was allowed only to make a closing statement. It said her lawyers argued that none of the information cited by prosecutors was secret, and that she had been in ill health in detention.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, parliament has approved laws that make public actions aimed at “discrediting” the army illegal and ban the spread of “fake news” about the armed forces.

Russian courts have also jailed lawyers who took on politically sensitive cases. In January 2025, a court sentenced three lawyers of the late opposition leader Alexey Navalny to between three and a half and five and a half years on “extremism” charges, in a case widely seen as an effort to discourage defence lawyers from taking political cases.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1032774/pr.text:
Nvidia is looking for a new CEO, and President Trump says the former Apple CEO would be ‘a great candidate.’

Nvidia is looking for a new CEO, and President Trump says the former Apple CEO would be ‘a great candidate.’

Jensen Huang resigned this morning as Nvidia’s CEO following reports of affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Right now, the company is being led by its CFO on an interim basis. But President Donald Trump is already throwing around one person he thinks should take over the chipmaking giant: former Apple CEO Tim Cook, who stepped down from leading the company on September 1st and moved into an executive chairman role.

Shortly after Huang’s resignation was announced today, Trump posted his idea about Cook on Truth Social: “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump said. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”

In a new episode of Stephen A. Smith’s Straight Shooter podcast published today, Trump made his pitch for Cook again, saying that Apple “would never be what it is today” if Steve Jobs was still “around”:

Can [Huang] be replaced?

Well, you know, the expression, Anybody can be replaced? So it’s very hard to replace him, but I had an idea this morning that I sort of just released: Tim Cook. He just sort of semi-retired from Apple. He’s done one of the greatest jobs in the history of business.

I think if Tim Cook, who built Apple… If Steve Jobs were around, Apple would never be what it is today. Tim Cook took a lot of these brilliant ideas and designs and everything else from Jobs and others, and he made it into one of the great companies of the world in a fairly short period. I think Tim Cook would be a great candidate to run Nvidia.

Apple and Nvidia didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. Cook is well-known for his ongoing relationship with President Trump, including gifting the president a 24k gold and glass statue last year. (Trump, after Cook announced his transition plan earlier this year, posted a story about having “the head of Apple calling to ‘kiss my ass.’”)

During the podcast, Trump said he spoke to Huang yesterday and that Huang is “going through hell”:

Should [Huang] have stepped down?

Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy, and I don’t know if that’s been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes, if the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.

But I can tell you this. Somehow, he’ll end up on his feet. I mean, I know him, I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man.

I spoke to him yesterday. He’s going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That’s what he is, really… that’s what he told me. I’m president, and he called me. And he said, What I’ve done to my wife and family is... That’s what he talked about.

Trump, on the podcast, called Huang a “tremendous talent.” Other tech leaders have also publicly supported Huang following his resignation.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed a new entry in the Wolfenstein series with a brief tease.

It’s been nearly a decade since Bethesda’s MachineGames released Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus in 2017, and now Xbox is ready to announce a sequel from the studio. Wolfenstein 3 was officially announced today, just days after Bethesda also confirmed that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel.

In a post, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the name and a photo of a script. “Looking forward to sharing more,” she said. MachineGames also announced the game in a post, saying the game is “in production” and sharing a photo from a motion-capture session. IGN reports that Brian Bloom (who plays protagonist William Joseph “BJ” Blazkowicz) and Debra Wilson (who plays Grace Walker) are reprising their roles, and they appear to be the featured actors in the photo.

Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at @MachineGames. One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more. pic.twitter.com/YyX8LrbTvh

The last mainline entry, Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus, launched in 2017 and continued the story of Blazkowicz in an alternate 1960s where Nazi Germany had won the Second World War. Wolfenstein: Youngblood also debuted in 2019 as a co-op spinoff, starring Blazkowicz’s twin daughters.

https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1032630.title: Whoop launched a social network where every user has a ‘verified heartbeat’

https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1032630.text:
Whoop’s new Humans platform is like Instagram Stories with updates from your friends’ fitness tracker data.

Whoop’s new Humans platform is like Instagram Stories with updates from your friends’ fitness tracker data.

Starting Thursday, Whoop members can share their data from its wearables on the app’s new Whoop Humans social network. Users can make their metrics, activities, and achievements visible to other Whoop wearers, post Story-like “Moments” with photos and captions, and add comments and reactions on other members’ posts.

Whoop claims its platform is “entirely human,” unlike other social media platforms that are “saturated with artificial intelligence, automated accounts and bots, and manufactured content.”

Whoop CEO Will Ahmed says Humans is “the most verifiably human network ever launched. Every account represents a real person with a verified heartbeat.” Whoop says its existing Teams social feature “will remain available,” allowing people to share strain, recovery, and sleep data along with group leaderboards.

In the Community tab in Whoop’s app, users can scroll through Moments from people they’re following, like tapping through your Stories feed on Instagram but with your friends’ fitness tracker data. In one of Whoop’s examples, swiping up on a user’s Moments post with a photo from their run shows a map with their route and details like their pace and distance. The Community tab also shows cards for people in your “community” with their sleep, recovery, and strain scores.

Whoop says users choose which activities, achievements, and metrics they want to share on Humans, including Recovery, Strain, Sleep, HRV, and resting heart rate. Any activities marked as sensitive aren’t shared by default. There’s also an option to keep Moments posts private and a “Stealth Mode” for temporarily hiding health and performance data without changing your sharing settings.

A new look for the Humble Bundle storefront is missing an important security feature that was previously there.

A new look for the Humble Bundle storefront is missing an important security feature that was previously there.

The Humble Bundle storefront for buying games and other software recently got a new look, but on the settings page, it no longer offers a way to add or update two-factor verification methods, as reported by Kotaku. PC Gamer also points out that there are Humble Bundle support pages discussing two-factor verification, and the writer for the publication said that they had set up two-factor verification on the old version of the site.

However, it does appear that, at least as of now, there is some form of two-factor verification. When I tried logging into my Humble Bundle account while writing this article, I was prompted to check my email for an access code before I could access my account. While logged in, I was able to update my password, but I didn’t have to enter my old password to be able to do so.

For what it’s worth, my passwords app also shows that I set up a rotating two-factor code for Humble Bundle at some point. I was not asked to input that at any part of my login process today.

Humble Bundle owner IGN Entertainment and IGN parent company Ziff Davis didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

https://www.wired.com/story/nvidia-emplo.title: ‘Bring Back THE Boss’: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return
https://www.wired.com/story/nvidia-emplo.author: Paresh Dave, Zoë Schiffer
https://www.wired.com/story/nvidia-emplo.text:
SOME NVIDIA EMPLOYEES are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.

“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.

“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.

One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”

The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.

Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.

Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.

It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.

One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.

Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”

Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”
https://www.wired.com/story/nvidia-emplo.summary: Internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED shows internal emails from Nvidia employees calling for Jensen Huang's return. The resignation of Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, has cost the company $1 trillion in market value.

https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.title: Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.author: Ericka Chickowski
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.text:
News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Most organizations haven't sorted out their cryptographic estate enough to even know where they'd start with post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

The pressure is mounting for security leaders to get serious about their post-quantum cryptography (PQC) transition plans, but most organizations aren't even ready to get ready for PQC.

Studies show that, yes, CISOs today do see PQC as a priority they've got to plan for. However, the bulk of organizations don't have a detailed enough cryptographic inventory to help them sketch out a roadmap of where to get started.

"When it comes to post-quantum cryptography, every company, no matter which ones you talk to are kind of stuck in the discovery phase," says Dr. Anurag Swarnim Yadav, founder and CTO of the startup QubitAC.

Recent numbers back up his observations. According to a July study by DigiCert, while 87% of organizations say they're planning, testing, or implementing PQC, only 44% have developed transition plans or created inventories. That mirrors another study by Ponemon Institute that found only 43% of organizations have full visibility of their cryptographic estate. Those respondents reported that their inability to discover those assets and improve that visibility is their number one greatest concern about PQC migration.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

Cryptography sits in web servers, certificates, VPNs, code signing, vendor products and all nature of assets in between. Getting every encryption use case ready for a post-quantum world will be a sweeping transition, and the latest research suggests developments in quantum computing are proceeding on a much faster timeline than originally anticipated. If an enterprise can't enumerate all the cryptography impacted, it means they're not toeing the start line for this footrace.

Getting all of those assets into post-quantum readiness will be a generational effort easily on par with the Y2K effort. Unlike with Y2K, however, there's no set-in-stone deadline for post-quantum.

The closest thing is Q Day, the point when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) can break the public-key cryptography behind key exchange and digital signatures. The big problem with building a widespread sense of urgency is that nobody knows exactly when Q Day will arrive.

Yadav says estimates for when Q Day will come run from 2030 to 2040 and beyond, but his own bet is that attackers could pull it off by 2029 based how the research is shifting. The expected window until Q Day arrives keeps compressing as quantum researchers perfect their craft. Last year, Google researchers calculated that breaking 2048-bit RSA encryption would take a quantum computer 20 times smaller than they had estimated in 2019. And in March Google set a 2029 target for its own PQC migration, influenced by such research and recent progress in quantum hardware.

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

Global governments are also starting to get firm about their own timing expectations for PQC transition in the run-up to Q Day. NIST finalized its PQC transition roadmap in late October, and a June executive order requires federal high-value assets and high-impact systems to move key establishment to post-quantum algorithms by 2030 and digital signatures by 2031. The United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre recommends that large organizations complete discovery and assessment and build an initial migration plan by 2028, then finish migrating by 2035.

Even if we don’t know exactly when Q Day will come about, the math behind what will happen after that day is well understood. Public-key cryptography lets two parties who have never met agree on a secret and prove who they are. It works because some math is easy to run forward and impractical to reverse. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring huge numbers, while elliptic curve cryptography and Diffie-Hellman key exchange rely on a related problem called the discrete logarithm.

Quantum computers use subatomic particles instead of transistors to represent data. This gives them an edge in how they process the ones and zeros of computing. Cryptography experts for years have warned that a sufficiently advanced enough quantum computer could use that edge to factor huge numbers and solve discrete logarithms at a rate of efficiency unheard of from even the most advanced classical super computers.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

Worthless Now, Priceless Later

There's also a more immediate deadline that's brewing from what attackers are likely doing today to prepare for Q Day. It's fairly trivial for the bad guys to vacuum up high-value encrypted traffic today with the promise that they might have a chance to decrypt it at a later date. For long-lived information like financial or health details, or secret sauce intellectual property, the long-game of this harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL) is worth the effort for future-minded criminals.

"The data is worthless to attackers right now, but becomes priceless later," Yadav explains. He offers credit card numbers as a classic example. They stay valid for years, so a cache of encrypted numbers harvested now could still be good if Q Day lands inside that window.

In its recently finalized roadmap, the National Institute of Standards and Technology named HNDL as one of the main reasons the transition is so urgent. NIST mathematician and cryptographic expert Andrew Regenscheid says HNDL reframes the whole PQC timeline for critical information stores across industry and government systems.

"This information may need to remain secret for years, or even decades, into the future," he explained in a NIST Q&A this summer. "For that kind of information, waiting until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives is waiting too long."

Considering that the most isolated cryptographic migrations can still linger for upwards of a decade or longer, even a conservative 2040 estimate for Q Day should be enough to have security experts scrambling to plan PQC transitions. The scale of changes needed will take significant planning and prioritization that will need to be phased in.

"Changing these algorithms is something that’s been done before. It’s a complex process that takes years," Regenscheid said. "Based on our experience and the challenge of navigating the post-quantum world, we expect this process to be the most challenging one yet. The breadth of these systems and the complexity of the change will dwarf what we’ve done before."

The destination, at least, is defined. In 2024, NIST finalized three post-quantum standards, one for key exchange (ML-KEM) and two for digital signatures (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA), built on math that's expected to hold up against quantum computers. The harder job is finding every place RSA and elliptic curve cryptography still run, and planning how and when to swap out each use case. Because of HNDL, NIST suggests the first transition phases should be prioritized around data that is particularly sensitive or has to stay secure for a long time.

In a September study on PQC readiness, Frost & Sullivan analysts emphasized how important risk-based prioritization like this will be for PQC readiness.

"A non-compliant cryptographic asset supporting a low-value application may represent limited immediate risk, while the same technology supporting sensitive information or a critical business process could require urgent remediation," they wrote.

Sorting through all the assets and ranking them depends on having a solid inventory on hand, though. This is why the discovery is so crucial. Frost &Sullivan concurred that the discovery process is proving to be trickier than many thought it would be.

"The inventory needs to extend beyond simply identifying algorithms to understanding the dependencies between cryptographic assets and business-critical applications," they explained.

Tools — commercial and open source — designed to assist organizations in their PQC journey are already available. These tools have their own approaches and have varying levels of maturity. One such tool is AC Scanner, which Yadav and QubitAC co-founder Joseph Wilson demoed at Black Hat Arsenal last August. The free open-source tool is purpose-built to kickstart the inventory process, Yadav says. It's a fast, lightweight tool that runs from command line, scans for outward facing TLS and SSH services, and creates an inventory for the IP range it's pointed at.

"You start with nothing but a domain name and by the end you get a complete cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM)," Yadav says. The CBOM is an inventory of the algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols in use, and the scanner pairs it with two scores, one for overall security health and one for post-quantum readiness based on NIST's post-quantum standards.

It also doubles as an outside check on HNDL exposure. Every encrypted session starts with a key exchange, where the two sides agree on a secret. If a public-facing endpoint still uses a classical exchange, traffic an attacker records today could be unlocked later by a quantum computer. A hybrid exchange that adds post-quantum math protects that traffic, provided the client uses it too, and the scanner reports which kind each endpoint offers.

Classical endpoints are the ones most exposed to HNDL, and Yadav sees AC Scanner as giving organizations a starting point for making HNDL-aware transition plans.

Of course, any security professional will be quick to point out that a scan is just an informational snapshot. It's what happens after that information is in hand that really counts. Scanning tools can kickstart discovery, but organizations need to follow up what they find with a migration plan and start executing on it. NIST’s Regenscheid says the sooner organizations can get to these plans, the better.

"Given how long these transitions take, the organizations that start planning and begin moving to post-quantum products and services now will be in a far stronger position later," he says, stating that this is an opportunity to modernize a lot of the process. "Many steps must occur in sequence, which is why an early start is crucial."

Contributing Writer, Dark Reading

An award-winning freelance reporter with nearly two decades of experience covering B2B cybersecurity, Ericka Chickowski has tackled every angle of security and risk for Dark Reading since 2009. Her coverage has spanned the full range of cyber topics important to every kind of cybersecurity stakeholder, including cybersecurity practitioners, CISOs, security-minded business managers, and security-aware board directors. She specializes in going deep on topics, breaking down how the technology trends affect real people, and how risk impacts the bottom line.

Some special areas of focus include: adversarial AI; AI risk and resilience; AI and agentic governance; application security (AppSec); governance, risk, and compliance (GRC); cloud security; network security; software supply chain risk; cyberinsurance; DevSecOps; enterprise risk management; and CISO career development.

In addition to Dark Reading, Ericka has written for many different IT and business publications over the years. Her byline has appeared in dozens of trade and consumer magazines, including Baseline, Consumer Digest, Channel Insider, CIO Insight, CSOOnline.com, DevOps.com, eWeek, Entrepreneur, Forbes, InformationWeek, SC Magazine, and SecurityBoulevard. https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers.

One possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A new study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it.

Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies

To investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance.

Solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly important.

The researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed.

Another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place.

Brain Activity Reveals New Clues to Math Difficulties

The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences.

They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems.

The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change.

Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method.

The Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies.

However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide new evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties.

Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children

An important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes.

As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes."

By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students.

The findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago. Yet the fossil record tells only part of the story. Fossilization is exceptionally rare, meaning that just a tiny fraction of the organisms that once lived on Earth have been preserved. Even when fossils survive, scientists can only discover them if the rock layers containing them are accessible today.

As a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps. Some geological periods and parts of the world have produced abundant fossils, giving scientists a detailed understanding of the life that existed there. Other periods and regions remain largely unexplored. Because fossil excavations require considerable time and resources, knowing where to search could make a major difference in uncovering new evidence of ancient life.

To help solve this problem, Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History (SNSB) and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna have developed a new tool for guiding fossil research. The two paleontologists analyzed the geographic distribution of fossil discoveries from animals that inhabited shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the regions of the world where fossil information is missing, providing a clearer picture of where future discoveries may be possible.

Mapping 540 Million Years of Ancient Marine Life

To build their map, the researchers examined records from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), the world's leading freely accessible repository of fossil information. The database contains a substantial portion of the paleontological findings published by scientists around the world.

Using these records, the team reconstructed where fossils from ancient shallow marine environments have been documented throughout Earth's history. They also examined how fossil research has developed over decades and centuries, measuring how frequently investigations in different regions have produced new scientific information.

The researchers then compared these findings with geological information from the Macrostat database. This allowed them to assess not only where fossils have already been discovered, but also where suitable rock formations could provide opportunities to fill important gaps in the fossil record.

Where Earth's Missing Fossils May Be Hiding

The analysis revealed a surprising imbalance in our understanding of prehistoric life. The Early Mesozoic (approx. 252 to 66 million years ago) and the Palaeozoic (approx. 539 to 252 million years ago) have already been studied extensively. According to the researchers, additional fossil discoveries from these periods are unlikely to produce a substantial increase in scientific knowledge in the near future.

The greatest opportunities for expanding the fossil record may instead lie in more recent geological history. Although scientists have already collected extensive evidence from the Cenozoic Era (beginning 66 million years ago), the analysis suggests that its shallow marine deposits still contain significant untapped potential for fossil discoveries.

To help researchers investigate this period, the team identified locations around the world where previously unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found. Crucially, these are also places where the appropriate geological layers are exposed or otherwise accessible, making actual discoveries possible.

A Treasure Map for Future Fossil Discoveries

By highlighting regions where important evidence may still be waiting, the new approach could help paleontologists plan more productive expeditions and make better use of limited research resources. Rather than concentrating on areas that have already been explored extensively, scientists can focus on locations with the greatest potential to reveal something new about Earth's prehistoric ecosystems.

"The fact that many regions of the Earth remain unexplored offers hope for valuable new discoveries," says SNSB paleobiologist Neubauer.

"But precisely because expanding the fossil record is quite challenging and progresses only slowly, our work can help researchers worldwide to focus their research specifically on these still largely unexplored areas. We provide a valuable guide for planning future projects and excavation campaigns. The same applies to the examination of existing museum collections awaiting scientific analysis. Through sensible prioritization, we can fill gaps in the fossil record strategically."
