https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/glu.title: Glutathione Supplements: Health Benefits or Just Hype?
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/glu.text:
Michael van den Heuvel

Glutathione supplements are marketed for detoxification, protection against oxidative stress, and even cancer prevention. Manufacturers promote glutathione as an effective antioxidant with a wide range of health benefits. In fact, this naturally occurring molecule plays an important role in cellular protection and the body’s natural detoxification processes; however, clinical evidence has not established that supplementation provides these health benefits. What do the studies actually show?

Glutathione is composed of three amino acids: glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. It is found in most human cells and is one of the most important intracellular antioxidants. Concentrations of these substances are particularly high in the liver, which breaks down foreign substances and prepares them for excretion.

The body produces glutathione itself, primarily depending on the availability of the amino acid cysteine. Fruits, vegetables, and meat also provide glutathione. However, the amount of dietary glutathione that enters cells after digestion and whether individual foods can raise glutathione levels to a clinically significant extent remain unclear.

Within cells, glutathione is predominantly found in its reduced form. When it neutralizes peroxides, it is oxidized to glutathione disulfide. The enzyme glutathione reductase converts it back to its reduced form using NADPH (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate). This cycle plays an important role in maintaining cellular balance.

Glutathione does more than neutralize free radicals. It also influences numerous signaling pathways, regulates protein function, and contributes to cell division.

Manufacturers often promote glutathione for its detoxifying effects. This molecule participates in important detoxification processes. Glutathione S-transferases catalyze the conjugation of reduced glutathione with foreign substances and metabolic byproducts, forming compounds that are more readily processed and eliminated by the body.

One well-known example is N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine, a toxic metabolite of paracetamol. Under normal conditions, glutathione neutralizes this metabolite. However, after a paracetamol overdose, the liver’s glutathione reserves can become depleted.

The fact that glutathione performs these functions does not imply that additional glutathione intake improves detoxification in healthy individuals. Convincing evidence is lacking for claims that supplements eliminate unspecified “environmental toxins,” support detoxification regimens, or provide general cleansing.

A critical review found insufficient evidence that detox diets remove toxins from the body. Similarly, randomized trials have not established that glutathione supplements provide specific health benefits, such as reduced exposure to pollutants or lower disease risk.

Oral glutathione was long considered poorly absorbed because digestive enzymes can break down the tripeptide in the gastrointestinal tract. However, studies have shown mixed findings.

In one randomized study, 40 healthy adults took 500 mg glutathione twice daily for 4 weeks. Neither the oxidative stress markers nor the glutathione status in red blood cells changed significantly.

A longer placebo-controlled trial reported different results. In that trial, 54 healthy nonsmokers received 250 mg/d or 1000 mg/d of glutathione or placebo for 6 months.

In the high-dose group, glutathione concentrations increased by an average of 30%-35% from baseline in red blood cells, plasma, and lymphocytes. Concentrations in buccal cells increased by 260%. The lower dose also increased glutathione levels in whole blood and red blood cells, although to a lesser extent. One month after supplementation was discontinued, the levels returned to baseline.

However, an increase from the baseline did not necessarily represent a treatment effect compared with placebo. The study suggested that oral glutathione changed certain measured levels, but whether these changes improved detoxification or prevented disease remains uncertain.

Manufacturers offer liposomal and other encapsulated formulations intended to improve absorption. One pilot study evaluated 12 healthy adults aged 51-72 years, including 11 women. Participants took 500 mg/d or 1000 mg/d of liposomal glutathione for 4 weeks.

Glutathione levels increased after 1 week and peaked after 2 weeks. Compared with the baseline, levels increased by 40% in whole blood, 25% in red blood cells, 28% in plasma, and 100% in mononuclear blood cells. Simultaneously, the oxidative stress marker 8-isoprostane in plasma decreased by up to 35%. Natural killer cell activity also increased at certain measurement points.

However, these peak values came from different dose groups and measurement timepoints. Overall, the study found no difference between the two doses.

Several limitations restrict the interpretation of the findings. The study included only 12 participants and had neither a placebo group nor a direct comparison with conventional glutathione. In addition, the company that supplied and marketed the tested product provided most of the funding for this study. Therefore, the findings did not establish whether liposomal glutathione was better absorbed or provided greater health benefits.

Randomized crossover studies have also examined the bioavailability of different oral formulations. For example, a 2026 study found that a micellar formulation achieved a higher glutathione concentration in the blood than conventional glutathione, despite using a lower dose. The authors emphasized the need for larger, longer-term studies.

Glutathione is a component of a complex network of endogenous antioxidants. With the help of glutathione peroxidases, it helps break down hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides. It also influences signaling pathways that respond to changes in the cellular redox state.

Oxidative stress is associated with aging, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders. A protective effect from higher glutathione levels is therefore biologically plausible. However, whether supplementation translates this potential into a health benefit is another question.

Some studies have suggested possible effects in individuals with pre-existing diseases. A randomized study in older adults with type 2 diabetes found that longer-term glutathione supplementation increased glutathione stores and reduced oxidative damage. At the same time, A1c levels also decreased.

However, A1c is a surrogate marker. Larger studies are needed to determine whether these changes lead to fewer complications or other long-term health benefits.

Studies used different biomarkers, tissues, and measurement methods, and the durations of the study varied considerably. These differences limit comparisons. Most importantly, higher glutathione levels should not be equated with proven protection against oxidative damage or disease.

Claims that glutathione can prevent cancer or support cancer treatment should be approached with caution.

Glutathione protects healthy cells against oxidative damage and helps neutralize potentially carcinogenic substances. These functions suggest a possible preventive effect from a biological perspective.

Tumors can also benefit from antioxidant defense mechanisms. Many cancer cells alter their glutathione metabolism to survive adverse conditions. High glutathione levels can help cancer cells neutralize reactive oxygen species, cope with metabolic stress, and evade certain forms of programmed cell death. The effects depend on the tumor type and metabolic state, among other factors.

A review article has shown that glutathione-dependent signaling pathways can promote tumor growth, cancer cell survival, and drug resistance. Glutathione peroxidases and glutathione S-transferases, among other enzymes, contribute to these processes. Some of these enzymes can inactivate certain anticancer drugs or alter how cancer cells process them.

High glutathione levels in tumor cells have been associated with a poorer response to treatment in various types of cancer. Glutathione, therefore, does not have an exclusively protective role in the context of cancer.

Glutathione During Chemotherapy: Protection or Risk?

Researchers have also examined whether glutathione can reduce chemotherapy-related adverse effects, particularly peripheral neuropathy associated with platinum-based chemotherapy drugs.

In relevant studies, patients received glutathione primarily through intravenous administration at specified doses as part of their cancer treatment. These findings cannot be extrapolated to over-the-counter oral supplements.

A Cochrane review evaluated seven studies of glutathione, involving 387 participants. The authors found only modest, statistically borderline evidence of a neuroprotective effect. Most studies were small and relied primarily on subjective assessment scales; therefore, the evidence was insufficient to establish a benefit.

The American Society of Clinical Oncology explicitly advises against the use of glutathione to prevent chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy in patients receiving paclitaxel and carboplatin. This recommendation applies specifically to combination therapy and should not be automatically extended to all chemotherapy regimens. More generally, the guideline does not recommend any agent for preventing chemotherapy-induced neuropathy in the absence of high-quality evidence.

Another concern is the potential effect on cancer treatment itself. Some therapies work, at least in part, by generating reactive oxygen species. Antioxidants could theoretically protect tumor cells as well as healthy cells. A review article in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute addressed concerns about taking antioxidant dietary supplements during chemotherapy or radiation therapy.

Adverse Effects: Generally Well Tolerated Short Term, but Long-Term Data Are Lacking

In small studies involving healthy adults, oral glutathione was generally well tolerated at the doses and durations examined. The researchers did not report an increased incidence of serious adverse effects.

However, these findings do not establish the long-term safety of these treatments. Most studies included only a few dozen participants and lasted from a few weeks to 6 months. But rare adverse effects, risks in individuals with chronic conditions, and the consequences of taking high doses for years remain largely unknown.

Glutathione infusions also raise different safety concerns compared with oral capsules. In 2019, the US Food and Drug Administration issued a safety warning after several patients became ill following injections of contaminated glutathione. The agency reiterated its warning in August 2026. At least 30 patients developed fever, chills, and circulatory problems, including shock-like reactions, after intravenous glutathione injections. Some required hospitalization. Bacterial endotoxins in glutathione intended exclusively for use as a dietary supplement were considered the likely cause.

Reliable studies on the interactions between oral glutathione and medications are limited. However, the lack of evidence does not establish that supplementation is generally safe.

Particular caution is required during cancer treatment. Glutathione metabolism influences cellular redox regulation and may contribute to resistance to certain anticancer drugs.

Clinically relevant interactions have not been established for every formulation or medication, but they cannot be ruled out. Therefore, there is insufficient scientific evidence to support routinely adding glutathione supplements during cancer treatment. The National Cancer Institute’s dietary interactions guidance provides further information for patients considering dietary supplements during treatment.

Glutathione plays an important role in cellular protection and the body’s natural detoxification processes. Its biological functions have been extensively studied, and some human studies have shown that supplements can increase glutathione levels under certain conditions.

However, studies have not convincingly established whether these changes improve health, prevent diseases, or enhance detoxification.

The available evidence does not provide sufficient reasons for healthy individuals to routinely take glutathione supplements. A balanced diet is a more reasonable way to support the body’s own glutathione production. Adequate protein, along with plenty of vegetables and other plant-based foods, provides important building blocks for metabolism.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/tk-8/.title: Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/tk-8/.author: Morgan Chittum
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/tk-8/.text:
Jane Street, one of Wall Street’s leading quantitative trading firms, more than doubled its Nvidia holdings in the third quarter, according to regulatory filings released Thursday and reviewed by Fortune. The securities filings show the firm’s positions as of Sept. 30—just over six weeks before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The scandal has led Nvidia shares to fall nearly 13% over the past five days, reaching a 17-month low intraday Thursday. The regulatory disclosure, known as a 13F, doesn’t reveal exactly when Jane Street purchased the shares, or how much the firm has gained or lost on its bets though.

The market maker held 23.8 million shares worth about $5.44 billion at $228.38 at quarter end, according to the 13F. That’s over double the 11.8 million shares held, worth $2.4 billion, in the second quarter. Nvidia was its second-largest holding behind SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. Jane Street did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

The filings show what Jane Street held in late September, not what it owns now, and leave out short positions. Jane Street traders could, in theory, have shorted Nvidia after the reporting period ended and made money from the subsequent decline. The filings alone cannot tell us whether they did, though.

Options add another layer of complexity to this. The 13F also discloses that Jane Street holds a large amount of puts and calls, which are reported using the value of the underlying shares, rather than the market value of the options themselves. Those notional figures can make positions look far larger than the sums actually invested, while revealing little about the firm’s overall exposure once offsetting trades are taken into account. A large reported position, in other words, is not necessarily a huge directional bet.

Huang stepped down on Thursday after more than three decades at the helm of the company he started in 1993. In his place, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO. Huang’s departure comes days after bombshell media reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former exec at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence authorities suspect of working for Beijing.

In a message to employees on Sunday, Huang admitted that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized. He also said he supported an independent investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

The bad news didn’t stop there for Huang, though. Just three days later, the New York Times reported that the 63-year-old also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Reuters reported Thursday, citing two people familiar with the matter, that he had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, as well.

Reuters reported in August, citing a person familiar, that Jane Street had so far generated more than $40 billion in trading revenue in 2026. That surpassed its $39.6 billion total for all of 2025 and comfortably beat trading revenues for the nation’s largest banks.

Still, there have been some signs of cracks. That same Reuters report over the summer said Jane Street took a $15 billion hit, partly from its exposure to AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness. Situational Awareness, started by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, sold the bulk of its equities portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel after the market downturn triggered margin calls. Jane Street told employees that the drawdown had left its investment roughly flat for the year, though it remained profitable over the full period, per Reuters. Jane Street has not confirmed this report.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/10/lalota-ga.title: A tabloid scandal bankrolled a Long Island Democrat, mostly with out-of-district money. A Hollywood-linked tycoon backed a Republican who beat him.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/10/lalota-ga.author: Aris Alexander
https://fortune.com/2026/11/10/lalota-ga.text:
Leaked photos were supposed to end Chris Gallant’s campaign. Instead, they bankrolled it. After the New York Post published archived images of the Democrat modeling bondage gear for a San Francisco leather retailer, his fundraising took off.

In the quarter the photos surfaced, Gallant raised more than the incumbent. His October quarterly FEC report shows $929,825 in receipts for July through September. Rep. Nick LaLota reported about $609,000 for the same period.

The money bought a close loss, not a win. LaLota won a third term in New York’s 1st Congressional District last Tuesday, 51.1% to 48.9%, a margin of nearly 7,000 votes with 560 of 561 election districts reporting. Gallant first held out for absentee ballots, then conceded Wednesday. LaLota’s margin shrank from about 11 points in 2024 to about two, in a year Democrats swept to control of Congress.

Nor was the money especially local. A Fortune review of both campaigns’ raw 2026 FEC filings through Oct. 14 found that in-district donors accounted for about 16% of LaLota’s money from named individuals and just over a third of Gallant’s.

The post-leak surge followed the same pattern. In the 32 days after the Post story ran on Sept. 13, Gallant reported $276,055 in itemized contributions. Only $65,997 of it, about 24%, came from individuals inside NY-1, and almost half of that came from 62 donors in the Hamptons. Donors in Manhattan and California gave $73,606 combined, more than every donor inside NY-1 put together.

In NY-1, the people who funded the race and the people who voted in it were often different. Both campaigns were bankrolled mostly by donors outside the district, including major Wall Street, Hollywood and tech names. Even the men on the ballot live beyond its lines: both reside near Amityville, on Long Island’s South Shore, which means neither could vote for himself.

NY-1 runs from Suffolk County’s North Shore villages to the East End, with vineyards and farms on the North Fork and the Hamptons on the South Fork. In between lie Smithtown and Brookhaven, where suburban neighborhoods give way to woods and residents are largely commuters, law enforcement and small-business owners.

Each summer, the South Fork fills with the people who run Wall Street and corporate America. That makes the district one of the country’s busiest political ATMs, where financiers and industry titans host fundraisers for both parties. Suffolk County donors gave more than $45 million to campaigns in the 2020 cycle alone, according to OpenSecrets data CNBC cited.

In August, Vice President JD Vance raised more than $5 million from young Republican donors at the Southampton home of Omeed Malik, president of 1789 Capital and a prominent Trump donor.

LaLota, a Navy veteran and former Suffolk County elections commissioner, was first elected in 2022 to succeed Lee Zeldin and was re-elected in 2024, defeating former CNN anchor John Avlon by about 11 points. In that race, LaLota criticized Avlon for his dual residency in both Sag Harbor and Manhattan.

Gallant, 37, is an Army National Guard Black Hawk pilot, a former FAA air traffic controller at JFK, a former union leader and a volunteer firefighter. He won the June primary with about 63% of the vote, defeating Lukas Ventouras, a 25-year-old law student and district resident who had raised about $124,000, mostly in unitemized small-dollar donations. Gallant later picked up endorsements from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

After the Post story, Gallant’s attorney, Sara Azari, who previously represented former Rep. Eric Swalwell after misconduct allegations, confirmed the photos were authentic and consensual. Gallant told the New York Times he hoped it could be his “Kim Kardashian moment,” and the campaign began selling “Make Politics Sexy Again” merchandise. LaLota stuck to calling Gallant “weak and woke” and needling him for declining to debate.

Asked by Fortune about the surge, Gallant answered through Slingshot Strategies, a consulting firm that promises “a proven track record of shifting the conversation” for candidates facing “overwhelming odds” and “difficult fights.”

He said the Post story “backfired on them” and that the Times interview let voters see “a proud gay man who refused to be ashamed of his identity, and it resonated.” On LaLota’s outside money, he said, “I never had to rely on outside interests to try and buy this seat.” About a third of his own money from named donors came from inside the district.

LaLota cast the surge as a product of the controversy itself. “On the same days my opponent was backing out of debates, he was monetizing his BDSM and pornographic modeling past,” he said in a statement to Fortune. “Instead of boasting how kinky he is, as he did to the Times, he owes Long Islanders an explanation for choosing vanity and fundraising over debates and accountability.”

Fortune analyzed itemized contributions dated in 2026 in both campaigns’ raw FEC filings through Oct. 14, so the comparison covers the same stretch of the race for both candidates. Repeat donors were counted once, refunds subtracted and conduit entries adjusted so no gift was counted twice. The FEC does not require campaigns to name individuals who give $200 or less in a cycle, so those donors are excluded. Fortune placed donors inside or outside NY-1 based on the mailing city they listed, which may differ from where they vote. Individuals may give $3,500 per election this cycle, or $7,000 for the primary and general combined. Fortune tallied the filings by hand, then used Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, to clean the raw files and check the calculations.

LaLota had the bigger war chest. Through Oct. 14, he had raised $4.5 million and had $2.31 million in cash on hand. Gallant had raised $1.7 million and had $426,000 on hand.

The sharper contrast was where the money came from. Of the 785 named donors in LaLota’s 2026 filings, 29% listed mailing addresses in the district. Together they gave $207,161, only 16% of what he raised from named individuals. PACs and other committees supplied $1.18 million, about a quarter of his total for the cycle.

Gallant’s support was more local, but not by much. Of his 1,031 named donors in the 2026 raw file, 390 (38%) listed addresses in NY-1 totaling nearly $300,000, about a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals this year. Counting gifts from 2025, his itemized individual total for the cycle is $1.15 million.

Half of that in-district money, about $159,000, came from the Hamptons and Shelter Island, the East End enclaves where wealthy New Yorkers have long kept second homes. In East Hampton Town, half of the 22,562 housing units are no one’s usual residence, according to the Census Bureau’s 2020-2024 American Community Survey, which counts second homes as vacant. In Brookhaven, the figure is only about 9%.

Outside the district, 218 Manhattan donors gave Gallant $215,600 and 85 Californians gave about $93,000. Thirteen listed San Francisco.

The photos worked as a fundraiser, just not a local one. Between Sept. 13 and Oct. 14, Gallant reported 677 itemized contributions totaling $276,055: $229,050 from 484 individual donors and $47,005 from PACs, party committees and other sources.

That haul, all in the campaign’s final month of reporting, is about 16% of the $1.7 million he raised this cycle and nearly a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals in 2026. About a third of it arrived in the first four days after the leak.

On Sept. 15, two days after the leak, the New York State Democratic Committee transferred $25,025 to the campaign. That same day, the campaign paid Sara Azari, the celebrity attorney who specializes in crisis and media strategy.

Among the contributions that followed: $500 on Sept. 15 from Howard Sacarob, head of U.S. Tax at Royal Bank of Canada, and $3,500 on Oct. 4 from Ryan Fitzpatrick, Corcoran’s regional vice president for Downtown Manhattan.

On Oct. 7, the New York Times published its own analysis of the photo scandal. That day, Robert Saum, the World Bank Group’s regional country director for Eastern Europe, a role based in Kyiv, gave $1,000. He lists an Arlington, Va., address.

Steven Holley, COO of the New York investment manager Select Equity Group and former Sullivan & Cromwell partner, gave $1,000 on Oct. 9. Sacarob, Fitzpatrick and Holley all list New York City addresses, outside the district.

The San Francisco-based CEO of Mr. S Leather, the retailer behind the photos, gave $1,000 on Oct. 10.

Not all of Gallant’s best-known donors gave after the Post story. Fortune checked the names below against the dates in his filings.

Wall Street: Stephen Mandel, who founded the Greenwich hedge fund Lone Pine Capital, gave the $3,500 maximum on Sept. 14, the day after the story ran. Susan Mandel of Greenwich, listed as not employed, gave $3,500 the same day.

Old money and real estate: Katharine Rayner, the Cox Enterprises heiress whose fortune of about $4.9 billion (Forbes) rests on her estimated 17% stake in the family company, gave $3,500 on Sept. 15. She had also given $2,000 in July, and her cycle total is listed at the $3,500 limit.

Another maximum gift came on Sept. 26 from Michael Raynes, a developer who restores architecturally significant properties in Miami. In late 2022, he sold a historic estate in Southampton for $20 million. He lists a Miami Beach mailing address.

Wall Street: Charles Myers gave the $3,500 maximum at the end of 2025, when Gallant was still facing a primary. He is founder and chairman of Signum Global Advisors, a geopolitical research firm that advises financial institutions and touts “representation across the political spectrum.” He previously served as vice chairman at Evercore ISI and advised Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign.

Jason Carroll, co-founder of the high-frequency trading firm Hudson River Trading, gave $3,500 on Sept. 8, five days before the leak. Eric Knight, a senior trader at Jane Street, gave $7,000, covering both the primary and the general.

Hollywood and media: Kevin Huvane, co-chairman of Creative Artists Agency, gave $3,500 on June 30. Jeffrey Bewkes, the former Time Warner chairman and CEO who sold the company to AT&T in 2018, gave $3,500 on Aug. 12.

Local: Nancy Goroff, an organic chemist and former chair of Stony Brook University’s chemistry department, gave the maximum on June 29, days after Gallant’s primary win. Goroff lives in a modest New England saltbox overlooking Stony Brook Harbor, valued at about $1.1 million. She ran for a similarly drawn seat in 2020, losing to Lee Zeldin, now President Trump’s EPA administrator.

Goroff also backed “Team KCQ,” North Fork educator Kathryn Casey Quigley’s progressive bid to oust Suffolk County Democratic Chairman Rich Schaffer. Casey Quigley won about 43% of the weighted county committee vote on Sept. 22. Her campaign accused Schaffer of “backroom deals” with the local Conservative Party, which had harshly condemned Gallant’s photos.

Wall Street: Charles Schwab, founder of the brokerage bearing his name, a Fortune 500 company, gave LaLota $13,600 over the past two cycles, the maximum allowed. His mailing city: Palm Beach, Fla.

Crypto and defense: Faryar Shirzad, Coinbase’s chief policy officer and a deputy national security adviser under George W. Bush, gave $3,500 from a Washington, D.C., address. Palmer Luckey of Newport Beach, Calif., who founded defense contractor Anduril after selling Oculus to Facebook for about $2 billion, gave $7,000.

Global money: Leonard Blavatnik, the Ukrainian-born British American billionaire (Forbes) behind Access Industries, gave LaLota $3,500 in March. FEC reports list another $7,000 in aggregate from his wife, Emily.

“Though I have never met him, I appreciate his support,” LaLota said. His spokeswoman suggested Blavatnik may be drawn to LaLota because Russia’s Foreign Ministry put LaLota on a May 2023 list of 500 Americans barred from the country, a distinction the congressman “wears as a badge of honor.”

Blavatnik’s recent contributions also include Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and the Equality PAC, which backs LGBTQ+ candidates.

His contribution forms give an address of 40 W. 57th St. in Manhattan, about 105 miles from the estate the press calls his.

The July 2025 sale of 408 Further Lane in Amagansett, which Behind the Hedges reported as the most expensive residential sale in Hamptons history, lists Brise Lointaine LLC as the new owner.

The seller, Terry Semel, ran Warner Bros. when Stanley Kubrick filmed his masked Long Island society for the studio. Semel had bought the property from Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman in 2005 for $43 million.

Property records from the real estate data service PropertyShark, reviewed by Fortune, list the arm’s-length price as $115,000, three zeros shy of the reported $115 million. East Hampton’s 2026 tax roll still billed Semel’s Windsor Digital Studio LLC. The town assessor’s office said it did not update the roll until July 2026.

The East Hampton Town Clerk’s office confirmed Brise Lointaine LLC’s ownership to Fortune and said deed updates take “very long” to process, along with the Suffolk County Clerk’s office.

Press accounts, though not the paperwork, identify the buyer as LaLota donor Len Blavatnik: Behind the Hedges, citing a source, and The Real Deal. Blavatnik owns Warner Music and holds a stake in A24, the arthouse studio behind Lady Bird (2017), Queer (2024), the gay BDSM romance Pillion (2026) and Backrooms (2026).

The tabloid framing of the race borrowed from Eyes Wide Shut (1999), but the sex and the masks were bait. Kubrick’s real horror was a gated order where wealth and power circulate in a closed circle, insulated from consequences.

In his year, the guest list was paper: electronic filing stayed voluntary for most committees until 2000, so a donor was a scanned page, not a spreadsheet. In NY-1, the circle is no secret.

In an age of metadata, AI-scanned social feeds and Flock cameras, nobody wears a mask for long. The leather shoot was archived, authenticated by an attorney and sold back to voters as merchandise. Every FEC filing is a digital fossil Kubrick’s guests would never have left behind.

The economics were another matter. LaLota raised about 84 cents of every named dollar from outside the district; Gallant, nearly two-thirds. What stayed masked on Election Day was not Gallant’s leather photos but the money, and how much of it came from outside NY-1.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ch.title: Nvidia abruptly changed how it reported revenue in Singapore last year, adding to questions about its relationship with Megaspeed
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ch.author: Sasha Rogelberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-ch.text:
A sudden change in how Nvidia reported some of its financial results last year is getting renewed attention, raising questions about its relationship with Megaspeed, a major Nvidia client at the time and now at the center of chip smuggling allegations.

The financial change under scrutiny involves Nvidia’s accounting for revenue from Singapore, where Megaspeed is based.

Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of the semiconductor chip giant on Thursday, following stunning revelations of his affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation), a woman suspected of being an operative for China. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress will lead the company in the interim, Nvidia announced on Thursday.

Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest buyers in Asia, has been suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced chips to China, in violation of U.S. export laws. Megaspeed, and its Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatric, moved at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China, tech news site The Information has reported.

Singapore authorities said on Thursday that they investigated Megaspeed and its former executive Alice Huang beginning in February 2025 and did not find sufficient evidence of espionage. However, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country. The U.S. is also investigating Megaspeed for export control violations. Jensen Huang has previously said there is no evidence of Nvidia chips being smuggled to China, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.

In June 2025, Nvidia added Megaspeed to its internal block list, prohibiting sales to the company, according to the Wall Street Journal. Around the same time, Nvidia stopped reporting revenue from Singapore, one of the five geographic areas Nvidia had previously listed in its breakdown of global revenues (they were U.S., Singapore, Taiwan, China, and “Other”).

In the fiscal quarter ending in July 2025, Nvidia reported $10.2 billion in revenue from Singapore, 22% of the company’s total revenue, and an 81% increase in year-over-year revenue from the country. In the next quarter’s earnings report, for the three months ending in October 2025, Singapore had disappeared from Nvidia’s geographic revenue breakdown, which now listed only four markets: U.S., Taiwan, China, and Other.

According to the October 2025 earnings report, Nvidia was now separating out markets based on “location of the customers’ headquarters” instead of “customer billing location.” The change was made even though Nvidia’s previous earnings reports had clearly stated that “customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere.”

Nvidia did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment, including an inquiry if the change in how it reported its earnings was at all connected to it adding Megaspeed to its block list.

Shiva Rajgopal, a professor of accounting and auditing at Columbia Business School, told Fortune correlation is not causation, and it is impossible to say with just public information whether concerns around Megaspeed’s export control adherence or Alice Huang’s alleged espionage caused Nvidia to change how it reported revenue. However, he noted, Nvidia’s changes in the filings will no doubt become part of the Department of Justice or Department of Commerce’s investigations into Nvidia’s export control compliance.

“The timing is curious,” Rajgopal said. “Even if it is not curious, people are going to raise questions given all this information now.”

Auditors will likely look at what Nvidia knew about where the Megaspeed chips were ending up, how Nvidia checked and documented customer end-use, and if Huang’s affair was related to Nvidia’s business with Megaspeed. But they will also look at whether investors were given an accurate picture of the risks associated with potential smuggling in China and Southeast Asia. Rajgopal made it clear that as CFO, Kress’ role in how finances were disclosed publicly, will certainly be scrutinized, but based on public filings alone, there does not appear to be evidence at this time showing Kress was aware of whether an earnings reporting change could have potentially been related to Megaspeed.

“I wouldn’t say Kress must have known,” Rajgopal said. “These are just financial statements. Nothing is illegal. It’s disclosed.”

Rajgopal argued Kress’s biggest challenge has little to do with the company’s past or immediate finances. Finance executives who take interim chief executive roles in tech companies rarely stay because they lack the buy-in of the tech community, he said. Nvidia’s priorities will soon shift from sustaining its financial momentum today to working to recreate or build upon the forward vision Huang gave the company, which is a decidedly different role than a finance head.

“A CFO running a tech company is not a good idea,” Rajgopal said, “especially something that’s so deeply tech-heavy.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/a-dark-da.title: ‘A dark day’: Jensen Huang’s sex drive threatens to pop the AI bubble, and the industry isn’t sure what’s next
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/a-dark-da.author: Emily Forlini
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/a-dark-da.text:
Welcome to Eye on AI. Emily Forlini here, filling in for Beatrice Nolan. In today’s issue:

Before we get to the news, can I just say, you are not going to want to miss this year’s edition of Fortune Brainstorm AI San Francisco.

We have an exceptional line-up of speakers for you: OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman will both be onstage. Once the closest of partners, their two companies are increasingly, competitors, so I’m eager to hear how differently they see the road ahead. AI pioneers Fei-Fei Li, now of World Labs, as well as Andrew Ng, now of LearnVector, will be discussing their view of AI’s future too. Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora will talk about AI and cybersecurity. Greylock partner Reid Hoffman, CapitalG’s Jill Chase, and Kleiner Perkins’ Mamoon Hamid and Ilya Fushman will weigh in on where the money is going. Recursive Superintelligence’s Richard Socher will talk about RSI and automating AI research.

Plus, we’ve got Nick Fox from Google. We’ve got Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao. We’ve got Cerebras’ Andrew Feldman, Vanta’s Christina Cacioppo, Unconventional AI’s Naveen Rao, Brex’s Pedro Franceschi, Maven Clinic’s Kate Ryder, Box’s Aaron Levie, Atlassian’s Mike Cannon-Brookes, New Work Foundation’s Clara Shih, Twilio’s Khozema Shipchandler, Rubrik’s Bipul Sinha, Harvey’s Winston Weinberg, Dynamic Creatures’ Marc Theermann, SendCutSend’s Jim Belosic, Apptronik’s Jeff Cardenas, Accenture Song’s Ndidiamaka Oteh, and Senra Systems’ Jordan Black. It’s going to be epic. So please join me and many of my Fortune colleagues at the St. Regis in San Francisco on December 7th and 8th. You can apply to attend here.

Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation as Nvidia CEO may be the biggest story in AI we’ve seen since the launch of ChatGPT almost exactly four years ago. Not only because it’s a stunning, swift downfall, but also because it’s the end of the first major phase of AI development as we’ve known it. At Fortune, we’ve been following the story closely over the past two days. You can check out our coverage by following the links in the “Fortune on AI” section of this newsletter.

It turns out, one man might just be able to single-handedly pop the AI bubble by not keeping it in his pants, with not one but three affairs—at least that we know about so far. But in all seriousness, this is a sad story. It’s a visceral betrayal for Huang’s family, his wife of 41 years, Lori, and their two children, both of whom work at Nvidia.

Huang has disappointed just about everybody in his orbit, from shareholders to customers, to people who held him up as a role model. Martin Casado, an investor at the prominent firm a16z called today a “dark, dark day,” and a “horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world.”

“It’s very sad by every dimension,” Penny Herscher, a longtime executive in the semiconductor industry, told me today. “It’s sad for his family, for the employees, for the customers. Jensen’s a remarkable person, and it’s sad to see such a remarkable person in this horrible situation—self-inflicted, but horrible.”

“I am extremely sad today as I see Nvidia without Jensen Huang,” one Nvidia employee posted. Several others have made similar public remarks.

My hunch is Nvidia will prevail, given the immense amount of money and geopolitical stability hanging on the health of its GPU business. But there will likely be a period of uncertainty, both in the boardroom and in Washington. America’s position at the top of the AI industry hangs in the balance, and stricter regulation may be more likely, especially given the Democratic Party’s sweeping midterms wins. As Jeremy Kahn wrote in Tuesday’s edition of Eye on AI, Huang had been a leading voice opposing both U.S. export controls on AI technology and government regulations on open models, and now that community has lost their main champion.

“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day!” posted Clement Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, the open source repository Nvidia acquired for nearly $13 billion in September. “But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!”

There is much more to the story yet to unfold. Huang has agreed to appear before Congress. More investigations are likely to ensue. Meanwhile, rumors are swirling that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei may have orchestrated Huang’s downfall. Amodei has warned that open models can serve as uncontrolled weapons that bad actors can harness to incur serious societal harm, and is in favor of industry-wide slowdowns. I’m not quick to believe that theory, mostly because there is not yet any proof, but also Anthropic had every incentive to wait until after its IPO if it was going to take down Huang. The dark cloud his ousting has cast over the AI industry threatens Anthropic’s valuation as investors enter arguably the greatest period of instability we’ve seen yet in AI.

“My expectation is a 10–15% valuation haircut, potentially approaching 20% if Nvidia’s leadership crisis raises doubts about its $10 billion anchor commitment,” Jonathan Tower, managing partner at the VC firm Catapult, tells Fortune. “Anthropic’s underlying business hasn’t changed overnight, but investor confidence has. I expect the anchor to hold, but investors will demand a greater margin of safety. The larger question is whether this marks the beginning of a broader repricing of AI risk.”

The big unknown is how the stock market will react. Nvidia shares are trading down 4% at the bell today, a modest dip.

As far as silver linings go, there will be a few winners to come out of Huang’s downfall. Nervous Nvidia customers could place bigger orders with other chipmakers, such as Google, Amazon, AMD, and Broadcom. Another winner could be Nvidia’s next CEO, who stands to score the role of a lifetime, and perhaps propel the company into a new and even more successful era. That search is already underway. But given the allegations against Huang at this time, particularly that he may be complicit in funneling chips to China via Megaspeed, the shell company helmed by his paramour Alice Huang—there could always be more executives involved.

The biggest story in AI since ChatGPT is far from over.

With that, here’s more AI news.

Emily Forlini
emily.forlini@fortune.com
@emilyforlini

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.title: As Nvidia reels from Huang's affairs, who stands to gain?
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.author: Lee Ying Shan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.text:
Nvidia’s leadership crisis is creating an opening for its rivals — and a major partner.

AMD to Broadcom and even TSMC sees greater investor interest as they rotate out of Nvidia.

Nvidia
’s leadership crisis is creating an opening for its biggest rivals as well as partners, as investors bet that Jensen Huang’s departure could loosen the AI chip giant’s grip on an industry it has long dominated.

From AMD
 to Broadcom
 and even partner TSMC
, chipmakers are emerging as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval, with market watchers pointing to a possible redistribution of manufacturing capacity and a narrowing of Nvidia’s technological lead.

“What you’re seeing in markets now is a bit of a rotation into other advanced chip design companies, on the assumption that this will enable other companies effectively to catch up,” said Mark Franklin, head of multi-asset solutions for Asia at Manulife Investment Management.

That shift comes as Nvidia grapples with the fallout from Huang’s resignation, following revelations about his multiple affairs including with a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy.

Huang’s departure could give competitors an opportunity to close the gap as Nvidia navigates leadership uncertainty, Franklin highlighted, adding that the rotation was already helping fuel positive momentum in other semiconductor stocks.

Farzin Azam, managing director of equities trading at Mizuho Americas, said the shift was evident on trading desks, with investors moving toward chipmakers less exposed to Nvidia’s management turmoil.

“Names such as TSMC, names such as Broadcom, names such as Advanced Micro will come as winners of this because they don’t have this overhang of a management disruption,” Azam told CNBC.

Nvidia shares have plunged 11% so far this week, while rivals AMD and Broadcom have gained 30% and 24%, respectively.

TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia’s most advanced processors, has also rallied 11% over the same period, as it stands to benefit, irrespective of which chip designer gains or loses. A rotation away from AI names perceived as risky also positions TSMC as a relatively safer play for those bullish on the overall theme.

The rotation away from Nvidia has also extended into less speculative corners of the semiconductor industry, including analog chipmakers such as Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Infineon, as investors adopt a more defensive stance, he said.

Texas Instruments has climbed about 13% this week, while Analog Devices and Germany’s Infineon have advanced 12% and 14%, respectively.

Beyond the immediate market reaction, Huang’s exit could fundamentally reshape competition across the AI supply chain, according to Dylan Patel, chief executive at semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis.

Patel said Huang had personally cultivated relationships with manufacturers and component suppliers, helping Nvidia secure scarce production capacity ahead of rivals.

That advantage could now come under pressure as companies including Google and Amazon strive to expand AI chip production.

The two hyperscalers were already gaining ground in securing supply-chain capacity relative to Nvidia, Patel said, and could accelerate those efforts without Huang’s influence over suppliers.

“If Nvidia can’t muster the supply chain, then technology is the only competitive advantage. And without Jensen, can they maintain technology advantages? Given they’re only a year ahead of their biggest competitors, it’s not like the gap is massive,” Patel said.

The challenge is particularly acute as hyperscalers increasingly develop proprietary AI chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, while AMD and other semiconductor companies race to capture a larger slice of the market.

Yet the upheaval doesn’t necessarily signal an end to the broader AI investment boom.

Franklin noted that major technology companies are projecting higher AI spending in 2027, with further increases possible in 2028, signaling the investment cycle remains structurally intact even as investors reassess which companies stand to benefit.

The bigger question is whether growing competition and the proliferation of open-source technologies eventually commoditize AI capabilities, putting pressure on chip prices and investment returns, he said.

For Nvidia, the immediate outlook may depend less on its earnings than on whether its next leadership team can reassure investors.

Azam said the stock appeared inexpensive relative to its earnings growth prospects, but warned that ongoing investigations and management uncertainty could limit any sustained recovery.

He expects Nvidia’s earnings due Nov. 17 to remain strong, with investors likely to focus more closely on management’s plans for navigating the crisis.

The result could be a reshuffling of winners within the semiconductor industry, with Franklin saying that investors were becoming more comfortable staying invested while rotating and diversifying their portfolios, instead of abandoning the market altogether.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-s.title: Why Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investors
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-s.author: Greg Iacurci
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-s.text:
Nvidia stock dropped sharply during early trading Thursday after Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO.

Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China. Reports also said he had a separate extramarital relationship with a direct report, Kimberly Powell, the chipmaker’s vice president of healthcare.

Many popular ETFs have a roughly 6% to 8% stake in Nvidia.

Nvidia stock plunged in early trading on Thursday after Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO. Huang co-founded the chipmaker 33 years ago and built it into a behemoth at the center of the artificial intelligence boom.

Since Nvidia
 is among the largest publicly traded companies by market capitalization, its stock is, by default, a substantial holding in several popular mutual funds and exchange-traded funds.

Many investors therefore hold the chipmaker’s stock in their portfolios — and may worry about their exposure.

But mutual fund and ETF investors’ exposure to Nvidia stock is likely relatively low, data shows — and any big swings in its stock price are likely to have a fairly muted impact on investor portfolios, financial advisors said.

“This is just a very contemporary, sensational case of risk,” said Philip Chao, a certified financial planner and chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth, based in Cabin John, Maryland. “But that is part and parcel to stock investing.”

Read coverage of CNBC’s 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors:

Nvidia’s stock fell more than 10% early Thursday on news of Huang’s resignation.

Huang stepped down following his admission to having an affair with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China, and after reports that he had a separate extramarital relationship with a direct report, Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare at Nvidia. Reuters also reported Thursday that Huang had an “intimate relationship” with a second Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter.

The stock has since pared some of those losses, and was down more than 5% as of roughly 2:50 p.m. EST.

However, investors “shouldn’t worry” about their exposure, Chao said.

For example, if Nvidia were 5% of an overall fund’s holdings and the stock dropped 10%, the fund’s value would decline 0.5%, assuming all else was equal, Chao said.

“It’s not a big deal,” he said. “Most people are just reacting to the sensational aspect of this [news].”

A flash poll of members of CNBC’s Financial Advisor Council and Financial Advisor 100 on Thursday showed 18 respondents are planning to hold their Nvidia allocations steady in client portfolios. Three are increasing their stake, and six do not own the chipmaker. None of the respondents are decreasing their ownership. The online poll, conducted from 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, was sent to 122 firms and 27 responded.

Let’s look at some of the most popular stock ETFs for some specific examples of why investors likely have limited exposure.

Nvidia stock is the largest holding in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO
).

The fund, as the name suggests, tracks the performance of the S&P 500 U.S. stock index and had a market capitalization of $1.7 trillion as of Sept. 30, according to the most recent Vanguard data.

On that date, Nvidia stock accounted for about 8.4% of the entire portfolio.

Assuming that weighting carried forward to today, a 5% decline in Nvidia’s stock would only cause the fund to lose about 0.42% of its value, all else equal, according to an analysis by Experiential Wealth for CNBC.

A 10% decline would lead the fund to drop by 0.84%, according to the analysis.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ
) is an ETF that tracks the performance of the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index.

The fund held about $473.8 billion as of Nov. 10, according to Invesco data.

Nvidia was its second-largest holding, at 6.8% of the overall portfolio. Apple was No. 1, at about 8.4%.

Based on that weighting, the fund would lose just 0.34% of its value if Nvidia’s stock lost 5%, all else equal, according to the Experiential Wealth analysis. A 10% Nvidia loss would equate to a 0.68% loss for the overall fund.

Nvidia stock was the largest holding in the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI
).

The fund had $1.8 trillion as of Oct. 31, according to Vanguard.

Nvidia stock accounted for about 7.13% of the fund, as of Sept. 30.

According to that weighting, the overall fund would lose roughly 0.36% of its value if Nvidia’s stock lost 5%, all else equal, according to Experiential Wealth’s analysis. A 10% Nvidia loss would equate to a roughly 0.71% loss for the overall fund.

“There’s a difference between [stock] volatility and substantial losses you cannot recover,” Chao said.

The Nvidia stock moves fall in the former camp, not the latter, he said.

Across all mutual funds and ETFs, “large growth” funds have the largest average weighting to Nvidia stock, according to Morningstar data. These are funds that tend to hold shares in fast-growing U.S. stocks with large market capitalizations.

Large growth funds had an average 10.34% weighting to Nvidia stock as of Wednesday, according to Morningstar. Funds that focus on the technology sector had a 7.31% average weighting to the stock, the second-largest exposure, it found.

Of course, Nvidia stock doesn’t exist in a vacuum, financial experts said.

“A 10% Nvidia drop would usually pull down other semiconductor and AI-linked names, such as AMD ... and Micron,” Chao said.

And that means mutual fund and ETF losses could be larger than Nvidia holdings might otherwise suggest, he said.

“This event could easily add further pressure to already stretched AI-related stock valuations,” Renée Friedman, global head of research at EXANTE, a brokerage firm, wrote in an e-mail.

However, that’s not a foregone conclusion, experts said.

The S&P 500 index and the Nasdaq Composite
, for example, were down slightly for the day as of about 2:50 p.m. EST.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-j.title: Cramer says Jensen Huang betrayed Nvidia shareholders. How to pick up the pieces
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-j.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-j.text:
CNBC’s Jim Cramer criticized former Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday for putting the chipmaker’s future at risk.

“Did he betray you, the shareholders?” Cramer asked. “Yes. End of story.”

Huang resigned Thursday morning following reports of an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Hours later, Reuters reported that he had an “intimate relationship” with a second employee. These revelations came days after Huang admitted to an affair with an executive at a Singapore-based cloud computing company whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China. Longtime CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO of Nvidia. Cramer said Huang’s departure was necessary to protect Nvidia from further fallout.

Shares ended Thursday down more than 4%, but at its lows of the morning, the stock was off over 14%. The decline in Thursday’s session brings Nvidia’s losses this year to 12%.

While questions remain about what comes next for the AI chipmaker, Cramer argued that Nvidia’s future extends beyond the executive who helped build it into one of the world’s most valuable companies. “There won’t be a better Nvidia, just a different one [without Huang],” Cramer said, envisioning a company that is better organized and more disciplined about its investments.

Under Huang, Nvidia built an extensive equity investment portfolio that included a $5 billion investment in Intel
 in 2025 and a $2 billion investment in AI cloud provider CoreWeave
 earlier this year. The investments, and many others, were part of Huang’s strategy to strengthen Nvidia’s position across the AI industry.

During the CNBC Investing Club’s Morning Meeting livestream Thursday, Cramer recalled urging Kress to reduce the company’s stakes in Intel and CoreWeave, only to be told that Huang preferred to maintain them. Cramer suggested that new leadership could take a more disciplined approach to capital allocation, potentially cashing in on some of those investments and returning the proceeds to shareholders through even bigger stock buybacks.

Cramer expressed confidence in Kress, praising her deep understanding of Nvidia’s operations and financials. He argued that the longtime finance chief is well positioned to provide stability as the company navigates the investigations surrounding Huang, which stretch from the boardroom to Washington, D.C.

Nvidia didn’t respond to CNBC’s request for comment on Cramer’s remarks. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not respond to CNBC’s request for comment.

Going forward, Nvidia’s underlying business remains strong, Cramer said, pointing to its substantial cash reserves and expectations for a robust earnings report Tuesday evening. But he cautioned that even strong quarterly results might not be enough to reassure investors during this time of lingering uncertainty.

Investigations into Huang’s conduct and possible violations of U.S. chip export restrictions could result in sanctions that hurt Nvidia’s international business. Meanwhile, competitors, including Advanced Micro Devices
, are making progress with their own AI chips, potentially threatening Nvidia’s market dominance. AMD shares surged almost 6% on Thursday, extending their winning streak to five straight sessions.

Those risks have prompted Cramer to take a more cautious approach to Nvidia stock, particularly after the substantial gains shares have delivered over the years for Cramer’s Charitable Trust, the portfolio of 32 stocks managed by the Club. On Tuesday, as Huang’s future at Nvidia looked more and more in doubt, the Club downgraded Nvidia to a hold-equivalent rating.

“Don’t ever turn a successful investment into an unsuccessful trade,” he said, urging longtime shareholders sitting on big gains to consider taking some profits. “You don’t want to give up all of your gains if the stock falls further. It fell further today after many of the analysts jumped ship and downgraded the stock from buy to hold. There could be more ahead.”

At the same time, Cramer cautioned against giving up on Nvidia altogether, pointing to the company’s extensive engineering expertise and multiyear product roadmap as reasons to believe it can continue competing at the forefront of AI without Huang.

The “Mad Money” host also drew parallels to Apple’s
 leadership transition from Steve Jobs to Tim Cook, suggesting that Nvidia could benefit from a similarly capable successor who brings a different management style without sacrificing the company’s technological edge.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/us-india.title: Inside India newsletter: Trump's poll setback fuels hope for U.S.-India trade deal by year end
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/us-india.author: Priyanka Salve
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/us-india.text:
After the loss in the midterm polls, U.S. President Donald Trump is keener to make a trade announcement, and India is the most likely candidate.

Democrats are mounting pressure on Trump’s tariff policies.

The trade deal could be signed in December, on the sidelines of the G20 summit in December, where Modi and Trump will be present, experts said.

This report is from this week’s “Inside India” newsletter, which brings you timely, insightful news and market commentary on the emerging powerhouse — Subscribe today

Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from India.

Welcome to the latest edition of “Inside India” — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world’s fastest-growing large economy.

After months of being weighed down by high energy prices, trade uncertainty and foreign investor exodus, India has had plenty to celebrate this Diwali. Foreign investors returned to its market in November and, now, it seems the long-awaited U.S.-India trade deal could be around the corner.

Experts say that the two sides are closer to signing on the dotted line following the U.S. midterm election results than they were before.

Any thoughts on today’s newsletter? Share them with the team.

The U.S.-India trade deal, which has been riddled with uncertainty since February, is likely to get a final push to the finish line, thanks to U.S. President Donald Trump’s electoral setback in the midterm polls.

Experts told CNBC that Trump could lean toward closing some of the pending trade deals to promote them as policy achievements to the American public, and the pact with New Delhi is a “prime candidate.”

They added that Trump and Indian Prime Minister Modi are likely to sign the trade pact when they meet in December for the G20 leaders meeting, as negotiations have largely concluded.

The U.S.-India trade talks “are far along and there seems to be a gentlemen’s agreement between Trump and Modi” that the deal should be concluded when the two meet at Mar-a-Lago in December, Mark Linscott, former assistant U.S. trade representative and senior advisor at the U.S.-India Strategic Partnership Forum, told CNBC.

Trump has used tariffs as a pressure tactic to clinch trade deals with several countries, even as that approach has drawn the ire of his political opponents who have flagged that export levies have increased costs for American households. Cost of living was the top concern for American voters in the midterms.

“The election was a verdict on the cost of living, and tariffs are now a liability the President cannot defend on the numbers,” Ronak D. Desai, visiting fellow at Hoover Institution of Stanford University, told CNBC.

“Congress will not hand him an affordability win, but a trade deal is one he can announce on his own,” Desai said, adding that an announcement of a deal with India is “more likely than it was before the election.”

India’s commerce and external affairs ministries and the U.S. Trade Representative’s Office did not respond to CNBC’s requests for comment.

When asked about how U.S. midterm election results will reshape the ties with New Delhi, a spokesperson for India’s Ministry of External Affairs on Tuesday said that the relationship between the two countries “enjoys bipartisan support in the United States.”

Trump insists Americans do not share the burden of his tariffs, but according to estimates from Tax Foundation, a nonprofit, the duties raised the average U.S. household’s tax burden by $820 in 2026 and $1,000 in 2025.

As a result, the Democrats, within days of taking control of both the houses of Congress are preparing to challenge Trump’s signature tariff policy. A trade deal at this time could be seen as a validation of Trump’s tariffs-led approach to business.

“The president may lean more into getting deals done – seeing them as policy achievements that he can promote to the American public,” Atman Trivedi, partner at Washington-based DGA Albright Stonebridge Group, told CNBC. He added that the Trump administration would like to get a deal done with India by the G20 leaders’ summit in December.

While American voters are more affected by import duties on Canadian goods, experts said that a trade deal with India could blunt criticism about tariffs as an effective bargaining chip.

In February, Trump announced a deal with India, claiming that New Delhi had agreed to “Buy American” at a much higher level after the U.S. agreed to slash tariffs to 18%. Trump had earlier imposed a 25% tariff on imports from India, along with an additional 25% duty on goods from New Delhi for buying Russian oil.

But that deal has since been awaiting final approval, especially after the Supreme Court struck down Trump tariffs, giving India space to demand preferential tariffs that give it an edge over competitors.

While American and Indian officials at the start of October said that the negotiations had reached an impasse, Trump on Oct. 20 said that the two sides were “pretty close” to a final deal. As per Indian media reports, the country’s Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal confirmed that discussions on the trade deal had largely “concluded.”

“We have been hearing for weeks that a deal is close to be settled,” Aryan D’Rozario, associate fellow and chair on India and Emerging Asia Economics at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CNBC, adding that Modi’s visit to the G20 summit in December “will provide the perfect stage to formalize an agreement.”

India as an AI hedge? The country’s stocks could see robust inflows as markets globally tank
The Indian stock market is emerging as an attractive hedge as investors seek refuge from a brutal sell-off in the artificial intelligence trade, making it a strong contender for global capital. If global investors “neutralize” their underweight positions on India, it could lead to foreign inflows of $115 billion, as per JPMorgan.

India billionaire Adani’s firm buys Dutch firm Evos to gain foothold in Europe
Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone
, India’s largest port operator, will acquire Netherlands-headquartered Evos from Igneo Infrastructure Partners in an all-cash deal at an enterprise value of 2.56 billion euros.

Nov. 12: India CPI inflation for October.

Nov.15: India unemployment rate for October.

S. midterm election results. India's stock market is emerging as an attractive hedge as investors seek refuge from a brutal sell-off in the artificial intelligence trade.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.title: Watchdog Coverage Prompts Texas Oil Regulator to Walk Back Restrictive Public Comment Policy
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.author: By Martha Pskowski, Texas Reporter
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/11112.text:
Many of our impact case studies cover ongoing stories that Inside Climate News continues to actively cover. The impact reflected here is current as of publication and may be updated as the situation develops.

I have watched every open meeting of the Railroad Commission of Texas, the state’s oil and gas regulatory agency, since I started reporting for Inside Climate News.

Every month, the three elected commissioners meet in Austin to vote on agency business, and members of the public can register for a three-minute slot to give public comments. Concerns about conflicts of interest have long plagued the Railroad Commission. Residents have told me their best opportunity to be heard is speaking directly to the commissioners during these open meetings.

At the August meeting, Commissioner Wayne Christian introduced a new public participation policy that had not been circulated. The commissioners hastily passed the new policy, which removed the standing public comment period from the monthly agenda. Going forward, public comment would be at the discretion of the commissioners.

We were the first to break the story. Outlets across the state republished our reporting, and I appeared on Austin’s local NBC station, KXAN, to discuss the story. Backlash from concerned citizens and elected officials promptly followed.

State Rep. Drew Darby, a Republican, urged the Railroad Commission to restore the original policy. Darby, who chairs the House Energy Resources Committee, called on Commissioner Christian to testify before an oversight hearing of his committee on September 15. Christian didn’t show at the hearing and doubled down on his position in a letter.

Then on November 10, after months of public pressure, Christian reversed his position. He informed Rep. Darby in a letter that the commissioners will restore the original public participation policy at their December open meeting. Once again there will be a standing agenda item for public comment every month.

Rep. Darby praised the decision in a press release. “Numerous constituents called my office expressing serious concerns with removal of the standalone comment period.”

Incoming Railroad Commissioner Jon Rosenthal, the first Democrat to win a seat on the commission in more than three decades, also reacted to the situation after my first story was published. He has expressed support for protecting the public comment period and making the agency more accessible.

With public comment restored, I will continue attending Railroad Commission open meetings and listening to the Texans who travel from around the state to participate.

Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.

That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.

Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.

Donations from readers like you fund every aspect of what we do. If you don’t already, will you support our ongoing work, our reporting on the biggest crisis facing our planet, and help us reach even more readers in more places?

Please take a moment to make a tax-deductible donation. Every one of them makes a difference.

https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.title: Major Microsoft Outlook outage disrupts services in 74 countries
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.text:
Microsoft Outlook suffered a major outage across the world Thursday, with tens of thousands of users struggling to access their email as the company said it was working "aggressively" to reduce the impact.

The disruption, which Microsoft attributed to "elevated load" on its infrastructure, dragged on for much of the US workday and also affected other company products such as Teams and the AI assistant Copilot.

The disruption went global within a span of an hour, knocking out Microsoft products in 74 countries and territories, outage tracker Downdetector reported.

A map posted by Downdetector on X showed the outage affected users across the Americas, and parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.

Microsoft initially said it was investigating outage reports "in the Americas," but later confirmed that the issue apparently affected "Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region."

Microsoft 365 is the company's cloud-based subscription service that includes popular applications such as Outlook and Teams.

"We've determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors," the company wrote on X.

"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," it added.

"We've paused all deployments, we're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service."

In the United States, around 130,000 users reported issues with Outlook shortly after 1 pm Eastern Time (1800 GMT), according to Downdetector.

Outage reports have since declined, with about 37,000 users reporting experiencing issues with Outlook as of 6 pm Eastern Time (2300 GMT).

Thousands of users also reported issues with Teams and Copilot, according to Downdetector.

As the outage dragged on for hours, Microsoft posted a series of updates on X, detailing continued but unsuccessful efforts to restore full service.

In one update shortly after 6 pm Eastern Time, Microsoft said it was "observing limited recovery" as it sought to route user traffic away from affected servers.

"As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect," the company added.

The disruption was blamed on "elevated load" on its infrastructure, which Microsoft attributed to "eLevated load," it said. Microsoft says it is working "aggressively" to reduce the impact.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Pope Leo XIV meets abuse victims in Peru, says Church must make 'amends'
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
Pope Leo XIV met six victims of clerical abuse in Peru on Thursday, including some linked to the once-powerful and now-disbanded Catholic society, Sodalitium Christianae Vitae.

The US-born pope is on a nostalgic return to the nation he calls his "homeland", and knows the abuse scandal well from the nearly two decades he worked in Peru as a missionary and bishop.

Leo spent over an hour with the victims, meeting "each person individually, listening to their stories of suffering and their pain," and "thanked them for their invaluable testimony," the Vatican said.

Together, "they reflected on how to foster a shift in mindset – by listening to victims, seeking the truth, pursuing paths towards healing, and committing to the creation of safe environments," it said.

Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (SCV), a lay society founded in the 1970s that was widespread in Latin America, was shut down in 2025 by Leo's predecessor Francis after years of allegations of sexual, physical and psychological abuse, as well as corruption.

Before he was elected Pope Leo XIV, Robert Francis Prevost was the bishop designated to hear from SCV victims, who said he was supportive of their claims.

In an address to bishops earlier Thursday, Leo described the "pain" caused by Catholic clerical abuse and said the Church must make "amends" to victims and foster "a culture of prevention and protection."

Clerical abuse, a global scourge, was "a reality that has caused us so much pain," the 71-year-old said.

In April 2026, the Vatican announced plans to set up a "listening channel" in Lima for victims, and use assets seized from the lay movement to compensate them.

Renzo Orbegozo, a 50-year-old victim, told AFP they were seeking "comprehensive reparation."

"Many require psychological and medical support, as well as social reintegration – all of which, ultimately, translates into financial assistance," he said.

On the eve of the pope's South America tour, the US-based non-profit Bishop Accountability presented a list in Lima of 77 members of the Peruvian clergy it said had been publicly accused of abusing minors.

Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of the group, called on Leo to implement "zero tolerance" of abusers.

The head of the 1.4 billion Catholics has not shied away from tackling sensitive political and social topics during his three-nation Latin American tour.

Pilgrim Pedro Campos said Leo was "a member of our country who ... knows the needs of all Peruvians."

At a speech later to some 40,000 people on the challenges facing Peruvians, the pontiff slammed "machismo" attitudes and said violence against women was "a reality that wounds all of humanity."

There was no excuse for "an unequal sharing of domestic responsibilities or the subordination of one spouse to the other," he said.

Chicago-born Leo was given a raucous reception by crowds lining the streets, chanting his name.

Thousands of people – including children dressed as the pope or as bishops – lined up for a glimpse of the pope as he drove by in the popemobile.

At a prayer vigil attended by some 60,000 young people in Lima's national stadium, the pope made his way around on foot to greet people, as thousands held up their phones as torches.

The intense trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru comes just weeks after the pope had surgery for lung cancer, but he shows no sign of flagging.

In his speech, Leo made fond references to Peru's landscape and culture, telling the Catholic clergy to think of their mission as a difficult but rewarding walk, like the path that leads to Machu Picchu.

He compared the Catholic mission to the "steep ascents" of the Inca Trail in Peru.

The trail, an ancient network of routes that traverses much of the Andes, "is not to be walked alone," he cautioned.

READ MORE
Pope Leo XIV returns to second homeland Peru and a nationwide welcome

During his tenure in Peru, Prevost worked in poor and remote northern areas, and remained close to local communities during periods of hardship, visiting them sometimes on horseback.

"Walking together fosters communion," he said.

Six days in Peru will see Leo travel from the deep Amazon to the high Andes. He will visit Cuzco, at more than 3,400 metres (11,000 feet) elevation, which will test his recovery from lung surgery.

He will also make an emotional return to Chiclayo, the northern city where he was bishop for a decade.
