https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Haitian police retake national stadium from gangs after two years
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
Haitian security forces regained control Thursday of the country's main stadium that had been under gang control for two years, forcing the national football team to play elsewhere.

The Haitian National Police said in a statement that it had taken "full control" of the venue with the Task Force, a private security group serving the government, after which it left the stadium under the guard of Salvadoran soldiers.

The operation is part of the deployment of some 2,000 soldiers ordered by El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, who announced last Tuesday that his men had destroyed the "headquarters" of 400 Mawozo, one of Haiti's main gangs.

READ MORE
Haiti's PM praises Bukele after Salvadoran troops help destroy gang headquarters

Bukele, who has gained attention for bringing Salvadoran gangs to heel but been accused of human rights violations, ordered the dispatch of the contingent to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers who went missing after an ambush on October 18 in Port-au-Prince.

The four soldiers are part of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a multinational group backed by the UN that distances itself from the actions of the troops sent for the rescue mission.

READ MORE
Amnesty urges El Salvador to disclose terms of Haiti troop deployment

The Haitian police added that after retaking the Sylvio Cator Stadium, the Salvadoran military took charge of security there.

Salvadoran state-run television said Salvadoran forces "took up position" in the stadium on Thursday.

In 2024, the 10,000-capacity stadium fell into the hands of gangs that control much of the country, the poorest in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The violence forced the Haitian national football team to play World Cup qualifying matches in Curaçao rather than at home.

The team, consisting virtually entirely of players who do not live in Haiti, won qualification to the World Cup in 2026 but were eliminated in the group stage.

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/spo.author: François PICARD
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/spo.text:
His decades of pastoral experience in Peru, amid political instability, terrorism, state violence and profound social inequalities, have shaped a religious outlook rooted in cultural openness, solidarity with the marginalized and an intimate understanding of human suffering.

Central to this interpretation is the enduring legacy of liberation theology and its "preferential option for the poor." Far from representing a marginal or exclusively Latin American theological current, Kazai suggests that its ethical commitments have become integral to the contemporary Catholic Church's understanding of its mission. Yet this inheritance also demands institutional self-examination. "We have betrayed the poor and the vulnerable," he observes, recalling the Church's historical failures to defend those suffering from violence and injustice.

The interview also explores the tension between the Pope's extraordinary popular appeal and the political consequences of his teachings. In a society where religious authority continues to shape public morality, papal denunciations of corruption, inequality and xenophobia may carry greater resonance than conventional political discourse. But admiration does not necessarily translate into action.

"They cannot just say 'amen' and look away," Casallo warns, challenging political leaders who publicly embrace the Pope while disregarding the ethical implications of his message.

Ultimately, the interview raises a question that extends far beyond Peru: Can the moral authority of religious leadership help restore dialogue in polarized democracies, or will its calls for justice be absorbed into the rituals of political spectacle?

For Casallo, the significance of Pope Leo's visit lies not simply in the enthusiasm of the crowds but in whether that enthusiasm can inspire greater solidarity, accountability and a renewed commitment to living together.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.author: Cam Wilson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Home Affairs minister Tony Burke and Microsoft’s President of Global Affairs, Lisa Monaco established a framework for cooperation on cloud infrastructure in June. (Supplied)

A top national security official warned months ago that the country's reliance on Microsoft risked a "disproportionate impact" if the tech company suffered an outage.

And just last week, the federal government ran a simulation of a cyber security incident with its agencies and private companies, including Microsoft, to identify and prepare their responses in the event of a crisis.

Speaking on a podcast in August, Home Affairs national security head, Hamish Hansford, referenced Australia's deep reliance on Microsoft services, and directly warned of a "disproportionate impact" if the company was hit by an outage.

"[Big tech providers] underpin our national security. They underpin the functioning of the economy, and they are individually important for how we operate," he said.

Microsoft outage live: For the latest on the issues impacting the tech giant's apps read our blog.

Mr Hansford's comments — and the cybersecurity simulation — follow numerous recent reports and alerts by government agencies of the potentially "catastrophic" consequences of outages from major tech suppliers like Microsoft, which secured more than $1 billion in federal government contracts this year.

Both the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) confirmed they were impacted by today’s outage, along with millions of Australians.

A government-commissioned review released in February highlighted how dependence on a small number of technology suppliers could threaten critical services.

Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today.

The Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) commissioned an independent review of "single-seller" relationships, which are deals negotiated by the agency for buying technology on behalf of the government.

The review assessed single-seller vulnerabilities as rare but potentially catastrophic in their impact with an overall risk assessment of "medium".

It identified the cost and complexity of changing providers as one of the factors driving towards single-seller deals, and ultimately supported keeping these arrangements.

Similarly, Home Affairs' Critical Infrastructure Security Centre renewed older warnings about concentrated technology dependencies in a risk review released as recently as November 2, 11 days before the outage.

Microsoft told the ABC there was no indication the problem was caused by malicious activity. (Reuters: Gonzalo Fuentes/file)

At Senate estimates last month, the Australian Cybersecurity Co-ordinator, Lieutenant General Michelle McGuinness, said the government was working to survey its dependence on providers like Microsoft.

"We will map that critical dependency that we see across both critical government systems and critical infrastructure systems," she said.

The same month as the review, the DTA announced a new five-year whole-of-government deal with Microsoft.

Several government agencies signed multi-year deals with Microsoft in June and July, including a $720 million arrangement with Defence, a $163.4 million deal with Services Australia, and a $151 million deal with the Australian Tax Office.

The deals include everything from licenses for Microsoft products like Office 365 to cloud computing contracts, and the published values may differ from the final spend.

Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke and Microsoft's Lisa Monaco signed a memorandum of understanding.

While acknowledging the need for diversity of tech providers, Mr Hansford also said it was "unrealistic" for Australia to find alternatives to major US providers, and that it should instead seek closer ties with the company.

He cited a Department of Home Affairs's first-of-its-kind agreement with Microsoft Australia signed in June.

The deal outlined a number of commitments, including a promise to collaborate on initiatives to "strengthen the resilience of Australia's digital technology stack".

It also included a pledge to, "work together to prioritise the recovery of Australia's digital economy as soon as possible from significant technology outages or digital disruptions within the Microsoft Corporation ecosystem".

It was through this deal that last week's resilience exercise was first imagined, with the goal to test both government and Microsoft's readiness.

Spokespeople for Microsoft and Home Affairs confirmed this satisfied the relevant part of the agreement with Home Affairs.

On Friday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the government had activated a provision in that deal that required Microsoft to prioritise Australia's recovery from an outage.

Microsoft was investigating recent configuration changes as possible contributors to the problem. (Flickr: Peter Wood)

"That agreement has in fact been activated today, to make sure that we get appropriate prioritisation of Australian interests in this," he said.

Asked whether Australia should diversify its reliance on Microsoft, Mr Burke said diversity was relevant across software, trade and other areas.

But he said that should not detract from the security work done with the company.

"There is very significant good work that is done between Australia and Microsoft in terms of making sure we have high levels of security," he said.

A spokesperson for Home Affairs said the department was aware of the outage and was working with Microsoft to prioritise the recovery of Australia’s digital economy as soon as possible.

Kalyn Ponga and Reece Walsh are the two dominant players heading into the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer and Mark Metcalfe)

The Golden Boot hasn't gone to the best player in the world for many years now but if it did you can still make the case it should have ended up in Reece Walsh's hands.

The Australian fullback is not always the best, but when he is at his best there's nobody better and his performances for the Kangaroos has been a scorching reminder that nobody in rugby league is as made for the fast lane.

These days the Golden Boot goes to the best player in Test matches for the year and by giving it to Kalyn Ponga after just 150 minutes in international football, the credibility of the award is on the line in Sunday's World Cup final.

There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

If New Zealand wins and Ponga plays well, two things that feel inextricably linked, it retroactively becomes a better decision. The outcome will be correct even if the process was flawed.

If Australia wins and Walsh plays well, it highlights the farce of giving out an accolade for international player of the year before the biggest international game of the year.

In a perfect world, or even an imperfect one given it just makes sense, the Golden Boot wouldn't be awarded until after full-time on Sunday, by which time Ponga could be a worthy winner, but as it stands Walsh should have won the trophy.

He has as many man-of-the-match awards in this tournament than Ponga has completed games and after a premiership hangover with Brisbane that could have killed a brown dog, the Australian jersey has banished the demons and brought Walsh roaring back to life.

Reece Walsh has been in brilliant form through the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Sometimes he spins out of control, such as when he lost sight of a Samoa bomb in the semifinal, leading to a Stephen Crichton try, but when he stays on the road it's an exhilarating sight.

From his length-of-the-field try in the tournament opener against New Zealand to his five try assists against Cook Islands and a hat-trick against Samoa, Walsh's football over the past month has been reminiscent of the form he showed in leading Brisbane to the 2025 premiership.

It has served as a reminder of his game-bending abilities for anyone who needed it after a title defence to forget, and it's all the more impressive given his initial selection in this squad was far from guaranteed.

The loyalty of coach Kevin Walters played a major part and if James Tedesco had not played in the grand final, there's every chance he would have started against New Zealand in the tournament opener.

But right from the beginning, where Walsh won a brilliant duel with Ponga, he has made the spot his own and shaped Australia's fortunes along the way.

Ponga's win on awards night is just the prelude, with both men shaping as their country's best and most important players in Sunday's World Cup final.

It caps a year that has pulled back and forth between two of the biggest names and best players in the sport, and this last battle will determine who wins the war.

Ponga got the early running when he beat Walsh to the Queensland fullback job only for Walsh to strike back in their showdown three weeks ago that left both of them with stuffed highlight reels and Ponga with a broken arm.

The return from that injury has no doubt played a part in Ponga winning the award and while it's too early to be handing out Golden Boots there is no denying that his 150 minutes on the field for New Zealand has been exemplary.

On Sunday, opposing fullbacks James Tedesco and Kalyn Ponga will lead their teams into the NRL grand final. It's about the only thing their paths have had in common.

Ponga linking up with the Kiwis wasn't possible until the Test eligibility laws were changed earlier this year, and what he's done since fits in with the wider journey he's been on this season.

It mirrors his run to the grand final with Newcastle, where he changed from being someone who could play great into a great player and it was a transformation based on emotion more-so than any technical improvement.

That evolution has continued through the World Cup, where he has proven the black and white jersey calls to him in a way the green and gold never did or could.

When the chance to represent Australia came up in the past he opted to stay home and prepare for the next NRL season.

When finally offered a shot for New Zealand not only did he accept, he rushed back from a serious injury and threw himself in front of Tongan freight trains without fear.

That feeling has unlocked something inside Ponga, which comes out as the most whole-hearted and inspiring play of his career.

He becomes what he was always said to be when he fully committed to a cause greater than himself.

That was not always possible in Newcastle, where Ponga's star power once overpowered the entire club, but it was this year and the same has been true for New Zealand throughout this tournament even as the new guy doubles as the most famous face on the team.

Where once he was cool and impenetrable to the point of being unknowable, now Ponga is throwing himself into contests heart first which is what makes his contrast with Walsh so compelling.

The Queensland teammates will fight it out for the right to be world champion.  (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Bronco is all bleeding edges, all the time. What Ponga has learned to do is something Walsh does by compulsion. He could not hide his emotions if he tried and he never tries.

They come bursting out of him, as chest-beating when he rounded Ponga over the sideline against New Zealand or as acrobatics when he scored against Samoa.

He is desperate to excel, to strike fast and hard and deadly and most of all to win and sometimes Walsh wants it too much and chases it too hard, but it's one of those things you'd rather have too much of than not enough.

There will be a galaxy of stars fighting it out for the World Cup in Brisbane on Sunday, where the end of so many stories will be told.

Casey McLean, another Golden Boot nominee, is off to the fastest start for world domination since Alexander the Great and Jamayne Isaako is kicking goals from the middle of hurricanes.

Half of Isaah Yeo's chest is ripped apart and he's made 109 tackles while only missing two all tournament and he'll have to pull off a similar job if Australia is to slow New Zealand's astonishing forward pack.

Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semi-final was a reminder of Goliath's power.

Jahrome Hughes and Cameron Munster, whose playmaking genius is so often paired together with Melbourne, will fix both of their minds on the destruction of the other.

But nobody will have a greater impact on the winning and losing of it than Ponga and Walsh, two players who are so different yet have arrived in the same place as they both burn white hot.

If their meeting in Sydney was high noon, the sequel at Lang Park may as well be a one-horse town that ain't big enough for the both of them.

After they meet with guns drawn and the dust finally settles it'll prove a Golden Boot is one thing but being able to call yourself a world champion is quite another.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Binna Burra Lodge chairman Steve Noakes says the return of overnight visitors has been "a long time coming". (ABC Gold Coast)

Binna Burra Lodge was destroyed in a 2019 blaze, along with 11 homes.

It has reopened to overnight guests after a seven-year rebuild.

The new site has been designed to better protect against future disasters.

Perched high in the Gold Coast hinterland, surrounded by ancient rainforest, Binna Burra Lodge has captivated generations of visitors.

But in September 2019, that all came crashing down when devastating bushfires ripped through Lamington National Park.

The blaze devoured 6,000 hectares of rainforest, reducing the heritage-listed site, as well as 11 homes, to ashes.

Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition

But after enduring years of setbacks, including a pandemic and a cyclone, the treasured landmark has finally reopened to overnight guests.

"Recovery from disaster is not a short term process," Binna Burra Lodge chairman Noakes said.

"In our case, it's been seven years, and it's just fantastic today to be welcoming people back to Binna Burra Lodge.

"Binna Burra's a place of a lot of intergenerational connection for the last almost 100 years and we hope that with this new lodge there'll be a whole lot of new generational connections."

Steve Noakes says the lodge is a treasured landmark. (Supplied: Binna Burra Lodge)

Binna Burra Lodge was founded by conservationists Arthur Groom and Romeo Lahey in the 1930s.

The two men wanted to create a place where people could soak up the region's lush natural beauty, while being inspired to protect the rainforests into the future.

Arthur Groom and Romeo Lahey founded Binna Burra Lodge. (Supplied: Binna Burra Lodge)

"Over generations, lots and lots of people from around Australia and around the world have had the opportunity to experience the location," Mr Noakes said.

The bushfire tore through Lamington National Park. (ABC News: Jennifer Huxley)

But on September 8, 2019, a blaze tore through the area, leaving a trail of destruction in its wake.

Evacuated three days before, Mr Noakes still remembers the moment he discovered the lodge was gone.

"[An] ABC report was the first time we had confirmation the lodge had been destroyed," he said.

Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition

Police initially reported the blaze may have been sparked by a discarded cigarette.

But an internal Queensland Fire and Emergency Services report, obtained by the ABC, found the fire was more likely started at a mystery shooting range in bushland.

The fire burnt through 6,000 hectares of rainforest. (Supplied: Binna Burra Lodge)

The report also contained evidence claiming that, during the fire, firefighters left one containment point, logging it as being "under control" when it was not.

The blaze then raged out of control, consuming the lodge and surrounding homes.

Several homes were lost in the bushfires. (AAP: Glenn Hunt)

Mr Noakes said while the reopening had been "a long time coming", there was "never a question" the lodge would be rebuilt.

"I wasn't sure how we were going to do it," he said.

The new lodge has been designed to protect against future disasters. (ABC Gold Coast)

Mr Noakes said the new facility was designed with concrete structures wrapped in timber facades to ensure better protection against future disasters.

"It's very different from the old lodge which was beautiful old heritage timber, but of course when bushfire comes through it just all gets sizzled up," he said.

"If the worst thing ever happened and a fire did finally get through, the basic infrastructure would still be there to enable repair."

The rebuild has taken seven years. (ABC Gold Coast)

Gold Coast architect and bushfire-mitigation expert Eldon Bottcher said while building design was crucial, it was only one piece of the puzzle to prevent future disasters.

"We've got to look at how we manage our vegetation around the building," he said.

"We need to make sure we can get firefighters in around the place and we need to make sure we've got a dedicated water supply for those firefighters.

"There's a whole pile of things we've got to do."

Pat Cummins spoke for 70 minutes at a press conference today. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

If nothing else, nobody can ever say that Pat Cummins didn't front up and face the music.

For 70 minutes he stood there, smiling through whatever other emotion was boiling inside of him, disarming with charm and eloquence and just enough humour for the situation at hand. He took the questions until they dried up.

He lifted the lid on cricket's uncomfortable history with ball tampering, detailing specific examples he had seen within Test and Sheffield Shield cricket. He said he believed Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were punished much too harshly by Cricket Australia.

Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

He spoke to the 2018 Australian team's "ugly underbelly", addressed allegations of systemic racism within the sport, and spoke about the culture of casual verbal abuse that stretched all the way to suburban club cricket.

Cummins provided a detailed floor plan of the Newlands dressing rooms, and mustered a laugh despite his obvious distaste for the cameras which captured he and his wife conversing on the street.

He pledged to be as open as possible, to dig into the game's nuances — he used that word a lot — to explain as much of what happened in that Cape Town Test match as he could.

And his verdict, repeated multiple times and with precise wording, was clear: Pat Cummins did not know sandpaper was being used to tamper with the ball, and Usman Khawaja's version of events is incorrect.

Pat Cummins rejected allegations made by Usman Khawaja in his book Sabr. (ABC News)

Was he telling the truth? Who really knows. David Warner says he wasn't.

The technicality Cummins and his fellow bowlers have relied upon since they released their first statement of denial in 2021 was that they did not know "sandpaper had been brought out onto the field". Those words have been repeated often this week, presented carefully each time.

By Khawaja's version of events, as printed in his book Sabr, that leaves some wriggle room in which perhaps there was wider knowledge sandpaper was being used on the sidelines in breaks of play when the umpire had left the ball on the boundary.

Usman Khawaja's revelations on Sandpapergate may have come eight years after the fact, but time has not changed Australia's response to the cricket scandal.

But Cummins was questioned about that too, and once again had a firm and unflinching answer.

"That was news to me this week. I had no idea," Cummins said.

"Even chatting to a couple of the guys, that was a revelation to ourselves. That was one of the things that really surprised us because that doesn't happen anymore; the umpires give the ball to you out in the middle."

The good news is that is a fact someone will be able to check.

Somewhere in the SuperSport archives there will surely be footage of the players coming onto the ground after the breaks in play during that series, and surely in that it will be clear to see precisely when the ball is exchanged between umpire and players.

The bad news is that is just about the only fact that can be checked. Everything else is hearsay, one man's word against another, a civil war whose weapons are alternate offerings of "my truth" and "my story".

Cummins suggested the past eight years have weighed on Khawaja, and hinted that may be because, as Khawaja expressed in his book, he specifically knew about the plan to bring sandpaper onto the field and even warned Cameron Bancroft to be careful.

What does Khawaja think about that pretty loaded suggestion? We will surely find out soon enough, either on Instagram or on the next stop on the book tour.

David Warner says Pat Cummins threw Usman Khawaja under the bus. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

We already know what Warner thinks. He said he believed Cummins threw Khawaja under the bus.

This just days after Khawaja had to deny he had thrown Cummins and co under the bus. At this point, there is not a member of the Australian cricket team who does not reside beneath a bus.

Warner said on Fox Cricket he would not be able to move on until the truth came out. The truth, he says, is what is written in Khawaja's book.

Warner was given the opportunity to expound on that truth in his own words, but did not take it, suggesting instead a future book of his own would eventually do that job.

It's all a total mess. Social media reaction to Cummins's conference suggests the Australian public, growing increasingly fatigued by it all, has long since made up its mind on what really went on in Cape Town and is past the point of being swayed by new information.

At some point, most likely when all of these players are comfortable in retirement and these squabbles make up part of the nostalgia tour rather than dominate the discourse, we may wonder what all the fuss was about.

The biggest error of the Cummins Q and A was his belief that his appearance would allow everyone to draw a line under the affair and move on.

That's not happening. We're dealing with hurt feelings here, fractured relationships and bruised egos and nebulous concepts of truth and justice. You better pick your side, if you haven't already, because this is never going away.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Conrad Lardner was found guilty of manslaughter in August 2026. (Facebook)

A man who fatally stabbed his cousin has been sentenced to eight years and three months in prison.

The court heard the pair clashed over an "inferior" supply of drugs.

Conrad Lardner will be eligible for parole in 2031.

A man who fatally stabbed his cousin during an argument over low-quality drugs on the NSW Mid North Coast has been sentenced to more than eight years' jail.

Conrad Lardner was initially charged with the murder of his cousin David Vale in 2023.

In August this year, Lardner, 51, was found not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter by Justice Stephen Campbell in a judge-alone trial in the Supreme Court at Port Macquarie.

The court heard on March 1, 2023, Lardner stabbed his cousin David Vale outside a Kempsey property after he demanded a refund for "inferior quality drugs" supplied by Lardner.

During sentencing on Friday, Justice Campbell told the court Mr Vale started the fight when Lardner continued to "defy" him.

"The offender expected to have money to repay the deceased some time that day, [saying] 'I'll have a couple of dollars for you, as soon as I get it I'll come up to your place'.

"That did not happen."

Lardner gave evidence during the trial that after a series of blows between the pair, he picked up the knife that had fallen out of Mr Vale's pocket.

Conrad Lardner was charged with murder in 2023, but a judge-alone trial found him guilty of manslaughter in 2026. (Supplied: NSW Police)

During sentencing, Justice Campbell ruled he was satisfied on the balance of probabilities the knife came into the offender's possession after it fell onto the driveway.

"It makes it more likely the offender stabbed the deceased as a spontaneous reaction," he said.

Justice Campbell told the court Lardner had the intent of inflicting serious grievous bodily harm on Mr Vale when he stabbed him.

"The offender took the most extreme step available and plunged it into the deceased twice," he said.

Justice Campbell found Mr Vale was the initial aggressor and that he was determined to fight if there was no refund forthcoming for the drugs.

"The offender's response to the perceived threat was unreasonable," Justice Campbell said.

"He could have neutralised it by throwing [the knife] away from the deceased or moving it away.

During sentencing, Justice Campbell took into account Lardner's deprived childhood, a diagnosis of anti-social personality disorder, and childhood sexual abuse.

The court also heard Lardner has cardiac disease and type 2 diabetes.

He was sentenced to eight years and three months in prison, but will be eligible for parole in 2031.

Justice Campbell took into account the fact Lardner had earlier pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the local court.

Although that plea was not accepted by the prosecution, it did result in a 25 per cent discount on Lardner's sentence.

Outside court, Mr Vale's partner, Jessica Howard, told the ABC she thought the sentence was a "disgrace".

Warner emphatically rebuked Cummins's claims about the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

David Warner has hit back at Pat Cummins after the Australia captain's sensational 70-minute press conference earlier today.

Warner stood by Usman Khawaja's revelations about the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal, saying Cummins threw Khawaja "under the bus" in denying them.

Warner also described the blame levelled at him and fellow suspended players Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft a "life punishment".

Former Australia opener David Warner has stood by Usman Khawaja's revelations about the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal, saying Australia captain Pat Cummins threw Khawaja "under the bus" at a press conference in Sydney this morning.

Cummins had said Khawaja's claims that the entire Australian camp knew about ball tampering in Cape Town were "complete and utter nonsense".

Warner, who was vice captain at the time of the incident and who received a year-long ban for his involvement, said he was "very disappointed" by his former captain on Fox Cricket's coverage of the opening ODI between Australia and England in Perth.

"I feel the captain today threw Ussie under the bus and I'm very, very disappointed by that," Warner said.

Warner said Cummins threw Khawaja "under the bus" at this morning's press conference. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett/Cricket Australia)

Warner also stood by his assertion that the initial investigation had been "botched", and that he, along with fellow suspended players Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft, had no choice but to bear the blame.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence. I feel like it was a botched investigation," Warner said.

"It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us and we had to move on and just accept responsibility, the three of us, and we ultimately did.

"We don't have that opportunity to go there and speak again. [Cricket Australia CEO] Todd Greenberg squashed that the other day. There probably are going to be conversations behind the scenes after this."

Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

Warner, a childhood friend of Khawaja's, also said he expected the truth about the saga to come out eventually.

"It's inevitable. Everyone writes a book at the end of their career but for me it's about accepting the truth and I just don't think this will rest," Warner said.

"It's very, very difficult with the acceptance of the consequences that we live day to day in our lives."

Warner described the blame levelled at him, Smith and Bancroft a "life punishment", saying he and wife Candice experienced a miscarriage in the aftermath of the incident.

"All three of us have paid a big price in this and I hadn't spoken about it in eight years, but at the end of the day, we've got to live with these consequences daily," Warner said.

"And we've been served a life punishment. So when other people talk about that they've been affected by it, there's nothing worse than for me, Steve and Cameron, who have to walk over there every single day and we cop abuse.

"Yes, we accepted it, but at the end of the day, my wife and I as well pay the greatest price.

"We lost a baby during that time. And that's why it really hurts me the most until the truth is accepted."

Earlier today, Cummins claimed he could not explain why Khawaja's and Warner's recollections of the incident were so different to his.

"That sounds like a pretty good question for those two," Cummins said.

"Again, there's quite a few different accounts here, so they've got two accounts.

"There's 11 players in that room, so that means there's nine other guys who I think it's appropriate you give an equal amount of weight into their story as well."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/i.author: Tim Little and Abbey Halter
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Federal and state governments have agreed to fund a feasibility study into a new research facility in Mount Isa. (ABC News: Harriet Tatham)

A business case for a $145 million critical mineral research hub in Mount Isa has secured funding for a feasibility study.

The centre will provide early analysis and testing for prospective mines trying to scale operations in the region.

The federal and state governments have agreed to tip in $241,250 each to fund trials, with an additional $482,500 to come from Mount Isa City Council.

Mount Isa's push to reinvent its regional economy with a new mineral research hub has secured state and federal backing for a feasibility study.

Mount Isa City Council and the University of Queensland released a business case earlier this month for a $145 million critical minerals research centre.

The facility would allow mining companies to analyse rock samples from local mineral deposits to see what minerals were present and if they would be viable to mine.

The $145 million centre is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs.  (Supplied: Mount Isa City Council)

In July 2025, Mount Isa's underground copper mine closure saw nearly 500 workers sacked in the 19,000-strong community, forcing the council to search for economic alternatives.

While Mount Isa's economy has been affected, exploration and investment across the wider North West Minerals Province has boomed, with about 85 critical minerals projects underway.

Sustainable Minerals Institute director at the University of Queensland Rick Valenta said the proposed hub would allow industry to scale operations quickly.

Rick Valenta (right) says the facility will help mines understand what minerals are in deposits and how they could be mined. (ABC Rural: Eric Barker)

"The reason you can't just find a deposit and put it into production in a year is because you've got to answer … 'What's the content of the metal that you're after? And … how do we get the metals out of that rock?'" Professor Valenta said.

"[At the moment], those rocks would be going elsewhere in Queensland … Australia or the world … [and] that involves a cost and a delay.

"This centre is aimed at providing a local solution to that sort of thing."

The proposed research centre would be situated between the George Fisher Mine and Mount Isa Airport. (Supplied: Mount Isa City Councill)

Mount Isa Mayor Peta MacRae said she hoped the research hub would help future-proof the city by giving mining companies a dedicated site to research problems locally.

"[Currently] minerals are just going to be ripped up and shipped," she said.

"What we want to do is add the value and do as much processing as we can … to help us secure the future for our communities."

Peta MacRae hopes the project will centralise some of the regions' mining investment into the town's economy.  (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

The proposed hub is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs and would be located near the Mount Isa Airport.

On Friday morning, Federal Assistant Minister for Resources Anthony Chisholm confirmed funding would be released to consider the proposal.

"We want to make the most of these opportunities … and ensure that Mount Isa remains a great place to live and work and attract people at the same time," he said.

"We know that there is enormous potential, but it's about proving that and then also ensuring that we can attract the industry investment."

Anthony Chisholm says the cenrre is about proving Mt Isa's potential and attracting industry investment. (ABC News: Tim Little)

The federal and state governments have agreed to tip in $241,250 each to fund a feasibility study, with an additional $482,500 to come from Mount Isa City Council.

If successful, the hub would operate in conjunction with similar facilities in Mackay and Townsville.

Initial testing and analysis would start at Mount Isa's centre, before small-scale piloting took place in Mackay followed by large-scale trials in Townsville.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.author: Kenji Sato
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police arrested two men over the theft of copper wiring from Town Square Redbank Plains. (Supplied: QPS)

Police have arrested two men over the theft of copper wiring from Town Square Redbank Plains.

Officers say security equipment was sabotaged over a period of nine days.

Police say more colluders could be at large.

Police have arrested two men who stole 239 kilograms of copper wire in an Ipswich shopping Centre heist, after one of the men tried to hide in a closet.

Detective Inspector Mick Manago said Town Square Redbank Plains security equipment was sabotaged over nine days in a "coordinated" attack.

Inspector Manago said police alleged around 11pm on November 1 a masked man was captured on CCTV deliberately damaging a security camera at the site before leaving.

Detective Inspector Mick Manago said police were searching for more possible colluders. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

He said on November 5, offenders allegedly cut through perimeter fencing before forcing a door open using a crowbar.

He said inspection of the site on November 9 identified extensive damage to electrical infrastructure, including a severed main earthing cable and additional wiring.

Inspector Manago said two Redbank Plains men had been arrested, a 42-year-old and a 46-year-old.

Inspector Manago said police were investigating the possibility that there may have been other people involved.

"There was some planning, which is quite concerning for us," Inspector Manago said.

"I would expect that amount of copper cabling would need a vehicle to remove it, so we're appealing to anyone in the area at the time who saw any suspicious vehicles to come forward.

"There is every chance that further persons will need to be held to account for what's occurred."

The 46-year-old was arrested by police after hiding in a closet. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

The 42-year-old has been charged with two counts of possessing tainted property and fraud, one count each of entering premises to commit an indictable offence, possessing dangerous drugs, possessing property suspected of having been used in the commission of a drug offence, and possessing utensils.

He was remanded in custody and is due to appear in Ipswich Magistrates Court on December 2.

The 46-year-old was arrested by police after trying to hide in a clothes closet.

He was charged with three counts of possessing tainted property, two counts of fraud, and one count each of entering premises to commit an indictable offence, and possessing utensils.

He was remanded in custody and is due to appear in Ipswich Magistrates Court on January 8.

Inspector Manago said copper theft was a serious offence.

"The financial impact of this type of offending extends well beyond the value of the copper stolen.

"There are businesses that face costly repairs, but also they face a financial impact due to the loss of trading."

The copper theft caused most of Town Square Redbank Plain's shops to lose power on Tuesday, causing businesses to close and food to spoil.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/n.author: Olivana Lathouris
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The NT teen appeared in the youth court today charged with terrorism offences. (Unsplash: Jay Wennington)

A Northern Territory teenage girl charged with serious terrorism offences could return home to her family after her lawyer made a bid for bail.

The 15-year-old was arrested and charged earlier this month with making or collecting documents likely to facilitate a terrorist act.

The judge adjourned his bail decision until Monday.

The diary entries of a 15-year-old Northern Territory girl charged with a terrorism related offence allegedly reveal she "had plans to shoot her school", a court has heard.

The 15-year-old girl, who applied to be released on bail today, has been in custody since being charged with collecting or making documents likely to facilitate a terrorist act 10 days ago.

Commonwealth prosecutor Hadi Mazloum opposed the bail application, telling the court the main concern was a risk to community safety.

"That's because of the risk of the infliction of ideologically motivated violence and an online presence which could be seen to encourage extreme violence," he said.

The girl was charged with collecting or making documents likely to facilitate a terrorist act. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Mr Mazloum referenced diary entries allegedly made by the teenager which he said included plans to carry out a school shooting and while the proposed bail conditions were strict, parental supervision would be "inadequate".

Mr Mazloum acknowledged detaining a young girl was a "grave step" and said her writing showed "a child in real distress with a history of being bullied".

However, he opposed the characterisation of the diary entries as that of a "young girl who was bullied and venting, not planning".

"She writes that she and the other young person had plans to shoot her school.

"All of this happened within the family home."

Mr Mazloum also raised concerns about the teenager's access to online devices which he said would be difficult to control through parental supervision in a home environment.

The girl's lawyer, Brooke Houen, put forward a plan she described as "extremely stringent" and would impose conditions akin to "house arrest" including "24/7 parental supervision" and electronic monitoring.

Ms Houen said her client's young age and her "psychological circumstances" were important considerations for the court.

Australian Federal Police are involved in the joint counter-terrorism investigation. (Supplied)

The court heard the teenager had been diagnosed with ADHD and was likely to be diagnosed with autism.

Ms Houen said her client's "educational difficulties" and "psychological needs" were unlikely to be met due to "rolling lockdowns" at the Holtze Youth Detention Centre.

"This is a matter where part of the issue is [the youth] has tendencies to be isolated, disaffected and struggling personally and putting her on remand in a youth detention facility is not the way to address those issues," Ms Houen said.

"The way to address those issues is through structured psychological supports which are now in place, returning her to her family, allowing them to support her."

The court heard the case was likely to proceed to a jury trial in the NT Supreme Court which Ms Houen said could take more than a year.

She also told the court guns owned by family members had all been removed from the property and the girl would have "no access" to any firearms.

Ms Houen emphasised that her client was "well aware" of the seriousness of the charges and the strictness of the bail conditions.

The AFP has warned of a 'tsunami' of youth crime is hitting the country, due to rapid online radicalisation (Unsplash: Gilles Lambert)

"Her primary goal is returning home to her family and she is willing to do whatever is necessary to achieve that," she said.

The girl was supported in court by a group of family members, including her mother, and at one point during the hearing Judge Greg Macdonald asked the girl how she was.

"Good," the girl said.

Judge Macdonald explained the bail conditions would include "lots of rules".

"Are you willing to stick with them, to comply with them, to follow the rules and not break them?" Judge Macdonald asked.

"Yes," the girl said.

Judge Macdonald said he required additional time to consider all the submissions from the prosecution and defence before deciding whether to release the girl from custody.

The girl was remanded in custody and the matter adjourned until Monday.

"I know detention is very hard, it hurts, but I have to remand you until at least Monday morning," Judge Macdonald said.

The girl cried as she was led away.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Bob Bramley was flying to pick up passengers for a return trip when his plane crashed. (Supplied)

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has released its preliminary report on the August crash of pilot Bob Bramley.

Bramley is believed to have died when his plane dived into the water off Groote Eylandt, in the Northern Territory.

His body has not been found.

Fishermen witnessed young Tasmanian pilot Bob Bramley's plane crash in waters off the Northern Territory in August "at very high speed", a report has revealed.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) today released its preliminary report into the crash in the Gulf of Carpentaria on August 25 this year, which is believed to have killed 23-year-old Bramley.

Northern Territory Police conducted extensive marine and air searches at the time, which recovered parts of the plane, but Bramley has never been found.

At the time, 23-year-old Bob Bramley was working as a charter company pilot. (Supplied.)

As a teenager, he became a passionate advocate for suicide prevention, and sought to raise awareness by becoming the youngest person to circumnavigate Australia solo by plane.

Friends and family expressed their shock and sadness in the wake of the crash, remembering Bramley as a "beacon of hope", and for his love of flying.

The ATSB report detailed the circumstances of the August crash, but noted the investigation is continuing and that a final report will be published at its conclusion.

The report, which refers to "the pilot" but does not identify Bramley, details his movements on the morning of August 25, as he prepared to fly between the small communities of Gove and Nambulwar in the Northern Territory.

At the time, Bramley had been working as a pilot for aviation operator Air Frontier for more than a year, and had been the company's senior base pilot for the Arnhem region since April.

The report noted that after fuelling the plane and lodging a flight plan, the Beechcraft 58 Baron plane departed from the Gove Airport at about 11am, with only the pilot on board.

"The flight plan for the return to Gove indicated four passengers were to be on board," the report noted.

The ATSB's map of Bob Bramley's final flight on August 25, 2026. (ATSB/Google Earth)

About half an hour later, at 11:27am, fishermen in a boat south-west of Isle Woodah in the west of the Gulf of Carpentaria watched the plane pass overhead.

"They expected the aircraft to pull up; however, it did not change trajectory, and it impacted the water at very high speed.

"The witnesses motored to the impact point and found a fuel/oil slick on the water surface along with many small floating fragments of shattered airframe."

NT Police image of wreckage underwater at the crash site. (NT Police)

The report noted that the Baron was not fitted with, and was not required to have, a flight data recorder or a cockpit voice recorder.

The ATSB said the flight wasn't detected by radar, and data tracking the flight was recorded by Bramley's iPad, which it was transmitting to the online platform OzRunways.

The final data point was transmitted at 11:24am, about 23 kilometres north of the crash site.

Bramley made two radio broadcasts during taxi and take-off, and phone records indicated "maintained a messaging stream with their partner" throughout the flight.

The report noted Bramley's qualifications to operate the Baron aircraft, that he held a valid medical certificate and that he had completed a multi-engine instrument proficiency check the previous month.

Bramley had more than 1,138 hours total flight time, more than 300 of which were in the Baron.

The Baron itself was initially built in 1978 and had been serviced most recently in June in Darwin.

The report noted no significant weather activity was observed on the day, consistent with the witnesses and other pilots flying in the area.

The report noted Bramley made two radio broadcasts during taxi and takeoff, and "maintained a messaging stream with their partner" throughout the flight. (Supplied: Lachlan Bennett)

In August, NT Police Acting Assistant Commissioner Peter Malley said the search for Bramley and the crash site had been particularly difficult, adding that "tiger sharks and crocs" had complicated efforts.

NT Police confirmed today human remains had not been found.

Police divers had to contend with sharks and crocodiles during search efforts. (Supplied: NT Police)

The ATSB report said diving operations recovered parts of the aircraft at a depth of 17 metres, and some of Bramley's personal items including his logbook, flight crew licence and "a significantly damaged iPad".

Included in the report was a photo of the plane's engine, which was found "embedded into the sea floor".

Other parts of the plane, including the cockpit area, parts of the wing, the fuselage and the vertical stabiliser were also found.

The ATSB said the investigation was ongoing, and that it will examine aircraft maintenance records, aircraft and pilot documentation, items recovered from the crash and similar occurrences.

A further report will be released at the end of the investigation.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.title: Vandals increasingly targeting Melbourne's bus shelters, data suggests
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.author: Toby Hussey
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Public Transport

Bus shelters are the most commonly vandalised infrastructure on Victoria's public transport network. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

The app Snap Send Solve has recorded a doubling in the number of public transport vandalism reports from its users over the past 12 months.

The Victorian government says targeting of bus shelters is the most common type of vandalism across the public transport network.

The Department of Transport says it is cracking down on vandalism including using drones along train routes.

Reports of vandalism across Victoria's public transport network have increased by 50 per cent over the past year according to a popular app.

The creator of Snap Send Solve claims it received more than 5,700 reports of vandalism and graffiti on public transport across Victoria between October 2025 and last month.

That was up from 3,760 the year prior.

Bus shelters were the most common target for vandals, with nearly 3,700 reports received in the past 12 months — double those of bus shelter vandalism reports from the previous year.

Bus shelters are commonly damaged in Victoria. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

"This isn't a general rise in vandalism, and it isn't app growth," said Snap Send Solve chief executive Danny Gorog, whose app launched in 2013.

Vandals were targeting "shelters specifically", he said.

Snap Send Solve's bus shelter figures include all reports of vandalism or graffiti to the app in Victoria which describe bus shelters or stops.

Mr Gorog said they received about two million reports annually for issues ranging from potholes to graffiti, from some 1.25 million registered users across Australia and New Zealand.

In Melbourne, suburbs in the north-east and south-east recorded the highest number of bus shelter vandalism reports.

Graffiti and broken glass were the issues most frequently flagged by users.

The Victorian government confirmed bus shelter vandalism was the most common type of vandalism across the state's public transport network, but did not provide a figure for the repair cost.

It said about $10 million was spent each year removing and repairing graffiti on the train network.

Public Transport Users Association spokesperson Daniel Bowen said bus shelter vandalism was a particular nuisance, especially during hot and wet weather extremes.

"Anecdotally, there are too many cases of vandalism," Mr Bowen said.

Bus shelters are often spray-painted or scratched by vandals. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

While bus shelter vandalism accounted for fewer than half of all public transport vandalism reports Snap Send Solve received in 2024-25, it was nearly two-thirds of reports in 2025-26.

"There's clearly a problem there," Mr Gorog said.

Responsibility for repairing or removing bus shelter vandalism across Melbourne varies between location.

Shelters with electronic billboards are often the responsibility of the advertising company leasing them.

A local cricket club in the south-western suburbs has expressed dismay after its turf pitch was destroyed by suspected vandals on e-bikes.

The ABC contacted several local governments within the areas with the highest number of bus shelter vandalism reports made to Snap Send Solve.

Most declined to comment and deferred to the Department of Transport and Planning, or to oOh!media, which leases shelters for advertising.

Mr Gorog said one theory was that lingering damage, such as graffiti not immediately removed, could encourage further vandalism.

"There is a thesis that there's this repair lag ... and when something has deteriorated and has been vandalised, it creates a bit more vandalism," Mr Gorog said.

The Shire of Nillumbik, which contains suburbs including Eltham and Diamond Creek, is in the north-east of Melbourne where the highest number of shelter vandalism reports originated.

The Shire said it had received 130 vandalism reports since January — roughly one every two days.

It said shelters were inspected and cleaned twice weekly, "with graffiti removed as quickly as possible".

Officials at Frankston City, in Melbourne's south-east, said they had removed more than 37,000 square metres of graffiti across all property types last financial year.

The council has been running a trial offering locals $500 if their graffiti reports result in a guilty finding in court.

Another scheme offered offered free graffiti removal supplies to locals.

Public Transport Users Association spokesperson Daniel Bowen said "there are too many cases of vandalism" on Victoria's bus network. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

The Department of Transport and Planning said it used more than 14,000 CCTV cameras across the public transport network.

A spokesperson said the department was "cracking down" on vandalism using drones and "new tracking technology" along train routes.

“We encourage anyone who sees vandalism or damaged property on our network to report it to Victoria Police," the spokesperson said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.title: Government back to the drawing board on backpacker crackdown
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.author: Holly Tregenza
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The government is reconsidering its controversial overhaul of the working holiday visa scheme. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The government is reconsidering its controversial overhaul of the working holiday visa scheme.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says he is also looking at ways to reduce the number of British backpackers coming to Australia.

Business leaders are urging the government to provide certainty to industries that rely on backpackers to fill jobs.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has all but confirmed the government is going back to the drawing board on its proposed backpacker crackdown, as it grapples with the twin issues of a surge in UK working holiday-makers and pressure to rein in overall migration.

On Friday, Mr Burke said Australia must "find a way" to reduce the number of UK backpackers arriving and staying in the country under a free trade deal introduced in 2023, which allows British citizens to live in Australia for up to three years without specific work requirements.

"We can find a way to bring that back to something more sensible and in the national interest, without jeopardising the other parts of the free trade agreement," he said.

In August, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ruled out imposing regional work requirements on backpackers from the UK, which apply to other working holiday-makers seeking to extend their visas beyond 12 months.

The favourable treatment has led to a steep increase in the number of British backpackers coming to Australia, up from 47,238 in 2023/24 to 79,412 in 2024/25 according to Home Affairs data.

"The conversations with the United Kingdom continue," Mr Burke said.

The government had also proposed introducing a ballot system for non-British backpackers seeking to extend their stay into a second or third year, to dramatically reduce visa numbers.

The Australian newspaper reported the government was now considering delaying the rollout of the ballot system until early next year, after farming, tourism and hospitality groups warned the changes could cripple their industries.

The report suggests the government is considering lifting the cap on third-year visas from the proposed 5,000 to 20,000 (down from the current 31,000) and imposing longer regional work requirements on visa-holders.

Mr Burke said the government was continuing to engage with industry stakeholders, but the "parameters" around reducing the overall number of working holiday-makers were unchanged.

"The total number of working holiday or backpacker numbers that I've announced at the National Press Club, I cannot shift from," he said.

He described potential changes to the implementation as "tweaks" that would allow businesses to "get the best possible use out of people, while they are here".

"I am completely open to that," he said.

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said there had been "extensive discussions" between the government and affected industries about the backpacker issue.

He warned the original proposal risked disrupting businesses outside major cities, particularly in regional areas that relied on working holiday-makers to fill jobs.

"And those regional areas really need those people to be coming out there and to be undertaking that work, supporting work in those areas," he said.

Andrew McKellar says the government must move quickly to grant businesses certainty. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr McKellar said business groups wanted the government to "make a decision", warning the "clock is ticking" for businesses seeking certainty ahead of summer.

"Let's ensure that those people who are already here can continue with their plans … and that there's a fresh set of rules for anyone else who's coming in," he said.

Community Strong MP Allegra Spender said growing uncertainty was becoming increasingly painful for businesses.

"What I'm seeing in the migration system more broadly is very slow processing times and not real honesty about where this is all going," she said.

"When you're employing someone where you've in the past been able to get some money in pretty quickly, and now it's taking months, there's that uncertainty that is really damaging for businesses".

The government paused working holiday-maker visa applications from 24 countries in August.

Mr Burke said the government was "very close" to a resolution.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/r.title: Victorian Labor MP 'sick to death' of council approach to new Maryborough pool
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/r.author: Coco Veldkamp
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

The Maryborough Municipal Olympic Pool was closed in 2022 following an assessment of its condition. (ABC Central Victoria: Sarah Lawrence)

Labor and the Coalition have pledged $5 million to demolish and rebuild the Maryborough outdoor pool.

Labor's promise came with conditions, including that the council explain its costings.

The council says it will consult with the community on the project when funding is secured.

Labor's Ripon MP Martha Haylett has called on Central Goldfields Shire Council Mayor Ben Green and CEO Peter Harriott to "reconsider their positions" amid controversy surrounding the redevelopment of Maryborough outdoor swimming pool.

The pool has been closed since 2022 after an independent assessor deemed it was at "end of life".

The Labor MP announced yesterday if re-elected, the government would match a Liberal Party promise of a further $5 million to fund the Central Victorian pool under "very strict conditions".

"We will not release a single cent of taxpayer funding until the council is able to explain how they have so dramatically mismanaged this project, and provide the community with a fully transparent and detailed plan as to how they intend to actually deliver it," Ms Haylett said.

"We are sick to death of this council repeatedly coming and asking for further money.

Martha Haylett has accused the council of mismanaging the Maryborough outdoor pool project. (Supplied)

"Due to ongoing issues, we think it is appropriate that Liberal Mayor Ben Green and CEO Peter Harriott reconsider their positions."

Yesterday, Liberal Party candidate Megan Read pledged $5 million to demolish the existing pool and build a new 50-metre outdoor pool.

$9 million in funding has already been secured for the project, comprising $4.5 million federal commitment, $3 million from the state government and $1.5 million from the Central Goldfields Shire Council.

Nationals candidate Jo Armstrong has also promised to "deliver the pool to the community".

Ben Green is the Central Goldfields Shire mayor. (Supplied)

An assessor previously recommended the Maryborough pool be demolished and rebuilt, estimated to cost $9 million.

Last year, the estimated cost of reopening the pool jumped to about $14 million, which the council attributed to soaring construction prices and site complexities.

The 50-metre pool is the only outdoor facility of its kind for the town of 8,000 residents.

Maryborough is facing its fourth summer without an outdoor pool. (ABC News: Sarah Lawrence)

Central Goldfields Shire Council did not respond to the ABC's questions about the call for the mayor or CEO to resign or to allegations the council had "dramatically mismanaged" the pool project.

In a statement to the ABC, a Central Goldfields Shire Council spokesperson welcomed the Coalition and Labor's commitment to provide $5 million for the pool.

"Additional community engagement will occur around all aspects of the project when funding is secured," the spokesperson said.

"After the election outcome is known, we'll seek the local member's support to work collaboratively and get on with delivering."

Speaking to the ABC this morning, CEO Peter Harriott said the $5 million commitment was "fantastic", but he denied wrongdoing.

"There has been no mismanagement of this project. If you are talking about the costs … look at some of the tunnels in Melbourne that go [over the budget]. We are nowhere in the league of those increases," Mr Harriott said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/q.title: 'That's on you': Queanbeyan council defends caravan parking policy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/q.author: Niddal Mustafa
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Vehicles smaller than 7.5 metres will be allowed to park for up to 28 days. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

The Queanbeyan-Palerang Council has banned large vehicles from parking on residential streets for more than an hour.

The council says the vehicles are often left parked for months.

Australia's largest caravan and motorhome club warns the restrictions could discourage people from owning a large vehicle in the area.

The Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council has begun enforcing strict residential parking rules banning large caravans, boats, and trailers from long-term parking in residential streets.

The push is part of the council's effort to crackdown on large vehicles being left for long periods of time in prime parking spots.

Under the new rules, which came into effect last month, vehicles longer than 7.5 metres cannot park in residential streets for more than an hour.

Vehicles smaller than 7.5 metres will be allowed to park in residential streets for up to 28 days before being required to move.

The council's push is aimed at reclaiming street space, and is being met with mixed reactions. (ABC News: Ruby Thomas)

Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council Mayor Kenrick Winchester said the issue was prominent in the NSW town of Googong, where he said people were using on-street parking to store large vehicles.

The mayor said people had "bought houses where they can't fit their boat or their trailer in their own backyards, or sheds, or driveways, and so they're parking them randomly throughout the suburb".

The new council rules also ban any vehicles from parking on the verge — the area between the road and the boundary of a property.

The council's pursuit to reclaim street space has been met with mixed reactions.

The council is concerned that vehicles are being left for long periods of time in prime parking spots. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Local couple, Sarah and Parveen, have lived in Googong for nine years and said they had recently seen more caravans parked on their street, for months at a time.

The couple said they now referred to their street as a "caravan park".

Googong residents Sarah and Parveen welcome the enforcement of strict residential parking rules, targeting caravans, boats, and trailers. (ABC News)

"In the beginning it was not bad, but now this whole street sometimes is full of caravans," Sarah said.

"Most of the year they just stay there, except the few times people will take them for holidays."

Parveen said the vehicles, which he speculated were not always owned by people who lived on the street, created a safety hazard.

But the move has also resulted in some not-so-happy campers.

The Campervan and Motorhome Club of Australia (CMCA) has criticised the crackdown as heavy-handed and unnecessary.

Chief executive Richard Barwick said people would now have to pay for storage sites for the vehicles, on top of rising fuel costs.

Vehicles longer than 7.5 metres can no longer park in residential streets for more than an hour. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

"Don't pick a certain market because they think it's an easy target and that they are wealthy because not all people that own an RV or that own a boat are wealthy people," he said.

Mr Barwick said he also did not believe that the area had the population or density to warrant the new rules, saying there was likely plenty of parking available for local residents.

"I know Queanbeyan reasonably well; to me there'd be parking. Drive around the corner, don't be afraid to exercise."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.title: Sheep price records continue to tumble
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.author: Angus Verley
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Lachlan and Olivia James, and their children Florence and Scarlett, were at the sale in Naracoorte on Thursday to watch their sheep set a national record.  (Supplied: James family)

Sheep prices have hit another national record.

First-cross ewes at a sale in Naracoorte on Thursday sold for an unprecedented $650-a-head.

Those in the industry expect prices will remain high for some time, given the historically low national sheep flock.

Sheep price records continue to tumble at saleyards across the country, in a golden age for sheep producers.

A line of 1.5-year-old ewes set a new record at the prestigious selling centre at Naracoorte in South Australia yesterday.

They sold for $650-a-head, overtaking the previous record of $641 set at Corowa in New South Wales only last month.

Sheep values have risen significantly this year, reflecting an excellent season in many areas, as well as strong demand and a critical flock shortage.

Drought conditions in key livestock areas in recent years led to a big sell-off of sheep, exacerbating the long-term trend of declining flock numbers in Australia.

The record-breaking ewes at Naracoorte belonged to the James family, who farm up the road at Mundulla West.

Trevor James said he felt a great sense of accomplishment, but was keeping it in perspective.

"It's a thrill, but you don't take long to reflect on why you get there," he said.

"We enjoy the support of buyers, and repeat buyers who keep buying our sheep, and that's a humbling experience.

"This is our 50th year selling first-cross ewes, and no-one ever thought we'd be at $650, or even in the 500s."

The James family's record-breaking sheep were also named 'best presented' at the Naracoorte sale.  (Supplied: James family)

It was only three years ago livestock values fell so sharply that some sheep were almost worthless, and Mr James said that was fresh in his memory.

"We need the return, because the last few years have been difficult, for one in price — the 2023 spring fell away quickly, and a couple of tough seasons in terms of feed costs, and now costs in general," he said.

He said he was not sure what the future would hold, but expected continuing strong demand while the sheep flock remained low.

"The shortage of sheep is now playing out and I would imagine it will take some while to rebuild numbers," he said.

"We're hoping it's not a bubble, because we're hoping to get a little bit more out of it."

There was a huge amount of interest in the James family's record-breaking sheep.  (Supplied: James family)

Almost all sheep prices have been hitting new highs in recent months.

The national first-cross record has been broken numerous times, and at a state level, the Victorian record was also broken yesterday, with ewes at the Edenhope sale selling for $625-a-head.

Only a week before, the national first-cross lamb record was broken, with a pen of lambs at the Bendigo sale selling for $595.

In the Merino industry, a new ewe record of $515-a-head was set at the Hay sheep sale in September.

These records all refer to breeding animals, but they also reflect extraordinary and unprecedented demand at the saleyards for sheep and lambs for slaughter — lambs have sold for up to $500, and sheep have topped $400.

Livestock specialist with stock agency AWN, Wayne Driscoll, said his clients had done the hard yards through tough years, sticking with sheep, and deserved to be rewarded.

"It's a wonderful time — it's great reward for persistence," he said.

"We're so pleased for the vendors who have stayed in it, because there was a lot of heartache a couple of years ago, they went through a lot and it certainly took people out of the industry, so let's not forget that."

Nigel Starick says he never dreamed sheep prices would reach the levels they have.  (Supplied: Elders Bendigo)

Elders Bendigo livestock manager Nigel Starick said he never expected to see prices so high.

'It's fantastic to see people get rewarded for sticking with something that hasn't always gone their way, but the ones in it now are getting well rewarded," he said.

"It's as good as I've ever seen it in 25 years in this job — never in my life did I think I'd see those prices. It's just phenomenal.

"When you actually get up and auction those sheep and command that sort of value for producers, it's a good place to be."
