https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.title: The US has been holding secretive talks with a regime it accused of genocide
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.author: Karishma Vyas
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Min Aung Hlaing, pictured in Malaysia, has been trying to rehabilitate Myanmar's image. ( Reuters: Azneal Ishak/Pool)

The United States has reopened direct talks with Myanmar, raising alarm among advocates and analysts.

It marks a reversal of efforts to isolate the military junta after it took power in a 2021 coup.

Analysts believe the US's desire to access Myanmar's rare earths could influence diplomacy.

As US President Donald Trump prepares to meet Asian leaders in the Philippines next week for the 49th ASEAN Summit, his administration is holding secretive talks with Myanmar's military-backed government, the same regime the US has accused of genocide.

Five years ago, Washington imposed sanctions on Myanmar's military leadership and downgraded diplomatic ties following a 2021 coup that ousted an elected government.

This year, however, senior Trump administration officials have travelled to Tokyo and Myanmar's capital, Naypyidaw, for talks with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing.

The goals of the diplomacy include countering China's influence in the region and potentially gaining access to Myanmar's "bountiful rare earth resources", according to a US State Department document.

But the outreach has raised concerns among human rights advocates that Washington's pursuit of strategic interests could help rehabilitate a military leadership accused of widespread atrocities.

Debbie Stothard believes pressure on Myanmar's government should not be weakened, with attacks on civilians ongoing. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

"It's pretty shocking and almost illogical that the US would engage in secret talks with a sham president elected by a sham election," said Debbie Stothard, chair of the International Network for Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.

"The military junta views engagement at this level as something that's encouraging and positive for them.

"They see this process as legitimising them, and that is very bad news indeed for civilians on the ground and for regional security."

The diplomatic opening followed the detention of an American businessman at Yangon airport on June 11 by Myanmar authorities.

Adam Castillo, 40, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, was detained for three months after being accused of financial impropriety, allegations he denied.

Adam Castillo was detained in Myanmar earlier this year. (Supplied)

A former US Marine, Mr Castillo was reportedly lobbying Washington to lift sanctions against Myanmar in exchange for negotiating American access to the country's vast rare earth deposits. He also ran one of Myanmar's largest security companies.

Mr Castillo's detention provided an opening for Washington to establish direct contact with the military leadership, said Hunter Marston, director of the Lowy Institute's Southeast Asia Program.

"A delegation of US representatives travelled to Naypyidaw to secure the release … that was the supposed setting or context for the US delegation to visit Myanmar," Dr Marston said.

"But it also paved the way for more substantive discussions about changing US policy and engaging with the Myanmar military regime.

"It seems like his detention was essentially hostage diplomacy, and the release was used tactically to secure talks with Washington.

"I think that played right into the hands of the Myanmar regime, but I think it also served as a useful pretext for Washington to engage in discreet talks with the military."

Myanmar, still the invisible war

Analysts believe the discussions surrounding Mr Castillo's release may have opened the door to broader negotiations over access to Myanmar's rare earth minerals, potentially in return for a normalisation of relations.

Since his release in September, meetings between senior US officials, led by Michael Vance, the Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research, and Myanmar's military-backed government have continued. The latest took place in Tokyo in October.

Rare earths are essential to manufacturing a wide range of modern technologies, from computer screens and electric vehicles to solar panels and advanced weapons systems.

Clusters of rare earth mines along the Lwe River network in Myanmar. (Reuters: 2025 Planet Labs PBC/Handout)

They are also crucial for producing the semiconductors or chips that power artificial intelligence, Dr Marston said, making them "really important to a number of US business interests".

"Whoever supplies today has the upper hand in the race for artificial intelligence," he said.

While the US remains a leader in technological innovation, it is heavily dependent on foreign suppliers for the minerals needed to manufacture many of these products.

Myanmar has emerged as a major source of supply, with more than 600 rare earth mines, according to the Stimson Center. Much of its output is exported to neighbouring China, which dominates the global processing of rare earths.

Rare earths are used to manufacture everything from smartphones to wind turbines. Here's where they can be found.

That dominance has become a growing concern for Washington as competition with Beijing intensifies, and the Trump administration seeks to diversify critical mineral supply chains.

But securing access to Myanmar's deposits will be difficult. Many of the mines are located in Kachin State, near the Chinese border, in areas controlled by ethnic armed groups fighting the military government.

Dr Marston said China's entrenched position in the industry would make it difficult for Washington to establish an alternative supply chain.

"It controls something like 90 per cent of the world's global rare earth production. So it's unlikely that the United States is going to succeed in circumventing Chinese control over these supply chains," he said.

For Min Aung Hlaing, however, the renewed US engagement represents a significant diplomatic breakthrough.

The former military chief ousted the elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021 and became president this year following elections widely dismissed by opposition groups and international critics as a "sham".

Since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild relations with regional and international powers, including India, Russia, China and Myanmar's South-East Asian neighbours.

Xi Jinping shakes hands with Min Aung Hlaing in Beijing in 2026.  (Reuters: Lintao Zhang/Pool)

Vladimir Putin meets Min Aung Hlaing in Moscow in 2025. (Reuters via pool: Pavel Bednyakov)

Myanmar's efforts to improve its standing with the US began in July 2025, when the government hired a US lobbying firm, the DCI Group, for more than $US3 million ($4 million) a year.

The US lobbyist Roger Stone, a longtime friend and ally of Mr Trump, is listed as a consultant for the firm. In 2019 he was convicted of obstructing a congressional investigation into whether the Trump campaign colluded with Russia to win the 2016 election, but was later granted clemency by the president.

According to documents filed under the US Foreign Agents Registration Act, Mr Stone "provided public affairs services" to Myanmar's Ministry of Information, aimed at "rebuilding relations between … Myanmar and the United States".

Donald Trump pardoned Roger Stone in 2020. (AP: Andrew Harnik)

Ms Stothard believes those lobbying efforts have made an impact.

With Mr Trump seeking access to Myanmar's strategic mineral resources, analysts believe the president could also press regional leaders to reconsider the country's exclusion from high-level ASEAN meetings in Manila next week.

The diplomatic developments come as the conflict inside Myanmar continues to intensify.

Since the coup, fighting between the military, pro-democracy resistance groups and ethnic armed organisations has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced millions more.

The ABC visited Myanmar ahead of its first election in more than five years — and signs of the junta's menacing presence were everywhere.

In September, weeks after US officials held talks with Myanmar's leadership in Naypyidaw, the military launched an air strike on a crowded marketplace in Rakhine State, killing more than 50 people, according to local reports.

Human rights advocates say renewed engagement with the generals, particularly any consideration of easing sanctions, risks weakening international pressure on the military to end its campaign against civilians.

"It's going to harm the US just as much as it harms the rest of us," Ms Stothard said.

"The UN and all legitimate human rights organisations have very clearly documented war crimes and ongoing genocide against the Rohingya and crimes against humanity in Burma."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.title: Gazans desperate to create shelter from rubble in 'miserable' conditions
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.author: Matthew Doran and Cherine Yazbeck
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Palestinians are sourcing material for makeshift housing from damaged buildings. (ABC News)

The UN has urged Israel to allow 150,000 tents into flood-hit Gaza.

Israel maintains Hamas has been stealing aid and using it for its own purposes.

The flooding is the result of the first heavy rains of what will be a long and wet winter.

Palestinians in Gaza are desperately trying to find new ways to prop up flimsy tents and shelters ahead of the long and wet winter, pulling material out of destroyed buildings to reinforce tarpaulins and sheeting.

Last weekend, the first heavy rains of the season hit the war-ravaged strip, flooding the sprawling tent camps where hundreds of thousands of people live.

A woman and three children were killed by a collapsing sand bank, according to local health authorities.

Heavy rain causes significant flooding in Gaza, with thousands of Palestinians living in tents bearing the brunt of the sudden burst of winter weather.

The United Nations said more than 40,000 tents had been damaged, leaving more than 200,000 people without safe and dry accommodation.

In many instances, floodwaters had mixed with sewage, with much of Gaza's infrastructure destroyed during the war, fuelling concerns of fresh outbreaks of diseases in the overcrowded ramshackle communities.

Sharif Abu Shaar, 45, was among the Palestinians sourcing material like reinforcement bars from damaged buildings in Khan Younis, in an attempt to strengthen existing shelters against storms.

Sharif Abu Shaar says the rain seeps through the holes in his makeshift tent. (ABC News)

"We lived in miserable conditions, with water, wind and rain. It was a catastrophe," he told the ABC.

"When we heard that metal could be salvaged from the rubble of destroyed buildings, we started rebuilding with it.

"Unfortunately, the sheets have holes, allowing rain to seep inside. We still need to repair them."

Samah Abu Shaar, 40, said the heavy rains were "devastating" for the tent camp where she lives in the Al Mawasi area, closer to the Mediterranean Sea.

Samah Abu Shaar says rain is devastating to tent camps in Gaza. (ABC News)

"Water gets into the mattresses and it is frightening. The little ones started crying," she told the ABC.

"My daughter tells me that water fell on her while she was sleeping, soaking her clothes, the mattresses and the duvet."

Topic:Unrest, Conflict and War

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Topic:
World Politics

The situation has enlivened an intense debate between humanitarian agencies, the Israeli government and the US-backed Board of Peace as to who is responsible for the crisis.

Heavy rain floods camp for displaced Palestinians in Gaza.

Gaza is about to enter its fourth winter since the war began and its second since President Donald Trump declared a ceasefire had been imposed.

Since the ceasefire came into force in October 2025, local health authorities said more than 1,600 Palestinians had been killed and more than 5,800 injured as a result of ongoing Israeli strikes.

Many of them are civilians, including women and children.

Palestinians lost their shelter and belongings in the floods. (ABC News)

On Monday, the Board of Peace labelled the situation "an immediate humanitarian emergency", and chastised Israeli authorities and Hamas for having "impeded progress" in improving the situation for civilians living amongst the rubble.

"We have specifically urged the Israeli government to authorise the entry of essential materials for temporary shelter, water and sanitation infrastructure, waste management, drainage and sewage material," it said in a statement.

"At the same time, we have repeatedly pressed Hamas to agree to lay down its arms, relinquish governing authority, and fulfil its obligations."

Men recover metal from the rubble of ruined buildings to be used to prop up shelter. (ABC News)

It said the steps being taken by Israeli authorities to fix the situation and prepare for the depths of winter, "remains insufficient" and suggested that had also slowed the process of Hamas laying down its weapons.

"We likewise call on Hamas's leadership to abide by its commitments without further delay," the Board of Peace said.

"Recent military activity in civilian areas and near Israeli positions endangers civilians and undermines the humanitarian progress of the last year."

Salvaged metal is used to reinforce the shelters. (ABC News)

Israel blamed Hamas for the situation, repeating its claims that Hamas had been stealing aid and using it for its own purposes.

"Hamas has done what it has always done: lie, steal, exploit, and rearm," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office posted on X.

"As long as Hamas remains in power, it will use every dual-use item entering Gaza to entrench its terror regime and expand its military arsenal.

"Hamas alone is responsible for the suffering of the people of Gaza, and it is now cynically exploiting that suffering to shift blame onto Israel once again."

Mr Netanyahu's office insisted more than 91,000 tents had been allowed into Gaza ahead of the winter season, and more than 8,200 trucks carrying items like tarpaulins and blankets had also entered the strip.

People salvage materials from the rubble of buildings in Khan Younis. (ABC News)

Allegations have also been raised of Hamas blocking engineers from working on shelter projects in a bid to exacerbate the crisis, after a social media post from one man named Ahmed al-Tallouli said he had been forced by Hamas to stop work.

A tent camp in Al Mawasi, where people are using salvaged materials to prop up their shelters. (ABC News)

The United Nations humanitarian agency OCHA has said there are more than 150,000 tents waiting to be let into Gaza, which have been held up because of Israeli restrictions and funding shortfalls.

UNICEF's Toby Fricker told the ABC that demand for shelter in Gaza was still outstripping supply.

"The needs are immense and vast, and for any UNICEF or any agency to provide for everyone, it's such a huge task and undertaking because there are so many needs inside Gaza," he said.

"We have been bringing in tents, we have been bringing in tarpaulins, but it's nowhere near enough.

Toby Fricker says UNICEF is trying to restore sanitation and water supplies. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

"The ceasefire announcement brought some more stability, let's say, for children and families across the Gaza Strip, but what it really needs to do now is deliver on the recovery."

He pointed to work UNICEF was trying to do in restoring sanitation and water supplies being impeded by equipment restrictions.

"There's Sheikh Radwan, which is a stormwater basin; it's meant to hold rainfall so it doesn't flood the local community in Gaza City," he said.

"Now it's filling up; it's also contaminated with sewage, which could be a huge public health risk for children and families in that area.

"But we don't have the equipment to fix that and to pump the water out quickly enough."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.title: Award-winning photographer lets once-incarcerated teens tell their own story
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Fine Art Photography

Hoda Afshar's National Photographic Portrait Prize-winning work Untitled #01. (Supplied: National Portrait Gallery)

In late 2023, artist Vernon Ah Kee contacted Iranian-born Melbourne-based photographer Hoda Afshar and writer and human rights defender Behrouz Boochani with an invitation to work on a project to address the mass incarceration of Indigenous youth in Far North Queensland.

Artist Hoda Afshar, whose work is the subject of a exhibition, titled a/part, at Buxton Contemporary in Melbourne.  (Supplied: Diana Pfammatter/DAAD Artists-in-Berlin Program)

Ah Kee, who was born in Cairns, and belongs to Kuku Yalandji, Waanji, Yidinji and Gugu Yimithirr peoples, stressed the issues his community faced were "too big, too hard to deal with" alone.

Although Indigenous children aged 10 to 17 make up only 6 per cent of the population, they are 20 times more likely to be imprisoned.

Ah Kee said he wanted to build "forms of solidarity and communities that could help us fight these systems", Afshar recalls.

Vernon Ah Kee wanted to highlight the incarceration of Indigenous youth in Far North Queensland. (Supplied: Joe Ruckli)

A year later, with the support of Change The Record, an organisation that works to reduce incarceration rates of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and Youth Empowered Towards Independence (YETI), which works with Indigenous youth caught up in the criminal justice system, Afshar had established a temporary portrait studio in YETI's backyard in Cairns.

All she needed was subjects.

"Nine days I stayed in the area, returning every day, to set up the big, large-format camera in that backyard," she says.

Over time her subjects, who rely on YETI for a range of support services, were drawn to Afshar, her camera and the props she brought in.

Hoda Afshar used a large-format camera for the portrait sessions, prompting curiosity from the subjects, who were formerly incarcerated teens in Cairns. (Supplied: Hoda Afshar and Milani Gallery)

"Eventually they started engaging," asking me, 'Can I help you? Can I take a photo? Can I be your assistant?'" she says.

Those photographs became the basis of Code Black/Riot (2025), now on display at Buxton Contemporary in Melbourne, in the exhibition a/part: Hoda Afshar.

The show, a product of a co-commission by Buxton Contemporary and the Biennale of Sydney, brings together three series, Agonistes (2020), Remain (2018) and Shafaq (2026), which confront themes such as "incarceration in contemporary Australia".

In Code Black/Riot, the subjects have used Afshar's props, which include fresh flowers, a handmade mask, Heath Ledger's iconic Joker make-up, and a piece of clothing or an outstretched arm from someone outside the frame, to remain anonymous to the viewer.

Through that simple act they retain agency over their own image.

"So much changes in the way that we frame things, in the way that what we leave outside of the frame and what we include in it," Afshar says.

In one photograph, a young man, and a senior member of the cohort Afshar photographed, is draped in an Aboriginal flag. Apart from one eye peering back at us, his face is concealed. In another, a young man holds a mask of Melpomene, the teary-eyed Greek symbol of tragedy, to replace his own.

In the next room is the companion piece, a four-channel video installation displayed across eight suspended screens. Their lived experience is so "complex and layered" that their "testimonies are lost" in the static photographs, Afshar says. The video "is a way of bringing that narrative forward, of confronting people with that reality".

The 33-minute video installation begins with vignettes of children sitting in the boughs of jacaranda trees that bathe the gallery in a warm tropical glow. However, this soon makes way for images of a coastal town with orderly streets, manicured lawns and a sprawling youth prison on its outskirts.

Current and former prison staff paint an unforgiving portrait of life inside the facility, including the various colour codes used by staff to describe incidents involving inmates; "Code olive is when they climb," one says.

A moment later a young boy readies himself for his interview. "Can you see my whole face or just my mouth?" he asks. Although only 14 years of age, he's been incarcerated five times, including once for over a year.

An installation by Hoda Afshar begins with idyllic images of jacaranda trees and launches into testimonials from juvenile detention. (Supplied: Hoda Afshar and Milani Gallery)

Presently his voice is joined by other anonymous young people, who detail physical assaults by prison guards and prolonged periods of "night mode", when the prison is plunged into near total darkness.

A former female inmate berates the prison guards' treatment of inmates.

"Would they go home and do that to their own children?" she asks.

Upstairs the exhibition continues with Agonistes (2020), which features portraits of whistleblowers: former employees or members of private, public and religious organisations, who made the decision to speak out after witnessing or experiencing violence, abuse and corruption.

The whistleblowers include community and military lawyers, care workers, a general practitioner and two former employees of the Australian government's refugee processing centre at Manus Island in Papua New Guinea.

To protect their identity Afshar has photographed sculptures printed from scans of their heads and shoulders. Hung in a row on a red, painted wall, these busts take on the appearance of a court of noble leaders carved from marble.

This work, from the 2020 Agonistes series, is called An Officer and Lawyer in the Australian Special Forces. (Supplied: Hoda Afshar and Milani Gallery)

In the accompanying video the whistleblowers divulge the miscarriages of justice they witnessed and outline the motivation behind their decision to speak out. "What I left behind at Manus, I often felt I was in my own prison anyway," one says.

When the Australia government closed the Manus Island facility in 2017, many former detainees remained on the island as they awaited resettlement. It was during this period that Afshar flew there to meet and photograph some of these men.

It took time to "build up that relationship," Afshar recalls.

The resulting series of photographs became Remain (2018), 11 of which are included in a/part, along with a two-channel video installation.

In one image, her longtime collaborator Behrouz Boochani stares back at us as a small fire rages behind him; in another water is poured over a former detainee's head as an outstretched arm sits on his shoulder.

Installation view of a/part: Hoda Afshar featuring the Remain series.   (Supplied: Christian Capurro)

According to Afshar, what connects the three series is the "process of dehumanisation" that is "used against certain people and bodies and skin colours that has led us to this moment and allows this to happen" in our own backyard.

Shafaq (2026) is a singe channel video installation featuring images the artist took in the Northern Territory last year. "It's the most personal work I've made because it came at a time I wasn't even planning to make it," Afshar says.

US military strikes against Iran meant she was unable to contact her family who were at the "centre stage of the war", she says.

During a ceasefire she travelled to the Northern Territory, only to find herself in a landscape that bore a striking resemblance to parts of southern Iran.

As fighter jets flew overhead in Operation Pitch Black, a joint military exercise between Australia and its allies, "It really started feeling like the world inside me is reflected in the world outside," Afshar says.

Shafaq is the most introspective work in the exhibition and marks a new direction for the artist.

a/part: Hoda Afshar is on at Buxton Contemporary in Melbourne until April 24, 2027.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/r.title: The village on wheels helping mums combat post-birth isolation
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/r.author: Oliver Brown and Stephanie Nitschke
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Parenting Babies

The mothers' group meets weekly to foster connections and navigate isolation post-birth. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

A woman from SA's Riverland has created a social group for mothers experiencing isolation post-birth.

Participants said the River Mamas group had helped them connect with community and manage mental health struggles.

A local psychologist said more support systems were needed for rural mothers experiencing postnatal depression.

Welcoming her second son was meant to be one of the happiest times of Stacey Wurfel's life, but instead it made her feel at her most vulnerable.

The 40-year-old's second son, Oakley, was born seven months ago, nine years after she had welcomed her first child.

She said it raised unexpected feelings of isolation because many of her friends of a similar age were moving into a different stage in their lives.

"My partner works away, my family's an hour away or more, and it was extremely lonely and the walls were closing in on me. [It was] very isolating," Ms Wurfel said.

Stacey Wurfel says she felt isolated from friends and family after the birth of her second son, Oakley. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

The South Australian government facilitates short-term early parenting groups through its Child and Family Health Service (CaFHS).

Ms Wurfel said while it was a start, she had been looking for other sources of connection, especially while experiencing signs of postnatal depression.

She soon realised she was not alone.

"I was just going to coffees every day, sometimes by myself. I was looking around and noticing that there was a lot of other mums on their own," Ms Wurfel said.

Stacey Wurfel says she and other mothers now  catch up over coffee and other events. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

The solo coffees and feelings of loneliness sparked an idea for Ms Wurfel to create a mothers' group of her own in her home community in South Australia's Riverland.

Within weeks of launching River Mamas Co on social media, Ms Wurfel said she was overwhelmed by the response from hundreds of women.

"[Something] we all crave is connection, and that's what I started this for."

While the group has an online presence, it also hosts weekly walking groups and coffee catch-ups that rotate between the Riverland's four major town centres.

Sunnefa "Sunny" Yeatman is one of the mums who has found important connection within the group.

Sunnefa Yeatman (centre) says the group helped her connect with community after moving to the Riverland earlier this year. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

The 37-year-old moved to the region while still pregnant with her now six-month-old son and said she feared being lonely in early motherhood.

"[Isolation] was my biggest concern moving up here and I felt it quite acutely until this group," Ms Yeatman said.

"I was struggling and was not that pleased to, necessarily, live here and be part of this community.

"But now I feel like there's some possibilities and a way forward."

Renmark mother Kosanna Sinc has also enjoyed making new, like-minded connections after going through what she described as a traumatic birth.

Kosanna Sinc says she loves the sense of connection she and her son have through River Mamas. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"[I had] postpartum depression, anxiety, the whole lot," the 34-year-old said.

"[It] definitely helped so much making those connections and just having other mums to talk to who have been through similar [experiences]."

Topic:
Retail Industry

Topic:
Livestock Farming

A national charity's latest report found 42 per cent of its survey respondents did not have access to a local mothers' group.

Motherland's survey of more than 1,000 mothers also showed 68 per cent of respondents had experienced postnatal depression or anxiety.

Elise Thompson says navigating mental health is more challenging for mothers in regional areas. (Supplied: Elise Thompson)

Riverland clinical psychologist Elise Thompson said getting support for postnatal depression or similar mental health conditions was more difficult in regional areas.

She said it made groups like River Mamas Co crucial.

"We have less services here in the country so if you're particularly wanting face-to-face mental health support, that often comes with a really lengthy wait," Ms Thompson said.

For Ms Wurfel, who feels immense pride about what her group has already achieved for many mums in her community, there are still plans to do more.

"I would really like to touch base on postnatal depression and support networks that are around and maybe collaborating stories of other local mums and their journeys," she said.

Stacey Wurfel (left) says she is proud of the sense of community that has naturally evolved at River Mamas.  (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/n.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang scandal brings China's spy networks into view
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/n.author: Bang Xiao
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

The alleged affair between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang has sparked worldwide scrutiny of Chinese intelligence networks. (Reuters: CTI)

It sounds like the opening of a spy thriller. Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to being unfaithful, with reports he had three extramarital affairs.

One is said to have been with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, who was reportedly suspected of working for Beijing.

The US Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws by facilitating Chinese access to restricted AI chips.

It has not been established yet what exactly Ms Huang provided to China's intelligence network. However, it has already rattled investors and brought wider scrutiny to Nvidia's business with China.

The tech giant's stock hit a 14-year low relative to earnings this week, while facing a proposed shareholder class-action lawsuit alleging it misled investors over Mr Huang's relationship with Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang, the founder of global artificial intelligence giant Nvidia, has resigned from his position as CEO.

The crisis also led to Mr Huang's resignation as Nvidia chief executive and director, ending his 33-year leadership of the company.

When romantic relationships become intertwined with national security, private lives are inevitably drawn into geopolitical rivalry.

During the Cold War, the East German intelligence service ran so-called "Operation Romeo", in which male agents were instructed to develop romantic relationships with women in the West German government to gain access to classified information.

Today, intelligence activities may also leverage commercial networks and professional channels, making it increasingly difficult to distinguish legitimate connections from potential espionage activity.

China's spy network may help Beijing gather information, but over-relying on it can also erode the relationship China needs with the West.

The cost may be that the people and relationships connecting China and the West are pushed aside, leaving both sides with fewer ways to understand each other amid an intensifying China-US competition.

To understand why, we need to look at how China's intelligence system operates.

According to The New York Times, US intelligence concluded that Ms Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) to gather information on Mr Huang and Nvidia, and potentially to influence the company's position on selling advanced AI chips to China.

The MSS is China's principal civilian intelligence and counterintelligence agency. It gathers human intelligence through covert operations and contacts, cultivating relationships in government, business, academia and Chinese communities overseas.

There is no publicly available figure for the size of the MSS's overseas network.

The UK parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee found that people cultivated as contacts by the MSS may not necessarily be aware they are dealing with intelligence officers.

Nvidia AI chips are widely used to develop AI models. (Reuters: Ann Wang)

Beijing's intelligence system is not just one network. It also has the People's Liberation Army (PLA), which gathers military intelligence, and the Ministry of Public Security (MPS), which is responsible for policing and domestic security.

These branches can also work through private technology companies and contractors, where their activity is not automatically attributed to one agency.

US court documents allege that the MSS and MPS have used Chinese hacking groups to collect information and obscure the government's role in the actions.

In one case, the US Justice Department said a Chinese contractor stole data by hacking emails, phones and servers linked to government agencies and dissident groups. It sold or attempted to sell the data to at least 43 MSS or MPS bureaus across 31 provinces and cities.

Ministry of State Security

Ministry of Public Security

Chinese Communist Party

This shows how an intelligence system can draw on private firms, though it doesn't mean that all Chinese technology companies or contractors are part of a spy network.

The MPS also has Network Security Police Offices in major Chinese internet companies and digital platforms. They can gather online intelligence from user data to support investigations into cybercrime and national security threats.

More than 1,000 offices are embedded in at least 10 major technology firms, including Tencent, Baidu, Sina and Alibaba.

Allegations of espionage between China and the US are nothing new. But a target as big as Jensen Huang could change who wins the AI race.

Similarly, these offices are established in the country's major telecoms, such as China Mobile and China Telecom, monitoring unlawful activities and investigating cases that could be linked to national security.

These overlapping structures between multiple state departments, companies and professional networks can make it difficult for people working between China and the West to know when an ordinary contact may carry national security risks.

Public reporting does not establish exactly when Ms Huang was recruited, what she knowingly did, or what information she passed on.

She may have had direct contact with the MSS, or may have acted as an intermediary for people linked to it. Neither possibility has been substantiated publicly.

There has also been scrutiny over whether Ms Huang was the ultimate owner of the assets and businesses associated with her name.

She reportedly worked as a journalist before moving into private banking and investment, and later became involved in corporate acquisitions and cross-border transactions.

She was involved in a project to build the Shanghai AI Computing Centre, and continued to oversee Megaspeed's daily operations after its shares were transferred through companies in the British Virgin Islands and Singapore, according to the New York Times.

An image shared by software company Net Thunder on LinkedIn in 2024 shows Alice Huang sitting next to Jensen Huang at an event in Taiwan. (Supplied: NetThunder/LinkedIn)

These details point to her role as a cross-border intermediary, with financial expertise and connections to investors, companies and clients acting behind the scenes.

The term "white glove" is used for an intermediary who holds or manages assets on behalf of another party. It is a common approach used by Chinese offshore companies to separate the registered shareholders, the actual controllers and the ultimate beneficial owners.

In some documented cases, offshore businesses have been linked to relatives or associates of China's political elites.

The fallout after Jensen Huang steps down as Nvidia boss

Public information has not established who ultimately controls Megaspeed, or who uses the advanced Nvidia AI chips.

However, the allegations involving Ms Huang, along with her romantic relationship with Mr Huang, have amplified the open secret in these opaque business networks.

Western businesses have long been attracted to commercial incentives and the access to the lucrative Chinese market, often accepting complex ownership structures to avoid political involvement.

Now, they are reassessing how to manage risks, particularly those related to ownership transparency, and ensuring that they remain resilient to political factors such as the downfall of senior Chinese officials or Western sanctions.

It's not just "white gloves" who have worked between Chinese investors and American clients.

China's United Front Work Department (UFWD) is actively building relationships with overseas Chinese communities and influential figures to promote Beijing's interests.

But the line can become blurred when the groups and individuals are used to advance political agendas, leaving some worried that their associations or public views could attract unwanted suspicion.

As national security concerns have expanded from traditional military, diplomatic and intelligence spheres to include technology, data and rare earths, more people working across China and the West — in sectors that once involved routine professional and personal interactions — are also feeling the pressure.

Cooperation in the fields of scientific research, academia, AI and critical minerals — once relatively unrestricted — is increasingly being constrained by national security concerns.

There will likely be a lot of tense conversations next week when Donald Trump and Xi Jinping both attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting. (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov/Pool)

The allegations surrounding Alice Huang and Jensen Huang have made these concerns more tangible.

Westerners in China collaborating with Chinese partners, as well as mainland Chinese people working overseas, may worry that legitimate and lawful exchanges of information or commercial connections could be perceived as a risk without their knowledge.

This also hinders engagement between China and the West, and may make it harder for both sides to understand each other as strategic competition deepens.

In the field of China studies, the West relies on people with first-hand experience of China to understand the country's complexities and prevent misunderstanding. China, in turn, benefits from foreign scholars and journalists living in the country to explain its society and politics to the outside world, and to foster the exchange of knowledge across borders.

But under growing pressure from national security concerns, these channels may narrow further.

The US investigation into Megaspeed, as well as the scrutiny of Ms Huang, will likely add to tension between the two nations.

Beijing has denied the allegations of espionage, while extending the export-control waivers on some of its rare earth minerals — which are crucial for producing AI chips — until January.

With US President Donald Trump expected to attend the APEC leaders' meeting in Shenzhen next week, it remains unclear how the case will affect bilateral discussions.

Whatever the outcome of the case, its effects on trust may deepen and prove difficult to reverse.

The concrete wall fell onto the rear part of the neighbouring house.  (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

A construction company has been fined after a 30-tonne concrete wall fell on a neighbouring property.

A mother and her baby sustained minor injuries.

Smart Builty Pty Ltd has been convicted and fined $150,000.

A construction company has been fined $150,000 after a 30-tonne section of a concrete wall fell on to a house in Adelaide's inner south, injuring a mother and her baby.

According to a ruling handed down by the South Australian Employment Court, the concrete wall was not properly secured and fell onto the rear of a neighbouring property at Wayville on November 28, 2023, during severe weather.

It fell onto the back 60 centimetres of the home and most of its outdoor living area.

The ruling said the principal contractor at the site, Smart Built Pty Ltd, was constructing a three-storey residential development which included 10-metre high precast concrete wall panels.

It said the panels had been supported by temporary "propping" but the company had requested its removal about two weeks earlier to allow for better access to parts of the construction site.

"No inspection of the precast panels or their permanent structural support was undertaken by any engineer prior to removal of the temporary propping," the ruling said.

The ruling noted that victim impact statements had described the "profound impact the offending" on the mother and her baby, who both suffered minor injuries.

The mother required stitches to her knee, while her baby "sustained superficial cuts only", but the court said those injuries could have been more serious.

"Other section[s] of the inadequately supported wall loomed over the rest of the … family's home," the ruling said.

On the day the wall fell, flooding and storm damage were reported around Adelaide, including at Wayville. (Supplied: Spence Denny)

The court said the cost of structural damage to the home amounted to $85,413.82 and a further $19,211 damage to its contents.

"The defendant [Smart Built Pty Ltd] paid $10,000 to the neighbours affected by the collapse to compensate them for the inconvenience of ongoing building works," the ruling said.

It said the defendant had helped with practical steps to facilitate repairs, which were being arranged through the family's insurer.

The ruling said the removal of the propping meant the wall was not "connected to other significant structural elements".

"The design drawings clearly state … that the precast panels are to remain propped until the wall bracing is installed," the ruling stated.

The court said it accepted "the offending did not involve deliberate or reckless conduct" but that the "poorly controlled risk of harm … was of death or extremely serious injury to multiple people".

"I conclude the offending involved mid-range objective seriousness rather than a lower level," the ruling said.

"I accept the defendant's evidence of its subsequently changed safety systems … I also accept the defendant's current intention is to not use precast panels again."

The court imposed a conviction and fined Smart Built Pty Ltd $150,000.

Pat Cummins calls Usman Khawaja's ball tampering claims 'utter nonsense'

Pat Cummins said Usman Khawaja's claims that everyone knew about ball tampering in 2018 were "complete and utter nonsense".

In a press conference that lasted more than an hour, the Test skipper said Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Cummins also said he had seen ball tampering in Sheffield Shield, but would not elaborate on who or which team.

Pat Cummins has labelled Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering allegations "utter nonsense", revealing he has received legal advice that the claims are "probably defamatory".

In an extraordinary 70-minute press conference on Friday, Australia's Test captain ruled out legal action against his former teammate, but was scathing in response to the bombshell revelations in Khawaja's book.

Cummins repeated he and the bowlers' stance that he had no prior knowledge of plans for illegal ball tampering, until Cameron Bancroft was caught with sandpaper during a Cape Town Test match in 2018.

Sandpapergate live updates: Cummins says Khawaja's ball-tampering claims '100 per cent wrong'

He agreed the bans handed down to Bancroft, David Warner and Steve Smith were too harsh after an investigation found they were the only players behind the plot, but rejected Khawaja's assertion that the entire team knew.

"When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins told a packed press conference in Sydney.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

Pat Cummins has rejected Usman Khawaja's claims that everyone knew about ball tampering in 2018. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"But Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper.

"That's complete and utter nonsense."

Cummins said he did not remember any conversations around the team taking collective responsibility, as Khawaja said in his book he had pushed for.

The 33-year-old said he had exchanged some messages with Khawaja over recent days and planned to speak to him at some point.

Pat Cummins says Usman Khawaja has been "casual" with people's lives. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

But the pair's relationship is now considerably rocky.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," Cummins said.

"In his book, Uzzy's been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket.

"I support his right to tell a story. I'm really glad that he feels like he can. But we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Cummins said it was up to Cricket Australia whether they would reopen the investigation into the matter, something the organisation has already ruled out.

Cricket great Usman Khawaja could barely walk and thought he had a terminal illness when he was just starting out his Test career. He was soon diagnosed with a crippling disease, which he has kept secret for 17 years.

But he made it clear he wanted to move on from the scandal, declaring his willingness to take every question on Friday should make it the last time he has to speak about it.

"I did get advised this week that some of the things that were said are probably defamatory," Cummins said.

"But I won't be doing that. Like, you've got to move on. It's been eight years.

"We're moving on. You've got to draw a line at some point."

Now the Australia Test captain, Cummins pointed out that at the time of the scandal in South Africa, he was a 24-year-old just 13 Tests into his career.

Cummins said he had also not yet spoken to Warner since his backing of Khawaja's claims, and could not explain why their position was so different to his.

"That sounds like a pretty good question for those two," he said.

"Again, there's quite a few different accounts here, so they've got two accounts.

"There's 11 players in that room, so that means there's nine other guys who I think it's appropriate you give an equal amount of weight into their story as well."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/f.title: Advocates warn FIFO standards are slipping on mine sites
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/f.author: Alistair Bates and Bryn Wakefield
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Mining and Metals Industry

FIFO workers face long shifts away from family, with accommodation playing a crucial role in their wellbeing. (ABC News: Cody Fenner)

Researchers say minimum accommodation standards are dropping on mine sites around the country.

As a result, FIFO workers are more likely to experience psychosocial hazards like isolation and harassment.

A code of practice for worker's accommodation is set to be endorsed by the WA government next year.

With six years' experience as a WA fly-in fly-out (FIFO) worker, Vicky Pellowe still remembers the creeping sense of loneliness at the end of a 12-hour shift.

"If you have had any kind of challenge or if there's anything going on at home, you are very much isolated with your own thoughts in your room," she said.

"It needs to be comfortable, clean and connected."

Mining camps are often built up with demountable "dongas". (ABC: Jessica Shackleton)

As the Australian resources sector has exploded with year-on-year production records, advocates warn basic accommodation standards on remote mine sites are slipping.

Ms Pellowe says the options range anywhere from extravagant camps to motel-style overflow to "donga" demountables.

Ms Pellowe, executive director of the FIFO Family Project, represents one of 50 organisations that submitted to the WA government about a draft code of practice for workers' accommodation.

Vicky Pellowe heads the FIFO Family Project, an advocacy group she founded after working in the mining industry. (Supplied)

The code outlined best practice for amenities, including deadbolts on doors, better lighting in outdoor areas, king-single beds and reliable Internet connections.

Triggered in part by revelations of widespread sexual harassment on site, it closed for feedback in June.

The Department of Local Government, Industry Relations, and Safety says the code will receive final endorsement next year.

Once the code of practice is in place, mining companies will not be legally bound to follow it, but it could be admissible in court if a hazard has not been properly managed.

Ms Pellowe said there remained critical gaps when it came to connecting workers with their loved ones back home.

She called for a mandated 24/7 contact point for families to raise welfare concerns.

"They can be a real part of the safety net if they're included in these conversations about psychosocial wellbeing of workers," she said.

Architectural sociologist Jack Tooley, who also entered a submission, said mining companies had failed to connect the challenges to their bottom line.

In a study published last month by journal Safety Science, Dr Tooley identified a reluctance to grant access to outside researchers, a lack of trust in survey data and an over-reliance on "wellbeing washing" like swimming pools.

Mid-tier operator Mineral Resources built luxury-style Mungala Resort for its Pilbara workers in 2021. (Supplied: MinRes)

Dr Tooley attributed 60 per cent of the psychosocial issues faced by mine workers to the built environment around them.

Modelling by Dr Tooley's consultancy found simple improvements that lifted a worker's experience to a "neutral standard" — things like a better bed or noise-cancelling acoustics — could generate about $1.6 billion in annual revenue.

Some advocates say the disparity is growing larger between rudimentary camps and resort-style accommodation. (Supplied: Courtney Mason)

In 2025, Mineral Resources grabbed headlines by opening its $140 million Mungala Resort at Ken's Bore mine in the Pilbara, which boasts a pool and accommodation built for couples.

The mid-tier miner has spruiked the 45-square-metre accommodation as three times the size of traditional FIFO rooms.

The problem is not specific to WA.

Erin Turner delivers mental health training at Queensland mine sites and says growing workforces mean FIFO workers often feel shunted from room to room.

"What that means is that people can't have their photos, they can't have certain homelike things that they would usually have," she said.

Ms Turner said "creature comforts" were important to navigate the isolation and recover from long hours.

Researchers from Edith Cowan University found employees in WA's Pilbara region were scared to speak up about the issues.

They approached 20 for in-depth interviews across FIFO and residential rosters.

Senior lecturer Heidi Vivian argued a wave of industrial action at BHP's iron ore and port operations earlier in the year was a reaction, having spoken with union-affiliated workers.

Research found basic improvements could boost workforce value significantly. (ABC: Charlie McLean)

Dr Vivian said a culture of silence shrouded dissatisfaction with pay and conditions as well as allegations of bullying and harassment.

A 2022 parliamentary report found nearly three-quarters of women in mining had experienced sexual harassment at work and it was widely accepted as part of the job.

Class actions have been launched in the Federal Court against BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue.

"They're asked to suck it up, toe the company line," Dr Vivian said.

"I believe that's probably part of the reason that some of the organisations are in the situation that they are now."

A BHP spokesperson told the ABC the company recognised "FIFO work asks a lot of our people".

"We regularly review worker accommodation, services, and amenities across our operations and we welcome the input of our workers," the spokesperson said.

Rio Tinto said it refurbished 3,000 of more than 1,900 FIFO rooms last year, along with mess halls, showers, laundry blocks and gyms.

Fortescue Metals Group was also contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/a.title: What is green steel and why is everyone racing to make it?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/a.author: Jon Daly
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Australian companies are racing to build green steel mills powered by renewables. (Supplied: Nucor)

As companies race to build Australia's first green steel mills, questions remain whether costs, technology and logistics will stop the industry's loudest advocates fulfilling their promises.

The race to Australian green steel production is hotly contested, with at least five aspiring projects across Western Australia, New South Wales and Queensland targeting production by 2030.

Their race matters because conventional steelmaking is a heavy emitter, accounting for 8 per cent of the world's greenhouse gas emissions.

Dominic Meagher, an economist and research fellow from ANU's Crawford School, puts it plainly:

Traditional steelmaking is a heavy producer of greenhouse gases. (Supplied: Francisco Fernandes on Unsplash)

"You can't stabilise the climate without dealing with the greenhouse gas emissions from steel," he said.

"The basic situation is that it is very important to get this done, but it takes a long time and we don't have that much time."

Green steel is produced in various ways, each promising significantly lower emissions than traditional steelmaking.

The chosen method of several leading local projects is to melt scrap metal in an electric arc furnace powered by renewables, an approach proponents say could reduce the carbon footprint by up to 90 per cent.

That recycled steel is known as secondary steel.

Australia has traditionally focused on primary steel, using iron ore that is melted in a coal-fired blast furnace.

Further processing turns that iron into a steel billet, or bar.

Established electric arc furnaces already recycle scrap at Laverton in Victoria and Rooty Hill in New South Wales.

What is "green steel" and could it be a reality for Australia?

Generation Steel is among the hopefuls trying to build the next generation of secondary steel mills in the West Australian town of Collie, 200 kilometres south of Perth.

"It's almost a little bit incomparable between the Australian facilities and what we're doing," co-founder Rajan Aggarwal said.

The "continuous" facility is designed to turn scrap metal directly into new reinforcement steel, which will remove the need for a billet or a blast furnace.

"Rather than producing a billet using energy, then cooling it down, then transporting it somewhere else, then rolling it, you can actually do that all in a continuous process," Mr Aggarwal said.

"And that itself increases the energy efficiency by about 80 per cent."

Green steel projects are trying to rival and replace cheap imports of rebar for construction. (Supplied: Nucor)

Australia's traditional steelmakers are struggling with aging infrastructure, cheap imports and the formidable challenge of decarbonisation.

Since the permanent closure of the coal-fired blast furnace at Whyalla, South Australia, Australia has become increasingly reliant on imports for reinforcement steel, commonly known as rebar.

Australia's construction sector uses millions of tonnes of rebar a year to build bridges, homes and just about anything with concrete.

This domestic steel market is where Mr Aggarwal and others have set their sights, targeting price parity with imported and tariffed rebar from Asia.

The blast furnace at the Whyalla steelworks was shut down permanently earlier this year. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Mr Aggarwal said there was a misconception that green steel was a premium-priced product.

"That's a little bit unfortunate, but you have to break some of those barriers," he said.

He argues green steel has competitive advantages, namely the abundance of scrap metal created by heavy industry and low-cost power from renewables.

WA exports almost all its scrap metal overseas — almost 600,000 tonnes were exported out of Fremantle Port in 2025–26.

Some of it may inevitably return in imported steel products.

Steel production accounts for 8 per cent of the world's carbon emissions. (Supplied: Morteza Mohammadi on Unsplash)

The same is true in Queensland, where roughly 60 per cent of the state's scrap is exported overseas, according to Rohan Richardson, chief executive of Future Forgeworks.

Mr Richardson believes his company's proposed green steel mill near the city of Ipswich, outside Brisbane, could compete with cheap imported rebar.

"If our scrap metal right now leaves QLD, it goes all the way to Asia; it's processed there," he said.

Green steel has a drastically lower carbon footprint than traditionally made steel. (Supplied: Nucor)

"With logistics reduction and the modern processing facility, our production costs can compete with Asia."

But with three rival projects in QLD alone, Mr Richardson acknowledged there was only so much scrap metal to go around.

"It would create an imbalance in supply and demand, but I'll leave it at that," he said.

Greensteel Australia is the only company to lock in final investment for the first stage of its mill at the former BHP Newcastle Steelworks in NSW.

Its production methods differ somewhat, and it will initially use imported steel from South East Asia rather than domestic scrap.

But future plans for clean iron processing could require billions of dollars in further investment.

While the concept and its associated benefits have drawn significant publicity and funding, they are yet to be proven financially viable.

The South Australian steelmaking town of Whyalla was a case in point, where steel tycoon Sanjeev Gupta took over in 2017.

He promised to transform the aging facility into a global hub for green steel by 2030.

What followed was severe financial losses and job cuts, and the eventual closure of the Whyalla blast furnace.

WA mining magnate Andrew Forrest has also faced criticism over whether his vision for green iron would withstand commercial realities.

Fortescue's green iron pilot plant at Christmas Creek in the Pilbara region reached the technical milestone of first molten metal earlier this year.

Beyond the immediate race for secondary production of green steel is the broader global contest for green iron, or low-emissions primary steel production.

Green iron, or direct reduced iron, is made in a "direct reduction furnace", replacing the traditional coal-fired blast furnace.

These furnaces use hydrogen or natural gas (methane) instead of coking coal to remove oxygen from ore.

The method is better suited to higher-grade, magnetite iron ore, which is significantly harder to extract and process than the lower-grade hematite iron ore largely targeted by Australian miners.

Generation Steel recently struck a deal with Rio Tinto to process small amounts of green iron from a pilot plant in Kwinana at its mill in Collie.

Tim Buckley, director of the think tank Clean Energy Finance, calls green iron the "holy grail".

Tim Buckley says green iron is the "holy grail" for Australia's exports. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

"For decades, Australia has been relying on our world-leading mining industry, but it has been a dig-and-ship mentality," he said.

"That could potentially double or triple the value per tonne of the iron ore we're exporting."

Mr Buckley said global interest in green iron was growing, pointing to the European Union's recent introduction of a carbon tax applied to imports at the border.

Last year, the Chinese government also expanded its own national emissions trading scheme to its heavy-emitting steel sector.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.title: 'Insufficient evidence' to charge Sydney Swans players with sexual assault
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.author: Danny Tran, Olivia Jenkins, and Emma D'Agostino
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

James Jordon, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney (clockwise from top left) will not face criminal charges. (ABC News/Getty Images)

Four Sydney Swans players involved in a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault will not face charges.

Player Isaac Heeney welcomed the news, saying the past three months had been "incredibly difficult" for his family.

Lawyers for the three women involved have confirmed they are still pursuing civil lawsuits related to the allegations.

Sydney Swans players embroiled in a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault in a Melbourne hotel will not face criminal charges.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Nick Blakey had been under a police investigation over the alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel in late August.

Several adult entertainers are understood to have joined players at the East Melbourne hotel after being hired in the hours after the Swans' win against Essendon on August 17.

The ABC understands the investigation centred on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

The police investigation centred on events at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne in August. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

Multiple police sources previously told the ABC they understood an arrangement was reached in the hotel room for players to pay extra to take drugs, believed to be cocaine, from the women's breasts and buttocks.

It is unclear how many players, or which players, had allegedly participated.

It is understood a woman was seen leaving the hotel room in a distressed state in the early hours of the morning, with a Triple Zero (000) call made to police soon after.

This morning, Victoria Police confirmed no charges would be laid over the incident.

"Following a thorough investigation and based on legal advice, Victoria Police will not proceed with criminal charges due to insufficient evidence," a police spokesperson said.

Victoria Police said due to an "ongoing civil matter", no further comment would be made.

Sydney Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich told a press conference today it had been a difficult period for everyone involved and affected by the hotel incident.

"We appreciate and understand that everyone has been dealing with it in their own way, and we thank them for their support during that time," he said.

Matthew Pavlich says the outcome of the police investigation marks a moment to move forward. (ABC News)

"We've been in constant contact with the players through the whole process.

"Today's a moment for them to move forward. It's a time for everyone to move forward, and at some point, they'll be back here at training, back with their teammates, and that's going to be an important step."

The players were sidelined by the Sydney Swans in the days after the incident, for staying out late drinking and inviting women back to the team hotel in breach of club standards.

Fellow Swans player Riley Bice, who was also stood down for breaching club standards, was earlier cleared in the police investigation.

In an earlier statement today, Sydney Swans management said they stood by the decision to stand down the players "because their conduct fell short of the standards of behaviour expected at the club".

"The club was clear from the outset that this decision was separate from the police investigation, and it stands by that decision.

"The club has commenced a comprehensive examination of its AFL program and is committed to acting on the findings and implementing meaningful change to build an environment that players, staff, members, supporters and corporate partners can be proud of," the statement said.

Pavlich said that work was the club's express focus.

"This is not a day for anyone to really celebrate — we're still looking very hard at the program and understanding where we need to get better for the future and examining that in real thorough detail," he said.

"I can guarantee everyone out there that we'll be doing everything we can to restore the standards and behaviours that this club has held for a long period of time."

Blakey last month moved from the Swans to North Melbourne football club, apologising for "the events that led up to my exit from Sydney".

"I know I have to win back the trust of the broader community, football and otherwise," he said at the time.

The police update came as lawyers confirmed three women were still pursuing civil lawsuits related to the allegations.

Lawyers representing one of the women who alleges she was sexually assaulted said she was "devastated" by the decision.

Slater and Gordon lawyer Jackson Pannam said what had occurred had a "profound impact" on her.

"She reported the incident immediately, provides a formal statement and cooperated fully with the investigation," he said.

"She has shown enormous courage in coming forward."

Mr Pannam confirmed the woman would proceed with a civil case, which must be proved on a "balance of probabilities" rather than the higher criminal standard of "beyond reasonable doubt".

"Slater and Gordon Lawyers is continuing to prepare a civil claim against the relevant parties and will continue to support our client through this extremely difficult time."

Victoria Police said a thorough investigation into the incident concluded there was insufficient evidence to lay charges. (ABC News)

John Karantzis from Carbone Lawyers, who is acting for two of the women in a civil claim against the club, said his clients were "very disappointed and distressed" over the outcome of the police investigation.

He said the women would still forge ahead with their civil claim.

"My clients' civil claim is based on a different burden of proof, it is based on the balance of probabilities," he said.

"We will vigorously pursue this claim."

Asked about how the club might handle related civil claims, Mr Pavlich contained his comments to the outcome of the police investigation.

"Any future aspects, we'll deal with that as it comes," he said.

In a statement, Heeney welcomed the police announcement.

"The past three months have been incredibly difficult for my family, Steffie and those close to me," Heeney said.

"Watching my family carry the weight of this has been heartbreaking.

"To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice.

Swans player Isaac Heeney was among those spoken to by police during the investigation. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"To those that have never doubted me and stood by my side in solidarity — thank you. I know it has not been easy in the face of such intense public scrutiny. I will never forget your support.

"To the entire Sydney Swans Club — my teammates, coaches, the board, our sponsors, and our loyal members and fans — thank you for keeping faith in me.

"The Swans have given me an opportunity to live out a childhood dream and I am fully focused on repaying that faith by being the best person and player I can be."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: U.S. Congress steps up scrutiny of Trump and Nvidia after Huang exit
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Robin Legrand
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
WASHINGTON – Key U.S. lawmakers on Thursday called for clarity on what the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump knew about Nvidia chief Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, after the artificial intelligence chip giant announced his departure.

Huang, now Nvidia’s former CEO, had pushed for looser rules on sales of U.S. chips to China — crucial in the AI race — and the controversy has reenergized advocates of a hard line on Beijing, days before Trump travels to China.

“Despite Jensen Huang’s resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk,” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said on social media.

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset,” he added.

Huang, a co-founder of the AI chip giant, on Sunday acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. The two are not related.

U.S. intelligence suspects her of working for Beijing, which has strongly denied the allegations.

According to The New York Times, Trump was informed of the suspicions last year, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed them to him in May.

Trump said on Monday he knew “the FBI is looking into” the affair, adding that he expected Huang to be “in good shape.” He said Huang had told him he did not know the woman was a spy.

Huang was ultimately brought down by the scandal on Thursday, when the company’s board announced his departure, effective immediately.

Lawmakers are also raising questions about Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s alleged reluctance to impose restrictions on exports of the chips to China.

Three Republican House committee chairmen had already said they wanted to hear from Huang behind closed doors on Nov. 18.

Democrats, who will take control of both chambers of Congress in January after winning the midterm elections, have also said they intend to look more closely into the affair.

The top Democrats on the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees told Lutnick in a letter on Thursday that they were investigating the administration’s “scheme to approve and tax” Nvidia chip exports to Chinese firms linked to Beijing’s government and military.

They accuse Lutnick and Trump of ignoring the “obvious national security threat” posed by the ties between Huang and a suspected Chinese intelligence agent, even though they had reportedly been informed of them.

Senate Republican leader John Thune told reporters on Thursday that a congressional investigation “would make sense” given the national security interests at stake.

Schumer, who will succeed Thune as the Senate’s most powerful lawmaker in January, demanded answers from the White House: “Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” for a state visit to China in May.

Beyond the national security questions, Democrats could also look for signs of corruption.

According to The Washington Post, Nvidia pledged $25 million toward the ballroom Trump is building at the White House, a few months after chip sales to China resumed. The company says the donation was unrelated to its business interests.

“The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump administration, Chinese spies and AI billionaires, the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt,” Democratic Sen. Chris Coons wrote on X last week.

“Congress will investigate and get answers.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang resigned after an affair with a former executive at a data center company. Huang had pushed for looser rules on sales of U.S. chips to China. The controversy has reenergized advocates of a hard line on Beijing, days before Trump travels to China.

WASHINGTON – Cade Cunningham racked up 52 points as the Detroit Pistons edged a double-overtime thriller 144-140 against Washington on Thursday.

The Wizards twice extended the game with clutch scores in the dying seconds, but could not repeat the trick a third time as the Pistons held their nerve to claim an epic road win.

Cunningham became the first player in NBA history to score 50 points and add 10 assists with zero turnovers, while Ausar Thompson had a triple-double with 17 points, 11 assists and 11 rebounds.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: “Yankii” fashion for coming-of-age ceremony showcased in London
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
LONDON – Japan House London on Wednesday kicked off an exhibition displaying exuberant yankii rebellious youth fashion seen at coming-of-age ceremonies in the city of Kitakyushu in Fukuoka Prefecture.

Running until April 18 next year, the “Tradition/Rebellion” exhibition at Japan House London, a hub for promoting Japanese culture established by the Japanese government, showcases both the yankii fashion culture centered on standing out from the crowd and the originality and diversity seen in Kitakyushu.

The exhibition highlights the culture’s rebellious spirit through haori traditional Japanese overgarments adorned with flashy embroidery and what is known in Japan as a Regent hairstyle, a blend of a pompadour and a ducktail.

Along with the history of Kitakyushu, the event features a video introducing the unique attires of eight newly minted adults.

Sota Yamaguchi, who curated the exhibition, said that the striking fashion came about through craftsmen’s trial and error to capture the new adults’ resolve to surpass those close to them and their seniors.

Some within Japan are opposed to calling the attention-seeking behavior a “culture.” Still, Kitakyushu Mayor Kazuhisa Takeuchi, who visited Britain for the event, promoted his city’s famous coming-of-age ceremonies, saying, “All cultures are born amid controversy.”

He added that the exhibition will help discover the values of Kitakyushu’s culture from a new global perspective.

Japan House London’s Simon Wright said the exhibition probably could not have been staged in Japan and stressed the importance of looking beyond appearances and valuing individuality.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Japan House London exhibition showcases yankii fashion culture at coming-of-age ceremonies. Exhibition highlights the culture's rebellious spirit through haori traditional Japanese overgarments adorned with flashy embroidery.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: El Nino, climate change supercharged Indonesia fires, study says
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: Mary Hui
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
A strong El Nino and human-induced climate change fueled the hot and dry weather over Indonesia this year that sparked the country’s worst wildfire season in a decade, according to new research.

El Nino was the driver of the severe lack of rainfall, while climate change was the cause of high temperatures, a report by World Weather Attribution shows. Human-induced warming made hot and dry conditions about three times more likely, as well as more intense, researchers said.

Indonesia’s worst fire season in years cloaked local towns and neighboring countries such as Singapore and Malaysia in toxic smog, prompting schools to close, straining diplomatic ties and crimping palm oil output. Poor rainfall from June through the end of October left the landscape bone-dry, making blazes often linked to slash-and-burn agricultural practices harder to contain.

“El Nino turned off the taps, but fossil fuel emissions turned up the heat,” said Friederike Otto, a professor of climate science at Imperial College London and a co-author of the study published Friday. “Without rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels and strengthened land-management protections, we will see more and much worse fire seasons like this in the future.”

Climate change amplified the hotter conditions from August to October, making the seasonal heat about 1.6 C hotter and more likely to occur, according to the study. Parts of Indonesia have also seen decades of deforestation and peatland draining, significantly increasing the fire risk, the authors wrote.

The ongoing El Nino is estimated to have reduced Indonesia’s seasonal rainfall by about 50% this year, and together with higher temperatures, the country experienced “record breaking fire weather,” the report said.

“Our analysis shows that climate change acts as a force multiplier during El Nino years,” said Theodore Keeping, an extreme weather and wildfire researcher at Imperial College London and lead author of the study. “When a strong El Nino hits, global warming makes the resulting fire weather significantly hotter, drier, and harder to contain.”
