https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Sheep-shearing and puffer fish among items in Japan’s New Year lucky bags
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Major Japanese department stores will sell fukubukuro lucky bags in their New Year’s sale next year, with many featuring frozen foods and gourmet ingredients.

The focus on food reflects department store operators’ aims to generate interest in their products as a proposed cut in the consumption tax rate on food next April is expected to boost demand for dining at home.

Stores are also offering sheep-themed food and experiences because 2027 is the Year of the Sheep in the 12-year Chinese zodiac cycle.

Takashimaya has prepared a ¥20,270 ($126) bag containing 30 servings of frozen foods, including its store-brand sweet-and-sour pork and hamburg steaks, along with a 121-liter freezer.

The company will also offer a ¥2,027 set consisting of lamb meat and a grill for jingisukan, a mutton barbecue dish. Both offerings will be available to five customers each through a lottery.

Matsuya will sell 200 lucky bags containing items worth up to ¥27,000 at its Ginza store in Tokyo for ¥5,000 each. The items will include crab and puffer fish, as well as meal vouchers.

At its Asakusa store, Matsuya will offer 10 lucky bags for ¥5,500 each, containing ¥3,000 worth of vouchers redeemable at its basement food hall and two vouchers for lunch at nearby restaurants.

Tobu Department Store will sell 10 lucky bags for ¥10,000 each at its Ikebukuro main store in Tokyo and its Funabashi store in Chiba Prefecture. Purchasers will have the opportunity to experience shearing sheep and other activities carried out by animal keepers at Tobu Zoo in Saitama Prefecture.

The Funabashi store will also offer a lucky bag that allows customers to experience herding sheep at Mother Farm in Chiba.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Japanese department stores will sell fukubukuro lucky bags in their New Year's sale next year. The focus on food reflects department store operators' aims to generate interest in their products. 2027 is the Year of the Sheep in the 12-year Chinese zodiac cycle.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Putin agrees to European participation in next round of Ukraine peace talks
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Andrew Osborn
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
MOSCOW/DUBLIN – Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed on Thursday that European representatives could join the next round of Ukraine peace talks, a U.S. envoy said, though the Russian leader said Washington must work with its European allies to understand if they want peace or war in Ukraine.

The move to give Europe a seat at the negotiating table at the next round of talks, announced by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, could mark a breakthrough. But Putin’s comments underlined how difficult the negotiations could become, given sharp differences between Moscow and European capitals over the way the war should end.

“The Europeans will join at the next meeting, which we consider to be a very important moment because they are our partners and it’s important to us that they take part,” Witkoff told Russian state TV after meeting Putin in the Kremlin.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Finance Ministry looks to rein in defense spending push amid funding concerns
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Nobuhiro Kubo
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Japan has warned defense contractors of deep cuts to expected orders as fiscal constraints threaten to scale back a military buildup that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government says is ​needed to counter China, four people familiar with the matter said.

Finance Ministry officials last week ‌proposed spending between ‌¥50 trillion ($313 billion) and ¥60 trillion on defense over ​the five years starting in April 2027, the people familiar with the proposal said.

That would exceed the current ¥43 trillion five-year plan but fall well short of the ¥80 ⁠trillion advocated by some defense officials and ruling Liberal Democratic Party lawmakers.

The gap would leave Japan short ⁠of its target of raising defense outlays to 2% of gross domestic product (GDP), as U.S. President Donald Trump presses Washington’s allies to spend more ​on their militaries.

The 2026 U.S. National ⁠Defense Strategy calls for allies worldwide to spend 3.5% of GDP on their armed forces and a further 1.5% on broader security needs.

The revised ⁠spending proposal could mean ​cuts by as much as half in planned purchases of some ​missiles and aircraft, including U.S.-made F-35 stealth fighters, the people said.

The people spoke ​on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

“The advisory panel on security and defense has not yet discussed matters at that level of detail either, so I don’t think we are at a stage where I should comment,” Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told reporters when asked about the revised spending proposal.

The Defense Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Finance Ministry officials argue that a steeper increase would be difficult to fund alongside Takaichi’s commitments to invest in economic growth and cut the sales tax on food, which would squeeze ​government ​revenue, three of the sources said.

The sales tax cut would leave ​an annual ¥4.3 trillion revenue shortfall that Takaichi would need to fill through other funding sources, ⁠potentially including foreign exchange reserves.

The Finance Ministry’s defense proposal, however, is likely to face resistance from security hawks in Takaichi’s party, setting up a clash over how much Japan can afford to spend to bolster its defenses.

“A contingency could occur at any time. If the goal ​is to build the capabilities necessary to deter and prevent such a contingency, a figure in the ¥50 trillion range is out of the question,” one ruling party official familiar with the discussions said, requesting anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: The yen is becoming too difficult for some investors to trade
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: John Cheng
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
After a year of wild swings, the yen surprised traders by settling into a tight range clustered near ¥158 per dollar over recent months. But this week, it broke out again, unexpectedly breaching the key ¥160 threshold before rebounding on speculation that officials would intervene to support the currency.

The sudden moves underscore just how difficult Japan’s currency has become to trade. Traditional signals such as interest-rate differentials have become less reliable guides, while Bank of Japan (BOJ) tightening, persistent capital outflows and unprecedented intervention have pulled the yen in competing directions.

The stakes extend far beyond Japan. The yen is one of the world’s most heavily traded currencies, changing hands in some $1.6 trillion of transactions each day. Its direction can make or break the fortunes of global investors, while its longer-term trajectory has implications for everything from Japanese inflation to the flow of the nation’s vast pool of savings into overseas markets.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: The yen broke out again, unexpectedly breaching the key ¥160 threshold. The sudden moves underscore just how difficult Japan's currency has become to trade. The yen is one of the world’s most heavily traded currencies, changing hands in some $1.6 trillion of transactions each day.

WASHINGTON – Senior White House officials are discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out amid a spy scandal surrounding Nvidia’s now-former CEO Jensen Huang, two people familiar with the situation said on Thursday.

A growing number of lawmakers criticized Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key U.S. trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China.

Criticism of Lutnick’s actions predates Thursday’s resignation of Huang, who said he would step down as CEO of the leading AI chipmaker after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. But the charge that Lutnick has not done enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China has emerged as the fallout from Jensen Huang’s actions grows.

The government is considering arranging a meeting between Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and International Criminal Court President Tomoko Akane, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Thursday.

Akane, a Japanese national, and the ICC have been targeted by sanctions imposed by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Kihara said that the Japanese government would like to make an advance payment of its contribution to the ICC for 2027 within this year.

He made these remarks when he received a proposal from Gen Nakatani and Yasue Funayama, co-chairs of a suprapartisan parliamentary group on human rights diplomacy, calling for Takaichi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi to meet Akane when she returns to Japan later this month.

At a later news conference, Kihara said it had yet to be decided whether to make the advance payment, adding, “The government will continue to consider what financial measures it can take.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Yasutaka Tamura
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
SmartNews is seeking to raise ¥11.2 billion ($70 million) in an initial public offering in Tokyo next month, at a valuation that’s 80% lower than its latest major funding round in 2021.

The news aggregator app developer’s founder and backers plan to offer 8.1 million shares at an indicative price of ¥1,390 each, according to a regulatory filing Thursday.

Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities, Morgan Stanley MUFG Securities and Nomura Holdings are the underwriters of the share sale. Books will open on Nov. 30 and pricing is expected on Dec. 7, with trading to begin on Dec. 15.

The indicative price implies a market value of about ¥43.1 billion, compared with about ¥219 billion in the company’s F series funding round, based on the exchange rate at the time.

It is also lower than the valuation of about ¥50 billion that the company was reportedly seeking in the IPO after exploring a trade sale but failing to find a buyer. The valuation may yet change during the process as some companies launch deals with a conservative pricing indication.

The deal highlights the struggles of what was once one of the most best-regarded startups in the country. Founded in 2012, SmartNews gained traction in the U.S. and Japan with its news aggregation app and became one of the few unicorns in Japan.

But the rise of artificial intelligence has made its valuation ambitions harder to justify as more people turn to AI as a gateway to news, resulting in the mismatch between the company’s lofty valuation and what investors are willing to pay.

Still, the debut will inject some momentum to Japan’s IPO market after the number of deals shrank to a 13-year low. The deal flow dwindled as the bourse effectively narrowed the window of new listings for smaller firms after investors criticized the underperformance of such stocks.

Hillhouse Investment Management-backed luxury villa operator Nota is among the startups looking to debut in December.

A survey released earlier this month found that junior high school students were increasingly negative about immigration. More than 40% of those surveyed opposed the notion that “an increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.author: Shaun Mckenna
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.text:
It’s a wonderful time of year for word nerds. Last week, the organizers of the annual 新語・流行語大賞 (Shingo Ryūkōgo Taishō, New Words and Buzzwords of the Year) unveiled 30 nominees for its 2026 edition. The top 10, along with the grand prize winner, will be announced Dec. 1.

But why should we leave it to the grown-ups to decide which words matter? Personally, I’m much more interested in learning how Japan’s Gen Z speaks, and, lucky for us, ギャル (gyaru, gal) magazine egg has its own annual buzzword awards, one that’s perhaps a bit closer to the internet’s collective brain.

Founded in 1995, egg became one of Japan’s best-known chroniclers of ギャル culture, documenting the fashion, makeup and attitudes of young women, particularly in Tokyo’s Shibuya neighborhood. After suspending its print edition in 2014, the magazine returned online in 2018 and has found a new audience on social media. Its annual buzzword awards can give us a snapshot of the language ギャル are currently using, and this year’s list, announced Nov. 1, includes everything from ギャル social dynamics to the perils of endless scrolling.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is heading for a showdown with potential replacement Gadi Eisenkot, who fears the caretaker leader may renew strikes on Iran under false pretenses in an effort to cling to power.

https://www.dw.com/en/us-disrupts-north-.title: US disrupts North Korea's $400 million crypto scam, FBI says
https://www.dw.com/en/us-disrupts-north-.text:
The US has seized servers linked to a North Korean scam that used fake video meetings and deepfakes to steal more than $400 million in crypto, and has moved to seize $1.2 billion that was taken from Binance.

The United States Justice Department said Thursday it had seized cloud infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a video-call scam that has stolen more than $400 million (€361 million) in cryptocurrency over 18 months.

It also said it had court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion taken in the recent Binance hack.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation calls the scam "FaceStealer."

According to the Justice Department, hackers sent meeting invitations from accounts taken over from earlier victims. Once a target joins, the hackers record their webcam video and play a prerecorded clip of a previous victim the target knows, so trusted contacts appear to be present. The FBI says hackers are also starting to use AI-generated deepfakes of well-known crypto figures.

The hackers then stage a fake technical error and offer a link to "fix" it, which installs malware, the department said. In some cases, they waited months, or over a year, before stealing funds.

After that, they use the victim's contacts to find new targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Most targets work in crypto and other internet-related fields, and the hackers are increasingly going after open-source software developers, apparently to enable supply-chain attacks, the department said.

Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos of victims.

"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough," said Patrick Grandy, who heads the FBI's Los Angeles field office.

The FBI ties FaceStealer to a hacking cluster known as Sapphire Sleet or UNC1069. It is separate from the North Korean military hackers blamed for the Binance theft.

In the Binance case, the FBI said the group known as TraderTraitor stole more than $6 billion (5.4 billion euros) on or around October 29. AP put the figure at about $6.3 billion (5.7 billion euros) and called it the biggest crypto heist on record. US agencies and private firms have since frozen more than $2.7 billion (2.44 billion euros), the department said.

Authorities usually file a forfeiture claim in court, after which a judge decides who has a rightful claim to the recovered funds, AP reported.

"North Korea's government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,"  said M. Scott Proctor, the department's principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security.

North Korea has denied involvement in the Binance hack.

https://www.dw.com/en/microsoft-works-to.title: Microsoft works to restore Outlook and Teams after global outage
https://www.dw.com/en/microsoft-works-to.text:
A Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook and Teams worldwide, with reports from scores of countries and territories. Problems from 74 countries and territories within about an hour.

Software giant Microsoft on Thursday said it was working to fix a global outage affecting its Microsoft 365 apps, including Outlook and Teams.

Outage tracker Downdetector received reports from 74 countries and territories within about an hour.

The outage, which blocked users from accessing their e-mail and other services, also impacted Microsoft 365 connectors used by the companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which said tools were not working as expected.

Downdetector logged nearly 130,000 US reports of Outlook problems shortly after 1 p.m. EST (1800 GMT). Some customers reported having trouble sending and receiving e-mail; others said the program was entirely inaccessible.

Outages of the Teams workplace messaging app were also reported, as well as other Microsoft 365 services such as the AI assistant Copilot.

Microsoft initially said on X that it was aware that users were "experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas," noting that part of its infrastructure was "experiencing elevated load" that was "likely contributing to connectivity errors."

"We are aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," it added.

Microsoft said some restarted servers stopped responding again once traffic returned. In an update at 0254 GMT Friday, the company said its latest changes had not worked as expected and that it was looking for other ways to restore service.

https://www.dw.com/en/darth-vader-strike.title: Darth Vader strikes back at auction as his lightsaber from two original Star Wars films reclaims the record from Luke Skywalker's prop
https://www.dw.com/en/darth-vader-strike.text:
Darth Vader's lightsaber sold for nearly $5 million, breaking the record set by Luke Skywalker's in July. The hilt, made from a 1950s camera flash attachment, was used in two of the original trilogy's duels.

A lightsaber prop made for "Star Wars" villain Darth Vader sold for $4.875 million (€4.4 million) on Thursday, setting an auction record for a collectible from the franchise, according to Dallas-based Heritage Auctions.

The iconic prop was used in two defining duels between Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker in the original "Star Wars" trilogy.

Vader wielded the lightsaber in the climactic Cloud City duel in "The Empire Strikes Back" (1980), where he cuts off Luke's hand. When Luke accuses him of killing his father, Vader replies with one of the saga's most famous lines: "No. I am your father."

The same lightsaber returned for their final duel in "Return of the Jedi" (1983). This time, Luke cuts off Vader's hand but refuses to kill him.

Vader's lightsaber set an auction record for a screen-used "Star Wars" prop in 2025. Luke's lightsaber from the same Cloud City duel broke it in July. In the latest twist, Vader struck back to reclaim the record.

Actor David Prowse and stunt performer Bob Anderson both wielded the saber as Darth Vader. It may also have been used in the original 1977 "Star Wars" film, but the auctioneers could not confirm that.

"Star Wars" creator George Lucas drew on Errol Flynn swashbucklers and the legends of King Arthur. He imagined the Jedi as peacekeepers guided by chivalry and honor and wanted a weapon that suited that role.

In the original "Star Wars," Luke's Jedi mentor, Obi-Wan Kenobi, gives him his father's lightsaber, describing it as "not as clumsy or random as a blaster" and calling it "an elegant weapon for a more civilized age."

Lucas first imagined the Jedi carrying ordinary swords. He gave them futuristic blades that could deflect blaster fire. As he put it in the Lucasfilm featurette "The Birth of the Lightsaber": "A laser sword in a world of ray guns would be a perfect defensive weapon."

The hilt began life as a 1950s British camera flash attachment. Prop makers added black plastic grips and tiny magnifying lenses from a calculator display. Heritage described it as "built to perform rather than merely to be seen." The crew reinforced the hilt to hold interchangeable wooden blades and screwed the grips into place after they came loose during fight scenes.

For "The Empire Strikes Back," the crew initially covered the wooden blades in reflective material and later painted them white. After filming, the effects team used the rods as a guide, tracing their movements frame by frame to create the blazing red blade seen on screen.

Heritage matched a distinctive bend in the hilt's belt ring to a production photo from "The Empire Strikes Back" and a dent at its base to a close-up in "Return of the Jedi."

https://www.dw.com/en/fifa-loses-bid-to-.title: FIFA loses bid to block UEFA evidence gathering against Infantino
https://www.dw.com/en/fifa-loses-bid-to-.text:
A New York judge has dismissed soccer governing body FIFA's attempts to shield its president from investigation. Europe's UEFA is seeking evidence of wrongdoing by Gianni Infantino.

New York Federal Court Judge Jeannette Vargas on Thursday rejected a bid by US subsidiaries of soccer's global governing body FIFA to block Europe's governing body UEFA from gathering evidence tied to FIFA President Gianni Infantino's attempts to sell shares of the  World Cup and other tournaments to private investors.

UEFA filed for discovery in the case in August with the intent of removing Infantino from office and has said it will file a criminal complaint against the embattled soccer boss in Switzerland if it finds evidence of financial wrongdoing.

UEFA is seeking discovery of evidence from Infantino's partners in the so-called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, a plan that instantly sparked fierce backlash when it became public in July.

The court's ruling means UEFA can now request the right to obtain documents tied to the deal from the US bank JP Morgan and the investment firm Thrive Capital, which is owned by Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and son of US Ambassador to France Charles Kushner, a convicted felon whom Trump pardoned before appointing him to that post.

Two FIFA subsidiaries had sought to block UEFA's efforts, but Vargas ruled they had no "direct, substantial and legally protectable interest" in the case, which is specifically aimed at Infantino and his dealings.

"Nothing in this record indicates that the US FIFA parties, or even FIFA itself, will be parties in the contemplated criminal proceedings," according to Vargas.

In an eight-page ruling issued from the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, Vargas wrote, "Certainly the US FIFA parties have not alleged facts suggesting they would be defendants in such a proceeding."

FIFA lawyers countered by saying, "The court has not addressed the merits of UEFA's application and no documents are required to be produced."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Infantino came under intense fire for seeking to set up FFE to manage FIFA's commercial interests in the World Cup and other competitions by allowing private investors to purchase minority stakes, with three continental soccer confederations rejecting the plan and UEFA threatening to boycott future FIFA tournaments if the plan was not scrapped.

The 211 member federations of FIFA, which effectively own the Zurich, Switzerland-based not-for-profit outfit, were offered $20 million (€18.1 million) payments each to approve the project.

Infantino initially pushed back but was eventually forced to abandon the plan in August.

UEFA has continued to push for Infantino's ouster since then and has demanded answers about the details of his scheme, for instance, questions about how Thrive was selected to head the investor group.

In what is the biggest challenge Infantino has seen in his 11-year stint as head of FIFA, UEFA has filed requests for discovery in multiple states in an effort to ascertain whether there was wrongdoing on his part.

Infantino has been accused of seeking retribution against those opposed to his leadership and in September FIFA told a judge in Florida, where the governing body has offices in a Miami suburb, that UEFA's legal pursuits amount to harassment of Infantino.

Infantino has shown no sign that he is willing to vacate his post and instead plans to run for reelection as FIFA president.

To do so, he must pass an eligibility and integrity check conducted by a FIFA-appointed panel.

So far, only one person, Japan's Kohzo Tashima, a member of FIFA's 37-member ruling council since 2016, has declared his candidacy.

UEFA is expected to propose another challenger and is currently seeking to get FIFA Head of Global Development and former Arsenal London coach Arsene Wenger to stand against the Swiss incumbent, who is also his boss.

Anyone wishing to challenge Infantino must declare by next Wednesday, November 18.

UEFA is also seeking evidence from Infantini's partners in the so-called FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.title: What we know about the global Microsoft outage
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.text:
A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems, or in some cases disabled entire services, including emails and artificial intelligence products.

Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues have so far been largely unsuccessful.

Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.

Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".

Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.

Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues.

More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.

The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening.

The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting.

Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.

Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.

From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.

Courts from Los Angeles to Texas warned that communications might be delayed.

In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.

The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.

Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.

Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack and attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure.

The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do.

In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these.

On Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.

The company added it is focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" and warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue".

In an earlier statement, the tech giant had said that its attempted fixes were "not taking as expected".

Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming for some, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.

Professor James Ferryman from the University of Reading said the details the company has disclosed provides some clues.

"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.

"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.

"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.

"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."

The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.

Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".

He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.

Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.

"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75.title: UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over Iran nuclear site
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75.text:
The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.

Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.

In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material.

Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.

Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.

Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.

The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.

The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.

"The Agency's lack of information about [Iran's] nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said in the latest report.

Iran announced plans for the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) on 12 June 2025, shortly after an IAEA resolution which declared Iran had failed to meet its nuclear safeguards obligations.

Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after Israel launched attacks the following day.

The IAEA's latest calls come almost a year after it made a similar appeal to Iran. At the time it said it had only inspected some of the 13 nuclear facilities that were "unaffected" by the attacks and none of the seven that were.

The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons - something Iran has consistently denied seeking. It says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckly.title: African Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckly.text:
Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.

Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.

"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.

Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.

Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.

"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.

Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.

The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.

In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances.

"Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.

Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.

The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them.

Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa.

"I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.

Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."

In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico.

She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"

The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.title: Nigerian university in mourning after four students die at post-exam party
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.text:
Four Nigerian students have died after attending a party in the south-eastern town of Nsukka to celebrate the end of their final exams.

The cause of death has not been confirmed but police spokesman Daniel Ndukwe said the two men and two women had reportedly fallen ill after consuming alcoholic drinks at the party.

The University of Nigeria Nsukka has declared three days of mourning, during which academic and social activities will be suspended.

The tragedy comes amid a wider crackdown on fake and adulterated alcoholic drinks in Nigeria, where the food and drug regulator has been raiding suspected producers of unsafe food and beverages.

The university's Vice-Chancellor, Professor Simon Ortuanya, said the university had received a distress call at 22:00 on Wednesday, and sent security personnel to a house party at Praise Lodge, outside the campus in Nsukka's Hilltop area.

"The preliminary investigation and interim report point to alleged alcohol abuse or drug paraphernalia and things like that. But we are not conclusive on those matters," he said.

He described the deaths as "tragic and painful".

"As a community, we mourn, not just alone, we mourn with the families, the parents that have suffered these years to train the men and women in their studies," he said.

Ortuanya also announced a ban on signing-out celebrations, which are commonly held by final-year students to mark the completion of their studies.

The celebrations often involve parties, dancing, photographs and friends signing one another's shirts. He urged students to use graduation as a time to reflect on their university experience and prepare for life beyond campus.

The university said it was working with security agencies to establish what had caused the deaths.

The police have also launched an investigation. They said alcoholic drinks had been recovered from the scene and the bodies taken to a mortuary for autopsies.

The investigation comes amid wider concerns about unsafe alcoholic drinks in Nigeria.

In September, dozens of people fell ill after consuming locally made alcoholic drinks and herbal mixtures in communities across Ondo State, south-west Nigeria.

More than 11 people died in the Araromi-Obu area, while more than 50 others were hospitalised.

Investigations found that some of the drinks had been contaminated with methanol, a highly toxic form of alcohol that can cause blindness and death.

Nigeria's food and drug regulator, Nafdac, reported more than 150 cases, including 48 confirmed deaths. More than 80 people were hospitalised, and five lost their sight.

The regulator has been carrying out raids across the country, targeting facilities suspected of producing fake or adulterated alcoholic drinks, food and beverages.

Nigeria has long struggled with the sale of unsafe and adulterated products, which campaigners warn pose a serious threat to public health.

The cause of death has not been confirmed but police say the two men and two women had fallen ill. The university has also announced a ban on signing-out celebrations.
