https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674.title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674.text:
How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.

But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?

That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.

A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.

Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.

There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.

This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.

Now the political pressure is building.

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.

And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.

Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.

Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.

The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.

It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".

That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.

There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?

The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.

The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.

This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.

Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674.summary: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c670.title: Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c670.text:
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.

Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.

But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.

"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."

A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.

Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.

His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.

Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."

"I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.

Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.

There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.

And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.

"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.

"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."

Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.

In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field.

"I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."

However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.

David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".

Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.

But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.

And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.

Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".

"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.

"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."

He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.

He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.

"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.

Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.

Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.

But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."

As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.

"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."

Few people think he'll get his wish.

"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.

"I don't know what the outcome will be."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c670.summary: Pat Cummins says he doesn't want to talk about sandpapergate again. Former teammate Usman Khawaja has released a memoir about his involvement in the scandal. The book has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.title: Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.text:
For the last few weeks, in addition to its usual payload of passengers, medicine, and supplies, Alaska Seaplanes has carried some unique cargo: midterm election ballots.

The regional airline is a piece of a complex logistical puzzle that sees Alaskans' ballots cast by mail and in person carried across the vast expanse of America's largest state, which is primarily connected by water and air rather than roads.

This considerable task explains why, a week after most US states knew their results in the midterms - in which the Democrats won back both chambers of Congress from the Republicans - Alaskans are still waiting for the Senate race to be called.

The victor in this close contest between the incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, former congresswoman Mary Peltola, could remain unknown until 18 November, when officials expect to have counted all eligible ballots.

"We do feel a sense of pride of making sure we do the job right - the really complicated job of getting all these ballots across thousands of miles in Alaska," Andy Kline, the marketing director of Alaska Seaplanes, which serves the south-eastern part of the state, told the BBC.

"We feel like we're part of the last leg of that journey of those ballots."

Some precincts in Alaska are able to communicate their initial results to centralised election offices on election night, allowing state officials and news outlets to report some preliminary vote tallies.

But it takes some time for the full picture of how people have voted to emerge.

As well as having the logistical challenge of counting votes from across a state more than six times the size of the UK, there is a delay waiting for mail ballots to arrive, says Charles Stewart, an election expert at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

These ballots can arrive up to 10 days later, or 15 days for overseas voters, if postmarked by election day.

Stewart said that election officials had "chosen to err on the side of getting it right rather than a rush to report the second and third tranches of ballots that get counted".

Regardless of whether ballots were cast in person or by mail, all of them eventually wind up in the state capital of Juneau – which is only reachable by plane or boat – for scanning and counting.

While more urban districts can get their materials on a plane late on election night, it takes longer for smaller or more remote parts of Alaska.

In some places, "you get someone who's basically running the election for their family and their neighbours because it's such a small village", says Scott Kendall, an election lawyer who previously worked on two campaigns for Alaska's other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski.

In these smaller areas, ballots are sealed up in special envelopes or containers and sent it through the mail - which is where companies like Alaska Seaplanes comes in.

Ballots are put on the planes and sent to Juneau, where they then get dropped at the post office and delivered.

"It's part of our daily routine, just another couple of boxes," Kline said.

Once all the in-person and absentee mail ballots reach Juneau, election officials will complete their review.

If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote in the first round, officials will quickly use ranked-choice voting to re-allocate votes from the lowest-scoring candidates to their voters' second choices.

Then Alaska will finally declare a winner for its Senate race, as well as contests for governor and US House of Representatives.

Adding to the suspense of who will win the Senate race is the question of whether another Republican candidate called Dan Sullivan, who was allegedly recruited by Democratic operatives, would affect the outcome. Results released so far suggest a low probability.

This week, President Donald Trump alleged Alaska's Senate election had been "rigged" due to the second Dan's involvement. His administration is appealing its rejected lawsuit to halt certification of the election over the issue, which a lower court dismissed.

Meanwhile, a judge has denied an attempt by Peltola's campaign to get information about how many absentee ballots election officials rejected, as well as information about those voters.

The state argued it had no obligation to share this data, and doing so would violate voter privacy.

While the result of the election is of the greatest importance to many, for people like Kline the process is also key.

"We're all citizens," he said of himself and his colleagues.

"We all feel like we have skin in the game to make sure that our elections are accurate and timely."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.summary: Alaska Seaplanes carry ballots across the state's vast expanse of Alaska. The state's election officials are waiting for the Senate race to be called. The winner could remain unknown until 18 November, when officials expect to have counted all eligible ballots.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art.title: Whatever happened to the $300,000 diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art.author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art.text:
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?

If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.

A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.

Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?

Someone, somewhere, knows something.

The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.

Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.

"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.

"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."

His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.

They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.

"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.

"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."

Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.

The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.

Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.

What happened next, though, was not part of the script.

There was huge media interest in the appearance of the Hollywood stars

While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.

The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.

Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.

Jaguar were given two different types of diamond for the weekend - one for promotional purposes (on the left) and one to be welded into the cars (on the right)

Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.

Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.

In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.

Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.

It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.

"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.

He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.

"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.

"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."

By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.

But there were plenty of theories.

Theory: it was not a real diamond

Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.

"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.

"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.

"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."

Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.

"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.

"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.

"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."

Theory: someone pocketed it

"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.

"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].

"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.

"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."

There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.

Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.

"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.

"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.

"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.

"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."

Theory: Klien crashed on purpose

Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.

And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.

"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.

Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.

"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.

"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.

"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."

While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.

His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.

"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.

"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."

In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.

"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.

"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."

Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."

Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.

"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.

Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art.summary: A 1.4 carat diamond was stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix in 2004. The diamond was not found until 22 years later. F1 team boss Purnell says the diamond was stolen from Christian's car.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp9.title: Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp9.text:
At least 74 countries have been affected by the Microsoft outage since it was detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on Thursday.

Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and artificial intelligence software Copilot, are experiencing "connectivity problems", the company said.

From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption has been widespread. Here's what's been happening around the world.

In the US, staff with the House of Representatives told Politico their work had been halted by the outage.

"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."

Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems.

OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.

Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.

Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.

Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.

The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.

"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."

In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto had declared a code grey, indicating an infrastructure failure.

The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.

In Japan, some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.

"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times.

The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.

"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.

Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".

Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.

In the Philippines, the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".

In India, the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.

People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.

"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.

Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.

Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.

China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.

Australia's spy and federal police agencies have been affected by the outage, though officials have suggested the impact is minimal.

"The impact that they are dealing with is very much on email system", the head of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, Mike Burgess, told reporters.

Other Australian public service providers also confirmed they had been affected by the outage, but similarly said this was mostly limited to emails, and the BBC understands there were no major impacts across New South Wales' primary services in health, education, transport, and emergency services.

European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reports.

In the UK, GPs, police and pharmacies are among services affected.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.

Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.

"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."

Some parts of Asia, Europe and Africa remain unaffected, according to Downdetector. These include Russia, where the use of Microsoft applications is heavily restricted, or phased out in favour of domestic alternatives.

However, this could also be a case of under-reporting in some countries, where Downdetector is among the websites blocked due to censorship.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp9.summary: outage detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) in the US. In Japan, some companies are among the websites blocked due to censorship.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.title: GPs, police and pharmacies among UK services affected by Microsoft outage
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.text:
GPs, police and pharmacies are among UK services affected by a global outage on some Microsoft platforms.

NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report. MPs have also been affected.

Microsoft has said the problem was caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers but that systems were now showing "early signs of stabilisation" as work continued on a fix.

Major airports and UK intelligence services have been unaffected by the outage, while a minister said officials were assessing the extent of the impact on government services.

Sir Ciarán Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some NHS services including emails.

NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.

Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111, 111 online or their local pharmacy.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.

A spokesperson for the National Pharmacy Association said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".

Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and North Yorkshire Police have all issued statements saying online forms may be affected by the outage. They have urged people to call 101 with time-critical but non-emergency reports.

South Wales Police and Dyfed-Powys Police have also reported similar issues and are asking people to call if they need to get in touch. Police Scotland said there may be delays responding to forms submitted in the past 24 hours.

The London Ambulance Service's critical platforms do not use Microsoft so are unaffected by the outage.

The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" across ambulance and NHS trusts.

"Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos," she said, though "emergency and life threatening call outs appear to be unaffected".

Heathrow, Manchester and Stansted airports are operating as usual.

Defence minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that the government was "assessing the impact" of the outage on its systems and would issue a statement once this was completed.

A government spokesperson said it was "working closely" with Microsoft to assess "any impact on government services" by the company's outage.

It is understood that UK intelligence operations have been unaffected. While some elements of the security services use Microsoft tools, they have a separate system for secret operations.

MPs are unable to access their parliamentary accounts, however. A spokesperson said alternative arrangements were in place to allow the day's business to go ahead.

Some teachers have reported being unable to access their calendars, emails and files on cloud servers, while parents in several parts of Scotland being told to call to report absences rather than using email.

Northern Ireland's Education Authority said its schools were unable to access email accounts.

Royal Mail also said some of its online services were unavailable and that email notifications about deliveries may be delayed or unset, but that post was still being collected and delivered as normal.

Microsoft and cyber-security experts have ruled out a cyber-attack being the cause of the outage, which has affected Outlook, Teams and Copilot.

The tech firm said a large number of its servers had become "unexpectedly available", meaning traffic was sent to the servers that remained online, putting them under strain.

"Just like on a motorway, when you block one lane, you have to put all of the excess traffic through just, say, one or two lanes," Jake Moore, a cyber-security adviser at ESET, explained.

"Everything goes and backs up. It slows down, and that's what we're seeing here."

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this incident should "hammer home" the need for contingency communication networks that are "independent of others".

"Unfortunately, we just put so much emphasis on just a few providers - so when one big one like this goes down, the knock-on effects are just huge."

His sentiment was echoed by Nicky Choo, who said his cyber-security firm Mimecast used Microsoft tools but had built-in alternatives to prevent disruption.

Moore added that "good old-fashioned phone lines" seemed to be "the strongest form of communication, especially today".

Caroline Wade, who runs her own PR agency in Kent, told the BBC that the outage had caused "huge disruption" to her work, including one client with an exhibition launch and another running a large public art project in central London.

"You feel that this is something that you can rely upon - it's quite incredible that it's not been sorted yet," she said.

But others were initially glad to hear about the Friday 13th outage - especially as it has occurred just before the weekend.

Martin told the BBC that waking up to no new emails was "absolute bliss" until he realised "today is a crucial day to conclude a business deal".

Meanwhile, one Radio 1 listener described it as "equivalent to an adult snow day".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.summary: NHS England says patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise. NHS trusts in England are enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services. NHS Scotland and NHS Scotland are also affected by the outage.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqy4.title: Heat pumps: How much heat does your home really need?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqy4.text:
Floorplans. Air duct diagrams. Heat pump specifications. Most people in the market for a new heating system probably don't want to think about this level of detail.

But, perhaps surprisingly, some do want to think about those things. In extreme depth.

Every day, roughly 150 new users sign up to an app called Cool Calc, which works out the heat requirements of properties in the US.

Just over one third of those new users are not tradespeople but private homeowners, says founder and chief executive Bill Fiore.

When choosing a heating system, people can find themselves bombarded with information – how powerful a heat pump do they need, for example? It isn't always easy to take a tradesperson at their word.

"As an overall trend, we are seeing homeowners be more informed," explains Fiore. "They want to do a calculation on their own."

A heat loss calculation is a figure, usually measured in watts, that defines how much heat a home loses during cold weather. It's worked out room by room and is a key part of designing an efficient heating system.

This estimate is especially important to get right when installing a heat pump, which is sized fairly precisely, according to the projected heat loss.

Should that calculation be off, the heat pump will likely perform poorly. You could be left with an underpowered device that struggles to warm your property, for example. Given the costs involved, homeowners are often anxious to ensure installers avoid such mistakes.

Certain new technologies are not, for the moment, helping, adds Fiore. "People are going to AI and they're getting a lot of misinformation because it's not backed by anything credible," he says. Cool Calc is planning to integrate with AI chatbots to try and improve the quality of the advice they spew out.

It is probably a good idea to be cautious about your new heating system's design, says Kevin Kircher at Purdue University. He and colleagues recently conducted a study, yet to be published, examining the heat loss calculations provided by tradespeople to roughly 75 US homeowners.

"We were surprised," says Kircher. "The heat loss calculations often led to overestimating the design heat loads by a factor of two or more." That would result in oversized systems that use much more power than necessary.

Not only that, some people reported charges of more than $1,000 (£745) – and in one case as much as $2,500 – just for a heat loss survey, adds Kircher.

Besides using excessive amounts of energy, an oversized heating system can also feel uncomfortable, says Dan Dempsey, a former senior engineering fellow for a major heating and cooling provider in the US.

Dempsey, who took part in Kircher and his colleagues' study, lives in Indiana. He says it is his retirement hobby to monitor the performance of heating and cooling systems in the homes of friends and family members, by analysing data from their smart thermostats.

"I spent five years manually downloading everything, every week," he says. He points out that oversized systems tend to cycle a lot, meaning they switch on and off again in quick succession.

This leads to discernible swings in temperature: rooms that fail to remain at their target temperature of, say, 20C, but rather fluctuate, which feels uncomfortable, says Dempsey.

For people seeking a better understanding of their home's heat loss, various free or partially free apps, including Cool Calc and AutoHVAC, are available. There are options for UK homeowners, too, such as web app Heatpunk.

Many things can influence the heat loss figure, including the amount of insulation in your home, whether the building has double or triple glazing, and also the size of your radiators.

Heatpunk allows people to draw a floor plan of their home and input data about the property in order to estimate its performance. Thousands of people use it every month, mostly professional installers, says Andy Rankin, founder and managing director of Midsummer Energy.

The web app also suggests specific heat pump models for each property, based on the results of the calculation. Naturally, these are models available through Midsummer Energy. "It's been a very effective marketing tool," says Rankin.

Dwellow, another company that offers heat pump installations in the UK, is keen to follow suit. The firm recently launched its own heat loss estimator.

While professional heat loss calculations remain essential, getting people to do their own "self surveys" first could ultimately reduce how much time professional heating engineers must spend analysing properties says Ian Mclaren, Dwellow's co-founder and director.

"Going into a home and just being able to check the information rather than start from scratch could turn a survey into a half-hour trip – far more efficient and less costly," says Mclaren.

There's no substitute for engineers doing a good job when it is their turn, however, stresses Maurizio Sibilla, of the Centre for Advanced Built Environment Research at the University of West England, Bristol.

"The solution is better installer practice, clearer customer-facing evidence, and improved methods, not expecting homeowners to do the engineering themselves," he says, adding that providing homeowners with information about the calculation and also data on heat pump performance post-installation can reassure them that the system works as expected.

Doing your own heat loss calculation may end up "over-intellectualising" things, says Adam Chapman, chief geek at heat pump training firm and installer network Heat Geek.

"I don't personally see what a homeowner would gain from it," he says. "We will guarantee the efficiency with way less radiators and pipework upgrades than any other system out there."

Chapman points out that only the most careful of surveys will capture a home's heat loss well.

He says it is common for Heat Geek installers to discover retrofitted windows that haven't been foam-insulated into their openings, leaving draughty gaps, or cavity walls that a homeowner thought had been insulated – but which were actually missed by the builder.

"It's stuff you can't see," he says. "What we actually need is home surveys that go and spot for these sorts of things."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqy4.summary: A heat loss calculation is a figure, usually measured in watts, that defines how much heat a home loses during cold weather. Heat Geek says only the most careful of surveys will capture a home's heat loss well.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj1d.title: Summer heatwave put bin crews lives at risk, says council worker
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj1d.text:
Some bin collections were missed over the summer in a county partly because the heatwave became so serious it posed a risk to the lives of workers, a council worker has said.

Flintshire County Council's Chris Goddard said crews faced a "perfect storm" of challenges during the UK's record-breaking hot weather, causing a spate of widespread missed collections.

During the summer, drought was declared in all of Wales and wildfires caused devastation in parts of the country.

Goddard said: "We do have to make some difficult decisions but ultimately if there is a fatality in the workplace because of a decision I've made, that's something that I would have to live with – and probably defend."

Despite the missed collections the council remained on target to hit the Welsh government's national 70% waste recycling target this year, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

Goddard, the council's streetscene service manager, said: "We had maybe five or six operational challenges that all came at the same time in a perfect storm this summer.

"Unfortunately, the heatwave was one of them and it was a contributing factor. We do have to prioritise staff safety above all else.

"My number one job every day is to make sure that everybody goes home safely and we take that really seriously within streetscene. That was only one of several contributing factors.

"That level of change is naturally going to cause a few bumps in the road, particularly with staff being asked to do a little bit more. There were some staffing issues during that period too."

Councillors praised Flintshire residents for largely embracing three-weekly residual waste collections and ensuring that the authority remained on-target to hit its statutory recycling rate.

"Three-weekly was very controversial at the time it came in," said Saltney councillor Richard Lloyd.

"It's quite clear to see now that the three-weekly black bin collection has been a good new factor. Recycling has improved at the kerbside."

Councillors said in the authority's meeting the change to three-weekly bin collections meant the council should still hit target despite the disruption.

The council also cut the amount of waste it sent to landfill or Parc Adfer by 6,467.49 tonnes between 2024 and 2026, and that improvement continued this year despite problems this summer.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj1d.summary: Flintshire County Council says crews faced a "perfect storm" of challenges during the summer. Council says heatwave was one of them and it was a contributing factor. Council remains on target to hit the Welsh government's national 70% waste recycling target.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg.title: National Trust takes back land for nature restoration
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg.text:
A 370-acre (150-hectare) area of land on the edge of Cambridge has been returned to the care of the National Trust - for the first time in 60 years.

The area - known as Northfield - runs alongside the opposite side of Quy Road towards Bottisham, seven miles (11km) from the city and close to Anglesey Abbey.

The National Trust hopes to restore the natural site to create new wildlife habitats and improve community access to green space.

Emma Ormond-Bones, general manager of the National Trust's North Cambridgeshire Portfolio, said: "We want Northfield to become a place where nature can thrive, helping wildlife recover and building resilience to a changing climate."

The project comes at a time when Cambridgeshire remains one of the most nature-depleted counties in the UK, where demand for accessible green space is increasing as the county's population rapidly grows.

Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the tenants.

The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".

There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.

The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.

Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".

Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."

The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.

Community drop-in sessions about the vision will be held between Saturday 21 November and Friday 27 November.

Feedback will be used to help inform the next stage of planning before proposals are developed during 2027.

Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below.

Follow Cambridgeshire news on BBC Sounds, Facebook, Instagram and X.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg.summary: 370-acre area of land on edge of Cambridge returned to the National Trust for first time in 60 years. The area - known as Northfield - runs alongside the opposite side of Quy Road towards Bottisham. The National Trust hopes to restore the natural site to create new wildlife habitats and improve community access to green space.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6gr.title: World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6gr.text:
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.

They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.

The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.

The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.

"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.

The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves.

Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.

The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.

Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, different styles are linked to particular periods.

The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.

Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old.

"Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."

Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.

Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue.

"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.

The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae.

"It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said.

"It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."

The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.

The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.

They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.

Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.

There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaeology Association specialises in finding and studying them.

Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel.

"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years.

"We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."

The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months.

The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.

Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.

The oldest known intact shipwreck, where the wood is still preserved, was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6gr.summary: The shipwreck is the world's oldest shipwreck, dating to 4,400-4,700 years old. It was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rm.title: My physical deformity left me feeling invisible - but one surgeon saw me
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rm.text:
As a teenager at school, Charlie Clarke "felt awful" in her uniform, with a physical deformity leaving her so self-conscious that she hid from her classmates.

At home, she wrapped her dressing gown tight around her chest, hoping it would conceal her condition - and didn't even tell her parents about it.

Now 26, Charlie has lived with pectus excavatum - a congenital chest wall condition that can make the chest appear sunken or hollow - for years.

As she awaits surgical treatment, she said the emotional and physical effects of the condition were "unimaginable and unignorable".

"Having pectus excavatum, which is a disability and a deformity under my shirt, was at times hell," she said.

Her worst memories from her teenage years are of hiding in the school bathroom during PE so other girls would not comment on her having "four breasts".

"I got to a point where I felt awful wearing my school uniform because of how I looked, also because of how people looked at me and made comments about my chest," said Charlie, from County Down.

The condition, which affects one in every 200 people, means Charlie's heart and lungs are compressed, which triggers breathlessness and an increased heart rate that can cause her to lose consciousness.

Charlie is one of 85 people in Northern Ireland who are waiting for surgery for pectus conditions.

Many of them have been waiting for their operation for less than two years - but five have been on the list for longer than five years.

The Department of Health said it acknowledged that some patients in Northern Ireland "have endured lengthy waits", adding that the volume of patients combined with "other demands on the thoracic surgery service have contributed to pressures on waiting times".

But it said it had secured extra funding for more surgeries in order to reduce the amount of people on the waiting list, resulting in additional pectus procedures in the last three years.

It also said it had agreed a further proposal "which should help to reduce both the number of patients waiting and the length of their waits".

If diagnosed early, patients can often be treated without surgery.

But getting that early diagnosis is key - and treatment depends on the type of pectus, how severe it is and the patient's age.

Charlie said she was previously "misdiagnosed, including [being] told I had anxiety".

"It wasn't until I had my shirt off in front of a clinical technician and she said they were unable to see my heart in a scan, it was compressed, and only then was I referred to a thoracic surgeon."

That was when she was 23 years old, which is considered too old for non-surgical treatment.

A breakthrough came when Charlie met someone who truly understood her experience.

Niall McGonigle, a Northern Ireland-based consultant thoracic surgeon, specialises in chest wall deformities.

What makes his expertise particularly unique is that he suffered from a pectus deformity himself as a child and underwent surgery at 17.

"I was called freak and a mutant at school," he said.

"It drove me away from sports because of changing for PE - I was bullied.

"It is what started my interest in medicine... I was profoundly interested in surgery and specifically pectus."

McGonigle said the condition was not recognised in Northern Ireland, and patients are often dismissed as asking for cosmetic surgery, which is not the case.

"There is a lot of evidence to show there are restrictions on the lungs and heart, which can be debilitating," he said.

"If this is diagnosed early, patients can be treated with non-surgical services.

"But Northern Ireland doesn't provide this and our young people are having to go to England instead."

McGonigle said Northern Ireland's limited pectus surgery service had been undermined by inconsistent funding.

Charlie's surgery will involve two metal bars being placed in her chest and a metal plate in her sternum, allowing her heart and lungs to return to their natural positions.

She said she was speaking out to raise awareness of the condition and to help others who have it, including her 11-year-old sister.

"I don't want her to have to wait this long and for her life to be paused and for her condition to become life-threatening," Charlie said.

Pectus excavatum, also known as "funnel chest", is different for everyone. Most who have the condition were born with it.

A patient's breastbone curves inwards, with a dip the ribs, which can leave the chest appearing sunken or hollow.

It is usually more noticeable in childhood or teenage years.

One treatment is vacuum bell therapy, using a suction device that sits over the sunken part of the chest to gradually lift the breastbone forwards.

It works best in younger people with a flexible chest wall and a relatively shallow deformity.

Another treatment, compression bracing, involves a specially fitted brace and is most effective in teenagers - but generally less so once the chest becomes rigid in adulthood.

In its statement, the Department of Health said work it carried out in 2023 led to the commissioning of a service for "non-surgical bracing of pectus carinatum".

It added it is understood this "can, in appropriately selected patients, negate the requirement for surgery".

"The impact of this service will be evaluated, including its potential to free up theatre capacity for those conditions which can only be resolved surgically."

Last month, patients and health professionals from across the UK met in Belfast to discuss the condition.

Simon Kendall, of the charity Pectus Matters, said early treatment saves the health service money in the long term.

"If you get that treatment when the patient is young and chest wall is more flexible you can avoid the big operations in the future."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rm.summary: Charlie Clarke, 26, has pectus excavatum - a congenital chest wall condition. Condition can make the chest appear sunken or hollow. She is one of 85 people in Northern Ireland waiting for surgery for patients and health professionals.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2l.title: Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2l.text:
Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016.

The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November.

Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire".

The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".

While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.

Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit.

Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line.

"But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line."

Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too".

He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016."

Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards".

On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill."

The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.

The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy8.title: US inflation higher than expected in October - here's what is happening with prices
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy8.text:
US inflation rose at a faster-than-expected pace in October, according to official figures.

Prices rose by 0.4% in the month, which was lower than the 0.6% increase in September.

However, analysts had expected prices to rise by 0.3%, and the higher-than-expected pace could add to arguments for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting in December.

The new figures come a week after the midterm elections which were fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

Over the month of October, prices rose by 0.4%, driven by increases in housing, food and energy costs.

However, the pace of energy price rises, at 0.7% in October, was much lower than the 5.2% increase seen in September.

While the Bureau of Labor Statistics would normally provide figures for the 12-month change in prices, it did not collect data in October 2025 so it could not provide that estimate.

For the 12 months to September, inflation was 3.7%.

The US Federal Reserve has a target for keeping annual inflation at 2%.

When inflation is too high the Fed tends to raise interest rates in order to encourage people and businesses to save more and spend less money in the hope this will slow price rises.

While there was no annual figure published for inflation this month, analysts say the fact inflation was higher in October than expected increases the chance of an interest rate rise at the Fed's December meeting.

Federal Reserve governor Chirstopher Waller, who spoke before the latest inflation figures were published, also suggested he was leaning towards a rate increase in December even if October's figures were slower than expected.

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

While inflation is currently above where the Federal Reserve would like it has been much higher in previous years.

During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.

Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.

Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

The value of social security benefits is changed to largely keep up with inflation, protecting people's ability to purchase their usual goods and services through the cost-of-living adjustment.

Shortly after September's inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.

The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.

The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy8.summary: Prices rose by 0.4% in October, lower than the 0.6% increase in September. Social Security benefits will rise by 3.6%, Social Security will rise 3. 6% in 2027. The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqj9.title: Politicians back focus on cost of living
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqj9.text:
Politicians have backed the Government of Jersey's key priorities for the next political term which includes action on the cost of living.

States members adopted the Common Strategic Policy which lays out the Council of Ministers' priorities for the political term until 2030.

The priorities are centered around four pillars including targeted action on the cost of living, restoring Jersey's competitiveness, investing in homes and infrastructure and maintaining financial stability.

Chief Minister Lyndon Farnham said the government was determined "to make Jersey a more affordable place to live" but Reform Jersey co-leader Lyndsay Feltham said the policy lacked "real action".

The policy was backed with 31 votes in favour, 10 against and two abstentions.

Ministers first published the proposed policy in September and this week politicians debated a number of amendments proposed by backbenchers.

This included adding a priority about government transparency and promoting democracy, bringing the total number of priorities up from 11 to 12.

Deputy Feltham's amendments to add actions to the policy about household affordability and employment rights were rejected and members also voted not to include reference to rental stress.

The Reform Jersey co-leader said she was worried about the gaps this left behind.

"What I really wanted to see from government was something more sustained and a sustained commitment to reduce everyday cost of living," said Feltham.

"They've committed to a review of household affordability. A review doesn't put food on the table or a roof over somebody's head.

"I am really concerned that ministers aren't going to actually take any action."

However, the chief minister said the policy recognised islanders' concerns such as affordability, housing, economic growth, investing in infrastructure and protecting the environment.

In his closing speech, Farnham said their contributions "reflected a shared commitment to securing the best possible future for our island".

He said the policy "will send an important message to islanders that we are putting their interests before our political disagreements".
