https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5zj.title: Cider makers fear future for orchards as costs grow
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5zj.text:
Rising costs could force the cider industry to reduce their reliance on British-grown apples, according to several well-established businesses.

Higher alcohol duty, energy bills and packaging costs are making it harder to stay profitable, according to a producer in Somerset.

The government said it was supporting the sector by increasing the value of Small Producer Relief, which provides lower alcohol duty rates for some smaller and medium-sized producers.

Matilda Temperley, director of Burrow Hill farm near Martock, said it would be a "tragedy" to stop using its own apples due to climbing costs.

Temperley, whose farm has been growing apples for 300 years, said recent increases had added to pressures already facing the industry, adding at 6% alcohol, their traditional cider is taxed at a higher rate than mass produced cider.

"By next February, we will have seen a 61% increase in tax on our standard 50cl bottles," Temperley claimed.

She welcomed the rise in Small Producers Relief but said other mounting costs outweighed it.

"We've got huge, energy costs, then almost a 90% increase in tax costs since 2020."

"The thing that will happen is that if you're a big cider maker, you're going to look to cut your costs and the only way to cut costs is to stop using British apples," she said.

"That's a real tragedy because cider should be made from these beautiful orchards".

Isaac Stell, a financial analyst at Wealth Club in Bristol, said that having pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax, national insurance or VAT for working people, the recent budget focused on other areas to "help plug the fiscal hole."

He said producers were also dealing with higher employer National Insurance contributions and increases in the minimum wage.

"Inevitably, some of those additional costs will find their way through to the pubs, clubs and restaurants that producers supply, and ultimately to an already squeezed consumer. "

The Showerings family, known for producing Babycham, has been making drinks in Shepton Mallet for more than 14 generations.

"Our business has grown a lot in the last ten years - we've gone from having 80 employees to around 350 now," the firm's managing director Matthew Showering said.

"We've had a good couple of years, we're making drinks that are popular and growing."

While acknowledging rising costs, Showering said he would rather see less government intervention.

"We don't want any help from the government, we'd rather they keep out of things as much as possible."

Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider in Low Ham said the size of his operation means he will be eligible for the Small Producer Relief but adds he will not see a huge benefit as the Alcohol Duty is a "fairly substantial" part of his monthly outgoings.

Gillett remains optimistic, and said he would not consider importing pulp or concentrate to cut costs.

"We are a craft producer here in Somerset and are proud of the fact we take from local orchards, traditional orchards, and use the fruit that is available here in this county."

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The cider industry makes a vital contribution to our rural economy and communities, and cider continues to benefit from significantly lower duty rates than other alcoholic drinks.

"But we know the industry is facing continued pressures, which is why the Budget provides additional support by cutting costs for pubs and bars that are vital customers for the industry and poured pints continue to benefit from draught relief."

Follow BBC Somerset on Facebook and X. Send your story ideas to us on email or via WhatsApp on 0800 313 4630.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmkg.title: Firm offers to fake artworks for wealthy migrants seeking UK 'talent' visas - BBC investigation
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmkg.text:
Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.

The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.

Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.

Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years.

We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee.

A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation.

No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than £100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said.

In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work.

A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists.

"There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood.

Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected.

The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the £100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation.

A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system".

They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused".

The man who told us artwork could be created in China for clients said he was from a company called iCareer Consultancy UK, based in Canary Wharf. That is also where its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, which is registered with the government regulator to offer immigration advice, is based.

Social media posts by iCareer employees pitch Global Talent visas as a route for wealthy Chinese nationals to come to the UK, without the need to speak English.

During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us:

iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address.

We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath of our first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims, when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum.

The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching.

A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu.

In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artist… Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approval… We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well."

In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement".

Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said.

While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud".

The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained.

Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration.

About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025.

Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year.

The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories.

Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent".

Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said.

"We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK.

Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London.

Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained.

To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time.

During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes.

Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win.

The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor.

It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges.

Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experience… online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English.

This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf.

Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter.

The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029.

The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about £98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling.

During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application.

The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass.

"There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result."

He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer.

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law".

When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made.

"We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us.

iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporter - adding that the company strongly denied "offering any visa services whatsoever".

"The meeting described by the BBC was not authorised by iCareer," it said. "We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him."

The company added it had been unaware that Peter and another employee had made social media posts promoting these services and would investigate.

It said that ADArt, which has the same owner as iCareer and was described by Peter to the undercover reporter as another division within the iCareer group, "signs artists and helps them curate exhibitions and develop professional relationships".

Peter continued to be listed as an employee on iCareer's website, and on his own LinkedIn profile, until the company was contacted by the BBC, which iCareer described as an oversight.

Our undercover meeting with him took place in the same Canary Wharf building where iCareer and ADArt are based, a co-working space. He also provided us with an iCareer brochure and sent a contract with a corporate iCareer email contact address.

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal says he has no doubt that some fraudulent claims will get through.

We have learned that the two Nigerian men purporting to be fine art photographers - whose visas have now been revoked because of our investigation - successfully obtained talent visas on the basis of faked evidence.

Their deception first came to light when art critic Molara Wood discovered articles reviewing their work in the Nigerian Tribune - which were under her byline despite the fact she had not written them.

The articles were taken down after she alerted the paper's editors.

The Tribune told us it had identified a "staff member who had posted the articles on our website without authorisation".

It said the employee admitted that "an individual outside the organisation had supplied the articles" but that he had denied being paid for it.

Wood said the criticism attributed to her was of poor quality, as were the artworks.

"It is writing that I would not want associated with me," says Wood. "The images were not worthy of comment."

Other critics have also had the same thing happen to them, she says.

Artists applying for the Global Talent visa have to provide at least two examples of recent press coverage reviewing or profiling their work.

The two men who were supposedly reviewed by Wood - Silva Ndifon and Adanu Emmanuel Okoko - are now thought to be living in the UK.

While one of them does boast an online portfolio, it does not feature the kind of fine-art photography described in the article that Wood did not write. The other appears to have little to connect him to photography, or any other kind of art, beyond the article Wood found.

Neither responded to the BBC's requests for comment. After the Home Office was contacted by the BBC, it is now understood their visas are in the process of being revoked.

If you would like to contact our team about this story you can email on: politicsinvestigations@bbc.co.uk

Additional reporting by Ruhua Xianyu
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmkg.summary: iCare employee Peter told undercover reporter she could get visa for artists who show "exceptional promise" Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd.title: Piddington to bring legal challenge over asylum base plans
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd.text:
The government will face a legal challenge over plans to house more than 1,200 asylum seekers at a former military site near Piddington, the parish council chairman has said.

Planning permission for the development at the MoD Bicester site near the Oxfordshire village was approved by the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner after the Home Office used a fast-track route for projects deemed to be urgently needed and of national importance.

Opponents have six weeks to challenge the decision. Parish council chairman Tim McNally said ministers should "absolutely" be ready for a legal challenge.

Defence minister Luke Pollard said the government would continue to engage with the community.

Piddington, a village of about 350 people, symbolically voted to leave the UK in September over the planned use for the site, and last month the group Wrong Plan Wrong Site appealed for a judicial review into the proposals.

McNally told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the village could also apply the new Hillsborough Law.

Once passed, the law would create a legally enforceable duty of candour which compels public officials and authorities to act transparently when investigations and inquiries take place.

McNally told the programme: "Last night, [Prime Minister] Andy Burnham was on a podium talking about the violence, sexual violence towards women, and bringing it upon the media industry as their responsibility to manage.

"But the reality is, is that this is exactly what the government is doing to us here."

Asked how the village would respond, he said: "There's going to be many actions, you will see. We will disclose that as we move forward.

"Today is a day of reflection, and we'll work out where we plan to go from this point. But I will say, the Hillsborough Law is there for a reason, and we're going to apply it."

Asked if ministers should be braced for a legal challenge, he said: "Absolutely, absolutely."

A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against and one in support.

It also said Rayner had ruled permission via an Urgent Crown Development application should be granted because "national demand for asylum accommodation remains high".

The permission allows for demolition of existing buildings, the building of new modular accommodation, and provisions for health and welfare facilities.

Melise Witkin, who has lived in Piddington for six years, told the BBC that she was "extremely disappointed but not surprised" to hear the plans had been approved.

She said she moved to the village because she wanted "tranquility" and to live in a community, which she said "we have".

"I think people are angry but scared," she said.

"Where are they [the asylum seekers] going? We've got no pavements, we've got no street lights, we've got no pub, we've got no shop, so what are they going to do?"

She added: "It's just the wrong site

"It's wrong for them, and it's wrong for us."

Jo Haw-Cook, who has lived in the village for 56 years, said she is "saddened" but "not surprised".

Speaking to the BBC earlier, she said: "There's still a long way to go, and we're still going to fight on.

"I think the mood is reasonably positive, obviously we are disappointed, but we're resilient, and we are a community, and we will come together to fight this as a community."

Defence minister Luke Pollard told LBC: "It's pretty obvious that there's a strong sense of feeling from the community around Bicester, especially in Piddington.

"The Home Office continues to engage with those.

"There's still a few more stages to go here, so it's not yet fully locked in and delivered, so that we can understand where the concerns are, so they can be mitigated.

"I recognise that any change for the people around MoD Bicester will be a concern, and that's why it's so important that the Home Office engages with the community."

A Home Office spokesperson said on Thursday: "Planning permission allows us to continue to progress the use of MoD Bicester. However, a final decision to proceed is yet to be taken.

"The Government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election.

"This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

"These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community."

In a statement posted on social media, Bicester Town Council said it is "deeply disappointed" by the government's decision to grant planning permission.

"This decision was taken through the Urgent Crown Development process, bypassing normal local planning scrutiny, despite strong and well-founded objections... regarding the suitability of the site, infrastructure capacity, community safety, and the lack of meaningful consultation," it said.

The council said it will now prepare a formal response to the government "setting out its continuing concerns and seeking clear assurances on the issues raised".

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the plans were a "betrayal of the women of Piddington" and "emblematic of Labour and Angela Rayner's disregard for the law and women and girls' safety".

She said on social media: "When I visited Piddington I met a village terrified of what was about to land on their doorstep.

"The Government said it was listening, instead it's completely ignored this community's concerns.

"The 1,000+ male migrants that Labour are about to deposit in Oxfordshire are in Britain illegally. They should be deported as soon as possible, not housed in areas completely unsuitable for the task."

Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said Piddington has become "ground zero for the invasion of Britain".

Speaking in Piddington, he told broadcasters: "Despite an enormous campaign from local residents demanding that the government doesn't dump 1,200 illegal migrant men into their village, Angela Rayner has approved it. It's absolutely shocking."

On whether using the former military site to house asylum seekers is a better use of taxpayers' money than using hotels, Yusuf said: "The only thing that should be happening with these people is them being detained and deported back to the country from which they came."

Additional reporting by Press Association.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd.summary: Planning permission for development at MoD Bicester site near Oxfordshire village approved. Home Office used fast-track route for projects deemed to be urgently needed. Opponents have six weeks to challenge the decision.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6p3.title: Smart glasses banned from Welsh Parliament after ruling they could be used for speeches
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6p3.text:
The Senedd's presiding officer has in effect banned the use of smart glasses in the Welsh Parliament, days after it emerged he would allow them to be used as a teleprompter.

Huw Irranca-Davies had ruled that using them in such a way was OK - provided he was alerted first - but Members of the Senedd (MS) have now been told he "will not be considering any other requests" to use the devices.

Reform's Jason O'Connell made headlines earlier this year after using the glasses to help him make a speech.

O'Connell, whose glasses do not include a camera, said he had voluntarily agreed not to use his device until a review into using them on the Senedd estate ends.

O'Connell previously said he had started using glasses as a teleprompter to improve his speaking skills and to avoid looking down at his notes.

A letter from Irranca-Davies from 20 October, published in committee papers last week, said he had "determined that members may use smart glasses as a teleprompter in the chamber, provided that they give me advance notice".

On Tuesday, an official working for the presiding officer told MSs that "he will not be considering any other requests to use AI-equipped glasses in the Siambr until the review has reported".

They said: "Following further helpful discussions, no members will be using the technology until the review has been completed."

The official said the next stage of the Senedd Commission's review would include a consultation with MSs and staff, and would be completed by the end of 2026 with recommendations "brought forward in the new year".

O'Connell told BBC Wales after the decision: "I've voluntarily agreed to stop using the ones I'm using as a teleprompter until the review completes."

Asked how he felt about the matter, he said: "I'm ambivalent. They were a useful tool to be used on occasions.

"I was no way reliant on their use. But I look forward to using them again once the Senedd approves them."

The Senedd declined to elaborate on the statement to MSs after being asked why the presiding officer's stance had changed.

Reform is currently holding an unrelated boycott of Senedd proceedings, after its member Joe Martin was barred from speaking by Irranca-Davies, after Martin claimed in parliament that white people were being "replaced" in the UK.

The smart glasses decision was issued to MSs before the presiding officer's ruling on Martin was issued.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6p3.summary: Huw Irranca-Davies ruled that using smart glasses in the chamber was OK. But members of the Senedd have now been told they will not be using them until a review is completed. Reform's Jason O'Connell made headlines earlier this year after using the glasses to help him make a speech.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zj.title: Youth scheme branded 'failure' over success rate
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zj.text:
Less than half of young people supported by two government-backed youth schemes in London went on to take up further education, employment or training (Neet) opportunities, according to new data.

Only 1,100 of 2,600 young Londoners supported by the £20m Youth Guarantee Trailblazer scheme moved into further opportunities.

Former youth worker and Conservative peer Shaun Bailey said the scheme was a "failure" and called for more support for employers but Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was helping young people furthest from the labour market and that it was still "early days".

A major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out proposals for tackling the problem next week.

Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training, according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics.

London is one of eight Youth Guarantee Trailblazer areas in England already exploring ways to help young Neets.

More than £20m in government funding is being spent on a variety of initiatives across London, from youth hubs to mental health support.

The money is funding two trailblazer projects in London, one focused on care-experienced young people in 12 boroughs, and a broader scheme that works across the capital.

The Greater London Authority (GLA), which leads the projects, has shared the initial results from year one of the two schemes with the BBC.

By the end of June 2026, London's two trailblazer schemes had offered support to more than 2,600 young people.

The programme offers a range of support, including access to mental health and wellbeing services at colleges and universities, help moving into further education, work experience, careers events, mentoring and practical help finding a job.

The programme is funded for two years until the end of March 2027.

Mattie Davies is a 19-year-old from London.

He recently left college, and since then, has struggled to find work.

"I applied to a good few thousand and it's constant rejections," Davies said.

He has found work as a delivery driver but he says the wage is not enough to pay his bills.

"Uber will take anyone and that's what I didn't want," he said. "I wanted a job I could go into and break down all of my barriers and build myself up as a person."

He has not been receiving support from London's two Youth Guarantee Trailblazer schemes.

Instead, he's been getting support from Millwall FC, where he plays football, and its youth programmes.

Lord Bailey said the government should instead focus on helping businesses employ young people.

"Sixty per cent of young people not moving into full-time employment or education show you it's actually a failure," Lord Bailey said.

"That money would be better spent giving businesses some headroom so that they can actually afford to employ young people."

The skills minister said London's Youth Guarantee Trailblazer schemes were helping young people who face several challenges, such as mental health difficulties or experience of the care system.

"The fact that a lot of them are succeeding at the first opportunity is a good result," the minister said.

"It's worked exactly in the terms we set for it, which is young people who were furthest away from the labour market able to get back into the labour market, and learning about how we engage with some of those young people."

The eight Youth Guarantee Trailblazers in England have received a total of £90m in central government funding over the two years of the programme.

The trailblazers were part of the Labour government's plan to help 16 to 24-year-olds classed as Neet, whose number has been rising in recent years.

There were 125,949 Neets in London at the end of 2025, the highest number of any region in England, according to government data.

Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, X and Instagram. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zj.summary: London's two youth schemes have offered support to more than 2,600 young people. Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training. London is one of eight Youth Guarantee Trailblazer areas in England already exploring ways to help young Neets.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.title: Young, Welsh and into politics - but with different views on independence
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.text:
Cerys and Patrick have a lot in common. They're both young, Welsh, and very interested in politics.

The one thing they don't agree on is Wales' future within the United Kingdom.

A leading academic said the conversation around Welsh independence "has become normalised" amongst young people.

This week, the Plaid Cymru Welsh government set up a new body to consider the case for Welsh independence, as well as more devolution for Cardiff Bay.

For Patrick, he thinks his country is better off in the UK with more devolved powers, while Cerys believes an independent nation could offer more opportunities to people.

Nationalist party Plaid formed a government in Wales for the first after winning 46 seats during the May 2026 Senedd election.

While it hasn't called for a referendum on independence, the second line of its constitution says: "As the National Party of Wales, the party's aims shall be: to secure independence for Wales in Europe."

Pro-union party Reform UK is the second biggest in the Senedd after winning 34 seats in May's election.

Its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said voters "do not want to see Wales ripped out of the United Kingdom" and said the commission was "ridiculous".

A recent poll by Survation for the pro-independence group YesCymru suggested people under 35 in Wales were more in favour of independence than their older peers.

"People feel left behind, especially my age," said Patrick, a 20-year-old student from Newport.

He added that he could understand why people were "energised and enthusiastic" about independence because of issues such as "student loans, the cost of living, the geopolitical scene".

But he said: "As of right now, I just do not think there is a case for it."

However, Patrick, said he would support further devolved powers for Wales within the union.

He said that "practical elements" such as whether there would be a border between Wales and England remain unanswered questions for him.

For Cerys, learning to speak Welsh as an adult and broadening her understanding of history led to a "realisation" that Wales "in reality deserved a lot better than we had been given in the past and in the present".

"I think if we were independent, we could offer people more opportunity here," said the 35-year-old from Bridgend.

She added she'd like Wales to have further powers over policing and justice - a policy area currently controlled by Westminster.

"People seem to be kind of dangling the carrot of more devolution and never actually giving it to us," she said.

"More powers would be great but I will believe in those powers when I see them and until then, I think our best option is independence."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he was open to the idea of giving the Welsh government control of policing in Wales.

A leading academic from Cardiff University said "it's staggeringly important" that "young people are a majority in favour of independence".

"They see nothing strange or impossible about Wales becoming independent in the future," said Prof Laura McAllister, from the Welsh Governance Centre.

She said that there was "great scepticism" around the topic when you look at the opinions of people aged over 65, adding there was a "real demographic schism".

"There's going to need to be something much closer to support at least half the population supporting independence before there is any chance of a referendum being won," McAllister believes.

She added nobody "can afford to be complacent about the future of the union" because "the concept of the United Kingdom has no God-given right to survive in its current form".

"What we've seen in politics in recent times is that the potential for change is intrinsic to everything that happened," she said.

In 2024, McAllister co-chaired a commission which concluded Wales leaving the United Kingdom is a "viable" option.

With polling suggesting between 20% to 30% of people in Wales would be in favour of independence, academics have compared the current situation to Scotland in the years leading up to the independence referendum in 2014.

"In some ways the situation here looks similar to Scotland in 2007," said Dr Jac Larner, a pollster and political analyst from Cardiff University, reflecting on when the Scottish National Party [SNP] took power.

"You might think now we have a party like Plaid Cymru, there's this inevitable march to this endless 50-50 that you see in Scotland, right?

"What's different here [in Wales] is that we still have a lot more hostility to the idea of devolution.

"You have about a third who want to get rid of the devolution altogether, maybe just less than a third who want independence."

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "I have a vision for Wales, I support an independent Wales."

He said it was about "improving a lot of the people of Wales, tackling injustices, tackling unfairness, tackling inequalities, creating prosperity".

He added: "In the here and now, I deal with those issues dealing with the UK prime minister."

In October, the first ministers of Wales and Scotland met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Glasgow for the National Economic Council, where devolution and funding were discussed.

Ap Iorwerth said there was "a new understanding of the injustice of rail expenditure in Wales" from Burnham, as well as "a realisation that this hasn't been given enough attention politically by UK governments in the past".

Following the 2026 Autumn Budget, ap Iorwerth told BBC Wales there were "paltry sums of money coming on rail, when they've said there's £14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services".

A UK government spokesman said: "The prime minister passionately believes in our union and is optimistic about the future of the United Kingdom.

"Our position on referendums is clear - the prime minister is focused on practical solutions to help people with the cost of living and make a positive difference in people's everyday lives, not constitutional questions.

"Through the convening power of No10 North, the prime minister will build a constructive working relationship with each devolved government to explore how we can together contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

Additional reporting by Gwenno Robinson
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.summary: Pro-union party Reform UK is second biggest in the Senedd after winning 34 seats in May's election. Leading academic says conversation around Welsh independence "has become normalised" Autumn Budget, ap Iorwerth says there's £14bn on the way for rail rail.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3.title: More women make allegations against Russell Brand
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3.text:
More women have come forward to make allegations about disgraced entertainer Russell Brand, in interviews with the Times and a new Netflix documentary.

Brand was jailed earlier this week after being found guilty of one count of rape and three of sexual assault at a trial in London.

Allegations against him first emerged after an investigation by the Times, the Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches in 2023.

The Times has now reported accusations of what it called sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by a further six women, which the newspaper said could not be reported until the criminal case had ended. He has denied non-consensual sexual activity.

The Times report was published on Thursday evening, and a Netflix documentary, titled Russell Brand: Open Secret, was made available on Friday morning.

The programme included an interview with a woman referred to as Emily, not her real name, who said she was in a relationship with Brand when she was in her twenties.

On one occasion, she said she "literally begged" Brand to stop after he refused to wear a condom during sex.

Emily, who was portrayed by an actress in the documentary, said: "I said to him, 'No, Russell, please, let's just use protection.' I kept saying 'No'. I said, 'Stop Russell, stop, please don't, please.'

"I begged him. I literally begged him. I tried to kick him off, I tried to draw my knees back, to kick him in his belly, but he was too strong for me."

But he "just pinned my hands back behind my head" before forcing himself upon her, she alleged.

"When it happens you just feel like, is this... is this rape? Because I'm with this guy [in a relationship]," she said, according to the documentary.

"I know I said 'No', but you question yourself and you think, did I do something wrong?"

She "left his as quickly as I could" and told one friend what had happened, but "back then women felt shamed", she said.

"You didn't talk about it. I just felt completely violated and unseen and unheard. I was saying 'No'. I kept saying, 'No, stop, please, stop, stop, no'."

Another ex-girlfriend, Jordan Martin, claimed in the documentary that Brand sexually assaulted her and smashed her phone in a hotel after she had spoken to an ex to arrange to collect her belongings.

"He snatched my phone out of my hand and broke it apart into pieces," she said.

Brand then followed her into a different room, she said. "He didn't say anything. He put his hand down the front of my jeans and he inserted a finger and then he walked away."

She added: "I look at myself back then and I feel sorry for myself. And not in a bad or pitying way, I just feel like it wasn't very fair."

Martin also said Brand was jealous and controlling, and had made her "brush her teeth until gums bled".

"He wanted me to taste anonymous," Martin said. "And so he was asking me to brush my teeth, but it just was never enough. And so he's standing over me and I'm brushing and I'm brushing, and then I'm seeing my teeth bleeding."

The Times and Sunday Times reported that at least five sexual partners said Brand had forced them to brush their teeth, including the fifth complainant in the trial, whom he was convicted of raping in 2009.

Among the new claims reported by the paper is one from a woman referred to as Alex, who claimed she had asked Brand to stop having sex after noticing he wasn't using a condom.

"I said, 'No, stop', and I started to sort of try and move. And... that wasn't happening," she said.

When he continued, she decided "I'm not going to fight", she said, because "who knows what he could do?"

Alex said Brand apologised in person and by text message after the alleged incident.

"I justified it in my head by saying to myself, at least he admitted it," she told the Times.

A woman called Vicky also claimed she had asked him to stop twice after they started having sex without any build up.

"My body wasn't ready for this and it was painful", she remembered.

"An uneasy wave hits me and I'm scared. And I say, 'It's painful' and he doesn't stop. And then it gets worse and it's really painful. And I say 'Stop' and he doesn't stop."

She added that it had felt like he "just wasn't present".

She claimed he said afterwards: "Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn't want to do."

Another woman named Zoe said Brand was "annoyed" after she turned up to his hotel late.

"He basically sort of just grabbed me and manhandled me around a little bit and he put his hand on my throat," she told the Times.

"And then he shoved his other hand down my trousers and penetrated me with his finger.

"I didn't resist. I just sort of let it happen."

On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison following his trial. He is expected to serve seven years.

He denied the charges and was acquitted on two further rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Police have said Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women.

The Metropolitan Police have said they are also "assessing" information from several people who contacted them during the trial "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".

Brand has been placed inside HMP Wandsworth. BBC News has asked his legal representatives for a response to the latest allegations.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3.summary: Russell Brand: Open Secret, made available on Netflix on Friday. Ex-girlfriend, Jordan Martin, said she was in relationship with Brand when she was 20. She said she begged him to stop after he refused to wear a condom during sex. BBC News has asked his legal representatives for a response to the latest allegations.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.title: Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya prank Rylan Clark for Children in Need
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.text:
Timothée Chalamet and his Dune co-stars will be seen pranking Rylan Clark during this year's Children in Need on Friday.

The Oscar-nominated actor will be seen making the presenter sweat with suggestions from children behind-the-scenes in an Impractical Jokers-style set-up, during an interview with Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy about the third installment of the film franchise.

This year's Children in Need show will also feature Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans and a "challenge squad" of young people completing feats in the name of charity.

Last year's appeal raised more than £45m to help children and young people across the UK, and this year's TV event will be broadcast from 19:00 GMT.

The three-hour show will be hosted live from Salford by Alex Jones, Mel Giedroyc, Rylan, Sara Cox and Tyler West.

They will welcome Wyn Evans, who has been the latest Radio 2 DJ to put himself through a gruelling challenge for Children In Need, following in the footsteps of the likes of Sara Cox and Paddy McGuinness.

Wyn Evans completed his 400-mile four-nation cycle ride through England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and his native Wales - finishing in Cardiff on Friday.

He raised more than £3.8m along the way.

Wyn Evans was joined on his final leg on Friday by 22-year-old Harri, who is living with hidden lasting effects of a brain tumour.

Harri is part of The One Show's "challenge squad" - four young people who have signed up for a series of personal missions for the charity.

The others are 16-year-old Zoe, who has Down's syndrome and who will be seen dancing with the cast of High School Musical, Ana, also 16, who has a rare physical condition and is doing a three-day kayaking challenge, and 22-year-old Serena, who will perform live in memory of her late brother and a childhood friend.

The theme of this year's Children in Need is Challenge Yourself 2026, which has also seen Morning Live presenters Michelle Ackerley and Gethin Jones learn instruments.

Joe Wicks and Emma Bunton are among the other stars who have been involved, while landmarks including the Blackpool Tower, London Eye and Titanic Belfast will be lit in yellow for the occasion.

Children in Need supports more than 1,600 local charities and projects across the UK.

Children In Need is on BBC One and iPlayer from 19:00-22:00 GMT on Friday

The three-hour show will be hosted live from Salford by Alex Jones, Mel Giedroyc, Rylan, Sara Cox and Tyler West. Wyn Evans completed his 400-mile cycle ride through England, Scotland

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr3e.title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr3e.text:
Spanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux.

The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.

La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.

Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."

The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."

Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.

She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc.

The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.

It was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.

He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.

Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.

Dosanjh superfan Divanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution".

"It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.

She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.

Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".

Accepting the prize for record of the year, Milo J seemed surprised to have won ahead of strong competition from Karol G, Jorge Drexler, Carin León as well as Rosalía.

The 20-year-old took home four trophies in the end and gave a shout out to Argentine folk music.

He described Niño as the song "I'm most proud of out of everything I've created so far".

"Long live Argentine folk music," he added.

Elsewhere, ARIA VEGA was named best new artist and songwriter of the year went to Sara Schell.

Additional reporting by Abu Bakar Yasin

Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr3e.summary: Rosalía wins five trophies, including two for her track La Perla. She also wins best alternative music album for her project Lux. The Spanish singer is the first woman to win the best album award at the Grammys.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.title: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.text:
Fast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursday - a record for a British female solo artist

The BBC Sound of 2026 winner is set to overtake rapper Little Simz, who headlined three nights at the legendary south London venue in 2021.

It will cap an incredible few years for Brit Award nominee Newman, 23, who performed at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Sunderland last month.

Speaking to BBC News's Mark Savage ahead of her record-breaking run, Newman said it had given her "goosebumps and chills". She added: "It's crazy. My jaw drops all the time. I feel honoured to be the first woman, and I don't take it lightly."

Born in south-east London, the "loud, raw and strikingly honest" Newman - according to our music correspondent - exploded onto the scene last year when her debut single, Hairdresser, went straight into the top 20.

The follow-up, Family Matters, reached number five in June. It was the first time a female artist had made the top 20 with their first two singles since Ella Henderson in 2014.

The husky-voiced soul and R&B singer has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour, and been called "incredibly talented" and "something else" by Sir Elton John.

During her opening night in Brixton, Newman debuted her new song Survival and was also joined by fellow London soul-pop singer Gabrielle for a duet of her 1993 hit Dreams.

Now she stands on the shoulders of pop giants.

Historically, US pop-punk icon Debby Harry and Romy Croft, frontwoman of the band The XX have also enjoyed big Brixton residencies, as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Chappell Roan and Tash Sultana.

But after three more gigs this weekend and an extra date next weekend, Newman will newly lead the way for UK female solo stars at one of the country's most prestigious venues.

She also insists on having an all-female band on stage with her.

"Women are the centre of my world," she said. "They're the people that built me. They allowed me space to grow and find myself. So, I definitely had to take that out on stage with me.

"I had to stand by what I stand by. It's quite scary at the minute how much social media is [affecting how women are being treated] so I'm just really big on trying to keep women everywhere."

She continued: "If I can have a woman in place, I will. I'll give a job out. I'll give my helping hand always."

Newman recently paid tribute to another soulful London singer to have graced the same space back in 2007, the late Amy Winehouse, with a rendition of her song Addicted during a special Back to Black anniversary gig for the BBC.

"The thing with Amy's music is it's so incredible that you don't want to touch it," she admitted.

"No-one would ever do it like Amy, and I think it was definitely scary for all of us... that feeling of, you've got to live up to that expectation. You've got to fill her shoes, and they're big shoes to fill.

"But I think we all smashed it, and I think it was honestly the most beautiful, inspirational day I've had in a very long time."

After more gigs in Brixton, Brighton and Manchester, she will head off to Australia with Harry Styles next month for a series of support slots, which the childhood One Direction fan says is "surreal", and something she agreed to with "no questions asked".

"'Whatever I've got, cancel it'," she joked she had told her team on hearing about the request.

"It felt like a dream because I was the age of One Direction [fans], so that was around when I was a child and obviously I loved them and Harry and Zayn were my favourites.

"So then now to go and support Harry Styles is just mental."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.summary: Skye Newman is set to break the record for a British female solo artist. The 23-year-old singer is set for three gigs at Brixton Academy on Thursday. She will be the first female solo singer to make the top 20 with two singles. She has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.title: Blink-182 to make Download debut as 2027 festival headliners
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.text:
Blink-182, Evanescence & Bring Me The Horizon have been announced as headliners of next year's Download Festival.

The trio are among more than 100 rock and metal acts set to play the event at Donington Park, Leicestershire from 9 to 13 June.

Other acts on the bill include The Prodigy, 5 Seconds of Summer and a special performance by heavy metal legends Mötley Crüe.

US pop-punk band Blink-182 will be making their Download debut, while Evanescence will become the festival's second female-fronted headliner.

The American rock band were founded by singer Amy Lee in the mid-1990s and had a UK number one with their best-known single Bring Me to Life in 2003.

It's the second year in a row a female-led band has headlined the festival, after Linkin Park topped the bill in 2025.

The nu-metal group have reformed with Emily Armstrong as their lead singer, after the death of former frontman Chester Bennington, who took his own life in 2017.

The choice of Emily upset some fans, who pointed to her alleged ties to the Church of Scientology and past support for convicted rapist Danny Masterson - someone she distanced herself from.

Next year's Download will be a first for Blink-182, who emerged from the California skate punk scene in the 1990s.

They've had two UK top 10 singles and had their first number one album in 2016, 21 years after their first record.

Their drummer Travis Barker is married to Kourtney Kardashian and survived a plane crash in the US that killed four people in 2008.

British rockers Bring Me The Horizon are more familiar to Download regulars, headlining for the second time in five years.

The four-piece band, formed in Sheffield, announced earlier this year they're celebrating 20 years of the debut album Count Your Blessings by re-recording it.

That 2006 record was in the deathcore genre, known for its heavy and aggressive sound, but the band have since moved towards metalcore, pop and electronic rock.

Some fans questioned if the original lyrics, which frontman Oli Sykes admitted could be interpreted as misogynistic, were still appropriate.

But the 39-year-old lead vocalist told the BBC Radio 1 Rock Show that going back to their roots was "a lot of fun" as they "got to remake the album how we wanted it to sound back then".

Download bills itself as a festival "spanning the full spectrum of rock, metal, punk, emo, hardcore, alternative and classic rock".

It called this year's line-up "bigger, better and bolder than ever" and said it features "something for everyone, from huge artists to electric newcomers".

Other acts announced include Turnstile, Faith No More, Body Count ft. Ice-T and Malevolence - with the festival saying more will be revealed.

Some pre-sales are currently available but tickets go on general sale at 10:00 GMT on Sunday.

In recent years Download has also featured pop acts and surprise guests, with the Vengaboys an unlikely addition to 2024's line-up.

And Dogstar - the band formed by actor Keanu Reeves - performed in 2026.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck7v.title: Brand will face 'hell on earth' in Wandsworth prison, says former inmate
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck7v.text:
Russell Brand will face "hell on earth" inside HMP Wandsworth, a former inmate at the London prison has said.

Brand, 51, was convicted a week ago of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and was sentenced on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison.

He is currently being held at the South London jail, which is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons.

Chris Atkins, who served eight months at HMP Wandsworth for tax fraud, described the prison as "hell on earth".

He continued: "The first month is hands-down the worst. The mental shock is absolutely colossal. It was colossal for me and it's going to be 10 times worse for him because of the nature of his offences and the height from which he's fallen.

"He has to come to terms with it and the pure physical shock of suddenly being trapped in a dungeon for weeks on end with nobody to talk to most of the time is ghastly."

A source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing in the prison.

A member of staff at Wandsworth said there had been "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival.

"Prisons are boring and Russell Brand being in their space has given them some fun - they've been slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. He is a rapist, so there's also been some anger about what he's done.

"We're very aware of that feeling," they said.

Brand is likely to still be in a cell on his own. It would usually have a bed, a basin and a toilet. He may have a television and kettle, depending on where in the prison he is housed.

On arrival, Brand's possessions will have been confiscated. That will include his mobile phone, clothing and any other valuables. He will have been issued with a grey prison tracksuit - a uniform that has been described by some of those who have been inside as "itchy" and "often the wrong size".

The former media personality and comedian will have been given a night pack. It contains items such as biscuits, teabags, a small bag of cereal, some sugar and a carton of milk. This is to help inmates until they can buy goods from the prison shop, according to the charity Prison Reform Trust.

Brand, who has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, would be able to register for the weekly Sunday service in the prison chapel, former inmates said.

"Many sign up just to get out of their cell," one added. They said Brand could probably get regular time with the prison chaplain if he wanted.

Inmates receive money through prison work or from their family. But several former prisoners have told the BBC that there were a limited number of jobs in places like workshops, laundry rooms and libraries.

They say it is much harder for sex offenders to get work because their conviction means they are more at risk of assault while mixing with other inmates.

Staff at other prisons say Brand's fame and the offences of which he has been convicted could make him a target for other inmates.

Sex offenders are often among those most at risk of being attacked. One prison governor said: "When a trial gets plenty of publicity it highlights the crimes the offender has committed.

"This in turn makes him vulnerable to the inmates own 'justice' system of arbitrary beatings and assaults, especially where sex crimes are involved."

The prison paperwork is also said to be a huge challenge for newcomers. Getting permission to make phone calls and filling out visitor requests can take a long time and these have to go through the system to be signed off.

Atkins said: "He won't have anyone set up on his visitor account - visitors need a series of checks. Phone numbers need to be approved. These checks are not quick and you need to know how to make these applications.

"There is often nobody there to tell you how this all works so you have to work it out." Atkins said it took five weeks to see his young son when he went inside.

It's just days since Brand was sentenced to more than a decade in prison.

At this stage, nobody knows what the future holds for him. In time he may be transferred to a different jail with a less harsh regime and more modern facilities.

The guidelines state that offenders jailed for four or more years for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case, that would be seven years.

He was convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault last week. He is currently being held at the South London jail, which is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.title: Global Microsoft outage affecting NI schools, councils and other services
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.text:
Schools, councils and other organisations across Northern Ireland are among those impacted by a global Microsoft outage.

Problems with the software giant started on Thursday, with monitoring website Downdetector seeing problems reported in more than 70 countries.

Microsoft has said it is seeing "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe, and North America is "improving", but adds "some users may still experience intermittent issues". Earlier, it said the issue wasn't caused by a cyber-security breach

Public bodies such as the Education Authority said on Friday: "Outlook is currently unavailable to NI schools and the Education Authority. Emails cannot currently be sent or received."

The South Eastern Health Trust said there will be "no impact on clinical services".

Northern Ireland Ambulance Service said that patient services are not impacted by the outage.

Some councils in Northern Ireland have said that their emails systems have been impacted.

Belfast City Council said it is experiencing issues "receiving and responding" to emails.

"Our website and phone lines are operating as normal however, and customers can still log requests."

In a statement Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council said they are aware of the "ongoing global disruption" and will share "further updates if necessary".

Causeway Coast and Glens Borough Council confirmed they have been impacted and said the majority of council services are unaffected however there is disruption to staff's ability to send and receive emails.

Queen's University Belfast also said they are experiencing email disruption on Friday.

"Our students and staff are currently unable to receive or send emails and may experience difficulties accessing.

"As always, staff and students should not use personal email accounts to send, receive or store university-related communications or information."

The Police Service of Northern Ireland have issued a statement to say its services are unaffected.

Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".

Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.

Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues.

More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.

The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening.

The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting.

Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.

Microsoft 365 services including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot are affected. Some councils in Northern Ireland have said their emails systems have been impacted.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.title: Laughter and learning at BBC Children in Need-backed homework club
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.text:
In a community hall in east Belfast, chatter and laughter fills the air as children play pool, draw cartoons and finish schoolwork with friends.

This is Ledley Hall Boys and Girls Club, which runs an after-school homework group with the help of BBC Children in Need.

"It's a safe space for them," says Caitlin McAlinden.

She is a special needs teacher but also gives each afternoon from Monday to Thursday to working as a part-time teacher at the homework club - and says it is of big benefit to the area.

The centre has running since 1942, providing services and activities for the local community.

For the past three years, with funding from BBC Children in Need, the centre has been able to help children up to the age of 15 with their homework, four days a week.

About 45 children are registered, with between 10 and 30 attending each day.

Children go to the club for a variety of reasons: their parents are still in work; they come for support with their homework; or just to spend time with their friends.

"They benefit from it being in an informal environment, which works for a lot of young people who maybe don't like being in school a whole lot," says senior youth worker Michelle Fullerton.

"It provides support for parents who either don't have the confidence to do homework or are at work.

"They come home from work and the homework's already done and it's been supervised by someone who is a teacher."

Ledley Hall received a three-year grant of about £34,000 in 2023, funding the salary of a part-time teacher and a classroom assistant to provide a homework club.

It is one of about 100 projects in Northern Ireland that BBC Children in Need supports with £5.5m of funding, reaching more than 25,000 children and young people.

This year's appeal on Friday aims to raise millions more pounds to help organisations like Ledley Hall carry on their work.

Fullerton says the club would not be possible without the help of BBC Children in Need.

"We charge 50p, and that's a nominal fee, but if parents were paying to have support for their kids after school to complete homework by someone who's a teacher it would cost a lot more," she says.

She says educational statistics in the area are "really poor", adding: "This is our attempt to try and bring up the educational standards of the young people."

The children who go to the homework club are pupils at nearby schools.

"They know what the rules are about how we work in here and I think just having that safe space for them to come," she says.

"They know that [we are here] if they need food, if they need support, if they need someone to talk to, if they just want somewhere to come and see their friends."

The children benefit both academically and socially from the club, says McAlinden, and the need for groups like it is "huge" in areas such as east Belfast.

"If we don't get our funding... then where do the kids go?" she asks.

"It's a place for them to make friends.

"They make friends from other schools, they get to maybe make friends with people in their school who they wouldn't usually talk to or anything like that."

Holly Hamilton, Connor Phillips and Pudsey Bear will host this year's BBC Children in Need 2026 in Northern Ireland, filmed at St Teresa's Youth Centre in Belfast.

You catch watch it on BBC One Northern Ireland and BBC iPlayer at 15:50 GMT on Sunday 15 November.

The club has been running since 1942, providing services and activities for the local community. BBC Children In Need has been able to help children up to the age of 15 with their homework, four days a week.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.title: Caught Between Killers: Ebola on One Side, Islamic State on the Other
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.author: Declan Walsh and Daniel Berehulak
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.text:
So many people are dying of Ebola that their bodies have been stacked, one atop the other, on makeshift racks in a shed by the hospital gate.

The town’s main cemetery is full, so fresh graves are being squeezed in between palm trees by the side of the road.

Medicine, IVs and basic protections have been so scarce that three-quarters of Ebola patients in this besieged Congolese town have died.

Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province.

It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hot spots as it moves through one of the world’s great rainforests.

Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain.

Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

“We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.”

And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State.

Declan Walsh is the chief Africa correspondent for The Times based in Nairobi, Kenya. He previously reported from Cairo, covering the Middle East, and Islamabad, Pakistan.

Daniel Berehulak is a staff photographer for The Times based in Mexico City.

Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected. But infections are soaring elsewhere, with the Islamic State becoming a threat.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.title: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.author: Amanda Taub
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.text:
From India to France, the implicit meritocratic bargain that underwrote stable societies by providing advancement to new generations is breaking down.

Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.

In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.

In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.

In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.

It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.

The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

Subscribe to The Times to read as many articles as you like.

Amanda Taub writes the Interpreter, an explanatory column and newsletter about world events. She is based in London.

Students in India and French have protested over the failure of their schools and the government. The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.title: Europe Agrees on a Team to Represent It in Talks With Russia
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.author: Jeanna Smialek
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.text:
After coveting a seat in the Ukraine war discussions, Europe is poised to get one. The continent wants to fill it with a six-member team.

Reporting from Dublin, where European leaders are meeting, and from an airfield near the city where Americans and Ukrainians debriefed on Thursday night.

European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. They learned this week that they would get one, and simply needed to decide which official should sit in that chair.

Instead, they decided on six.

European Union leaders concluded in Dublin on Friday that they will tap a group of major nations — Britain, France, Germany, Poland, and Italy — along with a representative from the E.U’s leadership arms, the European Council and European Commission.

In some ways, the choice of a crowd plays into jibes Americans have made about the continent’s indecisiveness: “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said earlier this week.

Europe’s failure to pick one negotiator leaves open the possibility that its fragmentation will diminish its influence. Even so, Europeans have underscored that they are a democracy of many nations and that many voices must be represented.

“We decide on who represents us, and that is what we have done today,” said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission.

“We need to work as a team,” António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, said at a news conference on Friday, noting that America itself has two envoys.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.title: After Xi Purges China’s Generals, a Military Inquisitor Rises
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.author: Chris Buckley
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.text:
The rise of Zhang Shengmin suggests that China’s top brass remains embroiled in investigations, potentially complicating preparations for war over Taiwan.

When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, endorsed the expulsion of dozens of disgraced officials at a recent Communist Party meeting in Beijing, one man stood out as a clear winner.

Taking his new place at the front of the meeting was Gen. Zhang Shengmin, the somber-faced enforcer of Mr. Xi’s purges inside the military. He had been promoted to the Politburo, the party’s top leadership council, the latest step in his improbable rise from low-profile inspector to a position second only to Mr. Xi in China’s military hierarchy.

General Zhang has been the principal overseer of Mr. Xi’s campaign to purify the People’s Liberation Army. His latest elevation signaled that the investigations, indoctrination drives and loyalty tests could continue for years, as Mr. Xi searches for officers he believes are irreproachably loyal, experts and officials said.

“Twist the blade inward, with strict measures to cure disorder,” China’s main military newspaper said after the party meeting that was held late last month, referring to the continued discipline campaign.

Three officials in Taiwan said they believed Mr. Xi’s loyalty campaign would keep the Chinese military focused on its own problems. That could hinder preparations for possible war over Taiwan, the self-governed island democracy that Beijing claims. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal assessments.

The leadership uncertainty comes as China’s military has continued to pressure Taiwan. Dozens of P.L.A. ships held unannounced drills in seas off the Chinese coast in recent weeks, with some, including a carrier strike group, still remaining, Joseph Wu, the secretary-general of Taiwan’s National Security Council, posted on X on Thursday.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.title: Border Crossings Have Plummeted. Stephen Miller Isn’t Satisfied.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.author: James Wagner and Jack Nicas
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.text:
U.S. Immigration Crackdown

Mexico has cooperated to significantly slow the flow of migrants. The new White House chief of staff insists it is not enough.

By James Wagner and Jack Nicas

Reporting from Mexico City

Since President Trump resumed office, the number of illegal crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border has dropped to the lowest point in decades.

For one of Mr. Trump’s top policy advisers, that is not enough.

In conversations with both American and Mexican officials over the last several months, Stephen Miller has insisted that illegal border crossings must be reduced, according to officials in both countries familiar with the private conversations but not authorized to discuss them.

Mr. Miller’s goal, they said, is zero crossings. Mexican officials have said that, with a nearly 2,000-mile border, that is simply not possible.

In his new role as chief of staff, Mr. Miller is expected to continue driving that agenda.

One of the main forums for Mr. Miller’s demands has been his near daily calls with the U.S. ambassador to Mexico, Ronald ​Johnson, some of the officials said. On calls with staff, Mr. Miller, previously the deputy chief of staff, frequently rails about the number of border crossings, despite their low figures, the officials said.

That has been especially true in recent months, they said, as border crossings increased slightly, to the highest point in Mr. Trump’s second term.

Note: Includes encounters outside official border crossings.

Source: U.S. Customs and Border Protection

Sergio Peçanha/The New York Times
