In a written message from Vakilabad prison in north-eastern Iran, he said: “I accept this award in the name of all those who, for the ‘crime’ of aspiring to a free Iran, have been imprisoned, tortured, threatened, or sentenced to death; in the name of my comrades in the resistance units and the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives.”

He added: “The regime demands repentance, televised confessions and surrender from us. But our answer is clear: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’”

Vafaei Sani, 31, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and accused of supporting an opposition group, the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK).

He was convicted of “corruption on Earth” and sentenced to death for a third time in September 2024 after “a grossly unfair trial”, according to Amnesty International. The supreme court upheld his death sentence on 4 October 2025. Since his arrest he has been tortured and held in solitary confinement for extended periods.

His continued imprisonment has drawn widespread international condemnation from prominent sportspeople, human rights organisations and legal experts who have called for his immediate release and the annulment of his death sentence.

The Magnitsky awards are named after the Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody after exposing government corruption. They began in 2015 as a way to recognise journalists, politicians and activists in the field of human rights.

Sir William Browder, head of the Magnitsky Justice Foundation and the chair of the awards committee, said Vafaei Sani’s case was emblematic of the plight of many Iranians who face execution for standing against the regime. “Most important, Mohammad Javad is still alive,” he said. “That is why this award matters. Every time the world pays attention, it becomes harder to kill him quietly.”

According to the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, at least 710 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, including 79 political and religious prisoners.

In an October report, the organisation documented at least 106 death sentences against January protest detainees, 35 of whom had already been executed. In Vakilabad prison, where Vafaei Sani is detained, five people have been executed linked to the protests and 15 others are facing death sentences.

Vafaei Sani’s award comes at a time when there are growing fears for imprisoned Iranian athletes, who are considered role models in the country. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, founder of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The situation is really dire … We have seven athletes at risk of execution now, including Vafaei Sani.”

Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a mountaineer, was executed on 14 October after the anti-government protests. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, earlier that month, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May.

Abdollahkhani said people had been celebrating Vafaei Sani’s award. “Even people who don’t support his political view are supporting him to be heard,” she said. “I find it very inspiring that different political groups are coming together to say no to execution.”

In his message, Vafaei Sani said he wanted “a free and democratic Iran … where the people vote freely, women and men are equal, there is no discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or belief, and no one is imprisoned or executed for political opposition”.

He added: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran are free.”

A news conference in Piddington has descended into a shouting match between Reform’s Zia Yusuf and the Conservative’s Chris Philp.

The two men, who are both home affairs spokespeople for their respective parties, appeared alongside Piddington parish council leader Tim McNally at a media event designed to outline local opposition to government plans to for a local accommodation site for asylum seekers.

But the united front did not last long and soon ended up with the pair bickering in front of the cameras. Yusuf asked Philp:

Would you like to actually apologise for the things that you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?

Are you going to take the opportunity to apologise to the people of Piddington and to the country?

Philp responded by saying that the residents of the military base would be asylum seekers who had arrived recently.

He said that “rather than engaging in point scoring”, Yusuf should “read the room”. However, Yusuf said the Tories failed to “secure our borders” during their 14 years of government.

Before that, McNally had accused prime minister Andy Burnham of “failing to step up”. He said:

[Burnham hasn’t] extended to us as simple as courtesy of consideration of what we are going to have to consider, to receive here as our new incumbent guests that you have targeted for us - 1,250 men.

Meanwhile, Downing Street has defended plans to convert the site at MoD Bicester near Piddington into asylum seeker accommodation.

Responding to questions around public safety, a spokesperson said such sites are “designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community”, the Press Association reported.

The spokesperson added: “As the prime minister himself has said, we do not want a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers who believe all parties to play their part.”

The spokesperson said the safety of the public “will always be our top priority”.

The Home Office underspent its Prevent counter-terror scheme budget by nearly a third last year, despite the number of referrals reaching record levels, the public spending watchdog has said.

The National Audit Office (NAO) said the Home Office underspent its £23.4 million Prevent budget by 28% for 2025-26, continuing a six-year pattern in which it underspent by an average of £5.6 million (17%) a year in real term, PA reported.

The government-led, multi-agency programme aims to stop individuals becoming terrorists. It has faced significant criticism after it failed to intervene in the case of Southport attacker Axel Rudakubana, who had been referred three times.

Demand for Prevent has grown significantly with referrals increasing year on year since 2020, and reaching a record 10,293 in the year ending September 2025.

Officials believe the referral spike might be down to more awareness of Prevent after the Southport Attack in July 2024.

Ministers will face a legal challenge over plans to convert a Ministry of Defence site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington into accommodation for more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers.

It emerged on Thursday that Angela Rayner, the housing and communities secretary, has approved full planning permission, a decision welcomed by the Home Office, who want to end the use of asylum hotels.

Tim McNally, the local parish council chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today Programme there would be “many actions” by villagers, and that ministers should “absolutely” be braced for a legal challenge, which would need to be lodged within the next six weeks.

Ministers have faced opposition over the plans from villagers, who even made a symbolic attempt to declare the village independent from the rest of the country after a referendum of its 350 residents. Asked how the village would respond, McNally said: “There’s going to be many actions, you will see. We will disclose that as we move forward.”

Asked if ministers should be braced for a legal challenge, he said: “Absolutely, absolutely.”

Campaigners could also apply the new Hillsborough law, which is being considered by parliament. Once passed, the law would create a legally enforceable duty of candour that compels public officials and authorities to act transparently when investigations and inquiries take place.

After the summit, Burnham plans to go further in exploring options for the UK’s future ties.

The prime minister’s remarks in recent weeks have fuelled questions about the prospect of the UK returning to the EU or adopting its freedom of movement rules, but he has insisted voters would ultimately be “the boss” of any changes.

Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.

There will be a “growing pressure” for parliament to scrutinise EU legislation under new deals on food and emissions to be sealed ahead of the UK’s summit with the bloc next week, a Lords’ committee has warned.

Prime minister Andy Burnham is due to meet EU leaders in Brussels next week and sign agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4%. This includes a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal on food and farming, as well as one on emissions trading and another for a youth mobility scheme.

A deal is also expected to be struck on a health security agreement to help address shortages of drugs such as antibiotics and ADHD medication, which have got worse since Brexit, according to a draft text seen by the I newspaper.

It will mark a significant shift in the Britain’s post-Brexit relationship with the EU as they will require dynamic alignment, the process of matching laws to the bloc’s evolving legislation, the House of Lords European Affairs Committee said in a new report.

The committee of peers says this will mean parliament needs to set up a “robust, consistent and adequately resourced cross-departmental system” to manage the UK’s dynamic alignment commitments. See the published report here.

The committee chairman, Jock Stirrup, said:

Although important details remain to be determined of the legal and institutional form that dynamic alignment will take, its introduction will mark a major change to the nature of the UK-EU relationship as it exists under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement.

As the UK aligns with more EU law, parliament will face growing pressure to scrutinise significant volumes of EU legislation.

The food and farming deal alone could generate at least 780 pieces of in-scope EU law every year, the committee heard.

Meanwhile, the I reports that the government is close to securing a deal with Europe to help tackle post-Brexit medicine shortages, including antibiotics, ADHD medication and epilepsy drugs.

Experts on post-Brexit health policy have reportedly described the deal as “significant’” and a “good first step” in addressing shortages that have hit both sides in recent years.

It comes as prime minister Andy Burnham said he believes a “win-win” deal could be done with the EU that could be “more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016”.

The prime minister was meeting fellow leaders at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, ahead of the summit next week, where he hopes to bring Britain closer to Europe.

I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe.

The deal is not done, and there’ll be some long nights ahead in the next seven days.

In other developments:

Some young people with disabilities will lose their personal independence payments and will have to apply instead to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment, Alan Milburn’s review will recommend.

Sadiq Khan has become the most high-profile Labour figure to weigh into the increasingly fractious debate over what the government should do with its electric vehicle targets.

Nigel Farage appeared on Russell Brand’s US podcast nine months after the comedian was investigated by police over allegations of sexual assault, the Guardian has learned.

The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/n.author: Miatta Mbriwa

Ministers consider banning under-16s from online marketplaces amid reported misuse of messaging functions and users’ photos

In June, Hannah* listed her seven-year-old daughter’s pink swimming costume for sale on Vinted, hoping other parents surfing the reselling site would snap up the £1 offer. Her inbox pinged.

“So a little girl wore this yh [yeah]?” wrote a user with a male handle.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“She did yes,” Hannah replied.

After sending back a barbed “What do you think?”, Hannah swiftly blocked the user and reported the incident to Vinted. She described the exchange as “disgusting” and “disturbing”.

Her experience is just one of the many innocuous listings of children and young people’s secondhand clothes on reselling apps that are attracting sexualised comments through their direct messaging function.

The Children’s Society has said some young users of resale sites are increasingly being asked for indecent photos in exchange for money or gifts. Some photos of young users posted on the platforms have been AI deepfaked into nudes without their consent.

In response, ministers are considering banning under-16s from platforms such as Depop, eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to the Sunday Times, over mounting fears that their private messaging functions are the latest frontline in child exploitation. Vinted, which has a minimum age of 18, would have to join the other sites in gating access with strict age verification features.

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said on Sunday that the government was “looking seriously” at expanding the under-16s social media ban to include online marketplaces. It is understood the regulations were sent for cabinet signoff this week, with Nandy expected to present them to parliament in December.

Young women have posted on TikTok and Reddit about their concerning interactions with buyers. Those exchanges include asking the seller if the item will come with used underwear if they buy it, or unsolicited sexual comments about their appearance.

Lucy* started reselling her pre-loved clothes on Depop when she was 15 and has been subject to many unsettling experiences. Once, she listed an item of clothing for about £10 and a user requested to raise the price. “The person had changed it to £30 and said: ‘If you include your pants I’ll pay more’,” she said. “That made me feel like, oh my God, awful.”

She then discovered that images of her taken when she was under the age of 18, posted to advertise her clothes, had been scraped from Depop and were circulating on Reddit.

“These pictures are actually still being resurfaced on these Reddit pages, which is quite frustrating,” she said. “It would be me at 17 trying to sell a bikini, and these men have screenshotted these images … It’s not just me, it’s hundreds of other girls.”

About two years ago, Lucy came across another social media platform, Discord, where she found users had stolen her old Vinted and Depop photos and manipulated them using AI to make deepfakes of her “fully nude”. She said: “It’s deplorable that people think it’s acceptable to take people’s images and make them into AI porn – I felt really, really upset.”

after newsletter promotion

Vinted says minors can only access the site under the supervision of adult account holders, while Depop says users must be aged 13 or over to set up an account, and over 18 to use PayPal and the Depop payment systems. However, the UK communications watchdog, Ofcom, has found that 15% of eight to 14-year-olds use Vinted each month, while another report has suggested that some children are able to bypass checks and access age-restricted online services.

Some child safety campaigners have expressed fears a sweeping social media ban could exclude children from the internet entirely. Karen Garland, the head of policy at the Marie Collins Foundation, a charity that supports victims of technology-assisted child sexual exploitation, said: “We need to make spaces for children and young people that are safer by design. And so, in some ways, extending a ban into other spaces may not be the best route overall.”

Despite her experience, Lucy is conflicted about the ban. “It’s a real shame because there are probably very young girls that maybe are from different backgrounds … that maybe really need that money.”

However, she acknowledged that there could be “extremely dangerous” consequences to selling clothes on Vinted. She said that as she was now 25 and has continued to find sexualised images of herself online,, the risk did not end at 18.

A Vinted spokesperson said: “We have zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content and use a combination of dedicated moderation teams and detection tools to spot and remove activity that breaks our rules. When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities.”

An eBay spokesperson said: “We have clear policies and safeguards to protect our community, including encouraging people to keep conversations on eBay, avoid sharing personal contact details and report any suspicious or inappropriate behaviour. Where we or our customers identify policy violations, we take appropriate action.”

Depop said: “Using someone’s images without their permission is a violation of our terms of service, which explicitly prohibits users from using or sharing another user’s content without their consent, whether on Depop or elsewhere. We take the safety of our community extremely seriously and we have robust policies, controls and processes in place to protect our users.”

*Names have been changed

NHS suffering ‘serious’ and widespread disruption, while people are told of possible delays in receiving prescriptions

Microsoft outage – live updates

Hospitals, GPs and police forces across the UK have been hit by the global Microsoft outage, which is also expected to disrupt schools, businesses and some travel.

Key public services battled to get systems back online amid “widespread” and “serious” disruption to NHS services, as staff resorted to using patient’s paper records after being unable to access email and other IT facilities used to deliver healthcare.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Downing Street said it was seeking to establish the “full picture” of Microsoft outages and urged the public to follow advice on “alternative ways to get in touch” where services were disrupted.

The disruption sent some sectors back to the 1990s amid reports of court staff looking for fax machines and rail travellers being warned they may not be able to rely on digital tickets.

Patients getting their prescriptions were also cautioned about possible delays, schools and universities were unable to access emails, and there were reports that ambulance services had been affected by the outage.

The problems began late on Thursday afternoon and users have been unable to access many of Microsoft’s most popular services. Thousands worldwide reported they were unable to send and receive emails through Outlook.

The Microsoft executive vice-president Charles Lamanna said the outages did not appear to be the result of a cyber-attack. On Friday morning, the firm said it was seeing “early signs of stabilisation”, later issuing an update that it was seeing email traffic being gradually restored.

NHS staff arriving at work on Friday morning reported being unable to access email, affecting their ability to deliver healthcare in hospitals and surgeries, amid warnings that the outage would be highly disruptive through the day.

In some cases, staff said they were able to use their phones to access Microsoft Teams, which is heavily relied upon in the healthcare sector, but meetings were having to be cancelled across the board.

An NHS England spokesperson said: “Local NHS services are enacting longstanding measures to manage IT outages and ensure critical services and appointments can continue for patients today – including using other IT systems or paper records where possible.”

Rachel Harrison, the GMB national secretary, said: “The Microsoft data outage is having a serious impact across ambulance and NHS trusts. Luckily emergency and life-threatening callouts appear to be unaffected.”

Pharmacists warned there would be delays in the issuing of some prescriptions as a result of the incident, which disrupted the ability of some pharmacies to communicate with GP practices and patients.

While there was no early sign of widespread travel disruption, National Rail warned that people may not be able to access tickets that have been emailed to them. “If you’re unable to locate or access your tickets through your email due to this issue, you may still be able to access your tickets by visiting the website or app where you purchased your tickets from and logging into your account,” it said, recommending that passengers do so before travel.

The already backlogged court system was hit with juries in some cases being sent home early, or prisoners not being sent to court. At Minshull Street crown court in Manchester, Judge Maurice Greene said staff had been looking for a fax machine earlier in the morning.

“I would say sorry but it’s not my fault. It’s Mr [Bill] Gates’s fault,” he told jurors before sending them home, referring to the cofounder of Microsoft, who officially resigned from Microsoft’s board of directors six years ago.

Businesses, meanwhile, were braced for the impact of economic damage while the UK’s top financial regulators, the Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority, were hit by the Outlook outage, although a spokesperson for the bank said “all critical operations” were running normally.

However, the turmoil comes on the busiest day of the week for mortgage completions and there were also warnings that digital tickets for events could be affected, with Cheltenham racecourse urging visitors to arrive early.

Engineers from the government were working with Microsoft to assess the impact of the outage, according to a minister, while the Welsh government said it was putting contingency plans in place.

A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister was being kept updated on the situation, while individual departments would be able to rely on contingency plans where necessary.

They declined to say whether Downing Street itself had been affected, adding: “There are contingency measures in place at No 10, as there are with all government departments, to ensure that work can go on as usual.”

Asked about the effect specifically on the NHS, they said it appeared all clinical and operation systems were working effectively.

However, Britain’s minister for defence readiness and industry, Luke Pollard, said earlier in the morning that the Microsoft outage demonstrated the need for “greater resilience” against technology failures.

Pollard told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “My appetite for disruption when it comes to using my phone is virtually zero. I imagine that’s the case for every one of your listeners, that people want it to work all the time, every time, and we’re seeing more disruption from those tech companies. That’s partly because we’ve become more dependent on technology.”

Police forces across the country, including Britain’s largest, the Metropolitan police, said the outage was having an impact on the ability to report crimes using official websites. Access to Microsoft products used by MPs was also down.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: “We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.”

School inspections in England were disrupted after Ofsted said it was unable to receive emails, as hundreds of schools, colleges and universities across the UK were affected.

The higher education sector was braced to be the hardest hit, with many UK universities relying on Outlook, OneDrive and other Microsoft services for administration and communications, although Teams appears to be functioning for some online meetings.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: NHS England said it was enacting measures to manage IT outages. Police forces across the country said outage was having an impact on the ability to report crimes using official websites. Access to Microsoft products used by MPs also down.

Police called to Huddersfield University on Tuesday after women reported being ‘approached and grabbed’

A 29-year-old man has been charged after seven women reported being sexually assaulted on the Huddersfield University campus over a 30 minute period.

West Yorkshire police said Sophan Akbash had been charged with nine counts of sexual assault and would appear at Leeds magistrates court on Friday. Security staff called officers to Huddersfield University on Tuesday evening after reports of a man approaching and sexually touching women on and near the campus, police said.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Oxfordshire villagers to launch legal fight against asylum centre plan
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Parish council of Piddington, which symbolically voted to leave UK over plan, says it will ‘absolutely’ take legal action

UK politics – live updates

Ministers will face a legal challenge over plans to convert a Ministry of Defence site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington into accommodation for more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers.

It emerged on Thursday that Angela Rayner, the housing and communities secretary, had approved full planning permission, a decision welcomed by the Home Office, who want to end the use of asylum hotels.

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Tim McNally, the local parish council chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme there would be “many actions” by villagers, and that ministers should “absolutely” be braced for a legal challenge, which would need to be lodged within the next six weeks.

Ministers have faced opposition over the plans from villagers, who even made a symbolic attempt to declare the village independent from the rest of the country after a referendum of its 350 residents. Asked how the village would respond, McNally said: “There’s going to be many actions, you will see. We will disclose that as we move forward.”

Asked if ministers should be braced for a legal challenge, he said: “Absolutely, absolutely.”

Campaigners could also apply the new Hillsborough law, which is being considered by parliament. Once passed, the law would create a legally enforceable duty of candour that compels public officials and authorities to act transparently when investigations and inquiries take place.

“Today is a day of reflection, and we’ll work out where we plan to go from this point. But I will say, the Hillsborough law is there for a reason, and we’re going to apply it,” he said.

Luke Pollard, a defence minister, said the government would continue to engage with the community. He told LBC: “It’s pretty obvious that there’s a strong sense of feeling from the community around Bicester, especially in Piddington.

“The Home Office continues to engage with those. There’s still a few more stages to go here, so it’s not yet fully locked in and delivered, so that we can understand where the concerns are, so they can be mitigated.”

A Home Office spokesperson said a final decision to proceed had yet to be taken. “The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election.

“This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community.”

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative party leader, said the plans were a “betrayal of the women of Piddington” and “emblematic of Labour and Angela Rayner’s disregard for the law and women and girls’ safety”.

She said on social media: “When I visited Piddington I met a village terrified of what was about to land on their doorstep. The government said it was listening, instead it’s completely ignored this community’s concerns.

“The 1,000+ male migrants that Labour are about to deposit in Oxfordshire are in Britain illegally. They should be deported as soon as possible.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Van Hollen takes aim at Schumer as Democrats face first big test after midterms – US politics live
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Shrai Popat (now) and Taz Ali (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
Good morning, and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Barely a week after sweeping to a stunning midterm victory, Democrats have found themselves facing an altogether different battle, one within their own ranks.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has launched a challenge to Chuck Schumer, of New York, for the Senate’s top Democratic leadership post. Announcing his decision during an interview with MS Now last night, Van Hollen argued that last week’s midterm election results showed Americans wanted a fundamental change in Washington, and that Democrats needed new leadership in order to deliver that.

We saw a huge outburst of democracy on election day – red states, blue states, purple states – and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption, his wars and his cruelty, it was also about a call for a larger change, to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favour of the very wealthy against working people, and it’s fuelled by a corrupt political system.

The call was to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual, and to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

His challenge came just days after Democrats secured control of the Senate, winning at least 55 seats in what has been a remarkable election cycle for the party. Winning the leadership contest requires a majority of the caucus, about 28 or 29 senators, with an election scheduled for next month.

The caucus votes behind closed doors by secret ballot, but Van Hollen told MS Now that he had the support of “more than 10” Democratic senators.

Progressive heavyweight Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont who caucuses with the Democrats, has already publicly declared he will not support Schumer, saying “the time is now for change”. Endorsing Van Hollen, Sanders said: “The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families.”

Incoming Democratic senator Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan, has also openly backed Van Hollen, saying he was “proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority”.

The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called [Van Hollen] to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now.”

Responding to Van Hollen’s leadership bid, Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since January 2017, said he welcomed “a discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead”, but that he had the votes to be re-elected as leader.

There has been a wave of calls from Republican lawmakers in Congress for commerce secretary Howard Lutnick to testify on Capitol Hill, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia.

Senator Tim Scott, the Republican chair of the banking committee has sent a letter to Lutnick, calling for him to appear before his committee to discuss the national security concerns about chip export regulations in light of Huang’s relationship with data company executive and suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen).

This also comes amid a New York Times report that the commerce department, under Lutnick’s leadership, has taken a more relaxed stance on Nvidia’s advanced chip sales to Asia given Lutnick’s close relationship with Huang.

Earlier this week the Times reported that a commerce department investigation into whether Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s company, was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, withered after an intervention from Nvidia’s general counsel.

Donald Trump is in Washington today, and will stay in the capital throughout the weekend.

He’ll spend the day in closed-door meetings on Friday, but we’ll let you know if anything opens up and we hear from the president in person.

Will JD Vance run for president in 2028? It’s a question that seems to have two rather different answers, depending on which news outlet you read.

Drawing on interviews with about a dozen people close to the US vice-president, CNN reported that his path to the Republican nomination has become less certain following the political fallout from the Republicans’ disappointing midterm performance.

One source said: “I wouldn’t be surprised by any decision he makes.” The same source pointed out that, at 42, Vance has plenty of time to pursue the presidency in future, adding: “It just may not be his time.”

A central concern appears be the consequences of Trump’s war with Iran. As one Vance ally put it: “The question isn’t if JD can do it. It’s: If the Iran war is still happening, can any Republican do it?

“If they don’t end the war in Iran, no Republican has a shot at 2028.”

While CNN painted a picture of a vice-president seriously weighing his options, the Washington Post offered a different perspective. In its report, based on conversations with more than a dozen people in Vance’s orbit, the newspaper said he remained more likely to run than not.

One person close to Vance said: “Two years is such an eternity in politics, and people are very easily prisoners of the moment.”

The Post reported another salient point:

People around Vance have embraced criticism from Republican backers of the war. Vance’s goal has long been to make “the right enemies,” and he is doing so now, another ally said.”

• Understand what it all means beyond the headlines and listen to articles on-the-go..

• Keep up with leading voices on the move with the Stateside podcast

Dozens of protesters with the Sunrise Movement, a youth climate organization, were arrested after staging a sit-in inside Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer’s Washington DC office on Thursday.

According to the Sunrise Movement, 54 people were arrested, among a few hundred who joined the protest from across the country, including some from New York, which Schumer represents. On its Instagram, the group is fundraising $24,000 to cover the bail fees and any potential legal fees for those arrested.

Capitol police were not immediately available for comment.

In a clip on the Sunrise Movement’s Instagram, with over 40,000 likes at the time of publication, young people sitting on the office floor chanted: “Hey hey, ho ho, Schumer has got to go!” Protesters, including children, held signs reading “The filibuster kills,” “Stop the climate crisis,” and “Schumer: Step up or step aside.”

There have been murmurings of a possible leadership challenge in recent days, with a number of Democrats questioning whether Schumer is the right person to lead the party into its next chapter.

Among the most outspoken was Kansas senator-elect Adam Hamilton, who warned Schumer was seen by many people in his state as a “polarising” and “divisive” figure.

“What I’d be looking for is a leader who can lead from the centre,” he told NBC on Sunday. “Somebody who can bring Republicans and Democrats together, somebody who can bring the various factions in the Democratic party together. Somebody with fresh ideas.

“No disrespect for Chuck Schumer, just it feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us.”

Senator Elissa Slotkin, of Michigan, has also made clear she does not support Schumer as leader.

“I think whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they’re going to govern differently, what they’re going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people’s pockets and then in particular how they’re going to communicate differently,” Slotkin said on Tuesday, adding that she was not actively seeking the position herself.

Speaking alongside her at the joint press conference, independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, praised Schumer’s role in the party’s success in the midterms but argued such victories should not entitle him to another term in the leadership.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer,” Sanders said.

“But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New York is running out of room for its waste even with Statue of Liberty sized landfill
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Oliver Milman
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades

A
s a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents.

The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“All around the lakes is pretty flat until you see this monster of a hill,” said Mark Pitifer, a marketing administrator at Waterloo Containers, a glass packaging company that sits next to the landfill and is dwarfed by its neighbor. “I mean it’s incredible, it’s like being in downtown New York City only instead of a building, it’s trash.”

Locals in the nearby towns of Waterloo and Seneca Falls, the latter famed as the birthplace of the women’s rights movement in the US, had hoped the bulging landfill would be closed when its permit expired last year. But the operator, Texas-based Waste Connections, has proposed elongating the life of the landfill for several more decades via 47 acres of newly lined disposal cells and adding another 70ft to the trash heap’s height.

As New York state authorities mull whether to grant this expansion, the landfill has become a central point of grievance over the pungent smell, water pollution and planet-heating pollution given off by the places we dump our rubbish. Seneca Meadows is now the largest source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, in the state, according to a study last year based on researchers using aircraft measurements.

The operator, Waste Connections, did not respond to questions from the Guardian; it defends its environmental protections measures and record in statements on its website.

The increasing size of landfills also raises uncomfortable questions about how much waste we produce and what to do with it. Seneca Meadows receives around 6,000 tons of trash each day from across New York, with 1,500 of those tons originating from New York City, which sends its rubbish to landfills hundreds of miles away that are rapidly filling up and are set to be completely full within the next 16 to 25 years.

If burning rubbish or casually dumping it into rivers and the ocean is too environmentally harmful, what is to be done with our waste beyond continually supersizing landfills to the point they become a major climate, as well as local, hazard?

“We are at the precipice of a crisis,” said Emily Gallagher, a Democratic member of the New York state assembly who recently took a tour of the Seneca Meadows site and has convened a hearing on the state’s waste storage policies.

“There is this huge mountain of trash that is off gassing almost 24 hours a day … contaminating the Finger Lakes, contaminating the groundwater,” she said of the site. “People we met in town are in really bad shape, we need to shut this expansion attempt down now.”

Gallagher said intense lobbying and donations from interests aligned with the plastics and fossil fuels industries has stymied strict measures to reduce waste and enforce more recycling – she estimated 80% of the Seneca Meadows contents could be recycled. But she added there needed to be a broader societal reckoning with the tsunami of trash, much of it from cheap and disposal items, we create.

“We say throwing away but there is no away,” said Gallagher, whose district includes a part of New York City’s borough of Brooklyn. “The problem is that it will take a culture change that people won’t want to do until it is forced in their faces. We used to have a much more circular economy, where people reused and rewashed everything, but we have been indoctrinated into a convenience culture, even if it then causes us more inconvenience.”

Dealing with trash is “gross problem”, Gallagher acknowledged. “But we need a much deeper conversation about it rather than continuously pushing it to the side because it’s uncomfortable and it confronts our human desire for comfort and our laziness,” she added.

The municipal government of New York City has pointed to recent efforts to reduce its waste, such as the pickup and composting of organic matter, which makes up around a third of what is left as trash in the city.

Yet New York City residents still create around 12,000 tons of trash a day and it will need to go somewhere. The city does not send residential trash to Seneca Meadows – although some private contractors do – but will be sending it further and further from the city, which has not hosted its own waste for several decades.

“As capacity continues to shrink in the region, we will likely export trash to further locations,” said a spokesman for the city’s sanitation department. “Our commitment to rail export makes this much easier than trucking.”

Yvonne Taylor, co-founder of Seneca Lake Guardian environmental group, stressed she didn’t want other communities to suffer living near growing landfills like hers had.

Residents routinely text her to say that they have had to remove their children from the nearby school because the smell had sickened them, or of ruined outdoor birthday parties and other gatherings, she said. Pitifer, of Waterloo Containers, said the company has had to install filtration equipment to help employees deal with the overpowering stench of the landfill.

“We don’t need to use plastic grocery bags, we don’t need to use plastic toothbrushes, toothpaste, shampoo bottles, and laundry detergent bottles – all of those things can be packaged in other materials that don’t wind up in a landfill,” said Taylor.

“So the solutions are out there. We just need the political capital to turn this around.” In the meantime, though, the Seneca Meadows expansion must be halted, she said.

“We certainly don’t want to push this burden onto another community and say, “Oh, we just don’t want it here. You guys take it.” That’s not our philosophy at all,” Taylor said. “Our philosophy is that we need to start somewhere, and that somewhere is with Seneca Meadows.”

The New York state department of environmental conservation and Waste Connections were both contacted for comment and did not respond.
 
 
 Waste Connections says on its website that it is “dedicated to the preservation and advancement of the environment” and has an “exemplary compliance record”.

Its environmental protections include a “double composite liner” and a collection system for rainwater that has contacted waste. Landfill gas is captured and burned to generate electricity, it says, and there is ‘state of the art’ equipment and practices to capture odors which it says air monitoring data shows is effective. It says the gas is 50 per cent methane and it is collected and controlled, and the system is monitored to evaluate its effectiveness.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty. It is the largest active landfill in the state and is now the largest source of methane. The landfill is located in the Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Martin Belam
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Users of Microsoft Teams and Outlook in businesses and public services reporting problems. Plus would you like to spend time as a helpful furry little post delivery service?

Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. A global outage of vital Microsoft systems has crippled businesses and public services around the world. The tech company said it was seeing “early signs of stabilisation” after the failure affected millions of users for more than 12 hours on Thursday and Friday.

Some but not all users were reporting problems with services including Microsoft Teams and Outlook email. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use Copilot, Microsoft’s AI chatbot, according to the company. Microsoft said that there were no indications that the outage had been caused by a cyber-attack. We are covering the recovery efforts and continuing impact in this live blog.

One of Donald Trump’s top lieutenants could reportedly soon be fired, as criticism mounts over the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick’s apparent lack of action over the Nvidia spying scandal. Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, after reports emerged of his multiple affairs, most importantly with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Who are the main people involved? For more information on the cast of characters, Dan Milmo has this profile of outgoing Huang, who went from washing dishes at Denny’s to becoming the rock star of AI, and Dara Kerr has this piece answering the question: who is Colette Kress? And yesterday my newsletter colleague Hettie O’Brien had this excellent breakdown of what we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang. We also have this timeline of how the scandal unfolded.

New York officials have confirmed at least eight deaths, six adults and two children, in the collapse of a building in Flatbush, New York. At least 18 people have sustained non-fatal but serious injuries. Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, confirmed officials were working with the department of buildings to investigate 100 other sites in the city with connections to the building that gave way.

Red Cross set up a supply center at the Flatbush YMCA down the street from the collapse, providing temporary housing, social services and mental health support. “The last time I saw something like this was when I went to work at 9/11,” one witness said.

In an apparent snub to the vice-president, who had been closely linked to negotiations with Tehran, Trump has said that the US is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered JD Vance to focus on domestic politics instead. Vance last week blamed the conflict for the historic rout dealt to Republicans in the midterm elections.

What is the latest on terrorist threats to US bases in Britain? A suspect held in a New York jail, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, has been linked to an alleged handler behind Iran-linked operations in Britain, including what was suspected to be an attempted attack on US forces stationed at RAF Fairford.

How has Pete Hegseth reacted to being reprimanded by a guard? After video of the defense secretary and his aides being admonished by a guard near the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier went viral, Hegseth has awarded a Joint Service Commendation Medal to the soldier who called him out, saying: “We love standards. Well done.”

Dan Hicks, NBC’s voice of golf and Olympic swimming, has died aged 64. His wife, the ESPN broadcaster Hannah Storm, said: “Our family is heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected passing of Dan.” Hicks enjoyed a 35-year career at NBC Sports.

Family Dollar is to pay $63m to settle overcharging allegations. The settlement with the FTC and state officials comes after the Guardian’s exposé of its pricing practices.

The father of a South Carolina baby who survived being buried alive has been charged with attempted murder. The child was found crying and covered in dirt in a dog crate by rescuers after being left there for about 24 hours.

Donald Trump Jr is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company has said.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The datacenter industry is using propaganda to fight opposition | Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation and jargon to obscure the harm the facilities can cause to communities

“Antifa”. “Commies”. “Chinese bots”. Everyone from tech leaders to the president has called datacenter resistance a “documented psyop” and a “Chinese PR thing”.

But why do they make these claims? Our new research finds that the datacenter industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition.

Big tech’s opening pitch about datacenters was typical: they told Americans that these facilities brought jobs and tax revenue. They spread this message through mailers, text messages, TV spots and targeted digital ads.

But much of the spending behind these multimedia campaigns flowed through opaque non-profits and dark money groups with tech industry ties, hiding the source of these efforts. Groups like “Elevate New Mexico” have passed themselves off as local initiatives while obscuring their connections to corporate entities in the datacenter space.

As environmental concerns mounted, the industry turned to misdirection and jargon to obscure datacenters’ impact.

Developers continue to use terms such as “closed-loop cooling” and “behind-the-meter power” to deflect concerns about water and power consumption. But while these approaches can mitigate consumption, the effect is smaller than often implied: closed-loop systems may simply shift demand for water up the supply chain to power plants, while behind-the-meter generators still rely on the grid for backup and stability while competing with it for components.

And those industry figures about job creation? They are often presented without any context.

To give an example, an ad by Build American AI – an industry advocacy group connected to Lead the Future, an industry Pac funded by OpenAI and Andreessen Horowitz – boasts that datacenters have created 57,785 jobs in Texas.

But industry figures can also be misleading: of the promised jobs, how many are permanent jobs remaining after construction? How many are cafeteria workers, landscapers, and custodial staff – who often work for subcontractors without benefits? And are those subcontractors included when industry reports the average salaries for the jobs they do create?

A similar story applies to other tax benefits. When companies mention the tax revenue they bring to communities, they rarely include the exemptions and abatements they received.

Those incentives are often unnecessary to attract projects and eat directly into budgets for schools and social services. Some jurisdictions even track the precise number of dollars they forgo through such abatements.

But even when agreements allow communities to claw back money from underperforming projects, local leaders are often hesitant to do so because they don’t want to admit a project has failed. In other words, accountability is rare.

The industry fights to keep critical details about projects under wraps, sometimes working with local authorities to do so. In The Dalles, Oregon, for example, Google paid the city’s legal fees after it withheld records about a datacenter’s water use. (The city agreed to release the information in a settlement with the Oregonian newspaper.) Most datacenters do not report their water consumption at all, hampering policymaking. As for the public, their visibility into the process is limited by non-disclosure agreements.

Local and state officials, operating in a low-information environment and starved of resources by anti-tax policies, welcomed these facilities at first. The public has been more skeptical. With time, some government officials have joined them.

Yet, local organizers and activists told us that they now see decisions about their economic future as pre-determined by big business and opaque governments. They criticized the lack of transparency, the late stage at which the public was consulted, and community benefits agreements they felt were inadequate compared to the burdens they were being asked to bear: higher electric costs, air pollution, noise, water depletion, and a change in the character of their communities.

Industrial tycoons have historically manipulated leaders, laws, and regulations to their advantage. This time, though, resistance has been fierce.

Perhaps that is why the industry has stooped to smearing its opponents as useful stooges of foreign propaganda. In May, Kevin O’Leary – the millionaire Shark Tank star who is developing one of the world’s largest datacenters – called two activists “proxies for the Chinese government”. He later admitted he had “no evidence”. Even so, similar theories have gained traction among tech executives and Washington policymakers. And it has percolated to the local level, where activists and organizers tell us they face this invective – and much more – online.

The irony is that datacenter proponents are often the ones relying on disinformation and other information manipulation tactics to make their case. Government decision-makers should not give credence to top-down claims from Silicon Valley or the broader datacenter industry suggesting community opposition is somehow propelled by China.

Instead, policymakers should create and enforce mandatory transparency requirements and other provisions forcing datacenters to keep their promises and provide critical data about resource consumption, job creation and other matters of public concern. Those transparency requirements should extend to the permissive environment for advertising and campaign finance in which disinformation and coordinated astroturf movements thrive.

As usual, sunlight is the best disinfectant.

Samuel Woolley is the Dietrich chair of disinformation studies and directs the Communication Technology Research Lab (CTRL) at the University of Pittsburgh

Dean Jackson is a senior fellow at the Communication Technology Research Lab and a contributing editor at Tech Policy Press

Maia Woluchem is the director of Data & Society’s Trustworthy Infrastructures Program and a research fellow at the Communication Technology Research Lab

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Democrats fumbled the Hegseth impeachment. That could be a blessing in disguise | Claire Finkelstein
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Claire Finkelstein
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The failed move could lead to a more robust effort against the defense secretary in the next Congress. Here’s how it could look

A
traffic jam, combined with disorganization on the part of Democrats, enabled House Republicans to scuttle the representative Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.

While recriminations are now flying among Democrats, the fumble may have been a blessing in disguise. Democrats can now refocus the articles against the defense secretary, possibly to better effect.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The first four of Massie’s articles of impeachment addressed the Iran war, asserting that the Department of Defense overstepped presidential war powers authority. The first three accused Hegseth of failing to respect congressional authority and the War Powers Resolution. And the fourth claimed that that the Pentagon failed to mitigate harm to civilians in its operations, resulting in the tragedy of the US strike on the girls’ school in Minab, Iran.

Inclusion of the first four articles of impeachment, however, might ultimately have backfired in the Senate, and maybe even in the House in the final vote.

The US has a long history of presidents ignoring Congress’s role in decisions to engage in military force. From Nixon’s invasion of Laos and Cambodia, to US-led Nato intervention in Kosovo and Serbia under Bill Clinton, to US military intervention in Libya under Barack Obama, among others, presidents and their secretaries of defense have flouted Congress’s role in authorizing military operations for years.

The same can be said about harm to civilians in US operations. It was mistaken strikes against civilians during the Obama years that inspired Secretary Mattis, followed by Secretary Austin, to establish the now-shuttered Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response program. Dismantling the program was a Hegseth initiative and one of Massie’s concerns.

A more targeted set of articles in the new Congress might stand a better chance of success.

Three causes for impeachment stand out as most likely to garner bipartisan support. The first is one that did not even appear in Massie’s articles: Hegseth’s egregious handling of classified communications in the infamous Signal chat conversation regarding a planned military operation in Yemen, when the editor-in-chief of the Atlantic, Jeffrey Goldberg, was inadvertently included on the thread.

“Signalgate”, as it has been called, identifies one of the worst cases of mishandling classified information ever to occur by a higher-level official in the defense department. A Pentagon report itself suggests that Hegseth put troops in danger in this incident.

Hegseth and other members of the administration continued to exchange classified information on Signal even after the initial revelation by the Atlantic. Hegseth then embarked on extensive internal investigations, using polygraph testing to search for leakers, and ultimately firing Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a member of the joint staff. Yet the secretary himself, or at least his lax practices, may well have been the source of some of the very leaks he is investigating.

Second, boat strikes directed against civilian vessels in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific stand on a different footing from the articles relating to the Iran war. This use of US military force has been virtually unanimously condemned by legal experts as an indisputable violation of the laws of war, or, more accurately, as murder.

Third, an article of impeachment addressing the vindictive campaign of retribution against the senator Mark Kelly for a controversial video he made with five other members of Congress could well garner support from Republicans, some of whom may rise to the occasion to defend their colleague.

As I made clear in a brief in support of Mark Kelly, the video, which reminded troops they may refuse to follow illegal orders, merely restated textbook training to servicemembers regarding the law of superior orders. The attack on Kelly was not popular with either Democratic or Republican members of Congress.

As I recently wrote about possible impeachment charges against Trump, Congress’s heightened investigatory powers during an impeachment inquiry provide a critical benefit of the process.

A Hegseth impeachment could force release of the Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) memo justifying the boat strikes. OLC lawyers should be called on to testify – presumably behind closed doors – to explain the process by which they came to support the strikes.

An investigation of the OLC is long overdue in any event, and a more general inquiry should be conducted by the House and Senate judiciary committees.

Hegseth’s attack on Pentagon lawyers should also be investigated and should possibly form a fourth article in newly refocused impeachment charges against him.

Starting with the firing of the top Judge Advocate Generals and moving on to incursions into the role played by rank-and-file Jags, Hegseth has sought to undermine fidelity to the rule of law and the role of lawyers in reviewing military operations.

While Congress has heard some testimony on these matters, such as that of Adm Frank Bradley, who took the hit himself for certain of the boat strikes in a likely attempt to protect Hegseth, many questions remain unanswered.

Most critically, impeachment proceedings against Hegseth will provide an opportunity for Congress to strengthen its oversight authority.

Hegseth will likely invoke either presidential “testimonial immunity” or “deliberative privilege”, doctrines made up by the executive branch over time that have rarely been tested in article III courts.

While it is true that presidents need to be able to consult with members of their cabinets confidentially without fear of public revelation, these doctrines have served more to interfere with congressional oversight and block transparency than to further sound presidential decision-making. Congress must work to cut these outsized claims of presidential authority down to size.

There will also likely be assertions that information cannot be shared with Congress due to classification concerns.

Here, too, Congress must stand firm and focus on rebuilding its oversight authority. Members of the two armed services committees have robust classification privileges that make sharing information with Congress behind closed doors entirely legal and appropriate.

Leaders of the 120th Congress will have the opportunity to lead critical impeachment inquiries as well as conduct extensive oversight in the new year, but they must play their cards carefully and keep their eyes on the prize – long-term restoration of democratic norms and the strengthening of checks and balances in the federal government.

Claire Finkelstein, a contributing opinion writer for the Guardian, is the Algernon Biddle professor of law and professor of philosophy at the University of Pennsylvania. She is also the founder and faculty director of Penn’s Center for Ethics and the Rule of Law (CERL). She is a fellow in residence at the Edmond & Lily Safra Center for Ethics at Harvard University during the 2026-27 academic year

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Democrats need to fix these three weaknesses before 2028 | Dustin Guastella
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Dustin Guastella
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Progressives should be careful not to get comfortable. There is work to be done

D
emocrats had a great midterms result. Big wins in Ohio, Georgia, Iowa, Maine and Texas show the potential for a majority coalition that reaches well beyond traditional liberal strongholds. That’s a good sign for the party’s chances come 2028.

Not surprisingly, the story of the midterms was “affordability”. Surveys showed that the economy was the top issue for the election, with a third of voters citing cost-of-living concerns as their number one issue, and nearly 40% of voters claiming their personal financial situation has worsened over the past year. It’s clear that voters don’t approve of Donald Trump’s economic management.

That’s good for Democrats in the short term, but voters kicking out the party in charge doesn’t mean they’ve been convinced by progressive appeals, nor that they will stick by the party come 2028. Remember, 2024 was also an “affordability” election, one that Democrats lost.

In fact, despite the victories, the midterms revealed a few troubling signs for Democrats.

While populist, pro-worker candidates in purple districts such as Sherrod Brown, Brian Poindexter and Bob Brooks did have a great showing in blue-collar districts, overperforming expectations, these “Bernie-dog” candidates are few and far between.

The reality is only 47% of voters without a college-degree pulled the lever for Democrats, as compared with 51% of whom voted for Republicans. That’s an improvement over 2024, but there is a long way to go.

Democrats did win (53%) the lower- and middle-income brackets ($30,000-$99,000 per year). But the party performed best among higher-income voters – about 60% of those who make more than $300,000 voted blue. These are worrisome signs that despite “affordability” concerns the party’s reputation among working-class voters is still in rough shape. Repairing it should be the major priority for these next two years.

To do so, Democrats need to address three key weaknesses before 2028.

First, it’s good that Democratic candidates were able to endlessly hammer Republicans on their failures to address pocketbook issues; that’s a step in the right direction. Unfortunately, it’s no substitute for an economic program that can actually address the problems we face.

There is a real danger that, thanks to the success of “affordability” politicking, Democrats will neglect building a credible, and ambitious, economic program. Fixing our lopsided, K-shaped economy is going to require major new investments in domestic infrastructure, industrial policies to revive manufacturing, crackdowns on corporate gouging, and new means to generate public funds.

Worryingly, despite all the populist sounding rhetoric, many “affordability” ideas proposed by leading liberals point in the opposite direction.

Consider the cheap anti-tax pseudo-populism on offer by the senator Cory Booker. Booker campaigned to exempt all residents making under $75,000 from federal income tax –that would mean a $5tn dollar tax cut, enough to make Grover Norquist blush.

Of course, this kind of cash-in-hand promise can win blue-collar votes in a cost-of-living crunch but it won’t win their loyalty in the long run. Democrats need to address the affordability issue as a wage and job crisis, not just a price problem, and that means it’s an expensive problem to fix.

A better message: pledge to balance the budget on the back of rich tax cheats, big pharma, Silicon Valley and Wall Street, all of whom have grown fat off taxpayer largesse. Reinvest the lost revenue in American industry, American infrastructure and the American worker.

Democrats need a post-Trump economic model for shared prosperity, it won’t be built on policy gimmicks.

Relatedly, there is a danger that in reaction to Trump’s tariffs, Democrats might end up ignoring the worldwide working-class revolt against globalism.

In 2016, liberals were blindsided by Trump’s attacks on free-trade; he excoriated Nafta and the “American carnage” that unfettered globalism wrought. Then, in 2024, Trump again capitalized on Democratic aloofness by attacking Biden’s border failures. Both issues, and they are linked, suggest a hunger for a step back from hyper-globalization.

And yet, despite a decade of experience, Democrats spent no effort making a positive case for a post-free-trade, post-neoliberal economy.

In fact, according to the Wall Street Journal, Democrats spent more than $58m on ads bashing tariffs and exactly $0 on making a positive case for a new trade agenda. Obviously, Trump’s tariffs have failed to bring good jobs home, and nary a Republican will defend them today.

But without making a positive case for a world beyond free-trade, beyond the neoliberal global order, Democrats are unable to address one of the central concerns that propelled Trump to power in the first place. If the anti-tariff message hardens into an embrace of the economic status quo ante, Democrats will be in trouble.

The same goes for immigration. While the cost-of-living was the dominant concern this cycle, immigration was number three on the list. And it remains among the only issues where voters still trust Republicans more.

Democrats are right to decry the brutality and illegality of Ice tactics, but they should not conflate anti-Ice sentiment with a sudden embrace of liberal border policies. Working-class voters want humane border enforcement and a path to citizenship for peaceable residents. But if Democrats can’t make the case that they can reduce illegal immigration, they will suffer.

Finally, Democrats are still far from working-class voters on many moral-cultural issues. While leading progressives have signaled a retreat from the liberal-to-the-max approach of the recent past – as evidenced by AOC’s admission: “Woke 1 was crazy” – the shift is tactical and superficial, designed for political expediency.

No doubt, some social liberals in the party will take yesterday’s results as reason to reanimate the spirit of 2020. That’s a mistake.

As Jared Abbott and Joan Williams show in an important recent report from the Center for Working-Class Politics, the “biggest single contributor” to winning blue-collar voters “is embracing cultural positions that resonate with the working class”.

Now, working-class voters are not uniformly conservative on social issues, and in many cases they have moved significantly to the left in recent years.

However, professional-class voters are far more socially liberal than the working class as a whole, and they are more liberal than they were just a few years ago. And because many of the operatives in Democratic politics come from professional-class, uniformly liberal, social worlds. They simply don’t know many (or any) blue-collar people or their views and values. That’s a liability.

If professional-class progressives fail to reckon with how different their own views are from those of working-class voters – on gender, abortion, crime, climate, immigration, etc – and adjust their appeals (if not to adopt working-class values, at least to accommodate differences) they will fail.

Democrats have been gifted a victory thanks to Trump’s economic mismanagement. They ought to accept it with some humility and spend the next two years hammering out a political vision that can actually win voters’ loyalty for the long haul.

The good news is there is time yet to demonstrate to working people that Democrats can represent both their values and their economic interests.

We need big new investments in American infrastructure to provide high-wage jobs for the left-behind parts of the country. We need a new post-global plan for trade so that we can begin to rebuild American manufacturing – and the industrial unions that made those jobs good.

We need to expand Medicare, social security, and provide new programs to make life easier for young families. We need better public schools for our students, free community college and trade programs, and a slew of new workplace rights.

In other words, we need candidates that can marry working-class populism with progressive economic policies in a way that can reach deep into Trump-country and win over enough independents to deliver a commanding majority in 2028. That work starts now.

Dustin Guastella is a research associate at the Center for Working Class Politics and the director of operations for Teamsters Local 623

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Progressives are still so pessimistic, but why? The populist right can and will be defeated | Andy Beckett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Andy Beckett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
From the US midterms to Brazil and Hungary, extremists are floundering yet the left still overestimates their power. Reality is on our side

F
rom Brazil to Hungary and Britain to the US, why are so many people so surprised by the right’s election defeats? Flávio Bolsonaro, Viktor Orbán, Reform UK, the Tories and a vast array of Republican candidates have all been rejected in national or local contests this year, even in usually reliably conservative Mississippi. Apparently impregnable incumbents and populist insurgents alike have been beaten, often by big margins. The supposedly ascendant global right has been out-organised, out-thought, outmanoeuvred and outnumbered.

Yet each time this happens – which is more often than the usual gloomy narrative of our politics allows – many liberals and leftists absorb and share the good news almost with wonderment. Rightwing governments such as Donald Trump’s may have been struggling for many months, having made countless impossible or incompatible promises and strategic blunders, and opinion polls may have been consistently pointing towards a meltdown, but their actual election defeats are seen as miracles: unexpected moments of joy in the morning news, often followed over subsequent months by a creeping conviction that the right’s supremacy will inevitably return.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

A similar progressive pessimism follows the right’s victories, whatever their scale. The 52% vote to leave the EU in the 2016 Brexit referendum set off years of centrist and leftwing soul-searching about why the right supposedly had a better understanding of the whole country. Boris Johnson’s 2019 general election win with a medium-sized majority of 80 seats – less than half the size of Tony Blair’s in 1997 and 2001 – was widely described as a “landslide” and a sign the Tories would stay in office for many years to come.

Then came Trump’s hugely hyped 2024 presidential victory. Despite him having run against a last-minute, less than compelling Democrat candidate, being ahead by just 1.5 points in the popular vote, and achieving an electoral share below 50%, his win was seen as signalling a profound shift to the right, not just in politics, but in American culture and society, from how young men thought to whom Latino voters supported. A brash but socially conservative, confrontational but entertaining counter-revolution was said to be surging in the US and far beyond, ideally suited to the online world.

The midterms haven’t made this movement disappear. But they are the latest evidence that its strength has been overestimated. Some of that error originates in the ultra-confidence of rightwing populists. Especially when amplified by a powerful rightwing media, it can convince some voters for a while, as the blustering Johnson’s relative popularity from 2019 to 2021 demonstrated. In democracies riddled with doubt and with a recent history of tentative leaders, the performance of certainty can be seductive – until its bluffing and self-delusions are revealed.

Many voters and journalists want to see politics in clear narratives. Believing that the right, or the left, is dominant is simpler and more emotionally resonant than acknowledging that many western democracies are closer to political stalemate, and have been for a long while. Over the past 50 years, the Republicans have won the US presidency seven times and the Democrats six, with the 2000 Republican win achieved only through a highly contentious ruling by the supreme court – itself a symptom of deadlock.

In truth, the battle for power in any democracy is much more complex and multi-dimensional than national contests suggest. Electoral politics happens at many different speeds and scales. Then there are public protests such as marches, riots and strikes; elite private lobbying operations; slow but potent changes in popular attitudes; culture wars in the media and other institutions; battles between ideas in books and online; shifting power dynamics within personal relationships; and evolving assumptions inside people’s heads.

If an ideology or political party significantly shapes many of these processes simultaneously, then it has achieved hegemony, as the term was understood and refined by the still influential Italian thinker Antonio Gramsci during the 1920s and 1930s. This century’s recurring transatlantic tendency to see the right as establishing a new era of dominance is a misapplication of this theory: a mistaken belief, across the political spectrum, that modern conservatism has come up with a formula as potent as those of the right’s last two hegemonic leaders, Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher, almost half a century ago. Yet unlike them, the right’s current icons such as Trump, Nigel Farage and the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, only seem able to achieve a year or two of decisive political momentum at a time, and even then never manage to shed their deep unpopularity.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

With national elections looming in two important countries where the populist right is currently strong – France and Spain – it’s possible the movement will finally start reshaping societies for the long term. But even if the populists get into office, it feels more likely that their governments will quickly become incoherent and intensely disliked, as Trump’s has. Scapegoating migrants, “woke” elites and minorities can be an effective campaign strategy, but doesn’t solve a country’s cost of living problems.

The modern overestimation of the right also has consequences for left-leaning governments. It can make them too cautious, as if they are impostors who believe that society’s natural rightwing rulers will soon replace them.

So far, Andy Burnham has largely avoided this psychological trap, clearly relishing being prime minister, referring to Reform and the Tories strikingly little in his speeches, and ambitiously promising a 10-year plan, to be revealed next month. However, in some of his policies, such as on immigration and prisons, a deference towards the populist right and its worldview can still be discerned.

Successful centre-left politicians, from Blair to Bill Clinton to Burnham, have always argued that their illiberal moves are responses to voters’ concerns. But where do those concerns come from? Often, from the right’s fear-mongering about modern life, its exaggerations about migrant invasions and the extent of crime. This dystopianism needs to be called out by conservatism’s opponents, and the association of the right with realism – social, economic or electoral – needs to be broken, or at least weakened. After years of failed rightwing governments all over the world, it’s well past time.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist
