https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Pochettino to take charge of two final USMNT matches

He has signed two-and-a-half-year United contract

Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from the US men’s national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday.

The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades. United have won one of their past 11 games and are in the Premier League’s relegation zone.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

United made Pochettino their first-choice target after it became clear Carrick would be dismissed. They only held talks with the Argentinian, despite interest in the former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann. United’s leadership group selected Pochettino over other candidates and had the decision to appoint him signed off by Sir Jim Ratcliffe this week.

The club were attracted to Pochettino based on his personality, hoping he can turn things around at United by building a strong culture within the dressing room. United sought a more experienced coach after Carrick, feeling Pochettino’s long-term record of player development and clear philosophy would suit the needs of United at the moment.

Pochettino signed a new four-year contract with US Soccer in August, an expansive deal that offered the Argentinian greater control over youth development and the overall direction of the men’s programme. To secure his services, United have paid the US federation about $10m (£7.5m), with an additional fee paid to secure the services of Pochettino’s longtime assistants.

United’s players not on international duty were told on Thursday they did not need to return to training until next week. With the second of the US’s two games against Haiti finishing in the early hours of Wednesday GMT, Pochettino’s first day with United is expected to be Thursday.

“The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honours of my career. We are so grateful to the players for their commitment, to the fans for their belief, and to the federation for always supporting our staff and creating the opportunities to impact the culture of soccer in this great country,” Pochettino said on Friday.

“We want to thank Cindy Parlow Cone, JT Batson and Dan Helfrich for their partnership and incredible working relationships throughout our time here. There is tremendous talent in the US player pool from the youth teams through to the senior team, and it’s one of the reasons we have so much belief for the future of US Soccer. You will always have a special place in our hearts, and we will be supporting the teams whenever they step on the field.”

Pochettino was hired by US Soccer in September 2024, brought on to steer the US through their first home World Cup in 32 years. Over the ensuing two years he compiled a 21-12-2 record and guided the team to the World Cup last 16, results that stack up favourably alongside other US coaches.

He earned praise in the US for his enthusiasm and for putting together the US men’s greatest group stage at a World Cup, a performance that included a 4-1 dismantling of Paraguay that will go down as the team’s best 90-minute performance at the tournament. All of that early progress, though, was wiped out by a 4-1 loss to Belgium in the last 16, a result marred by the federation’s – and Pochettino’s – handling of the red card controversy surrounding US forward Folarin Balogun.

It was not his only lowlight: there was the shocking fourth-place finish in the 2024-25 Nations League and a bitterly disappointing loss to Mexico in the 2025 Gold Cup final. The US were thrashed by top-level competition in friendly matches, and Pochettino sometimes struggled to connect with players, primarily the Milan midfielder Christian Pulisic. Others, such as Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie, found themselves in and out of the picture on a regular basis.

Pochettino leaves the US with a glimmer of hope for the future. Across his tenure, 75 players earned at least one cap for the US. In the months after signing his extension, he did well to integrate more than a dozen newcomers into the squad during a four-match international window during which the US went undefeated across four matches.

Steve Cherundolo, head coach of the US U-23 national team, will lead the senior team’s December camp, which will feature a roster of primarily Major League Soccer players.

United’s captain, Bruno Fernandes, has rejected a second offer of a new contract but the club are confident of getting the midfielder to commit his future. The 32-year-old’s deal runs until the end of the season but United have the option to trigger a further year.

Fernandes would be allowed to speak to clubs abroad in January if United have not activated that clause. He has previously had interest from Saudi Arabia and Galastasaray.

Fernandes won the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s player of the year award last season after helping United to third in the league with a record-breaking 21 assists but his form has dipped. He took aim at Carrick’s tactics after last month’s defeat by Como in the Champions League.

On Friday Carrick posted a message of thanks on Instagram to the fans, squad and staff. “I want nothing but success for Manchester United,” he wrote, thanking the players for their “efforts and the moments we’ve shared”.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: NFL quarterbacks are under more pressure than ever from rushers. Why?
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Arif Hasan
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Despite all the advantages offenses have secured over the years, defenses are better at pressuring the QB than any other time in recent history

T
he Baltimore Ravens are preparing to start their fourth quarterback this year, Jacoby Brissett, against the beleaguered Los Angeles Chargers on Monday, because of injuries to Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley and Joe Fagnano. That puts them dangerously close to the NFL record of five within a single season (a record shared by the 1984 Bears and 2023 Browns when excluding the 1987 strike season).

Jackson, Huntley and Fagnano were all injured after taking hits in games. And if it seems like quarterbacks are taking punishment more often this year, your eyes aren’t deceiving you. Through nine weeks, quarterbacks have been hit on 15.1% of their dropbacks, the most we’ve seen since 2006, when hits were first logged in official box scores.

That may be why more quarterbacks have started games through nine weeks in 2026 than in almost any other year in recent memory. This year’s 47 starters only fall behind 2019 (48 through nine weeks), 2010 (48) and 2007 (49) over the past 20 years, and the expected starts for Carson Beck, Kyle McCord and Fernando Mendoza will push the total up further.

It turns out that, despite all the advantages offenses have been given over the years, defenses are better at pressuring the quarterback than at any other time in recent NFL history.

Pro Football Focus has measured the pressure rate this year at 36.1%, the highest in their dataset going back to 2006. Sports Info Solutions’ dataset goes back to 2016, and this year’s rate is the second-highest by their count, falling just behind 2025. Next Gen Stats’ data goes back to 2018 and finds something similar: the third-highest in their dataset, just slightly below 2023 by 0.1%.

So, quarterbacks are under seemingly more pressure than ever. But why?

One may think it’s because offensive line play has declined. This has been a talking point for years – the theory goes that the best athletes go to the defensive side of the ball, more football happens in seven-on-seven and in camp environments, development is a dying art, etc.

But it’s hard to look at the top offensive linemen in the NFL and argue they’re any worse than in previous eras. I’d put Trent Williams, Penei Sewell, Creed Humphrey, Quenton Nelson, Tristan Wirfs and Jordan Mailata against almost any other period’s top linemen. Quantitatively, we haven’t seen offensive line pass-block win rates – either from PFF or ESPN’s measures – change much over the years. This measure, along with its mirror, pass-rush win rate, tells us how often a pass protector loses their rep within the first 2.5 seconds of play. That may not result in pressure because the quarterback could be getting rid of the ball, pass protection help could arrive or the quarterback is just too far away from the pass rusher to be affected, but it does give us a better snapshot of how a player executed their assignment than just “pressure”.

The bottom of the NFL performance charts for offensive linemen isn’t meaningfully different from previous years either; the lowest PFF grades to offensive linemen are actually higher now than they have historically been. Again, that matches the eye test – watching underperformers this year like Austin Jackson and Cam Jurgens, one would have difficulty arguing that their play is remotely comparable to the mediocrity we saw from John Michael Schmitz Jr in 2023 or Scott Quessenberry and Kenyon Green in 2022.

So where else should we look for a reason behind the rise? It could be that blitz rates are peaking – and not just because the Vikings are doing so at absolutely obscene rates. The median team’s blitz rate is higher than we’re used to seeing, too. But it’s not the highest we’ve ever seen. Median blitz rates were higher in 2009, 2010, 2011, 2013, 2014, 2019 and 2020. The pressure rates on blitzes this year are a little high (42.7%), but not drastically so. This only accounts for a small percentage of the noticeable uptick in pressure. We’re also seeing the rise in pressure even when we’re only looking at unblitzed downs.

There’s also little evidence that this uptick is due to inherent talent increasing on the pass-rushing side of the ball. Pass-rush win rates haven’t increased this year. In fact, they’re lower than ever. On top of that, quick pressure rates – that is, how often pressure appears in under 2.5 seconds – are the same as they’ve always been.

So, if it’s not more blitzing, poor offensive linemen, or better pass rushers, what is it?

The answer? Time in the pocket.

Quarterbacks are holding on to the ball longer than ever before. The average time to throw is 2.83 seconds, the longest it’s been since the stat has been charted. This isn’t a product of quarterbacks extending plays after pressure arrives, either – clean-pocket time to throw is higher than it’s ever been (2.45 seconds, up from an average of 2.38 over the previous 10 years).

The share of dropbacks lasting 2.5 seconds or longer is 57.6%, again the highest we’ve ever seen. This is significant; dropbacks over 2.5 seconds have historically been pressured at a 50.5% rate, while quick dropbacks see a pressure rate of just 16.6%.

One could point to the increasing prevalence of scrambling passers like Caleb Williams, who leads the league in time to throw. We can think of scramblers as quarterbacks most likely to extend plays after the pocket breaks down or attempt to run for yardage more often. About 45% of quarterback dropbacks in the NFL fit that criteria today. In 2009, that number was 10%. Not only that, throws on the run have increased (12.5% of all throws compared to 7% in 2022), as have throws outside the pocket.

That’s one contributing factor, but time to throw for non-scramblers is up, too – the highest rate in the dataset at 2.81 seconds on average.

Are offenses dropping back deeper in the pocket and attempting to dial up shot plays downfield? Sort of. Dropback depth has steadily increased over the years after dipping substantially in the late 2010s, with the share of dropbacks setting up nine yards away from under center increasing.

This explains some of the recent increase, but it can’t explain the pressure differences we’re seeing against 2010s- or 2000s-era offenses, where dropbacks were deeper than they are now.

Instead, offenses want to throw deep but can’t. Average depth of target has actually decreased over the years. This most recent five-year stretch is the shallowest in our throw-depth data.

Part of that is the decrease in man coverage (usually “Cover 0” with no safety help up top and “Cover 1” with one safety deep) and single-high safety shells (In addition to Cover 1, this includes “Cover 3” with one safety and two cornerbacks deep).

Teams are parking two safeties up top (Cover 2 and Cover 4) and deterring deep shots at a greater rate than any other time in the past 20 years. We can see this on the play-to-play level; teams throw over 20 yards against Cover 4 at a 9.1% rate and Cover 2 at a 10.3% rate.

But Cover 0 is at 10.7%, Cover 3 at 11.5% and Cover 1 at 14.8%. The expansion of these two-high looks over the past several years has meant that teams going big-game hunting have to turn down their deep shots for checkdowns and other shallower routes.

On top of that, coverage is getting better. Quarterbacks are declining their first read much more often – according to both FTN Fantasy and the PFF QB annual, the lowest rate in the last six years (which is as far back as this charting goes) and that almost always means a shorter pass because the first reads on plays tend to be the explosives.

We can also see this improvement in coverage in another way: Next Gen Stats logs something called “tight-window throws”, where throws are made with the defender within one yard of the receiver. That tight-window rate is at its highest since 2020. Contested targets (logged by both FTN and PFF) are up as far back as the data goes – 52.4% of targets this year have been contested. Only one other season in PFF data has a rate over 50% (2024 – 50.1%).

So why is quarterback pressure increasing? Part of it is because quarterbacks are better at extending plays and invite pressure when they do so. Part of it has to do with a slight increase in blitz rates. Part of it has to do with natural variance in how the game evolves. But most of it? NFL teams are better at stopping deep passes.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.summary: The pressure rate this year is 36.1% of the NFL's top quarterbacks have been hit on 15.1%. That's the highest rate we’ve seen since 2006, when hits were first logged in official box scores. Quarterbacks are better at extending plays after the pocket breaks down or attempt to run for yardage

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Washington Commanders 24-21 New York Giants

Stefon Diggs’s TD seals win in final minute

Jayden Daniels threw his third touchdown pass of the game, a 32-yarder to Stefon Diggs with 57 seconds left, and the Commanders rallied to defeat the New York Giants 24-21 on Thursday night in what was essentially a must-win game for Washington.

Daniels’ connection with Diggs in the final minute came after the quarterback had thrown his first two interceptions of the season to end the previous two drives. He was 23 of 33 for 249 yards and also had TD throws to Ben Sinnott and Antonio Williams.

Coming back keeps hope alive for the Commanders (3-5-1), who moved two games back of the NFC East-leading Giants (5-3-1) and now own the tiebreaker after the teams tied last month.

Daniels getting picked off by Jevon Holland and Ar’Darius Washington looked like it would haunt Washington, who allowed JJ McCarthy and Isaiah Likely to hook up for a 66-yard, go-ahead TD midway through the fourth quarter.

But the Giants were unable to move the ball effectively enough on the ground to run down the clock. Jameis Winston tried to get the Commanders to jump offside with a hard count of “Who Let the Dogs Out” – with a series of barks – but that did not work and New York kept giving Daniels the ball back by punting multiple times.

Washington’s quarterback rose to the opportunity, aided by a pass-interference call that moved Daniels and the offense closer. McCarthy threw for a career-high 293 yards in his first home start for New York since a trade from Minnesota in late September but was intercepted by Rasul Douglas in the final minute, sending fans to the exits.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.title: Microsoft outage live: millions still affected as disruption stretches beyond 18 hours
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.author: Graeme Wearden (now), and  Achol Arok , Jordyn Beazley and Josh Butler (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.text:
Across Europe, millions of Microsoft customers will have woken up to the news that the company is strugging to get its services back online.

The disruption, which began around 6pm GMT on Thursday, has disrupted key Microsoft services such as Outlook, Teams and Copilot. Initially mainly affecting US users, it has gone on to cause disruption across the Asia-Pacific region.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by issues with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running. It says it doesn’t believe it is suffering a cyber attack.

And it became clear that the problem was pretty serious when the company admitted that the fix was “not taking as expected”.

The outage hit government agencies in Australia, Japan and the United States, as well as companies including two massive AI companies – OpenAI and Anthropic.

In Japan, the economy, trade and industry minister said the disruption had had a “major impact,” on the world’s fourth-biggest economy.

Australia’s spy agency and federal police were among the organizations reporting disruption there, with billions of dollars of damage predicted.

The latest word from Microsoft is that it is seeing “positive results for server stability” after applying a software patch.

But despite that, the company still reports “Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise) and Microsoft consumer products”.

Simon Azzopardi, CEO of security firm CoreView, says IT teams need to do three things following the Microsoft outage:

“Confirm that security and compliance controls such as data loss prevention, sensitivity labelling and Intune compliance policies are working as intended.

Review every emergency change made during the outage, because workarounds made under pressure tend to become permanent gaps.

And treat delayed email with extra caution: Microsoft warned that Safe Links might not be able to check URLs during the disruption, and attackers routinely use outages as cover.”

“Our sympathy goes out to every IT team that has spent their time keeping their organisation running without email, calendars and, in many cases, their security and compliance tools.”

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to support our crucial year-end fundraiser. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

Over on the Sysadmin section of Reddit, people are discussing what to call the Microsoft outage.

Suggestions include “Microsoft 364” (although this might be downgraded to “Microsoft 363” if the problems drag into Saturday!), “Microsoft No-Pilot”, “Friday the 13th: Nightmare on One Microsoft Way”, and “Microsoft Long Weekend” (a nod to how today has been a write-off for some companies around the world).

More people who’ve been affected by the outage have been getting in touch with The Guardian, including students, teachers and others who work in education.

Jenny is a teacher in SEN [special educational needs] school in Norfolk, England and teaches a four day week. Ordinarily Friday is her rest day and in the morning, she says she logs in and gives access to her colleagues to teach lessons she has pre-prepared and also responds to emails.

“I realised there was a problem at 5:30am when I tried to give access to a powerpoint presentation my TA [teaching assistant] needed for a maths lesson. I had to download this, recreate it as a pdf and then upload it to the cover planning folder. It was not a quick fix.”

She also had to keep in contact with my TA via WhatsApp rather than email.

It’s made her rest day a lot more stressful, Jenny explains:

“I was wrestling with this issue until 9am when I gave up as school had then started.”

Jenny believes we should invest in European technology firms. “I find it very worrying that we are so reliant on US technology as we are seeing this has affected so many areas of our society today.”

Meanwhile Tracy, a nursing student at the University of South Wales, says the outage has disrupted her studies, “particularly as university emails are not working”.

This has made it difficult for her to access important communications from lecturers, receive updates about assignments, and stay informed about placement arrangements. “As nursing students, we rely heavily on timely communication,” she says, “especially when balancing academic work with clinical placements. The outage has caused uncertainty and made it harder to keep up to date”.

On the bright side, this might help nursing students to prepare for similar situations in the future, she says.

“We can see how to handle not being able to access the information. We can write everything down, we can pass on notes verbally or on paper - it’s back to the old-school days.”

We’re seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe.

We’re also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific, although some users may continue to experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation progresses across the remaining affected infrastructure.

UK house moves are being disrupted by the Microsoft outage, it appears.

David Strank, who runs Kent-based Stranks Removals & Storage, said that the moves of two customers had been disrupted today while the exchange of another client was also delayed. The hold up could derail their planned move date.

“We’ve got two crews that are waiting for keys at the moment,” Strank told the Guardian.

“They are loaded and sitting outside but can’t do anything. We’ve got a move that we’re supposed to start on 23 November and he’s rung to say that they can’t exchange today because they can’t send any emails.”

For consumers, Microsoft says users may be unable to access or perform several actions in Microsoft 365 services.

But, the software firm says its recovery efforts are “progressing” (which seems to be a gentle way of saying the issue isn’t fixed yet!)

This issue affects Outlook.com, OneDrive, OneNote, Microsoft To Do, Teams, and Microsoft 365 for the web.

Readers in the US may be surprised to wake up to the news that Microsoft's outage is not fixed!

While North America was asleep, there has been widepread disruption around the world – from schools, courts and public services in Australia, to companies and government services in Japan, and then schools, the police and the NHS in the UK.

The cause of the mega-outage, which began around 18 hours ago, is still not known.

Microsoft says it has “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident” at this time.

Reminder, it reported around 45 minutes ago that the situation was improving in Europe, Japan and North America.

Many Microsoft 365 services are affected, for example:

Problems with Exchange Online mean users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web

Microsoft 365 Education features including Assignments, Reading Progress, and Speaker Progress may be impacted.

Microsoft Copilot 365 – users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses in the web and desktop apps

The Microsoft To Do app may not load, and users may see operation failures.

On Teams, Microsoft says:

Most of the core functionality including joining calls, meetings, group chats, and channel messages are not impacted. Scenarios that depend on Exchange Online, including Calendar related failures with scheduling, invites, viewing, and meeting edits. Creation of Live or Virtual events fail. Failures with Copilot responses for outlook, calendar, or M365 files, read history, or adding to new chats.

Navigating to App chats, adding new contacts or syncing contacts in settings fail. Standard channels are working fine but users may experience the inability to create or delete private or shared channels.

The UK government say it is seeking to establish “the full picture” of Microsoft outages.

The prime minister’s deputy spokeswoman said:

“We’re working with departments and with Microsoft to establish the full picture, and where services are disrupted, departments have contingency arrangements in place.

“You’ll obviously appreciate this is an ongoing situation, but in the meantime, people are encouraged to follow advice on the services they require for alternative ways to get in touch.”

Some UK doctors have been getting in touch, reporting that their emails are now coming back online after being disrupted by the Microsoft technical problems today.

That suggests there’s progress bringing Outlook back online.

Ofqual, the exam regulator for England, is the latest educational institution to be hit by the Microsoft outage. This morning it advised users that its complaints service was not functioning:

“We are currently experiencing issues with this service, related to the global Microsoft outage.

“We are currently unable to receive complaints, whistleblowing and malpractice submissions.”

It said any urgent enquiries should come by telephone.

The continued disruption at Microsoft shows the importance of building some resilience into your IT setup, points out Steven Watt, Professor of Practice in Cybersecurity at the University of St Andrews:

Organisations should be able to answer some basic questions. Which of our critical processes depend on a single supplier? How long could we operate if that supplier were unavailable? What is our fallback for communicating with staff, customers and regulators? Have we tested it, or do we simply assume it exists?

A continuity plan that relies on the same platform that has just failed is not a plan. Remember manual workarounds – these don’t work any more!

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.title: Farewell, Cybertruck: why the winding down of the ‘Maga hat on wheels’ is a sign of the times
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.author: Matthew Cantor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.text:
Eccentric and overhyped, Tesla’s Cybertruck became a stand-in for Elon Musk during his ascent in the Republican party. It will join the ranks of other vehicles symbolic of their eras – for better or for worse

Three days after a historic blue tsunami changed America’s political landscape, Elon Musk announced Tesla would end production of its hulking Cybertruck next year.

Was it a coincidence? Maybe. Musk said the move was “to make room for increased Cybercab production”, referring to Tesla’s Robotaxi. But the combined circumstances felt highly appropriate: it was the end of an era.

Eccentric and overhyped, the Cybertruck became a kind of automotive stand-in for Musk himself amid his political ascent. Like so many of his projects, it was massively promoted, heavily delayed, and ultimately fell short: Musk once predicted he could sell 250,000 a year but ultimately sold 70,000 in three years, losing $1.9bn in the process, according to Quartz.

The design seemed to prioritize science fiction over robust engineering: the unveiling was in November 2019, when the film Blade Runner was set, as Musk proudly pointed out – but it didn’t arrive on the roads until four years later. At that unveiling event, Musk infamously showed off the Cybertruck’s durability by having a designer throw a ball at its window, which cracked. While Musk called it apocalypse-proof, it often seemed like the opposite: Cybertrucks suffered at least five vehicle fires, four of them deadly – making them deadlier than the notorious Ford Pinto, according to an analysis. They were subject to 11 recalls amid technical issues, including a loose pedal that could get stuck and cause unintentional acceleration. They routinely got stuck in the snow.

Like its creator, the Cybertruck was highly divisive. Many observers were repulsed by its bizarre, boxy appearance and its road-hogging size (a parallel parking nightmare). “It is the ugliest vehicle I think I have ever laid eyes on,” the automotive expert Mike Caudill told Fox Business. Others, however, were deeply devoted to their Cybertrucks. “I’ve got 6,000 miles on my Cybertruck; I’ve had zero issues,” Matt Holm, president of the Tesla Owners Club of Austin, told the Houston Chronicle.

Indeed, the Cybertruck had its strong points, according to experts. “People at Tesla were rightly proud of the engineering they put into it,” said Ezra Dyer, a senior editor and columnist at Car and Driver. But “a lot of the engineering problems they solved were self-imposed” – driven by the need to incorporate Musk’s super-epic design choices.

“Why is that important to you that it be bulletproof?” Jay Leno asked Musk during a test drive. “Because it’s badass and super cool,” the CEO replied.

All this, of course, coincided with Musk’s political rise in the Trump administration. The truck, as the Guardian’s Andrew Lawrence put it, became essentially “a Maga hat on wheels”, indicating its driver’s political beliefs – or at least the politics onlookers would ascribe to them. The archetypal Cybertruck driver was a guy, “probably with some kind of goatee, likely compensating for something, so desperate for attention that he will take negative attention”, as an automotive analyst told the New York Times. Many drivers of various Tesla models rushed to distance themselves from the CEO with bumper stickers that say, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.”

The Cybertruck, meanwhile, “became this totem and symbol of Elon Musk himself”, says Dan Neil, an auto columnist for the Wall Street Journal.

While Cybertrucks took to the streets, Musk was taking a literal chainsaw to the US government as head of the department of government efficiency (Doge), which bore plenty of similarities to the truck, beginning with the empty promises. Musk said Doge could cut $2tn from the federal budget; its website now claims it has cut just $215bn. In the process, hundreds of thousands of workers left the government due to workforce reductions, early retirement and other reasons – before, in a move reminiscent of the Cybertruck’s recalls, many were rehired. And like the Cybertruck, it all came to an embarrassing end: Musk left government under a cloud as he feuded with Donald Trump over spending in his “big, beautiful bill”.

Now, when it comes to the Cybertruck, “you’ve got this expensive luxury product with a very off-putting aesthetic and all this political baggage,” Dyer says (the 2026 model runs from about $72,000 to $102,000). So it’s little surprise that sales have struggled. “It’s following the trajectory of any cult vehicle,” Dyer says. The hardcore fans line up, but once they’ve all got theirs, demand fizzles.

As it reaches the end of its short road, the Cybertruck – outwardly mighty, inwardly fragile, a poorly conceived product of an increasingly oligarchical system – feels alarmingly apt as a symbol of Trump 2.0 Phase I. Ten years from now, spotting an ageing Cybertruck on the street will serve as a reminder of the bad old days.

It will join the ranks of other vehicles symbolic of their eras – for better or for worse.

The Cybertruck is to the 2020s what the Volkswagen Transporter – AKA the VW Bus – is to the 1960s. In many ways, the two are opposites: the VW Bus calls forth images of peace and music, flower decals, and a crowd of well-meaning hippies packed inside. Sixty years after the summer of love, the Cybertruck suggests an isolated middle-aged man hiding from the apocalypse.

The vehicles do have a few things in common, however. One is drugs, but while the VW conjures cannabis, the Cybertruck is more ketamine. The other is a reputation for putting looks over safety.

A few decades later came another icon of its era – in many ways the progenitor to the Cybertruck: the Hummer H2, introduced in the early 2000s. Like the Cybertruck, the Hummer was inconveniently enormous and associated with a certain kind of aggressive masculinity.

And with its military ties and gas-guzzling reputation, it was bound up with imagery of the Iraq war. “It became a lightning rod for pro and con militarism, and so people drove them or bought them as a political statement as much as a style statement,” says Neil.

A similar perception may have plagued the Cybertruck, as Tesla showed off its ability to withstand bullets. “All of that was childish,” Neil says. “It didn’t speak with any seriousness to the mindset of people preparing to put down $80, $90,000.” The Cybertruck “represented a kind of a militarized vision of the future” to an American public tired of war.

As for Tesla’s clientele, “the wager was they were emotionally immature and it looked like a toy-slash-weapon,” Neil adds. Indeed, as the Guardian’s Arwa Mahdawi put it, the Cybertruck “looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old”. In that sense, it might best be compared to another icon of American vehicle design: the Little Tikes Cozy Coupe, the plastic red and yellow car that was for a time the bestselling vehicle in the world.

But perhaps that’s unfair. To Neil, the Cybertruck represents both a “failure of management” and “a phenomenal piece of engineering.

“Its ambition and its vision and its willingness to break the mold of convention – that I think is its legacy,” he says.

Dyer agrees. “I’m glad in a way that it exists because it’s interesting, and I’m in favor of more interesting cars. Period,” he says. In this case, however, that difference “is a towering monument to overconfidence.

“There’s never been anything like it,” Dyer adds, “and I guess there never will be again.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: The sinister power of Friday 13th: how this maligned date affects our lives
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Leah Harper
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Property sales that complete on this day have a lower median price. Air fares are cheaper. Weddings are non-existent. And motor collisions increase. How did it become so mired in superstition?

“I
have only worked one Friday 13th wedding in my 14 years in business,” says Caroline Smyth, a photographer and celebrant based in Larne, Northern Ireland. “I definitely think it is down to the fact that it’s a date surrounded by superstition. People are maybe afraid it’s a bad omen for their marriage.”

Smyth’s sole Friday 13th wedding, in September 2013, was the first she ever photographed – and it kickstarted her career. But for many businesses, the date is not so auspicious. From weddings to flights, job interviews to elective surgeries, many people avoid booking anything of significance on this date, believing it to be bad luck.

Today is the third Friday 13th in 2026 – the maximum number of times this date can occur in any year in the Gregorian calendar, and the only such year this decade. The last year with three Friday 13ths was 2015. But where does western wariness of this date come from – and is there any evidence that it does bring bad luck?

The origins of the superstition are not entirely clear. Some believe the number 13 to be unlucky in itself, thanks to a mix of religious, folkloric and cultural traditions. In Norse mythology, for example, triskaidekaphobia – fear or avoidance of the number 13 – can be traced back to the story of Loki, a “trickster” or god of mischief, who crashed a banquet in Valhalla, becoming the 13th guest and then murdering the host’s popular servant, Fimafeng.

In Christianity, there is also the idea that Judas, the disciple who betrayed Jesus, was the 13th to sit at the table for the Last Supper, with Jesus’s crucifixion the following day (and which is itself believed to have taken place on a Friday).

Others attribute Friday 13th’s supposed bad luck to the Knights Templar, hundreds of whom were arrested for heresy on Friday 13 October 1307. Superstitions around the date seem to have become particularly prevalent in 19th-century France: in 1834, literary magazine Revue de Paris published a piece referring to a Sicilian count who killed his daughter on Friday 13th. The article reportedly stated: “It is always Fridays and the number 13 that bring bad luck!” The same year, the French play Les Finesses des Gribouilles (The Finesse of the Scribble), by Edmond Rochefort and Philippe François Pinel Dumanoir, included the line: “I was born on a Friday, 13 December 1813, from which come all of my misfortunes.”

More recently, there was Black Friday – a stock market crash that occurred on Friday 13 October 1989, and is sometimes referred to as “the Friday 13th mini-crash”. Friday the 13th has also become widely associated with the American horror franchise featuring fictional serial killer Jason Voorhees.

“I don’t think Friday 13th is the biggest superstition but it definitely is still prevalent and reflected in the commercial world,” says Stuart Vyse, psychologist and author of Superstition: A Very Short Introduction. “Many airports skip gate 13 – they don’t want people sitting at gate 13 waiting to board their plane. In the US, almost 80% of buildings that could have a 13th floor don’t have one. That may actually be one of the reasons the superstition continues,” he says. “People are not forced to confront their fear and thereby get over it.”

The wedding industry appears to be particularly affected by such nervousness. A survey in 2015 found that nearly a third (31%) of respondents would avoid getting married on a Friday 13th, reducing bookings for venues, florists and photographers, among others.

“We’ve had zero weddings booked for a Friday 13th this year, next year, 2028 or 2029!” says Sky McGuire, wedding and event coordinator at Burnham Beeches hotel in Buckinghamshire. “I remember a couple earlier this year who wanted to get married on a Friday in August that was during the same week as their anniversary … However, it fell on the 13th, so they booked for the 14th instead.”

Wedding cake vendors, too, are among those who have noticed a hesitancy. “After months or even years of planning, it’s understandable that even those who aren’t usually superstitious might think twice about tempting fate, whether that’s unexpected rain or the dreaded thought of the wedding cake taking a tumble!” says Tara Cunningham, head of marketing at bakery chain Cake Box. And when Friday 13th comes around, there is even a shift, she says, “in how customers choose to shop, particularly when it comes to wedding cakes. Some couples may prefer the convenience of ordering online rather than venturing out on a supposedly unlucky day.”

New research from independent residential buying agency Homebuyer.Agency also found that homes completing on Friday 13th consistently fetch less than the average median sale price (as do properties at number 13). So far in 2026, properties completing on Friday the 13th have sold for a median price of £275,000 – 5.2% below the wider annual median of £290,000.

What makes otherwise rational people heed such apprehensions when it comes to any kind of “big day”? “Superstitions may help reduce anxiety,” says Igor Radun, a researcher in the department of psychology at the University of Helsinki. “We have evolved to look for patterns and causes, and sometimes, perhaps too often, we perceive connections that are not really there. When people feel that events are beyond their control, rituals can provide comfort and a sense of predictability. Confirmation bias then strengthens these beliefs, because we tend to remember the occasions when a superstition appears to ‘work’ and forget the many times it does not.”

For some, the fear of Friday 13th becomes a phobia, known as paraskevidekatriaphobia. This also tends to be a learned behaviour, says Vyse: “No one is born superstitious; you have to be taught. Most people who are superstitious as adults were brought up in a family where this was part of the lore.”

It’s not all bad news, though. For those not put off by having an “unlucky” date on their boarding pass, flying on Friday 13th could mean a cheaper air fare. Flight prices are largely based on demand, so with fewer people willing to take to the skies, costs are likely to drop. “Last year, flights departing on Friday 13 June were 16% cheaper on average compared with the rest of June,” says Rachel Mumford, a travel expert for flight comparison website Kayak. Customers benefited, she says from, “savings of about £66, so less superstitious Britons may have secured a better deal”.

“That’s the thing about flying; we are not in charge,” says Vyse. “Exercising a superstition gives people an illusion of control. There’s a sort of double consciousness: one half is the rational mind that calculates and reasons, and then there’s the intuitive half which is quick-acting and sometimes emotional. The two can be in conflict with each other – you say to yourself: ‘I know this is silly, but I’ll just feel better if I do it.’ That’s a very common confession that people make.”

But could there be any truth to the idea that travelling on Friday 13th carries an increased risk? According to a 2013 analysis by the Aviation Safety Network, the average number of fatal accidents on Friday 13th was 0.067 compared with 0.091 on any other date – meaning that, statistically, it’s very slightly safer. But in 2014, Aviva looked at a decade’s data and found that motor collision claims increased by an average of 13% on Friday 13th, compared with other days in the same month. In terms of academic studies, however, the jury’s out. “A belief in bad luck can itself breed anxiety, even behind the wheel,” says Radun. “A driver who is anxious about driving on Friday 13th may experience more difficulty concentrating in traffic than usual on that day,” he says. “However, research on the relationship between anxiety and involvement in traffic accidents provides only small-to-moderate and inconsistent evidence of an increased risk.”

Friday 13th is not considered universally unlucky. In Spain and Greece, Tuesday 13th carries similar superstitions, whereas in Italy it’s Friday 17th that leaves people feeling anxious (due to the fact that the letters in the Roman numeral for 17 – XVII – can be reordered to spell the Latin word vixi, meaning “my life is over”). In Japan and China, it’s more specific: 4th April, or the fourth day of the fourth month, is thought to be unlucky because the word for the number four sounds like the Japanese and Chinese words for “death”; many hotels in these countries do not have a fourth floor.

Of course, some have found Friday 13th to be a particularly good omen. Pop star Taylor Swift cites having celebrated her 13th birthday on Friday 13th as one of the reasons for her affinity with the number 13. “My first album went gold in 13 weeks; my first No 1 song had a 13-second intro … Every time I’ve won an award I’ve been seated in either the 13th seat, the 13th row, the 13th section or row M, which is the 13th letter,” she told Jay Leno in 2009.

For Smyth, the wedding photographer, it’s also become something of a “lucky” number: in 2005, her youngest daughter was born at 13:13 and she has since personalised her car number plate to include the number 13, too.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: A super El Niño brings life and death to the California coast: ‘like nothing we’ve ever seen’
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Gabrielle Canon in Monterey Bay, California
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Water temperatures are climbing the charts, high tides are swallowing the shoreline and vital parts of the food web that feed ocean diversity are disappearing

On a picturesque autumn afternoon last week, the beaches of California’s Monterey Bay were teeming with life and death.

A cadre of shorebirds charged and retreated in a synchronized dance with the raging surf. Nearby, the receding tides had deposited lifeless bundles of feathers and bone, tangled in piles of glistening kelp. Swollen sea lion carcasses, their teeth bared in a quiet grimace, dotted the sand as beach picnickers and dog walkers enjoyed the warm, cloudless day.

The effects of a historic El Niño have officially reached Monterey Bay, according to scientists, and the mortality on display here may be a grim harbinger of more to come. The waters that hug California’s central coast are already undergoing startling changes.

The climate phenomenon, defined by unusually warm equatorial ocean conditions, is rapidly heating and expanding parts of the Pacific. Water temperatures are climbing off the charts, from the ocean’s depths to its surface. Record-smashing high tides are swallowing more of the shoreline. Plus, vital parts of a vibrant food web that feeds ocean diversity are disappearing, starving scores of species throughout the system.

These changes are compounding the impacts from the climate crisis and extreme marine heatwaves that have already stressed ocean ecosystems and their inhabitants.

“It is like nothing we’ve ever seen,” said Dr Jono Wilson, the science director for The Nature Conservancy’s oceans program. “We just are trying to figure out how to wrap our heads around the sheer scale of this event.”

Visual reports from divers, underwater cameras, and beach-goers have showcased how deeply underwater environments are changing. Waters clouded with nutrients cleared as they warmed, and an unusual array of visitors arrived from the southern seas.

The central coast has played host to schools of halfmoon fish that ventured far past their southern California range, translucent winged comb jellyfish generally spotted on dives near Hawaii, and Humboldt squid that are usually found in the eastern equatorial Pacific. Whale sharks common in the Sea of Cortez were seen in Malibu and juvenile garibaldi fish – brilliantly orange speckled with glowing electric blue splotches – were seen for the first time in Monterey Bay.

Despite the visible impacts near the shore, El Niño anomalies are even easier to spot at depth. A buoy moored at the mouth of Monterey Bay laced with sensors has been providing scientists like Dr Francisco Chavez, a senior scientist who leads the biological oceanography group for the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI), with insights from farther below.

Temperatures in the ocean layer called the thermocline, which acts sort of like a transition space between the sunlight-filled surface and the dark deep ocean, have been steadily rising in recent months. Chavez said they’ve now reached 8C (46.4F) above average. That rivals what is being observed at the equator, where El Niño signals tend to be the strongest.

Researchers had to add more height to their graphs to accommodate how sharply the heat has risen. “It’s almost at room temperature 200ft below the surface,” said Dr Henry Ruhl, director of an ocean observing collaboration housed at MBARI. Meanwhile, scientists watched as important phytoplankton populations plummeted alongside the rising temperatures.

It’s not unusual for the waters to become less productive in winter, but the change was pronounced. “That’s a real indicator of the amount of biomass that’s there to supply marine food webs,” Ruhl said, adding that it dropped by an order of magnitude.

Warm water with fewer nutrients has had a pointed effect on kelp forests, essential ecosystems along the California coast that are still suffering from the last strong El Niño roughly a decade ago.

“Kelp is the key foundation species and it enhances the whole biodiversity of the system,” said Dr Scott Hamilton, a professor at San Jose State University and director at the Moss Landing Marine Laboratories just north of Monterey Bay. “We know when you lose the kelp, you can lose about 40% of the species that live in the kelp forest.”

The kelp is very sensitive to abrupt changes in its environment. Warm waters, fewer nutrients, and big wave events are all disruptive. During El Niño years, these are more likely to occur – sometimes all at once.

“We lost a lot of kelp just because the temperatures are just so crazy warm,” Hamilton said, adding that the air temperatures were cooler than the water. The kelp held on at first, but as the water warmed, it began to disintegrate and die off. “Last week, a lot of it just kind of melted,” Hamilton said.

When the kelp forest takes a hit, it’s like the first domino falling to set off a cascade of effects. And once the kelp is in decline, it has a much harder time bouncing back. Hungry sea urchins, deprived of their normal levels of nutrients, “start actively grazing around like little lawn mowers on the reef – any little baby kelp that pops up, they just mow it down”, Hamilton said. “That then keeps this very sort of food-limited system and no habitat for species, and it can perpetuate itself for long periods of time.”

Rising temperatures are also upending the food chain on the ocean’s surface and shore. Starved or starving seabirds have washed ashore between San Francisco and Los Angeles by the hundreds over the last few months.

Scientists believe that warming temperatures are driving the fish these birds depend on into deeper waters, but the exact cause of the mass mortality will take time to understand. Experts are afraid this may just be the beginning of an exceptionally challenging winter.

Brown pelicans and Brandt’s cormorants are being heavily impacted, and common murres have been among the hardest hit. The tuxedoed seabirds that resemble penguins and are related to puffins struggled in warming conditions even before El Niño conditions began to drive their food sources deeper. Marine heatwaves have had catastrophic impacts on their populations before.

During another exceptionally warm period between the summer of 2015 and spring of 2016, roughly 62,000 dead or dying murres were found on beaches stretching from California to Alaska, during a mass-mortality event that would ultimately claim an estimated loss of 4 million birds.

“We have already seen a lot of murres along the beaches,” Chavez said. “The fish they feed on are moving deeper.”

Experts won’t be able to track the full-scale impacts on these populations and many other species until next spring. Between now and then, Chavez said, it’s still hard to predict how events will unfold. But excessive warmth isn’t expected to fall off much over the next few months and that alone could wreak havoc on a variety of species, including fish, mammals, and birds. “Some will move,” he said, “and some will perish”.

Back at the Monterey Bay, Kriss Neuman pointed her foot at a pile of kelp – a large tangle of wobbly brown ribbons and bulbs lying limp on the beach – momentarily disbanding a cascade of tiny black flies, as she quickly jotted observations on to a clipboard.

As a principal ecologist for the scientific conservation organization Point Blue, Neuman’s research primarily focuses on the Pacific population of western snowy plovers – tiny tufts of white that speed across the sand on stilted legs or blend into the dunes.

Charting changes and impacts to their populations, which are federally protected under the Endangered Species Act, sometimes means counting the fresh piles of kelp on which they indirectly depend. “Kelp not only has this amazing productive life when it’s in the ocean – it has a second life when it comes to shore,” Neuman said.

Invertebrates and insects that come with the kelp or eat it when it’s on the sand feed the birds. “But it’s not enough to just have kelp in the system,” Neuman added. “There has to be a beach that is wide enough and high enough. In order to receive that kelp and for it to persist and kind of fire up the sandy beach food chain.”

The dueling challenges come to a head in El Niño years, as temperatures and nutrient declines take out the kelp forest and sea level rise chews away at the shrinking shoreline. But there’s a third element that could wreak havoc on bird populations that depend on the beaches: an issue Neuman refers to as “coastal squeeze”.

The coast has been armored with seawalls, steep berms, and other forms of protective hardscape added as cities and communities try to keep the rising tides from swallowing infrastructure. This has a negative impact on sandy beach ecology, which is also getting hammered by strong surf.

As their habitats get squeezed, “we expect to have fewer birds, less kelp on beaches driving the food web, and really narrow beaches,” Neuman said. “The predictions for sandy beach loss in California are pretty dire.”

Just north of the beaches, a small room lined with petri dishes, beakers, and buckets – and emitting a strong briny smell – may be the key to softening some of the threats to California’s coastal ecosystems.

Moss Landing Marine Laboratories research technician Bennett Bugbee held up a glass jar swirling with soft, small green kelp spores. Contained within them is the future of the food web.

Hundreds of plants could be grown from what’s in one little beaker, according to Bugbee. “And there are – what – thirty beakers on this table? So, there’s a lot of kelp we have at our disposal.”

As they grow, the kelp is moved from their beakers to tanks. Once they get about 4 to 6in long, they are relocated to basins outside near the shoreline so they can adapt under more variable conditions. For the final step, they are woven into ropes rigged to PVC pipes and placed in the ocean.

Even with careful cultivation in the lab, El Niño is adding obstacles to the process. Seawater the team pipes in for their tanks is becoming far too warm – Bugbee described it as feeling “like bathwater”. They are also having to think about how to move the tanks now housed near the shore farther inland if the tides continue to rise.

Even with the challenges ahead, Bugbee is cautiously optimistic. “Because we’ve been out there doing the work, seeing what’s going on, we’ve been able to adapt with the changing conditions,” he said. “ I think there is still hope to save at least some of them.”

The restoration process has already had successes. Kelp forests were decimated during the last El Niño, especially in the northern parts of California dominated by a species called bull kelp, of which more than 90% has been lost. “But there are some areas that have persisted,” Bugbee said of the work to rehabilitate the essential plant. “Just last year at our restoration site we had over 700% increase in kelp canopy, relative to control sites.”

It’s not just the kelp that could be spared the worst outcomes. Scientists in a range of fields are working diligently to build resilience into the most at-risk systems. Their findings will also add insights for how to protect communities on land and sea as the world continues to warm.

Research done during previous strong El Niño events and other marine heatwaves has provided a head start. “For the past 10 years, we have just been doing an incredible amount of work to prepare California and the West Coast for future El Niño’s and we’re at a much better spot right now,” Wilson said. “We have a lot of the tools and resources at the ready to help us recover.”

The climate phenomenon is rapidly heating and expanding parts of the Pacific. The effects are compounding the impacts from the climate crisis and extreme marine heatwaves.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 live: ‘I will never give up’ UN chief tells climate summit ahead of last address
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Activists from civil society – representing Indigenous peoples, women, trade unions, young people and others – are in the plenary room celebrating the work of António Guterres, the outgoing secretary-general of the United Nations, who is attending his last Cop (at least in this role) this year. Guterres has championed climate action in often fiery speeches over the years, and highlighted the injustices faced by the most vulnerable people in society.

“You pushed me to go further, to do more, and I am grateful for that,” he told the assembled civil society representatives.

“Dear friends, even in a divided world cooperation is possible,” he added. “You prove that every day.”

To widespread applause, he concluded with the following: “When I leave, I will keep standing with you as an advocate and ally. And I can assure that I will never, ever give up.”

Guterres wraps up: “We face lobbies, we face powers, that are pushing pressure on governments. Civil society must put the counterpressure so governments understand that things must change and so we win the battle against climate change.”

The session comes to an end with chants in the room of “make the polluters pay”.

Guterres has said the voice of civil society is more important than ever, but told those in the room that the praise he has received is not justified.

“I just did my duty. I just did what I was supposed to do. And the duty of the secretary-general is to tell the truth. The duty of the secretary-general is to fight for justice. The duty of the secretary-general is to be completely at the service of those that suffer, those that are discriminated [against], those that are victims of injustice in our world.”

A feature of Cops is you can sometimes find yourself talking to a random observer one minute, and having a brush with a world famous figure the next.

Waiting outside one of the plenary rooms here earlier, I was talking to the president of last year’s Cop, Brazilian diplomat André Corrêa do Lago, when the former US vice-president Al Gore walked by.

They spotted each other. There was a big hug between old mates and some inquiry over each other’s families. All very human and normal.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to support our crucial year-end fundraiser. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

As plaudits for Guterres come rushing through, the host urged her colleagues to keep their statements to a single minute. “We are very used to keeping it to one minute in this process,” she said, in a nod to the sidelining of marginalised voices that activists have long complained plagues UN climate negotiations.

Mohamed Adow, founder of Power Shift Africa, has called Guterres “the best climate spokesperson the world has had over the last ten years” – challenging hypocritical fossil fuel producers, making climate justice “central” to the climate conversation rather than an afterthought, and speaking out when others remained silent.

“That is a legacy worth protecting and one we have a responsibility to carry forward.”

On behalf of Climate Action Network (CAN), he invited Guterres to “cross the floor” and join civil society by attending next year’s Cop wearing a CAN badge.

“Dear friends, even in a divided world cooperation is possible,” he added. “You prove that every day.”

To widespread applause, he concluded with the following: “When I leave, I will keep standing with you as an advocate and ally. And I can assure that I will never, ever give up.”

Far away from the conference centre, Norway’s supreme court has declared the state’s decision to award three permits for oil and gasfields in the North Sea invalid, as it had not accounted for the harm caused by burning the fuels.

The decision, hailed as a win by climate campaigners, does not automatically revoke the permits or demand an immediate shutdown of the fields, but will force the government to consider the global impacts of pollution before awarding licenses. It comes two days after the Norwegian prime minister, Jonas Gahr Stør, told fellow leaders at Cop31 that “Norway will do its part” in a speech that did not mention the country’s ongoing expansion of oil and gas infrastructure.

Tessa Khan, executive director of Uplift, which led legal challenges against the UK’s Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfields, called it a “historical ruling” that would be noted by decision-makers around the world.

“Today’s decision affirms what scientists and campaigners have been saying for years: burning more oil and gas is incompatible with a healthy and secure planet,” she said. “As Europe’s largest petrostate is forced to account for its climate harms, and with El Niño looming large, it is a timely reminder to all governments that their obligation to protect the public from climate harms is not up for political discussion. It is a legal requirement.”

Norway has argued that its oil and gas is produced more cleanly than many other major fossil fuel exporters, and that limits to its production would lead to more European dependence on countries with dirtier fuel and worse human rights. Studies estimate that for every 10 barrels of oil Norway stops producing, other suppliers will make six to nine more.

Climate campaigners have dismissed this argument as “the drug dealer’s defence”, arguing that almost every fossil fuel exporter is trying to be the last one to keep extracting dirty fuels, with justifications that range from the relative cleanliness of extraction processes to the right for poorer countries to exploit their natural resources.

My colleagues Fiona Harvey and Oliver Milman spoke today with Al Gore, the former US vice-president who championed global climate action with his documentary An Inconvenient Truth twenty years ago.

If the world were to meet 35% of final energy demand with electricity by 2035 – one of the key goals proposed at this Cop – it would represent one of the cheapest ways of getting to net zero greenhouse gas emissions, new data has shown.

The findings are from Climate Trace, a non-profit supported by former US vice-president Al Gore, which examines global emissions data. The analysis found that achieving the goal would result in emissions cuts of about 4bn tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per year, or about 7% of global emissions, even if the electricity were not generated entirely from renewable sources. If clean energy was used, the potential emissions cuts would be about 8bn tonnes a year, or 14% of global emissions.

As electricity is much more efficient than fossil fuels, and fossil fuel prices remain high, this would also represent a lower cost per tonne of removing carbon dioxide than other methods.

Gore told the Guardian in an interview: “You could double the emissions reductions at a fraction of the cost, if they simply do it in the right way.”

Electric cars are key to meeting the electrification goal, but Gore said there should also be more emphasis on buildings and homes. “If we electrify cooking and heating and use heat pumps, we can have a very large reduction in emissions,” he said.

Capping landfill sites that are leaking methane, which is a particular problem in Turkey as the Guardian has revealed, would also be a quick and cost-effective solution, he added.

Halving emissions of methane, a greenhouse gas about 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, which comes from oil and gas production, from animal husbandry, and from waste, could reduce global temperature increases by about 0.3C. The Turkish co-presidency has included in its voluntary “action agenda” a goal for halving the increase in the amount of solid waste produced globally by 2035. But Gore said there was room to do much more.

“The solid waste goal is an excellent goal but if we add to that the better management of existing landfills [we could achieve more],” he said. “The emissions from uncovered landfills are greater than all of the datacentres, AI and others, in the world. And it’s not a hi-tech challenge to manage these landfills. It’s shovel-ready – you just need sand or clay, to stop the methane.”

‘I want governments to put human rights at the centre of decisions’

During this first week of Cop31 I’ve been speaking to young climate activists at the UN summit. Today I spoke to Selma Bichbich, 25, from Algeria, who campaigns for climate education and greater youth participation in climate policymaking.

“In my region, we’ve seen water become scarcer, and heatwaves become more intense. When wildfires hit my family’s region in 2021, people lost crops and livestock. We don’t have enough resources to deal with these impacts, while many of the countries that contributed most to climate change have more capacity to respond.

“I worry about whether people in my region will be able to keep farming and stay in the places they call home. If governments won’t even recognise climate displacement, how are we supposed to support the people facing it? That’s why I’m at Cop31. We’re still debating adaptation and loss-and-damage finance while communities wait for support. I want to see more funding reach the people who have already suffered losses and more investment in water and agriculture.

“If I could change one thing about Cop, I’d give young people a real say in shaping the policies that will affect our future. That means speaking in our own words and helping to write the decisions. At this Cop, I feel young people from war zones have been completely overlooked, so I call on everyone to pay attention to the young people who couldn’t be here because of war, genocide, or occupation.

“Young people should be there for one another. I hope we make room for communities affected by climate change and conflict to shape these decisions with us. I want governments to put human rights at the centre of the decisions they make here.”

Given Sheldon Whitehouse’s often lonely climate advocacy in American politics, it is grimly suitable that he is the only US senator here at Cop31.

The Rhode Island lawmaker is with a group of other Democrats who are, in a sort of unofficial way, representing the US. Donald Trump has, for the second year in a row, not sent a delegation to Cop and has recently spent time talking about solar panels frying animals to death and how he won’t allow any “loser” wind turbines.

Whitehouse is attempting to bypass this stance with contentious new legislation to speed up approvals of energy projects that is currently being fiercely debated in the US over whether it will be a win for the environment or not.

Speaking to the Guardian, Whitehouse said that he has three priorities here at Cop: pushing for a price on carbon pollution to “end the free to pollute business model”, to highlight the economic havoc caused by the climate crisis including the “full meltdown” of real estate and insurance markets and finally to explicitly denounce the fossil fuel industry.

“If we’re going to win this fight, we’ve got to go at the villains in the fight,” Whitehouse said. “They are the climate denial fraud operation of the fossil fuel industry and the dark money corruption operation of the fossil fuel industry, which we’ve allowed to work semi-covertly for far too long.

“We should put a bright spotlight on those operations so that everybody sees what’s going on. This wasn’t something that happened. This was something that was done.”

Not making this clear is, Whitehouse added, “like telling the story of Little Red Riding Hood, but leaving out the wolf. It misstates the story, it makes it boring, and it’s wrong.”

The race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s Cop. Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), told the Guardian yesterday that the world is now in an “age of electricity”.

But what does life look like in some of the world’s most highly electrified countries? We spoke to people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out.

The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said.

Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war.

Transport is being electrified at an unprecedented rate: outside China, sales of electric cars have risen by 60% in the last nine months, the IEA has found. The growth of AI datacentres is also spurring electricity generation, as is the rapid growth in air conditioning, according to Birol, as heatwaves grow more intense and more frequent under rising global temperatures.

“We will still use oil and gas, but the dominant source of energy is becoming electricity,” Birol told the Guardian in an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey. “One staggering number [is that] in the last 10 years, the world has added about 5,000 gigawatts of electricity. And we expect, in a very conservative way, in the next 10 years, about 12,000 gigawatts, more than two times more than what we had in the last 10 years.”

Governments from 185 countries are meeting this week and next in Antalya for the annual talks, where the turn to electrification in place of fossil fuels is one of the key topics. A resolution to derive 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 is on the table, which if it succeeds, could be one of the most important ways of achieving the needed decarbonisation of economies by mid-century.

Electricity now fulfils about a quarter of most energy needs while three-quarters of final energy worldwide is supplied by fossil fuels, mostly for transport, heating and industrial uses. Global electricity was increasingly generated by renewable sources and that process would speed up even faster over the next decades, Birol said.

Greenpeace has unveiled a 6-metre tall Trojan horse next to a town hall in Antalya to draw attention to the fossil fuel industry’s expansion through plastic.

The installation, by Danish artist Thomas Dambo, has bags of plastic rubbish spilling out of the horse’s stomach, and a sign that reads: “Stop Plastic. Big Oil’s Trojan horse.”

Petrochemicals are an attractive opportunity for oil companies anxious that their core business – selling fuels to burn – will be destroyed by the green transition.

Plastic production worsens the climate crisis through the extraction of hydrocarbons, during which planet-heating methane often leaks into the atmosphere, and the energy-intensive process of turning fossil fuels into consumer products. Large volumes of plastic are then burned as waste, pumping even more CO2 and other lung-scarring chemicals into the air.

The UK government still has no plans to publish an explosive report showing the national security risk from the collapse of ecosystems around the world – even after handing the key official behind the report a new advisory role.

Andy Burnham addressed the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey on Thursday and said the UK was determined to reach net zero by 2050 and work with its partners to build a clean energy future.

The prime minister also announced the appointment of Madeleine Alessandri, a long-serving civil servant and the former head of the UK’s joint intelligence committee, to be adviser on climate security. The JIC is the committee of the UK’s spy chiefs, which oversees the work of MI5 and MI6.

Alessandri spearheaded the publication of the climate report, which found that food shortages, food price rises, mass migration and nuclear conflict overseas could result from the failure to prevent the collapse of key ecosystems, including the Amazon rainforest.

The report was supposed to be launched at last year’s Cop, but was suppressed by Keir Starmer’s government. The Guardian revealed – through a leak – the key contents of the report ahead of its intended launch last year, and early this year a redacted version was put out. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has briefed foreign governments on the findings and the report clearly influenced Burnham’s decision to appoint Alessandri, but the report itself remains under wraps.

China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.

Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”

China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.

Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.

Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.

The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.

“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.

“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”

Good morning. Nearly all of the more than 90 world leaders who descended on Antalya in the past three days have now packed up their suitcases and lit out, some of them for the EU’s AI summit in Dublin. Anthony Albanese and the UN secretary-general are among the few to linger but will also head off later today.

With the departure of the circus, the real negotiations can begin, and a first draft of the cover decision for this Cop could come as soon as today, though over the weekend or Monday are still more likely. Look out for wording on the “overshoot” of 1.5C, climate science, the all-important transition away from fossil fuels, the electrification target and finance. The current “wishlist” can be perused here.

As double-hosted Cop31 gathers steam, the quest is also on for a venue for Cop33. Next year’s event will be in Ethiopia, and according to the complex systems of the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the meeting after that should be in Asia. But who will host?

As the Guardian revealed last night, it will not be China – a shame, according to many experts, who had been hoping that the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and second biggest economy would step up. China is undergoing a massive economic transformation, swapping reliance on coal and oil for electricity generated from renewable sources. This has proved a boost to the country’s economy, as the clean and low-carbon sectors now make up more than a tenth of its GDP.

India also considered hosting Cop33, but dropped its early-stage proposal months ago. That leaves the field open, with Uzbekistan, Thailand, Korea and Indonesia also cited as potential bidders. No decision on the hosting is likely to be made at this Cop, as countries are likely to need more time to develop their bids.
