https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: More than 100 companies and groups linked to fossil fuels represented at Cop31, study says
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Oliver Milman in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Delegations outnumber those of some countries most vulnerable to climate impacts, such as Nepal, which suffered glacier collapse

Cop31 live – latest updates

More than 100 corporations and industry groups linked to fossil fuel interests have sent delegations to the UN climate talks in Turkey, according to an analysis.

The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is thought to be the largest ever in the three decades of the annual gatherings, with more than 92,000 delegates registered to attend talks aimed at shifting the world away from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

This swell of people includes numerous groups that support or are influenced by coal, oil and gas interests, the review has found. In total, 103 groups with a track record of obstructing climate action or furthering fossil fuel interests are at Cop31, according to the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition, which comprises about 450 environmental organisations.

The groups include 60 fossil fuel industry bodies, 16 financial companies that fund fossil fuels, six industrial agriculture and foods products groups, three big tech groups and 20 cross-sector organisations.

Among the largest delegations are the International Emissions Trading Association, which has 29 people at Cop and has been accused of helping provide legitimacy to fossil fuel companies, BNP Paribas, HSBC and Amazon. The oil firm Exxon has a delegation of 13 people in Antalya, TotalEnergies has five and BlackRock, another big financier of fossil fuel projects, has five.

These delegations outnumber the national delegations sent by some of the countries most vulnerable to climate impacts. Nepal, which suffered a devastating, deadly glacier collapse this summer that has been linked to global heating, has just a sixth of the number of delegates of these groups.

Prakash Dalal from Pro Public/Friends of the Earth Nepal said: “Big polluters have caused loss of livelihood, emotional damage, trauma and survival challenges for our people.

“We cannot tolerate the disproportionate space given to them compared to civil society and our country delegations.”

Large numbers of fossil fuel lobbyists have long been a feature of the UN climate talks, with one in every 25 participants at last year’s summit in Brazil a fossil fuel lobbyist. Environmental advocates have called for better transparency and conflict of interest disclosures for those attending, and influencing, the climate talks.

Sheldon Whitehouse, a US senator and prominent climate advocate who is at Cop31, said: “The ticket to entry to this badge should be a disclosure form in which you lay out exactly who you funded in the climate space with how much, when.

“I think it’s important to know who the infiltrators are, who the moles are in the climate conversation and who are the legitimate participants. If people want to come they’ve got to come clean about their bad behaviour and they can’t hide it out in the real world and then come here and act like they’re responsible.”

Unlike previous years when the Kick Big Polluters Out group counted the overall number of fossil fuel-aligned delegates, this time the organisation highlighted the companies and associations it says have slowed or blocked action on the climate crisis.

Large banks, for example, continue to provide major financial support for coal, oil and gas projects, and 30 banks with delegations at Cop31 account for more than $2.2tn (£1.6tn) in fossil fuel financing over the past five years. Among the largest banks at the summit are JPMorganChase, Citigroup, Mitsubishi UFJ Financial, Bank of America and Barclays, all of which provide many billions of dollars in funding for fossil fuels.

Kathy Mulvey, a campaigner at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said: “Unfortunately, big oil, other polluters, their front groups and enablers running amok at the international climate negotiations has been the rule rather than the exception.

“The outsize presence of these corrupt influencers is all the more egregious in a year of record-breaking heat and devastating floods.”

The designations of those at Cop can be somewhat opaque. Nearly one in five participants at the Antalya talks chose not to disclose their relationship to the delegation they were attending with, according to Transparency International. Notably, BlackRock is in France’s delegation this year, while Darren Woods, the chief executive of Exxon, is with the US Chambers of Commerce.

While many at Cop31 have had complicated journeys to the Antalya venue, taking budget flights from developing countries and cramming on to trams and buses, others have arrived more luxuriously.

There have been 94 private jet flights to Antalya since Saturday, 23 times more than average, according to Oxfam. Many of them have carried some of the world’s wealthiest people, with 18 registered attenders considered billionaires by Forbes.

This group, with a combined wealth of nearly $200bn, includes business leaders who advocate for climate action such as Michael Bloomberg and Andrew Forrest. But it also includes the Turkish mining magnate Ahmet Çalık and the Indian fossil fuel executive Pranav Adani.

IETA, Total, Exxon and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change were contacted for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: El Niño will increase risk of death in childbirth for millions, say midwives
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Emily Maclean in Nairobi
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Effects of extreme weather expected in countries that already have high maternal and newborn death rates

El Niño stokes a higher risk of death in childbirth for millions of women in the world’s harshest crisis zones, midwives have warned.

Converging waves of weather – floods, cyclones and extreme heat – forecast to peak in the coming months will prove fatal for many, especially pregnant women, who face being cut off from hospital when in labour.

Sign in now – it’s free, painless, takes just 30 seconds, and you’ll never be interrupted by this box again

Not signed in before? Create a free account

About 15 million babies are due to be born in November and December in countries rated as high risk for El Niño – that represents two in every three births worldwide.

They include Nigeria, Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan, Somalia and Afghanistan, which already have some of the world’s highest maternal and newborn death rates. About 260,000 women die in pregnancy and childbirth every year, mostly of avoidable causes, with sub-Saharan Africa carrying 70% of the burden.

“If you’re female, pregnant, socially deprived and in a climate catastrophe zone, the odds are stacked against you before you even conceive,” said Anna af Ugglas, chief executive of the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) today. “El Niño is coming on top of other health risks – and for many this will become the difference between life and death.”

In Bangladesh, maternity teams are braced for floods.

“Childbirth does not stop during a cyclone, flood, heatwave or landslide,” said Christine Ewoi Eloto, a midwife mentor in the Rohingya refugee camps of Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh. “Even a short delay in reaching a facility during an obstetric emergency can cost a mother or her baby’s life.

“During previous flash floods and landslides, women could not reach health facilities. Roads were submerged and our vehicle got stuck.”

In southern Malawi, a heatwave is keeping women from antenatal care. A failed rainy season has left farming families unable to afford bus fares to a clinic – so issues go untreated.

“At present we’re facing temperatures above 40C most of the week,” said midwife Judith Mgogo. “Antenatal attendance is expected to be low since women cannot travel in such hot weather. We are having electricity blackouts every day.”

When electricity fails, midwives deliver babies in sweltering wards or by torchlight, said midwife Madalitso Malekano, of Phalombe district. “Extreme heat is causing dizziness and fatigue in many women – and that includes myself.”

Previous strong El Niño events have left more than 4 million Malawians short of food. “There will be malnutrition, which will lead to low birthweight babies and heavy maternal bleeding – a consequence of anaemia,” said Malekano.

The World Health Organization rates malnutrition “almost certain” in drought zones, a “very high” risk, noting this as a particular hazard for pregnant and breastfeeding women.

Emmie Mang’anda, a Malawian midwife, said: “When households struggle to provide basic necessities, some girls may resort to risky survival strategies, including transactional sex, in order to obtain money or food.”

In Chile, where floods knocked out communities and hospitals this year, midwife Natalia Acha Godoy, of the Maternity Foundation, said: “What stays with me is how quickly reaching a hospital can become uncertain. I can’t help thinking about a pregnant woman going into labour in an isolated community, or a newborn requiring urgent care when roads are blocked.”

ICM has issued a manual on surviving extreme heat – which it calls an “invisible disaster”. A single day of overheating can raise the risk of premature birth, birth defects, high blood pressure and dangerous overheating in newborns.

On days of life-threatening heat, midwives are told to hang red flags outside clinics – telling women to stop farm work and stay at home if possible. Women should have a “heat action plan”: a cool shelter, someone to take on chores and at least 15 litres of drinking water stored.

“Extreme heat does not leave behind immediate physical destruction, making its severe physiological toll easy to overlook,” said Neha Mankani, an ICM adviser.

Campaigners say the harm from El Niño – a periodic Pacific warming thought to be made worse by global heating – shows why governments must act at the UN’s climate summit Cop31 in Turkey this week.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Digested week: Do we really have to see Liz Truss at the Cenotaph for the next 30 years? | John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
At some point even Liz won’t remember why she’s there. Meanwhile, Nige wants more air time, and Boris Johnson couldn’t have made less effort

Like most people, I assume, I had always thought the Remembrance Sunday service at the Cenotaph was a time to think of those who died in the two world wars and later armed conflicts. It turns out that Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform, sees it differently. I was listening to Dicky being interviewed on the Jeremy Kyle show on TalkTV – yes, I know, I’ve only myself to blame – when suddenly he went into a tirade on the BBC’s coverage of the service. His principal complaint was that Nigel Farage had not been given enough air time, though he later morphed into a rant about antisemitism. I never did quite work out how the two were meant to be linked. I’m sure the BBC will reflect seriously on this lapse of judgment in its debrief of the programme and will next year have several cameras trained on Nige throughout the service. It should be renamed: “A Nation Mourns with Nigel.”

On the subject of rethinking the ceremony, it could now be time to dispense with the tradition of inviting every former prime minister. We’re now up to nine, and it’s more a roll call of shame than of honour. The idea of seeing Liz Truss in the lineup for the next 30 or 40 years is likely to give some of us PTSD. Those who can remember who she is. There will come a time when even Liz won’t remember why she’s there. But it says something that Liz wasn’t even the biggest embarrassment. That fell to Boris Johnson, looking as if he’d just got out of bed. He couldn’t have made less effort if he had tried. A shambles of disrespect. If he had been a former Labour prime minister, the rightwing press would have had a field day.

We have a new dog. Stella, a five-year-old cockapoo, whom we adopted 10 days ago. It was love at first sight. She seems to enjoy all the things we like doing, she can walk off the lead on Tooting Bec Common and she is already a firm favourite at the local cafe. She is adorable, loves a snuggle and is sitting next to me as I write, every now and then giving me a nudge with her nose. We found Stella thanks to those of you who read this column. Back in the summer, I wrote about how there was a dog-shaped hole in our lives. How we were finally ready to love again after the death of our beloved Herbert Hound in April last year. But there were many obstacles. We knew we couldn’t get a puppy, as Jill’s illness and my job meant we just wouldn’t be able to devote the necessary time to training her properly. And we also knew we wanted another cockapoo because that was what Herbie had been.

To cap it all, we didn’t want a dog that had had a tough life and might be emotionally scarred: again, our lives were complicated enough. Now try finding an adult cockapoo who has come from a loving home. You can’t. No one wants to part with their cockapoo. However, one couple emailed me to say that they were heartbroken that their family circumstances had changed, and they were reluctantly looking for a new home for Stella. I would love to name them and thank them here for the trust they have shown in us by giving us something so precious. But they may not want to be identified. So from Jill and me, a huge anonymous thank you.

It’s probably not the most politically correct response to a man who has been found guilty of eight counts of fraud by misrepresentation and one count of fraud by a failure to disclose, but I can’t help having a sneaking admiration for Kashim Chowdhury. We hear so much these days about people claiming benefits and unable to find work, yet here we have a man who – at one point in 2023 – held no fewer than five full-time public sector jobs at the same time. That makes him borderline Stakhanovite.

It goes without saying that Chowdhury did this by mainly working from home – even he couldn’t manage to be in five places at the same time. But even so. Quite how he got away with working simultaneously for Defra, the Department of Health, the UK Health Security Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency is a mystery. Maybe Chowdhury was just one of those people you find in most organisations, usually in a side office. No one can remember quite what it is he is meant to be doing but everyone is too polite to ask, so they leave him alone to get on with doing what he does best. Which in Chowdhury’s case, is getting another job. You can only imagine that he is an absolute ace at job applications. Gets called for an interview every time and knows how to charm AI and real people. Can sound convincing when he insists that his greatest strength is as a team player. Someone prepared to go the extra mile. Who will work all hours. Even if that work is somehow doing no work. It does make you wonder if any government agency actually took up his references. “Mr Chowdhury hasn’t been seen for a while … though he appears to be an expert multi-tasker.” It seems that Chowdhury is facing a prison sentence. Let’s see how many jobs he wangles for himself inside.

Most cricket fans will remember when the Australian Cameron Bancroft was caught on TV tampering with the ball during the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018. It was the biggest cricketing scandal of the century. The captain and vice-captain, Steve Smith and David Warner, were sent home in disgrace along with Bancroft and were suspended from cricket for 12 months. Bancroft got a nine-month suspension. After serving his time, Smith has been a virtual ever-present in the national side ever since. His tear-stained press conference long since conveniently forgotten. Until now. The Australian opening batter Usman Khawaja has now given his version of the events in his autobiography – and they don’t square with the one the governing body Cricket Australia (CA) would have had us believe for the past eight years. Far from being a one-off aberration, he says, the ball-tampering was done with the knowledge of the whole team and had been used in previous Tests. (On Friday the Australia Test captain Pat Cummins described Khawaja’s claims as “complete and utter nonsense” and “100% wrong”.)

We have been told the tampering was all a mystery to the bowlers, and that they hadn’t noticed that the ball they had been using five minutes previously had changed shape. Strange. Every bowler should know the exact condition of the ball. It’s literally their job. But maybe CA wanted to minimise reputational damage and avoid suspending key players from future matches? Maybe that’s not the question. Will we see CA bluff this one out and hope the scandal goes away? Or will it suspend the rest of the team for a year? More importantly, will it look into whether the rest of the team lied about their involvement? Don’t hold your breath.

One of the pleasures of doing live shows is the questions from the audience. Several times now, I have been asked what essentials I would like to stockpile. Something I had never previously given much thought, having been a child in the 60s when you used to get government information films instructing you to sit under the kitchen table in the event of a nuclear attack. Even to my 10-year-old mind, that seemed like an exercise in futility. But now we have moved on and it makes some kind of sense to have a small stash of essentials to get you through a cyber-attack.

Sea levels are going to have to change massively for Tooting to be submerged by floods. Apart from water and some tinned tuna – the nice stuff from Ortiz, not the ones that taste like cat food – and tinned peaches, what I really would like is something to keep me entertained. I’m guessing if we’re in the middle of a national emergency then all football will be postponed. Currently, that counts as a blessing, as Spurs’ prime purpose in life is to torture me. So it must be a book. I don’t fancy M John Harrison’s Booker-winning The End of Everything. A publishing friend says it’s a book that creeps up on you on third reading, but I’m not sure I want to read the same book three times inside a week. On the other hand, I am loving Luke Kennard’s Black Bag. That should do it. And if you want to ask me anything else, there are still a handful of tickets left for my last show of the year at the Huntingdon Hall, Worcester on 26 November. Please come along.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve | Simon Jenkins
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Simon Jenkins
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
For all the supposed improvements, inspectors still obsess over statistics and adjectives, but surely school success depends on teachers and parents

T
he government regulation of state schools by Ofsted in England is a fiasco. Following the 2023 suicide of the Reading headteacher Ruth Perry, after her school was downgraded from outstanding to inadequate, Ofsted appears to have referred to a dictionary. Single words were replaced by colour-coded report cards, which use a wider range of different adjectives to grade abstractions such as personal development and wellbeing, achievement and leadership. Never has the concept of “education” seemed so empty.

The reaction of the teaching profession to the new code has itself been devastating, as highlighted in a recent survey that showed more than half of headteachers in England polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are now considering early retirement as a result of the experience. This sense of misery was also illustrated in a poll conducted by the National Education Union one year on from the introduction of the new framework, with 65% saying it is the same as or worse than before.

It is no wonder that the leader of the National Association of Head Teachers, Paul Whiteman, has called for an immediate halt to Ofsted’s visits. “The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it,” he said. “It poses a real and present danger to the well-being and mental health of school leaders and teachers, possibly even a risk to life.” Even the new education secretary, Lucy Powell, has said she takes the reaction to the inspections “incredibly seriously” and said she wanted to see a system that was “more supportive” to staff. We have yet to see what that means.

Schools used to be local institutions that belonged to the community. Bringing state-maintained schools under central government control in England and Wales began in 1988 with Thatcher’s national curriculum reforms. In 1992, John Major created Ofsted to enforce it. He also began a national league table of secondary schools, which were to be judged by their exam results. It is hardly surprising that the whole dynamic of secondary education became “to teach the exam”. Sports, art, music were shamelessly sidelined.

By the time of Tony Blair, the resulting avalanche of Whitehall regulations was said by a teacher friend to fill a wheelbarrow every school term. Vocational and technical education were demoted in favour of academic and university-oriented subjects. The nation’s performance in the international Pisa league tables became as competitive as the Olympic Games.

Now, Ofsted inspectors descend on schools, usually once in four years, with usually just 24 hours’ notice. They are armed not with advice or money but with exam statistics and adjectives. They have reduced the teaching profession to a production line.

The trauma experienced by staff has been an inevitable consequence. Perry’s sister says she has been contacted by 12 other heads saying they too have felt suicidal after glib dismissals of their work. How could such a brief inspection take account of considerations as important as a child’s health, the local job requirements and tutoring resources? An inspector merely needed to sniff the air, decide “not good enough” and stroll back to Whitehall. Would we judge our doctors, lawyers or bankers that way?

The naivety of the inspection regime is a classic of overcentralised government, of the relentless search for standardisation. I can find no evidence that relates a pupil’s or a school’s exam results to an individual’s wealth or happiness in later life. They are measuring for measuring’s sake.

The one great fault of comprehensive education in Britain from the 1960s onwards was its devoting so much of the secondary syllabus to academic subjects. Powell has already shown herself open to reforming this. She has banned GCSE preparation from the first two years of secondary school, and is determined to end the denial of vocational education for those who fail maths GCSE. Her proposal to teach subjects such as health and social care is welcome. So too is her enthusiasm for oracy and verbal confidence. If Powell means what she has said, she must put an end to Michael Gove’s generation of ministers and their obsession with academic league tables and to preparing pupils for university.

Possibly Britain’s currently most disgraceful statistic is that since the outbreak of Covid about 20% of children in England in year 9 – their mid-teens – are “persistently absent” from school. We need look no further for the cause of the current Neets crisis. The failure is glaring.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The success of a school, primary or secondary, is largely a function of its relationship with its local area. It depends on the reputation of its staff and their collaboration with parents. When schools were locally owned and run prior to Thatcher’s nationalisation these relationships were built into their governance. A school’s success was a feature of local pride. Of course this meant some worked better than others. But I find it significant that the UK was recently rated only the 16th “happiest country” in Europe. In part I sense it reflects its distant and heavily centralised public sector.

Nobody needs Ofsted. Andy Burnham should move to devolve schools to the communities they serve and on which they should in future depend. Inspecting the professional quality of their work should be a local matter. We need only to look abroad to see that this works.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘Never thought I’d eat that’: how vegetable prescriptions are helping Britons with diabetes
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Steven Morris
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
WellFed participants in Cornwall report better blood sugar levels with help of free veg boxes, cooking and gardening

T
he participants admitted that throughout their life, their food choices had been far from ideal: egg and chips, hearty roasts, raw fry – a Cornish one-pan dish of bacon, potatoes and onions, often fried in lard and once beloved of miners and fishers.

But here they were, at a community orchard in the harbourside town of St Ives in south-west Cornwall, massaging Swiss chard (to soften the leaves), dicing carrots, adding lentils into a pot to create a low-GI, high-fibre – and tasty – shepherd’s bake.

The six people who worked together on the bake were taking part in a pioneering “veg on prescription” programme for patients with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, in which participants are given free weekly veg boxes and access to group cooking and gardening sessions.

Many of the more than 100 people who have taken part in the WellFed scheme have reported improvements in their blood sugar levels, their weight and their feeling of wellbeing.

Chris Longthorp, 74, one of those in the St Ives “chop and chat” session, said he had been surprised when he had been diagnosed with type 2, saying it had “crept up” on him. He described his usual diet as “standard fodder … meat and two veg, quite a lot of sweet things”.

Since joining WellFed, Longthorp, who used to work in the pharmaceutical industry, said his HbA1c – blood glucose – level had dropped from 50 to 42. Diabetes UK says having a HbA1c over 48 risks complications such as problems in eyes, kidneys and feet. “I feel fitter and coming to these sessions is fun,”’ said Longthorp.

Another of the St Ives cooks was Johanna Evans, 85, a retired shop owner and a lifelong fan of raw fry. She said she had been surprised at how much she had enjoyed some of the meals they had prepared.

The week before, they had created – with the help of their facilitator – a sprouted bean, edamame, shredded sprout and sesame bento box. “I never thought I’d eat anything like that,” Evans said.

Claire Judd, the WellFed project lead, said the pilot programme was believed to be the first of its kind in England, taking into account the range of support provided and the geographical reach – sessions are run at 20 sites across Cornwall, from the border town of Launceston in the east to the Isles of Scilly about 28 miles (45km) off the mainland. GPs from more than 20 surgeries have put forward patients.

A preliminary impact report carried out by the Centre for Climate Change and Social Transformations is encouraging. It said: “WellFed participants described eating a healthier diet, feeling more confident about their health condition and how to manage it, and how their wellbeing improved.”

The report added: “Notably, most participants reported a reduction in their HbA1c and the average HbA1c level decreased from the diabetic range to the pre-diabetic range over the intervention period.”

WellFed is delivered by Volunteer Cornwall, funded by Cornwall council public health and the NHS in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly. If the final results are as positive as the preliminary ones, the hope is that it will be rolled out more extensively and health chiefs in other parts of the UK are keeping an eye on the impacts to see if they should replicate it.

Dan Rainbow, a St Ives GP, said he was delighted at the impact so far. “We spend so much of our time treating disease and illness but this is about creating health.”

He said that places such as St Ives were often perceived as well-to-do, but there were significant pockets of deprivation there and in many other parts of Cornwall. The number of people with pre-diabetes in Cornwall is also particularly high compared with the rest of England, a sign that more trouble is on the way.

“This project is just the sort of thing we should be doing,” said Rainbow. “We haven’t been told to do it by the government, rather it’s come from the community here, which is great.”

A few miles up the road from St Ives, A WellFed cooking and gardening session was taking place at Community Roots, a community garden in Porthtowan.

Mike May, 68, a retired engineer, said his HbA1c level had reached 78 at one point but had dropped to 43, which he put down to a combination of the WellFed project and other medical interventions.

Michael Waller, a 64-year-old former clay worker, who has been attending sessions at Chaos farm on the Roseland peninsula, said he had not wanted conventional medication when he was told he had diabetes. His HbA1c level has now dropped from 64 to 47. He said: “I was eating a lot of chocolate, ice cream and flapjack. At the farm it’s all vegetables and salad and peas and beans, pulses.”

Tracey Lyne, 67, a childminder from Truro, who has also been attending the Roseland sessions, said: “It was a combination of wellbeing – to be out getting your hands dirty – and a green gym, where we’re pushing wheelbarrows, stretching, digging.”

Lyne said she had previously fallen into the habit of microwaving “plastic” meals.

“You convince yourself that sticking it in the microwave is easy, whereas in 10 minutes you can produce something really lovely with a veg box.”
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.summary: WellFed participants in Cornwall report better blood sugar levels with help of free veg boxes. Participants in the scheme have reported improvements in their blood sugar level, weight and wellbeing. Pilot programme is believed to be the first of its kind in England.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.title: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.author: Sanya Mansoor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.text:
The privacy issues over the company’s surveillance cameras have caused protests in schools all over the country

Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people.

Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. Since April, at least ten university campuses across seven states, have scrapped contracts with Flock. That includes Cornell University, Penn State University, Elgin Community College, Emory University, Binghamton University, Kent State University and the University of Wisconsin’s Madison, Milwaukee and Oshkosh branches. Last week, the University of Buffalo announced an indefinite pause on its plans for a 60-day pilot program.

Elgin Community College tried, unsuccessfully, to cancel its Flock contract before it expired in April. School officials said they resorted to placing black plastic trash bags over the cameras “out of an abundance of caution” until the company removed the cameras after the agreement lapsed.

A few schools – Appalachian State University and the University of North Carolina’s (UNC) Charlotte and Chapel Hill campuses – have kept Flock contracts but restricted national access to the cameras’ records. UNC Charlotte made the change after local news outlet WBTV found that the Houston police department had searched the school’s Flock camera network more than any other agency between March and May 2026: a total of 183,000 times.

Schools that haven’t yet restricted what agencies can access Flock or dropped contracts are feeling the pressure. At the University of Florida and Florida State University, activists have turned to protests, online campaigns and petitions to express their discontent. The state of Florida recently banned Flock cameras and other license plate readers from its highways, but those laws don’t extend to private property or local rights-of-way.

The uproar on campuses reflects a broader uprising. This year, dozens of cities have deactivated, canceled or rejected Flock contracts. Vigilantes have damaged and destroyed the devices to the delight of their social media followers.

Flock Safety said in an emailed statement that its cameras help solve crimes and increase public safety by giving campus police credible leads. The company highlighted cases in which local law enforcement said Flock cameras helped track down a shooter at Brown University, arrest a person who shot a gun in the parking lot of a high school in Colorado and find a suspect in an investigation about more than $100,000 in stolen equipment from an on-campus construction site at UNC Charlotte.

“We understand that schools and universities must evaluate public safety technology, and we respect each institution’s authority to make those decisions, but taking away these tools could impact the safety of students,” the company said in an emailed statement.

Flock also denies that its cameras fuel mass surveillance and that it partners with federal immigration authorities, although news reports have documented indirect ways that local police have used the network to help US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. This summer, Flock also introduced updated policies around auditing, as well as data retention and sharing.

Student protesters are confronting many of the same challenges organizers in cities that have dropped Flock have faced: most commonly, a pivot to license plate readers from other vendors.

Stanford is already installing replacement automatic license plate recognition (ALPRs) from the Canadian company, Genetec. Nguyen, the Stanford student, still counts the move away from Flock as a win but says there’s still work to be done, as student organizers’ goal is “to prevent any possibility of mass surveillance on campus”. She’s speaking with the university’s transportation department to push for transparency around who can access the data captured by the cameras.

On the opposite coast, in New York state, Binghamton University has announced a switch to Axon, an even larger police tech company, after dropping Flock. Claims of police abuse have not dogged Axon’s cameras in the same way as Flock’s, although many activists still have data privacy concerns.

Hatim Husainy, a junior at Binghamton who canvassed in dining halls to get more supporters for a petition to drop Flock, said removing the company was a “huge win” but added that students’ goals are to push the university to end the use of any ALPRs.

At UW-Madison, Bradley Keenan, who protested Flock on campus, has said the devices are “a signal from the police and university that everybody is under suspicion”. But the sophomore didn’t celebrate when he learned that his university had dropped its contract with the company because UW-Madison indicated that it would be immediately looking for alternatives.

Keenan said organizers have since updated their demands to push the university not to pursue a contract with any ALPR company.

Stanford did not respond to a request for comment but has said that Genetec, a Canadian company, will continue to store data on its internal servers for 30 days and that the new system is “designed for use within a single institution”. UW-Madison did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Binghamton University, Ryan Yarosh, said in an emailed statement that school officials have met with concerned faculty and students, and respects their “right to express their concerns”.

High schoolers are getting in on Flock activism, too.

In northern Colorado, high school senior Gabe Sayer and a friend started a petition to ban Flock cameras in the city of Loveland, and took particular issue with devices placed outside three high schools, including his own. Gabe said he first learned about Flock last year in his government class when discussing constitutional rights. His research led him to believe that the network is a dragnet that violates the fourth amendment. Sayer has been tabling outside a local grocery store to get signatures on the petition and meeting city councillors to share his views on Flock cameras.

In Georgia, two seniors at Alpharetta high school created a petition to remove Flock cameras from their campus. Aditya Manchanda and Henry Jones, who are part of their school’s Young Democratic Socialists of America chapter, made a video on TikTok about ALPRs and their petition attracted local news coverage.

“Schools should be a safe place, and we don’t feel safe,” Aditya said. “We feel our privacy being violated with the presence of these cameras.”

After gathering signatures, the duo emailed the school’s principal. “I know he wasn’t too pleased because we got media attention, and that’s not a great look,” Aditya said. The principal referred the boys to Fulton county school board members. Their emails have so far gone unanswered, so they’re planning to show up to an upcoming board meeting to relay their concerns.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.summary: At least ten university campuses across seven states have scrapped contracts with Flock. High schoolers are getting in on Flock activism, too. Two Georgia seniors created a petition to ban Flock cameras in the city of Loveland.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Kenyan building collapse near Nairobi kills six people
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The collapse of an unfinished eight-storey building in Kenya has killed six people.

The structure fell on Friday morning in Syokimau on the outskirts of Nairobi. Coming on the heels of a similar recent incident in the capital, the accident has revived calls for stronger safety oversight.

Construction workers were reportedly at the site when the building’s uppermost concrete slab gave way, bringing down part of the structure, according to a preliminary report from Nairobi City County’s emergency team. The report did not establish why the slab failed.

The Kenya Red Cross initially reported that three people had been rescued and one person was reported missing. TV reports later said that five people had been pulled alive from the rubble and taken to hospital.

The emergency report said the number of workers present when the building fell had not been confirmed, leaving open the possibility that others were trapped.

Firefighters and specialist rescue teams were continuing to search for survivors.

Patrick Makau, a member of Kenya’s parliament representing Mavoko, the constituency that includes Syokimau, urged rescue agencies in a post on social media to act quickly.

“Every second counts,” he wrote, offering condolences to the victims’ families.

The accident follows a similar deadly building collapse in the city on October 23, which killed eight people. The twin disasters have prompted calls for tougher construction oversight.

The Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, a state research body, has identified poor workmanship, inadequate supervision, substandard materials and faulty designs as wider causes of building collapses.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Construction workers were reportedly at the site when the building's uppermost concrete slab gave way. The accident has revived calls for stronger safety oversight.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: France slams Israel’s ‘demagogic’ ban on left-wing leader Melenchon
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Paris has condemned Israel’s “demagogic decision” to bar French opposition figure Jean-Luc Melenchon from entering the country.

Late on Thursday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot slammed Israel’s earlier announcement that Melenchon, leader of the France Unbowed party (La France Insoumise), was not welcome.

Israel barred the party’s parliamentary group chair Mathilde Panot, alongside Melenchon, due to the “extreme anti-Israel stance” of the party and “outrageous statements” made by its leaders.

“This demagogic decision, coming from a government that has repeatedly violated international law, plays into the hands of those who, like La France Insoumise, make a living out of exploiting the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” Barrot, who belongs to the centrist ruling coalition, wrote on social media.

“France will continue tirelessly to work toward a two-state solution and peaceful coexistence between the Israeli and Palestinian peoples,” the minister added.

Israel accused Melenchon and Panot of making “blood libel” statements against Israel.

At the weekend, Melenchon had said that if he was victorious in the upcoming presidential election in April 2027, he would order French ships to escort flotillas taking aid to Gaza.

The Israeli military has previously raided such fleets and detained activists.

“Israel will respond firmly to those who seek to harm it and will not allow individuals who act against Israel and incite against its citizens to enter the country,” a statement from the Israeli Foreign Ministry said.

Speaking to French radio, Melenchon said that he had been “banned from entering a territory I did not ask to enter”.

The Israeli move came after France barred a prominent Israeli settler last week.

Yossi Dagan, a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, who heads one of six Israeli regional councils in the occupied West Bank, was denied permission to enter France after landing at Charles de Gaulle International Airport.

France’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that Dagan was barred “due to his active role in implementing Israel’s settlement policy,” which violates international law.

France was one of several European countries this year to step up restrictions on Israeli settlers, spurring outrage from Israeli officials.

Earlier this year, France banned far-right Israeli ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who are both members of Netanyahu’s cabinet and have encouraged accelerated settlement in the West Bank and pogroms targeting Palestinians.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Mauricio Pochettino announced as new Manchester United manager
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Manasi Pathak
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Manchester United have appointed ⁠⁠Mauricio Pochettino as the new manager to replace the ⁠sacked Michael Carrick, as the Premier League ⁠giants sit in the relegation zone after their worst start to a league ‌campaign in 40 years.

Pochettino will lead the United States national team in their upcoming matches against Haiti before joining ⁠Man United, US ⁠Soccer said on Friday.

“The club has reached an agreement with the US ⁠Soccer Federation for Mauricio and ⁠his staff to ⁠be released after the conclusion of their responsibilities with the ‌US Men’s National Team,” United said in a ‌statement.

Pochettino, a former Chelsea, Paris Saint-Germain, Tottenham Hotspur and Southampton manager, was the favourite for the managerial role at Old Trafford ever since rumours about Carrick’s departure hit the headlines.

The 54-year-old arrives at Old ⁠Trafford with United having earned one win and eight points from 10 Premier League games. They are 18th in the standings, one point above bottom side Crystal Palace.

United have won only three of their 15 matches across all competitions.

Pochettino, who returns to club football, had been in charge of the USA national team since 2024, and under him, the cohosts reached the round of 16 at the 2026 FIFA World Cup in North America.

“The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honours of my career,” Pochettino said in a statement.

British media reported United would have to pay substantial compensation to release Pochettino from his US Soccer contract, which had been due to run ⁠until the 2030 World Cup.

Pochettino becomes the eighth permanent man in charge at Man United since Sir Alex Ferguson’s departure in May 2013 after more than 26 years in the job.

United said in their statement that their new manager is known for “his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players”.

Pochettino took charge of Spurs from 2014 to 2019, leading the North London club to the Champions League final in the season before he was sacked.

He guided Spurs to the League Cup final in his first full season and to a runners-up finish in the Premier League in 2017.

Pochettino also spent a season at French giants PSG, leading them to the Ligue 1 title that year, and later guided Chelsea to a League Cup runner-up finish in 2023-2024.

He inherits a Man United squad assembled at considerable expense ⁠but lacking confidence and identity, with supporters booing the players off the pitch after the Bournemouth defeat.

United’s hierarchy, which has often attracted the fans’ criticism, will hope his experience can help stabilise one of football’s most scrutinised clubs.

Pochettino’s first assignment at his new club will be a trip to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool in the league on November 22.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Manchester United have appointed Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager. The 54-year-old will lead the United States national team in their upcoming matches against Haiti. Pochettinos was the favourite for the managerial role ever since Michael Carrick's departure.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Why is Ukraine attacking Russian warships in the Baltic Sea amid talks?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Nils Adler
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Finland’s military says it detected “a strike” on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, as Ukraine sent waves of drones towards Russia’s northwestern Leningrad region.

The strike came as Russian and Ukrainian delegations met in Abu Dhabi for their first United States-brokered talks since February.

It was a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea.

So why is Ukraine taking the war to the Baltic, and why now? Here’s what we know:

“The Finnish Defence Forces detected… a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation,” a military spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in an emailed statement.

The spokesperson said Finland was not under any immediate military threat, but declined to say where or when the incident happened, or how it had been detected.

It was not immediately clear whether there were any casualties. Estonian media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship that later returned to St Petersburg.

On Wednesday, drones also caused a fire in the Russian port area of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers, regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania told citizens to take shelter as drones strayed into their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response.

The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members, that extends east to St Petersburg. Ust-Luga, on its southern shore, is a key export outlet for Russian oil and grain.

Several Ukrainian drones deployed towards the Leningrad region have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic states, raising fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia.

Finland’s Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen said Helsinki had raised the strike with Kyiv.

“We have told the Ukrainians this time, and a little earlier too, how sensitive this narrow stretch of the Gulf of Finland, right between us and Estonia, is in terms of environmental safety and the safety of civilian shipping,” he said, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle.

But he said the spillover effects in the surrounding region stem from Ukraine’s defensive fight and assured the public the Baltic Sea around Finland was still safe.

“You can still cruise with peace of mind,” he said.

Ilya Timtchenko, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera the strike was thought to be the first by Ukrainian forces on a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic used by civilian traffic.

“Ukraine and its European allies are showing that they are unified in their approach to fighting off the Russian threat,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ukraine’s Security Service said it attacked the Buyan-M-class small missile ship, Naro-Fominsk, as part of a special operation, according to Yle.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff said the strike on Ust-Luga had damaged five fuel tanks.

“According to preliminary information, as a result of drone strikes on the port’s oil infrastructure, the tank network suffered the most damage,” it reported on Telegram.

On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Ireland and praised their mediation efforts.

Russia, Ukraine and the US held two days of talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. The last such talks took place in February this year.

The talks produced no breakthrough, apart from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners. Russia’s state-run TASS news agency said the exchange should happen in two to three weeks.

Territory remains the main sticking point.

Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to control all of Ukraine’s Donbas region.

Moscow’s demands reach beyond Ukraine as well, focusing also on the expansion of NATO.

Russian negotiators proposed in Abu Dhabi that Finland, which joined the alliance in 2023, leave NATO and that the alliance be barred from having military bases in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the German newspaper Bild reported on Friday.

The informal proposals, shared with European representatives, also called for arrangements to guarantee freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea, Bild reported.

On Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow, where the two sides agreed to continue the talks, before the envoys met Zelenskyy in Ireland.

To keep up the pressure on Moscow.

“Kyiv continues to demonstrate two points simultaneously: That it is willing to negotiate and that it has a position of strength,” Timtchenko said. “In parallel with any peace talks, Ukraine will likely continue to strike Russia’s military and the sources of funding for Russia’s war machine.”

Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries, ports, and energy infrastructure to raise the economic cost of Moscow’s war effort.

But the strikes have drawn criticism from Washington. Trump has blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy infrastructure for rising diesel prices, and last month he waived sanctions on Russia that Congress had overwhelmingly approved.

Timtchenko said the strikes still gave Kyiv leverage. “Long-range strikes considerably strengthen Ukraine’s hand at the negotiating table, which is why Russian officials keep bringing them up,” he said.

Russia has not commented publicly on the reported strike on its warship.

Governor Drozdenko said 150 drones were shot down over the Leningrad region during Wednesday’s attack, which also cut off a power station.

“Moscow might voice harsh rhetoric and try to blame the Ukrainians for undermining the peace talks,” Timtchenko said. “However, this is nothing new, since Russia has done this numerous times before.

“Despite Moscow’s pretence of seeking an end to the war, Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s military, critical infrastructure, and civilians,” he added.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Finland says it detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland. The strike came as Ukraine sent waves of drones towards Russia's Leningrad region. Russia has done this numerous times before, Timtchenko says.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Pakistan military reports it killed 74 ‘terrorists’ during raids
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Pakistan’s army has reported that it has killed 74 armed fighters in multiple raids in areas along the country’s borders with Afghanistan.

Thirty-one “terrorists” have been killed in the southwestern Balochistan province since November 3, with multiple weapons, explosives and ammunition recovered, the military’s news division said in a statement posted on social media on Friday.

Balochistan is the site of an armed rebellion waged by the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), which seeks independence from Pakistan for the region.

Another 35 fighters were killed in the past two days during separate raids on Mir Ali, while eight were killed in Orakzai, and weapons were recovered, the force added in an update.

Both districts are in the northern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where the Pakistan Taliban, known as the TTP, and several other armed groups are based.

Islamabad accuses India and Afghanistan of backing the armed groups, although Delhi and Kabul deny involvement.

“The security forces’ continued successes in the war against terrorism reflect national resolve and professional capabilities,” President Asif Ali Zardari said in a statement. “Operations must continue against externally sponsored terrorist elements seeking to undermine Pakistan’s security.”

The army identified the fighters as “Khawarij”, a term it uses to refer to fighters it says are backed by Afghanistan, including the TTP.

Although separate, the TTP is allied with the Afghan Taliban, which took power in 2021.

Pakistani authorities believe the group operates from areas on Afghanistan’s side of the border and is responsible for increased attacks on Pakistani territory in recent years.

The issue has strained relations between Islamabad and Kabul and led to armed confrontations resulting in civilian deaths.

At least 11 policemen were killed, and another 12 were wounded after alleged TTP fighters ambushed a convoy in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Thursday, authorities said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: UN watchdog calls on Iran to reopen nuclear facilities to inspection
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The United Nations nuclear watchdog has urged Iran to allow it to resume inspections of its nuclear facilities.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called for Tehran to restore access for its inspectors in a report circulated by the watchdog among member states on Friday, insisting the move is essential to carry out its remit to monitor the Iranian nuclear programme.

Iran has allowed only very limited IAEA inspections since the United States and Israel launched attacks on the country’s nuclear facilities in June 2025. The report said Tehran had told the organisation that it was not possible to allow the inspections to continue amid the current security situation.

The IAEA said the lack of information about Iran’s atomic sites and nuclear material is “a matter of proliferation concern” that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency,” The Associated Press news agency reported.

The watchdog noted that it is “fully prepared to resume its safeguards activities in Iran at short notice”.

The report expressed particular concern about an underground uranium-enrichment plant near Isfahan in central Iran, according to the Reuters news agency.

Tehran declared the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant in 2025 but has not permitted the IAEA access to inspect the facility.

Inspectors still do not know the plant’s precise location, whether it holds nuclear material, or its status under international monitoring rules. The report did not establish that uranium enrichment is taking place there.

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi urged Iran to consider limited technical measures that could make inspection visits possible and help restore routine monitoring, the AFP news agency said.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news conference in Tehran on Monday that Iran remained committed to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which seeks to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.

But he blamed US and Israeli attacks for limiting cooperation with the IAEA. Since the bombing of the nuclear facilities last year, the watchdog has been unable to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of near-weapons-grade uranium, the report noted.

The IAEA withdrew its inspectors for safety reasons, and Iran later passed a law suspending cooperation with it.

The IAEA’s inspections are intended to verify that nuclear material is not diverted towards weapons. Without direct access to sites such as Isfahan, the agency cannot independently establish what is happening at those facilities.

However, the report notes that Iran told the IAEA this month that discussion on resuming inspections in the country cannot resume amid “persistent, explicit, and public threats by the President of the United States of America … to commit further acts of armed aggression”.

Iran said that the issue would not be resolved “until the root causes of the present situation are addressed and the essential requirements for normal safeguards implementation are restored,” the report added.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.title: Live: Microsoft struggles to restore services as outage hits global users
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.author: Nils Adler,Heba Habib
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.text:
Andrew Cullen, AI and cybersecurity consultant at EthiCan, told Al Jazeera that Microsoft likely released a patch to make a change to its systems, and “it hasn’t worked as they expected”.

Here are the latest developments:

Walter Pasquarelli, a strategy adviser to governments on AI and affiliated researcher at the University of Cambridge, says the outage shows how dependent governments and businesses have become on a few centralised platforms.

“What we do know so far is that this is first and foremost a communication risk,” Pasquarelli told Al Jazeera. “It’s not just workers across businesses who cannot get access to it, but there’s lots of government services and lots of government infrastructure that actually relies on that.”

He said the evidence so far pointed to a technical failure rather than a cyberattack, but that the cause was not yet clear. “Even without hackers, even without an AI overload, these things can still happen,” he said.

Pasquarelli said the outage should lead organisations to rethink their exposure without abandoning digital tools. “I don’t think that we’re now all going to go offline again. I think that that’s completely utopian,” he said. “But there is a realisation that fundamentally these outages can happen to anyone at any time.”

Microsoft has said its 365 services and email delivery are improving across Europe, according to the company’s Service Health Status page.

Services are also improving in North America, the company said, adding that “some users may still experience intermittent issues”.

It said that Japan “remains comparatively more stable”.

Germany expects an outage affecting ⁠Microsoft services ⁠to have a significant impact on ‌German businesses, a Digital Ministry spokesperson said on ⁠Friday.

There have been ⁠no reports of ⁠major outages ⁠in ⁠Germany’s federal administration, though, the ‌spokesperson added.

The Philippine Supreme Court says the global Microsoft outage has affected the judiciary’s email and online systems, warning that responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed.

In a post on X, the court said the outage had hit the Philippine Judiciary platform, including Microsoft Outlook.

“The Supreme Court is working closely with Microsoft to restore all affected PJ365 services and will provide updates as necessary,” it said.

As Microsoft engineers work to repair its systems and companies and institutions worldwide scramble to find workarounds, social media has been filled with memes and light-hearted observations about the outages.

Many centre on the idea that being offline, or unable to access work emails, could be a welcome break from today’s fast-paced, internet-driven world.

Jurors at a Manchester trial were sent home early, and told the Microsoft global outage had caused “all sorts of delays”.

They were due to hear evidence in the northern English city in the ongoing case of nine men accused of various offences in connection with the drugging and raping of a woman by her husband.

Judge Maurice Greene told them: “What we are learning is the dangers of our [reliance] on computer systems and platforms, and so on.

“Many institutions rely on Microsoft 365 as do the court and various institutions connected to the court, so there have all been sort of delays because of this.

“I would say sorry but it’s not my fault … It may be Mr Gates’s fault but I don’t think he is going to come and apologise.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.summary: Microsoft outage has affected the Philippine Supreme Court's email and online systems. The outage has also affected the Philippines Supreme Court. The company says its 365 services and email delivery are improving across Europe.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Henry and Young shine as New Zealand thrash India by 244 runs
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Matt Henry took six wickets and Will Young struck a century as New Zealand thrashed a ragged India by 244 runs in the fourth ODI at Mount Maunganui on Friday.

Henry removed Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer, all without scoring, in the first over of India’s chase to tear the top order apart. The visitors needed a massive 334 for victory.

New Zealand made 333 all out in the last over after being asked to bat, with Young punishing two simple drops by Indian fielders to bring up his fifth ODI hundred.

India never stood a chance of chasing the total after Henry’s heavenly opening over.

Rohit edged his first ball to slip, Kohli was bowled facing his fourth ball, and then Iyer was pegged on his back leg to fall lbw.

India’s rebuild never happened, with Ishan Kishan top-scoring with just 27 as India were rolled for 89.

Henry ended with 6-27 and Matthew Fisher took 3-31.

New Zealand’s imposing total came off the back of Young’s 125 from 108 balls, including 14 fours and four sixes.

Young and Tim Seifert combined for an 85-run opening partnership.

While Young rode his early luck – dropped twice in two balls when on five in the second over, first by slip Rohit and then by wicketkeeper Kishan – Seifert played the aggressor with a brisk 39-ball 50.

When Seifert fell for 58, Nick Kelly and Dean Foxcroft soon followed, playing reckless shots.

Young found better support in Finn Allen, the pair putting on 90 runs in just 65 balls as they seized on wayward Indian bowling.

Young’s first 50 came from 49 balls, and his second from just 39 balls as he hit regular boundaries through the middle overs.

Allen made 41 from 30 deliveries, including five fours and two sixes.

Axar Patel took 2-39 from 10 overs as India pulled the innings back late, while Auqib Nabi had 2-59 and Gurnoor Brar 2-69.

New Zealand trail India 2-1 and can no longer win the five-match series, but they can avoid defeat if they ⁠win the final match at the same venue on Sunday. The third match was abandoned due to rain.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Why is Trump saying ‘no deal necessary’ with Iran as he sidelines JD Vance?
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.author: Yashraj Sharma
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Just hours before Iran claimed it hit the United States military’s early warning radar system in Bahrain early on Friday, US President Donald Trump said he had told his country’s lead negotiator, Vice President JD Vance, that, “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”

Instead, Trump said, he has told Vance to focus on unearthing what the president says is corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled cities and states – after Democrats stunningly took over Congress in the midterm elections.

Vance is a known critic of the US-Israeli war on Iran. He has blamed Trump’s military strikes on Iran and the subsequent energy crisis and inflation in the US for the Republicans’ losses in Congress.

Meanwhile, several commercial vessels trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz have hit naval mines, or were struck by the Iranian military, over the past week – but Trump continues to claim that Washington controls the critical waterway nonetheless.

So, where is the war headed – and is Vance being sidelined by Trump?

Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that he had asked Vice President Vance “to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he added. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

The Trump administration has appeared increasingly divided on the foregoing arc of war on Iran since the midterm losses.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that Washington’s economic pressure campaign against Iran is proving effective, so a resumption of large-scale military operations is unnecessary.

“The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added.

Trump has given mixed messages about his plans for the war. Despite threatening that he might “destroy” Iran last week, this week Trump has said that further strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely”.

Vance favours a deal with Iran, which Trump believes is not possible currently.

Vance led the US negotiations in April in Islamabad, where he helped secure the June memorandum of understanding with Iran. That quickly collapsed over glaring gaps in each side’s understanding of what had been agreed, however – particularly in reference to control of the Strait of Hormuz.

The US vice president also led direct talks with Iran in Switzerland and is part of renewed diplomatic efforts, engaging Qatari and Pakistani mediators and seeking continued negotiations with Iranian officials.

On November 4, following sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections, Vance publicly questioned whether the war had been worth the political and economic costs. In a post on X, he wrote: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” endorsing diplomatic resolution as sound advice.

He added: “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”

Political analysts say Vance’s rather blunt assessment is also an effort to distance himself from Trump’s war on Iran, when the president is facing his all-time low career approval ratings.

On June 17, speaking at the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France – when both parties had just signed the Islamabad MoU – Trump told reporters: “This way, if it works out, I’m going to take the credit. If it doesn’t work out, I’m blaming JD. You better be careful, JD.”

The next day, Vance told reporters he believed the president was “joking”.

On Friday morning, Tehran said it had attacked and destroyed an early-warning radar system belonging to the US military in Bahrain, in what it said was retaliation for an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran’s port city of Sirik.

Meanwhile, on Thursday, Trump said Washington’s allies in the Middle East had asked him to hold off on renewed large-scale attacks against Iran. He added that the US could destroy Iran’s energy infrastructure, bridges and manufacturing facilities within three days, if it wanted to.

“Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while,” he said at White House, adding that Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain preferred the current approach.

Asked whether he would have launched further attacks without those requests, Trump replied: “Yes, I would.”

Though Trump acknowledged that rising fuel prices caused by the war contributed to the Republicans’ defeat in the midterm elections, he defended his decision to attack Iran.

Meanwhile, Brigadier General Ali Reza Belaili, an adviser to the aerospace force of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said an order by Iran’s supreme leader to strike “enemies” without geographical limits will be implemented “at the appropriate time”.

Iran’s Mehr news agency quoted him saying that “the more Americans persist, the more they will sink into this swamp they created themselves”.

This week, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator, told Al Jazeera that the Strait of Hormuz will “never return” to its status before the US-Israel war on Iran. That was when all commercial shipping was able to pass through the strait freely without having to pay tolls.

Iran in effect closed the strait, through which one-fifth of global oil supplies were shipped in peacetime, in early March following the start of US-Israeli strikes. That sent global energy markets into turmoil.

Ghalibaf said Tehran has sent a clear proposal for a ceasefire and for the reopening of the strait to Washington via Qatari mediators, laying out seven conditions, and added that Iran is now waiting for an official response from the US.

“The ball is now in the American court,” he said.

Iran’s conditions include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.

The US has previously refused to agree to these demands without an agreement on Iran’s nuclear programme in place first. Iran wants to negotiate that separately.

Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, an associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the Chatham House think tank, told Al Jazeera: “We are still in a situation which is ‘no war, no peace’, and it’s unlikely to move for the time being.

“Major strikes are unlikely to happen in the imminent days, but things are likely to shift one way or the other in the next couple of weeks,” she said. “The Gulf countries are not necessarily endorsing this as a new normal, even if they prefer this to the prospect of a renewed war.”

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Ghalibaf said this week that “there are no ‘free waters’ [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply” to the Strait of Hormuz. The strait does, in fact, run solely through the territorial waters of Iran and Oman.

“The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it,” he added, reiterating Iran’s position that it is tightly controlling the waterway.

Tehran has said that multiple “offending” vessels – which it says have used an “illegal” route, referring to the southern corridor of the strait – have caught fire during attempts to transit the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has previously told approved ships to use a northern route which passes closer to its own coastline.

At least 12 tankers have been hit in the past 12 days, according to Iran.

The US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) says it has been “working round the clock” to keep the strait open.

On Wednesday, CENTCOM claimed that at least 4,000 ships had crossed the waterway with the US military’s assistance, carrying more than 1.7 billion barrels of crude oil.

However, all maritime agencies continue to advise against travelling through the strait, and insurers have raised prices sharply for such journeys, or are refusing cover at all.
