https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/.title: Specialized’s Tarmac SL9 S-Level is built to wreck your Zone 2 ride
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/.author: Eric Bangeman
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/.text:
Specialized’s second-fastest bike may be the smart buy.

I love a good Zone 2 ride. There’s nothing like getting on the bike, settling into a groove, and letting the miles (and hours) flow by. But sometimes when I hopped on the Specialized Tarmac SL9 S-Level, Zone 2 would turn into a tempo ride. It was like having a little imp—the stereotype dressed in red with the pitchfork—on my left shoulder whispering into my ear: “Go fast. This bike was built to go fast. Speed is good. You can do a Zone 2 ride tomorrow.” Normally, I’d count on the good imp—the dude with the harp and wings—on my right shoulder to restrain these urges. But the Tarmac is so seductive that he would just shrug and say “he’s got a point.” And in a moment of weakness, I would drop the hammer and head into the red, just because the SL9 makes that so rewarding.

The Tarmac SL9 is Specialized’s aero road bike, with the S-Level sitting just below the S-Works in Specialized’s top tier of carbon, aero road bikes, where it replaced the Tarmac SL8 Pro. After it got an update this year, I spent several weeks riding it, putting nearly 1,000 miles on it

Specialized offers the Tarmac SL9 in four models, all available with SRAM and Shimano drivetrains (Ars tested the SRAM version). Notably, you don’t need to buy the top-of-the-line bike to get the top-of-the-line groupset. Here’s the breakdown of the Tarmac SL9 lineup (note that the Shimano versions of the Expert is 20 g lighter and Comp is 70 grams heavier than the SRAM versions):

The $10,500 S-Level offers the top-of-the-line SRAM Red groupset and integrated cockpit, just like the $14,000 S-Works. But the frameset, wheelset, and saddle differ. The major difference is the frame: the S-Level gets the same carbon-fiber FACT 10r frame as the Expert and Comp. At 822 g for a 56 cm frame, the FACT 10r is 135 g heavier than the FACT 12r used on the S-Works. Despite the weight difference, Specialized says the FACT 10r offers the same stiffness and comfort characteristics as its lighter sibling. Along with the frame, different wheelsets and saddles make the S-Level 500 g heavier than the S-Works. With bottle cages, a Garmin mount, and my preferred Shimano XTR XC PD-M9200 MTB pedals, the S-Level I tested weighed in at 7.98 kg. By way of comparison, my own road bike—a Gen 8 Trek Madone—weighs in at 7.71 kg.

I rode the S-Level all around the Chicago suburbs as well as in central Illinois. Unlike the Diverge 4 Pro, I wasn’t able to test its climbing ability in the Rocky Mountains. All we’ve got in most of Illinois are short, punchy climbs … and a lot of long flats. I rode The S-Level on everything from freshly laid asphalt to freshly laid chipseal, including a couple of 60-mile-plus rides on the country roads downstate.

Visually, the S-Level is striking. The blue-on-white with gray striping is one of Specialized’s better-looking colorways. And it looks aerodynamic. Indeed, Specialized says the Tarmac SL9 is the most aerodynamic road bike it has ever made. Notable changes from the previous-generation Tarmac SL8 to SL9 involved tweaking the head tube, rerouting the rear hydraulic brake hose to accommodate the narrower head tube, and moving to a dropped-down tube for improved aerodynamics. But the most visually striking change is the Win Fin. As the seat tube rises from the bottom bracket, it deviates from the vertical to follow the curve of the wheel as it approaches the seat stays. When riding with just a single water bottle on the downtube—common in pro races where a full bottle is just a team car away—Specialized claims Win Fin saves riders half a watt.

The S-Level I tested came with Specialized’s 30 mm Specialized Cotton TLR tires—used by Red Bull-BORA-hansgrohe on the UCI World Tour—in a tubeless setup. According to Bicycle Rolling Resistance, the Cotton TLR outperforms the much-loved Continental GP 5000 S TR tires when it comes to rolling resistance (at 28 mm). Using Silca’s tire pressure calculator, I rode with the tires inflated to 73 psi in the front and 75 psi in the rear, a departure from the 62/64 setting on my 32 mm Contis—and there is a slight, but noticeable difference in ride comfort between the S-Level and my own road bike. Mounted on the Roval Rapide CL III carbon wheels with 21 mm internal width, the Cotton TLR tires measured 30.2 mm wide (my 32 mm Contis are a hair over 33 mm).

On every surface shy of brand-new chipseal, the Tarmac felt comfortable and balanced, with the bike absorbing some of the punishment meted out by uneven pavement. Fresh chipseal is another matter entirely, as it feels more like gravel, which felt jarring on the SL9 S-Level. What was particularly impressive about the SL9 is how great it feels on long rides. Some manufacturers are skilled at building aero bikes that feel great on hours-long rides, and the Tarmac is just as good as the Trek Madone SLR 9 AXS Gen 8 I reviewed in this regard.

When you’re ready to drop the hammer, the S-Level is your willing accomplice. It’s twitchy in all of the good ways, with instantaneous response to the rider’s effort. The SRAM Red AXS groupset makes shifting buttery smooth (and the bonus buttons on the brake hoods allow the rider to change screens on the bike computer without releasing the brake hoods), and the drivetrain (50t/37t chainrings and a 10t-36t cassette) offers gear ratios for every type of terrain.

The first few seconds of a climb on the Tarmac SL9 S-Level feel like they come for free. Whether I stayed seated or cranked out watts in an upright position, there was no lag or flex as the bike snapped forward. Descents were amazing, and cornering on the S-Level is sublime—I felt balanced and in control at all times.

There are a few nits to pick. The reach to the brakes in the drops felt excessive on my first couple of rides, and I had to adjust them slightly to brake easily on descents. Also, I would prefer shorter cranks on the Tarmac. The trend among professional riders has been toward shorter cranks because it makes holding an aero position easier and reduces hip and knee flexion. To its credit, Specialized reduced the crank length from 172.5 mm on the 56 cm SL8 to 170 mm on the same-sized SL9, but I run 165 mm cranks on my road bikes and noticed the difference on the S-Level. One demographic that buys expensive road bikes is middle-aged dudes with empty nests and disposable incomes, and they are the ones most likely to appreciate shorter cranks.

The 3D-printed Power Pro Mirror is a fine saddle, but there’s a reason I ride with a Specialized S-Works Power with Mirror on my Trek—it’s more comfortable and offers noticeably more padding around the cutout. And if I owned the S-Level, I’d move to 32 mm tires as soon as I wore out the 30s for better compliance.

Specialized brags that the Tarmac SL9 S-Works is the fastest bike ever made, and it claims the S-Level is the second-fastest bike ever made. I can’t speak to that claim, but the SL9 S-Level checks all of the boxes for an aerodynamic road bike. It’s lightweight, it’s fast, it’s responsive, and it’s great on rollers and punchy climbs. And it’s nice to get a SRAM Red groupset without springing for the absolute top-of-the-line model. $10,500 is a hefty sum for a road bike, but I’d be a lot more willing to forego the weight savings from the lighter components (frame, wheels, seatpost, bottom bracket, and bearings) of the S-Works—and spend $3,500 less. The real selling point, though, is how often it made me want to go harder just for the fun of it. That little imp has a point: Zone 2 can wait until tomorrow.

The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers.

Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.

Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think.

Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China.

The act is drawing renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair. Find out what the proposed tracking measures would involve.

https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.author: Jessica Hamzelou
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.text:
People with experimental brain implants are pushing for more recognition and respect.

Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”

Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.

He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it.

The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough.

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”

In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition—an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.

The guidelines, published on Tuesday, lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”

As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.

The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants.

Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data. Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.

The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.

“It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”

The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago, he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.)

Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.

Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will—an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.

Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.

Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low. The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference.

“This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”

https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.author: Aaron Zamost
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.text:
Tech executives traded their reputations as visionaries for short-term political gain.

The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda.

Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers, the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs.

For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.

What were they thinking?

The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else.

In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die.

Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “violence and death to our enemies” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”?

I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand.

There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “masculine energy,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats.

In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.”

“Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida, they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones.

Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next.

Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

https://www.zdnet.com/tech/essentials-an.title: Attention, Android power users: This app unlocks 30+ features you won’t find in Settings
https://www.zdnet.com/tech/essentials-an.author: Jack Wallen
https://www.zdnet.com/tech/essentials-an.text:
Tech
>
Services & Software
>
Operating Systems
>
Mobile OS
>
Android

Is Android Settings not delivering enough power? The Essentials app features 30+ mods and tweaks - but you won't find it in the Play Store

November 12, 2026, 1:15 pm ET

Most Android owners know of the Settings app, which gives them all the power Google assumes they need. Then there’s the Developer Options feature that can be enabled to give users even more power.

Also: I turned an old Android phone into a server for my LAN

If that’s not enough, there’s now Essentials, a power-user’s toolbox that includes 30+ mods and tweaks for things like button remapping, app freezing, Google Maps battery saving modes, sound and haptics, wallpaper, widgets, status bar icon customization, edge lighting, flashlight pulsing, notification management, Always-On Display, and more.

The only requirement for most Essentials features is Android 8 or newer. There are a handful of advanced features that require shell providers like Shizuku or even root access, but the majority of features most users will want to enable have no requirements beyond the minimum.

Essentials isn’t found on the Google Play Store. Instead, Essentials must be sideloaded from the APK available on its official GitHub Repository. Keep in mind that Google has changed the way apps are sideloaded.

Also: How to sideload Android apps on your phone now

Make sure you understand the new sideloading process before you proceed. You’ll also need to change some permissions, depending on the feature you want to use. For example, to change lock screen shortcuts, you have to enable it in Accessibility Services.

As well, you have to enable restricted settings, which is done with Settings > Apps > See all X apps > Essentials. On that page, tap the three-dot menu and then tap “Allow restricted settings.”

Without that feature enabled, Essentials will be hamstrung by Android’s permissions system.

Essentials is fairly simple to use. You open the app, search for the feature you want to enable, and enable it. One thing you’ll discover is that you have to enable a lot of permissions for Essentials. It seems every time I go to enable or customize a feature, I have to grant yet another permission. I know it sounds like a hassle, but given the extra power you gain, it’s worth it.

Also: How to turn on Android’s Private DNS mode

Let me walk you through a feature found in Essentials you’ll wish were baked into Android. The feature is App Lock, which lets you require authentication for specific apps. This is a handy option, especially if someone gets ahold of your phone while it’s unlocked and tries to open certain apps you’d prefer to keep private (such as your banking app). To use this feature, you have to grant Essentials permission for Accessibility features, which you’ll be prompted to do when you go to enable it.

App Lock is found in Essentials > Security and Privacy. Once there, click the On/Off slider to enable App Lock, and you’ll be prompted to grant the necessary Essentials permission in Accessibility. After enabling the feature, tap it, and you’ll be prompted to authenticate with fingerprint, face, or password/PIN (whichever you have set up).

On the next page, tap “Select locked apps,” and you’ll be prompted to select the apps that require authentication to open. For instance, I want to make sure that Authy (my 2FA app of choice), my bank app, and Messages require authentication before they open. To do that, I tap the On/Off slider for those apps until they are in the On position. The next time I go to open any of those apps, I’ll be required to authenticate via the fingerprint sensor.

Also: This silent Android feature scans your photos for ‘sensitive content’

Another handy feature is found in Notifications and Alerts, where you can enable notification lighting, flashlight pulse, notification snoozing, and snooze system notifications. You can enable notification lighting and then select which apps it applies to. I enabled notification lighting for Messages and Phone, so I will never miss a message or call, even if my phone is on silent mode. You can also enable flashlight pulses, so it doesn’t matter if your phone’s screen is facing up or down — you’ll be notified of your messages.

That’s essentially how Essentials works. Do remember two things: you’ll be met with a barrage of permission requests, and some of those permissions aren’t possible unless you have root access or Shizuku (an open-source Android tool that lets third-party apps use system-level APIs and ADB (Android Debug Bridge) privileges without requiring you to fully root your device. Also, note that Shizuku requires you to enable wireless debugging to start the service. Once you install Shizuku (from the Play Store), you’ll find detailed (and lengthy) directions on how to do this.

Also: 5 ways I speed up your Android phone beyond clearing system cache

If you want considerably more control over your Android device, I highly recommend adding Essentials, as you won’t find most of these options in any other tool.

Essentials isn’t found on the Google Play Store

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/when-a.title: When an AI Agent Goes Wrong, Can You Stop It?
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/when-a.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/when-a.text:
Suppose an AI agent is asked to sort support tickets and look up account details. A ticket contains instructions that lead the agent to export records to an unfamiliar destination. The agent can make the request because its identity has access to the records and its connected tools allow the action.

That kind of scenario raises a response question: what does “stop the agent” actually mean? A team may be able to pause the model while a workflow, credential or existing connection remains active. Those pieces can require separate controls.

An October 2026 roundup from the OWASP GenAI Security Project describes evaluation agents reaching beyond their intended scope and recommends testing whether containment can revoke both credentials and network access. The roundup is a selected collection, not an exhaustive survey of incidents.

An AI agent is usually part of a larger system. A model may choose an action, but an orchestrator runs the workflow, an identity supplies access and tools or APIs carry out the work. Network rules determine where those tools can connect.

The details vary by deployment. In one system, disabling the agent may stop its current task. In another, queued jobs, retries or an already established session may continue. Revoking one credential may not invalidate a different token or connection. A model endpoint can be offline while a separate service continues to process work it already received.

That is why “kill switch” is best understood as a tested set of controls. It may need to stop active and queued runs, revoke the credentials they use, disable access to tools and restrict network paths. The right sequence depends on the architecture and the risk of interrupting other services.

An unexpected action does not automatically mean an agent has been compromised. A changed workflow, a software defect, a bad configuration or an unusual input can produce behavior that looks suspicious. Teams should investigate the signal and its context.

Signals that warrant a closer look include:

The agent’s own logs can help explain what it attempted, but they are only one source of evidence. Security teams should compare them with identity-provider, API, application and network records. A log entry showing an attempted action does not necessarily prove that the action succeeded.

Stop the active run and suspend its triggers, retries or queue where possible. If the agent shares infrastructure with other services, isolate the affected workflow rather than taking down unrelated systems, provided you can do so safely.

A prompt telling the agent to stop is not a containment control. The response should act through the system that runs the workflow.

Identify the credentials, sessions, grants and service identities associated with the run. Disable or revoke the access that is no longer trusted. If there is evidence that a secret was exposed, rotate it and review where else it is used.

Revocation behaves differently across systems. Some tokens expire quickly; others may remain valid until a session ends or a specific service invalidates them. Teams should confirm that the affected access is no longer usable instead of assuming that disabling the agent handled it.

Disable the tool or integration involved in the activity, or apply an access policy that blocks the agent from reaching the affected resource. If data may be moving outside the organization, network controls can limit further connections while the investigation continues.

This control should sit outside the agent’s own instructions. OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance recommends least-privilege tool access, explicit authorization for sensitive operations, audit trails and ways to interrupt or roll back agent operations.

Record the agent identity, run or session ID, timestamps, tool calls, authorization decisions and affected resources. Preserve relevant identity, API and network logs before normal retention or rotation removes them. Avoid copying secret values into incident notes or general-purpose logs.

Then determine what the agent actually changed or accessed. Check for files read or modified, records exported, permissions changed, messages sent or credentials retrieved. Separate completed actions from attempted ones, and confirmed facts from assumptions.

If the agent accessed a sensitive account or resource, assess that resource on its own. Revoke additional access, remove unauthorized changes and involve the relevant system owner. If data may have left the environment, follow the organization’s incident, privacy and notification processes.

Stopping the agent limits further activity. It does not undo actions already completed.

Before restarting the workflow, identify the cause. It may involve unsafe input, overbroad permissions, a compromised integration, a configuration change or a defect in the agent’s surrounding system. Fixing the prompt alone will not address a problem in credentials or network policy.

Restore access with the smallest scope the task requires. Test the workflow in a controlled environment, verify that high-impact actions receive the required authorization and monitor its tool calls and access after it resumes. Where an action could expose sensitive data or make an irreversible change, a human review step can give the team time to catch errors before execution.

An incident response plan is only useful if teams know which controls to use and can reach them under pressure. For each production agent, organizations should know:

Those procedures should be tested. A tabletop exercise can expose gaps, but teams should also verify that revoking credentials and disabling tools work in the actual environment. NIST’s incident response guidance treats preparation, response and recovery as part of cybersecurity risk management, not as steps to improvise after an event.

An effective response starts with knowing which credentials an agent can use and how to revoke its access. KeeperPAM® brings secrets management, access controls and auditing together to help organizations govern the credentials behind AI-driven workflows.

With Keeper Secrets Manager, teams can give agents access to only the secrets their tasks require, retrieve credentials at runtime and review secret-access events. These controls support containment alongside tested procedures for stopping workflows, terminating sessions and restricting network access.

Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Aranza Trevino at Keeper Security.

An unexpected action does not automatically mean an agent has been compromised.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/silent.title: SilentAir Hijacks Asian Telecom Networks to Intercept SMS 2FA Codes and Spy on Taiwanese Users
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/silent.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/silent.text:
A newly identified spying group used hacked equipment inside Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected people, mostly in Taiwan.

Enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software company based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week. It assessed with high confidence that SilentAir is a state-level actor, but linked its activity to China only with low confidence.

The company has told the operators where it found SilentAir sources. It said SilentAir has been disrupted for now but could return. The report does not say whether those operators have cleaned up the hacked equipment.

Mobile operators use the SS7 and Diameter protocols to exchange signaling messages that route calls and texts and enable roaming. This traffic crosses a shared network called the IPX, which runs on a high level of trust between operators. SilentAir sent its attacks into the IPX from the hacked equipment.

For interception, SilentAir sent the target's home network an UpdateLocation message, or its Diameter equivalent. The message claimed that the hacked equipment was now serving the target's phone. If the home network accepted it, calls and texts for that person would be diverted to the attackers.

Some of these attacks worked. For some targets, the company observed two-factor authentication (2FA) codes being intercepted immediately after the diversion took effect. That points to an attempt to break into other accounts registered to those people.

The report gives no similar evidence for voice calls, and it does not say whether any account was taken over.

Interception made up 18.3% of the attacks the company saw from SilentAir. For a typical surveillance company, the kind of firm behind most signaling attacks, the share was 2.1% in the company's earlier research.

Some targets were political and government VIPs in their own countries. In rare cases, SilentAir equipment in several countries worked together against such targets, which the company said points to a single controller.

The attacks came in bursts, from one or a few subscribers to several thousand over a month, with gaps of up to several months or longer between bursts.

Outside Taiwan, targets were mostly in other Southeast and East Asian networks, and at times in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. People using the hacked operators' own networks may also have been targeted, but the company could not see that traffic.

The company spotted SilentAir by studying attacks on the links between operators. Since early 2025, it has tracked unusual attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes Diameter, from some Asian operators that would not normally send attacks. Later analysis found suspicious activity even earlier.

The networks hosting SilentAir handled follow-up messages for diverted targets in odd and inconsistent ways, according to the company's technical report. That left two explanations: someone outside was faking those networks' signaling addresses, or equipment inside each network had been taken over.

The company then saw equipment inside one operator both send and receive attack commands, which confirmed the second explanation. That equipment behaved exactly like SilentAir sources in other networks.

Detecting and blocking the attacks was hard at first because the attackers understood mobile networks and signaling defenses well. After the attacks were contained, the company recovered traces of unauthorized access. It could not analyze the malware it believes SilentAir used.

The report does not name the countries, the operators, or any of the targets. In some countries, SilentAir attacks came from more than one operator.

SilentAir also sent silent SMS on a very large scale, mainly to subscribers in Taiwan. These are texts that the phone does not display or alert on.

During the day, most silent SMS went to subscribers on other networks, such as Southeast Asian networks. One of their main uses appears to have been checking whether a diversion had worked, the company said.

If the test text reached the hacked equipment instead of the phone, the attackers knew they were getting that person's texts.

Most silent SMS went out at night, and most of those went to people in Taiwan. The company said the purpose of those messages is not confirmed. They may be a bulk check that earlier diversions were still in place, since phones are least likely to re-register to their real location at night.

The silent texts carried spam-like motivational or promotional lines, often in English. The company believes the text was a disguise. If an operator along the way stripped a message's silent setting, the recipient would see it as spam and ignore it.

The company's low-confidence link to China rests on several signs. SilentAir focused on Taiwan and did not target Chinese networks or subscribers.

Its tracking and interception attacks also followed a working day in UTC+8, which is China Standard Time. They started at 9 a.m., almost stopped on weekends, and paused or slowed around Chinese holidays.

The company also considered a link to Liminal Panda, a group behind earlier telecom intrusions. It called the link possible but unconfirmed and does not tie the two groups together for now.

In several hacked operators, SilentAir attacks happened during a known Liminal Panda infection. At other times, the two showed no sign of working together. They also went after operators in the same part of Asia, though Liminal Panda has no known focus on Taiwan.

SilentAir's behavior also partly matches that of SCTPE, a little-known Linux trojan that runs in the kernel and is designed to send and receive SS7 and Diameter traffic.

Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has described the same tool in a government advisory. There, the tool is called SIGweaver. The agency said CrowdStrike identified it on January 21 and links it to Liminal Panda with moderate confidence.

But Enea said SilentAir answered messages it had not sent itself, which the known SCTPE program cannot do. SilentAir's operational security also seemed far better than Liminal Panda's.

Separately, the company's GTP firewall has detected Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators since the first quarter of this year. The company blocked the group's GTPDoor traffic there and saw Liminal Panda infections, or strong signs of them, in at least 5 to 10 operators.

The GTPDoor backdoor, first documented on February 27, 2024, hides commands within GTP-C, the protocol that establishes mobile data connections between networks. The company also found evidence of a new version that hides commands in GTP-U, the part of GTP that carries users' data. GTP-U traffic is harder to inspect, though the company believes the new version serves mainly as a backup.

The company said any attacker could reuse these techniques, and it told operators to:

The report does not advise people whose calls and texts may be targeted.

The company says SilentAir has been disrupted for now but could return. The group has been identified as a state-level actor, but linked its activity to China only with low confidence.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/operat.title: Operation Endgame Takes Down Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC Servers, Seizes 6.4M Stolen Logins
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/operat.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/operat.text:
An international police operation took down servers behind Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC this week. Criminals used the three malware tools to gain access to computers, steal passwords, and launch ransomware attacks.

Police also seized about 6.4 million stolen logins belonging to more than 40,000 victims, according to Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA).

Gootloader is a loader: once on a computer, it could download other malware, especially ransomware. It spread through fake legal documents placed on hacked websites, often WordPress sites. Criminals used SEO poisoning to push those sites high in search results.

Gootloader has infected at least 25,000 computers worldwide since 2018, the U.S. Justice Department said. Its operators used those computers to infect more computers, then sold access to the new ones to ransomware criminals. In the U.S., Gootloader was used in ransomware attacks against at least 44 victims, resulting in about $28.8 million in losses.

German police gave a much higher count in their statement in German. Based on what investigators know so far, Gootloader has infected millions of computers worldwide since it first appeared in 2020.

Across the three tools, police seized 235 servers and 257 domains, according to an operation summary from Europol, which supported the action. The takedown is part of Operation Endgame, an international police campaign against malware criminals use to access victims' computers.

For Gootloader, police took down 14 servers and 218 domains and removed malware from 681 hacked websites.

With court approval, U.S. agencies and their international partners removed Gootloader from more than 100 servers, including hacked WordPress sites. They also seized U.S. domains used to deliver and control the malware, according to the Justice Department announcement.

CastleRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) known since 2025, allows attackers to control an infected computer remotely. Police seized 120 of its servers and 39 domains.

StealC is an infostealer that exfiltrates passwords and other login credentials from infected computers, allowing criminals to sell or misuse them. Police took down its servers again this week, after a June operation against it.

After that June action, its operators changed their infrastructure and brought it back online to stay out of investigators' reach, German police said. Some of StealC's key infrastructure ran on Virtualine/Omegatech, a bulletproof hosting service that advertised its services to criminals.

Police shut that hosting service down in a late-October takedown.

No arrests were announced in this week's action. Dutch police also carried out further investigations targeting Gootloader's main suspect, according to their news release.

Dutch police have loaded data stolen by CastleRAT into Check your hack, a police service where people can enter an email address. If the address is in the data, the police send an email within a few minutes with steps to remove the malware. If it is not, no email arrives.

More data will be added in the coming weeks. The service checks single addresses, not whole domains, but organizations can join No More Leaks, a police project that shares data with private partners. The stolen data is also being shared with services including Have I Been Pwned and the Shadowserver Foundation.

Emails that claim to come from the police and ask people to check the data are fake. The police never send emails with links.

Even after police seize the data, criminals may still have the stolen logins, the police say in their frequently asked questions. As long as the malware stays on a computer, criminals may also keep getting its passwords.

The Shadowserver Foundation is working with internet service providers and computer security incident response teams (CSIRTs) to find infected computers and notify their owners, the Justice Department said. In Germany, the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) is helping notify victims, according to the BKA.

Denmark's National Special Crime Unit (NSK) helped clean the 681 websites. In a statement in Danish, the unit said it believes the attackers got into the sites with stolen passwords that came through criminal channels. They then installed a backdoor.

Officers removed the attackers' code and access, and left a message for the site owners with advice on securing their sites.

Police in Denmark and the Netherlands advise WordPress site owners to take these steps, several of which are set out in a Dutch advice sheet:

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.title: Hackers Exploit PHP2Shell Flaws in Check Point Gateways to Deploy TSGA Backdoor and Wipe ESXi Files
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.text:
An unknown threat actor has been observed targeting unpatched Check Point Security Gateways to obtain initial access via the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and then a previously unreported local privilege escalation flaw in Gaia OS to deploy a backdoor called TSGA.

The activity, detailed by Check Point, began on October 30, 2026, and targeted Israeli organizations, with a broader follow-up wave on November 2, 2026, that targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors. Some of the organizations singled out in the first wave have also been at the receiving end of destructive actions that include the deployment of wiper malware.

"PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039," Check Point said. "The attackers then deployed PHP web shells, the persistent TSGA backdoor, and its embedded TSProxy networking component."

"The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage."

CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score: 7.8) is a missing authorization flaw that could enable privilege escalation to root in the DynamicCLI process, enabling any authenticated local user to run arbitrary commands by writing a single request to the socket.

"The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point said, adding it "observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers."

The issue impacts versions R82.20, R82.10, R82, R81.20, R81.10, and R81 of the following products -

"In late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways," Check Point said.

"Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619."

After obtaining initial access, the unknown hacking group is said to have escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by weaponizing CVE-2026-123039 and deploying PHP web shells with an aim to establish persistent access. The web shells support command execution and file upload capabilities.

The November 2, 2026, wave is said to have targeted some Israeli organizations that had already been targeted in the first wave, alongside other organizations worldwide, without demonstrating any specific geographic or sector preference, indicating an opportunistic initial-access effort.

The access afforded by the web shell paves the way for TSGA, a standalone passive backdoor that also includes a second component called TSProxy. TSGA, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, has been described as a Linux gateway implant with Check Point-specific functionality, offering encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

"[TSProxy's] injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue," Check Point said. "This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services."

Some of the other post-exploitation actions observed are listed below -

Both TSGA and TSProxy are assessed to be Check Point-specific components of a toolkit dubbed PhiliKit that was first documented by ESET in June 2026, attributing it to a China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221).

Other factors that point to the involvement of a possible China-aligned threat actor include the use of LightNode VPS infrastructure and the fact that scanning activity was concentrated between 12 and 9 a.m. UTC, coinciding with typical Chinese working hours.

However, the cybersecurity company said it does not have enough evidence to link the latest campaign to the threat actor or other known Chinese-nexus groups, citing the following reasons -

"Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation," Check Point said. "Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen."

The November 2, 20 26, wave is said to have targeted some Israeli organizations that had already been targeted in the first wave.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.title: Hackers Exploit N-central Flaws to Infect 21 Servers, Including 19 Running Hotfix 2
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.text:
N-able on Thursday said it's taking additional precautions in the wake of public disclosure of a new set of flaws tracked as 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell.

"We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," the company said in a Thursday update. "These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers."

The following actions have been applied to Hosted environments -

Hosted customers are also being recommended to follow N-able's previous guidance to upgrade Agents and Probes on N-central version 2026.4 HF1 and above, as the update introduces changes in how the Probe and Agent communicate.

"N-able N-central 2026.4 HF1 updates legacy components of the Agent and Probe, which changes how the two communicate," it said. "As such, upgrading both Agents and Probes in your N-central server is a MUST to ensure all managed devices are communicating and patched."

On-premises customers are being urged to upgrade Agents and Probes and ensure Legacy API access is disabled in the environment, if it has been previously turned on.

"Our teams are actively assessing the new disclosures, developing additional remediation, and working to safely restore affected functionality," N-able said. "Protecting our partners and their customers remains our highest priority, and we will continue to take precautionary action where necessary."

The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed two new sets of flaws called 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell that work against the latest version of N-central and can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions.

Multiple threat intelligence reports show that 4EverAble2Shell has moved beyond preliminary probing to active exploitation efforts, with threat actors leveraging it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

The attacks have been found to string together a critical Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8), with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to obtain root-level access.

"An unauthenticated exploit chain in N-able N-central, disclosed as 4EverAble2Shell, is reported to allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary operating-system commands with root privileges," Previdian, which is tracking the flaw as VULN-2026-0009, said.

"The chain exploits unsafe class instantiation during SOAP fault processing in the bundled Apache Axis component. A crafted request causes an attacker-selected JLine class to process malicious input, resulting in command execution as the nable service account."

In an exploit chain detailed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to download and execute a shell script ("jup.sh") from an attacker-controlled server at "157.20.241[.]16," while sending back diagnostic information and command output to the server.

Cybersecurity company Huntback has also revealed that the same IP address is weaponizing the 4EverAble2Shell flaw, deploying an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner on 21 N-central servers via the aforementioned shell script -

The miner is designed to use only half of the available CPU cores, likely in an effort to fly under the radar. The compromised N-central servers are concentrated across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden.

"The miner is the only payload we have seen, but the escalation hands the operator root on a host that manages your customers' endpoints," Huntback said. "Treat a hit as a full compromise, not a cleanup job. Applying Hotfix 2 is not enough on its own: 19 of the victims here were already running it."

https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.title: Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.author: Robert Lemos
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.text:
News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Blockchain complexities, such as attacker-deployed sweepers, hobble security controls designed to limit the damage of an exchange compromise.

On Oct. 29, cyber thieves transferred around $6.34 billion in various cryptocurrencies from at least 11 wallets owned by exchange Binance to attacker-controlled addresses. Binance seemingly had not put in place security controls to quickly detect malicious authorizations and disable them through a pretested kill switch, experts say — which should put other crypto firms on notice.

While Binance's internal security systems issued an alert in minutes, the attackers exploited a feature of Ethereum smart accounts — a relatively new type of account abstraction introduced to Ethereum with the EIP-7702 proposal in 2025 — to essentially install malicious code, known as a "sweeper." The sweeper code transferred all the funds held in a primary treasury wallet at Binance — consisting of more than five dozen cryptocurrencies totaling approximately $2.5 billion — to the attacker's address created minutes before.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

In the end, the wallet was left with a single ETH coin, according to an analysis by blockchain security firm BlockAid.

Large transactions from other wallets to the same address, initiated by the attackers, triggered internal alerts at Binance. The company took countermeasures, but the smart-account authorization continued to function for about four hours, siphoning additional funds.

"An EIP-7702 authorization [is] a standing delegation," says Ido Ben-Natan, co-founder and CEO of BlockAid. "Once it is on-chain, attacker-controlled code can move that hot wallet's funds, and anything later deposited to it, until the same wallet ... [revokes the authorization]. It carries no amount and no destination, so withdrawal controls never see it."

Despite a sweeper function enabled through EIP-7702 authorization being a known threat, Binance noted in a Nov. 3 post-mortem report that the authorization hobbled the companies efforts to stop transactions from flowing out onto the blockchain.

"Once established, these authorizations enabled the attackers to continue moving assets independently of Binance's normal withdrawal infrastructure," the company stated in a post-mortem report. "Binance needed additional transactions to revoke these on-chain authorizations ... suspending withdrawals and shutting down hot wallet services did not automatically invalidate existing on-chain authorizations."

Developers were the initial weak point, enabling the EIP-7702 authorization attack to occur. One developer downloaded a compromised version of Homebrew, an open source package management tool for Macs, while a second developer fell for a fake job interview, during which they were given a software "assignment" that compromised his system, according to Binance's post-mortem.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

In the end, the attackers used their compromise of the two developers' systems — as well as a third developer's system — to gain signing privileges, creating 50 presigned authorizations to flood the targeted wallet, known among blockchain analysts as "Binance 14," at the right time.

The same targeting of developers happened during the ByBit Ethereum heist on Feb. 21, 2025, says Avi Sambira, vice president of North America at incident-response firm Sygnia. In that case, cyber thieves compromised the Mac of a Safe{Wallet} developer nearly three weeks before the actual theft, according to Sygnia's analysis of that incident. Safe{Wallet} is used by Ethereum and other decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) to enforce multisignature security.

"[A]n AWS token was used and attackers operated inside Safe{Wallet}'s cloud environment for roughly two weeks before modifying the signing interface," Sambira says. "Binance's disclosure appears consistent with the same model, with initial reporting indicating endpoint and internal-tool compromise preceded credential, token, and[/or] container access to wallet signing."

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

Like that incident, the FBI placed blame directly on North Korean cybercriminal operators, releasing a list of more than 600 Ethereum addresses, 19 Bitcoin addresses, and 1 SOL address linked to TraderTraitor, a moniker for the group behind the attacks.

Exchanges and crypto-finance firms need to treat their developers, vendors, and suppliers as critical elements of their infrastructure. Attackers are increasingly looking to compromise developer identities, repositories, CI/CD pipelines, cloud control planes, and third-party integrations, Sambira says. Those assets sit only one or two trust boundaries away from withdrawal authority.

"TraderTraitor's evolution is less about abandoning old techniques than combining them into a more sophisticated trust attack," he says. "Fake recruiters and malicious coding assignments establish the foothold, [while] stolen sessions, cloud credentials, and trusted interfaces turn that foothold into transaction control."

When the cyberattackers used their pregenerated authorizations, they sent 50 at the same time because every transaction needs a valid nonce — a sequential counter — so the attackers used a window of 50 authorizations and needed only a single one to match.

The nonce spray to install a malicious sweeper is a new, but known, threat. In a paper presented at the USENIX Security conference in August, researchers from Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and two other Chinese schools revealed that at least 924 malicious smart contracts had been enabled through the EIP-7702 mechanism, leading to at least $2.3 million in losses.

In its own research, BlockAid saw at least $1.1 million in losses across four instances. It predicted that the first 10-figure attack would arrive before the end of 2026. The firm was off by a factor of 100.

The attacks can be stopped — or at least blunted — by a combination of controls. Any company processing cryptocurrency transactions in real time should use simulations to detect malicious rules, enforce policies on the allowed size of transactions and their destinations, issue alerts based on detecting a burst of large transactions, and deploy a fast kill switch that has been prebuilt to pause signing and stop wallet refills, says BlockAid's Ben-Natan.

Binance seemingly had none — or only some — of those controls in place. In the end, it took nearly four hours — the attack started at 20:05 UTC and the last transaction was recorded at 23:56 UTC — for the company to stop transactions from being recorded on the blockchain, subsequently freezing and recovering about $2.85 billion in attempted stolen assets. The company did not respond to requests for comment.

Binance highlights the importance of having good monitoring and the ability to detect anomalous transactions.

The difficulty in responding to the attacks underscores the problems that cryptocurrency exchanges and infrastructure firms face to combat theft and fraud. In many ways, Binance had created an overlapping set of controls to detect attacks and block transfers in near real time. However, the state-sponsored attackers found a way to bypass those controls through the EIP-7702 sweeper.

The pressure on cryptocurrency firms will only rise because attackers can exfiltrate the funds quickly, says Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs and a former federal prosecutor and US Treasury official.

"For years we've seen hacks against large financial institutions, tech companies, and even government agencies — the difference is that in crypto you can steal funds in real time," he says. "There's no clawback window, and the money is gone in minutes."

Crypto-finance firms need to have visibility across four domains: identity and authority governance, infrastructure and execution integrity, custody and transaction authorization, and on- and off-chain detection, says Sygnia's Sambira. Companies that only monitor transactions on the blockchain are seeing changes too late, he adds.

In addition, crypto firms should rigorously track all identities and systems that can initiate, approve, modify, or execute transactions and be ready to suspend those accounts' privileges, he says.

"Controls with the greatest containment value involve the preauthorized ability to revoke identities and tokens, pause transfers, isolate wallets, and rebuild affected infrastructure within minutes," Sambira says. "Those capabilities must be tested before a crisis hits and retested regularly."

Testing and practicing these controls are critical because companies need to know that they will work in real time, says TRM Labs' Redbord.

"The actionable part for any company touching crypto is that these patterns are recognizable. If you watch in real time, you can act in the first moments, when it matters most," he says. "This is all about speed."

Monitoring transactions can detect suspicious activity quite quickly and, in the case of the cryptocurrency thefts targeting Binance and ByBit, can stop attacks before too much value is lost. The keys to adequate responses are speed and relationships to the various stakeholders, says Redbord.

"Issuers like Tether and Circle can freeze the addresses holding stolen tokens and then burn those tokens and reissue the same amount to the rightful owner," he says. "The funds don't have to be chased down. They can be made whole on-chain."

Nearly all issuers, exchanges, blockchain intelligence firms, and many global law enforcement agencies are part of the Beacon Network, created by TRM Labs and other industry players, for early detection of and intelligence sharing about cryptocurrency incidents. In addition, cryptocurrency-reliant businesses should ensure that any exchange with which they do business has withdrawal limits and allowlists, isolates their signing systems on computers reserved for that purpose, and constantly trains their engineers against social engineering, Redbord says.

Organizations should also reduce measures of time to detect, time to contain, and time to freeze to seconds. The approval of major transactions should require multiple signatures from systems that are used for only that purpose, and businesses need to have a response plan that keeps them operational while they recover.

Binance has taken some of these steps, including identifying the affected systems, cleaning or replacing them, and replacing wallets, it stated in its initial incident report. It has also completed "enhanced" security scans across employee devices, rotated credentials, and deployed enhanced AI-based behavioral anomaly detection, the company stated.

"There are a number of security measures we have implemented and are implementing that will remain private to prevent malicious actors from compromising our security," the company stated.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
A major new study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks. However, the findings also point to a possible increase in risk over a longer period, making the decision more complicated than it initially appears.

The independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago. The annual conference brings together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, emerging evidence, and advances in clinical care.

An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes. Statins are widely prescribed to lower cholesterol and reduce these risks, including in people who have never experienced a cardiovascular event. This preventive approach remains a central part of the American Heart Association's 2026 joint guideline on dyslipidemia.

Do Older Adults Need to Keep Taking Statins?

Although statins are an established treatment for reducing cardiovascular risk, questions remain about how much benefit they provide when people reach their 70s and beyond, particularly if they have never had a heart attack or stroke.

"While the Association's recent joint guideline recommends lifestyle and potentially medication for people with high LDL-C at younger ages to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, recent studies question the health benefits of continuing statins in the later decades of life," said study author Rita F. Redberg, M.D., M.Sc., FAHA, professor of cardiology and the Araxe Vilensky Endowed Chair in Cardiology at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. "A few previous studies assessed the safety of discontinuing statins for primary prevention at age 70 and later, and they found no difference in mortality. One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins. Whether it is safe to discontinue statins to prevent a first CVD event in the elderly remained unclear and the question we explored in our study."

To investigate, researchers enrolled nearly 1,900 adults aged 70 and older who were taking statins specifically to prevent a first cardiovascular event. Every participant also had at least two chronic medical conditions, such as a history of cancer or lung disease.

Participants were divided into two groups. One group stopped taking statins, while the other continued their prescribed treatment. Researchers tracked their health for approximately two years, with additional follow-up extending as long as four years. They examined rates of heart attack, stroke, and death, along with changes in quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and muscle wasting (known as sarcopenia).

What Happened When Older Adults Stopped Statins?

The initial findings were largely reassuring. After approximately two years, participants who stopped taking statins did not experience a statistically significant increase in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths compared with those who remained on the medications.

Stopping treatment also did not produce measurable improvements in the other outcomes researchers examined. Quality of life, muscle discomfort, falls, and muscle wasting were similar in both groups.

There was, however, a small difference in cardiovascular outcomes. Over the first two years, the results indicated approximately one additional cardiovascular event for every 40 people who discontinued statins compared with those who continued treatment.

The longer follow-up revealed a more concerning pattern. Over a period of up to four years, 12.7% of participants who stopped statins experienced a heart attack, stroke, or death, compared with 9.2% of those who kept taking the medications.

Longer Follow-Up Reveals a Potential Risk

Redberg explained that the higher rate of serious outcomes during the four-year follow-up represents a new finding in research on statin discontinuation among older adults. She suggested that the difference may have emerged because this trial included more participants and tracked them for a longer period than earlier studies.

These results complicate the question of whether older adults should continue cholesterol treatment indefinitely. While the findings suggest that stopping statins may be a reasonable option for many people in this age group, they also indicate that remaining on treatment could offer some protection over time.

"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," she said. "There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event."

Study Design and Important Limitations

The trial involved 1,880 participants aged 70 and older (average age of 77; 53% men, and 47% women), all of whom had at least two chronic health conditions. Individuals with established cardiovascular disease or a previous cardiovascular event were not eligible to participate.

Researchers conducted the study between November 2021 and April 2026 across 24 medical centers in Switzerland, France, and the Netherlands. Of the participants, 938 were assigned to discontinue statins, while 942 were assigned to continue taking their medications.

Throughout the trial and subsequent follow-up, researchers recorded heart attacks, acute ischemic strokes, and deaths from any cause. Participants also completed surveys assessing their overall quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and sarcopenia.

One limitation was that some participants did not remain in their originally assigned groups. Some people instructed to stop statins eventually resumed treatment, while others assigned to continue taking statins stopped using them. Altogether, approximately 14% of participants switched from their assigned treatment approach during the study.

To determine whether these changes affected the findings, the researchers performed several additional statistical analyses. The results remained unchanged.

Taken together, the findings suggest that discontinuing statins may be an option for many adults over 70 who have not previously experienced cardiovascular disease, especially when considering outcomes over the first two years. However, the higher rate of heart attacks, strokes, and deaths during longer follow-up underscores why stopping treatment should be an individualized decision made with a healthcare professional rather than a general recommendation for all older adults.
