https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: Watch SpaceX attempt a historic Starship launch and double-catch landing today (Nov. 13)
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Mike Wall
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
Liftoff is scheduled for 5:45 p.m. ET today (Nov. 13).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.

Starship is scheduled to launch on its 15th test flight today from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). SpaceX plans to bring both of Starship's stages back to Starbase for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something it has never done before.

You can watch it all live here at Space.com. And there should be a lot to see: Starship Flight 15 will last more than 22 hours, if all goes according to plan.

Starship consists of two elements: a huge booster known as Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship, or Ship for short. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight.

The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said.

SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy, pulling the feat off on three previous Starship test flights. But it has never tried to do so with Ship, which flies farther and faster than the booster and is therefore a more challenging vehicle to recover.

So today's flight is a pretty big deal for SpaceX.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," the company wrote in a Flight 15 mission description.

The action will unspool over two days, if all goes to plan. Super Heavy will return to Starbase for a touchdown just 6.5 minutes after launch, but Ship will continue on to low Earth orbit.

The upper stage will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, during a 42-minute stretch beginning about 35 minutes after liftoff. This will be just the second batch of V3 spacecraft to reach orbit, after the 26 that went up on Flight 14 on Sept. 28.

Ship will then stay aloft for nearly a full day. The mission plan calls for the upper stage to return to Starbase for its chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), about 22.5 hours after liftoff.

There's no guarantee things will go according to plan, however. SpaceX will call off a Ship catch if the vehicle experiences any issues during Flight 15. If something crops up, the company will steer Ship to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, either near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

So it'll be a busy weekend for SpaceX, and for space fans who want to keep tabs on the mission. And we can help you out there, with our Flight 15 updates page.

On this week’s episode of “The Readout LOUD”: the failure of two closely followed heart disease drugs and how these setbacks may impact the future of cardiovascular drug research. Plus, drug safety concerns weigh on some of the biggest companies in the sector.

For years, it was widely believed that a deeper understanding of genetics was going to speed the development of newer and better medicines for patients with heart disease. But then came this year’s American Heart Association meeting, which was dominated by presentations of clinical trials that showed no benefit whatsoever for two drugs long thought to be genetically validated.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/sena.title: Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on restoring trust in science, the state of public health, and RFK Jr.
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/sena.author: Nicholas Florko
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/sena.text:
Abdul El-Sayed will soon become the first epidemiologist in the Senate at a moment that would keep anyone with a public health background up at night. More than 5,000 Americans have been sickened by the measles this year and the United States is expected to lose its formal measles elimination status by the end of the month. Dengue fever is spreading in Florida, respiratory virus season is underway, and the United States just weathered a foodborne illness outbreak that sickened more than 20,000.

In a wide-ranging interview with STAT, the Michigan Democrat emphasized that he is hopeful the United States can fix its growing trust-in-science problem, but he expressed frustration — at Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., at drug and insurance companies, and at the field of public health — for leading America down this path.

“We’ve created the space for a few grifters to come in and in effect lie to the public,” El-Sayed said. “To create a level of distrust in science and in public health that has had disastrous consequences.”

By Mandy Cohen and Ellen Montz

By Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper

Eli Lilly has been featuring a telehealth company called Counsel Health on a list of providers for patients seeking a GLP-1 prescription.

On Tuesday, Counsel said it would be acquired by the smart ring maker Oura, allowing Counsel clinicians access to the data gathered through the ring so they can help customers understand the data and then diagnose or treat any conditions.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/fert.title: 5 takeaways from STAT’s investigation of the sprawling ‘three-parent IVF’ industry
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/fert.author: Megan Molteni
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/fert.text:
The investigation started with a tip from a British couple.

After trying to have a second child for several years, they had signed up with a U.S.-based company called International Fertility Group (IFG), paying tens of thousands of dollars for access abroad to an experimental fertility procedure illegal in the U.S. and tightly regulated in the U.K. The procedure, known as MRT — for mitochondrial replacement techniques — is sometimes called “three-parent IVF,” because it involves creating embryos that combine the genes of a mother and father with a bit of DNA from the mitochondria of a third person.

In the U.K., MRT is allowed at only one academic medical center, and only for the purposes of lowering the risk of passing on mitochondrial disease. But according to IFG, the procedure could also help older women overcome issues that make the odds of IVF go down significantly after the age of 40. Despite being a doctor herself, the woman in the couple had been taken in by the hope of a miracle.

By Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper

In 1976, at the dawn of the modern Alzheimer’s era, the neurologist Robert Katzman, champion of efforts to extract Alzheimer’s from senility and “normal aging,” concluded his short essay “The prevalence and malignancy of Alzheimer disease” with this notably qualified call to action:

“In focusing attention on the mortality associated with Alzheimer disease, our goal is not to find a way to prolong the life of severely demented persons, but rather to call attention to our belief that senile as well as presenile forms of Alzheimer are a single disease, a disease whose etiology must be determined, whose course must be aborted, and ultimately a disease to be prevented.”

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/phon.author: Isabella Cueto
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/phon.text:

MILWAUKEE — Kat Zilka sat on the floor of her living room, beside a glowing Christmas tree and a pile of essays, and felt like weeping. It was late in 2022, and she had asked her 12th grade digital journalism students to reflect on their relationships to devices.

“The things they were writing were deeply disturbing,” she said.

Teenagers quietly enduring online abuse, using their phones all night without their parents’ knowledge, or trapped in a cycle of deleting and redownloading social media. Their words made real what Zilka had been observing for years — how the light in students’ eyes was dimmer, especially since Covid — and revealed the astonishing magnitude of the problem.

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/onc.title: Oncotype DX Helps Avoid Unnecessary Chemo in Breast Cancer
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/onc.text:
Real-world data from France suggest that genomic testing with Oncotype DX can help many patients with early-stage hormone receptor-positive (HR-positive), HER2-negative breast cancer avoid chemotherapy without compromising outcomes. The findings come from the second interim analysis of the French FREDO-ODX study, presented at the European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress in Madrid, Spain.

According to Elsa Curtit, MD, PhD, principal investigator and oncologist at Besançon University Hospital in Besançon, France, “thanks to genomic tests, 75% of patients can be spared chemotherapy, if we consider the entire FREDO population. At 5 years, their recurrence-free survival rate is very good, and it is as good as in cases where chemotherapy has been given.”

In a press release, Curtit said: “For patients who may appear to be at high risk based on traditional clinical factors, having additional information about the biology of their individual tumor can provide greater clarity when it comes to deciding whether chemotherapy is needed. These findings reinforce the importance of integrating genomic information into therapeutic discussions so that care can be tailored to each patient.”

Curtit noted that the test is intended only for a subset of patients with HR-positive breast cancer, which accounts for about 70% of cases. When a tumor is small and detected early, surgery followed by endocrine therapy may be sufficient. More aggressive disease clearly warrants chemotherapy. Between these two extremes, however, about 20%-33% of patients fall into a gray area, where the benefit of chemotherapy is uncertain and treatment is often offered out of caution.

The analysis included 2289 patients treated at 17 centers in France. At study entry, 64% had node-negative disease and 73% had grade 2 tumors. The median age was 58.7 years, and 71% of patients were postmenopausal. Recurrence Score results were ≤ 10 in 19% of patients, 11-25 in 64%, and > 25 in 17%.

The findings showed a notable gap between traditional clinical risk assessment and genomic risk. After testing, endocrine therapy alone was selected for 75% of patients, whereas 25% received chemoendocrine therapy. Even among patients considered at high clinical risk, only 27% had a posttest treatment decision in favor of chemotherapy.

With a median follow-up of 3.6 years, the estimated 5-year invasive disease-free survival was 88.5%. These outcomes were broadly consistent with those reported in the TAILORx and RxPONDER trials.

Muriel Dahan, MD, research and development director at Unicancer, said the study supports the use of genomic testing in routine care and suggests it can help refine prognosis and reduce the use of chemotherapy in patients who are not at high risk. She also said the findings complement earlier evidence from TAILORx and RxPONDER and support a scientifically justified therapeutic de-escalation in appropriate patients.

The study is expected to continue until 2028, with a target enrollment of 4500 patients and outcome reporting over 10 years rather than 5.

The test is included in major international breast cancer treatment recommendations, including those of ESMO, the St. Gallen International Breast Cancer Conference, the American Society of Clinical Oncology, and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network in the US. However, despite full coverage for eligible patients in Germany, the UK, and Netherlands, access remains uneven in France.

The test costs about €1800 and is partially reimbursed to hospitals through RIHN (Référentiel des actes innovants hors nomenclature), a transitional French funding mechanism for innovative tests and procedures not yet included in the standard reimbursement system. Because hospitals must still absorb part of the cost, availability varies across the country.

Curtit said the main value of real-world data is to determine whether results from large prospective randomized trials such as TAILORx and RxPONDER can be reproduced in routine practice in a population that is less selected than those enrolled in clinical studies.

She said: “The aim is to ensure that the results in terms of recurrence-free survival are comparable to those reported in TAILORx and RxPONDER, and therefore that the therapeutic de-escalation strategies enabled by the use of the test remain safe when applied to a larger and more heterogeneous population.”

She added that these data also help researchers analyze practice patterns across centers, including how the test is prescribed and how it affects treatment decisions, thereby confirming that the benefits seen in trials are also found “in real conditions of care.”

Curtit said the main remaining barrier in France is reimbursement. “The main obstacle remains related to the financing and reimbursement of these tests in France, which are still based on a partial coverage system by the Health Insurance, with a balance to be paid by health establishments.”

She also noted differences between US and European recommendations. In Europe, and particularly under ESMO guidance, genomic signatures are mainly recommended in situations of uncertainty about the need for chemotherapy, especially when prognostic factors are discordant or suggest high clinical risk. This leaves room for clinical judgment, but also for variability in interpretation across centers.

Looking ahead, Curtit said the currently used genomic signatures were developed about 20 years ago and could likely be improved, especially through new molecular approaches and through stronger predictive, rather than only prognostic, performance.

However, she cautioned that there is not yet enough evidence to support replacing current assays in practice. “To date, we do not have clinical data with a sufficient level of evidence to validate the use in routine practice of next-generation tests that could replace the currently available signatures.”

Curtit added: “The challenge is not only to develop more effective tools from a biological or prognostic point of view, but above all to demonstrate their clinical utility, in particular their ability to guide therapeutic decisions in complete safety, with a level of evidence comparable to that which we have today for Oncotype DX.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/life-afte.title: Life after Jensen: What Nvidia’s shakeup means for private AI
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/life-afte.author: Allie Garfinkle
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/life-afte.text:
This time last week, AI without Jensen Huang seemed impossible. Today, that’s the world we live in.

Granted, it’ll have been less than (or about) 24 hours into that new world by the time you’re reading this, and there’s so much we don’t know about what a Jensen-less AI landscape looks like. One thing we do know: It will affect the private markets.

“Nvidia matters more to private AI markets than any single investor because it has three roles,” said Harrison Rolfes, PitchBook senior research analyst, who was among many who answered my feverish reporting calls yesterday. “It’s the largest corporate investor in U.S. AI. It’s the main supplier for AI startups, and it’s the main [benchmark] public stock investors use to judge the AI market.”

Now, in the near term at least, how Nvidia and new interim CEO Colette Kress will handle dealmaking is in question. Rolfes pointed out to me that Nvidia invested $189 billion in 2026, making it AI’s top U.S. corporate backer. This broke down somewhat expectedly: OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI account for $172 billion, and 27 other deals make up the remaining $17 billion. Kress, and any Huang successor, could be more circumspect moving forward. (Indeed, worth noting: Nvidia’s blockbuster $12.93 billion buyout of open-source startup Hugging Face hasn’t yet closed.) And some companies will struggle more than others, especially neoclouds, for which Huang was dealmaker and guarantor.

“If they’re dependent on Nvidia to bankroll them, like [CoreWeave] or Lambda Labs or some of these neoclouds, then I think you could be really screwed,” one early-stage VC told me.

Much will move forward, nevertheless: My colleague Beatrice Nolan and I reported that Anthropic’s IPO is high-stakes but (for now) very much on, and some VCs told me that, yes, this could pressure AI valuations—and so what.

“I think the valuations were ridiculous anyway,” said Rob Biederman, managing partner at Asymmetric. “I don’t think it would be the worst thing for the tech world if there was a little bit of a reset shakeout because a lot of things are getting funded right now that aren’t especially good ideas.”

For startups wondering what’s next, Rolfes had some advice: Nvidia will invest less for now, but (on the bright side) it’s possible GPU prices will also drop.

“If you’re a startup, maybe don’t reach out to Nvidia in the short term to get investment cash,” he said. “What they should do is reach out to go get compute, go buy the chips…If some of these startups can get a hold of cheaper chips, then they can build out their product, which means we’ll probably start to see an influx of seed-stage [and] Series A-stage startups moving up.”

Here’s our larger feature contemplating life in AI after Jensen.

Allie Garfinkle

Email: alexandra.garfinkle@fortune.com

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/navy-rese.title: Our bank accounts had exactly one signer. Then the Navy called
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/navy-rese.author: Keith Presley
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/navy-rese.text:
In October, the company I co-founded pitched on the main stage as a top 20 finalist at TechCrunch Disrupt, drawn from thousands of applicants. I was not in the audience or in the wings, because four days earlier the Navy had sent me mobilization orders. While Matt Chase, our senior vice president of global sales, delivered the most important pitch in our company’s history, I was in Norfolk, Virginia preparing to deploy. The mobilization was eventually canceled before I deployed, but, by that time, Matt was already being mic’ed up to get onstage.

I have thought about that week every day since, and I have come to believe the orders were the most honest test a CEO can face: proof, on a date I did not choose, of whether I had built a durable company or a team that could not function without me. The startup world quietly treats reserve service as a liability, but my experience that week convinced me the industry has it backwards.

There’s not much I can say about the mobilization itself, so this is a story about what the orders demanded of the company rather than where they were sending me.

Orders arrive via phone call with a report date and no room to negotiate. Questions a leader would normally settle over several quarters had to be settled in days. Investor relationships I had managed personally moved to Jonathan Sperber, my cofounder and our chief strategy officer. Decisions that existed only in my head had to be written down and handed to people I trust to make them without me. The handoff that nearly broke was signature authority on our accounts, which existed in exactly one name until that week.

Matt took over the pitch I had expected to give and tried to make the script his own. He delivered it well: the sales and investor conversations the pitch opened are still running today. The biggest moment in our history ended up in the hands of our head of sales rather than one of my co-founders. None of it resembled the continuity plan that sits untouched on our Google drive, because it happened on a clock, with Disrupt approaching and the real possibility that I would be unreachable for six months.

Every CEO assures investors that the company would survive without them, but almost none of us are required to prove it. The succession conversation is the one that slides to next quarter because the founder is healthy and nothing forces the issue, and mobilization orders are the rare event that forces it on a schedule the founder does not set. The test showed me precisely which parts of the company had real owners and which parts had been held together by my personal attention, and that knowledge has outlasted the orders themselves.

Every founder eventually gets pulled away, whether by a health crisis, a family emergency or another distraction. And usually with less warning than the Navy gave me. A reservist is simply a founder who receives the test in writing and is obligated to prepare for it in advance.

My civilian work involves identifying foreign influence campaigns as they move through American online conversation, so I have never thought of military service and company building as entirely separate worlds. The numbers say people who hold both roles are becoming rare.

Fewer than 1% of Americans serve in uniform today, across the more than 1.2 million on active duty and the roughly 800,000 of us in the reserve components. The veteran share of new entrepreneurs fell from 12.3% in 1996 to about 6% by 2011. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York has found that veteran-owned businesses have a harder time accessing capital than comparable companies. In my own fundraising conversations my reserve commitment has come up, politely and more than once, as a key-person risk. We announced a $7 million seed round in October, and we are not raising now.

I understand the instinct, since the investors asking are stewards of other people’s money, but I believe they are mispricing what they see. A founder who maintains a reserve commitment practices the one discipline most companies pay consultants to simulate, which is the readiness to hand the operation to someone else on short notice.

There is an obvious objection here, and it deserves a straight answer: a chief executive who can be ordered away at any time is a genuine operational risk, and no board should pretend otherwise. My own orders proved as much, because the company absorbed real disruption in those weeks. But the risk of losing a CEO exists at every company in some form.

The reservist is the only leader required to prepare for it before it arrives, and that preparation is the difference between a disruption and a collapse. The cancellation, when it came, was a change in the Navy’s needs that I controlled no more than I had controlled the original orders. It changed nothing about the test, because by the time word came, the handover was complete and the company had already stood on that stage without me.

The company came out of October stronger than it went in, because the delegation we built under pressure has stayed in place. Other founders should run this drill before circumstances run it for them, starting with hiring leaders whose judgment they trust. Investors can help by changing what they read into a founder’s service record.

Veterans Day is approaching, and the tributes it brings are welcome, but the more useful form of gratitude would be to treat reserve service as evidence of operational discipline rather than a liability to be priced in.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/ford-rebi.title: This Ford sculptor has carved cars out of clay for 40 years. AI and VR just cut his work time in half
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/ford-rebi.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/ford-rebi.text:
John “Rex” Allen is 68, wears cowboy boots, a black baseball cap, and he’s spent four decades building life-size cars out of clay. These days he builds inside a virtual-reality headset, too.

He does his work upstairs at Ford Motor Company’s gleaming new headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan, where the bird sounds in the yard aren’t even real. Just over four miles away, the 109-year-old Rouge Plant looks much the way it did in the 1920s, except with 3D-printed parts patching the factory together and a “Green Roof” overhead that is one of the world’s largest.

The new Ford World HQ opened in November 2025 as a 21st-century expression of the Ford Rouge logic, according to Ford Land CEO Jim Dobleske. World HQ stacks modern teams vertically the way Henry Ford stacked steel and assembly at the Rouge. It used to take 30 minutes to move a car from one end of the old design center to the other; now it takes “just over three minutes.” The birdsong in the courtyard is piped in, predator calls included, to keep Michigan’s ever-present geese away from workers wolfing down their lunches. “Those are not real birds,” Dobleske said, “that’s all fake.”

Fortune visited Ford in 1947 to document the “rebirth” of the company, when founder Henry Ford died and his grandson, Henry Ford II, was leading the postwar modernization of the iconic American manufacturer. Nearly eight decades later, Detroit as a whole is 13 years on from its historic bankruptcy process, but General Motors was the only member of the “Big Three” auto firms to post a net profit in 2025.

All three OEMs, or original equipment manufacturers, announced major pullbacks in their electric-vehicle strategies in 2025 as the federal government scrapped subsidies, prompting Ford CEO Jim Farley to (accurately) predict that the EV market would be cut in half as a result. In December, Ford announced about $19.5 billion in charges and pivoted to another rebirth: a race against the calendar.

Upstairs at Ford World HQ, Allen is looking at his clay cars, his monitors, his plastic models and his virtual reality glasses.

The Ford modeling studio is massive, with ceilings 25 to 30 feet high and a wide-open, blank space that feels like an empty Hollywood studio, awaiting a Gilmore Girls set or a replica of the Titanic.

Allen, with his thin white mustache complementing his mane of white hair, is doing what he’s always done: building cars out of clay.

Like most Michiganders who still work in auto manufacturing, Allen has an unimpressed air about his remarkable, unusual career. Asked how he joined the ranks of elite auto sculptors, he explains that he felt forced into it by fear of automation. “I used to be a machinist, and then it started becoming robotic, so I got out of that business real quick.” He reasoned that he’d always been a “bit of an artist,” and in high school loved comic books and cars and ran a side hustle airbrushing the “Rat Fink” mascot and other Kustom Kulture motifs onto T-shirts for other kids. Sort of a Mickey Mouse by way of R. Crumb, Rat Fink was a neon-green rodent mascot that exemplified the proto-punk vibes of Southern California car culture of the 1960s, but Allen said his tastes also ran a bit less gonzo — he used to carve Disney characters out of wood and clay for extra credit in art class, along with watercolors and oil paintings for extra credit in art class. “I made good money in high school,” Allen shrugs. “I loved doing that stuff.”

He didn’t set out to become a clay-man, either. “Somebody told me they created cars out of clay,” he explains, “which I had no idea of, so he introduced me to a guy that owned a business. And I mean, I fell right into it.” Allen recalled that he “tried it once” and the results spoke for themselves. He was 26 and soon found himself working 100 hours a week, pulling down roughly $100,000 a year.

Allen wasn’t in-house at Ford, then. At that time, Detroit had a dense web of small model shops that handled overflow work for the Big 3 — Ford, General Motors and Chrysler (now Stellantis), along with their suppliers — and Allen worked at a half-dozen of them. Work was steady. “You could grab a job any day of the week in one of these places,” he said, recalling that he worked on the original concept for the Dodge Viper at a Chrysler satellite studio. He’s now been at Ford for 24 years.

So, why clay? Allen and his colleagues, Nick Navarro, Shawn Fairall and Michael Smith, explained that it’s been that way for nearly a century. “Having the physical property in front of you to have the conversation with multiple people has always been a key part of the process,” Fairall said. “There’s always kind of this general misconception that computers have taken over car design,” Fairall said. “Clay has never really gone away.”

Smith, who leads research and development for Ford’s design team, always describes it to interns the same way. “We don’t sell pretty pictures of cars,” he said. “We sell vehicles.” He said a director might look at the clay and say, “you need to pull this back three more inches.”

It used to take about two weeks for one modeler to sculpt one full-size model, Allen said, and every change meant more weeks of work to do by hand. About six years ago, that changed with virtual reality and 3D printing. Now Allen can knock out a design’s theme in five days.

Allen said he’s seen a lot of upgrades in 40-odd years. First came “sweeps,” templates that modelers could drag along a car’s side. “That was a wow factor there for a while,” Allen said. Then came machines that could map the body, cut pieces out of it, and eventually shape an entire side. Now the team can rough out a car in clay, scan it in about 20 minutes, put on a headset to refine the shape digitally, and have a mill carve out the new surface over a few shifts, then continue working the surface by hand for the finishing touches. They call it hybrid sculpting. “This one is leaps and bounds,” Allen said, “further than anything we’ve ever done.”

“Because of technology, we’ve reduced the people over the years, so there’s less and less of us,” Allen said, adding, “we still have the same amount of work.” He said he thought this “virtual reality way of working would help keep us employed, basically, and it seems like it has, because we’re able to flip more designs now because of it.”

Those saved weeks matter because of what Ford is trying to pull off.

So what is the shape of the new Ford being born? The answer is in four parts. Ford sold about 650,000 fewer vehicles in the U.S. than GM last year, yet brought in slightly more revenue: $187.3 billion to $185 billion. The difference is mainly Ford Pro, the commercial arm that sells trucks and vans to businesses and governments earned $6.8 billion before interest and taxes in 2025 at a 10.3% margin. That’s more than double the earnings of Ford Blue, the gas and hybrid business, which made $3 billion, while the EV unit called Model e, lost $4.8 billion.

Kumar Galhotra, Ford’s chief operating officer, explained to Fortune how Ford’s next plan for Model e started with a skunkworks operation in California. “We tore down multiple Chinese OEM vehicles,” he said. “It was clear that because of the labor advantage and certain subsidies and battery areas, that their batteries are cheaper than ours.” So the team stopped trying to win on battery cost and designed around a smaller battery instead, with cleverer aerodynamics, fewer frictional losses and more efficient motors. “In the end, we’re pretty much equal in total system cost,” he said of Ford’s projection against China’s BYD, calling it “first principles thinking.”

The first vehicle on Ford’s new Universal EV platform is the Fathom, a $28,350 midsize electric pickup due in 2027. Ford says it will be able to send more than 10 kilowatts into a house during a blackout without the expensive wall-mounted inverter the F-150 Lightning needed. Asked how Ford makes money on that, a spokesperson said: “We see it as a compelling reason to buy Fathom.”

The rebirth includes a brand new business, Ford Energy, built to get a return on the billions Ford has sunk into batteries. By around March of 2025, veteran executive Lisa Drake could see that her battery plants just “weren’t full,” but Ford had already licensed lithium-iron-phosphate cells from China’s CATL and was building batteries in Marshall, Michigan. The same chemistry turned out to be close to ideal for energy storage for utilities and power developers racing to meet demand from data centers and an aging grid. “We actually were very fortunate,” Drake told Fortune. “I had a license for the best tech on the planet and the right tech for storage.”

In December, the board gave her $2 billion to start Ford Energy and she is retooling a Kentucky plant that used to make F-150 Lightning batteries, reusing about 30% to 40% of the equipment, with production set to begin in late 2027. The target customers are utilities, renewable energy developers and even data centers and hyperscalers, which don’t buy batteries directly but need power.

It’s part of Ford’s giant race against the calendar — Galhotra said Ford will end up “refreshing about 80% of our North American portfolio” between 2027 and 2029. And that’s where Rex Allen comes in. Every week saved in the clay studio will get to that refresh quicker.

Allen isn’t the only unlikely face of innovation at Ford. Over the river in Dearborn, another wears a giant Luigi-shaped mustache. His name is Greg Foresi.

The Ford Rouge Plant shows its age in a good way — a living museum, the first fully integrated auto factory in the world, still turning out cars in minutes through a century-old assembly line. And walking around, like a friendly engineer beat cop, is Foresi, the 3D-printing guy.

Foresi, who wears the horn-rimmed glasses of a Buddy Holly or a young Elvis Costello, got his signature look when he shaved off his eight-inch beard to play Luigi to a friend’s Mario one Halloween. When “mustache guy” shows up, he takes random requests from nearly everyone on the factory floor. That’s because he manages the 3D-printing lab, where roughly a dozen machines whirr away, steadily adding to nearly 300 tools and components in Foresi’s database, including about 50 individual socket covers.

“I’m out on the floor all day talking to people, trialing tools, evaluating equipment,” said the 35-year-old Foresi. Sometimes he gets five requests in one day, and sometimes nothing for five days. Foresi and his team point me toward a factory-floor wheel that isn’t black like the other ones, but a bright royal blue. This is a specialized part that filled a gap in availability during a supply-chain disruption. When Foresi saw the shortage coming, he printed his own.

Foresi explained that they didn’t have time to test the part. The choice was either trying the blue wheel and potentially creating a line stoppage — or not trying and definitely creating a stoppage. Some versions of the wheel failed, but Foresi said iterative improvements were made. “We avoided the problem entirely,” he said. Galhotra explained that Ford makes a new F-150 every 54 seconds at the plant, making Foresi’s blue wheel a hugely important component, but also not inherently scalable.

“One of the most radical things about 3D printing is that it decentralizes your logistics,” Foresi said. Galhotra put the limits plainly, saying that right now it’s “good for patches here and there,” like when a part is back-ordered or only can be flown in from somewhere else. Foresi agrees: “It’s not remotely close to replacing our conventional supply chain,” he said, adding that he gets “crazy requests” he has to turn down constantly. Some people think 3D printing is a joke, and other people “think that you can just 3D-print anything.”

Foresi had his own doubts at first. After stints at a supplier and a Ford stamping plant in Kansas City, he landed at the Dearborn truck plant as the only mechanical engineer in the final assembly department — ”a pretty intense job,” he said. “I’ve seen everything in the plant break and fixed everything,” Foresi said, recalling a line of people always waiting outside his cubicle. So when his talent was recognized as a fit for 3D printing (his “boss’ boss asked,” he said), his first instinct, like Allen’s, was fear for his job. His first instinct was that the job wouldn’t last, that 3D printing would lose favor and he’d be moved to a new role.

“I was worried that it was just a fad with the company and that it would lose energy and I would get laid off or something,” Foresi said. “They were like, ‘Too bad, you’re doing it anyway.’” Foresi hastened to add that he never felt pushed into taking the job or truly feared that he would be laid off; but he did think he might get reassigned. “After two or three months it became clear both to management and myself that printing was becoming so useful that a full-time position was needed.”

Mike Aragon and Alicia Boler Davis are both newcomers to Ford’s C-suite. The two Amazon veterans said have grown close, Aragon said, as their teams depend on each other and they bond over similar big-tech career transitions. Aragon recalls showing up for a leadership meeting five minutes late and CEO Jim Farley turning to him and saying, “Hey Mike, I want you to take on this AI initiative.” Boler Davis, a Detroiter who spent nearly 25 years working at GM before seven years out of manufacturing, said her return was like “drinking out of a firehose” and that she’s still “relearning the language, learning the culture.”

Boler Davis described the services and efficiencies that come from her use of smart data connected to a nationwide fleet and said she’s working toward a Ford Pro that can predict when a car will need a repair, or provide AI-enhanced advice to customers. As president of Ford Integrated Services, Aragon leads the teams that develop and scale digital products. “This is another reinvention on top of the reinvention that we already had to do,” he told Fortune.

At the Ford Accelerate event in Detroit in late September, Farley described to Fortune during a media briefing how Ford Pro actually uses AI to help dealership technicians, citing the example of an engine removal from a Ford Super Duty truck. “It’s like a two-day job” to take apart a Super Duty, he said, and AI is invaluable in walking customers through the process. “We are using AI for them to say, ‘Okay, do this, do that,’” he said. “They’re good mechanics, they just don’t know. They’ve never done it before.”

Galhotra was more measured about how far Ford has to go. There’s the AI that software companies talk about, on the one hand, and then “AI that’s going to change factories of how we build physical things, and in that second category, I haven’t seen really good execution yet. And even ourselves, we’re at the beginning of that journey.”

Boler Davis said some of Ford Pro’s fleet customers have pushed back. “We have some customers that, you know, don’t want you monitoring the vehicle or connected or don’t want to use the AI,” she said. Stressing that the cost of downtime can be hundreds, even thousands of dollars per vehicle on a given day, she said Ford Pro wants to empower fleet managers to help unlock the potential for their business. The tool isn’t to “get rid of the fleet manager,” she said, but to “make their job easier.”

Part of Ford’s pull for Aragon is personal. He said he remembers being driven to school in his grandfather’s 1963 F-100 truck. “I just remember the smell, which is like the smell of the nylon, and the dust — and then the Camels [cigarettes].” He said he’s planning to rebuild a model from the early ‘70s, which he’s planning to drive to work every day.

He’s not the only one at Ford with a project in the garage. Fairall restores old Volkswagens — he’s finished an ‘84 Westfalia Bus and is working on a ‘65 Split Window Bus. Allen is building his own car on the side, and he’s 3D-printing its front end. Asked whose intellectual property that makes it, Allen immediately responds, “It’s my car. “

Allen once feared the future enough to steer his son away from clay, though. Years ago, he brought his son, Derek, into a satellite studio and paid Derek to work six hours a day for him. “He started heading down this path,” Allen said, “he was getting pretty good at it. But I wanted him to be much more than just a modeler because I was worried about where modeling was going.” He steered him into engineering instead. “I always thought virtual reality would be there, but not in my lifetime,” he said. “I didn’t think I’d be part of it exactly.”

Allen says he thought he was ready to retire eight years ago, but now he’s excited to train the next generation of modelers in both virtual reality and clay. “I’m very excited about this whole chapter in my life,” he said. “I hop out of bed in the morning so I can come to work.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/detroit-c.title: Detroit’s innovation lesson: what kids hear about careers vs. what they actually do
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/detroit-c.author: Anika Goss, Angelique Power
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/detroit-c.text:
Some of America’s most influential leaders will soon gather in Detroit for the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum to discuss innovation, the pace of change and what it takes to compete. In classrooms across the same city, the workers their companies will need a decade from now are hearing about careers they may never get to try.

When Detroit Future City and The Skillman Foundation surveyed 83 young Detroiters in 2025 about career exposure, 78 percent said they had heard from a guest speaker or professional mentor. Fewer than half had done an internship or paid work experience. Just 35 percent had received hands-on training.

Detroit’s teenagers are not short on talk about work. They are short on chances to do it.

Jordan, a composite of students in our focus groups, shows what that costs. At 14, she loved sketching buildings, rooms and imagined cities. But no one suggested her interests might point toward a career in architecture or design. She discovered architecture years later, by accident, and realized there were pathways she could have explored in middle school.

Her story is common. A student who loved performing did not learn about physical therapy until nearly graduating. A true crime enthusiast had no idea criminology was a career. Students in skilled trades programs wished they had discovered those opportunities earlier.

Some youth are best suited for college, while others may pursue careers directly after high school. Both need opportunities to explore options and find a path forward.

Across the country, employers report trouble finding the right skills and experience. In a 2025 U.S. Chamber of Commerce survey, just 38 percent of hiring managers said finding candidates with the right skills was easy; 37 percent said the same about experience. The report, produced with the College Board, also found that 84 percent believe most high school graduates are not workforce-ready.

That points to a blind spot. Workforce programs focus on the late stages: choosing a major, enrolling in training, applying for a job. By then, young people like Jordan have already formed assumptions about which careers exist and where they belong.

Our May 2026 report, which Skillman funded, started with young people themselves: surveys and focus groups with nearly 200 Detroit youth, along with conversations with educators, employers and community leaders.

What we heard was consistent: Young people want earlier career exposure, mentors to explain different pathways and opportunities to connect school with the world beyond it. They are not asking adults to decide their futures. They want the possibilities to be more visible and accessible.

That is not just a Detroit challenge. According to NAF’s 2025–2026 Student Survey, 47 percent of students who did not participate in work-based learning cited a lack of awareness of available opportunities. Meanwhile, 79 percent of students who participated said those experiences helped them identify and develop skills for their future careers.

Exposure alone is not enough. In Detroit, talk is plentiful and practice is scarce.

Businesses can build on Career and Technical Education programs by offering workplace exposure, mentors, internships, apprenticeships and other forms of work-based learning. These experiences help students test their interests, build skills and understand career requirements.

Apprenticeships show the payoff. According to the U.S. Department of Labor, more than 800,000 people participate in apprenticeship programs annually nationwide. And the department’s April 2026 ApprenticeshipUSA fact sheet reports that 93 percent of apprentices who complete their programs retain employment, demonstrating the value of connecting education with hands-on experience and career opportunities.

Business cannot do this alone; educators, workforce organizations, higher education, philanthropy and community partners all have roles. The goal is to help young people see their options, not steer them toward one path.

Detroit Public Schools Community District’s High School Redesign strengthens connections between education, career exploration and life after graduation. Beginning in the 2026–27 school year, it expands advising, academic supports and college- and career-connected experiences across neighborhood high schools.

Henry Ford Health’s RYSE MED program offers another example, providing hands-on opportunities to explore careers in medicine and health care. From 2022 to 2026, the program enrolled 120 high school students, including 45 who attended DPSCD schools.

If businesses want stronger pipelines tomorrow, they cannot wait until students graduate to begin building them. They need to become visible earlier, in classrooms, in after-school programs, in summer internships, in middle schools, through meaningful opportunities for young people to learn by doing.

Detroit’s executives will spend the Forum talking about innovation. The students in the city around them are already hearing plenty. What they need is the chance to try the work, and business can give it to them.

Names and some identifying details have been changed to protect the privacy of youth research participants. Jordan is a composite based on real focus group accounts from the authors’ research and does not depict any one participant’s account verbatim.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/ai-insura.title: Baldwin Group CEO: The biggest AI disruption in insurance is the advisor
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/ai-insura.author: Trevor Baldwin
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/ai-insura.text:
Artificial intelligence is going to disrupt insurance brokerage. There is not much question about that. The question that matters is what gets disrupted, and how differently firms are preparing for it.

Most firms are approaching AI the way they approached every prior wave of technology: take the work as it exists and do it faster. But AI is dramatically changing the economics of gathering information, comparing coverage and facilitating transactions. A firm whose value lives in those activities is competing in a race to the bottom.

A firm built on specialized expertise, deep client relationships and experiential human judgment can change the paradigm, turning risk into opportunity for clients. Firms that make that leap go from being a vendor of downside protection to a business partner that helps a client achieve the fullness of their ambition. Their value becomes constrained only by what their clients can achieve.

Showing up that way requires the fortitude to completely rebuild how the work gets done. At Baldwin, alongside our partners at Dell Family Office and Sequence Holdings, we have launched into that journey. We call it Refounding.

Consider a middle-market renewal: gather exposure data, prepare the submission, market it, compare quotes, build the proposal, and present. Weeks of cycle time, most of it waiting on the next hand-off. Apply AI to each step and you compress each one a little. Redesign the work around what AI does well and you compress the entire cycle, and you hand the recovered time back to the client advisor for the only parts a client will pay a premium for: understanding the business, anticipating what could go wrong and structuring solutions that unlock potential.

That is the work underway through Catalyst, our firm-wide transformation program. Over 17 weeks, we completed more than 47,000 AI-assisted tasks at quality rates above 98 percent while standardizing 27 processes in our Client Experience teams. Those numbers matter only for what they free up: capacity redeployed into advisory work, not simply banked as cost savings.

Three things happen when you make that shift. Cycle times compress meaningfully. Throughput rises because the same team carries more complexity. And complex knowledge work gets sharper. In one early claims-review application, AI identified coverage gaps in minutes that led to $71,000 in additional claim payment for a client. A professional still had to evaluate what the technology surfaced and decide what to do. That is the model: technology ingests and processes; the human provides the judgment; and experienced professionals remain accountable for every decision that carries real financial consequences for a client.

AI drives the marginal cost of information toward zero, and when information is free, the premium shifts to what you do with it. Clients will have more data than ever. What they will not have is someone who has seen 200 versions of their problem, who knows which carrier will actually show up when a claim is contested, and who will tell them the uncomfortable truth about a coverage gap before the loss rather than after. That is judgment, earned through experience. The relationship that lets a client hear that perspective and act on it with conviction is earned the same way.

It is also why insurance advice has to move earlier in the conversation. Too often, insurance enters the discussion after the consequential decisions about risk have been made. With AI compressing the mechanics, the best advisors will move upstream into the room where those decisions happen, helping clients understand how risk affects their investments, their capital and their growth. That is where the advisor’s value was always supposed to live. The transactional work got in the way.

For generations, early-career insurance professionals built judgment by doing the foundational work: reviewing policies, preparing submissions and sitting beside experienced colleagues. That apprenticeship was never efficient, but it worked. AI will eliminate the tasks it is built on. Remove those tasks and do nothing else, and we will produce a generation of advisors who can operate the tools but cannot challenge them. Judgment comes from working through hard situations, seeing the consequences of decisions and learning from people who have been there before. We have to redesign the apprenticeship for a world where the old on-ramp no longer exists.

At Baldwin, we are transforming how we work, and early-career colleagues are among the first to benefit. They now encounter real client challenges sooner than the traditional path allowed. We have begun retooling our internal university, The Azimuth Institute, using AI as a training environment where a new advisor can pressure-test a coverage program, or ask why a senior colleague structured a placement a certain way, and get a substantive answer in seconds. Because AI absorbs time-consuming tasks, these colleagues are now beginning to learn higher-level insurance concepts earlier and spend more time on client relationships and complex coverage questions. We are also committed to more structured mentorship, not less, because experienced advisors are best placed to teach how to rigorously interrogate what the technology produces. And we are rethinking performance: when a day’s work takes an hour, the question is no longer how fast a task was completed, but how well the day was spent on problem-solving and critical thinking for client solutions.

Five years from now, the role of the insurance advisor will look substantially different, and I expect the advisors who meet that moment to be more valuable than any generation before them, because what they bring is the one thing the technology cannot: experience, judgment and a relationship the client trusts.

The firms that win will not be the ones that focus on AI purely to drive efficiencies. They will be the ones that changed the work, then built the people who could do the new work well. That is the work in front of us, and we intend to get it done.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/senate-ba.title: Senate Banking Committee asks Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify over ‘significant national security concerns’ next month, or face subpoenas
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/senate-ba.author: Eleanor Pringle
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/senate-ba.text:
Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have been asked to appear before the U.S. Senate Banking Committee next month to address national security concerns.

Senator Tim Scott (R-SC), who leads the committee, confirmed overnight that Huang and Lutnick have been asked to appear on December 3.

“Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” he said. “The American people deserve answers.”

Senator Scott’s letter added a weighty conclusion: If either fails to appear before the committee voluntarily, it is “prepared to use all tools at our disposal, including subpoenas, to conduct this legitimate and necessary oversight.”

The Banking Committee hearing is the latest in a series of inquiries into the conduct of Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia. Huang resigned from the company he’s spent the past 30 years building after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Reports have since surfaced that Huang had an affair with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. Reuters reported yesterday that the entrepreneur had a second affair with a member of staff, quoting unnamed sources.

Nvidia’s CFO, Colette Kress, has been named interim CEO following his resignation.

President Trump told reporters earlier this week that the FBI is investigating the affair between Huang and Alice Huang (no relation), the alleged Chinese spy. China has denied its involvement. Nvidia’s board has also said it is conducting its own independent investigation and has hired Joon H. Kim, former acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to lead the review.

Senator Scott laid bare the Senate Banking Committee’s authority to request both Huang and Lutnick, a member of the president’s cabinet, to appear before it. His letter to Huang says the committee has “jurisdiction over matters relating to ‘export controls,’ including their application to NVIDIA’s exports of advanced semiconductors.”

The committee is “seeking answers to questions that raise grave national security concerns,” it added in a post on X.

Chairman @SenatorTimScott has requested that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang appear on December 3 and Commerce Secretary Lutnick on December 10.

The Committee oversees advanced semiconductor export controls and is seeking answers to questions that raise grave national security concerns. https://t.co/HpSxJH213J

Members of the committee have suggested Lutnick had allowed loopholes to persist that allowed high-end chips to continue to be sold to China.

Senator Jim Banks (R-IN) told Fox News last night that he believed Lutnick had “defied President Trump’s directive not to sell these high-end chips to China or to allow them to be sold to Chinese customers, that ended up happening anyway.”

“Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military,” added Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), currently the ranking member on the committee.

Huang is also likely to face disbelief from Senator John Kennedy (R-LA). Senator Kennedy told CNN in an interview last night: “I’m not naive; I’m not Bambi’s baby brother. I know people have affairs; I wouldn’t recommend it, but if you do, you ought to make sure it’s not with a Chinese spy. I mean, check their LinkedIn page for God’s sake.”

Senator Kennedy referred to the debacle as an “intergalactic freak show,” adding: Here’s a man, head of one of the most powerful companies in the world, more than anybody else in the private sector; he’s been making AI policy for America, and certainly with respect to our relationship with China. And then we learn about this.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/dusquesne.title: Duquesne’s Michael Buckley says young investors skip over learning these critical skills. They could prove to be invaluable in the AI boom
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/dusquesne.author: Emma Burleigh
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/dusquesne.text:
As investors race to identify the next big winners in the AI boom, standing out requires more than just spotting the next breakthrough. Michael Buckley, managing director and head of equities at investment firm Duquesne Family Office, says young investors often overlook the fundamentals of corporate finance. In the age of AI, that could give them an edge.

Buckley has built a diverse investing résumé. He’s worked across private equity, venture capital, and public equities—and his early days in debt and credit helped set him apart. Right after graduating from Harvard, Buckley learned the ropes of accounting and corporate finance at Sankaty Advisors, the now-renamed credit arm of private equity giant Bain Capital. With credit as the focus, Buckley poured himself into capital and corporate structures, as well as bonds and loans. His responsibilities unwittingly set him up to be recruited for one of America’s top private investment firms.

“I learned the importance of things like capital structure and debt, which I think a lot of people—for example, that start out their career in things like equities—oftentimes will skip that stuff over,” Buckley tells Fortune. “It’s because it’s tedious and it can be complicated,” he added.

Early-career analysts who have their heads buried in stock charts, earnings growth, and revenue projections could get a leg-up by returning to those basics. There’s a simple reason: The AI boom hinges on debt. Buckley explains that in this new ecosystem, debt is suddenly very important not only to distressed debt companies, but also to public markets and venture firms. As AI companies and their infrastructure partners take on more borrowing to finance data centers, chips, and computing capacity, investors need to assess how quickly a business might grow—and whether they can afford to pay back what they owe. It particularly stands out for those involved in data centers or funding next-generation labs, Buckley adds; tech hyperscalers issued more than $100 billion in corporate bonds last year, according to the Bank for International Settlements.

Buckley recognizes that doors opened thanks to his debt and credit expertise. During his two-year stint as an analyst at private equity firm CPMG, a headhunter came calling; Duquesne was looking to hire a credit and equities wiz to work under the family office’s founder and leader, legendary macro investor Stanley Druckenmiller, whose claim to fame was helping George Soros make $1 billion betting against the British pound in 1992. He joined as an analyst at 27.

Today, at Duquesne, he’s steering some of the firm’s biggest wins. Over the past 11 years he’s leaned into investments in AI, as well as healthcare and biotech—which he believes will vastly innovate over the next decade. Recently, Buckley says the firm backed pharma company Formation Bio. As a self-proclaimed “non-dogmatic” investor, he’s continuing to keep his horizons open, a philosophy shared by Druckenmiller: Keeping a broad perspective on the market—and a set of skills to meet the moment—could mean the difference between spotting an opportunity or missing it entirely.

“Now, we’re seeing that in the AI venture world, these concerns about credit and interest rates suddenly have this big impact on AI infrastructure, private companies, and the venture community,” Buckley says. “I think it’s something I’ve learned from Stan, to always be thinking about the top-down and the bottom-up.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/inside-th.title: Inside the dismal final days of Jensen Huang: a broken man heard saying things like ‘whatever’ and ‘I don’t care’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/inside-th.author: Jim Edwards
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/inside-th.text:
We’re getting some extraordinary reporting on what it has been like inside Nvidia during Huang’s last days. Before his forced resignation, Huang had given up, Bloomberg says, and was heard saying things like “whatever,” “I don’t care,” and referring to himself as a “piece of sh--.”

That, of course, was in stark contrast to how Huang historically ran the company. Huang had “imperial control,” and ran it like a “feudal system,” according to the FT. “I can’t tell you what a cult this place is,” a source told the paper. General counsel Tim Teter wore a leather jacket just like Huang’s, the source said: “Jensen is a god, and that’s how he’s worshipped.”

Noteworthy: In addition to having no board chair, the company also did not have a compliance officer, the FT says.

Interim CEO Colette Kress and whoever replaces her as permanent CEO will have messy office politics to deal with, according to the FT. Huang’s daughter Madison Huang is a senior director of marketing at the company, but she acts like her father’s de facto chief of staff, the FT says. Nvidia also employs her husband Nico Caprez and Huang’s son Spencer.

Kress, meanwhile, sometimes did not get Huang’s respect, the WSJ reported. He once called her “a deer in the headlights” and a “reporting CFO” (as opposed to a strategic leader) during a meeting in which they were discussing Nvidia’s agreements “to provide billions of dollars of guarantees to companies that couldn’t afford its chips,” the WSJ said.

Kress struggled to rein in Caprez, who had made multiple offers of financing to cloud providers and data-center builders in return for shares of revenue.

Lenders relied on the Huang family's backing for AI financing when structuring deals with AI providers. Without Huang at the top, “that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago, that puts those neocloud businesses at risk,” Joe Kaiser of Switchyard Partners, an AI financing company, told Fortune’s Catherina Gioino.

Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and commerce secretary Howard Lutnick have been called by Sen. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) to testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee, the NYT reports. The hearing will be conducted next month. “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” Scott said.

That’s a reference to Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company that bought Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling them into China in violation of U.S. export controls.

As for Lutnick, Republicans are furious at what they perceive was the special treatment he gave Nvidia in terms of its access to the Chinese market and in his foot-dragging on the enforcement of export bans to China, the FT says.

Lutnick shielded Nvidia from the White House’s attempts to restrict export of the U.S.’s best technology to China, the NYT reported.

All matters related to Nvidia were routed through a deputy to Lutnick, Jeff Kessler, who rarely took action without Lutnick’s approval, the NYT said.

Inside the White House, senior Trump administration figures largely blame Lutnick for being asleep at the wheel in terms of the threat Nvidia posed to national security, given its ties to Chinese importers, the WSJ reported.

​​Alice Huang: Those concerns will get extra momentum on the news that Jensen Huang’s affair partner, suspected spy Alice Huang (no relation) of Megaspeed, had a relationship with Huawei, China’s biggest competitor in China, according to CNBC.

Alice Huang allegedly ran a complicated network of companies to do deals with Nvidia that resulted in its chips ending up at Chinese companies, per Bloomberg.

Before Megaspeed, there was Supermicro: The other Nvidia partner tied to China chip smuggling—and to Jensen Huang - Amanda Gerut

CFOs face a tough choice on AI spending as borrowing costs rise, expert warns - Sheryl Estrada

Nvidia shares fell 4.34% yesterday but gained 1.84% overnight as some traders bet on the dip. S&P 500 futures were flat this morning after the index fell yesterday. It’s looking like another difficult day for stock investors, as the price of oil ticked up and markets largely fell across Asia and Europe.

This chart shows how traders are rotating out of tech stocks into non-tech companies. The S&P 500 “equal weight” index (which nominally tracks each stock as if it were valued equally) is up 15% this year. By contrast, the real S&P 500—heavily skewed by the massive market caps of tech companies—is up only 11%.

This chart visualizes what stocks retail traders—meaning individual investors, not institutions—are buying and selling on a month-by-month basis in the S&P 500. Arun Jain and his colleagues at JPMorgan broke it out into Magnificent Seven tech stocks, an “AI 30” set of stocks linked to AI, and the S&P 470—all the non-tech companies.

Perhaps the most interesting trend is that retail traders clearly lost interest in non-tech stocks somewhere in 2022.

One central question about the Anthropic IPO is: how can this company grow revenue if its product prices—as measured via tokens—are in a race to the bottom? Turns out that piling it high and selling it cheap works in AI the same way it works in groceries, as these charts from Alpine Macro’s Noah Ramos show.

“While token prices have declined dramatically, overall customer spending continues to scale. This reflects both users extracting more intelligence per unit of compute and inference optimizations that make it economically viable to consume substantially more tokens. Lower token prices are expanding consumption rather than reducing spending,” he said in a note.

—Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives, expressing the head-spinning pace at which Jensen Huang went from indispensable founder to excess baggage at his own company, Nvidia. “The old Jensen, the black leather jacket, the Godfather of AI, the rock star viewed as the face of the AI boom, is over and in the past; his value to the company pre and post this week is dramatically different, and the board did what we said it needed to do, which is rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him after this dark moment for Jensen and Nvidia.”

Ives also has an eyebrow-raising suggestion for who could replace Huang as CEO: Apple’s Tim Cook. He could be “a dark horse candidate in our view given the global importance of Nvidia to the overall U.S. tech industry.” The proposal makes sense given that Cook just retired as CEO of Apple, and although he is now its chairman, he does, in theory, have time on his hands. And frankly, who knows more than Cook about stewarding the most important tech company of its day to further success following the loss of an “irreplaceable” founder?

It goes without saying that the stakes are high. Remember what happened at HP and Intel, warn Wedbush’s Matt Bryson and Tuo Ma: “Both [HP’s] Mark Hurd and [Intel’s] Brian Krzanich departed their posts relatively abruptly following affairs with no clear successors in place. And for both Intel and HP, we believe these transitions played some role in disastrous periods that saw the companies lose their respective leadership positions in technology, with HP eventually breaking apart and Intel still struggling to prove it can regain the fab and chip design expertise it seemingly lost during its failed 10nm transition.” Ouch!

For decades, the markers of extreme wealth were easy to spot: the second home, the fancy cars, the Ivy League education. New analysis of Federal Reserve data points to a subtler one: a third child.

Mike Konczal, vice president of policy and research at the Economic Security Project and a former White House economist, studied households headed by 45- to 64-year-olds in his analysis of the Fed’s Survey of Consumer Finances, pooling five surveys from 2013 through 2025. He found that 49% of top-1% earners have three or more children, compared with about 40% of the rest of the top 10%.

Families with four or more kids are about as common in both groups, so the gap comes down to the third child: 34% of the 1% stop at exactly three, versus 24% of the merely affluent.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/hilton-ce.author: Diane Brady
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/hilton-ce.text:
Good morning. On one level, the best leadership strategies can sound obvious. “There’s nothing proprietary about it,” says Chris Nassetta, president and CEO of Hilton Worldwide. “It’s about grinding it out, investing in people, having the top-down purpose-driven north star, getting everyone unified, and doing the ground-up granular work. It’s about doing it and doing it and doing it and doing it. And then, when you-know-what hits the fan, it’s about continuing to live the values of the company.”

In a world of shorter cycles, faster innovation and an increased urgency to transform and adapt, Nassetta preaches the power of playing the long game. He became CEO of Hilton in 2007 and told me that transforming a fragmented hotel company into a cohesive high-performing culture took years. It has paid off as Hilton was just named the No. 1 World’s Best Workplace by Fortune and Great Place To Work for the third time and second consecutive year. Leadership, or the lack thereof, is top of mind. Running a founder-led tech company like Nvidia is obviously different from managing a people-centric global hospitality company like Hilton.

We’re paying a lot of attention this week to the perils of tech titans who make it all about themselves. Let’s also look at the playbook of a very different style of leader. We don’t just pick who gets on the Best Workplace list. It’s determined by data like employee engagement, where Hilton scored 93% in a company of more than 500,000 workers across 9,600 properties. And 93% of the leaders across those properties got their start in frontline jobs. They get training, perks, and opportunities to rotate in different roles.

What matters most is who’s in charge. Nassetta thinks a lot about the art and science and execution of leadership. He talks about the need for humility, agility and communicating a “vision in unique and different ways so that people feel part of something bigger than themselves.”

And of course he thinks about AI. “There’s so much money and time being spent trying to scare people as opposed to trying to educate people about where … the different possibilities are,” he told me. “AI, as well as other forms of technology we’ve used, have been tools that we can put in the hands of our frontline team members that help them do their job better, faster, easier.”

Is he replaceable? You bet. He believes building a bench of talent is part of the job, arguing “you take way too much risk trying to bring somebody in from the outside.”

And there’s no shortcut when it comes to listening, learning and building a great workplace. As with diet and exercise, it can take years to see the full results. “If you said to me, you have five years to ring the bell, high-five it, and you’ve totally rebuilt the culture, based on what I know now, I would have said, not possible,” he said. “It’s a marathon, not a sprint.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/ppi-infl.title: Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/ppi-infl.author: Jeff Cox
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/ppi-infl.text:
The producer price index, a measure of wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, slightly less than the 0.4% forecast.

On an annual basis, PPI surged 6.5%, the biggest increase since November 2022.

Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon.

The producer price index, which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.

Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations.

On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022.

The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve’s next policy meeting Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank’s key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike.

Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed.

Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected.

The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn’t collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI.

However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal.

“Today’s PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed’s approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.

Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump’s tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched.

“We’ve had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row,” Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. “If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it’s not just that we’re above the target and have been for some time. It’s that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you’re still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way.”

Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October.

Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022.

Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight.

“We’ve been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we’re not making any progress, and if anything, it’s going the wrong way,” Goolsbee said. “Inflation is rising; it’s it’s proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks.”

Other items in the PPI report also showed multi-year gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/us-infla.title: Bessent: Treasury has wanted Megaspeed restrictions for months, but Commerce is in charge
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/us-infla.author: Kevin Breuninger,Lim Hui Jie
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/us-infla.text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his department and others have long supported slapping restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce is in charge.

Jensen Huang, who just resigned as Nvidia CEO under a cloud of scandal, had pushed to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported slapping restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s spy-sex scandal.

But the Commerce Department is in charge, “and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent told CNBC’s “Squawk Box.”

The Cabinet secretary’s comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed.

Lutnick has “repeatedly stood in the way” of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported.

Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had “no such conversation” in the Situation Room.

Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, “We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room.”

But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all “were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months.”

Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, “I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s.”

“And so any leakage is very frustrating” because it “hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage,” he said.

Huang, seen as one of Trump’s closest corporate ally before resigning as Nvidia CEO under a cloud of scandal Thursday morning, had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales.
