https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.title: What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.author: Michelle Fox
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.text:
Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO raises questions about the company’s role in AI financing.

Investors are watching whether a leadership change alters Nvidia’s role in backing AI companies.

Smaller AI infrastructure companies may be more sensitive to any pullback in Nvidia’s support.

Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang’s departure hasn’t produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company’s role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

“Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point,” Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang’s resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can’t repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia’s 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.77%, nearly 6% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Thursday with the Nasdaq 100
 closing down 0.3% as markets digested the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Thursday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It’s the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave
, Nebius
 and IREN
 are all in Nvidia’s portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.75% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped 18% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia’s support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

“We don’t know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side,” he said.

“However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it’s likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate,” he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang’s departure, that Nvidia “is not one person.”

“There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking,” he said in an interview with “Squawk on the Street.” “They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us.”

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn’t see any big changes in terms of Nvidia’s relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

“Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they’re holding all the cards,” he said. “When they decide that the game is over, that’s it — it’s going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies.”

— CNBC’S Kif Leswing and Isabel O’Brien contributed reporting.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/trump-cu.title: Trump says he wants to ‘get Cuba done’ before leaving office, would consider military force
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/trump-cu.author: Sam Meredith
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/trump-cu.text:
Trump said he wants to “get Cuba done” before leaving office in 2029 and would “certainly consider” a short U.S. military operation.

The comments come as Washington intensifies economic pressure on Cuba, including new sanctions targeting oil tankers and shipping companies.

Cuba is grappling with severe fuel shortages, blackouts and economic strain, while analysts see further economic pressure as more likely than military action.

U.S. President Donald Trump has said he wants to “get Cuba done” before leaving office in 2029, adding that he would “certainly consider” military intervention against the communist-run Caribbean island.

In an interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, Trump said his administration was monitoring the situation in Havana “very closely” and described Cuba as a “failed” state.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump said. His comments marked the first time he has put a timeline on possible military intervention to topple Cuban authorities, according to Politico.

Trump said Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents are from Cuba, “would love to do it” and said he would “certainly consider” a short military operation.

It comes as the U.S. continues to enforce a comprehensive economic embargo against Cuba, a campaign which has contributed to a deepening energy and economic crisis on the island. Cuba has suffered repeated nationwide blackouts in recent months, as well as fuel and food shortages.

The Cuban Embassy in Washington, D.C., estimated on Thursday that the cost of the U.S. blockade to Cuba between March 2025 and February 2026 amounted to $8 billion.

Earlier this month, the Treasury Department imposed further sanctions on Cuban oil tankers and shipping companies and threatened to target any international entity or person doing business within its marine or maritime industries as part of a push “to end the Cuban regime’s malign activities, both in Cuba and across our hemisphere.”

In response, Cuba’s Embassy in Washington, D.C., said these steps “deepen an energy siege that already leaves hospitals without reliable power and families facing blackouts. The blockade is not targeted at a government. It is collective punishment that hits ordinary people every day.”

Trump has previously talked up the prospect of a “friendly takeover” of Havana and said the White House could turn its sights on Cuba after the Iran war. The U.S. president has also said he could do anything he wanted with the country, adding that he thinks he will have the “honor” of “taking Cuba.”

In May, Cuban Energy Minister Vicente de la O Levy said the country of roughly 10 million had run out of fuel oil and diesel, describing the country’s predicament as “extremely tense.”

Analysts have typically been skeptical about the prospect of a U.S. military campaign against Cuba, suggesting that further economic pressure against the island’s authorities appears more likely.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/us-seize.title: U.S. seizes $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/us-seize.author: Jenni Reid
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/us-seize.text:
DOJ said it obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance.

U.S. government and private-sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion of the more than $6 billion stolen from Binance on Oct. 29.

DOJ also disrupted cloud infrastructure tied to FaceStealer, a separate social-engineering campaign it says stole more than $400 million over 18 months.

U.S. authorities have seized around $1.2 billion in virtual assets stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last month, the Department of Justice said Thursday, as it vowed action to tackle cyberscams originating from North Korea.

Over $6 billion was stolen from industry giant Binance on Oct. 29, which the DOJ attributed to actors linked to the North Korean military.

Collective efforts between the U.S. government and private sector have resulted in more than $2.7 billion of that amount being frozen.

The FBI blames the attack, which shook confidence in crypto market security, on members of the North Korean military it refers to as “TraderTraitor.”

The DOJ said it was taking coordinated action against what it called the North Korean government’s “schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.”

That includes “the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance,” it said.

DOJ units, law enforcement partners and virtual asset service providers have been working to intercept the stolen assets.

But efforts to track and freeze the assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder them through various cryptocurrency channels.

Authorities have also seized cloud-based infrastructure used in a massive identity impersonation scam known as “FaceStealer,” which has seen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen over 18 months, the DOJ said.

The scheme sees hackers set up fake video meetings using stolen accounts and recordings of people known to the target by using AI-generated deepfakes. The hackers then say a technical problem requires a fix, install malware on a computer and take over the victim’s communications, steal their cryptocurrency and target their contacts — sometimes months or more than a year after the initial compromise.

Individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries are prime targets.

Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy, of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, called FaceStealer “a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user.”

“It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough,” Grandy added.

“North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said in a statement.

“America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/cnbcs-of.title: CNBC's Official NHL Team Valuations 2026: How the 32 franchises stack up
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/cnbcs-of.author: Michael Ozanian
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/cnbcs-of.text:
For the first time, hockey team valuations have crossed the $4 billion threshold.

CNBC’s NHL valuations are led by the Toronto Maple Leafs, at $5.4 billion, the New York Rangers, at $4.7 billion, and the Montreal Canadiens, at $4.1 billion.

The average NHL team is now worth $2.71 billion, 23% more than a year ago.

For the first time, hockey team valuations have crossed the $4 billion threshold, with CNBC’s NHL valuations led by the Toronto Maple Leafs, at $5.4 billion, the New York Rangers, at $4.7 billion, and the Montreal Canadiens, at $4.1 billion. The average NHL team is now worth $2.71 billion, 23% more than a year ago.

Don’t be fooled by the lone NHL control sale to close over the past 12 months: the $1.8 billion sale of the Pittsburgh Penguins to the Hoffmann family. Although the transaction was approved by the league in June, the price was negotiated about 18 months ago.

Look instead at the latest minority stake transactions. In March the NHL approved the sale of a 12.5% stake in the Carolina Hurricanes by Tom Dundon in a transaction that valued the team at $2.66 billion. Scott Malkin and other shareholders are close to selling a 15% stake in the New York Islanders at a $3 billion valuation. Sports bankers tell CNBC these deals are representative of what control stakes in the two teams would sell for given the hot market for sports teams.

“Like the other major sports leagues there is a strong demand to own hockey teams because their media content values are high and there is a scarcity of teams,” said Sal Galatioto, whose firm, Galatioto Sports Partners, advises clients on both the buy and sell sides of sports team transactions. “Capitalism and technology are creating more wealth and the NHL, like the NFL, NBA and MLB, is an industry with a very long product life cycle, a hedge against risk in AI.”

The NHL’s current national media rights deals with Walt Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery are worth a combined annual average of close to $650 million through the 2027-28 season, but given the league’s strong television ratings last season, a big increase could be in the offing.

“The 2025-26 NHL regular season averaged 546,000 viewers across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports, up 25% from last year and the highest average in more than a decade,” Sports Media Watch wrote. “The 25% increase is on the high end of a general rise in sports viewership that includes gains of 35% for the NBA, 19% for men’s college basketball and 10% for the NFL.”

Sports Media Watch also wrote that the 2026 NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs averaged 1.8 million viewers in the U.S. across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports. That’s up 68% from 2025, and it’s the highest average on record for the playoffs on American television, going back to 1994, it said.

The NHL is pondering adding teams in cities such as Houston and Atlanta, and another factor fueling NHL valuations is the belief that the expansion fees paid by the new teams would surpass $2 billion. The Seattle Kraken, the NHL’s most recent expansion team, paid a $650 million fee to join the league for the 2021-22 season.

According to CNBC’s figures, revenue for the league’s 32 teams averaged $257 million for the 2025-26 season, 6% more than the previous year, while EBITDA — earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — averaged $48 million per team, a decline of 11% due to arena expenses. The league’s profitability should rebound as money spent on hospitality, concessions and merchandise stores boosts revenue.

In April 2025 the NHL and Rogers Communications agreed to a 12-year national Canadian media rights deal worth $7.79 billion, based on exchange rates as of Nov. 24, that will begin with the 2026-27 season. That’s more than twice the amount the league is getting from its existing 12-year deal with Rogers. This will help push up the league’s hockey-related revenue — which includes media rights, sponsorships, premium seating, tickets, concessions and parking — to around $7.25 billion for the 2026-27 season, 7% more than last season.

CNBC’s Official NHL Team Valuations are current enterprise values — equity plus net debt — calculated using revenue multiples, and include the economics of the team’s arena, including non-NHL revenue that accrues to the team’s owner. The valuations are meant to represent what a control stake valuation would go for in an arm’s-length transaction and do not include the value of the arena or the real estate it sits on.

Revenue figures are net of revenue sharing and the 35% of home playoff non-premium gate revenue that goes toward the league’s revenue-sharing pool. Revenue multiples are based on historical transaction prices, as well as what investors, league executives and bankers say about the current market.

CNBC values exclude other businesses related to the teams with separate financial statements, such as the Edmonton Oilers’ mixed-use real estate project. For teams that sell their own merchandise, such as the Oilers, CNBC deducts the cost of goods sold from merchandise sales. Likewise, CNBC excludes the market value of affiliates/equity method investments to ensure consistent enterprise value-to-revenue and enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiples. Debt figures are the latest available and include both team debt and stadium debt.

CNBC incorporates the value of a pending new arena in our valuations if construction has begun and financing has been secured. For example, the $2.25 billion valuation for the Calgary Flames incorporates their new arena, which is scheduled to open in time for the 2027-28 season. Likewise, CNBC valuations anticipate a substantial increase in the NHL’s next U.S. national broadcasting deal, which would begin with the 2028-29 season.

Revenue and EBITDA figures are for the 2025-26 season and net of revenue sharing and player escrow. CNBC presents revenue and operating income figures on a cash basis, rather than an accrual basis. CNBC figures are different from the league’s official hockey-related revenue because we include non-NHL arena revenue that goes to the teams. When the owner of the arena also owns both the NHL team and NBA team that play in the same building — as is the case for several teams, including Toronto’s Maple Leafs and Raptors, who are both owned by Rogers Communications and play in Scotiabank Arena — we divide revenue from non-sports events held at the arena evenly between the two teams.

All valuation figures are in U.S. dollars. The exchange rate for revenue and EBITDA is based on a one-year average, from June 2025 to June 2026, of CA$1 = US$0.72, and the exchange rate for team values and debt, as of Sept. 21, is CA$1 = US$0.71.

Sources for CNBC’s Official NHL Team Valuations include team owners, investors and executives, as well as sports bankers and league consultants; public documents such as stadium lease agreements, stadium authority budget audits and credit rating reports; and sponsorship and broadcasting industry executives. Certain figures were provided by league executives who spoke to CNBC on the condition of anonymity because agreements are private and they do not have permission to speak about them publicly. Figures that could not be confirmed with sources are CNBC estimates.

— CNBC’s Jungwoo Ethan Kim contributed to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/canada-s.title: ‘We will sue them’: Canada threatens Stellantis as Trump trade war reshapes Jeep production plans
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/canada-s.author: Sam Meredith
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/canada-s.text:
Canada gave Stellantis 30 days to address alleged breaches of a federal funding agreement or face potential legal action.

The dispute escalated after Stellantis signed an agreement to sell its idled Brampton assembly plant to Canadian defense manufacturer Roshel.

A Stellantis executive said the company would return $24 million in federal support, while Ottawa says the automaker could owe hundreds of millions of dollars.

Canada has threatened to sue auto giant Stellantis
 over the planned sale of an idled assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario, alleging breaches of a federal funding agreement after the carmaker announced plans to shift production to the U.S. amid President Donald Trump’s trade war.

Speaking at a news conference on Thursday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the government had served Stellantis with a formal notice of default, giving the company 30 days to address its concerns or face legal action.

“We sent a notice of default and, basically, they have 30 days — or else, of course, we will sue them,” Joly told reporters in Toronto.

Joly said Stellantis had violated its contractual commitments to the Canadian government and the workers at Brampton by announcing an agreement to sell the plant to armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel earlier in the week. She added that the company was now “on the hook” for hundreds of millions of dollars over the move.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the situation at the Brampton plant as “unacceptable” and a “betrayal” of its workers.

The standoff comes as the U.S. and Canada remain locked in a bitter trade dispute, with Trump repeatedly putting pressure on automakers to move vehicle production south of the border.

Stellantis, which owns auto brands including Dodge, Fiat, Chrysler and Peugeot, had scrapped plans to build its Jeep Compass at the Brampton plant and shifted future production to a factory in Illinois amid U.S. auto tariffs and other market pressures.

Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley said in a statement shared with CNBC that the company would return $24 million it received in government support for the Brampton Assembly’s original retooling plan. This amount, however, falls significantly short of the Canadian government’s own estimate of what the company owes.

“We recognize the disappointment and uncertainty surrounding the future of the facility. While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use,” Longley said.

“As Canada’s largest automotive employer, this decision also allows Stellantis to focus its resources on sustaining competitive manufacturing operations in Canada in the face of challenging market realities,” he added.

Stellantis said Monday that it had agreed to sell the Brampton assembly plant to Roshel for an undisclosed amount.

It also acknowledged its obligations to employees at the facility and said it remains prepared to work with Unifor, Canada’s largest private sector union, to negotiate a settlement to assist union-represented employees.

Stellantis stock has fallen sharply since the start of the year, with its Milan-listed shares down more than 60% for 2026 so far.

— CNBC’s Michael Wayland contributed to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-n.title: Nvidia stock inches higher as investors continue to weigh Jensen Huang’s departure
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-n.author: Arjun Kharpal
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-n.text:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after coming under scrutiny for two extramarital affairs.

Nvidia shares hovered near the flatline in premarket trading on Friday.

Nvidia
 shares were slightly higher in premarket trading on Friday as investors navigate the fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation after reports of at least two affairs.

It follows a wild day for the stock on Thursday, which dropped sharply before recovering to close just over 4% lower.

Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia.

Huang was already under scrutiny following an investigation by the board into his relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.

Reuters reported on Thursday the existence of another affair with an Nvidia employee, which the news agency did not name. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request for comment.

Shares of Nvidia were 1.7% higher as of 8:13 a.m. ET.

Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that his departure could cost Nvidia as much as 20% of its market value, given how critical he has been to the company’s success. Nvidia’s stock is already down more than 20% over the last month.

A lot of the company’s success has been built around Huang, said Stephane Houri, head of equity research at ODDO BHF.

It’s about more than just Nvidia, but also about the “architecture of the AI industry that really depended on the vision” and expertise of Huang, Houri told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe” on Friday.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.title: Huang's downfall may undo cozy ties between business and government: analysis
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.author: Steve Liesman
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.text:
Jensen Huang’s exit and the recent election results could make corporate leaders more cautious about close public ties to the White House.

The two developments may also create pressure for increased regulation of companies.

A poll of midterm voters showed 90% identified corruption as a crucial or major issue in their voting decision.

The resignation of Jensen Huang, together with the results of the recent congressional election, could make this a watershed moment in the relationship of American business to government, one that sees the pendulum swing back toward greater regulation and greater separation of finance from politics.

Corruption topped the list among issues that motivated voters in the overwhelming and nationwide midterm election victory for Democrats, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. It showed 90% identified corruption as a crucial or major issue in their voting decision, a percentage point higher than the cost of living.

When voters were asked which party was best able to deal with the corruption issue, Democrats led Republicans 37% to 30% — though, significantly, 32% said neither party.

It’s impossible to know exactly what voters mean when they say corruption, but there are hints it involves the relationship of business to government. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey, taken two weeks before the election, asked respondents if elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, should personally own or trade stocks in companies that have contracts with the federal government. An overwhelming 93% said it should not be allowed. A similarly bipartisan 89% objected to the president’s family members receiving government contracts.

The upshot: The very close relationship between business and the government, which has existed under both political parties but has come plainly and brazenly to the fore in President Trump’s second administration, is now a major issue for voters.

The Huang affair encompasses all of that. Nvidia, along with several other large corporations, made large donations to the president’s ballroom. Meanwhile, there are allegations that the administration did not act when informed of potentially illegal sales of Nvidia chips to China. It may be that the president ignored warnings from inside his own administration that Huang was involved with a woman who was reportedly a potential Chinese spy, instead bringing Huang on a state visit to China and giving him say in U.S. export policies for chips.

The Trump era has seen the virtual creation of the CEO Statesman: Huang and other tech execs draped around the president during foreign trips, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff negotiating with Russia, Elon Musk deciding who the federal government fires.

Could the Huang affair be the end of that phenomenon?

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., wasted no time in signaling the new Congress was ready to get tough on tech execs.

“It’s clear that the American people cannot rely on Big Tech billionaire CEOs to put our national security above their bottom line – which is why Congress must pass the AI Overwatch Act and other bipartisan bills to keep advanced American AI technology out of China’s hands.”

The enormity of Huang’s fall cannot be overstated. Imagine J.P. Morgan resigning — or Jack Welch or Steve Jobs or Tim Cook. Few have stood astride the pinnacle of political and corporate power during their era like Huang during the AI boom.

This comes at a time of massive wealth increases for the elite that have helped undermine faith in capitalism. The CNBC Voter Poll showed 56% with a strong or somewhat favorable opinion of capitalism, with 32% reporting an unfavorable opinion and 12% saying they don’t know.

But those numbers are overwhelmingly driven by older Americans. Younger Americans, ages 18 to 34, have a deeply negative opinion. Those aged 35 to 49 are favorable toward capitalism by only a 46%-41% margin.

What could this mean for business?

For starters, it could result in a return to more traditional separation of business and politics, where business has less of a direct say in policy. But this could be the start of a more significant change.

In the wake of the Great Financial Crisis, the banking system was put under such strict regulations, many of which exist to this day, that one commentator remarked it was “in receivership in everything but name only.” One can go back even further to more extreme measures taken when the public was deeply dissatisfied with business — to the fallout from the robber baron era when the trusts were busted up, or the wake of the Great Depression when the government put stricter regulations on banks and Wall Street and gave unions more power.

Democrats will be limited, even with large gains in both houses, in their ability to overturn presidential decisions with veto-proof majorities. But executives themselves may decide that it’s not a good look any longer to be seen being too cozy with the White House. And some Republicans, especially those from swing states, may read the change in the electoral winds and side with Democrats on some of the most populist issues, like the data centers, the environment and even regulation.

The irony is that Trump ran, among other things, on a strong deregulatory agenda, one that business welcomed as unshackling overregulation during the Biden administration. With potential support from the public, and an overwhelmingly Democratic Congress, the pendulum may be about to swing the other way.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.summary: Jensen Huang's resignation and recent election results could make corporate leaders more cautious about close public ties to the White House. The two developments may also create pressure for increased regulation of companies.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.title: Jensen Huang scandal casts doubt on Nvidia’s AI dominance — how we got here
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.author: Katie Tarasov
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.text:
Nvidia
 is facing one the biggest crises in its 33 year history, with founder Jensen Huang resigning as CEO Thursday after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Now CFO Colette Kress has taken the helm as Nvidia’s interim CEO.

The implications of Huang’s affair with Alice Huang run far deeper than infidelity. That’s because her ties to Nvidia customer Megaspeed put her in the middle of a sprawling effort to accumulate AI chips across Southeast Asia. And Megaspeed is under investigation for possibly diverting restricted Nvidia chips into the hands of Chinese companies.

The relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang dates back to 2023, according to The New York Times. That was a “turbulent” period for Nvidia, Jensen Huang told CNBC during an interview at the time. Nvidia was in the midst of redesigning some chips to comply with the first in a series of strict export controls imposed by the U.S. government that restricted sales to China.

“The regulation is going to be just fine. We’re going to be able to work through it,” Huang told CNBC from Nvidia’s headquarters in February 2023. The interview was for a documentary about how Huang created Nvidia and built it into the backbone of the AI boom.

That same day, CNBC also interviewed Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair.

It’s not the first time Nvidia has faced an uncertain future. The company nearly went bankrupt in the early years after it was founded in 1993.

“Every company makes mistakes and I make a lot of them,” Huang said in the 2023 interview. “And some of them put the company in peril.”

In the early months of the AI boom, after OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022, Nvidia was on the precipice of historic growth. Jensen Huang told CNBC he’d like to keep running the company for “three or four decades,” as long as “I feel that I’m making a real contribution to the company.”

Less than four years later, Jensen Huang is out, and we’re taking a look back at our interviews with the Nvidia co-founder and other company executives as the chipmaker enters this next critical chapter. Watch the video for the full story.

WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huang

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.title: Apple, Alphabet and Uber survived major founder transitions. Nvidia will be a harder test
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.author: Arjun Kharpal
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.text:
Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation leaves Nvidia facing an unusually difficult transition after losing its founder CEO.

Companies like Apple, Alphabet and Uber have prospered after losing high-profile leaders, but those transitions were generally less abrupt.

Nvidia’s next permanent CEO will need to manage the fallout from Huang’s departure while maintaining its competitive position as rivals develop their own chips.

Jensen Huang is not the first CEO to leave a company he helped build.

But experts told CNBC that his sudden resignation from Nvidia
 at a critical juncture is unique and leaves his eventual successor with challenges in leading the company that’s powering the artificial intelligence boom.

In 33 years, Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a spy for China, made the company he co-founded the world’s most valuable.

Former Goldman Sachs
 CEO Lloyd Blankfein wrote on X that he was “indispensable” but “the graveyards are filled with indispensable men,” referencing a quote attributed to French leader Charles de Gaulle.

While the board looks for a new CEO and CFO Colette Kress does the job temporarily; analysts say Huang’s charisma and bullish drive will be hard to replicate.

“I’m not sure we’ve seen a situation quite like this, where the founder and CEO of one of the world’s largest companies faces such a sudden departure amid scandal,” Michael Withers, professor of management at the University of Notre Dame’s Mendoza College of Business, told CNBC.

Whoever follows will “face challenges that go well beyond those of a typical CEO replacing a founder,” he added.

Apple
’s image was inseparable from Steve Jobs when he resigned in 2011. But unlike Nvidia, the company had had other CEOs — and an internal successor.

Tim Cook invested in Apple’s chip strategy and services business and became a key corporate diplomat in dealings with the U.S. and Chinese governments. He was known as an operator who controlled Apple’s supply chain.

Cook had “considerable preparation” for becoming CEO, Withers said. Apple’s market cap went from about $350 billion to $4 trillion in his 15-year tenure.

Larry Page and Sergey Brin left their executive roles at Alphabet
 in 2019, 21 years after founding Google.

Page and Brin’s departures were expected. Page said at the time that it was the “natural time” to simplify the company’s management structure. Alphabet shares are up more than 300% since then under Sunder Pichai.

Travis Kalanick left Uber
 in 2017 after mounting pressure over a series of scandals and governance concerns.

But his departure “unfolded over several months, and while it certainly attracted attention, it pales in comparison to what Nvidia is currently facing,” Withers added.

Former Expedia
 CEO Dara Khosrowshahi repaired the organization and found a path to profitability.

Withers said successor CEOs often struggle “under normal circumstances” to juggle maintaining what made a company successful while establishing their own leadership.

“It becomes considerably more difficult when the transition follows such a high-profile scandal involving the company’s founder,” he added.

Huang had an extraordinary 60 direct reports, as part of a flat structure that favored fast communication over layered hierarchies.

Withers told CNBC Nvidia did not appear to have a succession plan for Huang, who is also often described as inextricably linked to the company.

“We’re talking about a company that was, until recently, the largest in the world by market capitalization. That’s a pretty remarkable situation,” he added.

As well as having to “step out of his shadow,” the new CEO will have to deal with the “scandal” arising from Huang’s conduct and “the extent to which it sticks with Nvidia,” Withers said.

Huang’s successor will also have to tackle the longer-term business strategy, while picking up the relationships he managed.

Huang cultivated a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump and accompanied him to China in May. Huang consistently pushed for the U.S. to relax export restrictions that prevent Nvidia from selling its chips to the world’s second-largest economy.

He also managed close relationships with the bosses of the company’s key suppliers, from SK Hynix to Samsung.

Storm Uru, co-head of the Global Innovation team at Nvidia investor Liontrust Asset Management, said two key priorities were changing company culture and managing the supply chain.

The supply chain was “where Jensen was able to provide a vision for the future and able to bring people to the table and to expand capacity to enable the build-out of this technology,” Uru told CNBC, adding it mattered especially “when supply chains are already so tight.”

Nvidia continues to face rising competition from rivals such as AMD
 and hyperscalers, which are ramping up efforts to develop their own chips.

Investors noted that the new CEO will have a roadmap of products for the next few years, unaffected by Huang’s removal.

“We have to look beyond Jensen ... there are thousands upon thousands of engineers,” Joanne Feeney, partner and portfolio manager, Advisors Capital Management, told CNBC on Thursday, as pressure was mounting on Huang to go.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/cftc-cha.title: CFTC Chair Selig tells CNBC crypto industry is embracing agency rules as legislation hopes fade
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/cftc-cha.author: Talia Kaplan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/cftc-cha.text:
CFTC Chairman Michael Selig says major crypto exchanges and new entrants are showing interest in using the agency’s federal oversight framework.

The CFTC published an advance notice on Oct. 5 seeking comment on a framework for retail crypto commodity transactions after the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act on Sept. 15.

Democrats’ 2026 congressional gains are expected to bring greater scrutiny of crypto regulation and President Donald Trump’s crypto ties in 2027.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules governing digital assets, according to Chairman Michael Selig.

The commodities regulator in October proposed rules aimed at preventing abuse in crypto markets and codifying crypto transaction rules under a federal rulebook. In the announcement, Selig said the move was a “critical step” in ensuring the United States remains the crypto capital of the world.

Speaking this week at Cantor Convergence, an annual FinTech conference held in Miami Beach, Selig told CNBC in an exclusive interview that many of the major crypto exchanges are already registered with the CFTC because they offer financial derivatives, including perpetual futures, on their platforms and would now be able to add spot trading.

“We’re also getting interest from new entrants who say, ‘Look, signing up with 50 different state regimes is tough. We’d rather come to one regulator and get a license at the CFTC’ so those new entrants are lining up to come register with us as well,” he added.

After the Clarity Act, a comprehensive market structure bill that established a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate in September, the CFTC and the SEC moved to establish federal frameworks using their existing statutory authorities.

“We need to protect our markets and protect our customers using those markets so we’ll continue to do exactly that in the wake of the Clarity Act failing to get the votes it needed to get to the president’s desk during the current Congress,” Selig said.

“Our statute does provide for authority of the agencies to register exchanges that want to offer margined, leveraged, or financed crypto assets or other types of commodity trading so we’re utilizing that authority to allow our existing exchanges to begin offering these products under a regulated framework,” he said.

Selig added that the oversight is opt-in for exchanges that are not currently offering margin leveraged financing, which is not permitted under existing state regimes.

But the CFTC’s new rules could face new scrutiny and oversight in 2027, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate after the midterms. Selig told CNBC he hopes the U.S. won’t see a wave of software developers moving offshore, as many crypto businesses threatened to do under the Biden administration.

“I really hope that we learned lessons from the last several years in this space,” he said.

Crypto firms were at odds with Washington during the Biden administration, asking for clear operating rules, while also facing lawsuits brought by the SEC under former chair Gary Gensler’s leadership. That shifted after President Donald Trump’s 2024 victory.

“I do hope that we can work together with both sides of the aisle to protect software developers who want to do the right thing,” Selig said, adding that those looking to commit crimes and engage in fraud should be held accountable.

When asked whether he’s prepared for increased scrutiny from Congress in 2027, Selig said, “Congress will do its job investigating where it needs to investigate.”

“I’m happy to answer any questions that Congress has for me just as I would answer Congress’ questions today as I’ve done before hearing committees several times already,” he said.

Selig has also faced heat from Democrats for his handling of prediction markets. In February, 23 Democratic senators sent a letter to Chairman Selig urging him to reverse the agency’s greenlighting of prediction markets.

Selig has argued that prediction platforms are federally regulated as more states try to rein them in. The CFTC has sued several states to defend what the agency views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate event contracts, which it classifies as swaps.

“We’re going to fight this up to the Supreme Court if that’s where it’s going,” Selig said. “Our view on the statute is that we have exclusive jurisdiction over these markets, and I will not allow for states to go bring lawsuits against our exchanges, claiming that they’re unlicensed gambling.”

CNBC’s Tanaya Macheel contributed to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nhls-nex.title: NHL’s next media deal will test the league’s strength
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nhls-nex.author: Alex Sherman
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nhls-nex.text:
The NHL can begin formally negotiating a new media rights deal with its incumbent partners — Disney/ESPN and Skydance, the new owner of TNT Sports — on Jan. 1.

How much the NHL can extract from its media partners will likely set the bar for other media rights set to come to market, including MLB.

One of the biggest developing stories in entertainment and sports is how the world’s biggest media companies judge the value of non-NFL rights — and the NHL is giving us our first window into this new era in media values.

My colleague Mike Ozanian is out with his new NHL valuations this morning. See the full list here.

The NHL can begin formally negotiating a new media rights deal with its incumbent partners — Disney/ESPN and Skydance, the new owner of TNT Sports — on Jan. 1. Sources tell me the league wants an increase in overall rights fees between 50% and 100% over its current deal. The NHL inked a 7-year, $4.5 billion deal with ESPN and TNT Sports in 2021.

Whether the league actually gets that type of increase is still unclear — and that will be one of the most watched data points in the world of sports business next year.

The bull case for the NHL

National media rights for the NHL currently make up about 13% of its annual revenue, which is around $8 billion, according to CNBC estimates.

I’m told both Disney/ESPN and Skydance want to renew a deal with the league. Both companies have engaged in preliminary conversations with the league in the past few weeks, and while there’s still work to do in terms of price, there’s mutual interest in getting something done.

In its current deal, ESPN has access to 100 exclusive games for the 2026-27 season. Fifty-three of them air on ESPN or ABC, and the other 47 exclusive stream on ESPN. Under current terms, the league’s playoffs are split between Disney and TNT Sports.

I’m told Disney is particularly interested in acquiring the rights to more playoff games. The NHL had its most-watched playoffs on record last season, averaging 1.8 million viewers per game. The Stanley Cup averaged 5.2 million viewers — the largest audience since 2019. It was played between the Carolina Hurricanes and the Vegas Golden Knights — not exactly marquee NHL franchises.

Last year’s regular season averaged 546,000 viewers across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports, up 25% from a year ago — the highest average in more than a decade.

The sport is also having a moment culturally. Earlier this year, HBO Max said its hockey-romance series “Heated Rivalry” averaged a whopping 10.6 million viewers per episode.

International hockey competitions, such as the league’s annual “4 Nations Face-Off” midseason tournament and the 2026 Winter Olympics, have drawn huge ratings. The last “4 Nations Face-Off” game — 2025′s U.S. vs. Canada final — drew 9.3 million viewers.

This year’s Gold Medal men’s hockey game between the U.S. and Canada averaged a stunning 26 million viewers on NBC and Peacock in the U.S., according to Nielsen data. That made it the most-watched sporting event in U.S. history with a start time before 9 a.m. ET.

“We think we’ve got the best content,” NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman said on CNBC last month. “Our ratings have continued to increase. We were up dramatically into the double digits last year. So we view ourselves coming into the marketplace in a very strong position. Having said that, the marketplace is extremely competitive and extremely fragmented. But, I believe that with fierce competition that’s going on between traditional television and the newer media platforms that there’ll be a great opportunity for us to both expand our reach and get paid what we think is an appropriate reflection of our value.”

Recent history suggests the NHL will get the rights increase it wants. The NBA nearly tripled its national media rights revenue, signing an 11-year, $77 billion contract with Disney, Amazon and NBCUniversal in a deal that started last season.

The NHL also renewed its TV rights deal in Canada just last year with Rogers Communications, scoring an increase of more than 100% annually when adjusting for currency fluctuations.

But recent history may not match up to present reality.

While I’ve been told Skydance is interested in getting a deal done, sources also tell me Skydance’s top two priorities are paying down debt and saving money to pay for what’s going to be a huge NFL rights increase — potentially $1 billion per season or more.

Skydance is dead set on renewing the NFL, I’m told. Those talks will likely occur in 2028, as the league has an opt-out clause at the end of the 2029-30 season.

The NHL was a meaningful sports property to Warner Bros. Discovery. The company could use its loyal fanbase and sizable playoff ratings to help justify distribution fees to pay TV providers while marginally adding some subscribers to HBO Max.

Now that Paramount and WBD have been pushed together, the NHL isn’t as important to Skydance for distribution leverage, which already has premier sports media rights such as the NFL, The Masters, college football, March Madness, UFC and UEFA Champions League.

That’s not to say the NHL isn’t a priority for Skydance. Sources both from Skydance and the NHL tell me they’d like to get a new deal done. Skydance still needs programming for the cable networks it owns to keep that business chugging along. But relative to WBD, it’s not as much of a must-have.

“As it relates to future rights, we’ll be disciplined,” Skydance CEO David Ellison said during an earnings conference call this week — perhaps hinting at his company dropping not only NHL but also other rights from the WBD portfolio in the coming months and years. “Every right has to earn its place.”

Perhaps Skydance remains a partner but buys fewer NHL games. This potentially opens the door to new bidders. I’m told CNBC’s own parent company Versant would be interested in a slice of NHL games. Amazon sniffs around just about every national sports property that comes to market.

Netflix? Regular season NHL games are certainly not events. Fox? NBCUniversal? Both companies need to worry about how much it’s going to cost to renew the NFL. A big package of NHL games may not fit the strategy.

How much the NHL can extract from its media partners will likely set the bar for other media rights set to come to market, including MLB, which could be delayed by labor negotiations. New York Yankees President Randy Levine told Ozanian this week that “I don’t know whether they’ll reach an agreement or not.”

Disclosure: Versant Media is the parent company of CNBC.

The CNBC Sport newsletter with Alex Sherman brings you the biggest news and exclusive interviews from the worlds of sports business and media, delivered weekly to your inbox.

Subscribe here to get access today.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-s.title: Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-s.author: Natalie Feary
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-s.text:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to appear voluntarily before the Senate Banking Committee after Chairman Tim Scott asked him to testify on Dec. 10, according to NBC.

Lawmakers are scrutinizing the Commerce Department’s oversight of Nvidia chip exports to China and its enforcement of export controls.

Scott also asked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear on Dec. 3 as lawmakers examine national security concerns tied to recent reporting about Huang and Nvidia.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies.

Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security.

Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding “recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce’s role that raises national security concerns.”

“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment.

The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy “raise significant national security concerns.”

Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday.

There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary’s approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia’s exports thoroughly enough

Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick “appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur,” in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday “Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military.”

In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved.

Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities.

Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick.

Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump’s administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China’s AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June.

Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/russia-o.title: Russian crude production rebounds after Trump diesel deal, IEA says as oil markets return to surplus
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/russia-o.author: Hugh Leask
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/russia-o.text:
Russia’s crude oil production rose by 210,000 barrels a day to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, according to the IEA.

Global oil supply rose to 105.4 million barrels a day in October, lifting supply above demand for the first time since the Iran war began.

Diesel supply remains constrained because attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and Middle East disruptions continue to limit product exports.

Russia’s crude oil production rose to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, a 210,000-barrel-a-day surge, as a rebound in Gulf shipments pushes oil markets into a surplus for the first time since the Middle East conflict began, the International Energy Agency said Friday.

Global supply and stocks have both swelled, though Middle East disruptions and attacks on Russian energy infrastructure tightened diesel supply, according to the agency’s latest monthly oil market report.

“Persistent attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to choke off the country’s diesel supplies to international markets, adding to losses from the Middle East,” the IEA noted.

U.S. President Donald Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to supply diesel to global markets on Oct. 9. The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a general license authorizing certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027.

Crude supply can rise even as diesel remains tight, with refinery capacity and refined product exports still constrained.

Global oil supply reached 105.4 million barrels a day in October, up 2.3 million barrels a day from September, the IEA said, adding that supply rose by an “extraordinary” 5.3 million barrels a day since August, despite ongoing attacks on energy infrastructure and tankers.

Inventories also rose for the first time since June, with observed global stocks increasing by 52 million barrels in October, or 1.7 million barrels a day.

“The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” IEA analysts observed.

Higher export flows have strengthened supply expectations for the fourth quarter, with Middle East and Russia losses partly offset by growth from the U.S., Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana, which together are set to boost output by 1.6 million barrels a day this year.

The IEA has raised its fourth-quarter supply estimate by 3.3 million barrels a day, and now forecasts a 6.6 million barrels per day increase in 2027.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/kraft-he.title: From Jell-O to Philadelphia cream cheese, Kraft Heinz is putting a new spin on old favorites
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/kraft-he.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/kraft-he.text:
Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane is betting on new products, including cheesy ramen and protein-packed Jell-O pudding, to revive growth at the packaged food giant.

Cahillane has invested an additional $700 million in the business and halted plans to split the company.

Kraft Heinz
 is giving some of America’s most familiar grocery staples an unexpected makeover in a bid to revive long-slumping sales and win back support from Wall Street.

The packaged food giant — known for brands like Heinz, Kraft, Philadelphia Cream Cheese, Lunchables and Oscar Mayer — is reinventing its decades-old brands to appeal to changing consumer tastes, particularly growing demand for protein and convenient foods, CEO Steve Cahillane told CNBC’s Jim Cramer on Thursday.

“I think the mistake that was made at Kraft Heinz before I arrived in the last several years is this notion that there’s a ‘forever brand,’ that brands can just live on the history of their past,” Cahillane said after Kraft Heinz held an investor day earlier Thursday. “That’s not true. But equally, brands that existed for a long time are not necessarily destined for the dustbin of history.”

“You have to innovate. You have to bring new news. You have to bring excitement with your brand,” he added.

That philosophy is central to Cahillane’s turnaround strategy. Since taking the helm at the start of 2026, he has directed an additional $700 million toward the business and hired 400 employees. He also paused plans to split Kraft Heinz into two companies. At Thursday’s investor day, Kraft Heinz projected that it would return to top- and bottom-line growth in the second half of 2027. The company’s revenue has declined on an annual basis in back-to-back years, with analysts also projecting a 1% drop in 2026, according to FactSet.

“I saw a lot that was fixable,” Cahillane said. “If we spent all of this year separating the business ... we would have ended up with two suboptimal businesses.”

He argued that the company’s resources could be put to better use revitalizing the company’s brands.

One of the clearest examples of that strategy is Kraft Mac & Cheese. The nearly century-old brand has returned to growth following the introduction of products including PowerMac, which packs 17 grams of protein and six grams of fiber, and Restaurant Edition, which brings restaurant-inspired flavors to the classic boxed format.

Perhaps an unexpected innovation is Kraft Mac & Cheese Cheesy Ramen, which debuted in Canada in July to overwhelming demand. “We sold out three months’ worth of stock in a week,” Cahillane said, adding that the company plans to bring the cheesy noodles to U.S. shelves next year.

Jell-O is also joining the protein craze, which has been fueled in part by fitness influencers and the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss medications. Kraft Heinz plans to introduce pudding with 10 grams of protein, giving the nostalgic dessert a nutritional boost. Cahillane said the company’s research and development team worked to overcome the taste and texture challenges that often come with adding protein to familiar foods.

“Our R&D team has cracked the code,” he said. “The chocolate’s my favorite. Chocolate Jell-O pudding with protein, I think, is going to be a real hit.”

Philadelphia cream cheese is next in line for a protein-packed makeover, following the introduction of new flavors of the regular spread in September. Cahillane said Kraft Heinz plans to introduce new products under the brand next year. “We’ve got a big opportunity to drive protein, to steal some share from cottage cheese, and that’s going to come through the Philadelphia name,” he said.

Kraft Heinz shares have struggled for years, but investors are showing signs of renewed optimism. The stock has gained 7% this quarter, outperforming the broader market, even as its roughly flat performance for the year trails the S&P 500′s 11% advance.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.title: How the Jensen Huang affair changes the outlook for U.S.-China relations
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.author: Evelyn Cheng
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.text:
Fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has drawn comparisons to historical periods of tension.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet again next week alongside the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting from Nov. 18 to 19.

“The Nvidia scandal has destroyed the credibility of the biggest corporate lobbyist against U.S. export controls on China,” said Arthur Kroeber, partner, Gavekal Dragonomics.

BEIJING — Prolonged U.S. Congressional scrutiny of former Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy raises the stakes for already tense relations between the world’s two largest economies.

Nvidia’s Huang resigned Thursday, and agreed to testify before Congress sometime before Thanksgiving on Nov. 26. House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told reporters there could be “public hearings for other people or other things down road.”

“I worry this incident will deteriorate the atmosphere dramatically in Washington against China, and also export control matters, and also the Trump administration in its way of dealing with China,” said a Beijing-based foreign policy researcher, who requested anonymity as academics risk discipline or even removal for speaking to the media.

The researcher warned of a possible return to a situation like that in the 1990s, when a “Chinese-American” nuclear physicist was suspected of sharing nuclear secrets with the Chinese government, resulting in a federal prosecution. The court ultimately dismissed all but one of 59 counts.

Now the bilateral relationship, supported by a fragile trade truce, faces another espionage allegation. And this time it’s around the tech executive at the heart of the U.S.-China competition over artificial intelligence.

“This isn’t really about Jensen,” said Mitch Presnick, non-resident honorary fellow on the Chinese economy, Center for China Analysis at the Asia Society.

He noted how some in Washington prefer measures to exclude China and disagreed with the semiconductor executive’s message that American technology needed to be used in China in order to remain relevant to global tech development.

Washington started to restrict Nvidia’s ability to sell advanced chips to China in 2022. But the Trump administration eased many Biden-era restrictions in 2025.

Meanwhile, Nvidia’s Huang advocated his views across a spectrum of markets from the U.S. to China to Taiwan to Germany.

At the peak of his influence, he shared a banquet table in September with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in Washington, D.C. The two presidents are next expected to meet alongside the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting from Nov. 18 to 19 in Shenzhen, China.

The political landscape has swiftly changed, with Democrats sweeping U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 and turmoil over subsequent reports about Huang’s alleged Beijing spy connection. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair over the weekend.

It remains unclear whether any sensitive information was shared.

China’s Foreign Ministry has called the “Chinese spy” allegation unfounded “smears against China.”

“The U.S. should stop fabricating the “Chinese spy” narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions,” spokeswoman Mao Ning said Thursday, according to an official English translation.

But the immediate outcome, analysts predict, is more of the U.S. restrictions that China doesn’t want.

“The Nvidia scandal has destroyed the credibility of the biggest corporate lobbyist against U.S. export controls on China,” said Arthur Kroeber, partner, Gavekal Dragonomics. “There is now a good chance that Congress will tighten up those rules before the end of this year.”

Looking ahead, Kroeber warned Beijing could cut off supplies of rare earths or chipmaking materials if the U.S. tried to restrict China further with the MATCH Act or Affiliates Rule. The measures could, respectively, limit Beijing’s access to key tech suppliers in the Netherlands and Japan, and drastically expand export controls to include many subsidiaries.

“So when Trump and Xi meet next week in Shenzhen they will probably agree to keep the uneasy U.S.-China truce going,” Kroeber said. “It will just keep getting more and more uneasy.”

Pressuring China has been a rare area of bipartisan agreement in Washington. Beijing has meanwhile ramped up homegrown alternatives to U.S. tech since Washington restricted Nvidia’s ability to sell advanced chips to China in 2022. And even Trump’s approval of some Nvidia sales had yet to translate into meaningful orders from China.

“We are going to see the two countries start to decouple again in terms of technology,” George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice, The Asia Group, said Thursday, noting “China will double-down on self-reliance.”

“I begin to feel the Jensen Huang case feels like more like another ‘spy balloon’ case,” he said.

In early 2023, during the Biden administration, the U.S. shot down what it described as a Chinese surveillance balloon. Beijing called it a weather balloon that had blown off course. But the incident delayed then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken’s trip to China by more than four months, following limited engagement amid Covid-19 travel restrictions.

Fast-forward to the Huang affair, and “the timing is no accident here,” Presnick said. “We’re talking about a very curious set of coincidences, and also the fact that the information came through unnamed sources, and there were other things that were strange about it.”

Days after the U.S. midterms, The Financial Times and The New York Times reported, citing sources, that U.S. government intelligence believe China’s Ministry of State Security recruited businesswoman Alice Huang to gather information on then-CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang.

“Obviously somebody was looking to do this, and they wanted to ... make the discussion about espionage, and not about American competitiveness,” Presnick said.

“The U.S. is thinking [in terms of] U.S. and China, but that’s not what China is thinking,” he said, pointing to Beijing’s trade with fast-growing non-Western economies in Africa and Southeast Asia.

—CNBC’s Samantha Subin contributed to this report.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/jensen-h.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday, and agreed to testify before Congress. He says Beijing is trying to make the discussion about espionage, not about American competitiveness.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.title: Why Singapore keeps turning up in the fight over Nvidia chips and China
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.author: Anniek Bao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-j.text:
Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country in February 2026 after authorities said she provided inaccurate information about her role in Megaspeed.

The country repeatedly sought intelligence on Super Micro from U.S. authorities, but received “limited information or assistance,” the ministry said.

Singapore has faced international scrutiny over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China.

Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia
 sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington’s push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO’s scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight.

The Southeast Asian nation said Thursday that it had barred Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of a scandal that catalyzed the end of Jensen Huang’s run as Nvidia CEO, from re-entering the country.

A fifth person was handed 41 charges on Friday in a Singapore fraud case involving computer servers that might have contained Nvidia chips and were exported to Malaysia. The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year.

The investigations into several companies and key officials, including Megaspeed International, began in February 2025 and remained ongoing as of Thursday.

Authorities have been examining whether servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the domestic market were subsequently rerouted to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement late Thursday.

Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China.

The U.S. has imposed export restrictions on Nvidia’s most cutting-edge AI chips to China since 2022 to curb Beijing’s surging AI development.

Nvidia’s revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country’s trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker’s revenue.

Experts have pointed to gaps in enforcement of U.S. export restrictions and Singapore’s corporate system that make it hard to trace where advanced Nvidia chips ultimately end up.

Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. Chinese companies can also legally gain remote access to the most advanced AI chips hosted in data centers outside China rather than buying the hardware directly.

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. national security official, said that Southeast Asia has become “a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention,” importing tens of billions of dollars’ worth of AI chips per year.

Singapore has stepped up efforts to police suspected chip diversion since last year, including investigations involving alleged fraud and money laundering.

Authorities acknowledged the potential “blind spots between separate monitoring of trade flows and banking flows,” said Alvin Camba, lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, an Austin-based AI risk assessment firm. Correlating physical shipments with related financial transactions can be “challenging,” he added.

“Singapore’s strong corporate secrecy regulations, which offer extensive protections for foreign investors, can also make it difficult to rapidly identify the true recipients of goods,” Camba said.

Those challenges can be exploited to “obfuscate financial flows and potentially circumvent global restrictions on technology transfers,” he added, urging constant adaptation from regulators.

Singapore said it had received limited help from U.S. authorities in its yearlong investigation.

Police sought information on Super Micro Computer Inc., a U.S. server supplier relevant to the probe, but the company provided limited cooperation, according to the Thursday statement.

The city-state first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025, and has repeated its request on several occasions since September last year. “Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” it said.

Police interviewed Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident who was then Megaspeed’s CEO, chairperson and a key controller, in June 2025.

In February 2026, authorities concluded that there was insufficient evidence that she had committed offenses related to the declarations under investigation. She was nonetheless barred from re-entering Singapore after being found providing inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed.

The country does not enforce “unilateral export controls” imposed by other countries, the ministry said in Thursday’s statement, but it expects companies operating there to take foreign export rules into account in their international business activities.

Megaspeed, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming company, became Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customer in less than three years and has bought more than $4.8 billion worth of its chips since June 2024, according to The New York Times, though the company has denied any wrongdoing.

Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing, served as managing director at Megaspeed for eight months in 2023 but has reportedly continued to play a leading role at the company.

Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, ending 33 years at the helm after revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, plunging the chipmaker at the heart of the global AI boom into crisis.

Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.
