Authorities say she provided inaccurate information about her role in Megaspeed. Singapore has faced international scrutiny over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/tech-dow.title: I interviewed Huang at peak ‘Jensenmania.’ Three weeks later, Nvidia is grappling with a world without him
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/tech-dow.author: Arjun Kharpal,Caleigh Keating
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/tech-dow.text:
The departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia has sent shockwaves through the tech sector.

CNBC’s Arjun Kharpal, who interviewed Huang just a few weeks ago at GTC Berlin, unpacks how everything came crashing down for the popular CEO.

In other news, Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its IPO next week, priced between $70 and $78 per share.

I was the last person at CNBC to do a live broadcast interview with Jensen Huang.

At the time, Huang still seemed untouchable. But weeks later, Nvidia is confronting a question investors hadn’t had to confront in more than 30 years: What does the company look like without him?

I sat down with the company founder on Oct. 22 at Nvidia
’s GTC event in Berlin, Germany, just weeks before he admitted to an affair with a woman that U.S. intelligence alleges could be a spy for China.

“Jensenmania,” as I like to call it — which had come to characterize the CEO’s appearances — was in full force at the Berlin event. The Nvidia merchandise store featured clothing with Huang’s face on it, huge cheers erupted when he appeared on stage, and attendees were doing their best to secure a picture with the Nvidia founder.

Huang had somewhat of a rockstar persona with a fandom to match in every city he visited around the world. In 2025, I followed Huang around on his visit to Europe. At an event in London, an attendee who was eagerly waiting to catch a glimpse of Huang compared the Nvidia boss to “Iron Man,” referencing the popular character of the Marvel superhero and tech billionaire inventor Tony Stark.

These moments that I experienced really embodied what Huang had become – a larger-than-life personality who was central to the excitement around artificial intelligence. Less CEO, more AI hype man, evangelical about the technology and its transformative power.

He had the credentials to back it up. Since he co-founded Nvidia in the early 90s, Huang helped shape the company from a startup taking on incumbents to a dominant player for AI chips. Over the last three decades, he saw the shifts coming, investing to turn what were initially chips designed for rendering gaming graphics – GPUs – into general-purpose AI computing semiconductors, along with the software that gave Nvidia its strong position.

The near 500% rally in Nvidia’s shares over the past five years has been driven by its incredible growth, but also the backing of Huang’s vision.

“Nvidia without Jensen is something which we’ve never really considered,” Storm Uru, co-head of the global innovation team at Liontrust Asset Management, which has been invested in Nvidia since 2017, told me.

Now it is a reality. Huang is out and he has left some of the biggest shoes to fill in tech history – without a clear succession plan in place.

But perhaps it’s the right time for someone new, such an operator-type leader. We’ve seen it before at tech giants like Apple
 or Alphabet
, where visionary leaders step down, and new CEOs take over, bringing the businesses to new heights — at least if you look at the share prices. Sure, they may not be the flamboyant founders, but they innovate in other ways.

Nvidia’s roadmap of new products is set for the next few years. The reality is that AI firms and hyperscalers are still yearning for computing power, which is in short supply. Nvidia also remains the gold standard for its AI chips. Yes, there is rising competition, but the market dynamics that have supported Nvidia are not going to disappear overnight. That gives any permanent successor some breathing space.

“While he and the company must respond to his actions, he has already left an indelible mark on Nvidia and it will be successful in many years to come as a result,” Ben Barringer, head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, told me.

This report is from this week’s The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here.

Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy with whom Huang had an affair, owned stakes in businesses benefiting Chinese competitor Huawei while she was in business with Nvidia, CNBC’s Eamon Javers exclusively learned.

Microsoft
 suffered a widespread outage Thursday and Friday that impacted Outlook and other services across multiple regions.

Amazon’s
 Ring unveiled an indoor home security drone camera and a patrol robot for businesses in its latest foray into the intelligence sphere.

Ukrainian defense tech startup UFORCE is now valued at $6 billion after raising $700 million in its latest funding round, showcasing investor appetite for battle-tested autonomous drones.

CoreWeave
 CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC that he has cancelled his planned share sale program, also known as a 10b5-1. He faced criticism for his stock sales amid the company’s recent struggles.

Nvidia’s interim CEO will be Colette Kress, the current CFO and a 13-year veteran at the company.

Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia raises serious questions about the future of the AI industry, and not just because of his status as a “singular figure.”

Nvidia’s interconnected status as the “central bank of AI” raises the possibility that trouble inside the chip giant could have wide-reaching implications for the AI boom, my colleague Matt Peterson writes. Nvidia has made, or committed to, hundreds of billions of dollars in investments to firms in the industry, including OpenAI and Intel
.

If Nvidia can’t honor its commitments, this circular financing model could spell trouble for AI companies supported by Nvidia and banks that lent money in the AI buildout.

— Caleigh Keating, Digital Rotational Associate
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/tech-dow.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has left the company, which is set to offer 825 million shares in its IPO next week. Huang was the last person to do a live broadcast interview with the company founder.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-w.title: Nvidia without Jensen Huang. What lies ahead for Asian chipmakers?
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-w.author: Jenny Lee
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-w.text:
Nvidia’s Asian chip partnerships are expected to remain intact, analysts said.

Longer-term uncertainty remains over Nvidia’s product roadmap, according to Daol Securities.

ASUS is watching for potential supply chain impacts under new leadership, its co-CEO told CNBC.

Nvidia’s
 leadership shake-up is unlikely to cause immediate disruption for major Asian semiconductor suppliers, such as Samsung Electronics and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., but Jensen Huang’s departure has raised questions about the company’s longer-term product strategy and supply chain relationships.

The bigger issue for investors and suppliers is whether Nvidia can maintain the pace of innovation and close ties with key partners that Huang helped drive as the company built its dominance in artificial intelligence chips.

In a Friday research note, Nam Dae-jong and Kim Yeon-mi, analysts at South Korean brokerage Daol Investment & Securities, said Huang’s departure was unlikely to affect the semiconductor industry’s near-term outlook.

However, they flagged uncertainty over Nvidia’s medium- to long-term product roadmap, including how its new leadership would coordinate with partners across the AI ecosystem.

For chipmakers in Asia, one key question is whether Nvidia’s relationships with its manufacturing partners could change under new leadership.

Nam and Kim expect Nvidia’s foundry relationship with TSMC to remain unchanged, given the companies’ established partnership.

They also expect Nvidia’s relationship with Samsung’s foundry business to continue, citing growing cooperation between the companies, including manufacturing involving Samsung’s 4-nanometer process and work on next-generation high-bandwidth memory technology.

The analysts said custom AI chips, or application-specific integrated circuits, or ASICs, are emerging as alternatives to Nvidia’s graphic processing units and could accelerate diversification in the AI chip market.

However, they cautioned against interpreting growing competition as a sign of weakening demand for memory semiconductors, particularly high-bandwidth memory, or HBM.

Still, uncertainty remains over Nvidia’s longer-term product roadmap, given Huang’s central role in shaping the company’s business strategy and allocating resources.

SK Hynix, another key supplier to Nvidia, reversed earlier gains to close 3.03% lower on Friday.

In a research note earlier in the day, Shinhan Securities said investors had initially looked past concerns over Nvidia’s leadership change and focused instead on the broader outlook for the AI industry.

South Korea’s Kospi also reversed earlier gains Friday. In a research note, iM Securities said the impact of Nvidia’s leadership change on the broader semiconductor sector appeared limited, pointing to gains in AMD and Broadcom shares in the previous U.S. session and continued investment demand for AI companies.

ASUS Co-CEO S.Y. Hsu told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” that Nvidia’s leadership change was unlikely to alter its competitive advantages in the near term, though the company would monitor any impact on product quality, service costs and deliveries.

“I think Nvidia’s product and the total AI ecosystem, the advantage will not change overnight,” Hsu said.

ASUS, which works with Nvidia across graphics cards and AI servers, has yet to interact with interim CEO Colette Kress, Hsu said, adding that the company was seeking a meeting to better understand any potential strategic changes.

Over the longer term, Hsu said Huang had played a key role in helping Nvidia and its partners accelerate innovation, and that he would be watching to see whether the company could maintain that pace without him.

Nvidia”s leadership shake-up is unlikely to cause immediate disruption for major Asian semiconductor suppliers, such as Samsung Electronics and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-s.title: Nvidia on track for longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.6 trillion
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-s.author: Ari Levy
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-s.text:
Nvidia shares are down 11% this week, as of Thursday’s close, and are headed for their sixth straight weekly decline.

That will be the longest losing streak since 2012.

The chip giant has lost roughly $1.6 trillion in market cap since the slide began in early October.

Nvidia
 investors turned bearish before this week’s Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock toward its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.

The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world’s most valuable company, has lost 29% of its value over that stretch as of Thursday’s close. That’s a drop of roughly $1.6 trillion in market cap, and it fell below Apple
 in the process.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor.

Nvidia shares fell 4.3% on Thursday, bringing their loss for the week to 11%. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being “unfaithful to my wife.” The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair, this one with the company’s vice president of health care.

By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump’s top allies in the corporate world.

“With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months,” Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. “We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition,” he wrote.

Last week, prior to Huang’s departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout.

In the weeks before the election, Nvidia’s stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets.

Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That’s up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.

Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, “we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term.”

“The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang,” they wrote.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.title: Data Center Outrage Swept Pennsylvania Democrats Into Office. What Comes Next?
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.author: By Emily Rizzo
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.text:
Last week, Pennsylvania Democrats won competitive state legislative races, taking control of the State Senate for the first time in more than three decades. One key issue at the core of their campaigns: opposition to data centers.

“I’ve never in my career seen anything as unpopular as data centers,” said Molly Parzen, executive director of Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania.

Newly elected state senators and representatives who flipped their seats from red to blue say data centers played an important role in their wins. Now they are preparing to act on that mandate.

In the next legislative session, they say they want to address Pennsylvanians’ concerns about  the lack of transparency around the AI buildout, study environmental impacts, ensure costs don’t land on electric ratepayers, push for moratoriums, codify data center regulations, empower local governments to reject proposals and repeal tax breaks for data center developers.

A number of bills related to data centers that fell short during split control of the legislature could be re-introduced in the state House and Senate in the next session. In the last year, Sen. Katie Muth introduced a three-year statewide moratorium, Rep. Paul Friel introduced a bill that would allow municipalities to set 180-day local moratoriums on all data center applications and Rep. Greg Vitali introduced legislation that would repeal the data center tax exemption.

Notably, Gov. Josh Shapiro pivoted on his data center stance in the last year—from fast-tracking developments to signing an executive order that established stricter guardrails. Advocates say the order is a step in the right direction but are calling for stronger protections that only legislation could provide. The order still allows room for developers to press on without complying with some standards, such as using clean energy.

People in the Poconos want to preserve their natural land, said Democrat Brian Wrightson, who won a key senatorial race in the 40th District and flipped a Republican seat, with data center resistance fueling his campaign.

The region has seen roughly 24 data center proposals, according to the Data Center Tracker. Wrightson wants a complete halt in Northeastern Pennsylvania. Come January, he would support a moratorium, whether it’s 180 days for municipalities or three years statewide. He’d love a retroactive one pausing projects already underway so municipalities can get answers they need before development moves forward.

“I’m never gonna close my mouth about it,” Wrightson said in an interview with Inside Climate News.

“Is [180 days] enough? No. Is it something to get it started, to continue the conversation? If that’s what it takes to get the conversation started and slow down and give a six-month breathing room to people, then that’s where we need to go.”

Along with a pause, he wants to modify the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code. Right now, it essentially says municipalities must allow for every type of development.

David Masur, executive director of PennEnvironment, is just one of the environmental advocates pushing for changes to the code. He said it’s essential to stopping data centers in Pennsylvania at the local level. While Shapiro’s order requires developers to gain approval from local authorities before they can receive state permits, Masur argues that local officials need more tools at their disposal.

Wrightson plans to find out if there’s a way a municipality can reject a proposal on the basis that it changes the town’s character.

“ Ultimately, I’d love to never see one of these built in Pennsylvania, period,” Wrightson said.

Democrat Jeff Warren, who flipped Pennsylvania’s 137th House District in Northampton County, also wants to change the planning code, so local governments have the “autonomy to make decisions for their own community in the way that they want to.”

Warren supports the tighter data center regulations within Shapiro’s executive order and wants them to become law.

He said data center developers should take care of their infrastructure responsibilities so costs don’t land on residents. “They need to pay for their own power, they need to generate their own power, distribute their own power,” Warren said. “ We cannot let them tap into the grid and let utility costs continue to increase for consumers in our communities. It’s unacceptable to me.”

Despite energy costs rising in the state, Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, has denied data centers are the cause. In a statement to Inside Climate News, Diorio said the industry is “committed to advancing Pennsylvania’s digital infrastructure, supporting energy reliability and affordability, and promoting long-term, responsible economic development.”

He added that the trade group “looks forward to working with federal, state, and local policymakers, communities, and other stakeholders to earn trust, support responsible data center growth, and help build a stronger economic future for every Pennsylvanian.”

Shapiro’s order only asks data centers to comply with the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development standards, which tasks them with providing 100 percent of their own electrical energy (and use 32 percent renewables by 2035). But developers could still move forward without consenting, though that path would be more difficult. Wrightson worries this could lead to companies relying on gas power rather than renewables.

“ The ‘bring your own power’ scares me,” Wrightson said. When Shapiro’s GRID plans were circulating, he said, developers added natural gas plants to their data center proposals.

He already lives near a 1.4 megawatt natural gas plant in Jessup. “I hear it start up, I can smell it and I can see it,” Wrightson said. Now developers are proposing more on the other side of the valley. “So what air do we breathe? That’s unacceptable.”

There are 27 data center projects in some stage of the state’s permitting process, including three approved by the Department of Environmental Protection. On Nov. 10, agency Secretary Jessica Shirley said the state is “actively negotiating” with a number of developers over compliance with Shapiro’s GRID standards but did not say any have signed on yet.

Warren has already taken a stance against tax breaks for data centers—pointing to his Republican opponent, who voted in favor of the sales tax exemption in 2021. He said he’d support legislation repealing the exemption, which the state government has estimated could cost the commonwealth about $2 billion in revenue by mid-2031. Warren believes Shapiro might work with legislators on that.

“ I think the governor is on board with saying, ‘You know what? Perhaps at the time that was the best course of action, but over time, we’re learning that those tax breaks for developers obviously were not,’” Warren said.

Under Shapiro’s order, developers can still receive the exemption if they meet his responsible-development requirements.

“ I don’t believe in tax breaks for billionaires,” said Democrat Sara Agerton, who flipped the state House 88th District seat in Cumberland County. “We need to fight back against that.”

Agerton wants municipalities to have the opportunity to set a longer moratorium than 180 days. She and Warren both believe that isn’t long enough, saying local governments need more time to examine proposals and navigate the complexities.

“Here’s the crux of this whole thing with data centers and AI: Nobody ever asked for this,” Warren said. “So if the legislative leadership decides to bring up a two-year [pause], a five-year [pause], I’m gonna vote in favor of it.”

Agerton said the state needs time to fund and complete independent environmental impact studies and further tighten data center regulations for projects already underway. She also said local officials need more guidance. “Because it’s hard. … We need more tools, more science, deeper understanding.”

If development has to happen, Agerton said, it should be done without damaging the environment or costing ratepayers. She wants to lean on scientific evidence, and pointed to the data centers left abandoned in China.

“We need affordable housing,” she said. “We don’t need abandoned warehouses.”

Democrat Eileen Hartnett Albillar, who flipped a state Senate seat in Bucks County, said protecting ratepayers from rising utility costs and ensuring responsible development and transparency are her priorities.

Whether it’s 180 days or three years,  Hartnett Albillar said, ”we need to give communities time to be able to revisit their township ordinances and decide if, when and how they would like data centers to be built in their communities.” That entails gathering community feedback, she added, which can take a while.

Prohibiting non-disclosure agreements between data center developers and state agencies and asking for community outreach plans are aspects of Shapiro’s executive order. Parzen, of Conservation Voters, is confident that codifying those policies into law will be an immediate priority for the Democrats in the new session.

Despite the blue wave, it might be challenging to pass progressive policies on data centers in the Senate, said Masur. With such a slim majority, he thinks Democrats will move delicately.

“If you lose a single Democrat in the Senate, you can’t pass anything,” Masur said. “And when you look at the makeup of the current caucus, the political spectrum is huge.”

Still, across the aisle, lawmakers would have to be “tone deaf” to not tread thoughtfully, Masur said. “If I were an elected official and looking at the lay of the land, I’d go, ‘Big money in politics can’t save you on this issue.’”

https://grist.org/transportation/the-aff.title: The affordability election delivered billions for public transit
https://grist.org/transportation/the-aff.author: Benton Graham
https://grist.org/transportation/the-aff.text:
In an election dominated by concerns about affordability, voters across the country overwhelmingly agreed to raise taxes to preserve or expand public transit.

Out of 27 ballot measures supporting transit, 22 passed on November 3, representing $27.4 billion in funding to rescue faltering systems and expand or build new ones. Some of the biggest wins of the night included voters in the San Francisco Bay Area staving off enormous cuts to Bay Area Rapid Transit and other regional systems, Coloradans backing new regional rail, and residents of Seattle and nearby Pierce County favoring expanded bus service.

“It’s an indication that the public is willing to pay for these public transit improvements,” said Sohail Husain, a policy analyst at the Eno Center for Transportation. “That’s very telling –– especially in a world like today where people are concerned about affordability. I think people are still also concerned about mobility and having options to move.”

Public transit has now fared well in the red wave of 2024 — when 19 out of 25 measures supporting transit passed — and this year’s blue wave. Although few candidates campaigned on the issue, the results could significantly alter policy. At the state level, transit advocates see opportunities to advance projects or simply get the government out of the way. Meanwhile, a Democratic majority in Congress will shape a major transportation infrastructure law that is up for renewal. Together, the results could remake how Americans get around.

States have broad discretion to fund transportation as they see fit, which is why Democratic wins in red states and Democratic control of the governorship and both legislative chambers in 22 states have many public transit advocates excited about what comes next.

Pennsylvania is one of those states. It has endured a bitter battle over the finances of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, which serves the Philadelphia area. When the agency faced 45 percent service cuts last year, Governor Josh Shapiro directed the state Department of Transportation to allow the agency to shift nearly $400 million from its capital to operational budget. He also made another $220 million available to the system.

Now, with Democrats taking control of both chambers of the state legislature, transit advocates say SEPTA can look beyond self-preservation. Stephen Bronskill of Transit Forward Philadelphia pointed to projects including trolley modernization, new fleets to replace vehicles from the 1970s, more frequent regional rail service, and fully accessible stations.

“This is a once-in-a-generation moment to invest in public transit –– safe, reliable, accessible transit that Philly needs, but all of Pennsylvania deserves,” he said.

The prospects are less straightforward in Texas, where Republicans still control the Senate. Jay Blazek Crossley, executive director of Farm&City, a nonprofit focused in part on road safety, has spent more than a decade trying to nudge GOP lawmakers toward less violent and less polluting transportation options. Every legislative session has seen him unsuccessfully push legislation that would make it easier for cities to reduce speed limits on residential streets. He sees new hope for that measure and, more broadly, a future that might include additional public transit funding, which accounts for just 0.72 percent of the transportation department’s budget. State Republicans have generally been more interested in moving more cars more quickly, primarily by building bigger highways, while pushing back against some city-led public transit efforts.

“At the very least, the state, I believe, will get out of the way on things like building good light rail and transit,” he said.

There’s hope for bigger projects too. State Representative John Bucy III has again filed legislation directing the Texas Department of Transportation to find a public-private partnership for a high-speed rail line linking Dallas and San Antonio. He believes the bill will appeal to lawmakers whose constituents would benefit from an alternative to driving on the heavily congested Interstate 35 corridor.

“I think the voters spoke loud and clear that they want a Texas government that is going to work on kitchen table issues,” he said. “I think that’s healthcare, education. It’s also mobility and transit, and how do we get around this big, vast state?”

Georgia is another state where Democrats took the governorship and flipped the House, but Republicans still control the Senate. That could be a challenge for Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who has called for dedicated state funding for the Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority and other systems that have historically relied heavily on local and federal support.

The election could have even greater implications at the federal level, where Congress must soon decide how much spending to allocate to transit and passenger rail. The BUILD America 250 Act passed out of a key House commitee with bipartisan support in May, but left public transit advocates concerned about funding cuts. With Democrats taking control of Congress, the legislation is likely to look different. Representative Jerry Nadler of New York, the lone Democrat on the committee to oppose advancing the legislation, sees an opportunity to change its direction.

“Unlike the current Republican proposal, next year’s bill should not prioritize one mode of transportation at the expense of others. This bill must make robust investments in rail and public transit, to connect communities, create good-paying jobs, lower transportation costs for families, and reduce the cost of moving goods across the country,” he said in a statement.

But rewriting the bill won’t necessarily happen quickly. Rebecca Higgins, the Eno Center for Transportation’s vice president of policy, said lawmakers will face some urgency because Congress is already relying on an extension to fund transportation. At the same time, she expects lawmakers to give their newly elected colleagues a chance to weigh in. One major question is what happens to money for intercity passenger rail that was included in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act but dropped from BUILD America 250.

Whatever happens in Washington, the local and regional measures voters approved will have a more immediate impact. In the Bay Area, a 14-year regional sales tax is expected to raise about $1 billion annually to preserve service on BART and other systems that had been facing steep budget shortfalls. Colorado voters approved a 0.333 percent sales tax to build, operate, and maintain passenger rail connecting Pueblo and Colorado Springs with Denver and Fort Collins.

In Seattle, voters doubled an existing sales tax over the next decade, generating an additional $138 million per year largely for transit service. In nearby Pierce County, voters also approved a sales tax increase to expand bus service.

The Pierce County win is particularly notable because voters there hadn’t increased public transit investment since 2002, said Kirk Hovenkotter, the executive director of the Transportation Choices Coalition. The fast-growing region also faces an affordability crisis. The American Public Transportation Association estimates that relying on public transit rather than owning a car can save a household more than $14,000 annually.

Hovenkotter makes a similar argument about the costs facing residents of the Pacific Northweest. “The average cost of car ownership in Washington state is about $12,000,” he said. “The fastest way we can put $12,000 back in someone’s pocket is making it easier for them to live without a car or with one fewer car.”

The election results suggest that, for a wide swath of voters, transit funding isn’t competing with affordability concerns. It’s an answer to them.

https://grist.org/culture/cozy-radicalis.title: The cozy radicalism of repair cafés
https://grist.org/culture/cozy-radicalis.author: Johnny Kauffman
https://grist.org/culture/cozy-radicalis.text:
On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with tool boxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”

Lilly Pettus’s broken chair gets a hand from attendees at the Decatur repair café​. Nearby, a sign tracks repair progress during the event. Johnny Kauffman / Grist

This is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies selling everything from hiking boots, smartphones, and hot water boilers, that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throw-away economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.

Yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés as more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy.

At the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.

Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus said. “We are a big family.”

The newlyweds settled on a simple table and six chairs — two “host style” with arms, four without — from the local Ethan Allen store. The furniture came to feel more like home than the many houses where Pettus, her husband, and their children lived. They moved the table and chairs with them from Florida to Connecticut, then to Indiana, Michigan, Texas, and finally to Georgia. “ I don’t know anyone’s chairs that I like more than my own,” Pettus said.

But after absorbing shakes of laughter during countless games of Hearts, and fidgets of anxiety at family meetings about upcoming moves, one of the chair’s joints finally cracked. “We had the chair just sitting in the corner,” Pettus said, “but no one actually sat in it.” She didn’t know how to fix the chair, but if she sent it to a landfill that would mean trashing a reminder of her fondest memories from the last 30 years.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely.”

Pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair, and decided to give it a second chance.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” said Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a new item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”

Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash — with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma said. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”

Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste — the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft — according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.

Postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.

In 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and New York passed “right to repair” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products.

“ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she said.“I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.”

According to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics.

“If the world ends, at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”

On a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reasons, and more so they could keep using them.

Gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines said, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries.

Pines recently graduated, but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a new $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines said. “I don’t really have a very big support network outside of my friends.”

One of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying new stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines said.

When a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the airfryer, they quickly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair. Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself.

“ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really important to me, and something that I try to do as well,” Pines said. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.”

Another volunteer, Lew Lefton, said he thought that the satisfaction humans draw from making and fixing things has largely been lost, but apocalyptic threats like climate change and artificial intelligence have driven many people toward rediscovering more basic, human skills that are key to survival. People who come to a repair café have a different way to view the future, according to Lefton, especially if they learn something or volunteer themselves. “If the world ends” he said, “at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”

Back in Decatur, Pettus left the repair café with a newly sturdy chair. A screw and some glue fixed the crack around the joint, but the chair still needed upholstery work. Someone Pettus met at the café, who had provided one of the sets of hands that held her chair together as the glue set, advised her on where to buy fabric. Pettus thought she might bring the chair back to the repair café for help reupholstering its seat cushion.

“The beauty of it,” Pettus said, “was that I actually was able to learn more about the chair. It was a great experience to know that — I’m not gonna say I birthed it, I of course did not — but I actually had something to do with helping to get it put back together.”

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Pope Leo XIV visits South America, regional leaders gather at the Ibero-American Summit in Spain, and Chile’s Atacama Desert feels the effects of El Niño.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Pope Leo XIV visits South America, regional leaders gather at the Ibero-American Summit in Spain, and Chile’s Atacama Desert feels the effects of El Niño.

Sign up to receive Latin America Brief in your inbox every Friday.

Pope Leo XIV began a 12-day tour through South America last Friday. It is the longest trip yet of his papacy, taking him to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru. He’s getting a rock star reception: The Chicago-born pope became a Peruvian citizen after working as a missionary in the country, making this trip a homecoming for him, Gene Kuleta wrote in Foreign Policy last month.

In Argentina, Leo made headlines on Sunday when he called for the kind of strong social welfare state that runs counter to President Javier Milei’s austerity measures. Milei nevertheless praised Leo through tears when he bid him farewell. Argentina experienced a national “collective empathy” during Leo’s trip, Clarín’s Héctor Gambini wrote.

Leo’s itinerary underscores a clear set of foreign-policy ideals, said Massimo Faggioli, a historian at Villanova University, the pope’s alma mater. Chief among them is the idea that the Catholic Church can be a guardian for multilateralism as it comes under attack from the United States.

While the Vatican’s support for the United Nations system is not new, “what has changed is that U.S. foreign policy has become more muscular, more unilateral, and so you see more visibly now the difference between American foreign policy and that of the Vatican,” Faggioli said.

Leo was outspoken after the United States captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January and again after the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, according to Faggioli. The pope publicly suggested that both actions could be unlawful; he has since visited multiple small countries and spoken about how they play crucial roles in the international system.

“The gift of smallness,” Leo said on a trip to Monaco in March, means putting “your prosperity at the service of law and justice, especially at a historical moment when the display of power and logic of oppression are harming the world and jeopardizing peace.”

This focus on small states helps explain why Leo chose to start his trip in Uruguay, which is one of Latin America’s least religious countries, Faggioli said. The pope was celebrating Uruguay’s strong civic and diplomatic traditions, not just its small Catholic population. A plurality of the country’s population has no religious affiliation.

“Persevering in respect for law, for negotiation, and for the patient search for agreements is a service that Uruguay can continue to offer to its neighbors,” Leo said in Uruguay’s capital of Montevideo last Friday. The orchestra that welcomed him played Afro-Uruguayan candombe.

Latin America’s Catholic population is shrinking—dropping from 80 percent of the total population in 1995 to only 55 percent today, losing ground to evangelicals and people with no religion, according to pollster Latinobarómetro. But the same survey suggests that the decline has slowed in the last half decade.

“That might be part of the Pope Francis effect,” Faggioli said, referencing Leo’s popular Argentine predecessor.

Leo has continued Francis’s focus on seeking out the poor and marginalized in his travels. Judging by the crowds welcoming the pope in Argentina, the country has fully embraced him as a continuation of Francis’s spirit.

Leo arrived in Peru on Wednesday. On Friday, he will return to his adopted hometown of Chiclayo.

Friday, Nov. 13: Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla concludes visit to China.

Friday, Nov. 13, to Tuesday, Nov. 17: Pope Leo XIV ends his tour with a visit to Peru.

Wednesday, Nov. 18, to Thursday, Nov. 19: Chilean President José Antonio Kast, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.

Monday, Nov. 23, to Friday, Nov. 27: Polish President Karol Nawrocki visits Argentina and Chile.

Paraguay’s bank scandal. As this newsletter covered last week, a dramatic bank collapse in Paraguay toppled President Santiago Peña, who was removed from office on Nov. 6 after announcing plans to resign the day before. It was the country’s largest political crisis since the 2012 removal of leftist President Fernando Lugo.

Lugo was one of the few Paraguayan leaders of the last 70 years who did not hail from Peña’s right-wing Colorado Party. Peña was replaced by his vice president, Pedro Alliana, who is expected to hew closely to Colorado’s orthodoxy, the Paraguay Post reported. That includes trying to create a business-friendly environment and staying aligned with the United States, Israel, and Taiwan.

Alliana signaled that he would focus mostly on domestic policy, saying in remarks to Congress that “too much time has been spent overseas.” Paraguay’s next presidential election is set for 2028.

Slavery reparations? The United Kingdom’s King Charles III faced protesters demanding reparations for slavery during a trip to the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda that wrapped up last week. The island nations remain part of the Commonwealth of Nations, an association of 56 countries, mostly former British colonies.

Unlike fellow Caribbean community member Jamaica, the three countries that Charles visited have not filed a formal legal petition on reparations to the United Kingdom. But the protesters’ demands still prompted a formal response from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who attended a Commonwealth Heads of Government summit last week.

Burnham committed to beginning a “structured dialogue” with Caribbean countries affected by the slave trade, Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne said. Though Burnham recently wrote in the Guardian that he did not believe financial reparations were appropriate, last week he voiced openness to debt restructuring for some Commonwealth countries.

An aerial view of blooming wildflowers in the Atacama Desert near Copiapo, Chile, on Sept. 18.JAVIER TORRES/AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES

Desert bloom. Chile’s Atacama Desert is covered in bright pink, purple, and yellow desert flowers this month. They spring to life every few years, when the area receives high amounts of rain. This year’s display is a result of the weather irregularities linked to the so-called Super El Niño climate phenomenon.

El Niño has hit various parts of Latin America differently. Nearby Bolivia has seen severe droughts and has declared a state of emergency, FP’s Christina Lu reported. The toll on Chile has also been tragic: A storm that scientists say was exacerbated by the weather pattern killed 13 people in July, some of them in the same region as the Atacama Desert.

While Chileans are celebrating the desert blooms, many are also calling for better preparedness for extreme climate events.

In addition to the Atacama Desert, which of the following is also a desert in Chile?

Though most of Patagonia is in Argentina, some of it extends into southern Chile.

Argentina’s President Javier Milei and other leaders attend the 30th Ibero-American Summit at the Royal Collections Gallery in Madrid on Nov. 5. THOMAS COEX/AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES

Last week, seven Latin American heads of state gathered in Madrid for the Ibero-American Summit, which has been held nearly every year since 1991 and unites Latin American countries with Spain, Portugal, Andorra, and Equatorial Guinea.

Presidential attendance increased since the last summit in 2024, as did the number of countries that signed on to a joint declaration—albeit with some disagreements in the footnotes. The event is the latest evidence that Latin American leaders are trying to strengthen their network of relationships beyond just the United States and China, which are the top trade partners for many of them.

Notably, most of the Latin American presidents at the summit were right-wing leaders who have signaled alignment with U.S. President Donald Trump. Brazil, Mexico, and Uruguay—all led by left-wing presidents—sent their foreign ministers instead.

In his speech, Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz marked independence from the United States both by congratulating Brazil on its democratic election—which Trump has still not recognized—and by proposing the creation of an Ibero-American “center for strategic and security thinking” in Bolivia.

The proposal was accepted, Paz said afterward. It is an indication that as his and other right-wing governments don’t want anti-crime cooperation to be restricted to the Trump-led Shield of the Americas initiative.

It’s not the only recent sign that Latin American countries are turning to Europe for partnership. Since the Mercosur-European Union trade deal took provisional effect in May, exports to the bloc have risen by around 30 percent from Brazil alone, according to Brazil’s trade ministry.

Like many U.S. presidents before him, Donald Trump is responding to a final midterm election drubbing by heading for foreign shores—to a region that has been far from top of mind over the past two years.

Trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines and China next week to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. At the latter, he will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping for the third time this year. In Manila, Trump is expected to meet with the other leaders in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue—between the United States, Australia, Japan, and India—for the first time in his second term.

Like many U.S. presidents before him, Donald Trump is responding to a final midterm election drubbing by heading for foreign shores—to a region that has been far from top of mind over the past two years.

Trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines and China next week to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. At the latter, he will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping for the third time this year. In Manila, Trump is expected to meet with the other leaders in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue—between the United States, Australia, Japan, and India—for the first time in his second term.

Trump will make those trips under the shadow of his political diminishment at home, with last week’s elections leading to the Democratic Party’s control of Congress starting in January and giving them the ability to block Trump’s legislative agenda.

“It is often the case when a president ventures to a major trip in Asia, a long domestic shadow casts its darkness over the trip,” said Kurt Campbell, chairman and co-founder of The Asia Group, a geopolitical advisory firm in Washington, D.C. “This is another case of just massive overhang from domestic politics that are going to shape everything that he does,” added Campbell, who previously served as deputy secretary of state and Indo-Pacific coordinator on the National Security Council under former U.S. President Joe Biden.

But Trump is equally likely to try and push past that dynamic, said Mike Kuiken, vice chair of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a bipartisan panel that advises U.S. lawmakers on China. “The reality is that Trump is weaker at home politically, so I think he’s going to feel very motivated to project power and confidence,” said Kuiken, who is also a distinguished visiting fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution.

Trump “loves pomp and circumstance, and these kinds of events present an incredible opportunity there,” Kuiken said. “There’s going to be red carpets, and flowers, and parades, and military equipment all over the place, so this is the kind of thing that plays to his insecurities in a way that he’ll very much enjoy.”

Substance, there may be less of.

Experts predict that in his meeting with Xi, Trump will seek to maintain the status quo between the world’s two largest economies—whether with their trade truce (which the two countries just extended until mid-January), their nascent dialogue on artificial intelligence, or their tit-for-tat export controls on U.S. semiconductor chips and China’s critical minerals.

“I think at least the Chinese expect that he will be more desirous of preserving calm on the diplomatic front now that he is politically weakened and presumably will not want to see the stock market dips or other things that would erode his position even further,” said Hal Brands, a professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies who also serves on the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission. The commission, incidentally, is set to publish its annual report to Congress on Wednesday—the same day that Trump is scheduled to touch down in Shenzhen.

The midterm result “probably makes Trump more interested in getting big, good international headlines to help him restore a sense of momentum around his presidency,” said Brands, who is also a frequent Foreign Policy contributor.

Trump’s semiconductor position may also be muddied by the turmoil around Nvidia, the chipmaking giant at the center of the U.S. export control debate. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned on Thursday after news emerged of his extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy as well as with one of his subordinates at the company.

Huang’s resignation has big implications for the global AI race.

Reshaping a globally competitive auto industry needs a hard rethink on deals.

Elections have consequences overseas, too.

Huang cultivated close personal ties with Trump and attended both of his previous meetings with Xi in Beijing and Washington along with other tech CEOs. Last December, Huang successfully petitioned the Trump administration to relax some restrictions on sales of the company’s second-tier chips to China—giving the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of some sales in the process.

The Nvidia drama is already causing tension in the U.S.-China relationship. “The U.S. should stop fabricating the ‘Chinese spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing on Thursday.

But the Nvidia elephant in the room is likely to be mutually ignored—or quickly swept under the rug—when Trump and Xi meet. “There’s no gain for Trump in making an issue of this and even less gain for Xi in making an issue of it, and so I would be kind of surprised if it came up in their bilateral meeting,” Kuiken said. However, Xi is likely to stress that any further tightening of chip export controls through proposed legislation would invite retaliation from Beijing. “I wouldn’t be shocked if Xi were to try to find ways of reminding President Trump: ‘Oh, it’s wonderful what we’ve achieved together over the last year, would be such a shame if anything were to happen to disrupt this productive relationship,’” Kuiken added.

There’s also the prospect of a trilateral meeting of Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump said that he thinks he will meet the two leaders in Shenzhen to discuss “a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he said on Sunday. But Beijing appears to be wary of the implications of such a meeting, given its long-standing reluctance to commit to arms control.

“If the Xi-Putin-Trump meeting happens, it will only happen because the Chinese have received sufficient guarantees that it’ll be utterly devoid of substance,” Brands said. “The things that Trump wants to discuss are a settlement in Ukraine and nuclear arms control. The Chinese have no intention of being put on the hook as a responsible party in bringing the war in Ukraine to an end, and they have no interest in a trilateral nuclear arms control negotiation,” he added. “They would want to make this as scripted and formulaic as possible.”

For Beijing, simply having and hosting the meeting holds a degree of appeal. “When we were in China, we heard over and over again about how the Chinese really liked President Trump’s ‘G-2’ framework,” Kuiken said. “What happens when it becomes sort of a G-3 framework where China effectively has two seats at the table? Because you know Putin’s seat is essentially China’s seat.”

Putin, as the leader who first floated the meeting, appears more amenable to discussing both nuclear weapons and Ukraine but will likely look to focus more on the latter, said Edgard Kagan, a senior advisor and chair of China studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C. “This was originally a Putin idea,” Kagan told reporters in a briefing earlier this week. “I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like.”

Then there’s the Quad, which will be convening a leaders’ meeting on the sidelines of ASEAN before Trump heads to Shenzhen. It will mark the first and likely final time that Trump meets the other leaders of the security grouping—Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi—together in his current term.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been the flag-bearer for the Quad thus far, having attended and convened multiple meetings with his counterparts over the past two years. Trump’s participation is unlikely to amount to more than a box-checking exercise, experts said.

“I don’t think the president can hide the fact that he’s not terribly enthusiastic about the gathering,” Campbell said, adding that the Trump administration’s notable lack of preparation for meetings with traditional U.S. allies and partners will not be lost on their leaders. “If you compare how he prepares and thinks about a meeting with Putin or Xi, or even potentially with [North Korean dictator] Kim Jong Un, there just is a noticeable difference, and that’s not lost on Asian interlocutors,” Campbell added.

There are limits to what the other countries that form ASEAN will seek to extract from Trump—to the extent that they get to engage with him at all. “They have probably learned by now that the most effective place to engage this administration is never in a multilateral format but is actually a bilateral format, so I think that the more interesting meetings are the sidebars,” said Kuiken. “These meetings are probably more likely to be the places where these countries choose to engage, as opposed to trying to box in the U.S in some sort of larger regional discussion or engagement.”

The White House has not yet released a full schedule for Trump’s visit, though a bilateral meeting in Manila with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appears to be in the cards and others could materialize closer to the date.

Trade is likely to be high on Asian leaders’ lists of priorities. “Some of the tariffs that he has imposed on these countries are pretty staggering, and so I think those countries now may feel emboldened to compel or urge Trump to revisit these things,” Kuiken said. “It’ll be interesting to see if they decide to play that card in this first meeting, or if they decide to hold back for a later engagement that’s sort of quieter and a little more underneath the radar.”

According to Campbell, the big question on every leader’s mind will be the resolution of a conflict that none of them are directly involved in. “We all know that the Iran war had an impact on this [U.S. midterm] election, but it is starting to have very substantial impacts across Asia,” he said, mentioning supplies of key industrial inputs such as helium, sulfur, and diesel that have been disrupted by the war. “When the war started eight months ago, it was at a moment in which most countries had maximum reserves in many of these areas. Those reserves are now gone,” he added. “So [Trump] is going to be in countries and meeting with leaders—the Philippines, Indonesia, other Southeast Asian countries that are being battered by higher costs associated with energy and the like.”

Ultimately, however, Campbell said those leaders will already be starting to look past Trump.

“I think what they see [from the midterms] is a pretty clear rejection of a style of politics in the United States and a rejection of the United States as an authoritarian leader-led country,” he said. “And so, the biggest manifestation is going to be Asian interlocutors seeking out other power sources in Washington.”

Rishi Iyengar is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @iyengarish.bsky.social X: @Iyengarish Instagram: @iyengar.rishi

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.title: The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.author: Charles Kupchan
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.text:
CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

How to Avoid Another Yalta

In just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm plan has yet been announced, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons wrote on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”

These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats while turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting may ultimately yield little progress on major issues.

Nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another, but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

If he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core issues that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flash points of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

Our editors’ top picks, delivered free to your inbox every Friday.

* Note that when you provide your email address, the Foreign Affairs Privacy Policy and Terms of Use will apply to your newsletter subscription.

I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a new concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus-building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

But the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

Yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

If they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flash points. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung laid out an ambitious plan for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

Lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they may be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Seoul and Pyongyang. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a plan for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

The prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer, but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia, and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a new round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

Xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi can advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

Trump and Xi can press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, may convince Putin to relent on at least some of these issues.

Trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to issue maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

Neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

As a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

Xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop, or at least slow, the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

Xi can also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf and release frozen Iranian assets and remove economic sanctions. Washington may well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiation of a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi can help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

Beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Putin and Xi. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, New START, ended in February. There are currently no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

In October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon projects that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it nearly in the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

Realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

Trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area where cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Yemen or Gaza. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

Yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force upon Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a new Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

Trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

A summit next week will not usher in a new era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It may not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump will begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.
