BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Northern Tasmania

The court heard Davis waited until the shoebox had burnt completely, then went inside to prepare lunch for his father. (Supplied: Paul Worsteling)

A Tasmanian man has been convicted and fined over a fire he lit in the state's upper east coast that later destroyed two homes.

Michael John Davis was found guilty of lighting a fire without taking reasonable precautions to prevent it from spreading.

Davis was fined a total of $3,000 on two charges, one relating to drink driving.

A Tasmanian man has been fined for lighting a fire that destroyed two houses and burnt through 1,200 hectares of vegetation in the state's upper east coast.

Michael John Davis, 56, was found guilty in the Launceston Magistrates Court this week of lighting a fire on December 9 last year without taking reasonable precautions to prevent it from spreading.

He also pleaded guilty to a low-range drink-driving charge.

The bushfire at Stieglitz could be seen across the water from St Helens. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

According to his lawyer, James Oxley, Davis could not appear in person as he lives in Indonesia, and so appeared via videolink.

The prosecution said on December 9, 2025, Mr Davis was at his parents' property burning a shoebox filled with tax records inside a fire pit while smoking cigarettes.

Davis sat with the fire until the box had burnt completely, then went inside to prepare lunch for his father, who was bedridden at the time.

The December 9 bushfire was captured by a NASA satellite. (Supplied: NASA/MODIS)

When he went back outside 30 minutes later, he discovered bushland on the northern boundary of the home, metres from where he burnt the receipts, was on fire.

Davis attempted to extinguish the fire with buckets of water and asked his mother to call the fire brigade when she returned home.

The fire had spread through bushland to the north, and as a result, two residences on St Helens Point Road were destroyed.

TasNetworks and Telstra infrastructure were also damaged as a result of the fire.

Topic:
Fishing and Aquaculture Industry

Mr Oxley said he confirmed with the Tasmania Fire Service that a total fire ban had not been issued on the day, and no fire permits were required in that area.

He said the total number of documents burnt had fit into a shoebox, and that the fire was not large.

"He did everything he could once he saw the fire had spread to put it out."

The bushfire sent plumes of smoke over St Helens. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Mr Oxley asked Magistrate Simon Brown to consider Davis' visa status in his decision, and asked for Davis to be fined without a conviction, as that could hamper his chances at renewing his visa with the Indonesian government.

"That process will involve him producing his Tasmanian record to the Indonesian government," he said.

"His plan is to remain there with his wife for the foreseeable future, and in my submission there is a real risk that this could come back to haunt him in that application process."

Two houses were destroyed in the blaze at Stieglitz. (Supplied: John Sullivan)

However, Magistrate Brown said there had been "catastrophic consequences" as a result of Davis' negligence.

"In fairness, I don't think I'm minded to not convict," he said.

"I accept the defendant's degree of negligence. His moral culpability here is plainly at the lower end of the scale.

"Of course, lighting a fire outside in Tasmania in the summer months in December is something that should be done with real care.

"Whilst the defendant did watch the fire and believed it to be out, he took no steps to ensure it could go absolutely nowhere by wetting down or stamping on it."

Magistrate Brown convicted Davis and fined him $1,000 for the drink driving charge, as well as suspended his licence for six months.

He was fined $2,000 in relation to the fire, totalling $3,000.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Tara Morrison was murdered in the Busselton home of her former partner, Hannah Louise Glover.  (Supplied: Facebook)

A man accused of murdering a woman in WA's South West is set to face a retrial, after a jury could not reach a verdict.

James Anthony Sorgiovanni had been accused of stabbing Tara Morrison to death.

The jury had been deliberating since Monday.

The jury in the trial of a man accused of murdering a woman whose body was found stuffed in a wardrobe at a house in WA’s South West has been unable to reach a verdict.

WARNING: The following story contains details that may distress some readers.

James Anthony Sorgiovanni, 29, had been on trial for the murder of Tara Morrison, whose body was found in his Busselton house in 2024.

Ms Morrison had been visiting the house Mr Sorgiovanni shared with his girlfriend Hannah Louise Glover, who had also been charged with murder but pleaded guilty part-way through the trial.

Her guilty plea followed the evidence of an inmate who said Glover — who was formerly Ms Morrison's girlfriend — had confessed to the killing in prison.

A court sketch of Hannah Louise Glover and James Anthony Sorgiovanni, (ABC News: Anne Barnetson)

The court was earlier told Ms Morrison was killed in a frenzied attack arising from a “love triangle”.

The jury started deliberating on Monday afternoon but after days of discussing the case, could not reach a unanimous verdict on the charge of murder and was discharged today.

Glover gave evidence describing how she stabbed her former girlfriend multiple times, in several locations inside the house she shared with Mr Sorgiovanni.

She told the jury Mr Sorgiovanni held Ms Morrison while Glover attacked her, but that he was the last one to stab the victim.

The court had heard Ms Morrison was planning to stay at the house, and methylamphetamine and GHB were used on the night of the murder.

James Sorgiovanni’s defence lawyer, Lisa Boston.  (ABC News: David Weber)

Mr Sorgiovanni’s lawyer Lisa Boston told the jury he was under the influence of drugs at the time, woke to find Glover attacking Ms Morrison, and could not effectively prevent it.

Under cross-examination by Ms Boston, the prisoner who Glover confessed to said Glover made "no mention" of Mr Sorgiovanni initially.

Tara Morrison was stabbed multiple times.  (Supplied: Facebook)

She said Glover told her Mr Sorgiovanni had grabbed her in a "bear hug" and tried to drag her away.

During closing submissions to the jury, prosecutor Michael Cvetkoski showed a photo of Tara Morrison's left hand, with a serious injury which he described as a defensive wound.

Mr Cvetkoski put it to the jury that Ms Morrison's right hand was being restrained and could not be used as a "defensive mechanism".

Hannah Louise Glover pleads guilty to stabbing Tara Morrison to death in Western Australia's South West after a murder trial hears about her prison confessions.

"Likely, this was an ongoing struggle," Mr Cvetkoski told the jury.

The court was shown crime scene photos with blood on the floor and walls of the house.

Mr Sorgiovanni now faces a retrial.

It is not known when Glover will be sentenced.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.title: How the Microsoft outage is affecting Australia
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.author: Georgie Hewson and Ahmed Yussuf
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

More than 120,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook. (Reuters: Gonzalo Fuentes/File Photo)

Australians woke up this morning to a global outage affecting numerous Microsoft products used in hundreds of millions of workplaces around the world.

Throughout the day, the tech giant worked to fix the issue causing disruptions to Outlook, Teams and Authenticator, and the many other programs businesses, institutions and services rely on.

Microsoft outage live: For the latest on the issues affecting the tech giant's apps, read our blog.

While some enjoyed a reprieve from responding to emails at work, the outage has exposed how reliant Australians are on technology the country does not control.

Australian Catholic University's IT discipline head Niusha Shafiabady said the outage exposed how dangerous that was.

"When systems fail overseas, Australian businesses can feel the consequences almost immediately," she said.

"We are making our systems more intelligent in Australia, but not necessarily more resilient. Even the smartest systems are useless when the infrastructure they depend on fails."

Here's what people told the ABC about how they experienced the outage.

A widespread outage hit Microsoft software, including Outlook, with many users having trouble accessing their email accounts and encountering other errors across the tech giant's suite of applications.

Some small businesses have lost up to $30,000 in one day.

On Microsoft's Service Health Status site, the company confirmed users may be unable to connect to multiple 365 services, including Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot 365, Defender, Planner, To Do, Intune, Purview and Power BI.

The company posted an update just after 9am AEST saying it had begun a "gradual recovery" of access to email and other online services.

An hour later, another update was posted saying restored servers were becoming unresponsive again.

Microsoft explained this was due to a process on the affected servers "responsible for establishing secure connections" becoming overwhelmed, causing the servers to stop processing requests.

In the hours after the outage, there have been reports of a gradual return but no "long-term fix" has been found by Microsoft.  (AP: Lindsey Wasson)

The company said it was preparing a solution to "address this behaviour" and if successful it would then "gradually reintroduce additional traffic".

A further update said: "We've monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they're not taking as expected."

As of Friday night, Microsoft said access was "being gradually restored" in the Asia-Pacific region, with improvement also seen across Europe and the US.

Beyond the immediate impact to inboxes, businesses and government agencies reported cascading effects on day-to-day administration.

Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today.

Stores lost email-based sales, patients have lost access to telehealth services and long-distance schools have shut for the day.

With Microsoft's two-factor authentication app Authenticator down, Peter Roche in Adelaide said he could not process invoices or access accounting software.

"[It's] very difficult to do work, losing thousands of dollars because we aren't getting the orders in and the invoices out. Bloody Microsoft."

Manny Flores in Melbourne had to miss a job interview.

"[I] couldn't access Teams for a job interview, it has been rescheduled for next week," he said.

"I suppose I should be grateful for the extra time to prepare, but after almost a year unemployed, getting to a final interview is huge, and the sooner I get an answer about my success or otherwise, the better."

The Microsoft outage has hit students across schools and TAFE. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

The outage has affected students in the midst of their end-of-school exams.

Emilie Yu from Melbourne said she had been unable to study for her two remaining VCE language exams.

"Due to the Microsoft outage I now cannot access help and work from my teachers, on top of the VCAA website still being down for the past two days," she said.

"How are we expected to study like this? This isn't fair for hardworking students who are now losing resources."

Susan Wallace in Lismore said: "Lucky it's Friday because all of us using Teams for Virtual Classrooms at TAFE NSW and elsewhere, wouldn't be able to attend classes."

People have reported not being unable to access medical appointments following the outage. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Occupational therapist Lauren Van Ingen in Melbourne said she was unable to care for patients with neurological conditions due to being locked out of her Outlook account.

"This will affect my ability to work today, which includes helping clients with MND, Huntington's, and other conditions get the equipment they need to remain living safely at home.

"Fingers crossed it's up and running soon."

Maria Derosa is a patient in Melbourne who couldn't get medical scans done after a car accident.

"Medical scans have been cancelled due to both myself and the clinic not being able to access referrals via email or fax," she said.

"Doctors don't give paper referrals anymore so everything has been cancelled/delayed.

"I was in a car accident and I can't have the relevant tests to make sure I'm OK."

Some people reported flight delays after the outage. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Livinia Drummond from Sydney said her colleague's flight to Papua New Guinea was delayed as the captain's pre-flight documents were sent via email on Outlook.

"Passengers were advised to wait on the bus at the tarmac for someone on foot to bring printed documents," she said.

"Our reliance on these systems is terrifying."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/y.title: Teen sentenced for 'vicious' attack on woman sleeping rough
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/y.author: Eva Blandis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/y.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The now 18-year-old was sentenced in Adelaide's Youth Court. (ABC News: Stephanie Richards)

An Adelaide teenager has been sentenced for attacking a woman who was sleeping rough near a public library in 2025.

The sentencing magistrate said the attack was "sustained and vicious".

The teenager will remain in detention until March and will spend a year under supervision after his release.

A teenager who subjected a woman sleeping rough in Adelaide's inner south to a "repeated, persistent and forceful" nine-minute attack will be released from detention early next year.

The now-18-year-old was today sentenced in the Adelaide Youth Court over an attack on a 64-year-old woman near the Mitcham Memorial Library, on Belair Road at Hawthorn, on November 13, 2025.

The teenager, who cannot be identified, has already spent a year in detention.

He previously pleaded guilty to causing harm with intent, and to a charge of serious criminal trespass for a series of break-ins after the attack.

In an almost hour-long hearing on Friday, Magistrate John Wells said the then-17-year-old's "violent offence" against the "vulnerable" woman was "unambiguously serious".

"The youth attacked a homeless woman … in a sustained and vicious manner," he said.

"The violence was repeated, persistent and forceful."

The attack on a homeless woman took place near the Mitcham Memorial Library.  (ABC News)

Magistrate Wells said the teenager also recorded portions of the attack, and had made comments to the woman that were "aggressive" and "callous".

He said the victim suffered several injuries including broken ribs, a fractured eye socket, a scalp haematoma and a fractured jaw.

The court previously heard the teenager had a "cocktail of substances" in his system at the time of the offending and was in a state of "dysregulation" at the time of the offending.

It had also heard the youth had since been diagnosed with alcohol use disorder, autism and severe ADHD.

Magistrate Wells sentenced the teenager to a further four months in detention, and ordered he be under supervision for one year following his release in March next year.

He said the teenager would be ordered to spend three months and 16 days in detention if he re-offended during his supervision period.

The teenager's mother and a support person were present at the hearing but declined to comment to the media as they exited the court building.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/u.author: Kirstie Wellauer, Tahnee Jash, and Joanna McCarthy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/u.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Indigenous Policy

Albert Barume says the Commonwealth must be willing to override states and territories on Indigenous rights. (ABC News: Geoff Kemp)

Australia’s failure to protect Indigenous rights is damaging the country’s global reputation, a UN special rapporteur has warned.

Albert Barume was barred from visiting youth detention centres in Queensland and the NT during his two-week visit to Australia..

Dr Barume will present his report to the UN Human Rights Council in September next year.

A UN special rapporteur has urged the Commonwealth to set national minimum standards for Indigenous rights, calling the current state "embarrassing" for Australia's international reputation.

"I'm convinced Indigenous peoples' rights … are unsafe in the hands of states and territories," Albert Barume told reporters in Sydney.

"I really think the current generation of Australians have a responsibility to face, and this is for their own international reputation, whether on the left or on the right, they need to face the responsibility.

"The state of protection of Indigenous peoples' rights is a bit embarrassing."

The Special Rapporteur for the Rights of Indigenous Peoples has just wrapped a two-week visit to Australia, during which he was denied access to youth detention centres in Queensland and the Northern Territory.

Albert Barume met with community members in the Torres Strait Islands. (Supplied: United Nations)

In his preliminary findings, Dr Barume urged the Commonwealth to legislate national mandatory standards for First Nations rights that were consistent with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

Without these, he said, Australia's human rights obligations were easily ignored by states and territories.

"A change in the government could wipe out those human rights gains," Dr Barume told the ABC.

"It means those rights are not really secured, they are unsafe, and it's like they are optional. Human rights should not be optional."

He criticised states and territories for passing punitive bail and sentencing laws and failing to raise the age of criminal responsibility, which he said had fuelled the over-incarceration of Indigenous children.

First Nations children account for nearly two thirds of those in youth detention.

Indigenous people also make up 37 per cent of the prison population, up from 24 per cent in 2009.

Albert Barume spent two weeks travelling the country. (Supplied: United Nations)

Dr Barume's report said incarceration could not "be understood separately from the continuing effects of colonisation, dispossession, structural racism and inequalities".

He also criticised Queensland and the Northern Territory for abandoning treaty processes, and the Victorian opposition for its promise to scrap treaty if it wins government.

"Fundamental rights cannot be contingent on electoral outcomes or the priorities of successive governments," the report said.

Dr Barume said he heard "disturbing accounts of heightened racism and hate speech" during and after the Voice referendum, and called for a national representative voice for First Peoples.

"Some section of public opinion tended to understand the failed referendum as a 'no' to Indigenous peoples' rights and as an open door to expressing those prejudiced, racist views," he said.

Albert Barume wants the federal government to enact national minimum standards to protect Indigenous rights. (ABC News: Geoff Kemp)

Dr Barume said he had "grave concern" about the rates of missing and murdered Indigenous women and children, and the high rates of children in out-of-home care.

"I was particularly concerned by accounts by First Peoples women who, despite being survivors of violence, are misidentified as perpetrators by law enforcement agents," his report said.

"Women also described fear that seeking assistance or reporting abuse could lead to the removal of their children."

Dr Barume said Australia had made some progress on Indigenous rights, including the expansion of Aboriginal community-controlled organisations, Indigenous ranger programs, language revitalisation and native title rights.

He met with Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy and said he had requested a meeting with the prime minister.

"I'm really asking the prime minister … to explain to the wider Australian population that it is in their interest to fix Indigenous peoples rights," Dr Barume said.

"It's a collective responsibility and a collective international reputation."

A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland told the ABC the government welcomed Dr Barume's visit.

They said human rights in Australia were protected through a range of laws state and federal laws, common law and the constitution.

Dr Barume will present his findings to the UN Human Rights Council in September next year.

The jury delivered its verdict in Rory Amon's indecent assault and sexual intercourse of a minor trial on Friday. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Former NSW Liberal MP Rory Amon has been found guilty of the rape and indecent assault of a 13-year-old boy in 2017, after meeting him on a dating app.

The ex-member for Pittwater stood trial in the NSW Supreme Court this week on charges of indecent assault of a person under 16, and having sexual intercourse with a person between 10 and 14-years-old.

The court heard Amon connected with the victim on a dating app and first met him in person in July 2017, when they went into the toilet of an underground car park.

The jury deliberated for about four hours, and found the boy was raped and indecently assaulted at that meeting.

Amon had argued he thought the boy was 17.

The matter is listed for sentence hearing later this month.

Amon remains on bail.

The former MP faced trial in March on 10 charges relating to the same victim, but was found not guilty on eight of those charges.

At the time, the court heard those eight charges related to a second alleged meeting between the pair, which Amon denied ever happening.

The jury was hung on two of 10 of the charges, which led the Director of Public Prosecutions to call for this week's retrial on those counts.

The first trial heard Amon and the boy met near the boy's apartment block, and then went into the public bathroom, where Amon had the victim to perform oral sex on him.

Amon did not dispute that there was sexual activity at that first meeting, but said he believed the victim was 17, because that is what he had told him.

The victim said he told Amon he was 15, but was in fact 13.

Amon resigned from NSW parliament in August 2024 after being arrested.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.title: Tasmanian premier apologises for 'outcome' of Christmas post
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.author: Josh Duggan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Premier sorry for 'effect' of Christmas remarks

Premier Jeremy Rockliff says he's "sorry" for the fallout over a Facebook post that shamed a Tasmanian school's attempt to rename its Christmas event.

Mr Rockliff incorrectly claimed all references to Christmas were being removed, attracting social media vitriol against the school and its acting principal.

Mr Rockliff says it was not his "intention to have an outcome such as this", but says he stands by his expectations.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff has apologised "for the effect" of a Facebook post in which he incorrectly claimed all references to Christmas were being removed from a school's end-of-year celebrations.

Trevallyn Primary School became embroiled in a social media firestorm last month, following a move to rename its end-of-year event from "Christmas on the Hill" to "End of Year Extravaganza".

Is this Rocky's last Christmas as Premier?

Mr Rockliff took to Facebook on October 14, to say he was aware of "efforts made to remove all references to Christmas in end-of-year school celebrations".

He had since refused to apologise, saying he had a right to express the view that Christmas was an important part of our way of life.

While his post did not identify the school involved, it and the acting principal were identified in the comments, and in media reports.

Topic:
Fishing and Aquaculture Industry

At a media conference today, Mr Rockliff was asked again about the saga, following Australian Education Union (AEU) members from Trevallyn Primary School passing a no confidence motion in him.

"What was a very simple constituent concern.. I made my expectations clear to the secretary of the department and I've made two very measured public statements of which I have not mentioned the school or indeed any individuals at all.

"Now, there's been a lot of discussion and… I'm sorry for the outcome that it has created, and it was never my intention to have an outcome such as this. So I'm sorry for the effect on individuals, teachers and schools — that was never my intention.

"But I stand by my expectations and my expectations are very clear, they have been very clear, and I am remaining true to those expectations but also feel for the people that have been involved the local school the local teachers as well.

"There is no place in our community for vitriol, for personal attacks in any setting including social media so I'm very sorry for that. I wish that we have a very measured discussion that's all, what I've always wanted, in setting those very clear expectations."

The union has been contacted for comment.

Jeremy Rockliff has apologised for his remarks, saying: "it was never my intention to have an outcome such as this, so I'm sorry for the effect". (ABC News)

Following the premier's post, Trevallyn Primary School was forced to call security due to online abuse.

The acting principal also took leave.

The AEU had called for an apology, calling the post "reprehensible" and calling the impact "significant".

It had barred all politicians from end-of-year events at schools until the premier offered an apology.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff made a social media post saying he was aware of "efforts made to remove all references to Christmas" in school celebrations the same day the education department wrote to his office to say Christmas remained an important part of the event — but he says he did not see the letter until the next day.

"Parents and educators across the state are aghast that Premier Rockliff has not only refused to apologise for his action but has doubled down," the union's Tasmanian president David Genford said.

The Tasmanian Principals Association also said it was "outraged" by the premier's actions.

Mr Rockliff's apology did not acknowledge that he had falsely claimed all references to Christmas were being removed from schools.

Correspondence tabled in parliament revealed Education Department secretary Ginna Webster wrote to the premier on the day of his post, informing him that Christmas remained an important part of Trevallyn Primary School's event.

A post on social media by Tasmania's premier decrying an apparent attempt to "remove references to Christmas" has spiralled into a culture war.

"Rather than remove Christmas, the school is seeking to balance longstanding traditions with an inclusive approach that enables all students and families to participate in a way that is respectful of their individual beliefs and circumstances," Ms Webster wrote.

Mr Rockliff has said he did not receive this letter until the day after, but that it was clear changes were being made.

His original post on Facebook received more than 2,000 comments, generally supportive of his stance.

Multiple Liberal MPs posted to Facebook in support of the premier, reiterating the importance of Christmas.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/l.title: Locusts wreaking havoc across South Australia's pastoral land
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/l.author: Tahlia Fahey and Isabella Kelly
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Agricultural Pest Control

This composite image captures locusts swarming across Bridget Wood's station. (Supplied: Bridget Woods)

Producers in South Australia's Mid North and Flinders Ranges are reporting significant locust outbreaks.

One pastoralist said she had been communicating with PIRSA for five weeks before it began aerial spraying earlier this week.

The department said it would continue to monitor locust numbers across the state and spray where possible.

Locust outbreaks are reaching new highs in parts of South Australia, as landholders raise concerns that the time for effective control has passed.

Outbreaks have occurred across SA, with producers reporting higher numbers this year than in previous years.

The Department of Primary Industries and Regions (PIRSA) began surveying the outbreaks in early September and has completed aerial spraying for locusts over 115,000 hectares around the Flinders and Mid North regions.

A locust in a paddock at Bugle Hut in South Australia's Riverland. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Peterborough livestock producer Bridget Woods said she filed a report with PIRSA after first noticing locusts on her property about five weeks ago.

"There were thousands of them everywhere that were about half a centimetre in size," she said.

"There's not much left there for them to eat now, but while we still had clover, they ate all the plants, just leaving half-formed seed pods behind."

Bridget Woods said watercourses on her station were covered by "a black cloud" of locusts.  (ABC Rural: Brooke Neindorf)

Since then, the pests have grown, both in size and population.

"We had the rain, and they've hatched. The volume of them is like nothing I've seen. It's incredible," Ms Woods said.

Though PIRSA has regularly monitored the station, Ms Woods said it took about five weeks before the department began aerial spraying on Thursday.

Locusts have taken to the air at Bridget Wood's station near Peterborough. (Supplied: Bridget Woods)

"They kept telling us … that we didn't have enough grasshoppers; we needed to have between 80 and 500 per square metre per 100 hectares," she said.

SA's locust commissioner, Michael McManus, said survey teams had been at Peterborough regularly, but swarms of adult locusts had infested the area in the past week, triggering the aerial spraying.

He said several factors had to be evaluated when considering aerial spraying, including the target's size and the landscape.

Michael McManus said the department had to consider several factors when determining where and if to conduct aerial spraying. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

"We need to be efficient and effective with our locust response," he said.

"We're trying to control very large areas, so we focus on those big targets where we can effectively take out large populations."

South Australian Mallee farmers believe aerial spraying at this stage in the season is too late as locusts take flight and harvest is in full swing.

Earlier this month, the state government backflipped on its outbreak management approach when it sprayed parts of the Mallee despite previously saying the region was unsuitable for spraying.

Further north at Mount Little Station in the Flinders Ranges, pastoralist Peter Zadow said the locusts had been "out of control" this year.

Mr Zadow said the best time to control locusts was at the banding stage a few weeks after hatching, when the pests gather in large groups.

"They'll all be millions of grasshoppers all combined together in one area, and they'll just hop around," Mr Zadow said.

Mr Zadow said PIRSA had been monitoring his property, but the outbreak did not meet the threshold for aerial spraying.

The locusts at Mount Little Station have been "out of control" this year. (Supplied: Peter Zadow)

He was instead told about the department's Plague Locust Chemical Rebate.

"That doesn't help if you haven't got any machinery and misters to go out there and actually do the job," he said.

Mr McManus said while locusts are harder to control in the adult stage, concerned producers could try to control the pests in the morning or evening when they settle.

He said PIRSA would continue to monitor locusts in the Flinders Ranges and Mid North, while aerial spraying where possible.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/l.title: 'They absolutely destroy a cherry': Lorikeets wipe out Perth orchard
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/l.author: Emma Wynne, Kate Forrester, Mark Gibson, and Olivia Thorn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Agricultural Pest Control

Damaged cherries at the Perth Hills orchard (Facebook: Irymple Orchard)

Thousands of rainbow lorikeets have stripped a Perth Hills orchard of its cherries over the past five days, with the owner fearing more losses to come.

Birdlife WA says the pest population, which grew from about just 10 birds in 1968, is now too large to eradicate.

Birdlife WA says authorities need to focus on containment and management, as growers consider netting their orchards to protect the fruit.

A tiny flock of rainbow lorikeets introduced to WA in 1968 has bred into an almighty problem for growers across the south-west of the state — with their latest attack taking out all the cherries at a Perth Hills Orchard.

Over the past five days, Linda Moore watched helplessly as thousands of rainbow lorikeets took off her entire cherry crop.

"We're just letting our poor customers know that our early cherries just won't be there," Ms Moore told Mark Gibson on ABC Radio Perth.

"We're really hoping that we will still have mid cherries and late cherries. But these birds even got into green cherries. They absolutely destroy a cherry."

Not only has she already sustained thousands of dollars in losses, but she also fears this is only the start of the problem.

"This is just the beginning of stone fruit season, so it's only people with very early nectarines, apricots and cherries that have noticed it at this stage," she said.

"But of course, these flocks aren't going to go away."

While rainbow lorikeets are native to the east coast of Australia, they were introduced to Western Australia and are now a declared pest.

"All the birds that we see today [in WA] have stemmed from a population of about 10 escaped or released birds in about 1968," Tegan Douglas, program manager at Birdlife Australia, said.

"Since the late 60s, they've become a really big problem."

Dr Tegan Douglas says the pest lorikeet population is now too large to eradicate. (ABC Radio Perth: Emma Wynne)

Despite not being native to the landscape, the lorikeets have proven remarkably adaptable and clever at finding food.

"Because they are social, they're smart, they seem to adapt well to our urban lifestyle and that enables them to explore places like Roleystone and places in the Perth hills," she said.

"Once they switch onto something new, they can easily switch from feeding on the lemon-scented gums in the Perth metro on to things like grapes, and in this instance, it seems like cherries and potentially other stone fruit."

Dr Douglas said that the population is now so large that eradication is unfeasible and authorities need to look at containment and management strategies.

"When it comes to impact on primary producers, looking at controlling those birds where they are or deterring them from hanging around in areas where there are tasty, vulnerable crops is going to be the best management approach," she said.

"You can generally scare them out of a single property, but that just makes them your neighbour's issue and nobody wants to be that guy, so what tends to be most effective is where growers and property owners have the capacity to work together."

Rainbow lorikeets may be beautiful to look at but they are a huge pest for agriculture. (ABC News: Daniel Johnson)

There are a range of options, from lethal control to deterrents like lasers, loud noises or gas guns open to landowners, but Dr Douglas warns the birds are also very adaptable.

"These are birds that have been living in the Perth Metro for decades, so they are used to bright lights, they're used to loud noises, they're used to people being in close proximity to them. It's definitely a marathon. It's not a sprint."

Citrus crops in the Wheatbelt have also been targeted by flocks of up to 100-strong of the declared pests.

Grower Shane Kay said his blood orange orchard in Bindoon, 75 kilometres north-east of Perth, had copped a lot of damage.

Shane Kay, Sue Middleton and Liz Brennan from Moora Citrus.  (Jo Prendergast)

Mr Kay estimates he has lost up to 7 per cent of his blood oranges to lorikeets during picking in July-August this year, which cost him about $5,000 a hectare.

He said there was a missed opportunity to effectively control lorikeet populations when they started to soar around the Perth metro area in recent years.

"There was the opportunity to get rid of them and it wasn't done, so now it's been let go for everyone to try and manage," he said.

Mr Kay said orchard netting was a potential solution but cost-prohibitive for growers at roughly $60,000 a hectare.

"It'll help multiple industries for multiple reasons if access to netting is made easier," he said.

In the meantime, Linda Moore is surveying the wreckage and weighing up her next move.

"Maybe we do have to net a whole orchard, but netting cherries is really tricky because you have to get into that tree about four or five times in a season," she said.

"How do you do that and lift a net each time? As soon as you lift the net, the lorikeets come in."

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Government

Doris Stuart Kngwarraye is a senior Arrernte elder. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

Construction began last week on a multi-million-dollar multicultural centre in Alice Springs.

The local Arrernte people say they were not consulted, but the NT government says it is covered under prior sacred site approval.

Construction is due to be complete by late next year.

The Northern Territory government has rejected criticism that it should have consulted with traditional custodians over the development of a culturally sensitive site at the Anzac Hill precinct in Alice Springs.

In February, the government made public its plan to locate an $8.8 million multicultural centre at the old Alice Springs High School site.

But senior Arrernte elder Doris Stuart Kngwarreye said the first she heard of the project was when bulldozers started their engines last week.

The heavy machinery has already arrived to excavate the site. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"No-one said to me 'come to hear'," she said.

"I said before, it's a women's site.

Jodie Clarkson was one of group of concerned residents who broke the news to Ms Stuart and her family, and has been visiting the area since to "bear witness to what's happening".

"Two of the senior [Aboriginal] women had no idea this was happening until we told them," she said.

"I spoke to the foreman and he showed me his AAPA [Aboriginal Areas Protection Authority] certificate, which is a 2018 certificate for the ATSIAGA [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art Gallery of Australia].

Bron Wintermilne (left) and Jodie Clarkson are among the concerned Alice Springs residents. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"So they're working to a certificate that's not for this multicultural centre, it's not been updated," she said.

Announced in 2017, the National Aboriginal Art Gallery, later rebadged ATSIAGA, was at the centre of controversy over a proposal to locate it in the same precinct as the multicultural centre and demolish the local Anzac Oval sports ground in the process.

The AAPA certificate lists rocky outcrops, corkwood trees and vegetation that must be protected.

In Alice Springs on Wednesday, NT Chief Minister Lia Finnochiaro said it was "perfectly fine" to recycle the certificate for the multicultural centre and argued there was no need to consult with custodians.

"That's the process — we don't have to, why would we?" she asked.

The site at the Anzac Hill precinct is culturally sensitive. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"There was a high school there. It's now demolished.

"We are not impinging on any sacred sites in the area and we need to build a multicultural hall on Northern Territory government land, of which that is."

Ms Finocchiaro said the development would go ahead despite the women's concerns.

"This is a great construction investment, let alone a community asset, so we're not going to let people stop progress — this has got to happen.

An artist's impression of the planned new multicultural centre now being built at the Anzac Hill precinct. (Supplied)

"And we're not talking about a greenfield site here — this is literally a demolished piece of land," Ms Finocchiaro said.

Ms Stuart said Arrernte people were upset when Alice Springs High School was built in between Anzac Hill and the Todd River in 1953.

"Of course we were … [there was] no permission [from traditional owners]," she said.

"All they [the government] want is what they can get out of it, they're not listening to what I'm saying.

"They're going ahead with whatever they want to do.

Multicultural Community Services Central Australia (MCSCA), which is one of the groups that will make use of the new centre once construction is complete, declined to be interviewed.

The Northern Territory treasurer says the federal government will not support the proposed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art gallery in Alice Springs in its current form.

In a statement, an MCSCA spokesperson said the organisation was concerned to learn the location chosen was "in the same area as a women's sacred site".

"We are engaging with traditional custodians to clarify any misunderstandings about MCSCA's role as an advocate, to listen and learn and to discuss how we can work together to promote harmony in our community," they said.

An NT government spokesperson said construction would be complete in 2027.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.title: Lamarre-Condon pressed on 'lies' in fiery end to cross-examination
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.author: Isabella Ross and Anton Rose
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Beau Lamarre-Condon denied the deaths of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies were "murder plain and simple". (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied he "executed" his former love interest and then killed his new partner to "eliminate him as a witness".

Prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC on Friday went methodically through what he described as Mr Lamarre-Condon's "lies" to the jury.

In picking apart Mr Lamarre-Condon's explanations on the stand over the past six days, Mr Hatfield said his actions were "murder plain and simple".

In a fiery end to his cross-examination, former police officer and accused double murderer Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied the deaths of his former love interest and his new partner were "murder plain and simple".

Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to murdering his former partner Jesse Baird and Mr Baird's new boyfriend Luke Davies at a Paddington terrace home on February 19, 2024.

He maintains both men died during separate struggles over Mr Lamarre-Condon's police pistol.

On Friday, prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC repeatedly pushed Mr Lamarre-Condon on his account of how Mr Baird and Mr Davies died inside the home.

Multiple times, Mr Hatfield suggested the former police officer "executed" Mr Baird as he put to Mr Lamarre-Condon in forensic detail the alternative versions of events.

Mr Hatfield went step-by-step through the inconsistencies in Mr Lamarre-Condon's explanations to the jury in finishing a tense cross-examination on Friday afternoon.

"You murdered Jesse Baird didn't you?" Mr Hatfield asked.

"I did not," Mr Lamarre-Condon answered.

"What you did was totally inconsistent with manslaughter. It was murder plain and simple," Mr Hatfield said,

"It was not," Mr Lamarre-Condon replied.

"You then murdered Luke Davies to eliminate him as a witness," Mr Hatfield then said.

"I did not," Mr Lamarre-Condon again replied.

The afternoon's evidence began with Mr Hatfield asking about the location of a knife Mr Lamarre-Condon said Mr Baird pulled on him inside the home.

The prosecutor claimed "this was a lie".

"You just made that up after seeing it in the brief didn't you?" Mr Hatfield asked.

Luke Davies and Jesse Baird died inside a Paddington terrace on February 19, 2024. (Instagram)

In another exchange, Mr Hatfield said the accused double murderer wanted "to make it look like [Jesse] disappeared".

The prosecution claims Mr Lamarre-Condon then used Mr Baird's phone to message the TV presenter's housemates that he was going to Perth that day.

Mr Lamarre-Condon, when asked, denied his actions after the shooting showed that he was trying to cover up a double murder.

"I would have two stolen cars and a firearm that is not linked to me," Mr Lamarre-Condon said.

"I know exactly how to do it [get away with murder] I work with youth gangs."

Mr Lamarre-Condon stated to the jury several times Luke Davies died during a second struggle in the hallway after being pushed by the prosecutor that he was shot through a bedroom door while calling police.

When taken to messages Mr Lamarre-Condon sent to friends the day the couple were killed, the former police officer denied they showed he was planning a murder.

In one he told a friend he "valued your friendship" and that he was deleting his social media.

He argued they were about his mental health struggles and contemplations of suicide.

"We're not talking about 'this is great I'm about to go and commit a murder allegedly'," he said.

"This is clearly not me going 'yay im going to commit a murder and we'll have a glass of wine and laugh about it'."

Asked about his actions after the alleged murders, including a trip to a sushi restaurant with a younger man who wanted to join the police, Mr Lamarre-Condon said he was "trying to make things appear normal".

New CCTV footage of Beau Lamarre-Condon a day after Jesse Baird and Luke Davies's deaths has been released.

Mr Hatfield said Mr Lamarre-Condon appeared in security vision to be laughing at the lunch and also bought a chicken burger and a frappe after the murder.

"I'm not laughing at anything happening you can see my hands are on my head," Mr Lamarre-Condon replied.

The 21-year-old friend at the sushi restaurant, the prosecutor said, was an "immature young man" who looked up to Mr Lamarre-Condon.

Mr Lamarre-Condon claims it was that young man who gave him advice about how to dispose of the bodies.

"Mr Lamarre is that seriously your evidence?," Mr Hatfield said, after telling him he was a police officer who had experience of investigating dozens of crime scenes.

Asked whether he was going to use a chainsaw to dismember the bodies, Mr Lamarre-Condon said: "No. Not ever."

The prosecution alleges this footage shows Beau Lamarre-Condon trying to cover up deaths. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

He denied a suggestion he was willing to do "terrible things to the bodies" to "save yourself".

Earlier on Friday, Mr Lamarre-Condon denied accusations his movements and conversations with friends in February 2024 are evidence he was preparing to kill Mr Baird.

Mr Hatfield put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that Mr Baird had been on his mind in January.

"No I disagree. He only came up in conversations when I was asked, or general conversations about past relationships," he said.

The Crown said Mr Lamarre-Condon told a friend how he "couldn't help myself" when previously breaking into Mr Baird's phone to unfollow a man on Mr Baird's Instagram.

"Yes I said I unlocked his phone, and yes I said the things she stated, yes," he said.

Mr Lamarre-Condon said he did not know of Luke Davies prior to the alleged murders.

"I have never been aware of Jesse and Luke … until after the incident," he said.

"Prior to this date, I was never aware, I had never seen anything on social media."

Mr Hatfield put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that he was still angry with Mr Baird.

"You're still angry with him rejecting you aren't you?" he claimed.

"I am not," the accused responded.

Mr Lamarre-Condon and Mr Baird were in a brief, casual relationship previously. (Instagram)

On January 15, 2024, Mr Lamarre-Condon purchased an Amaysim sim card under the false name Bob Ballard to use in what the Crown described as a "burner phone".

Mr Lamarre-Condon disagreed with the second phone description.

He said he had ordered the sim card with the plan to contact media with allegations of workplace bullying in the police force.

"It had nothing to do with Jesse Baird," Mr Lamarre-Condon said of obtaining the sim card.

The Crown suggested Mr Lamarre-Condon's reasoning was false.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to murdering Mr Baird and Mr Davies. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

The weekend of January 26, 2024, the former police officer started using the sim card.

"You were thinking about murdering Jesse Baird around this weekend weren't you," prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC said to Mr Lamarre-Condon.

"I never thought about murdering Jesse Baird, no," the accused replied.

He said he used the sim card to contact people on encrypted messaging app Signal.

The court was shown a call log, which recorded Mr Lamarre-Condon having contacted a man whose Bungonia family farm was the location Mr Baird and Mr Davies's bodies were taken to.

He said the purpose of the call was to catch up, but when he tried contacting the man, he did not receive a reply.

The accused denied he was calling the man to ask about the farm.

Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield (right) cross-examined the accused in court this week. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

On January 23, 2024, Mr Lamarre-Condon hired a car from Hertz in his own name.

In late January, he asked a friend if hired cars could be tracked.

Mr Lamarre-Condon said he was asking in regards to "dial-a-[drug] dealers" in his capacity as a police officer, and said it had nothing to do with him having a hire vehicle.

Mr Lamarre-Condon was asked whether he was searching on Decathlon for what could be used as a "body bag" on February 2, 2024.

"I was looking at multiple things I wanted to buy, which was a chest press … I didn't type anything about a body bag," he said.

Mr Lamarre-Condon later used surfboard bags bought from a Decathlon store to transport the bodies of Mr Baird and Mr Davies.

CCTV showed Mr Lamarre-Condon buying a surfboard bag with cash. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

On February 3, 2024, Mr Lamarre-Condon spent $60.52 at online retailer AliExpress.

Mr Hatfield asked Mr Lamarre-Condon whether he purchased a motorcycle helmet from AliExpress.

The Crown suggested the helmet formed part of Mr Lamarre-Condon's food delivery worker disguise used on the day of the alleged murders.

"I bought a laser hair removal kit, things for my swimwear line, for my business — but not a helmet," Mr Lamarre-Condon said.

He previously said he took the helmet, jacket and gloves from a food delivery worker's motorbike before entering the Paddington house.

Mr Lamarre-Condon was wearing a helmet as part of a food delivery driver outfit he says he found. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

Also in early February, the accused and a friend were involved in an acting class.

Mr Hatfield: "Did you make a comment to her or ask a question, 'Would you help me hide a body?'"

Mr Lamarre-Condon: "I made a very similar comment, a joking banter comment, yes … the joking banter was in line with the play [we were acting out]."

Mr Hatfield: "Is it the case that you asked her that, because you planned to murder Jesse Baird?"

Mr Lamarre-Condon: "Absolutely not. I have said comments like this hundreds and hundreds of times."

The female friend was the second person Mr Lamarre-Condon tried to call after the alleged murders on February 19.

"Yes I called her. It was definitely not a plan to ask her to help me hide a body," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.author: Josh Duggan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Firmus is currently Tasmania's largest data centre proponent. (Supplied)

Further details have been provided on Tasmania's AI data centre deal that would compel companies to pay into community benefit funds.

Businesses are required to pay $3,000 per megawatt of contracted energy each year.

The government says the expectations will be binding.

Tasmanian data centre proponents would each run their own community benefit funds under a proposal from the state government.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff announced his government's statement of expectations for data centres on Friday, which includes rules for the community funds.

Once a facility is operational, proponents would be required to pay into their own funds, at a rate of $3,000 per megawatt (MW) of contracted energy each year.

The requirement to pay into community funds is included in the Tasmanian government's statement of expectations. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

For Tasmania's largest AI data centre company, Firmus, its 104MW facility at St Leonards would contribute $312,000 per year.

It also has a proposed 288MW centre planned for Long Reach, near Bell Bay, and a 40MW centre at Wesley Vale in the state's north-west.

Last month, Premier Rockliff announced plans for a singular local community benefit fund, but did not release the cost or structure.

Jeremy Rockliff (left) has since released more details about the community funds that would impact companies such as Tim Rosenfield's (centre) and Oliver Curtis' Firmus. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

At Friday's press conference, further details were announced.

The premier and Industry Minister Felix Ellis spoke of a single fund governed by "local people" and "local representatives" who would allocate grants to "community groups and other eligible organisations".

They did not reveal that there would be several funds or that companies themselves would control the funds.

The statement of expectations outlines "transparent governance arrangements" and requires public reporting.

Topic:
Fishing and Aquaculture Industry

Greens MP Tabatha Badger said she was "very curious" about how the community funds would be run.

Premier Rockliff announced plans for the fund in the days following Firmus's scrapped IPO, which unravelled due to investor concerns about the company's finances, expansion plans and social licence.

He said today that the expectations document would be reviewed within six months.

"In our view, [data centres] are a good investment for Tasmania and we welcome that investment," Mr Rockliff said.

Unnamed companies are looking at setting up six data centres in Tasmania, a parliamentary document reveals.

Mr Ellis said proponents who did not follow the expectations "won't be able to proceed".

"There are already many statutory rules that the data centre developers are required to meet in areas such as planning and environmental requirements," he said.

The state government has been under pressure to step up its regulation of the burgeoning sector, following Firmus unveiling plans for multiple data centres in the state.

Opponents to data centres have raised concerns about where the energy and water used by the AI data factories will come from.

Proposals for AI data centres in Tasmania have been met with some local opposition. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

For the Firmus factory at St Leonards, state energy company Aurora has contracted energy supply through the initial stage, but it does not have a long-term deal.

Energy Minister Nick Duigan said proponents were "required" to partner with new renewable energy projects, but they could do that "through" Hydro Tasmania.

"So Hydro would go out and contract with the new renewable energy providers and act as an aggregator to provide a firmed energy product to the data centre," he said.

Russell Kelly, chief executive of technology sector advocate TasICT, said the expectations "put the onus" on data centre proponents to build trust with the community.

Russell Kelly says the fund will help AI data centre companies build trust. (ABC News: Cameron Atkins)

Mr Kelly said the amount proposed for the Local Community Benefit Fund was in line with other proposals in the nation.

"We can see a pipeline of young Tasmanians getting jobs in technology. We can see closer association between the University of Tasmania and TasTAFE."

Fiona Turner of start-up hub Enterprize welcomed the expectations.

"Giving skills back to locals around AI is very important, especially with these data centres here," she said.

Emergency services were called to the property just after midday on Friday. (ABC News)

South Australia Police say a man has died in a workplace incident at Vista, in Adelaide's north-eastern suburbs.

A portion of Leopold Street was taped off on Friday afternoon after emergency services responded to the incident about 12:15pm.

Police say a 26-year-old Linden Park man died at the scene.

There were several police vehicles parked outside the suburban home, while multiple SES workers were also at the scene. 

An SA Power Networks truck arrived about 2.30pm and workers were seen examining a power pole at the end of the street.

Police attended the scene at Leopold Street. (ABC News)

A SafeWork SA spokesperson told the ABC it was notified of the incident earlier today, and that an investigator and inspector were attending the scene to make enquiries.

Police will prepare a report for the coroner.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/n.author: Carly Cook and Giselle Wakatama
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The group Rising Tide has staged protests in the Port of Newcastle for more than a decade. (ABC News: Romy Stephens)

The NSW Supreme Court has rejected a challenge from the state's police commissioner to a climate protest planned in Newcastle.

The protest, organised by Rising Tide, is set to see hundreds of activists paddle out in the Port of Newcastle.

The court heard the flotilla will stretch across the harbour, blocking the shipping channel for up to 40 minutes.

A climate protest on Newcastle Harbour will go ahead as planned after the Supreme Court rejected an application by NSW Police to stop it.

Rising Tide's Paddle for the Plant flotilla is set to see hundreds of people in kayaks take to the water tomorrow.

Handing down his judgement this afternoon, Justice Edward Muston said he had to balance the interests of the public with the concerns of police.

"The public interests in the facilitations of political expression through assembly outweighs the legitimate concerns which have been expressed by the commissioner," he said.

Protest organisers in NSW must submit a notice of intention to hold a public assembly to the police commissioner, known as a Form 1.

The NSW Police Commissioner opposed this application and asked the Supreme Court to prohibit the event due to safety concerns for those attending and other users of the harbour.

Without a Form 1, protesters run the risk of being charged by police for offences including obstructing people, vehicles or vessels.

Police have argued their resources have been stretched on the water and land during previous anti-coal events. (ABC Newcastle: Carly Cook)

The court heard up to 785 people on kayaks and other watercraft would enter Newcastle Harbour tomorrow morning to unfurl a 20-metre-long series of connected floating letters that will read "Coal Exports Equals Climate Chaos".

They also plan to form a continuous line spanning the harbour for about 30 to 40 minutes, blocking the shipping channel, before returning to shore.

On Wednesday, barrister David Hume SC, who acted for NSW Police, told the court transport officials and police predicted dire consequences.

"Everyone has looked at this [event] saying it poses an unacceptable risk," Mr Hume said.

The Assistant Police Commissioner echoed those calls, citing an incident last year where protesters were washed hundreds of metres down the harbour.

Police watch on as protesters previously demonstrated against fossil fuels at Newcastle's port.  (ABC News: Romy Stephens )

"I have not seen any Rising Tide event run safely yet," Assistant Commissioner David Waddell said.

The number of watercraft will be capped at 785 — more than double previous anti-coal protests in the port.

Rising Tide's barrister Michael Green told the court the event would have a kayak safety team, swimming in the channel would be banned, and life jackets mandatory.

He said people attending would also be briefed on hand signals they could use to raise the alarm if they get into trouble.

Rising Tide's Anne Hodgson told the court it would be a family-friendly event and ruled out the prospect of civil disobedience.

Ms Hodgson told the court it was hoped global media would cover the event.

The world's biggest coal port in Newcastle has been a focus for groups fighting climate change. (ABC Newcastle: Carly Cook)

"Yes, as the COP31 meetings are on, we would like that," she said.

COP31 is the United Nations Climate Conference — the largest international summit to negotiate and advance global cooperation on climate change.

On the eve of the court action, Newcastle City councillors banned Rising Tide from protesting on community land "now and into the future", sparking fears among activists about their right to peacefully protest.

Newcastle's Lord Mayor Gavin Morris used his casting vote on Tuesday to pass a motion opposing the use of community land for the purpose of Rising Tide's events and protests.

Newcastle Lord Mayor Gavin Morris used his casting vote this week to ban Rising Tide from protesting on community land. (ABC News: Keely Johnson)

"The constant request for them [Rising Tide activists] to remain within the boundaries has been broken, and it's been a constant breaking of promises," he said.

"Sadly, they keep pushing the boundaries beyond the realms of safety and something just needed to be done."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.title: Salmon farm antibiotic use impact 'completely unfair' cray fisher says
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.author: Loretta Lohberger and Jano Gibson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Fishing and Aquaculture Industry

Kodey Rolston says "fishermen are being impacted so deeply by what salmon farming has done". (ABC News: Jano Gibson)

A Tasmanian cray fisher says the wild-caught fishing sector has been "impacted so deeply" by salmon companies' use of antibiotics.

Following salmon company Tassal's use of an antibiotic, two commercial fishing areas are being closed from Sunday until February 14 to protect export markets.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff says it is important "we get the balance right".

A commercial fisher says the impact of salmon companies' antibiotic use in Tasmania is "completely unfair" on smaller, wild fishers.

Kodey Rolston, who works as a deckhand on a cray fishing boat, said while he was a supporter of the salmon industry, "fishermen are being impacted so deeply by what salmon farming has done".

The Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) is closing two commercial fishing areas from Sunday until February 14.

Commercial rock lobster and dive fisheries in parts of Tasmania's south-east will be closed for three months to "mitigate trade risks" linked to antibiotic use.

The commercial taking of rock lobster and the setting of rock lobster pots will not be allowed within parts of the Southern Channel "therapeutic management area" (TMA).

Commercial divers will not be allowed to take short-spined sea urchins, long-spined sea urchins and periwinkles in the Northern Channel TMA.

Under the state government's Aquaculture Therapeutant — Wild Fisheries Market Access Management Plan, released last month, wild fisheries near salmon pens treated with antibiotics get temporarily closed.

The closures are to protect export markets as some countries have zero tolerance for antibiotics in wild-caught fish.

The two new closures are linked to salmon company Tassal's recent use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline (OTC) at its salmon farms at Great Taylors Bay and Meads Creek in the lower D'Entrecasteaux Channel.

The company said the closure accounted for 1.6 per cent of the state's historical rock lobster catch.

A map showing the areas of the rock lobster fishery that will be closed from Sunday. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

But Mr Rolston said the closure area was "vital to the crayfishing industry".

"Down south is our safe haven for abalones, for crayfish.

"It's a multi, multi-generational fishing ground and it's being locked off all together because the salmon farms want to just dump as much antibiotics in the water as they can to try and save their own arse and not cooperate with other businesses," he said.

"I actually don't have anything against the salmon farms.

"In all honesty, I'm very much for them — they provide a lot of jobs all around the state.

Tassal says the rock lobster fishery closure accounts for 1.6 per cent of Tasmania's annual rock lobster catch. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

Tasmanian Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff said the government was expecting the wild-caught fishing industry to "do all the heavy lifting".

"Wild fishers have been sidelined and the interests of big salmon companies have been put first by the government," Ms Woodruff said.

"They've refused to put in place any regulations to constrain the operations of salmon farming in the Channel."

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said it was important "we get the balance right".

"The industry is in a transition and a very quick transition in terms of antibiotic use because of the investment that's going into breeding, for example, will mean that in future years there'll be less reliance on antibiotics if at all, and that's the space we need to get to.

"We're in a transition time now and I know it's difficult … I feel for industry outside of the salmon industry very much.

"It's important that all industries work together, we get the balance right."

In a statement yesterday, Tassal said the closure was a "precaution to protect export market access".

"Public Health has confirmed swimming and recreational fishing remain completely safe.

"We recognise the consequences for any affected commercial rock lobster fishers and are working with the wild fisheries sector on appropriate support, with monitoring underway to support reopening as soon as possible."

Tassal has been administering OTC by injection, rather than orally through medicated food.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.title: Outlook outage expected to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.author: Liana Walker
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Microsoft outage has been ongoing for more than 12 hours.  (Reuters: David Ryder)

Experts say the Microsoft outage is likely to cost businesses billions.

RSM Australia Risk Advisory partner, Ashwin Pal, says small business will be hit the hardest.

The financial impact is expected to last weeks.

The Microsoft outage is calculated to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars, with experts warning small businesses will be the hardest hit by the technology failure.

A widespread outage, which started about 3:15 am AEDT, has hit platforms including Outlook, with many users having trouble accessing emails and encountering errors across the Microsoft suite of products.

Workers across multiple types of businesses have reported being unable to access email or SharePoint, with some resorting to using fax machines to keep operating.

Microsoft outage live: For the latest on the issues affecting the tech giant's apps, read our blog.

RSM Australia Risk Advisory partner Ashwin Pal said the cost to professional service businesses, such as lawyers or accountants, would be hundreds of thousands of dollars per hour.

"It's not just the initial downtime, it's more actually about then the catch up effort because that costs money," he said.

"Because now when things do normalise, you're going to have to spend money to actually catch up because of all the backlog."

Ashwin Pal says Monday's backlog of work will be costly.  (Supplied)

He said the impact of the outage was amplified by the 3.9 million businesses globally that used the Microsoft suite, with many not having backup systems, resulting in huge costs to the economy.

"This is what happened with CrowdStrike. So when the outage happened, because of where we are in the world in terms of time zones, we felt the impact first.

"As the US and Europe come online, and they can't operate, it's going to get worse. So you're going to have a multiplier effect."

Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today.

He said the repercussions would be most keenly felt by small businesses, due to operating on thin margins.

"You take a CBA as an example, they'll be able to absorb an impact like this a lot easier than the five-person accounting shop down the road," he said.

"They were already actually working on very thin margins. All of a sudden they're actually out for three, four, five days or whatever it takes for them to recover. That could be the final straw."

Owner of small Queensland business Regal Shower Screens, Tracey Tucker, said the lost day of business would cost at least $30,000, but there were numerous flow-on effects.

"I'm paying my girls sitting in here in the office to do nothing," she said.

"The phone rings, they can't order anything.

"Then it puts undue pressure because if it's back online on Monday, everything we missed Friday, we're going to try to catch up on."

Experts say the outage will hurt small business the most.  (Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration)

She said the outage meant the business would struggle to meet its promoted deadlines because the glass manufacturers would also be inundated on Monday.

"It's going to put pressure on everybody down the track because our girls are going to get yelled at, like, 'You just said my shower's going to be two weeks now, it's two and a half weeks', all because we can't send the order through today."

Service delivery manager with telecommunication company Hubify, Chloe Mombeshora, said she had received numerous calls from less tech-savvy clients who were unsure what was happening.

"They're thinking that their internet is down, they don't know what to do," she said.

She added some clients had raised concerns the inability to communicate could impact their businesses' reputations.

Some Outlook users were receiving notifications for emails they could not open. (ABC News: Liana Walker)

IT support specialist James Coates said he had been inundated with requests for help but was unable to reply through his helpdesk because it used Outlook.

"We actually have to call each client individually, every single personal phone number, every single Teams number, hope it gets through and update them that way because the email service is just not working on their end either," he said.

He said he also could not do other work over concerns it would not be saved.

Liam Jones from the Australian Chamber of Commerce & Industry said the outage would have some businesses reconsidering using Microsoft.

"This is a reminder of just the increasingly digital nature of the modern economy and disruptions like this can occur.

"They need to be worked through. We need to get to the bottom of what's occurred here and work out steps to ensure that disruptions like this don't occur into the future where they can be avoided."

He warned there would be ripple effects.

"But this is the digital world. This is the digital economy in which we live," he said.

Innes Willox says time is money. (ABC News: Dan Fermer)

Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox said the outage demonstrated how important technology was to the modern economy, especially on a Friday when many hybrid workers would work from home.

"What the outage tells us is that technology is great until it isn't," he said.

He said the biggest issues would be communication and delays.

"Time is money and that disruption will be very difficult for some businesses, more difficult for some than others because it will represent lost opportunities," he said.

"So it's too early to even contemplate the impact, but this has global ramifications so it will lead to a significant downturn in productivity as well. And that will be of concern at a time when we need to drive productivity as much as possible."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.title: Outback cattle flown to Kazakhstan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.author: Matt Brann
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Beef Cattle Farming

Ben Hayes (second from right) alongside livestock agent Tim McKean, inspecting cattle with Kazakhstan buyers. (Supplied: Undoolya Station)

A buyer from Kazakhstan has taken nearly 300 head of cattle from the Northern Territory after flying out to inspect them.

Cattle producer Ben Hayes says Kazakhstan's government has an initiative to boost its national herd.

Federal data shows Kazakhstan imported more than 1,000 head each of cattle and sheep in October.

Nearly 300 head of cattle from a station near Alice Springs have been flown to Kazakhstan, in what local producers hope is the start of a new market.

The distance from Alice Springs in the middle of Australia to Kazakhstan is roughly 10,000 kilometres.

Ben Hayes from Undoolya Station said he got a call from his livestock agent one day with an interesting offer.

"He asked if we had some heifers for this Kazakhstan job and we did," he said.

"The buyer from Kazakhstan actually flew out here [with an interpreter], took a quick look and ended up taking them.

"They got trucked down to Melbourne, where they stayed in quarantine for about a month and were then loaded into crates and onto the plane."

Cattle from Undoolya Station ready for export to Kazakhstan. (Supplied: Undoolya Station)

Mr Hayes said the animals were flown from Melbourne to Singapore and then onto Kazakhstan.

"There was a weight limit on them of about 180 to 250 kilograms and they had to be preg-tested empty."

He said the money paid for the animals was "on-par" with what he would normally receive in the Australian market.

But he said the chance to be involved in the sale to Kazakhstan was "very special".

"To know that our heifers are now becoming breeding stock for Kazakhstan is a feather in our cap, in Australia's cap," he said.

ABC Landline has been told some cattle from Mt Riddock Station in the NT were also purchased for the consignment.

According to data from the Federal Department of Agriculture, there were two flights of breeder cattle out of Victoria last month totalling 1,252 head.

Another flight to Kazakhstan took 1,617 breeder sheep.

It is understood Australia last exported cattle to Kazakhstan in 2019.

It is a long way from Alice Springs to Kazakhstan. (ABC Landline)

This is not the first time Undoolya Station has flown cattle to a distant market.

In 1981, Undoolya steers were flown direct out of Alice Springs to Korea.

"I was only a little fella at the time, but my father and grandfather flew steers out of Alice Springs on a Flying Tiger aircraft, straight to Korea" Mr Hayes said.

"I don't know why they wanted steers, but that's what happened, Alice Springs is an international airport, it was a good opportunity."

Undoolya Station is the Northern Territory's oldest pastoral lease. Established in 1872, the property has been owned by the Hayes family since 1906.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police are investigating the sudden death of James Reilly at a property in Kuranda. (ABC News: Sharnie Kim)

James Reilly was found dead and his sister, Peta Reilly, critically injured in a home at Kuranda on Thursday morning.

Ms Reilly was taken to Cairns Hospital with facial injuries and her condition is now stable.

The siblings' sister has flown to Cairns to be with Ms Reilly, as police investigations continue.

Relatives of two siblings have expressed shock after one was found dead and the other critically injured in a Far North Queensland home.

Police went to the home of James Reilly and his sister Peta Reilly, both aged in their 60s, at Kuranda on the Atherton Tablelands just before 10:30am on Thursday.

Mr Reilly was found dead and Ms Reilly was found with significant facial injuries.

She was taken to Cairns Hospital in a critical condition, but is now in a stable condition.

The siblings' sister has planned to fly from interstate to be with Ms Reilly, who has undergone facial reconstruction surgery.

It is understood the siblings lived at the property together since the 80s. (ABC News: Sharnie Kim)

Police remained at the house and the family were waiting for answers about what may have happened inside the home.

The siblings' nephew, Tim Reilly, said his uncle and aunt had been living in their late mother's home since the 1980s.

He said they were well liked.

"He was very social and generally very well liked," he said about his uncle, James Reilly.

"Peta [has been] a very reclusive artist all her life."
