https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.title: Inexpensive ways to approach weeding your garden
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.author: Anna Chisholm
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-13/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Removing and managing weeds comes with gardening, but getting started doesn't need to feel overwhelming. (ABC News: Sonya Gee)

Some gardening tasks can feel like a lovely way to spend time. Weeding is rarely one of those.

But there are some simple and inexpensive ways to remove those weeds from your garden and prevent them from coming back.

We've looked through past stories to bring you some of the strategies that horticulturists and passionate gardeners have previously recommended.

Admittedly this is obvious, but if you have spiralled into overthinking it could be worth pointing out that simply pulling unwanted plants out of the ground is an option.

Warmer weather is great for spring-time growth, but it also means more weeds.

It's simple, inexpensive and doesn't involve using chemicals.

Nipaluna/Hobart horticulturist Louise Sales says common weeds varieties that pop up seasonally and are known as annuals.

"With annual weeds, the key is to get rid of them before they go to seed," she says.

"If you are trying to work out which weeds to target first, it's the ones with the flowers on them."

For those with taproots, such as capeweed and dandelions, she says it's important to dig out the root to stop them regenerating.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

If there's a particularly pernicious patch of weeds in your garden, the boiling water and vinegar methods might be a more effective choice.

Meanjin/Brisbane-based horticulturist and gardening coach, Kate Wall says "boiling water and vinegar are both very effective" at killing weeds.

"The vinegar burns off the foliage [but] it's not being absorbed into the plant, so it's not systemic."

Ms Wall says weeds with large underground stems will be more resistant to this approach.

"It won't affect those underground parts, so it's not effective against those sorts of weeds. However, any plant that you constantly take the top off of so that it can't photosynthesise will eventually die."

Gardening Australia suggests adding salt to the vinegar too.

In spring, Koren Helbig — a sustainable city living educator in Tarntanya/Adelaide — uses her weeds to help fertilise the soil and prepare for hungry crops ahead.

This includes "chopping and dropping" by "cutting them at their roots and layering the leaves across the soil's surface.

She then adds handfuls of fertiliser pellets (she opts for organic varieties) and sprinkles in activated biochar, which helps retain water and nutrients.

Ms Helbig says many nutrient-rich common weeds can also be added to compost once they've been pulled up.

Koren Helbig recommends "chopping and dropping" to create no-dig layers. (Supplied: Koren Helbig)

Managing weeds can be a tedious task, but prioritising prevention will help cut out a lot of that work.

Ms Helbig employs strategies to naturally suppress weeds in her garden. For paths, she lays down cardboard — sourced for free from local businesses — and tops it with about 4cm of bark mulch.

Koren Helbig says she uses free cardboard on garden paths to suppress weeds. (Supplied: Koren Helbig)

"I've created natural barriers on garden paths using thick layers of overlapping cardboard," she says.

"This blocks sunlight and smothers weeds."

Ms Sales also endorses the use of cardboard in the garden.

"If you've got lots of weeds [laying cardboard down] is a really good way of suppressing them," she says.

Ms Helbig also plants out her gardens with ground cover to help outcompete the plants she doesn't want.

"I grow edible ground covers such as marjoram, thyme, nasturtiums and warrigal greens for a living mulch barrier."

It's an approach Ms Wall recommends too.

"If you don't want weeds to grow in that empty space, put a plant in it," she says, adding that choosing plants that suit your conditions will help them beat the weeds.

Agapanthus can spread easily through seed dispersal and dumping garden waste. (ABC News: Jessica Schremmer)

It's also important, to choose plants that won't create their own weed problem.

There are lots of common garden plants that can become hard to manage and contain.

Agapanthus, morning glory, gazania and foxglove are all considered weeds in some states and can spread quickly across your garden — and beyond.

Ms Wall says "almost every local council has a list on their website of plants considered weeds in that area. That's probably the first place to look for plants you shouldn't grow locally."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Malaysia weighing how to aid AirAsia without risking public funds, ex-minister says
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Julie Zhu
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia is weighing how to support AirAsia without risking public funds and will not simply pump money into the private airline, said Anthony Loke, who resigned this week as the nation’s transport minister.

The finance ministry, not the transport ministry, is still reviewing various options to financially aid Southeast Asia’s largest low-cost airline as it grapples with high jet fuel prices and currency swings, Loke said, citing discussions at cabinet meetings.

AirAsia, unlike state-owned Malaysia Airlines, is a private company, Loke said, and any support would have to take a regulated form. “It has to be a formal kind of arrangement,” he said. “Government is not going to pump in money just like that.”

He declined to provide details about the options under consideration and said Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who is also finance minister, would decide on any conditions.

The finance ministry and AirAsia did not respond to requests for comment.

Loke made the remarks in an interview on Wednesday, a day after he resigned in protest of a High Court decision that allowed former Prime Minister Najib Razak to be released from prison and serve under house arrest the rest of his sentence over his role in the 1MDB scandal.

AirAsia, which controls about 60% of Malaysia’s domestic aviation market, had current liabilities of 18.4 billion ringgit ($4.52 billion) as of June 30.

With AirAsia, the Malaysian government is aiming to strike the right balance, Loke said, “without jeopardizing public funds, but at the same time maintaining air connectivity, which is important.”

Tengku Zafrul Aziz, a senior political adviser to Anwar who chairs the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, said in a separate interview that any government rescue of a private company must protect the business and its workers, not its shareholders.

The right policy for any government “is not to interfere in the commercial sector,” Zafrul said, adding that any government support for a company considered strategic to the country must be justifiable.

Zafrul, who was responding to questions about AirAsia, spoke  in general terms about government intervention in private companies and described his comments as his personal view.

AirAsia has said it is looking to raise up to $1 billion from international debt markets plus 700 million ringgit in local credit facilities. AirAsia co-founder Tony Fernandes said last month he expected the $1 billion fundraising to be completed between December and February.

At the time, Fernandes denied asking the government for financial assistance, though he said AirAsia would not turn away help if offered.

The finance ministry said last month it had made no agreement or commitment to provide financial assistance to AirAsia, whether in the form of guarantees, loans or public fund injections.

Loke said the transport ministry coordinated modest relief for airlines this year, including longer credit terms on aviation charges. The Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia extended the credit period for aviation fees and charges from 30 days to 60 days from May 1.

Loke said the measures were “not major” but gave airlines “some breathing space” as they dealt with high jet fuel prices.

The ministry was inclined to help because fuel costs are passed on to passengers through pricier tickets, which dampens demand and hurts tourism and the wider economy, he said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Malaysia weighing how to support AirAsia without risking public funds, says Anthony Loke. AirAsia is a private company, unlike state-owned Malaysia Airlines, and any support would have to take a regulated form. Loke resigned this week as the nation’s transport minister.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Japan team creates ‘planimal’ hybrid plant-animal cells in world first
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
A Japanese team said that it has become the first in the world to create hybrid plant-animal cells, dubbed “planimal” cells, by fusing a unicellular alga called Cyanidioschyzon merolae into cultured animal cells.

According to the team from the University of Tokyo, the Institute of Science Tokyo, Kindai University and others, all of C. merolae’s DNA was integrated into the animal cells’ chromosomes.

But the hybrid cells were, in terms of function, animal cells because C. merolae’s DNA was suppressed and chloroplasts, which conduct photosynthesis, were degraded during fusion.

“We hope to introduce chloroplasts and activate C. merolae genes to generate oxygen through photosynthesis,” said Sachihiro Matsunaga, professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Frontier Sciences.

The team’s findings were published in the international journal Nature Communications.

Matsunaga had been working on the production of planimal cells since he proposed the creation of such a hybrid in 2018.

If cells that produce useful animal and plant proteins can be cultured in large quantities using photosynthesis, it could provide a new means of producing drugs and cultured meat. In this experiment, the cultured animal cells were derived from Chinese hamster ovaries, which are used to produce drugs and other products.

While plant cells have walls outside the cell membrane, C. merolae has no cell walls because it is primitive. In addition, its genome is very small.

Matsunaga and other members of the team fused C. merolae into cultured animal cells using a conventional method involving polyethylene glycol, in order to put the alga’s DNA into the animal cell nucleus.

Although the success rate was low, they produced planimal cells in which all of the alga’s DNA was integrated into the animal cells’ chromosomes.

The integrated DNA was frozen by a mechanism called methylation, acting as an “off” switch for gene expression. Like ordinary cultured animal cells, the planimal cells continued to divide and multiply for more than 150 generations.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Japan yet to make full use of nuclear power equipment export treaty with India
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
NEW DELHI – No concrete progress has been made in exporting nuclear power plant equipment from Japan to India since the two countries signed a treaty of cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy a decade ago.

This is despite India having established a legal framework that made it easier for foreign firms to supply nuclear plants to the country as the government seeks to expand the installed capacity, or the maximum potential output of electricity, of nuclear plants.

The treaty, which allows Japan to export nuclear power technology and equipment, was signed in November 2016 and took effect in July 2017. One of the factors hindering Japan’s nuclear power plant exports had been India’s nuclear liability law.

The law stipulated that not only plant operators but also equipment suppliers would be held liable for damage from nuclear accidents. The provision discouraged companies from entering the business.

In December last year, India established a law that allows equipment vendors to avoid liability unless they explicitly assume it through contractual agreements. The law also partially allows companies, including foreign firms, to build and operate nuclear power plants.

“Export opportunities may expand, including through collaboration with foreign manufacturers,” said an official at Japan Atomic Industrial Forum, an industry group. The group said that Japanese firms have a track record of supplying equipment to U.S.-made nuclear power plants.

Currently, 24 nuclear reactors are in operation in India, with a total installed capacity of approximately 8.78 gigawatts. The administration of Prime Minister Narendra Modi has a goal of boosting that capacity to 100 gigawatts by 2047, when India marks its 100th year of independence.

The Modi administration also aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero by 2070.

“Nuclear power, with negligible operational greenhouse gas emissions, is indispensable to that pathway,” said Daya Shankar, associate professor at Woxsen University in the Indian city of Hyderabad.

The nuclear cooperation treaty caused a controversy in Japan at the time of its signing because this meant that Japan, the only country hit by atomic weapons, would be allowed to export nuclear plants to India, a nuclear state that is not a member of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).

“Antinuclear sentiment remains strong within Japan’s domestic politics” following the 2011 nuclear accident in Fukushima Prefecture, Shankar said. Any “move to export nuclear technology to a non-NPT signatory invited sharp domestic criticism,” he added.

Environmentalist E.A.S. Sarma, a former Indian government official who opposed the Japan-India treaty, said, “Please ponder over the disruption that a nuclear power plant will cause in the lives of the local communities and how it exposes vast stretches of thickly populated areas to the scourge of a Fukushima-like disaster, as and when it happens.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: India has established a legal framework that made it easier for foreign firms to supply nuclear plants to the country. The treaty, which allows Japan to export nuclear power technology and equipment, was signed in November 2016. The law stipulated that not only plant operators but also equipment suppliers would be held liable for damage from nuclear accidents.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Sumitomo Mitsui, Mizuho raises annual profit forecast and announces share buyback
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Taiga Uranaka
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Two of Japan’s biggest banks raised their profit forecasts and unveiled share buybacks, after cashing in on rising interest rates and robust loan demand that put them on course for another record year.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
TAIPEI – China carried out a large, unannounced military exercise across the western Pacific and around Taiwan in early November, in what officials in Taipei have described as a campaign of “silent intimidation” aimed at pressuring Taiwan and other governments before major international meetings.

A senior Taiwan security official, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, said China’s military and coast guard had at one point massed more than 100 vessels in the region early this month, conducting drills that included simulated attacks on other militaries and cities including Taiwan’s.

The naval deployment was larger than “Justice Mission 2025,“ China’s last formally named drills targeting Taiwan nearly a year ago and one of the largest Chinese naval deployments to date, the official said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Oh and Kuriyama call for change as Japan’s baseball landscape shifts
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Jason Coskrey
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
If Japanese baseball legend Sadaharu Oh, who hit a world-record 868 home runs during his career with the Yomiuri Giants from 1959 to 1980, had played today, he might have been among the many players to leave Japan for MLB.

The trend that began in earnest with Hideo Nomo’s move to the Los Angeles Dodgers in the mid-90s has only grown since then, with NPB’s top stars leaving Japan and an increasing number of amateur players bypassing the Japanese game.

The outflow of young talent has sounded alarm bells for many about the future of Japanese baseball. But former NPB manager Hideki Kuriyama, whose protege Shohei Ohtani is the player so many of the MLB hopefuls are trying to emulate, says that instead of fighting against the tide, Japanese baseball should use the current moment as a way to make itself better.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Indonesia’s Prabowo rushes end of Jokowi era with son’s ouster
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The ultimate target of Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s shakeup at the top of his country’s politics may be the man who helped propel him to power after leading the country for a decade: former President Joko Widodo.

The resignation on Thursday of his eldest son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, as vice president strips Widodo of his most important remaining foothold in Prabowo’s administration. It also gives Prabowo control over the shortlist for Gibran’s successor, helping him shape the vice presidency and the contest for power in 2029.

“Nobody can beat Prabowo except Jokowi,” said Made Supriatma, visiting fellow in the Indonesia Studies Program at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, using the name by which Widodo is popularly known. “So just get rid of Jokowi and his family forever.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Joko Widodo's son Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigns as vice president. Widodo is the ultimate target of the shakeup at the top of Indonesian politics.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Opposition in Upper House seeks to expand relief during and after food tax cut
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Kenji Yoshida
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
An Upper House special committee began deliberations on the food tax reduction bill Friday, as the opposition seeks to further broaden relief for households during and after the cut.

The ruling Liberal Democratic Party and its coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party (also known as Nippon Ishin no Kai), are four seats short of a majority in the chamber and are likely seeking support from major opposition parties Komeito or the Democratic Party for the People (DPP). Both opposed the bill when it passed the Lower House last week.

The bill would lower the consumption tax on food and nonalcoholic beverages from 8% to 1% for two years starting in April 2027. Income-linked cash payments for low- and middle-income workers would start alongside the cut to offset the remaining 1%, with the program expanding its support measures when the tax rate returns to 8%.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: The bill would lower the consumption tax on food and nonalcoholic beverages from 8% to 1% for two years starting in April 2027. Income-linked cash payments for low- and middle-income workers would start alongside the cut to offset the remaining 1%.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: Chinese filmmakers at TIFF take risks and reap rewards
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Mike Fu
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
Exploring themes of food, philosophy and forbidden love, Chinese directors brought experimental visual styles and emotional depth tinged with raw eroticism to the Competition section of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF).

Two of three competing titles received accolades at the closing ceremony on Nov. 4. Tellingly, none of the films were officially sanctioned by the China Film Administration; instead, they were made with production partners from across Asia, Europe and the Middle East.

Hu Ling received the best actress award for her leading role as a middle-aged dormitory manager who enters into a furtive love affair with a university student in “The Night That Binds Us,” the debut feature from Wang Jiangyong. Sun Xun’s “Magic Atlas,” a mixed-media extravaganza of animated woodblock prints, paintings and other visual forms, was awarded the Special Jury Prize.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
CHIBA – An outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza has been confirmed at a chicken farm in Asahi, Chiba Prefecture, the prefectural government said Friday.

It is the second bird flu case at a Japanese poultry farm this season.

The prefecture will cull about 40,000 egg-laying chickens at the farm and prohibit the transportation of 5.62 million chickens at 49 farms within a 10-kilometer radius from the Asahi farm.

The Chiba government received a report from the Asahi farm Thursday that the number of dead chickens was rising there. A simple test produced a positive result, which was confirmed early Friday through genetic testing.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Second bird flu case at Japanese poultry farm this season. Chiba Prefecture will cull about 40,000 egg-laying chickens at the farm.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
Public broadcaster NHK unveiled the lineup for the 77th edition of its New Year’s Eve music extravaganza “Kohaku Uta Gassen” on Friday, with 41 acts set to perform on the program, including seven making their debut on the show.

The announcement was made at the NHK Broadcasting Center in Tokyo’s Shibuya Ward, where all of the first-time performers were revealed onstage with the drop of a large white curtain.

The newcomers in this year’s “Kohaku” reflect the ongoing boom in idol music that J-pop has embraced over the past years. They include male outfits Ae! Group, Ebidan and Monaki and colorful female groups Cutie Street and =Love. https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Tadahito Iguchi could not have scripted a better start to his tenure as Samurai Japan manager.

Tomoya Masaki picked up where he left off in the Japan Series, leading off Japan’s game against Taiwan with a home run to help launch the Iguchi era in a 5-0 victory at the Asia Professional Baseball Championship at Tokyo Dome on Thursday night.

Masaki, the Japan Series MVP for the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks last month, hit another home run in the third inning and added an RBI single in the fifth. Rui Muneyama finished with a solo homer and a pair of doubles, and Misho Nishikawa had an RBI single among his two hits. Yumeto Kanemaru dominated from the mound with seven scoreless innings.

Stefon Diggs’ late touchdown secured a tense 24-21 Washington Commanders win over the New York Giants after Cam Skattebo had rushed for two touchdowns Thursday.

Commanders QB Jayden Daniels, who had not thrown an interception all season, threw two on consecutive drives while seeking a comeback in a wild fourth quarter, before finding veteran receiver Diggs with a minute remaining for the go-ahead touchdown.

Daniels finished with 249 passing yards and three TDs, with Antonio Williams and Ben Sinnott also reaching the end zone for Washington.

Workers and companies in Japan are grappling with the effects of a globally crippling outage that has struck Microsoft 365 and its widely used apps Outlook, Teams and AI software Copilot.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Ariana King
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
GMO Internet Group said Friday it is facing a ¥3.05 billion ($19.1 million) loss, to be recorded in the fourth quarter, as a result of last month’s data breach that led to unauthorized transactions and exposed personal data.

“This incident has damaged the trust placed in us by our customers, shareholders, investors and society as a whole,” said Masashi Yasuda, group vice president and chief financial officer, during an online news conference announcing its quarterly financial results. “We take it very seriously.”

Of the losses, ¥50 million (of ¥130 million maximum) has been claimed in goodwill payments for about 11,000 cases so far. The company promised a uniform payout of ¥5,000 to all customers “in respect of the inconvenience and anxiety this matter has caused.”

Cybersecurity companies in Japan are reporting a rapid increase in demand for a wide range of security services in recent weeks, as the number of cyberattacks rises and awareness grows following a series of high-profile incidents.

Digital Data Solution (DDS), which offers data recovery, digital forensics, security operations center protection and vulnerability testing, is especially busy these days, said Managing Director Masashi Kumagai.

“The forensic team responds to cyber incidents whenever a cyberattack occurs,” said Kumagai. “Their cases have doubled.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Ian King
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
At the end, Jensen Huang looked broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted.

After weeks spent denying the allegations of infidelity and fighting to remain in his job as Nvidia’s chief executive officer, his surrender late Wednesday night was unconditional. Huang’s usual take-charge demeanor had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and he’d started using phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.”

For the decades he spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth, Huang was famous for his attention to the tiniest of details, from chip architecture to the compensation packages of even the most junior employees at the company. Now, in the eyes of the people in the room, he had given up.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Japan can fund the ICC. But can it save the court?
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Imran Khalid
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
Tomoko Akane did not walk to the podium when she presented the International Criminal Court’s annual report to the United Nations General Assembly last week.

The court’s president, a former Japanese prosecutor, appeared instead in a prerecorded video from The Hague, the first time a court president has addressed the Assembly that way since the pandemic. U.S. sanctions now cover her personally and, since Oct. 9, the court itself. She asked all 193 U.N. members to take concrete action in its defense. Within days, her own government answered in the one currency the sanctions are really aimed at.

Tokyo is considering paying its 2027 contribution to the court ahead of schedule, possibly through a second supplementary budget for fiscal 2026. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara has said the government would “consider what financial measures we can take.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Jessica Speed
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Japan bucked a broader decline in long-term immigration experienced across other developed economies in 2025, a report released Thursday found.

The OECD International Migration Outlook 2026 found that Japan welcomed 192,000 new long-term or permanent immigrants last year, including people who changed their residence status, with labor migrants accounting for 63% of the total.

Japan recorded a 9.5% year-on-year increase in long-term immigration in 2025 while other OECD member countries saw a 1.6% decline, marking the second consecutive annual drop.

https://www.dw.com/en/is-the-ai-bubble-b.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
https://www.dw.com/en/is-the-ai-bubble-b.text:
The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI) bet started paying off. Instead, it’s turning into a test of nerves.

In the first half of the year, many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.

Two of the largest AI players — Anthropic and OpenAI — announced plans for public listings, following SpaceX's much-hyped IPO in June, which briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire.

AI models, meanwhile, got noticeably better at difficult tasks in the race to beat human intelligence.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty. While the stock of Nvidia, a chipmaker, pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen their stock prices gyrate wildly.

Then last week, after the Democrats secured control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections, technology stocks sold off dramatically, with the Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — losing more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit this week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days. The sell-off followed news that Nvidia's board — alongside the FBI — is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

On Thursday, Huang resigned from the chipmaker when a second alleged marital affair was revealed, sending Nvidia's shares lower still.

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending. Growing pressure on US lawmakers to curb the expansion of AI data centers has added to those doubts.

In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, told DW, meaning that times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "show me the money."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other analysts think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks last week's rout was a "healthy correction."

"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

While OpenAI has delayed its public listing until next year, Claude-maker Anthropic still plans its IPO later this month. On Tuesday, the company said it would offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 per share.

Dick said Anthropic’s decision to go ahead amid the market sell-off left him scratching his head. “Is this the best timing?” he asked.

While Anthropic had originally targeted a valuation of over $2 trillion, it now thinks the firm could be worth around $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion.

Dick said the valuation depends on whether Anthropic can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of over $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."

Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude-maker's prospects.

“Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company,” Seth told Bloomberg this week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. “Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize.”

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported last week.

"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."

That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.

Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers.

This summer, New York and Texas temporarily paused new data center approvals. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who takes office in January, wants new laws to stop data centers’ heavy power and water use from pushing up household bills.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railroads, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.

Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.

"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-nmecha-w.title: Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-nmecha-w.text:
Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp says that midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-leaders-gather-.title: EU leaders gather for first ever AI summit
https://www.dw.com/en/eu-leaders-gather-.text:
The summit comes as worries about the artificial intelligence's global impact mount and Europe seeks a role in its development and regulation.

European Union leaders are meeting in Dublin on Friday at the first ever summit on artificial intelligence (AI). The meeting comes at a critical moment, as the bloc seeks a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology.

"Given the rapid pace of AI development, ​I ‌believe that a first dedicated discussion, at leaders' level, is now needed on the opportunities presented by AI, as well as on its transformative effect on our economies and societies," European Council ‌President Antonio Costa wrote in a letter to EU leaders last week.

The meeting is taking place in Dublin's Convention Center, which was also the meting place of the European Political Community summit this week.

French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch, as well as Nobel-prize winner and researcher Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," are expected to speak to EU leaders at the summit.

The summit will take place a time of mounting worries about the emerging technology, which promises to transform ‌industries, labor markets and societies.

It also comes in the wake of a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months and the wider discussion about how the technology could harm humanity.

Tech leaders behind the technology have also fallen under scrutiny. As recently as this week,Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign after it was revealed that he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company.

During the summit, a discussion about where Europe fits in within the AI movement is expected.

Leaders face questions on how to unlock AI's potential, how to catch up with China and the United States in the race for the technology, but also how to protect against the risks it poses to individuals and businesses.

The governments of Estonia and Finland wrote in a letter ahead of the summit that Europe must "establish EU-level arrangements for responding to serious AI incidents," calling for "developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly."

Meanwhile, Mistral has pushed back on calls to slow down AI development, urging Europe to push ahead.

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-updates-ru.title: Ukraine updates: Russia hit with second car bomb attack in two days
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-updates-ru.text:
A second car bomb in two days exploded in Moscow, targeting an exiled Ukrainian political aide, according to Russian media. Meanwhile, Ukraine and Russia exchanged deadly strikes overnight. DW has more.

Here are the latest developments from the Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, November 13:

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday asked US President Donald Trump to not make any "surprises" on Ukraine with the Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump is expected to meet with Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders' summit in China next week.

Speaking on the sidelines of the European Union meetings in Dublin, Merz said that "some here ⁠in ⁠fear this could turn into a 'second Anchorage moment'."

The Russian and US presidents held talks in Anchorage, Alaska, last summer, the outcome of which European side views as favoring Putin.

"I ‌therefore want to state our message to the United States very clearly: Please, no surprises. Continue to ‌play as part of 'Team Europe' and 'Team Ukraine'," Merz said.

He also stated that Europe does not need to talk about security arrangements with Russia.

"Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that, it already exists," he said.

Merz also said it was a "given" that his country would involved in the next round of Ukraine talks.

Kyiv residents are bracing for another difficult winter as Russian airstrikes continue to target the Ukrainian capital’s energy infrastructure. Long and unpredictable power and water outages are disrupting daily life, forcing families to rely on batteries, portable power stations and improvised routines.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.

Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

Read more about the uncertainty over Europe’s representation in the Ukraine peace talks

Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia needs clarity on the European Union's "real intentions" for joining the Ukraine peace talks before making a decision on whether to expand the trilateral format.

US negotiators ‌said on Thursday that ‌President ​Vladimir Putin had agreed to an EU seat at the table, but Peskov's remarks indicate that the Kremlin has not yet agreed.

"Once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format," Peskov said.

"If the Europeans really do have someone who is at least authorized in some way to talk, and if the Europeans really do have the desire to do so, then, of course, we will be ready to talk to them," he said.

Speaking after the latest trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, Russia's lead negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, claimed that "Russia did not receive single concrete peace proposal from European countries."

The European Union (EU) foreign affairs chief, Kaja Kallas, said Russia did not want ​"anybody strong" at the negotiating table because "they ​want to ​push through their maximum ​demands."

Arriving at an EU summit in Dublin, Kallas told reporters that Moscow had no say over who represented the European Union in the US-mediated Ukraine-Russia peace talks.

"First we need a ceasefire. If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us, which is that we divert the attention away from that there is no ceasefire," she said.

EU leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent the European Union in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the bloc will be present at the next meetings.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa.

As yet, the EU hasn't been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

Overnight drone attacks killed several people in both Ukraine and Russia.

In the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa, authorities said two people had been killed and five others injured. One person was reportedly injured in an attack on a hospital, according to reports from the capital city of Kyiv.

A Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia in the southeast killed a 17-year-old boy, acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said.

Meanwhile, In the Russian city of Volgograd, four people were killed and two others injured, regional government said.

Russia's Investigative Committee has launched an inquiry into the explosion of a car belonging to an exiled Ukrainian political aide in Moscow, media reported.

The car reportedly belonged to Sergei Zavorotniy, a former spokesman for Mykola Azarov, who served as Ukraine's prime minister from 2010 to 2014. He fled to Russia from Ukraine amid anti-government protests in 2014.

According to the Russian newspaper Kommersant, Zavorotniy was hospitalized. Both Ren TV and the 112 Telegram channel reported that he lost his left arm in the attack and sustained a concussion, rib fractures, and other injuries.

Meanwhile, Azarov told Russia's TASS state news agency on Friday that he does not know anything about the explosion except that Zavorotniy survived.

This is the second reported car explosion in Russia following the death of a Russian serviceman in a car explosion in Saint Petersburg on Thursday.

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

EU leaders are set to convene in the Irish capital, Dublin, for an informal European Council meeting on Friday. They are under pressure to nominate someone to represent the European Union in the Ukraine peace talks.

In other news, a car bomb exploded in Russia, targeting a former aide to the pro-Russia Ukrainian politician Mykola Azarov.

Follow along for the latest updates on the peace talks and other news from Ukraine.
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-updates-ru.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz asks US President Donald Trump to not make any "surprises" on Ukraine with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Merz says Europe does not need to talk about security arrangements with Russia. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas says Europe will be present at next round of Ukraine peace talks.

https://www.dw.com/en/humanitarian-situa.title: Humanitarian situation in Gaza worsens amid political deadlock
https://www.dw.com/en/humanitarian-situa.text:
In war-battered Gaza, heavy rain flooded and damaged thousands of tents. Several people died. Could pressure by Trump's Board of Peace on Israel and Hamas help to ease the humanitarian crisis amid stalled peace talks?

This autumn's heavy rain and falling temperatures are exacerbating the humanitarian situation for civilians in Gaza. Torrential rainfall over the weekend killed at least six people, including children, according to UNICEF. Local authorities said at least 70,000 tents were flooded and more than 200,000 people affected.

"Over the past two days, we have been trying to stabilize our tent with sand and rubble to keep water from seeping inside," Rawan Al-Omari, a mother of two, told DW on the phone.

She and her children share a tent west of Jabalia in northern Gaza. "The entire area around us has turned into mud, so even leaving the tent has become difficult," the 33-year-old said. "Everything is exhausting."

The rain also soaked the tent and everything 45-year-old Radi Amin and his three children own.

"For three consecutive days, we have been trying to dry our clothes while my children were shivering in the cold," he told DW. "Only on Wednesday, with the sun finally out and warm enough, our belongings started to dry."

Amin said that "the heavy rain served as a stark reminder of our truly dire state."

Aid teams meanwhile have started to clear blocked sewer lines and stormwater basins at 60 locations, benefiting an estimated 30,000 families, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported on Wednesday.

However, OCHA's humanitarian partners also warned that there is not enough space to relocate people living in flooded areas or war-damaged buildings. "Israeli authorities are restricting Palestinian access anywhere behind the so-called 'Yellow Line,' which means that most of Gaza's land remains off limit," OCHA said.

Following the Hamas terror attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, the ensuing war in Gaza has destroyed most of Gaza's infrastructure and housing. More than 74,600 people were killed in the Gaza Strip, according to figures from Gaza's Health Ministry. Israel controls about two-thirds of the territory, which is marked by a military demarcation line, the so-called Yellow Line.

Hamas continues to exercise governing authority in much of the remaining territory close to the Mediterranean Sea, where most of Gaza's roughly 2 million residents live. Most of them have been displaced several times and live in tents, camps for displaced people or in houses that are deemed unsafe. Hamas is classified as a terrorist organization by Germany, the EU, the United States and others.

As part of the US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025, US President Donald Trump established the Board of Peace (BoP) committee to oversee the ceasefire's implementation as well as Gaza's postwar governance and reconstruction. According to a joint assessment by the World Bank, United Nations and European Union published in April 2026,Gaza's recovery and reconstruction will require an estimated $71.4 billion (€64.2 billion) over the next decade.

However, little progress has been made as negotiators have been failing to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its troops from the territory. Despite the ceasefire, Israel continues to carry out airstrikes on Gaza. On Thursday, Israel carried out a strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis against alleged Hamas members.

For Nathan Brown, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University in the US, the current rainfall exemplifies the deadlock of Trump's peace plan for Gaza.

"The failure of the Board of Peace to advance reconstruction, or even secure reliable relief, is fundamentally due to Israeli objections based on the insistence that Hamas has to completely disarm first," he told DW.

Until the recent elections in Israel, the Board of Peace showed little interest in challenging that view, Brown added: "Now it is willing to go public, though not in very confrontational terms."

On Monday, the Board of Peace issued a statement saying that Israel's steps to improve the humanitarian situation ahead of the coming winter remain insufficient. "We call on the leadership of the current Government of Israel to act immediately to authorize and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterization and humanitarian supplies."

Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) said the same day that among other equipment, 12 sewage vacuum trucks for the International Committee of the Red Cross arrived in Gaza and that 91,000 tents and more than 8,200 trucks carrying tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothing had entered Gaza in recent months.

In its statement, the Board of Peace also called on Hamas to abide by commitments under the ceasefire, including laying down its weapons and transferring governing authority. Hamas promptly rejected the criticism in a statement and accused Israel of obstructing implementation of the peace plan and withholding urgently needed humanitarian supplies.

The United Nations as well as numerous international agencies have accused Israel of systematically preventing the import of prefabricated shelters into Gaza. The UN said around 150,000 tents were outside Gaza and ready to be dispatched, pending the necessary approvals, a claim Israel rejects.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is serving as caretaker prime minister while a new government is being formed following the October 27 elections, denied that Israel was responsible for the worsening conditions and blamed Hamas instead.

He warned that "as long as Hamas remains in power, it will use every dual-use item entering Gaza to entrench its terror regime and expand its military arsenal."

For Gaza's population, this deadlock amid the approaching winter spells ongoing hardship.

"Children and families are facing devastating conditions, with around 1.2 million people, including more than 560,000 children, living in critical or catastrophic shelter conditions," Ahmad Alhendawi, regional director of the aid organization Save the Children, told DW.

The amount of available winter clothing remains critically insufficient in Gaza, he added.
