https://www.dw.com/en/china-s-influence-.title: China's influence in the gaming industry is growing
https://www.dw.com/en/china-s-influence-.text:
Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."

Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.
https://www.dw.com/en/china-s-influence-.summary: More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. Games are not allowed to be shown in China because of government requirements. Games can be shown without the need to be censored or banned from the market.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.title: Climate action discussed at youth COP meeting
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.text:
School children are taking part in an event aimed at inspiring climate action, to coincide with the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey.

Hosted at the Kingston Maurwood campus, the first Dorset-wide Youth COP has brought children from 14 schools together to discuss issues including future careers.

Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said young people should be "given a voice" over dealing with climate change.

A Dorset COP 2026 event is also being held on Saturday as world leaders and delegates gather at Antalya in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit.

The Dorset Youth COP event includes discussions about how young people feel about climate change as well as a panel session introducing them to the range of jobs and careers in the climate and energy sectors.

Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said: "Young people are inheriting the climate and ecological emergencies that previous generations have created and need to be given a voice in jointly developing and implementing the solutions to these issues."

"The Youth COP aims to raise awareness, inspire and support them to take action now and into the future."

The main Dorset COP 2026 event takes place on Saturday also at the Kingston Maurward Campus near Dorchester.

The fourth annual event brings together community groups, environmental organisations, experts and political leaders.

The programme will explore how Dorset can respond to climate change, nature loss, food resilience, pollution and other environmental challenges.

The programme will also feature an exhibition of over 30 local organisations and a Question Time-style panel bringing together Dorset MPs, council leaders and independent climate experts.

Giles Watts, chair of Dorset CAN said the event's focus was on making "a lasting positive impact" on climate and nature local areas.

"We want to bring people together, listen to different perspectives and energise local communities and politicians to act more quickly on the pressing challenges we face," he added.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.summary: Dorset Youth COP event is being held at Kingston Maurwood campus in Dorset. Event aims to inspire young people to take action on climate change. Event also being held as world leaders and delegates gather at COP31 climate summit in Turkey.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr9d.title: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr9d.text:
Conservative MP Chris Philp and Reform UK's Zia Yusuf had a blazing row at a joint press conference, as they joined villagers protesting against asylum accommodation plans.

The pair clashed when sharing a platform in Piddington to oppose converting a former military site at MoD Bicester into accommodation for more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers.

The two politicians were invited to make speeches about the plans, but things became heated after Yusuf asked Philp to apologise for the Conservatives' record on immigration.

Philp, the shadow home secretary, told Yusuf to "calm down" and accused him of "cheap politics", an assertion Reform's home affairs spokesman dismissed.

A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation.

The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.

There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council.

In September, Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire.

Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners.

Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it was opened by Labour.

Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives.

He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government.

"So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?"

Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power.

He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring".

Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room."

Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government.

Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics."

Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power.

As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging."

Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people".

McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent."

While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters.

Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party as replacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives, and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform to secure power.

Government ministers want to use former military bases as part of efforts close all asylum hotels.

Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also previously said it should not just be the poorest communities receiving dispersed refugees and asylum seekers.

Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller told the BBC he was "very disappointed" but not "surprised" by the government's decision to grant planning permission.

Miller, whose constituency of Bicester and Woodstock includes the military site, said "the government was marking the government's application".

He said the decision "lays bare the weakness of the application and the many, many problems with it, because this is not a suitable site and it is not the right place to put a large-scale asylum centre".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.title: Reform could try to remove Senedd presiding officer over member's speaking ban
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.text:
A senior Reform politician says a no-confidence vote in the Senedd's presiding officer is "not off the table", after a party member was banned for claiming white people are being "replaced".

Llŷr Powell, Reform's chief whip in Cardiff Bay, said his colleague Joe Martin had the right to raise "legitimate concerns" that were being "infringed upon".

Martin was told he would not be called to speak in the Welsh Parliament until he apologised for the remarks made on Tuesday, which Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies called "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Reform withdrew from most Senedd proceedings on Wednesday in response.

Powell, who as chief whip enforces party discipline in the Senedd's Reform group, was asked on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast if his party would put forward a no confidence vote in Irranca-Davies.

He said: "I'm not going to say that we're going to do that now, but what I would say it's not off the table right now because freedom of speech and the right of members to raise legitimate concerns should be the main priority.

"And for us, right now, we see that as being infringed upon."

Powell denied Martin had made any connection to a far-right conspiracy theory that the white population was being deliberately replaced by the immigration of other ethnic groups.

"Joe was asking a legitimate question based on demographic changes," Powell said.

"The idea that he was framing some far-right theory is false.

"He was talking about legitimate concerns that is out there for data for all to see."

During business questions on Tuesday, Martin had asked Welsh government minister Heledd Fychan for a "statement from your government on the demographic replacement of white British people taking place in the UK".

"Mass immigration and differing birth rates mean that, in just 37 years' time, in 2063, we will be a minority in our own country," he said.

Fychan had asked the deputy presiding officer, who had been chairing the session, whether the question broke Senedd rules.

Irranca-Davies later called Martin's statement "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive" and "clearly discriminatory" when he issued the speaking ban.

He said that unless Martin apologised to the Senedd chamber "we will not be calling him to speak".

Aliya Mohammed, chief executive of the charity Race Equality First, criticised Martin on Wednesday, saying "the idea that white people are being 'replaced' is linked to a conspiracy theory that creates division and wrongly portrays people from minority ethnic backgrounds as a threat".

Martin, a Member of the Senedd (MS) representing Caerdydd Penarth, was accused by Plaid Cymru of dangerous rhetoric in June when he claimed attacks from Sudanese asylum seekers were inevitable.

The next day MSs walked out during a speech where Martin joked that Welsh students were unable to read, and Indian nurses were taking Welsh jobs.

He was later accused by the presiding officer of making offensive remarks in a debate about the crisis-hit Welsh Gender Service.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.summary: Reform's chief whip Llŷr Powell says no-confidence vote in presiding officer is not off the table. Joe Martin was banned for claiming white people are being "replaced" by other ethnic groups. Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies called Martin's remarks "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr86.title: 'Hardest challenge of my life' - Owain Wyn Evans completes Children in Need ride
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr86.text:
Presenter Owain Wyn Evans has completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need.

The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show rode almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff on Friday.

The challenge started on 9 November in Scotland and over the next five days, Owain rode through Northern Ireland, England and Wales and raised £3,853,530 in the process.

Reflecting on his journey, he said: "This has been the hardest challenge of my life, 100%.

"I can't believe I'm here. It's overwhelming, all the love and passion and commitment people have shown."

The BBC said Owain's challenge would be the "greatest-ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.

He crossed the finish line in Cardiff's Central Square just after 11:00 GMT, and was greeted by a crowd cheering him on before he was met by his husband, Arran Rees.

Owain, 42, whose bike was named Shania Chain, and decked out in Children in Need colours - Pudsey's favourite yellow with coloured spots - said: "Thank you so much everyone, from me and Shania.

"Honestly, this has felt so far away for such a long time. I can't believe that I'm here with this welcome and the sun's out."

Hollywood actor Luke Evans announced the route to Owain each day on BBC Radio 2.

During the 640km feat, he was also surprised with the premiere of Steps' brand-new version of their debut hit 5, 6, 7, 8, retitled 5, 6, 7, donate, which featured new lyrics and extra vocals.

It was recorded to help boost Owain's spirits on the longest day of his challenge.

When the challenge was announced, Owain, who is originally from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, said: "I'm ready to give it absolutely everything I've got."

He said colleagues Sara Cox, Paddy McGuinness and Vernon Kay had previously achieved "extraordinary things" for Children in Need so he ad "a lot to live up to".

Owain was undertaking his second challenge for the BBC charity fundraiser, following his 24-hour drumathon in 2021.

During the ride Owain received a heartwarming message of support from his primary school teacher Cath Adams.

Speaking to his parents on Radio 2, he recalled having a pink Care Bears lunch box while in reception because he loved the programme.

He said some classmates laughed at him and it prompted his "first feeling of shame", so he hid his lunchbox.

He added: "I remember Cath Adams bringing it out and telling the other kids that this is alright.

"And she was probably, probably my first ally. And I never realised at the time but I love you Cath Adams, you're amazing."

Asked how he was feeling, Owain said: "There are so many children who need our help and who will be helped by all the donations."

Speaking to Kay, he spoke about the gruelling nature of the challenge.

"You train so hard, me and Shania Chain going around the streets, but the reality of it, it's so hard.

"It's been amazing every step of the way and that's been super emotional as well."

Owain previously admitted he "never enjoyed exercise at school" because of bullying, ahead of his four nations biking challenge.

The broadcaster also expressed his gratitude for the support of Radio 2 listeners.

His messages of support from public figures included one from the Princess of Wales, who recorded a message for him in Welsh, saying: "Hi Owain, it's Catherine, you're doing so well. Keep going. Wishing you all the very best."

Shania Twain was so impressed that the bike had been named after her that she sent a message of good luck before the challenge.

She said: "Hi Owain, Shania Twain here. You're about to take on an incredible challenge for BBC Children in Need, cycling 400 miles through all four nations.

"As you set off in Glasgow, I just want to say: 'Let's Go, Owain!' We'll be cheering you on all the way. Good luck."

She sent him another message when he finished, saying: "Congratulations on completing your incredible challenge for Children in Need. You're still the one my friend, sending you all my love."

Helen Thomas, head of Radio 2, said: "Owain truly captured the hearts of the nation this week as he battled through his epic four nations Challenge.

"On behalf of all the Radio 2 listeners as well as the thousands of children and families who will benefit from his Herculean fundraising efforts we simply can't thank him enough. Diolch Owain! "

Evans began his broadcasting career in Welsh-language television when he presented the children's news programme Ffeil.

He later presented the weather on BBC Wales Today and began hosting BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show in 2023.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/techn.title: Nvidia Lost Its Founding C.E.O. Can It Keep Its Momentum?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/techn.author: Steve Lohr
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Throughout the years, tech giants have had mixed records after losing visionary founders who propelled their success. Successors with tech expertise helps.

Advice to Nvidia’s board: Choose a techie.

As the chip giant’s directors seek a replacement to Jensen Huang, the history of successions at Silicon Valley companies suggests that the odds of long-term success are better with a person steeped in technology and product development rather than finance, sales or marketing.

Replacing a founder is a defining moment for any company, whether it’s been planned for years or a sudden departure, whether the company is thriving or faltering. For Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and former chief executive, the fall came remarkably quickly. He resigned on Thursday after the disclosure of affairs with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy and with an executive who reported to him.

Nvidia’s business as the leading chip supplier to artificial intelligence data centers is flourishing. Mr. Huang’s hasty exit, analysts say, will have little near-term effect on the company’s business, despite a big stock-market reaction. (The company’s shares have fallen 14 percent in the last five days.)

But the best tech leaders steer their companies toward opportunity. At Nvidia, founded in 1993, Mr. Huang recognized more than a decade ago that chips used mainly for image-processing in computer games could be repurposed as the hardware engines for A.I. software. It was a huge bet for the small company — and paid off.

“You can coast on the founder’s work for years with good execution,” said Steve Blank, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and investor, who is an adjunct professor at Stanford University. “But you can lack the founder’s vision to see over the horizon and identify what’s next. That’s why the best successors have a lot of technical acumen as well as business acumen.”

Over the years, the results for tech companies replacing founding executives have been decidedly mixed.

NASA’s Artemis III Mission

SpaceX could still try to catch the rocket’s upper stage tomorrow. Progress toward a fully reusable rocket remains mixed.

SpaceX will have to wait until its next test flight of Starship to recover all parts of the giant rocket in a single mission.

The company had hoped to execute a milestone “double-catch” maneuver during the flight that launched on Friday from South Texas. That will be a key step toward SpaceX’s goal of developing a fully reusable rocket.

Until recent years, rockets have generally been expensive, single-use throwaways. If all of Starship, which is the largest rocket ever built, can be repeatedly flown, it would revolutionize the space industry, enabling launches of bigger, heavier satellites and other cargo at lower costs.

In addition, NASA is counting on a version of Starship to serve as a lunar lander for its Artemis program. The catches are not needed for NASA’s Artemis III mission next year, but any failures would make it even more unlikely that NASA could meet its goal of landing astronauts on the moon in 2028.

Starship launched on schedule at 5:47 p.m. Eastern time from its Starbase site outside Brownsville, Texas, into a clear azure sky, even as the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for air travel.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/your-.title: Deed Theft Is Rising, Along With Property Values
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/your-.author: Ann Carrns
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/your-.text:
The victims are often older people or immigrants, with thieves going after vacant land or unoccupied homes. But there are ways to protect yourself.

A dying woman with dementia. A doctor from Long Island. A couple renovating a home in Florida.

The three fell victim to a type of real estate fraud known as deed, or title, theft, in which someone forges documents or fakes an identity to take ownership of a home or vacant land. Criminals may impersonate the true owners and sell the property to unsuspecting buyers, or use it as collateral to obtain loans.

The rise in home property values, and, therefore, home equity, have made deed theft potentially lucrative, experts say. Homes owned by older people, homes that show signs of financial distress, and vacant homes or land may be especially vulnerable.

It’s not clear how common deed theft is nationally but awareness of the fraud is mounting, especially in the Northeast. Earlier this month, a Queens man became the first person convicted under a New York deed theft law passed in 2024. And New York City has created a special office of deed theft prevention to detect and investigate such fraud.

Reports of real estate crime in general rose by 32 percent in 2025, to more than 12,000 complaints, and associated financial losses rose to more than $275 million, according to the F.B.I.’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. The F.B.I. estimates it received 66 complaints about deed or title theft in 2025, representing $5.9 million in losses, compared with 75 complaints representing losses of almost $7 million from January through October of this year.

The National Association of Realtors surveyed real-estate executives nationally in 2025 and found that nearly two-thirds reported being aware of this type of fraud in their area within the past year, with awareness highest — 95 percent — in the Northeast.

But the fraud isn’t confined to one region. “It happens everywhere,” said Craig Haskins, president of the American Land Title Association, a trade group for title insurers and agents and real-estate closing professionals. The group’s survey this year of 245 title professionals in 40 states found that nearly three out of five had experienced at least one incident of attempted “seller impersonation” fraud, up from about a quarter two years earlier.

https://www.npr.org/sections/world-cafe/.title: Queens of the Stone Age try something new on 'Perfecth'
https://www.npr.org/sections/world-cafe/.author: Raina Douris
https://www.npr.org/sections/world-cafe/.text:
When I walked into the studio for my interview with Queens of the Stone Age frontman Josh Homme, he was fiddling with something on his belt. So the first thing I asked him was, "What are you doing?"

He looked up at me, holding a tiny metal cross charm on a hoop, and laughed. "I'm just trying things lately," he said.

Turns out, at that moment, he was trying out belt charms.

But that also sums up the new Queens of the Stone Age album, Perfecth, which finds the band branching out in new musical directions.

As you'll hear in our conversation, that attitude of "I'm just trying things lately" goes way beyond accessories for Josh.

He's been through a tumultuous few years in his personal life, including a couple of health scares, and he's come out of it seeming wiser, lighter and with a renewed sense of adventure.

As a person and a musician, he refuses to be boxed in.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Banned books from Ireland’s room of ‘evil literature’ finally see the light of day
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Censored books spanning 1926-96 contained themes ‘likely to corrupt or deprave’, or references to contraception or violence

For almost a century, an Irish government building in the heart of Dublin has hosted a secret sanctum: the banned books room.

The department of justice, on St Stephen’s Green, did not grant public access, because the shelves contained 12,000 books deemed indecent or obscene.

It was a graveyard for titles condemned by the Censorship of Publications Board, a guardian of public morals which guillotined anything that smelled of sex or other corruptions.

Harold Robbins was interred. So too Ian Fleming, Edna O’Brien, Brendan Behan, Oscar Wilde, DH Lawrence, JD Salinger, John Updike, Iris Murdoch, F Scott Fitzgerald and many more.

Exhumation, however, is nigh. The entire collection is to be moved to the National Archives as part of the repeal of Ireland’s censorship laws. The censors’ notes, minutes and ledgers that detail why each book was banned will be made publicly available for the first time – a trove for researchers of social history and state control.

“The censors prohibited works that they saw as contravening or subverting public morality – anything that was seen as unwholesome or suggestive of sexual immorality,” said Orlaith McBride, the director of the National Archives. “It was often just the innuendo of something that could have been perceived as likely to corrupt or deprave.”

The volumes span 1926 to 1996 and encompass pulp fiction, high-brow literature and academic texts. References to family planning, contraception and violence were likely to elicit bans, said McBride.

So too did suggestive imagery, such as the cover of O’Brien’s groundbreaking 1960 novel, The Country Girls. “It’s very subtly done but you can see the contours of the female form. The issue wasn’t just the contents but the image,” McBride said.

Banned titles included classics such as Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray, Behan’s Borstal Boy and Lawrence’s Lady Chatterley’s Lover, as well as pulpy paperbacks with titles such as The Baby Doll Murders, A Doctor and his Mistress and Torrid Tale of a Wicked Town.

Scholarly tomes such as Sexual Life in England Past and Present and arcane works such as The Collected Works of Pierre Louÿs, a Belgian poet of the early 20th century, also ended up in what was informally called the banned books room.

The censorship board adopted a broad definition of indecent and obscene, said Brian Hughes, a history lecturer at the University of Limerick’s Mary Immaculate College.

“I think people would be very surprised seeing these books or reading some of these books to think that they were banned at all in the first place, because attitudes are quite different now. I think it suggests that certainly in terms of printed matter, the written word, there’s a much more liberal society. It is a more secular society as well; that’s part of it. But I think it’s a wider process of attitudes towards sex, sexuality changing.”

In 1926, soon after independence, the nascent Irish Free State established the Committee of Evil Literature, a five-man panel tasked with protecting public morals. It recommended a strict system of vetting that led to the Censorship of Publications Board – which, for a time, was led by a Catholic priest – and an appeals board.

The censors reviewed material that was submitted by members of the public and customs and revenue officers. They also sourced books through a subscription to the Times Book Club.

The periodicals and books that accumulated at what is now known as the department of justice, home affairs and migration will be moved after Christmas to the National Archives, where they will be conserved, catalogued and stored.

“Many are first editions, and because of sheer age in a vulnerable state, so they won’t be available to the public,” said McBride. People could source them online “and in all good bookshops”, she said.

The censors’ registers and notes, plus letters from the public and interest groups, were transferred this week, and are undergoing conservation in advance of becoming publicly available. McBride said: “They are the most interesting because they record the decisions and reveal the thinking behind the bans.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Jennifer Rankin in Dublin
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Kaja Kallas says Moscow is trying to divert attention from its aggression by raising issue of European security

Europe live – latest updates

The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.

“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”

In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US were held this week in Abu Dhabi.

Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.

European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.

Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.

The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.

The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.

Despite more than two years of on-off talks, the EU has not settled on a choice. But there is a growing view that Europe should not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent.

Paris and Berlin support a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: the European Council’s president, António Costa, and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.

Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.

after newsletter promotion

Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”

Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing, a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.

Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Eleanor Donaldson, wife of former DUP leader, placed on sex offender register
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Judge imposes three-year treatment order on Donaldson for aiding and abetting sexual offences by her husband, Jeffrey

Jeffrey Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, has been placed on the sex offender register for five years for aiding and abetting sexual offences by her disgraced husband.

Eleanor Donaldson appeared via remote link at Newry crown court to hear the order on Friday one month after her husband, the former Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, was convicted of abusing two women when they were children.

The 60-year-old bowed her head and cried as Judge Paul Ramsey imposed a three-year supervision and treatment order as well as placing her on the sex offender register. Asked if she understood the court order, she nodded and said yes.

In June her husband was convicted of 18 sexual offences, including one count of rape, spanning 1985 to 2008. The case stunned Northern Ireland and destroyed the career and reputation of a politician who had been the leading voice of unionism. In October he was sentenced to 15 years.

His wife faced a trial of the facts after being deemed unfit to participate in a conventional trial on mental health grounds. A jury found that she had aided and abetted her husband’s abuse.

She could not be given a prison sentence, only a hospital order, a supervised treatment order or a discharge. Two experts, one for the prosecution and one for the defence, told the court that a supervised treatment order was the most appropriate option.

The victims, known as Complainant A and B, were in court for the hearing on Friday. The prosecutor, Rosemary Walsh KC, told the court that “pain permeated” their statements.

Donaldson’s three-minute appearance on screen was the first time she had been seen in court since 2025. Wearing a black jumper, and with close-cropped hair and two cuts on her forehead, she cast her eyes down and held a tissue.

The judge told the court the medical evidence about her was unchallenged and that a supervision and treatment order was “inevitable”. Donaldson would be under the supervision of a social worker from the Craigavon community mental health team for three years, he said.

This would require attending appointments, treatment and home visits, said the judge. She will be subject to the notification provisions of the sex offender register for five years.

Bronagh Muldoon, the assistant director for the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children Northern Ireland, said aiding and abetting abuse required consequences.

“It is right and important that the role she played in these terrible crimes has been recognised in court today. The women involved in this case have shown incredible bravery in coming forward to ensure the Donaldsons have both been held accountable.”

The former DUP leader is appealing against his convictions and his wife is appealing against the jury verdict.

In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help at Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helpline International

Her husband Jeffrey was convicted of 18 sexual offences, including one count of rape, spanning 1985 to 2008. She was placed on the sex offender register for five years for aiding and abetted sexual offences by her disgraced husband.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Nigel Farage’s security paid for by Reform UK despite claim over £5m gift
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Anna Isaac and Ben Quinn
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Exclusive: Sources reveal party is covering costs – raising new questions about leader’s explanation for billionaire’s gift

Nigel Farage’s personal security has been paid for out of Reform UK’s central funds despite his claim that these expenses would be covered by an undisclosed gift of £5m from a billionaire donor, sources have told the Guardian.

The Reform leader has had the central party pay for a team and two cars ever since a reduction in the security provided by the taxpayer after a review in 2025.

The disclosure raises fresh questions about Farage’s explanation of the £5m he was given by the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

After the Guardian revealed the gift, Harborne said it was intended “to support Nigel’s security not just now but for the rest of his life”.

Farage initially said: “This money was given to me so that I would be safe and secure for the rest of my life.”

He suggested that the Home Office did not offer him any security support. In fact, though it was reduced in scale, he was offered a bodyguard, a driver and car – similar to the provision made for Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the official opposition.

Farage refused this, and since then his security has been paid for from central party funds. These costs have amounted to more than £150,000 in the past year, sources said.

The arrangement has caused consternation for some within the party. “It’s completely at odds with the narrative he’s tried to sell the public,” a Reform source said.

Asked about Farage expensing the party, a spokesperson for Reform UK said: “As a standard practice, we do not comment on security matters.”

The party refused to answer questions about whether Farage had spent any of the £5m on security costs to date. It also refused to address questions about why Farage had refused the offer of a taxpayer-funded package.

The Guardian understands that the party makes a distinction between security required as a result of its leader’s political activities, which it pays for, and his potential longer-term personal security needs, which the gift was intended to provide for.

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Nigel Farage’s excuses over his secret £5m ‘gift’ have fallen apart. You can’t trust a word he says. From secret gifts, to police investigations into Reform’s finances, to donations from a convicted fraudster – Reform are up to their necks in sleaze and scandal. Farage and his party are simply not fit for office. It’s time for him to get his story straight and be honest with the public.”

A Conservative party spokesperson said: “Nigel Farage variously described his fishy bung from an overseas crypto billionaire as a reward for Brexit, cash he can spend on Ferraris or the horses if he wants, the list goes on. It is no wonder people are asking questions, and the public are entitled to a straight answer. Nigel Farage should come clean about where the £5m has gone and what it was really for.”

Zia Yusuf, Reform’s spokesperson for home affairs, complained publicly that the party was having to seek fresh support from donors to meet Farage’s security costs in October 2025.

Harborne gave Farage £5m shortly before he stood as an MP in the 2024 general election. On becoming an MP, Farage was offered and accepted taxpayer-funded security, which he used until the autumn of 2025.

Harborne had been the dominant party donor in recent years until he was joined by his fellow crypto tycoon Ben Delo in donating a further £36m each in September.

Costs charged to Reform by Farage have included security changes to his properties, including ones used by his family members, according to sources.

The security team funded by Reform has also been used by Farage for personal activities, sources said.

Since Harborne’s initial claim that the gift was intended to fund his security arrangements, Farage’s account of what the £5m gift was for has varied. He has said he could spend it on Ferraris, or that it was a reward for Brexit campaigning, and at other times he has tried to suggest it was not political but for his security for life.

Footage gathered by the undercover reporting group Verbatim and shared with the Guardian last month appeared to show that Farage’s close aide Dan Jukes believed it was a PR mistake for Farage to suggest it was for anything other than security.

“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said, after Farage suggested the money was a reward for his political campaigning in an interview with the Sun.

Jukes has since stood down from Reform and he denies any wrongdoing.

Lawyers for Harborne have previously said he “expected nothing in return” for the money and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.

The timeline for the gift is disputed. Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024. According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.

The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in 2024.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Siberian rubythroat was thousands of miles off course from its route to winter in south or south-east Asia

A bird that flies south from its breeding grounds in Siberia to winter in south and south-east Asia has been found thousands of miles off course in Cumbria. Regrettably, it was found by a cat.

Chris Hind, Cumbria’s county recorder for birds, said it was “extraordinary” that a Siberian rubythroat was found on his patch, albeit dead. There have been only 17 recorded instances of the bird in the UK, 15 of those in the northern Scottish isles.

Hind was contacted by the RSPB at the weekend after a woman who lives in a remote north Cumbrian valley reported the bird. She had recognised it was out of the ordinary and put the dead bird in her freezer.

“She realised that it was something unusual,” Hind said. “She probably didn’t realise how incredibly unusual it is. There are only two accepted records of it from mainland Britain.”

The woman, who wants to remain anonymous, told the BBC she had “heard the cat flap go” and her heart sank when her cat “brought her a bird and trotted off”.

“I saw the bird’s distinctive, beautiful orange-red feather patch under its beak but I couldn’t recognise the species,” she said.

Quite why the bird appears to have headed west, rather than south, is a mystery although Hind pointed to the puzzle of yellow-browed warblers that have been spotted in the UK in increasing numbers in recent decades.

“It used to be thought that these are birds which had just got lost but there are academics now thinking that it may be something rather more purposeful,” he said.

Hind said the bird brought in by the cat was very underweight, weighing 28 grams (just under 1oz). Textbooks say it should be about 73 grams.

Siberian rubythroats were also extremely secretive, he said. “They tend to creep around in the vegetation and the place where it was found was a place hugely vegetated, lots of trees, lots of bushes, lots of hedges in a remote little valley.”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: ‘So lovely’: Stevie Wonder surprises Stalybridge restaurant with late-night visit and £1,000 tip
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
Singer, 76, was in Manchester with his band for penultimate UK show of his Songs in the Key of Life anniversary tour

When Stevie Wonder’s team just called to say: “Can we all come to your restaurant in Stalybridge at 11pm on a Sunday?” Ryan Robinson, of course, said yes.

First the band turned up, and then – at 12.30am – the man himself arrived. Hours later, staff at the Cafe Continental were sharing a £1,000 tip.

It was, the co-owner admitted, “all a bit mad”, as he praised Wonder as someone who was happy to chat to everybody, and the team around him as down to earth and extremely polite.

Wonder, 76, was in Manchester with his band for the Sunday night gig at Co-op Live on his Songs in the Key of Life 50th anniversary tour.

It was the penultimate night of a 13-date European leg of the tour in which Wonder performed all 21 songs from his most celebrated album, which includes Have a Talk With God, Sir Duke, Joy Inside My Tears and Isn’t She Lovely.

Robinson told the Manchester Evening News that some of the musicians on the tour had already been in a few times, “as they often tour with other artists”.

“Every time they’ve visited, they’ve been like: ‘Stevie might come’, and we were always just thinking that it would be amazing but we never expected anything from it.

“His band visited again on Saturday and then we got the call to say they wanted to come again with Stevie’s youngest daughter after their show in Manchester, and they said again that Stevie might come. We stayed open late for them, and then he turned up – it was all a bit mad!

“We normally just do a roast service on Sunday, so it was a bit of a scramble to make it all happen and ensure we had the full menu ready for them, but everybody was so lovely. Stevie is actually a really nice guy and was happy to pose for photographs and have a chat.”

Among the late-night diners was Wonder’s daughter Aisha, for whom he wrote Isn’t She Lovely when she was a newborn. Robinson said: “His daughter, his family, and his entire team are just all down to earth and very polite. You wouldn’t think they were these massive global superstars. I just kept looking over being like: ‘Is this actually happening?’ We’ve still not come to terms with it now!”

Cafe Continental describes itself as a neighbourhood restaurant in the heart of Stalybridge, “offering a modern, day to night dining experience”.

The superstar and his musicians dined on steak and seafood and before leaving they gave a £1,000 tip, which was shared among staff, Robinson said. After the visit the restaurant posted on Facebook: “Surreal things happen now and again. This is one of them! Pleasure to welcome Mr Stevie Wonder to the restaurant to close off his tour!”

Robinson said he thought the band had found the restaurant on social media. “If it wasn’t for social media, they more than likely may have Googled something nearby and it might have led them to the city centre,” he told the BBC. “But it’s brought them out here into the suburbs and it’s really nice to see. “It’s good for the area. For a small independent business like us to receive so much traction from this … getting a major celebrity to this town itself, it does a lot.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: US terrorism case sheds light on RAF Fairford arrests mystery
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Suspect held in New York jail has been linked to handler behind Iran-linked operations in Britain

When the US took custody of Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi in May, investigators hoped the string of terrorist and arson attacks he was accused of promoting and directing against American and Jewish targets in the UK and Europe on behalf of Iran would stop. They were wrong.

An updated indictment, released on Tuesday by the US Department of Justice, describes some of what happened next. It reveals that al-Saadi has two allies, believed to be in Iran, also trying to provoke fear and chaos in the UK, one of whom is accused of orchestrating the September incident at RAF Fairford.

Al-Saadi described himself as “a prisoner of war” when he first appeared in a Manhattan courtroom in June, accused of being the man behind a new terrorist group called Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia (Hayi) as well as a commander with Kata’ib Hezbollah, an Iraqi group backed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Yet, as al-Saadi awaited trial from a jail in New York, he was nevertheless able to make calls to his family. During the calls, according to the 26-page indictment, al-Saadi sought to pass on “coded messages” to two associates in Iran. On or about 24 September, he asked after one of them, named Ali. Ali had been transferred to the “international section”, family members said, as the FBI listened in.

Digesting this, al-Saadi gave an instruction – “Give him money so we can do it” – though it was not immediately obvious what he meant. In any event, Ali had already been busy, according to the US. Within days, Ali’s efforts had come together, directing the incident in a Cotswold village right next to RAF Fairford, the indictment says.

Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, told MPs in mid-October that the IRGC was “almost certainly” behind Fairford. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, added: “Our assessment is that it is highly likely to have been coordinated by a known individual based in Iran, and almost certainly directed by Iran’s IRGC.”

A fortnight later, two Britons from London were charged by UK police. They await trial, accused of assisting Iranian intelligence in breach of the 2023 National Security Act, and are yet to plead.

Last month Westminster magistrates court in London heard that the men in the vans had been directed to drive to Fairford by a handler called Ali.

But it was not until last night that Ali was given a full name by investigators. The US indictment said he was Mohammed Ali al-Hassani, a 35-year-old Iraqi who had lived in Britain – it is unclear for how long – and was now using contacts and associates “to carry out terrorist attacks in the UK”.

Al-Hassani was said to be one of two associates of al-Saadi in the low-level campaign conducted by Hayi in March and April, along with Mohsen Mohajeri. A video obtained by US prosecutors shows Mohajeri telling al-Hassani: “We need to get focused on London” on 6 April, as they look at a map of the capital on a laptop. Six attacks in the capital followed shortly after.

In one case, all three men are accused of directing an individual in real time to attack a premises linked to an educational charity called Jewish Futures in Hendon, north London, on 17 April. Late that Friday, a man lit a plastic bag containing bottles of fluid outside the front of the building before fleeing.

Video evidence recovered by US prosecutors shows the three are linked to the individual via a FaceTime video call, its image projected on a large screen against the Hayi logo. During the call, al-Hassani appears to direct the perpetrator’s actions, telling them to take a lighter and “light one in your hand”, “light it” and “throw the fourth one”, according to the US.

after newsletter promotion

The arson attack was basic, but the string of Hayi-linked arson attacks in London in March and April, on synagogues and other Jewish community sites, had a wider impact.

Roger Macmillan, a former head of security at Iran International, an independent London-based TV channel, whose staff have been the focus of threats and harassment from Tehran, argues it matters less whether Iran has the capability to kill or hurt people because “terrorism is not always about massive attacks, it is about instilling fear”.

Al-Saadi was arrested in Turkey in May, and extradited to the US within a couple of weeks. But al-Hassani and Mohajeri remained at liberty – and in August al-Hassani was back, this time accused by the US of orchestrating the preparations of the alleged plot against RAF Fairford.

It will be for the British courts to determine what happened at Fairford, but what the US indictment does demonstrate is that there remain other IRGC-linked individuals interested in orchestrating sabotage and terror plots in the UK.

Britain’s role in the US-led bombing of Iran may have been limited to allowing the US to use its airbases, but the UK has become a theatre of the now simmering conflict, a psychological arena in a war started by Donald Trump.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrats won big in the US midterms. Now, organizers want them to deliver
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Fabiola Cineas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
After Tuesday’s election, ‘everyone must have a Wednesday agenda,’ experts say

T
he bright blue map that emerged on election night in the US was unthinkable two years ago. When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, many Democratic voters curled up in bed and doomscrolled, fatigued and fearful about the direction of the country. Any desire to fight back was dampened by the enormity of the loss.

But the mood gradually shifted over the following two years, culminating in a generational shift on election day: Democrats flipped five governors’ seats and took control of the House and Senate by wide margins. Voters were angry about the rising cost of living, the war in Iran, masked immigration agents in their neighborhoods and datacenters rising in their backyards.

But anger alone didn’t boost turnout. That required years of building coalitions, developing local campaigns and expanding movement infrastructure that turned frustration into organized action – and, eventually, votes.

Now, these same organizers are determining where to go next. The goal was never about any one party or politician. To continue to build power, movements must diversify their tactics, make clear demands, put pressure on the newly elected and keep building community-based networks, movement experts said. And they must be unrelenting.

“Elections themselves don’t achieve what it is that people want,” said Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor, an African American studies professor at Princeton University and the author of From #BlackLivesMatter to Black Liberation. “They set the table for the possibility of change.”

The national No Kings protests have been some of the most visible actions in the second Trump administration. The coalition, made up of dozens of groups and partner organizations, emerged in the middle of 2025 as intentionally leaderless and decentralized, its marches designed to be a container for the variety of grievances that millions of people wanted to express, from anger over gas prices and federal workforce cuts to frustration over war.

The marches provided an entry point for people who were new to activism, and now, after the midterms, the coalition is regrouping.

“One thing is clear: the work of protecting our democracy doesn’t begin or end with this election,” said Ezra Levin, co-founder of Indivisible, which helps power No Kings.

But drawing attention to injustice or sounding the alarm isn’t enough, said Jamila Raqib, executive director of the non-profit Albert Einstein Institution, which studies nonviolent action.

“People are more engaged than ever before,” said Raqib. “They’re taking action in response to the crises we face, but they’re less often achieving concrete objectives.”

Movements need to adapt tactics to keep up with authoritarian governments, she said. Many governments have learned that brutal crackdowns on nonviolent action tend to backfire, so they rely on “smart repression” – selective arrests, legal harassment, surveillance, disinformation, funding restrictions and job losses – to wait movements out. Governments simply outlast demonstrators who eventually have to return to school and work.

That’s why movements must map the “pillars of support” that any government depends on, including courts, businesses, media and religious institutions, Raqib said. They can then decide which of those pillars to win over, which to weaken and which to replace.

Activists should prepare to organize within workplaces, government agencies, businesses and congregations, where an opponent’s support actually lives, Raqib said. Mutual-aid networks, community defense groups and independent media can sustain a movement through a long fight, too. Preparing for smart repression also means treating digital security as a basic organizing skill, planning for the arrest of key leaders and training successors before a crackdown comes.

Several of those ideas showed up in Minnesota in January. A general strike, sit-ins at corporate headquarters and pressure on employers to speak out weakened Trump’s Operation Metro Surge in ways a single march could not. After federal agents killed two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, tens of thousands of people marched in subzero cold under the banner “No Work, No School, No Shopping”. Trump ended the operation the following month.

The response rested on years of labor, faith and community organizing, said Doran Schrantz, a longtime Minnesota organizer who founded the Organizing Lab. Thousands had trained as legal observers starting in January 2025 through immigrant rights groups like Unidos and the Immigrant Defense Network. Groups like Defend the 612 built an efficient rapid-response system to observe and document ICE agents, and the Ice Out Now coalition linked all groups on the ground, Schrantz said.

To resist, “not everyone has to march in the streets”, Raqib said.

The fight over datacenters has united Americans across party lines, showing what is possible when resistance is local and personal and outlines clear demands.

“There is an authentic local response to these datacenters,” said Schrantz. It was something that people felt they had agency over, she said: “It’s concrete: ‘I can stop that datacenter.’”

That clear target allowed groups that normally agree on little else to work together. The coalitions included environmental groups, farmers, retirees, school parents and “Maga moms”, Schrantz said. The tactics were simple and repeatable: residents packed council and county commission meetings, filed public records requests and gathered signatures for moratoriums and referendums. Across the country, the demands were clear enough to fit on a petition: pause construction until the impacts are studied, make developers pay the full cost of grid upgrades instead of passing it on to taxpayers, end tax breaks for the projects and give communities a vote before anything gets built.

On election day, the steady groundwork paid off. Voters weighed in on 41 datacenter measures in 10 states and sided against the industry in all but a single measure.

Another demand that people have rallied around during Trump 2.0 is “ICE out”. Executing that demand has proven more complicated. Still, organizers have remained steadfast to get justice for people killed by ICE and to pass legislative measures that would get officers off the street.

Three days after the Texas governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, claimed victory on election day, Houston mayor John Whitmire signed an executive order barring police from contacting ICE during vehicle stops when the drivers aren’t arrested, even if they have immigration warrants.

Whitmire’s order mirrors the ordinance activists first advocated for last year. Empowered by Republican governor Greg Abbott soon leaving office, three council members have filed a measure to write it into city law, said Jasmine Khadem González, the co-chair of the Houston Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

“We’ve been going and having meetings with city council members, telling them, teaching them about the local police collaboration with ICE,” said Khadem González.

It took months of pressure – and the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant who had lived in Houston for nearly 35 years, during a traffic stop – before city leaders publicly admitted the collaboration was happening, she said. Organizers canvassed businesses and helped them make safety plans for workplace raids, posting “employees only” and “ICE is not welcome here” signs . They met with faith leaders and held community teach-ins on how Houston police were delivering people to ICE, often through traffic stops. Now, the Harris county district attorney is taking the Salgado Araujo case to a grand jury.

“We can prosecute every single ICE agent who murdered people on our streets,” she said, “and so I’m excited to see some justice come to that family.”

Khadem González’s demands for the new Democratic majorities in the state go well beyond Houston. She wants lawmakers to repeal SB4, the state law that bans sanctuary cities, to end police collaboration with ICE across the entire state of Texas.

“Now that Democrats are in power, we have to show what good governance looks like,” she said.

This drives home the greater point: movements need to keep putting pressure on Democrats, newly elected or otherwise, to get their demands met.

Celebration can’t be the endpoint, Taylor, of Princeton, warned. “Everyone who is connected to an organizing project, to organization politics, must have a Wednesday agenda,” she said, noting the need to keep pushing after Tuesday’s election. “What are we doing now to push the political representatives who solicited our votes?”

Only sustained pressure will move anything, she said, and no elected official is off-limits.

The DSA has a slate of priorities it wants its affiliated candidates to push through when they get into office: an arms embargo on Israel; an end to foreign wars and on sanctions on Cuba, Venezuela and Iran; Medicare for All; abolishing ICE. The organization said its five nationally endorsed candidates, from Melat Kiros in Colorado to Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, will represent the largest bloc of democratic socialist candidates in Congress in the nation’s history.

“This election is a reminder that the electorate is not fixed and that organizing and investment can transform what’s possible,” said Katrina Gamble, a political scientist turned social impact strategist at Sojourn Strategies.

For example, in Mississippi, where Democrats just flipped a Senate seat and elected the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, Black voters made up 3% more of the electorate than they did in 2024; nearly 21% of the state’s voters in this election didn’t vote in 2024.

But Gamble also warns that “these wins are fragile”. The work now is to keep engaging people and ensure electeds deliver on what they promised voters.

“It can’t just be that the blue wave comes and we’ve done our jobs,” Taylor said. “The blue wave is just the beginning.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Houston Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) wants lawmakers to repeal SB4, the state law that bans sanctuary cities. The coalition, made up of dozens of groups and partner organizations, emerged in the middle of 2025 as intentionally leaderless and decentralized.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Marlon Brando cool to Jensen Huang joke: how the black leather jacket became a meme
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Chloe Mac Donnell
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Once the ultimate symbol of Hollywood rebellion, the former Nvidia chief’s signature look is now being mocked as a midlife crisis cliche

For nearly two decades a black leather jacket has been a key part of Jensen Huang’s look. Now it has become a punchline.

As the founder and chief executive of Nvidia resigned this week after reports of multiple affairs, his affinity for a leather jacket, an item of clothing typically associated with a man in midlife crisis mode, has become widely mocked.

The Cut ran a story suggesting a clear line between his penchant for a luxury leather jacket and his extramarital affairs. “Jensen Huang’s leather jackets confessed before he did” read the headline. Writing in the New York Times, the author Anand Giridharadas asked “is an expensive leather jacket on a middle-aged man the new symbol of a honeypot victim?”

Meanwhile, the internet is rife with memes, including an AI-generated image of a leather jacket flying at half mast outside Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX. There was also another fake image, this time of Huang in a studded leather jacket, that many people believed was real.

Elsewhere, there are plenty of divorced dad jokes doing the rounds. “Jensen leather jacket discourse reminds me of the time two years ago when I wore my beloved moto jacket to a party and my good friend said “great jacket, sorry you got divorced”, wrote one user on X.

Similar to Steve Jobs’s black rollneck and jeans or Mark Zuckerberg’s Latin-sloganed T-shirts, Huang’s black leather jacket has become a visual trademark. He likes to pair a leather jacket (always black) with a black T-shirt and black jeans.

In September, in an interview with CBS, Huang explained he had 30 to 40 leather jackets. He credited his wife, Lori Huang, with choosing them. They vary from motorcycle-inspired jackets with a tighter fit and plenty of zips to collarless croc-embossed jackets and clean-cut tailored versions. He has worn them to trade shows, to parties and to give keynote speeches at developer conferences. In 2021 he appeared on the cover of Time magazine in a black leather jacket from Tom Ford. In July, another Tom Ford jacket worn and signed by Huang sold at a charity auction at Sotheby’s for $960,000, more than 10 times its original price.

“The leather jacket is Huang’s way of borrowing some cool,” says Peter Bevan, a writer and stylist. Bevan points to the leather jacket’s “rebel history” as part of the appeal.

Marlon Brando led his biker gang wearing an asymmetric zip jacket in 1953’s The Wild One; James Dean zipped around off-screen in a similar style while following his Berlin era; David Bowie wore a black leather jacket on the cover of his Heroes album in 1977. Patrick Swayze in Dirty Dancing, John Travolta in Grease and Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones also made a leather jacket an enduring symbol of Hollywood style.

By choosing a black leather jacket rather than a corporate suit, it suggests that Huang is unconventional, a leader rather than a conformist.

“It’s basically Huang saying: ‘I’m not a regular billionaire boss, I’m a cool billionaire boss’,” Bevan says.

When asked by CBS in October why he wore a leather jacket day in, and day out, Huang said it helped him avoid decision fatigue. “Black is the absence of choice,” he said. “It’s nice to wear the same thing every day because no surprises. For everybody else, they probably have to make three or four decisions. I took that off my plate. The moment I wake up, I could be thinking about important things.”

It’s a look that has not gone unnoticed by his fellow tech giants. In 2024, Zuckerberg posted a photo of Huang swapping jackets. Later in the year, at a Siggraph conference in Colorado, Zuckerberg presented him with another jacket. “It’s black and leather and shearling,” Zuckerberg said describing the coat. “It’s a vibe. I mean, get this guy a chain.” In return, Huang gave him the black leather jacket he was wearing, explaining that Lori had bought it for him to commemorate that year’s conference. “This is worth more because it’s used,” Zuckerberg said as he slipped it on.

after newsletter promotion

Bevan says that while Huang’s choice of designer jackets are “the kind that most fashion insiders would rate”, a box-fresh leather jacket “feels try hard” and as a result, “tips into midlife crisis territory fast”.

The biggest mistake men make when buying a leather jacket Bevan says is choosing one that is “too shiny, too new and too tight.”

The list of those who get it wrong is long – including Jeremy Clarkson, who likes to wear a black leather jacket with bootcut jeans.

For Bevan, the men who have mastered a leather jacket are those who “look like they’ve owned it for ever”.

Lenny Kravitz who, like Huang, is in his 60s, prefers a battered leather jacket. John Malkovich, who is a decade older, likes a brown oversized leather jacket, while the rapper A$AP Rocky, who is in his 30s, has made a bomber leather jacket his style staple.

For those without youth or “rock-star DNA” on their side, Bevan suggests ditching a leather jacket for a cotton Harrington style that he describes as “having the same cool but none of the leather-clad midlife baggage”.

As for Huang, he may have to reconsider his default wardrobe for next week. While he managed to pull off a leather jacket at tech conferences, it may be harder to pull off at a congressional testimony.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: UK’s biggest insurer hit by rise in subsidence claims after record hot summer
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Increase reported by Aviva after Hastings Direct said claims were up 140% in August and Axa said it had been a ‘surge year’

The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis.

Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows.

It follows two record hot summers in the UK; August this year was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world. Drier summers cause the ground under houses to shrink, which undermines a property’s foundations. It then expands in wetter winters, which can further damage homes.

Aviva experienced a “peak subsidence period” between July and September, with claims continuing into October, its chief executive, Amanda Blanc, told Bloomberg in an interview on Friday. Aviva would not provide any further detail on the scale of the increase in claims.

Blanc said homeowners could reduce the risk of subsidence by keeping a close eye on drains, pipes and gutters, and fixing any leaks that could affect the ground under homes. “It’s about managing trees and plumbing,” she said.

A number of fellow insurers have also experienced a rise in claims in recent months. Hastings Direct said it received record subsidence claims in August, up 140% compared with a year earlier. Axa, one of the UK’s biggest home insurers, has said it has been a “surge year” for subsidence.

The value of claims have also hit a record high. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a high of £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers. Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year.

Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, according to the British Geological Survey, which estimates that up to 11% of UK homes – more than 4.2m houses – could be at risk by 2070. Older properties with shallow foundations and those built on clay-rich soil are facing the biggest threat, with areas including London, Essex, Kent and areas around Oxford among the most vulnerable.

But despite the rise in subsidence claims, Blanc said Aviva was in rude health, having reported a 19% rise in general insurance premiums to £11.8bn in the third quarter.

“Aviva is in great shape,” she said in a statement released alongside the company’s financial results. “Our performance has been excellent in the first nine months of 2026, demonstrating once again the benefits of scale across our diversified business. We continue to deliver strong, profitable growth, particularly in the capital-light areas of general insurance and wealth.”
