https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: A global Microsoft 365 outage has hit millions – what happened and when will it be fixed?
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Josh Taylor, Mark Sweney and Aisha Down
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Problem affects businesses, government agencies and even tech firm’s own employees

Microsoft scrambles to fix global outage affecting Teams and Outlook

Microsoft outage – live updates

Tell us: have you been affected by the Microsoft outage?

Millions of people were unable to access their emails, Teams chats or meetings on Thursday night and Friday morning after a Microsoft 365 outage brought down services across the globe.

The incident affected businesses, government agencies and even Microsoft employees. Businesses, government agencies and vital services around the world have all reported issues, from the US House of Representatives to an Australian spy agency and airlines in India. In the UK, police services, ambulances and hospitals reported issues with email services and online form submissions.

The outage has affected millions but is also patchy; some users are still able to access some aspects of Microsoft’s service, and service is resuming in some parts of the world faster than others. Microsoft and independent internet researchers have reported incremental improvements in service during Friday.

Experts say that the outage has laid bare the dangerous dependence of countries such as the UK on a few US tech companies.

What happened and why – and what does it say about online services in 2026?

At about 6pm GMT on Thursday, the outage website Down Detector showed an increase in users reporting issues with Microsoft 365, the suite of cloud software that includes Teams, Word Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook.

The outage has lasted for more than 19 hours at the time of reporting, with Microsoft working to bring services back.

By Friday morning, Microsoft had narrowed down most of the problems to Microsoft Exchange, the email service behind Outlook. Teams meetings and chats had returned to service.

By midday UK time, Microsoft said there was “encouraging recovery progress in Europe”, improvements in North America and Asia Pacific, and Japan was “stable”.

So far, the problem appears to be a configuration update that resulted in some servers becoming overloaded and taken offline, Microsoft indicated.

When the company attempted to apply a fix, servers that had come back online again became unresponsive when traffic began returning to them.

As some servers went down, traffic was funnelled on to the remaining servers, causing traffic problems for those remaining online.

To understand what was bringing down the servers, the company began limiting the traffic that could reach affected servers in specific locations, and on some servers rolled back to an earlier software configuration to see if it fixed the problem.

An outage that runs for so long for a service as critical as Microsoft 365 is unusual. The company has not said why it has lasted this long, but a clue might be in its updates: as servers returned to being unresponsive after being fixed, engineers had to work through alternative solutions, taking longer than expected to get servers back up and running.

In the UK, police services, the Bank of England, vital health services – such as ambulances and the NHS – and schools have been affected. In Australia, many people who rely on Microsoft 365 were reporting being unable to access their inboxes, including in councils, state and federal government agencies, courts and schools.

Across Europe, government agencies in the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany and France reported issues, with a French municipality instructing residents to phone instead in case of need.

In Japan, government services and private companies were widely affected, with some employees saying they were switching back to sending faxes. The shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and railway stations, while Taisho, a big pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

In the US, a court in Maine, the US House of Representatives, and cities in Colorado and Florida are among those reporting issues.

The UK government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on government services, adding that there were “robust contingency plans in place to minimise disruption”.

The NHS, which in England has a five-year deal to use Microsoft 365, said a range of services had been disrupted.

The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies said fund management services had been disrupted.

In financial markets, some portfolio managers have been unable to use email to authenticate their access to some trading platforms.

Given the recent OpenAI agent attack on Medicare, and the spate of cyber-attacks in Europe bringing down internet-connected fridges, some quickly guessed the global outage might be a new attack on critical infrastructure. Microsoft quickly hosed down the idea, saying there was no indication it was a cyber-attack. There is also no indication presently that it came from AI, although AI tools have been fingered as a source of other high-profile recent outages.

UK politicians and experts have said that outages such as this underscore the world’s reliance on cloud services provided by a few massive US tech companies – Amazon, Google and Microsoft. This reliance has been a growing source of unease through each high profile outage. It has grown more pronounced because of the hostility of the Trump administration towards Europe, which has prompted some governments to consider alternatives to its software.

As the name Microsoft 365 implies, the world has quickly become accustomed to online services being available 24/7. Given software is no longer solely downloaded to individual PCs but is also stored on a server owned by a company, outages such as this will happen. Most of the time they are brief but sometimes they are not.

Outages in recent years from telecommunications providers, from the PHP incident to the Crowdstrike incident, show just how varied the sources and causes of a massive outage can be.

There are many different pieces of the puzzle keeping services online – but the effect of one of those services going down is much greater than it ever has been.

An associate professor at Australia’s RMIT University, Mark Gregory, said it was important for organisations to thoroughly test updates before rolling them out to the live network. That is in addition to the extra security testing companies must carry out to ensure their services are protected from threat actors armed with AI tools that can find vulnerabilities quicker than ever before.

Gregory said companies that relied on services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options such as Google’s Gmail in the event of an outage.

Others have suggested the free and open-source Office alternative LibreOffice.
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.summary: Microsoft 365 outage has lasted 19 hours and has been reported by experts. Microsoft has narrowed down most of the problems to Microsoft Exchange. Outages in recent years have been caused by software being stored on a server owned by a company.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Johana Bhuiyan
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia, the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years.

Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.

China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns.

Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive.

A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements.

Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd. At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg.

Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry.

Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.

Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered. The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband, Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times. The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba.

The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips.

Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office.

The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after.

The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reportes that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier.

The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this.

Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy. Trump still invites Huang on his trip to China, saying in a social media post that he is honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip.

At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary.

In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement.

Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him, and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished.

At a press conference, Trump says the FBI is investigating Jensen Huang but adds that he thinks Huang will be “in good shape”.

“And I asked him about that, and he … said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president says at a press conference. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’”

“I really believe him,” Trump says.

Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects.

The New York Times reports that Huang also allegedly had an affair with the company’s vice-president of healthcare.

At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO.

Huang steps down, ending his 33-year tenure leading the company he co-founded in 1993. The board starts a search for the company’s next CEO while the company’s chief finance officer, Colette Kress, serves as interim CEO.

Meanwhile, shares in the company continue to plummet.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: If you’re wondering what a Reform government might look like, just look at its chaotic record in Wales | Will Hayward
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Will Hayward
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
As the main opposition in the Senedd, the party should be taking politics seriously. Spoiler alert: it’s not

I
n May 2026, Reform UK became the official opposition inside the Welsh Senedd. It was the best result the party had ever received in a national parliament – and since that time it has been a wild ride. Given that its leader, Nigel Farage, claims he expects to one day lead the UK government, how it performs in Wales matters more than just for the people of Cymru; it gives the rest of the UK a sense of what it could expect if Reform does well in the next general election.

Just to give you a taste, here are two developments. In September, Reform’s leader in Wales, Dan Thomas, resigned after he was arrested and released on bail on suspicion of assault and coercive or controlling behaviour. (Thomas said that he had done “nothing wrong” but resigned to avoid becoming a “distraction”.) It has also lost one of its members in a bizarre defection from the rightwing Reform (which has been sceptical about even the existence of the Welsh parliament) to the leftwing Plaid Cymru (which wants more devolution and ultimately an independent Wales).

To mark six months of Reform holding more than a third of seats in the Senedd, two colleagues and I decided to undertake a deep-dive investigation into the party in Wales, which we published on my newsletter. We spoke to several Senedd members and staffers who all agreed to speak to us on the condition of anonymity. They took us inside Reform WhatsApp groups and revealed a world of paranoia, leader worship and an obsession with “disruption”, rather than a party of serious opposition or government in waiting. Our findings flew in the face of the Reform UK Wales deputy leader’s claim in September to be the “most effective, professional and united opposition the Senedd has ever seen”.

Our investigation found that out of 100 Senedd committee meetings held between 8 May and 21 October, there have been 31 times when at least one Reform MS has been absent. For context, here are the figures for the other parties: Plaid, eight times; Labour, nine; the Tories, nine; the Greens, six; and the Lib Dems, one. Committee meetings are a key way for MSs to hold the Welsh government to account, and the number of Reform MSs to have missed meetings is almost as many as all the other parties’ absent members put together.

But what was most striking was the total aversion to scrutiny and the dictatorial way that the party’s MSs are managed. According to the members we spoke to, there is a “banned list” of organisations and journalists whom Reform Senedd members are forbidden to talk to. These include Oxfam and the Books Trust charity. I must now admit a certain amount of professional pride that I too have managed to make the list.

For example, back in the summer I sat inside the Senedd canteen eating lunch. The number of MSs increased by more than 50% at the last election, so space is at a bit of a premium. There was a seat free on my table and a Reform MS came up with his tray and asked: “Do you mind if I join you?”

He sat down and we ate our food in silence. After a minute he looked up at me, paused, and said: “You’re Will Hayward.”

He then looked panicked, like a man who had just clicked on a link in a phishing email. “I am not allowed to be here or talk to you,” he said.

I said: “You are a grown man and an elected representative on £80,000 a year, you are allowed to talk to who you want.” He stood up, glanced around and squeezed his way on to a packed table elsewhere.

But is it surprising that they behave like this? Sources told us that there is a large picture of Farage on the back of the Reform group’s office door in the Senedd. More significantly, the power of the leader is captured by the fact that the Welsh Reform constitution states that he must give permission for the Reform group to work with any other party.

However, the fear of journalists within the party pales into insignificance compared with how paranoid the Reform higher-ups are about Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain. As one MS told us: “Everything the party is doing is about countering Restore. HQ are obsessed.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

This drive to defend their right flank has manifested itself inside the Welsh parliament in just the past week, when the Reform MS Joe Martin made claims that white British people were being “replaced” and would be a minority in the UK by 2063 (the definition of “white British” used by Reform is so narrow it would exclude King Charles).

The speaker in the Senedd told Martin that he would not be called to speak again until he apologised for his comments. This prompted one of the most surreal press conferences I have ever attended where Reform’s leader in Wales, Helen Jenner, said that the rest of the party would be boycotting the Senedd in solidarity.

And if you really want to know what a large Reform group could be like in Westminster, look no further than the WhatsApp message Jenner posted when talking about attending a group in the Senedd established to develop policy to tackle the issues affecting women in parliament and wider society.

“Sort of makes me feel like we should go along and disrupt,” she wrote.

By the way, I put everything we found out in our investigation to Reform UK to comment. They said, “These claims are blatantly outlandish, ridiculous and unsubstantiated.” We sought clarification on which of the 13 different points we put to them they were referring to. Despite repeated attempts, they did not reply.

At a time when Wales is crying out for a credible and serious opposition, we are left with disruption for disruption’s sake. To quote Succession’s Logan Roy, these “are not serious people”.

Will Hayward is a Guardian columnist. He publishes a regular newsletter on Welsh politics
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: Reform UK became official opposition inside the Welsh Senedd in May 2026. It was the best result the party had ever received in a national parliament. Since that time it has been a wild ride.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Portugal vs Denmark: UEFA Nations League – predictions, how to watch, teams
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Manasi Pathak
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Who: Portugal vs Denmark
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A4
Where: Braga Municipal Stadium, Braga, Portugal
When: Saturday, November 14, at 7:45pm (19:45 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream

A new chapter in Portuguese football starts on Saturday, as the national team moves on from the departure of their record scorer and longstanding captain, Cristiano Ronaldo.

Ronaldo ended his 23-year association with the Selecao last week, announcing his retirement in a lengthy video on social media, weeks after a public rift with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.

The 41-year-old, a polarising football icon who wore the much-adored No 7 shirt for his country, said it was now time to “pass it on to the future”.

Playing their first game without their biggest star, Portugal face Denmark in Saturday’s home fixture, having already confirmed their spot in the quarterfinals.

With three goals each, forwards Goncalo Ramos and Joao Felix have orchestrated Portugal’s attacking play in Ronaldo’s absence, while Denmark’s charge has been led by Rasmus Hojlund, who has netted three of his team’s seven goals so far.

Two-time holders Portugal will be confirmed as group winners if they avoid defeat against Denmark, who are second in the standings.

The Danes have a bit more complicated path to secure their spot in the last eight on Saturday – they need to win against Portugal and hope that neighbours Norway do not beat third-placed Wales in a clash of the bottom two.

Portugal have a perfect record in the competition, with four wins out of four.

They began their title defence with a 1-0 home win over Wales before beating Norway 2-1, a game in which Ronaldo was an unused substitute.

Shortly afterwards, Ronaldo stormed out of the national camp, but his absence did not trouble the team as they thrashed Denmark 4-2 in another away game before winning 2-1 at home against Norway to reach the quarterfinals.

Denmark have won two games and lost two.

Their campaign started with a 3-2 loss in Norway, but they bounced back with a 2-0 home victory against Wales.

The third match saw them fall 4-2 at home to Portugal before they beat Wales 1-0 away.

Goals from Joao Cancelo, Goncalo Ramos, Vitinha and Felix gave Portugal a 4-2 win over Denmark on October 1.

Mikkel Damsgaard and Rasmus Hojlund scored for the hosts in that game at Copenhagen.

Opta’s supercomputer has given Portugal a 59.4 percent probability of victory, while Denmark’s odds stand at 19.4 percent.

There is a 21.2 percent chance the game ends in a draw.

(Last five matches, latest game first)

Cancelo and Francisco Conceicao are suspended, while Rafael Leao, Nuno Mendes and Nuno Tavares are out with injuries.

Probable Portugal XI: Diogo Costa; Diogo Dalot, Ruben Dias, Renato Veiga, Flavio Nazinho; Ruben Neves, Vitinha, Bruno Fernandes; Joao Felix, Goncalo Ramos

Denmark will be without Patrick Dorgu, and they will have to be cautious with six players one booking away from suspension.

Probable Denmark XI: Mads Hermansen; Rasmus Kristensen, Joachim Andersen, Oliver Provstgaard, Joakim Maehle; Morten Hjulmand, Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg; Gustav Isaksen, Mikkel Damsgaard, Mohamed Daramy; Rasmus Hojlund

You can find your regional broadcaster on UEFA’s official broadcaster listing.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Can Netanyahu launch a strike on Iran before he leaves?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Stephen Quillen
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Despite losing its majority in last month’s parliamentary elections, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is still in power in a caretaker capacity.

That will continue until a new governing majority is formed – a process that could take months as Israel’s opposition struggles to form a coalition.

And while he may be politically weakened, Netanyahu is reported to be weighing new military action against Iran, despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and the politicians vying to replace him.

But does Netanyahu’s caretaker government actually have the authority to send Israel back to war, and how would such a move be received at home?

Officially, Israel’s caretaker government has the same authority as a regular government. Article 30 of the country’s Basic Law states that an interim government continues to carry out the same duties until a new one takes its place.

However, Israel’s Supreme Court has previously ruled that an outgoing government must avoid irreversible policy moves unless they are urgent – a principle known as the “duty of restraint”.

In practice, Netanyahu can still initiate military action with the approval of his caretaker government, which he could present as “urgent and in the national interest”, Neve Gordon, a professor of international law at Queen Mary University, London, and the author of “Israel’s Occupation”, told Al Jazeera.

Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, told the Reuters news agency that security issues generally are “the clearest exception” to a caretaker government’s duty of restraint.

“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset [parliament] ⁠⁠convenes and before its committees are formed,” said Asher.

“A caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran,” he added.

Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera the government’s caretaker status raises the “political burden of proof”.

“Netanyahu would be asking the country to accept the consequences of a decision that could outlast his government,” he said.

On Wednesday, Israeli media reported that the security cabinet chaired by Netanyahu had ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran.

“The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” public broadcaster KAN reported.

That followed reports that Netanyahu has been repeatedly calling US President Donald Trump to press for a new military campaign against Iran, conversations that on at least one occasion became heated, according to Israel’s Ynet News site.

On Thursday, a US military official was quoted by KAN as saying that Washington had told Israel to get ready for a potential new round of confrontation. But the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) later dismissed the reports, telling Al Jazeera they were “mere speculation”.

According to Israel’s Channel 13, the Israeli military establishment sees no urgent need to attack Iran. It said that assessment had been presented to Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next government, during a briefing on Wednesday.

The opposition has demanded that Netanyahu avoid any military action unless it is critical.

Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, a member of the opposition bloc, said the prime minister’s caretaker government must not “make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full agreement of all security officials”.

Eisenkot echoed this sentiment in a letter to Netanyahu on Wednesday, saying that deploying Israeli forces “without a direct and immediate threat that cannot wait could have devastating consequences for Israeli democracy and public trust in the institutions of government”.

The Israeli premier responded by insisting the government makes all decisions based only on “security considerations”.

There would be serious divisions.

“Obviously, those who voted for Netanyahu and parties from his coalition would be in favour, while most of those who supported the so-called change bloc would be upset at Netanyahu’s use of the war to try to remain in power and block their electoral success,” said Gordon.

But ultimately, he said, most people who voted against Netanyahu’s bloc would “rally around the flag” if he resumes hostilities.

Jabareen agreed that Israelis would likely rally if a new war breaks out and missiles are incoming. But he said that “tells you very little about whether they think Netanyahu was right to start another round [of conflict]”.

“And the harder test comes when reservists are called up again, families are back in shelters and the government has to explain what the campaign can achieve that the previous one didn’t,” he added.

Jabareen said the debate in Israel over any new confrontation on Iran would likely centre on “why now?”

“If the case for urgency is weak, especially if Washington is opposed and senior Israeli commanders have reservations, the decision could be seen as an attempt to change the political agenda while Eisenkot is trying to form a government,” he said.

Beyond domestic considerations, an obstacle to Netanyahu restarting attacks may be the position of Israel’s main ally, the US, which has said it is doubling down on its economic pressure campaign against Iran rather than pursuing more large-scale military action.

“Netanyahu’s problem … is not the Israeli public, but what seems to be a loss of appetite in the US,” said Gordon.

Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, said it would be easier for Netanyahu to pull off a new military campaign if it is undertaken jointly with the US.

But “the more openly Netanyahu provokes Iran, and the less support he receives from Trump, the harder it will be for him to get away with it – and for the Israeli public to accept it”, Persson told Al Jazeera.

Yes. And in one case, the government was led by Netanyahu himself.

In May 2021, weeks after his party lost seats in legislative elections and while negotiations for a new government were under way, the prime minister launched an 11-day war in Gaza that killed at least 260 people in the Palestinian enclave. Thirteen people also died in Israel.

While that conflict temporarily stalled efforts to replace Netanyahu, a new government, led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, was formed the following month, ending a 12-year run as prime minister.

Former Israeli prime ministers Ehud Olmert and Yair Lapid also ordered military action in Gaza while serving in a caretaker capacity. The 2008 war directed by Olmert was by far the most deadly, killing about 1,400 Palestinians.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Supreme Court has previously ruled that an outgoing government must avoid irreversible policy moves. Anders Persson says it would be easier for Netanyahu to pull off a new military campaign if it is undertaken jointly with the US.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Ukraine claims record 3,000 Russian casualties in one day as war drags on
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: John T Psaropoulos
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
As Ukraine, Russia and the United States engaged in their first peace talks since February this week, the front lines continued to deteriorate for Moscow as its casualties rose to a possible new record without any significant territorial gains.

Ukraine’s military said it had caused more than 26,000 Russian casualties – meaning those killed and seriously wounded – in the first 10 days of November, suggesting this month’s figure could mark a new record topping October’s 54,400.

On November 9, Ukraine also claimed a new daily record of 2,980 Russian soldiers killed or wounded. That marked the fourth reported daily record this year.

Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty claims by either side.

This cluster of new casualty records in the autumn, accompanied by a lack of any significant territorial gains by Russia, suggested that Moscow was not coming any closer to its goal of seizing the last remaining quarter of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region this year.

A group of pro-Ukrainian hackers from Belarus said they had accessed records of the Russian state statistical service, Rosstat, and discovered an official tally of 450,000 Russian fatalities for the entire full-scale invasion, since 2022.

Independent assessments indicate that Russia has seized a net 117sq km (45sq miles) this year, a poor showing for its pains.

Yet, Russia was as defiant as ever at peace talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11.

Presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, told Vesti television after the talks concluded that he would be satisfied “only when we win and sign a peace agreement on our terms”.

Russia has demanded territory Ukraine is not willing to surrender, and said NATO needs to pull out of all the former Soviet bloc countries which joined it since 1997.

Medinsky called for “a new, comprehensive, and just security system in Europe,” because the one put in place after World War II “is functioning very poorly, and, in fact, the entire system is sick. In Ukraine, a festering wound has simply burst.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saw it differently.

“When the Russians now talk about a security architecture for themselves … What they really want is to freely interfere in the affairs of other countries, and to use force whenever they want, and to make sure that no one can support liberty inside Russia,” he told the Danish parliament, the Folketing, on the day the talks concluded.

Although US negotiators agreed to table the subject of a European security architecture at Abu Dhabi, the three European powers present – Germany, France and the United Kingdom – did not, and they were excluded from the proceedings.

“We did not communicate with them. We don’t really understand what their status is here,” Medinsky said.

Europe agrees with Ukraine that such a discussion puts the cart before the horse.

“The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is a complex and potentially dangerous one,” Zelenskyy said on the eve of the talks. “First, we must discuss how to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. Second, what the security infrastructure will be for Ukraine.”

Ukraine has asked for an ironclad guarantee of military intervention if it is attacked again, as offered in NATO’s Article 5.

Instead, Zelenskyy said, the Trump administration offered “something similar to NATO”.

Russian President Vladimir Putin received the US negotiating team in Saint Petersburg after talks in Abu Dhabi, and repeated the Russian position that the presence of European peacekeepers in a post-war Ukraine would also be “absolutely unacceptable”.

Zelenskyy attributed Russia’s absolutism to its inaccurate understanding of realities on the ground.

“Putin lives in a different reality,” he told journalists in Copenhagen on November 11. “When I received the second report from our negotiating group after the meetings in Abu Dhabi, they told me that the Russians believe and claim that they have already occupied half of the [part of the] Donbas region which is actually under our control. These were military officers, Russian intelligence.”

Russia’s defence ministry has claimed to have seized 3,600sq km (1,400sq miles) of Ukraine this year, and Putin has repeated the claim.

Still, Abu Dhabi did produce some results.

Russia and Ukraine said there would be a new POW exchange of at least 1,000 or possibly 1,500 prisoners on each side. And Zelenskyy said de-escalation steps were discussed.

In the run-up to Abu Dhabi, Russia pounded Ukraine’s cities.

“For 10 days and nights, Ukraine faced constant alarms,” said its General Staff. During that period, Russia launched 3,519 drones, and Ukraine managed to intercept 3,068 of them, they said, including 83 percent of the jet-powered drones, which now comprise roughly half of the swarm.

On the night of November 7, Russia unleashed 36 ballistic missiles into Ukraine, including some reportedly manufactured by North Korea, striking energy infrastructure.

Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi has asked European allies to provide generators and battery packs for homes, as well as mobile shelters and buses to keep urban transport moving during blackouts.

On November 12, Ukraine reported it was experiencing renewed restrictions on its use of the Starlink satellite service, which it needs to coordinate interceptors to incoming Russian drones.

“This directly impacts our ability to intercept Russian kamikaze drones,” said Zelenskyy. “Due to the speed limitations, we simply cannot intercept them in time.”

This came as Ukraine continued its own strikes inside Russia, targeting ballistic missile launchers and factories as a forward defence.

On November 7, a fire burned almost a hectare of storage space next to an Almaz factory in Rostov, which makes communications equipment. It was unclear whether Ukraine caused it. On the same day, Ukraine fired Neptune missiles into the Proton-Electrotex conglomerate which makes parts for Kormoran cruise and Iskander ballistic missiles, and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers.

On November 9, Ukraine struck the Morozov plant near St Petersburg, which makes solid rocket fuel for ballistic missiles, and the Redkino plant in Tver, which makes chemical products used in missiles.

On November 10, Ukraine struck the 123rd Aircraft Repair Plant in Novgorod, which services Russia’s increasingly rare A-50 early warning and targeting aircraft.

On November 11, Ukraine struck the Naro-Forminsk cruiser, which launches Kalibr and Onyx cruise missiles.

“We are acting asymmetrically,” Ukrainian defence minister Yevhenii Khmara told his Dutch counterpart. Ukraine had struck a total of 12 ballistic missile launch sites inside Russia, he said without specifying the timeframe, and said the strikes on factories were reducing Russian production capacity.

Zelenskyy renewed his call for German Taurus missiles with which to strike Russian launchers.

Ukraine also struck a series of refineries during the past week, including the Afipsky, Saratov, Kirishi, Ust-Luga and Omsk refineries. Russian military reporters said three Russian helicopters had been downed by friendly fire during attempts to defend the Ust-Luga refinery.

Since the end of October, its General Staff said, Ukraine had struck Russia’s five biggest refineries.

Sources told Reuters that Ukraine has destroyed at least 30 percent of Russia’s refining capacity.

The purpose of refinery strikes is to diminish Russian export revenue for petroleum products and to disrupt its economy. Those goals appeared to be working last week, as Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported Moscow projecting a $63bn-$67bn deficit for 2026, double its intended figure, and Russian media reported staff layoffs at the parliament, or Duma, and the Russian Federation Council.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Yashraj Sharma
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old cofounder and face of the chipmaking company which has become the backbone of the modern AI industry, has shaken the US’s Silicon Valley.

Nvidia, valued at nearly $4 trillion, is a critical pillar of the US economy where AI and tech companies make up some 40 percent of stock market valuations. The furore over Huang’s extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the company’s market value, dragging down the S&P 500 and Nasdaq.

While CFO Colette Kress has temporarily stepped into the top job at Nvidia, the search for cofounder Huang’s successor continues.

What happens next at one of the world’s most valuable companies will have repercussions far beyond Silicon Valley. So, what’s next for Nvidia?

On October 29, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies suspected a Chinese businesswoman and executive associated with Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed International, Alice Huang, had been tapped by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information from Nvidia’s Huang.

The newspaper reported that the two were involved in an intimate relationship, later confirmed by the cofounder of the company in an internal memo. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote in an internal memo to Nvidia staff.

The business links go beyond just the affair, however, fuelling further concerns. Megaspeed purchased more than $4.8bn of Nvidia chips over roughly two years. Separately, The Information reported that Alice Huang facilitated at least $7.5bn in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, raising even more questions about skirting US export controls.

Then, on Wednesday, the NYT reported a second alleged affair between Jensen Huang and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him.

The next day, Huang was forced out of the company and off its board.

Hours later, Reuters reported that Huang had allegedly been involved in a third affair with another Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter.

In simple terms, if Nvidia sneezes, the AI industry and modern computing catch a cold.

Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for advanced AI chips which are used to train frontier AI models, giving it an extraordinary degree of influence over the global AI industry and the infrastructure powering it.

Observers say the company holds the keys to next-generation computing. Its customers include tech giants such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, which rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate their AI data centres.

That’s also why Washington has restricted Nvidia from selling chips to China.

Nvidia’s Huang has spent years lobbying in Washington against such restrictions, arguing that restricting sales would surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors.

That puts him at odds with US lawmakers who view access to Nvidia’s advanced chips as a national security risk, particularly given their potential military applications.

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing has “always opposed the abuse of export control measures”, as pressure gains momentum yet again in Washington. Beijing has rejected allegations that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as “baseless”.

In China, investors have been selling shares in Chinese AI-linked companies over worries that recent developments at Nvidia could deepen the technological divide between Beijing and Washington.

On Friday, shares in Z.AI, one of China’s top AI model developers, tumbled more than 10 percent in Hong Kong while shares in rival MiniMax hit record lows.

A Reuters review identified more than $3bn in Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia’s restricted processors – despite the American chipmaker claiming that US export controls effectively shut it out of the AI data-centre market in the world’s second-biggest economy.

The examination shows projects stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, and underscores how deeply Nvidia’s technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.

Nvidia shares rose 1.8 percent in premarket trading on Friday after losing around 11 percent of their value this week up to Thursday, when Huang exited the company he built.

The company is on course for its longest streak of weekly losses since October 2012.

US President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, next week in Shenzhen at the APEC leaders’ summit.

Similarly, shares in Nvidia’s customers, such as South Korea’s Naver, fell more than 5 percent. Nasdaq futures and S&P 500 futures fell 0.4 percent and 0.15 percent, respectively.

“Jensen has obviously been a singular force in many ways so the impact will likely be felt far and wide,” UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri told Reuters.

“The company has become a key source of funds for a host of AI industry participants including neo-clouds, LLM developers, ecosystem partners, and suppliers, and we have always seen Jensen as a key driving force for this effort,” Arcuri said.

“Even if a new leader ultimately maintains a similar approach, there is likely to be some ‘pause’ in the company’s willingness and ability to continue pursuing these deals in the near term,” he added.

From washing dishes at a Denny’s to building a $4 trillion technology giant, Huang has led Nvidia for nearly 33 years – and made one of Silicon Valley’s defining entrepreneurial stories.

But the “cult-style” leaders at Silicon Valley – including Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk – also reflect the concentration of market power that tech companies enjoy. Technology stocks now account for nearly 40 percent of the S&P 500’s total market value.

That is likely to rise when AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI also go public.

And in the absence of a clear succession plan, things could go awry, sending jitters among investors – a concern which Nvidia highlighted itself in its annual review for this year.

Under the risk factors dealing with its dependence on key personnel, Nvidia’s report noted that the company is “highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team”.

“Failure to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions involving executives and key employees could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success,” it said.

Nvidia’s board has begun searching for a permanent successor to Huang, tapping CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Meanwhile, President Trump, who has defended Huang as a “genius”, shared his two cents, too. He suggested former Apple chief executive Tim Cook could take over Nvidia. “A Legend replaces a Legend,” Trump wrote.

Nvidia has said it will consider candidates from both within and outside the company.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/uber-c.author: Zack Whittaker
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/uber-c.text:
Uber is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California, the ride-hail giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data.

The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider.

TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets.

Online productivity startup Notion confirmed its data was also stolen in the Fireworks hack.

“The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch, deferring our questions to Fireworks.

Uber did not say how many customers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident. A spokesperson for Fireworks did not respond to questions about the incident.

According to data breach notices seen by TechCrunch, the stolen data includes driver’s licenses of 2,567 individuals in Massachusetts, 3,430 people across South Carolina, and 1,873 residents of Rhode Island. A filing with Illinois showed that some state residents had their driver’s license information stolen, but that the number of affected people was pending. Uber also notified drivers who live in California, but did not say how many had their information stolen.

The number is expected to rise as more data breach notifications roll in.

Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs.

No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft.

This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/eleven.title: ElevenLabs’ new app combines meeting note-taking and dictation for teams
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/eleven.author: Ivan Mehta
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/eleven.text:
In the last few months, Fireflies, Wispr Flow, and Granola have all released competing capabilities in the dictation and meeting note-taking space. The newest entrant in that category is voice AI giant ElevenLabs, which this week released an experimental app called ElevenAI that combines meeting note-taking, dictation, and agent integration.

Launched during its 11/11 Summit in New York, ElevenAI is still in preview, and you have to sign up for early access instead of just downloading an app. ElevenLabs, valued at $22 billion, is very much positioning this as a product that lives within a team as compared to a productivity tool for an individual.

ElevenAI packs all the features typically found in other apps in the category. It can take meeting notes across your meetings and notify other participants that the conversation is being recorded. Users can query data across meetings and get live assistance during a chat, helping them recall a key detail from older conversations. ElevenLabs also allows companies to integrate ElevenAgent and take follow-up actions such as writing a draft email based on meeting notes.

Plus, there’s a dictation feature, which lets users convert speech to cleaned-up text in any app with support for over 90 languages. The company said that the app is capable of understanding industry-specific terms across dictation and meeting transcription.

ElevenAI allows the company to use its own model as a showcase and also utilize its agent platforms for better context funneling. The startup’s positioning might not be to directly compete in the productivity market, but rather to give enterprise teams an option to not buy licenses to a notetaker and use its solution instead. All meeting-related tools are rushing to become central knowledge hubs for companies while aiming to automate knowledge extraction and follow-up actions

In the last week, the company also launched its v3 series of Scribe speech-to-text models with live transcription capabilities and the ability for companies to fine-tune models using their own data, a tool to pick the right language model based on use case, and a routine creator that automates tasks based on the transcript.

Meta has ticked off academics on all sides of the social media and mental health debate.

Three years ago, Meta apparently considered a plan to turn public opinion against one of its most influential opponents, Jonathan Haidt. But since the proposal was revealed in court filings last month, it’s backfired. In fact, if there’s one thing Anxious Generation author Haidt and his critics can agree on, it’s being mad at Meta.

Recent court filings in California revealed that Meta employees had discussed in 2023 a “Whisper strategy” to “turn academics against Haidt,” who would soon publish a bestselling book arguing that platforms like Meta’s were hurting kids. Haidt had spent years popularizing his theory that social media and smartphones are to blame for the decline in teens’ mental health, including in his 2018 book The Coddling of the American Mind and before Congress in 2022. To counter it, Meta apparently considered a “Below-the-line campaign,” including one idea to “Get Gellman to write a take-down piece” — possibly a reference to Columbia University statistics and political science professor Andrew Gelman, who’d previously publicly critiqued Haidt, though the spelling differs.

Duet is a decent helper, if a little jumpy at times.

Normally, the products I test don’t offer to help me write up my experience with them. Duet is different.

Claude Duet is Anthropic’s AI agent for consumers, the latest attempt by an AI company to try to convince us that agents can be useful for people who don’t write code. It’s been an interesting couple of months: Instinct gave us an impressive text-based assistant, Meta offered us its cute little guy, Muse, to help us buy things, and OpenAI gave us the more work-oriented Dots. Claude Duet is even more focused on work than those. It’s also more consumer-friendly than Claude Cowork, which was more consumer-friendly than Claude Code — the coding agent that kicked off a whole hype cycle earlier this year. I’ve been testing it over the past week as I navigate a busy travel and work schedule. At turns it has been truly useful, kind of a nag, and very eager to write about itself.

Duet is still a “research preview” according to Anthropic, and access is limited to Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers in the US, with a waitlist to join. It’s not here to order you burritos, either; it’s for “professionals and small business owners” and is meant to use its judgment about what needs your attention most.

Like Meta’s Muse, Duet has its own app. (If you’re keeping score at home, yes, it has been updated to fully support the iPhone Duo).

https://arstechnica.com/culture/2026/11/.title: Screenless GPS: Slate Auto says, "Remember the road atlas"
https://arstechnica.com/culture/2026/11/.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
https://arstechnica.com/culture/2026/11/.text:
What’s more fitting than a spiral-bound map for a bare-bones two-door pickup?

Whether it’s nostalgia or a sense that technology has gotten a bit too pervasive, there’s no denying that Slate Auto appears to be tuned into the particular moment. The startup has a simple pitch: an affordable electric truck with just the basics, leaving owners to DIY and BYOD for everything else, all for a sub-$25,000 starting price.

Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. But there is a solution to getting lost, and it’s called “Screenless GPS.” Even though we don’t have a Slate truck to test it with, the OEM sent us a unit to review.

That’s right, it’s a good old spiral-bound road atlas! “We believe you should use the devices you know and love,” Slate says, and it reckons that maps worked just fine for past generations, so they should still work now.

The Rand McNally 2027 Road Atlas isn’t quite as detailed as the maps being made for automotive navigation by companies like HERE. Those are designed to be read by computers, not people, with rich data on not just places of interest but also live traffic, road conditions, and the accuracy required for assisted and autonomous driving systems. Any OTA updates to the atlas must be applied by Post-it note, and its 154 pages cover the United States, Canada, and Mexico, in full color.

The system is entirely portable, and it’s vehicle-agnostic: you can use it as easily in a Ford, Ferrari, or Fisker as in a Slate. Some might find the idea a little contrived, but having spent some time behind the wheel of the refreshingly simple truck, I think it fits the vibe perfectly. The automaker has added its screenless GPS system to its store for a limited time, and the review copy Slate sent Ars, along with the sticker pack, will be up for grabs in our end-of-year charity drive.

https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.title: Scientists warn 1.5°C climate change threshold could arrive by 2029
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.author: Bob Berwyn, Inside Climate News
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.text:
Climate action has stalled for five years as fossil fuel development keeps growing.

ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.

Climate Action Tracker, a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5 degrees Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicusclimate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.

“This striking change suggests that global warming has accelerated in recent years,” the EU scientists wrote. Even without understanding every aspect of the recent rapid global temperature increase, “It is clear that the ever-growing concentrations of greenhouse gases emitted by human activity in the atmosphere remain the main driver of this trend.”

The current level of warming has already triggered deadly and destructive floods, wildfires and catastrophic glacier collapses, said Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who is attending the U.N. “Conferences of the Parties” climate talks, for the first time since 2021.

“The climate crisis is a matter of life and death,” she said. “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”

Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, said governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.

“Our message is a stark one,” Heck said. “Collective government action on climate change has stalled for the fifth consecutive year.” Efforts to speed up the shift away from fossil fuels have been negated by new oil and gas drilling projects and governments that are “delaying, weakening or rolling back their climate policies.”

Even under the most optimistic scenario, assuming full implementation of existing policies and promises, global temperatures would rise 3.4 degrees Fahrenheit above preindustrial levels by 2100, an increase climate scientists consider extremely dangerous.

While there has been progress on developing renewable energy sources, the “brutal truth is that these positive developments have not yet added up to bend the curve fast enough,” said Niklas Höhne, a researcher with The New Climate Institute. Developing new oil and gas projects is a bit like discovering your food is burning and then turning up the stove instead of turning it off, he added.

Getting into the specifics of the current negotiations at COP31 surrounding global renewable goals, he noted that conference co-hosts Turkey and Australia have so far opposed including the word “clean” in connection with electrification targets.

“It’s very hard to understand, and the only explanation I can think of is their interest in fossil fuels,” Höhne said.

Australia is one of the world’s biggest coal exporters, and Turkey is a major coal consumer, with its power sector still highly dependent on the most climate-damaging fossil fuel. Even as they host this year’s climate conference, neither country has offered any specific plans to transition away from fossil fuels.

Bill Hare, the CEO of Climate Analytics, called out wealthy, developed countries for their lack of leadership on climate action, noting that European Union Commission President Ursula von der Leyen failed to mention anything about transitioning away from fossil fuels during her speech this week at COP31.

“Governments … at this COP have a stark choice,” Hare said. If they continue supporting fossil fuels, “it would consign humanity and our ecosystems to insurmountable economic damage and irretrievable loss.”

Bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

European Union's Copernicusclimate change service: Global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris agreement. Climate Analytics: Governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/fbi-sa.title: FBI Says North Korean Hackers Stole Over $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/fbi-sa.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/fbi-sa.text:
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has established that threat actors tied to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK aka North Korea) have stolen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency as part of a social engineering scheme codenamed FaceStealer in the last 18 months.

As part of a coordinated set of actions announced by the U.S. government, the cloud-based infrastructure used to pull off the "hard-to-detect" campaign has been seized.

In tandem, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen by the North Korea-linked TraderTraitor actors following the hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. The plundered digital assets are used to fund Pyongyang's illicit weapons program, the DoJ added.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman in a statement.

"North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months."

According to the Justice Department, FaceStealer relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and deepfakes to facilitate cryptocurrency theft. Some aspects of the activity dovetail with a campaign documented by Kaspersky under the name GhostCall in October 2025.

The activity is linked to a prolific North Korea-linked financially motivated threat cluster tracked as BlueNoroff, which is also known by the cryptonyms APT38, CageyChameleon, CryptoCore, DangerousPassword, Nickel Gladstone, Sapphire Sleet, Stardust Chollima, and UNC1069.

The campaign involves luring targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from stolen accounts belonging to prior victims. Targets who join the meeting have their video stream recorded, while simultaneously serving an authentic, prerecorded webcam video of a previous victim or victims known to the target to build trust.

"The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective," the DoJ said. "Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target's trust."

A few seconds into the meeting, a mock technical error is presented to the victim, claiming that they cannot be heard, and they are provided a link to address the non-existent issue. The fix is a ClickFix-style lure that's designed to install malware on the victim's workstation and steal cryptocurrency, as well as abuse the target's privileges to other computer infrastructure.

In an extensive report shared with The Hacker News in July 2026, JUMPSEC revealed how the social engineering operation is built atop a phishing kit designed to impersonate videoconferencing platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams. The cybersecurity company has characterized FaceStealer as a victim acquisition platform that involves using compromised trusted contacts as a pathway to fuel a self-propagating attack chain via Telegram.

This includes hijacking social media and communications accounts such as Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord for extended periods of time, and then accessing the victim's contact list to target the victim's personal and professional circles.

The entire attack plays out as follows -

Attacks mounted by BlueNoroff are known to specifically single out individuals working in the cryptocurrency and Web3 industries, along with individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.

The goal is to obtain access to the developers' devices and the software repository accounts they control to facilitate software supply chain attacks. Notably, the FaceStealer scheme was put to use in targeting the maintainer of the popular Axios npm package earlier this year to push a trojanized version that delivered a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT).

More than 900 victim webcam video recordings used by the threat actors to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks have been seized by the FBI. The agency said it's "aware of several other attempts by North Korean hackers to target software developers, maintainers, and software libraries with significant download volume."

In a report published in April 2026, Arctic Wolf said the targeted social engineering campaign had targeted over 400 victims across more than 20 countries, with most of them concentrated in the U.S., Singapore, the U.K., Hong Kong, South Korea, and the U.A.E.

"A full 80% of identified targets operate directly in cryptocurrency/blockchain finance (54%) or adjacent finance and investment sectors (26%)," the cybersecurity company noted at the time. "CEOs and founders alone account for 45% of the target set – nearly half. This underscores BlueNoroff's singular operational focus: individuals with access to cryptocurrency assets, wallet infrastructure, exchange platforms, or investment decision-making authority."

The activity has since expanded in scope, with 677 targets identified across 58 countries. More than 80% of the targets are founders and C-suite executives. Besides introducing new lure themes such as a fake Chrome PDF Viewer update, the campaign incorporates generative AI technology from ChatGPT, Google, SpaceXAI Grok, and Wondershare AI Content Generator (AIGC) to supply the attackers with artwork, avatars, and convincing synthetic participant videos.

"Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate," the company added. "Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims' webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person's likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves."

Each new victim offers a pathway to further the attack. The cyclic modus operandi still remains the beating heart of the social engineering operation.

"Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff's efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships," Arctic Wolf said.

It's worth emphasizing here that the FaceStealer campaign is distinct from ClickFake Interview, an iteration of Contagious Interview that also employs ClickFix-style tactics to trigger the execution of malware as part of recruitment-themed campaigns.

Like FaceStealer, this involves the attackers approaching prospective targets by posing as recruiters on platforms like LinkedIn and sharing a "technical assessment" designed to run malware. In a post shared on LinkedIn, Alina Krasavina, an engineering manager at Delivery Hero, detailed how she was targeted in October 2026 by two fake recruiters on the same day, 13 minutes apart.

"The first one sent a 'technical assessment': a Next.js project of 113 files. At the end of next.config.js, after 204 spaces, there was a backdoor," Krasavina said. "The second one didn't send any ZIP. On a video call, a 'Member of Technical Staff' asked me to share my whole screen, download a repo, and run it. When I said no, he told me it was 'a requirement to continue.' After the call, I wrote to the recruiter and asked for another interview format. About a minute later she blocked me."

"The two attacks were built in opposite ways. The first one put the effort into the code and almost none into the recruiter. The second one put it into the people, and I never even saw its code."

According to a joint cybersecurity advisory published by cybersecurity and intelligence agencies from Japan, the U.S., Australia, and Germany in late September 2026, the long-running campaign is estimated to have compromised at least 30,000 devices located in 100 countries.

The attacks experiment with multiple delivery methods to convince victims to run malicious code -

Last month, Sophos disclosed that an employee's corporate macOS device had been compromised in mid-September 2026 after they cloned a public code repository presented as a job interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code.

"The repository contained a weaponized VS Code workspace settings file that replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile," the cybersecurity company said. "When a terminal opened in the workspace, the modified profile silently downloaded and ran a multi-stage payload."

The payload in question is BeaverTail, a JavaScript loader that's used to deliver a Python backdoor referred to as InvisibleFerret. Both malware families are attributed to Contagious Interview.

Sophos said the malware ran in memory on the device for about 26 hours, right from its execution on September 14, 2026, until it was rebooted a day later. The incident did not affect any of its products or services, or customer data or their systems, it added.

What's more, recent research from JFrog has uncovered that the threat actors linked to the campaign have even set up a decoy company named AccuraSoftHire, complete with a careers site, client testimonials, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards, and verified recruiters in an attempt to lend credibility and ultimately deceive candidates into running malware through a rigged take-home test and a video verification step.

"Our research shows these lures are built to pass the checks people rely on: a professional website, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards and recruiters with LinkedIn's verified badge," Guy Korolevski, senior security researcher at JFrog Security Research, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"Developers and other employees with system access can't be expected to catch that on their own, so employers need to set the rules. Interview assignments with downloads should only ever run in a disposable virtual machine, never on a work laptop. Security teams should also warn employees about downloading unknown files, even from a source they think they can trust. Developers can also check when a recruiter’s profile was created and whether the company's location is the same on every page."

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/trezor.title: Trezor Confirms Hidden Implants in CryptoBilis-Sold Wallets That Can Steal Recovery Phrases
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/trezor.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/trezor.text:
Three Trezor Safe 5 wallets bought from the reseller CryptoBilis contain an implant, an extra circuit board that can copy their recovery phrases, hardware wallet maker Trezor said yesterday.

The implant reads the phrase from the wallet's screen and sends it over the mobile network to a server controlled by the attackers. The company examined one of the wallets in its lab, identified the other two from photos their owners sent, and has had no reports of lost funds.

A firmware update released earlier this week, version 2.13.1, stops the implants found so far from capturing anything on wallets that run it, the company said, but “the update can’t protect a wallet backup that was captured before it.”

The company has not changed its advice to anyone who bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March, including from the reseller's stores on Tokopedia and Shopee:

Version 2.13.1 was released for the Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3 and Model T, according to the company's firmware changelog. The company will not publish technical details that could help attackers or put customers at risk, it said in an investigation update.

Its engineers extracted and analyzed the implant's firmware from the first wallet it reported. The implant sits between the Safe 5's main board and its screen and changes nothing on the wallet itself, including its firmware and Secure Element, the company found.

The implant copies the recovery phrase when the wallet shows it during backup creation, and when someone types it in to restore an existing wallet to the device. It also copies a passphrase if one appears on the screen. It encrypts the data before sending it, and if it cannot connect, it keeps the data and tries again until it succeeds.

The company first warned of a suspected implant on October 30, two days after a buyer reported it and before its lab had seen the wallet.

CryptoBilis served as an official reseller for the company's wallets in Southeast Asia until October 9, when the company removed it. That was the day Ledger, another hardware wallet maker, began investigating losses of funds among the reseller's customers.

Ledger later confirmed an unauthorized implant in a wallet the reseller sold. Attackers had fitted genuine Ledger devices with hidden components designed to capture the recovery phrase during setup, then drained wallets in a single coordinated operation, Ledger said in an incident statement.

Trezor says the implants in its wallets work the same way as those found in Ledger devices, adapted to the Safe 5's display. It has not said who fitted the implants or where in the supply chain that happened.

The three wallets were bought between August 20 and September 23. So far the company has found implants only in Safe 5 wallets sold by the reseller, and none in wallets from its other resellers or in its other models.

After the October reports, it asked people who bought a Trezor from the reseller to get in touch, and 48 have done so. It is checking their wallets in its lab or from photos of the insides, and has not said how many it has checked so far.

The company says none of the three owners has lost funds. Trezor wallets are self-custodial, so it cannot see anyone's balance.

The company says it has cut its reseller network by about 80%, dropping trustworthy partners that posed no immediate threat but did not fit its stricter new rules. It first announced the reduction on October 13 in a post on X, more than two weeks before the first report of an implant in one of its own wallets.

In a partner letter that day, it told the dropped resellers that they would get no new stock, could sell what they had until January 1, 2027, and would then be removed from its list of authorized sellers.

It is still investigating. It will post an update if it confirms an implant outside the reseller's wallets or the Safe 5, receives a report of lost funds linked to the implants, or releases new protections.
