https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.title: As Test Takers Turn to AI for Answers, Exam Security Must Catch Up
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.author: Arielle Waldman
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.text:
Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

It's hard to detect whether someone is using artificial intelligence (AI) to cheat on IT certification exams, but new tools and processes are emerging to boost trust.

Certifications play a critical role in keeping up with the latest industry metamorphosis, but artificial intelligence (AI) is now muddying the verification process.

From Meta Glasses to AI browsers and deepfakes, exam administrators face a growing list of risks to monitor — and organizations need to know that the person they hired can actually do what their certification says they can.

Score legitimacy has become harder to assess as test takers use AI to fill in the blanks. As a result, the industry is shifting toward more in-person testing and stricter fraud-detection protocols to keep certifications credible.

Certifications range from entry-level cloud and cybersecurity knowledge and cover Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services updates. In some industries, like government, banking, and financial services, certified IT departments are required to stay current on compliance regulations.

Cheating is a risk that has existed for as long as testing has. But AI has significantly changed the testing game for IT certification, explains Marielle Carlos, data forensics scientist at Caveon.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Traditional threats, like harvesting pre-knowledge, plagiarism, or collusion proxy testing, have evolved as people use AI as an unauthorized aid, she says, and it has become an incredibly challenging problem.

However, the problem is still in its infancy stage — so much so that Caveon added a new category to its testing security threats taxonomy: unknown.

"It makes it hard to know if your exam is measuring actual competence or if it's measuring someone's ability to use AI to answer the question," Carlos tells Dark Reading. "It really challenges the usefulness of that exam."

Carlos spends her day interpreting test results to help programs decide whether anomalies warrant any additional attention or professional review. Over the past two years, she has seen how AI has changed the way certification programs monitor metrics to assess cheating. Previously, it may have been enough to look at speed and score separately to flag a case for review. Now attention has shifted, as administrators take numerous variables into account since AI can combine multiple cheating tactics.

During her research, Carlos noted a "huge boom of people" who are testing fast and receiving high scores. No concrete data exists that says it's all due to AI, but there is enough organizational interest and concern over that trend's growth that Carlos says she and her team will look at it more.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

But uncertainty hasn't stopped other organizations from taking action. Widespread irregular exam results and verified cheating attempts discovered during ISC2's online proctoring pilots led the nonprofit to require in-person testing, says Casey Marks, chief operating officer at ISC2. The consortium also implemented "the most stringent security protocols available to analyze each result and detect irregularities," including biometric and identity verification.

The testing environment mirrors the most stringent conditions used by licensed professions, such as doctors, to provide the highest security available in the industry, Marks says. Regarding AI use, the fact that ISC2 is exclusively a test-center based for all exams ensures no access to outside resources or technology during exam administration, he adds.

"The candidate, the employer, and every other professional holding that credential depend on the credibility of the process," Marks tells Dark Reading.

Regardless of AI introducing new risks, certifications remain one of the most universal ways for employers to validate a candidate's necessary knowledge and skills when making hiring or promotion decisions, Marks adds.

Carlos agrees but urges programs to have conversations around protecting score validity across the entire process.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

"That includes secure exam design, control during administration, analysis of results, and a clear process for responding to your security concerns," Carlos adds.

A layered approach is crucial because while there are "tools to indicate possible AI use, it's hard to pinpoint exactly." Carlos points to research by Sarah Toton, director of data forensics at Caveon, as an example. Toton conducted an experiment comparing AI and human test taking based on test results and response patterns.

"She has seen some distinct differences in response timing. When someone uses AI, they're often six to 48 times faster compared to an individual test taker," she explains. "That said, AI can get some things wrong sometimes, particularly the questions that involve some realm of human judgment."

In an ironic twist, the same technology people use to cheat on exams is also becoming one of the most in-demand certifications employers rely on to validate real skills.

Many certifications, like ISC2's Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), have and continue to evolve to address how AI is impacting security best practices, Marks says. That's in addition to new AI-specific security certifications that are also entering the market.

For example, the Computing Technology Industry Association launched SecAI+ to help organizations secure, govern, and responsibly integrate AI into their cybersecurity operations.

"As certifications evolve, especially with AI now playing a key role in so many facets of our work, the value of certifications for employers is increasing," Marks adds.

Features Writer, Dark Reading

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: This AI ‘mechanic’ can peer inside the black box of other neural networks
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Elizabeth Gibney
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Some AI models behave like mechanics — fixing issues in other models that they neither designed nor fully understand. Credit: Mint Images/Getty

Researchers have used an artificial-intelligence model to read and tinker with the internal workings of another AI network — offering a new way to peek into the ‘black box’ of AI.

Computer scientists usually improve models by training them in tiny increments or by building them from scratch. A team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge has demonstrated how an AI model called GPT-6 Astra can interpret the raw internal values of some other models well enough to predict what different parts of the systems do. It can then edit the models to make improvements — including boosting their mathematical abilities. The authors reported their findings in a preprint1 on 2 November.

ChatGPT is a black box: how AI research can break it open

Frontier AI models are “showing early sparks” of an ability to treat neural networks like files that they can read, reason about and change, says co-author Rikiya Takehi, a machine-learning researcher at MIT.

The results do not mean that Astra, developed by OpenAI in San Francisco, California, can explain or understand how a given AI network works. But the findings suggest that general-purpose AI models — such as ChatGPT or Claude — might be able to modify a network in useful ways, like a mechanic who can identify and fix issues in an engine that they neither designed nor fully understand.

Researchers already try to interpret how different components of a network create its outputs. The preprint shows that it is possible to automate some of these ‘interpretability’ methods, says Fazl Barez, an AI-safety researcher at the University of Oxford, UK.

Researchers hope that better understanding models in this way will help to create safer AI systems, although Barez cautions that this assumption is “largely untested”.

It remains unclear if Astra is going beyond applying information and techniques learned in its training. Barez says he would be surprised if Astra is able to read and interpret models in ways that go beyond existing human abilities.

Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

Still, if developed further, such ability to reprogram models might be an asset in developing AI for science, says Marinka Zitnik, a computer scientist and bioinformatician at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. For example, it could help to spot errors in a model ahead of real-world testing, she says.

Frontier AI systems are based on massive neural networks — brain-inspired architectures in which layers of processing units, or neurons, are linked by billions of ‘weights’, values that represent the strength of connections inside a model. The strength of each weight is slowly nudged during training to make the model better at, for example, predicting a protein structure or the next word in a sentence.

The complex way in which a model’s features link to its outputs means they are often described as black boxes. Interpretability researchers run experiments to work out, for example, which weights are activated under specific conditions. Researchers have also previously developed custom models that can learn to edit other models2.

Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. https://www.space.com/stargazing/skywatc.author: Jamie Carter
https://www.space.com/stargazing/skywatc.text:
The StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a great model to learn the basics of manual telescope operation and get great views of your chosen targets, thanks to intuitive smartphone integration, but it isn't as easy to set up as you might think.

Superb for finding objects

Sharp, high-contrast 150mm optics

Excellent wide-field views

Difficult and heavy to lift and move

Awkward tabletop design

Basic focuser and eyepieces

Why you can trust Space.com  Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a new telescope.

Finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit.

It was a stunning view, and exactly the kind of experience a beginner needs from a first telescope. There was no frustration and no wondering whether I was looking in the right place. StarSense took me straight there — but, crucially, I moved the telescope myself. I’ve always liked that combination of hand-holding and DIY observing that Celestron’s StarSense tech gives you.

I’m less convinced by the tabletop telescope it’s attached to. Although this $599 RRP (£379) model is significantly smaller than the Celestron StarSense Explorer 8-inch Dobsonian telescope I’ve previously reviewed, it still weighs 25 lbs (11.33 kg). You need to place it on something sturdy before you can use it comfortably. After living with it in my backyard, I’m not convinced the tabletop format is the advantage it initially appears to be.

I’ve used Celestron’s StarSense Explorer system on a variety of telescopes and have always been impressed by how easy this type of smartphone navigation is to use. The technology works just as well here and, for me, it remains one of the best ways of making a traditional optical telescope accessible to a complete beginner.

This isn’t a computerized GoTo telescope. There are no motors to slew across the sky automatically and no tracking system to keep an object centered. Instead, a smartphone sits in a dock attached to the telescope, and its camera looks at the sky via a small mirror. Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app analyzes the reflections of the stars it sees, works out exactly where the telescope is pointing and tells you which direction to push it to reach the object you want to observe.

My iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted perfectly into the dock, and the initial alignment process was identical to what I’d used before. Once that was done, I used StarSense to find the Pleiades (M45), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Double Cluster in Perseus and Saturn. It worked every time, with the target appearing in the eyepiece when the app told me I had reached it.

I can find all of those objects without an app, but that’s not really the point. Beginners often struggle to translate a star chart or an astronomy app into actual telescope movements. StarSense gives you confidence that you’re heading in the right direction while still requiring you to operate it physically.

That makes it a useful way to learn the night sky. After repeatedly pushing the telescope from one familiar object to another, you begin to understand how everything fits together. That’s very different from pressing a button and watching a GoTo or smart telescope move itself, and it’s why I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, even on a relatively wide-field telescope like this one.

The StarSense system may be the headline feature, but the reason to buy any Dobsonian is aperture. This one uses a 150mm (5.9-inch) parabolic primary mirror with a 750mm focal length and a relatively fast f/5 focal ratio. That combination gives it fairly low-power, wide-field views that are particularly well suited to large star clusters.

The Pleiades was one of my favorite views. At 30x through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, the telescope gave me a sharp field of stars and a particularly good view of what I call “Carter’s Whip” — the curving line of stars running through the cluster. I saw little obvious softness towards the edges, and focusing was straightforward.

The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) was a different proposition. From my light-polluted backyard, I could see Andromeda’s bright core, but not its outskirts or its satellite galaxies. That’s largely a consequence of observing a galaxy from a city, not a criticism of a 150mm telescope, but it’s a useful reminder of what visual astronomy is actually like. Don’t expect the colorful, detailed views of galaxies and nebulas you see in astrophotos, such as the stacked images a smart telescope can give you.

Saturn was more rewarding, but I would have liked more magnification when the seeing was this good. Add a Barlow lens if planets are a priority — it can double the magnification of any eyepiece you use it with.

Overall, I was impressed by the telescope’s optics. The views were sharp and contrast-y, and there’s enough aperture here to make a serious start in visual astronomy. However, the two supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces are decidedly entry-level — and obvious candidates for upgrading in the medium term.

The focuser is a weak point. It’s a fairly basic 1.25-inch rack-and-pinion design, but I noticed some wobble and vibration while using it. That’s a shame because the focuser is one of the parts of a telescope you constantly interact with, and something smoother and more precise would make the entire instrument feel more accomplished.

The tabletop design isn’t necessarily as convenient as it sounds. I expected this scope to feel considerably more convenient than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Dobsonian. The base has built-in grab handles, but the assembled telescope's shape and weight make it awkward to lift onto a table — I certainly wouldn’t recommend it to anyone with a bad back. You could move the optical tube and base separately, but that starts to cancel out the convenience of owning a relatively compact tabletop telescope.

You also need to choose your table carefully. It has to be sturdy enough not to introduce vibrations, but not so large that you have to stretch across it to reach the eyepiece as the telescope points to different parts of the sky. I found myself bending and stretching into some awkward positions.

Once it’s in position, the Dobsonian mount worked well. The balance was good, and I didn't need to adjust the altitude tension, while the movements offered a useful mix of resistance and fluidity as I followed StarSense around the sky. At 75x, however, keeping Saturn centered was more difficult than I expected. It was easy to over-nudge the telescope, then correct in the opposite direction.

Celestron sells an optional tripod for the telescope, and after using the tabletop base, I can see why that might be attractive. However, I’d personally rather put the money towards a larger Dobsonian whose base is designed to sit directly on the ground.

This scope doesn’t arrive in one piece. Assembly took about 90 minutes, and it required all manner of screws and screwdrivers. The main problem was getting the screws into the holes in the Dobsonian base, which took so much effort that I ended up with a blister on my hand. That’s not what I expected from a telescope aimed at beginners, especially when almost everything about using it has been designed to make things easy.

Once built, things improved considerably. My review sample arrived well collimated, so I didn’t have to adjust the mirror alignment. The tube rings, phone dock and general construction were all good enough for a telescope at this price, and nothing about the telescope felt particularly fragile. Once the telescope is outside, on a suitable table and aligned, it’s an impressively straightforward instrument to use.

The more I used the StarSense Explorer 150mm Dobsonian, the more I wondered who really benefits from the tabletop format. It’s certainly smaller than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Explorer Dobsonian, but it’s still a substantial object to store, and I didn’t feel any more inclined to grab it for a quick observing session.

Going bigger offers an optical advantage. An 8-inch/203mm aperture collects about 83% more light than a 150mm aperture, which matters when you’re observing faint deep-sky objects. The 8-inch StarSense also had a much nicer 2-inch Crayford focuser, and generally felt like a telescope with a little more room to grow into.

Dobsonians are the perfect companion to smart telescopes. The latter have completely changed what beginners can photograph from their backyards, particularly under light pollution. They can reveal galaxies and nebulas that are extremely difficult or impossible to see visually. I use them all the time. But they are no substitute for navigating to and actually seeing objects in the night sky with your own eyes.

The two approaches don’t need to compete. A smart telescope has to be pointed and then left alone for an hour or four to stack images. That time could be spent pushing something like the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian around the sky, and actually looking through an eyepiece at the same objects. One shows you far more than your eyes can detect, but the other lets you see the photons yourself — and make a human connection with the night sky.

At $599 RRP (£379), the StarSense Explorer 150mm sits in an interesting part of the beginner telescope market. There are smaller tabletop Dobsonians like the Celestron Moon Mission 100mm without smartphone navigation, but I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, particularly for a first-time telescope owner.

If you mainly want to observe planets and the moon, a refractor like the Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ also makes sense. However, if you want to go relatively large, I do recommend the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian — with an important qualification. Its optics are good, StarSense is superb, and it’s an excellent way for a beginner to learn their way around the night sky, but I’m not convinced that 150mm is the sweet spot for this particular design. It’s too big to feel genuinely convenient as a tabletop telescope, yet not big enough to deliver the full advantages of a larger Dobsonian.

If space is tight, this is a very capable first telescope. If you have room for the 8-inch StarSense Explorer, I’d go bigger.

He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: Astronaut Suni Williams rides through NYC as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade | Space photo of the day for Nov. 13, 2026
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Chelsea Gohd
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
Navy veteran Suni Williams leads in a longstanding astronaut tradition.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

New Yorkers got a space-y surprise on Wednesday (Nov. 11): Retired NASA astronaut and U.S. Navy Captain Sunita "Suni" Williams rolled down 5th Avenue in the back of a classic convertible wrapped in patriotic decals as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade.

On Wednesday, New York City's 107th annual Veterans Day Parade made its way through Manhattan to the cheers and respectful nods of thousands of onlookers.

The parade is an annual tradition on the holiday, which honors veterans of the U.S. armed forces. As part of the parade, veterans, active-duty soldiers, firefighters, marching bands, youth cadets and more march through the city and honor those who have served and sacrificed in the U.S. military.

This year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join New Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event.

Williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025. She spent 608 days in space during her astronaut career, the second-most by an American astronaut behind Peggy Whitson, who racked up 695.

Williams also had an extensive career in the U.S. Navy. She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017.

During this time, Williams supported relief efforts following Hurricane Andrew, trained within the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and gained a wealth of further experience flying as a military pilot.

Williams is part of a longstanding tradition of astronauts serving in the U.S. military. From test pilots to naval officers and more, there's a strong link between the U.S. armed forces and NASA's astronaut program.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music

https://www.space.com/news/live/spacex-s.author: Tariq Malik
https://www.space.com/news/live/spacex-s.text:
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX is counting down to make history with the launch of its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13, with liftoff scheduled for 5:45 p.m. EDT (2245 GMT) at Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land both Starship Ship and Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever full recovery of an orbital rocket and spacecraft, if successful.

Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which will also deliver 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.

Flight 15 livestream | SpaceX | Starship | Starship V3 explained

Good morning, Space Fans, it is launch day for SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 and the world's largest rocket is now hours away from attempting its first double landing test flight. Liftoff remains on target for today, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) from SpaceX's Starbase launch site in South Texas. You'll be able to watch the Starship Flight 15 launch on this page, as well as on Space.com's homepage and our YouTube channel VideoFromSpace. Our live webcast will begin at 5:15 p.m. EST (2215 GMT).

Last night, SpaceX rolled the Ship 42 upper stage out to the Starship launch pad and stacked it atop its Super Heavy booster. The Ship's number was accompanied by a fun sci-fi message - "Don't Panic" - in a nod to the Hitchhiker's Guide To The Galaxy books by Douglas Adams. Elon Musk's Tesla bore the same message when SpaceX launched it into space on the first Falcon Heavy mission.

Space.com's Josh Dinner is on site at Starbase and will be providing updates as possible from Starbase, which we'll share here as they're received.

Here's an update from Josh from the launch pad:

A post shared by Space.com (@spacedotcom)

SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 is the 15th test flight of Starship, the world's largest and most powerful rocket. SpaceX has designed the rocket to be fully reusable, and has landed its massive Super Heavy first stage booster several times.

Flight 15 is SpaceX's first attempt to land both the Super Heavy booster and its Ship upper stage by returning them to their launch pad and catching them in the pad's metal "Chopstick" arms. The landings will be about 22 hours apart, with Super Heavy landing minutes after launch and the Ship upper stage returning to Starbase on Saturday afternoon.

We'll be updating this page throughout the day with news from Josh, SpaceX and Starbase for this unprecedented 22.5-hour test flight. Here's our full timeline for SpaceX Starship Flight 15.

SpaceX is now less than 24 hours from the planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 mission, with liftoff on track for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). The test flight will attempt land both the Starship Super Heavy Booster 22 and its Ship 42 upper stage.

Because the mission will last 22.5 hours, Starship will likely be visible in the night sky to stargazers hoping to see the giant spacecraft in orbit. Space.com's Skywatching Writer Anthony Wood has a great guide on how to see Starship in the night sky.

"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station, but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," our skywatching columnist Joe Rao told Wood.

Check out the full story:
SpaceX's Starship megarocket will launch to orbit on Nov. 13. Will you be able to spot it in the night sky?

STARBASE, Texas — We are one day until launch of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15, and Space.com is onsite here in Texas prepping cameras and coverage.

Liftoff is currently targeted for tomorrow (Nov. 13), during a 75-minute window opening at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT).

This flight could be a historic one for SpaceX and the space industry. For the first time, SpaceX will attempt to catch both stages of its massive Starship rocket — Super Heavy just minutes after launch, and the Ship upper stage roughly 22 hours later, following several orbits around Earth.

I'll be covering the action from here in Texas, so stay tuned to Space.com for updates as we count down to liftoff!

Happy Wednesday, Space Fans. We are now T-2 days away from SpaceX's planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 test mission, so I wanted to take a moment to give you a run down on what to expect.

Today, you can read my full guide to SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch here, which goes over what time and where to watch the launch online. Liftoff is on track for Friday, Nov. 13, at 4:45 p.m. CST, which is 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). But it ALSO (and this is new) includes what time to tune in a day later for the planned Starship upper stage (Ship) landing and catch by the metal "Chopstick" arms of its landing pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility in South Teas.

If you're wondering how the rocket's assembly is going, our Spaceflight Editor Mike Wall has this update on the Starship Flight 15 Super Heavy booster going through final catch tests yesterday. Flight 15 will mark the first time SpaceX will attempt to land and catch both the Super Heavy booster (which it has done several times) and the Ship from orbit.

If successful, it will be the first full recovery of an entire orbital rocket from space.

Hello, Space Fans, and welcome to our coverage of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight, the first ever to attempt twin landings of the Starship Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage.

SpaceX has officially set the launch date for Flight 15 for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EDT (2145 GMT). That puts launch just about 3 days away and Space.com will provide live coverage of the potentially historic flight, the first full recovery of an orbital rocket.

Space.com Spaceflight Writer Josh Dinner will be reporting live from near SpaceX's Starbase , Texas site for the launch, with myself (Tariq Malik), Spaceflight and Tech Editor Mike Wall and other team members tracking the flight remotely for you here. SpaceX has already test-fired the engines on its Starship Flight 15 vehicles.

Today, SpaceX moved Super Heavy Booster 22, the first stage for Flight 15, to the launch pad for vehicle stacking. Here are some photos of that move:

Super Heavy moved to the launch pad at Starbase. Booster 22 is the first Super Heavy V3 booster planned to return to the launch site for catch and was used for final catch testing upon arrival, including a suspended squeeze test at catch height https://t.co/iYTX1e6DEHNovember 10, 2026

We'll be updating this page regularly in the days ahead counting down to SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch (and landings). So check back for updates each day.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/orga.author: Tarvez Tucker
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/orga.text:
I watched Hailey’s chest without pause, searching for the slightest movement, a tiny intake of breath, any sign of life.

Hailey (not her real name) was 22 years old, a college student who had suffered a catastrophic brain injury in a traffic accident. She lay before me in our neuroscience intensive care unit, her heart beating steadily, her skin warm, a ventilator breathing for her. I was performing an apnea test, the final step in determining whether she had died by neurological criteria. It’s part of my job as a neurointensivist at Oregon Health & Science University. The longest 10 minutes of my life are those I spend watching for any small chest movement as we remove a patient from a breathing machine. I can’t let my eyes wander. I can’t blink. Hailey never took a breath; she was brain dead.

Her parents sat vigil for two days, waiting for her sister to arrive from overseas so she could say goodbye. When they finally accepted that their daughter had died, the organ donation team took over.

Takeda reported that its narcolepsy pill, the first treatment to target the underlying cause ​of the rare sleep disorder, is now available in the U.S. after ‌the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration removed the final regulatory hurdle for its rollout, Reuters notes. The DEA has classified Orzeyful as a Schedule IV controlled substance, a category considered to have a ​low potential for abuse and dependence. The U.S. list price has been ⁠set at $16,500 per 60-tablet bottle, across all strengths. About ⁠120,000 people in the U.S. have the disorder.

Pfizer will no longer sell its hormone replacement therapy Premarin, which has been available as a vaginal cream and three strengths of oral ​tablets, in Canada following an internal review, Reuters reports. Premarin vaginal cream, used to treat ‌symptoms of menopause, has been in shortage in Canada since June and no further batches will be supplied. Demand for hormone replacement therapy has been ​rising, particularly in the U.S., where prescriptions have increased after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration removed long-standing safety warnings a year ago. Some other hormone therapy ⁠products to treat menopause symptoms are also facing supply constraints in Canada.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/usps.author: Chelsea Cirruzzo
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/usps.text:
WASHINGTON — Two senators are introducing a bill Friday to rein in conflicts of interest on an influential federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services.

The bill, from Sens. Angus King (I-Maine) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), follows reports that a number of members picked by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. could profit from the decisions they make on the panel, known as the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. It would codify standards for membership on the panel and for avoiding conflicts of interest.

The bill comes after STAT reported that members of the panel hold stock in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and that two of them own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care. The New York Times reported on the financial investments as well. Federal officials granted all members blanket waivers, allowing them to remain on the panel, though they could still be required to recuse themselves from particular matters. The panel has not met in more than a year.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Entresto may reduce AF recurrence after ablation in some patients
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — Compared with valsartan, sacubitril/valsartan was linked to reduced risk for atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence after catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation, according to the results of the SUPERIOR trial.

For the SUPERIOR trial, presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, Wei Zhang, MD, PhD, cardiologist in the department of cardiovascular medicine at the Shanghai Institute of Hypertension at Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, and colleagues enrolled 320 patients aged 55 to 79 years with AF and high blood pressure who underwent catheter ablation for AF (mean age, 68 years; 58.8% men; mean clinic BP, 135.6 mm Hg systolic/84.4 mm Hg diastolic). After the procedure, patients were randomly assigned to valsartan or sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto, Novartis).

“Hypertension contributes to atrial remodeling and increases risk for atrial fibrillation recurrence after catheter ablation,” Zhang said during a press conference. “Sacubitril/valsartan provides dual angiotensin receptor blockade and neprilysin inhibition, with potential cardiovascular effects beyond those of conventional [angiotensin receptor blocker] therapy. The hypothesis is that sacubitril/valsartan reduces documented atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence compared with valsartan in patients with hypertension undergoing atrial fibrillation catheter ablation.”

Using ECGs and 24-hour heart monitors, each patient’s heart rhythm was checked at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months after the procedure, and patients were encouraged to use a handheld ECG at least twice a week and whenever they felt symptoms of an arrhythmia, Zhang said during the press conference, noting that two physicians confirmed which episodes lasted more than 30 seconds.

The primary outcome of ECG-detected atrial tachyarrhythmia (AF, atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia) between 91 and 365 days after the procedure occurred more often in the valsartan group compared with the sacubitril/valsartan group, Zhang said.

In the sacubitril/valsartan group, the primary outcome occurred in 18% of patients during 138.5 person-years of follow-up, for an incidence rate of 20.9 events per 100 person-years of follow-up, and in the valsartan group, the primary outcome occurred in 28.3% of patients over 124.6 person-years of follow-up, for an incidence rate of 36.1 events per 100 person-years (HR = 0.58; 95% CI, 0.36-0.9; log-rank P = .03), he said.

“The results suggest that medication choice after atrial fibrillation ablation may influence the likelihood of [AF] recurrence” in this patient population, Zhang said during the press conference. “What remains uncertain is whether the benefit lasts beyond 1 year and whether similar results would occur for other patient populations.”

In a discussion during the press conference, Ratika Parkash, MD, MSc, FRCPC, FHRS, professor of medicine (cardiology) at Dalhousie University and Queen Elizabeth II Health Sciences Center in Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada, said ablation “treats the trigger, and it may halt the progression, but we really need something to target that atrial tissue before it reaches the point of no return, to actually reverse progression once it’s started.”

She said the SMAC-AF study did not find that lowering BP prevented AF recurrence after ablation, but “there were two groups that did benefit: older patients and those who had prior very well-controlled blood pressure coming into the trial. Sacubitril/valsartan ... may actually target the atrial substrate. Neprilysin breaks down natriuretic peptides. When you have more natriuretic peptides floating around, you actually have less atrial stretch, less inflammation, less fibrosis and fewer triggers. There may actually be some benefit for this particular molecule to modify the substrate.”

Zhang W, et al. LBS.04. Innovations to optimize arrhythmia care. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Parkash reports receiving research grants from Abbott and Medtronic. Zhang reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.title: Experts weigh in on liability over AI use in healthcare
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.author: Lucas Laboy
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

ORLANDO — Developers, hospital systems and clinicians may be liable when AI makes a mistake, although the ultimate decision about legal accountability will be determined in court, according to experts at AIMed26.

In a panel discussion, Leo Anthony Celi, MD, MSc, MPH, clinical research director and principal research scientist for the laboratory of computational physiology at Massachusetts Institute of Technology, asked participants about how clinicians can identify an AI mistake and who is liable when a mistake occurs.

“Today, liability lands mostly on the clinician who acted on the output and the hospital that deployed the tool,” Celi told Healio. “Developers are rarely held to account, and I think that is backward. The clinician at the bedside usually had no say in buying the system and could not see how it was trained. Responsibility should be shared with the developer and the health system, in proportion to what each party could have known and controlled.”

During the panel discussion, participants responded to a question about identifying mistakes made by an AI tool.

“One of the problems we have right now with AI and healthcare is that we tend to sort of hold it to this extremely high standard of performance because it’s a computational intervention,” Philip Payne, PhD, chief health AI officer at for BJC Healthcare and Washington University Medicine, said during the discussion. “We need to be careful not to assume that anything short of perfection is a failure of AI.”

Ruhy Patel, MBBS, surgeon and global lead, medical affairs, at Olympus Corp., said during the discussion that holding AI to perfection makes identifying errors more difficult.

“What we should be looking at is where should we improve?” Patel said. “Where can AI deliver upon standardization and consistency? Where does AI augment us?”

Clear guidelines around liability in AI use are also needed, but establishing them in real-world scenarios will be difficult, according to Payne.

“The likely best-case scenario from an ethical and moral standpoint ... [is] we share responsibility around these tools and capabilities,” Payne said. “Then there’s the reality ... that it will almost exclusively be dictated by case law, and we’ll sort of emerge from cases that we’ve not yet seen.”

“What happens is going to happen at the court of law,” Nina Kottler, MD, MS, chief AI officer at Mosaic Clinical Technologies, said during the panel discussion. “The decision's being made there. And frankly, probably everyone gets sued.”

Kottler proposed a different question, looking at who should be accountable when AI makes a mistake.

“The accountability question is one that we can answer and we should answer,” she said. “That is our responsibility as clinicians, and that is not a single person, because AI has a life cycle.”

For clinicians using AI tools, understanding where the data come from is important, according to Celi.

“Ask what data the tool learned from, whether patients like yours were in that data and how it has performed at your own hospital,” Celi told Healio. “The patients most likely to be harmed by an AI error are the ones who were poorly served before AI arrived, because the models learn from records of that care.”

Celi said hospitals should make reporting potential errors “easy and free of blame” to “protect clinical judgment.”

“When an error happens, the patient should be told and the event should go through the same safety review as a medication error,” Celi said. “That review should ask whether the error was a one-off or part of a pattern affecting a particular group of patients. The findings should go back to the developer and to other hospitals using the same tool. Many clinical AI tools fall outside any shared adverse event reporting system; and we need one.”

Patients and community members should also be involved in evaluating AI tools before clinical use, Celi said.

“They are the ones who live with its mistakes,” he said.

Leo Anthony Celi, MD, MSc, MPH, can be reached at nephrology@healio.com.

Celi L, et al. Who is liable when AI gets it wrong? Presented at: AIMed26; Nov. 11-13, 2026; Orlando.

https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.author: Joseph Hostetler
https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.text:
By 6:30 a.m. Eastern Time on November 12, 2026, oil had reached $94.58 per barrel, measured using the Brent benchmark. That’s $1.14 less than it cost yesterday morning and about $31.50 above its price a year earlier.

Check Out Our Daily Rates Reports

Oil prices are inherently unpredictable. While many variables come into play, the basic push and pull of supply and demand is what ultimately matters. In times of heightened concern about recession, war, or other major disruptions, oil can swing suddenly.

Each gallon you pay for at the pump bundles together several costs. Crude oil is one piece, but you also pay for refineries, wholesalers, government taxes, and the price markup set by gas stations.

Because crude oil usually accounts for more than half of the price per gallon, it tends to move the needle the most. Sharp increases in oil almost always show up quickly at the pump. Declines in the price of oil, on the other hand, often translate into slower, more delayed drops in gas prices—the “rockets and feathers” effect.

When an emergency arises, the U.S. has a reserve of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its chief function is to secure energy during disasters like sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also help take the edge off brutal price spikes when supply gets hit.

It’s not a solution for the long haul. It’s more of an immediate safety net to support consumers and keep crucial sectors of the economy running (think key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and the like).

Oil and natural gas are two of the main fuels that keep the world running. A big change in oil prices can end up affecting natural gas. As an example, if oil prices increase, some industries may sub natural gas for certain areas of their operations wherever possible. This can increase demand for natural gas.

The oil market typically tracks two benchmarks:

Between the two, Brent offers a clearer view of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the preferred gauge for tracking historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark over multiple decades, you’ll find oil has been anything but stable. It’s seen sharp rises due to factors like wars and supply cuts, along with steep declines tied to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

Bottom line, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. It’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-cf.title: Nvidia CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO—but the succession question remains
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-cf.author: Sheryl Estrada
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-cf.text:
Good morning. Nvidia is the latest Fortune 500 company to name its CFO interim CEO.

The AI giant appointed CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, replacing Jensen Huang, the company’s co-founder and longtime leader, who resigned Thursday after admitting to an affair that raised national security concerns. Kress will continue serving as finance chief while taking the helm of Nvidia.

Kress is “very much the right interim CEO,” Scott W. Simmons, co-managing partner of executive search firm Crist Kolder Associates, told me. As CFO for 13 years, she knows the company’s story “front and back” and is a highly respected spokesperson with credibility among investors, Simmons said.

Nvidia’s transformation during Kress’s tenure has been extraordinary. Since she joined in 2013, revenue has grown from $4.13 billion in fiscal 2014 to $130.5 billion in fiscal 2025, while its market capitalization has climbed from about $9 billion to nearly $4 trillion today—an increase of roughly 44,000%. Kress ranks No. 49 on the Fortune 2026 Most Powerful Women list.

When I first interviewed Kress in 2022, we discussed her previous roles at Cisco, Microsoft, and Texas Instruments, as well as how Nvidia attracted and retained employees.

“I think my career background did serve me well at Nvidia,” she told me. “When I started at Nvidia, it was the smallest company that I’d ever worked for. It’s gotten quite large, but the focus is on how do you think about the future and make sure we’re ready for it to scale?”

She also discussed her approach to leadership, emphasizing the importance of surrounding herself with “people that you can learn from; people that can help lead.”

The company had no publicly disclosed succession plan. Replacing a founder-CEO is especially challenging, said Simmons, who has worked in executive recruiting for almost 30 years. At Nvidia, whose longtime leader has achieved celebrity status, the task is even more complicated, he said.

“When you’re talking about cutting-edge technology that’s evolving at light speed, you’re trying to find someone who could pick the ball up and carry it down the field, and that’s difficult,” he said.

As interim CEO, Kress must help steer Nvidia through a leadership transition at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. The company plays a crucial role in shaping the technology’s future in the U.S. and beyond.

Whether she could eventually become the company’s permanent leader is another question. Simmons expects Nvidia’s board to look for a technologist to succeed Huang. Meanwhile, Nvidia has named Harvey Jones chair of the board. Jones has worked in technology, including semiconductors, for more than 30 years, Fortune’s Emily Forlini reported.

If the board decides to select a technologist as Huang’s successor, one potential internal contender, Simmons said, is Ian Buck. He joined Nvidia in 2004 and is now vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing and a key architect of its AI business.

For leading analysts’ picks of potential outside successors to Huang, you can read my article here.

Have a good weekend.

Sheryl Estrada
Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com

Fortune 500 Power Moves

Andrew Murray was named CFO of Albertsons (No.57), effective Jan. 17. Murray succeeds Cody Perdue, who has served as interim CFO since Sept. 30 and will continue as SVP of treasury, investor relations and risk management. Murray joins Albertsons from Fonterra Co-operative Group, the world's largest dairy exporter, where he has been group CFO since 2024. He also oversees strategy, M&A, transformation and IT there. Before Fonterra, Murray was CFO of Simplot Australia, led global finance transformation at Toll Group, and held senior finance roles at Mondelez International.

More notable moves this week:

Karen Burgess was named CFO of HubSpot (NYSE: HUBS), a customer relationship management software company, effective Feb. 11. She will succeed Kate Bueker, who will retire and remain in an advisory role through December 2027. Burgess will join HubSpot on Nov. 30 as executive vice president of finance before assuming the CFO role. She joins from Adobe, where she serves as senior vice president and CFO of its Creativity & Productivity business unit. Since joining Adobe in 2002, Burgess has helped support its business model transformation.

Richard Dziadzio was named CFO of AmeriLife Group, a life and health insurance distribution, wealth management and retirement solutions company. Dziadzio succeeds Jim Quinn, who has been CFO since 2017 and moves into the newly created role of president and chief transformation officer. Most recently, Dziadzio was interim CFO of Sterling Check during its acquisition by First Advantage.

Adrian Wood was appointed CFO of BHP Group Limited, a global resources company, effective Feb. 17. He will succeed Vandita Pant, who will step down following the release of BHP’s half-year results on Feb. 16 and remain with the company through March 29. Wood currently serves as VP of projects, minerals Australia. He joined BHP in 2015 and previously served as VP of finance, minerals Australia, and group investor relations officer.

Jacqueline Maxwell was named CFO of Prolink, a Cincinnati-based workforce solutions firm, the company announced. She succeeds Jennifer Prospero, who becomes chief administrative officer. Maxwell has been with Prolink since 2012, most recently as vice president and corporate controller. Before that, she was a controller at Mary L. Shiley, LLC. Prospero joined Prolink as interim CFO in March 2024 and was named CFO in January 2025.

Dev Ahuja was appointed CFO of QXO (NYSE: QXO), a building products distributor, effective in January. He will succeed Ihsan Essaid, who will become vice chairman, an executive role, at the same time. Ahuja brings more than two decades of experience. He joins from aluminum producer Novelis, where he has served as CFO since 2016. Previously, he held CFO roles at Novartis for Alcon North America, Alcon Japan and the company’s South Korean business.

Mike Barna was named CFO of Advantive, a provider of software for specialty manufacturing and distribution businesses. Barna brings more than two decades of finance and operating leadership across software and data businesses, most recently as CFO of Lone Wolf Technologies. He has also held leadership roles at CoreLogic, Information Services Group and The Nielsen Company.

Adrian Bartella was named CFO of Medical Solutions, a health care workforce solutions company. Bartella brings more than 20 years of finance leadership experience, including serving as CFO of Upstream Rehabilitation, The Fresh Market and Hudson Group.

JLL’s 2026 Global Real Estate Investor AI Survey, covering 837 senior decision-makers across 12 countries, finds that AI adoption is widespread but has yet to consistently deliver the investment edge investors seek.

About 83% have scaled or embedded AI in at least one business area, and 80% report benefits, yet 43% still struggle to achieve their goals. While investors prioritize investment outperformance and proprietary analytics in capital deployment, the strongest reported results come from operational improvements in asset and property management.

JLL argues that widely available AI tools and market data can improve productivity but offer limited differentiation. Durable returns will come from applying AI to boost net operating income and building customized workflows that integrate proprietary data, institutional knowledge and relationships to strengthen existing competitive advantages, according to the report.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/paul-rabi.title: Fresh off a $100 million raise, Paul Rabil takes pro lacrosse to the basketball courts of Venice Beach
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/paul-rabi.author: Robert Gray
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/paul-rabi.text:
The Premier Lacrosse League is taking a stripped-down, pick-up version of the sport to the streets of Los Angeles. On Saturday, Nov. 14, the league’s Street Lacrosse Pro Tour makes its first L.A. stop, on the basketball courts at Venice Beach, with a festival vibe and a 5-on-5 format that looks more like street basketball or hockey than the field game.

The goal is to keep growing the sport and build buzz before its long-awaited return at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, about 600 days away. Lacrosse last appeared as a medal sport in 1908. It has appeared since only as a demonstration sport, including at the 1932 L.A. Games and, most recently, in London in 1948.

Men’s and women’s pros will share the court with special guests, including streetball star The Professor and influencer Cameron Elliott Schmidt.

Paul Rabil, widely regarded as one of the best players in the sport’s history, co-founded the PLL and its sister circuit, the Women’s Lacrosse League (WLL). He is president of the parent company; his brother, Mike, is CEO. In June, the league closed a $100 million Series E led by Ares and Joe Tsai, with ESPN taking a minority equity stake.

Rabil, who has previously shared his leadership playbook with Fortune, sat down with us to discuss the Street Lacrosse Pro Tour and the sport’s state in the run-up to the Olympics.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Fortune: Lacrosse has grown quickly this century, well beyond its traditional hotbeds in New England and along the East Coast. Since 2000, the number of NCAA lacrosse programs has more than doubled to 917, while high school participation has increased by more than 353%. In 2024-25, 212,988 high schoolers played on 6,670 boys’ and girls’ teams nationwide.

Team lacrosse has surged. So how does the Street Lacrosse Pro Tour fit into the PLL portfolio?

Rabil: We’ve done a lot with our Assists program, our 501(c)(3). We donate equipment, provide coaching opportunities, and playing opportunities for kids who otherwise don’t have access.

Street Lacrosse came [in 2023] when Rich Kleiman and Kevin Durant invested in the PLL. Kevin and I grew up in the DMV [the Washington, D.C., area], and we both played hoops, so we knew you had to play pickup to get better as a player. That was always around and available for basketball, but a sport like lacrosse, that’s not always available to you.

So street lacrosse was born—basically playing a version of lacrosse on a basketball court. All you need is a stick and a tennis ball, no helmet, pads, and all that other stuff.

We felt like if we could lift off Street Lacrosse, get the pros to play it, create a ton of exciting media around it, that would start penetrating the subconscious of a young kid who wanted to try lacrosse and not worry about signing up for a rec team or club team.

Ultimately sport should be egalitarian. If anyone wants to try something, they should be allowed to try it, and if they fall in love with it, they can commit to playing it and potentially pursue a life in it.

Fortune: Both pro field leagues, which play 10 a side, just finished strong seasons. The PLL posted its most-watched season ever in its eighth year, and the WLL set women’s pro attendance records in its inaugural season. Where does the next leg of growth come from?

Rabil: We’re in a territory where professional lacrosse has never been, and that’s exciting. We’ve raised our Series E around the prospect of having growth over the last eight seasons, and now we’re pouring on growth capital to potentially take the next step into the mainstream spotlight of where the big five or six sports live.

We have a major media deal with ESPN, they’ve invested in our league [in the Series E round], and we have title sponsors across the major categories that never touched lacrosse in the past. That’s because we have real distribution of viewership [on ESPN and sister network ABC], our audience is highly sought after—families and younger generations—and we have a built-in production team that creates content that’s bespoke on behalf of our players, teams, and our partners.

We’re in the middle of producing a five-part documentary series with ESPN [releasing next spring]. I like to say we’re a league and a media company, which has been our focus since we raised our first dollar.

Fortune: All PLL and WLL teams are owned and operated by the leagues. Are you considering expanding, or bringing in individual owners like in other team sports?

Rabil: Because we own the whole thing, it makes less fiscal sense to expand in the PLL [now]… There’s room for expansion of the WLL from four teams up to eight, same as the PLL, but no plans right now that I can announce.

Lacrosse being back in the Olympics in 2028 is a very attractive time for a big shift in our operating model [to possibly selling teams to individual owners].

Fortune: What’s your biggest challenge at the moment?

Rabil: It has to be getting people to decide in today’s environment to pay for a ticket, drive to a game, pay for parking, show up in the heat of the summer for a game broadcast on ABC at one o’clock. That’s a challenge for any league, but lacrosse, in my point of view, outside of the college Final Four, has never really conditioned its fans to attend games.

This is the best lacrosse I’ve ever seen in my life, but conditioning a fan from scratch is a journey. We’re eight years into that journey and seeing a lot of success, but it takes a long time to condition human behavior.

Fortune: What’s your advice to someone starting a sports league?

Rabil: You have to understand the attention economy if you’re trying to grow an otherwise niche sport. You have to do a lot of things really well: education, storytelling around athletes, community investment of your teams, and you have to be omnipresent across mobile devices and televisions, and video boards.

You should approach your business, and find the right investors, metaphorically to think that you’re building a New York City skyscraper. That means you have to dig really deep into the ground first, which comes at an unattractive P&L, but that gives you a strong enough foundation to build upward.

People look at the skyline and say, ‘How beautiful is that!’ They don’t understand the structure that lives underneath it and the investment that went underneath it. It’s a long game.

If you’re starting a football, baseball, basketball, or hockey league, my advice is basically: don’t do it!

Fortune: The PLL and WLL are helping stage the first Lexus Global Lacrosse Games, a new international tournament set for Dec. 8-13 outside Washington, D.C., to build toward the Olympics. It will include men’s and women’s national teams from lacrosse powerhouses the U.S., Canada, Australia, and the Haudenosaunee, who originated the game centuries ago.

Rabil: The ’28 Olympics are an incredible opportunity for our sport and our players. It’s one the sport has never had.

We’re setting up a version of the 4 Nations Face-Off tournament the NHL had that built momentum around the USA and Canada through the Winter Olympics. Over the next two years we’re going to try and build as much attention and awareness around international lacrosse so that when summer 2028 comes in LA, people will be champing at the bit to see a U.S.-Canada final.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/the-weakn.title: The weaknesses that cost Binance $6.3 billion are already hitting Europe’s banks
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/the-weakn.author: Sam Birchall
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/the-weakn.text:
When hackers drained $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, on October 29, it was tempting to treat it as a crypto problem. Less than a week later, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, a French lender, disclosed that hackers had made off with roughly €100 million ($112 million).

The back-to-back attacks highlight the threat of cyber heists to traditional banks. “If a company like Binance can lose billions of dollars, the threats facing banks are overwhelming,” said Ryan Kirkley, cofounder and CEO of Global Settlement, which develops blockchain infrastructure for banks. Speaking at the Digital Asset Summit in London on November 10, he said: “It is impossible for the average bank to stay secure.”

Binance’s founder and former CEO, Changpeng Zhao, went further. “If a crypto exchange can be hacked, banks are in a worse position, in my opinion,” he told CoinDesk days after the heist.

The Binance hackers used a combination of social engineering and malicious software to take over crypto wallets and drain them of funds. This involved arranging a series of fake job interviews to persuade a Binance engineer to inadvertently download malware which allowed the hackers into the company’s systems.

The FBI has seized $1.2 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency, while Binance confirmed it had “replenished” approximately 98% of the total impacted amount.

The weaknesses hackers exploited to steal funds on Binance are not unique to crypto and the same vulnerabilities are present in traditional financial institutions, said Katerina Mitrokotsa, professor of cybersecurity at the University of St. Gallen in Switzerland. “Banks are not automatically safer just because they are regulated.”

Regulators on both sides of the Atlantic have raised concerns. In the U.S., the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency began calling banks on November 2 to ask about unusual activity and service disruptions, Reuters reported.

In July, the European Central Bank wrote to the chief executives of 110 banks warning about the risks of frontier AI models, which are making it “quicker and cheaper to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IT systems.” .

Banks have some advantages over crypto platforms, according to Vivien Mura, chief technology officer of Orange Cyberdefense, the cybersecurity arm of French telecoms group Orange. The EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act, or DORA, which has applied since January 2025, requires banks to test their defenses and report cyber incidents. “They also benefit from mechanisms crypto platforms lack, such as the ability to block or reverse payments and close cooperation with supervisors and law enforcement,” Mura said.

Yet he acknowledges that those advantages only go so far. “Banks are better placed to absorb and recover from a major attack, but they are not necessarily better at preventing one.”

Mitrokotsa highlights two weak spots: The long chain of outside suppliers banks rely on, which DORA tries to address by bringing the most critical providers under direct EU supervision, and the aging technology many banks still run.

In the Crédit Mutuel Arkéa case, hackers used the bank’s own account to carry out transactions after gaining access through an unnamed service provider. The bank told customers the incident had “no impact” on their assets.

“Compromised suppliers, staff with privileged access, fake job approaches and the misuse of internal tools have been recognized risks for years and are not unique to any one sector,” Lee Elliott, director of resilience and cyber at UK Finance, the British banking industry body, told Fortune.

Banks benefit from the sector’s practice of sharing threat intelligence through initiatives such as the Financial Sector Cyber Collaboration Centre, he adds.

Attackers are already exploiting Europe’s aging IT systems. Since October, hackers have hijacked internet-connected refrigeration systems at supermarkets in more than a dozen countries and at three French blood banks. Danfoss, which made the electronic temperature controllers, has said most affected units were older models that no longer receive security updates.

“A fridge doesn’t look like a security risk, and that’s exactly why attackers like it,” Mitrokotsa says. “Banks have the same problem. Many still run core systems that are decades old, next to old servers, building control systems and suppliers’ remote access.” Her advice is for banks to start by knowing every device connected to their networks, then make sure that the ones with no need to reach core systems are cut off from them.

Banks could even learn from crypto, Mitrokotsa added. “Some exchanges split control of a key between several parties, so no single computer can approve a transfer on its own, much like a vault that needs two keys turned at once. An attacker who compromises one laptop gets only part of what they need.”

Personal AI agents also present a new risk for financial institutions to grapple with. Increasingly, consumers are using digital assistants—such as Meta’s Muse—to make purchases or pay bills on their behalf.

Citigroup and Bank of America have restricted agents from accessing customer accounts., JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon has urged financial institutions not to allow autonomous AI agents to handle banking payments, warning of their “treacherous” risk. U.K. banks HSBC, Nationwide, NatWest, Barclays, and Lloyds have also blocked AI agents from accessing their accounts. However, some European lenders are taking a more cautious middle path. Santander and ING let agents make payments, but only within limits the customer sets in advance or after the customer approves each purchase.

With the number of cyber threats mounting, the Crédit Mutuel Arkéa hack is unlikely to be the last attack on Europe’s financial sector.

https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.title: Current price of oil as of November 13, 2026
https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.author: Joseph Hostetler
https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.text:
At 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil was priced at $98.45 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s a gain of $3.87 compared with yesterday morning and around $35 higher than the price one year ago.

It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast.

Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business.

Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.”

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas.

To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks:

Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/spacex-fa.title: I booked the first used Falcon 9 booster. Where will satellite operators go when SpaceX retires it?
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/spacex-fa.author: Martin Halliwell
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/spacex-fa.text:
In 2016, I agreed to put a communications satellite owned by SES on a Falcon 9 booster that SpaceX had already flown. No commercial customer had ever done such a thing before, but as chief technology officer at SES, I had overseen the work our engineers had carried out with SpaceX. Their engineers had shown us how they tested the engines, checked the electronics, and prepared the booster for a second flight. I was confident in SpaceX’s ability to deliver, and they did. In March 2017, they used the booster to launch our satellite.

I would oversee six Falcon 9 launches during my time at SES. But today, as an investor in growth-stage space companies, I find myself wondering what company I would book if I still had that job. SpaceX is setting aside the Falcon 9 and turning its attention to Starship, a much larger rocket; and from my conversations with people working at SpaceX, I can see why the company wants its engineers to change their focus. Most of the remaining Falcon 9 slots up to around 2030 are already booked up. So what happens now if you need to get to space?

Those companies that have managed to secure a booking with SpaceX before 2030 will be glad for their foresight. In October 2025, the team at K2 Space, one of our portfolio companies, announced that they had booked a 2027 Falcon 9 flight for three satellites, having secured their place more than a year in advance. But even operators who book that far ahead can lose their place. Suppose a supplier calls you just before launch because a different customer has found a fault in a component on which you depend. Though your engineers may need just a few days to look into things, everybody else sharing the rocket has a customer waiting too. Under SpaceX’s rideshare terms, you could put the money you have paid towards another flight and pay a rebooking fee of 5% to 10%. You could work out the fee to the dollar and still have no real idea when you might start earning money from whatever it is that you have put into orbit.

Those building satellites that weigh 100 kg or less may find themselves particularly exposed after 2030. On a SpaceX Transporter flight, such a company shares the rocket with dozens of other customers and buys only the space it requires. For a shared flight around Earth that passes near both poles, SpaceX advertises $350,000 for the first 50 kg and $7,000 for each additional kg. At those rates, a founder with a satellite weighing 100 kg can pencil in $700,000 for the ride. After 2030, it is hard to see how a space company could get to orbit on anything like those terms.

In March, K2 Space launched its two-tonne Gravitas satellite on Falcon 9. Because it costs less to build than traditional satellites of similar power, K2 co-founder Karan Kunjur has argued that it still makes economic sense to launch such a spacecraft at a cost of roughly $7.2 million, compared with an estimated $600,000 if Starship delivers the promised savings. But K2 is a highly unusual case. Most satellite operators will struggle to offset higher launch costs with savings of that kind.

At ICEYE, another of our portfolio companies, the team is looking at an alternative way to launch satellites for its European government customers. In September, its executives agreed with Arianespace to explore using Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket for future missions. Neither company announced a launch date. For now, ICEYE continues to fly with SpaceX. In October, the team launched four radar satellites on one SpaceX flight and four more on another just 19 days later.

If your usual provider postpones a launch, the question is whether anyone else can take your satellite at short notice. Say you plan to launch a satellite on Neutron and Rocket Lab postpones the flight. How long can you afford to wait? You still have to pay your engineers, and until you get the satellite into orbit, you can’t sell whatever services you provide. You could try booking a flight with Blue Origin, provided its team can offer you a place on New Glenn in time; but even after engineers fly a new rocket for the first time, they may need years to build enough of them to fly regularly. My estimate is that Rocket Lab and Relativity Space may take until 2033 or 2034 to reach that point with Neutron and Terran R.

At SES, we agreed to fly our satellite on a Falcon 9 booster that SpaceX had already used. Before we made that decision, our team worked alongside the people who had tested the booster and prepared it to fly again. Today, as an investor, I’d ask the people running a satellite company three questions: Which flight have you booked, how much have you agreed to pay, and what will you do if you lose your place? If I were one of their customers, I’d want those answers before I counted on having the satellite or payload in service by a particular date.
