https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/openai-c.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its 'dots' AI agents to make purchases for users
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/openai-c.author: Ashley Capoot
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/openai-c.text:
OpenAI announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its “dots” AI agents to make purchases on behalf of users.

ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available to OpenAI’s Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old.

OpenAI built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and it allows those customers to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections.

OpenAI
 on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its “dots” artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.

The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express
, Mastercard
 and Visa
, and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.

OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user’s card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a “payment token,” which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.

“Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that’s safe and easy to use,” Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.

ChatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta’s Muse offering topped the App Store charts.

Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kickstart a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents.

OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an “Instant Checkout” feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products.

Nayak said ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI’s previous efforts, particularly around product discovery.

“We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they’re really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint,” she said.

ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to OpenAI’s Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old. The limited rollout is intentional, and the “right approach to make sure things are working,” said Luke Gebb, executive vice president and global head of innovation at Amex.

OpenAI’s ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter. With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to “turn up the volume” on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to.

“It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there,” Gebb told CNBC in an interview.

Merchants and vendors are still reckoning with the rise of personal AI agents, and some companies have opted to forgo them entirely. United Airlines
 said Wednesday that it will block agents from accessing its systems to book tickets, and Amazon
 prevents the agents from purchasing products on its platform.

OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its “early days,” and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition. The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren’t inadvertently blocking OpenAI’s agents, for instance.

“It’s going to take time for the ecosystem to build the right infrastructure to be able to make this experience really amazing and seamless across all of their sites,” Nayak said. “Really, who we are speaking to here is the networks and the merchants.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/chicago-.title: Chicago Fed's Goolsbee says central bank 'has definitely got work to do' on inflation
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/chicago-.author: Jeff Cox
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/chicago-.text:
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday that the central bank is getting further away from its inflation goal and “has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility.

In a CNBC interview, the policymaker indicated that inflation is beginning to spread.

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee expressed concern about the latest inflation data, telling CNBC on Friday that the central bank likely will need to take action.

“I believe that the the central bank has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility,” the policymaker said during an interview on “Squawk Box.”

His remarks came shortly after the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the producer price index, considered a proxy for wholesale prices, posted a 0.3% increase in October, which was slightly less than expected, but also indicated a 6.5% annual gain, the highest since November 2022.

With data in hand earlier in the week showing that the consumer price index rose a bit more than expected during the month, Goolsbee said the Fed is slipping further away from its 2% inflation target.

“We’ve been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we’re not making any progress, and if anything, it’s going the wrong way,” he said.

“Inflation is rising. It’s proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks, and now we’re adding this old-fashioned demand overheating coming from the AI data center buildout, that looks like it’s starting to spread out of its lane,” Goolsbee added.

Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase when the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets next on Dec. 8-9. There also is a better than 10% probability of a half-point hike, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch gauge of futures markets. Goolsbee is not currently an FOMC voter but will be in 2027.

Earlier in the week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller indicated he would entertain a 50 basis point move depending on this week’s inflation data.

Goolsbee did not speculate directly on whether the Fed might need to be more aggressive.

“It’s it’s all going to be about this ... question: What is happening to inflation, and are we on path back to 2%?” he said. “My feeling is, right now we’re not.”

https://www.cnbc.com/investingclub/2026/.title: Jim Cramer's top 10 things to watch in the stock market Friday
https://www.cnbc.com/investingclub/2026/.author: Jim Cramer
https://www.cnbc.com/investingclub/2026/.text:
1. Futures are higher this morning after the October producer price index came in lighter than expected, rising 0.3% month over month versus the 0.4% consensus. Dow futures are up 200 points, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq are also set to open higher. Still, the hottest annual PPI in nearly four years. Bond yields are up.

2. Colette Kress is not a “deer in the headlights,” contrary to what Jensen Huang, according to The Wall Street Journal, said about her during a meeting. The Nvidia CFO and now-interim CEO is a heavyweight finance executive. What if Kress was just asking questions of Huang around all these backstops and financing deals that nobody else was willing to ask?

3. After dropping 4% yesterday on news of Huang’s resignation, Nvidia shares are trying to mount a little rally this morning. Up over 2% premarket. Still plenty we don’t know about the affair scandal, specifically around Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. But what I know for sure is that Huang had to go as CEO. Just because someone is brilliant doesn’t mean he can do whatever he wants.

4. Cisco
 is off 3% this morning despite a nice beat in its fiscal first quarter. Guidance for the current quarter looked good, and the networking giant hiked its full-year outlook. So why the selling? Some analysts are pointing to slowing order growth ex-hyperscalers and maybe a peak in hardware. Going to get to the bottom of it with CEO Chuck Robbins on “Squawk on the Street” this morning.

5. AI chipmaker Cerebras Systems
 is up over 11% after reporting better-than-expected third-quarter results and issuing guidance for the December quarter ahead of expectations. Cerebras also announced with Microsoft, adding to its deals with Amazon and OpenAI. Worth noting that there’s tons of short interest in Cerebras, which went public in May. Focused on AI inference.

6. Applied Materials
 is down slightly premarket after a top- and bottom-line beat. Solid guidance too. You need AMAT’s machines to manufacture semiconductors, including memory chips, so they’re a hot commodity. But multiple questions on the call about whether demand is slowing at all. CEO Gary Dickerson argued demand is “very, very strong,” and that customers want them to ship equipment “as fast as we can.” Still, many price target cuts as valuation multiples compress across the group.

7. Costco nearly did it. Finished just under its May 19 record-high close. Another session of gains for the Club stock yesterday after Tuesday night’s special dividend and buyback announcements. The stock is steady this morning. Bank of America raised its price target to $1,257 from $1,095. The analysts came away from an investor meeting with CFO Gary Millerchip feeling good about continued upside.

8. Palo Alto Networks
 caught an upgrade from KeyBanc ahead of next week’s earnings. The analysts went to buy from hold. They expect growth in cybersecurity budgets at companies to accelerate next year, seeing Club name Palo Alto Networks as a big beneficiary.  I have said over and over that cyber is essential in the age of AI. No company can afford to skimp. We also own CrowdStrike. Both stocks have cooled off since October after a blistering rally that began in the spring.

9. Piper Sandler trimmed its price target on Club stock Home Depot
 to $371 from $378, saying supplier discussions indicate a slowdown in spending on home projects. Shares are up about 18% from October lows, including a nice postelection boost last week on hopes a new Congress could help the sluggish housing market. Home Depot needs lower rates. Piper also cut its Lowe’s
 PT by five bucks to $260. Home Depot reports earnings on Tuesday; Lowe’s on Wednesday.

10. Tractor Supply
 was downgraded to hold from buy at Evercore. Analysts said the rebound in discretionary spending activity that the retailer needs to realize stronger earnings growth hasn’t materialized. Also worried about freight and product cost pressures. Tractor Supply had been an excellent performer for a few years, as people moved to the suburbs and rural areas. But shares topped out last August and have lost over 40% of their value since then.

https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-s-wireta.title: Indonesia's wiretapping scandal opens a political fault line
https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-s-wireta.text:
Senior police officers are accused of illegally monitoring President Prabowo Subianto, exposing rival networks within Indonesia's security establishment and renewing concerns about political misuse of surveillance.

For decades, Indonesia's police and intelligence agencies have been accused of spying on politicians, journalists, and activists, Now, a widening scandal involving some of the country's most senior police officers has brought those concerns to the heart of government.

Earlier this month, Indonesian police named four senior officers as suspects in an alleged illegal surveillance operation targeting President Prabowo Subianto and other prominent figures.

Former national police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is not related to the president, was among the senior officers arrested. The ex-police chief became the president's chief of staff in October, just weeks before the scandal broke.

Investigators claim that officers intercepted communications without proper authorization in 2025 and 2026 and then tried to delete records of the operation.

Suyudi Ario Seto, the new police chief, told a parliamentary panel this week that the surveillance targeted the president, officials within the presidential palace, ministries, state institutions, lawmakers, political party figures, governors, anti-corruption officials, activists and students.

A parliamentary commission is investigating the motive behind the wiretapping operation and trying to uncover whether other senior figures were involved. Meanwhile, the police have opened an investigation into possible treason-related offenses.

Amnesty International has called for investigations to also determine whether the wiretap operation was used to intimidate government critics and weaken civil liberties.

The government has responded by ordering an additional 20,000 troops to Jakarta as a precaution, although there had been no indication that the wiretap is part of a larger campaign intended to bring down Prabowo's administration.

The affair has intensified tensions between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo, commonly known as Jokowi, while exposing deeper problems with the powers and political loyalties of Indonesia's security establishment.

"The use of surveillance is actually pretty widespread," Yohanes Sulaiman, an associate professor at Universitas Jenderal Achmad Yani, told DW.

"While there are laws and regulations, they are flouted since there is no regulation on eavesdropping, especially by law enforcement agencies," he added.

Officially, Indonesia's Electronic Information and Transactions Law prohibits unauthorized interception, while other legislation permits surveillance for specified law enforcement and intelligence purposes.

Despite these safeguards against illegal interception, Sulaiman said it could be argued, "that the police and intelligence are essentially unconstrained."

Indonesia's intelligence agencies and law enforcement have long played a role in political competition, Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told DW.

Under Suharto's authoritarian New Order regime, which collapsed in 1998, intelligence agencies were central in monitoring political opponents and suppressing dissent.

After democratization, controversies persisted. In 1999, a leaked recording of a telephone conversation involving then-President BJ Habibie raised concerns about surveillance within the presidential palace itself.

In 2024, the elite counterterrorism unit, Densus 88, was caught surveilling Deputy Attorney General Febrie Adriansyah, who at the time was overseeing major corruption investigations.

But what makes the latest allegations particularly significant is "their apparent scale and the suggestion that surveillance capabilities may have been deployed outside established legal procedures and against the sitting president," Priyandita said.

Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo, a former special forces general, has sought to consolidate his authority over the country's political and security institutions.

Critics accuse him of accelerating the militarization of civilian government, including through legislation expanding the military's ability to occupy civilian posts.

However, the president inherited a security establishment partly shaped by his predecessor.

In 2024, Jokowi, who couldn't run for office again, backed Prabowo's presidential campaign and his eldest son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, became Prabowo's running mate and subsequently vice president.

The Jokowi-Prabowo alliance was decisive for Prabowo's electoral victory, but it also left him governing alongside officials and political networks cultivated during Jokowi's decade in power.

On Thursday, Jokowi's son Gibran resigned as vice president amid a growing controversy over his educational credentials.

Indonesia's Constitutional Court and the country's Supreme Court found that Gibran's overseas high school qualifications fell short of legal requirements for vice presidential candidates, and had been wrongly accepted by election authorities.

The academic credentials probe was apparently not related to the investigations into the wiretapping scandal.

A series of government reshuffles in recent months has also been interpreted as Prabowo's attempt to strengthen his control, especially against some Jokowi loyalists. Listyo, appointed police chief by Jokowi in 2021 and long regarded as close to the former president, was replaced in October.

"Prabowo may have consolidated his political authority since taking office, but that does not necessarily translate into complete control over institutions whose senior leadership and internal networks were shaped under the previous Jokowi government," Priyandita said.

Also, Prabowo may emerge politically stronger if the investigation weakens rival networks within the police. However, replacing one set of political loyalties with another would do little to resolve the underlying problem in the country's security apparatus.

The controversy has renewed calls for reforms that would prevent police surveillance capabilities from becoming instruments of political competition.

Because the latest wiretapping controversy targeted not only the president but also political elites and key civil society actors, "surveillance goes beyond mere politics," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Jakarta, told DW.

"It is a calculated and systematic abuse of power," he added.

Fahrizal argued that a fundamental problem lies in the National Police's constitutional and institutional position, which answers directly to the president.

This increases the risk that the police respond to presidential political interests rather than solely to the law.

In November last year, Prabowo established a police reform commission to investigate longstanding concerns about professionalism, governance, and accountability.

However, Fahrizal said former police chief Listyo failed to implement meaningful reforms, with the latest allegations showing the consequences of inadequate oversight.

Fahrizal called for Indonesia to bring its fragmented surveillance regulations together under a unified legal framework, with tighter controls over the interception powers of the police's Criminal Investigation Agency and the Intelligence and Security Agency.

"Internal police reform must urgently address this by restoring professionalism and a proper institutional ethos," Fahrizal said.

Without such changes, divided political loyalties risk becoming a "dangerous virus" spreading through the police and other security institutions, he added.
https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-s-wireta.summary: Indonesia's police chief says former police chief Listyo failed to implement meaningful reforms. Four senior officers were arrested earlier this month in an alleged illegal surveillance operation.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg.title: Bessent blames Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to block Megaspeed
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg.text:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, of failing to properly oversee the export of high-specification Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.

Jensen Huang left the company he co-founded after revelations he had an affair a former Megaspeed executive. The firm had been buying advanced chips from Nvidia.

Megaspeed had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling those chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.

Bessent told CNBC several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".

"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.

Bessent also said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.

"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.

Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times.

There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.

However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.

"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme.

"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?

"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."

Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blames Commerce Department for delays in putting Megaspeed on export control list. Bessen says he is "frustrated" by delays in adding the firm to the list.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/techn.title: Wall Street Braces for Anthropic’s Spending
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/techn.author: Cory Weinberg
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/techn.text:
Artificial Intelligence

The company’s financial picture may get murky as it deals with employee stock compensation and the growing costs of artificial intelligence.

Reporting from San Francisco

Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, introduced his artificial intelligence company to potential stock market investors this week with a sublime vision. He predicted the end of cancer and mental illness within a decade, and a transformation of cognitive work. “If we do this right, we can create an age of miracles,” he said in a marketing video for Anthropic’s initial public offering.

Wall Street is grappling with how much it may cost to get to utopia.

Stock analysts at Goldman Sachs, the investment bank leading Anthropic’s I.P.O., have told investors privately this week that they forecast the company will burn through more than $65 billion next year, and another $41 billion in 2028, said two people familiar with those discussions. Those totals would make Anthropic’s spending among the most aggressive corporate bets on funding the giant A.I. infrastructure build-out.

“We are in aggressive investment mode,” Krishna Rao, Anthropic’s chief financial officer, said in the video, without discussing specific spending forecasts.

That spending would create a drastically different financial picture than Anthropic has shown recently. The company generated cash from its business in the first nine months of this year, its I.P.O. prospectus shows, a feat in the expensive business of A.I. model development. It has barely spent the $141 billion it raised privately from investors.

The listing on Nasdaq, expected next Thursday, could value Anthropic at $1.4 trillion. It would not only cement its status as one of the world’s most prominent companies but hand it additional firepower to help it pull further ahead of well-heeled rivals like OpenAI and Alphabet. The I.P.O. would deliver Anthropic an additional $100 billion to spend, and make it easier to raise even more money to fund those huge commitments.

But Anthropic’s public debut will lead to costs that don’t appear today. It said in the prospectus it anticipated about $40 billion of expenses in the coming years tied to preexisting stock grants it has given employees that haven’t yet hit its accounting books.

Dario Amodei, the company’s chief executive, publicly frets about the dangers of artificial intelligence and has made enemies of his peers along the way.

Credit...
Timo Lenzen

By Kalley HuangMike Isaac and Cecilia Kang

Kalley Huang and Mike Isaac reported from San Francisco, and Cecilia Kang from Washington.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, was becoming a nuisance for his fellow technology industry executives.

Anthropic and OpenAI, the leading artificial intelligence companies, were lobbying the White House to prevent some A.I. models from being developed and widely shared because, they argued, they were too dangerous. But companies like Nvidia and Microsoft saw those A.I. models as a big business opportunity.

At the end of July, Satya Nadella, chief executive of Microsoft, and Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, intervened. They emailed each other drafts of a letter saying those A.I. models should remain open, according to four people familiar with the discussions. When they asked other technology executives whether they’d like to sign on, two dozen companies quickly agreed before the letter became public. Over the next week, 200 more companies — including a chastened OpenAI — signed onto the letter.

Dr. Amodei has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A.I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A.I. systems in the world. Frustration has turned to hostility as Anthropic leaped into the lead in A.I. development, experienced stunning revenue growth and moved toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever later this month.

Along the way, Anthropic — which has cultivated an image as a company that tries to do the right thing — has also gained a reputation for playing hardball with customers and competitors. It has cut some off from its service and lobbied against other companies’s free alternatives to its A.I.

Over the last year, other technology companies and investors have organized to push back, according to more than 20 people in the technology industry, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve their relationships with Anthropic.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Right to make green challenges to planning decisions under threat, say UK lawyers
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Matthew Pearce and Pippa Neill
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Exclusive: Government in ‘private meetings’ about removing cost cap protections under Aarhus convention

UK politics live – latest updates

The government is considering stripping back legal protections that limit the costs community groups face when challenging planning decisions that threaten nature.

The Aarhus convention, an environmental treaty that was signed into law by the UK in 2005, guarantees the legal right to participate in democratic processes on environmental matters – such as sewage pollution, new roads or datacentre developments.

Under the treaty, when an individual brings an environmental legal claim, they are protected by a cost cap that means they pay only £5,000 of the other side’s costs if they lose. For organisations, the cost cap protection is £10,000.

The purpose of this is to ensure legal challenges about the environment are not prohibitively expensive for individuals and public interest groups.

According too environmental lawyers, the Ministry of Justice has been holding private meetings with “select” stakeholders on plans to remove these cost cap protections and distance the UK from the convention.

Other possible changes include doubling cost caps at each stage of a challenge and removing the costs protection where a court finds a “misuse of judicial review”.

Another potential change would allow groups that crowdfund legal challenges to face costs of up to 70% of the money they raise if they lose.

Proposals to change the way environmental judicial reviews worked began under Keir Starmer’s government, which repeatedly referred to nature as a blocker to growth. Starmer singled out the activist Dr Andrew Boswell as an example of the “nimbys and zealots” bringing “vexatious” legal claims that thwart growth, including a two-year legal fight against the expansion of the A47 in Norfolk that he ultimately lost.

Boswell said Starmer was “putting a target” on his back and that his campaign against the A47, which was funded by £73,000 in crowdsourcing from 2,000 individuals, “brought the community together in Norfolk”.

Carol Day, a senior environmental solicitor at Leigh Day, said the changes would “bring environmental litigation almost to a halt”.

“If they had a bank of cases where they could point to legal action holding things up, I think we could try and have a sensible discussion about it. But we have nothing from them, no kind of hard and fast evidence.”

Another environmental lawyer said the changes being proposed would “fundamentally undermine access to environmental justice deliberately” and mean “potentially really terrible decisions” would not be challenged.

“Local community objectors are often at the cutting edge of challenges that expose widespread government failures in relation to national and international obligations,” the lawyer said.

Sarah Finch, an environmental campaigner whose grassroots judicial review over an oil well in Surrey changed UK climate law, said the government’s proposals would have prevented her group from bringing the case.

after newsletter promotion

“If we ran the risk of paying the other side’s fees, we would have never brought this legal action,” she said. “It’s completely despicable for the government to take this right away. It’s a proposal to restrict people’s access to environmental justice.”

Lawyers fear the private meetings signal the government is accelerating towards leaving the convention, which the government denies. Day said: “The UK government say they don’t want to leave the convention, but [potential changes] would put them in a very difficult position because they would be very significantly non-compliant with it.”

Kyle Lischak, the head of the environmental law charity ClientEarth UK, said: “The right to challenge unlawful decisions is one of the few ways people can hold those in power to account …

“Whether it’s datacentres or intensive livestock production, people too often find their rights and their environment on the chopping block in favour of rapid industrial buildout – and these people need the safe, affordable route to court to protect themselves, and nature, that the law should guarantee them.”

Niall Toru, a senior lawyer at Friends of the Earth, said: “The government seems determined to find someone to blame for slow growth, and environmental campaigners and community groups make an easy target. But nature isn’t holding the economy back. Floods, droughts, pollution and climate breakdown are costing people and businesses billions.

“These proposals will not fix those problems. Instead, they will make more people feel that decisions are being imposed on them without any meaningful way to challenge them.”

A government spokesperson said: “The government is committed to upholding its obligations under the Aarhus convention, including maintaining access to environmental justice that is not prohibitively expensive. There are no plans to remove costs protections for well-founded claims.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Doctor named as DC gym shooting suspect confessed, detailing dispute over living conditions, police say
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna Betts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Gunman killed one person and injured at least four others in and around condo building not far from the White House

More details were emerging on Friday about the previous morning’s shooting in north-west Washington DC, as a manager in the shooter’s residential building told how he was angry over living conditions there and confessed to the killings.

The gunman killed one person and injured at least four others on Thursday in and around the condominium building in the Logan Circle neighborhood of the capital, not far from the White House, where he lived.

Police identified the gunman as 55-year-old Matt Lambert, a doctor who had been involved in an ongoing legal dispute with his building’s management. The person killed was identified as James Stuart, 46, a manager at the condominium complex.

According to police, Lambert fatally shot Stuart inside a gym in his building just before 8am ET, before returning to his apartment, where he fired at four people from his balcony. Those victims were taken to hospital, and as of Thursday, one was in critical condition. Lambert then barricaded himself inside his unit, and was found dead with a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Charelle Ferguson, another building manager, recalled speaking with Lambert by phone at around 9am that morning, around an hour after the shooting began, she said in an interview with the Washington Post.

Ferguson told the newspaper that she had been calling residents to check on their safety after shots were fired, when Lambert answered. During the conversation, she said that he told her that he was tired of mold and water damage in his apartment.

“The only way people will pay attention, you have to do something,” Ferguson said that he told her. She said that he then confessed over the phone to her to shooting the five people.

“I never thought he’d do something like this,” Ferguson told the Post. She also said that he had previously told her about the issues in his unit, and she said she had been sympathetic to his concerns.

Court records seen by the Guardian show that Lambert sued his condo association in 2025, alleging it had failed to address water damager, mold and moisture issues in his apartment, which he alleged began after exterior work was carried out on the building. The association denied allegations of negligence and denied responsibility for the damage, in court filings, and the litigation remained ongoing.

Lambert’s attorney in the civil matter, Joel Braithwaite, said at a news conference on Thursday that he was “deeply shocked” by what happened and that he had last spoken with his client on Tuesday and said that he had sounded fine.

“I can’t tell you how surprised I am because the person I knew as a client is someone who is in the business of healing people,” Braithwaite said.

On Thursday evening, residents gathered at a vigil in the neighborhood, lighting candles and showing support for those affected by the shooting.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Gunman killed one person and injured at least four others in and around condo building in Washington DC. Gunman identified as doctor Matt Lambert, 55, who had been involved in an ongoing legal dispute with his building's management. Lambert told a building manager that he was angry over living conditions there and confessed to the killings.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Young men were key to the blue wave. Our research offers a reason why | Brigid Schulte and Haley Swenson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Brigid Schulte and Haley Swenson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Amid concerns over the influence of the manosphere, our findings show that young men are concerned about caregiving

When young men helped propel Donald Trump into the White House in 2024, the administration doubled down on a brand of toxic masculinity popular in the so-called manosphere.

They touted high testosterone, male supremacy, and a “biblically-based family” where men work and provide, and deferential women stay home to bear children and care for others.

In a complete reversal, on 3 November, young men powered the blue tidal wave that swept away Maga’s hold on political power. Men 18 to 29 shifted nearly 40 points to help Democrats capture both Houses of Congress, flip seats in state legislatures, and win some unexpected governorships.

Turns out, young men may not be so toxic after all. So what do they want?

The election results made clear that young men want financial stability at a time when the cost of living is soaring and jobs have become precarious, disposable and threatened by AI. But they also want time to give care.

That’s according to recent research we produced with NORC at the University of Chicago on men’s attitudes and experiences with care, based on a nationally representative survey of more than 3,000 Americans, with an oversample of young men 18-29.

We found that more than six in 10 young men value caregiving as much as paid work, even though many of them are not yet fathers or caring for a loved one.

Thirty percent of young men identify as caregivers, including 44% of young Hispanic men, who swung for Democrats by 47 points from 2024. Nearly six in 10 young men who have worked while giving care have reduced their work hours. Providing care while still earning enough to live is a major concern.

“Everything is so expensive these days that a young person can’t even consider taking care of someone, as they can barely take care of themselves,” a 23-year-old male caregiver from Ohio shared in the survey.

Eight in 10 say that being an involved father is an important part of being a man. Seven in 10 say they’d be at least somewhat interested in being a stay-at-home parent if they had the choice.

In fact, six in 10 young men, compared to about four in 10 young women, said they’d be at least somewhat interested in being a full-time caregiver – hardly the answers politicians pandering with UFC fights on the White House lawn might have expected.

Abdul, one of our survey respondents, began caring for his chronically ill father at age 19 because no one else in his family was available, and they couldn’t afford the high cost of paying for care. He missed classes, quit his job, and moved in with his extended family in order to care for his father until his death.

“It was always nice for me to be there for my father, because he was there for me when I was young,” Abdul, now 26, told us. “I have no regrets. I would do it again.”

Our survey did find that some young men hold traditional views on gender.

Men ages 18 to 29 are nearly three times more likely than women of the same age group to say that it’s OK for men to do some care work, but women are better suited to do most of it (32% versus 12%). Young men are also more likely than young women to say that men’s role in the family should be providing financial support while women run the household (32% versus 14%).

Still, these are minority viewpoints. More than 70% of young men say that care should be divided equally between men and women. Sixty percent said mothers and fathers do an equally good job of caring for a newborn, compared to just 52% of men over 30. And young men are more likely than young women to say gender does not play a role in who is best suited to care for an adult.

Half of young men said they are “somewhat” or “very” likely to need paid leave from work to care for a child in the future, about the same share as young women, and 44% anticipated needing leave to care for an adult family member.

Among young fathers who took paid leave to care for a child, 70% said having access to paid leave through their employer or state was a major reason they took it.

And when we asked men who wanted to take caregiving leave from work, but didn’t, the most common reasons were that they couldn’t afford it, worried their careers would suffer, or that their workplaces weren’t supportive. Just 5% said taking leave wasn’t “manly”.

Nearly one-third of young men say they have “no control” over their work schedules, and while 33% work from home at least some of the time, 68% would prefer to, a 35-percentage-point gap between what young men have and what they want.

Perhaps what young men want is what we all want: good work with living wages that ensure the ability to have and care for a family.

Instead of disgruntled Republicans working to thwart Democrats at every turn in the next Congress, policymakers would do well to raise the minimum wage, help all families cover the high cost of care, and pass federal paid family and medical leave, and measures to give workers more flexibility and control over their schedules.

Evidence suggests young men are moving beyond toxic masculinity and the politics of division.

If they want to stay in power in 2028 and restore hope for the future, it will be up to policymakers to deliver instead on what the newly elected Texas senator James Talarico calls the politics of love.

Brigid Schulte is an award-winning journalist for the Washington Post and the Washington Post Magazine and was part of the team that won the 2008 Pulitzer prize. She is director of the Better Life Lab at New America

Haley Swenson is a PhD social scientist and senior Writer and researcher at New America’s Better Life Lab

If they want to stay in power in 2028 and restore hope for the future, it will be up to policymakers to deliver instead.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.author: Simon Burnton (now); David Tindall and Dominic Booth (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.text:
Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from the US men’s national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday.

The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades.

Just to prove we’re not completely fixated with Manchester United today’s Football Daily is not about Manchester United:

Hello everyone! I begin my time at the helm with some reaction to, yes, Pochettino’s appointment by Manchester United. Here are the thoughts of Henry James “Harry” Redknapp:

Someone said to me today, ‘What a bad time to take the job’, I said, ‘I could never think of a better time to take over the Man United job’. They are rock-bottom. There’s only one way, it’s up. It isn’t like David Moyes following Alex Ferguson. David Moyes is a great manager, but following Fergie was impossible. Now he [Pochettino] takes over a club that is in a real mess at the moment, and he can only take one take them one way, and that is going to be up. I like him. He’s a great character, very clever manager, knows the game, and I’m sure he’ll do a good job. But it’s going to be two or three years before you see Man United anywhere near what you’d hope they would be.

And here are the thoughts of Harry’s son, Jamie Redknapp:

He’s an elite manager. I’m sure that [sporting director] Jason Wilcox, [chief executive] Omar Barada are probably thinking to themselves, ‘Are we lucky to keep our jobs?’. I think the answer to that would be yes, if they are to stay with that structure and regime. He’s coming into an environment now that’s going to be so difficult, he’s probably going to think after a few months, ‘Wow, have I made the right decision here?’. One of the biggest clubs in the world, but for the last few years has been so poorly run.

I regret to report that the thoughts of Jamie’s children Charley, Beau and Raphael are currently unknown.

Time to hand the blog to Simon Burnton for further Pochettino reflections and more. Here he is…

Pochettino is doing his best not to talk about Manchester United – yet. But he does finally give away something.

I think we will have time next week to talk about Manchester United, but now I think it is much better to talk about us, about USA Soccer, and of course, USA Men National Team, and we have two games ahead, and now it is focus complete on this.

However, when pressed about why he’s leaving after just signing a new deal with the USMNT, he does throw us a little nugget.

There’s not too many opportunities that happen in your career like a side of Manchester United and, of course, when that arrives it is difficult to turn down.

Pochettino is asked if he’s satisfied about what he achieved during his time at USMNT.

I think it’s difficult in that business, always you want more, and then you are a critic, and you say, ‘oh, I could be better, I should do better things, do better things’.

Always it’s being brave, take the best decision, to get the experience from that decision, what happened, and try to adapt again, and to try to make better decisions for the future.

I don’t like to use satisfaction, being satisfied of what happened in the past. That’s always, I think, in our mindset, it’s always we try to do better, and do better and try to find a way to, maybe in this similar situation, act in the always best way.

Pochettino composes himself. Aware that this is U.S. Soccer goodbye rather than a Manchester United hello, his focus is on his time in charge of USMNT. He dodges the question on what appealed about the United job.

I want to thank the fans for the support, for everything. And of course, always, it was a tough moment.

Like I said before, it’s a really tough decision. But at the same time, we are excited for that step forward. But now it’s not the moment to talk, it’s the moment to be committed, like always we are. And care, because we really care. And always we are going to care about the federation and the players and all the people that are here.

It’s to be focused in the next game because it’s really important for the federation. The players are amazing and they know how to manage this type of situation. It’s true that it’s not ideal, but it’s never an ideal situation when this type of thing happens.

But in life, football is quick to move. That is why we need to move forward, I think. To keep that relationship and all the memories that we share. I think we were amazing.

Mauricio Pochettino is giving a surprisingly emotional press conference as he officially announces his departure from the USMNT for Manchester United following their next two games. When thanking officials for the opportunity he was given, his voice cracks and out comes a tissue to wipe away the tears.

If you want your Football Weekly in video form, this is the link for you.

An interesting take from Suzanne Wrack as Chelsea host Manchester City in the WSL on Saturday lunchtime. We’ll have a live MBM blog on that one by the way.

We’re all aware now that Pochettino’s first game in charge is at Anfield. But what comes after that? His first six matches comprise four in the Premier League and two in the Champions League.

22 Nov: Liverpool v Man Utd
25 Nov: Sporting v Man Utd
28 Nov: Man Utd v Brentford
2 Dec: Newcastle v Man Utd
5 Dec: Man Utd v Coventry
8 Dec: Man Utd v RB Leipzig

Three away games in the first four isn’t ideal or perhaps it is. Poch can start to bed in on the road where the away fans will perhaps give him more leeway. Sporting away is tough given that the Portuguese side have won three of their first four Champions League matches in the group phase. But Leipzig are down in 29th while Coventry and Newcastle are in the bottom half of the Premier League. Brentford sit 12th in the six-match EPL form table after two wins, two draws and two defeats. In other words, there are opportunities to turn the ship around.

Cheers Dom. That seems a fair summation of my plans. I’ll start with some Poch…

Right, I shall hand back to David Tindall who will no doubt provide much more United/Pochettino chat, with the occasional post about something else.

Valérien Ismaël has been appointed as Le Havre coach until the end of the season, with the club sitting rock bottom in the Ligue 1 standings.

The 51-year-old former defender, who was hired as a replacement for Didier Digard, will face a huge task to keep Le Havre in the French top tier. Still winless in Ligue 1, Le Havre have two points from 10 matches.

The much-traveled Ismaël has coached teams in Germany, Greece, Austria, Turkey and England, and was most recently at Blackburn. Le Havre said in a statement yesterday that he has handled “emergency situations” in the past, “which could prove very useful in the coming weeks.” AP

Will Carlos Baleba become a key man for United under Pochettino? Much has been made of the Argentinian’s desire to see his teams run, run, and then run some more. In the space of one season at Chelsea, Pochettino improved their running stats.

Baleba looks to be the only current United midfielder with the legs to cover large spaces. Pochettino often prefers a 4-2-3-1, so surely it stands to reason that the former Brighton player will fit in as one of two deep-lying midfielders? Kobbie Mainoo would appear to be the ideal partner for Baleba – and we know Pochettino likes to promote young homegrown talent. What that means for summer signings Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, it remains to be seen. But the news that Bruno Fernandes probably won’t sign a new contract, could mean a shift in the structure of United’s midfield.

Santos was loaned out by Chelsea to Nottingham Forest and Strasbourg during Pochettino’s sole campaign at Stamford Bridge. United may well look to recruit more hard-running midfielders in January or the summer to suit Pochettino’s preferences.

Let’s recap some of the Guardian’s most relevant reads to Manchester United, Carrick and Pochettino.

Just watching Carrick’s end-of-season speech on the Old Trafford turf from May, after a 3-2 win over Nottingham Forest.

I suspect he won’t be repeating his praise of the United playing staff, but that connection with the Stretford End is most certainly evident.

Japan head coach Hajime Moriyasu will step down next week, the country’s football association revealed today, cutting short his tenure in the wake of the 2027 Asian Cup’s postponement.

Moriyasu, Japan’s longest-serving coach, was originally set to lead the team at the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia in January before handing the reins to current Under-23 boss Go Oiwa.

But the Asian Football Confederation announced last week that the tournament would be pushed back to December 2027 due to “exceptional circumstances” in the region, following Houthi attacks on the host country.

That left Moriyasu in limbo, with Japan Football Association (JFA) chiefs last week declining to clarify when the coaching handover would take place.

They said that Japan’s friendlies in Singapore against Brazil on Saturday and Paraguay on Tuesday would be Moriyasu’s last games in charge. AFP

The former head coach has taken to Instagram to address United fans and his departure from the club.

Dear United fans, I’ve had the immense privilege of leading Manchester United, the football club that I love. There are very few who get to live that and feel it, and for that I am incredibly grateful.

With that comes huge responsibility, and to be at Manchester United you need to understand exactly what that means. It’s different to anywhere else.

Ultimately you need to push to be the best, but there is a culture, there are values and there are behaviours that you have to live by and respect, which have been built over a long period of time …

I want to say a big thank you to the supporters. I must say, you are a special rare breed …

I just wanted to give you something back. That love never dies. I know we’ve not had the results lately, but you’ve shown me nothing but love and support in times when the easiest thing … would be to turn the other way. That means more than a win or two …

I want nothing but success for Manchester United. This club has been such a big part of my life and that will never change. I’ll always be proud to have played my part and I’ll always want the very best for it.

He was linked with the post as far back as 2016, also coming close to being appointed in 2018, 2021 and 2022. He has long had an admirer in Sir Alex Ferguson, who praised Pochettino in a 2016 interview when the Argentinian’s Spurs team were approaching their apex.

“This lad has composure,” said Ferguson.

“You never see him ruffled and the way his team play is a testimony to the work he is doing.

“The most important thing for English football is how many English and young players are in his team. He understands the advantage of playing young people. They won’t let you down and they have been fantastic.”

We want to thank Cindy Parlow Cone, JT Batson and Dan Helfrich for their partnership and incredible working relationships throughout our time here. There is tremendous talent in the US player pool from the youth teams through to the senior team, and it’s one of the reasons we have so much belief for the future of US Soccer. You will always have a special place in our hearts, and we will be supporting the teams whenever they step on the field.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Will Democrats try to strip US-Israel initiative from Pentagon funding?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Joseph Stepansky
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Washington, DC – After a commanding performance in the United States midterm elections, advocates say Democrats are uniquely positioned to strip a controversial measure from a Pentagon funding bill that would codify integration of the US and Israeli military industries.

Earlier this year, Democratic leadership had already opposed the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), a sprawling $1.15 trillion package that, along with supplemental bills, includes funding for much of President Donald Trump’s military wishlist, including the “Golden Dome” missile shield and his so-called “Trump-class” battleship plan.

Top party officials, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, had attached their opposition to the Trump administration’s war with Iran and wider affordability issues facing US citizens. Advocates say the leadership must also send the message that the US-Israeli defence production integration is a non-starter.

The current Senate version of the bill, under Section 219, calls for the creation of a so-called “United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative” that would “expand and accelerate bilateral defense technology research, development, testing, evaluation, coordination, and industrial cooperation”.

Cavan Kharrazian, senior policy adviser at Demand Progress, told Al Jazeera that “Democrats need to make it clear right now that their votes for the NDAA depend on substantial changes, including US-Israeli military integration and Iran war prohibition”.

Opposition to Pentagon funding has historically been politically fraught, with lawmakers wary of appearing to not support the US military. But while a version of the funding package passed the Republican-controlled House of Representatives in May, Democrats delayed the Senate version via a procedural vote in July.

They now face a December 11 deadline when current stopgap funding ends, meaning they would need to pass another stopgap measure or the full NDAA to maintain Pentagon funding.

Because the NDAA requires 60 votes to pass, Democrats can exercise outsized leverage in the remaining days of this congressional session, Kharrazian explained. Republicans, meanwhile, face a ticking clock before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress in January.

“[Democrats] have the leverage to filibuster the NDAA until these provisions are stripped out and they need to commit to blocking NDAA consideration until those changes are secured,” Kharrazian said.

“An amendment vote alone is insufficient if Democrats then let the bill advance with the provisions intact.”

To be sure, Democrats, eager to show they are delivering on voter affordability concerns, have signalled they will seek some overhaul to the current NDAA and related supplemental bills. Defence industry analysts have predicted a major constriction in Pentagon funding, which also includes a stalled $360bn supplemental package.

However, it has been unclear if that would extend to the US-Israeli military development initiative.

“We must push for the development of a more realistic and sustainable approach to our national security – one that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or one paid for with draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Representative Adam Smith, currently the ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said in a statement shortly after the November 3 election results rolled in.

He echoed Schumer, who wrote in a July “dear colleague” letter that Republicans were seeking a Pentagon funding bill “that would dump billions more into the defense industry while long overdue investments in American communities wait”.

Smith had initially supported, but later opposed, the provision to integrate US-Israeli military development. But Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who are both seeking to retain their leadership positions in their respective chambers, have not publicly stated their positions.

Critics have long warned that the initiative would establish an opaque new avenue for the Pentagon to provide US tax-funded support to Israel via joint development ventures, while dodging congressional oversight. It would also make future policy pivots more difficult, entrenching Israeli-developed technology into US military programmes.

Some have characterised the initiative as the next phase of Washington’s decades-long military support for Israel, with both US and Israeli officials acknowledging direct military aid has become increasingly politically fraught.

“The whole point of Section 219, let’s understand, is to move the US-Israel aid relationship … further outside the purview of Congress, which is to say to sort of inoculate it from democracy,” said Matthew Duss, the executive vice president at the progressive Center for International Policy think tank. “I think Democrats and others who are opposing this measure in the NDAA are on firm ground to hold a hard line.”

“But I think it’ll be tough, especially with this leadership that remains very strongly pro-Israel,” he told Al Jazeera. “I think both Schumer and Jeffries have shown signs they recognise that their respective caucuses are in a very different place ideologically than they are on this issue.”

A growing number of senators have publicly opposed the measure. In July, Senator Chris Van Hollen joined six colleagues in rejecting the provision.

A total of 12 senators have since signed on (PDF) to a new letter released earlier this week, including progressive stalwarts like Bernie Sanders and more centrist figures like Ron Wyden and Tammy Duckworth.

Hamid Bendaas, the communications director for the Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) Policy Project, said the senators represent “a broader range of the Democratic Caucus”.

“So I think that’s a good sign that a good amount of Democrats are ready to really stand against those provisions in the NDAA,” he told Al Jazeera.

Bendaas also pointed to public opinion polls suggesting widespread opposition to US military support for Israel, fuelled by the genocide in Gaza. Both President Trump and Vice President JD Vance have acknowledged that the current state of the US-Israel relationship has become politically fraught.

“I wouldn’t want to be a Democrat or a Republican who votes yes on the text that we’ve seen,” Bendaas said. “For one of the first major bills to pass post-midterms to be a bill that directs the Pentagon to send taxpayer funds to Israel, or, I should say, Israeli companies, some of which are government-owned companies … I think that’s about the worst thing that they could possibly do right now.”

In their letter, the senators wrote the provision would “expand and accelerate the US-Israel defense relationship, including technology sharing, co-production of weapons systems, and bilateral research and development across multiple domains of warfare such as biotechnology, quantum, autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, cyberwarfare, and others”, surpassing integration even with some US NATO allies.

That could, in turn, “threaten US national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology” and “create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the US defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement”.

“To do so in this instance would be unwise,” the lawmakers wrote. “Especially as the Government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with US interests and values.”

You can preorder several of the devices today, with shipping expected to start in mid-December.

The first few smart home devices and accessories that Apple co-developed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric for its new Apple Home Collection are now available for preorder through the company’s online store, with delivery expected in mid-December. Apple announced the collection a month ago as part of a stronger push into the smart home space that’s led by its new Siri AI-powered HomeView smart display which is also now available starting today.

Of all the Apple Home Collection devices currently listed on its online store, only a handful of LG accessories are available for preorder. These include the $299.95 LG Outdoor Cam and $199.95 Indoor Cam, plus the $249.95 LG Video Doorbell, which all show an estimated shipping timeline of December 11th to December 17th. The rest of the collection, including the $399.95 LG Floodlight Cam, $349.95 LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, $199.95 LG Smart Thermostat, $199.95 Schneider Home Smart Thermostat, and $39.95 Schneider Home Room Sensor, aren’t yet available for preorder and don’t have an estimated ship date.

The devices in the Apple Home Collection don’t include exclusive features or functionality, but through the partnership, Apple has streamlined the setup process so it’s as easy as tapping them with your iPhone to get them running. The devices in the collection also use Thread to remain connected should they lose access to the internet or your Wi-Fi network, and they can automatically update their network credentials if you make changes to your wireless network.

Cape believes that private, secure communications are essential to free expression.

For too long, cell phone users have accepted the idea that sacrificing privacy is part of staying connected. Sharing and tracking one’s location, keeping a record of call logs and browsing history, and using a singular phone number as a digital identifier are par for the course to participate in the modern age.

Yet, as network-level cyberattacks and data breaches occur with greater intensity and frequency every year, cell phone privacy is more significant and under threat than ever. The statistics are grim: According to a 2024 survey, 36 percent of American journalists reported facing threats of or experiencing physical violence, while 97 percent of U.S. advocacy programs for domestic violence reported their clients have been harassed or monitored through technology. Victims often experience stalking and coercion through personal technology devices — a digital betrayal compounded by the constant flow of data that often includes sensitive medical, banking, and social media information, as well as access to friends and loved ones.

This is where Cape comes in. Its founders identified that threats of digital attacks go beyond the modern privacy stack: encrypted chat apps, VPNs (virtual private networks), private browsing, or phone-level settings like roaming and 5G.

“Even the most operationally diligent cell phone users still call and text their grandparents, schools, doctors, and banks, revealing patterns of life and allowing persistent tracking,” says Cape CEO John Doyle. “If advances in tech are supercharging the bad guys, we need to be innovating on behalf of regular people who don’t want a gradual erosion of privacy to be the price of technological progress.”

Cape’s privacy approach begins with collecting the minimum amount of data needed to provide service, then deleting it in days rather than keeping it stored indefinitely, or worse, selling it to data brokers. From there, the goal of Cape is to reduce a user’s digital footprint, which can reveal the patterns of a user’s life and allow for persistent tracking or leaks of sensitive metadata. Standard solutions like burner phones and encryption apps no longer cut it; instead, disruptions to privacy are ingrained within the foundation of cellular architecture itself.

Defending user privacy involves controlling the “mobile core,” the central brain of a cellular network that governs how devices authenticate and transmit data. These are some of the key ways Cape is working toward just that.

Every phone has an IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity), a 15-digit number assigned to your phone by a mobile carrier, which appears whenever your phone connects to a network. With sufficient access from carriers, governments, or bad actors, your location and travels can be tracked and surveilled over time. Cape offers the rare ability to rotate this network identity on a daily basis to all its subscribers—a feature previously only available through the purpose-built Cape Obscura device.

Like a driver’s license or passport, one’s phone number has become a form of identification. While it’s convenient for signing up, logging in, or two-factor authentication, it carries myriad risks that range from spam calls to privacy data breaches. Cape offers two additional alias phone numbers for every user, which can be used to sign up for newsletters or online shopping, while leaving one’s real number private and reserved for friends and loved ones. Cape’s Secondary Numbers are also middle-to-end encrypted, so they’re safe to use for things like 2FA codes. It’s a step above common services like VoIP (Voice over IP), whose numbers are rarely encrypted and often insufficient for authenticating with apps.

Your call log can reveal a lot about you: who you talked to, how long you spoke, and where you called from. Most calls can be easily forgotten, but the data can live on within a carrier’s database for up to five years. Instead of retaining this data (i.e., for monetization purposes), Cape deletes call logs after 24 hours. Because Cape runs its own mobile core, unlike other MVNOs (mobile virtual network operators), Cape is able to produce its own logs and delete them soon after. Not only does this policy prevent your call log data from being sold, but it also shields it against all-too-familiar data breaches that affect hundreds of millions, conducted by hackers who don’t even have to try very hard these days.

We take the network coverage on our cell phones for granted, with easy access to the major operators that control the physical cellular towers across the U.S. However, access to just one network isn’t always optimal, as it makes your traffic easier to trace. Enter Cape’s Multi-Network Coverage. Cape offers subscribers access to two major domestic roaming networks, Alpha and Tango, and allows users to seamlessly switch between the two within the Cape app with the press of a button. Spreading your traffic across two domestic roaming networks not only makes it harder to be tracked, but it also enables better coverage: If you lose signal on one network, Cape will automatically try the other, so you stay connected more often, especially in rural areas.

To make Cape available to more of the people who need it the most, like journalists and activists, Cape works with the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which has promoted digital privacy and free expression since 1990, to provide free Cape service. Cape also provides its subscribers with discounted access to Proton Unlimited or Proton VPN Plus.

Cape’s service costs $99/month, which is comparable to rates from today’s major carriers. But early adopters who switch to Cape this year get their monthly service cost reduced to $70/month and retain those savings for life. The plan includes benefits you expect from major carriers, like unlimited talk and text, but its host of additional features could ensure that you can take control over a key aspect of your modern life: genuine digital privacy.

Governments, hospitals, courts scrambled by global Microsoft outage.

A global outage taking down a wide range of Microsoft 365 services remains ongoing Friday morning.

The outage started midday Thursday, impacting users of Microsoft email, cloud, and AI services. Microsoft has documented the full list of services impacted by the error, while moving early Friday morning to protect customers around the world from losing emails during the extended disruptions.

“Recovery actions are ongoing,” the Microsoft 365 Status account confirmed on X. “To help preserve delayed mail during this event, we’ve extended email timeout to 48 hours.”

Similar to recent world-shaking outages of widely used tech like Amazon Web Services and CrowdStrike, the Microsoft disruption looks like “one of the biggest outages of all time,” Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News. Possibly even “worse,” he suggested.

Businesses, hospitals, police departments, and schools were among those scrambling to work around the outage. In Japan, it disrupted government IT infrastructure, according to deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki. NBC’s report documented various harms, noting that “few public bodies were immune from the outage.” In some cases, doctors couldn’t send patients “important” updates on medication changes or follow-up care.

The financial sector suffered, too, with people blocked from making bank transfers since they couldn’t receive verification codes.

Justice systems were also hobbled. The Supreme Court in the Philippines saw its legal work derailed, NBC reported. And one US sheriff’s office in Colorado reported that the outage made it difficult for people to post bond for prisoners’ immediate release.

It’s unclear how many users were affected, but Microsoft estimated in January that the total number of paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions exceeded 450 million.

On a status page, Microsoft said “we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident” and promised to “share a full Post-Incident Report with root cause and defense-in-depth actions after mitigation is complete.”

“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” Microsoft said on X.

But Microsoft’s public statements make clear that the tech giant was blindsided by the outage and struggled for hours to find mitigations that could reliably restore user access.

Shortly after detecting the outage, Microsoft confirmed that the main issue was “a portion of infrastructure” that “is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions.” This was not caused by increased traffic, Microsoft said, but “a problem that’s causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”

Once it became clear that the failed health checks were to blame, Microsoft said it took steps to prevent additional server outages while validating alternate health check methods. But four hours later, the company admitted that it was still in the weeds.

“We’re opening all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” Microsoft said. “We found a core process on affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, causing capacity loss. To validate a potential recovery, we’re isolating a portion of infrastructure, restarting affected components, and reintroducing traffic to confirm the services remain stable before applying the change more broadly.”

Even small wins seemed to turn into new setbacks. As Microsoft worked to resolve the issue, some of the servers it brought back online would “become unresponsive again once they receive traffic,” giving the company yet another problem to solve.

Realizing that no quick solutions were coming, Microsoft moved to extend email timeout to 48 hours. As “encouraging” recovery efforts remained ongoing, Microsoft advised users that “some intermittent issues may continue” when traffic is restored.

Microsoft’s most recent updates confirmed that it’s seeing “broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific.”

“Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure,” Microsoft said. “Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods.”

DownDetector, which tracks user reports of service issues globally, showed that connectivity losses peaked Thursday afternoon and dropped off substantially by Friday morning.

In comments, an Outlook user described the pains of monitoring email recovery, complaining that outgoing messages seem to send fine but incoming messages are received inconsistently. Some Copilot users seemed distressed that access wasn’t restored as quickly as Outlook. One Microsoft 365 user pondered, “How many offices had people with practically nothing to do? How much has this cost?”

https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.author: Jennifer Ouellette
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.text:
Heinz von Foerster thought population would grow exponentially and “squeeze” us all to death.

As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday’s global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It’s not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point.

It’s not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus—one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever.

Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn’t starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, “they will be squeezed to death,” he wrote.

Plenty of scholars objected at the time, dismissing von Foerster’s conclusion as “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd.” The global population did not keep accelerating at an exponential rate; the baby boom petered out just a few years after von Foerster published his paper.

“He got the picture right just as that picture ceased to be right,” mathematical biologist Joel Cohen of Rockefeller University and Columbia University recently told Popular Science. “The all-time peak happened in the early 1960s.” Nor did von Foerster foresee the impacts of longer life expectancy and the sharp decline in child mortality rates.

Nevertheless, the paper was highly cited and received a fair amount of media coverage at the time. As Alan MacEachern, a historian at Western University, pointed out at The Conversation:

The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate—at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were better than those of most demographers throughout the 1970s and 1980s.

Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter and the global population began falling behind the forecasts—because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.

Doomsday predictions are nothing new; they date at least back to the first century CE, when an ascetic sect interpreted the Jewish uprising against the Romans in 66-70 as a harbinger of the coming Messiah. The Christian religion has produced a ton of incorrect predictions of the end times; among those making them was Martin Luther, who believed the world would end no later than 1600.

Puritan minister Cotton Mather kept updating his predictions, first calling for the end in 1697, then 1716, then 1736. (He would probably have kept updating them had he not died in 1728.) My personal favorite is Mary Bateman, an Englishwoman in Leeds who claimed in 1806 that her hen was laying eggs inscribed with the words “Christ is coming.” It was a hoax: Bateman had actually used a corrosive ink to etch the eggs before putting them back inside the hens.

Astrologers have come up with their fair share of doomsday predictions, usually involving rare planetary alignments and comets, but scientists have not been immune. Jacob Bernoulli thought the Earth would be destroyed by a comet on April 5, 1719, for example. And in 1974, astrophysicist John Gribbin co-authored The Jupiter Effect, which predicted several catastrophes arising from the combined gravitational force of aligned planets. (Gribbin has since distanced himself from that hypothesis.)

There hasn’t been a successful doomsday prediction yet. So relax, once Microsoft is up and running again, we’ll probably all be fine—at least until 2060, which none other than Isaac Newton believed could herald the end of the world. Or maybe it won’t happen until 2129 or 2239 (based on interpretations of the Talmud) or 2280 (based on interpretations of the Qur’an). Or we can cling to the prophecy of a mystic named Baba Vanga, who thought the world won’t end until 5078.

DOI: Science, 1960. 10.1126/science.132.3436.1291  (About DOIs).
