https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.title: Asking the right questions: How to design fairer, more rigorous observational studies
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.author: Regina Schaffer; Nandita Mitra, PhD
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Observational studies remain a valuable way to assess real-world relationships and long-term outcomes, but confounding variables, selection bias and poor design can make for spurious associations that perpetuate misinformation.

The most difficult step for researchers designing an observational study is not choosing a statistical method, Nandita Mitra, PhD, professor of biostatistics and codirector of the Center for Causal Inference at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, said during a keynote presentation at the Dermatology in Pharma Educational Collaborative (DPEC).

Before analyzing any study, Mitra said, the hardest questions come first: “What are we trying to learn, and can the data we have answer that question?”

Causal inference, Mitra said, changes how people think about evidence by moving beyond observing patterns and toward understanding cause-and-effect relationships.

“If I have a headache, I take aspirin and my headache goes away an hour later, that is not a causal claim,” Mitra told Healio. “What I would have to then think about is what would have happened to me had I not taken aspirin? Would my headache still have gone away? Inference relies on these hypothetical, counterfactual situations.”

Healio spoke with Mitra about the questions researchers should ask when designing an observational study, which variables to adjust for and why, and the importance of including a credible comparison group. DPEC, hosted by Penn’s Center for Clinical Sciences in Dermatology and led by Healio Dermatology Chief Medical Editor Joel M. Gelfand, MD, MSCE, FAAD, is an academic-industry collaborative program that promotes continuing education for professionals working on clinical research.

Healio: What is a causal question?

Mitra: The causal question compares two potential outcomes for the same patient. For example, an outcome with treatment vs. an outcome without treatment. The difference between these two outcomes is the causal effect for that patient; the unobserved alternative is the counterfactual.

Most clinical questions — Does this treatment work? Does it cause harm? Would another treatment have been better? — are causal questions. The problem is we can never observe both outcomes for one person at a particular point in time.

People sometimes confuse causation with association. Often, you find there is an association or correlation between a medication and a particular outcome, but that does not necessarily mean that the medication caused that outcome.

Because we cannot observe the counterfactual, we must estimate it. We look for patients who can tell us what might have happened otherwise. The comparison group must be a credible stand-in for the missing counterfactual.

Healio: During your talk, you referred to a study that assessed whether GLP-1 receptor agonists cause hair loss , as reports of alopecia have increasingly appeared in real-world cohorts. What were you trying to convey with that example?

Mitra: I picked the topic because it is timely and relevant. The data seem to say yes. A systematic review and meta-analysis showed 40% higher odds for nonscarring alopecia with GLP-1 use. Should we believe it?

When you are conducting these types of observational studies, you cannot randomize people who receive a GLP-1 vs. those who do not just to assess hair loss. Were the patients in the comparison group comparable to begin with? Before treatment, they may differ in obesity severity, age and sex, health-seeking behaviors, healthcare use, nutritional status and use of other medications. This is confounding. Simply adjusting for all the different factors that you have collected does not necessarily mean you now have a causal effect.

Healio: What should researchers be adjusting for? What should they not be adjusting for?

Mitra: In my talk, I described what a confounder is. A confounder is a common cause of both the treatment and the outcome. People who start GLP-1s may be different from those who do not. These differences confound the association between GLP-1 use and hair loss. If you don’t adjust for confounders, you could end up with a spurious association between the treatment and the outcome. So, we do want to adjust for confounders. However, you may not have measured all confounders so your study may still be susceptible to unmeasured confounding. In addition, there are other types of variables you must think about very carefully.

There are mediators, variables that occur after treatment and are on the causal pathway to an outcome. If certain variables result from GLP-1 use, we often do not want to adjust for that if we want to estimate the total effect of GLP-1s on the outcome. Weight loss, for example, is a mediator. If we adjust for weight loss, we are no longer estimating the total effect of GLP-1 treatment. We have changed the causal question. But we might be interested in the indirect effect of weight loss. In those cases, we might want to then conduct a different type of analysis to assess that mediated effect.

Colliders are a common effect of treatment and outcome, and we usually do not adjust for those variables. Selection bias is an example.

Healio: How can researchers avoid selection bias?

Mitra: Continuing with this example, those taking GLP-1s may be more likely to see a dermatologist. Those who have hair loss may be more likely to see a dermatologist. If you subset to investigating only patients who saw a dermatologist, that is selection bias or conditioning on a collider. By doing this, you might end up with a population of people that are not generalizable.

Importantly, a statistician cannot make these decisions in a vacuum. When we think about causality and different types of variables, that information is coming from collaboration with a domain expert. When I work on dermatology studies, it is critical that I am working very closely with a dermatologist who can help me think through all the variables, how the treatment progresses and how data are collected.

Healio: How can researchers design a fairer comparison?

Mitra: When you are thinking about, specifically, an observational study where all of these issues can come into play, clinicians will often come to me and say, I want to use these statistical methods, like propensity score weighting or instrumental variable methods, because I want to make a causal claim. What I usually say first is, “Let’s go way back in the process. Imagine the trial you wish you could run. First, what is the question you want to answer?

Causal inference is not a statistical method. It is a way of thinking about evidence. You must ask the right question, design the right comparison and be honest about what you do not know.

Can you answer the question that you want to answer using the data you have? Also, think very carefully about the design of the study. The next step is to think about the different causal assumptions. Do we have a clear comparator group that could be thought of as that counterfactual world? And then, we finally get to the statistical methods.

The methods have changed enormously over my career, but the questions I find myself asking have changed remarkably little.

Nandita Mitra, PhD, is professor of biostatistics and codirector of the Center for Causal Inference at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania. Mitra can be reached at nanditam@pennmedicine.upenn.edu.

Mitra N. Causal inference in the real world: A matter of life and death. Presented at: Dermatology in Pharma Educational Collaborative; Nov. 6, 2026; Philadelphia.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/democrats.title: Democrats won Congress. Now they must win back trade policy
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/democrats.author: Desirée LeClercq
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/democrats.text:
Days after winning Congress, Democrats are debating whether and how to restore congressional authority over tariffs. Some in the party are focusing on reining in Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs on allies like Canada, while others hope that a 2029 Democratic President might direct Trump’s expansive tariffs toward progressive priorities, such as raising labor standards. This debate is missing two things. First, it blames trade failures on Trump, when both the Trump and Biden administrations pursued similar trade policies that failed workers. Second, it focuses on taking tariff power back from the president but overlooks Congress’s role in setting trade objectives.

I have spent my career trying to make trade work for American workers. As a progressive, I urge congressional Democrats to take stock of the lessons from both the Trump and Biden administrations, which requires a course correction, even if it means restraining a future Democratic president.

Both administrations, acting unilaterally, have cost us. Congress once shared control over trade policy. Under Trade Promotion Authority (TPA), it linked its up-or-down vote on trade agreements to its negotiation objectives that included enforceable labor and environmental standards. Both administrations essentially ignored it.

Trump used it once, for the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Biden never used it, let it lapse, and redirected resources into domestic production. Both relied on decades-old tariff statutes that alienated allies and raised consumer prices. The results? Partners turned to [Al%20Jazeera,%20Oct.%2028,%202025]China, and allies have signed trade agreements without us. Under Biden’s domestic policies, U.S. factory production fell and manufacturing jobs stalled. Unilateralism, even under Biden’s “worker-centered” trade policy, didn’t work. Here’s why.

When I was a trade negotiator in the first Trump administration, we were pressured by both Democrats and Republicans to use tariffs and other sanctions to get countries to treat their workers better at home. The theory was that market leverage would force better labor and environmental standards in partner countries and level the field for U.S. businesses that meet those standards.

We tried that theory. It didn’t work for us, and it hasn’t since.

Trade partners have valid reasons to resist U.S. trade pressure. They don’t want to appear weak to their constituents. And our market leverage isn’t the silver bullet we think it is. Governments can turn to China for financial support. In Cambodia, while the United States and the European Union considered withdrawing trade benefits in 2019 over worker-rights violations, China pledged $588 million in aid. While we waited for Cambodia to give in to trade pressure, The Wall Street Journal reported in July 2019 on a draft agreement granting China’s navy a 30-year lease at Cambodia’s Ream base.

Progressives rightly champion workers who are losing jobs to global trade. Tariff policy doesn’t protect workers in the United States from job loss; it taxes them at the grocery store and when their jobs depend on a steady, affordable supply of steel and aluminum. The average hourly wage for manufacturing production workers rose 6.6 percent from January 2025 to October 2026, which is only slightly higher than 5.8 percent inflation.

By letting its trade authority lapse, Congress gave up its main say in trade negotiations. The result has been rushed deals with unrealistic commitments. The Agreement on Reciprocal Trade between the United States and Cambodia, negotiated in months in 2025, committed Cambodia to protect internationally recognized labor rights, including freedom of association and prohibitions against forced labor. The International Labor Organization recently found that Cambodia still violates those standards. If we want trade commitments to translate into action, we need deliberative consultations at home and abroad. The deal with Cambodia would have been more realistic if Congress had required Cambodia to amend its laws before the deal could be finalized.

Patient efforts under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, by contrast, paid off. With time to debate the labor-rights commitments domestically, Mexico passed critical labor legislation to protect independent trade unions.

A new Democratic majority must focus on reviving deliberative processes in trade policy. It should require transparent, participatory consultations at home, including trade-sector workers and their representatives. It should also require trade partners to consult their businesses and workers before agreeing to labor and environmental commitments. Congress should start in January by requiring its approval for new tariffs, as Democratic leaders now promise. They must also enact a new TPA centered on participation by workers and other stakeholders at home and abroad. President Trump will likely veto both, but doing so would put on record that he prefers unchecked trade power over new agreements that would benefit U.S. companies and workers. Congress would still have drafts ready for whoever takes power in 2029.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/clean-ene.title: Climate Advisers director: The U.S. needs a clean energy standard for AI data centers
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/clean-ene.author: Matt Piotrowski
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/clean-ene.text:
Voters delivered a verdict on data centers in the midterm election. In an NBC News exit poll, 56% said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, and voters passed more than 40 local measures restricting data centers. Lawmakers now face a choice. They can answer with bans, or with rules that decide who pays for AI’s power but ignore where it comes from. Either would be half a policy. Voters want lower bills and cleaner air, and clean energy can address both. Ireland, Singapore and China have already tied data center growth to clean power. The United States should too.

Residents outside Memphis have seen the alternative. xAI has run dozens of gas turbines across the state line in Southaven, Mississippi, to power its Colossus 2 data center, drawing lawsuits and complaints over air quality. More are coming. Global Energy Monitor counts 189 GW of natural gas tied to data centers in development as of mid-2026, with about 17 GW already under construction. Gas appeals to AI companies because it can provide reliable, around-the-clock power, but turbine shortages and equipment backlogs could delay projects or cause them to be scrapped. This gives policymakers time to shape what will power most AI data centers in the coming years.

For now, clean energy is winning on the grid. This year, solar, batteries and wind make up more than 90% of planned U.S. capacity additions, according to the Energy Information Administration, with developers racing to qualify for federal tax credits before they phase out. Without policy, that may not last.

So far, when it comes to AI data centers, Washington and the states have focused mostly on costs. President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge is voluntary, and The Ratepayer Protection Act, which stalled in the Senate this fall and could return in the next Congress, would protect consumers from higher bills but says nothing about clean energy.

States have moved faster, with moratoriums and rules that make data centers pay for grid upgrades, but few tie data centers to clean power. Lawmakers at both levels should close that gap by pairing strong ratepayer protections with a phased clean energy standard for new data centers.

Other countries show how. Ireland requires new data centers connecting to the grid to meet 80% of their annual demand with new renewable energy built in Ireland. Singapore requiresapplicants for new data center capacity to power at least 50% of proposed capacity with green energy. Japan offers subsidies up to 50% of investment costs to data center operators that run entirely on decarbonized electricity. China, whose data center capacity is forecast to nearly double by the end of the decade, has set a requirement of 80% green power at its newly built main data center hubs. These countries compete with the U.S. for AI investment, and they are already ahead.

A clean energy standard would also serve AI companies. Wind and solar are competitively priced, can come online quickly, and offer protection against energy price swings. Even a Bank of America Securities analyst who sees gas as the fastest way to secure power describes solar as “the lowest-cost marginal energy.” Clean power isn’t free, but neither is the alternative.BloombergNEF estimates that powering a 500-megawatt data center with on-site gas can cost upwards of $140 per megawatt-hour, substantially more than purchasing electricity at industrial grid rates. A phased standard that lets developers buy clean power from the grid, rather than build it all on site, would keep costs down without slowing construction. The industry is already a willing buyer. Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft signed about 80% of corporate renewable power contracts in 2025, making them natural allies for a standard that rewards the investments many have already made.

Households and communities would benefit too. Paired with cost protections, a clean energy standard would keep data center costs off electricity bills at a time when the EIA expects residential electricity prices to rise nearly 5% this year. And it would mean cleaner air for neighborhoods like those outside Memphis.

Critics warn that a clean energy standard could push investment abroad, to less regulated markets. That risk is smaller than it looks. The U.S.’s top competitor, China, already requires clean power for new data centers in its national computing hubs, and other jurisdictions, such as India’s Gujarat state, have their own clean power conditions. A phased-in standard, with compliance timelines and flexibility in how developers secure their supply, would give companies time to adapt. Ireland’s six-year compliance period offers one example of how such a transition can be structured.

The U.S. leads the global AI race, and AI infrastructure development will remain a major source of electricity demand. This means that U.S. clean energy policy has to keep pace. Congress and state governments should phase in clean energy requirements for new large data centers, prioritize additional clean generation, account for grid reliability, and enforce safeguards that keep infrastructure costs from shifting to consumers. The country cannot afford to treat AI development and energy planning as separate challenges. A clean energy standard for new data centers would help the U.S. pursue technological leadership while building an affordable and sustainable electricity system. Lawmakers have written half a policy. It’s time to finish it.

The 10-year Treasury yield stayed over 5% on Friday after October’s producer price index, a measure of wholesale prices, came in slightly less than expected.

The yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 5 basis points to more than 5.15%.

The 2-year Treasury note
 yield, typically more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was higher by less than 1 basis point, at 4.872%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond
 yield, sensitive to geopolitical risks, was more than 5 basis points higher, at 5.481%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.

October’s producer price index rose 0.3% versus September, less than the 0.4% expected by economists polled by Dow Jones. But on an annual basis, PPI rose 6.5% over the past 12 months, the biggest annual increase since November 2022.

There was “no silver lining” in the inflation report, said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, adding that core PPI — which excludes food, energy and trade services — increased 0.5% in October.

“It is economics 101 that producer prices lead consumer prices and right now it looks like consumers will be on the hook for a fresh burst of factory inflation,” he said.

The moves come after 10-year Treasury yields jumped more than 13 basis points to more than 5% in Thursday’s session, with the 2-year yield soaring more than 15 basis points.

Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. Odds of a quarter percentage point hike now stand at 86%, with the chance of a half point increase at around 14%.

Energy inflation remains a key part of the puzzle, with oil set for its second weekly decline as prospects of renewed strikes by the U.S. against Iran fade. Prices were choppy in early trading Friday. U.S. West Texas Intermediate
 futures for December delivery were down 0.1% at $88.63 per barrel. Brent crude
, the international oil benchmark, was higher by 0.3% at $96.11.

The second Trump administration has placed significant strain on U.S. treaty alliances. It has directly threatened the sovereignty of long-time allies such as Canada and Denmark and wielded tariffs as a weapon of first resort. Moreover, the administration has sought major force posture changes, often without allied consultation and reportedly based on ideological considerations rather than military requirements. And it has attempted to interfere in allied domestic politics, championing far-right parties and individuals.

To demonstrate that the administration’s turn against allies is not a settled fact of U.S. political life, the new Democratic majority in Congress should reassert powers as a co-equal branch of government. Rhetorical steps, such as reassuring statements and letters of concern, will not be enough even if they garner bipartisan support.

The second Trump administration has placed significant strain on U.S. treaty alliances. It has directly threatened the sovereignty of long-time allies such as Canada and Denmark and wielded tariffs as a weapon of first resort. Moreover, the administration has sought major force posture changes, often without allied consultation and reportedly based on ideological considerations rather than military requirements. And it has attempted to interfere in allied domestic politics, championing far-right parties and individuals.

To demonstrate that the administration’s turn against allies is not a settled fact of U.S. political life, the new Democratic majority in Congress should reassert powers as a co-equal branch of government. Rhetorical steps, such as reassuring statements and letters of concern, will not be enough even if they garner bipartisan support.

Instead, the next Congress must take practical steps to remove obstacles to defense industrial base integration and make it harder for the administration to take unilateral steps that sabotage alliances.

Current Senate Democratic leadership has telegraphed that working to improve the domestic economic situation in the United States is one of its top priorities for the new Congress. In this context, reasserting congressional authority over foreign policy in general and alliances in particular is not only a national security imperative, but also a part of the Democrats’ affordability agenda: President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Washington’s closest allies have added to Americans’ woes, while economic integration with allies can spur growth and jobs.

Amid rapidly increasing allied defense spending, everyone would benefit from integrating allies into the U.S. defense industrial base. Many of the Trump administration’s actions, however, have soured commercial relationships and pushed allies toward domestic or alternative suppliers. Congress can take concrete steps to help establish a more cooperative allied industrial relationship that ultimately improves intra-alliance burden-sharing.

First, Congress could treat more allies as part of the U.S. defense industrial base. This would involve adding more countries to the National Technology and Industrial Base and putting funding behind it; extending to other allies the exemptions to the International Traffic in Arms Regulations that Australia and the United Kingdom receive through AUKUS; designating additional key allies as domestic sources under Title III of the Defense Production Act (as Section 1080 of the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act did to add Australia and the U.K., alongside Canada); and raising the dollar thresholds for congressional notification on sales to close allies to match the increased price of modern high-tech weapons.

Before doing this, Congress would need to vet each ally’s technology protections and compliance with existing U.S. law on issues such as human rights—but for most treaty allies, this wouldn’t create a problem.

Second, Congress should facilitate allies building more together. It could increase funding for co-production of critical capabilities such as the Patriot PAC-3 and other air defense interceptors as well as counter-drone capabilities. To ensure that the Pentagon follows through, Congress could withhold a share of funds until the Defense Department certifies progress, the same mechanism that the Senate Armed Services Committee has proposed to ensure access to a second source for Patriot interceptor rocket motors.

The legislature could consider complementing bipartisan U.S. maritime security efforts, such as the SHIPS for America Act, with additional exemptions to 10 USC. 8679 for allies in Europe and the Indo-Pacific that can make major shipbuilding contributions.

Here, the Icebreaker Collaboration Effort Pact among the United States, Canada, and Finland offers a template: Finnish shipyards are building the first new U.S. Coast Guard icebreakers in decades as domestic U.S. production capacity ramps up. Any change must be coordinated closely with domestic interest groups, such as unions and industry, to protect American workers.

To pay for these steps, Congress could pass a supplemental appropriation aimed at building munitions production in the United States and allied countries. Such a supplemental could include a requirement that allies co-fund each co-production initiative they decide to join, which would go beyond existing proposals such as the nonbinding expectation in the fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) that Baltic countries match U.S. funding for the Baltic Security Initiative.

The party should start with investigations and subpoenas, then prepare for more substantial campaign finance reform.

Beyond specific measures related to the defense industrial base, Congress could examine authorities preventing deeper or more rapid cooperation, including limitations on how much allies can do with and for U.S. forces to support their readiness and operations. For example, Congress could extend foreign repair exemptions under 10 USC. 8680 to include South Korea and Japan, as the statute already permits under specified conditions for U.S. submarines in Australian and U.K. shipyards.

Other problems stem not from missing authorities but instead from open-endedness in existing authorities. For instance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly not completed the required paperwork for allies to transfer their own Patriot interceptors to Ukraine. Any similar approval requirements that lack a deadline will give any administration an implicit veto over allied cooperation even if that cooperation advances U.S. interests.

Congress could consider reviewing these authorities systematically and develop more serious accountability mechanisms, such as instituting automatic approvals if the executive branch has not acted within a specified period and, at a minimum, establishing standing consent for transfers among treaty allies.

In other areas, Congress has already begun building the tools to create a bulwark against the administration’s efforts to undermine U.S. alliances. Section 1249 of the 2026 NDAA bars U.S. troop reductions in Europe below 76,000 without independent certification from both the commander of U.S. European Command and the secretary of defense that includes consultations with NATO allies. Congress should now overcome the administration’s objections to extend these provisions and establish similar limits on U.S. troop reductions in South Korea in the final version of the 2027 NDAA.

After the Supreme Court confirmed in February that presidents can impose tariffs only when Congress has clearly authorized them, the administration shifted to a temporary surcharge and then to Section 301 tariffs that include allies. Congress could consider passing into law a bill similar to the bipartisan Trade Review Act, which would make any new tariff lapse after 60 days without congressional approval.

Members have also proposed various ways to limit potential military action against allies, including a bipartisan bill that would prohibit the departments of Defense and State from using funds for military action or annexation of the sovereign territory of a NATO member state. Although the worst of the Greenland crisis, which inspired these legislative proposals, has passed for now, the administration could attempt to once again coerce allies at any point. Moving forward, Congress should learn from the fact that its efforts to rein in Trump through stand-alone bills and appropriations amendments have stalled. Instead, lawmakers should consider adding new protections to must-pass legislation.

Legislation is not the only tool, however. The Senate’s advice-and-consent powers allow it to withhold approvals on confirmations, and both chambers can conduct oversight hearings and expand investigations. For example, the Senate can resist confirming nominees selected for posts in Europe, up to and including all pending ambassadorial nominees or potential new cabinet nominees, until the administration accounts for its attempted interference in allied domestic politics. Next term’s committee leaders could also develop a joint hearing agenda early in the term that prioritizes alliance issues, including interference in allied politics.

Enacting fixes, however, is just the first half of the challenge. Ensuring that the administration complies is the other, perhaps harder, half—as the past 22 months have illustrated.

In October, a bipartisan group of senators wrote a letter to the secretaries of defense and state, urging the “swift obligation” of Baltic Security Initiative funding, following up on their similar letter sent in May that appears to have gone unheeded. In September, the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that the administration could not lawfully let congressionally appropriated funds expire unspent.

Congress can make its legislative priorities bite by withholding funds until the administration certifies progress, as several of the provisions discussed above do, setting firm obligation deadlines and authorizing multiyear procurement that is harder for any one president to unwind.

But while compliance mechanisms might be able to force the administration’s hand, they cannot force allies to continue investing in a partner that they no longer trust. Whether allies ultimately believe that they still have a partner in the American people depends on how muscular the next Congress decides to be.

John Drennan is a visiting fellow, Europe in the world program, at the Egmont  Royal Institute for International Relations in Brussels, with the support of a Council on Foreign Relations Robert A. Belfer international affairs fellowship in European security. He is also a nonresident fellow at the Transatlantic Dialogue Center in Kyiv.

Ariane Tabatabai is the vice president of research, security, and defense at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs and a contributing editor at Lawfare. Previously, she served in a number of roles in the U.S. Department of State and Department of Defense, including as deputy assistant secretary of defense for force education and training. https://www.dw.com/en/why-does-el-salvad.title: Why does El Salvador's Bukele have troops in Haiti?
https://www.dw.com/en/why-does-el-salvad.text:
Haiti's Prime Minister congratulating El Salvador's President for a gang crackdown in Haiti has shone a light on the relationship between the two countries. What's going on, and where does the US stand?

Haiti has been engulfed in crisis since 2018, with protests, a presidential assassination and widespread gang violence bringing the country to its knees.

But earlier this week, Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime hailed a major win in the battle against the violence, thanks to "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs."

El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele had earlier said a joint task force between the countries had "destroyed" what he called "the house of Lanmo San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters." He also tweeted out an as-yet unverified video of helicopters firing on a sprawling property.

A number of Salvadoran troops have been stationed in Haiti, nearly 2,000 kilometers from their homeland, since the beginning of 2025, mostly in an attempt to curb gang influence.

Last month, Bukele dispatched more than 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti, ostensibly to rescue four Salvadorans who were ambushed on October 18 and have not yet been found.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Writing on social media platform X, Fils-Aime thanked the Salvadorean military for helping "the fight against gangs." The two nations are, he added, working alongside the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), in an attempt to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority."

The GSF has been operating in Haiti since 2016. But there are doubts to the legitimacy of El Salvador's presence.

"Where the lines are and where the coordination begins and ends between a bunch of distinct entities and security forces is a huge concern about how this actually plays out, and El Salvador are trying to frame it as their choice, their action," Jake Johnston, a Haiti expert and director of international research at the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR) in Washington, told non-profit news agency The New Humanitarian this week.

A UN report about Haiti released on Thursday described "bloody turf wars, sexual violence and other horrors, noting that serious violations and abuses continue to be committed across the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and in the Artibonite and South-East departments."

It further found that between July and September 2026, at least 1,167 people were killed and 459 injured, with more than half of that violence stemming from "ground or aerial operations carried out by security forces against gangs, sometimes with the support of a private military company using drones."

For many observers, this chaos is a major part of the appeal for Bukele, who appears to wish to export his mano dura (iron fist) policy on to foreign soil. The policy saw gang members jailed on a huge scale and a significant drop in the murder rate of a country once notorious for homicide. But Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a Haiti expert from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, told DW earlier this month that Haiti's gang problem is more entrenched. He says using the same tactics as in El Salvador may not have the same result.

"Haiti does not currently have the conditions to replicate the Salvadoran model: Its prisons were emptied in 2024, its justice system is largely paralyzed and criminal groups resemble militias more than gangs, with territory, taxes, weapons of war and political networks that protect them," Le Cour Grandmaison said.

Despite El Salvador being on Donald Trump's list of "shithole countries" that the US president disparaged in 2018 in notorious remarks which he later partially denied, relations between the US and El Salvador have improved markedly during Trump's second term.

The number of migrants deported to El Salvador from the US rose by 98% at the start of 2026 and Le Cour Grandmaison said the US plays "a central, albeit very discreet, role in public life" in El Salvador.

Bukele's move to position himself as an ally of Trump has seen the US president offer him a level of endorsement and autonomy to do what Bukele deems necessary to protect El Salvador's security and that of its troops.

"He said that he has a big problem with Haiti. I said: 'Look, you're running your country. You have to do what you have to do,'" Trump said in November.

Iran claimed it struck US radar systems in Bahrain, while the US said it had intercepted the attacks. Clashes continue in the Strait of Hormuz, as the war remains in a state of de-escalation.

Iran said its forces hit a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday. However, the US military denied the claims and said it shot down two Iranian attack drones.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) initially said in a statement that its air force targeted and destroyed the radar on the island of Bahrain.

They claimed this was a retaliatory attack in response to an US attack on a telecommunications tower in the Iranian county of Sirik, on the shores of the Strait of Hormuz.

Several hours later, the US military's Central Command, denied the IRGC's claim that the radar was destroyed and said it stopped two "one-way attack drones" targeting Bahrain by the militant group.

It reported no casualties or damage.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran war, started by the US and Israeli strikes on February 28, is currently undergoing a de-escalation as main issues remain unresolved.

Both US and Israel are holding off major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.

On the other hand, Tehran has continued seeking to control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where reports of burning ships came through.

Before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump said on October, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes, without giving any timeframe.

Trump is expected to meet Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders' summit in China next week and discuss ending the ​war in Iran.

Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to reach a conclusion.

https://www.dw.com/en/beijing-faces-its-.text:
China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image at the global stage.

An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen next week.

China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.

The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.

At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.

In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.

A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies, most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.

Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.

For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.

As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues, Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.

The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.

"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.

She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.

For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival,  and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.

"Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added.

Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012.

The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades.

At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends.

Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods.

While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome.

"China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa.

"Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added.

In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine.

Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body.

However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas.

Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is  concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea, which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy.

But for now, the benefits of alignment remain.

MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage."

"China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added.

Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare.

"Strategic distrust between the two sides, particularly Russia's concerns about economic dependence on China, will continue to limit the scope of their cooperation," Insisa said.

https://www.dw.com/en/cyber-attacks-and-.title: Cyber attacks and hybrid warfare: Germany gives sweeping powers to its police and intelligence services
https://www.dw.com/en/cyber-attacks-and-.text:
Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic and foreign sources?

Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday.

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany.

Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies.

Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The president of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch this week again pointed out that today's hybrid attacks pose a new challenge to the organizations safeguarding the country's security. At his organization's annual meeting in Berlin this week, he said the "hybrid attacks" are challenging the "separation principle," which means that the police conduct investigations while intelligence services gather information. The exchange of data between the two is permitted only under strict conditions.

Münch has long objected to this strict division of responsibilities. He has been calling for expanded powers for the police and closer cooperation with the domestic intelligence agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which is responsible for countering espionage and sabotage.

The separation principle results from lessons learned from the Nazi dictatorship, when the Secret State Police (Gestapo) operated largely outside judicial constraints and served as the regime's central instrument of terror, used to oppress and murder Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, communists, social democrats, and many others. The Allied powers that defeated Nazi Germany in World War II then decided that the police and intelligence services should remain institutionally separate and be granted different powers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Historian Sönke Neitzel of the University of Potsdam considers the separation principle understandable in its historical context. At the BKA's autumn conference, however, he described it as "nonsense" in light of today's threat landscape and said it was no longer necessary in a country that has been a constitutional democracy for decades.

While Neitzel considers the separation principle outdated, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the center-right Christian Social Union (CSU) wants to preserve it in its essential form. In his view, even a more extensive exchange of data does not violate the principle. At the same time, however, he has made clear that he wants to transform the domestically focused Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the foreign intelligence agency, the Federal Intelligence Service(BND), into "real intelligence services."

This legislative reform brings Dobrindt a significant step closer to that goal. Parliament pproved the interior minister's plans with the votes of the governing coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dobrindt insisted that Germany intends to take an active approach to defending itself against cyberattacks: "Anyone who attacks us in this way must know that we are prepared to strike back. They must know that their digital infrastructure, their server infrastructure, and their software will also be targeted by us."

BKA President Holger Münch welcomes Dobrindt's determination and points to the growing threat posed by cyberattacks. The line between criminal and state-sponsored actors is becoming increasingly blurred, he argues. As a result, both intelligence services and law enforcement agencies face the same challenge.

To underscore the scale of the threat as he sees it, Münch cited two statistics: in the first six months of 2026, crime originating from abroad rose by 24% compared with the same period the previous year. What concerns him most is that fewer than 5% of these cases are solved. The BKA chief considers this trend more dangerous than ever: "The state's promise of security can become fragile. Confidence in the ability of its institutions to act effectively and remain steadfast is declining."

This article was originally written in German.

The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.title: The U.S.-Israel Relationship Is Broken. Here’s How Eisenkot Could Fix It.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.author: David M. Halbfinger
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/world.text:
Former Israeli and U.S. ambassadors, lawmakers and analysts largely agree on steps Gadi Eisenkot could take if he becomes prime minister. But they are risky.

By David M. Halbfinger

Reporting from Jerusalem

Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who has been given a chance to form Israel’s new governing coalition and replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is by no means assured of success.

But if he does take power, another hugely daunting challenge would immediately confront him: how to undo the vast damage done to Israel’s relationship with the United States, its closest and most important ally.

It’s hard to imagine things getting much worse.

Many Americans have turned against Israel over its devastating military campaign in Gaza, and even more so over its role in pressing for war with Iran, which led to soaring gas prices.

President Trump announced this month that he would cut off billions of dollars in annual U.S. military aid to Israel by the end of the year and blamed Israel in part for Republican losses in the midterm elections. Democratic control of Congress could quickly lead to sanctions on violent Israeli settlers and on new settlement construction in the occupied West Bank, as well as to new conditions on arms sales.

In the past, Israel could always turn to Congress for support in clashes with the White House, said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to Washington and deputy prime minister under Mr. Netanyahu. But no longer.

“For the first time in the history of our relationship with the United States, we have no recourse,” he said. “We have to start from scratch. We have a lot of fence mending to do and with no guarantee of success. Zero.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/busin.title: Fewer Fed Meetings Raise Stakes of Warsh’s Communications
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/busin.author: Colby Smith
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/busin.text:
The Federal Reserve will vote on interest rates less frequently beginning next year as part of a plan by the central bank’s chairman, Kevin M. Warsh, to overhaul how it operates.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

When officials at the Federal Reserve meet next month to vote on interest rates, they will have only a partial snapshot of the economy in hand. Fresh inflation data comes out the day after policymakers finalize their rate decision, leaving them without insight into whether price pressures in November continued to accelerate or showed signs of easing.

This predicament underscores why officials at the central bank broadly appear on board with a plan hatched by Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, to reduce the number of meetings convened each year to vote on interest rates.

The changes will be ushered in gradually, beginning next fall. In a revised schedule released on Thursday, the Fed confirmed that its policymakers will meet eight times in 2027, but that the Oct. 25-26 gathering will be “dedicated to the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues.”

By 2028, there will be just six meetings accompanied by policy votes, with two others focused on strategy.

Meeting less frequently, and at more evenly spaced intervals, has the clear benefit of giving officials a more consistent flow of economic data to parse when they gather to debate their policy settings. But there are trade-offs that will put more onus on Mr. Warsh to communicate openly about how the Fed is approaching its rate decisions and its thinking about the outlook, something he has so far resisted even as the central bank has embarked on raising rates this year.

“The decision process is more important than the timing,” said Esther George, who served as president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City from 2011 to 2023. “And this committee is struggling a bit with how to communicate what exactly they mean.”

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/g-s1-1533.title: How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/g-s1-1533.author: Jonathan Lambert
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/g-s1-1533.text:
Senator Chris Van Hollen speaks at a rally outside of the U.S. Capitol in support of USAID — the United States Agency for International Aid — on February 5, 2025. The Maryland Democrat has just announced that he will challenge Senator Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.

"We need new leadership," says Senator Chris Van Hollen, who on Thursday announced he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic majority leader. Van Hollen has garnered support among Democrats for his sharp criticism of the Trump administration, including their upheaval of U.S. programs to promote health and end poverty around the world.

In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, two days before his announcement, Van Hollen spoke to NPR about his plans to "shine a light on all the harm and damage the Trump administration's done to our country and our interests around the world" — and what the Democrats hope to accomplish with foreign aid.

As the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department and what's left of the United States Agency for International Development, he could have considerable sway over how Congress investigates and legislates on foreign aid.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length. NPR reached out to the State Department for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

You've taken a strong stand against the Trump administration's shakeup of foreign aid. You led protests against the dissolution of USAID and in a hearing last year told Secretary of State Marco Rubio that "People died because of those actions, mothers, fathers and children." You've also authored statements condemning a range of actions, including tying health aid to mineral deals. In the majority, what's the first step you'd take on the aid front?

Priority number one is to do an analysis of all the harm the Trump administration has done.

There have been very credible analyses showing that over 700,000 people around the world died between January 2025 and January 2026 because of cuts to USAID. If these trends continue, you're talking about millions of people dying in the coming years.

One of the great benefits of being in the majority, is you actually have a gavel and can call a public hearing, and use that as a spotlight to help educate people around the country.

We can do that to show the consequences of Elon Musk taking a chainsaw to USAID. I remember to this day a scene at the White House [in February 2025] when Donald Trump was at his desk and Elon Musk was standing behind him, and a reporter asked Elon Musk about the cuts to fighting Ebola, and Elon Musk's response was essentially, "Whoops, yeah, we missed that." And then he claimed that they'd restored it. Well, we know that they've not restored it adequately — there's good evidence that the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could have been better contained if the United States had not made big cuts to public health.

We can investigate what they did, not for the purpose of putting it back exactly as it was but understanding the damage that has been done, fully, with an eye toward reforming it.

You've already been speaking out against a lot of this in the minority. What kinds of actions can Democrats take as a majority that they couldn't before?

Being in the majority makes a big difference. Now we have many more tools available, specifically through the power of the purse.

One of the things the Trump administration has done is essentially sit on funds appropriated by the Congress for public health here at home but also for international health programs. So there's an example where we can much better safeguard the will of the Congress now that we're in the majority.

Can you give an example?

One of the things the Administration did was to rescind over $500 million in funds for global health. In other words, they cut it, and you had a rubber stamp majority in the Congress. Republicans, go along with that. You would never get Democrats to agree.

There's another ongoing example right now, which is a number of years ago, we passed about $1.5 billion in funds for [global] public health, and it appears that they're using those funds not for public health but to wind down USAID. So this is an area where we could say no, you may not use these funds to wind down USAID.

The administration has been ignoring a lot of these "no's" so far. What gives those "no's" more weight in the majority?

When we in Congress provide a sum of money, for say public health, we say this money should be spent on these specific items, like vaccinations or clinics. That's guidance, that's direction. It's technically called report language, and this report language used to be respected by Democratic and Republican presidents.

The Trump administration has ignored report language because it's not technically legally binding, and Republicans in the Congress have let them get away with it. And the more they let them get away with it, the more they do it.

So we're going to have to convert what used to be report language into real law to prevent this administration from taking those actions. We Democrats have been trying to do that, but since we've been in the minority, we haven't been able to get that passed.

What if the administration still tries to hold up funds or ignore or veto Congress' actions?

This has been a lawless president, and he's still in the White House. But being in the majority will give us more leverage. If we're able to codify the safeguards that would prevent the Trump administration from diverting funds from their intended purpose to something else, that would be legally binding. Then you can go to the courts and say, you know this isn't simply report language. This is not just guidance. This is legally required, and so that does provide the safeguards that we would need.

Now we may have a back and forth and fight with the administration over providing those safeguards, but we're in a much stronger position now than we have been.

If the Democrats win the presidency and keep control of Congress in 2028, would the fate of USAID be revisited? Might the agency return? Or are there parts of the Trump administration's global health policy that you think are worth preserving or building on?

I don't think there's anything the Trump administration has done that's worth preserving or building on. That does not mean that I'm in favor of simply returning to the status quo prior to this administration.

I am a big believer that the role that USAID performed was both helpful to protecting the health of Americans but also helpful to developing good relations with other countries and the people of other countries. I think we need to develop our plan for how we perform this very important role as part of our foreign policy and as part of our health policy. But I'm not saying we would just go back exactly to the way USAID was.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews.
Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/chatgp.title: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/chatgp.author: Sarah Perez
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/chatgp.text:
ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots, help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express.

OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction.

The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app.

Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf.

It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own.

To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant.

The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions.

The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously.

It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead.

To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/nvidia.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/nvidia.author: Amanda Silberling
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/nvidia.text:
Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.

U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.

The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.

By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia.

Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.”

Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making.

In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy.

“Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states.

That same evening, Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) requested that Huang and Lutnick both testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

“The American people deserve answers,” Scott wrote on X.

After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia.

Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress, will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang.

Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993.

Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26.

“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”

The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed.

After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days.

Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said. The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan.

The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO.

According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year.

Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed.

The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.

Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.

Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.

In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.

On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.

When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”

Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.

Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.

An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.

Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.

The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump, has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.

Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.

Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.

Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.

These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.
