The subscription fee for newly launched Paprika 4 is well worth the price. And the free version is better, too.

The subscription fee for newly launched Paprika 4 is well worth the price. And the free version is better, too.

Nearly 10 years after the launch of Paprika 3, the recipe-managing, pantry-organizing, grocery list-making app has gotten a big upgrade that adds more functionality to nearly every corner of the experience. I tested Paprika 4 for several weeks while it was in open beta, and the update recently launched across Android (the version I’ve been using), iOS, Windows, and macOS.

Where Paprika 3 was a one-time purchase per platform, accessing most of the new features in Paprika 4 requires an annual subscription fee of $14.99 (it can also be gifted). With the subscription, you can access the app on any supported platform. New users, as well as those who bought Paprika 3 (or previous versions) but don’t want to pay for the subscription, will be moved to a free version of Paprika 4, which comes with a smaller selection of features that were available to test in beta, plus the ability to save up to 50 recipes.

Together, the new features locked behind the paywall make it possible to import recipes from social media and from physical cookbooks, scan product barcodes to organize your pantry or shopping list, and connect with other cooks via the app to share notes and recipes. They’re good, for the most part, and makes the subscription feel worth it. But the free version is upgraded in ways that make it worth trying if you’re hearing about Paprika for the first time.

My favorite of the new subscription-exclusive features solves a conundrum I often find myself in: My wife sends me a lot of recipe videos on Instagram.

Cape believes that private, secure communications are essential to free expression.

For too long, cell phone users have accepted the idea that sacrificing privacy is part of staying connected. Sharing and tracking one’s location, keeping a record of call logs and browsing history, and using a singular phone number as a digital identifier are par for the course to participate in the modern age.

Yet, as network-level cyberattacks and data breaches occur with greater intensity and frequency every year, cell phone privacy is more significant and under threat than ever. The statistics are grim: According to a 2024 survey, 36 percent of American journalists reported facing threats of or experiencing physical violence, while 97 percent of U.S. advocacy programs for domestic violence reported their clients have been harassed or monitored through technology. Victims often experience stalking and coercion through personal technology devices — a digital betrayal compounded by the constant flow of data that often includes sensitive medical, banking, and social media information, as well as access to friends and loved ones.

This is where Cape comes in. Its founders identified that threats of digital attacks go beyond the modern privacy stack: encrypted chat apps, VPNs (virtual private networks), private browsing, or phone-level settings like roaming and 5G.

“Even the most operationally diligent cell phone users still call and text their grandparents, schools, doctors, and banks, revealing patterns of life and allowing persistent tracking,” says Cape CEO John Doyle. “If advances in tech are supercharging the bad guys, we need to be innovating on behalf of regular people who don’t want a gradual erosion of privacy to be the price of technological progress.”

Cape’s privacy approach begins with collecting the minimum amount of data needed to provide service, then deleting it in days rather than keeping it stored indefinitely, or worse, selling it to data brokers. From there, the goal of Cape is to reduce a user’s digital footprint, which can reveal the patterns of a user’s life and allow for persistent tracking or leaks of sensitive metadata. Standard solutions like burner phones and encryption apps no longer cut it; instead, disruptions to privacy are ingrained within the foundation of cellular architecture itself.

Defending user privacy involves controlling the “mobile core,” the central brain of a cellular network that governs how devices authenticate and transmit data. These are some of the key ways Cape is working toward just that.

Every phone has an IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity), a 15-digit number assigned to your phone by a mobile carrier, which appears whenever your phone connects to a network. With sufficient access from carriers, governments, or bad actors, your location and travels can be tracked and surveilled over time. Cape offers the rare ability to rotate this network identity on a daily basis to all its subscribers—a feature previously only available through the purpose-built Cape Obscura device.

Like a driver’s license or passport, one’s phone number has become a form of identification. While it’s convenient for signing up, logging in, or two-factor authentication, it carries myriad risks that range from spam calls to privacy data breaches. Cape offers two additional alias phone numbers for every user, which can be used to sign up for newsletters or online shopping, while leaving one’s real number private and reserved for friends and loved ones. Cape’s Secondary Numbers are also middle-to-end encrypted, so they’re safe to use for things like 2FA codes. It’s a step above common services like VoIP (Voice over IP), whose numbers are rarely encrypted and often insufficient for authenticating with apps.

Your call log can reveal a lot about you: who you talked to, how long you spoke, and where you called from. Most calls can be easily forgotten, but the data can live on within a carrier’s database for up to five years. Instead of retaining this data (i.e., for monetization purposes), Cape deletes call logs after 24 hours. Because Cape runs its own mobile core, unlike other MVNOs (mobile virtual network operators), Cape is able to produce its own logs and delete them soon after. Not only does this policy prevent your call log data from being sold, but it also shields it against all-too-familiar data breaches that affect hundreds of millions, conducted by hackers who don’t even have to try very hard these days.

We take the network coverage on our cell phones for granted, with easy access to the major operators that control the physical cellular towers across the U.S. However, access to just one network isn’t always optimal, as it makes your traffic easier to trace. Enter Cape’s Multi-Network Coverage. Cape offers subscribers access to two major domestic roaming networks, Alpha and Tango, and allows users to seamlessly switch between the two within the Cape app with the press of a button. Spreading your traffic across two domestic roaming networks not only makes it harder to be tracked, but it also enables better coverage: If you lose signal on one network, Cape will automatically try the other, so you stay connected more often, especially in rural areas.

To make Cape available to more of the people who need it the most, like journalists and activists, Cape works with the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which has promoted digital privacy and free expression since 1990, to provide free Cape service. Cape also provides its subscribers with discounted access to Proton Unlimited or Proton VPN Plus.

Cape’s service costs $99/month, which is comparable to rates from today’s major carriers. But early adopters who switch to Cape this year get their monthly service cost reduced to $70/month and retain those savings for life. The plan includes benefits you expect from major carriers, like unlimited talk and text, but its host of additional features could ensure that you can take control over a key aspect of your modern life: genuine digital privacy.

Black Friday is still a couple weeks away, but you can already save on 3D printers, chargers, robot vacuums, and more.

Black Friday is still a couple weeks away, but you can already save on 3D printers, chargers, robot vacuums, and more.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The countdown to Black Friday is on, and the discounts are starting to appear. Although the shopping holiday isn’t officially until November 27th, retailers are already dropping early deals on some of our favorite tech. Of course, with prices rising across the board, a good discount doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting a historically low price. But we’re still seeing worthwhile discounts on a host of tried-and-tested gear, with more expected in the coming weeks.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best early Black Friday deals we’ve found so far. Prices could drop further as Black Friday approaches, as is always the case, but these deals are worth considering if you’d rather shop early and beat the holiday rush. We’ll continue to update this guide as more retailers launch their holiday sales, too, so be sure to check back regularly as we get closer to the main event.

The SN850P M.2 SSD with a heatsink is a great, competitively-priced option for PlayStation 5 and PC owners alike. It offers fast performance and a bunch of extra storage at a price we don’t commonly see these days.

You likely won’t find wireless earbuds with a more striking appearance than Nothing’s Ear 3A. Additionally, these sound fantastic, and boast active noise cancellation. Read our review.

The Quest 3S is a standalone VR headset with the same chipset as the pricier Quest 3, but with the same lenses and screen resolution as the Quest 2. There are plenty of great Meta Store VR games, and it can also be connected to a gaming PC to play demanding games like Half-Life Alyx. Read our review.

This more affordable, more streamlined version of the Max has a slightly smaller battery (16 hours versus 20), and lacks external power bank functionality, but is otherwise the same as the pricier Max, and just as good at delivering excellent audio.

Despite being an entry-level variant of the B6 OLED, this model features four HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, a capable processor, and pixel-perfect image quality and contrast for any content you want to watch. Lower brightness is likely the biggest compromise with getting a cheaper OLED.

Ember’s latest smart mug is designed to keep your coffee at the ideal temperature for up to three hours, with five temp settings between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The third-gen version is similar to prior models; however, you can now adjust the heat settings directly on the mug and throw it in the dishwasher, which wasn’t the case before.

Hisense’s 2026 CanvasTV is a 4K QLED TV that doubles as wall art when you’re not watching. It features a matte, anti-glare display and runs on Google’s excellent TV software; it’s also a great pick for gamers thanks to its snappy 144Hz variable refresh rate and a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports.

The Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo is a beginner-friendly 3D printer that supports four filament spools. It features an enclosed build chamber, automatic bed leveling, and a large touchscreen, making it easy to produce reliable prints.

Moft’s Trackable Tripod Wallet is a MagSafe-compatible wallet that holds two cards and folds into an adjustable phone stand or small tripod. It also supports both Apple’s Find My network and Google’s Find Hub, offers Qi wireless charging, and includes a detachable shutter remote for taking photos.

Govee’s Christmas lights offer over 130 preset lighting effects, though you can also create your own custom light displays. The IP65-rated lights feature Matter support, so they’ll work with any major smart home platform, and are sold in lengths up to 328 feet with up to 1,000 LED beads.

Govee’s Table Lamp 2 is way more fun than your average table lamp. The color-changing device boasts built-in scheduling and more than 60 dynamic lighting effects, including preset scenes for various holidays. You can even create custom color combos for when “Dandelion” and other presets just aren’t cutting it.

Birdfy’s metal smart bird feeder features a wide-angle 4K camera that lets you get an up-close look at visiting birds, along with a 1.8-liter seed capacity and a built-in solar panel for charging. It also offers free AI-powered recognition of more than 6,000 bird species.

Tessan’s universal travel adapter delivers up to 205W of combined USB charging power and can charge up to eight devices, including a pair of laptops, at the same time. It features six USB-C ports, including two that can deliver up to 140W individually, a USB-A port, and an AC outlet. It also works in over 200 countries and regions.

Bambu Lab’s P2S Combo is a 3D printer that can print in multiple colors and automatically dry its materials to help improve print quality. It also features a 5-inch touchscreen, a built-in camera for monitoring prints remotely, and AI-powered tools that can detect printing problems.

The Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets, thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets.

Eight Sleep’s Pod 6 automatically adjusts your bed’s temperature based on your sleep patterns, heart rate, and breathing. It features a redesigned hub that’s half the size of its predecessor and adjusts temperatures faster. The system also tracks sleep quality, detects snoring, and lets couples control the temperature on each side of the bed independently.

Flextail’s Zero Pump 2 might weigh a mere 1.7 ounces, but it can quickly inflate and deflate a sleeping pad. It comes with six nozzles and a replaceable battery that recharges via USB-C, allowing you to inflate up to 30 pads on a single charge.

The last-gen Litter-Robot 4 can monitor your cat’s visits, track their weight, and automatically separate waste from clean litter after each use, so you can go up to eight days without emptying your cat’s litter box. The so-called starter bundle also includes 20 pounds of litter, 25 waste drawer liners, a host of odor-control accessories, a litter-trapping mat, and a three-year warranty.

Headspace makes it easier to build mindfulness into your everyday life, whether you’re looking to manage stress, improve focus, or get a better night’s sleep. An annual subscription gives you access to hundreds of guided meditations, breathing exercises, and other tools for beginners and experienced users alike.

Part of Casetify’s early Black Friday sale, which offers up to 50 percent off select phone case styles, this Moonaries Illo case features playful artwork from the illustrator behind Mocha Cat. It’s available for the iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro, and other iPhone models.

The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Which science fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Emily H. Wilson
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
New Scientist has always been interested in science fiction and its attempts to imagine the future. In 1958, when the magazine was 2 years old, it published an article by Ian S. Menzies in which he wrote: “Like every other form of literature, s. f. ranges from excellent to awful. But the best of science fiction today is far superior to much other fiction.” Elsewhere in the feature, Menzies talked about the risks of the “rapid catching up of reality with fiction”.

It’s true that some of the sci-fi he was reading then was rapidly overtaken by events and, in the process of that, rendered redundant. What Menzies couldn’t know was that other works from that same period would still be regarded as prescient, important or relevant, or even all three, decades later.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dreaming of a bright and shiny future filled with personal jet packs, levitating autos, and automated gadgets straight out of "The Jetsons?" Add in a gritty mystery, a notorious private eye, double-crossing aliens, and a bombshell diva framed for a killing, and you’ve got the perfect recipe for "Ray Gunn."

Oscar-winning director Brad Bird ("The Incredibles," "Ratatouille") returns to our screens with his new big-budget animated sci-fi project, "Ray Gunn," and this latest trailer has us primed.

"In Metropia, a gigantic city in an alternate future as seen from 1939, private eye Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell) is drawn into a case involving aliens, murder, and a multimedia starlet named Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson)," states the official synopsis.

Netflix Films and Skydance Animation's "Ray Gunn" is a stylistic pastiche of classic film noir tropes populated by down-and-out detectives and femme fatales living in the inspiring air of technological optimism viewed through a pre-war America lens.

Think "The Fifth Element" meets "Who Framed Roger Rabbit?" and "The Maltese Falcon," and you’re going to be close to this sci-fi whodunnit's vibe, which is intended for more mature audiences and rated PG.

This energetic new preview is locked and loaded with dazzling visuals by Cinesite, freaky creatures, streamlined flying cars, and a blistering pace. And if you listen very closely, The B-52s' "Planet Claire" can be heard playing in the background, which is one of the touchstones that inspired Bird to begin his 36-year journey to bring "Ray Gunn" to life. Was it worth the wait? We'll have to find out.

Also starring the vocal talents of Tom Waits, Bobby Cannavale, Alan Tudyk, Matt Berry, and Michelle Rodriguez, "Ray Gunn" opens in select theaters and 70mm screenings Dec. 4. After that, it lands on Netflix on Dec. 18... a date you might want to circle on your calendar, as that’s also the release slot for "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Dune: Part 3."

It's going to be a busy day for sci-fi fans. "Strap in, buster!"

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: ‘Give back to yourself’: Flourishing as a provider
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

ORLANDO — Self-care can help healthcare providers truly flourish, according to a speaker here.

In her keynote presentation at the annual ACLM conference, Dawn Mussallem, DO, DipABLM, chief medical officer of Fountain Life in Jacksonville, Florida, discussed the importance of a healthcare provider’s vitality both for themselves and their patients.

Although flourishing is something that providers “aren’t very good [at] in our own lives,” Mussallem said that, if their own self-care is neglected, providers can carry exhaustion into the exam room with them.

In 2023, 45.2% of physicians reported burnout, according to one study Mussallem cited. Plus, physicians had an 82% higher likelihood of burnout than those in other occupations (OR = 1.82; 95% CI, 1.63-2.05). A 2022 study published in BMJ highlights the consequences of this: physician burnout was associated with double the patient safety incidents.

“We have to show up for ourselves,” Mussallem said. “I know we’re each in these unique experiences of being pulled in so many different directions, but we have our own unique life that we can’t lose sight of.”

However, she also highlighted that burnout levels move throughout time; for example, in the same 2023 study, researchers reported that 62.8% of providers felt burnt out in 2021, so the 45.2% number can be seen as an improvement.

“Five percent of the blood that the heart beats, it keeps for itself. You’ve got to show up for yourself in life,” she said. “Ninety-five percent of what it does is it’s feeding the rest of the body. And in life, that’s what each of you are doing. You are serving others. You are showing up for others in a way that you will never truly understand the impact of.”

But keeping that 5% is what makes giving the 95% possible, Mussallem said.

“Give back to yourself; 95% is showing up for the needs of others through that lens of love for humanity, and service and compassion,” she said. “When you take your own medicine, others are going to follow you because you’re going to be the biggest source of inspiration, and that’s going to move every single life you touch.”

Mussallem D. Keynote: Choose fully alive: Lifestyle medicine and the science of restoration, resilience and human flourishing. Presented at: Lifestyle Medicine Conference; Nov. 8-11, 2026; Orlando.

https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.title: Speaker: Cybersecurity becoming important aspect of AI governance
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.author: Lucas Laboy
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

ORLANDO — Cybersecurity has become a critical component of AI governance, according to a speaker at AIMed26.

Dennis Chornenky, founder and CEO of DomeLabs, discussed how the rapid evolution of AI is correlated to an increasing need for cybersecurity awareness and control.

“When AI governance is narrowly defined as a compliance checklist, cybersecurity and value realization remain siloed, creating critical gaps where the greatest risks often emerge,” Chornenky told Healio. “Today’s rapidly evolving AI landscape demands an integrated approach to governing, securing and continuously measuring the value of AI systems.”

According to Chornenky, AI is being used defensively to improve threat detection, for incident responses and investigative needs, among others. Conversely, AI is also being used for malicious attacks, including phishing scams, deepfakes, malware and AI-enabled autonomous attacks, he said.

As a result, AI-related cyberattacks have exponentially increased, Chornenky said.

“AI-related cyber incidents are growing at a rate of 10 times faster than regular cyber incidents,” he said.

Chornenky highlighted several risks that may impact individuals and hospitals as AI adoption increases at a rapid rate, including data leaks and model theft. He cited one particular risk to look out for: shadow AI.

“Shadow AI is ... people using consumer or personal instances of AI and putting organizational information into those personal instances in order to try to make their work more efficient,” Chornenky said. “It’s not necessarily malicious intent, but it’s a huge security problem.”

Overall, Chornenky said AI cybersecurity is “a core component of AI governance and not a separate afterthought.”

Chornenky highlighted areas for hospital systems to keep track of and adopt AI, starting by developing an AI cybersecurity framework, AI use policies and ensuring transparency and exit options with AI vendors.

“Clinicians are essential partners in this shared responsibility, helping identify risks, evaluate real-world performance and ensure AI delivers meaningful improvements in patient care,” Chornenky told Healio.

Chornenky D. Why AI governance is not enough. Presented at: AIMed26; Nov. 11-13, 2026; Orlando.

Disclosures: Chornenky reports being CEO of DomeLabs. Healio is an official media partner of the AIMed26 conference.

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/t%C.author: Marc PERELMAN
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/t%C.text:
Salih, a former Iraqi president who was himself once a refugee, took the helm of UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, in January. He regretted that the war in Sudan, now in its fourth year, has displaced millions and that "hundreds of thousands of people have been killed and maimed and traumatised".

"For this to happen in the 21st century is really embarrassing, to say the least. It's shameful," he said, calling for "a political solution to bring this conflict to an end".

Salih said the impact of US funding cuts had been "drastic", while noting that the EU had increased its support to his agency. He outlined how the funding cuts complicate UNHCR's mission. In Adré, Chad, the agency could only provide refugees with "eight litres of water per person per day", he explained, and a community of some 60,000 refugees in Gambela, Ethiopia, has "only one doctor". "This is not acceptable," the UN refugee chief said.

Salih warned that the asylum system was "under threat" amid a debate he described as "politicised and even weaponised". "Asylum is not competing with immigration control. They are in fact complementary," he argued.

https://www.dw.com/en/ice-hockey-russia-.title: Ice hockey: Russia threatens against Canada and Germany over exclusion from tournaments
https://www.dw.com/en/ice-hockey-russia-.text:
A fortnight after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak added after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed on Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to play in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Canadian Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said in a statement. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following last month's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling, in which it said that the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient – the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

Norway then said it had been bumped from the World Juniors and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated that they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14. With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport said on Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the (German) ice hockey federation (DEB), nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a World Championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport—and ice hockey in particular—find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hardline on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to pointing the way forward for the men's tournament in Germany next May.
https://www.dw.com/en/ice-hockey-russia-.summary: Russia threatens to take legal action against two tournament hosts. Russia has threatened to impose sanctions on Canada and Germany. Canada confirmed on Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to play in the IIHF World Junior Championship. Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and Canada.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrk.title: Education minister cleared over Israel trip
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrk.text:
The Education Minister Paul Givan did not breach the ministerial code over a trip to Israel, according to the Assembly Commissioner for Standards.

The week-long trip, paid for by the Israeli government in October 2025, led to a no-confidence motion in Givan in the assembly.

However, the motion failed to get cross-community support.

In a statement following the publication of the commissioner's report, Givan accused those behind the no-confidence motion of "an attempted political lynching".

During his trip, Givan visited a school in east Jerusalem, and a post about the visit was put on the Department of Education (DE) website and social media.

The minister also faced criticism from the body which represents Northern Ireland's main teaching unions over the trip.

The Assembly's Commissioner for Standards investigates complaints against members of the legislative assembly (MLAs) and ministers in the Northern Ireland Executive.

They launched an investigation into Givan's Israel trip following a number of complaints and questions.

Those included whether Givan had taken the trip in his role as minister or as an MLA, the use of Department of Education resources and public funds, and whether the trip had breached the political impartiality of the civil service.

But the commissioner did not uphold the complaints and found that Givan had not breached the ministerial code by going on the trip to Israel.

MLAs on Stormont's cross-party Standards Committee had also asked the commissioner to investigate whether Givan had attended the trip as an MLA as "his letter to the Israeli Minister of Foreign Affairs accepting the invitation was as minister of education and on DE headed paper".

The committee also queried why officials in the minister's private office had supported him by "requesting travel options, checking luggage allowance on flights, finalising travel details and relaying itinerary information".

The committee said that could breach the political impartiality of the civil service.

But the standards commissioner found that Givan had gone to Israel in his capacity as an MLA, and that the work on the trip by departmental officials was "negligible and not inappropriate".

"Mr Givan, in interview described the visit as a cultural, fact-finding exchange and an opportunity to experience and hear from people," the commissioner's report said.

"The press release issued by Mr Givan on the department website contained no political opinion or commentary."

Givan has welcomed the commissioner's report and the conclusion that he had not breached the ministerial code.

In a strongly-worded statement on the DE website, Givan said the assembly had been "turned into a kangaroo court," when the no-confidence motion against him had been debated.

"The commissioner's report carefully examines every aspect of the trip and exposes the falsehoods at the heart of the motion that was tabled," he said.

"In a rush to judgement by nationalist MLAs and the Alliance Party, all objectivity was set aside and instead they opted for an attempted political lynching."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrk.summary: Education Minister Paul Givan was paid for by the Israeli government in October 2025. A no-confidence motion in the assembly failed to get cross-community support. Givan accused those behind the no- confidence motion of "an attempted political lynching"

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/techn.title: Jensen Huang’s Resignation From Nvidia Worries the A.I. Start-Up World
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/techn.author: Erin Griffith and Cory Weinberg
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/techn.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

Mr. Huang championed start-ups, with Nvidia holding $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July.

By Erin Griffith and Cory Weinberg

Reporting from San Francisco

For years, Jensen Huang was a frequent presence at Silicon Valley start-up events, networking with founders, judging pitch competitions and showing up at “demo” days.

The Nvidia chief executive became a godlike figure in the start-up ecosystem, not just because the industry idolized him as one of the world’s most successful entrepreneurs. Mr. Huang, 63, also made it his mission to help start-ups gain a foothold against the industry’s biggest and most powerful tech companies, providing funding and computing power.

“As many good ideas as we have, you don’t have all the world’s good ideas,” he said on the Acquired podcast in 2023.

So Mr. Huang’s abrupt resignation from Nvidia on Thursday has investors and start-up founders nervous that they have lost a powerful ally.

“Nvidia is the central bank of A.I. and all of a sudden, the Fed chairman is out,” said Tomasz Tunguz, an investor at Theory Ventures, which funds young start-ups.

Nvidia held $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including large stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July, according to securities filings. It more than doubled its start-up investments in six months.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: UK-EU deal will ‘dissolve’ £60m a year of costs for plant trade, says Angela Eagle
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Joanna Partridge
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Signing of agreement to smooth movement of food, plants and animals next week will not recoup huge sums firms were forced to spend

The removal of border checks and paperwork on plant imports will “dissolve” £60m of annual costs for the horticulture industry when the UK and EU’s new post-Brexit deal comes in, the environment secretary has said.

Before the UK-EU summit on 20 November, Angela Eagle said she hopes paperwork headaches for importers will “disappear” after the changes, although the move will not help businesses recoup the large sums they spent to deal with border controls.

“If we get the ink dry on 20 November, which I very much hope we will … all of that uncertainty, the extra cost, the paperwork and the potential problems if things get stuck at borders would all disappear,” Eagle told the Guardian during a visit to a plant nursery in Kent.

“The cost, that £60m, can just dissolve and people’s potential to both export back into the EU and get their imports in … gets easier and more predictable.”

The UK’s departure from the bloc triggered the introduction of border checks on imports and exports of plants, food and animal products, from sausages and cheese to trees and leather goods.

Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit, according to analysis by the National Farmers’ Union, with egg, chicken and potato producers badly affected.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal, largely agreed between the two sides in May, is due to be signed at next week’s summit. It will permit the removal of the vast majority of physical checks and most of the accompanying certificates and paperwork.

This will save businesses in the horticulture sector the current cost of trading with Europe, including plant health inspection fees, phytosanitary certificates, document and ID checks, port fees, agents’ fees, additional labour costs and extra haulage costs.

These costs total £60m a year, according to calculations by the industry body the Horticultural Trades Association (HTA), but do not include late delivery penalties or sales lost because of port delays or damage to goods.

These savings should put “downward pressure on food prices”, Eagle said, although she would not confirm the deal would lower the cost of food in the UK.

The promise of the deal was welcomed by Provender Nurseries, one of the UK’s largest wholesale nurseries, which sells thousands of plants, trees and shrubs to local authorities, parks and landscapers from its base at Swanley in Kent.

However, the company has already spent at least £500,000 on building a post-Brexit control post on its eight-hectare (20-acre) site, which will become obsolete once the deal is implemented.

Richard McKenna, the managing director of Provender, said the business constructed the “sealed building and bought four electric forklifts to operate in it” to allow inspections of lorry loads of valuable trees and shrubs imported from the continent.

The company decided to build the site to reduce the “delays and damage” it has experienced when smaller loads are inspected at government-run border control posts such as Sevington.

“It cost a lot for a barn, but it gave us security as a business,” said McKenna.

Despite this, McKenna hopes the SPS deal will convince some of Provender’s European suppliers, previously deterred by the paperwork and potential pitfalls of post-Brexit trade with the UK, to restart exports.

“We need to see the small print on the agreement,” he said. “It could have been sooner, but we are pleased that it is happening.”

The deal is not expected to be implemented until the first quarter of 2028, meaning businesses such as Provender will still be subject to the current border arrangements for more than a year.

In the meantime, Fran Barnes, the chief executive of the HTA, called for “some easements as a transition arrangement that are pragmatic” to help horticulture businesses, such as fewer or no checks on imports of lower-risk products.

Eagle conceded the implementation date was later than the mid-2027 targeted when former prime minister Keir Starmer announced his EU “reset” deal in May 2025.

Starmer’s replacement by Andy Burnham led to a “pause” in negotiations with Brussels, said Eagle, with the upcoming November summit pushed back from July.

The original target was “always a very, very ambitious timescale,” she said. “That extra time has meant we could deal in more coherent way with some of the knottier, thornier issues on things like pesticides.”

The UK has continued to use some pesticides and fungicides that are banned in the EU.

This has prompted industry concerns that British potatoes grown in 2027, treated with pesticides banned in the EU, could need to be thrown away if the resulting frozen chips went on sale after the deal’s implementation.

“We are very well aware of these kinds of issues and the EU is also very aware it doesn’t want to be seen to be wasting food,” Eagle said.

British exporters of produce including seed potatoes and some mussels also hope the SPS deal will allow trade halted by Brexit to restart.

“We have been waiting for this moment, but it all depends on the timing of the deal,” said Adam Taylor, a director of Taylors Bulbs in Lincolnshire, which supplies tulip, daffodil and other bulbs to garden centres and nurseries across the UK and Ireland.

A Brexit certification disagreement halted exports of British seed potatoes, particularly from Scotland, to the EU. Taylors underwent the “laborious and expensive” work of setting up an Irish business in order to keep suppling the Republic of Ireland.

“When things go back closer to how they were before Brexit, I hope our Irish customer base will reflect on the loyalty given to them,” he said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Truck and bus crash in India’s Assam state kills at least 24 people
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
At least 24 people have been ⁠⁠killed and 11 others injured, after a container truck collided with a bus in ⁠⁠India’s northeastern state of Assam, police said.

The crash happened on Friday on a highway in Golaghat district, near Kaziranga National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site famous for its one-horned rhinos, about 225km (140 miles) east of the state capital, Dispur.

Several children and the bus driver were among the dead, officials said, as Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said on X he was “deeply distressed by the tragic accident”.

“The scale of this loss has shaken all of us, and my heart goes out to every family that has lost a loved one. No words can ease their pain, but I want them to know that they are not alone. All of Assam stands with them in this hour of grief,” Sarma said.

He added that local authorities were at the site and “personally overseeing the relief arrangements … to make sure the injured receive the best possible medical care without delay”.

Swapnaneel Deka, superintendent of police of Golaghat district, told the Reuters news agency that “it is likely the death toll will increase”. He said the bus ⁠⁠was travelling to a neighbouring district, with about 30 people on board.

India has one of the highest rates of road fatalities in the world, with accidents happening regularly in part due to poorly maintained roads and vehicles.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: The bus was travelling to a neighbouring district, with about 30 people on board. The bus driver and several children were among the dead, officials said. India has one of the highest rates of road fatalities in the world, with accidents happening regularly in part due to poorly maintained roads and vehicles.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Europe seeks seat at Ukraine peace talks but lacks unified voice
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
European nations are debating who may be their representative in Russia-Ukraine peace talks while the continent’s leaders spar with Russia over their participation in future negotiations.

Whether Europe should be represented by one person or a team – and who should take on the role – was debated on Friday as leaders of the 27-nation European Union (EU) met at a summit in Dublin, Ireland. Senior EU officials and politicians have been suggested, but there is no consensus yet.

What the job might entail is also unclear and contested. However, EU leaders have broadly agreed on the need for Europe to join the ongoing trilateral negotiations between Washington, Kyiv and Moscow.

The EU is concerned that a United States-backed process will allow Moscow and Washington to decide the fate of a war that has embroiled the continent.

After talks in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, US envoys said that Europe would join future negotiations – but the Kremlin appeared to slam the brakes on that plan, saying no decision had been made.

German ⁠Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday pleaded for ⁠US President Donald Trump to create no ⁠surprises during expected talks with Putin in China next week.

“Some here in Dublin fear this could turn into a ‘second Anchorage moment’,” ⁠said Merz on ⁠the sidelines of the EU meeting, a reference to the Alaska summit where they were stunned by Trump’s overtures to the Russian leader in the absence of Ukrainian or European envoys.

“I therefore ⁠want to state ⁠our message to ⁠the United States very clearly: please, no surprises. Continue ‌to play as part of ‘Team Europe’ ‌and ‘Team ‌Ukraine’.”

Kyiv is eager for support from European allies, but Russia does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, arguing they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort.

European leaders have discussed whether Europe should be represented by one person or a team.

Supporters of a single envoy, like Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, argue that the absence of a united European voice has allowed individual countries or small groups to engage in freelance diplomacy.

“There are too many different groupings discussing the issue,” she said.

The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, laid claim to the envoy role on Friday, saying, “I’m the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy.”

“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but, you know, do we have a say, ‘Who is representing Russia?’” she said. “We can’t send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending.”

Al Jazeera’s Milena Veselinovic, reporting from the summit in Dublin, said: “Kaja Kallas is putting herself forward for that role and for many she would be the natural choice – she is the voice for the EU on foreign policy.”

However, “there isn’t unanimous support behind her”, as Kallas is seen by many as “uncompromising” on Russia, she added.

Kallas is far from the only player in this game; European Council President Antonio Costa is also a top contender for the role.

US and Russian diplomats have criticised Europe for not being united.

After the US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia in the United Arab Emirates this week, US envoy Jared Kushner said that “if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.”

Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said the Kremlin has not confirmed that Putin agreed to expand the trilateral talks to include Europe.

Even though Russian officials say they are ready to talk with European leaders, they have also criticised Europe, our correspondent said, noting that Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has even compared European leaders to “spiders in a jar”.

“During the Thursday meeting here at the Kremlin, the Russian side spoke about a revision of security architecture in Europe,” Shapovalova said. But “at the same time, Moscow refuses to keep EU leaders at the negotiating table during the peace talks,” she noted.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: EU leaders have discussed whether Europe should be represented by one person or a team. The EU is concerned that a United States-backed process will allow Moscow and Washington to decide the fate of a war that has embroiled the continent. The Kremlin has not confirmed that Putin has agreed to expand the trilateral talks to include Europe.

https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1024777.title: The Verge’s 2026 gift guide for dads
https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1024777.author: Ryan Waniata
https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1024777.text:
This year, why not get Dad a gift or two he won’t expect?

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Gone are the days when you could just buy your father a random tie or some leather-clad alcohol vessel or a shaving kit. Dads want — nay, deserve — something memorable. Luckily for you, it’s not that hard to find something special that he’ll approve of, and we’re here to guide you.

We’ve curated this year’s gift list with the modern father in mind, whether he’s a gamer, creator, chef, or simply a gadget lover. There’s a lot in here we think he’ll like, from noise-canceling headphones like the Sonos Ace Ultra and an autonomous drone to a brilliant QD-OLED monitor and a nifty light that’s perfect for illuminating his next campsite. Whatever your dad is into, we’ve got you covered.

Antigravity’s A1 is the ultimate gadget for the dad who dreams of owning the sky. The compact drone comes with specialized goggles that will make him feel like he’s in the cockpit, and it records always-on, 360-degree 8K video. It’s an exhilarating flight experience and an excellent creator’s tool in one slick package.

Cleaning gadgets like Dyson’s PencilVac FluffyCones are never cheap, but they’re often worth the cost and a pleasure to use. The lightweight, broom-replacing stick vacuum doesn’t do carpets, but its rolling bars pack incredible cleaning power for touching up hard floors, including stairs.

For those who love travel but hate the constraints of a hotel TV, Belkin’s ConnectAir is a slick solution. Plug the transmitter into any device with a USB-C video-out port and the receiver into the TV’s HDMI port, and voilà, you’re easily (and wirelessly) connected.

Sonos raised its headphones game on all fronts with the Ace Ultra, which deliver better noise canceling, improved sound, and the feature we’ve all been waiting for: Wi-Fi support. With the ability to bounce audio across your Sonos ecosystem, including from a TV via newer Sonos soundbars, Dad’s sonic sanctuary is finally complete.

Werewolf’s affordable dongle kit provides an almost magical way to power nearly any DC device from a USB-C charger or portable battery. Program it from a mobile app, connect it to your old gear, and everything from a PC monitor to an original Game Boy can accept USB-C charging.

Who would have thought a simple hook could make roaming the city with a backpack so much more convenient? After testing Peak Design’s well-designed bags, we’re convinced the clever addition is a game-changer for anyone who doesn’t want to leave their bag on the filthy ground.

WiiM’s first soundbar builds on its seamless Sonos-esque connectivity with a sleek design, detailed sound, and up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. It also pairs with other speakers for surround sound through a no-fuss setup process, including ones you already own that are linked to one of WiiM’s amplifiers.

Your dad needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.

If your dad is still reading books on his phone (or aging e-reader), it’s time for an upgrade. The latest in Amazon’s series of waterproof, auto-dimming e-readers loads books faster than the prior model and offers a slick aluminum upgrade. No matter which you choose, it’s a better way to bring the library along.

Give your father a little nostalgia and a lot of convenience in one package with this stylish USB-C dock and SSD combo gadget. The cassette-shaped Sharge Disk Pro 2 works as a hub with support for HDMI at 4K, SD and microSD card slots, USB-A and USB-C ports, along with up to 8TB of storage stored within.

Smart TVs are often pretty dumb. If your dad is always complaining about his TV, or if you want to get ahead of it, grab the latest Apple TV 4K. Although it’s not cheap, it stands out with built-in mics for Siri AI, lots of power, HomePod surround sound support, and a simple, ad-free interface.

The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.

Oura didn’t reinvent the wheel with the Ring 5, but it did reshape it into a slimmer, thinner, more wearable design that could make all the difference. Inside are the same extensive health and fitness tracking features for charting everything from sleep to heart health, backed by long battery life.

The CS-Pro will make your dad feel like a private eye in the early ’80s. The retro-inspired digital camera serves up 16-megapixel stills and offers four filters accessible from its tactile dial, plus USB-C charging, a high-quality Xenon flash, and a 4GB SD card for plenty of vintage photo fun.

BougeRV’s fancy, compact lamp will spark joy for the glamper in your life, as well as everyone else. Its powerful, foldable spread of LEDs provides a blast of light anywhere plug-ins can’t reach, from the beach to the shed where that scary spider holds court, with up to 60 hours of light on low power.

The Rival Pro offers plenty of thoughtful extras, including swappable batteries and an ultra-wideband base station for a seamless, low-latency connection. The gaming mouse’s lightweight design and 8,000Hz polling rate also deliver both accurate and ergonomic performance for up to 16 hours per charge.

It’s time to help Dad ditch his collection of plastic reusable cups, which have clearly seen better days. NotNeutral’s hand-pressed, timeless tumbler offers ’70s vibes with a modern twist, making it the perfect vessel for whatever Dad twists into his favorite drink.

Give the gift that fixes past home improvement transgressions. These handy Japanese-made pliers from Vampire Tools have one fundamental purpose — to remove stripped screws — and they’re damn good at it. The best part? Watching Dad’s face light up seconds before he sprints to the garage for them.

For the manga or live-action Netflix show lover on your list, this fashionable Pirates jersey, inspired by Monkey D. Luffy from the seminal pirate adventure series One Piece, will be as surprising as it is delightful.

If you’re after a cheap, useful stocking stuffer, Trond’s reliable three-prong extension cord is a practical pick that’s available in leftward or rightward configurations to fit nearly any outlet. Dad will probably say, “Oh, I’ve always wanted one of these,” and this time he’ll mean it.

Zero Company, a strategy game set in the twilight of the Clone Wars, is a fun way to get lost in the Star Wars universe. The single-player, turn-based title lets players command a diverse team of characters across a gorgeous expanse of worlds, offering hours of solitary entertainment.

If your father already owns an Apple Watch, the Nomad Stratos is a foolproof upgrade idea. The refined watch band features titanium links with a rubbery interior for durable comfort, and it comes in an array of subtle color options that make it as suitable for the office as it is for the slopes.

We fell for Apple’s handy iPhone strap due to its effortless accessibility and comfy design, which uses flexible magnets to keep excess segments in check. From biking to hiking to concerts, it’s a great way to sling your iPhone 18 Pro, assuming you have a compatible phone case.

The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.

Most of us have thousands of photos in the cloud, but if a photo never makes it into the real world, did it really happen? Existentialism aside, the Cricut StickerPix offers a new way to play with photos, providing you with everything you need to turn any picture into a pro-quality print or sticker.

This battery-powered fan is a big upgrade over your average plug-in job. As a 3D circulator, it can tilt to push air in all directions. It can be controlled from an app and even detaches from its stand to sit on a desk or tabletop. Quiet, powerful, and versatile, it’s equipped for nearly any adventure on or off the grid.

Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.

If your favorite cinephile is looking to get off the streaming carousel, the Kaleidescape Strato E is the key. The premium player lets library builders locally store and play their favorite films and TV shows in lossless 4K resolution with Dolby Atmos for sterling entertainment that’s all theirs.

Once The Great British Baking Show becomes an obsession, only a serious stand mixer will do for replicating recipes at home. This mixer’s timeless design adds new features in what KitchenAid calls its biggest upgrade since 1955, with a new half-speed setting and a control lever that lets you set speeds between its standard settings.

The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.

When it comes to jotting down notes, there’s nothing like a pen and paper. At least, that’s what we thought before we tried the Remarkable Paper Pure. Offering a strikingly realistic writing experience that saves everything in the digital realm, this tablet is a brilliant way to bridge the gap and save paper.

Electronics are becoming more sustainable, and Fairphone is leading the way. The Fairphone 6 Plus may seem like a regular Android phone on paper, but the ability to repair and replace its internals, from the screen to the battery, makes it anything but average.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/new-mi.title: New Mior and Skyfall Attacks Let Rogue Cloud Hosts Steal Secrets From AMD SEV-SNP VMs
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/new-mi.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/new-mi.text:
Two attacks made public this week allow a malicious host to read data inside AMD SEV-SNP-protected virtual machines (VMs), which are built to keep the server's operator out.

One of them, Mior, can also modify a VM's memory and fake the signed report confirming which software it runs. Both need control of the server's hypervisor, and Mior also needs control of the server's BIOS. Researchers showed both in lab tests on AMD EPYC server processors.

AMD, which makes the processors, lists SEV firmware for Mior and microcode for Skyfall, both dated August 12. It plans to give server makers platform firmware in November for Skyfall and in December for Mior, and fixes for embedded chips later. Customers are told to get the BIOS update from their server maker.

SEV-SNP brings confidential computing to AMD EPYC server processors. It uses hardware-enforced memory encryption and access control to protect a VM, even from the host's hypervisor.

The ETH Zurich team behind Mior attacked SEV-SNP while it was starting up. During start-up, a security co-processor on the chip, the Platform Security Processor (PSP), fills in a table called the Reverse Map Table (RMP). The RMP records who owns each page of memory and what they may do with it.

The team redirected the PSP's writes to the memory of a graphics card it controlled, instead of to main memory. The team used a card because it believes the PSP reads the values back to check them, and the card could return them. Start-up then finished without errors, but part of the real RMP, including the entry that protects the table itself, stayed uninitialized.

That let the hypervisor rewrite the RMP's protections. The team then enabled debugging on a confidential VM that had it disabled and used the PSP's own debug commands to read and write the VM's memory. This worked in all 1,000 attempts across both test runs.

SEV-SNP also measures a VM's software image when the VM starts, and the PSP signs attestation reports that include this measurement. In a second test, the team copied a harmless VM's measurement into a malicious VM, so the malicious VM's attestation reports described the harmless image instead.

The attack needs control of the hypervisor and the BIOS (also called UEFI), plus a PCIe device such as a graphics card, the Mior paper says. For the tests, the team modified the BIOS to leave the chip's memory-routing settings unlocked.

"We operate in AMD’s threat model defined for SEV-SNP. AMD explicitly distrusts the UEFI, thus an attacker can modify the UEFI," the researchers say.

Ordinary VMs already trust their host and its firmware, so Mior gives an attacker nothing new against them, the team says.

The team ran Mior on one EPYC 9135, a Zen 5 chip. It considers Zen 3 and Zen 4 chips potentially affected but did not test them because it had no setup that allowed it to change their BIOS.

The debugging and attestation tests both worked with ciphertext hiding turned on. That optional SEV-SNP feature stops the hypervisor from even reading encrypted VM memory.

Two earlier attacks by some of the same researchers, the Fabricked attack and the RMPocalypse attack, also corrupted the RMP as SEV-SNP started up. Mior is a separate flaw, unrelated to Fabricked and to the fix for it, the team says. It also worked on older firmware from before that fix.

Skyfall comes from a team at ETH Zurich and Google. It builds on Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA), a group of flaws in AMD processors that can leak data through instruction timing. TSA was first disclosed on July 8, 2025.

The team found that when a hypervisor intentionally causes a VM to fail to start, the processor has already cached part of the VM's saved state. That data is left behind without the usual cleanup, and the hypervisor can read it through TSA.

This way, the team recovered a VM's saved register values and a disk-encryption key from a test VM. For the key, it changed the VM's kernel to pause at the moment the key sat in registers. In a real attack, the team says, a hypervisor can instead use a technique called SEV-Step to step through the VM until the key reaches the registers.

Skyfall can also read VM memory, but only three fixed cache lines in a page it targets, at offsets 0x0c0, 0x380 and 0x3c0. The rest of the page stays out of reach.

The attack needs a malicious host or hypervisor, but no tampering with the hardware. The team tested it on an EPYC 7313, a Zen 3 chip, and on EPYC 9124 and 9334 chips, which are Zen 4. It did not show the leak on Zen 5 chips.

Beyond VMs, the Skyfall team read decrypted microcode updates on all three test chips. It also recovered register values stored in System Management Mode (SMM) memory, which even the operating system kernel normally cannot read. Both of these attacks need privileged software on the machine.

The program committee of the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, which accepted the Skyfall paper, said it overlooks what a realistic attack on VMs would need. That includes a processor core free of other activity, failing VM starts and performance-counter reads at high speed, and a VM that does not crash or time out during the attack.

AMD tracks Mior as CVE-2026-0462 and rates it 5.9 on the CVSS 4.0 scale in a security advisory. It tracks Skyfall's VM leak as CVE-2026-40671, rated 4.9, in a second advisory that describes the flaw as exposing VM register data.

For Mior, the company lists only SEV-SNP as affected, not the earlier SEV and SEV-ES versions.

It lists the same five EPYC server lines for both flaws, with these fixes:

The two advisories give the same TurinPI_1.0.0.C package different target months. Microcode for Skyfall is dated August 12 for each of these lines. The Instinct MI300A accelerator has a Skyfall patch dated September 21, and fixes for embedded EPYC models are due between January and April 2027.

The Mior team says updated firmware that mitigates the flaw is already out, and the Skyfall team says new microcode has been released. The advisories do not say whether those updates work on their own or only as part of the BIOS updates, and they list no workaround.

Supermicro, a server maker, has published a BIOS fix list covering flaws in dozens of its H12, H13, and H14 motherboards. The same pages say the boards also need a BMC firmware update and that the company is still testing affected products.

Because the fixes are implemented in the host's firmware, customers who rent confidential VMs depend on their cloud provider to install them. The advisory covering Mior also lists TCB (trusted computing base) values for SNP attestation next to each fixed firmware version. It does not say how VM owners should check them.

Neither advisory says whether the flaws have been used in attacks. Both teams have published code, and the Mior proof-of-concept code needs a BIOS patched to leave the memory-routing settings unlocked.

The EDK II project assigned Skyfall's SMM leak CVE-2026-18448 and rates it 5.6. AMD's EDK II bulletin traces it to missing TSA mitigations in EDK II firmware code.

The bulletin lists EPYC and Ryzen chips, including embedded models, and recommends the company's earlier TSA mitigations plus an EDK II patch when one is available.

For the five EPYC server lines listed above, the bulletin lists only that patch, due in November. Platform firmware with the fix is already available for other chips, including the EPYC 4004 and 4005 models. The EDK II project's own advisory lists no patched version as of today.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/us-nation.title: U.S. debt now equals the whole economy — and tax cuts since 2001 added over $10 trillion
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/us-nation.author: Hinckley Jones-Sanpei, The Conversation
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/us-nation.text:
Democrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy.

Clocking in at $32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living.

Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes. Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt.

The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found.

The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar, I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact. But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper, the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts.

I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing.

Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise.

U.S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen.

At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan think tank, noted.

President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis. The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth.

Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts.

While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1.5 trillion. That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025.

But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts.

The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3.4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034.

A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not.

If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable. The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well.

This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts, the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office.

In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats.

It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century.

Hinckley Jones-Sanpei, Public Policy Researcher, University of Denver

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwx2.title: Police investigating David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwx2.text:
The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over "alleged serious sexual offences".

It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITN and The Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".

When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".

"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.

Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."

Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.

Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/busin.title: Bessent Faults Commerce Dept. for Failing to Blacklist Megaspeed
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/busin.author: Ana Swanson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/busin.text:
Artificial Intelligence

The Treasury secretary blamed the department for not sanctioning the Singaporean firm and said that Nvidia employees should be held accountable if they sidestepped the law.

Reporting from Washington

Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, blamed the Commerce Department on Friday for the government’s failure to sanction the Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed, saying that other departments had pushed for the measure but that Commerce “has the pen.”

The Treasury, Defense and State Departments and the U.S. trade representative were all in favor of putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist called the entity list for months, but the Commerce Department is in charge of that authority, Mr. Bessent said on CNBC on Friday.

“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said, adding, “Treasury and my deputy has been pushing for this for months at the deputies level.”

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” he said. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

Frustration is boiling over within the administration and on Capitol Hill about Megaspeed, the company led by a woman U.S. intelligence deemed to be an asset for the Chinese government.

The woman, Alice Huang, had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang. Mr. Huang resigned from his company on Thursday in the wake of revelations about that and another affair, sending the company’s stock price cratering.
