Fox has officially acquired Roku and there are CONSEQUENCES. For one, the "Marine Aquarium" screensaver will no longer be available. One person posted on the "Mildly Infuriating" subreddit: "I can't believe it I love my fish what am I gunna do."

Jim Sachs' screensaver

The artist behind that screensaver, Jim Sachs, is NOT renewing his license due to Fox's acquisition. "It seems that Fox simply wants another venue for spreading their philosophy, which I consider repugnant. I can't stand the idea of my artwork being used to lure even one person down that rabbit hole," Sachs told Ars Technica. The licensing deal will have big personal consequences for Sachs, who relies on the $80,000 per year licensing deal. Another comment on the subreddit posted, "This is the last straw, Apple TV for me."

What to Know: Over the past decade, European countries have become increasingly reliant on U.S. technology to support their air defense systems. We're talking fighter jets & missile defense systems like the Patriot, which can intercept ballistic missiles. It seemed like an obvious choice: these are high-quality pieces of technology, they're readily available, and buying American keeps the U.S. committed to European defense. Here's the problem: the whole "readily available" thing doesn't seem to be true. There is a MAJOR backlog of missiles while demand just keeps going up. That's due to both production delays and the U.S.' own military needs in Iran. PLUS!! European countries that bought technology like the Patriot are now locked in to American equipment. They can't just switch to another supplier to get missiles.

Visitors queue to take a closer look at a Patriot missile launcher during the Armed Forces Day at the Airbase in Laage, Germany, on June 06, 2026. Along with nine other locations, Laage hosts the Armed Forces Day 2026.

Why this matters: You kind of want to know if you're not gonna get a few hundred missiles on time. While the U.S. is focused on the Iran war, threats from Russia still loom large in Europe. And now, many European nations are at the whim of these defense contracts panning out… having to put up with delays and higher costs. The article's authors look back and see a missed opportunity in 2022 for investment into homegrown systems: "Calls to Europeanise the funding and ordering of air defense systems were ignored and the strategic gap is now all too visible."

Business journalist and friend of the show Paddy Hirsch adds: "No one could have predicted the extent to which Trump would damage the relationship between the U.S. and Europe. But the fact is that Trump isn't the first president to beat the drum about European over-dependence on the US. He's just the first to really force the issue. And guess what? He was doing Europe a favor! Europe desperately needs to wean itself off the U.S. teat, and not just because of the unpredictability of a Presidential whim. But because there's no telling how U.S. and European interests will diverge over the next few decades."

What to Know: Spain has one of the lowest fertility rates in the world. It's currently at 1.1, meaning 100 women birth 110 children on average. To maintain the current population, rates would need to sit at 2.1. Immigration has kept the population from dropping dramatically since 2000, but the author offers a DIFFERENT solution to Spain's childbearing woes: more housing. Spain, like many countries, has struggled with expensive housing: prices have risen 81% between 2015 to 2025. The average age of leaving the parental home in Spain is 30.2 compared to 23.8 in France and 24.1 in Germany. The author asks: could an influx of public housing incentivize partners to start families earlier?

How realistic is this?: There's no hard evidence in the Elcano article showing more housing actually leads to a higher fertility rate. That said, Planet Money co-host Jeff Guo says the evidence for this argument does look stronger outside the U.S. There was literally a paper about this topic IN SPAIN that came out a few weeks ago. The paper found a 10% rise in local housing prices LOWERS birth rates by about 3% for women 20-34. In fact, the authors deduced that higher housing prices account for roughly HALF of the 2014-2022 implied fertility rate decline. In short: more expensive housing = fewer kids.

If you HAVEN'T listened: We all know the old adage "the stock market doesn't equal the economy." Well, lately, maybe it does!! At least more than usual. The "new era" economy (AI, tech etc.) has an outsized impact on the growth of both the stock market AND economic growth. That's all well and good, except hyper-concentration means hyper-risk. If AI stocks start to tumble, it could have a negative chain reaction on the economy in a uniquely problematic way. Two non-profits in the episode warn that the AI bubble is a thing. In short, the economy depends on the market! A downturn there is more likely to mean an economic downturn too. Diversification is important, people.

LISTEN TO THE FULL EPISODE

If you HAVE listened: You know that the economic risk isn't just about a market downturn. It's about the impacts that follow. Consumer spending is driving much of economic growth, and that's led by wealthy spenders. Another downstream risk: pension funds hold debt related to the AI buildout, according to the report from the Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund. They argue this has exposed pension funds and even ordinary workers to dangerous risk! Reporter Wailin Wong says, "That's something I wasn't able to get into in the episode, since we were focused on stocks and not debt. But certainly the credit markets are a huge part of this story too."

Reporter Ricky Mulvey read A Violent Masterpiece

It's a profane, no-holds-barred thriller. Jordan Harper wrote on TV shows in Hollywood before getting disillusioned with the industry and writing about some of its seedier parts in novels.

A Violent Masterpiece follows three storylines that converge around a suspicious death in a jail cell. It's Eyes Wide Shut meets LA Confidential.

Two things I really admire about Harper's work.

A Violent Masterpiece is a perfect book to rip through on a plane if you are traveling for the holidays. A genteel reader should stay far away, and sickos should pick it up. The story is far from perfect; you'll see why at the ending. I loved it.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Jasper Jolly
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
JLR chief executive calls for EU and Britain to join forces amid competition from Chinese electric carmakers

Jaguar Land Rover has reported a £451m quarterly loss as it counts the cost of cutting 4,000 jobs, while its chief executive has called for the EU and Britain to work together in the face of competition from China.

Britain’s largest automotive employer reported revenues rising to £5.9bn between July and September, but it recorded £530m in costs from the job cuts announced near the end of that period amid tough trading conditions.

JLR said it expected the vast majority of the job cuts to be achieved via voluntary redundancies, with 3,000 already confirmed. Most of those people will leave at the end of November.

JLR said it had scraped into profit from its operations if it ignored the restructuring costs, but it was hurt by falling sales in China and the Middle East.

Many European carmakers are struggling as they face competition from Chinese rivals at the same time as they invest in electric car production.

PB Balaji, JLR’s chief executive, said on Friday the “onslaught of competition” from China meant the UK and EU should stop plans for new post-Brexit trade barriers on each other.

The automotive industry is lobbying the UK and EU intensely to delay the implementation of “rules of origin” on 1 January, which threaten to impose 10% tariffs on UK-EU electric cars that use batteries from Asia. The EU is also considering “made in Europe” rules that would lock UK-made cars out of subsidies.

“Now is the time for actually fostering this entire electrical ecosystem,” Balaji said. “It’s so important for us that we all hold hands, stick together and ensure that we get the system to evolve into the world of electrics.”

He added: “We just need time to ensure all these plans start coming into fruition.”

The company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata, previously sought to target China for growth, only to write off billions in investments in 2019 as a new wave of Chinese carmakers led to massive overcapacity in the country.

JLR, which was last year hit by a devastating hack, is targeting growth in the US, where it is in the process of agreeing a deal for the Chrysler owner, Stellantis, to manufacture Land Rovers for the first time.

JLR has started to produce electric Land Rovers, beginning with its flagship Range Rover, built in Solihull in the West Midlands. Electric versions of its cheaper, higher-selling Range Rover Sport, Defender and Defender Sport will follow.

It also produces the luxury electric Jaguar Type 01, and Balaji said JLR was working on a new version of the Discovery.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Police say allegations of sexual misconduct are separate from those made by multiple women in Guardian and ITN investigation

The Metropolitan police have announced a criminal investigation into David Walliams over alleged sexual misconduct.

In reports by the Guardian and ITV News, Walliams, 55, has been accused by multiple women of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex.

Details of the allegations were revealed after a court rejected a legal attempt by Walliams aimed at preventing publication. He has denied any wrongdoing.

Walliams is one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and top-selling children’s authors.

In a statement announcing the criminal investigation, the Met said the serious allegations it was investigating were separate from those reported by news organisations. “In recent days, the Met has received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s.

“Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers.

“The allegations are separate from those reported by ITN and the Guardian. However, as part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences.”

Det Supt Mike Cagney, whose team is leading the investigation, said: “We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

“We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process.”

People could report information to police by calling 101 and providing the reference 4900/10NOV26, or by contacting the complex sexual offences unit on 0207 175 2738.

https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11.author: Dan Goodin
https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11.text:
“SignDrop” exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.

Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.

On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.

The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.

By manipulating Windows Object Manager symbolic links, the attacker causes Defender to open the CLFS container in the security context of the antimalware engine. If an associated authentication file is missing, CLFS creates it using Defender’s System privileges. Because CLFS assigns the newly created file the Discretionary Access Control List of the original file, the attacker may gain access to a file created with System privileges, allowing the file-creation operation to be abused as part of a privilege-escalation attack.

Ironically, the vulnerability stems from a security measure Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to prevent attackers from exploiting other vulnerabilities in CLFS.

“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation [of] privileges,” Nightmare Eclipse wrote. “Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.”

The researcher continued:

What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR.

Nightmare Eclipse said the exploit worked against Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental. People can see if their systems are vulnerable by checking the CLFS authentication mode. If it’s in learning mode or enforcement mode, the system is vulnerable, and the PoC supplied in the post should spawn a SYSTEM shell. Nightmare Eclipse has published numerous other Windows zero-days in recent months.

Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there’s a catch, he said.

“The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems,” he explained. “That is, you can’t just take a new 26H2 system and install updates and have it work.”

For a system to be vulnerable, Dormann said, the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode
value must be 0 or 1.” Out of the many machines Dormann uses, only a single one met this requirement.

Microsoft does staged rollouts of Windows updates, such as 26H2, so it’s not clear how many people have it. You can check by running the “winver” command. Microsoft representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking comment.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Device shows benefit in severe tricuspid regurgitation
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Transcatheter tricuspid valve repair improved health status and reduced tricuspid regurgitation severity vs. optimal medical therapy alone in patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation, a speaker reported.

Mortality and heart failure hospitalizations did not differ significantly, but the CLASP II TR trial was not powered for mortality, according to results presented at TCT 2026.

As Healio previously reported, the FDA approved the system (Pascal Precision, Edwards Lifesciences) for patients at elevated surgical risk with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation despite optimal medical therapy.

Approval was based on the 1-year results of the CLASP TR trial, in which researchers evaluated the system in 65 patients with severe symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation despite optimal medical therapy. The repair system was associated with significant improvement in tricuspid regurgitation and durable outcomes out to 1 year.

“The Pascal Precision system is the same delivery system and implant technology as the mitral [transcatheter edge-to-edge repair] system,” Charles J. Davidson, MD, executive vice chair for clinical affairs in the department of medicine at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine at Northwestern Memorial Hospital, said during a presentation.

The system features a nitinol design with atraumatic clasping, central spacer and contour paddles and retention elements, according to the presentation.

Researchers enrolled 450 patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation despite medical therapy who were randomly assigned 2:1 to tricuspid valve repair plus optimal medical therapy or optimal medical therapy alone. Follow-up visits were conducted at 30 days, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months with an annual follow-up planned for 5 years.

The researchers reported the trial met its 6-month primary endpoint, showing superiority of the transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement system vs. control group, with a win ratio of 1.98 (95% CI, 1.47-2.67; P < .001).

“Patients treated with Pascal were approximately twice as likely to have a benefit than those in the control group,” Davidson said. “The device group won 48% of all comparisons and the control group 24%, largely driven by improvements in [Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall summary score].”

The 30-day composite of major adverse events rate in the device group was 6.9%, mainly driven by single leaflet device attachment (3.4%) of patients and severe bleeding (3.1%), and with low rates of CV mortality and stroke (0.3% each). The 1-year composite major adverse events rate was 20.1%, according to the presentation.

Researchers reported the system significantly reduced tricuspid regurgitation severity, with 79.9% of patients in the valve repair arm achieving moderate or less regurgitation at 1 year vs. 30.4% among controls (P < .001).

At 1 year, the estimated rates of all-cause mortality was 8.8% in the device group vs. 4.6% in the control group.

“The difference between groups was nonsignificant,” Davidson said during the presentation. “There were disproportionately more noncardiovascular deaths in the device group, with nine deaths compared to one in the control group. There was no difference between groups in heart failure hospitalization at 1 year.”

The rates of tricuspid valve intervention at 6 months were similar between the device and control groups; however, separation emerged within 1 year with 15.8% of controls undergoing interventions vs. 5.5% of the device group (P = .001).

“This was due to significant control group attrition that occurred coincident with commercial approval of the two alternative transcatheter technologies,” Davidson said.

The device was associated with an early 13.7-point improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) overall summary score at 30 days vs. controls, which persisted through 6 months, according to the presentation.

Moreover, researchers noted that a greater proportion of patients in the device arm were alive and well at 6-month follow-up (64% vs. 51%), with a number needed to treat of 5.4 patients.

“The CLASP II TR trial met its 6-month primary endpoint, demonstrating superiority of the Pascal system compared to [optimal medical therapy] alone, in symptomatic with greater than or equal to severe [tricuspid regurgitation] in patients, primarily driven by KCCQ. There was no difference in mortality or heart failure hospitalization,” Davidson said during the press conference. “Treatment with the Pascal system resulted in significant [tricuspid regurgitation] reduction, with 80% achieved less than moderate [tricuspid regurgitation] at 1 year vs. 30% in the control group. There was substantial improvement in patient-reported health status that was evident by 30 days and persisted through 1 year. The trial demonstrates the safety and efficacy of the Pascal system to improve health status in symptomatic patients with greater than or worse severe [tricuspid regurgitation].”

Davidson CJ, et al. Late-breaking clinical trials: Session II: In collaboration with The New England Journal of Medicine. Presented at: TCT Scientific Symposium; Oct. 31-Nov. 3, 2026; San Diego.

Disclosures: Davidson reports receiving research support from Abbott, Cardio Mech, CroiValve, Edwards Lifesciences and V-Dyne, and holding equity in ReValve. CLASP II TR was funded by Edwards Lifesciences.

https://www.dw.com/en/what-s-going-on-wi.title: What's going on with the polar vortex?
https://www.dw.com/en/what-s-going-on-wi.text:
Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it mean for the weather?

High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.

If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.

Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.

It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.

So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.

This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.

It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.

Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.

For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-leaders-urged-t.title: EU leaders urged to 'act now' to stay AI competitive
https://www.dw.com/en/eu-leaders-urged-t.text:
EU leaders in Dublin were called on by an AI leader to move quickly in the tech race with the US and China. EU official Metsola, however, expressed frustration with the idea that the bloc is behind in AI development.

European Union leaders met in Dublin on Friday at the first ever summit on artificial intelligence (AI). The meeting came at a critical moment, as the bloc seeks a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology.

The meeting took place in Dublin's Convention Center, which was also the meeting place of the European Political Community summit this week.

French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch, as well as Nobel-prize winner and researcher Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," spoke to EU leaders at the summit.

"Europe has all the technology and the talent to lead the AI race," Mensch said during the event. "What it needs is speed, financing and a strong coordination between member states."

Mensch urged the leaders to "act now" to stay competitive with the US and China in regards to AI development.

The summit took place at a time of mounting worries about the emerging technology, which promises to transform ‌industries, labor markets and societies.

It also came in the wake of a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months and the wider discussion about how the technology could harm humanity.

Tech leaders behind the technology have also fallen under scrutiny. As recently as this week,Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign after it was revealed that he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company.

During the summit, a discussion occurred about where Europe fits in within the AI movement.

"AI is the most important technology of our time," European Council ‌President Antonio Costa said in a post on X regarding the summit. "Europe must make the most of its benefits, from higher productivity to better public services. We must also manage the risks and changes it will bring — and help set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI."

European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she frustrated with the notion that Europe had "somehow lost the AI race."

She noted that the EU has "world-class talent, technological expertise and industrial experience to lead in AI."

"What we need now is to ensure that our ideas have the financing they need to grow and succeed in Europe," she added.

Leaders face questions on how to unlock AI's potential, how to catch up with China and the United States in the race for the technology, but also how to protect against the risks it poses to individuals and businesses.

The governments of Estonia and Finland wrote in a letter ahead of the summit that Europe must "establish EU-level arrangements for responding to serious AI incidents," calling for "developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly."

Meanwhile, Mistral has pushed back on calls to slow down AI development, urging Europe to push ahead.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2.title: What we know about the ground stop and what to do if you're affected
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2.text:
The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks.

The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe.

The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.

The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.

The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.

All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended.

There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.

Passengers travelling from the UK have been warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning.

A number of flights to the US from Heathrow airport were cancelled and delayed, but Manchester airport said no significant disruption was expected. Flights were operating as normal from Gatwick airport.

Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, had grounded all US-bound flights, but scheduled flights are now expected to depart as planned.

Air Canada also cancelled flights between the US and Canada.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference on Friday night that the outage would cause a ripple effect for a few days.

"It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.

Tens of thousands of people were stranded in airports around the country, many of them "without any knowledge of where they're going to sleep tonight", Duffy said.

Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations.

American Airlines said it was "focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening". JetBlue said it would resume flights on Saturday morning.

British Airways, which has had a few US-bound flights affected, advised passengers to check their flight status but to travel to the airport as planned.

In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness.

As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems.

But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws.

Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly.

It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund.

In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers.

However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights.

Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason.

If your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.

The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.

Duffy said a legacy air traffic control communications system became overloaded.

"So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," Duffy said.

He said this had affected communications and radar. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50bn price tag.

"It's going to continue to fail," he said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the news conference that there was "zero evidence" it was a cyber-attack.

He also ruled out any link to the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday.

Mullin said the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system had overwhelmed it.

Both cabinet secretaries insisted the public was never in danger during the stoppage.

It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.

"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.

Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.

"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.

The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published and flights were grounded until that system was restored.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2.summary: FAA says ground stop was due to communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres. More than 8,500 flights delayed and 8,000 cancelled on Friday. All flights departing within the US will be grounded until further notice.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.text:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The Ukrainian president's comments on Saturday come after US envoys visited Moscow and an EU summit in Dublin as part of ongoing efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance as a condition of any peace deal to deter future threats, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.

Zelensky has also consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory, despite Moscow's demands for it to cede the Donbas.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.

Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

There have, however, been recent signs the two can find common ground: last month, US First Lady Melania Trump was able to broker a temporary ceasefire in the the Kherson region to allow for evacuations and aid deliveries.

US officials had previously said that Ukrainian Nato membership was off the table.

Zelensky said on Saturday that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".

But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

Ceding the small portions of land Ukraine still controls there would be symbolically significant for Kyiv because it would constitute an acceptance of the Donbas being Russian.

Zelensky has previously spoken of retaking Russian-controlled territory in four of Ukraine's regions, as well as the Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which US President Donald Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices, which have been rising since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.

Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz7.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz7.text:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.

It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing have yet to comment.

No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.

The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.

Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.

Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.

Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.

But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.

Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.

The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.

Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.

Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz7.summary: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week. The two-day summit will take place in Shenzhen, the White House says. It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw20.title: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw20.text:
Contains upsetting scenes.

Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.

The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort should go to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help".

"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.

Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.

Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side, Moreno said.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.

The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

US President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue had been an "incredible job".

Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.

Ships have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what had occurred.

Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he had seen the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision.

"It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."

Holford added that he had seen passengers and crew "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.

The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.

Built in 2015, the vessel has at least four decks.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw20.summary: Cruise ship American Heritage hit by cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt in Mississippi River. 32 people left in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckre.title: Setback for SpaceX Starship rocket's double-catch test
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckre.text:
SpaceX has aborted its attempt to catch the bottom part of its huge Starship rocket during its latest test flight.

The company had aimed to catch it using the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on the launch tower as it returned to Earth, but instead it was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames as it came down.

The top part of the rocket is now continuing its journey to space and SpaceX will decide whether it will try to catch this rocket stage at about 15:15 local time (21:15 GMT) on Saturday.

It is the aerospace firm's first attempt to fully recover its rocket, paving the way for making Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.

The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:45 local time on Friday.

The launch tower there was supposed to catch the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six-and-a-half minutes later when it returned, but it was instead diverted to the ocean.

During a livestream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each manoeuvre safely."

The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, is continuing its journey to space, where it is deploying 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet.

The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off, where a second catch may be attempted.

SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.

But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks.

Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space.

If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.

Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.

In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.

Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.

But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society.

"Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.

"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."

After SpaceX became a public company earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will Nasa.

The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.

SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.

But it is not the only company working with Nasa. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touchdown.

Both companies will also play a key role in the Artemis III mission, which is currently planned for summer 2027 - another challenging schedule.

Four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft will attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers during the voyage.

Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.

But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.

Blue Origin had said its spacecraft would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.

Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said the US was in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

The company had aimed to catch it using the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on the launch tower as it returned to Earth. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rr.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rr.text:
Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption.

The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected.

The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.

Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent.

Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.

Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.

Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge.

In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected, as were some schools and police forces.

UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network.

In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.

In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.

Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.

In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.

The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.

Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill".

His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.

"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said.

"We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible."

Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.

It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.

By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.

Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.

Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.

"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.

Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.

"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rr.summary: Microsoft says services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide. The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services. Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckjw.title: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckjw.text:
Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor Orbán, authorities have said.

Miklós Seszták, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.

Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.

On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".

Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into Seszták, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.

The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said.

The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the Orbán rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".

Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many Orbán-era policies since entering office.

Allegations of corruption and cronyism have long dogged Orbán, who during the course of his tenure turned Hungary into what the EU characterised as an "electoral autocracy".

His government faced accusations of offering lucrative government projects to allies. Orbán has strongly denied the claims.

Two of his former ministers, including Seszták, and the former central bank chief Gyorgy Matolcsy have been under arrest since September over accusations of graft in separate investigations. They all deny wrongdoing.

On Monday, Hungarian authorities also detained Orbán's brother and three others as part of a people-smuggling case.

The former prime minister ​dismissed it as political revenge, saying: "In this dirty game, ​the aim is the elimination of the political opponent and the establishment of a one-party system.

"I am the target, my younger brother is just a tool."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckjw.summary: Miklós Seszták is accused of accepting bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing. Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq39.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq39.text:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.

That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.

And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?

The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."

Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.

What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".

That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.

But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.

"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.

"Our proposals were almost laughed at.

"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".

"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."

Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.

Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.

This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.

After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.

But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.

"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.

The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.

And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.

And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.

Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.

But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.
