https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmr4.title: Bluetongue virus confirmed on County Down farm
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmr4.text:
The first case of Bluetongue in Northern Ireland this season has been confirmed on a farm in Kilkeel, County Down.

Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) said the virus had been detected in three sheep.

There will be no additional movement restrictions or disease control zones, because the virus has been present in Northern Ireland since November 2025.

It presents no risk to public health.

The minister, Andrew Muir, said the discovery of the virus was "disappointing but not unexpected", given the spread of the disease in Great Britain and Ireland.

The Chief Veterinary Officer, Brian Dooher, urged local farmers to be alert to any symptoms in their livestock.

The confirmation of the virus in Kilkeel comes after more than 100 cases across the Republic of Ireland in recent months.

Cases in England have been increasing, with 2,950 now confirmed.

There have been 512 cases in Wales and 57 in Scotland.

The mild winter means more of the biting midge that spreads the disease are likely to have survived and become infectious this season.

Muir said awareness was key, adding: "Continued vigilance and strict biosecurity measures remain of paramount importance and I would once again urge all farmers to report any suspicion of disease to Daera.

"It is important that I reiterate that Bluetongue poses no threat to public health nor to food safety – milk and meat are safe to consume."

Dooher said any suspected cases on farms should be reported to Daera.

"Active surveillance is ongoing at abattoirs alongside post-import testing of susceptible animals imported from mainland EU countries.

"I also want to stress the importance of safe and responsible sourcing of animals."

The disease was first detected in Northern Ireland near Bangor in County Down in November 2025.

A number of other herds along the eastern coast of Northern Ireland have also been affected.

Farmers have been urged to vaccinate their animals.

The disease affects ruminants such as cattle, sheep, goats and deer.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.title: What could El Niño mean for winter weather in the US and Canada?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.text:
Montreal, Canada was badly hit by the Great Ice Storm of 1998 which was blamed, in part, on El Niño.

The developing El Niño - already the strongest on record by some measures - continues to grow and could have profound effects on the weather across North America this autumn and winter.

The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon sees trade winds over the Pacific Ocean, which usually blow from east to west, weakening or reversing with warm water instead spreading eastwards.

This releases heat into the atmosphere which can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.

Impacts in the US and Canada are varied, with a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south.

There is also some evidence that El Niño can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter.

No two El Niños are the same and the impacts are not guaranteed - the odds are just shifted in favour of certain outcomes.

UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact

The eastward shift of warm ocean waters associated with El Niño can cause the Pacific jet stream to move south and extend eastwards, directing rain-bearing weather systems across the southern USA.

This typically leads to wetter winters during El Niño years.

The likely impacts of El Niño on winter weather vary across different parts of North America.

The latest three month forecast
, external
 from the US National Weather Service (NWS) suggests this is a likely outcome for the winter of 2026-2027.

South-eastern states, including Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas, have the greatest chance of seeing above-average rainfall.

The El Niño winter of 1997-1998 brought significant flooding in the south-east and spun up tornadoes for Florida.

Severe flooding hit Long Beach, California in February 2024.

California could well find itself in the firing line with forecasts suggesting a wet winter is likely.

Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency
, external
 ahead of anticipated floods and mudslides.

Areas scarred by recent wildfires are particularly susceptible, with the effects of climate change exacerbating the risks.

Many past El Niños have been wet here, with winter 2023-2024 bringing relief from drought. However this is not always the case. In the strong El Niño of 2015-2016, California actually had below-average rainfall.

Coastal erosion and large waves could be worsened by a rise in the overall sea level driven by so-called Kelvin waves.

This is where ocean water which sloshes eastwards across the Pacific due to El Niño reaches the west coast of the Americas, where it can travel no further.

It causes a large-scale wave which then spreads along the coast over a period of weeks and months, raising sea levels by 15cm (6in) or more.

The shift of the Pacific jet stream generally leads to warmer and milder winters in the north-west USA, Northern Plains and Ohio Valley - as well as western and central Canada.

This lessens the risk of flooding, but reduced rainfall can leave groundwater and river levels low, fuelling drought and wildfires in spring and summer.

Ski resorts can also suffer from a lack of snow.

Long-range predictions suggest a dry, warm winter is more likely than usual this year.

However, El Niño does not guarantee this. For instance, the winters of 1982-1983 and 2015-2016 were wetter than normal in the north-west USA.

In much of the northern USA, and large swathes of Canada, a greater chance of dry and warm weather makes snow less likely.

Further south, however, above-average precipitation typically leads to big snowfalls in the Californian mountains and southern Rockies - good news for water stocks.

It can also increase the probability of snow at lower levels in the southern and eastern USA - but only if enough cold air is in the mix.

The area around Washington DC often receives more snowfall than usual in an El Niño winter - but not always.

Snowfall caused chaos in Washington DC in February 2010.

The winter of 2009-2010 delivered record-breaking snowfall that brought the city to a standstill, while widespread blizzards affected much of the US east coast in 2016.

However, some of Washington DC's least snowy winters have also occurred during El Niño events, including 1972-1973 and 1997-1998 which brought just 0.1in (0.25cm) of snow.

Higher winter temperatures in eastern Canada and the north-east USA can mean precipitation that might normally fall as snow gives rain instead.

This can increase the chance of freezing rain events, with the so-called Great Ice Storm of 1998
, external
 being blamed partly on the effects of El Niño.

It is worth saying that snowfall amounts are decreasing overall in most places due to human-induced climate change, meaning predicting the impact of El Niño is even more complex.

An added complication is the possible impact of El Niño on the polar vortex, a ring of strong winds that circles the North Pole in winter, around 10-30 miles (16-48km) up in the stratosphere.

It holds cold, dense air in place above the Arctic but sometimes it can weaken and disrupt, and there is some evidence that the energy released into the atmosphere by El Niño makes this more likely.

Disruptions to the polar vortex sometimes ripple down through the atmosphere, weakening the polar jet stream and opening the door for cold air to spill across Canada and the USA.

However this does not always occur and the links are far from clear.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6qj.title: Extreme weather leaves gardeners hedging their bets
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6qj.text:
Gardeners in one of the most drought-hit parts of the UK have said they are adapting their planting strategies amid increasingly extreme weather.

West Sussex - like most of the country - experienced an unprecedented summer marked by record-breaking heatwaves and severe drought.

The conditions have put immense stress on many traditional plant species, with some seriously struggling or dying completely.

Iain Parkinson, head of landscape and horticulture at Kew Wakehurst near Ardingly, said he had seen a "big change" in climate over the some 40 years he has worked there.

"We've had trees die," he added.

Meanwhile, senior gardener at High Beeches near Haywards Heath, Elliot Chandler, said some rhododendrons had died off this year.

"That's probably going to continue," he said.

"We'll do what we can for the plants...but if they're not surviving, then we need to plant different things.

"That's the only way we can really maintain the garden and keep it full of interest and flowers."

Joe Whelan, head gardener at Nymans in Handcross, warned another year of drought could be "quite detrimental" on larger, more mature trees.

The gardeners said planting a greater diversity of species will be key to climate resilience, with plants from North America, southeastern Europe, central Asia, South Korea and Japan potentially faring better in future.

Chandler added it will not be a case of ripping out old plants and planting new species "in one go" but rather a gradual change over time with a "really diverse mix of things".

Whelan said it will be difficult to predict what will do well in the future.

It will be about "experimenting and accepting that some things probably aren't going to make it", he continued.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70.title: Woman with terminal cancer gets dream wedding on hospital ward
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70.text:
A woman with a terminal cancer diagnosis married her partner of 15 years in the hospital where she is receiving palliative care - and her horses even made the ceremony.

Maggie Heginbothom, 68, who has advanced liver cancer, thanked staff at Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor for organising a wedding ceremony on Monday, just two days after her partner Mark proposed.

The horse lover and former clinical scientist with Public Health Wales, described hospital staff as being "like family to me".

"It was so beautiful and I honestly never thought it was going to be possible, especially seeing both my horses there as well," she said.

Heginbothom, originally from the Vale of Glamorgan, was admitted to hospital nearly three weeks ago after becoming unwell while riding one of her horses.

After her partner proposed from her hospital bedside, staff on the Tegid Ward volunteered to pull together a celebration that included flowers, decorations, a harpist, food, cake and Heginbothom's beloved horses Ozzy and Quiosque.

The horses were brought to the hospital by Pen Llŷn Stud and Riding School, where Heginbothom rode and competed for many years.

"From the beautiful decorations to all the little touches that made our wedding so special, I cannot thank them enough," she said.

Ward manager Rachel Parry said her team were determined to get things right.

"On the morning of the wedding, we transformed Maggie's room with white sheets and fairy lights to create a beautiful space for the ceremony, while the relatives' room became a reception area," she said.

"Everything ran like clockwork, and some of our colleagues even came in on their days off to help make it happen.

"It was such a special and emotional occasion.

"There wasn't a dry eye in the room, and it was particularly lovely that some of the other patients Maggie has got to know during her time on the ward were able to join the celebrations."

Matron Ceri Newell said it was an example of the compassion and dedication shown by NHS staff.

"Nursing is about so much more than treating illness," she said.

"It is about compassion, kindness, humanity and recognising that sometimes the most important thing we can do is help make someone's wishes come true.

"What the team achieved for Maggie and Mark in such a short space of time was truly remarkable, and I could not be prouder of every single person involved.

"Everyone went above and beyond, working together to create something incredibly special for a couple going through such a difficult time.

"Moments like these remind us why we do what we do, and I am so proud of what the team achieved."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm20.title: 'I cycled across America in memory of my wife - I know she's proud of me'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm20.text:
Declan Faulkner and his wife Patrina always intended to return to the United States, a place they visited shortly after getting married almost 30 years ago, and maybe make a cross-country trip.

But, as is sometimes the case, life had other plans.

They moved close to Patrina's home village of Ballygawley, County Tyrone, developed their careers, raised three children – and then Patrina was diagnosed with breast cancer. Four years later, in 2017, she died.

But Declan never forgot the journey they were meant to take together – which is why the 55-year-old just spent seven weeks cycling coast-to-coast across the US, from Portland, Oregon on the west coast to Portland, Maine.

"When things got tough throughout the journey, I just had Patrina's voice in my head and I dug deep thinking about what she and other cancer patients go through," he said, reflecting on one of the hardest but more rewarding challenges of his life.

It was during Patrina's illness that Declan found an outlet in the form of endurance sports, setting him on a path to his 3,800-mile (6,115km) epic cycle across the US.

"I've always been a keen runner and love to cycle, and even when she was sick Patrina would give me the green light to go off to the Mourne mountains for the day," he said.

"I just loved the serenity of running and cycling there and I suppose mentally it really helped me hold things together at the time.

"I'd remembered talking to Patrina about this idea I had in my head of going back to America and cycling coast to coast.

"Ten years had passed since she died and the kids have grown up, and I just thought wouldn't it be great to see America on two wheels with the memory of Patrina on my shoulder along the way."

So at 55 years old, Declan, who is a financial adviser by day, decided to take a short career break to fulfil a lifelong dream, while raising cancer awareness along the way.

He was joined on the road by his friend from Cork, Donncha O'Brien, another keen cyclist.

Declan said: "We had met a few years back on cycling trip in Kerry and had become great friends and thank God he was there because he kept pushing me.

"There were days when you felt like your body was just shutting down and you were sore all over, because we were spending sometimes 10 hours a day on the bikes without a break."

The men spent 43 days on their bike and averaged 85 miles (137km) a day, but on some days cycled up to 120 miles (193km).

They cycled 45,000m of elevation, the equivalent of five-and-a-half Mount Everests.

The journey took them through some of the most spectacular landscapes in North America - over the Big Horn Mountains in Wyoming and along the Great Lakes.

Declan said he had several pinch-me moments throughout the trip.

He said: "Cycling into Devil's Tower, Wyoming, which I think was one of the first national parks inaugurated in 1906 and it's just this big volcanic plug - we cycled there on a beautiful day.

"Seeing that for the first time was special.

"Then coming into Vermont in the autumn and some of the colours of the trees were just stunning.

"And we cycled through this amazing lightning storm in upstate New York in the dark, with the lightning strikes just lighting up the whole place."

There were also many hard days along the way too.

"Cycling through the strongest winds I've ever experienced in South Dakota was probably the toughest.

"Leaving South Dakota Badlands National Park we actually ran out of water and my sugar levels just dropped and I nearly fell of my bike a number of times, I was just exhausted."

Declan's journey started at the Pacific Ocean and ended at the Atlantic Ocean.

He says seeing the Atlantic coast is something he will never forget.

"Our final destination was this beach right on the Atlantic Ocean, and the last 20 miles to it just went in a flash, and taking the bikes down to the water on that last day was totally surreal.

"I wasn't overly emotional until that evening when a friend sent me a picture of Patrina and I from 30 years ago when we were at a party at college.

"That just brought the tears because I was looking at that picture and felt like she was with me the entire way."

As part of the cycle, Declan raised almost £20,000 for Charis Cancer Care, which runs a specialist care centre on the banks of Lough Fea in County Tyrone where Patrina spent many days after her diagnosis.

The centre in the foothills of the Sperrin Mountains, just outside Cookstown, provides a free-of-charge service offering emotional, physical and practical support to people with cancer.

Arlene McAvoy from the charity said: "With Declan doing this cycle in Patrina's memory and raising awareness, it's just amazing what he has achieved.

"Each year we have about 1,400 people who come to our centre.

"It's not just for the person who is going through cancer, but it's also for their families and carers as well, and I know this was a special place for Declan also."

Now that Declan is back home, he says it is taking a bit of getting used to.

He added: "You wake up thinking: Have I pumped the tyres? Have I greased the pedals? Are the lights charged?'

"It's mad because you've been in that cycling bubble for so long.

"But now that I'm looking back on it, I am very proud, and I do think about what Patrina would think.

"She'd probably laugh and say: 'You're not wise' - but I know she'd be proud too."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm20.summary: Declan Faulkner and his wife Patrina always intended to return to the United States. But they never forgot the journey they were meant to take together. The 55-year-old spent seven weeks cycling coast-to-coast across the US.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv8e.title: Hospital doctors to strike as pay dispute continues
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv8e.text:
Hospital doctors in Northern Ireland are to strike in November over pay.

It comes after the Royal College of Nursing announced that it is also balloting its members on potential strike action.

The doctors will stage two separate 24-hour strikes on 20 and 23 November.

The British Medical Association (BMA) has warned doctors are prepared to escalate the strike action if progress is not made in addressing the pay issue, which they say has seen doctors' pay drop from upwards of 26% over the past 18 years due to below inflation pay awards.

The Department of Health (DoH) has been approached for comment.

Resident doctors will hold a full 24-hour strike starting at 07:00 BST on 20 November until 07:00 the following morning.

Consultants and specialist, associate specialist and speciality grade (SAS) doctors will also take 24-hour action from 07:00 on 23 November until 07:00 the following morning.

They will provide what is known as Christmas Day cover, which means that most routine and elective services will be cancelled but full emergency cover will remain in place.

Resident doctors are fully qualified medical practitioners who are completing postgraduate clinical training in a hospital or general practice under the supervision of a senior doctor.

SAS doctors are specialist doctors employed by health trusts.

The three branches of hospital doctors also took strike action in June.

The BMA said if Health Minister Robbie Butler was serious about transforming the health service and addressing the waiting list crisis he needed to value doctors by paying them fairly.

Dr Clodagh Corrigan, chair of BMA's Northern Ireland SAS committee, said: "We have been clear to avoid further industrial action we need a credible offer from government that makes meaningful progress towards full pay restoration.

"We met with the new health minister recently, hopeful that we could begin fresh discussions on agreeing a credible pay offer. Regrettably, this did not happen."

She said the minister was unable to confirm if the minimum annual pay uplift for 2026/27, which has been paid to doctors elsewhere in the UK, would be paid "this side of Christmas, or indeed at all".

"We were informed that the decision ultimately lay with the executive," she said.

"Therefore, we have been left with no alternative but to announce more dates for industrial action and we are fully prepared to escalate action if no progress is made."

Dr David Farren, chair of BMA's NI consultants committee, said pay was central to recruitment and retention of doctors and hindered the delivery of a sustainable and safe health service.

"There is palpable anger among our members at continuing sub-inflationary, late pay awards while we work beyond capacity in under-supported services," he said.

"This annual uncertainty over when we will receive our pay award reinforces the widespread feeling that we are not valued, and leads to doctors seeking better paid roles elsewhere."

He said this impacted service delivery and it was "unacceptable that our government continues to let this happen".

It comes after the Royal College of Nursing announced on Wednesday that it will ballot its members on industrial action and strike action over pay.

The union said the move came after many months of inaction on the pay award.

Earlier this year, the NHS pay review body recommended a 3.3% pay increase for staff across all pay bands.

While nurses and healthcare workers in England and Wales have received their award, nursing staff in Northern Ireland have not.

In a statement the DoH said the health minister was clear that the 2026/27 award should be implemented and pay parity with colleagues in NHS England restored as soon as possible.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv8e.summary: Doctors will stage two separate 24-hour strikes on 20 and 23 November. British Medical Association warns doctors are prepared to escalate action if pay issue is not addressed. Royal College of Nursing also balloting its members on potential strike action.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5dj.title: As Christmas rush looms, how do China-made toys find their way to the US?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5dj.text:
On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures.

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show.

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.

Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5dj.summary: Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn) China's toy industry is about to have its busiest time of the year by far. The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck20.title: Football kit giveaway aims to boost participation
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck20.text:
Former England captain Millie Bright has helped hand out new kit to grassroots football teams in Leeds as part of an initiative aimed at keeping girls in sport for longer.

Thirty teams based in communities facing social or economic challenges were chosen by anti-discrimination charity Kick it Out for the donation.

Bright, who began her career at Doncaster Belles, said it was "vital" to keep girls playing sport.

"Every young girl deserves a kit, no matter what level they play at, and, whilst the top of the game is doing really well, real life still exists. People can't afford to give their children kits, but that doesn't mean they should go without."

Craig Gilmore set up Champions CIC, in Beeston, six years ago, to provide free Saturday morning training for children in the local area, as well as breakfast and lunch.

"With the cost of living, football's expensive [and] bills come first," he said.

"We work with a lot of families that can't afford the direct debits and the ongoing costs of grassroots sport nowadays.

"The new kit is amazing. It gives them that sense of belonging, that team pride, it's a massive boost for them."

The new kit was provided by Kick it Out, in partnership with the Morrisons Foundation.

They hope it will inspire these girls to continue sport as young women and adults.

"Girls' participation struggles with drop-out rates," said Gemma Clark, from Kick it Out.

"One of the barriers is kit. We want to remove that barrier so that more local girls can keep playing."

Bright told the BBC she was fully behind the campaign.

"As a girl or a woman, it's about feeling wanted and equal," she said.

"We deserve to have kits. I don't want to see any girl dropping out of the game because they don't feel valued or comfortable.

"These are the days that really make a difference. Hopefully this shows the girls that the people at the top care. The power of having a kit is a small gesture, but has a massive impact."

Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck20.summary: Millie Bright has helped hand out new kit to grassroots football teams in Leeds. The former England captain is behind the initiative to keep girls playing sport for longer. The new kit was provided by anti-discrimination charity Kick it Out.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.title: What do Christmas market traders say about rising prices?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.text:
Mention Christmas markets these days and the conversation often turns to rising prices – from £8 bratwursts, £11 Yorkshire pudding wraps and even £5 for a few marshmallow sticks.

But what do the people behind the stalls think? Are they benefiting from the hikes or are their own profits being squeezed?

Traders at Manchester's Christmas markets told the BBC they were feeling the pressure of increasing bills for staff, ingredients and energy, with some saying they were making less money despite charging more.

One trader said it costs at least £4,000 a day to run each her four stalls, while another has cut prices to keep customers coming back.

Nils Borstel, 25, helps run Bratwurst King, a family business which has operated at the markets since 1999.

He said a sausage that previously cost £3.50 now sold for £8, with much of the increase taking place over the past five or six years.

"But we don't earn more money," he said.

Borstel, whose family operates four stalls across the city centre, said rising costs for meat, electricity, staffing and accommodation had forced the business to increase prices.

About 15 workers travel from Germany to help run the stalls, alongside staff recruited in the UK.

He said that despite busy crowds and dry weather during the opening weekend, people appeared more cautious about spending than in previous years.

For example, some customers were now buying one portion of food to share, rather than purchasing one each, he said.

Borstel said he had seen a change in spending habits since 2019, when customers were more willing to buy food and drinks without worrying about the cost.

He acknowledged that prices were high and did not want to increase them, but said the they were necessary to cover expenses.

Among those questioning the costs were Neve and Poppy, both 18.

Neve, a student, said she had spent about £15 on one dish, while Poppy, who is taking a gap year, paid £11 for a Yorkshire pudding wrap.

"I think it was pricey for what it was," Neve said.

Poppy also felt she had not received much food for the money, although said it was tasty.

Both said they enjoyed going into the city and looking around the markets, while Neve sympathised with traders, saying she thought the cost of renting space could force businesses to raise prices.

Charlotte Whittle, director of CT Catering, has been trading at the markets for 10 years and now operates four stalls.

She said each stall cost at least £1,000 a day to run, bringing her total daily operating costs to at least £4,000.

Whittle, who employs a range of staff, said customers often underestimated the work and expense involved.

Before the markets opened, her business spent two weeks preparing its stalls, with another two weeks needed to dismantle them after Christmas.

She said the costs included staff wages, accommodation, deliveries, storage, packaging and card payment fees.

Parking three vans in Manchester city centre could cost £100 a day alone, she said, with the vehicles needed to replenish stock throughout busy trading periods.

"They think that you're just selling cookies," she said.

Whittle, who began her business selling homemade cakes at street food markets, said the cost of stock and packaging had increased significantly over the years.

Although she had increased some prices, she said she had chosen to absorb part of those costs rather than risk putting customers off.

"We've had to take a massive cut on profits," she said.

She also argued that the standard of street food had improved and customers were receiving food comparable in quality to that served in restaurants.

But not every trader has responded to rising costs by putting up prices.

Clark Murphy, whose family has traded at the markets for 22 years, runs Mr Crimble Crumble, which sells fruit crumbles from two stalls.

He said the business had kept most prices unchanged for three years and had reduced the cost of its largest portion by £2.

Murphy said cooking oil and biodegradable packaging had become more expensive, but the business wanted to retain customers who returned each Christmas.

"We haven't increased our prices for three years now," he said.

He said the business remained profitable, although margins were under pressure and card payments added to operating costs.

At another food stall, a notice offered customers £1 off each drink or dish when paying cash.

"Card fees are crazy – help us keep it simple," it said.

Meanwhile, a gift trader calling himself Ernie the Elf, who sells handmade Christmas decorations in Albert Square, said visitors could still find affordable products.

His decorations cost £4 each or three for £10, while metal signs were priced at £9.

Ernie, who is in his second year at the Manchester markets, said traders faced substantial expenses, including accommodation and parking.

But he believed the markets offered good value, pointing out that people could enjoy the festive atmosphere without having to spend money.

Tyler, from Australia, and Rebecca, from Hong Kong, were enjoying their first Christmas in England with their daughter.

Rebecca bought four brownies for £10, while Tyler paid £6 for a meat pie, which he said was not unreasonable compared with some other prices.

However, he described another stall charging £5 for three marshmallow sticks as "outrageous".

The couple said the markets were part of enjoying their first Christmas in England with their daughter.

Despite questioning the cost of some products, Tyler said the experience was worthwhile.

"I think if you don't buy anything, it's still great to come," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c670.title: Food bank sees donations drop by 10% each year
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c670.text:
A food bank that has seen a drop in donations of about 10% each year since 2023 is hoping government stockpiling advice will not affect the public's generosity.

Someone eats a meal provided by Cambridge City Foodbank "every two minutes" and it claims to have provided more than 260,000 in the past year.

In October, the government launched its "Be Ready" campaign and encouraged households to stock up with enough non-perishable food and water to survive for three days in case of an emergency.

Chief executive Steve Clay says he does not know if this will affect the Christmas appeal - their busiest period - but confesses: "It is a concern."

A government spokesperson said it had "no serious evidence of stockpiling or indeed a supply shortage" with the campaign and it had worked with voluntary organisations and charities to address any concerns.

The food bank team estimates it will provide more than 45,000 meals to people in the city between 13 November and 15 January.

Clay says that with cold weather and pressure on spending, Christmas is "more difficult" than the rest of the year.

"Budgets are tighter, more has to be spent on fuel and energy," he said.

"So people are contacting us all the time for emergency support and we need to make sure that the support is always there and is continuing to be there."

Donations are used to purchase emergency hampers, treats or provide advice and assistance.

While the food bank's doors close on Christmas Day, meals they have provided mean more people can enjoy the festivities.

Every pound donated, up to the first £15,000, would be doubled as part of a match-funding commitment.

Dr Liam Loftus, development director of the food bank, said: "As we head into winter and the cold draws in, thousands of individuals and families will be forced to make the heart-breaking choice between heating or eating.

"This winter, can you take two minutes of your time to support our Winter Appeal?

"You'll be helping restore hope and dignity to people facing hardship and providing one of your neighbours with their next meal at what should be one of the happiest times of year."

The government spokesperson said of the Be Ready campaign: "We've worked hand-in-hand with voluntary organisations and charities, including food banks, to address any concerns and ensure the guidance is as accessible as possible.

"Where households can act, that frees up emergency services to prioritise those most in-need during any emergency."

The food bank says it has provided more than 260,000 meals in the past year. The government launched its "Be Ready" campaign in October. It has worked with voluntary organisations and charities to address any concerns

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c69v.title: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c69v.text:
Young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support, the author of a major review of youth unemployment has told the BBC.

Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister whose proposals on welfare and young people will be unveiled on Tuesday, said those who refuse to take up the help could lose their benefits.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Milburn called for a radical shift in government spending away from benefits for young people to measures that support them into work.

He claims spending on benefits for young people is 25 times as much as spending on employment support, and believes the ratio should shift to two to one.

That would mean significant cuts to benefit spending and significant extra taxpayers' cash for training, education or other forms of support.

Milburn said "the pendulum's swung far too far from the one to the other - £25 to one, and we can take everything to £2 to one".

He added: "To do that, we've got to invest, less in benefits, so we've got to be paying out less in benefits."

The former MP acknowledged that would mean some young people losing out on benefits, arguing the system should focus on helping people into work rather than keeping them dependent on welfare.

Milburn said the government is already spending £22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive, and that money needs to be spent differently.

He has already said that the under 25s should no longer be able to claim some health benefits – the personal independence payment and the health element of Universal Credit.

In his other major announcement, Milburn spoke of the proposal he calls an "opportunity guarantee" for young people.

This would put a legal duty on government to ensure young people have access to a route into employment.

He said: "It should be a guarantee for a young person. Because at the moment the only guarantee they've got is a very simple thing. To get a benefit. What sort of life is that?"

The "opportunity guarantee" might work similarly to the way that councils have a legal responsibility to offer homeless people accommodation or advice, or accommodate children in care.

Milburn argues previous employment schemes have been temporary, and says a permanent legal entitlement is needed to tackle the long-running problem of young people not in education, employment or training.

The government is expected broadly to welcome the proposals, which will be published in full on Tuesday, with a statement in Parliament and draft laws early next year.

Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training - otherwise known as Neet - according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Milburn's forthcoming report as a "watershed moment," but stopped short of committing to implementing its recommendations in full.

Burnham also insisted paying for the reforms would not mean "more money" but "spending differently" in government when pressed on the large upfront investment they are expected to require.

Asked whether he would accept the politically sensitive report in full, Burnham declined to provide that "blanket assurance".

Speaking to reporters in a trip to Dublin on Thursday, he said: "We will have to wait until the report is published. It's a wide-ranging report, and obviously we'll set out our response next week.

"But I think it's really important to see the report as quite a watershed moment I think in terms of how we think about supporting young people and supporting young people into work."

Lord Blunkett, a former Labour home secretary, told the BBC that money from cutting benefits spending should be reassigned to supporting employment "at least in the immediate future".

Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, he said reforms should focus on "transferring resource that currently goes into paying for failure, keeping youngsters at home, isolated, lonely, into actually putting the money in and the resource and the commitment in to making those jobs available".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail.

Her party and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.

Reform economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "This review is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away.

"It cannot be right that this continues for another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."

The Liberal Democrats want the government to introduce a 100-hour work experience guarantee and a careers coach for every young person.

They believe this would equip youngsters with the best possible skills before they leave school.

The Green Party has warned against "demonising" young and disabled people and wants the government to address the "structural inequalities stacked against them".

Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c69v.summary: Alan Milburn says young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support. Former Labour minister says spending on benefits for young people is 25 times as much as spending on employment support. Milburn's proposals on welfare and young people will be unveiled on Tuesday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr5y.title: Tories pay artist for Burnham images after legal threat
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr5y.text:
The Conservatives have agreed to pay an artist who threatened to sue the party after it used his illustration of Andy Burnham to mock the prime minister.

Stanley Chow posted on Facebook that the party had used the picture - which Burnham has used on social media - without permission.

He had sought legal advice and threatened to take action against the party. It is understood the Tories agreed to pay a £1,000 fee for use of the image - and contributed an unknown sum to Chow's legal fees.

The Conservatives had distributed water bottles with the image on them - accusing Burnham of being a "bottler".

Chow posted on Facebook: "The Conservative Party have settled after their recent indiscretion of using my image without my permission."

He added: "Maybe ask first… admittedly I would have said no, but it would have been a damn sight cheaper for the Tory Party if they just hired any illustrator to do their take on a cartoon of Burnham… hopefully this a lesson learned. Copyright matters."

A Conservative spokesman said: "The Conservative Party values the importance of intellectual property in the creative industries. We consider this matter closed."

Manchester United fan Chow, a Labour supporter, has previously created images of footballers, including Wayne Rooney, Edgar Davids and Ronaldinho.

He has also exhibited a series of portraits of "Great Northerners", which featured the likes of actress Maxine Peake, suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst and poet Lemn Sissay, and recently curated an art trail for the Brit Awards' arrival in his home city.

He has also drawn Eric Cantona and presented a picture of Sir Alex Ferguson to the former Red Devils manager.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr5y.summary: Stanley Chow posted on Facebook that the party had used the picture without permission. He had sought legal advice and threatened to take action against the party. The Conservatives had distributed water bottles with the image on them - accusing Burnham of being a "bottler"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jr.title: Welsh Labour leader says party focused too much on powers for Senedd
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jr.text:
Labour lost its connection with previously loyal voters at May's Senedd election, the party's leader has said.

Officials will publish on Saturday a review of Labour's historic election defeat in the May Senedd election.

Speaking to BBC Wales, Ken Skates said it was "absolutely obvious" that the party needed to rediscover its purpose and reconnect with people the "length and breadth of Wales".

Labour was thrown out of power at the election when it was reduced from 30 seats in the Welsh Parliament to nine.

It is holding its first party conference since the party went into opposition, and Plaid Cymru took over the Welsh government.

After years of trailing Labour, Plaid won the largest number of seats, allowing party leader Rhun ap Iorwerth to become first minister.

Labour had led the Welsh government since devolution began 27 years ago.

Skates, who took over as leader following the election, said: "According to the review, it's absolutely obvious that we needed to rediscover our purpose".

He said the party needed to "strengthen" its "soul" and "reestablish that powerful contract between us as a movement in Welsh Labour and the people of Wales who share our values".

He said he could not disclose what the review, by Prof Anand Menon of King's College London, will say the day before conference.

"But I can say this - that people still believe that we share the fundamental values that they have and that they hold dear."

Asked what he stood for as leader, Skates said: "My passion has always been quite fundamental that no young person should be left behind because of disadvantage when growing up, that every person in life should have the best opportunity to succeed."

He said he and Prime Minister Andy Burnham "share a huge number of similarities".

"Catholic influences, strong community influence, we support the same football team, [we] went to the same university, we both enjoy running."

"I was determined to ensure that this review is dispassionate, independent and objective," he said.

"We don't have a version of the truth, we have the objective truth. And I would hope that no matter how tough it is, people will accept the findings and will be part of the movement that will build again."

Since becoming prime minister, Burnham has lobbied the Welsh government to devolve more powers to Wales' regions.

The policy has been criticised by some former Welsh ministers. Lee Waters, former transport minister, said it "just doesn't work" in a Welsh context.

The Plaid Welsh government has promised a green paper looking at the powers of councils, with legislation possibly after the next election in 2030.

Skates said people in Wales were telling the party they wanted more powers for their communities.

"We want more powers to come to the Senedd, to Cardiff Bay, but we also want more powers out of Cardiff Bay in our communities," he said. "That's what people want."

He said the review would make clear "about what people in Wales want most, which is more power in their communities."

Skates is expected to address the conference on Saturday.

He says it is "absolutely obvious" that the party needed to rediscover its purpose. Labour was thrown out of power at the election when it was reduced from 30 seats in the Welsh Parliament to nine.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmg4.title: Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmg4.text:
It's an ugly acronym. And it's an even uglier situation.

The reality of so-called "Neets" in the UK - young people who haven't got jobs, aren't studying or being trained up - has seen hundreds upon hundreds of thousands of Brits in their late teens or early-20s struggle to find a decent future for well over a decade.

It costs the taxpayer billions. And the human cost is variously described as a disaster, a national shame, even a moral crisis.

When the phrase Neet was first coined by Tony Blair's Downing Street in 1999, the focus was on 170,000 or so teenagers who were not in education, employment or training. After many attempts at solving the problem, add in a pandemic and years of a sluggish economy, it's acute - with nearly a million under-25s in that situation.

A tome full of proposals to try and fix it once and for all will be published on Tuesday, after a year in the making.

How the government reacts will test its appetite and capacity for radical change, and the prime minister's real, not rhetorical, hunger for tricky political arguments.

The canny smooth talker behind the huge review, former Labour MP Alan Milburn, wants you to know that Andy Burnham knows exactly what's coming.

Speaking to me in Liverpool, where in Merseyside 14.5% of 16 to 24-year-olds are unemployed, he tells me: "All the way through, the prime minister, the chancellor, all the ministers, they know what's going on. It won't be a surprise to them when this is launched and that gives it a fighting chance of actually being implemented."

But his collection of proposals is not for the faint-hearted.

On top of a plan to stop under-25s claiming the main sickness and disability benefits, Milburn will argue for a dramatic shift in the balance of what the taxpayer spends on benefits for young people compared to what is spent on support to help them get into work.

He says the amount spent on young people's benefits is 25 times as much as that on employment support - and he wants to shift it to a drastically different two to one.

He won't put specific numbers on it yet, but accepts openly that means a significant number of young people losing their benefits or facing cuts.

But that would come with a chunky expansion of the amount of further education, training, health support and likely jobs subsidised by the taxpayer too. A big cut to state support on one side of the ledger, but a big increase on the other.

And to make sure that government gets really serious about improving the mess, Milburn is asking for a new law that would give young people a guarantee of help and support - a job, an apprenticeship, a training place, or perhaps health treatment so they are able to work - an "opportunity guarantee".

He told me he won't fall into the "elephant's trap", where a feisty teenager could sue the prime minister if they didn't get the job they fancied. But the idea is to put a legal duty on the authorities in a similar vein to councils' obligation to look after children in care, or to provide accommodation or advice to homeless people.

Westminster jargon often describes earnest sets of recommendations published in reports like this as "wide-ranging". This review genuinely is, arguing for changes not just in welfare, but in the health and education systems.

It's a real expansion of the state's involvement in the next generation, from one of the Blairites still standing, with the expensive Paul Smith knitwear to match.

He is not the first government veteran nor is Burnham the first PM, to try to sort out this problem.

But what Milburn and his allies say is different this time round is they're pushing for a whole new system that's permanent, not just another scheme that gets introduced by one secretary of state, then is dropped or scrapped by the next one that turns up.

And the notion of a legal guarantee is designed to make the state, likely through local councils or mayors, take responsibility for making sure young people have something useful to do when they emerge from school – for good.

The recommendations apply to the whole UK, but the precise way the powers might be used in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will be worked out when it gets to the finer details of draft laws.

The scale of the practical challenge can be seen from space. New research from the Lib Dems this weekend suggests that if nothing is done, the number of Neets would hit 1.26 million by 2031.

And Milburn himself cites figures that puts the cost of the issue at £22bn a year.

No politician would argue for the status quo. But agreement that something must be done doesn't automatically translate into consensus over what that something is.

For all Milburn's talk of grand ambition – his plans will not, any time soon, make much difference to the ballooning costs to welfare.

His plan will take as long as a decade before making a real dent in the benefits bill. And it will require taxpayers' cash at the start, although not the £6bn guesstimates that have done the rounds.

He's still coy about the upfront cost, but it will be billions over the years.

And he says plainly there are many young people who are capable of working but don't, although tiptoes carefully around any accusations that some take advantage of the system, saying he's convinced the vast majority of young people do want to work.

The Conservatives and Reform have both put saving tens of billions from the welfare bill, and fast, at the top of their list.

The Tories said Milburn was right that benefits must be cut - but that "unlike Labour, our plan goes to the root of the problem" including by halving employer National Insurance for young people and creating 100,000 new apprenticeships. Reform said the review "is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away" and it cannot be "another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."

Milburn and the government can expect sustained criticism that it's not acceptable the plans would take so long to start cutting the enormous bill for the taxpayer. There is no question the expected increases in benefit payments are absolutely eye-watering.

The opposition from that quarter, and indeed from the Greens on the left arguing already that what they have seen so far is "cruel", is entirely predictable to Downing Street. What's harder to read, and therefore more difficult to contend with, is how Labour MPs will respond.

Keir Starmer tried, and painfully failed to make changes to welfare, sabotaging his own authority when he backed down in the face of backbenchers.

That's why Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, has spent hours and hours talking to Labour MPs in the last year, trying to patiently make the case for this plan.

And why Milburn, as he was keen to point out, has continually been in touch with No 10 and 11, trying to get Burnham on board even before he made it to Downing Street. A government source said hopefully, this time "we've done the ground work – it's not a rushed Treasury process driven by numbers".

As my colleague Iain Watson has written, the signs are healthier for Milburn, with a few key critics from last time showing more than an open mind to the new plans.

The political climate is completely different with Labour, for now, cheerier about the polls, and backbenchers reluctant to make trouble.

Burnham still is in possession of course, of the enormous majority that Starmer won.

There will, without doubt, be voices on the left of the party, concerned perhaps about opposition from the Greens or the SNP in their constituency who will never sign up to anything that would mean a cut to payments for anyone on benefits now.

"Look at the chaos Starmer got into," one source on the left warned, saying Burnham wouldn't be so "boneheaded" to do the same as "he wants to be everyone's friend".

So a possible fault line may become whether the reduced benefits apply to those already claiming, as Milburn believes, or only those in future.

A No 10 source is plain the plans would have to apply to those on benefits now, warning they must act as soon as they can, although new laws will take time.

They told me "an argument on welfare is an argument we are happy to have". Let's see if that sentiment stands the test of time.

The Milburn review was set on its path by Starmer. But it will emerge blinking into the light under a different leader, and in a very different political moment.

Perhaps, some in Labour wonder, Milburn's ideas are arriving at a time when a newish prime minister has big rhetoric but perhaps is short of big concrete ideas, mocked by his opponents for reportedly bringing in private consultants to fill out his much-vaunted 10 year plan.

Burnham is widely expected to adopt most of Milburn's genuinely radical ideas. Months of arguments lie ahead, however settled the political picture appears right now.

But Milburn's ideas just might have come around at the right time for a relatively new government . As one senior Labour figure believes: "You need some meat on the bones that isn't just, 'nationalise everything' – this could be it."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn7.title: Brand, Walliams and MAFS: Is this a reckoning for the entertainment industry?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn7.text:
This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.

On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women.

By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him.

Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show.

These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry.

So why is this all happening now?

In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence.

All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago.

From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting.

"The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me.

In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court.

Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry.

It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him. The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations.

What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave".

When looking at what’s driving more women to speak up, much can be traced back to the revelations about Harvey Weinstein and the #MeToo movement.

It changed the perception of whether victims would be believed.

In the past, women alleging this sort of behaviour faced barriers - being seen as opportunistic, fearing retaliation, believing they might be the only one.

Now, there can be a snowball effect. Once one, two or three come forward, that prompts others to revisit their experiences - which they may have dismissed or subdued.

"There is more of a sense that you will now be listened to," said Freeman.

It's also clear that when women see action taken, it can encourage others to speak up as well - as it helps counter the widely-held assumption that reporting abuse results in nothing.

When another high-profile man, MasterChef presenter Gregg Wallace, faced accusations of a very different and much lesser order, relating mostly to inappropriate sexual language and humour, the reaction was similar.

Last summer, an independent inquiry upheld dozens of claims against him, and he was sacked. Wallace said "none of the serious allegations" against him had been upheld but that he was "deeply sorry for any distress caused".

One young woman I spoke to in my investigation into Wallace texted me at the time, to give her reaction to his sacking.

"I really believe this will encourage young girls going into the TV industry to have the courage to speak up, if they feel something is wrong," she told me.

But unions say it is still difficult for junior freelance workers, who often find their income unstable and unpredictable, to speak up.

Vulnerable workers "continue to fear raising concerns", said head of broadcast union Bectu, Philippa Childs.

She's echoed by Freeman, who said an "attitude of protecting the talent" remained.

"There will always be wealthy famous predators," she said. But, she added: "Hopefully more and more people at TV stations and movie studios are willing to hear these young people and will take them seriously”.

For more senior people in TV, raising the alarm can also be difficult.

Earlier this week, comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News: "The reason high-profile people are not saying anything is because they lose work, because you're seen that you might be a trouble causer. It does need to be said that there needs to be some intervention."

Social media has also played a role in encouraging people to speak up.

And policing investigations have had to keep pace - and adapt - with media scrutiny often prompting authorities to investigate.

Attitudes towards women who speak up are also starting to change – although not always.

Some of what unfolded in court during the Russell Brand case felt like a throwback to how rape cases used to be conducted.

Many have commented on Brand's lawyer's defence tactics against the accusers on the stand - behaviour Freeman said would have been "standard" in the past.

But Freeman noted it was heartening to hear the judge’s remarks in summing up the case - which have also been widely shared by women online and praised for dispelling rape myths.

When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Brand to ten-and-a-half years, he told him: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no."

"I think attitudes have changed,” said Freeman. “It doesn't mean those assaults don't happen any more but attitudes around them have changed.”

So where does this go from here?

Events of the past few weeks highlight how figures who rose to prominence in the nineties and noughties did so in an era with different standards.

Lad culture and celebrity status shielded Brand and others from scrutiny.

Now, behaviour once dismissed as eccentricity or womanising is increasingly being reassessed and called out. Times are catching up with some men of that era.

However, it would be an error to assume this sort of behaviour is confined to the past.

"This is not just about nineties/noughties culture," Wark told me. "It can't be dismissed as a hangover of the past, this is about right now and the industry changes that must happen.

"There will be more cases to come, sexual abuse, coercive control, verbal and physical abuse. It is not OK, and it never was OK."

This week, comedian Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women were "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.

And in the past few days, I've had tip-offs about other celebrities allegedly abusing their power. No doubt other journalists have too.

None of those is reportable, yet. As Freeman said: "There are other names out there, but you and I couldn't name them as we'd be sued".

But one "cheering thing", she said, was that the sort of jokes and innuendos from the nineties and noughties, or even the optics of seeing a much older man with a younger girl would no longer be "glossed over".

"It wouldn't be laughed at, and it wouldn't be 'nudge nudge'," Freeman said. "That kind of open, in your face, weirdness won't happen any more".

"On the downside, that may make it harder to identify predators, if it means these things are kept more in the shadows."

Then there’s the use of gagging orders and other legal routes often used by celebrities and media organisations to stop women speaking out.

Last week, a High Court judge rejected an injunction request by Walliams, clearing the way for him to be named.

"There are lots of barriers to speaking out, and those that have access to wealth or fame will often use legal measures to deter alleged victims from doing so," Harriet Wistrich, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told me.

That too, may be starting to change.

This week, multiple government ministers have spoken against non-disclosure agreements and called for further restrictions on their use.

Change could come in other areas too.

Next week, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will convene industry leaders to urge them to improve safeguarding practices - while Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front an MPs on Tuesday.

When MAFS UK was cancelled, Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom's broadcasting code.

There is growing recognition that those at the top of media organisations have a responsibility to root out abuse. It can't just be down to the victims.

"People in positions of power have a duty to speak up too," said Wark.

"Broadcasters, production companies and those financing productions all have a responsibility to ensure protections are upheld," added Josephine Brassey, from Women in Film and TV, while Philippa Childs urged the creative industries to accept that their current internal reporting mechanisms were "inadequate".

What everyone seems to agree on is that this can't be another empty tipping point with no real, lasting change.

Maybe this time it could really be a watershed moment.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones says US move humbled her before big break with Steven Spielberg
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm.text:
Catherine Zeta-Jones has said she had an ego check after moving to America in the 1990s.

The Swansea-born star had become a household name in the UK, but Hollywood quickly provided a reality check for the rising star and she was even asked by casting agents if she had any acting experience.

It was during her stint on CBS mini-series Titanic that she was seen by Steven Spielberg who suggested she go for a role in The Mask of Zorro, which he was producing.

"Five days later I got the job, and three days after that, I was down there starting my sword-fighting lessons," she said.

Zeta-Jones had become a star in the UK thanks to her breakout role in The Darling Buds of May that originally aired from 1991 to 1993.

But when she touched down in California, she was no longer recognised by the public and had a six-month visa to "give America a shot".

She told Business Insider it was "good" for her to have her ego knocked down a bit.

It was only when the Spielberg saw the Titanic series that she was given a major opportunity.

"I was shipped down to Mexico to screen test with Antonio Banderas," she said.

She credits it as her breakthrough into A-list territory and it was rumoured that she beat actors such as Salma Hayek and Jennifer Lopez to the part.

Zeta-Jones went on to work with Sean Connery in Entrapment which cemented her stardom, and she refers to the late James Bond actor as a "dear force of nature".

"I just never wanted to stop acting with him, because we were such good buddies," she said.

"He was so incredibly protective of me, like a daughter he never had, and he said that to me."

Zeta-Jones is currently starring in Kill Jackie, a revenge thriller based on the 2018 novel The Price You Pay by Nick Harkaway.

She stars as the titular Jackie Price, a Welsh high-end art dealer with a shady past in the drug trade who discovers a hit has been put out on her.

In September, Zeta-Jones made headlines for revealing that it was the first time she had used her Swansea accent for a role.

After decades of working on accents including English, American and Scottish she said the opportunity to speak in her native accent was both "liberating and cathartic".

As well as returning to her Welsh roots, the series' ultra-violent scenes have been a blast for Zeta-Jones, who relished the chance to go off the rails.

"I love this character," she said.

"I wanted the audience to come along on this ride with me and root for her. In all the craziness."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.title: Why so much love between Ireland and Garth Brooks?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text:
Fans of Garth Brooks will be brushing off their Stetsons and polishing their cowboy boots after the country music superstar announced he will be performing in multiple cities across Ireland in 2027.

The tour includes Belfast, Galway, Kilkenny, Limerick and Cork and will be the first time he has played in Northern Ireland since his King's Hall gig in November 1998.

The singer has said in the past that Ireland is his favourite place in the world to sing, and the love appears to be mutual as his first two Belfast concerts sold out, with an extra date already added.

So why has an American country music star remained so popular with Irish fans for so many years?

Cathy O'Reilly, who is originally from County Monaghan but lives in Belfast, managed to get her tickets for the very first show of Garth Brooks' tour on 21 May 2027 at Boucher Road Playing Fields.

She has already seen Brooks perform live before - twice during his run of concerts in Dublin in 2022 and her love of his music was passed on from her parents and uncles.

"It's growing up listening to him it brings me back to my childhood. My uncle gave me his cd, he didn't even buy me one - just gave me his because I loved him so much."

She believes the Irish link to the US and the fact that fans on the island give the best welcome to performers, are the reasons for Garth Brooks' popularity in Ireland.

"He [Garth Brooks] gives us energy and we're giving it back ten-fold nearly, and we're just so welcoming so he really enjoys coming here."

Peter Aiken, from Aiken Promotions, told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the new Belfast gig is "red hot".

"There could be a fourth show in Belfast," he said.

Brooks is the biggest selling artist in US history and is the only artist to pass 200 million albums sold.

In 2014 about 400,000 fans booked tickets to five concerts he had planned for Dublin's Croke Park but Dublin City Council only granted permission for three of them.

Brooks said he would only perform all five concerts or none at all and so the shows were cancelled.

He returned to Dublin in September 2022.

Stephen Butler from Newtownabbey performs as a Garth Brooks' tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls.

His love for the musician also goes back to his childhood.

"My mother was a fan when I was younger, she was always playing his music and buying his albums so I loved the songs.

"I knew, with me loving Garth and there being such a following in Ireland, I knew it was the right thing to do."

He went to the Dublin concert in 2022 and while he hasn't yet got tickets for the Ireland dates next year, he hopes to get tickets to at least one of them closer to the time.

"I was able to get four or five tickets about a week or two before the Croke Park shows, I'll definitely go - I have to go.

"His band is amazing, he's amazing, and his songs - he's got an endless amount of anthems."

Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music".

"I'm not saying I'm as good as Garth Brooks, but I definitely have his enthusiasm.

"I talk about him and how much I love him throughout the songs and I just identify with them as much as I can.

"My job is easy, I just have to go on there and get everybody singing along with me."

Butler says he thinks the reason Garth Brooks remains so enduringly popular in Ireland is because the people here identify so strongly with his songs.

"Everybody loves Friends In Low Places, people of Ireland love it, they love Callin' Baton Rouge.

"I speak to a lot of people after I play the shows and a lot of people identify with some of the words in the songs, they tell me about a relative that's passed and they seem to have some kind of identification with the songs Tomorrow Never Comes or Unanswered Prayers - it talks about love and about how Garth feels.

"And in amongst Thunder Rolls and the big hits that Garth has, he sings big rocky country rock and ballads, so it's exciting and it's sad - it's an emotional roller coaster," he said.

"And he's such a down-to-earth, genuine, caring person, he seems to be a good soul and I think people people identify with his personality.

"It's a big working-class country and they love someone that's genuine and that talks from the heart."

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.title: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.author: Jason Horowitz
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.text:
As retirees live longer, governments need to spend more on pensions. That makes it harder to fund other services, spurring protests like those in France.

Reporting from Madrid

Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.

“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.

But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.

“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”

This disagreement embodies a broader question for Europe, one at the heart of the mass antigovernment demonstrations that returned to France on Saturday, as well as recent protests driven by frustrated young people in countries including Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy and Portugal. As Europeans live longer, should the needs of the young be eclipsed by their parents’ and grandparents’ pensions, routinely the largest items in Europe’s national budgets?

“It’s a generational clash,” said Jorge Galindo, the director of EsadeEcPol, an independent think tank in Spain, which has some of the most generous pensions in Europe.
