https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-604.title: Old tech blamed for the ground stop that caused flight chaos: 'It got overloaded'
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-604.author: Joel Rose
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-604.text:
Flight are listed on a board inside a terminal at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Friday.

The nationwide ground stop that paralyzed the U.S. aviation system on Friday has ended, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

The rare stop, which lasted about four hours, grounded thousands of flights at all U.S. airports in one of the biggest disruptions of the nation's air travel system since the September 11th attacks.

In a Friday night news conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that air traffic control facilities had experienced "intermittent" outages of their radar and communications systems beginning earlier in the afternoon. Duffy blamed outdated technology for the failures.

"We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It's an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded," he said.

But when pressed by reporters on exactly why those systems would become overwhelmed on an otherwise normal travel day, Duffy did not have a ready answer.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin joined Duffy in the White House briefing room and said there was no evidence the issue was due to an attack.

"We have seen zero evidence this is a cyber attack," he said.

A flight board showing delayed flights is pictured at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Friday.

As of 9 p.m. ET, more than 8,000 flights had been delayed Friday and 7,000 had been canceled in the U.S., according to FlightAware, a flight tracking site. The turmoil comes on the heels of nearly 7,000 flight delays on Thursday.

The FAA said the issue affected Air Route Traffic Control Centers — the regional air traffic control centers across the country that handle high-altitude traffic.

FAA leaders did not brief the media at the White House press conference, and did not provide any further detail on the communication outages that led to the ground stop.

This was only the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001. The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.

That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.

Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) released a statement late Friday evening calling for a "prompt, penetrating investigation" into the causes of Friday's ground stop.

"A widespread communication outage of this scale is highly alarming — a clear danger to national security, as well as safe, convenient travel close to the holidays. The Department of Transportation owes Americans credible, accurate action and factual disclosure," the statement read.

The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.

"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.

The nationwide ground stop caused chaos in airports and headaches for travelers — many of whom are already too familiar with flight delays and cancellations during the holiday season.

At the Friday night press conference, Duffy said flights would resume but would take time to clear.

At Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Regina Harling said she waited hours — long past when her flight was supposed to depart — before she learned of the nationwide grounding by checking the news on her phone.

"There's still a sign right in front of me that says we're boarding in 16 minutes," she said Friday afternoon.

An airline worker shows people how to apply for a refund at LaGuardia airport on Friday.

Harling needed to travel last minute to San Diego for a family emergency. Stuck at the airport, she said she was thinking about how soon she could make it to her family, but she's not optimistic.

"I was just thinking to myself that it always feels like it's getting harder to travel than it used to be," she said.

At Chicago O'Hare International Airport, Giliann Karon was on board a plane when the ground stop was ordered. Karon said she had already experienced a flight delay the day before due to bad weather in New York City, where she is heading.

"It's just kind of like, 'Oh, of course this is happening,'" she said.

Deepa Shivaram contributed to this report.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-604.title: With his challenge to Schumer, Van Hollen forces a debate over Democrats' mandate
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-604.author: Elena Moore
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-604.text:
Democrats say they have a mandate to deliver change, but as the party gets ready to retake the majority in both the House and Senate, there are divides over who should lead it.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Democrats say they have a mandate to deliver change next year, but as the party gets ready to retake a majority in Congress, there are divides over how far that change should go and who should lead it. It's a debate playing out in the Senate where minority leader Chuck Schumer now faces a challenge from fellow Democrat Chris Van Hollen for the top job next year. Here to break down what we know is NPR's Elena Moore in the studio with me. Hi, Elena.

ELENA MOORE, BYLINE: Hey, Sacha.

PFEIFFER: So last night, Van Hollen announced he's running. For people who don't know him, what should we know about him?

MOORE: Yeah, he's had a pretty long career in Washington, representing Maryland in the Senate since 2017 and serving more than a decade in the House before that, where he held some leadership roles. Ideologically, he's seen as more progressive than Schumer is, and he's tried to position himself in recent years as someone who pushes back hard against the Trump administration. Notably, last year, he lobbied for the release of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland man who was wrongly deported to a prison in El Salvador, and Van Hollen actually traveled there to meet with him.

PFEIFFER: And what is Van Hollen's argument for why he should have the Senate's top job?

MOORE: Well, he argues that the midterms showed how much voters want Democrats to reject the status quo. You know, speaking to reporters earlier today at a Democratic conference in Colorado, he argued he's the best person to usher in that change.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

CHRIS VAN HOLLEN: This is about answering the call of the American people because what I'm very afraid of is that their calls to end political corruption, their calls to end a rigged economic system, will require that we organize the Senate in a different way.

MOORE: And, Sacha, those talking points may sound kind of familiar because we kind of just heard them on the campaign trail. Van Hollen is really embracing much of the same messaging used by successful Democratic Senate candidates this cycle, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who made, you know, their campaigns all about this idea of rejecting the establishment, which, in many ways, Schumer has long embodied.

PFEIFFER: And that message has been successful for some candidates, but...

PFEIFFER: ...In many ways, Van Hollen kind of embodies older school politics. So what makes him think he is an embodiment of change right now?

MOORE: Yeah, and also he's only eight years younger than Schumer, which I think is also kind of important to mention. But it is an important question. On the issues, it's worth noting that he and Schumer are pretty aligned on the party's big-picture priorities. They've both emphasized the need to lower costs, you know, end the war and reverse some of the Trump administration's funding cuts.

I think the bigger difference between the two politicians is how they talk about reforming the Democratic Party. You know, Van Hollen has talked about the Senate being taken over by special interest groups, which hits on a pretty big rift within the caucus right now about campaign donations from super PACs as well as pro-Israel lobbying groups like AIPAC, which is a group that has supported Schumer in the past.

PFEIFFER: And I know that Van Hollen has said he hopes to rally support from the party's left flank. But can you tell if the opposition to Schumer is being driven mainly by progressives, or is there broader appetite for an alternative inside the party?

MOORE: Yeah. It's important to say Schumer is by no means universally loved inside the party, right? You know, towards the start of Trump's second term, he was actually criticized both within the halls of Congress and from voters who argued he wasn't doing enough to fight back against Trump.

Yes, some of that frustration is coming from progressives, like, you know, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, for example. But, Sacha, it's not just the party's left flank. You know, earlier this week, Sanders actually held a press conference alongside Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who's way more of a moderate, I would say. And the two both announced that they wouldn't be backing Schumer for the job.

And, you know, when looking at the broader caucus, dissatisfaction with Schumer may not translate to a victory for Van Hollen, per se, but, you know, he knows he's the underdog here. Schumer says he's confident he has the support needed. But there's also time for both of these politicians to try to make gains. Ultimately, this is going to come down to a secret ballot vote in early December.

PFEIFFER: That is NPR political reporter Elena Moore. Thank you.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-603.title: The government says it will close a beloved D.C. park Sunday. Will a judge step in?
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-603.author: Rachel Treisman
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-603.text:
The National Park Service wants to close most of East Potomac Park, far more than just the golf course. The perimeter loop is beloved by runners and cyclists.

Federal judge Ana Reyes grilled the government on Friday about its plans for East Potomac Park, and indicated she could order it to remain open despite President Trump's renovation wishes.

Washington, D.C.'s most beloved parks could close indefinitely on Sunday unless a judge decides to intervene. East Potomac Park is home to the municipal golf course that President Trump wants to redevelop into what he calls a championship-level venue. But at a hearing today, administration lawyers argue that repairs are needed not only to the golf course but to the entire recreational area around it. NPR's Rachel Treisman watched the hearing and joins us now. Hey, Rachel.

RACHEL TREISMAN, BYLINE: Hey, Scott.

DETROW: Did the judge indicate how she'll rule?

TREISMAN: District Judge Ana Reyes sounded like she is likely to take action, but she seemed to be grappling with what exactly she can tell the government to do. The government is arguing it needs to close almost the entire park on Sunday for two main reasons. That's the day the lease expires with the golf course's current operator and because it wants to repair the park's seawall, which has been deteriorating for years. Reyes didn't really seem persuaded by that. The government chose to end its operator lease on November 15, which is the day President Trump has said the park would close. And the government acknowledged it doesn't yet have a plan to repair the seawall or a contract to redevelop the golf course. Reyes suggested she'd rule on Saturday. We'll have to see whether she orders the park to stay open or goes even further and tells the government to keep the golf course open, too.

DETROW: You've been listening to this since 10 in the morning. What are some of the main sticking points from today?

TREISMAN: Yeah. There was a lot of discussion about how Trump's proposed redesign would change a space that so many people here in D.C. just love. Critics say the scale of the course would make it less accessible for beginners, and it would eliminate the perimeter loop that joggers use every day and also for big races, like the Cherry Blossom 10 miler. I spoke to event director Rob Wolfe, who is still hoping the race can take place in April.

ROB WOLFE: It's really important that people understand that if this roadway goes away, hundreds - thousands of people on a daily basis will lose out.

TREISMAN: The government has recently started arguing that the park needs to be closed because the seawall poses a safety issue. At one point, the lawyer mentioned a risk of unattended children falling into the Potomac River at night. The judge seemed pretty incredulous. She kept asking why those concerns hadn't been addressed sooner and whether the whole park really needs to be closed for that.

DETROW: How final are these golf course plans? I mean, all of this seems so up in the air.

TREISMAN: Totally. The government has already submitted this proposal to two different federal commissions, but it still needs to go through environmental reviews and get public input. Reyes has really pressed the government's lawyer on whether it's too late for them to change course, especially given how much people here are opposed to the plan. Reyes says she's gotten death threats over the case. There have been protests by cyclists and birders. At one point, Reyes asked people in the courtroom how many of them were there because they care about East Potomac Park and almost all of them raise their hands.

DETROW: And I think that gets to a bigger storyline here. You know, one reason the case has gotten so much attention is because of the tension between the judge and the government and because of the pointed rulings that the judge has made saying you're not cooperating. Tell us about that.

TREISMAN: Yeah. Reyes has been very vocal about feeling misled by this administration - by officials, by its lawyers. Two weeks ago at the last hearing, she announced she'd open an investigation into potential attorney misconduct, and that there's a long history there with the administration cutting down hundreds of trees in October after telling her they wouldn't, administration officials telling her that there was no final plan to close the course, despite the president saying so online. Reyes has chosen a first-term Trump administration lawyer to lead that probe, but today, the government opposed that, which means Reyes will probably lead that investigation herself.

DETROW: The golf course is, you know, as you've been covering, one of several of these projects that are playing out in court right now. You've got the proposed arch. You've got the Kennedy Center he wants to make the Trump Kennedy Center. What are other possible checks on these projects?

TREISMAN: Well, Democrats have said they hope to use their incoming congressional majority to push back. That could be blocking funding or holding oversight hearings. Judge Reyes actually opened today's hearing by referencing some recent CNN reporting saying the interior department has destroyed documents related to Trump's construction projects, which it denies. Now, Reyes has asked the government's lawyer if he'd heard anything about that. He said, no, and she said if she finds out otherwise, there will be consequences in a zeptosecond. That, she said, is the shortest measurement of time ever recorded in a lab.

DETROW: NPR's Rachel Treisman. Thanks so much.

TREISMAN: Thank you, Scott.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-604.title: Microsoft outage disrupts work and gives some a chance to unplug
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-604.author: Andrea Hsu
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-604.text:
Millions of individuals, organizations and businesses were left without access to Microsoft's Outlook email on Thursday. Some people celebrated a day without email, while others work around obstacles.

Microsoft says it is seeing broad recovery and stability following a massive outage of its Outlook email system and other applications yesterday. The company says it was a technical issue not related to AI agents. The outage hit millions of Microsoft users in more than 70 countries. NPR workplace correspondent Andrea Hsu hit the phones to find out how people weathered the disruption.

ANDREA HSU, BYLINE: As president of the Global Healthy Living Foundation, Seth Ginsberg spends long days communicating with patients, doctors and government officials in the U.S., as well as Canada, Australia and Japan.

SETH GINSBERG: It does feel like a constant back and forth.

HSU: Some 200 emails a day. But starting midday yesterday, for 20 hours, he heard nothing. For someone who's dedicated his career to improving the quality of life for people with chronic illnesses, it was jarring.

GINSBERG: It was almost like an existential crisis because I went from feeling incredibly productive to wondering whether anyone needed me anymore.

HSU: Once his tech team assured him that his emails would come through eventually, he settled in with pad and paper, worked on some follow-up notes from a rheumatology conference last week.

GINSBERG: The funny part is how we're all so conditioned to respond to email that when it stops, we assume something terrible has happened. And apparently now, like, peace and quiet is a technical malfunction.

HSU: Now, even without email, people couldn't stay away from their devices. Social media was flooded with posts. On TikTok, Reba McEntire shared a song as she wondered why her inbox was quiet.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "WHY HAVEN'T I HEARD FROM YOU")

REBA MCENTIRE: (Singing) Tell me, why haven't I heard from you? Why haven't I heard from you?

HSU: Lots of people liken the outage to a snow day. Others wax nostalgic about a time before email. Someone surfaced an image of one of those yellow interdepartmental mail envelopes, you know, where you cross out the name of the previous recipient and write in the new one.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "WHY HAVEN'T I HEARD FROM YOU")

MCENTIRE: (Singing) Oh, why haven't I heard from you?

HSU: Now, the outage did bring some serious disruption to some institutions, like the U.K.'s National Health Service, which relies heavily on Microsoft for communications and scheduling. They had to revert to paper records and phone calls. In Colorado, the Arapahoe County Sheriff's Office couldn't process online bond payments. They said anyone looking to post bond for immediate release had to do so in person. Caroline Berdzik, an employment and labor attorney with the firm Goldberg Segalla, says yesterday was a good reminder that there are other tools.

CAROLINE BERDZIK: How about picking up the phone or walking down to, you know, the office a few doors down? A lot of the email traffic we get is internal.

HSU: She remembers at her first law firm job how she'd stand by a fax machine waiting for a reply. Back then, there was room to think and deliberate. Now...

BERDZIK: Everything just seems to be so much more sped up. It almost seems like it's a hot potato situation. It's just, like, folks can't wait to say, OK, I'm done with this. Now it's passed along to the next person to do something.

HSU: Berdzik says, fortunately, she wasn't trying to file anything in court yesterday. That would have been a problem. Instead, she had a really productive day drafting motions, revising briefs, just focusing.

BERDZIK: Without the constant dinging of emails coming in, which I think, naturally, it's almost like a Pavlovian dog response that you hear the ding and you immediately respond to it.

HSU: Efficiency is a good thing, she says, but so is pressing pause from time to time and reflecting. Yesterday's outage, she says, was inconvenient and yet glorious.

Andrea Hsu, NPR News.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-603.title: Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-603.author: Michel Martin
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-603.text:
Jensen Huang delivers a keynote at Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin on Oct. 21, 2026.

A suspected intelligence scandal, reports of multiple extramarital affairs and the abrupt departure of one of Silicon Valley's most influential CEOs. It's been a dizzying week for Nvidia and the AI industry.

Jensen Huang helped bankroll the AI boom. Now, after 33 years at the helm of the leading company in AI, he's out, leaving questions about the future of an industry that has relied heavily on his company's financial backing. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO.

"Nvidia has put itself basically in a position of being a bank, backstopping everything," Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI researcher, told Morning Edition.

He was describing circular financing: Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use the money to buy Nvidia's chips. OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave have relied on that funding, he said, even as many AI businesses struggle to turn a profit.

"Jensen was kind of a swashbuckler, willing to make bets of arbitrary size," Marcus said.

Unlike Huang, whose background is in engineering, Kress comes from finance and appears more cautious about making large financial bets, potentially changing how Nvidia backs the wider AI industry.

Kress will also have to contend with potential federal and congressional investigations into Nvidia's dealings involving China, leaving her to "clean up that mess," Marcus said.

He said lawmakers need answers about what information Huang may have shared with Alice Huang and why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had not intervened earlier.

"Why didn't Lutnick shut some of this down when he was asked to?" Marcus said.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.title: Men on a mission: U2 is back, again. Are they cool this time?
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.author: Ann Powers
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.text:
U2's 16th album, Carnaval De Luz, clatters through the band's history with unapologetic delight.

This essay first appeared in the NPR Music newsletter. Sign up for early access to articles like this one, listening recommendations and more.

He may be thanking the stars in the Dublin sky or his political consultants — either way, Bono must be feeling pretty fortunate these days. U2 is back, and not just because they've insisted on reentry into the zeitgeist. No major rock band has faced as tumultuous a twilight era as this one, now half a century into its reign as rock's quintessential try-hards, a status that grew increasingly unmanageable as age and wealth pushed its members farther away from pop's shifting conversation and toward the dreaded status of nostalgia act. Chasing relevance, U2 made some spectacular mistakes; leaning into its fans' goodwill, the Irish foursome kept making money while slipping ever farther into irrelevance. Bono, the most extroverted rock star since Mick Jagger, watched his kids replace him in the celebrity pages and tended to his health problems. But the celestial bodies have realigned, and Carnaval De Luz is proving to be the lucky 16th album that's made U2 admirable again, if not exactly cool.

Despite a few naysayers, this collection of dance tunes and 2 a.m. reflections again justifies U2's place as a blockbuster band able to startle, engage and generate happiness. It follows two recent EPs that hit like renewal ceremonies and several singles that made clear that the band is here to play, in both the musical and disruptive sense. An engagement with Latin music, signaled by a smattering of Spanish foreshadowed by the album title and Bono's revelation that one track was named after his latest platonic muse Rosalía, have, on the album itself, thankfully proven to be less like weird appropriation than a reinforcement of the Eurotrashy cosmopolitanism the group first introduced on 1992's Achtung Baby. (Her reported response, an amused "Do I have to sing on this?" suits the song's message: They can barely touch the hem of her garment, but will gush anyway.) At times U2 has tried to seize the moment by engaging with awkwardly fitting trends, but here, a core commitment to its own historic innovations feeds an immediacy that feels earned, not forced.

Before the singles showed they'd be back on their old stomping grounds, the Edge had whispered about a "sci-fi Irish folk project," but beyond an uptick in the guitarist's pedals-happy noise generation, this music isn't at all experimental. It does, however, benefit from a certain investment in time travel. Like a self-referential version of Terry Giliam's Time Bandits, Carnaval De Luz clatters through U2's history with unapologetic delight. Opening track "Go (Carnaval De Luz)" starts with a wash of noise that points back to Achtung's "The Fly." The slice of Edge's guitar against Adam Clayton's bass on "Silencio" calls back to "Two Hearts Beat as One," from 1983's War. "The Greatest Show on Earth" is a ballad that harkens back to the band's Wim Wenders era and "Glorify" sizes down the strut of 2004's "Vertigo" to fit a more direct invocation of grace. Bono makes the rounds of his various techniques: beat-poet rapping, an unctuous falsetto, a broken croon, that wail. Larry Mullen Jr. shows what expensive physical therapy can do by banging the drums with machine-gun force.

Religious and profane, aggressive and generous, the songs on Carnaval De Luz add new layers to U2's defining preoccupations: what it means to have a sense of mission in an instant-gratification oriented world, and how hard and good it can be to keep searching for meanings of the word soul.

On that topic, it's notable that Bono's lyrics have grown more direct in their outright expressions of Christian faith. He's still a sucker for a goddess — the unnamed "face of the future" in "La Reina" joins a harem of his divine feminine muses — and an anti-dogmatic believer, as "Torn," apparently the last song Dolly Parton recorded, makes evident. That particular goddess shared Bono's stubborn conviction that people are essentially good, especially when enriched by faith, and that loving your neighbor remains possible; their collaboration will move some hearts, but pushes the limits of mawkishness as it laments the loss of the ecumenical ideal.

Faith remains the point of this band, and clearly feels more urgent to Bono now than back in the '90s, when he first openly indulged in the lemon squeeze of earthly pleasure. We're closer to heaven now; this is an older man's album, reflective and repentant. "Street of Dreams" begins with the very Psalm-ish phrases, "God, hear me shout" and in "Glorify" he addresses those who reject the spiritual with the ultimate Jesus flex, snarling, "There's nothing you can do to keep me from loving you." Casual fans who are not religious may be uncomfortable with such fervor. Those who don't mind a little preaching will appreciate the way he continues to play with that tradition, as on "Midnight Sunshine," a bubblegum soul number that turns on the pantheistic punchline, "You say God no longer cares for us / I say the stars are only there for us to shine." Banal on the page, Bono's words gain the light they need from a melody that feels like a mnemonic tool or, yes, a prayer. This is something that he's said before, a tiny pep talk to stay connected. Dogma breaks things, but the night is illuminated; let's dance.

U2 tries to maintain that nimbleness throughout Carnaval De Luz, and mostly pulls it off. Doing so, the time bandits meet the moment in which they've now landed. Whether dumb luck or Spidey sense had U2 choose a release date right after the U.S. election midterms that have solidified the return of liberal confidence, this music runs on a similar energy. As in many of the campaigns that recently made an impact, humor plays a key role in making U2's bolder messages palatable. Sometimes it takes the obvious form of wordplay, as when Bono quotes Ernest Hemingway's famous quip about his favorite cocktails in "Silencio," but mostly it's in the music itself. This is where the bass playing of career-long secret weapon Adam Clayton makes a difference. Motown's bop and the bubbling syncopation of lovers rock inform his style; here those rhythms act as a counterpoint to the drive of Mullen's drums, and to Bono's impassioned declarations. Bono knows how to turn a phrase in Clayton's direction as Edge's guitar creates static around both, so that his heavier pronouncements fizz a bit and shift their meanings. This playfulness among bandmates is what makes a song like "The Mirror Maker (Rosalía)" not a cringeworthy come-on but a genuine expression of awe at a younger artist. Longtime studio allies Brian Eno and Jacknife Lee make sure the atmosphere's right for this interplay. Instead of the big skies of the Daniel Lanois era or even the Eno-helmed, overlooked 2009 gem No Line on the Horizon, this album's production stresses agility and fun.

Even the big ballad "The Greatest Show on Earth," an homage to the illuminated cathedrals that U2 makes of stadiums when it plays "With or Without You" on its world tours, has enough antic energy running through it to save it from navel-gazing ponderousness. Bono's take on Peggy Lee singing "Is That All There Is," with Courvoisier in hand, the song meditates on the many marriages that make up a life. Naming heartache and productive codependence, he may be talking to his actual wife, Ali, who's been with him as long as he's gone by that ridiculous name. Regarding a dream that's gone dusty, he seems caught up with his bandmates, cajoling them into the spotlight one more time. But when he sings "Breathe on me and I'm love and I'm lust," it's a force beyond those intimates he welcomes — on the one hand, the spirit that guides him, and on the other, the fans he still insists on making a congregation. Clayton and Mullen turn that spotlight into pinpoints, keeping Bono from settling too firmly into his grandiose gestures, and the Edge offers up the soaring guitar lines that made them work in the first place. This torch song turns into a soul invocation, redolent of Aretha and the Sweet Emotions; all he can do, Bono realizes, is say that little prayer. For himself, for the band, for the moment where we're stuck and — even if you're not a fan — for you.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global outage that could have billion-dollar impact on Australia
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Henry Belot and Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Experts say disruption exposes ‘Australia’s reliance on foreign technology’ as software giant says services being restored

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Microsoft outage could be a disaster for the Australian economy that forces some small businesses to close, with costs expected to run into the billions of dollars, experts have warned.

The US software company has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.

The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.

Experts have said the outage exposes “Australia’s reliance on foreign technology” and that people unable to be paid, send an invoice, or access government services “are entitled to be worried”.

The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began on Friday morning, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.

Ashwin Pal, a partner at the risk advisory firm RSM Australia, said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn’t have a fallback.

“A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for smaller entities,” Pal said.

Pal said Microsoft had obviously struggled to recover, which raised bigger questions.

“I’m a technologist and I’m actually flabbergasted as to how something like this could have happened … they pushed out a change which should have been tested,” Pal said.

The Australian Computer Society has renewed calls for the federal government to urgently review which critical IT systems rely on a single provider, and where backup options could keep the economy running.

The society’s chief executive, Prins Ralston, said the outage had “exposed Australia’s reliance on foreign technology”, particularly on small businesses.

“Australians who couldn’t get paid, couldn’t send an invoice, or couldn’t reach a government service this morning are entitled to be worried,” Ralston said.

Australian hospitals and health clinics were affected by the outage, although the Australian Medical Association (AMA) on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care.

“We’ve had some facilities return to using paper for scripts because authentication to get into lots of prescribing software requires multifactor verification, which requires you to be able to access your Microsoft-supported email,” said the AMA’s president, Dr Michael Bonning.

Courts in South Australia and Victoria reported that the outage had affeced its email system. Many schools across the country were also affected.

Service NSW, the one-stop shop agency for residents, drivers, and business owners to access government services, encouraged customers to delay their visits to its service centres.

Federal government departments have also been maffectedy the outage, including national security agencies.

The head the domestic spy agency Asio, Mike Burgess, on Friday said the organisation’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.

The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.

In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.

Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”

US flight outage – live updates

Some US-bound flights from Sydney airport were grounded or delayed on Saturday after American authorities halted departures and delayed landings at all US airports.

Flights from Melbourne airport were also affected, with travel for passengers expected to depart for Los Angeles shortly after 10am being delayed by almost three hours.

Sydney airport confirmed the US ban on flight arrivals was lifted shortly before 1pm, although it was not known how this would impact delays.

Earlier, the airport confirmed some US-bound flights had been grounded.

“We are aware of the nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration and are monitoring the situation closely,” the spokesperson said.

“Passengers travelling to or via the United States should check with their airline for the latest information regarding their flight.”

Passengers on US bound flights from Sydney Airport reported being stuck on the tarmac for three hours before eventually departing. One plane required extra fuel after running air-conditioning for several hours while waiting.

The FAA announced the nationwide pause in response to “a temporary telecommunications outage”. It has since lifted the grounding order, as it continued to investigate the cause of the outage.

Passengers on two US-bound flights from Melbourne airport, which were due to depart at 12pm and 12.45pm, were also delayed due to the situation in the US.

A flight to Dallas, scheduled for 10am, departed at around 1pm, shortly after the US ban was lifted.

By 3pm Saturday, all delayed flights from Melbourne had departed.

“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we [are] going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”

In an apparent allusion to the “great replacement theory”, a far-right conspiracy theory that white westerners are being actively “replaced” by minority ethnic immigrants, he continued: “That’s the socialist plan, is to destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation.”

The comments sparked a wave of criticism, but the party has shown no signs of taking Bonds off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. One Nation did, however, dump one candidate this week: the Victorian branch disendorsed a lower-house candidate over an old social media post describing Hitler as the “GOAT”, an acronym for greatest of all time.

The rally was not a one-off. On a podcast released on Monday with the rally’s organiser, the Australian Lobby Group, Bonds appeared to double down on the remarks. He did not challenge host Scott Challen’s assertion that Labor governments were building “ethnic voting blocks with Middle Eastern and subcontinent people … to stack the numbers to entrench power for themselves”, instead responding: “Mate, and that’s why we’re going to get rid of all of the multicultural grants, right?”

On Wednesday, in an interview with ABC Upper Hunter, Bonds responded to questions about his comments by citing Australian Bureau of Statistics data that shows the proportion of Australians born overseas has trended upward since the end of the second world war, from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. He did not mention that the proportion of Australians born overseas was at its highest – 32.4% – in 1891, the first year of available data.

Bonds said with the Australian birthrate beneath the 2.1 required to replace the population, “I would just like to know what people assume is going to happen.”

“Where are these people going to come from?” he said.

NSW Labor pounced on the rally comments immediately, with the state’s premier, Chris Minns, calling them “frankly outrageous and racist”. The government passed motions in both houses censuring Bonds, not yet a member.

The Coalition followed four days later. On Wednesday afternoon, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said Bonds’ language was “clearly divisive”.

But she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement with One Nation after the March state election.

“We will not form a coalition with One Nation, [but] we’ll work with anyone post-election if we’re in a minority government,” she told reporters.

The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a Coalition with One Nation. And with the Coalition consistently polling behind One Nation, that makes Bonds not a fringe candidate, but a potentially influential figure.

The ABC’s former election analyst, Antony Green, said the remarks played straight into Labor’s hands.

“This will certainly be something the Labor party uses in all those multi-ethnic seats in Sydney,” he said – seats like those on the rural fringes of Sydney, which One Nation said it plans to target.

Indeed the deputy premier, Prue Car, who has Indian heritage and whose electorate of Londonderry is one of the seats in question, gave an impassioned critique of Bonds’ comments in question time on Tuesday.

“Who’s he [Bonds] talking about when he talks about this?” she said. “I tell you who he’s talking about – he’s talking about families like mine, and families that I represent.”

after newsletter promotion

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a director of polling group Redbridge, said that while the comments likely won’t play well in Sydney seats – including alienating moderate Liberal voters worried about the party going into Coalition with One Nation – “you might be able to get away with it in certain parts of NSW”.

And Bonds, a former coalminer, has made his base in the Hunter.

Samaras said One Nation could “clean the deck” in the regions, including Labor-held seats in the Hunter, and “pretty much anything else the Coalition hasn’t got bolted down to the ground”.

The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, who in September said he “made a mistake” when he told a Sydney rally he wanted to stop abortions, did not respond directly when asked if he agreed with Bonds’ comments or if he would rein in his first-placed upper house candidate.

“What I will say is that what Stuart Bonds is a patriotic Aussie. He’s a coalminer. He has very, very strong views,” he said on Tuesday.

Newman, who previously rejected claims that One Nation was racist, said on Tuesday: “What we want to do is … protect Australian values, and that is the fundamental thing that Stuart Bonds is pushing for. It’s about assimilation.”

The NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, whose parents immigrated to Australia from India in the 1970s, told the ABC that Bonds’ comments were not grounded in reality.

“I think he’s saying that there is a deliberate conspiracy to use migrants to replace the way he puts it, native-born Australians for political reasons,” Mookhey said.

The quota for election to the upper house is 4.5%, making Bonds all but guaranteed to be elected, with One Nation polling in the high 20s and low 30s in recent months.

Green expects the party to pick up four or five seats in the upper house; so far it has only named three candidates: Newman, Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer who is second on the upper house ticket.

But unlike Victoria, NSW has optional preferential voting, which means when that state goes to the polls in March, lower house preference flows aren’t guaranteed.

But Bonds has downplayed whether he may have jeopardised a future preference deal with the Coalition.

“If the Coalition have a problem with facts, the same as the Labor party, then maybe it will,” he told the ABC.

“But I’m not here to impress the Coalition.”

But his party has shown no signs of dumping him off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. NSW treasurer Daniel Mookhey says his comments are not grounded in reality.

https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.title: UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.text:
Eurotunnel owner Getlink wants to replicate ‘airport experience’ at Folkestone and Calais, without making people get out of cars

Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais.

In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

Not signed in before? Create an account

Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further.

Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais.

Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate.

In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore.

The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years.

EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France, have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues.

It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal.

Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting.

But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting.

Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time.

“This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?”

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said.

The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent.

Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche.

He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars.

The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint.

Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they are can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question was are asking all the time.”

This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: University hounded out of Hungary by Orbán reaches out to new government
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Prospect of partial return to Budapest by Central European University suggests confidence in Hungary’s future

A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to expanding its presence in Budapest, in a mark of confidence in the country’s democratic future.

Carsten Q Schneider, the interim president and rector of Central European University (CEU), said it was interested in increasing its programmes in Budapest, as long as this did not damage the student experience.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

So far the CEU has not held formal talks with Hungary’s new government, which has promised to restore academic freedom, “but our hand is reaching out, their hand is reaching out – it is just that they have many things to do”, the academic told the Guardian.

The CEU relocated its main activities to Vienna from Budapest in 2019, after pressure from the previous government led by Orbán. But the outlook changed when Péter Magyar won a landslide victory in April pledging to root out corruption and reform the state.

The CEU, founded by Hungarian-American financier and philanthropist George Soros in 1991 to entrench democratic change in the region, was forced to cease awarding degrees in Budapest in response to a law widely seen as targeting the institution.

The EU’s highest court struck down Hungary’s “Lex CEU” in 2020, finding that it violated the EU charter of fundamental rights, but the verdict came too late for the university. The CEU retains 312 staff in Budapest, mostly administrative, but the majority, 476, and all its teaching, are in Vienna.

Schneider said upgrading the status of the CEU, which is privately funded, in Budapest would be “a symbol for academic freedom [and] of resilience” but depended on goodwill and funding independent of the Hungarian government. He said a decision on its future in Hungary would be taken by the CEU’s 13-member board, whose members include Soros and his son, Alexander Soros.

“We don’t want special treatment,” Schneider said. ‘“We are a great asset, so let’s work out something.”

But the CEU, which he said was “thriving tremendously” in Vienna, does not plan a wholesale return to Budapest. Any change would have to ensure the quality of the student experience, for instance, assuring that students would be able to combine courses, say in economics and history, without having to travel the 200km-plus distance between the two cities.

Focused on social sciences, law and humanities, the CEU has more than 1,400 students from 103 countries, mostly doing master’s and PhD programmes.

According to Schneider, for the first time in the CEU’s 25-year history, students from the US now make up the largest cohort of master’s students (10%). The CEU has seen an increase in US applicants since Donald Trump returned to the White House and launched a sweeping campaign against elite universities, including slashing federal funding and seeking to exert control over internal policies.

The CEU rector has had informal talks with US academics on how to maintain academic freedom under pressure from rightwing populists. He described his message as: “Don’t be naive for a second. These people have a plan, so it’s not by accident that they attack universities. They want to have cultural hegemony.” He added, however, that Trump and allied movements, such as Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland, have identified “real problems”, such as in the US how universities have entrenched “a reproduction of elites”

When coming under political pressure, he said universities needed “to look for allies”, among other academic institutions, students, alumni and parents. Institutions also had to stand up for disciplines under attack, such as gender studies, Schneider added.

He recalled the outpouring of support for CEU – when tens of thousands of people protested in Budapest in defence of the university – as “one of the most humbling experiences I have had”.

Schneider, a German political scientist who specialises in the study of democracies and regime transition, said Magyar had successfully used Orbán’s political machine against him.

“Nobody has a better idea than [Magyar] how to defeat the most potent and the most skilled illiberal populist [Orbán]. So he knows something.” He added: “The people and skills that you need to bring a non-democratic regime down are not the same and sometimes the opposite of what it takes to establish a democracy. So the question now is whether he [Magyar] has the skills to basically reinvent liberal democracy for the 21st century.”

Schneider said Hungary could be the world’s first “post-illiberal democracy” – a model for democratic restoration, just as Orbán inspired rightwing populists around the world. But he also raised doubts about this thesis, saying there were questions about how Magyar and his Tisza party might develop in the context of Hungary’s “very difficult economic situation”.

The test would be, he suggested, when Magyar faces losing support and, eventually, defeat at the ballot box. “So what happens when he loses support and then cracks in his movement appear? Will he be the visionary leader who manages … to establish a three, four, five-party system, where people compete? That is to be seen.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Hungary seizes $19.5m in cash found buried in forests amid graft inquiry
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: AFP
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Anti-corruption agency carried out searches as part of investigation into Orbán-era minister accused of taking bribes

Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) buried in forests and hidden elsewhere while investigating an ex-minister of nationalist former leader Viktor Orbán’s cabinet.

Miklós Seszták, Hungary’s minister of national development between 2014 and 2018, is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, purchasing secondhand buses at inflated prices.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The prime minister, Péter Magyar, won a landslide election victory in April, ending Orbán’s 16 years in power after promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during his rival’s rule.

Seszták, two other Orbán-era ministers and the former premier’s brother have been taken into custody in different cases as graft inquiries have gathered pace in recent weeks.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), an anti-graft body with sweeping powers established as part of Magyar’s accountability drive, said it searched several locations on Thursday and Friday as part of the criminal proceedings against Seszták.

“During the search, investigators found large amounts of cash: buried in forests, hidden in agricultural and warehouse buildings as well as residential properties, and stored in high-value safes in secluded locations,” the statement said.

“The total amount of cash found during the two-day search was 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and US $1,257,100,” it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m.

NVVH said its staff deposited the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury’s account.

“Upon receipt, 12 Treasury employees spent 8 hours counting the money using 5 counting machines,” the finance minister, András Kármán, said on Facebook.

Magyar hailed the seizure as a potential turning point.

“This officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” he said in reference to Orbán’s former governing coalition.

The former leader did not react to the latest development. Orbán had previously denounced the probes targeting his inner circle as “political persecution” aimed at imprisoning him.

Mohammed Alfatih rearrested over alleged plot to target Israelis in Europe while detained for attack on bailiff

A former Hamas bodyguard convicted of knife crime in the UK is wanted in Germany for allegedly plotting to murder Jewish people.

Details of the alleged plot can now be reported after Mohammed Alfatih, also known as Mohammed Naim, was found guilty on Friday of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his home in Birmingham.

The 40-year-old was found guilty by a majority verdict of unlawful wounding, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of the more serious charge of wounding with intent.

He was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit when he attacked the bailiff last year.

Alfatih, the son of a senior Hamas official, could not be named during his trial because of reporting restrictions.

He had been photographed working for a former leader of Hamas before being granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.

While detained for the attack on the bailiff in Birmingham, he was rearrested after authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged plot to attack Israeli targets in central Europe.

Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK, with his connection to Hamas stated in the German extradition request.

German prosecutors charged seven suspected Hamas members in September over an alleged plot to target Jews or Israelis in Germany or Austria around the second anniversary of the 7 October attack on Israel.

They said “Mohammed A” played a prominent role in transporting and storing weapons but was being prosecuted separately after UK authorities arrested him in London and noted he had not yet been returned to Germany.

German authorities said he was connected to Hamas’s leadership and was said to have produced a video in advance to take responsibility for the attack on its behalf.

The attack was disrupted by Germany’s domestic intelligence service after a tipoff from the Mossad, Israel’s secret service.

During a two-week trial at Birmingham crown court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October 2025.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Eisenkot condemns Netanyahu’s ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: William Christou
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Prime ministerial hopeful calls Arab minority ‘an integral part of the Israeli story’ as he seeks to form government

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot condemned a “racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation” against the country’s Arab citizens, after the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accused Arab parties of electoral fraud without evidence.

Netanyahu has repeatedly targeted Arab parties and Palestinian citizens of Israel after his party received a disappointing electoral showing, accusing them of manipulating the election and being linked to Hamas. Israeli electoral authorities have rejected these claims as not being backed by evidence.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Arab citizens of Israel, the vast majority of them of Palestinian descent, comprise more than 20% of the country’s population.

Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security branch, sought to question four Arab lawmakers, including the Arab-majority Ra’am party head, Mansour Abbas, leading to accusations that the security agency had become politicised.

“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story. The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of statesmanship,” Eisenkot said in a statement on Friday.

Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis.

The statement also reflected political realities in Israel, as Arab parties found themselves kingmakers after the latest election. The two Arab-majority parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, secured 19 seats in the October election.

They have the potential to help Eisenkot form a governing coalition and become Israel’s next prime minister. If Eisenkot cannot form a coalition within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, the mandate to form a government would pass to another lawmaker, potentially Netanyahu.

Eisenkot has to balance the competing interests of several parties if he hopes to form a coalition. Rightwing elements of the opposition have pledged to drop their support of the prospective PM if he cooperates with Arab parties.

His statement on Friday portrayed a more statesman-like approach to ruling than his more rightwing, demagogic opponents who have used Arab parties and citizens as political scapegoats over the last three years.

“[Arab citizens] have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” Eisenkot said in his statement.

“The prime minister of Israel is the prime minister of all Israeli citizens, including those who did not vote for him,” he added.

Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” after its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.

In a speech, Netanyahu falsely claimed that the two Arab lists sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.

During the same ceremony, the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, heckled Joint List’s leader, Yousef Jabareen, during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.

“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.

President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.

Israeli media has reported that Eisenkot has also been reaching out to the country’s ultra-Orthodox parties for a potential alliance. The issue of the ultra-Orthodox not serving in the Israeli military was one of the hot button issues during the October election, with Eisenkot previously saying they should also be included in the country’s mandatory draft.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Gadi Eisenkot condemned a ‘racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation’ against the country’s Arab citizens. Israeli electoral authorities have rejected these claims as not being backed by evidence.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Phillip Inman
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% last month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Pill told the Financial Times: “My view would be, we will see evidence that motivates further rises,” adding that the central bank would “do ‌what is necessary to get inflation back to 2% through time”.

The chief economist is one of a number of the Bank’s policymakers who believe the UK economy has gained in strength over the last year, handing workers the power to bid up wages.

Recent figures showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, to give an annual rate of growth that was only surpassed by the US among the G7 group of wealthy countries.

With inflation expected to rise to 5% in spring next year, driven by high oil and gas prices as a result of the Iran war, Pill expects public and private sector workers to demand substantial pay rises, which would keep inflation high for a longer period.

Pill said he considered an end to the US-Israeli ‌conflict with Iran and a fall in energy prices to be a “very low probability”, signalling to the newspaper that he was poised to vote for another ​quarter-point increase next month.

“My bias, for what it’s worth, is that I worry about the inflationary impact being magnified by second-round effects,” he said, adding that he believed the central bank should have acted sooner to combat inflation. “In my ⁠view, we waited too long.”

While the Bank has not seen evidence of wage increases or companies being able to pass on higher costs to consumers, Pill said the absence of evidence was not evidence of absence.

“As we go into next year, we will begin to see some evidence, and it could play out in one direction or another – we’ll see.”

after newsletter promotion

Financial markets expect UK interest rates to rise to almost 5% in 2027. Pill said these expectations were “not outrageous”, hinting that he could vote for more substantial increases in the cost of borrowing at the next meetings of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) because the “ability to be ​modest [in the scale ​of rate rises] has diminished”.

City analysts have interpreted the increasingly hawkish comments of Pill and other MPC members as making an interest rate rise in December almost inevitable. But there is disagreement about the strength of the economy, with many concerned that further increases in the cost of borrowing will hit the manufacturing sector and the construction industry, which has contracted for much of the year.

Households are also likely to cut back on spending in the new year, when the energy price cap is expected to rise to almost £2,000 for a typical home and council tax bills increase by an average of almost 5%.

Tech company says operations restored to all customers and regions affected by one of worst IT failures in years

Not signed in before? Create an account

“Further updates can be found at MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center.”

The outage, which began on Thursday, affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hours-long episode had affected some of their operations.

In the UK, where NHS England has a five-year deal to use Microsoft 365, vital public services were hit, with hospital staff resorting to paper records and one union reporting that ambulance services had suffered a “serious impact”.

The already backlogged court system was also hit, with juries in some cases being sent home early or prisoners not being sent to court, while at Minshull Street crown court in Manchester staff scrambled to locate a fax machine.

In the US, school districts told parents they must reach out by phone or online apps to contact their child’s school, while staffers at the House of Representatives told Politico they had lost a day of work.

One detention facility in Colorado said they were unable to take online bond payments to release detainees and told anyone needing to post bond for immediate release to do so in person at the jail.

In Australia, many people who rely on Microsoft 365 reported being unable to access their inboxes, including at councils, courts and schools. The federal police and Asio, Australia’s national domestic security and intelligence agency, were also affected by the outage.

Asio’s director general, Mike Burgess, said the agency’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.

Across Europe, government agencies in the Netherlands, Belgium and France reported problems, with a French municipality instructing citizens to use the phone instead of emailing.

In Japan, government email services became unavailable and staff resorted to text messaging. The shipping firm Sagawa Express was unable to accept some online reservations while Taisho, a major pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies told Reuters that fund management services had been disrupted.

Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.

Approximately 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems began at about midday on Thursday in the US and at 6pm in the UK.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

The Washington-based company apologised on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents. It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” after a recent network change.

The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when multiple communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. The outage has fuelled concerns in the UK about an overreliance on a small number of tech companies.

Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London, told the Guardian an outage of this size was usually “the result of some surprising interaction between systems. Each of the systems is normally quite well understood but interactions between them are complex and frequently the cause of large outages like this.

“It’s very hard to build a complex system without there being some risk of some failure.”

Tim Clement-Jones, a former chair of the House of Lords artificial intelligence select committee, said the widespread outages of vital government services were an “I-told-you-so moment” highlighting Britain’s dependence on US tech.

Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science, said: “This problem serves to emphasise the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”

The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450m paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.

Government agencies in the Netherlands, Belgium and France reported problems.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Greenpeace boulders may delay building of £12bn windfarms in North Sea
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Activists dumped rocks off Norfolk coast on site of Burnham-backed project in protest against seabed trawling

The giant offshore windfarms backed by Andy Burnham this week may face unexpected stumbling blocks after Greenpeace activists unwittingly dumped about 15 tonnes of boulders on to the site as part of a campaign against seabed trawling in the North Sea.

Greenpeace created the “boulder barrier” to safeguard harbour porpoises off the Norfolk coast by dropping giant stone blocks, each weighing up to 2 tonnes, on to the sea floor to prevent a method of fishing known as bottom trawling.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The barrier will pose an additional challenge for the green energy developers because most of the boulders were dropped on to the site earmarked for one of the UK’s biggest planned windfarms, known as the Norfolk Vanguard project.

Greenpeace began dumping boulders on to the site, without consent from the marine authority, days before the prime minister told the Cop31 summit that the UK would invest £1bn of public money in the Vanguard West and Vanguard East windfarms in what is believed to be the biggest investment of its kind in UK history.

The Guardian understands that Greenpeace checked the seabed for any existing cables, pipelines or shipwrecks, but it was not aware of the plans to build the Vanguard East windfarm.

The creation of the underwater barrier in one of “the most heavily trawled” areas of the southern North Sea was timed to coincide with the premiere of the BBC’s Blue Planet III documentary, narrated by Sir David Attenborough.

Some boulders bear the signatures of celebrities including Simon Pegg and Benedict Cumberbatch, who have voiced marine conservation documentaries, and agreed to support the Greenpeace campaign.

However, they are likely to be removed within months after renewable energy developers agreed a £12bn deal alongside the UK government to begin building the offshore windfarm next year. Industrial fishing activities, including bottom trawling, are also likely to move elsewhere to avoid the construction area.

The Guardian understands that the offshore wind developer, the German utility company RWE, is in talks with Greenpeace to verify the exact placement of the boulders so that they can update the seabed surveys they began last summer. The company is also investigating any potential impact to the construction of the project or its undersea cables.

after newsletter promotion

A spokesperson for RWE described its communication with Greenpeace as “constructive” and said the company would “continue to investigate the precise implications” for the Norfolk Vanguard East project.

Will McCallum, the co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said any suggestion that the boulders would cause a genuine obstacle was “absurd”.

“Anyone familiar with offshore wind in the North Sea knows that energy companies routinely move naturally occurring boulders from the seabed before building windfarms,” he said.

“Some of these boulders can be 10 times heavier than those we placed.

“Greenpeace has long championed offshore wind and will continue to do so. While we wait for this windfarm to be built, our boulders will provide an essential barrier to destructive bottom trawlers that are decimating the seabed in this protected area.”
