https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Torture survivors may have been sent to Sussex asylum camp unlawfully, documentary reveals
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Diane Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Undercover ITV report also shows inadequate welfare checks at ex-military base run by firm of asylum camp billionaire Graham King

Asylum seekers accommodated at a controversial military base in East Sussex have been subjected to inadequate welfare checks, and torture survivors may have been placed there unlawfully, a new undercover documentary for ITV has revealed.

Mass accommodation sites are central to the government’s plan to end the use of hotels to house asylum seekers. For the documentary Inside The Asylum Camp, ITV’s undercover reporter got a job as a welfare officer at Crowborough and covertly filmed inside the former military training camp. The documentary claims that poor screening and welfare checks are having serious consequences for some of the asylum seekers.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Last May, the high court ruled that a Home Office policy change forcing torture survivors to share rooms was unlawful. The accommodation at Crowborough is in large dormitories.

The Home Office’s decision to accommodate asylum seekers on two former military sites – Crowborough, and Wethersfield in Essex – have triggered opposition from local residents. Plans to use three other sites – Bicester, Barnham and Linton-on-Ouse – have caused a similar outcry, mostly around fears about asylum seekers causing a rise in violent crime. However, very low levels of even minor crimes have been recorded by police at Wethersfield and Crowborough among asylum seekers at the two camps.

The Crowborough site is run by Clearsprings Ready Homes. According to its latest accounts, it is generating millions of pounds in income every day from its asylum accommodation contracts. Its boss, Graham King, has become the first asylum accommodation billionaire.

The documentary footage shows that, although two comprehensive welfare checks are supposed to be carried out each month by Clearsprings welfare officers, some staff appear to admit cutting corners and not asking all the questions they are required to ask of asylum seekers. On one occasion a welfare officer is filmed telling the undercover reporter “you don’t need to go in too deep”.

Staff appear to admit to falling behind on the 1,000 welfare checks they are supposed to carry out each month saying: “We’re so fucked.”

Concerns about an asylum seeker can be flagged on their file. A welfare officer is filmed telling the undercover reporter: “Those flags mean nothing” and that “nobody ever looks at them again”. When asked by the undercover reporter if some asylum seekers fall through the net due to brief welfare checks carried out, the welfare officer replies: “Oh, absolutely.”

The undercover reporter says he has identified four or five survivors of torture who should not have been sent to the military camp.

Louise Calvey, the executive director of the charity Asylum Matters, raised concerns about the findings of the undercover documentary. Her organisation has a campaign to accommodate asylum seekers in communities not camps. “The reports of torture survivors being accommodated on military barracks are appalling,” she said. “Brave survivors endure appalling experiences arriving to a country where they thought they’d be safe – a supposed civilised country, placing them in camps without the support they desperately need.

“People being held in isolation for prolonged periods of time without access to sufficient water demonstrate just how far we have fallen as a country. That government contractors can fail so resoundingly in their duty of care to people seeking safety in our country demonstrates how much our system dehumanises refugees.”

Calvey said the government needed to urgently review its use of the camps, which she described as “a choice to punish people for having the audacity to exercise their lawful right to seek asylum here”.

The Home Office and Clearsprings have been approached.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Health is wealth? Polymarket and Kalshi now host bets on measles and other US health crises
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Experts warn of risks of platforms hosting bets tied to US public health – including vaccine mandates and drug trials

The sign was pasted on a construction fence next to an elementary school in the Brooklyn borough of New York City. “Vaccines,” it proclaimed in bold capital letters against a blue star-spangled background – appearing, at first glance, to be like any other public health message on the importance of getting vaccinated.

But at the bottom of the sign, in smaller letters, it read: “Will any state end vaccine markets?” It was accompanied by the logo for Polymarket, an online prediction market where users can log in to wager on the outcomes of nearly any event – including, now, public health.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Polymarket joins Kalshi, another online prediction market, which began offering health-related predictions over the summer. Users can wager on when the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) will approve a skin-cancer vaccine, or whether the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) will change its vaccine recommendations. They can also bet on drug trial outcomes and approval; they can bet on how many cases of measles the US might see in 2026 and whether it will lose its measles-elimination status this year.

“I am not surprised,” said Matthew Eisenberg, professor and chair of health policy and management at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “Kalshi and Polymarket will list contracts on anything with a checkable outcome.”

Despite being functionally “identical” to regulated gambling, prediction markets are largely unregulated, said Lia Nower, a professor and the director of the Center for Gambling Studies at Rutgers University.

“Gambling right now is like the wild, wild west,” she added. “There’s no federal regulatory body that’s really prescribing any limits on any of this, or just minimum guidelines for states to follow – so anything’s possible.”

Prediction markets position themselves as financial derivatives, rather than traditional bets, in a regulatory loophole, Nower said – which means they operate under federal commodities laws, with oversight from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and are not regulated by states as gambling operations. Several states have filed lawsuits against the companies alleging that they function as gambling sites.

Advocates, officials and lawmakers could place bets on ending vaccine mandates at the state level, for instance, and then introduce new laws or policies to do so; there don’t appear to be any laws against that, Nower said. There are bets on when certain officials will leave health agencies, which could be affected by resignation or termination decisions.

Predictions could also affect how drugs are tested and regulated, critics say. Trial participants could purposefully change their behavior to affect outcomes; drug companies could change the timing of trials.

Predictions on FDA decisions and trial endpoints “create a payoff for anyone with nonpublic information”, like agency reviewers, trial investigators and legislative staff, Eisenberg said. Prediction markets may create their own safeguards, like employment checks at sign-up, “but the risk isn’t necessarily that a reviewer takes a bribe – it’s that the market now rewards leaks”, he said.

Polymarket did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the potential consequences for public health or medicine. Kalshi did not respond on the record to the same questions, but spokesperson Dani Lever argued that the predictions on drug trials and approvals would improve transparency.

“Kalshi’s clinical trial markets are a pilot program aimed at a structural problem in drug development: the people who best know whether a trial will succeed are scattered, and their insight rarely reaches the public,” Lever said in a statement. “Public markets avoid those barriers.”

Problem gambling is itself a rapidly growing public health concern.

Gambling is a “big public health issue” that disproportionately affects people who are younger, Black or Hispanic and lower-income, Nower said. She co-authored a new report showing that more than half of young people, between the ages of 13 and 27, gambled in the past year – and among the young gamblers, 39.5% had some degree of gambling-related risk and 10.3% were high risk for problem gambling.

Eisenberg’s research on online sports betting found that legalization is followed by measurable increases in treatment for depression and anxiety among young men. There have been some discussions after such findings to create state-level consumer protections – like deposit limits, self-exclusion, rules about advertising and funding for treatment paid out of state betting taxes, he said. “But the prediction markets sit outside all of that.” Very little of the revenue flows to states through taxes to support such treatment.

“In effect, these are gambling products that have exited the only regulatory system designed to limit gambling harm,” Eisenberg said.

Prediction markets are “really something that the government needs to clamp down on”, Nower said. Yet “the federal government still has no federal regulatory body,” she added. There are no research centers at the National Institutes of Health focused on gambling, as there are for alcohol and drug abuse.

“It’s just unaddressed at the federal level,” Nower said.

States like New Jersey are moving to restrict the markets – and concerns include consumer protection and the potential for insider trading, Nower said.

“People with inside information or control over an outcome could potentially profit from what they call ‘event contracts’,” another word for the predictions, she said.

This is the future, Eisenberg said: “Gambling on everything, everywhere, with fewer and fewer consumer protections.”

Yet he pointed out that public-health propositions on the markets were small, and he cautioned against seeing them as any sign of public sentiment. “Prices that small can be moved by a single trader and shouldn’t be read as public opinion,” Eisenberg said. “A few-hundred-dollar contract on the childhood vaccine schedule is not a forecast of anything.”

Within a week, the Polymarket sign in Brooklyn was vandalized. The bottom, with the Polymarket logo and the text on placing a prediction, was ripped away.

Now the sign simply reads: “Vaccines.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Polymarket joins Kalshi, another online prediction market, which began offering health-related predictions over the summer. The sign was vandalized within a week.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Enough is enough’: rising number of deadly ebike battery fires spark fear in New York City
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
City has failed to build infrastructure that could reduce threat, and saw 400 fires, 83 injuries and 12 deaths this year

F
ires from lithium-ion batteries, which power ebikes and scooters, have become regular occurrences in New York, causing deaths and fear among residents, but the city has failed to build infrastructure that could reduce the threat.

New York has seen a dramatic uptick this year in fires from the batteries. In 2025, there were 292 fires, 51 injuries and one death, according to the New York fire department (FDNY). This year, there have already been more than 400 fires, 83 injuries and 12 deaths.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

In late October, four members of a family, including an 11-year-old boy, died in a fire caused by a battery in an ebike that was in the pathway to an exit of an 11th floor apartment in a public housing building in the Bronx.

Then recently in a fire at a home in Brooklyn, six people died and nine were injured, including three firefighters and two police officers. Investigators discovered lithium-ion batteries at the scene but have not determined whether they caused the fire, the city council speaker, Julie Menin, said in a statement.

“The presence of lithium-ion batteries at the scene is a serious concern, and more must be done to encourage and mandate safe storage practices. Enough is enough,” Menin stated.

London and Toronto have also recently seen a dramatic increase in lithium-ion battery fires, which are often caused by overcharging and defective or damaged batteries.

Some of that trend is simply because ebikes, often used by food delivery workers and commuters, have become more popular.

But in New York, the city has not executed its plan to build outdoor charging stations which would prevent people from plugging in the batteries in their apartments, where an overheated or defective battery poses a greater risk, experts say.

“There is a ton of red tape around this sort of new technology, and while it’s well intended to not let something new roll out too quickly, I think in this case, it is time to do something quickly,” said Laura Kavanagh, former commissioner of the FDNY.

In 2025, there were 2.2m ebikes imported into the United States, according to Light Electric Vehicle Association, double the number from just three years earlier.

In response to the increased usage and related increase in fires, the New York City department of transportation conducted a 2024 pilot in which it hired companies to offer battery-swapping cabinets where delivery workers could exchange exhausted batteries for charged ones.

The riders did more than 12,000 swaps over six months, and among participants, there was a 35% reduction in charging batteries at home, according to the city.

Following its success, the city announced that it would install 25 charging sites but not until 2027. The city first needed to “gather feedback on site selection, design and implementation”.

In April, New York mayor Zohran Mamdani asked residents to provide feedback on where they would like the 25 cabinets. The city planned to make them available in 2028, the announcement stated.

In 2023, the city also announced that it received a $25m federal grant to build 173 electric-micromobility charging and storage stations at 53 public housing developments.

“This means that residents will no longer need to charge their ebikes in their apartments, what we find to be extremely dangerous,” Mayor Eric Adams said at the time.

At the time, the deputy mayor, Meera Joshi, said residents would start “seeing evidence” of the stations in early 2024.

Three years later, none have been built.

Even though the Biden administration allocated the $25m for the infrastructure, the federal government has not actually provided the funds, according to the New York department of transportation.

Asked why the process has moved slowly, a transportation department spokesperson stated in an email: “The city’s strategy to reduce the risk e-bike battery fires focuses on getting unsafe devices off our streets and providing safe and convenient e-bike charging options” and the “outdoor battery swapping cabinets will make charging safer and more accessible for the thousands of delivery workers who rely on these devices to serve New Yorkers. With the public feedback we gathered this summer, we’re finalizing locations for our public e-bike charging program before advancing to the design phase and remain on pace to launch the service in 2028”.

Meanwhile, Popwheels, one of the companies in the successful pilot, has installed about 45 cabinets around the city, according to CEO Baruch Herzfeld.

He wants to install hundreds more around the city but has been stymied by a permitting process that he describes as “ludicrous”. He said it often takes six months for the city to approve one cabinet.

“If I want to put a cabinet that they approve in a parking lot, I have to use an architect to do a drawing, and then they have to come and do an inspection of a drawing of an ebike battery cabinet in the parking lot,” Herzfeld said. “This permitting process is why kids are dying.”

The city also often issues tickets to the owners of properties where Herzfeld has installed the cabinets, he said, for minor infractions like a fire extinguisher not having the proper tags or trash at the site.

Amanda Farinacci, the FDNY deputy commissioner public information, stated in an email that the tickets were not for “minor infractions but instead significant concerns”.

“The FDNY has been very serious partners with the micro-mobility/charging cabinet industry, being very accessible and collaborative to achieve solutions,” Farinacci stated. “We are a public safety agency and our mission is public safety. To conflate our regulatory responsibilities with causing people to charge their batteries indoors is entirely misplaced and inaccurate.”

Kavanagh, who spent a decade at FDNY before leaving in 2024, argued that the department is focusing on “too narrow of a concern”.

“I respect whatever concerns they have about the cabinet as real, but that is asking the wrong question,” said Kavanagh, who now works as a visiting urbanist at New York University. If “a battery failed in that cabinet outside, it is almost certain that would do no more than property damage. You are comparing that to” 10 New Yorkers dying in fires in the last three weeks.

“This is just appreciably worse, and so I think we need to frame it that way,” she added.

The latest fire may spur the city to expedite its approval process. On Friday, Menin announced that the city council would hold an emergency meeting on 20 November to conduct oversight to ensure the city is properly enforcing existing laws and that the public is educated on best fire safety practices and lithium-ion battery storage.

Ebike fires “are something that can cause people to lose their lives as well as their livelihoods”, Mamdani said on MS Now after the Brooklyn fire. “And so, we are really looking at every avenue we have to keep them safe.”

In 2023, the city received a $25m federal grant to build 173 electric-micromobility charging and storage stations at 53 public housing. FDNY deputy commissioner says department is focusing on “too narrow of a concern

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: SpaceX not being honest about ‘political’ reasons for slowing Starshield, says Zelenskyy
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Luke Harding in Kyiv
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Throttling of Elon Musk’s military-grade satellite system affecting whole frontline, says Ukraine’s president

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of not telling the truth over restrictions to Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system, saying the decision to impose speed limits appears to be “political” rather than “technical”.

Speaking on Friday, Ukraine’s president said the restrictions affecting Ukrainian drones had been in place for five days. They could no longer fly at speeds of more than 161km/h (100mph), he said, with connections at higher speeds lost.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

As a result, incoming jet-powered Russian Shahed drones could no longer be intercepted. Ukraine’s own mid-range strikes against military targets in Russian-occupied territory were also severely affected, he said.

Speaking to the Guardian and other journalists at the presidential palace in Kyiv, Zelenskyy said he had asked his military leadership to raise the issue with Elon Musk’s company SpaceX, as well as with the Pentagon and the US state department.

There was “no clear explanation” as to why Ukraine’s operations were being throttled. He said SpaceX had told Kyiv that there were “no restrictions”. The claim, Zelenskyy suggested, was untrue with problems detected across the “entire frontline”.

“There have been discussions with the company at the institutional level. The ministry of defence spoke with SpaceX. They replied: ‘We are not imposing any restrictions.’ They say it is some kind of technical issue. We do not believe that is the case,” Zelenskyy said.

He added: “The question is not whether we believe them or not. There may be some further checks. But every day, we test this in different directions. Every day, we get the same confirmation. So these are not isolated cases; they are widespread.”

Ukraine suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US tactic, designed to put pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin. It follows a similar issue last month, and coincided with US-brokered talks last week in Abu Dhabi featuring Ukrainian and Russian representatives.

The Kremlin insists Ukraine give up the entire eastern Donbas region.

But Zelenskyy categorically ruled out giving away further land to Russian “terrorists”. He also revealed that US negotiators, Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and real estate developer Steve Witkoff, had asked if Ukraine was willing to give up the Donbas in exchange for membership of Nato, or Nato-like security guarantees.

Details of the proposal were vague, Zelenskyy said. They did not appear to involve US peacekeeping troops on the ground, he added. He said the war could only end with a ceasefire agreement, alongside meaningful security guarantees, underwritten by western partners.

Zelenskyy also dismissed an offer by Putin for a “humanitarian mission” in the eastern city of Kostiantynivka as a ploy. Russia has called for a five-day ceasefire, modelled on a truce last month in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, from where civilians were evacuated.

“It’s an absolutely primitive move. Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” Zelenskyy said. He said civilians had already fled the area as fierce street-by-street fighting continued, with huge Russian losses.

Zelenskyy said he had proposed repeating the Oleshky truce in nearby Russian-occupied villages and towns in south Ukraine, along the Dnipro River. Putin rejected this. His true goal was to swallow up Kostiantynivka and the Ukrainian garrison cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Zelenskyy said.

He also called Russian attempts to discuss Europe’s security architecture – a topic raised last week by the Trump administration – as “concerning”. The Kremlin has called for Nato to return to its pre-1997 configuration, before eastern European countries including the Baltic states joined the alliance.

Putin first made this demand in 2021, in the runup to his big Ukraine invasion. Its revival after nearly five years of full-scale war, Zelenskyy said, was an alarming signal, indicative of imperial thinking. “Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact,” Zelenskyy said, stressing: “We cannot turn everything upside down.”

Ukraine’s president said his recent conversations with European leaders who met in Dublin had brought tangible results. They included pledges from Denmark to supply ammunition for F-16 jets – used to shoot down Russian drones – as well as energy support packages for Kyiv and other cities.

Russia was “betting everything” on its winter campaign, he added. In recent months Moscow has escalated its attacks on Ukrainian cities, in an attempt to make civilians capitulate. The US Congress could pressure Putin to de-escalate by passing laws on sanctions and giving Ukraine weapons, Zelenskyy said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘We must deliver’: jubilant Democrats gather in Denver to chart way forward
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio in Denver
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
At party’s ‘What’s Next’ conference, consensus is they need to act quickly, but over affordability or accountability is the question

What’s next for Democrats?

It’s the question thousands of Democrats, including lawmakers, strategists, pollsters, creators, organizers, staffers and 2028 presidential hopefuls are trying to answer at a three-day gathering in Denver, after a sweeping victory in the 2026 midterm elections.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

But the answer remains vague.

“We must deliver immediate, bold relief during this affordability crisis,” James Talarico, the senator-elect from Texas, said at the “What’s Next” conference on Thursday.

“Now, we’ll have the collective responsibility to really get to work, fighting for an affordable America, working hard to drive down the high cost of … groceries, high cost of gas, high cost of housing,” Hakeem Jeffries, the congressman of New York, said on Friday.

The consensus is Democrats need to act quickly when they become the majority in January. But the how in that is much more complicated.

There’s a looming question of whether lawmakers should focus more on accountability and pursuing investigations into the administration or focus on moving legislation forward to make life more affordable for Americans.

Rob Sand, the governor-elect of Iowa, told reporters on Thursday he thought the focus should be on delivering tangible economic relief.

“Every time I read, right now, about more investigations of things that have already been reported on in the media, I’m thinking: ‘Why do we need to investigate that? It’s already been reported on.’ Why don’t you do something actually productive or better people’s lives,” Sand said.

Jamie Raskin, the congressman from Maryland who is expected to lead the House judiciary committee, told reporters he believed lawmakers could do both.

Not to mention, there’s a fight brewing over party leadership in the Senate. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is now challenging Chuck Schumer, the party’s longtime leader, as Senate majority leader.

“I’m not voting for senator Schumer,” Elissa Slotkin, a senator for Michigan, told reporters on Friday.

Yet the mood at the Democrats’ de facto victory party – which was planned months in advance by a new group called Majority Democrats – was mostly celebratory. Attendees reveled in the massive wins in longtime Republican strongholds that handed the party sizable majorities in both chambers of Congress and expanded Democrats’ control of governorships and state legislatures across the country.

A six-piece jazz band welcomed attendees to a spacious outdoor plaza on Thursday afternoon. Attendees hugged and congratulated one another. The plaza was packed with smiling Democrats, some wearing “Talarico for Texas” shirts and “Jamie Ager for Congress” pins, others wore “pay your taxes” hats.

Most of the attendees were young. Many of the organizers and strategists are people who joined Democratic groups or campaigns in or after 2016, when Donald Trump was first elected.

Multiple attendees described the event like a class reunion.

The crowd was filled with hugs, laughter and selfies of overjoyed organizers who have spent the last decade working toward a Democratic sweep.

“I think it is important to debrief elections, win or lose. I think we saw the negative ramifications of not properly debriefing an election after 2024,” said Danielle Butterfield, the executive director of Priorities USA, a Democratic-aligned Super Pac.

By 4pm on Friday, alcoholic beverages were flowing and what seemed like an endless stream of happy hours began.

Yet, beneath the excitement appeared to be a fear that Democrats would fail to seize the moment.

“We can’t fuck this up,” one Democratic strategist said.

Reminders of simmering tensions within the party were present throughout the weekend. Leftist protesters interrupted Jeffries multiple times during his Friday event on the main stage. They called him a traitor, accused him of not pushing back enough on the Trump administration and of ignoring younger Democratic voters.

Outside of the event venue, a small group of protesters called on Democrats to reject Schumer and elect new leadership. Another larger group of protesters expressed support for Palestine and denounced billionaires.

Progressive Democrats, whose presence on the main stage was few and far between at the “What’s Next” conference, have expressed deep frustrations with establishment Democrats.

Throughout the event, some Democrats alluded to those frustrations.

Anderson Clayton, the 28-year-old chair of the North Carolina Democratic party, questioned why Democrats had not invested in the South, especially in Black districts where voters cast their ballots for Democrats.

“We say that Black voters are the base of our party. Then I ask why are we not investing in a region of the country that on Tuesday night, just proved everybody wrong of what is possible,” Clayton said on Thursday.

Aftab Pureval, the mayor of Cincinnati, warned Democrats not to take the recent wins as a sign that the Democratic party was popular.

“Victory has a nasty tendency of clouding our judgment. It turns our eyes inward, tempting us to believe that, we here in this room, saved democracy. That the American people finally came around to our way of thinking. But the truth is, they didn’t come around to us,” Pureval said.

“Last week, they gave us one more chance to come around to them.”

But when asked about the potential split in Democratic factions, many attendees dismissed concerns, believing Democrats will rise to the occasion.

“The progressive – moderate binary in this moment in our politics is insufficient for understanding the moment that we’re in,” Yasmin Radjy, the executive director of Swing Left, a progressive grassroots organization, told the Guardian.

“Among the attendees, there is a pretty dynamic mix and while this conference is branded as a moderate conference, when you look more specifically at both the main stage messaging and the ways that a lot of leaders here are talking, there is a different thing that’s happening,” Radjy said.

“There’s more talk about what it means to embrace the politics of addition, what it means to really make sure that Democrats deliver in a major way.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The Democratic conference is being called a moderate conference. But many attendees dismissed concerns about the potential split in Democratic factions. ‘The progressive – moderate binary in this moment in our politics is insufficient for understanding the moment that we’re in,' says Yasmin Radjy.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Will Trump’s lame duck presidency push him further beyond constraints of the law?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Midterm elections have defanged the US president – leaving critics to worry about his next move in his ‘fat Elvis’ stage

It was just before 3am when Donald Trump entered a crowded Manhattan ballroom, greeted by chants of “USA! USA” and theme music from the Hollywood film Air Force One. On stage, two red “Make America great again” (Maga) caps were mounted in glass cases like holy relics.

That was the scene 10 years ago this week when Trump, a businessman and reality TV star, stunned the world by beating Hillary Clinton to the White House. A decade later an unlikely president is serving an unlikely second term. But in the wake of a humiliating vote of no confidence in last week’s midterm elections, he now enters an endgame wracked with uncertainty.

“Trump is about to get even weirder and, sadly, more dangerous,” tweeted Clinton, who has been a wry commentator on the Trump years, predicting that the president will deflect blame, become more unhinged, demand even greater loyalty from Republicans and potentially launch fresh attacks on Iran.

Political obituary writers have been swift to describe him as a lame duck, defanged lion or cornered animal in the wake of the midterms. Democrats’ 13 percentage point victory was the second biggest of any midterm election since 1942, and the party conquered the Republican bastions of Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas.

The causes of the Republican rout were plain: an eight month war in Iran that sent fuel prices soaring, persistent cost of living pressures and a backlash against masked immigration raids that turned deadly in Minneapolis.

The 80-year-old president’s response has swung wildly between conciliation, aggression and farce. He told the CBS network’s 60 Minutes program that his deportation push was “too tough” while declaring that no amnesty would occur and appointing immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

He publicly invited the job of White House press secretary to “violent fighter and warrior” Dana White of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), brought him into the briefing room to play out the scenario, then insisted it had all been a joke. He threw his weight behind the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, who survived an impeachment resolution brought by a maverick Republican in Congress.

All the while he has retreated into architectural vanity projects, including a White House ballroom and triumphal arch in Washington, and increasingly wayward rhetoric that included ruminations about men’s posteriors, speeches punctuated by strange guttural sounds and a lengthy social media post about comedian Bill Maher.

Miles Taylor, founder of Defiance.org, a non-profit aimed at countering government corruption and abuses of power, agrees with Clinton’s analysis about the finale of the Trump show. He said: “It will certainly be weirder because Donald Trump was always going to end the administration with the bottom of the barrel appointees.

“Like any wannabe autocrat, you end up in the figurative bunker at the end of the regime with the most hardcore loyalists, which tend to be the people who are willing to contort themselves into whatever shape the leader wants. These are the people who have no scruples and are willing to carry out the president’s most extreme edicts and, in some cases, are the ones who have been goading him for almost a decade to do the most extreme things.”

Miller is the prime example. He has championed expansive presidential power, branded the Democratic party a “domestic extremist organisation”, advocated suspending habeas corpus to speed deportations and asserted that the US has a right to Venezuela’s oil and Greenland’s territory. He supplanted Susie Wiles, whose more measured approach had been seen as a potential restraint on Trump’s darkest impulses.

Taylor, a former chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security during Trump’s first term, said: “In my experience with Stephen, he was a guy that was all too willing to walk up to the line of the law and then leap over it and dare the courts to rein us in. That was literally the type of thing he said to me on multiple occasions.

“One of my biggest fears about this next two years is: will Donald Trump cause the ultimate constitutional crisis by defying judicial orders, including from the supreme court, if he doesn’t get his way? I see it as very possible because he’s got a team around him that might be willing to make the case of why that would be justified.”

There is another way for an embattled president to seek a place in history: foreign policy. Presidents approaching the end of their time in office have often turned to diplomacy and international affairs as a means of burnishing their legacy. After Democrats suffered heavy losses in the 2014 midterms, Barack Obama announced the restoration of diplomatic relations with Cuba, secured a nuclear agreement with Iran and helped broker the Paris climate agreement.

Trump has already placed an emphasis on global affairs since returning to the White House last year. Even as Democrats prepare to rein in the president when they take control of Congress in January, Trump will retain considerable latitude to pursue his ambitions on the world stage, from Iran and Israel to Ukraine and China.

Taylor commented: “What he did in the first two years on the foreign policy front could potentially pale in comparison with what he does in the latter two years and that’s saying something because he launched this war in Iran.

“But here are things to look for. Does Nato survive this period? Does the United States actually try to go seize more territory? Both of those are things that Donald Trump has talked about doing and been walked back by advisors on over the course of two terms. I’m not sure that’s the case anymore.

“But then there’s other areas of the world that might be worried about Trump administration inaction being just as bad or worse than Trump administration offensive action, if the Russians try to seize more territory and if the Chinese take Taiwan. On the world stage I would warn our allies, it’s about to get very, very bad. And I would say to our adversaries, this is probably the luckiest two years you’re ever going to get.”

Despite the historic losses, there is little sign of a Republican revolt against Trump. On Capitol Hill this week the party effectively killed the attempt to impeach Hegseth while also electing Jim Jordan, a pugnacious ally of the president, as its minority leader for the next Congress. Most Republicans who survived the midterm bloodbath are from safe red districts and staunchly pro-Trump. The outcome could be more Maga, not less.

Olivia Wales, a spokeswoman for the White House, said via email: “President Trump will continue to enact his commonsense, America First agenda that has delivered the most secure border ever, the largest working-class tax cut in history, the lowest murder rate since 1900, the sharpest drop in prescription drug prices in more than 60 years, and a stock market that has hit record highs.

“As the President said, he is willing to work with anyone who wants to strengthen our economy, lower costs for American families, protect our national security, and improve the lives of hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the best interests of the American people.”

Some commentators believe that, given Trump’s ideological fluidity, a deal with Democrats might be possible.

Bill Whalen, a research fellow at the Hoover Institution thinktank in Stanford, California, said: “If Trump wants to work with Congress, the question is what do they have in common? If I’m running the Democratic caucuses right now, I might think 70-30 or 80-20 is what I want in terms of a compromise, because the president wants to sign something to show he’s still relevant.”

Whalen suggests an intriguing parallel: “Is Donald Trump at his heart really that conservative, or will he turn out to be a little bit more of a moderate Democrat? Similar to [former Republican governor]Arnold Schwarzenegger here in California, where he gets chastised, and then in his second term, he’s governing very much like a moderate Democrat.”

Others suspect that Trump, who has placed a red baseball cap saying “veto” on his desk in the Oval Office, indicating his willingness to block Democratic legislation, intends to go out with all guns blazing. Newt Gingrich, a former House of Representatives speaker, predicts an aggressive counter attack rather than a chastened administration winding down.

“I recommend everybody read Trump’s book The Art of the Comeback, which explains what he’s like when he’s right at the edge of being destroyed, pivots and rebuilds overnight,” Gingrich said. “You have to assume that he and Stephen Miller are methodically thinking through the comeback. I suspect the State of the Union [address] will be chock-full of things that the American people want that the Democrats will be taunted about passing.”

For Democrats, the uncertainty of whether Trump will offer a fight or flight response poses a conundrum. Speaking at the Center for American Progress thinktank in Washington this week, congressman Jim Himes said: “We just don’t know which Donald Trump is going to show up. Is it the dealmaker, or is it the Stephen Miller pugilist? On any given day we’re not going to know which president is sitting in the Oval Office.”

For Rick Wilson, a veteran political strategist and co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, the president has crossed a threshold into volatile decline. “The impulsivity has come not only from his age but from the understanding now that he is an island unto himself,” he said.

“He doesn’t have that enormous backstop of congressional impunity to work from. That is going to make him do a lot of lashing out and things like we’ve seen the last few days – going to the podium in the press room and just riffing.”

Wilson believes that Trump has reached his “fat Elvis” phase. “He’s trying to recapture the old magic. He’s trying to get back the old mojo and it just isn’t quite there. The crash out of his approval, the loss of his congressional shield wall and the lack of any adult supervision around him now – it’s a toxic combination where he’s going to feel desperate and angry and crazy.”

While Trump grapples with immediate constraints, political gravity is already shifting toward the presidential succession in January 2029. JD Vance, the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, and Texas senator Ted Cruz were all quick to weigh in with opinions on what went wrong in the midterms. Former state governors Glenn Youngkin and Chris Christie are among other potential contenders.

Can Trump endure sharing the stage in 2028? Wilson foresees a messy spectacle. “He has been the centre of that political gravity for 10 years now. Because he’s the devil, he’s going to go in and piss on Vance one day and raise him up the next. He’ll piss on Marco [Rubio] one day and raise him up the next. He’ll try to be the kingmaker.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.summary: Donald Trump is expected to become more unhinged, demand even greater loyalty from Republicans. Political obituary writers have been swift to describe him as a lame duck Donald Trump. Despite the historic losses, there is little sign of a Republican revolt against Trump.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Hegseth survived impeachment bid but reprieve may be temporary: ‘He can’t escape justice forever’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robert Tait in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The reprimand the defense secretary endured at US military’s most sacred shrine epitomizes his disrepute

The sentinel who bawled out Pete Hegseth for apparent disrespect at the Tomb of the Unknown Solider seemed to be speaking for more than just himself.

Nothing quite epitomizes the disrepute into which the US defense secretary has fallen than the reprimand delivered to Hegseth and his party after they conversed and laughed loudly while visiting Arlington national cemetery on Wednesday to mark Veterans’ Day.

Yet in a week that was especially turbulent even by his standards, that public indignity was the least of Hegseth’s problems.

The self-anointed “secretary of war” found himself in the line of fire from his own side when Thomas Massie, the outgoing Republican representative from Kentucky, introduced eight articles of impeachment that alleged he was guilty of “high crimes and misdemeanors”. The articles focused on his stewardship of the war against Iran, deadly strikes against alleged drug traffickers off the coasts of South America, the seizure of the former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, and attempted retribution against Mark Kelly, a Democratic senator, for urging armed services members to disobey illegal orders.

In the event, Hegseth dodged a bullet when the House of Representatives voted by 211 to 204 against advancing the articles to a committee – a margin that could have been overcome if 11 absent Democrats, some of whom attributed their non-appearance to being “caught in traffic”, had turned up to vote.

But the strength of feeling, combined with the Democrats’ thumping triumph in this month’s congressional midterms, suggests that Hegseth’s reprieve may be temporary.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the Democratic House speaker when the new Congress assembles in January, vowed in a video produced by a military veterans organization that “we are going to run Pete Hegseth out of town.”

Military veterans and commentators believe the threat is serious – and deserved.

“He will not survive impeachment once the new Congress is seated,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US National Guard and a member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former senior military officers.

“I give it 100% probability he’ll be the first secretary of defense to be impeached.”

Joe Cirincione, a veteran military analyst and former congressional aide to the House armed services committee, said: “He is the worst secretary of defense in American history. Nobody else comes close.

“The Democrats will take this up and and probably have a more rigorous process. They will vet the articles of impeachment more and build support for the resolution before they introduce it.

“By then, even the Republican caucus will be greatly decreased in number and perhaps be more willing to vote against Hegseth.

“Hegseth may have slipped the noose this time, but he can’t escape justice forever.”

The ultimate sanction would be removal from office, an outcome that would require a two-thirds vote for conviction in a Senate trial.

With the Democrats holding a maximum of 56 seats – the Alaska race is still to be called – the chances of that appear slim.

However, Kevin Carroll – a former army intelligence officer who served in the defense secretary’s office under Donald Rumsfeld – predicted that a Senate trial could pose a serious threat to Hegseth.

“I think several Republican senators will vote to convict,” he said. “A lot of Republican senators have said they felt burned by voting to confirm Hegseth due to the enormous pressure brought by Donald Trump when he was at the height of his powers.

“Newly re-elected Republican senators will have another six years before they have to face voters – and Trump’s going to be far in the rearview mirror at that point.”

Hegseth’s many critics charge that he is incompetent and unqualified to be in charge of the Pentagon, a vast bureaucracy with a trillion dollar-plus annual budget.

They also accuse him of committing “extrajudicial killings” tantamount to murder by ordering strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats in the Caribbean and Pacific that have killed around 200 people. Hegseth insists – without providing evidence – that the victims have drug traffickers engaged in narco-terrorism.

“The boat strikes against shipwrecked sailors are clear violations of the law of war. We hanged Nazis who did the same thing to shipwrecked sailors,” said Carroll, who called Hegseth’s impeachment “a life and death matter”.

Hegseth also stands accused of facilitating civilian deaths in the war on Iran, by openly deriding “stupid” rules of engagement and calling for “no quarter” in combat operations, rhetoric critics say paves the way for committing possible war crimes.

Manner accused him reducing accountability by slashing the number of military judge advocate generals (JAGs) and inspector general in the US armed forces’ Central Command – responsible engagement in the Middle East – who would investigate accidents and potential war crimes.

More than 165 people, including 120 children, were killed in a strike on a girls’ school in the southern Iranian city of Minab on the first day of the war last February. Washington has not acknowledged responsibility, although independent investigations have concluded that it was a US strike. Carroll called the deaths “negligent homicide”.

Hegseth was sufficiently perturbed by Massie’s impeachment move to stage his first Pentagon press briefing in six months at which he dismissed the articles as a “political stunt” that handed a propaganda victory to the US’s enemies.

But Janessa Goldbeck, chief executive of the Vet Voice Foundation – a military veteran’s group – said they had widespread support.

“There is a overwhelming sense from the veterans and military community, that Pete Hegseth is well deserving of impeachment,” she said. “We are coming to this in the context of an unconstitutional and illegal forever war and he has been the most unqualified and incompetent Secretary of Defense at the helm. And along with all of that, the Iranian regime is more entrenched than ever.”

She added: “He is seeking to tie the impeachment articles as an indictment of President Trump and the strategy in Iran. But that’s not what these impeachment articles are about. They are about conduct that fits the standard of high crimes and misdemeanors. The question is whether he used the powers of his office in a way that damages the constitutional system itself.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Pete Hegseth is accused of facilitating civilian deaths in the war against Iran. Heg set to be impeached by a Republican representative in the House. He is accused by a sentinel of apparent disrespect at the Tomb of the Unknown Solider.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: All passengers and crew accounted for after New Orleans boat crash in ‘miracle on the Mississippi’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas and Lucy Campbell in New Orleans
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
No passengers or crew killed or critically hurt after tanker collides with river cruise ship on Mississippi, officials say

In what the city’s mayor declared a “miracle on the Mississippi”, all passengers were accounted for – with none killed or critically hurt – after a tanker collided with a river cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon.

Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals after the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck American Cruise Lines’s American Heritage at about 12.30pm – but none of their injuries were considered critical, New Orleans’s mayor, Helena Moreno, said at a news conference.

Zero passengers or crew members were unaccounted for, Moreno said. She attributed that fact to a hectic but effective multi-agency rescue effort after the American Heritage was struck and a number of people ended up in the river, whose waters are cold and its currents are infamously perilous.

That “truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said near the scene of the crash, as a group of fellow officials around her applauded.

The American Heritage had 197 passengers onboard when it was hit, Port of New Orleans press secretary Kimberly Curth said in a statement.

About two hours before that, the American Heritage had docked at the port to begin passenger disembarkation, Curth said.

Thirty of those reported injured were on the American Heritage, and they were said to have mostly had bumps and bruises. Two others among the injured were harbor police officers who were on the river boat after the crash participating in rescue efforts.

Officials did not immediately provide details about what caused the crash. But New Orleans’s US coast guard commander Melanie Burnham said the tanker apparently had “some type of loss of steering” – as an emergency response source had indicated earlier.

The website MarineTraffic.com showed the Atlantic Asphalt’s path was seemingly uneventful as it went around the difficult bend in the Mississippi River near New Orleans’ Algiers Point neighborhood. It had just made it past the Crescent City Connection bridge linking New Orleans’ central business district and the community’s Algiers section when it began heading generally to its starboard – or right – side.

Video provided to Guardian reporting partner WWL Louisiana showed the Atlantic Asphalt then T-boned the side of the American Heritage. The cruise ship eventually slowly rolled on to its side where it was struck, according to the video, which the CBS affiliate obtained from Barry Kern, proprietor of Mardi Gras World, a tourist attraction near the scene of the crash.

One witness, Jamie Holford, told local NBC News affiliate WDSU that it took 15 minutes “from impact to where it rolled over”.

“Surreal,” Holford said. “That’s what that was.”

Maritime law expert Martin J Davies of Tulane University told the Associated Press that local pilots are onboard ships such as the Atlantic Asphalt as they travel on the Mississippi River. Those pilots know the river’s waters and the ships they are on well, Davies said.

Davies said videos circulating online of the crash suggest there was some kind of catastrophic system failure on the tanker – and some “super bad luck” for it to strike the American Heritage as passengers disembarked.

The Atlantic Asphalt was traveling slowly against the current upriver, Davies said to the AP. He added: “For something like this to happen for an upbound ship indicates that something must have gone really badly wrong.”

Separately, Davies said to local Fox affiliate WVUE that the Atlantic Asphalt was fortunate to have not hit the Crescent City Connection, which could have endangered motorists on a two-span, cantilever, steel truss bridge that is estimated to carry about 160,000 cars daily.

“This is obviously a really bad incident,” Davies said. “But it could also have struck the bridge, which it didn’t.”

A video from WDSU showed crew members of a tugboat working to pull people in lifejackets or holding on to flotation rings out of the river. An emergency response that drew in firefighters, crews of tug vessels in the vicinity, US Coast Guard helicopter and boat personnel, as well as port and city police – among others – also helped pull out people who ended up in the water in plain view of cameras and stunned eyewitnesses.

One image on social media showed people climbing on the side of the cruise boat – specifically, on stateroom balconies – after it was struck, with chairs and tables strewn about after it evidently took on water.

Blake Paterson, an independent New Orleans journalist who publishes Perdido Street.News, interviewed 65-year-old American Heritage passenger Tamara Carrasco about what she saw at the time of the crash.

The retired Atlanta elementary school teacher told Paterson that she was dining on the first floor of the riverboat when she saw the tanker careering toward the American Heritage. The tanker dropped its anchor, and she could see its crew running away on its deck, according to what Carrasco told Paterson.

Carrasco began running to the other side of the river boat, but she was knocked to the ground when the tanker hit. She said water began pouring into the dining room, making her think it was “like the Titanic”.

An employee at the Ernest N Morial Convention Center next to the scene of Friday’s crash said she realized something was awry when she could see from her vantage point that the tip of the American Heritage was tilted. She then grasped the nature of situation when she heard desperate shrieks.

“People were screaming for help,” said the employee, who asked to not be named. She recalled how she and colleagues assembled wheelchairs, water and other items in case survivors would soon need them.

Moreno said many people lost their IDs, car keys, cell phones and other belongings in the disaster. The mayor said most were from out of town.

She said the city and its partner organizations were working to ensure affected passengers had “food, hotel rooms, transportation” – and access to their prescription medication.

The American Heritage’s passengers were brought inside the New Orleans port’s administration building, next to the convention center, after the crash.

At the news conference where officials then confirmed there were no casualties, Louisiana governor Jeff Landry echoed Moreno in invoking the term “miracle”, especially “when you think about the population that was on that cruise ship – and the ability for us to get them off and out of the water”.

“The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond,” Landry said. “There were challenges out there.”

With everyone accounted for, Burnham said the focus would shift to re-opening the river to traffic. It had been closed from mile markers 93 to 96 to facilitate rescue efforts.

US House majority leader Steve Scalise, a suburban New Orleans Republican, said on Friday that the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) would investigate the crash. But Scalise said the investigative team had been slowed by a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop on Friday that had delayed or canceled more than 11,000 US flights.

The NTSB late on Friday said it would send investigators by ground to the scene of the Atlantic Asphalt-American Heritage crash.

A statement from American Cruise Lines on Friday said “guests and crew were evacuated” from the American Heritage but did not elaborate. “We are deeply concerned for everyone involved,” the cruise operator’s statement added.

The American Heritage, a 300ft paddle-wheel ship, was built in 2015 and previously sailed as the Queen of the Mississippi. It has more than 80 staterooms and operates cruises on the Mississippi River, including ones which depart from New Orleans.

The Atlantic Asphalt is a oil tanker built in 2017 measuring approximately 525 feet (160 meters) in length and has a deadweight of 17,764 metric tons. It flies the flag of the Marshall Islands and is owned and commercially operated by Nave Shipping SA, a company registered in Liberia. Its maintenance, technical and safety operations are overseen by Singapore-based Thome Ship Management, according to online records.

The vessel’s next recorded destination was Singapore, and it had last departed from Paulsboro, New Jersey, on 26 October. It specializes in hauling large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

The Atlantic Asphalt not appear on the international sanctions lists checked by maritime tracking services, including Magic Port.

However, it was previously fined C$7,800 by Canadian authorities for a violation of the Canada Shipping Act and related vessel pollution regulations.

The penalty, recorded on 11 August 2020, stemmed from an officer failing to properly carry out their duties while supervising a transfer operation aboard the tanker, according to the Canadian government.

To many in New Orleans, the crash involving the Atlantic Asphalt called to mind an episode nearby – nearly 30 years earlier – when a cargo ship struck a wharf adjacent to the city’s Riverwalk shopping center and Hilton Riverside hotel.

No deaths resulted from that case, which occurred on 14 December 1996 after the Liberian-registered Bright Field lost propulsion power, an NTSB report later said. But there were more than 60 injuries reported, including four which were considered serious.

Maya Yang contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The American Heritage was hit by the Atlantic Asphalt-American Heritage on Friday. No passengers or crew were killed or critically hurt, but none were considered critical. The NTSB will investigate the crash, but it has been slowed by a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘It’s frustrating’: chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Edward Helmore in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Travelers and crew feeling ‘pissed’ or ‘lucky’ depending on level of upset amid nationwide ground stop

T
he US Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights on Friday threw airports and travel plans into chaos across the country, as passengers on planes and in airport terminals were suddenly thrust into limbo.

At New York’s John F Kennedy airport, passengers found their travel plans abruptly cancelled – some even after they’d boarded.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Steve Honberger, heading home to Portland, Oregon, with his wife and daughter, said he’d been on a plane about to take off when the shutdown was announced.

“They didn’t seem to know what’s happening, and they wanted to hold off as long as possible,” Honberger said. The plane sat at the gate for an hour and 40 minutes.

They realized they were just going to be sitting at the gate, so they eventually asked to deplane and rebook.

Many still thought it worth showing up despite the uncertainty of when flights would resume. Rashid Kahn, heading for Miami, said he’d “heard about the ground stop on the news, but the airline said we might take off 10 or 11pm”.

“I am hopeful,” he added. “But maybe it’s something to do with the date. I’m not super serious, but it’s Friday the 13th.”

Tom Rolenaitis, returning a Shiba Inu show dog named Tsuki to Finland, said it was frustrating. “It’s cutting into a three-day trip and I have to get him back to his owner. We have no idea what’s happening.”

A flight attendant headed for Barcelona, who declined to give his name, said he had been told his American Airlines flight would be slightly delayed and all incoming international flights were being allowed to land.

Another crew member from the flight said cheerfully: “Things happen. Hopefully it will all be resolved.”

As the day wore on, passengers on international flights began to be boarding, prompting applause to erupt at the gates. “It’s moving, so that’s good,” said an airline representative. “But only international is going.”

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, citing a communications problems at regional air traffic control centers, according to an FAA notice. Four hours later, FAA sent out an advisory lifting the stop.

“You can’t moan about this kind of thing ... it’s such a first-world problem,” said Laura, a woman who lives in New York and was heading for San Francisco when her JetBlue flight was grounded. She still hoped her flight would go. “That what I have to figure out,” she said, sitting on the floor of the terminal.

With the lifting of the ground stop, more chaos followed. “My flight was cancelled, then I go to a kiosk, put my information in and it says I’m leaving at 3am. Then I talk to the desk and they know nothing,” said Larson Welsh, heading to Las Vegas from Paris.

The outage has nonetheless caused upheaval for thousands of passengers. There have been 10,343 flight delays within, into or out of the US so far, according to the website FlightAware, and 1,479 cancellations. More than 1,000 aircraft were bound for US when the ground stop was announced, according to Flightradar24.

Only two national ground stops have previously been issued: on 11 September 2001, after the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center; and in January 2023, after a communications failure.

The ground stop also snarled the sports world, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams stranded as they tried to reach their destinations before a big weekend of games. It also was unclear whether referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would make it on time.

Back at JFK, travelers expressed frustration and resignation.

“My flight to California was cancelled with no information and no rebooking. My flight was cancelled last night as well due to bad weather. Now I’m missing a family event,” said a man who gave his name only as Andy. “It’s frustrating. And I’m pissed.”

Honberger, meanwhile, tried to stay optimistic, saying: “There are people sitting on tarmac, so we count ourselves lucky and we were able to book ourselves a hotel for the night.”

Tom Johnson and agencies contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: US Federal Aviation Administration's decision to ground all flights on Friday threw airports and travel plans into chaos across the country. More than 1,000 aircraft were bound for US when the ground stop was announced.

New York City mayor says deal will allow bodegas and convenience stores across the country more time to comply

Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, has struck a deal with Donald Trump to secure a 90-day delay on new rules for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap), so that bodegas and corner stores across the country have time to comply.

The extension, Mamdani said, starts Friday as a result of conversations he had with Trump and Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary.

The new guidelines, implemented by the US agriculture department, which retailers would have had to meet by 4 November, require stores to stock at least seven varieties within each staple food category: dairy, grains, protein and fruits or vegetables. Retailers would also have to ensure that they offer perishable items in three of the staple food categories.

The new guidelines threw the lives of “more than a million New Yorkers” and “tens of milllions more across America” into “chaos”, the mayor said at a press conference on Friday.

“People already reckoning with a shortage of affordable places to buy what they need for their home, soaring costs at the register, and food deserts across the five boroughs, now feared that the few places they could shop would no longer be able to accept their benefits,” Mamdani said.

Several advocates were concerned that the new rules would mean people relying on Snap would be unable to buy groceries at their only accessible store. According to the Food Research and Action Center, bodegas, convenience stores and small grocery stores make up roughly 70% of Snap retailers.

Given the tight timeframe to adjust their stock and meet the new requirements, small retailers ran the risk of going out of business if they couldn’t accept Snap benefits, the mayor said.

“For so many of our fellow Americans, whether they shop at a general store in Michigan or a convenience store in Missouri, would have struggled to use their benefits and feed those they love.”

More than 100 bodega owners reached out to Mamdani’s office with concerns about the new rule. According to the New York City department of city planning, there are more than 10,000 bodegas and corner stores across the five boroughs.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: New Orleans boat crash: all passengers and crew found alive in ‘miracle on the Mississippi’ – as it happened
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
A tanker collided with a river cruise liner, the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage, carrying 129 passengers plus crew in New Orleans on Friday. It began turning on its side and taking on water.

All passengers and crew are alive and have now been accounted for in what New Orleans mayor Helena Moreno called “truly a miracle on the Mississippi.”

It is unclear exactly what caused the collision. Melanie Burnham, commander of the US Coast Guard sector in New Orleans, told reporters that “there seems to be some type of a loss of steering,” in regards to the tanker.

Louisiana governor Jeff Landry, addressing reporters during a news conference, said he will be launching an investigation into what led to the collision to ensure it will not happen again.

Moreno said the tanker ship narrowly missed striking a bridge carrying around 160,000 vehicles daily.

Thirty-two people are being treated at a local hospital. Those include two New Orleans Harbor Police officers who went into the water to rescue people after the cruise ship began sinking.

Several photos and videos circulating around social media show different angles during the moment the ship was falling on its side into the water. Passengers were seen climbing onto the balconies’ railing to avoid sliding into the river as the ship turned horizontally.

Louisiana governor Jeff Landry, addressing reporters during a news conference, said he will be launching an investigation into what led to the collision to ensure it will not happen again.

Landry said the Mississippi river is “not some quiet pond” and praised state and local officials for their quick response to the incident. He added that first responders risked their lives to save those in the water.

Captain Melanie Burnham, commander of the US Coast Guard sector in New Orleans, told reporters that “There seems to be some type of a loss of steering,” in regards to the tanker.

“The exact reason why - we don’t know that,” she said.

LCMC Health, a major New Orleans-based healthcare system, said they had received around two dozen patients following the incident.

“University Medical Center New Orleans and other LCMC Health hospitals have received an estimated two dozen patients following the reported maritime incident,” LCMC said in a statement shared with media outlets. “Our medical teams are currently evaluating patients and providing appropriate care while coordinating with emergency responders.”

An employee at the Convention Center, who did not want to be named, said she was on the ground floor when she looked up and noticed that, beyond the brick wall that separates the building from the Mississippi, the very tip of the river cruise ship was tilted. Then, she heard screaming. “People were screaming for help,” she said.

She and colleagues assembled wheelchairs and water and other items to be sent in the direction of survivors. “I’m just glad I didn’t see anything, I already hold this deep fear of water.”

New Orleans mayor Helena Moreno said all passengers and crew have been accounted for in what she called “truly a miracle on the Mississippi.”

She added the ship narrowly missed striking a bridge carrying around 160,000 vehicles daily.

Thirty-two people are now being treated at a local hospital. Those include two New Orleans Harbor Police officers who went into the water to rescue people after the cruise ship began sinking.

Witnesses in New Orleans described a scene of chaos as the liner listed on its side and took on water.

Devon Flanagan was at his job nearby at the Port of New Orleans when workers began rushing down the dock. He got out of his truck and noticed the American Heritage on its side and passengers in the water.

“It was just chaos,” he said. “You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water.”

“Surreal — that’s what that was,” witness Jamie Holford told WDSU-TV. “Fifteen minutes from impact to where it rolled over.”

A tanker collided with a river cruise liner, the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage, carrying 129 passengers plus crew in New Orleans on Friday.

The cruise liner was taking on water as it rapidly turned on its side, and videos showed people climbing on to the railing to avoid falling in the water.

New Orleans mayor Helena Moreno’s communication team said multiple individuals have been rescued, and search-and-rescue operations remain ongoing. Helicopters were seen in the air along with ambulances waiting nearby.

It is currently unclear if there are any fatalities and whether all passengers and crew are out of the water.

It is also unclear exactly what caused the collision. A source told the Guardian that it was possible the tanker had lost power before striking the cruise liner. Maritime experts speculated the incident may have been caused by either steerage failure or engine failure.

Officials said they would be holding a news conference, originally scheduled for 3pm CST, that has now been delayed. We are still waiting for it to begin.

Congressman Troy Carter, the representative for Louisiana’s 2nd congressional district, said in a statement that he was devastated by news of the crash.

“I am monitoring the situation closely and praying for the swift rescue of survivors and for all emergency crews responding to the situation,” he wrote on social media.

A video circulating around social media shows a different angle during the moment the ship was falling on its side into the water. Passengers can be seen climbing onto the balconies’ railing to avoid sliding into the river as the ship turned horizontally. Several uniformed people can be seen running away from the scene, likely to gather equipment that would help rescue efforts.

Martin J Davies, a maritime expert at Tulane University, told local news outlet Fox 8 that he suspected the incident was caused by either steerage failure or engine failure.

“This ship is headed upriver and for it to have lost the ability to avoid the moored vessel, there must have been some fairly substantial failure, with the steering gear or the propulsion of the ship to prevent them from avoiding the vessel on shore,” Davies said.

“Given that the pressure of the water going down river is sufficiently strong that the upbound ship would have been going fairly slowly,” he said. “So that’s my first thought upon looking at the footage.”

Davies also noted how close the vessels appear to be to the bridge above, suggesting the ship was lucky to have avoided also hitting the bridge. He said: “This is obviously a really bad incident, but it could also have struck the bridge, which it didn’t.”

Pictures are now coming in from the news wires. Emergency personnel and crews can be seen on the scene after a tanker crashed into a river cruise in New Orleans. The cruise liner can be seen lying on its side:

Officials said they will be holding a news conference at 3pm CST, to begin in about ten minutes, providing further updates on the collision. We will bring you those latest updates as they come.

A statement from the US coast guard also announced that the river “is closed to all vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96,” encompassing the area where Friday’s crash occurred. That is so to assist responders as they “assess the situation and conduct response operations”, the coast guard’s statement said.

The New Orleans Regional Transit Authority said in a statement on social media that ferry service across the Mississippi River has been temporarily suspended as a precaution following the collision. Travelers are encouraged to seek alternate routes.

New Orleans mayor Helena Moreno’s communication team said multiple individuals have been rescued, and search-and-rescue operations remain ongoing, according to a local Fox News affiliate.

Photos are circulating on social media of people climbing out and onto the balconies of the ship that is now turned completely on its side.

Local media is reporting that multiple people have already been rescued, and helicopters were seen in the air along with ambulances waiting nearby. Several people can be seen in the river wearing life jackets.

Videos circulating across social media appear to show the moment the Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashes into the side of the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage while the cruise ship is docked on the Mississippi River. The ship then falls to its side towards the open water and begins sinking rapidly.

An emergency response source said that there were efforts underway to rescue people from the water. That source said it was possible the tanker had lost power before striking the American Heritage.

Images on social media showed the American Heritage on its side. It was docked on the Mississippi River outside the port of New Orleans’s administrative building when it was hit.

A tanker has collided with a river cruise liner carrying more than 130 people in New Orleans, authorities have said.

The governor of Louisiana has confirmed an incident in the Mississippi River. Jeff Landry said on X he was in contact with local officials and law enforcement.

The cruise liner was taking on water, local media reports said, and rescue efforts are under way.

The Port of New Orleans press secretary said the tanker collided with the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage around 12:30 pm local time on Friday.

There were about 129 passengers onboard as well as crew, Port authorities told local media.

This is breaking news story. We’ll bring you the latest updates as we get them.
