Maritime experts believe the tanker lost power before striking the cruise liner. It is unclear if there are any fatalities and whether all passengers and crew are out of the water.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: As Van Hollen wages a challenge, Senate Democrats are torn on whom to elect as their leader
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Maryland senator’s bid against Chuck Schumer for leadership could decide direction of the Democratic party

US politics live – latest updates

Ever since Donald Trump returned to the White House, Democratic officeholders and voters alike have been divided over whether their leader in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, is up to the task of taking the president on.

That debate intensified on Thursday, when the Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen announced he will challenge Schumer for the post of Democratic Senate leader, which will become one of the most powerful jobs in Washington when the party takes control of Congress’s upper chamber next year.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The contest between Schumer and Van Hollen is the party’s first major test of unity after its triumph in last week’s midterm elections, in which voters gave Democrats their biggest majorities in both the Senate and House of Representatives in years. Now the party will be forced to confront the two veteran lawmakers’ differing visions on how to use their newly expanded power to confront Trump, advance the party’s agenda and address divisive issues such as the question of aid to Israel.

“Trump’s policies have been fired, but we are still in the position where we need to take advantage of this opportunity. So that does mean closing the trust deficit? … And I don’t think you can close the trust deficit by simply returning to the status quo,” Van Hollen said at a press conference on Friday.

Progressive groups have cheered the 67-year-old Van Hollen’s candidacy, and he’s picked up a handful of endorsements in the hours since he made his bid official. But his prospects are unclear: the senator said he is an “underdog” in the contest, which is set to be decided at a behind-closed-doors caucus meeting scheduled for 1 December.

Schumer, meanwhile, has expressed confidence he’ll win the Democratic caucus’s nod again, and has the support of senators from across the party’s ideological spectrum.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer, 75, wrote on X after Van Hollen announced his bid. “I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.”

A New York City native, Schumer won election to the House in 1980, then the Senate in 1998. He became the top Senate Democrat in 2017, when the party was in the minority at the beginning of Trump’s first term. Four years later, Schumer became majority leader under Joe Biden, and managed to win passage of parts of his legislative agenda even though the Democratic caucus was so small it could not lose a single vote on party-line bills.

Trump returned to power in 2025, and it was not long after that Schumer’s leadership came into question. In March of that year, Congress faced a deadline to approve new government funding or cause a shutdown. Though many Democrats believed they had leverage over Trump to win concessions, perhaps over the gutting of the federal government by the “department of government efficiency”, Schumer opted to advance a GOP-backed spending measure, arguing that it was a bad time to shut down the government.

The compromise triggered an explosion of anger at Schumer both from Democrats in the House of Representatives who had rejected the funding compromise, and activist groups who saw it as a sign that Schumer was no longer fit to be leader.

“Senator Schumer has contributed to and led many important accomplishments that Indivisible is grateful for. But with our democracy on the line, he let us, the country and the Democratic party down,” said Ezra Levin, co-executive director of the network of progressive groups.

“Senator Schumer should step aside as leader. Every Democrat in the Senate should call for him to do so, and begin making plans for new leadership immediately.”

The relationship between Schumer and the party base – including some Democratic lawmakers – has yet to recover. Another wave of calls for Schumer to step down arrived later that year, when dissident Senate Democrats decided to end a record-long government shutdown without Republicans meeting any of their demands on healthcare.

Schumer did not publicly endorse their deal, but it was widely believed to have his backing. By the time campaigning for the 2026 midterms began, several candidates were making their opposition to him prominent in their platforms.

In some ways, the tension is a unique consequence of the differences in power between the minority party in the House and Senate. In the former, the party out of power has little recourse to block legislation, but in the latter, the filibuster’s 60-vote threshold makes Schumer a major figure in deciding whether his party plays along with the 53 Republicans in the majority, or obstructs them.

At the same time that Schumer’s standing among Democrats was growing rocky, Van Hollen’s star was ascending. Elected to the Senate from the House in 2016, Van Hollen made national news when he traveled to El Salvador to meet Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadorian who had been wrongfully deported from Maryland in the early days of Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

after newsletter promotion

He has joined in criticizing Israel, amid a wider backlash among Democratic voters towards the US ally fueled by accusations it committed a genocide in Gaza. Van Hollen voted against providing bulldozers and bombs to the country, and after a visit to the Gaza-Egypt border in 2025, co-released a report accusing Israel of planning to ethnically cleanse the territory. In September, the senator led an unsuccessful resolution to force the state department to issue a report on violence in the West Bank.

Schumer’s criticism of Israel has been comparatively muted – he did not vote for the efforts to cute off arm sales, but did support Van Hollen’s resolution on the state department report. When he was majority leader in 2024, and thereby the highest-ranking Jewish official in the US government, Schumer called on the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, to step aside.

Last week’s sweep of the midterm elections seems to vindicate his leadership of Senate Democrats – after all, the party won just about every state it was contesting, and some where it had invested few resources. Yet Van Hollen said Schumer could have done better, noting that several candidates he had backed in the primaries wound up being rejected by voters.

After the election, reports emerged that Van Hollen was not planning to challenge Schumer, fueling speculation that he would instead run for president in 2028. He now says he’s not interested in a presidential run, and announced the bid for party leader just as activists again called for Senate Democrats to replace Schumer.

“Our members are tired of politicians content with incrementalism – they want bold, creative leadership that will help Democrats usher in affordability and accountability without delay or compromise in the next Congress,” said Joel Payne, the executive director of liberal group MoveOn.

“We welcome and will support any potential Senate leader willing to meet the moment.”

A small number of Democratic senators have publicly backed Van Hollen since he announced his leadership bid, including Bernie Sanders, the independent progressive who caucuses with the party, and incoming senators Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota. Others, such as Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, incoming senator Adam Hamilton of Kansas and Juliana Stratton of Illinois, said the party should choose a new leader, but have not said who that should be.

Schumer, meanwhile, retains considerable sway in the party, and has been endorsed by progressive and moderate senators alike. Those who have backed him argue he’s been effective, and point to last week’s results as proof.

“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” asked Angus King, the Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, and endorsed Schumer.

The contest is the party's first major test of unity after its triumph in last week’s midterm elections. Van Hollan has joined in criticizing Israel, amid a wider backlash among Democratic voters.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Ecuadorian fishermen who survived US boat strikes sue Trump administration
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US military has killed nearly 250 people in attack on ‘narco-terrorism’, and on 17 March, sank the 16 plaintiffs’ boat, leaving two with serious burns

More than a dozen Ecuadorian fishermen are suing the US government after they survived a military drone attack in the Pacific ocean earlier this year that sank their boat and left two of them with serious burns from the explosions.

The 17 March attack on the La Negra Francesca Duarte II was part of the Trump administration’s Operation Southern Spear campaign, announced in November 2025 ostensibly to counter “narco-terrorists” it said operated in the Caribbean and Pacific.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The Washington office on Latin America (Wola) said as many as 250 people have been killed by the US military in subsequent attacks. The group considers the actions extrajudicial executions because the government has provided no proof that the victims were engaged in trafficking.

In the lawsuit seen by the Guardian, to be filed in US district court for the western district of Pennsylvania on Monday, the 16 fishermen insist they had no connection with the drug trade and were illegally targeted by the crew of an unidentified US military vessel about 385 nautical miles from the port of Manta as they returned from a two-week fishing trip.

Two armed drones, the filing states, exploded on their boat, setting it ablaze and destroying it completely, and two of the crew “were themselves set on fire and burned on their legs, arms and back”.

The men say they jumped overboard and into small emergency boats that they rowed towards the vessel, pursued by a surveillance drone. They were greeted by US military personnel in camouflage uniforms who, they said, restrained them with zip ties and placed plastic hoods over their heads.

In an interview in June, the boat’s captain, Hernán Flores, described the moments after the boat he commanded for about 20 years was set alight. “Some guys looked for an extinguisher, but the fire was already spreading,” he said. “So some of our crew leapt into the water.”

The lawsuit seeks unspecified financial compensation for the attack, and for their subsequent “kidnapping and torture” that they say occurred when they were taken to a detention center in El Salvador and imprisoned for several weeks.

“They go out fishing, they don’t come home for a month, they’re like in a migrant detention center in El Salvador, and as we know those centers are not so nice,” said Dan Kovalik, a Pittsburgh-based attorney who is filing the lawsuit on behalf of the men.

“So there’s a lot of trauma there. It was catastrophic for them. They are home now, but they are struggling financially, and the two guys who were hurt bad are still dealing with that.”

Kovalik said the loss of the fishing vessel meant none of the plaintiffs had been able to work or support their families, and they were angry that, until their lawsuit, there was no recourse against the US authorities for what happened to them.

“They would also like the US to stop these boat strikes. That’s another goal of all this, and I think the US public and the media have been, honestly, not outraged enough about these strikes.”

The lawsuit states that the “manifestly unlawful” attack on the fishermen came soon after Ecuadorian authorities inspected the boat for themselves and determined it was not carrying drugs, nor its crew affiliated with any cartels.

It said the attack was illegal because, as with other strikes during Operation Southern Spear, it was conducted without congressional authority.

Additionally, the lawsuit alleges, “the wanton, willful and outrageous attacks upon, and kidnapping and torture of, plaintiffs at sea constitute torts under general admiralty and maritime law.

“There is no actual armed conflict that could justify the use of military force against the boats, nor was there one on March 17 when the attack took place. The US’s campaign of bombings against defenseless vessels and individuals violates long-standing and well-accepted international law.”

A spokesperson for the department of defense said in a statement on Friday: “As a matter of policy, the department does not comment on pending or ongoing litigation.”

In June, after details of the attack on the La Negra Francesca Duarte II first emerged, the Pentagon and US Coast Guard denied participating in operations involving Ecuadorian fishing vessels.

“We have no knowledge of, nor were Department of War forces involved in, the incidents described in those reports,” a spokesperson for US Southern Command (Southcom) said in a statement.

“US forces conduct operations under established legal authorities and hold its forces to the highest standards of professionalism, safety, and compliance with US and international law.”

Kovalik said he expected the government to contest the lawsuit, filed in a Pennsylvania district he said had “experience in admiralty cases”.

But he said it would help shine a light on the policies and actions of the Trump administration at a time when the Democratic party was about to take over control of Congress and launch its own investigations.

“Some of the Democrats that we met with are very interested in doing hearings on these boat strikes,” he said.

“We hope this case will encourage the Democrats when they get sworn in in January to start some hearings. I think it will have that impact.”

The fishermen’s lawsuit will join previously filed, similar litigation against the Trump administration. In January, the families of Chad Joseph, 26, and Rishi Samaroo, 41, Trinidadian fishermen killed in a US military strike in the Caribbean three months previously, filed a first-of-its-kind suit in Massachusetts.

The American Civil Liberties Union is among advocacy groups demanding an end to what it calls “a terrifying, lawless killing campaign at sea”.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Flights slowly resume after US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Abené Clayton
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Transportation secretary Sean Duffy says the airspace is now open and the problem has been identified

Chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt

What to know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA

Flights in the US have slowly started resuming after being grounded for several hours on Friday due to a major communications outage, but authorities have warned that a return to normal operations will take time.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop about four hours after it was declared on Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware, and throwing airports into sudden chaos.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website. “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon.”

Duffy said the federal government had “identified the problem” that brought down the US air traffic control system on Friday and the system “is operational right now”.

At a White House briefing on Friday evening, Duffy said the trouble began at 3.36pm, when air traffic control centres experienced ​instability in radar and communications systems.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” he said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”

But the briefing on Friday evening with Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, quickly turned into a plea for funding from Congress to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”.

A notice from the FAA had earlier said the ground stop was imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.

Duffy said more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued.

Mullin said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.

“There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters.

The flight grounding caused widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo. Footage from airports around the country showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways. Passengers thronged concourses, desperate for information about an outage that had thrown their plans into chaos.

As news of the airspace reopening trickled down to airline passengers on Friday evening, not all greeted the news with joy. A woman at John F Kennedy airport in New York who gave her name as simply Lola said she was frustrated. She had already rebooked her flight to Atlanta for another day and was going home. “I don’t like it,” she said.

Amid the earlier confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations.

“Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day.

In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary.

“There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. We just need communication from them. If they were there every hour briefing the American public, it would help and give us a sense of a timeline.”

According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway international airport and rippled across the rest of the US.

The FAA said in a statement that they “thoroughly tested” their systems to confirm they were stable and reliable before clearing flights to resume.

San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart.

John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport.

US airlines including United, Delta, Southwest and American Airlines announced they were resuming flights on Friday night after the ground stop was lifted.

United said it was restarting operations, “including some Friday night flights”, while American Airlines said it was focused on “operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening”.

British Airways cancelled a flight to New York that had been due to take off from Heathrow at 10.30pm on Friday night, and a spokesperson for Manchester airport confirmed three US-bound flights scheduled to leave on Saturday morning – all operated by Virgin Atlantic – were likely to be affected if the issue was not resolved soon.

A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air.

This is the third time all departing flights have been grounded in the US. The first time was on 11 September 2011; the other was in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours after a pilot notification system malfunctioned.

The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data.

Last week, the FAA announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US were officially operational in Alaska and Florida, as part of a modernization project intended to reduce flight delays and improve the flow of air traffic.

Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.

US congresswoman, who has been caught up in repeated controversies, loses re-election bid to Democrat Eileen Laubacher

Lauren Boebert, the firebrand conservative Republican Colorado representative whose three terms in Congress have been marred by multiple controversies, was defeated in her re-election bid.

The gun rights advocate, born-again Christian and one-time QAnon fan lost to Democrat Eileen Laubacher by a less than 1% margin, according to the Associated Press.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“I’m honored by the trust the people of Colorado’s fourth district have placed in me. This campaign was never about party labels. It was about putting people first,” Laubacher said in a statement. “To those who voted for me, thank you, I will strive to make you proud. To those who didn’t, I’ll fight just as hard for you and hope to earn your support.”

This district, which spans the eastern plains of Colorado, is one of the state’s most conservative seats and has long been a Republican stronghold. Laubacher is a retired two-star navy rear admiral, who was deployed to Afghanistan and later worked on the national security council under the Biden administration.

Laubacher just became a registered Democrat in 2025, saying in a debate with Boebert the Republican party had become “nearly unrecognizable”. She focused her campaign on decades of military and national security service.

In a statement congratulating Laubacher, Suzan DelBene, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, declared: “Lauren Boebert’s sideshow is over.”

Both Laubacher and Boebert moved to Colorado’s fourth congressional district in recent years. Boebert accused Laubacher of moving there and changing parties in order to run for Congress. Likewise, Boebert has been questioned for her move to the district in 2024 after barely eking out a win in the third district’s previous election.

Boebert said the move was because of “dark money” flowing from Hollywood to “steal” district three’s congressional seat: “It’s coming from Hollywood … when you have Barbra Streisand coming in and donating to the Democrat, when you have Ryan Reynolds coming in and donating to the Democrat … It shows you that Hollywood is trying to buy their way into Congress.”

Boebert’s tenure in Congress has been racked with controversy. She decried the 2020 presidential election as being rigged, demanded to carry a handgun on the House floor and was accused of helping incite the January 6 insurrection by tweeting “Today is 1776” the morning of the riots, among other actions. Boebert later condemned the attack on the Capitol.

She went viral in 2023 when she was filmed groping her date, vaping and being escorted out of a Beetlejuice musical in Denver in 2023. Initially, Boebert joked that she would “plead guilty to laughing and singing too loud”, but the incident later led to her publicly apologizing and divorcing her husband (who was not her date).

And just weeks before the election, she was hit by an ethics complaint over allegations she had sexual relationships with three staffers and had paid one to stay silent, allegations she has denied and called “politically motivated”.

Despite the dust-ups and being a Maga loyalist, Boebert did occasionally stand up to Trump. She was one of the most vocal members of Congress calling for the release of the Epstein files, even after the White House tried to persuade her to remove her name from a discharge petition for the documents.

This earned the ire of Trump, who has called Boebert a “carpetbagger” and “dumb”. The president’s first veto of his second term was for a bill sponsored by Boebert that would have funded a drinking water project in district four. The bill had passed the House and Senate unanimously.

“Nothing says ‘America First’ like denying clean drinking water to 50,000 people in south-east Colorado many of whom enthusiastically voted for him all three elections,” Boebert said in a statement at the time.

“But hey, if this administration wants to make its legacy blocking projects that deliver water to rural Americans; that’s on them.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: What the choice between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen for Senate leader is all about | Bernie Sanders
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Bernie Sanders

This is not a personality contest. This is a debate about the future of the Democratic party

The election for Democratic Senate leader between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen must be understood for what it is.

This is not a personality contest. This is a debate about the future of the Democratic party. It is a debate about whether the Democratic party remains a top-down party dominated by billionaire campaign contributors, inside-the-beltway consultants and 30-second TV ads, or whether we can transform it into a grassroots party of, by and for the working families of our country.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The election for Democratic Senate leader will determine whether we continue to tinker around the edges and maintain status quo policies, or whether we finally have the courage to take on enormously powerful special interests and address the unprecedented crises that we face.

Do we address the issue of oligarchy, obscene income and wealth inequality, and the reality that never before in the history of our country have so few people held so much wealth and so much power?

Do we address the issue of a corrupt campaign finance system and their Super Pacs, which enables billionaires to buy elections and undermine our democracy?

Do we address the issue that, in the wealthiest country in the history of the world, 60% of our people live paycheck to paycheck, we have the highest rate of childhood poverty of any major country and millions of seniors are unable to retire with dignity

Do we address the reality that our current healthcare system is dysfunctional, wildly expensive and that we are the only major country on earth that does not guarantee healthcare for all as a human right?

Do we address the reality that artificial intelligence, the most transformative technology in history, is being pushed down our throats by a handful of big tech billionaires who couldn’t care less about the wellbeing of ordinary Americans?

Do we address the reality that climate change is causing deadly heatwaves, massive forest fires, drought and extreme weather disturbances and will only get worse if don’t transform our energy systems away from fossil fuels and into energy efficiency and sustainable energy?

Do we address the reality that our immigration system is broken and that we have, with ICE, a domestic army that has killed Americans in cold blood and has acted in cruel, illegal and unconstitutional ways?

Do we address the reality that the wars in Vietnam, Iraq and the current war in Iran were based on lies and that we need to fundamentally rethink our foreign policy, including continued military funding to the extremist government in Israel?

Bottom line: whether we like it or not, our country faces some extraordinary and unprecedented crises. Do we seriously address these difficult challenges, and restore the faith of the American people that their government can improve their lives, or do we continue the same old, same old politics?

In large measure, that is what this Senate Democratic leadership election is all about.

Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on press freedom: authoritarians target journalism because it matters | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
From Cairo to Moscow to Washington, governments are turning up the pressure on media workers

L
ina Attalah is an influential Egyptian journalist. Yet until last month, even she was unaware of a major and concerning piece of news: her own conviction. In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October, resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month.

Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. Their lawyers say that they have been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

On Monday, Russia finally succeeded in silencing the famed Novaya Gazeta, which had spent decades battling growing repression. Six of its journalists, including Anna Politkovskaya, paid for their coverage with their lives. But the newspaper continued until, stripped of its newsroom, donation platforms and right to publish, it was forced to turn the lights off. (The separate Novaya Gazeta Europe, founded by many of its alumni, continues.)

These cases are part of a wider pattern. Press freedom is at its lowest ebb for a quarter of a century, Reporters Without Borders said this spring, judging more than half of the 180 countries it surveys to have “difficult” or “very serious” conditions for journalists. The rising tide of war worldwide is also increasing the pressures and dangers: the Committee to Protect Journalists recorded a new peak of 129 deaths of reporters and other media workers in 2025. Unesco said last week that almost nine out of 10 killings of journalists go unpunished.

High-quality journalism has never been more necessary in a world of rising conflict, AI slop and malicious fabrications spreading on platforms run by big tech firms who barely nod to ethical responsibilities. As Ms Attalah herself has pointed out, the disappearance of professional media organisations enlarges the space for conspiracies and disinformation.

Yet while the US previously pressed the case of threatened journalists overseas, sometimes helping to ease their conditions, it is now led by a man who has called news media “the enemy of the American people”, whose FBI raided a correspondent’s home in January, and who is currently pursuing a $10bn lawsuit against the BBC. Donald Trump has also sought to dismantle federally funded organisations which were an important source of independent reporting on many repressive nations.

This week, an appeals court panel ruled that the administration had illegally fired the head of Voice of America. VoA, Radio Free Asia and Radio Free Europe have all struggled on thanks to dedicated staff, though hugely diminished. Recent elections in Serbia, Brazil and the US are evidence that journalism, alongside activism, can stem the erosion of democracy. Thousands of people protested in Turkey last month against Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s media crackdown. Large parts of the public still want the truth and, against the odds, courageous journalists worldwide persist in finding it out and sharing it. That authoritarians target them so relentlessly only testifies to their importance.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Nationwide flight shutdown disrupts team travel in US

Mississippi v Oklahoma football game moved to Sunday

Cavaliers face tight turnaround after Miami travel delay

The Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights nationwide for several hours on Friday threw the US sports world into disarray, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams scrambling to reach their destinations in time for a packed weekend of games.

Transportation officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications issues at regional air traffic control centers for the stoppage. Some teams were left searching for hotel rooms, others rescheduled flights, leagues adjusted start times and several college football programs took the unusual step of chartering buses rather than waiting for the ground stop to end.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“We’re going to allow for general aviation, those larger movements, to take place as a priority. Smaller movements will take lower priority,” the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said after the ground stop was lifted on Friday night in Washington.

No 19 Mississippi’s football game at Oklahoma was moved from Saturday to Sunday at 1pm ET because of travel issues. Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny criticized the decision, saying the Southeastern Conference had threatened Oklahoma with a forfeit if it did not agree to the change.

“I understand that difficult decisions sometimes must be made under extraordinary circumstances,” Denny said in a statement on X. “Put simply, this decision isn’t fair to our athletes, our institution or to Sooner nation.”

Most college football teams playing on Saturday travel the day before their game, and the stoppage left several schools – including No 2 Utah, No 8 Texas and No 9 Tennessee – at a standstill as they prepared to depart for road games. The Utes visit No 22 Arizona, the Longhorns travel to No 24 LSU and the Volunteers face Texas A&M in three of the weekend’s biggest matchups.

“The Southeastern Conference is aware of the FAA’s nationwide ground stop and the potential impact on team travel,” the league said. “The safety and well-being of student-athletes, coaches and team personnel remain our highest priority.”

Texas and Tennessee both returned to their campuses during the stoppage. Once it was lifted following more than four hours of uncertainty, the schools began making plans to fly out as soon as possible, allowing them to arrive before game day.

Auburn opted to take a bus to Mississippi State, with the SEC pushing back Saturday’s kickoff from noon ET to 4.15pm to give the Tigers more time to reach Starkville. Purdue likewise decided to travel by bus from West Lafayette, Indiana, for their game at Iowa.

Other schools affected by the stoppage included Baylor, Washington, Kansas State, Minnesota and Arizona State.

The Big 12 moved the Kansas-West Virginia game from 5.30pm ET to 3.30pm because the Jayhawks had arrived in plenty of time. That allowed the conference to push the Arizona State-UCF game from 2.30pm to 5.30pm, giving the Sun Devils an additional three hours after their flight from Arizona to Florida was delayed.

Washington spokesman Kurt Svoboda said the Huskies returned to campus when their flight was grounded, but officials remained in contact with their airline partners and the flight crew stayed in place. Washington eventually departed late on Friday for their game at Michigan State on Saturday, which was pushed back 75 minutes to 5.30pm ET.

There were also concerns about whether referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would be able to reach their destinations. The Big Ten said all of its officials had arrived for their scheduled assignments on Saturday.

Several teams managed to depart before the stoppage began, including all those traveling in the Atlantic Coast Conference; Missouri, who were flying to top-ranked Georgia; Duke, who were visiting fifth-ranked Miami; and No 10 Texas Tech, who posted images on social media of their arrival for a game at Oklahoma State.

NFL teams playing on Sunday typically travel the day before their games and were expected to fly as planned on Saturday.

In the NBA, the Cleveland Cavaliers played in Miami on Friday night but were forced to postpone their return flight until Saturday morning, leaving them scheduled to land about eight hours before their home game against the Dallas Mavericks.

NBA teams rarely fly on the day of a game, although exceptional circumstances, often involving severe weather, have occasionally forced such arrangements.

At least two other NBA teams had Friday night flights pushed back to Saturday morning, although neither were scheduled to play that evening. Cleveland, meanwhile, scrambled to rebook hotel rooms in Miami after checking out earlier on Friday.

“It’s part of it. You just adapt,” Cavaliers coach Kenny Atkinson said.

The NHL has 14 games scheduled for Saturday, with the Florida Panthers among the majority of teams who reached their destinations before the stoppage began. The San Jose Sharks, who were left waiting to see whether they would be able to travel, eventually arrived in Utah late on Friday.

In women’s college basketball, JuJu Watkins and her third-ranked Southern California teammates were attempting to reach South Carolina for Sunday’s marquee matchup against the top-ranked Gamecocks.

The Trojans had just boarded their flight at Los Angeles International Airport when the ground stop was issued. After an extended wait, passengers were told to disembark and the team returned to the Galen Center.

The disruption also reached soccer. The Utah Royals were already in the Washington DC area ahead of Saturday’s National Women’s Soccer League semi-final against the Washington Spirit, but the Kansas City Current were scheduled to depart on Friday for their semi-final against Gotham FC in New York on Sunday. Team officials were uncertain when their flight would be cleared to leave.

The US men’s national team’s match against Haiti on Saturday in Miami was unaffected. Both teams and match officials had already arrived for the first leg of their two-match Concacaf Nations League quarter-final.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Scientists find blood biomarker that opens door to CTE diagnosis in living patients
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Sean Ingle
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Condition is prevalent in rugby and American football

Scientists are optimistic of significant breakthrough

Scientists have moved a step closer to diagnosing the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy in living people, after a study found a blood biomarker that identifies an advanced form of the disease.

As things stand CTE, which is caused by repeated trauma to the head and is especially prevalent in collision and contact sports such as American football, rugby and football, can be diagnosed only after death by examining brain tissue.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

However, scientists at Washington University School of Medicine in St Louis have now identified a protein fragment in blood – eMTBR-tau243 – that is elevated not only in Alzheimer’s disease but also in other brain diseases that share the same type of toxic protein buildup, including CTE.

“We are potentially opening a new door for diagnosing and treating CTE in living patients,” said Kanta Horie, the co-senior author of the study in the medical journal JAMA Neurology.

When researchers tested blood from 11 people whose CTE was confirmed at autopsy, they found that levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher than in healthy people and rose with the severity of the brain disease.
 
 
 Yet while the test could distinguish people with advanced CTE from healthy people with high accuracy, it could not reliably identify early-stage CTE.

The test has not yet been validated for diagnosing CTE. However, the scientists say that if large studies confirm their findings, clinicians could use such a blood test to monitor people at risk from CTE and enable trials of drugs that could help the condition.

“Our study shows that an Alzheimer’s disease biomarker can be applied to other tauopathies, including CTE,” the neuroscientist Chihiro Sato, who co-authored the study with Horie, said. “This is not going to be a standalone biomarker. But if someone has a history of repeated head injury, tests negative for Alzheimer’s and this biomarker comes up, it might be CTE.”

CTE continues to be a major focus of concern across science and sport. In one recent study of nearly 400 NFL players whose brains were donated for examination after their deaths, 93.5% showed evidence of CTE.

More than 350 NFL players have been diagnosed with CTE after their deaths, including Mike Webster, a hall of fame center; Junior Seau, whose 20-year career included two Super Bowl appearances, and Frank Gifford, who was a former MVP and prominent broadcaster.

Legal action is continuing from a number of living former rugby union and league players who have been diagnosed with Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome (TES), including the England World Cup winner Steve Thompson. The boxer Ricky Hatton also had a mild CTE diagnosis after his death.

Earlier this year, the Professional Footballers’ Association recommended that professionals should not head a ball more than 10 times a week in training sessions, and children under 12 not at all, as part of a CTE prevention protocol.

CTE is caused by repeated trauma to the head and is prevalent in contact sports such as American football, rugby and football. Scientists say they could use such a blood test to monitor people at risk from CTE.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: USA hammer Denmark 14-0 with record 85 shots to reach women’s hockey worlds semi-finals
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Americans set tournament record with 85 shots on goal

Harvey and Winn score twice each in 14-0 rout

Canada edge Czechs 3-2 to set up Sweden semi-final

Defending champions the United States marched into the semi-finals of the women’s ice hockey world championship with a crushing 14-0 victory over hosts Denmark on Friday.

The Americans stormed out of the blocks, racing into a 5-0 lead inside eight minutes before stretching their advantage to 10-0 by the end of the second period in the first-ever meeting between the teams.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The US will face Finland in Sunday’s semi-finals.

Taylor Fox opened the scoring just 57 seconds into the game, skating into the slot to put the Americans ahead. Fox finished with a goal and three assists in a four-point performance.

Caroline Harvey and Haley Winn each scored twice and added three assists, while Kelly Pannek had two goals and two assists. Hannah Bilka contributed a goal and two assists, while Casey O’Brien, Grace Zumwinkle, Laila Edwards and Hayley Scamurra each finished with a goal and an assist. Alex Carpenter and Jesse Compher also scored.

Gwyneth Philips needed to make just eight saves to secure the shutout.

Denmark pulled starting goaltender Emma-Sofie Nordstrom before the third period after she had stopped 51 shots. Her replacement, Caroline Bjergstad, made 20 saves.

The Americans’ 85 shots on goal set a single-game tournament record, surpassing the previous mark of 82 set by the US against Sweden in 1997.

Elsewhere, Canada survived a scare against the Czech Republic, edging a 3-2 victory in Herning to book a semi-final meeting with Sweden.

Sarah Fillier, Rebecca Leslie and Renata Fast scored for Canada, while goaltender Eve Gascon made 14 saves.

Kristýna Kaltounková, the No 1 overall pick in last year’s PWHL draft, scored twice for the Czechs, who managed more than one goal against Canada for the first time in six meetings across all competitions.

Fillier broke the deadlock 1:29 into the second period, pouncing on a rebound to score for the third straight game after missing Canada’s first two preliminary-round contests with an upper-body injury.

She leads Canada with 23 goals and 38 points in 38 career appearances at the world championships.

Leslie doubled the lead on a power play less than three minutes later before Kaltounková pulled one back with a power-play goal of her own.

Fast restored Canada’s two-goal advantage with 3:13 remaining in the second period, but Kaltounková struck again in the third to set up a tense finish.

The Czechs pulled goaltender Klára Peslarová with 42 seconds remaining in search of an equalizer, despite Kaltounková being in the penalty box, but Canada held on.

In Esbjerg, Sweden secured their place in the last four with a 1-0 victory over Switzerland, Sara Hjalmarsson scoring the game’s only goal.

Finland, last year’s bronze medalists, also advanced with a 6-0 shutout of Germany. Petra Nieminen led the way with a goal and two assists.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Alex Bellos
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems

The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.

After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.

Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.

Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.

The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.

“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”

Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.

In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.

In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.

“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.

“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”

after newsletter promotion

Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.

Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.

The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.

“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”

Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”

In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].”

Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”

Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”

Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.summary: Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. His work is said to contain hundreds of proved theorems.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas

SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket, but ultimately fell short.

Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas.

The rocket, which is on its 15th flight, is composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 Raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top.

As smoke plumes wafted from the launch site, SpaceX employees erupted into cheers.

SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted, and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. The cause of that diversion remains unknown.

“That certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” said Kate Tice, SpaceX’s director of quality management, but she noted the booster’s return was in line with “rigorous safety checks”.

Early in the webcast, SpaceX simulated the return. The entire rocket was expected to be grabbed in the launch tower’s “chopstick” mechanical arms.

Friday’s test did not rise to the double-catch mantle, which Elon Musk had described early in November as a “critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary”.

Still, the flight is still poised to mark another milestone for the company. If all goes to plan, it would be the first time SpaceX has caught the rocket’s 171ft upper stage.

Previous tests focused on the retrieval of the booster.

The Starship, meanwhile, has continued to sail through space at over 26,000 km/h at an altitude of 270km.

The launch went on as scheduled despite a nationwide ground stop that disrupted hundreds of flights.

Flights to the west coast from Hawaii were temporarily paused, then resumed on Friday due to space debris from the launch, according to the island’s transportation agency.

As in the past, Starship carried satellites for Starlink, SpaceX’s internet service wing, three of which were fitted with cameras to analyze the rocket’s heat shield. The data plays a role in determining if the spacecraft is ready to return.

SpaceX chief executive Musk has sought to advance Starship’s “rapid reusability” as a vehicle, which he hopes will take humans to the moon and, controversially, to Mars.

Nasa has contracted SpaceX, along with Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, to provide the lunar landers that will return astronauts to the moon in 2028.

Musk has cast his reusable rocket as a buffer against the enormous costs associated with future space travel.

SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights in recent years, some of which have resulted in explosions that signaled major design flaws.

In September, the most recent flight test, SpaceX notched a victory, sending the spacecraft into Earth’s orbit for the first time, although its engine failed during the ascent.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Hundreds of children in England prescribed weight-loss jabs, figures show
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Exclusive: investigation finds prescriptions for children under 12, as experts stress need for specialist supervision and long-term monitoring

Hundreds of children in England are receiving prescriptions for GLP-1 medications, including some younger than 12, the Guardian can reveal.

GLP-1 medications were initially developed to help people with type 2 diabetes control their blood sugar levels, but have since become a popular slimming aid, with products such as Wegovy and Mounjaro becoming household names.

While social media is awash with adults who have lost weight with GLP-1s, data shows a number of children are also being prescribed them.

A Guardian investigation has revealed that in the financial year 2025-26 there were 419 prescriptions issued to children under the age of 18, 10 of which were for children under the age of 12.

And in the four months from April to July this year, 341 prescriptions for GLP-1s were issued to children, 15 of whom were under the age of 12.

The figures, obtained from the NHS Business Services Authority through freedom of information requests, relate to prescriptions in England and dispensed in a community setting anywhere in the UK.

However, they do not cover those prescribed and dispensed via private prescriptions, in prisons, and in hospitals, meaning the figures are likely to be a considerable underestimate.

One private clinic for children has previously revealed it has more than 200 patients receiving the jabs. It is also unclear whether the GLP-1 figures reflect medications that are being given primarily for weight loss.

Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, said the number of prescriptions was still small relative to the scale of childhood obesity, but those taking the drugs needed long-term change to their lifestyles.

He said: “The important thing is that children who start them do so within specialist services, with support for diet, growth and wellbeing, and a plan for the long term.

“That includes regular monitoring of growth and puberty, nutritional intake, mental health and eating behaviours, and side effects. This matters partly because we know weight tends to return when the drugs are stopped, and partly because we still have limited data on use over many years in growing young people.”

The rising use of GLP-1s comes as levels of childhood obesity are increasing. Figures from the National Child Measurement Programme show that 10.7% of reception-year children (ages 4 and 5) are obese, while that rises to 22.8% for children in year 6 (ages 10 and 11).

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 400 million children and adolescents aged between five and 19 were overweight in 2024, including 170 million living with obesity.

As part of efforts for early intervention, the NHS began piloting Complications from Excess Weight (CEW) clinics from 2021, aimed at children aged two to 16 with severe obesity.

In May, NHS England revealed almost 6,500 children have since been referred to such clinics, including more than 400 younger than four.

Hundreds of young people have received weight-loss medications through such services – although only some CEW clinics can access funding to offer GLP-1s, and these are typically dispensed through hospital pharmacies.

Dr Dunia Ismail, a consultant paediatrician who runs a CEW clinic, said experts were now looking at widening the use of GLP-1s in such settings. “We have been sticking to 12 [years], although now we are looking at expanding that to eight-plus once licence-approved,” she said.

Last month, new global guidelines from the WHO stated obesity medications, including GLP-1s, should not be given to children under the age of 10.

However, recent data from a trial involving 165 children aged 6 to under 12 – run by the pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, which produces Wegovy and Victoza – has suggested GLP-1s can help young children with obesity.

Julian Hamilton-Shield, a professor in diabetes and metabolic endocrinology and a clinician at the Bristol Complications CEW clinic, said typically children who receive semaglutide at CEW clinics had been unable to lose weight through standard dietary and nutritional advice and psychological support.

“Probably, in the vast majority of cases, they have a secondary comorbidity such as type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnoea, liver disease, intracranial hypertension – you name it, they’ve got it,” he said. “So it’s been used as an adjunct after standard therapies haven’t really helped. However, it is used quite frequently and it is a very effective drug.”

Hamilton-Shield stressed GLP-1 medications were given to children who have very high excess weight. “You’d call it morbid obesity if you were classifying it as adults,” he said.

The use of GLP-1s in children has reignited a debate about the drivers of childhood obesity, but experts say it is important to avoid blaming patients or their families.

“We’re a health service that delivers health to the people who require it. We’re not one that makes moral judgments about people,” said Hamilton-Shield. “Nobody’s saying that every child who’s a bit heavy should have a GLP-1.”

Hamilton-Shield added: “These children and young people are from very complex backgrounds, have enormous lack of self-esteem. They’re not attending school. They’ve got all these complications. They’ve got all the stigma. And when you actually give them a drug that helps them to lose maybe 25, 30kg, [it is] the first time they feel they have any agency in their lives at all, and that will have a transformative effect in its own right.”

Ismail also stressed the importance of GLP-1s for children. “We know now that obesity is not a choice, it’s a condition,” she said. “We’re giving them GLP-1s because there is nothing else you can do at this stage. Otherwise, they will die young, they will have heart disease, they will have diabetes … It’s just terrible what could happen to them if we don’t.”
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.summary: 341 prescriptions for GLP-1s were issued to kids under the age of 12 in the four months from April to July this year. GLP1s are used to help people with type 2 diabetes control their blood sugar levels.

Kai Wright of the Guardian podcast Stateside will speak with author and environmentalist Bill McKibben – and we’d like to hear your questions

Was the climate crisis one of your top political priorities during the midterm elections? We want to hear from you: what do you want political leaders to do about it in 2027?

Democrats will control the House and Senate in the new year, and they have a long list of priorities ahead of them. But it remains to be seen just how much they will focus on one of the most pressing issues of our times: the climate crisis. The UN declared this summer that, despite some progress, it is now “unavoidable” that the globe will heat past the point that scientists say will threaten human health. Despite these terrifying predictions, the US remains absent from global efforts to limit the impacts of the climate crisis.

Environmentalist and Guardian columnist Bill McKibben has been ringing the alarm for decades. But in his most recent book, Here Comes the Sun, he’s argued that we’re at a unique moment of opportunity. The science and the markets have given us the tools to solve the crisis – we just need the politics to catch up. So what does he think is politically possible now? And what would you like to ask McKibben about this moment of peril and opportunity?

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: California governor Gavin Newsom endorses global fossil fuel phaseout
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Mark Hertsgaard
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the Trump administration continues to boycott

The leader of the world’s fourth biggest economy, California governor Gavin Newsom, has explicitly endorsed a global phase out of the fossil fuels that drive climate breakdown.

Newsom told the Guardian that California is “100%” behind the efforts of the so-called Santa Marta coalition, a group of more than 50 countries that includes many of the world’s largest economies, to transition away from oil, gas and coal toward solar, wind, batteries and other non-carbon energy sources.

Speaking at the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday, Newsom said: “When you have a product that is obviously superior, which clean energy is for the climate and the economy, why wouldn’t you make that shift as quickly as possible?”

As the head of America’s most populous and economically powerful state, Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the administration of US president Donald Trump continues to boycott.

Newsom, a Democrat, is widely expected to run for president in 2028. His statement raises the possibility that the US, the world’s biggest economy and largest historical emitter of planet-warming gases, could join the Santa Marta coalition if he wins the presidency two years from now.

More than 80 countries wanted last year’s COP30 to begin to develop a global “roadmap” to phase out fossil fuels. A handful of petrostates led by Saudi Arabia blocked that effort, relying on the disputed notion that decisions at UN climate summits can only be made by consensus. Undaunted, countries favoring a roadmap met in April in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin designing a phase out on their own.

“Love it,” Newsom said of the challenge that this Santa Marta “coalition of the willing” is posing to the US and other states intent on keeping the world burning fossil fuels.

The coalition is in effect no longer allowing petrostates to employ procedural tricks and endless talk to prevent what scientists say is imperative: rapidly phasing out fossil fuels. Instead, this critical mass of countries, which includes Germany, France, Brazil and The Netherlands – with additional countries, perhaps including the UK, expected to join later in Cop31 – is proceeding on its own with roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels, hoping that its example and economic power will lead others to follow suit.

“You don’t ask drug dealers to vote for Prohibition, and you won’t get petro-states to agree to phase out fossil fuels,” said Mohamed Nasheed, the former president of The Maldives, who once convened a cabinet meeting underwater to dramatize the plight of low-lying island nations like his. “Countries wishing to phase out fossil fuels should just go ahead and do it,” Nasheed told the Guardian.

Newsom’s statement could add momentum to a CopP31 summit that has been widely expected to yield modest progress at best. The governor’s comments follow two political earthquakes that also raised hopes of a new era in global climate politics. First came the surprising re-election of president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil in October, then the crushing rebuke of Trump and his Republican Congress in the US midterm elections in early November.

What makes the Santa Marta coalition’s vision more than a pipe dream is the coalition’s economic might. Collectively, the 80-plus countries that wanted a phase out roadmap at Cop30 amount to the biggest economic superpower on earth.

If the coalition can begin implementing a credible transition away from fossil fuels, it “would send an unmistakable message that the age of oil, gas and coal is ending, and the smart money is shifting,” Mohamed Adow, director of the nonprofit Power Shift Africa, said in an interview. Governments and financial markets around the world would be put on notice that staying invested in fossil fuels will be an increasingly risky proposition that could leave them holding trillions of dollars of stranded assets.

Thus far, Germany, the world’s third biggest economy, has committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045. France, the world’s sixth biggest economy, and The Netherlands, the 18th biggest, have released phase out roadmaps as well.

California’s clean energy track record aligns with the one policy goal that, analysts say, Cop31’s final agreement might endorse: a commitment to obtain 35% of the world’s energy from electricity by 2035. California’s economy has run on 100% clean electricity nine out of every 10 days during much of 2026, with batteries emerging as “a game changer”, as Newsom described it. As the costs of clean energy continue to fall, Newsom expects more counties to follow California’s example because “the markets are moving in our direction”.

The midterms also brought to power scores of climate champions at the state and local level. In Texas, the US’s second largest state economy after California, the new governor is Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who shunned contributions from the fossil fuel industry that has long dominated her state. In all, 29 states will have Democratic governors who, among other things, could block datacenters.

Humanity is in “a final battle against the evil forces” trying to keep the world burning fossil fuels, said Johan Rockstrom, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research. As the Nepal glacier disaster and 50,000 extreme heat deaths in Europe this summer illustrate, climate breakdown is already wreaking terrible damage. Nevertheless, Rockstrom added, “89% of citizens across the world trust science [and] want action. We are a majority power that can have confidence we have a collective global community that really wants this to succeed--and that it isn’t too late.”

Mark Hertsgaard is the executive director of Covering Climate Now and the environment correspondent for the Nation. He has covered UN climate summits since the 1992 Earth Summit

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to bring shoppers back

The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?

Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Central to this, the study says, is trying to banish, or at least tame, motor traffic, because too often urban centres are places “designed to be driven through, not for time to be spent in”.

As well as citing a lack of imagination, the report, which is co-produced by bike storage company Cyclehoop, blames planning regulations that favour conformity and clutter and too often treat speeding cars as a given, to which everything else must adjust.

“The default high street is engineered for traffic and furnished from a catalogue: a tarmac pavement, guardrails penning people at the kerb, litter bins ordered from a procurement catalogue, a row of plastic planters – public investment that is joyless,” it says.

While planners have traditionally focused on car access as a metric for thriving town centres, calculations for the Create Streets report suggest that replacing parking with other kerbside infrastructure, including bike spaces or outside drinking and dining areas, creates more economic value.

It found that one parking space in the high street of a market town is typically used by about 3.5 vehicles a day, bringing in just over £73,000 a year in spending to nearby shops.

But the same 12 square metres, if used to hold nine share e-bikes, generates an average of 13 trips a day, with over £146,000 a year in spending, even taking into account the lower average spend per person.

In a busier city, where share bikes would be used more frequently, the estimated total annual spend rises to more than £300,000.

Repurposing the space for outside dining brings less dramatic gains, but in a city centre it can still amount to about £120,000 in extra annual spending.

The report calls for a cultural rethink involving low-cost tweaks that rip away ugly and unnecessary street furniture and make better use of kerbsides.

Calling use by families “the indicator species of a healthy high street”, the report cites what is known as “the wrist test” – whether it feels safe to let go of a young child’s wrist so they can roam with some freedom.

This is best done, it argues, by removing the threat of speeding motor vehicles and not by trying to mitigate their impact. It calls the removal of pedestrian guardrails next to roads “the most cost-effective upgrade for the majority of high streets”, saying they are an eyesore with minimal safety benefits.

The report says “the absurdity of modern public realm management” is exemplified by Secured by Design, policy guidelines on cutting neighbourhood crime. These can, critics point out, mean benches and plants are removed on the advice of police, supposedly to discourage antisocial behaviour.

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has pledged to try to reverse the decline of high streets, announcing in September a £210m regeneration fund.
