Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

However, the bulk of the money will go into buildings: turning old shops into shared workspaces or community cafes, or keeping pubs and clubs in business.

The report argues that renovating buildings is pointless if the street outside is unappealing. To reduce clutter, it says, there should be “a presumption of removal where an item cannot be justified”.

The effects can be dramatic, the report says, pointing to examples including Altrincham in Cheshire, where the creation of a walkable, car-free urban area helped see retail vacancies fall from over 30% to 7% in less than a decade.

Such initiatives do not have to be expensive, it claims, noting the example of an unused patch of land next to a church in Grimsby which was turned into a park for less than £20,000.

“Streets that are ugly are not so because councils lack the desire to change them, but because the system is counting the maintenance liabilities, not the benefits,” said David Milner of Create Streets.

“What works is cheap: trees in the ground, benches people want to sit on, clutter taken away.

“So much of what is built now seems to be temporary, looking more like road works than public realm improvements, so we encourage the concept of permanence; more trees in the ground, not in giant plant pots, for example.”

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We support local leaders to make decisions on pedestrianisation based on their communities’ needs.

“Our Hope on the High Street strategy will help local people revive town centres by protecting community assets, bringing derelict buildings back into use and tackling the spread of vape and gambling shops.

“Funding is available for local leaders to spend on their priorities, including pedestrianising and regenerating their high streets if they so wish.”
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.summary: Report says too often urban centres are places ‘designed to be driven through, not for time to be spent in’ It says planning regulations favour conformity and clutter. Local leaders can spend on their priorities, including pedestrianising and regenerating their high streets.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘You cannot build peace on a burning planet,’ UN chief tells Cop31 in farewell speech
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey, Oliver Milman and Graham Readfearn in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
António Guterres says climate action central to every aspect of UN’s work, as leaders depart Cop31 and talks go on

Tackling the climate crisis is central to all of human life and must be at the forefront of global governance, the outgoing UN secretary general has said in an emotional farewell address at the Cop31 climate summit.

“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” António Guterres said at his final climate press conference as secretary general on Friday. “You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it. You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Guterres has been the most forthright secretary general yet on the subject of the climate, returning to it again and again to castigate fossil fuel companies and recalcitrant governments.

He leaves office at the end of December and his successor is still unknown after Donald Trump tried to interject his preferred choices into the process. There are widespread fears that the next incumbent will downplay the climate crisis in favour of other issues.

In a clear message to his successor, Guterres spelled out why the UN must continue to place the climate at the top of the global agenda. “Climate change does not stay in its lane,” he said. “It drives anger and displacement around the world. It wipes out development gains built over decades. It pushes countries deeper into deficit. It aggravates competition for land and water.

“It fuels instability. And increasingly, it threatens the very existence of communities and countries. For all these reasons, I have never viewed climate action as just one of many other issues. Climate action is central to every aspect of the work of the UN.”

Guterres was one of the few world leaders left at Cop by Friday afternoon as most of the more than 90 who had attended returned to their capitals, leaving negotiators to get down to tackling issues such as the electrification of the global economy and a just transition out of fossil fuel industries for workers.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, flew out after hosting a meeting between major international investors and Australian renewable energy companies, followed by a meeting with Taneti Maamau, the president of the low-lying Pacific nation of Kiribati. Albanese made raising the plight of his country’s Pacific neighbours a major part of his two and a half-days at the talks.

The Australian co-presidency of the 31st “conference of the parties” to the UN framework convention on climate change issued a list of “reflections” that encapsulated the proposals countries had expressed since the talks began on Monday. This will form a loose basis for a first draft of the “cover decision”, the final negotiated document gavelled through at the end of the summit, which is likely to be the central outcome of Cop31.

Recent cover decisions have produced significant progress: at Cop28, in Dubai in 2023, the cover decision included a global pledge to “transition away from fossil fuels”, and at Cop26, in Glasgow in 2021, a cover decision produced a requirement to “phase down” coal.

This year, hoped-for resolutions include a target of deriving 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035, seen as one of the most important ways of decarbonising the global economy, and pledges to cut methane emissions, make progress on the phase-out of fossil fuels, and ensure adequate finance for developing countries hit by climate disaster.

after newsletter promotion

The “reflections” document gave a clear sense of how difficult it will be for Australia – which, in an unusual sharing arrangement, is presiding over the negotiations while Turkey hosts the talks – to forge an agreement before the scheduled end next Friday night.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and the president of the negotiations, said: “We are making sure parties are being listened to as we progress negotiations. The reflection text is not a negotiating text. Nothing in it is prejudged, locked in or necessarily to be included in the final decision.”

Countries will have until late on Saturday to respond, with an official draft cover decision text not expected until early next week.

More than 100 companies and groups linked to fossil fuels were present at the talks, research revealed on Friday, despite efforts to clamp down on the presence of lobbyists in recent years.

Prakash Dalal, of Pro Public/Friends of the Earth Nepal, criticised their presence. “Big polluters have caused loss of livelihood, emotional damage, trauma and survival challenges for our people,” he said. “We cannot tolerate the disproportionate space given to them compared to civil society and our country delegations.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past

“S
cience fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize.

Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t want to break out of the ghetto; he wants to break it down. “I really hate categories, and I really hate being categorised,” he said.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Set in an unnamed seaside town in an unspecified future, The End of Everything depicts a disintegrating Britain after the invasion of an alien species called the iGhettis, rumoured to have “come out of the internet”. Capitalism, ecological disaster, AI, Brexit – the cause of “the crisis” is unclear. All we know is that “it’s ongoing and unresolved. It never ends.”

Ahead of Cop31, Ed Miliband this week claimed that “the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences”. With news of Microsoft outages, cyber-attacks on supermarket freezers, not to mention national stockpiling, the Booker judges’ decision couldn’t be more timely. As Atwood has said, science fiction is “always about now”.

From Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein to Isaac Asimov’s Robot series to Nobel laureate Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun (a new film adaptation of which has been panned by critics), writers have been fascinated by non-human intelligence. Science fiction responds to anxieties about the impact of scientific and technological discoveries on society and the human psyche. Harrison’s great hero, JG Ballard, described his move away from classic sci-fi as a rejection of outer space for “inner space”.

Harrison has dismissed science fiction’s world-building as “the great clomping foot of nerdism”. The End of Everything is about a world breaking down, and as rationality and communication have collapsed, he had to break down the rules of fiction, including science fiction. There are no explanations or solutions, no salvation. He wants the reader to feel as confused and destabilised as his characters.

For some, this lack of answers is bewildering, and will confirm the Booker’s reputation for tricky winners. Others have an alien aversion that no amount of fine writing can overcome. The Wasp Factory author, Iain Banks, published his science fiction novels under the name Iain M Banks to distinguish them from his mainstream work. This is no longer necessary.

Whether the novel’s win marks a new frontier for publishing and literary awards remains to be seen. One thing is certain – there will be no shortage of fiction confronting a bleakly precarious future. As Harrison has said, we are living “in an age of fantasy”. The End of Everything is a novel for our times. Today’s polycrisis demands a polyphony of genres. Be it speculative fiction, science fiction, horror, fantasy, satire, dystopia - or a mix – the question of whether such fiction deserves a capital L belongs to a bygone age.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jonathan Freedland
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world

F
or politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices.

Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya, promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

That’s where things get tricky. Last month Burnham’s government approved the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, dismaying climate activists. Soon there will have to be a decision on Rosebank, the much bigger proposed new oilfield northwest of Shetland. There are also signs that ministers are preparing to weaken the targets set for the car industry to shift to electric vehicles. And this week, the chancellor, John Healey, declared himself fully “behind building a third runway at Heathrow”. Small wonder that campaigners are talking of hypocrisy and the government’s “crumbling” credibility.

What is Burnham to do? He has Healey in one ear, telling him that a thriving airport is an engine for economic growth, doubtless alongside the oil, gas and car industries. And in the other he has the climate scientists, reminding him that global carbon emissions are at record levels and the planet is getting hotter every year. What option does he have, except to keep putting off the moment of choice, buying himself time by saying, for example, that Rosebank is a “quasi-legal decision” that cannot be hurried?

Naturally, there are advocates for each of the binary options, whether it’s green activists demanding he put the planet first, regardless of the impact on jobs or prices, or business leaders insisting it be the other way around. But he is in a different position from each of those warring sides – because he has to come up with something both can live with. The answer might just be an arresting blend of pragmatism and radicalism – both, and at the same time.

Such an approach would begin with saying a couple of things campaigners might not want to hear. First, that the most reliable route to reducing the use of fossil fuels lies not with curtailing supply – blocking production – but with slashing demand. Or as Michael Jacobs, who served as the climate and energy adviser to Gordon Brown in Downing Street, told me this week: “We need to destroy the demand for oil and gas.” On that goal, there has been remarkable progress, whether measured in the shift to renewable sources of power, such as wind and solar, for the generation of electricity or the move to electric vehicles: last month just under one in two new cars registered in the UK were either fully electric or plug-in hybrids.

The second message Burnham might deliver to a wary, green audience would be: symbols matter, but they should not obscure the thing they are meant to symbolise. In that context, and given that destroying demand is more important than curbing supply, he could argue that the green light he gave to Jackdaw should not be overplayed. That project is relatively small and has an expected lifespan of only about 10 years. Yes, it became a signifier, but the bigger picture is what matters.

It would be much harder to make that argument for Rosebank, which is bigger than Jackdaw and set to last for 25 years, and harder still for Heathrow, not least because emissions from aviation are stubbornly difficult to reduce: you can’t shrink demand for aviation fuel, because, as of now, there are few readily available alternatives. So a third runway means a serious increase in the UK’s emissions of CO2.

But what if Burnham felt he could not rebuff the growth lobby on Heathrow and Rosebank, especially if he also stands firm on his electric vehicle targets despite the howls of protest from UK carmakers? Is there a bone he could throw them, while not enraging the climate-concerned voters he needs to keep on side?

One option would be to grant reluctant consent to Rosebank – but follow it with a blanket policy that says any fossil fuel production in the North Sea must engage in carbon capture and storage, or CCS, essentially sending the equivalent amount of carbon that will be released by burning the extracted oil or gas back into the ground from which it came. It’s an expensive process, with vehement critics, and such a move would have to be phased, but it is possible. Norway has been running a CCS operation at the Sleipner field in its part of the North Sea for 30 years.

The UK government has set aside about £21bn to subsidise CCS, but here’s where the radicalism comes in. Healey should tell the fossil fuel companies, whatever the decision on Rosebank, that if they want to drill in the North Sea, they will have to pay to capture and store the carbon themselves. It’s the most elementary principle: the polluter pays. What’s more, it will free up that £21bn to be spent on schools, hospitals, defence – anything more worthy than subsidising the fossil fuel industry.

after newsletter promotion

I’m told such a move is under “live” consideration by ministers and so it should be, not least because government estimates suggest CCS would create about 50,000 UK jobs in the 2030s, many more than lie in further extraction. It would represent a one-two punch of pragmatic radicalism: granting consent for some fossil fuel extraction, such as Jackdaw, while limiting the wider industry’s impact on the planet. Sure, it lacks the purity and simplicity of a wholesale ban that would keep fossil fuels in the ground – but it would be the next best thing, keeping an increasing amount of carbon deep in the earth. If it worked, Jacobs believes the likes of the EU or Norway might follow suit, imposing a similar CCS demand on their own oil and gas producers – thereby making good on Burnham’s promise of a “new era of British leadership”.

It’s just one example of a possible approach for a government that needs to find a way through the dilemma that confronts it – and governments like it across the globe. If it can’t say no to every move that entails emissions, then it must not say yes to all of them either. It will have to explain its logic on each specific case – even as it makes the broader argument about the necessity of preventing a climate breakdown and the most effective ways to do it.

It won’t be easy, not least because there are always more novel, more eye-catching issues to discuss. Climate breakdown at least used to have the market in existential, apocalyptic threats to itself – now it has to compete for that attention against the menace of AI. Charting a path ahead and having the public follow will require a nimble, trusted communicator, unafraid of nuance and complexity. It could be one of Andy Burnham’s biggest tests.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Microsoft outage shakes up companies, schools and local governments across US
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Gaya Gupta in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Local officials warn some services remain unavailable even as Outlook starts to resume normal operations after outage

Microsoft outage – live updates

The Microsoft Outlook outage has shaken up companies and local governments across the US that use its suite of email, calendar, video conferencing and cloud storage systems.

Even as Outlook started to resume normal operations Friday morning, local leaders from across the country, including in Miami, Maryland and Los Angeles, warned residents that certain staff or services were still unavailable due to the outage that started around 1pm ET on Thursday.

In Colorado, one local detention facility in Arapahoe county said that they were unable to take online bond payments to release detainees because of the outage.

“Until Outlook email is restored, anyone needing to post bond for immediate release must do so in person at the jail,” the office said in a social media statement.

The Los Angeles county sheriff’s department also warned that it was experiencing disruptions in its email and other communications platforms.

Emergency management services in Fredericksburg and Gillespie county in Texas said they were unable to receive emails and encouraged residents and partners to call instead.

Around Maryland, the Washington suburban sanitary commission, which provides safe drinking water and sewer treatment to parts of Maryland, said that its technicians may be delayed due to the outage, and some customers may have trouble making their water bill payments.

In Washington DC, congressional staffers continued to lament the outage’s impact during the lame duck session of Congress. Some told Politico that the disruptions were particularly disruptive as their offices were in the middle of negotiating pending legislation before the end of the year and planning for the next Congress.

“Shall we start conducting all official business via DM?” wrote Sharon Eliza Nichols, the director of communications for congresswoman Eleanor Holmes Norton of Washington DC.

Some school districts in Richmond, Virginia, and Port Washington, New York, also told parents on Friday morning that they were experiencing outages, and asked them to reach out by phone or through other online educational platforms to reach their child’s school, while the Albany school district said that it had restored its services.

The Colorado School of Mines encouraged “faculty to be flexible with assignment deadlines and understanding of students who cannot complete assignments due to unavailability of Microsoft tools”, though many of its systems were on unaffected platforms such as Google Workspace and Canvas.

Claude, whose developer, Anthropic, is gearing up for its upcoming stock market debut with a valuation of up to $1.4tn, also said that it was starting to see signs of recovery from the Microsoft outages, but warned that some users may still receive errors. OpenAI also said it was still investigating issues with “Microsoft connectors” that were degrading performance.

“We’re investigating an issue with Microsoft connectors where new connections may be broken and tools are not working as expected. We’ll share an update when we know more,” the company said.

On Wall Street, Workhorse Group, an industrial manufacturer, rescheduled its Q3 earnings call that was scheduled for Thursday afternoon because of the outage.

In a social media post, Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said late Thursday that “there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity”.

On Friday morning, Microsoft noted “improvements in service availability” but noted that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as a recovery continues”.

By the end of the day, most of the issues seemed to be ironed out. Schools and businesses appeared to be coming back online, congressional staffers reported “improvements to Outlook’s functionality”. The Colorado detention facility said it is “now receiving email notifications when online bond payments are made”.

And the emergency management services in Texas said they were starting to see emails trickle back in, saying: “Thanks for your patience with the worldwide outage!”

Dara Kerr and Johana Bhuiyan contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Local officials warn some services remain unavailable even as Outlook resumes normal operations. The outage started around 1pm ET on Thursday and has shaken up companies and local governments across the US.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Global oil supply returns to surplus for first time since start of Iran war, says IEA
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Lauren Almeida
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October as market shows ‘tentative signs of rebalancing’

The world’s oil supply is swinging back to a surplus for the first time since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said.

Oil supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October, the Paris-based agency said, as “Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand”.

The market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran”, the IEA reported.

It comes after months of disruption to the global oil market as the Middle East conflict blocked shipments via the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes.

The conflict has triggered a rise in energy prices this year. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, traded at about $72 a barrel in February, before the conflict began, and hit $126 a barrel by the end of April.

However, this week prices fell to their lowest level since late August, at $89.66, after the US president, Donald Trump, told reporters that the war with Iran was “effectively over”. Brent crude was trading at about $95 a barrel on Friday.

There are still concerns around continued attacks on oil tankers in the Middle East, and this week reports emerged that senior Iranian officials believe the US could be planning further military strikes.

However, the IEA said it expected global oil supply to average 105m barrels a day in the final three months of the year, 1.7m higher than forecast demand. The agency had previously expected a deficit in the fourth quarter.

The recovery in global oil supplies has also eased pressure on emergency stockpiles, which have been diminished by the Iran conflict. The IEA said its members would speed up the release of remaining emergency oil stockpiles pledged earlier this year, adding a further 71m barrels to the market by the end of February. The stocks are held in refineries, oil terminals, power stations and at offshore fields in the North Sea.

The Opec+ oil cartel said this week that it had pumped 41m barrels a day of crude in October, up from about 2m in September and at 97% of its prewar volumes.

Global oil demand is also expected to fall by 2.68m barrels a day this year to 103.2m a day, the IEA reported. Consumption is forecast to rebound next year but is still expected to remain below 2025 levels, with growth mostly in petrochemical feed stocks as the market for vehicle fuel is hit by “high prices, electrification and fuel efficiency”.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: UK tells blind Nigerian pensioner to go to India for medical treatment
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Diane Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Woman who has lived in UK for 26 years refused indefinite leave to remain under Home Office’s new settlement rules

A blind Nigerian pensioner who has lived in the UK for 26 years has been told by the Home Office she can safely go to India, a country she has never visited, for medical treatment.

Comfort*, 67, arrived in the UK in 2000, and shortly after suddenly went blind due to acute glaucoma.

After living here for 20 years, she was granted leave to remain under long residence rules. Those allowed to stay on this route have to renew their visa every 30 months for 10 years and after that can apply for indefinite leave to remain. Under the new settlement rules announced by Shabana Mahmood this week, it is likely Comfort will now have to keep renewing her visa for the next 20 years before she will finally, when she reaches her 80s, be eligible for indefinite leave to remain.

Due to her age and disability, lawyers at Refugee and Migrant Justice applied to the Home Office for her to be granted indefinite leave to remain now rather than having to wait two more decades before becoming eligible. There is a provision to fast-track indefinite leave to remain applications in exceptional circumstances.

However, the Home Office rejected this application, telling her in the first part of the letter that she could return to Nigeria because there are services there for blind people. But the refusal letter concluded: “Your circumstances are not so severe or lacking in potential treatment in India that it would warrant indefinite leave to remain in this case.”

Numerous migrants’ rights’ organisations have raised concerns about the increase in the period of time some will now have to wait for settlement here, after the home secretary’s announcement. For some, the amount of time they have to wait has increased sixfold.

According to freedom of information data obtained by Refugee and Migrant Justice, many people of pensionable age have applied for settlement but, due to their age, are likely to die before satisfying the new, more stringent Home Office wait times. One person on the Home Office data disclosure is a woman from Pakistan aged 103, who will not be eligible for settlement until she is 123 years old.

“In 2022, I got my permission to stay here based on long residence in the UK,” said Comfort. “I’m very disheartened that I may now need to wait nearly 20 years to get indefinite leave to remain.

“I have been living in this country for 26 years. I have found my home here and settled well. I have my friends, my church and do voluntary work. I’m a good citizen, not a law-breaker and am begging the Home Office to have mercy on me and grant me indefinite leave to remain now, rather than making me wait 20 more years.

“I don’t know why the Home Office said I could go back to India. It’s a country I have never visited and have no connection with.”

Nick Beales, head of campaigning at Migrant and Refugee Justice, who is supporting Comfort, said: “This woman is blind, in her late 60s and has lived in the UK for a quarter of a century. She meets the rules to remain here and there is no public interest in making her continue to renew her visa.

“Rather than viewing these vulnerable people as human beings, the government is fixated on appearing tough. Shabana Mahmood’s plans to double settlement routes will clearly make these problems even worse, especially as her decision-makers cannot even differentiate between India and Nigeria.

“Government data shows that people over 80 are applying to enter these settlement routes. While it’s unlikely many of these people would survive a 10-year period, Mahmood has not explained what she hopes to achieve by making these octogenarians and older wait two decades before having settlement. The government should admit that their earned settlement model is cruel and counter-productive and scrap these plans once and for all.”

Home Office sources said that corrective action was being taken to re-issue an updated letter to the woman.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on individual cases. All applications for permission to stay in the UK are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the immigration rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.”

* Name has been changed.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Andy Burnham urges Labour to ‘rearm’ for Kemi Badenoch comeback
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Pippa Crerar and Jessica Elgot
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
No 10 sources say PM wants party to refocus on Tories as electoral threat after prioritising Reform and Greens

Andy Burnham has instructed the Labour party to “rearm” to fight the Conservatives at the next election amid concern inside government that they must take the prospect of a Kemi Badenoch-led recovery seriously.

Downing Street sources said the prime minister wanted Labour headquarters to refocus on the Tories as an electoral threat after more than two years of prioritising Nigel Farage’s Reform and, on their left flank, the Greens.

“Andy is well aware of how volatile electoral support is. Just because the Tories are trailing in the polls now, their trajectory is upwards and they could bounce back ahead of the election. We can’t be complacent about our old foe,” one source said.

The Conservatives took 24% of the vote at the last general election, before support dipped to 18%. But last week this had risen to 25%, according to polling from More in Common, the first time in 18 months they had exceeded their vote share at the time of their record election defeat.

Many Tory MPs who had felt their party’s situation was existential, now believed they had a route back, with Badenoch finally appearing to recognise that the economy, rather than culture wars, presented her with an opportunity, especially among core supporters.

A senior Downing Street figure said Burnham did not want party officials to take their eyes off Reform – which has dipped in the polls amid ongoing scrutiny of party finances – but felt they should be planning for a potential Tory resurgence as well.

A third No 10 insider told the Guardian: “Kemi is running a party base strategy with policies aimed at higher earners, mostly in the south. It won’t be enough to win at the next election but it does put them more in contention. We need to be ready for that. We need to rearm.”

Cabinet ministers including the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, the chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, and the Europe minister Hamish Falconer have Tory-facing seats, while Labour MPs across Hertfordshire, Kent and parts of London, including Finchley and Harrow, could also be at risk.

One tactic under discussion is talking up the prospect of a Tory-Reform pact, with MPs suggesting voters would only return in earnest to the Tories if there was a genuine chance they could win a majority, but that they could stay with Labour if they were worried about Farage getting close to power.

Another is to focus on the Tory brand – including the shadow cabinet – more generally. While Badenoch’s personal ratings are relatively strong, the Conservatives overall lag way behind. Only a third of people who told More in Common they believed Badenoch was doing a good job said they would vote for her party.

Labour officials insisted that, as the Conservatives were the official opposition, they still had them in their sights day to day. But they acknowledged they needed to step up their wider strategy.

The party is understood to be preparing to devote more resources to taking on the Tories from January, in the run-up to the May elections. “We did really well at this set of elections last time, so it will be a real test point for whether the Tories have got their act together,” one said.

A group of London MPs has urged Burnham to refocus on Badenoch’s party, which in some polls has overtaken Reform into second place, warning him that Labour HQ was “getting caught out” by “obsessing” about Reform and the Greens.

One minister with a slim majority said they had been “banging this drum” inside government for a while. “It’s time to wake up about it, frankly. I think lots of my colleagues under threat from Reform have seen some of us in more traditional Tory seats as having it easy but by the next election it could be the other way around.”

One former Keir Starmer staffer said: “Every arm of the Labour party has been refocused to take on Reform; all the strategic decisions have been taken with that in mind. That can change if the party starts the work now but it does need to start properly.”

Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common, said Burnham was right to broaden the party’s focus. “Starmer was fighting on one front, but Labour now has two fronts on its right flank. They need to prepare for all outcomes,” he said.

“Reform has shown an ability to squeeze the Conservatives but it definitely has limits, so they’re definitely going to be on the pitch at the next election.”

Tryl suggested the biggest risk to Labour was “self-sorting” by voters, with Reform winning right-leaning votes from Labour in the “red wall”, while the Conservatives took them in affluent parts of England, including the south-east.

“Because of the shallow but broad nature of Labour’s support at the last election, there are more seats that could end up being Labour-Tory fights than you might think,” he said, adding that the Tories were also currently taking more votes from the Lib Dems than the other way around.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Aletha Adu political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Anneliese Midgley surprises colleagues after Burnham said whips’ office should not be ‘something to be feared’

If Andy Burnham has been accused of being a people pleaser by his critics, the same most certainly cannot be said of his chief whip.

“I’m not going to take any shit and I don’t fuck about,” said Anneliese Midgley, the Labour government’s newest head of party discipline, shedding some light on her direct approach to keeping MPs in line.

Midgley, the MP for Knowsley, who is one of the prime minister’s closest friends in government, has surprised some Labour MPs with her strikingly “frank yet glam” interview in Vogue in which she said she was determined to win. She also highlighted her unlikely journey from a deprived Liverpool housing estate via the arts world to the heart of government.

But it was her honesty in regards to being tough that caught attention from her Labour colleagues who hoped Burnham’s reign would be marked by an end to Keir Starmer’s strict party management style.

Burnham wrote to MPs back in July: “I want to create a different culture where MPs are happy and fulfilled doing their jobs, where everyone has a part to play and where opinions and approaches are respected, even where there’s difference … the whips’ office should be our HR department, not something to be feared or where discipline is used to stifle debate.”

At the time many Labour MPs, particularly those on the party’s left wing, breathed a sigh of relief – until he appointed Midgley as his chief whip, with some even going as far as saying they would be in “her bad books” because “I’m not one of her buddies she hangs and drinks with on the parliamentary terrace”.

Midgley, who worked as Jeremy Corbyn’s deputy chief of staff and Starmer’s senior special adviser, criticised the former prime minister’s approach to managing the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) and praised Burnham’s approach – a man she said she “would run through the walls for”.

On party discipline, Midgley said: “These are grown-ups who should be treated with absolute respect, who’ve got a wealth of ideas and advice – not just treated as a number to go through a voting lobby.”

When challenged on whether she thought Starmer had treated MPs “as a number”, the chief whip replied: “Yeah, I do think that.”

Despite her celebration of Burnham’s collegiate approach, Midgley told the magazine: “I’m very determined. If there’s things I want to do, I will do them. Basically, I will win,” she said, laughing, according to the magazine.

“Obviously, I said all of that stuff before about team-building, and that’s absolutely right. But like, I’m not going to take any shit and I don’t fuck about. Do you know what I mean?”

One MP described the interview as striking, not just because chief whips usually keep their heads down and far away from the spotlight, but because Midgley managed to articulate herself as an MP bringing a new era into the “dark arts” of “chief whipping”, being one that has artistic taste, fashion sense and the determination to rise from child poverty to being an influential minister.

The interview appeared to mark another way in which Burnham’s government was attempting to start a new phase in Labour politics, or simply making itself appear more human, while “scaring the shit out of the PLP”, according to one senior Labour MP.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor

Exclusive: Plans to replace key disability benefits for young people with work and training could affect adults

Downing Street is considering whether plans to replace key disability benefits with work and training for people under-25 should be expanded to older age groups, the Guardian has learned, in a move that risks reigniting Labour tensions over welfare changes.

Andy Burnham and other cabinet ministers are looking at applying the idea of “participation first” to all people of working age, meaning spending billions more on support to enter the workplace while cutting or removing some disability benefits.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The move would be politically risky given the difficulties that Keir Starmer faced in getting changes to health and disability benefits past the Labour parliamentary party last year, with a rebellion leading to a major U-turn.

The government is preparing to accept recommendations from its adviser, Alan Milburn, next week on overhauling the benefits system for young people.

In his report, Milburn will propose that under-25s should get training and support instead of the universal credit health element. Under the plans, young people with disabilities will also lose their personal independence payment (Pip) but will be able to apply to a local fund for specific short-term expenses and equipment, rather than an ongoing payment. Those with the most extreme needs who cannot work will have their entitlements protected.

This week, cabinet ministers looked at whether the arguments could be applied more broadly to over-25s, and were considering an intervention from the prime minister or Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, to make the case that the principles should apply to all. This could happen within weeks of both the Milburn review and the Stephen Timms review into disability benefits being published.

Some government sources said they believed the idea of expanding the welfare changes to over-25s would ultimately not survive given the probable backlash from some parts of Labour. Others said they believed Milburn had successfully made the case that the system needed to change and that the public were behind his efforts.

Burnham has repeatedly said the changes would not be “crude cuts”, but some backbenchers have said they are sceptical and worried about the impact on young disabled people.

If the changes were expanded to the over-25s, it could yield more savings as the cohort is much larger than the under-25s and the level of support needed to get people back into employment would probably be lower.

Ministers have said they believe any system for the over-25s would need to reflect the different circumstances of older people, many of whom had families or caring responsibilities, and more complex health needs. However, there was a belief that many of the core problems, including detachment from the workplace and a need to encourage greater participation, were the same for under- and over-25s.

A government source said: “The support offer and benefit changes Alan has set out were devised for young people and the specific circumstances they face. But the Timms review has set out that Pip is no longer fit for purpose, and the government will respond to that review when it reports.”

Milburn, a cabinet minister under Tony Blair, has promised his report is about giving billions more in support to young people to help them into work. The Guardian has learned there has been consternation within some government departments – including the Department of Health and the Department for Education – that the upfront funding for Milburn’s extra support will come from within their budgets.

Some estimates have put the cost of Milburn’s proposals at around £6bn. However, it is understood the report will not commit to a level of spending that high, even though it will provide some costings for the upfront funding needed and a trajectory for projected savings.

Milburn told the Guardian this week that the support for young people outlined in his report would create 440,000 employment and education opportunities by 2036 and raise the net incomes of young people by more than £2bn.

He said the main finding of the review was not a lack of ambition from young people but a lack of opportunities. “I have not met a single young person who wanted to be Neet [not in education, employment or training]. Not one. They want independence, they want to earn their own money and they want someone to give them a chance,” he said.

after newsletter promotion

The Guardian revealed last month that ministers were working up sweeping plans for welfare changes, including scrapping key disability benefits for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.

Charities are nervous about how the proposals will affect young people. The Joseph Rowntree Foundation said the proposals could significantly weaken the safety net for hundreds of thousands of young people with a disability or health condition, leaving many of those on universal credit living on a basic rate of support of about £80 a week.

“Cutting someone’s income when they’re already struggling to afford food or the bus to college makes it harder for them to stay in education or find work,” said Iain Porter, the charity’s senior policy adviser.

More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities have warned ministers against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people.

In their joint letter to Milburn and McFadden, they said cutting support or bringing in sanctions risked pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.

Polling suggests that while the public favours cutting the welfare bill overall, they believe that tackling the root causes of joblessness instead of cutting benefits is the best way to do it. Welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving roughly 55% of the budget, and young people, including Neets but not children, about 2.5%.

A government spokesperson said: “The Milburn and Timms reviews are due to be published shortly, and we will respond to their recommendations in full.

“We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work. But the prime minister has been clear that we need a wholesale change in the way we support young people to grow up in this country, where we invest in their success rather than paying for failure.”

Move risks reigniting Labour tensions over welfare changes. More than 40 charities warn ministers against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people. Welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving 55% of the budget.
