https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.title: The abortion doctor who leads with her faith: ‘God is forgiving’
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.author: Melissa Hellmann with photographs by Idara Ekpoh
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.text:
Dr DeShawn Taylor runs Arizona’s only Black woman-owned abortion clinic amid rapid legal changes

When gynecologist and abortion provider Dr DeShawn Taylor has conversations with patients about the afterlife, they ask her if they will be condemned for their choices. To quell their concerns, she shares with them bible verses about free will. “If God wants that vessel, that spirit to get here, God will choose another vessel. You get to say, ‘I’ll pass,’” Taylor said at her clinic one spring afternoon, her short curly hair matching the color of her maroon scrubs. “I think that makes people feel a lot better with that understanding.”

As the founder and CEO of Desert Star Institute for Family Planning in Phoenix, Arizona, Taylor heads the only Black woman-run abortion clinic in the state, which also boasts a staff of women of color. On a Tuesday in March, pop music wafted throughout the waiting room filled mostly with Black and brown women, some with their children in tow. Bilingual posters about abortion care taped to the wall reflected the diversity of the clinic’s staff and clientele. On 6 February, an Arizona judge struck down state laws requiring patients to receive an ultrasound and to wait at least a day before receiving an abortion. With abortions now more accessible, a steady stream of clients poured into the office the week that the laws were repealed. By mid-March, appointments had petered out to a more manageable about 10 services a day.

Following the supreme court’s overturning of the constitutional right to terminate a pregnancy in Dobbs v Jackson Women’s Health Organization in 2022, states have independently held the authority to regulate abortion access. In the aftermath, Arizona placed restrictions on abortions that advocates fought against in court. Two years later, Arizona voters enshrined the right to abortion in the state constitution.

Amid the rapidly changing tides of the legal system, Desert Star Institute for Family Planning – one of nine brick-and-mortar abortion clinics throughout the state – has remained at the forefront of providing abortion care and gender affirming services to a diverse client base. Taylor, along with some of her staff, are Christian women who sometimes provide support to their religious clients by joining them in prayer prior to a procedure. Taylor’s faith has undergirded her resolve in continuing to operate the clinic. “How did abortion become the one sin that you can’t repent for?” Taylor said. “Granted, I don’t think abortion is a sin, but even if you think it’s a sin, it’s still forgiven. God is forgiving already.”

In states with abortion restrictions, marginalized people are dying, said Loretta J Ross, an associate professor of the study of women and gender at Smith College. In a post-Dobbs world, people are traveling out of state or are turning to abortion pills. Taylor is “special”.

“She’s choosing to put her career and her license on the line to serve the people who have the least access, and the most need,” Ross said. “In my 50 years of working in the movement, it’s usually those doctors that have that particular passion for serving the underserved that risk … at least losing their license, and having their families attacked. In many ways, they’re the heroes of the movement.”

The clinic is also unique because, along with abortions, clients can also receive wellness exams, checkups for routine gynecological issues, and birth control. “Abortion is healthcare,” Taylor said, “so when people come to have an abortion, they should just feel like they’re at the doctor’s office.” Over the past six years, the clinic has also offered gender-affirming hormone therapy. “It’s been a struggle to keep the clinic open, and I’ve had consultants come in and try to change the model. Of course it’s less expensive to just concentrate on one thing,” Taylor said. “But if we ever did that, then why should this clinic be here? Then it becomes no different than any other abortion clinic. We’ve created something here that is very special. And patients recognize that.”

Taylor wanted to be a medical doctor since she was six years old. In middle school, she participated in a program for Los Angeles youth interested in healthcare, where she decided that she’d become a brain surgeon. But after reading the book Gifted Hands by Ben Carson while she was a sophomore at the University of Southern California, Taylor said she learned that “I didn’t believe it to be my personality, that I could do the best I can for someone and they could die anyway.” After further contemplation, she decided to dedicate her career to taking care of women. Taylor pursued a doctorate of medicine at the University of California, Los Angeles and completed a residency in obstetrician gynecology because she loved being in the operating room, she said: “What I love about it is I can actually fix people’s problems.”

As a child-free and single physician living in California, Taylor bought a home in Arizona when her mother retired there. At first it was her vacation home, but then she decided to move to Arizona to work for a statewide reproductive health organization until she founded her own clinic in 2013. Taylor, 51, ran the clinic on her own for ten years until she sold it to her nonprofit at the end of 2023 so that it could receive grants and host fundraising campaigns to foster self-sustainability. She’s also created another stream of income through speaking engagements and advisory boards, which allows the nonprofit to be less encumbered by her salary.

Through the nonprofit, she also trains future abortion providers, including residents, interns and physician assistants. Last year, the nonprofit started a birth justice hub where it convenes birth workers, abortion doulas (who provide emotional and physical support to people throughout their abortions), and activists to meet in person every four months to discuss how they can work together to support their communities. As Taylor has grown in her career, she’s butted against anti-abortion Christians who have questioned her belief system. She grew up in a spiritual, but non-religious family that sometimes visited Kingdom Halls, worship centers for Jehovah’s Witnesses, because her dad enjoyed the teachings. Taylor said: “We didn’t go knocking on doors.”

While some of her extended family were evangelicals, Taylor’s parents encouraged her to embrace her own ideologies. “I actually got baptized as an adult,” Taylor said. “My mom told me that she didn’t baptize us because she wanted us to come to that decision on our own.” Taylor’s faith didn’t initially inform her work until she realized that “this is a political issue that people religiously conscientiously object,” she said. “I call BS, because I sleep fine at night, in my Christian beliefs and providing abortion.”

But then in the spring of 2017, the anti-abortion group the Center for Medical Progress released undercover footage of Taylor at a Planned Parenthood conference. In the secretly recorded video, Taylor talked with Center for Medical Progress investigators who claimed to be buyers from a biotech company. The group edited the context of her quotes about fetal tissue being used for medical research, describing it as evidence that abortion providers possibly covered up infanticide. “That ignited me”, Taylor said. As someone who had studied the Bible, she was indignant that Christians used their faith to justify harassing her as an abortion provider. “I’m about to be a Christian provider out loud.”

When she published her book Undue Burden: A Black, Woman Physician on Being Christian and Pro-Abortion in the Reproductive Justice Movement in 2023, Taylor wanted to make a statement about the identities that she brings into her profession. “Faith and abortion is the conversation that everybody wants to have,” Taylor said. “I’m no theologian; I’m a Christian working on my own salvation.” Earlier this year, Taylor also published the workbook Beyond Choice: An Essential Workbook for Personal and Community Transformation Through Reproductive Justice. The book uses prompts, exercises and case studies to help readers connect their spiritual beliefs with reproductive choice and to stave off burnout in their political action.

A turning point for the clinic came more than seven years ago when a patient asked her if she believed in God and if she would pray for her before she received the medication for a surgical abortion. As the woman lay on the exam table, Taylor held her hand, and they both closed their eyes to pray to God aloud. Since then, patients have occasionally asked to be prayed for prior to services. “It has created safety for my patients of faith who have comfort in the knowing that their doctor also has a faith,” Taylor said. “Sixty per cent of people who have abortions have a faith, and there aren’t many providers who, one, outwardly communicate that they have a faith, and two, actually have a faith.”

While it is sometimes surprising for the public to learn that an abortion provider is religious, people of faith have long supported abortion, said Dr Carole Joffe. She’s a professor in the Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology and Reproductive Sciences at the University of California, San Francisco. Some clinics have even hired chaplains on their staff to counsel patients.

Christianity and abortion have a long intertwined history. The Catholic church accepted early-term abortions as a way to save a woman’s life until 1869, when Pope Pius IX forbade terminating a pregnancy at any stage. The narrative that many Christians are against abortion became widespread 50 to 60 years ago, after states began leading the charge in legalizing abortion.

“It was clear something like Roe was going to happen, and one of the first groups to mobilize against it was the Catholic church. They became very, very active in leading the forces opposing it,” Joffe said. Then in the late-1980s, evangelical Randall Terry founded Operation Rescue, a militant group that blockaded clinics through sit-in demonstrations. “The most high-profile opponents of abortion were very strongly associated either with the Catholic church or with the evangelical movement. But that doesn’t mean that there were no supporters of abortion.”

In 1967, six years prior to Roe v Wade, a covert group of ministers and rabbis formed the Clergy Consultation Service on Abortion to help women safely terminate pregnancies after seeing people die or be injured from unsafe abortions. The faith leaders helped an estimated 500,000 women by negotiating lower costs with doctors and referring them to abortion providers. After abortion was legalized in 1973, a new group grew out of the service, Religious Community for Reproductive Choice, where people of faith advocate for access to safe abortions by lobbying politicians and blessing abortion clinics.

What makes Taylor unique is that, along with being an abortion provider, she writes about her experiences through her books. “She’s really a spokeswoman within the African American community and beyond of what it means to be a person of faith providing this service,” Joffe said. Taylor’s role as a Black abortion provider is also significant in light of the racist origins of anti-abortion propaganda, said Regina Mahone, the co-author of Liberating Abortion: Claiming Our History, Sharing Our Stories, and Building the Reproductive Future We Deserve. The American Medical Association, composed of white male physicians, launched its first anti-abortion campaign in 1857, in part, to delegitimize midwives. At the time, Black, Indigenous and immigrant midwives provided most reproductive healthcare, including abortions. White male physicians sought to wipe out the competition of Black midwives by portraying them as unhygienic. The doctors encouraged state lawmakers to ban abortion, resulting in the creation of at least 40 anti-abortion laws in the late 19th century.

Anti-abortion sentiments in the late 1800s were “rooted and deeply tied to these racist and sexist ideas of controlling the fertility of women to preserve the numbers of white people in this country. And also continuing to control Black women’s bodies after slavery, because these physicians who are pioneering this field of obstetrics and gynecology were savagely experimenting on Black women … to heal white women’s bodies,” Mahone said. “And so it was never, and has never been about this argument about the right to life.”

The anti-abortion campaign continues to affect Arizona politics more than 150 years later. Following Dobbs, Arizona prohibited abortions past 15 weeks of pregnancy, with no exception for rape or incest. To ward off continued restrictions, Arizona voters chose to enshrine the right in their legal framework. In 2024, Arizona became one of seven states to establish abortion access as a fundamental right in its state constitution, while 13 states now have total bans on abortion.

In recent years, the American Civil Liberties Union of Arizona and Arizona healthcare providers have filed lawsuits against the state to strike down several longstanding abortion restrictions. In March 2025, a Maricopa county superior court judge lifted a ban on abortions past 15 weeks in Reuss v Arizona, ruling that the prohibition violated the 2024 constitutional amendment. Then in February 2026, a court permanently blocked the law requiring a 24-hour wait, laws prohibiting abortions for fetal conditions, as well as a ban on telemedicine in Isaacson v Arizona.

But the fight isn’t over, said former ACLU of Arizona senior staff attorney Lauren Beall. “There are many folks in the legislature who are still seeking to restrict abortion access in whatever way they can, despite the voters approving this amendment, despite a very clear message that this is not a partisan issue,” Beall said, adding that the Arizona Legislature spent more than $800k of taxpayer money to uphold abortion restrictions in Isaacson v Arizona. “The people of Arizona want a fundamental right to abortion.”

Along with being vocal about her religious beliefs, Taylor has also embraced politics in recent years. She convened the coalition Arizona Proactive Reproductive Justice Alliance, consisting of community-led groups such as the local Black Lives Matter chapter and the ACLU of Arizona, to fight abortion restrictions in the state. She and other coalition members worked with lawmakers Senator Analise Ortiz and congresswoman Sarah Liguori to draft legislation including repealing parental consent for minors seeking abortion care, though the Republican-controlled legislature has continuously stalled the bills.

As political volatility remains at play outside the clinic, Taylor’s staff and clientele view Desert Star Institute for Family Planning as a safe haven. Annie Nguyen, a 27-year-old Vietnamese woman, joined the clinic as a registered nurse last December after being inspired by Taylor’s speech about a woman’s right to choose at an abortion rally last winter. She wanted to work with a woman of color who was vocal about her beliefs.

Originally from Louisiana, one of the first states to ban abortions in 2022, Nguyen long dreamed of working as an abortion provider. She’d assisted many of her friends in accessing safe abortions by identifying other states they could travel to for their procedure or helping them pay for the service. “Ever since I was younger, I always loved the history of feminism and Roe v Wade,” Nguyen said. “I grew up in a Catholic school all my life, and it was always so frowned upon to say abortion. And so I just thought: ‘Then who can speak for these people?’”

“You can tell Dr Taylor really cares,” Nguyen said, who appreciates her patient-centered approach. “I don’t think any of our patients ever feel pressured. Dr Taylor is so good at learning every single one of her patients that walks through the door and listens to what they say. It’s their choice.”

Waiting in the consultation room, a 31-year-old Mexican American client who chose to be anonymous, said that the Black and brown staff “makes me feel more comfortable”. Another aspect of the clinic that helps people feel more at ease, said Nguyen, is that because of its secluded location, where it’s sandwiched between other businesses, there are no protesters outside.

In the spring, Elizabeth, a family medicine resident, temporarily joined the staff as part of a three-week elective at her school in another state to gain experience in abortion services. “I can tell how much it means to the patients to have quality care from people that look like themselves,” said Elizabeth, who is using a pseudonym out of fear that funding for her residency program could be jeopardized. An Asian American woman, Elizabeth said she was drawn to Taylor’s clinic for its diversity and reputation as providing a well-rounded approach to abortion care. “With all of the injustices that we’ve been seeing with ICE and immigration so far”, Elizabeth said, “it’s very important to be able to uplift our immigrant communities and let them feel that they are valued.”

The staff’s religious background, some of whom are Christian, helps them empathize with their patients. Rose Espericueta, a 29-year-old Hispanic woman, has worked as the clinic manager for five years. She decided to join the clinic to offer support to Spanish-speaking patients, since most of the clientele are Latina. A practicing Catholic, Espericueta helps provide solace to religious patients who question whether abortion aligns with their spiritual beliefs. “I always tell my patients who struggle because of their faith, there’s people doing actual crimes out here,” Espericueta said. “I don’t think God is judging you for having an abortion.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.summary: Dr DeShawn Taylor runs Arizona's only Black woman-owned abortion clinic. She is the founder and CEO of Desert Star Institute for Family Planning in Phoenix, Arizona. The clinic has also offered gender-affirming hormone therapy.

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.title: She gets 16 pelvic exams a day – so yours don’t hurt
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.author: Carmen Rising
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.text:
Molly Callahan, a gynecological teaching assistant, helps medical students practice pap smears and breast exams

On her busiest days, Molly Callahan, has 16 speculums inserted into her vagina. She works full-time as a gynecological teaching assistant (GTA) – a layperson who helps medical students practice pap smears and breast exams before they work with actual patients.

It’s not as unpleasant as you might think. In fact, the point is to help students learn how to do it without causing discomfort. Contrary to common belief, pap smears – tests that screen for cervical cancer – don’t have to be painful.

“I don’t ever really feel physically in pain even after the longest week of work,” she said. “If [your] reaction to my job is that it sounds like torture, I hope you feel scammed,” added Callahan, 30, who is also the president of an international association for GTAs and MUTAs (male urogenital teaching associates). “I hope you go fire your gynecologist.” (While students practice speculum exams with her throughout the day, she says that the actual pap smear – the collection of cells from the cervix – is a little abrasive and she “definitely could not do 16 of those in a row”.)

Pap smears have reduced cervical cancer–related deaths by 86%, but many women avoid them due to confusion around guidelines, perceived lack of symptoms and, most commonly, speculum discomfort and embarrassment. One large study of US cancer statistics data found that from 2005 to 2023, 32% of women aged 21-29, and 15% of women aged 30-65, had never had a pap smear.

The negative association isn’t surprising. Looking at the cervix for indications of cancer became more common in the early 20th century, said Dr Kirsten Gardner, director of medical humanities at the University of Texas San Antonio, and methods centered innovation over comfort.

“So much of that conversation [on pap smears] was about the medical possibilities, not about the impact on the female patient,” said Gardner. “And when it did talk about impact, it was very much in the language of early cancer detection. It was never in the language [of]: ‘How does a woman feel? Is this painful? What can we do about the pain?’”

GTAs exist in part to answer that question. Pelvic exams and pap smears were historically performed on anesthetized patients until the 1970s, when GTAs became more commonplace in an effort to improve the ethics and educational quality of such exams. While GTAs teach medical students the basics, they also provide real-time reactions and feedback.

“They center the patient’s voice,” Gardner said. “Getting an experience with the GTA just reminds practitioners that they can talk to patients.”

Currently, more than 90% of medical schools in the US and Canada utilize GTAs – Callahan, who lives in Queens, teaches at 30 universities and hospitals. But despite the flexible schedule and pay rate – almost $100 per hour – Callahan estimated that there were only about 40 GTAs in the tri-state area, where there are more than 15,000 medical students.

GTA trainees learn anatomy and the tactics of breast and pelvic exams: how to swab the cervix, check for abnormalities, find the ovaries. They practice on a qualified GTA, then each other. It requires two months of training and a final test to ensure they are able to teach the exam to medical students.

Callahan became a GTA because of her mother, an actor, director and producer who was looking for additional income when a friend suggested it. Eight years ago, Callahan, who also went to theater school, was cobbling her life together after graduation. “She was like: ‘You’d be so good at this,’ which is a strange thing for a mom to say to a daughter,” said Callahan.

One stormy evening, I went to Teaneck, New Jersey, to observe Callahan teaching two labor and delivery nursing students from Fairleigh Dickinson University. Inside a fluorescent-lit classroom, Callahan sat upright on an exam table wearing a patient gown.

“I talk a lot about preserving people’s modesty and privacy as much as possible,” she said. “But to me? No, I don’t really care. It’s just parts. It’s just my meat suit.”

Callahan spent a few hours with the students – likely their only lesson on pelvic and breast exams during school, as is common for nursing students. First, she talked them through breast exams; the students doused their hands with sanitizer and sat at the base of the table. Callahan dropped her gown and explained that since appointment times are often short, they would be focusing on the areas of the breast where malignancies are most common: the outer tissue and in the underarms. They took turns gently pressing their fingers in a circular motion on Callahan’s chest.

“Don’t tell patients they look ‘good’ or ‘perfect’,” said Callahan. “Use positive but clinical language.”

She moved on to pelvic exams, holding a small mirror so she could see their movements. The student cautiously placed the back of her hand on Callahan’s inner thigh, a gesture Callahan teaches for consent and calming the patient before proceeding.

Then Callahan issued instructions: First, place two fingers on the labia and check for redness. Gently expose the clitoral hood to check for adhesions, which can indicate infections or skin diseases, and check the vestibular glands for cysts. Insert fingers, nail side down, to gauge speculum size. Explain what you’re doing at every step; if the patient winces, you are causing pain.

A proper exam is a collaboration that begins even before the appointment starts, Callahan said. For patients, it can be helpful to know the intricacies of a pap smear and what evidence-based care looks like. Patients can read guidelines and recommendations from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) to stay informed on key information like how often to get a pap smear. There is also knowing your own body: what does your vulva look like? Do you experience pain during sex? Is your breast tissue naturally firm?

This is important because you may change providers between exams, or a provider may not remember you, Callahan said. By tracking any differences over time, “you can tell when something’s changing and not healing so you have really concrete [information]”.

One of the best things people can do is think about their own experiences with providers, especially negative ones, and identify what would make it better and more comfortable, said Callahan. Then ask for what you want at the beginning of an appointment.

“If you, the patient, know that there’s a certain part you really hate – like speculum exams are really painful – could you ask for the smallest size possible?” she said. (Speculums come in different sizes: small, medium, large and pediatric.) Larger speculums are sometimes used by default simply because “the more tissue you push away, the more you can see”, said Dr Corey Babb, medical director of the Haven Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Additionally, patients may request a blind swab, which omits the speculum, or to insert the speculum themselves.

For additional comfort, Babb said, speculums can be warmed and should be well-lubricated. Patients can also ask to be put under nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, if available.

A provider who makes you comfortable and is invested in your wellbeing is worth holding onto, Callahan said. And if the experience is negative, you can provide feedback, or file a complaint for more distressing cases.

On one of her days off, I met Callahan at Hex House, a members-only warehouse in East Williamsburg, where she sometimes conducts GTA training. In her studio, Callahan gestured toward a three-tier cart full of medical books.

“I love this one,” she said, pointing at a 1981 publication called How to Stay Out of the Gynecologist’s Office, by the Federation of Feminist Women’s Health Centers.

“Going to the gynecologist was such a nightmare [at the time]. So it guides you through doing a self-pelvic exam, how to treat yeast infections, how to do a vacuum-assisted abortion,” she said, flipping through images. “Full bush, obviously.”

Gynecology emerged in the 20th century as a male-dominated field that displaced midwives, Gardner said. In the 1950s, biologist and sexologist Alfred Kinsey conducted a study that became known as the Kinsey report. In his research, he gently stroked the cervix of patients with a cotton probe, which only 5% of 878 participants could feel. When he tried a larger object, 84% reported feeling a sensation. Yet only the former result made it into the final draft, and he concluded that the cervix was insensitive. J Marion Sims, “the father of gynecology”, practiced on enslaved women and never used anesthesia. Body parts like fallopian tubes, Bartholin’s glands and the G-spot were named after male doctors.

“They think they discovered these things,” said Callahan, who prefers location-based names, such as “uterine tubes” and “vestibular glands. “Give me a break.”

At the end of the teaching session, the two nursing students admitted that neither of them had ever experienced a slow, gentle pelvic exam themselves. Callahan put her clothes back on as the students waved goodbye.

Once home, Callahan said, she would let a hot stream of water wash away the long evening of being touched – her hips and back get stiff from all the sitting, and the work can be exhausting. It can be taxing to unteach conventions of the past.

“It’s wonderful to be a good example for all of the students,” she said. “The healthcare providers assume everyone hates this, and it’s so horrible and it’s so weird – and it doesn’t have to be that way. I think it’s really great to show them that you can treat [physical exams] with consideration and respect.”

Carmen Rising is a writer based in Brooklyn
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.summary: Molly Callahan, a gynecological teaching assistant, helps medical students practice pap smears and breast exams. Pap smears have reduced cervical cancer-related deaths by 86% but many women avoid them due to confusion around guidelines.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: How SAF successes in Sudan’s Kordofan could turn tide against the RSF
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Khartoum, Sudan – The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) gained control over several strategically important villages and localities in west Kordofan this week, shifting the war against the rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in its favour.

On Friday, the Sudanese army took control of al-Khuwai, according to local media. This is one of the main towns in West Kordofan and a strategically important site in the army’s ongoing campaign against the RSF in the resource-rich state, which began several weeks ago.

So far, the offensive by the SAF and allied Darfur forces has succeeded in breaking the RSF siege on al-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, and surrounding areas.

It has also opened up new routes for the army in central and southwest Sudan, paving the way for significant SAF advances in South Kordofan, all the way to Babnusa and the approaches to North Darfur, including an important road linking al-Nuhud, the site of gold mines, and al-Khuwai.

The RSF, alongside its alleged allies in the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdelaziz Al-Hilu, still holds al-Nuhud and parts of South Kordofan. But its recent defeats in southern and western Sudan could weaken the paramilitary’s ability to coopt tribal groups in the region.

“The RSF’s shift from attack to defence will alter its military composition, which was built on demanding rapid tribal support,” Mohamed Ali, an independent Sudanese analyst, told Al Jazeera.

“The Kordofan region is not a social stronghold for the RSF; therefore, it is expected to withdraw from the region and reposition its forces in Darfur. This would give the army a strategic advantage in Kordofan and could make Darfur the new epicentre of the conflict sooner than expected.”

The RSF’s main social and tribal support base is among the Arab communities of south and east Darfur, including areas around Nyala and el-Daein, along with border areas with neighbouring countries.

The RSF has relied heavily on mobilising tribes and civilians in areas under its control, said Mohiedeen Mohamed, an expert on Sudanese military affairs. This is particularly true when the paramilitary comes under attack from several fronts and reinforcements are desperately needed to hold the line.

But this informal coalition is also vulnerable to the changing circumstances in the war, with a number of tribal and other groups defecting from the RSF in recent weeks, as the SAF gains ground.

“When the RSF expanded into parts of the Kordofan region, it established alliances with certain tribal groups and local communities,” Mohamed told Al Jazeera.

“However, these alliances can be understood, at least in part, as arrangements driven by military and political necessity, rather than necessarily reflecting the longstanding social and historical integration.”

After the downfall of former Sudan President Omar al-Bashir in 2019, a power struggle between General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the head of the SAF, and his former ally in the RSF, Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo, emerged, developing into a nationwide conflict between the two sides in April 2023.

Fighting between the SAF and RSF has resulted in one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with about 150,000 people killed and more than 14 million of Sudan’s 53 million population displaced in the ongoing war.

Following SAF’s military successes in Khartoum and other areas, fighting has focused on the remote, impoverished but oil-rich and strategically important Sudanese provinces of Darfur and Kordofan.

The recent battles in Kordofan form part of a broader struggle over geography, economic resources, and supply routes connecting Sudan’s central regions with Darfur and beyond.

The RSF still consolidates control across all five states in Darfur, including el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, which fell to the RSF in October 2025 after a brutal siege and bloody reprisals that saw thousands of civilians killed, tortured, detained or raped.

The United Nations has identified Kordofan as the epicentre of Sudan’s conflict and said fighting in the area is complicating an already dire humanitarian situation.

Continued fighting has seen about 4.5 million civilians flee to Chad, Egypt, South Sudan, and other neighbouring countries.

Civilians are paying the highest price in the war, with drones targeting them and civilian infrastructure, including homes, schools, health facilities, power and water plants.

About 160 people were killed in drone attacks over several days in October in western regions of Sudan.

While both sides have been accused of using drones, analysts see the RSF’s use of drones as part of a wider strategy of intimidation and economic disruption, aimed at spreading fear and paralysing daily life in government areas.

“However, the military balance in Kordofan is shifting. The SAF’s growing air superiority, extensive use of drones, and changing ground tactics have enabled advances along unexpected routes, as demonstrated by the capture of Al-Khuwei,” said Mohamed. “These developments significantly reduce the RSF’s chances of regaining lost territory.”

Most humanitarian assistance operations in the region have halted due to the deteriorated security situation.

Omer Yousif, 55, a driver who works in aid delivery for an organisation called Tasami, said travelling through his native Kordofan has become an increasingly dangerous task. But he believes the humanitarian and security situation might improve if the SAF campaign in the region is successful.

“We were travelling to all of Kordofan region despite the danger because we wanted to help our people. I was captured last August by the militia and I was beaten. Some of my colleagues were tortured and killed,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Restoring the Kordofan region [to the SAF] means more aid can be delivered to both Kordofan and Darfur region.”

Al-Rasheed Mohamed, a military expert, told Al Jazeera the SAF offensive in Kordofan appears to have had some success in consolidating their gains in central Sudan, and opening a new route towards Darfur.

“Of course, the current operations along the western strategic axis are part of a broader military strategy linked to the overall plan to reclaim control of the entire country and restore Sudan’s sovereignty over every inch of its territory,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Although the advances have varied across different fronts, the overarching strategic objective remains the same – the army is now advancing and taking the initiative across these fronts, while the RSF has been pushed into a defensive position.”

Control of Kordofan also brings considerable economic and strategic benefits, with the region being rich in agricultural products, including sesame seeds, groundnuts, hibiscus and gum arabic.

It is also home to the strategically important Heglig oilfield, a major oil processing and transit hub for Sudanese and South Sudanese crude, as well as gold.

“Ultimately, restoring state control and stability across Kordofan is not merely a territorial or security objective; it is a critical economic and national sovereignty priority,” Mohamed al-Nayer, a professor of economics at the University of Sudan, told Al Jazeera.

“It would enable [the] Sudan [government] to regain control of its natural resources, revive exports, restore oil production, increase foreign currency revenues, and lay the foundations for sustainable economic recovery in the short and long term.”

Kordofan’s proximity to South Sudan also gives it control over key border crossings, trade routes, pastoral corridors and critical oil infrastructure.

Whoever controls Kordofan would thus gain significant economic leverage and strategic influence with neighbouring South Sudan.

“Kordofan’s stability is equally important to South Sudan, whose oil exports depend on transportation through Sudanese territory to Bashayer Port,” said al-Nayer.

“Both countries therefore share a strategic interest in securing oil infrastructure, protecting border areas, and restoring cross-border trade.”

Of particular importance are the area’s strategic oil fields, particularly Heglig and Balila in West Kordofan, which produce 90% of Sudan’s oil. Control over these resources also grants the government linked to the SAF added national and international significance and legitimacy.

“Securing these fields and restoring oil production would help reduce Sudan’s dependence on imported petroleum products, strengthen public revenues, and support economic recovery,” alNayer added.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Sudanese army took control of al-Khuwai, a strategically important town in West Kordofan. The region is home to the Heglig oilfield, a major oil processing and transit hub for Sudanese and South Sudanese crude.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting at APEC: What to expect
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Shola Lawal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, the White House has confirmed.

On Friday, Washington also confirmed Trump’s attendance at the summit, which will take place from November 18-19.

Talks will focus on nuclear proliferation, the White House said. But they come amid significant global turbulence: Russia’s war in Ukraine, the US-Israeli war on Iran and ongoing trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.

“I think what we’ll see is some pretty impressive photo-ops with a lot of really bombastic rhetoric from Trump,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at the UK’s Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. However, he added, the three “collectively or unilaterally, are not able to bring about an end to the conflict in Iran or Ukraine”.

So what does each side want and what will be the likely outcome?

Each leader has his own priorities, but there are some issues all will want to discuss.

A top issue for Russia and the US is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February. The treaty was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.

Russia currently possesses the largest number of warheads, followed by the US and then China, which is rapidly building up its own arsenal.

Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.

China is understood, however, to be reluctant to join an agreement it was not involved in forming.

A senior Trump administration official told Reuters this topic will start the conversation but that “we do not expect to get any kind of agreement”.

Officials also say the world leaders will discuss the Iran war, which the US and Israel launched on February 28. While full-scale strikes have, for now, ceased, the conflict remains in a deadlock.

After more than 100 days, the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed, and oil and gas prices are still volatile as ships in the strait continue to face Iranian strikes and seamines. One-third of China’s crude oil supply transited the strait before the war. The conflict is also hampering demand for Chinese exports.

Russia, meanwhile, has profited from rising energy prices and recent sanctions relief from Washington amid supply crunches – particularly of diesel.

Trade wars and the race to control microchips used to power artificial intelligence are straining relations between Beijing and Washington.

Trump hit China with a 145 percent tax hike last year, while Beijing retaliated by imposing 125 percent levies on US imports. Tensions mounted further over China’s restrictions on exports of rare earth minerals needed to manufacture advanced chips and other technology.

The two countries have since reduced tariffs and struck several deals following Trump and Xi’s meetings in South Korea and Washington However, the recent scandal at chip firm Nvidia has prompted the US to allege that China was spying on CEO Jensen Huang. Beijing denies this.

It is very unlikely. A Trump administration official told reporters the US president will not bring up Russia’s war on Ukraine, although Kremlin officials previously suggested the conflict could be discussed.

China, an ally of Moscow’s, has said the Ukraine war is a European issue.

US officials also note that Washington is pursuing peace talks, with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visiting both Ukraine and Russia this week. “China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” an official told reporters.

President Trump has accused Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of “not wanting” to end the war, while Kyiv has reiterated allegations that the US has restricted its Starlink satellite connection that allows it to operate attack drones. Trump has also blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices because of its strikes on Russian oil facilities.

At the same time, Trump has feted Putin, agreed to allow Russian diesel into global and US markets, and lifted oil sanctions on Moscow.

For President Putin, the meeting could provide a positive photo opportunity and a platform to project power while sidelining the Ukraine conflict, analysts say.

It will give him a “first among equals” position that he can display at home to show that he can influence Europe’s security architecture following the Ukraine war, Alexander Bratersky, a Moscow-based journalist and political analyst, told Al Jazeera.

Beijing has already been pushing for a resolution to the US war on Iran, which has impacted its own energy supplies.

China will also want to avoid being pulled into a nuclear treaty it had no part in establishing.

Last month, China’s Foreign Ministry said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.

Trump’s priority is to include both China and Russia in a new nuclear proliferation treaty, according to administration officials. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told reporters.

The president could also use the meeting to project his administration’s diplomatic influence, as Iran refuses to capitulate to US demands for ending the war and hand Washington a win.

Trump has also sought closer ties with Xi, Putin and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, all seen as “strongmen”, and is likely to be perceived as influential in such circles, analysts say.

“I think it will be more performative – Donald Trump playing global statesman rather than peacemaker,” said Mabon.

Trump’s Republican Party’s crushing defeat in midterm elections last week could undermine his leverage, experts note, as a new Democrat-led Congress is likely to support Ukraine more staunchly.

Pyotr Tolstoy, chairman of the Russian parliament’s foreign affairs committee said it could lead to a “new Yalta”.

The 1945 conference in Yalta, in the then Soviet Union, saw USSR President Joseph Stalin, the US’s Franklin D Roosevelt, and the United Kingdom’s Winston Churchill divide Germany and establish the United Nations in what was seen as the template for a new world order.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, called the trilateral meeting now taking place between the leaders of the US, China and Russia as “extremely significant” but pointed out that any agreements reached at the meeting cannot be imposed on other nations.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Trump, Xi Jinping and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's Shenzhen. Talks will focus on nuclear proliferation, but they come amid significant global turbulence.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Three killed in Russia as Ukraine claims US floated NATO membership option
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
A Ukrainian drone attack has killed a mother, father and their 24-month-old daughter at their home in Belgorod, a Russian region bordering Ukraine, according to Russian authorities.

The deadly attack came on Saturday in Proletarsky, about 20km (12 miles) from Ukraine’s border as Russia’s Ministry of Defence claimed the army intercepted 29 Ukrainian drones overnight, including several over the Moscow region.

In turn, Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched 96 drones from Friday evening, of which 81 were shot down or electronically suppressed as of early Saturday. It reported hits at eight locations and falling debris at two others, while a local power supplier reported outages in parts of northeastern Sumy.

Meanwhile, in Friday’s comments to reporters that were under embargo until Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said United States negotiators had asked during this week’s Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, the transatlantic military alliance.

Zelenskyy said the question had been raised for the first time but that no concrete offer existed. Zelenskyy maintained that Ukraine would not withdraw its troops but could put the issue to a referendum if Kyiv received firm security guarantees, funding for its armed forces and money for reconstruction.

“NATO is back on the agenda,” he said.

Donbas comprises Donetsk and Luhansk, two eastern Ukrainian regions partly occupied by Russia.

Moscow demands a Ukrainian withdrawal from areas Kyiv still controls, while also opposing Ukraine joining NATO, whose members pledge to defend one another.

Zelenskyy said on Friday that he would not amend Ukraine’s constitution to make it neutral, arguing the move would not guarantee lasting security.

Ukraine has been defending itself, with Western assistance, against a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022.

This past week brought a resumption of US-mediated direct talks between the Russians and Ukrainians, which raised hopes of an early end to the war.

However, apart from renewed prisoner exchanges, there appears to have been little progress. European representatives are set to take part in the next round of talks.

Zelenskyy said the European Union and NATO are Europe’s “only real security” and that Moscow’s bid to review the continent’s security was “dangerous because … it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Eight sentenced to jail over Nurmagomedov-Dvalishvili Abu Dhabi hotel brawl
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Manasi Pathak
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
The Abu Dhabi Criminal Court has convicted 10 people over a mass brawl ⁠involving mixed ⁠martial artists Usman Nurmagomedov, Merab Dvalishvili and their teammates at a hotel.

The brawl broke out ahead of a wrestling event organised ⁠by Real American Freestyle (RAF), where Usman Nurmagomedov’s brother Umar and Dvalishvili were scheduled for matches against different opponents.

“An Abu Dhabi court has convicted 10 defendants in connection with a brawl ‌inside a hotel and has sentenced them to six months’ imprisonment … along with deportation from the country,” read the announcement from the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department on Friday.

ESPN reported that six members of Team Nurmagomedov were sentenced to six months in prison, fined 300,000 dirhams (approximately $81,600) and ordered to be deported after serving their sentences.

According to Abu Dhabi-based The National newspaper, former UFC bantamweight ⁠champion Dvalishvili and a friend were fined 50,000 dirhams ($13,600) for “disturbing public security and assaulting others”.

Two additional people were handed six-month prison sentences for privacy violations after they filmed the ⁠brawl and published the footage online, the reports added. The court also ordered the confiscation of their phones and deletion of the footage.

The brawl broke out on Wednesday when Georgian Dvalishvili, who was scheduled to appear at RAF Abu Dhabi on Saturday, was being interviewed in the lobby of the Yas Hilton.

PFL lightweight champion Usman – the cousin of retired MMA legend Khabib Nurmagomedov – and his associates approached Dvalishvili. Videos shared online showed ‌Usman coming in from behind and slapping Dvalishvili, which started the melee.

Usman was not scheduled to feature at the RAF Abu Dhabi card but travelled to the UAE capital to accompany his older brother, Umar, who was scheduled to face Urijah Faber.

Later on Friday, the event organisers removed Umar from the card, replacing him ‌with ‌Saba Lazishvili, Dvalishvili’s friend who was also involved in the brawl.

RAF cofounder Chad Bronstein said Dvalishvili has been released from custody. He remains available for his scheduled match with Marlon Moraes.

“I’m pleased to share that Merab Dvalishvili is back with us in Abu Dhabi,” Bronstein said in a statement. “We would like to express our sincere appreciation to the relevant authorities in Abu Dhabi for their professionalism and support.”

Dvalishvili posted several videos on social media after the incident and released his personal statement on X, saying: “Just want to let everyone know I have been released, and I am good, healthy and ready to go.

“I want to thank everyone in Abu Dhabi for your help in resolving this matter … I do hope that they release everyone; I would not press charges. I want peace and the best for all,” he added.

Wednesday’s incident wasn’t the first time Dvalishvili and Team Nurmagomedov clashed. Tensions also escalated in January last year after Dvalishvili defeated Usman’s older brother Umar in a UFC bantamweight title fight. They also had a smaller altercation at an RAF event in Georgia in July.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Abu Dhabi Criminal Court has convicted 10 people over mass brawl in hotel brawl. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Ukraine, Russia race to build military satellite networks as war rages on
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Mansur Mirovalev
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Kyiv, Ukraine – Looking like a tiny desktop tower with wing-like solar panels, the Obria Nano satellite is a small step that could herald a giant leap for Ukraine’s military.

Launched by Himera, a Ukrainian company known for ergonomic military radios, and GomSpace, a Danish small-satellite manufacturer, the first Obria Nano could eventually grow into Kyiv’s own constellation of military satellites, its creators hope.

The nanosatellite marks Ukraine’s “first historical step toward establishing resilient and sovereign satellite communications capabilities,” the company said on October 27, almost four weeks after the Obria Nano had reached orbit.

In mid-October, Kyiv also signed up two Finnish companies, the Nokia telecoms giant and the ICEYE space startup that owns a “self-illuminating” radar technology for obtaining high-resolution satellite imagery in any weather, to look into developing a network of military satellites.

Kyiv’s efforts are rooted in one concern – the nearly total dependence of Ukraine’s military communications on SpaceX, Elon Musk’s satellite communications giant that operates Starlink, a constellation of more than 10,000 low-orbit satellites.

On Thursday, the speeds of Starlink and Starshield, its military component operated by the Pentagon, were limited for Ukraine, leading to “significant disruptions” of their operation along the front line, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Before this, Starlink was also disrupted last month.

Kyiv realises that “it’s possible to create an absolutely new system, but it will take several years,” Anatoly Zak, a US-based space expert, told Al Jazeera. “In the nearest year or two, Starlink and [its military-grade component] Starshield are absolutely necessary.”

Since 2022, Ukraine developed a love-and-hate relationship with Musk, his volatility, shifting loyalties and political demands.

“Musk’s mood swings play a significant role,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “There were times when Musk helped Ukraine, and times of very negative reactions.”

Ukrainians hailed Musk’s decision to provide Starlink services and modems to Ukraine free of charge. The military, hospitals and government agencies operating critical infrastructure quickly made a backbone of their communications.

But in late 2022, Musk refused to activate Starlink coverage in Russia-occupied areas, slowing down or stopping Ukraine’s successful counteroffensive.

The world’s wealthiest man also said that Kyiv should remain “politically neutral” in the future, officially cede Crimea to Moscow and conduct United Nations-supervised referendums on Russia-occupied territories.

“If you want to understand what Russia has done here, come to Ukraine and you will see it all for yourself,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in response. “And then you will tell me how to end this war, who started it and when it can be ended.”

Meanwhile, Russia has reportedly smuggled thousands of Starlink terminals and used them for comms and drone attacks. This February, Musk put an end to the practice by allowing only certified modems to operate in Ukraine.

Kyiv’s attempts to find an alternative to Starlink followed the October 14-24 speed limits for Ukrainian drones imposed without prior warning by Starlink and Starshield.

Drones and drone interceptors moving faster than 60km/h (37mph) lost signal and could no longer reach their targets.

Musk accused the Pentagon of limiting the speed and admitted that the decision was his only after The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk had personally authorised the slowdown.

Both Musk and Kyiv realise that Starlink and Starshield are the Ukrainian military’s survival tool.

When it comes to his highly publicised position towards Ukraine, Musk has to balance his own emotional outbursts and the interests of SpaceX, the crown jewel of his business empire that comprises two-fifths of his net worth, analyst Fesenko said.

“If he tries to throw Ukraine under the bus, it may work as very negative advertising for his business, including the Starlink system,” Fesenko said.

Another factor is Russian President Vladimir Putin’s calculated flattery towards Musk – on October 28, he called him a “real genius”.

“Putin apparently wants to use the methods he’s used towards [US President Donald] Trump – flattery, unlimited flattery,” Fesenko said.

Putin mentioned Musk while talking about Russia’s attempts to create its own version of Starlink.

“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it’s very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.

The attempts have not been very successful so far.

The military satellites for the upcoming Rassvet (Dawn) constellation turned out to be Qianfan satellites, which are similar to first-generation Starlink satellites and manufactured in China.

Bureau 1440, a Kremlin-controlled space company that runs the Rassvet system, plans to have 900 satellites in orbit by 2035.

In August, the Institute for the Study of War, an international military think tank, claimed that more than a third of Rassvet satellites failed to reach “sustainable operational altitudes”.

By early November, Moscow lost two of the 32 Rassvet 3 satellites launched in the past seven months.

The second satellite that burned in the Earth’s atmosphere on November 1, failed to launch its propulsion to correct its position, according to The Defence Express, a Ukrainian military publication.

Ukraine can also try negotiating a switch to Starlink’s rivals, but they are smaller and less effective.

The US-based Iridium has 66 satellites flying at about 800km (497 miles) above Earth.

OneWeb, operated by the French Eutelsat company, has up to 650 satellites that orbit the Earth at 1,200 kilometres (746 miles). But it is not authorised to be used for military drone strikes.

An average terminal in Ukraine sees five dozen Starlink satellites simultaneously – and only 11 OneWeb satellites. A light, compact Starlink terminal costs up to $500; a much heavier and bulkier OneWeb one costs $9,000.

According to Pavel Luzin, a space and military analyst with the Jamestown Foundation, a think tank in Washington, DC, Kyiv has two options to get its own satellites.

It could work towards heavy and pricey satellites in geosynchronous orbit – or Earth-centred – that could serve for up to 20 years and cover all of Ukraine’s military needs.

Or option two is a focus on launching a system of hundreds of cheaper low-orbit satellites that will need propulsion engines to maintain position, but they will eventually fall down because of contact with the upper atmosphere, and will constantly need to be replaced, he said.

Kyiv can also use much cheaper alternatives such as stratostats or stratospheric drones that serve as “quasi-satellites,” he told Al Jazeera.

A satellite fleet necessary to provide coordinates to long-range drones makes each drone strike pricier, and AI-driven drones that can be “taught” to recognise their targets could bring the price down – and make the satellites unnecessary.

The development of ballistic missiles is another alternative, because they do not need satellite connection but can cause damage equal to the boom from several drones that have gotten through Russia’s air defence system, he said.

“Such decisions are made with all calculations considered, not because Starlink – that depends on current political trends in Washington – needs to be replaced with an alternative,” Luzin said.

“I don’t rule out that Ukraine won’t have to create any alternatives, because SpaceX is definitely interested – even if someone in the company doesn’t realise that – in Ukraine using it further,” he said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: South Sudan postpones first-ever national elections until February
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
South Sudan has delayed its first-ever presidential and parliamentary elections until February, the latest in a series of delays to the long-sought vote, as ethnic and political tensions deepen.

The country’s election commission announced on Saturday that the polls would be held on February 11 next year, instead of December 22 this year. It did not give any reason for the decision.

The world’s youngest country, which continues to grapple with violence despite a 2018 peace deal that ended five years of civil war, has delayed the vote at least three times since setting 2022 as its election year.

In September, South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government and appointed a caretaker administration. That step allowed the country to move towards elections without first completing a permanent constitution or census – two processes that were previously tied to the transition.

But analysts and watchdogs warned that move dismantled a key power-sharing arrangement, consolidating power in Kiir’s hands and raising the risk of renewed widespread conflict.

“This amounts to a constitutional coup through legislative reforms,” Yasmin Sooka, chair of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, said in October.

“Whether elections take place or not, South Sudan will still need an inclusive political settlement, protection for civilians and institutions capable of preventing further violence,” she added.

Kiir’s government forces and followers of detained former Vice President Riek Machar have been involved in escalating, deadly confrontations in recent months.

Other ethnic tensions and cattle-rustling battles have also complicated the picture in one of the world’s poorest countries.

South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011, but Kiir’s and Machar’s forces fought a civil war from 2013 to 2018 that killed at least 400,000 people.

Machar has been under house arrest since last March, accused of crimes against humanity.

Under the new election timetable, voter registration is due to begin on Saturday, November 14 and continue until November 28.

A 45-day election campaign period will run from December 27 to February 9, followed by a one-day silence period before the February 11 poll.

Gabriel Bol Deng, chairman of the National Elections Commission, said a total of 3,161 registration centres have been set up across the country, with more than 22,000 staff recruited for the operation.

According to the World Bank, about 90 percent of South Sudan’s 15 million inhabitants have no state-recognised identification, complicating their registration.

Such people, particularly in rural areas, will be identified by community leaders and issued an “identification form” enabling them to vote, Deng said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: South Sudan has delayed its first-ever presidential and parliamentary elections until February. The country’s election commission announced on Saturday that the polls would be held on February 11 next year. The world’Sudan has delayed the vote at least three times since setting 2022 as its election year.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Sabalenka crashes out of season-ending WTA Finals after losing to Svitolina
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Elina Svitolina overwhelmed Aryna Sabalenka in the deciding set to seal a ⁠6-3, 3-6, 6-1 upset on Friday and reach the semifinals of the season-ending WTA Finals in Indian Wells, where she will face Linda Noskova.

Svitolina absorbed and redirected Sabalenka’s power effectively, breaking the ⁠Belarusian six times before sealing her first victory over her opponent in more than six years with a forehand winner on her fourth match point.

With the win, Svitolina improved to 2-6 against Sabalenka in their career meetings.

“It was a bit of a roller-coaster match,” Svitolina told reporters.

“I played well in ‌the first set but lost a little bit of rhythm. She played well in the second and served much better. I was really happy with the way I could come back in the third after losing the first game.”

The Ukrainian again did not shake hands with Sabalenka after the match, maintaining her policy of not doing so with Russian and Belarusian players following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Svitolina, the 2018 WTA Finals champion, will face Noskova on ⁠Saturday for a place in the final.

The defeat ended Sabalenka’s season ⁠on a disappointing note.

The second seed won Brisbane International in January and then Indian Wells and the Miami Open in March to complete the “Sunshine Double” but did not claim another title after that.

Sabalenka also surrendered the world number one ⁠ranking to Elena Rybakina at the US Open.

She had entered the season finale among the favourites after Rybakina withdrew on the eve of ⁠the tournament because of illness.

Sabalenka declined to speak to the ⁠media following Friday’s loss.

Earlier in the day, tournament debutant Andreeva continued her impressive run with a 6-2, 6-1 win over fellow Russian Diana Shnaider, her third straight-sets victory of the week.

Shnaider, Andreeva’s friend and doubles partner, replaced Karolina Muchova, who ‌withdrew before the final day of round-robin matches with a gastrointestinal illness.

Andreeva had already secured her place in the semifinals before facing Shnaider and will meet American Jessica Pegula on Saturday.

The eight-day, $10m ‌tournament was moved from Riyadh to Indian Wells Tennis Garden due to the United States-Israeli war on Iran. The event will be played in Charlotte starting next year.

Svitolin will face Linda Noskova in the final on Saturday. The Ukrainian will face the Russian on Saturday for a place in the semifinals.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Netanyahu may fall, but his far-right legacy in Israel is going nowhere
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Simon Speakman Cordall
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
As Israel’s opposition looks to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, speculation has centred on the possible fate of the current government’s more hardline, right-wing elements, including the parties led by the unapologetically pro-settler Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, convicted of inciting terrorism.

While all members of Netanyahu’s cabinet, with the unflinching backing of the opposition politicians hoping to supplant them, have supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and attacks on regional states, it is Smotrich and Ben-Gvir who have been the focus of international attention and lightning rods for criticism by Western governments.

With talk of Netanyahu looking to form a unity government with Eisenkot, both ministers have publicly opposed a government led by the former chief of staff.

In the run-up to the vote, Ben-Gvir took the unusual step of claiming that Netanyahu now has a choice of selecting himself to “save Israel”, or Eisenkot.

Smotrich, meanwhile, has warned his ultra-Orthodox political allies against entering negotiations with Eisenkot, saying he will “dump them” once he uses their votes to oust Netanyahu.

Netanyahu formed a coalition government with Ben-Gvir’s far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) and Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party in 2022, giving both several of Israel’s most important cabinet positions. Smotrich became finance minister, granting him control over the Israeli budget and a number of institutions in the occupied West Bank, while Ben-Gvir was named national security minister.

Drawing on a wellspring of hardline Zionism, Jewish supremacy and what critics describe as unapologetic racism, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have exploited their political leverage to advance Israel’s most hardline policies over the past three years. They have also transformed their ministries to reflect their hardline ideological projects.

Both have been enthusiastic proponents of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, repeatedly threatening to withdraw their support from the government when it appeared Netanyahu might falter in the face of international pressure about the huge number of civilians killed, famine, and withholding of aid.

In September 2025, Ben-Gvir threatened to bring down the government if Hamas remained in existence following the release of the captives under United States President Donald Trump’s proposed Gaza plan. Both ministers have repeatedly called for the annexation, settlement and ethnic cleansing of Gaza.

Smotrich has encouraged the expansion of illegal settlements within the West Bank and, in the eyes of his opponents, bears culpability for the explosion of settler violence and pogroms across the occupied territory.

In June 2025, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir were sanctioned by a wave of Western countries. Ireland and the Netherlands imposed travel bans on the two ministers, while other countries froze their assets. Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin said these measures were taken due to their shared “desire to see the elimination of Palestinians from Palestine”.

However, analysts said the ministers and their movements should not be treated as a homogeneous entity or be isolated from Israeli policy in general.

“I would argue that we should not treat Ben-Gvir and Smotrich as a single bloc, since exclusion from government would affect them in opposite ways,” Arie Perliger, of the University of Massachusetts Lowell, who has led studies into the far right in Israel, Europe and the US, told Al Jazeera. “Ben-Gvir’s power is populist and performative, and opposition suits him.”

Ben-Gvir’s roots in the outlawed Kahanist movement had, in tandem with many right-wing movements, relied upon their historical exclusion from power as evidence of a betrayal by the establishment, he added.

Smotrich, meanwhile, had used his position as finance minister to co-opt part of the settlement programme and force through his explicitly Zionist agenda. This means he would have more to lose if he were “cut off from budgets, portfolios and control over settlement policy”.

“Smotrich’s case is the reverse. His achievements were bureaucratic rather than rhetorical,” Perliger said.

Both figures have been accused of transforming their ministries in ways that will linger long after they leave government.

As part of the 2022 deal with Netanyahu that secured his finance portfolio, Smotrich was given the additional role as a minister in the Ministry of Defence. This gave him sweeping powers over much of the occupied West Bank’s Israeli-led civilian administration.

From there, he used his position to establish a separate Settlement Administration and to rapidly accelerate illegal settlement expansion across the occupied territory. In August 2025, he announced the revival of the E1 settlement plan, which he boasted would bury “the idea of a Palestinian state”.

Ben-Gvir has been accused of rapidly politicising the Israeli police force under his command and essentially fashioning it to mirror his own hard-right outlook. He has also introduced sweeping changes to the prison service, including severe restrictions on the conditions and rights of Palestinian prisoners, whose institutional legacy could last for years.

“These are personnel, procedures and facts on the ground and reversing them requires sustained political will,” Perliger added. He is sceptical that an opposition government would override the changes introduced by the ministers.

Ejecting the pair from the mainstream of Israeli politics was also unlikely to dent support for the groups, according to Roi Zur, an assistant professor in the Department of Government at Essex University.

Smotrich’s Religious Zionist movement goes back to the war of 1967 and, together with Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit, has the support of about 10 percent of the Israeli electorate.

“They are stable and will be there for many years … [They] cater to very similar kinds of people in Israel,” Zur told Al Jazeera.

Their lasting legacy may be the official sanction of hatred towards Palestinians which, long festering, exploded in the wake of the Hamas-led October 7 attacks. Through their actions, and those of other right-wing members of Netanyahu’s coalition, the value of Palestinian lives in the eyes of Israelis has sunk to unprecedented lows.

The widely publicised killing of more than 74,000 people in the genocidal war on Gaza, the willful neglect of Palestinian townships within Israel’s borders, where crime and murder have become a virtual epidemic, and the brutal conditions imposed on Palestinian prisoners have not been hidden so much as celebrated. Ben-Gvir was a leading figure in the passage through the Knesset of a death penalty law that solely targets Palestinians.

Meanwhile, the pogroms against Palestinians and their property across the occupied West Bank have continued without any meaningful government sanction.

“Violence is a constant danger,” said Aida Touma-Suleiman, the Palestinian former member of parliament for the left-wing Hadash party. “People are scared on the street, on the bus, everywhere. You have to be careful just to speak Arabic, wherever you are.”

Under the most recent Netanyahu government, apartheid against Palestinians, which had long existed in Israel, had become engrained and a version of fascism, Touma-Suleiman said.

“Apartheid is a series of laws that discriminate on the basis of race. Fascism is when the discrimination and the racism are carried in the soul,” she told Al Jazeera.

“Netanyahu and his allies haven’t just given permission to be racist; they’ve made it almost proof of patriotism – it’s expected.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir have been the focus of international attention. Both ministers have been enthusiastic proponents of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. They have been accused of transforming their ministries in the past three years.
