SpaceX succesfully launched its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:47 p.m. EDT (2247 GMT) from Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land its Ship upper stage for the first time, but did abort a landing pad catch of its Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever recovery of an orbital Starship upper stage, if successful. See launch video above and live views from SpaceX.

Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which also deployed 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.

Flight 15 landing livestream | Flight 15 video | SpaceX | Starship

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

Good morning and happy Saturday, Space Fans! Today is Flight Day 2 for SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight and SpaceX reports that its Ship 42 spacecraft is in good health as we near the 14-hour mark of its 22.5-hour test flight.

About 7 hours into the mission, SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot confirmed that flight controllers gave the go-ahead to forgo an early return window for a splashdown off the coast of Chile and proceed for the full 14-orbit flight. Starship is on track for a landing attempt, its first-ever from orbit, today (Nov. 14) at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT). Space.com's livestream of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 landing will begin at 2 p.m. EST and you can see it at the top of this page.

"Starship's going to stay in space. We are one step closer to an eventual return to launch site," Huot said in the update. "So that's great news."

Huot also reported that Starship's tile-covered heat shield appears in good shape for today's landing attempt. SpaceX used long-range ground-based cameras and cameras on some of the 26 Starlink satellites the Ship deployed to check its heat shield after liftoff.

"Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a re-entry and return to the launch site," Huot said.

Huot also said it was likely a guidance and navigation control issue that caused the Booster 22 Super Heavy first stage to abort its landing attempt after liftoff on Friday. The giant booster plunged into the Gulf of Mexico instead of making a landing patch catch at Starbase, Texas.

The next "early return" check will come about 20 hours into the mission, around 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT), when flight controllers will have to decide for hte last time whether to press ahead with the landing attempt or send Starship to a splashdown off the coast of Hawaii.

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft Ship 42 is flying over Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean as it continues its long coast 260 kilometers above Earth.

You can actually try to spot Starship in the night sky using our guide here.

SpaceX's livestream is showing the position of the spacecraft, giving you an idea of where and when to look. You should be fast though, as Starship is moving at about 26,442 km/hour.

If you do see Starship in the night sky, let us know! Send us a note on what you saw and your photos here: spacephotos@space.com.

SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 Ship vehicle has successfully deployed all 26 Starlink satellites and has now entered an extended coast phase of its mission that should last well into tomorrow. Here's our launch wrap with video and photos from Josh Dinner at the launch site.

The Ship 42 spacecraft deployed all 26 Starlink V3 internet satellites by the 1-hour, 17-minute mark of the mission.

Flight controllers then decided to forgo an "early return" option to land Starship early with an ocean splashdown off the coast of Hawaii. The option, at the 90-minute mark of the flight, is the first of three "early return" options fopr Starship in case something goes wrong.

So far, Ship 42 is performing well in orbit. The next early-return checkpoint is about 7.5 hours into the mission, which will occur around 1 a.m. EST (0600 GMT).

"That means this is now going to be the longest Starship mission we've ever flown," SpaceX's Dan Huot said. "We're going to surpass the point that we had to come home on Flight 14. So that's already exciting."

Huot and other SpaceX commentators will return in a few hours with a status update. So for now, Starship is just coasting in space.

It's been one hour since SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch and Starlink satellite deployment is underway.

So far, the Ship 42 upper stage has deployed 12 of 26 Starlink V3 internet satellites, with more popping out of its Pez-dispenser like payload bay every few minutes.

Ship is flying over a brilliant blue Earth, with the camera views from the spacecraft relayed to Earth via SpaceX's Starlink satellite constellation.

SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 Ship upper stage has begin deploying its 26 Starlink internet satellites into orbit.

Three satelllites have already been deployed, with the Ship performing a slow rotation to allow the cameras on one of the Starlinks capture imagery of the spacecraft's heat shield.

"It will be about 40 minutes all told to get these satellites out the door," SpaceX's Dan Huot says.

SpaceX's Ship 42 has successfully performed its orbital insertion burn and is now orbiting the Earth. It is only the second time SpaceX has reached orbit with Starship. The first time was September's Starship Flight 14 test mission.

"We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX’s Dan Huot says. "That’s a really great moment."

The next major milestone will be Starlink satellite deployment, which should start at the 35-minute mark and last about one hour.

Here's our full guide and Starship Flight 15 mission timeline for the full 22.5-hour mission.

SpaceX's next big milestone after today's mostly successful Starship Flight 15 launch with be orbital insertion, when the Ship will fire up a Raptor engine to enter orbit around Earth.

That engine burn is scheduled for about 26 minutes after liftoff and will last about 20 seconds.

"We are go for orbit," SpaceX's Dan Huot says.

If all goes to plan, Ship 42 should end up in an orbit about 275 kilometers above Earth and spend up to 22 hours orbiting Earth 14 times before returning to Earth tomorrow.

Deployment of the 26 Starlink V3 satellites in Ship's payload bay is scheduled to begin at the 35 minute mark.

SpaceX's Booster 22 has splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico after it aborted the planned launch pad catch. It was unclear the exact cause of the landing catch abort.

"We'll dig in to what caused that abort during its flight back to the tower," SpaceX's Dan Huot says.

The Ship upper stage, meanwhile, successfully completed its ascent and has shut down its 6 Raptor engines. It is now in orbit, with the payload deployment of 26 Starlink satellites to come next.

The Starship Flight 15 Super Heavy Booster 22 has successfully separated from the Ship upper stage and is beginning its return to Earth. One of its 33 engines may have dropped out, but its upcoming 13-engine boost back burn is coming up.

Ship 42 is continuing its ascent with all 6 engines firing.

LIFTOFF! SpaceX launches its Starship Flight 15 test flight on the company's first-ever attempt to land both Super Heavy and Ship!

Fueling is now complete for Starship flight 15, SpaceX's Dan Huot reports.

SpaceX is now less than 5 minutes away from its Starship Flight 15 launch at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT). Fueling will end in about 2 minutes.

"T-5 minutes and we are tracking no issues," SpaceX's Dan Huot said. "We have no holds on the board right now."

SpaceX is expected to be chilling down its 33 Raptor engines on the Super Heavy first stage on the Starship Flight 15 rocket.

The fueling process is ongoing and will continue until just over 2 minutes to liftoff.

The launch remains on track for 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT).

SpaceX just revealed that YouTube icon Mr. Beast has put his personal touch on today's Starship Flight 15 launch. He installed a heat shield tile on part of the spacecraft, and it's verified all set for launch.

A reminder, too, that SpaceX is launching 26 Starlink V3 internet satellites on Flight 15. They will be deployed in orbit by the 90-minute mark after launch.

Today, the heatshield tile that @MrBeast installed flies to space https://t.co/e5D82pYy0BNovember 13, 2026

SpaceX has officially begun fueling its massive Starship Super Heavy Booster 22 and Ship 42 for today's Flight 15 test launch. Liftoff is on track for 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT).

The Super Heavy and Ship require nearly 12 million pounds of liquid oxygen and liquid methane for launch.

Super Heavy Booster 22 will be the first V3 Starship booster to attempt a landing, though SpaceX has performed the feat several times before. Ship 42 will be the first upper stage to attempt a landing when it returns to Earth on Saturday.

"We are not currently tracking any technical issues, any range issues and definitely no weather issues for today," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said.

SpaceX has a new launch time for Starship Flight 15 today. It is two minutes later than previously announced.

Liftoff is now set for 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT). SpaceX has a 75-minute launch window for today's test flight.

SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 livestream has begun at the T-45 minute mark for today's launch. Liftoff is still targeted for 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT).

SpaceX does have a 75-minute window for today's launch, assuming it is not affected by the FAA groundstop to aircraft nationwide.

SpaceX has given the "go" to begin the fueling processes for Starship.

"Go for propellant load. Teams will soon begin loading Starship with ~12 million pounds of liquid oxygen and liquid methane," SpaceX reported in a launch update.

SpaceX is now T-1 hour and counting to the planned launch of its SpaceX Starship Flight 15 test flight and our launch livestream will begin soon. Liftoff is on track for 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT).

One thing that has happened in the last few hours: The FAA has issued a rare national groundstop for all aircraft due to a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," Sean Duffy, Secretary of Transportation, said in a social media post. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue."

It is unclear if the groundstop will affect the reentry plans for Starship Flight 15, given the recent FAA approval for the launch.

SpaceX says it's still on track: "On track for Starship’s 15th flight. The 75-minute launch window opens at 4:45p.m. CT. Live coverage of the mission begins ~42 minutes before launch.," the company wrote on X.

SpaceX is officially "go" to proceed with its Starship Flight 15 launch attempt today (Nov. 13). The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) gave the green light this afternoon — pretty late in the game for an approval to come in.

Flight 15 is scheduled to launch during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). You can watch here at Space.com, starting at 5 p.m. EST (2200 GMT).

The test flight will make history, if all goes according to plan: SpaceX plans to catch both of Starship's stages back at the Starbase launch site using the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something that has never been done before. The booster catch will come just 6.5 minutes after launch, while the upper-stage snag is scheduled for Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), after 22.5 hours post-liftoff.

SpaceX is now less than 5 hours away from the planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 test flight from Starbase, Texas, with liftoff still on track for 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). The company is still awaiting FAA approval for today's launch, so that could be a hurdle for the flight.

SpaceX has updated its start time for today's Starship Flight 15 launch webcast. Instead of starting 30 minutes before liftoff, it will now begin at 4:58 p.m. EST (2158 GMT), according to the company's livestream schedule on X. Our livestream will begin at the same time.

SpaceX has a 75-minute launch window for Starship Flight 15. Based on road closure announcements from Starbase officials, backup days may be available on Saturday and Sunday.

Good morning, Space Fans, it is launch day for SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 and the world's largest rocket is now hours away from attempting its first double landing test flight. Liftoff remains on target for today, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) from SpaceX's Starbase launch site in South Texas. You'll be able to watch the Starship Flight 15 launch on this page, as well as on Space.com's homepage and our YouTube channel VideoFromSpace. Our live webcast will begin at 5:15 p.m. EST (2215 GMT).

Last night, SpaceX rolled the Ship 42 upper stage out to the Starship launch pad and stacked it atop its Super Heavy booster. The Ship's number was accompanied by a fun sci-fi message - "Don't Panic" - in a nod to the Hitchhiker's Guide To The Galaxy books by Douglas Adams. Elon Musk's Tesla bore the same message when SpaceX launched it into space on the first Falcon Heavy mission.

Space.com's Josh Dinner is on site at Starbase and will be providing updates as possible from Starbase, which we'll share here as they're received.

Here's an update from Josh from the launch pad:

A post shared by Space.com (@spacedotcom)

SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 is the 15th test flight of Starship, the world's largest and most powerful rocket. SpaceX has designed the rocket to be fully reusable, and has landed its massive Super Heavy first stage booster several times.

Flight 15 is SpaceX's first attempt to land both the Super Heavy booster and its Ship upper stage by returning them to their launch pad and catching them in the pad's metal "Chopstick" arms. The landings will be about 22 hours apart, with Super Heavy landing minutes after launch and the Ship upper stage returning to Starbase on Saturday afternoon.

We'll be updating this page throughout the day with news from Josh, SpaceX and Starbase for this unprecedented 22.5-hour test flight. Here's our full timeline for SpaceX Starship Flight 15.

SpaceX is now less than 24 hours from the planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 mission, with liftoff on track for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). The test flight will attempt land both the Starship Super Heavy Booster 22 and its Ship 42 upper stage.

Because the mission will last 22.5 hours, Starship will likely be visible in the night sky to stargazers hoping to see the giant spacecraft in orbit. Space.com's Skywatching Writer Anthony Wood has a great guide on how to see Starship in the night sky.

"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station, but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," our skywatching columnist Joe Rao told Wood.

Happy Wednesday, Space Fans. We are now T-2 days away from SpaceX's planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 test mission, so I wanted to take a moment to give you a run down on what to expect.

Today, you can read my full guide to SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch here, which goes over what time and where to watch the launch online. SpaceX has officially set the launch date for Flight 15 for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EDT (2145 GMT). That puts launch just about 3 days away and Space.com will provide live coverage of the potentially historic flight, the first full recovery of an orbital rocket.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration announced Friday that it is giving states an additional six months to begin enforcing Medicaid work requirements.

States have been racing to prepare their Medicaid systems by Jan. 1 to include the work requirements passed last year in the One Big Beautiful Bill. The legislation required states that expanded Medicaid after Democrats passed the Affordable Care Act to ensure all working-age recipients without dependent children are employed, in school, or volunteering at least 80 hours each month, unless they are disabled, caring for young children, or “medically frail.”

A federal judge recently rejected the federal government’s medical frailty definition and ruled that states did not have adequate time or resources to overhaul their eligibility systems.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/13/mede.text:
Clinicians first noticed medetomidine in the Philadelphia drug supply during the spring of 2024. There was a cluster of overdoses one weekend, leaving patients more sedated and with lower heart rates than normal after receiving the reversal medication naloxone.

It raised some red flags, but amid a constantly changing drug supply, not many. None of the patients died, and most went home from the hospital the same day. It wasn’t until autumn, when patients started coming in with excruciating withdrawal symptoms, that doctors knew something had dangerously shifted.

“It took a while for our patients to consistently have a supply that was exposing them to this enough so that when they stopped, they would rapidly develop withdrawal,” said Jeanmarie Perrone, an emergency medicine physician and director of the Penn Medicine Center for Addiction Medicine and Policy. “It’s the withdrawal that has caused so many problems.”

Despite all the setbacks, Boston Scientific won’t stop pushing the Watchman.

The medical-device giant committed hundreds of millions to acquire the tiny heart implant more than a decade ago, and then endured a years-long debate at the Food and Drug Administration over whether to approve it.

When that approval finally came through, for a limited pool of patients, Boston Scientific was prepared with a plan for something much larger.

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/fda.title: FDA Approves Durvalumab With Enfortumab Vedotin for MIBC
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/fda.text:
M. Alexander Otto, MMSc-PA

The FDA has approved durvalumab (Imfinzi, AstraZeneca) in combination with enfortumab vedotin (EV) as neoadjuvant treatment, followed by single-agent durvalumab as adjuvant treatment after radical cystectomy, for adult patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) who are ineligible for or who have refused cisplatin-based chemotherapy.

The approval comes almost a year after the agency gave the green light to rival immunotherapy pembrolizumab with the antibody-drug conjugate for the indication, but with both given before and after surgery.

The durvalumab/EV approval was based on the VOLGA trial, which randomized 695 patients to radical cystectomy alone or neoadjuvant durvalumab/EV followed by adjuvant durvalumab, with or without peri- and postoperative tremelimumab.

Event-free survival (EFS) at 24 months was 45.1% in the surgery-alone group vs 63.5% in the durvalumab/EV arm and 60.1% with durvalumab/EV/tremelimumab. Overall survival at 24 months was 78.4% with durvalumab/EV vs 69.4% with surgery only. Overall survival was not significantly different between triple therapy and surgery alone.

In the KEYNOTE-905/EV-303 trial, which won pembrolizumab its MIBC with EV approval, the estimated 2-year EFS was 74.7% with the combination vs 39.4% with surgery alone.

Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in half of the surgery-alone group in VOLGA compared with 71.1% of patients treated with durvalumab/EV. The rate of grade 3 or higher events in KEYNOTE-905 with pembrolizumab/EV was 71.3%.

The most common adverse reactions with durvalumab/EV in VOLGA, occurring in more than 20% of patients, were increased aspartate aminotransferase, increased alanine aminotransferase, decreased hemoglobin, rash, increased creatinine, pruritus, decreased calcium, increased lipase, increased potassium, urinary tract infection, increased amylase, fatigue, decreased sodium, decreased lymphocytes, diarrhea, decreased leukocytes, constipation, decreased appetite, increased alkaline phosphatase, dysgeusia, nausea, peripheral neuropathy, musculoskeletal pain, and alopecia.

Durvalumab prescribing information includes warnings and precautions for immune-mediated adverse reactions, infusion-related reactions, complications of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and embryo-fetal toxicities.

Durvalumab dosing is weight-based and delivered every 3 weeks for the new indication in combination with neoadjuvant EV 1.25 mg/kg on days 1 and 8 for three cycles prior to surgery, followed by durvalumab every 4 weeks for up to nine cycles after surgery.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/alpha-sch.title: Wealthy parents pay $75,000 for Alpha’s two-hour AI school day. Half of its K-8 students missed the math target
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/alpha-sch.author: Muskaan Arshad
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/alpha-sch.text:
Alpha School, the network of AI-driven private schools charging parents up to $75,000 a year, has won backers from Silicon Valley to the Trump administration. Its own data show most of its students aren’t reaching the model’s central promise.

Only 42% of Alpha students met the network’s goal of learning twice as fast in both math and reading, according to internal data first reported by The New York Times. The findings land as Alpha pushes into public schools, where districts are adopting its software in hopes of fitting more learning into less time.

Alpha has no traditional teachers. It employs what it calls “guides,” whose job, according to the company’s marketing materials, is to “make every student feel valued and motivated.” Guides don’t plan lessons or grade homework, Fortune reported in September.

The core of the pitch is that students will “learn twice as much as their peers in two hours of academics a day” using TimeBack, an app Alpha markets as an AI tutor. Cofounder MacKenzie Price says the app personalizes and accelerates learning for each student, freeing the rest of the school day for workshops on skills such as public speaking and relationship building.

The network has grown fast. A spokesperson told Fortune in September that Alpha had more than 1,200 students. The Times put the figure at about 1,500 across roughly 50 campuses, in line with the expansion plans Alpha announced in August.

That pitch has drawn AI optimists. “I definitely think using AI well is a skill in the future, if not the skill, so it’s kind of a disservice not to have that in school,” Sarah Cone, a venture capitalist whose 8-year-old daughter attends Alpha’s New York campus, told Fortune in September.

In September 2025, U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon toured Alpha’s Austin campus and called its model “the most exciting thing I’ve seen in education in a long time.” LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and hedge fund manager Bill Ackman have both publicly backed Price and Alpha on X. Even the X account of Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder serving more than 11 years in prison for fraud, praised Price.

Math is the bigger gap. About half of K-8 students at Alpha’s private campuses missed the goal of learning math twice as fast, and roughly one in five missed their reading targets, according to the Times‘ review of the network’s data.

Students who started behind fared worse. About a fifth of Alpha’s private school students scored at or below the 50th percentile nationally in math last fall, and only 37% of that group met the network’s 2x growth goal by winter, the Times found.

The two-hour premise is also in question. Guides and parents told Wired that students worked late into the night to meet the school’s goals. One parent of a 13-year-old reading at an 11th-grade level said reaching those goals came with “stress and anxiety.”

Former employees told 404 Media that Alpha’s AI generated faulty lesson plans, which internal documents said sometimes did “more harm than good,” and that the company scraped other online courses without permission.

More than 2,600 public school students in Texas and South Carolina now use Alpha’s platform, according to company documents reviewed by the Times. That is a tougher test: public schools can’t remove struggling students, the Times noted, and they lack the prize incentives Alpha uses at its private campuses.

The Houston Independent School District, the largest in Texas, is piloting the software at two schools. Superintendent Mike Miles told the Times that students spent more time on Alpha’s apps than planned, cutting into other activities. He still wants AI in the district’s toolkit, calling it an important tool for students to be “successful in a different world and workplace.”

Alpha’s expansion comes as schools grapple with falling math and reading scores and growing evidence that how students use AI matters as much as whether they use it.

A study of 26,811 secondary students in central China found that homework scores rose 18% after students adopted generative AI tools, while closed-book exam scores fell 20%. The OECD’s latest PISA results found that daily AI users scored lower in science than nonusers, while moderate users performed about the same.

Professors have told Fortune that students who lean on AI summaries struggle with sustained reading. “Today, if you assign that amount of reading, they often don’t know what to do,” Timothy O’Malley, a theology professor at the University of Notre Dame, told Fortune‘s Preston Fore in June.

“It’s not even an inability to critically think,” Jessica Hooten Wilson, a professor of great books and humanities at Pepperdine University, told Fortune. “It’s an inability to read sentences.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-corrup.title: The case of Nvidia and the growing risk of AI and corruption
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-corrup.author: Susan Ariel Aaronson
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-corrup.text:
In 2025, the UN Office of Drugs and Crime and the Organization of American States co-convened a panel (slideshow & video) which examined whether AI is the biggest corruption risk in history. In November 2026, the panelists’ deepest fears about the AI-corruption relationship came true, but not in the way they expected.

The panelists feared that AI would enable corruption by making it easier to launder money, give bribes, or produce disinformation. Instead, they learned that the corruption of AI did not start inside the technology itself but with its leaders, heads of state, government officials, and tech CEOs, steering the direction of AI governance. As we see today, America’s approach to AI governance, using export controls to regulate the supply of AI and its components, is fueling corruption. We utilize Transparency International’s definition herein– the abuse of entrusted authority for private gain.

I believe that one company, Nvidia, has become the poster child for corruption in the U.S. Last year, the Trump Administration restricted sales of chips to China under U.S. law out of fears that would provide the Chinese military with an advantage or could undermine U.S. leadership in AI. The now former CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, used flattery and donations to influence the Trump Administration’s AI export policies. And in December, Mr. Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell the H200, an older but still powerful A.I. chip, to China, as long as the U.S. government was given a cut of the sales. (Another company AMD also received an exemption). In so doing, the U.S. gained a financial incentive for loosening controls of AI infrastructure to China However, the Congressional Research Service reported that .”Article I, Section 9, Clause 5 of the U.S. Constitution,prohibits the federal imposition of export taxes and duties (not user fees), and 50 U.S.C. §4815(c), which prohibits BIS from collecting fees for considering or issuing export licenses.”

Additionally, last year, Nvidia’s General Counsel, Tim Teter, seemed to interfere in an investigation of Nvidia’s sales to Chinese and Malaysian entities. And now we’ve learned that although senior administration officials such as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were warned about the dangers surrounding Nvidia and its now former CEO, they took no action. This corruption and inaction puts U.S. national security and the American people at risk.

While export controls may be useful and necessary, they are particularly vulnerable to corruption because they sit at the intersection of high-value restricted goods, bureaucratic gatekeeping, in customs, business, and trade policymaking agencies, and complex cross-border supply chains. When governments restrict access to lucrative technologies, including dual use items such as chips or AI, they can create massive financial incentives for bad actors to bribe officials or exploit regulatory blind spots to bypass the rules. Export control systems rely on government officials to issue licenses, classify goods, and clear shipments through customs. This concentration of discretionary power allows corrupt officials to solicit bribes in exchange for faster approvals or looking the other way. At the same time, U.S. agencies struggle to coordinate trade, customs, and anti-corruption efforts, which are controlled by different agencies.

Export controls also create situations of artificial scarcity and high profits, particularly for dual use items such as AI systems. Some buyers may be willing to pay extremely high prices to receive a limited supply of AI services. Not surprisingly, both competitors of Nvidia that produce high speed chips such as Google, and, as well as Open AI, Amazon, Anthropic, and Microsoft—three of Nvidia’s biggest clients—support legislation that would further limit Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China.

Finally, export controls often involve opaque national security exemptions. Because export decisions often involve classified intelligence or sensitive defense deals, licensing and procurement processes frequently lack transparency and accountability. Such situations make it difficult for independent watchdogs to spot irregularities However, the Trump Administration fired many inspector generals in 2025, including at the Department of Commerce, along with antiorruption prosecutors. .

Given these problems, export controls are not the best tool to prevent our adversaries from acquiring advanced AI systems or chips because they present many opportunities for corruption. Yet Politico has reported that it is almost impossible for members of Congress to support loosening export controls. Studies have shown such controls are rarely effective. Hence, Congress should weigh a different approach Morreover, current export control implementation can harm U.S. economic and technological competitiveness. . While there are no easy answers, , the U.S. should work with its Western allies to to manage technology transfers that might threaten our shared security interests

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/new-congr.title: A warning for the new Congress: Don’t stop at ‘affordability’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/new-congr.author: Samantha Tweedy
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/new-congr.text:
It was a night of historic wins for the candidates who understood that “affordability” was at the heart of this election. But the lesson of this election is bigger than the price of eggs and gas, and every candidate – Democrat and Republican – who won should be careful not to miss the point of what voters really want.

As Black business leaders who are experts in navigating and building economic opportunity when the system doesn’t deliver, we had a hunch “affordability” wasn’t telling the whole story. So we spent months before Election Day asking voters and confirmed we were right.

Through internal polling conducted by Workbench Strategies during July 2026 of 1,400 voters, including an oversample of 400 Black voters, and our two-way texting conversations with voters, we found that they gravitated toward a combination of solutions that provide immediate relief from rising costs and build pathways to help them get ahead. For example, nearly half of all voters chose both caps on medical and prescription costs (45 percent) and increasing wages to keep up with the cost of living (43 percent) as a top-three priority. Black voters were even more focused on higher wages, with 56 percent choosing it as a top-three priority.

And over and over again, voters in focus groups conducted by HIT Strategies said that they wanted to take control of their own economic futures and for leaders to remove barriers to opportunity.

It was easy to see leading up to the election that candidates who recognized these concerns and built agendas around addressing both affordability and economic opportunity would be rewarded at the ballot box. Now that we can sit with the results of the election, it’s clear that what voters were calling an affordability crisis is also an economic mobility crisis. And now, the newly elected Congress has only 18 months to demonstrate it understands the difference and begin to deliver on both.

Yes, lowering prices matters – but that only helps Americans get to the end of the month.

Helping Americans really get ahead will take solutions that make it possible to own a home, finance a business, compete for a contract, and turn a lifetime of work into lasting financial security for their children and grandchildren – in other words, it will take building pathways to work, wages, and wealth.

This conversation matters for more than economic reasons: our democracy is still on the line.

A growing body of research finds links between economic inequality, institutional distrust, and democratic backsliding. If elected officials fail to create meaningful pathways for far more Americans to get ahead – making sure work pays, wages rise, and wealth can be built – they should not be surprised when voters look elsewhere for answers in 2028 and beyond. Nor should they expect trust in our economy, our institutions, or our democracy to rebound on its own.

Fixing this requires a bold, affirmative economic plan – and for our leaders to realize they’re on the clock with voters to deliver. The good news is that there are solutions that address both sides of the challenge: actions that can help families manage rising costs today while expanding the pathways that help people get ahead over the long term.

Lawmakers should lower costs where families feel the greatest pressure. That means promoting competition in prescription drugs, lowering grocery costs, and expanding proven tax credits that help working families keep more of what they earn.

But lowering costs alone is not enough.

Leaders must also expand pathways to work, wages, and wealth by increasing access to homeownership, supporting entrepreneurship and small business growth, expanding opportunities for workers to own a piece of corporate profits, raising wages, and ensuring that economic growth reaches communities too often left behind.

Finally, leaders must restore trust that the economic rules are fair. That means increasing transparency in concentrated markets, enforcing fair competition, and ensuring tax regulations do not disproportionately reward those who accumulate wealth.

If leaders do not take immediate steps to address rising costs and make the country’s founding promise of opportunity a reality for more Black Americans, and consequently all Americans, we’ll continue in a downward spiral: lack of faith in economic opportunity causes lack of faith in democracy, which harms the whole economy.

Every leader who won in 2026 should take this warning seriously and signal to voters that they understand the mandate underpinning those wins. The clock starts now.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/walmart-c.title: When Walmart pulls out of town, the stores next door don’t pick up its shoppers — their sales are down 20% a year later
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/walmart-c.author: Vivek Astvansh, Preetinder Kaur, Pushpinder Gill, The Conversation
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/walmart-c.text:
Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate.

Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road.

But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger?

We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026.

This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor.

Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business.

Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect: Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants.

Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop. But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest. What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes.

A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area.

This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough.

We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open.

We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes.

That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared.

In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally.

Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand.

Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales.

Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed.

These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure.

A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores.

That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits.

For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s.

Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area.

Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic.

Vivek Astvansh, Associate Professor of Quantitative Marketing and Computational Data Science, Binghamton University, State University of New York; Preetinder Kaur, Assistant Professor of Marketing, University of Guelph, and Pushpinder Gill, Assistant Professor of Marketing, Toronto Metropolitan University

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/gta-vi-bi.title: From Gen X to Gen Z, ‘unicorn game’ GTA VI’s multigenerational pull is a threat to Hollywood’s holiday blockbusters
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/gta-vi-bi.author: Andrew McGowan
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/gta-vi-bi.text:
Thirteen years after its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrives on Nov. 19. The sixth installment in Rockstar Games’ open-world crime series launches on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, and its pull is likely to be felt well beyond gaming, wherever other entertainment competes for the same audience’s time.

When Grand Theft Auto V came out in 2013, it generated $800 million in sales in its first 24 hours. It has since sold nearly 235 million units, according to parent company Take-Two Interactive’s latest earnings release.

The new game is on pace to crush those numbers. Sensor Tower estimates GTA VI had logged about 12.1 million digital preorders worth roughly $1.18 billion as of the morning of Nov. 13.

If it were a movie, GTA VI would already be one of the year’s top-grossing films. Its preorders alone top the roughly $1.01 billion that The Super Mario Galaxy Movie has grossed worldwide, according to The Numbers’ 2026 worldwide box office chart.

The stakes for Take-Two are enormous. Analysts estimate the publisher has spent $1 billion to $1.5 billion on the game, as Fortune has reported on CEO Strauss Zelnick’s bet. Earlier this month, Take-Two held its forecast of $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings for the fiscal year ending in March, saying preorders were running well ahead of its expectations.

Fans are clearing their calendars. In a survey of nearly 1,500 users by digital marketplace G2A.com, 29% said they had already requested time off from work or school to play the game. G2A also says its preorders surged 152% week over week in the most recent seven days.

That kind of planned absence has fueled viral estimates of what GTA VI will cost the U.S. economy, though economists told Fortune those fears are overblown.

G2A founder Bartosz Skwarczek tells Fortune, “GTA VI is much more than a game launch. It’s a global cultural moment that shows just how deeply gaming has become part of people’s lives.”

Zelnick has called GTA VI the “most anticipated entertainment property of all time,” and the rest of the industry seems to agree. Publishers have largely moved their releases out of its way, leaving this quarter unusually quiet.

“This Fall has been the most depressed Fall we’ve ever seen in terms of game volume,” Colan Neese, senior vice president of gaming at research firm Screen Engine/ASI, tells Fortune. “Basically every game that was going to come out this Fall tried to release in September and then it just fell off a cliff in October.”

The only other major releases this month look like counterprogramming. Blizzard launched World of Warcraft: Forever on Nov. 4, and Nintendo released its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 on Nov. 5.

The former is a PC and Mac game, platforms GTA VI won’t reach at launch. The latter is family-friendly and sells to a different crowd than GTA does.

GTA VI’s shadow could stretch into the new year. “It’s going to be really hard for a game to break through in December,” says Neese. “And then the question goes, how long does that shadow last? Does it go into January? Does it go into February?”

Neese points to Sony, which pushed God of War Laufey from Feb. 16 to May 20, 2027, a move he reads as steering clear of GTA VI. Sony’s Santa Monica Studio said the extra time would go toward “putting in the finishing touches.”

Hollywood may feel the squeeze, too. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens Nov. 20, the day after GTA VI, in what Fortune has called a thin November box office that GTA VI is set to test. In December, Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three both open on the 18th, each vying to be the entertainment event of the year.

Little do they know that their greatest competitor might be a video game with a vast, multigenerational audience.

“Grand Theft Auto VI is a unicorn game because it’s reaching elder millennials and young Gen Xers who grew up on Grand Theft Auto III through Grand Theft Auto V. It was a decade where they released multiple Grand Theft Autos and we all grew up with the game, played it constantly, and then it culminated with GTA V, and then it just went away when we went into our thirties.

“Now, we’re in our forties and all of a sudden, we have a new Grand Theft Auto and we’re all excited to ride the nostalgia,” explains Neese.

“Then you have an entire generation who only had one Grand Theft Auto game, which is Gen Z,” Neese continues. “They grew up with Grand Theft Auto V streamer culture on Twitch and YouTube. They had Grand Theft Auto V and then Grand Theft Auto Online, which has also brought in early Gen Alpha.

“So, you have this really interesting moment where multiple generations are just going to be sucked into this thing.”

Rockstar has a track record that justifies the anticipation. Between GTA V and VI, the studio released Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018, which has shipped more than 89 million units and remains one of the best-selling games of all time.

GTA VI itself was delayed twice, first from fall 2025 to May 2026 and then to Nov. 19, giving Rockstar more time to polish what Neese sees as a landmark.

“They purposely built a new engine. They’ve made it incredibly realistic,” says Neese. “They did a lot of research into the Southern Florida setting and culture and tried to bring this world to life.

“They put a lot of research, time, and technology into making this and it’s the pinnacle of game creation for humans. It’s like the Sistine Chapel or the Notre-Dame of what a game can be made by humans, and candidly, I don’t know if we’ll ever see the likes of this again.”

Former Take-Two CEO Ben Feder made a similar case in Fortune this week, arguing that GTA VI will be the last pre-AI blockbuster video game of its kind.

If 2013 doesn’t seem like that long ago, consider that the gap between then and now is longer than the stretch between the first and last Harry Potter movies, or between Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith and The Force Awakens. It’s also longer than the full runs of era-defining shows like Game of Thrones, Breaking Bad, The Office, Friends, and Seinfeld.

Meanwhile, the gaming industry has boomed. Americans spent $60.7 billion on video games in 2025, according to the Entertainment Software Association’s 2026 Essential Facts report, nearly triple the roughly $21 billion they spent in 2013.

The same report counts 212.3 million Americans who play video games, about two-thirds of the population. By comparison, 53% of U.S. adults told the Pew Research Center in 2025 that they had seen a movie in a theater in the past year.

Mainstream entertainment companies seem to be waking up to gaming’s potential as its core audience comes of age. Earlier attempts to adapt video games for the big screen were poorly received, but this year The Super Mario Galaxy Movie has grossed more than $1 billion worldwide and Resident Evil about $410 million.

TV series such as The Last of Us, Arcane, and Fallout have proved successful, too.

“Part of the challenge with gaming adaptations for the longest time was that you had a generation of people who never actually played or experienced the IP. Now, they have a relationship to it,” concludes Neese.

If traditionalist attitudes still siphon video games into a niche corner of the entertainment industry, Nov. 19 may be a referendum on that outlook. GTA VI stands to show how much a single game can disrupt the broader entertainment business and hold an audience’s attention for months at a time.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/nyc-city-.title: NYC is spending $70 million on 5 city-run grocery stores that will price essentials 30% below retail — and bodegas are fighting back
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/nyc-city-.author: Nevin Cohen, The Conversation
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/nyc-city-.text:
New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses.

What explains this pushback?

As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.

It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.

If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.

New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.

While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.

In this respect, the stores offer a “public option” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.

At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”

Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.

These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.

This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.”

Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.

Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.

To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.

Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.

The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.

Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.

Nevin Cohen, Chair of the Department of Health Policy and Management, CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Public Policy
