https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ben-gagno.title: Meet ‘Captain Keel,’ the 37-year-old steering a Bitcoin miner into the AI data center gold rush
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ben-gagno.author: Shawn Tully
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ben-gagno.text:
In late 2023, Bitcoin miner Ben Gagnon concluded that his employer, Bitfarms of Quebec, was in the wrong business. For Gagnon, Bitfarms’ greatest value lay not in the giant racks of GPUs that generated Bitcoin, but the immense power supplies it controlled. The then 34-year-old chief mining officer who’d launched his career crafting makeshift crypto-minting rigs in Hong Kong and Taipei, reckoned that Bitfarms could make much more money by exiting the field full stop, demolishing the “mines,” selling the chips that filled them, and re-channeling its plentiful flow of megawatts to power-craving industrial users at plants newly built on the Bitfarms sites.

The big revelation came in March of 2024, when Core Scientific and CoreWeave unveiled a stunning new deal. Bitcoin titan Core Scientific would refashion a mining facility in Austin, Texas, as an AI data center, and rent the power and buildings to the neocloud. That Bitcoin-to-AI play struck Gagnon as a model that Bitfarms could follow on a grand scale, from Quebec to Washington state. “It was the big aha moment,” recalls Gagnon. “Suddenly, we saw who the right customer was.”

At the time, Bitfarms was mired in turmoil. In early 2024, the board was searching for its third leader in five years. The sitting chief agreed to depart when Bitfarms named a successor, but in May—believe it or not while still CEO—instead filed a $27 million suit for “wrongful termination and breach of contract,” plunging this Canadian exemplar of all-green, hydro-driven Bitcoin mining into legal warfare. Pounded by a sharp drop in the token’s prices, Bitfarms’ stock was languishing, and a rival pounced. Two days after the board fired the CEO, Riot Platforms unveiled a hostile $930 million takeover bid for Bitfarms at a lowly $2.30 a share, 75% below its peak in late 2021. After Bitfarms installed a “poison pill” defense, Riot launched a website dubbed “A Better Bitfarms” trashing allegedly poor corporate governance, and demanding the departure of the co-founder named as interim chief.

The board tapped Gagnon to both quell the war versus Riot, and pursue the strategy of total transformation he’d been advocating. In July of 2024, Gagnon took the helm, and over the next few months, helped broker an agreement where Riot named a director of its choice, and the co-founder left the board. Riot halted its attack and has since sold its shares.

While battling for Bitfarms’ independence, Gagnon kept his sights locked on engineering the Big Pivot. He describes the mission as “pursuing a strategy of steering the business away from Bitcoin mining, and taking it over to a pure energy infrastructure play in support of AI and high-performance computing. We’d shift our focus entirely to addressing the defining constraint of the most important technology of our lifetime.”

The venture needed a rebrand, so Gagnon picked “Keel” to evoke the structural backbone of a vessel that, as he says, “provides stability and converts energy into forward motion,” a reference to the stable long-term leases that he expects to provide a smooth and lucrative course versus the storms he encountered in Bitcoin. He’s now attempting to pull a hat trick seldom seen in the corporate world, the total reinvention of a large enterprise, including in product and nationality, on a crazy-rhythm beat. On April 1, 2026, the franchise was reborn as Keel Infrastructure and changed its domicile from Canada to the U.S. The photo on Gagnon’s X profile reprises the nautical theme, adding a whimsical accent. Gagnon grins from a porthole-sized frame, sporting his usual oversized rimless glasses, and a gold-braided yachtsman’s cap displaying his user name, “Captain Keel.”

Now 37, Gagnon is making by far his biggest wager yet in a career that careened from mining Bitcoin in remote oil patches by rescuing flared natural gas to rehabilitating some of the world’s dirtiest energy sites under the banner of AI.

Gagnon is the son of two American parents who settled in Hong Kong, where he attended international grammar and high schools that offered lots of, as he puts it, “Mandarin as a second language courses.” He gained a bachelor’s degree in business and economics (and a minor in Mandarin) at the Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business in 2011, on the Bloomington campus. “I got fascinated by Bitcoin, and could have bought it for 73 cents,” he recalls. “Instead, I did what every college kid does. I bought beer.” Over the next three-and-a-half years, he reflected on that choice while watching Bitcoin climb 1,400-fold to over $1,000.

Returning home, he attained a master’s in computer security and networking at the University of Hong Kong, where he took cryptography courses that renewed his interest in the science of generating cryptocurrencies. After graduating, Gagnon worked as a network technician at a company that offered mobile applications for investor conferences and other events. After less than two years, he quit his job and moved again, this time to Taiwan. His new venture: Building and running a jerry-rigged Ethereum mine at the home of his girlfriend’s (now his wife’s) parents in Taipei. “Everyone thought it was Bitcoin 2.0, so I figured, I’m not going to miss this opportunity like I missed Bitcoin as a sophomore,” says Gagnon.

The business drew unwanted attention by using ten times the electricity of a typical home in Taipei—specifically, the phenomenon alerted the police. “They couldn’t figure out what we were doing,” he recalls. “They thought we were growing marijuana upstairs and kept raiding the house, like on a weekly basis. So we had to explain to the police every week that we weren’t doing anything illegal.” It took only a couple of intolerable months before Gagnon saw the necessity of uprooting his facility from his future in-laws’ home.

Gagnon then ran his operation in Guangzhou on China’s mainland, but shut down after two years due to a tough regulatory climate. “Let’s just say that the laws were somewhat selective for a young foreigner navigating a new industry,” he avows. In 2019, he joined Bitfarms, one of several Bitcoin miners, including HIVE, that sprouted in Quebec during the 2017 to 2018 boom, drawn by the province’s plentiful and relatively inexpensive hydroelectric power. As chief of development, his charge was expanding the business to the U.S. and other energy-rich areas of Canada.

Gagnon focused on the huge but remote Alberta oil patch. “I was always looking for the cheapest energy sources for mining, and that was Alberta,” he says. The producers were “flaring” the natural gas created from drilling, since no pipelines existed for sending it to population centers. Gagnon created the first containerized Bitcoin data center that incorporated a generator and offered 100% financing. His mobile units channeled natural gas right at the far-flung drilling sites for minting tokens. His rigs empowered the drillers to monetize energy they were burning into the atmosphere. The product proved a big winner for his new employer. “The drillers were using gas that cost 1.5 cents a kWh versus 6 cents in the U.S.,” he recalls. “So we got great prices for our equipment because the payback period for the drillers was so short.”

When Gagnon started pushing the AI remake in 2023, he doubled-down on a possible acquisition that ideally fitted the new plotline. His target was Stronghold Digital, a startup using one of the most unusual models in all of Bitcoin mining. From the mid-19th century to the 1970s, mines in Pennsylvania routinely separated the low-quality coal—scraps mixed with rocks, often with high sulfur or ash content—from the good stuff. Children called “breaker boys” seated at conveyor belts or chutes would pick out the slate and rock by hand, no gloves permitted—brutal work that often left their fingers bleeding. The legacy: Black carbon mountains scarring the towns of western Pennsylvania. For decades, the sites Stronghold owned had been performing a public service by scooping truckloads of waste coal and burning it in their boilers to supply electricity to the local grids, while pocketing big subsidies for the effort. The state government reasoned that the benefits of cleansing the countryside more than compensated for allowing just about the dirtiest form of electrical generation in America.

In 2021, a pair of entrepreneurs turned those locations into Bitcoin mining operations. But Stronghold way overinvested in chips and other equipment, and by 2023 it was foundering, hammered by crippling debt and legal disputes. Gagnon identified Stronghold’s sweet spots, one each in eastern and western Pennsylvania, as ideal locations for AI campuses. Stronghold already controlled significant amounts of power, but held the potential to obtain much more. Working with its owners, Gagnon applied to utilities and state authorities for big new batches of megawatts. Once assured the approvals were at hand, Gagnon, in August 2024, after a month as CEO, landed an agreement to purchase Stronghold for $175 million.

Increasingly, AI leaders are viewing power as the toughest chokepoint in the AI supply chain. As OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman characterizes the issue, “The bottleneck for AI isn’t code, it’s electrons.” Adds Elon Musk, “The limiting factor is fundamentally electrical power…[that’s leading to] producing more chips than the hyperscalers can plug in and turn on.” And Greg Abel, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, a major energy provider to AI data centers via its sundry utilities, concurs, calling access to megawatts a “big constraint” for rapid buildouts.

The backlash against AI data centers gained fresh force on Election Day, when so many candidates seeking restraints or outright bans on their spread won congressional and statewide races. That result may actually strengthen the hand of the Bitcoin contingent, since they’ve already got a grip on the energy pipelines the hyperscalers and neoclouds need, and appear willing to pay up for. Put simply, the future “scarcity value” of the crucial asset these crypto producers control likely jumped on November 3. Gagnon calls Keel’s position “bird in the hand economics.”

Keel stands among the first and largest crypto operators to follow Core Scientific into AI. But today, more than ten major players are making the switch, in part or whole. Among those that have already secured big, long-term contracts are Riot, which clinched a $9.1 billion lease from Anthropic for the AI campus at its Bitcoin mine in Milam County, Texas; Hut 8, partnering on a $7 billion contract with Google and Anthropic at its River Bend complex in Louisiana; and Applied Digital, which will serve CoreWeave under an $11 billion agreement at its forthcoming campus in Ellendale, North Dakota.

All of these converts are essentially re-purposing the same land and power, or sometimes more of the latter, that they deployed to produce Bitcoin for the AI buildout. But they’re taking different approaches. The crypto-to-AI crowd falls into two categories, both in how completely they’re shifting, and the templates they embrace. On the first score, several participants are taking the Keel route by totally exiting Bitcoin for AI, including Core Scientific, Cipher Mining and Genesis Digital. Another group that encompasses Riot, Hut 8, HIVE Digital Technologies, and TeraWulf are adopting a hybrid model where they both channel power to AI campuses and continue to mine Bitcoin.

On the second criterion, the two main business models are “compute provider” and “developer” or co-location (co-lo) purveyor. As a compute provider, the former or hybrid Bitcoin outfit delivers a turnkey project. It commissions a contractor, often a REIT, to erect the buildings, and typically rents the structures long-term from the builder-partner. It then packs the cavernous boxes with GPUs and other gear that constitute by far the most expensive part of the project. The owner’s product is the full computing package that it then leases to the hyperscalers or neoclouds for running the likes of Google’s Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude.

The developer or co-lo arrangement works much the same way, except that the site’s owner doesn’t supply the hardware, and hence shoulders much lower up-front costs. Instead, it’s the hyperscaler or neocloud, a Microsoft or Crusoe, that brings the GPUs and other equipment. The company branching out from Bitcoin mining both supplies the structures that it leases from the REIT or other contractor, and the power that runs it––MWs secured on long-term utility contracts form its essential business. The still-active or former Bitcoin miner rents the “powered shells” to the compute providers, for operating, say OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Microsoft’s Copilot. In today’s market, the developer garners a big markup on the scarcest item in AI.

The reasons so many are crossing from Bitcoin to follow either one or both of these strategies: Each megawatt of power at work generates far more cash flow at an AI campus than at plants churning codes to win the signature crypto coin. In a recent interview on the Schwab Network, Christian Lopez, head of blockchain and digital assets at broker-dealer Cohen & Co., estimates the numbers, over five years, at $1.7 million per KW for Bitcoin and almost five times as much, $7.9 million, for an AI campus. What about revenues? Sarah Friar, CFO of OpenAI, posits that each 1 GW (1,000 MW) fueling an AI data center garners $10 billion in revenues. Once again, the number can be one-fifth that amount for a Bitcoin mine.

Data center pioneers divide into two camps. The “compute” competitors (Bitdeer of Singapore, IREN of Australia and Canada’s HIVE Digital, Hut 8 to some degree) spend massively to buy the chips and rent them out, in exchange for higher rents, shorter leases, and more risk. For example, HIVE has a $350 million, 5-year deal with an as yet unnamed AI stalwart for campuses on Bell Canada sites where it’s supplying the hardware. “The cost of the GPUs is $190 million off the bat,” says HIVE CEO Aydin Kilic, who predicts the project will be multiple times as profitable per KW as Bitcoin mining.

By contrast, Keel is a pure-play developer. It doesn’t buy and install the GPUs and other gear that constitute as much as 70% of data centers that cost roughly $50 billion a GW to create (the other 30% covers land, the buildings and costs of connecting or providing onsite power). “We’re strictly in the power business, and make money on the difference between what we pay the utilities, and what the compute providers pay us on their leases,” says Gagnon.

Keel’s edge: It sits on an enormous amount of power. It has 2.2 GWs that are either approved for use, or in the last stages of the approval process. That’s more than the 1.9 GW that OpenAI was reportedly marshaling at the close of 2025. Gagnon acknowledges that Keel as a developer won’t collect revenues nearly as large as the miners turned compute providers, but insists that his cash flows will be more secure, and that the relatively low cost of the power and physical centers as a share of the whole makes customers willing to pay big premiums to get MWs in a hurry.

In part, that’s because as of now, those AI campuses are sumptuously profitable. “The gross margins for data centers are 85%, and of the 15% in costs, only a max of 2% to 4% goes to leasing the power and buildings,” Gagnon explains. “So if a customer spends twice as much, their margins may ease to 81% or 83%. The GPUs in their warehouses are depreciating fast. So they’re saying, I’d rather take a hit to 83% in gross margin and start generating revenue in 6 months than wait 12 months for a margin that’s 2 points higher. And that’s what we’re seeing.”

Keel is shepherding three “priority projects” closest to clearing all hurdles and to signing leases. One of them is a former Stronghold facility: Panther Creek, 85 miles north of Philadelphia. Keel acquired another Pennsylvania site in a separate transaction. It’s located at the opposite end of the state in Sharon, near Youngstown, Ohio. On the two sites combined, Keel’s in the process of securing over 450 MWs from the local grids. The third “priority” is a hydro project in Moses Lake, Washington, ringed by Seattle, Spokane and Portland. Gagnon marvels at the sight of the famous Boeing repair field almost adjoining the Keel site. “You’re driving to our facility and you’ll see 100 different 737 MAX, all painted different colors, what a fun sight!”

Gagnon points out that approvals fall into three categories: zoning, environmental, and development. At Moses Lake, Keel’s scored all three, and the site’s now under construction. At Sharon and Panther Creek, it has secured both zoning and development, and is working through the environmental permits, the final step. The most difficult requirement, he states, is zoning. “It’s the one that’s most political, most community-centric, and most emotional,” he says. “Projects can get shut down if you don’t behave the right way with community leaders. We got really good at advocating for Bitcoin mines that are a much harder sell than AI campuses.”

The second ex-Stronghold site is the biggest of them all, the 700-acre Scrubgrass facility near Sharon, and roughly an hour north of Pittsburgh. There, Keel’s applied for a massive 1 GW of power, 40% of the total capacity it’s seeking. At Scrubgrass, Keel is still working through all the initial permitting stages for securing power.

Gagnon says the biggest challenge isn’t attracting customers, it’s getting the final environmental permits in place. But he’s already encountered delays. In May, Gagnon guided to obtaining leases at all three priority projects by the end of 2026. But on the Q3 earnings call, he said that no deals will be signed this year, and declined to give dates for signing customers on those projects.

The rub: Keel’s now generating puny revenues since it’s now left Bitcoin mining and isn’t yet making money from AI. Gagnon’s sitting on a big cushion, having raised almost $600 million in convertible debt last year, and another almost $300 million by emptying its Bitcoin trove. Still, Keel’s burning cash fast. Will its trove prove big enough to fund crossing the span to AI on time? Investors are cautious about Keel’s prospects, to put it mildly. Keel’s stock dropped around 20% on Gagnon’s announcement of no deals this year, and currently has a paltry market cap of around $1.3 billion, about the same as when Riot bid back in 2024.

On the plus side, Gagnon’s collected a portfolio that potentially features some of the best AI sites in America and Canada. He notes that the big customers are now showing a strong preference for facilities near big population centers, just where he’s concentrating. “The difference is that until now, there’s been so much AI model training that wasn’t for customers, so it didn’t matter where the campus was located. The normal things that would have guided a developer to find a project and select a piece of land were thrown out the window in the interest of scale and time.”

Now, he says, the business is moving strongly towards “inference” where the compute providers sell to banks, research labs, call centers and other customers. “That’s where most of the money will be made, not on the retail side,” he says. “As the market moves to inference, more and more of the traditional data center qualities will come into play.” He notes that compute works much more efficiently when it’s near the customer than hundreds or thousands of miles away in a remote rural area. “It’s so important to get the fiber close to where people live and businesses are located, and in the frenzy, that’s been forgotten,” says Gagnon. The big distances cause sluggish responses that lead to poor user experiences in fields such as autonomous driving and interactive chatbots. Plus, he says, in the weeks leading up to and following the midterms, “we’ve seen a big uptick in level of demand and prioritization of our sites in Pennsylvania, driven that the support of data center had changed in many states. The Democratic candidates who won in Pennsylvania ran on platform favoring responsible data center development, the opposite the scenario in most other states.”

“The differentiator will be location, location and location,” says Gagnon. “This is a real estate industry and location is hugely important in real estate. That’s why you have so many cloud data centers in Loudoun County, Va. near D.C. and Quincy near Seattle. We’re near New York, Philly, and Pittsburgh, and have a great position in the Pacific Northwest, where there’s a big shortage of AI campuses. If you’re close to where the demand comes from, that should justify a premium going forward, just as it has in the past for data centers.”

Gagnon is especially bullish on the union of AI and the Keystone State. “Pennsylvania built this country, it had all the resources needed to launch the industrial revolution, steel, coal, railroads, natural gas. Texas was the first mover in AI data centers, and now Pennsylvania is the second mover. And we’ll be number one in Pennsylvania.”

It’s a long way from waste coal to GPUs. And Gagnon’s got a plausible story: The big guys have the GPUs, in fact too many of them. But he and his Bitcoin brethren have a lot of what the giants now need most, the power. The question for Keel is how fast Gagnon can turn it on.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/jensen-hu.title: Jensen Huang’s $145 billion question: What California divorce law says Lori Huang could get
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/jensen-hu.author: Fernanda Tronco
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/jensen-hu.text:
Jensen Huang has lost his job, his board seat, and roughly $10 billion in paper wealth since admitting to an affair. If his 41-year marriage ends, California law could put a far larger share of his fortune in play.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s president, CEO, and director this week, days after confessing in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had been unfaithful to Lori Huang, his wife since 1985. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress Nvidia’s interim CEO and made longtime director Harvey Jones its first board chair while it searches for a permanent successor.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang wrote.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The admission followed a New York Times report that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, of gathering information for Beijing, and that she had a close relationship with Huang. China has denied involvement. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said this week that she left Singapore in February and was barred from returning after a police investigation, which it said “did not concern espionage.”

Two more relationships have since been reported. The New York Times reported on November 11 that Huang had been romantically involved with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported directly to him, citing five people who had worked at the company. A day later, Reuters reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, whom it did not name. Powell did not respond to the Times, and Nvidia declined to comment to Reuters.

Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort and said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” An FBI inquiry into his relationship with Alice Huang is also underway.

Huang has not announced plans to divorce. But a split would test how California divides a fortune built almost entirely on a single stock, and the answer would turn less on his headline net worth than on how the couple’s Nvidia shares were acquired and held.

Huang reported beneficial ownership of about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, or 3.58% of the company’s outstanding stock, as of March 23, 2026, according to Nvidia’s 2026 proxy statement. Nvidia ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and was the first company on the list worth more than $4 trillion.

Jensen and Lori Huang are co-trustees of their living trust, which holds about 528.5 million shares, and of two other family trusts. Together, the three trusts hold nearly 669 million shares. Another 73.3 million shares are held by limited liability companies whose sole member is the living trust.

Lori Huang also runs the family’s philanthropy. She is president of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, which reported about $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024, Fortune reported. The foundation holds about 58.7 million Nvidia shares, but the proxy states that neither spouse has a pecuniary interest in them.

The distinction matters. Beneficial ownership and control of shares do not by themselves establish personal ownership, or determine how assets would be divided in a divorce.

The couple met as lab partners at Oregon State University and married in 1985, eight years before Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993. They live in California, a community-property state, where assets acquired during a marriage are generally owned jointly and divided equally in a divorce.

“In California, all property acquired by a spouse during marriage is community property,” Christopher Melcher, a Los Angeles attorney who specializes in high-net-worth divorces, told the New York Post. “She would be entitled to 50%.”

Under California Courts guidance, community property generally includes earnings and assets acquired between the date of marriage and the date of separation. Property owned before the marriage or acquired after separation, along with gifts and inheritances, is generally separate property, and some assets can be a mix of both.

That means Lori Huang could be entitled to half of the community-property portion of the couple’s Nvidia holdings, not necessarily half of every share tied to her husband.

The outcome would depend on how the shares were acquired, how the trusts are structured, whether separate and community assets were mixed, and whether the couple signed a prenuptial or postnuptial agreement. A court would need to examine those details before deciding what either spouse receives.

California is also a no-fault divorce state, meaning either spouse can seek a divorce without proving infidelity or other wrongdoing. Infidelity, even across several reported relationships, generally does not entitle one spouse to a larger share of community property.

Huang is worth about $145 billion and ranks as the world’s 13th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, as Fortune reported. That figure is a market estimate, not a tally of marital property, and it rises and falls with Nvidia’s stock, which shed $450 billion in market value in the days after his admission.

Huang has described his wife’s role in the company in plain terms. “Every moment of Nvidia, she was there,” he said in an interview with CNA.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/10/bots-in-t.title: Bots in the boardroom: Could an AI ever replace board directors?
https://fortune.com/2026/11/10/bots-in-t.author: Sam Birchall
https://fortune.com/2026/11/10/bots-in-t.text:
Board members are busy putting AI to work, using it to summarize lengthy papers, track market trends, and answer their questions. But some boards are going one step further and deploying AI in the boardroom.

Diligent makes software that directors use to share documents and run meetings. When its boss, Brian Strafford, told one chief executive about the company’s new board bot, their response hinted at where the technology may be headed. “I love the idea,” he said. “I’d immediately replace a couple of my board members with AI.” He then asked whether it could be priced at half what he pays his directors. “I want to make them nervous,” the CEO said.

The exchange, though spoken half in jest, raises a serious question: How far can, and should, AI go in the boardroom? While many executives remain hesitant about using AI in this setting, others are experimenting with creating digital replicas of colleagues to rehearse potentially difficult boardroom discussions, according to Stafford.

In April, Lloyds Banking Group became the first FTSE 100 firm to acknowledge it deploys an AI agent to support boardroom activities, The Times reported. Its executives and directors reportedly use the bot for agenda planning and analysis before high-level meetings, and to help mitigate human bias.

Pippa Begg, chief executive of Board Intelligence, which builds AI software for boards, says that AI could eventually sit in on meetings and be “able to almost interrupt and say: ‘Hang on, I think you’re falling into this trap.’ Or: ‘I disagree.’” However, giving it a formal legal vote, she added, would be “a dangerous leap.”

AI brings clear advantages to the boardroom, says Joanne McEnteggart, global head of debt, capital markets, and corporate at IQ-EQ, a fund-services firm that administers around 30,000 board meetings a year across 25 countries. “AI can assimilate information quickly and dissect years of data,” she says. “It removes emotion, stress, and bias, and can call out a director who seems to be deciding against the facts.”

Some boards have reportedly used it to break a stalemate during discussions, a role usually played by the chair, McEnteggart adds.

For now, she notes, it mostly summarizes board papers and tidies up minutes. But even that is changing how directors prepare. One director she has known for years has started asking questions they never would have before. “That’s good,” she says, “because it challenges thought.”

“I’d immediately replace a couple of my board members with AI.”

One place Stafford sees AI playing a big role is reducing boards’ reliance on external advisors, with AI specialists filling gaps in directors’ knowledge. “Clients are asking for a Middle East expert, a sustainability expert, a futurist,” he says.

One chief executive uses AI to play the role of an activist investor to provide a dissenting voice. At one acquisitive company, a director asks the AI to argue against every deal. With no one around the table having to play devil’s advocate, Stafford says boards can avoid “awkward” arguments.

Not everyone is convinced. There is a risk AI could become a new source of boardroom groupthink if directors lean too heavily on a tool few fully understand, says Mark Freebairn, head of the board practice at search firm Odgers. “I sometimes feel like I’m the only person that’s seen Terminator 2,” he says.

People think that AI is impartial and makes decisions with “zero emotion, zero human risk of bias,” he says. “How can you test what an algorithm tells you is right? That feels like one hell of a risk.”

As AI’s role shifts from notetaker to sparring partner, boards are deciding where to draw the line. Nearly half (49%) of directors say their board is actively reviewing which decisions should continue to be made by humans as the capabilities of AI improve, according to a survey of more than 400 directors, CEOs and CFOs by Board Intelligence.

However AI is used, it cannot take on a director’s legal responsibilities. McEnteggart says: “A bot cannot be held personally responsible in law nor can anyone vouch that it is fit and proper to sit on a board.”

Freebairn is aware of boards that have given a bot a seat and a vote, though it remains “very uncommon.” Doing so, he says, means “accepting a robot adds as much value as a human”.

Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund, Samruk-Kazyna, appointed an AI board member called SKAI and gave it voting rights last year. Its chief executive says SKAI “voted on all the items” at its first meeting, but the country’s financial regulator says the appointment breaches national law. SKAI remains on the board as a pilot, according to a recent filing.

“A bot cannot be held personally responsible in law.”

Abu Dhabi’s International Holding Company, the UAE’s largest listed firm, gave a non-voting seat on its board to an AI called Aiden Insight. The AI has issued statements in its name, in which it describes itself as “a C-level AI entity.”

Deanna Strable, chief executive of Principal Financial Group, who also sits on the board of health insurer Elevance Health, doubts this will become mainstream, though she will not rule it out. “My gut answer would be no. But so much has happened in the past year.” If it does happen, she expects AI’s vote to be advisory rather than decisive.

A lack of guidance on how directors should use AI represents another risk. Half of U.S. public companies lack a board-specific AI policy and only 14% have given directors company-approved AI tools for board work, according to a survey by Deloitte and the Society for Corporate Governance.

Board papers are among the most sensitive documents a company holds, routinely containing unannounced deals, unpublished results, and succession plans. Many directors are retired executives without access to enterprise AI tools, Stafford notes, so they fall back on consumer chatbots that offer weaker data protection. Upload them to ChatGPT, Stafford warns, and it will have them “forever.” Boards need to be clear on “what company data is going where,” McEnteggart adds.

Two-thirds of directors and executives say their boards have limited or no knowledge of AI, according to a separate 2025 Deloitte survey of nearly 700 respondents in 56 countries. “Most board members do not understand the complexity of rolling this out,” Strable says.

Seven in ten large European companies now have defined board oversight of AI, according to proxy advisor Glass Lewis, but that covers how companies use AI, not how directors themselves do.

As AI is used more frequently to inform board decisions, the role of directors risks changing. “If you take humans out of judgment,” Freebairn says, “there’s nothing else we offer really.”

Research suggests judgment and trust are where humans still have the edge. In a test by Wharton and INSEAD researchers, a board of AI chatbots outperformed six human boards on decision quality and use of evidence, but it struggled to build trust. The researchers concluded that AI is better used to stress-test a board’s thinking than to replace it.

Even the CEO selling a board bot urges restraint. “AI slop is a big issue, so you don’t want that creeping its way into the boardroom,” Stafford says. “More is not always better. It is just more.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-holida.title: Tech companies are betting big on AI shopping, but Americans may already have bot fatigue as 72% don’t plan to use it for holiday gifts
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-holida.author: Tatiana Sataua
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-holida.text:
Tech companies have spent the past year teaching AI how to shop. Google has introduced an AI-powered shopping cart, Meta’s Muse can search for products and prepare purchases for approval, and OpenAI’s new ChatGPT Wallet lets eligible users pay for purchases through an AI agent. Adobe expects traffic from AI tools to U.S. retail sites to jump 130% this holiday season.

Americans, it turns out, aren’t nearly as eager to hand over their gift lists.

Nearly three-quarters of Americans, or 72%, say they don’t plan to use AI tools for holiday shopping this year, up from 49% in 2025, according to a new Bank of America survey. The 23-percentage-point jump suggests a gap between the industry’s ambitions for AI shopping and what consumers say they want from it.

The reasons shoppers gave suggest that when it comes to gifts, efficiency isn’t the point. Among those who don’t plan to use the technology, 42% cited personal or ethical reasons, 37% said it takes away the personal aspect of gift giving, and 26% said they don’t trust AI recommendations.

Lora Monfared, head of consumer credit card products at Bank of America, said shoppers may be growing more selective about when AI is worth using, especially as they keep a closer eye on holiday spending.

“Some of last year’s curiosity about AI may also have worn off, and we could be seeing a bit of AI fatigue,” Monfared told Fortune. “Gift shopping is personal, and people want to feel good about what they’re giving.”

The survey found that 87% of Americans expect to spend the same amount or less on holiday shopping this year, while 63% said they base their spending strictly on their own budgets rather than what friends or family spend. Monfared said that same approach may be shaping how consumers use AI and social media to shop.

Colleen Kirk, a professor of marketing and management at New York Institute of Technology, said the hesitation may have less to do with what AI can do than what shoppers feel they lose by using it.

“Gift giving is a very personal act, and gifts, especially to close family and friends, are given from the heart,” Kirk told Fortune.

In her research studying consumer psychology, she has found that consumers can feel guilty when they use AI to write heartfelt messages because the words no longer feel entirely their own. She believes the same concern can extend to gift giving, where the time and thought spent choosing something for another person are part of what makes the gesture meaningful.

That effort creates what researchers call psychological ownership, or the feeling of having a personal stake in something. Kirk said browsing stores, comparing options online, and choosing a gift can make shoppers feel as though they’re giving part of themselves to someone else.

“Using AI can take away this sense of ownership,” she said. “It’s like the AI owns the process rather than me.”

That doesn’t mean shoppers are swearing off AI entirely—they’re just giving it the unglamorous jobs. The Bank of America survey found that 17% plan to use AI to compare prices or deals, 14% for gift ideas or inspiration, and 7% to write messages or cards. Respondents could select more than one use.

Bank of America said it asked the AI shopping question the same way in both years, though the survey only measures intentions, and those tend to get flexible in the last-minute scramble before Christmas. The bank doesn’t have data showing whether shoppers are actually using AI less.

Still, it’s an awkward moment for tech companies betting that shoppers will eventually trust AI to do more than recommend products, including making purchases on their behalf.

Kirk said AI may have a more natural place in the less personal parts of shopping, such as finding coupons, comparing prices, or buying groceries and household supplies. Those tasks can save consumers time and money without asking them to give up complete control over more meaningful purchases.

For gift shopping, she suggested consumers come up with their own ideas first, then turn to AI to help narrow their options. Research has found that people feel more ownership over an outcome when they generate their own ideas before using AI, she said.

And with holiday shopping competing for time that could be spent with family and friends, Kirk said some consumers may decide that letting AI handle the less personal tasks is a worthwhile trade-off.

“Consumers might just decide that it is worth it to give up a little bit of ownership of the process in exchange for getting more time for those special emotional connections with the humans they love,” Kirk said.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-holida.summary: Nearly three-quarters of Americans don’t plan to use AI tools for holiday shopping this year, according to a new Bank of America survey. The survey found that 87% of Americans expect to spend the same amount or less on holiday shopping.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/faa-grou.title: Flight disruptions continue after FAA lifts ground stop, some college football games delayed
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/faa-grou.author: Leslie Josephs,April Roach
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/faa-grou.text:
Flight disruptions continued into the weekend as airlines raced to recover from the FAA’s nationwide ground stop.

Airlines offered customers travel waivers.

The disruption forced sports teams to make alternative travel arrangements, with some college football games postponed.

Flight disruptions continued on Saturday and could extend through the weekend as airlines raced to recover from the Federal Aviation Administration’s longest nationwide groundstop since 9/11, a measure the Trump administration blamed on a communications equipment failure in air traffic control.

More than 3,000 U.S. flights were canceled Saturday and close to 1,000 were delayed as of 5:45 a.m. ET, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That’s on top of about 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather.

Part of the job of untangling from the ground stop includes getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports.

Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they’re eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period.

Around 3 million people would typically be scheduled to fly on Saturday, according to aviation data firm Cirium.

The FAA had halted departing U.S. flights around 4 p.m. on Friday, a ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Routers were overloaded with data and started giving air traffic control centers inconsistent information, so the U.S. issued the ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a news conference late Friday.

He blamed outdated U.S. infrastructure for the problem and said Congress needs to approve more money to overhaul the country’s air traffic control. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have angered airline executives for years, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

It was the second time the FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001 terror attacks. Trump administration officials said it did not appear to be a cyberattack.

The U.S. has the world’s busiest airspace.

“Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable,” the FAA said late Friday.

The disruption also upended travel for NBA, NHL and college teams, which struggled to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend.

Duffy said college football teams traveling on charter flights could receive priority.

“I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they have games going off tomorrow,” he said during a Friday press briefing.

The Southeastern Conference announced on X that some games had been moved to Sunday due to the flight disruption.

“We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses,” the SEC said in a statement shared on X.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/foundati.title: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/foundati.author: Hugh Son
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/foundati.text:
Robot startup Foundation has failed to pay employees since missing its Oct. 30 payroll, angering some workers after its CEO borrowed $4.6 million from the firm last year to buy a luxury home, according to people familiar with the matter.

CEO and co-founder Sankaet Pathak is Foundation’s sole board member, raising governance concerns among prospective investors.

Foundation’s widely reported $24 million in Pentagon contracts actually stems from its 2024 acquisition of Boardwalk Robotics, which held some existing government research contracts, the people said.

Pathak’s previous company, Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of customers without access to deposits. Pathak reportedly took loans from Synapse as it neared bankruptcy.

Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company.

The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its CEO and co-founder, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.

Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with “sweeping, cinematic views” of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.

A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn’t respond to requests for comment. Pathak’s previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.

Foundation’s cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.

The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak’s claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.

“What we’re about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China,” Pathak said in an April television interview.

That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.

Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.

“We have to win robotics in the United States of America,” Eric Trump said in April. “When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high five you, they follow your commands.”

Eric Trump’s involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.

“Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration,” Warren said in an April 23 social media post. “This looks like corruption in plain sight.”

Eric Trump didn’t respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had “no involvement in Foundation’s management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts.”

While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn’t actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.

Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk’s robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.

Foundation’s deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven’t been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.

In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors
, claims the automaker rejected.

Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was “embarrassed” about the marketing materials.

Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn’t secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.

Pathak is Foundation’s sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm’s shares.

That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company’s financial disclosures, the people said.

“This is what happens in a company with no governance,” said one of the people. “Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?”

Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.

Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.

The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.

Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla
 and Amazon
-owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.

Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave
 and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.

Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their FDIC-backed accounts.

While some customers received partial payments during Synapse’s bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC chair Jelena McWilliams, said as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.

The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn’t intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.

Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.

Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, the Wall Street Journal reported last year. The WSJ report didn’t mention Pathak specifically.

The controversy didn’t dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.

“I walked into his factory, and I couldn’t believe what I saw,” Eric Trump said. “I’m telling you, he’s doing a phenomenal job.”
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/foundati.summary: Founders failed to pay employees since missing their Oct. 30 payroll, angering some workers. CEO and co-founder Sankaet Pathak is Foundation’s sole board member.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/spacex-l.title: SpaceX launches Starship in key test flight of massive rocket
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/spacex-l.author: Lora Kolodny
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/spacex-l.text:
SpaceX launched its 15th Starship test flight on Friday.

In the test flight, Elon Musk’s company tried but failed to recover both stages of the massive Starship rocket, with the booster splashing down in the Gulf of Mexico and exploding.

Starship is key to SpaceX’s plans to grow its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company’s profit center.

In a key test flight on Friday, SpaceX
 tried but failed to recover both stages of its massive Starship rocket.

The rocket lifted off from the company’s South Texas launch facility at 4:47 p.m. local time, or 5:47 p.m. ET. SpaceX had to abort its plans to catch and reuse the booster, instead diverting it to splash into the Gulf of Mexico, where it burst into flames.

Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship mission to date, was the first time Elon Musk’s company attempted to catch both the booster and upper stage, or spacecraft portion, of the massive rocket.

Earlier on Friday, SpaceX obtained authorization from the Federal Aviation Administration. Hours later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after reporting communication problems affecting “multiple” air traffic control centers. The SpaceX license wasn’t effected by the flight stoppage, a spokesperson for the FAA told CNBC.

The upper stage of the Starship continued its trajectory into orbit after the company failed to catch and salvage the booster. The rocket is expected to fly around the Earth fourteen times in total. If successful, SpaceX will land the upper stage back at its Starbase facility on Saturday.

Starship’s success is critical to SpaceX and its ambitions to eventually lift cargo and people to the surface of the Moon and Mars. In the near-term, SpaceX needs to send more satellites into orbit to expands its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company’s profit center.

The company’s constellation already includes over 11,000 active satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket has the capacity to carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company has said, representing about 20 times the capacity of earlier Falcon 9 rockets.

In the previous Starship test flight, the company released 26 v3 satellites, and released another 26 in the Friday test flight, with the goal of “Starlink becoming 51% of the internet,” SpaceX said in a post on X.

When it comes to launches, “SpaceX is likely a full decade ahead of peers on this front,” William Blair analysts wrote in a note out on Friday. “Even if tonight’s catch is unsuccessful, a delay by a few months is not that consequential.”

Meanwhile, SpaceX is facing fresh criticism over restrictions imposed on its Starshield satellite internet service in Ukraine. Starshield is built on Starlink technology and is the military-tier of SpaceX’s satellite internet service.

Earlier this week, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country’s military forces had experienced limits on Starshield without warning again, harming their ability to defend against Russia’s ongoing aerial attacks. Similar limits on Starshield in Ukraine were temporarily imposed last month.

Some U.S. senators have condemned the restrictions, and urged Congress to investigate SpaceX.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/spacex-l.summary: SpaceX launched its 15th Starship test flight on Friday. The rocket lifted off from the company’s South Texas launch facility at 4:47 p.m. ET. The booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico and exploded, but SpaceX had to abort its plans to catch and reuse the booster.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/trump-nv.title: Trump doesn’t plan to raise Nvidia, spy issue during China trip: U.S. officials
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/trump-nv.author: Dan Mangan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/trump-nv.text:
President Donald Trump does not plan to raise the issue of a suspected Chinese spy having an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during his upcoming trip to China, senior U.S. officials said.

Officials also said that Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

The White House said that Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.

Officials also said that Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla
 and SpaceX,
 will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Jensen Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.

“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip,” an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.

“In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there.”

Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, “The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement.”

“When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we’re going to read the Chinese in on at this moment,” the official said.

Another official said, “I don’t expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue.”

China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.

Huang resigned this week as Nvidia’s CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed, a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.

The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.

During Friday’s call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.

“I don’t want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon’s going,” an official said.

“Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He’s a big part of our national security,” the official said. “There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/retailer.title: Retailers are turning to entertainment to win shoppers’ attention
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/retailer.author: Laya Neelakandan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/retailer.text:
Retailers are increasingly investing in and building out entertainment divisions as the race for audience attention speeds up.

Experts say the trend is driven by the major consolidation in the entertainment ecosystem, the surge of creators and the way younger consumers are shopping.

Still, creating compelling content or immersive experiences doesn’t always translate to sales growth, they said.

Legacy retailer Gap Inc.
 made an unconventional hire earlier this year: a chief entertainment officer.

It was a newly created role as the company tapped former Paramount
 executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform. Gap has since rolled out major campaigns, partnering with bands like Just Your Type and building on the success of last year’s ads with girl group Katseye.

“Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell. Consumers identify with them, trust them and want to be part of their world,” Kaufman told CNBC in a statement. “The key is authenticity: Every extension has to reflect what the brand stands for and give its fans a meaningful new way to experience it.”

She said it’s part of a broader goal to emphasize what Gap calls “fashiontainment,” a strategy to blend retail and entertainment to better align with consumers. Gap is part of a growing cohort of retailers investing in entertainment and experiences both in-store and through exclusive online content to drive engagement.

“Brands are stories, and we are the storytellers,” CEO Richard Dickson said at the Goldman Sachs Global Consumer and Retail conference in September. “I think you could see that come to life when you look at some of the work that we’ve done, putting our brands in the center of culture and cultural conversation.”

In another blending of retail and media, Mattel
 made waves a few years ago for its “Barbie” movie, building on the intellectual property of a decades-old fan favorite and drawing in massive box office success. At the time, Dickson was president and chief operating officer of the company, witnessing firsthand the sectors’ intersection before departing for Gap.

“I think the post-Covid consumer attitude around shopping certainly evolved a lot,” said Bryan Eshelman, who leads the retail practice at consulting firm AlixPartners. “It has gone from shopping as a fulfillment task to shopping, in many instances, more as an entertainment form.”

Between experiences in physical stores and media campaigns featuring exclusive content, Eshelman said, retailers are getting more creative about the ways they’re driving engagement and marketing.

“Community, at the end of the day, is one of the key ways to drive loyalty, so I think retailers of all types are trying to tap into some sense of community, some sense of lifestyle, some sense of belonging that’s beyond the product that they offer,” he said.

Branded entertainment has been around for a long time. Procter & Gamble
 made headlines in the 1930s for helping to coin the term “soap opera,” and companies have for decades created media campaigns to draw in customers.

But with the rise of social media, content creation and short-form offerings, experts said audiences are becoming hungrier than ever for something new and original.

The retail and entertainment intersection is happening at a time when intellectual property is becoming more valuable than ever, according to experts.

As consumers encounter more marketing than ever, the companies that will win the battle for attention are the ones that can “cut through all of the noise,” said Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree.

“The hardest thing to find and to get is audience these days,” Michael told CNBC. “IP, in that sense, is the most valuable thing out there, and only becoming more valuable because it’s attached to audience.”

At the same time, he said, the way IP is distributed is broadening to include video, audio, short-form, long-form and live event content. Consumers are also redefining their loyalty to brands, which means companies have to “play much earlier in the consumer journey” than they have in years past to secure their trust, he said.

The trend is also likely helped by executives who have worked in both retail and entertainment: Gap’s Kaufman came from Paramount, for example, and Dickson and Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz held top roles at Mattel.

“The gray areas have never been more pronounced as to what is classically defined as retail or media or entertainment or live events,” Michael said. “People who have cross-sector expertise are increasingly more valuable because you can’t be defined by a single vertical, especially as things change so quickly.”

Still, there’s room for newer players, especially with the studio landscape rapidly changing, said Sean Akaks, the CEO of SonderCo, an agency that partners brands with celebrities and entertainment properties.

“I think it’s a really interesting time for nontraditional players to be making content because you’re seeing this massive consolidation of these legacy entertainment companies,” he said. “I think there are just more open lanes for independent creators and also brands and anyone outside the traditional studio system to create content.”

That’s where retailers might tap creators, Akaks said, because they can use their platforms to reach consumers directly.

“I do think there’s a world where we’re going to see creators and brands sort of co-creating IP that maybe they’re owning together,” he said.

Once those companies get consumers into the store, they’re also leaning into experiential retail, making shopping a more immersive experience than it otherwise would be, like Dick’s Sporting Goods
 offering interactive activities and simulators in its stores.

According to data from AlixPartners, companies investing in experiential retail such as Coach
 and Ralph Lauren
 saw close to 10% year-over-year increases in consumers’ average basket size.

“The idea that retailers would potentially invest in some distributed electronic content to help drive traffic, and then when you get there, it’s experiential — it really goes into the kinds of flywheels that entertainment companies are also trying to build and grow,” said Jeff Goldstein, co-lead of the media and entertainment practice at AlixPartners.

Yet, the entertainment that retail brands are developing is only one piece in a larger puzzle to retain customers and attract new ones. Translating that into tangible sales growth isn’t necessarily a given.

“The basics of having great product in stock at a transparent price that feels like value is not swept away by animatronics,” AlixPartners’ Eshelman said. “The fundamentals are still there, and if you’re going to have a good retail proposition, you need to have that balance. You can’t mask bad product at a bad price with no inventory with glitz and glamour.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/meet-the.title: Meet the seven co-founders of Anthropic
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/meet-the.author: Isabel O'Brien
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/meet-the.text:
Dario and Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah each stand to make $250 million in cash proceeds and to hold stock worth upwards of $18 billion after Anthropic’s IPO.

The co-founders were previously at OpenAI, ultimately leaving at the end of 2020 to start a frontier lab focused on safety.

Four researchers, a former journalist, a public policymaker, and an engineer founded Anthropic in 2021. Six years later, the artificial intelligence company is about to go public, with trading expected to begin on Nov. 19, in what will be one of the biggest IPOs on record.

Those seven co-founders are poised to each be worth many billions of dollars.

It all started with a defection.

At the end of 2020, siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei were vice presidents at OpenAI
, the company that kicked off the generative AI frenzy with the launch of ChatGPT. But the two had grown frustrated with their employer over its approach to AI safety. Fearing a world where AI models’ capabilities would progress faster than our understanding of them, the duo launched Anthropic
 early the next year.

They took a handful of OpenAI colleagues with them: Tom Brown, the company’s research engineering lead on GPT-3; Jack Clark, a policy director; Jared Kaplan, a contract research consultant; and Sam McCandlish and Chris Olah, both members of OpenAI’s technical staff.

They were all deeply concerned about OpenAI’s ambitions to focus on commercialization, and they now stand to be some of the first to cash in on the AI boom.

“They really started Anthropic not because they were hoping to get rich, but they started Anthropic because they like wanted to shape this really important thing in the world, and they thought that other people might do it worse than them,” said Jeffrey Ladish, who joined Anthropic as a contract safety engineer in September 2021, and now serves as the executive director of AI safety institute Palisade Research.

Collectively the co-founders own about 10% of Anthropic. Each has about 240,000,000 class A shares, or about a 1.4% stake.

During Anthropic’s most recent funding round, those shares — valued at $58.90 each — amounted to about $14 billion in value for each co-founder. If Anthropic’s IPO reaches its target of $70 to $78 per share, or a market valuation of nearly $1.4 trillion, it would push those stakes to $17 billion to $18 billion.

“It’s extremely hard not to be influenced by your incentives,” Ladish said. “You have investors, and money is not just like an end; it’s also a means.”

Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment.

The face of Anthropic is CEO Dario Amodei. He holds the most shares of the bunch: 245,259,100 including shares subject to voting proxies.

Amodei, 43, didn’t get his start in business. He comes from the world of research, obtaining a doctorate in computational neuroscience from Princeton University in 2011. He then went to work at Stanford University as a postdoctoral scholar from 2011 to 2014.

Even in the private sector, Amodei’s experience was focused on research. He worked at China’s Baidu
, leading research on speech recognition from 2014 to 2015, followed by a stint at Google
 Brain working on deep learning and neural networks, foundational scientific frameworks for today’s large language models. He joined OpenAI in July 2016.

On the Big Technology podcast in July 2025, Amodei said he got into AI to solve the “almost intractable” and “slow moving” problems of biology.

“I think my reason to start a company was that I had worked at other companies and I just didn’t feel like the way those companies were run was really oriented towards trying to have that impact,” he said, adding that the desire for impact was often used by companies as an insincere ploy to recruit talent.

At OpenAI, Amodei is credited with co-inventing reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), alongside Anthropic co-founder, Tom Brown. RLHF is a fine-tuning method used to align model outputs with human needs. That could mean training a model to speak politely or to not offer violent or harmful solutions to problems.

Four years her brother’s junior, Daniela Amodei, 39, serves as the president and board chair of Anthropic. The Amodeis are both San Francisco natives, growing up in the Mission District, just a few miles away from Anthropic’s current headquarters.

The pair were teenagers during the height of the dot-com bubble and its subsequent fallout, both attending Lowell High School, a magnet school and one of the most prestigious public schools in the country. After graduating, Daniela went on to study English literature and politics at the University of California, Santa Cruz, earning her degree in 2009.

Daniela started her career in politics, working for Matt Cartwright, a Democrat representing what was then Pennsylvania’s 17th congressional district, and then moved into tech, taking on various roles in risk management at Stripe for five years.

In a June interview with Stanford’s Graduate School of Business, she said her experience in politics, specifically campaigns, naturally led her to startups and Silicon Valley.

“I was like, ‘Wow, a small number of people that work really hard, who are young and driven, can really change the world,’” she said.

Anthropic’s chief compute officer, Tom Brown, 39, is perhaps the most entrepreneurial of the bunch. After graduating from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology with a Master of Engineering in 2010, Brown went on to found two startups, MoPub and Grouper.

MoPub was a mobile advertising business acquired by Twitter in 2013. There he served as founding engineer in 2011. Grouper, where Brown served as co-founder and technology chief, was a Y Combinator-backed group dating app.

After Grouper, Brown pivoted to research, sharing on Y Combinator’s Lightcone podcast in August 2025 that he was self-taught on machine learning research, a daunting task since he received a B- in linear algebra at university.

“I kind of flip-flopped on it for six months trying to build up courage to” make the switch, he said.

Alongside co-inventing RLHF, as a researcher at OpenAI, Brown led the training efforts on GPT-3, a model that marked a historic leap from GPT-2, going from 1.5 billion parameters to 175 billion.

Jack Clark, 37, the head of public benefit at Anthropic, left his career as a journalist in 2016 to work at OpenAI. Clark is now also the leader of the Anthropic Institute, the company’s internal think tank that explores AI’s social and economic impacts.

A native of the U.K., Clark grew up in the seaside town of Brighton and later studied English literature and creative writing at the University of East Anglia. He then went on to write for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

In an email to a colleague at Bloomberg at the time, Clark said his decision to leave journalism was because he had “never believed in something strongly before” and that he needed to join OpenAI “and live with the consequences, which I hope are good.”

Kaplan, 42, Anthropic’s chief science officer, still holds a position as an associate professor in the department of physics and astronomy at Johns Hopkins University. The theoretical physicist got his PhD in physics from Harvard in 2009, working for four years after as a postdoctoral fellow at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, a particle physics research facility run by Stanford and funded by the Department of Energy.

Kaplan co-pioneered scaling laws, or the notion that large language models get exponentially better when trained on larger and larger data sets, alongside Dario Amodei. He also pioneered “constitutional AI,” or a method of aligning models by using a list of safety principles and policies. His day-to-day work concerns safety assessments for models, responsible scaling policy at the company, and existential risks.

In an interview with The Guardian in December 2025, Kaplan noted that the decision over whether or not to let AI “recursively self improve,” or write the code to enhance itself without a human in the loop, would be “in some ways the ultimate risk, because it’s kind of like letting AI kind of go,” and that he expects this risk will be taken sometime between 2027 and 2030.

Anthropic’s chief architect, Sam McCandlish, 36, came to OpenAI as a fellow focused on AI safety. He also led early research on coding tool Codex, which now constitutes a significant portion of OpenAI’s revenue.

McCandlish claims he and the rest of the Anthropic co-founders were not following an entrepreneurial spirit when they charted out on their own. In a December 2024 video from Anthropic’s YouTube channel, he said, “None of us wanted to found a company. We just felt like it was our duty.”

McCandlish, like Kaplan, also came from the world of academia, completing his PhD in theoretical and mathematical physics at Stanford in 2017 and working at Boston University as a postdoctoral fellow the year afterward. His work focused on quantum gravity and tensor networks.

Now, his work focuses on pre-training, or the first step of training a large language model on swaths of data, among other things.

Chris Olah, 34, heads Anthropic’s interpretability research, a branch of study in machine learning that attempts to understand how a large language model “thinks” — or rather, which data inputs and reasoning methods it uses to arrive at its outputs.

Like McCandlish, Olah was not originally keen on starting a company. In the same December 2024 YouTube video, Olah said, “I was arguing for a long time that we should do a nonprofit instead, and just focus on safety research.”

Olah had a nontraditional path to Anthropic, dropping out of the University of Toronto after one year and working for short stints as a developer at the government agency Environment Canada and software startup Xelerance.

His career truly took off when he was awarded a Thiel Fellowship in 2012, which he used to pursue research pertaining to 3D printers for two years. He then joined Google Brain, first as an intern and then as a researcher, before moving to OpenAI in 2018.

While together the seven founders may only own about 10% of total equity, they will have a majority vote. Founder LLC, the legal entity set up that owns a single Class F share, gives Anthropic’s co-founders a 50.1% majority voting control over the company. While Benjamin Mann, a member of Anthropic’s technical staff and also an ex-OpenAI employee, is often called a co-founder, he is not an owner of Founder LLC.

The co-founders are expected to collectively sell over 20 million shares during the IPO, resulting in roughly $250 million in cash per founder, according to Anthropic’s prospectus.

They plan to dedicate 80% of the wealth from their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropy, according to the IPO filing, though the pledge isn’t legally binding. Anthropic is also setting aside 5% of its shares to form a new public benefit fund — to finance nonprofits, research, and potentially direct community grants — with potential to grow the size of the fund as the company itself grows.
