https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/data-cen.title: Why the data center slowdown concern is overblown. Two stocks to buy amid the fear
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/data-cen.author: Brian Sullivan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/data-cen.text:
No, the data center boom isn’t over.

Not one utility CEO we spoke with at the EEI conference is anticipating a slowdown in electricity growth expectations.

Power Insider exclusive: Two utility stocks that stand to benefit if data center business leaves Texas.

Our exclusive with Texas billionaire and U.S. Ambassador to Italy Tilman Fertitta.

GET THIS IN YOUR INBOX FIRST: Subscribe to CNBC’s “Power Insider” newsletter.

The demise of data centers has been greatly exaggerated. So says every utility CEO and energy-focused investor we spoke with at the Edison Electric Institute’s annual conference in Arizona. Here’s why...

There is a lot of misleading, misdirected, or straight-up incorrect information floating around about data centers and the AI buildout. I’m not going to dive into the old water-use story — you can do your own research on that — but rather focus this week on what the insiders know: Some newly elected politicians either don’t have the power to stop the buildouts or, if they do, the buildout will likely just continue somewhere else.

Ohio and Georgia are important states to watch with their new incoming political class, but for the sheer importance in size and scope, I’ll focus on the energy and data center capital: Texas.

Incoming Governor Gina Hinojosa and incoming Senator James Talarico both campaigned on promises to go after what they believe to be affordability issues around data centers. I say “what they believe to be” because it’s unclear how much data centers may raise your electricity bill, if at all.

First and foremost, data centers are largely a state issue, meaning officials elected to federal office have little control over outcomes, at least for now. In Texas, any cancellations or moratoriums on new builds will come from the statehouse in Austin. That’s where current Governor Greg Abbott has already, and rather quietly, put his own “pause” on data center permitting. That delay has been underway for a few weeks. Also, in Texas, the Governor has less direct power than in some other states. The power the governor does have largely derives from the authority to appoint those in charge of the all-important permitting process.

In the Lone Star State, that power lies with two agencies: the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the even lesser-known Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ). The PUCT regulates Texas’ electricity, telecom, and water industries. It helps oversee growth of anything electricity-grid-related. So if a data center wants to connect to the public utility grid, it needs the commission’s approval. Its chair — a pro-growth chap named Thomas Gleeson —is also on the board of Texas’ electric grid powerhouse ERCOT and will serve his term with the utility commission through September 2029. Yes, three years from now.

That agency gets involved when a data center or power provider wants to connect to the electricity grid. But what about facilities that are off the grid and have their own dedicated power sources? Texas has less control over what happens then. That said, it does have to authorize certain environmental permits, and that responsibility largely lies with the TCEQ. The TCEQ was “BBI” (my own little term for “boring, but important”) until data centers came along. It’s not exactly the Alamo, but this obscure group — run by a regulator named Brooke Paup — is largely the “last stand” for permitting on those new builds. Paup was also appointed by Gov. Abbott and serves through next year. In other words, unless she and Gleeson step down or there is some way to oust them, the regulatory environment in Texas may not change much.

The bottom line in this brief foray into the Texas regulatory swamp is to highlight that there are things for investors to consider around the data center/energy world that may not be at the top of the headlines.

Important Note → Be mindful that I am an East Coast-based financial broadcaster and journalist, not an expert on Texas regulation or how the state operates. There may very well be things I don’t know, things my sources aren’t aware of, or other ways in which the new Governor and state House can assert power. For one, she recently said she may try to freeze electricity rates. Hint: that would be a terrible idea unless you want to damage the growth of badly needed new power sources like wind and solar.

Disclaimer is done. Let’s assume I am wrong on Texas and there is a larger push to slow or stop data center growth in the state. Conversations with some pretty smart people lead me to believe that if those facilities aren’t built in that state, they will be built in another: Louisiana, Oklahoma, or another state. Sources tell me that Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry and his team are already working the phones, telling companies that his state would love to welcome new business. Same for Oklahoma. Both are gas-rich, have plenty of power, and are only too happy to grab any data center dollars.

Let’s acknowledge that not all data centers are going to be built… and never were. There are way too many plans to make them all happen. Some DCs were shelved before the election. Some others may soon be canceled, either for reasons of public pushback or otherwise. It’s also not clear if we even need all the planned compute. There will be a time when companies realize they have enough — or at least enough for now — and turn off the spending taps.

Goldman Sachs lays it out in a new note late this week:

“The midterm election results pose only modest risks to AI investment, for now. We expect newly elected Democratic governors in states that account for over a third of planned US data center capacity to impose moratoria on new data centers. However, these will likely only impact projects not yet permitted, leaving the vast majority of planned 2027 construction unaffected. We therefore expect data center construction spending to remain strong next year, though moratoria that are stricter or longer-lasting than we expect pose downside risks.”

The firm adds that it still sees spending on AI-related hardware coming in around $1.4 trillion by the end of next year. In other words, the spending boom is going to keep going, at least for now.

Another key point for all you energy- or utility-focused investors out there: While data centers are one huge driver of electricity demand, they aren’t the only one. Electric cars, reshoring manufacturing, and the “electrification of everything” will also grow the need for more gigawatts. This is why we asked every utility CEO we spoke with at the EEI conference if they saw any slowdown in their internal electricity growth estimates. All gave the same answer: no. Not one hinted at a downturn. Not Exelon’s Calvin Butler. Not Entergy’s Drew Marsh. And not Drew Maloney, head of EEI. Of course, power demand is about more than just data centers, but it’s still important for investors to hear it from the top.

Side note: Many of you think I’m wrong about my “hot take” on data centers and the election. If you missed last week’s Power Insider, this is how you responded to my X poll on the election and energy.

So… why am I writing this week about AI and data centers? Because, as I’ve said before and will keep saying, AI and data centers are just energy stories in disguise. If they grow, energy demand grows. Demand for solar, wind, and natural gas grows. The economy grows. Because, after all, energy is the economy.

Oh, and in the past week, I’ve flown from Newark to Rome to Chicago to Phoenix and back to Newark. My brain may be a little mushy, so bear with me.

So now that my big take on data centers and regulation is over, let’s get granular. What energy stocks do you buy right now?

Let’s get the “1-2-3” on six stocks: one in solar, two in power, and three in oil and gas.

One: William Blair is upgrading First Solar (FSLR) to Outperform. The election result is part of the story. Analyst Jed Dorsheimer and his team believe the new Congress and certain state governorships will benefit local support for utility-scale solar, and that First Solar is best-positioned, though he does caution investors that it may take “some time to show up in the bookings.” He adds that Texas is the largest builder of solar, so the shift in state-level leadership is a big deal. Fair warning, however: upgrades do not mean the stock will go higher. Deutsche Bank upgraded FSLR back in early July — an upgrade I wrote about — and the stock has fallen 22% since.

Two: Staying with the macro power theme, Barclays’ Nicholas Campanella is particularly optimistic on two utility names. He tells Power Insider that he “really likes NiSource (NI) and Xcel Energy (XEL) right now.” It has to do in part with what I just wrote about above. Campanella says the political outcomes in states such as Texas and Georgia may drive investors into utilities in other areas, particularly those with “more stable and established data center policies in place.” That would fit with Indiana-based NiSource and Minnesota-based Xcel. While Minnesota may have a Democratic tilt, the company operates in eight different states. It is also working with Alphabet (GOOGL) on a massive new data center, and CEO Bob Frenzel told us that he is confident they can successfully navigate it all.

Three: Now to the “3”… three picks on what powers some of the power: oil and natural gas.

In an interview on CNBC, Bernstein analyst Bob Brackett says he likes ExxonMobil (XOM), calling it a great “barbell” play between natural gas and refined products. Brackett — a former Exxon employee — also believes it’s a relatively “safe” stock to own right now in the volatile and headline-driven world of energy. Brackett has an Outperform rating and $186 target on the stock, giving it about another 10% upside from here.

Brackett also likes the lesser-known Expand Energy (EXE). If you’re not familiar with Expand Energy, don’t worry; it’s still relatively new. The company is the combination of Chesapeake Energy and Southwestern Energy. It’s a natural gas behemoth, and Brackett says the gas story is a “great long-term story” that’s trading below a “midcycle price,” and Expand fits right into it. Brackett also notes that Expand has a new CEO. He has a $139 target on the stock, making him one of the more bullish analysts on the Street. Expand has a median price target of $123.54.

Meanwhile, the chart looks tasty on another energy name: Cheniere Energy (LNG). Piper Sandler technical guru Craig Johnson likes the stock, and while he isn’t a fundamental energy analyst, he was one of the few to upgrade the entire sector back in February when the Iran war began. Cheniere — along with Venture Global (VG) — is a pure play on why I was just in Europe: the worsening European energy crisis. Cheniere exports massive quantities of U.S. natural gas to customers in Europe, Asia, and other parts of the world. Johnson likes Cheniere in part because it recently broke out of a “very big base,” and he wants to buy stocks that are on the upswing.

Cheniere is a well-run, rather quiet company with a fantastic CEO in longtime energy executive Jack Fusco. Jack has forgotten more about running an energy business than most will know, and the company continues to expand production. As I’ve pointed out for over four years, without American natural gas, Europe would be in dire straits and cutting demand even more than it already is. It’s not hyperbole to say that American natural gas is — literally — keeping the lights and the heat on across Germany, Italy, and other countries.

Remember this incredible stat: just one tanker of LNG can produce a year’s worth of power for over 100,000 average-sized European homes. Next year, Europe is still planning to stop buying LNG from Russia. That means demand for American natural gas is only going one way: up.

This week’s Inside Line is with Amrita Sen, founder and director of market intelligence at Energy Aspects. Amrita is one of the smartest and most well-connected energy experts in the world, and she took a few minutes from her constant travel to answer a couple of questions.

This week’s Take A Look is a little outside the norm, but an important interview nonetheless. It’s with the U.S. Ambassador to Italy, business magnate, and former star of CNBC’s Billion Dollar Buyer, Tilman Fertitta. In a wide-ranging interview from the ambassador’s residence in Rome, we talked about that day’s stock market crash, business, the consumer, and, of course, energy. Full disclosure: Tilman and I have been friends for over 15 years.

This Washington Post article was published a few days after the election. The underlying research from Harvard University and the University of Pennsylvania that it was based on is here and is worth a read. The study came out on October 9 (and yes, I missed it as well).

Not blaming data centers for higher energy costs is definitely random, but interesting!

Catch up with more on energy including interviews and video content from CNBC and Power Insider.

Read the last issue of Power Insider here.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-h.title: Nvidia hasn’t selected search firm for permanent Huang replacement, board tells CNBC
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-h.author: Seema Mody,Annie Palmer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-h.text:
Nvidia hasn’t chosen a search firm to identify potential candidates to replace former CEO Jensen Huang, the company’s board told CNBC.

Speculation has swirled around who the board will select to permanently succeed Huang.

“We have not formally engaged any potential candidates,” the board said in a statement.

Nvidia
 hasn’t yet selected a search firm to work with in identifying a successor for former CEO Jensen Huang, the company’s board told CNBC.

“We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role,” the board said in a Friday statement. “We have not formally engaged any potential candidates.”

The comments come after speculation has swirled about who might be tapped to replace Huang. Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang would step down as CEO of the chipmaker after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman purported to be a Chinese spy.

Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO and said it will begin a search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, adding that it will consider both internal and external candidates. Kress conducted her first meeting as interim CEO on Thursday afternoon with high-level executives at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named in order to discuss internal details.

The Financial Times reported Friday that Nvidia’s board has approached Arm
 CEO Rene Haas in its search for Huang’s successor, citing people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia’s board said, “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature.”

Before joining the SoftBank-backed chip company in 2013, Haas spent seven years at Nvidia, serving in a variety of roles including vice president of its computing products business.

Nvidia shares fell more than 2% on Friday, dragging the company’s market cap below $4 trillion as investors digested the news of Huang’s departure, and the specter of ongoing probes into his conduct.

On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Wachtell Lipton to investigate allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, following revelations that its then-CEO had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang, who several outlets reported is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.

Three House committees have asked Huang to appear for briefings, and renewed those calls even after the CEO’s resignation. The Senate Banking Committee has also requested that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify to discuss “serious concerns about our national security,” and how the company’s top AI chips have reportedly ended up in China.

The comments come after speculation has swirled about who might be tapped to replace Huang.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.title: A Wildland Firefighter Ends Montana Democrats’ Three-Decade Drought in the US House
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.author: By Mosabber Hossain
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.text:
For three decades, Montana voters had not elected a Democrat to the U.S. House of Representatives. That changed earlier this month when Sam Forstag, a former wildland firefighter and union leader, defeated Republican Aaron Flint in Montana’s 1st Congressional District.

During his congressional campaign, Forstag, 32, who as a leader in the National Federation of Federal Employees represented some 800 U.S. Forest Service workers in the Lolo, Bitterroot and Gallatin national forests, promised to strengthen federal land management agencies and improve wildfire preparedness.

In an interview with The Wild Idea Podcast before the election, Forstag called for simplifying the permitting process for prescribed burns and increasing wildland firefighters’ base pay to reduce their dependence on overtime. He argued that investing in measures such as prescribed burning and forest thinning could reduce the risk of destructive wildfires and save taxpayers money. He also proposed pursuing standalone legislation to fund those efforts.

Forstag has also expressed support for the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act, which would strengthen workers’ rights to form unions and bargain collectively. Democratic Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia introduced the bill in the House in March 2025, with a companion bill introduced by independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont. The legislation remains in committee and has not passed either chamber of Congress.

In a post-election email to supporters, Forstag outlined four priorities for his first term in Congress: affordable housing, healthcare, reducing the cost of living and campaign finance reform. Although wildfire preparedness and Forest Service staffing were central to his campaign, neither appeared among the four priorities listed in that email. But, in a separate message thanking supporters, Forstag reaffirmed his commitment to protecting Montana’s wild places for future generations.

Forstag has already begun challenging the Trump administration’s plans for federal public lands. In a Facebook video posted Nov. 12  from the U.S. Capitol, he criticized a new Interior Department proposal to reduce federal land holdings.

“They’re trying to sell off our public lands, but we won’t let them,” Forstag said. He also said he had reached out to Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, whom he is replacing, hoping the outgoing congressman would oppose any effort to sell federal lands. Zinke’s office separately confirmed his opposition to federal land sales and transfers.

Forstag has also expressed interest in working with Republican Rep. Troy Downing, who represents eastern Montana. In a Facebook post, on Nov. 11, Forstag identified protecting public lands as an area where the two lawmakers could find common ground, despite their political differences. “”We can get so much more done for Montana when we work together in Congress,” he wrote.

Forstag said he would seek a position on the House Natural Resources Committee after taking office in January, giving him an opportunity to influence federal land policy. The Interior Department’s five-year strategic plan proposes selling some federal lands to states, tribes and local governments, although officials have not identified specific parcels. Whether Forstag can influence the administration’s plans will depend partly on congressional cooperation and the legal limits on such sales.

During freshman orientation in Washington, D.C. last week, Forstag said he was seeking congressional committee assignments that would give western Montana a stronger voice on housing and rebuilding federal public lands agencies. He also said he planned to join both the moderate Blue Dog Coalition and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, hoping to work across different wings of the Democratic Party to advance economic policies that benefit working people.

In a separate Facebook post, Forstag congratulated the newly elected members of Montana’s American Indian Caucus, which will have a record 14 Native American lawmakers into the state’s 2027 legislative session, and expressed support for tribal sovereignty, treaty rights, and Tribal water and land rights. He said the caucus would be an important voice for Native communities in the state Legislature.

Forstag’s victory marks a historic political shift in Montana, where Democrats have not won a U.S. House election since 1994. His win also brings a former firefighter to Washington at a time when federal workforce cuts have raised concerns about wildfire preparedness, Forest Service staffing and public lands management. During his campaign, Forstag pledged to restore staffing at federal land management agencies and expand fuels reduction crews as well as simplify the permitting process for prescribed burns and increase the use of such treatments to prevent costly wildfires.

While supporters hope his experience will help address those challenges, political observers caution that turning campaign promises into federal policy will not be easy for a first-term congressman.

“Forstag by himself cannot do much, of course,” said University of Montana political scientist Abhishek Chatterjee.

His ability to influence federal policy will depend on cooperation with other lawmakers, said Chatterjee. Other newly elected lawmakers may share Forstag’s goals to increase funding for wildfire prevention, he added, but presidential veto power and Senate filibusters could limit such efforts.

Chatterjee also expects Forstag to be a part of increased congressional opposition to certain proposals involving public land swaps or transferring federal lands to state governments.

The Forstag campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

According to unofficial results from the Montana Secretary of State, Forstag received 132,003 votes, or 50.34 percent, compared with Flint’s 122,694 votes, or 46.79 percent. Libertarian Nick Sheedy received 7,522 votes.

Forstag’s victory ends a three-decade absence of Democrats from Montana’s U.S. House delegation. Pat Williams, the last Democrat elected to Montana’s U.S. House delegation, retired in 1996.

County-level election results show that Forstag received strong support in several of western Montana’s larger population centers.

In Missoula County, he received 41,232 votes, or 68.24 percent; in Gallatin County, which includes Bozeman, he took 59.42 percent: and in Silver Bow County he garnered 61.55 percent.

Together, Missoula and Gallatin counties gave Forstag a combined advantage of 35,226 votes, helping him overcome Flint’s leads in several rural counties of the district.

Forstag’s personality may have contributed to his success, said Bill Hallinan, a member of Montana Conservation Elders and Wild Montana who noted that he was not speaking on behalf of either organization.

Hallinan described Forstag as “sincere and relatable” and suggested that his campaign may have been better organized in larger cities. Forstag may have better addressed economic concerns that influenced voters, he suggested, while Flint presented himself as a loyal supporter of President Donald Trump.

Several factors may have contributed to Forstag’s victory, Chatterjee said, including his background as a wildland firefighter and union leader, federal workforce cuts under the Trump administration and broader dissatisfaction with the administration’s policies and economic conditions.

“Gas prices in particular would have played a role,” Chatterjee said in an email to Inside Climate News.

Before entering politics, Forstag worked as a wildland firefighter with the U.S. Forest Service, including as a smokejumper, parachuting into remote areas to fight wildfires. He also represented workers in the National Federation of Federal Employees.

That experience became central to his campaign as it focused on protecting federal employees and challenging workforce reductions under the Trump administration.

Forstag’s victory has raised expectations among environmental advocates who believe his firsthand experience could help bring attention to the challenges facing federal land management agencies.

His campaign platform outlines several proposals to strengthen wildfire protection, protect federal jobs and improve public lands management. He has pledged to expand federal land management agencies, rather than just return them to the staffing levels they had prior to the second Trump administration’s cuts, and increase funding for forest management and operations to reduce loads of vegetation that can fuel severe wildfires, creating more jobs while shifting resources toward wildfire prevention. He also supports responsible timber harvesting and federal grants to modernize Montana’s timber mills, while opposing the use of emergency authorizations and fast-track programs to bypass environmental protections in forest management projects. Forstag’s platform calls for ending the use of emergency authorizations and fast-track programs that bypass environmental protections, while improving the review process for forest management projects.

Amy Cilimburg, executive director of Climate Smart Missoula, a nonprofit organization, said Montana could benefit from having a representative who understands wildfire response and the importance of federal agencies.

“Congress has the power of the purse, and federal agencies, including scientific bodies, need to be consistently staffed and funded,” Cilimburg said in an email. “The needed response to climate risks like reduced snowpack, hotter temperatures, longer fire seasons, and drought is to lean into credible science and rebuild our public agencies and work forces,” she said.

Hallinan also hopes Forstag will support stronger Forest Service staffing and continued federal grants for wildfire preparedness and education.

“More forest service staff means more hands to organize, assist, coordinate and administrate,” Hallinan said.

He emphasized the importance of protecting communities in the wildland-urban interface, where homes and developed areas meet flammable forests and open spaces.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.title: An Obscure Utility Calculation Is Putting a Thumb on the Scale for Gas in Georgia
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.author: By Ryan Krugman
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.text:
The growth of data centers and rapid electrification is driving Georgia Power toward another major expansion of its electric grid. The state’s largest utility is preparing to add between 2,000 and 6,000 megawatts of new capacity to its grid for 2032 and 2033. The utility is considering a mix of resources, including natural gas and battery storage, to meet its future electricity needs.

But how much each resource counts toward that expansion depends on a calculation called Effective Load Carrying Capability, or ELCC. It is the “critical renewable energy concept you’ve never heard of,” according to the Union of Concerned Scientists. And the way Georgia Power is using that calculation in its latest effort to secure new power generation is drawing scrutiny from renewable energy advocates across the state.

Prior to the rise of renewable energy, determining how much capacity a new power project added to the grid was relatively simple. Utilities projected peak electricity demand and ensured they had enough power plants available to meet it.

But because renewable resources like solar and wind are variable, planning grid expansions has become more complex. The sun is not always shining and the wind is not always blowing, making it more difficult to determine how much reliable capacity renewable projects actually add to the grid.

ELCC is a way of measuring how much capacity a power resource can reliably contribute to the grid. A resource with a 100 percent ELCC can be counted on for its full capacity when determining how much electricity the grid can reliably support. Natural gas typically has an ELCC near 60 to 80 percent, while solar and wind projects without battery storage can have ELCCs between 4 to 40 percent. With batteries, renewables can have ELCCs around 95 percent, but that value can fall as more batteries are added to the grid.

In its previous planning, Georgia Power assigned battery storage an ELCC of 95 percent for its first 3,000 megawatts of capacity, 75 percent for the next 3,000 megawatts and 50 percent for the next 3,000 megawatts. As more batteries are added, they become less valuable during peak demand because they increasingly compete to provide power at the same time.

Based on the amount of battery storage on the grid and planned for the future, the utility’s previous calculations suggest the current ELCC should be set at around 75 percent. The latest procurement, however, uses a much lower figure.

According to Bob Sherrier, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center and the Advanced Power Alliance, which both testified about the issue to Georgia regulators, Georgia Power is now using an ELCC of just 20 percent for battery storage in its upcoming procurement. That means a 1,000-megawatt battery project would count for just 200 megawatts toward the utility’s capacity needs. A 1,000-megawatt natural gas plant with an 80 percent ELCC, by comparison, would count for 800 megawatts.

ELCC calculations are based on modeling under different conditions and assumptions. Georgia Power did not provide details on the calculations but did tell Inside Climate News they have been consistent and are committed to accurate evaluations of all resources. In response to  additional questions about the request for proposal, a company representative said “the company is in the middle of several ongoing resource procurements and cannot comment on specifics of requests for proposals.”

The steep drop in ELCC from Georgia Power’s previous calculations could put battery storage at a disadvantage as the utility evaluates projects for its planned 2,000 to 6,000-megawatt expansion, Sherrier said. With a lower ELCC, developers would need to build more battery capacity to earn the same capacity credit as a natural gas project.

He called the change a “thumb on the scale for gas,” arguing that it makes battery storage artificially less valuable in the procurement.

“Batteries are going to look significantly more expensive than gas,” Sherrier said. “We know that is not the case anymore.”

Recent cost estimates show that utility-scale solar can be cheaper than new natural gas generation. Pairing solar with battery storage raises the cost, but can still make it competitive with gas while allowing electricity to be stored for use when it is needed.

If the ELCC for batteries remains unchanged, Sherrier fears the new expansion could once again be dominated by natural gas.

For its 2029-2031 expansion, Georgia Power planned nearly 10,000 megawatts of new capacity, including roughly 6,000 megawatts from natural gas, with the remainder coming from solar and battery projects. At the time of planning in 2024, the utility’s planning assigned battery storage an ELCC of 95 percent for its first 3,000 megawatts of capacity.

More than 6,000 megawatts of natural gas capacity, if operated at full output year-round, could produce an estimated 20 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, roughly the same emissions as 4 million cars.

If the 2032-2033 procurement goes the way Sherrier expects, Georgia Power could lock in millions more tons of annual emissions.

Georgia Power is reviewing proposals for its 2032-2033 expansion, with battery storage still assigned an ELCC of 20 percent. But the issue is not settled. The utility and regulators are expected to discuss which projects to move forward with early next year.

According to Sherrier, however, some of the damage may already be done. By assigning batteries a lower capacity value, Georgia Power may have discouraged battery developers from submitting proposals in the first place. The impact of the ELCC calculation will become clearer when the utility’s selected projects are submitted for regulatory approval in mid-2027.

If the issue is not resolved in this procurement, SELC and the Advanced Power Alliance plans to push for a higher ELCC in the next round of expansion planning, which is expected to begin in 2028.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.title: A Clean Air Advocate Will Represent Part of America’s Oil Capital in Congress
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.author: By Lauren Nutall
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.text:
Leticia Gutierrez’s upset victory in a Houston-area congressional district means an environmental-health advocate will represent part of the country’s oil capital, and environmental groups say that could help communities choked for years by petrochemical pollution.

Gutierrez, who spent more than a decade as Air Alliance Houston’s government relations director, pledged to support policies to improve air quality and regulate AI data centers’ water consumption and electricity usage. The Democrat beat a vastly better-funded former oil-industry executive whose contributors included petrochemical companies and Elon Musk.

“There is now, dare I say it, a green Houston congressional contingent,” said Jennifer Hadayia, executive director of Air Alliance Houston. She counts Reps. Christian Menefee, Sylvia Garcia and Lizzie Fletcher, all of whom won re-election in their Houston-area districts, among that group.

“We know that they understand Houston is the energy capital of the world,” Hadayia said. “That also means we’re the pollution capital of the world, and I feel very confident that that group together is going to advocate for our best interests when it comes to things like efforts by the current EPA, [which] has been stripping the community of its rights to weigh in on pollution decisions.”

Gutierrez’s 9th Congressional District was among those redrawn by Texas Republicans in 2025 in an unsuccessful effort to maintain the party’s control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Instead, the blue-wave election last week swept numerous Republicans out of office in Texas and nationwide.

The redrawn district includes parts of Harris County and the Houston Ship Channel, a major source of pollution lined with hundreds of petrochemical facilities. During the campaign, Gutierrez pointed to the health consequences of living near those facilities. The Texas Department of State Health Services, studying part of east Harris County near the ship channel and other pollution sources, found higher-than-expected rates of certain cancers in 2015, and a 2025 update still found notably higher rates.

Advocates were heartened by her election because they say people in the region need representatives pushing for pollution control.

“I think a really big issue for Harris County and for District 9 is how we’re treating our national emission standards for hazardous air pollutants,” said Clara Goodwin, staff attorney at the Environmental Integrity Project.

Last year, the Trump administration invited companies to email requests for “presidential exemptions” to a number of rules designed to reduce Americans’ exposure to air pollution hazards, including cancer-causing chemicals. Goodwin estimated that 30 facilities in the district have sought such exemptions.

Hazardous material dredged from the Houston Ship Channel and moved to dump sites in the region also pose risks to residents in parts of Gutierrez’s district. In 2024, sample testing of dredge material from part of a channel expansion that began in 2022 found toxic substances, including high levels of cancer-causing arsenic. Despite this finding, current U.S. Environmental Protection Agency policy does not treat dredge material from ship channel expansions as dangerous, Goodwin said.

Gutierrez will join a Congress in January newly under Democratic control. New laws controlling pollution may be impossible for the next two years—President Donald Trump can veto them—but Hadayia said there will still be opportunities to act. The major rollbacks of EPA rules that began last year are an environmental injustice, because the harms fall unequally across the country, she added.

Democrats “can hold ethics investigations and expose some of the corruption that’s going on, including the destruction of the Environmental Protection Agency by the Trump administration,” said Josiah Rector, an associate professor and urban environmental historian at the University of Houston.

He also thinks there’s room for action on tax breaks for petrochemical companies along the Houston Ship Channel that contribute to local air pollution. Rector said those policies have left school districts and other public entities with inadequate funding while people, many of them lower income, pay with their health.

“Now with the defeat of [Gov.] Greg Abbott and the GOP in Texas, there’s a real opportunity for Democrats, both in the congressional delegation representing Harris County but also in the Texas state Legislature, to start phasing out these tax breaks for corporate polluters to incentivize renewable energy,” he said.

Some advocates are tempering their expectations about how quickly Gutierrez can act on her campaign promises.

“Obviously, she’ll be a freshman,” said Luke Metzger, executive director of Environment Texas, “and it’s difficult to be able to immediately have an impact when you’re a freshman, but I think I’m excited to see what committee she gets appointed to and what she does to hold the EPA’s feet to the fire.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.title: A New Top Priority for House Democrats? Restoring Science
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.author: Interview by Steve Curwood and Jenni Doering, Living on Earth
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/14112.text:
From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by host Steve Curwood and Jenni Doering with U.S. Rep. Zoe Lofgren.

As Democrats prepare to take control of the House in January, they’re gearing up to advance a long list of priorities.

One key player in that effort will be the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, which oversees federal grants and research at the National Laboratories and agencies like NASA and NOAA. U.S. Rep. Zoe Lofgren represents California’s 18th district and, as the most senior Democrat on the committee, is in line to become its next chair. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

STEVE CURWOOD: What was your reaction on election day and after, as you understood that the Democrats would take control of both the House and Senate with sizable margins?

ZOE LOFGREN: It’s huge, and it’s a wonderful opportunity that we have to deliver for the American people on the things that matter to them. Obviously, the cost of living was top of mind for many, many voters. People are concerned about the corruption of this administration, which in many cases is related to the costs spiking. Everything from healthcare costs to energy costs and the like, and each committee in the Congress will have a piece of the remedy that we need to bring to bear as best we can.

JENNI DOERING: You are currently the ranking member of the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology in the House, and may become the chair in January. What issues fall under that committee?

LOFGREN: The entire science enterprise, primarily anything with the research, is related to the Science Committee. We have jurisdiction over the space program as well [as] some of the issues that we’ve worked on in fusion energy research and quantum computing. AI has been a focus of the committee, as well as just basic science research.

We do touch over into issues that relate to climate and in the science portfolio, it’s a broad jurisdiction. We’ve looked at some of the things that EPA has done, which have really been outrageous, as well as the Department of Energy. It’s a fun committee; my predecessor [U.S. Rep.] Eddie Bernice Johnson used to call it the committee of the future.

CURWOOD: What are your top priorities as you assume this position? The things that have been undone or moved ahead by the Trump administration—that list is fairly long. What’s at the top of yours?

LOFGREN: We need to do two main things. One is oversight—to put a spotlight, and in some cases, to uncover what the administration has done that has damaged the science enterprise in this country. We also need to do legislation to change policies that will better serve the American people.

The committee has a long history of bipartisanship, and it certainly has even in this Congress when it comes to legislation. I will say the Republicans have not been active in criticizing the administration, but we have worked collaboratively to pass a number of bills. I think all the bills that we passed were either unanimous or close to it, and so I’m hoping that that spirit of bipartisanship can continue on some of the bills that we need to enact in our subject area.

In terms of oversight, the administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency has done tremendous damage. Twenty percent of the agency’s workforce has quit, retired or been fired. They’ve shut labs down. The Office of Research and Development was completely wiped out. We’ve made multiple requests for records and documents, and they haven’t produced a single one.

Their science capacity has been gutted, and the science integrity is really impaired. It’s an industry-capture event, and climate denialism is rampant in the agency. It’s pathetic. Their basic mission is to use the best available science to protect health and the environment, and they’ve not done so.

We’re preparing our letters right now to [EPA Administrator Lee] Zeldin to renew our oversight requests. I sent a similar letter to the Department of Energy secretary, [Chris] Wright, last week. We need to know about their reorganization plans, the Endangerment Finding, and a number of other things. That’s first on the agenda.

DOERING: We wanted to ask you about what’s been happening at the National Science Foundation. We’ve reported in the past on how the Trump administration has targeted vital American science establishments by freezing and canceling grants, and also refusing to release obligated funds at the National Science Foundation. How might your committee go about investigating those missing funds and ensuring they’re returned?

LOFGREN: We’re going to get to the bottom of what has happened. The NSF was the crown jewel of our government’s support for discovery science across all fields of science and engineering. The president asked for a $3 billion cut in fiscal year ’25 and ’26, and it’s worth reminding ourselves that in a bipartisan way, Congress said no to that cut.

We enacted and funded the agency close to the fiscal year ’24 level, but as you mentioned, the money does not appear to be going out. There are whistleblower accounts that the administration is sort of taxing up to 30 percent of funds for some kind of slush fund [for] their politicized priorities, not science, but maybe funnel it into tech firms. We’re not sure. That would be in complete contravention of the law.

But looking forward, and I’ve discussed this with the incoming chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee, [Rep. Rosa DeLauro], I think Congress needs to consider and take a look at how we might be more prescriptive in the crafting of authorizations and appropriations so that the opportunity for mischief is severely curtailed, and the opportunity for court orders is significantly enhanced.

CURWOOD: Can you talk to us a bit more about what’s gotten frozen at NSF? I’m thinking of the National Center for Atmospheric Research, or NCAR, and then also over at NOAA. I think the biggest grant under NSF was going to the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution to deal with climate stuff, and that simply got stuck.

LOFGREN: It’s not going, and the interesting thing is the courts have been the sole branch of government that didn’t cave, with the exception of the Supreme Court. The trial courts have been pretty good about ordering the administration to comply with the law. But of course, it takes a long time, and so by the time the courts make their decisions, the damage has been done and they slow-walk the compliance, or it’s too late to undo it. So yes, we’re going to take a look at NOAA, which is so important across the board.

Every part of America needs NOAA and relies on adequate weather information. Whether you’re in agriculture or whether you’re in a Gulf Coast state worried about hurricanes, or in the West dealing with droughts. We need to know all of that, and they have impaired that capacity. They’ve not only impaired that, they’ve impaired the satellite capacity to capture data where they’ve illegally made changes. We’re going to put a spotlight on all of it, try to unwind the misconduct and prospectively be in a legislative posture that will make it more difficult for them to engage in misconduct in the future.

DOERING: To drill down on the climate aspect of this, when it comes to places like the National Center for Atmospheric Research or NOAA, how important is it at this moment in time when the U.N. is telling us we are surpassing 1.5 degrees Celsius, this critical threshold? How important is it to have that data as weather disasters mount?

LOFGREN: It’s hugely important. We went into an effort to preserve the data. There was an effort to destroy all the data that had been accumulated, and working with scientists in Europe to try and portal some of the data so it would not be lost once this administration is gone. There was some success there, but the new collection of data and the gaps that are being created are not good for science.

Of course we know that climate change is real. Unfortunately, some of my colleagues on the right wing in the Congress say it, well, it’s just weather. They don’t believe that there is actually climate change. Every farmer in America can tell you that there’s climate change. So we need to do something about this. …

The cheapest energy is solar at this point, but we also need to recapture carbon not only from the air but from the sea, which is the biggest carbon sink. That’s a more difficult challenge, but it is a doable challenge if we’re going to try and be successful in preserving a livable planet.

CURWOOD: What about research funds for universities? I hear a lot of complaints that those have been really slashed, and that the applications for Ph.D. programs that require grant support are down some 20 percent.

LOFGREN: There is a lot of concern, and I don’t think we have had an adequate complete accounting of that yet. The Democrats, on our Science Committee website, have a portal for people to tell us if their grants have been canceled. That’s how we’re getting information from the grantees. This does tremendous damage to our country.

Since World War II, we had a system in place. Was it perfect? No, and it could be improved. But destroying it is not improving it. There would be bipartisan support for basic research that was primarily university-based, and then from those wonderful discoveries, there would be commercial development and prosperity.

And it was the envy of the world. Everyone was trying to copy what we were doing, and [the Trump administration] dismantled that through stupid political moves, mindless destruction. I’ve talked to so many university presidents who’ve told me that they have not admitted otherwise admissible doctoral and postdoctoral students because they don’t know how to pay for the research. Those students are either going into another field or going to another country.

Another part of this issue is the steep decline in foreign students. If you take a look at the Americans who won Nobel prizes, somewhere between 40 and 50 percent are Americans who were born in another country—Americans by choice. The pattern has been that [the] best and the brightest in the world want to come to America. They get their doctorates. They love America. They become Americans, and then they win the Nobel Prize for America. Well, there’s been a close to 70 percent drop-off in foreign students coming into the U.S.

DOERING: A lot of Americans are concerned about the rapid pace of how artificial intelligence is developing. What do you think the Science Committee might be able to do to impose regulations or slow down the rapid pace of AI?

LOFGREN: It’s not clear what the leadership on the Democratic side wants to structure the approach to AI. Right now, three committees have most of the jurisdiction over AI, and that’s the Science Committee, the Judiciary Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee. I’m on two of the three, and we could approach it collaboratively. There’s been a discussion among some whether we should do a separate select committee. I don’t know if that would be a wise approach, since it’ll take six months to get staffed up and organized, but AI has tremendous possibilities.

It also poses tremendous challenges, and there do need to be constraints and controls. And we need to assign responsibility and liability to the developers of AI for harm that is caused. … We’re ready to serve, and to do what the American people need to make sure that this technology serves their needs, not the needs of the tech bros.

CURWOOD: You have written that, as Science Committee chair, you will work to put a stop to Trump’s politicization of science. Why is taking the politics out of science so important, from your perspective?

LOFGREN: I’ll just give you an example. Ted Cruz and his staff put together a little report [targeting] DEI in science, which was crazy. They did a word search, and then it looks to me that DOE and NSF and NIH just took that document and started canceling grants based on it. I’ll give you an example of a researcher who was doing research on dementia in a university, and she had people who were part of the study, but the people who surrounded the university were all high-income Asian and Anglo individuals, and she needed a broader sample to validate the sample. That’s not DEI. That’s science. They canceled the grant based on the keywords. Stupid stuff. The idea is, and always has been in American science, is if your idea is peer reviewed, it could stand up to review, that’s the measure of valid science. It’s not somebody saying, “I don’t like blue states.”

When the secretary of Energy came before the committee, we asked about energy grants, but also research grants. Were they canceled based on politics? And he testified that they had not been canceled because of politics. At the same time, the lawyers were in court, swearing under oath that the decision had entirely been made by which states voted for Trump and which states hadn’t.

We did refer the secretary to the Department of Justice for review of whether that is a felony, to lie to Congress. I don’t fool myself that [Attorney General] Todd Blanche is … going to pursue that. But the statute of limitations is five years, so that referral has already been made.

We’ll see what Trump does in terms of pardoning his entire criminal enterprise of an administration. But we’re going to be very busy with our oversight activities in crafting legislation that diminishes the opportunity for bad conduct and trying to get this science enterprise back on track and better.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.title: Fisheries Commission Lowers Chesapeake Bay Menhaden Cap But Advocates Remain Worried
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.author: By Aman Azhar
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.text:
Atlantic fisheries managers this week agreed to lower the cap on industrial menhaden fishing in Chesapeake Bay but stopped well short of imposing deeper coastwide cuts.

At its annual meeting, held from Nov. 9–12 in Newport, Rhode Island, the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission’s Menhaden Management Board reduced the coastwide catch limit by about 9 percent in 2027 and another 9 percent in 2028. The Chesapeake Bay cap was also reduced by 27 percent in 2027 and 34 percent by 2028.

Menhaden are small, oily fish that filter plankton and in turn feed predators along the coast, from ospreys to striped bass and bluefish. The Chesapeake Bay is a critical nursery for the species.

The multibillion dollar aquaculture industry has made the omega-3 and fatty acid-filled menhaden a prime commodity for producing fishmeal to feed farmed fish, fish oil and other products, a process known as reduction fishing.

Industrial fleets, aided by spotter planes and small aluminium chase boats, are deployed to encircle dense schools of menhaden with a vertical wall of netting, including in the lower Chesapeake Bay. Though researchers have not proven these industrial fleets are the cause of predators’ food depletion, some conservationists point to them as an important factor.

Ospreys’ declining population have become the most obvious warning sign.

As Inside Climate News previously reported, researchers have documented acute food stress and poor breeding performance in the Bay. The 2026 survey by the Center for Conservation Biology at William & Mary found that 81 percent of monitored nesting pairs in the Bay’s saltier waters failed to raise a chick this year. Ospreys in fresher parts of the Bay, where other fish are available, have fared better, according to Bryan Watts, the center’s director.

Under the new limits, the coastwide total allowable catch, covering the commercial fishery from Maine to Florida, including the Bay, will drop from 186,840 metric tons this year to 170,000 metric tons in 2027 and to 155,000 metric tons in 2028. That follows a 20 percent reduction in 2026.

The commission said it measured the ecological benefits of leaving more menhaden in the water against economic harm to harvesters and fisheries that rely on menhaden for bait.

But the commission’s projections paint a different picture. Its technical committee found that a 39 percent cut, to 114,200 metric tons in 2027, would give managers a 50 percent chance of meeting the ecological fishing target. That target is designed to leave enough menhaden to keep striped bass at healthy levels but does not account for ospreys or measure how many menhaden are available in the Bay.

The commission acknowledged that the new limits will very likely allow more fishing than the target. But it said they carry no risk of overfishing, which it measures against a looser limit that allows heavier fishing than the ecological target.

Actual catches are another point of contention. The commission’s fishery review puts last year’s commercial catch at just under 147,000 metric tons, below both of the new adopted limits. That means the 2027 limit leaves room for about 50 million pounds more than the industry caught last year.

In the Chesapeake Bay, the board tied the reduction fishery’s cap to 21.8 percent of the coastwide limit. That lowers the cap from 51,000 metric tons to 37,123 metric tons in 2027 and 33,847 metric tons in 2028. The cap cannot exceed 51,000 metric tons even if the coastwide limit rises, and the board decided to revisit it at least every three years. The Bay cap applies to reduction fishing, not the bait fishery, which catches menhaden to be used as bait for recreational and commercial fishing.

The new coastwide limit will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, while the Bay cap takes effect May 1.

The board did not adopt seasonal quota periods, which supporters said would spread the Bay harvest across the fishing season and ease pressure on menhaden while ospreys feed their chicks. Debate over whether to redistribute the coastwide quota among states was put off until January.

Virginia holds about 75 percent of the coastwide quota and is home to the Atlantic coast’s only active menhaden processing plant. Maryland, North Carolina, Florida, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and New York backed deeper coastwide cuts, according to the nonprofit Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership, but they were outvoted.

In the Bay, the majority of the menhaden fishing is done by Ocean Harvesters, which supplies Omega Protein’s processing plant in Reedville.

In emailed comments, a spokesperson from Ocean Harvesters said the company was disappointed with the cuts.

“[T]he consequences will be felt by the fishermen, processing workers and families who depend on the fishery, as well as businesses,” he said. “The commission should have allowed the newly funded research to proceed before imposing additional restrictions.”

The representative disagreed that the commission’s decisions to impose new catch limits struck the right balance, and questioned “whether additional restrictions will produce the benefits being claimed.” The company said it supports ongoing research and will keep working with scientists to better understand menhaden in the Bay, adding that its future depends on a healthy bay and a sustainable fishery.

The commission’s latest assessment, based on data through 2023, found menhaden are not overfished along the coast. But it acknowledged it lacks the data to say how many menhaden are in the Bay or how fishing affects the population.

The Chesapeake Bay Foundation has pointed to falling catches in Maryland, Potomac River and Virginia waters as examples of low menhaden availability. Chris Moore, CBF’s Virginia executive director, said menhaden caught in the Bay are younger and lighter than they used to be, a sign of a population under stress.

“While we are encouraged by the Chesapeake Bay cap reductions in particular, this was unfortunately another year of the ASMFC failing to manage menhaden according to its own ecosystem-based science,” said Jaclyn Lunaas, forage fish program manager for the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership.

Allison Colden, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation’s Maryland executive director and a Maryland representative on the menhaden board, criticized her fellow board members for rejecting seasonal quota periods. “Reducing the Bay cap overall is a significant win and a step in the right direction,” she said. “But it still leaves the door wide open for the industry to catch everything in the three-week time period in the summertime when both our fisheries and our predators really need it.”

Virginia has approved $2 million over two years for menhaden research to inform a scientifically tested Chesapeake Bay harvest cap. Moore said his foundation will keep pressing Virginia lawmakers to put observers on fishing vessels. Earlier this year, Congress approved $2.5 million for Bay-specific research that could inform future management decisions.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.title: Mishandled Data Means No One Knows if California’s New Pesticide Regulation Protects Workers
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.author: By Liza Gross
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.text:
Just before 5 p.m. on the last day of September, Jane Sellen and her colleagues at Californians for Pesticide Reform learned that regulators had to toss out nearly nine months’ worth of air-monitoring data for two deadly fumigants.

California’s Department of Pesticide Regulation, or DPR, said the state laboratory that analyzes its samples was “recalling and voiding” all the monitoring results for 1,3-dichloropropene, or 1,3-D, and methyl bromide from Oct. 24, 2025, through June 30, due to a quality-control problem.

How can pesticide regulators say they’re protecting anyone from 1,3-D or methyl bromide if they don’t know how much of these toxic gases entered the air? asked Sellen, development director for Californians for Pesticide Reform, a statewide coalition of public-interest groups.

Methyl bromide was one of the most widely used pesticides on California farms until the Environmental Protection Agency banned it for all but “critical uses” in 2005 to protect Earth’s ozone layer. A potent neurotoxin, the gas can also cause severe neurological disease, multisystem organ failure and death. Even so, California farmers have long received a critical use exemption, and apply about 1.6 million pounds of the noxious gas each year to fields that produce nut trees, berries and other crops.

Growers also apply more than 7 million pounds of drift-prone, cancer-causing 1,3-D each year on almonds, grapes, strawberries and other billion-dollar crops. The pesticide is banned in 40 countries to protect public health and the environment.

DPR collects air-monitoring samples and sends them to a laboratory at another state agency to keep track of how much of these and other pesticides escape from treated fields. To measure concentrations in a given sample, labs rely on what’s called a reference standard, a manufacturer-certified sample of a chemical of interest used to ensure accurate readings. The reference standards for methyl bromide and 1,3-D had “significantly degraded,” between 18 percent and 96 percent, over nine months, the agencies reported.

Losing the 1,3-D data is particularly vexing for pesticide-reform advocates. They say the data is critical for gauging the effects of a new rule regulators said would limit agricultural workers’ exposure to the dangerous chemical but health and environmental advocates believe is flawed.

“DPR muscled through regulations for 1,3-D that we don’t believe adequately protect communities,” said Sellen, whose organization has gone to court four times to compel state regulators to pass rules that are “consistent and effective” at protecting workers and their communities from 1,3-D.

Sellen said her conviction that DPR’s rules aren’t effective is reflected in Californians for Pesticide Reform’s lawsuits and the lab’s failure “to actually even partially characterize what communities are being exposed to.”

Over the past two years, state pesticide regulators enacted two different 1,3-D regulations, one for people who live near treated fields and another for those who work near them, even though most farmhands live and work in the same region.

The rule that went into effect in January 2024 says it’s safe for residents of farming communities, who are largely low-income and Latino, to be exposed to 1,3-D air concentrations that are 14 times higher than the level experts at the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment, or OEHHA, say is safe. The other rule, for workers, which went into effect in January, set a safety target five times higher than OEHHA scientists said reduces a person’s lifetime cancer risk from exposure to the pesticide.

Pesticide regulators maintain that both rules mitigate the lifetime cancer risk for people living and working near 1,3-D treated fields.

Inside Climate News asked the Department of Pesticide Regulation and the California Department of Food and Agriculture, which analyzes the air samples, how it could take so long to notice a problem with the analytical results and if any ditched data could be salvaged. DPR spokesperson Amy MacPherson deferred to CDFA to explain the lab problems but did not address whether any data could be recovered.

A CDFA spokesperson was not able to provide an immediate response because its experts were traveling or on vacation.

Sellen is upset by the loss of so much air-monitoring data, which she says is an important way to audit the regulation’s effectiveness.

She’s worried that emissions increased, like they did after the residential bystander rule went into effect in 2024. A draft 1,3-D report DPR released in October shows that after that rule was implemented, both applications and emissions of the fumigant rose following a multi-year decline.

“DPR and CDFA have agreed on additional quality-control measures to make sure future air monitoring data is not compromised by similar problems,” DPR stated when it announced the problem.

Chemist Susan Kegley said such tests should be routine.

Good laboratory practice requires knowing the standards are correct, and there are several methods for doing that, said Kegley, principal scientist and CEO of the Pesticide Research Institute, an environmental consulting firm. “Running regular quality-control tests is the centerpiece of understanding how correct your method is.”

Caroline Cox, a retired pesticide scientist and former research director at the nonprofit Center for Environmental Health, doesn’t understand how it took state officials nine months to notice a problem with the standards. “It should be something that you notice virtually right away,” Cox said.

Even under the best circumstances, the agency typically releases air-monitoring results at least six months after collecting samples, Cox said. The delay is frustrating because it means she and others have to tell people in the community about potential risks months after they happened. “That just makes people really angry,” she said, “because what can they do?”

Plus, because DPR takes just one 24-hour sample of the pesticides it monitors each week, Cox said, “we actually have no idea if the concentration was really higher or lower in the days before or after they took the sample.” That’s particularly troubling, she said, because all of the state’s air monitors at some point detect 1,3-D emissions above the level OEHHA says is safe.

Handling standards for highly volatile chemicals like methyl bromide and 1,3-D is tricky, allowed Anne Katten, director of California Rural Legal Assistance Foundation’s Pesticide and Work, Health, and Safety Project. “But that’s no excuse for taking nine months to find the problem.”

DPR has proposed replacing the lost data with modeled values, which raises additional concerns, Sellen said. The methods behind the model aren’t clearly laid out, she said. And when Sellen and Cox ran the agency’s model by an independent researcher, he confirmed their concerns that it underestimates higher values.

DPR’s MacPherson said the agency’s modeling approach has been peer-reviewed and is “scientifically supported, including the level of accuracy for this type of analysis.”

But Cox believes air-monitoring data is much more important than modeled numbers. She and Katten are trying to figure out if any of the air-monitoring data can be salvaged.

Sellen sees the lab failure as one more example of regulators’ inability to safeguard communities.

“It just further undermines public confidence in DPR’s willingness to protect communities from these hazardous chemicals,” she said.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.title: Top Aide for a Senator Pushing a Permitting Bill Was Also on Staff at a Pipeline Company
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.author: By Lauren Dalban, Nicholas Kusnetz
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.text:
When U.S. Sen. Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma started work this year on legislation to speed approval for infrastructure projects, he hired the chief lawyer at one of the nation’s largest gas pipeline developers to lead his Senate office.

Armstrong had previously led the Williams Companies, stepping down before entering public office. But his new chief of staff, T. Lane Wilson, maintained his position at the company even while serving in the Senate.

During his nearly three-month stint in the Senate, Wilson kept the title of senior vice president and general counsel at Williams, a company spokesperson said. That means Wilson’s colleagues at Williams were lobbying his new colleagues in the Senate on pipeline permitting reform.

A chief of staff is typically second-in-command in a Senate office, supervising staff and advising on policy. While a Williams spokesperson said Wilson did not take his corporate salary while serving on the Senate staff, he maintained a significant financial stake in the company.

Delaney Marsco, director of ethics at the nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center, said it is highly unusual for such a high-level staffer to maintain outside employment. She said the fact that Armstrong was working on legislation that would affect Wilson’s company raised “serious questions.”

Wilson’s 89-day tenure may have allowed him to avoid restrictions that generally prohibit Senate staffers who serve 90 days or more from serving as an officer at, or affiliating with, corporations.

Craig Holman, the government affairs lobbyist for watchdog group Public Citizen, called the arrangement “an obvious conflict of interest,” even if Senate ethics rules did not prohibit it.

Armstrong, a Republican, was appointed in March by Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt to finish the Senate term of Markwayne Mullin, who was tapped to lead the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. At the time, Armstrong was serving as executive chairman of Williams and had previously served as the company’s chief executive. Oklahoma law barred Armstrong from running for a full term and he is now slated to serve until Nov. 30, when the newly elected Republican Kevin Hern will be sworn in.

As soon as he took office, Armstrong touted his experience leading Williams as an asset in advancing permitting legislation through the Senate.

“I am retired from the industry,” Armstrong said in his first Senate speech. “I am here because I have seen how this system strangles our great country.”

Armstrong introduced a bill in June with provisions that would have restricted the ability of states, tribes and others to challenge pipelines. While the legislation never came to a vote, it drew 20 cosponsors. Armstrong celebrated the inclusion of similar provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the permitting bill that cleared an initial Senate vote on Monday.

The bill includes a range of measures to accelerate permitting, including provisions that would limit states’ authority to reject or impose conditions on planned interstate gas pipelines and transmission lines. Williams stands to benefit from those provisions.

Wilson was Armstrong’s chief of staff from April 13 to July 10, according to Blake Jackson, a Williams spokesperson. Jackson said Wilson did not receive a salary from the company during this period. Wilson also shifted his responsibilities and communications to avoid potential conflicts of interest, Jackson said, including separating himself from the company’s government affairs team and recusing himself from any meetings between that team and Armstrong or his staff.

A spokesperson in Armstrong’s Senate office declined to comment.

Upon entering the Senate, he held more than $20 million in company stock, according to a securities filing. Wilson also continued making regularly scheduled stock sales under a pre-arranged broker agreement, selling nearly $450,000 worth of stock from May through July. Since leaving the Senate, Wilson has sold an additional $1.5 million in Williams shares, including nearly $1 million in two transactions made outside the pre-arranged agreement, according to a securities filing.

Experts said it is unclear whether Wilson’s dual employment violated Senate ethics rules. One provision prohibits outside “employment for compensation which is inconsistent or in conflict with the conscientious performance of official duties.” Wilson may have complied with this rule by not taking a salary from Williams while working in the Senate.

Wilson did not file a financial disclosure report. A Williams spokesperson said he was not obligated to do so. Senate rules say all staff with annualized salaries of at least $151,661 must file reports. Williams did not disclose Wilson’s salary there, and staff salaries for the period have not yet been published. But a Congressional Research Service report said the minimum salary for a Senate chief of staff last year was just over $163,000.

Experts say another key question is whether the Senate Select Committee on Ethics approved the terms of Wilson’s employment. Jackson, the Williams spokesperson, said the committee had signed off, but he declined to provide a copy of any advisory letter. Such letters generally remain confidential unless a recipient makes them public.

Neither the Ethics Committee nor the office of Republican Sen. James Lankford, the committee chairman and Oklahoma’s senior senator, replied to questions for this article. The office of the committee’s vice chairman, Sen. Christopher Coons (D-Delaware), also did not reply to inquiries.

“Everything might be, by the letter of the law and the Senate rules, totally above board, but it doesn’t solve the problem of looking really bad,” said Marsco, with the Campaign Legal Center. “And in the ethics world, that’s just as bad.”

The Ethics Committee website says it has long interpreted its rule on outside employment “as applying to both actual conflicts of interest and the appearance of a conflict of interest.”

Marsco said appearances are important because democracy relies on public trust. “If a reasonable person can draw these conclusions that something might be a conflict of interest,” she said, “it calls into question in the mind of the public whether or not these people are actually working on the public’s behalf or if they’re working for their own bottom line or the bottom line of a special interest.”

From 2007 to 2025, the Senate’s Ethics Committee received reports of over 2,000 alleged ethics violations. None led to sanctions, according to its records.

Donald Sherman, chief executive of the nonprofit government watchdog organization Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, said in an email that “Armstrong’s ability to appoint T. Lane Wilson to his staff is emblematic of why the Senate Ethics Committee needs reform.”

He called for the Senate to establish an independent ethics body to investigate issues like Wilson’s employment, following the House of Representatives’ example.

“The results of the recent midterms have made clear that the American people are overwhelmingly tired of government corruption,” Sherman said. “These kinds of revolving door arrangements should be impermissible; [the] potential for conflicts of interest are obvious to anyone paying attention.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.title: Trump Administration Stalling Protections for Imperiled Fish Near Massive Alabama Data Center, Groups Say
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.author: By Dennis Pillion
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.text:
The Birmingham darter, though only recently discovered by science, is a survivor.

The roughly two-inch long fish, adorned with red spots and stripes along translucent fins, has survived 100 years of coal mining, steel-making, quarrying and suburban development along the rolling Appalachian foothills running southwest from Birmingham to Tuscaloosa.

But the fish might not survive the new 4.5-million square foot hyperscale data center planned just upstream from one of the six known locations where it still survives.

“Clearly they’re endangered in fact, if not by law, because their populations are so small,” Charles Miller, policy director for the Alabama Rivers Alliance, said in an interview. “They’re only found in Jefferson County, and so the loss of even one of those populations can be devastating for the species as a whole.”

The Rivers Alliance, along with the Center for Biological Diversity and Black Warrior Riverkeeper, petitioned the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service nearly a year ago to consider whether the species should be listed under the Endangered Species Act, a move that would likely force developers of the Project Marvel data center to make accommodations to save the fish.
