Now, after nearly a year with no action and crews already clearing land for the data center, they are threatening to take the matter into court.

On Thursday, the groups sent a notice of intent to sue the Fish and Wildlife Service and the Department of the Interior, saying they will file suit if the FWS does not respond within 60 days. The groups are required to give 60 days notice before filing a lawsuit under the Endangered Species Act.

Laurel Jobe, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the FWS missed a legally required 90-day deadline to issue an interim decision on the darter’s status, and that time is of the essence.

“Birmingham darters don’t have time for the Fish and Wildlife Service to slow-walk this decision,” Jobe said in a news release. “Every day these darters spend waiting for protections brings them that much closer to extinction.”

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and data center developer QTS did not immediately respond to requests for comment for this story.

The data center, called Project Marvel, was announced in 2025 as having 18 warehouse-style data center buildings spanning 4.5 million square feet on 700 undeveloped acres in the city of Bessemer, just west of Birmingham.

Since then, developers purchased an additional 900 acres of property surrounding the original site plan. Virginia-based data center developer QTS purchased the project for $432 million in June, according to local media reports.

Recent municipal elections in Bessemer installed a new mayor and city councilors, after strong public backlash against the data center. The previous mayor and other officials signed non-disclosure agreements with the original developer that even required them to destroy records that the developers deemed confidential.

In October, new Bessemer Mayor Louise Alexander asked QTS to pause development operations until a scheduled meeting with city officials. According to AL.com, the company responded saying it would continue clearing the site, which had already been permitted by the city.

QTS has offered to buy homes surrounding the site from residents, and subcontractors have sent letters to residents informing them they are within a half mile of a potential blasting site, seeking to conduct “pre-blast inspections” on structures in that radius.

When completed, Project Marvel will be one of the largest users of electricity in the state, needing an estimated 1,200 megawatts of power. That’s almost half the total capacity of Alabama Power’s James H. Miller Jr. Electric Generating Plant, a coal-fired power plant located about 20 miles away.

The darter is surviving, but definitely not thriving. The species has already been extirpated from parts of its range, in a number of streams feeding into Valley Creek, a Black Warrior River tributary. The clear, spring-fed streams that it needs to survive have been impacted by urban runoff and industrial pollution.

According to the groups’ notice, there were populations of the Birmingham darter in Fivemile Creek, just east of the data center site, that have seemingly been wiped out due to quarrying operations in the area. The groups say darters haven’t been seen there since 2006.

“Birmingham was the center of a coal and an iron and steel industry that really messed with these streams,” Miller said. “The darters that we have left are so precious because they represent individuals and species that were really put through the wringer.”

Now, the darter is facing threats from the development of the new data center, as well as the controversial Birmingham Northern Beltline highway project, which is planned to run directly through the area. The highway is being built not to alleviate traffic problems, but in an attempt to spur economic development through sparsely populated areas north and west of Birmingham.

The route will take it directly through many forested and undeveloped areas, clearing hundreds of acres of wetlands, critics say, imperiling the Birmingham darter and numerous threatened and endangered species in the area. The project’s estimated total cost is more than $6 billion in 2026 dollars, though the road is not expected to be completed for several decades.

These two massive new developments on top of the existing pressures on the darter threaten its survival as a species.

“We’re seeing this new form of industry come in that is posing threats to our natural environment in similar ways as mining did back in the day,” Miller said. “And we’ve got to make sure that these species can survive this next revolution in terms of AI and data centers.”

Alabama is a well-recognized hotbed of biodiversity, boasting more freshwater aquatic species than any other state, thanks to its wide range of habitats from the Appalachian foothills to coastal plains, Piedmont, and the Mobile-Tensaw Delta, one of the richest wildlife areas in North America.

These diverse ecosystems in Alabama are home to at least 300 species of freshwater fish, 186 species of mussels, 31 species of turtles, 97 species of crayfish and 200 species of freshwater snails, according to The Nature Conservancy in Alabama.

There are numerous species of darters in the Birmingham area that are found nowhere else in the world, including the vermilion and watercress darters. The Birmingham darter was initially thought to be part of another species until biologists documented it as a distinct species about two years ago.

“It’s incredible, and I think a lot of people living in Jefferson County, like I do, don’t even know this,” Miller said. “But we have all of these cool little endemic darter species that only live here, and that are found nowhere else on Earth.”

But Alabama is also among the national leaders in extinctions, with more than 100 documented species lost since European settlers arrived.

Miller said action is needed to prevent the Birmingham darter from becoming another lost species, and that protecting any of the six remaining populations would have a big impact.

“Any one of those fish in any one of those populations that we can save contributes a great deal to the genetic biodiversity of the species as a whole, and increases its chances of survival,” Miller said.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.title: Conservation Programs in the Colorado River’s Upper Basin Inch Forward, Despite Thorny Questions
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.author: By Jake Bolster
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.text:
New voluntary water conservation programs in the Upper Colorado River Basin appear on track after the 320th meeting of the Upper Colorado River Commission concluded this week. But Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and the federal government have yet to agree on how any conserved water would be credited and stored.

These questions, experts say, may not come with easy answers.

This June, the federal Bureau of Reclamation put $100 million on the table for the four states in the Upper Basin to fund their own voluntary water conservation programs, which usually entails paying ranchers and farmers to use less water. Overuse and drought-diminished flows on the Colorado River threaten the water supply of roughly 40 million people, 30 tribes, seven states and Mexico.

Most Upper Basin states are planning to implement programs in 2027 (Utah already has one running), and their success could be crucial to the states’ assertion that they should only have to ease the pressure on the Colorado River through voluntary measures. This fall, the federal government implemented new mandatory reductions on the Lower Basin, and Nevada, later joined by Arizona, sued over the potential for even deeper cuts.

“It’s … important to recognize, and I say this in a positive way, a complimentary way, the audacious ambition of attempting to put this together in the time frame that we have,” Wayne Pullan, the Bureau of Reclamation’s Upper Colorado Basin regional director, told negotiators from the Upper Basin states at the virtual meeting.

Colorado made it clear that its program can only move forward with an agreement from Reclamation that conserved water would remain under the state’s jurisdiction.

“We really need to get some credit for the upper division states through a program like this,” said Amy Ostdiek of the Colorado Water Conservation Board, who presented the state’s conservation program. “What that means in Colorado is seeing that that water is treated as operationally neutral, and not simply passed downstream.”

“Operationally neutral” water is conserved by one state and stored in federal reservoirs for future use by that state. Arizona, California and Nevada, the Lower Basin states, have banked water in Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, with the option to withdraw it for future use. But the Interior secretary is the legal water master in the Lower Basin and has the ability to allocate surplus water there. The secretary does not play the same role in the Upper Basin.

Pullan said that Reclamation is “able and willing” to keep working on how the government would credit and handle water conserved by the Upper Basin. Some observers wondered how the Upper Basin’s condition would sit with the federal government, which built and financed the dams that store the water.

“They don’t like to turn over the keys of the car to the states,” said James Eklund, a partner at Taft Law and Colorado’s Colorado River negotiator from 2013 to 2019.

The Lower Basin would also need to agree that water conserved in the Upper Basin could be stored for the upstream states’ use, something Kathryn Sorensen, director of research for Arizona State University’s Kyl Center for Water Policy, had a hard time envisioning.

The Lower Basin states “would expect some sort of quid pro quo for that type of arrangement,” she said.

The Upper and Lower basin negotiators from each of the seven Colorado River states had years to agree on new guidelines for the federal government to implement. After they missed several deadlines, Reclamation implemented its own new operating plan this year, and the states appear no closer to an agreement.

The possibility of one of the seven basin states suing another before the Supreme Court looms over the basin.

Various conservation programs in the Upper Basin are in different phases of development. Utah’s program saved about 5,500 acre feet of water in 2025, Amy Haas, executive director of the Colorado River Authority in Utah, announced at the meeting.

One acre foot of water can supply anywhere from three to six homes for a year, depending on the region’s climate and urban density.

New Mexico and Wyoming made their programs compatible with other funding sources, like state appropriations or grants from nonprofits, should they become available, state representatives said.

The Upper Basin uses less water than the Lower Basin, which recently reined in its consumption after years of drawing more water than it was allocated, though it has plans to divert yet more water from the river. In its operating guidelines released this summer, Reclamation modeled up to 200,000 acre feet of voluntary conservation annually in the Upper Basin—if hydrology allows.

Eklund, who attended the virtual meeting, said it’s disappointing the seven basin states still can’t agree on a solution to the problems plaguing the Colorado River. “If this system collapses, it doesn’t really matter what we’re legally entitled to,” he said.

“If Phoenix sneezes, the Upper Basin catches a cold,” he added. “We’re very, very connected economically to each other, and if we don’t start governing the system like we’re all part of one country and not seven different sovereign countries, then we’re A: only going to have ourselves to blame, and B: we’re not going to like the results.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.title: UN Leader Says People Power Is the Secret Weapon Against Global Warming
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.author: By Bob Berwyn
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13112.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—Despite the lack of progress toward the goal of curbing global warming, outgoing U.N. Secretary General António Guterres urged climate activists and environmental justice advocates at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference here not to give up hope.

“You pushed governments to face up to the role of fossil fuels,” he said during his speech Friday to about 800 representatives of civil society groups from around the world. “You fought for finance for communities facing the worst impacts of a crisis they did little to cause. But let’s be clear. We face powerful lobbies that are pressuring governments. So civil society must put the needed counter-pressure against that.”

Guterres, former prime minister of Portugal, said a big part of the effort is to protect future generations who can’t influence today’s decisions. He said it’s essential to “do everything to make sure that those responsible for essential decisions create the conditions for a rapid, drastic reduction of emissions.”

While cutting carbon dioxide emissions is the only proven way to stop warming, this year’s Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, once again is far from addressing the issue of fossil fuels.

A voluntary global pledge to increase electrification holds the most promise for reducing emissions, but even that has become contentious, as some countries are resisting using the term “clean electrification,” which means producing electricity from renewables, rather than fossil fuels. Converting systems to run on electricity doesn’t reduce emissions if the electricity is produced by burning coal, oil or gas.

And there is a danger the U.N. process could backslide. Observers at some of the closed-door sessions this week said several countries, mainly Russia and Saudi Arabia, may be trying to block adoption of a final conference decision document—an outcome that could lead to the summit being widely perceived as a failure, even if such a text is not procedurally required.

All decisions and documents at the conference must be adopted by consensus, and Saudi Arabia’s 30-year history of obstructing efforts to address fossil fuels is  well documented.

Guterres’s 10-year term as U.N. secretary-general ends Dec. 31. He has been outspoken about global warming and environmental justice. Even though international cooperation on climate and other issues has deteriorated recently, he has an abiding faith that collective action can overcome seemingly intractable social and political circumstances.

That belief, he has said, is rooted in part from his experiences during Portugal’s 1974 Carnation Revolution, when citizens arose against the country’s military dictatorship to establish what has become one of Europe’s most stable democracies.

“We are losing ground to climate change because we are not doing enough,” Guterres said. “We must turn the promise to transition away from fossil fuels into clear commitments … with clear timelines and real support for the workers and impacted communities.”

Shamini Selvaratnam, director of international climate and clean energy at the Ocean Conservancy, applauded Guterres’ leadership on climate change.

“Secretary-General Guterres has been a tireless champion for climate action and a powerful voice for protecting our ocean and the communities that depend on it,” she said. “His unwavering belief that cooperation is possible, even in a deeply divided world, was the message many of us needed to hear.”

Selvaratnam said his promise to keep up the fight after leaving office affirms that  ”none of us can give up on protecting our oceans and our planet.”

https://grist.org/indigenous/indigenous-.title: Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action
https://grist.org/indigenous/indigenous-.author: Joseph Lee
https://grist.org/indigenous/indigenous-.text:
The annual United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change gathering drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance in Belém, Brazil last year, leading some to dub it “the Indigenous COP.” But the event was marked by frustration and protest, with many Indigenous leaders calling it little more than a continuation of a longstanding pattern of exclusion from international negotiations.

This year’s gathering in Antalya, Turkey, is billed as an “implementation” conference focused less on sweeping new pledges than on the procedural work of turning previous agreements into action. For Indigenous advocates, that makes COP31, which started November 9, a test of whether the promises made last year translate into tangible changes, including greater authority over climate action.

“It is still a struggle,” said Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. “I’m yet to really determine whether there will be any more progress that is made in terms of realization of the rights of Indigenous people.”

Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on their commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on 400 million acres in tropical forest countries, provide $1.8 billion in funding, and respect rights to free, prior, and informed consent in the energy transition.

Despite those pledges, funds have been slow to reach affected communities and Indigenous land defenders say their rights and lives remain under constant threat. Porokwa said that he feels that responsibility to address climate change continues to fall on smaller countries and Indigenous peoples.

The stakes have been particularly stark over the last year. In Nepal, massive floods and landslides in August killed more than 1,500 people and destroyed entire villages. In Canada, a historic wildfire season saw millions of acres burned, causing thousands of evacuations. And in Indonesia, wildfire smoke alone has caused thousands of deaths and led to school closures and other emergency measures across Southeast Asia.

“The recent large-scale mountainside collapse on the border of Nepal and Tibet should serve as a wake-up call to the global community,” said Biswash Chepang, who is a founder of the Institute for Indigenous Affairs and Development in Nepal.

Climate-driven threats to Indigenous peoples and their lands continue to mount as a historically powerful El Niño threatens to drive famine, heat-related deaths, and other catastrophes across the globe.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The conference comes in the wake of a recent United Nations report that said it will be virtually impossible to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees, the goal set under the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. Indigenous delegates find that reality particularly frustrating because they see it as a direct result of decision makers ignoring their knowledge and all the ways their stewardship has been proven to benefit the environment and climate.

“For over 30 years we have brought Indigenous knowledges and sciences to these negotiations,” Māori activist Quack Pirihi said in an opening statement on behalf of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. “Yet emissions continue to rise, putting 1.5 degrees C beyond reach.”

While the work of reducing emissions and protecting Indigenous rights in the energy transition continues, securing funding for nations and communities most impacted by climate disasters is also a priority. In October, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage approved $21.6 million for Nepal — its first disbursement and less than 1 percent of the nearly $5 billion in damage the country sustained. But the process to receive and administer those funds is ongoing, and Indigenous leaders say the fund must work faster. Their push comes as wealthy countries face renewed scrutiny over climate-finance pledges they have failed to deliver.

“Loss and damage is not simply a question of humanitarian assistance,” Chepang said. “It is also a question of climate responsibility, historical emissions, equity, and the right of affected communities to recover with dignity.”

Indigenous peoples also hope to hold polluters to account. Bianca Ranson, who is Māori and a board member of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network, is attending COP31 in part to highlight the landmark climate case her father Mike Smith led against major emitters in New Zealand. The case, which uses Māori customary law, has been blocked by the national government.

Despite the logistical, financial, and political hurdles of attending an event like COP, Ranson said there is value in global spaces. “I think that with the geopolitical moment that we’re in, with the rise of the far right and fascism and war, and the struggles that Indigenous peoples are facing across the globe, it’s a really important place for us to be able to come together to connect, to strengthen our solidarity,” Ranson said.

As negotiations continue through November 20, Indigenous advocates will continue their push for all the discussions to lead to tangible actions. “Now I think it is not time only to talk about the commitment,” Porokwa said. “It is time to change the commitment into practice.”

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/11/13/eu-.title: The EU’s First AI Summit
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/11/13/eu-.author: Alexandra Sharp

My FP: Follow topics and authors to get straight to what you like. Exclusively for FP subscribers. Subscribe Now | Log In

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the European Union’s artificial intelligence ambitions, dual car bombings in Russia, and an alleged Iranian strike on a U.S. radar system.

European Union leaders convened in Dublin on Friday for the bloc’s first-ever summit on artificial intelligence. With the continent expected to fall short of its chip-manufacturing goals, the conference may be a pivotal opportunity for the EU to develop a unified policy that aims to catch up with the world’s AI powerhouses: the United States and China.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the European Union’s artificial intelligence ambitions, dual car bombings in Russia, and an alleged Iranian strike on a U.S. radar system.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

European Union leaders convened in Dublin on Friday for the bloc’s first-ever summit on artificial intelligence. With the continent expected to fall short of its chip-manufacturing goals, the conference may be a pivotal opportunity for the EU to develop a unified policy that aims to catch up with the world’s AI powerhouses: the United States and China.

The 2023 European Chips Act sought to double the continent’s semiconductor production global market share from roughly 10 percent to 20 percent by 2030 and attract billions of dollars in foreign tech investment. This legislation was a way for Europeans to say, “we want to be serious about this, and the only way to be competitive is to engage in the same practices, because otherwise you’re just never going to get manufacturing back to your shores,” Bruce Andrews, then-Intel’s corporate vice president, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar in 2024.

Since then, though, the EU has emerged as a more passive actor in AI’s advancement. A March report by Eurostat, the bloc’s statistics office, found that 1 in 5 EU enterprises used at least one AI technology in 2025, compared to less than 1 in 10 businesses a few years ago. Yet, in installed data center capacity alone, the bloc, with its 11.92 gigawatts, remains double-digits behind the United States (53.73 gigawatts) and China (31.9 gigawatts).

Such stagnation has EU leaders concerned that the continent is being left behind. “AI is the most important technology of our time,” European Council ‌President António Costa wrote on X on Friday. “Europe must make the most of its benefits, from higher productivity to better public services. We must also manage the risks and changes it will bring—and help set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI.”

Yet the summit’s AI agenda may be derailed by other issues—particularly, who will represent European interests in future Russia-Ukraine peace talks.

On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin told U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that he would allow European officials to join the next round of negotiations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who is also in Dublin this week for talks with EU leadership, applauded Putin’s concession. However, who will represent the continent’s delegation remains unclear.

“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Kushner said on Thursday. Among the names floated as possible options are Costa, EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is also likely to steal the summit’s attention. Huang stepped down on Thursday over his alleged extramarital affairs, including one that he admitted to with a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia is the world’s leading producer of the advanced semiconductor chips used to power AI and data centers.

Assassination attempts. Russian authorities are investigating a series of assassination attempts this week, after two separate car bombings in as many days targeted senior pro-Kremlin officials. It is unclear who was responsible for the incidents; however, Ukraine’s intelligence agency has previously used similar operations to attack dozens of Russian officers and operatives. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for a few of these operations, including the killing of Lt. Gen. Igor Kirillov in December 2024, but it has not commented on this week’s bombings.

On Thursday, local media reported an explosion in St. Petersburg’s Pushkinsky District, an area known for housing Russian military personnel. The attack killed a senior Russian military official believed to be a colonel in the country’s air force. The following day, a car bomb in Moscow severely wounded Sergei Zavorotniy, a former senior aide to exiled former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, who fled Kyiv in 2014 after Ukraine’s Maidan revolution toppled the country’s pro-Russian president.

Both attacks occurred following a new round of U.S.-mediated Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. Those negotiations made little headway, apart from an agreement to exchange prisoners. However, Putin later expressed his willingness to hold a future round of dialogue with European representatives present.

Alleged U.S.-Iran strikes. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Friday to have destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar system in Bahrain in what would be Tehran’s first direct attack on a U.S. military installation in months. The IRGC said the operation was in retaliation for a recent U.S. airstrike on an Iranian communications tower overlooking the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Central Command, however, denied that its radar system was damaged, instead claiming to have intercepted two Iranian drones that were heading toward Bahrain.

The alleged radar system strike came the same day that a tanker carrying liquified natural gas (LNG) reportedly hit a naval mine in the strait. The IRGC navy told state media that the ship was using an “unauthorized and dangerous route” when it came into contact with the underwater explosive and that it had ignored repeated warnings to avoid the area.

As traffic through the critical passageway has started to return, the number of maritime incidents has also climbed. October was the busiest month for LNG exports from the Persian Gulf region since war first broke out in late February. According to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, though, last month also saw the highest number of attacks on ships in the strait.

Vance’s new mandate. U.S. President Donald Trump directed Vice President J.D. Vance to move off the Iran portfolio on Thursday and instead focus his “complete and total attention” on alleged corruption in Democratic Party-run states and cities. The shift comes after Vance blamed the administration’s handling of the Iran war for Democrats’ sweeping wins in recent midterm elections.

Vance has long had a heavy hand in U.S.-Iran negotiations. Despite being a skeptic of the war, the vice president has helped shape the conflict’s objectives, led the charge for a precarious memorandum of understanding, and engaged with top Iranian hard-liners to try to revive peace talks. Moving him off the Iran agenda therefore marks a significant shift in how Trump appears to want to handle the conflict.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

The change-up also signals the White House’s concerns about a looming Democrat-run Congress. Incoming Democratic lawmakers have vowed to investigate Trump’s business dealings and other potential avenues of corruption when they take power in January. In response on Thursday, Trump accused Democratic Party leadership—particularly in the states of California, Illinois, and Minnesota—of stealing billions of dollars every month, without citing evidence.

Finland already has a reputation for being the happiest country in the world. Now, Helsinki is hoping to share that wealth with 16 lucky singles from around the world. In February, Finland will host a four-day, food-oriented group date alongside local Finnish residents also looking for love. Participants will taste some of the country’s most iconic dishes, from sautéed reindeer to bread cheese; relax in traditional saunas; and explore the Nordic nation’s cultural landmarks.

FP’s World Brief writer can personally attest that the Finnish sauna experience alone provides an almost unparalleled level of relaxation. Just follow the golden rule: What is said in the sauna stays in the sauna.

B. It marked the party’s worst-ever results.

No party won an outright majority, a further sign that South Africa’s political landscape is fragmenting, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.

Some of the most enduring theories of power were born in its absence. Thucydides, exiled from Amphipolis for failing to ward off the Spartans, surmised that “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” Thomas Hobbes, forced to flee an England consumed by civil bloodshed amid an ailing monarchy, argued that only absolute authority can tame humanity’s primal “state of nature.” Machiavelli, tortured and driven from political life by the Medicis, opined that successful rulers must sometimes be ruthless. Circumstances vary, but when the right observer falls into the pits of powerlessness, they can see in human nature what others cannot.

This is a motif that features heavily in David M. Sacks’ The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power, a meticulously researched biography of the man who made international relations theory a field in its own right—by putting power at its theoretical core.

Thucydides, exiled from Amphipolis for failing to ward off the Spartans, surmised that “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” Thomas Hobbes, forced to flee an England consumed by civil bloodshed amid an ailing monarchy, argued that only absolute authority can tame humanity’s primal “state of nature.” Machiavelli, tortured and driven from political life by the Medicis, opined that successful rulers must sometimes be ruthless. Circumstances vary, but when the right observer falls into the pits of powerlessness, they can see in human nature what others cannot.

The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power, David M. Sacks, Henry Holt & Co., 528 pp., $36.99, November 2026

This is a motif that features heavily in David M. Sacks’ The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power, a meticulously researched biography of the man who made international relations theory a field in its own right—by putting power at its theoretical core.

The Realist starts with a cold open: summer 1922 in Coburg, Germany, on a day Morgenthau would later describe as the worst of his life. A high school junior ranked second in his class, Morgenthau was slated to address his peers as part of a celebratory academic tradition. “But what should have been a triumph quickly turned to humiliation,” writes Sacks. The townspeople turned their backs, spat on Morgenthau, and barraged him with antisemitic vitriol for having the gall to participate in a “Christian Day” ceremony. All because, in their eyes, he was no more than a “stinking Jew.”

While that day would leave an indelible scar on Morgenthau, it wasn’t his true awakening. Later that year, he would attend one of Hitler’s gatherings in Munich to witness with his own eyes the antisemitic tide said to be sweeping across all of Germany. It was “one of the most profound experiences of my life,” Morgenthau recalled. Soon after, the same scene played out in his own backyard: In defiance of local law, the führer sallied into Coburg with 800 stormtroopers and delivered two fiery philippics, whipping up a public paroxysm of threats, assaults, and mass street brawls, with tacit support from town police.

In just two days’ time, Morgenthau’s sleepy, parochial hometown became one of the Nazis’ earliest political proving grounds. From this, Morgenthau “drew a clear lesson,” writes Sacks. “He, and other powerless individuals, could not rely on the law or abstract ideals for protection.”

Nazis in Coburg, Germany, in 1922. UNIVERSAL HISTORY ARCHIVE/UNIVERSAL IMAGES GROUP VIA GETTY IMAGES

In one sense, The Realist is, as its title suggests, a study on an -ism—the school of thought that every international relations major must acquaint themselves with during their baptismal power-skim of Morgenthau’s 750-page syllabus staple, Politics Among Nations. The book sketches all the contours of political realism: Nations pursue power above all; peace depends on a healthy balance of it; and moral values must align with national interest and practical constraints.

But the basis of this framework, Sacks writes, was not incubated in an ivory tower; it was forged from a story of Sturm und Drang. Growing up Jewish during the rise of the Third Reich, Morgenthau endured a traumatic crescendo of antisemitism that “molded one’s whole life,” he wrote. He was the target of constant bullying and abuse, finding respite only in schoolwork, and sank into isolation and embitterment at a young age. Morgenthau’s father, too, was not spared: A doctor, he lost his medical license after the Nazis falsely accused him of professional misconduct, wiping away what little standing the family had left in Coburg.

After Morgenthau left for Frankfurt to pursue philosophy and law, he drew on the brutishness he’d seen among the common German volk—that “primitive” and “irrational” impulse—to elaborate his grand theory of power, one that was, in a sense, post-traumatic in character. It demanded constant hypervigilance and self-preservation. It doubted the durability of security commitments, and expressed a healthy skepticism toward rules, norms, and laws. And it saw the world’s default state as anarchy, ready to rear its ugly head yet again at any time. “The distribution of power,” as Morgenthau warned, “is always precarious.”

In the lead-up to World War II, this distribution of power wasn’t just skewing toward Germany; it was careening dangerously in Hitler’s favor. Few observers at the time saw this as lucidly—or as urgently—as Morgenthau, and Hitler’s expansionist designs were proof of concept.

But despite this prescience, it seems, Morgenthau mostly floundered as a young academic. He took whatever teaching jobs he could find in a Europe ravaged by the Great Depression with little appetite for his ideas, let alone his ethnic heritage. In Geneva, Sacks writes, colleagues found his Cassandra-like rhetoric a “disturbing influence.” At Brooklyn College, students felt his anticommunism was befitting of a hysterical “Hearst reporter.” In Kansas City, which Morgenthau called an “overgrown cow town,” his émigré ambition clashed with a culture in which academic standards were relatively modest—or, again in his words, “virtually non-existent.” Even when he first arrived at the tony University of Chicago, where he’d be a fixture for the next three decades, Morgenthau’s emphasis on theory over practice and empiricism put him at odds with his department.

Why Do People Hate Realism So Much?

The school of thought doesn’t explain everything—but its proponents foresaw the potential for conflict over Ukraine long before it erupted.

ARGUMENT 

|

 STEPHEN M. WALT

The school of thought doesn’t explain everything—but its proponents foresaw the potential for conflict over Ukraine long before it erupted.

What emerges from this account is a portrait of a man who was not just politically persecuted but constantly intellectually embattled. Yet he was never cowed by power. By Morgenthau’s own admission, he refused “to play the role of the suffering martyr,” and it’s hard not to agree. The book makes clear that Morgenthau met nearly every criticism he faced with an equal and opposite reaction. This is someone who took to prestige media to publicly pillory his detractors with a revolutionary’s zeal (“trash,” “hatchet man,” “fanatical wrongheadedness”), as if their objections were affronts to his own lived experience.

And perhaps they were. After all, Sacks spills relatively little ink on the thinker’s life outside of work. In this respect, the book seems to imply by omission that Morgenthau’s personal and intellectual identities were, by dint of his traumatic upbringing, fused. We are teased with tidbits about Morgenthau’s wife, who softened his hard edges among friends and whose family supported them financially; his mother, the “closest companion throughout his life”; his authoritarian father, who believed he would never amount to anything; his son, who appeared to suffer from various ailments; and his extramarital affairs, which were far from passionless.

But for the most part, these read like brief digressions with little bearing on the bigger story. This is a weak point for a first-ever biography of such a fascinating figure, let alone one whose intellectual mission clearly seemed to color his personal life in a number of ways, and vice versa. Consider, for example, Morgenthau’s sudden interest in the Jewish question: The theorist had never been observant, did not know his Hebrew name, and was largely agnostic on Israel and the plight of the Soviet Jewry until his early 60s, believing that the Jewish state fell outside his sphere of interest. But by the late 1960s, after his forced retirement from the University of Chicago, Sacks writes, something “elemental” had shifted in Morgenthau. Feeling “disillusioned and cast aside,” he suddenly found great meaning and purpose in the Jewish community. His personal involvement with Chabad in particular fueled a political zeal for aiding Soviet refuseniks as well as a fierce insistence on Israel’s right to self-defense following the Six-Day War. This is a highly intriguing turn in Morgenthau’s story, but it’s, again, one The Realist gives little airtime.

Similarly, the book also could have lingered a bit more on Morgenthau’s bond with Hannah Arendt, another Jewish German émigré who fled the Nazis. The duo’s epistolary exchanges are rich with romantic intrigue—he may have proposed to her while still married—and intellectual compatibility. After all, they were both strangers in a strange land, hacking their way through the U.S. garden of liberal rationalism. When Arendt unveiled her infamous theory of the “banality of evil” while covering Adolf Eichmann’s trial in 1963, she provoked an intellectual maelstrom among colleagues at the University of Chicago, many of whom shunned her in response. Morgenthau, meanwhile, stood by Arendt and wrote to her gushingly, “Reality has protruded into the protective armor of illusion and the result is psychological havoc.” His use of the word “reality” was likely no coincidence.

Morgenthau addresses an audience in Washington, D.C., on May 15, 1965, while taking part in a national, 15-hour teach-in on the Vietnam War.ASSOCIATED PRESS

Over the past several years, conflicts from Gaza to Ukraine to Iran have prompted a great deal of debate among observers about whether the world is seeing the supposed return of realism. However, it’s worth remembering that aggression alone is not a good proxy for the presence of realism, which, as John Mearsheimer notes, is in large part predicated on restraint. Rather, the violence exposes a core realist truth: With no mechanism of holding great powers to account, the international rules-based order is still only as strong as those who abide by it.

The Realist, for its part, wisely avoids wading into contemporary politics, instead letting the resonance of realism’s history speak for itself. Nowhere is that more striking than in the book’s account of the Vietnam War.

One might assume that Morgenthau—who called for a very muscular posture toward the Soviet-backed Castro government during the Cuban missile crisis—was all for U.S. intervention in communist North Vietnam. However, Sacks goes to great lengths to show that he was an outspoken opponent from the jump: For two decades, Morgenthau waged a war of words with officials in the Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon administrations, including McGeorge Bundy, Robert McNamara, Walt Rostow, and Henry Kissinger (a frenemy of sorts). By the mid-1960s, as the conflict became clearly unwinnable, Morgenthau grew deeply distressed by the carnage on moral grounds. But his original argument had always been one of narrow political strategy: that the growth of communism in North Vietnam “simply was not a vital interest,” as Sacks writes. We must only intervene “where our national interest requires it and where our power gives us a chance to succeed,” Morgenthau wrote. “If the United States applies this standard, it will intervene less and succeed more.”

To say that the United States has done just the opposite would be a great understatement. In the aftermath of 9/11, President George W. Bush’s anti-terror war in Iraq created the conditions for the world’s deadliest terror organization to flourish, while the war in Afghanistan—which spanned four presidents—began and ended with Taliban rule. Though U.S. officials justified both interventions on the basis of national interest, prominent members of the neorealist school vehemently opposed them. Broadly speaking, this was because the conflicts were driven less by narrow strategy and more by either quixotic (nation-building) or chimeric (eliminating weapons of mass destruction) goals. When those goals could not be realized, the U.S. mission crept, and officials resorted to sunk-cost fallacies about credibility instead of retrenchment; the very same tack was taken by Kissinger, who attempted to argue on realist grounds that the United States would lose international “prestige” by pulling out of Vietnam. As for the current war in Iran, declared on the all-too-familiar pretext of imminent nuclear capability, the United States seems woefully bound to repeat the same cycle, and no amount of victory declarations from our commander-in-chief will change that.

To be sure, these military misadventures do not suggest that realism reigns supreme in international relations. Instead, they point to one of its key weaknesses: the malleability of “national interest”—especially, and perhaps ironically, in the face of trauma.

When Morgenthau published his first book, Scientific Man versus Power Politics, in 1946, Sacks notes that some critics found the term “national interest” too nebulous—a gripe that Morgenthau actually took in stride. U.S. military misadventures in the Middle East reveal that this problem remains in full effect. The country’s collective trauma after 9/11 gave the U.S. government a pretext to widen the aperture of “national interest” so much so that temporally or geographically distant threats—like simmering political instability in a region many Americans could not point to on a map—suddenly became existentially urgent. “As long as the Middle East remains a place where freedom does not flourish,” as Bush said in 2003, “it will remain a place of stagnation, resentment, and violence ready for export.” The United States met this specter of violence in much the same way it did Vietnam’s communism: with real violence. After two decades, our efforts to install a democratic regime resulted in nothing more than hundreds of thousands of civilian casualties. “The evil we wanted to prevent,” as Morgenthau wrote of Vietnam, was “nothing compared with the evil we left behind.”

It may be tempting to see the “return” of realism in a world where the United States continues to pursue power brutally, by any means necessary. Yet if realist thought now predominates among U.S. foreign-policymakers, it is a far cry from the realism of Morgenthau’s making. Instead, it is a realism in which national trauma has turned national interest into an empty signifier, used for vengeful wish fulfillment at the expense of sober statecraft. If “great nations” like the United States are truly great because “they married … power to purpose,” as Morgenthau believed, then what has that purpose been over the last quarter-century of foreign policy? It’s hard to think of anything other than power itself.

What does a citizen owe to their country? And what if that country is Russia?

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile.

What does a citizen owe to their country? And what if that country is Russia?

Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Loktev’s protagonists, almost all women, fled as Russia imposed censorship laws that made their already dangerous jobs punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Within days of Dozhd’s disbandment, sometimes hours, they scooped up their laptops, pets, children, and underwear and flew wherever they could without a new visa—Istanbul, Tbilisi, Prague, Tel Aviv.

They resisted Russian President Vladimir Putin and his government, yet wherever they go, they remain citizens of a country that is invading and killing its neighbors and are held responsible for the war it wages in their name.

“You feel like it’s 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew” says journalist Anna Nemzer, as she reloads her vape cartridge.

Loktev’s subjects are buffeted by cognitive dissonance and must constantly explain themselves—to their Georgian and Latvian hosts, who urge them to “tell Putin to stop the war”; to their Ukrainian sources, who resent the very language that they speak; to their Russian parents who tell them to stop writing anti-government “bullshit” and come home; and even to themselves, wondering what they could have done differently to stop their country’s slide into fascism, and whether their work matters when Russian missiles continue to rain down on Ukraine.

Loktev, who shot the film herself on an iPhone, gives these questions room. At six hours, this film is even longer than its predecessor—a bold choice—but the sheer accumulation of ordinary moments makes this exploration of exile intimate and compelling. For viewers willing to grapple with existential dilemmas and lucky enough to live near an art-house cinema, the movie’s length may be a boon. After all, its central questions are ones that take a lifetime to sort out.

Perhaps no one takes up these questions more bluntly than Elena Kostyuchenko of the recently shuttered Novaya Gazeta, where, during her tenure, four of her colleagues were murdered. “All of us … spent many years, thoroughly, in great detail, in very good, well-written articles describing the coming of fascism in Russia,” she says. “Well, there you fucking go. So we wrote all those articles.” Elsewhere, she is just as unsparing about the failure to stop Putin from turning Russia into what it is today: “We didn’t want to sacrifice our comfort.”

Alesya Marokhovskaya expresses similar unease as she recalls watching someone get beaten at a protest. “My job is to film,” she says. “You don’t rush in to defend the person. You film them, because, well, that’s your job.”

Despite those doubts, the journalists keep doing journalism. They provide truthful coverage of the war to Russian-speaking audiences through YouTube channels, podcasts, and eventually live broadcasts from Riga, Latvia, where Dozhd secured a broadcasting license. But they are walking on eggshells. A series of on-air missteps that led to questions about the station’s allegiances ultimately cost Dozhd its initial broadcasting license, forcing it to relocate to the Netherlands, where it operates today.

Irina Dolinina continues to work in exile from Prague.Cinetic

The hope of finding safety outside Russia does not last long. Alesya and her best friend Irina Dolinina, investigative journalists with IStories (or Important Stories), now based in Prague, receive oddly specific anonymous threats. The senders know their passport numbers, flight reservations, even about Alesya’s “snorting” bulldog. New friends are not always who they say they are: A supposed human rights lawyer Irina befriends previously worked for Moscow police. Alesya’s father, meanwhile, doesn’t understand why his daughter left. The war is in Ukraine, he says, not Russia.

But for most of these women, war is everywhere. From a temporary shelter in a Swiss village, where cathedral bells mark the hours of another peaceful day, Kostyuchenko recounts the symptoms of what she believes was a deliberate poisoning in Munich in October 2022: foul sweat, disorientation, nausea, swollen extremities.

Months before, reporting from the Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv, Kostyuchenko had visited a morgue overflowing with victims of Russian shelling, which she wrote about with brutal clarity. “In the fridge, the bodies are stacked in layers. Two girls lie on top of each other. They’re sisters. The older one is 17—in the heap of bodies, all I can see is her hand, long thin fingers with a neat pink manicure. The younger is 3—she lies on top of her sister. … Her body is dotted with red shrapnel wounds. The girl looks alive.”

Despite atrocities that should have stopped the world in its tracks, life goes on, and Loktev’s film captures that well. Kostyuchenko loves, and loves deeply. Her partner is Yana Kuchina, a Moscow book editor turned disability-rights advocate who followed Kostyuchenko into exile. A newcomer to Loktev’s saga, Yana delivers some of the film’s most chilling insights into how Russia treats its own. Her cerebral palsy, she says, is considered an “intellectual inadequacy” in the eyes of the authorities, barring her from getting a driver’s license, becoming a doctor, or adopting a child.

You’d have to be fearless or a fanatic to persist in journalism in Russia. These women are both.

So-called realists arguing for Ukraine’s surrender can’t let go of the past.

How Moscow broke with the West—and unleashed a more chaotic world.

Ksenia Mironova and co-director Julia Loktev speak after a screening of My Undesirable Friends: Part II: Exile at the New York Film Festival on Sept. 27.Michael Loccisano/Getty Images

Besides Yana, Kostyuchenko loves her mother—whose birthday she is missing for the first time—and her country. Her life there, she felt, was real. “I worked at the best newspaper on Earth. … All around me was my country, which I … value and love still.” Her love is definitely not blind, but for Ukrainians, whose country Russia is destroying, it may be difficult to comprehend, much less forgive.

Unlike Elena and Yana, former Dozhd reporter Ksenia (Ksyusha) Mironova walks the road of exile alone, a melancholy kaleidoscope of taxi rides, dark staircases, and endless rented rooms; her fiancé, the journalist Ivan Safronov, is still being held in a Moscow prison on fabricated charges of high treason. Ksyusha returns to Russia for his sentencing, a trip Loktev also documents. Ivan gets 22 years.

In the midst of so much loss, there are brief moments of tenderness. In a rented apartment abroad, Ksyusha and her Dozhd friends sing along to a Russian song: “When you return … I hope we recognize each other … and I am not your wife and not even your girlfriend.” It is probably the most Russian scene in the entire movie—elegiac, haunting, yet oddly hopeful.

After leaving Russia with her family, Anna Nemzer spent time in Tblisi, Georgia.Cinetic

Ksyusha is neither a victim nor a tragic heroine; behind her soft, girlish looks is a rod of steel. No longer with Dozhd, she moves from country to country, taking whatever freelance jobs she can find to keep herself afloat and working as an independent journalist covering political prisoners, their families, and the lives of Russians in exile. In 2025, we see her in the United States reporting on President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. “It’s really strange I’m now in America and the same things are happening here,” she says. She now works with Nemzer to archive independent journalism, including to preserve two decades of coverage in Russia against the Kremlin’s attempts to erase it.

Sonya Groysman, another Dozhd journalist, finds ingenious ways to report on Russia from exile, directing anonymous camera operators, including wedding videographers. One of her reports features Sasha Skochilenko, an artist who was sentenced to seven years in prison for replacing price tags in a St. Petersburg supermarket with anti-war messages. The camera zooms in on a black-and-white tag above the coffee cans reading “Russia’s Army bombed Mariupol art school where 400 people hid from shelling.” It’s yet another reminder that in Russia, the price of truth is your freedom.

Or your life. A sizable part of the documentary is devoted to the 2024 death of opposition leader Alexey Navalny. Dozhd, broadcasting from Amsterdam, ran videos of him from the day before his death, where he looks energetic and fairly healthy. In their coverage, the presenters called his death in prison what many in Russia knew but were afraid to say: a killing. Navalny went to prison to change people’s minds, says tearful Valeria Ratnikova, a Dozhd news anchor, between the airings of her show. He was a beacon for many. Now, all she sees is “total blackness ahead.”

Valeria Ratnikova stays in a hotel in Istanbul after fleeing Russia.Cinetic

The only characters spared this Dostoyevskian moral anguish are, unsurprisingly, Ukrainian. “We don’t have the energy and time to worry and panic,” says Nataliya Gumenyuk, a prominent Ukrainian journalist and war correspondent who is married to a longtime former Dozhd journalist. “We live in our own country and continue to do our work.” Among the movie’s most striking images is that of Ukrainians dancing in a square in Kharkiv, where entire blocks are flattened by air strikes, the sound of Ukrainian folk songs mixing with the howling of the air raid sirens. Nataliya’s Russian husband, Peter, resolved his moral dilemma by joining the Ukrainian army and now records his Fuck the War! podcast between missions.

This article is featured in the FP Weekend newsletter, a curation of our best book reviews, deep dives, and other reads that take a step back from the drumbeat of the news. Get the lineup directly every Saturday.

From its new home in the Netherlands, the “optimistic channel,” as Dozhd was once known, still reaches 13 million as of 2023, according to Dozhd. Because coverage of the war not aligning with Kremlin narratives has been all but silenced, most watch through VPNs and proxies. For journalists, reporting on Russia’s war means living the Russian reality. This makes integration into their new countries nearly impossible; they are neither here nor there. But going home is not an option. Ratnikova, for one, was sentenced to seven-and-a-half years in prison in absentia by a Moscow court. Loktev records her hearing over a video call, where “witnesses” explain how the “false information” about the war “confused” them. This is how Russian justice works.

For now, Ratnikova has a visa, a job, a place to stay. That could change overnight. Political exile is not war, but that’s a low bar for young men and women who could have lived a relatively normal life. By reporting independently, first in an increasingly authoritarian state, then from exile, often at considerable risk to themselves, they have given more to their country than its perpetually silent majority.

One of Ratnikova’s colleagues likens their mission to Sisyphus pushing his stone uphill: not as punishment, but by choice. They keep at it, hoping their work might still change minds in a country that seems irretrievably lost. Loktev’s immersion in their lives leaves us with hope for them, if not for Russia’s future.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief. Today’s special edition comes in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia over multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief. Today’s special edition comes in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia over multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Sign up to receive China Brief in your inbox every Tuesday.

In another world, recently resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s infidelities would be a private embarrassment. In this one, however, a powerful man’s poor judgment could steer the U.S.-China technology relationship onto the rocks.

Huang admitted to marital infidelity; he reportedly engaged in affairs with at least three women, including two Nvidia employees. His relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman and alleged Chinese asset, has drawn the most scrutiny. But why is the relationship, and his resignation on Thursday, so potentially explosive?

Broadly speaking, U.S. policy toward China has long been divided into two camps. The caution camp, exemplified by national security hawks, worries about China’s record of intellectual property theft, its control of critical supply chains, its economic might, and its potential to leapfrog the United States in key technologies such as artificial intelligence.

The opportunity camp focuses instead on what the relationship with China could offer: selling technology, tapping vast Chinese markets, and finding ways for cooperation and mutual investment. The tension between the two can produce good policy, especially when each side argues smartly against the other.

But this healthy debate depends on good faith, on both sides believing that they share a basic set of U.S. national interests. It depends on caution not curdling into racist paranoia and on opportunity not turning into personal greed.

The Nvidia debate is particularly intense because there is no hotter resource in the U.S.-China relationship right now than compute: raw processing power, which depends on advanced chips.

Unlike most other domains of U.S.-China competition, such as supply chains or critical minerals, this is the rare case where the United States holds the upper hand: roughly 75 percent of global compute, compared with China’s 15 percent. That edge rests on the U.S. alliance with Taiwan, home to chipmaker TSMC, as well as on companies, such as Nvidia, that design and sell these chips.

For years, the argument over how to manage China’s access to advanced chips swayed between caution and opportunity.

The opportunists argued that Chinese dependence was a good thing. If China could buy everything but the most advanced chips, it would remain reliant on U.S. firms; if China were cut off, it would build its own industry. But the cautious approach—that Beijing should be kept from buying the most advanced chips, thereby locking in the U.S. advantage—generally prevailed.

The deal that Nvidia struck with U.S. President Donald Trump last year blew a hole in all of those arguments and in the assumption of good faith.

Nvidia was allowed to sell the extremely advanced H200 chip to China not because it won a reasoned debate but because the White House was offered a cut: 25 percent of the sales revenue, with no apparent oversight of the money. Huang via Nvidia also donated $26 million to pro-Trump causes, including construction of the White House ballroom.

The deal was rotten from the start, but national security hawks, fearing retaliation from Trump, were quieter than they might have been otherwise. Now the situation is reversed. An incoming Democratic Congress, backed by those Republicans who still care about national security, is poised to scrutinize these deals relentlessly.

The spy allegations against Alice Huang have supercharged that scrutiny, as has the White House’s apparent disregard of earlier warnings about her. If it emerges that Trump profited by shorting Nvidia stock after a second warning, the case becomes far worse. Even if Alice Huang never influenced Jensen Huang’s decisions, it will be easy to portray him as swayed by Beijing.

Huang’s downfall lets opponents of chip sales depict companies such as Nvidia as tools of the Chinese state and the White House as their willing accomplice. Trump’s doubling down on support for Huang only hands them more ammunition. With Republicans reeling from the U.S. midterm elections, companies can no longer afford to bet solely on Trump’s protection.

In the long run, the scandal might expose a wider circle of corruption and sanctions evasion surrounding the $4 trillion company.

Nvidia’s most advanced family of chips, Blackwell, is still banned from export to China, yet signs of its usage are all over Chinese AI, and Chinese firms are working hard to acquire it. Some U.S. national security officials appear to have been waiting for the right moment to leak incriminating documents.

Alice Huang’s firm, Megaspeed, somehow jumped from $33 million in assets in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, which suggests possible Chinese state investment and use as a vehicle for sanctions evasion. (Megaspeed denies any wrongdoing and has promised full cooperation with U.S. criminal investigations.)

The United States had already started prosecuting companies believed to be evading sanctions, but a full federal investigation into both Jensen Huang’s and Alice Huang’s activities could turn over many more stones.

China, as usual, denies any involvement in espionage and urges the United States not to impose new tech restrictions. But those restrictions, and much tighter scrutiny of deals involving chips or China, now look inevitable. Hopefully, Beijing will accept that as part of the game and not retaliate by tightening its own already extensive anti-sanctions regulations or cutting off U.S. supplies of critical minerals.

On the U.S. side, there is also a risk of overindexing on a single case—a recurrent habit of intelligence services. The recruitment of one young American by the Chinese intelligence services in the early 2000s, for instance, made the security clearance process far harder for every U.S. citizen who had worked or studied in China.

At worst, that overindexing could mean racial bias against anyone of Chinese descent working in sensitive technology in the United States. At the very least, it should make any U.S. businessperson more cautious about dealing with their Chinese counterparts, let alone sleeping with them—and perhaps that is for the better.

In mid-July 2006, NPR’s foreign editor dispatched me to Beirut. Israel and Hezbollah were waging an all-out war after militants launched a cross-border attack from Lebanon, killing eight Israeli soldiers and capturing two more. Israeli bombs pounded Lebanon’s ports, roads, and bridges, while Hezbollah rained missiles down on northern Israel. Believing his country had the upper hand, Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert wanted to finish off Hezbollah once and for all and had convinced the George W. Bush administration to hold off calling for a ceasefire.

I was in my hotel room working on a story with a Lebanese translator when then-U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice appeared on TV, suggesting the conflict was an opportunity to remake the region. She added that the attacks—which had already led to more than 300 Lebanese deaths and would go on to kill over 1,000 people in Lebanon and 121 Israeli soldiers—were the “birth pangs of a new Middle East.”

In mid-July 2006, NPR’s foreign editor dispatched me to Beirut. Israel and Hezbollah were waging an all-out war after militants launched a cross-border attack from Lebanon, killing eight Israeli soldiers and capturing two more. Israeli bombs pounded Lebanon’s ports, roads, and bridges, while Hezbollah rained missiles down on northern Israel. Believing his country had the upper hand, Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert wanted to finish off Hezbollah once and for all and had convinced the George W. Bush administration to hold off calling for a ceasefire.

I was in my hotel room working on a story with a Lebanese translator when then-U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice appeared on TV, suggesting the conflict was an opportunity to remake the region. She added that the attacks—which had already led to more than 300 Lebanese deaths and would go on to kill over 1,000 people in Lebanon and 121 Israeli soldiers—were the “birth pangs of a new Middle East.”

The translator looked up from her computer and turned to me. “Birth pangs?” she asked, shaking her head. “Why does Lebanon always have to be the midwife?”

The Best Kind of American: A True Story of Murder, War, and America’s Undoing in the Middle East, Kim Ghattas, Henry Holt and Co., 496 pp., $32.99, October 2026

For five decades, Lebanon has been a key Middle East battleground, caught in the geopolitical crosshairs of Israel, Iran, Syria, and the United States competing to shape or control the broader region. In her new book The Best Kind of American: A True Story of Murder, War, and America’s Undoing in the Middle East, Kim Ghattas contends that many of the policies and conflicts playing out across the region today were established in Lebanon during the 1980s, particularly Israel’s 1982 invasion. It’s a prescient argument given where the Middle East now finds itself, with Israel continuing to vie for security and land, Iran using Hezbollah to project power, and Lebanon remaining a fragile state.

Ghattas, a Lebanon-born journalist and commentator, unfolds the story of the country’s turbulence around the 1984 murder of Malcolm Kerr, a U.S. scholar of the Middle East and president of the American University of Beirut who was gunned down outside his office. The book begins with an email from Kerr’s widow, Ann, asking Ghattas if she had discovered new information about his assassination while writing an earlier book. Ann had clues about who had killed her husband, but no clarity as to why.

Kerr was born and spent most of his childhood in Lebanon. Ghattas portrays him as an Arabist with a deep knowledge of the Middle East and an intuitive understanding of the role of religious fanaticism in the region. This was in striking contrast to successive U.S. administrations that, Ghattas writes, have been out-maneuvered time and again by Iran, Israel, and Syria.

Lebanon was embroiled in a brutal civil war in the 1980s, which provides a vivid backdrop for Ghattas’ search to identify Kerr’s killer and the reason for his death. Regional powers pursued their own deadly agendas in the country, while Israeli tanks swept through southern Lebanon and did not stop until they reached Beirut. Kerr’s death was considered just one of many wartime losses and thus was not investigated. The book provides rich, well-researched profiles of a patchwork of deadly rivals—militants, religious fanatics, assassins, and governments—operating in Lebanon during this time. These included the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), which had been based in the country since the early 1970s; the pro-Iranian Islamic Amal militia; and Syrian President Hafez al-Assad and his son and successor, Bashar, who brutally controlled Lebanon for decades.

Ghattas also humanizes a wide cast of characters affected by the hijackings, car bombs, hostage taking, and civil war that marked the era: a wife searching for her husband who was kidnapped, a celebrated Lebanese diva refusing to sing until the killings stopped, and the agony of those who lost loved ones, including the Kerr family.

One of the more striking consequences of the 1982 war was that it led to the emergence of Hezbollah, one of Iran’s most powerful proxies. That June, Israel invaded Lebanon in a bid to dislodge Yasser Arafat and his PLO, which had been launching sporadic attacks against Israel. At the same time, Iran’s new Islamist regime sent several hundred fighters and volunteers, along with a handful of clerics, to Lebanon via Syria. They set up training camps for local Shias around Baalbek and other areas in the Beqaa Valley. More fighters and paramilitary forces arrived, taking up the name Hezbollah, or Party of God.

Initially, Hafez al-Assad was cautious about allowing Iran to funnel troops and weapons through Syria, even though the two countries had become allies after the 1979 Iranian revolution. But Assad came to view Hezbollah as a powerful deterrent against Israel and a way to help consolidate his grip on Lebanon.

                The ‘Super-Terrorist’ We Still Can’t Escape            


    
    	Carlos the Jackal left behind a violent, celebrity-obsessed world.

    Juliette Kayyem

What a scandal involving movie star Alain Delon can—and can’t—tell us about French society.

In a new book, Sally Hayden considers how journalists can puncture the detachment of the privileged.

Carlos the Jackal left behind a violent, celebrity-obsessed world.

In Ghattas’ telling, the Ronald Reagan administration made a strategic mistake by acquiescing to the 1982 invasion. It was sold to the United States by then-Israeli Defense Minister Ariel Sharon as a limited operation to remove the PLO from Lebanon, not the broad incursion into Beirut it turned out to be. There are remarkable moments in the book highlighting Israeli sway over Washington. The U.S. ambassador to Lebanon, Robert Dillon, urgently called the State Department to say he was watching Israeli tanks and troops moving into Beirut, only to be told by the switchboard operator that Tel Aviv had given its assurances that the Israeli military was not there. A few weeks later, Philip Habib, Reagan’s special Middle East envoy, rang Washington to say Israel had broken a ceasefire and was pounding Beirut. When Washington told him Israel denied that claim, Habib held his phone out the window as two tanks fired off rounds, thereby making his case.

The United States was pulled into the Lebanon morass to help control the blowback from the Israeli invasion, which the White House worried could spin into another Arab-Israeli war. Washington deployed Marines in August 1982 as peacekeepers to help oversee the withdrawal of the PLO from Lebanon to Tunisia, and to control fighting between various Lebanese factions. A second deployment of Marines came after the massacre by Lebanon’s Israeli-backed Phalange militia in the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps in September 1982, which killed roughly 3,500 Palestinians and Lebanese Shia in Beirut over the course of three days.

U.S. Marines deploy in Beirut on Aug. 25, 1982, during the Lebanese Civil War. Dominique Faget/AFP via Getty Images

Yet U.S. involvement in Lebanon, marred by tragedy, ultimately punctured Washington’s aura of invincibility. In April 1983, a pickup truck filled with explosives rammed into the U.S. Embassy in Beirut, killing 63 people, including 17 Americans. That October, barracks housing U.S. Marines collapsed after a suicide bomber detonated a truck loaded with explosives, leaving 241 U.S. service personnel dead. Four months later, Reagan announced the end of the mission.

Washington’s reputation took another hit with the Iran-Contra affair. In 1986, it came out that Reagan had secretly authorized a plan to sell U.S. weapons to Iran with the aim of getting seven hostages held by Hezbollah released. U.S. officials had also siphoned profits from the sales to help fund the Nicaraguan Contras in their fight against the leftist Sandinista government. The scandal embroiled Washington for months and left lingering questions among allies about U.S. trustworthiness. It also made clear that hostage-taking was lucrative and gave Hezbollah leverage when dealing with the United States.

While this played out, Malcolm Kerr’s family continued to search for clues to his killing. Andrew Kerr, his youngest son, stumbled across classified information while working as a junior staffer on the National Security Council during the Clinton administration. It was a transcript of an intercepted conversation in which two Iranian operatives told the Iranian ambassador in Damascus, Ali Akbar Mohtashemipur, that they had killed Kerr. The document, which directly proved Iran’s involvement, contained the means and methods of his father’s death, but no definitive answers about the motive.

To this day, no one has stood trial for the killing, but in researching her book, Ghattas discovered a link between Kerr’s murder and his investigation into the kidnapping of a university colleague, David Dodge. Still, for all that Ghattas has uncovered, the central mystery of Kerr’s death remains.

U.S. President George W. Bush walks to Marine One as he departs the White House on July 11, 2005. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

In the decades since, Ghattas observes, Iran’s covert activities and deadly ambitions have continued unabated, often in concert with other players. She writes that Bush’s decision to invade Iraq not only further eroded the United States’ standing in the region, but also consumed its attention, leaving Iran “effectively unshackled, from Baghdad to Beirut.” This allowed Hezbollah to build up its fighting force and consolidate power and legitimacy in Lebanon. In 2006, Hezbollah fighters ambushed Israeli soldiers, in part to force the release of Lebanese and Arab prisoners held in Israeli jails. Israel viewed the attack as an opportunity to eliminate Iran’s powerful proxy force, but the month-long war ended in a ceasefire.

The Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, gave Israel, under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, another opportunity to remake the region, just as Sharon had done in 1982. Shortly after the Iranian-backed militant group launched its assault, killing approximately 1,200 people in Israel and kidnapping 251, the Israeli military launched devastating assaults on Gaza, razing whole neighborhoods and cutting off electricity, food, and fuel to Palestinians.

A second front in the war opened after Hezbollah launched a cross-border attack. Israeli forces moved into southern Lebanon, destroying much of Hezbollah’s military capabilities and killing several of its leaders, including Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah. It bombed Iranian weapons depots and other targets in Syria. A weakened Hezbollah was unable or unwilling to help prop up Bashar al-Assad’s regime, which quickly fell. Iran’s network of proxies was unraveling.

A shaky 2024 ceasefire between Lebanon and Israel was broken after the United States and Israel launched a war of choice against Iran in February with a series of strikes that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Hezbollah launched a barrage of missiles at Israel in support of Iran, and the Israeli military retaliated with a brutal offensive into southern Lebanon. At least 4,300 Lebanese have been killed and more than 1 million displaced in the ongoing operation, which has drawn parallels to Israel’s 1982 invasion.

Iran—by far the weaker military force—has had leverage in the conflict with Israel and the United States because of its control of the Strait of Hormuz. Now in its ninth month, the war has led to a global energy crunch, shaken up alliances, and undercut U.S. credibility. Lebanon remains embroiled in conflict orchestrated by outsiders. Hezbollah is again rebuilding its forces. History has a way of repeating itself in the Middle East.

A woman holds a portrait of a killed fighter as she attends a ceremony commemorating Hezbollah Martyrs’ Day in Beirut on Nov. 11. Joseph Eid/AFP via Getty Images

What Washington is sorely missing as it navigates this quagmire is someone like Kerr, an individual whom the historian Kamal Salibi, his friend and colleague, once called the “best kind of American who came to the Middle East”—one who was devoted to, and clear-eyed about, the region and its relations with the United States.
