Your all-access pass to FP

The semiconductor manufacturer Nvidia, which had until recently been the most valuable company in the world, was thrown into turmoil this past week. Company founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned upon allegations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and subsequently intervened to sell Nvidia chips to her China-tied company, despite U.S. regulations in place to prevent China’s access to the technology. The scandal has put a spotlight on the widespread international practice of economic espionage—and also on the Trump administration’s susceptibility to corruption.

What is the difference between industrial espionage and economic espionage? Is the tech elite particularly vulnerable to this type of spying? And will China be successful at incorporating any AI technologies that it managed to steal?

The semiconductor manufacturer Nvidia, which had until recently been the most valuable company in the world, was thrown into turmoil this past week. Company founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned upon allegations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and subsequently intervened to sell Nvidia chips to her China-tied company, despite U.S. regulations in place to prevent China’s access to the technology. The scandal has put a spotlight on the widespread international practice of economic espionage—and also on the Trump administration’s susceptibility to corruption.

Prefer to listen? To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts.

What is the difference between industrial espionage and economic espionage? Is the tech elite particularly vulnerable to this type of spying? And will China be successful at incorporating any AI technologies that it managed to steal?

Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Cameron Abadi: What are the differences exactly between industrial espionage, economic intelligence, and economic espionage?

Adam Tooze: In general understanding, industrial espionage is above all targeted at particular businesses by, more often than not, other businesses but sometimes by governments. And it’s about accessing commercial secrets, business secrets, business strategies, business technologies. And it involves various types of subterfuge or illegal action.

Economic espionage is sort of blurred into that zone, because it also involves various types of subterfuge. But when we say economic espionage, one immediately thinks of governments. Why is that? I think because when we think of businesses, we think of private economic activity and profit. But when we use the word “economy,” we immediately start thinking about GDP and national interest. And so, the sorts of information that are being targeted there might be more to do with technologies of general strategic interest. So that will be different from industrial espionage or purely commercial espionage.

And then an example of economic intelligence would be, say, wartime efforts on the part of the British who are aiming a strategic bombing program against Germany and therefore need to understand how the German economy functions and built an economics intelligence wing of the British military war effort so as to organize that. And that ranged from people who were architectural historians who knew which cities would be inflammable if you dropped incendiary bombs on them all the way through to an understanding of the input-output diagram, the supply chains.

And it involves, more often than not, open-source information. It doesn’t involve any subterfuge at all. And so economic intelligence kind of blurs into the world that we’re in, of economic reporting, of newsletters, of regular updates. The Economist magazine has what it used to call the Economist Intelligence Unit, which was presumably very well-connected journalists doing studies.

And I think the allegation in the Nvidia case sits most squarely in the domain of economic espionage. Yes, it targets a particular business and the top man in that particular business, the charismatic figurehead, indeed, of the entire hardware side of AI. So it would seem that it sits somewhere on that boundary.

I don’t think the allegation, however, is that Jensen Huang’s lover was doing this with a view to commercially profiting herself. I think the suggestion is that it’s MSS, the Ministry of State Security, which is doing this on behalf of the Chinese state.

CA: Jensen Huang is said to have fallen prey to a honey-trap method of espionage, in which a spy creates a sexual relationship to later exploit it. Is our current economic elite in tech companies particularly susceptible to this form of espionage?

AT: It’s impossible not to speculate about the ego makeup of Silicon Valley engineers. It wouldn’t, after all, be surprising if there was a desire for compensation for a whole variety of inhibitions, which no doubt are introduced at various stages in many people’s careers during their extraordinary efforts in very recondite zones of technical expertise. So, the nerd gone wild at the head of a company, the loneliness of people in that kind of position, all of this, I think, no doubt plays a role.

But then I was thinking, actually sociologically, and I came to this strange realization, because I spend quite a lot of time in hotels because of this weird existence that I have. And I was thinking to myself, if a senior soldier goes to a hotel, on the face of it, you’re kind of wondering what the senior soldier is doing in a hotel, right? If a senior civil servant, pretty much whichever government they work for, goes to a really glamorous hotel, again, you’d be asking yourself, how can they afford that? That’s not really where they belong, right?

So suddenly, you realize that the whole zone of high-end, expensive, relatively exclusive hospitality that presumably provides the most attractive zone for this kind of entrapment, the actors for whom it arouses zero legitimacy issues, zero need for explanation at all, in fact it’s completely normal and taken for granted, are high-level business figures.

In fact, the entire conference circuit, where people stay, the blending in those spaces of leisure and business activity, including pools and gyms and eating and drinking as a matter of course, in fact, isa kind of mandate for many businesses. I’ve gone to a lot of these investor conferences, and it’s quite clear that networking is an absolutely required option, right? There’s no excuse for just withdrawing to your room and getting on with your life, which I’d want to do most of the time.

And so presumably, this is precisely the world in which this works. I mean, business people systematically expect to be wined and dined. They expect to be courted. They constantly struggle to draw the line between reasonable inducements and bribery. That is an essential part of their business. And many of them, of course, have very strict codes of ethics. But it’s a matter of record that those shift all the time.

And they’re much more like, in that sense, the Chinese Communist Party than they are like, you know, conventional civil service jobs in the West, where it’s just quite clear that accepting any kind of gift in any form is just off-limits. No one in the civil service is regularly invited to glamorous parties where there’s a mixture of more or less formally clad, in some cases scantily clad, different types of interaction. And so it’s a kind of recipe for stress on this fault line, I would have thought. And it’s purely sociological, it’s not a matter of psychology at all.

CA: There’s clearly a distinction between pursuing the acquisition of technologies through espionage of this kind versus productively absorbing that technology upon having acquired it. How does that distinction apply right now to China?

AT: I think this is the whole game, actually. The real reason to be worried is that China has a demonstrated and extraordinary capacity to incorporate. In other words, it’s a near-peer. And that’s precisely what makes it so alarming to Western security officials, is that there’s absolutely every reason to think they can, yeah. And furthermore, leapfrog, even. Give them half a chance and there’s every single reason to think that they can generalize it, make it cheaper, speed it up.

There are differences, obviously, because what Nvidia does or what Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company does or what the lithograph makers do is literally special source. Like, no one has ever done that anywhere, ever, in the entire world in the history of humanity. So whether you can replicate that is an open question. But that’s presumably what the Chinese aren’t going to do anyway. They’re going to make their own version that’s more suitable to their circumstances.

And it’s critical to know—and we don’t know what’s actually happened in this case—but there are certain critical problems that it’s interesting to know how other people solve them, because it helps you to think about how you should solve them in your own terms. And that is why I think the Chinese case is so significant, because they have a demonstrated capacity to do that. And it really varies—in regard to transport engineering, cars, railways, solar, batteries, there has already been hugely successful leapfrogging; the game is over. With regard to chips, it’s a slightly different story, and I think that speaks to the fact that the technological demands are just so mind-blowingly high.

But that does contrast very significantly with the Soviet Union, which at different periods in its history demonstrated greater- and lesser-degree capacity to incorporate technologies that it acquired through espionage. So around the atomic bomb program, there was a quite a high capacity to incorporate. Then of course in rocketry, they become world-leading. And they do that like the Americans by capturing German rocket scientists and then incorporating their knowledge into what was already a high-functioning military industrial system in the Soviet Union that was wasteful of people’s lives but was generative of a whole series of incredibly innovative, very, very powerful and effective weapons.

But more generally, it’s a remarkable instance of just how little can get transferred, because after all, the Soviet Union was the beneficiary, after ‘45, of a huge wave—this is the untold story of German reparations after World War II, absolutely gigantic, and they take the form principally of dismantling. So vast amounts of German equipment are shipped to the Soviet Union where, I don’t think it’s merely apocryphal to say, an awful lot of it just rusted and was not fully incorporated into the Soviet system.

Now, in earlier stages, they had done much better. So in the ‘30s, the Stalinist industrialization program is heavily dependent on American expertise and on German expertise funded in part by export guarantees from the Weimar Republic that helped to fund this flow.

So it wasn’t consistently rubbish at incorporating, but it certainly wasn’t the powerhouse of creative imitation, adaptation, modification, and improvement that China is, to an extent that nowhere else in the world can match, right?

That’s the extraordinary thing. They can iterate, they can modify, they could incorporate at a pace that no one else in the world—in almost all areas of production—no one else can match. And so, then if you feed that with privileged insider information, then you’d expect really large-scale effects.

Cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi

Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze

During NATO’s formative years, the U.S. military commitment to the old continent was a tenuous thing. Dwight Eisenhower, appointed the first supreme allied commander of Europe in 1950, argued—amid a vicious debate in Washington over committing additional divisions to Europe—that American forces should only act as a bridge until Europe stepped up to defend itself. If the United States still had troops in Europe 10 years hence, he said in 1951, then the trans-Atlantic project would be a failure.

Ike’s forecast, it seems, was wrong on both counts. Seventy-five years on, roughly 80,000 U.S. troops remain on the continent. Yet few would regard the alliance as a failure. The U.S. military commitment succeeded in guaranteeing Europe’s freedom and keeping the Soviets at bay. But Europe never fully shouldered the burden of its own defense.

During NATO’s formative years, the U.S. military commitment to the old continent was a tenuous thing. Dwight Eisenhower, appointed the first supreme allied commander of Europe in 1950, argued—amid a vicious debate in Washington over committing additional divisions to Europe—that American forces should only act as a bridge until Europe stepped up to defend itself. If the United States still had troops in Europe 10 years hence, he said in 1951, then the trans-Atlantic project would be a failure.

Germany Rearmed: The Return of War and the End of Illusions, Liana Fix, Oxford University Press, 216 pp., $34.99, November 2026

Ike’s forecast, it seems, was wrong on both counts. Seventy-five years on, roughly 80,000 U.S. troops remain on the continent. Yet few would regard the alliance as a failure. The U.S. military commitment succeeded in guaranteeing Europe’s freedom and keeping the Soviets at bay. But Europe never fully shouldered the burden of its own defense.

Old assumptions, however, are finally changing. Squeezed by both a volatile Washington and voracious Moscow, Europe has finally awoken to its security dilemma: Its defense spending has nearly doubled in six years in real terms, from 242 billion euros in 2020 to 454 billion euros in 2026. If by 2035 Europe fully meets its NATO military expenditure target—spending 3.5 percent of GDP on defense (compared to the little more than 2 percent that it spends today)—then the surge in annual spending will rival the scale of the Marshall Plan relative to Europe’s GDP.

As Council on Foreign Relations scholar Liana Fix argues in her incisive new book, Germany Rearmed, the central protagonist in this story is Berlin. Germany has doubled defense spending since 2021 and accounts for more than a quarter of the European Union’s increase over that period. Based on its current budget, by 2029, Germany will spend more on its military than France and the U.K. today spend combined.

But is a rearmed Germany, in fact, a good thing for Europe and the world? Fix makes a compelling case that Berlin shedding its “myth of pacifism” is in the best interest of both Europe and the United States. But risks abound. A militarily empowered Germany has centrifugal potential, threatening friction with prickly France and anxious neighbors in Central and Eastern Europe if the rearmament is not executed within a broader European framework. And if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party eventually takes the reins of what will be one of the world’s most powerful militaries, it would reawaken historical nightmares.

Germany Rearmed gives proper airing to the consequences and challenges of German rearmament, often left unanalyzed amid general backslapping about surging European defense spending. The U.S. commitment to Europe is ultimately unsustainable at current levels as Washington focuses on growing threats in the Pacific—and given its isolationist spasms at home. And Europe, with Germany as its backbone, has the overwhelming means to check a revanchist Russia—Germany’s economy is roughly two times the size of Russia’s, and the EU’s is nearly 10 times its size.

But policymakers in Europe and Berlin should take heed of Fix’s advice. She argues that Germany needs to do a better job of Europeanizing its rearmament—in force structure, spending on a Europe-wide military industrial base, and joint funding—or it risks undermining European cohesion as the United States draws down.

West Germany participates for the first time as NATO’s 15th member in Paris, France, on May 9, 1955. AFP via Getty Images

Germany’s recent rearmament push, at first blush, may appear as a sudden break from the past. In popular perception, the allied occupation after World War II underwrote an enduring German aversion to military power, just as in Japan—whose own story of U.S. occupation and political transformation is beautifully told in John W. Dower’s Pulitzer-winning Embracing Defeat. The Western security architecture during the Cold War then reinforced German passivity: Lord Hastings Ismay, NATO’s first secretary-general, allegedly described NATO’s purpose as to “keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down.”

This “myth of pacifism,” according to Fix, has permeated German history ever since: from Chancellor Willy Brandt’s Ostpolitik of the 1970s to the Wandel durch Handel (“change through trade”) approach to Russia and China adopted under both Chancellors Gerhard Schröder and Angela Merkel. At seemingly every opportunity, Germany prioritized diplomacy and economic engagement over military power, believing the former to be more attuned to the future. This belief hardened after 1989, when Germans concluded (correctly) that the Soviet collapse owed more to Mikhail Gorbachev’s reforms than to U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s military flexing.

Crucially, as Fix observes, the German body politic has no grand military tradition to lean on, unlike its European neighbors. The United Kingdom can look back nostalgically to its days of ruling the waves. France’s defiant Gaullist military tradition is having its moment in the sun in the wake of Julian Jackson’s masterful book De Gaulle, adapted into a recently released blockbuster biopic. Germany, for obvious reasons, can’t draw from its 20th-century military history; even Prussian militarism is viewed skeptically with the hindsight of what followed.

But Fix provides nuance to this myth of pacifism, arguing that Germany was in fact no stranger to hard power after WWII. West German defense spending surpassed 3 percent of GDP through the mid-1970s, and even after the Cold War, the Bundeswehr fought in out-of-area operations in both the Balkans and Afghanistan, where it lost 55 soldiers—a fact little remembered in Germany today.

Quibbles aside, Germany has undeniably entered a new relationship with its military. In addition to the doubling of defense spending over the past five years, polling from fall 2024 showed that 73 percent of Germans wanted to invest more money in European security and 65 percent supported a spending target of 3 percent of GDP or higher.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and U.S. President Donald Trump speak at the G-7 summit, in Evian, France, on June 16.Christian Hartmann / POOL / AFP via Getty Images

While many commentators would gladly attribute this wake-up call to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s brutal invasion of Ukraine, Fix inconveniently but convincingly credits U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House as the real catalyst.

After Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz claimed grandiloquently in his “Zeitenwende” speech that “the world … will no longer be the same as before.” But while his 100 billion euro special defense fund was a good first step, disbursement was slow, and it wasn’t followed by other bold moves.

Only in 2025, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz facing a hostile Washington, did Germany finally turn a corner. Between 2025 and 2029, Germany plans to spend a total of 649 billion euros and reach annual spending of 3.5 percent of GDP—up from just 1.15 percent in 2015, the year after Russia’s annexation of Crimea.

Referring to Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the United States’ reelection of Trump in 2024, Fix memorably writes that “history had to repeat itself twice for Germany to abandon the ‘myth of pacifism’ and to seriously begin rearmament.”

It’s a remarkable feature of our turbulent era that the breakneck rearmament of Germany is considered, in the main, a beneficent thing. Economists surveying the many challenges of slowing European growth and flagging competitiveness point to continental rearmament as a sole bright spot: a fiscal stimulus surpassing COVID-era spending that may boost sagging European productivity growth by 0.25 percent per every 1 percent of GDP spent on defense, if focused on research and development as well as equipment rather than military pensions and personnel, according to estimates from the Kiel Institute.

And Germany is undoubtedly the most consequential player in the story of Europe’s broader rearmament. With French bond markets quaking, Germany is one of the only countries with the fiscal headroom to spend, with a debt-to-GDP ratio of 64 percent. Germany’s contribution to increased spending will also invariably be Europe’s largest, given that its economy is a third larger than that of the U.K. and 50 percent larger than France. And its industrial prowess positions it well to play the role of Europe’s arsenal.

But what kind of military power will Germany be? Here Fix rightly throws up notes of caution. Thus far, Germany’s rearmament has largely been a national one, with spending at the German rather than EU level and funding largely going to German defense players. This trajectory risks fragmenting Europe’s military production, while also enhancing Germany’s own preeminent power within the continent—inviting suspicion and potentially exacerbating European divisions. It’s hard to envision outright conflict between Germany and its neighbors, but a more assertive Germany backed by hard power may more forcefully push its own foreign agenda over, say, Poland or France. The U.S. security blanket helped keep a lid on these rivalries since World War II; if Washington retreats from the continent, competing national priorities may sharpen with the steel of military spending.

Fix’s solution, which is a compelling one, is for Germany to rearm inside either a more European NATO or a broader European security architecture: spending at European level where possible on shared platforms, inside a more integrated European command, and across a continent-wide military industrial base. Such “Europeanized” spending would allay concerns about the contortions in power caused by German rearmament. It would also reassure allies wary of an AfD ascension in Berlin: tied into a NATO or European architecture, a remilitarized Germany would have a harder time pursuing an overtly nationalistic military agenda.

The question of Washington’s future role on the continent still presents a broad conundrum. Fix wrote Germany Rearmed in 2025 and early 2026, and the rawness of the Trump administration’s provocations on trade and Greenland shines through. She argues that Washington is “never going back” and that the future trans-Atlantic relationship under either Democrats or Republicans will resemble “a patron-client relationship more than an alliance, with no preferred treatment for Europeans.”

This likely over-indexes on the wrecking ball of the Trump administration’s first two years. After the Republicans’ drubbing in the midterms, and considering that Trump’s favoritism toward Putin’s Russia and Xi Jinping’s China is idiosyncratic even within his party, the possibilities of U.S.-European reconciliation are higher than she lets on. Brussels and Washington will still have overwhelming shared interests come a new U.S. administration in 2029, especially as Europe finally awakens to the threat of surging Chinese exports and barrels into a trade conflict with Beijing over the coming years. More likely is a United States that is less bullying and extractive, whether a Republican or Democratic administration, and remains committed to NATO and Article V—even if it pushes for Europe to shoulder more of its defense burden while gradually winding down its troop commitment.

New reservists of the Bundeswehr train at Camp Aulenbach near Baumholder, Germany, on Sept. 15. Andreas Rentz/Getty Images

This matters because it should inform how Europe rearms. Replacing core U.S. enablers, such as space-based intelligence and integrated air and missile defense systems, would be a costly endeavor that would eat up a tremendous amount of European capacity and take up to a decade. The International Institute for Strategic Studies puts the cost of fully replacing US capabilities at more than $1 trillion.

A more prudent wager is that a future United States will maintain its nuclear umbrella over Europe and the backbone of critical NATO capabilities while Europe builds capacity in complementary areas such as ground forces, missiles, unmanned systems, and munitions. Betting on even limited U.S. staying power may seem foolhardy at the moment, but the alternative would be an expensive distraction that Europe can ill afford.

The greater threat to European security and cohesion is more likely to come from within. The AfD now leads every national poll in Germany, averaging 29 percent to the Christian Democratic Union/Christian Socialist Union’s 19 percent. Its path to the chancellery as German elections approach in 2029 remains narrow given that Germany maintains a strong political firewall against the party in light of history. But the AfD agenda should terrify us: The party has an affinity for Russia and China, and it advocates for even greater defense spending of 5 percent of GDP in pursuit of national sovereignty.

However unlikely an AfD-run Germany may be, populist convulsions within Europe are certain. Fix spends little time on the rise in France of the far-right National Rally, which appears poised to win the French presidency in the spring. How a right-wing France in the engine room of Europe would affect broader rearmament is a question that should be top of mind in Brussels today.

The implications of German rearmament are vexing, and the recent surge in spending represents easy yards. But for a remilitarized Germany to truly enhance European security, it must surrender more of its own power, decision-making, and even defense-industrial spending to the rest of Europe. Otherwise, Europe will have answered Eisenhower’s challenge 75 years on only to produce a more fractured continent as the United States pulls back.

1. On Sunday, South African authorities announced the results from Nov. 4 local elections. Why was the election a historic one for the African National Congress party?

The party won a majority in every province except one.

It marked the party’s worst-ever results.

The party won a majority in the Western Cape province for the first time.

Two-thirds of the party’s election winners were women.

No party won an outright majority, a further sign that South Africa’s political landscape is fragmenting, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.

2. This year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference kicked off on Monday in Antalya, Turkey. How many people are part of the official delegation from the United States, the world’s biggest cumulative carbon emitter?

U.S. President Donald Trump has withdrawn the country from the Paris Agreement at the start of both of his presidential terms. He has also tried to intimidate countries that want to take action on the climate, Noah Gordon wrote in January.

3. Which former leader requested new identity papers from their home country on Monday?

Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina

Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban

Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte

Thai Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra

Hasina has been living in exile in India since fleeing Bangladesh in the wake of mass protests in 2024, FP’s Michael Kugelman reports in South Asia Brief.

4. French sports star Teddy Riner announced on Monday that he was joining the country’s presidential race. In what sport did Riner compete?

The three-time Olympic gold medalist expressed concern about the rise of the country’s far right, which has broken through the French political establishment’s long-standing firewall, Robert Zaretsky wrote in March.

5. Israel’s Knesset swore in its new class of lawmakers on Tuesday, but they still haven’t formed a government. Who was tasked this week with leading coalition-building negotiations?

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett

Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu

Democrats party leader Yair Golan

Eisenkot’s clearest path to power is joining forces with the country’s Arab parties—something that has only happened once in Israel’s history, FP’s Steven A. Cook writes.

6. Pope Leo XIV was greeted by massive crowds during a visit to Peru that began on Wednesday. According to estimates from local authorities, roughly how many people took to the streets in the capital of Lima to see him?

Leo became a naturalized Peruvian citizen after serving as a missionary in the country. His 12-day South America trip is the longest yet of his pontificate, with two earlier stops in Uruguay and Argentina, FP’s Catherine Osborn reports in Latin America Brief.

7. On Thursday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned just days after admitting to having an affair with Alice Huang, a woman believed by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy. Alice Huang was formerly an executive at a data center company called what?

Nvidia stock has plummeted this week in the wake of the scandal, which could have implications for the wider artificial intelligence industry, FP’s Rishi Iyengar writes.

8. This week’s resignations don’t end there. Following months of scrutiny, what prompted Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka to submit his resignation to parliament on Thursday?

He was unable to prove that he graduated high school.

He also had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

He was implicated in a major vote-buying scandal.

He faced allegations of spying for Russia.

The move throws a wrench in the tenuous truce between the government and Gibran’s father, former President Joko Widodo, FP’s Alexandra Sharp reports in World Brief.

9. Also on Thursday, Russia agreed to allow which actor to participate in the next round of peace talks for the war in Ukraine?

Officials from the International Atomic Energy Agency

European representatives

From bomb threats to drone incursions, hybrid threats from suspected Russian operatives have stoked fear in Europe in recent months, Beniamino Irdi writes.

10. Which embassy unexpectedly received attention around the world on social media this week after briefly closing on Tuesday for a staff event?

The Brazilian Embassy in Berlin

The Egyptian Embassy in New Delhi

The Greek Embassy in Ottawa, Canada

The Finnish Embassy in Canberra, Australia

Thousands of the embassy’s adoring fans shared jokes and commiserated over the closure—which prompted the embassy to celebrate its reopening the next day with a ribbon-cutting ceremony, the Guardian reports.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: US proposed Ukraine cedes Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, Zelensky says
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said that the United States proposed Ukraine cede land to Russia in exchange for joining NATO and that his government was in talks on "specific" security guarantees from the West.

He said that US negotiators had floated a question about Ukraine's potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for ‌joining the alliance, following the ⁠latest round of peace talks with Russia in ‌Abu Dhabi.

Zelensky reiterated his position that ⁠Kyiv was not willing to retreat from its territory. He said that if Ukraine received a ‌comprehensive security package, that includes security guarantees, a strong and well-funded Ukrainian ‌army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a referendum.

"The Americans raised a question: "What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He said the EU and NATO are Europe's only "real security", warning the Kremlin's bid to change the continent's security architecture could lead to more wars.

"This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations," Zelensky told reporters Friday in comments under embargo until Saturday. "Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe."

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: Live: France deploys 70,000 police for new wave of anti-government protests
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
From treating tear gas exposure to tending to injuries, street medics have become an increasingly common sight at protests all over the world.

But who exactly are they and when did they start showing up at demonstrations? ⬇️

Between 50 and 60 marches are expected throughout the country on Saturday, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who plans to mobilise as many police officers as during the three previous rounds of weekend demonstrations since October 24, calling on around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes.

A police source told AFP that between 30,000 and 60,000 people were expected in Paris, including possibly “300 to 600 high-risk individuals.”

The Paris demonstration is due to set off from Place de la République at 1.00 pm toward Place de la Nation, passing through Bastille. This is intended to allow families with children to leave the march before the dispersal and to avoid the clashes with police that often occur during dispersals.

The "Yellow Vests" coordination group, which has helped organise Saturday demonstrations across France since October 17 to protest the “high cost of living,” listed 338 demonstrations nationwide on its website Friday afternoon for Saturday’s day of action.

The march in Paris is set to begin shortly at 2pm at Place de la République, heading toward Place de la Nation via Bastille. This route allows families with children to leave the march before it concludes, helping them avoid the clashes with police that frequently occur as crowds disperse.

Shortly before noon, dozens of musicians could be seen preparing to rehearse, cordoned off by barrier tape at the base of the statue in Place de la République.

Karl Ghazi, general secretary for Paris of the CGT,  France's major labour union CGT, noted a "real sense of activist fatigue, which we have to take into account".

The union did not issue a national call to demonstrate, but its regional branches in the Île-de-France area have called for participation in the movement.

French police have made extensive use of tear gas during protests that have roiled France in recent weeks, sometimes causing grievous injuries.

Thousands of accounts of women experiencing acutely painful periods and increased bleeding are further challenging assumptions that the chemical irritant carries only minor consequences.

Lacrymos du sang (tear gas of blood), a collective comprising activists and health workers, has in recent weeks collected thousands of testimonies from protesters and bystanders who reported changes to their menstrual cycles after exposure to tear gas. It plans to release its findings on November 17, but some reports are already visible on the group's Instagram account.

Read Ben Dodman's feature for more.

A total of 21 station closures will affect Paris métro lines today, at the request of the Paris's prefectural police.

Both Châtelet and Les Halles have been closed since 10am.

Stations near the Champs-Élysées will close from 11am, including Charles de Gaulle–Étoile station.

Meanwhile, stations along the route of the procession – between Filles du Calvaire and Reuilly-Diderot, will also be closed.

A Spanish neo-Nazi activist suspected of planning an attack in Paris was arrested last Friday.

Spanish daily El País reported that Spanish authorities discovered dozens of weapons and Nazi-related items in the possession of Isabel Peralta, a spokesperson for a far-right fringe group. According to the Spanish daily, she had planned to travel to Paris to "open fire" amid ongoing social unrest and student protests.

She was arrested on Friday, November 6, along with thirteen other members of the organisation Núcleo Nacional.

"Society's in bad shape," said Claire Bourdille, from a collective battling violence against children and teenagers. "We can't focus on one cause more than another," she told AFP.

Activists have in recent months demanded better protection for children against sexual abuse.

Others will be protesting against a new bill in parliament to grant police who use their weapons a presumption of legitimate self-defence.

Activists argue the bill, approved by the lower house and soon to go to the Senate, amounts to a "licence to kill". They say it would make holding security forces accountable even harder in a country where most cases of alleged police brutality rarely reach a criminal court.

Its backers, including the far-right National Rally party of presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen, say it is necessary to avoid police being automatically suspected of using disproportionate force.

Helicopters and drones monitoring protests are both a sight and sound that have become almost commonplace since October 17.

From the FRANCE 24 office in Issy-les-Moulineaux, the sound of the helicopters that will be monitoring this afternoon’s demonstration can already be heard... ⬇️

A drone pilot from the Paris Prefecture’s aerial unit practices operating his device at the police academy in Paris, September 27, 2023, © Joel Saget, AFP file photo.

Welcome to this liveblog covering the protests happening across France.

Follow our Liveblog for the latest updates.

https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.text:
Microsoft ⁠said ​on Saturday that ​services had fully recovered across Teams, ​Outlook, ‌Copilot and ⁠other applications, ending a ‌global outage ‌that ​crippled online communications across businesses and ​governments ​for ​over 24 hours.

"We have completed ‌our efforts to ​address the underlying issue of the incident ​and restored ​service to ​the remaining impacted customers ​and regions," the company posted on X.

The company earlier apologised for the shutdown affecting online software including Outlook, Copilot and certain features of Teams, which since Thursday had impacted at least 74 countries across the Americas, Europe, Asia and Africa.

The technology ‌giant earlier said it was "monitoring the backlog of email messages accrued ‌during this event" across its enterprise services before announcing the issue was resolved.

The US Homeland Security chief in Washington also confirmed that there was no link between the Microsoft issue and Friday's US air stoppage. Microsoft earlier said it had no indication that the Federal Aviation Administration nationwide ground stop is related to the service disruption that took Outlook and other services offline Thursday, a spokesperson for the company said.

Microsoft had said server ​issues were behind the incident that ‌also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out AI as the cause.

Outlook and Teams are two of ⁠the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.

It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines ‌to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements.

Organisations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.

https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.title: China to host first-ever trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin next week
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.text:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday.

Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran – but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, US officials said.

WATCH MORE
China keeps a close eye on US midterm shake-up

The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.

One of the major conflicts dominating Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the US officials said.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.

The meeting calls back to the 1945 Yalta summit in the Soviet Union, where then-US president Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain's Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin laid out the post-WWII settlement and new territorial boundaries in Europe.

Zelensky has raised the alarm that the meeting in Shenzhen could be a Yalta-like "redistribution of spheres of influence" for the 21st century.

The Trump administration has sought to reassert US dominance over the "Western hemisphere" – including by capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January – but splitting the world among great powers like it's 1945 may not guarantee security.

Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday – their fourth meeting since the US president's return to power last year.

But Trump is not scheduled to have a separate one-on-one with Putin.

The US also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: US flights resume after nationwide ground stop lifted
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday night that airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop that Trump administration officials blamed on “overloaded,” “outdated” systems.

Even with the order being lifted, the airlines will not be able to return to normal operations immediately because so many of their planes and crews are out of position.

The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system overwhelmed it. He couldn't rule out another outage.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

There was no indication the communications failure was related to a cyberattack. The consequences were profound, disrupting potentially thousands of planned flights through at least late Friday night and upending travel plans for passengers.

“It’s frustrating. This certainly sounds like it’s going to be more than the usual run-of-the-mill delay. I look forward to finding out why,” said Jeff Dubner, a Washington attorney whose Alaska Airlines flight home from Los Angeles was already half an hour late and taxiing to the runway when the plane came to a halt.

International flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Mullin, with some seen taking off Friday evening.

Asked whether Mullin could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, he said: “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way.” He said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that it appears to be “mechanically driven,” adding that officials were still looking for the cause.

At least 827 flights were diverted so far as a result. As of 7:05 pm EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

The airports where many of the flights ended up being diverted included Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport and Nashville International Airport.

Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 pm EST, raising the likelihood of more cancelations and flight diversions.

At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday afternoon, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board.

Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.

Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals. Her friends, she said, had already arrived there.

“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer, who took a week of vacation for the trip. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”

Austin Curtis and his wife were rethinking their trip from South Bend, Indiana, to a friend’s baby shower in Denver after getting delayed during a layover in Chicago.

They had boarded a flight to Denver from O’Hare International Airport when they were told to get off the plane.

“We did see them taking luggage off our plane and others, so we’re assuming it’s going to be a pretty substantial delay,” Curtis said.

They were unsure whether to get a hotel room or keep waiting out the delay at the airport. With care already in place for their two young children at home, they might stay the weekend in Chicago, he said.

READ MORE
US flight authority orders national ground stop over air traffic control 'communication issue'

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.

Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.

FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it is prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.

US airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods – from letters to packages -- to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

Despite the nationwide FAA ground stop, SpaceX launched its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday afternoon on its latest test flight.

Mullin had said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, DC, and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centres.

The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.

But much work remains. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”

Friday’s ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.summary: FAA blames “overloaded’ systems for the delay. Hundreds of flights were diverted. The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control outage in September.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Passengers face further cancellations as US flights slowly resume after ground stop
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
More than 2,000 flights were cancelled Saturday as airlines across the US worked to dig out from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, which stranded passengers and forced professional and college sports teams to scramble for alternate transportation.

Trump administration officials said new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours.

A limited number of domestic flights departed after the stop was lifted around 8:15pm ET (01:15 GMT Saturday). But the effects could be felt for days, with officials saying the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The incident marked only the second time such an alert had been issued in US airspace – which is among the busiest in the world – since the 9/11 attacks.

Federal Aviation Administration officials reopened the airspace on Friday night "after restoring full functionality" at air traffic control facilities, according to Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy.

"It will take us time (to) resume normal operations... Our top priority is the safety of you and your family when you fly," Duffy said.

Administration officials blamed the incident on telecommunications issues with decades-old equipment, adding there was no evidence of foul play.

"This is a legacy system problem," Duffy said. "We have old, old switches, old routers.

"We use 1980s little copper lines. It's an old system that went down, and went down everywhere. It got overloaded."

Duffy had formally asked Congress on Thursday for $30.1 billion in funds to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control System.

As the ground stop was lifted, he repeated his plea.

"I'm going to say it a million times: the Congress has to give the resources to the president so he can finish this bill," he said.

There were almost 6,000 flights cancelled, including some international routes, according to FlightAware, a tracking platform.

Footage from airports around the country showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways.

Passengers thronged concourses, desperate for information about an outage that had thrown their plans into chaos.

"We're trying to debate whether or not we need to reschedule or drive or what, but if the whole country is stopped, that means the highways are going to be jammed too," said Joseph Anderson, 72, who was trying to fly from Las Vegas to Oakland, California.

A nationwide ground stop is highly unusual.

There was one such stop in January 2023 when a pilot notification system failed, but the only other national stop happened in the wake of the 9/11 attacks in September 2001, when no aircraft took to the skies for days.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stressed there was no evidence of any hostile action on Friday.

"We've seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack or (AI) attack," he told a news conference.

He also ruled out any connection with the outage that affected Microsoft this week, knocking email systems offline for millions of users, public services and businesses worldwide.

The stop caused misery at airports around the country.

At New York's LaGuardia Airport, Tiara Johnson said she had been trying to get to Orlando for a concert with a friend.

"They just keep delaying it... So it started out at 7:55. Then it went to 8:30, 9:30. Now it's at 10:30. So we don't know when it's gonna leave," she told AFP.

"I feel very frustrated because you know, you come to the airport and then all of a sudden your whole plans have changed and you don't know when you're leaving. We're kind of stuck."

Some travelers said they had been told their flight was delayed because of wind, while others were left to gather what information they could.

Boards at the airport continued to show departures leaving as normal, while mobile boarding passes held by those stuck on the ground appeared to show their flight was underway.

Stranded passengers were scrambling to find alternatives, with long lines forming at rental car counters at the airport in Las Vegas.

Susan Sardina said she had boarded her flight back to Orange County, California when staff told passengers there was a problem.

"We were already on our flight to leave and we were told to get off," she told AFP as she stood in a lengthy queue for a rental car.

For those looking on the bright side, the delay was a chance to extend a break.

Kathy Sommers was on her way home from visiting friends in Las Vegas when her flight got cancelled.

"We're blessed that our friends are coming back to pick us up," she said. "So one more night to play cards."

(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP).

Officials say new technology being added to air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment. The incident marked only the second time such an alert had been issued in US airspace since the 9/11 attacks.

https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.title: France secures thrilling Nations Championship victory over South Africa
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.text:
France pulled off a stunning and nervy 21-19 victory over world champions South Africa in the Nations Championship on Friday.

A brilliant first-half display and gutsy second-half showing amid a flood of cards handed Les Bleus only their second win over the Springboks in their last 11 Tests.

Captain Antoine Dupont was named man of the match in a pulsating encounter that contrasted the running invention of the French with South Africa's bludgeoning force.

And in the end, the only difference was a missed conversion by Springboks replacement fly-half Manie Libbok.

France, though, were almost undone by wayward kicking, especially from half-back Maxime Lucu.

The hosts' backs sparkled in the first half with wings Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang and Louis Bielle-Biarrey, and full-back Theo Attissogbe scoring a try each in a scintillating first half.

But South Africa's brute force and forward power kept them in touch, scoring two catch-and-drive tries.

Tries from hookers Jan-Hendrik Wessels and Malcolm Marx, and a close-range effort from replacement scrum-half Cobus Reinach, helped them storm back from a 21-7 half-time deficit, but it was not enough.

It was South Africa's first defeat in the tournament and hands the initiative to New Zealand in the southern hemisphere pool.

France, though, ensured that they will maintain their lead in the northern hemisphere section ahead of next weekend's clash against Argentina, keeping them in pole position to reach the final at Twickenham in two weeks' time.

The build-up to the match had been peppered with mind games.

Having been named on the team sheet at fly-half, Dupont played at scrum-half with Lucu outside him.

And an hour before kick-off, South Africa coach Rassie Erasmus swapped his entire starting front row with the three players initially named on the bench.

France blew two early chances to open the scoring as Lucu kicked for the corner instead of the posts.

The first time he fluffed his lines and South Africa won a penalty at the subsequent scrum.

And the second time, the Springboks stole the line-out.

But things turned in France's favour on 13 minutes as Bok lock Lood de Jager saw yellow for a high tackle on Lucu.

Grandidier-Nkanang made them pay after 15 phases of play by diving over in the corner, with Lucu converting.

And before De Jager returned, Attissogbe pounced on a lucky ricochet off Kalvin Gourgue's head to score a second.

South Africa hit back on the half-hour mark with a classic tactic.

Their scrum won a penalty, which they kicked to the corner before mauling hooker Wessels over for the try.

But France hit back immediately as hooker Peato Mauvaka, who was a last-minute replacement for Julien Marchand, broke from a ruck and Dupont sent in a delectable grubber for the electrifying Bielle-Biarrey to notch his 30th try in 29 Tests.

Erasmus changed his entire front row five minutes before half-time, and moments later, Lucu was yellow-carded for a high tackle.

Kurt-Lee Arendse seemed to have scored a second Boks try on the stroke of half-time, but he was denied by an offside call.

Things swung back in France's favour as Boks No.8 Jasper Wiese was given a 20-minute red card early in the second half for a dangerous clear out.

But soon after, Grandidier-Nkanang was sent to the bin for a deliberate knock-on.

South Africa were quick to strike as Reinach jutted over from close range.

The visitors tried to turn the screw with their forward power and Lucu missed a crucial penalty attempt that would have given France a 10-point lead.

Then a yellow card to Regis Montagne for yet another collapsed scrum looked to have cost the hosts with just over 10 minutes to play.

The punishment was doubled as South Africa drove Marx over from a rolling maul.

But heroic defence and a steal by Dupont helped France see out a famous victory.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP).
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.summary: France beat South Africa 21-19 in the Nations Championship. Captain Antoine Dupont was named man of the match in a pulsating encounter. It was South Africa's first defeat in the tournament and hands the initiative to New Zealand in the southern hemisphere pool.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: France among five major powers to represent EU in Ukraine talks
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Europe will send a team of diplomats from the European Union and five individual countries to the next round of Ukraine talks, a top EU official said Friday, following a summit focused on how to avoid being shut out of US-led negotiations on ending the nearly five-year war.

European Council President Antonio Costa said the continent will be represented by officials from the 27-nation EU bloc and five members of the “Coalition of the Willing” that backs Ukraine: the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.

“We need to integrate all of us. And for this it's essential to have a team and to speak with only one voice,” Costa said.

European leaders have been concerned that a US-backed process will leave them sidelined and Kyiv vulnerable as Moscow and Washington decide the fate of a conflict that has roiled the continent.

Ukraine is eager for support from its European allies. It's reluctant to leave the talks solely in the hands of a US administration that has often seemed to lean toward Moscow’s views. Russia, for its part, does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort.

European leaders also distrust US President Donald Trump to negotiate on their behalf after a series of tense standoffs over trade, Greenland and conflicts in Iran and Ukraine.

“Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin. “There is no more US support.”

“At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans,” he said.

European leaders fear Russian President Vladimir Putin will press Trump to back a peace settlement that weakens not just Ukraine but broader European security. Putin has demanded NATO troops be pulled back from Russia’s borders and that no European forces be deployed in Ukraine.

As envoys from Washington, Moscow and Kyiv met this week in Abu Dhabi, several European countries, including the UK, France and Germany, attended discussions nearby, but not the main talks.

READ MORE
Abu Dhabi peace talks show US, Europe and Ukraine are ‘aligned’, NATO chief says

US envoy Jared Kushner and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said after they met in Dublin late Thursday that Europe would be part of the next round of talks. Zelensky said Europe would send a negotiating team, adding that “they will have a voice".

“We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” Kushner said, adding that Putin was “willing to give it a try.”

European leaders are united in wanting a place at the table. But they have tussled over whether Europe should be represented by one person — as Russia has demanded and the US suggested it would prefer — or a team, ultimately opting for the latter.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that “the Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar” and that they should name a representative.

Supporters of a single envoy, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, argued that the absence of a united European voice has allowed individual countries or small groups to engage in freelance diplomacy.

“There are too many different groupings discussing the issue,” she said.

The question of who represents Europe is an old one. Europe itself is loosely defined. Is it the 27-nation EU, the 32-nation NATO military alliance made up mostly of European countries, the 29-nation Schengen zone, or the 47-nation European Political Community?

That has long frustrated Washington.

After this week's US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia in the United Arab Emirates, Kushner said that “if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.”

That echoes the famous question often misattributed to former US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger: “Who do I call if I want to call Europe?”

The decision to send a team, rather than an individual, allows for participation by members of the “coalition of the willing”, a group of nations that have pledged to underpin a future ceasefire with military support. That includes the UK, which left the EU in 2020.

Poland is a voice for nations on the EU's eastern flank that face constant hybrid threats from Russia, including influence campaigns and disruptive drones.

It was not immediately clear who would represent the EU's institutions. Speculation had centred on Costa and the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas.

Earlier this year, Costa faced criticism within the EU after his office set up a hush-hush back-channel with Moscow.

Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, laid claim to the envoy role Friday, saying, “I’m the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy.”

“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but, you know, do we have a say, who is representing Russia?” she said. “We can’t send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending.”

READ MORE
Exclusive: EU's Kallas says US 'can't negotiate on our behalf' on lifting Russia sanctions

Meanwhile, some leaders are pessimistic about the talks.

“In my opinion, calling them negotiations is an exaggeration,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Thursday. “We will not build a new security architecture simply because the Russian president, or someone in the United States, wishes it.”

With Trump due to head to Beijing next week to meet Putin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said European leaders feared another “Anchorage moment”, a reference to the Alaska summit where they were stunned by Trump's overtures to the Russian leader in the absence of Ukrainian or European envoys.

“Please, no surprises,” Merz said. “Continue to play in team Europe and in the team with Ukraine.”

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs noted that Europe is larger than Russia in population, economy and military might. “We as Europe have to grow some bigger balls," he said.
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.summary: European leaders fear Russian President Vladimir Putin will press Trump to back a peace settlement. European leaders are united in wanting a place at the table, but they have tussled over whether Europe should be represented by one person.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24

The US Federal Aviation Administration grounded all departing flights nationwide on Friday after a communications ​failure hit ‌air traffic control centres across the country, disrupting ⁠thousands of flights.

The announcement means planes in the air may land, but those on the ground ‌cannot take off. Flight tracking service FlightAware said nearly 7,000 ⁠flights were delayed or cancelled due to the nationwide ground stop.

“The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all US airports ​following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic ‌Control Centres. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

The disruption is the ‌latest sign of strain on the US air traffic control system, which has been beset by ​equipment failures, communications problems and shortages of controllers while the FAA tries to replace ageing infrastructure. Congress approved $12.5 billion for the overhaul last year, and ​the FAA and White House asked lawmakers on Friday for another $30.1 billion.

Shortly ​before the announcement, the FAA halted traffic in Chicago ​due to air traffic control communications issues. The agency said, "All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further ​notice." The FAA said it would manage international flights on a case-by-case basis.

Friday's halt was the second nationwide ground stop of all departures since the September 11, 2001, attacks. The other happened in January 2023, when ⁠the FAA paused all domestic departures for less than two hours.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/k.title: 'We're still standing': King Charles jokes with Elton John in birthday clip
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

King Charles joined Elton John for an episode of his Rocket Hour radio show. (Supplied: Apple Music/Handout via Reuters)

King Charles joined Sir Elton John for an episode of the singer's radio show which was aired on the monarch's 78th birthday.

In it, the king joked that they both were "still standing".

The special edition episode of Elton John's Rocket Hour was to celebrate 50 years of The King's Trust.

Britain's King Charles has joked that he and Sir Elton John were "still standing" in a clip recorded for the singer's radio show which was aired on the monarch's 78th birthday.

King Charles had joined Sir John for a special edition of the singer's Elton John's Rocket Hour on Apple Music to celebrate 50 years of The King's Trust and musicians who have supported his youth charity.

During the episode, which was first broadcast on Saturday to coincide with the king's birthday, the pair discussed benefit concerts held in support of the Trust.

This included a Rock Gala held at Wembley Arena in 1986 where Sir Elton performed his 1980s hit, I'm Still Standing.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience," King Charles said.

Sir John, who turns 80 in March, replied, "I'm still sitting now, though", prompting laughs from the king.

"With occasional bits dropping off here and there," King Charles said.

"I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

Both men have suffered well-documented health problems in recent years, with the king still undergoing treatment for cancer and Sir Elton suffering problems with his eyesight.

King Charles and Sir Elton John at the Royal Variety Performance in 2024. (Reuters: Toby Melville/Pool/File Photo)

When he was the heir, King Charles founded the Prince's Trust in 1976 using his Royal Navy severance pay to help disadvantaged young people prepare for work, find jobs or start businesses.

It was renamed the King's Trust after Charles became king in 2022.

The charity says it has supported more than one million young people since its launch.

Rocket Man came at a vital time in Elton John's then-burgeoning career, saving him from being written off as a one-hit wonder.

"Music has always been at the heart of The Prince's, and now The King's Trust," King Charles said, adding that the program offered a chance to showcase performers who had supported the charity and newer artists it had helped launch.

The pair recalled benefit concerts stretching from Wembley Arena's rock galas in the 1980s to shows in Hyde Park and at the Royal Albert Hall.

Among them is British rock band Muse, which received a grant to buy sound equipment when it performed under its former name Rocket Baby Dolls.

The group later held a sold-out Royal Albert Hall concert in aid of the Trust in 2018, Buckingham Palace said in a statement.

"If you champion a young artist and show you believe in them, it makes all the difference," Sir Elton said.

Sir Elton received the Order of the Companions of Honour from Charles, then Prince of Wales, at Windsor Castle in 2021 for services to music and charity.

One of the best-selling artists of all time, with hits including "Goodbye Yellow Brick Road", "Rocket Man" and "Your Song", Sir Elton was knighted by Queen Elizabeth in 1998.

Rocket Hour is a weekly show that has aired globally on Apple Music 1 since 2015.

Women’s Big Bash League

Lily Bassingthwaighte finished with 3-25 off her four overs. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Defending WBBL champions, the Hobart Hurricanes have slumped to 0-6 after a 10-wicket loss to the Brisbane Heat.

The Hurricanes were dismissed for just 88 inside 18 overs, which the Heat chased down in just 5.4 overs.

Heat opener Grace Harris top-scored with 52 off just 22 balls.

Brisbane have continued their stunning WBBL rejuvenation in spectacular style, annihilating hapless Hobart by 10 wickets with a staggering 86 balls to spare.

After skittling the Hurricanes for just 86 in 17.5 overs at Bellerive Oval on Saturday, the Heat wasted no time securing themselves a fourth win in six matches, taking just 5.4 overs to race to 0-88 in reply.

Grace Harris (52 not out off 22 balls) and Charli Knott (34no off 12) looked like they were batting on a different deck to Hobart's confounded batters, who struggled to hit the ball off the square.

The 'Canes hit just six boundaries. Harris and Knott, in contrast, combined for 12 fours and four sixes.

Brisbane's 62-run powerplay set a new competition record.

Their intent was obvious as they crushed 17, 18, 20, seven and 13 off the five completed overs, Harris teeing off from the outset, before Knott applied the finishing touches, raising victory with back-to-back fours.

After going winless for 706 days, the Heat have now notched four victories in the past 10 days to consolidate third position on the ladder.

Meanwhile, reigning champions Hobart have crashed to a 0-6 record.

When captain Nicola Carey was castled by Lily Bassingthwaighte, the Hurricanes were staring down the barrel at 3-11 inside their own powerplay.

That soon became a perilous 6-42.

No 9 Lauren Smith top-scored with 20 before being bowled by Knott, ending Hobart's disappointing innings.

Bassingthwaighte (3-25) was the early destroyer, while Sianna Ginger (2-8), Lucy Hamilton (2-15) and Sarah Glenn (2-16) shared the spoils.

Darcy Vescio kicked two goals in her 100th game as Carlton progressed to a preliminary final clash with Melbourne. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick/AFL Photos)

Darcy Vescio starred in her 100th game as Carlton defeated Hawthorn in their AFLW preliminary final.

Sydney upset Geelong by three points at Kardinia Park, marred by a serious head injury to Cats ruck Piper Dunlop.

Geelong will face Melbourne and Sydney take on North Melbourne in the preliminary finals.

Carlton has claimed a thrilling five-point semifinal win over Hawthorn, with 100-gamer Darcy Vescio starring as the Blues set up an AFLW preliminary final against Melbourne.

Hawthorn started fast at Princes Park, but the Blues fought back, with Vescio slotting the match winner to deliver a 6.7 (43) to 6.2 (38) win in front of 4,701 fans.

Hawthorn star Aine McDonagh could have kicked the winner with two minutes left but missed everything from close range.

Earlier, Sydney pulled off an upset, defeating Geelong by three points in the other semifinal to progress to a final-four clash with North Melbourne.

Hawthorn was without Eliza West for the pivotal final moments after the star on-baller suffered a left knee injury.

West was clearly best on ground and had 25 disposals, 10 tackles, 14 contested possessions and three clearances in the first half alone, before finishing with 31 touches.

Defender Jenna Richardson was important while Jac Dupuy kicked two goals and had an entertaining duel with Carlton's Harriet Cordner (six marks, 11 intercepts).

Carlton skipper Abbie McKay lifted and had 29 disposals and nine clearances.

The Hawks dominated the early exchanges, at one point leading clearances 10-1, kicking three goals to race to a game-high 19-point lead in the first term.

Carlton stopped the rot when Tara Bohanna cut the quarter-time margin to 11.

Lila Keck sparked Carlton before Lily Goss made the most of a contentious 50-metre penalty against Casey Sherriff to cut the half-time deficit to four.

Then, in the third quarter, Vescio won a free kick and kicked truly to put Carlton in front for the first time.

Mackenzie Eardley restored Hawthorn's lead before Vescio forced the ball forward and Sophie McKay spun on a dime in the square, beating three Hawks to put the Blues back in front.

Eardley struck again to make for a thrilling finish, but Vescio took a strong contested mark then snatched victory with her second goal of the game.

Piper Dunlop collapsed after what looked like a glancing blow in a head knock with Tanya Kennedy. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

Earlier, there were concerning scenes as Geelong ruck Piper Dunlop was stretchered from the field on a motorised cart in the Cats' shock loss to Sydney.

Dunlop went down after a head clash with Sydney's Tanya Kennedy during the third quarter at Kardinia Park.

She initially returned to her feet before becoming unsteady and falling on the edge of the centre circle, caught by Sydney's Lexi Hamilton before trainers sprinted onto the ground to attend to her.

The game was stopped for nine minutes as medical staff gathered on the field, Dunlop eventually leaving the field on the motorised cart.

Geelong has since said Dunlop was taken to hospital for "further precautionary assessment".

Forward Chloe Molloy was the star for the Swans, kicking three goals and taking a key late mark to see her side through to its first-ever AFLW preliminary final.

The 8.2 (50) to 7.5 (47) victory means Sydney will face two-time defending premiers North Melbourne next weekend.

Geelong, meanwhile, bows out of the finals series in straight sets after just one loss in the regular season.

The Swans led by 16 points early in the final quarter, but goals to Chloe Scheer and Jacqueline Perry cut the deficit to four points minutes later.

Scheer proceeded to hit the post, with her behind proving the final score of the game.

Geelong experienced a torrid afternoon on the injury front.

In addition to Dunlop's concerning head knock, the Cats lost Amy McDonald to a hamstring injury in the shadows of half-time, Rachel Kearns was absent for most of the second half, and star midfielder Georgie Prespakis spent time off the field after a heavy collision.

All three of Molloy's goals came in the first half, including one spectacular effort in which she gathered and snapped from an acute angle on the right.

Young key forward Maddie Quinn (22 disposals, one goal) was also impressive for the Swans, while Scheer finished with three majors for Geelong.
