BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Father Christmas's annual arrival in Adelaide was met with adoration. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Thousands have lined the streets for the Adelaide Christmas Pageant, marking the start of the festive season in the city.

Pageant-goers flocked to the city early to secure good spots, ahead of the arrival of Father Christmas.

While the David Jones collapse has left a cloud over the Magic Cave, the popular Christmas attraction remains open.

More than 300,000 people are estimated to have lined the streets for this year's Adelaide Christmas Pageant, the 94th edition of the annual yuletide parade.

Pageant-goers arrived in the city early, along with hundreds of performers who gathered near South Terrace and King William Road, ahead of the much-loved parade.

Young faces lined the CBD streets to watch the floats pass by, ahead of the arrival of Father Christmas. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Five new floats were added to this year's line-up, including The Magic Hat and A Bumper Christmas.

"Seeing all the floats go past, they love it," one parent said while sitting with his family.

Hundreds of performers took part in the event. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Organisers believe about 335,000 people turned out for the event, which culminated with the much-anticipated arrival of Father Christmas.

Beneath grey skies, a slight shadow was cast on proceedings by the collapse of David Jones, whose Adelaide store has hosted the children's Christmas attraction, the Magic Cave, for almost three decades, although it will continue operating for the time being.

But, overwhelmingly, there were beaming smiles along the event's route.

Five new floats were added to this year's line-up. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Renowned children's entertainer Emma Watkins, better known by her stage name Emma Memma, said she was thrilled to be back after making her debut last year.

This year Watkins was part of the float The Sounds and Signs of Christmas, a reference to her push to help make entertainment more accessible for deaf and and hearing children alike.

Emma Memma says she is thrilled to be back for the Christmas Pageant. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

"Today is the first time that my co-performer Elvin Lam is actually joining me in the pageant," she said.

"It's his first Christmas pageant ever, and Elvin is profoundly deaf, and he will be signing throughout the whole parade."

Kunal Dhingra and his family were among those who rose early to secure good spots.

"I can see a lot of people are here from different backgrounds. All the kids are really happy," he said while holding his slightly tired infant daughter.

"We're here from 6am, she woke up pretty early."

Kunal Dhingra and his family were among the early risers. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

A cross-section of the community was present at the time-honoured parade, with young pageant-goer Miabelle saying she relished "spending time with my cousins" and seeing the floats.

"There's one big teddy bear I'm looking forward to," she said.

Another attendee, a local grandmother, said her connection to the event went back decades.

"Now I get to enjoy it with my grandchildren.

"I just love it. I think I'd come without the kids, if I had to."

The event brings Christmas magic to the streets of Adelaide. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The Magic Cave, currently held in David Jones at the Adelaide Central Plaza, has been part of the city's Christmas landscape since the 1890s. David Jones took over in 1998 when its original host John Martin's closed down.

While the Magic Cave welcomed Father Christmas this year, questions have emerged about what lies ahead for the attraction.

Last week, David Jones went into voluntary administration, with 19 of its 38 stores slated for closure across Australia and New Zealand.

Organisers estimate more than 300,000 people attended. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

In SA, stores in Westfield Marion and Westfield West Lakes will shut down by the end of the year.

But the store in Rundle Mall will remain open, and locals are keen to keep the Magic Cave as part of Adelaide's Christmas festivities.

"It's an Adelaide icon, bringing my now baby like when I was a kid, and now letting her do it," local woman Erin said.

"We need David Jones … we need the Magic Cave, the kids love it, it's one thing they look forward to."

Entertainers were everywhere to be seen on the city's streets. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Mahli Beardman celebrates the wicket of England's Joe Root during his stunning debut at Optus Stadium. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Fast bowler Mahli Beardman's 6/24 against England was the best ODI debut performance of all time by an Australian bowler.

Beardman, 21, played his initial and representative junior cricket in Dampier in WA's Pilbara.

Cricket figures hope his performance encourages the next generation of country cricketers.

While Mahli Beardman's record-setting demolition of England may have stunned the visitors, those who watched his development as a junior say it's no surprise.

On a day when fresh hostilities in the Sandpaper scandal dominated the headlines, the West Australian fast bowler's 6/24 skittled the visitors and gave Australian cricket a much-needed bit of good news.

But for West Pilbara Cricket Association secretary Christy Reed, Beardman's talent was always obvious.

Beardman (right) receives a representative cap while playing junior cricket in WA's Pilbara. (Supplied: Christy Reed)

While hailing from Cowaramup in WA's South West, the 21-year-old played his initial junior and representative cricket for Dampier in WA's Pilbara.

Initially spotted by scouts at a talent clinic in Karratha in 2017 as a 12-year-old, Beardman progressed quickly through the junior representative ranks, eventually landing at WA Premier Cricket Club Melville when he moved to Perth.

Ms Reed said he made an impression early.

"He was a tiny little kid, but his bowling was absolutely natural talent," she said.

Beardman (left) was identified early as a talented young bowler. (Supplied: Andrew Hayes)

"So fast for his size, and he absolutely loved his cricket.

She hoped Beardman's success would show other talented junior cricketers across the Pilbara what could be achieved.

"For years it was really hard for kids to have a pathway through to that upper level, but I imagine this would get more kids interested in the sport," Ms Reed said.

"I couldn't be happier for him, his family and for Cricket Australia."

WA Cricket country area manager Andrew Hayes was working in the Pilbara around the same time Beardman and fellow Dampier quick Josh Vernon were making their way through the system.

"To take six wickets against our old foe on debut is an incredible achievement, and we couldn't be prouder," he said.

Mahli Beardman (back row, second from right) representing the West Pilbara at Junior Country Week. (Supplied: Christy Reed)

The pride was echoed in Cowaramup, who are keen to embrace Beardman as a favourite son despite competing claims from nearby Dunsborough and Margaret River.

Cricket: Mahli Beardman would love to consistently bowl over 150

Cowaramup Cricket Club stalwart and secretary Bob Biddulph coached a six-year-old Beardman before his family moved north.

"Unfortunately, he was only there for one year … but it was the start of his cricket journey, so we're very proud of him," he said.

"We're claiming it down at Cowaramup that's for sure; I think everyone associated with the cricket club is very proud of that."

Mahli Beardman walks off Perth Stadium after taking 6/24 on debut for Australia in ODI cricket. (ABC News: Sam Tomlin)

Mr Biddulph echoed the importance of seeing regional cricketers performing well at international level.

"It just goes to show that it doesn't matter where you are; if you start off and you enjoy the game and stick at it and keep practising, the sky is the limit," he said.

"We've got quite a few junior teams this year, so for them to actually see one of their own making it on the big stage is quite exciting."

Game two of the three-match ODI series is at Adelaide Oval on Sunday.

Topic:
Protests and Demonstrations

Rising Tide says more than 900 people registered for the paddle-out protest. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

More than 600 kayakers took to Newcastle Harbour as part of "Paddle for the Planet", protesting coal exports.

No arrests were made after NSW Police had tried to block the event.

A larger protest is being planned for February 2027.

Protest organisers and NSW Police say no arrests were made as hundreds of kayakers took to Newcastle Harbour in New South Wales, to protest against coal exports and fossil fuels.

Climate activism group Rising Tide began promoting its "Paddle for the Planet" event in August, but Newcastle Council this week moved to ban the group from holding any of its events on council land.

NSW Police attempted to block the protest, citing safety concerns and potential resourcing pressures.

However, the court dismissed the application on Friday, deciding the event was in the public interest.

The Supreme Court of NSW dismissed an application by NSW Police to stop the on-water protest. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

Speaking after the paddle-out, Rising Tide spokesperson Joe Hallenstein labelled Anthony Albanese "hypocritical", as the prime minister and climate change minister engage in the COP31 summit.

"[Albanese] is over in Türkiye telling the world that Australia is a leader in climate action, when the opposite is true," Mr Hallenstein said.

"Both Albanese's federal Labor government, and Chris Minns's state Labor government continue to approve new coal and gas projects, which is the opposite of action on climate change."

Rising Tide spokesperson Joe Hallenstein spoke out at the event. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

The event was held off Horseshoe Beach, which is managed by Transport for NSW.

A NSW Police spokesperson confirmed, by the completion of the event, officers had not made any arrests.

Organisers say more than 900 people registered for the event, with more than 600 taking to the water.

Hundreds more lined the shore of Horseshoe Beach for the hour-long demonstration.

"I'm tired of governments, from the federal government down to the local government, not doing enough about reducing [climate impact]," attendee Scott Alcorn said.

"I can see there's plenty of enthusiastic people who feel just the same way as I do."

Protesters formed a line across Newcastle's harbour during the one-hour paddle-out. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

A limited police presence, mostly on foot, attended the protest.

In the Supreme Court hearing, Assistant Commissioner David Waddell and NSW Police's legal representative argued there were serious safety concerns for large amounts of people on the water.

A cap of 785 vessels was placed on the event.

The Port of Newcastle did not run any shipping movements between 10am and 2pm.

NSW Greens spokesperson for climate change and justice Sue Higginson said climate change and fossil fuel projects must be a key concern in the NSW election, scheduled for March 13, 2027.

She argued while the cost of living is the biggest issue for voters coming into the campaign period, it "does not mean people are not also concerned about the health of their local environment".

"Labor and the Coalition, all they want to do is talk about One Nation … what we are doing is providing the people with a real alternative and a real vision for their future."

NSW Greens MLC Sue Higginson declared her support to the Rising Tide movement. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

Ms Higginson also referred to a recent decision by the Minns government to make legislative changes allowing the Mount Pleasant coalmine in the Upper Hunter to increase its life and output.

The premier announced the move despite a High Court ruling relating to the mine that concluded global climate emissions must be considered in approvals.

"[The government] is literally carving laws that defy the High Court's ruling because a coal company is threatening to lay off workers before Christmas," she said.

Ms Higginson said the matter is set to be debated in NSW parliament next week.

A Rising Tide spokesperson confirmed the group plans to hold a larger on-water protest at the end of February on Newcastle Harbour, a fortnight before the election.

Topic:
Scams and Fraud

Bookeasy says it has engaged cybersecurity experts to investigate the breach. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Some Canberrans have reported "suspicious messages" after a cybersecurity breach of a booking portal the government uses for campgrounds and other attractions.

The platform, Bookeasy, says that so far it believes only personal details and no credit card details have been compromised.

The ACT government has temporarily disabled the platform, but people can still book sites directly.

The ACT government is stressing vigilance after a cybersecurity breach of a booking platform for campgrounds in territory parks and reserves.

The government said another of its departments, VisitCanberra, used for accommodation and attraction bookings in the ACT, had also been compromised.

The third-party platform, Bookeasy, processes bookings and permits for the National Parks booking system in the ACT and other Australian states, storing personal data from emails to addresses and phone numbers.

It comes as systems in Queensland, Victoria and South Australia were hacked this week.

In a statement, Bookeasy said it was continuing to investigate, and so far had identified potential compromising of customers' personal and booking information.

The platform says it has not identified any breaches of financial details. (Supplied)

"Following a security alert, we were able to take immediate containment action. This included engaging cyber experts to assist with our investigation and provide advice," Bookeasy said.

It said it had not detected any access to credit card details.

The ACT government said it has emailed around 6,000 users, warning them of attempts to scam or phish in the wake of the breach.

The territory government said some Canberran campers had received "suspicious messages via email of WhatsApp applications".

"We urge extreme caution and to consider that there is a risk of being scammed," the department's executive group manager Bren Burkevics said.

Mr Burkevics said the government has temporarily disabled the platform while it assessed the fallout.

The National Parks booking system for Queensland, Victoria and South Australia has suffered a data breach, with hackers stealing personal user information.

"Bookeasy has notified the ACT government that they have incurred a cyber incident and potentially the unauthorised release of information," he said.

"So in the abundance of caution, the ACT government has suspended the use of that website."

Mr Burkevics said people could make bookings directly via the parks government website.

"The usual message is that avoiding scams is critical in these times," he said.

"Further information is available from scamwatch.gov.au, but avoid clicking on links and providing sensitive information, particularly credit card information, to third-party applications."

By Myles Houlbrook-Walk

David Warner has lashed Cricket Australia's investigation of ball tampering in 2018. (Getty Images/Gallo: Ashley Vlotman)

David Warner has posted on social media that bowlers Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood were not interviewed in the Cape Town ball-tampering investigation.

A source close to the bowling group has told the ABC the "comments are just not true", while Pat Cummins already said he was part of the 2018 inquiry.

Warner said the investigation was "shoddy" and "stinks of a cover-up".

All four bowlers from the 2018 Cape Town Test spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into ball tampering, the ABC understands, running counter to claims by former opening batter David Warner.

Warner wrote on social media that Cricket Australia's investigation — which saw him and Steve Smith banned for a year, and Cameron Bancroft rubbed out for nine months — was poorly handled and had a pre-determined outcome.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation. If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?" Warner wrote.

But sources connected to the bowling group said Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc were interviewed. The other front-line bowler from Cape Town, current Test captain Pat Cummins, said during a marathon press conference on Friday that he spoke to investigators.

Sources close to the bowlers said they all spoke to investigators. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour/Cricket Australia)

"They were all interviewed. [Warner's] comments are just not true," one source told the ABC.

The ABC also understands Tim Paine was interviewed as part of the investigation.

In his detailed 70-minute press conference, Pat Cummins said he hoped he could draw a line under the brewing Sandpapergate civil war. David Warner quickly proved that won't be happening.

After Cummins's press conference, Warner said Cummins had "thrown [Usman Khawaja] under the bus" by rejecting Khawaja's claims that more people were responsible for sandpaper entering the field of play than Warner, Bancroft and Smith.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence," Warner said on Fox Sports before Friday's ODI between Australia and England.

"I feel like it was a botched investigation. It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us [Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft] and we had to move on and just accept responsibility."

Usman Khawaja (right) said it wasn't fair for three players to bear all the responsibility for ball tampering. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

And Warner has doubled down on social media.

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that bowlers had no idea," he wrote.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Cricket Australia said in response: "As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since.

"Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players right to provide their own version of events."

In his new book, Khawaja said he was never spoken to despite sitting next to Cameron Bancroft during discussions about using sandpaper on the ball.

Much has been written and said about Usman Khawaja's new book — but what's actually in the pages of Sabr?

Cummins on Friday said he spoke to investigators and there were calls at the time for anyone with more information to come forward.

On Tuesday, Starc was one of the first players to be asked about Khawaja's claims and said there were "differing opinions of eight years ago".

"We were heavily grilled through the process at the time and since," he said.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021."

In 2021, Bancroft implied in an interview that the bowlers likely knew what was going on.

"Obviously what I did benefits bowlers and the awareness around that, probably, is self-explanatory," he said.

Starc, Cummins, Lyon and Hazlewood released a joint statement in response, saying they were disappointed to have their integrity questioned.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands," they wrote five years ago.

By Kristy Sexton-McGrath

Adelaide woman Trish Crabb is stranded at JFK Airport in New York after thousands of flights were cancelled and delayed.  (Supplied: Trish Crabb)

A major air traffic control outage in the US has disrupted thousands of flights, leaving Australians stranded and warnings about global flow-on impacts, including international delays.

Airlines are working to clear the backlog as US authorities investigate what caused the outage.

Australians have been caught up in widespread flight disruptions across the United States after a communications outage forced aviation authorities to ground flights nationwide.

More than 11,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, with passengers left stranded at airports across the country after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an unprecedented ground stop.

The grounding has since been lifted, but airlines are warning it could take time to clear the backlog, with disruptions also affecting flights departing Australia for the US.

Look back on our live blog for the latest on the issues affecting flights in the US and Australia.

Sydney Airport said flights to the US would now resume from Mascot after being temporarily grounded on Saturday morning, and urged passengers to contact their airlines.

The disruption has affected travellers at major airports including New York's JFK, Los Angeles International Airport and San Diego.

Adelaide traveller Trish Crabb snapped this photograph while in line at JFK airport in New York. She was among thousands of travellers caught up in US flight cancellations.  (Supplied: Trish Crabb)

Trish Crabb, from Adelaide, was among those caught up in the chaos after her flight from New York to Miami was grounded.

She and her husband were due to fly out of JFK Airport when they discovered their Delta flight had been cancelled.

The couple are holidaying in the US and had planned to drive from Miami to Fort Lauderdale to board a cruise.

"My husband is going to try and find us a hotel room somewhere close by, and hopefully we will be able to get a flight out at some stage," she said.

Despite the disruption, Ms Crabb said passengers appeared to be keeping their composure.

"Everyone was very calm," she said, adding most people were taking the situation in their stride.

Rivkah Brown, from Myrtleford in Victoria, was stranded at San Diego Airport after her Delta flight was cancelled.

Rivkah Brown from Victoria was stranded at San Diego Airport following a cruise in the US. She's now boarding a bus to get to Las Vegas.  (Supplied: Rivkah Brown)

Ms Brown had just disembarked from a cruise and was stopping over in San Diego before travelling to Las Vegas, where she was due to meet her fiancé.

She said she would now take a bus to Las Vegas instead, a journey of almost 10 hours.

"It's disappointing but it is what it is," Ms Brown said.

The FAA ordered the nationwide ground stop on Friday, local time, after communications problems affecting air traffic control centres across the United States.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the issue was affected all Air Route Traffic Control Centres, with technicians investigating the cause.

Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage.

The FAA said the decision was made because of "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety".

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said preliminary investigations pointed to a telecommunications outage, with no immediate indication of a deliberate attack.

"There's no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now," he said.

The outage affected the 22 regional air traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft between airports across the country.

At least 600 flights had been diverted, including aircraft sent back to their departure airports or redirected elsewhere.

The order to ground all departing US flights was finally lifted after more than five hours. (AP Photo: Tony Gutierrez)

About 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to depart US airports after 4pm Eastern time on Friday.

Planes already in the air were able to continue to their destinations, with authorities prioritising their safe landing.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a computer system failure at the FAA caused thousands of delays. It was also only the second nationwide grounding since the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001.

Australian travellers caught up in the disruption are being urged to contact their airline or travel agent if they are due to fly within the next 72 hours.

The Australian Travel Industry Association (ATIA) says those passengers are being prioritised, while people travelling later are being asked to hold off contacting travel providers so urgent cases can be dealt with first.

Travellers should also check their airline's website or app for flight updates.

ATIA chief executive Dean Long said passengers travelling soon should contact their provider if they had not already heard from them.

"We know this is unsettling for travellers. Our members are there to help, and we are monitoring the situation closely."

The Federal Government's SmartTraveller website is telling Australians to monitor media and contact airlines for updates and to reschedule flights.

It advises travellers to exercise "normal safety precautions" in the US.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/m.author: Simon Smale
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Matt Hauser finishes second, capping off a superb year. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

Matt Hauser finished second in the rescheduled Abu Dhabi leg of the World Triathlon Championship Series.

Fellow Australian Luke Willian finished fifth, earning valuable points in quest to qualify for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.

Next year, the World Triathlon Championship Series will be rebranded to create the Triathlon World Tour.

Australia's leading triathlete Matt Hauser has claimed a silver medal in the season-ending World Triathlon Championship Series race in Abu Dhabi.

Gold Coast-based Hauser finished 18 seconds behind Brazil's Miguel Hidalgo, with New Zealand's Paris Olympics silver medallist Hayden Wilde in third.

The result confirms Hauser's second place finish in the overall season standings, with newly crowned world champion, Vasco Vilaça of Portugal, not racing in Abu Dhabi.

"I could really feel the legs in the back end of that race, I think I could feel the whole year in the back end of that race to be honest," said Hauser, who won four golds this season, as well as the Noosa Tri earlier this month.

"Miguel had too much out there today, you could tell he was really locked in and credit to him he did a lot of work on the bike as well.

"So all round a really great race and good to see him back on top as well."

Despite being Australia's first male triathlon world champion in 20 years, Matt Hauser is still building the blocks towards his aim of Olympic success in 2028.

The race, originally scheduled for March but postponed due to security concerns in the region, took place after the grand final in Pontevedra.

However, the competition still provided valuable qualifying points for the LA 2028 Olympic Games.

"I always think about LA, it's always in my mind, without overexposing my thoughts. It would be silly not to think about it," Hauser told AusTriathlon in the lead up to the Abu Dhabi event.

"It's a process and journey we've been on since Paris, I'm really focused on performing well at those Games."

The qualification period runs until May 18, 2028, with an athlete's 12 best results until then counting towards their overall ranking.

Fellow Australian Luke Willian came home in fifth place, with Luke Schofield 29th, Brandon Copeland 35th and Cal McClusky 40th.

"[It was good to see] Luke Willian having a sprint finish for fourth and fifth," Hauser said

"I'm just really stoked on the podium, it's been a big year and a long year at that."

Hayden Wilde (right) is shaping up as one of Matt Hauser's biggest challengers for Olympic gold in LA. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

In the women’s race, Matilda Offord was the best placed of the Australians finishing in 35th, with Sophie Malowiecki not finishing.

Russia's Diana Isakova claimed her first World Triathlon Series victory, surging away from Luxembourg's Jeanne Lehair, with American Gwen Jorgensen in third.

The race marks the end of the World Triathlon Series Championship races, as the tour combines with the Professional Triathletes Organisation to form a new Triathlon World Tour.

The new circuit will combined the existing T100 Triathlon World Tour and the World Triathlon Championship Series (WTCS), rebranded as the T100 World Championship Tour and T50 World Championship Tour respectively.

The Professional Triathletes Organisation (PTO) and World Triathlon today announced what the Triathlon World Tour brand will look like to fans and athletes when it starts next year, as well as the initial 2027 T50 and T100 World Championship Tour calendars.

"Our sport was really fragmented from a competition and commercial perspective, which was holding it back," World Triathlon president Antonio Arimany said earlier this year.

"We could have waited until the end of the current Olympic qualification before making the changes, but the changes we're making were too important to wait.

"By introducing the Triathlon World Tour now, we are creating one unified structure and brand, which can unify as many events as possible, creating a win-win situation for all of us in the sport."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/w.title: What we know so far about why US flights were grounded
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/w.author: Audrey Courty
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Information and Communication

The order to ground all departing US flights was finally lifted after more than five hours. (AP Photo: Tony Gutierrez)

The United States has lifted its order to ground departing flights nationwide as a major communications outage continues to disrupt air travel.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage.

Thousands of flights into and out of the US were delayed or cancelled, leaving airlines and passengers scrambling to work out their next steps.

Look back on our live blog for the latest on the issues affecting flights in the US and Australia.

The ABC understands the US "ground stop" has caused some delays to a small number of US-bound flights from Australia.

Here's what we know about the unfolding situation so far.

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has attributed the disruption to a telecommunications issue with air traffic control centres.

"It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now," Mr Mullin told reporters at the White House earlier on Friday, local time.

It is not yet confirmed what specifically caused the communications failure.

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says authorities are investigating the issue.

Mr Mullin had earlier said investigators would examine whether there was any connection to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence (AI) system designed to help identify problems and reroute aircraft.

However, the system operates from a single location near Washington DC and provides recommendations to air traffic control centres.

US President Donald Trump has also rejected suggestions the new AI technology was responsible for the disruption.

In his latest press conference, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed "old technology" for the outage.

"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," he said.

"We have analogue telecoms, our routers actually got overloaded with data … and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data … because of that we shut the system down," he says.

Speaking to ABC News, Shawn Pruchnik, an associate professor in Ohio State University's aviation department, said officials made the right call by grounding departing aircraft as a precaution.

"We have this significant problem of airplanes at higher altitudes that cannot communicate with air traffic control, so the solution to that is less airplanes up there," he said.

"Keep everyone down, let everyone land."

Mr Mullin said there was currently no indication the outage was the result of a nefarious attack.

However, he later added:

"We're not ruling out anything at this point.

"The first thing is [to make sure] everybody that is flying in is safe."

In a subsequent press conference, Mr Mullin reiterated that there were no signs pointing to a cyber attack for now.

"Typically, somebody's going to raise their hand up and say, 'Hey, we did that'. There's no chatter. We haven't seen any footprints … of people that have got into the system," he said.

"It appears this was mechanically driven. However, we are still looking."

Microsoft has denied any known connection between its recent global outage and the FAA's nationwide stoppage.

"We have no indication that the FAA's nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services," the company said on X.

The statement came amid speculation about a possible link to Microsoft's 21-hour global outage, which was resolved earlier on Friday.

Mr Mullin also dismissed the suggestion of a connection, telling reporters: "I don't see any reason to connect those two at all."

The FAA's order applied to departing flights across the US, grounding nearly all aircraft scheduled to take off during the five hours it was in effect.

The agency also asked Eurocontrol, its European counterpart, to suspend flights to the US from its 42 member states, including Türkiye, Morocco and Israel.

Aircraft that were already in the air when the order was issued were allowed to continue safely to their destinations.

The order to ground flights resulted in mass delays and flight cancellations. (AP Photo: Mike Stewart)

The full scale of the disruption is still emerging, but the impact has already been felt by tens of thousands of travellers.

Flight-tracking website FlightAware reported about 9,814 delays on flights into and out of the US, alongside more than 4,749 cancellations. Those figures are continuing to change as the disruption unfolds.

Meanwhile, the ABC understands Australian airlines are dealing with a backlog of delayed flights.

Thousands of flights have been delayed or cancelled across the US, leaving Australian travellers stranded at airports.

Before the US order was lifted, a Sydney Airports spokesperson had said all US-bound flights from Sydney were grounded.

Since the order was lifted, the spokesperson said:

"Flights scheduled to depart Sydney for the United States are expected to depart as planned. Passengers should continue to check with their airline for the latest information."

The ABC is continuing to stay in touch with Sydney Airports for further updates.

Yes. Aviation experts say pilots and air traffic controllers are trained to manage communications failures.

Skip Bailey, an aviation professor who spoke to The Associated Press, said pilots were expected to maintain the headings and instructions given by air traffic controllers before communications were lost.

If the outage continued, they could revert to their filed flight plans.

Airlines and passengers were left scrambling to work out their next steps. (AP Photo)

Pilots may also be able to communicate with other aircraft over the radio, even if they cannot reach air traffic controllers. Commercial aircraft also have their own radar systems.

"It's not mass chaos out there," Professor Bailey said.

"There are plenty of ways to try to communicate."

He said preventing additional aircraft from taking off had been crucial to avoiding further complications.

"We don't want to put more aircraft into a system that's already having an issue."

Mr Duffy said US air space was reopened at 8:15pm Eastern Standard Time, about five hours after the grounding order was issued.

However, he warned that flights could be "slow" to take off again.

"If you are watching, if you are at an airport, check with your airline; it depends on [if they] have crews available," Mr Duffy said in his latest press conference.

"We are going to try to move as many of those [flights] as we can tonight if we have capacity.

"If not, we are going to start tomorrow morning with our airline partners to move those aircraft, but it is going to take us some time to unwind what has happened this afternoon."

The FAA has assured travellers the country is now safe for air travel.

"Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," it said in a statement.

Australians travelling to the US should expect to hear from their airlines or travel agents as the disruption continues, the Australian Travel Industry Association said.

"We're absolutely expecting the domestic network within America to be disrupted for at least the next 24 hours," the industry body said in its latest statement.

"If you have a stand-by ticket, the reality is you probably aren't getting on a plane, but if you've got a confirmed ticket, you can rest assured those planes will be taking off safely and on time."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/p.title: 'Plastic farmers' in Indonesia unaware of the dangers of burning waste
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/p.author: Natasya Salim
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Recycling and Waste Management

Plastic waste was regularly burned in limestone kilns in Sumberejo, a village in East Java. (Supplied: Brawijaya University)

Ahmad Yani spent hours each day sifting through piles of rubbish, searching for recyclable materials to sell to help make ends meet.

For decades, his family and other people in his village in East Java, in Indonesia, would buy truckloads of waste residue from factories recycling imported paper and cardboard.

They would spread the waste on the ground, and separate plastics from paper and cardboard.

The paper would be sold back to the recycling factories and most of the plastics to industries that needed fuel for furnaces.

"It had become a source of livelihood for many low-income residents," Mr Yani said, adding he would make about 300,000 rupiah ($24) a month.

Any plastics still left over would be used in his village to fire limestone kilns, to produce building materials to sell or use.

Ahmad Yani says plastic waste from overseas has been coming to his village for decades. (Supplied: Brawijaya University)

Mr Yani said among the rubbish he noticed food sachets and cat and dog food packaging with Australian labels, as well as labels of countries in Europe.

While burning plastic has helped support the family's livelihood, the smoke from their home and neighbouring households may be having a devastating impact on health.

Mr Yani said some people he knew who had operated the limestone kilns had died from respiratory diseases and causes were never determined.

He said the burning of plastics in his village was no longer happening. It stopped about a year ago.

Several local media reported companies had stopped distributing waste to his community to sort, which had sparked anger among locals who lost their source of income.

The ABC couldn't independently verify the reasons for the change.

But health concerns for people who have been exposed to air pollution from burning plastics remain.

Women sort through waste in East Java. (Supplied: Brawijaya University)

Researchers from the Climate and Health Centre at Brawijaya University were investigating the health effects of air pollution in East Java when they found locals were burning plastic waste.

One of the researchers, Sekar Aqila Salsabilla, said pre-screening tests earlier this year on those in their study produced some worrying findings.

She said at least 20 per cent of the more than 4,000 participants across six East Java villages were at high risk of cardiovascular disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

Sekar Aqila Salsabilla has been researching the health effects of air pollution in villages in East Java. (Supplied: Sekar Aqila Salsabilla)

"When we first entered these communities, one of the most distressing findings was that many people were unaware of the dangers associated with burning plastic waste," said Ms Salsabilla, who, as part of a broader study, worked with more than 30 researchers, the majority of whom had medical backgrounds.

People earning money from sorting waste, known as "plastic farmers", knew their health was "slowly declining" but did not understand the source of the problems, she said.

"Despite the income they generate, many do not realise that the long-term health burden they may face is likely to be far greater than the money they earn from handling and burning this waste," Ms Salsabilla said.

Environmental activists say Australian plastic waste was in this rubbish heap in East Java, Indonesia, in 2024. (Supplied: Ecoton)

Most plastic waste was no longer burned in people's homes but rather converted into refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and burned in a designated facility, she said.

"But I think this only relocates the problem rather than actually solving it," Ms Salsabilla said, adding the facility still required humans to sort the waste.

Emissions from open waste burning, such as burning plastics, include a variety of air pollutants, some of which have particularly harmful effects on both the climate and health, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

"Exposure to these pollutants, whether short or long-term, can lead to adverse health effects such as coughing, skin irritation, respiratory diseases, and other negative outcomes," the WHO says on its website.

Environmentalists say plastic waste from Australia is often found in East Java. (Supplied: Ecoton)

Ms Salsabilla said the waste imported to East Java was coming from places including Australia, the US and Europe.

Agus Rusly, the waste reduction director at Indonesia's Ministry of Environment, told the ABC the lack of accessible waste management services, irregular waste collection and limited recycling facilities had contributed to open waste burning in Indonesia.

Mr Rusly said the environment ministry was working to improve waste governance, in collaboration with regional governments, through a national framework "aimed at achieving comprehensive waste management by 2029".

In 2019, Indonesian environmentalists called on Australia to tighten its regulation and enforcement of waste exports to foreign countries, saying Australian exporters were effectively "smuggling" huge amounts of plastic and waste paper supposedly sent for recycling.

Daru Setyorini, executive director of local environmental activist group Ecoton, said plastics with Australian labels could still be found in East Java and people in villages were still "secretly" burning plastics.

Environmentalists have long called for Australia to tighten waste exports to countries such as Indonesia. (Supplied)

"To this day, it [the plastic waste] still exists, although it has decreased significantly compared to 2024 and the years before that," she said.

"The monitoring and enforcement are still weak. Ideally, these imports from Australia should just be stopped altogether."

Australia exported 701,000 tonnes of paper and cardboard to Indonesia in the recent financial year, according to Joe Pickin at Blue Environment who analysed data from Australia's Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW).

While Australia can legally export recyclable plastic waste to Indonesia, concerns have centred on plastic contaminants in paper and cardboard exports.

Environmentalists in Indonesia claim that among the thousands of tonnes of paper bales sent to East Java are household waste items including faeces-contaminated nappies.

Indonesia applies a 2 per cent contamination limit on paper waste imports, meaning contaminants such as plastic, food residue, soil and other non-paper materials must not exceed that threshold.

A spokesperson for Australia's Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) said it took "allegations of unlawful waste exports seriously".

"The National EPA assesses allegations of non-compliance with Commonwealth environmental laws and takes a proportionate, risk-based approach to determining appropriate regulatory responses," the spokesperson said.

Many Australian material recovery facilities have invested significantly in upgrading their operations to meet these standards and ensure materials exported for recycling meet appropriate quality requirements, according to the Australian Council of Recycling.

"Failure to enforce these rules not only risks environmental harm but also disadvantages operators doing the right thing, undermining their investments," CEO Suzanne Toumbourou said.

Ms Setyorini said each country should be responsible for its own plastic waste.

"Indonesia has got enough waste problems, so developed countries like Australia shouldn't export their waste here," she said.

The DCCEEW has been contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/t.title: The Townsville creatives making their own queer community
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/t.author: Isabella Garrido and Emma Jones
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Michael Smith and Lij Bolden found the community they had been looking for through CROOKED. (Image: Emma Jones, ABC North Queensland) (ABC News: Emma Jones)

Townsville is known for humidity, rugby league, and its unofficial status as North Queensland's capital.

Its queer culture is less visible, but that is changing as more people create the communities they once had to leave regional Queensland to find.

Michael Smith knows that experience well.

The professional dancer grew up in Gladstone before moving to Brisbane.

"Growing up as a queer person in a regional place, I didn't have any elders or community members to paint a picture of what a queer life could be," they said.

Mx Smith grew up in Gladstone before moving to Brisbane, but later returned to regional Queensland. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Years later, Mx Smith returned to regional Queensland.

"There's actually a really large queer and trans community in Townsville," they said.

"There just aren't many things that are overtly visible that bring everyone together."

Finding a queer community did not necessarily mean Mx Smith found where they felt most at home.

Rather than leave, they began wondering how else a queer community could look.

With writer P. Eldridge, they created CROOKED, an independent queer publication — due to launch on November 14 — rooted in Gurambilbarra, the traditional Wulgurukaba name for Townsville.

The project quickly revealed there were others also looking for a different way to connect.

Lij Bolden was one of them.

Lij Bolden participated in writing workshops to prepare their written piece for CROOKED. (ABC News: Emma Jones)

Writing for CROOKED gave Mx Bolden the chance to tramp down memory lane.

"It's peppered [with] vignettes of my life and realising I'm queer and discovering other people like me," they said.

They reflected on the parts of themself they had once kept hidden.

"I got to sit in that space and relive my queerness in a place where I did feel lonely and unseen, but realising that maybe I've had that queerness in me this entire time," Mx Bolden said.

Greater visibility, however, can come with risk.

"With the amount of political divisiveness and extremity in the world, it takes effort to be neutral," Mx Smith said.

That risk became reality at a Townsville Pride event in June 2025, where Mx Smith was preparing to perform when a small group disrupted the event.

An attendee who asked the group to leave was allegedly assaulted.

"It had been a long time since I had felt that kind of hostility targeted towards a specific group of people," Mx Smith said.

The experience reinforced for them why visible signs of safety mattered.

"As a young queer person in a regional place, you can be hypervigilant in public, constantly assessing every room you step into, looking for danger and looking for safety," they said.

"If someone has gone to the effort of putting up a [pride] flag, it takes a little of that social anxiety and pressure off your shoulders."

Queensland Council for LGBTI Health chief executive Rebecca Reynolds agreed visible signs of welcome mattered but said what followed was just as important.

Rebecca Reynolds says belonging also means having room to be the whole of who you are. (Supplied: Queensland Council for LGBTI Health)

"Visible inclusion needs to lead to something people can use: a welcoming person, clear information, an activity they can join or help reaching the right support," she said.

Research suggests knowing a community exists is not necessarily the same as feeling part of it.

A 2025 University of Southern Queensland study of 87 LGBTQ+ people in the Toowoomba region found participants wanted safety, support, acceptance, friendship and connection.

Ms Reynolds said everyday recreational groups could foster connection across the year, beyond larger moments of visibility such as pride events.

"These spaces can take many forms, shaped by the people who use them. What matters is that people can find somewhere that feels right for them."

For Ms Eldridge, those spaces should grow from the places they serve.

Writer P. Eldridge helped create CROOKED, an independent queer publication. (Supplied: P. Eldridge)

"I'm deeply suspicious of the idea that interesting queer culture only happens in capital cities because it doesn't," they said.

"Gurambilbarra has its own queer histories, its own ways of surviving and making community that I think we, as a culture and a movement, can benefit from listening to.

"CROOKED came from wanting to listen to that rather than parachuting in with an idea of what regional queer life should look like."

Ms Eldridge said trans and queer writing had its own lineage, one that was still being defined, shaped and expanded.

"I believe that means there's no reason to confine ourselves. We can pretty much make anything new whenever we want," they said.

"I don't want to mitigate how dangerous regional life can be because of the backward turn toward fascism, but I will say that in the midst of so many crises, there is even more strength, solidarity and hope."

CROOKED, an independent queer publication, is due to launch on November 14. (Supplied)

Mx Smith said they felt a responsibility to make visible what they could not see growing up.

"CROOKED is the messier version of queerness," Mx Smith said.

"It's brash and it's not polished.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/science/2026.title: Predicting weather in the Southern Hemisphere is challenging. Here's why
https://www.abc.net.au/news/science/2026.author: Jacinta Bowler
https://www.abc.net.au/news/science/2026.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Weather Forecasts

Weather forecasts have become much more reliable over the past century. (ABC)

It's not easy to forecast the weather in the Southern Hemisphere.

Atmospheric scientists such as Kimberley Reid from the University of Melbourne face a number of unique challenges that make observing weather trickier here than in the Northern Hemisphere.

"The Northern Hemisphere has … so much more land mass. There's more people and more funding for observations, and more major cities," Dr Reid said.

"In the Southern Hemisphere … we don't have as many surface observations, or as many weather balloons, which are all necessary for working out what's going on."

Despite this, in recent years the Southern Hemisphere has narrowed the forecasting gap, with accuracy that almost matches our northern counterparts.

This isn't due to extra weather stations or balloons but rather an increase in data provided by international satellites, according to the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM).

Accurate forecasting can lead to more time to prepare, which can help save lives. (ABC News: Tahlia Davis)

While this has provided a wealth of data for weather forecasting around the world, experts warn that satellites can't help forecast everything.

And as weather gets more extreme, forecasters are turning to new technologies and techniques to keep up.

Humans have been trying to predict the weather for thousands of years, but it's only in the last few decades that forecasters could peer into the future with any kind of certainty.

Short-term forecasts between one and three days are reasonably accurate, but the further into the future the forecast looks — up to five or so days — the less dependable they are.

According to Dr Reid, this is because weather is particularly chaotic, and tiny variables can end up having "large flow-on effects" over just a couple of days.

This compounds when there are fewer locations to collect data points.

This has historically been the case in the Southern Hemisphere where Dr Reid said there just isn't enough land for equipment.

"We can't stick weather stations in the ocean," she said.

Each weather forecast is the culmination of centuries of science, mathematics and technology.

This lack of data was visible in the historical accuracy gap between the two hemispheres.

In the 1980s, a three-day forecast was about 90 per cent accurate in the Northern Hemisphere, but just over 80 per cent in the Southern Hemisphere.

Michael Logan, general manager of decision support services at the BOM, said this improved over the next two decades, but the Southern Hemisphere still lagged behind into the 2000s.

The introduction of data from specialised weather satellites helped close the gap.

Australia doesn’t have its own weather satellites, but instead uses data from 40 satellites owned by countries including the US and Japan.

While some satellites orbit the Earth, others stay above one location by following the planet's rotation.

The copious amount of globally shared information produced by these satellites is vital for groups like the BOM, providing more than 90 per cent data for weather forecasts.

Weather satellites like Japan's Himawari 8 and 9 are very important for modern weather forecasting. (Wikimedia: Himawari89/Japan Meteorological Agency/CC BY 4.0)

"For the Bureau, even just what we use in our weather predictions, it's of the order of 13.5–14 million observations every day coming in from these satellites," Mr Logan said.

"That's contributed an enormous amount of data that really helps with the numerical computing models."

But according to Martin Jucker, an atmospheric climate scientist at the University of New South Wales, many of the satellites are coming towards the end of their life.

"The really big [worry] is new satellites that were supposed to replace old ones have been cancelled," Dr Jucker said.

"So these satellites will reach their end of life and replacements will be late."

Forecasting extreme weather events has become increasingly important as the world's climate changes.

"We're making sure that we're improving the skill of predicting the big weather events, whether it be cyclones or really extreme rainfall or extreme heat," Mr Logan said.

Along with using satellite data, forecasters are turning to AI to hone their models.

The apocalyptic El Niño we didn't see coming

"AI … has been around for a fair while," Mr Logan said.

BOM, for example, already uses Google DeepMind's forecasting system for cyclones.

In 2024, the system was shown to predict the weather 15 days ahead and more accurately than the best system currently in use.

"It's impressive what it can do," he said.

Despite advances in AI, accurately predicting some extreme weather phenomena is still a major challenge.

Dr Reid's research focuses on atmospheric rivers, which produce large amounts of rainfall or snowfall over a region when they hit land.

"An atmospheric river is a long, narrow region of enhanced water vapour transport in the lower atmosphere," she said.

Understanding when and where weather patterns created by atmospheric rivers will hit well in advance can help limit damage and casualties.

In 2022, an atmospheric river caused both the Brisbane and Lismore floods.

"Having more observational data has the potential to improve the timing and location of extreme rainfall forecasts so that people have plenty of time to evacuate if needed."

To get more data you need to get up close to these sky rivers.

Hurricane hunter planes are able to get much more information than a satellite or weather station. (Wikimedia: Lieutenant Commander Andrew Utama/NOAA Corps/Public Domain)

In the US, air crews known as hurricane hunters, fly airplanes directly through atmospheric rivers to gain data.

This extreme close-up information can be used alongside satellite data and modelling to provide more accurate forecasts.

"They've got some good results showing these improved observations improve [forecasting for] where and when these atmospheric rivers will hit," Dr Reid said.

"The more information you have at the present time, the better your forecast will be."

Awhina Hetet and Rita McRae Kingi became friends in Brisbane but their families bonded 100 years ago through New Zealand's rugby league team. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Awhina Hetet and Rita McRae Kingi share a drink on a blistering November day, on the balcony of Awhina's Logan business.

The women and their families met and became close mates in Brisbane, after moving to the city from Rotorua and Marton and in New Zealand.

But the families' close bond was first forged more than a century ago, on the rugby league fields of New Zealand.

Awhina's great-great-great grandfather Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet was the team manager for the Māori All Stars in 1909.

Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet was the team manager for the Maori All Stars in 1909. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Rita's great-great grandfather Nirai Whareure "Ned" McRae was a coach, captain, and player.

The players had all anglicised their names before making the trip across the ditch for the campaign 117 years ago.

Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet (far left) was the team manager for the Maori All Stars in 1909 and Nirai Whareure "Ned" McRae (far right) was a coach, captain, and player. (Supplied)

"New Zealand was a nation of union players," Awhina says. "When they came over in 1909 to Australia … we brought with us our haka, our culture. They had two guides with them … they came with a campaign to show, 'this is who we are, we're Māori. We love this game.'"

"You see how proud they are and I think our people absolutely displayed that proudness when they put on the shirt."

Rob Hetet, Awhina Hetet, Rita McRae King, Te-Kapua Rahoroi Kingi and Harley Kingi. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

One of the guides was Mākereti "Maggie" Papakura, a Māori-English translator who was posthumously awarded a Master of Philosophy in Anthropology from the University of Oxford.

Mākereti "Maggie" Papakura, a Māori-English translator, was a guide. (Supplied)

At the time, rugby league was struggling financially in Australia. But the Aussie-Kiwi clashes attracted more than 30,000 to their games.

The Maori side left victorious, taking the cup back to New Zealand. It is now in the care of Awhina's family "in an undisclosed location," she laughs, in New Zealand.

Rob Hetet with the 1909 cup. (Supplied)

"That cup's still standing, it's one of the oldest rugby league cups in existence," she says.

"Beautiful history," adds her father, Rob Hetet. "That's probably why I am really passionate."

The Hetet family also has distant links to star Kiwi player Kalyn Ponga, who is part of the starting side for the World Cup Final in Brisbane this Sunday.

Te-Kapua Rahoroi Kingi, Harley Kingi and Rob Hetet. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

The Hetet and McRae families will be in the stands at Lang Park, with a closer link to the game than most other revellers.

"It's been 13 years since we were in the finals," says Awhina.

"Our boys have been amazing throughout this whole campaign … may the best team win!"

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/n.title: Minns vows to open 100 long-day childcare centres if re-elected
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Early Childhood Education and Care Services

The Minns government has committed to building and opening 100 long-day childcare centres (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The NSW Labor government has pledged to open 100 new long-day childcare centres if re-elected in March.

It is on top of an existing promise from the Minns government to build and open 100 new preschools by January.

The government expects 8,000 families will benefit from 5,000 new placements at long-day childcare centres.

The NSW government will open and operate 100 new long-day childcare centres to address demand if it wins the state election in March.

The centres are in addition to an existing government pledge to build 100 new preschools and have them operational from January next year.

In the private sector, long-day centres offer early childhood services for children from birth to four years old and operate between 7am and 6pm.

The announcement on Saturday from the Minns government will deliver the first publicly owned long-day childcare centres in NSW, providing 5,000 places for about 8,000 families.

Chris Minns expects many long-day centre locations to open up in Western Sydney.  (ABC News)

Premier Chris Minns said the centres would be built on existing public primary school sites and in areas deemed so-called childcare deserts.

He said the government would "not be indiscriminate" about new locations and that he expected many to open in Western Sydney and regional NSW.

"The reality is, for us in New South Wales, if we want a productive economy, we want to make sure that we're giving every family the opportunity to get ahead," Mr Minns said.

Prue Car says families are in desperate need of extended child care hours. (ABC News)

Deputy Premier Prue Car said families desperately needed the extended care hours the centres would provide.

"That will end the double drop off and it will make it easier for parents to get back into the workforce," she said.

"It will also create an opportunity for high quality early learning as children transition into kindergarten and primary school."

The government will also extend the transitional funding period for community run preschools.

As part of the NSW government's early childhood education reforms, the Universal Preschool Funding Program will replace the Start Strong arrangement from January 1.

According to the government, 10,000 families are missing out on the community preschool places, which are not-for profit.

"We have listened to the concerns of the sector, and we've responded to that by guaranteeing their funding for two years," Mr Minns said on Saturday.

The opening of a new preschool in Sydney's south-west has raised questions over plans to expand preschools in NSW.

"That will freeze their funding at, at least, last year's level.

"So that will give community preschools a funding guarantee that they will not go backwards while we work with them on how we can get more children into their high quality preschool."

Carol Matthews from the Independent Education Union of Australia said preschools had been "extremely worried" about losing thousands of dollars in funding next year, and prior to today's announcement had started to shed staff.

"Now obviously, this reprieve is really going to help, but nevertheless, there's been significant damage done already," the union's NSW ACT branch secretary said.

While the union welcomed the election promise, Ms Matthews said there was "more work to do on the details of the model".

"We want them [the NSW government] to sit down with us, and actually negotiate an outcome which would enable some sort of stability and security in staffing going forward.

"That means recognising the actual staffing needs of preschools."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/p.title: PearlBone gets FDA clearance for world's largest orthopaedic market
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/p.author: Rachel Jackson and Jess Baker
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Scientific Research

The PearlBone FDA approval follows years of testing, evaluation and development. (Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls)

A bone graft substitute made from Kimberley pearl shells has received clearance from the US Food and Drug Adminstration (FDA).

The product is the first of its kind to repair bone fractures using nacre, commonly known as mother-of-pearl.

Marine Biomedical says there is more to be done before the product can treat patients, but regulatory approval is an important first step.

Mother-of-pearl harvested in Western Australia's north could soon be used to fill bone fractures for patients in the United States.

WA biotech company Marine Biomedical has received clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its bone graft substitute, PearlBone.

A manufacturing facility for PearlBone was built in Broome in 2022. (Supplied: Rolee Kumar)

The product is the first of its kind to be developed from nacre, commonly known as mother-of-pearl.

The iridescent material has been used for ornamental items, jewellery and even buttons.

But Marine Biomedical chief executive Rolee Kumar said it was also effective for bone repair and regeneration.

PearlBone will be used to repair bone fractures for patients in the United States. (Supplied: Rolee Kumar)

"The material of what the mother-of-pearl is made out of, all of these are actually building blocks of our bone too," she said.

"So in a way, it's not surprising when we do these studies we see PearlBone facilitates bone healing."

The United States is the world's largest orthopaedics market, with the bone grafts and substitutes sector valued at $US1.1 billion ($1.5 billion).

Ms Kumar said FDA clearance was an important first step in entering the US market, but there were more hurdles to be overcome before it could be sold.

Rolee Kumar says PearlBone is as safe and effective as existing bone repair materials. (Supplied: Rolee Kumar)

"We've gone through a process where PearlBone was compared against another existing bone graft that's established itself in the market," she said.

"We've been able to demonstrate PearlBone is as safe and efficacious as the predicate device."

She said the company also hoped to bring the product to Australian customers in future and expand into other treatments like dental work.

Marine Biomedical was established in 2021 through a partnership with local Broome pearling business Willie Creek Pearls and research expertise from the University of Western Australia (UWA).

Paul Birch says shells are prepped at the farm before being transported to the manufacturing facility in Broome. (Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls)

Willie Creek chief executive Paul Birch said the collaboration was an exciting opportunity for the pearling industry.

"And with more research, there might be other parts of the oyster that can be used for other biomedical technologies."

The shells farmed by Willie Creek for pearl production undergo cleaning and preparations before being transported to the Marine Biomedical manufacturing facility in Broome.

Mr Birch said there was an abundance of pearl shell available at the farm to meet current requirements, but this could change as the product demand increased.

"So hopefully at one point in time, it might be something the entire industry is able to be involved in and supply to Marine Biomedical," he said.

The shell is harvested at Willie Creek Pearls, off the Kimberley coast. (Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls)

UWA biomedical and health innovation director Kevin Pfleger said it was an exciting time for medical research in WA.

The professor said it was common for products to gain approval in the United States market before returning to Australia.

"One of the big reasons is because even though we're a very large country geographically, we've got a relatively small population," Professor Pfleger said.

"So if we get approval in the US first, it means it's much more economically viable for us to then come back and market in Australia."

Willie Creek Pearls, based on the outskirts of Broome in WA's north, will provide the product for PearlBone. (ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins)

Professor Pfleger said the clearance was an "inspiring" achievement for others in the industry.

"The next point is obviously making sales, getting patients and benefiting from that and getting surgeons using it," he said.

"But regulatory approval is critical."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/d.title: Do Australians actually want cheaper housing? We're finding out fast
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/d.author: Tom Crowley
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-14/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Housing Policy

Australia's housing crisis has entered new territory. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Australia's housing crisis has entered a new phase: a little less conversation, a little more action.

The first seeds were planted three years ago, with a landmark national agreement to build more homes. The target, 1.2 million in five years, is likely doomed. But what mattered was that a target was set at all. After years of lip service, leaders had promised to act on the root cause.

Then there was last year's economic roundtable. After much fanfare, the closed-door event had seemed like a fizzer. But for Treasurer Jim Chalmers, it helped build the case that Labor's old policy to wind back negative gearing could be reinvented, and framed as a leg up for homebuyers over investors.

A policy to boost supply and a policy to slash demand. Throw in the highest interest rates in 18 years, and all of a sudden a housing market that seemed as if it would never turn is turning very fast indeed. This week saw the steepest drop-off in new home loans ever recorded.

Unit values outperform houses in most capital cities as rising interest rates shrink borrowing power and reshape demand.

Commentators had long wondered whether, for all the hand-wringing about the housing crisis, Australians would actually want a solution when it came, since, one way or another, cheaper homes for the young can only mean less valuable homes for those who already own them.

But no more need to wonder: we're finding out. A tumbling market may not have been federal Labor's ideal pathway to affordable housing, but after months of dithering, the government took a tentative step this week towards embracing the chaos, framing it as a win for homebuyers.

In the coming weeks and months, Labor governments in Australia's two largest states will put their own higher-density plans to voters. At federal and state levels, Liberals are betting voters will dislike the prescribed cure worse than the sickness.

Topic:Housing Construction Industry

Topic:
Housing Construction Industry

Topic:
World Politics

Topic:
Property Prices

Topic:
Indigenous Culture

Labor did not expect its changes to the capital gains tax and negative gearing to tank house prices. Treasury analysis predicted prices would still grow, but by 2 per cent less. Chalmers has repeatedly said he is "not targeting a particular price".

Nor did it want prices to tank. In 2024, Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said it was her "strong view" that falling prices would be bad.

"Our policies are not going to reduce house prices. We want house prices to grow sustainably," she said then.

Clare O'Neil has been caught between championing affordability and protecting people's investments. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

But now they have fallen. The median national house price is 5.6 per cent below its March peak, and 3.9 per cent for apartments. The drop-off has been sharper in Melbourne and Sydney, and some analysts predict double-digit declines.

Other indicators point in the same direction. The auction clearance rate has plunged below 50 per cent, compared to its long-run average of 60 per cent. And new figures this week showed a record 15 per cent dip in new loans between June and September.

The chill was evident across the board, but it was clearly worse for investors (31 per cent) than for homebuyers (5 per cent). First home buyers (8 per cent) fared worse than established homebuyers, but still far better than investors.

High rates have clearly played a role. But they do not explain why investors are falling away by "so much more than in previous interest rate increasing cycles", as Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock observed last week.

"[That] suggests something else is going on here, and [that] is the tax changes," she said. In other words, the tax changes are doing what they were designed to do: discourage investors.

Until this week, the government had been skittish about embracing that. Even after opinion polls suggested a majority of Australians believed that prices needed to fall, ministers were nervous about embracing the nosedive.

But on Wednesday, O'Neil ditched the script and stopped equivocating.

Research shows nurses, teachers and social workers can only afford a small percentage of rental listings across Australia.

"We've had a housing market geared towards investors for a generation, and where did it get us? Plummeting ownership, out-of-control house price increases, and a generation losing hope," she said.

"These numbers show the balance is shifting back … It is absolutely the case that volumes are down, as you would expect in a period where prices are softening. But these figures also clearly show a strong shift away from investors and towards Australians buying a home to live in."

It is a risky gambit. First home buyers may be getting a leg up — CBA's Matt Comyn said yesterday their share of new loan applications doubled last month. But a fast-falling market is a risky one to enter, especially with high rates, and it can also chill housing supply.

Liberal housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg seized on the comments, calling them "strange".

"People would look at what Clare O'Neil says and think, 'Well, what planet is she living on? Why is she saying fewer loans is good?' Fewer loans is bad. We need to see more lending."

A chorus of real estate moguls and personal finance celebrities agree. A prominent example is podcaster Mark Bouris, who predicted in The Australian this week "the longest downturn in our history" and warned: "We're going to have a serious structural hit to people's wealth."

The comments are revealing, hinting at what motivates many critics. Not affordability, but wealth.

That cannot be said of Bragg, one of a handful of politicians who have publicly embraced the idea that lower house prices could be welcome if they happen via a supply boom, not a demand chill.

But for many home owners, wealth is front of mind, and this is just as true on the supply side as it is on the demand side, as state governments are finding out.

In Victoria, the Labor government has pursued the most aggressively pro-supply policy in the country, designating several Melbourne suburban hubs as so-called activity centres, where high-density towers will be allowed in narrow strips and medium-density in wider surrounds.

Typical of the cynical political style of former premier Daniel Andrews and his successor Jacinta Allan, many zones are in places Labor will never win, including in Brighton and state Liberal leader Jess Wilson's Kew.

Jess Wilson said a Coalition government would shift the focus of high-rise development to Melbourne's inner city. (ABC News)

Locals have been whipped into a frenzy by dystopian artists' impressions of amorphous black skyscrapers invading their leafy shopping strips, a feature of media coverage.

Kew and Brighton will hardly shape the election, which pundits predict Labor will lose for other reasons, but Wilson has vowed to scrap the plan and give local councils a veto if elected.

A similar dynamic is emerging in Sydney, where the Minns Labor government will face voters early in the new year and where designated density zones in suburbs such as Woollahra and Crows Nest are also opposed by the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane.

Sloane, echoing Wilson and many Teal MPs, says she supports more housing but frames her complaint as one of consultation, and is also promising a council veto.

The argument has a reasonable-sounding guise — "We just want locals to have a say" — but to pro-supply campaigners including Peter Tulip, it is an all-too-familiar smokescreen for building fewer homes, since councils make decisions for existing residents, not potential new ones.

"[The] households who move in would be better off. As would renters and homebuyers who benefit from improved affordability. They greatly outnumber the opponents, but they don't get to vote for the local politicians who are biased against new housing," he said last week.

If Tulip is right, the political numbers game should favour Labor governments at federal and state levels if their policies really do make housing more affordable: they would lose Kew and Crows Nest, but win the country.

In different economic and political circumstances, that reckoning might have come gradually. Instead, we are hurtling towards it.
