More than 30 people were hospitalized, but all passengers survived and were accounted for. The paddlewheel cruise boat, called The American Heritage, capsized after the impact with the much larger cargo vessel.

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-updates-eu.title: Ukraine updates: Europe to send united front to potential peace talks
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-updates-eu.text:
Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland — as well as the EU itself — will jointly represent Europe in possible peace talks. Meanwhile, a second car bomb in two days has exploded in Moscow.

These updates have been closed. Below, you can review developments from the Russia's war in Ukraine from  Friday, November 13:

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Friday directly contradicted US envoy Jared Kushner's Thursday statement that President Vladimir Putin had voiced willingness to have European representatives join upcoming talks designed to end his war of aggression against Ukraine.

Responding to a request for comment from Germany's DPA news agency, Zakharova said, "As far as Russia's Foreign Ministry is aware, the issue was not discussed during the talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow."

No Foreign Ministry representatives were present during a Thursday meeting between Putin and US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff according to Russian state media, which said Putin was accompanied by his own foreign policy advisor Yuri Ushakov, Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky and envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday said the EU will take part in future peace talks aimed at ending Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and will jointly represent Europe with France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK.

"Europe must speak with one clear voice and united voice in all discussion that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent. And this is ultimately a team effort," Costa said after a European leaders' meeting in Dublin.

European and Ukrainian leaders have long insisted on the format, while Russia has rejected the idea and the US appeared indifferent under the Trump administration.

The situation appears to have changed slightly, with US envoy and presidential son-in-law Jared Kushner saying late Thursday, "We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table," adding that Russian President Vladimir Putin "is willing to give it a try."

Despite consensus about wanting peace after nearly five years of Russia's war of aggression, Europe lacks unanimity as to who should be representing the interests of the continent and member states.

Russia and the US have called for one single representative to be present, whereas several nations have called for a diplomatic team.

The question of who will represent the EU itself remains unresolved.

The bloc's foreign affairs boss Kaja Kallas — a staunch critic of Russia and its war — said Friday, "I'm the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy." Adding, "I know that the Russians don’t want me, but, you know, do we have a say, who is representing Russia?"

With frustration growing over Russian aggression on Europe's doorstep, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs put things in perspective. Pointing to the fact that Europe is more populous, richer and more militarily powerful than Russia, he said Friday, "We as Europe, have to grow some bigger balls."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said no clear explanations have been given for recent speed issues with Starshield.

The Ukrainian president said on Thursday that Ukraine's military faced new "systematic restrictions" to tech billionaire Elon Musk's Starshield satellite internet.

Zelenskyy doubled down on his comments on Friday, saying the issue remained unsolved.

He said the connections were only working when devices were moving slower than 161 kilometres (100 miles) per hour.

"This makes it impossible, in particular, to use interceptors against jet-powered 'Shaheds.'" he added. The Ukrainian president also said he instructed his ministers to step up contacts with the US side.

The Starshield military communications system — the military-grade version of satellite-based communication network Starlink — is operated by Musk's SpaceX and plays a key role for frontline communications.

Ukraine first flagged issues with Starshield last month after a dispute between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump over a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk "capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network."

Tech billionaire and US president both denied throttling Ukrainian access, but Musk later accused Ukraine of using the service for military purposes while Trump said Musk had "put it back."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday asked US President Donald Trump to not make any "surprises" on Ukraine with the Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump is expected to meet with Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders' summit in China next week.

Speaking on the sidelines of the European Union meetings in Dublin, Merz said that "some here ⁠in ⁠fear this could turn into a 'second Anchorage moment'."

The Russian and US presidents held talks in Anchorage, Alaska, last summer, the outcome of which European side views as favoring Putin.

"I ‌therefore want to state our message to the United States very clearly: Please, no surprises. Continue to ‌play as part of 'Team Europe' and 'Team Ukraine'," Merz said.

He also stated that Europe does not need to talk about security arrangements with Russia.

"Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that, it already exists," he said.

Merz also said it was a "given" that his country would involved in the next round of Ukraine talks.

Kyiv residents are bracing for another difficult winter as Russian airstrikes continue to target the Ukrainian capital’s energy infrastructure. Long and unpredictable power and water outages are disrupting daily life, forcing families to rely on batteries, portable power stations and improvised routines.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.

Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

Read more about the uncertainty over Europe’s representation in the Ukraine peace talks

Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia needs clarity on the European Union's "real intentions" for joining the Ukraine peace talks before making a decision on whether to expand the trilateral format.

US negotiators ‌said on Thursday that ‌President ​Vladimir Putin had agreed to an EU seat at the table, but Peskov's remarks indicate that the Kremlin has not yet agreed.

"Once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format," Peskov said.

"If the Europeans really do have someone who is at least authorized in some way to talk, and if the Europeans really do have the desire to do so, then, of course, we will be ready to talk to them," he said.

Speaking after the latest trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, Russia's lead negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, claimed that "Russia did not receive single concrete peace proposal from European countries."

The European Union (EU) foreign affairs chief, Kaja Kallas, said Russia did not want ​"anybody strong" at the negotiating table because "they ​want to ​push through their maximum ​demands."

Arriving at an EU summit in Dublin, Kallas told reporters that Moscow had no say over who represented the European Union in the US-mediated Ukraine-Russia peace talks.

"First we need a ceasefire. If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us, which is that we divert the attention away from that there is no ceasefire," she said.

EU leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent the European Union in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the bloc will be present at the next meetings.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa.

As yet, the EU hasn't been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

Overnight drone attacks killed several people in both Ukraine and Russia.

In the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa, authorities said two people had been killed and five others injured. One person was reportedly injured in an attack on a hospital, according to reports from the capital city of Kyiv.

A Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia in the southeast killed a 17-year-old boy, acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said.

Meanwhile, In the Russian city of Volgograd, four people were killed and two others injured, regional government said.

Russia's Investigative Committee has launched an inquiry into the explosion of a car belonging to an exiled Ukrainian political aide in Moscow, media reported.

The car reportedly belonged to Sergei Zavorotniy, a former spokesman for Mykola Azarov, who served as Ukraine's prime minister from 2010 to 2014. He fled to Russia from Ukraine amid anti-government protests in 2014.

According to the Russian newspaper Kommersant, Zavorotniy was hospitalized. Both Ren TV and the 112 Telegram channel reported that he lost his left arm in the attack and sustained a concussion, rib fractures, and other injuries.

Meanwhile, Azarov told Russia's TASS state news agency on Friday that he does not know anything about the explosion except that Zavorotniy survived.

This is the second reported car explosion in Russia following the death of a Russian serviceman in a car explosion in Saint Petersburg on Thursday.

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

EU leaders are set to convene in the Irish capital, Dublin, for an informal European Council meeting on Friday. They are under pressure to nominate someone to represent the European Union in the Ukraine peace talks.

In other news, a car bomb exploded in Russia, targeting a former aide to the pro-Russia Ukrainian politician Mykola Azarov.

Follow along for the latest updates on the peace talks and other news from Ukraine.
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-updates-eu.summary: Russia and US have called for one single representative to be present in Ukraine peace talks. EU leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine talks. Car bomb in Russia targets former aide of pro-Russian politician Mykola Azarov.

https://www.dw.com/en/david-walliams-uk-.title: David Walliams: UK police launch sex offense probe into comedian
https://www.dw.com/en/david-walliams-uk-.text:
The "Little Britain" star and "Britain's Got Talent" judge has been accused of engaging in sexual misconduct and inappropriate behavior towards young women and girls. Walliams denies the allegations.

London police on Friday said they are opening an sexual offenses investigation into British actor, comedian and children's author David Walliams.

The Metropolitan Police said they "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offenses involving a man now in his 50s."

It comes after British outlets ITV News and The Guardian paper reported that Walliams misused his power and celebrity status to prey on women and girls over a period of more than 20 years. The media outlets produced an hourlong video documentary on the allegations against Walliams, entitled "David Walliams: Power and Silence."

The documentary reported on a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Walliams when she was 15. The outlets also highlighted sexual harassment and inappropriate conduct allegations regarding "Britain's Got Talent," where he was a judge, and his book publisher HarperCollins.

"We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offense to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened," said Detective Mike Cagney, who is in charge of the Met Police investigation.

The Met Police investigation is based on allegations against Walliams that are separate from those reported by the two news outlets.

Neither Walliams nor his lawyer have responded to the Met Police investigation. However, Walliams did respond earlier to the ITV and Guardian report about him.

"I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me," Walliams told the outlets in a letter. "Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something I never did."

The allegations against Walliams have already have already had repercussions on his career. The BBC took down content featuring Walliams from its platforms, including comedy sketch show "Little Britain."

Walliams' publisher, HarperCollins UK, dropped him last year after The Telegraph newspaper reported on inappropriate behavior towards women at the publishing firm.

The allegations come as several male comedic and literary figures in the UK have faced either sexual assault charges or accusations in recent years.

Media personality and actor Russell Brand on Monday was sentenced to 10 years and 6 months imprisonment after he was convicted of rape and assault.

In 2024, children's book author Neil Gaiman was accused of sexual assault, leading companies such as Disney and DC Comics to drop adaptations of his works. Gaiman denies the allegations.

"The media industry will need to look at itself and ensure whether it is taking all of the steps needed to protect the safety of woman and girls who work within the industry," British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Thursday.

British Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy is expected to meet with entertainment industry leaders next week, where she will deliver a warning that the UK government could intervene if they do not protect those who blow the whistle on sexual assault and misconduct.

https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-celebrate.title: Pope Leo celebrates Mass in his former diocese of Chiclayo, Peru
https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-celebrate.text:
Over a million people have gathered for Mass with Pope Leo XIV on Friday. The event in northern Peru, where he served as bishop before becoming head of the Catholic Church, is the centerpiece of his South American tour.

Pope Leo XIV was greeted by another enormous crowd on Friday as he arrived at Pampas de Pimentel, a vast desert park outside the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo, to celebrate an outdoor Mass in a diocese that he served as bishop for eight years before being summoned to Rome in 2023, where he was later elected pontiff.

The Vatican estimates that roughly 1.5 million faithful braved scorching sun and heat of 31 degrees Celsius (87 degrees Fahrenheit) to attend.

The event was the centerpiece of Leo's 12-day South American tour, throughout which an estimated 12 million people have turned out at stops in Uruguay and Argentina and now Peru.

Pope Leo, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, Illinois, had already referred to Peru, where he served as a missionary for some 20 years, as his homeland in remarks delivered on Wednesday.

Beyond US and Vatican citizenship, Leo also holds a Peruvian passport.

Leo, whom locals still refer to as "Padre Roberto" and "amigo," arrived from the capital Lima on Friday morning in a plane adorned with stickers reading "Leo XIV flies home." The leader of the Catholic Church's 1.4 billion members will remain in Chiclayo until Sunday.

An agricultural and commercial hub on the Pacific coast, Chiclayo is Peru's fourth largest city and has a population of 700,000. Beyond locals, many of those attending Mass on Friday told reporters that they had journeyed from far-flung regions and even neighboring countries to receive the pope's blessing.

The crowds that Leo has attracted throughout his trip, undertaken shortly after he underwent surgery for lung cancer in Rome, have grown along the way, with the largest gathering coming in Lima on Wednesday, where an estimated 3.5 million people turned out.

Though normally reserved, Leo has openly displayed his emotions since returning to Peru — laughing, singing and tearing up while interacting with crowds of faithful both young and old.

After making his way through the massive crowd to celebrate Mass on Friday, Leo began his sermon with words of thanks.

"What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo!" Leo said at the start of his homily, "It is a blessing for me to be with you once again."

"As I look your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers, especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," Leo told the crowd.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Friday afternoon, the pontiff will deliver a speech at Chiclayo's St. Turibius de Mogrovejo Catholic University, where he once served as chancellor.

The institution is named after a sixteenth century Spanish missionary who would become the first archbishop of Lima. He served as a role model for Leo during his own ministry.

Mogrovejo was known to travel long distances on horseback to spread the gospel, as well as for standing up for the rights of indigenous and enslaved peoples.

Leo, too, is remembered for his outreach and for championing human rights and social justice, especially for the poor.

https://www.dw.com/en/the-dangers-of-rev.title: The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture
https://www.dw.com/en/the-dangers-of-rev.text:
Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.

But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.

"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.

He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.

US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years.

Kushner said he was looking at a "broader" European architecture before he flew to meet with Russian and Ukrainian representatives in Abu Dhabi.

European diplomats immediately pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine because they feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.

Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.

Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.

They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.

The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.

"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.

During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.

But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.

"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."

Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.

The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

"Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.

"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.

He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.

Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.

Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-braces-for.title: Czechia braces for massive protest against public media reform plans
https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-braces-for.text:
A fast-tracked bill to cut public media funding has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is planned for Prague on Sunday.

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.

The right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism."

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country."

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.

But this could come at a cost.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.

"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

Babis is aware of the danger.

The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation."

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.
https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-braces-for.summary: The government's fast-tracked bill to cut public media funding has sparked protests and strikes. The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y4.title: Bonnie Tyler remembers loved ones in posthumous Christmas single
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y4.text:
Bonnie Tyler sings of "love, light and peace" and remembers "the ones who still live on inside our hearts" on her posthumous Christmas single, which was released on Friday.

The popular Welsh powerhouse singer, born Gaynor Hopkins, died in July aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year.

Fans were able to hear the Total Eclipse of the Heart singer's husky tones one more time on the festive track titled "Love, Light and Peace".

The last song Tyler recorded features sleigh bells and angels and an ad-libbed farewell: "To all, goodnight."

The lyrics about grief and loss take on new meaning following her death.

Tyler sings: "Blessed are the ones who still live on inside our hearts.

"Here's to the best of them."

The song was written by Chrissie Hammond and Grammy-winner Terry Britten, who played guitar on Tyler's debut album, The World Starts Tonight in 1977.

Nearly 50 years later, he returned as a writer and producer for the last song she recorded.

Tyler's husband of more than 50 years, Robert Sullivan, previously said she would have wanted fans to hear the music she was working on, and gave his blessing for the song's release.

Tyler was born in a Neath council house where she grew up with a love of music before being discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.

After finding fame she was dubbed "the female Rod Stewart" for her husky vocals, and launched a career that spanned 50 years.

In August, fans travelled to Swansea to line the streets as a celebration of life service was held for her at Swansea Minster.

https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/.title: Asian love ballads test Eurovision’s winning song formula.
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/.author: Francesca Regalado
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/.text:
Bangkok9:34 p.m. Nov. 14

The high-camp event is underway in Bangkok, with performers in feathered capes and sequined corsets. Will it appeal to fans in a vast new market?

The Eurovision Song Contest will crown its first Asia champion in Bangkok on Saturday, in an event that will test whether a high-camp singing competition with an ardent fan base can appeal to audiences in a new market.

The inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia includes artists and original songs from 11 countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. It will be live-streamed on YouTube at 8:30 p.m. local time (8:30 a.m. Eastern) and broadcast by television stations across the region.

Eurovision has been a fixture of the European cultural calendar since it began in 1956. Past winners include Sweden’s ABBA and the Canadian chanteuse Celine Dion, who represented Switzerland in 1988.

Asian artists have readily embraced the kitschy outfits and spectacular sets that are part of Eurovision tradition, with costumes that include traditional dress, as well as feathered capes and sequined corsets. Malaysia’s performer plans to enter the stage in a giant teardrop.

But the Eurovision format has not been tested in Asia. Fans and regional partners have expressed concern in recent weeks that budget constraints, production issues and weak audience demand could imperil the spinoff. Organizers say the contest could take time to build an audience.

“It would be profoundly arrogant to think that just because we have a heritage brand and a huge global audience for the European show, that we would walk in and demand it to be the same here,” said Martin Green, the European Broadcasting Union’s director of the Eurovision Song Contest. “Like any new thing, it needs to find its roots.”

Two previous attempts to take the competition to Asia were abandoned by the European Broadcasting Union, which owns Eurovision, and its partners in the region. A Eurovision spinoff in the United States, NBC’s American Song Contest, ran for one season in 2022.

The Asian edition kicking off on Saturday is far smaller than its European counterpart. Eurovision organizers said they were in talks with more countries to join future seasons. They include China, Japan and India, whose music industries have global reach.

“Bringing the world together through music is a fundamentally good idea,” Mr. Green said. “Europe shouldn’t keep it to itself.”

Here’s what we’re covering:

Politics: Geopolitics have long intruded on the European edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, but they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia. Read more ›

Voting process: Each artist will receive half their scores from professional juries in each country, and the other half from public voting on the Eurovision Asia website. Viewers are allowed to vote for artists from at least three other countries — not their own.

Thailand’s entry, Mang and Daou, is the only duet in tonight’s show.

Piyatida Lekklang, whose stage name is Mang, debuted as a member of the co-ed group Bamm in 2021 and started her solo career three years later. Pittaya Saechua, who goes by Da-Ou, is an actor who has performed with the boy band LAZ1.

Their hit song “Aroma” tells the story of someone aching for a departed loved one, hoping to meet them again – even if only in a dream – to share an embrace and say a final goodbye. The song’s title can also be translated from the Thai as “Night Scent” or “Aroma of the Night.”

The home crowd knows their favorites are next. A tree is rolled out onto the stage for Mang and Daou, the Thai duo.

In Beatmosphere’s song,“Tumi Ele,” which is about the adrenaline rush of a new love, the group is singing and rapping in Bengali while using their voices to mimic traditional instruments like the stringed dotora and the tabla drum.

“We have a very percussive culture,” Beatbaksho, a member of the group, said in an interview before the final.

Beatmosphere has the audience dancing to its a cappella hip-hop track, “Tumi Ele.” Even the artists in the green room are on their feet!

Beatmosphere is a Dhaka-based a cappella hip-hop group with six members: Ishtiyak Zobayer (Zardo), Sayed Ahnaf Tahmid (Glizmo), Sidratul Mursalin Bhasha (Bhasha), Mahi Bin Ashraful (Sykoverse), Moktadir Dewan (BeatBaksho) and Mahi Hossain Khan (Invalíd).

The group formed in 2019 at Beatbox Bangladesh, a community of beatboxers that hosts beatboxing battles. They took different paths to beatboxing. Invalid, for example, was a classically trained singer, Zardo learned beatboxing on the internet, and Sykoverse started by joining hip-hop jam sessions in his neighborhood.

Beatmosphere from Bangladesh are trying to bring beatboxing back to pop music in a way not seen since Justin Timberlake’s 2002 hit “Cry Me A River,” an era of pop music I feel may sadly have passed

The hosts are interviewing Dara, this year’s Eurovision winner from Bulgaria. In a brief onstage interview, she briefly sang a line from Loreen’s “Believe,” a catchy dance track that won Eurovision 2012. It seemed to go down like a lead balloon, based on the silence on YouTube.

Three fans were chosen to play a Eurovision trivia game. The winner will get a trip to Burgas, Bulgaria, the site of the next European contest in May.

Carmelle is the only artist whose lyrics are about self-belief (“If I’m too much for you / Maybe you’re just not enough for me”). That surprises me, as that kind of lyrical choice is normally an easy way to win the European edition of the show. Eurovision winners who have adopted the strategy include Russia’s Dima Bilan in 2008 and  Israel’s Netta in 2018. In “Believe,” Bilan sang about how “Even when the world tries to pull me down,” he won’t’ succumb. In “Toy,” Netta sang the refrain “I’m not your toy / You stupid boy.”

When they sat down to plan the final show of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest in Asia, the organizers faced a challenge: How could they introduce variety when most of the entries were slow-paced love songs?

Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers.

“Europeans tend to prefer songs with a crescendo, a hook and a grand ending, but also a strong social message,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of contemporary Europe at the University of Luxembourg who is an authority on Eurovision.

“The audience doesn’t want to see an innocuous pop song,” he said.

Electro-pop and dance songs have featured heavily on the list of Eurovision winners over the past decade. In May, Bulgaria’s Dara won with “Bangaranga,” a dance-pop song inspired by her diagnosis with attention deficit hyperactive disorder. Nemo, from Switzerland, won in 2024 with an EDM opera about their nonbinary identity, while in 2018, Israel’s Netta won with “Toy,” a pop anthem about female independence.

Some countries hold a nationwide contest to select an artist and a song to represent them in Eurovision, while others leave the choice to Eurovision’s local broadcasting partner. Audiences in the Philippines voted for Carmelle in a televised competition, for example, while Vietnam Television chose Toc Tien.

The two are considered front-runners in the Asian edition, with their high-energy folk-pop songs about female empowerment.

Malaysia’s Aina Abdul, another early favorite, will showcase her powerful vocals in “Bluest Sky,” a ballad with an orchestral arrangement that is about a troubled relationship. The track is reminiscent of “Wasted Love,” an opera-techno song that won Austria the European title in 2025.

Pratik Himal Rai of Nepal, who got married this summer, said love was easy to sing about because it can be understood across borders and languages.

“It is love that holds the world together,” he said in an interview.

He will sing “Ananta Maya” in Nepali. Other Eurovision Asia artists blend English lyrics with their national languages.

In Europe, every winning song after 2022 has been in English. That year’s champion, Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra, sang in their own language on “Stefania,” a hip-hop track that interspersed a Ukrainian lullaby with rap verses and traditional woodwind instruments.

Winning songs tend to blend a country’s national instruments and musical motifs with internationally trendy pop, Mr. Vuletic said.

A traditional Bhutanese flute can be heard in “Lhayi Semo,” Nyendra’s love ballad. Monetrey’s “I Let You Go” uses a Cambodian bamboo xylophone and a tro, a string instrument played with a bow. A kulintang, a percussion instrument made of eight brass gongs, keeps the fast beat in Carmelle’s “Sobra-Sobra.”

Carmelle Collado was born in Camarines Sur, a province southeast of Manila, to a family of singers.

When she was 12, she finished second in a kids’ edition of The Voice Philippines. That same year, she won seven gold medals in the World Championships of Performing Arts, an international competition for young musicians held in the United States.

Her song, “Sobra-Sobra,” is a female-empowerment anthem that challenges traditional notions that a woman should be demure, gentle and quiet. Her vocal performance spans belting riffs and rap verses.

The cheers for Carmelle were deafening. At 19, she is the youngest performer in Eurovision Asia stage, but she has one of its biggest voices.

Luigi Abreu, 23, a member of the Carmelle Collado Fanatics group on social media in the Philippines, said she was praying for the singer’s success.

“We love you very much,” she said. “Thank you for representing the Philippines. Forward, woman.”

Carmelle is dressed in a feathery cape by the Filipino designer Axel Que. She looks like a Sarimanok, a mythical rooster with multicolored wings that is a symbol of wealth and good fortune. The cape flies off to reveal a sequined corset reminiscent of a Filipino superhero, Darna.

The crowd began cheering for Carmelle, the Philippines’ entry, before she appeared onstage. Many Filipinos have flown into Bangkok for this show.

I really like Bhutan’s Nyendra, a singer who has said he never traveled by plane or train before going to this contest. He has described himself as a big Justin Bieber fan, and his cute pop song has early Bieber vibes.

Nyendra’s song “Lhayi Semo” is a romantic ballad about falling deeply in love with someone who seems heavenly. It captures the beauty, longing and uncertainty of loving someone who feels too extraordinary to be real. The title can be translated as “The Angel” or “Daughter of the Gods.”

Tandin Dorji, a Bhutanese music director and composer, said that he feels proud and emotional to see a Bhutanese singer representing his country on an international stage. “For those of us who have spent years composing, recording and nurturing local talent, moments like this are especially meaningful,” he said.

Nyendra, 24, grew up in a small town called Phuentsoling, on Bhutan’s southern border with India. After winning his country’s national selection, he has left Bhutan for the first time to travel to the Eurovision final in the Thai capital, Bangkok.

“I wasn’t famous in Bhutan,” he said in an interview before the show. “This has changed the entire course of my life.”

The youngest of four siblings, he started writing songs and singing in school when he was 13. He said his parents, siblings and grandparents were his favorite part of life. He left his town when he was 19 to study mass communications and journalism in Thimphu, the Bhutanese capital.

Bhutan’s Nyendra sings a love song to an angel as a dancer in white floats around the stage. He is wearing a gho, the traditional garment of Bhutanese men.

Artists who have performed are sitting on sofas with their teams in the green room, an elevated platform to the side of the stage. They will stay there for the rest of the show until the winner is announced.

These performances are so much better than they were for the national qualifiers when most acts simply sung while standing stock still. Take Mongolia’s “Beck.” For his national contest, he wore a white suit and sang like he was a hotel entertainer. Here, he’s wearing a traditional Mongolian outfit that’s flowing in the (fake) wind, there are dancers and some onstage pyrotechnics

The crowd erupts as Beck ends his song, “Chamguigeer,” on a high note. The love ballad was a last-minute replacement, after Beck’s first song was disqualified because it was released before July.

Geopolitics have long intruded on the Eurovision Song Contest. But they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia for the first time.

That was still true as of Saturday evening, as the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia was about to start in Bangkok.

Over the decades, Eurovision organizers have insisted that the contest is nonpolitical. Its organizers impose rules governing lyrics, political symbols and what can be broadcast. Even so, wars and diplomatic disputes have shaped who gets to sing, who stays home and what broadcasters are willing to air.

“Politics is why we watch Eurovision,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of the show at the University of Luxembourg.

Here are some examples of geopolitics bleeding into the European edition of the contest:

In 2009, less than a year after fighting a war with Russia, the former Soviet republic of Georgia planned to send a disco song called “We Don’t Wanna Put In” to Eurovision. Eurovision’s organizers said that the apparent dig at Vladimir Putin, then Russia’s prime minister, had to go. Georgia pulled out instead of changing it.

In 2017, Russia pulled out of the contest in Kyiv after Ukraine barred its singer from entering the country. And five years later, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Eurovision barred Russia altogether.

In 2024, the war in Gaza triggered mass protests over Israel’s participation. A bitter dispute over government influence on voting followed in 2025, and there were boycotts of the contest by five countries in 2026, the biggest crisis in Eurovision’s 70-year history.

The 11 Asian countries that sent artists to Saturday’s show have plenty of offstage geopolitical friction.

Cambodia, for example, is set to sing in Thailand’s capital less than a year after a border war between the two neighbors killed dozens and displaced hundreds of thousands. As fighting picked up last year, Cambodia withdrew its athletes from the Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, citing safety concerns.

But none of that has translated into a Eurovision controversy.

Mr. Vuletic said he expects Eurovision Asia to become a more visible platform for politics if the event continues over the next few years, drawing a wider audience and raising the stakes for countries taking part.

For now, some of Asia’s biggest powers are conspicuously absent from the lineup. Broadcasters from China, Japan and India discussed participating but did not sign up before the entry deadline, said Assaf Blecher, the contest’s executive producer. Pakistan and Indonesia are also absent.

China’s relations with Japan have been strained by a diplomatic dispute over Taiwan, which spilled into pop culture last year when Beijing canceled Japanese concerts and restricted films. China also has overlapping maritime claims in the South China Sea with the Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia — countries that are all competing on Saturday.

Taiwan’s absence spares the organizers potentially sensitive decisions about names and flags. Beijing claims the self-governing island as its territory and opposes its treatment as an independent country. Such symbols have proved contentious at Eurovision, which in 2024 barred its audience from carrying Palestinian flags while permitting those of participating countries, including Israel.

Eurovision’s organizers have said the competition is “not a contest between governments.” But maintaining that distinction involves decisions about both what performers can sing and what broadcasters air.

The European contest’s rules prohibit political lyrics, speeches and gestures, and entrants may be asked to submit new songs or rewrite offending words. In 2024, organizers required Israel to change the title and lyrics of “October Rain,” which appeared to reference the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attacks. The song became “Hurricane.”

For all the trouble it can bring, the breadth of representation has also been part of Eurovision’s appeal since its founding in 1956, as an experiment in international television and an effort to bring Cold War Europe together. Bosnia and Herzegovina debuted in 1993 while Sarajevo, its capital, was under siege. Its singer, Fazla, told The New York Times in 2022 that he had escaped barefoot under sniper fire after his shoes became stuck in the mud.

“Eurovision is about representing your nation,” he said, “about giving yourself a platform to bring your story into the living rooms of normal people.”

Eurovision is not the only song contest to offer that platform. Russia revived the Cold War-era Intervision contest in 2025, after its exclusion from Eurovision over the invasion of Ukraine. It promoted the new competition as a showcase for what the Kremlin calls “traditional values.”

Vietnam’s Duc Phuc won that contest in Moscow.

On Saturday in Bangkok, another Vietnamese pop star, Toc Tien, will be first onstage at Eurovision Asia.

Thailand’s entry, Mang and Daou, is the only duet in tonight’s show.

Their hit song “Aroma” tells the story of someone aching for a departed loved one, hoping to meet them again – even if only in a dream – to share an embrace and say a final goodbye. The song’s title can also be translated from the Thai as “Night Scent” or “Aroma of the Night.”

The home crowd knows their favorites are next. A tree is rolled out onto the stage for Mang and Daou, the Thai duo.

In Beatmosphere’s song,“Tumi Ele,” which is about the adrenaline rush of a new love, the group is singing and rapping in Bengali while using their voices to mimic traditional instruments like the stringed dotora and the tabla drum.

“We have a very percussive culture,” Beatbaksho, a member of the group, said in an interview before the final.

Beatmosphere has the audience dancing to its a cappella hip-hop track, “Tumi Ele.” Even the artists in the green room are on their feet!

Beatmosphere is a Dhaka-based a cappella hip-hop group with six members: Ishtiyak Zobayer (Zardo), Sayed Ahnaf Tahmid (Glizmo), Sidratul Mursalin Bhasha (Bhasha), Mahi Bin Ashraful (Sykoverse), Moktadir Dewan (BeatBaksho) and Mahi Hossain Khan (Invalíd).

The group formed in 2019 at Beatbox Bangladesh, a community of beatboxers that hosts beatboxing battles. They took different paths to beatboxing. Invalid, for example, was a classically trained singer, Zardo learned beatboxing on the internet, and Sykoverse started by joining hip-hop jam sessions in his neighborhood.

Beatmosphere from Bangladesh are trying to bring beatboxing back to pop music in a way not seen since Justin Timberlake’s 2002 hit “Cry Me A River,” an era of pop music I feel may sadly have passed

The hosts are interviewing Dara, this year’s Eurovision winner from Bulgaria. In a brief onstage interview, she briefly sang a line from Loreen’s “Believe,” a catchy dance track that won Eurovision 2012. It seemed to go down like a lead balloon, based on the silence on YouTube.

Three fans were chosen to play a Eurovision trivia game. The winner will get a trip to Burgas, Bulgaria, the site of the next European contest in May.

Carmelle is the only artist whose lyrics are about self-belief (“If I’m too much for you / Maybe you’re just not enough for me”). That surprises me, as that kind of lyrical choice is normally an easy way to win the European edition of the show. Eurovision winners who have adopted the strategy include Russia’s Dima Bilan in 2008 and  Israel’s Netta in 2018. In “Believe,” Bilan sang about how “Even when the world tries to pull me down,” he won’t’ succumb. In “Toy,” Netta sang the refrain “I’m not your toy / You stupid boy.”

When they sat down to plan the final show of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest in Asia, the organizers faced a challenge: How could they introduce variety when most of the entries were slow-paced love songs?

Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers.

“Europeans tend to prefer songs with a crescendo, a hook and a grand ending, but also a strong social message,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of contemporary Europe at the University of Luxembourg who is an authority on Eurovision.

“The audience doesn’t want to see an innocuous pop song,” he said.

Electro-pop and dance songs have featured heavily on the list of Eurovision winners over the past decade. In May, Bulgaria’s Dara won with “Bangaranga,” a dance-pop song inspired by her diagnosis with attention deficit hyperactive disorder. Nemo, from Switzerland, won in 2024 with an EDM opera about their nonbinary identity, while in 2018, Israel’s Netta won with “Toy,” a pop anthem about female independence.

Some countries hold a nationwide contest to select an artist and a song to represent them in Eurovision, while others leave the choice to Eurovision’s local broadcasting partner. Audiences in the Philippines voted for Carmelle in a televised competition, for example, while Vietnam Television chose Toc Tien.

The two are considered front-runners in the Asian edition, with their high-energy folk-pop songs about female empowerment.

Malaysia’s Aina Abdul, another early favorite, will showcase her powerful vocals in “Bluest Sky,” a ballad with an orchestral arrangement that is about a troubled relationship. The track is reminiscent of “Wasted Love,” an opera-techno song that won Austria the European title in 2025.

Pratik Himal Rai of Nepal, who got married this summer, said love was easy to sing about because it can be understood across borders and languages.

“It is love that holds the world together,” he said in an interview.

He will sing “Ananta Maya” in Nepali. Other Eurovision Asia artists blend English lyrics with their national languages.

In Europe, every winning song after 2022 has been in English. That year’s champion, Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra, sang in their own language on “Stefania,” a hip-hop track that interspersed a Ukrainian lullaby with rap verses and traditional woodwind instruments.

Winning songs tend to blend a country’s national instruments and musical motifs with internationally trendy pop, Mr. Vuletic said.

A traditional Bhutanese flute can be heard in “Lhayi Semo,” Nyendra’s love ballad. Monetrey’s “I Let You Go” uses a Cambodian bamboo xylophone and a tro, a string instrument played with a bow. A kulintang, a percussion instrument made of eight brass gongs, keeps the fast beat in Carmelle’s “Sobra-Sobra.”

Carmelle Collado was born in Camarines Sur, a province southeast of Manila, to a family of singers.

When she was 12, she finished second in a kids’ edition of The Voice Philippines. That same year, she won seven gold medals in the World Championships of Performing Arts, an international competition for young musicians held in the United States.

Her song, “Sobra-Sobra,” is a female-empowerment anthem that challenges traditional notions that a woman should be demure, gentle and quiet. Her vocal performance spans belting riffs and rap verses.

The cheers for Carmelle were deafening. At 19, she is the youngest performer in Eurovision Asia stage, but she has one of its biggest voices.

Luigi Abreu, 23, a member of the Carmelle Collado Fanatics group on social media in the Philippines, said she was praying for the singer’s success.

“We love you very much,” she said. “Thank you for representing the Philippines. Forward, woman.”

Carmelle is dressed in a feathery cape by the Filipino designer Axel Que. She looks like a Sarimanok, a mythical rooster with multicolored wings that is a symbol of wealth and good fortune. The cape flies off to reveal a sequined corset reminiscent of a Filipino superhero, Darna.

The crowd began cheering for Carmelle, the Philippines’ entry, before she appeared onstage. Many Filipinos have flown into Bangkok for this show.

I really like Bhutan’s Nyendra, a singer who has said he never traveled by plane or train before going to this contest. He has described himself as a big Justin Bieber fan, and his cute pop song has early Bieber vibes.

Nyendra’s song “Lhayi Semo” is a romantic ballad about falling deeply in love with someone who seems heavenly. It captures the beauty, longing and uncertainty of loving someone who feels too extraordinary to be real. The title can be translated as “The Angel” or “Daughter of the Gods.”

Tandin Dorji, a Bhutanese music director and composer, said that he feels proud and emotional to see a Bhutanese singer representing his country on an international stage. “For those of us who have spent years composing, recording and nurturing local talent, moments like this are especially meaningful,” he said.

Nyendra, 24, grew up in a small town called Phuentsoling, on Bhutan’s southern border with India. After winning his country’s national selection, he has left Bhutan for the first time to travel to the Eurovision final in the Thai capital, Bangkok.

“I wasn’t famous in Bhutan,” he said in an interview before the show. “This has changed the entire course of my life.”

The youngest of four siblings, he started writing songs and singing in school when he was 13. He said his parents, siblings and grandparents were his favorite part of life. He left his town when he was 19 to study mass communications and journalism in Thimphu, the Bhutanese capital.

Bhutan’s Nyendra sings a love song to an angel as a dancer in white floats around the stage. He is wearing a gho, the traditional garment of Bhutanese men.

Artists who have performed are sitting on sofas with their teams in the green room, an elevated platform to the side of the stage. They will stay there for the rest of the show until the winner is announced.

These performances are so much better than they were for the national qualifiers when most acts simply sung while standing stock still. Take Mongolia’s “Beck.” For his national contest, he wore a white suit and sang like he was a hotel entertainer. Here, he’s wearing a traditional Mongolian outfit that’s flowing in the (fake) wind, there are dancers and some onstage pyrotechnics

The crowd erupts as Beck ends his song, “Chamguigeer,” on a high note. The love ballad was a last-minute replacement, after Beck’s first song was disqualified because it was released before July.

Geopolitics have long intruded on the Eurovision Song Contest. But they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia for the first time.

That was still true as of Saturday evening, as the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia was about to start in Bangkok.

Over the decades, Eurovision organizers have insisted that the contest is nonpolitical. Its organizers impose rules governing lyrics, political symbols and what can be broadcast. Even so, wars and diplomatic disputes have shaped who gets to sing, who stays home and what broadcasters are willing to air.

“Politics is why we watch Eurovision,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of the show at the University of Luxembourg.

Here are some examples of geopolitics bleeding into the European edition of the contest:

In 2009, less than a year after fighting a war with Russia, the former Soviet republic of Georgia planned to send a disco song called “We Don’t Wanna Put In” to Eurovision. Eurovision’s organizers said that the apparent dig at Vladimir Putin, then Russia’s prime minister, had to go. Georgia pulled out instead of changing it.

In 2017, Russia pulled out of the contest in Kyiv after Ukraine barred its singer from entering the country. And five years later, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Eurovision barred Russia altogether.

In 2024, the war in Gaza triggered mass protests over Israel’s participation. A bitter dispute over government influence on voting followed in 2025, and there were boycotts of the contest by five countries in 2026, the biggest crisis in Eurovision’s 70-year history.

The 11 Asian countries that sent artists to Saturday’s show have plenty of offstage geopolitical friction.

Cambodia, for example, is set to sing in Thailand’s capital less than a year after a border war between the two neighbors killed dozens and displaced hundreds of thousands. As fighting picked up last year, Cambodia withdrew its athletes from the Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, citing safety concerns.

But none of that has translated into a Eurovision controversy.

Mr. Vuletic said he expects Eurovision Asia to become a more visible platform for politics if the event continues over the next few years, drawing a wider audience and raising the stakes for countries taking part.

For now, some of Asia’s biggest powers are conspicuously absent from the lineup. Broadcasters from China, Japan and India discussed participating but did not sign up before the entry deadline, said Assaf Blecher, the contest’s executive producer. Pakistan and Indonesia are also absent.

China’s relations with Japan have been strained by a diplomatic dispute over Taiwan, which spilled into pop culture last year when Beijing canceled Japanese concerts and restricted films. China also has overlapping maritime claims in the South China Sea with the Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia — countries that are all competing on Saturday.

Taiwan’s absence spares the organizers potentially sensitive decisions about names and flags. Beijing claims the self-governing island as its territory and opposes its treatment as an independent country. Such symbols have proved contentious at Eurovision, which in 2024 barred its audience from carrying Palestinian flags while permitting those of participating countries, including Israel.

Eurovision’s organizers have said the competition is “not a contest between governments.” But maintaining that distinction involves decisions about both what performers can sing and what broadcasters air.

The European contest’s rules prohibit political lyrics, speeches and gestures, and entrants may be asked to submit new songs or rewrite offending words. In 2024, organizers required Israel to change the title and lyrics of “October Rain,” which appeared to reference the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attacks. The song became “Hurricane.”

For all the trouble it can bring, the breadth of representation has also been part of Eurovision’s appeal since its founding in 1956, as an experiment in international television and an effort to bring Cold War Europe together. Bosnia and Herzegovina debuted in 1993 while Sarajevo, its capital, was under siege. Its singer, Fazla, told The New York Times in 2022 that he had escaped barefoot under sniper fire after his shoes became stuck in the mud.

“Eurovision is about representing your nation,” he said, “about giving yourself a platform to bring your story into the living rooms of normal people.”

Eurovision is not the only song contest to offer that platform. Russia revived the Cold War-era Intervision contest in 2025, after its exclusion from Eurovision over the invasion of Ukraine. It promoted the new competition as a showcase for what the Kremlin calls “traditional values.”

Vietnam’s Duc Phuc won that contest in Moscow.

On Saturday in Bangkok, another Vietnamese pop star, Toc Tien, will be first onstage at Eurovision Asia.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.author: Brent Crane
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

President Trump and U.S. tech executives are expected to gather for a major summit in Shenzhen next week. On the agenda: a stalled trade war, expanding export controls, and suspected spy games.

U.S.-Chinese business relations were thrown a curveball ahead of a major C.E.O. summit in Shenzhen, China, next week. On Thursday, Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia after it was revealed that he had affairs with an executive at the company and a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

One of the architects of the artificial intelligence boom, Huang was also perhaps the strongest proponent in Washington for U.S. companies selling A.I. hardware to China — an issue that has become central to the countries’ fraught economic relationship. Huang, who has a close relationship to President Trump, has also promoted open A.I. models, an approach favored by many Chinese firms.

China hawks in Congress have already seized on the scandal, using it to push for three bills that would put more restrictions on technology exports to the country.

Next week’s summit, which is hosted by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, has the potential to advance policy talks. Trump and the Chinese leader Xi Jinping (and perhaps President Vladimir Putin of Russia) are expected to meet. On the sidelines, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will take part in a bilateral dialogue on A.I.

But observers have low expectations for big changes. “The Chinese would like to prolong this fragile stability for as long as they can,” Ryan Hass, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who advised President Barack Obama and White House officials on U.S. policy toward China, told DealBook.

Still, amid a stalled trade war, expanding export controls, legal tussles and suspected spy games, the conversation may have just gotten a little more complicated. Here are the biggest questions looming about the world’s most important economic relationship.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-603.title: Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-603.author: Ashley Lopez
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-603.text:
A voter walks into a booth at the Valley Bible Chalet to cast his ballot on Election Day, Nov. 3, in Indian, Alaska.

A ballot measure that would have repealed Alaska's nonpartisan primary system and ranked choice voting has failed, according to an overnight race call by the Associated Press.

This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly.

This year, though, Alaska's system was under intense nationwide scrutiny, due to the inclusion of two candidates with the same name on the four-person U.S. Senate general election ballot. That race appears likely to move on to a ranked-choice tabulation.

"Alaskans of all political stripes have spoken: They want the freedom to vote for any candidate, regardless of party, in every taxpayer-funded election," Nick Troiano — the executive director of Unite America, a philanthropic venture fund that invests in nonpartisan electoral reform — said in a statement before the AP call. "At a time when most general elections across the country are essentially coronations, the Last Frontier is showing that a better way is possible. It is time to honor the voters' decision and move forward."

Just a few states have nonpartisan primary systems that allow voters of all political affiliations to vote on the same primary ballot. While California and Washington's systems allow the top two vote getters to advance to the general election, Alaska's system allows the top four candidates to move on. Then, if no candidate gets a majority of the general election vote, ranked choice voting is used to determine the winner.

Opponents of Alaska's elections say the current system is confusing and can be manipulated.

Those opponents seized on this year's closely watched Senate race, in which an independent candidate named Dan Sullivan was alleged to be a Democratic-backed spoiler recruited to siphon votes that were meant for the Republican incumbent, also named Dan Sullivan.

Democrats denied recruiting the independent Sullivan, who made the top-four general election ballot and has defended his candidacy.

However, proponents of Alaska's system have said that the state's ranked choice voting system could blunt the effects of any confusion. Voters had the ability to rank both Dan Sullivans and not rank Democrat Mary Peltola, for example.

Massachusetts voters this year decided not to switch to a top-two nonpartisan primary system. And during the last election cycle, in 2024, several states considered measures that would create a nonpartisan system similar to Alaska's. Voters rejected all of those ballot measures.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-602.title: Perspective: A new kind of White House press secretary
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-602.author: Scott Simon
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-602.text:
Dana White, UFC president and CEO, speaks in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington.

There has been no White House press secretary for almost a month. But have you really noticed?

Katie Zacharia held the position for 5 days in the middle of October, but her lone briefing was … brief and not well-reviewed.

After several secretary-less weeks, President Trump declared in an online post that he would ask Dana White, the head of the UFC, to take the job, calling him "a violent Fighter and Warrior." Reporters imagined how the CEO of a martial arts league might answer a sharp question with a swift kick to their journalistic chops. "What's the President's plan to bring down inflation?" Then, Bang! Thwap! Ooof!

The president later clarified that he, "was only kidding," about Dana White. He added wistfully, "You wouldn't mess around with him so much."

Even as the number of White House press briefings has declined during the second Trump administration, the president himself has had almost 500 "interactions" with the press: in interviews and press conferences, or impromptu Q&As at a ceremony, aboard Air Force One or while walking to the new White House helipad.

And, really, what is the need for a press secretary when a chief executive can announce whatever they want directly to millions of people on social media at any hour? President Trump posts dozens of times a day on his Truth Social platform, without those pesky reporters around to interrupt his message with fact-checking, contrary opinions or context.

I'd like to float another idea. Why not make the next White Press secretary an AI chat bot? That's how so many corporations now respond to customer complaints and inquiries.

They could call the new White House spokesperson Ben. As in Ben Franklin. Who doesn't like Ben Franklin?

When reporters call or log in to Robo-Ben and ask, "What is the president's response to President Putin's latest statement?" Ben might mellifluously reply, "I'm glad you asked that. I understand your interest." And nothing else. If White House reporters snap back, "But Ben, you're not answering the question!" Robo-Ben might respond, soothingly, "I understand your frustration. Thank you for your patience. Please stay on the line for our Media Satisfaction Survey."
