https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Choking fires, deadly heat and devastating floods: 2026 in extreme weather
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Jonathan Watts; graphics by Sara Fiorillo
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
People around the world have contended with unprecedented weather events and their fatal effects caused by the climate catastrophe

A
fter the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.

As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.

Extreme heat fuels wildfires in Australia
As temperatures jump nearly 20C (68F) above average, Victoria and other southern states register new heat records, including 50C in Port Augusta and the tiny opal mining town of Andamooka. Melbourne hospitals report a 25% increase in heat-related illnesses, while authorities in many areas struggle with wildfires. Scientists say the supercharged climate has made the heatwave five times more likely. Heatwaves already cause more deaths in Australia than all other natural hazards combined.

Mudslides kill 72 in Brazil after record rain
The city of Juiz de Fora in Minas Gerais records its wettest ever month, triggering landslides that sweep away hundreds of homes in poor communities on unstable hillsides. Floods also disrupt Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. More than 10,000 people are displaced.

Devastating floods across much of the world
In Ethiopia, at least 131 people are killed in floods and mudslides that bury entire villages. Eighty die in Kenya and 18 in Tanzania. The Arabian peninsula is battered by fierce winds and heavy downpours that flood the streets of the desert kingdom. Hailstones the size of tennis balls fall in Oman and lightning storms leave cities in the UAE inundated with water. Many areas report record rainfall. At least 30 die in Afghanistan as heavy rains trigger landslides. Hong Kong is soaked in twice the usual monthly precipitation. Flood waters in southern Russia submerge homes and leave more than 300,000 without electricity. Huge tracts of farmland are left underwater in Argentina and Chile.

World’s energy imbalance accelerates rapidly
The World Meteorological Organization reveals an alarming buildup of energy in Earth’s system. More than 90% is stored in the oceans, where warming has more than doubled over the past two decades compared with the average over the previous 45 years. This makes weather more extreme and threatens health and food supplies. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, says: “The global climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red.” Guterres urges the world to cut fossil fuel emissions as rapidly as possible to minimise future risks. However, CO2 in the atmosphere continues to rise.

Super typhoon tears through Micronesia, Guam and Saipan
At peak intensity on 12 April, Sinlaku registers a wind speed of 295km/h (183mph) – roughly the same as a Shinkansen bullet train and the joint highest recorded by a storm in the western Pacific basin so early in the year. It is also the deadliest in decades, killing 12, leaving 43,000 without power, forcing mass evacuation and causing $1.5bn (£1.1bn) in damages. This will remain one of the most powerful storms of 2026, superseded only by Super Typhoon Champi that will strike Taiwan and Japan in October.

Hundreds of millions endure deadly heat in south Asia
At least 47 heat-related deaths are reported in southern Asia as temperatures soar above 45C in several Indian and Bangladeshi cities, and hit a peak of 52C in Pakistan’s southern province of Sindh. Scientists warn that the climate crisis is exposing hundreds of millions of people in south Asia to longer, deadlier pre-monsoon heat.

Ocean heat enters uncharted territory
Sea surface temperature graphs begin to jag upwards and away from all previous highs on 21 June, starting a trend that will worsen over the rest of the year. This alarms scientists because oceans absorb more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system. If the seas start to release that heat then the land and air will get warmer more quickly. This coincides with the emergence of the latest El Niño, which is confirmed on 2 June.

Arctic and Antarctic swelter in unprecedented warmth
Instead of the usual winter snow and ice, scientists at the Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula of Antarctica are astonished to see rain and dirt outside their windows after an eight-day heatwave that peaked with a record temperature of 15C on 6 June. At the other end of the planet, the Arctic experiences its warmest ever June. Beliy Island, Siberia, registers 28.3C on 25 June, the highest temperature ever recorded that far north in the Eurasian Arctic.

West African deluge takes heavy toll
Relentless rains claim almost 100 lives in west Africa from May to June. Record downpours of up to 140mm (5.5in) in a single day are made five times more likely and 23% more intense by the human-caused climate crisis. Floods and mudslides kill 59 in Côte d’Ivoire, 35 in Ghana and five in Togo.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

Fires choke Canada and Europe
Almost 1,000 wildfires sweep across Canada, charring 3m hectares (7.4m acres) and sending a haze of smoke as far as New York. On 15 July Toronto registers the world’s worst air quality as a result of the haze. Smoke kills 4,000 people in Canada each year, almost four times as many as at the start of the century. Meanwhile, in Europe, prolonged droughts create tinderbox conditions for wildfires in Greece, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain and France. They burn 686,000 hectares in Europe, twice the average of the past 20 years.

Extreme weather disrupts US 250th birthday festivities and the World Cup
Half of the US population is under a heat alert before 4 July independence celebrations, disrupting Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington and other events. Dozens of heat-related deaths are reported and thousands experience power cuts.

At least nine World Cup games are played in potentially dangerous heat and humidity, while fierce storms delay three matches by more than an hour, including Mexico v England.

Nepal glacier collapse kills at least 1,300
Lhende Khola river valley communities are swept away after a 2 sq km (0.8 sq miles) slab of rock and glacier ice falls 1,400 metres (4,600ft) in the Himalayas, triggering a flood of water and debris. More than 5,000 people are missing and 8,600 need medical attention. Scientists say unusually warm temperatures and long-term permafrost degradation owing to the climate crisis were among the likely causes of the catastrophe.

Europe’s murderous heat forces reactor shutdown
The UK and France are among a host of nations that swelter through the warmest summer (June to August) in European history. The heat kills an estimated 50,000 people in cities across the continent. Two-thirds of those excess deaths are attributable to the climate crisis. Many more are likely to have died in rural areas. As droughts spread, Romania is forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because the cooling system could not be replenished by low water levels in the Danube River.

Record heat and deadly storms lash Asia
Hundreds are killed and millions evacuated as the world’s most populous continent experiences its hottest September and severe storms. Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 10 people in Japan, with violent winds of 144km/h and 832mm of rain in only 48 hours on the island of Izu Oshima. Three die in a mudslide in eastern China during Typhoon Saudel. At least 102 are killed in India and Nepal amid rain that is nine times the norm in some places. Eight die and half a million are affected by flooding in Bangkok, Thailand.

Governments warned to brace for peak El Niño
The UN disaster relief agency urges countries to prepare for an unprecedented “wrecking ball” El Niño that is forecast to peak around the end of the year. UK authorities advise households to stockpile a few days of basic supplies. Climate scientists project more than 450,000 people globally will die by February as a result of the additional heat brought by the super El Niño.

Protests in Indonesia after deadly fires
Demonstrators in Jakarta protest against Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, which has scorched almost 2m hectares of forest – more than twice as big an area as last year. The choking haze is estimated to have killed 3,560 people in one month alone.

Roads turn to rivers in Chile
After the heaviest October rainfall in 76 years, the Chilean government declares the Santiago district of Las Condes a “disaster zone”, with more than 1,000 people evacuated from their homes, some by helicopter.

Drought and fire in the Amazon rainforest
Months of drought leave some of the world’s mightiest rivers, including the Rio Negro, Madeira and Tapajós, close to record low levels, curtailing the water transport of essential goods. This coincides with a sharp rise in fire activity in the central and eastern Amazon region, releasing so much smoke that the city of Manaus registers the second-worst air quality in the world on 12 October.

2026 is forecast to be one of the hottest years in history

Global temperatures tie an all-time record of 2.04C above preindustrial levels, which was set in 2023. This year is forecast to be one of the four warmest years in history, along with 2023, 2024 and 2025. Sea surface temperatures are so high that the climate scientist Eliot Jacobson calculates the odds of being this far above the norm at 33tn to one. Meanwhile, the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere reaches a peak not seen in 2m years. On the plus side, global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Milder weekend forecast in UK as autumn freeze eases off
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Daniel Lavelle
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Met Office says overnight frost to give way on Saturday to ‘fine day with some sunshine’ in most regions

The UK should have a milder weekend as the unusual autumn freeze eases off, after cold health alerts were issued and temperatures plummeted overnight, forecasters have said.

After frost on Saturday morning, most of the UK should enjoy a “fine day with some sunshine”, the Met Office said. However, it will not be blue skies for everyone, as torrential rain and showers are predicted to move in from the west, bringing patchy rain and strong winds across the north and far west of the UK.

Snow is also on the cards for north-west Scotland, the Met Office said. Temperatures on Saturday morning were expected to vary between 5C (41F) in Norwich and Manchester and 11C in Plymouth.

The mild reprieve will be welcome to many Britons after temperatures on Friday night fell as low as -6.6C in Sennybridge, near Bannau Brycheiniog in south Wales, and -6.5C in Shap, a village near Penrith in Cumbria.

The first yellow cold health alerts of the season were issued this week by the UK Health Security Agency for the West Midlands and the north-west, and remained in place until midday on Saturday.

These alerts indicated the weather was “likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services”, including an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life to vulnerable people, the agency said.

Eastern parts of England should have drier conditions on Saturday evening, with clear spells and some frost. But other parts of the UK would be cloudy, with passing showers, the forecaster said.

On Sunday, temperatures are expected to stay above freezing in the morning. Sunshine is expected to brighten things up in the east, and the UK’s far north and west will also be treated to a bit of sunshine later in the day.

However, people elsewhere should expect plenty of cloud and wind, as well as rain, some heavy, and potential hill snow in Scotland and the north of England.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Bomb found at Illinois ethanol plant, prompting evacuations
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Peoria officials said a bomb was found at BioUrja Renewables and later defused; FBI said it is investigating

Residents were ordered to evacuate parts of an Illinois community on Friday after the mayor there said authorities found a bomb at a local ethanol- and alcohol-production plant.

The discovery reported at BioUrja Renewables in Peoria triggered a mandatory evacuation over a one-mile evacuation zone encompassing sections of that city as well as the adjacent municipality of East Peoria.

“It is real – this is a real thing,” Peoria’s mayor, Rita Ali, said, according to local news outlet WMBD. “We know that is a real threat. We know it is a bomb.”

Peoria’s police chief, Brad Dixon, said at a news conference early on Saturday that bomb technicians had rendered the object in question safe.

But Dixon asked for the public’s patience as investigators searched BioUrja Renewals’ expansive facility for other explosive devices, as the Peoria news outlet WEEK reported.

“We don’t know if there are other devices,” Ali remarked.

Meanwhile, Ryan Presley of the FBI, who is in charge of the bureau’s field office about an hour away in Springfield, Illinois, said agents would pursue whoever was responsible “tirelessly” and “bring them to justice”.

At about 7.05pm local time on Friday, the Peoria police department had announced that officers were “actively investigating a reported bomb threat at BioUrja Renewables”. The agency then urged “anyone who lives or works within a one-mile radius of the facility to immediately evacuate their homes and businesses until further notice”.

The police’s statement said the evacuation notice had been “issued out of an abundance of caution while officers and emergency personnel investigate the threat”, which officials initially referred to as a suspicious package. The city offered the Manual Academy school as a temporary shelter, and police said anyone who needed assistance evacuating their home or business could call for help.

In a separate statement, the municipal government of neighboring East Peoria acknowledged that the evacuation zone associated with the package at BioUrja Renewables extended into part of that city. The East Peoria government said it expected to provide an update at about 9am local time on Saturday, but in the meantime all evacuations would remain in place.

“This is not a hoax,” the Illinois state senator Dave Koehler said during the early Saturday news conference. “This has gone beyond that … This is serious. This is serious.”

Friday’s BioUrja Renewables case came amid a particularly chaotic day in the US marked by a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration-ordered nationwide ground stop at US airports that was in effect for about four hours, canceling or delaying more than 11,000 US flights.

The country’s nerves were also frayed by a tanker which struck a cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon. First responders had to rescue passengers from the river’s water after the cruise ship turned on its side, and there were more than 30 injuries reported. But none of those injuries were critical, and there were no fatalities reported in association with the crash.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Bomb was found at BioUrja Renewables in Peoria, Illinois, and defused. The discovery triggered a mandatory evacuation over a one-mile evacuation zone. The FBI said it is investigating the incident and will pursue whoever is responsible.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump ‘whiplash’ on deportations putting Afghans in turmoil: ‘People already survived a war’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sanya Mansoor in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Members of Congress and advocates warn that returning people to their home countries could be a death sentence

Dozens of Afghans who are currently in the US but fear being deported back to Afghanistan along with a larger group and possibly killed by the Taliban are experiencing “fragile relief” this weekend after it appeared that the Trump administration had put on hold plans to remove them within days.

Members of Congress and advocates have repeatedly warned that the deportations could effectively be a death sentence.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

A flight originally scheduled to transport the group out of the US on election day earlier this month had stayed grounded after a federal judge issued a court order temporarily blocking its departure to Afghanistan or neighboring Pakistan. The whole group numbers more than 150 Afghans, the New York Times reported. And the AP previously reported that the federal government intends to route these detainees to their home country via Pakistan.

Then, as the temporary court order expired last weekend, immigration advocates battling to prevent the deportations talked of dreading that the detainees could be forced to leave the US during the week of 16 November . This prospect was based on a rescheduled removal date given for at least one Afghan man currently in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention who was due to be on the flight.

As that date loomed, suddenly there was another development amid frantic advocacy efforts.

Late on Tuesday, it was learned that that detainee, along with a handful of other detained Afghans on the original flight manifest, now no longer had a specified departure date issued by the US government.

Some immigration lawyers also reported that their Afghan clients had been moved from staging facilities to long-term detention facilities, suggesting they would not be forced onto a deportation flight in the coming days after all.

Amid some confusion and often few details from the administration, Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the US non-profit coalition #AfghanEvac, said that a sensation of “fragile relief” had descended on the people involved.

Some of the Afghans in the targeted group have relatives who assisted the US war on Afghanistan after the terrorist attacks on the US on 11 September 2001 that drove out the Taliban, VanDiver said. He had already called Donald Trump’s efforts to remove Afghans from the US cruel and being done in “a heinous matter” as a scare tactic against others.

“In a matter of days, these allies were told they were being sent through Pakistan into the hands of the Taliban, then told they were safe, then told that nobody knows. That isn’t immigration policy. It’s whiplash inflicted on people who already survived a war,” he said. “These men and women kept their promise to America, and it’s time we kept ours by ending these removals for good.”

VanDiver has slammed any option to use Pakistan as a conduit for “forced rendition”.

Immigration advocates are hoping continued pressure will result in further delays and the ultimate cancellation of that flight and any others planned for the coming weeks. In the meantime, #AfghanEvac is pushing what will become the newly Democratic-controlled Congress in January to pass a bipartisan bill that has been drafted and would give Afghans who are already in the US temporary protected status (TPS) through July 2029, with a vetting process. The US supreme court in June allowed the Trump administration to strip such protections, including from Afghans.

Such legislation would “keep people we already vetted and brought here from being sent back to the Taliban while their cases are decided”, VanDiver said.

Among the passengers reported to be on the blocked flight were Afghans whose relatives helped American troops, women, at least one gay man and members of the minority ethnic Hazara group – some who have said they were previously beaten by the Taliban.

Human Rights First, the US-based human rights group, has warned about “grave, systematic dangers” for Afghans returned to Afghanistan. That includes “arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging, and retaliatory violence”, as well as restrictions on basic freedoms for women and girls.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in response to questions and a request for comment that the agency complies with all lawful court orders and that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) does not comment on or confirm prospective removal operations, for operational security reasons, and the safety of its officers.

Sari Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said that the Trump administration’s targeting of Afghans reflects a broader trend of creating arrangements with other governments to send people back to war zones, security crises and countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with the US.

The US suspended relations with Afghanistan after the Taliban government took over in 2021, forcing a scrambled US evacuation.

The Trump administration has held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians via a third country, and last Sunday an attorney reported that the US deportation flight of Iranian nationals headed to Iran via Pakistan was abruptly canceled, according to the AP.

The Trump administration also is increasingly deporting immigrants to such “third countries”. The supreme court is still litigating in what circumstances the federal government can deport people to regions they have no connection to, though in late September, the court ruled on an emergency basis, allowing Trump to continue this practice.

Federal law is designed to prevent the US government from forcing someone to return to a country where they are likely to face torture.

The DHS said in a statement that immigrants sent to a third country “receive notice and an opportunity to challenge their removal unless the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries” that they would be safe upon return.

More than 60 concerned lawmakers in Congress signed a letter to the DHS and the state department, citing relevant law and also calling for the cancellation of any deportation flights of Afghans or Iranians to their home countries, either directly or through any other country. “The United States is also bound not to return anyone to a country where they would face torture, and that obligation does not disappear because a flight makes a stop along the way,” the letter stated.

In another letter, New York congressman Gregory Meeks and US senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, both Democrats, wrote to Pakistan’s ambassador to the US, urging the Pakistani government not to collaborate in any operation to fly Afghans to Pakistan and then expel them over the border to Afghanistan. The Pakistani embassy did not respond to a request for comment.

The Afghans targeted are believed to have final removal orders, which means the US can legally deport them. But the fact that an immigrant failed to get asylum or prove to the Trump administration that they have a credible fear about returning to their home country does not mean they don’t face serious risks in their native country, critics argue.

The US state department advises Americans: “Do not travel to Afghanistan for any reason,” warning of “civil unrest, crime, terrorism, risk of wrongful detention, kidnapping, natural disasters, and limited health facilities”. The risks for returning Afghans are seen as much greater.

“We are talking about people who’ve already been tortured, people who came with evidence – some of the most compelling claims – and the idea that they could find themselves on this flight is pretty horrifying,” said Sarah Mehta, deputy director of immigration policy at the ACLU. “Why would we send Iranians to a war zone or Afghans to one of the most repressive regimes in the world knowing, indeed, that they are going to be targeted because of the very vulnerabilities that led them to flee in the first place?”

One Afghan national expected to be on any deportation flight, who has been detained in ICE custody since late 2024, fears returning because his wife is a former member of Afghanistan’s military before the Taliban took over, according to court documents. He is also part of the Hazara Shia group and said he has previously been severely beaten by the Taliban while they searched for his wife.

Shaw Drake, assistant professor of law at the University of New Mexico School of Law and co-counsel for the man, said the immigration judge’s not being swayed by these risk factors was “absolutely absurd”. Drake argues that his client had no notice or opportunity to present a claim of fear of persecution or torture in Pakistan.

The man’s mental health deteriorated when he was transferred to detention in El Paso, Texas, so much so that a federal court in New Mexico issued a stay for 14 days to ensure the government had enacted safeguards to protect him from the risk of suicide.

Another Afghan who could be put on a flight is a Hazara man who testified to immigration officials that he worried about being killed by the Taliban because he reported them to the police when they killed his father, according to US government documents. He said that a few years ago, he was captured, detained, tortured and threatened with death by the Taliban, whose members electrocuted him and beat him with sticks. US federal asylum officers acknowledged the detainee’s testimony but concluded there was insufficient evidence to show the Taliban would inflict severe mental or physical harm towards him if he were sent back.

Madhavi Narayanan, a lawyer at Human Rights First, who represents him, said: “It’s another confirmation that our immigration system is not equipped to help those who are fleeing persecution and genuinely seeking safety.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The group was due to fly out of the US on election day earlier this month. The group numbers more than 150 Afghans. The federal government intends to route these detainees to their home country via Pakistan.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Underwater salt mine closure in Ohio raises safety and supply concerns for winter
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Stephen Starr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Questions remain about reason for leak, safety of drinking water and where salt can be sourced for roads during winter

When water last month began gushing through a crack in the ceiling of a Morton Salt mine in Ohio, the company had only one option: shut the mine down for good.

For locals in and around Fairport Harbor, it means the loss of 77 jobs; but for the wider region, which depends on its salt reserves to keep roads ice- and snow-free every winter, it could mean travel chaos.

On top of that, in the weeks since the mine’s closure what’s been concerning mining experts and residents alike across the Great Lakes region is the mine’s location – about 2,000ft (610 meters) underneath Lake Erie. And that is sending broader warning signals across the region among activists and environmentalists, as to whether the issue could eventually hit other mines underneath the Great Lakes.

At the Fairport Harbor facility, one of 12 rock salt mines that Morton Salt runs around the world, around 1.3 million tons of rock salt were mined from underneath the lake every year.

Last winter’s colder and snowier than average weather ate into road salt stockpiles at hundreds of municipalities across the region.

Situated 30 miles (48km) from the now-shuttered mine, Trumbull county’s 200,000 residents relied entirely on the Fairport Harbor mine for road salt.

Trumbull county’s location downwind of Lake Erie means its roads and highways are particularly affected by lake-effect snowstorms and the freeze-thaw process for up to five months a year.

“We get about 30,000 tons [of salt] a year from the mine. But we have a stockpile of around 14,000 tons,” says David DeChristofaro, the Trumbull county engineer.

“We are waiting for the Ohio department of transportation [to see about acquiring additional road salt supplies]. If necessary, we will mix salt with aggregate, one to one, as was typically done 15 years ago, to stretch our supply of salt. But that adds to cost because it needs to be swept up at the end of winter.” Trumbull county gets around 4.5ft (1.4 meters) of snowfall every winter.

Authorities in a township in a neighboring county have had to issue a warning to motorists about potentially hazardous driving conditions this winter because of the salt shortage.

While the mine closure could mean transportation problems for more than a million residents in a region of Ohio that experiences especially harsh winter conditions, the water intrusion has also raised safety questions.

With five salt mines situated partly or entirely underneath Great Lakes waterways – in Fairport Harbor, Detroit and Cleveland, and two over the Canadian border in Ontario – a growing concern is that weeks later, Morton Salt officials say they still can’t find the source of the water intrusion.

The salt is extracted by drilling and using explosives, and while the distance between the bed of Lake Erie and Morton’s Fairport Harbor mine is in excess of 1,000ft (305 meters), decades of blasting and the presence of underground aquifers could contribute to significant subterranean rock movement, say experts.

“Blasting can fracture rock near an excavation, and removing rock changes the stresses carried by the roof, pillars and surrounding layers. For water to enter, there must also be a connected pathway from a water source to the mine,” says Xiong “Bill” Yu, a professor of engineering at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland.

“A nearby aquifer could supply that water through a fault, connected fractures, or a compromised shaft or seal. More than 1,000ft of rock is meaningful separation, but the engineering question is whether the layers provide a continuous barrier and whether anything crosses it.”

While the likelihood that the lake is the source of the water entering the Morton salt mine appears to be remote, local voices have begun calling for an investigation into just how safe salt mines carved out from under large bodies of water are and whether drinking water resources may be affected.

“Could the rock roof be breached, creating saline water swamps in a Lake Erie that’s the source of drinking water for millions in both the US and Canada?” an editorial in the Cleveland Plain Dealer asked this month.

after newsletter promotion

In 2017, the much larger Cargill-run Whiskey Island salt mine 30 miles (48km) west of Fairport Harbor experienced a water intrusion event that also saw dangerous levels of hydrogen sulfide gas released. That facility, which is one of the largest of its kind in the world, producing up to 4m tons a year and supplying road salt for states across the Great Lakes and midwest, spreads out 16 sq miles (41 sq km) beneath Lake Erie. More than 200 employees work 12-hour shifts there every day.

In 1994, one of the largest salt mines in the world, located in western New York, was inundated with aquifer water and collapsed. And in 1980, Lake Peigneur in Louisiana was accidentally drained when an oil rig breached the roof of an underwater salt mine 1,300ft (396 moeters) under the surface of the lake. No salt miners were injured in either incident.

The Mine Safety and Health Administration, a federal agency, oversees health and safety operations in US mines. But under the Trump administration, a deregulation drive has been enacted that includes, among other measures, eliminating diesel particle matter exposure levels in mines.

In 2022, under the Biden administration, a Morton Salt mine in Louisiana was placed on the Department of Labor’s pattern-of-violations notice for “a high number of significant and substantial violations and other safety and health compliance problems”. That notice was lifted in April 2025.

Emails sent and calls made by the Guardian to Morton Salt asking how often the Fairport Harbor mine underwent a full perimeter inspection for water intrusion before its closure, whether the company knows the source of the water intrusion, and if it is scheduling any new or improved safety measures at other mines it operates were not responded to.

Emails sent to Cargill inquiring about any potential additional safety steps it may be taking at its Whiskey Island mine, in light of the Morton Salt mine closure, were also not responded to. In 2020, two miners at a Cargill salt mine in Louisiana died while trying to prevent water from flooding the mine, according to lawsuits filed by family members.

Miners employed at the Fairport Harbor mine contacted by the Guardian declined to be interviewed, citing restrictions in a non-disclosure agreement.

For industry observers, the almost immediate decision to close Morton’s Fairport Harbor mine means that it might be time for monitoring authorities to step in.

“I would support a targeted, regulator-led review of water-intrusion risks at operating salt mines beneath the Great Lakes,” says Yu.

“[The Morton mine] incident is reason to check how each mine detects and responds to unusual seepage, and to review the condition of shafts and seals, the stability of roofs and pillars, and any known pathways from water-bearing rock.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Indigenous students retrace Lewis and Clark’s historic journey: ‘We can’t protect what we cannot see’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ashley Stimpson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Two centuries after the expedition, Indigenous students are conducting a new wildlife survey along the route

I
n 1804, when Thomas Jefferson dispatched Meriwether Lewis and William Clark and their Corps of Discovery to explore the newly acquired land west of the Mississippi, the president’s primary aim was political: Americans needed to establish presence, power and trade routes in these territories before the Europeans beat them to it.

But Jefferson, an ardent naturalist, had a secondary agenda. He ordered that the expedition also survey the flora and fauna of these landscapes. On their two-year jaunt across the western half of the country, Lewis and Clark kept meticulous journals of the animals and plants they encountered: bison, horned lizards, sage grouse, prairie dogs, wild licorice and catfish, among them. These observations were pivotal in shaping an early understanding of North American biodiversity.

These “discoveries” were hardly new to the Indigenous tribes who had occupied the Great Plains and west for millennia, however. While European Americans tend to see the Lewis and Clark expedition as a triumphant achievement, many Native Americans remember it as an invasion, the bugle blast of forced removal and relocation.

“There are a lot of negative feelings about that history,” says Dan Buresh, a recently retired environmental science professor at Sitting Bull College on the Standing Rock Sioux reservation just outside Fort Yates, North Dakota. Nevertheless, when Buresh learned that ecologists with the Smithsonian National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute would be conducting another wildlife survey along Lewis and Clark’s historic route – this time using thousands of motion-triggered trail cameras installed by partner institutions across the country – he wanted his students to be a part of it.

Staff at the Smithsonian were on the same page. Unlike the first survey, when the many Native contributions to the Lewis and Clark expedition – which relied on tribal partners for navigation, diplomacy and protection – were downplayed or unacknowledged, the Smithsonian wanted to prioritize Native participation this time around. “Early on, we reached out to every tribal college along the trail,” says Brigit Rooney, the re-survey’s project coordinator. “Tribes were critical to the success of the Lewis and Clark expedition and we wanted to recognize those contributions by including current tribal members in the re-survey.” The Smithsonian’s Women’s Committee also raised money to enroll tribal students as paid interns, the only re-survey volunteers to receive a stipend.

In the end, seven tribal colleges signed up to run cameras, manage data and interpret the changes that have occurred over the last two centuries on their reservations, where this type of ecological knowledge is transmitted orally but rarely published.

“There are a lot of elders that are passing this information on from their childhood memories,” Buresh says. “This project allows us to ground-truth some of that, and to get the real-time data.”

At first, some residents of Standing Rock, which spans both Dakotas and is home to the Lakota and Dakota Nations, were hesitant about opening up their lands to outsiders. Buresh heard concerns from elders that the data would be used to, for instance, locate prime hunting spots. Others said they had felt burned in the past by scientists who had come to collect data and then not included tribal members on resulting studies.

“Sometimes, in the past, when we’ve shared this information, we didn’t really have full control over it afterwards,” says Tamiera Garter, a junior in environmental science and project intern who helped deploy the cameras. But Garter and fellow intern Precious Yellow Fat came to believe that gathering contemporary data was integral for their community, offering an opportunity to confirm or update the traditional ecological knowledge held by their elders. Some residents, for example, worry about the impact of climate change on the reservation’s wildlife, a concern that’s difficult to validate or address without data.

“We cannot protect what we cannot see or don’t understand,” says Yellow Fat, who recently graduated with a bachelor’s degree in environmental science. “Having those cameras out there will help us get insight on how we can manage the land and the species that live on it.”

“At the end of the day, it will protect our sovereignty,” Garter adds. “It will allow us to have more autonomy with decisions we make around management and conservation.”

The re-survey, which received funding from the Smithsonian’s Our Shared Future initiative, a commemoration of the country’s semiquincentennial, kicked off in early 2025 when Smithsonian staff digitized Lewis and Clark’s journals, geolocating hundreds of wildlife observations the survey party made along the way. In spring 2026, more than 50 research partners in 15 states activated camera arrays across the original route. Buresh, Yellow Fat, Garter and fellow students installed 16 across the 2.3m-acre (931,000-hectare) Standing Rock, which required several field days and a lot of hiking.

Before the photos even started rolling in, the experience was revelatory, say Yellow Fat and Garter, both members of the Lakota tribe.

“We saw a side of nature we don’t usually see,” says Garter. “I never saw the hills and grasses be so animated.” In addition to admiring chest-high grass and running from fearsome hailstorms, the students learned to identify birds and harvested quills from a dead porcupine to use in regalia and earrings. They got to spend time in sacred and historic sites they had learned about from their parents and teachers.

When the cameras began capturing images, Yellow Fat and Garter found stark ecological differences between the two watersheds – the Grand River in South Dakota and Cannonball River in North Dakota – on the reservation where they had spent much of their lives. They’ve seen close-up snaps of typically elusive bobcat and mule deer. They’ve puzzled over why certain animals show up at certain times, whether they’re looking for mates, food or cover. “We aren’t really just taking pictures,” Garter realized. “We’re trying to understand these animals.”

Bill McShea, the Smithsonian wildlife ecologist who conceived of the re-survey project, hopes the initiative will allow its tribal partners to get some overdue credit for taking good care of the wildlife in their charge. Indigenous tribes manage more land than the National Park Service, and previous studies have shown higher biodiversity on acres overseen by Indigenous stewards compared with other entities.

“If we look at where the bison are right now, where the good carnivore populations are right now, they’re on Indian reservations,” McShea says. “It’s because they have a better ethos toward wildlife than we do,” he adds, pointing to the spiritual role that animals play in many tribal cultures.

The re-survey is an extension of Snapshot USA, a nationwide wildlife-monitoring project McShea helped to launch in 2019 that partners with institutions around the country to track long-term trends in mammal population using camera traps. The ecologist modeled the program, in part, after the popular app eBird, which has gathered more than 200bn observations of birds since 2002 with the help of more than 100 million users.

“I was so jealous of the bird people. Bird people know everything about birds because they have 10,000 binoculars going out there every year and writing down what they see,” McShea says. “We had almost none of that information about mammals.”

To date, Snapshot USA has logged more than 1m records of mammals across all 50 states. These images are identified by AI and validated by volunteer scientists. The project has been largely successful in filling in gaps about mammal distribution, diversity and behavior, McShea says, except in sparsely populated parts of the country. “There just aren’t a lot of people in the Great Plains, so we have holes in our data there.”

When the semiquincentennial came along (as well as funding to celebrate the US’s natural history), McShea saw a poetic way to address those holes. The re-survey could commemorate Lewis and Clark’s original contribution to science, while also gathering data in parts of the country that Snapshot USA wasn’t capturing.

So far, re-survey partners have captured more than 5.5m images of a confirmed 67 species. There have even been some heartening findings among them, according to Rooney, the project coordinator: a slew of photos of American beavers, for example, a species that was being slaughtered for their fur by the millions in the early 19th century, resulting in their near extinction. Fishers – another small mammal in the weasel family – have shown up in Pennsylvania, where they were once completely wiped out by trappers. “The story we have in our heads about conservation is usually negative,” says Rooney, “but there are many positive stories to find.”

The trail cams took their last snaps at the end of October, and volunteers across the nation are now identifying the species that appear in each one uploaded to a dedicated project page. McShea says that once the project is complete, the data will be free and available to anyone who wants it, including land managers in charge of hunting regulations or scientists endeavoring to support endangered species.

Yellow Fat and Garter may be two of those scientists. Both are planning careers in natural resource management. Being part of this project, they say, has allowed them to hone their science chops while providing their tribes some of the recognition they deserve.

“I have no disdain for Lewis and Clark. I simply see them as researchers,” says Garter. “But we were some of the first stewards of the land, who understood how everything connected. So, for this opportunity to come back to us today, despite all we have been through as a people, it feels full-circle.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Smithsonian wants to use motion-triggered trail cameras to collect data from Native Americans. The project will help the Smithsonian understand the changes that have occurred on their reservations.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Corporate Democrats are weaponizing identity politics to smear progressives | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
House members have responded to legitimate criticism with cynicism. Let’s not have another ‘Bernie bros’ moment

B
efore we get started, some ground rules. You are, of course, completely free to disagree with everything I have to say here. However, doing so might mean that you’re racist, homophobic and/or sexist. (Not to boast, but I have a lot of oppression cards to play.) So, you might want to tread carefully, OK?

That might sound ridiculous, but I don’t make the rules: I’m just taking a page from the corporate Democrat playbook. From Haley Stevens to Hakeem Jeffries, cynically weaponizing identity politics to ward off reasonable criticism seems to be all the rage.

Let’s start with the soon-to-be-irrelevant Stevens who, as you may have noticed, is an adult human female. The Michigan representative is also a sore loser who attempted to torpedo Abdul El-Sayed’s senate campaign by endorsing his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, at the 11th hour.

But don’t you dare quibble with her about any of that or she’ll cry sexism. In a softball interview with conservative commentator Scott Jennings before the midterms, Stevens seemed to imply that sexism played a part in why she wasn’t invited to an El-Sayed campaign event.

“I gave [El-Sayed] an opportunity ... to unite around something that everyone could agree on, and then I got disinvited instead,” Stevens told Jennings. “This is what happens to women.”

Stevens must have been born with an inability to experience embarrassment because, after El-Sayed won, she doubled down on this cringe weaponization of feminism. “For me, living my beliefs was never measured by who would win at the ballot box,” she posted in a lengthy essay on Twitter/X. “As a woman, I have the right to make a decision and to change my mind.”

As a woman, I have the right to change the subject now and move on to Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next speaker of the House.

Not everyone is thrilled by this for a number of reasons. There is the fact that he is very chummy with Aipac (the American Israel Public Affairs Committee), for example. Not only has he received money from the group, but Aipac has publicly boasted about supporting him. And on Thursday, Jeffries refused to say whether he supported or opposed controversial efforts to integrate the US and Israeli militaries.

Jeffries also said this summer that he opposes Medicare for All, reversing his earlier position, and putting him at odds with a number of progressive Democrats who campaigned on the platform.

He’s been consistently hostile to the progressive faction of his party, refusing to endorse Mamdani for New York City mayor for months. And it was recently revealed that Jeffries met with Jared Kushner in private before the midterms, which did not go down very well.

“The American people demanded impeachment!” one protester yelled at Jeffries during an event on Friday. “Your version of accountability is shaking hands with the Trump family!”

Many progressives view Jeffries as an establishment figure who offers no hope for meaningful change and want someone less beholden to corporate interests to be speaker. Jeffries and some of his allies, meanwhile, have suggested that denying him the opportunity to become the first Black speaker in US history would be, to quote Bloomberg, “racially insensitive”.

During the June congressional primaries, when a picture of Jeffries came up on the screen at a victory party for Claire Valdez, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, the crowd yelled: “You’re next!”

“It was very interesting to me, as observed by others, that there was almost zero diversity in that crowd,” Jeffries said in a CNN interview this week.

I don’t know about that crowd, but there’s plenty of diversity amongst DSA-affiliated politicians. Zohran Mamdani, the first Muslim mayor of New York, is a DSA member. So are Nithya Raman and Janeese Lewis George, who just got elected as the respective mayors of Los Angeles and Washington DC. DSA members David Morales and Yousef Rabhi are going to be the next mayors of Providence, Rhode Island, and Ann Arbor, Michigan.

If we’re going to continue to play identity politics, I should note all six of the DSA candidates elected to the House were Black, brown, or from marginalized backgrounds. You can certainly argue that DSA supporters skew white, but painting it as some sort of racist organization, as Jeffries seems to be doing, is intellectually dishonest.

And we’ve seen this craven use of identity politics to smear progressive politics before, haven’t we? It’s the Bernie bros playbook all over again.

Despite the fact that some polls found that young women supported Bernie Sanders in greater numbers than young men in the 2016 primaries, Sanders’ supporters were portrayed as misogynistic bros. Hillary Clinton’s campaign may not have coined the term, but they leaned heavily into this bad-faith narrative.

Let’s not have a Bernie bros 2.0 moment, please. While a petition to make the progressive Massachusetts congresswoman Ayanna Pressley the speaker of the House reached around 100,000 signatures on Friday, Jeffries faces no real challengers. He is almost certainly going to be the next speaker.

Instead of responding to criticism with identity politics, Jeffries has an opportunity to listen to reasonable concerns about his leadership and build a broad coalition that includes progressives instead of sidelining them. And that’s my opinion as a woman.

“We are proposing a comprehensive package of measures to curb all forms of violence against women, for the safety ⁠and dignity of Hungarian women,” the prime minister Peter Magyar said on Thursday. Magyar put an end to 16 years of soft autocracy by the far-right Viktor Orbán when he won a resounding election victory in April.

Sign up to The Week in Patriarchy

Get Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equality

after newsletter promotion

“While there is no publicly announced restriction on male dentists treating women, a ban appears to have spread across the country,” the Guardian reports. “In most provinces, male doctors have also received orders and directives from the Taliban instructing them not to examine female patients.”

“It just shows the hypocrisy behind so-called Saudi reform,” the activist Maryam Aldossari told the Guardian. “We know MBS [Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince] has been trying to show the world that Saudi is becoming a modern country that empowers women, yet we see the court sentence a mother to 100 lashes.” Large swathes of the western press have been complicit in whitewashing Prince Mohammed (who has been described as a “psychopath” by an exiled intelligence officer), when it’s always been clear his “reforms” are a hollow PR exercise.

“People describe it as a sudden dysphoria … that follows nipple stimulation,” the Guardian writes. There’s not much scientific research into it, and it’s not an official medical diagnosis, but there are a lot of interesting theories.

“It is all too convenient to cast Netanyahu – wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity – as the bogeyman,” writes Owen Jones. “But the dehumanisation of Palestinians is so extreme that even their youngest, most defenceless members are regarded as legitimate targets by leading figures in both government and opposition.”

Following revelations of Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman thought to be a Chinese spy, that phrase is everywhere. “The story behind the phrase is that a good, hardworking man was minding his own business when a serpent of a woman lured him off the righteous path by dishonest means and propositions he, being a man, simply couldn’t refuse,” writes Laëtitia Vitaud for FastCompany. “Can a 63-year-old billionaire CEO really be supposed to have no say over his sex life? Like a bear wouldn’t be able to resist honey?”

While prenups may be all the rage right now, guess who doesn’t appear to have one? Jensen Huang’s wife.

Remember poor Peanut the squirrel? He was euthanized by New York authorities and turned into a parable about Democratic government overreach by JD Vance. Now the squirrel’s former owner has been detained by ICE and may be deported. Is Vance going to come to her rescue? Somehow I do nut think so.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Mauricio Pochettino asked the US to believe in his project. Did he believe in it himself?
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The coach’s tenure with the USMNT brought a whiplash of highs and lows. He met some goals but also left many with the impression he never truly bought in

It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing.

He’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“We need to believe that we can win,” Pochettino said that day in September 2024. “That we can win not only a game: We can win the World Cup.”

It is the type of belief that feels almost alien to observers of the US men, the type of statement that American fans yearn to hear so badly from a coach yet also roll their eyes at. For years, fans of men’s soccer in the US have been desperate to taste glory, and for years they have developed an inferiority complex spurred along not only by results but by international perception. Even in the present day, with American players playing in Europe at the very highest level, the idea that the US could win a men’s World Cup feels borderline preposterous.

That never stopped Pochettino from espousing his belief that the US should believe they could make a miraculous run in 2026 and win the whole thing. It was a mantra he returned to frequently during his time leading the team, publicly and privately, even in the weeks leading up to the tournament. Pochettino even told Donald Trump that the US could win it all, perhaps planting the seeds for an assist turned own-goal down the line.

Belief is something that could attract even the most casual US fans, the type of newcomers whose previous experience with an American soccer coach came from Apple TV. Unfortunately for US fans, Pochettino’s actions never quite lined up with the inspirational speech.

There was the near-constant stream of rumors attaching Pochettino to clubs in England, rumors he never really went out of his way to quash even before they tied him to the Manchester United job he has now accepted. In many ways this type of thing is unavoidable and understandable: bringing on a high-profile coach and expecting peace and quiet is the footballing equivalent of dating a supermodel and expecting no one else to make an advance. Yet too often it felt as if Pochettino was the one stoking the fire; it was not uncommon to wake up in the States and find social media feeds populated with clips of the Argentinian espousing the valor of the Premier League and even floating the idea of returning someday.

This was never really shocking or unexpected and was far from offensive. Professional sports are fickle and players, coaches and administrators alike are wise to keep their options open and their bridges intact. Yet it was a bit galling to hear from someone brought in to galvanize the US’s players and fans ahead of a generational event: a home World Cup.

Pochettino also seemed sometimes frustrated by the very thing he was in part brought in to help change: American soccer’s sometimes awkward place in America itself. After losing the 2025 Gold Cup final to Mexico in Houston, he went out of his way to criticize the idea that the US would play in front of a pro-Mexico crowd on home soil, an issue that predates Pochettino by decades and may well never be solved, one even the most cursory research would’ve revealed prior to arrival. He fairly criticized the lack of stakes in Major League Soccer and suggested that US players are coddled throughout their youth development while at the same time butting heads with media who dared question the effects of a group-stage loss to Turkey at this summer’s World Cup. In reality, he faced far less pressure as the head coach of the USMNT than he would have in most any other major footballing nation.

All of it too often gave observers the feeling that Pochettino was never truly bought in. But then, there was the whiplash, which was palpable. As soon as one began to feel that way, there’d be a fresh injection of dopamine – the US’s 4-1 demolishing of Paraguay, for example, far and away their best-ever performance at a World Cup. And there was Poch, nearly in tears and belting out Country Roads, then speaking glowingly about America, American football and everything else that comes along with it. A few weeks later, they’d suffer a 4-1 drubbing at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 that will go down as among the worst-ever performances by the US at a World Cup. Certainly the most traumatic.

Athletes and coaches hate being asked about their legacies, in general. The question in and of itself sounds moribund, as if the person asked is about to ascend into the ether. Legacies, too, are tricky things – they often take years to materialize, and they’re sometimes just as quickly erased by shifting perceptions or the accomplishments of successors.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

Pochettino does not seem to be the kind of person who would mind being asked about his legacy; he actually seems more like one who would already have one in mind before departure. Yet when asked by the Guardian on Friday to define his lasting impact, he struggled to do so at first. “I am not arrogant,” Pochettino replied with a smile and a laugh. “Well, not arrogant enough. I am a little bit arrogant.”

Eventually he relented. Pochettino’s lasting impact, the coach said, was largely down to relationships, to having done things the right way, in his mind.

“The most valuable feeling that we get isn’t one victory, or that we helped in the program,” he said. “It is that relationship in the program – even when you cross the sea, you look and smile because I think you share the values that are very important in life, more important than anything else. That is our principal that we respect always.”

Pochettino has always thought in big, broad, ambitious strokes and has executed those visions over the course of his career with varying degrees of success. In the United States, he arrived with varying goals: ensure a proper showing at a home World Cup, help change the perception of the game to the general public and lay down roots for long-term growth.

In some ways, Pochettino certainly succeeded. In others, he’s left the whole of American soccer wanting. It’s a fitting end for a coach who wanted so many people to believe – yet might never have felt that way himself.
