But critical federal support to keep the effort going for at least a decade was running out, and its renewal was uncertain — grant applications had been met with silence for months. And just two weeks before Juarez and Maunakea landed on Maui, state funding they were counting on fell through.

Now, here they were at what might be their last big event to understand how survivors were doing and what help they needed.

Juarez was distraught: It felt like the end. But Maunakea, usually the pessimist of the pair, refused to believe it. He felt the study had to continue. The need was too great. They would find a way.

At the health center that Saturday morning, Maunakea greeted Lisa and Nilsson Panis, a pair of siblings born and raised in Lahaina. As he checked them into the study, he explained what they’d do that day. Urine samples to track environmental exposures. Saliva collection for biomarkers of stress and aging. Blood tests for metabolic function. Two assessments of lung health. Recordings of blood pressure, height, and weight. A mental health screener.

At the end of it all, they’d meet with a volunteer physician who would help them understand their test results, and they’d each walk away with $100, compensation for their time.

“We’re trying to do this every year,” Maunakea told the Panises.

He was determined to make that happen.

The lobby of the health center had a dark stain on its ceiling where water had leaked in just a month before.

The building — run by the state’s Department of Health and loaned to MauiWES for the weekend — sits near the base of the sprawling West Maui mountains. That weekend, the foothills above the center were covered in dry, yellowing grass that was nonetheless much greener than usual, courtesy of recent Kona low storms.

The storms swept water damage into construction sites and homes that had just been rebuilt. They busted up highways and caused torrential flooding, triggering millions of dollars in damage across the county. They also kicked off an unusually verdant spring, with flowers blooming on the trees outside the center and along the highway below. Wetness that early can heighten the fire risk later in the year, fueling grass and brush growth that dries out and becomes plentiful tinder, susceptible to heat and strong winds.

Lisa Panis, a participant in the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, has struggled with her mental and physical health since the fires, and her family is still in temporary housing. Keerti Gopal​​

Lisa Panis had an appointment with MauiWES that day, but she was hoping they’d have room for her older brother, too. In a fluorescently lit room just beside the center’s main lobby, she introduced Nilsson to Maunakea and explained that he had been a first responder after the wildfires, cleaning up debris in the burn zone. Maunakea immediately instructed the Ph.D. students working the check-in desk to sign him up, along with Nilsson’s girlfriend, another survivor.

MauiWES had limited resources, especially with funding so up in the air. But on an island already suffering from a severe healthcare provider shortage, Maunakea and Juarez didn’t like turning anyone away.

Maunakea listened to Nilsson explain what his life looked like in the months after the fires:12-hour days, seven days a week, clearing the burn zone for a construction company. He wore full-body gear to keep as much of the dust out as possible, but he still ended each day coated in grime. Though he’d never been tested, Nilsson felt confident the constant inhalation of ash and the debris that covered his body as he worked had impacted his health.

“We tried to push all the dust down with water,” Nilsson said to Maunakea, describing the cleanup. “But you cannot get everything.”

“Are you still doing that, or pau?” Maunakea asked.

“Pau,” Nilsson replied. Finished. Now he was working as a mason, bringing his sister on whenever he could. It wasn’t steady. He hoped jobs would pick up in the summer.

The Panis siblings’ father is descended from Filipino immigrants who came to the island to work on the sugar plantations more than a century ago, during a period when American and European companies brought indentured laborers from the Philippines to work under brutal conditions for extremely low pay. The plantations, established before Hawaiʻi’s illegal annexation by the United States and continuing another century after, sucked water out of Lahaina’s once green and fertile hills.

That set the stage for modern-day wildfire risks, now worsened by climate change, and cemented a pattern of local disenfranchisement that continued as the tourism industry took hold.

For years, the Panises had experienced the harder realities of life in Lahaina, like gentrification and unstable housing and employment. On the day of the fires, Nilsson was meant to fly back from Las Vegas to spread the ashes of two siblings who had passed away just weeks apart that spring. Lisa was living with an aunt whose home would not survive. She remembers standing on the field next to the post office where she and her brothers played football as kids, watching as flames engulfed the town above and below her.

After they finished checking into the study, the Panis siblings moved through the stations, a sort of medical assembly line: urine samples, then blood tests, then blood pressure, then spitting into a tube. A few feet away, Juarez coached another participant on how to blow into a spirometer to test lung function.

“Sigue, sigue, sigue,” he said, reminding the man to keep breathing out. Throughout the day Juarez greeted Spanish-speaking participants, acting as one of a handful of interpreters who walked people through the study’s tests in English, Spanish, and Tagalog.

Juarez was pulled into Maui’s recovery because of his connections to Lahaina’s abundant immigrant community. One-third of Lahaina residents were born outside the U.S., many in Asia or Latin America. Juarez moved from Mexico to Houston for a doctorate at Rice University, then to Oʻahu for a job at the University of Hawaiʻi. There, he met Maunakea, and as neighbors in the university’s faculty housing, they fell in love.

When they met, Juarez’s research was focused on social networks and Maunakea’s on health disparities in disease. After the fires, Maunakea was drawn to Maui by his connections with people working to address the disproportionate public health burdens faced by Native Hawaiians across the islands. Although he lives on Oʻahu, his great-grandmother, a Native Hawaiian healer, was born in Kula, an upcountry Maui community that was also badly impacted by the 2023 fires.

He and Juarez met with community leaders and healthcare workers on Maui soon after the fires. They became part of the MauiWES advisory board, consulting on design and implementation. For many study participants, that grounding made a big difference.

Mikey Burke, a Native Hawaiian mother of four who grew up in West Maui, remembers an influx of mental health practitioners from the continent who swarmed to Maui after the fires. They roamed the lobbies of hotels where she and other displaced families were sheltered. But though they were well-intentioned, they felt largely unapproachable. She gravitated toward local organizations like Maui Medic Healers Hui, which was working with MauiWES. It was something in their mannerisms, the way they spoke to her, the normalcy and familiarity they offered.

In the months after they lost their home, Burke, her husband Rob, and their four young sons were shuttled between temporary shelters, family homes, and rental properties. She could see that her twin boys, just 8 years old when the fires hit, were struggling. But it wasn’t until they got screened by MauiWES that addressing their mental health shot to the top of her lengthy to-do list. The study team told her that both boys were showing serious signs of post-traumatic stress disorder, and got them connected with a free therapist right away.

The Burkes aren’t an anomaly. The study found widespread emotional distress and trauma in adults and children, and connected many with therapists.

During a weekend collection event in May, the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center was bustling with families, healthcare workers, and researchers. MauiWES has seen 2,500 participants in three years. Keerti Gopal​

On an island with a severe shortage of physicians, MauiWES was also most early participants’ first time seeing a doctor after the fires. Over the past three years, the team made some big saves.

In August 2024, one year after the fires, a former trauma nurse named Amy Jackson had such a low hemoglobin count that it wasn’t registering on MauiWES’ testing system. The team urged her to go to the emergency room immediately. Jackson had signed up for the study because the cash would be a good birthday present for her daughter. If it wasn’t for that, she wouldn’t have gotten checked out at all.

At the hospital, she remembers a doctor telling her he was amazed she was still alive. She was admitted and treated, and she credits MauiWES with saving her life.

In February 2024, another participant presented with symptoms suggesting a serious lung infection. Volunteer physicians were concerned and said she needed medical attention right away. But she was an undocumented immigrant and one of the 10 percent of study participants who had both lost their jobs in the fire and weren’t eligible for state insurance.

Juarez coordinated with Roots Reborn — a local organization supporting Maui’s immigrant community — and reached out the next day to ask an insurer with a charitable health coverage program to consider an emergency enrollment.

She got the insurance and then the treatment she needed. She’s one of more than 200 participants Juarez estimates have been connected with private insurance via Kaiser Permanente because of interventions from MauiWES and Roots Reborn. He was happy to see her now, in good spirits and good health, coming in for her follow-up at the May collection event. He thought the immigrant population had the most to lose from the study ending.

The team still had so much to do.

After her lung test, Lisa Panis stood underneath the stain on the lobby’s ceiling and waited for her brother. The Panis siblings stay strong for one another. But she’s experienced depression since the fires, like many other survivors, and her tests revealed elevated levels of several toxic metals in her body.

In their first, smallest cohort, about six months after the fires, Juarez, Maunakea, and their colleagues found that about half of study participants were experiencing breathing problems that suggested ongoing, residual impacts from wildfire smoke. They’ve also found that poor lung function was linked to elevated levels of heavy metals in participants’ urine, including some of the same metals the health department found in the burn zone.

After looking at so many test results, Maunakea can guess with considerable accuracy what neighborhood a participant lives in just by seeing the distribution of metals in their body. Some of that contamination may predate the fires. But the health implications are the same.

Before Nilsson Panis left for the day, Juarez gave him a T-shirt with the MauiWES logo — a sun rising behind the island — and a hundred-dollar bill. Then he ushered him over to the front desk, where a case manager who works for the Department of Health was waiting.

She asked Nilsson if there was anything he might need help with.

He paused for a moment before answering. Maybe some assistance with food, he said. He also asked about opportunities to volunteer and help other survivors.

The case manager took down his email.

The next day Maunakea supervised a group of staff and volunteers administering lung function tests. A participant wearing a neon-yellow baseball hat and flower-patterned shorts walked in and took a seat.

“It’s unfortunate that you guys didn’t get more additional funding from the legislative session this time,” Ekolu Lindsey said to Maunakea as he took a break from breathing hard into a plastic mouthpiece.

It had been MauiWES’ most recent funding attempt: A bill sponsored by the state senator for West Maui, Angus McKelvey, would have allotted $3 million to keep the study going and expand the number of children it could serve. But at the last minute, the bill failed to make it through.

“I get it, they went for the bigger-ticket items, but the health part is also a big-ticket item that didn’t take precedence,” continued Lindsey, who is the president of a grassroots land trust organization on Maui. “I don’t think they understood, because probably none of them went through it.”

Maunakea agreed. He had thought that public health would be more of a priority in the wildfire recovery, especially in a state with a doctor as a governor. But funding MauiWES has been an ongoing challenge.

The study’s first cohort, in early 2024, began with charitable funding from the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation and Kaiser Permanente, while the researchers pursued government support. That summer, they got $2.3 million from the state. And almost one year after the fires, they received a $1.4 million grant from the National Institutes of Health’s minority health disparities program.

That support quickly turned precarious after Donald Trump retook office and slashed funding for programs focused on diversity or health disparities, along with a wide swath of academic research.

The MauiWES researchers hoped to renew their federal funding and keep the study going for at least a decade. But heading into the May event, applications they submitted to the agency had been languishing without a decision for more than a year. By that time, the NIH had lost 23 percent of its staff under the Trump administration, almost double the reduction across the entire federal government, according to an analysis by Inside Climate News.

The MauiWES researchers started getting national recognition in the disaster recovery space, speaking on panels and presenting at conferences on the mainland, hoping that might drum up more cash. But private funding wasn’t enough to keep the study going, and the speaking engagements had yet to pay off. More state funding seemed like Juarez and Maunakea’s best hope.

Initially, the team had strong backing from the state’s Department of Health, which wrote enthusiastic letters of support for federal grants. But as the study progressed and the researchers began publicizing their results, the agency pushed back.

The Department of Health had earlier screened 557 West Maui residents for lead in their blood, saying in May 2024 that so few had elevated levels that it was not necessary to screen the general population for toxic substances identified in the burn zone.

“On the basis of these results with lead as an indicator of exposure, we do not expect to find health impacts caused by toxins in the wildfire ash,” agency director Kenneth Fink said in a statement at the time.

But lead is just one of the toxic substances the department found at elevated levels in burn zone ash, and it’s undetectable in people’s blood relatively quickly after exposure, unlike some other substances found in the burn zone. Environmental health experts questioned why the department used a limited sampling of lead to draw broad conclusions about the burn zone as a whole.

Then MauiWES found elevated levels of heavy metals associated with heart and lung issues and cancer risks in a cohort of more than 1,200 fire survivors.

The findings seemed to contradict the Department of Health’s assertion that the burn zone was safe. Emails and letters Inside Climate News obtained through public records requests suggest that agency staff quickly moved into damage-control mode.

The day after Honolulu Civil Beat published a story about the preliminary findings last year, a naturopathic doctor on Maui emailed state toxicologist John Jacob for information about the effects of heavy metals like arsenic, nickel, cadmium, mercury, and lead on psychological function. Her clients had been tested by MauiWES and registered high levels of those metals, she wrote.

Jacob forwarded the email to colleagues at the Department of Health.

“I don’t want to affirm what UH is stating,” he wrote, referring to the University of Hawaiʻi. “The panic has begun!”

A few days later, agency staff discussed whether to stop assisting MauiWES with data collection. Fink, the director, said staff could continue for now, but he felt the department’s recommendations on study design had been either inadequate or disregarded. “If the latter, I would need to reevaluate our involvement,” Fink wrote to colleagues.

In October, the Department of Health sent a letter to the University of Hawaiʻi, criticizing MauiWES’ reliance on sampling survivors who showed up — as opposed to a randomized cohort — and its findings of elevated heavy metals in their urine.

The university defended the research in its response and explained that MauiWES was not claiming a definitively causal relationship between the fires and the heavy metals.

Although the team remained committed to working with the state, Juarez said he saw the Department of Health’s letter as an attempt to censor their research. Academics not involved with MauiWES told Inside Climate News the exchange seemed unusual for a university and a state agency, and they did not think the health department’s dismissal of burn-zone dangers was warranted based on the limited information it had collected.

The agency’s director said in a statement to Inside Climate News that discussions about the best way to approach research “are a normal and healthy — and often essential — aspect of scientific collaboration.”

“While our perspectives may differ, both DOH and UH remain committed to respectful dialogue and evidence‑based inquiry,” Fink wrote in his statement. “Most importantly, the public needs clear, accurate, and consistent information about how the wildfires may have affected their health. Residents deserve timely communication they can trust — free of speculation and grounded in the best available data.”

In an emailed statement to Inside Climate News, Jacob acknowledged that the researchers’ approach was acceptable but said that not disclosing limitations could “result in confusion among the general public.”

In defense of the agency’s own approach to quantifying post-wildfire health risks, a department spokesperson said in an email that a structured soil sampling technique allowed staff to use the lead screening as a “reasonable indicator for population exposure.”

In internal emails in January, agency staff discussed a bill with funds earmarked to keep MauiWES alive. They agreed to keep a close watch on the effort. “Especially since we are not satisfied with their science,” wrote Jacob, the toxicologist.

In the end, a department subagency was among those submitting testimony in support of the funding. But that wasn’t enough to push it through. When the bill fell short with still no word on federal money, it looked like the end of MauiWES.

At nearly 5 p.m. on Sunday, the team packed up while finishing tests for the last few stragglers. Most of the staff and volunteers had to catch a flight back to Oʻahu in a couple of hours, but Christopher Knightsbridge, a therapist working on the study’s research team, would stay on Maui a few more days to see patients in person.

Knightsbridge was overcome with pure frustration. All weekend, he’d done mental health check-ins with participants still focused on getting by, day by day. He felt certain the study was having an impact. He saw it every week. And he was still concerned about what he’d been hearing in his sessions. He wanted his patients to wake up and feel like they were living, not simply fighting to survive. For that, they needed more support, not less.

Knightsbridge poured everything he had into supporting survivors’ mental health in recovery. He spent half of most weeks away from his wife and young children on Oʻahu to see patients still dealing with ongoing crises: survivors in temporary housing and unstable employment, people with cancer diagnoses, young children whose lives were turned upside down by the fires. He’s seen serious PTSD symptoms, depression, and even suicidal ideation from kids as young as 6.

That same week, he sat in his video gaming group for kids at the health center with two of Mikey and Rob Burke’s sons, the twins dealing with PTSD. Knightsbridge was seeing both boys for therapy and organized the gaming group as another form of support, a low-stakes place for kids to open up. But the federal emergency grant supporting his position — separate from MauiWES’s funding — was also about to run out.

On the other side of the lobby, Juarez stood in a doorway, gutted. The study had made painfully apparent the gaps in healthcare access on the island, and it felt like their work was just beginning. The thought brought him to the brink of tears. Throughout the weekend, he heard from worried participants who asked if the study was going away. He didn’t want to let them down.

Near the entrance to the courtyard, Maunakea carried a table from the hallway back into one of the offices, tired but heartened by how many people had come through. Sitting with returning participants, learning about their recovery journeys and watching how they were putting the pieces back together was energizing for him. Healing is a communal task in Lahaina. The study leaned into that.

Maunakea knew the next disaster was just around the corner. He believed Maui could adapt and offer a model to the rest of the world for building resilience to the steep challenges climate change brings.

Maybe, he thought, that would be the ultimate lesson from the study: that documenting and addressing health inequities in the wake of a disaster helps communities withstand what they cannot escape.

Toward the end of the day, more survivors arrived without appointments after hearing about the study from family and friends. By closing, he estimated the team had turned away more than a dozen new people, taking down their names in case funding came through. Maunakea met people that weekend who said they’d known about the study for several years but hadn’t felt ready to participate until now. It hammered home to him how crucial it was for their work to go on.

The team would find a way to continue the study, Maunakea felt certain. He didn’t know how, but he saw no other choice. If his great-grandmother was alive, she would have said: ‘O ka pono ke hana ‘ia a iho mai nā lani. Continue to do good until the heavens come down to you.

He believed that this study is pono, and that the community wanted and needed this service. So, somehow, iho mai nā lani. The heavens would come down.

Inside Climate News’ Peter Aldhous contributed to this story.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: 'I never imagined my father was a Nazi': Born in a German-run 'baby factory'
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: Stéphanie TROUILLARD
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Adopted as a child, Édith Pagot had no idea she had been born in a Nazi-run Lebensborn (“fount of life”) maternity home until earlier this year, when her daughter began looking into their past.

“This photo is of a baby about 18 months old. It has my first name and surname on it,” says Édith, holding a black-and-white photo in her fingertips.

Until a few months ago, Édith had never seen a picture of herself as a baby.

“I look nice. I look very well-behaved,” she says, a little wistfully.

However, behind the image of the chubby-cheeked infant lies a dark story.

“It was taken at the Indersdorf orphanage in Germany in 1945. They photographed us holding a sign with our first names and surnames on it, to try to find our families," Édith says. "It’s a bit difficult to see that sign,” she adds.

At the time, the baby girl in the picture was still called Édith de Vicar. It was the name under which she was born on April 11, 1944, in a Lebensborn home in France's Oise department, before a journey that would take her to Germany and then back to France.

The Lebensborn project was created in 1935 with the aim of producing “perfect Aryan children”, according to the criteria of Adolf Hitler’s regime.

“They were Nazi maternity facilities, and the man behind them was Heinrich Himmler. He wanted a ‘pure race’,” the 82-year-old explains. “There were French women who had affairs with Germans. That’s how these babies came to be born.”

All her life, Édith was unaware of this painful chapter of her past. Placed with a couple in France's northeastern Lorraine region in 1948, she knew nothing of her origins.

“My adoptive parents told me right away that I’d been adopted, but nothing more. I asked several times, but I was never told anything else.”

With no answers, she simply imagined “a mother who had abandoned her”, without necessarily thinking of any connection with the war. She built her life around what was left unsaid, becoming a healthcare manager and the mother of two children herself, a boy and a girl.

Years later, her daughter decided to investigate.

“Ever since I learned she’d been adopted, I always wondered where she came from. So I asked Mum for permission to do some research,” says Émilie Ruffra, Édith's daughter, who also works in healthcare.

The Lebensborn programme: When Nazi Germany sought to create an Aryan elite

One day, a friend told her about a book she had read. "Le Fardeau" (The Burden), by Matthieu Niango recounts his investigation into the past of his mother Gisèle, who was born in a Lebensborn home in Belgium. Émilie came across her own mother’s birth name – the only information she had up until then – several times in the book.

“Through Matthieu’s and his mother’s stories, I discovered there were similarities with my own mother’s story. So I contacted him in the spring of 2026, and he was the one who confirmed that Mum had also been born in a Lebensborn home.”

For Émilie, the discovery was a bombshell.

“It was difficult. It took me a little while to take it in, and certainly to accept it,” Émilie admits. “When I told Mum, I was afraid she’d hold it against me,” she adds.

For Édith, learning about the long-buried secret also came as a shock: “I’d never imagined my father was a Nazi.”

Despite the upheaval the discovery brought to the family, Émilie kept digging. She contacted the German archives and the local branch of the National Office for Veterans in the region where her mother had been placed with her adoptive parents. Little by little, piece by piece, she retraced her mother’s path.

Édith was born in a manor house in the Lamorlaye commune of France, near Chantilly. It was there that the Nazis opened Westwald in February 1944, the only Lebensborn home on French soil. Around 10 such homes were set up in Germany, as well as in Norway, Poland, Denmark, Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

The racial origins of mothers who had relationships with SS officers were subjected to close scrutiny at these facilities, including genealogy and physical appearance. According to a report from French services in Germany and cited by journalist Boris Thiolay in his book, "Lebensborn, la fabrique des enfants parfaits" (Lebensborn: The Making of Perfect Children), “young women were admitted, at the father’s request, six weeks before the due date and had to remain [at Lamorlaye] for six weeks after the birth to breastfeed their child. After that, they either had to sign a deed of abandonment in favour of the German authorities, or they agreed to leave for Germany.”

Twenty-three children were born at the facility in France. Nothing is known about Édith's mother, apart from the surname “de Vicar” and the fact that she was French. Her father’s identity is a mystery, as is whether her mother had a love affair with a German soldier.

“There are no documents. Everything was burned,” Émilie says.

As the Allies advanced and the Germans sensed the tide turning in the summer of 1944, the children at the Lamorlaye manor were taken to Germany. After a long journey, Édith arrived in April 1945 in Steinhöring, Bavaria, at the very first Lebensborn home the Nazis had created. After the war in Europe ended later that year, she was transferred in August to the refugee centre at Indersdorf, near Munich.

It was there that the photo of her was taken, along with footage shot by the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, which provided aid in Europe after the Liberation. The little French orphan appears to be mischievous among other children her age, squabbling over a cake or a cuddly toy.

But Édith's journey was not over. A year later, on August 5, 1946, she was finally repatriated to France, arriving in Commercy with about 10 other children. She has only a vague memory of that time: “I can see myself getting off a train, that’s all.”

She and the other children were in poor health and were hospitalised for several weeks. They were also given new first names to erase their origins. Édith was now to be called Georgette. The French state also decided to change their places of birth: all of them were now recorded as having been born in Bar-le-Duc.

Two years later, after a stay with a foster family “where she felt happy”, the little girl was suddenly handed over to a childless couple. “I saw them once, and a month later they came back. My suitcase was packed and I left with them. It was hard.”

They formally adopted her in 1951 and decided to keep her original first name, Édith – a decision, she says, that continues to cause issues with routine administrative appointments in France.

“When I went to renew my identity card not long ago, they asked me whether I was actually Georgette.”

By going through her mother’s adoption file at the departmental archives, Émilie has been able to uncover new details and flesh out her timeline, but she has learned nothing more about the identity of her biological grandparents. With no other options, she has turned to DNA testing through a genealogy website.

“They confirmed that we have German ancestry. There are also matches with potential cousins. Will this reveal our origins and connect us with family? I don’t know yet.”

Édith has let her daughter carry on the search. She understands her wish to know more but feels no “emotional need” to find her biological family. “What I mostly want is to understand what happened when my mother fled," she says. "Why was I abandoned?”

After months of intense investigation, Édith is shaken, but she also feels freed of a burden.

“It was hard to hear, but I’m not responsible for it, and I’d rather know where I come from,” she says.

Thanks to her daughter’s research, Édith was able to meet Gisèle Niango, who arrived in Commercy on the same convoy in 1946. In an unlikely coincidene, both women live in Nancy.

“She’s a year older than me. We’ve had the same life story. It’s extraordinary. She now thinks of me as her sister.”

The two women speak on the phone regularly. They took part in commemorations in Commercy last October to mark the 80th anniversary of their return to France.

The experience has also brought Édith and Émilie closer.

“Mum has always been a strong, determined and courageous person. She amazes me. I really admire what she is still overcoming to this day,” Émilie says proudly.

In the meantime, mother and daughter continue to face the past together.

“The story isn’t complete, because we’re still missing a lot of pieces. But telling her story is already helping her a great deal, to accept the past and move on with her life.”

https://www.france24.com/en/environment/.title: 'Climate action is alive': Triumphant Democrats attend COP31 summit shunned by Trump
https://www.france24.com/en/environment/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/environment/.text:
Fresh from their US midterm election triumph, an emboldened group of Democratic lawmakers descended on the COP31 climate talks shunned by President Donald Trump on Saturday to signal their commitment to tackling global warming.

The 18-strong delegation joined the annual UN conference in Turkey after their party regained control of both chambers of Congress in a landslide victory last week cheered by climate campaigners.

READ MORE
Why the Democrats routed the Republicans in the US midterm elections

"Many of our allies and partners across the world think the United States has not been predictable or dependable. So we have a lot of trust to earn back," Florida Representative Kathy Castor told AFP.

"We have so much work to do. And yes, I hope the United States gets back on track with urgent climate action," she said after the group took photos in front of a large COP31 sign in a sprawling expo centre.

The election has been a topic of discussion at COP31 in Antalya, with hopes that Democrats can restore some clean energy policies and that a pro-climate president can be elected in two years.

"What happened in the US is remarkable, and a much needed shift that we all needed, not only from a climate perspective, but overall," Harjeet Singh, strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told AFP.

Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has rolled back some of the clean energy policies of his predecessors, promoted oil drilling, pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement and kept his country out of the UN's climate negotiations.

"It is absolutely shameful that the Trump administration operates this way, that this is an administration that is filled with climate deniers, that is beholden to big oil in the United States," Yassamin Ansari, an Arizona lawmaker, told AFP.

Ansari and other members of the delegation spoke at a panel focused on the midterm elections, attracting a crowd that overflowed outside the "America Is All In" pavilion.

The group reminded COP31 delegates that, while Trump has rejected clean energy, US states and local governments have continued to promote renewables and other pro-climate policies.

A group of US mayors and governors visited COP31 earlier this week, along with former US vice president Al Gore and former US climate envoy and secretary of state John Kerry.

"Despite the setbacks that we're experiencing through this Trump administration, climate action is alive in America," California Congressman Raul Ruiz told the panel.

The president's Republican party was handed a resounding defeat last week in large part due to anger over soaring energy prices and Trump's costly war with Iran.

Democrats have vowed to use their majority in the House and the Senate to launch investigations into the administration's climate policies and propose clean energy legislation.

But Trump still has two years left in office and has vowed to wield his veto power.

"At a time where Americans from all political backgrounds want to see their energy bills reduced, this administration will be very hard pressed to veto legislation that will bring down costs for the American people," Ansari said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/u.title: US floated NATO membership for Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/u.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says NATO membership is back on agenda for Ukraine. (Reuters: Marko Djurica)

The US has raised the possibility of a security framework for Europe to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says.

It's the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised, the president said.

Mr Zelenskyy reiterated that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory.

US negotiators raised the idea of Ukraine's potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, the president said.

"That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

Mr Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia's full-blown invasion in 2022.

Mr Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory.

Mr Zelenskyy and Ireland leader Micheal Martin (right) attend the summit in Dublin. (Reuters: Cathal McNaughton)

But he also said that if it received a comprehensive package, including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum.

Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Mr Zelenskyy dismissed Russia's call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine.

"This war must be ended first."

Mr Zelenskyy also dismissed Mr Putin's suggestion for a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, saying it reflected Moscow's inability to take the city by force.

Mr Putin wants Uranians to leave Kostiantynivka, Mr Zelenskyy says. (Reuters)

Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added.

"Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way," he said.

Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other frontline settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Mr Zelenskyy said.

Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war.

The two days of US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough.

The sides agreed to a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Mr Zelenskyy said.

The final numbers for the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added.

US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with Mr Putin at a meeting in Moscow on Thursday, Zelenskyy said, but there was no news of any progress after their talks.

Mr Zelenskyy met Mr Witkoff and Mr Kushner on Thursday in Ireland after their talks in Moscow.

He said the US negotiators had told him that all sides had agreed for Europe to have a seat at the negotiating table in forthcoming peace talks.

In Abu Dhabi, delegates from Europe — which is now Ukraine's largest financial and military backer — had talks with US and Ukrainian officials but did not sit at the table with Russia.

At the summit in Ireland, EU leaders agreed that Europe's team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers — non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland — as well as EU officials.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw80.title: Noel Fielding 'appalled' by jokes he made with Russell Brand
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw80.text:
Noel Fielding has said he is "appalled" by jokes he made alongside Russell Brand when the pair appeared together on TV and at live shows.

The Great British Bake Off presenter said in a statement to the Sun he was "horrified and deeply disturbed" to learn of Brand's crimes, after the disgraced comedian was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Footage of Fielding and Brand joking about rape with TV presenter Jonathan Ross on an episode of Channel 4's Big Fat Quiz of the Year in 2007 has resurfaced in the aftermath of Brand's conviction.

Fielding described "some of the jokes" he made as "horrible and inappropriate", and said he had not been in contact with Brand "for many years".

"I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand's crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice," Fielding said.

"I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years," he added.

"Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them."

The BBC has contacted Fielding for comment.

Ross has also released a statement distancing himself from the remarks, saying that his "thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."

Among the resurfaced footage is a clip of Brand and Fielding laughing on an episode of The Russell Brand Show, which aired on BBC Radio 2 in 2007. In it, Brand joked about kissing and holding an underage grasshopper.

"How do you even know if it's a child or an adult? You don't even care, do you," Fielding responded.

Brand can be heard replying: "It's a mistake I've made. I've had a lot of problems in the past, because I thought a grasshopper was above age. Before I know it, I'm in it, right, I'm kissing it, I'm holding it. Then it turns around and looks at me with onyx eyes and says: 'I'm 12.'"

Brand and Fielding also performed charity gigs together as The Goth Detectives.

Brand was jailed for 10 and a half years for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others.

Further allegations against him have materialised in recent days. More women have made allegations about him in interviews with the Times and a Netflix documentary.

The Times said it could not publish the investigation until the criminal case ended. Brand has denied non-consensual sexual activity.

Police have said Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women.

The disgraced entertainer is being detained at HMP Wandsworth. BBC News has asked his legal representatives for a response to the latest allegations.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Napping Kansas driver whose truck sped on to soccer field and killed two won’t be charged
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Authorities declined to file charges against napping woman whose truck accelerated on to field during youth game

A soccer mom napping in her pickup truck when it suddenly accelerated on to the field at a Kansas youth tournament where her child was playing, killing two people, won’t face criminal charges, a prosecutor has said.

Investigators believe the 34-year-old woman had failed to put the Chevrolet 1500 in park and likely put her foot on the gas pedal while sleeping at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita on 17 October. They conducted multiple interviews and even ran a test in the same parking spot with a similar vehicle.

“I cannot prove she consciously disregarded a tremendous risk to people on that field,” the Sedgwick county district attorney, Marc Bennett, said on Thursday.

He acknowledged the public might find his decision strange. Bennett’s 28-page report listed possible crimes that might be triggered when a person causes the death of another person but said none fit the soccer field tragedy under Kansas law.

“If I could charge somebody, why wouldn’t I?” Bennett said at a news conference. “But I also have an obligation to stand up and say, ‘It’s not here.’”

The two people killed at the scene were Cole Adrian, six, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both from McPherson, Kansas, police said. Ten others ranging in age from five to 68 were reported injured and treated at area hospitals.

The Wichita police chief, Joe Sullivan, said his department spoke to victims and families before the report and other information were released publicly.

“Every lead was examined. Every piece of evidence was reviewed. Every reasonable avenue available to us was pursued … Our responsibility is not to fill gaps with assumptions or speculation,” Sullivan said.

The report said the day started with the woman driving to the soccer field with three children. After two games, they left the Stryker complex for a meal and returned by 2.30pm for another game.

While one child went to a field to play, the mom and her two other children remained in the pickup truck. She said she was going to take a nap, and a daughter covered the windshield with a two-panel sunscreen, the report said. Less than an hour later, the vehicle began to move.

“There is no evidence to support the conclusion that she knew the truck was still in drive, or evidence to explain what motive she would have had to do so,” the report said.

Wichita police detectives ran an identical test. They parked a Chevy 1500 in the same stall and also in drive mode – and “the truck stayed in place until the accelerator was pressed,” the report said.

“We sat there and waited and waited,” Bennett said at a news conference. “After about 15 minutes we went, ‘This truck isn’t moving.’ … Tires against a 7in curb and it did not move.”

Investigators said they interviewed more than 30 witnesses. Blood tests showed no evidence of drugs that would have impaired the driver’s judgment, the report said.

The report said the woman awoke to screams inside and outside the truck and the feeling of the vehicle moving.

Bennett said people who immediately pulled the driver from the truck found her sleepy, “sobbing, at turns described as frantic, hysterical, saying, ‘I’m sorry, I’m sorry. What have I done?’”

According to Bennett, the case could be tried in civil court.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.title: Why US Democrats are expected to keep Schumer and Jeffries in power
https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.author: Evan Semones
https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.text:
Over a week after Democrats rode a historic wave of support to retake the United States Congress, divisions within the party seem to be threatening to undermine its newfound political momentum.

Despite growing calls for a change in Congressional leadership, Democrats Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries appear likely to remain at the helm of their respective US Senate and House caucuses.

After amassing the most Democratic power in Washington since 2009, the two New Yorkers are seeking to retain their leadership positions as their party prepares to take control of both chambers in January.

Schumer, the US Senate’s 75-year-old minority leader, is vying to lead Democrats’ new majority in the chamber, a post he previously held during Joe Biden’s presidency. On the other side of the US Capitol, the 56-year-old Jeffries, as the current minority leader in the US House, is seeking the top role of speaker, placing him second in the line of succession for the US presidency.

But the prospect of keeping Schumer and Jeffries in charge has frustrated some Democrats, exposing long-running tensions between Democratic lawmakers who want to maintain continuity and those who believe their midterm victories offer an opportunity to fundamentally reshape the party’s priorities.

Here’s why Schumer and Jeffries could prevail:

Perhaps the biggest reason the top two Democrats in the US Congress will hold onto their posts: the party’s massive electoral gains.

Schumer’s supporters argue he helped Democrats secure at least eight Republican-held Senate seats, including victories in traditionally conservative states. The party is poised to hold as many as 56 seats in the next Congress, giving it a substantial majority not seen since former President Barack Obama’s first term in office.

“When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract”, Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego, with Schumer by his side, told reporters on Tuesday. “And this has been a really good election cycle for us”.

Schumer also played a central role in recruiting candidates who could compete in states where Democrats have struggled in recent elections, including former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown and former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper.

Adam Jentleson, a longtime US Senate aide and author of, Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power, argued Schumer’s electoral success makes it difficult for critics to mount a successful challenge.

“It’s hard to argue with somebody who just oversaw the biggest election the Democrats have had since Watergate,” Jentleson said during an interview with public radio station WBUR earlier this month.

“The only people who matter are the members of the Democratic caucus,” Jentleson said, explaining that lawmakers who had recently benefitted from the midterm results would have little incentive to remove the person who helped deliver those victories.

Schumer’s allies have made a similar argument. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who oversees the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, credited Schumer’s candidate recruitment and fundraising efforts for helping the party reclaim the US Senate.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership,” she said.

Schumer himself has expressed confidence that he has enough support to retain the position.

In an interview with The Washington Sun on Wednesday, he said he had secured more than enough backing from his colleagues.

“I am going to be elected leader, OK, and we’re united on the issues,” Schumer told the Sun. “We’re united.”

Not every Democrat believes last week’s victories are enough to anoint Schumer as the party’s leader in the Senate in the next Congress.

Senator Chris Van Hollen announced on Thursday he would mount a challenge for the role after factions of the Democratic base, particularly progressives, have called for new leadership.

The Maryland Democrat attracted attention at the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term after he travelled to El Salvador to meet with his constituent, Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who had been deported to the country despite a judge’s ruling barring his removal.

That, according to a senior Senate Democratic aide who spoke with Al Jazeera, exemplified “the fight Schumer just doesn’t have”.

“This is not about any one individual, but it is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen said during a Thursday appearance on MSNOW, adding that US voters sent a message to “reject the status quo and to reject business as usual”.

Another Senate aide, who would only speak on condition of anonymity to talk freely about an internal matter, suggested Van Hollen’s bid may be more about extracting concessions from Schumer, like a promise to serve as a short-term “bridge” to a new generation of Democratic leadership.

An analysis by Al Jazeera showed that 12 Democratic senators have publicly committed to backing Schumer in next month’s leadership election. At least 10 senators, including independent Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, have said they will not. However, only half of those opposed to Schumer’s leadership have backed Van Hollen’s challenge.

In an interview with The Nation published on Wednesday, the Vermont independent senator acknowledged knowing Schumer for decades and even liking him personally. But he argued that personal relationships should not determine who leads the party.

“In this moment in American history, Chuck’s views are way out of touch with where the American people are at — and especially with where [the base of] the Democratic Party is,” Sanders said.

He added that Schumer was not in tune with Democratic voters on the issues, arguing the party needed a new and more ambitious direction.

Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin has also questioned Schumer’s leadership, calling for a concrete plan outlining how Democrats intend to use their newly won congressional power.

Slotkin went further on Tuesday, suggesting to reporters at the US Capitol that senators withhold a quorum — the minimum number of lawmakers required to conduct official business — if Schumer runs unopposed, until he presents a plan that gives members a meaningful voice in setting the party’s priorities.

Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock has also declined to commit to supporting Schumer, telling CNN on Tuesday that Democrats are at an “inflection point” and any senator who believes they should lead deserves an opportunity to make their case.

Still, there is a difference between public dissatisfaction and the votes needed to remove a leader. Senate Democrats select their leader through a private ballot, requiring only a simple majority of the caucus.

Tre Easton, vice president for public policy at the Searchlight Institute and a former deputy chief of staff for Democratic Senator John Fetterman, has also questioned the timing of the push against Schumer, arguing calls for new leadership would have carried more weight following the Democrats’ losses in 2024 rather than immediately after their electoral successes in 2026.

“The job of the leader in each legislative chamber here in the U.S. isn’t to articulate a vision for the party”, Easton said in a social media post. “It’s to keep each respective caucus together and count votes. Dassit”.

The outlook is considerably clearer for Jeffries, who is seeking to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes on January 3.

Unlike Schumer, Jeffries does not face a prominent challenger for his leadership position, despite criticism from some progressives over his approach to Trump and his longstanding support for Israel.

His backing from moderate Democrats has been particularly visible.

The New Democrat Coalition, a group of Democratic centrists representing 142 current and newly elected lawmakers, issued a statement on Tuesday endorsing his bid for speaker.

“Hakeem Jeffries is the right person at the right time to lead our party”, the group said. “He’s smart, strategic, and action-oriented, with strong relationships across the Democratic caucus”.

The coalition added that it “can’t wait to vote for Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker of the House on January 3, 2027”.

But support from the party’s moderate wing has not eliminated dissatisfaction among progressives.

Representative Pramila Jayapal, a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said she is withholding her support for Jeffries unless he commits to advancing Medicare for All, a proposal to establish a government-funded universal healthcare system.

Jayapal has also acknowledged that the lack of an alternative candidate complicates the leadership debate.

“You can’t beat somebody with nobody,” the Washington state Democrat told Talking Points Memo, adding that the emergence of a challenger would change the calculations of lawmakers considering whether to support Jeffries.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, meanwhile, was asked by CNN whether she supported Jeffries.

“The race is unopposed. Yeah,” she responded, suggesting that the absence of a challenger was an important factor in the debate.

The tensions in the US House have also been illustrated by the case of Don Leonard, an incoming Democratic congressman from Ohio who said he will withhold his support for Jeffries unless the party commits to specific policy changes.

Leonard, who has called for an end to US support for Israel and the war in Iran, alleged in a video posted to social media that senior House Democrats threatened to make his life a “living hell” in Washington and undermine his chances of re-election in 2028 if he continued attaching conditions to his support for Jeffries.

He has not identified the lawmakers involved, and the allegations have not been independently verified. House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar told reporters on Tuesday he did not know which senior Democrats Leonard was referring to.

Jeffries, who has denied reports that US House Democrats have been receiving calls to oppose his bid for the speakership, spoke to reporters on Thursday about frustrations within the party over his leadership.

“We take nothing for granted, because all of us in the House of Representatives are on a two-year employment contract”, Jeffries said. “And we have to continue to make our case both with respect to our track record up until this point, as well as, perhaps even more importantly, our vision for the future”.

The leadership contests are scheduled for November 18 and 19 for House Democrats and at an unannounced date in December for Senate Democrats.

If elected, both Schumer and Jeffries will likely continue to face competing demands from progressives seeking more aggressive action against Trump and from moderates representing districts and states where a more centrist approach may be politically important.

They will also have to contend with the practical limitations of governing. Even with control of both chambers, Democrats will not have the 60 Senate votes generally required to overcome a filibuster, meaning they will need Republican support for much of their legislation.

For now, however, the party’s electoral gains have given Schumer and Jeffries an argument for continuity.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote in an X post on Thursday. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.”

Black Friday has become a shopping season of its own, with retailers once again offering discounts well ahead of the actual shopping holiday. We’ve already rounded up some of the best early Black Friday deals we’ve come across, but if you’re looking to save on outdoor gear or pick up something for an upcoming trip, REI’s annual Holiday Sale, which runs through November 23rd, is worth checking out.

The Kelty Low Loveseat is a sturdy, low-profile camp chair built for two. It features a steel frame, a padded seat, and extra-large cup holders for your drinks or gear. It also includes a padded roll-tote storage bag, making it easy to transport when it’s folded down.

The Siesta prioritizes comfort with a roomy rectangular shape that gives you space to stretch out. The synthetic sleeping bag features an insulated hood — one that’s spacious enough to accommodate a real pillow — along with multiple zipper configurations so you can vent your feet or fully unzip it into a quilt-like blanket.

Rumpl’s classic lightweight blanket features synthetic insulation for warmth, a weather-resistant outer shell, and a stuff sack. It also comes in an array of attractive designs and pairs with Rumpl’s Cape Clip, so you can wear it hands-free.

Sea to Summit’s small toiletry bag lets you keep all of your essentials close at hand for weekend getaways. It features a water–resistant fabric and a convenient hanging hook, along with internal mesh pockets so you can quickly find whatever it is you need.

Sea to Summit’s lightweight, inflatable camping pillow features a soft memory foam layer, adjustable firmness, and a curved design that cradles your head. It’s also quick to inflate and includes patches to keep it from sliding while you sleep.

Mpowerd’s solar-powered string lights are perfect for camping or a backyard shindig. The 18-foot string can display six colors and last up to 15 hours on a single charge; the case also doubles as a charger, allowing you to top off your phone in a pinch.
