https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: SpaceX says Starship Flight 15 booster aborted 'chopsticks' landing catch after launch due to guidance issue (video)
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Tariq Malik
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
SpaceX had hoped for a historic double-catch landing for the Starship Flight 15 booster and Ship. The booster didn't make it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX has an idea why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster.

The giant Starship rocket, a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight. The goal: To land both the Super Heavy first stage and the Ship upper stage, for the first full Starship recovery — and the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system in history.

The Super Heavy stage, called Booster 22, came back to Earth mere minutes after liftoff as planned. Instead of returning to its launch tower to be caught mid-air by the tower's metal "chopstick" arms, however, the rocket veered off shore and detonated its flight termination system. A guidance issue appears to be the reason, SpaceX now says. Follow our Starship Flight 15 live updates for the latest on the mission.

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

"We were initially 'go' for a catch," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during live commentary about seven hours into the mission. "But in the later stages of the coast, the booster aborted itself for a GNC issue that it detected, and that put it into its contingency landing offshore." Super Heavy exploded a few feet above the waves of the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

GNC is short for Guidance and Navigation Control, a criticial system used by rockets to control their flight and ensure they remain on their planned course. Such a system is vital for any landing attempt by a Starship Super Heavy or Ship upper stage to ensure the vehicle returns to its landing site safely and doesn't veer off course to damage SpaceX's Starbase or surrounding populated areas.

Super Heavy is powered by a cluster of 33 Raptor rocket engines that fire simultaneously during liftoff to send the 41-story Starship megarocket into orbit. During Friday's launch, all 33 engines fired as planned for the ascent, Huot said.

One engine did drop out after stage separation, when Super Heavy dropped away from Ship and flipped over for a "boostback" burn to begin its trip back to Earth, Huot said.

"We had 32 out of the 33 booster engines lit for boostback, which started sending it back here to the launch site," he added.

The guidance issue for Super Heavy appeared to occur during the booster's landing burn, when it fires 13 Raptor engines to slow itself for its tower approach before shifting to fewer and fewer engines. In SpaceX's launch video, the 13 engines can be seen activating, followed by the abort and the booster steering itself to a contingency landing zone in Gulf waters.

"It did that hover, cut the engines off, the FTS — the flight termination system — triggered, and it splashed down in the water," Huot said. (The FTS is designed to destroy a booster in the event of an emergency.)

As its name suggests, Starship Flight 15 is SpaceX's 15th test flight of the giant rocket, but it will be the first to attempt to catch a Ship upper stage with the chopsticks. SpaceX has successfully caught Super Heavy boosters on three test flights to date.

Flight 15's Ship vehicle is in good health and will orbit Earth a total of 14 times before landing back at its launch pad in Starbase at around 4:20 p.m. EST (1920 GMT) today, if all goes well.

"Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground-tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a reentry and return to the launch site," Huot said in the mission update. (Flight 15 hauled 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites to orbit, and a few of those spacecraft carried cameras for heat-shield inspection.)

SpaceX designed Starship to be fully reusable, with the company banking on that reusability to make it an affordable heavy-lift booster capable of a wide range of missions to low Earth orbit, the moon and eventually Mars.

NASA has picked Starship as one of two commercial landers to carry Artemis astronauts to the moon in 2028, and SpaceX sees the rocket as vital to building out a 100,000 constellation of Starlink V3 internet satellites, as well as a new AI data center network in orbit called Starmind.

But first, SpaceX has to successfully land a Starship upper stage from orbit. That's the next step for Flight 15.

Huot says flight controllers will make one last check at the 20-hour mark in the mission to decide whether to proceed with the landing at Starbase or make an "early return" splashdown off the coast of Hawaii.

That final check is expected by about 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT). Space.com's Starship Flight 15 landing livestream will begin at that time, and will be carried on our live updates page, Space.com homepage and our VideoFromSpace YouTube page.

He is an Eagle Scout and Space Camp alum with journalism degrees from the USC and NYU. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast on the TWiT network. https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Hanneke Weitering
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program.

The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad, commander, and Alan Bean, the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon, the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms.

The previous moon mission, Apollo 11, drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3. Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.

The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old.

Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions.

To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible.

The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13.

The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program.

After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

https://fortune.com/article/delta-ceo-ed.title: Delta CEO says air traffic control systems are so outdated that some commercial flight routes were faster in the 1950s than they are today
https://fortune.com/article/delta-ceo-ed.author: Sydney Lake
https://fortune.com/article/delta-ceo-ed.text:
Last year, chronic flight delays and cancellations at Newark Liberty International Airport revealed a litany of problems with antiquated air traffic control systems. Today, those problems persist and are even more illuminated thanks to the FAA’s nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Even Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy admitted last year that some of the decades-old computer equipment air traffic controllers use looks like it came off the set of Apollo 13, and compared it to a 1967 Volkswagen Beetle.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian also revealed last year that, due to aging air traffic control systems, it actually takes longer today to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when the airline opened that route.

“That’s the air traffic control system. It’s very slow. It’s congested,” he told TODAY in May 2025. “If you modernize the skies, you can kind of bring greater efficiency.”

By modernizing the skies, the airline chief means using satellite technology, the latest state-of-the-art equipment, and GPS. But currently, air traffic controllers have to use a radar point-and-shoot system from the 1960s.

“The screens look like something out of the 1960s and ‘70s,” Bastian said. “Our controllers and our operators need the best in order to keep us safe and make sure it maintains its safety record.”

Despite a barrage of emergency landings, machinery failure, a collision, and other air traffic control failures in the airline industry reported this year, he insists it’s still safe to fly.

“It is absolutely safe. It’s the safest form of transportation in the world,” Bastian said. “The most skilled aviation professionals in the world work and operate the U.S. airspace. So it is absolutely safe.”

But just because it’s safe doesn’t mean it’s acceptable for the U.S. to have such antiquated technology operating its airspace, Bastian said.

Although there is bipartisan support to modernize America’s air traffic control system, it’s a process that requires a lot of time and money. On May 8, 2025, Duffy and President Donald Trump announced a plan to build a brand-new air traffic control system “that will be the envy of the world.”

The plan includes replacing outdated infrastructure with wireless and satellite technologies at more than 4,600 air traffic control sites, building six new air traffic coordination centers, and replacing towers and terminal radar approach control (TRACONs).

“Our antiquated air traffic control system is affecting our workforce,” the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. “As Secretary Duffy has said, we must get the best safety technology in the hands of controllers as soon as possible.” Reuters reported in late March the FAA was short about 3,500 air traffic controllers.

On Friday, Duffy called on Congress to appropriate $50 billion for modernization. The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, though, estimates it could cost $12.5 billion. The Modern Skies Coalition, an umbrella group for aviation industry groups, estimated it would cost $31 billion or more.

But in the short term, the airline industry is making adjustments to improve flight delays and cancellations that result from air traffic control problems. Many airlines are pulling down their operations at Newark, Bastian said, which reduces some of the congestion at the airport.

“Now, that’s not good in the long run. It’s not good for consumers,” Bastian said. “It’s not good for the airport itself, but it’s the only thing that we have in the meantime.”

A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on May 16, 2025.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/faa-groun.title: Air traffic control, phone systems and emails are all down following China’s AI espionage scandal — is there a common answer?
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/faa-groun.author: Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, Cedric Leighton, Vito Errico, Steven Tian
https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/faa-groun.text:
An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random.

The United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days. The timing is almost too coincidental to be a coincidence – coming on the heels of the removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO amidst an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, widespread recriminations about chip exports to China, and demands for tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China.

Could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S. infrastructure? It’s too early to know for sure, but the country deserves far more transparent answers than we have received so far.

At 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday, November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every departing flight in America, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the third nationwide ground stop ever ordered. The first came on Sept. 11, 2001; the second more than 20 years later, on Jan. 11, 2023.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would say only that “a communication issue” had struck every one of the 22 centers that guide planes across the country, and that technicians were investigating. A subsequent press conference by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did little to reassure anyone, with no answers about what happened and little reassurance that it would be fixable anytime soon, with airports sending travelers home and communicating that flight cancellations would persist for many hours at a minimum, if not days.

It was the second time in two days that critical infrastructure the country cannot function without simply stopped, potentially for very nefarious reasons. The day before, Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot went dark in 74 countries and stayed down for hours. Both blackouts struck within a day-and-a-half of the most damaging China espionage story in years.

The last nationwide ground stop, in 2023, lasted about 90 minutes and still delayed more than 10,000 flights and canceled 1,300. Friday’s lasted hours with no resolution imminent on the horizon. At the four-hour point of this latest ground stop, 10,243 flights were already delayed and 3,234 cancelled, with flights grounded not only at single regional airports but across the entire nation, suggesting systemic breakdowns rather than localized issues.

Microsoft’s failure began at 11:17 a.m. ET on Thursday and spread across 19 Microsoft 365 services. Within an hour, complaints about Outlook were running at more than 2,000 times their normal level. Microsoft counts more than 450 million paid commercial seats, with many millions of those users locked out entirely from their inboxes and other critical services.

The casualty list reads like a roll call of essential services: the U.S. House of Representatives was substantively incapacitated; a federal appeals court that could not send or receive email; Britain’s Parliament and its National Health Service, where the failure threatened patients’ prescriptions; Australia’s spy agency and federal police were sent offline as well.

When a botched CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines in 2024, the Fortune 500 alone lost an estimated $5.4 billion. One risk adviser already puts Microsoft’s bill in the billions for Australia alone, not to mention the lost economic value in the U.S. or the rest of the world. This was the first time in history so many users were locked out for so long – with shifting and unsatisfactory explanations. Similarly, this is the first time in global aviation history where there has been a nationwide ground stop with no satisfactory, clear explanation and immediate fix.

Microsoft wrote the playbook for false comfort. For a full day it insisted there was “no indication” of malicious activity while its own bulletins showed it did not know what had broken. If it did not know for sure, then how could they know for sure there was no indication of anything malicious amidst shifting explanations?

First it blamed elevated load, then servers that had unexpectedly dropped out. It found no recent change that lined up with the failure. Hours later, it was rolling back a network change that did. Early Friday, engineers were still trying to “pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx.”

Only on Friday afternoon did Microsoft name a culprit: a flaw introduced during a network capacity upgrade, “not related to cyber.” That sequence is as nonsensical as it is falsely reassuring. No patient would trust a doctor who swears it is not an infection before he can diagnose the fever. You cannot rule out what you cannot yet explain, and nobody can feel particularly reassured from this disturbing sequence of events and shifting explanations.

On Thursday morning, Nvidia, whose board failures we dissected in Fortune this week, announced the resignation of Jensen Huang, the chip industry’s loudest advocate for selling to China, after he admitted an affair with a businesswoman U.S. officials suspect of spying for Beijing. Beijing has been vocal in calling it a smear amidst a rapid escalation of U.S.-China tensions. Lawmakers in both parties are demanding testimony and tighter export controls. Within three hours, inboxes went dark from Capitol Hill to Canberra. A day later, planes stopped and were grounded.

Could that really be a coincidence?

Perhaps we are being too conspiratorial, but there is a certain uncanny resemblance to Beijing’s favorite playbook, which is to divert from negative news stories by shutting down internet services and diverting public attention.

For example, in 2011, a petition to free Ai Weiwei got Change.org knocked offline. In 2012, exposés of the family fortunes of Xi Jinping and Wen Jiabao got Bloomberg and The New York Times blocked in China and targeted by hackers. In 2014, as Hong Kong marched for democracy, a newspaper and a voting site were buried under one of the largest attacks the internet had ever seen. In 2015, China’s “Great Cannon” hammered GitHub for days for hosting banned news. In 2019, Telegram and the LIHKG forum were swamped as Hong Kong marched again. In 2022, news of the zero-COVID protests on Twitter drowned in a deluge of spam. Maybe this pattern of untimely hacks was merely a coincidence – or could it have been more than coincidence?

Microsoft knows this adversary better than anyone. Hackers tied to Beijing tore through its customers’ Exchange servers in 2021 and stole some 60,000 State Department emails through its cloud in 2023, a breach a federal review board blamed on a “cascade of security failures” at Microsoft. Just three weeks ago, Microsoft itself said a China-aligned group had turned AI agents loose on more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 customers.

Whatever the cause, the lesson is identical. Some cyber experts are warning about potentially economically destabilizing cyberattacks, with researchers warning that AI-enabled hacking is spreading like a virus: attacks on previously unknown flaws have roughly doubled since capable open-source models arrived.

U.S. agencies say China’s Volt Typhoon hackers have already burrowed into American communications, transportation, energy and water networks, in some cases for five years, positioning themselves to disrupt them. They sat inside one small Massachusetts electric and water utility for more than 300 days. If the inbox and the skies can go dark on consecutive days, why not the grid, or the tap? Is it time for every business and household to buy storage batteries, water tanks, MREs and porta potties?

Of course, regardless of whether this was a Chinese or foreign malevolent actor attack, or whether it was merely the coincidental degradation of antiquated and outdated infrastructure systems, all of this takes place against the backdrop of the substantive hollowing out of U.S. government counterintelligence and cyber capabilities, with more than 1,500 special agents having departed the FBI and almost 1,000 staffers—about one-third of the workforce—have left the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) since Trump returned to office. Domestic commentators point out that this comes despite $1 trillion in Pentagon spending; and that the upgrades needed for aviation infrastructure would have cost $40 billion.

Legendary Intel CEO Andy Grove’s renowned book was titled, “Only the paranoid survive”, suggesting paranoia is not entirely unwarranted. The poet Delmore Schwartz said in 1966 that “even paranoids have enemies.” And everyone from Joseph Heller to Henry Kissinger to Kurt Cobain has repeated some variation of “just because you’re paranoid, doesn’t mean they’re not out to get you.”

Sometimes, superstition that seems delusional can connect authentic facts. And sometimes it behooves us to look at “worst case” scenarios in an effort to avoid them.

https://fortune.com/article/former-goldm.title: Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein says Peter Thiel is wrong: College is worth it because it makes you a ‘complete person’
https://fortune.com/article/former-goldm.author: Emma Burleigh
https://fortune.com/article/former-goldm.text:
Business leaders are butting heads over whether the college degree is dead, arguing over its usefulness and overall value. Palantir cofounder Peter Thiel is meanwhile luring young entrepreneurs with $200,000 grants to ditch the “corrupt institution” of higher education and “build new things.”

But Lloyd Blankfein, former CEO of Goldman Sachs, is hitting back with his own two cents for budding workers.

“I strongly disagree with the technology investor Peter Thiel,” Blankfein wrote in an excerpt from his memoir, Streetwise, shared with Vanity Fair earlier this year. “To succeed in a career, you have to know the technical minutiae of your field, of course. But you also need to be a complete person—the kind of person other people want to engage with.”

One of the best ways aspiring professionals can grow as individuals and set themselves up for career success is by going to college, Blankfein advised.

The longtime executive is an alum of both Harvard University and Harvard Law School, and in remembering his undergraduate years recalled he “survived” the experience more than he enjoyed it. Blankfein conceded the Ivy League school might not be a perfect fit for everyone, but it undeniably opened doors for his future career and was “the best place to have gone.”

The ex–Goldman Sachs leader says the school nurtured his confidence, writing skills, love of history, and engagement with current events. And he might have missed out on that growth if he’d skipped the experience altogether; Blankfein recognizes the value in a liberal arts education.

“Your undergraduate years are your best opportunity to make yourself uncomfortable in a way that can help make you more curious and interesting,” Blankfein added.

Blankfein’s vocal appreciation for the college experience comes at a time when some tech leaders are challenging the efficacy of higher ed.

Just last spring, Palantir launched its Meritocracy Fellowship: a four-month, paid internship for recent high school graduates not enrolled in college. During their stint at the company, Gen Zers learn about U.S. history and foundations of the West, and work alongside Palantir’s full-time employees in solving technical problems and improving products.

The gig was advertised as a way to “get the Palantir degree” and “skip the debt. Skip the indoctrination.” Cofounder and CEO Alex Karp added that the internship was created to combat the “shortcomings of university admissions.”

“Opaque admissions standards at many American universities have displaced meritocracy and excellence,” the Palantir job posting said. “As a result, qualified students are being denied an education based on subjective and shallow criteria. Absent meritocracy, campuses have become breeding grounds for extremism and chaos.”

Palantir cofounder Thiel has been disrupting the college-to-job pipeline for much longer. Since 2011, the Thiel Fellowship has been handing out sizable grants to young people who are willing to drop out of college and launch their businesses.

The program has minted around a dozen unicorns so far, with notable fellowship alumni including Figma cofounder Dylan Field and Scale AI creator Lucy Guo.

The former Goldman Sachs CEO isn’t the only business leader espousing the value of college degrees. Cofounder of AI giant Anthropic Daniela Amodei believes the liberal arts won’t fade into the background in an increasingly tech-driven world—they’ll actually be pushed to the forefront of innovation.

“I actually think studying the humanities is going to be more important than ever,” Amodei said in a 2026 interview with ABC News. “The ability to have critical thinking skills and learn how to interact with other people will be more important in the future, rather than less.”

Even leaders who achieved massive success outside of corporate life advise aspiring professionals to stay in school.

Multimillionaire music icon Usher did not attend college himself, but he still recognizes the value of attending university. However, he cautions that one slip of paper won’t carry them far—budding workers need to work hard and put their skills to good use once they set foot off campus.

“A diploma still matters, yes of course it matters, but it’s not the paper that gives the power, it’s you, you create the value behind that degree,” Usher told graduates of Emory University in 2025. “It is your ambition, it is your integrity, it is your hustle, it is your heart; that’s how you lead, that’s how you serve, that’s how you choose to show up when no one else is watching.”

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on February 20, 2026.

https://fortune.com/article/jensen-huang.title: Jensen Huang had a strict no one-on-one meetings rule for his 60 direct reports—and Nvidia’s interim CEO has a similar mantra: ‘We don’t waste a dime’
https://fortune.com/article/jensen-huang.author: Orianna Rosa Royle
https://fortune.com/article/jensen-huang.text:
Former Nvidia CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang famously avoided unnecessary meetings, prioritizing efficiency over routine check-ins. Even with, at one point, 60 direct reports, he refused to do catch-ups. Now that he’s resigned, the question is whether his successor (currently Colette Kress who has stepped up on an interim basis) will keep the rule.

Speaking at Stanford University, Huang once disclosed his aversion to frequent catch-ups. “I don’t do one-on-ones with any of them,” he said.

Huang argued frequent meetings would clutter his schedule. He said they would also get in the way of the broader team’s ability to address challenges, work effectively, and stay transparent.

“They never hear me say something to them, that is only for them to know,” he said. “There’s not one piece of information that I somehow secretly tell the staff; I don’t tell the rest of the company.”

“In that way, our company was designed for agility. For information to be to flow as quickly as possible. For people to be empowered by what they are able to do, not what they know,” he added.

But that doesn’t mean he had no time for his team. Huang insisted he still regularly caught up with his executives. They just didn’t need to set time aside in their diaries to be on the same page.

“I write no reviews for any of them,” he added. “I give them constant reviews and they provide the same to me.”

And when an employee genuinely needed a moment of his time, Huang insisted he’d “drop everything for them.”

Stepping into Huang’s shoes (for now) is CFO Colette Kress. The interim CEO, who has an estimated net worth of $1.2 billion according to Forbes, holds a bachelor’s in finance from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University.

After nearly three decades’ worth of financial roles at companies such as Texas Instruments, Cisco, and Microsoft, she joined Nvidia in September 2013.

Since then, she guided the company’s finances through a significant transformation, from a business largely focused on video game hardware to a chipmaking powerhouse at the center of the AI boom—and watched its market cap soar from about $9 billion to, at its peak, $5 trillion. Its since dropped below $4 trillion upon the news regarding Huang.

She hasn’t revealed whether she’ll ditch one-on-ones too. But the 59-year-old, who has spent 13 years as Huang’s right hand on Nvidia’s finances, seems to share his affinity for efficiency.

“We do not waste a day, we don’t waste a dime,” Kress said in 2024. “And those two things are really important about us, our agility to move fast, but our ability to not waste things along the way.”

Huang isn’t the first leader to argue that meetings aren’t the best use of time.

Pandora’s former CEO Alexander Lacik told Fortune too many meetings result in every department or company issue getting “equal attention”—whether or not it needs it. He limited his catch-ups with management.

“There’s only one, two, three activities that actually draw disproportionate value and the rest is just background noise,” he said. “As time has gone by and I’m getting towards the end of my career, I’m much more clear on trying to insert myself where I make a high impact.”

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby caps his meetings at four hours a day, and wants the ones he does attend to be “quick” and “almost all conversational.”

E-commerce giant Shopify took one step further and actually axed all meetings involving more than two people in 2023, in a company-wide “calendar purge” meant to give employees more time to work on other tasks.

And even Amazon founder Jeff Bezos—a big fan of “messy meetings”—mandates a strict protocol to ensure they’re actually useful, complete with a six-page memo instead of a PowerPoint (because they’re too vague) and half an hour set aside at the start of the meeting to silently read it together before having “a really elevated discussion.”

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on June 12, 2024.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/real-est.title: Rising rents draw Wall Street money to industrial outdoor storage lot investments across the U.S.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/real-est.author: Kevin Williams
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/real-est.text:
Brookfield and Blackstone, two of the world’s largest alternative asset managers, are among the institutional investors moving in on what the industry calls “industrial outdoor storage.”

Ownership of lots used to store industrial equipment is fragmented in markets across the U.S., which the Wall Street giants plan to capitalize on.

But real estate experts say local investors can still find opportunities to invest, especially in lots of three to five acres in size, and it is a market where rents have doubled since 2020.

Nondescript lots holding idle bulldozers, trucks and other industrial equipment are a common sight in local real estate markets across the U.S., and increasingly, a focus for Wall Street private investment giants.

If you haven’t noticed them, it’s probably because they so easily fade into the landscape, just another non-branded bit of land in the miasma of suburbia. But Brookfield and Blackstone, two of the world’s largest alternative asset managers, are among the institutional investors moving in on what the industry calls industrial outdoor storage, or IOS. Investors are eyeing these lots as the AI build-out increases the demand for heavy equipment.

“We have strong conviction in industrial outdoor storage, which plays a critical role in our supply chain,” said Devin Barnwell, a managing partner and co-leader of Brookfield’s logistics business.

He says that up until now, the segment has been fragmented, but Brookfield sees that changing.

“We see significant opportunity to bring institutional capital and operating expertise to this fragmented sector, improving the quality and efficiency of these assets while strengthening the resilience of our industrial supply chains,” Barnwell said.

Brookfield spent $1.2 billion earlier this year to take Peakstone Realty Trust private, a deal completed in May that gave it a portfolio of more than 70 industrial properties, most of them outdoor storage yards.

Blackstone is also ramping up in the sector, mainly as a lender. Its real estate debt arm has made six loans to outdoor storage owners totaling more than $1.1 billion, including a $244 million loan in June to Alterra IOS to buy 37 properties.

Despite the billions being bet on the market by Wall Street, there is still opportunity in the market for individual investors and local entrepreneurs looking to park their money where others park their equipment.

“1,000 percent yes,” said Adam Petrillo, an executive managing director at Newmark, a commercial real estate advisory firm, who co-leads its industrial outdoor storage practice.

Petrillo said smaller, non-institutional investors, still control a significant amount of well-placed storage in secondary markets. “The good news for smaller investors and mom and pops is that a good individual IOS site isn’t necessarily 50 acres,” Petrillo said.

Lots as small as three to five acres in primary or secondary markets can still yield a robust return, he said.  “At that bite size, an individual can step in. We are not talking about tens of millions ... a three-acre, well-located IOS with multiple use cases can be found, marketed, leased,  and stabilized,” he added.

The numbers help explain the appetite.

Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses.

Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically.

The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren’t uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial.

Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah’s IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah’s container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025.

Petrillo said that there is still plenty of room left for values to increase, so an investor jumping in now hasn’t missed the game. “We are still in the very early innings,” Petrillo said.

Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots.

“It comes down to supply and demand,” he said. “If you need a warehouse you can usually find one. Properly zoned infill IOS sites are much harder to find and every year more of them are converted to warehouses and other uses,” he said, referencing multifamily housing units. The scarcity makes tenants sticky. “So a limited supply keeps shrinking. And because so much of the value is in the land itself, owners keep the option to redevelop the site as the area grows,” Cheema added.

Because of the imbalance of supply and demand, rents and prices are rising across the board, according to Cheema, but no two IOS properties look alike, which has kept the door open for smaller investors.

“Big institutions want exposure to IOS, but ownership is fragmented across mom-and-pop owners and small businesses, so it’s hard to deploy large amounts of capital without first aggregating these assets into portfolios,” Cheema said.

Unlike traditional warehouses, there’s no standard spec like square footage or clear height to compare them. “That lack of standardization along with the ongoing growth of the asset class, means there’s still runway for small investors to find opportunities,” Cheema said.

“Financing has improved as more lenders have a better understanding of IOS, but it’s still largely local and regional banks,” Cheema added.

Zoning is the biggest challenge.

“If you don’t understand the city’s plans for the area, you may end up owning a use they’re trying to phase out,” Cheema said.

CanTex Capital works with the city and neighborhoods before buying to ensure the impact aligns with the community’s plan for its future.

Alex Sutterer, an executive vice president at NAI Hiffman, a Chicago-area commercial real estate firm, said that beyond being a place to store big equipment, IOS attracts investors for two main reasons: lower capital expenditure requirements than traditional industrial or multifamily properties and the potential for higher yields.

“Capital improvements are also less specific to individual tenants, so owners can direct spending toward the property’s overall functionality,” Sutterer said.

For private investors, IOS typically trades at a yield around one percentage point higher than traditional industrial properties, helping attract smaller investors and family offices. “We believe that gap will continue to narrow as more institutional capital enters this space,” Sutterer added.

Even for industrial properties with similar yields, he said the credit profile of tenants is generally stronger for IOS.

Shallow-bay, multitenant industrial properties — industrial facilities that tend to be much smaller than big-box distribution warehouses — have comparable yields. But unlike the local businesses that tend to fill up shallow-bay sites, IOS tenants range from local businesses to those with investment-grade credit ratings, offering investors the potential for both yield and creditworthy tenants.

And institutional money is making IOS more competitive.

“Institutional capital has increased competition in IOS, and property values and lease rates have risen overall,” Sutterer said.

He added smaller investors can still find opportunities below institutional deal-size thresholds, although that does not mean every smaller deal is priced fairly. “We see opportunities to add value and earn yield in deals below $3 million–$5 million,” Sutterer said.

For local investors, that means there is the ability to build a portfolio at a smaller scale and hold the assets for cash flow, or aggregate more than $10 million in assets and seek a portfolio premium when selling to institutional capital.

But buyers need to understand what they are getting into. Due diligence on tenant demand by site and site function, and tenant turnover ratio, are important factors in buying the right asset. Market diversity can also provide protection, Sutterer said.

“In Chicago, no single user category accounts for more than 18% of IOS tenants, helping insulate the market from industry-specific slowdowns,” he said. Tenants’ tendency to stay and tight vacancy rates nationally are current advantages of the asset class. In Chicagoland, for example, vacancy is below 3%.

Still, all the due diligence in the world can’t protect investors from some variables.

“No one outside the Federal Reserve can control the cost of debt,” said Kellie McIvor, vice president of acquisitions at Redwood Living, an Ohio real estate development firm. She said that right now, the cost of debt for light industrial uses is lower than, say, for residential construction.

“However, interest rates are still high, with no relief in sight,” McIvor said.

The Fed is expected to raise rates in December in its effort to tame inflation, and after this week’s latest hot October CPI report, potentially hike twice more in early 2027, according to some Wall Street forecasts.

“Because lenders view them as riskier than a large institutional investor, smaller buyers can face more expensive debt and may be asked to bring more equity to the deal. That can make financing a small acquisition disproportionately expensive. ... More expensive debt means less room for error in execution,” McIvor said.

A small buyer looking at a small site that requires no improvement may be able to fund the deal all on his own. “That’s the dream! Own your business and the land it’s on, outright!” she added.

Ross Blankenship, who owns two fenced contractor and fleet yards in Colorado’s Vail Valley through Wins Parking, said the math has to work today. In a mountain market where little land is zoned for the use, he rents spaces for $210 a month for a car or pickup and $265 for a box truck or trailer, and charges $1,250 to $5,500 a month for contractor zones. Blankenship also runs Park Graph, the parking software he uses to rent the spaces.

The swing factor is vacancy, he said. “A full yard throws off more cash per dollar of capex than a small retail or office building. An empty one earns nothing,” he said.

His advice for a first-time buyer: call 10 local contractors and ask what they pay for space.

But he still likes the opportunity.

“A small investor can still buy, but the deal has to work on rents you can collect today, not on what an institution might pay you later,” Blankenship said.

https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.title: DR Congo, Rwanda clash over Francophonie leadership as Macron seeks compromise
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.text:
The Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, already mired in cross-border conflict, clashed on Saturday over who should next head a key group of French-speaking states and governments.

The next secretary-general of the 53-member Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), which begins a summit in Cambodia on Sunday, has become a major bone of contention.

French President Emmanuel Macron, who arrived Saturday in the capital Phnom Penh, has requested that Rwanda withdraw its candidate for the job, current leader Louise Mushikiwabo, in favour of a compromise choice.

Mushikiwabo has been standing for another term against three other candidates, including DR Congo's Juliana Lumumba, the daughter of national hero Patrice Lumumba.

Following a story in Jeune Afrique magazine reporting Macron's move, Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe said his country had "rejected" the request.

DR Congo, the world's second-largest French-speaking country, has threatened to quit the organisation in the event that Mushikiwabo is re-elected on Monday, according to several sources.

Kinshasa accuses Rwanda of supporting the M23 armed group's activities inside DR Congo, which Kigali denies.

READ MORE
Ceasefire verification mission deploys to eastern DR Congo

DR Congo stated on Saturday it was ready to withdraw Lumumba if Rwanda did likewise in favour of a third candidate who could deliver consensus and unity.

"We have called on all member states to work towards a consensus and, in that spirit, we would be prepared to withdraw our candidate's nomination in order to facilitate the emergence of a consensus," said DR Congo's Foreign Minister Therese Kayikwamba Wagner in Phnom Penh.

https://www.dw.com/en/werner-holzer-priz.title: Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim
https://www.dw.com/en/werner-holzer-priz.text:
DW journalist Jaafar Abdul Karim and Russia correspondent Katja Gloger have been awarded the prestigious Werner Holzer Prize for international journalism.

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.

The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

"I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.

Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set new standards," the jury stated.

So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue."

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from."

This article was originally written in German.

First prize went to Russia correspondent KatjaGloger, who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin. Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafars Abdul KarIM.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.title: Meet the Fans Who Traveled to Bangkok for Eurovision Asia
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.author: Francesca Regalado
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.text:
Some were Asia-based Europeans chasing nostalgia. Others were Americans eager to experience their first edition of the song contest.

By Francesca Regalado

Simon Robinson, one of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday, said that his history with the competition is nearly as long as its seven-decade run.

He was eight years old when he first watched it with his family in Yorkshire, England, when Britain's Mary Hopkin finished in second place behind Ireland’s Dana.

“I really liked the concept of bringing Europe together after the war,” said Mr. Robinson, 63, who now lives in Melbourne, Australia. He described the contest’s annual broadcast as a social activity for his family and neighbors.

“Eurovision helped to create the European identity,” he added.

Other fans had their own motivations for traveling to see the contest’s first Asian edition.

Some are Europeans living in Asia, on the hunt for nostalgia, while others are Americans who were eager to experience their first Eurovision.

Lee Hudson, an American television executive based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, said that he gets emotional when he talks about Eurovision, which he has watched since 2012.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.title: Asia’s Eurovision Contest Is Missing China, India, Pakistan, Indonesia and Japan
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.author: Alex Marshall and Francesca Regalado
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.text:
China, India, Pakistan, Indonesia and Japan aren’t joining the singing contest. That leaves some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix.

By Alex Marshall and Francesca Regalado

For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia has several notable absences.

For starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — won’t be there. Even Japan, a country globally considered a cultural powerhouse, is absent.

That leaves some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix. India has Bollywood hits. China has produced both Mandopop and Cantopop, the genre associated with Hong Kong pop stars. JPop was once huge across Asia.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How a US extradition bid over Hamas allegations put a wealthy activist before a Spanish court
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Timothy Pratt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, a Cox Enterprises heir, faced a two-hour hearing about alleged support for Hamas

A two-hour hearing in Spain’s high court Friday on the US extradition request of wealthy leftwing activist and philanthropist James “Fergie” Chambers turned out to be a study in contrasts.

Chambers’s defense took most of the session to query the US citizen and detail irregularities in the Trump administration’s extradition request – several of which the Guardian has reported on – as well as the figures of Spanish law that would lead the three-judge panel to deny the request; while the prosecutor sped through his case, head down, asking Chambers no questions at all.

Notably, neither the judges or the prosecutor asked Chambers to address the insinuation in the extradition request that the wealthy activist had supported Hamas. Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money laundering charge and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

But the defense’s queries did allow him to speak for the first time since his 10 July arrest in Ibiza about events at the center of the case: 2023 protests against Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit in Massachusets and New Hampshire and 2024 transfers of $7.2m to Tunisia, where he lived at the time. The latter was buttressed with testimony from a financial expert.

On the whole, Chambers painted a picture different from the depiction contained in the extradition request, that of a violent backer of Hamas on the run from the US. At one point, he noted that his family’s next door neighbor in Tunis was the US ambassador.

The court will decide next week on extraditing Chambers. If the decision is affirmative, Spain’s council of ministers can reverse the court’s decision. This means Chambers’s extradition may be among the last decisions made under Pedro Sánchez, the socialist prime minister, before national elections on 29 November.

Friday’s hearing began with Chambers’s defense asking about his wealth. A self-described communist and anti-imperialist, Chambers sold stock back to his family’s business, Atlanta-based Cox Enterprises, worth about $250m in mid-2023.

Then he started a foundation, he told the court. He and the foundation’s three-member board decide on funding and ensure that no projects seeking support are under US sanctions, Chambers said. The foundation has funded an estimated 100 progressive and humanitarian projects in 20 countries, according to his partner, activist and actor Stella Schnabel – including, Chambers said Friday, organizations in Gaza working on issues such as “medical treatment for children, transportation out of dangerous areas and clean water and food”.

Two of the request’s three charges – riot and conspiracy to riot – are related to the late-2023 protests against Elbit.

Chambers detailed his participation in the protests: locking himself to a door, marching in the street and – in New Hampshire – standing in the road, speaking to the media and paying bail for four protesters who were eventually found guilty of misdemeanor charges and served 30 days in jail.

As for the $7.2m, the defense and a financial expert serving as a witness laid out how ten bank transfers from the US to Tunisia mostly went to sponsor the football club Club Africain – described by Chambers as “one of the largest football clubs in Africa” – and a sporting business Chambers launched while living in Tunisia.

“Is there any indication that the money went to support terrorist activities?” asked defense attorney Aitor Martínez. “None,” said financial expert Albert Deulofeu Schilt.

Then, in about 15 minutes of rapid-fire monotone, prosecutor Juan Hernández Villalba laid out a wholly different picture of Chambers as backing “an organized structure … aimed at repeatedly committing illegal acts … together with funds destined for terrorist organizations”.

He accused the defense of laying out the facts of the case “in a fragmented way … when what’s most relevant is an evaluation of the whole picture”.

“The extradition petition isn’t based on ideology or political statements, but on actions [Chambers] organized, financed and carried out, causing material damage,” Hernández Villalba asserted.

The actions against Elbit “were presented as a simple protest”, he said. “Nevertheless, the actions described by the US were planned for days … with objectively violent content.”

Given all this, the prosecutor said, “there are more than enough indications to consider … that [Chambers’s] funding was aimed at terrorism”.

Among the 100-plus people in varying time zones following Friday’s hearing on the court’s YouTube channel was Irish film-maker and journalist Sinéad O’Shea, whose documentary on Chambers called All About the Money makes its New York premiere this weekend. It covers the time period cited by the FBI affidavit underpinning the US request. O’Shea said that extradition case “builds a false narrative which begins with the protest in New Hampshire – a piece of vandalism at worst and for which people ended up serving 30 days. I saw myself the football club in which he invested in Tunisia and his donations to Palestinian and other charities are a matter of public record. It is impossible not to see this as a politically motivated case.”

Chambers’s views have been extensively profiled in US media. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”

Dressed in dark jeans, a grey-blue shirt, a black jacket, with a close-cropped haircut and mustache, Chambers got the last word during the hearing.

“To this day I cannot understand why I have been in prison since July for what amounts to speaking emotionally and committing minor offenses of public disturbance,” he said.

“I’ve never had any contact with any terrorist organization. I’ve certainly never financed any terrorist organization … and for this my family has been torn apart. I missed my grandmother’s funeral last week. My five-year-old son asks where I am every day. And my wife will give birth, God willing, in March – and I don’t know if I will be by her side.”

“[All] because I have spoken my mind, and I had a lot more money than others who have spoken their mind, in my country. And that’s all it amounts to.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, a Cox Enterprises heir, faced a two-hour hearing in Spain’s high court Friday. Chambers says he has never had any contact with any terrorist organization.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: US air travel slowly recovers from nationwide flight ground stop as chaos continues
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Anna Betts
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Thousands of flights still canceled as officials blamed ageing air control system for nationwide grounding

Travel chaos continued across the US on Saturday morning as airlines scrambled to recover from a four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or canceled thousands of the flights.

On Saturday morning, more than 3,000 flights within, into or out of the US had already been canceled, according to FlightAware.

The longest nationwide group stop in 25 years left passengers stranded at airports across the country, with no certainty about exactly when they may reach their intended destination.

The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, on Friday blamed the ground stop on an ageing air control system, saying that the air traffic communications equipment became “overloaded with data and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers”.

“Because of that, we shut the system down,” the Trump administration official said.

The US homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said on Friday that there was “no indication as of yet” that the communications failure had been caused by “a nefarious attack against us”.

Duffy warned that it would “take us time” to “resume normal operations”.

“Our top priority is the safety of you and your family when you fly,” he said.

The rare flight grounding caused widespread disruptions, throwing travel plans into disarray as more than 8,000 flights across the country were canceled on Friday.

Among those affected by the fallout from the ground stop were sports teams traveling for games over the weekend. In college football, the Southeastern Conference announced that Mississippi’s game against Oklahoma had been rescheduled to Sunday – a day usually reserved for the National Football League (NFL).

Meanwhile, a men’s college basketball game between the University of North Carolina Greensboro and Cornell University, scheduled for Saturday, was postponed.

And although flights began resuming after the FAA’s decision to lift the ground stop, the aftermath still appears to be affecting passengers around the country. There were reported flight disruptions at airports in major cities including Boston, Washington DC, New York and Miami.

In a statement on Saturday, Duffy said that “operations are slowly returning to normal this morning” – but he added that “you will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most”.

“Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible,” he said.

Duffy said he planned to hold a news briefing at 10.30am ET.

The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) also issued a statement on Saturday morning warning that “while US flights have resumed, there may be some follow-on disruption as airlines work to re-book affected passengers and get all services back to normal”.

The statement added: “Anyone due to travel on flights between the UK and USA should check with their airline for the latest information before heading to the airport.”

During the news briefing on Friday evening, Trump administration officials urged Congress – which until January is controlled by the White House’s Republican allies – to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”.

Friday marked the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA this century. The first occurred after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks. And the second took place in January 2023, after a pilot notification system went down.
