https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Progressive versus moderate? Democrats deny party rift as they head into new Congress
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Rachel Leingang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Incoming lawmakers have more in common with each other than they have divisions, even across ideological factions

D
emocrats who won in the midterms, including those in places previously considered off the blue map and those in Democratic strongholds, crafted their campaigns around economic populism and accountability.

Lawmakers in the anti-establishment incoming congressional class have more in common with each other than divisions, even across ideological factions. Voters sent a resounding message to work on affordability and rein in the Trump administration, and Democrats across the party have many more shared goals than Republicans, who face a more existential level of discord.

The challenge comes when this class of newcomers meets a Washington machine that they view as stuck to the status quo, and as they confront institutional barriers – and a president with a veto pen at the ready – that could prevent them from installing the tangible changes voters demanded.

But, political operatives and officials said, the shared agenda is clear, and Democrats need to stay focused on it, lest they lose the seats they just won in parts of the country where they previously weren’t getting traction.

“They got to just keep being who they are,” said Joe Maxwell, president of Farm Action Fund, a non-profit focused on building back rural communities. “There’s a whole different rhythm and politics and narrative to be able to be effective in Washington DC.”

Before the new lawmakers take their oath of office, they will have to decide whether to keep their party’s leaders. In the US Senate, Chris Van Hollen announced a challenge to longtime leader Chuck Schumer. On the House side, Hakeem Jeffries so far appears to have the speaker job.

In a speech at the Democrats’ meetup in Denver on Friday, Van Hollen said his bid was a response to voters’ calls for a political system that serves them.

“We should not be preserving our institutions if they are not delivering for the American people,” he continued. “And we should be making delivering for the American people the single mission of our government, even when that means shaking things up.”

Disagreements over a leader don’t mean there are deep disagreements on the path forward, though, Democrats insist.

“There’s a very small set of consultants and self-interested commentators and donor-aligned op-ed writers who are crashing out on the internet right now,” said Maurice Mitchell, the leader of the Working Families party. “I think it would be a distraction to focus on a factional fight that they are so thirsty for, when Tuesday suggested that you should be past the narrow politics of factionalism inside the Democratic party.”

This month’s wins present a “generational opportunity” to deliver results for the American people, Mitchell said, and trying to fit that into a “narrow framework” that pits moderates versus progressives misses the point.

“We just want to get things done, and we think that there’s a big terrain to get things done,” he said.

The Democratic party once again becomes a big tent, full of people from different parts of the country with varying life experiences. Because so many different Democrats got elected, there is an “interesting mix of basically a slice of America governing”, said Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party.

“For me, that means we’re going to have a much more durable party,” she said. “It’s not going to be a one-note party.”

As former CBS News journalist John Dickerson put it: “A party big enough to win everywhere has to hold people who disagree. The tension comes with winning. When coverage treats that tension as a crack-up or a flaw, it mistakes how the game works for a threat to the game. Tackling isn’t an obstacle to football. Tackling is football.”

Newly elected Democratic lawmakers have expressed a willingness to talk to anyone. They’ve highlighted speaking with voters who disagreed with them on the campaign trail and ran against how both parties do politics. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive who won the US Senate race in Michigan, has said Trump can call Medicare for All “Trumpcare for All” if he wants, as long as it makes it into law.

Some new members will join multiple Democratic caucuses that may seem to have competing ideologies. Indeed, the various caucuses announced big increases in membership after the election, from the progressive to the centrist New Democrats. Sam Forstag, a smoke jumper who flipped a congressional district in Montana, joined both the Progressive and Blue Dog caucuses, saying he would be one of few Democrats sitting in both. Being in both rooms would give him “a chance to fight for populist economic policies that are actually going to help working people and finally put us all back at the front of the line”, he said.

“What you realize once you get elected is that you now are the establishment,” Kleeb said. “So I think you’ll see a reopening of what the establishment means, and I do think it’s really good that the DC traditional establishment does get shook up.”

Affordability, affordability, affordability: the campaign’s theme will become the clear frontrunner on a shared Democratic agenda.

That includes working to end the war in Iran to lower gas prices, rolling back tariffs, restoring subsidies on the health insurance exchanges that have pummeled people with massive cost increases, and reversing upcoming cuts to social services.

“I haven’t heard any Democrat with a different position on those,” said Glenn Ivey, a Democratic representative from Maryland. “Everybody wants to end the war. Everybody wants to roll back the tariffs. Everybody wants gas and grocery prices to go down. Everybody wants to help expand healthcare tax credits and restore Medicaid and the like.”

Other bills are more niche, but could be simple ways to respond to affordability. Maxwell, of the Farm Action Fund, said there’s already a bipartisan bill filed to address consolidation in the meatpacking industry, which would help lower meat prices.

Sign up to Breaking News US

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

The second-most-frequent refrain from voters was to bring accountability to the Trump administration. Amanda Litman, the founder of progressive candidate pipeline Run for Something, said it would be a mistake for Democrats to forgo any oversight in the name of putting the past behind them. This doesn’t mean a revenge or retribution campaign like Trump undertook in his second term, but an effort to show voters that there needs to be respect for the law, she said.

“At the very least, we’ve killed how many people in fishing boats off the shore?” she said. “It would be useful to have some hearings.”

There’s also consistent support for institutional reforms that would help restore public trust in Congress. A group of 50 incoming freshmen sent a letter to Democratic leadership to call for a stock trading ban, a frequent campaign promise for Democrats – and some Republicans – this year.

“A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them,” the group wrote in its letter. “This rule would be a down payment on much-needed reform to prevent elected and appointed government officials and their spouses from trading stocks. We promised our communities we would clean up this place. In January, we should do just that.”

At the post-election Democratic confab in Denver this week, Jeffries said banning congressional stock trading was on the menu. He also said he supported new rules that would limit how long members of Congress can serve as leaders on committees in an effort to give new, younger lawmakers a chance at leading.

Procedurally, Maxwell, of the Farm Action Fund, said Democrats should work on single-issue or pared-down bills rather than weighty omnibus measures that obscure the work that lawmakers do. People need to see movement, he said.

This also sets up Republicans to vote up or down on specific issues, then Trump to have to veto, or, possibly, not. Mitchell, of the Working Families party, said lawmakers shouldn’t hedge their bills against whether Trump will veto them.

“They voted people in to fight for them,” Mitchell said. “It’s their job to pass the legislation in line with what the voters want, and dare the president not to sign that legislation.”

Democrats flipped state legislatures in several states and now have new governing trifectas that make policy wins much more possible at the state level, which could serve as a balm to the partisan gridlock common in Washington. When these states pass new laws, “we need to communicate governing wins”, said Kleeb, the Nebraska party chair.

Communication will be key, Democrats said. If a piece of legislation meets a roadblock in Congress, name it, said the Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan. If Trump vetoes a bill, make it clear that he’s responsible for that.

Voters understood that this election was not “business as usual”, Flanagan said, and they demanded change. Some people in power may now “sort of be kicking and screaming along the way with this change”, but Flanagan said her job is to represent the Minnesotans who shared their deeply personal struggles.

The social media prowess of the incoming class means that each lawmaker functions as their own small media entity, Litman said. They can use this massive reach to show the work they are doing to fight for the agendas they ran on, she added.

“I do think it is really, really important for Democrats in Congress to get caught trying,” Litman said.

The stakes are high for Democrats to show the cross-partisan group of voters who elected them that they can govern, or they will face the same rebuke Republicans got this year, Mitchell said.

“They will not be kind to Democrats,” Mitchell said of the voters who are sick of the status quo. “On the flip side, if Democrats actually deliver, we could be talking about the beginnings of a realignment in this country.”

Shrai Popat and Ariana Baio contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: A group of 50 incoming freshmen sent a letter to Democratic leadership to call for a stock trading ban. The group said it would be a down payment on much-needed reform to prevent elected and appointed government officials from trading stocks.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How ICE raids in Kansas meatpacking country sparked fury – and turned voters against Trump
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
In region where migrants have settled to work at abattoirs and feedyards, harsh raids pushed people to vote Democrat

J
osé Del Real looked over the crowd from the stage in a park, at hundreds of his neighbors with furious signs tucked under their arms, voicing their anger at immigration agents who had descended on their town and started rounding up their friends and family. His daughters, in the front row, were crying.

Del Real, an army veteran who served two tours in Iraq, hadn’t voted in a decade. He thought it would not matter in this ruby red corner of Kansas. But the midterm election was weeks away. He draped an American flag over his shoulders, put on his Iraq veteran cap and ended his speech with a message: “None of this matters if you do not vote. Let’s go vote.”

They did. This county and two of its neighbors in south-western Kansas, Republican strongholds where a steady stream of immigrants have settled over the decades to work at feedlots and slaughterhouses, swung wildly to the left. The shift helped elect a Democratic US Senator from Kansas for the first time in nearly a century, signaling the limits of Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation agenda.

Since Democrats won back control of Congress in a decisive rebuke to Republicans, Trump has sent mixed messages about how he plans to handle immigration enforcement going forward. He suggested that his approach to deportations was too harsh but also named hardliner Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff. Both parties will be recalibrating their approach ahead of the next presidential campaign.

Here in Kansas, late September raids ignited a maelstrom of rage, turning many who had been apathetic, like Del Real, into determined voters.

Masked officers in tactical gear banged on doors before dawn. They stopped cars in the middle of intersections. Businesses shuttered. Families feared leaving their houses. Children stopped going to school. Some live-streamed themselves being detained. One man pleaded “God help me” in Spanish, his hands shaking, as he asked anyone watching to let his family know.

The resistance came not only from Democrats or the Latino population, which has grown to about two-thirds of Dodge City. Kansas’s embattled Republican senator, Roger Marshall, who would lose his reelection bid to Adam Hamilton, issued a statement pleading with the administration to consult local officials before launching raids.

Del Real regrets he didn’t vote in 2024, when Trump roared back into office pledging mass deportations.

“We had to see it in front of us,” Del Real said. “I had to see it in the flesh.”

This corner of Kansas is responsible for much of the country’s beef. The gates leading into Dodge City boast that it’s the “Queen of the Cowtowns” Its main street is named after the classic western set here, Gunsmoke. Murals celebrating cowboy history mix with evidence of a changing culture: storefronts showcasing quinceañera dresses, Mexican bakeries, city signs printed in both Spanish and English.

Del Real’s family came from Mexico when he was a kindergartner. Like most here, they came to work. The area – Dodge City and the region’s other hubs, Garden City and Liberal – is known as the Golden Triangle of Meatpacking, responsible for about a quarter of the US beef supply.

Some here thought their importance to the nation’s food might spare them from the administration’s deportation campaigns, said Amy Soberanes, a 25-year-old local organizer.

Soberanes, the daughter of Mexican immigrants, said she and others tried for years to get people – particularly their young, Latino neighbors – engaged.

But, from rural Kansas, immigration raids in places like Minneapolis and Chicago felt abstract.

Then they saw their own streets in social media videos.

People were furious, said Soberanes, who worried the daily protests could get out of hand. They told people not to slash tires or break windows, to store up their anger and take it out on election day.

“We’ll see them at the ballot box,” she recalls repeating.

Her phone rang and rang. People she’d hassled to vote for years asked: how do I register?

“If ICE hadn’t come, we would still be red, 100%,” she said. “And so I thank Donald Trump for sending immigration here.”

No one knew immigration officers were coming.

Dodge City commissioner Rick Sowers said he and other city officials found out just like everyone else, through social media or masses of unmarked trucks on their neighbors’ lawns.

They scrambled to get answers from the federal government – who they were looking for, who was in charge, how long they would stay – and never did.

The Trump administration issued statements naming five “heinous criminals” they said had been arrested. But the Wichita Eagle dug into that claim and found none of those people were actually apprehended during the surge: Four had been deported months before and the fifth was already in prison, the newspaper found.

The agency said it detained 104 people from south-west Kansas.

Local officials have still never seen a list, Sowers said.

Local Republican chairman Scott Fischer, who describes himself as a supporter of strong borders, was surprised by the operation’s intensity.

“There was a little showmanship,” he said. “I don’t know why it was like that.”

He said he still considers the county red – it voted, narrowly, for Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson. The Associated Press called that race on Thursday: Masterson lost to Democrat Cindy Holscher .

But some Dodge City Republicans abandoned the party in the US Senate race.

Russell Arben Fox, political science professor at Friends University in Wichita, said swings as dramatic as that one couldn’t have happened without some white, moderate Republicans changing their minds.

More than half of Kansas voters in the Senate race disapprove of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is handling its job, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. That’s consistent with the 61% of voters who say this nationally.

Most of the Latino immigrants here are hard-working, family-oriented, faithful people – a perfect fit for conservative Kansas values, Fischer said, so local Republicans tend to have a nuanced view on immigration.

Some public officials have for years begged the federal government for reforms to provide a pathway for these workers who run the region’s economy.

“In general terms, mass deportation is not practical,” Fischer said. “When we say send them all home, what does that mean? Who is them?”

To many here, “them” this time meant relatives and friends. In this small town, nearly everybody is connected to everybody else, so they did what they could to help.

Oscar Soto delivered food to people afraid to leave home during the deportation raids.

He started calling it “the black week” after the black plague. That’s what it felt like to him, a pestilence that arrived suddenly.

His mother came here from Mexico, he said, and though she is here legally, she was terrified.

“It seemed unreal,” he said. “It was stuff that’s never been seen here, and it was day after day after day.”

He works at a family-owned grocery, and strung a garland of flags from around the world above the counter when it opened. Most customers are from Mexico and Guatemala, he said, but he wanted to signal that the store was for everyone.

Then he hung a big American flag from the ceiling. It means to him that anyone, from anywhere, can come here, work hard and build a life, free from fear.

That belief in the American dream was shaken for him when ICE arrived.

So he registered to vote for the first time aged 39.

He stood in line to cast his ballot, amazed by how many young, Latino voters were waiting along with him.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 to hit new space distance record of one light-day
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
NASA has announced that its Voyager 1 probe will soon become humanity’s first object to travel one light-day from Earth.

On Wednesday, the robotic space probe will hit the milestone of travelling at least 16 billion miles since its launch in 1977, a distance equal to one light-day, or how far light can travel in 24 hours.

The probe completed its Saturn flyby in 1980, the end of its primary planetary mission, and is currently travelling at roughly 36,000 miles per hour (58km/h) in interstellar space, the vast gap between stars.

NASA expects it to take 18,000 years to travel a full light-year, and double that before it nears another star.

Plutonium-powered Voyager 1 was launched shortly before another probe, Voyager 2. Both continue to relay data back to Earth daily, including readings on the strength and direction of the magnetic field as well as on the surrounding pressure, dust and galactic cosmic rays.

Voyager 2 is expected to hit one light-day from Earth in 2035.

Both are kept active by a skeleton team of NASA engineers who send commands roughly once a week, and more if the probe gets into trouble.

In October, the team briefly lost communication with Voyager 1, and they have not yet figured out why.

Voyager 1 project manager Suzanne Dodd described Voyager 1 as “a national treasure” and told The Associated Press news agency that the two probes’ activities are akin to that of weather satellites.

The probe’s cultural impact has been significant. The famous “Pale Blue Dot” photo of Earth was taken by Voyager 1 in 1990.

“All of us — everyone on Earth — have been touched by these missions,” the Planetary Society’s Bill Nye said in a statement.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Voyager 1 will hit the milestone of travelling at least 16 billion miles since its launch in 1977. The probe completed its Saturn flyby in 1980, the end of its primary planetary mission. Voyager 2 is expected to hit one light-day from Earth in 2035.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Canada’s Stelco to recall 175 workers after government pressure
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.author: Tamara Khandaker
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Canadian steelmaker Stelco says it will recall all 175 workers laid off at its plant in Hamilton and pay them retroactively, following a weeks-long standoff that pitted workers and the Canadian government against its owner in the United States.

The announcement on Friday came shortly after Canada’s Industry Minister Melanie Joly said she would seek a court order to force Cleveland-Cliffs to sell Stelco unless she heard from management by the end of the day.

The company said in a statement on Friday that it had reached agreements with enough customers to restart its finishing operations and that workers would be recalled on December 1. They would receive back pay for the standard wages they would have earned while laid off.

The president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, Ron Wells, welcomed the announcement and credited pressure from workers, the union and the government.

At a news conference, he called the layoffs “illegal” and “immoral” which should never have happened.

Alongside him was Joly, who said the outcome sent a message to investors that Canada was “a country of the rule of law and that the law applies to everyone, notwithstanding the size of your wallet.”

“This fight was absolutely worth it,” she said.

Cleveland-Cliffs, which bought Stelco in 2024, announced in late September that up to 500 workers would be laid off at Stelco’s plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ontario, citing weak demand and difficult market conditions for cold-rolled and coated steel products used to make everything from cars to appliances.

It blamed US President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel, which made it more expensive in the US, as well as competition from cheaper foreign steel, which it argued was eating into domestic demand for Canadian steel.

Ottawa said the layoffs violated binding commitments the company made when it bought Stelco, including keeping the same number of Canadian unionised employees through 2029.

The government and the union also argued that Cleveland-Cliffs’ CEO Lourenco Goncalves violated a commitment to advocate for policies that would benefit the steel industries in both Canada and the US when he publicly supported Trump’s tariffs on steel, including Canada’s.

Goncalves’ open support for the tariffs raised questions, given that he also blamed them for Stelco’s financial troubles.

In its statement, Cleveland-Cliffs said its customers had committed to supporting its operations in Hamilton “despite the lack of response from the federal government to address the shortfalls in their tariff response program.”

It didn’t provide details on the agreements it had reached with customers or explain what had changed to make restarting operations viable.

Cleveland-Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
France's judo champion turned presidential candidate Teddy Riner on Saturday sought to distance himself from President Emmanuel Macron, calling the head of state's rare endorsement a "poisoned chalice".

The centrist president said on Monday that Riner joining the 2027 election race could "only benefit the country" after the popular judoka announced he was running.

READ MORE
Judo star Teddy Riner announces bid for French presidency

"I'm not the president's envoy," said the 37-year-old, who has won five Olympic gold medals.

"If I had to describe the president's congratulations, it would be more like a poisoned chalice," he added as he visited a trade fair of products made in France.

Riner said in his announcement on Monday he feared France could soon become deeply divided. He appeared to cast himself as a candidate for voters unwilling to choose between two political extremes — the far right and the hard left.

The sportsman from the French overseas territory of Guadeloupe has said he is neither from the left nor the right, but some have accused him of seeking to follow in Macron's footsteps.

Macron's popularity is the lowest it has ever been since he first became president in 2017, according to recent polls, as nationwide protests rock the country.

Opinion polls project far-right candidate Marine Le Pen as winning the first round of next year's vote, with hard-left hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon qualifying to face off against her in a second round.

READ MORE
Poll shows French far-right leader Marine Le Pen widening lead ahead of 2027 presidential vote

The centre-right has struggled to produce a single candidate with a decent shot at the top job. Former prime minister Edouard Philippe has slipped from second to third place in surveys in recent months.

Riner has hinted in an interview with Le Parisien newspaper that he would be in favour of a pension reform and a reduction in social security contributions, which could appeal to voters on the centre-right.

But he has also deplored that "a young person's future can be shattered just because they don't have the right connections, the right name or the right skin colour," which could attract leftists.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmz6.title: Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmz6.text:
Nigeria's government has cautioned its citizens, in particular those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia's main airport due to its altitude.

The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.

The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capitals in the world. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year.

Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk.

The Nigerian foreign ministry did not disclose the identities of the travellers it said had died, nor the cause of death.

It urged anyone with a health condition exacerbated by high altitudes to "exercise caution" when planning a journey via Addis Ababa and "obtain appropriate medical guidance" before doing so.

The ministry stressed that it did not want to discourage Nigerians from travelling through the Ethiopian capital.

Visiting an area at a high altitude can be dangerous for people with heart and lung diseases, as the air is thinner and so less oxygen can get into the bloodstream, experts say.

This means the heart has to work harder to get enough oxygen to different parts of the body, which can sometimes lead to heart failure among those with existing conditions, according to the American Heart Association.

The lack of oxygen at high altitudes can cause adverse effects such as dizziness, fatigue and shortness of breath among healthy people - which can cause complications for people with lung disease, studies show.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
PM accuses Tories of burning ‘all our bridges’ and says deal he is pursuing with EU will ‘get food prices down’

Andy Burnham has said the UK has “lost more than we gained” since leaving the EU, the prime minister’s latest in a string of comments criticising Brexit.

Outlining his desire to form closer ties with Brussels, Burnham accused the Conservative party of having “burned all our bridges” with the bloc after Brexit and said a new deal he hopes to secure with the EU next week will “get food prices down” and put more money in the pockets of British exporters.

The prime minister is due to meet European leaders at a summit next week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. He will also “explore options” for a different long-term relationship with Brussels.

Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said: “We need to be willing to take difficult decisions to get the cost of living down.

“It’s why, in a few days’ time, I will head to the next UK-EU summit and I will be working hard as we move towards it to get to a new deal on food and farming between the UK and the EU. Why am I doing that? Because I want to help Welsh businesses.

The prime minister added: “I think we’ve lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years, and, actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016, because they burned all of our bridges in the aftermath, with the EU, and so I’m going to lead as prime minister on this issue, and I’m going to go and try and get the best deal I can for Wales, for those here who could benefit, Welsh farmers, exporters of Welsh shellfish and Welsh lamb.”

Burnham has recently said he is open to rejoining the single market, customs union or to “go all the way” by rejoining the EU, but on Saturday he said voters would ultimately be “the boss” of any changes.

He reiterated his commitment to Labour’s manifesto “red lines” – which rule out returning to the customs union, single market or free movement. “People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that’s what makes us who we are,” he told the conference.

“And, yes, working with the European Union, as I said, but at the same time respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum, the referendum result. So, that’s the spirit, everybody, that I will take forward.”

The government has already made several announcements that would tie the UK closer to Brussels. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees, if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.

Earlier this week, Hamish Falconer, the cabinet minister in charge of EU talks, said Britain was willing to discuss paying towards infrastructure schemes in poorer parts of the EU in return for access to the European electricity market.

Despite Burnham’s recent pro-EU comments, senior figures in Brussels have said they want to see the UK begin to start paying for access to the European schemes it says it wants access to.

The EU’s former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier told the BBC last week: “There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market.”

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and António Costa, who leads the European Council, will meet Burnham on 20 November in Brussels for a summit where deals on food and drink, carbon emissions and youth exchange could be signed.

Barnier said the UK could not rejoin the single market “à la carte”, when speaking to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg last Sunday, adding: “I said very, very often during these negotiations, the Brexit, there is no cherrypicking.”

On Episode 236 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize.

When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms.

But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/nvidia-a.title: How Nvidia turmoil and a Democratic Congress could reshape the AI trade, according to ETF experts
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/nvidia-a.author: Julian Torres
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/nvidia-a.text:
The largest technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade could stand to benefit the most from Nvidia's woes and a Democratic-controlled Congress pushing back on data centers, according to investing experts interviewed on CNBC's "ETF Edge" earlier this week.

"We may have been put in an environment, as much as investors have sort of been looking for areas outside of Big Tech, where net-net Big Tech ends up as the winner once again," said Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza, whose firm manages the Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS
).

Part of his bull case: Other players in the AI trade are positioned to fill Nvidia's chip demand if investors lose trust in the company after a tumultuous week that saw its iconic founder and CEO Jensen Huang resign.

"If we get into an environment where people can't trust … Nvidia, they're going to look for other sources for these chips because they need them," Mazza said during the "ETF Edge" interview, which occurred Monday as the Nvidia scandal grew but before Huang had resigned.

Discussing recent fund flow activity for the MAGS ETF, as well as for the Roundhill Neocloud ETF (NCLD
) — which focuses on smaller market cap, specialized cloud computing companies — Mazza said, "In a weird way, [hyperscalers] may continue to benefit from this because they have the compute available. It's going to be more valuable if the demand is there."

The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF ended the week in the green, albeit with a gain of less than 1%, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF was up over 1%, though earnings from top holdings Coreweave and Nebius presented a mixed picture.

CoreWeave had its best day since April 2025 on Wednesday after its latest quarterly results, while Nebius shares sank after its Thursday report. The neocloud ETF remains deeply in the red since its August 2026 launch, down 39%, amid concerns about balance sheet strength, which could linger given Nvidia's role in financing the AI buildout. CoreWeave shares sank again on Friday, and Nvidia posted its longest losing streak since 2012 after its latest weekly losses.

Nvidia's interim CEO and current chief financial officer Colette Kress will have her first opportunity to reassure the market when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," Kress said in a statement issued on Thursday morning when the company announced Huang's exit.

Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives said on "ETF Edge" on Monday that the market will remain optimistic about other AI chip players, like AMD and Alphabet, if Nvidia faces prolonged headwinds. Ives helped create the Dan IVES Wedbush AI Revolution ETF (IVES
) while at Wedbush Securities, where he served as the managing director and global head of technology research before departing Wedbush to form his own firm earlier this year.

AMD finished trading this week up close to 13%, with Broadcom posting similar gains.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index posted its best week since August as Nvidia's slump reshuffled the AI trade.

Yorkville Ives lowered its price target on Nvidia to $225 from $300 on Thursday after Huang's resignation, but maintained a buy rating on the stock, which finished the week at $162.85 per share.

"Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," Ives wrote in a note to investors on Thursday. "The strategic roadmap is already essentially built around the next few family of chips and physical AI with 42k employees driving it. ... Valuation at roughly 10x 28 EPS is way too cheap once Nvidia gets through this storm and emerges on the other side."

The compute that does exist could become even more indispensable against the backdrop of a potential slowdown to the data-center buildout by Congress after the Democratic Party gains of Nov. 3 swept control of Congress, Mazza said.

Ives estimates that the "blue tidal wave" in Congress could mean 10% of planned data centers won't materialize on the low end, and 15%-20% on the high end, but he added that demand still outstrips supply four to one. "The compute is just that much more valuable in the capacity today than it was a week ago. So I could argue just more and more bullish, strong, get stronger," Ives said.

"The game is going to change for Big Tech. It will slow it down. But there's no overbuild, no bubble concerns. And I view that as actually a positive thing," he added.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.title: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.author: John Bartlett
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.text:
A masked demonstrator prepares to throw a Molotov cocktail as police use a water cannon to disperse students protesting education policies, rising living costs and reduced sentences for people convicted of sexual offenses against minors in Santiago, Chile, Nov. 5, 2026.

SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.

José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.

It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.

But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.

"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.

"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.

Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.

Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.

Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.

But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.

In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.

Trucks are parked along a road as drivers protest rising fuel prices and operating costs on the outskirts of Santiago, Chile, Nov. 12, 2026.

This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.

On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.

It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.

Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.

In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.

At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.

"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.

Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.

To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.summary: Chile's ultraconservative president has just 24% approval in the polls. President José Antonio Kast has been criticized for his policies on social issues. He has been in power for eight months but has shown little sign of doing so. In Chile, rising living costs and rising fuel prices have hit him hard.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: A rapid interest rate rise seems inevitable – and households are expected to pick up the tab
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Phillip Inman
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Raising borrowing costs too far risks laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy

A
head of steam is building up behind the Bank of England raising interest rates again. With the latest forecasts by the central bank showing inflation rising to 5% next spring, another increase in the cost of borrowing seems inevitable, and may come as soon as next month.

A growing number of analysts predict the Bank’s policymakers will don Scrooge masks when they meet on 17 December to deliver a message of austerity and sacrifice.

So sclerotic is the economy, so lacking in flexibility or productive spare capacity, that even the burst of growth experienced by the UK over the last year, defying most forecasters, must be calmed down with higher interest rates or else inflation will rip.

Huw Pill, the Bank’s chief economist, told the Financial Times on Saturday that more than one rate rise was almost certain.

This is not a message anyone who borrows money will want to hear, especially when the festive season is in full swing. If interest rates edge up from 4% to 4.25%, mortgage deals will rise and business loans will become more expensive.

The central bank expects businesses to react to the higher costs of doing business by hitting their customers with price hikes. It is an argument that presumes consumers have money available to pay higher prices, despite plenty of evidence to the contrary. Only households in the top half of the income scale have spent more this year and that has depended on running down their savings.

Consumers are also battle-hardened after the greedflation period following the pandemic that morphed into its evil cousin, shrinkflation. They know about grifting retailers and consumer product suppliers that try to build a narrative about the inevitability of surging inflation to disguise their own price hikes.

The Bank says its business surveys have failed to detect efforts by the corporate sector to increase prices. It’s just that a majority of policymakers are convinced pressure is building and inflation will be more than double their 2% target in a few months.

But if consumers don’t have any spare cash, or have become more savvy about how they spend it, there is still a weak link – a special kind of consumer who could aid corporates in pushing up prices.

The weak link is the state, or government in all its forms. The NHS is a big purchaser, so is local government and the many agencies that are funded by government, from Homes England to National Highways. Government expenditure on goods and services accounts for 25% of overall consumption in the economy.

Everything from concrete and medical supplies to food and furniture will cost more, and sellers will be prepared to justify the rise with a wide range of excuses.

Corporates will blame the war in the Middle East for an increase in transport costs and the impact of climate change that makes growing stuff harder. They will even accuse the government of raising costs by introducing new worker protection rules.

Let’s add another one: contractors will say they can’t get the skilled staff and so must pass on the cost of higher wages.

After 15 years of austerity and job cuts, there is a question mark over whether the public sector has the nous and resolve to push back to keep costs in check.

Budgets on the London to Birmingham high-speed rail line (HS2) have spiralled out of control. The costs of the next largest infrastructure project in England, the 14.5-mile (23km) lower Thames crossing linking Essex and Kent via two tunnels, have more than doubled to £11bn.

Government spending on consultants reached £3.7bn in 2024-25 from £2.9bn in 2022-23 and there seems to be no end to their uses, from advisers on artificial intelligence to strategies for reaching net zero.

The public sector is also notorious for commissioning plans for new town or city developments for which there is no funding, except for the inflationary bill from consultants.

These public sector organisations have huge clout, and should use it. If they do, there will be knock-on effects to inflation deals struck within the business community, which in many cases can only ramp up prices knowing the public sector is the ultimate buyer.

Inside Threadneedle Street, policymakers expect everyone – consumers, government and business – to cave in to sellers’ demands. And that many of the UK’s 33 million workers will subsequently demand big pay rises to compensate.

Yet it must be possible that all three consumer groups will adopt the slogan Can’t Pay, Won’t Pay, limiting the rise in inflation and eliminating the need for elevated pay rises.

Even if the poor, financially bombed-out household consumer is the only one to take a stand against greedy corporates, inflation will not hit the heights forecast by the Bank of England. In the meantime, it might have raised interest rates too far, laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy.
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.summary: Bank of England has forecast inflation to rise to 5% next spring. But it is not clear if the economy is sclerotic or productive spare capacity. The Bank ofEngland is raising interest rates again to curb inflation.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: LGBTQ+ protesters defy crackdown in Turkey to march with Cop31 activists
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Damien Gayle, Graham Readfearn and Gabrielle Canon in Antalya, Turkey
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Civil society campaigners form protective cordon around LGBTQ+ campaigners as they unfurl flags and placards

Queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march on Saturday in the city hosting this year’s climate summit.

Turkey’s LGBTQ+ groups have faced increased persecution since September, with police targeting activists in their homes or at the offices of the NGOs that advocate for their rights.

But on Saturday afternoon, civil society campaigners from around the world that had gathered in Antalya for the UN climate summit formed a cordon around them as they unfurled rainbow flags.

Őzgǔr, a 20-year-old Turkish LGBTQ+ activist, marched defiantly with a rainbow flag wrapped over her shoulders. She said holding the flag “feels a bit dangerous” and that usually police would not allow it.

“It feels like I am living in a prison in this country. I am running all the time,” she said. “We can do this because the eyes of the international media are here.”

Another activist, who gave her name only as Beren, added: “I feel very excited about being able to wave the flag, but I would love my friend to be here. She is detained right now because she is trans.”

Turkish police ran a massive security operation around the march. Attenders were frisked twice and had bags searched on the way into Aydin Kanza Park, where the protest gathered. The entire route was cordoned off with steel barriers to prevent anyone entering or leaving until the end.

Police examined the slogans on protesters’ placards and in some cases photographed them. “We have all been told we have to bring our passports,” said Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. “Our bags are being searched.

“It’s a very, very difficult time for Turkish movements who have faced a wave of repression. And so this is an important moment for us as the international movement to create some space for Turkish voices to be heard.”

The inclusion of LGBTQ+ activists on the march was carefully planned in advance. Protest organisers ensured that flags would be available, but they were not unfurled until the activists were safely surrounded by civil society groups and media.

Lucia Posteraro, a consultant at the International Federation of Human Rights, said: “The international organisations have been closely following the LGBT block to make sure there will not be any coercion actions from the security forces.”

Turkish environmental activists who joined the march said it also gave them space to highlight issues. “This march is very important because there are active local grassroots movements who are fighting to protect their villages, their forests, and they need to see the solidarity and the support from the international community,” said Özlem Katısöz of Climate Action Network in Turkey.

Activists from around the globe chanted, danced to trombones, walked on stilts and unfurled giant banners. “We defend life,” read one. A gold-plated bronze statue showed a naked Donald Trump being carried on the shoulders of a diminutive man, to represent the rich world’s exploitation of the poor.

“It’s so hot,” Greenpeace volunteer Ufuk Anil said, pulling off the large head of his polar bear costume. He had travelled from Istanbul to march in the head-to-toe animal suit, and in the midst of a muggy afternoon rainstorm he said it carried a dual message: “It is getting hotter and hotter every day,” Anil said, wiping sweat from his face. “We need to keep 1.5 alive.”

Anil said he was marching to call attention to an underwhelming climate agenda in Turkey and the continued import of plastics. But mostly he came on behalf of his young daughter. “I would like her to live in a much greener planet – much cooler,” he said. “We have to do it now – we don’t have much time.”

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

The protest was also an opportunity for activists from other countries with restricted civil space to draw attention to their campaigns. Triana Kurnia Wardani, of the Indonesian democratic women’s organisation Seruni, said she was marching to draw attention to the forest and land fires in her country that had been burning for months.

“Indonesia is burning right now. We have so many victims of the haze,” she said. “When we take action in our country, we get harassed by police. Our social media posts get blocked, so it is blocked from international attention.”

The march comes as the Cop31 summit reached its halfway point, with little progress yet made on substantive issues. Aditi Tiwari, the youth engagement leader at Voice of Aroha, said she still felt Cop could make a difference.

“Despite all the controversies, I think this is where we have the most influence, where we can make our voices heard by the world leaders who make those influential decisions,” she said. “So here’s to hoping that this Cop is way different than the rest and we can [have] some hopeful outcomes.”

Louise Hutchins, a co-convener of the Make Polluters Pay international coalition, said: “Yesterday, we stood with the UN secretary-general, who told us: ‘You’re on the right side of history. Keep going.’

“Today, we’re back on the streets at Cop31 with thousands of people from around the world, demanding that governments make polluters pay. We promised to keep up the fight. And we won’t stop until we win climate justice.”

Negotiations were still under way at the conference centre. Simon Stiell, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, urged countries to “move swiftly to the hardest issues to avoid tactical delays”.

“There is no collective success without compromise from every party,” Stiell said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: EU calls for immediate humanitarian access to Gaza
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The European Union has urged Israel to reopen all Gaza border crossings and grant “immediate, unimpeded access” for aid groups to provide humanitarian relief in the territory following devastating flooding in Gaza this week.

Civilian infrastructure and medical facilities in Gaza “must be protected,” said an EU statement released on Saturday by the office of Kaja Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and the Vice-President of the European Commission.

The EU call came as an Israeli drone attack killed two more Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday.

The drone struck them as they walked down a street in Jabaliya on the northern edge of Gaza City, according to Mohamed Abu Selmiya, director of Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, where the casualties were taken. The American field hospital said several other people were wounded but did not provide a number.

The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas “militants” in the area.

An Israeli air attack on Thursday at the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza killed at least six Palestinians, including a surgeon, and left dozens wounded.

“The EU underlines the need to respect international law, including international humanitarian law, at all times,” the 27-nation bloc said on Saturday. “This includes the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as medical personnel and facilities. The recent airstrike on the Nasser Hospital is deeply alarming,” it added.

Damage from Israeli attacks on Gaza’s infrastructure has worsened floods caused by heavy rain, which have submerged large areas of the enclave, local officials and the UN said this week. Gaza’s media office reported that more than 700km of Gaza’s sewage network has been destroyed.

Heavy rain has directly affected at least 106,000 people in Gaza in recent days, according to the UN children’s agency, UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged and latrines overflowing into camps.

In response, the EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies, and humanitarian organisations including NGOs, and comply with all its obligations under international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law.”

The EU reaffirmed “its commitment to the two-state solution” and called for “the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza” as it called for “sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance and early recovery support at scale” to ease the worsening humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/asian-.title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/asian-.author: Kate Park
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/asian-.text:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.

On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed.

Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry.

China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday, a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.

Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters’ review of procurement notices, investment plans and corporate disclosures. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain.

In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration.

In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing.  The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case.

South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects.  Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report.

Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media. Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project.

In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwn8.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwn8.text:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.

The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment.

Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/po.title: Ground Stop Highlights Chronic Vulnerabilities in Air Traffic System
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/po.author: Karoun Demirjian
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/po.text:
U.S. Flight Disruptions

The Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure has had several disruptive failures in recent months, as officials have sought to make upgrades.

Reporting from Washington

The ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure, which has had several disruptive failures in recent months.

Two months ago, a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line.

The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the F.A.A. has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures. Officials said it was prompted by efforts to replace an outdated router, which caused circuits in the national air traffic network to become overloaded and fail, interrupting communication lines between air traffic controllers and pilots.

By Saturday, thousands of flights had been canceled, and airports were still crowded with stranded travelers. The recovery will most likely take days, as airlines rebook passengers and reposition planes.

Friday’s breakdown, and the earlier episodes, have underscored the structural vulnerabilities that hamper controllers’ ability to safely manage flight traffic, even after improvements. And they have raised questions about whether federal authorities have done enough to create backup systems to prevent disruptive or catastrophic failures.

Friday’s incident touched off a blame game in Washington. Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, accused Congress of failing to pony up for systemwide upgrades.

Karoun Demirjian is a breaking news reporter for The Times.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Italy fines Meta $880m over photo privacy
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Italian regulators have fined Meta 805 million euros ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their consent.

The Facebook app on Android devices “accessed photos, videos and associated metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without specific consent and without informing them”, Garante, the Italian data privacy authority, said Saturday.

The issue relates specifically to the “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook” feature, which suggests photos and videos from the phone’s gallery for posting while browsing.

This feature violates the Italian law implementing the EU’s ePrivacy directive, the authority said.

Garante said the app’s process for collecting consent is too generic and does not allow users to fully understand the specific permissions they are allowing by accepting. The suggestions option was also enabled by default.

The figure of 805 million euros is by far the largest fine ever imposed by the Italian regulator.

Garante said Meta must fix the unclear consent notification and disable it being set by default, suggesting that roughly 20 million Italian Android users could have been affected by it.

The regulator also highlighted a “lack of cooperation” by Meta and said an earlier violation, which resulted in a 2019 fine, was a contributing factor in their decision.

The amount is roughly 0.47 percent of Meta’s global turnover.

The proceedings did not address the possible use of content to train artificial intelligence, which Meta denies.

Meta has not yet publicly commented on the matter, and it has the right to appeal the regulator’s decision.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.author: Matthew Mpoke Bigg
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.text:
Analysts had warned that the vote, originally set for December, faced a legitimacy crisis. South Sudan has not held a national election since gaining independence in 2011.

By Matthew Mpoke Bigg

Reporting from Nairobi, Kenya

Officials in South Sudan, the world’s youngest state, said on Saturday that its first national election would be postponed, raising new questions about a vote that analysts had already said could not yield a credible result.

The National Elections Commission said in a statement that the presidential and legislative elections, which had been scheduled for Dec. 22, would be held on Feb. 11 instead. The country’s information minister, Ateny Wek Ateny, said the postponement would allow more time to register voters and educate them about the process.

South Sudan has never held a national election. Since gaining independence from Sudan in 2011 after decades of war, it has been ruled by President Salva Kiir, and it has faced seemingly intractable political difficulties.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.title: FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.author: Ava Berger
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.text:
A person looks at a departures board showing delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City.

Friday's nationwide ground stop was declared after an error occurred while a contractor was updating an old Federal Aviation Administration telecommunication line, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.

L3Harris, a long time contractor for the
Federal Aviation Administration, was doing routine maintenance in at least one of FAA's remote locations changing copper wire to fiber, he said. Duffy said the routers in these facilities were manufactured in 2001. These updates have been happening in American institutions for decades, Duffy said.

"Virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital," Duffy said. "Just maybe the FAA is the last one to be doing this work because the investments haven't been made, but this is not complicated."

L3Harris did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment.

Duffy said the FAA is still investigating the exact error that started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system.

"It's pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location. So what we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?"

Bryan Bedford, the FAA administrator, who joined Duffy at the briefing said there was no evidence of anything nefarious happening or AI-related issues.

Tens of thousands of passengers across the U.S. are still stranded Saturday after a rare ground stop halted all flights.

The chaos is expected to linger for days.

The aviation system is back online and slowly returning to normal Saturday morning, but delays and cancellations will continue after yesterday's nationwide ground stop, Duffy said in the press briefing Saturday.

"Based on everything that we're hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they'll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday," Bedford said.

Duffy told reporters Friday night: "I think we're going to be back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving."

For about four hours on Friday, thousands of flights at U.S. airports were grounded in one of the biggest disruptions of the nation's air travel system since the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001.

Nearly 25,000 flights were delayed, and over 9,000 were cancelled on Friday, according to FlightAware, a flight tracking site. The disruption seeped into Saturday morning with more than 4,000 cancellations recorded. That's 14% of flights departing the U.S., according to data from Cirium, which tracks aviation analytics.

Duffy said Friday that air traffic control facilities had experienced "intermittent" outages of their radar and communications systems beginning earlier in the afternoon. Duffy blamed "old switches, old routers" for the failures. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin joined Duffy in the White House briefing room and said there was no evidence the issue was due to an attack.

Flight boards at airports across the country Saturday morning continued to be riddled with red cancelled marks. At Tampa International Airport in Florida, people in the main terminal area before security curled up in chairs to grab a wink of sleep.

On Friday night, a flight board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in D.C. showed dozens of flights delayed into the early morning hours or cancelled.

Passengers Erin and Jake Britt spent half the day at the airport in D.C. on Friday. Their plane to Fort Lauderdale, Fla. boarded at 3 p.m. By 5:30 p.m., they were getting off the plane — but they were still in D.C.

"Overall, our plane was definitely annoyed, but reasonable," Erin Britt said, as the couple left the airport at 8pm. "People being upset and asking like, 'Well, how are you not prepared for this?' And it was like, 'Well, no one was prepared.'"

She said neither the pilot nor flight attendants had any more information than passengers."They seem just as in the dark," she said.

The pair decided to cancel their weekend trip, but the night didn't end there. They spent over nine hours overnight waiting on the JetBlue customer service call line to be reimbursed. "I was setting alarms in 20 minute intervals in case I fell asleep," Erin Britt said.

For people who had events or plans over the weekend – the delay added an extra layer of stress. Joe Romano and Maddie Cabana had a cruise leaving Orlando, Fla. Saturday afternoon.

"It was a big eye roll. I mean, I travel a lot for work already, so I'm constantly dealing with flight delays," Romano said. "When this happened, I was just like, 'Of course, it always happens to me.'"

"Just rather inconvenient and frustrating," Cabana added, as the pair contemplated checking their bags or going home. "Hopefully, everything will be fine. It'll all work out. It always does."

And it did – eventually. After their JetBlue flight was ultimately cancelled, they quickly booked another one on Southwest Airlines and made it early Saturday morning.

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, DC on November 13, 2026.

Others, like Suze DiPietro decided flying wasn't worth it anymore. Her husband drove about four hours down from Ocean City, New Jersey to pick her up in D.C. Luckily, they had friends in the area where they spent the night.

"My husband, my hero, is driving down from New Jersey to come get me," DiPietro said.

Other alternatives included people switching to Amtrak trains as they struggled to get to their destination. Although, even Amtrak's system had a brief outage Friday night.

This was only the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001. The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.

That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.

The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.

"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.
