He was investigated in 2003 over alleged sexual misconduct involving female colleagues. He had been given a financial penalty of two weeks' pay, and was suspended on full pay.

https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/.title: Democrats push back on Duffy’s demand for $50 billion to upgrade air traffic systems.
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/.author: Annie Karni
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/.text:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said work to transition from copper to fiber optic cable in a remote facility caused a router to overload the system. It was unknown if the flaw was with the equipment or installation, he said.

Karoun DemirjianNiraj ChokshiHari Raj and Ryley Ober

Federal officials said the cascading communications failures that forced the government to shut down flights across the United States on Friday started with a contractor upgrading air traffic control equipment, replacing copper wire with fiber optic cable.

The upgrade set off communications failures across the facilities that manage the national air space, the officials said. Alarmed at the scope of the problem, the Federal Aviation Administration decided to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for several hours.

Speaking at news conference in Washington, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the specific problem with the upgrade, which took place in what he called a “remote” facility, was not yet known. The contractor, L3Harris, has worked for the Federal Aviation Administration for decades, he said.

Mr. Duffy said his agency was trying to determine whether the problem had been caused by the contractor’s incompetence or faulty equipment. “We haven’t determined what the fault was,” he said. He added, “We’re going to hold people accountable.”

The F.A.A. administrator, Bryan Bedford, said there was no evidence the communication problems had stemmed from a cyberattack or the use of artificial intelligence.

Mr. Bedford said that he expected the system to be back to normal by Sunday night. “The worst is behind us,” he said.

But even though the system came back online Friday evening, the effects of the shutdown were vast and continued on Saturday.

Travelers across the United States were still facing delays and cancellations on Saturday as airlines and airports struggled to recover from the ground stop.

At least 3,000 flights scheduled for Saturday were canceled, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. At Chicago O’Hare International Airport, a ground stop was issued for United Airlines flights.

Mr. Duffy again called on lawmakers to fully fund upgrades that he said were needed to prevent similar failures. To upgrade aging air traffic facilities and technology, he said, he wanted another $50 billion from the Republican-controlled Congress, which last year approved $12.5 billion for the project.

Here’s what else to know:

If your flight is canceled: You are entitled to a refund if your flight is canceled in the United States, regardless of the reason, or if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and you decide not to take it. Here are other travel tips that might be helpful. Read more ›

Handling the chaos: Radio transmissions between air traffic controllers and pilots at major airports offered a peek at how they navigated the ground stop. Read more ›

Rare halt: Friday’s nationwide ground stop was only the third that the F.A.A. has issued this century. It ranks as the second-longest, after the stop issued in the wake of the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001. There was a shorter one on Jan. 11, 2023, because of an outage in the F.A.A.’s safety-alert system. Read more ›

Democrats’ response: Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House’s top-ranking Democrat, said the stop was “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents” under the Trump administration. He added that Americans deserved timely answers about how and why it happened.

Reporting from Washington

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, on Friday requested $50 billion for a “complete overhaul” of the aging air traffic control system, laying much of the blame on Congress after flights across the nation were halted for hours.

Mr. Duffy’s demand thrust the funding issue to the forefront of the final days of Republican control on Capitol Hill.

Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Saturday morning that he would seek to add more funding for the Federal Aviation Administration into an “aggressive legislative package” he planned to put forth in the lame-duck session of Congress.

Democrats said the Trump administration had plenty of money it could put toward improving an outdated air traffic control system — funds it was using instead for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. They said Congress needed to begin investigating the failures of the Trump administration.

Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion to help pay for upgrades to the air traffic communications system. Republican lawmakers have introduced the Modern Skies Act in the House and Senate, a bill that would authorize another $30 billion in upgrades.

That bill seeks to allocate $10.1 billon for air traffic control modernization, $10 billion for control towers and airport improvements, and another $10 billion for an aging terminal pilot program.

But the bill has no Democratic co-sponsors. And on Friday night, Democrats said the airport crisis was caused by how the Trump administration had allocated money and overseen the F.A.A.

Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said that Mr. Duffy’s request for another $50 billion was alarming, given that Republicans had “showered ICE with billions in funding.”

He added that “if this administration is serious about aviation safety, it should stop making excuses and work with Congress to put taxpayer dollars where they’re actually needed.”

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, blamed the breakdown on the Trump administration.

“From Day 1, instead of taking responsibility, MAGA extremists have fired and scapegoated hard-working federal employees whose job it is to keep our skies safe, particularly women and people of color,” he said.

House Democrats promised an investigation next year into how air traffic was brought to a standstill. “Preserve all documents and emails,” Democrats on the committee overseeing homeland security and the Transportation Security Administration wrote online. “Oversight is coming.”

Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, the senior Democrat on the subcommittee overseeing aviation, demanded a thorough investigation into the F.A.A.

Mr. Johnson, however, said that “we don’t really need any investigation to understand we need further investment.”

At a news conference on Friday night, Mr. Duffy said the issues were not partisan.

“It’s not Democrat, it’s not Republican. It’s American,” he said. “Give us the money to fix it.”

Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs

At the Detroit airport — long one of my favorites because of the bright red tram and, more recently, a chance run-in with ex-NBA star Jalen Rose — travelers have packed the food courts and bars as they wait for flights, delayed or otherwise.

The televisions next to the airport outpost of Buddy’s, which lays claim to inventing Detroit-style pizza, are playing the Saturday afternoon slate of college football games, including, of course, the University of Michigan’s matchup with Oregon.

On Saturday afternoon, San Francisco International Airport still showed the effects of a ground stop called by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday. Crowds were moderate, travelers were sleeping in gates and hallways of the airport and the screens showed many delays and cancellations.

Thousands of passengers scrambled to update their travel plans on Saturday as air traffic slowly unsnarled after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but a number of travelers had already arrived at their destinations on flights left unaffected by the order.

Dozens of international flights took to the skies even as airports across the United States coped with only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration this century. Certain flights were also permitted to depart from the West Coast to Hawaii during the stoppage.

Here’s why some air travel was allowed to proceed even as flight systems were hampered.

More than 8,200 flights were canceled nationwide on Friday — over 31 percent of those scheduled — according to Cirium, an aviation data firm.

But more than 60 flights bound for overseas left the United States during the stoppage, according to Flightradar24, an aviation tracking site.

There are 21 air traffic control facilities, 20 in the contiguous United States and one in Alaska, that oversee swaths of regions throughout the country, according to the F.A.A.

As some of those centers recovered, flights were “allowed to depart through coordination with the Air Traffic Control System Command Center,” the F.A.A. said in an advisory less than two hours after the ground stop was ordered.

Flights departing for Europe from the Midwest or the East Coast can communicate with the Canadian authorities, said Dan Bubb, a former commercial pilot and an aviation history professor at the University of Las Vegas, Nevada.

Additionally, air traffic over the open ocean is less congested compared with that of the contiguous United States, he said.

Nick Daniels, the president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, said that for planes traveling such a large distance over oceanic airspace, “they have process procedures, different standards of separations, than what we do to run the volume of air traffic” in the lower 48 states.

At 3 p.m. Pacific Standard Time on Friday, about two hours before the nationwide ground stop was lifted, San Francisco International Airport said that Pacific-bound flights, including to Hawaii and Asia, had been cleared for departure.

Why were passengers flying west so fortunate?

Those pilots generally will talk to one of the regional centers until reaching cruising altitude, Dr. Bubb said.

Centers handling air traffic headed to Hawaii or Asia are outside the contiguous United States, and therefore could avoid long delays from the ground stop, he said. At a certain altitude, a pilot could swap communications with California controllers for those in Hawaii or Alaska, he added.

Flights within Alaska, those from the West Coast to Hawaii and international flights from Honolulu were also exempt from the ground stop, Alaska Airlines said in statement.

Areas like Alaska, Guam and Hawaii are far enough removed that they can remain stable even as systems are affected in the contiguous United States, Mr. Daniels said.

“If they would have seen any kind of risk in the system there as well, then they would have reacted the same to reduce the capacity,” he added.

During ground stops and delays, emergency and medical aircraft are given clearance to take off.

Life Flight Network, a medical transport service, said in a social media post on Friday that “EMS aircraft are exempt from this restriction,” and its services were operating normally.

“Above all is medevac and law enforcement,” Mr. Daniels said. “They get a priority movement throughout the system, and we move other aircraft out of their way, versus, they need to get in line with everyone else.”

Pilots and controllers have many tools to communicate, Dr. Bubb said.

Pilots can talk to one another, their companies and ground control through different messaging systems even if one fails.

“There are redundant systems where pilots can talk to each other, and we can sequence ourselves, but we follow the instructions that we were given by air traffic control,” Dr. Bubb said.

At about 11 a.m. inside the Tom Bradley international terminal at Los Angeles International Airport, the check-in area flight boards showed no delays and things appeared to be moving smoothly.

L3Harris, the federal contractor that was updating air traffic control equipment prior to the nationwide outage, said in a statement that they took the nationwide ground stop seriously. The contractor said it had completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. The company added it was supporting the F.A.A. in its investigation.

Madison Malone Kircher

The National Football League said this weekend’s games would go forward as planned, but that the league had “adjusted its officiating assignments” by “reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” Brian McCarthy, a spokesman, wrote in an email.

Madison Malone Kircher

As the effects of Friday’s ground stop continue to ripple outward, Princess Cruises said it would delay departure times for three ships set to leave from U.S. ports on Saturday to allow passengers extra time to account for travel delays. The postponed sail times would not affect cruise itineraries, a spokesperson wrote in an email.

Madison Malone Kircher and Miles G. Cohen

Travelers across the United States on Saturday morning were still feeling the frustrating, plan-ruining aftershocks of the ground stop that halted air travel for hours on Friday.

“I’ve been right here for 20 hours,” said Jasmine Harp, a passenger at Kennedy International Airport in New York. “I have not showered, I have not slept. It’s torture.”

Ms. Harp, 25, was going on 48 hours of travel, trying to get home to Detroit after spending a week in Paris for her birthday.

She had just sat down in her airplane seat on Friday when the pilot told passengers to deplane. A few hours later, the flight was canceled. She described a mad dash to the baggage claim, where passengers worked to secure their luggage.

“They just dumped everybody’s bags off all at once,” she said. “It was chaotic.”

To make matters worse, Ms. Harp had left the gate area but still had to wait for her rebooked flight, which was to depart at 3 p.m. the next day. That meant no restaurants, no shops and, most uncomfortably, no seats. She found a luggage counter to perch on.

“I wish they would let me in the lounge,” she said Saturday morning, as she broke out some trail mix that she had rationed throughout the night.

Antonio Alemán, 39, whose transfer to Lima, Peru, was canceled late on Friday, spent an uncomfortable night at the same airport. The airline, Latam, rebooked him on a flight for Tuesday. “I don’t know where I will stay until then,” he said.

Further south, the scene at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport looked, at first glance, as if it might have been a typical Saturday morning, with passengers checking bags and waiting at security checkpoints.

A closer inspection, however, revealed travelers sleeping in the airport’s quiet corners, departure screens speckled with cancellation and delay notices, and backups at customer service desks.

Barefoot and sprawled out on the carpeted floor in Hartsfield-Jackson’s central atrium, Glory Agunbiade, 16, and her mother, Itanola Agunbiade, 56, had managed to steal four or five hours of sleep after their Friday flight to Indianapolis was canceled.

From their makeshift campsite — they each used their bags as pillows — the pair bickered over how the federal government had handled Friday’s ground stop. While the elder Ms. Agunbiade saw the decision to halt flights as a necessary precaution and said it was “not anybody’s fault,” her teenage daughter was more frustrated.

“It’s like all we know is that the problem was about communication,” the younger Ms. Agunbiade said. “I feel like we’re entitled to more information.”

In Chicago, Pedro and Aorbys Vasquez were resting at O’Hare International Airport on Saturday, more than 12 hours after their connecting flight to Paris was supposed to leave. Their original flight was delayed six times before it was finally canceled. By that point, they could not find an available hotel room.

The couple slept in seats with nothing more than neck pillows to comfort them. Their new flight is scheduled for 6:45 p.m., 24 hours after they were originally scheduled to depart.

Looking at the bright side of an experience he called exhausting, Vasquez joked, “at least we shouldn’t have a problem sleeping on our flight.”

Robert Chiarito and Sean Keenan contributed reporting.

Randy Near, 58, a home inspector from Washington State, was furious on Saturday as he waited with a pile of luggage, while his 24-year-old son Charlie stood in the line at Terminal 3 at Los Angeles International Airport with dozens of people, hoping to get them on the next flight home to Seattle.  He hadn’t slept in 36 hours.

“Look, our entire infrastructure, from the highway system to the F.A.A., is a joke,” he said. “You go to any other Western country, and they have Wi-Fi, fiber optics, good freeways, good bridges, and we are here living in the freaking dark ages and being force-fed this lie that we are somehow the greatest country in the world.”

“Both parties pay a lot of lip service to bills that support infrastructure in this country, and as soon as soon as they get elected, that sort of stuff gets forgotten,” he added.

The communications failures that prompted Federal Aviation Administration officials to issue a nationwide ground stop started when L3 Harris, a contractor managing the agency’s telecoms network, made a standard upgrade at a remote air traffic location, federal officials said Saturday.

The contractor was conducting work on Friday that was needed to replace aging analog copper wire with more modern fiber optic cable, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, told reporters. The “routine” task was being done at a location remote and small enough that officials assumed a Friday afternoon upgrade would pose no meaningful disruption to the air traffic, he said.

That presumption proved wrong, as the changeover from copper to fiber started flooding the system with levels of data it could not handle, triggering a cascade of communications failures across the air traffic facilities that manage the national air space. Officials, alarmed at the scope of the problems, decided to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for hours.

As of Saturday morning, administration officials still have not determined whether L3 Harris or shoddy equipment was at fault.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning it was user error or installer error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router?” Mr. Duffy told reporters. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

Representatives for L3 Harris did not immediately return email and phone requests for comment on Saturday.

L3 Harris has been managing the F.A.A.’s effort to shift its antiquated communications system of analog copper lines to a nationwide network of fiber optic cable. Earlier this month, the company boasted that they had completed such upgrades at 70 percent of air traffic control facilities, a figure that F.A.A. administrator Bryan Bedford echoed at Saturday’s news conference.

Such upgrades — which Mr. Bedford characterized as “sustainment,” not modernization — are vital to ensure that the air traffic control system can operate safely, he and Mr. Duffy told reporters.

Officials were sure, Mr. Duffy said, that they had identified the origin of the problem; for instance, when they isolated the location and took it offline, the system’s functionality was restored. There was no evidence that nefarious activity, or the agency’s recent efforts to outfit its air traffic control facilities with assistive A.I. technology, had played a role in triggering Friday’s problems, he and Mr. Bedford added.

But the episode raises serious questions about how well the F.A.A. understands the potential vulnerabilities of their existing network as it makes patches and upgrades to antiquated technology.

The routers in air traffic control facilities, which became overloaded with over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, were mostly manufactured in 2001, Mr. Duffy said, and were out of service by 2006.

“Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration? Or was it just a bad piece of faulty technology?” Mr. Bedford said, without offering a conclusion.

He added that officials would have to reassess their protocols, and “pivot” in the future to avoid causing similar sweeping problems when upgrading equipment.

Traffic at Los Angeles International Airport was robust on Saturday, with travelers being dropped off curbside. Airplanes appeared to be taking off and landing at a slower pace than on a normal day. Inside Terminal 3, Delta check-in counters were jammed with travelers dropping off bags. The departures and arrivals screens showed several canceled flights, but a majority of flights were listed as boarding, at the gate or on time.

The near-total shutdown of the nation’s airspace ended on Friday evening, but its ripple effects continued into Saturday as airlines canceled thousands of flights.

By Saturday morning, almost 15 percent of the day’s flights had been scrapped, and the number was still climbing. The recovery will most likely last for days as airlines work to juggle their schedules, rebook passengers and reposition planes.

Aviation functions like a relay race. To work well, many things have to align in the same place at the same time, including the availability of planes, crews and an open airport gate.

On Friday, thousands of planes were pulled from the air, filling up limited space on the ground. Many returned to the airports they had just left, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. Jets at crowded airports weren’t allowed to depart and sat idle while flight crews quickly hit their legal working limits.

Pilots are generally limited to eight or nine hours of flying and a total shift length of 9 to 14 hours, though union contracts and airline policies often shrink those windows. Flight attendants are also governed by limits on the length of their shift. Both must receive lengthy breaks in between shifts, too.

For instance, a pilot who was scheduled to fly from New York to Miami on Friday night could easily have timed out while waiting for the ground stop to end. That would have left the airline struggling to find replacement pilots not only for the flight from New York, but also for the flight that pilot was scheduled to operate out of Miami on Saturday. Multiply that by hundreds and airline schedules can quickly implode.

Take N865DN, the tail number for a Boeing 737 operated by Delta Air Lines. It started Friday flying from Charleston, S.C., to Atlanta. From there, it made round trip flights to Louisville, Ky., and Norfolk, Va., returning to Atlanta, according to Flightradar24, a flight-tracking service.

The plane was supposed to fly on to Savannah, Ga., back to Atlanta, and then to Chicago, where it would start the day on Saturday. But it never made those last three flights.

Delta rebuilt its Saturday plan, with the plane scheduled to fly from Atlanta to Spokane, Wash., and on to Salt Lake City and Raleigh-Durham, N.C.

For minor disruptions, airlines can play catch-up by restarting flights and trying to make up for lost time. But bigger disruptions, such as the one that occurred Friday, often require resetting the network by proactively canceling many flights.

We're standing at the gate in Charlotte waiting on one flight attendant for our flight to Dallas. The rest of the flight crew is waiting with us, neither the captain nor the gate agents can get through to scheduling even though five attendants have volunteered to take the empty slot. As delays stack up, the flight crew waiting with us is at risk of timing out if scheduling cannot get a flight attendant assigned to our flight in time, then the cycle will restart.

Here is a case study - Yesterday Friday, United had 3 flights to Frankfurt from SFO.  1:50pm flight was cancelled at 4:50pm (crew timeout?). 2:45pm flight operated by partner Lufthansa departed at 4:30pm. 6:45pm flight departed at 7:15pm — including a handful of passengers from the cancelled flight. Today Saturday, the SFO-FRA flights are on time (so far) and packed full, no empty seats. Every Saturday morning connection to Houston, Chicago, or Washington Dulles was cancelled (due to no aircraft or no crew?). So no good way to connect through to FRA today. Bottom line - two and one-quarter flights worth of originally scheduled passengers got to Frankfurt on yesterday’s two flights.  Perhaps a handful more from yesterday got onto today’s flights.  International carriers were able to get out more or less on time yesterday. In my view, the airlines have done an amazing job of handling chaos and desnarling a thicket of misplaced crew, planes, and passengers.

My wife and I dealt with a very short weather related ground stop at DFW a few years ago.  I think the total time flights were affected was about one hour.  Our American flight was delayed and then eventually canceled as a result. No matter how many times we were rebooked, the flights we were supposed to take never showed up due to ripple effects throughout the American Airlines system or if the plane did make it, the flight was canceled because the crew hours had timed out.   We spent three nights at the airport, two on our dime to buy a local motel room, and one sleeping on the carpet on the skytrain level.  This was just one airport, one just short ground stop, and just one airline. My advice to the folks who are experiencing a far greater systemwide disruption that may take weeks to get everyone to their ultimate destinations?   Go to the rental counter right now, rent the cheapest car you can find, and drive home.Nick in Palm Springs

At long last, the line to pick up luggage checked for Friday flights is shrinking, baggage claim carousels are whirling, and departure screens are becoming slightly less colorful. The Atlanta airport is starting to look like its old self.

The balcony in Hartsfield-Jackson’s central atrium remains a sort of campsite for weary travelers whose flights have been delayed or canceled. Some bought neck pillows and blankets downstairs. Others claimed the airport’s complimentary wheelchairs. Most slept on their luggage.

The security line at O’Hare’s Terminal One, from which United Airlines operates, was virtually nonexistent Saturday at 10:50 a.m. local time. Possibly because most United Airlines flights appear to be delayed or canceled.

The F.A.A. has not extended a ground stop for United Airlines flights at Chicago O’Hare International Airport, which was scheduled to end at 11 a.m. Eastern, according to an agency alert. About 13 percent of the 616 United flights scheduled to depart from the airport have been canceled as of 11:20 a.m., according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. United is headquartered in Chicago.

As of 11:30 a.m. Eastern, over 3,900 flights — or about 17 percent of total departures scheduled for Saturday — have been canceled nationwide, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, repeatedly stressed throughout his news conference that he would choose safety over inconvenience, acknowledging that passengers will miss weddings, birthday parties and work trips this weekend.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, has now twice mentioned that college football games have been disrupted by the fight cancellations and delays caused by Friday’s ground stop.

Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administator, said no air traffic facilities went entirely dark, but the F.A.A. received reports of certain frequencies going in and out. The issue popped up in more than 10 facilities. That’s when the F.A.A. realized something larger was going on and ordered a national ground stop.

Madison Malone Kircher

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said his agency was able to isolate the location where the faulty upgrade work was done and take it offline. “We feel very comfortable that was the root cause,” Duffy said. “It wasn’t a foreign actor.” He said what happened Friday raised questions for the contractor, L3 Harris, about what went wrong. “We’re going to hold people accountable,” he said.

Madison Malone Kircher

The F.A.A. administrator, Bryan Bedford, said his agency had ruled out the possibility of a cyberattack as the cause. “We’ve all concluded it’s not a cyber issue,” he said.

The nationwide ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening has highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure that has had several disruptive failures in recent months.

Officials called the rare ground stop after outdated communications lines became overloaded and began to fail, interrupting communication lines between air traffic controllers and pilots, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

The breakdown occurred less than two months after a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush International Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line.

The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the F.A.A. has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures. The F.A.A. has yet to identify precisely what caused communication lines to falter.

But the successive episodes have underscored the structural vulnerabilities that continue to hamper air traffic controllers’ ability to safely manage flight traffic, even after concerted efforts to make improvements. And they raised questions about whether the federal authorities have done enough to create backup systems and redundancies to prevent disruptive or even catastrophic failures.

For decades, the air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks and alphabetical keyboards so old that the F.A.A. has difficulty sourcing spare parts. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding to help pay for upgrades, after a series of outages in air traffic control facilities, including the one serving Newark Liberty International Airport, caused alarming losses of radar and other communications capabilities.

Earlier this month, L3 Harris, the primary telecoms contractor tasked to manage the system upgrades, boasted on its website that it had converted about 70 percent of the copper line to fiber optic cable; last week, the F.A.A. announced it would begin to phase out floppy disks.

But the disruptions in recent weeks showed that those upgrades had serious vulnerabilities themselves.

In September, when a circuit at a regional air traffic facility failed, operators had no backup options beyond the fiber line, 600 feet of which they discovered — to their surprise — had been severed by a construction crew in New Jersey working on Amtrak project. More than 430 flights were canceled before the system was fixed several hours later.

A similar incident occurred in October at the Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina, when a contractor working on plumbing accidentally severed a fiber line. The airport was forced to issue a ground stop for several hours. Just one day after that, officials were forced to issue a ground stop at George Bush International Airport, when yet another contractor inadvertently severed a fiber line.

The fiber line upgrades themselves, Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, told reporters at the time, were not enough to save the system from failure.

Ideally, the F.A.A. wanted to put data into cloud services, he told reporters then, so that “when you have a fiber cut, you have multiple pathways of backup.”

“Today we have physical fiber and when it’s cut, there’s one redundancy, and when we lose that, there’s no more redundancy,” he added.

Friday’s national ground stop revealed that the lack of redundancies in the F.A.A.’s system could trigger catastrophic failures in other ways and touched off a blame game in Washington. Mr. Duffy seized on the chaos to hammer Congress, saying it had failed to pony up enough funding to pay for systemwide upgrades.

“How many more times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?” he told reporters at the White House Friday night, asking that lawmakers approve $50 billion in emergency funds for the project. Their lack of action, he said, had forced his department to pursue patchwork upgrades that were insufficient. It was a dramatic increase in his demand for additional money, which for the past several months has hovered at $30 billion.

But lawmakers in both parties are raising questions about how efficiently Mr. Duffy and the F.A.A. have been spending the money they have already been given.

“Today’s unprecedented breakdown is the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents under the Trump administration’s failed leadership,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, said in a statement issued shortly after Mr. Duffy’s news conference, accusing the administration of failing to take responsibility for its failures in “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents.”

Madison Malone Kircher

“What we saw was instability, and we couldn’t explain the instability,” the F.A.A. administrator, Bryan Bedford, said. “That’s when we made the decision to ground stop out of an abundance of caution.”

Madison Malone Kircher

“We’re making transition not because we want to spend money, but because it is safer and more resilient,” Bedford said, answering a question about changing from copper wire to fiber optic cable.

Madison Malone Kircher

The F.A.A. administrator, Bryan Bedford, stressed that the problems were caused by an equipment issue with zero evidence of an A.I. issue.

Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, started his remarks by offering “a sincere apology to the American traveling public.” Duffy had thanked travelers for their patience in enduring Friday’s ground stop earlier in the news conference. Beford said that they expected to be back to normal by Sunday night. “The worst is behind us,” he said.

Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia.

Reporting from San Francisco

Many of Silicon Valley’s executives and investors are rallying behind Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday after revelations that he had affairs with an employee and with a woman whom U.S. officials believed to be a spy for China.

In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board of directors, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia. Mr. Huang’s exit, they argued, would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race. And they blamed Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive and the richest person in the world, said in a social media post on Saturday. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

The support put a spotlight on Nvidia’s role as the linchpin of the A.I. boom and on Mr. Huang’s leadership as the company grew into one of the most valuable in the world. Nvidia, which started making computer chips for video games, now controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy. Along the way, Mr. Huang became Silicon Valley’s consummate dealmaker, turning Nvidia into a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding.

“We believe the board should avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders,” Brad Gerstner, the chief executive of Altimeter Capital Management, and Gavin Baker, the chief investment officer of Atreides Management, wrote in a letter sent on Friday. The investors, whose firms are Nvidia shareholders, asked the company’s board to consider “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

An open letter to Nvidia’s board, titled “Stand With Jensen,” asked the board to reinstall Mr. Huang as chief executive, to conduct an independent investigation and to explain its actions. The Starship spacecraft safely landed back at the Starbase launch facility, a major step in SpaceX’s quest to build fully reusable rockets.

The latest test flight of Starship, SpaceX’s spacecraft, made history on Saturday afternoon, when its orbital craft re-entered Earth’s atmosphere and, for the first time, returned to the launchpad where it started.

At about 4:20 p.m. Eastern time, it slowed to a hover next to the launchpad tower and slid between two giant mechanical arms called “chopsticks,” which grabbed it out of midair.

This maneuver was a crucial step in SpaceX’s quest to make reusable rockets.

The launch: Liftoff from SpaceX’s Starbase launch site in South Texas occurred at 5:47 p.m. Eastern time on Friday. It was almost flawless. Once in orbit, the upper-stage Starship spacecraft deployed 26 of the company’s next-generation Starlink satellites. Read more ›

No booster catch: SpaceX had hoped to catch the bottom half of the rocket, the giant booster stage known as Super Heavy. After finishing its part of the flight two minutes after liftoff, the booster dropped away and headed back toward the launchpad. However, the booster detected a problem with its guidance and navigation control and instead performed a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico.

Heat shield: In an overnight update on its webcast, SpaceX reported that data from cameras on the ground and on two of the deployed Starlink satellites showed that the tiles that protected the underside of the Starship spacecraft from the fiery temperatures of re-entry were in good condition.

Today’s catch is a breakthrough for the possibility of fully reusing rockets, but experts say SpaceX has a long way to go before it can catch and launch again, given the potential damage to the heat shield and engines caused by falling through the atmosphere.

That was an amazing view, seeing the spacecraft drop out of the clouds, pivot to vertical, hover and then slide between the chopstick arms.

The catch was successful. Starship hovered next to the launchpad tower and slid between two giant mechanical arms called “chopsticks,” which grabbed it out of midair.

We’re hearing sonic booms.

SpaceX has decided to attempt the catch.

Starship has slowed to subsonic speeds.

The spacecraft has survived passage through maximum heating. It is now passing over Mexico and is eight minutes away from landing.

How can you land a rocket to use it again? On four legs? Or with parachutes?

What about … giant chopsticks?

SpaceX is on a quest to make spacecraft run like trains and airplanes. As part of this vision, it is counting on a tower with two mechanical arms called the “chopsticks” to catch its Starship spacecraft when it returns from orbit on Saturday.

If all goes according to plan, Starship will travel through the atmosphere faster than the speed of sound before being steered back into the tower it launched from in South Texas. There, the mechanical arms will squeeze it safely into place, like chopsticks holding a piece of sushi.

The company has already proved the arms can catch a rocket booster minutes after liftoff. But the Saturday attempt will be the first such landing for the upper-stage spacecraft, which is also called Starship but is often shortened to Ship.

The latest mission had to cancel an unprecedented “double-catch” attempt after its rocket booster was diverted on Friday for a water landing in the Gulf of Mexico.

Although catches will not be part of NASA’s Artemis III mission next year, a successful one on Saturday would be seen as a breakthrough for the potential of rockets to be repeatedly flown.

“But if something goes really wrong with Starship, it could take out the whole tower,” said Alistair John, director of the aerospace engineering program at the University of Sheffield in England. “It’s higher risk, higher reward.”

Joseph Gonzalez, a professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who worked on the Artemis II mission, said the arms offer a better chance to save a rocket for reuse than more traditional forms of landing.

Landing the rocket on legs tacks on weight and thus a need for more fuel. Parachute landings can add on days for an ocean recovery, Gonzalez said. The tower holds the promise of catching Ship in the exact place from where it could be launched again.

“Time is always of the essence, especially if you’re talking about rapid reusability,” Gonzalez said.

Still, John said, SpaceX has a ways to go to catch both parts of its rocket and launch them into space again.

The rocket’s heat shield will “take a beating” on its way down through the atmosphere on Saturday, and SpaceX will have to prove next that it and other key components like the engines are “OK to go again,” he said.

In the modern space race, China has successfully caught a rocket booster with giant nets. SpaceX already has a partially reusable Falcon 9 rocket, which can rapidly send satellites into orbit. Its booster lands on legs.

At the press viewing site, a SpaceX employee just handed out foam ear plugs. The returning spacecraft is expected to create a loud sonic boom.

So how will Starship make it home? SpaceX will fire the spacecraft’s engines to slow it down, so it can fall out of orbit. Then it will fall through the atmosphere, “a bit like a skydiver,” said Alistair John, the aerospace engineering director at the University of Sheffield in England.

Similar to a skydiver moving his arms and legs, four flaps deployed on the spacecraft will allow for slight steering. Air resistance slows it down in a big belly flop through the atmosphere. At the end, the engines will relight to flip the spacecraft vertically into a hover — and then hopefully right into the tower’s mechanical arms.

SpaceX’s Starship is slated to participate in its first NASA mission sometime in the second half of next year, as part of the space agency’s efforts to return humans to the moon.

NASA’s Artemis program aims to land astronauts on the lunar surface by the end of 2028, but the next mission, Artemis III, will stay in orbit around Earth. The main objective of this flight is to practice docking with two prototype lunar landers.

Artemis III is similar to what NASA did half a century ago with Apollo 9. That often overlooked mission provided a crucial check that the lander would work as designed.

During Artemis III, which is expected to last 14 to 17 days, four astronauts will launch inside the Orion capsule atop a Space Launch System rocket from Florida. Once in orbit, Orion will try to dock with the Blue Moon spacecraft built by Blue Origin, the space company started by Jeff Bezos. The astronauts will be able to enter a crew cabin on Blue Moon.

On the sixth day of the mission, SpaceX will launch a Starship. This spacecraft will largely be a run-of-the-mill version pulled off SpaceX’s assembly line, but with a docking port attached at the top.

The spacecraft will not include modifications like a crew cabin or a life support system, which will be needed for the lunar lander version. That means the Artemis III astronauts will not be able to enter Starship.

However, a successful docking will offer data on a change that SpaceX is seeking for the moon mission. Instead of Starship and Orion traveling separately to lunar orbit and docking there, SpaceX wants the two spacecraft to dock in low-Earth orbit, and then Starship would provide the propulsion to get them to the moon.

On the eighth day of the mission, Orion is expected to dock with Starship for two hours, in order to test whether the combined spacecraft will perform, considering that Orion was not originally designed for that configuration.

“It gives us critical data and allows us to really understand the forces of docking, how we’re going to push, how we’re going to work together,” Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, said during a news conference in October.

Parsons said he was also interested in another crucial demonstration that was planned for early next year, showing that ultracold liquid methane and liquid oxygen propellants can be transferred from one Starship to another.

Because Starship uses up most of its propellant just to reach orbit, it will need to refill its tanks before heading to the moon.

“This is going to be a first-of-its-kind SpaceX mission where they’re going to launch two starships in quick succession,” one from Texas and one from Florida, Parsons said.

You might notice “DON’T PANIC” on the side of Starship. This is a reference to Douglas Adams’s “The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy.” This particular ship is No. 42 off the production line, and in Adams’s book, 42 was the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe and everything.

Unlike yesterday’s launch weather, which was warm with cloudless skies and bright sunshine, today is cool, breezy and gray. It seems there are fewer spectators.

Dan Huot, the SpaceX commentator, says SpaceX has another option to avoid flying over land, if the team determines it’s risky for the spacecraft to fly over populated areas. SpaceX could command Starship to tumble into the atmosphere, which would bring it down in the Pacific.

On Friday, SpaceX gave reporters a rare tour of its Starship manufacturing facility in Texas, named Starfactory.

SpaceX did not allow any photographs or videos to be taken during the visit. But it is hard to imagine the million-square-foot factory that builds Starship without walking through it.

Each rocket is more than 400 feet high and 30 feet wide, and the numbers do not convey the immensity.

Even though it is building the biggest rocket ever, Starfactory is more like a toy factory or an automobile assembly line than a traditional aerospace factory, said Justin Styer, senior director of Starship launch at SpaceX.

“Traditionally, rockets, airplanes, whatever, have been these extremely precious, artisanal, one-off creations,” Styer said. “SpaceX works really differently. Our whole idea is to kind of incorporate automotive methods, incorporate just general, more mass-manufactured things, to the rocket space.”

“We’re trying to make it very normal, very sort of pedestrian with its consistency so that humanity can take advantage of it like any other transport system,” he added.

The SpaceX factory in Hawthorne, Calif., where the company makes its Falcon 9 rockets, was originally a factory for airplane fuselages. The Texas site was built from the bottom up for the company’s rockets.

In the Starfactory entrance lobby, a giant globe of Mars hangs from the ceiling, a reminder of Elon Musk’s ultimate destination for Starship.

Five floors of office space in the front of the building include walkways that overlook the bright, cavernous space of Starfactory. Almost everything, including the floors and girders rising to the ceilings, is gleaming white, with some swaths of black. It seems that an unofficial uniform for SpaceX employees consists of a black T-shirt and jeans.

Pieces of the rocket in various stages of manufacture line up along the assembly line. Half of the factory is devoted to the Super Heavy booster and half is “Shipland,” an area set aside for building the upper-stage spacecraft that goes into orbit. A wide-open aisle extends the length of the floor between the two.

It takes seven to eight months to complete one booster or one Ship, but there are so many under construction simultaneously that one booster is completed every four weeks and one Ship every two weeks, said Danny Fain, director of booster production.

Once finished, they are taken to nearby tall buildings known as megabays where the Raptor engines are installed.

Fain said it used to take five to six hours to attach one engine. Now, SpaceX has sped up the process to 30 minutes, he said.

SpaceX’s goal is to make space travel seem “extremely lame,” Styer said — something ordinary and common, not rare and expensive.

“We hope to unimpress you with the normalcy after seeing a lot of rocket parts,” he told the reporters.

One of Starship’s engines just fired briefly. That was enough for the spacecraft to drop out of orbit.

About an hour ago, SpaceX gave a final “go” for trying to catch the Starship spacecraft at its Texas launch site. If anything had looked wrong, there was one last opportunity to re-enter early and splash down in the Pacific near Hawaii. If anything goes wrong at this point, Starship could still divert its path and come down in the Gulf of Mexico, as the booster did yesterday.

In 2019, the first time I drove out of Brownsville, Texas, east along State Highway 4, there was almost nothing here among the marshy grasslands. I remember seeing something tall and silvery in the distance, “like a giant, shiny and pointy grain silo,” I described it.

This was a prototype of Starship — just the top part, the upper stage that is now often referred to as Ship — sitting outside next to the highway. The factory was basically just a tent, a supersize version of a wedding pavilion.

Next door was a clump of about 30 houses named Boca Chica Village. For the residents, this was a quiet refuge surrounded by a wildlife sanctuary. It was so far from anything else that it was easier for the county to truck in water, filling up big black containers on the front lawns, rather than build water lines.

It is very different now.

Instead of a tent, SpaceX now has Starfactory, a gleaming, million-square-foot manufacturing facility that churns out Starships like an automobile assembly line.

“On any given day, there’s around 8,000 people working somewhere on campus,” said Sheila McCorkle, a SpaceX vice president who serves as the general counsel for local issues.

The surrounding area is now Starbase, an official city that was incorporated in May last year. It includes a police department, a fire department and a soon-to-open public library. Brand-new houses have popped up. Water lines have been installed.

“Everything you see here, SpaceX has built from the ground up,” McCorkle said. “It was a sandbar when we started. I like to think of it as a little bit ‘Mad Max’ back in the day. People living in tents and building rockets in tents. Now we have schools, clinics.”

Starbase has about 800 full-time residents, mostly SpaceX employees, although a few of the original Boca Chica residents remain. Most of the city employees are spouses of the SpaceX employees, McCorkle said, adding that her husband runs the economic development corporation for the city.

“Sometimes I call it like a capitalist commune,” McCorkle said. “We’re well funded, so the commune part actually works. Like we’re all in it together.”

SpaceX will have to wait until its next test flight of Starship to recover all parts of the giant rocket in a single mission.

The company had hoped to execute a milestone “double-catch” maneuver during the flight that launched on Friday from South Texas. That will be a key step toward SpaceX’s goal of developing a fully reusable rocket.

Until recent years, rockets have generally been expensive, single-use throwaways. If all of Starship, which is the largest rocket ever built, can be repeatedly flown, it would revolutionize the space industry, enabling launches of bigger, heavier satellites and other cargo at lower costs.

In addition, NASA is counting on a version of Starship to serve as a lunar lander for its Artemis program. The catches are not needed for NASA’s Artemis III mission next year, but any failures would make it even more unlikely that NASA could meet its goal of landing astronauts on the moon in 2028.

Starship launched on schedule at 5:47 p.m. Eastern time from its Starbase site outside Brownsville, Texas, into a clear azure sky, even as the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for air travel.

You can watch SpaceX’s coverage in the player above.

As the booster headed back to the launchpad, the commentators on SpaceX’s webcast said the attempted catch was called off. Instead, the booster made a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico, which ended with a loud explosion.

At 407 feet tall, Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever built. It consists of two pieces: a powerful booster stage with 33 engines known as the Super Heavy, and an upper-stage spacecraft, also called Starship and often shortened to Ship.

“It’s designed for not just full reusability but also rapid reusability, like an aircraft,” Elon Musk, the founder and chief executive of SpaceX, said in September during the All-In Summit, a business and technology conference.

A previous Starship test flight in September was the first to enter orbit around Earth. The mission successfully deployed 26 of SpaceX’s newest Starlink satellites, which will become operational pieces of the internet communications network.

This is the 15th test flight of Starship. After launching from the southern tip of Texas, the rocket headed eastward over the Gulf of Mexico.

The SpaceX webcast commentators said they did not know why the booster catch attempt was called off.

The upper-stage Ship continued upward to orbit, about 170 miles above Earth, where it deployed another batch of 26 Starlink satellites.

After 22 hours and about 14 trips around the planet, Ship will drop out of orbit and head back to the launch site, where it is to be caught by the mechanical arms on the launch tower.

During Flight 14, SpaceX showed that it could restart an engine on the upper-stage Ship, allowing the craft to first enter a circular orbit and then to drop out of orbit.

If something on the spacecraft is not performing quite as expected, the return schedule can be moved up so that it will land in an empty swath of the Pacific Ocean.

That is what happened during Flight 14. Although SpaceX was not going to try to catch the Ship, it did plan to re-enter over the United States and then simulate a landing over the Gulf of Mexico. However, because one of the upper-stage engines had failed during ascent, SpaceX decided to be cautious and have the Ship return early, splashing down in the Pacific.

Flight 16 could be the first Starship launch from SpaceX’s revamped launchpad at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The launch site in Texas is not sufficient to serve SpaceX’s planned acceleration of Starship launches. Another Florida launchpad is under construction at the nearby Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, and SpaceX has announced plans to build a huge launch complex in Louisiana.

SpaceX could also hit a major milestone next year if it can launch two Starships in quick succession, dock them together in orbit and then move liquid methane and liquid oxygen propellants from one Starship to the other.

The refueling maneuver is essential for Starship to leave low-Earth orbit and head to more distant destinations like the moon and Mars. That is because by the time the upper-stage Ship reaches orbit, its tanks are almost empty.

SpaceX’s plan is to put up the equivalent of an orbital gas station. A series of tanker Starships will bring propellants to fill up the station. When it is full, the Starship that is headed to the moon or elsewhere beyond low-Earth orbit will launch, dock with the gas station, refuel and then continue on its journey.

In the second half of 2027, NASA plans to undertake its Artemis III mission. That trip will not go to the moon but will remain in orbit around Earth to practice docking procedures. Like the Artemis II mission that flew to the moon and back this year, the Artemis III astronauts will sit inside an Orion spacecraft, launched atop of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket.

After they reach orbit, the astronauts will practice docking with prototype moon landers, first with the Blue Moon spacecraft built by Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin company and then with Starship.

NASA has not yet decided which lander it will use for Artemis IV, which will try to land two astronauts on the moon near its south pole.

In March last year, Mr. Musk said on X that Starship would be heading to Mars by the end of 2026. The two planets line up to provide an optimal trajectory every 26 months.

On board would be Optimus humanoid robots built by Tesla, Mr. Musk’s car company.

But failures during Starship test flights last year meant that the craft would fall behind schedule. The Optimus robots have appeared in demos but do not appear to be ready for official space missions, either.

An earlier version of this article misstated the status of the Starlink satellites deployed during the Starship test flight in September. They are not yet operational.

At about 4:20 p.m. Eastern time, it slowed to a hover next to the launchpad tower and slid between two giant mechanical arms called “chopsticks,” which grabbed it out of midair.

This maneuver was a crucial step in SpaceX’s quest to make reusable rockets.

The launch: Liftoff from SpaceX’s Starbase launch site in South Texas occurred at 5:47 p.m. Eastern time on Friday. It was almost flawless. Once in orbit, the upper-stage Starship spacecraft deployed 26 of the company’s next-generation Starlink satellites. Read more ›

No booster catch: SpaceX had hoped to catch the bottom half of the rocket, the giant booster stage known as Super Heavy. After finishing its part of the flight two minutes after liftoff, the booster dropped away and headed back toward the launchpad. However, the booster detected a problem with its guidance and navigation control and instead performed a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico.

Heat shield: In an overnight update on its webcast, SpaceX reported that data from cameras on the ground and on two of the deployed Starlink satellites showed that the tiles that protected the underside of the Starship spacecraft from the fiery temperatures of re-entry were in good condition.

Today’s catch is a breakthrough for the possibility of fully reusing rockets, but experts say SpaceX has a long way to go before it can catch and launch again, given the potential damage to the heat shield and engines caused by falling through the atmosphere.

That was an amazing view, seeing the spacecraft drop out of the clouds, pivot to vertical, hover and then slide between the chopstick arms.

The catch was successful. Starship hovered next to the launchpad tower and slid between two giant mechanical arms called “chopsticks,” which grabbed it out of midair.

We’re hearing sonic booms.

SpaceX has decided to attempt the catch.

Starship has slowed to subsonic speeds.

The spacecraft has survived passage through maximum heating. It is now passing over Mexico and is eight minutes away from landing.

How can you land a rocket to use it again? On four legs? Or with parachutes?

What about … giant chopsticks?

SpaceX is on a quest to make spacecraft run like trains and airplanes. As part of this vision, it is counting on a tower with two mechanical arms called the “chopsticks” to catch its Starship spacecraft when it returns from orbit on Saturday.

If all goes according to plan, Starship will travel through the atmosphere faster than the speed of sound before being steered back into the tower it launched from in South Texas. There, the mechanical arms will squeeze it safely into place, like chopsticks holding a piece of sushi.

The latest mission had to cancel an unprecedented “double-catch” attempt after its rocket booster was diverted on Friday for a water landing in the Gulf of Mexico.

Joseph Gonzalez, a professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who worked on the Artemis II mission, said the arms offer a better chance to save a rocket for reuse than more traditional forms of landing.

Because Starship uses up most of its propellant just to reach orbit, it will need to refill its tanks before heading to the moon.

Unlike yesterday’s launch weather, which was warm with cloudless skies and bright sunshine, today is cool, breezy and gray. It seems there are fewer spectators.

Dan Huot, the SpaceX commentator, says SpaceX has another option to avoid flying over land, if the team determines it’s risky for the spacecraft to fly over populated areas. SpaceX could command Starship to tumble into the atmosphere, which would bring it down in the Pacific.

Each rocket is more than 400 feet high and 30 feet wide, and the numbers do not convey the immensity.

Even though it is building the biggest rocket ever, Starfactory is more like a toy factory or an automobile assembly line than a traditional aerospace factory, said Justin Styer, senior director of Starship launch at SpaceX.

In the Starfactory entrance lobby, a giant globe of Mars hangs from the ceiling, a reminder of Elon Musk’s ultimate destination for Starship.

Five floors of office space in the front of the building include walkways that overlook the bright, cavernous space of Starfactory. Almost everything, including the floors and girders rising to the ceilings, is gleaming white, with some swaths of black. Pieces of the rocket in various stages of manufacture line up along the assembly line. Half of the factory is devoted to the Super Heavy booster and half is “Shipland,” an area set aside for building the upper-stage spacecraft that goes into orbit. A wide-open aisle extends the length of the floor between the two.

If anything goes wrong at this point, Starship could still divert its path and come down in the Gulf of Mexico, as the booster did yesterday.

In 2019, the first time I drove out of Brownsville, Texas, east along State Highway 4, there was almost nothing here among the marshy grasslands. I remember seeing something tall and silvery in the distance, “like a giant, shiny and pointy grain silo,” I described it.

This was a prototype of Starship — just the top part, the upper stage that is now often referred to as Ship — sitting outside next to the highway. The factory was basically just a tent, a supersize version of a wedding pavilion.

The latest test flight of Starship, SpaceX’s spacecraft, made history on Saturday afternoon, when its orbital craft re-entered Earth’s atmosphere and, for the first time, returned to the launchpad where it started.

At about 4:20 p.m. Eastern time, it slowed to a hover next to the launchpad tower and slid between two giant mechanical arms called “chopsticks,” which grabbed it out of midair.

This maneuver was a crucial step in SpaceX’s quest to make reusable rockets.

The launch: Liftoff from SpaceX’s Starbase launch site in South Texas occurred at 5:47 p.m. Eastern time on Friday. It was almost flawless. Once in orbit, the upper-stage Starship spacecraft deployed 26 of the company’s next-generation Starlink satellites. Read more ›

No booster catch: SpaceX had hoped to catch the bottom half of the rocket, the giant booster stage known as Super Heavy. After finishing its part of the flight two minutes after liftoff, the booster dropped away and headed back toward the launchpad. However, the booster detected a problem with its guidance and navigation control and instead performed a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico.

Heat shield: In an overnight update on its webcast, SpaceX reported that data from cameras on the ground and on two of the deployed Starlink satellites showed that the tiles that protected the underside of the Starship spacecraft from the fiery temperatures of re-entry were in good condition.

Today’s catch is a breakthrough for the possibility of fully reusing rockets, but experts say SpaceX has a long way to go before it can catch and launch again, given the potential damage to the heat shield and engines caused by falling through the atmosphere.

That was an amazing view, seeing the spacecraft drop out of the clouds, pivot to vertical, hover and then slide between the chopstick arms.

The catch was successful. Starship hovered next to the launchpad tower and slid between two giant mechanical arms called “chopsticks,” which grabbed it out of midair.

We’re hearing sonic booms.

SpaceX has decided to attempt the catch.

Starship has slowed to subsonic speeds.

The spacecraft has survived passage through maximum heating. It is now passing over Mexico and is eight minutes away from landing.

How can you land a rocket to use it again? On four legs? Or with parachutes?

What about … giant chopsticks?

SpaceX is on a quest to make spacecraft run like trains and airplanes. As part of this vision, it is counting on a tower with two mechanical arms called the “chopsticks” to catch its Starship spacecraft when it returns from orbit on Saturday.

The company has already proved the arms can catch a rocket booster minutes after liftoff. But the Saturday attempt will be the first such landing for the upper-stage spacecraft, which is also called Starship but is often shortened to Ship.

The latest mission had to cancel an unprecedented “double-catch” attempt after its rocket booster was diverted on Friday for a water landing in the Gulf of Mexico.

Although catches will not be part of NASA’s Artemis III mission next year, a successful one on Saturday would be seen as a breakthrough for the potential of rockets to be repeatedly flown.

“But if something goes really wrong with Starship, it could take out the whole tower,” said Alistair John, director of the aerospace engineering program at the University of Sheffield in England. “It’s higher risk, higher reward.”

Joseph Gonzalez, a professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who worked on the Artemis II mission, said the arms offer a better chance to save a rocket for reuse than more traditional forms of landing.

Landing the rocket on legs tacks on weight and thus a need for more fuel. Parachute landings can add on days for an ocean recovery, Gonzalez said. The tower holds the promise of catching Ship in the exact place from where it could be launched again.

“Time is always of the essence, especially if you’re talking about rapid reusability,” Gonzalez said.

Still, John said, SpaceX has a ways to go to catch both parts of its rocket and launch them into space again.

The rocket’s heat shield will “take a beating” on its way down through the atmosphere on Saturday, and SpaceX will have to prove next that it and other key components like the engines are “OK to go again,” he said.

In the modern space race, China has successfully caught a rocket booster with giant nets. SpaceX already has a partially reusable Falcon 9 rocket, which can rapidly send satellites into orbit. Its booster lands on legs.

At the press viewing site, a SpaceX employee just handed out foam ear plugs. The returning spacecraft is expected to create a loud sonic boom.

At the end, the engines will relight to flip the spacecraft vertically into a hover — and then hopefully right into the tower’s mechanical arms.
