https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/.title: Here’s the latest.
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/.author: Kenneth Chang
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/.text:
The Starship spacecraft safely landed back at the Starbase launch facility, a major step in SpaceX’s quest to build fully reusable rockets.

The latest test flight of Starship, SpaceX’s spacecraft, made history on Saturday afternoon, when its orbital craft re-entered Earth’s atmosphere and, for the first time, returned to the launchpad where it started.

At about 4:20 p.m. Eastern time, it slowed to a hover next to the launchpad tower and slid between two giant mechanical arms called “chopsticks,” which grabbed it out of midair.

This maneuver was a crucial step in SpaceX’s quest to make reusable rockets.

The launch: Liftoff from SpaceX’s Starbase launch site in South Texas occurred at 5:47 p.m. Eastern time on Friday. It was almost flawless. Once in orbit, the upper-stage Starship spacecraft deployed 26 of the company’s next-generation Starlink satellites. Read more ›

No booster catch: SpaceX had hoped to catch the bottom half of the rocket, the giant booster stage known as Super Heavy. After finishing its part of the flight two minutes after liftoff, the booster dropped away and headed back toward the launchpad. However, the booster detected a problem with its guidance and navigation control and instead performed a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico.

Heat shield: In an overnight update on its webcast, SpaceX reported that data from cameras on the ground and on two of the deployed Starlink satellites showed that the tiles that protected the underside of the Starship spacecraft from the fiery temperatures of re-entry were in good condition.

Today’s catch is a breakthrough for the possibility of fully reusing rockets, but experts say SpaceX has a long way to go before it can catch and launch again, given the potential damage to the heat shield and engines caused by falling through the atmosphere.

That was an amazing view, seeing the spacecraft drop out of the clouds, pivot to vertical, hover and then slide between the chopstick arms.

The catch was successful. Starship hovered next to the launchpad tower and slid between two giant mechanical arms called “chopsticks,” which grabbed it out of midair.

We’re hearing sonic booms.

SpaceX has decided to attempt the catch.

Starship has slowed to subsonic speeds.

The spacecraft has survived passage through maximum heating. It is now passing over Mexico and is eight minutes away from landing.

How can you land a rocket to use it again? On four legs? Or with parachutes?

What about … giant chopsticks?

SpaceX is on a quest to make spacecraft run like trains and airplanes. As part of this vision, it is counting on a tower with two mechanical arms called the “chopsticks” to catch its Starship spacecraft when it returns from orbit on Saturday.

If all goes according to plan, Starship will travel through the atmosphere faster than the speed of sound before being steered back into the tower it launched from in South Texas. There, the mechanical arms will squeeze it safely into place, like chopsticks holding a piece of sushi.

The company has already proved the arms can catch a rocket booster minutes after liftoff. But the Saturday attempt will be the first such landing for the upper-stage spacecraft, which is also called Starship but is often shortened to Ship.

The latest mission had to cancel an unprecedented “double-catch” attempt after its rocket booster was diverted on Friday for a water landing in the Gulf of Mexico.

Although catches will not be part of NASA’s Artemis III mission next year, a successful one on Saturday would be seen as a breakthrough for the potential of rockets to be repeatedly flown.

“But if something goes really wrong with Starship, it could take out the whole tower,” said Alistair John, director of the aerospace engineering program at the University of Sheffield in England. “It’s higher risk, higher reward.”

Joseph Gonzalez, a professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who worked on the Artemis II mission, said the arms offer a better chance to save a rocket for reuse than more traditional forms of landing.

Landing the rocket on legs tacks on weight and thus a need for more fuel. Parachute landings can add on days for an ocean recovery, Gonzalez said. The tower holds the promise of catching Ship in the exact place from where it could be launched again.

“Time is always of the essence, especially if you’re talking about rapid reusability,” Gonzalez said.

Still, John said, SpaceX has a ways to go to catch both parts of its rocket and launch them into space again.

The rocket’s heat shield will “take a beating” on its way down through the atmosphere on Saturday, and SpaceX will have to prove next that it and other key components like the engines are “OK to go again,” he said.

In the modern space race, China has successfully caught a rocket booster with giant nets. SpaceX already has a partially reusable Falcon 9 rocket, which can rapidly send satellites into orbit. Its booster lands on legs.

At the press viewing site, a SpaceX employee just handed out foam ear plugs. The returning spacecraft is expected to create a loud sonic boom.

So how will Starship make it home? SpaceX will fire the spacecraft’s engines to slow it down, so it can fall out of orbit. Then it will fall through the atmosphere, “a bit like a skydiver,” said Alistair John, the aerospace engineering director at the University of Sheffield in England.

Similar to a skydiver moving his arms and legs, four flaps deployed on the spacecraft will allow for slight steering. Air resistance slows it down in a big belly flop through the atmosphere. At the end, the engines will relight to flip the spacecraft vertically into a hover — and then hopefully right into the tower’s mechanical arms.

SpaceX’s Starship is slated to participate in its first NASA mission sometime in the second half of next year, as part of the space agency’s efforts to return humans to the moon.

NASA’s Artemis program aims to land astronauts on the lunar surface by the end of 2028, but the next mission, Artemis III, will stay in orbit around Earth. The main objective of this flight is to practice docking with two prototype lunar landers.

Artemis III is similar to what NASA did half a century ago with Apollo 9. That often overlooked mission provided a crucial check that the lander would work as designed.

During Artemis III, which is expected to last 14 to 17 days, four astronauts will launch inside the Orion capsule atop a Space Launch System rocket from Florida. Once in orbit, Orion will try to dock with the Blue Moon spacecraft built by Blue Origin, the space company started by Jeff Bezos. The astronauts will be able to enter a crew cabin on Blue Moon.

On the sixth day of the mission, SpaceX will launch a Starship. This spacecraft will largely be a run-of-the-mill version pulled off SpaceX’s assembly line, but with a docking port attached at the top.

The spacecraft will not include modifications like a crew cabin or a life support system, which will be needed for the lunar lander version. That means the Artemis III astronauts will not be able to enter Starship.

However, a successful docking will offer data on a change that SpaceX is seeking for the moon mission. Instead of Starship and Orion traveling separately to lunar orbit and docking there, SpaceX wants the two spacecraft to dock in low-Earth orbit, and then Starship would provide the propulsion to get them to the moon.

On the eighth day of the mission, Orion is expected to dock with Starship for two hours, in order to test whether the combined spacecraft will perform, considering that Orion was not originally designed for that configuration.

“It gives us critical data and allows us to really understand the forces of docking, how we’re going to push, how we’re going to work together,” Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, said during a news conference in October.

Parsons said he was also interested in another crucial demonstration that was planned for early next year, showing that ultracold liquid methane and liquid oxygen propellants can be transferred from one Starship to another.

Because Starship uses up most of its propellant just to reach orbit, it will need to refill its tanks before heading to the moon.

“This is going to be a first-of-its-kind SpaceX mission where they’re going to launch two starships in quick succession,” one from Texas and one from Florida, Parsons said.

You might notice “DON’T PANIC” on the side of Starship. This is a reference to Douglas Adams’s “The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy.” This particular ship is No. 42 off the production line, and in Adams’s book, 42 was the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe and everything.

Unlike yesterday’s launch weather, which was warm with cloudless skies and bright sunshine, today is cool, breezy and gray. It seems there are fewer spectators.

Dan Huot, the SpaceX commentator, says SpaceX has another option to avoid flying over land, if the team determines it’s risky for the spacecraft to fly over populated areas. SpaceX could command Starship to tumble into the atmosphere, which would bring it down in the Pacific.

On Friday, SpaceX gave reporters a rare tour of its Starship manufacturing facility in Texas, named Starfactory.

SpaceX did not allow any photographs or videos to be taken during the visit. But it is hard to imagine the million-square-foot factory that builds Starship without walking through it.

Each rocket is more than 400 feet high and 30 feet wide, and the numbers do not convey the immensity.

Even though it is building the biggest rocket ever, Starfactory is more like a toy factory or an automobile assembly line than a traditional aerospace factory, said Justin Styer, senior director of Starship launch at SpaceX.

“Traditionally, rockets, airplanes, whatever, have been these extremely precious, artisanal, one-off creations,” Styer said. “SpaceX works really differently. Our whole idea is to kind of incorporate automotive methods, incorporate just general, more mass-manufactured things, to the rocket space.”

“We’re trying to make it very normal, very sort of pedestrian with its consistency so that humanity can take advantage of it like any other transport system,” he added.

The SpaceX factory in Hawthorne, Calif., where the company makes its Falcon 9 rockets, was originally a factory for airplane fuselages. The Texas site was built from the bottom up for the company’s rockets.

In the Starfactory entrance lobby, a giant globe of Mars hangs from the ceiling, a reminder of Elon Musk’s ultimate destination for Starship.

Five floors of office space in the front of the building include walkways that overlook the bright, cavernous space of Starfactory. Almost everything, including the floors and girders rising to the ceilings, is gleaming white, with some swaths of black. It seems that an unofficial uniform for SpaceX employees consists of a black T-shirt and jeans.

Pieces of the rocket in various stages of manufacture line up along the assembly line. Half of the factory is devoted to the Super Heavy booster and half is “Shipland,” an area set aside for building the upper-stage spacecraft that goes into orbit. A wide-open aisle extends the length of the floor between the two.

It takes seven to eight months to complete one booster or one Ship, but there are so many under construction simultaneously that one booster is completed every four weeks and one Ship every two weeks, said Danny Fain, director of booster production.

Once finished, they are taken to nearby tall buildings known as megabays where the Raptor engines are installed.

Fain said it used to take five to six hours to attach one engine. Now, SpaceX has sped up the process to 30 minutes, he said.

SpaceX’s goal is to make space travel seem “extremely lame,” Styer said — something ordinary and common, not rare and expensive.

“We hope to unimpress you with the normalcy after seeing a lot of rocket parts,” he told the reporters.

One of Starship’s engines just fired briefly. That was enough for the spacecraft to drop out of orbit.

About an hour ago, SpaceX gave a final “go” for trying to catch the Starship spacecraft at its Texas launch site. If anything had looked wrong, there was one last opportunity to re-enter early and splash down in the Pacific near Hawaii. If anything goes wrong at this point, Starship could still divert its path and come down in the Gulf of Mexico, as the booster did yesterday.

In 2019, the first time I drove out of Brownsville, Texas, east along State Highway 4, there was almost nothing here among the marshy grasslands. I remember seeing something tall and silvery in the distance, “like a giant, shiny and pointy grain silo,” I described it.

This was a prototype of Starship — just the top part, the upper stage that is now often referred to as Ship — sitting outside next to the highway. The factory was basically just a tent, a supersize version of a wedding pavilion.

Next door was a clump of about 30 houses named Boca Chica Village. For the residents, this was a quiet refuge surrounded by a wildlife sanctuary. It was so far from anything else that it was easier for the county to truck in water, filling up big black containers on the front lawns, rather than build water lines.

It is very different now.

Instead of a tent, SpaceX now has Starfactory, a gleaming, million-square-foot manufacturing facility that churns out Starships like an automobile assembly line.

“On any given day, there’s around 8,000 people working somewhere on campus,” said Sheila McCorkle, a SpaceX vice president who serves as the general counsel for local issues.

The surrounding area is now Starbase, an official city that was incorporated in May last year. It includes a police department, a fire department and a soon-to-open public library. Brand-new houses have popped up. Water lines have been installed.

“Everything you see here, SpaceX has built from the ground up,” McCorkle said. “It was a sandbar when we started. I like to think of it as a little bit ‘Mad Max’ back in the day. People living in tents and building rockets in tents. Now we have schools, clinics.”

Starbase has about 800 full-time residents, mostly SpaceX employees, although a few of the original Boca Chica residents remain. Most of the city employees are spouses of the SpaceX employees, McCorkle said, adding that her husband runs the economic development corporation for the city.

“Sometimes I call it like a capitalist commune,” McCorkle said. “We’re well funded, so the commune part actually works. Like we’re all in it together.”

SpaceX will have to wait until its next test flight of Starship to recover all parts of the giant rocket in a single mission.

The company had hoped to execute a milestone “double-catch” maneuver during the flight that launched on Friday from South Texas. That will be a key step toward SpaceX’s goal of developing a fully reusable rocket.

Until recent years, rockets have generally been expensive, single-use throwaways. If all of Starship, which is the largest rocket ever built, can be repeatedly flown, it would revolutionize the space industry, enabling launches of bigger, heavier satellites and other cargo at lower costs.

In addition, NASA is counting on a version of Starship to serve as a lunar lander for its Artemis program. The catches are not needed for NASA’s Artemis III mission next year, but any failures would make it even more unlikely that NASA could meet its goal of landing astronauts on the moon in 2028.

Starship launched on schedule at 5:47 p.m. Eastern time from its Starbase site outside Brownsville, Texas, into a clear azure sky, even as the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for air travel.

You can watch SpaceX’s coverage in the player above.

As the booster headed back to the launchpad, the commentators on SpaceX’s webcast said the attempted catch was called off. Instead, the booster made a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico, which ended with a loud explosion.

At 407 feet tall, Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever built. It consists of two pieces: a powerful booster stage with 33 engines known as the Super Heavy, and an upper-stage spacecraft, also called Starship and often shortened to Ship.

“It’s designed for not just full reusability but also rapid reusability, like an aircraft,” Elon Musk, the founder and chief executive of SpaceX, said in September during the All-In Summit, a business and technology conference.

A previous Starship test flight in September was the first to enter orbit around Earth. The mission successfully deployed 26 of SpaceX’s newest Starlink satellites, which will become operational pieces of the internet communications network.

This is the 15th test flight of Starship. After launching from the southern tip of Texas, the rocket headed eastward over the Gulf of Mexico.

The SpaceX webcast commentators said they did not know why the booster catch attempt was called off.

The upper-stage Ship continued upward to orbit, about 170 miles above Earth, where it deployed another batch of 26 Starlink satellites.

After 22 hours and about 14 trips around the planet, Ship will drop out of orbit and head back to the launch site, where it is to be caught by the mechanical arms on the launch tower.

During Flight 14, SpaceX showed that it could restart an engine on the upper-stage Ship, allowing the craft to first enter a circular orbit and then to drop out of orbit.

If something on the spacecraft is not performing quite as expected, the return schedule can be moved up so that it will land in an empty swath of the Pacific Ocean.

That is what happened during Flight 14. Although SpaceX was not going to try to catch the Ship, it did plan to re-enter over the United States and then simulate a landing over the Gulf of Mexico. However, because one of the upper-stage engines had failed during ascent, SpaceX decided to be cautious and have the Ship return early, splashing down in the Pacific.

Flight 16 could be the first Starship launch from SpaceX’s revamped launchpad at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The launch site in Texas is not sufficient to serve SpaceX’s planned acceleration of Starship launches. Another Florida launchpad is under construction at the nearby Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, and SpaceX has announced plans to build a huge launch complex in Louisiana.

SpaceX could also hit a major milestone next year if it can launch two Starships in quick succession, dock them together in orbit and then move liquid methane and liquid oxygen propellants from one Starship to the other.

The refueling maneuver is essential for Starship to leave low-Earth orbit and head to more distant destinations like the moon and Mars. That is because by the time the upper-stage Ship reaches orbit, its tanks are almost empty.

SpaceX’s plan is to put up the equivalent of an orbital gas station. A series of tanker Starships will bring propellants to fill up the station. When it is full, the Starship that is headed to the moon or elsewhere beyond low-Earth orbit will launch, dock with the gas station, refuel and then continue on its journey.

In the second half of 2027, NASA plans to undertake its Artemis III mission. That trip will not go to the moon but will remain in orbit around Earth to practice docking procedures. Like the Artemis II mission that flew to the moon and back this year, the Artemis III astronauts will sit inside an Orion spacecraft, launched atop of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket.

After they reach orbit, the astronauts will practice docking with prototype moon landers, first with the Blue Moon spacecraft built by Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin company and then with Starship.

NASA has not yet decided which lander it will use for Artemis IV, which will try to land two astronauts on the moon near its south pole.

In March last year, Mr. Musk said on X that Starship would be heading to Mars by the end of 2026. The two planets line up to provide an optimal trajectory every 26 months.

On board would be Optimus humanoid robots built by Tesla, Mr. Musk’s car company.

But failures during Starship test flights last year meant that the craft would fall behind schedule. The Optimus robots have appeared in demos but do not appear to be ready for official space missions, either.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.title: She Was a CBS News Producer When Few Women Were
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.author: Richard Sandomir
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.text:
Linda Mason started in an entry-level job at CBS Radio in 1966 and rose through the news division’s ranks to senior vice president. She was 84.

Linda Mason, an Emmy Award-winning journalist at CBS News who was the first female producer at “CBS Evening News” with Walter Cronkite and who was put in charge of reinforcing the division’s standards after a botched “60 Minutes” report on President George W. Bush’s military service, died on Oct. 28 at her home in the Bronx. She was 84.

Her husband, Cary Aminoff, said the cause was dementia.

Ms. Mason stood out for her long rise through the male-dominated news division. She started as a desk assistant at CBS Radio before moving into jobs of increasing responsibility, including senior producer of “CBS Evening News”; executive producer of “CBS News Sunday Morning” and the documentary news series “CBS Reports”; and vice president of public affairs, developing programming and overseeing standards.

She was also known as a mentor to other women at the network.

“We took it for granted that every woman was going to be a secretary or a researcher, and she had made it to the exalted position of producer,” Marcy McGinnis, who started at CBS News as a secretary and later became a producer and senior vice president of news coverage, said in an interview. “I looked to her as my North Star. Oh, I wanted to be like her. And she was nice to me and other people like me who didn’t matter at the time.”

In 2004, as a vice president, Ms. Mason was CBS News’s liaison to an independent review panel convened by the network to investigate a flawed “60 Minutes Wednesday” report about Mr. Bush, which was broadcast two months before his successful campaign for re-election. It purported to raise serious questions about the president’s Vietnam-era Texas Air National Guard service and whether he had received preferential treatment because of his family’s political connections.

Her role was to answer questions from the panel — led by Louis D. Boccardi, a former chief executive of The Associated Press, and Dick Thornburgh, a former attorney general of the United States — about CBS’s reporting methods.

“For months, I felt as if I were in isolation, quarantined,” she wrote in her memoir, “Speak Up: Breaking the Glass Ceiling at CBS News” (2023). “It was a very difficult time for me since I was used to being involved in all the events CBS was covering and talking with my colleagues.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.title: How Some Flights Were Exempt From the Ground Stop
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.author: Emmett Lindner
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.text:
U.S. Flight Disruptions

Dozens of international flights departed from the United States during Friday’s nationwide ground stop. Some planes also left for Hawaii from the West Coast.

Thousands of passengers scrambled to update their travel plans on Saturday as air traffic slowly unsnarled after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but a number of travelers had already arrived at their destinations on flights left unaffected by the order.

Dozens of international flights took to the skies even as airports across the United States coped with only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration this century. Certain flights were also permitted to depart from the West Coast to Hawaii during the stoppage.

Here’s why some air travel was allowed to proceed even as flight systems were hampered.

More than 8,200 flights were canceled nationwide on Friday — over 31 percent of those scheduled — according to Cirium, an aviation data firm.

But more than 60 flights bound for overseas left the United States during the stoppage, according to Flightradar24, an aviation tracking site.

There are 21 air traffic control facilities, 20 in the contiguous United States and one in Alaska, that oversee swaths of regions throughout the country, according to the F.A.A.

As some of those centers recovered, flights were “allowed to depart through coordination with the Air Traffic Control System Command Center,” the F.A.A. said in an advisory less than two hours after the ground stop was ordered.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/g-s1-1537.title: SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/g-s1-1537.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/g-s1-1537.text:
SpaceX's mega rocket Starship lifts off for a test flight from Starbase, Texas, on Friday.

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.

Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.

The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster's messy miss.

"Can you believe it?" shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot.

SpaceX officials said Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, intended for moon and Mars travel. Although Friday's booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday's news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk's ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.

The world's largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission's one to two laps.

It was SpaceX's 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster's guidance system sensed it wasn't in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA's next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

Artemis III's four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity's first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/g-s1-1537.title: Bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois forces evacuations
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/g-s1-1537.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/g-s1-1537.text:
A bomb was found near an ethanol plant in central Illinois, sparking evacuations of those who live near the industrial site as law enforcement officials investigate, authorities said Saturday.

The bomb was found Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria. While officials say the device has since been "rendered safe," as of Saturday morning, all residents within a 1-mile radius remained under an evacuation notice as officials continued to scour the facility for any other bombs and evidence.

Meanwhile, shelters have been set up for those displaced by the threat, authorities said.

"This is a credible threat," Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon told reporters just after midnight Saturday. "We need to take the blast radius seriously."

FBI Special Agent Ryan Pressley said his agency was investigating, but declined to provide further details.

"We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice," he said.

No arrests have been made at this time and no injuries have been reported.

Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday that BioUrja is "a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that's what alarms us."

It's not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don't result in a credible threat even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims.

Just earlier this week, hundreds of airline passengers in Europe had their flights diverted or given military escorts after a series of bomb threats that officials have since declared were malicious hoaxes.

"We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests," said Dixon. "We're asking for the public's patience while we work to make this area safe."

Peoria, with a population of around 110,000, is located about 150 miles (about 240 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.

The BioUrja plant is located along the Illinois River. The company acquired the ethanol plant in 2021.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-603.title: 'We can't let them down' -- After midterm wins, Democrats turn to charting path ahead
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-603.author: Barbara Sprunt
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-603.text:
Texas Senator-elect James Talarico speaks at the Mission Ballroom during the What's Next Denver political convention on Nov. 12, 2026.

DENVER — Democrats descended on Denver for a two-day conference that was half victory party, half sober look at the road ahead on delivering for the voters who elected them.

The "What's Next" conference, hosted by the group Majority Democrats, was scheduled long before Democrats outperformed expectations with their best electoral performance since Watergate. It brought together rising stars — like incoming Gov. Rob Sand in Iowa and Sen.-elect James Talarico in Texas — along with strategists, organizers, state and federal lawmakers and potential presidential contenders.

Held at a concert hall, with colorful artwork of party heavy hitters dotting the venue, Democrats attended sessions like "What Voters Want" and "What Needs To Change." The overwhelming emphasis from speakers was that Democrats have to earn back trust.

A compilation of posters on display at the What's Next conference in Denver on November 12, 2026.

"We won races in places where we haven't won in a long time, even in some places where we've never won. And the message shouldn't be that [voters] are fully embracing the Democratic Party," said Colorado Rep. Jason Crow in an interview.

"It took us decades to dig ourselves in a hole and to push people away from us, and it's going to take us more than one cycle to earn that trust," said Crow, who is one of the party's recruitment co-chairs.

Attendees cheer during the What's Next summit. Following the midterm elections, prominent Democrats and political insiders gathered for the event to evaluate election results, and debate party strategy.

Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party, took the party to task for not investing more in the South and in Black voters.

"When we say that Black voters are the base of our party, then I ask why are we not investing in a region of the country that on Tuesday night just proved everybody wrong of what is possible," said Clayton to much applause. "Rural America deserves the investment from the Democratic Party and we must run towards communities that our party has run away from."

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg said Democrats shouldn't rest on their laurels.

"I think we are adequately politically traumatized by the last few cycles, so that we will not draw the wrong lessons from all of this," Buttigieg said. "Because here's the thing: it is yet to be written whether what we just experienced is one more oscillation from one side to the other and back, or whether it is the beginning of a tectonic movement changing American politics."

He said Democrats can learn from the current White House on two fronts, by having: "a bias towards action and a readiness to get things done coming out of the gate and at the very same time a readiness to plan for the long-term," adding Democrats should come out of the gate strong, with a rapid-fire series of bills to lower the cost of living.

Presumptive next Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries told the audience he has plans to do just that, with a robust agenda that includes reversing Medicaid cuts, banning congressional stock trading and mid-decade redistricting, establishing a statutory right to abortion, and overturning the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision that did away with limits on political spending by corporations and unions.

The conference itself was peppered with potential presidential contenders, including Buttigieg, New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, and California Rep. Ro Khanna, one of the few progressive speakers.

No one announced an official run, but many gave previews of their theory of the case.

"I do think it's important that whoever we hire to be the chief executive of this country knows how to run something, knows how to get stuff done, knows how to not just have a vision but knows how to deliver on it," Shapiro told reporters.

Someone who was previously kicking the tires for a possible White House bid — Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen — told reporters he's no longer considering it, as he instead pursues the top leadership post in the Senate.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., speaks during the What's Next summit on Nov. 13 in Denver.

Throughout the conference, Democrats debated whether and how to work with the Trump administration in order to deliver meaningful change for voters.

"If slapping Trump's name on it and putting it in gold letters would get it through — hell yes, I would do that," said Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

"The American people cannot wait two years for change, so we must work with President Trump," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any American presidency."

But New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill added a note of caution, describing the president as a bad faith actor.

"The art of the deal to Trump is he figures out what you want, he leverages the you know what out of you, and keeps taking, taking, taking, and never delivers," Sherrill said. "My advice to Sen. Talarico is if Trump wants to work with us, we will lay out the agenda, and he can sign it."

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Philippines’ Carmelle wins first Eurovision contest in Asia
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Raphael Rashid
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
Filipino entry, pop and rap song Sobra-Sobra, takes 19-year-old to victory at grand final in Bangkok

Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’ entry, Sobra-Sobra, to victory in Bangkok on Saturday night, at the first regional edition of the contest to be staged outside Europe.

Eleven countries competed at the One Bangkok Forum in central Bangkok, and the show ran for two and a half hours including advertising.

The winner, who performs under the single name Carmelle, finished on 211 points, 41 clear of the hosts Thailand, with Vietnam third. She received the most votes from both the national juries and the public ballot.

Carmelle, 19, grew up beside the railway tracks in the Bicol region of south-eastern Luzon and has been competing in televised talent contests since she was 12.

Sobra-Sobra mixes pop and rap, is supported by traditional Philippine instruments, the kubing and kulintang, and is sung in Tagalog and English.

After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women”.

“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told the Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”

“It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are,” she told the Guardian before the final. “It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas.”

The show opened with a routine celebrating the host country, in which Muay Thai fighters shared the stage with drag performers on street food carts. The 11 acts were then driven on in tuk-tuks, each carrying their national flag.

Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên, a star at home for more than 20 years, performed first, among dancers costumed as lotus leaves. Mang x Daou represented Thailand, a duo assembled for the contest in the host country who performed a duet staged like a musical number.

Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai gave one of the most conventionally Eurovision performances of the night with Ananta Maya, a rock ballad staged with fire imagery and a large heart-shaped structure behind him.

He ended it by appealing for support for his country, which he said was “going [through a] very hard situation”. More than 1,500 people were killed and more than 5,000 were reported missing after a rock and ice avalanche near the Chinese border triggered catastrophic flash floods in August.

Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, originally a nine-member a cappella and beatbox group, sang without a single instrument. Three of their members were left out of the final due to a rule capping each act at six performers on stage.

Nyendra from Bhutan sang dressed in the gho, his country’s national dress for men, against a backdrop of Himalayan peaks. Mongolia’s Beck performed in a reinterpreted deel, also a national costume.

Half the result was decided before the show began. The 11 national juries voted at a dress rehearsal on Friday night and put the Philippines at the top with 93 points, ahead of Vietnam and Malaysia.

The other half came from viewers around the world, who could vote online but not for their own country, and who were given eight free votes each and the option to buy 10 more.

Laos’s entrant, Thinla, was unable to hear her own music during her performance, and her dress rehearsal was aired once all live performances were over. She finished fifth, with the night’s third-highest public score.

Carmelle receives no prize money but does get a trophy presented by Dara, the Bulgarian singer who won this year’s European contest, and will perform at Eurovision 2027 in Burgas.

Organisers have said the right to stage future editions will not automatically go to the winner, on the grounds that smaller countries lack the infrastructure.

Some of the clearest echoes of Eurovision’s camp traditions came through those who announced the votes.

South Korea’s jury points were read by Jo Kwon, a veteran pop star who has played Adam in the Korean production of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and the title role in Everybody’s Talking About Jamie.

The Philippines’ were read by Vice Ganda, a gay comedian who is one of the biggest stars on Philippine television.

Meanwhile, the guest performer was the Thai singer Jeff Satur, who reached a wider Asian audience through KinnPorsche, a 2022 series in the genre of male same-sex romance dramas that has a large following across Asia.

Organisers intend the Bangkok show to be the first of many regional editions, with the executive producer, Assaf Blecher, saying that 16 or 17 territories had expressed interest in competing next year, among them China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Even Labor MPs are at a loss over the Victorian premier’s ‘tough love’ plan for youth offenders
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Benita Kolovos
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
MPs across factional lines share concerns about policy that legal expert says ‘paints the imprisonment of children as therapeutic’

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Until December last year, Meena Singh was the Victorian commissioner for Aboriginal children and young people, a role that saw her advocating for some of the state’s most vulnerable children.

She had held the role since 2022. In all that time, she says, nobody from the Victorian government had approached her with a proposal like the one the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, announced last week: a $204m “tough love” plan to send children who commit low and mid-level offences to secure facilities, including the former Malmsbury youth justice centre, for schooling, drug and alcohol treatment and life skills.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“If you are on the trajectory of committing crime like carrying a knife or looking to steal cars, you can expect to be detained and be put in this new mandatory detention in Malmsbury,” Carroll told reporters last Sunday.

“We have seen how, where you break the cycle, it can turn young lives around.”

Singh says she was “quite horrified” by the announcement.

“It is very misleading to try and paint the imprisonment of children as therapeutic,” Singh, now a professor at Monash law school, tells Guardian Australia.

“Children who are getting in trouble with the law, there are reasons behind it … Imprisoning these children is effectively imprisoning them for traumas they have experienced rather than the behaviours they are displaying.”

She is far from alone in her criticism. The Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service called the announcement “mandatory sentencing dressed up as political leadership” and the Justice Reform Initiative said it was a “dramatically disproportionate response”. The same organisations were among the legal and human rights groups that lashed other Labor changes introduced this term in an attempt to bring down the state’s crime rate – including “adult time for violent crime” and tougher bail laws.

Even the state’s union movement has criticised this proposal, with the Trades Hall secretary, Luke Hilakari, taking to his personal social media account to publicly rebuke the government.

“Honestly thought the policy of locking up children for a year for shopping lifting [shoplifting] or vandalism was from the Liberal party,” he wrote, adding that one of the most common items stolen was groceries.

“How about we fix disadvantage rather than deepening it.

“And if you want to win an election, could we leave issues in the Liberal party frame to the Liberals.”

Hilakari finished his post by sharing a DemosAU poll, released on Monday, showing Labor on a primary vote of 18% – the lowest figure in its history. That same day, Carroll was in South Melbourne spruiking a $70m plan to hire police reservists to reopen police stations Labor has closed over the term and $300m to build and renovate stations.

Half a dozen MPs from across the party’s factional lines, not authorised to speak publicly, also shared their concerns with Guardian Australia. Some said Labor was handing the Liberals a free kick by choosing to campaign on crime after presiding over rising crime rates and the closure of police stations.

Others say they gritted their teeth and supported the earlier measures, hoping it would be enough to stem the bleeding on the issue. This hasn’t eventuated – a separate RedBridge poll, released on Wednesday, had the party at a 23% primary vote. And it said Labor was 18 points behind the Coalition on crime.

“How are we here?” one MP said.

Another Labor strategist, who requested anonymity to speak freely, described the announcement as “a metaphor for the complete lack of clarity regarding our identity and message for Victorian voters”.

The strategist was particularly disturbed to see Davydd Griffths, Labor’s candidate in Melbourne – a seat currently held by the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell – standing behind the premier for the press conference.

“What targeted Melbourne voter would support that policy? The focus on crime this week has scrapped any chance of winning Melbourne off the Greens,” they said.

For MPs on the right of the party, it’s “too little too late”. They say crime disproportionately affects working-class communities, particularly in the outer-suburban seats Labor needs to retain – and other MPs would’ve known this earlier if they were actually in touch with their constituents.

“This is a reflection that, since the campaign started three weeks ago, they’ve been copping it out door knocking, at street stalls, shopping centres on crime,” one MP said.

Those on the left say the proposal is further proof Labor has abandoned its values. Carroll has pitched himself as a “centrist”, an “economically conservative, socially progressive premier”. He’s also sought to distance himself from a government he has been part of for more than a decade. The slogan printed on the rear of his big red campaign bus is anything but subtle: “New Premier, New Direction”.

The strategy appears to be based on the idea that voters want a decisive break with the past. But there are concerns that, in trying to disown the government’s record, he is also disowning the Labor movement’s achievements over the past 12 years. It risks giving voters little reason to remember why they voted for them in the first place.

One MP said a growing group of colleagues were “furious” that the new leadership had “overseen the trashing of the government’s legacy and instead delivered an election campaign focused almost exclusively on the Big Build royal commission and law and order – two issues losing votes for Labor”.

“Having lost all but our most rusted-on Labor voters to other parties, it looks like they are now happy to see how far we can push before they leave us as well,” the MP said.

There’s evidence this is happening. Monday’s DemosAU poll had the Greens at a record high 17%. This was prior to Labor’s move to run an open ticket in Prahran, which has angered progressives.

The Greens responded on Friday by confirming they will be running their version of an open ticket – urging people to put the Greens first and One Nation last rather than direct preferences.

There’s no doubt this will hurt Labor in a number of seats, capping off another difficult week on the campaign trail.

Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent. Henry Belot contributed to this reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.summary: The Greens are running an open ticket in Prahran, which has angered progressives. Meena Singh was the Victorian commissioner for Aboriginal children and young people. She says she was ‘quite horrified’ by the announcement.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Art ‘must not be sacrificed on the altar of corporate profit’ Liberal senator says as AI policy debate rages
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Tess Ikonomou and Josh Butler
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Andrew McLachlan says he chooses ‘real forests over virtual ones’ as he urges Labor government to consider AI’s impact on artists and environment

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Outspoken Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan has raised the alarm about the approach of his party and the Labor government to AI, urging artists’ copyright not be “sacrificed” for investment and that building new datacentres must not be prioritised above environmental concerns.

As Labor considers copyright changes in an AI policy suite including datacentres, online safety, energy resources and economic benefits, the South Australian backbencher added weight to mooted constitutional challenges as to whether watering down copyright law would be an illegal acquisition of property.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“The works [artists] create must not be sacrificed on the altar of global corporate profiteering,” he said.

“Artists’ property rights must be respected and protected. It is unimaginable that as a nation we might value the machine over beauty created by the artist”.

Although the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has previously declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, some AI companies have rejected making agreements under existing copyright laws, arguing it is too difficult.

AI companies have said they need legal certainty on the copyright issue before investing in Australia, with Anthropic putting foward an “opt out” model which would allow it to scrape music, books and journalism unless a rights holder signals an objection.

Leading voices in the recording industry have raised alarm about any changes to weaken existing copyright law.

McLachlan said the work of artists “nourishes the soul of our nation”, and demanded art be prioritised over the demands of big tech.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“The principle of fair pay for a fair day’s work must not be forgotten in the age of social media platforms, datacentres and artificial intelligence. AI provides amazing opportunities for our nation. If there are trade-offs then the costs must be clearly articulated and understood.”

Labor and the Coalition have largely agreed on AI-related issues; senator David Pocock has complained about a major party “stitch-up” on AI regulation. This week, the shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, and the shadow cybersecurity minister, Aaron Violi, said in a statement that AI was “too important to become an unnecessarily partisan political contest”, saying they’d “engage constructively” to ensure an “enduring and multipartisan approach” to the technology.

But fellow Coalition members Ross Cadell and Michaelia Cash have backed concerns raised by Aria that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government; the constitutional imperative that the government must acquire property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern in the copyright debate.

McLachlan said any potential compensation arrangements must be considered on an individual basis for each artist, adding it would be difficult to ensure an industry-wide scheme would be fair.

“As a Liberal, I believe property rights are foundational to a healthy democracy and a strong economy,” he said.

“The state should never seek to compulsorily acquire or trade away an individual’s property rights except in very limited circumstances and not without just compensation.”

Labor and the Coalition are both in favour of attracting more AI investment and datacentres to Australia, but the opposition has warned the government against “selling out” Australian rights holders in a rush to secure investment.

The growth of datacentres in Australia is expected to increase emissions and power costs for households, prompting backlash from environmental groups and some communities.

McLachlan, who has spoken strongly on conservation and environmental issues, said: “Datacentres must not be built at the expense of our biodiversity.

“We must explore ways to build sovereign AI capability in a sustainable way.

“I choose real forests over virtual ones.”

Earlier this week, Labor announced it will set up a new AI safety regulator and implement six key obligations on AI companies after a breach of government sites by OpenAI.

Labor’s AI package is expected to be unveiled before the end of the year.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Family of Watford woman set alight ‘desperate for answers’ after attack
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Raphael Boyd
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Appeal for information comes after Brenda Raymond, 80, was set on fire outside her flat on Monday

The family of an elderly woman who was set on fire outside a block of flats in Watford have said they are “desperate for answers”.

Brenda Raymond, 80, was found set alight outside her flat on Caractacus Cottage View on Monday. She was taken to a nearby hospital, where she is in critical condition.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Hertfordshire constabulary have said a 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson with intent to endanger life but has been released on bail with strict conditions.

Raymond’s family said the attack had left them in “complete shock” and that they were confused over why she was targeted.

In a statement issued via Hertfordshire constabulary, they said: “Words cannot describe how distressing the past few days have been for us as a family.

“Our beautiful, chatty, fun-loving and much-loved Brenda, who loves to keep fit and dancing, has suffered catastrophic injuries in the most devastating of circumstances; circumstances which have left us all in complete shock.

“We simply cannot understand why anyone would have wanted to hurt her in this way. Someone out there knows something. They know what happened to Brenda. We are desperate for answers and are pleading for anyone with information to please come forward.”

The family also asked for their privacy to be respected during this “unimaginably difficult time”.

Police believe that Raymond was attacked as she returned home at around noon, with her attackers pouring some kind of flammable liquid on her before setting her alight. Detectives said that an accelerant was also poured through the letterbox of a nearby flat, but they have not officially linked the two events.

The decision to publicly name Raymond was made by police with the blessing of her family on Wednesday in the hope it would lead to anyone with knowledge of the attack coming forward.

DI Adam Bridges, from the major crime unit, said: “This was an appalling and deeply distressing attack on an elderly woman who suffered horrific injuries after being set alight outside her own home.

“Our thoughts very much remain with Brenda and her family as we continue to do everything we can to find out what happened and who is responsible.

“Her family are understandably distraught and have taken the step of releasing her name and photograph to help jog people’s memories around this distressing and highly unusual incident.

“Someone out there knows something. You may have witnessed suspicious activity, heard a conversation, noticed unusual behaviour, or captured something on CCTV or dashcam footage without realising its significance.

“Please do not assume that what you know is too small or unimportant to tell us about. It could be a seemingly insignificant piece of information that provides investigators with the breakthrough they need.

“If you know anything about what happened to Brenda or think you may have information that could assist our inquiries, please come forward. Your information could be crucial in helping us find answers and bring those responsible to justice.”
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Brenda Raymond, 80, was found set alight outside her flat on Monday. She was taken to a nearby hospital, where she is in critical condition. Police say 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Mike Johnson: ‘Leaders have to take responsibility when things go wrong’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna Betts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Republican House speaker not running for re-election contrasts sharply with president who avoids accountability

In his first interview since the midterm elections, the US House speaker, Mike Johnson, said that the Republican party’s crushing losses during the 3 November elections prompted his decision to step away from party leadership.

“Leaders have to take responsibility when things go wrong,” Johnson said on Fox News on Saturday.

The Republican leader, who informed aides on 4 November that he would not seek re-election for House leadership, said on Saturday that he reached the decision “pretty quickly after election night”.

“We worked around the clock, left it all on the field to win. We had to defy history, as you and I both know, it’s only happened twice in 90 years, but we did everything that we could to make that happen,” Johnson said. “But, you know, this was the a year where history was not defied …

“We don’t like the results,” he said. “But, real leadership, I’ve always believed, you lead from the front, and leaders have to take responsibility when things go wrong whether it’s individually deserved or not, that’s part of it …

“I’m going to remain in this fight, but from a role different than as minority leader in the next Congress,” he added.

Johnson’s decision came after Republicans suffered historic losses in this year’s midterm elections, with Democrats flipping key seats in Republican strongholds, including Texas, to seize control of both the Senate and House. It stood in sharp contrast to the reaction of Donald Trump, who has deflected all responsibility for the devastating losses suffered by his party, including defeats for at least 10 Republican Senate candidates in states where he held rallies in the closing weeks of the campaign. That number could rise to 11, should Alaska’s incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, be defeated.

As it stands, come 3 January, Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate, and Republicans will have 44. In the House, Democrats will have at least 256 seats, while Republicans will have at least 169. Each party leads in four of the eight House races where votes are still being counted, and the final two seats will be determined in runoff elections next month in Louisiana. The Senate race in Alaska has not yet been called.

On Tuesday, House Republicans elected the congressman Jim Jordan, of Ohio, to replace Johnson next year, when Republicans will be the minority party in both chambers of Congress. Senate Republicans, meanwhile, re-elected the senator John Thune, of South Dakota, to continue as their leader.

Democrats have not yet voted on who will lead their party in the House and Senate when the new Congress convenes in January. The representative Hakeem Jeffries, of New York, currently serves as House minority leader for the Democrats, and is expected to become the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, while the senator Chuck Schumer, also of New York, currently leads Senate Democrats.

However, the contest for Senate leadership has intensified in recent days, after Chris Van Hollen, of Maryland, announced a challenge to Schumer for the position.

Sign up to Breaking News US

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority leader.”

Bernie Sanders, the progressive senator from Vermont, said this week that he would not support Schumer’s bid to serve as the Democratic leader in the Senate, saying that “the time is now for change”. Sanders then endorsed Van Hollen and outlined the stakes of that contest in a Guardian opinion article.

Senate Democrats are scheduled to hold a closed-door vote on 1 December.

Currently, Jeffries does not face a challenger, but he has faced resistance from some members of his party, including from several Democrats elected earlier this month.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: US House speaker Mike Johnson said that the Republican party’s crushing losses during the 3 November elections prompted his decision to step away from party leadership. “Leaders have to take responsibility when things go wrong,’ he said on Fox News on Saturday.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Canadian lineman died Friday after medical incident

Three-star prospect committed to Georgia in June

High school postpones game as coach pays tribute

Marcellus Young Casario, an 18-year-old Canadian high school football player who had committed to Georgia, died Friday following what his school described as a medical emergency.

Casario, a senior defensive lineman at Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School in northeast Georgia, was taken to hospital after an incident Friday morning. The school announced his death later that day but did not identify him until Saturday. No further details about the circumstances were released.

“Rabun Gap immediately followed our emergency response protocols, and local emergency personnel responded, transferring the student to the hospital,” the school said in a statement.

The school postponed its state semi-final playoff game against Cannon School scheduled for Friday night.

Originally from Halifax, Nova Scotia, Casario moved to Georgia to pursue a college football scholarship. The 6ft 5in, 255lb defensive lineman committed to the Bulldogs in June after receiving offers from several major programs.

Rated a three-star prospect, Casario was ranked the No 49 defensive end nationally by ESPN and was part of Georgia’s 2027 recruiting class.

“He was everything a coach wants in a player,” Rabun Gap coach Derek White said. “He was known for his relentless dedication, and his journey as a student-athlete was marked by hard work and true brotherhood with his teammates.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to move peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.

Kushner told reporters Saturday that “both sides” know that compromises will be necessary to end the war, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were now working on next steps.

Trump son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a prisoner exchange.

The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders agreeing on Friday to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not think it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.

The Kremlin has signalled an openness to negotiations with Europe, but it has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.

The five countries attending are the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland – the five countries that have signalled readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.

In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said that the bloc must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.

Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.

Zelenskyy said Friday that US negotiators had asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO.

The war has raged while negotiations continue. November leaks from Russia’s official statistics agency showed that Russia’s war effort has so far cost the lives of at least 450,000 soldiers.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: More than 100,000 rally across France in new Yellow Vest protests
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France in another round of cost-of-living rallies organised by the “Yellow Vests” and various youth movements.

Saturday’s protests saw a decline in turnout compared with previous weekends and stayed largely calm, authorities said.

The Ministry of the Interior reported that 106,000 people took part in protests nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris – down from 146,000 people nationwide and 46,000 in Paris last week. Student unions place Saturday’s protest numbers higher, at 200,000 people, including almost 100,000 in the capital.

The country has been gripped by high-school blockades, mass demonstrations, and strikes for more than a month, with protesters rallying against falling educational standards, cost-of-living increases, low wages, and police violence.

A number of demonstrators also carried signs targeting President Emmanuel Macron, who has faced significant criticism from protesters.

Some rallies in recent weeks have seen violence at the fringes, and the first major protest on October 17 saw looting in cities across France. Since then, police presence at rallies and controls on transport and permits to protest have been expanded.

Marseille, France’s second-largest city, banned protests over the weekend, but the prefecture announced that some 3,500 people still took to the streets. Local media reported that tear gas and a water cannon were used against protesters and shared images of fires burning in a popular local square.

In Lyon, local media reported that roughly 8,000 people took to the streets. They shared images of masked protesters chanting in front of fires lit in the street and police charging and using tear gas.

Tear gas use was also reported in Nantes, Bordeaux and Paris.

Unions have called for a new day of strikes on Tuesday after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent as “crumbs”.

If the demonstrations go ahead, they will take place on the eighth anniversary of the Gilet Jaune – which translates to “Yellow Vest” in French – movement, which rocked the beginning of the Macron government in 2018 with two years of protests triggered by rising fuel prices.

On Tuesday, the Yellow Vests will “celebrate their eight years where it all started: on roundabouts and toll booths all over France”, Yellow Vest protest tracking website 17octobregiletjaune.net writes.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: 106,000 people took part in protests nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris. The country has been gripped by high-school blockades, mass demonstrations, and strikes for more than a month.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Tens of thousands march in latest Portugal housing protests
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of more than 30 towns and cities in Portugal to protest against surging rental prices, demanding urgent government action to address the country’s worsening housing crisis.

Organised by the Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) platform, demonstrations on Saturday took place under the slogan “They will not steal our right to a home,” with protests in Lisbon, Porto, Faro, Portimao, Coimbra, Braga and other locations. It was the biggest national demonstration since the social movement began weeks ago.

Participants, ranging from teenagers to retired people, walked behind large banners, with the Lisbon march punctuated by drums, music, and chanting. Protesters called for caps to be placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing. They also demanded the reversal of proposed changes to rental legislation.

One woman on a protest march in Lisbon told Al Jazeera that she was a business owner, “and I can’t afford a house.”

“I can’t say much more than this. I’m forty-years-old, I can’t go to a bank and just buy a house with my money,” she added.

Another woman told Al Jazeera that she had joined the march to protest “for a better life, for all of us, not just the young people, all of us, because we deserve to have a home.”

One man told Al Jazeera “we have been suffering this for the last three or four years, and I have many friends and family in this situation, they had to move because they cannot afford the rent. If you earn, for example, a thousand euros, and you have to pay rent of six hundred, seven hundred, then you cannot live, it’s impossible.”

Casa Para Vivir brings together approximately 100 housing associations and grassroots organisations, is seeking tighter regulation on rental contracts, short-term tourist accommodation, and vacant properties.

The protests come after parliament approved the government’s proposed changes to provide greater flexibility in rental contracts and accelerate eviction procedures.

Housing campaigners warned the changes could weaken tenant protections amid rising rents and limited housing availability.

House prices in Portugal have risen much faster than incomes in recent years, statistics show. Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal posted the biggest jump in the European Union in the home price-to-income ratio, with an increase of 61 percent, followed by the Netherlands with 34 percent, the EU statistical office Eurostat said last week.

There is no indication that the rise in housing costs is slowing. Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, property prices rose by almost 20 percent, the National Statistics Institute, a government agency, said last month.

Rental prices, too, have climbed significantly, recording a 68 percent increase since 2020, according to the government. Much of this jump in real estate costs has been fuelled by foreign buyers and investment funds, as the country’s relaxed climate near the ocean has attracted many remote workers and retirees.

The government has responded to the protests by lowering taxes on new construction, restricting short-term rentals, and promising to build 145,000 new homes, but it acknowledged that the effects will not be immediate, as Prime Minister Luis Montenegro was urged by Casa Para Viver representatives to engage directly with them.

The protests in Portugal in recent weeks took their cue from demonstrations in neighbouring Spain last month over similar issues around housing and forced evictions. A wave of youth-led protests has swept Europe in the latter half of this year, with demonstrators across the continent denouncing rising prices and a lack of future prospects.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Thousands of people have taken to the streets of more than 30 towns and cities in Portugal to protest against rising rental prices. Protesters called for caps to be placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction. They also demanded the reversal of proposed changes to rental legislation.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Pope Leo urges end to violence in Peru during visit to remote Andes town
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Pope Leo XIV has called for an end to the violence gripping Peru, urging people not to respond to injustice with brutality, as he visited communities he once served as bishop.

“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, he said, speaking at his former cathedral in Chiclayo.

Peru’s homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reported extortion cases rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official figures cited by The Associated Press.

Security was a top concern for Peruvians in the last election. Conservative President Keiko Jujimori took office in July after promising to tackle crime. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.

She has also pursued closer ties with Washington, bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’ a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.

Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.

“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.

He also drew attention to the suffering of rural communities he used to serve, where migration and declining birth rates are emptying villages.

“Let us think, for example, of the suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future for themselves and their families in the great coastal cities,” he said.

Originally from Chicago in the United States and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo arrived in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba by helicopter and was welcomed by a local band singing “Pope Leo, welcome home.”

He’d made the journey to the remote area many times before during his time as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, driving himself along winding mountain roads in a pick-up truck.

The pope, who holds both US and Peruvian citizenship, spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US blames system upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The top United States transportation official has said work being performed on an antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for a rare, hours-long US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that halted all air traffic inside the country.

At a news conference in Washington, DC, on Saturday, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy spoke about routine maintenance that was performed on Friday to upgrade a router from copper to fibre at a “very remote location”.

Duffy said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router in question to start flooding other ones in the country’s air traffic control system.

“We had 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” he told reporters at the Department of Transportation.

When those connection issues caused disruption in radar feeds and communications between air traffic controllers and aeroplanes, Duffy said a ground stop was ordered.

“When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” he said.

The Transportation Department identified the contractor of Friday’s maintenance as L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company that has been tasked with modernising the communications system for the FAA.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

Duffy added that L3Harris, which he said had performed decades of work for the FAA, “didn’t meet the moment”.

“They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”

In response to Duffy’s allegations, L3Harris told Al Jazeera it has been working “in close coordination with the FAA” and places safety and reliability as its “highest priorities”.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the November 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” a spokesperson for the company said. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

Amid concerns that Friday’s ground stop was the result of a cyberattack, the US government said Saturday it did not “believe” that was the cause.

“Once we were able to isolate the work being done at this location, all of our systems came back online,” Duffy said. “So, we don’t believe this was cyber at all.”

The head of the FAA, who also spoke at Saturday’s news conference, echoed the transportation secretary’s remarks, saying the system outage was caused by an equipment error.

“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said.

A root cause analysis would be shared with the public when it is available, he added.

As airlines and thousands of travellers begin the process of digging out from Friday’s groundstop, the longest and only second nationwide stop since 9/11, the FAA said full schedule integrity is expected by the end of Sunday.

“We have crews and aircraft that are out of position for 12,000 flights that were lost,” Bedford said. “These crews, pilots and flight attendants need to get to their points of reconnection with their schedules.”

Bedford said the FAA expects about 4,000 to 5,000 flights out of the 41,000 scheduled on Saturday to be cancelled.

“That will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” he said. “I do think the worst is behind us.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said work being performed on antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop. Duffy said the router in question was to blame. The FAA said Friday’s ground stop was the result of a cyberattack.
