https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/elon-m.author: Anthony Ha
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/elon-m.text:
A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.

The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.

“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says.

Huang resigned on Thursday, several days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive identified by U.S. intelligence as a suspected Chinese spy. News reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs.

Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock fell 2% on Friday, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/tesla-.title: Tesla opens Cybercab pre-orders ‘for personal use,’ with geo restrictions and a $299 monthly fee
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/tesla-.author: Anthony Ha
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/tesla-.text:
Tesla said on Friday evening that “select customers” now have the opportunity to pre-order the company’s autonomous, golden Cybercab “for personal use.”

More details became clear as those select customers looked at the order page. Tech reviewer Marques Brownlee posted that buyers “must accept delivery” in one of a handful of Texas cities and that the Cybercab will only operate in certain geofenced areas. The estimated delivery date is December 2026.

In addition to the $29,990 price tag, Cybercab owners will need to pay $299 per month to operate their vehicle.

In response to Brownlee’s post, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the Cybercab “will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval.” He added that the monthly fee is “too high”: “Should match the cost of Tesla [Full Self-Driving] and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

Tesla’s Ashok Elluswamy offered more information about the geofencing, saying that Cybercab will work “unsupervised inside all the same geo locations as @robotaxi, just serving the owners’ needs.”

After falling far short of projected sales, Tesla recently announced it will cease Cybertruck production next year and use the additional factory capacity to build more Cybercabs.

SpaceX captured Starship using the arms of ‘Mechazilla’ its launch and catch tower for the first time.

SpaceX captured Starship using the arms of ‘Mechazilla’ its launch and catch tower for the first time.

After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15’s booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its “Mechazilla” launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ‘chopstick’ catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that “success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” While not a complete success, in that the company was unable to recover the entire launch vehicle, it still stands as a milestone for the Starship program. And, since it has previously caught boosters on previous launches, there is reason to believe the failure today was not an insurmountable obstacle. SpaceX is still trying to determine what caused the booster to abort its landing and detonate over the Gulf of Mexico.

In the video above, you can watch Starship plunge through the clouds, flip vertically, and, with surprising grace, ease itself between the waiting arms of Mechazilla at around 4:20 PM ET.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/jensen-hu.text:
In October, in a converted church in West London, Jensen Huang stepped onto a stage to preach to a packed congregation. The then–Nvidia CEO had a gospel to share with the politicians, tech executives, and journalists, Fortune among them, crowding the room: The AI boom was only getting started, and Nvidia was in town to help bankroll it.

“I’m gonna invest in you! I’m gonna invest in you!” he shouted at the founders in the crowd. “We’re not your largest investor, but we are your best investor.”

Huang’s London visit was one stop on a European charm offensive that also swept through France, Sweden, and Germany. At the time, the trip had the feeling of a victory lap. Nvidia is the default supplier of the vital chips that are fueling the AI industry’s rapid growth, and with a market cap that, at one point, topped $5.7 trillion, had seeded an entire ecosystem that came to depend on Nvidia’s support.

If the AI boom is a kind of religion, then Huang had been its high priest—proselytizing to investors and policymakers, ministering to the faithful, and doling out alms to needy startups, AI labs, and neoclouds. Nvidia was the world’s most valuable company, and Huang was one of the world’s most powerful men.

Just three weeks later, that victory lap across Europe looks more like a last hurrah. The man who sold the world his vision of an AI future was soon fighting for his own future—and on Thursday morning, the seismic news broke: Jensen Huang had resigned from his role as CEO.

His abrupt departure followed reports that U.S. intelligence agencies believed Huang had been involved with a woman who was working as a Chinese intelligence asset: Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that had bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips.

For the once seemingly untouchable founder, the fall from grace came fast. Within a week, Huang had sent a memo to Nvidia’s 42,000 staffers acknowledging he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and was “deeply sorry.” Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation; U.S. congressional leaders summoned Huang to answer questions; and federal agencies said they were investigating the matter. Nvidia shares tumbled, and prediction sites began to take bets on whether Huang would resign.

The other shoe dropped when the New York Times reported allegations of a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to Huang. By the next morning, Nvidia’s CEO of 33 years had submitted his resignation. Nvidia’s brief announcement of that fact—and of the appointment of chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO—gave no reason for his departure.

The timing couldn’t have been worse for Nvidia or for the AI industry in which Huang played such a central role. Worries about rising interest rates, dire warnings about AI’s extinction-level risks, and Americans’ opposition to data centers—on display in November’s midterm elections—have already put the AI boom’s foundations on shaky ground.

Critics have long warned that Nvidia’s AI investments had created a risky “circular” web in which Nvidia pours money into AI labs and data center companies, which in turn buy Nvidia chips. The company said that as of the end of July it had invested nearly $50 billion into leading AI model companies alone, including stakes in OpenAI, Anthropic, and Elon Musk’s xAI, and its equity investments across the AI ecosystem totaled twice that amount. The company has increasingly stepped in to use its investment-grade credit to help AI companies and so-called neocloud data center providers obtain financing. In total, it has pledged $170 billion on commitments of this kind, including guarantees valued at $105 billion to OpenAI for just one facility in Ohio. Additionally, Nvidia has been in talks with a consortium of Wall Street lenders to help backstop a $500 billion plan to turn AI chips into tradable securities.

This “central bank of AI” role, as some have characterized it, masked weak demand and inflated a dangerous financial bubble, critics argued. Just as worrisome, it positioned Nvidia as a single point of failure that could destabilize the entire industry. But even the company’s harshest critics didn’t expect the biggest threat to Nvidia to come from the man at the center of it all.

To be clear: Even with its charismatic founder no longer in the CEO role, Nvidia’s core business isn’t going anywhere. Its chips remain the industry standard; its supply is sold out and contracted through the next year. The company can survive “independent of his cult of personality,” says Francine McKenna, an investigative journalist and expert on corporate governance and accounting. But Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners, warns that Nvidia risks losing what made it exceptional: Huang’s willingness to make big bets and keep moving even when some—like Nvidia’s ill-fated effort to make chips for mobile phones—failed. “If they lose that,” he says, “they’re going to become just another chip company.”

Indeed, for all its dominance, Nvidia was never invincible: Some of its best customers were already turning to rival chips or building their own, and governments were pushing for “sovereign AI” that doesn’t depend on American tech.

The AI boom is bigger than any one company, but the sector has yet to prove it can thrive without Nvidia—and Nvidia has yet to prove it can thrive without Huang. Can the industry outgrow its dependence on its most powerful evangelist, or will Huang’s departure from the company he built expose how much of the boom was built on faith?

In a wide-ranging interview with Fortune in London—before news of the affairs broke but months after concerns about Nvidia’s dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed first surfaced—Huang was still going full speed even though he’d only eaten “half of a half sandwich” all day.

He was behind schedule for his next engagement in the church across town, but waved his hand dismissively. “I’ve been late all day,” he said. This was a man who knew very well: The show couldn’t go on without him.

Huang was characteristically optimistic about the future of AI, and about another topic: China. The opportunity there “is large and growing,” he said, wearing his signature black leather jacket in the sweeping lounge of a Central London office building that had just hosted an Nvidia-sponsored hackathon. “We should provide, and we do provide, the best, the soonest, and the most to American companies,” he said. “However, we should compete.”

To understand what happened to Huang, one has to understand Nvidia’s history with China, which has long been a major part of the Santa Clara, Calif.–based company’s business. That business took a hit in 2022 when the Biden administration barred Nvidia from selling its most advanced AI chips there, in an effort to slow Beijing’s progress in the AI race. Successive rule changes forced out even Nvidia’s scaled-down chips. And Beijing started discouraging Chinese AI companies from buying American chips.

Huang—who once publicly complained that U.S. export controls had shrunk Nvidia’s share of China’s AI chip market from 95% to zero—lobbied hard to roll back the export controls. He argued that allowing Nvidia to sell its chips in China would help make American tech the global standard—and crowd out Chinese competitors who were advancing quickly.

When Donald Trump won a second term in 2024, Huang donated $1 million to his inaugural fund and began making frequent pilgrimages to Mar-a-Lago. By all accounts, the two men became close. Trump once phoned while Huang was onstage at a summit in Los Angeles; Huang put him on speaker, and the pair dismissed fears about AI to the crowd.

In late 2025, Huang won a key compromise: Nvidia would be allowed to ship a second-tier chip model to approved Chinese customers. In an unprecedented arrangement, the U.S. government would take a 25% cut.

Huang’s lobbying proved “very effective,” said Ed Mills, a policy analyst with investment firm Raymond James. “There was an ‘in Jensen we trust mantra’ within D.C. and a push within the tech industry to pivot away from seeking to restrict what China got, to seeing if we could get China hooked on our technology.”

It emerged after the scandal broke that Megaspeed had long been suspected of helping Chinese firms dodge export controls. People briefed on U.S. intelligence told the Times that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information on American AI chips and to persuade Nvidia to push for its advanced chips to be sold in China.

China hawks in both U.S. political parties have accused Nvidia of downplaying chip smuggling and overstating the strength of China’s homegrown chips to win looser rules. Huang’s affair with a suspected China asset gave them fresh ammunition to question his motives. “This episode makes clear what we have been alleging the whole time, which is that Nvidia is deeply compromised,” said Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a group that lobbies for regulation of the tech and AI industry. “At best they turned a blind eye to smuggling of their chips into China. At worst, they were complicit in it.”

Meanwhile, China called the allegations “groundless speculation and slander,” and Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe” firm secrets or national security were compromised. (Nvidia did not respond to multiple questions from Fortune seeking additional comment after news of the affairs and eventual resignation.)

Later reporting revealed that a U.S. Commerce Department probe into whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chips into China was halted and passed to the Justice Department after Nvidia’s general counsel contacted the agents running it. An Nvidia spokesperson told the Times that the company had contacted officials “to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field,” and to seek guidance.

Soon after news of Huang’s affair with Alice Huang broke, President Trump called the Nvidia CEO “very aboveboard” but described the situation as “very complex.”

The scandal has also exposed a rift inside the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent took to CNBC this week to suggest Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department had stalled efforts to restrict Megaspeed, saying Treasury, Defense, and State had “for months” favored putting the company on the entity list. Bessent said that the focus on Huang’s personal life missed the point. “The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage?” he said.

Reports have also emerged that Bessent had pressed Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over his resistance to export controls (a Commerce spokeswoman later denied this). Alongside Huang, Lutnick has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about the department’s handling of Nvidia chip exports and the Megaspeed case.

At Nvidia’s flagship GPU Technology Conference (GTC) in Berlin a few days after Huang’s London visit, his keynote hit capacity almost two hours before he took the stage. In his speech, Huang was relentlessly upbeat about the AI boom. He urged Europe to embrace its AI future and build more AI “factories”—Huang’s preferred term for data centers. He wrapped the show with a Eurovision song contest performed by AI agents.

But despite Huang’s onstage enthusiasm and his rock-star reception, the AI boom was already showing signs of strain. “He is a cheerleader for a market, and he is cheerleading it,” Paul Miller, a principal analyst at Forrester, said at a crowded Berlin coffee shop after Huang’s event. “But even he’s not blind to the problems that this sector faces.”

Those ranged from concerns about an AI bubble to fears that AI could pose catastrophic risks to humanity. And by November, a new problem had emerged for the industry: the U.S. midterm elections. Democrats, many of whom had campaigned on reining in AI and data center development, won control of Congress, and voters overwhelmingly backed ballot measures aimed at restricting new data centers. AI stocks tumbled following the blue wave elections, as investors braced for a tougher regime of regulation.

Meanwhile, an even more pressing threat to Nvidia is emerging: Its best customers want to build their own AI chips to reduce their costs and to give themselves more control over chip supply.

Google already trains its Gemini models on its own TPU chips instead of relying solely on industry-standard GPUs. Amazon is pushing its Trainium chips. OpenAI is designing its own silicon with Broadcom. Anthropic increasingly uses Google TPUs, AMD’s GPUs, and Amazon’s Trainium chips, too—although it also uses Nvidia’s. AI itself is making it easier for Nvidia’s customers to switch, with developers using frontier AI coding agents to handle the otherwise difficult and time-consuming work of migrating AI workloads between different chip types.

Countries including the U.K. are also trying to develop their own chips and pursuing AI models that might be able to run on “heterodox compute”—which mixes chips of different types in a single data center—to lessen dependency on American tech like Nvidia’s.

This is all bad news for Nvidia. Hyperscalers and large cloud providers account for about half of its data center revenue, which makes up more than 90% of its total sales.

Huang was in Europe in part to play out his defense strategy and counter the continent’s sovereign AI push, pitching Nvidia as the solution: Europeans could run any model they liked, including open-source ones like those from French AI company Mistral, as long as it ran on Nvidia chips. Huang and Nvidia have heavily backed open-source AI, or models whose underlying “weights” are published for anyone to download, modify, and run on their own hardware. (Anthropic and OpenAI, in contrast, keep their weights secret and sell access only through their own apps and cloud services.) The reasoning, for Nvidia: A thriving open-source ecosystem full of companies that need Nvidia chips and its CUDA software to run their models would offer the chipmaker a hedge for if and when the leading closed labs start getting their chips elsewhere. And it’s good for the world, Huang argued in London: “Our business model is so transparent,” he said. “We benefit when the world uses AI. Period. Whether it’s closed or open.”

But not everyone is convinced. Aldo Podestà, CEO of Italian AI startup Giotto.ai, calls Nvidia’s strategy a “Trojan horse.” The company gives away free software that works best on its own chips, he says, so the more people use it, the more they end up relying on Nvidia. “Some dependence is easier to accept when it arrives in the language of freedom,” he says.

Nvidia controls an estimated 80% of the global market for AI chips, and its hardware fills the data centers that tech giants are racing to build. At GTC Berlin, the AI industry’s reliance on Nvidia was on full display.

Beyond the robot demos and packed panels, Nvidia’s partners, including many neocloud companies, took up much of the floor. These newer cloud companies, including Nebius and CoreWeave, buy Nvidia chips in vast quantities, pack them into data centers, and rent the computing power to AI labs and businesses. Many of them count Nvidia as a supplier, an investor, and in some cases, a customer. (Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company at the center of the recent scandal is also a neocloud.)

As of late July, Nvidia held about $99 billion in investments across what Huang calls AI’s “five-layer cake”: energy companies, data center operators, chipmakers, model builders, and the apps that sit on top. In several cases, those deals come with promises from the labs to spend heavily on Nvidia’s chips.

To Huang, this was all just good business. “Every single one of the layers we’ve selected are very strategic and really high-quality companies to invest in,” Huang said. “Everybody we invest in are connected into Nvidia’s ecosystem, and so we’re making our platform more vibrant.” But to critics like Michael Burry—the investor famed for betting against the U.S. housing bubble—Huang is inflating a dangerous financial bubble in AI with “circular financing” deals.

In his interview with Fortune, Huang dismissed the idea that Nvidia is propping up the AI boom. The company, he said, only takes minority stakes in a given venture, meaning other investors have to believe in the companies, too. He insists that Nvidia’s investments are necessary since AI, unlike earlier software booms, requires enormous amounts of capital upfront. “We’ve created an industry that the VCs alone cannot fund,” he said. And the bets, he added, “have returned fabulously.”

The neoclouds exhibiting in Berlin make a similar case. “If it’s all going to come down to Nvidia’s capital, we would have run out already,” says Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nvidia-backed neocloud Nebius. But even he acknowledges that “many companies out there … have more extreme financial relationships with Nvidia than we do.”

Of course in boom times, the vulnerabilities in the system are easy to ignore. But, McKenna says, “Nvidia’s role propping up much of the AI sector puts enormous pressure on weak links if demand ends up less than the very rosy forecasts.”

The worst case is that several big customers such as OpenAI or CoreWeave can’t earn enough to cover their bills. If that happens, Nvidia could find itself losing chip sales and its equity investment in these companies, and find itself on the hook for some of their debts. Such fallout would cause widespread carnage in the financial markets, starting with Nvidia’s own share price.

It’s worth remembering Cisco, whose routers and switches carried much of the early internet’s traffic. It was a “picks and shovels” operator in the dotcom bubble, holding a place similar to the one Nvidia occupies now—and it too engaged in vendor financing to seed the market for its networking hardware. When the bubble burst in late 2000, Cisco didn’t go out of business. But its market value plunged more than 85%, and to this day, it has never touched those levels again.

“Weak links come from unexpected places and create systemic risks that can ripple through supply chains and sales cycles,” McKenna said in an interview in late October. Now, the vulnerability has emerged at the very center of that web. How far the damage will spread remains to be seen.

It wasn’t just Nvidia’s pile of cash or its investment-grade credit rating or its advanced chips that helped fuel the AI boom: It was also Huang’s good name. Huang was well-regarded long before AI made him a corporate celebrity.

His personal story gave him an underdog credibility few tech billionaires can claim: His first job was as a teenage dishwasher at Denny’s, and he and his cofounders later sketched out the idea for the chip company in one of that restaurant chain’s booths. They founded it in 1993, and Nvidia chips went on to become the go-to for the video gaming industry. Huang steered Nvidia through a near-death experience in its earliest days, when the company almost ran out of money. He built it into the engine of the gaming industry and a Fortune 500 company—then, two decades later, was early to spot the opportunity in artificial intelligence.

If Nvidia is the linchpin of the AI industry, Huang was the linchpin of Nvidia, and his sudden absence exposed just how much of the company’s success rests upon him. In trading following his resignation, Nvidia stock dove as much as 14%, briefly pushing the company below a $4 trillion market cap for the first time in more than a year—then recovering somewhat.

Huang put himself squarely in the middle of a company that still operates “like a startup,” says Laura Fay, who reported directly to Huang for a decade at Nvidia before retiring in July. His management style is famously flat: He has said that at one point he had around 60 direct reports.

That structure helped Nvidia move at what Huang likes to call the “speed of light.” It has also left the company unusually dependent on one man. At the time of his resignation, Nvidia had no president, no chief operating officer, and no obvious No. 2. Its board had no executive chairman.

Nvidia may feel Huang’s absence most acutely in Washington, where he maintained chummy relationships and spent years bending policy in the company’s favor. In May, Trump even brought Huang aboard Air Force One to China—joking at the time to Fortune that he was surprised Huang didn’t have his own private jet. That was reportedly around the same time Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed the president on the suspected spying operation. (Trump has since said that warning “didn’t make much of an impact on” him.)

The company has pushed back hard on think tanks that advocated tougher chip export controls, and some customers, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have avoided taking public positions on the issue for fear of angering the chipmaker, according to a report from The Information. In a statement to the outlet, an Nvidia spokesperson defended the company’s stance against export controls: “America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide.”

Some in the industry have called Nvidia a bully and complained that anyone who disagrees with its stances could be put in “Jensen jail” and cut off from much-needed chips. Others say that clout is just a function of the company’s success: Nvidia “make[s] the best chips, and companies want them a lot and are afraid of doing things that could anger [Nvidia],” says Nathan Calvin, general counsel and VP of state affairs at Encode, a nonprofit that advocates for regulation of AI and Big Tech. “They have a lot of influence and leverage that they can use to advance their favored policy positions.”

It remains to be seen what will happen to that leverage. Huang was Nvidia’s most effective advocate in Washington, and with him gone, the company has lost its loudest voice opposing the tightening of rules on chip sales to China. New export controls are probable, even before the new crop of lawmakers is sworn in. Huang’s departure “guarantees new export controls,” said Raymond James analyst Mills. Three bills proposing new export controls on AI chips and advanced semiconductor equipment are attached to the defense authorization bill awaiting passage on Capitol Hill. The Nvidia scandal “is the accelerant to push [the legislation] over the finish line,” Mills said.

What remains uncertain, he said, is how far those restrictions will go and how robustly the Trump administration will enforce them. The bills still have a loophole for “remote access” in which Chinese AI companies can access Nvidia chips in data centers located in other Asian nations, he noted. That access is exactly what Alice Huang’s former neocloud company, Megaspeed, reportedly provided to Chinese firms. Mills said such loopholes could be closed by policies that would require Nvidia and other chipmakers to implement know-your-customer policies and, in the case of resellers and cloud companies, to identify who their customers’ customers are.

It is also possible that Washington will enact licensing requirements or restrictions on open-source AI models, measures Huang had advocated against. Because the best open-source models have been created by Chinese AI labs, “open-source equals China” in the minds of many lawmakers, Mills said. “If Washington is serious about trying to win the AI race against China we need to see regulations on open-source.”

For investors, policy questions run second to a more immediate one: With Huang gone, who keeps the AI boom intact?

The companies most exposed in the wake of his departure are the neoclouds. The future of all those ventures now looks unclear. Some of Huang’s most ambitious plans to finance these companies, including the more than $500 billion financing platform Nvidia announced with Wall Street firms in August, had already faced resistance at senior levels inside Nvidia, according to Goldberg of Seaport Research Partners. “Nobody at Nvidia could replace Jensen’s role in bringing that together,” he said. Without Huang, he expects many neocloud projects simply won’t get funded.

Following Huang’s exit, investors may also start to scrutinize the numbers Huang used to justify Nvidia’s complex web of investments, said Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business. “Is ‘Jensen’s Math,’ the term used for the complex financial entanglements of these AI firms … about to collapse?” Schloetzer asked rhetorically. “What else has he covered up? What else is lacking candor?”

Nvidia’s partners may also find they have more leverage. Companies that once took Nvidia’s money on Nvidia’s terms could start pushing back. “Maybe they’ll drive a harder bargain,” McKenna said.

The rest of the industry won’t escape unscathed. AI has the momentum to keep going, Goldberg said, but it will become “much more vulnerable to political pressure,” especially amid the backlash against data centers. Anthropic, which is set to go public just days after Nvidia reports its first-ever quarterly earnings without Huang, will be the industry’s first taste of a world after Jensen. Nvidia has agreed to buy about $10 billion of shares as part of a $26 billion private placement alongside the listing, and investors expect that commitment to go ahead without Huang. But his departure could raise the stakes for the wider industry and put some of the companies’ partners under the microscope. Schloetzer, for example, said he expects “much closer scrutiny of [Anthropic’s] ties to Nvidia and customers associated with Nvidia.”

The likely winners are Nvidia’s rival chipmakers. The turmoil, Goldberg says, is “really good for AMD, and it’s really good for Broadcom.” Google’s TPUs are likely to benefit from any concerns about Nvidia’s long-term prospects. AMD, Nvidia’s longtime archrival in the GPU market, will probably see some market share gain, too.

Since the scandal broke, one of the loudest voices in tech has gone quiet. Huang pulled out of public appearances, and his only public statement has been an apology to his staff. “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” he wrote. “I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security.”

The chastened tone was a far cry from the bombastic man on the sofa in London. What Huang was selling then was the rosiest possible vision of our AI future. The technology, he argued, would give a small local business the same software firepower as a tech giant. “As a result, everybody will become more ambitious,” he said. “And so I’m excited about that.”

The AI boom has run, in large part, on faith in Jensen Huang and the story he has been telling. He promised that demand for his chips would keep climbing, that AI’s risks could be engineered away, and that the companies building the future-shaping technology could be trusted to police themselves. And for so long, investors, customers, and global leaders happily took that leap with him.

But now that faith has been shattered. The AI boom’s high priest is gone, and the world is waiting to see if the entire AI church he helped construct comes toppling down with him, steeple and all.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-indust.title: The hottest job in AI right now may be counterintelligence as companies pay former spooks $500,000 to protect trade secrets
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-indust.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-indust.text:
The scandal that brought down Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, the AI chip giant he cofounded, has highlighted the growing demand for protection against industrial espionage.

Last weekend, he admitted to a romantic affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. While the U.S. intelligence community raised alarms about their relationship, Huang continued to enjoy access to President Donald Trump and his top administration officials.

Nvidia’s board launched an investigation but doesn’t think that national security or company secrets were compromised.

Still, U.S. officials believe Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, and surveillance revealed that she was feeding information to Beijing, according to reports. China has denied any espionage.

The case came a month after an OpenAI engineer was arrested for planting a listening device in a company conference room. The Justice Department alleged he was communicating with a member of the Saudi royal family.

Given the high-stakes race to achieve AI supremacy, the technology has been deemed a matter of national security, and protecting trade secrets has become especially critical.

AI firms like OpenAI, Anthropic and Nvidia have started hiring for counterintelligence roles in recent years, with most salaries ranging from $200,000 to $500,000, according to workforce data tracker Revelio Labs.

Revelio data compiled by Reuters shows that Anthropic alone has hired 33 employees for counterintelligence functions so far this year, up from 14 last year, and nine in 2024. In 2025, Anthropic appointed former CIA deputy director David Cohen and former National Security Agency cybersecurity director Dave Luber to its national security advisory council.

OpenAI’s counterintelligence hiring jumped to 22 in 2026 from nine in 2025. And in 2024, OpenAI named former National Security Agency director Paul Nakasone to its board.

Despite the Nvidia scandal, the company actually hired 16 people for counterintelligence this year.

“The AI firms have snapped up a lot of security talent,” ​Christopher Falkenberg, a former U.S. Secret Service agent and current president of Insite Risk Management, told Reuters.

“There are some very sophisticated people out of government thinking about security for these businesses… Demand outstrips ​the supply of people with relevant experience.”

Top tech firms are looking for even more talent. OpenAI is seeking a senior global ​security investigator with counterintelligence listed as a key skill, Anthropic is advertising for a ‌threat-intelligence security ⁠engineer, and ASML is in the hunt for ​a Taiwan-based intelligence officer, according to Reuters.

Eric O’Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative, told Fortune‘s Tatiana Sataua this week that protecting executives should include teaching them to recognize manipulation—and giving others a way to intervene when the boss won’t listen.

He said an approach rarely begins with someone asking an executive to hand over company secrets. It may start at a conference, through a business introduction, over drinks, or even on a dating app.

Warning signs can be subtle: a relationship that moves unusually quickly, persistent questions about sensitive business matters, requests to meet influential colleagues, or encouragement to keep secrets. Those signs are harder to recognize when the person under scrutiny is someone the executive trusts.

“By the time a security professional raises concerns, the executive may already be emotionally invested and unwilling to listen,” O’Neill said.

Of course, the private sector isn’t alone in identifying the need to guard against industrial espionage. The U.S. defense and intelligence communities are getting more aggressive.

Sources told the Washington Post last month that the Pentagon is planning a spying program that deploys “nonofficial cover officers” who pose as executives—a covert effort in a larger economic warfare campaign.

Politico also reported that the Defense Department is quietly building an elite agency to covertly sabotage foreign technology programs that could threaten U.S. military superiority.

The Technology Support Office was established in April by reorganizing two classified intelligence programs that have been secretly carrying out technology sabotage at a smaller scale since 2023.

The Pentagon has denied the reports.

Other signs point to the U.S. taking economic warfare more seriously. In September, CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis said the U.S. is expanding espionage against China by targeting companies in sensitive areas like AI, biotechnology and chips.

Also this year, the Pentagon formed the Economic Defense Unit for “deterring, denying, disrupting, and helping to defeat adversaries through economic means,” sources told DefenseScoop.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/faa-groun.title: FAA telecom problems that triggered the ground stop were so alarming the White House situation room and national security apparatus went into action
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/faa-groun.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/faa-groun.text:
The country is on edge as freezers and email go haywire, and the federal government wasn’t taking any chances either when the FAA saw a communications issue.

On Friday, the regulator ordered a nationwide ground stop for several hours, forcing airlines to delay and cancel thousands of flights, after a communications problem affecting air-traffic control was detected.

Officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or other nefarious activity, but the speed with which the telecom issue spread was alarming enough to briefly elevate it to the highest echelons of government.

During a press briefing on Saturday, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the White House situation room and the entire national security infrastructure were activated, noting that the FBI was also in facilities to investigate.

“I think we’ve all concluded that it’s not a cyber issue,” he declared.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said FBI Director Kash Patel, the director of national intelligence, and the Defense Department participated in a conference call because they were concerned there was a cyberattack from another country.

But they didn’t see any online chatter to indicate a hacking attempt, Duffy added. And once the FAA isolated the location where the telecom problem originated and took it offline, then the system began functioning properly again.

“We feel very comfortable that that was the root cause of the impact on our system,” he said. “It wasn’t a foreign actor.”

Still, cybersecurity has been top of mind lately. Hackers raised the temperatures in freezers across Europe and at U.S. military bases, making food go bad.

Last month saw so many cyberattacks that it was dubbed “Black October.” Cybersecurity experts also rushed to fix vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language that’s used in nearly 70% of all websites.

After the U.S. launched its war on Iran, the regime warned it would retaliate via cyberspace and threatened to cut undersea cables that carry internet traffic.

Meanwhile, consumers are still grappling with the aftermath of a Microsoft outage that shut down email, collaboration and AI functions. The company said Friday it had no indication that the ground stop was related to its global outage.

What actually caused the problem was more mundane.

It began when a contractor with L3Harris was doing routine maintenance at a remote FAA location to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber optics, according to Duffy.

But the changeover caused routers across the air traffic control system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, he explained. Because it disrupted some radar feeds, the FAA ordered the ground stop to ensure safety.

“So what we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router,” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was. Was it the router or were they not doing great work for us at L3Harris?”

He later pointed out that the company owns the legacy telecom network, while the department is working with “the greatest telecom companies in the world,” like be AT&T, Verizon, and Lumens to build a new architecture.

Duffy also stressed again that L3Harris owns the network and is the prime contractor, warning that the department will hold people accountable.

“Many of our contractors, many of our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us,” he complained. “And we have demanded more. We’ve demanded better because the American people deserve better. And we’re getting better performance from everyone who’s doing business with us now. We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job.”

An L3Harris spokesperson said the company has been modernizing the communications infrastructure for the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA.

Along with its telecom partners and the FAA, L3Harris added that it has completed more than 70% of the conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/faa-groun.summary: The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop for several hours Friday after a communications problem. The problem was caused by a contractor with L3Harris, which is the company that is the prime contractor. The FAA says it has no indication the problem was related to its global outage.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/spacex-p.title: SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/spacex-p.author: Lora Kolodny
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/spacex-p.text:
SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit.

Elon Musk’s aerospace company made the historic catch using its “chopsticks,” mechanical arms attached to a launch tower, at its Starbase, Texas, facility.

During the first phase of the flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the rocket’s booster, instead diverting it to splash down in the Gulf of Mexico, where it exploded before hitting the water.

After a booster explosion on Friday, SpaceX
 successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit on Saturday — a triumphant milestone for the company.

SpaceX made the historic catch using its “chopsticks,” mechanical arms attached to a launch tower, at its facility in Starbase, Texas.

Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship test yet, marked the first time Musk’s company attempted to catch both the rocket’s booster and upper stage.

During the first phase of the test flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the booster, instead diverting it to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded before hitting the water.

The rocket’s upper stage then continued into orbit and flew around the Earth 14 times before successfully landing on SpaceX’s launch tower, nicknamed Mechazilla.

The Hawaii Department of Transportation issued a temporary pause on some West Coast flights Friday, due to debris risk from the flight. Separately, the FAA issued a rare, nationwide ground stop due to telecommunications system failures. (Both of those orders have since been lifted.)

Making Starship a reliable and fully reusable rocket is critical to SpaceX’s ambitions. In the near term, the company needs Starship to send more satellites into orbit to expand its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company’s profit center.

SpaceX is also expected to use Starship to bring astronauts and cargo from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface and back for NASA. Musk also has a grand vision to use Starship to “colonize Mars” and “make humanity multi-planetary.”

During Test Flight 15 on Friday, SpaceX released another 26 of its newest Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, growing its commercial satellite internet network.

The company’s constellation already included over 11,000 satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket can carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites, the company has said.

During the first phase of the flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the rocket’s booster, instead diverting it to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded before hitting the water.

https://www.france24.com/en/spacex-stars.title: SpaceX's Starship completes first-ever mid-air catch after return from orbit
https://www.france24.com/en/spacex-stars.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/spacex-stars.text:
SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.

Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.

The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss.

“Can you believe it?” shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot.

SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, intended for moon and Mars travel. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.

The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

READ MORE
SpaceX's supersized Starship rocket reaches Earth orbit for the first time

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.

It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

READ MORE
Want to live on the moon? NASA opens recruitment for Artemis programme

Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Netanyahu renews call for Israeli government unity as Eisenkot dismisses 'tricks'
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Israel's caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday reiterated his calls for a national unity government with his opponent Gadi Eisenkot, who in turn dismissed the appeal as a ruse.

The latest exchange comes as Eisenkot is in the midst of negotiations to form a government, after he was tapped for the post of premier on Sunday.

READ MORE
Israel's new parliament to be sworn in as Eisenkot prepares government

A meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday "only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government" to guarantee Israel's security, Netanyahu said in a video statement, adding that such a government could "eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all".

He said this government would be made up of parties that recognise Israel "as a state for the Jewish people".

It would address security challenges, he added, most notably Iran which he claimed would "not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us".

The outgoing prime minister warned against Eisenkot's plan to form a minority government, presented as a "national emergency government".

Such a plan would see the 48 lawmakers in Eisenkot's bloc vote in favour of his government, against the 46 Netanyahu backers. The 26 other members of parliament, from Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties, could abstain, allowing the government to be approved without an absolute majority in the Knesset, which has 120 seats.

"Instead of trying to form a weak and dangerous government... let's meet in one room, without preconditions, put aside all our disagreements and all the boycotts, and reach agreements for the security and the future of the state," Netanyahu urged.

Minutes later, Eisenkot responded by saying Netanyahu "knows he lost the election", accusing him of playing "tricks" by appealing for a unity government.

"Netanyahu is calling for negotiations while they are already underway; he claims to want unity but... sows division and stokes tensions as if there were no tomorrow," the former army chief said, adding that "these tricks don't work on me".

Eisenkot was tapped on Sunday to form a new government within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension.

Negotiations are expected to be difficult, especially as Netanyahu has waged a campaign to discredit Arab-Israeli parties, which gained a record number of seats in the election.

Netanyahu's proposed unity government would be made up of key Jewish parties ranging from the centre to the right, while excluding the Arab parties.

READ MORE
Eisenkot pushes October 7 inquiry as Netanyahu targets Arab parties in tense new parliament

Eisenkot has indicated he would be open to forming a government with members of Netanyahu's Likud party, as well as outgoing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism, provided their commitment to unity is "sincere".

But a unity government with Netanyahu himself remains unlikely, particularly after Eisenkot denounced his "racist" campaign against Arab parties on Friday.

Eisenkot on Saturday reiterated his calls for a "break with the extremists", notably supporters of far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir, as a condition for any participation in a government under his leadership.

Another point of contention is the election on Tuesday of the speaker of the Knesset, a post currently held by Amir Ohana, a close Netanyahu ally. The opposition has put forward Matan Kahana, a former officer in the Israeli army who was fifth on Gadi Eisenkot's list, to replace him.

"If they (Likud and its allies) are truly seeking a sincere political partnership, as they claim, they must allow the democratic process to unfold normally... and instruct their members of parliament to support the appointment of Matan Kahana," Eisenkot said.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Macron says limiting Ukraine aid would pave way to 'another war'
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
French President Emmanuel Macron said Saturday that countries seeking to limit aid to Ukraine want to impose an "unjust peace" and warned that it was a recipe for another war.

The French leader's statement posted on social media comes as the United States mediates talks between Ukraine and Russia in a bid to end the war that started with Moscow's 2022 full-scale invasion.

"Those who want to ration aid to Ukraine wish underneath it all to force an unjust peace on it" and, by extension, all of Europe, Macron said.

"That is the spirit of defeat. That is a recipe for another war. That cannot be France's position."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in comments released Saturday that Washington has suggested Kyiv cede land to Moscow in exchange for Ukraine joining NATO.

READ MORE
US proposed Ukraine cedes Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, Zelensky says

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky separately on Thursday, after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi which ended with no breakthrough.

Negotiations did, however, lead to agreements that European countries will join future talks on ending the war.

On Friday, in Dublin, Europe chose five countries – France, Germany, Italy, the UK and Poland – to send representatives to the talks.

"Europe must take full part" in the work to bring about a "fair and lasting peace" in Ukraine, Macron said.

"What happens in Ukraine concerns us directly... Helping Ukraine defend itself is protecting France and the French."

READ MORE
France among five major powers to represent EU in Ukraine talks

The French president said that Ukraine's allies must clearly set out, including to Russia, its postwar vision and "we must also detail what we expect of the United States for Europe's long-term security".

Macron added that he believed "Vladimir Putin does not want to negotiate" and was trying to break Ukraine by stepping up drone and missile strikes against civilians and energy infrastructure as winter closes in.

"That means we must keep up our financial backing and helping Ukraine protect its population, its power plants and its grids," he said.
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron says countries seeking to limit aid to Ukraine want to impose an "unjust peace" He says those who want to ration aid to the country want to force an " unjust peace" on it. The French president says that Ukraine's allies must clearly set out, including to Russia, its postwar vision.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:

Ellie Carpenter (right) provided the assist for Chelsea's only goal of the game in the victory over Manchester City. (Getty Images: Bryn Lennon)

Chelsea moved above Manchester City in the WSL table with a 1-0 at Stamford Bridge.

Ellie Carpenter provided the assist for Chelsea's goal.

Chelsea next play Paris Saint-Germain in the women's Champions League in midweek.

Ellie Carpenter has continued her thunderous campaign for Chelsea, helping set up the winner in the Blues' table-topping Women's Super League (WSL) victory over champions Manchester City.

By assisting on Sandy Baltimore's stunning goal that sealed the 1-0 win at Stamford Bridge on Saturday (Sunday AEDT), the on-song wing back also earned the bragging rights over Matildas' teammate Mary Fowler, who was taken off by City with half an hour to go after a much more ineffective afternoon.

By inflicting City's first league defeat of the season, Chelsea went back to the top, leapfrogging the champs to go a point clear after 10 matches.

And as usual this season, the energetic 26-year-old Carpenter, who has looked one of the best players in the WSL this term, was at the heart of the win, already having caused plenty of problems with her crossing from the right flank even before her key contribution deep into stoppage time in the first half.

Carpenter found Baltimore in the box with a short pass and then sped off to take the return pass while dragging her defender with her.

That simply opened up more space for French international Baltimore, who had time to set her sights and curl home a superb left-footed strike beyond keeper Ayaka Yamashita.

It was Carpenter's first assist of her exceptional league season to go with her four goals.

However, across all competitions she's the club leader with nine goal involvements, five goals and four assists.

City looked as if they could eke out an equaliser but their hopes were finally dashed with a quarter of an hour left when Yamashita was sent off, losing out in a race to the ball with Alyssa Thompson and clumsily bringing her down.

Fowler, whose recent form has helped her really nail down a starting spot at City, had already been taken off by that point, replaced by fit-again WSL legend Vivianne Miedema, but the visitors still could not find an equaliser, Lauren Hemp missing a sitter from point-blank range in the 64th minute.

It was City's first defeat in any competition since April 25.

Elsewhere, Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier marked her 150th appearance for the club with a goal in a 2-0 victory at Crystal Palace that moved them to fourth, while Tottenham drew 0-0 at home to Everton and Liverpool won 3-0 at Brighton.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/y.title: A slowing economy could mean higher youth unemployment, economist warns
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/y.author: Fiona Blackwood
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/y.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Lachlan Riddell says he has applied for hundreds of jobs over the past three years. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Economists are watching to see if youth unemployment rises further as the economy softens.

Young people are increasingly competing with multiple job holders for work.

University students are being encouraged to engage with the job market well before they graduate.

Young people struggling to find work can be the canary in the coal mine for the rest of the jobs market.

And a recent rise in the youth unemployment rate could be a sign of things to come.

Australian Bureau of Statistics data from September showed youth unemployment at 11.1 per cent compared with the overall unemployment rate of 4.7 per cent.

While still lower than before the pandemic, a slowing economy could mean youth unemployment rises further in the coming months.

"We tend to see younger workers affected more heavily when there is a slowdown," chief economist at jobs website SEEK, Blair Chapman, said.

Commonwealth Bank economist Harry Ottley said the youth unemployment rate was "definitely rising more quickly than other cohorts".

Topic:Women’s Big Bash League

Topic:
Women’s Big Bash League

Lachlan Riddell has experienced what he describes as "job hunting depression".

"I started to fall into a bit of a slump, [asking myself], 'why am I even doing this'," he said.

The 24-year-old estimated he had applied for hundreds of jobs over the past three years, from collecting supermarket trolleys to retail and hospitality roles.

"I feel like there is a mentality that … generation Z don't want to work, that they're very selective about what they want to do, which is simply not true," he said.

Lachlan Riddell says without a permanent job, he's struggling to make ends meet. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Riddell has a Diploma of Music and works casually as an audio-visual technician, but shifts are sporadic.

He said that despite having wide-ranging work experience, he rarely received a response from employers, and most job applications were online.

He has concerns that success in Tasmania's small jobs market can depend less on what you know than who you know.

Lachlan Riddell has applied for jobs, including in hospitality. (ABC News: Sam Ikin)

As he continues his search for more permanent work, Mr Riddell said he was struggling to make ends meet on his Jobseeker payment and relied on support from his fiancee.

Graduate job ads have been trending down after post-pandemic highs, according to SEEK.

"There is anecdotal evidence that several larger firms have reduced their graduate intakes in recent years," Mr Chapman said.

"The big four accounting firms are a good example of this as they reduced their intakes in response to declines in demand."

Blair Chapman says the number of graduate jobs has been trending down. (ABC News: John Gunn)

He said he suspected a slowdown in demand for graduates would continue in Australia as the economy softened.

But it is not all bad news.

The rise in youth unemployment has come alongside continued job growth for young people.

Harry Ottley says there are more young people in the labour market looking for work. (Supplied)

"The share of young people in work [the employment-to-population ratio] is 63.6 per cent, down from a peak of 66.7 per cent in November 2022, but well above its 2019 average of 59.7 per cent," Mr Ottley said.

He said youth participation was also high at 71.4 per cent compared with 67.7 per cent in 2019.

Blair Chapman says younger workers are often more heavily affected when there is an economic slowdown. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

There have been fears that the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) could lead to a jobs apocalypse, particularly for young people and white-collar workers.

But a study by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations found the technology was not yet causing broad disruption to Australia's labour market.

The study, released in July this year, also found that jobs for people aged 20 to 24 had grown slightly faster than those for people aged 25 and over since the introduction of ChatGPT, while young graduate outcomes remained resilient.

But the report did cite evidence from the US suggesting young people have experienced slower employment growth than older people since the introduction of generative AI tools, especially in occupations more exposed to AI.

Qantas last week announced 850 job cuts and plans to accelerate its use of AI.

Qantas is cutting jobs. (ABC News: Evelyn Manfield)

"We do think there'll be some job disruption at the margin, let's say, over the next five years," Mr Ottley said.

Federal Skills and Training Minister Andrew Giles said AI was mostly augmenting jobs, "so changing the way in which a job is done rather than completely automating a job".

"We've got to really focus on our skill to make sure workers are equipped to manage this transition," Mr Giles said.

Young people are also facing increasing competition for positions from existing job holders.

One million people in Australia have multiple jobs.

SEEK's Blair Chapman has some advice for young job seekers, particularly university graduates.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/v.title: Young Victorian voters torn between disillusionment, optimism
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/v.author: Andrew Mangelsdorf
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Andrew Mangelsdorf

Ollie Edens is frustrated by the lack of tertiary education options in Mildura. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

Young voters across regional Victoria say the issues that matter most to them are close to home, but they are getting little information about state politics, often relying on social media and word of mouth.

Many the ABC spoke to said they were not satisfied with the political status quo and were turning to alternative parties.

The Victorian Electoral Commission (VEC) said people aged between 18 and 44 would be pivotal to the outcome of this month's state election, making up 44 per cent of the vote.

Mildura Rural City youth council deputy mayor Ollie Edens wants the youth voice to be heard.

The recent high school graduate said that while a generation ago, young people voted in line with their parents, "very few" of his peers will do so.

Political parties are laying out their visions for the state's future, as voters prepare to head to the polls on November 28.

He said social media was driving young people to make their own voting choices.

"I've seen young people getting more of an independent conscience when it comes to politics, and they're very determined on that," he said.

Mr Edens is travelling to Melbourne as he has not found the training course he needs in Mildura, and would like to see a greater focus on supporting young people to stay in regional areas.

Ollie Edens says local education options are limited, with the local university campus offering few courses. (ABC Mildura-Swan Hill: Alexandra Treloar )

Wodonga student Jack Dumsday relies on his wheelchair to get around and said he was concerned about Wodonga's public transport system.

"Wodonga is not a small town by any means, and we have an abysmal bus network. I'd love to see that improve," he said.

Charlie Bradbury, who lives in the Ovens Valley electorate in north-east Victoria, said she would be "picking the lesser of the evils".

The 22-year-old is on the youth advisory committee at the North East Support & Action for Youth (NESAY) community agency, which works with young people and families to provide safe housing, education and employment.

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Despite her dissatisfaction with the political landscape, Ms Bradbury said the Greens' policies around rent freezing and publicly owned local supermarkets were appealing.

She said she would approach her vote with a "gender-based" focus.

"[That's] purely because the present violence against women epidemic is absolutely abysmal," she said.

Charlie Bradbury says some issues are not being properly addressed by political parties. (ABC)

Since 2025, One Nation has surged in polls across Australia, recently claiming four lower house seats in the South Australian election.

Ms Bradbury said she had seen this rise and while she noticed it more in "older generations", it was not limited to that demographic.

"It does kind of feel like we've taken a step backwards — the younger generation," she said.

Monash University associate professor of politics Zareh Ghazarian said there would be "thousands" of first-time voters who will have a "huge impact" in determining the outcome in this election.

Dr Ghazarian studied how young and first-time voters approached their first time at the ballot box.

Zareh Ghazarian says young and first-time voters could have a "huge impact" in determining the outcome of November's Victorian state election.  (Supplied)

"We identified that, of course, young people have rich and many different reasons as to who they decide to vote for," he said.

"And they do reflect in broad ways the sorts of strategies and preferences older voters demonstrate."

He said young voters could be divided into two categories: those who research candidates, their policies and ideas, and those who look at how their parents and friends voted.

"When you have such a high proportion of young people in Victoria, the decisions they're going to make may potentially be the key to the major parties or any party, any candidate in any electorate winning the seat," Dr Ghazarian said.

Conal Feehely, the Victorian campaign director for GetUp, which is an independent movement of more than one million people aiming to bring participation back into our democracy, said young people were "frustrated".

"Young Australians are facing the prospect of having a lower standard of living than their parents had, and that's a really heavy burden," he said.

"They're [also] facing enormous student debt … enormous increases to their rent and still don't see a prospect of owning a home."

Conal Feehely says young voters are frustrated with a range of issues heading into this year's state election. (ABC)

Mr Feehely said young people "want a type of politics that's hopeful and gives them answers and they're not seeing a lot of that right now".

Dr Ghazarian said it was unsurprising young people were tackling the current political landscape through protests, saying this had long been the case in Australia and abroad.

"Many young people are leading figures in international movements such as those concerned with environmental protection, conservation and social justice," he said.

Not only did young people lead political debate, but they also responded to it, he added.

Hamish Knight and Dylan Stockwell organised a rally against One Nation last month, which saw about 100 students march through Bendigo.

Hamish, 17, is concerned the party is dividing Australia and believes people need to "start fighting back".

Mr Feehely said he believed young people tended to be "a bit more blank canvas than other demographics".

He said this "opens the door" to influence, especially online, where young people were spending "more time … being influenced by algorithms".

But NESAY youth advisory committee's Sarah Clayton has a different take.

The 21-year-old Benambra voter said she felt uninformed about politics and saw that reflected among her peers.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog.

Ms Clayton did not watch television and often received information through social media or word of mouth.

"I think the biggest reason [for a lack of knowledge on politics] is within my social media algorithms. It's not something that pops up very much," she said.

She said the donkey vote had become "popular" in her generation and she wanted to see more education in schools about politics.

Young people often receive election information via social media. (ABC News)

Ms Clayton said it was common for young people to be on the receiving end of smart remarks from mates when politics was brought up.

"You're not supposed to talk about politics — it's meant to be a private thing, and it frustrates people — but I think that's exactly why it needs to be spoken about," she said.

"People are passionate about things, and this is how we get and make changes in our world. I think there is a huge lack of understanding within youth and a lot of the Australian population in general about the importance of voting."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/q.title: The Brisbane buildings made from sandstone touched by dinosaurs
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/q.author: Lucy Loram
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

This dinosaur footprint was unearthed in the same quarry that supplied sandstone for some of Brisbane's most iconic buildings. (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

Some of Brisbane's oldest heritage-listed buildings are harbouring clues about the prehistoric past.

Fossilised footprints belonging to 230-million-year-old dinosaurs have been unearthed in Brisbane, indented into the same sandstone that constructed the city's most recognisable buildings, like the General Post Office.

"These buildings certainly capture my eye, and I do glance twice to see what evidence might be hidden within their own architecture," Palaeontologist Dr Anthony Romilio said.

Iconic Brisbane landmarks like the General Post Office were built with sandstone from the same quarry. (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

Dr Romilio said two separate pieces of Brisbane-mined sandstone handed over to the University of Queensland's Dinosaur Lab, appear to display the tread-marks of the Sauropodomorph.

"Instead of walking on all four legs, they walked on their back legs. They still retained a very long neck and tail, but they were more ancient than the more typical than the brontosaurus," he said.

One of the footprints was discovered by a teenager over six decades ago at Petrie's Quarry.

Palaeontologist Anthony Romilio identified the footprints as likely belonging to a sauropodomorph. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Before the inner-north neighbourhood of Albion became the sought-after suburbia of today, it was Petrie's Quarry.

Educator Sue-Belinda Meehan said the Petrie family opened the quarry in the 1860s, 30 years after the family settled in Brisbane, which was then known as the Moreton Bay Penal Colony.

"If the Petrie's hadn't recognised the quality of that sandstone, we wouldn't have the sandstone that literally built Brisbane," she said.

A woman at Petrie's Quarry, which would one day become the suburb of Albion. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

The General Post Office, All Hallows School, and the Old Customs House were all made up of the creamy, white stone.

"When you think about the number of buildings that were constructed from it, it's quite extraordinary … it's probably easier to mention buildings that weren't made from it, then buildings that were," Ms Meehan said.

St Stephen's Cathedral, St John's Cathedral, and St Paul's Presbyterian Church are among the other builds that feature Petrie sandstone.

Sue-Belinda Meehan says the quarry supplied the sandstone that "literally built Brisbane". (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

"They were very much equal opportunity builders. It didn't matter what brand of religion you were, the Petries would build you a church," she said.

All the while, they were working with stone that had been touched by dinosaurs.

The General Post Office, located on Queen Street, was built in 1875. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

As quarrying ceased, the site was often visited by adventurous school children and aspiring geologists, before the suburb of Albion slowly started to build around it.

But Ms Meehan said remnants of the once active quarry remained today.

"If you go out to Albion and drive down Crosby Road, and look up to St Margaret's, you can see the scar in the mountain that was Petrie's Quarry."

Layers of white sandstone are still visible in Albion today. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

Dr Romilio said the white hills of Albion are made up of layers of sand that were deposited when the landscape was traversed by dinosaurs.

"If you were to travel 230 million years ago, you would find a very flat area. There wouldn't be much in the way of trees in that immediate area, because you're looking at a very wide river," he said.

"It would have been shallow enough for a two-legged dinosaur to walk past."

But the Sauropodomorph was not the only pre-historic creature walking the now streets of Albion.

"It would have also been an environment in which aquatic creatures lived as well. So giant salamander like animals are known to have existed in that same time as well," Dr Romilio said.

Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition

Both pieces of sandstone etched with the dinosaur footprints were discovered during the 1950's.

Dr Romilio said he is often approached with information about Brisbane's Petrie Quarry site.

"It may seem unusual in a capital city, that we find evidence of dinosaurs, but really all you need is the right aged material and a keen eye, and some conviction to investigate," Dr Romilio said.

St Stephens Cathedral today, sitting in a forest of modern buildings.  (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

Ms Meehan said not all dinosaur discoveries are reserved for outback Queensland.

"Queensland is just awash with wonderful dinosaur relics from the past, and to know that we have them here in Brisbane, just makes it an even more fabulous city," she said.
