https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/u.title: US officials say copper wire replacement caused national ground stop
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/u.author: Jason Dasey
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/u.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Air Transport Industry

The chaotic scene in Atlanta as travellers awaited news of rescheduled flights over the weekend. (Reuters: Elijah Nouvelage)

Flights in the US have resumed, but airlines are struggling to clear a backlog.

A communications failure, which officials blame on the replacement of old copper wires, forced a nationwide grounding of US departures for about five hours until Friday evening.

Nearly 29 million passengers are expected to fly on US airlines during the Thanksgiving travel period from November 20–30.

As air travellers across the United States face further disruptions this weekend following a nationwide grounding of flights, the US government has blamed on a program to replace copper wires with new fibre wires.

Airlines are struggling to clear a backlog of delayed and cancelled services after a major air traffic control communications failure forced authorities to suspend departures across the country for about five hours on Friday, local time.

Flights have since resumed, but airlines are warning it could take days for services to return to normal.

The US government says it may have been the fault of a single router installed by a government contractor.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters on Saturday, local time, that contractor L3Harris had been replacing a section of the air traffic control system's old copper wire with new fibre wire, and that work somehow caused the system overload.

Mr Duffy said the work caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps.

He said officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty router was the cause.

"Our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment," Mr Duffy said.

L3Harris said it took the issue seriously, and were "supporting the FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the ground stop of our nation's air travel."

The issue began overloading communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centres across the country, which prompted the authority to issue the ground stop because it could not identify a root cause.

Mr Duffy said the new routers started flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, which sparked communications issues with planes and radar at FAA facilities.

The FAA is still trying to understand the root cause of what went wrong.

It said communications did not go down but led to instability in data at the centres, and it did not lead to centres going dark.

Mr Duffy said the routers being replaced were about 25 years old and were supposed to be replaced in 2006.

The FAA spends $US1 billion annually to maintain its old copper wire system and is racing to replace it with modern fibre-based communications.

"We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job," Mr Duffy said.

"Virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fibre, from analog to digital."

L3Harris noted it has completed more than 70 per cent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fibre-optic system.

The disruption comes less than a week before the Thanksgiving travel rush, with industry group Airlines for America forecasting nearly 29 million passengers will fly on US airlines between November 20 and 30.

Almost 10,000 flights were cancelled, including 1,800 on United Airlines. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

While officials expect operations to return to normal before the holiday rush, Mr Duffy warned that the process would be gradual.

Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for a communications outage.

Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed, leaving passengers stranded at airports across the country and forcing airlines to rearrange aircraft and crew schedules.

Nearly 10,000 flights had been cancelled during the disruption, including more than 2,200 each at Delta Air Lines and American Airlines, and 1,800 at United Airlines, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.

Some aircraft at major airports were forced to wait more than five hours for a gate, the website reported.

US airlines will not be required to compensate stranded passengers because the disruption was caused by failures in the Federal Aviation Administration's systems rather than the carriers themselves.

Flights in Europe were also impacted by the problems in the US. (AP Photo: Mike Stewart)

The impact extended beyond the United States, with European aviation authorities asked to suspend US-bound departures during the emergency.

The disruption also affected a small number of flights from Australia, with airlines working to clear a backlog of delayed services.

The Australian Travel Industry Association warned that disruption to domestic flights within the US could continue for at least 24 hours.

Thousands of flights have been delayed or cancelled across the US, leaving Australian travellers stranded at airports.

The grounding was the longest nationwide shutdown of US flight departures since the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001.

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack and sought to reassure passengers about the safety of air travel.

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says authorities are investigating the issue.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/d.title: Two rappers went into youth detention. What they heard surprised them
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/d.author: Dan Condon
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Kobie Dee has seen the power of music through his time working with youth in detention. (Supplied)

Kobie Dee knows the power of music as a positive force that can steer young people towards a less destructive path. He knows the road they're on.

"I was very fortunate that I didn't end up in jail," he tells Double J's Michael Hing.

"I was very much walking down a road that was leading that way. For me, it was, 'If I don't get my life right, if I don't get myself help, these opportunities aren't going to last for me.'

Start your weekday with the songs that soundtrack your life, thrilling new releases and fun chats. Michael Hing hosts Mornings from 9am Monday to Thursday, on Double J.

"There were so many opportunities that came when I was heavy in addiction, and all the stuff I was doing. I missed out on so much stuff. There were big shows that I was supposed to do that I didn't do because I was heavy in addiction."

The 29-year-old Gomeroi man and award-winning musician has recently spent weeks working as part of the Hear Me Out, Music Behind Bars initiative from the Australian Children's Music Foundation, an intensive six-week songwriting pilot for those detained at the Cobham Youth Justice Centre.

He was joined by Rhyan Clapham, a Filipino Murrawarri musician who performs as Dobby. Both rappers believe there are few more powerful and accessible ways to escape.

"We've seen the power of music play out again and again with young people," Dobby says. "It's a platform with which to express themselves, and also to just make dope music."

Both rappers are Indigenous men and take seriously the responsibility of being put up as examples of the power of music in one's life.

"We are so over-represented in these centres," Kobie says. "So, to have other black fellas come in and to be able to speak to stuff that they can be working towards outside, showing them how to make music…

"They got to watch Dobby do his thing in there. Those young fellas' minds were blown. To see that it's also accessible for them to be doing too, I think it's so important."

“It’s not just about me anymore.”

"You've got to see it to be it," Dobby agrees. "It's representation.

"It's also self-fulfilling. When you create something that you can own and hold and say, 'That's my song,' it gives you a sense of pride and motivation to keep creating. I think creativity cannot be taken seriously enough."

The two rappers know creating music needs a safe environment conducive to accepting self-expression in whatever form it takes.

"We're helping create a space in which they feel safe enough to share their story and bring it out in a musical way, whether it be rap, whether it be singing or playing the guitar or whatever," Dobby says.

"Because we're fostering that environment, they're able to sharpen their sword and practice their skills and become a better musician.

"That should be afforded to anyone. It doesn't matter what situation you're in doesn't matter who you are. Music is a universal language, and we can all speak it. It's one of the most powerful forces of energy that we have here to work with."

Music as escapism becomes especially profound when talking about youth in detention. No one wants to be in jail, and Kobie says making music provides a momentary but powerful escape.

"They're completely in the moment of creating and expressing themselves and speaking about things they probably wouldn't be speaking about in everyday life within these centres."

Rap and incarceration have been closely aligned for decades; countless hip hop classics reference prison and the behaviours that will land you in there.

When Aboriginal-Filipino rapper DOBBY made his ARIA award-winning album Warrangu: River Story, it set him on a journey of spiritual self-reflection. Now he's using his voice to send a powerful message around climate, racism and injustice.

"I'm very biased as a rapper, but I think it's one of the most influential forces," Dobby says. "It's so direct.

"It helps tell their story. I mean, hip hop is famously a counter narrative against the mainstream, against the government, against wider Australia in this context.

"Where racist stigma and stereotypes are put upon them, hip hop is a place where they can say, 'No, that's not me. This is my story, let me tell you the real side of what it is'. That's incredibly powerful."

Some preconceptions about the music being made in these sessions are natural, but that doesn't mean it's always correct.

Rap wasn't the only sound participants gravitated towards. And not every song was born from anger.

"When I walked in, I was expecting to hear a rap song," Kobie says. "I was expecting to hear some drill music, just from my own experience of doing workshops in juvies in different states. It's mostly what the kids want to be making.

"I walk in and they're singing a love song, and it was beautiful.

"This is the stuff that is on their minds already."

Making such a song requires a level of vulnerability that can be hard for any young person to access, let alone when in a prison environment.

The program provides a level of safety that hopes to allow participants the chance to air the gamut of their feelings.

"To be able to provide a space where they can let that out like that, I think it's just so important that we're doing this for these young people," Kobie says.

Both Dobby and Kobie know the limitations of a program like this. They know they won't influence everyone, and that those they affect won't always carry these lessons with them.

That doesn't mean it's not worth doing. As active members of Australia's music industry, they see the opportunities that exist.

"Showing these young people, 'This is out there for you. You have the opportunity to change your life through music,'" Kobie says.

"It doesn't have to be being on stage or anything like that; they could even be doing what we're doing right now and teaching other young people music.

"Showing the different opportunities and showing the different avenues."

Vitally, they know the most influential people in a child's life are their peers.

"You could do workshops with 20 kids, and there might be only one kid that comes out with that thought," Kobie says.

"But changing that one kid is so powerful, because that one kid can then go on to start his own programs and save another five or six kids from that lifestyle.

"It's more about showing them what's possible and telling them, like, 'If you want this in your life, there are some things that need to change.' It's sowing those seeds."

Hear Michael Hing's full chat with Kobie Dee and Dobby on Double J Mornings, Monday from 9am.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/b.title: Artists relish flying the flag for WA's biggest remote community
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/b.author: Ruby Littler
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art

Some of the recent artwork produced from Bidyadanga, WA's largest remote Aboriginal community. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Artists from Western Australia's largest remote community are increasingly securing their own unique place in the state's vibrant northern arts scene.

Bidyadanga, about 2,000 kilometres north of Perth, is home to about 850 people.

Its unique location between the red dirt of the West Kimberley and clear blue water of the Indian Ocean gives the community's artists a unique perspective.

Bidyadanga, about 180 kilometres south of Broome, is home to 850 people. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Jenny Butt was painting long before the community's award-winning arts centre opened its doors.

She said Bidyadanga's artistic reputation continued to grow in scale and reach.

"It's been touching; painting, representing your identity with your family's connection to country," she said.

"And inspiring for us too, as we think of back where we've been.

"We grew up near the coast [and have] lived in the desert with family, so we've got two connections."

Jenny Butt makes a sale on opening night. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Butt said it was particularly heartening to see the next generation of young artists getting involved.

The work highlights the connection of different cultures and everything that made Bidyadanga what it is, according to artist Marika Jadai.

The centre hosts an exhibition in Broome twice a year, giving locals the opportunity to buy artworks direct from the artists themselves.

The artists keep part of the proceeds, while the arts centre also directs some of their take back into the Bidyadanga community.

Sifting through the reams of artwork at Redbill Studio Gallery. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Behind the scenes, the process of hauling the reams of pieces from Bidyadanga to Broome is no small feat, especially in stifling summer weather.

In the days leading up to the show, artists and staff began cataloguing and listing the pieces, ready to be rolled, packed up and driven to Broome.

Augustine Bada has taken up a position working at the art centre and helps to coordinate the showcase.

Augustine Bada says he was proud to have the pieces on display. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Mr Bada said he was excited about what next year would bring, with high hopes for the studio.

"It's really important here, because by doing art, we're sharing stories, passing down knowledge and painting country as well."

Jenny Butt says Bidyadanga artists have the rare opportunity to represent both the ocean and desert in their work. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

The opening night of the show, at Broome's Redbill Studio Gallery, attracted a crowd of hundreds.

Attendees sifted through the vast quantity of paintings on display from more than 80 Bidyadanga artists.

Daisy (far right) says the work she buys will remind her of her time in the Kimberley.  (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler )

"We're probably moving on soon, so we really wanted something that captured the earthy colours and reminded us of our time up here," shopper Daisy said.

"I work out in Bidgy as well; I know a lot of these artists, so it feels really special."

Redbill Studio Gallery has hosted the Bidyadanga artists twice a year for the past four years. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Redbill Studio Gallery co-owner Melissa Foster said the connection with the remote community and hosting their art shows in Broome came about through "word of mouth".

"It's great for them to have a platform in Broome. They have a lovely following of community," she said.

"We definitely get a lot of good feedback. We always have people come up and ask when the next Bidgy sale is."

The Starship vessel returned safely to its launch pad where it was grabbed by a giant pair of mechanical ‘chopstick’ arms

SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft on Saturday returned from its longest ⁠flight in orbit yet to the ⁠Texas launch tower it was launched ⁠from a day prior, showing the first key recovery of the rocket system’s centrepiece vessel in the company’s decade-long effort to develop a fully reusable rocket.

The towering two-stage rocket’s Super Heavy booster – the rocket’s bottom half – carried Starship to space on Friday, lifting off from SpaceX’s Starbase, Texas, facilities. ‌

That booster had failed to make a similar return to the launch pad some 10 minutes after lift-off, nixing SpaceX’s plan to recover both parts of the rocket for the first time.

https://www.dw.com/en/spacex-carries-out.title: SpaceX carries out first-ever spaceship capture
https://www.dw.com/en/spacex-carries-out.text:
The successful recovery of the SpaceX Starship marks the first recovery of a spaceship.

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned from its longest-yet flight in orbit on Saturday to the tower it was launched from on Friday.

The spaceship descended and smoothly slipped between the mechanical "chopstick arms" above Launch Pad 2 in the US state of Texas. It was the first key recovery of the rocket system's centerpiece vessel in the company's decadelong effort to develop a fully reusable rocket.

"Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted. "Look at her! Baby, she’s back!"

It was the 15th test flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket system. SpaceX had intended to also capture the Super Heavy booster that launched the Starship, but the lower stage recovery was aborted and it exploded over the Gulf of Mexico shortly after launch on Friday.

The successful return of the craft's upper stage after orbiting Earth 14 times for over 22 hours, during which it deployed 26 Starlink satellites, marked a ​key milestone in the multibillion-dollar development of Starship, which billionaire Elon Musk sees ​as key to SpaceX's satellite business and ambitions to put humans on the moon and eventually Mars.

NASA welcomed the news. The US space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base.

"It was almost magic," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote on X.

As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon. The booster's guidance system sensed it was not in the correct position and initiated the self-destruction protocol. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-2027-bud.title: Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-2027-bud.text:
The 2027 federal budget proposal has finally been hammered out and is set for a vote in parliament. What are the government's policy priorities in defense, infrastructure, the economy and social spending?

It was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.

Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).

But here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

If the new debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

This development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.

To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social issues, security and geopolitics.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding new investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.

What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.

Russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary."

The rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.

Nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are plans for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

People born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

The pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.

The Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.

Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.

The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

At the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

This would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an important point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.

At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year."
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-2027-bud.summary: The budget proposal is set for a vote in parliament on November 27. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027. Germany is still in relatively good shape compared to other countries.

https://www.dw.com/en/nigeria-s-upcoming.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
https://www.dw.com/en/nigeria-s-upcoming.text:
As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.
https://www.dw.com/en/nigeria-s-upcoming.summary: Nigeria's electoral body has released its preliminary voter's register. The body is investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use. Country's return to democratic rule in 1999 was only 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

https://www.dw.com/en/south-sudan-pushes.title: South Sudan pushes back elections amid violent flare-ups
https://www.dw.com/en/south-sudan-pushes.text:
South Sudan has been independent from Sudan since 2011, and has not yet held national elections. Since then, the country faces cycles of violence after a civil war led to a tenuous peace deal.

South Sudan on Saturday pushed back its first national elections from December to February next year, as the country faces flare-ups of violence and political strife.

Presidential and legislative elections are now slated for February 11, 2027.

"We didn't postpone the elections. We have just adjusted the time to allow other processes to be implemented and that is according to the law," National Elections Commission spokeswoman and Commissioner Josephine Achiro said.

"Article 57 of the National Elections Commission gives us authority to adjust the elections timelines," she added.

Achiro said the postponement of the election date is for voter registration and civic education purposes.

According to the World Bank, the vast majority of South Sudanese lack state-recognized ID, creating challenges for voter registration. Thousands of centers have been established across the country to register voters.

South Sudan became independent from Sudan in July 2011 following a referendum. The country has some 12 million people and is one of the impoverished nations on the planet.

From 2013 to 2018, forces backed by President Silva Kiir, a member of the Dinka ethnic group, fought against troops supported by Vice President Riek Machar, who hails from the Nuer tribe. More than 400,000 people died in that conflict.

A fragile peace agreement was achieved between the two sides in 2018, with a national unity government established in 2020.

Kiir dissolved South Sudan's transitional government in September ahead of elections, and has since ruled by decree in a caretaker administration. He fired Vice President Machar, who had earlier been charged with treason and is under house arrest.

Despite the peace deal, there are also frequent clashes between the Dinka and Nuer groups loyal to Kiir and Machar.

The head of the UN Mission in South Sudan, Anita Kiki Ghebo, said earlier in the week that violence is increasingand added that approximately 10 million people in South Sudan need some form of humanitarian assistance. She also noted that 1.4 million people have entered South Sudan due to an ongoing conflict in Sudan.

"If left unaddressed, political, security, and humanitarian challenges risk reinforcing one another, further exacerbating tensions adn vulnerabilities across the country," she said.

She has urged renewed dialogue "to focus on establishing clear and credible roadmap for completing the outstanding provisions of the Revitalized Peace Agreement," the formal name for the 2018 peace deal.
https://www.dw.com/en/south-sudan-pushes.summary: South Sudan has not yet held national elections since 2011. The country faces flare-ups of violence and political strife. The World Bank says the vast majority of South Sudanese lack state-recognized ID. The UN Mission in South Sudan says 1.4 million people have entered South Sudan due to an ongoing conflict in Sudan.

https://www.dw.com/en/us-duffy-says-inco.title: US: Duffy says 'incompetence' or bad tech to blame for flight haltings
https://www.dw.com/en/us-duffy-says-inco.text:
Air carriers in the US canceled some 16,000 flights over the past 24 hours in the biggest such grounding since 9/11. Officials hinted that incompetence or faulty equipment, not malfeasance, is the cause.

US Federal Aviation Administration officials and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday said that investigations are ongoing in an attempt to find the cause of the largest mass grounding of flights in the country in over 25 years.

Stranded passengers scrambled to find hotel rooms or buses and trains that could take them to their destinations, others hunkered down in the nation's airports in the first such nationwide grounding since January 2023 and the largest since the September 11, 2001, terror attacks.

International carriers were also forced to cancel flights to the US, and the massive backlog prompted, among other things, the rescheduling of dozens of college and professional sporting events — a staple of many Americans' weekends.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that a total of 16,000 flights had been delayed on Friday and Saturday, adding that he hoped flight schedules would be back to normal sometime Sunday, saying the "worst is behind us."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said no evidence of malfeasance had been found, before pointing his finger at numerous possible culprits, starting with the previous administration, then Congress and eventually settling on possible "contractor incompetence."

Duffy said the issue may have been a faulty router installed when workers from "legacy contractor" L3Harris replaced aged copper wire with new fiberoptic cable or that they had somehow caused a system overload while updating the wires.

During a press conference that was itself plagued with technical problems, Duffy said, "We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning, was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said, adding that either way, "Our contractor didn't meet the moment."

He was also asked why such complicated updates would be undertaken on a Friday afternoon when air travel is at its busiest rather than on a Saturday night, for instance, when far-fewer planes are in the air. He replied by saying the scheduling of such updates will be reevaluated moving forward.

Since the decision was made to update the very old infrastructure currently in use, Congress has approved $12.5 billion (€11.3 billion) to fund the changeover. The Trump administration had been seeking a further $30 billion to complete the job but Duffy on Friday called $50 billion instead, saying, "This is an emergency."

Despite the pain and frustration endured by customers, there is also a massive financial component to the groundings.

Since the groundings were ordered by the FAA, airlines are not legally responsible for compensating passengers whose flights were cancelled.

On Saturday, Administrator Bedford said the FAA is "working with aviation stakeholders" to make things right, saying, "everyone will either be reaccommodated (sic) on a flight or they'll get a full refund."

Investors are already beginning to calculate potential losses to airlines — which will compound the sting of sky-high fuel prices brought on by the Trump administration's war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz — with shares of American, Delta and United Airlines falling between 1% and 2% late Friday.

Shares in JetBlue as well as contractor L3Harris were down 3%.
https://www.dw.com/en/us-duffy-says-inco.summary: FAA officials say they are investigating the cause of the largest mass grounding of flights in the country in 25 years. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford says 16,000 flights were delayed Friday and Saturday. The FAA is working with airlines to make things right, says the FAA is "working with aviation stakeholders"

https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-iranian.title: Fact check: 'Iranian' content farms reach millions
https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-iranian.text:
Several social media accounts claiming to represent the Iranian military show signs of being part of so-called content farms. DW Fact Check looks at how they operate and how users can spot them.

As fears of regional escalation grew after US strikes on Iran, US President Donald Trump claimed the US-Israel war with Iran was "effectively over" on November 9 at a White House briefing. "We're just keeping it the status quo."

Periods of heightened public interest, such as the conflict involving Iran, create fertile ground for so-called content farms. Following Trump's statement, posts on the Iran war surged online again. And a growing network of accounts claiming links to Iran's military has accumulated millions of views.

DW Fact Check examined a number of these accounts and found recurring signs of content farm behavior. Experts who reviewed the accounts DW provided describe them as part of a broader ecosystem of pro-Iran content aggregators that connect across multiple social media platforms.

Content farms are websites or social media accounts, or a network of either, producing large amounts of cheap content in a short time span. They may be driven by economic incentives, but they can also serve as vehicles for political influence campaigns.

The internet watchdog NewsGuard has found 165 false claims about the Iran warthat collectively have been watched hundreds of millions of times. Only a few of them originated from Iranian state media.

NewsGuard identified the majority as pushing a pro-Iran agenda, shifting toward AI-generated images, and increasingly claiming that accurate stories from authentic media are AI-generated and false.

An analysis by the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) identified pro-Iran networks of X accounts which revealed signs of coordination, cross-promotion and engagement tactics while spreading misleading and AI-generated war content. It found no links to state-affiliated actors.

Several accounts identified by DW Fact Check use the Iranian flag as their profile picture and a variation of "Iran Military" in their username. While ownership cannot always be verified, they share recurring characteristics commonly associated with content farms.

Content farms use repetitive and formulaic posting formats, as they are cheaper and easier to produce. Their posts frequently start with the word "BREAKING" and imitate the appearance of news updates on the conflict.

One account, called "Iran Military Media," is linked to a Facebook account that Iranian state media have verified as authentic. It has built a substantial audience across multiple social media platforms, with over 290,000 followers on X, 597,000 on Facebook and 17,200 followers on Instagram.

It posts a handful of times a day, often sharing AI-generated or AI-enhanced videos and frequently adopting the "BREAKING" format. Since late 2025, it has published more than 1,600 posts on X, generating over 150 million views and 3.6 million likes.

"The accounts discussed are a central part of this ecosystem as they distribute the pro-Iranian content, state and non-state allied media at relatively low cost and generate millions of views," said Moustafa Ayad, an expert in online influence operations at the ISD.

Ayad examined 10 similar "Iran Military"-themed accounts during the same period, and their combined reach is even greater. Together, they accounted for 12,588 posts, 353 million views and 6.6 million likes.

This network is replicated on Facebook in numerous languages. According to Ayad, this strategy is part of what the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei outlined as "soft war."

Ayad said the accounts' reach is amplified when they are paired with other accounts. Only a small share of "Iran Military Media's" 150 million views came from reposted content.

A second account, "Iranian Force," has amassed more than 248,000 followers. It typically posts around 10 times a day, though on some days the volume exceeds 30 posts.

Like "Iran Military Media," it frequently relies on "BREAKING" alerts and AI-generated content. It also includes genuine footage, often framed through a pro-Iran lens.

X lists the account as being based in Pakistan and its profile history shows six username changes. In a break from the Iran-related content, one post suddenly defends a Pakistani TikToker and includes an appeal in Urdu to the government in Pakistan.

Charlene Lin, an analyst for the internet watchdog NewsGuard, told DW it had flagged this account for multiple false narratives. According to Lin, it is also linked to another account that spreads the same false narratives in coordination.

A third account, called the "Iran Army," posts a handful of times a day, including AI-generated videos. Its posts regularly reach tens and at times hundreds of thousands of views.

Like "Iranian Force," it distributes videos from official briefings by the Iranian Armed Forces while also using the "BREAKING" format to drive engagement. One post claiming "the war has officially started" received over 41 million views.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While these accounts differ in reach and post slightly different content, they share many characteristics. The accounts repeatedly share cheaply produced images, at times coordinated between accounts, and make sensational and unverified claims portraying Iran as militarily powerful or politically influential.

Several accounts in this wider ecosystem have faced restrictions. Since March, a number of prominent "Iran Military"-themed accounts have been suspended on X, including "Iran Military Monitor," which had close to 2 million followers before its removal.

Earlier this year, Iranian state media issued a statement distancing itself from a range of "Iran Military" accounts circulating on social media, stating that only one account was authentic.

Yet for social media users, distinguishing that account from the others may not be straightforward. The verified account uses the same "Iran Military" branding and a similar profile picture, while also sharing AI-generated content and frequent "BREAKING" updates.

Despite differences in authenticity and affiliation, many of these accounts consistently adopt a pro-Iran framing. They portray Iran as militarily capable, able to retaliate against adversaries and enjoying international support, while rarely highlighting information that contradicts that image.

DW Fact Check found repeated postings of the same content close in time across the accounts and different platforms. The "Iranian Force" and "Iran Military Media" accounts have, for example, posted the same image (here and here), with the same caption on the same day, as have accounts in the wider "Iran Military Media" network.

"The pro-Iranian ecosystem online is large, multi-layered and cuts across almost all of the various popular social media platforms and messaging services," said the ISD's Ayad. "[It's] a key component to the Iranian government's ability to withstand challenges to its rule both from within and outside, while generating sympathy and connections with other online communities."
https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-iranian.summary: DW Fact Check looks at how social media accounts operate and how users can spot them. The accounts are part of a broader ecosystem of pro-Iran content aggregators. They are driven by economic incentives, but they can also serve as vehicles for political influence campaigns.

https://www.dw.com/en/italy-slaps-meta-w.title: Italy slaps Meta with €805mn fine over access to Android photos
https://www.dw.com/en/italy-slaps-meta-w.text:
Italian regulators say Meta accessed photos and multimedia content from Italian users via the Facebook application for Android devices. Meta has not yet commented on the fine or the allegations.

Italy's data protection agency said on Saturday that it was imposing a €805 million (around $887.3 million) fine on Meta for violating the privacy of Italian users.

Italian regulators say Meta accessed the photos and videos from Italian Android phone users via the Facebook app. The regulators said the privacy infringement was due to a feature on the Facebook app which suggests photos from users' personal galleries which they can then post on the social media platform.

The data protection agency said Meta did this "without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them."

The fine, which is equal to 0.4% of Meta's annual turnover, is the largest-ever imposed by Italian regulators on a big tech company.

Meta has 60 days to disable the camera roll suggestions feature and to separately ask for permission from Facebook users for just that function.

Italy's data protection agency said there a "high number of people affected" by Meta's data privacy infringement "which is still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regulators first launched the investigation into Meta in July 2025, and say the big tech giant has not cooperated during the probe.

Meta has not yet commented on the fine or the allegations made by the Italian authorities, but it could file a legal appeal against the financial penalty.

The company has also previously denied using the camera roll feature to train AI models, although this aspect was not being probed by Italian regulators.

Meta's European headquarters is in Ireland and the company has previously argued that the data privacy case should fall under Irish legal jurisdiction.

Italian regulators have rejected this claim.
https://www.dw.com/en/italy-slaps-meta-w.summary: Italian regulators say Meta accessed photos and videos from Italian Android phone users via Facebook app. The company has not yet commented on the fine or the allegations. The fine is equal to 0.4% of Meta's annual turnover, the largest-ever imposed by Italian regulators on a big tech company.

https://www.dw.com/en/ice-hockey-impasse.title: Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany
https://www.dw.com/en/ice-hockey-impasse.text:
Two weeks after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak said after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's secretary of sport, said in a statement on Wednesday. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

On November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors tournament and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14.

With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport, said Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the [German] ice hockey federation [DEB], nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a world championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport — and ice hockey in particular — find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hard-line on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to finding a solution for the men's tournament in Germany in May.
https://www.dw.com/en/ice-hockey-impasse.summary: Russia threatens to take legal action against two tournament hosts. Russia has threatened to impose sanctions on Canada and Germany. Canada confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship. Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and Canada.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cwlym2.title: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cwlym2.text:
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.

"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.

The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.

But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.

The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:27 local time (21:27 GMT) on Saturday and was successfuly caught.

The city said it will provide additional training for bus drivers after CCTV footage revealed the moment the horses and their riders walk onto the bus.
