https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3r.title: Alleged Russell Brand rape victim wants age of consent law changed
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3r.text:
A woman who has alleged that she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity and is campaigning for a staggered age of consent in an interview with the Sunday Times.

Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. She was known under the pseudonym 'Alice'. Brand denied the allegations at the time.

None of the women in the 2023 media investigation were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

On Monday the entertainer was sentenced to 10 and a half years for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

The Sunday Times reported that Latter had initially described the allegation about Brand to them as a sexual assault and that is how they reported it in their 2023 investigation.

Latter, 37, "now calls this allegation rape", the paper said.

Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time, when she was on her way home from a shopping trip. She said Brand was working at MTV.

She told the paper: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power],"

She said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.

It was towards the end of their relationship that Latter was allegedly orally raped by Brand, according to the Sunday Times.

Latter said that she was now campaigning for the introduction of a "staggered" age of consent that would prohibit relationships between 16- and 17-year-olds and adults.

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other," she told the paper. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

She also told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.

In her interview with the Sunday Times she said that the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but the police wanted her to be part of a "subsequent trial".

A Met Police spokesperson said: "Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.

"Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.

"This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."

A spokesperson for the Crown Prosecution Service said it would "continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible".

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Although booster exploded, company caught upper stage for first time in campaign to make megarocket reusable

SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight.

The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22hr mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times.

Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the sea as with some previous test flights.

The hulking spacecraft is composed of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship.

Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico.

The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) system triggered the no-go.

“It was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, it detected that the booster was not in the place it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday.

This week’s test flight was still a victory for SpaceX, marking the first time that the company caught its upper stage.

The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface. The agency has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin for the mission.

SpaceX has plans to ramp up its Starship test flights to a weekly, then twice-weekly cadence, chief executive Elon Musk said on a recent earnings call. He has sought to make Starship rapidly reusable so that it can land and take off much like standard airplanes.

Beyond another Moon landing, Musk has also pushed a plan of carrying humans to Mars.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.summary: SpaceX's megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday. The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms. The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’S plan to return humans to the lunar surface.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Netanyahu says only a unity government can guarantee Israel’s security
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his call for a national unity government with his rival, Gadi Eisenkot, saying only such a government can guarantee Israel’s security.

In a video statement on Saturday, Netanyahu said a meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government”.

The prime minister said such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all”, claiming Tehran would “not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us”.

“Let’s meet in one room, without preconditions,” he said.

Within minutes, however, Eisenkot dismissed the appeal as a ploy.

A former army chief, Eisenkot said Netanyahu “knows he lost the election”.

“Netanyahu is calling for negotiations while they are already underway,” he said. “These tricks don’t work on me.”

Neither side won a majority in the October 27 election. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc took 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s four-party bloc got 48 seats, and Arab-led parties won a record 19.

President Isaac Herzog last week tasked Eisenkot with forming a government, after 67 lawmakers, including those from Arab-led parties, endorsed him, while 46 backed Netanyahu.

Eisenkot has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. He has ruled out including Arab-led parties in his government.

Under Eisenkot’s plan for a minority “national emergency government”, his bloc’s 48 lawmakers would vote in favour against the 46 Netanyahu supporters, while the 26 lawmakers from Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties could abstain. It would allow his government to be approved without an absolute majority in the Knesset.

Netanyahu has warned that such a government would lead to Israel’s “collapse”.

Netanyahu’s version would include Jewish parties from the centre and the right and exclude Arab parties. He and his allies have made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties “stole” the election.

On Friday, Eisenkot called Netanyahu’s campaign against them “racist”.

Eisenkot has said he could work with members of Netanyahu’s Likud party and with Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism if their commitment to unity is “sincere”, but he insisted on a “break with the extremists”, notably supporters of far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

The Knesset will elect its speaker on Tuesday. The post is currently held by Netanyahu ally Amir Ohana, and the opposition has put forward Matan Kahana, a former military officer, in his place.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Netanyahu says only a government can guarantee Israel's security. Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc took 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's four-party bloc got 48 seats, and Arab-led parties won a record 19.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Explosion near Syria’s capital kills father and child
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
A blast from a suspected explosive device planted inside a car in a suburb of the Syrian capital, Damascus, has killed at least two people, including a child, and wounded one.

The explosion in Jaramana, on the southeastern edge of Damascus, on Saturday killed a man and his daughter, while a third person, said to be the wife of the man, was seriously injured.

Syria’s Internal Security Forces said they sealed off the area and opened an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the blast.

Jaramana is home to a large community of the Druze religious minority and has seen tensions between some Druze members and the Sunni majority backing President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s government.

Witnesses described the vehicle as a Kia Rio parked between two apartment buildings in Jaramana, which is largely considered a quiet residential area, said Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett, reporting from the blast scene.

Pett said the security situation in the capital remains complex, despite improvements since the regime of former President Bashar al-Assad fell two years ago.

“In the last couple of months, there were two very high-profile incidents,” she said, including a double-tap attack in July during French President Emmanuel Macron’s visit, which Syrian authorities attributed to a cell affiliated with ISIL (ISIS).

“There was also a deadly attack on what’s known as the Lawyer’s Cafe, near the Palace of Justice, which has been the scene of these high-profile trials of former members of the Assad regime,” Pett said.

She added that most of the bombings and security incidents have not necessarily targeted civilians but members and locations of security forces, which authorities have also blamed on ISIL.

Last year, Damascus joined the US-led international coalition against ISIL. The coalition was formed in 2014 and has carried out operations against the group in Syria and Iraq.

On September 27, the security forces said they had arrested four members of an ISIL cell involved in planning and carrying out several attacks in different parts of the country.

Last month, Syria’s security forces said they foiled a plot to target a police patrol in the Damascus countryside, saying an ISIL cell was preparing to carry out the attack, Syrian state television reported.

They said the group was responsible for explosions and assassinations in Raqqa, Aleppo, Idlib and Homs.

Total sales at Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Phillips are expected to be around $2.4 billion, which would equal last year’s total, according to ArtTactic.

Sotheby’s alone is expected to pull in over $1.1 billion, with a single collection from The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection estimated at $450 million.

The collection includes the two big headliners of the week: Vincent van Gogh’s landscape “Châtaigniers en fleurs,” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million and Paul Cézanne’s “Arlequin,” estimated at $120 million.

A version of this article appeared in CNBC’s Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions straight to your inbox.

The art auctions in New York next week could top $2 billion, as a treasure trove of masterpieces comes to the market for the first time in decades.

Total sales at Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Phillips are expected to be around $2.4 billion, which would equal last year’s total, according to ArtTactic. Sotheby’s alone is expected to pull in over $1.1 billion, with a single collection from The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection estimated at $450 million.

The collection includes the two big headliners of the week: Vincent van Gogh’s landscape “Châtaigniers en fleurs,” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million and Paul Cézanne’s “Arlequin,” estimated at $120 million. Neither has been seen in public for a half a century.

Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart said demand is strong in the art market, especially for the highest quality blue-chip works, as rising stocks markets and private wealth boost the confidence of collectors.

“There’s been enormous wealth creation and a lot of confidence in markets,” Stewart said. “It’s a global phenomenon. We’re seeing recovery and greater interest across Asia and something really exciting happening from the Middle East across to Singapore and Europe and the U.S.”

Christie’s star of the week is Wassily Kandinsky’s “Betonte Ecken,” estimated at $60 million to $80 million. Christie’s CEO Bonnie Brennan describes the market is “confident but discerning, rewarding truly exceptional works.” She said recent gyrations in the stock market and fears of an AI bubble aren’t likely to deter serious collectors.

“At the very highest end of our market, collectors tend to take a much longer-term view,” Brennan said. “They understand that the opportunity to acquire a masterpiece may come only once in a generation, and that can be far more important than what the stock market has done in any particular week. In uncertain moments, the very best can actually become even more compelling.”

The art market has continued to rebound this year after declines in 2023 and 2024, with auction sales in the first half up 70% over last year, to $6.8 billion, according to Bank of America.

Drew Watson, head of art services at Bank of America, said blue-chip art is outperforming, with Impressionist & Modern sales up 133% in the first half.

“Our outlook for the art market this November is cautiously optimistic,” Watson said. “Improving liquidity, combined with an unusually strong concentration of fresh-to-market private collections, creates a favorable backdrop for the marquee sales.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/e.title: Author Tim Winton says Exmouth wrong place for a port
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/e.author: Yousuf Shameel
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/e.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Tim Winton has been advocating for Exmouth Gulf since the inception of the port proposal. (ABC News: Courtney Bembridge)

A deepwater industrial port in a northern WA tourist town is facing a backlash from locals and conservationists.

The Exmouth Chamber of Commerce backs the plan and says it will provide plenty of benefits to the community.

If approved, construction of the port is scheduled to begin in early 2029 if approved.

A proposed deepwater industrial port in northern Western Australia has been described as unnecessary, unjustified and unacceptable by locals and conservationists worried about the impact on marine animals.

The Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex is proposed to be built just outside of Exmouth, 1,230km north of Perth, where it will feature a single jetty wharf, bulk fuel storage, a solar farm, and a seawater desalination plant.

The port is proposed to be built 10km south of the township. (Supplied: Gascoyne Gateway Ltd.)

The port will be designed to service cruise liners, defence and commercial supply vessels.

The proposal has caught the attention of conservationist and famous author Tim Winton who has opposed the project.

Exmouth local Brinkley Davies also said she was concerned about the port's location so close to town and World Heritage Ningaloo.

"It is worrying because it is my front yard, but also the marine ecosystem that is at risk is a major factor," Ms Davies said.

Having worked in marine conservation herself, Ms Davies has been involved in the campaign against the port since its initial proposal in 2020.

Brinkley Davies walking her dogs at the Exmouth Gulf. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

"It was not widely spoken about then and in the last five or six years, the town has really boomed and there is a lot more people living here and more people standing up for the place," she said.

"There are a few key species that really have an importance in this area, one of them is dugongs.

"There is a very important seagrass meadows where they are feeding and they also come in here to nurse their calves and rest, and that area is at direct risk of being covered in silt if they are going to dredge."

Signs with messages opposing the port have been placed around town. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

Fellow Exmouth local Violeta Brosig said she was concerned the port could impact the humpback whales that rely on the Gulf.

"My main concern is it is going to be right in the middle of the parts of the humpback highway in Exmouth Gulf," she said.

"It needs to be preserved and protected instead of destroyed."

However, the Exmouth Chamber of Commerce president David Gillespie said it was an opportunity of a lifetime for locals and there would be flow-on benefits for the community.

"There will be upgrades and roads, jobs, " he said.

"There's for and against on both sides with businesses that agree to disagree, but I just get back to what the positives are from an economic perspective and what that will do for the town, for increased housing and population."

Exmouth Gulf is now the chosen site for the Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

Gascoyne Gateway CEO Daniel Jackson said there had been extensive community consultation and believed the majority of locals and businesses were in favour of the port.

"We certainly acknowledge that there's seasonal windows, we're talking a few months of the year in which higher degree of risk mitigation is required to manage interaction between vessels and fauna, as it does now.

"There's commercial vessels operating there today that are moving in and out and around fauna in the Gulf."

The project is still undergoing approvals, with the WA Environmental Protection Authority currently undertaking public consultation.

World renowned author, conservationist and patron of Protect Ningaloo, Tim Winton, said the Exmouth Gulf was the wrong place for a port.

"It is one of the world's most important humpback whale nurseries and the idea of building a wharf a kilometre long into the whale refuge and to bring up to 600 vessels a year into the whale nursery just seems fundamentally wrong," Mr Winton said.

"We're of the view that this is unnecessary, unjustified and unacceptable in its impacts to the Ningaloo estate."

While this proposal could be approved by and started by 2029, the Exmouth Gulf is also being considered for National Heritage Listing, with that decision not expected until 2030.

The WA government is also looking to establish a new marine park covering the entire Exmouth Gulf.

Exmouth Gulf is also currently undergoing an assessment to be added to National Heritage List. (Supplied: Australia Marine Conservationist Society)

"Exmouth Gulf, is about to become a marine park, it is currently being assessed for national heritage status, which is obviously a pathway to world heritage protection," Mr Winton said.

Protect Ningaloo has so far gathered over 74,000 signatures for their submission to the EPA.

Mr Jackson said a large portion of the environmental review submission focused on dredging during the construction phase and it would be done in a controlled manner to ensure the seabed was not overly disturbed.

If approved, construction on the port is expected to begin in 2029 and be operational by end of that year.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/l.title: How distance and old-fashioned phone calls grew love for Amber and Kirsty
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Family and Relationships

Amber and Kirsty have travelled the world together, and with their daughter, over their 27 years together. (Supplied)

Kirsty and Amber Sayers-Hunt met when they were both living in WA's Pilbara region and only one of them was openly gay. Nineteen years and one child later they were married at their home in the Northern Territory town of Humpty Doo and had to kick out the last of the guests weeks later.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

These are Amber and Kirsty's words.

Amber: We officially met at a Baby Animals concert. We went back to my brother's house. That was kind of the first time I think we ever talked.

I'd come out to my folks, but I was living in a mining town, in Port Hedland, so you can only be so out there.

Kirsty was a friend of a gay friend. Within that community there are untouchables. Untouchables are the girlfriends or friends of gay people who aren't gay. So I didn't really have that kind of attraction straight away. I stuck to the rules.

Just before I left Port Hedland, Kirsty sent me a rose and put her phone number on it. It was about three weeks before I left Port Hedland and I was like, you're joking, all this time!

I was like, "You know I'm leaving town, right? I'm moving 1,200 kilometres away to Karratha." I think Kirsty said, "Oh, well, you know, I had to do it." So we chatted on real phones for a while and then we kind of lost contact for a bit.

Amber: I actually hadn't spoken to Kirsty, maybe for a couple of months. But I knew that she'd moved to Exmouth and I knew that a cyclone was coming, because it'd just gone past Karratha. It was pretty big so I rang her. And I was like, "Are you OK?" And she said, "I've just run down the corridor. I've watched my roof come off. I'm in my bathroom. I need to get off the phone, because my phone's going to go flat."

I hung up and thought, holy shit. It actually quite affected me. I think that's when I realised that I had true feelings there.

Talking through everything and knowing when to just focus on their relationship and their family is what Kirsty and Amber say sustains their love. (Supplied)

Kirsty: I definitely was not seeing myself as being gay or queer or lesbian or anything like that. I was born and bred in Port Hedland, so I had no choice.

At first it was just regular phone calls. I think the relationship grew because you actually had to have genuine conversations. It wasn't relying on texts and emojis and all of that stuff. You learn a lot about someone when you can just have an open dialogue for hours on end on a landline. It was really raw talking.

Amber: I'd lived in Perth. She'd lived in Port Hedland. We didn't want to go to Broome. We wanted to go somewhere a bit bigger. We had one friend that lived in Darwin, and I rang her. I said, "What's it like getting a job up there?" And she said, "You'll have a job tomorrow if you come."

I don't know that we decided we were just going to spend the rest of our lives together. It was just one of those things that once we kind of started seeing each other and then one thing led to another, we moved in together and that was it.

If we were ever allowed to marry, we would marry. So, I think it was about two weeks after the same-sex marriage legislation passed I went and bought a ring and I proposed.

Our wedding day was pretty special. It was bigger than Ben-Hur. We invited everyone we knew from everywhere around Australia and the world because we thought, well, they're not going to come because it's a long way to come. They all came. We had 250 people at our house, and it was massive.

Kirsty and Amber's wedding was held at their home in Humpty Doo, a small town near Darwin in the Northern Territory. (Supplied)

Kirsty: Until the legislation passed, I didn't really want to entertain the thought, or to get too excited. We had a child, we had a mortgage, we've had all of the usual family trials and tribulations and so I just didn't want to get our hopes up that we could actually then have a wedding and have everything else that everyone had.

There were people there, and we knew their prior opinions on marriage equality, who ticked yes because, oh, we want to see the girls get married, that would be a bloody great party in Humpty Doo. Some people stayed a month and some people we had to kick out after six weeks.

I wore a big white dress and Amber had a beautifully tailored white suit on and we were just in our garden that we had prepped and preened for months. We had made the bar out of old bits of corrugated iron. We had painted and decorated the shed with lights. It was a very DIY everything wedding.

I can't remember who, but someone said, when you're standing there in front of all your friends and family, just take a moment to stop and look back at all their faces. And so I think that was probably my most favourite memory, just seeing everyone's faces and knowing what we had to do to get to that day and seeing everyone just in tears and smiling and joy.

For Kirsty and Amber, getting married brought another level of security and sacredness to their relationship. (Supplied)

Kirsty: We come home and we sit outside on our balcony and chat, and just debrief every day. I think that when you reflect on it, it probably comes back to those very first days in Port Hedland and Exmouth when it was all just conversations. It's just listening and having the conversation and having someone there that probably knows you inside and out sometimes more than you do, to be there with you.

Amber: I think the best part is just being with someone that you love and that you know. We're very busy people, but we also know when to spend time just by ourselves; shut off all our notifications on our Messengers and just be with us, our little unit.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.title: What does Japanese wine taste like? Start with a Koshu.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.author: Weiwen Lin
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.text:
When I told friends I was visiting wineries across Japan in 2016, many of them thought I meant sake breweries. They were surprised to learn I was referring to the actual drink made from grapes.

“Japan makes wine?” they’d say.

Ten years later, Japanese wine has gained international recognition, winning awards at competitions such as the Decanter World Wine Awards and appearing on the wine lists of top restaurants around the world.

These days, I’m more often asked, “What does Japanese wine taste like?”

It’s a broad question, much like asking what French wine tastes like. But France’s established appellation rules and winemaking traditions make it easier to generalize about regional styles, with Bordeaux and Burgundy serving as familiar reference examples. Japanese wine is harder to pin down.

Japan has five prefectures designated as geographical indications (GIs): Yamanashi, Nagano, Osaka, Yamagata and Hokkaido. Producers must follow specific standards, like using at least 85% of the grapes from the designated region, to use a GI label on their wines. However, they can grow any grape variety they want. This is in stark contrast to France, where planting cabernet sauvignon in the pinot noir territory of Burgundy would make you an outcast.

Since no single area in Japan has an identifiable wine style, it’s not easy to link a wine’s flavor profile to a particular region. At least, for now it’s not.

To answer the question of what Japanese wine tastes like, though, let’s start with the indigenous grape that serves as its de facto flagbearer: Koshu.

Koshu grapes are grown primarily in Yamanashi’s Koshu Valley, which accounts for 95% of domestic production of the grape. DNA analysis has found that Koshu is 71.5% Vitis vinifera — the species behind most Old and New World wines — and the remainder Vitis davidii, a wild East Asian species.

Koshu is light-bodied, with fruit and citrus flavors. It has an acidity that ranges from medium to high depending on harvest conditions and winemaking techniques. I’d place it somewhere between a semillon and a riesling: It has the roundness of the former and some of the crisp acidity of the latter.

Anzu Kojima, founder of the Japanese wine bar Three Grapes in Tokyo’s Yoyogi neighborhood, says Koshu’s smoothness reminds her of a pinot gris. To see how Koshu’s different styles compare, I visited Three Grapes and picked three styles from its list: a sparkling wine, an unoaked wine and a barrel-fermented wine.

The first, a Lumiere Sparkling Koshu 2023 (¥1,900 per glass) from Yamanashi-based Lumiere winery, underwent secondary fermentation in the bottle and was aged for 20 months. It’s crisp and citrusy, with tiny bubbles that fade gently on the palate. A light saline aftertaste gives it a savory finish.

Kojima says that for those trying Koshu for the first time, a sparkling wine is a good introduction because it’s refreshing. “I’ll pair it with oysters and sushi,” she says.

Next up, from Miyazaki Prefecture, is a Tsuno Wine Makiuchi Private Reserve Koshu 2025 (¥1,900 per glass). The wine was briefly aged in stainless steel tanks with no barrel maturation, preserving its crisp acidity. It has notes of tropical fruit, reflecting the region’s subtropical climate. The vines are planted on a plateau 200 meters above sea level, where cooler conditions help mitigate the intense heat that poses a challenge to grape growing. I find the wine itself to be delicious and easy-drinking.

My final glass is a Grace Wine Koshu Toriibira Vineyard 2024 (¥2,100 per glass) from Yamanashi made from grapes grown on a slope at an altitude of 450 meters. A sloping vineyard offers better drainage, encouraging roots to penetrate deeper to search for groundwater and nutrients. That stresses the vines and produces smaller, more concentrated grapes.

Fermented in old French oak barrels for three months, the wine has round acidity, citrusy notes, umami and a touch of pepper. It has a fuller body than Tsuno’s wine, making it robust enough to pair with yakitori.

These three wines showcase Koshu’s versatility. Although they each embody a different style of winemaking, all three have an approachable flavor profile that is unique to the grape. The French and Italians will tell you that they make wines to pair with their regional dishes. In this regard, Koshu fits the bill of what a Japanese wine should taste like in that it pairs well with sushi, sashimi and tempura. For newcomers, it’s a sure crowd-pleaser.

The same can’t be said for Muscat Bailey A, however, Japan’s signature red wine grape. It tends to have what oenophiles call a “foxy” flavor, which tastes like an odd combination of musk and strawberries. Fans of red wine may find it a bit offputting.

With top-quality grapes, careful maceration and proper barrel aging, however, Muscat Bailey A can be delicious. One of my favorite wines representing the grape is Yamagata’s Domaine Takeda’s Bailey A, Vieilles Vignes, L’elevage en fut 2022. Its grapes come from vines that are nearly 80 years old — a rarity in Japan. Such vines have deeper roots that tap into water reserves and minerals to produce wines with more concentrated and complex aromas.

Aged for a year in barrels, Domaine Takeda’s medium-bodied red is a whirl of raspberry, soy, pepper and chocolate notes all lifted by moderate acidity. Its foxy flavor is very subtle, just enough to lend a deceptively earthy hint to its finish. In a blind tasting, the wine might be mistaken for a New Zealand pinot noir.

That’s a statement I would never have made 10 years ago. For me, Japanese wine today tastes less unfamiliar when compared with its New and Old World counterparts. It’s in a middle-of-the-road territory — and that’s a nice place to explore.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.title: Tim Anderson’s latest ‘JapanEasy Kitchen’ is more than forced fusion
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.author: Simon Daly
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.text:
Here’s a secret many novice home cooks struggle to master: With just a handful of kitchen staples, you have the basis for most dishes — and not necessarily just from the Japanese canon.

“JapanEasy Kitchen: Simple Recipes Using Japanese Pantry Ingredients” is the latest cookbook from former “MasterChef U.K.” champion Tim Anderson and a continuation of his now four-volume “JapanEasy” series. The newest book from the perennially busy author highlights more than a dozen ingredients across nine chapters, and the recipes within are case studies for how to use these building blocks in expected and surprising ways.

There are Japanese dishes, but the majority are not. This is not forced fusion; rather, Anderson paints a picture of the modern, eclectic global kitchen with a Japanese-tinted palette.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.title: A relative newcomer, ‘hakusai’ cabbage is now entering peak freshness
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.author: Makiko Itoh
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.text:
Hakusai, also known as napa or Chinese cabbage, is available year-round, but its peak season is late fall to winter when frost makes the leaves especially tender and sweet. It’s a must-have vegetable in hot pots, soups and stir-fries.

Hakusai actually has a surprisingly short history in Japan, only being introduced in the late 19th century around the time of the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95. It is said that Japanese troops on campaign ate the leafy vegetable and brought back plants and seeds with them to their villages.

However, the vegetables were pollinated in mainland China by bees and butterflies that did not exist in Japan, so the plants brought into Japan never propagated. This meant that they had to continue to be imported at high costs.

It wasn’t until the 1930s that Kichibei Numakura, a scientist from Miyagi Prefecture, was able to breed a stable species of hakusai that could be reliably pollinated by native Japanese insects. Even today, Numakura is remembered as the father of Japanese hakusai.

The recipe is for a refreshing pickled mix based on hakusai. Shio-kombu (salted shredded kombu) adds an umami boost while chili peppers add spice. It is far quicker to make than kimchi — and vegan to boot.

Use this as a side dish for a traditional Japanese meal.

Prep time: 30 minutes

Pickling time: Several hours or overnight

Cut the root ends off the hakusai, separate the leaves and wash well. Pat completely dry very, then slice into 4-centimeter-long pieces. Sprinkle each piece on both sides with salt.

Cut the shio-kombu into 3-centimeter pieces. Remove the seeds from the chili peppers and slice into small pieces with kitchen scissors.

Layer the salted cabbage, shio-kombu and chili peppers in a ziplock plastic bag. Squeeze the air from the bag and seal it up. Put the bag on a baking sheet or a plate and weigh it down with another sheet or plate. Place another weight on top (a few books or a couple of cans of food do the trick).

Several hours later (or overnight, if you have the time), take the contents out of the bag and drain any extra moisture. Arrange in a bowl, sprinkle with sesame seeds and serve.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.title: Family Dollar to Pay $63 Million Settlement for Overcharging Customers
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.author: Rebecca Chao
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/busin.text:
Since 2023, the discount retailer has been overcharging shoppers “millions of dollars” at checkout, according to a complaint filed by federal regulators and 17 states.

Family Dollar has agreed to pay a $63 million settlement after federal and state authorities filed complaints against the company for charging customers more than amounts advertised in mailers and displayed on store shelves.

The settlement, which was announced by the Federal Trade Commission on Thursday, came alongside a same-day order, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia.

The order seeks to prevent the retailer from continuing its deceptive pricing practices and would require it to create a “pricing accuracy program,” to be independently certified on an annual basis.

“Today’s order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices,” Christopher Mufarrige, the director of the F.T.C.’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in the announcement.

The agreement is the result of a complaint filed by the commission and 17 states on Thursday, which claimed that Family Dollar had overcharged consumers “millions of dollars” since January 2023.

The F.T.C. and Family Dollar did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday. In the order, Family Dollar said that it neither admitted to nor denied any of the allegations in the complaint.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: David Jones’ future looks grim. Is Myer next?
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Jonathan Barrett Business editor
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down.

Except, this isn’t David Jones, the embattled upmarket retailer that is shutting half its 38 stores.

This is its longtime rival, Myer, where entire floors are seemingly permanently on sale.

With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question: is Myer next?

At first glance, Myer’s headline numbers seem to defy the retail gloom, with double-digit sales growth to $4.1bn last financial year.

That lift, however, was not driven by surging demand, but by adding sales from the newly acquired apparel chains, Just Jeans, Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti and Jacqui E, bought from billionaire businessman Solomon Lew’s Premier Investments.

Meanwhile, to keep registers ringing, Myer employed “higher than planned promotional activity to stimulate demand”, according to its annual report, which reduced its profitability.

The department store has also slashed the value of its brands, down more than $200m in one year alone, in an admission that its labels are worth far less than they once were.

Department stores have faced a “sustained erosion of relevance over the past five years”, according to IBISWorld market researchers, as online platforms win over bargain-hunters and specialists like beauty retailer Mecca prove more nimble in capturing shifting tastes.

DJs and Myer, on the other hand, have been weighed down by long-running physical property leases tied to underperforming stores in their sprawling networks.

The era of Australian families being fiercely loyal to either David Jones or Myer is long gone, replaced by a grim battle for both chains to stay relevant.

The stress on big department store profitability has been exacerbated by a period of cost of living pressures that have “entrenched deal-hunting behaviour, reshaping how and when consumers engage with department stores”, according to IBISWorld.

Myer was contacted for comment.

Myer, however, has a critical advantage over David Jones: time.

While DJs fell into administration under mounting debts, Myer finished last financial year with a $100m net cash buffer, buying management breathing space to fix the business.

It has been reducing store numbers and with it lease liabilities – down to 56 stores from 60 before the pandemic – which is something David Jones is only doing now that it has collapsed into administration.

For the moment, Myer is leaning into the discounts demanded by shoppers, in the hope that more profitable trading conditions will emerge.

Richard Hemming, the editor at Under The Radar Report, says in retail “volume is everything”.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

“If you get the volumes through, that customer base will eventually be in a position to pay more, and when volumes and margins both improve, you get that double effect,” Hemming says.

While analysts have mixed views on whether permanent discounting is a smart survival tactic or a slow-motion way to go bankrupt, department stores do need to move huge volumes of stock to keep cash flowing and clear seasonal goods.

They can use those discounts to get more people signed up to their loyalty programs – such as the successful Myer One program – in the hope they will become long term customers.

Hemming sees the upside in Myer’s current pain, noting the retailer is “cleaning house earlier than rivals” precisely because investors have long priced it “like it’s going to go broke”.

Myer is revamping the business to aggressively pursue online sales.

Myer shares have been heavily sold down over the years, and now hover around the 24c mark, representing a fraction of its $4.10 float price from 2009.

It did, however, receive a price bump on the day DJs fell into administration.

With roughly two in five Myer stores sharing a shopping centre with a David Jones outlet, investors are betting the coming closure of 19 DJs sites will hand Myer an easy market-share boost, even as its own long-term turnaround demands further store cuts.

In the short term, the pain is likely to intensify for Myer as the David Jones stores marked for closure are under orders to clear stock with widespread promotions, luring customers.

Broader retail sentiment is also souring, as a string of interest rate rises and escalating cost-of-living pressures force cash-strapped shoppers to pare their discretionary spend.

The Retail Doctor Group’s chief executive, Brian Walker, says the main long-term advantage Myer has over its old rival is financial flexibility.

“Whereas David Jones was incredibly encumbered, Myer doesn’t have that issue right now,” Walker says.

“As we sit here today, Myer is financially stronger, but strategically still pretty vulnerable.”

https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.author: Michael Monostra
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. — Adults with obesity who used either semaglutide or tirzepatide at baseline were able to maintain weight loss at 2 years across four separate treatment regimens, according to data presented at ObesityWeek.

In an analysis of data from adults with obesity who were using either injectable once-weekly semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy, Novo Nordisk) or tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound, Eli Lilly) at baseline, researchers compared changes in body weight and other cardiometabolic parameters among different management strategies. While adults who underwent bariatric surgery achieved the largest weight loss at 2 years, those who switched between semaglutide and tirzepatide had a greater weight loss than those who remained on their baseline medication. All four groups who continued some form of obesity therapy had greater weight loss at 2 years than the group that stopped treatment.

“Our study highlights the importance of continued obesity management,” Hamlet Gasoyan, PhD, investigator at the center for value-based care research at Cleveland Clinic and assistant professor of medicine at Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine of Case Western Reserve University, told Healio. “These results could support patient-clinician discussions about alternative therapy options in patients who consider switching or stopping injectable semaglutide or tirzepatide.”

Researchers used electronic health record data from Cleveland Clinic to conduct a target trial emulation. Data were obtained for 20,486 adults with type 2 diabetes or obesity using either injectable once-weekly semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy, Novo Nordisk) or tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound, Eli Lilly) from 2021 to 2025 (mean age, 56.7 years; 63% women). Adults were assigned to one of five treatment strategies:

Of the study group, 68% had hypertension and 65.7% had type 2 diabetes. Semaglutide was prescribed for 73.4% of participants.

According to the per-protocol analysis, adults who continued their original medication had a 10.9% weight reduction at 2 years, those who switched between semaglutide and tirzepatide lost 16% of their body weight, adults who switched to another obesity drug reached an 8.1% weight loss, those who underwent bariatric surgery lost 26.6% of their weight and adults who stopped treatment had a weight decline of 3.9%.

For adults who received semaglutide at baseline, switching to tirzepatide was linked to 3 kg greater weight loss at 2 years than continuing semaglutide. Among those using tirzepatide at baseline, continuing with the original drug resulted in 4.5 kg greater weight loss than switching to semaglutide.

Changes in HbA1c and systolic BP occurred in a similar pattern as body weight change, according to the researchers.

Even though there were differences in weight reduction between the treatment groups, the study participants who continued some form of obesity treatment maintained weight loss at 2 years, including those who switched to older drugs, Gasoyan said.

“Our findings encourage future real-world evaluation about alternative therapy options in patients who consider switching or stopping their GLP-1 based medication,” Gasoyan said. “We will continue our research in this area to help patients choose treatments based on their individualized expected benefits and risks and aligned with their preferences.”

Hamlet Gasoyan, PhD, can be reached at gasoyah@ccf.org; or on X @HamletGasoyan.

Gasoyan H, et al. Oral-021. Presented at: ObesityWeek; Nov. 14-17, 2026; National Harbor, Maryland.

Disclosures: Gasoyan reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/root-cau.author: Tobias Burns
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/root-cau.text:
The inability to pinpoint the reason for the infrastructure malfunctions led the FAA to take actions that resulted in the grounding order, Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters.

Officials reported issues with routers and networking equipment on Saturday, citing products and services from Cisco and L3Harris Technologies.

“Until I can build [the new architecture], I’m stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

The root cause of the longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 remains unclear after a Saturday press conference by U.S. transportation officials.

Routers and networking equipment appeared to be involved in the technological disruption that grounded flights across the country, but a definitive cause has not been established as of Saturday afternoon.

The inability to pinpoint the reason for the infrastructure malfunctions led the Federal Aviation Administration to take actions that resulted in the grounding order, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, told reporters.

“Because of our lack of identifying the root cause, we were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a sensor losing connectivity with aircraft,” he said.

“What we saw was instability. We couldn’t explain the instability,” Bedford added.

Officials reported issues with routers and networking equipment on Saturday, citing products and services from Cisco
 and L3Harris Technologies
.

“Until I can build [the new architecture], I’m stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

In a statement on X, L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” the statement said. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

On Friday, Duffy and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin called for an air travel overhaul, with Duffy requesting $50 billion from Congress.

FAA administrator Bedford said that router updates were a matter of regular business for his agency and distinct from modernization allocations.

“We are constantly replacing 2,000, you know, Cisco 600 routers with Juniper routers, right? So this is ordinary course of business stuff. This is not part of the … FAA $12.5 billion modernization efforts. So let’s not conflate those two things,” Bedford said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/m.title: Journalist urges federal government to intervene in NT 'social catastrophe'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/m.author: Jane Bardon
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

In his new book, Murray McLaughlin outlines years of government failures in the NT and argues it "will never right itself".  (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

A veteran ABC journalist has delivered a searing analysis of Northern Territory politics in a new book that chronicles how government policies have worsened life outcomes for Aboriginal people in the NT.

Murray McLaughlin's new book is out now. (Supplied)

In his new book The Northern Territory: A Litany of Failure, Murray McLaughlin — who worked as an ABC TV current affairs journalist and later as an adviser to the Northern Land Council (NLC) — argues the federal government has been mostly passively complicit in the welfare of the Territory's Aboriginal citizens declining over five decades.

As well as a critique of failure, the book serves as an appeal to the federal government to intervene in a territory McLaughlin describes as a "beguiling and bewitching place, a unique wonderland".

"While Canberra's reluctance to dictate prevails, one certainty remains: the Territory will never right itself.

"A mendicant jurisdiction beholden to the Commonwealth is allowed to bring embarrassment and shame upon the whole country with policy agendas that disproportionately impact on Aboriginal people while it lavishes benefits on the non-Aboriginal population."

He says the Albanese government "has done little to avert the social catastrophe unravelling before its eyes".

"As Canberra pours billions of dollars into the Territory to shore up northern defence systems and the petrochemical industry prepares to prosper from the bountiful gas fields to be fracked in the immense Beetaloo Basin south-east of Darwin, housing, health and education markers continue to deteriorate for the Territory's Aboriginal population, especially those living in remote communities."

Patrick Dodson wrote the foreword to The Northern Territory: A Litany of Failure. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

In the book's foreword, former Labor senator Patrick Dodson, for whom McLaughlin worked as an adviser, reinforces its central message: That the NT's self-government in place since 1978 has been "a failed experiment" which has hastened "a collapse of social order".

But Mr Dodson writes that he and McLaughlin share hope that the Commonwealth will use "a rare political window … to show leadership and imagination in rebuilding the Territory and redirecting its troubled course".

Much of the book's conversational, accessible political history of the Territory is told from McLaughlin's firsthand reporting experience, and then from the sidelines of fights between the NLC and NT governments on policies affecting the rights of Aboriginal people.

He takes readers on an evocative journey through the Territory, analysing the policy blows Country Liberal Party (CLP) and Labor governments have delivered to Aboriginal people, focusing particularly on how successive CLP governments, aided at times by Canberra Coalition administrations, have tried to erode federal NT Aboriginal land rights laws.

The book claims successive governments from both major parties have failed Aboriginal people in the NT. (Torsten Blackwood, AFP)

He writes the Territory's first CLP chief minister Paul Everingham's 1978 administration opposed Aboriginal land rights and "ruthlessly" challenged almost every land claim.

This continued through to the 2013 CLP Adam Giles administration, McLaughlin writes, as they tried to persuade the Commonwealth to hand control of the land rights law to them.

McLaughlin documents how "Aboriginal incarceration rates have grown exponentially", starting with 1995 CLP chief minister Shane Stone's administration introducing mandatory sentencing for a range of offences.

"The law, predictably, had a disproportionate impact on Aboriginal people, and its impact had been cynically calculated," he writes.

The book also chronicles a series of Labor government policies during the early 2000s that harmed Aboriginal interests, including the 2001 Clare Martin administration's approval for Xstrata to dig through a sacred site to expand its McArthur River Mine in 2006.

The book uses the approval to destroy a sacred site at the McArthur River Mine as an example of how governments have ignored Aboriginal interests. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

McLaughlin labels this as "a conspicuous example of how governments have brutally brushed aside Aboriginal interests when development proposals take priority".

He writes how the following 2007 Paul Henderson Labor administration wound back bilingual education in Aboriginal community schools, concentrated government funding into larger Indigenous communities and amalgamated 53 remote local government councils into eight "super shires".

"Worse, the resultant changes coincided with the Howard government's Intervention, with communities never recovering from that double calamity," he writes.

McLaughlin analyses how both a "flawed" ABC Lateline story about an alleged paedophile ring in Central Australia and Clare Martin's "failure to respond with boldness and urgency to the Little Children Are Sacred report" resulted in the NT National Emergency Response — the Intervention.

John Howard and his Indigenous affairs minister Mal Brough launched the Intervention, with Mr Brough visiting Mutujulu in 2007. (Ian Waldie, file photo: Getty Images)

Seventy-three communities were identified as primary sites for intervention and the army and police were brought in from other jurisdictions.

"The scope of the Intervention was extraordinary and its impact on Aboriginal people cataclysmic," he writes.

"Although Aboriginal men were offended because the Intervention had branded them child molesters and, as traditional owners, they felt threatened about the Commonwealth's compulsory leasing of community lands, the most troubling policy … was compulsory income management, facilitated by the suspension of the Racial Discrimination Act 1975.

"Federal Labor, not wanting to be wedged, embraced the Intervention."

The 2013 Adam Giles government's treatment of youth prisoners, including the use of tear gas, mechanical restraints, spit hoods and indefinite detention isolation, that was exposed by the ABC is scrutinised in the book.

Youth detainees were shackled and hooded the day after tear gas was used on them at Don Dale. (Supplied)

"The brutalisation of children and their bastardisation in detention were painfully illustrated by the treatment of a 14-year-old Aboriginal boy, whose explosive behaviour on 21 August 2014 precipitated the tear-gassing of him and other detainees," McLaughlin writes.

McLaughlin analyses how the 2016 administration of Labor's Michael Gunner — summed up as "an uninspiring and shallow chief minister who promised plenty but delivered little" — "slithered and dithered" over recommendations of the royal commission into youth justice abuse.

He writes that Mr Gunner toughened bail laws "in the full knowledge that incarceration rates, especially of Aboriginal people, would blow out beyond already record-breaking numbers, and his commitment to a treaty began to fade".

Murray McLaughlin describes Michael Gunner as "an uninspiring and shallow chief minister". (ABC News: Che Chorley)

McLaughlin also accuses the Gunner government of attacking Aboriginal land rights by passing laws making it easier for pastoralists to develop cattle stations for other uses without native title holders having to be consulted or compensated.

"Gunner's government would soon resort to drawing from the same well of prejudice against Aboriginal land claims as had nourished the Country Liberal Party," he writes.

The veteran journalist follows the NT right up to the current CLP government, documenting how Indigenous incarceration continued  to dramatically increase with tightened bail laws following the 2023 murder of a bottle shop worker, Declan Laverty.

"By August 2025, the government was boasting that more than 3,300 people had been refused bail, a 44 per cent increase over the same period in 2024," the books reads.

McLaughlin's chronicle finishes with current Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro's appointment of former NT Cattlemen's Association President David Connolly earlier this year, and her determined defence of that after racist social media posts he had previously made were exposed.

Territorians protested David Connolly's appointment as administrator earlier this year. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"Obduracy and disdain for proper process marked Finocchiaro's announcement," he writes.

"Albanese's refusal … to reject the Territory government's egregious recommendation of a man with a record of racist commentary to be the Territory's Administrator … spoke of a deliberate avoidance of responsibility."

McLaughlin told the ABC he hoped the federal government was starting to understand that the Territory's Aboriginal people were facing a crisis so severe that it must now intervene.

Despite its 'litany of failure', Murray McLaughlin is hopeful the federal government will intervene.

"The Commonwealth has got to recognise that it's got responsibilities here," he said.

"It's going to take something like a Marshall Plan to just catch up.

"Something has to happen — these remote communities are on their knees.

"[Independent NT politician] Yingiya Guyula said it when he resigned, that Aboriginal culture is being destroyed in front of our eyes.

"Things are deadly serious."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Kaylee McKeown is back in action after being "wiped out" by glandular fever. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Kaylee McKeown returned to competition at the Swim GP after an illness-ravaged 2026.

Mollie O'Callaghan missed the event due to an infection.

Australia's Dolphins are tipped to star at the 2027 World Championships in Budapest.

Battered by illness and injury, a trio of Australian Olympic swimming stars are being backed to be ready for Los Angeles Games.

Between them, Kaylee McKeown, Mollie O'Callaghan and Kyle Chalmers have won 11 Olympic gold medals.

McKeown returned to competition over the weekend at the inaugural Swim GP in Melbourne, having not raced since last year because of glandular fever.

Chalmers was poolside at the event, in the midst of a six-week break from swimming as he manages long-term back problems.

O'Callaghan, who nursed back and shoulder injuries through the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, was a late withdrawal from the Swim GP because of a skin infection.

McKeown said the one positive of her illness was that it had happened this year, not next.

Australian swimming head coach Rohan Taylor echoed that sentiment about the three stars in the context of the four-year Olympic cycle.

Mollie O'Callaghan missed competing at Swim GP due to an infection. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"No-one will remember what happens in 2026 [in terms of injury or illness]. You can't worry about that now," Taylor told AAP.

"You have to get them right, you have to remember their talent won't go anywhere.

"It's about getting them healthy and then letting the fitness build. We know they can race and we just have to get ourselves to the arena fit and healthy, then we will be right."

McKeown made a successful return to racing at the Swim GP and Taylor was pleased with the backstroke queen's progress after the illness knocked her flat.

"I live on the Sunshine Coast, so I get to see it up close and see the progression," Taylor said.

"It's really good to see her back racing. She's such a competitor.

"She just looked back to her normal self, competitive, focused when the race was on, but enjoying herself.

"She just has to build momentum back."

McKeown gave a glimpse of her blistering backstroke speed on Saturday night, storming home after the staggered start to beat Ella Ramsay's breaststroke in the 50m skins champions race.

It was her first racing since the world championships in July last year.

Kaylee McKeown is one of Australian swimming's biggest stars. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"I've been doing some pretty solid sessions, but it's hard to come into these races — not racing all year — and then my body just hasn't recovered as quickly as it would," McKeown said.

"It's good, nice practice and gives a bit of confidence that I'm still swimming well.

"It's great there are no times, which takes the pressure off. It's just about racing."

As McKeown notes, glandular fever affects people differently and in her case, "it just really knocked me flat".

So competing for the Tsunami team at the Swim GP, with nothing riding on the results, was an ideal stepping stone as McKeown looks to next year's world championships and then the 2028 Olympics.

"It's really good fun and I'm glad we can race in this format," she said.

"It's taken a long time to build back and then I have to build to where I was, which is even more of a gap.

"I'm lucky it was this year and not next year, when it counts, so it's a blessing in disguise. I've had some nice time at home."

Swim GP is a points-based competition in a 25m pool, with no official times recorded and a variety of relay and individual race formats.

The Wahoo team, lead by Meg Harris and Sam Short, dominated the two-night Swim GP and comfortably won on 222 points.

McKeown's Tsunami were next on 173, ahead of Kraken (170) and KingTide (149).

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/a.title: The parade of high-profile men doing wrong is getting exhausting
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/a.author: Annabel Crabb
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Sexual Offences

Russell Brand has been jailed for 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assault. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

This coming Thursday is International Men's Day. Unaware of it? So are most carbon-based life forms, even though it's been around for about three decades now.

Google Trends advises that the term "International Men's Day" bumps along at low rates of interest most of the year, with two identifiable annual spikes; one smaller, one larger.

The smaller occurs around now, in the lead-up to the day itself — November 19.

The larger spike occurs in early March, around International Women's Day. It doesn't take an expert to decode the March spike; men who've just seen a poster for International Women's Day (IWD) and want to know why there isn't a day for them, or women juggling a tray of IWD-themed cupcakes who've just been asked that question by a male colleague and are googling it with the other hand to confirm their vague recollection that it's not that there isn't one, it's just that nobody organised a brunch and a speaker for it.

It's coming along, though, and there are events planned for Thursday, a day on which we are encouraged to reflect on the broad patterns of male experience that are visible from space: higher suicide rates, shorter life span, higher likelihood of violent death, lower performance at all levels of education.

This year's theme? "The Future is Everyone."

How awkward, then, that the November pre-sizzle to International Men's Day has so far consisted of a daily, multi-nation parade of high-profile men for whom the future — and indeed the present, and the past too — are mainly organised around a far more specific and compelling figure: ME ME ME.

The disgraced British entertainer-turned-conspiracy theorist charted a course towards fame and notoriety before a criminal trial in London found him to be a sexual predator.

In the United States, there's a president for whom even a crushing performance review from 125 million constituents cannot dislodge his conviction that what struggling Americans really want is more detail about the chandelier-count in his billion-dollar ballroom.

Or Jensen Huang, the "godfather of AI" who over three decades single-handedly built a company silicon-paving humanity's path to a future in which we either lounge about doing craft projects on a living wage or are torn apart by robot dogs (nobody's quite sure which), only to undo it all using only his penis.

In the UK, formerly beloved TV stars and writers Russell Brand and David Walliams are confronted with the carefully catalogued consequences of their actions and conclude that the real victim is … themselves.

And in Australia this very week, we find ourselves once more ensnared in an intense argument among Australia's best-known cricketing men about exactly who knew what, and when, about whether sandpaper was going to be secreted in the jocks of a bowler in Cape Town eight years ago.

What purpose does this new outbreak of finger-pointing, flounce-outs, self-justification and mic-drop moments serve? Apart from ensuring that a fresh new generation of junior cricketers can be as confused and disappointed as their predecessors were back in 2018?

You can dress it up as the pursuit of justice, or the righting of wrongs, or the promotion of a book, but let's call it what it is: a handful of guys who feel they were personally wronged by the way the last village-burning went, and are now torching the joint again to correct the record.

This whole month feels like one of those old choose-your-own-adventure novels, where every single storyline leads to a dude who has let everyone down but still wants to go for a coffee about it.

So, what is it about this parade that has caused anyone with an internet connection and two X chromosomes to want more than usual to go for a lovely lie down in the snow and never get up?

I think it's the shamelessness. The relentless, insistent, main-character energy that leads some humans — having done a wrong or been proved wrong — to argue the toss or return to the scene in the garb of a victim, rather than do the normal human thing, which is to go to bed indefinitely in a soup of self-loathing and hope that someone else will soon take the heat off you by doing something exponentially worse.

In a way, it's transfixing. Also, to a bone-deep level, exhausting.

Let's go to the details, starting with Russell Brand, whose conviction and 10-year sentence for rape rather crystallises the speculation that has mounted around him over the course of this century. This may or may not have inspired him to move to America, convert to Christianity, be baptised by Bear Grylls and engineer an entrée into the kind of conspiracy theorist circles where a sexual assault allegation is a fungible token of victimhood.

The re-Branding exercise allows this story to continue to be — for Russell Brand and his remaining fans — about Russell Brand, rather than the young women he groped, raped or abused.

Asked if he had anything to say to the women his son was convicted of assaulting, Brand's dad Ronald snapped at reporters outside court this week:

"The victim? What, Russell? The girls, you mean, who chased him and harassed him? Is that what you mean?"

Multiple people have now alleged David Walliams groomed teenage fans and harassed women. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

Or David Walliams, another British TV star and writer long reputed to have used his celebrity as a pretext for approaching young women. Confronted with allegations of this behaviour after several journalists worked for years with multiple women, Walliams demanded their stories be suppressed, as their publication would — given his fame — cause him distress to the point at which he was likely to kill himself.

Fame, in other words — having for years delivered this guy just about whatever and whomever he wanted — could now be repurposed as victimhood.

In Walliams's public statement, the key paragraph ran to 36 words, five of which were "I" or "me":

"I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Spare a thought for the other victims, though. Like fellow celebrity Jonathan Ross.

Jonathan Ross said he was "as horrified by the revelations … as the rest of the nation". (Supplied: ITV News)

As MC of the 15th British Comedy Awards in 2004, Ross got a big laugh by likening the comedy gong to any other 15-year-old: "It's drunk, it's unpredictable and it's probably going home with David Walliams."

Four years later, co-hosting a BBC Radio show with Russell Brand, Ross was recorded shrieking "He f***ed your grand-daughter!" as Brand left voicemail after voicemail for actor Andrew Sachs (famous for playing Manuel in Fawlty Towers). In one of the messages, Brand croons: "It was consensual … and she wasn't menstrual …"

Ross would now like everyone to know that he didn't know anything about any of it, and someone else wrote the joke for him, and had he known his pals were actual creeps, he absolutely would have done something about it.

This is part of the exhaustion, for any normal member of the public who's bought the tickets, bought the T-shirts, bought the books, taken their kids along to the live events or the games or in any way boarded the bus, liked and subscribed, only to discover there's a whole VIP lounge up the back where everyone's necking champagne and braying at a joke from which cattle class have been excluded.

Finding this out is bad enough. But when the charlatans involved still think they can talk you back onto the bus? And would like you to consider just how rough this has all been for them? My God. Where does this level of shamelessness come from?

Britain's culture secretary describes the reported allegations against David Walliams as "the latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" in the entertainment industry.

Not to dwell too grimly on the misdeeds of chaps we've actively invited into the lives of our children, but this Big Me Energy was unmistakeable in Australian writer Craig Silvey's 9,000-word apologia, published on Substack this month as he trudged off to prison convicted of possessing and distributing child exploitation material.

I haven't counted how many times the words "I" and "me" were deployed in this screed, mainly because doing so would involve Nvidia chips and I don't want to get pregnant, but they certainly appeared a lot.

Silvey devoted the bulk of his unsolicited essay to a discussion of his own trauma: sexual and physical abuse in his childhood; a brother who defrauded him; a lifetime of never feeling enough; a father whose transgressions are rather exhaustively listed, ranging from violence, to betrayal, to the lesser offences of coldness and being nicer to other kids at footy training.

These are deployed as "context" for Silvey's own transgression, which warrants one clipped and euphemistic sentence: "In January this year, while participating in an awful and inappropriate online conversation with another adult, I downloaded and sent an image of CEM."

Craig Silvey was found guilty of possessing and distributing child exploitation material. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

A reader would have to cross-research quite doggedly through the court records to find that Silvey's online activity was not restricted to one conversation. That his lengthy consideration of paternal failing excluded, for instance, the court's chat room transcripts of Silvey confiding he was aroused by the idea of mothers having sex with their boy children, or that a child of eight was "the perfect age".

The essay rounds off with an assurance that Silvey has done the work in therapy and now is prepared to love himself again. All of which is welcome news. But there is no doubt who continues to be the main character of this story, and it's certainly not the children harmed by the material Silvey sought out and/or shared.

Nor is it Silvey's own wife and three children, from whose silkily present-tense mention in the essay ("people I love and care about devotedly") it might be inferred that the family unit remained supportively intact.

It fell to Silvey's wife to take a minute or two out of sole-parenting a toddler and twin babies to pen a rather more economical note, clarifying that "we separated as soon as I learned of his crimes".

Enough of all this! Humans are poor, sometimes damaged creatures, and we all fail in some way. Usually every day. And for powerful men who are accustomed to being the main character in their own lives, it's very hard to relinquish that role, even when they screw up incredibly badly.

To hedge against this terrible possibility, they are prepared to do extraordinary things. Brand changes his entire persona. Walliams threatens to kill himself. Silvey unveils a lifetime of suffering sufficiently grim to rival that of the children affected by his online activities.

It's too early to say how Jensen Huang, Destroyer of Worlds, will jump. Will we never see him again? Or will he be on the cover of next month's GQ, "speaking out" about his pain from the depths of a billionaire python-skin jacket (RRP $20,000)?

Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia after 33 years. (Reuters)

(Honestly, one hates to pre-empt the inquiry into how elite Chinese spycraft came to identify Huang as a promising target for a honey trap, but his practice of wearing a leather jacket every single day, at 63, cannot have been immaterial.)

Is there a more biblical parable than Huang's? He builds a company with the express aim of immortalising and super-proliferating human intelligence, only to knock about a trillion dollars off its value with the most conventional bit of human stupidity imaginable.

It kind of makes you proud in a weird way, doesn't it? That artificial intelligence can scrape the entire universe of human wisdom but still get caught out by the undigitised impulses of man's least governable muscles — the heart and the one to the south of the heart? Bless us all, in our fleshy imperfection.

International Men's Day could not come at a better time, with its quiet reminder that men in general are not reducible to the antics of an ego-obsessed few.

In Becoming a Man, a thoughtful new collection of essays by men published this month by HarperCollins and edited by writer Julia Baird with her teenage son Sam Baird Sparks, several contributors deal specifically with the phenomenon of men who place themselves at the centre of everything.

British-born WA creative director Sam Harris describes this creature as "spotlight man".

Becoming a Man is edited by Julia Baird and her son. (Supplied: HarperCollins)

"A spotlight man will blind others with his talent, fame, wealth and success," Harris writes.

"He feels most alive when he's the centre of attention, with crowds cheering his name. But you'll see the real shape of spotlight man when the light's not on him, leaving him in a black hole of shadows. His dreams are more important than anyone else's — if you take his spotlight, he'll pull you into his black hole too."

Arne Rubinstein, founder of Rites of Passage, defines the transition from boyhood to manhood specifically around the changing sense of self. While boys might believe "I am the centre of the universe … I am always right and I will lie rather than admit I am wrong", manhood is about realising that everything is not, in fact, all about you.

"A problem arises when we end up with leaders and people in power who still have boy behaviours running their lives," Dr Rubinstein writes.

"Unfortunately, I believe a lot of our global leaders are boys, and that is a massive problem that puts the future of the world at risk."

So. This International Men's Day, let's understand properly that the victims of toxic masculinity are not just women.

Let's recognise the men who have completed the journey from boyhood to manhood and as a result are tough enough to confront the harshness of life — even its unfairness, even its humiliations, even their own inevitable mistakes — without requiring the world to drop everything to pity or exonerate them.

Men who have evolved past the childish notion that winning at life means having all the toys, all the praise, all the power. Who care for the people around them at work and at home, through good times and bad, not so they can be named Man of the Year, but because they're smart enough to work out that this is the most durable path to happiness.
