https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Pulisic double leads US to 6-0 rout of Haiti in Pochettino’s farewell tour
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
US take 5-0 lead in Nations League quarter-final

Hall, 18, scores again as Pochettino prepares for exit

Pulisic goes into fourth on all-time US scoring list

When Mauricio Pochettino named his US roster for the November window, few could have expected that the games would double as his brief lame-duck era. A week of camp instead brought constant media coverage, efficient negotiations and questions about the future of the national team. Come Wednesday, his day job will take him far from the federation’s headquarters in Fayetteville, Georgia, as he hopes to make sense of Manchester United.

Saturday finally allowed Pochettino and his players to get on with the intended purpose of this window, and they took to the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals with aplomb. The US opened their two-leg series against Haiti with a dominant 6-0 victory in front of a considerably pro-Haitian crowd in Miami. Auston Trusty provided the first half’s only goal before Julian Hall, Christian Pulisic, Weston McKennie and Folarin Balogun contributed to the eventual rout.

Concacaf allowed Haiti to host the match in Miami under an “exceptional hosting arrangement” because of the ongoing political unrest and gang violence in Port-au-Prince.

Pochettino’s penultimate lineup as US manager built on the momentum fostered during the previous international window. Tyler Adams retained the captain’s armband after being named permanent skipper in September, a decision on which Pochettino’s successor would be foolish to renege.

Trusty partnered Chris Richards between the first-choice full-back tandem of Antonee Robinson and Alex Freeman. Pulisic and McKennie made their first international appearances since the World Cup. Diego Kochen and Hall started in goal and at striker, respectively, as two members of a rising generation who debuted en masse in the previous window.

One major evolution under Pochettino led to the game’s opening goal. Midway through his tenure, Pochettino cut into Pulisic’s ownership of dead-ball duties, opening the door to alternatives after the Milan winger had too routinely sent his deliveries into the first defender. Malik Tillman made the most of the change, scoring a pair of direct free-kick goals in the World Cup knockout rounds. It also helped Sebastian Berhalter establish himself in a prominent role, transforming from an uncapped outsider when Pochettino arrived into an every-game option capable of filling multiple roles in midfield.

In the ninth minute, Freeman drew a free kick on the right flank roughly 30 yards from goal. Berhalter stood over it as players congregated in the penalty area, curling his delivery around the crowd and beyond the far post. Trusty arrived without a defender in tow, steering the ball back toward the right post for his second international goal.

VAR took some time to confirm that Trusty had stayed onside for such an unobstructed run, and the Celtic defender had plenty to reflect on in the interim. It was his first on-field action in nearly a month, having last played on 15 October following the death of his father, Walt. The decision was met with a series of emphatic claps from Trusty as his teammates returned to celebrate with him for a second time.

Still, Les Grenadiers threatened the US with greater attacking ambition than Mexico or Canada had shown in the previous window. Backed by raucous support, Haiti sustained an intense, swarming press whenever the Americans had possession in their defensive third. In the 16th minute, Danley Jean Jacques fashioned a powerful effort after a quick Haitian break, but Kochen parried the shot away from any would-be follow-up. Lenny Joseph found another opening shortly after the half-hour mark, only for Richards to time his sliding block expertly.

The teams converged near midfield around the 40th minute after an exchange between Adams and Josué Casimir, with the Haiti attacker appearing to attempt to slap Berhalter in the face after the US midfielder intervened on his captain’s behalf. Guatemalan referee Walter López ultimately showed yellow cards to Casimir and Berhalter, and the remainder of the half unfolded in disjointed fashion as neither side looked willing to back down.

The second half sustained that intensity, with both teams leaving a little extra in their challenges. Haiti felt they had earned an attacking free kick in the 52nd minute after Tillman brought down Casimir from behind. As the home-away-from-home faithful booed, the US broke down the flank with a decisive sequence of passes, Pulisic carrying into the final third before slipping the ball left to Robinson.

The left back sent it back into the box for the onrushing Hall, whose movement had afforded him time to pick his spot. The 18-year-old comfortably dispatched his effort into the net. Despite making his debut only in September, Hall already has four goals from five appearances for the US, a tally he looks poised to build on for years to come. Only two other American men have scored four international goals before turning 20: Pulisic and Gio Reyna.

Hall’s appearance on Saturday also officially cap-tied him to the United States, ending any possibility of a one-time switch to Poland, who had courted the teenager.

Hall continued to torment Haiti’s center-backs. Five minutes after his goal, he drew defenders toward him before playing a clever backheel into Pulisic’s path. Carlens Arcus tripped the Milan attacker as he tried in vain to reach the bouncing ball. It was a straightforward penalty decision for López.

Pulisic made no mistake from the spot, opting for power as he drove his effort straight down the middle while goalkeeper Alexandre Pierre dived helplessly away. The American star peeled toward the corner flag for a smiling celebration with a group of young fans before exchanging high-fives with his teammates.

It was his 34th international goal, drawing him level with Eric Wynalda for fourth on the program’s all-time scoring chart. Their shared position lasted just 32 seconds.

Haiti squandered possession from the ensuing kickoff, handing the Americans the ball inside their own half. Freeman swept a pass into the middle, where Pulisic collected possession and fashioned a shooting opportunity from more than 20 yards out. Pierre could do little to stop it, and suddenly the US were four goals to the good with more than two hours still to play across the two legs.

Much of Pochettino’s tenure has been spent imploring his players never to let up regardless of the scoreline, and the US took that message to heart. McKennie separated himself from Joseph at a 68th-minute free kick, heading home his 13th international goal and his first since 28 March.

Haiti still tried to claw back some of the deficit, catching the young Kochen in no man’s land a few minutes later with a lofted ball over the high US defensive line. The nominal home support erupted as Casimir collected the long ball and found Joseph in the box for a comfortable finish. But VAR determined that Casimir had strayed offside by the narrowest of margins, his big toe enough to negate the consolation goal.

In truth, there was little left to be decided. Balogun appeared to score his first US goal since his ill-fated last-16 appearance against Belgium, only for VAR to controversially rule it out for an apparent infraction. Balogun needed no contact with defenders to make amends five minutes later, gliding between two opponents before strolling into the box and nutmegging Pierre.

Both the disallowed first effort and the legitimate second prompted the same celebration from a smiling Balogun: a pantomime tap of his watch, “it’s about damn time” in so many words.

The rest of the year will likely feel similarly free of stakes. US Soccer is not expected to appoint Pochettino’s successor until the new year, with Olympic team coach Steve Cherundolo poised to handle December’s friendly window on an interim basis. There is something of a somber party atmosphere around the team at present, attacking with fearlessness and showing considerable fight when games get thorny. All that remains for Pochettino before taking over at Manchester United is to see out a 6-0 advantage in Tuesday’s second leg in Cincinnati.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/j.author: Ewa Staszewska
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Government

Jacqui Lambie says the government needs to consider access to existing subsidies as it looks to make budget cuts. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Senator Jacqui Lambie suggests the government consider means testing existing subsidies, including child care and for electronic vehicles, as it looks for cuts ahead of December's budget update.

She says it should also have the "courage" to look at a new tax on gas exports as a way to raise billions of dollars in revenue.

The government will face a political battle this week to pass its gas reservation bill, which currently does not have the support of the Greens or Coalition.

Independent senator Jacqui Lambie says the government should means test several subsidies, including child care, as it looks at ways to tighten its budget.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers is facing growing pressure to rein in government expenditure ahead of December's budget update due to cost-of-living pressures including persistent inflation and a fifth interest rate hike this year.

The Tasmanian senator has suggested one possible lever for the government is to better target assistance at those who need it most.

"We've got to target better in this country," she told Insiders on Sunday.

She proposed different levels of subsidy for child care depending on income, using a couple with $500,000 income between them as an example.

As the government pursues savings "across the board" ahead of the mid-year budget update, an ABC analysis shows only a handful of ministers have managed net savings so far this year.

"Why aren't we means testing you? Why aren't we doing what we used to do and say, you can have 10 per cent rebate. Not this much rebate," she said.

Asked whether that principle would apply to other subsidies like those on electric vehicles, Senator Lambie said, "Means test it all, why not? That's where you'll get some money from."

Senator Lambie stressed that she had not seen her constituents under such financial strain since the COVID-19 pandemic, with some turning to putting meat "down their pants and walking out" of supermarkets to feed their children.

"I don't see this financial situation turning around overnight. And I think we've got a couple of more years of it," she said, pointing to uncertainty across several issues like the war in the Middle East.

As politicians return for the final sitting fortnight of the year, the government hopes that it can pass its nationwide gas reservation scheme which it says will put downward pressure on prices.

The scheme would force liquefied natural gas exporters to keep up to 20 per cent of their product for Australia's domestic market and address consistent threats of shortfalls on the east coast.

Senator Lambie says she will support the legislation when it is debated in the Senate but has called on the government to have "enough courage" to put a 20 per cent tax on export gas.

"Start taking our resources back into our own hands, but we're actually making money off out of them," she said.

The idea is supported by members of the crossbench including the Greens and independent senator David Pocock, who state a 25 per cent tax on gas exports could raise billions of dollars in annual revenue.

The proposal has been repeatedly rejected by the government who argue it needs to protect trade relationships with Asian partners and points to the existing petroleum resources rent tax, which has upwards revisions in forecast revenue.

Shadow Minister for Defence James Paterson said the opposition was concerned about the future of gas investment in Australia as it works constructively with the government, not revealing where it has landed on the gas reservation bill.

"We do want to have more gas here for Australians to access, particularly for industry whose prices have been driven through the roof on Labor's watch," he told Sunday Agenda.

"And we want to see more gas extracted here in Australia. But the government has not done anything to make that easier."

Police are investigating the suspected stabbing death of a man in Melbourne's south-east.

Emergency services were called after a man with suspected stab wounds was found on the corner of Leonard and Beach streets in Frankston at about 1:20am today.

After efforts to revive him, including CPR, the man, who is yet to be formally identified, was declared dead at the scene.

Homicide detectives are probing a potential connection between the man's death and an earlier incident at a property in Lucerne Crescent.

They have set up crime scenes at both locations.

A woman was arrested at the scene of the man's death in relation to another matter.

Police allege the people involved were known to each other.

Anyone with information that may assist the investigation is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or online.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: U.S. floated idea of Ukraine ceding Donbas for NATO membership
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
KYIV – U.S. negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine’s potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, following the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelenskyy said in remarks to reporters released by his office Saturday.

“The Americans raised a question: ’What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’” he said.

“That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard (Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation.”

Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.

Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum.

Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskyy dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine.

“We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said on Saturday that the two sides had set out “maximalist positions” in the talks last week, but in private discussions both “understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war.”

“Serious and constructive work continues among those of us committed to finding solutions,” Kushner said in a social media post.

Zelenskyy also dismissed Putin’s suggestion for a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, a hotly contested city in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, saying it reflected Moscow’s inability to take the city by force. Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added.

“Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” he said.

Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other front-line settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Zelenskyy said.

Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war.

The two days of U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough, though the sides agreed to a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Zelenskyy said.

The final numbers for the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added.

Kushner and fellow U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff had pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with Putin at a meeting in Moscow on Thursday, Zelenskyy said, but there was no news of any progress after their talks.

“Putin personally does not support a ceasefire,” he said.

Zelenskyy met Witkoff and Kushner on Thursday in Ireland after their talks in Moscow. He said the U.S. negotiators had told him that all sides had agreed for Europe to have a seat at the negotiating table in forthcoming peace talks.

In Abu Dhabi, delegates from Europe — which is now Ukraine’s largest financial and military backer — had talks with U.S. and Ukrainian officials but did not sit at the table with Russia.

At the summit in Ireland, EU leaders agreed that Europe’s team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers — non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland — as well as EU officials.

Kushner said the U.S. focus was now on “facilitating direct engagement between Moscow and European partners and preparing the agenda for the next round of trilateral talks.”

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn8.title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn8.text:
It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach.

"I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering.

Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar.

This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa.

Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use.

"I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid."

Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated.

High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight.

And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out.

But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier.

"I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist.

She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product.

"For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales."

Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice.

"I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items.

"And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy."

Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing".

So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to?

Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and beauty expert, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them.

"Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous.

"But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it."

This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it.

In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do.

"The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says.

With additional reporting from Kris Bramwell
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn8.summary: Beauty advent calendars are popular with women who want to try out new products. But some say they are too expensive to buy them and are not worth it. Kim Kardashian's beauty calendar was criticised for its quality after being criticised on social media.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw77.title: Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw77.text:
You might know her as a pop star, endorsed by everyone from Taylor Swift to Sam Fender, but Holly Humberstone has a secret double life.

In her spare time, the singer-songwriter is literally a cat burglar.

"We've stolen one of our neighbours' cats by accident," she laughs, in a Zoom call from her fixer-upper in New Cross, south-east London.

"He's a tiny little black cat who's come into our garden and simply chosen us."

Under the slightest scrutiny, however, her story crumbles like a biscuit in a hot cup of tea.

"OK, we've been coercing him into the house with treats," she admits. "He's just so cute.

"But we're not trying to keep him. We literally push him out every night."

Humberstone's excuse for this feline felony is that, last year, her parents sold her childhood home in Lincolnshire and moved to Wales – taking her pets with them.

One, a cat called Tsuki, had even been immortalised in the song Lucy as a confidante who listens to her problems but "never judges".

"Oh, she knows some secrets!" laughs the singer. "I'm so glad she can't talk."

"We actually tried to bring her to London with us, but she's a countryside cat and she hated it so much. We had to send her to Wales where she can be free and frolic."

Her parents' relocation was disruptive for the human Humberstones, too.

Their house, a "freezing cold, falling down" property 20 minutes outside of Grantham, played a huge part in the singer's success.

Her early EPs were all written there, inspiring the "wonky sonics" of her indie-leaning pop sound. The 2021 single Haunted House is even dedicated to the "friendly" spirits who inhabited the property.

"It's a place I always felt I could go back to, to remind myself of who I am," she says.

Instead, she spent 2025 "packing up 23 years of stuff my family and I had accumulated", from her old ballet shoes and poetry books to forgotten bits of jewellery.

The process was unsettling. Already grappling with the idea of leaving childhood behind, Humberstone found herself literally throwing away her past.

"I felt uprooted. I was having some sort of identity crisis almost weekly," she says.

So she did what she's always done, and poured those feelings into her second album, Cruel World, which entered the UK charts at number four earlier this year.

"Writing these songs felt like building myself a little shield and a kind of safety bubble," she says. "There's an escapist, fantasy element to so much of the album."

Maybe that's true, but Humberstone has always had the ability to locate a song's emotional core, and the lyrics on Cruel World don't disappoint.

"To lose somebody is to know you're only human, honey," she sings on To Love Somebody, soothing her elder sister as she endures an agonising break-up.

Undeterred by that heartbreak, she throws herself headfirst into a new affair on Die Happy, declaring: "Hit the gas, I want it fast, want it reckless."

But the most revealing song is the closing track, Beauty Pageant.

Fragile and raw, it's the sound of Humberstone in her dressing room, addressing the woman in the mirror who'd "die for the applause" but who struggles with the impossible beauty standards imposed on female artists.

"That's a song that I wasn't really setting out to write," she confesses.

"Writing about other people often feels easier than turning the magnifying glass on yourself."

The lyrics, she says, draw on a "very specific" mindset she acquired at her all-girls school in Grantham.

"It was drilled into me: You're all in competition. You're only rewarded if you're the best. And if you're not, you're worthless."

The experience "really warped the way I view other girls", she says.

Musical success made it worse. After winning the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, Humberstone found herself competing with megastars, even though her music leaned towards the alternative side of pop.

"I'm a very small fish and I recognise that, but suddenly I was in meetings being compared to all these people on my label's roster, who are on a completely different scale," she says.

"It's something I really, really struggled with in the early days and it's something I've really had to unlearn."

Nowadays, Humberstone has stopped benchmarking herself against her peers, recognising that the need for validation never fades.

"I don't think that there's a point I could get to, or an award that I could win, where these feelings would disappear," she says.

"Everybody feels like they've still got something to prove, so I'm done with setting myself goals - because then I lose sight of the real reason that I'm doing this, which is to write music that represents me, and have other people feel understood through that music."

That mindset comes to fruition in the new, expanded edition of Cruel World, whose five new songs were largely written after the original album was handed in.

"I was super proud of Cruel World and, when you've got that in your back pocket, there's room to experiment and break some of your usual parameters."

The new tracks find Humberstone embracing a new persona – more confident, more flirtatious, a little salty – with music inspired by a playlist featuring Abba, Madonna and Robyn.

The single Too Cute To Be Lonely is a will-they/won't-they story set at a house party.

"Don't leave a girl upset, in such a pretty dress," she teases the object of her affections.

Terminally Yours takes place a couple of weeks later, when Humberstone realises she's fallen head-over-heels in love.

"Your stupid face is my sorry fate," she harrumphs, cross at herself. "For [expletive]'s sake, I'm in love."

Silver Sky, a gorgeous acoustic ballad, tells another side of the story, as she settles into her lover's arms and drifts into blissful reverie.

"I wrote that on a kind of Hail Mary trip, seeing what fell out of the air in Nashville," she reveals.

"We went over to [co-writer Maddie Diaz's] house, took a guitar into the garden and wrote Silver Sky outside, while all of these gorgeous red cardinals were singing around us.

"I usually write a lot about my mental health struggles, but I was just in the mood to write something that made me feel good."

Not that her mental health issues are in the rear view mirror. Humberstone admits her stage nerves have only intensified since the release of Cruel World.

"It's the proudest I've been of any of my work and, for that reason, I struggled with shows because I felt a lot of pressure to go out and deliver it to the standard that I think people are expecting.

"But on the other hand, it's totally fine if you mess up or sing a wrong note. People can't connect to a pop star that feels too robotic and polished.

"So maybe my strength is that vulnerability, and I need to recognise that more."

That vulnerability has won Humberstone millions of fans, even if a hit single has (so far) eluded her.

And her audience keeps growing. In May this year, her breakout single Falling Asleep At The Wheel was awarded a silver disc... five years after its release, indicating that her songs have staying power in an era of disposable hits.

Astonishingly, this is news to Humberstone, who learns about the accolade during our interview. But it helps to clarify a thought that's been knocking around her head.

"If I'm going to be doing this for years to come, I've just got to keep making music that feels right, trusting my gut and realising there's no end point," she says.

"Reaching an end point would mean I've 'made it', but I think, maybe, that's a myth that doesn't really exist."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw77.summary: Holly Humberstone's first album, Cruel World, entered the UK charts at number four. She has been writing for years and has been struggling with her mental health.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.title: Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.author: Marissa J. Lang
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.text:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (shown here in October) signed the anti-DEI law that Delray Beach officials say prohibits them from putting on cultural celebrations, like a St. Patrick's Day parade.

One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick's Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.

The city of Delray Beach announced this week that it was canceling its popular St. Patrick's Day festivities in compliance with a new law that takes effect on Jan. 1. The city will also withdraw its sponsorship of LGBTQ Pride celebrations in June, officials said.

The law, backed by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is part of the state's ongoing crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that the governor has called discriminatory and said have "no place" in public institutions.

The city lawyer for Delray Beach, a community in southeast Florida with picturesque beaches and a historic downtown, told the mayor that any government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that are not a national holiday (for example: Independence Day) could run afoul of the new anti-DEI law. So, Mayor Tom Carney said, he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city's biggest events of the year.

In past years, the parade, an annual event since 1970, wound its way through the downtown core of Delray Beach with spectators lined up several-people deep along the route. Local businesses and organizations sponsored floats and giveaways. School bands played as they marched through the streets. Participants included members of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the largest and oldest Irish Catholic organization in the country.

"I've said it's engrained in the DNA of Delray and I do mean that. It's one of our signature events," Carney, a Republican, told NPR.

The mayor said he's hopeful that the city can find a path forward — and a way to preserve the event.

If a private sponsor were to volunteer to take over the St. Patrick's Day parade, or the June Pride celebrations, Carney said, the city would gladly hand over the reins and support the continuation of these festivities.

"These types of events we should be celebrating because in this country, people can have these events. In other countries, you can't do this. We have great freedoms here," he said. "And if the community wants something and it's not against public policy then I would support them to do it if they're using private dollars. If we can do it, we should do it."

Carney, who is of Irish descent, said the parade was privately run until about eight years ago — so returning to a private-sponsorship model would be a callback to the parade's origins. His own family, he said, was involved in keeping the parade going during the 1980s and 1990s.

Delray Beach officials said they have been inundated with emails, calls and social media messages from constituents who are angry that the community's decades-long celebration had been axed.

"It was kind of a call to action to me," Carney said. "The community really wants to have it, so we should go ahead and have it, we just need to get it privately funded."

The governor, meanwhile, has accused Delray Beach of weaponizing the new anti-DEI measure to make a political point. DeSantis said the city was "engaging in "malicious compliance" in a message he posted on X following the city's cancellation announcement.

"What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law," the governor wrote. "It's just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We've seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat."

The mayor said the city is merely trying to stay out of trouble with the law. The measure, SB1134, asserts that any official that violates the provision could face civil or legal consequences.

"The legislation has unintended consequences. The governor may genuinely believe what he believes and I take him at his word; our city attorney came up with a different conclusion," Carney said. "I'm going to leave it at that."

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/where-.title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/where-.author: Connie Loizos
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/where-.text:
Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.

At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.

Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.

Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.

Not all of those relationships are the business of the security team. Relationships with subordinates typically fall to HR, legal, and the board. But an affair with an executive at a company under federal investigation is a different animal. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.) Security specialists say affairs can create vulnerabilities that foreign intelligence services look to exploit.

Catching that kind of exposure isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.

Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week. (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.

Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.

Many companies also define security very narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”

Still, some of it is beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.

What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”

The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.

Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers are one example. These devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more.

Eftimiades says no one knows yet if these were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But either way, what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, should become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.

In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/where-.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships. Security specialists say affairs can create vulnerabilities that foreign intelligence services look to exploit.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/federal-r.title: The Fed’s battle against inflation risks turning into a forever war—and may last as long as Operation Iraqi Freedom while Iran ‘status quo’ drags on
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/federal-r.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/14/federal-r.text:
In a few months, the Federal Reserve will be able to count six years that inflation has been above its 2% target, and central bankers’ own forecasts put “mission accomplished” sometime in 2029.

That means the Fed could fall short on the price-stability portion of its dual mandate for eight straight years—or as long as Operation Iraqi Freedom lasted.

Despite the obvious differences with the bloody Iraq war, the Fed’s inflation fight is also driven by events in the Middle East, this time in Iran.

Inflation was trending lower at the start of the year, as the initial spike from President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year was wearing off. Then crude prices soared after Iran closed off the Strait of Hormuz and attacked regional energy infrastructure in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes.

While oil exports have rebounded with the help of U.S. military protection, supplies of refined products like gasoline and diesel remain tight, inflicting more pain at the pump for consumers.

At the same time, GDP growth is running hot as the AI hyperscalers pour hundreds of billions of dollars a year into the economy, adding more pressure on prices.

This past week’s consumer price index for October came in hotter than expected and showed that inflation is spreading beyond energy categories into more goods and services, alarming Fed officials.

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the data “borderline disturbing,” and fellow policymakers have indicated more rate hikes are needed, possibly even a jumbo-sized increase of 50 basis points.

Meanwhile, the Iran war shows no signs of ending soon. Trump has backed down from repeated threats to restart major combat operations, but has also shot down negotiations, saying the U.S. doesn’t need a peace deal with Iran.

“We’re just keeping it the status quo,” Trump told reporters on Monday.

With the Iran conflict dragging on indefinitely, the Fed may have to readjust its inflation outlook again and get more aggressive on rates.

In September, the Fed’s summary of economic projections put down 2029 as the year when inflation is expected to fall back to 2%, pushing it back from a 2028 forecast made in June, as energy prices stayed high.

To be sure, there have been several shocks outside the Fed’s control since inflation first exceeded 2% back in early 2021. The pandemic saw supply-chain snarls and massive fiscal stimulus. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 sent oil and gas prices soaring. Then came Trump’s trade war last year and his Iran war this year.

But the Fed has also provided monetary stimulus, and Chairman Kevin Warsh has argued that high inflation is a “choice,” suggesting shocks are no excuse. And the longer inflation stays above target, other central bankers have said they are less willing to be patient about rate hikes and “look through” short-term spikes.

Their fear is that an extended period of high prices will eventually cause consumers to lift their long-term inflation expectations and change currency spending patterns that fuel even more inflation.

That’s why the Fed has sounded more hawkish lately as policymakers look to ensure inflation expectations remain anchored and prevent consumers from believing there’s more tolerance for higher prices.

“I believe that the central bank has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility,” Goolsbee told CNBC on Friday. “We’ve been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we’re not making any progress, and if anything, it’s going the wrong way.”

On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller offered a similar message, saying a 50-basis-point rate hike should be considered at the Fed’s December meeting if October core consumer prices rose by 0.3% or more. In fact, they did rise 0.3% from the prior month.

“Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,” he explained.

Also on Tuesday, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said in separate remarks that it “may be possible to move more rapidly” than what September’s quarter-point hike and October’s hold have implied. She warned the ​current 3.75%-4.00% policy rate is too low and adds to inflationary pressures.

Diane Swonk, chief economist and managing director at KPMG, noted Fed hawks are coalescing as inflation has been too hot for too long—and moving higher.

“Fed is losing its inflation fighting credibility,” she posted on LinkedIn this week. “Consumers who rely mostly on wages, not their stock portfolios, are paying the price.”

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Tens of thousands of protesters paraded in the streets of France on Saturday, some clambering up statues with French flags as they vented on issues ranging from the rising cost of living to a proposal to give police greater legal protection.

The European Union's second-largest economy has been gripped by high-school blockades and mass demonstrations for more than a month, with the far right leading in the polls to win presidential elections next year to replace Emmanuel Macron.

Around 106,000 people took to the streets nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said, in the lowest turnout in recent weeks.

Student unions put the number of demonstrators at 200,000, including almost 100,000 in the capital.

Arrest figures were also noticeably lower than at previous mass protests, with the ministry saying 219 people had been detained across the nation. Paris prosecutors said 45 were arrested in the capital.

"No justice, no peace," a protester shouted into a megaphone in Paris as people including students, unions and Yellow Vest activists demonstrated for the fifth Saturday in a row.

Others called for the president to resign, or cried "Everybody hates the police", as a group carried a giant puppet whose hat read "Lord Macron".

Some of the largely peaceful rallies in recent weeks have seen fringe violence, as well as accusations of police brutality, including against young teenagers.

Adrien, a 20-year-old cello player in a volunteer orchestra at the Paris rally, said the focus of the day was a new bill in parliament to give police who use their weapons further protection.

"We're scared when we come to a protest, and this will only make us even more afraid if their impunity is strengthened," he said, after tear gas fell on protesting musicians last month.

Backers of the new police bill – including the far-right party of leading presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen – say a new law presuming police acted in self-defence is necessary to avoid officers being automatically suspected of using disproportionate force.

Activists argue it would amount to a "licence to kill", as it would hamper the opening of investigations and make holding security forces accountable even harder in a country where alleged police brutality cases rarely reach a criminal court.

Others nationwide demanded better learning conditions, more children's rights or simply sang for a better France.

In the southwestern city of Bordeaux, 72-year-old Josette belted out the protest song "I have two passions: brass bands and revolution".

"My children didn't want me to come," she said. "But I'm so grateful to the youth for starting this movement."

"They're giving us hope at a time when it feels like we're heading straight for disaster, with a planet that keeps getting hotter and far-right movements that are increasingly unapologetic."

Macron's popularity is the lowest it has ever been since he first became president in 2017, according to recent polls, and the government has little leeway to respond to protester demands as it struggles to reduce its debt.

Polls project hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon as runner-up in next year's elections, with the centre-right struggling to present a single strong contender.

In the southern city of Toulouse, Kenza, a 28-year-old asylum law specialist, denounced the government's response to the social unrest.

"The repression of protesters is unacceptable – even more so when they are children," she said.

Lawyers last week said police violence at recent protests had led to "mutilations" including hand, foot and eye injuries.

Police had to intervene in the city of Lyon to protect a team of television reporters after protesters attacked them, local authorities said.

Unions have called for a new day of strikes on Tuesday, after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent as "crumbs".

The largest protests in recent weeks occurred during a union-led strike on Thursday last week, when more than half a million people took to the streets nationwide, according to official figures.

Student unions put the number of demonstrators at 200,000, including almost 100,000. Arrest figures were also noticeably lower than at previous mass protests.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Global powers converge on Manila as ASEAN summit kicks off
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
MANILA – A key regional summit opens on Sunday in Manila, with Southeast Asian heads of state facing questions on trade, security and an ongoing energy crisis while playing host to a who’s who of global leaders.

U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive on Tuesday near the summit’s conclusion, a visit expected to include a sideline meeting with fellow “Quad” countries India, Japan and Australia — the first of his second term.

The meeting of the Quad — a grouping broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence — would come days before a historic sit-down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

Brazil’s recently reelected Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, meanwhile, is set to attend a plenary session of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Sunday, while Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will sign a new defense pact with host country the Philippines.

Nearly 20,000 police officers have been deployed around Metro Manila for the summit, with progressive groups predicting a turnout of thousands on Tuesday for an anti-Trump march on the summit site.

Much of the uproar targets the U.S. Pax Silica program — a supply-chain initiative designed to counter China’s dominance in semiconductors and rare earths — whose flagship Philippine project, a 1,620-hectare AI manufacturing hub north of Manila, threatens to displace Indigenous families.

U.S. Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said last week that a widely rumored November target date for a deal signing timed to Trump’s visit was never in the works.

A day of early meetings kicked off on Saturday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announcing a Philippine trade deal, and ASEAN leaders huddling on key issues including haze from Indonesia and potential fuel-sharing schemes as members struggle with Iran war-driven shortages.

But two issues that have vexed ASEAN leaders for years — a languishing South China Sea “Code of Conduct” and their relationship with war-torn Myanmar — look to be Singapore’s problem when the bloc’s rotating chair passes to the city-state in 2027.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level ASEAN meetings since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand, which shares a border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations, last week called for Naypyidaw’s foreign minister to be allowed back into meetings.

But Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro told reporters on Saturday there was “no easing” of the approach being taken with Myanmar, which faces an international ruling later this week on whether it committed genocide against its marginalized Muslim Rohingya minority.

Hopes of achieving a Code of Conduct in the disputed South China Sea between ASEAN states and China during Manila’s year in the chair, meanwhile, have flagged.

A Southeast Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations said he did not expect a code to be signed at the summit.

Lazaro indicated as much on Saturday, saying negotiations were “80%” complete.

“If it happens, then it’s a small miracle,” said Siew Mun Tang, former head of the ASEAN Studies Center at Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute.

Beijing claims most of the South China Sea despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis, and its coast guard has clashed repeatedly with that of the Philippines.

The row has reared its head at inopportune times over the past year, with a July foreign ministers summit opening less than a day after Chinese and Philippine sailors engaged in a clash.

An ASEAN defense chiefs meeting last month saw Beijing send only an embassy defense attache, blaming “reckless” statements by Philippine politicians.

A week later, Manila issued a rare rebuke to its own public officials over comments about China, stressing the need for a unified voice as the two countries negotiate.

As the summit opens on Sunday, an annual seminar less than 5 kilometers away will be making the case against China’s South China Sea claims.

Philippine defense chief Gilberto Teodoro, sanctioned by Beijing this year for what it called “irresponsible remarks,” will give a keynote address.

The meeting of the Quad is aimed at counterbalancing China’Southeast Asian nations’ influence. The summit will be held in Manila on Sunday, with the first of his second term.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6dj.title: Judo champion shakes up French  presidential race with surprise candidacy
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6dj.text:
Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.

That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.

The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.

But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.

Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.

More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.

Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.

So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?

"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.

"But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."

For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.

But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.

The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.

So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.

It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.

Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"

In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.

All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices.

"People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said.

"Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."

It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers.

But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.

What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?

In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?

Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.

In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.

The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.

Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.

The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.

The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.

So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.

The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".

That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.

Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".

Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat.

In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".

If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form.

In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6dj.summary: Teddy Riner is running for the Élysée Palace in France. The 37-year-old is one of the most popular figures in modern-day France. He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.text:
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.

"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.

But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.

Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.

"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.

The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.

The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.

After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.

Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.

This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.

After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.

This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.

"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.

Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.

He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.

"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.

In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.

Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.

"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.

Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.

The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.

However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.

"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.

For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.

He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.

Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.

"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.

They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.

Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.

After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.

"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."

During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.

But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.

Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.

"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".

He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.

But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.

Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.

He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."

He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.

"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.

The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.

Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.

"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent.

Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica, on Facebook at BBC Africa or on Instagram at bbcafrica

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62.title: Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62.text:
Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer.

The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently took part in the second season of the Celebrity Traitors, said cancerous cells were discovered after she attended a cervical screening in 2020.

She underwent a hysterectomy, describing the experience to BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs as "horrific".

"As awful as that was, it had a full stop at the end of the sentence," the 42-year-old added. "I had my five-year clear the other day. I feel so unbelievably lucky."

In Sunday's episode, Fry told show host Lauren Laverne that she had delayed a cervical screening examination for months in 2020. After she attended one, the results "didn't come back for a few weeks," she said.

"Then I got a call from my GP telling me they needed me to come back and do another test, and they did a biopsy.

"I was trying hard not to panic but when they found it was in the lymphatic system… that was when it really started to come down."

The broadcaster said she was told that her chances of survival depended on the cancerous cells not having spread to her lymph nodes, although it was not clear "how bad it was at that point".

"It's all about, basically, how far into your lymphatic system has it got. If it had not got into any lymph nodes, then the odds were in my favour and I had a really good chance of survival," she said.

Fry explained that this meant "if it was in one it would drop to a 60% chance of survival and two – the odds would go against me and it would be a 40% chance".

While in isolation in hospital following her hysterectomy, Fry said a surgeon told her that four of her lymph nodes had appeared enlarged.

She added: "I was in this hospital bed on my own and no-one could come and visit me for over a week, with nothing but the sheer terrifying drop of the end of my existence in front of me – it was horrific."

Fry described not being able to "think back to happy things that... have already happened because it is sad", while also not being able to "look forward to things you are hopeful about because it doesn't feel like it is there".

She also said she asked her then husband to set up FaceTime in the corner of a room so she could watch their two young daughters play while she was in hospital.

"I didn't want them to see me, it was too much," she said.

But she added: "Going through something like that I don't think I would swap it.

"I think it was honestly such a gift to have that experience when you're 36 and then come out the other side of it."

The presenter grew up in a working-class family and studied mathematics at University of College London.

She later completed a PhD in fluid dynamics, and last year became Cambridge University's first professor of the public understanding of mathematics.

Fry has fronted BBC science series including The Future with Hannah Fry and The Secret Genius of Modern Life.

She was banished in the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors after being exposed as a traitor.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62.summary: BBC presenter says she was told cancerous cells were discovered after a cervical screening in 2020. She underwent a hysterectomy and was told she had a 40% chance of survival. She said she was not able to "think back to happy things that have already happened"

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/so.title: After Her Baby Was Buried Alive, a South Carolina Mother Wonders Why
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/so.author: Eduardo Medina
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/so.text:
Koah Sharp, nearly 1, was rescued alive this week in a rural patch of central South Carolina. In her first interview, Koah’s mother explains what happened.

Reporting from Lexington County, S.C.

The detectives dug quickly but carefully, as the baby’s cries underneath the freshly packed dirt grew louder.

Koah Sharp, just shy of his first birthday, had been buried alive for about 24 hours in Lexington County, S.C., the authorities said, entombed in a dog crate wrapped with a dirt-smeared towel. Deputies unearthed the 11-month-old on Tuesday, amazed to find him breathing.

On Friday evening Koah was in the arms of his 25-year-old pregnant mother, Dezarae Sharp, who was still trying to make sense of what had happened to her boy as she caressed his plump baby cheeks again.

“I can’t believe it still,” Ms. Sharp said in the first interview she has granted since her child, who is expected to fully recover, went missing. “It’s something you would see in a movie. It’s something you would see on TV. And the fact that it happened to him — I don’t know.”

Michael Comer, Koah’s father and Ms. Sharp’s ex-boyfriend, was arrested and charged with attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary.

“I didn’t think he could go that far,” Ms. Sharp said.

Koah’s disappearance and his remarkable survival have shocked people well beyond Lexington County, a booming manufacturing hub that is part suburbia, part rural and near the capital city of Columbia.

Eduardo Medina is a Times reporter covering the South. An Alabama native, he is now based in Durham, N.C.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/scien.title: SpaceX Makes History With Successful Rocket Catch in Texas
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/scien.author: Kenneth Chang
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/scien.text:
NASA’s Artemis III Mission

The Starship spacecraft returned from orbit to the same spot where it lifted off, marking a key milestone in SpaceX’s vision of building fully reusable rockets.

Reporting from Starbase, Texas, Kenneth Chang watched the launch on Friday and the catch on Saturday.

SpaceX’s giant Starship spacecraft pulled off a remarkable feat on Saturday afternoon in the quest to build fully reusable rockets. For the first time, the spacecraft successfully returned from orbit to its launch site in South Texas, where it was caught between two mechanical arms on the launch tower.

For the past decade, SpaceX has successfully landed the boosters of its smaller Falcon 9 rockets and then reused them on subsequent launches. But the upper stages of the Falcon 9s are still thrown away each time.

The Starship rocket system is not only much larger than Falcon 9, but it was designed from the start to be fully reusable. Bringing back an upper stage from orbit is a major technical hurdle, and SpaceX was able to pull it off on its first try.

Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator, offered his congratulations on X. “Making more believers by the day….one step closer to,” he wrote, adding an emoji of the moon and the American flag. Starship is slated to serve as one of two lander designs that will take astronauts to the surface of the moon as part of NASA’s Artemis program.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX, posted a video on X showing a view of Starship from below, part of the post-landing inspection.

A few hours earlier, the spacecraft, which is about 170 feet long, had been traveling at more than 17,000 miles per hour at an altitude of 170 miles. Then, one of its engines fired briefly, nudging it out of orbit to begin its fall back to Earth.
