Deputy prime minister says change would be a massive step but ‘deserves proper consideration and scrutiny’

The government has said it will consider calls to change the age of consent after a woman waived her right to anonymity to publicly claim she was raped by Russell Brand as a 16-year-old schoolgirl.

Mia Latter, now 37, alleged she had been orally raped by the jailed comedian when she was a teenager and he was 30 years old.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, she called for the introduction of a staggered age of consent – which would make relationships between adults and teenagers aged 16 and 17 illegal.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, told the newspaper that Latter’s “heart-breaking story” meant a law change deserved consideration.

She said: “We need to listen to Mia and other victims like her who have been through these experiences because it’s really important that as lawmakers their experience is at the heart of what we consider.

“It clearly would be a massive step to change the age of consent, but it deserves proper consideration and scrutiny. I can absolutely understand why she is calling for it.”

Under UK law, adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds.

Latter said: “It’s shocking to me time and time again that whenever the news comes up again about him, it’s always in the comments about the relationship with a 16-year-old.

“That’s not the most heinous bit. But why is that the thing that everybody collectively gets stuck on? I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.”

Latter was referred to under the pseudonym of Alice in previous reporting by the Sunday Times, the Times, and Channel 4’s Dispatches documentary.

She was 16 when she first met Brand in Leicester Square, central London, while she was on her way home from a shopping trip.

He took her number and later messaged her, asking if she wanted to go for dinner, she said.

She told the newspaper that Brand – who was working at MTV at the time – still asked her to meet after she had confessed her age to him.

Latter alleges Brand orally raped her towards the end of their three-month relationship.

Brand denied all of the allegations made against him by Latter when they were first reported in 2023 by the Times.

She spoke to the police after the documentary, but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decided not to include her case in Brand’s trial at Southwark Crown Court.

He was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is now serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults.

Earlier this week, it was announced that a series of “serious” sex offence allegations against comedian David Walliams are being probed by the Metropolitan police after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.

One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”.

Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

Haigh went on to say that, in light of news that one of Walliams’s accusers was asked to sign a non disclosure agreement (NDA), the government should also look at banning them in cases of alleged sexual assault and harassment. She said: “When we consider the allegations against David Walliams, teenagers who were fans wouldn’t come under the current consultation.

“I do think there is a very strong case to look at banning NDAs in all circumstances where they relate to harassment or discrimination, to make sure that no victim, regardless of where it happened or what their relationship was with the perpetrator, should ever be silenced.”

It is believed MPs outside Labour may support a bill to change the age of consent laws, with Jess Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson, coming out in favour of reviewing them.

Commending Latter for the “extraordinary bravery” it took to waive her anonymity, Brown-Fuller said: “I think we must go further to increase protections for young women and girls, and looking at a staggered age of consent is an important step.

“We already have rules that recognise power imbalances in professions: between teachers and students, or barristers and junior colleagues. It’s time for the government to recognise the implicit power imbalance held by older men over teenage girls.”

Latter’s decision to come forward was also praised by Bridget Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, who said she “and thousands of others across the country will be in awe of her courage and determination”. She added that it is “up to all of us to send a message to women and girls who experience sexual violence: the shame is not yours. Women like Mia are leading the charge, but we can and must do more to make this a moment of change.”

Latter’s allegation was reported to the Met police, who said the investigation into the alleged rape remains ongoing.

A Met Police spokesperson said: “Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.

“Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.

“This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence.”

The CPS said: “The Crown Prosecution Service will continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible.”
https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov.summary: Mia Latter, 37, alleges she was raped by Russell Brand as a 16-year-old schoolgirl. She was 16 when she first met the comedian in Leicester Square, central London. CPS says delay has been distressing for victim-survivor.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: SpaceX’s Starship captured by launchpad arms in dramatic first
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
SpaceX’s Starship ‌spacecraft has returned to Earth, caught midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

The spaceship emerged from a cloudy sky on Saturday, descending slowly over Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2 in Texas – the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space.

Soon afterwards, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk congratulated his “incredible team”.

SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates Starship’s full reusability, crucial for rapid, low-cost recycling.

However, with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.

Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it was not in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA, which is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the Moon later this decade, welcomed the achievement.

“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on X.

Starship completed 14 laps around the Earth, 265km (165 miles), outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

Starship, a 124-metre (407ft) behemoth, is the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, intended for Moon and Mars travel.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months.

https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/wi.title: With Starship catch, SpaceX still shows it can dazzle the world
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/wi.author: Eric Berger
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/wi.text:
It felt like stepping into the future.

STARBASE, Texas—The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.

This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different, difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power, and be captured by the tower.

It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before, by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.

Nevertheless, it happened.

Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

The shuttles were engineering marvels. But during the return to Earth they acted as gliders, not igniting their engines. And their heat shields were delicate flowers, requiring painstaking refurbishment after each flight. At the outset of the shuttle program, the space agency contemplated sending dozens of humans into space at a time, and carrying cargo at a cost as low of $25 per pound.

Reality never matched these rosy projections. The crew space capped out at seven astronauts, and the cost-per-pound was closer to $25,000. Each orbiter cost an extraordinary amount of money to build; NASA only ever built five that went to space.

SpaceX has five Starships in an advanced state of development at Starbase today; and its factory houses the components for a dozen more. The company can currently manufacture a Starship upper stage in its South Texas Starfactory every three weeks. The factory was sized to produce a ship every three days. When SpaceX founder Elon Musk discussed these build targets in an interview five years ago, he sounded mad. But he no longer does.

The Space Shuttle was nearly a fully reusable space launch system, but it fell far short of low-cost, rapid launch. Over 30 years the vehicle made 135 flights. Within a few years SpaceX aims to fly 135 times a year, then thousands of times.

Such was the significance of Saturday. SpaceX aspires to fundamentally change the relationship between humanity and the heavens. The first step is to get the entire rocket back. SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. It will take time to reach a high rate of success with such landings, but Saturday’s safe return offered a proof of concept.

The landings will come with increasing frequency; and so will the launches. Over time SpaceX will perfect the heat shield that is likely to be the most difficult aspect of rapid reuse. And eventually, as difficult as it may be to believe, what we experienced with amazement this weekend will become routine. One day, we will take this all for granted.
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/wi.summary: SpaceX has returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. The rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Marine Incidents

All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship and tanker survived the collision. (AP)

The US National Transport Board has begun investigation a collision between a tanker and cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday, local time.

All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship and tanker survived the collision.

The investigation will include a team of 16 people, who will hand out a preliminary report in 30 days, and final report in 18 to 24 months.

The US National Transport Safety Board (NTSB) says it is on a "fact finding" mission to figure out how a tanker collided with a cruise ship that had more than 100 passengers.

A tanker has collided with a river cruise boat docked near the port of New Orleans with more than 100 passengers onboard.

All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship and tanker survived the collision in New Orleans on Friday, local time.

Officials said 32 people were taken to hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled, but none of the injuries were critical.

Eight remained hospitalised on Saturday.

The National Transportation Safety Board said the tanker's voyage data recorder had been recovered, and a 16-member team would spend a week in New Orleans investigating the incident.

Tanker collides with river cruise boat in New Orleans

NTSB member John DeLeeuw said the agency expected to release a preliminary report within 24 to 30 days, with the final investigation report expected in 18 to 24 months.

“We are still in the fact-finding stage. We look at the maintenance record, the history of the ship. We actually look at a number of things, but it is way too soon [to know what happened]," Mr DeLeeuw said.

The first warning Joe Knab, a passenger on the American Heritage cruise ship, had of the imminent collision was the tanker blasting its horn several times.

The hit was hard, and the cruise ship immediately started leaning. The crew quickly gathered everyone on the third deck, got them in life vests and started getting them off the boat.

But the vessel suddenly rolled and sent Mr Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River.

Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.

"It's fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time," Mr Knab told WDSU-TV, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud.

Emergency services help people out of the water after a tanker crashed into a cruise ship in New Orleans. (AP: Devon Flanagan )

Mr Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered after the incident. The rest of his belongings were in the river but somehow his phone still worked.

He said he was in the water for about 15 minutes, and joked that his 20 years in the navy likely helped him.

"They taught us not to drown," he said.

A lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $US1 million ($1.47 million) in damage to its terminal.

A judge issued a warrant on Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.

The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham told reporters on Saturday.

Emergency crews work at the scene of the collision. (The Advocate via AP: Enan Chediak)

She said the first step was to make sure the 60,500 litres of fuel on the boat were removed safely.

Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Captain Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: ‘A moral red line’? World on cusp of autonomous weapons revolution
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
PARIS – Lethal autonomous weapons powered by artificial intelligence are set to revolutionize warfare but there is no proper regulatory or legal framework governing the new technology.

A conference starting Monday at the United Nations in Geneva will discuss how to establish curbs and prohibitions on such weapons, called killer robots by some.

But some analysts doubt the discussions at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) will keep pace with the fast-changing weapons.

Here is a look at three key questions ahead of the conference.

Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) “can identify, select, and engage a target without the intervention of a human operator in the execution of these tasks,” said Jean-Marc Rickli, head of global and emerging risks at the Geneva Centre for Security Policy.

Autonomous weapons have long existed. An anti-personnel mine “is an autonomous weapon in the sense that it explodes when someone steps on it,” said Laure de Roucy-Rochegonde of the Centre for Geopolitics of Technology at the French Institute of International Relations.

But with the proliferation of AI-enhanced drones, such weapons are now “capable of selecting and engaging a target that was not predetermined, adapting to their environment without human intervention,” said Rickli.

So the critical issue for potential regulators lies in determining the level of human control over the decision to employ such a weapon.

The United States refers to “appropriate levels of human judgment” in the use of autonomous weapons.

France maintains that a human must remain in the decision-making loop and bans “lethal autonomous weapons systems” (LAWS) but permits “partially autonomous” systems, known as PLAWS.

“The human role is always ensured through what is termed ’appropriate control’ by a military commander — a concept that varies in scope depending on the system’s criticality and the operational context,” said Rear Adm. Vincent Sebastien, deputy director of the French defense ministry’s Agency for Defence Artificial Intelligence (AMIAD).

What are the ethical issues?

“We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: the autonomous targeting of humans by machines,” U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, and International Committee of the Red Cross President Mirjana Spoljaric warned in a joint statement in August.

But analysts said the Geneva discussions, while important, will touch only part of the issue.

Today, the diminishing role of humans is being driven by the growing use of AI in analysis and targeting.

Rickli said the scope of the agenda in Geneva is “very narrow.”

“It fails to encompass the full range of issues surrounding AI on the battlefield” — an area where its use is expanding, particularly in target generation.

He said this was seen in the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran this year “where the Americans engaged as many as 1,000 targets per day” inside Iran.

“There are a host of problems and unacceptable risks associated with targeting and decision-support systems,” added de Roucy-Rochegonde. “Part of this debate concerns systems that are already widely deployed on the battlefield.”

“What kind of human supervision is required to ensure that the operator is genuinely exercising their own judgment rather than simply providing a rubber stamp for the machine’s recommendations?” she asked.

How quickly is the situation changing?

The autonomous weapons to be discussed in Geneva are not yet in widespread use, although analysts have noted that they have been deployed by Russia in its invasion of Ukraine as well as U.S. attacks in Iran.

But the spread is inevitable.

“Autonomy will very quickly become a reality on the battlefield,” warned Sebastien.

“Autonomous weapon systems are not part of a distant future — a race towards greater autonomy in weapons systems is already well underway,” Guterres and Spoljaric said in their statement.

Yet significant doubts and dangers remain, Dario Amodei, head of the AI giant Anthropic, warned this year: “Today, frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.”

But ultimately, the incentive for major powers is too strong.

Swarms of autonomous drones — which “aim to neutralize an adversary through saturation” — would be highly effective, and some states view them as a crucial strategic advantage, said Rickli.

In January, the Chinese defense ministry described swarms of autonomous drones as the “new face of warfare.”

“In an era of sharp military competition, the first state to normalize fully autonomous lethal strikes will reset expectations for everyone else,” said Gerald Mako, a research affiliate of Cambridge University in the Small Wars Journal.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/un.title: Unlike Other Countries, America’s Government Funds Its Air Infrastructure
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/un.author: Pranav Baskar
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/un.text:
Despite handling the most flights in the world, the United States’ air traffic systems rely on 1980s-era computer equipment.

It took Canada two years to replace paper flight strips with electronic ones in air traffic control towers, a simple transition to avoid cascading delays. In the United States, the same project has taken more than four decades, and it is still not complete.

The example highlights an irony. Despite handling the most flights in the world, America’s air traffic control systems — still using 1980s-era equipment and prone to widespread failures — have lagged behind some global peers when it comes to improving technology.

A key difference, aviation experts say, is that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration relies on Congress to fund crucial upgrades, while other countries have privatized their air traffic control. That has meant more money, more consistently, to invest in improving systems in places like Canada and the European Union, both considered success stories in aviation management.

The F.A.A.’s issuing of a nationwide ground stop on Friday underscored America’s aging infrastructure, which experts have warned for years is in urgent need of modernizing, and which critics say has been chronically underfunded. For decades, U.S. air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks and alphabetical keyboards so old that the F.A.A. has difficulty sourcing spare parts.

Speaking to reporters after the outage, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, echoed those concerns, describing an air traffic control system stuck in the past, and demanding $50 billion from Congress to improve it.

“Canada and the European Union don’t have to worry about the public purse,” said John Gradek, an aviation management expert at McGill University. “They are masters of their own destiny.”

Pranav Baskar is an international reporter at The Times, based in New York.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Hundreds of men march in Switzerland to protest violence against women
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Hundreds of men have led a demonstration in Switzerland’s capital, Bern, to denounce misogyny and violence against women, saying men need to take a more effective role in fighting both.

The “Men Against Violence Against Women” rally outside parliament on Saturday follows persistent concerns that misogyny is too prevalent online among teenage boys and young men and that other men need to build a stronger counter-narrative.

The misogynistic views are pushed by the right-wing “manosphere” – a loose network of online forums and influencers that promote male supremacy and hostility to feminism. Such influencers were emboldened after Donald Trump won the US presidential election in 202 to justify and amplify misogynistic derision and threats online.

“We men are part of the problem – the problem being violence against women and queer people,” said Christoph Gosteli, a 42-year-old social worker who co-organised the rally with a group called maenner.

“That is why it is important for us to take a stand and say, ‘We no longer want to be part of the problem; we want to be part of the solution.’”

An academic and advocacy group survey released in June by the University of Zurich and MenCare, an umbrella group of Swiss men’s and fathers’ organisations, found that half of male respondents aged 18 to 24 held a “restrictive and dominance-based view of masculinity”, expressing concerns that “real men are increasingly marginalised in society”.

The study called for “a systematic and society-wide debate about ideals of masculinity that promote violence”, beginning in schools.

Swiss Justice Minister Beat Jans attended a conference earlier this month on the dangers of violent online abuse of women.

In a speech on November 2, he said that men commit four-fifths of violent crimes and that in rape cases, the share is “as high as 99 percent”.

“It is not all men. But we must also admit: It is almost always men,” Jans said. “Violence by men does not begin with the first blow; it begins with a disparaging remark. We men all have a duty.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/n.title: Carers of people with disability left exhausted navigating NDIS
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/n.author: Nick McAllister
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Amanda Solarino has been left stressed trying to secure more NDIS support for her son Alex. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

Caregivers of people with disabilities say navigating the NDIS to try to get more support for their loved ones is leaving them feeling exhausted and taking a toll on their mental health.

It comes as accessing the NDIS becomes increasingly difficult, after cuts in funding for some sectors began to be rolled out on October 1.

Amanda Solarino, who lives in Romsey just outside Melbourne, is the full-time carer for her 21-year-old son Alex, who is autistic, non‑verbal and has an intellectual disability.

Ms Solarino said she was continuously replacing furniture and fixing walls as a result of her son's escalating aggression, and she struggled to get the help she needed from the NDIS.

Some of the damage caused by Alex at home. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

"Alex's aggression isn't just directed at us or the furniture anymore — he's now turning it on Erica, his 19‑year‑old sister," she said.

"She's so anxious she won't walk down the hallway unless she knows exactly where he is."

Her son's disability also comes at a steep financial cost.

Amanda Solarino lives with several health conditions herself. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

"No one's paying to fix the furniture he breaks ... the $2,000 couch he breaks with his head or the two beds he's broken in the last 18 months," she said.

Ms Solarino said Alex had been kicked out of programmes providing day care in their area, and in a neighbouring town, leaving the family with one support worker who can only come for six hours every Monday.

Ms Solarino has had to plaster the walls after Alex damaged them. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

The stress is affecting Ms Solarino. She has chronic migraine disorder and requires injections every 12 weeks, and her arthritis has worsened.

"They're suspecting autoimmune problems, probably brought on by all the stress," she said.

After Alex's aggression worsened, the NDIS escalated his housing request to crisis level and eventually approved his specialist disability accommodation.

Ms Solarino said the new plan did not fulfil the provisions she had asked for, but she was too exhausted by the process to fight it.

She said all she wanted for Alex was for him to live with some dignity.

On the Sunshine Coast, the family of Breanna Medcalfe, a 24-year-old law student with a spinal injury and quadriplegia, has also faced challenges getting the NDIS help she needs.

Ms Medcalfe is completely paralysed from the neck down and relies on assistance for all activities, including driving and showering.

Breanna Medcalfe now relies on her parents for care. (ABC News: Josh Dye)

Ms Medcalfe has one support worker, but mainly relies on her 60-year-old parents to take care of her daily care responsibilities.

She would like more NDIS-funded support hours, but her requests have been declined.

"Because I have mum and dad and I live at home with them, they are like my informal supports, and they therefore can provide the main support, which is incorrect," she said.

Ms Medcalfe is lodging an appeal against a review of her NDIS plan.

"We haven't yet come to the point where we've run out of support hours, but we've been very restricted as to what we can do," she said.

"Why do we have to justify that we're disabled enough to need this funding?"

Ms Medcalfe says its not right that her parents have to care for her all the time. (ABC News: Josh Dye)

The NDIS refused to answer specific questions about supports provided by family members and the lack of resources in regional areas, referring the ABC to its website.

A spokesperson defended the agency's role in providing "critical, essential services" and confirmed that funding resets for social, economic and community participation and improved daily living supports had gradually rolled out from October 1.

The spokesperson said supports vital to the health, safety, and wellbeing of participants would be excluded from the changes, and added that new safeguards will protect participants with 24-hour care needs.

Ms Medcalfe and her support worker Katy-Lea Holmes.  (ABC News: Josh Dye )

Ms Medcalfe says she wants the NDIS to understand the real‑world consequences of its decisions.

"We're not asking for, you know, over the top things," she said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: SpaceX pulls off first-ever spaceship ‘catch’
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
STARBASE, TEXAS – Elon Musk’s SpaceX on Saturday carried out the first-ever recovery of a spaceship, pulling off a successful “catch” of its Starship vessel as it returned to its launch site after a day in orbit.

The spaceship emerged from a cloudy sky after withstanding the extreme heat of re-entering the Earth’s atmosphere, and descended slowly over Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2.

The feat marked a milestone in the space industry’s decadeslong pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems — a goal that can drastically reduce mission costs and make more frequent launches possible.

“That was the Holy Grail of space flight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship and now, everything changes,” SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot said.

Crowds gathered on the Gulf of Mexico beach near Starbase broke into cheers as the spaceship eased into its high-tech nest on the 15th test flight of the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket system.

This time the Starship spacecraft that gives the rocket system its name orbited Earth 14 times and deployed 26 satellites for Musk’s Starlink satellite internet constellation during its 22-hour journey.

Until now SpaceX had captured returning booster rockets three times. However, the “catch” of Starship was extraordinarily complex because the spaceship fell much faster and from a much higher altitude than boosters do.

Clayton Swope, an aerospace expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, called the mission a “huge technical achievement and proves the whole idea of Starship as a fully reusable spaceship can work.”

“Let’s see how quickly they can do it again,” he added.

The vessel’s path home was carefully mapped out by engineers.

“If you want to get back to the east coast of Texas, you have to fly over the entire continent to get back there. So inevitably, you’re flying over land and we spend a lot of time figuring out the safest way to do that,” senior SpaceX engineer Lars Blackmore said.

Starship flew over sparsely inhabited desert areas, wove over towns and then carried out a “giant swoosh maneuver” in its final approach, looping around the cities of Texas’ Rio Grande Valley and approaching its landing site from the east.

Some versions of Starship are designed to launch internet satellites and data centers into orbit, while other iterations will be made to ferry people to the moon and Mars.

U.S. space agency NASA is expecting Starship to serve as a lunar lander on its Artemis mission. On Saturday, Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated Musk and SpaceX.

“It was almost magic. ... Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (the moon),” he said on X.

Musk, the world’s richest person, has already revolutionized the space sector with the partially reusable Falcon rockets, which regularly launch satellites and carry astronauts to the International Space Station.

But the Starship project has been plagued by delays as SpaceX grapples with novel engineering challenges, including the unsolved problem of transferring fuel to the spaceship while in orbit — a requirement for any journey to the moon or Mars.

It will also need to further fine-tune the Super Heavy booster, which ran into a technical issue Friday on its descent, forcing a diversion to the Gulf of Mexico just off the launch site. It, too, was supposed to have been caught by the “chopstick arms.”

The booster automatically self-destructed — a fireball erupting from the booster — before hitting the water.

Following SpaceX’s high-profile stock market debut in June that raised about $85.7 billion, the company is investing heavily in production and launch capabilities.

During a tour of its 93,000-square-meter factory at Starbase on Friday, SpaceX officials told journalists it now has the capability to produce a spaceship every two weeks and a booster every four weeks.

https://www.dw.com/en/tens-of-thousands-.title: Tens of thousands continue to protest across France
https://www.dw.com/en/tens-of-thousands-.text:
Some 106,000 people marched through French cities for a fifth consecutive weekend of protests, marking the lowest turnout in recent weeks.

Tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday to demonstrate against the rising cost of living and strained public services, the Interior Ministry said.

Saturday's demonstrations drew their lowest turnout in recent weeks. Some 106,000 people marched through French cities, with 24,000 in Paris alone. The previous weekend, some 146,000 people had participated nationwide.

The number of arrests was also significantly lower. Police detained 219 people across the country, according to the Interior Ministry.

Although the demonstrations were largely peaceful, police fired tear gas in Paris, Bordeaux and the western city of Nantes, including after some protesters shot fireworks.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mass protests have swept across the European Union's second-largest economy for more than a month.

What began in September as student protests against teacher shortages and poor facilities has since evolved into a broader movement fuelled by anger over the rising cost of living, strained public services and police brutality.

In mid-October, around 565,000 people took to the streets across France, as riots, looting and clashes disrupted demonstrations in several cities.

As France entered its fifth consecutive weekend of nationwide unrest, President Emmanuel Macron's approval ratings fell to the lowest level since he took office in 2017, according to recent polls.

The French government doesn't have much room to respond to the protesters' demands due to its high debt.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.title: FAA ground stop disrupts college football
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.author: Chandelis Duster
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.text:
Byrum Brown #17 of the Auburn Tigers looks to pass during the first half against the Mississippi State Bulldogs at Davis Wade Stadium on Saturday in Starkville, Miss. The game was delayed because of the FAA ground stop on Friday.

The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop on Friday has led not only to travel headaches, but also schedule changes and delays in college sports.

Many college football teams were in airports Friday on their way to upcoming games when the nationwide ground stop was issued and thousands of flights were canceled. The FAA on Saturday said airports were returning to normal operations, but that delays and cancellations would continue through the day.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the ground stop's impact on college football. Several games on Saturday were delayed for hours.

"If you look at the cost of what happened yesterday, we're talking if you like football — I know we've had some disruptions to the college football schedule. Some games are being moved," Duffy said during a news conference Saturday. "That's not the most important thing, but we do want to move teams around the country so we can have playoffs happen."

Utah, ranked No. 2 in the College Football Playoff Rankings, will kick off against Arizona in Tucson at 8:30 p.m. local time — a three-hour delay. The Auburn vs. Mississippi State game was pushed back more than four hours to start at 3:15 p.m. local time in Mississippi because of the ground stop. The Florida Atlantic Owls were also unable to fly to Oklahoma on Friday ahead of their game against the Tulsa Golden Hurricane. Saturday's game, which was supposed to begin at 2:30 p.m. local time, was moved to 6:15 p.m. local time.

While other college teams were able to arrive at their destinations and proceed with games on Saturday, the University of Mississippi did not.

Ole Miss, ranked No. 19, was not able to fly to Oklahoma as planned on Friday for its matchup with the University of Oklahoma Sooners. The game between the two teams, which was scheduled to occur Saturday, will now take place on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET, according to the Southeastern Conference. The game will compete with several NFL games that will be televised at the same time. NFL teams were largely unaffected by the ground stop.

In order to help alleviate fans' frustration, the Sooners on Saturday announced "fan appreciation" promotions for the rescheduled game. Oklahoma students can go to the game for free with their student ID and there will be reduced prices on concession items such as $2 for popcorn or a 16-ounce beer.

Hamas has confirmed that Rafah brigade commander Samir Abu Younis was killed in an Israeli air strike on the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis, southern Gaza.

Israel’s military and Shin Bet security agency earlier said in a joint statement that they had targeted a senior Hamas military commander in a drone strike in Khan Younis on Saturday.

The attack that hit a tent sheltering displaced people wounded two others.

The casualties were taken to Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, medical personnel told Al Jazeera on Saturday.

Video footage verified by Al Jazeera and posted by Palestinian journalists from the vicinity of the hospital showed ambulances inside the grounds and stretchers that appear to be stained with blood.

Al-Mawasi, a coastal strip on the Mediterranean, is crowded with displaced Palestinians living in tents. Israel has repeatedly attacked the area despite previously designating it a humanitarian zone.

Gaza’s Ministry of Health said in its latest update on Saturday that Israeli attacks have killed 16 people and injured 68 others over the past 48 hours.

Since the “ceasefire” in Gaza took effect on October 11, 2025, Israel has killed at least 1,643 Palestinians and injured 5,964. At least 850 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

Since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, at least 74,695 people have been killed and 176,093 injured, according to the Health Ministry.

The ministry also reported that the number of deaths related to cold has risen to 11 after a nine-month-old baby died from hypothermia, the first this winter.

Gaza’s residents, most of whom have been displaced, are living in tents and damaged buildings as water damage from recent heavy rains has set in.

Israeli attacks have escalated across Gaza, despite the October ceasefire.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.text:
Cacao is a 6-year-old Pomeranian surrendered to ARK this spring when his family, for no fault of his, could no longer keep him. Cacao was, to put it mildly, not happy with the decision, in which he had had no say. When he first arrived at ARK, he was an angry little fellow and even refused to have a lead put on him.

That was seven months ago and the transformation has been magical.

Cacao is affectionate and loves having his fur brushed. He also loves to run. He’ll race around full of energy and joy.

That said, Pomeranians are said to be spirited and confident, and those two traits can spell trouble if their wishes are not taken into full consideration. Simply said, Cacao wants to be heard. He wants to “participate” in decisions that affect him.

He’s independent and he’ll play all by himself, but he also likes your presence and expects you will be just as smitten by him as he is of you.

Cacao wants a family or a friend that, largely, wants to do what he does. He’s not at all difficult for the right person: Someone loyal, someone who will dote on him, someone whose life will revolve around him (only when he’s looking is fine). Does that sounds like someone you know? Then Cacao is your boy!

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Italy pitches Germany observer status in fighter jet program
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Italy has formally proposed giving Germany observer status in a fighter jet program it is developing with the United Kingdom and Japan, rejecting a report that it opposed Berlin joining the group.

Rome, London and Tokyo are driving the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP), which aims to put a sixth-generation stealth fighter jet into service by the mid-2030s.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said earlier this month that he expects a decision by the end of March on whether to join GCAP, after scrapping the Future Combat Air System project with France earlier this year.

Earlier Saturday, the Financial Times reported that Italy had rebuffed a U.K. move to explore bringing Germany into the program, saying it was instead pushing for a “low-level” observer status that would give it no role in the aircraft’s design or development. The newspaper said Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto strongly opposed allowing Germany an equal role in the multibillion-dollar program.

The Italian ministry of defense said the Financial Times report doesn’t reflect the nation’s position.

“Italy has always expressed its full willingness to welcome Germany” into GCAP, the ministry said in a statement Saturday. “Precisely to facilitate and accelerate this process, Italy proposed that Germany join as an observer, as an immediate, program information-sharing enabler towards subsequent full membership.”

The ministry said its proposal was not intended to limit Germany’s future role in the program.

The U.K. said any discussions on adding new nations to the program would be undertaken with its GCAP partners.

“We are open to exploring credible options for future participation by other nations, while keeping the program on track and delivering our future military capabilities,” a spokesperson for the U.K. ministry of defense said in a statement.

GCAP has itself experienced budget strains, though respective national leaders have maintained it remains on track.

Still, Japanese officials have already questioned whether adding another partner would further push back a program that is already facing delays, as a renegotiation of the already-agreed-to division of labor becomes inevitable.

Tokyo seeks to field the sixth-generation fighter by 2035.

During a recent visit to Japan, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz expressed an interest in participating in GCAP, telling a joint news conference with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi after their meeting that Berlin would like to explore “cooperation” in fighter jet production.

Takaichi, however, made no mention of GCAP at the news conference.

Asked earlier this month about Merz’s comments, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi also offered a lukewarm response, noting the importance of the trilateral framework and saying that Japan intends to “work closely” with the U.K. and Italy, “while taking into account factors such as the development schedule and the impact on the defense industry.”

Germany’s Pistorius has said an alternative to GCAP would be for aerospace company Airbus to undertake a project in collaboration with other European partners aimed at the early 2040s.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Rally held for abductee Megumi Yokota 49 years on
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
NIIGATA – A rally was held in the city of Niigata on Saturday, a day ahead of the 49th anniversary of Megumi Yokota being abducted to North Korea at the age of 13.

Participants called for stepped-up efforts to realize an immediate return home of Yokota, who was kidnapped from the capital of Niigata Prefecture on Nov. 15, 1977, when she was a junior high school student.

Her mother, Sakie Yokota, who attended the gathering online, said, “Although I can’t push myself because I’m 90 years old now, I’m doing my best, praying for a reunion (with my daughter) while I’m still healthy.”

About 700 people attended the rally. Takuya Yokota, the 58-year-old younger brother of Megumi Yokota and head of the Association of Families of Victims Kidnapped by North Korea, said, “In my memory, Megumi still remains 13 years old, so I can’t imagine what she looks like now at the age of 62.”

He called on the Japanese government to realize a summit with North Korea to resolve the issue of Japanese nationals who were abducted to the reclusive nation decades ago, including Megumi Yokota.

Also among the participants was 67-year-old former abductee Hitomi Soga, who returned to Japan from North Korea with four other abduction victims in October 2022 following a historic summit between then-Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi and then-North Korean leader Kim Jong Il in Pyongyang in September the same year.

Soga was kidnapped to North Korea in 1978 with her mother, Miyoshi Soga, then 46. Miyoshi Soga’s whereabouts remain unknown.

“It’s painful that I can’t do anything as a daughter,” Hitomi Soga said of her mother. “Let me take care of my mother again.”

NEW YORK – Weary travelers braced for more flight disruptions through Sunday, as service resumed at U.S. airports after an hourslong stoppage that the Trump administration blamed on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.

Friday’s nationwide ground stop — meaning no planes can take off — sparked widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before they were due to depart by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events.

“Tired. Exhausted. Frustrated. Yeah, you know, it’s just a mess, right?” Lisa Beraid, 48, who works for an insurance company, said as she waited for a flight Saturday morning at New York’s La Guardia airport.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: NFL referee faces 112-mile dash on double-duty Sunday after FAA ground stop
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Don Willard faces 112-mile trip between NFL games

NBA scrambles to replace referees stranded by delays

College football games postponed as teams struggle

An NFL official will work two games on the same day Sunday after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide for several hours Friday, disrupting travel plans for professional and college teams across the country.

Don Willard will officiate the Miami Dolphins’ game against the Indianapolis Colts at 1pm ET before traveling 112 miles east to work the Pittsburgh Steelers’ Sunday Night Football matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals.

The NFL benefited from its Sunday schedule, with teams typically traveling the day before their games. But Friday’s flight stoppage forced adjustments across the league’s officiating crews and elsewhere in American sports.

The NBA also made changes to its officiating assignments as travel disruptions continued into Saturday.

Brian Forte was added to the officiating crew for the Chicago-Minnesota game, replacing Jason Goldenberg. Jenna Schroeder, meanwhile, replaced Forte for the Dallas-Cleveland game. The Brooklyn-Memphis game brought Michael Smith into the three-person crew late in the afternoon after another referee could not get there in time.

Brent Barnaky and CJ Washington were added to the Denver-New Orleans game on Saturday night after officiating a game in New Orleans on Friday night. Two other referees had been assigned earlier Saturday.

Major sporting events slowly returned to normal Saturday after the nationwide ground stop, although teams across the country continued to grapple with its effects.

Most college football teams playing Saturday travel the day before kickoff, and a number of games were delayed by hours to give visiting programs more time to arrive and prepare. No 2 Utah’s game at No 22 Arizona was pushed back three hours, as was Arizona State’s game at Central Florida. Other teams, like Auburn, opted for charter buses. One way or another, most teams found a solution.

There was, however, one major exception: the No 19 Mississippi game at Oklahoma was moved to Sunday, with kickoff scheduled for 1pm ET.

JuJu Watkins and her third-ranked Southern California teammates had just boarded their flight to face top-ranked South Carolina when the ground stop was issued. The Trojans women’s basketball team stayed in Los Angeles for the night after being deplaned, and their departure for Greenville was pushed to Saturday afternoon.

Fairleigh Dickinson women’s basketball coach Stephanie Gaitley found out late Friday night that her team’s flight to Ohio State had been canceled. There was discussion about leaving immediately by bus and making a stop halfway, but Gaitley preferred to let her team get a better night’s sleep before setting out on a 10-hour bus ride on Saturday morning.

In women’s soccer, the Utah Royals were already in the Washington DC area ahead of their National Women’s Soccer League semi-final against the Washington Spirit on Saturday. The Kansas City Current were supposed to depart Friday for their semi-final against Gotham FC on Sunday in New York.

The Current told ESPN they were “collaborating with key stakeholders, including the NWSL and our charter partner, to identify next steps in order to arrive safely ahead of our match against Gotham FC on Sunday”.

There were 14 scheduled NHL games on Saturday, and the majority of teams made it to their destinations before the flight stoppage began. The San Jose Sharks, who were left waiting to see whether they would be able to travel, arrived late Friday in Utah.

In the NBA, most teams were, at worst, mildly affected by Friday’s events. Cleveland were the outlier.

The Cavaliers started their Saturday much earlier than usual, leaving Miami at 8.54am on a plane taking them to Cleveland, where they were set to play the Dallas Mavericks on Saturday night.

The Cavs couldn’t get out of Miami on Friday night as planned after a game against the Heat that capped a three-game road trip, then scrambled to rebook some hotel rooms. NBA teams typically don’t fly on the morning of a game, but exceptions have been made for unusual situations.

Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell said he would have preferred Saturday’s game to be rescheduled, but noted the team would “make adjustments, figure it out and go from there.”

“Back-to-back, three-hour flight, it was already a tough one,” Mitchell said. “But hey, they say we’ve got to play, we’ve got to play.”

Rescheduling the game against the Mavericks wasn’t an ideal option. Cleveland have a busy arena with a minor league hockey team, college games and other events scheduled; Saturday’s game falls in a stretch where the arena is playing host to events on 11 consecutive days.

“It’s part of it,” Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson said. “You just adapt.”

The Cavaliers listed Mitchell, James Harden, Peyton Watson and Jarrett Allen as questionable on Saturday night’s injury report shortly after their flight landed in Cleveland. All four started Friday’s game in Miami.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/q.title: Qld government reveals successful tenderer for $1.4b Brisbane Arena
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/q.author: Ned Hammond
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Urban Development and Planning

The Queensland government has announced the successful tender to build the new Brisbane Arena in Woolloongabba. (Supplied)

The Gather Brisbane consortium has been named as the successful tenderer to build Brisbane's planned sports and entertainment arena at Woolloongabba ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The government will make a one-off contribution of $600 million to the project after it's delivered, and hand the development rights for the former Gabba site to the consortium to build about 4,000 new homes.

Construction of the new arena and precinct is expected to begin in January.

Construction of Brisbane's new entertainment and housing precinct is set to begin in January, with the state government selecting a private sector building partner.

Deputy premier Jarrod Bleijie announced this morning construction consortium Gather Brisbane had been chosen as the successful tenderer for the $1.4 billion Brisbane Arena in Woolloongabba.

The consortium includes Live Nation, Oak View Group, Plenary and Webuild, and beat out the Brisbane Entertainment Alliance consortium for the deal.

The Brisbane Arena is planned to have a 17,000-seat capacity, increasing to 18,700 for concerts.

The Brisbane Arena will be adjacent to the new Cross River Rail station and have capacity for up to 18,700 people. (Supplied)

The arena is intended to replace the Brisbane Entertainment Centre at Boondall in Brisbane's north and will be adjacent to the new Woolloongabba Cross River Rail station.

Mr Bleijie said the Gabba stadium nearby would be decommissioned following the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games, giving way to "open public space" and almost 4,000 new homes.

He said the government had committed a one-off $600 million contribution to the project's projected cost of $1.4 billion, to be delivered following its completion, which is expected in 2031.

"To get the acts to come to Queensland, to get the sporting events, to get the music events, the concerts to come to Queensland, you need a venue that rivals the rest of the venues around the world," he said.

"Entertainment lovers will love it, public transport users will be able to access the Cross River Rail here once it opens and I can say confidently … we look to be on-site in January."

Jarrod Bleijie says work on the new arena is expected to begin in January. (ABC News: Josh McIntosh)

He said the state would continue to own the land in a long-term commercial arrangement with the arena operator.

"This is a 40-year deal and the maintenance [and] the obligations to maintain the arena will be [on] the consortia and the operator," Mr Bleijie said.

"There will be a commercial arrangement going forward with the operators, but as I said, it's over 40 years.

"That will be locked in before the end of the year, before construction starts on the new arena in January."

Brisbane live music stalwarts Lisa and Jess Origliasso — also known as The Veronicas — backed the new arena and said it would be an "incredible opportunity".

"We look around Brisbane and, you know, we have so many memories here — every part of our career has a sentimental attachment to different parts of Brisbane," Jess Origliasso said.

"That is why this is so fantastic — I think this is a dream coming true," Lisa Origliasso said.

The Veronicas described the new area as a "dream coming true". (ABC News: Josh McIntosh)

Mr Bleijie insisted the government was "not giving away the land" on which the Gabba stands.

"This is a very complicated commercial transaction," he said.

"Part of the process for getting the consortia to design, finance, and operate [the arena] without any government contribution until at least 2031, is to obviously have the ability that they know the investment [is] going forward.

The land the Gabba Stadium stands on will be handed to developers with plans to construct almost 4,000 new homes after 2032. (Supplied)

"We're not giving away the land, it's a commercial transaction and the commercial transaction that we've entered into is over a 40-year period."

He said the state government would be responsible for tearing down the Gabba after the 2032 Games, before handing the land to the consortium.

"The previous government had no plans to unlock this site," he said.

"In contrast, this government does, and we are very happy to partner with the private sector to get things done."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Fuel removal at Fukushima reactor going smoothly: workers
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
FUKUSHIMA – An operation to remove fuel from the building for the No. 2 reactor at Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings’ (Tepco) disaster-stricken Fukushima No. 1 nuclear power plant in northeastern Japan is progressing smoothly thanks to thorough preparations, workers in charge of the mission have said.

Tepco began in June to take nuclear fuel from the storage pool of the No. 2 reactor using remote-controlled equipment. The power station in Fukushima Prefecture was heavily damaged in the March 2011 major earthquake and tsunami, and is being decommissioned.

Unlike the No. 1 and No. 3 reactors, the No. 2 unit did not experience a hydrogen explosion and therefore suffered no major damage to the building housing the reactor, but radiation levels around the spent fuel pool have been high.

An opening was made in the wall of the reactor building, and workers use specialized remote-controlled equipment consisting of three cranes to place fuel assemblies removed from the pool into a container called a cask, which is then taken out through the opening.

A worker who is from a company cooperating with the plant decommissioning and responsible for loading the fuel into the casks told reporters that workers had repeatedly practiced beforehand using mock fuel assemblies that were almost identical with real assemblies in shape and weight.

“We have been able to carry out the work safely by drawing on our experience,” the worker said.

According to Tepco, the length of the crane arms is adjusted by a few millimeters. An official of the power supplier said it takes less than an hour to remove each fuel assembly, adding, “We want to complete the mission by communicating with each other closely and steadily carrying out each task.”

Of the 615 fuel assemblies in the pool, including ones that have yet to be used, 126 have been removed so far.

The removal work has been suspended since Oct. 19 for equipment inspections and to secure a sufficient space in the plant’s common storage pool, to which the removed fuel is transferred.

Tepco plans to resume the operation around spring next year, aiming to complete the work by the end of fiscal 2028.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: TIFF director Shozo Ichiyama on bridging the gap with Chinese cinema
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Mike Fu
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
It’s no exaggeration to call Shozo Ichiyama a guru of Chinese cinema.

In addition to his role as programming director of the Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF), he has produced almost all of the features by Jia Zhangke, one of China’s leading contemporary filmmakers, since 2000 “Platform” (2000). Ichiyama has also worked on titles by independent directors Yang Lina, Wang Qi and Song Fang. His international footprint includes a string of collaborations with acclaimed Taiwanese auteur Hou Hsiao-hsien in the 1990s, notably the iconic “Flowers of Shanghai” (1998).

On a brisk November morning, the 63-year-old cineaste sat down with The Japan Times at TIFF’s headquarters in Tokyo’s Yurakucho neighborhood for a conversation about the past, present and future of Chinese filmmaking. With his memorable mane of white hair and easygoing manner, Ichiyama spoke freely and earnestly about his career and his relationships with Chinese artists.

That same evening, the Competition jury would award TIFF’s best actress prize to Hu Ling for her role in Wang Jiangyong’s “The Night That Binds Us” and the Special Jury Prize to Sun Xun for his mind-bending mixed-media animation “Magic Atlas.” A third film, Qiu Jiongjiong’s “Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting,” was also a contender in this year’s competition.

Chinese talent is well represented at TIFF nowadays, but this wasn’t always the case. When Ichiyama first began helping out in the early 1990s, he says “there was nobody in the programming department who knew about Asian cinema. … The Asian selection of the festival was very weak.”

Ichiyama had been working in the production department of Shochiku, the studio behind cinematic legends such as Yasujiro Ozu and Kenji Mizoguchi, when his boss dispatched him to TIFF. At first, he simply attended to the visiting overseas guests, but he was soon invited back in a more formal capacity.

Even though Ichiyama says he was no Asian film expert and just a “movie fan,” he began working as the programmer for TIFF’s Asian sidebars in 1992. It was this role that allowed him to meet Hou Hsiao-hsien when “The Puppetmaster” (1993) screened as the opening film in his section.

A native of Yamaguchi Prefecture, Ichiyama had been a student at the University of Tokyo before embarking on a career in the film industry. In the mid-1980s, Chen Kaige’s “The Yellow Earth” (1984) was released in Japanese cinemas and left a deep impression on Ichiyama.

“I read Nagisa Oshima’s review of the film in the newspaper,” Ichiyama recalls, adding that when he finally saw it, “it was a big surprise” and a “very cinematic and challenging film.”

Around the same period, when a friend was studying abroad at Beijing’s Renmin University, Ichiyama visited China for the first time. He would return frequently in subsequent decades for festivals in Shanghai, Hong Kong and Pingyao, as well as to work on projects with Jia Zhangke.

Though Jia’s films have increased in scale over the decades, he also had more modest beginnings as an independent director in the 1990s — perhaps not unlike some of the filmmakers that TIFF has been spotlighting in recent years.

“The Chinese films in TIFF (this year) were very different because all three films were not ‘official,’” Ichiyama says. “The filmmakers are from China, but they were financed by other countries.”

Despite its Shanghai setting, for example, “The Night That Binds Us” is a co-production between France and Hong Kong, while “Magic Atlas” was made through a Singaporean animation studio. “Fuxi” drew on funding from a range of Middle Eastern and East Asian partners.

“Usually, every year we receive entries from commercial Chinese films that were released in January or February, so they try to show the film in Tokyo as a world premiere,” Ichiyama says. “But this year, this kind of film was not submitted — maybe it’s because of the political situation between China and Japan. … So we were somewhat forced to show independent films in the main Competition, but I liked those three films very much, and it didn’t matter if they didn’t get (official) permission.”

Ichiyama praises “The Night That Binds Us” for being “a realistic film with very strong direction,” especially as Wang’s feature-length debut. He notes that “Magic Atlas” and “Fuxi,” both abstract and visually striking films, were made by artists.

“I like this kind of experimental film very much,” Ichiyama says, going on to muse that such films have the power to “encourage artists working in China.”

Ichiyama says the ongoing freeze in Sino-Japanese relations, which has had a significant impact across the cultural domain, is “a bad thing for both the Chinese and Japanese film industries.” With major titles like “Chiikawa” unable to screen officially in China, the economic losses have been undoubtedly significant.

“While political issues between Japan and China are ever-present, there are people in China who enjoy Japanese films and animation, just as there are audiences in Japan who are interested in Chinese cinema,” he says. “It is important to bridge the divide between nations through this kind of cultural exchange, and I believe that movies play a significant role in doing so.”

Besides his work as a film programmer, Ichiyama began teaching at Tokyo University of the Arts (Geidai) in 2013 and has been a professor at the Graduate School of Film and New Media since 2024. In this capacity, he supervises student productions, reading scripts and offering advice. The producing course enrolls a relatively small cohort of students, including several from China.

In recent years, TIFF has screened the works of emerging Chinese directors who graduated from Geidai, such as Yang Liping (“Ashes”) and Cai Ronglin (“Miracle Summer”). Both Yang and Cai have made films set in Japan, with all-Japanese or majority-Japanese casts.

Ichiyama says the students have told him that “in China, it’s not easy to make independent films. … It’s very difficult to finance.” And, of course, there’s the matter of censorship. Sometimes, getting approval for a completed film is a feat in itself. As Ichiyama puts it, “(The director) must change many things in order to bypass censorship. That’s why they try to explore careers in other countries.”

When he first started at Geidai, “many Chinese students graduated and returned to their home country to work in Chinese film studios or film companies. But recently, many have decided to stay in Japan. They’re probably trying to explore making the films that they want to make.”

In 1998, Ichiyama stepped away from TIFF to join Office Kitano, the production company led by auteur Takeshi Kitano, and founded Tokyo Filmex, a smaller-scale festival focused on independent and arthouse cinema. When he returned to lead TIFF in 2021, creating a forum for film education was one of his priorities.

“My first mission is to select good films,” he says, “but I insisted that (TIFF) should do something different, like educational programs or programs that support filmmaking. … This kind of thing has been lacking for a long time.”

He points to the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Film Academy as an example of an initiative that has had a lasting impact on filmmakers from around the region. The Asian Students’ Film Conference, launched in 2025, is TIFF’s version of a program to nurture emerging talent.

“For the film industry to thrive in the long term,” he says, “there needs to be a variety of films beyond just commercial ones.”

In China, the system of institutional funding to help smaller films reach the festival circuit isn’t as robust as it is in other countries. Censorship, too, remains a concern.

“While it’s unlikely that censorship will disappear overnight, easing these standards — thereby allowing a broader range of films to be shown domestically — is essential for the continued development of Chinese cinema,” Ichiyama says.

For a growing number of emerging Chinese filmmakers, Tokyo offers an alternative place to develop their work and find an audience. Ichiyama, meanwhile, is always looking for the next generation of talent.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/po.title: Judge Blocks Immediate Closure of East Potomac Park for Trump Golf Project
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/po.author: Zach Montague
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/po.text:
Judge Ana C. Reyes, who has been overseeing combative litigation, said the Trump administration would not be responsible for operating the course while the case proceeded.

Reporting from Washington

A federal judge on Saturday temporarily blocked the Trump administration from shuttering East Potomac Park in Washington, finding that the proposed closure appeared to be intended to start the process of transforming the area into a championship golf course.

President Trump had announced that the municipal golf course and park would close on Sunday, ahead of the renovation work that he had called for. The ruling by Judge Ana C. Reyes of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia means the park will remain open for now.

Her decision was the latest setback to Mr. Trump’s renovation projects in the capital, which have repeatedly become tangled up in lawsuits. In her 30-page order, Judge Reyes said that the Trump administration would not be responsible for operating the course while the case proceeded. But she required the golf courses, paths and picnic areas in the park to remain “open and accessible to the public.”

Judge Reyes has for months been overseeing combative litigation over the future of the Washington park and golf course. A preservationist organization and local golfers sued in February, arguing that the project threatened to destroy a historic course that remained a cheap and accessible option for recreational players.

She had issued a series of rulings focused on a narrower dispute over whether the administration could clear out trees at the site. Saturday’s order was her first blocking work more generally at the park.

It came amid a larger standoff in which Judge Reyes has repeatedly accused administration officials of concealing their efforts to move forward with Mr. Trump’s ideas.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Andrew Messenger
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Party’s NSW leader Mike Newman says contenders are ‘people from the real world’ and not ‘career politicians’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The failed federal Liberal candidate Katherine Deves, who campaigned to exclude transgender women from women’s sport, will stand for One Nation at next year’s New South Wales election.

Deves was among four NSW Legislative Council candidates announced by One Nation’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, on Sunday.

The other candidates were Arnon Wither, a construction worker from the Hunter region who works as an electorate officer for Senator Sean Bell; Manti Steele, a farmer, teacher and mother of eight from Dubbo; and Daniel Hill, a surf lifesaver from the state’s south coast.

The NSW election will be held on 13 March.

Newman said on Sunday the upper house candidates were “authentic”, “people from the real world” and not “career politicians”.

One Nation has only announced a single lower house candidate – Newman, in the electorate of Cessnock – but he said the party would run candidates in all 93 lower house seats.

“We want to make sure that these people bleed orange, and like I said, they’re all from the real world,” he said.

“That’s the that’s the type of person we’re aiming at … people from the real world who understand business, who understand their pinch points and pain points, understand the cost of living, understand cashflow.”

Deves was handpicked by the former prime minister Scott Morrison to run in the federal NSW seat of Warringah in 2022. Her candidacy was marred by controversy, including when she likened anti-trans activism to standing up against the Holocaust.

On Sunday she said she joined One Nation “because I wanted to be a part of the rescue, recovery, and restoration of our nation”.

“We are seeing cost of living skyrocket, whether it’s fuel, housing, energy, and we are watching a government that is so wedded to destructive ideologies like DEI and net zero that they are prepared to impoverish us all,” she said.

If elected, she would look to make changes to state laws regarding “discrimination, hate speech, vilification, birth certificates, etc”.

“Where we can restore clear and accurate language around biological sex, men and women, and ensure that women and girls are safe and have spaces for services, sports, etc, where it’s inappropriate for males to be there.”

One Nation has required candidates at state elections to sign non-disclosure agreements preventing them from discussing their potential candidacy with the media.

News24 reported last month that Deves would run as an upper house candidate in the NSW election. She announced that she joined One Nation in September.

When Guardian Australia contacted Deves about her potential candidacy in October, she directed inquiries to Vikki Campion, the NSW party’s part-time media adviser. The party provided a statement saying it had confirmed only three candidates at that time – Newman, the lead upper house candidate, Stuart Bonds, and a Tamworth firearms manufacturer, Jeff Bacon.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Thunderstorms, giant hail and powerful winds forecast for NSW as wild weather hits east coast
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Stephanie Convery
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Volatile weather predicted after storms on Saturday, with a man in his 20s struck by lightning while swimming on NSW Central Coast

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Dangerous and severe “supercell” thunderstorms with the potential for giant hail and destructive winds were forecast for parts of New South Wales on Sunday, as volatile weather continued in the eastern states over the weekend.

Storms dumped heavy rain across large parts of northern and eastern NSW and much of Queensland on Saturday, with strong winds recorded up to 98km/h in Goulburn and rainfall totals of between 30mm and 50mm in the Coffs Harbour area.

A man in his 20s was struck by lightning while swimming at Ettalong beach on NSW’s Central Coast on Saturday afternoon. He was pulled from the water by fellow swimmers and given CPR by first responders until NSW Ambulance paramedics arrived. He was taken to Gosford hospital in a serious condition, and later transferred to Royal North Shore hospital.

The young man was in a critical but stable condition on Sunday morning, a hospital spokesperson said.

Witnesses said while there was storm activity visible in the distance towards Gosford, the area around the beach was clear and sunny and that the lightning bolt appeared to come “out of nowhere”.

Lightning can strike up to 30km from the centre of a storm cell.

Sunday was expected to be “another big storm day”, with “very dangerous and severe thunderstorms” likely for north-eastern NSW, said Sarah Scully, senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology.

Those storms could bring hail with a diameter greater than 5cm, and winds in excess of 120km/h.

“That’s being driven by a southerly change that’s pushing up the New South Wales coast,” Scully said. “It’s a potential trigger for these supercell high-end thunderstorms.”

Severe thunderstorms with 2cm hail, wind gusts in excess of 90km/h, heavy rainfall and flash flooding was possible on Sunday through a broader area of NSW extending down towards inland parts of the ranges to the east of Sydney, and pushing up into south-east and central parts of Queensland.

Storms were expected in Sydney on Sunday, but were likely to be less severe than further north, though rain was likely. The forecast temperature was 23C. Showers and thunderstorms were expected in Brisbane with a top of 31C.

The BoM expected to release more severe weather warnings throughout Sunday as the storms develop.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

On Monday, the risk of high-end severe thunderstorms would move into the NSW northern rivers and south-eastern parts of Queensland, including Brisbane, the Gold Coast and the Sunshine Coast, again with the potential to bring giant hail, destructive winds, and intense rain that could lead to life-threatening flash flooding.

“That again is being driven by that trough that’s pushing up the coast combined with the very humid conditions that eastern Australia has been experiencing the last few days,” Scully said.

A coastal trough with a low-pressure system appeared to be developing off the north coast of NSW near the Queensland border, which had the potential to bring even more rain onto the coast.

“How much rainfall accumulates is highly dependent on how close that trough sits to the coast, and also how long it lingers there,” Scully said.

“At this state we’re only expecting moderate rainfall totals during tomorrow from that coastal trough, between 30mm to 70mm, easing into Tuesday morning. But we are watching it very closely as rainfall totals associated with these coastal troughs are notoriously challenging to predict. If they just move that little bit closer to the coast they can sometimes dump a whole lot of rain.”

Elsewhere, there were showers developing in Melbourne on Sunday with a forecast top of 17C. There was a high chance of showers in Hobart, with 13C expected, and cloudy in Adelaide with a mild 20C forecast. It was partly cloudy in Canberra, where they were expecting 24C, and in Perth, with an expected top of 28C. Darwin was expecting 34C and an afternoon storm.
