https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Iraq PM sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran stronghold
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has dismissed nine senior security officials over an alleged oil smuggling operation in the Jurf al-Nasr area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group.

Al-Zaidi chaired an emergency security meeting to review the findings of a committee investigating smuggling in Jurf al-Nasr, Babil province, military spokesperson Sabah al-Numan told the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The move follows an investigation that uncovered illegal oil refineries and evidence of manipulation linked to the smuggling activities.

“In light of the investigation’s findings, [the prime minister] ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary,” al-Numan said.

The prime minister “also ordered the dismissal” of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil, he said.

The police chief of Babil province was among those dismissed.

Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-aligned paramilitary group and one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, has recently issued several sharp statements against the prime minister, threatening his government and accusing him of corruption.

Senior Iraqi politicians previously told the AFP news agency that al-Zaidi had repeatedly said he was ready to confront groups refusing to disarm.

Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, said previous Iraqi governments had been careful not to address the issue of an alleged oil smuggling network worth up to $30m monthly.

“This area had effectively been run as a state within a state until now,” Smith said. “But that seems to have changed, with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi saying that no inch of Iraq will be allowed to have oil smuggling operations like this.”

Two strategic oil pipelines running through the south of the country, just south of Baghdad, “had effectively been tapped into”, Smith said, citing a leaked intelligence report. “Oil was being siphoned off, stolen, and then sold on the black market in an operation worth tens of millions of dollars every month.”

On Wednesday, the INA reported that “intelligence documents” containing satellite images “showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction” in Jurf al-Nasr, accusing an unnamed group of tapping into a pipeline there.

Al-Numan said the investigating committee “confirmed the accuracy” of the information.

Akeel Abbas, a senior non-resident fellow at the Iraq Initiative within the Atlantic Council, told Al Jazeera that oil smuggling by various political factions and armed groups “is common in Iraq” due to “commercial rather than political or strategic” gains.

Abbas said the latest crackdown has more to do with “militia disarmament”.

“The prime minister cleverly decided to frame it as anticorruption. That is why a few days ago, there was a report leaked by the government about this operation,” he said.

The prime minister wants to “cut off the financial lifeline to this particular group that has been so resistant” to the government’s “militia disarmament” initiatives, he added.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/c.title: Legal but not available: Who decides what healthcare is on the table?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/c.author: Lucy Barbour
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Hundreds recently gathered at Newcastle's Civic Park to protest against the changes to healthcare access. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

Accessing IVF, abortion or voluntary assisted dying (VAD) can be difficult and complicated. It can be harder still in rural and regional areas, where specialist shortages, long delays, distance and conscientious objection already limit access.

That is why a Catholic provider's decision to stop offering these services at Newcastle Private hospital in regional New South Wales has alarmed many clinicians and the community.

A local issue has exposed the potential for national implications. Calvary, a Catholic not-for-profit, is poised to take over 14 private hospitals from Healthscope, effectively doubling its private hospital network across the country.

Catholic providers already run about 6 per cent of Australia's public and private hospitals. If the latest Calvary deal clears regulators, that footprint will grow, and so will doctors' fears that access to legal healthcare will shrink.

These healthcare services have long attracted irreconcilable world views. But in 2026, they're legal. The debate now has moved beyond what should be lawful, to who decides what care should be available.

The catalyst for the Calvary controversy was a Teams meeting held Wednesday before last. Obstetricians and gynaecologists at Newcastle Private met with their incoming Calvary leadership team.

Most were stunned when they were informed that IVF, abortion, VAD, gender affirming care, contraception, vasectomies and tubal ligation — to prevent fertility — would all be off the table within a few weeks.

Calvary is a Catholic not-for-profit health, aged-care and community-care organisation in Australia. It forms part of the ministry founded by the Sisters of the Little Company of Mary. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

The doctors had assumed they'd have time to negotiate terms or find a solution to keeping these services on the hospital site. No such luck.

They would also have to sign a document pledging to practise in line with the Code of Ethical Standards for Catholic Health and Aged Care Services in Australia. The code calls abortion "morally wrong" and says procedures that substitute for the "marital act" are "not morally permissible".

Calvary has acknowledged the "concerns and uncertainty within the community" and, late on Friday, more information was provided on its website.

"Where a requested intervention cannot be offered, we remain committed to treating every person with dignity, providing clear information and supporting access to appropriate ongoing care … Where a service is not offered, we will work with the treating specialist to support appropriate pathways."

The Catholic church has been unwavering in its teachings for hundreds of years. Even as arguments on issues such as IVF and abortion have shifted, its stance has remained constant.

The code that guides decision-making in Catholic hospitals describes itself, in its preface, as "a crucial resource for the Church's mission in health care". In practice, that means the church expects that its core and fundamental beliefs on sanctity of life and medical intervention should be upheld in a hospital setting.

But critics say that approach can create more barriers to clinical care.

Moments before surgery, Hayley Deniss was told about a potential disruption to her IVF care.

IVF Australia's Dr Veronica Knight calls Calvary's latest decision, "discrimination based on religious ethos".

The Royal Australia and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) is framing the issues as a matter of access, not ownership.

"We have no objection to Catholic ownership of hospitals," RANZCOG President Dr Nisha Khot told the ABC.

"What we're saying is that the law of the land says that all this health care is legal, and it should be available in every hospital. It should not be defined by the faith of the organisation that owns the hospital."

The competition regulator recently cleared Calvary's takeover of Hobart Private Hospital, where reproductive health, gender-affirming care and VAD were also due to be wound back.

RANZCOG'S concern is one of concentration. Dr Khot warned of scenarios "where the local public hospital and the private hospital are both Catholic", leaving no hospital access for reproductive sexual health care or voluntary assisted dying.

Newcastle already offers a preview of what happens when VAD care meets a Catholic operator.

The region's only public hospice sits within a hospital already run by Calvary as a public-private partnership. The hospital does not allow patients to have VAD drugs administered on-site, so patients who choose VAD must be moved to another bed — in another location — to die on their own terms.

Newcastle Private and Hunter Valley Private, the two hospitals Calvary is set to take over, have been making beds available where possible. If — or when — they stop offering that option, the pressure on health workers to find alternative beds will increase.

It's likely that Newcastle Private Hospital will no longer be able to take VAD patients, after being taken over by Calvary. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

One VAD doctor, who cannot be named because of their contract with NSW Health, says the result could be waits that "blow out by several days".

"There have already been cases where patients have been waiting for a couple of hours to transfer to another facility, in the final hours of their lives — sometimes in significant pain," the doctor said. "And the longer they must wait, the risk is that patient loses the capacity to consent to taking the medication."

Calvary's decision to end services at Newcastle Private and Hunter Valley Private would leave patients to rely on workarounds.

Clinicians typically go to great lengths to make those succeed, and most Newcastle patients will likely still get care, but with more administration, delay and frustration.

Dr Nisha Khot is concerned about the dangers of delays in healthcare for vulnerable people. (ABC News: Margaret Burin)

Delay comes with risks. RANZCOG's Dr Khot raises an extreme scenario, in which a woman at 18 weeks has her waters break at a Calvary hospital.

"She's 18 weeks at a Calvary hospital, isn't told about abortion as an option and doesn't realise her life is at risk until sepsis sets in," she said. This is hypothetical, but she says she's "genuinely concerned" about it happening.

Abortion access is already uneven, particularly in rural and regional NSW, where public hospitals have turned women away.

In public hospitals, governments have levers. After ABC reporting revealed that Orange Hospital had told staff to stop providing terminations of pregnancy, the NSW health minister stepped in and reinstated the service.

The answer is less clear when the hospital is private, whether it is Catholic or not.

Calvary's supporters, and even those who reject its doctrine, argue the Catholic health sector is worth protecting. Its roots go back to nuns who began caring for the sick and dying in Sydney in the late 1800s.

Federal Labor MP and doctor Mike Freelander puts the practical question bluntly: "What's the alternative?"

In other words, if Calvary doesn't take over Healthscope's hospitals, who will, and who has the money to do it?

Dr Freelander says Catholic hospitals provide quality care, but is concerned the "Catholic ethical system is not keeping up with modern healthcare".

Labor MP and doctor Mike Freelander says we need Catholic providers to keep the hospitals going.  (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Some have called on NSW Health to refuse to transfer the hospital licence unless Calvary keeps providing the services it plans to end. The Health Minister and Premier have ruled that out, saying the services will be available elsewhere, including at an already stretched public hospital.

That has done little to reassure providers working to avoid scenarios like eggs for IVF being driven across town because women can no longer have them retrieved at the private hospital next door to the clinic where embryos are created.

The ACCC is still assessing Calvary's national expansion, but its test is whether the deal would substantially lessen competition, not whether patients lose access to services.

That leaves open the question: when care is legal, who decides whether or not it is provided?

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author

NEW YORK – A U.S. resident who fled Lithuania during World War II on a visa issued by Japanese diplomat Chiune Sugihara received an award Friday from the Japanese consul-general in New York for her efforts to preserve the late renowned diplomat’s humanitarian legacy.

Sylvia Smoller, 94, received the Consul-General’s Commendation at the official residence of the consul-general in the U.S. city.

Warsaw-born Smoller and her family escaped Nazi persecution of Jewish people after obtaining visas issued in Lithuania by Sugihara, who was stationed in the country at the time, and traveled to the United States via Japan. Such visas issued by Sugihara are often called “visas of life.”

At the award ceremony, Smoller stressed the importance of younger generations upholding the spirit of “benevolence and compassion” that Sugihara valued.

“Sugihara’s message is more important today than it ever was,” amid ongoing conflicts around the world and increasingly dire conditions for immigrants, she told reporters.

Satoshi Katahira, Japan’s consul-general in New York, thanked Smoller, saying that Sugihara’s legacy has continued to inspire people across cultures and generations due to many years of her dedications.

The ceremony was also attended by Masanori Kaneko, mayor of the town of Yaotsu in Gifu Prefecture, Sugihara’s hometown. Kaneko presented Smoller with a replica of the visa Sugihara issued to her father. The original visa was donated to the town by Smoller in 1993.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Political jockeying over a bill to reduce the number of proportional representation seats in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber of the Diet, the country’s parliament, is expected to intensify.

The ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and its coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party (JIP) also known as Nippon Ishin no Kai, are aiming to launch Lower House deliberations on the bill as early as Tuesday and pass it through the chamber within this month.

Opposition parties — aside from the Democratic Party for the People (DPP) — are preparing to mount strong resistance to the bill.

The expected standoff may affect deliberations in the Upper House on a bill to cut the consumption tax rate on food and beverage products from 8% to 1% for two years from April 2027, leaving the ruling bloc struggling to manage the situation.

In talks with reporters Friday, Keitaro Ono of the LDP, the ruling side’s leader of the board of the Lower House’s special committee on political reform, stressed his party’s intention to launch deliberations as soon as possible.

The current extraordinary Diet session is scheduled to end Dec. 12. Some within the LDP have called for sending the seat cut bill to the upper chamber by Nov. 27, taking into account the fact that the ruling bloc lacks a majority in the chamber.

However, the special committee already has three bills on a review of political donations from corporations and other organizations, which have been carried over into the current Diet session, and the ruling and opposition sides have yet to reach agreement on which legislation should be given priority.

At a meeting of the special committee’s board on Friday, the ruling bloc proposed starting deliberations on the Lower House seat cut bill Monday after holding a vote on the political donation bills.

The Chudo parliamentary group in the Lower House, mainly comprising the Democratic Reform Party and Komeito, both opposition parties, rejected the proposal, saying it would effectively bring discussions on reviewing political donations to an end.

The ruling bloc plans to resume talks with opposition parties soon with the aim of beginning Lower House deliberations on the seat cut bill Tuesday.

The bill mainly calls for shedding 31 of the 176 proportional representation seats in the 465-seat Lower House. Enacting the legislation during the current Diet session is nonnegotiable for the JIP, which has placed a seat reduction at the heart of its reform agenda since forming the ruling coalition with the LDP in October 2025.

The ruling bloc agreed to measures including a plan to allow the creation of joint proportional representation candidate lists by multiple parties in order to woo the DPP, and the three parties jointly submitted the bill to the Lower House on Thursday.

Other opposition parties have strongly opposed the bill, with Komeito policy chief Hiromasa Nakano arguing that reducing only proportional representation seats would increase the number of wasted votes.

Criticizing the ruling coalition for abandoning efforts to build consensus and voicing his determination to block the enactment of the bill, Democratic Reform Party chief Junya Ogawa said, “There are no rules that allow unilateral changes to the playing field (for democracy).”

Some ruling bloc members have argued that they should not hesitate to force a vote if opposition parties refuse to cooperate.

During the previous extraordinary Diet session that ended in July, however, opposition parties boycotted deliberations in protest against the ruling side’s referral of a similar seat reduction bill to a parliamentary committee, making Diet proceedings deadlocked.

There are concerns that repeating the same mistake could jeopardize the passage of the consumption tax cut bill, which is currently under deliberation in the Upper House.

Yoshitaka Saito, Diet affairs chief of the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan, warned Friday that developments regarding deliberations on the seat reduction bill may impact talks on the tax cut bill.

Some ruling coalition members envision enacting the consumption tax cut bill in early December and then pushing through the seat reduction bill before the current Diet session ends. But it is uncertain whether this could be achieved as a vote on the tax bill may be delayed.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/t.title: Neil the seal has new management plan unveiled
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/t.author: Loretta Lohberger
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Neil the seal is a southern elephant seal that has been visiting Tasmania twice yearly since his birth on Turrakana/Tasman Peninsula in October 2020.

Neil has become a social media sensation and has attracted crowds during his time ashore.

The Tasmanian government's new management plan includes a minimum approach distance of 30 metres.

New measures to protect Tasmania's favourite elephant seal Neil will require onlookers to stay at least 30 metres away from him when he spends time on land.

The new rules are included in an updated management plan released today.

"Everyone loves Neil, he's very popular, but we've also got to respect Neil," Premier Jeremy Rockliff said.

"We want to ensure we're protecting Neil's safety, of course, and the safety of the community as well."

An interim protection order has also been made under the state's Threatened Species Protection Act to provide "additional legal protections for southern elephant seals and their habitat when they haul out in key coastal areas of southern Tasmania".

The elephant seal has been attracting onlookers in southern Tasmania, as well as a growing social media audience, but fears for his wellbeing and concerns that some people aren't keeping their distance have led to calls to better protect Neil.

The order includes a minimum approach distance of 30 metres, requirements to keep dogs under control and away from seals, restrictions on parking vehicles close to seals, and separation distances for vessels and drones.

Breaching such an order could lead to a conviction and a fine.

The management plan states that "compliance action may be taken where unlawful disturbance, harassment or interference with an elephant seal is identified".

Topic:
Women’s Big Bash League

At six years of age, the southern elephant seal known affectionately as "Neil the seal" was estimated to weight around 1,000 kilograms when he last "hauled out" in June and July and spent time in and around south-east Tasmanian coastal communities.

Adult male southern elephant seals can weigh more than 3,000 kilograms.

Neil the seal is a regular visitor to south-east Tasmania. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Since his winter visit, 110,326 people have signed a petition in support of creating restricted access zones around Neil's known habitats, and introducing fines for people who get too close.

The updated management plan, while developed in response to Neil, will also apply to other southern elephant seals.

"We know Tasmanians love Neil and enjoy following his adventures, but Neil is a [member of a] threatened species and wild animal, so it is important we all do our part to keep him safe," Environment Minister Guy Barnett said in a statement.

Mr Barnett said the plan had been informed by scientific advice and consultation with councils, Tasmania Police and other stakeholders.

The new measures come after the premier said in July that his government was not considering strengthening Tasmanian laws.

"Common sense is what is key here; we don't need to legislate for common sense," Mr Rockliff said at the time.

"There are very clear guidelines around Neil the seal: make sure your dogs are leashed, make sure you have at least a 20-metre buffer."

Neil the seal's antics have a large audience on social media. (Supplied: Sam Volker Photography)

Today, Mr Rockliff said he remained "committed to the fact that we do need a common sense approach around all our wildlife, not just Neil".

"But given the popularity of Neil we do need again those guardrails in place which is why we have the management plan," he said.

Greens MP Cecily Rosol said her party would be "looking at the detail" of the management plan.

"We'll be speaking to local communities and local councils and just assessing that management plan in consultation with communities to make sure that it includes everything it needs to keep Neil the seal safe," she said.

Neil has hauled out twice a year in south-east Tasmania, generally in November-December to moult and in the middle of the year to rest, according to the state's Natural Resources and Environment Department (NRE).

"He has an exceptional public profile that extends well beyond Tasmania, attracting significant local, national and international media coverage, extensive social media engagement and widespread public interest," an NRE document about Neil states.

Councils, police and the state's environment department are all invovled in protecting Neil when he comes ashore. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Neil is expected to continue to return to Tasmania for the rest of his life, but, according to NRE, "his movements and behaviour are becoming increasingly variable", as he has entered the sub-adult stage of life.

Southern elephant seals are a threatened species.

The updated management plan states that while much of the use of Neil's name and image has been positive, and helped enforce conservation and animal welfare messages, there was also "evidence of individuals and businesses seeking to monetise his popularity or commercially exploit his name and identity".

NSW Fair Trading recently fined the operator of a former website that sold Neil the seal merchandise after it found the website "falsely" claimed links with conservation organisations.

Brand Tasmania is working to trademark the "Neil the Seal" identity.

"Securing appropriate trademark protection would strengthen the State's capacity to manage commercial use of the 'Neil the Seal' brand in relation to the goods and services covered by those registrations," the management plan states.

"It would provide a clearer basis for licensing approved commercial uses and, where appropriate, taking action against unauthorised use of the protected trademarks."

Mr Rockliff said local artists would still be able to create Neil the seal merchandise under the trademark.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/s.title: How Swim GP may have given a glimpse of the future of para-sport
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/s.author: Simon Smale
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Lakeisha Patterson says para-swimmers' involvement in Swim GP is important. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swim GP's made for TV, all-action racing format has proven a hit with swimmers and spectators alike.

But the biggest benefit may well be the innovations that placed para-swimmers front and centre of the competition at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatics Centre.

In front of a sold-out crowd, four teams: Kraken, Wahoo, King Tide and Tsunami, competed in a variety of races ranging from skins events through to mystery medley relays.

Times are not important. It's all about who touches the wall first.

"It is an opportunity for our athletes, our Paralympic team and our Olympic team, to come together and really showcase what they do," Swimming Australia Paralympic head coach Mel Tantrum said ahead of Saturday's evening events.

"This is about building the brand, building the profile of the athletes, swimming in prime time in preparation for the next six years."

The Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre was sold-out for day two. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swim GP is not a new idea, and indeed has built on the concepts reintroduced at last year's Australia vs the World in Brisbane.

However, crucially, Swim GP has seen para-swimmers take a leading role.

Swimming Australia chief executive Rob Woodhouse told ABC Sport that involving the para-swimmers "was one of the most important factors" and a "no-brainer" in Swim GP's planning for a couple of reasons.

"Both our head coaches, Mel Tantrum and Rohan Taylor, they absolutely want a packed stadium for our trials, ideally Sydney next year, but particularly the Olympic/Paralympic trials in '28 in Chandler, one of the reasons being, for the Olympics, SoFi Stadium, with 40,000 screaming Americans and Long Beach for the Paralympics," Woodhouse said.

"Some of those [para-]athletes do have sensory issues, so for them to have some experience coming out to all of that noise and those bright lights, the flashing lights and all those sorts of things is really, really important.

"So there's quite an important benefit from Swim GP for those para-athletes that do have to deal with those things to get more accustomed to a noisy venue, to a bright flashy venue and things like that.

"[Also] that aspirational view that these athletes can provide, whether they're para-athletes or able-bodied athletes, to the young kids at home, and there's a lot of kids with various disabilities that don't have opportunities to get into a pool or to even just get involved in the other sports. So, just being able to showcase our amazing para-athletes and what they do is a really critical factor."

A big atmosphere is vital for Australia's swimmers to prepare for LA Olympic Games in 2028. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Tantrum agreed, saying integrating the two programs was vital.

"Swimming Australia is really inclusive in terms of the parity between Olympic and Paralympic programs and making sure our swimmers across both programs are really profiled and really supported," Tantrum said.

"The athletes are loving being part of a bigger team. Those sort of innovative, creative competitions make the athletes feel they're part of an elite team.

"It's not just para, it's not separate, it's part of being the Australian Dolphins swim team and both programs coming together.

"The athletes are fully integrated team members. They don't sit separately. They've got the same uniform, same bleachers, same team meetings.

"And I think that's, for the athletes, it's a chance for them to really showcase their athleticism.

"It's not about, oh, you're a para-athlete, it's about elite swimming at its best.

"The world's best swimmers are here in the pool. And yeah, whether you're Olympic or Paralympic, you know, able-bodied or have a disability, it doesn't matter. You're an elite athlete first and you're here to perform."

Victoria Belando Nicholson (right) was a member of the King Tide team. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

One of the biggest challenges in para-sport when there are a limited number of athletes, is integrating multiple classifications and how to accurately, and fairly, ensure a level playing field.

In a standard multi-class meet, swimmers with varied impairments all start their races at the same time, with the winner determined by how close a swimmer gets to the world record in their particular classification.

That's all well and good but, for spectators, it can get confusing as to who as actually won because the winner does not always touch the wall first.

Swim GP gets around this by having a staggered start, with lights on the blocks for each swimmer.

The time-gap is determined based on a swimmer's season best in a particular distance and should result in a blanket finish — far more appealing for spectators.

"I think it's a really good idea to then see everyone come up towards each other and finish pretty closely," Paralympic legend Lakeisha Patterson told ABC Sport.

"It makes it an exciting race, I think, towards the end.

"I think for an event that isn't preparing for a world champs or a major international meet, this is really good for fans to see how multi-class swimming works."

Lakeisha Patterson said she was nervous before her race, perhaps made more so when Ben Hance literally ripped the shirt off his back when walking out. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson competed in, and won, Saturday night's opening race, a multi-class, mixed 100m event where each swimmer swam a different stroke, with Patterson unusually swimming butterfly, which she noted "definitely" won't be on her program for next year's world championships.

Perhaps she should reconsider. Patterson, who is classified as an S9 swimmer, swam a PB to blitz the field, although the other three swimmers; Tim Hodge (S9), Ben Hance (S14) and Keira Stephens (S10), were far closer together.

"It doesn't matter what their classification is and, in some cases, what their gender is," Tantrum explained.

"It's some new tech that we're trialling for the first time on the block so that athletes, no matter what their class or their gender, they can race together.

"With this [Swim GP] format, it's basically who touches the wall first is the winner.

"These staggered starts and close finals make the crowd get right into it. It makes it exciting if someone's got a 20-second stagger to catch up on in 100 metres. It makes for exciting racing, and the crowd really got into that last night and you could feel the crowd lift.

"That's what swimming should be, right? It should be exciting."

Lakeisha Patterson (right) and Rowan Crothers (second right) were key members of Team Tsunami. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson noted that giving para-swimmers the same platform was crucial for the development of the sport.

"I think it's incredibly important to showcase that our athletes aren't just here for participation," she said.

"We are athletes showcasing what is possible, and I think Australia is leading the way in that inclusion space and how we can involve our entire team.

"Leading into Brisbane we can really build on that and hopefully have all of Australia behind us, and showing to the people watching at home that they may have a space in Paralympic sport as well."

Fully integrated competitions remain a rarity for para and able-bodied sporting events, the Commonwealth Games being a notable exception.

Given the success of this format, Tantrum said that innovations like the staggered starts seen in Swim GP could inspire more innovation elsewhere, perhaps even adding more athletes to future Commonwealth Games fields.

"If we could influence Commonwealth Games Federation … we could potentially have a greater number of athletes and a greater number of classes competing together," Tantrum said.

"We left a number of athletes at home [from the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games] because they simply didn't have events for those classes.

"So something that is more of a multi-class format for Commonwealth Games would be a great innovation to at least consider.

Birmingham 2022 celebrated the largest para sport program in history, but there's still a large gap between wealthy and developing nations. What should integration look like?

"There's potential there that we could make this more integrated, fun, with exciting finishes and more athletes involved from Australia."

Perhaps even other sports could take note?

"Our immediate purpose is to showcase swimming," Tantrum said.

"But you know, if we can lead other sports and things like track and field to follow a similar format, where the para-athletes are standing alongside their Olympic athlete colleagues?

"You know, it's humans, right? It's human story, it's humans doing the best that they can do.

"If other sports such as athletics or cycling, want to come in and do what we're doing, if we're the trailblazers of that space, we'd love others to join in as well."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr4g.title: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr4g.text:
On a visit to an isolated Andean village in his former diocese, Pope Leo XIV has spoken about the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future", which he said had left communities under threat.

About 6,000 people live in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, which is located in a remote part of the Andes mountains in northern Peru, but the Pope's visit drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican.

At an outdoor Mass, Pope Leo spoke of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages," and the unequal distribution of the land's resources.

Over 40% of the population in the Cajamarca region, where the town is located, live in poverty - the highest figure in Peru, according to official data.

Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.

In his sermon, Pope Leo thanked those who had made the journey to him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.

Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where Pope Leo served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population.

On Saturday he returned by helicopter, where he was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, where he waved to people who had travelled from across the region to see him.

Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the Pope said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again.

"It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said.

Rev. Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz.

He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert,' as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father."

Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the leader of the Catholic church, who was elected in May 2025.

The 12-day trip has included stops in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in Peru carries personal significance.

The US-born pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.

The pontiff is set to leave Chiclayo on Sunday, when he will head to Cusco, and then on to a Peruvian sector of the Amazon rainforest. His tour of the region will conclude on Monday, at which point Pope Leo will return to Rome.

He spoke of the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future" The Pope's visit drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6j9.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6j9.text:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington DC.

US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.

Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park or its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.

Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.

In a 30-page decision issued on Saturday, Reyes said the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual, and that the government violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline."

"The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.

She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".

Her order will last until the 28 November.

The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.

The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital.

The legal fight then escalated in October, when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin.

After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes.

Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.

"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post to Truth Social.

Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether the justice department attorneys "have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".

That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans was "done in bad faith" and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.

She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr62.title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr62.text:
Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.

For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.

"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.

While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".

Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.

The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.

Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."

The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.

Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.

When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.

In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.

Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.

This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.

"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.

The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.

Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.

But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.

Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.

Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.

In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.

A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.

"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."

The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.

The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.

This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"

Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.

Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.

Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.

Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."

The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.

Whatever technology is used, it can be hard to keep everyone happy, as smells are so subjective. "Unfortunately, the general rule is that the nastier we perceive the odour to be, the more sensitive towards it we are," says Johan Lundström, a professor in the science of smell at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/fl.title: What to Know About Continued Flight Disruptions
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/fl.author: Sejal Govindarao
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/fl.text:
U.S. Flight Disruptions

After a nationwide ground stop Friday, travelers are still encountering snags, and it could take several days for flight schedules to return to normal.

Effects of a nationwide ground stop on air travel Friday evening, which stranded thousands of passengers and caused widespread delays, rippled into Saturday as airlines canceled thousands of flights and airports struggled to recover.

The air traffic control system, which faced a faulty upgrade that caused communications failures leading to the ground stop, is expected to be back to normal by Sunday night, said Bryan Bedford, who leads the Federal Aviation Administration. Flight schedules could take several days to return to normal.

Federal officials are still trying to determine who is at fault and have called for congressional funding to prevent similar failures. There is no evidence that the problem was caused by a cyberattack, officials have said.

L3Harris, a contractor managing the F.A.A.’s telecoms network, made a standard upgrade at a remote air traffic location, federal officials said Saturday. L3Harris was conducting a routine task — replacing copper wire with more modern fiber optic cable — that was expected to pose no significant disruption to air traffic, said Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary.

But the switch from copper to fiber overwhelmed the system with levels of data it could not handle, prompting widespread communications failures across air traffic facilities that manage the national air space. Alarmed at the scope of the problems, officials issued a rare nationwide ground stop for hours.

Administration officials say it’s still unclear whether L3Harris or faulty equipment was to blame. L3Harris said in a statement on Saturday that it was supporting the F.A.A. investigation and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts two missiles, two drones in Riyadh
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis have said they intercepted two missiles and two drones targeting Riyadh, allegedly launched by the Houthis, as fighting intensifies across various front lines in Yemen.

“Air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward Riyadh,” Turki al-Maliki, the Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, said in a post on X early on Sunday.

Earlier on Saturday, al-Maliki said two suspected Houthi drones “were intercepted and destroyed” in the Riyadh and southern regions.

At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to the kingdom’s authorities.

The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid International airport, as well as the East-West pipeline and oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia.

The interceptions come as the Saudi-led forces supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government also said they intercepted several drones launched towards the Yemeni city of Marib.

Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said government forces had made gains against the Houthis during heavy fighting in the al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf, as fighting intensified in Marib.

Al-Nuzaili said 321 Houthi leaders had been killed or wounded in 723 targeted operations by Saudi-backed forces in the Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf governorates, and that 117 military vehicles used by the Iran-allied rebel group had been destroyed.

The coalition carried out at least 37 air strikes and 56 drone attacks, as well as 541 artillery strikes.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Saudi-led coalition had launched 72 air strikes against the Houthis in the Saada, Taiz, Lahij and al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.

Saree said the Houthis targeted Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of the Lahij governorate with ballistic missiles.

Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported that two women and two children were injured as a result of artillery shelling by Saudi-backed forces in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa.

More than 340,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

As the fight between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalates, the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans in the kingdom to exercise “heightened vigilance”, citing an increased threat of Houthi attacks.

The embassy said Houthi attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia had “caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions”, warning that hostilities could spread “rapidly”.

“Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia,” it said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/e.title: Central coast man in critical condition after 'blue sky' lightning strike
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/e.author: Charles Rushforth and Ben Clifford
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/e.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Disasters, Accidents and Emergency Incidents

Emergency services were called to Ettalong Beach yesterday after a swimmer was struck by lightning.  (Supplied)

A man struck by lightning on the New South Wales Central Coast remains in a critical but stable condition in hospital.

Bystanders pulled the man from the water at Ettalong Beach yesterday afternoon.

More thunderstorms are forecast across NSW today.

A man is in a critical but stable condition at a Sydney hospital after a "blue sky" lightning strike on the Central Coast yesterday afternoon.

The man, believed to be in his 20s, was swimming at Ettalong Beach when he was struck about 3:00pm.

A NSW Ambulance spokesperson said bystanders pulled the man from the water and performed CPR until paramedics arrived.

Brandon Duffy witnessed the "chaotic" scene after arriving shortly after the strike for a morning swim.

"They were commencing CPR when I arrived. There were a lot of bystanders looking on," he said.

"People were very concerned. When the lightning strike happened, it was pretty clear."

The man was taken to Gosford Hospital by ambulance, but has been moved to the Royal North Shore Hospital in a critical but stable condition.

The incident follows severe storms across Greater Sydney, resulting in about 250 calls for help across NSW.

Taylor Lee Quimby said she was visiting the beach with her three children on Saturday when she heard a "massive bang" about 200 metres away.

"We were shocked it was so loud, considering none of the dark clouds were above us," she said.

"All along the beach was so sunny."

Emergency services attended the beach to assist the man after the lightning strike. (Supplied: @nswccincidentalerts)

Arriving home a short time later, Ms Quimby said she was shocked to learn that someone had been struck by lightning despite the clear skies.

"My youngest is seven months old. She was laying with my eldest son under the umbrella on the beach when it happened," she said.

Senior meteorologist with the Bureau of Meteorology, Sarah Scully said "blue sky" lightning strikes have been recorded up to 30 kilometres away from the nearest storm system.

"[Blue sky lightning] develops because thunderstorms are really really tall, sometimes they push up to 30,000 feet into the atmosphere," Ms Scully said.

"Lightning can occasionally shoot out at the top and travel through the clear air before it strikes the ground, sometimes 15 to 30 kilometres away."

More thunderstorms across NSW are expected today, with the weather bureau forecasting potentially dangerous storm cells across the state's Mid North Coast and Northern Rivers.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/d.title: Liberals announce plans for teen prison bootcamp for young offenders
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/d.author: Philippe Perez
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The facade of Dhurringile mansion in northern Victoria, located on the prison property. (Supplied: Hugh McGowan)

Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson has announced a plan to allow courts to send young offenders to the former Dhurringile Prison for a new bootcamp program if the Coalition wins November's state election.

The program would include daily physical tasks such as farm work or cleaning.

The site closed in September 2024, but local environmental and Aboriginal organisations were negotiating a purchase before the election.

The Victorian opposition says it will send young offenders to a bootcamp program near Shepparton if elected in November

Under the Coalition plan, courts could send offenders aged between 14 and 17 to the program as an alternative to a community corrections order or other custodial sentence.

The former Dhurringile Prison near Murchison would serve as a base for the program, where those sentenced would undertake daily tasks including farm work, cleaning, maintenance, cooking and education.

Unlike existing youth justice custodial orders, young offenders sent to the bootcamp would be required to take part in the daily program.

Political parties are laying out their visions for the state's future, as voters prepare to head to the polls on November 28.

Opposition leader Jess Wilson announced the new bootcamp program at the Coalition's campaign launch today and criticised Labor for having no plans for the facility.

"This is about instilling the discipline and respect that so many young offenders have not learned throughout their life, and crucially, giving them the skills they need to get on the right path," she said.

Jess Wilson made the announcement of the new bootcamp at her party's election launch on Sunday. (ABC News)

Nationals candidate for Shepparton Shane Sali said the program would benefit the local community.

"Bringing new activity to the facility will create opportunities for the local area, while helping address an issue that is affecting families, businesses and communities right across the Goulburn Valley," he said.

A similar program for older prisoners currently runs in Langi Kal Kal, in Victoria's west, focusing on agricultural work and preparing prisoners for life in the community.

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Labor criticised the announcement and said it was a "half-baked thought bubble" and that their own mandatory rehabilitation detention plan had been successfully tested in other countries.

"Labor has a fully costed $204 million plan, a clear legislative pathway and the facilities to start putting our plan in place immediately."

Premier Ben Carroll did not specifically respond to the plan at the Labor Party's launch today but focused on his record, saying he had built frontline services.

Ben Carroll told supporters on Sunday that a second police academy will be established if Labor is re-elected. (ABC News)

"We focused on community safety, boosting police powers as well as committing to hire another 1,500 more police and build a second police academy in Melbourne's west," he said.

In April last year, the Goulburn Broken Catchment Management Authority and the Yorta Yorta Nation Aboriginal Corporation were negotiating to purchase the site, but were awaiting a costing from the Victorian government.

Greater Shepparton City Council had also expressed interest in purchasing the site early last year, but withdrew its interest.

In October last year, it was revealed in parliament that maintenance at the site had cost just over $2 million for the year after the prison closed.

No income had been generated from leasing or farming activity since then.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.title: A Mexican Artist Sang Some of His Hits. Authorities Stopped the Show, Then Arrested Him.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.author: James Wagner
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world.text:
A concert by the singer Gabito Ballesteros was suspended after he sang songs that supposedly glorify cartel culture. The action has renewed a debate over culture and free speech.

Reporting from Mexico City

A popular Mexican singer’s concert was halted on Friday night because he performed songs considered to be glorifying cartel culture, making him the latest and most high-profile artist to be ensnared in a government crackdown on the genre known as narcocorridos.

He was later arrested by the federal authorities in relation to an unrelated investigation.

Gabito Ballesteros, 27, whose songs have billions of streams, was performing at a fair in Querétaro State in central Mexico when authorities escorted him off the stage.

Before the show, his set list was reviewed and approved by state officials and event organizers, according to a statement issued by the fair. Songs that glorified criminal activities were explicitly excluded, in accordance with state regulations, the fair said.

Last year, the state joined several other states and municipalities throughout Mexico that effectively prohibit the public performance of so-called narcocorridos, a version of traditional Mexican ballads that celebrate drug cartels instead of historic events and everyday life. Violations were punishable with fines or even jail time.

The actions — and the genre itself — have sparked much debate in Mexico, which has been wrestling with both the effects of organized crime, particularly amid pressure from the Trump administration to crack down on cartels, and its identity as defined through popular culture. The discussion also has became a referendum on free speech.

On Friday night, Mr. Ballesteros performed an unauthorized song and local authorities took him offstage to remind him of his prior agreement, the fair said. When he returned, the fair said Mr. Ballesteros started to perform another unauthorized song, “AMG.” The 2022 hit, which references the luxurious lifestyles and fancy cars of cartel members, has nearly one billion streams on Spotify.

James Wagner covers news and culture in Latin America for The Times. He is based in Mexico City.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/po.title: Key Witness in Comey Case Attests to Justice Dept.’s Aggressive Tactics
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/po.author: Alan Feuer
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/po.text:
A former aide to James Comey at the F.B.I. said the government had engaged in a “harassment campaign” in its efforts to secure witness testimony.

For more than a year, the Justice Department has gone hard after James B. Comey, the former F.B.I. director, using an array of rule-bending tactics in an effort to satisfy President Trump’s drive to see him charged.

In the three cases filed against Mr. Comey so far, prosecutors have improperly used search warrants to get evidence, made glaring errors in front of a grand jury and enlisted a mafia hit man in an effort to prove that Mr. Comey had broken the law.

They also considered treating The New York Times as Mr. Comey’s co-conspirator in a leak prosecution in what appeared to be a bid to breathe new life into accusations that might otherwise have been barred by the statute of limitations.

On Friday night, a new court filing added additional details to a portrait of belligerence, showing just how far investigators have been willing to roam in their pursuit of Mr. Comey.

This summer, the filing said, prosecutors hauled two workers at a New York apartment building in front of a grand jury in Florida after they refused to let an F.B.I. agent inside to serve a subpoena on one of its residents — a longtime confidant of Mr. Comey’s from whom the government wanted testimony.

The prosecutors also threatened to charge the confidant, Daniel C. Richman, with obstruction of justice for supposedly evading the subpoena, though he says that his lawyers had already agreed to accept it on his behalf.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Victor Wembanyama and why we crave sports villains
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Victor Wembanyama is a singular talent, one of one.

Wemby, as the 224-centimeter Frenchman with Congolese roots is affectionately known, can do things on a basketball court that most humans have experienced only on a Nerf hoop attached to a closet door.

He dunks from seemingly impossible distances or without even leaving the ground. Most players his size lumber. He’s uncannily graceful and quick. Wemby dribbles, spins, and sinks 3-pointers better than players who reach his armpits. He’s also the first NBA player ever to receive every first-place vote for Defensive Player of the Year.

The 22-year-old phenom led his San Antonio Spurs to the NBA Finals last June. But something surprising happened to the new star during that playoff run: Wembanyama was suddenly hated.

He was ejected from a second-round playoff game for elbowing a Minnesota Timberwolves opponent in the throat. The slow-motion replays made it look like a blow from a John Wick film. In the Finals, he shoved New York Knicks star Jalen Brunson to the floor, then laughed as Brunson protested.

Wembanyama is built like a streetlamp, willowy and strong, with a 243-cm wingspan. Brunson may be an All-Star, but he stands barely above 183 cm, far more ordinary and earthbound. When the Knicks won the series, with Brunson the Finals MVP, many people cheered David slaying Goliath.

During the series, the cover of the New York Post featured Wembanyama in a “Wanted” poster. He caught more heat for skipping the post-series handshakes and telling reporters in the news conference after the final game, “See you all never.”

“Is Wemby the quickest hero-to-villain arc in sports history?” a reader asked the Ringer’s Bill Simmons, one of the NBA’s most influential tastemakers.

“I think you can make the case [that] the Finals alone changed how people looked at him entirely,” Simmons answered.

Wembanyama remains the frontrunner for MVP this year in just his fourth season in the league. He’s also found himself cast in the classic role of the bad guy.

“Now there’s a lot of places in the NBA where people don’t love you anymore,” a reporter said to Wembanyama this fall. “They vilify you.”

Wembanyama replied that he was fine with fans of other teams viewing him as the enemy.

“We are fighting for the top spot on the mountain, and we are going to have to move people in our way,” he said.

This supposed heel turn, when a likable star athlete gets reclassified as a villain, got me thinking about how sports villains are made. Some athletes deliberately cultivate the role. Others earn it through their behavior. And some find themselves cast as the bad guy whether they want the part or not.

The idea of the heel turn comes from the scripted dramas of professional wrestling. But athletes from other sports have recognized that to be a superstar who fills stadiums and captures the fascination of fans as well as marketers, talent often isn’t enough. It also helps to become a character in a morality play.

Muhammad Ali was the greatest at this — as he was the first to remind people while performing — as the world’s most boastful boxer.

The heavyweight champion revealed in a 1969 interview that he learned about the value of adopting an arrogant persona from a conversation he had with a wrestler known as Gorgeous George, who was famous for his over-the-top, staged narcissism.

“He told me people would come to see me get beat,” Ali said. “Others would come to see me win. I’d get ’em coming and going.”

Ali took on a more polarizing and riskier persona as well — that of the athlete activist. In 1967, with public opinion about the Vietnam War dividing the nation, he refused to be drafted into the military. He was stripped of his title and banned from fighting for over three years.

He was celebrated and reviled by people on opposite ends of the political divide, in much the way Colin Kaepernick was when he took a knee during performances of the national anthem before NFL games in 2016 to protest police killings of Black civilians.

The Indiana Fever’s Sophie Cunningham became a flash point of controversy this past WNBA season both for her hard fouls and her opinions in the Trump-era culture wars on topics like transgender athletes. Her nickname: MAGA Barbie.

There’s another bad guy archetype, that of the rule-breaking bully, that players — or even entire teams — have leaned into to gain an advantage over their opponents.

The intimidating Detroit Pistons of the late 1980s, with Bill Laimbeer and Dennis Rodman, called themselves the Bad Boys and played basketball like they were in a bar fight. Argentina won the World Cup four years ago with a classically beautiful style of play. This summer, with an older and less talented roster, they deployed a slugging, physical, fouling strategy — which led them all the way back to the finals.

Joakim Noah understands both sides of the villain role. The retired Chicago Bulls center is another big man originally from France, having moved from Paris to New York when he was 12. He enthusiastically played the “black hat” when he saw it as a means to motivate his teammates or irritate opponents. Noah says some players are wired to feed off the negative energy of tens of thousands of opposing fans raining boos on them.

“I felt like it was us versus the world, and I loved that,” he says. “I always played my best.”

The same could be said of Dillon Brooks of the NBA’s Phoenix Suns (known as Dillon the Villain), as well as “bad guy” racecar drivers of the past, such as NASCAR’s Kyle Busch or F1’s Michael Schumacher.

To see Wemby as only a heel, however, is to overlook much else about him.

Not that it registered with most Americans, but this fall he spoke out in support of the hundreds of thousands in France who’d taken to the streets to protest neglect of the country’s public education system.

And unlike nearly all of his peers and every major professional sports league, Wemby has refused to work with betting companies or prediction markets.

“I will never do that,” he told reporters. “Honestly, I think it’s very sad to see some players promote it.”

For a 22-year-old, let alone one of the greatest athletes alive, he’s intellectually and culturally curious. While on the road for a game in New York in 2024, Wemby  played chess against fans in Washington Square Park. He spent part of his offseason in 2025 in a Chinese monastery training with Shaolin monks — meditating, hiking, practicing kung fu. It was like Batman’s hero’s journey.

There’s a video that went viral from the 2025 NBA All-Star Game of Wemby in the locker room with a book. Three-time MVP Nikola Jokic teases him.

“I read before every game,” Wemby replies. “Is that crazy? It’s not like I brought an octopus or something.”

He and teammate Harrison Barnes, who is 12 years older, started a team book club, and the San Antonio Public Library launched the “Read Like Wemby” initiative so people can check out his reading list. It includes George Orwell’s 1984, the Dune series, lots of fantasy.

In her TED talk, the Nigerian novelist Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie doesn’t bring up basketball or Wembanyama, but she focuses on what’s missed when someone’s humanity is reduced to a single story: “The single story creates stereotypes, and the problem with stereotypes is not that they are untrue, but that they are incomplete. They make one story become the only story.”

Wembanyama told 60 Minutes recently that he learned from his immature outbursts during last year’s postseason: “It showed my limits more than anything else. Going out there, you need to play basketball. You don’t need to beat the s--- out of people — if you want to win, at least.”

Wemby should remain in the spotlight for years to come. I suspect the heel label won’t stick, even among opposing fans. He may break their hearts, but he doesn’t need to play a character to dominate on the court.

“Hate it or love it,” Noah says, “we are blessed to be able to watch what the future of the NBA is, and it’s him.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Oliver Holmes and Rebecca Bailey
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings

The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.

Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.

The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy.

Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.

“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”

Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines, starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.

While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.

Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea, where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.

The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.

For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.

The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.

Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.

Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.

“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.

Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.

China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.

Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas. Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.

A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore.

Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration. Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.

Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

Additional research by Yu-chen Li
