https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Anthony Albanese apologises for hot-mic gaffe after Coalition criticises ‘locker-room talk’
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Tom McIlroy in Manila
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Prime minister says he and Chris Bowen were having ‘light-hearted banter’ when they were caught discussing where they keep their phones

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese has apologised for a hot-mic gaffe at the UN climate talks in Turkey, saying he regretted being overheard discussing mobile phone radiation and “dicks” in a candid conversation.

“I of course regret that. I apologise,” Albanese said during a visit to the Australian warship HMAS Stalwart in the Philippines on Sunday.

Enter your email to keep reading – for free. It takes just 30 seconds

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“This was a private conversation, we thought, between two friends having a bit of light-hearted banter.”

Ahead of a meeting at the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya on Friday, Albanese and the climate change minister, Chris Bowen, were caught on camera discussing which pocket they use to keep their mobile phone.

Albanese can be heard telling Bowen that he should store his phone away from his heart because “it can interfere with your rhythm”. Laughing, Bowen asks whether the advice was because a phone can be “a little bit radioactive”.

Albanese says “it makes absolute sense”, before Bowen replies that he was more conscious of putting his phone in his pants pocket. The prime minister asks: “Because of your dick?”

Bowen agrees and says: “Arguably more important than the heart.”

On Sunday, Albanese played down the incident which occurred ahead of a meeting with business leaders in Antalya.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“No one was hurt or harmed. We weren’t having private banter which criticised anyone,” he said.

The speedy apology is in contrast to previous gaffes by Albanese, including long-running controversy over comments about the gift of melons from Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, on a podcast.

Albanese previously apologised for saying he would “shag” Australian singer Kylie Minogue in the same episode of the Bush Deep podcast.

Sign up to Politics, really

Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you

after newsletter promotion

The melons comment risked becoming an international incident, as Albanese repeatedly insisted the comments and his corresponding hand gestures were not a reference to breasts.

Japan’s government sent a diplomatic cable to Australia in July, days after the podcast originally aired, claiming there had been “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” and saying they detected no “ill intention” in Albanese’s statement.

The Coalition on Sunday criticised Albanese and Bowen’s comments.

Opposition frontbencher James Paterson said the remarks were unfortunate, telling News24 they could damage impressions of Australia on the world stage.

“That locker-room talk like that has a time and a place and it’s not at international summits when you’re the prime minister of Australia talking to your energy minister,” he said.

But the employment minister, Amanda Rishworth, dismissed the criticism, saying the comments were a joke.

“This is a private conversation in between meetings,” she said.

“I know that a hot-mic incident is very exciting for people ... but really, there are bigger issues to tackle and discuss.”

Earlier a spokesperson for the prime minister said the hot-mic comments were “a joke in between meetings”.

Albanese is in the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit and high-level diplomatic meetings, including with the US president, Donald Trump.

He will hold formal bilateral talks with the Filipino president, Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr, on Sunday and visited a Jollibee fast food restaurant to celebrate the chain’s expansion to Australia.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/h.title: Australian doctors say health anxiety is being fuelled by social media
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/h.author: Scout Wallen
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Ashley Bowden says about half of his patients are dealing with some form of health anxiety. (Supplied: Ashley Bowden)

Doctors say health anxiety is being fuelled by social media content.

Advertisements for predictive medical tests and longevity tools are trending online.

GPs say people should talk to a doctor before spending money on these trends.

Ashley Bowden spends a large part of his workday counselling patients for their health anxiety in his regional NSW practice.

"It almost feels as if it's 50 per cent of the patients I see; we end up touching on health anxiety," he said.

"There's certainly a number of patients that have quite severe anxiety around their health."

Ashley Bowden is a GP in regional NSW. (Supplied: Ashley Bowden)

Dr Bowden said social media was fuelling the issue.

"I absolutely love talking to patients about what they've seen online … what they're worrying about and what's causing them to spiral," he said.

Olivia Loughnan completed her PhD on the link between social media and health anxiety. (Supplied: Olivia Loughnan)

Psychologist Olivia Loughnan said social media played a "significant" role in triggering health anxiety.

She said algorithms reinforced health-related fears by responding to what users watched, searched for and engaged with.

"Someone who watches a video about the early warning signs of a serious illness, they may subsequently be exposed to more content about related symptoms," Dr Loughnan said.

"It can create the impression that serious illnesses are increasingly common or personally relevant to them."

Dr Bowden said the online marketing of predictive medical tests and health screenings, such as full body MRI scans or blood tests, was also playing a role.

"I have a lot of patients that are on supplements or they're undertaking private tests at huge expense," he said.

The products are part of the world of longevity, biohacking and health optimisation, which has a strong following online.

Biohacking and anti-aging science are raising hopes of living longer. What's hype and what shows promise?

Dr Loughnan said the trends could be positive by encouraging people to be more proactive about their health and wellbeing.

"However, the concern is that pursuit of that optimal health can become excessive," she said.

"When people are constantly exposed to information about hidden diseases, prevention scans, biological aging … they can begin to feel that being healthy is simply not enough."

She said it reinforced the idea that people should be constantly monitoring their bodies for symptoms.

"Psychologically, this can create heightened need for control, increased body monitoring and difficulty tolerating uncertainty," she said.

A woman at a biohacking conference in New York City. (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

Australian Medical Association president Michael Bonning said the tests were increasingly popular around the country.

"We see more patients seeking frequent or increasingly, not just comprehensive, but almost fringe investigations," Dr Bonning said.

"It's sometimes very difficult for a doctor to push back and say, 'No, you really shouldn't have that,' even though it is very clear that intervention or investigation doesn't have an evidence base to it."

It’s good to be on top of your health – but how far would you go to ensure you’re staying healthy?

An example of one of these tests being advertised online is full body MRI scans, which cost thousands of dollars and do not use radiation.

"It's really tempting to think that surely that's going to give us more information … we'll find the bad thing if it exists, whether it's a lump or a cancer," Dr Bowden said.

Dr Bonning and Dr Bowden said they were more likely to catch incidental findings, which could lead to false positives and invasive tests.

Dr Bowden said if people were concerned by something they had seen online, or were thinking about taking one of the tests, they should speak to a trusted GP.

"They can say, 'I've seen this online' or 'I've put it into an AI bot,' because that gives us a point of the conversation to talk around," he said.

He also said it was important to be critical of ads.

"Is the person marketing that in any way interested in improving their health, or do they have an ulterior motive like making money?" he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/t.title: Tim Winton talks Rinehart, rage, climate change and Cloudstreet
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/t.author: Courtney Bembridge
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Courtney Bembridge

After more than four decades as a published author, Tim Winton is looking back with a collection of personal essays.  (ABC Arts: Nina Otranto)

Tim Winton has been publishing books for more than 40 years, but there's one that stands out.

Cloudstreet — recently voted Australia's favourite book in an ABC poll — was a defining moment in Winton's career, but it's a book that almost never was.

In the late 1980s, Winton was in Europe with his wife and young son.

A young Tim Winton in 1998.  (Supplied)

"We were in transit carrying all our earthly goods, and we were catching a bus to the airport in Rome, and we got off the bus," he said.

"We were just going into the terminal, and just before we got to the glass doors, this Italian guy started tugging on my sleeve … he's really quite insistent," Winton recalls.

"I stopped eventually, and he was pointing back at the bus and … there was one little grey sports bag in there, and I just couldn't believe it. It was all the manuscripts, all the type scripts, all the carbon copies, all the notes, my entire novel to that point about to head off into Rome unaccompanied.

"If it hadn't been for just the decency of that guy … I could have kissed him because, in a way, he saved our lives because that was the book that saved our lives."

The opening passage of Cloudstreet is set on the banks of Perth's Swan River, or Derbal Yerrigan. (ABC News: Courtney Bembridge)

Cloudstreet follows the fortunes of two families — the Lambs and the Pickles — over two decades in mid-20th-century Perth.

The book has been adapted for radio, theatre, opera and television, and in the 35 years since it was released, it has never been out of print.

"I can't really get my head around the life that the book has had," he said.

"I do have people coming up to me almost every day."

The opening passage from the book reads as follows:

"Will you look at us by the river! The whole restless mob of us on spread blankets in the dreamy briny sunshine skylarking and chiacking about for one day, one clear, clean, sweet day in a good world in the midst of our living." — Cloudstreet, 1992

Winton told 7.30 people told him the book reminded them of a gentler time, a kinder country.

"Probably the most consistent thing that people say to me seems to be about the kind of decency that they see in it, a kind of a yearning for solidarity and neighbourliness," Winton said.

Tim Winton's Cloudstreet was voted Australia's favourite book in an ABC poll. (ABC News: Jack Stevenson)

Winton's latest book, Songs from the Firefront, is a collection of personal essays exploring how people find meaning, community and hope in an era marked by climate change, rage and social upheaval.

"The book is me reflecting on my own anguish and my own rage," he said.

He says the rise of big tech and the way algorithms seize on people's rage is feeding dangerous rhetoric, and those in charge need to be held accountable.

"People are profiting from our rage," Winton said.

"This is the thing that kills me. This is essentially a business model to make us angry, to make us scream at each other, to make us want to own each other, to destroy each other in public.

"I think the way our government at the moment is threatening to adopt a very supine attitude to those tech bros is a cause of deep concern … these bro-ligarchs or, as somebody very wisely has called it, the 'Nerd Reich'.

"I just think we need to be more assertive."

Big tech bosses are not the only ones who come in for criticism in his book.

He writes about his view of mining magnate Gina Rinehart in these words: "She does not value or understand: the natural world, tenderness, mercy, fellow feeling."

Tim Winton describes Gina Rinehart as a "lonely oligarch".  (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Given Mrs Rinehart has a lot of power, Winton is asked if writing about her makes him nervous?

"I think everybody's nervous and careful in speaking about that person for those reasons, because there's just so much form," he said.

Winton went on to say it was hard to explain to people outside of Western Australia the influence that Mrs Rinehart, and her father Lang Hancock, had had "on every element of society in politics, in the media, in communications. The amount of fear and awe that they generate".

In June One Nation leader Pauline Hanson told the ABC that she consulted Mrs Rinehart on policy and considered her a friend.

And it was revealed in July that Mrs Rinehart paid for Senator Hanson's flights from London to Sicily earlier this year and arranged for her to attend high-end fashion shows.

Winton said he was concerned about Mrs Rinehart's growing political influence.

7.30 approached Mrs Rinehart for a response through her company. A spokesperson for Hancock Prospecting disagreed with Winton's views and suggested the author was promoting socialism.

"Tim needs to better understand, the socialist style causes he espouses, which are the very opposite of caring. And the very opposite of tenderness and mercy," the spokesperson told 7.30 in a statement.

"And Tim needs to understand, what does enable better outcomes: investment, innovation, and the opportunities these bring, lifting the standards of living of those fortunate enough not to live in his uncaring, merciless socialist utopias.

The spokesperson also stated that Mrs Rinehart and her companies had paid "$25 billion" in taxes over the past decade, which they said helped "provide for nurses, hospitals, police, veterans, the elderly, emergency services, defence and so much more for her fellow Australians".

"Sadly, Mrs Rinehart and Tim are likely to always disagree on the governments most important responsibility, defending our country and its citizens."

Acclaimed author Tim Winton on why now is the right time for a memoir. (Courtney Bembridge)

Winton has been considering how the world should respond to rising temperatures for decades.

His 2024 novel, Juice, imagines a world where most of Australia is uninhabitable due to extreme weather.

"We had a generation to take swift and decisive climate action. We haven't done that.

Scorched land after bushfires that took place in Lancelin, Western Australia, 2023. ( ABC News: James Carmody )

"The best we can do now is to adapt and to mitigate the bits that we can. And sadly, we know that we're going to lose ecosystems, we're going to lose species, and a lot of people are going to live in more anguish and more straightened circumstances than needed to.

"And when you come from a prosperous country like ours, I don't think that's a tragedy. I think that's an outrage."

Tim Winton says the lack of action on climate change has been an "outrage".  (ABC News: Courtney Bembridge)

As to why he wrote a memoir,  a strange deviation for someone who is known to be very private, Winton said it was the right time.

"It's just a way of trying to sift through that stuff and figure things out and give an account of myself to myself as much as for anybody else," he said.

Tim Winton's mother with his young daughter. (Supplied)

"It's not really a proper memoir; it's just a sort of set of thoughts and reflections in the mode of memoir.

"You get to a sort of fulcrum point in your life where you realise there's more time behind you than years ahead of you, and that makes you reflect on where you've been … and what's most precious to you. And obviously that's the kids and their kids."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Concerns arise as Takaichi’s X posts not kept as records
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi makes active use of X, formerly Twitter, to communicate on behalf of the government.

The government says, however, that posts from her personal account are not administrative records under the public records and archives management law. No legal provision requires the posts to be preserved, and critics warn that they may not be available for later scrutiny.

From the launch of her administration in October last year through Oct. 12 this year, Takaichi posted 843 times on X. That is more than two posts a day on average, an unusually high rate compared with her predecessors.

Some of her posts are about her private life, while others are made as president of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party. Most, however, concern official duties, including explanations of government policies and legislation, reports on summit diplomacy and messages to the public during disasters.

Her most widely shared post since she took office was a photo of herself with U.S. President Donald Trump during his visit to Japan in October 2025. It was reposted more than 55,000 times.

In August this year, Takaichi posted a series of messages explaining her government’s measures against rising prices. She also sometimes communicates directly with foreign leaders by replying to their posts on X.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara has said the posts come from a personal account and are therefore not public records.

Noriko Ishigaki, an Upper House member from the opposition Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan, asked in writing whether the prime minister’s posts represent the government’s official positions. In its written reply, the government said the posts were “not from an account operated by the government” and that it was “not in a position to answer.”

Takaichi, however, has said of her use of X: “There are times when I want to provide timely updates on government initiatives, and I can also hear directly from the public. It has a certain value.” Her remarks suggest that she sees X as a way to communicate as head of the executive branch.

The public records and archives management law defines administrative records as documents “created or obtained by employees of administrative agencies in the course of their duties” and “held for organizational use.”

According to the Cabinet Office’s records and archives management division, posts on X by the Cabinet secretary for public affairs meet this definition, but posts from lawmakers’ personal accounts do not.

Trump is another national leader who makes active use of social media. In the United States, the Presidential Records Act requires the president’s posts on official matters to be preserved and managed as public records, even when they come from a personal account. Records of edits and deletions are also kept, and the National Archives later makes an archive of them public.

Hajime Sebata, a professor of Japanese political history at Ryukoku University and an expert on public records management, called it “a gap in the law” that the prime minister’s social media posts are not covered by the public records and archives management law.

“We live in an era when the prime minister’s social media posts carry significant political influence. Records must be kept so that the politics of the day can be examined later,” he said. “The prime minister and Cabinet ministers hold public positions while in office, so their posts should be preserved as public records regardless of their content.”

The law describes public records as “an intellectual resource to be shared by the people in supporting the basis of sound democracy.” It also seeks to ensure the accountability of the state and incorporated administrative agencies “to the public for their various activities in both the present and future.”

With the prime minister’s social media posts becoming more prominent, how to preserve and manage them is likely to draw closer scrutiny.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Zimbabwe’s HIV gains face a test among young people
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Harare, Zimbabwe – When Shaun Moyo started nursing at Parirenyatwa Hospital in Harare in the late 1990s, the effects of the HIV epidemic were visible in the hospital wards and beyond them. Patients filled the wards, she recalls, while funerals had become a familiar part of everyday life.

Nearly three decades later, the picture has changed. Antiretroviral treatment has transformed the lives of people living with HIV. Condoms, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) and other prevention options also give young people more ways to protect themselves.

But Moyo, now a 48-year-old nurse working locum shifts at two major public hospitals in Harare, worries that some young people may not fully appreciate the risks.

Her concern reflects a wider challenge for Zimbabwe: how to protect hard-won progress against HIV while ensuring that young people understand, can access and are willing to use the prevention tools available to them.

Dr Misheck Ruwende, a Zimbabwean family physician and advocate for reducing HIV stigma, shares that concern. In a public address on Twitter in September, followed online by Al Jazeera, members of the public and other local journalists, Ruwende warned that the country risked losing some of the gains made over decades.

“The sad part is that this is coming at a time we have the best options to prevent HIV, from rapid testing, PrEP, condoms, PEP to injectables,” Ruwende said.

“It wasn’t like that in the late 90s to early 2000s. It looks like we are now reversing all this huge success we had notched in recent times,” he added.

The scale of Zimbabwe’s progress is clear in the national figures. UNAIDS estimates that annual new HIV infections fell from 79,000 in 2010 to 15,000 in 2023. Among people aged 15 to 24, infections declined from an estimated 27,000 to 4,400 over the same period.

But falling infections do not mean the threat has disappeared. The challenge is to sustain those gains among young people navigating relationships, economic pressures and uneven access to youth-friendly health services. It is a challenge shared across a region that continues to carry a heavy burden of HIV.

For Moyo, the contrast between the epidemic she witnessed as a young nurse and the attitudes she encounters today can be difficult to accept.

“Seeing today’s youth who are blessed with condoms, ARVs and PrEP meds makes me furious,” she said. “In the 90s every weekend was a trek to cemeteries, not weddings.”

She believes the availability of effective treatment has changed how some young people perceive HIV. Because the virus is no longer the immediate death sentence it was once widely understood to be, she worries that some underestimate the consequences of infection.

Moyo recalled conversations involving her son and his friends on Facebook, where one comment suggested that “getting blood pressure is worse than HIV”.

Her observations are personal, not scientific evidence of changing attitudes among young people. But they point to a difficult public health task: explaining why prevention remains important even though treatment has made HIV a manageable chronic condition for many.

The concern is not confined to Zimbabwe. UNAIDS estimated that 210,000 adolescent girls and young women aged 15 to 24 acquired HIV worldwide in 2023. Some 160,000 of those infections were in sub-Saharan Africa, while nearly 60 percent of the global total occurred in Eastern and Southern Africa.

South Africa, Zimbabwe’s neighbour, illustrates the continuing scale of the epidemic in the region. UNAIDS estimated that 7.7 million people were living with HIV there in 2023.

Data from Gauteng province also point to concerns about sexually transmitted infections. Between April and December 2023, 167,109 males attended public health facilities in the province, and 67,400 were treated for Male Urethritis Syndrome (MUS), which is associated with sexually transmitted infections. The provincial health department reported that MUS incidence increased from 12 percent in 2020 to 15 percent in 2023. The condition is not itself a measure of HIV infections.

For Dr Linda-Gail Bekker, a South African HIV physician-scientist and co-author of the report on the PURPOSE 1 clinical trial, the response must combine scientific advances with prevention messages that speak to young people.

The Phase 3 trial examined lenacapavir, an injectable HIV prevention drug administered twice a year. In its primary analysis, none of the 2,134 women who received the drug acquired HIV.

The results highlighted the potential of long-acting prevention, but Bekker argues that medical advances must be matched by communication that resonates with young people.

“Beating the old drum about the horrors of HIV, and shouting to youths about condoms is not necessarily going to cut it,” she said.

She believes prevention efforts need to move beyond fear-based messages and give young people accurate information, accessible services and the freedom to make informed decisions without judgement.

That task has become more difficult amid funding pressures. UNAIDS reported in March 2025 that disruptions to US-funded HIV programmes in Zimbabwe had affected services for key populations, including access to PrEP, testing and counselling.

Bekker has also raised concerns about whether prevention information reaches young people in ways they find relevant. Traditional pamphlets and warnings about abstinence or faithfulness may fail to engage those already making decisions about sex and relationships.

She argues that public health workers need to acknowledge young people’s realities and provide practical information about reducing risk, including through PrEP. Services must also be adolescent-friendly, allowing young people to ask questions and seek help without feeling judged.

In Harare, 23-year-old peer educator Angela Gutu is taking that message beyond the clinic.

Working with the Harare municipality, the health ministry, nongovernmental organisations and churches, she helps organise pop-up health services at markets, transport hubs, university campuses and sporting events. These are places young people already visit, bringing information and services closer to them rather than expecting them to navigate a formal health facility.

The distinction matters, Gutu says. For some young people, asking for an HIV test or screening for a sexually transmitted infection at a clinic can be intimidating. Fear of judgement or harsh treatment by health workers can discourage them from seeking help.

At the pop-up clinics, young people can access HIV self-testing kits and condoms, while mobile health workers provide referrals for PrEP and other services. Peer educators can help make those conversations less daunting, giving young people an opportunity to ask questions in an environment where they feel more comfortable.

“It’s about speaking young people’s lingo, taking away the HIV stigma,” Gutu said.

Her work reflects a growing recognition that making prevention services available is not enough. They must also be approachable, confidential and responsive to the concerns young people bring with them.

Zimbabwe’s health authorities say they are also working to bring prevention and treatment closer to communities.

Dr Innocent Hove, Provincial Medical Officer for Harare Metropolitan Province, told reporters, including Al Jazeera, at an August meeting that tackling HIV among young Zimbabweans was an urgent priority.

The government is decentralising services including PrEP, PEP, HIV testing and treatment, as well as screening and treatment for sexually transmitted infections and tuberculosis.

Hove also pointed to mobile healthcare trucks being used to reach people in areas where conventional health facilities are difficult to access, including informal mining communities and remote artisanal gold-mining sites.

Such outreach could help people whose work, distance from clinics or financial circumstances make regular visits difficult. But its impact will depend on whether services are consistently available and reach those most in need.

For young people, access means more than knowing that PrEP or HIV testing exists. It means being able to obtain services without prohibitive costs, long journeys or fear of stigma.

Bongani, who plans to volunteer as a peer educator through the health ministry’s programme in January, wants to help make prevention information more accessible to his generation.

“My generation was born with the best array of HIV prevention tools. It’ll be a tragedy if AIDS deaths make a dramatic comeback due to our reckless behaviours,” he said.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have identified two brain regions that show signs of deterioration earlier than the hippocampus, the area commonly examined for evidence of the disease.

The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.

By examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus. These changes may offer important new clues about how Alzheimer's develops and how it could be detected before significant cognitive decline occurs.

"We have found that there are early changes in the brain manifesting the clinical biomarkers of atrophy as much as a decade before there are clinical symptoms," said biomedical engineer and senior author Michael Miller. "It's at least a 5-to-10-year play where your brain is changing. Imagine if we could start to treat the neurodegenerative changes at the 2, 3 or 4-year point rather than after 15 years when the changes are manifesting in memory symptoms. That's the great promise here for your loved ones who are at risk."

The findings were recently published in NeuroImage Reports and are being presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

Detecting Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss Begins

Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, but the disease does not begin when someone first experiences forgetfulness or confusion. Changes associated with Alzheimer's can accumulate in the brain for decades before noticeable symptoms emerge.

Scientists believe this long period of silent progression may provide a crucial opportunity for treatment. Interventions that begin before extensive damage occurs could potentially do more to preserve memory and other cognitive abilities. However, taking advantage of that opportunity requires reliable ways to identify the disease in its earliest stages.

One promising approach involves biomarkers, measurable biological changes that can indicate the presence or progression of a disease. In Alzheimer's research, these markers could help reveal who is developing the condition before symptoms become apparent.

"Our goal is to be able to treat individuals before the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease develop so that they may delayed or even stopped," said Marilyn Albert, co-author and director of the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.

Two Brain Regions Reveal Earlier Warning Signs

To investigate where the earliest detectable changes occur, the researchers examined hundreds of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans collected through two independent research projects: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study.

The scans followed people at different stages of Alzheimer's disease over time, including individuals without symptoms, those experiencing cognitive impairment, and patients who ultimately died from the disease.

In both groups, the researchers observed a consistent pattern. The entorhinal cortex and amygdala, which are located near the hippocampus, showed greater relative tissue loss during the early stages of Alzheimer's than the hippocampus itself.

This distinction matters because the hippocampus plays a central role in memory and has traditionally been a major focus when doctors look for Alzheimer's-related brain damage.

The two newly highlighted regions perform important functions of their own. The entorhinal cortex helps retrieve previously stored memories, while the amygdala contributes to emotional memory, including how emotional experiences are processed and remembered.

Their earlier shrinkage suggests that examining these structures together could reveal signs of Alzheimer's that might be less apparent when attention is focused primarily on the hippocampus.

Brain Shrinkage Linked to Alzheimer's Tau Protein

The researchers also found an important connection between the loss of brain tissue and tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Under normal conditions, tau helps maintain the internal structure of nerve cells. In Alzheimer's, however, tau can accumulate abnormally and form tangles that interfere with healthy brain function.

Using PET imaging and digital pathology, the scientists found that areas of gray matter shrinkage overlapped with regions showing tau-related changes. Gray matter contains large numbers of nerve cell bodies and is essential for processing information throughout the brain.

This relationship strengthens the possibility that changes in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala could serve as useful indicators of early Alzheimer's disease.

The team believes that measuring tissue loss in both regions, rather than relying primarily on changes in the hippocampus, could eventually improve predictions of who is likely to develop cognitive decline.

As brain imaging becomes more accessible and less expensive, this approach could also become increasingly practical. For people with a family history of Alzheimer's or other risk factors, researchers envision a future in which doctors might examine these regions as early as a person's 30s or 40s.

"As biomarkers and treatments become increasingly available, knowing who is going to have cognitive decline is going to be really important," said co-author Meaghan Morris, a neuropathologist who studies Alzheimer's and other dementias. "This could really play into better risk stratification for identifying who is going to have cognitive decline in the near future -- and treating people earlier and earlier to hopefully slow the course of the disease."

A Potential New Path Toward Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment

Although the findings are promising, more research is necessary before doctors can use these brain changes as a reliable diagnostic tool. The study identifies potential early biomarkers, but it does not yet establish a clinical test capable of predicting Alzheimer's years in advance.

The next step is to investigate what happens within these regions at a much smaller scale. The researchers want to understand the molecular changes surrounding abnormal tau accumulation and how those changes contribute to the progressive loss of brain tissue.

Identifying the biological processes involved could eventually reveal new targets for therapies designed to interrupt Alzheimer's before extensive damage occurs.

"Our future work is to better show the molecular neighborhoods associated with these Tau protein changes as localized by these clinical biomarkers of atrophy," Miller said. "Once we know more about the molecular neighborhoods, we can develop therapies."

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.

Quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.

Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.

Launched in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.

"These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," says Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so quickly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics."

Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars

Until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.

Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.

"Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting."

Among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.

Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn

Two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.

These discoveries establish new records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.

"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," says Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.

The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.

"The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a big step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level."

Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies

One of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.

Their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where new stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an important glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.

These quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.

"Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," says ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.

How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants

Euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.

"Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.

"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground."

All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.

Although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.

As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide new clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Big Bang.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean. New research suggests that marine resources washed onto prehistoric beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey millions of years ago.

Today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food. Scientists call this process marine subsidization (MS). It is especially common in coastal environments and can become more important when food on land is limited, such as during droughts.

A new study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs. By examining chemical signatures preserved in fossils, researchers found evidence that ocean resources contributed to prehistoric food chains.

"We show that coastal terrestrial organisms in the greenhouse climates of the Cretaceous relied on marine resources to supplement their diets in a similar way that modern organisms do," said first author Dr. Clayton Forster, a geologist at the University of Arkansas. "We can identify that marine resources are passed along the food chain and incorporated in the minerals of bones and teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, and fish."

Mysterious Chemical Clues in Dinosaur Teeth

The discovery helps explain a longstanding mystery involving the chemical composition of dinosaur teeth.

Plants contain two forms of carbon known as isotopes: 'light' (C-12) and 'heavy' (C-13). Scientists can measure the relative amounts of these isotopes, expressed as δ13C, to identify a chemical fingerprint that passes from food into the animals that consume it.

As animals eat, this carbon signature becomes incorporated into their tooth enamel. The δ13C value in enamel is typically higher than that of the food consumed, with living animals generally showing an increase of between 11 and 13 parts per thousand.

However, previous measurements of dinosaur teeth have consistently revealed unusually high values. These readings also exceed what scientists would expect from animals that ate only plants growing on land, which generally have lower δ13C values than most marine plants.

One possible explanation is that dinosaurs, or the animals they consumed, were obtaining some of their nutrients from the ocean.

"By determining the carbon isotope composition of dinosaur, fish, and crocodile tooth enamel, we can determine what their primary dietary source was and if they were different between regions," explained Forster.

Fossils Reveal a Prehistoric Ocean Food Source

To investigate, researchers examined fossils from (once) coastal locations bordering the Western Interior Seaway and the ancient coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. Around 100 million years ago, the Western Interior Seaway was an enormous inland sea that divided North America into two separate landmasses.

The team also analyzed fossils from locations farther inland, allowing them to compare animals that lived near the ocean with those that occupied landlocked environments.

The fossil deposits formed during two intervals of the Cretaceous Period: the early Albian (around 113-107 million years ago) and the early Cenomanian (approximately 100-96 million years ago).

Researchers used powdered fossil material to measure carbon isotope signatures from both periods. They also determined the latitudes where the animals had lived to investigate whether geography influenced the results.

A clear pattern emerged. Fossils from coastal environments consistently contained higher δ13C values than those from the inland formation. Remarkably, the coastal signatures remained similar across different locations, regardless of latitude or geological age.

These findings provide the first evidence of marine subsidization in prehistoric ecosystems, indicating that nutrients originating in the ocean were entering food chains on land millions of years ago.

Seaweed May Have Been on the Dinosaur Menu

The researchers next considered what ocean food source could explain the widespread chemical signatures.

"Coastal-dwelling organisms must have eaten some kind of organic matter from the ocean, or prey that had done so. This pattern is shared from fish to megaherbivores and indicates that the extra carbon source must have been low in the food-chain to affect both aquatic and terrestrial animals," Forster explained.

For the same chemical pattern to appear in such a wide variety of animals, the marine food source would likely have entered the food chain near its base. It also needed to be something that existed along coastlines but was absent farther inland, while remaining available for millions of years.

Seaweed emerged as the most likely explanation.

"Few organisms meet these criteria besides marine macroalgae or macrophytes - seaweeds," said Forster. "Given the almost ubiquitous behavior of large coastal herbivores today to supplement their diet with seaweeds, it's likely that most of the sampled herbivorous dinosaurs were no different."

Modern plant-eating animals living near coastlines often consume seaweed to supplement their diets. The fossil evidence suggests that many herbivorous dinosaurs may have behaved similarly, with marine nutrients also passing to other animals through the food chain.

Not Every Dinosaur Had a Taste for the Sea

Despite the widespread evidence of marine nutrients in coastal food webs, the researchers found that not every dinosaur took advantage of these resources.

One notable exception was Tenontosaurus tilletti, a large plant-eating dinosaur whose fossils have been discovered at numerous locations dating to the Cretaceous Period.

Its tooth enamel contained δ13C values comparable to those of modern animals that feed on plants growing on land. This suggests that Tenontosaurus tilletti did not rely on marine food sources, even though other dinosaurs apparently did.

The difference also strengthens the researchers' interpretation of the fossil evidence. If geological processes occurring after death had altered the carbon signatures in dinosaur teeth, the same unusual values would be expected more broadly. Instead, the variation between species suggests that the elevated readings reflect genuine differences in diet.

An Ancient Connection Between Land and Ocean

Although the findings provide strong evidence that marine resources supported the coastal ecosystems examined, important questions remain.

The available fossils do not include specimens from polar or equatorial regions during the early Albian and early Cenomanian. As a result, scientists cannot yet determine how widespread this feeding behavior was across different latitudes.

Additional studies will also be needed to establish whether similar relationships existed during other geological periods, including the earlier Jurassic Period and the later early Cenozoic Era.

Beyond revealing a surprising possibility about what dinosaurs ate, the discovery highlights how closely life on land has been connected to the ocean throughout Earth's history.

"Our study emphasizes the connections between terrestrial and marine ecosystems," concluded Forster. "They are deeply intertwined and have been for hundreds of millions of years. It highlights the importance of environmental linkages across time and space and protecting them where they exist today."
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: Scientists examined fossils from coastal locations bordering the Western Interior Seaway and the Gulf of Mexico. They found evidence that ocean resources contributed to prehistoric food chains. Scientists call this process marine subsidization (MS)

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Physicists at Auburn University have discovered how to use brief bursts of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions hidden inside a crystal. Their findings shed new light on a mystery that has puzzled researchers for decades and demonstrate how lasers can influence the material's electrical behavior. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists explore faster ways to process and store information.

The research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter Endowed Associate Professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil. Their paper, "Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition," received an Editors' Suggestion designation from Physical Review Letters. Scientists at Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology produced the crystals used in the study.

A Decades-Old Mystery Hidden Inside a Crystal

The researchers investigated a modified version of strontium titanate, a material with an unusual combination of electrical characteristics. Although electrons can travel through the crystal, it also contains extremely small regions with positive and negative electrical sides. Known as polar nanoregions, these microscopic "islands" can point in different directions or become aligned with one another. Understanding how and why this alignment occurs is essential to explaining the material's properties and learning how to manipulate them.

Scientists have spent decades trying to determine what happens when these regions become organized. One possibility is that atoms move together to produce the polarized state. Another is that the tiny electrical islands are already there and simply begin pointing in the same direction as temperatures fall. The distinction is similar to the difference between assembling a group of people and asking people who are already gathered to turn and face the same way. Because the regions are extraordinarily small and produce very weak signals, determining which explanation is correct has been a persistent challenge.

Laser Experiments Reveal How Electrical Order Emerges

To investigate, the Auburn researchers developed an exceptionally sensitive system that uses lasers to measure subtle changes in the crystal. By studying how the material altered incoming light, they were able to monitor the orientation of its electrical regions while repeatedly heating and cooling the sample.

The measurements revealed a clear pattern. At warmer temperatures, the tiny regions pointed in seemingly random directions. When the crystal cooled, however, they began adopting preferred orientations. This behavior provided compelling evidence that the electrical islands existed before becoming aligned, supporting the explanation that cooling organizes regions already present in the material.

A Flash of Light Creates Order in a Trillionth of a Second

The team went beyond observing this natural process. Researchers also demonstrated that short laser pulses could temporarily align the electrical islands, even at higher temperatures when the regions would ordinarily remain disorganized. Using an optical measurement, they were able to detect the pattern produced by the laser light.

The effect was extraordinarily brief, lasting approximately one picosecond, or one trillionth of a second. Nevertheless, the ability to create and detect this electrical alignment using light provides a promising approach for studying how information might be controlled at extremely high speeds.

Three Years of Experiments Lead to a Breakthrough

Achieving these results required considerable patience and technical refinement. The collaboration began at the 2023 American Physical Society March Meeting, where Jin met Japanese researchers capable of producing the specialized crystals needed for the experiments.

Back at Auburn, the team spent almost a year refining its equipment before it could reliably detect the weak optical signals from the tiny electrical regions. The next obstacle was even more demanding: measuring the extremely short interval during which laser illumination caused the regions to align.

"The breakthrough came in 2025, when Mohamed finally observed the disordered polar regions becoming aligned under laser illumination," Jin said. "Seeing that signal emerge was a thrilling moment for the team."

The achievement also represents an important personal milestone for Kandil, whose first published research paper reflects three years of dedicated experimental work.

"This experiment has truly been Mohamed's odyssey," Jin said. "It took him three years of dedication to complete the work and achieve his first publication."

New Possibilities for Ultrafast Information Technology

The discovery provides important evidence about how electrical order develops in this unusual crystal while also establishing a method for manipulating that order with light. Rather than simply observing the material's internal behavior, researchers can now briefly influence its microscopic electrical patterns and detect the resulting changes.

Although practical applications remain a future possibility, the experiments offer a new way to investigate the rapid electrical processes occurring inside quantum materials. By revealing how light can control these previously elusive patterns, the Auburn researchers have opened another avenue for exploring technologies that could one day transform how information is processed and stored.
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: Researchers at Auburn University have discovered how to use brief bursts of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions hidden inside a crystal. The breakthrough could help scientists explore faster ways to process and store information. The researchers investigated a modified version of strontium titanate, a material with an unusual combination of electrical characteristics.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
A new study from the University of Otago, Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka, has revealed a surprising divide in the fortunes of one of New Zealand's least understood penguin species. Although Erect-crested penguins breed in just two remote island groups, their populations are experiencing dramatically different outcomes.

Published in PLOS ONE, the research found that one population has remained stable for at least 25 years, while the other has declined by more than 40 percent over the past three decades.

The study was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, which brings together scientists from the university's Departments of Zoology and Marine Science. Researchers also collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.

Drone Surveys Reveal a Surprising Penguin Population Divide

Erect-crested penguins breed exclusively on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two isolated island groups located approximately 800 kilometers southeast of New Zealand's South Island.

To determine how many penguins remain, researchers conducted extensive drone surveys between 2022 and 2024. They photographed and counted every breeding colony across both island groups, producing the first comprehensive population survey of the entire species.

"The results overturn a long-standing assumption," Dr. Mattern says.

"The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species' stronghold."

The difference in population trends was even more unexpected. Despite their small size, the Bounty Islands have maintained a relatively consistent number of breeding penguins for decades. Meanwhile, the much larger Antipodes Islands have experienced a substantial decline.

"Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.

"The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995."

Why Are Penguins Disappearing From the Antipodes Islands?

Researchers believe several overlapping pressures may explain why the two populations are heading in opposite directions. Natural predators, increasingly destructive storms, and differences in where the birds travel and feed could all be contributing.

One particularly troubling factor involves skuas, native subantarctic birds that prey on penguin eggs and chicks. As penguin colonies become smaller, the birds lose some of the protection that comes from nesting together in large numbers.

"As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further."

Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that changes involving another penguin species may have intensified this pressure.

Eastern Rockhopper penguins suffered a "catastrophically" severe population collapse during the second half of the 20th century. Similar declines occurred across their Southern Ocean breeding range, likely driven by warming ocean waters. Today, fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs remain on the Antipodes Islands.

"As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead," Dr. Pütz says.

Stronger Storms and Different Migration Routes Add to the Threat

Predators are not the only challenge facing the Antipodes penguins. Increasingly powerful storms, consistent with wider climate trends across the Southern Ocean, have caused landslides that break up breeding colonies and leave the birds more vulnerable.

Differences in ocean habitats and seasonal movements may also help explain why the two populations have experienced such contrasting outcomes.

According to Dr. Mattern, penguins breeding on the Antipodes Islands migrate considerable distances into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone when the breeding season ends. In contrast, birds from the Bounty Islands remain closer to their nesting grounds, where the surrounding waters are more sheltered and may offer more abundant food.

These differences could leave the two populations exposed to very different environmental pressures, despite belonging to the same species.

The Strange Paradox of Schrödinger's Penguin

The researchers have named this unusual situation "Schrödinger's Penguin," drawing inspiration from the famous physics thought experiment involving a cat inside a sealed box.

In that experiment, the cat is imagined to be both alive and dead until the box is opened and its condition is observed. But Dr. Mattern explains that the penguin discovery turns the familiar concept around.

"With Schrödinger's cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.

"With Erect-crested penguins, it's the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.

"Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn't one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands."

In other words, looking at the species as a whole can conceal what is happening within individual populations. Only by examining both island groups separately did researchers uncover how dramatically their circumstances differ.

A Hidden Conservation Crisis for Endangered Penguins

The Erect-crested penguin is currently one of only four penguin species worldwide classified as "Endangered" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another New Zealand penguin, the hoiho/yellow-eyed penguin, shares that designation.

However, the two species have received very different levels of attention. While the plight of the hoiho has attracted ongoing public interest and conservation efforts, the Erect-crested penguin has remained relatively overlooked.

Dr. Mattern explains that the species' current conservation classification relies on population estimates from the 1970s that were considerably inflated. When the new survey results are considered, the "Endangered" designation remains broadly appropriate for the declining Antipodes population, but not for the stable Bounty Islands population.

This creates a difficult conservation dilemma. If the two populations are combined into a single assessment, the species' overall threat classification could actually improve, even though one population continues to decline sharply.

"Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to "Vulnerable," masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species' last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing."

The researchers warn that a more favorable overall classification could create a misleading impression of security. Although the Bounty Islands population remains stable, it may still face significant threats, particularly from industrial fishing activity.

"A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger's box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs," Dr. Mattern says.

The findings highlight why conservation efforts must account for the circumstances of individual populations rather than relying exclusively on a species' global status. For Erect-crested penguins, recognizing the differences between the two island groups could be essential to protecting their future.

The study received funding from the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust and from the Global Penguin Society. The research was carried out under permits issued by the New Zealand Department of Conservation.
