https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss

The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict

Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening

Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans. The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms. Researchers hope to use the algorithm to help doctors direct preventive treatments toward patients most likely to benefit.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/f.title: Fix failings that led to Floreat murders, DV advocates say
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/f.author: Blake Kagi
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Jennifer and Gretl Petelczyc were shot dead by a gunman who entered their Floreat home searching for his ex-wife. (Supplied)

Advocates for domestic violence victims and survivors in Western Australia want improvements to the systems and data used to track potential offenders and protect those at risk.

The request follows a five-day coronial inquest into the 2024 murder of Jennifer and Gretl Petelczyc at the hands of Mark Bombara, which revealed police errors and missed opportunities to save the women's lives.

The state government has said it would carefully consider any recommendations from the coroner, who is due to release the inquest's findings next year.

The best way to honour the deaths of Jennifer and Gretl Petelcyzc is to ensure nobody else succumbs to the police errors and missed opportunities revealed by the coronial inquest into their shocking 2024 murders, advocates for victims and survivors of family violence say.

Mark Bombara had been looking for his estranged wife Rowena when he shot and killed her best friend Jennifer, and her teenage daughter Gretl, before turning the gun on himself in the affluent suburb of Floreat in Perth's west.

Over the past five days, the inquest heard how unheeded pleas to police for help, several Triple Zero calls left on hold and failings by the authorities to review gun licences had contributed to the tragedy.

Alison Evans (left) and Donna Chung (right) hope the Floreat murder victims' deaths will trigger change.   (ABC News: Blake Kagi)

"A critically important way to honour Jennifer and Gretl is to address the serious systematic gaps and missed opportunities that have come to light through the coronial inquest," said Alison Evans from the Centre for Women's Safety and Wellbeing.

With the acting state coroner Sarah Linton's findings set to be released next year, advocates hope the tragedy will lead to improvements in the system and data used to keep track of potential offenders and protect those at risk.

Curtin University social work professor Donna Chung, who, like Dr Evans, gave evidence at the inquest, called for more stringent measures to assess the risks posed by potential domestic violence perpetrators like Mark Bombara.

She highlighted how the inquest revealed that those in authority can miss warning signs, and that perpetrators of family violence can often hide in plain sight.

"He was one of the people that's able to be pleasant to community, pleasant outside the home, and unpleasant and abusive to his partner. It is something that's often not well understood," she said.

About two months before the murders, police escorted Mark Bombara's estranged wife to the family home to collect her belongings. She and her daughter Ariel had previously warned police about him several times.

The women were shot dead in their Floreat home. (ABC News: David Weber)

The inquest heard from Constable Shaun King, who accepted a cup of tea from the gunman, saying he thought Bombara "seemed like a nice guy" and that he was impressed by his opulent home.

A coronial inquest into the deaths of Jennifer Petelczyc and daughter Gretl puts police errors under the microscope.

Professor Chung said this was an example of the various systemic failures to understand the risk Bombara posed.

"It's really critical in the first instance that if in doubt, we assess something as being higher risk than it may be, because the consequences of underestimating are huge and significant," Professor Chung said.

The inquest has highlighted several police errors. (ABC News: Julian Robins)

The state government has pledged to strongly consider all the recommendations from the inquest. The murders helped trigger an overhaul of Western Australia's gun laws, which are now among the most stringent in the country.

Australian cricket's Sandpapergate saga has continued, with David Warner doubling down on social media while a former squad member declares he is comfortable saying the entire team knew about the infamous ball-tampering scandal.

Khawaja sent the cricket world into a spin last week when he claimed in his memoir, Sabr, that the ball-tampering scandal in Cape Town in 2018 was everyone in the team's responsibility.

David Warner, who was suspended with Cameron Bancroft and then-captain Steve Smith over the incident, backed Khawaja's account in Sabr, saying it was "100 per cent accurate", and on Saturday claimed he took the brunt of punishment without having all of the facts.

Sources connected to the Australian bowling group say they all spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into Cape Town ball tampering, which runs counter to claims by David Warner.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," he wrote on Instagram.

"If that's correct then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning … ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Multiple media outlets, including ABC Sport, have reported the bowlers were interviewed by Cricket Australia.

On Sunday, Warner then doubled down on his criticism of Cricket Australia and supported his previous post.

"Just to clarify 'As far as I am aware' was the POINT," he wrote.

"I was never told the bowlers had been interviewed or provided statements.

"That information would've been pretty useful when I was forced to make decisions back in 2018.

"Why weren't we given all the evidence by CA?"

Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball during the Test match in Cape Town, with an investigation determining he, Smith and vice-captain Warner were responsible for the ball tampering.

The trio was suspended, while the bowlers in that Test have always denied knowledge that sandpaper was being used on the ball.

Chadd Sayers, who was part of the Australian touring squad in 2018, said ahead of Australia's second ODI against England in Adelaide on Sunday that he was comfortable saying every member of the team knew sandpaper was being used.

"I'm comfortable saying where I'm sitting now that everyone knew what was going on [in South Africa in 2018]," Sayers said on the SEN broadcast.

"It [sandpaper] was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in change rooms … I'm not taking sides; it's just my recollection of what took place."

In his memoir, Khawaja claimed he knew sandpaper was being used on the ball and told Bancroft to be careful.

Khawaja also said ball-tampering was commonplace in cricket.

Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

"When he says 'we all knew', if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins said on Friday.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years; I did not know that was happening.

"But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper; that's complete and utter nonsense.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper. That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman that has been part of the team that's helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations. In his book Ussie's been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell a story, 100 per cent. I'm really glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: The COP31 talks showcase a disastrous post-American world
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Andreas Kluth
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
If you want to glimpse the fate of our world after the abdication of American leadership, as humanity struggles to cope with its biggest problems, cast your eye toward Antalya, Turkey. This is where delegations from some 200 countries have gathered for COP31, the 31st conference of the United Nations treaty to slow down climate change.

You’ll see some Americans walking around that conference, including congressmen, governors, mayors and other state politicians. But for the second year in a row, you won’t run into a delegation from the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump. Because there isn’t one.

Trump is boycotting not only the conference but the entire global effort to limit climate change. For the second time, he has withdrawn the United States from the Paris Agreement of 2015, the pact in which the parties of the U.N. framework convention pledged to cap global warming at about 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. He’s even pulled the U.S. out of that framework convention itself, an exit that takes effect in February and a step that no other country has ever taken.

The leader of the nation that is historically and cumulatively the largest emitter of greenhouse gases, and nowadays the second-largest after China, is sabotaging humanity’s attempt to clean up the mess Americans have helped to make.

And that attempt does seem to be failing: In September, the U.N. Environment Program confirmed that “overshooting” the goals set at Paris is now “unavoidable.” That collective failure has many causes in many places. But Trump is a big one.

Scientists call his policies for the past 22 months an “all-out assault” against clean energy. The administration has halted or defunded offshore wind projects and other efforts to get more energy from renewable sources. And it has eliminated swathes of regulations by the Environmental Protection Agency that were meant to limit emissions from vehicles and power plants. The gist is to favor fossil-fuel industries.

Because America is so huge, this policy U-turn makes a global difference. The U.N.’s latest “emissions gap report,” issued in October, finds that in 2025, the first year of Trump’s second term, the increase of emissions in the U.S. (of 133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) “far exceeded that of all other countries.”

The authors also quantify the future consequences of Trump’s policies so far: American emissions projected for 2030 are now 0.9 gigatons of CO2 equivalent (GtCO2e) higher than projections based on policies in place during the administration of Joe Biden. (The unit means billions of metric tons of carbon dioxide or the equivalent amount in other greenhouse gases.) For comparison, America’s additional emissions will amount to 1.4 times the total emissions of Germany last year.

Because Trump has pulled out of the framework convention and the Paris Agreement, moreover, the report’s authors assume that he isn’t done. As part of its exits, America has also scrapped its previous emissions targets. That could translate into an additional 1.7 GtCO2e a year by 2030 (more than an entire Indonesia, Brazil or Japan), and 2.2 GtCO2e by 2035 (almost a Russia).

What matters is of course the increase in warming that Trump’s policies are likely to cause. The U.N. now projects that by the end of the century we will be 2.5 C to 2.6 C warmer than we were in the pre-industrial era (an increase that at the time of the Paris Agreement was still considered a catastrophic scenario). That estimate is 0.2-0.3 C higher than it was only a year ago. And about half of that increase is due to Trump’s policies.These seemingly small increments are misleading. Weather (as opposed to climate) is like the two proverbial statisticians: One freezes to death and the other burns to death, but on average they’re comfortably warm. In reality, these warming scenarios blow apart any attempts to model disasters such as storms, droughts, floods, fires and the rest. What we can say is that the future will be more volatile, weird and extreme than we imagined.

A notable irony is that one particular Trump policy is currently causing an unintended and temporary blip of relief: His war against Iran has led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and a global disruption in oil and gas usage. As countries burn less of those fossil fuels, they’re also emitting a bit less. But that won’t last.

Another unintended consequence of Trump’s policies is to make authoritarian China, the largest emitter, look exemplary in comparison. It’s still burning a lot of coal, but it also continues its full-bore push to replace gas-guzzlers with electric cars and trucks — and to feed those vehicles with energy from the sun and wind.

And there you have it, the world after the Pax Americana: As Homo sapiens, we keep hurtling toward disaster and our last best hope is the Chinese Communist Party.

The most perplexing aspect may be the suddenness with which climate change has become unfashionable as a topic, especially in America under Trump. Democrats just repudiated the president across the country and will control both chambers of Congress come January. But to win, they were advised: “The First Rule About Solving Climate Change: Don’t Say Climate Change.”

If they intend to turn their triumphs into good governance — an old-fashioned notion, I admit — they’ll need to ignore that advice, and not only say “climate change,” but start doing something about it.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-604.text:
Temporary fencing is seen at East Potomac Park, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington.

WASHINGTON — A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that "We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons." He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild "a World Championship Public Facility."

Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. "They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it," she wrote. "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

Reyes said her order "ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction."

The judge said the order is in effect "through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first."

The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. "Nothing in the Court's order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue," it said. "The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration's agenda in court."

Catherine Carroll, a senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs, praised the ruling. "We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration's pursuit of another one of the president's vanity projects," she said. "The administration's inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced."

The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.

Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.

Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.

Temporary fencing is seen at East Potomac Park, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington.

Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes "doesn't want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous." He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on "any and all Rates charged" and that the redevelopment would "evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!"

Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs' requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.

Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.

Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.

Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her "egregious behavior" and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself.

The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing.

She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/t.title: Three people including schoolboy seriously injured in Scenic Rim crash
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Road Accidents and Incidents

Three people, including a young boy, have been seriously injured in a crash in the Scenic Rim.

Emergency services were called to Boonah Fassifern Road on the Cunningham Highway near Aratula at about 11:30am after reports of a collision between a car and a truck.

A primary-school-aged boy has been taken by ambulance to the Queensland Children's Hospital in a potentially life-threatening condition.

A man in his 20s has been airlifted to Princess Alexandra Hospital with potentially life-threatening chest, abdominal, pelvic and limb injuries.

A woman in her 70s was treated at the scene.

The man driving the truck was not injured.

The Cunningham Highway is closed in both directions near the scene of the crash, with motorists urged to avoid the area if possible.

Investigations are underway into the cause of the crash.

A search and rescue crew responded to a call for help from two bushwalkers in the Western Arthur Range. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

Two bushwalkers have been rescued from a track in Tasmania's remote south-west.

Police say the two women, from South Australia, called for help "due to conditions".

Police say while the pair was equipped for the walk, they are reminding anyone venturing into the bush to ensure they're prepared.

Two bushwalkers from South Australia have been rescued from the Western Arthur Range in Tasmania's remote south-west.

Tasmania Police said the women, aged 58 and 26, activated a satellite device about 8pm yesterday, and reported they needed help "due to conditions".

They were rescued from a track at Haven Lake.

Police said the weather conditions meant the rescue helicopter was unable to reach the women.

A search and rescue crew was dropped by the helicopter on Arthurs Plains at 5am today, and then walked to the women.

The two women did not need medical treatment. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

"The rescue team located the pair about 8am and are in the process of transporting them back to Hobart," police said in a statement this afternoon.

"The pair was checked as a precaution and do not require medical treatment."

Police said the pair was equipped for their planned overnight camping trip, and their personal locator beacon ensured a quick response from emergency services.

"It's a timely reminder for bushwalkers in remote areas to carry sufficient food, water, communication equipment and emergency shelter for unexpected delays," Senior Constable Cameron Rennie said.

'It's also really important to ensure all gear, such as equipment and clothing, is independently stowed so it keeps dry."

Weather conditions meant the rescuers had to walk from Arthurs Plains. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/l.title: Rival promises as parties rally at Victorian election campaign launches
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/l.author: Sian Johnson and Larissa Ham
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Liberal leader Jess Wilson and Labor leader Ben Carroll have addressed party faithful at campaign launches in Melbourne. (AAP: Joel Carrett/ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The Liberal Party has officially launched its election campaign in the city, while Labor has held its event at Moonee Ponds.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson urged Victorians to consider a "fresh start" while announcing a policy to set up a bootcamp for youth offenders.

Premier Ben Carroll described Labor as "up for the fight" as he unveiled a new public health policy to slash elective surgery wait times and bolster specialist appointments.

Victoria's two major parties have held their campaign launches in Melbourne, ahead of what aspiring premier Jess Wilson has described as the "most consequential election in decades".

At the Liberal Party's launch at The Glasshouse on Olympic Boulevard, Ms Wilson promised a tough new bootcamp for young offenders aged 14 to 17, to be established at the former Dhurringile Prison near Shepparton.

The camp would act as an alternative to a community corrections order or other custodial sentence, and would include a daily program of physical and other activities, such as cleaning, maintenance, agriculture and education, she said.

Meanwhile, Premier Ben Carroll addressed a sea of red at Labor's campaign launch in Moonee Ponds, declaring his party "up for the fight".

At the Liberal launch in the city, Ms Wilson said that, after 12 years of Labor, Victoria was at a crossroads.

"Labor have completely forgotten both the privilege and the responsibility of government," she told supporters.

"They have spent their time focused on the lives of themselves and their mates, not the lives of Victorians."

Victorian Liberal Party leader Jess Wilson with her young son Patrick. (AAP: Jay Kogler)

She told the party faithful, including three former premiers, that the November 28 election was a choice "between a Labor government that has increased taxes, wasted your money and let crime and corruption take over".

"Or, a fresh start with lower costs, reduced crime and a government that works."

In just 13 days, Victorians will head to the polls to decide how the next four years will look after three consecutive terms of Labor government.

At the Liberal launch, Ms Wilson spoke of what she claimed the state had lost, including $15 billion under alleged corruption in the Big Build, a sense of safety, and money from 70 increased or new taxes and charges.

"They have robbed us of something more fundamental too — they have sucked the life, the light, the vibrancy from this state," she said.

The opposition leader said Labor had also let the state's pothole-riddled roads "fall into rack and ruin".

Ms Wilson has promised a Liberal government would make Victoria safer. (AAP: Jay Kogler)

Among her promised solutions were a vow to hire 3,000 extra police, return protective service officers (PSOs) to train stations and recruit another 200 PSOs to patrol high-risk shopping centres.

Political parties are laying out their visions for the state's future, as voters prepare to head to the polls on November 28.

She has also promised to repeal Victoria's treaty, halve elective surgery waiting lists, bring back technical colleges, scrap activity centres and build three new select-entry public high schools.

Ms Wilson promised that a Liberal government would implement "adult crime, adult time" laws before Christmas, for 25 serious offences including arson and motor vehicle theft.

"We'll end the tobacco wars because Victorians are sick of waking up to firebombings every single day," she said.

Other pledges include no new or increased taxes, scrapping the controversial emergency services tax and exempting first homebuyers from stamp duty on properties up to $1 million.

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

At Ben Carroll's campaign launch, the focus was squarely on health, as the premier announced his party's promise to halve the state's planned surgery waiting list.

Before the premier spoke, Mr Carroll's wife Fiona Rothville introduced him and recounted their family's experience with the health system during life-threatening pregnancy complications ahead of the birth of their daughter, Madeleine.

"Public healthcare saved the life of my daughter and the life of my wife," Mr Carroll said.

"Those doctors saved my family. That's the truth."

Premier Ben Carroll addresses the party faithful at his Moonee Ponds campaign launch. (ABC News: James Oaten)

The pledge to fund an extra 100,000 planned surgeries in public hospitals would cost $1.17 billion, while a complementary promise to fund an extra 500,000 specialist appointments would involve a $195 million spend.

"It's all very well to fund additional surgeries, but we also need to make sure that people can get in and see the specialists that they need to see to determine whether surgery's a requirement or not," Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said.

She also said 30 per cent of the surgeries would take place in regional Victoria.

To learn more about the key electorates, candidates and swing seats in the coming election, head to this guide from the ABC's Chief Elections and Data Analyst Casey Briggs.

A Coalition policy to halve elective surgery waitlists announced in early October differs in its use of private hospitals to reduce wait times.

In the lead-up to the election, Labor has already promised to set up 20 free dental clinics and hire 750 more nurses across 12 emergency departments.

"We'll slash ED waits by 20 per cent, slash surgery waitlists by 50 per cent, and slash dental care costs by 100 per cent," Mr Carroll said.

"I will make healthcare more affordable. Liberals will make healthcare more American.

"Labor has always been the party of Medicare and the party of public health.

"We're going to be the party of free dental."

Mr Carroll unveiling his party's latest election promise after the Labor campaign launch. (ABC News: James Oaten)

Former premiers Steve Bracks and John Brumby attended the launch, along with federal Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles.

As the country tunes into the biggest race day of the year, Victorians will become one step closer to the state election finish line.

Despite Mr Carroll's efforts since taking over as leader to distance himself from the leadership of former premiers Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews, he received rounds of applause as he listed some of the party's achievements since it gained power under Mr Andrews in 2014.

"Victoria has been moving fast and making things since 2014," Mr Carroll said.

"[We're] catching up with our biggest ever population boom and building generational infrastructure like the Metro Tunnel, like the 121 brand new schools and the 12 brand new hospitals.

"Thanks to Labor, we now have half a trillion dollars' worth of assets coming online and those assets are the platform for future growth and prosperity."

He said the government had boosted frontline services and "hired thousands more nurses, thousands more teachers and police".

"But building for the future isn't always easy, never has been, never has been smooth sailing. We did face significant headwinds, significant global headwinds, and yes we could've done some things better," he said.

"These are tough economic conditions but we are up for the fight."

The party faithful gathered at Moonee Ponds to officially launch Ben Carroll's bid to remain premier after the state election. (ABC News: James Oaten)

He accused the Liberal Party of being irresponsible by "promising the world to everyone and knowing you can't deliver it".

"That is what Jess Wilson's done," he said.

He said Liberal policy would "hurt working people".

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/a.title: Protesters drive home message to data centre company
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/a.author: Evelyn Leckie and George Yankovich
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Rally organiser Magdalene Lippett says the community does not want to see just a "pause" to the Tungkillo data centre plan. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

More than 250 people rallied at SA Parliament on Sunday, calling for plans for a data centre in the Adelaide Hills to be scrapped.

Quantum DC announced earlier this week it would pause its plans to build a data centre at Tungkillo, following a strong community backlash.

The SA government says it is working on developing legislation that will "comprehensively deal with the rollout of data centres".

Hundreds of protesters have doubled down on their message to data centre company Quantum DC that its plans for a 1,200-megawatt AI data centre are not welcome in the Adelaide Hills.

It comes after the company announced it would pause its plans for the development at Tungkillo earlier this week, after deep frustration, anger and protests from the surrounding community.

At least 250 people rallied on the South Australian steps of parliament on Sunday, with various political parties including the SA Liberals, Greens, One Nation and independent federal MP Rebekha Sharkie in support of the protest group.

Campaign organiser Magdalene Lippett said the community was hopeful it had won the fight against the development.

Local farmer Kym Gladigau said the proposed area was prime land for food production.

"The Adelaide Hills is a food production area, that's what it's all about," Mr Gladigau said.

Kym Gladigau says there is limited prime agricultural land and the area should not be put at risk of bushfires. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

"We're losing farmland at Mt Barker, we've lost it at Virginia.

"The risk with this data centre, is that we lose that.

"If this thing goes wrong … we cannot afford another big bushfire in the Adelaide Hills, and who is going to tackle it?"

Liberal leader Ashton Hurn, who spoke at the rally, agreed the proposed area should be reserved for farming.

Ashton Hurn says Tunkillo is prime agricultural land that should be protected. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

"We keep hearing that data centres are a part of our future, there are of course economic opportunities, but we also need to make sure the community is brought along for the ride as well."

Greens leader Robert Simms said he wanted to see the Tungkillo plans rejected if they reached the government.

"That's why Greens are moving a motion calling on the government to reject this proposal," he said.

"We're also calling for a statewide moratorium on data centres. We don't want to see South Australia become the test dummy for the nation."

An estimated 250 people were at the rally. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis said he was "very disappointed" with the Tungkillo developers, referencing the company's poor method of community engagement.

"I mean, they have behaved in a way that has really lit this fire," he said.

Mr Koutsantonis said the developers had not approached government at all about the plans.

"I'm the energy minister and the treasurer. They've never spoken to me, and you would've thought the first door you'd knock on is the government's," he said.

"Data centres are an essential part of our future. There's no world where Australia cannot have data centres.

"If we don't have our own data centres, we'll be price takers rather than price setters."

Mr Koutsantonis said the government was working on developing legislation that would "comprehensively deal with the roll-out of data centres".

"Data centres have got to have almost no impact on the grid for them to operate in South Australia, and until that time is achieved, we won't license them."

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.title: Malaysian plan to let refugees work spurs advocates’ call for safeguards
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.author: Vincent Tan
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.text:
Thailand has introduced a similar scheme that has reportedly allowed 6,000 refugees from Myanmar to join the workforce over a year

On October 30, Malaysia’s home ministry said refugees could be granted conditional access to formal employment under its refugee registration document programme, known as DPP, a system introduced in January to register refugees, verify their identities and determine their status.

Employment would be temporary, restricted and subject to federal approval, the ministry said, adding that the arrangement was intended to address labour shortages while prioritising Malaysian workers. It stressed that DPP registration did not automatically confer the right to work or offer a pathway to permanent residency or citizenship.

Nur Sadek, a Rohingya refugee who has experience in humanitarian work, communications and community advocacy, said Malaysia’s plan offered the prospect of more secure employment for refugees who currently had no means of working legally.

Uncertainty over documentation continued to limit opportunities and weaken refugees’ ability to negotiate with employers, he said.

“Even when you are qualified for a position, employers may be reluctant to hire you because of your documentation. This means that people sometimes have to accept jobs below their qualifications or work in sectors where they have very limited protection,” Nur Sadek said.

Chuah Hui Yin, a Malaysian refugee researcher, said Thailand’s experience offered lessons in practical arrangements needed for refugees to work, including coordination between government agencies, employers, humanitarian organisations and refugee-led groups.

According to Malaysia’s home ministry, eligibility would be limited to refugees who were in the country before January 1, 2023, and documentation from the UN refugee agency would not automatically qualify someone.

The ministry classifies the DPP card as a temporary special pass under immigration laws, subject to conditions and possible withdrawal.

Cardholders’ movements are limited to designated zones, with travel between states requiring the immigration department’s permission, according to a written parliamentary reply on October 27 by Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail. Their cards must be renewed annually.

For refugees trying to understand how the programme would work, basic information remains scarce, Nur Sadek said.

“As far as I know, I have not encountered anyone from the Rohingya community who has received DPP documentation,” he said.

People were unsure how to apply, who would qualify and when registration would be available outside detention centres, he added, calling for transparent application procedures and information in languages to help refugees understand.

Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said on October 26 that the programme remained in its first phase, covering people held in immigration depots, and could extend to UNHCR cardholders living outside the depots “in the near future”.

On November 3, Deputy Foreign Minister Lukanisman Awang Sauni said in parliament that “about 147 refugees had been registered since January”, citing a shortage of government staff.

A study by a civil society coalition, the End Detention Network (EDN), has described DPP as the most significant shift in Malaysian refugee governance in decades. It recommended publishing DPP procedures and opening registration to asylum seekers living in the community.

Chuah said her understanding was that DPP functioned primarily as a registration exercise, while the associated rights were still unclear. Without firm legal grounding, arrangements could be changed or withdrawn, she added.

Formalising work, Chuah said, could reduce exploitation among refugees who turned to informal work to survive, but she questioned whether they would easily trust a process administered by immigration authorities they associated with arrest and detention.

Moreover, legal employment was only one aspect of protection, and income by itself would not resolve other barriers like schooling, medical bills or their legal status.

“I think livelihood is only really, like one part of overall protection,” she said.

Nur Sadek said: “For many refugees, reporting an employer for exploitation or unpaid wages is not simply an employment decision. It can also raise concerns about their immigration status and personal safety.”

He called for written contracts, fair wages and a way to report abuse without risking detention, and for workers to be able to change employers. The EDN study similarly recommends mobility between employers, enforceable labour protections and access to remedies.

In a UNHCR statement, over 6,000 refugees from Myanmar had “entered the workforce” in Thailand by September 10, a year after Bangkok allowed long-staying refugees to work. Identity cards issued this year also opened access to banking and telecommunications.

“The right to work is the foundation, not the finish line,” said Hai Kyung Jun, UNHCR’s regional director for Asia and the Pacific.

Leon de Riedmatten, executive director of the non-profit The Border Consortium (TBC), cited figures from Thailand’s department of employment showing that there were over 7,000 refugees currently working outside the camps and supporting their families. De Riedmatten described the past year as a “historic and overwhelmingly positive step forward” after decades without a legal right to work.

Some refugees had left their jobs and returned to camp because they were unhappy with the work or accommodation, or over other employment-related disputes, he said. Many had since found new employers and resumed working.

Access remained uneven, he said, as refugees without the Thai interior ministry’s registration could not participate, and female refugees had fewer opportunities because many jobs were in construction and agriculture.

“Yet many employers are still unaware that they can legally hire refugees at all,” he said, noting that camp residents included teachers, health workers and administrators.

De Riedmatten welcomed changes proposed by ministries on November 6 to allow work within the districts holding the refugee camps and extend permission for the employment period from one year to two. Working closer to home would particularly help women and people with care responsibilities, he said.

Currently, TBC still provides monthly food help to more than 15,000 refugees, including older people and those unable to work because of disabilities or chronic illness.

De Riedmatten cautioned against drawing direct comparisons between Thailand and Malaysia, whose refugee populations lived under different circumstances.

Chuah noted that refugees in Malaysia were already working informally, without the camp-based aid system available to those in Thailand.

The two countries also appeared to have different priorities in opening employment to refugees, she said.

Chuah viewed Thailand’s policy as driven partly by labour demand, including the departure of Cambodian migrant workers during the 2025 border conflict. Shrinking humanitarian funding and recognition that refugees would remain in the country long-term were also factors, she said.

“For Malaysia, it’s about security,” Chuah said, pointing to official messaging on control, repatriation and resettlement. “[In Thailand,] the solution is not to send them back. But for Malaysia, we still think like, OK, the solution is they will go back one day.”

Whatever the motive, she said, policies needed to factor in the family and community ties of refugees. If formal employment offered little additional security, refugees could see little reason to leave the informal economy.

“The easiest way is really just to look at how many people sign up for it and how many people stay,” she said.

Nur Sadek said he would judge the programme by job stability, wages, contracts and access to remedies rather than the number of registrations.

“If a refugee is tied to one employer and cannot leave an abusive workplace, then formal employment could unintentionally create another form of vulnerability,” he said.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.title: Is Italy the Model for Europe’s Future?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.author: Jason Horowitz
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.text:
Over more than a quarter-century, I’ve watched Europe’s politics become more like Italy’s, with all the resulting instability, as the far right came in from the cold.

Jason Horowitz, previously bureau chief in Rome, is now bureau chief in Madrid. This article is adapted from his recent book, “The Italian Job: A Memoir of an American Reporter in Rome.”

When I first moved to Rome, I spent my time living in the past.

At the turn of the century, I drifted through a vintage postcard of postwar Italy: old women sitting around tables they had dragged into the street, old men playing cards in caps, cats arching their backs on the hoods of snub-nosed Fiats.

As newspapers filled with talk of Silvio Berlusconi, a media mogul with ambitions and appetites worthy of a Roman emperor, my meanderings inevitably took me toward Tiber Island, a sliver of land in the middle of the river that divides Rome.

An ancient bridge on the island’s left bank had a strange statue of weather-beaten faces positioned back-to-back as if they couldn’t stand one another. The heads rose out of the shared torso of a square pillar and represented Janus, Rome’s god of the past and future, the deity of transitions and change.

Back then, I didn’t see the change around me, but now, more than a quarter-century later, after spending decades reporting on Italian politics and changes across Europe, I have come to understand that I was living in the future.

In the time since, I have seen an Italianization of politics all around the continent, with coalitions of small parties resulting in instability, with fed-up voters desperate for new saviors. But more than anything, I have seen — in Britain, France, Germany — countries following the Italian model by allowing the far right into the political mainstream.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.title: In Europe, an Emboldened Iran Contributes to a Sense of Anxiety
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.author: Michael D. Shear
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.text:
War in the Middle East

Prosecutors and government officials believe Iran or its proxies are behind a series of security breaches and threats in Britain and Europe, unsettling the region.

Reporting from London

On Veterans Day this past week, President Trump declared that his decision to go to war with Iran had been a complete success.

“When this conflict is over, and it will be soon,” he said, speaking on a blustery morning from Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington, “the entire world will be a much safer and better place, more peaceful place.”

That is not how it feels in Europe.

A growing number of attempted terrorist attacks across the continent and in Britain, including a foiled plot against a major American military base, arson attacks on Jewish community sites and cyberattacks that raised temperatures in refrigerators and blood banks are rattling national security officials and unnerving the public. Many have been attributed to Iran or to proxies acting on its behalf.

The sense of global unease was heightened when the U.S. government grounded all air travel for hours on Friday in what officials later said was a technical issue.

European residents had already grown frustrated before the most recent round of turmoil. The economic consequences of the war that Mr. Trump and the Israeli government started against Iran in February have piled up: Gas prices are higher because of disruptions of oil deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz. Groceries cost more. Heating homes in winter has become far less affordable.

And in recent weeks, the effect has grown darker as security officials have accused Iran or its proxies of conducting a series of terrorism-related plots. In September, U.S. prosecutors say, an Iraqi man, an Iranian operative and a senior operative for an Iran proxy group in a New York jail plotted to attack R.A.F. Fairford, an air base in England used by American bombers. They did not succeed, but the effort prompted a major security incident.

Bear 122 has survived a train, cars and rival bears. Some fear the biggest threat to his life now is his own fame.

“The Boss,” the near mythical grizzly bear king of Banff National Park.
Credit...
All in the Wild Photography

Reporting from Banff National Park, Canmore and Dead Man’s Flats, Alberta.

To the scientists and wardens of Banff National Park he is grizzly bear 122. But to everyone who lives in or near Canada’s oldest national park, and many of its 4.5 million annual visitors, he is the Boss.

He has been struck by a freight train without apparent ill effect. He has shrugged off being hit by cars. Scientists have confirmed that he killed and snacked on a black bear at least once, and he is believed to have fathered many, if not most, of the bears in his 2,000-square-kilometer territory.

Most of all, the Boss has become Canada’s 700-pound celebrity bear king. When he strolls along the Trans-Canada Highway looking for dandelions, “bear jams” swiftly follow. His battles with a rival bear known as Split Lip are legendary. (He caused the split lip.) His annual awakening from hibernation, usually in March, is reported by news outlets across Alberta.

Galleries in Banff and neighboring Canmore ship giant photos of him worldwide. His image appears on fridge magnets, T-shirts and tote bags. A local restaurant is named for him, its main dining room dominated by a scrap metal sculpture of the bear.

But despite his fearsome demeanor, enhanced by four-inch claws, few bear experts consider the Boss a threat to park visitors or residents. Rather, they fear his celebrity and the legions of fans it have created, may be the biggest threat to his life and his dominance.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US judge blocks Trump’s plan to renovate historic DC golf course
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Order by judge Ana Reyes is the latest instance of the federal judiciary pushing back against Trump’s efforts to redesign the nation’s capital

A federal judge has ordered a temporary suspension of any work at a historic Washington public golf course, in the latest setback for US president Donald Trump’s plan to turn it ⁠into a championship-level course.

In a 30-page decision, US district judge Ana Reyes temporarily blocked the federal government from moving forward with a plan that would have closed East Potomac Park on Sunday. Trump said in an 18 ⁠October social media post that the closure would last 15 months and transform the park’s golf offerings into “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World”.

Reyes ruled that the Trump administration’s stated reasons for closing the park were “pretextual” ⁠and that the government violated at least two federal laws “to meet an arbitrary deadline”.

“The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all ​stripes, indefinitely,” Reyes wrote.

The plaintiffs argue that Trump’s plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the president denies.

Although Reyes ordered that the park – near the Jefferson Memorial, ‌2 miles (3km) south of the ‌White House – remain open, the Trump administration does not have to maintain golf operations at the site, the judge wrote. But the government “cannot use the absence ‌of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public,” she added.

The ruling by Reyes, who was appointed by Joe Biden and whom Trump has called a “lunatic”, is the latest instance of the federal judiciary pushing back against Trump’s sweeping efforts to redesign the nation’s capital through major construction projects.

Many of his projects, including plans for a huge ballroom at the White House, the installation of his own name on the Kennedy Center and construction of a massive arch, have been challenged in courts.

The ruling came in a lawsuit brought by the DC Preservation League, a historic preservation group that says Trump’s plan to redevelop the park violates various federal regulations and statutes.

The group’s lawyers earlier won a ruling from Reyes that blocked the National Park Service, part of the Interior Department, ‌from cutting down trees at the park or making other irreversible modifications without advance notice.

Democracy Forward, which is representing the preservation league and two local residents in the case, said in a statement it was grateful that Reyes stopped “another one of ​the president’s vanity projects”.

The group’s senior legal adviser, Catherine Carroll, said: “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced.”

The Interior Department, Justice Department and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The lawsuit has produced several heated confrontations between Reyes and Justice Department lawyers. The judge said last month that the government’s removal of hundreds of trees from the course and failure to tell the preservation group ⁠about the work “has cost the government all of its credibility” in the case.

Reyes has ordered an ethics investigation into ​whether government lawyers have repeatedly misled her about the timeline for ​the park’s closure.

The Justice Department has accused Reyes ​of overstepping her authority and inappropriately belittling government lawyers. It demanded her recusal from the case, a request she denied.

Trump, ​who owns golf courses globally, has ‌focused on the East Potomac ​Park renovations as part of his ​larger ambition to leave an architectural legacy across Washington.

The park has three golf courses totalling 36 holes, a miniature golf course and a paved loop popular with cyclists and runners. The proposed redesign would turn the area into a single 18-hole championship course that Trump has said could hold world-class events, such as the US Open and the Ryder Cup, while remaining open to the public.

With Reuters and Associated Press

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/r.title: Mia Tattler alleges Russell Brand raped her as a 16-year-old
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/r.author: Scout Wallen
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Sexual Offences

Mia Tattler spoke to journalist Rosamund Urwin in an interview with The Sunday Times about her allegations against Russell Brand. (Supplied: Youtube, Times Radio)

One of the women who spoke to UK media about Russell Brand's alleged sexual misconduct before his criminal trial has waived her right to anonymity.

Mia Latter says Brand raped her while the pair were in a relationship when she was 16.

She is fighting for changes to the UK's consent laws.

A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand while in a relationship with him as a 16-year-old says he was a "monstrous person" who would refer to her as "the child".

Warning: This article includes allegations of sexual assault some readers may find distressing.

Mia Latter was known as 'Alice' in a 2023 joint investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4 about Russell Brand.

She alleged that Brand groomed her, was emotionally abusive, controlling and sexually abused her. He denied those allegations at the time.

On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years in prison for rape and three counts of sexual assault in relation to separate complaints.

In the UK, victims and alleged victims of sexual offences are automatically entitled to lifelong anonymity, but can choose to waive that right.

Mia Latter says the alleged abuse has impacted her entire life. (Supplied: Instagram, @mialatter)

Ms Latter, who was not a complainant in the trial, decided to reveal her identity in an overnight interview with the Sunday Times.

"Feeling incredibly nervous about it [speaking] because I know that it will open me up to lots of unwanted commentary, but it also feels incredibly important," the 37-year-old told the newspaper.

Ms Latter said she met Brand in London when she was 16 and he was 30, when he approached her and asked her on a date.

She said she told him she was 16, and that he replied that he did not care, but just needed "to know where I stand legally."

Ms Latter said their relationship lasted around three months, during which he allegedly orally raped her.

Brand faced trial at London's Southwark Crown Court, but Ms Latter was not a complainant in the case. (Reuters: Julia Quenzler)

"People around me … they begged me not to see him, and it felt like an extra humiliation when he did assault me," she said.

"He's a monster … a monstrous person."

Ms Latter said Brand fetishised her for being young.

"He carried me around wrapped up in a towel like I was a baby, called me 'the child' or 'his little dolly', and would put me in the bath and bathe me," she said.

In April, Brand acknowledged that he had been in a sexual relationship with a 16-year-old, in an interview with Megyn Kelly.

"I did sleep with a 16-year-old when I was 30, but when I was 30, I was a very different person," Brand said at the time.

Ms Latter said following that interview, the police decided to remove her from the trial.

"They didn't want it to become the 'Alice show'," she said.

"I took it very badly, I was in a bad place … it just felt so unfair."

Mia Tattler spoke to journalist Rosamund Urwin. (Supplied: Youtube, Times Radio)

Ms Latter said she was asked to be part of a second trial, but has removed herself from the process.

"I just don't know what capacity I have to give years more of my life to this, for my head to be occupied with these awful crimes," she said.

"There were other women that shared their stories as part of the investigation, and I feel like justice has been served."

The Sunday Times reported that in a statement, the Metropolitan Police said they launched an investigation in January into an allegation of rape, but that investigation was ongoing.

"We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence," they said.

One of the main reasons Ms Latter said she was speaking out was to advocate for a staggered age of consent.

The current age of consent is 16 in the United Kingdom, regardless of gender, and there are added protections for those under the age of 18.

Ms Latter wants the age of consent increased when the partner is older.

"If you're in your 30s, 40s, and 50s and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it's a criminal offence," she proposed.

The trial of Russell Brand received international media coverage. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

Ms Latter said if added measures had been in place when she was 16, her parents could have stopped her from being with Brand.

"It would have been illegal for me to be staying at his house, [for him to] be having a sexual relationship with me, so the subsequent sexual assault would never have happened," she said.

"My parents did all the things; they took my phone away from me, my mother grounded me … but they can't keep me under lock and key the whole time, which they tried to do, but they failed."

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.title: Hong Kong must expand trade, not wait for ‘luck’ as AI exports could slow: commerce chief
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.author: Theodora Yu
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.text:
Algernon Yau says city must explore other ways to grow trade networks and not rest on laurels of recent peak in export growth rate

Hong Kong must proactively expand trade networks and not “wait for luck to come our way”, as the recent growth in artificial intelligence exports may gradually slow down, the city’s commerce minister has said.

Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah said on Sunday that Hong Kong’s September export growth rate – the highest monthly figure in more than 40 years – was driven by an increase in re-export volume equivalent to 1.4 times the city’s gross domestic product.

It boosted Hong Kong’s annual re-export trade value to over HK$5.49 trillion (US$700 billion).

“Re-export trade acts as a ballast point for our export sector, stabilising overall exports,” Yau said on a radio programme.

He noted that the current upwards trend driven by AI development may gradually slow down, and stressed the need to explore new opportunities to maintain the city’s status as an international trade hub.

“We must closely monitor overall global trends, and in turn make preparations regarding how to strengthen ourselves, how to adjust our strategies and how to expand our trade networks … we cannot simply wait for luck to come our way,” Yau said.

He said 75 per cent of the city’s air cargo volume and 80 per cent of sea freight were re-exports.

“A lot of re-export trade goes from mainland China through Hong Kong,” he said.

There is also demand for finance, legal services, accounting and certification in the re-export sector, which alone supports 100,000 to 200,000 jobs, he said.

To raise the city’s competitiveness, Yau said Hong Kong should align with the mainland’s 15th five-year plan to consolidate its status as an international trade centre.

“It starts with our closely interconnected financial centre, maritime centre, aviation hub and innovation and technology sector … and to keep pace with international advancements in AI,” he said.

On expanding opportunities in Central Asia, Yau said a Kazakhstan fund was preparing to issued bonds in Hong Kong, while another airport company in Uzbekistan had signed a cooperation agreement with a Hong Kong firm to help develop the airport there.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu led a delegation on a five-day trip to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in June, at the end of which 96 cooperation agreements and memorandums of understanding across government and business sectors were signed.

“We are also keeping a close eye on [Central Asia], hoping to explore and develop new markets, and have more cooperation with new economies,” Yau said.
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.summary: Algernon Yau says recent growth in artificial intelligence exports may slow down. He says Hong Kong must explore other ways to grow trade networks.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Francophone summit opens in Cambodia amid Rwanda-DR Congo rift
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Leaders of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) are meeting in Cambodia amid a dispute between the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda over who should lead the association of French-speaking nations, which threatens to split the group.

The OIF is holding a three-day summit in the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, through Monday. A loose confederation of 90 states and governments where French is spoken or widely used, the OIF has 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers.

French President Emmanuel Macron, who chaired the last summit in 2024 and will hand the chair to Cambodia, arrived on Saturday and met Prime Minister Hun Manet, The Associated Press news agency reported.

About 20 leaders are expected, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Vietnamese President To Lam, Rwandan President Paul Kagame and DRC President Felix Tshisekedi.

On Monday, leaders will choose the organisation’s next secretary-general for a four-year term.

Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo, who has led the OIF since 2018, is seeking a third term.

The DRC, however, which accuses Rwanda of backing the M23 armed group in the country’s east, has threatened to leave the OIF if she is re-elected. Congo, the United States and United Nations experts say Rwanda backs the M23, one of about 100 armed groups in the mineral-rich region.

Rwanda denies the allegations.

On Saturday, the DRC withdrew its candidate, Juliana Lumumba, the daughter of independence hero Patrice Lumumba, and backed Romanian former Prime Minister Dacian Ciolos to allow “consensus around a unifying candidacy”.

Rwanda’s foreign minister, Olivier Nduhungirehe, said Mushikiwabo would stay in the race. Mauritania’s Coumba Ba, a former minister, is also running, the AFP news agency reported.

Macron’s office said that most members agreed on the need for consensus and that he would take it up with his African counterparts. France is the biggest contributor to the OIF’s 2026 budget of 71.7 million euros ($79m).

Rwanda has said Macron asked Kagame to withdraw its candidate and that Kigali refused, AFP reported.

The DRC has a population of more than 110 million, roughly 40 million more than France, and is the most populous country where French is an official language. Its exit would be a blow to the organisation, which lost Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso, which announced their withdrawals in March 2025 following suspensions over military coups.

The summit’s slogan is “Reinvest in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability”. Activists see it as a chance to press Cambodia, a de facto one-party state, on rights.

UN Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews urged delegates to press for the release of detained activists. “No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions,” he said.

Macron arrived as France faces widespread protests at home. He is due to visit the Angkor World Heritage Site on Monday before leaving for Malaysia.
